## 1:1 Introduction: In Which: I. The Emphases of the Words and the Genuine Meaning of the Sayings Are Elicited
IN WHICH: I. The emphases of the words and the genuine meaning of the sayings are elicited from the sources, the context, and the analogy of Scripture: II. The principal versions are compared with the Greek text, the sincerity of which is vindicated everywhere:

III. The expositions of both the ancients and the moderns are weighed, the truer ones of the Fathers themselves, of B. Luther, and of other theologians are established in their own words: IV. Textual, historical, genealogical, and other doubts are resolved: V. Apparent contradictions are discussed: VI. Various theoretical and practical questions are solved: VII. Most classical passages are treated expressly: VIII. The corruptions of heretics and others are clearly refuted: IX. Grotian depravations and ψευδερμηνείαι are subjected to a just examination and exploded;

AND SO IT IS ESPECIALLY AND DILIGENTLY AIMED AT, THAT THE SINGLE LITERAL SENSE OF SCRIPTURE BE ASSERTED AND CONFIRMED FROM EVERY SIDE,

Latin:

IN QUIBUS Emphases vocum ac mens dicto- rum genuina e fontibus, contextu & analogia Scripturae eruuntur: II. Versiones praecipuae cum Graeco textu, vindicata ubique

hujus sinceritate, conferuntur: III. Expositiones cum veterum, tum recentiorum interpretum expendun- tur, veriores Patrum ipsorummet, B. Lutheri, & aliorum Theologorum propriis verbis stabiliuntur: IV. Du- bia textualia, Historica, Genealogica, & alia, expediuntur: V. Contradictiones apparentes discutiuntur: VI. Quaestiones variae, Theoreticae & Practicae, solvuntur: VII. Loca Classica pleraque ex professo tractantur: VIII. Corruptelae Haereticorum, & aliorum luculenter retunduntur: IX. Grotianae depravationes & ψευδερμηνείαι justo examini sistuntur, & exploduntur;

ADEOQUE ID IMPRIMIS SEDULO AGITUR, UT UNICUS LITERALIS SCRIPTURAE SENSUS UNDIQUAQUE ADSERATUR, ET CONFIRMETUR,

With the following prefixed: a newly composed Evangelical Harmony, prefaces and partitions of each book, as well as the argument and distribution of every chapter, with the inclusion also, according to the wish of the learned, of ALL THE ANNOTATIONS OF GROTIUS, whether they contribute to the understanding of Scripture, or deserve observation, or have been recalled for censure,

SO ADORNED THAT THEY MAY SERVE AS A PROPER COMMENTARY: With a very rich fivefold index added finally at the end.

VOLUME I. EXHIBITING THE HARMONY OF THE EVANGELISTS AND ANNOTATIONS ON THE BOOKS OF THE EVANGELISTS AS ALSO THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES.

By the work and study of D. ABRAHAM CALOVIUS, PRIMARY PROFESSOR IN THE ACADEMY OF WITTENBERG, AND GENERAL SUPERINTENDENT OF THE ELECTORATE OF SAXONY.

DRESDEN AND LEIPZIG, At the expense of Johann Christoph Zimmermann

HILDBURGHAUSEN, PRINTED BY BALTHASAR PENSOLD, IN THE YEAR 1719.

OF THE MOST SERENE AND MOST POWERFUL PRINCE AND LORD, LORD JOHANN GEORG II, DUKE OF SAXONY, JÜLICH, CLEVES, AND BERG, ELECTOR AND ARCH-MARSHAL OF THE HOLY ROMAN EMPIRE, BURGGRAVE OF MAGDEBURG, LANDGRAVE OF THURINGIA, MARGRAVE OF MEISSEN AND OF BOTH UPPER AND LOWER LUSATIA, COUNT IN THE MARCH AND RAVENSBERG, LORD IN RAVENSTEIN, &c. &c., HIS MOST CLEMENT LORD, AS IT WERE A GRANDFATHER, A MOST MUNIFICENT FOSTERER, MOST BLESSED BY THE GOVERNMENT OF DOGMA AND PRUDENCE AND SALOMONIC TRANQUILITY, A MOST GLORIOUS PRINCE, A GREAT DEPOSIT OF HEAVEN,

ALSO OF THE MOST SERENE PRINCE AND LORD, THE LORD JOHANN GEORG III, DUKE OF SAXONY, JULICH, CLEVES, AND BERG, LANDGRAVE OF THURINGIA, MARGRAVE OF MEISSEN AND OF BOTH LUSATIAS, COUNT IN THE MARK AND RAVENSBERG, LORD IN RAVENSTEIN, &c. &c., HEIR TO THE ELECTORATE, HIS MOST EXALTED MOST CLEMENT LORD AS HIS MOST EMINENT PARENT.

TO THE MOST HIGH AND MOST ILLUSTRIOUS PRINCES AND LORDS, THE LORDS JOHANN GEORG IV AND FRIEDRICH AUGUST, DUKES OF SAXONY, JULICH, CLEVES, AND BERG, LANDGRAVES OF THURINGIA, MARGRAVES OF MEISSEN AND OF BOTH LUSATIAS, COUNTS IN THE MARK AND RAVENSBERG, LORDS IN RAVENSTEIN, &C. &C., RESPECTIVELY MOST PRAISEWORTHY NEPHEWS AND SONS; TO MY MOST GRACIOUS LORDS

I PRAY WITH ALL MY HEART FOR THE PERENNIAL GRACE OF GOD THE FATHER, THE GLORIOUS PEACE OF JESUS CHRIST THE PRINCE OF PEACE, AND THE GRACIOUS GUIDANCE OF THE HOLY SPIRIT, THE SPIRIT OF COUNSEL AND OF THE FEAR OF THE LORD.

MOST HIGH PRINCES OF YOUTH, MOST GRACIOUS LORDS.

Most worthy of commemoration is the admonition of the Lord of Lords and Prince of the Kings of the earth, which He gave through the Great Emperor of the people of Israel, when he asked for a King, as to what the chief duty should be of him who was to govern such a people, a Royal priesthood of God: This, indeed, He commanded: Let the King describe for himself the law in a volume, and let him have it with him, and read it all the days of his life, that he may learn to fear the Lord his God, and to keep His words and ceremonies, which are commanded in the law.

It is the opinion of Bellarmine, who attempts to extend his fringes, that Cardinals are to be equated with Kings in the Kingdom of the Anti-Christ. How much more are Electors compared with Kings in the Kingdom of Christ? To them, nothing should be more sacred, nothing more primary and ancient, than the reading of the Holy Code, which Cardinals—often, and more than too much, Carnals—neither read, nor would they understand it if they did read it. Not once only, but twice was the law of the Lord to be described by the Kings of Israel when they sat on the Royal throne, unless the law had already been described by them before their elevation. Interpreters inquire whether the law had to be described by their own hand? Which most affirm, and not undeservedly. For what great thing would this be, if they at least took care for it to be described, how could the law of the Lord stick in the memory through description, unless they applied their own hand to the work? Than which work, indeed, nothing is more excellent, nothing more worthy of supreme Heads: For this reason, the Law of the Lord is to David, a King after God's own heart and most approved, a treasure far more precious than gold and silver, the best treasure, making the King wise, above all fathers, the highest and inestimable inheritance: In the judgment of Solomon, the wisest of Kings, wisdom, which is had from the word of God, is far more excellent not only than gold, but also than pearls and most excellent gems, which no mortal is able to value sufficiently, no one is able to extol with worthy praises,

Nor indeed is the divine Law to be turned over by hand only by night and by day, but it is to be cherished in the faithful heart perpetually, nay, to be expressed by the work itself, and holily fulfilled, as far as it can be done, through the whole space of the reign: It is commonly said, but it is most true, especially concerning Holy Scripture, A reading read pleases, repeated ten times it will please. But indeed this command of the Lord is to be inscribed in golden letters upon the hearts of Princes: After the King of Israel shall have sat upon the throne of his kingdom, let him describe for himself this repeated law in a volume, taking a copy from the Priests of the Levitical tribe: And he shall have it with him, and shall read it all the days of his life, and shall learn to fear the Lord his God, and to keep the words and ceremonies Of that which is prescribed in the law. Nor let his heart be lifted up in pride above his brethren, nor let him turn aside to the right hand or to the left, that he himself, and his son, may reign a long time over Israel. Let Theologians therefore prescribe the laws of a happy, the just Jurists of a long-lived, the Prudent Philosophers of a well-governed [reign]: this one Rule, which the Lord Himself gave, provides all those things most abundantly—a kingdom happy, just, long-lived, prudent, and in all respects most auspicious and most desired. Therefore, Jehoiada the high priest ordered the book of the law to be delivered to the royal Joash at his solemn inauguration, albeit a seven-year-old one, such as is almost JOHANN GEORG IV, FIRE OF THE LORD, worthy to be called so because of his fiery zeal toward the word of GOD, so that he might intimate that the King must diligently study it.

There is nothing in this Rule about a twofold description of the Law: yet Rabbinical traditions add it: Nor is this without cause: because that which is written down repeatedly is more strongly impressed upon the mind. And when the law is described by the hands of the King, into the hands of the one describing, because the description is repeated, it flows so much more strongly into living practice, since it is not, like human laws, in the minds, but animated and living, spirit and life, when it is received with a faithful heart and cherished.

If any of the Princes in the Christian world is found to whom this more religious care of describing the law has belonged, your Grandfather, most praiseworthy Princes, the most glorious example and likeness of Princes, whose name is therefore to be consecrated to eternity, he is to be considered JOHANN GEORG II. He not only has all the letters of Scripture, by the number of the Masoretes, even without the aid of memory, in the written tables in counted order, which we have not easily heard of a Prince speaking: but he also curiously searches out the sense, which is the soul of Scripture, and does not, with the Anti-Christ and his worshippers, think it alien to a Prince's care to search out the sense of Scripture through the diligent reading of Scripture, which for that reason is called Reading by the Hebrews. With what a devout mind also he is wholly occupied in this, that his life may express what he has embraced in his mind, let the idea of his life teach: which he keeps hidden from no one, allowing it to be an illustrious court, so that all may behold it: for it will surely be a most splendid mirror for all. Certainly, never would such wicked names—Pius who was truly Impious, Clemens who was anything but Clement, Eugenius who was destitute of all generosity, Martius who was consecrated much to Mars besides his sacred office, Innocentius who was devoid of all innocence, Urbanus who was most alien to all urbanity—in a word, monsters of men, horrible, have sat on the throne which is believed to be most holy, if the reading of Scripture had been held by them at its just value. Therefore, the most blessed Prince will confound those little saints on the last day, when he will shine in the firmament like the Sun, but they, even by his own reckoning, placed on the judgment throne, will be condemned to eternal darkness.

Well done in Heroic Virtue, Prince JOHANN GEORG III. May you furthermore be heard as heir, as of your paternal virtues, so also of heroic zeal against the Sacred letters and their holier observance. Well done, most Serene former Successor JOHANN GEORG IV, most eminent Prince of Youth. Well done, most High Duke FRIEDRICH AUGUST, ONCE ADJUNCT TO THE MOST GLORIOUS LIEUTENANT, TRULY AUGUST, may this omen and ancestral vow, which the ELECTOR superior to all praise, JOHANN GEORG II, most prudently conceived with these titles, be yours—heir in full of paternal virtue, surpassing his ancestor, most happily reflecting his great-grandfather. Be such as the most glorious Grandfather desires, with the most high Grandmother, the most praiseworthy Parent, with the AUGUST Mother, a most shining and utterly incomparable mirror of royal matronly virtues: such as so many provinces, nay, the whole Holy Roman Empire, certainly hope for; What? The entire world.

The zeal for the Evangelical faith, diffused through the whole world and all the climates of the earth. These deposits of such great heaven have been granted again, after an almost desperate restoration of life, by divine Clemency, so that by most pious prayer, most religious education, and Royal instruction, they may render successors truly worthy of the throne by the virtues of their ancestors of both lineages. O may heaven hear the entire Lutheran Church vowing the same, and seeking the same heaven with outstretched hand, and may it render it as one seeking it: And that I may embrace many things in few, may it grant all those things which are the vows of a pious and Christian Prince, and may it at length receive them to itself with those most Serene heads to be crowned with an unfading crown.

Which vow, or rather that which I shall certainly obtain from heaven with my daily prayers, most graciously admit as my most humble gift, in the manner of a New Year's present, most gracious LORDS, and vibrate the structures of your Clemency upon me and my poor dwellings; Thus, what alone I can, not as is fitting, for who could do that, but to the best of my ability I will consecrate your AUGUST & GLORIOUS names to eternity. Which I strive for entirely by this address, I exhibit for the most part the History of the Example of Examples, of the virtue of virtues of our sweetest LITTLE JESUS, clearly described by the Four Amanuenses, alongside the course of the life and proclamation of that pair of truly equal exalted luminaries of the world, ST. PETER, not the Roman, but the Antiochene Bishop, Doctor of the Jews, and ST. PAUL, the Roman, or rather the Apostle of the whole world, especially of the Gentiles. Thus also I shall be cheerfully excited, if I have pleased such great Princes, which is not the least praise, to set before the public the study of the sacred works undertaken, and among these, after the Biblical Annotations are completed, of a Theological System, and if God grants, of a Paraphrase of the entire Biblical Code, in Latin-German, to be dedicated to your glory, although I know that nothing can be added to it by me, who rather strive for this most earnestly, that what is lacking in light and glory in these works of mine may be poured upon them by such great Names and Divinities. Thus, above all, I shall continue to weary heaven with prayers, that these holier deposits of heaven may not be returned to heaven until after late years, and that the Heroes may triumph eternally in heaven after countless victories. He who rules well in this age, as Isidore predicts in book III of The Chief Good, chapter XLVIII, reigns without end forever, and passes from the glory of this age to eternal glory.

OF YOUR MOST SERENE NAMES

WITTENBERG, on the very Kalends of January in the Year of the Redeemed World 1676.

MOST HUMBLE WORSHIPPER, MOST SUBJECT SERVANT, PERPETUAL INTERCESSOR,

ABRAHAM CALOVIUS, D.

To the illustrious Estates of the Electoral line of Saxony, to all the Orders of the lands, to the most reverend Prelates, to the most illustrious and most excellent Counts and free Barons, to the most noble and most distinguished Knights, to the Council of Nobles, shining most brightly with the most splendid images of their ancestors, to the most famous, magnificent, likewise most ample and most wise Consuls, Proconsuls, Senators, representing the civic state, my lords to be humbly celebrated, patrons to be observantly venerated, and supporters to be dutifully esteemed,

He prays from the heart for abundant health of soul and body, from God the Father of lights, along with the most desired course of the year begun in Christ, the Prince of Peace, in tranquility, and the most happy recurrence of many years, and the ever-assisting Spirit of counsel.

GRACIOUS MAECENASES, SUPREME PATRONS, GREATEST SUPPORTERS,

The Prophetic maxim, נדיב נדיבות יעץ, which I have chosen from my youth as a symbol, is worthy of always resounding in our ears, nay, of being written in golden letters upon our hearts. The Vulgate has rendered it: The prince will think the things that are worthy of a prince. Osiander (for that was the name of the theologian) does not amend it, according to his custom and practice, but he takes the word נדיב by antonomasia, concerning the Prince of the kings of the earth, Christ Jesus, Apoc. 1:5, who is to be opposed to the fool, that is to say, the Anti-Christ, whom he wishes to be regarded here, especially on account of his notorious Epicureanism, described in Psalm 14:1 ff. For who will be opposed to him more rightly than Wisdom itself hypostatically, the Son of God, Prov. 8:23, 9:13, Luke 11:49. The fool will speak foolish, that is, impious, perverse things, and his heart will work iniquity, he will not piously and well administer the Republic: that he may perform simulation, or hypocrisy, that he may speak fraudulently to the Lord, that is, he will do this: that he may instruct a hypocritical religion, and that he may make empty the soul of the hungry, and take away drink from the thirsty: that is, all things will be arranged so that he may exhaust the wealth of his own miserable subjects, and let them hunger and thirst, as the Osiandrine paraphrase has it. Perhaps, and not inappropriately, it may be understood of spiritual hunger and thirst, from Amos 8:11 ff., Zech. 9:17, Deut. 8:3, Matt. 4:4. For to provide for this is the work of a Prince, and that most princely, Isa. 49:23, Ps. 24:7, in which the King of Kings, Lord of Lords, goes before, Apoc. 17:14, 19:16. To the Ruler, to Princes, to all Lords, Job 6:15, 27, 32 ff., Prov. 19:5, Isa. 55:2, Apoc. 2:17, Isa. 30:20, 21, Jer. 3:15. Psalm 23:1, Apoc. 7:17. The Prophet adds: And he himself shall stand over the leaders; or princes (the Apostles), that is, he shall be eminent above the Apostles, and all others, especially the Doctors of the Church: For they all shall sit at His feet, as the only Master, Matt. 23:10, Acts 22:3. Lyranus, Thomas, Hugo, Vatablus, B. Luther, Cramer in the Summaries: Sanctius, Cornelius à Lapide, Menochius, Tirinus, Adam Sasbouth, Emanuel Saa, concerning Hezekiah, and now Hugo Grotius (comparing it very poorly with Isa. 9:6). Jerome, however, Procopius, Cyril of Alexandria, Haymo, Brentius, Osiander, Hutter in the Summaries, the Vinariean Paraphrasts: likewise Oecolampadius, Zwingli, Calvin, Piscator, Junius, the Belgian Paraphrasts, Amama, and others, concerning Christ. Tirinus interprets it concerning Hezekiah as the type, and concerning Christ as the antitype, and the leaders as the Apostles, whom the sacred Psalmist thus calls in the Epithalamium of Christ, Thou shalt make them princes over all the earth, Ps. 45:17, and Ps. 68:28, The princes of Judah their leaders. Osiander, as I have said, wishes the Anti-Christ, the ringleader and chief of the impious, to be noted most especially in the antithesis, who above others is נבל a fool, or Epicurean, and greedy, whose cupidity the world has hitherto been unable to satisfy, and also the worst of hypocrites: although perhaps he does not exclude others.

But the saying is general in its first sense. The word נדיב is used of any munificent person, Exod. 35:5, 22. Of the holy people of the Lord, Ps. 110:5, Thy people shall be עמר נדבות liberality, or spontaneous, Ps. 119:108, Accept now, O Lord, the spontaneous offerings of my mouth (τὰ ἑκούσια): Therefore Vatablus and Musculus have interpreted these things generally: The former, the liberal man devises liberal things: the latter, the beneficent man thinks of beneficent things. Nor otherwise in his translation Megalander: Princes should have princely thoughts: Which that Davidic [verse], he dispersed, he gave to the poor, altogether becomes. His Latin Commentary also tends to this: He has liberal thoughts, how he may benefit and accommodate all. For he feels that he is instituted for this reason, that he may BENEFIT rather than RULE, that he may serve rather than dominate. These are subordinate, not opposite, interpretations. What is said in general about the good, why not

DEDICATORY EPISTLE.

may it be permitted to apply to the best? Or if I should speak strictly of the idea of a Prince, or of the best of Princes, what prevents me from understanding this of all, since all ought to compose themselves according to that pattern? Thus elsewhere, those who take the noun נדיב generally, have translated it as ἄρχων, Prince, Job 12:21, ch. 21:28, ch. 24:18, Ps. 46:9, 82:10, 106:40, 112:7, 117:9, 145:2, Isa. 13:2; βασιλεὺς, King, Prov. 19:6; τύραννος, Tyrant, Prov. 28:16 (where, however, Aquila and Theodotion have ἐξουσιαζόμενοι, and B. Luther has 'the kings'); or πρόθυμος, Prompt, 1 Chron. 28:21, 2 Chron. 29:31; or καταδεχόμενος, looking up to, Exod. 35:5; or δίκαιος, Just, Prov. 17:7. In our text they vary: they explain the former word as οἱ ἐυσεβεις, the pious, and the latter as συνετὰ, wisdom or prudence. There is also a place where they interpret it as ὁι δυνάται, the powerful, Judg. 5:9, 1 Sam. 2:8, Prov. 17:27, ch. 25:7. and the cognate verb ισχύει, IT IS VALUED. Deut. 16:10; they rendered the word נדיבה ἡγεμονικῶς, princely, Ps. 51:13; B. Luther explained it as 'holy': in the words immediately following here, it pleased the 70 interpreters to translate it βουλὴν, counsel. But he who takes it more correctly in the same sense as the former is ὁ πάνυ. But how did it happen that they once interpreted it as ἡ ἐλπὶς, hope, namely Job 30:15, or that they translated it ὁμολόγως, manifestly? Which, however, I observe more than once in the most useful Kircherian Concordances, Hos. 14:5. Likewise: that they chose ὁμολογίαν, confession, Deut. 12:6, Ezek. 46:13, Amos 4:1; προσφερόμενα, offered, Exod. 36:2; σφάγιον, victim, Lev. 22:23; δῶμα, gift, Deut. 23:24, 2 Chron. 31:14, I do not understand, unless perhaps they had regard to the fact that heresy is chosen with will and counsel. And, to return to the beginning, PRINCE, I say, ἀρχὴν, beginning, Ps. 109:4, or because these things ought to be voluntary, and ἀφαίρεσμα, a separation, Exod. 35:27, as also αἵρεσις, Election, Lev. 22:18, 21. For otherwise, it very frequently pleased them to use τὸ ἑκούσιον, the voluntary, Lev. 7:6, ch. 23:38, Num. 29:39, Ezra 1:4, 6, ch. 8:26, Ps. 54:6, 68:10, 119:107, and καθ̔εκούσιον, Num. 15:3. From which, if you compare them with our aphorism, many things could be sought, whether for the sake of similarity or examples, for clarifying the sense and for the amplification of the things said, which do not make for an unpleasant result; and it cannot be denied that this custom, if applied opportunely, is not ungrateful to the audience, but both sweet and fruitful for great and ingenious Ecclesiastical Orators (for for application, not so much judgment as a conjectural talent is required).

But to the Prophetic apophthegm! Kircher diligently collects the principal meanings of the word, as is his custom: נדיב, Spontaneous, liberal, munificent, beneficent, having a heroic spirit for doing good. He added: Magistrates and Princes are commonly called so, who are stirred up by God to show themselves beneficent and liberal toward their subjects. The verb יעץ is to propose in the mind, to counsel, or to enter into counsel, to consult, to deliberate, to decree, which counsel is as it were a layer or covering upon which actions rest, βουλεύειν, συμβουλεύειν, συνάγειν, συνετίζειν, ἀγγέλλειν, ἀπαγγέλλειν, γινώσκειν, according to the version of the Seventy. Most of those are cognate: For when counsel is announced, it comes into knowledge: Nor can it be unknown when it is decreed, nor can consultation be instituted with another without the manifestation or announcement of the mind's senses, nor do we deliberate with ourselves without proposing something to our mind, nor do we decree without establishing or weighing in our mind whether it should be chosen or not? Therefore, it is the proper virtue of a Prince, and of any reborn person who, instructed by the Holy Spirit (the principal Spirit said to David, Ps. 51:12) and prepared and ready to offer sacrifices to God, whether Levitical or mystical, is πρόθυμος, that is, ready and prepared—voluntary, I say, and spontaneous, which alone, if they are presented through faith, are pleasing to God—to be liberal and munificent in promptly counseling what will be of use, both public and private, and in contributing to the matter what may serve others who are in need of counsel or help.

Such ἄρχοντες (rulers) are also the Doctors of the Church, although they ought not to be as the ἄρχοντες τῶν ἐθνῶν (rulers of the nations) who lord it over them or exercise authority, but as spiritual Princes or Leaders who are ἐυεργέται (benefactors). Matt. 20:25, Luke 22:25, mindful of that saying of Peter, 1 Ep. 4:10, 'as each has received a gift, ministering it to one another, as good stewards of the manifold grace of God': And what Paul has in 2 Cor. 9:7, 'God loves a cheerful giver': Most especially, however, what Christ, proposed to us as an example, that true נדיב, as Paul records in Acts 20:35, said: 'It is more blessed to give than to receive.' Those who neglect this are to be considered twins to the pagans, from whom Timocles of Delos, praised in Athenaeus book 8, chapter 11, made his own maxim contrary to the נדיב: ἀνόητος ὁ διδὺς, ἐυτυχὴς δὲ ὁ λαμβάνων: 'Insane is he who gives, happy is he who receives.' What? They are worse than the sounder Heathens, whose mind Plutarch expressed in his work On Love of Wealth: 'They would rather be rich, even while suffering, than become blessed by giving money.' Demosthenes, indeed, when asked what men had that was similar to God, replied, 'to do good,' as Maximus testifies in sermon 10. Xenophon's saying was also by no means pagan: 'It is much more noble and praiseworthy to leave behind a multitude of benefits than of trophies.' The truth of the word of Jesus, which to the children of this age is truly a paradox, and was once among the unwritten sayings, is confirmed, and they excite us to the practice of the aphorism, the reasons for which are to be properly recalled here, which it is helpful to express in the words of others. Then well, as Gregory the Great, book 28 of the Morals, chapter 6, excellently warned, the manifold grace of God is dispensed when the received gift is believed to be also for him who does not have these things, when it is thought to be given to oneself for the sake of him upon whom it is spent. This is the sum, says the other Gregory, the Theologian, Bishop of Nazianzus, regarding the Doctors, in his first Apologetic oration, that they may be able to be purified first, then to purify, to be instructed in wisdom, and thus TO RENDER OTHERS WISE, to become a light, & TO ILLUMINATE OTHERS, to approach God, and to lead others to Him, to be sanctified, & to bring holiness to others. Lord more than that which is spent on His poor, and where He finds the care of mercy, there He recognizes the image of His own piety. Let there be no fear of a lack of resources in these expenses, since kindness itself is a great substance, nor can the material for generosity be wanting where Christ feeds and is fed. In all this work that hand intervenes, which increases bread by breaking it, and multiplies it by distributing it. Let the distributor of alms be secure & cheerful, because he will have the greatest profit when he has reserved the least for himself, as the Blessed Apostle Paul says: 'He who provides seed to the sower, and bread for eating, will provide and multiply your seed, and will increase the fruits of your righteousness, in Christ Jesus our Lord.' To give is a sign of abundance, to receive of poverty, says Augustine in book III against Maximinus, ch. 14. And therefore the generosity of the giver is more blessed than the poverty of the receiver, and Cassian has this in book X on the renunciation of justice, ch. 18, 19. For according to Vallesius, Sacr. Phil. ch. 88, the end of liberal giving is not the emptiness of goods, but the addition of better things, such as honesty and honor. But the receiving is of poverty. For he who gives is more honorable, he who receives is viler, as Jerome teaches in his letter to Nepotianus. On the contrary, if I may add this παραφυαδικῶς (as an aside), in evils & injuries it is more blessed to receive than to give. Concerning which St. Chrysostom published homily no. LXXVIII to the people of Antioch. That it is better to suffer an injury than to inflict one. For heaven refers the whole right to the sufferer, makes him a citizen of the saints, absolves him from sins, and crowns him with justice. Do this, therefore, the golden-mouthed one advises, and looking to heaven, consider that you have been made like Him who sits there above the Cherubim. Therefore, not less truly than elegantly, Artaxerxes ὁ μακρόχειρ, called Longimanus, whom many chronologists—not going where one ought to go, but where the path leads—have made the husband of Esther, but without merit, along with Josephus, Sulpicius Severus, Nicephorus, and a Cardinal from the Society of Jesus, falsely and by antiphrasis so called, who is commonly believed to be named after another's initial, and who easily excels the rest of this century in erudition, namely Bellarmine, as well as his twin in the purple, and other Jesuits (you might more correctly call them Efavitas), such as Sanctius, Petavius, Salianus, Henricus Philippi, and also the author of the Gothan Chronological Historical Compendium—have done: when they ought rather to have followed the Blessed Luther here with Brentius and Funccius, because this glory of piety and munificence should be left to Darius Hystaspes, the chief restorer of the temple and the protector of the Lord's people. For they have more truly determined that Artaxerxes Longimanus—whose edict and munificence, spent on divine worship, is altogether ἀξιομνημόνευτος (worthy of memory) and worthy of such a King, and is celebrated by the Holy Spirit Himself, and is set as an example to other princes (פריצים) in Esther VII—is the one, as most ancient chronologists like Julius Africanus, Eusebius, Jerome, and not a few Greek and Latin Fathers, as well as more recent writers of history, both Papist and Reformed, such as Ussher, Bayly, Lansberg, and Samson, and Evangelicals like Chytræus, Christian Matthiæ, Joh. Cluverus, Gottfried Vogelius, Schillingius, Langius, and the authors of the Ernestine Compendium of Church History, have established: concerning whom there is enough in our sacred Chronicle. He is said to have said, as Plutarch commemorates in his Apophthegmata Regum: That for him as a prince, the hand for giving, namely the right, was very long, but the left was contracted and very short: for it is more kingly to add than to take away. For God also is long-handed for giving, but short-handed, or rather no-handed, for receiving.

Generosity of this kind will without doubt be recognized by grateful minds in the communication of the Illustrated Bibles of the Old and New Testaments, in the exhibition of the System of the Holy Scriptures, and in other works, both exegetical and polemical, especially against the Innovators, such as the Socinians, Arminians, and Calixtines, who revive the 'middle-way' buskin from the underworld, Grotius, Nicolai, and other fanatics, which have been given to the public light: Let the readers estimate with prudent comparison how much these cost, and yet how little they now sell for: for it is harder to strike the throat of the Innovators, without ambiguity, than to resist the ancients. For in this conflict others have led the way. But there, one had to fight without a leader, where the slipperiness of the adversaries often did not even permit the versatile and variegated antagonists to be recognized.

With the same generosity I present to the Church, I present to our illustrious Saxony, I present to your most Excellent Names the FOURTH VOLUME OF THE ILLUSTRATED BIBLES, both begun and brought to an end in these Saxon lands—to God alone be honor and glory! After I had dedicated the first to the MOST POWERFUL ELECTOR JOHN GEORGE II—may he live in this clamorous time, and may the Prince most necessary to the Church flourish as long as possible like the Rue! I dedicated the second to the MOST SERENE HEIR TO THE ELECTORATE, JOHN GEORGE III. May the divine hand preserve him, restored to life, for the consolation of the Church most happily! The third to the most Illustrious and High Princes of the Youth, JOHN GEORGE IV and FRIEDERICUS AUGUSTUS, names of good omen! The one FULL OF GRACE or GRACIOUS, BECAUSE HE IS PERPETUALLY WATCHING FOR THE FATHERLAND, the other called RICH IN PEACE, that is, in all-encompassing salvation, and ALWAYS AUGUST. May He grant such men for the salvation of the Saxon lands, the Empire, and the universal Church, I pray, and shall never cease to pray, as long as the Spirit rules these limbs; what remained, but that I should dedicate the FOURTH to the Illustrious Estates, should I dedicate to those most high, holily devoted, and humbly submissive Heads? By which very act I might both publicly render thanks for the benefits shown to me, and indeed reverently aspire to further grace, with my studies and strength exhausted in this old age, and as I trust, humbly aspire. I am certain, Illustrious Orders, that you acknowledge with the highest and never sufficiently to be praised grace, that these Electoral lands above other kingdoms and provinces have been especially affected, because from these shores, and indeed initially from this Academy, the light of true religion spread throughout the whole world, and emerged again from the midst of the darkness of the Babylonian Confusion: because it was asserted by the same from Stygian darkness for more than a whole century and a half into the tenth year: because it was vindicated from the Syncretistic Gloom, which lay upon the neighborhood: You will undoubtedly venerate the clemency of the King of Hosts, who granted that the Holy Bible, by the care and incredible diligence of the Blessed Luther, truly a God-man, most elegantly and most effectively, not without the assisting Spirit, might be read in the German idiom, while the Roman Capitol thundered in vain against it. You will undertake that which even today in the sources, just as it was done in the previous century by divine gift, if not more happily, may be read. You will also value at some price the successes granted by God, because it was permitted to vindicate the entire Scripture of the Old and New Testament in the Electoral Saxon University and in countless and most grave [works] of a Man, great in both deed and name, but an unhappy Advocate of the Roman curia, a more unhappy Aristarchus of the Scriptures, a most unhappy interpreter, and to restore them to their pristine luster, and to have set forth all the Prophetic Scriptures, all the Historical books of the Old Testament, likewise of the New Testament, with the whole Epistle to the Romans, truly golden and gem-like, a part of the former to the Corinthians, a part of the latter Epistle to the same Church, and also to the Thessalonians, and finally even the Johannine Apocalypse in public disputations, by an example which I believe is unheard of. Not to us, O Lord, not to us, but to your name, O Lord, be glory; again and again I vow. All of which I have endeavored to execute with all my might, so that everywhere, with the analogy of faith exposed from the parallels of the entire Scripture on the sole disk, the sounder interpretations of the holy Fathers, and also the explanations of more recent Doctors, especially of the Great-man Luther, might be asserted against the depravations of any heretics and fanatics whatsoever from the very sources, and so that the heavenly deposit of our Churches might be placed in safety. Whether I have achieved this, I piously commit to the judgment of the Church. That I have followed this everywhere, I can assert with a joyful conscience; that I have attained it everywhere, far be it that I should be so full of myself as to ever claim, which I am most certain can be thought of no mortal. The Roman Bishop alone ought to be able to do this, and because he ought, he is about to render thanks to God that he is at the same time able, [and one must ask] why he does not execute it, that is, why he does not adorn a perpetual gloss on the whole Holy Scripture, and from the Chair, in which he wishes to be infallible, promulgate it for all without any contradiction, just as Sixtus V and Clement VIII in their Bulls pronounced concerning the Vulgate edition without any error, to the great seduction of the world devoted to them, if indeed the Clementine and Sixtine editions clash with each other in more than a thousand places, they dared to proclaim. Therefore, one of these Pontiffs must have lied profusely: and this is that decanted infallibility, the unique and highest principle of the faith of the Roman Church.

Receive, O generous and pious souls, this work, whatever it is, dedicated to your Fatherland, and do not disdain to look upon me graciously. Thus may Divine grace look upon you again, and command your counsels, which are never not salutary, to be at the good pleasure of the Great Prince, and for the excellent Public, flourishing in this century, which is huge in all wealth, honors, and most happy things, and in the most praiseworthy gifts of yours, in the vigor of increments, so that you may live blessed and shine forever in the other century.

Of your Illustrious and Most Ample Names

Perpetual Worshipper, Indefatigable Intercessor before God,

ABRAHAM CALOVIUS, D.

L. S. B. I. D. I.

It is a mark of ingenuous candor and a grateful spirit not to be silent about the person through whom you have made progress. And in sacred studies especially, it matters much not to be, or to wish to appear, αὐτοδίδακτον [self-taught]. For those who are such love to be singular. This is to be avoided in these writings, which more than others require ὁμοψήφους [those of one mind]. Therefore we are commanded not to despise prophecies, and that the spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets. This was the reason why I have always loved the CATENAE, as the ancients called them, woven together from Greek and Latin authors: and why I have wished that these works of ours should exhibit some likeness to them: and to that end [I have used] the words of the authors, which it would have been so easy to change for my own, had I not chosen to save time in transcribing them, a task which, as it was most burdensome to me, I devolved upon an amanuensis, not without the expense of funds. Those things are more pleasing and sweeter which gush forth from the very fountains. Nor can any injury be done to authors in such a way, nor even be presumed by others, who can thus also more easily do without them, and have no need to go to expense on their account: Thus also mistakes, which often tend to arise from an ἀνεξερευνήτω [unexamined] manuscript, can be more avoided. The authors who have been employed are not deprived of their praise by that method: and when they had to be noted with censure, which was indeed always courteous and friendly, as was especially fitting among the orthodox, and such as everyone would wish for himself when the occasion arises, it was applied. Then, too, justice and equity demanded that I attribute to the Heterodox their due, whether in refuting errors or in the reckoning which they deserved. The consensus of whom often serves to confirm the truth and to reconcile others to it, and their dissensus serves to illustrate the same truth ἐκ ἐναντίας [from the opposite]. I therefore ordered them to speak ἰδίᾳ γλώσσῃ [in their own tongue], lest they complain that they are not understood. Nor have the ὀι ἀμφίβιοι [amphibious ones] been neglected, or deprived of their honor when they have touched the nerve. For sometimes even a gardener has spoken very opportunely. It seemed that pains should be taken so that the Fathers, especially GREGORY, CHRYSOSTOM, JEROME, ARETHAS, ANDREW OF CAESAREA, THEOPHYLACT, might be perceived αὐτολέξει [word for word], and among them our Blessed LUTHER ὁ πάνυ [the great], truly a most accurate interpreter. This was demanded by the emphases, the elegance of the speech, the gravity, the sweetness, and the harmony, by their own right. To him, in the explanation of Genesis, the Psalms, the Epistles to the Romans, to the Galatians, and the Apocalypse, it is fitting to attribute in great part the genuine sense of the holy Apostles: just as the Blessed Gerhard rendered the palm ambiguous for others in what he expounded in the Harmony of the Evangelists, and in Genesis, as also in the Song of Songs, and not least in the earlier [commentaries] on Romans, in both Petrine [epistles], and in the Apocalypse, upon which Blessed Cluverus also bestowed excellent effort, and the Weimar Paraphrase, which faithfully followed him (I mean Gerhard) regarding the last writing: [and] Blessed Dorschäus in his ἀνεκδότοις [unpublished works] on the Epistle to the Hebrews, Dr. Sebastian Schmid on Job, Blessed Aegidius Hunnius on the Pauline and Johannine Epistles, Blessed Hülsemann on chapter II of James, and Blessed Brockmand on the whole Epistle. Not without merit are to be added to them WELLER, OSIANDER, CHEMNITZ, POLYCARP, and WILHELM LYSER, GERHARD, πολλῶν ἀντάξιος ἄλλων [worth many others], and his son JOHANN ERNST, the HUNNIUSES, MYLIUS, PHILIPP NICOLAI, GESNER, RUNGIUS, BALDUIN, WINCKELMANN, HOE, HÜLSEMANN, ἀκριβείᾳ [in precision] second to none, and his twin in the same, DORSCHÄUS, BROCHMAND, CLUVER, HOPFNER, MENTZER, MEISNER, BEHM the elder, especially in Chronology (the younger abandoned the footsteps and orthodoxy of his parent), FEUERBORN, MYSLENTA, TARNOV, DANNHAUER, ὀι νῦν ἐν ἁγίοις [those now among the saints], Dr. GEIER, SCHMID, and others, whose MS. ἀνεκδότοις [unpublished works] I have also used in part with a grateful hand and mind, all of whom, now triumphing in heaven, I venerate as Fathers in Christ, not to mention others now, whom the index at the end will not fail to note.

But in particular, those who elsewhere bore a certain symbol in refuting GROTIUS were to be heard: RIVET, MARESIUS, BAILLIE, and others who happened to occur, and the rest produced in the Catalog of Authors.

Now if anyone says that few things here are mine, he will not find me denying it. I have already brought forward the reason why I prefer to be a follower of others rather than αὐτοδίδακτος [self-taught]. If [he says they are] vile and of no great moment, let him know that nothing is vile and small in the Scriptures, and that it is enough if they are recognized as not useless, and how much more so if they are recognized as necessary, just as these are valued by not a few on account of the corruptions of Grotius, for the judging of which not all have equally exercised senses. Finally, I make that saying of Jerome in the Prologue to the Galeatus to the XXXV. [chapters] of Exodus my own here: In the temple of GOD everyone offers what he can, some gold, silver, and precious stones, others fine linen and purple: it goes well with us if we have offered skins and goats' hair.

I have called it a NEW-ANCIENT HARMONY: New, because I have seen none adorned in this way: Ancient, because I judge it uniquely to be the true one: for everything most ancient is most true. Ancient, because I have read the footsteps of the Fathers, as the Canons handed down concerning harmony; Ancient, because although it is nowhere found ὀλικῶς [wholly] in that way, yet κατὰ μέρη [in parts], as far as that part is concerned in this one, and as far as another part is concerned in that one, it is founded upon the ancients. I judged that the Gospel commentaries hardly needed [my work], after Grotius seemed to have shed some light upon them with his very learned annotations; But in the censure, when it had to be applied ὡς ἐν παρόδῳ [as if in passing] as the matter required, and as the occasion allowed, I compared the opinions of others, and I chose the one which I believed to be truer, and I confirmed it with the words of the authors whom I found to be ὁμοψήφες [of one mind], or by authority, designated by a bare citation, no less than by textual reasons: sometimes I also discussed the contrary reasons of their own, but always those of Grotius, when he seems to dissent not without some reason: I also considered it not superfluous or useless to bring forward sporadically some things from our own writings not yet published for a richer elucidation of the texts, with defenses against those who dissent. Moreover, the concatenated labors here and there did not allow me to seek out with care all the more recent opinions into which I happened to fall. To the heretics I opposed a just refutation, instituted ἀποτόμως [severely] according to the admonition of the Apostle; to the orthodox I showed the due modesty. Nor did I fear τὰ ἴδια ἀνερεῖν [to retract my own things]: And to amend those things which I wrote otherwise when reviewed. To which end I added the years in which each was published to the portrait prefixed. For day has taught day, and my name among those who write proficiently, I do not hesitate to report. I have rarely produced an ἰδίαν ἐπίλυσιν, or my own meditations, and not unless I was certain that they were in agreement with the intention of the Holy Spirit, which indeed are not even to be considered an ἰδίᾳ ἐπιλύσει. For I have always striven to be a stranger to the pursuit of singularity, observing that Chemnitian maxim: Τὰ κοινὰ κοινῶς, & τὰ καινὰ κοινῶς, I have gladly used my own words and a didactic style, which the Apostle requires, not one that is curled with tongs or obscured by an excessive affectation of tropes and figures. To this kind of teaching I have been accustomed from my tender years, as is approved by Chemnitz, Gerhard, and other great men. I have studiously avoided barbarisms and solecisms, unless the terms of the arts were required to be called into use ἐξ ἀνάγκης, or had been called so by others. And to these things I have devoted my effort. After the Chronology of the Old Testament and the Chronotaxis prefixed to the Acts of the Apostles, I did not think that the historical [parts] required such a lengthy commentary, and the reason for the συνεχείας, which is apparent in the Gospels or from the Harmony; where, however, they did require it, I did not fail in the parts of my duty: therefore the Acts could be dispatched in shorter lines; but in the commentaries on the Epistles of Paul and the other Apostles, because of the assertion of the dogmas of faith, there was need of greater care. And the GROTIAN opinion is clearly singular and novel in most respects, not only concerning the Anti-Christ, but also concerning Christ, His kingdom, the Church, and His enemies, both spiritual and corporal: therefore a new refutation, a new study, and one that is the more accurate, seemed to be demanded, the more ornately the Great Man adorns his Helen, lest the αἴτησις τῇ ἐν ἀρχῇ of the refutation be justly objected; but in order that πολυλογία might be avoided, it did not seem appropriate to repeat those things which had already been said or treated in one or two places, concerning which the places of Scripture observed by Grotius or in our notes, or the indices, will generally be able to give notice, unless perhaps when the prior treatment has slipped from memory. That nothing was given by me to party spirit in choosing the truer opinions will be evident from the fact that I have just as easily added the calculation to heterodox authors, when they have attained the sense of Holy Scripture, as to those who are associates of our faith: for that saying of Primasius pleased me: 'Indeed, I have even culled from the Donatist TICONIUS those things which were in agreement with a sound sense, and from those things which were to be chosen, I have tempered them for Catholic moderation, repressing the redundant, cutting back the importunate, and composing the unpolished: but just as a precious gem found in dung by a prudent man ought to be collected and restored to its innate dignity, so wherever truth may shine forth, it is to be claimed for Catholic unity.' My only intention was not to deviate from the sense and intention of the Holy Spirit. If I have attained this, which I would not dare to hope or presume in all things, give thanks to GOD with me; if not, you will attribute it to human infirmity. However, if any errors appear, I would not wish them to be imputed to me: perhaps not even to the Corrector or the Amanuensis, for I readily concede that the ἀυτόγραφον could not always be read equally well. Sometimes Grotius himself, or the printer, or the copyists were at fault. In the proofreading I applied the effort that I could, but because it sometimes had to be done in haste, it may have happened that errors were left without correction. The reason for the συνεχείας was not always rendered, especially where it seemed clear from our explanation, or the Grotian one, or was to be elicited from the sense of Grotius, and was believed by me not to be inconvenient. Whose annotations I for the most part tacitly approve, when I have not noted them with an adverse censure, whether ἐπ᾿ ἀυτοφώρῳ or in another place. I have left minor matters without censure, either because they were to be left in the middle, or because the praetor does not concern himself with trifles. Trifles, that is, with regard to Grotian matters: for in the Scriptures nothing of the sort is to be estimated: 'Whoever shall break the least point in the law, Holy Scripture, shall be called the least in the kingdom of heaven,' that is, nothing. 'He who is guilty in one is guilty of all': for all things are from one, of one truth, of one authority, equally infallible and divine, and therefore equally inviolable. I have treated the principal dogmas in their primary seat or classic places, so that it is possible from this to adorn Commonplaces throughout the whole Theological System in the manner of the index of Tirinus, or of our Dn. D. OLEARIUS, a supreme Theologian and intimate Brother, to be honored in the highest place, as observed in the Commentaries of the Blessed Balduinus, and to prove them solidly, as I am persuaded in the Lord, with each one fully recalled and digested to its own place and from all the sayings pertaining thereto, so that I may be able to supersede the continuation of the System, if by chance old age should cut short its thread: which, however, with the final hand placed upon this Biblical work, I shall undertake, God willing, hoping that it may be completed in the same tenor in which it was begun. For not only will my opinions from thence, and their foundations, be collected, but also the ἀντίθεσis and ἔλεγχος of the adversaries, as much as is sufficient. Most have been adduced, if you depart from the recent fanatics: for both the names and often the opinions of these are obscure. Nor was it granted to compare them, either because they could not be had among us, or because I was excluded by time when I was referred to them. But I must not be silent here, but must celebrate with the due praise of more exquisite diligence my former listener and συζητητής, a most industrious man, the very Reverend Dn. M. Ioh. Andr. Lucius, Court Μεσεκκλησιαστὴς of Dresden, whose help in annotating the Interpreters I profess to have used not rarely. Furthermore, a certain distinguished man [has] an index of that System from the Anti-Grotian [parts] of the former edition, who, if he should continue, or should not be burdened to transcribe the very διήγησιν at the same time, with both my words and those of Grotius, although it is a work of great labor; I promise, however, that it will also be of great use: for whose sake amanuenses will altogether have to be employed, not without expense, but I promise a return to them and to the τῇ ἐργοδιώκτῃ. But first this entire index must be completed and shared with me; I promise its use not only to the collector, but also to any reader whatsoever. For what is more useful than Biblical Theology? Without Scripture, Theology does not even deserve to be called Theology. Let the Theologian blush to speak without Scripture: the Physicist without nature, or the document of nature: unless Scripture supplies its place. What ἀποδειξις is then sufficient, not merely Topical arguments: as some sciolists today, not without contempt for Scripture, think: Moreover, I have used the means τῆς ἑρμηνείας, which our blessed Franzius praised in his writing concerning the interpretation of Scripture, on account of certain oracles, although handed down with tedious prolixity, not uselessly; on account of which the authority of great men was sometimes to be postponed. I have added the argument of the chapters, with the partitions of both books and sections, everywhere. I have studied accuracy rather than elegance of words. If this, adorned with a paraphrase woven from a Biblical work, and where perhaps that is lacking, supplemented by the elucidation of the text from Osiander or Vlnarius, were to be published, with verses added to the argument corresponding to the text, which were omitted through haste (for any argument exhibits the whole text or chapter almost in summary), that little work, in my judgment, would be neither useless nor ungrateful: I myself will meditate on such a thing, under the title of Summaries and Partitions of Scripture, if divine kindness keeps me alive. For by that method, the Biblical series will be able to be imprinted on the memory more easily in a cursory reading of the Bibles, with those things always repeated, and the literal sense of Scripture will be obtained more correctly in an accurate one. Which has been my only wish, my only study. That, if I have obtained it by means of this, is that for which I congratulate not so much myself, as the Church, for whom these things are intended. Such a compendium, God granting, a Harmony, in which parallel texts are only cited, not written out, but the texture is shown at the same time through the Evangelists teaching the same things, will also be able to follow harmoniously, so that even with the copies distributed in a smaller form, an appendix to the Biblical Volumes APPARATUS with a SUPPLEMENT to the illustrated Bibles of both Testaments, comprising I. A BIBLICAL CRITIC, II. MOSAIC GENESIS exposed with a very rich commentary: III. Classical Dicta, vindicating the pre-existence of the Son of GOD before the Nativity from the Virgin Mary: such as Gen. III. 15. Jer. IX. 24. c. VI. 29. 57. Rom. VIII. 4. Heb. I. 22. c. IV. 1. Matt. XI. 17. c. VI. 28. 41. 42. 48. c. XVI. 5. c. VII. 3. c. IV. 25. c. XVI. 18. 50. 58. 62. 1. Cor. X. 4. c. X. 5. c. IV. 26. c. XVII. 5. c. VI. 39. 40. 44. c. X. 9. c. XI. c. IV. 29. John I. 1. et seq. c. VII. 16. 28. 29. c. XI. 3. c. XIII. c. VII. 1. c. I. 3. c. VIII. 23. c. XV. 47. 1. Pet. 1. 10. 11. Exod. XXXIII. 20. c. I. 9. c. VIII. 41. Gal. III. 23. 1. John I. 20. 1. Kings II. 19. c. I. 10. c. VIII. 58. c. IV. c. IV. 9. 10. 14. Job XIX. 25. c. I. 14. c. XI. 27. Eph. I. 22. c. V. 20. Ps. II. 7. c. I. 15. c. XVI. 28. c. III. 17. Jude v. 14, XVI. 8. chap. III. 15. c. XVII. 5. 7. Col. I. 16. 17. Rev. I. 8. XLV. 8 c. III. 17. c. XVII. 8. Heb. I. 22. c. I. 11. CX. 1. c. III. 13. 31. c. VIII. 32. c. II. 5. c. II. 8. Isa. IX. 6. c. V. 35. Acts VII. 56. c. II. 14. 15. c. III. 21. c. XLIII. 9. c. V. 14. 23. 24. 30. 37. c. X. 10. c. III. 7. c. XXI. 6. c. III. 16. c. XXII. 13.

IV. ROMAN APOSTOLIC THEOLOGY, or that which is handed down in the Epistle to the Romans through XXII oracles, clearly asserted against the various corruptions of the Papists, Calvinists, Socinians, and other heterodox persons. V. A VESTIBULE to the Epistle to the Hebrews, in which most things pertaining to the canonical authority, ministerial author, original language, occasion, scope, method, partition, and finally the excellence and dignity of this Epistle are unfolded, with a preceding oration on the prerogatives by which this Epistle stands out and excels above the other writings of the N. T.

Concerning the Apocalypse there would be many things which perhaps might not be mentioned ἀκαίρως (untimely) nor ἀκάρως (without effect). But the fair reader will see of his own accord that no less effort was applied to it than to the other Apostolic Epistles (since the ἀποκάλυψις [revelation] is also written and inscribed in epistolary form) so that the true sense might be rendered with continuous συνεχείᾳ (continuity), and the parallel passages not so much unrolled as hinted at. For it was thus adorned by the Holy Spirit, so that together with the visions, the prediction of the ἀποςασίας (apostasy) from the faith, and of seduction to heresies, both of others and especially of the Roman Anti-Christ, it might present and confirm the true doctrine and the eternal Gospel, just as from most of the chapters of the uniquely saving religion here not obscurely proposed, but clearly expounded: Sentences which were determined too ἐιδικῶς (specifically) or particularly by some, such as by D. Joh. Cocceius, as also by our own B. D. G. B. M. I. D. and others, but less περιςατικῶς (circumstantially), if I may use the word, are designated in the Apocalypse, e.g., concerning the army of the superior logisticians, concerning the Bohemian War, concerning the recent English parricide, concerning the Cromwellian shaking of the kingdoms of England, and the conflict with the Dutch, and likewise concerning the Swedish victories of the most glorious GUSTAVUS ADOLPHUS, and the repression of the Anti-Christian endeavor, etc., I pass over these ἐκ προαιρέσεως (by choice) and deliberately with a dry foot, lest I should seem to want to carp at others or to be occupied without reason in those things which I have judged to be entirely ἀσήπηκτα (unprovable) and merely ingenious human inventions. Thinking that I have performed my duty sufficiently if I should confirm more solidly those things which are entirely certain, such as those which the great Luther [Megalander] held, rather than laboriously toil over such clearly uncertain matters.

To all of which will not inconveniently be subjoined Academic explanations of prophecies and divine oracles, which were proposed here and at Königsberg by public programs, either for the sake of the Theological Faculty or the Academy, as they contribute not a little to illustrating and confirming the sense of Scripture more richly. And therefore a fuller treatment will be had here of most things which perhaps could still be desired from our more sacred store or furniture: and thus the illustrated Bibles will be completed in five Exegetical Volumes.

But lest I hinder my Polemical studies, since those things which pertained to the wars of the Lord, proposed through disputations in various places but easily scattered, cannot all be obtained, nor are they any longer found in the shops of booksellers, and yet are sometimes curiously sought by not a few: I am in the process of comprising in three Volumes the Elenchtic Writings, whether hitherto published or still unpublished, in the Latin and German idiom: and the same, if indeed I have already come to an agreement with a most upright man, a most famous bookseller in a certain Illustrious Republic, who is studious of propagating the glory of the divine name, I shall present to the Church in a more corrected form. I shall perhaps present a Biblical Epitome, the partitions of the Sacred Code, with summaries of the chapters, to be exhibited separately in a smaller form, which as an Enchiridion or manual can be carried more easily, or, since you perhaps seek it, it can already be taken from the Illustrated Bibles, and to the chapters beginning a new period of time, I shall at the same time add a Chronology, which is not so obvious to everyone: until all those things, together with the Biblical Paraphrase and the most useful, nay, most highly necessary appendix of the more important parallel passages, if GOD shall have granted life and grace, it will be permitted to add. Finally, lest the didactic names be left incomplete with the Parenetic ones, since from many of the Four Volumes of the Theological System (in which we have proposed Sacred instruction, or elements, as an Isagoge to Theology: theophany, or divine manifestation, according to nature, and especially the mystery of the most Holy) Trinitatis: κτισιογραφίαν, concerning the works of creation, and specifically concerning the Angels: as well as ἀνθρωπονομίαν, concerning man, in whom the law was both inscribed and prescribed) I see that a continuation is desired, and being provoked by almost daily reproaches to complete the same, I have set myself to that task also, ξὺν θεῷ, and by divine grace I have now dispatched the four following Tomes, namely παιδαγωγίαν νομικὴν, the legal leading of man alienated from GOD by sin, by which we are led to Christ as if by an injected hand, through the law as a schoolmaster, as it is called in Gal. III. 25,

& thus we are led back to God: geisognōsian, a just information concerning the person & office of Christ: ekklēsiometrían, concerning the Church, and its [history] according to ages, before the flood, after the flood, before the Babylonian captivity, about the same, after the liberation from the same: likewise under Christ in the days of his flesh, & the times of the Apostles, up to Constantine the Great, thence under the Anti-Christ, & from that to the Reformation of the Blessed Luther, finally from thence up to the consummation of the age, & the destruction and most recent punishment of the Anti-Christ, according to the religion, & condition of the faithful, under the varied appearance and figure of those different ages, and the status or different Monarchies, the measure, or Economy concerning the same divine, & mystēriosophían, heavenly wisdom concerning divine mysteries, of the Sacraments of both Testaments. There still remain three Volumes, namely the divine Nomocanon, or nomothesían; Christian Soteriology, which contains our calling to Christ, the illumination and conversion obtained from Christ, the donation of faith in Christ, with a more accurate explanation of the nature of faith, today highly necessary on account of the Arminian Syncretists, justification through faith in Christ alone, union with Christ, and indwelling, and the immanent joy and exhilaration of Christ in us, Sanctification in the Spirit, and preservation in holiness, and thus perseverance in faith; and the defection from faith or Apostasy from faith contrary to it, which finally degenerates into the sin against the Holy Spirit, and blasphemy of the Spirit: likewise repentance outside of the sin against the Holy Spirit, and finally eternal glorification. And sacred eschatologían, to which I also refer practical athanasían, or the art of dying well. It will be your task, Benevolent Reader, to assist and promote these my efforts, such as they are, and my life and health with pious prayers, just as I am prepared to assist and promote yours in your studies, in turn. May God thus make us both fruitful and safe by His grace! Given at Wittenberg, on the Day of the Lord's Epiphany, in the Year of the birth of Christ 1676.

ABRAHAM CALOVIVS, D.

To the most Reverend and Magnificent Man, Lord Dr. Abraham Calovius.

You marvel that Columbus was able to turn the whole world by the ship of his voyage across the sea, furrowing various waters through shallows and sandbanks, until he bravely obtained the ports he could: continue to marvel, Reader, behold a new Columbus, who is present, another far greater than the former. He who furrowed the sea, than which there is none deeper, which no sounding line is able to explore. Namely the Ocean, containing HOW GREAT mysteries! Which cannot be known, or grasped by reason. Indeed, which reason mocks with contempt, and at which, having been disgusted, it feels nausea with its own wit. So that at the same time they do not yield to the cliffs of the soul, which are not believed, just as on the contrary only those things which are believed are strong for life. What would one not be amazed at? Would one not call individual things abysses? And would one not count them among the waters above the heavens? And yet, compressed into this one volume, all that the HOLY BIBLE completes with its own sense; now thus illuminated by the study and labor of Calovius, by the progress of his pen, and by the rowing of his own effort. So that he who now sails the sea of Holy Scripture may fear nothing at all that might delay his journey, or perhaps leave an eclipse of understanding, and everything that was hidden before may now lie open. You, Reader, who handle the Bible, only stop your step, and look upon this work with your own eyes.

What do you wish me to lay aside? You will speak with me yourself, since behold, this new Columbus is here with his oars! Who traverses the straits, who the reefs, who the abysses of the divine mind, and shows a level path everywhere.

Thus Tobias Wagner, Doctor and Chancellor of the University of Tübingen, esteems the Biblical Work of the Lord Author, a most consummate Theologian.

O excellent Interpreter of Scripture and Prelate of sacred things, who feeds the young and the sheep with your writings and your voice: the holy Spirit has breathed upon you from the ethereal citadel, and rules your pen and tongue night and day: CALOVIUS, you reveal yourself to the world in such learned writings as rare ages produce. For many have explained the books of the Prophets, and the writings of the son of Jesse, beloved by the pious. But your holy Bibles, illustrated with new notes, now surpass the rest and deserve praise. Nothing remains, except that you may live on after death, and that rewards worthy of you may come from heaven. Johannes Meisnerus, Doctor, writes on the Biblical labors of the most honorable Lord Colleague.

Luther is the sublime pillar of the Chair, and CALOVIUS the first glory of the ridge of Zion; the divinely inspired harvest of writers, and exhausted labors, place an immortal name for WHOM in the world: what will finally be the limit of your merits? What hour will bring more pleasant leisure to your pen? Behold, GROTIUS, laid low, again offers you the grass, multiplying the certain trophies of his defeat. Let other things wither; let Fame, the aged woman, speak of this present Triumph worthily among the peoples. May the Church henceforth enjoy these palms, AND MAY THE GOOD FATES PRESERVE YOU FOR US FOR A LONG TIME!

Thus Johannes Andreas Quenstedt, Doctor and Public Professor of Sacred Theology, congratulates from his heart the most Reverend, Ample, and Excellent Lord Doctor ABRAHAM CALOVIUS, a man most illustriously deserving of the Church of Christ, his kinsman, fellow godfather, colleague, and in Christ Jesus his venerable and sincerely beloved brother, for his completed labor.

COmmemoratione dignissima est admonitio Domini Dominorum, & Principis Regum terræ, quam per Magnum Imperatorem Populi Israelitici dedit, cùm ille Regem posceret, quid præcipui ejus muneris esse debeat, qui tantum populum, Regale Dei sacerdotium, guber- naturus erat: Id nempe præcipiebat: Describat sibi Rex legis in volumine, habeatque secum, ac legat illud omni- bus diebus vitæ suæ, ut discat timere Dominum Deum suum, & custodire verba, & ceremonias Ejus, quæ in lege præcepta sunt.

Regibus æquiparari in Regno Anti-Christi Cardinales, Bellarmini, fim- brias suas extendere conantis, sententia est. Quantò magis in Regno Chri- sti componuntur cum Regibus Electores? Illis nihil sanctius, nihil prius, & antiquius esse debet, quàm lectio Sacri Codicis, quem Cardinales, sæpè sæ- pius plus nimio Carnales, neque legunt, neque si legerent, intelligerent. Non semel tantùm, sed bis describenda erat, Regibus Israeliticis lex Domini, cùm in throno sedebant Regio, nisi ante evectionem jam ab ipsis descripta lex fuerit. Disquirunt Interpretes, an propria manu lex deseribenda fuerit? quod plerique, nec immeritò, adfirmant. Quid enim magni hoc foret, si descri- bi saltem curarent, quomodo memoriæ hærere Domini lex per descriptio- nem posset, nisi manum ipsi operi admoverint? Quâ operâ profectò nihil præ- stantius, nihil summis Capitibus dignius: Idcircò enim Regis secundum cor Dei, & probatissimi, Davidis, Lex Domini auro & argento longè pretio- sior thesaurus optimus, sapientem reddens Regem, præ omnibus Patribus, hæreditas summa, & inæstimabilis: Judicio Regum Sapientissimi Salomo- nis, non auro tantùm, sed & margaritis, gemmisque præstantissimis longè excellentior sapientia, quæ ex verbo Dei habetur, quam nemo mortalium sa- tis æstimare, nemo laudibus condignis extollere valet,

Nec verò manu tantùm nocturnâ & diurna volvenda Lex divina, sed cor- de fovenda fideli perpetuò, imò opere ipso exprimenda, & sanctè implenda, quoad ejus fieri potest, per totum regiminis spatium: Vulgò dicitur, sed ve- rissimum est, de sacrâ maximè Scriptura, Lectio lecta placet, decies repetita placebit. At verò hoc præceptum Domini aureis literis cordibus Princi- pum inscribendum: Postquam sederit in solio regni sui Rex Israel, describat sibi iteratam hanc legem in volumine, accipiens exemplar à Sacerdotibus Leviticæ tribus: Et habebit secum, legetque illud omnibus diebus vitæ suæ, & discat timere Dominum Deum suum, & custodire verba, & ceremonias Ejus, quæ in lege præscripta sunt. Nec elevetur cor ejus in superbiam super fratres suos, neque declinet in partem dextram vel sinistram, ut longo tem- pore regnet ipse, & Filius ejus super Israel. Præscribant itaque Theologi leges felicis, JCti justi, Medici longævi, Philosophi Prudentis regiminis: hæc una Regula, quam Dominus ipse dedit, omnia illa præstat uberrimè, regnum felix, justum, longævum, prudens, omnibusque numeris auspicatissimum, & exoptatissimum. Idcirco Jojadas summus Sacerdos Regiis Joas in solemni inauguratione, etsi septennali, qualis ferè est JOHANNES GEORGIUS QUARTUS, IGNIS DOMINI, ab igneo zelo erga verbum DEI vocari dignus, librum legis tradi jussit, ut Regi diligenter illum evolvendum esse innueret.

Nihil in hâc Regulâ de geminâ Legis descriptione: Addunt tamen tradi- tiones Rabbinicæ: Nec id sine causâ: quia fortius imprimitur animo, quod inscribitur iteratò. Et cum manibus Regii describitur lex, in manus de- scribentis, quia iteratur descriptio, tantò fortius influit ad vivum exercitium, quandoquidem non sit, ut humanæ leges, in animis, sed animata, & viva, spiritus & vita, cum fideli corde excipitur, ac fovetur.

Si quis Principum in orbe Christiano reperitur, cui religiosior hæc descri- bendæ legis cura fuerit, AVUS Vester, Principes Laudatissimi, Exemplum & instar Principum gloriosissimum, cujus nomen ideò æternitati consecrandum est, is censendus est, JOHANNES GEORGIUS II. Non is solùm lite- ras omnes Scripturæ, Maseretharum numero, etiam extra subsidium memo- riæ, tabulas conscriptas in numerato habet, quòd non facilè de Principe fan- do accepimus: sed curiosè sensum etiam scrutatur, qui anima est Scripturæ, non verò cum Anti-Christo, ejusque adoratoribus, alienum à Principis curâ putat, scripturæ sensum per lectionem sedulam Scripturæ, quæ ob id Ebræis Lectio dicitur, scrutari. Quam devoto etiam animo in eo totus sit, ut vita exprimat, quod mente complèxus est, idea vitæ Ejus doceat: quam nemini clam habet, Illustrem aulam esse permittens, ut omnes intueantur: omnibus quippe speculum splendidissimum futuram. Non sanè unquam tam flagi- tiosa nomina Pii verè Impii, Clementis nihil minus quàm Clementis, Euge- nii, omni generositate destituti, Marti multum, præter munus sacrum con- secrati, Innocentis ab omni innocentia, Urbani, ab omni urbanitate quàm alienissimi, verbo, monstra hominum horrenda, in throno, qui creditur san- ctissimo, sedissent, si Scripturæ lectio in justo ipsis pretio fuisset. Confundet ergò in novissimo die Sanctulos illos Beatissimus Princeps, cum lucebit in fir- mamento instar Solis, ipsi verò ad tenebras æternas etiam calculo ipsius, in throno judiciario collocati, damnabuntur.

Macte Heroicâ Virtute Princeps JOHANN GEORGI III. Hæres porrò, ut Patriarum virtutum, ita & zeli Heroici adversus Sacras literas, earumque sanctiorem observationem audias. Macte Serenissime quondam Successor JOHANN GEORGI QUARTE, Princeps Juventutis Eminentissime. Ma- cte Celsissime Dux FRIDERICE AUGUSTE, ADJUNCTE OLIM LO- CUM-TENENTIS GLORIOSISSIMI, VERE AUGUSTE, omen hoc atque votum Avitum, quod cum titulis istis prudentissimè concepit ELE- CTOR omni laude superior JOHANN GEORGIUS II. Paternæ virtutis ex asse hæres, Avitam superans, Pro-Avum referens felicissimè. Sitis tales, quales exoptat Gloriosissimus Avus, cum Avia Celsissima, Parens Laudatissi- mus, cum Matre AUGUSTA matronalium Virtutum Regiarum speculum fulgidissimum, & prorsus incomparabile: quales certò sperant tot provinciæ, imò totum Imperium Romanum Sacro-Sanctum; Quid? Orbis universus

Evangelicæ fidei addi stus, per totum mundum, & omnia terræ climata diffu- fus. Donata iterum ista tanti cœli deposita, post desperatam fere vitæ restitu- tionem, divinâ Clementiâ, ut prece pientissima, educatione religiosissima, in- formatione Regia virtutibus Majorum utriusque stirpis verè augustis throno dignos reddant successores. O exaudiat cœlum universam Ecclesiam Lu- theranam idem voventem, & facta manu ob idem cœlum ambientem,reddat- que eam exambientem: Et ut multa paucis complectar, largiatur ea omnia, quæ pii, & Christiani Principis Vota sunt, feroque tandem ad se recipiat cum Serenissimis illis capitibus corona immarcessibili mactandos.

Quod votum, imo cœlitus id precibus quotidianis cum meis certo impe- traturus sum, donum meum humilimum, strenæ instar, gratiosissime admit- tite, DOMINI GRATIOSISSIMI, & structuras Clementiæ in me vibrate, ædesque meas pauperculas; Ita, quod unum possum, non prout par est, ec- quis enim id posset, sed pro virili nomina Vestra AUGUSTA & GLORIO- SA æternitati consecrabo. Quod hac compellatione omnino contendo, Historiæ Exempli Exemplorum, virtutis virtutum JESULI NOSTRI dulcis- simi per Quatuor Amanuenses luculenter descriptæ, juxta eum luminarium mundi excelsorum paris verè comparis, S. PETRI, non Romani, sed Antio- cheni Episcopi, Judæorum Doctoris, & S. PAULI, Romani, vel potius totius orbis, gentium maxime, Apostoli vitæ & præconii curriculo magnam partem exhibeo. Ita etiam excitabor hilaris, si tantis Principibus placuero, quæ non ultima laus est, studium ceptorum operum sacrorum, & inter hæc post expe- ditas Annotationes Biblicas, Systematis Theologici, ac si Deus concesserit, Paraphraseos totius Codicis Biblici, Latino-Germanicæ publico sistere, glo- riæ Vestræ nuncupandæ, etsi eidem per me nihil accedere posse, noverim, qui potius id molior summopere, ut quod deest luminis & gloriæ hisce me- is, à tantis Nominibus & Numinibus affundatur. Ita imprimis pergam pre- cibus fatigare cœlum, ut non nisi post seros annos, cœlo ista sanctiora cœli deposita reddantur, æternumque post innumeras victorias Heroës cœli triumphent. Qui in hoc seculo bene imperat, Isidoro l. III. de Summo Bo- no c. XLIIX. ominante, sine fine in perpetuum regnat, & de gloria hujus secu- li ad æternam gloriam transit.

SERENISSIMORUM VESTRORUM NOMINUM

ABRAHAM CALOVIUS, D.
