Whence it came about that the holy writers very often oppose the doctrine of Christ to law, and call it by the name of grace, or if ever they need to use the word law for it, they add seasonings that temper the rigor of its name, as when it is called the law of faith, not of works Rom. III. 27, and the law of liberty Jas. I. 25. Deservedly, therefore, did Christians, in order to commend the saving doctrine by the very sound of the name, prefer to prefix to it the title of covenant rather than law. Although, however, διαθήκη, as we have said, when it treats of Christian doctrine, has primarily the meaning of covenant, yet since the Greek word quite commonly denotes a testament, it is no wonder that this use of the word is also alluded to by the writer of the Epistle to the Hebrews IX. 17, especially since a Testament, particularly where an heir is instituted under a condition, or something is committed to his trust, approaches as closely as possible to the nature of covenants or agreements. Latin Christians, however, not for that not only in that place, but wherever διαθήκη is found in the New Testament, and indeed in the Old, even where διαθήκη Θεȣ is named, they have employed the word testament: not so much following the usage of law and the forum, as the nature and origin of the word, which is apt to embrace everything by which someone makes his will known: especially, however, that by which a certain totality of goods is conferred upon someone: in which sense the word heir is also accustomed to be taken, apart from the indication of death, as when we are called heirs of God. But since there were formerly many διαθήκαι Θεȣ, as appears in Rom. IX. 4, Ephes. II. 12, and circumcision itself κατ' ἐξοχὴν, just as ברית in the books of Moses and the Prophets and in the most received custom of the Jews, is so called in Greek διαθήκη in Acts VII. 8, and the promises also concerning Christ made of old come under this name in Luke I. 72, Acts III. 25. Gal. III. 15, 17, yet the new διαθήκη is properly and peculiarly opposed to that public and most solemn covenant which was begun at the departure from Egypt, and completed on Mount Sinai, and sanctioned by the application of the blood of animals: as appears in Jerem. XXXI. 32. And these are the two διαθῆκαι which Paul sets before our eyes as ἀντιδιῃρημένας in Gal. IV. 24, and just as he calls that one παλαιὰν διαθήκην in 2 Cor. III. 14, so he calls this one, in respect to it, καινὴν in verse 6, and in the same way the writer of the most noble epistle to the Hebrews calls that one the first, and this one now the new, now the fresh, and indeed the better, and likewise the eternal. It appears from this that this book cannot be called the New Testament in Latin, except in that looser and more recent acceptance of the word: not that what is contained in it is not properly a Testament (for it is the will of Christ confirmed by his own death) but that in that sense the old cannot be opposed to it: wherefore it must either be called a covenant, or the word Testament must be extended beyond the limits of old and common usage.

Latin:

PRÆLOQUIUM GROTIANUM DE TITULO NOVI TESTAMENTI:

Ἡ καινὴ διαθήκη.] Tribus modis homines hominibus ob- ligantur: lege, sponsione, testamento: quæ ita inter se distincta sunt, ut tamen communitate juris cohæreant: unde & legem συνθήκης nomine definivit Aristoteles ex Sophyssa Lycophrone, & post eum Demosthenes, quod Papinianus sponsionem transtulit, & pacta contractuum leges vocantur, & testatoris voluntas lex dicitur, natumq; hic verbum Testamenti proprium legare. Nam (ut erat in tabulis duodecim) uti quisque rei suæ legassit, ita jus esto. Apud Græcos verbum est quod tria ista complectitur δια- τίθεσθαι, quod de legibus usurpat Plato, de sponsione Ari- stophanes, de testamento Isocrates, alique. Cui conse- quens est nomen διαθήκη æque late patens: nam & testa- mentum frequentissime designat, & pro sponsione poni- tur apud eum quem dixi Aristophanem, & pro legibus u- surpatum est ab Orphicis & Pythagoristis. Nam hi præ- scriptas suo gregi vivendi normas διαθήκας vocabant. Com- munis quoque est legibus & sponsionibus sanctio. Nam pacta, præsertim publica quæ fœdera dicuntur, antiqui- tus sanciri solebant pecude cæsa, ipsaque vox sanciendi, ut recte à Servio est observatum, à sanguine deducitur, quæ causa Hebræos magistros movit, ut crederent ברית deductum à ברא quod pro succidere usurpatur, & Lati- nos, ut fœdus à feriendo derivarent. Atque hinc fœdus percutere, loquendi modus Hebræis, Græcis Latinisque pariter usitatus: qua de re iterum agendi ad caput XXVI. dabitur occasio. In legibus autem sanctio dicitur ea pars, quæ sanguinem delinquentis legi consecrat. Hinc Hebræi voces ברית & חוק sæpe alteram per alteram exponunt. Rursum lex cum testamento hoc habet commune, quod neutrum conventione indiget. Nam & hæres eo ipso, quod hæres est præstare debet factum defuncti, & subjectus alte- rius imperio eo ipso quod subjectus est, ejusdem legibus parere debet. Conventio autem in hoc cum Testamento congruit, quod & contrahendi & hæreditatis adeundæ ini- tium solet esse liberum: at subjectionis non item, ut quæ multis in locis ex origine sola descendat. Hæc cum ita sint, quæri potest, cur septuaginta Interpretes, quos secuti sunt omnes Hellenistæ atque inter eos viri sancti qui Evangelia atque Epistolas scripserunt, vocem Hebræam ברית inter- pretari maluerint διαθήκην quam aut συνθήκην ut fecit Aqui- la aut aliter etiam, quippe cum multas ejus significationis voces suppediter Græcæ linguæ ubertas, Videntur igitur mihi eo respexisse, quod latius pateret vox Hebræa ברית quam Græca συνθήκη, aut alia quæ vim similem obtinet. Nam συνθήκη ex consentienti duarum voluntatum testi- monio vinculi potestatem accipiunt. At quod Moses a- liique ברית vocant, plerumque est ejusmodi ut nullum partis alterius consensum requirat, cum obligandi vis ei adsit ex solo superioris, puta Dei, jussu atque imperio, qui tamen interdum sponte sua se quoque promittendo obliget: ut solent legum auctores quoties præmia addunt legibus. Quia vero vocem Hebræam unam una quoque Græca exprimere studebant senes eruditissimi, ideo et- iam ubi ברית ad conventiones mutuas pertinebat; ut 1 Reg. V. 12. atque alibi generali vocabulo διαθήκης uti maluerunt: Credo quod ipsam quoque vocem ברית ab alia notione vocis ברא natam arbitrarentur. Nam ברא ut proprie creare, ita similitudinis jure ordinare atque διατίθεσθαι significat: quo factum est, ut Judæi Helleni- stæ etiam τό κτίζειν, quod Hebræo ברא respondet, ad eum significatum produxerint. Neque enim aliter potest accipi illud apud Jesum Sirachiden, Eccl. XI. 16: πλάνη κὴ σκότος ἁμαρτωλοῖς συνέκτισται, & ΧΧΧΙΧ. 34. πῦρ κὴ χά- λαζα κὴ λιμὸς κὴ θάνατος· πάντα ταῦτα εἰς ἐκδίκησιν ἔκτισται. & ΧL. 1. ἀχολία μεγάλη ἔκτισαι παντὶ ἀνθρώπῳ. & ibid. 9. θάνατος κὴ ἒρις, κὴ ῥομφαία κὴ αἶμα, ἐπαγωγή λιμῦ κὴ συν- τρίμματος κὴ μάστιγος, ἐπὶ τὰς ἀνόμος ἐκτίσθη. Hinc & Petrus τὴν ἐξουσίαν ab hominibus institutam, aut ad res hu- manas vocat ἀνθρωπίνην κτίσιν. Voces autem διατίθεσθαι & διαθήκης latiore sensu ab Hellinistis usurpatas, quam quo vox συνθήκης posset extendi, indicio nobis est locus Luc. XXII. 29. multoque magis Ecclesiastici XXXVIII. 37. ubi διαθήκη κρίματος nih. l aliud est quam jus judicia- rium. Viso cur ברית Hellenistæ interpetati sint διαθή- κην, sequitur videamus, cur Christiani veteres hunc li- brum maluerint καινὴν διαθήκην appellare quam καινὸν νό- μον, præsertim cum Hebræi & Pentateuchum peculiari- ter, & communiter omnes libros ad sacrum codicem per- tinentes תורה sive νόμον appellaverint, & Christiana doctrina suo jure legis nomen sibi vindicet, ut Gal. VI. 2. Jac. II. 8. Existimo igitur Christianos veteres præcipue respexisse ad ipsa Christi verba, qui consummatissimam doctrinam morte sua sanciturus eam novi ברית nomine appellavit. Nam ea voce haud dubie est usus, pro qua Græci scriptores more septuaginta virûm posuerunt διαθή- κης vocabulum. Proprie autem fœderis notationem à Christo spectatam ostendit addita sanguinis mentio Matt. XXVI. 28. Marc. XIV. 24. Luc. XXII. 20. Quod accu- rate explicat scriptor Epistolæ ad Hebræos. Cujus dicti memores Apostoli διακόνους καινῆς διαθήκης dici haberique se voluerunt, 2. Cor. III. 6. Accedebat quod vox fœderis aliquanto dilucidius exponebat summam bonitatem & συγκατάβασιν Dei, ut qui misso ad nos Jesu Christo, non summo nobiscum jure egisset, ut solent legislatores, ne- que imperiofe & minaciter, quæ solet vox esse legum, sed blande admodum & cum magna comitate, planeque ut solent qui bona fide inter se contrahunt. Quo factum est, ut sancti scriptores sæpissime doctrinam Christi νόμῳ opponant, & gratiæ appellent vocabulo, aut sicubi eam legis voce indigeant, addant condimenta quæ nominis ejus rigorem temperent, ut cum dicitur lex fidei, non o- perum Rom. III. 27. & lex liberatis Jac. I. 25. Merito igitur Christiani, ut ipso nominis fono doctrinam salu- tarem commendarent, διαθήκης quam νόμο titulum præfi- gere ei maluerunt. Quanquam autem διαθήκη, ut di- ximus, ubi de doctrina Christiana agitur, fœderis potissi- mum habeat significationem, cum tamen Græca vox u- sitate admodum testamentum denotet, non mirum est ad hunc quoque vocis usum alludi à scriptore Epistolæ ad He- bræos IX. 17. præsertim cum Testamentum, imprimis ubi hæres sub conditione instituitur, aut fidei ejus ali- quid committitur, ad fœderum aut pactionum naturam quam proxime accedat. Latini autem Christiani non eo tantum loco, sed ubicunque διαθήκη invenitur in Novo codice, quin & in Vetere, etiam ubi διαθήκη Θεȣ nomina- tur, vocem adhibuerunt testamenti: non tam juris foris- que usum secuti, quam naturam originemque vocis, quæ apta est omne id complecti quo quis voluntatem suam te- statam facit: præsertim vero eam, qua bonorum quæ- dam universitas alicui confertur: quo sensu & vox hære- dis, citra mortis indicationem, sumi solet, ut cum hæ- redes Dei dicimur. Cum autem plures olim fuerint δια- θῆκαι Θεȣ, ut apparet Rom IX. 4. Ephes. II. 12. ipsaque circumcisio κατ' ἐξοχὴν ut ברית in Mosis & Prophetarum libris receptissimaque Judæorum consuetudine, ita Græ- ce διαθήκη appelletur Act. VII. 8. promissiones quoque de Christo olim factæ hoc nomine veniant Luc. I. 72. Act. III. 25. Gal. III. 15. 17. nova tamen διαθήκη pro- prie ac peculiariter illi fœderi publico maximeque solen- ni, quod in exitu Ægypti inchoatum, & in monte Si- nai peractum, adhibitoque pecudum sanguine sancitum est, opponitur: ut apparet Jerem. XXXI. 32. Atque hæ sunt δύο διαθῆκαι quas ἀντιδιῃρημένας nobis ob oculos po- nit Paulus ad Gal. IV. 24. atque ut illam παλαιὰν διαθή- κην 2. Cor. III. 14. ita hanc ejus respectu καινὴν vocat v. 6. eodemque modo scriptor nobilissimæ ad Hebræos epi- stolæ illam vocat πρώτην, hanc modo καινὴν, modo νέαν, quin & κρείττονα, itemque αἰώνιον. Apparet hinc Latine hunc librum Novum Testamentum dici non posse, nisi la- xiore illa atque recentiore vocis acceptione: non quod non proprie Testamentum sit quod eo continetur (est e- nim voluntas Christi morte ipsius confirmata) sed quod eo sensu vetus ei opponi non possit: quare aut fœdus di- cendum, aut Testamenti vox extra usus veteris atque communis terminos producenda est.

## 1:1 Introduction: Observations on Grotius's Preface
OBSERVATIONS ON GROTIUS'S PREFACE.

§. I. Grotius observes at the beginning that the word διαθήκης and Testament very frequently designate, and are used for a pledge among Aristophanes, and are used for laws by the Orphics and Pythagoreans, just as the verb διατίθεσθαι embraces those three things by which men are bound to men: law, pledge, and testament. But as to why the LXX interpreters and the holy men who wrote the Gospels and Epistles preferred to interpret the Hebrew word ברית as διαθήκη rather than συνθήκη, as Aquila did, or otherwise, he thinks this cause underlies it: that the Hebrew word extends more broadly than the Greek συνθήκη, which brings in a bond from the consenting testimony of two wills, whereas on the contrary that which Moses and others call ברית is for the most part of such a kind that it requires no consent of the other party, since the power of binding is present from the command and authority of the superior alone, for instance, God.

§. II. Although the word διαθήκης is altogether more convenient, and mutual consent does not intervene here in the divine διαθήκη, as it does in an agreement and covenant, one must not, however, acquiesce in the general meaning of the word, nor admit the meaning of law, as if ἡ καινὴ διαθήκη were a new law, but rather the common translation received by the Church, NEW TESTAMENT, should be retained, especially because the Holy Spirit urges the proper force of the word Testament in this case, because it attains its firmness upon the death of the testator supervening, Heb. IX. 16, the nerve of which argument is cut if διαθήκη signifies only law, not testament. Meanwhile, Flacius observes not without reason in the Preface to his gloss on the New Testament that the sacred covenant of God with men has a most sweet mixture and tempering of covenant and testament. For (1) in a testament the parties are for the most part most closely joined beforehand. (2) For a Testament there is no need of a conciliating mediator, who nevertheless appears in the divine Testament. (3) A testament is not confirmed by an oath, and can be made void by the surviving Testator as often as he pleases. But the New Testament is immutable and confirmed by a heavenly oath, Ps. 89. Flacius adds other things which the divine Testament either has in common with testaments or shares in the nature of a covenant, and thus he concludes that the divine διαθήκη is rightly called a covenant of Testament. The divine διαθήκη is certainly of a peculiar character, whether you look at the old or the new, and it is not to be estimated precisely from the nature of either covenants or common Testaments, but it participates in both, and especially approaches a Testament, because it is confirmed by blood and death. But perhaps the meaning of LAW pleases Grotius, because he believed a new law was handed down by Christ, not being alien to the tenets of Socinus and the Papists, who make Christ a certain lawgiver.

§. III. But the reasons he brings forward for his opinion are too weak. That the word ברית arises from ברא, which, just as it properly means to create, so by right of similarity it means to order, and to διατίθεσθαι, and that the words διατίθεσθαι and διαθήκης are used by the Hellenists in a broader sense than that to which the word συνθήκη can be extended. Luke XXII. 29, Ecclesiasticus XXXVIII. 37, and finally that Christian doctrine claims for itself by its own right the name of law. Gal. VI. 2, James II. 8. These do not deserve approval. For the word ברית is not correctly derived from ברא. Marcus Marinus in Arca Noae and Avenarius reduce it to no root. Forsterus derives it from ברר, to bring into the light, to choose, to declare, to purge, because pacts or covenants ought to be declared and ratified on both sides without any sophistry, with a public ceremony employed. Buxtorffius, Schindlerus, and Joh. Coccejus, Disputation 1 on the Covenant of God, thesis 1. They derive it from ברה, which is 'he chose' or 'he selected,' because it comes from election: because persons are chosen, among whom, and things and conditions on account of which, and according to which, the covenant is entered into: which etymology seems more approved to us. Others deduce it from the same ברה, insofar as it signifies 'he ate' or 'he consumed,' and by metalepsis 'he slaughtered,' either because covenants were formerly confirmed as it were by the solemnity of banquets, or because victims were slaughtered in the sanctioning of a covenant. And although the word διαθήκης is extended more broadly than συνθήκης, it is not used here in that broader and general signification, but in the way it serves to express a Testament, whether properly or by analogy, which signification also has a place in Luke 22:29. Finally, although mention is made of the law of Christ in Galatians 6:2 and of the Royal law in James 2:8, since the commandment concerning the love of one's neighbor was peculiarly claimed by Christ and figured for us by His own most eminent example in 1 John 3:16, it was not therefore to be designated by the name of a new law. The writing of the New Testament, in which the primary doctrine concerning the grace of God obtained through Christ holds sway; whence it happened that the holy writers very often, as Grotius admits, oppose the doctrine of Christ to the law, and call it by the name of grace, or if anywhere they point to it with the word 'law,' they add seasonings which temper the rigor of that name, as when it is called the law of faith, not of works, in Romans 3:27, and the law of liberty in James 1:25.

§. IV. Therefore, that signification of the word ברית and διαθήκης is more convenient in this place, which is deduced from the words of Christ in Matthew 26:28, Mark 14:24, Luke 22:20: mindful of which, the Apostles wished to be called and considered ministers of the new covenant in 2 Corinthians 3:6; Grotius rightly judges that the ancient Christians looked back to these in this inscription, but he hallucinates not lightly in this, that Christ there, about to sanction the most consummate doctrine by His death, called it by the name of a new ברית. For He did not call His doctrine there by the name of a Testament, nor is the matter there about the sanctioning of doctrine, but He said 'the blood of the New Testament,' because by it grace was acquired for us, sanctioned by a covenant and a new Testament, for the death of Christ was not a μαρτύριον, as if he wished to seal the truth of his doctrine with his blood in the manner of the martyrs, but it was a λύτρον & ἀπολύτρωσις of the human race. The blood, therefore, of the καινῆς διαθήκης is this: it is of the New not only covenant but also New Testament: because the New Testament is ratified by this blood. fits here: especially on the ground that a testament, where an heir is instituted under a condition, or something is committed to his faith, approaches as closely as possible to the nature of covenants or agreements, although he thinks that Latin Christians did not so much follow the usage of law and the forum, as the nature and origin of the word, in employing the name TESTAMENT, by which it is apt to embrace everything by which one makes his will attested, especially that by which a certain totality of goods is conferred upon someone. In which, however, we do not subscribe to him. For if Christians had used the word TESTAMENT only generally, both in the inscription of these sacred books and in rendering the passage Heb. IX. 17, why would they appeal to the requirements of a testament properly so called, which is often observed among them, or how would they satisfy the Apostle, who points to a testament properly so called, for which, in order to be firm, the death of the testator is required? For if, as Grotius wishes, the Apostle were only alluding there to this usage of the word, he would not be bringing forward a solid argument in a matter of such moment, since allusions have no power of proof. Nor is it beside the point that Andr. Rivetus observes this with Bellarmine & Ribera on Exod. XXIV. 4. in his Commentaries. Nothing prevents one and the same convention from being called and being both a covenant and a testament; that is, it is a mixed action in such a way that it is a confederation between two parties under certain conditions, and nonetheless a testamentary disposition of one, with death intervening; especially if such a condition is posited, which is fulfilled by the testator himself in another part, which is what happened here.

§. V. Furthermore, Grotius warns that, although there were formerly many διαθῆκαι Θεοῦ Rom. IX. 4, Eph. II. 12, and circumcision itself is so called Acts VII. 8, as are the promises concerning Christ formerly made Luke I. 72, Acts III. 25, Gal. III. 16, 17, yet a new διαθήκη is properly and peculiarly opposed to that public covenant most solemn, which was performed on Mount Sinai, Jerem. XXXI. 32, Gal. IV. 24, 2 Cor. III. 14, whence he thinks it appears that this book cannot be called the New Testament in Latin, except by that looser acceptance of the word, not because it is not properly a Testament which is contained in it (for it is the will of Christ confirmed by his own death) but because in that sense the old cannot be opposed to it. Concerning which we wish this to be observed: that this book is called by the name of Testament metonymically, because it exhibits not a New Testament improperly so called, but one of such a kind that it is a Testament κυριολέκτως, because it exhibits the will of Christ; not legal, as perhaps Grotius wishes, but Evangelical concerning the remission of sins, freely and by the death of Christ the testator both ratified and confirmed. For Christ the Testator has this peculiar and proper to himself, that while other testators do not by their death acquire those goods which they bequeath to heirs, that heavenly Testator not only wished to confirm and seal to us his will concerning the obtaining of the heavenly inheritance by his death, but also procured and acquired the same inheritance for us by his precious blood and his death. Although indeed in the Old Testament the death of the testator did not intervene, yet so that something might correspond to it by analogy, it had to be ratified by the blood of victims prefiguring the death of Christ.

Wherefore it is not necessary that we believe that by διαθήκη not only a covenant is designated, but it can be understood as a testament in the more received notion, although, as we observed before, it also participates in something of the nature of covenants, and the reason for this Testament is altogether peculiar, which, however, does not cause it to be called a testament only by that generality by which everything comes under this name by which one makes his will attested.

§. VI. Moreover, the testament which is pointed to here, with B. Hutter, our author in the cited places, defining it, is nothing other than a divine disposition, both concerning the legitimate dispensation of religion itself, and concerning the government of the Church, or the people of God, instituted with this end and purpose, that the people of God might not wander by their own will, and stray in any mere ἀταξία or confusion, but be contained within a certain polity distinct from all peoples. Whence the testament is not religion itself, or faith, or the doctrine itself, but something occupied about its legitimate dispensation. The Old Testament, therefore, is that most ancient solemn disposition by which God, having led the Israelite people out of Egyptian captivity amidst thunders and lightnings, delivered the entire administration of both religion and polity, described in a certain form of rites and laws or constitutions, on Mount Sinai.

The New Testament, however, is a new and solemn disposition, by which God, having abrogated the former Old Testament, announced to His people the universal promulgation of the Gospel and its most clear propagation throughout the whole world from Zion and Jerusalem, and instituted and ordained a new administration of evangelical doctrine through two Sacraments, Baptism and the Lord's Supper. Not, indeed, that the doctrine concerning the reconciliation of men on account of Christ was entirely unknown in ancient times, but that it has now been revealed in another mode of dispensation, more full and more plain. Others of our own call the Old Testament that covenant of the law entered into on Mount Sinai between God and the Israelite people with great solemnity and majesty, by which a temporary and eternal blessing is promised to the people if they perfectly observe the commands of God, but punishment and a curse in the present and future age is denounced against all who violate the law in any way, with the dedication and consecration of the covenant by the blood of bulls and calves accompanying it. The New Testament, however, is that gracious covenant of the remission of sins, righteousness, and eternal life in Christ, which God indeed entered into with our first parents and the patriarchs, yet it was ratified and confirmed by the death of the Son exhibited in the flesh, which was propagated and promulgated from Mount Zion into the whole world and all nations by the ministry of the Apostles. But the blessed Hutter rightly observes that the nature and proper affection of the New Testament does not look properly and uniquely to the thing itself that is proper to the Gospel, that is, the doctrine of our salvation itself, but to the mode of delivering this thing: just as, conversely, the nature and proper affection of the Old Testament looks indeed also to the law, or the decalogue, but not to the doctrine of the law itself considered in itself, but only to the mode of the thing being delivered, that is, the legitimate dispensation of the promulgated law, according to the form prescribed by God Himself.

§. VII. Therefore the blessed D. Joh. Friedericus König in Theol. Posit. Acroamat. §. 837, says that a divine Testament, as he abstracts it from Old and New, is a disposition of the most free will of God concerning divine worship, and the means of salvation, and the form of government in the Church, sealed and confirmed by the blood and death of the Testator, to the praise of divine grace and righteousness, and for the salvation of men. A Testament, however

The Old [Testament] defines it as the most free disposition of the will of God concerning religion and divine worship, and the goods of the Testament, partly published immediately by the Son of God himself ἄσαρκον, partly through the intervening ministry of Moses, solemnly, wrapped in shadows, burdensome, sealed with the blood of a typical animal, for the salvation and honor of the ancient people, and for the praise of divine justice and grace. The New Testament, however, defines it thus: that it is the most free disposition of the will of God concerning religion and divine worship, and the goods of the Testament, solemn, published partly by the Son of God himself ἔνσαρκον, partly by the Apostles, exhibiting the very body and complement in Christ, free from the yoke of the old, and sealed by the blood of the Testator himself, for the praise of justice and divine [grace], and the salvation of the heirs. Whoever wishes to compare the development of these definitions may do so in the cited place and in the inaugural dissertation on the Nature of the Old Testament. We have also spoken more fully concerning the name and definition of the Testament, and how the Old and New Testament are distinguished, in the General Prologue to the books of the sacred Code, page 1 et seqq., and we are about to speak especially concerning these things in the second part of the eighth chapter of the Epistle to the Hebrews, § 8. Let these things, therefore, suffice for the present concerning the Title. There follows

II. CONCERNING THE BOOKS OF THE NEW TESTAMENT.

The books of the New Testament exhibit not only the life of Jesus Christ, and both his Acts and Doctrine, as they were historically recorded by the amanuenses of the Holy Spirit up to the Ascension of Christ into heaven: but also the Acts of the Apostles, woven with a historical thread, along with the doctrine of the same, which was delivered primarily in the Apostolic Epistles directed to Churches or certain persons, or generally to the faithful: indeed, it also embraces the state of the Church, such as it was to be from the time of the Apostles until the consummation of the age, which for the most part is adumbrated in a Prophetic style. Therefore, Sacred Writings of a triple kind are contained in the New Testament: I. HISTORICAL; which embrace the life of Jesus Christ our Savior up to his Ascension into heaven, composed by the IV Evangelists, Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John, which writings have the name GOSPEL prefixed: verse 9. ἐυαγγέλιον κτ̓ Ματθαῖον, the Gospel according to Matthew, and so on: then the Acts of the Apostles, primarily of Peter and Paul, from the Ascension of Christ up to the first Roman captivity of Paul. Which, recorded by St. Luke the Evangelist, bear the title πράξεις τ̃ ἁγίων Ἀποτόλων. II. DOGMATIC, which exhibit the Evangelical doctrine didactically, written in the manner of Epistles: such are the Epistles of both St. PAUL and the OTHER APOSTLES. St. Paul's XIII Epistles are special, directed to a certain place or object, namely nine to certain Churches, one to the ROMANS, two to the CORINTHIANS, former and latter, one to the GALATIANS, one to the EPHESIANS, one to the PHILIPPIANS, one to the COLOSSIANS, two to the THESSALONIANS, namely the former and the latter: but the remaining four are to certain persons: namely two to TIMOTHY, former and latter, one to TITUS, and one to PHILEMON. To which is added the fourteenth Epistle of St. Paul directed to an entire nation, namely to the faithful HEBREWS. The writings of the other Apostles, which have been related to the Canon of the New Testament, are VII in number: namely their Epistles: one of St. JAMES, two of St. PETER, former and latter, three of St. JOHN, and one of St. JUDE: all of which are called Catholic, but concern the Church universally, with the exception of the second and third of John, which were directed to certain persons. III. The PROPHETIC Writing of the New Testament is the single APOCALYPSE OF JOHN, which is entirely composed in the Prophetic manner, and concerns the future state most of all. We have spoken of these writings of the New Testament generally in System. Theol. Vol. I. page 507 et seqq. and concerning the original text of the New Testament, that the Greek is the original text, and that no book of the New Testament was written in the original in another language, and that the language of the New Testament, if you look at the style, is Hellenistic, and delights in Hebraisms and Syro-Chaldaisms, with some things also mixed in from the Latin and Persian language, we asserted in the Critico Sacro Diatr. V., and we laboriously asserted the uncontaminated purity of the sources of the New Testament in the same Critico Diatrib. VI., having also vindicated the passages which are judged to be corrupted either through malice or through carelessness, and specifically those which are argued by Morinus to be corrupt. Which, having been proposed thirty years ago, when we were still performing the duties of a Theological professorship at the Regiomontana Academy, now recalled here to the anvil, whoever wishes may compare them, not without fruit. Then Thomas Gataker discussed the style of the New Testament among many others from the Reformed [tradition] in a dissertation on the style of the New Testament against Pfochenius, Johannes Vorstius in a dissertation and Commentary on the Hebraisms of the New Testament, from our own [scholars] Baeclerus on the language of the New Testament, Joh. Olearius in an inaugural Disp. and Philological-Theological dissertation on the style of the New Testament. Hottinger certainly, although more inclined to the opinion of Salmasius and less favorable to Hellenism, nevertheless acknowledges that the style can be called Hellenistic, or Hebrew-Greek, or even Hebraizing, which the LXX Interpreters used, in the Thesaurus Philol. p. 353, and he makes the style of the N. T. similar to it in Syst. Theol. l. 1. loc. III. q. 151. Most clearly (he says in the former place) Drusius against Serar. p. 89, Heinsius in the preface to the New Testament p. 12, Const. l'Empereur in the preface to Baba Kama, and Coccejus in Sanhedr. show by examples that certain things are so proper to the LXX Interpreters that external or profane authors contribute nothing at all to their explanation. Compare also Joh. Selden in the book on the succession of the Hebrew legates c. V. Salmasius himself on the cross page 465 confesses that the entire scripture of the N. T. teems with infinite Hebraisms.

III. ON THE AUTHOR OF THE WRITINGS OF THE NEW TESTAMENT.

The primary author is the Holy Spirit, because not only is πᾶσα γραφὴ θεόπνευστος, as the Apostle testifies in 2 Tim. III. 16, and holy men of God spoke and wrote φερόμενοι ὑπὸ πνεύματος ἁγίου in 2 Pet. I. 21, but for that reason also the Holy Spirit was promised to the Apostles by Christ, that He might lead them into ALL TRUTH, John XVI. 13, not only in preaching, but also in writing: add Luke XXIV. 49, Acts I. 4, 5, 8, to which end Christ also granted the Holy Spirit to them by breathing upon them, John XX. 22, and sent the Holy Spirit from heaven on the Feast of Pentecost, who gave the Apostles not only to speak, but also to record in writing the mighty works of God, Acts II. 4, whence the mystery concerning Christ is said to have been revealed to the holy Apostles by the Spirit, Eph. III. 5, and the Apostles announced the Gospel by the Holy Spirit sent from heaven, 1 Pet. I. 12, and what the Apostles say in the Scriptures, that the Spirit

The Holy Spirit, who spoke and wrote through them, is said to have said so, 1 Tim. IV. 1. Cf. Matt. X. 20. Mark XIII. 11. Luke XII. 12. John XIV. 26. Acts XV. 28. Rev. II. 11, 17, 29, ch. III. 6, 13, 22. Thus Peter commends Paul, because he wrote according to the wisdom given to him in all the epistles, 2 Epist. III. 15, 16; and Paul, with James, honors St. Peter and John with this eulogy, Gal. II. 9, that they were seen to be pillars: and he says that we are built no less upon the foundation of the Apostles in the New Testament than upon that of the Prophets in the Old, Eph. II. 20, just as also in the Apocalypse, ch. XXI. 14, the names of the twelve Apostles of the Lamb are said to be inscribed on the foundations of Jerusalem. Furthermore, since the command given to the Apostles to teach all nations concerns not only that doctrine which they provided in writing, but also that which was handed down by word of mouth, Matt. XXVIII. 29 [sic], inasmuch as it pertains not only to the men of that time, but also to the time to follow, even to the end of the age, since the presence (παρουσία) is promised until then, v. 20; just as their duty was to testify of Christ not only by teaching but also by writing, John XXI. 14, 1 John I. 3, 4, Rev. I. 2, 3, 11, 19, ch. II. 4, 8, 12, 18, ch. III. 13, 14, ch. XIV. 13, ch. XIX. 9, ch. XXI. 5, it is not to be doubted that God, by whose order and command they wrote, is the supreme author of Scripture. Whence St. Irenaeus, book III, against heresies, ch. I, says: The Apostles, he says, what they first preached, they later by the will of God handed down to us in Scripture.

The secondary or ministerial authors of the writings of the New Testament, therefore, were the Apostles: Matthew, John, James, Peter, Jude, and Paul; that they were impelled by the immediate inspiration of the Holy Spirit, there is no doubt: besides whom, indeed, both Mark and Luke wrote, but they are believed to have been from the number of the 70 disciples of Christ, and the history of Mark receives divine testimony from Peter, and that of Luke from Paul: whose great praise in the Gospel Paul mentioned, 2 Cor. VIII. 18. Irenaeus calls Luke a follower and disciple of the Apostles, book III, ch. 14; but Mark a follower of Peter, ch. 1. Eusebius, book III, Eccl. Hist. ch. 21, testifies that the Gospel of Luke, no less than those of Matthew and Mark, was approved by John; Jerome in the Catalogue of Illustrious Men. Mark, he says, the disciple and interpreter of Peter, according to what he had heard Peter relating, being asked at Rome by the brethren, wrote a short Gospel, which when Peter had heard, he approved, and published it to be read in the Church by his authority. But we shall speak of each one specifically in turn. Certainly the whole Church received the books of the New Testament as divine, and although the authors of some were doubted by some, such as the Epistle to the Hebrews and the Apocalypse, and it was ambiguous to some whether the Epistle of James was equal to the others, yet the reasons for doubting were not of great moment, and their divine and Canonical authority was acknowledged by others, and approved by the judgment of the whole Church for many centuries.

IV. ON THE COMMENTATORS ON THE NEW TESTAMENT.

Those who have illustrated the entire Sacred Code with commentaries or observations are designated in Volume I of the Bibliorum Illustratorum of the Old Testament. But those who devoted their effort to the New Testament, and indeed as regards those who illustrated all or at least most of the books of the New Testament, these are especially celebrated among the ancients: John Chrysostom, first a Presbyter of Antioch, finally Archbishop of Constantinople, around the year of Christ 400, whose commentaries, however, for the most part do not exist, and only homilies are generally had: but others have collected many things from his writings: Theodoret, Bishop of Cyrrhus, who adorned many commentaries on the Scriptures, having followed St. Chrysostom for the most part, in the year 450. Theophylact, Bishop of the Bulgarians, around the year 900, reduced to a compendium what Chrysostom had handed down more prolixly in exegetical writings, with commonplaces omitted: Euthymius Zigabenus, who around the year 1180 collected succinct commentaries from the writings of the ancient Fathers and especially of Chrysostom: Oecumenius, around the year of the Lord 800, compiled a Catena on the New Testament, in which these authors are read to have been employed: Papias, Clement, Methodius, Dionysius, Irenaeus, Origen, Hippolytus, Athanasius, Eusebius, Basil, Gregory of Nyssa, Acacius, Isidore, Photius, Chrysostom, Gregory of Nazianzus, Severianus, Gennadius, Arethas, Andreas, Cyril, Theodoret: to whom Oecumenius added his own. Thomas Aquinas in the year 1274 wrote on the whole New Testament: but on the four Gospels he collected an explanation from the Fathers, both Latin and Greek, which work he entitled a continuous work on the four Evangelists, called by more recent writers the Golden Catena. Augustinus Anconas in the year 1330 wrote on the whole New Testament with the zeal of a postillator. Johannes Bacco, an English Carmelite, explained the whole New Testament in the scholastic manner in twenty-seven books in the year of the Lord 1350. Johannes Capgravius, an Englishman, in the year 1364 likewise wrote on the whole New Testament. Laurentius Valla instituted a collation of the Latin Version in the New Testament with the Greek text in the same age. Erasmus of Rotterdam published learned Annotations on the New Testament at the beginning of the previous century, but to be read with judgment: to which Edward Lee, an Englishman, opposed his own Annotations on the New Testament at Mainz in the year 1520. Joh. Gagnejus, a Parisian theologian, in the year of the Lord 1550. composed Scholia on the New Testament. Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples compiled commentaries on the Gospels, the Pauline Epistles, and the Canonical Epistles. Nicolaus Tacitus Zigenus collected Scholia on all the books of the New Testament in the year 1540. Sixtus of Siena also named a certain Johannes Loppis, who wrote on the whole New Testament, but he did not designate his age. Alfonso Salmerón, one of the first ten Jesuits, wrote sixteen volumes on the New Testament, of which ten [are on the] four concern the Evangelists: For the first contains Prolegomena: The second the beginning of John concerning the Incarnation of the Word: The third the infancy & childhood of Jesus: The fourth the Evangelical History, & the life of Christ up to the last supper: The fifth is concerning the Sermon of the Lord on the mount: The sixth explains the miracles of Christ: The seventh expounds the parables: The eighth treats of the disputations of Christ: The ninth deals with the Sacrament of the H. Eucharist, & the last sermon of Christ at the supper: The tenth is concerning the passion & death of Christ: The eleventh is concerning the resurrection & ascension of Christ. Cornelius à Lapide expounded all the books of the N. Test. with proper Commentaries: Aloysius Novarinus also wrote on all the books of the N. T., but only Annotations. Of our own, B. Luther, although σποραδηνῶς throughout the Volumes of his works, interpreted almost the entire N. T. excellently. Philip expounded not a few things in the N. T. There exist also notes of Lucas Lossius on the N. T. as also of Erasmus Sarcerius. Joachimus Camerarius wrote learnedly on the figures of speech in the N. T. Matthias Flacius published a Gloss on the whole N. T. Erasmus Schmidius left annotations on the N. T. with a new version. From the Reformed, Beza composed his own version and learned notes on the N. T. Benedictus Aretius

Aretius prepared commentaries on the books of the New Testament, as did Mart. Bucer, Hem. Bullinger, Daniel Tossanus, and Thomas Cartwright. Jacobus Capellus left behind certain annotations. Daniel Heinsius wrote twenty books of Exercitations on the New Testament. Johannes Drusius [wrote] books of 'Preterita' on the N.T. Ludovicus de Dieu prepared annotations. Joh. Camero presented the 'Myrothecium Evangelicum' along with other things pertaining to the explanation of the N.T. occurring in his works: to which a 'Spicilegium' was added, by the author Ludovicus Capellus. Isaac Casaubon wrote succinct notes on the historical books of the N.T.: to which can be added those things which the same author has here and there in his Exercitations. Also on the whole New Testament. A chain or exposition, which he calls Catholic, was collected from more recent authors primarily by Augustinus Marloratus, such as Emssno, Philippo, Brentio, Sarcerio, Vito Theodore, Zvvinglio, Calvino, Bullingero, Bucero, Musculo, and others, with some additions also from the Fathers. And these are concerning the books of the N. Testament in general.

Latin:

OBSERVATIONES AD GROTIA- NUM PRÆLOQUIUM.

§. I. Vocem διαθήκης & Testamenti cum frequen- tissime designare, & pro Sponsione poni apud A- ristophanem, & pro legibus usurpari ab Orphicis, & Pythagoristis, initio observat Grotius, æque uti verbum διατίθεσθαι tria ista, quibus homines homi- nibus obligantur, legem, sponsionem, testamentum complectitur. Quod autem vocem Ebræam ברית LXX. Interpretes virique sancti, qui Ev- angelia, atque Epistolas scripserunt, interpretari maluerint διαθήκην, quam συνθήκην, cum Aqui- la, aut aliter, causam hanc subesse existimat, quod vox Ebræa latius pateat, quam Græca συνθήκη, quæ vinculum infert ex consentienti duarum volun- tatum testimonio, quum contra id, quod Moses, a- liique ברית vocant, plerumque ejusmodi sit, ut nullum partis alterius consensum requirat, cum obligandi vis ex solo superioris, puta Dei jussu, atque imperio adsit.

§. II. Quamquam vero convenientior omni- no sit vox διαθήκης, neque hic in διαθήκῃ divina consensus mutuus, ut in conventione, ac fœdere, in- terveniat, non tamen vel generali significatui vocis acquiescendum, vel legis significatio admit- tenda, quasi ἡ καινὴ διαθήκη sit nova lex, sed reti- nenda potius communis translatio, ab Ecclesia recepta, NOVI TESTAMENTI, maxime quia Spiritus Sanctus propriam vocis Testamenti vim in hac causa urget, quod firmitudinem suam consequitur morte testatoris accedente Ebr. IX. 16. cujus argumenti nervus inciditur, si διαθήκη solum legem, non testamentum significet. Interim haud abs re observat Flacius in Præfat. glossæ in Nov. Testam. Sacrum Dei cum hominibus fœdus suavissi- mam habere fœderis, & testamenti mixturam, at- que temperaturam. Nam (1) in testamento partes plerumque ante sunt conjunctissimæ (2) ad Te- stamentum non opus est mediatore conciliante, qui tamen in Testamento divino comparet. (3) Testamentum neque juramento confirmatur, & à superstite Testatore, quoties placet, irritum fieri potest. Testamentum vero Novum immutabile est, & juramento cælesti confirmatum Psal. 89. Addit alia Flacius, quæ aut cum Testamentis communia habet divinum Testamentum, aut de natura foederis participat, adeoque concludit, divinam διαθήκην recte Testamenti foedus appel- lari. Peculiaris certe indolis divina διαθήκη est, seu veterem, seu novam respicias, nec aestiman- da praecise, sive e foederum, sive e Testamentorum vulgarium natura, de utrisque vero participat, & imprimis ad Testamentum accedit, quia sangui- ne & morte confirmatur. Placet autem forte Grotio LEGIS significatio, quod legem novam a Christo traditam crediderit, haud alienus a Socini & Pontificiorum placitis, qui Christum quendam νομοθέτην faciunt.

§. III. Sed quas ejus sententiae causas adfert, infirmae nimis sunt. Vocem ברית a ברא oriri, quod ut proprie creare, ita similitudinis jure ordi- nare, atque διατίθεσθαι significet, vocesque διατίθε- σθαι & διαθήκης latiori sensu ab Hellenistis usurpa- ri, quam quo vox συνθήκη extendi possit. Luc. XXII. 29. Ecclesiastici XXXVIII. 37. denique Chri- stianam doctrinam suo jure sibi legis nomen vendica- re. Gal. VI. 2. Jac. II. 8. Haec calculum non me- rentur. Nam vox ברית non recte a ברא deriva- tur. Marcus Marinus in Arca Noae & Avenarius, ad nullam radicem eam reducunt. Forsterus a ברר in lucem producere, eligere, declarare, expurgare, deducit, quod pacta sive foedera sine omni sophisti- ca utrinque declarari, & radificari debeant, publica adhibita ceremonia. Buxtorffius, Schindlerus, & Joh. Coccejus Disp. 1. de foedere Dei th. 1. a ברה quod est elegit, delegit derivant, quod ex electione eveniat: quia eliguntur personae, inter quas, & res ac conditiones propter, & secundum quas foedus initur: Quae etymologia probatior nobis videtur. Alii ab eodem ברה deducunt, quatenus signi- ficat comedit, manducavit, & per metalepsin macta- vit, vel, quia conviviorum solemnitate foedera quondam quasi confirmabantur, vel quia in foe- dere sanciendo caedebantur victimae. Et licet vox διαθήκης latius extendatur, quam συνθήκης non ta- men hic ampliori, & generali illa significatione adhibetur, sed qua ad Testamentum sive κυριολεκ- τως, seu κατ' αναλογίαν exprimendum facit, quae significatio etiam Luc. XXII. 29. locum habet. De- nique quamvis legis Christi Gal. VI. 2. & legis Regiae Jac. II. 8. mentio fiat, cum mandatum de dilectio- ne proximi a Christo peculiariter vindicatum, & exemplo ipsius proprio longe eminentissimo nobis figuratum sit 1. Joh. III. 16. non tamen ideo legis novae nomine designanda erat. Scriptum Novi Testamenti, in qua to πρωτειον doctrina de gratia Dei per Christum parta obtinet; unde factum, ut sancti Scriptores saepissime, fatente Grotio, doctri- nam Christi νόμῳ opponant, & gratiæ appellent voca- bulo, aut sicubi eam legis voce indigitant, addant con- dimenta, quae nominis ejus rigorem temperent, ut cum dicitur lex fidei, non operum Rom. III. 27. & lex libertatis Jac. I. 25.

§. IV. Convenientior itaque hoc loco est illa vocis ברית & διαθήκης significatio, quae e verbis Christi Matth. XXVI. 28. Marc. XIV. 21. Luc. XXII. 20. deducitur: quorum memores Apostoli διακο- νοι καινης διαθήκης dici, haberique voluerunt 2. Cor. III. 6. ad quae etiam Christianos veteres in hac e- πιγραφῇ respexisse, recte censet Grotius, sed hal- lucinatur in eo non leviter, quod ibi Christus con- summatissimam doctrinam morte sua sanciturus, eam novi ברית nomine appellarit. Nam non doctrinam suam appellavit ibi nomine Testamenti, neque de sanctione Doctrinae illic res est, sed sanguinem Novi Testamenti dixit, quod eodem acquisita sit nobis gratia foedere, & Testamento novo sancita, non enim mors Christi μαρτύριον erat, quasi san- guine suo martyrum more, obsignare doctrinæ suæ veritatem voluerit, sed erat λύτρον & ἀπολύ- τρωσις generis humani. Sanguis ergo καινῆς δια- θήκης hoc est, Novi non tantum fœderis sed etiam Novi Testamenti est: quia sancitur hoc sanguine Novum Testamentum. Neque diffitetur Grotius Testamenti vocem hic congruere: præsertim eo no- mine, quod testamentum, ubi hæres sub conditione instituitur, aut fidei ejus aliquid committitur, ad fœderum aut pactionum naturam quam proxime accedat, etsi putet, Latinos Christianos non tam juris forique usum secutos, quam naturam o- riginemque vocis, nomen TESTAMENTI adhibuis- se, qua apta est omne id complecti, quo quis volun- tatem suam testatam facit præsertim eam, qua bono- rum quædam universitas alicui confertur. In quo vero eidem non subscribimus. Nam si tan- tum generaliter voce TESTAMENTI usi essent Christiani tum in inscriptione horum librorum sacrorum, tum in reddendo loco Ebr. IX. 17. Cur ad requisita Testamenti proprie ita dicti provo- carent, quod sæpe penes ipsos observatur, aut quomodo satisfacerent Apostolo Testamentum proprie dictum, ad quod, ut firmum sit, mors testatoris requiritur, indigitanti. Neque enim: si, ut Grotius vult, alluderet tantum ibi ad hunc vo- cis usum Apostolus, argumentum in re tanti mo- menti solidum adduceret, quum allusiones vim probandi nullam habeant. Nec præter rem cum Bellarmino & Ribera observat Andr. Rivetus ad Ex- od. XXIV. 4. in Commentar. Nihil obstare, quo minus una & eadem conventio fœdus & testamen- tum simul dicatur, & sit; id est, ita sit actio mixta, ut sit inter duas partes confœderatio sub cer- tis conditionibus, & unius nihilominus dispositio testamentaria, accedente morte; maxime si talis conditio ponatur, qua ab ipso testatore in alia parte impleatur, quod hic factum est.

§. V. Porro monet Grotius, cum plures o- lim fuerint διαθῆκαι Θεῒ Rom. IX. 4. Eph. II. 12. ipsa- que circumcisio ita vocetur Act. VII. 8. ut & promis- siones de Christo olim factæ Luc. I, 72. Act. III. 25. Gal. III. 16. 17. novam tamen διαθήκην proprie, ac peculiariter illi fœderi publico maxime solemni, quod in monte Sinai peractum, opponi Jerem. XXXI. 32. Gal. IV. 24. 2. Cor. III. 14. unde apparere pu- tat, Latine hunc librum Novum Testamentum dici non posse, nisi laxiore illa atque receptione vocis acce- ptione, non quod non proprie Testamentum sit, quod eo continetur (est enim voluntas Christi morte ipsius confirmata) sed quod eo sensu vetus ei opponi non possit. De quo id observari volumus: Librum hunc Testamenti nomine metonymice appellatum, quod Testamentum Novum non improprie ita dictum exhibeat, sed ejusmodi quod κυριολέκτως Testamentum sit, quia exhibet voluntatem Christi; non legalem, uti forte Grotius vult, sed Evangeli- cam de remissione peccatorum, gratis & salute mor- te Christi testatoris & sancitam, & confirmatam. Nam hoc peculiare sibi ac proprium habet Testa- tor Christus, quod cum alii testatores morte sua non acquirant bona illa, quæ hæredibus legant, cœlestis ille Testator non tantum voluntatem suam de consequenda cœlesti hæreditate nobis confirmare & obsignare morte sua voluerit, sed eandem hæreditatem etiam nobis pretioso sanguine, ac morte sua compararit, & acqui- siverit. Etsi vero in Testamento Veteri non in- tervenerit testatoris mors, ut tamen per analogi- am aliquid ei responderet, sanciendum illud erat sanguine victimarum mortem Christi præfigurante.

Quapropter necessum non est, ut per διαθήκην non solùm fœdus designâri credamus, sed notio- ne receptiori Testamentum intelligi potest, quam- vis, uti antea observavimus, etiam de fœderum na- tura aliquid participet, ac peculiaris omnino ra- tio hujus Testamenti sit, quæ tamen non facit, ut solum illa generalitate testamentum vocetur, qua omne id hoc nomine venit, quo voluntatem suam quis testatam facit.

§. VI. Est autem testamentum, quod hic indi- gitatur, B. Huttero, nostro in LL. CC. definiente, nihil aliud, quam dispositio divina, tum de ipsius re- ligionis legitimâ dispensatione, tum de gubernatione Ecclesiæ, sive populi Dei, hoc fine ac consilio institu- ta, ut ne populus Dei proprio vagetur arbitrio, & in mera quapiam ἀταξίᾳ sive confusione oberret, sed intra certam politiam à populis omnibus distin- ctam contineatur. Unde testamentum non est ipsa religio, seu fides, aut doctrina ipsa, sed aliquid cir- ca legitimam ejus dispensationem occupatum. Ve- tus itaque Testamentum est antiquissima illa sole- mnis dispositio, qua Deus populo Israëlitico ex capti- vitate Ægyptiaca educto inter tonitrua & fulgura, universam tum Religionis, tum politiæ administra- tionem, certa rituum ac legum, seu constitutionum forma descriptam in monte Sinai tradidit.

Novum vero Testamentum est nova & solemnis dispositio, qua Deus priori Veteri Testamento abrogato, po- pulo suo universalem Evangelii promulgationem, ejusque clarissimam propagationem in universum orbem terrarum ex Sion & Jerusalem annunciavit, & novam doctrinæ Evangelicæ administrationem per duo Sacramenta Baptismum & Cœnam Domi- nicam instituit, & ordinavit. Non quidem, quod doctrina de reconciliatione hominum propter Christum antiquitus prorsus fuerit ignota, sed quod nunc alio dispensationis modo, pliniore ac pla- niore fuerit revelata. Alii è nostris Vetus Testa- mentum pactum dicunt illud legis in monte Sinai in- ter Deum & populum Israëliticum magna solemnita- te & majestate initium, quo benedictio promittitur populo temporaria, & æterna, si mandata Dei perfe- cte observet, pœna autem & maledictio in præsenti & futuro sæculo, denunciatur omnibus legem ulla ra- tione violantibus, accedente pacti per sanguinem tau- rorum & vitulorum dedicatione, & consecratione. Novum vero Testamentum pactum illud gratiosum remissionis peccatorum justitia & vitæ æternæ Chri- sto, quod quidem cum primis parentibus & patribus inivit Deus, tamen morte Filii in carne exhibiti ra- tificatum & confirmatum est, quod è monte Sion in orbem terrarum & omnes gentes ministerio Aposto- lorum propagatum & promulgatum. Sed recte ob- servat B. Hutterus Novi Testamenti naturam, & affectionem propriam non rem ipsam Evangelii propriam, h. e. ipsam salutis nostræ doctrinam, sed rei hujus tradendæ modum proprie & unice respi- cere: quemadmodum vice versa Veteris Te- stamenti natura & affectio propria, legem quidem etiam respicit, sive decalogum, sed non ipsam do- ctrinam legis in se consideratam, verum tantum modum tradendæ rei, h. e. legis promulgatæ legiti- mam dispensationem, secundum formam à Deo ipso præscriptam.

§. VII. Ideo B. D. Joh. Friedericus König in Theol. Posit. Acroamat. §. 837. Testamentum di- vinum, prout à Veteri & Novo abstrahit, dicit es- se dispositionem liberrimæ Dei voluntatis de cultu divino, mediisque salutis, ac forma regiminis in Ecclesia, obsignatam & confirmatam sanguine & morte Testatoris, in gratiæ ac justitiæ divinæ lau- dem, & hominum salutem. Testamentum vero

Vetus definit, quod sit dispositio liberrima Dei vo- luntatis de religione & cultu divino, bonisque Testa- mentariis partim immediate per ipsum Dei Filium ἄσαρκον, partim interveniente Mofis ministerio so- lemniter publicata, umbris involuta, onerosa, ob- signata sanguine pecuino typico, in populi veteris sa- lutem ac decus, & justitiae ac gratiae divinae lau- dem. Novum vero Testamentum ita definit: quod sit dispositio liberrima Dei voluntatis de reli- gione & cultu divino, bonisque Testamentariis, so- lemnis, partim per ipsum DEI Filium ἔνσαρκον, partim per Apostolos publicata, ipsum corpus ac complementum in Christo exhibens, expers jugi ve- teris, ipsiusque Testatoris sanguine obsignata, in justitiae & divinae laudem, & haeredum salutem. Qui quoad harum definitionum evolutionem conferatur loco citato & in disputatione inaugu- rali de Natura Vet. Testamenti. Diximus & nos uberius de nomine ac definitione Testamenti, & quomodo Vetus ac Novum Testamentum distin- guantur, in Proloquio Generali ad libros Codicis sacri pag. 1. seqq. & dicturi cumprimis sumus de hisce ad partem alteram capitis octavi Epistolae ad Ebreos, § 8. Haec ergo in praesenti de Titulo sufficiant. Sequitur

II. DE LIBRIS NOVI TESTA- MENTI.

Libri Novi Testamenti exhibent non modo vitam Jesu Christi, ejusque tum Acta, tum Do- ctrinam, prout illa Historice consignata sunt ab amanuensibus Spiritus Sancti usque ad Ascensio- nem Christi in caelum: sed etiam Acta Apostolo- rum, Historico contexta filo, cum doctrina eorundem, quae imprimis in Epistolis Aposto- licis ad Ecclesias vel personas certas, vel gene- ratim ad fideles directis tradita est: imo comple- ctitur quoque statum Ecclesiae, qualis ille futurus erat a tempore Apostolorum usque ad consum- mationem seculi, qui maximam partem stylo Prophetico adumbratus est. Idcirco triplicis ge- neris Scripta Sacra in Novo Testamento conti- nentur: I. HISTORICA; quae tum vitam Jesu Christi Salvatoris nostri usque ad ejusdem Ascensionem in caelum complectuntur conain- nata à IV. Evangelistis, Matthaeo, Marco, Lu- ca & Johanne, quae Scripta EVANGELII nomen praefixum habent: vers. 9. ἐυαγγέλιον κτ̓ Ματθαῖον Evangelium secundum Matthaeum, & ita porro: tum Acta Apostolorum, imprimis Pe- tri, & Pauli inde ab Ascensione Christi usque ad captivitatem primam Pauli Romanam. Quae à S. Luca, Evangelista consignata titulum ge- runt πράξεις τ̃ ἁγίων Ἀποτόλων. II. DO- GMATICA, quae doctrinam Evangelicam Di- dactice exhibent, Epistolarum more conscri- pta: Qualia sunt Epistolae tum S. PAULI, tum ALIORUM APOSTOLORUM. S. Pauli Epistolae XIII. speciales sunt, ad certum lo- cum vel objectum directae, utpote Novem ad Ec- clesias certas, ad ROMANOS una, duae ad CO- RINTHIOS, prior & posterior, una ad GA- LATAS, una ad EPHESIOS, una ad PHI- LIPPENSES, una ad COLOSSENSES, duae ad THESSALONICENSES, prior nempe ac posterior: Quatuor vero reliquae ad personas cer- tas: duae sc. ad TIMOTHEUM, prior & poste- rior, una ad TITUM, & una ad PHILEMO- NEM. Quibus accedit decima quarta S. Pauli Epistola ad integram gentem, nimirum ad E- BRAEOS fideles directa. Caeterorum Apostolo- rum scripta, quae in Canonem Novi Testamen- ti relatæ sunt, numero VII. sunt: Eorum nempe E- pistolæ: una S. JACOBI, duæ S. PETRI, prior, & posterior, tres S. JOHANNIS, & una S. JU- DÆ: quæ omnes Catholicæ dicuntur, sed univer- saliter Ecclesiam concernunt, secunda & tertia Johannea exceptis, quæ ad certas personas dire- ctæ. III. PROPHETICUM Scriptum Novi Testamenti unicum est APOCALYPSIS JO- HANNIS, quæ tota more Prophetico concin- nata, ac statum futurum potissimum concernit. Diximus de hisce Scriptis Novi Testamenti gene- ratim System. Theol. Tom. I. pag. 507. seqq. & de textu primigenio Novi Testamenti quod Græcus sit textus originalis, neque ullus liber Novi Testam. in originali alia lingua scriptus sit, quodque lingua Novi Testamenti, si stylum respicias, Hellenistica sit, Ebraismis, & Syro-Chaldaismis gaudeat, ad- mixtis quoque nonnullis è Latina & Persica lin- gua, in Critico Sacro Diatr. V. ac puritatem fon- tium Novi Testamenti incontaminatam asserui- mus operose eodem Critico Diatrib. VI. vindi- catis etiam locis quæ vel per malitiam, vel per in- curiam corrupta censentur, & in specie illis, quæ à Morino corruptionis arguuntur. Quæ ante ipsos triginta annos, quum adhuc in Academia Regio- montana professione Theologica fungeremur, proposita, nunc sub incudem hic iterum revo- cata hic conferre, cui libuerit, non sine fructu, po- terit. Egit deinde de stylo Novi Testamenti in- ter alios complures è Reformatis Thomas Gata- kerus dissert. de stylo Novi Test. contra Pfoche- nium, Johannes Vorstius in dissert. & Comment. de Hebraismis Novi Testam. è nostris Bæclerus de lingua N. Test. Joh. Olearius in Disp. inaugur. dis- fert. Philologico-Theologic. de stylo Novi Te- stam. Hottingerus certe, etsi in Salmasii sententiam propensior Hellenismo minus faveat, agnoscit ta- men stylum dici posse Hellenisticum, vel Hebræo- Græcum, vel etiam Hebraizantem, quo usi sunt LXX. Interpp. in Thesauro Philol. p. 353. eique si- milem facit stylum N. T. in Syst. Theol. l. 1. loc. III. q. 151. Luculentissimis (inquit ille in priore loco) Drusius contra Serar. p. 89. Heinsius præf. in Nov. Test. p. 12. Const. l'Empereur præfat. in Baba Kama & Coccejus in Sanhedr. ostendunt exemplis, ita quæ- dam LXX. Interpretibus esse propria, ut ad eorum explicationem nihil plane conferant exteri aut profa- ni autores. Conf. & Joh. Seldenus in libr. de suc- cess. ableg. Hebr. c. V. Salmasius ipse de cruce pag. 465. fatetur, infinitis Ebraismis totam scriptu- ram N. T. scatere.

III. DE AUTORE SCRIPTORUM NOVI TESTAMENTI.

Autor primarius est Spiritus Sanctus, quia non tantum πᾶσα γραφὴ θεόπνευστος est, Apostolo teste 2. Tim. III. 16. & sancti Dei homines loquuti sunt, ac scripserunt φερόμενοι ὑπὸ πνεύματος ἁ- γίου 2. Pet. I. 21. sed ideo etiam Apostolis promif- sus à Christo est Spiritus Sanctus, ut duceret eos in OMNEM VERITATEM Joh. XVI. 13. non so- lum in prædicando, sed etiam scribendo: adde Luc. XXIV. 49. Actor. I. 4. 5. 8. qua fini quoque i- psis Christus insufflando Spiritum Sanctum con- cessit Johan. XX. 22. misitque de cælo Spiritum Sanctum in Festo Pentecostes, qui dedit Aposto- lis non eloqui tantum, sed etiam scribendo confi- gnare magnalia Dei Act. II. 4. unde mysterium de Christo dicitur revelatum Sanctis Apostolis per Spi- ritum Eph. III. 5. & Apostoli annunciarunt Ev- angelium per emissum è cælo Spiritum S. 1. Petr. I. 12. quodque Apostoli in Scripturis dicunt, id Spiritus

Sanctus, qui per eos loquutus est, & scripsit, dixi- se perhibetur 1. Tim. IV. 1. Conf. Matth. X. 20. Marc. XIII. 11. Luc. XII. 12. Johan. XIV. 26. Act. XV. 28. Ap. II. 11. 17. 29. c. III. 6. 13. 22. Sic Paulum com- mendat Petrus, quod κατὰ τὴν αὐτῷ δοθεῖσαν σοφίαν scripserit ἐν πάσαις ταῖς ἐπιστολαῖς 2. Epist. III. 15. 16. ac Paulus cum Jacobo S. Petrum & Johannem hoc elogio mactat Gal. II. 9. quod visi fuerint co- lumnæ: nosque extrui dicit non minus super Apo- stolorum in Novo Testamento, quam super Pro- phetarum in Veteri fundamentum, Ephes. II. 20. quemadmodum & in Apocalypsi c. XXI. 14. in fun- damentis Hierosolymæ nomina duodecim Apostolo- rum agni inscripta dicuntur. Adhæc quum do- cendi omnes gentes mandatum Apostolis datum doctrinam non minus illam, quam scriptis præsti- têre, quam quæ viva voce tradita est, concernat Matth. XXVIII. 29. utpote quæ non illius solum temporis homines attineat, sed etiam temporis sequuturi, usque ad consummationem seculi, quum eo usque παρουσία promissa sit v. 20. quemadmo- dum officium eorum erat non docendo tantum, sed etiam scribendo testificari de Christo Joh. XXI. 14. 1. Joh. I. 3. 4. Ap. I. 2. 3. 11. 19. c. II. 4. 8. 12. 18. c. III 13. 14. c. XIV. 13. c. XIX. 9. c. XXI. 5. non dubitan- dum est Deum cujus jussu & mandato scripserunt, autorem Scripturæ esse supremum. Unde S. Ire- næus l. III. adv. hæres. c. I. Apostoli, inquit, quæ pri- mum præconiaverunt postea per Dei voluntatem in Scriptura nobis tradiderunt.

Autores ergo secundarii vel ministeriales Scri- ptorum Novi Test. fuêre Apostoli, Matthæus, Jo- hannes, Jacobus, Petrus, Judas, & Paulus: quos immediato Spiritus S. afflatu impulsos fuisse, nul- lum est dubium: præter quos quidem & Marcus & Lucas scripsêre, sed illi è numero LXX. discipu- lorum Christi fuisse creduntur, & Historia Marci testimonium divinum à Petro, Lucæ vero à Paulo accipit: cujus laudem magnam in Evangelio esse di- xit Paulus 2. Cor. VIII. 18. Lucam sectatorem & discipulum Apostolorum dicit Irenæus l. III. c. 14. Marcum vero sectatorem Petri, c. 1. Eusebius l. III. Hist. Eccl. c. 21. Evangelium Lucæ non minus quam Matthæi & Marci à Johanne fuisse approbatum, te- statur: Hieronymus in catal. Illustr. Viror. Marcus, inquit, discipulus & interpres Petri, juxta quod Petrum referentem audiverat, rogatus Romæ à fra- tribus, breve scripsit Evangelium, quod cum Petrus audivisset, probavit, ac legendum Ecclesiæ sua autori- tate edidit. Sed de singulis dicturi deinceps su- mus specialiter. Universa certe Ecclesia libros No- vi Testamenti ceu divinos suscepit & licet de quo- rundam autoribus dubitatum fuerit à nonnullis, utpote de Epistola ad Hebræos & Apocalypsi, non- nullis etiam Jacobi Epistolam cæteris parem esse, ambiguum fuerit, rationes tamen dubitandi non magni fuêre momenti, & agnita ab aliis fuit au- toritas eorum divina & Canonica, totiusque Ec- clesiæ judicio multis seculis approbata.

IV. DE COMMENTATORIBUS IN NOVUM TESTAMENTUM.

Qui universum Codicem Sacrum commenta- riis vel observationibus illustrarunt, designati sunt Tomo I. Biblior. Illustrator. V. T. Qui vero operam suam contulerunt ad Novum Testam. & quidem quod ad eos, qui omnes aut plerosque saltim libros N. T. illustrarunt, hi potissimum ce- lebrantur è Veteribus Johannes Chrysostomus, pri- mo Antiochenus Presbyter, denique Archi-E- piscopus Constantinopolitanus circa ann. Christi cccc. cujus tamen Commentarii plerique non extant, & homiliæ fere tantum habentur: è scriptis autem ejus alii multa collegerunt: Theodoretus Cyrensis Episcopus: qui multa in Scripturas commentaria adornavit, magnam partem sequu- tus S. Chrysostomum, Anno CCCCL. Theophyla- ctus Bulgarorum Episcopus circa annum nongen- tesimum in compendium redegit quæ scriptis Exegeticis prolixius tradiderat Chrysostomus, o- missis locis communibus: Euthymius Zigabenus, qui circa annum cIo cxxC. è Scriptis Veterum Pa- trum & imprimis Chrysostomi commentarios succinctos collegit Oecumenius circa annum Do- mini octingentesimum concinnavit Catenam in Novum Testamentum, in qua isti autores legun- tur adhibiti: Papias, Clemens, Methodius, Dio- nysius, Irenæus, Origenes, Hippolytus, Athana- sius, Eusebius, Basilius, Gregorius Nyssenus, Acacius, Isidorus, Photius, Chrysostomus, Gregorius Nazian- zenus, Severianus, Gennadius, Arethas, Andreas, Cyrillus, Theodoretus: quibus Oecumenius sua ad- jecit. Thomas Aquinas Anno cIo CCLXXIV. in to- tum Novum Test. scripsit: in IV. vero Evangelia explinationem collegit è Patribus, iisque tum La- tinis, tum Græcis, quod opus continuum in IV. Ev- angelistas inscripsit, à recentioribus vocatur cate- na aurea. Augustinus Anconas Anno cIo CCCXXX. postillari studio scripsit in totum N. T. Johannes Bacco, Anglicus Carmelitanus, exposuit Schola- stico more totum N. T. libris viginti septem Anno Domini cIo CCCL. Johannes Capgravius Anglus Anno cIo CCCLXIV. in totum itidem N. Testam. scripsit. Laurentius Valla collationem Versionis Latinæ in N. T. cum textu Græco instituit eadem ætate. Erasmus Roterodamus Annotationes in N. T. eruditas edidit superioris seculi initio, sed le- gendas cum judicio: quibus Edvardus Leus An- glus suas in N. T. Annotationes Moguntiæ An- no cIo IDXX. opposuit. Joh. Gagnejus Parisiensis Theologus Anno Domini cIo IDL. Scholia in N. T. composuit. Jacobus Faber Stapulensis Com- mentaria in Evangelia, Epistolas Paulinas & Ca- nonicas concinnavit. Nicolaus Tacitus Zigenus Scholia collegit in omnes libros N. Test. Anno cIo IDXL. Nominavit Sixtus Senensis & quendam Johannem Loppis, qui in totum Novum Test. scri- pserit, sed ætatem ejus non designavit. Alphonsus Salmero, è primis decem Jesuitis unus, sedecim Tomos scripsit in N. T. è quibus decem IV. Evan- gelistas concernunt: Primus enim Prolegomena continet: Secundus initium Johannis de Incarna- tione Verbi: Tertius infantiam & pueritiam Jesu: Quartus Historiam Evangelicam, & vitam Christi usque ad ultimam cœnam: Quintus est de Sermo- ne Domini in monte: Sextus explicat miracula Christi: Septimus exponit parabolas: Octavus tra- ctat disputationes Christi: Nonus agit de S. Eucha- ristiæ Sacramento, & sermone ultimo Christi in cœna: Decimus est de passione & morte Christi: Undecimus est de resurrectione & ascensione Christi. Cornelius à Lapide justis Commentariis o- mnes libros N. Test. exposuit: Scripsit & Aloysius Novarinus in omnes N. T. libros, sed Annotatio- nes tantum. E nostris B. Lutherus, licet σποραδηνῶς per Tomos operum universum fere N. T. præcla- re interpretatus est. Philippus non pauca in N. T. exposuit. Extant & notæ Lucæ Lossii in N. T. ut & Erasmi Sarcerii. Joachimus Camerarius de figuris sermonis in N. T. erudite scripsit. Matthias Flacius Glossam in totum N. T. edidit. Erasmus Schmidius annotationes in N. T. cum nova versione reli- quit. E Reformatis Beza versionem propriam & notas eruditas in N. T. concinnavit. Benedictus Aretius

Aretius Commentaria in libros N. T. adornavit, ut & Mart. Bucerus, Hem. Bullingerus, Daniel Tof- sanus, & Thomas Carthuvrightus. Jacobus Capellus annotata quædam reliquit. Daniel Heinsius Exer- citationum ad Novum Test. libros XX. scripsit. Johannes Drusius libros præteritorum in N. T. Lu- dovicus de Dieu annotata adornavit. Joh. Camero Myrothecium Evangelicum cum aliis ad N. T. explicationem pertinentibus in operibus occur- rentibus exhibuit: cui spicilegium accessit, Ludo- vico Capello autore. Isaacus Casaubonus notas suc- cinctas ad libros N. T. historicos conscripsit: qui- bus addi possunt quæ passim idem habet in Exer- citationibus. In totum etiam Novum Test. Cate- nam vel expositionem quam vocat Catholicam è recentioribus imprimis collegit Augustinus Mar- toratus, utpote Emssno, Philippo, Brentio, Sar- cerio, Vito Theodore, Zvvinglio, Calvino, Bul- lingero, Bucero, Musculo & aliis, additis etiam quibusdam è Patribus. Atque hæc circa libros N. Testam. in genere.

## 1:1 Introduction: Grotius's Preface on the Gospel
GROTIUS'S PREFACE ON THE GOSPEL.

Εὐαγγέλιον.] Just as they received the word of the new covenant, so too did Christians receive this one from the supreme Teacher, just as he himself had received it from the Prophets. It is a Hebrew word בשׂר εὐαγγελίζεταy, whence the Syrians, by a metathesis that is sufficiently accepted, made סבר, and it is established that D and ש are equivalent. Isaiah LII. 7 had used the Hebrew word, which is sufficiently broad in its scope, so that although it signifies a message, he used it for the doctrine of Christ; Paul cites this in this sense in Romans X. 15. Now that doctrine is described in the Prophet by a double name, of peace and of the kingdom of God; and hence it is that this doctrine is frequently called by Christ himself, and by his Apostles, the Gospel of the kingdom, with the word of God sometimes added, Matthew IV. 23, IX. 35, XXIV. 14, Mark I. 14, and no less frequently the Gospel of peace, Ephesians II. 17, VI. 15, Acts X. 36. From which passages, when compared with one another, it appears that the Gospel is properly and primarily called that proclamation begun by John the Baptist (for the act of evangelizing is attributed to him also, Luke III. 18), but consummated by Christ, both by himself and through the Apostles (for Christ himself is said to have evangelized through them, even to the Gentiles, Ephesians II. 17), concerning the spiritual kingdom of God within us, and concerning the remission of sins obtained. For this proclamation, just as it is opposed to the Law and the Prophets as something greater and more perfect, so it is manifestly shown that the Baptist took his beginning from the pronouncement of Christ himself, which is in Luke XVI. 16, and that the proclamation of both the Baptist and Christ points, as it were, with a finger to that prophecy of Isaiah which we mentioned: for the first voice of John was, as it were: The heavenly Kingdom has arrived, Matthew III. 1 and Luke III. 3. Christ then, beginning his own announcement, starts with that same word: The heavenly kingdom, he says, has arrived, Matthew IV. 17, Mark I. 15, where this very thing is explained by the addition of the word 'Gospel': and Luke IV. 18 declares most openly that this is the very thing which is indicated by the word 'Gospel'. And hence it is that any doctrine differing from the doctrine of Christ is called a 'different Gospel' by Paul, 2 Corinthians XI. 4, Galatians I. 6, that is, a different proclamation. But because all the circumstances of his proclamation pertain to explaining, illustrating, and confirming the doctrine announced by Christ, therefore the history itself also received the name of Gospel, the scope of which is properly described by that time which intervened between the announcement of the Baptist and the ascension of Christ, as the words of Peter clearly indicate, Acts I. 22 and X. 37. Hence it is that Mark, beginning his narrative from the announcement of the Baptist, prefixes to it the title: The Gospel of Jesus Christ the Son of God: so that what Matthew and Luke discuss—the former concerning the birth of Christ, the latter indeed even concerning the birth of the Baptist—and likewise that comparison of the Baptist and Christ instituted by John the Apostle at the beginning of his book, are to be held in the place of a certain preface and introduction: which Luke himself also seems not obscurely to profess, Acts I. 1. In this secondary sense, which, as I said, embraces the coherence of the history together with the doctrine, Christ himself seems to have used the Hebrew word בשׂר or the Syriac סברא, which Mark translated as 'Gospel', chapter XIV. 9. For most just reasons, therefore, the ancient Christians inscribed these books concerning the things of Christ as 'Gospels': so that by the very name the reader might be admonished how much sweeter things this book contains than the prophecies of the Prophets, most of which prefix to themselves that sad name 'burden' (משׂא). That the title of Gospel is most ancient and derived from the Apostolic times themselves, Justin teaches us in his Apology for the Christians, which is undoubtedly his, where he says thus: 'For the apostles, in the memoirs composed by them which are called Gospels, have thus delivered...' It is added that not only the Latins, but also the Syrian and Arab interpreters, and the Churches of all languages, have called these books by this very word, the word by which Xenophon had inscribed those books in which he had noted the principal sayings and deeds of Socrates, according to Laertius: by which example you would rightly call these books in Latin 'commentaries concerning the things of Christ'.

TABLE OF CONTENTS OF GROTIUS'S PREFACE.

The homonymy of the Gospel is more correctly explained in this way, that although it specifically denotes the preaching of grace concerning the remission of sins to be obtained through Christ, or even more restrictively the joyful message concerning the advent of Christ the Savior, Luke 2:10, yet generally it designates either the whole doctrine handed down by Christ, or finally the entire history of the life and doctrine of Christ, which Justin in his Apology for the Christians called ἀπομνημονεύματα, just as Xenophon had titled those books in which he had noted the principal sayings and deeds of Socrates, as Laertius testifies: by which example, Grotius observes, these books are rightly called in Latin commentaries on the affairs of Christ.

These acceptations, however, must be especially distinguished. For otherwise a twofold error is easily introduced, from which even Grotius was not free: first, as if legal preachings also pertained to the Gospel properly so called. For if the whole preaching of the Baptist and of Christ be called the Gospel properly and primarily, the Gospel accepted in a proper and primary sense will contain at the same time legal doctrines, such as are not a few handed down by John and Christ, and it will be a Gospel, which is properly a preaching of grace, at the same time a preaching of wrath and repentance, which is a contradiction in terms. Then, if that preaching which began with John is finally called the Gospel properly, it must be confessed that the Gospel, or the proclamation concerning the spiritual kingdom of God and the remission of sins, did not obtain in the Old Testament: And the Socinian dogma will deserve approval, that the Scripture of the Old Testament was devoid of such promises, as those which only began with the auspices of the New Testament. But St. Peter teaches that all the prophets testified to the remission of sins in the name of Christ, Acts 10:43. And the Council of Jerusalem concludes that the ancients believed they would obtain salvation through the grace of Christ, just as we believe it, Acts 15:11. Therefore, the comparison of the Gospel with the prophecies of the prophets is not to be rashly approved, who, even if they sometimes deservedly prefix to themselves that sad name משא, nevertheless also contain many joyful things concerning the Messiah, his advent, kingdom, and the peace which he brings. Although those prophecies sometimes come under the word of promise, just as the fulfillment of them, which we have in the advent of the Messiah, is peculiarly called the Gospel. For which reason the kingdom of God is said to be preached from the time of John, Luke 16:16, not because the kingdom of God had not been preached in the Old Testament, because the ancient faithful also hoped for a heavenly country and eternal life, Heb. 11:10, 14, 16. But because the kingdom of God began to be preached most clearly, publicly, and throughout the whole world in the New Testament, when the mysteries were handed down more fully and openly, and because Christ the King has arisen over the house of Jacob, about to occupy the royal throne of his Father, as interpreted by the Angel, Luke 1:32, 33, to which he was to be raised, through exaltation to the right hand of God. For his kingdom was not of this world, nor was he to occupy the worldly throne of David, but a spiritual one: not to be a political King, but the head of the Church, as of his own mystical body. Wherefore the first voice, as it were, of John, and the same was the first voice of Christ, was not that the heavenly kingdom has arrived, but IT IS NEAR Matth. III. 2. Luc. III. 3. Matth. IV. 17. which had already arrived for the Protoplasts, when the crushing of the serpent's head was promised to them, but that the kingdom of God had begun to be nearer, on account of a more illustrious and fuller manifestation, and a more diffused propagation; unless by the kingdom of God we wish to understand a new form and manner of government, to be administered by Christ the God-man raised to the legal throne, or the economy of the kingdom of God proper to the New Testament. For this kingdom was then approaching, inasmuch as both the Messiah the heavenly King had been exhibited, and that manifestation of the economy of the New Testament was at the doors, the state of that happy Church under the government of the Messiah: whence the Holy Scriptures otherwise call this time the accepted time, and the day of salvation 2. Cor. VI. 2. of which Rom. XIII. 11. for now is our salvation nearer than when we believed. Which time was long ago promised by the Prophets Is. XLIX. 8. c. LXI. 1. and elsewhere throughout: in which God was both to exhibit the heavenly King, and to exert the power of the kingdom of heaven, both extensively, by diffusing it, and extending the boundaries of that kingdom, hitherto confined within the circuit of the Jewish nation, and intensively, by administering the fullness of light and spirit, in the fullness of time.

ON THE CAUSES OF THE WRITING, AND THE NUMBER, AND THE COMMENTATORS OF THE FOUR GOSPELS IN GENERAL.

Thomas Aquinas in the Catena recounts these causes of the writing, for which the Evangelists recorded the History of Christ; (1) that they might teach those whom they could not be present with, through the Scripture concerning the Gospel. (2) that those things which it is fitting to know concerning the words and deeds of Christ might be preserved in perpetual memory. (3) lest false histories or doctrines concerning Christ should be spread by heretics. How pregnant this last reason was, is taught especially by those pseudo-gospels, which have been scattered in great number: For not only did the Valentinians boast of more Gospels according to Iren. l. III. c. 11. Tertul. l. advers. hæres. and the Basilidians according to Ambros. preface in Luc. and Hieron. prolog. in Matth. and the Manichaeans, as witnessed by Augustine l. XXXI. against Faustus chap. 2. but also under the name of the Apostles many other Apocryphal Writings were sold as Gospels; namely the Gospel according to the twelve Apostles, of which Origen see book I. on Luke, and Jerome preface in Matthew.
