The Gospel of Peter the Apostle, the Gospel according to Andrew according to Eusebius l. III, c. 26. Hieron. l. c. Augustin. against the adversaries of the law and the Prophets c. 20. The Proto-Gospel, which is called, of James, which is seen among the Orthodoxographa of the Fathers: The Gospel of James which was of the Nazarenes according to Origen T. II. Tract. VIII. on John. Eusebius l. I. c. 25. The Gospel of Philip which was of the Gnostics according to Epiph. heresy XXVI. The Gospel of Bartholomew, according to Dionys. the Areopagite. The Gospel of Thomas, which the Manichaeans used: See Cyrill. Hieros. catech. The Gospel of Matthias, which favored the Marcionites and Basilides. See Euseb. l. III. c. 25. Clem. Alexandr. l. II. Strom. But also a Gospel was attributed to Judas the traitor, and was approved by the Cainite heretics. See Iren. l. I. c. 35. Epiph. heresy XXXVIII. Others were also bandied about

Gospels, such as that of Barnabas, in the book of Recognitions attributed to Clement, the Gospel of Nicodemus, in the Orthodox Fathers: the Gospel of Apelles according to Hier. Prol. Matth. The Gospel of the Egyptians, which was in use among the Valentinians and Sabellians. See Clem. Alex. l. III. Stromat. Epiph. heresy LXII. Hieron. l. c. All of which, however, betrayed themselves by their falsehood and futility, and therefore have been held by the Church as apocryphal and rejected.

But only the quadriga of the Gospels is received by the Catholic Church, as being recognized as genuine no less from internal criteria than commended by the divine authority of the Apostles to the Church, which, as regards the whole New Testament, was done by St. John, who was the last survivor of the Apostles. Concerning these Irenaeus l. III. c. 11. with testimonies produced from the four Gospels of Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John: So great, he says, is the firmness concerning these Gospels, that even the heretics themselves bear witness to it, and each one of them, departing from them, attempts to confirm his own doctrine. Nor are there more in number than these, nor again can there be fewer Gospels. For since there are four regions of the world in which we are, and four principal spirits, and the Church is disseminated over all the earth, but the pillar and foundation of the Church is the Gospel and the spirit of life, it follows that it has four pillars, breathing out incorruptibility on all sides, and vivifying men. From which it is manifest that the Word, who is the artificer of all things, who sits upon the Cherubim and contains all things, having been revealed to men, gave us a quadriform Gospel, which is contained in one spirit. St. Jerome, Epist. ad Paulin., applies here the chariot of the Lord, shown to Ezekiel c. I and to John, Apoc. IV. Augustine, l. I. de Consens. Evangel. c. VII, says it is that holy chariot of the Lord, by which, as if in a triumphal car, he was carried through the whole world, scattered the most abundant fragrance of knowledge, and subdued peoples to himself. The pious Ancients then apply the forms of the four living creatures to the four Evangelists, although not all by the same reasoning. The speculation of Jerome, whom Gregory the Great followed in homil. IV in Ezech. and Sedulius in l. 1 de opere Paschali, is not inelegant: The first, he says l. c., the face of a MAN signifies Matthew, because he began to write as if from a man, 'The book of the generation of Jesus Christ,' etc. The second, of a LION, Mark, in whom the voice of a lion roaring in the wilderness is heard, chap. I, 'The voice of one crying in the desert.' The third, of a CALF, Luke, because he took his beginning from Zacharias the Priest. The fourth, of an EAGLE, John, because having taken the wings of an eagle and hastening to higher things, he disputes about the Word of God.

There are commentators on the Gospels who have expounded them either absolutely and without comparison, or harmonically, that is, with a comparison of the Evangelical history instituted regarding its sequence and agreement: of these latter we shall speak specifically hereafter, on the occasion of the Evangelical Harmony to be prepared by us. Of the interpreters or commentators of the former kind, besides those who have written on the whole New Testament, are Diodorus of Tarsus, Chrysostom's teacher, who in the year of the Lord 360 prepared commentaries on the IV Gospels. Asterius of Scythopolis wrote brief commentaries on the IV Gospels in the year 380. Fortunatianus, by whom the same was done in that age: Ottfried, a student of Rabanus Maurus, Archbishop of Mainz, in the year 810. Richard of Middleton in the year 1210. John Balbus of Genoa is said by Sixtus of Siena, Bibl. S. l. IV, to have written a Postil on the IV Gospels.

In the year of our Lord 1580. At which time also Johannes Christophorus of the Order of Preachers wrote on the Evangelists: as also Michaël Maffensis in the year 1650. Johannes Majoria the Scot composed a Scholastic Postil on the four Gospels in the year 1600. Antonius Broickhus à Königstein published four books of narrations on the four Gospels in a style almost Scholastic, but somewhat more polished, in the year 1641. Guttierus Trejus of Plasencia, a Spaniard, elaborated commentaries on the four Gospels in the year 1650. Johannes Arobaeus of Laon, a Doctor of the Sorbonne, published Commentaries on the four Gospels at the same time. Finally, Didacus Stella, Perez, Perpinianus, Sylvester, and others also wrote on the Gospels. A Greek Catena was also collected, which Sixtus Senensis reviews in the aforementioned place, from Origen, Eusebius of Caesarea, Chrysostom, Victor the Presbyter, Titus of Bostra, Severus, Isidore of Pelusium, Basil, and Cyril, on the four Evangelists. Balduinus Walæus devoted almost similar effort to the four Evangelists and the Acts of the Apostles not so long ago among the Reformed, while he composed his own work from various Annotations under the title of a perpetual Commentary on the historical books of the New Testament, but chiefly from philologists: from whom he praises these: Theodore Beza, Isaac Casaubon, Joachim Camerarius, Franciscus Gomarus, Claudius Salmasius, Daniel Heinsius, Johannes Cameron, Fridericus Spanheim, Johannes Drusius, and Johannes Selden, Ludovicus de Dieu, Hugo Grotius, Benedictus Arias Montanus, Aloysius Novarinus, Johannes Pricaeus: to whom some others have been added, Thomas Bartholinus, Bochart, Budé, Buxtorf the Son, Calvin, Caninius, Ludovicus Capellus, Cheitomæus, Chemnitius, Croy, Cunaeus, Dallaeus, Fagius, Octavius Ferrarius, Fuller, Galatinus, Wilhelmus Langius, l'Empereur, Polyc. Lyserus, Montacutius, Paræus, Petitus, Piscator, Revius, Rivetus, Joseph Scaliger, Scultetus, Sibelius, Henricus Stephanus, Tarnovius, Tremellius, Valtesius, Gerhard Vossius, Antonius Walæus, Johannes Walæus. Theodorus Hackspan also wrote certain Philological-Theological notes on the four Evangelists. Not a few have also written on the Sunday and Festival Gospel Pericopes, both Postils, as they are called, and ἐξηγήσεις and annotations. Sixtus Senensis commemorates these from the Fathers and Papists in alphabetical order: Albert of Padua, Albinus, Antonius Bitontinus, Antonius Bruich, Antonius Gislandus, Aurelius Augustinus, Bede, Callistus, Caesarius, Cyril of Jerusalem, David, Ecbert, Ericus, Eusebius Emissenus, Flavianus, Franciscus Obsunna, Fridericus Nauseas, Fulgentius, Gvalterus Dissus, Georg. Vicelius, Gerardus, Streda, Gregorius Magnus, Gosscalcius, Gvërricus, Gvilhelmus Peckin; Haymo, Henricus Calteson, Henricus Consveldius, Henricus Harphius, Henricus Hebnesius, Henricus Langestein, Henricus Urimarius, Hermannus Petra, Hildegard, Honorius, Jacobus of Genoa, Jacobus Scapperus, Innocent III, Johannes Arundineus, Johannes Beeths, Johannes Castellenfis, Johannes Doceus, Johannes Dominici, Johannes Ferus, Johannes Gauver, Johannes Hofmeister, Johannes Justus, Johannes Maria, Johannes Nider, Johannes Nivecellensis, Johannes Regnus, Johannes Rojardus, Johannes Taulerus, Johannes Turrecremata, Judocus, Ludovicus of Granada, Mauritius of Paris, Maximus of Turin, Michaël Cefenas, Nicolaus Cusa, Nicolaus Herbron, Nicolaus Dunckelspulius, Petrus Chrysologus, Petrus Spirensis, Petrus Verberius, Sanctius, Sixtus, Smaragdus, Stephanus of Paris, Sylvester, Titus, Thomas, Hasselbachius; to whom, from the more recent Roman Catholic Postillers and narrators of the Gospels, many have been added, e.g., Franciscus Costerus, Thomas Stapleton, etc. From the Reformed, Gvalterus, Olevianus, Nehum, Zepperus, Lucius, Scultetus, Sebelius, etc. From our own, after the Blessed Luther, Philippus, Major, Chemnitius, Chytraeus, Selneccerus, Simon Paulus, Ægydius Hunnius, Siegfridus Saccus, and others of the previous century, almost countless ones of the modern century, Matthias Hoë, Fridericus Balduinus, Balthasar Meisnerus, Johannes Gerhardus, Johannes Tarnovius, Johannes Cluverus, Johannes Himmelins, Conradus Dietericus, Danhavverus, Salomo Glassius, Reinholdus, Backius, Mehlfürerus, Tauderstadius, etc.

Latin:

PRÆLOQUIUM GROTIANUM DE EVANGELIO.

Εὐαγγέλιον.] Sicut vocem novi fœderis ita & hanc Christiani à summo Magistro accepêre, ipse à Prophetis acceperat. Vox Hebræa est בשׂר εὐαγγελίζεταy, unde Syri per μετάθεσιν satis receptam סבר fecere D & ש con- stat esse ἰσοδύναμα. Vocem Hebræam late satis patentem, ita ut quamvis ἀγγελίαν significet, de doctrina Christi u- surpaverat Esaias LII. 7. quem in hunc sensum citat Paulus Rom. X. 15. Describitur autem ea doctrina apud Prophe- tam duplici nomine, pacis, & regni Dei; atque hinc est, quod hæc doctrinæ tum ab ipso Christo, tum ab ejus A- postolis crebro vocetur Εὐαγγέλιον τῆς βασιλείας, addita etiam interdum voce τοῦ Θεοῦ Matth. IV. 23. IX. 35. XXIV. 14. Marc. I. 14. neque minus frequenter εὐαγγέλιον εἰρήνης Ephes. II. 17. VI. 15. Act. X. 36. E quibus locis inter se col- latis apparet, proprie ac primario Evangelium dici, xή- ρυγμα illud à Johanne Baptista inchoatum, (nam & illi tribuitur τὸ εὐαγγελίζεσθαι Luc. III. 18.) à Christo vero tum per se, tum per Apostolos (nam per hos ipse Christus dicitur εὐαγγελίσασθαι, etiam gentibus Ephes. II. 17.) con- summatum, de regno spirituali Dei in nobis, deque parta remissione peccatorum. Hoc enim κήρυγμα, sicut legi ac Prophetis, ut majus ac perfectius quiddam, opponitur; ita manifeste ostenditur Baptistam sumfisse exordium ab ipsius Christi pronunciato quod est Luc. XVI. 16. ipsum- que tam Baptistæ, quam Christi κήρυγμα, ad id quod di- ximus, Esaiæ vaticinium quasi digitum intendit: Joannis enim quasi prima vox fuit: Adventavit Regnum cœleste, Matth. III. 1. & Luc. III. 3. Christus deinde suam an- nunciationem inchoans, ab eodem illa voce incipit: Ad- ventavit, inquiens, regnum cœleste, Matth. IV. 17. Marc. I. 15. ubi hoc ipsum explicatur addita εὐαγγελίου voce: id- que ipsum esse quod εὐαγγελίου voce indicetur, apertissime declarat Luc. IV. 18. Atque hinc est, quod doctrina quæ- vis à Christi doctrina discrepans ἕτερον Εὐαγγέλιον à Paulo vocatur. 2. Corinth. XI. 4. Galat. I. 6. id est aliud κήρυγμα. Quia vero ad explicandam, illustrandam & confirman- dam doctrinam à Christo annunciatam, pertinent omnes ejus κηρύγματος circumstantiæ, ideo ipsa quoque historia Evangelii nomen accepit, cujus ambitus proprie de- scribitur eo tempore, quod ab annunciatione Baptistæ ad Christi ascensum intercessit, ut clare indicant Petri verba Act. I. 22. & X. 37. Hinc est quod Marcus narrationem incipiens ab annunciatione Baptistæ, titulum ei præfigit: ἐυαγγέλιον Jesu Christi filii Dei: ita ut quæ Matthæus & Lu- cas, ille de Christi ortu, hic vero etiam de Baptistæ nata- libus edisserunt, itemque comparatio illa Baptistæ & Chri- sti à Johanne Apostolo libri sui primordio instituta, ante- loquii cujusdam & εἰσαγωγῆς habenda sint loco: quod ipse etiam Lucas non obscure videtur profiteri Act. I. 1. In hoc sensu secundario, qui, ut dixi, cum doctrina simul historiæ ipsius cohærentiam complectitur, ipse Christus vocem Hebræam בשׂר aut Syriacam סברא videtur u- surpasse, quam Marcus ἐυαγγέλιον transtulit, cap. XIV. 9. Justissimis igitur de causis, veteres Christiani hos libros de rebus Christi, ἐυαγγέλια inscripsere: ut ipso quoque nomine admoneretur lector, quanto dulciora hic libet contineat, quam Prophetarum vaticinia, quorum plera- que triste illud nomen משׂא sibi præscribunt. Esse autem antiquissimum & ab ipsis Apostolicis deductum tempori- bus Evangelii titulum, docet nos Justinus in Apologia pro Christianis, quæ non dubie ipsius est, ubi ita inquit: οἱ γὰρ ἀπόστολοι ἐν τοῖς γενομένοις ὑπ' αὐτῶν ἀπομνημονεύμα- σιν ἅ καλεῖται εὐαγγέλια, ὕτως παρέδωκαν Accedit quod non Latini tantum, sed & Syrus & Arabs interpretes, omnesque omnium linguarum Ecclesiæ hac ipsa voce hos libros vocavit, qua voce Xenophon eos libros inscripserat, quibus præcipua dicta factaque Socratis annotarat, Laërtio teste: quo exemplo Latine hosce libros commen- tarios de rebus Christi recte appellaveris.

ELENCHUS GROTIANI PRÆ- LOQUII.

Homonymia Evangelii rectius ita expeditur, quod etsi speciatim quidem notet concionem gra- tiæ de remissione peccatorum per Christum con- sequenda, vel etiam restrictis lætum nuncium de adventu Christi Salvatoris Luc. II. 10. generaliter tamen designet, vel doctrinam totam, à Christo traditam, vel denique historiam vitæ, & doctri- næ Christi universam, quam Justinus in Apol. pro Christian. ἀπομνημονεύματα vocavit, uti Xeno- phon eos libros inscripserat, quibus præcipua di- cta factaque Socratis annotarat, Laërtio teste: quo exemplo, Latine hosce libros commentarios de rebus Christi recte appellari, Grotius observat.

Quæ vero acceptiones apprime distinguendæ sunt. Nam facile alias error geminus invehitur, à quo etiam Grotius alienus non fuit: primo qua- si ad Evangelium proprie dictum conciones legales quoque pertineant. Si enim totum κήρυγμα Ba- ptistæ, & Christi, proprie ac primario Evangelium vocetur, Evangelium sensu proprio & primario acceptum complectetur simul legales doctrinas, quales non paucæ à Johanne & Christo traditæ, eritque Εὐαγγέλιον, quod proprie est concio gratiæ, simul concio iræ & pœnitentiæ, quod est ἀντικείμενον ἐν προσκαπήλῳ. Tum, si proprie Evangelium demum illud κήρυγμα dicitur, quod à Johanne cœpit, fatendum erit, in Veteri Testa- mento non obtinuisse Evangelium, vel præconium de regno spirituali Dei, & remissione peccatorum: Et Socinianum dogma, calculum merebitur, quod Scriptura Veteris Testamenti talium pro- missionum expers fuerit, utpote, quæ demum cœperint cum auspicio Novi Testamenti. At S. Petrus docet, remissionem peccatorum in nomine Christi omnes Prophetas testatos esse, Actor. X. 43. Et Concilium Hierosolymitanum concludit, Ve- teres credidisse: per gratiam Christi salutem se consequuturos, perinde uti nos id credimus A- ctor. XV. 11. Non ergo temere probanda compa- ratio Evangelii cum Prophetarum vaticiniis, qui, etsi quandoque triste illud nomen משא, meri- to sibi præfigant, multa tamen etiam continent læta de Messia, ejus adventu, regno & pace, quam affert. Quanquam illa vaticinia ἐπαγγε- λίας, seu promissionis voce nonnunquam ve- niant, uti complementum eorum, quod habe- mus in adventu Messiæ, ἐυαγγέλιον peculiariter vocatur. Quapropter à Johannis tempore re- gnum Dei prædicari dicitur Luc. XVI. 16. non, quod regnum Dei prædicatum in Veteri Testa- mento haud fuerit, quia sperarunt etiam ve- teres fideles patriam cœlestem, ac æternam vi- tam, Ebr. XI. 10. 14. 16. Sed quod luculentis- sime, publice, ac per totum terrarum orbem regnum Dei prædicari in Novum Testam. cœ- perit, quum mysteria plenius & apertius tradita sint, quodque Christus Rex super domum Jacob exortus sit, thronum Patris sui regium occupa- turus, interprete Angelo Luc. I. 32. 33. ad quem eve- hendus erat, per exaltationem ad dextram Dei. Regnum enim ejus non erat de hoc mundo, nec thronum Davidis mundanum occupare debuit, sed spiritualem: non Rex politicus futurus, sed caput Ecclesiæ, ceu corporis sui mystici. Quapro- pter prima quasi vox Johannis, eademque prima Christi vox fuit, non adventavit regnum cæleste, sed PROPE EST Matth. III. 2. Luc. III. 3. Matth. IV. 17. quod ad Protoplastos jam adventavit, cum contritio capitis serpentini promissa ipsis fuit, sed quod propius esse cœperit regnum Dei, ob illustrio- rem, & pleniorem patefactionem, ac diffusiorem propagationem; nisi per regnum Dei, novam regi- minis formam ac rationem intelligere velimus, per Christum θεάνθρωπον in thronum legalem eve- ctum, administrandam, vel œconomiam regni Dei Novo Testamento propriam. Hoc enim regnum tum appropinquabat, siquidem & Messias Rex cœlestis exhibitus erat, & manifestatio illa œco- nomiæ Novi Testamenti, erat præ foribus, status istius felicis Ecclesiæ sub regimine Messiæ: unde alias S. S. vocat tempus hoc tempus acceptum, & diem salutis 2. Cor. VI. 2. de quo Rom. XIII. 11. νῦν γὰρ ἐγγύτερον ἡμῶν ἡ σωτηρία, ἢ ὅτε ἐπιστεύσα- μεν. Quod tempus à Prophetis olim promissum Es. XLIX. 8. c. LXI. 1. & aliis passim: quo Deus & Regem cœlestem exhibiturus, & regni cœlorum vim exerturus erat, tum extensive, diffundendo illud, & regni illius pomœria, hactenus intra gen- tis Judaicæ ambitum coërcita exporrigendo, tum intensive, plenitudinem lucis & spiritus admini- strando, in plenitudine temporis.

DE CAUSIS SCRIPTIONIS, ET NUMERO, AC COMMENTATORIBUS QUATUOR EVANGELIORUM IN GENERE.

Causas Scriptionis has recenset Thomas Aqui- nas in Catena, propter quas Evangelistæ Historiam de Christo consignarint; (1) ut quos præsentes non possent, per Scripturam de Evan- gelio docerent. (2) ut in perpetua memoria con- servarentur, quæ de Christi dictis & factis non sci- re convenit. (3) ne per hæreticos falsæ historiæ vel doctrinæ de Christo spargerentur. Quæ po- strema ratio quam prægnans fuerit, docent impri- mis illa ψευδευαγγέλια, quæ sparsa sunt magno nu- mero: Nam non jactitarunt tantum Valentiniani, plura Evangelia apud Iren. l. III. c. 11. Tertul. l. ad- vers. hæres. & Basilidiani apud Ambros. præfat. in Luc. & Hieron. prolog. in Matth. & Manichæi, te- ste Augustino l. XXXI. contra Faustum cap. 2. sed sub nomine etiam Apostolorum alia plurima A- pocrypha Scripta pro Evangeliis venditata sunt; Evangelium nempe secundum duodecim Apostolos, de quo Origenes vid. libr. I. in Lucam, & Hieronym. præfat. in Matth. Evangelium Petri Apostoli, Ev- angelium secundum Andream apud Eusebium l. III, c. 26. Hieron. l. c. Augustin. contr. advers. leg. & Proph. c. 20. Prot-Evangelium, quod vocatur, Ja- cobi, quod inter Orthodoxographa Patrum visitur: Evangelium Jacobi quod Nazarenorum fuit apud Origen. T. II. Tract. VIII. in Joh. Eusebium l. I. c. 25. Evangelium Philippi quod Gnosticorum fuit apud Epiphan. hær. XXVI. Evangelium Bartholomæi, a- pud Dionys. Areopag. Evangelium Thomæ, quo Manichæi usi sunt: Vid. Cyrill. Hieros. catech. Ev- angelium Matthiæ, quod Marcionitis & Basilidi fa- vebat. Vid. Euseb. l. III. c. 25. Clem. Alexandr. l. II. Strom. Sed & Judæ proditori Evangelium tribu- tum, & Cainis hæreticis probatum fuit. Vid. Iren. l. I. c. 35. Epiph. hær. XXXVIII. Jactata & alia sunt

Evangelia, utpote Barnabæ, in libro Recogn. Clementi tributo, Evangelium Nicodemi, in Or- thodox. Patrum: Evangelium Apellis apud Hier. Prol. Matth. Evangelium Ægyptiorum, quod in usu fuit Valentin. & Sabellianis. Vid. Clem. Alex. l. III. Stromat. Epiph. hær. LXII. Hieron. l. c. Quæ vero omnia falsitate & futilitate sua se pro- diderunt, & proinde ab Ecclesia ceu apocrypha, & rejectitia habita sunt.

Sola autem quadriga Evangeliorum ab Ecclesia Catholica recepta, utpote non minus ex inter- nis κριτηρίοις genuina agnita, quam ab Aposto- lis Ecclesiæ autoritate divina commendata, quod quoad totum N. Testam. à S. Johanne, qui novis- simus Apostolorum superstes fuit, factum est. De his Irenæus l. III. c. 11. productis è quatuor Ev- angeliis Matthæi, Marci, Lucæ, & Johannis te- stimoniis: Tanta, inquit, est circa Evangelia hæc fir- mitas, ut & ipsi hæretici testimonium reddant ei, & ex ipsis egrediens unusquisque eorum, conetur suam confirmare doctrinam. Neque autem plura numero quam hæc sunt, neque rursus pauciora ca- pit esse Evangelia. Quoniam enim quatuor regio- nes mundi sunt in quo sumus, & quatuor principa- les spiritus, & disseminata est Ecclesia super omnem terram, columna autem & firmamentum Ecclesiæ est Evangelium & spiritus vitæ, consequens est quatuor habere eam columnas, undique flantes incorrupti- bilitatem, & vivificantes homines. Ex quibus ma- nifestum est, quoniam qui est omnium artifex Ver- bum, qui sedet super Cherubim & continet omnia declaratus hominibus, dedit nobis quadriforme Ev- angelium, quod in uno spiritu continetur. S. Hieronymus Epist. ad Paulin. huc accommodat quadrigam Domini, ostensam Ezechieli c. I. & Johanni Apoc. IV. Augustin. l. I. de Consens. Ev- angel. c. VII. dicit esse sanctam illam Domini qua- drigam, qua tanquam curru triumphali per orbem terrarum vectus, odorem cognitionis sparsit uberri- mum, ac populos sibi subegit. Applicant inde pii Veteres formas quatuor animantium quatuor Evangelistis, quamvis non una omnes ratione. Hieronymi, quem sequutus est Gregor. M. homil. IV. in Ezech. & Sedul. l. 1. de opere Paschali non inconcinna est speculatio: Prima, inquit l. c. HO- MINIS facies Matthæum significat, quia quasi de homine exorsus est præscribere, Liber generationis Jesu Christi &c. Secunda LEONIS Marcum, in quo vox leonis in eremo rugientis auditur cap. I. Vox clamantis in deserto. Tertia VITULI Lucam, quia à Zacharia Sacerdote sumsit ini- tium. Quarta AQUILÆ Johannem, quia sum- tis pennis aquilæ & ad altiora festinans de Verbo Dei disputat.

Commentatores in Evangelia sunt, qui vel absolute, & citra collationem eadem exposuêre, vel Harmonice, seu instituta Historiæ Evangeli- cæ collatione quoad seriem & convenientiam: de his posterioribus deinceps peculiariter dicturi sumus, occasione Harmoniæ Evangelicæ à nobis adornandæ. E prioris generis interpretibus vel Commentatoribus sunt præter illos, qui in Nov. Testam. totum scripsêre, Diodorus Tar- sensis, Chrysostomi præceptor, qui Anno Domini CCCLX. Commentationes adornavit in IV. Evan- gelia. Asterius Scythopolitanus brêves Commen- tariolos in IV. Evangelia scripsit Anno CCCXXC. Fortunatianus, à quo eadem ætate id factum: Ott- friedus Rabani Moguntini Archiepiscopi auditor Anno IƆ CCCCX. Richardus Mediavillanus Anno cIɔ CCX. Joh. Balbus Genevensis Postillam in IV. Ev- angelia scripsisse dicitur à Sixto Senensi Bibl. S. l. IV.

Anno Domini cIɔ cdxxc. Quo tempore etiam Johannes Christophorus ordinis Prædicatorum in Evangelistas scripsit: ut & Michaël Maffensis An- no cIɔ cdcL. Johannes Majoria Scotus Scholasti- cam Postillam in IV. Evangelia Anno cIɔ cdcC. concinnawit. Antonius Broickhus à Königstein in IV. Evangelia libros IV. enarrationum stylo fere Scholastico, sed aliquantulum cultiore edi- dit Anno cIɔ Iɔ XLI. Guttierus Trejus Placentia Hi- spanus commentaria in IV. Evangelia elaboravit Anno cIɔ IɔL. Johannes Arobaeus Laudunensis Sorbonicus Doctor eodem tempore Commenta- rios in IV. Evangelia edidit. Denique scripsêre etiam in Evangelia Didacus Stella, Perez, Perpinia- nus, Sylvester, aliiqve. Collecta etiam est Cate- na Græca, quam recenset Sixtus Senensis l. c. ex O- rigene, Eusebio Cæsar. Chrysostomo, Victore Presby- tero, Tito Bostreno, Severo, Isidoro Pelusiota, Basilio & Cyrillo, in IV. Evangelistas. Gemellam fére operam navavit in IV. Evangelistas, & Acta A- postolorum non ita pridem inter Reformatos Balduinus Walæus, dum è variis Annotatis sua concinnawit sub titulo perpetui Commentarii in libros Historicos Novi Testam. sed è Philologis potissimum: è quibus hos laudat: Theodoram Bezam, Isaacum Casaubonum, Joachimum Came- rarium, Franciscum Gomarum, Claudium Sal- masium, Danielem Heinsium, Johannem Camero- nem, Fridericum Spanhemium, Johannem Drusium, & Johannem Seldenum, Ludovicum de Dieu, Hugonem Grotium, Benedictum Aria- montanum, Aloysium Novarinum, Johannem Pri- cæum: quibus nonnulli accesserunt Thomas Bar- tholinus, Bochartus, Budæus, Buxtorfius Filius, Calvinus, Caninius, Ludovicus Capellus, Cheito- mæus, Chemnitius, Croyus, Cunæus, Dallæus, Fagius, Octavius Ferrarius, Fullerus, Galatinus, Wilhelmus Langius, l'Empereur, Polyc. Lyserus, Montacutius, Paræus, Petitus, Piscator, Revius, Rivetus, Josephus Scaliger, Scultetus, Sibelius, Henricus Stephanus, Tarnovius, Tremellius, Val- tesius, Gerhard. Vossius, Antonius Walæus, Johan- nes Walæus. Scripsit & Theodorus Hackspan no- tas quasdam Philologico-Theologicas in IV. Ev- angelistas. In Pericopas Evangelicas Dominicales & Festivas etiam non pauci scripsere cum Po- stillam, quas vocant, tum ἐξηγήσεις & annotatio- nes. ## 1:1 Introduction: In the Name of Jesus. Abraham Calovius' Evangelical Harmony, for the Composing of a New Mo
In the name of Jesus. Abraham Calovius' Evangelical Harmony, for the composing of a new Monotessaron.

Latin:

I. N. J. D. ABRAHAM CALOVII HARMONIA EVANGELICA, AD CONCINNANDUM NOVUM MONOTESSARON.

## 1:1 Introduction: In the Name of Jesus. Prolegomena Concerning Harmonic Writers and Certain Things to Be Obs
In the name of Jesus. Prolegomena concerning harmonic writers and certain things to be observed in a harmony.

Among all divine authorities which are contained in the Holy Scriptures, the Gospel deservedly excels; for what the Law and the Prophets foretold would come to pass, this is demonstrated in the Gospel as having been rendered and completed. With these words, the learned Aurelius Augustine began his most erudite books on the consensus of the Evangelists, calling the Gospel the history of the life of Jesus Christ, described by the holy quadriga of the Evangelists: which is truly a history of histories, whether we consider the dignity of the person whose life is described, or the majesty of the deeds which were performed, or the divinity of the form of writing, or the utility of the salutary fruits which redound from it, or even the authority of the writers themselves. For the Evangelists did not write so much as Christ wrote through them; therefore, St. Augustine, having at length in Book I of the Consensus of the Evangelists refuted the vanity of those who thought that the disciples of Christ who were writing the Gospel were to be despised because no writings of His own were brought forth by the faithful, concluded thus from the truth: Therefore, since they wrote what He showed and said, it is by no means to be said that He did not write it; since His members performed that which they learned by the dictation of the Head. For whatever He did not wish to be read concerning His own deeds and words, this He commanded them to write as if by His own hands.

I. Concerning harmonic writers.

However, since no light difficulties occur in the Evangelical history, as the four amanuenses of Christ vary quite frequently, as is apparent, great men have devoted no ordinary effort to arranging the same in order and to demonstrating or defending the harmony of the deeds and writings.

But I would easily agree with B. Chemnitius, who praises Theophilus, the seventh Bishop of the Church of Antioch after Peter the Apostle, who flourished under Marcus Antoninus Verus around the year of Christ 120 (as Jerome testifies in his Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers) and extended his life until the times of Commodus, as appears from his books to Autolycus (whence he is wrongly confused by William, Archbishop of Tyre, in Book IX of his Sacred History, with the Theophilus to whom St. Luke inscribed the Gospel and the Acts of the Apostles), as having first applied his hand to this most holy labor, and who counts him among those who wrote one out of four, if such a thing were established by better authority. But neither St. Jerome in his Catalogue of Writers, nor anyone else, mentions such a writing of St. Theophilus: but what is referred to in the letter of Jerome to Algasia, Question VI, Vol. III of his Works, page 163, that Theophilus, compiling the sayings of the four Evangelists into one work, left behind monuments of his genius, it is manifest from the fact that it does not pertain to a certain Monotessaron, but to the books of Commentaries or allegories on the four holy Gospels, which are found in the Library of the Ancient Fathers by Margarin de la Bigne, a Doctor of the Sorbonne, in the third Cologne edition of the year 1619, Vol. II, page 145 et seqq., because all the things which Jerome brings forward at length in the cited place concerning the unjust steward in Luke XVI are read in the third book of those Commentaries in the same words, in which indeed Theophilus devoted his effort not to an Evangelical Harmony, but to the parabolic explanation of certain sayings in the writings of the Evangelists.

Tatian, however, of an age similar to Theophilus, a disciple of Justin Martyr, a Christian from being a Platonic philosopher, and while his teacher was alive, of the same faith as him, was once of such estimation that Rhodon came to him in Rome, as he was teaching, from the East, as Eusebius testifies in Book V of his Ecclesiastical History, chapter XII; but afterwards, on account of the presumption of his mastership, he became a follower of heretics and the prince of the new heresy of the Encratites (see Irenaeus, Book I, chapter XXXI; Tertullian, On Prescription, chapter LII).

c. LII. Eusebius, book IV, Ecclesiastical History, ch. XXVII, seems to be the first of those whose memory survives who wove together one work from the four Evangelists: concerning whom Eusebius, in the aforementioned book, says: 'Tatian composed a certain gluing together and reconciliation, I know not how constructed, which he named Diatessaron, which some even now circulate.' And Theodoret, in the aforementioned book, Heretical Fables: 'Tatian also composed a Gospel, which is called Diatessaron, with the genealogies cut off, and other things which show that the Lord was born from David according to the flesh.' And not only those who are of that sect used it, but even those who follow the Apostolic dogmas, not recognizing the fraud of the composition, but using it more simply as a compendious book. Bishop Victor of Capua seemed to have found this work of Tatian, when by chance a similar writing fell into his hands without the author's name, which had the title Diapente, and he conjectures that Tatian, while still adhering to the side of Justin, had adorned it by merit of that learning. But Victor is mistaken in more than one way: for neither was the title of Tatian's work Diapente, nor was it called a Harmony of the Gospels, which inscription Victor made for it, but Diatessaron, as Eusebius, Theodoret, Nicephorus, and others declare with one voice: nor was Tatian an Alexandrian by nationality, as Victor's inscription has it, 'The holy Harmony of the four Gospels by Tatian the Alexandrian author'; but he was a Syrian by nation, as is evident from Clement of Alexandria, Stromata III, Epiphanius, heresy XLVI, and Theodoret: nor finally, which is of primary importance, do the characteristics of Tatian's work designated by Eusebius and Theodoret correspond to that book found by chance; for this is not to be held in such low esteem as Tatian's 'gluing together, I know not how constructed' is held by Eusebius: nor are the genealogies of Christ, whether of Matthew or Luke, or those things which pertain to Christ born of David according to the flesh, cut off in it, nor are there the hands of profane emendation, or rather corruption, brought upon that writing, which Victor himself says were brought upon Tatian's work, nor could it be held as a COMPENDIUM of the Evangelists, which Theodoret professes of Tatian's book, to be substituted in their place; because it exhibits the very words of the Evangelists, not merely encompassing their sentiments or arguments: all of which are exposed by the work falsely attributed to Tatian and published by Victor of Capua: just as it is exhibited with Victor's preface in Volume II of the Bibliotheca Patrum, page 183 et seqq. And how does that Victor of Capua not contradict himself, when he notes (however undeservedly) profane hands in his putative Tatian, and yet affirms that the work was produced by Tatian while still adhering to the side of Justin, before he defected from the Church? Nevertheless, others have followed Victor in asserting that writing to be Tatian's, such as Sixtus of Siena, book IV, Bibliotheca Sancta, under Tatian, and Georgius Ederus, book III, Oeconomia Bibliorum, and others; but the genuine work of Tatian is exhibited in Volume III of the Bibliotheca Patrum, page 22, from the translation of Ottomar Luscinius under the title 'Narrative of the four Gospels,' even though it falsely bears the author Ammonius of Alexandria, whose Harmony it was rashly thought to be, when it is easily evident that it is not the work of Ammonius of Alexandria, but of Tatian the Syrian; since all those things which Eusebius and Theodoret reported about Tatian's Diatessaron correspond to it exactly, as after Baronius at the year of Christ 174, Bellarmine in his Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers, and Possevinus in his Apparatus under the word Ammonius (although the latter contradicts himself when he says that Ottomar Luscinius translated the writing of Ammonius), it is noted in the praised edition of the Bibliotheca Patrum that Victor of Capua wrongly confused the Harmony of Ammonius and the Diatessaron of Tatian. Now, the work of Tatian begins with the prologue of John, and in a continuous series through succinct sentences from the Evangelists according to the order of events, it first assembles what they handed down concerning Christ up to the Baptism and temptation of Christ, and the proclamation in the borders of Zebulun and Naphtali, with both the genealogy of Christ of Matthew and of Luke cut off; then indeed it elegantly pursues the events in order through the three years of the Lord's preaching.

It has this beginning: 'In the beginning was the Word, through whom all things were created, in the end of time made flesh' (John 1). And this in a new manner of birth from the Virgin Mary given in marriage to a certain Joseph (Matthew 1). But pregnant by the message of Gabriel, the heavenly paranymph (Luke 1). Which matter drew her husband Joseph, ignorant of the mystery, into admiration, so that had he not been taught by a divine oracle, he would undoubtedly have fulfilled his plan of leaving the Virgin, just as he had conceived in his mind, etc. Concerning this work, B. Chemnitz, Harmony of the Gospels, prolegomena, ch. 3, has these things: 'Because we have previously shown clearly that that fragment which Luscinius published under the name of Ammonius is not his, I would not, however, wish to contend, just as I cannot affirm nor dare I, that these are Theophilus's. Yet because there is no doubt that it is of an ancient writer, and some use of it can be made for the purpose of our undertaking, let us indeed call it the Harmony of Theophilus.' However, a certain peculiar method is preserved in that Harmony; for the order of the histories is connected in a certain series of its own, but the histories themselves are not described in their entirety, but only their chapters or arguments are briefly recited, and the places where they exist in the Evangelists are noted. The great man rightly observed that that Harmony is not Ammonius's; but that it is not the same as that of Theophilus of Antioch or some other, but is Tatian's, has now been brought to light: but what B. Chemnitz ascribes to Tatian as a work is not Tatian's, but Ammonius's.

For AMMONIUS the Alexandrian, the teacher of Origen, half a century later, around the year of Christ 226, in the time of the Emperor Alexander—whom Sixtus of Siena in his Bibliotheca, along with Suidas and Volaterranus in book XIII of his Anthropologia, ridiculously claims to have had an ass, the most stupid of all animals, as a listener to his teaching—among many monuments of his genius and illustrious works, as Jerome records in his Catalogus, devised the Evangelical Canons, which Eusebius of Caesarea later followed. That others call these Canons an Evangelical Harmony, Bellarmine notes in his Ecclesiastical Writers, under the title Ammonius. But the thing itself teaches that the Evangelical Harmony of Ammonius the Alexandrian is one work, and the Evangelical Canons are another. Zacharias Chrysopolitanus, Bishop, illustrated the Harmony with commentaries five hundred years ago, which he adapted from the opinions of the Fathers woven into a single chain, and Victor of Capua, Bishop, published the same around the year of our Lord 450, woven from the words of the Evangelists alone. Although, as I have said, he falsely took it for the work of Tatian, which is itself presented in Volume II of the Bibliotheca Patrum, p. 184, and begins from the preface of Luke ch. I, 1-5, to which is joined the beginning of John ch. I, 1-5, and furthermore what Luke has in ch. I: Then the Genealogy of Matthew (to which certain things from the Genealogy of Luke are inserted) and the rest of Chapter I of Matthew, and then the nativity, and circumcision, and presentation in the temple from Luke ch. II, the history of the Magi is from Matthew II, with the consequences from the same chapter, etc. Regarding this, we append the ἐπίκρισιν [critique] of our blessed Chemnitz, even though he, the late lamented, following Victor of Capua, attributed that Harmony published among the Orthodoxographa at Basel to Tatian, along with the reasoning observed in it: He says, he attributes individual chapters to individual histories and sermons (as we commonly speak now) and thus divides the whole context into 181 chapters. But where the same history is described by other Evangelists as well, or with varied circumstances, he indeed retains the context of Matthew in most places, but adds and inserts into it, in their proper place, the principal circumstances noted also by others. For he is not anxious to count up the words of individuals or minor circumstances in the series or order of the histories; he did not bind his Harmony precisely to the context of any one Evangelist: but those things which were set forth in a discrete narrative by the four Evangelists, he reduced into the order in which he himself judged they ought to follow one another. He does not explain the reason for the order which he followed in placing and arranging individual histories in a certain place. And his order in most histories became the more disturbed because he concludes all the acts of the public ministry of Christ within the curriculum of one year, and twists those distinct feasts of the Passover in John II and VI to that single one which is described in Matthew XXVI. Many not useless admonitions about the order of the histories can, however, be taken from that Harmony of Tatian (it should have been said, of Ammonius). And thus, with blessed Chemnitz not denying it, it agrees with this harmony, which blessed Chemnitz later noted regarding the method observed by Ammonius of Alexandria, from Eusebius in his Epistle to Carpianus: namely, that Ammonius proposed to himself the context or order of Matthew, and from the remaining Evangelists, where either the same or similar things are described, he excerpted those things and, as it were, heaped them together and annexed them to the context of Matthew. These things, therefore, regarding the Harmony of Ammonius. But that his Evangelical Canons were far different can be established even from Jerome: who, in his preface to the four Gospels to Damasus, testifies that he expressed the Canons, which Eusebius, following AMMONIUS, arranged into ten numbers, just as they are held in the Greek; which tables of his are exposed to the eyes of readers in Volume IX of the works of Jerome; at the beginning; what sort of thing, or if you look at those ten Canons of Eusebius or the Tables of Jerome, nothing appears in the Harmony of Ammonius comprised in 181 chapters, as it is exhibited in the Bibliotheca Patrum: nor indeed did Victor of Capua find those numbers in the book into which he happened to fall; and therefore he himself attempted to add them to it; This Gospel, therefore, says Victor in his preface, when I had found it without the numbers which Ammonius found with wonderful study, and Eusebius, Bishop of Caesarea in Palestine, receiving them from him, diligently cultivated, by which things commonly said by the Evangelists are declared by their own little marks, with the Lord helping, I devoted the effort of my labor so that I might diligently affix the mentioned numbers in their appropriate places.

These, therefore, are the things which Eusebius, by arranging the Evangelical Canons of Ammonius into ten numbers, which Jerome, by interpreting the Canons of Eusebius, which Victor of Capua, by affixing the same to the Ammonian Harmony, contributed to this goal. But that the use of these numbers is not great now, blessed Chemnitz rightly warned, since the chapters of the Evangelists were then distinguished far differently than today in our editions; Whence nothing remains from antiquity that is relevant, except that Diatessaron of Tatian and the already mentioned Harmony of Ammonius: For as for Trithemius, in Possevinus under the entry for Tatian, attributing the Diatessaron to Victor of Capua, he was entirely mistaken in that, since that Victor only published the writing of Ammonius and added numbers to it, but did not adorn a peculiar Harmonic work.

However, St. Augustine also contributes to this from better antiquity, who flourished around the year of the Lord 420, as witnessed by Epistle XXI, which is to Hesychius, and left four illustrious books on the CONSENSUS of the Evangelists, in the first of which only general matters are held, but in the remaining three the histories are examined specifically and in order, and reconciliations of the Evangelists are instituted.

In later ages, however, there flourished especially Marianus of Fulda, a Scot by nationality, who in the year 1086 composed one book on the concordance of the Gospels. Petrus Comestor, author of the Historia Scholastica, around the year 1150, who adorned both the history of the whole Old Testament and also a Harmony of the Evangelical history: Thomas Aquinas wrote a continuous work on the four Gospels around the year 1270. Cardinal Bonaventura, who at almost the same time wrote a Meditation on the Life of our Lord JESUS CHRIST, in which he reduced the four Gospels into one history. Guido Perpinianus, a Spaniard and Bishop of Majorca, wrote on the Concordance of the Evangelists in the year 1320 in imitation of Augustine. Petrus Izuzquius from Navarre in Spain, of the Order of Preachers, compiled a series of the Holy Gospel of JESUS CHRIST from the four Gospels. Rupertus Goulletus, a Parisian Doctor, wrote a Tetramonon Evangelicum. Simon Cassianus arranged the four Gospels according to the deeds of the Savior in the year 1350. Around the same time: Ludolphus Saxo, a Carthusian in the Monastery of Strasbourg, collected one history of the life of Christ from the four Evangelists, praised no less by our blessed Chemnitz than by Sixtus Senensis. Johannes Ganuet, a Reader of the Carmelite Order, of Mainz, wrote on the concordance of the Evangelists in the year 1440. Dominicus Nanus Mirabellius, Doctor of Arts, in the year 1470 collected a Monotessaron, comparing the sayings of philosophers, and even of Mahomet, with the Evangelical sentences, as witnessed by Sixtus Senensis. Johannes Gerson, the most learned Chancellor of the University of Paris, adorned a μονοτέσσαρον [monotessaron] on the concordance of the Evangelists, continuing the order of Evangelical history begun by St. Augustine, having finished his life in the year 1419. Diego Deza, Archbishop of Seville, in the year 1500. He left a Monotessaron illustrated with commentaries; in it, preserved by Simon Corroyus, of the Cœlestine order, according to the same Sienese, in the same year 1500. He composed a Monotessaron on the Gospels, which he called an Evangelical Pandect. Antonius Brucchius of Königstein collected a brief Monotessaron of the Gospels in the year of our Lord 1541. Alanus Copius at Louvain in the year 1572. Paulus de Palacio in the year 1605. Severinus Lubomiltius, at Cracow in the year 1606. Gorwaldus Meschius &c. Andreas Osiander, who, with B. Chemnitius as herald, with the greatest effort and singular sharpness of wit by a completely new method, compiled a Harmony of the Evangelical History, in such a way that he is not compelled to move or transpose any history, except for two of Matthew's, concerning the plucked ears of grain and the healing of the withered hand, out of the context in which they are described in the individual Evangelists, who died in the year 1552 at Königsberg in Prussia. Whom, as was observed by the blessed Chemnitz, Molineus and Codomannus mostly followed, who indeed do not even wish for those two histories of Matthew XII, concerning the ears of grain and the withered hand, to be transposed, but maintain that they are different from those which are described by Mark and Luke.

To these must further be added from the Papists: Cornelius Jansenius, Bishop of Ghent, in his Evangelical Concordance; Sebastian Barradius, a Portuguese Jesuit, who expounded the History and Evangelical Concordance in a thick volume of four tomes, but with less judgment and ἀκρισίᾳ (lack of judgment); likewise Bartholomeus Riccius in the Life of our Lord Jesus Christ from the words of the Gospels, published at Cologne in the year 1610; and a certain Beaulxamis, praised by Antonio Possevino in his Apparatus under Ammonius; from the Reformed: Johannes Calvin, in his Evangelical Harmony composed from three Evangelists, published at Geneva in the year 1595; the Disposition and Pericope of the Evangelical History compiled by the four Evangelists, reduced to the form of a handbook from the Commentaries of Heinrich Bullinger; Gerhard Mercator in his Harmony, Wisburg of Cleves, in the year 1592; Theobald Meuschius in his Evangelical Harmony in the year 1604. Andreas Selmatterus in his New Symphony of the Evangelists, published at Basel in the year 1613. C. also mentions Daniel Tossanus in a letter given to Theobald Meuschius on November 23, 1549, regarding a Harmony which he says he is compiling, in which he counts no more than three Passovers in the course of Christ's ministry, whereas Mercator and Meuschius assign five. The same Tossanus mentions in the same place other authors of Harmonies: besides others, he says, a certain Codomannus wrote a German Harmony in quarto, which, however, I have not seen. This year, the Harmony of Johannes Rubus of Douai, a theologian, was reprinted, somewhat revised. A certain Harmony also appeared at Licha in the year 1605 by Bernhard Copius. Gerhard Johannes Vossius at Amsterdam in the year 1656. published three books of an Evangelical Harmony concerning the passion, death, resurrection, and ascension of Christ, in the preface of which he declares that he has dealt separately with the prophetic office of Christ, and has attributed to it both the preaching of the Gospel and its confirmation through miracles. From our own, D. Paulus Crellius, in the previous century in the year '66, professes that his Harmony was built upon the outline of the Harmony of the Evangelical History publicly proposed here by the blessed Pomeranus, which, prevented by death, he had left barely begun, which he adorned in both the Latin and German languages. However, the Harmony of the passion, death, and resurrection of Christ, received in these churches, was completed by the blessed Bugenhagen. The blessed D. Micrælius in his Syntagma Hist. Eccles. praises the Harmony of the Gospels of Erasmus Albertus, page 458 of book III, but which I have not happened to see. Georgius Wirth, Doctor of Philosophy and Medicine among the Leipzigers, described the life, or the Gospels of Jesus Christ from the four Evangelists, which work appeared at Frankfurt am Main in the year 1594. D. Eilhardus Lubinus, Professor of Theology at Rostock, also published a Harmony, to which he gave the title Quadripartita Evangelica Historia, at Monas in the year 1616; as well as M. Rupertus Erythropilus, Pastor of Hanover, who published in the German language a Historical Harmony of the four Evangelists, comprising the ministry

- & Vitam Christi. Published at Magdeburg in the year 1609. - The Harmony of Joh. Avenarius of the year 1583 is also commended. - That of Henr. Bünting 1592. Bartholomäus Radmann - Frankfurt an der Oder in the year 1600. Nicolaus Selneccer - Leipzig in the year 1604. Baazius of Linköping, etc. But the Evangelical Harmony of the blessed Joh. Cluver, most recently published and composed with vigor and solidity, easily carries off the palm from all of these. The blessed Christoph Althofer also adorned an Evangelical Harmony, which appeared in recent years. The Calix-tine Concord, on account of various errors impinging upon both the Harmony and History, as well as the dogmas of the faith, hardly comes into consideration. But the incomparable theologian Mr. Dr. Mart. has left the effort and diligence of all these predecessors in this study far behind him by a long interval. Chemnitz, whom, as in his other writings he surpassed others, so in his Harmony he surpassed himself, is not undeservedly judged by the learned to be our Great GERHARD, the parent, the blessed one, who judges from the truth. To whom, however, since he was prevented by death from putting the final hand to that golden work, he acknowledges that the equally most excellent theologian Dn. D. Polycarpus Lyserus the Elder, a man who has most excellently deserved of the Saxon churches, especially the Electoral ones, succeeded by divine providence in faithfully completing the Harmonic work, and he professes that great thanks are owed to the most Benign God for this, he who most happily put a conclusion to this most salutary labor, our never-sufficiently-praised blessed GERHARD: concerning which most excellent CHEMNITIO-LYSERO-GERHARDINE work of Evangelical Harmony, we wish the judgment passed in the name of the Theological College of this Academy in the year 1651, and prefixed to the new edition, and inserted into the Theological Counsels of Wittenberg, part I, Title I, no. IV, to be repeated here in its entirety, and thus we seriously commend that work again and again to all cultivators of the word of God, candidates of the Holy Theology and the Ministry, as an Evangelical Treasure, more precious than gold and gems.

II. ON THE METHOD OF OUR HARMONY.

But as no most praised authors wished their most holy works to be subject to an unanswerable law, from which they might never depart regarding the order they observe and the arrangement they institute throughout; or placed a barrier to the more accurate meditation and scrutiny of the sacred Harmony, so when in the defenses of the Evangelists against Hug. I was occupied with Grotius, with whom Vossius not rarely disturbs the Harmony to a wonderful degree, and tears apart the Evangelical μονοτέσσαρον; I judged that a simpler path should be observed, that a completely peculiar effort must still be applied to the Harmony, and that it could be most expeditiously elicited from the writers of the Lord's life alone, if they are compared more accurately among themselves, provided we bid farewell to preconceived opinions in some matters; which, by the grace of God, I now believe I have elicited, so far from doubting it, that I do not fear in the least to exhibit to the public judgment of the Church a distinguished HARMONY, most clear from the Evangelists alone, to be completed most easily by the mere joining together of the words of the divine amanuenses. In which I now at last discover that the hypothesis attributed a little before to Andreas Osiander, Molinaeus, and Codomannus in the words of the blessed Chemnitz, is common to me with them insofar as I had either read or observed that it had been their own, before I now, by the grace of God, had expedited the συνάφειαν συναγωγὴν, & εἱρμὸν τ᾽ ἀκολουθίας from the Evangelists alone, which I repeat again, namely, that no history outside the context in which it was recorded by the Evangelists is to be moved from its place and transposed. Although I cannot yet say whether they entered upon the same method in order and Harmony, or with what dexterity they arranged the Gospels, since I have not even been able to see, let alone compare, their μονοτέσσαρα or τετράμο- να: Except that while I write these things, there are offered to me the four books of the Evangelical Harmony of Andr. Osiander, in Greek and Latin, which perhaps, if time permits, I shall subsequently compare, to be subjoined somewhere in the commentaries. He distributes the Harmony into four books; the first of which is from the conception of John the Baptist until the ordination of the twelve Apostles: the second from the ordination of the Apostles until the migration from Galilee into Judea: the third, from the migration into Judea until the last sermon of Christ held in the temple: the fourth, from the last sermon until the passion, resurrection, ascension, and the sending of the Holy Spirit, until the beginning of the Gospel preached everywhere by the Apostles, [and] the just and genuine order of things

embraces the order of things done by Christ. Thus Osiander. Furthermore, I have relied in this my arrangement and Harmony, after the natural series of the Evangelists, which it is necessary to observe entirely, primarily upon those two eyes of HISTORY; namely, CHRONOLOGY and TOPOGRAPHY; and thus I have deemed that the account of the circumstances of time and place must be held in the highest regard. Where, therefore, I have noticed a diversity of time and place, even if certain circumstances are found to be similar among other Evangelists, I have been entirely compelled, since others establish the same history with an inversion of the Evangelical writings and of the circumstances which bind [the event] to this place and this time, to posit them as diverse histories; which, even if done more rarely, has brought significant light to the harmony and has established everything in a clear and plain state. However, there was a religious concern, since the diversity of place and time openly demanded it, according to the very letter of Holy Scripture, where everything flows in order most conveniently if one insists solely upon the footsteps of the holy men of God, to have [them] as one history, whether the other Evangelists will it or not, and to reconcile them through some forced recapitulation, which Augustine and Ticonius [call] a 'rememoration,' as Gerson calls it, whatever may have seemed otherwise to one or another of the Fathers. Which is to bring a sense into Scripture, not to bring it out of Scripture. For there is certainly no doubt, says the blessed Chemnitius in Prolegom. c. V., that the same sermons were often repeated by Christ, and various miracles which were similar were often performed by Him. Which is a GOLDEN rule or observation that must be properly fixed in our minds. Those things also please me, which the great Chemnitius excellently subjoins in the same place for the sake of illustration: Since it is also certain that not all things are diverse which have been described by different Evangelists, but that for the most part the same things, with circumstances slightly varied, have been repeated by different writers: therefore, UNLESS A KIND OF NECESSITY DEMANDS IT, of such circumstances as are so CERTAIN & MANIFEST that they seem not so much to persuade as to COMPEL [one] to a diversity, those things which the matter itself testifies are the same, must not be made diverse. For otherwise the comparison of circumstances, which exist in the description of the same histories among different Evangelists, which is the light of Evangelical History, perishes. But when MANIFEST circumstances show DIVERSITY, the APPEARANCE OF SIMILARITY ought not to cause CONFUSION OF ORDER AND HISTORIES. And what are more MANIFEST circumstances of DIVERSITY than TIME and PLACE? what [things] compel more, and impose a necessity to constitute diverse histories, even if some other circumstances present an apparent similarity? Whence the blessed Chemnitius prescribed this Rule, which is highly necessary to be observed, and never to be rashly violated, in Prolegom. c. V. §. 16: When, however, the PLACES, TIMES, PERSONS, OCCASIONS, & ENDS are diverse, then because of the SIMILARITY, those things which were repeated at DIFFERENT TIMES are not to be confounded, but distinguished. He illustrates this from Luke: In this way, a judgment is correctly formed concerning MANY Histories, which are described from the ninth chapter of Luke to the eighteenth, and have a great similarity with the preceding ones. An illustrious example is in the Leper in Mark c. I. 40. seqq. the healing described in Luke V. 12, and that which Matthew c. VIII. 1. seqq. exhibits: concerning which indeed the blessed Lyserus speaks hesitantly in Harm. c. LII.: that it is either an anticipation or a different history: But the blessed Chemnitius, without hesitation, for the sake of avoiding the convulsion of the order of histories, and for the sake of the account of time and place, confesses himself compelled to place those histories, although SIMILAR, yet distinct in the Harmony: so that the leper of Mark (and Luke) is one, and that of Matthew is another, although the doctrine of both is the same. Such things have been observed by the blessed Chemnitius, as also by the blessed Lyserus, and I add, by the blessed Gerhard.

The evident diversity of circumstances, especially of time and place, which compelled him to make such histories—however similar they may be in appearance in most words or deeds—different, compels me also to consider other histories, similar in many respects but entirely discrepant in individualizing conditions and circumstances, as different regarding the here and now and other περιστάσεις: where from that more accurate observation of circumstances a great light is added to the whole historical account, and to the order and sequence of the Evangelists, and no less to the Evangelical Harmony: which things, being preferable to preconceived opinions about the same histories recounted by recapitulation or ὕσερον πρότερον or πρωθύσερον, what sensible and pious reader will doubt? Such causes do not merely persuade, but compel me to assert that Peter's mother-in-law was freed from fever by Christ not once, but twice, as the diversity of time demands, once in Mark I. 29 and Luke IV. 38, and again the following year after the sermon on the mount in Matth. VIII; and that those whom the Lord healed having a withered hand were different, one in Mark III. 1 and Luke VI. 6 ff., the other in Matth. XII. 15; likewise that I should establish the paralytic, whom Mark II. 3 ff. and Luke V. 18 ff. narrate as being let down through the roof, as different from the paralytic of Matthew ch. IX. 1 ff., and a few other things of this kind, in which, because of evident necessity, it was necessary to depart from the Chemnitz-Lyser Harmony. For that Christ performed similar miracles more often AT A DIFFERENT TIME AND IN VERY DIFFERENT PLACES, there is no doubt, he himself says

& Lyserus, Harmony, ch. 52. And here the modesty of the blessed Chemnitz is to be praised, concerning the history of the Paralytic, Harmony, ch. 43, which he thought was handed down by Matthew, Mark, and Luke alike: Because the demonstrations are not entirely evident and necessary, but are only PROBABLE narrations, or CONJECTURES, I wished to propose them to the Reader not with the NECESSITY OF FOLLOWING, but with the LIBERTY of judging. Since, therefore, I have clearly found from the circumstances that the Paralytics are different, with all respect to the blessed Man, I here depart from his opinion. Such causes will also be placed παρ' ὅραμα (beside the vision/view) in our Harmony: whence all things will turn out clear and perspicuous in the Evangelical concord, which otherwise must remain intricate and by no means clear. This can be illustrated by the example of the two blind men, and the mute demoniac, alongside different Evangelists, on the occasion of which St. Augustine, book II, on the consensus of the Evangelists, ch. 29, handed down those same observations, and warned that they should be diligently noted: This concerning the two blind men, and the mute demoniac, Matthew alone (ch.

9) places. For those two blind men, about whom others also narrate, are not these, but nevertheless it is a similar event: so that if Matthew himself had not also remembered that event, it could be thought that this, which he now narrates, had been said also by the other two. Which we ought to diligently commend to memory, that there are certain similar events: which is proven when the same Evangelist himself commemorates both: so that if at any time we find such individual things in individual [authors], and in them a contradiction occurs to us which cannot be solved, [we should conclude] that this is not the same event, but another similar one, or one done similarly. Which St. Augustine again inculcates at the end of chapter 30. I warn again and again that it is necessary for the reader to remember, lest he need such an admonition very often, that the Lord repeated many things in different places of his sermons which he had already said elsewhere: lest perhaps the order of the places themselves, when it does not agree with one of them from another Evangelist, one might think from this that there is a contradiction: when he ought to understand that what had already been said elsewhere is being said again elsewhere: and that this ought to be observed not only concerning words, but also concerning deeds. For nothing prevents one from believing that this same thing was done again. But to slander the Gospel, while one does not believe that what no one proves could not have been done again was done again, is of sacrilegious vanity. Thus, from this observation, Augustine admits that the reproaches described in Matt. 11 & Luke 10 are different, even if they are similar, which the reason of time also compels: For although he brings here his own distinction between the order of the Evangelist's recollection and the order of the things themselves, he nevertheless inclines more to the fact that the reproaches are different, ch. 32, thus differing: Matthew follows, and says: Then he began to reproach the cities, in which his many mighty works were done, because they had not repented, etc., up to that point where he says: It will be more tolerable for the land of Sodom in the day of judgment than for you. Luke also commemorates this, joining these things also from his own mouth to a certain continued sermon of the Lord: whence it seems more that he himself commemorates those things in the order in which they were said by the Lord. Matthew, however, [is thought] to have kept the order of his own recollection: or if that which the same Matthew says, 'Then he began to reproach the cities,' is thought to be accepted in such a way that it is believed he wished to express the very point of time in that which was said, 'Then,' but not the time itself somewhat more broadly, in which these many things were done and said: whoever believes this, let him also believe that this was said twice. For since even in one Evangelist are found certain things which the Lord said twice: just as also in the same Luke concerning not taking a wallet on the way, and other similar things, it is found that it was said by the Lord in two places: what wonder if also something else is said twice, individually by individuals, in the same order in which it was said? And therefore a different order appears in individuals, because it was said both when that one, and when this one, commemorates it. Which very thing the blessed Polycarp Lyserus also observed concerning the reproach of Christ, Harmony, chapter 56, pericope 3. This part of the History, however, which deals with the rebuke of certain cities, is controversial as to in what place and order it is to be placed. For Luke, ch. 10, verse 13, noted that it was done then, when the seventy disciples were sent away to preach. And when they had returned, Luke adds an express notation of time: that at the same hour Christ said: I confess to thee Father, etc., so that it can seem that this present pericope of the eleventh chapter of Matthew, up to the end, is placed out of order by Anticipation, and is to be referred to that. And many follow that reason. But this pericope, as to the text and as to the sense, coheres so aptly and conveniently with the preceding and with the following [passages], that it seems it cannot be removed from there and transferred elsewhere without injury and obscuration of the sense and doctrine. For the sweetest exclamation of Christ provides the occasion: Come to me all, etc. & it paves a most beautiful way for the history of the sinful woman, Luke 7. Thus, with the Lord's help, we shall show later. I therefore approve the opinion of Augustine, who thinks that that same sermon of Christ was held twice: once as Matthew describes it: but afterwards at another time and on another occasion it was repeated, just as Luke describes it in chapter 10, verse 13. For sometimes the same Evangelist narrates that the same thing was said or done by Christ twice or several times. A clear example also occurs in Matt. 12:22 and Luke 11:14, where the blessed Lyserus has it thus in Harmony, chapter 59, in the reasoning of the order: But it seems to cast a scruple that Luke describes a similar miracle and contention, not in this order, but in the last journey of Christ, chapter 11, verse 14, and yet he relates all things in such a way that they seem to be entirely the same, and done only once in one place and time. But there will be nothing absurd if we understand the history which Luke describes in the stated place not to be the same as this one which exists in Matt. XII. verse 22 and Mark III. verse 22, but to have happened in the final journey of Christ. For in the following it will be manifestly discovered that all those things which Luke describes from chapter IX. verse 51 were done in the third year of Christ's ministry, although both the sermons and the miracles for the most part so agree with those which happened in the previous years, and are described in the same words, that they seem to be entirely the same. But who will doubt that the same things happened more often? Since even this very history agrees in many respects with that miracle which Matthew noted in chapter IX. verse 32, where he also testifies that Christ cast out a mute demon. And that from there followed the calumny of the Pharisees, that he casts out demons through the Prince of demons. Since, therefore, we read in one and the same Evangelist that the same miracle was done twice, and that in both places the same calumny arose from it: why should we not posit that words and deeds, even if similar, occurred at two different times, which by two

will be distributed to the Evangelists? Would that these very necessary warnings had always been observed by St. Augustine, as also by the blessed Lyser in his Harmony, since the consideration of time and place required the same; without doubt, a greater light would have shone in arranging and eliciting the Harmony. For one cannot place faith in the common Concordances appended to the Codices, as far as the method of order is concerned, which often only serve to show the consonance of the sentences: which is also detected in this apology of Christ proposed by Mark, chap. III, verses 22-30. For although the Concordances compare it with Matt. XII. 24, and even the blessed Lyser refers it to the same time, the order of the events teaches that it cannot be referred to the same time: since that apology follows the healing of the blind man who was also mute in Matthew, whereas that in Mark occurred already before the sending out of the Apostles, as it happened only in Mark VI. 2. But these and other things of this kind, in which there is an equal reason and an equal necessity, will be most clearly evident from our Harmony. One thing must still be warned in advance, that we have judged that the guide of the order should be chosen not so much as St. Mark, but Luke, so that those things which would otherwise be quite difficult and perplexed may be rendered easier. For I would not rashly say that it was proposed to Mark to reduce the Gospel of Matthew into order, as has seemed to some, since the Gospel of Matthew is sufficiently ordered, provided the series of events and times is correctly observed. But all these things will be placed in a clear light through the very investigation and connection of our Harmony. How I have clearly explained this privately, aided by divine tradition, while it sufficiently asserts itself, it would not be irrelevant, if by certain notes, especially Harmonic ones, or those concerning the sequence of the order, the reader is not rendered doubtful by the diverse opinions of others, which often render all the most certain things uncertain and involve them in the most brilliant obscurity, so that our monologue may be fortified and confirmed. It will, however, be worth the effort to discuss a little more laboriously in advance about the guide of the order, so that our mind and the foundation of our opinion may be more certainly established.

the symphony of the Evangelists, as he called it in his Isagoge to the symphony, published in the year 1613 at Basel with the approval of the Theological Order of Basel, they assert that either MATTHEW neglected the order and used the greatest liberty, but they are persuaded that Mark did this, to introduce order into his Evangelical History. Which neither befits the Holy Spirit, whose amanuenses, if not pens, the holy Evangelists were, as the author not of confusion but of order, nor are they worthy of the Canonical Writers, as if they had recorded without order a History which demands order entirely; and how piously or prudently this is imputed to the Holy Spirit, that through Matthew he first pushed out the Evangelical History as if confusedly, and then through Mark, his epitomizer, he did this, that some order might be procured for the undigested narrative of Matthew, we leave to be judged. Nor will that description of Selmætter be able to please the wise, which he indeed shares with Daniel Tossanus (in a letter to Theobald Meuschius given on January 4, 1598): that it was not proposed to the Evangelists (if you perhaps except John to some extent) to write the annals of Christ, much less his diaries, but to record certain things from that infinite number of divine sayings and deeds, as they HAPPENED, sufficiently for forming faith and life, while meanwhile all were hastening to the death of the Son of GOD, and from death to the resurrection to immortality, as the first and highest foundations of our salvation. It is certainly no wonder if any Jewish Rabbi, or any Manes, or Marcion, or Celsus, or Porphyry revived in modern atheists (to use the words of Selmætter), should despise such a method of writing if it had been used by the Evangelists, as unworthy either of suitable witnesses or of divinely inspired Writers, whose task it certainly is not to write down whatever HAPPENED, and to neglect order, and to hasten to death in recording the history of a life. Which are also easily refuted as false accusations by the very reading of the holy Evangelists. For the rest, we do not deny that St. MARK is also deservedly observed in the natural order of history, all other things being equal, and without prejudice to St. MATTHEW, whom our blessed POMERANUS followed in the delineation

III. ON THE GUIDE OF THE ORDER AND CERTAIN THINGS TO BE OBSERVED IN THE ORDER.

ST. LUKE, whose praise was great in the Gospel through all the Churches (II Cor. VIII. 18), and who followed everything accurately from above from the beginning, and recorded the Evangelical History in due order, inspired by the divine Spirit (Luke I. 3), is deservedly constituted the Guide of the order, who also alone noted those things which were to be said about the conception, birth, and circumcision of JOHN the Baptist and JESUS CHRIST, along with many other things, just as St. John, the Spirit of God directing, wrote down for the most part the sayings and disputes of Christ alone, when they had been passed over by others. Nor indeed do those deserve to be heard here who, with Andreas Selmætter, a Swiss Reformed minister of the word of God, in the Harmony publicly proposed here, claim that Mark excels in particular histories omitted by John and treated by the three prior Evangelists as regards their order, to whose elaboration his blessed analysis intervened, which indeed D. PAUL CRELLIUS explained, just as he observed St. MATTHEW's Diatessaron in the first place, and recalled the others to the same in most things which are common to others; which he would not have done if he had judged that his History was recorded disorderly and with frequent transposition. But concerning St. LUKE, the blessed Chemnitz did not observe it beside the point in his prolegomena. chap. 2. the same [author] prefaces that he will write this after others for this reason, that he may both begin the Gospel history HIGHER UP, and weave it together in a certain ORDER, just as he notes the order of the Histories in many places through circumstances, so that in most [places] they agree WITH ORDER with Mark, so that on that account it is not inelegantly called by Tertullian a DIGEST of the Gospel History: (however much he may have sometimes placed certain things, whose order is manifest from Matthew and Mark, in a place not their own on the occasion of his narrative, which we readily grant regarding a few certain things:) And that the little word καθεξῆς also implies that B. Chemnitius is not entirely disagreed with in the Prolegomena of C. V., namely because he wishes to add the rest subsequently in a continuous narrative, distinctly and distributed as if by degrees. The Vulgate renders it, in order. Beza notes that it is properly continuously, and adds not inconsiderately: This passage causes us to think that a certain order is kept in writing the harmony of the Evangelists, if those things which the others have in common are accommodated to Luke rather than Luke to the others. And this praise, having observed the same emphasis of this word, was long ago attributed to St. Luke by Ambrose, Bishop of Milan, namely that he wrote καθεξῆς, that is, distinctly and distributed, as those who bring some judgment to the writing of history are accustomed to do. And thus our Erasmus Schmidius also rendered the words of Luke: it seemed good to me also, after I have investigated everything exactly from the very beginning, to write (them) to you in order. That he wishes to begin the history HIGHER UP he had already indicated by the word ἄνωθεν, which is the same as ἀπ' ἀρχῆς in Acts 26:5, and is rashly taken by Gomarus as an adverb of place, and afterwards referred to God, as if it were hinted that Luke received these things from God as if from heavenly places. For it is said that he followed all things accurately from the beginning: not that he was curiously close to all the persons, as the Syriac has it, interpreted by Ludovicus de Dieu, but that he had followed all things with his mind, as the Arabic has it, not otherwise than if he himself had been present at those things being done, as Capellus weighs the emphasis of the word παρηκολουθηκότι. Which Theobaldus Meuschius, Inspector of Atzea, also acknowledges in his Evangelical Harmony, in the prolegomena: namely that Luke wrote for the most part in a natural series, according to the laws of history, and did not use transpositions, except for small and manifest ones, which he proves from his own preface where he says that he wrote everything from the beginning in order: Then, also from the fact that Mark proceeds conformably with him: which could not happen if both or one of them used an arbitrary method. Meuschius also refutes the contrary opinion of others, especially of his own D. Daniel Tossanus, though his name is suppressed; the refutation of which I am pleased to submit. Nor, he says, let it be objected to me that this natural series of Evangelical History can in no way be found, since none of the Evangelists kept it in narrating; but that individuals collected some of the deeds and sayings of Christ without a certain order, as they remembered them (these words are Tossanus's). For I deny that, and on the contrary I affirm that, from a diligent collation of all, the natural series of both the deeds and the sayings of Christ can be gathered most excellently. For the Evangelists wrote by the singular instinct of the Holy Spirit in such a way that where one or another has deflected a little from the natural series, there another weaves the narrative according to the law of history. Indeed (which is to be wondered at) although no one imitated another (I except John, who is said to have seen the others and to have written nothing but what was omitted) but each wrote for himself without another: yet they so succeed one another in narrating that where this one ends, that one begins. Nor is it difficult for one considering it to notice the counsel of the Holy Spirit: for He wished thus to sharpen our diligence in reading and joining together all the Evangelists, and thence to render us more certain of the truth of the whole history and doctrine. Namely, when we see that there is such a consonance between the Evangelists, who nevertheless, when read separately and incidentally, seem to fight entirely among themselves and to have collected only rhapsodies. Wherefore, for my part, there is no doubt that there is not only the highest consensus among the Evangelists concerning the things themselves: but also that individuals observed the law of history in such a way that from the collation of all, the natural series, and thus the consensus itself, can easily be gathered and demonstrated, however much individuals may seem to narrate separately in a perplexed manner. Moreover, I add this: without the collation of all and the investigation of the natural series, neither certainty nor the perfect meaning of individuals can be had, so that I wonder that so few Doctors, both ancient and recent, have labored on the Evangelical Harmony. All these things Meuschius: which we entirely approve. To which, however, how his hypotheses, upon which he relies as foundations, do not sufficiently agree, I for my part do not understand: such as that he says Matthew used an almost ARBITRARY order, especially from Chapter 5 up to 14, because the Evangelist often assumes for one sermon certain things from another and thus joins two different ones, similar however in regard to the subject or related. And that Matthew especially often collects sermons of different times into one place: which certainly agree neither with the natural series of history nor with Historiographical laws.
