III. 26. But that dignity, eminence, excellence, authority, and some right is also designated by that word, Matt. VII. 29, Apoc. XVII. 12, Rom. XIII. 1. He also rightly notes that τὸ γίνεσθαι signifies both to become and to be: which we admit regarding different places: since in one place both meanings cannot be admitted. Thus, therefore, we obtain the dignity that we may be the sons of God when we receive him through faith. The Syrian has the word שולטנא, authority, dignity, eminence, which is proper to those who rule. This, therefore, is implied: that to those who by nature are servants and slaves of sin and Satan, and children of wrath, that dignity is conferred, that they may be the sons of God, that is, not only that they be adopted into the family of God, but that they be adopted as sons of God. Namely, those who believe εἰς τὸ ὄνομα αὐτοῦ, in his name, who place their trust in him: in his name, by which he revealed himself in the Word; and thus through faith they receive and embrace him, just as he offers himself in the Word in respect of his person and office. Which dignity, however, they do not have from blood or carnal generation, even if they are of the most noble lineage, nor from the will of the flesh, i.e., the study and effort of the powers of the flesh or nature, nor from the will of man, or effort and study however excellent, such as that of brave men and heroes: as if to say, by no studies, works, or virtues, whether common or heroic, and merits can this ἐξουσία [authority] be obtained: but that there is need of a birth from God, and a spiritual regeneration, which is effected through the Word and the Sacraments: through which we are both gifted with faith by grace, and through faith are made the sons of God, 1 Pet. I. 23, John III. 5.]

§. IX. Concerning the incarnation of the Word, and his dwelling among men.

Vers. 14. And the Word was made flesh; and dwelt among us; and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father, full of grace and truth.

Now his arrival into the world and to us is explained more clearly; namely, through the ἐνσάρκωσιν [incarnation]. The particle 'And' is not inappropriately taken αἰτιολογικῶς [causally]: because through the incarnation, that ἐξουσία [authority] and we obtain generation from God: and therefore the Son of God was made flesh, that he might make us, who were born flesh from flesh, sons of God: But he was made flesh, not as we are flesh by reason of corruption, because he is like us in all things, yet excepting sin Heb. IV. 15. but because he was made a partaker of our flesh and blood by reason of nature and quiddity. or metonymically, either for carnal concupiscence, as John III. 5. or for human frailty, proper to mortals, as 1. Cor. XV. 50. although neither in that Pauline passage, nor anywhere else is bare frailty or corruptibility denoted by the word flesh abstractly, but the body as it is frail or corruptible: nor therefore is being made flesh to become frail, as the Socinians pervert it, or to be rendered mortal, and to wither like hay, as the Arians once caviled; since frailty or corruptibility and mortality do not fall upon the Word, who is the eternal God, much less was the Word made frailty or corruptibility; but substantially, and that synecdochically, as in the manner of Scripture flesh denotes man, or human nature, to the constituting of which with flesh or body the rational soul contributes: to which it happens and befalls to be frail and corruptible, since it was neither such in the state of integrity, nor will it be such in the state of blessed glorification, without prejudice to the truth of human nature: See Gen. VI. 12. Ps. CXXV. 21. Is. XL. 5. 6. Joel II. 28. Rom. III. 10. how the Son of God is said to be made a partaker of flesh and blood, just as his faithful children are partakers of the same, Heb. II. 14. to have assumed the seed of Abraham, v. 16. born of the seed of David according to the flesh, i.e., human nature Rom. I. 3. and from the Fathers c. IX. 5. And therefore the Catholic Church with the highest consensus has rendered the meaning of this aphorism in this way: That the eternal Word who is God, and the only-begotten Son of God the Father, was made man; not indeed by a mutation of Deity into humanity, nor by a conversion of the Word into flesh destitute of a soul, but by a union of the divine and human nature, or an assumption of human nature into the divine, as Athanasius says of the incarnation, the assumption of humanity into divinity. Gregor. Neocaesar. Orat. in Epiphan. You are God and man, you who were in the beginning, and who were made flesh, but not converted into flesh. Cyrill. Alex. in h. l. Finally, he openly enters into the discourse of the incarnation with these words. For he clearly teaches and plainly explains that the Son of man was made and called the only-begotten; for that is what that signifies, where he says, the Word was made flesh. For it is the same as if he said, the Word was made man. When he says this, he introduces nothing unusual or strange to us, since divine Scripture very often signifies the whole animal by the word flesh alone, according to that which is written in Joel: I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh. When I read, the Word was made flesh, in the Word, says St. Augustine, l. XIII. de Trin. c. 19, I understand the true Son of God, in the flesh I recognize the true son of man, and both together joined in one person by the ineffable grace and bounty of God. Greg. M. l. IX. Ep. 61. The Word, he says, we say was made flesh, not by changing what he was, but by assuming what he was not. Chrysost. homil. X. in Joh. For by the union and the conjunction, the Word of God and the flesh are one, not by a confusion occurring, nor by the disappearance of the substances, but by a certain ineffable and unspeakable union. But do not seek how, for it was made as he himself knows in an ineffable manner. Leo M. Serm. III. de pass. Dom. c. 1. This the Catholic faith hands down, that we should know that two natures have come together in our Redeemer, and with their properties remaining, such a unity of both substances was made, that from that time, when as the cause of the human race demanded, the Word was made flesh in the womb of the blessed Virgin, it is not permitted to think of that God without that which is man, nor of that man without that which is God. Eligius (circa An. 640) hom. I. That Word, which was in the beginning, and was with God, and the Word was God, through whom all things were made, and without whom nothing was made, in the end of the ages was made flesh, and dwelt among us, that he might become the Mediator of God and men, the man Jesus Christ, true God and true man in the unity of person. Conf. Ambros. l. de Dom. incarn. sacr. c. 6. Hilarius l. XI. de Trinit. Fulgentius lib. I. ad Thrasim. Reg. c. 18. Atticus Constantinopol. in Act. Conc. Ephes. T. II. c. 28. etc.

But the Evangelist preferred to use the word flesh rather than man, both because God's love toward us is more declared by the mention of flesh, and because for our sake he even lowered himself to the worse part, as Nazianzen has it, Epist. I. ad Cledon. and because according to Cyril, l. I. in Joh. c. 25, he wished to signify the reparation of the whole from the part most corrupted, but vivified by the union of the Word; so that the wound and the remedy, the sick and the physician, that which has fallen into death and he who raised it to life, that which yielded to corruption and he who removes corruption, that which was overcome by death and he who is superior to death, that which was bereft of life and he who bestows life, might be seen at once.

St. John continues, and he dwelt among us: which is understood either of the habitation in the flesh, or our nature, so that it is explained by that dwelling as incarnation, because the Word filled the tabernacle of the body, or humanity, with his Deity, Col. II. 9. just as formerly the majesty of God filled the Mosaic tabernacle, Ex. XL. 34. and the Solomonic temple 1. Kings VIII. 10. to which the interpretation of Cyril, Chrysostom, and Theophylact goes, that the Word dwelt personally in the assumed flesh, just as the soul is said to dwell in its own proper body as in a tabernacle, 2. Cor. V. 1. 2. Pet. I. 13. or of the habitation of conversation among men, and particularly among his own, i.e., the Jews, just as the Son of God promised Zech. II. 10. Behold I come, and I will dwell in the midst of thee; which sense we prefer as the simpler one with the blessed Chemnitz: because St. John wished to embrace the sum of the things said, inasmuch as they are completed by the incarnation of the Word, the conversation among men, and the manifestation of glory. By the word ἐσκήνωσε, i.e., he dwelt in a tabernacle, it is thus insinuated both that he was as it were a pilgrim on earth, just as pilgrims of old, such as the Patriarchs and others, dwelt in tabernacles; and that he came to wage war against our enemies, just as soldiers are accustomed to dwell in tabernacles, and he fixed his tent against the infernal power, that having won the victory he might ascend triumphing into heaven, leaving the world as a military tabernacle, so that he might one day transfer the militant Church from these military tabernacles to the triumphant Church, as the blessed Chemnitz beautifully advised.

Although, however, the state of humiliation and emptying is thus hinted at by the word ἐσκήνωσεν, yet in the same the glory and majesty of the Son of God shone forth, both in the doctrine of Christ, which was delivered with authority and with notable power, Matt. VII. last, John VI. 63, and in most illustrious miracles, and in divine revelations from heaven, and in the transfiguration of Christ on the holy mount; where St. John, with Peter and James his brother, saw his glory in a peculiar way, Matt. XVII. all of which he embraces in this place when he says: And we saw his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father: where that ὡς is not of likeness, but of truth, as the Kaf of truth is observed among the Hebrews; because not only similar, but the same divine and infinite glory, which is proper to the only begotten Son himself, shone forth in the incarnate Word made flesh; just as the Word is himself the only-begotten from the Father, alone begotten from the substance of the Father, the true, natural, eternal, and consubstantial Son. Cf. v. 18. Cyril of Alexandria observes this connection. Therefore, although the Evangelist says the Word was made flesh, he does not assert that he himself succumbed to the infirmities of the flesh, nor that he fell from that original virtue and glory of his, because he put on our infirm and inglorious body. For we saw his glory, he says, more sublime than any glory, and such as no one would fail to confess is fitting for the only-begotten Son from God the Father. For he was full of grace and truth.

That 'full of grace and truth' does not cohere with the immediately preceding words, 'we beheld his glory' etc., for those are to be read in a parenthesis; but with the words above, 'the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us, full of grace and truth.' Which refer not to the Word by reason of his essence, but by reason of the economy: for as to the essence of the Word, his Deity had already been described before, to which the 'fullness of grace and truth,' and whatever is of divine perfection, pertains. But here it treats of the Word, as he was made flesh and dwelt among men: of God manifested in the flesh, and of the fullness with which that very flesh or human nature was filled: in which it pleased all fullness to dwell. Col. 1:19. By virtue of the hypostatic union, 'all the fullness of the Godhead' dwelt [in him]. Col. 2:9. To which fullness indeed pertains the fullness OF GRACE AND TRUTH. For in God there is essentially a fullness of grace and mercy, since grace is an attribute proper and essential to God, and God is most truthful, and truth itself by essence; thus the fullness of both grace and truth belongs to the human nature assumed into the hypostasis of the Son of God through the hypostatic union: so that we may all receive from his fullness grace for grace, and so that we may draw all truth from the fullness of truth, as from an immense and inexhaustible fountain. For this communion of grace and truth is brought forward here primarily because of Christ's mediatorial office: because the human nature is therefore full of divine grace and truth, so that in the incarnate Word and Christ the God-man we may seek uniquely all the grace and all the truth that we lack—being otherwise prone to errors and entirely destitute and alien from grace and truth—in whom, as in an ark and repository, God has deposited grace and truth as all the treasures of mercy and knowledge, so that they may be sought there and received from there. Col. 1:19; ch. 2:3; Eph. 1:6; ch. 2:4, 7. From which fullness, therefore, rivulets are derived everywhere into all believers. For grace and truth would not have been made for us through him, nor could they have been, unless the assumed flesh had been full of grace and truth through the hypostatic communication: and therefore it pleased the divine goodness that all fullness should dwell in him; so that from his fullness we might all receive both grace and truth, or knowledge, through the intervention of his merit. Therefore, in the present truly golden aphorism, there is exhibited not only the communication of the hypostasis or subsistence of the Word, and the communion of the divine and human natures, but also the communication of idioms, and primarily of the divine glory made to the human nature: concerning which [see] in the Examination of Reformed Doctrine regarding the person of Christ.

Latin:

PROOEMIUM S. JO- HANNIS.

Quo summa capita Evangelii, λόγου æterni incar- natio, commoratio in terris, & manifestatio glo- riæ divinæ exhibentur, non neglecta Johannis prodromi testificatione de λόγῳ.

§. I. Λόγου æternitas, & vera Deitas.

JOHAN. CAP. I.

Vers. 1. In principio erat Verbum, & Verbum erat apud Deum, & Deus erat Verbum.

Vers. 2. Hoc erat in principio apud Deum.

[Summaria capita tradendorum in Evangelio sunt, de Verbi æterni incarnatione, & actis in terra: deque præcursoris Johannis de illo testificatione. De verbi itaque προϋπάρξει prææterna, & temporali ejusdem ἐνσαρκώσει, hoc S. Johannis proœmium imprimis agit: non neglecta, uti diximus S. Johannis Baptistæ de eodem testificatione: siquidem tum hujus Christi prodromi missio & testimonium, tum ipsius verbi adventus in mundum, & quæ salutis nostræ causa gesserit, describenda fuerint. Avolat ergo altius Evangelistarum Aquila S. Johannes ad ipsam VERBI æternitatem, existentiam apud DEUM Patrem, veram Deitatem, & præexistentiam apud Patrem æternam. In principio creationis rerum omnium non demum factum, aut genitum esse λόγον, Filium Dei, sed jam extitisse, adeoque vere æternum esse: extitisse autem apud Deum Patrem, utpote a quo τῇ ὑποστάσει, distinctus est, & in quo ab æterno fuit Filius, ὁ μονογενὴς υἱὸς, ὁ ὢν εἰς τὸ κόλπον τοῦ πατρὸς, v. 18. Ne autem Deitate a Patre diversum esse, vel τῇ ὀυσίᾳ, Verbum credatur, uti τῇ ὑποστάσει ab eo distinguitur, addit S. Johannes, καὶ θεὸς ἦν ὁ λόγος, & Verbum erat Deus, h. e. æque verus Deus ut Pater, vel potius, idem quoad essentiam Deus. Denique ne ullum supersit dubium, de prææterna & præexistentia, & distinctione a Patre, & Deitate τοῦ λόγου, omnia illa una sententia complectitur, ὗτος hic Deus (quod erat prædicatum in præcedente propositione, qui ὁ λόγος) ἦν ἀρχῇ πρὸς τὸν θεὸν, erat in principio, utpote æternus Deus, non vero demum factus in tempore, apud Deum Patrem. Deus apud Deum, λόγος apud Patrem, in cujus sinu erat. Distinguuntur ergo personis: sed quia æque λόγος, ut Pater, Deus, nec nisi unus est natura & essentia Deus, ideo Verbum & Pater non distinguuntur Deitate, vel essentia divina, sed unum sunt, Joh. X. 30. 1. Joh. V. 7.]

§. II. Per λόγον omnia creata sunt.

Vers. 3. Omnia per ipsum facta sunt, & sine ipso factum est nihil, quod factum est.

[Asserta Deitate æterna τοῦ λόγου, eundem esse verum omnium creatorem, quia verus Deus non est, nisi creator cœli & terræ, testatur: quod cum in principio Deus cœlum & terram creasse dicatur Gen. I. 1. λόγος Dei Filius cum Patre omnia creavit, non vero Pater sine λόγῳ quicquam condiderit. Per λόγον autem omnia condita dicit, non tanquam per medium vel instrumentum, quia in principio non erat quicquam extra Deum, & Verbum erat verus & æternus Deus: sed quod Pater per Filium tanquam coæternum & coëssentiale verbum hypostaticum, quod ab æterno apud Deum erat, quodque Deus erat, omnia condiderit: & quidem sine exceptione omnia: ideo additur, & sine ipso factum est nihil, quod factum est. Non ergo λόγος illis, quæ facta sunt, vel creaturis annumerari potest, utpote per quem omnia facta, & condita sunt in rerum omnium principio. Quo de vid. tractatus peculiaris de hoc, In principio erat Verbum, adversus Socinian. & Arianos prææternam existentiam & Deitatem Filii Dei adserens.]

§. III. In λόγῳ vita, quæ lux hominum, erat.

Vers. 4. In ipso vita erat, & vita erat lux hominum.

[A generali creationis opere ad ea, quæ in specie, tum viventia omnia, tum imprimis hominem concernunt, descendit: ob quorum vitam æter- nam hominem fieri voluisse λόγον dicturus erat S. Johannes, c. XXI. 31. Ideoque non tantum in ipso vitam fuisse ab æterno ὑσιωδῶς, utpote qui ipsa vita est; sed etiam ab ipso vitam esse omnium vi- ventium ἐνεργητικῶς, ut & lucem omnem, quæ in ho- minibus est, docet, h. e. ipsum esse autorem, & cau- sam vitæ omnis, nec non illuminationis, & lucis spi- ritualis; qui vitam imprimis spiritualem nobis conciliando, nosque ita vivificando illuminat, vel lucis nos participes reddit, & illuminando nos per verbum, vivificat: nec enim sine vita lux, vel sine luce vita spiritualis in homine esse potest. Ideo vere illuminamur ad æternam vitam, quia ille nobis lux est, in quo erat ab æterno vita, qui que est ipsa æterna vita, 1. Joh. I. 2. 5. c. V. 11.]

§. IV. Lux in tenebris lucens non apprehensa a tenebris.

Vers. 5. Et lux in tenebris lucet, & tenebræ eam non comprehenderunt.

[Jam cur plerique ab hac luce non illuminentur, causam exponit. Non ea in luce sita, quia λόγος lux hominum esse voluit; nec solum cum tenebræ adhuc nullæ essent in homine, utpote qui condi- tus erat ad imaginem Dei, in agnitione & sapientia, Col. III. 10. Gen. I. 26. Sed etiam cum per aposta- siam non nisi mera tenebræ essent in mundo: Lux enim illa lucet in tenebris: Φαίνει actum perpe- tuum infert: nunquam non, & nusquam non in tenebris lucet: in hominibus tenebris obrutis spiritualibus, qui tenebræ meræ erant, Eph. V. 8. omnis lucis spiritualis expertes: quorum vero il- luminandorum causa lucet, inde ab ortu tenebra- rum, lux illa, vera & magna, utpote omnem homi- nem illuminatura, quantum in ipsa est, v. 9. Quod autem plerique non illuminentur, causa est, quod tenebræ lucem non admiserint, aut receperint, οὐ κα- τέλαβεν. Uti Sol & pronus est, & potens ad suum lumen per omnia conclavia diffundendum, non- nulla tamen tenebricosa manent, sive ob fenestra- rum defectum; sive quod crassis obducta sint ve- lamentis; ita λόγος Sol justitiæ, lux illa vera & potest & gestit omnium hominum corda per Ev- angelii jubar illuminare, sed plerique in tenebris manent, non recipiunt lucem, vel quia fenestris carent, h. e. aures non habent ad audiendum, vel quia corda obducta sunt densis errorum, & vitio- rum linteamentis. Luc. VIII. 12. Tenebræ homines sunt, tenebris mentis, ignorantiæ & erroribus Job. XII. 35. Eph. IV. 18. tenebris cordis, vitiorum & peccatorum, quæ operæ tenebrarum, Rom. XIII. 12. tenebris afflictionis, Es.V. 13. Thren. III. 3. & te- nebris damnationis, quæ extrema sunt tenebræ, Matth: XXII. 13. obnoxii.

§. V. Johannes missus, ut de luce illa vera te- staretur, ut per ipsum crederent.

Vers. 6. Fuit homo missus a Deo, cui nomen erat Johannes.

Vers. 7. Hic venit in testimonium, ut testimo- nium perhiberet de lumine, ut omnes crederent per illum.

Vers. 8. Non erat ille lux, sed ut testimonium perhiberet de lumine.

Vers. 9. Erat lux vera, quæ illuminat omnem hominem venientem in hunc mundum.

[Quia lucem in præsenti dixit LUCERE in te- nebris, actum quidem continuum lucendi, sed imprimis etiam istius temporis, quo lux illa mundo exorta est, cum visitavit nos oriens ex alto, ἐπιφᾶ- ναι τοῖς ἐν σκότει, ἡ σκιᾷ θανάτου καθημένοις Luc. I. 79. respicit, quod de lucis illius in mundo peculia- ri ortu testari debuit Baptista, velut Phossphorus- Solis ortum imminere indicat. De eo ergo agit Johannes, ejus missionem & testimonium de hac luce, ceu officium, ob quod missus, finemque testificatio- nis, ut omnes crederent per ipsum, indicat: adeoque eundum a luce illa magna discriminat, quæ o- mnem hominem illuminat. Non ergo causa, quod non illuminentur omnes homines, vel in Deum, vel in Verbum Dei rejicienda, quum Deus præco- nes mittat Verbi, ut OMNES credant, eoque fine verbum prædicetur; nec in lucem illam magnam, quæ quantum ad gratiosam voluntatem, ad meri- tum illuminationis, ad media, quæ ob eandem de- stinata omnibus sunt, illuminat omnem hominem, etsi actu secundo non illuminentur omnes, pro- pria hominum culpa. Porro è tenebrarum antithefi illuminationem simplicissime intelligi, recte nota- tum B. Chemnitio: Nam 1. contra ignorantiæ tene- bras, revelatione verbi & illustratione spiritus ad ve- ram agnitionem, nos illuminat. 2. Contra peccati tene- bras, imputatione justitiæ, remissione peccatorum, & inchoata in hac vita renovatione, nos illuminat. 3. Contra tenebras iræ Dei, gratia, reconciliatione & adoptione faciem Dei super nos illustrat, sicut scri- ptura loquitur, Num. VI. 25.4. Contra tenebras mise- riarum, consolatione, mitigatione & liberatione nobis illucescat. 5. Contra tenebras exteriores mortis & da- mnationis, vita & salute æterna nos illuminat, 2. Tim. I. 10. Vitam illuminavit Col. I. v. 12. ad sortem sanctorum in lumine. Cæterum referri posset illud ἐρχόμενον εἰς τ᾿ κόσμον ad τὸ Φῶς τὸ ἀληθινὸν, ut indicetur adventus vero illius lucis in mundum hunc, quemadmodum vers. seq. statim dicitur in mundo fuisse, & v. 11. in propria venisse: ac v. 14. caro factus inter homines habitasse: qua de re l. c. diximus.]

§. VI. In mundo, per ipsum condito, erat. Sed mundus non cognovit eum.

Vers. 10. In mundo erat, & mundus per ipsum factus est, & mundus eum non cognovit.

[Illud in mundo erat vel de primordio statim lucis, quæ post lapsum luxit homini, intelligitur, siquidem exinde a paucis cognitus fuerit: vel po- tius de temporum plenitudine, cum in mundum ve- nit Filius Dei natus è muliere Gal. IV. 4. Mundus autem per ipsum factus dicitur, ut, quum ipse crea- tor mundi voluerit nostri causa in mundum veni- te, extrema rei indignitas notetur, quod mundus, maxima pars hominum in mundo, eum suscipere renuerit, ac ne cognoverit quidem. Ingrati ergo animi & stuporis, dicente hic Cyrillo, mundus hic postulatnr, qui & suum authorem ignoravit, & illu- minationis suæ fructum non bonum edidit.]

§. VII. Et quanquam in sua venerit, a suis ta- men receptus non fuit.

Vers. 11. In propria venit, & sui eum non rece- perunt.

[Εἰς τὰ ἴδια. Mundus pertinet ad τὰ ἴδια. Sed specialius ad τὰ ἴδια venit: ubi oi ἴδιοι eum non suspe- perunt; tum quoad homines in universum, quia ad homines venit, qui ei proprii sunt, præ aliis crea- turis: tum quoad Judæos imprimis, ad quos primi- tus missus erat, quiq; ejus erant peculium, & ei ἴδιοι, quos sibi segregaratin populum, & e quibus nasci voluit secundum carnem. Quo de Cyrill. Mirum nihil est, si mundus unigenitum non agnoverit, qui a recta intelligendi via deflexerit, quum ipse quoque po- pulus, quem sibi præ cæteris peculiarem elegit Deus in carne præsentem abjecerit, & eum qui ad omnium salutem advenerat, excipere noluerit. Addatur B. Chemnit. Cum primo dicit! mundus enim non re- cepit, ostendit tristem esse cæcitatem naturæ lapsæ, ut naturalibus viribus rationis non possit Christum agno- scere. Cum vero addit suos, qui verbum habebant, ad quos in assumta carne doctrina & miraculis ve- nit, eum non recepisse, ostendit cæcitati adjunctam extremam malitiam, quod Spiritui S. restiterint, vo- lenti ipsos illuminare dato verbo.]

§. VIII. De ἐξουσία eorum, qui λόγον rece- perunt, & quinam eum receperunt.

Vers. 12. Quotquot autem receperunt eum, dedit eis potestatem filios Dei fieri, his, qui cre- dunt in nomine ejus.

V. 13. Qui non ex sanguinib?, neq; ex voluntate carnis, neq; ex voluntate viri, sed ex Deo nati sunt.

[Distingui quidem fortassis possent verba κατα- λαμβάνειν v. 5. παραλαμβάνειν v. 11. & λαμ- βάνειν v. 12. Sed hic fere videntur Synonima: nam tenebræ dicuntur non comprehendisse, quæ non mo- do non comprehendere, sed nec apprehendere possunt lucem, quamdiu manent tenebræ: quem- admodum οἱ ἴδιοι non assumsisse dicuntur venientem εἰς τὰ ἴδια: credentes autem λαμβάνειν, recipere dicuntur filium Dei: unde utrumq; λαμβάνειν, & παραλαμβάνειν eadem voce קבל reddidit Syrus. Explicant autem sese mutuo hæc verba: ita reci- pere nos FiliumDei per fidem debere, ut eum vel- uti ad nos sumamus, cum nobis sese offert, & com- plecti, ac comprehendere totum annitamur. Ἐξουσία autem recipientibus datur ab ipso λόγῳ, ut fiant Filii Dei: quod argumentum est insigne Deitatis τοῦ λόγου: nam jus & dignitatem concedere, ut quis filiusDei fiat, non nisi Deo uni convenit: ubi præ- clare monuitB. Chemn. non potestatem innui vel fa- cultatem, ut si libuerit, virib. liberi arbitrii evadamus filii Dei; nam qui receperunt Filium Dei, actu jam sunt filii Dei: Omnes enim filii Dei sumus per fi- dem, Gal. III. 26. Sed dignitatem, eminentiam, excel- lentiam, auctoritatem & jus aliquod voce illa etiam designari, Matth. VII. 29. Apoc. XVII. 12. Rom. XIII. 1. Recte etiam notat, τὸ γίνεσθαι utrumque significa- re, & fieri, & esse: quod vero de diversis locis ad- mittimus: quum in uno loco utrumq; significatum admitti nequeat. Sic ergo dignitatem, ut simus Filii Dei, consequimur, cum ipsum per fidem recipimus. Syrus habet vocem שולטנא auctoritatem, dignita- tem, eminentiam, quæ dominantium propria est. Id itaque innuitur, illis, qui natura servi sunt, & man- cipia peccati, & Satanæ, ac filii iræ, dignitatem il- lam conferri, ut sint filii Dei, hoc est, non tantum in familiamDei adsciscantur, sed adoptentur in filios Dei. Qui scil. credunt εἰς τὸ ὄνομα αὐτοῦ, in nomen ejus, qui fiduciam in ipsum collocant: in nomen ejus, quo sese in Verbo revelavit; & ita fide eum susci- piunt, & amplectuntur, uti ratione personæ & officii sese in Verbo offert. Quam vero dignitatem non habent ex sanguine vel carnali, etiamsi generosissi- mæ propaginis sint, generatione, nec ex voluntate carnis, h. e. studio & conatu virium carnis; seu natu- ræ, nec ex voluntate viri, seu conare & studio quan- tumcunq; præclaro, quale virorum fortium & hero- um est: q. d. nullis vel vulgaribus, vel heroicis stu- diis, operibus, virtutib. & meritis hanc ἐξουσίαν ob- tineri posse: sed opus esse nativitate ex Deo, & re- generatione spirituali, quæ fit per Verbum & Sacra- menta: per quam & fide donamur ex gratia, & per fidem efficimur filii Dei, 1. Petr. I. 23. Joh. III. 5.]

§. IX. De Verbi incarnatione, & habitatione inter homines.

Vers. 14. Et Verbum caro factum est; & habita- vit in nobis; & vidimus gloriam ejus, gloriam qua- si unigeniti a Patre, plenum gratiæ & veritatis.

[Jam luculentius exponitur adventus in mundum & ad nos; nimirum per ἐνσάρκωσιν. Particula Et αἰτιολογικῶς vel causaliter non incommode accipi- tur: quia per incarnationem, ἡ ἐξουσία illa & ge- nerationem ex Deo consequimur: & ideo filius Dei factus est caro, ut nos, qui caro ex carne nati su- mus, efficeret filios Dei: Factus autem est caro, non uti caro nos sumus ratione corruptionis, quia per omnia nobis similis est, excepto tamen peccato Ebr. IV. 15. sed quia carnis nostræ & sanguinis parti- ceps factus est ratione naturæ & quidditatis. Caro enim hic non accipitur accidentaliter vel metony- mice, sive pro carnali concupiscentia, ut Joh. III. 5. sive pro fragilitate humana, mortalibus propria, ut 1. Cor. XV. 50. quanquam nec isto Paulino loco, nec uspiã alias voce carnis abstractive nuda fragilitas, vel corruptibilitas, sed corpus qua fragile, vel corru- ptibile, notetur: neq; ergo carnem fieri est fragilem evadere, ut Sociniani pervertunt, aut mortalem red- di, & instar fœni arescere, uti quondam Ariani ca- villati sunt; quum in Verbum, quod est æternus Deus, non cadat fragilitas aut corruptibilitas, & mortalitas, nedum factũ Verbum sit fragilitas aut corruptibilitas; sed substantialiter, idq; Synecdochi- ce, uti more Scripturæ caro hominem, vel humanã naturam notat, ad quam constituendam cum car- ne, vel corpore anima rationalis facit: cui accidit & contingit esse fragilem & corruptibilem, quum nec talis fuerit in statu integritatis, nec futurus talis sit in statu glorificationis beatæ, salva humanæ naturæ veritate: Vid. Gen. VI. 12. Psal. CXXV. 21. Es. XL. 5. 6. Joel. II. 28. Rom. III. 10. quomodo Filius Dei parti- ceps factus dicitur carnis & sanguinis, sicut ejusdẽ fideles pueri ejus participes sunt, Ebr. II. 14. assum- sisse semen Abrahæ, v. 16. natus ex semine David se- cundum carnem, i. e. naturam humanam Rom. I. 3. & ex Patribus c. IX. 5. Ideoque sensum hujus apho- rismi Catholica Ecclesia summo consensu reddidit ejusmodi: Verbum æternum quod Deus est, & uni- genitus Dei Patris Filius, esse hominẽ factum; non quidẽ mutatione Deitatis in humanitatem, nẽc con- versione λόγε in carnem anima destitutam, sed unio- ne divina & humana naturæ, vel assumtione huma- næ naturæ in divinam, uti Athanasius ἐν (άρκωσιν dicit πρόσληψιν τ̃ ἀνθρωπότητῶ εἰς θεότητα. Gregor. Neocæsar. Orat. in Epiphan. Deus es & homo, tu qui in principio eras, & qui caro factus es, sed non in carnem conversus. Cyrill. Alex. in h. l. A- perte demum his verbis ἐνανθρωπήσεως λόγον in- carnationis sermonem ingreditur. Clare enim docet σαφῶς ἐξηγεῖται filium hominis factum & appel- latum esse unigenitum; id enim significat illud, quo ait, Verbum carnem factum esse. Idem enim est, ac si di- ceret, ὁ λόγῶ ἄνθρωπῶ ἐγένετο, Verbum homo fa- ctũ est. Quod cum ait, nihil nobis inusitatũ aut peregri- num ingerit, cum plerumq; divina Scriptura soliu: car- nis vocabulo totum animal significet juxta illud, quod apud Joelem scriptum. Effundam de Spiritu meo super omnem carnem. Cum lego, Verbum caro fa- ctum est, in Verbo, inquit S. Augustin. l. XIII. de Trin. c. 19. intelligo verũ Dei Filium, in carne agnosco verum hominis filium, & utrumque simul in una persona Dei & hominis ineffabili gratia largitate conjunctum. Greg. M. l. IX. Ep. 61. Verbum, inquit, carnem dicimus factũ non immutando quod erat, sed suscipiendo quod non erat. Chrysost. homil. X. in Joh. τῆ γαρ ένώσεl, καὶ τῆ συναφείᾳ ἓν ἐσιν ὁ θεὸς λόγῶ κὴ ἡ σὰρξ ἐ συγχύσεως γενομένης, ὐδὲ ἀφανισμᾶ τ̃ ὐσιῶν, ἀλλ᾽ ἑνώσεως ἀῤῥήτε τινὸς ὠ ἀφράσε. τὸ δὲ ὅπως μὴ ζήτει, ἐγένετο γὰρ ὡς οἶδεν ἀυτὸς τρόπῳ ὅτι μοιοτρόπῳ. Leo M. Serm. III. de pass. Dom. c. 1. Hoc Catholica fides tradit, ut in Redem- torem nostrum duas noverimus convenisse naturas, & manentibus proprietatibus suis tantam factam unitatem utriusque substantiæ, ut ab illo tempore, quo ficut humani generis causa poscebat, in beata Virgi- ei nis utero Verbum caro factum, nec Deum illum sine hoc quod homo est, nec hominem sine hoc liceat cogi- tare quod Deus est. Eligius (circa An. 640) hom. I. Verbum illud, quod in principio erat, & apud Deum erat, & Deus erat Verbum, per quod omnia facta sunt, & sine quo factum est nihil, in fine seculorum caro fa- ctum est, & habitavit in nobis, ut Mediator fieret Dei & hominum homo Jesus Christus, verus Deus & ve- rus homo in unitate personæ. Conf. Ambros. l. de Dom. incarn. sacr. c. 6. Hilarius l. XI. de Trinit. Ful- gentius lib. I. ad Thrasim. Reg. c. 18. Atticus Con- stantinopol. in Act. Conc. Ephes. T. II. c. 28. &c.

Maluit autem Evangelista vocem carnis adhibe- re, quam hominis, tum quod ita magis Dei erga nos amor declaretur carnis commemoratione, & quod nostri causa etiam ad deteriorem partem sese dejecit, ut habet Nazianzen. Epist. I. ad Cledon. tum quod juxta Cyrill. l. I. in Joh. c. 25. ex parte ma- xime corrupta, sed unione Verbi vivificata totius re- parationem significare voluerit; ut una cerneretur vulnus & remedium, æger & medicus, quod in mor- tem prolapsum est, & qui excitavit ad vitam, quod corruptioni cessit, & qui corruptionem amovet, quod morte superatum est, & qui morte superior est, quod vita orbatum est, & qui vitam largitur.

Pergit S. Johannes, & ἐσκήνωσεν ἐν ἡμῖν, & habi- tavit in nobis: quod vel de habitatione in carne, vel natura nostra, ut explicetur per illam σκήνωσιν ἐνσάρκωσις, intelligitur, quia λόγος Deitate sua replevit tabernaculum corporis, vel humanitatis, Col. II. 9. quemadmodum quondam majestate Dei replevit tabernaculum Mosaïcum, Ex. XL. 34. & templum Salomoneum 1. Reg. VIII. 10. quo abit Cy- rilli, Chrysostomi, & Theophylacti interpretatio, quod λόγος in assumta carne personaliter habi- tarit, sicut anima in suo proprio corpore tanquam in tabernaculo habitare dicitur, 2. Cor. V. 1. 2. Pet. I. 13. vel de habitatione conversationis inter homines, ac peculiariter inter suos, i. e. Judæos quemadmo- dum promisit Filius Dei Zach. II. 10. Ecce ego venio, & habitabo in medio tui; quem sensum tanquam simpliciorem præferimus cum B. Chemnitio: quia complecti voluit S. Johannes summam dicendo- rum, utpote quæ absolvuntur Verbi incarnatione, inter homines conversatione, & gloriæ manifestatio- ne. Verbo ἐσκήνωσε, i. e. in tabernaculo habitavit, ita insinuatur tum quod peregrinus veluti fuerit in terra, quemadmodum olim peregrini, uti Pa- triarchæ & alii in tabernaculis habitarunt; tum quod militatum venerit adversus hostes nostros, uti solent milites habitare in tabernaculis, & ten- torium suum fixerit contra potestatem inferna- lem, parta victoria triumphans in cælum ascen- deret, relinquens mundum tanquam castrense ta- bernaculum, ut Ecclesiam militantem ex castren- sibus hisce tabernaculis aliquando transferat ad triumphantē Ecclesiam ut pulcre monuit B. Chemn.

Quamvis vero ita subinnuatur status humiliatio- nis, & exinanitionis voce ἐσκήνωσεν, in eodem ta- men effulsisse gloriam & majestatem Filii Dei tum in doctrina Christi, quæ cum ἐξουσία fiebat, & cum insi- gni ἐνεργείᾳ, Matth. VII. ult. Joh. VI. 63. tum in mira- culis illustrissimis, tum in revelationibus de cælo di- vinis, & in transfiguratione Christi in monte sacro; ubi peculiariter vidit S. Johannes, cum Petro, & Ja- cobo fratre gloriam ejus, Matth. XVII. quæ omnia complectitur h. l. cum ait: Et vidimus gloriam ejus, gloriam quasi unigeniti a Patre: ubi illud ὡς non si- militudinis est, sed veritatis, uti apud Ebræos Kaf veritatis observatur; quia non similis tantum, sed eadem divina & infinita gloria, quæ est ipsiusmet Filii unigeniti propria, effulsit in Verbo incar- nato; quemadmodum ὁ Λόγος est ipse unigeni- tus a Patre, solus ex substantia Patris genitus, ve- rus, naturalis, æternus, & consubstantialis Filius. Conf. v. 18. Observat hanc συνέχειαν Cyrillus A- lex. Itaque licet Evangelista Verbum carnem factum esse dicat, non tamen ipsum carnis infirmitatibus suc- cubuisse asserit, nec pristina illa sua virtute & gloria excidisse. eo quod infirmum nostrum & inglorium corpus induit. Vidimus enim gloriam ejus, inquit, omni a gloria sublimiorem, & qualem decere Filium ex Deo Patre unigenitum nemo non fateatur. Ple- nus enim erat gratia & veritate.

Illa πλήρης χάριτος & ἀληθείας non cum im- mediate præcedentibus, ἐθεασάμεθα τὴν δόξαν αὐτῶ &c. cohærent, ea enim in parenthesi legen- da; sed cum superioribus ὁ λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο & ἐσκήνωσεν ἐν ἡμῖν, Verbum caro factum est, & habitavit in nobis, Plenum gratia & veritate. Quæ respiciunt non λόγον Verbum ratione τῆς ὐσίας, sed ratione τ οἰκονομίας: nam quod ad essentiam Verbi, jam antea ejus Deitas descripta fuit, ad quam πλήρωμα χάριτος & ἀληθείας, & quic- quid est divinæ perfectionis, pertinet. Hic vero agitur de Verbo, qua caro factum inter homines habitavit: de Deo in carne manifestato, & de ple- nitudine, qua repleta fuit ipsa caro vel natura hu- mana: in qua quia placuit habitare omnem plenitu- dinem. Col. I. 19. vi unionis hypostaticæ πᾶν τὸ πλήρωμα τ θιότητος habitavit Col. II. 9. ad quod vero πλήρωμα pertinet plenitudo GRATIAE ET VERITATIS. Nam in Deo ὐσιωδῶς est gra- tiæ, ac misericordiæ plenitudo, quum gratia attri- butum Deo proprium, atque essentiale sit, Deus- que sit veracissimus, & ipsa veritas per essentiam, ita plenitudo & gratiæ, & veritatis humanæ na- turæ assumtæ in hypostasin Filii Dei convenit per unionem hypostaticam: ut e plenitudine ejus acci- pere possimus omnes gratiam pro gratia, utque e ple- nitudine veritatis omnem haurire possimus veri- tatem, ceu ex fonte immenso & inexhausto. Hæc enim gratia & veritatis communio inprimis hic adducitur, ob officium Christi mediatorium: quia ideo plena est divina gratia, & veritate humana natura, ut in λόγῳ incarnato, & Christo θεανθρώ- πῳ omnem gratiam, omnem veritatem, qua indi- gemus, extra ipsum ire tantum & erroribus obno- xii, & a gratia & veritate prorsus extorres, & alieni, quæramus unice, in quem tanquam in arcam & repositorium gratiam & veritatem ut thesauros misericordiæ & cognitionis omnes reposuit Deus, ut ibi quærantur, & inde accipiantur. Col. I. 19. c. II. 3. Eph. I. 6. c. II. 4. 7. e qua proinde plenitudine ri- vuli undiquaque in omnes credentes derivantur. Non enim gratia & veritas per ipsum nobis facta esset, aut fieri potuisset, nisi caro assumta plena gratia & veritate fuisset, per communicationem hypostaticam: atque ideo placuit divinæ bonitati, ut habitaret in ipso omnis plenitudo; ut de plenitudi- ne ejus omnes & gratiam, & veritatem vel cognitio- nem, interveniente ejusdem merito, acciperemus. Aphorismo ergo præsenti vere aureo exhibetur non tantum communicatio hypostaseos, vel subsisten- tiæ τὺ λόγα, & communio naturarum divinæ & humanæ, sed etiam communicatio idiomatum, ac inprimis divinæ gloriæ facta humanæ naturæ: quo de in Exam. doctr. Reform. de person. Christi.

## 1:1 Introduction: In the Name of Jesus. Evangelical Harmony Concerning the Life of Jesus Christ, for Compili
In the Name of Jesus. EVANGELICAL HARMONY CONCERNING THE LIFE OF JESUS CHRIST, FOR COMPILING A NEW MONOTESSARON.

FIRST SECTION CONCERNING THE ACTS BEFORE CHRIST'S PUBLIC MINISTRY. ARTICLE I. CONCERNING THE CONCEPTION, NATIVITY, AND THE CHILDHOOD AND YOUTHFUL AGE OF CHRIST. CHAPTER I. The parents of Christ's forerunner, St. John the Baptist, are described, and his Nativity and his forerunner office are announced by Gabriel.

§. I. After the designation of the time, St. Luke describes John's parents by their status, piety, and childlessness.

LUKE CHAPTER I.

Ver. 5. There was in the days of Herod, king of Judea, a certain priest named Zacharias, of the course of Abia; and his wife was of the daughters of Aaron, and her name was Elizabeth.

Ver. 6. And they were both righteous before God, walking in all the commandments and justifications of the Lord without complaint.

V. 7. And they had no son, for that Elizabeth was barren, and they both had advanced in their days.

[The days of Herod, commonly called the Ascalonite, or the Great, i.e., the times of his reign are designated, concerning which compare Sect. VIII. q. VII. p. 134 of the Sacred Chronicle. Zacharias was a ἱερεὺς [priest] from the course of Abia: not indeed the high priest or Pontiff. Concerning the courses we have spoken at Grotius on this passage.]

§. II. The foretelling of the Nativity of John made by the Angel Gabriel to his father Zacharias, and his office from Malachi: (c. IV. 5.) as a sign of which the father is made mute, returning home when the days of his duty were finished, and from that [time] she, having become pregnant, hid herself for five months.

Ver. 8. And it came to pass when he was performing the priesthood in the order of his course before God:

Ver. 9. According to the custom of the priesthood, he went out by lot, that he might offer incense, having entered into the temple of the Lord.

Ver. 10. And all the multitude of the people was praying outside at the hour of incense.

Ver. 11. And there appeared to him an Angel of the Lord, standing at the right side of the altar of incense.

Ver. 12. And Zacharias was troubled seeing [him], and fear fell upon him.

Ver. 13. But the Angel said to him: Fear not, Zacharias, for thy prayer is heard: and thy wife Elizabeth shall bear thee a son, and thou shalt call his name John.

Ver. 14. And there shall be joy to thee, and exultation, and many shall rejoice in his nativity.

Ver. 15. For he shall be great before the Lord: and he shall not drink wine and strong drink, and he shall be filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother's womb.

Vers. 16. And he shall turn many of the children of Israel to the Lord their God.

Vers. 17. And he himself shall go before him in the spirit and power of Elias: to turn the hearts of the fathers unto the children, and the incredulous to the wisdom of the just, to prepare unto the Lord a perfect people.

Vers. 18. And Zacharias said to the Angel: Whereby shall I know this? for I am an old man, and my wife is advanced in her days.

Vers. 19. And the Angel answering, said to him: I am Gabriel, who stand before God: and am sent to speak to thee, and to evangelize these things to thee.

Vers. 20. And behold, thou shalt be silent, and these things shall come to pass, because thou hast not believed my words, which shall be fulfilled in their time.

Vers. 21. And the people were expecting Zacharias, and they wondered that he tarried in the temple.

Vers. 22. But when he came out, he could not speak to them, and they realized that he had seen a vision in the temple. And he was making signs to them and remained mute.

Vers. 23. And it came to pass, that when the days of his ministry were completed, he went away to his house.

Vers. 24. But after these days his wife Elizabeth conceived, and she hid herself for five months, saying:

Vers. 25. Because thus the Lord has done for me in the days in which he looked upon me to take away my reproach among men.

CHAPTER II. The conception of Jesus announced and explained to the virgin Mary by the same Angel.

§. I. In the sixth month from the conception of John, Gabriel is sent to the Virgin Mary and announces the conception and birth of Jesus, and describes his person and especially his kingly office.

Vers. 26. And in the sixth month, the Angel Gabriel was sent from God into a city of Galilee, named Nazareth.

V. 27. To a virgin betrothed to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David, and the virgin's name was Mary.

Vers. 28. And the Angel entered to her and said: Hail full of grace: the Lord is with you: blessed are you among women.

Vers. 29. And when she had heard this, she was troubled at his speech, and was considering what manner of greeting this might be.

Vers. 30. And the Angel said to her: Do not fear Mary, for you have found grace with God.

Vers. 31. Behold, you shall conceive in your womb, and shall bring forth a son, and shall call his name Jesus.

V. 32. He shall be great, and shall be called the Son of the Most High, and the Lord God shall give unto him the throne of David his father: and he shall reign in the house of Jacob for ever.

Vers. 33. And of his kingdom there shall be no end.

§. II. Mary, inquiring how that can be done, since she has never known any man, is informed by the Angel concerning the conception by the Holy Spirit and the overshadowing of the power of the Most High, whence the holy thing born of her shall be the Son of the Most High.

Vers. 34. And Mary said to the Angel: How shall this be, because I know not man?

Vers. 35. And the Angel answering, said to her: The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you: and therefore also the holy thing which shall be born of you shall be called the Son of God.

§. III. Mary is confirmed by the fruitfulness of the barren Elizabeth, and by divine omnipotence, and submits herself to the divine will.

Vers. 36. And behold your kinswoman Elizabeth, she also has conceived a son in her old age, and this is the sixth month with her, who is called barren.

Vers. 37. Because no word shall be impossible with God.

Vers. 38. And Mary said: Behold the handmaid of the Lord, be it done to me according to your word. And the Angel departed from her.

[This happened in the year of the World 4000, on the 26th day of March.]

CHAPTER III. Mary visits Elizabeth, and being received by her as the mother of the Lord, she celebrates the Lord with a hymn, and serves her for three months.

§. I. Mary travels over the mountains into the city of Judah to the house of Zechariah, and Elizabeth being greeted, she is received by the leap of the fetus of John, enclosed in his mother's womb.

V. 39. And Mary rising in those days went into the hill country with haste, into the city of Judah.

Vers. 40. And she entered into the house of Zechariah, and greeted Elizabeth.

Vers. 41. And it came to pass, that she heard the greeting

of Mary, Elizabeth, the infant leaped in her womb.

[Mary walked for miles through the mountains of Gilboa, Gerizim, Ebal, and Ephraim, and into the mountains of Judea to the priestly city and city of refuge, Hebron: where Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob were once buried.]

§. II. Mary is proclaimed blessed, as the Mother of the Lord, and blessed because of her faith, and the fruit of her womb is proclaimed blessed by Elizabeth, who is full of the Holy Spirit.

Vers. 41. And Elizabeth was filled with the Holy Spirit.

Vers. 42. And she cried out with a loud voice, and said: Blessed art thou among women, and blessed is the fruit of thy womb.

Vers. 43. And whence is this to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?

Vers. 44. For behold, as the voice of thy greeting was in my ears, the infant leaped in joy in my womb.

Ver. 45. And blessed art thou that hast believed, because those things shall be accomplished that were told thee from the Lord.

§. III. The hymn of Mary, in which she celebrates the benefits shown to herself and to the whole human race.

Ver. 46. And Mary said: My soul doth magnify the Lord:

Ver. 47. And my spirit hath rejoiced in God my Saviour.

Ver. 48. Because he hath regarded the humility of his handmaid; for behold from henceforth all generations shall call me blessed.

Ver. 49. Because he that is mighty hath done great things to me; and holy is his name.

Ver. 50. And his mercy is from generation unto generations, to them that fear him.

Ver. 51. He hath shewed might in his arm: he hath scattered the proud in the conceit of their heart.

Ver. 52. He hath put down the mighty from their seat, and hath exalted the humble.

Ver. 53. He hath filled the hungry with good things; and the rich he hath sent empty away.

Ver. 54. He hath received Israel his servant, being mindful of his mercy:

Ver. 55. As he spoke to our fathers, to Abraham and to his seed for ever.

§. IV. Mary, having stayed with Elizabeth for three months, sets out for home.

Vers. 56. And Mary remained with her about three months, and returned to her own house.

[In the passing month of June: In the year of the world 4000. B. Bünting thinks this happened on the 2nd day of July, John the Baptist having already been born and circumcised: But others judge that her virginal modesty would not have permitted her to wait for the birth of John, in which matter little is at stake: because the Holy Spirit directed such things according to His pleasure.]

CHAPTER IV. The birth of John, the Hymn of Zacharias, with the growth and strengthening of John in the Spirit. §. I. The son of Elizabeth is born, and his circumcision with the imposition of the name, by which he was called not Zacharias, but John, Zacharias approving that name, the bond of his tongue being loosened to the admiration of all.

Vers. 57. Now Elizabeth's time was fulfilled for giving birth, and she brought forth a son.

Vers. 58. And her neighbors and relatives heard that the Lord had magnified His mercy with her, and they were congratulating her.

Vers. 59. And it came to pass on the eighth day, they came to circumcise the child, and they were calling him by the name of his father, Zacharias.

Vers. 60. And his mother answering, said: Not so, but he shall be called John.

Vers. 61. And they said to her, Because there is no one in your kindred who is called by this name.

Vers. 62. But they made signs to his father, what he would have him called.

Vers. 63. And asking for a writing tablet he wrote, saying: John is his name. And all wondered.

Vers. 64. And immediately his mouth was opened, and his tongue, and he spoke blessing God.

Vers. 65. And fear came upon all their neighbors, and throughout all the hill country of Judea all these words were spread abroad.

Vers. 66. And all who heard them laid them up in their heart, saying: What, do you think, will this child be? For the hand of the Lord was with him.

§. II. Zechariah, filled with the Holy Spirit, prophesies, celebrating God for the raising up of the horn of salvation.

Vers. 67. And Zechariah his father was filled with the Holy Spirit and prophesied, saying:

Vers. 68. Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, who has visited and wrought redemption for his people.

Vers. 69. And has raised up a horn of salvation for us, in the house of David his servant.

Vers. 70. As he spoke by the mouth of his holy prophets, who have been from of old.

Ver. 71. Salvation from our enemies, and from the hand of all who hate us.

Ver. 72. To perform the mercy promised to our fathers, and to remember his holy covenant.

Ver. 73. The oath which he swore to our father Abraham, that he would grant us.

Ver. 74. That we, being delivered from the hand of our enemies, might serve him without fear.

Ver. 75. In holiness and righteousness before him, all our days.

§. III. Furthermore, Zacharias prophesies concerning the prophetic and προδρομευτικῷ [forerunning] office of his son, and its end, the communication of the knowledge of salvation.

Ver. 76. And you, child, will be called the prophet of the Most High: for you will go before the face of the Lord to prepare his ways.

Ver. 77. To give knowledge of salvation to his people, in the remission of their sins.

Ver. 78. Through the tender mercies of our God, in which the sunrise from on high has visited us.

Ver. 79. To give light to those who sit in darkness and in the shadow of death: to guide our feet into the way of peace.

§. IV. John grows and is strengthened in the Spirit, remaining in the desert until the day of his ἀναδείξεως [manifestation] before the people. This is to be referred to the 30th year of his age, that is, to the year of the world 4030. This is added here, however, as a summary account of his life up to the time of his ministry, since the Holy Spirit wished to narrate nothing further about John until he described the beginning of his office.

Ver. 80. And the child grew, and was strengthened in the Spirit: and was in the deserts until the day of his manifestation to Israel.

CHAPTER V.

The genealogy of Joseph woven by Matthew: whom, when he wished to desert his pregnant betrothed, an Angel warned that what was born in her was from the Holy Spirit, and therefore he took Mary, until she brought forth her son Jesus.

§. I. The genealogy of Christ woven through three groups of fourteen starting from Abraham: The first up to David.

Vers. 1. The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham.

Vers. 2. Abraham begat Isaac. And Isaac begat Jacob. And Jacob begat Judah and his brothers.

Vers. 3. And Judah begat Perez and Zerah by Tamar. And Perez begat Hezron. And Hezron begat Ram.

Vers. 4. And Ram begat Amminadab. And Amminadab begat Nahshon. And Nahshon begat Salmon.

Vers. 5. And Salmon begat Boaz by Rahab. And Boaz begat Obed by Ruth. And Obed begat Jesse. And Jesse begat David the King.

§. II. The second group of fourteen extends from Solomon to the Babylonian captivity.

Vers. 6. And David the King begat Solomon by her who had been the wife of Uriah.

Vers. 7. And Solomon begat Rehoboam. And Rehoboam begat Abijah. And Abijah begat Asa.

Ver. 8. And Asa begat Josaphat. And Josaphat begat Joram. And Joram begat Ozias.

Ver. 9. And Ozias begat Joatham. And Joatham begat Achaz. And Achaz begat Ezechias.

Ver. 10. And Ezechias begat Manasses. And Manasses begat Amon. And Amon begat Josias.

Ver. 11. And Josias begat Jechonias and his brethren in the transmigration of Babylon.

§. III. The third group of fourteen extends from the transmigration of Babylon unto Christ.

Ver. 12. And after the transmigration of Babylon Jechonias begat Salathiel. And Salathiel begat Zorobabel.

Ver. 13. And Zorobabel begat Abiud. And Abiud begat Eliacim. And Eliacim begat Azor.

Ver. 14. And Azor begat Sadoc. And Sadoc begat Achim. And Achim begat Eliud.

Ver. 15. And Eliud begat Eleazar. And Eleazar begat Mathan. And Mathan begat Jacob.

Ver. 16. And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ.

§. IV. Joseph's purpose, and the divine command given in a dream by an Angel not to desert Mary; and the cause of it, the conception of Jesus the Saviour from the Holy Spirit.

[Joseph noticed that Mary was pregnant without a doubt, after she returned home from Elizabeth, whom she had attended for three months. For in the fourth month the signs reveal themselves. Therefore these things happened at the beginning of the month of July approximately.]

Vers. 18. Now the generation of Christ was in this wise: When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost.

Vers. 19. Then Joseph her husband, being a just man, and not willing to make her a public example, was minded to put her away privily.

Vers. 20. But while he thought on these things, behold, the angel of the Lord appeared unto him in a dream, saying, Joseph, thou son of David, fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife: for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost.

Vers. 21. And she shall bring forth a son, and thou shalt call his name Jesus: for he shall save his people from their sins.

§. V. Confirmation of the same from Isaiah concerning the virginal birth, Ch. VII. 14.

Ver. 22. Now all this was done, that it might be fulfilled which was spoken of the Lord by the prophet, saying:

Ver. 23. Behold, a virgin shall be with child, and shall bring forth a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel, which being interpreted is, God with us.

§. VI. Execution of the angelic command in the taking of Mary, whom Joseph did not know until she brought forth her firstborn, whose name was Jesus.

Ver. 24. Then Joseph being raised from sleep did as the angel of the Lord had bidden him, and took unto him his wife.

Ver. 25. And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son: and he called his name Jesus.

CHAPTER VI.

The birth of Christ, and his annunciation, and angelic celebration: with the journey, the investigation of the matter, and the pastoral proclamation. §. I. The birth of Christ is described, regarding the circumstances of time, the Edict of Augustus concerning the census under Quirinius, governor of Syria: of place, in Bethlehem, to which Joseph betook himself with Mary, because he was of the lineage of David: of manner, in a humble state: that he was born the first son of Mary, and wrapped in swaddling clothes and laid in a manger.

Ver. 1. And it came to pass in those days, that there went out a decree from Caesar Augustus, that all the world should be taxed.

Ver. 2. (And) this taxing was first made when Cyrenius was governor of Syria.

Vers. 3. And all went, that they might register, every one into his own city.

Vers. 4. And Joseph also went up from Galilee, out of the city of Nazareth, into Judaea, unto the city of David, which is called Bethlehem: because he was of the house and family of David.

Vers. 5. To register himself with Mary his espoused wife, being great with child.

[Indeed, that journey from Nazareth to Bethlehem was eighteen miles, and it was undertaken in the month of December.]

Vers. 6. And it came to pass, that, while they were there, the days were accomplished that she should be delivered.

Vers. 7. And she brought forth her firstborn son, and wrapped him in swaddling clothes, and laid him in a manger; because there was no room for them in the inn.

[The 25th day of December, in the year 4000.]

§. II. To the shepherds in the Bethlehemite field, in that same night, there is announced by an Angel of the Lord, surrounded by brightness, the great and universal joy of the Nativity in the city of David of the Saviour Christ, with the addition of the sign of the infant wrapped in swaddling clothes and placed in a manger.

Vers. 8. And there were in the same country shepherds abiding in the field, keeping watch over their flock by night.

Vers. 9. And, lo, the angel of the Lord came upon them, and the glory of the Lord shone round about them: and they were sore afraid.

Vers. 10. And the angel said unto them, Fear not: for, behold, I bring you good tidings of great joy, which shall be to all people.

Vers. 11. For unto you is born this day in the city of David a Saviour, which is Christ the Lord.

Ver. 12. And this shall be a sign unto you: You shall find the infant wrapped in swaddling clothes, and laid in a manger.

§. III. The hymn of the angelic host is sung in honor of the newly born Savior.

V. 13. And suddenly there was with the Angel a multitude of the heavenly host, praising God, and saying:

Ver. 14. Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men of good will.

§. IV. The shepherds set out for Bethlehem, find the mother and the little infant in the manger: and they make known the word preached by the Angel, while others marvel at it, but Mary keeps and ponders it in her heart, and returning to the fields, they celebrate God.

Ver. 15. And it came to pass, as the Angels departed from them into heaven: the shepherds spoke to one another: Let us go even to Bethlehem, and see this word, which has come to pass, which God has shown to us.

Ver. 16. And they came with haste: and they found Mary and Joseph, and the infant lying in the manger.

Ver. 17. And seeing, they understood concerning the word, which had been spoken to them about this child.

Ver. 18. And all who heard, wondered: and at those things which were told to them by the shepherds.

Ver. 19. But Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart.

Ver. 20. And the shepherds returned, glorifying and praising God for all the things that they had heard and seen, as it was told unto them.

CHAPTER VII.

The Circumcision & Naming of Jesus.

§. I. On the eighth day after his birth Christ was circumcised. [Namely, on the 1st of January, in the year of the world 4001.]

V. 21. And after eight days were accomplished, that the child should be circumcised: his name was called Jesus.

§. II. The name of Jesus, by which he was named before he was conceived in the womb, was imposed upon him.

V. 21. Which (the name Jesus) was called by the Angel, before he was conceived in the womb.

CHAPTER VIII.

The arrival of the Magi from the East, and their return by another way according to divine command.

§. I. Jesus having been born in Bethlehem in the time of King Herod, Magi from the East come to Jerusalem, and inquire where the newborn King of the Jews may be, whom they have come to adore, having seen his star.

Vers. 1. Now when Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judaea in the days of Herod the king, behold, there came wise men from the east to Jerusalem.

Vers. 2. Saying, Where is he that is born King of the Jews? for we have seen his star in the east, and are come to worship him. [We do not doubt that the Magi came from Persia. Now Susa, the academy of the Magi in Persia, is distant from Jerusalem 230 miles towards the East.]

§. II. Herod being terrified, along with all Jerusalem, having gathered the Council, it was investigated where Christ ought to be born, and Bethlehem was designated from Micah (ch. V. 2.)

Vers. 3. And when Herod the king had heard these things, he was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him.

Vers. 4. And gathering all the chief priests and scribes of the people, he inquired of them where Christ should be born.

Vers. 5. But they said to him: In Bethlehem of Judea. For so it is written by the Prophet:

V. 6. And thou Bethlehem, the land of Juda, art not the least among the princes of Juda: for out of thee shall come forth the captain, that shall rule my people Israel.

§. III. Having summoned the Magi, so that Herod might know at what time the star appeared, he sends them to Bethlehem, pretending that he also would worship the infant, to whom, as they were setting out, the star which they had seen went before them, until they arrived where the infant was: whom finding they adored, with gifts of gold, frankincense & myrrh offered.

[Which offering occurred on Jan. 6, in the year of the world 4001.]

V. 7. Then Herod, having called the Magi privately, learned diligently from them the time of the star which appeared to them.

V. 8. And sending them into Bethlehem, he said: Go, and inquire diligently about the child: and when you have found him, report back to me, that I also coming may adore him.

Vers. 9. Who when they had heard the King, went away: and behold the star, which they had seen in the East, went before them, until it came and stood over where the child was.

Vers. 10. And seeing the star, they rejoiced with exceeding great joy.

Vers. 11. And entering the house, they found the child with Mary his mother, and falling down they adored him: and opening their treasures, they offered him gifts, gold, frankincense, and myrrh.

[Bethlehem was distant from Jerusalem by one mile and a half.]

§. IV. The Magi, commanded in a dream not to return to Herod, return to their own country by another way.

Vers. 12. And having received an answer in their sleep not to return to Herod, they returned by another way into their own country.

[Through an interval of about two hundred and thirty miles.]

CHAPTER IX.

The presentation of Christ in the temple, and the testimony of Simeon and Anna.

§. I. When the days of purification were ended, Jesus was brought to Jerusalem, that he might be presented to the Lord according to the law (Exod. XXXIV. 19. Num. VIII. 17.) and that they might offer the appointed sacrifices (Lev. XII. 8.)

Vers. 22. And after the days of her purification according to the law of Moses were accomplished, they brought him to Jerusalem, to present him to the Lord.

Vers. 23. As it is written in the law of the Lord: That every male that openeth the womb shall be called holy to the Lord.

Vers. 24. And that they might give a sacrifice according to that which is said in the law of the Lord, a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons.

[Joseph and Mary brought the little Jesus from Bethlehem to Jerusalem, a mile and a half away, thirty-three days after the circumcision. That the arrival of the Magi preceded the presentation of Christ, and that this did not happen long after the presentation of Jesus (which Andr. Osiander maintains after Eusebius and Epiphanius, as does Anton. Alexandr.), we conclude with the blessed Chemnitz not only from the word παιδίον ἐν τῷ, Matt. II. 1., which is read concerning a newborn boy, Heb. XI. 23., and the particle idè: But also because the parents of Jesus are said to have moved to Nazareth, not Bethlehem, after the purification, Luke II. 39., whereas the Magi found the child with his mother in Bethlehem. And thus the order of the histories coheres perfectly, because meanwhile, while Herod expects the return of the Magi, the boy is presented in the temple of the Lord, and when the report concerning the testimony of Simeon and Anna spread not only through the city, but through all Judea, Herod understood from that, that he had been deluded by the Magi. Nor is it necessary to bring the Magi from the innermost or extreme recesses of Persia; who could easily have measured their journey within 30 days, if perhaps seven days are attributed to their stay in Jerusalem and Bethlehem, and thus have both arrived and departed before the time of purification.]

§. II. The description of Simeon and the oracle given to him, concerning seeing the Christ of the Lord, who, appearing in the temple by the instinct of the Holy Spirit, takes Jesus into his arms, celebrates God, and prays for his departure, because

he had seen with his own eyes the salvation (το σωτήριον) of the Lord, the light of the Gentiles and the glory of Israel: and blessing them while the Father and Mother marveled, he predicts to the mother that Jesus is set for the fall and rising again of many, and for a sign of contradiction, from which a sword is to pass through her own soul.

Vers. 25. And behold there was a man in Jerusalem whose name was Simeon, and this man was just and devout, waiting for the consolation of Israel, and the Holy Spirit was upon him.

V. 26. And he had received an answer from the Holy Spirit that he would not see death before he had seen the Christ of the Lord.

Vers. 27. And he came in the Spirit into the temple. And when his parents brought in the child Jesus, to do for him according to the custom of the law.

Vers. 28. And he took him into his arms, and blessed God, and said:

Vers. 29. Now you dismiss your servant, O Lord, according to your word, in peace.

V. 30. Because my eyes have seen your salvation,

Vers. 31. Which you have prepared before the face of all peoples.

Vers. 32. A light for the revelation of the Gentiles, and the glory of your people Israel.

Vers. 33. And his father and mother were wondering at those things which were spoken concerning him.

Vers. 34. And Simeon blessed them, and said to Mary his mother: Behold this child is set for the fall, and for the resurrection of many in Israel, and for a sign which shall be contradicted.

V. 35. And your own soul a sword shall pierce, that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed.

§. III. Anna the prophetess, daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Asher, a widow of 84 years, serving God perpetually in the temple, at the same hour preached the Lord, and spoke of him to all who were waiting for λύτρωσιν in Jerusalem.

V. 36. And there was Anna the prophetess, the daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Aser: she had advanced in many days, and had lived with her husband seven years from her virginity.

Vers. 37. And she was a widow until eighty-four years: who did not depart from the temple, serving with fastings and supplications night and day,

Vers. 38. And she, coming up at that very hour, gave thanks to the Lord: and spoke of him to all who were awaiting the redemption of Israel.

§. IV. When all these things were finished according to the law, they proceeded in turn into Galilee to their own city, Nazareth. [But soon on the way they are warned about the flight into Egypt, so that they might not have need to go through all of Judea, and Jerusalem itself, first to Nazareth, and from there, by taking up flight again, to pass through Judea and the royal seat of Herod, when they wished to withdraw the infant from the King. See Anti-Grot. on Luke II. 22. p. 37.]

Vers. 39. And when they had performed all things according to the law of the Lord, they returned into Galilee to their own city, Nazareth.

CHAPTER X. The flight into Egypt, and the infanticide of Herod, and upon his death the recall from Egypt, and the dwelling in Nazareth.

§. I. Joseph, being warned by an Angel in a dream to flee into Egypt until he should be recalled, on account of the threatened death of Jesus, immediately that night entered upon the journey with the infant and his mother, and betook himself there until the death of Herod, to fulfill the prophecy (Hos. XI. 1.) That this refers literally to the recall of the own Son of God from Egypt has been shown in Bibl. illustr. Vol. II. part II. page 743.

Vers. 13. Who (the Magi) when they had departed, behold the ange- l of the Lord appeared in a dream to Joseph, saying: Arise, and take the child, and his mother, and flee into Egypt, and be there, until I tell you. For it will come to pass that Herod will seek the child to destroy him.

Ver. 14. Who rising up, took the child and his mother by night, and withdrew into Egypt.

Ver. 15. And he was there until the death of Herod, that it might be fulfilled which was spoken by the Lord through the Prophet saying: Out of Egypt I have called my Son.

[Jerusalem is reckoned to be about seventy miles to Goshen, a region of Egypt.]

§. II. Herod, feeling himself deceived by the Magi, takes care that the males of two years old and younger in Bethlehem and its borders be killed. Where the prophecy of Jeremiah (Chap. XXXI. 15.) was fulfilled.

[We showed in loc. cit. Vol. II. part I. page 447 that Jeremiah there in the literal sense prophesies concerning the weeping arising from that infanticide.]

Ver. 16. Then Herod seeing that he had been mocked by the Magi, was exceeding angry, and sending, killed all the boys that were in Bethlehem, and in all its borders, from two years old and under, according to the time which he had inquired from the Magi.

Ver. 17. Then was fulfilled that which was spoken by Jeremiah the Prophet saying.

Ver. 18. A voice in Rama was heard, lamentation and great mourning: Rachel bewailing her children, and would not be comforted, because they are not.

§. III. Herod being dead, he was ordered by an Angel to return into the land of Israel, and when he heard that Archelaus his son was reigning, and feared for himself, by divine command he betook himself into Galilee, and dwelt in Nazareth, that it might be fulfilled which was spoken by the Prophets, He shall be called a Nazarene.

(Where we inquire into that saying in Anti-Grotian. ad h. l.)

[The return, however, occurred in the year of the world approximately 4002. Tatian says that Jesus spent a continuous seven years in Egypt; others choose four years, others two. But in Sacred Chronology, section VIII, question 7, we have shown that between the birth of Jesus and the death of Herod at most only a year and three months intervened; therefore, Jesus was left in Egypt for not much more than a year.]

(They returned, however, to the town of Nazareth at an interval of approximately sixty-six miles.)

Verse 19. But when Herod was dead, behold, an Angel of the Lord appeared in dreams to Joseph in Egypt;

Verse 20. Saying: Arise, and take the child and his mother, and go into the land of Israel: for they are dead who sought the life of the child.

Verse 21. Who rising up, took the child and his mother, and came into the land of Israel.

Verse 22. But hearing that Archelaus reigned in Judea in the place of Herod his father, he was afraid to go there: And being warned in dreams, he withdrew into the parts of Galilee.

Verse 23. And coming he dwelt in a city, which is called Nazareth: that it might be fulfilled which was said by the prophets: That he shall be called a Nazarene.

CHAPTER XI.

Concerning the progress of the boy Jesus, and the journey to the feast of the Passover, where he conferred with the Doctors, and the return to his homeland.

§. I. Jesus grows, and is strengthened, full of wisdom, and the grace of God was with him.

[Full of divine and infinite wisdom communicated through the hypostatic union: because in him dwelt all the fullness of the Godhead bodily, Col. II.

9. And all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge were hidden, v. 3. But he grows and is strengthened by the Spirit, not regarding that hypostatic communion of the gifts of the Spirit, for thus he had received the Spirit ουκ εκ μετρου not by measure, and therefore in an immense manner, namely infinite gifts, and truly divine ενεργηματα [mighty works], John III. 34. but regarding the participation of habitual wisdom, which was a gift of the Spirit to him as a man, in personal union indeed, yet not communicated through and because of the union of the person. But as he willed to be made, and had been made in ομοιωματι ανθρωπων in the likeness of other men, Phil. II. 7. He progressed, I say, regarding that wisdom which subjectively, actually, and formally inhered in his mind, not regarding that wisdom by which he possessed the whole fullness of the divinity σωματικως [bodily] and personally: see what we said in Exam. Doct. Reformat. on the person of Christ, Contr. VII. p. 369. Damascene distinguishes between those things which Christ as man had τη χαριτι by grace, as other men, and those which he had δια την προς τον λογον ενωσιν because of the personal union with the Word, and to these he refers the knowledge of all things. Bk. II. de Orth. fid. c. 22.

Vers. 40. And the child grew and was strengthened, full of wisdom: and the grace of God was upon him.

§. II. The parents of Jesus, going to Jerusalem every year for the feast of the Passover, bring with them their son who was twelve years old, but on the return they miss him, they seek him, and find him in the temple in the midst of the Doctors, with whom he was conferring, to the admiration of all; they rebuke him, but are warned that he must be in those things which are his Father's.

Vers. 41. And his parents went every year to Jerusalem, on the solemn day of the Passover.

Vers. 42. And when he was twelve years old, they going up to Jerusalem according to the custom of the feast day.

Vers. 43. And when the days were finished, as they returned, the child Jesus remained in Jerusalem, and his parents did not know it.

Vers. 44. But thinking him to be in the company, they came a day's journey, and sought him among their kinsfolk and acquaintances.

Vers. 45. And not finding him, they returned to Jerusalem, seeking him.

Vers. 46. And it came to pass, after three days they found him in the temple sitting in the midst of the doctors, hearing them, and asking them questions.

Vers. 47. And all who heard him were astonished at his understanding and his answers.

Vers. 48. And seeing him they were amazed. And his mother said to him: Son, why have you done so to us? Behold your father and I have sought you sorrowing.

Vers. 49. And he said to them: How is it that you sought me? Did you not know that I must be about my Father's business?

Vers. 50. And they understood not the word that he spoke to them.

§. III. He went down to Nazareth and was subject to them, and he advanced in wisdom, age, and grace before God and men.

[They are said not to have understood, v. 50, and yet his mother kept those words in her heart, v. 21. Even the word of the Lord that is not understood must be kept, until, God granting, we attain its understanding. Now Nazareth was distant from Jerusalem by an interval of sixteen miles. And these things pertain to the month of Nisan of the year 4013.]

Vers. 51. And he went down with them and came to Nazareth: and was subject to them. And his mother kept all these words in her heart.

Vers. 52. And Jesus advanced in wisdom and age, and grace before God and men.

SECTION I. ARTICLE II. CONCERNING THE NOTIFICATION OF CHRIST IN MANHOOD, AND HIS INAUGURATION TO OFFICE, AND PREPARATION.

CHAPTER I. John's baptism and proclamation, with the rebuke of the Pharisees and Sadducees, and the instruction of the people, primarily prophetic concerning Christ.

§. I. The title having been prefixed, Mark 1:1, the time of the Johannine calling is defined by reason of the rulers and high priests, Luke 3:1-2, and the place and office are designated, Luke 3:3, and its confirmation from Isaiah (Chap. 40:3 et seqq.), Luke 3:4-6. St. Matthew designates the time indefinitely, and the place in the desert of Judea, but he comprehends the sermon with the word μετανοεῖτε [repent], and with the reason added, ἤγγικε γὰρ ἡ βασιλεία τῶν ὀυρανῶν [for the kingdom of heaven is at hand], and he likewise seeks confirmation from Isaiah, Chap. 3:1-3, having subjoined the kind of clothing and food of John and the confluence of the people, who receive baptism having published a confession of sins, v. 4-6, from which St. Mark makes the beginning of the Gospel concerning Jesus Christ the Son of God, with another prophecy (Mal. 3:1) still added. Mark 1:1-7. (The beginning of the Johannine proclamation occurred in the year 4030, perhaps on the feast of trumpets on the first day of the seventh month, or Tishri, which corresponds to September.) Furthermore, concerning the designation of time made by St. Luke, see what has been said in the Sacred Chronology concerning the prophetic passages of Isaiah and Malachi, and what has been said concerning those in the Annotations.

Mark 1:1. The beginning of the Gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God.

Luke 3:1. Now in the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, Pontius Pilate being governor of Judea, and Herod being tetrarch of Galilee, and his brother Philip tetrarch of Iturea and of the region of Trachonitis, and Lysanias the tetrarch of Abilene.

Verse 2. Under the high priests Annas and Caiaphas, the word of the Lord came unto John the son of Zacharias in the wilderness.

Verse 3. And he came into all the country about Jordan, preaching the baptism of repentance for the remission of sins.

Matt. 3:1. In those days came John the Baptist, preaching in the wilderness of Judea.

Vers. 2. And saying: Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.

Vers. 3. For this is he who was spoken of by the prophet Isaiah, saying: The voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord: make his paths straight.

Luke III. v. 4. As it is written in the book of the words of Isaiah the prophet: The voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord: make his paths straight.

Vers. 5. Every valley shall be filled: and every mountain and hill shall be brought low, and the crooked shall be made straight and the rough ways plain.

Vers. 6. And all flesh shall see the salvation of God.

Mark I. v. 2. As it is written in Isaiah the prophet: Behold I send my angel before thy face, who shall prepare thy way before thee.

Vers. 3. The voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord, make his paths straight.

Vers. 4. John was in the desert baptizing, and preaching the baptism of repentance for the remission of sins. [Understand in Malachi 5) One of the Prophets is named, namely the older and principal one, and yet at the same time the prophecy of another Prophet is brought forward, as being not only ὁμόψηφον, but also

fixed upon the former, and as it were placing before the eyes the execution of the same, which is furthermore prefixed for this reason, so that the agreement of the conclusion of the Old Testament and the beginning of the Gospel of the New Testament may be more clearly exhibited.]

Matth. III. v. 4. But John himself had a garment of camel's hair, and a leather girdle about his loins: and his meat was locusts, and wild honey.

Vers. 5. Then went out to him Jerusalem, and all Judæa, and all the region round about Jordan.

Vers. 6. And were baptized of him in Jordan, confessing their sins.

Marc. I. v. 5. And there went out unto him all the land of Judæa, and they of Jerusalem, and were all baptized of him in the river of Jordan, confessing their sins.

Vers. 6. And John was clothed with camel's hair, and with a girdle of a skin about his loins; and he did eat locusts and wild honey.

[A leather girdle was the garment of the Prophets, 2 Kings I. 8. Zech. XIII. 4. Heb. XI. 37.]
