§. II. John specifically rebukes the Pharisees and Sadducees, and exhorts them to the fruits of repentance, lest they rashly boast of the Abrahamic lineage, since God can raise up children of Abraham from stones, and the axe is already laid to the unfruitful tree.

Matth. III. v. 7. But when he saw many of the Pharisees and Sadducees come to his baptism, he said unto them: O generation of vipers, who hath warned you to flee from the wrath to come.

V. 8. Bring forth therefore fruits meet for repentance.

V. 9. And think not to say within yourselves: We have Abraham to our father. For I say unto you, that God is able of these stones to raise up children unto Abraham.

Verse 10. For now the axe is laid to the root of the trees. Every tree, therefore, which does not bring forth good fruit, shall be cut down, and cast into the fire.

Luke III. v. 7. He said therefore to the multitudes that came forth to be baptized by him: Ye brood of vipers, who hath showed you to flee from the wrath to come.

Verse 8. Bring forth therefore fruits worthy of penance, and do not begin to say: We have Abraham for our father. For I say to you, that God is able of these stones to raise up children to Abraham.

Verse 9. For now the axe is laid to the root of the trees. Every tree therefore that bringeth not forth good fruit, shall be cut down, and cast into the fire.

[He called the Jews in general the brood of vipers, but specifically, however, the Pharisees and Sadducees. Conf. Matt. XXIII. 33.]

§. III. The people are instructed as to what needs to be done: primarily concerning beneficence, the publicans concerning avoiding avarice, the soldiers concerning rapine.

Luke III. v. 10. And the multitudes asked him, saying: What then shall we do?

Verse 11. And he answering, said to them: He that hath two coats, let him give to him that hath none; and he that hath meat, let him do in like manner.

V. 12. And the publicans also came to be baptized, and said to him: Master, what shall we do?

Verse 13. But he said to them: Do nothing more than that which is appointed you.

Vers. 14. And the soldiers also asked him, saying: And what shall we do? And he said to them: Do violence to no man, neither calumniate any man; and be content with your pay.

§. IV. To the people thinking that John was Christ, John answers that he baptizes with water; but that one stronger and more worthy than himself is to come, who will baptize with the Holy Spirit, Luc. III. 15-16. Marc. I. 8. Matt. III. 11. and will purge his floor, Luc. III. 17. Matt.

III. 12. with many other admonitions added. Luke III. 18. which indeed Herod, when he himself was also rebuked at some time on account of Herodias and other offenses, could not stomach, and therefore imprisoned John, which Luke mentions at the same time by way of πρόληψιν [anticipation] on this occasion, v. 19. 20.

Luke III. v. 15. And as the people were in expectation, and all men mused in their hearts of John, whether he were the Christ.

Vers. 16. John answered, saying unto them all: I indeed baptize you with water; but one mightier than I cometh, the latchet of whose shoes I am not worthy to unloose: he shall baptize you with the Holy Ghost and with fire.

Mark I. v. 7. And preached, saying: There cometh one mightier than I after me, the latchet of whose shoes I am not worthy to stoop down and unloose.

Vers. 8. I indeed have baptized you with water; but he shall baptize you with the Holy Ghost.

Matt. III. v. 11. I indeed baptize you with water unto repentance; but he that cometh after me is mightier than I, whose shoes I am not worthy to bear: he shall baptize you with the Holy Ghost, and with fire.

[The baptism of water is not denied to consist of the Spirit, see John III. 5, but the ministerial and principal cause is distinguished, because it is a matter of the dignity not of the baptism, but of the Baptist. John indeed dispenses the baptism of water as a minister; but Christ was to baptize with the Spirit and with fire, as the supreme cause, about to pour out the Holy Spirit upon the Apostles themselves, the chief ministers, at the feast of Pentecost in the visible form of fire, Acts I. 5 and II. 3, 4, and to purge his church in such a way that he will burn the chaff with eternal fire. Which is not the work of a minister, but of Christ himself, Matt. XIII, 40. seqq.]

Matt. III. v. 12. Whose fan is in his hand, and he will throughly purge his floor: and will gather his wheat into the garner; but the chaff he will burn with fire unquenchable.

Luke 3:17. Whose winnowing fan is in his hand, and he will purge his floor, and will gather the wheat into his barn; but the chaff he will burn with fire unquenchable.

Verse 18. And many other things exhorting, he preached unto the people.

Verse 19. But Herod the tetrarch, being reproved by him for Herodias his brother Philip's wife, and for all the evils which Herod had done,

Verse 20. Added yet this above all, that he shut up John in prison.

CHAPTER II. The baptism of Christ with the heavenly Θεοφανείᾳ [theophany], on the occasion of which the genealogy of Christ is woven.

§. I. At the same time, when the people were being baptized, Jesus also, coming from Nazareth of Galilee, took care to be baptized, John in no way refusing, who rather professed that he himself ought to be baptized by him, that he might fulfill all righteousness, Matt. 3:13-15. Mark 1:9.

Matt. 3:13. Then cometh Jesus from Galilee to Jordan unto John, to be baptized of him.

Verse 14. But John forbade him, saying, I have need to be baptized of thee, and comest thou to me?

Verse 15. And Jesus answering said unto him, Suffer it to be so now: for thus it becometh us to fulfill all righteousness. Then he suffered him.

Mark 1:9. And it came to pass in those days, that Jesus came from Nazareth of Galilee, and was baptized of John in Jordan.

[Jesus came, however, by a journey of thirteen miles from Nazareth to Bethabara at the Jordan.]

§. II. When Jesus was being baptized and was praying, heaven was opened, as Jesus was ascending from the Jordan, with the Holy Spirit descending in the bodily form of a dove, and a voice (of the Father) crying from heaven: This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased, Matt. III. 16. 17. Mark I. 9. 10. 11.

Matth. III. v. 16. And Jesus, when he was baptized, went up straightway out of the water. And lo, the heavens were opened unto him, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove, and coming upon him.

Vers. 17. And lo, a voice from heaven, saying: This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.

Mark I. v. 9. [And he was baptized by John in the Jordan.]

Vers. 10. And straightway coming up out of the water, he saw the heavens opened, and the Spirit like a dove descending, and remaining upon him.

Vers. 11. And there came a voice from heaven: Thou art my beloved Son, in thee I am well pleased.

Luke III. v. 21. Now it came to pass, when all the people were baptized, and Jesus being baptized and praying, heaven was opened:

V. 22. And the Holy Spirit descended in a bodily shape like a dove upon him: and a voice came from heaven: Thou art my beloved Son; in thee I am well pleased.

Which John also commemorates from the mouth of the Baptist, John I. 32. The variant of the Evangelists in reporting the heavenly voice, which Mark and Luke report as uttered in the second person, 'You are my beloved Son'; Matthew in the third, 'This is my beloved Son': Concerning which St. Augustine, Book II de Cons. Evangelist., says: that those who did not retain the same wording retained the same meaning, and that although each of the Evangelists held to the words of the heavenly voice, some nevertheless varied the words to explain the same meaning more familiarly: But it seems simpler and more correct to the blessed Chemnitz, Harm. c. XVII, and to us, that John It also pleased Gerson that that voice of the Father was repeated twice, first to Christ, as Mark and Luke have it, then to the Baptist and the rest, as Matthew reports, since that voice is described in the prophecies of the Prophets in both ways, as Ps. II. 7 in the second person: 'You are my son'; Is. XLII. 1 in the third, 'He is my elect, in whom I am well pleased': so that the Harmony has it thus: And immediately, when he was coming up out of the water (Jesus) saw the heavens being split open, and the Spirit descending upon him like a dove, and a voice came from the heavens saying: 'You are my beloved Son, in you I am well pleased.' And (the Baptist) saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove, and coming upon him. And behold a voice from the heavens saying: 'This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.' Which things agree better than if, with Osiander, annot. to book 1 Harm. c. XV. you say, that the voice of the Father heard from heaven, although it was unique, nevertheless generated different sounds in different ears, so that Christ heard: 'You are my Son' etc., and the others heard: 'This is my Son': just as the same Osiander also (but wrongly) determined that the Apostles, when they received the Holy Spirit and preached the magnificent works of God in one and the same speech, were heard to speak in a different sound and in different languages: and he greatly marvels that this miracle was observed by no one before in this place. St. Augustine warns that in certain Latin codices according to Luke, this voice sounded as what is written in the Psalm: 'You are my Son, today I have begotten you': But he reports that this is not found in the older Greek codices, from which those few Latin ones are to be corrected entirely, no less than from the collation of Mark.

§. III. Having commemorated the time of Christ's age, at which he was baptized, in about his 30th year, St. Luke weaves together his genealogy by ascending from Joseph all the way to Adam, c. III. 23-38. Christ was indeed baptized in the year 4030. Which perhaps was done on the feast of atonement, in the month of Thisri: See what we have said in Chron. sacr. Sect. VIII. Q. V.

Luke III. v. 23. And Jesus himself was beginning to be about thirty years of age, being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph, who was the son of Heli, who was the son of Matthat.

Verse 24. Who was the son of Levi, who was the son of Melchi, who was the son of Jannai, who was the son of Joseph.

Verse 25. Who was the son of Mattathias, who was the son of Amos, who was the son of Nahum, who was the son of Esli, who was the son of Naggai.

Verse 26. Who was the son of Maath, who was the son of Mattathias, who was the son of Semein, who was the son of Josech, who was the son of Joda.

Verse 27. Who was the son of Joanan, who was the son of Rhesa, who was the son of Zerubbabel, who was the son of Shealtiel, who was the son of Neri.

Verse 28. Who was the son of Melchi, who was the son of Addi, who was the son of Cosam, who was the son of Elmadam, who was the son of Er.

Verse 29. Who was the son of Joshua, who was the son of Eliezer, who was the son of Jorim, who was the son of Matthat, who was the son of Levi.

Verse 30. Who was the son of Simeon, who was the son of Judah, who was the son of Joseph, who was the son of Jonam, who was the son of Eliakim.

Verse 31. Who was the son of Melea, who was the son of Menna, who was the son of Mattatha, who was the son of Nathan, who was the son of David.

Verse 32. Who was the son of Jesse, who was the son of Obed, who was the son of Boaz, who was the son of Salmon, who was the son of Nahshon.

Ver. 33. Who was the son of Aminadab, who was the son of Aram, who was the son of Esrom, who was the son of Phares, who was the son of Judah.

Ver. 34. Who was the son of Jacob, who was the son of Isaac, who was the son of Abraham, who was the son of Thara, who was the son of Nachor.

Ver. 35. Who was the son of Sarug, who was the son of Ragau, who was the son of Phaleg, who was the son of Heber, who was the son of Sale.

Ver. 36. Who was the son of Cainan, who was the son of Arphaxad, who was the son of Sem, who was the son of Noe, who was the son of Lamech.

Ver. 37. Who was the son of Mathusala, who was the son of Henoch, who was the son of Jared, who was the son of Malaleel, who was the son of Cainan.

Ver. 38. Who was the son of Enos, who was the son of Seth, who was the son of Adam, who was the son of God. [We have treated this Genealogy abundantly in the Annotations on Luke III. 23.

CHAPTER III. The temptation of Christ in the desert, preparatory to his office.

§. I. Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returning from the Jordan, was driven by the Spirit into the desert, was tempted by the devil for 40 days, Luke IV. 1, 3, Matthew IV. 1, being among the wild beasts, Mark I. 12.

Luke IV. v. 1. And Jesus, being full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan, and was led by the Spirit into the desert.

Ver. 2. For forty days, and was tempted by the Devil.

Matth. IV. v. 1. Then Jesus was led into the desert by the Spirit, to be tempted by the Devil.

Marc. I. v. 12. And immediately the Spirit drove him into the desert.

Vers. 13. And he was in the desert forty days and forty nights: and was tempted by Satan: and he was with the beasts. [It is likely that he was led into the desert of Arabia Petraea, where Moses and Elijah fasted for 40 days, and from there to Mount Sinai, where the law was delivered, at an interval of 34 miles.

§. II. When after those 40 days he was hungry, the Devil attacked Jesus specifically first with the temptation of distrust, that, as the Son of God, he could not make stones into bread: which he repelled with the sentence of Scripture (Deut. VIII. 3.) that man lives not by bread alone, but primarily by the word of God, Luc. IV. 2. 3. 4. Matth. IV. 2-4.

Luc. IV. v. 2. And he ate nothing in those days: and when they were finished he was hungry.

Vers. 3. And the Devil said to him: If you are the Son of God, say to this stone, that it may become bread.

Vers. 4. And Jesus answered him: It is written, that man lives not by bread alone, but by every word of God.

Matth. IV. v. 2. And when he had fasted forty days and forty nights, afterwards he was hungry.

Vers. 3. And the tempter approaching said to him: If you are the Son of God, say that these stones may become bread.

Vers. 4. Who answering said: It is written: Not in bread alone doth man live, but in every word that proceedeth from the mouth of God.

§. III. Then the temptation of presumption followed, Christ being led to the pinnacle of the temple, that he might cast himself down from there, relying on the angelic support (Ps. XCI. 11.) promised, which was thus defeated, because we are forbidden to tempt God (Deut. VI. 16.) Matth. IV. 5-7. Luc. IV. 9-12. Where the words of Luke καὶ ἤγαγεν are to be rendered in the pluperfect: and he had led him into Jerusalem. For that this was done earlier is most clear from Matthew.

Matth. IV. v. 5. Then the devil took him up into the holy city, and set him upon a pinnacle of the temple.

Vers. 6. And he said to him: If thou be the Son of God, cast thyself down. For it is written: That he hath given his angels charge over thee, and in their hands they shall bear thee up, lest perhaps thou dash thy foot against a stone.

Vers. 7. Jesus said to him: It is written again: Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God.

Luc. IV. v. 9. And he brought him to Jerusalem, and set him on a pinnacle of the temple, and he said to him: If thou be the Son of God, cast thyself from hence down.

Vers. 10. For it is written, that he hath given his angels charge over thee, that they keep thee:

Vers. 11. And that in their hands they shall bear thee up, lest perhaps thou dash thy foot against a stone.

Vers. 12. And Jesus answering, said to him: It is said: Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God.

[From the desert and from Mount Sinai, Jesus was led an interval of 30 miles to Jerusalem to the pinnacle of the temple.]

§. IV. Thirdly, the Devil tempted Jesus with the temptation of apostasy: when, with the kingdoms of the world shown on a high mountain, the Devil offered them to Christ if, falling down, He would worship him; but being ordered to depart, because it is written (Deut. VI. 13, ch. X. 20) that God alone is to be worshipped, Matth. IV: 8, Luc. IV. 5-8. This temptation being overcome, and Satan routed, the Angels approached and served Christ, Matt. IV. 11, Marc. I. 13, and so the Devil left Him for a time, Luc. IV. 13. But Jesus was led from the first of the temple to the mountain, as it seems, Pisgah, in which formerly the whole promised land was shown to Moses across the Jordan through an interval of six miles.

[That this was the final temptation, as being the most grievous, and upon its completion, as Luke himself testifies, He said, ὕπαγε ὀπίσω με Σατανᾶ (which the Latin wrongly omitted) ch. IV. 8, Matthew testified: τότε then he left Him, the Devil, which was done finally when all temptations were completed, Luc. IV. 13, and upon his departing, behold, the Angels approached and served Him.

Matth. IV. v. 8. Again the Devil took Him up into an exceeding high mountain, and showed Him all the kingdoms of the world, and the glory of them.

Vers. 9. And said to Him: All these things will I give Thee, if falling down Thou wilt worship me.

Vers. 10. Then Jesus says to him: Get thee hence, Satan; for it is written: Thou shalt worship the Lord thy God, and Him only shalt thou serve.

Luke IV. Verse 5. And the Devil led him up into a high mountain, and showed him all the kingdoms of the world in a moment of time.

Verse 6. And he said to him: To thee I will give all this power, and the glory of them; for to me they are delivered, and to whom I will, I give them.

Verse 7. If thou therefore wilt adore before me, all shall be thine.

Verse 8. And Jesus answering, said to him: It is written: Thou shalt adore the Lord thy God, and him only shalt thou serve.

Matthew IV. Verse 11. Then the Devil left him: and behold Angels came, and ministered to him.

Mark I. Verse 13. And the Angels ministered to him.

Luke IV. Verse 13. And all the temptation being ended, the Devil departed from him, until a time.

[These temptations occur, as some conjecture σοχαςικω̃ς, in the eighth month, called Marcheshvan, corresponding to our October, in the year of the world 4030. After the fast and the temptations, however, Christ returned to John, by whom, having been adorned with distinguished testimonies, he gathered some disciples, with whom having set out into Galilee he changed water into wine, after which he returned from Galilee into Judea for the Paschal feast. Bünting in the Itinerary of our Lord Jesus Christ, page 67, [states that] in the thirtieth year of his age Christ came from Nazareth to Bethabara, and was baptized there by John on Friday, the seventh of October, on the very feast of atonement, in the middle of the last week, Dan. IX, when he was not yet thirty years of age complete: On the seventeenth of November, a Thursday, having completed forty days and nights, Christ at length hungered: From the Kidron valley up to the wall of the outer vestibule, upon which the pinnacles of the temple were placed, he calculates with Josephus, Antiq. book XV, ch. 14, a height of 400 cubits, from where the Devil wished to cast Jesus down: He thinks, however, that Christ rested in December (one of those three temptations having been completed) in Perea, that is, in the further region of the Jordan, not far from John: but that he had not yet begun to teach publicly, because he only completed his 30th year on December 25th, at which age, according to the law in Num. IV, they began to teach. He judges, however, that the miracle of the water changed into wine was performed not on January 6th, as Epiphanius wished, but not long before the feast of the Passover. Moreover, from Mount Nebo or Pisgah, where the Devil had shown Christ the kingdoms of the world, to the Jordan, where John baptized, near Bethabara, there are only two miles: There, in the month of March, John bore witness concerning Christ before the legates of the Jews, and on the two following days, with Christ himself present, pointed out the Lamb of God. Blessed Chemnitius, ch. IV, Proleg. Harm. p. 14, sets up this calculation of days a little differently, relegating the baptism of Christ to the end of November, but the first miracle to February 10th.]

CHAPTER IV. The first testimony of John concerning Christ.

§. I. John testified concerning Christ, whom he had predicted (Matt. 3. 11.) This was he of whom I spoke, John 1. 15.

V. 15. John bears witness of him, and cries out saying: This was he of whom I spoke: he who is to come after me, is made before me: because he was prior to me.

[While Christ was withdrawn from the sight of men into the desert and tempted, Blessed Chemnitius, Harm. ch. XX, thinks that the Baptist meanwhile testified concerning him, now manifested, during those forty days: by which preaching an occasion may have been provided for the following embassy: Which embassy Tattamus places before the baptism of Christ, as does also Ammonius Alexand.: But the particle of time, though not inconsistent, stands in the way of this opinion, connecting the testimony made before the legates with the testimony deposited by John when Christ came to John again, Behold the Lamb of God, John 1. 28. 29. which is said to have been promulgated τῇ ἐπαύριον, the day after the embassy was dispatched. Whence Blessed Chemnitius gathers that at that time, when the legates were setting forth their mandates to the Baptist, Jesus was on the journey from the desert: and came to the Jordan to John on the day immediately following the departure of the legates:] For τῇ ἐπαύριον is not some other day indefinitely, which is wont to be expressed by ἐν μιᾷ τῶν ἡμερῶν, Luke V. 17, but it designates the day immediately following. Jud. VII. 1. Acts XXV. 6.]

§. II. Of his fullness we have received grace for grace, etc.

Verse 16. And of his fullness we all have received, and grace for grace.

Verse 17. Because the law was given through Moses, grace and truth came through Jesus Christ.

Vers. 18. No one has ever seen God: the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has declared him.

[These words can be taken as the Evangelist's own, concerning himself and other Apostles, or the faithful who have professed these things, which is the opinion of Chrysostom and Cyril: in which way, however, it must be said that the preceding testimony in verse 15 is to be understood γυμνῶς (nakedly/simply) as indefinite, and still pertains to the Johannine prologue, by which the testimony of the Baptist is generally comprised: It is better, however, with Origen, Theophylact, and also Ammonius of Alexandria, to join these with the preceding verse, as they cohere through a copulative, and to refer them to the sermon of the Baptist, as the blessed Chemnitz and the blessed Cluver do not deny: so that the sermon of the Baptist held within those 40 days was very illustrious, and by it was shown that Christ far excels Moses and all the Patriarchs and Prophets (no less than John the Baptist) by reason of both person and office: to whom the Baptist numbers himself, because the law and the prophets were until John: Since, although the Patriarchs and other saints had the law, they did not obtain whatever spiritual gifts they had from the works of the law, but from the promise of the Messiah. For the only-begotten Son also ἐξηγήσατο (declared) God the Father to the Patriarchs and all the faithful, because no one knows the Father except the Son, and he to whom the Son wills to reveal him, Matt. XI. 27.]

CHAPTER V. The second testimony of John given to the legates of the council concerning himself and especially concerning Christ.

§. I. The question of the legates proposed to John: Who is he himself? And his answer (from Is. XL. 3.)

Vers. 19. And this is the testimony of John, when the Jews sent Priests and Levites from Jerusalem to him, that they might ask him: Who are you?

Vers. 20. And he confessed, and did not deny: and he confessed: That I am not the Christ.

Vers. 21. And they asked him: What then? Are you Elijah? And he said: I am not. Are you the Prophet? And he answered: No.

V. 22. They said therefore to him: Who are you, that we may give an answer to those who sent us? What do you say about yourself?

Vers. 23. He said: I am the voice of one crying in the desert: Make straight the way of the Lord, as the prophet Isaiah said.

Vers. 24. And those who had been sent were of the Pharisees.

§. II. Further inquiry: Why does he baptize? John declares that he baptizes neither as Christ, nor as Elijah, nor as a Prophet, but as the forerunner of Christ, who has already risen in their midst, of whom he professes himself a most unworthy servant. And this is said to have been done in Bethabara.

Verse 25. And they asked him, and said to him: Why then do you baptize, if you are not the Christ, nor Elijah, nor the Prophet.

Verse 26. John answered them, saying: I baptize in water: but there has stood one in the midst of you, whom you do not know.

Verse 27. He it is, who is to come after me, who was made before me: of whom I am not worthy that I should unloose his shoe latchet.

Verse 28. These things were done in Bethany beyond the Jordan, where John was baptizing.

CHAPTER VI. The third testimony concerning Christ, having been seen himself, promulgated by John.

§. I. The next day John saw Jesus coming to him, and said: Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world. This is he, of whom I said: after me comes a man, who was before me, because he is prior to me.

Verse 29. The next day John saw Jesus coming to him, and said: Behold the Lamb of God, behold him who takes away the sin of the world.

Verse 30. This is he, of whom I said: After me comes a man, who was made before me: because he was prior to me.

[He had said this the day before in verse 27. After me, by reason of the execution of office: Before me, by reason of subsistence: before me, in dignity; for he had not judged himself worthy to unloose the latchets of his shoe. After me, as man: before me, as God: above me, as God and man.]

§. II. He teaches that he himself (as to the individual) had not known Jesus before he was baptized, yet that he had been sent to baptize for the sake of making him known, but that he had seen the Spirit descend upon him like a dove, and it had been said to him, upon whom the Holy Spirit shall descend, he is the one who baptizes with the Holy Spirit: whence he testified that this is the Son of God,

V. 31. And I did not know him, but that he might be manifested in Israel, therefore I came baptizing in water.

Vers. 32. And John bore witness, saying: That I saw the Spirit descending as a dove from heaven, and it remained upon him.

Vers. 33. And I knew him not, but he who sent me to baptize in water, he said to me: Upon whom you shall see the Spirit descending, and remaining upon him, he it is who baptizes in the Holy Spirit.

Vers. 34. And I saw: and I bore witness, that this is the Son of God.

Furthermore, Augustine raises a doubt and explains this place in book II of De Consensu Evangelistarum, chapter 15. If he knew him then, when he saw the dove descending upon him, it must be asked how he said to him when he came to be baptized, 'I ought rather to be baptized by you': for he said this to him before the dove descended. From which it appears, although he already knew him: for he even exulted in his mother's womb when Mary had come to Elizabeth: yet he learned something in him which he had not yet known by the descent of the dove, namely that he himself would baptize in the Holy Spirit, by a certain proper and divine power; so that no man, who had received baptism from God, even if he were to baptize someone, could say that what he was handing over was his own, or that he could give the Holy Spirit from himself. B. Chemnitius, Harmony, chapter XVII. approves the explanation of Chrysostom, that he did not know him before he came from Galilee to John, but when he came to Baptism, he recognized Jesus through the Holy Spirit revealing him inwardly: but the confirmation and sealing of that interior revelation was that public manifestation which happened from heaven, so that the Messiah might be revealed not only to John, but to the whole people. To which opinion we add our own vote.

CHAPTER VII. The fourth testimony of John concerning Christ, and its consequences.

§. I. On the next day, when John saw Christ in the sight of two of his disciples, he pointed him out with his finger: Behold the Lamb of God: who followed him into the lodging: of whom one was Andrew, the brother of Simon Peter.

Vers. 35. The next day again John was standing, and two of his disciples.

Vers. 36. And looking upon Jesus walking, he says: Behold the Lamb of God.

Vers. 37. And the two disciples heard him speaking, and they followed Jesus.

Vers. 38. But Jesus turning, and seeing them following him, says to them: What do you seek? Who said to him: Rabbi, (which is interpreted Master) where do you live?

Vers. 39. He says to them: Come and see. They came and saw where he was staying, and they stayed with him that day: but it was about the tenth hour.

Vers. 40. Now Andrew, the brother of Simon Peter, was one of the two who had heard from John and had followed him.

[Therefore, one of the two was Andrew, the other, as it seems, was John the Evangelist: for he described this history accurately with its circumstances.]

§. II. Andrew announced to his brother Simon that he had found the Messiah, and brought him to Jesus: upon seeing whom, Jesus says: You are Simon the son of Jonah, you shall be called Kephas, which is rendered πέτρος.

Vers. 41. He first finds his brother Simon and says to him: We have found the Messiah (which is interpreted Christ).

Vers. 42. And he brought him to Jesus. But Jesus, looking at him, said: You are Simon the son of Jonah, you shall be called Cephas; which is interpreted Peter.

§. III. The next day, Jesus, intending to go into Galilee, finds Philip, and said to him: follow me. Philip finds Nathanael, and testifies to him about the found Messiah, Jesus of Nazareth: to whom he replies, how can anything good come from Nazareth? He advises: Come and see.

V. 43. On the next day he wanted to go out into Galilee, and he finds Philip. And Jesus says to him: Follow me.

Vers. 44. Now Philip was from Bethsaida, the city of Andrew and Peter.

Vers. 45. Philip finds Nathanael: and says to him: we have found Jesus the son of Joseph from Nazareth, of whom Moses in the law, and the Prophets, wrote.

V. 46. And Nathanael said to him: Can anything good be from Nazareth? Philip says to him: Come and see.

CHAPTER VIII. The conversation of Jesus with Nathanael, in which he makes himself known to him.

§. I. Jesus, having seen Nathanael, declares him a true Israelite, in whom there is no guile.

Vers. 47. Jesus saw Nathanael coming to him, and says of him: Behold a true Israelite, in whom there is no guile.

§. II. To Nathanael asking: whence he knew him? he answers: that he had seen him, before he was called by Philip, sitting under the fig tree: Whence Nathanael acknowledges him, and says: Rabbi, You are the Son of God, You are the King of Israel.

Vers. 48. Nathanael says to him: Whence do you know me? Jesus answered and said to him: Before Philip called you, when you were under the fig tree, I saw you.

Vers. 49. Nathanael answered him, and says: Rabbi, you are the Son of God, you are the King of Israel.

§. III. Christ predicts that he will see even greater things he will see: and heaven opened, and the angels ascending and descending upon the Son of man.

Ver. 50. Jesus answered and said unto him: Because I said unto thee, I saw thee under the fig tree, believest thou? thou shalt see greater things than these.

Ver. 51. And he saith unto him: Amen, Amen I say unto you, you shall see heaven opened, and the Angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of man.

CHAPTER IX. The return of Jesus into Galilee, and the miracle in Cana, with his stay in Capernaum.

§. I. Jesus returns in the power of the Spirit into Galilee, and the fame of him goes out into all the region.

Ver. 14. And Jesus returned into Galilee, and the fame went out concerning him through all the region.

[B. Chemnitius, Harm. ch. xxvi., thinks that Christ came into his own country, Cana of Galilee, on the occasion of Nathanael being brought to the knowledge of him: but since St. Luke testifies, ch. IV. 14, that he returned into Galilee not on that occasion, but in the power of the Spirit, I do not see why this account of Luke, as far as that 14th verse is concerned (for what follows in v. 15 pertains to another return into Galilee designated by John ch. IV. 43), should not be referred to this place: especially because after the temptations of Christ in the desert, into which he had been led by the Spirit, and the testimonies of John concerning Christ, by which disciples were drawn to him, and the taking of certain other disciples described in John I., the return into Galilee followed, and the miracle performed in it at the wedding in John II.] [Thus Ammonius of Alexandria appends this passage of Luke to the dialogue held with Nathanael: but he does not deserve approval in that he immediately leads Jesus from there into the synagogue of Nazareth, and only long afterwards to the wedding in Cana; namely, after the sermon on the mount was finished, and even after the miraculous catch of fish by Peter. Since indeed the first miracle of Jesus was performed at those weddings. Tatian more correctly commemorates those weddings after the particular calling of Peter and others in John I. He returned therefore accompanied by his new disciples Andrew, and John (the Evangelist), Simon (Peter), Philip, and Nathanael, from Bethabara through the vicinity of the town of Bethel, where Jacob saw the ladder of heaven, of which Jesus had spoken with Nathanael, on a journey of thirteen miles into Galilee, to Cana, which he deigned to honor with his first miracle.]

§. II. On the third day, being invited to the wedding in Cana, he is present, and when the wine failed, he turned water into wine: which was his first miracle, by which he manifested his glory, and his disciples believed in him.

Vers. 1. And the third day there was a marriage in Cana of Galilee: and the mother of Jesus was there.

Vers. 2. And Jesus also was invited, and his disciples, to the marriage.

Vers. 3. And the wine failing, the mother of Jesus saith to him: They have no wine.

Vers. 4. And Jesus saith to her: What is that to me and to thee, woman? my hour is not yet come.

Vers. 5. His mother saith to the waiters: Whatsoever he shall say to you, do ye.

Vers. 6. Now there were set there six waterpots of stone, according to the manner of the purifying of the Jews, containing two or three measures apiece.

Vers. 7. Jesus saith to them: Fill the waterpots with water. And they filled them up to the brim.

Vers. 8. And Jesus saith to them: Draw out now, and carry to the chief steward of the feast. And they carried it.

Vers. 9. And when the chief steward had tasted the water made wine, and knew not whence it was, but the waiters knew who had drawn the water; the chief steward calleth the bridegroom,

Vers. 10. And saith to him: Every man at first setteth forth good wine, and when men have well drunk, then that which is worse. But thou hast kept the good wine until now.

Vers. 11. This beginning of miracles did Jesus in Cana of Galilee; and manifested his glory, and his disciples believed in him.

§. III. Then he went down into Capernaum with his mother, brothers, and disciples, and stayed there for some days, until the Passover was near, at which he was going up to Jerusalem.

Vers. 12. After this he went down to Capernaum, he and his mother, and his brothers, and his disciples: and they remained there not many days.

Vers. 12. And the Passover of the Jews was near, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem.

[Cana was distant by an interval of five miles from Capernaum, to which Christ is said to have betaken himself with his brothers, by which name are usually specifically called James the Less, son of Alphaeus, (Matt. X. 3.) and of Mary (Mark XV. 40.) sister of Mary the Virgin (John XIX. 25.) and his brothers Joses, Simon (the Cananaean, Matt. X. 4. called the Zealot, Acts I. 13.) Judas (the Lebbaeus who is also Thaddaeus, Matt. X. 3. called Judas of James, Acts I. 13.), Matt. XIII. 55. Mark VI. 3. Jude v. 1. For these four were cousins of Christ, who in the phrase of Scripture are called brothers: See Matt. XII. 50. ch. XIII. 55. Mark VI. 3. Luke III. 20. Who, since they were from Cana, Matt. X. 4. It is likely that they were present at the wedding. His newly-admitted disciples were Andrew, and his brother, who perhaps was John (the Apostle), whom it seems likely that he also brought to Christ, as he did his brother James the Greater, for they were the sons of Zebedee and Salome, the sister of Joseph, to whom Mary was betrothed, and they are joined later in the call to the fishing of men with Simon Peter and his brother Andrew, Matt. IV. 18, 21. Among the newly-admitted disciples were Simon Peter here, the brother of Andrew, and also Philip from Bethsaida, and Nathanael the Cananaean (John XXI. 2.) from Capernaum, where they did not remain for many days, because the feast of the Passover was near, Jesus betook himself to Jerusalem through fourteen miles: which H. Buntingius, l. c. page 70, from Josephus, l. XV. Antiq. c. 14, and John ch. II. 20, surmises was done at the beginning of April in the 46th year after the restoration of the Jerusalem temple by Herod the Great, King of the Jews. For he says that this first Passover of Christ's ministry was celebrated on the sixth of April, a Thursday, and that this feast lasted until the thirteenth of April.

Osiander designates the third day thus, because Christ remained for two days in that place where John was baptizing, so that John, having seen him, bore witness of him both on the former and the latter day, but Christ departed on the latter day, so that he arrived in Cana of Galilee on the third day. Others understand the third day from Christ's departure from the Jordan. But H. Chemnitius is pleased that the third day from the entry into Galilee, or after Jesus had come into Galilee, is denoted. The Baptist had been staying in Bethabara beyond the Jordan: from where there is a double journey into Galilee: either through Peraea, so that the Jordan is crossed around Gennesaret, or so that the Jordan is crossed at Bethabara, and one passes through Samaria into Galilee: but Cana is in the region for those coming through Samaria, John IV. 46, and so it is likely that Christ passed that way then. But that journey could scarcely be completed in three days: and therefore the third day is most simply understood as the day after he had arrived in Galilee.

SECTION TWO CONCERNING THE ACTS OF CHRIST IN HIS PUBLIC MINISTRY UP TO THE σταυρώσιμον PASSOVER. ARTICLE I. THE ACTS OF CHRIST FROM THE FIRST PASSOVER OF HIS PUBLIC MINISTRY TO THE SECOND.

CHAPTER I.

The cleansing of the temple.

§. I. The first thing that Christ did in his public ministry according to the Evangelists was that he cast out those buying and selling along with the money-changers from the temple, and warned them not to make the house of his Father a house of merchandise.

Vers. 14. And he found in the temple those selling oxen, and sheep, and doves, and the money-changers sitting.

Vers. 15. And when he had made as it were a scourge of cords, he cast them all out of the temple, the sheep also, and the oxen, and he poured out the money of the money-changers, and overturned the tables.

Vers. 16. And to those who were selling doves, he said: Take these things away from here, and do not make the house of my Father a house of merchandise.

§. II. Seeing which, the disciples remembered that which is written (Ps. LXIX. 10.) Zeal for my house consumes me. (Which Psalm we have shown in its proper place in the illustrated Bibles to treat of Christ.)

Vers. 17. And his disciples remembered that it is written: Zeal for your house consumes me.

§. III. The Jews, however, demanded a sign of this authority, which he gave them, the ἔγερσιν or raising up of the temple of his body, which the disciples finally understood after his resurrection.

Vers. 18. The Jews therefore answered and said to him: What sign do you show us, since you do these things?

Vers. 19. Jesus answered and said to them: Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.

Vers. 20. The Jews therefore said: Forty and six years was this temple in building, and will you raise it up in three days?

Vers. 21. But he was speaking of the temple of his body.

Vers. 22. When therefore he was risen from the dead, his disciples remembered that he said this, and they believed the scripture and the word which Jesus had said.

§. IV. Christ nevertheless performed miracles at that Passover, on account of which many believed in him; but he did not entrust himself to them, inasmuch as he knew everyone intimately, without the testimony of any man.

Vers. 23. Now when he was at Jerusalem at the Passover, on the feast day, many believed in his name, seeing his signs which he was doing.

Vers. 24. But Jesus himself did not entrust himself to them, because he knew all men.

Vers. 25. And because he had no need that anyone should bear witness concerning man: for he himself knew what was in man.

CHAPTER II.

The instruction of Nicodemus.

§. I. Nicodemus, approaching Jesus by night, is instructed concerning regeneration in baptism.

Vers. 1. Now there was a man of the Pharisees, named Nicodemus, a ruler of the Jews.

Vers. 2. This man came to Jesus by night, and said to him: Rabbi, we know that you have come from God as a teacher: for no one can do these miracles that you do, unless God is with him.

Vers. 3. Jesus answered and said to him: Amen, amen I say to you, unless one is born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God.

Vers. 4. Nicodemus says to him: How can a man be born when he is old? Can he enter a second time into his mother's womb, and be born?

Vers. 5. Jesus answered: Amen, amen I say to you, unless one is born of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God.

Vers. 6. That which is born of the flesh is flesh: and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit.

Vers. 7. Do not marvel that I said to you: you must be born again.

Vers. 8. The wind blows where it wishes: and you hear its voice. But you do not know where it comes from, or where it goes: so is everyone who is born of the Spirit.

Vers. 9. Nicodemus answered and said to him: How can these things be?

Vers. 10. JESUS answered and said to him: Are you a teacher in Israel, and do you not know these things?

Vers. 11. Amen, amen I say to you, that we speak what we know, and we testify to what we have seen, and you do not receive our testimony.

Verse 12. If I have told you earthly things, and you do not believe: how will you believe, if I tell you heavenly things?

§. II. A fuller account concerning the descent of the Son of man from heaven, his heavenly and divine glory, and his ascent into heaven: and especially his exaltation (on the cross) as the antitype of the bronze serpent exalted in the desert, so that by looking upon him with faith, we may be saved.

Verse 13. And no one has ascended into heaven, but he who descended from heaven, the Son of man, who is in heaven.

Verse 14. And as Moses exalted the serpent in the desert: so must the Son of man be exalted.

Verse 15. That everyone who believes in him may not perish, but may have eternal life.

§. III. An explanation of the causes of salvation, of the universal love of God, of the merit of Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, and of saving faith, as well as the proper cause of condemnation, namely unbelief.

Verse 16. For God so loved the world, that he gave his only-begotten Son: that everyone who believes in him may not perish, but may have eternal life.

Verse 17. For God did not send his Son into the world, to judge the world, but that the world might be saved through him.

Verse 18. He who believes in him is not judged: but he who does not believe is already judged: because he does not believe in the name of the only-begotten Son of God.

V. 19. And this is the judgment: that the light has come into the world, and men loved darkness more than the light: for their works were evil.

Verse 20. For everyone who does evil hates the light and does not come to the light, so that his works may not be reproved.

Verse 21. But he who does the truth comes to the light, so that his works may be manifested, because they are done in God.

This conversation with Nicodemus at Jerusalem seems to have been instituted after the feast of the Passover, where B. Büntingius thinks that JESUS remained during this first year of his ministry until the month of October, in which he also celebrated the feast of tabernacles there, while John the Baptist in the meantime bore witness of him in the desert, and while many were regenerated to eternal life by the doctrine of the Gospel and the sacred font of baptism, so that this year thus had the two greatest and most excellent teachers of all, CHRIST the Son of GOD and John the Baptist, concerning whom see also Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews, book XVIII, chapters 4 and 7.

But if one prefers to listen to the blessed Chemnitz, Jesus did not remain long in Jerusalem, because it is said in John 2:24 that He did not entrust Himself to them, and after other feasts were finished He was not accustomed to remain long in the city; and so, since Nicodemus lived in the city of Jerusalem and was one of those Senators, John 7:50, he judges that this conversation took place when He had returned to Jerusalem from a retreat, conjecturing that it happened at the next feast after the Passover, that is, at Pentecost, Harm., chap. XXVII, p. m. 262. However, he thinks that He withdrew into that part of Judea, around Jerusalem, which, verging toward Samaria and Galilee to the north, belonged to the tribe of Benjamin: just as afterwards in John 3:22, after the conversation with Nicodemus, having left the city of Jerusalem, He came into that part which belongs to the tribe of Judah, situated to the south of Jerusalem, toward Idumea and Egypt: and there He stayed, teaching and baptizing, until the imprisonment of the Baptist, so that in the first year of His ministry Christ traveled through that whole land which is called Judea, on this side and beyond the Jordan, and is distinguished from Samaria and Galilee, and illuminated it with His teaching and miracles: Which opinion of the blessed Chemnitz we judge to be preferred.

CHAPTER III. A discussion concerning the purification of baptism, and the information of John's disciples concerning Christ.

§ I. While Jesus was promoting baptism with His disciples, and John was baptizing in Aenon, a dispute arose concerning purification, with the disciples of John asking why Jesus baptizes, and many flock to Him.

Ver. 22. After these things Jesus and His disciples came into the land of Judea: and He stayed there with them, and was baptizing.

Ver. 23. But John was also baptizing in Aenon, near Salim: because there were many waters there, and they were coming, and were being baptized.

Ver. 24. For John had not yet been sent into prison.

Ver. 25. But a question arose from the disciples of John with the Jews concerning purification.

Ver. 26. And they came to John, and said to him, Rabbi, He who was with you beyond the Jordan, to whom you bore witness, behold, He is baptizing, and all are coming to Him.

[Jesus is said to have come into the land of Judea from Jerusalem, where He had had the conversation with Nicodemus, not because He went first into Galilee and then into Judea, as it seemed to the author of the Historia Scholastica: But because He came into the land of the lot or tribe of Judah, which is specifically called the land of Judea, as in Ezra 2:1, chap. 7:14, 2 Chron. 11:14, chap. 20:17, chap. 36:10, just as Judea, Jerusalem, Samaria, Galilee, and the region around the Jordan are named in this distinct order by the Evangelists, Matt. 3:5, Luke 3:17, chap. 6:17, John 4:3, Acts 9:31. For Jerusalem is situated in the tribe of Benjamin, from where Jesus turned aside into the land of the tribe of Judah assigned to the south of Jerusalem. Ammonius Alexandr. adds this discussion to the confirmation of the Petrine vocation made through the miraculous catch of fish: But Christ was still acting here in Judea: He betook Himself to Galilee, where that miracle happened around the Sea of Gennesaret, only after the report about the imprisoned Baptist.

the same, Büntingius thinks in the place cited, into Judea, after the feast of tabernacles had passed; but B. Chemnitius [thinks it was] immediately after the feast of Pentecost, so that he remained in that land of Judea for nearly five or six months, John 4:35, since the word διατρίβειν signifies to draw out and to remain for a longer delay, and in that part of Judea the Patriarchs, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, for the most part resided, and there received the principal revelations and repetitions of the promise concerning the blessed seed, and died and were buried in the hope of the promise concerning the Messiah. Aenon, however, was not situated on the same bank where Bethabara was, but on the opposite, namely the western bank: near that Salem, into which Gen. 33:18 Jacob crossed, and which was the royal city of Melchizedek, Gen. 14:18, distant 4 miles from Shechem according to Bochart, proceeding towards the east to the Jordan: Therefore John, who had begun in the desert of Judea, which was on the western bank of the Jordan, Matt. 3:1, and having progressed from there to the Jordan from the south towards the north, had baptized across the Jordan in Bethabara: now having progressed further towards the north, having crossed the Jordan and Aenon to the borders of Galilee in the region of Shechem or Samaria, which was situated there, he baptizes. Therefore, the regions adjacent to both the eastern and western banks of the Jordan, which are called περίχωροι, the Baptist traversed with his ministry, and finally progressed into the dominion of Herod in Galilee, where he was captured; Salem was 10½ miles distant from Jerusalem.

§. II. Therefore John recalls his testimony concerning Christ to their memory, and warns them that He is the bridegroom, but he himself is the friend of the bridegroom: that He is from heaven, and above all, and testifies to those things which He has seen and heard. And he teaches that His testimony is divine, indeed that He himself is the Holy Spirit anointed without measure, and that all things have been delivered into His hands, and that eternal life is not had except through faith in the Son.

Verse 27. John answered and said: A man can receive nothing, unless it has been given to him from heaven.

Verse 28. You yourselves bear witness to me, that I said: I am not the Christ: but that I am sent before Him.

Verse 29. He who has the bride is the bridegroom: but the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices with joy because of the bridegroom's voice. This my joy therefore is fulfilled.

Verse 30. He must increase, but I must decrease.

Verse 31. He who comes from above is above all. He who is of the earth is of the earth, and speaks of the earth. He who comes from heaven is above all.

Verse 32. And what He has seen and heard, this He testifies: and no one receives His testimony.

Verse 33. He who has received His testimony has set his seal that God is true.

Verse 34. For He whom God has sent speaks the words of God: for God does not give the Spirit by measure.

Vers. 35. The Father loves the Son: and has given all things into his hand.

Vers. 36. He who believes in the Son has eternal life: but he who is unbelieving toward the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God remains upon him.

[This is the final sermon of John, inasmuch as he was imprisoned shortly after by Herod: concerning whom Luke treated briefly on the occasion, chap. III. 19. 20.

It comprises three things: I. The Person, where he says ἄνωθεν, that is, to have come from heaven, inasmuch as he is ἐπὶ πάντων, GOD over all Rom. IX. 5. The Lord from heaven I. Cor. XV. 47. He came, however, into the earth by assuming our nature, because the Word, which was with the Father in the beginning, was made flesh. II. The Doctrine: where he says: he who is of the earth, speaks of the earth: but he who has seen and heard, this he speaks, as if to say, Mere men understand nothing except earthly things from themselves II. Cor. III. 5. I. Cor. II. 14. But the Son of God, who saw, who heard, who was present at the secret counsel of God, brought forth his doctrine from the bosom of the eternal Father. III. The Office: that because the Father (for his sake) gave him the Spirit not by measure, and because he gave all things into his hands: that for this reason he loves him, because he undertook the work of redemption, so that in the beloved he might also love us Eph. I. 6.

CHAPTER IV.

Christ's conversation with the Samaritan woman.

§. I. John's imprisonment being known, and that a rumor had reached the Pharisees concerning the many disciples of Jesus, he himself, withdrawing through Samaria into Galilee, instituted a conversation on the journey with a Samaritan woman in Sychar, Matt. IV. 12. Mark I. 14. John IV. 1-6. and that on the occasion of water drawn by her from Jacob's well, concerning living water springing up into eternal life, John IV. 6-15.

Matt. IV. Verse 12. Now when Jesus had heard that John had been delivered up, he withdrew into Galilee.

Mark I. Verse 14. Now after John was delivered up, Jesus came into Galilee, preaching the Gospel of the kingdom of God.

John IV. Verse 1. When therefore Jesus knew that the Pharisees had heard that Jesus makes more disciples, and baptizes, than John.

Verse 2. (Although Jesus did not baptize, but his disciples.)

Verse 3. He left Judea, and went again into Galilee.

Verse 4. And he had to pass through Samaria.

Verse 5. He came therefore to a city of Samaria, which is called Sychar: near the plot of ground that Jacob gave to his son Joseph.

Verse 6. And Jacob's well was there. Jesus therefore, being wearied from his journey, was sitting thus by the well. And it was about the sixth hour.

Verse 7. A woman of Samaria came to draw water. Jesus says to her: Give me to drink. [Absurdly, Salmero ascribes Christ to the order of mendicants from this. For he did not beg for water, but requested that it be given to him, so that he might win over the woman, who was still alienated from the true Church and given to whoredom, and lead her to the thirst for living water, or the grace of God, by a suitable discourse, as Pelargus rightly says here: He who sought to drink, thirsted for the faith of the woman herself. Thus he thirsts for the faith of those for whom he shed his blood, says Augustine, Tract. XV. on John.]

Verse 8. (For Jesus' disciples had gone away into the city to buy food.)

Verse 9. That Samaritan woman therefore says to him: How is it that you, being a Jew, ask me to drink, who am a Samaritan woman? For Jews do not associate with Samaritans.

Verse 10. Jesus answered and said to her: If you knew the gift of God, and who it is that says to you, Give me to drink: you perhaps would have asked him, and he would have given you living water.

Verse 11. The woman says to him: Sir, you have nothing to draw with, and the well is deep: from where then do you have living water?

Verse 12. Are you greater than our father Jacob, who gave us the well, and he himself drank from it, and his sons, and his cattle?

Verse 13. Jesus answered and said to her: Everyone who drinks from this water will thirst again: but whoever drinks from the water that I will give him, will not thirst forever:

Ver. 14. But the water that I shall give him shall become in him a fountain of water springing up into eternal life.

Ver. 15. The woman saith unto him: Sir, give me this water, that I thirst not, neither come hither to draw.

[Beautiful are the things which Pelargus has here concerning the spiritual effects of the grace of God in comparison with water: 1. It cleanses, washing away the filth of sins, Ps. LI. 2. It quenches the heat of concupiscence: 3. It removes the thirst and desire for earthly things. 4. Through the affection of love, it binds man together with God and with his neighbor. 5. It makes the soul fruitful, rendering it fertile in good works. 6. And just as water of one and the same nature produces different effects in different things, and sometimes even contrary ones, as in the lily a white color, in the narcissus black, in the rose red, in the violet purple, in the fig it produces sweetness, in wormwood bitterness: So the grace of God bestows upon some especially the Spirit of humility and fear, upon others the Spirit of confidence and magnanimity; in some it stirs up the Spirit of sorrow and sadness, in others of joy and cheerfulness: some it raises to contemplation, others it keeps in the study of cultivating the active life, 1 Cor. XII. Rupertus in h. l. The water which Jesus gives extinguishes the eternal thirst of body and soul from the depths, so that you may not thirst burning among the damned, or burn while thirsting, but with the Lamb as your guide you may proceed to the fountains of the waters of life, and, cleansing all the need of the body with an eternal draught of blessedness, you may not lack any good thing forever. Furthermore, just as waters partly flow down from heaven, partly spring from the earth, and partly flow forth from the sea through hidden channels of the earth: So grace is from God alone in the heavens, and yet it is derived from that immense sea of the charity of Christ, and through the hidden channels, as it were, of the Word and Sacraments, to the souls of men. As living water, which is the comparison of St. Augustine, Tr. XV. in John, flows in such a way that it is joined to its own principle from which it has its origin: So the grace of the Spirit is always joined to its own principle, makes us joined, always depending on the Holy Spirit: Through which the Spirit himself also dwells in us, is united with us, so that we may be joined to him. Beautifully also again Rupertus: What, he says, is water, if not that which is received in baptism, the grace of the Holy Spirit? This water is the Holy Spirit, this water is God: This water is the fountain of life in the heart of God the Father, it is the river of grace and peace in the mouth of God the Son: In the blessed Angels it is a torrent of glory, in the elect of men it is the cleansing of life, which, by whomever it shall have been drunk, leaps back to its matrix, the abyss of eternal Divinity, deeper than hell, longer than the earth, wider than the sea, and higher than heaven.]

§. II. Jesus reveals to the woman the hidden things about her six husbands; whence she recognizes him as a Prophet, and asks about the place of worship, which Christ teaches is now truly everywhere, provided God is worshipped in Spirit and in truth.

Ver. 16. Jesus saith unto her: Go, call thy husband, and come hither.

Ver. 17. The woman answered and said: I have no husband. Jesus saith unto her: Thou hast said well, that I have no husband:

Verse 18. For you have had five husbands; and he whom you now have, is not your husband: this you have said truly.

Verse 19. The woman says to him: Sir, I see that you are a Prophet.

Verse 20. Our fathers adored in this mountain, and you say, that at Jerusalem is the place where it is necessary to adore.

Verse 21. Jesus says to her: Woman, believe me, that the hour comes, when you shall adore the Father neither in this mountain, nor in Jerusalem.

Verse 22. You adore that which you know not: we adore that which we know, for salvation is from the Jews.

Verse 23. But the hour comes, and now is, when the true adorers shall adore the Father in Spirit and in truth. For the Father also seeks such to adore him.

Verse 24. GOD is a Spirit: and they that adore him, must adore in Spirit and in truth.

§. III. To the Samaritan woman making mention of the Messiah, who is to declare all things, Christ testifies that he is the same.

Verse 25. The woman says to him: I know that the Messiah comes (who is called Christ) therefore when he is come, he will announce all things to us.

Verse 26. Jesus says to her: I am he, who speaks with you.

Verse 27. And immediately his disciples came: and they wondered, because he was speaking with the woman. Yet no man said: What do you seek, or why do you speak with her?

§. IV. The Samaritan woman announces this to her fellow citizens. Meanwhile, Christ preaches to his disciples about his food, which is to do the will of the Father, and, taking the occasion of the harvest that would be in four months, he preaches about the sowing for eternal life. Many of the Samaritans indeed believe in Christ because of the woman's speech; but as Christ stayed there for two days, they believed more because of his own speech.

Vers. 28. The woman therefore left her water jar, and went away into the city, and says to those men.

Vers. 29. Come, and see a man who told me everything that I have done: is he perhaps the Christ?

Vers. 30. They went out therefore from the city, and were coming to him.

Vers. 31. Meanwhile the disciples were asking him, saying: Rabbi, eat.

Vers. 32. But he says to them: I have food to eat, which you do not know.

Vers. 33. The disciples therefore were saying to one another: Has anyone brought him something to eat?

Vers. 34. Jesus says to them: My food is that I may do the will of him who sent me, that I may complete his work. [Hence we learn, says Cyril, how great is God's charity toward men; for he considers the conversion of lost men as his food, as it were.]

Vers. 35. Do you not say that there are still four months, and the harvest comes? Behold I say to you: Lift up your eyes, and see the regions, for they are already white for the harvest. - [That harvest, as Cyril says, was altogether splendid, when through the preaching of the Gospel so many peoples attached to earthly things were brought into the threshing floor of the Lord, that is, the Church.]

Vers. 36. And he who reaps receives a reward, and gathers fruit for eternal life: that both he who sows and he who reaps may rejoice together.

Vers. 37. For in this is the true saying: that one is he who sows, and another is he who reaps.

Vers. 38. I sent you to reap that for which you did not take pains: others have taken pains, and you have entered into their labors.

[He encourages the disciples with a threefold argument for reaping or teaching: 1. from the immense opportunity: because just as the harvest was then imminent in Judea, so the regions now seemed to be whitening for the spiritual harvest; 2. from the utility: for the reward will be great, Dan. XII. 3, Matth. V. 12, 1 Petr. V. 4, which remains for both the sower and the reaper, that is, for the Doctor of both the Old and the New Testament; 3. from the ease: for they themselves had not taken pains in sowing the seed: where there is less labor, there is greater delight, according to Chrysost. hom. XXXIII.

Ver. 39. Now many of the Samaritans from that city believed in him, because of the word of the woman testifying: That he told me all things, whatsoever I have done.

Verse 40. When therefore the Samaritans

Verse 41. And many more believed

Verse 42. And they said to the woman: Because

This conversation took place in the month of December in the year 4031, when Christ, having been informed of the imprisonment of the Baptist (Matt. IV. 12) and of the plots of the Pharisees (Joh. IV. 1), departed from the Jordan, and intending to return into Galilee, passed through the region of Samaria, where at the fountain of the Patriarch Jacob, near the town of Sychar (or Sichem), two and a half miles from the Jordan towards the sunset, He conversed with a Samaritan woman, four months before the harvest (Joh. IV. 35), and having entered the town, He remained there for two days, and afterwards, having returned into Galilee, He was kindly received by the Galileans. Furthermore, the blessed Chemnitius judged that the end of the first year of Christ’s ministry could be established at the imprisonment of John: he therefore refers the history of the Samaritan woman to the beginning of the second year. Meanwhile he leaves it free, so that according to the common opinion, which he himself also followed in his harmony, the end of the first year of the ministry is his departure from Judea through Samaria into Galilee, and the healing of the nobleman's son in Cana of Galilee, at which point Büntingius also ended the first year.

Sichem, shoulder by the force of the word, from the summit of Mount Garizim, to which it clung like a shoulder, or rather named from the Prince Sichem, son of Hemor, Gen. XXXIV, is here called Sichar, a sweet but intoxicating drink, שֵׁכָר; it was a city of the Levites and of refuge, Jos. XX & XXI. In its field the Patriarch Joseph was buried, Jos. XXIV. From the southern gate of Sichem, as far as a bow can shoot twice, is Jacob’s well on the way that leads to Jerusalem: above which is a high mountain having two heads or summits, on one of which is Garizim. Joshua recited Deuteronomy, when the blessing was made and the curse was present from the people standing by, and from the other summit of the mountain, Hebal, the response was heard. Upon that mountain Sanballat had built a Samaritan temple, which after two hundred years was utterly destroyed by John Hyrcanus.

CHAPTER V. The second miracle of Jesus in

§. I. Jesus, coming into Galilee, is received by the Galileans, who had seen the things which He had done at Jerusalem, John IV. 43-45. And the fame of Him spread throughout all the surrounding regions, and He taught in their synagogues, being glorified by all, Luke IV. 15.

John IV. 43. Now after two days he departed thence: and went into Galilee.

Ver. 44. For Jesus himself testified, that a prophet hath no honour in his own country.

Ver. 45. Then when he was come into Galilee, the Galilaeans received him, having seen all the things that he did at Jerusalem at the feast: for they also went unto the feast.

Luke IV. 15. And he taught in their synagogues, being glorified of all.

[To one coming into Galilee from Samaria, Nazareth occurs before Cana; but since Jesus wished to pass by Nazareth and head into Cana, he himself provided the reason, as interpreted by Cyril in John IV. 44, namely because a prophet has no honour in his own country, which sentiment he is read to have repeated often at different times, Luke IV. 23, Matt. XIII. 57. The reasons for this proverb are given as follows: (1) because it is almost natural for citizens to envy citizens: for they do not consider the works being done in the present, but recall the fragility of infancy, as Jerome has it in chapter XIII of Matthew. (2) because familiarity is accustomed to breed contempt. Chrysostom on this passage: We are accustomed to value little what is worn out and daily, even if it be great, says Cyril. (3) because on account of the perversity of the world, exotic things are preferred to domestic ones. But that Jesus came into Cana before his own country of Nazareth is evident from the fact that in his own country he testified that his fellow citizens had said: Whatsoever we have heard done by thee in Capernaum, do also here in thy country, Luke IV. 23. For although the Lord performed the miracle of the healing of the nobleman's son while staying in Cana, yet that was done to the son of the nobleman lying ill in Capernaum, and thus it truly happened in Capernaum. And since Christ, coming to Nazareth, himself testified concerning many things done in Capernaum, there is no doubt that he performed other miracles in Capernaum after the healing of the nobleman's son, even if those same ones have not been expressly reported (just as those are not recorded which are said to have been performed at the feast of the Passover, John II. 23, cf. ch. III. 2, ch. IV. 45), before he came to Nazareth.]

§. II. He comes into Cana, and restores to health the nobleman's son who was absent in Capernaum.

John IV. 46. So he came again into Cana of Galilee, where he made the water wine. And there was a certain nobleman, whose son was sick at Capernaum.

Ver. 47. When he heard that Jesus was come out of Judaea into Galilee, he went unto him, and besought him that he would come down, and heal his son: for he was at the point of death.

Ver. 48. Jesus therefore said to him: Unless you see signs and wonders, you do not believe.

Ver. 49. The nobleman says to him: Lord, come down before my son dies.

Ver. 50. Jesus says to him: Go, your son lives. The man believed the word which Jesus spoke to him, and he went.

Ver. 51. And as he was now going down, his servants met him and reported, saying that his son was living.

Ver. 52. He asked therefore the hour from them, in which he had fared better. And they said to him: That yesterday at the seventh hour the fever left him.

Ver. 53. The father therefore knew that it was that hour in which Jesus said to him: Your son lives: and he himself believed, and his whole house.

Ver. 54. This second sign Jesus did again, when he had come from Judea into Galilee.

Sichar was distant from Cana of Galilee by an interval of eight miles. Most identify that nobleman, a minister of Herod Antipas, whose son was lying ill in Capernaum, five miles distant from Cana, as Chuza, called the ἐπίτροπον (steward) of Herod in Luke 8:3. For because the first year of the ministry of Jesus ends in this history, it is helpful to observe with the blessed Chemnitius how he traveled through the principal places of Palestine in the first year, so that he scattered the seeds of his doctrine in them, which would be cultivated in the following years. For he set out from the Galilean city of Nazareth across the Jordan and was baptized there: led from the Jordan into the desert, from the desert he returned to the Jordan, into the region across the Jordan, which is called Perea, where he gathered his first disciples. Thence he set out to Cana of Galilee. From Cana he went down into Capernaum: thence he set out to Jerusalem for the Passover feast; from it he departed into the land of the lot of Benjamin, thence returning again to Jerusalem, where the conversation with Nicodemus was held. Furthermore, from Jerusalem he came into that part which is peculiarly called the land of Judea, and belongs to the tribe of Judah, and he remained there until the end of the year, until, having left Judea, he was about to set out into Galilee, he was present with the Samaritans for two days, and thus he spent the greatest part of the first year in Judea, yet he also scattered certain rays in Perea, Galilee, and Samaria.

CHAPTER VI. The Nazareth Sermon.

§. I. In the Nazareth synagogue he teaches that the prophecy of Isaiah concerning the anointing and mission of the Messiah (ch. 61:1 ff.) is fulfilled in himself.

Luke 4:16. And he came to Nazareth, where he had been brought up, and he entered according to his custom on the Sabbath day into the synagogue, and stood up to read.

Vers. 17. And there was delivered to him the book of the prophet Isaiah. And as he unrolled the book, he found the place where it was written:

Vers. 18. The Spirit of the Lord is upon me: wherefore he hath anointed me, he hath sent me to preach the gospel to the poor, to heal the brokenhearted.

Vers. 19. To preach deliverance to the captives, and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty them that are bruised, to preach the acceptable year of the Lord, and the day of retribution.

Vers. 20. And when he had closed the book, he gave it again to the minister, and sat down. And the eyes of all them that were in the synagogue were fastened on him.

Vers. 21. And he began to say unto them: This day is this scripture fulfilled in your ears.

[This is the first sermon which was delivered by Christ in Galilee, by which Christ demonstrated his calling and mission from Isaiah. For what is said in Luke IV. 15 to have been taught in the synagogues of Galilee is summarized in his preaching: the beginning of which was indeed made here in the synagogue of Nazareth: and that most appropriately, since it concerns the foundation of his office and also the credentials once written out by the Prophet, which deserved the first place of all.]

§. II. While all were wondering, Jesus recognizes that they themselves would demand that miracles, such as he had performed in Capernaum, be performed in his own country: to which, however, he replies that no prophet is accepted in his own country.

Vers. 22. And all bare him witness: and wondered at the words of grace which proceeded out of his mouth, and said: Is not this the son of Joseph?

Vers. 23. And he said unto them: Surely you will say unto me this proverb: Physician, heal thyself: how great things done in Capernaum, do also here in your own country.

Verse 24. But he said: Amen I say to you, that no prophet is accepted in his own country.

§. III. He proposes the example of Elijah, sent only to the woman of Zarephath, and of Elisha, who restored only Naaman, and not others, from leprosy.

Verse 25. In truth I say to you, there were many widows in the days of Elijah in Israel, when the heaven was shut up for three years and six months, when there was a great famine throughout all the land.

Verse 26. And to none of them was Elijah sent, except to Zarephath of Sidon, to a woman, a widow.

Verse 27. And there were many lepers in Israel under Elisha the prophet: and none of them was cleansed except Naaman the Syrian.

§. IV. The Nazarenes, stirred to anger, wish to cast Jesus down from the mountain; but he passed through the midst of them.

Verse 28. And all in the synagogue were filled with anger, hearing these things.

Verse 29. And they rose up, and cast him out of the city: and they led him to the brow of the mountain, upon which their city was built, that they might cast him down.

Verse 30. But he, passing through the midst of them, went his way.

[The Nazareth Sermon pertains to the beginning of the second year of Christ's Ministry, held for them in the month of January: Nazareth, however, is distant from Cana by two miles. Since therefore Jesus had the right of citizenship and a place of residence in Nazareth, and they were no longer willing to bear him among them, he migrated to Capernaum.]

CHAPTER VII.

The summary of Christ's sermon, and the calling of Simon and Andrew, as also of James and John: as also the deliverance of one possessed in Capernaum.

§. I. Jesus therefore betook himself to Capernaum, and dwelt there, that the prophecy of Isaiah might be fulfilled (chap. IX. 1.) Matt. IV. 12-16. and from it he preached: Repent, the kingdom of heaven has drawn near Matt. IV. 17. Mark I. 14. 15. About the sea of Gennesaret he calls Simon and his brother Andrew, and appoints them fishers of men: soon also calling James and John the brothers Matt. IV. 18-22. Mark I. 16-20.

[Capernaum was, however, three miles distant from Nazareth.]

Matt. IV. 12. Now when Jesus had heard that John had been delivered up, he withdrew into Galilee.

Ver. 13. And, leaving the city of Nazareth, he came and dwelt in Capernaum by the sea, in the borders of Zebulun and Naphtali.

Ver. 14. That it might be fulfilled which was spoken by Isaiah the prophet.

Ver. 15. The land of Zebulun, and the land of Naphtali, the way of the sea beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the Gentiles.

Ver. 16. The people who sat in darkness saw a great light: and to those sitting in the region of the shadow of death, light has sprung up for them.

Ver. 17. From that time Jesus began to preach, and to say: Repent: for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near.

Mark 1:14. Now after John was delivered up, Jesus came into Galilee preaching the gospel of the kingdom of GOD.

Verse 15. And saying: For the time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of GOD is at hand; repent and believe in the Gospel.

Matthew 4:18. And Jesus walking by the sea of Galilee, saw two brothers, Simon, who is called Peter, and Andrew his brother, casting a net into the sea (for they were fishermen).

Verse 19. And he said to them: Come after me, and I will make you to become fishers of men.

Verse 20. And they immediately leaving their nets followed him.

Verse 21. And going on from there, he saw other two brothers, James the son of Zebedee, and John his brother, in a ship with Zebedee their father, mending their nets: and he called them.

Verse 22. And they immediately leaving their nets and their father followed him.

Mark 1:16. And passing by the sea of Galilee, he saw Simon; and Andrew his brother, casting nets into the sea (for they were fishermen).

Verse 17. And Jesus said to them: Come after me, and I will make you to become fishers of men.

Ver. 18. And straightway, having left their nets, they followed him.

Ver. 19. And having gone a little further from there, he saw James of Zebedee, and John his brother, and them mending their nets in the boat.

Ver. 20. And immediately he called them. And having left their father Zebedee in the boat with the hired servants, they followed him.

[Christ had indeed come before this also into Capernaum, and had already performed many miracles there, Luke IV. 23, but now he betook himself there in such a way that he dwelt there, where he also obtained the right of residence and citizenship. Cf. Matt. IX. 1, chap. XVII. 24. Moreover, this calling of Simon and Andrew is not to be confused with that confirmation in their calling, described by the miraculous catch of fish in Luke V. 1: because this one happened only after the possessed man was freed, Luke IV. 33-37, Peter's mother-in-law was healed, ver. 38, 39, and many sick were restored, ver. 40, 41, and preaching in other cities of Galilee, ver. 44. Nor indeed is it to be thought that Peter and Andrew had abandoned this calling described by Matthew and Mark because they are read to have fished: for even after the resurrection of Christ, after they had already been confirmed in the ministry by Christ through the breathing of the Holy Spirit, John XX. 21, 22, they fished, chap. XXI. 1, seqq. and the blessed Johannes Gerhardus observes, on Matt. IV. 20, in the annotations, page 233, from Franciscus Lucas Brugensis: That if at any time after their calling they are read to have fished, this was not the fishing of those practicing a trade, but of those fleeing idleness, or relaxing a sorrowful mind. And that they had indeed left their former craft of life, but meanwhile had not immediately renounced all ownership of things. For the account of time compels us to distinguish the confirmation set forth by Luke from the calling handed down by Matthew and Mark: which has also been done by Lyranus, Fr. Toletus, Johannes Maldonatus, and B. Cluverus, and observed concerning Osiander, Molinaeus, Codomannus, and others in the Chemnitian Harmony, chap. XXXVI. Tatian and Ammonius of Alexandria still place the miraculous catch of fish before Christ's withdrawal into the borders of Zabulon and Nephthalim, and the final sermon of John handed down in John III. But wrongly, as is evident. Moreover, the team of four Apostles called here: Simon teaches us to obey Jesus calling, An drew to act manfully, Jacob to supplant the enemy: John to implore the grace of God for these things.

§. II. He teaches in the Capernaite school to the admiration of all, Mark 1:21, 22; Luke 4:31, 32.
