Ver. 28. For the earth bringeth forth fruit of herself; first the blade, then the ear, after that the full corn in the ear.

Ver. 29. But when the fruit is brought forth, immediately he putteth in the sickle, because the harvest is come.

Ver. 30. And he said, Whereunto shall we liken the kingdom of God? or with what comparison shall we compare it?

Ver. 31. It is like a grain of mustard seed, which, when it is sown in the earth, is less than all the seeds that be in the earth:

Ver. 32. But when it is sown, it groweth up, and becometh greater than all herbs, and shooteth out great branches; so that the fowls of the air may lodge under the shadow of it.

Ver. 33. And with many such parables spake he the word unto them, as they were able to hear it.

Ver. 34. But without a parable spake he not unto them: and when they were alone, he expounded all things to his disciples.

[These things may seem not to agree with one another, because Mark records that the Mother with his brothers came to Jesus before the parable of the seed, whereas Luke reports that arrival after the parable. But those words in Luke ch. VIII. 19. παρεγένοντο δὲ πρὸς ἀυτὸν can be understood in the pluperfect, 'They had come, however, to him': and thus the matter will be on firm ground.]

CHAPTER X. The calming of the storm at sea, and the deliverance of the two possessed men.

§. I. A scribe approaches Christ, who is about to cross the sea, intending to follow him; but he hears that the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head: and another, who however first wished to attend to the burial of his father.

Matth. VIII. 18. And Jesus, seeing great crowds around him, gave orders to go across the sea.

Vers. 19. And one scribe approaching, said to him: Master, I will follow you wherever you go.

Vers. 20. And Jesus says to him: Foxes have dens, and birds of the sky have nests: but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.

Vers. 21. And another of his disciples said to him: Lord, permit me first to go and bury my father.

Vers. 22. But Jesus said to him: Follow me, and let the dead bury their own dead.

§. II. When Christ had entered the boat with his disciples, a huge storm arises, which he himself, however, calms with a word, Matth. VIII. 23-27. Marc. IV. 35-40. Luc. VIII. 22-25.

Matth. VIII. 23. And as he was getting into the boat, his disciples followed him:

Vers. 24. And behold, a great disturbance arose in the sea, so that the boat was being covered by the waves, but he himself was sleeping.

Vers. 25. And his disciples approached him, and woke him, saying: Lord, save us, we are perishing.

Vers. 26. And Jesus says to them: Why are you timid, you of little faith? Then rising, he commanded the winds and the sea, and a great calm was made.

Vers. 27. Moreover the men marveled, saying: What manner of man is this, that the winds and the sea obey him?

Marc. IV. 35. And he said unto them on that day, when even was come: Let us pass over unto the other side.

Vers. 36. And sending away the multitude, they take him even as he was in the ship: and there were other ships with him.

Vers. 37. And there arose a great storm of wind, and the waves beat into the ship, so that the ship was filling.

Vers. 38. And he himself was in the stern asleep on a cushion: and they awake him, and say unto him: Master, carest thou not that we perish?

Vers. 39. And rising up he rebuked the wind, and said unto the sea: Peace, be still. And the wind ceased: and there was a great calm.

Vers. 40. And he said unto them: Why are ye fearful? have ye not yet faith? And they feared with a great fear, and said one to another: Who, thinkest thou, is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?

Luc. VIII. 22. And it came to pass on one of the days: and he himself went into a boat, and his disciples, and he said unto them: Let us cross over to the other side of the lake. And they set sail.

Vers. 23. And as they sailed he fell asleep, and there came down a storm of wind into the lake, and they were filling and were in jeopardy.

Vers. 24. And they came and awoke him, saying: Master, we perish. But he rising, rebuked the wind and the tempest of the water, and it ceased: and there was a calm.

Ver. 25. But he said to them: where is your faith? Who fearing, wondered, saying to one another: Who, do you think, is this, because he commands both the winds and the sea, and they obey him?

[Andreas Osiander does not admit this Harmony of the Evangelists, but establishes other and distinct histories, making Matthew's indeed the earlier, but Mark's and Luke's later by a long interval, lib. 1. Harmon. cap. 39. Codomannus, and Paulus Crellius, and others follow him: But there is no necessity to make these histories, so agreeing in circumstances, and differing neither in place nor time, diverse: And therefore in that part we subscribe to the ancients, and to B. Lyser, who hold them for the same history. See Harmon. Lyser. c. LXIV. Osiander confesses that UNTIL NOW, that is, up to his own times, they were held by ALL as the same, on account of their extreme similarity. For in both places, he says, they mention the crossing, but from where they set sail, even if it is certain here, it is certainly expressed there: in both places they relate in almost the same words that a storm arose, that Christ fell asleep, that the disciples awakened him and warned him of the danger, that the storm was calmed by his word, and that the disciples were rebuked for the smallness of their faith. Then in both places they narrate that a legion of demons was cast out and sent into the swine, and that the swine went headlong into the sea and were suffocated. Finally, in both places the herdsmen of the swine reported it to the city, the men came out and saw Christ, and asked that he depart from their borders. At length Osiander adds: For since there has been NO ONE until now, as far as I know, who has consistently thought them to be diverse histories, yet all these, who have attempted to prove them the same, have sweated no less than I see I MUST SWEAT, in order to prove them diverse. But there is no need for any sweat to teach that they are the same. Everything is plain and in the open; there is nothing intricate, nothing perplexed.

§. III. Across the sea in the borders of the Gergesenes he cast out demons from two possessed men, who precipitate the swine into the sea: whence the citizens urge that he depart from their borders.

[He crossed over, however, by one mile and a half into the region of the Gergesenes.) But the other of these possessed men, whom Luke specifically designated, because he wished to follow Christ as he was returning home by ship, is ordered to preach to them what GOD had shown him: which was also done by him. Matt. VIII. 28-34. Mark V. 1-21. Luke VIII. 26-39.

Matt. VIII. v. 28. And when he had come across the strait into the region of the Gerasenes, there met him two having demons, coming out of the tombs, exceeding fierce, so that no one could pass by that way.

Ver. 29. And behold they cried out, saying: What have we to do with thee, Jesus, Son of GOD? Hast thou come hither before the time to torment us?

Ver. 30. And there was not far from them a herd of many swine feeding.

Ver. 31. And the demons besought him, saying: If thou cast us out hence, send us into the herd of swine.

Ver. 32. And he said to them: Go. But they going out went into the swine, and behold the whole herd went with violence down a steep place into the sea: and they died in the waters.

Ver. 33. And the shepherds fled: and coming into the city, they told everything, and concerning those who had had the demons.

Ver. 34. And behold the whole city came out to meet Jesus: and when they saw him they besought him that he would depart from their coasts.

Mark V. 1. And they came across the strait into the region of the Gerasenes.

Ver. 2. And as he was going out of the ship, immediately there met him out of the tombs a man with an unclean spirit.

Vers. 3. Who had his dwelling in the tombs, and now no one could bind him even with chains.

Vers. 4. Because having been often bound with fetters and chains, he had torn apart the chains, and had broken the fetters in pieces, and no one could tame him:

Vers. 5. And always day and night he was in the tombs and on the mountains, crying out, and cutting himself with stones.

Vers. 6. But seeing Jesus from afar, he ran, and worshipped him:

Vers. 7. And crying out with a loud voice, he said: What have I to do with thee, Jesus, son of the most high GOD? I adjure thee by GOD, that thou torment me not.

Vers. 8. For he was saying to him: Go out, thou spirit, from the man.

Vers. 9. And they were asking him: What is thy name? And he says to him: Legion is my name, for we are many.

Vers. 10. And he besought him much, that he would not expel them out of the region.

Vers. 11. And there was there about the mountain a great herd of swine, feeding.

Vers. 12. And the spirits besought him, saying: Send us into the swine, that we may enter into them.

Vers. 13. And Jesus granted it to them immediately. And the unclean spirits going out entered into the swine: and the herd with great violence was cast headlong into the sea, about two thousand, and they were suffocated in the sea.

Vers. 14. But they who were feeding them fled, and reported it in the city, and in the fields. They went out to see what had been done:

Ver. 15. And they come to Jesus: and they see him who had been vexed by the demon, sitting, clothed, and in his right mind, and they were afraid.

Ver. 16. And they who had seen it told them how it had happened to him who had had the demon, and concerning the swine.

Ver. 17. And they began to beseech him that he would depart from their borders.

Ver. And when he was getting into the boat, he who had been vexed by the demon began to beseech him that he might be with him.

Ver. 19. And he did not admit him, but said to him: Go into thy house to thy own, and announce to them how great things the Lord hath done for thee, and hath had mercy on thee.

Ver. 20. And he went away, and began to preach in Decapolis how great things Jesus had done for him: and all were wondering.

Ver. 21. And when Jesus had passed over in the boat again across the strait, a great crowd gathered to him, and he was by the sea.

Luke VIII. 26. And they sailed to the region of the Gerasenes, which is opposite Galilee.

Ver. 27. And when he had gone out to the land, a certain man met him, who had a demon for a long time now, and he was not clothed with a garment, nor did he remain in a house, but in the tombs.

Ver. 28. He, when he saw Jesus, fell down before him: and crying out with a loud voice, said: What is it to me and to thee, Jesus, Son of the most high GOD? I beseech thee, do not torment me.

Vers. 29. For he was commanding the unclean spirit to go out from the man. For many times it would seize him, and he was bound with chains and fetters, being guarded, and having broken the bonds he was driven by the demon into the deserts.

Vers. 30. But Jesus asked him, saying: What is your name? But he said: Legion: because many demons had entered into him.

Vers. 31. And they were begging him not to command them to go into the abyss.

Vers. 32. Now there was there a herd of many swine feeding on the mountain: and they were begging him that he would permit them to enter into them. And he permitted them.

Vers. 33. The demons therefore went out from the man, and entered into the swine: and the herd went with force down a steep place into the lake, and was suffocated.

Vers. 34. When those who were feeding them saw what had happened, they fled, and reported it in the city and in the villages.

Vers. 35. But they went out to see what had happened, and came to Jesus: and they found the man from whom the demons had gone out, sitting at his feet, clothed and in his right mind, and they were afraid.

Vers. 36. And those who had seen it reported to them how he had been made whole from the legion:

Vers. 37. And all the multitude of the region of the Gerasenes asked him to depart from them: for they were seized with great fear. But he, getting into the boat, returned.

Vers. 38. And the man from whom the demons had gone out was begging him that he might be with him. But Jesus sent him away, saying:

Vers. 39. Return to your house, and tell how great things GOD has done for you. And he went through the whole city, preaching how great things Jesus had done for him.

[Whom as more noble and more famous Augustine, book II, On the Harmony of the Gospels, chapter 24; Bede and Strabo as more ferocious; Chrysostom, Theophylact, Euthymius and others think they are named by Mark and Luke. As for the other reasons Osiander has gathered, in order to invent different histories here as well, see them refuted by B. Lyserus, Harmon. CLXVI. Osiander is certainly too bold and reckless, not to say anything more severe, when in his annotations to Harm. Evang. bk. 1, ch. XXXIX, he says: 'I, indeed, unless it is established that what Matthew writes here about two demoniacs is something far different from what Mark and Luke report there about one, see no reason that can be devised why we should not confess that the Evangelists not only lapsed in memory, but also wrote down uncertain things for certain and false for true.' These are Osiander's words; yet he does not deny, when he can always prove diversity in other similar cases with solid arguments, that in this one place he has hardly anything besides those thin and uncertain conjectures. And yet it is wonderful how much he stirs up about this passage, and 'moves the Tyrian seas,' as the saying goes. But in vain. For the fact that Matthew connects this history with those miracles of Christ which were performed in the first year of Christ's preaching, while Mark and Luke connect it with those of the second, is easily refuted, as it is evident that all three refer to the second year. Nor does the argument regarding the diversity of the location of the land of the Gergesenes and Gadarenes have the strength that Osiander believed it especially possessed. Concerning this, see what was said on Mark ch. V.1. Gadara, from which come the Gadarenes, and Gergesa, or Geressa, from which come the Gergesenes, were different towns, yet both were situated on the Lake of Gennesaret, and their borders were so intermingled that, when Christ is read to have come into the region of the latter, he is to be understood as having come into that of the former as well. Tremellius, and following him Casaubon and Tossanus, says: 'Each town was situated on the other side of the Lake of Gennesaret, ἀντιπέραν τῆς γαλιλαίας, as Luke says.' And Pliny and Ptolemy mention Gadara in this tract. I pass over the fact that the Ethiopic and Arabic versions read 'Gergesenes' in all the Evangelists, and that March. Veles and the Stephanus Greek codices VIII and IX are cited, which read γεργεσηνῶν in Mark V. 1: and that Victor of Antioch, Theophylact, and he whose scholia are mixed with the scholia of Euthymius, as noted by Fr. Lucas in his notes on the Gospel of Mark, praise this reading as that of approved books. Whatever may be the case regarding this, since the Greek codices in Luke consistently have γαδαρηνῶν, those different towns situated bordering the Sea of Tiberias across the Jordan both stand well. In the geographical map of the Holy Land edited by the Amsterdam Jews, you have on the further bank of the Lake of Gennesaret the large and famous city גרגש Gerges, situated on a hill or cliff; and from it the region there is named the land of the Gergesenes ארץ הגרגשי. Not far from there, though more remote from the Lake of Gennesaret, is the city גדירה Gedirah, also situated on a hill, next to which is a marsh, which is called מקוחמים, a collection of waters, on the map: Since, therefore, Christ is said in one place to have come ἐις χώραν τῶν γηργεσηνῶν, and in another τῶν γαδαρηνῶν, one must not look to the cities themselves, but to the region in which these cities were situated. Which, whether it was named from the Gergesenes or the Gadarenes, was the same. Whence, when Matthew says, πᾶσα ἡ πόλις, 'all that city' went out to meet Jesus: Luke, who does not mention the city of the Gergesenes, but had made mention of the Gadarenes, does not speak of the city, but ἅπαν τὸ πλῆθος, not simply τῶν γαδαρηνῶν but τῆς περιχώρου τῶν γαδαρηνῶν, he says: you should not understand the citizens of the city of Gadara, but the inhabitants of the adjacent region. Cf. Ludov. de Dieu in h.l. Heidmann's Palaestina, ch. IX. §.76. Cluver's Introduct. bk. V. c. 22. B. Glass. Gram. S. p. 820.

In the Greek text v. 30, it is held, 'a herd of swine was far from them.' How wrongly Huntlaeus wishes to correct it from the Latin: 'not far.' Because all Greek codices agree and Mark has πρὸς τὰ ὄρη: nor is it likely that the swine were mixed with the men, Christ and the others, but were some distance away, not on the shore itself, but at the roots of the mountain. The Syriac and Ethiopic agree with the Greek text, which is so constant that not even one of those sixteen codices which were collated by the Parisians, nor of the sixteen others which were collated by the Marquis Velesius, Peter Faxardus the Spaniard, nor finally any of those which the English used in the preparation of the Polyglot Bibles, gathered from everywhere, departs from it or stands for the Vulgate: The Greek Fathers also agree, as do the Latin; Chrysostom, Theophylact, Hilary, Jerome, etc.

CHAPTER XI.

The healing of the paralytic and the repeated calling of Matthew.

§. I. To Christ coming into his own city, a paralytic is offered, whom he heals.

Matt. IX. 1. And getting into a boat, he crossed over, and came into his own city.

Vers. 2. And behold, they were offering him a paralytic lying on a bed. And Jesus, seeing their faith, said to the paralytic: Take heart, son, your sins are forgiven.

Vers. 3. And behold, some of the scribes said within themselves: This man blasphemes.

Ver. 4. And when Jesus had seen their thoughts, he said: Why do you think evil in your hearts?

Ver. 5. Which is easier to say: Thy sins are forgiven thee; or to say: Arise and walk?

Ver. 6. But that you may know that the son of man has power on earth to forgive sins, then he said to the paralytic: Arise, take up thy bed, and go into thy house.

Ver. 7. And he arose, and went into his house.

Ver. 8. And the multitudes seeing it feared, and glorified GOD, who gave such power to men.

[This paralytic of Matthew is different from the paralytic of Mark II. 3 and Luke V. 18, concerning whom see above Art. 1. Chap. XI. §. 2. For although most of the circumstances are similar, the time is nevertheless entirely different, so that they cannot be considered the same history. For it is manifest from the sequence of Matthew that the present paralytic was healed only after the sermon on the mount: but that paralytic was healed before that sermon. Nor was this paralytic of Matthew let down through the tiles on account of the crowd, as was that one of Mark and Luke: where many are said in Mark to have gathered at the house of Christ, so that the house or the doors could not contain them, of which nothing is held in Matthew. A great confusion is certainly introduced into the sequence and relation of Matthew, unless it is established that this paralytic is different from that one already mentioned above by Mark and Luke, healed a long time before, namely before the second Passover of Christ's ministry, and before the lame man healed at Bethesda.

§. II. Afterwards Christ calls Matthew again, and takes food with the publicans, and defends that, and resolves the question of John's disciples concerning fasting.

Ver. 9. And when Jesus passed on from thence, he saw a man sitting in the custom house, named Matthew. And he saith to him: Follow me. And he arose, and followed him.

Ver. 10. And it came to pass as he was sitting at meat in the house, behold many publicans and sinners coming, sat down with Jesus, and his disciples.

Ver. 11. And the Pharisees seeing it, said to his disciples: Why doth your master eat with publicans and sinners?

Ver. 12. But Jesus hearing it, said: They that are in health need not a physician, but they that are ill.

Ver. 13. Go then and learn what this meaneth: I will have mercy and not sacrifice. For I came not to call the just, but sinners.

Ver. 14. Then came to him the disciples of John, saying: Why do we and the Pharisees fast often, but thy disciples do not fast?

Ver. 15. And Jesus said to them: Can the children of the bridegroom mourn, as long as the bridegroom is with them? But the days will come, when the bridegroom shall be taken away from them, and then they shall fast.

Ver. 16. And nobody putteth a piece of raw cloth unto an old garment. For it taketh away the fulness thereof from the garment, and the rent is made worse.

Ver. 17. Neither do they put new wine into old bottles, otherwise the bottles break, and the wine runneth out, and the bottles perish. But new wine they put into new bottles: and both are preserved.

[We judge that this calling is repeated, from those things which we noted in the preceding article of Chapter XII, and from the very series of the Evangelical narrative; not to mention that the healing of the woman with an issue of blood followed this calling and the banquet and the discussion about fasting in the same place where those things were done, which some think did not dwell in Capernaum, but in Caesarea Philippi, because in that city, in memory of the event, two statues made of bronze were erected, namely of Jesus and of that woman, which Julian the Apostate tore down three hundred years later; as Buntingius reports here from Eusebius, Sozomen, and Nicephorus, p. 82. Nor indeed should it seem strange that a report of a certain banquet celebrated is likewise subjoined here: and of a similar ἐγκλήματι (accusation) of the Pharisees, and Christ's apology: For why could Matthew not have entertained Christ at a banquet a second time?] And since those accusations of the Pharisees, arising from envy and a prurience for calumny, were customary for them, it is to be believed that Christ deemed them unworthy of a new apology, who therefore replied to them again the same thing as before, and thus reminded them again and again of the cause and end of his coming, and consequently of his office. Which must likewise be held concerning the similar question about fasting and the similar response of Christ made on two occasions, although the question is not in all respects similar, but a certain diversity is observed on the part of those asking, who there were not the disciples of John themselves, about whom others were rather instituting the question, but here they are the disciples of John, just as a diversity is also detected here in the apology of Christ, since those words reported by Matthew v. 13, πορευθέντες δὲ μάθετε τί ἐστιν, ἔλεον θέλεω, καὶ ὐ θυσίαν (go and learn what this is, I desire mercy, and not sacrifice), are not repeated among the others. But primarily it is manifest from the consequences among the other Evangelists that this repeated calling of Matthew is not to be confused with that former one: For there, the plucking of the ears of corn on the second-first Sabbath and the healing of the withered hand on the following Sabbath followed the calling of Matthew, which do not follow at all in this place in Matthew, nor can they follow because of the reason of time: And that calling of Matthew happened before the sermon of Christ delivered on the mount, and before the election of the twelve Apostles: But this repetition of the calling is later than the mountain sermon, as also than the election of the Apostles.

CHAPTER XII. The resuscitation of Jairus's daughter, and the healing of the woman with an issue of blood, and also of two blind men, and of a mute, and of many others.

§. I. While he was saying these things (concerning fasting) the ruler of the synagogue came to him, seeking, that his daughter was now dead, and asks that he come and raise her: meanwhile while he goes there, on the way the woman with the issue of blood is healed by him, Matt. IX. 18-26. Mark V. 22-43. Luke VIII. 40-46.

Matt. IX. 18. While he was speaking these things to them, behold one ruler came, and worshipped him, saying: Lord, my daughter is even now dead: but come, lay thy hand upon her, and she shall live.

Ver. 19. And Jesus arose, and followed him, and his disciples.

Ver. 20. And behold a woman, which was diseased with an issue of blood twelve years, came behind him, and touched the hem of his garment.

Ver. 21. For she said within herself: If I may but touch his garment, I shall be whole.

Ver. 22. And Jesus turned him about, and when he saw her, he said: Daughter, be of good comfort, thy faith hath made thee whole. And the woman was made whole from that hour.

Ver. 23. And when JESUS came into the ruler's house, and saw the minstrels and the people making a noise, he said:

Ver. 24. Give place: for the maid is not dead, but sleepeth. And they laughed him to scorn.

Ver. 25. But when the people were put forth, he went in, and took her by the hand. And the maid arose.

Ver. 26. And the fame hereof went abroad into all that land.

Mark 5:22. And there came one of the rulers of the synagogue, Jairus by name: and seeing him, he fell at his feet.

Verse 23. And he besought him greatly, saying: My daughter is at the point of death: Come, lay thy hand upon her, that she may be safe and may live.

Verse 24. And he went with him, and a great multitude followed him, and they thronged him.

Verse 25. And a woman, who was in an issue of blood twelve years.

Verse 26. And had suffered many things from many physicians: and had spent all that she had, and was nothing the better, but rather grew worse.

Verse 27. When she had heard of Jesus, came in the crowd behind, and touched his garment:

Verse 28. For she said: If I shall touch even his garment, I shall be whole.

Verse 29. And immediately the fountain of her blood was dried up: and she felt in her body that she was healed of the plague.

Verse 30. And immediately Jesus knowing in himself the virtue that had gone out from him, turning to the multitude, said: Who hath touched my garments?

Verse 31. And his disciples said to him: Thou seest the multitude thronging thee, and sayest thou: Who hath touched me?

Verse 32. And he looked about to see her who had done this.

Verse 33. But the woman fearing and trembling, knowing what was done in her, came and fell down before him, and told him all the truth.

Ver. 34. But he said to her: Daughter, thy faith hath made thee whole: go in peace, and be whole of thy plague.

Ver. 35. While he was yet speaking, there come from the ruler of the synagogue, saying: Thy daughter is dead: why dost thou trouble the Master any further?

Ver. 36. But Jesus, having heard the word that was spoken, saith to the ruler of the synagogue: Fear not: only believe.

Ver. 37. And he admitted no man to follow him, but Peter, and James, and John the brother of James.

Ver. 38. And they come to the house of the ruler of the synagogue, and he seeth a tumult, and people weeping and wailing much.

Ver. 39. And going in, he saith to them: Why make you this ado, and weep? the damsel is not dead, but sleepeth.

Ver. 40. And they laughed him to scorn. But he having put them all out, taketh the father and the mother of the damsel, and them that were with him, and entereth in where the damsel was lying.

Ver. 41. And taking the damsel by the hand, he saith to her: Talitha cumi, which is, being interpreted: Damsel (I say to thee) arise.

Ver. 42. And immediately the damsel rose up, and walked: and she was twelve years old: and they were astonished with a great astonishment.

Ver. 43. And he charged them strictly, that no man should know it: and commanded that something should be given her to eat.

Luke VIII. 41. And behold there came a man, whose name was Jairus, and he was a ruler of the synagogue: and he fell down at Jesus' feet, beseeching him that he would come into his house.

Ver. 42. For he had an only daughter, almost twelve years old, and she was dying. And it happened, as he went, that he was thronged by the multitudes.

Vers. 43. And a certain woman was in a flow of blood for twelve years, who had spent all her substance on physicians, and could not be cured by any.

Vers. 44. She came behind, and touched the hem of his garment: and immediately the flow of her blood stopped.

Vers. 45. And Jesus said: Who is it that touched me? And all denying it, Peter, and they that were with him, said: Master, the multitudes throng and press thee, and dost thou say: Who touched me?

Vers. 46. And Jesus said: Somebody hath touched me: for I know that virtue is gone out from me.

Vers. 47. And the woman seeing that she was not hid, came trembling, and fell down before his feet: and declared before all the people for what cause she had touched him: and how she was immediately healed.

Vers. 48. But he said to her: Daughter, thy faith hath made thee whole: go in peace.

Vers. 49. As he was yet speaking, there cometh one to the ruler of the synagogue, saying to him: Thy daughter is dead, trouble him not.

Vers. 50. And Jesus hearing this word, answered the father of the girl: Fear not, believe only, and she shall be safe.

Vers. 51. And when he was come to the house, he suffered not any man to go in with him, but Peter, and James, and John, and the father and mother of the girl.

Vers. 52. And all wept and mourned for her. But he said: Weep not, the girl is not dead, but sleepeth.

Vers. 53. And they laughed him to scorn, knowing that she was dead.

Vers. 54. But he taking her hand cried out, saying: Girl, arise.

Vers. 55. And her spirit returned, and she arose immediately. And he commanded that something be given her to eat.

Vers. 56. And her parents were astonished, whom he charged that they should tell no one what had been done.

[There are those who make these different histories, one according to Matthew, another according to Mark and Luke, namely two girls raised from the dead, and likewise two women with an issue of blood healed; but the circumstances are clearly the same, not even excepting the περιςάσεως of time or even place (which are individuating conditions), which sufficiently prove them to be the same persons, not different ones: B. Lyserus, however, dissolves the contrary objections in chapter LXVII of his Harmony, where indeed, as far as time is concerned, there is no need to resort to anticipation or recapitulation here among the Evangelists: since everything flows in the correct order, as has been shown thus far. Osiander is therefore mistaken, who, although he admitted that the history is so similar that he does not know whether anyone before him existed who perceived that one was different from the other: since in both cases, while Christ is proceeding to the girl, a woman suffering from an issue of blood for twelve years, touching the garments of Christ from behind, is healed: in both cases the flute players are cast out from the dead girl: in both cases Christ says the dead girl is not dead, but sleeping: in both cases, having grasped the hand of the dead girl, he restores her to life: he contends, however, that it is not the same, but a different history. The diversity of time is rashly alleged here as a pretext, as is that of place. For the fact that Matthew does not place Christ by the sea as Mark and Luke do, but at a banquet, happened because they passed over that banquet, which we learn from Matthew had intervened: for the rest, it is entirely manifest from the preceding and following election of the Apostles, which are the same among all those three Evangelists, that the time was the same.]

§. II. Passing through Capernaum he heals two blind men.

Vers. 27. And as Jesus was passing on from there, two blind men followed him, crying out and saying: Have mercy on us, Son of David.

Vers. 28. And when he had come into the house, the blind men came to him. And Jesus says to them: Do you believe that I am able to do this for you? They say to him: Yes, Lord.

Vers. 29. Then he touched their eyes, saying: According to your faith let it be done to you.

Vers. 30. And their eyes were opened: and Jesus sternly charged them, saying: See that no one knows.

Vers. 31. But they, going out, spread his fame throughout all that land.

§. III. A certain mute man possessed by the Devil is brought to Christ, whom He frees and heals, and on account of this He is blasphemed by the Pharisees.

Vers. 32. And when they had gone out, behold, they brought to him a mute man, having a demon.

Vers. 33. And when the demons were cast out, the mute man spoke, and the crowds marveled, saying: Never has it appeared so in Israel.

Vers. 34. But the Pharisees were saying: By the prince of the demons he casts out demons.

§. IV. Coming again into his own country (Nazareth), he is despised there, when he was teaching in the school.

Mark VI. v. 1. And going out from there, he went into his own country: and his disciples followed him.

Vers. 2. And when the Sabbath had come, he began to teach in the synagogue: and many hearing were astonished at his doctrine, saying: Whence to this man all these things? and what is the wisdom which is given to him; and such mighty works, which are wrought by his hands.

Vers. 3. Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary, the brother of James, and Joseph, and Jude, and Simon? are not his sisters also here with us? and they were scandalized in him.

Verse 4. And Jesus said to them: A prophet is not without honor except in his own country, and in his own house, and among his own kin.

Verse 5. And he could do no mighty work there, except that he cured a few sick people by laying his hands upon them.

[It is no wonder that a similar contempt is read of here, which had previously befallen him in the same place, 'is this not the son of Joseph!' (although the words vary in that place) because his lineage was known to them, and he was thought to be the son of Joseph, whence the same taunt is also returned by Christ, that no prophet is accepted in his own country: however, the diversity of time clearly compels us to establish different histories. For that first sermon was held at Nazareth, and immediately after he came from the desert from temptation, Luke 4:13-16, and betaking himself thence to Capernaum, he freed one possessed and healed many sick, and that before the miraculous catch of fish and the sermon on the mount: but these things were done long after, as the whole series in Mark teaches: and after the descent from the mountain, the calming of the storm of the sea, and the raising of Jairus's daughter.

§. V. Christ going about teaches everywhere, and heals many, and commands them to pray for laborers to be sent out into the harvest, Matt. 9:35-38, Mark 6, v. 6.

Matt. 9:35. And Jesus went about all the cities and villages, teaching in their synagogues, and preaching the gospel of the kingdom, and healing every sickness and every infirmity.

Verse 36. And seeing the multitudes, he had compassion on them: because they were harassed, and lying like sheep having no shepherd.

Verse 37. Then he says to his disciples: The harvest indeed is great, but the laborers are few.

Verse 38. Pray therefore the Lord of the harvest, that he may send forth laborers into his harvest.

Mark 6:6. And he marveled because of their unbelief, and he went about the villages round about, teaching:

CHAPTER XIII. The sending away of the Apostles.

§. I. The Apostles are sent out with ϑαυματυργικῇ (miraculous) power, whose names Matthew recounts in ch. X. 1-4. Mark VI. 7. Luke IX. 1. 2.

Matt. X. 1. And having called together his twelve disciples, he gave them power over unclean spirits, to cast them out, and to cure every disease, and every infirmity.

Vers. 2. Now the names of the twelve Apostles are these: The first, Simon, who is called Peter, and Andrew his brother,

Vers. 3. James of Zebedee, and John his brother, Philip, and Bartholomew, Thomas and Matthew the publican, James of Alphaeus, and Thaddaeus:

Vers. 4. Simon the Canaanite, and Judas Iscariot, who also betrayed him.

Mark VI. 7. And he called the twelve: and began to send them out two by two, and gave them power over unclean spirits.

Luke IX. 1. And having called together the twelve Apostles, he gave them virtue and power over all demons, and to cure diseases.

Vers. 2. And he sent them to preach the kingdom of GOD, and to heal the sick.

That the Apostles were sent out at the second harvest, towards the end of which the feast of tabernacles was to be celebrated, Ex. XXIII. Lev. XXIII. so that they departed in the month of September, Buntingius determines in Itinerar. Christ. p. 80.

§. I. The instruction of the Apostles, Matt. X. 5-17. Mark VI. 8-11. Luke IX. 3-5.

Matt. X. 5. These twelve Jesus sent forth; commanding them, saying: Go not into the way of the Gentiles, and into the cities of the Samaritans enter ye not:

Vers. 6. But go rather to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.

Vers. 7. And as ye go, preach, saying: That the kingdom of heaven is at hand.

Vers. 8. Heal the sick, cleanse the lepers, raise the dead, cast out devils: freely ye have received, freely give.

Vers. 9. Provide neither gold, nor silver, nor money in your purses.

Vers. 10. Nor scrip for your journey, neither two coats, neither shoes, nor yet staves: for the workman is worthy of his meat.

Vers. 11. And into whatsoever city or town ye shall enter, enquire who in it is worthy; and there abide till ye go thence.

Vers. 12. And when ye come into an house, salute it, saying: Peace be to this house.

Vers. 13. And if the house be worthy, let your peace come upon it: but if it be not worthy, let your peace return to you.

Vers. 14. And whosoever shall not receive you, nor hear your words: going forth out of the house, or city, shake off the dust from your feet.

Vers. 15. Amen I say to you, it shall be more tolerable for the land of Sodom and Gomorrha in the day of judgment, than for that city.

Vers. 16. And behold I send you as sheep in the midst of wolves. Be ye therefore wise as serpents, and simple as doves.

Mark VI. 8. And he commanded them that they should take nothing for the way, but a staff only: no scrip, no bread, nor money in their purse,

Vers. 9. But to be shod with sandals, and that they should not put on two coats.

Vers. 10. And he said to them: Wheresoever you shall enter into an house, there abide till you depart from that place.

Vers. 11. And whosoever shall not receive you, nor hear you, going forth from thence, shake off the dust from your feet for a testimony against them.

Luke IX. 3. And he said to them: Take nothing for your journey, neither staff, nor scrip, nor bread, nor money; neither have two coats.

Vers. 4. And whatsoever house you shall enter into, there abide, and from thence depart.

Vers. 5. And whosoever will not receive you, when ye go out of that city, shake even the dust of your feet for a testimony against them.

§. III. Prediction of persecution, with the promise of the Holy Spirit, of divine providence, and of gracious confession before the Father.

Matt. X. v. 17. But beware of men. For they will deliver you up to councils, and they will scourge you in their synagogues:

Vers. 18. And you shall be led before governors and kings for my sake, for a testimony to them and to the Gentiles.

Vers. 19. But when they deliver you up, do not think how or what you are to speak: for it will be given to you in that hour what you are to speak.

Vers. 20. For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you.

Vers. 21. But brother will deliver brother to death, and father his child, and children will rise up against parents; and will put them to death.

Ver. 22. And you will be hated by all for my name's sake: but he who perseveres to the end, he will be saved.

Ver. 23. But when they persecute you in this city, flee to another. Amen I say to you, you will not finish the cities of Israel, until the Son of man comes.

Ver. 24. The disciple is not above the Master, nor the servant above his lord.

Ver. 25. It is enough for the disciple that he be as his master; and the servant, as his lord. If they have called the master of the house Beelzebub: how much more his household?

Ver. 26. Therefore do not fear them; for there is nothing covered, that will not be revealed; and hidden, that will not be known.

Ver. 27. What I say to you in darkness, speak in the light: and what you hear in the ear, preach upon the housetops.

Ver. 28. And do not fear those who kill the body, but cannot kill the soul: but rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in hell.

Ver. 29. Are not two sparrows sold for a farthing: and one of them will not fall upon the ground without your Father?

Ver. 30. But the very hairs of your head are all numbered.

Ver. 31. Do not fear therefore: you are of more value than many sparrows.

Ver. 32. Everyone therefore who will confess me before men, I also will confess before my Father, who is in heaven.

Vers. 33. But whoever shall deny me before men, I also will deny him before my Father, who is in heaven.

[Jansenius in Conc. Evang. cap. 135. Maldon. in Joh. p. 929. thinking that what is related here by Matthew was not said by Christ to the disciples at that time when he first sent them out, but when his passion was imminent, so that Matthew, on the occasion of that solemn mission described by him, gathered into one body, as it were, those things which were predicted by Christ to the Apostles separately and at different times and places concerning their future lot. But this gathering together (συναθροισμός) of various things from different times and places is foreign to the simplicity and order of the sacred historians; therefore, Toletus, Ribera, and others not undeservedly reject this opinion.]

§. IV. Admonition concerning preferring parents and children after, and following Christ, with the promise of life.

Vers. 34. Do not think that I came to send peace upon earth: I came not to send peace, but the sword.

Vers. 35. For I came to set a man at variance against his father, and the daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law:

Vers. 36. And a man's enemies shall be they of his own household.

Vers. 37. He that loveth father or mother more than me, is not worthy of me: and he that loveth son or daughter above me, is not worthy of me.

Vers. 38. And he that taketh not up his cross, and followeth me, is not worthy of me.

Vers. 39. He that findeth his life, shall lose it: and he that shall lose his life for my sake, shall find it.

§. V. He who receives the Apostles or even any least one, and shows him some benefit, shall not be deprived of a reward.

Vers. 40. He that receiveth you, receiveth me: and he that receiveth me, receiveth him that sent me.

Vers. 41. He who receives a prophet in the name of a prophet, shall receive a prophet's reward: and he who receives a just man in the name of a just man, shall receive a just man's reward.

Vers. 42. And whoever shall give to drink to one of these little ones a cup of cold water only in the name of a disciple: amen I say to you, he shall not lose his reward.

§. VI. The apostles, having been sent out, preach, cast out demons, and heal many, Mark VI. 12. 13. Luke IX. 6. Mark VI. v. 12. And going forth they preached that they should do penance.

Vers. 13. And they cast out many demons, and anointed with oil many that were sick, and healed them.

Luke IX. v. 6. And going forth they went about through the towns, preaching the gospel and healing everywhere.

CHAPTER XIV. The embassy of John to Christ and the testimony of Christ concerning John, as well as the rebuke of certain cities and the invitation of those who are weary and burdened.

§. I. Christ preaches here and there in the cities: whence John, remaining in prison, sends his disciples to him, who are ordered to report those things which they hear and see.

Matthew XI. v. 1. And it came to pass, when Jesus had made an end of commanding his twelve disciples, he passed from thence, to teach and preach in their cities.

Vers. 2. Now when John had heard in prison the works of Christ, sending two of his disciples.

Vers. 3. He said to him: Are you he who is to come, or do we look for another?

Vers. 4. And Jesus answering said to them: Go and report to John what you have heard and seen.

Vers. 5. The blind see, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead rise again, the poor have the gospel preached to them:

Vers. 6. And blessed is he who shall not be scandalized in me. [And here is the proper seat of the embassy of John to Christ, which was related proleptically by Luke ch. VII. 18. on the occasion of the fame of the widow's son raised in Nain, together with the consequences up to verse 36 exclusive. There is therefore no reason why we should establish a hysterology with Cornel. à Lapide in Matthew at this place, as if what he narrates here concerning John happened before the mission of the Apostles. For verse 1 of chapter XI opposes this, openly indicating the order.

§. II. The testimony of Christ to the people concerning John: citing Malachi (ch. III. 1.) and proclaiming the eminence of John.

Vers. 7. And as they were going, Jesus began to say to the crowds concerning John: What did you go out into the desert to see? A reed shaken by the wind?

Vers. 8. But what did you go out to see? A man clothed in soft garments? Behold, those who are clothed in soft garments are in the houses of kings.

Vers. 9. But what did you go out to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet.

Vers. 10. For this is he of whom it is written: Behold, I send my angel before your face, who shall prepare your way before you.

Vers. 11. Amen I say to you, there has not risen among those born of women a greater than John the Baptist: yet he who is lesser in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he.

Vers. 12. And from the days of John the Baptist until now, the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent take it by force.

Vers. 13. For all the prophets and the law, until John, prophesied:

Vers. 14. And if you are willing to receive it, he is Elias, who is to come.

Vers. 15. He that has ears to hear, let him hear.

§. III. Christ's complaint about the people, whom he compares to children sitting in the marketplace, because they received neither John nor the Son of man.

Vers. 16. But to what shall I liken this generation? It is like to children sitting in the marketplace, who crying to their companions

Vers. 17. say: We have sung to you, and you have not danced: we have lamented, and you have not mourned.

Vers. 18. For John came neither eating nor drinking, and they say: He has a devil.

Vers. 19. The Son of man came eating and drinking, and they say: Behold a man that is a glutton, and a drinker of wine, a friend of publicans and sinners. And wisdom is justified by her children.

§. IV. He rebukes certain cities, and says woe to Bethsaida and Chorazin, as also to Capharnaum.

Vers. 20. Then he began to upbraid the cities, wherein were done the most of his miracles, because they had not done penance.

Vers. 21. Woe to thee, Corozain, woe to thee, Bethsaida: for if in Tyre and Sidon had been wrought the miracles that have been wrought in you, they had long ago done penance in sackcloth and ashes.

Verse 22. But I say to you: it shall be more tolerable for Tyre and Sidon in the day of judgment, than for you.

Verse 23. And thou Capharnaum, shalt thou be exalted up to heaven? thou shalt go down even unto hell: for if the miracles had been done in Sodom that have been done in thee, perhaps it would have remained unto this day.

Verse 24. But I say to you, that it shall be more tolerable for the land of Sodom in the day of judgment, than for thee.

§. V. He preaches the Father, and invites to himself all that labor and are burdened.

Verse 25. At that time Jesus answering, said: I confess to thee, O Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because thou hast hid these things from the wise and prudent, and hast revealed them to little ones.

Verse 26. Yea, Father: for so it hath seemed good in thy sight.

Verse 27. All things are delivered to me by my Father. And no one knoweth the Son, but the Father: neither doth any one know the Father, but the Son, and he to whom it shall please the Son to reveal him.

Verse 28. Come to me, all you that labor, and are burdened, and I will refresh you.

Verse 29. Take up my yoke upon you, and learn of me, because I am meek, and humble of heart: and you shall find rest to your souls.

Verse 30. For my yoke is sweet, and my burden light.

CHAPTER XV. The defense of the disciples rubbing the ears of corn, and of himself healing on the Sabbath.

§. I. Christ, as the Passover approaches, passes through the cornfields, and excuses his disciples rubbing the ears of corn on the Sabbath.

Matt. XII. v. 1. At that time Jesus went through the cornfields on the Sabbath: and his disciples being hungry began to pluck the ears of corn, and to eat.

Vers. 2. And the Pharisees seeing it, said to him: Behold thy disciples do that which is not lawful to do on the sabbath days.

Vers. 3. But he said to them: Have you not read what David did, when he was hungry, and they that were with him:

Vers. 4. How he entered into the house of GOD, and did eat the loaves of proposition, which it was not lawful for him to eat, nor for them that were with him, but for the priests only?

Vers. 5. Or have you not read in the law, that on the sabbath days the priests in the temple break the sabbath, and are without blame.

Vers. 6. But I tell you, that there is here a greater than the temple.

Vers. 7. And if you knew what this meaneth: I will have mercy, and not sacrifice: you would never have condemned the innocent.

Vers. 8. For the Son of man is Lord even of the sabbath.

[That this history, although similar, is nevertheless different from the other which is described by Mark in chapter II. 23 and by Luke in chapter VI. 1, the very series of the Evangelical account sufficiently testifies: concerning which matter it has been spoken above in chapter II of this section and article.]

§. II. On the same Sabbath, Christ coming into the synagogue restored a withered hand, while the Pharisees raised a doubt in vain. Whence the Pharisees consult against him, to whom he yields.

Vers. 9. And when he had passed from thence, he came into their synagogue.

Vers. 10. And behold a man having a withered hand, and they asked him, saying: Is it lawful to heal on the sabbath days? that they might accuse him.

Vers. 11. But he said to them: What man shall there be among you, that hath one sheep: and if the same fall into a pit on the sabbath day, will he not take hold on it and lift it up?

Vers. 12. How much better is a man than a sheep? Therefore it is lawful to do good on the sabbath days.

Vers. 13. Then he saith to the man: Stretch forth thy hand. And he stretched it forth, and it was restored to health, even as the other.

Vers. 14. And the Pharisees going out made a consultation against him, how they might destroy him.

Vers. 15. But Jesus knowing it, retired from thence:

§. III. A great multitude follows Christ, and he heals them all, but that they should not make him known: that the prophecy of Isaiah might be fulfilled (Chap. XLII. 1. seqq.) and many followed him, and he healed them all:

Vers. 16. And he charged them that they should not make him known.

Vers. 17. That it might be fulfilled which was spoken by Isaias the prophet, saying:

Vers. 18. Behold my servant, whom I have chosen, my beloved, in whom my soul hath been well pleased. I will put my spirit upon him, and he shall shew judgment to the Gentiles.

Vers. 19. He shall not contend, nor cry out, neither shall any man hear his voice in the streets:

Verse 20. A bruised reed he shall not break, and smoking flax he shall not quench, until he send forth judgment unto victory:

Verse 21. And in his name shall the Gentiles trust.

CHAPTER XVI. The healing of the blind and dumb man, with an apology against blasphemy.

§. I. A blind man, who was dumb and possessed by a demon, is healed; which, when the people marveled at, the Pharisees slander as being done through Beelzebub.

Verse 22. Then was brought unto him one possessed with a devil, blind, and dumb: and he healed him, insomuch that the blind and dumb both spake and saw.

Ver. 23. And all the crowds were amazed, and said: Is this not the son of David?

Ver. 24. But the Pharisees hearing it, said: This man does not cast out demons, except by Beelzebub the prince of the demons.

§. II. Jesus, understanding their thoughts, institutes a defense: and warns concerning blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, that it is irremissible, gravely rebuking the Pharisees.

Ver. 25. But Jesus knowing their thoughts, said to them: Every kingdom divided against itself shall be made desolate: and every city or house divided against itself shall not stand.

Ver. 26. And if Satan casts out Satan, he is divided against himself: how then shall his kingdom stand?

Ver. 27. And if I by Beelzebub cast out demons, by whom do your sons cast them out? Therefore they shall be your judges.

Ver. 28. But if I by the Spirit of God cast out demons, then the kingdom of God has come upon you.

Ver. 29. Or how can anyone enter into the house of a strong man, and plunder his goods, unless he first binds the strong man? And then he will plunder his house.

Ver. 30. He who is not with me, is against me: and he who does not gather with me, scatters.

Ver. 31. Therefore I say to you: Every sin and blasphemy shall be forgiven to men, but the blasphemy of the Spirit shall not be forgiven.

Ver. 32. And whoever shall speak a word against the son of man, it shall be forgiven him: but he who shall speak against the Holy Spirit, it shall not be forgiven him, neither in this world, nor in the future.

Vers. 33. Either make the tree good, and its fruit good: or make the tree bad, and its fruit bad: for by the fruit the tree is known.

Vers. 34. Offspring of vipers, how can you speak good things, when you are evil? for out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks.

Vers. 35. A good man out of the good treasure brings forth good things: and an evil man out of the evil treasure brings forth evil things.

Vers. 36. But I say to you, that for every idle word that men shall speak, they shall give an account of it in the day of judgment.

Vers. 37. For by your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned.

[This apology with the miracle, if you consider the analogy of the sayings and deeds, seems to be the same as those which are presented by Luke Chap. XI. 14. ff., as also those which are handed down by Mark Chap. III. 20. ff., which Tatian also judged; but the miracle and apology of Luke are later than the transfiguration of Christ, the sending out of the LXX disciples, and the conversation with Martha and Mary, whence the blessed Lyserus acknowledges these to be different from the present history of Matthew, Chap. LIX. of the Harmony. Nor can those things which Mark narrates be considered as having occurred at a different time, nor as being the same as these present ones of Matthew, with the blessed Lyserus: For they preceded the calming of the storm of the sea, Mark IV. 35., as also the sending away of the Apostles, Mark VI. 7., Matt. X. 1., which indeed happened before this healing of the blind and mute, and his apologetic defense against blasphemies, described here by Matthew.]

§. III. To some who were replying and demanding a sign, he presents the sign of Jonah, and teaches concerning the Ninevites and the Queen of Sheba who were to accuse them.

Vers. 38. Then some of the Scribes and Pharisees answered him, saying: Master, we wish to see a sign from you.

Vers. 39. He answering said to them: An evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign: and a sign shall not be given to it, except the sign of Jonah the Prophet.

Vers. 40. For as Jonah was in the belly of the whale three days and three nights, so shall the son of man be in the heart of the earth three days and three nights.

Vers. 41. The men of Nineveh shall rise in the judgment with this generation, and shall condemn it: because they repented at the preaching of Jonah. And behold, something more than Jonah is here.

Vers. 42. The Queen of the South shall rise in the judgment with this generation, and shall condemn it, because she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and behold, more than Solomon is here.

§. IV. He predicts evils to this generation, because its latter state shall be worse than its former.

Vers. 43. When, however, the unclean spirit has gone out of a man, he walks through dry places seeking rest, and finds none.

Vers. 44. Then he says: I will return into my house from whence I came out. And coming, he finds it empty, swept, and garnished.

Vers. 45. Then he goes, and takes with him seven other spirits more wicked than himself, and they enter in and dwell there: and the last state of that man becomes worse than the first. So shall it be also to this wicked generation.

§. V. Someone pointing out the presence of his mother and brothers, he teaches that his mother and brothers are those who do the will of God.

Vers. 46. While he was yet speaking to the crowds, behold his mother and brothers stood outside, seeking to speak to him.

Vers. 47. But one said to him: Behold thy mother and thy brothers stand outside, seeking thee.

Vers. 48. But he answering the one who spoke to him, says: Who is my mother, and who are my brothers?

Vers. 49. And stretching forth his hand toward his disciples, he said: Behold my mother and my brothers.

Vers. 50. For whosoever shall do the will of my Father, who is in heaven, he is my brother, and sister, and mother.

[Something similar happened in Mark III. 31, Luke VIII. 19, but at a different time: not indeed, as Osiander wishes, on the same day before and after noon; but that in Luke and Mark was already before the sending out of the Apostles, whereas this was after the same, whence, although the same sayings occur, it must be determined from the diversity of times that they are different histories. It might cause a scruple that, just as Matthew immediately subjoined the Apology of Christ against the calumny concerning Beelzebub to the arrival of the mother and brothers of Christ, this was also done by Mark: but what prevents it, since Christ instituted a similar apology, that his mother and disciples arrived in a similar way, albeit at a different time. For we have previously shown that the Apology commemorated by Mark and Matthew is entirely different, even if in large part similar. The passage in Matt. VIII. 19. 20. 21. can be compared with Luke IX. 57. et seqq., where likewise two similar histories follow one another in both Evangelists concerning a certain man wishing to follow Christ, to whom He said: foxes have holes, and birds of the air have nests, etc., and concerning another, to whom, wishing first to bury his father, He said: Suffer the dead to bury their own dead: and in that similarity not only of the histories, but also of the sequence, we are nevertheless compelled by the circumstances of time and place to make them distinct histories; which B. Lyserus acknowledges in Harmon. c. LXIII.

CHAPTER XVII.

Many parables of Christ.

§. I. On the same day, having gone out to the sea, when many a crowd was gathering, he set forth a parable about the seed.

Ver. 1. On that day Jesus went out of the house, and sat by the sea.

Ver. 2. And great crowds were gathered to him, so that he went up into a boat and sat; and the whole crowd stood on the shore.

Ver. 3. And he spoke many things to them in parables, saying: Behold, the sower went out to sow.

V. 4. And while he was sowing, some fell by the wayside, and the birds of the air came and ate them.

Ver. 5. And others fell on rocky ground, where they did not have much soil, and they sprang up immediately, because they had no depth of soil:

Ver. 6. But when the sun had risen they were scorched: and because they had no root, they withered away.

Ver. 7. And others fell among thorns, and the thorns grew up and choked them.

Ver. 8. And others fell into good soil, and they gave fruit, some a hundredfold, some sixtyfold, some thirtyfold.

Ver. 9. He who has ears to hear, let him hear.

Ver. 10. And the disciples came and said to him: Why do you speak to them in parables?

Vers. 11. He answering said to them: Because to you it is given to know the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven: but to them it is not given.

Vers. 12. For he that hath, to him shall be given, and he shall abound: but he that hath not, from him shall be taken away even that which he hath.

Vers. 13. Therefore do I speak to them in parables: because seeing they see not, and hearing they hear not, neither do they understand.

Vers. 14. And in them is fulfilled the prophecy of Isaiah, who saith: By hearing you shall hear, and shall not understand: and seeing you shall see, and shall not perceive.

Vers. 15. For the heart of this people is grown gross, and with their ears they have heard heavily, and their eyes they have shut, lest at any time they should see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart, and should be converted, and I should heal them.

Vers. 16. But blessed are your eyes, because they see, and your ears, because they hear.

Vers. 17. For amen I say to you, many prophets and just men have desired to see the things that you see, and have not seen them, and to hear the things that you hear, and have not heard them.

V. 18. Hear you therefore the parable of the sower.

Vers. 19. When any one heareth the word of the kingdom, and understandeth it not, there cometh the wicked one, and catcheth away that which was sown in his heart: this is he that received the seed by the way side.

Vers. 20. And he that received the seed upon stony ground, is he that heareth the word, and immediately receiveth it with joy:

Vers. 21. Yet hath he not root in himself, but is for a time: and when there ariseth tribulation and persecution because of the word, he is presently scandalized.

Vers. 22. And he that received the seed among the thorns, is he that heareth the word, and the care of this world and the deceitfulness of riches choketh up the word, and he becometh fruitless.

Ver. 23. But he who was sown into the good ground, this is he who hears the word, and understands, and brings forth fruit, and produces some a hundredfold, some sixty, and some thirty.

[This parable about the seed seems to be the same as that which Luke described in ch. VIII, v. 4 ff. and Mark in ch. IV, 2. But the diversity of time proves them to be different: For that one in Mark and Luke was proposed before the storm was calmed and the Gadarene demoniacs were freed, and also before the sending out of the twelve Apostles: but this one was proposed after all those things: No other parables were joined to that one, which are joined here in great number. Nor indeed is it permitted to object here a certain ὑστερολογίαν (hysteron proteron), or an indefinite designation of time; for Matthew stands in the way of this exception, while he says in v. 1, ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ ἐκείνῃ, that these parables were spoken on that very day on which Christ came into conflict with the Pharisees, on account of the miracle of the cast-out demon, Matt. XII. 22, and on which his mother and brothers had visited him, v. 47. If, however, anyone considers the contents of those chapters of Matt. XI from v. 2, XII & XIII. to v. 53, which cohere with the sending of John's disciples to Christ (assuming the hypothesis that Matthew recorded it there out of natural order, so that he might join the instruction of his own disciples to the instruction of John's disciples, which St. Luke indeed recounted in the aforementioned place, ch. VII. 18), and thinks that the rest handed down there in order should be placed before the histories of Matt. IX. 18 and the following by a certain ὑστερολογίαν (hysteron proteron), he will indeed save the opinion of those who hold that these parables of Christ are the same in place and time as those which Mark describes in ch. IV. 1-34 and Luke in ch. VIII. 1-19: But not without great disturbance of the order observed by St. Matthew, for the sake of preventing which it seems that a different present parabolic discourse must be posited.]

§. II. The parable of the tares among the wheat.

Ver. 24. Another parable he proposed to them, saying: The kingdom of heaven is made like a man who sowed good seed in his field.

Ver. 25. But while men were sleeping, his enemy came, and oversowed tares in the midst of the wheat, and went away.

Ver. 26. But when the herb had grown, and had brought forth fruit, then the tares also appeared.

Ver. 27. And the servants of the householder coming, said to him: Lord, did you not sow good seed in your field? Whence then does it have tares?

Ver. 28. And he said to them: An enemy man has done this. And the servants said to him: Do you want us to go and gather them?

Ver. 29. And he said: No: lest perhaps in gathering the tares, you root up the wheat together with them.

Ver. 30. Let both grow until the harvest, and in the time of the harvest I will say to the reapers: Gather first the tares, and bind them into bundles to be burned, but gather the wheat into my barn.

§. III. The parable of the mustard seed.

Vers. 31. Another parable he proposed to them, saying: The kingdom of heaven is like to a grain of mustard seed, which a man took and sowed in his field.

Vers. 32. Which is the least indeed of all seeds: but when it is grown, it is greater than all herbs, and becomes a tree, so that the birds of the air come and dwell in the branches thereof.

§. IV. The parable of the leaven. The reason for the parabolic discourses is added from the Prophet (David Ps. LXXVIII. 2.)

Vers. 33. Another parable he spoke to them: The kingdom of heaven is like to leaven, which a woman took and hid in three measures of meal, until the whole was leavened.

Vers. 34. All these things Jesus spoke in parables to the multitudes, and without parables he did not speak to them:

Vers. 35. That it might be fulfilled which was spoken by the prophet, saying: I will open my mouth in parables, I will utter things hidden from the foundation of the world.

§. V. He explained the parable of the tares to the disciples privately.

Ver. 36. Then, having dismissed the crowds, he came into the house; and his disciples came to him, saying: Explain to us the parable of the tares of the field.

Ver. 37. He answering said to them: He who sows the good seed is the Son of man.

Ver. 38. And the field is the world. But the good seed, these are the children of the kingdom. And the tares are the children of the wicked one.

Ver. 39. And the enemy, who sowed them, is the Devil. But the harvest is the end of the age. And the reapers are the angels.

Ver. 40. As therefore the tares are gathered, and burned with fire: so shall it be in the end of the age.

Ver. 41. The Son of man shall send his angels, and they shall gather out of his kingdom all scandals, and them who do iniquity:

Ver. 42. And shall cast them into the furnace of fire. There shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth.

Ver. 43. Then shall the just shine as the Sun in the kingdom of their Father. He that has ears to hear, let him hear.

§. VI. A new parable concerning the hidden treasure, and the pearl.

Ver. 44. The kingdom of heaven is like unto a treasure, hidden in a field: which a man having found, hides, and for joy thereof goes, and sells all that he has, and buys that field.

Ver. 45. Again the kingdom of heaven is like to a merchant man, seeking good pearls.

Vers. 46. And having found one precious pearl, he went away, and sold all that he had, and bought it.

§. VII. The parable concerning the net enclosing good and rotten fish, and the explanation of the same.

Vers. 47. Again, the kingdom of heaven is like a net cast into the sea, and gathering together of every kind of fish.

Vers. 48. Which, when it was filled, they drew out, and sitting by the shore, they chose the good into vessels, but the bad they cast out.

Vers. 49. So shall it be at the consummation of the age: the angels shall go out, and shall separate the bad from the midst of the just,

Vers. 50. And shall cast them into the furnace of fire: there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth.

§. VIII. Concerning the Scribe instructed unto the kingdom of God.

V. 51. Have you understood all these things? They say to him: Yes.

Vers. 52. He says to them: Therefore every Scribe instructed in the kingdom of heaven is like a man, a householder, who brings forth from his treasure new things and old.

CHAPTER XVIII. Jesus in Nazareth, despised again.

§. I. These parables finished, Christ returns to his own country, teaching in their schools.

Vers. 53. And it came to pass, when Jesus had finished these parables, he passed on from there.

Verse 54. And coming into his own country, he taught them in their synagogues.

[At the beginning of the third year of Jesus' ministry, that is, the thirty-third of his age, Büntingius gathers from the Evangelists, in Itiner. p. 86, that he returned to Galilee at an interval of 14 miles from Jerusalem, and wintered there in the months of January and February, when, with Spring approaching, shortly after the death of John the Baptist, he crossed over the sea of Tiberias not far from the town of Bethsaida to the further bank of the Jordan, a little before the third Passover of his ministry, Matt. XIV, Mark VI, Luke IX. The journey of the twelve Apostles, who had been sent out by Christ in the month of August of the previous year and had passed through all of Galilee and Judea, teaching the Gospel concerning the Son of God, also lasted more than half a year to seven months: and John was killed in the month of March between the height of winter and Spring, not long before the feast of the Passover: John VI.]

§. II. While many were wondering, because of his known relatives, Christ testified to them that a prophet is not accepted in his own country, so that he performed no miracle there, such that they wondered and said: Whence has this man this wisdom, and these mighty works?

Verse 55. Is not this the carpenter's son? Is not his mother called Mary; and his brothers, James, and Joseph, and Simon, and Judas.

Verse 56. And his sisters, are they not all with us? Whence then has he all these things?

Verse 57. And they were offended in him. But Jesus said to them: A prophet is not without honor, except in his own country, and in his own house.

Verse 58. And he did not do many mighty works there, because of their unbelief.

[Some join here a similar account described in Mark VI. 1. seqq.: But this happened in Mark at another arrival in his country, which indeed took place before the sending out of the Apostles: but the present arrival happened after the sending out and many other intervening events. However, nothing prevents that not once, or twice, but three times a similar contempt happened to Christ in his country, with his lowly lineage being cast in his teeth, and the same taunt being returned by Christ about a prophet not being accepted in his country. For the difference in time does not suggest, but commands, that those different histories be left separate, not confounded. But at the first time at least it is recorded that he refuted that objection: Physician, heal thyself; and that he brought forward the example of Elijah and Elisha, and that his fellow citizens attempted to cast him down from the mountain, Luke IV, such as did not happen on the other occasions.] But that this taunt was familiar to Christ, that no prophet is accepted in his own country, appears, since he also used it when he was going into Galilee, John IV. 44.]

CHAPTER XIX. Christ, withdrawing into the desert on account of Herod, feeds 5000 men, and walks upon the sea.

§. I. The fame of Christ reaches Herod, who thinks that John is risen from the dead: on which occasion the account of the slaughter of John is given. Matt. XIV. 1-12. Mark VI. 14-29. Luke IX. 7-9.

Matt. XIV. Vers. 1. At that time Herod the tetrarch heard the fame of Jesus.

Vers. 2. And he said to his servants: This is John the Baptist, he is risen from the dead, and therefore mighty works are wrought in him.

Vers. 3. For Herod had apprehended John, and bound him: and put him in prison, because of Herodias, his brother's wife.

Vers. 4. For John said to him: It is not lawful for thee to have her.

Vers. 5. And having a mind to kill him, he feared the people: because they esteemed him as a prophet.

Vers. 6. But on Herod's birthday, the daughter of Herodias danced before them: and pleased Herod.

Vers. 7. Whereupon he promised with an oath, to give her whatsoever she would ask of him.

Vers. 8. But she being instructed before by her mother, said: Give me here in a dish the head of John the Baptist.

Vers. 9. And the king was struck sad: yet because of his oath, and for them that sat with him at table, he commanded it to be given.

Vers. 10. And he sent, and beheaded John in the prison.

Vers. 11. And his head was brought in a dish, and it was given to the damsel, and she brought it to her mother.

Ver. 12. And his disciples coming, took up his body, and buried it: and coming they told Jesus.

Mark 6:14. And King Herod heard, (for his name had become manifest) and he said: John the Baptist has risen from the dead: and therefore mighty works are wrought in him.

Verse 15. But others said: It is Elias. But others said: It is a Prophet, as one of the Prophets.

Verse 16. Which having heard, Herod said: John, whom I beheaded, he has risen from the dead.

Verse 17. For Herod himself sent and apprehended John, and bound him in prison, for the sake of Herodias, the wife of Philip his brother, because he had married her.

Verse 18. For John said to Herod: It is not lawful for you to have your brother's wife.

Verse 19. But Herodias laid snares for him: and wanted to kill him, and could not.

Verse 20. For Herod feared John, knowing him to be a just and holy man: and he kept him, and having heard him, he did many things, and heard him gladly:

Verse 21. And when a convenient day had arrived, Herod made a supper on his birthday for the princes, and tribunes, and chief men of Galilee.

Verse 22. And when the daughter of the same Herodias had come in, and had danced, and pleased Herod, and those who were reclining with him, the king said to the girl: Ask of me what you will, and I will give it to you:

Verse 23. And he swore to her: Whatever you shall ask I will give you, even to the half of my kingdom.

Verse 24. Who, when she had gone out, said to her mother: What shall I ask? But she said: The head of John the Baptist.

Vers. 25. And when she had come in immediately with haste to the king, she asked, saying: I will that forthwith thou give me in a dish the head of John the Baptist.

Vers. 26. And the king was struck sad: because of his oath, and because of them that were sitting with him at table, he would not displease her:

Vers. 27. But having sent an executioner, he commanded his head to be brought in a dish. And he beheaded him in the prison.

Vers. 28. And he brought his head in a dish: and gave it to the damsel, and the damsel gave it to her mother.

Vers. 29. Which his disciples hearing came, and took his body, and laid it in a monument.

Luke IX. Vers. 7. Now Herod the tetrarch heard all things that were done by him, and was in a doubt, because that it was said

Vers. 8. by some: That John was risen from the dead; but by some: That Elias had appeared; and by others: That one of the old prophets was risen.

Vers. 9. And Herod said: John I have beheaded: but who is this of whom I hear such things? And he sought to see him. [Herod had kept John imprisoned for a full year and three months: However, that his beheading took place not before the sending out of the Apostles, but about that time when they returned, is to be gathered from Mark and Luke: See B. Lyserus, Harmon. ch. LXXIV, where he makes the whole course of John's ministry two years and six months, so that he spent half the time before his incarceration, and completed the other half of the time in prison. §. II. Therefore Jesus betakes himself into the desert of Bethsaida: whom a great crowd follows with the returned Apostles: and they are fed by Christ miraculously, five thousand men with five loaves and two fishes, Matt. XIV. 13-22. Mark VI. 30-44. Luke IX. 10-17. John VI. 1-14.]

Matth. XIV. Vers. 13. Which when Jesus had heard, he retired from thence by ship, into a desert place apart: and the crowds having heard of it, followed him on foot out of the cities.

Vers. 14. And going out he saw a great crowd, and had compassion on them, and cured their sick.

Vers. 15. And when evening had come, his disciples approached him, saying: The place is deserted, and the hour has already passed: dismiss the crowds, so that going into the villages, they may buy food for themselves.

Vers. 16. But Jesus said to them: They have no need to go: give them something to eat yourselves.

Vers. 17. They answered him: We have nothing here but five loaves, and two fish.

Vers. 18. Who said to them: Bring them here to me.

Vers. 19. And when he had ordered the crowd to sit down on the grass, taking the five loaves and the two fish, looking up to heaven he blessed, and broke, and gave the loaves to the disciples, and the disciples to the crowds.

Vers. 20. And they all ate and were satisfied. And they took up the leftovers, twelve baskets full of fragments.

Vers. 21. Now the number of those eating was five thousand men, besides women and children.

Vers. 22. And immediately Jesus compelled the disciples to get into the boat, and to go before him across the sea, until he should dismiss the crowds.

Mark VI. Vers. 30. And the Apostles gathering together to Jesus, reported to him all things that they had done and taught.

Vers. 31. And he said to them: Come apart into a desert place and rest a little. For there were many who were coming and going: and they did not even have time to eat.

Ver. 32. And getting into the boat, they went away to a desert place by themselves.

Ver. 33. And many saw them going, and recognized them: and they ran together there on foot from all the cities, and arrived before them.

Ver. 34. And Jesus going out saw a great crowd: and he had compassion on them, because they were as sheep not having a shepherd, and he began to teach them many things.

Ver. 35. And when the hour was now late, his disciples came to him, saying: This place is desert, and the hour is now past:

Ver. 36. Send them away, that going into the next villages and towns, they may buy themselves food to eat.

Ver. 37. And answering he said to them: Give them you to eat. And they said to him: Shall we go and buy bread for two hundred denarii, and give them to eat?

Ver. 38. And he says to them: How many loaves have you? Go and see. And when they had found out, they say: Five, and two fishes.

V. 39. And he commanded them that they should make them all sit down by companies upon the green grass.

Ver. 40. And they sat down in ranks, by hundreds and by fifties.

Ver. 41. And taking the five loaves and the two fishes, looking up to heaven, he blessed, and broke the loaves, and gave to his disciples to set before them: and the two fishes he divided among all.

Ver. 42. And they all ate, and were filled.
