Lucas & revertentes (à mo- numento) paraverunt aromata, sed non eo sensu, quod statim postquam reverterentur, id factum sit: non enim determinationem addit temporis: nec id admittit breve illud spatium inter sepultu- ram Jesu, & occasum solis; imo explicat sese Lu- cas verbis sequentibus: & Sabbatho quidem silue- runt secundum legem: innuens exacto Sabbatho illam præparationem factam esse, quemadmo- dum S. Marcus docet, demum διαγενομένε Σαβ- βάτε mulieres comparasse aromata.

§. I. Finita septimana, cum primum se ostenta- ret lux primæ diei Sabbatorum, valde mane ex- currunt mulieres ad sepulcrum, portantes quæ paraverant aromata, Matth, XXVIII. 1. Marc. XVI. 2. Luc. XXIV. 1. Joh. XX. 1.

Matth. XXVIII. v. 1. Vespere autem sabbathi, quæ lucescat in prima sabbathi, venit Maria Mag- dalena, & altera Maria videre sepulchrum. Marc. XVI. v. 2. Et valde mane una Sabba- thorum veniunt ad monumentum, orto jam So- le. Luc. XXIV. v. 1. Una autem Sabbathi valde di- luculo venerunt ad monumentum portantes quæ paraverant, aromata. Joh. XX. v. 1. Una autem Sabbati, Maria Mag- dalena venit mane, cum adhuc tenebræ essent, ad monumentum: & vidit lapidem sublatum à mo- numento. [Καί τινες σὺν ἀυταῖς: quas voces temere o- mittit Vulgata Latina.

CAPUT II. Terræmotus, & lapis à sepulcro revolutus per angelum.

§. II. Solicitudo mulierum de lapide sepul- crali.

§. I. Terræ motus.

Matth. XXVIII. v. 2. Et ecce, terræ motus fa- ctus est magnus.

Marc. XVI. v. 3. Et dicebant ad invicem: Quis revolvet nobis lapidem ab ostio monumen- ti? Vers. 4. Et respicientes, viderunt revolutum lapidem: erat quippe magnus valde.

Non exprimitur diserte tempus ejusdem: sed è Mattheo colligitur, antecessisse eum adventum mulierum ad sepulcrum: quæ invenerunt jam Angelum super lapidem revolutum sedentem. In hoc terræmotu B. Lutherus censet Jesum descendis- se ad inferos, & à mortuis resurrexisse. Hilarius c. XXXIII. in Matth. circa finem: Motus terræ tem- pore matutino diei Dominicæ, resurrectionis est vir-

§. III. Mariæ cursus ad Petrum.

Joh. XX. v. 2. Cucurrit ergo & venit ad Simo- nem Petrum, & ad alium discipulum, quem ama- bat Jesus.

§. IV. Reliquarum ingressus in sepulcrum. Angeli conspectus & oratio. Matth. XXVIII. 5. 6. 7. Marc. XVI. 5. 6. 7. Luc. XXIV. 3-8.

Matth. XXVIII. Vers. 5. Respondens autem Angelus dixit mulieribus: Nolite timere vos: scio enim quod Jesum, qui crucifixus est, quæritis.

Vers. 6. Non est hic: Surrexit enim, sicut dixit. Venite, videte locum ubi positus erat Dominus.

Vers. 7. Et cito euntes dicite discipulis ejus quia surrexit: & ecce præcedit vos in Galilæam: ibi eum videbitis, ecce prædixi vobis.

Marc. XVI. Vers. 5. Et introeuntes in monumentum, viderunt juvenem sedentem in dextris, coopertum stola candida; & obstupuerunt.

Vers. 6. Qui dicit illis: Nolite expavescere: Jesum quæritis Nazarenum crucifixum: surrexit, non est hic: ecce locus ubi posuerunt eum.

Vers. 7. Sed ite, dicite discipulis ejus & Petro, quia præcedit vos in Galilæam: ibi eum videbitis: sicut dixit vobis.

Luc. XXIV. Vers. 3. Et ingressæ, non invenerunt corpus Domini Jesu.

Vers. 4. Et factum est, dum mente consternatæ essent de isto, ecce duo viri steterunt secus illas in veste fulgenti

Vers. 5. Quum timerent autem, & declinarent vultum in terram, dixerunt ad illas: Quid quæritis viventem cum mortuis.

Vers. 6. Non est hic, sed surrexit: Recordamini qualiter loquutus est vobis quum adhuc in Galilæa esset.

Vers. 7. Dicens: Quia oportet Filius hominis tradi in manus hominum peccatorum, & crucifigi: & die tertia resurgere.

Vers. 8. Et recordatæ sunt verborum ejus.

[Sive idem Angelus fuerit, qui lapidem devolverat, sive alius, parum refert; saltim non videntur mulieres sedentem super lapidem conspexisse, alias etiam Maria Magdalena vidisset eundem, imo introeuntes demum cæteræ, Marco teste, Angelum illum concionatorem, vel potius duos Angelos, è quibus unus eorum ipsis prædicavit, ut è Luca colligere est collatione, viderunt. Probabilius tamen censuerim, Angelum illum custodibus visum diversum fuisse ab hisce duobus, qui visi sunt mulieribus, uti diversa eorum fuêre munia, quæ expedierunt, & diversa apparitionis forma: quum illius aspectus horribilis fuerit: hic vero viri duo in veste fulgenti apparuerunt, vel, ut Marcus habet, in stola candida, non ut terrerent, & fugarent, sed ut consternatas mulieres erigerent, & ad discipulos ablegarent.]

§. V. Exierunt è monumento cum festinatione ad discipulos. Matth. XXVIII. v. 8. Marc. XVI. 8.

Matth. XXVIII. Vers. 8. Et exierunt cito de monumento cum timore, & gaudio magno.

Marc. XVI. Vers. 8. At illæ exeuntes, fugerunt de monumento: invaserat enim eas tremor & pavor, & nemini quicquam dixerunt: timebant enim.

CAPUT IV. Excursus Petri & Iohannis ad sepulcrum, ut & Maria Magdalena. §. I. Maria Magdalena apud Petrum & Johannem queritur de sublato Domino.

Joh. XX. v. 2. Et dicit illis: Tulerunt Dominum de monumento, & nescimus ubi posuerunt eum.

§. II. Illi currunt ad monumentum. Luc. XXIV. 12. Joh. XX. 3. 4.

Luc. XXIV. Vers. 12. Petrus autem furgens cu- currit ad monumentum.

Joh. XX. Vers. 3. Exiit ergo Petrus & ille alius discipulus, & venerunt ad monumentum.

Vers. 4. Currebant autem duo simul: & ille alius discipulus præcucurrit citius Petro, & venit primus ad monumentum.

§. III. Johannes videt solum linteamina.

Vers. 5. Et quum se inclinasset, vidit posita linteamina, non tamen introivit.

§. IV. Quæ etiam vidit solum Petrus cum su- dario Joh. XX. 6. 7. 8. 9. Luc. XXIV. 12.

Joh. XX. Vers. 6. Venit ergo Simon Petrus se- quens eum, & introivit in monumentum, & vi- dit linteamina posita.

Vers. 7. Et sudarium quod fuerat super caput ejus, non cum linteaminibus positum, sed separa- tim involutum in unum locum.

Vers. 8. Tunc ergo introivit & ille discipulus, qui venerat primus ad monumentum, & vidit, & credidit.

Vers. 9. Nondum enim sciebant Scripturam, quia oportet eum à mortuis resurgere.

Luc. XXIV. Vers. 12. Et procumbens vidit lin- teamenta sola posita.

§. V. Illis visis discedunt rursus. Joh. XX. 10. Luc. XXIV. 12.

Joh. XX. Vers. 10. Abierunt ergo iterum disci- puli ad semetipsos.

Luc. XXIV. Vers. 12. Et abiit, secum mirans quod factum fuerat.

[Quod secundum ὕστερον πρότερον retulit ibi Lucas ceu factum post apparitionem Jesu, quæ mulieribus contigerat: quam vero constat de- mum contigisse post apparitionem, qua dignatus est Dominus Mariam Magdalenam, utpote quæ omnium prima fuit JESU post resurrectionem apparitio.]

§. VI. Maria autem plorat ad monumen- tum.

Joh. XX. Vers. 11. Maria autem stabat ad mo- numentum foris, plorans:

[Redierat ergo cum discipulis illis ad monu- mentum, utpote à quo è primo excursu redux ipsis lapidem à monumento sublatum, & Domi- num ablatum indicarat Joh. XX. 2.

CAPUT V. Angelica apparitio Mariæ facta.

§. I. Mariæ apparent duo Angeli.

Vers. 11. Dum ergo fleret, inclinavit se, & pro- spexit in monumentum,

Vers. 12. Et vidit duos Angelos in albis, seden- tes, unum ad caput, & unum ad pedes, ubi positum fuerat corpus Jesu.

§. II. Quærunt de causa ploratus.

Vers. 13. Dicunt ei illi: Mulier quid ploras? Dicit eis: Quia tulerunt Dominum meum, & ne- scio ubi posuerunt eum.

CAPUT VI. Apparitio IESU Mariæ Magdalenæ facta.

§. I. JESUS apparet Mariæ, sed creditur hor- tulanus esse. Joh. XX. v. 14. 15. Marc. XVI. v. 9.

Joh. XX. Vers. 14. Hæc quum dixisset, con- versa est retrorsum, & vidit Jesum stantem: & non sciebat quia Jesus est.

Vers. 15. Dicit ei Jesus: Mulier, quid ploras? quem quæris? Illa existimans quia hortulanus esset, dicit ei: Domine, si tu sustulisti eum, dicitomihi ubi posuisti eum, & ego eum tollam.

Marc. XVI. Vers. 9. Surgens autem mane prima Sabbathi, apparuit primo Mariæ Magdalenæ, de qua ejecerat septem dæmonia.

§. II. Agnitus autem ab ea cum eam compellat nomine proprio Maria, non vult tangi ab ea, mittit eam ad fratres suos.

Vers. 16. Dicit ei Jesus: Maria. Conversa illa, dicit ei, Rabboni, quod dicitur Magister.

Vers. 17. Dicit ei Jesus: Noli me tangere: nondum enim ascendi ad Patrem meum: vade autem ad fratres meos, & diceis: Ascendo ad Patrem meum & Patrem vestrum, Deum meum & Deum vestrum.

§. III. Quæ annunciat discipulis se vidisse DOMINUM. Johan. XX. 18. Marc. XVI. 10.

Joh. XX. Vers. 18. Venit Maria Magdalena annuncians discipulis: Quia vidi Dominum, & hæc dixit mihi.

Marc. XVI. Vers. 10. Illa vadens nuntiavit his qui cum eo fuerant, lugentibus & flentibus.

§. IV. Sed ipsi non crediderunt ei.

Vers. 11. Et illi audientes quia viveret, & visus esset ab ea, non crediderunt.

CAPUT VII. Apparitio IESU aliis mulieribus a sepulcro revertentibus facta.

§. I. Et ecce, (cum mulieres currerent nuntiare discipulis angelicam visionem) Jesus occurrit illis.

Matth. XXVIII. Vers. 8. Currentes nuntiare discipuli ejus.

Vers. 9. Et ecce Jesus occurrit illis, dicens: Avete. Illæ autem accesserunt, & tenuerunt pedes ejus & adoraverunt eum.

§. II. Misit eas quod fratribus nunciare debeant.

Vers. 10. Tunc ait illis Jesus: Nolite timere. Ite, nuntiate fratribus meis, ut eant in Galilæam, ibi me videbunt.

§. III. Quod ab iis factum.

Luc. XXIV. Vers. 9. Et regressæ à monumento, nuntiaverunt hæc omnia illis undecim, & cæteris omnibus.

Vers. 10. Erat autem Maria Magdalena, & Joanna, & Maria Jacobi, & cæteræ quæ cum eis erant, quæ dicebant ad Apostolos hæc.

Vers 11. Et visa sunt ante illos sicut deliramentum verba ista, & non crediderunt illis.

CAPUT VIII. Mendacium de corpore Iesu furto ablato custodibus suggestum.

§. I. Custodum nuncium ad Sacerdotes.

Matth. XXVIII. V. 11. Quæ quum abiissent, ecce, quidam de custodibus venerunt in civitatem, & nuntiaverunt principibus Sacerdotum omnia quæ facta fuerant.

§. II. Consilium de eo habitum, ejusque conclusio.

Vers. 12. Et congregati cum Senioribus, consilio accepto pecuniam copiosam dederunt militibus,

Vers. 13. Dicentes: Dicite, quia discipuli ejus nocte venerunt, & furati sunt eum nobis dormientibus.

Vers. 14. Et si hoc auditum fuerit à Præside, nos suadebimus ei, & securos vos faciemus.

§. III. Conclusi exequutio.

Vers. 15. At illi accepta pecunia, fecerunt sicut erant edocti, & divulgatum est verbum istud apud Judæos usque in hodiernum diem.

CAPUT IX. Apparitio Iesu discipulis Emaunticis facta.

§. I. Apparitio Jesu in ignota forma. Marc. xvi. 12. Luc. xxiv. 13-16.

Marc. XVI. Vers. 12. Posthæc autem duobus ex his ambulantibus ostensus est in alia effigie, euntibus in villam.

Luc. XXIV. Vers. 13. Et ecce, duo ex illis ibant ipsa die in castellum, quod erat in spatio stadiorum sexaginta ab Jerusalem, nomine Emmaus.

Vers. 14. Et ipsi loquebantur ad invicem de his omnibus quæ acciderant.

Vers. 15. Et factum est dum fabularentur, & secum quærerent, & ipse Jesus appropinquans ibat cum illis.

Vers. 16. Oculi autem illorum tenebantur ne eum agnoscerent.

§. II. Colloquium cum discipulis institutum.

Vers. 17. Et ait ad illos: Qui sunt hi sermones quos confertis ad invicem, ambulantes, & estis tristes?

Vers. 18. Et respondens unus cui nomen Cleophas, dixit ei: Tu solus peregrinus es in Jerusalem, & non cognovisti quæ facta sunt in illa his diebus?

Vers. 19. Quibus ille dixit, Quæ? Et dixerunt: De Jesu Nazareno, qui fuit vir Propheta, potens in opere & sermone coram Deo & omni populo:

Vers. 20. Et quomodo eum tradiderunt summi Sacerdotes & principes nostri in damnationem mortis, & crucifixerunt eum.

Vers. 21. Nos autem sperabamus quia ipse esset redempturus Israel: & nunc super hæc omnia tertia dies est hodie, quod hæc facta sunt.

Vers. 22. Sed & mulieres quædam ex nostris terruerunt nos, quæ ante lucem fuerant ad monumentum:

Vers. 23. Et non invento corpore ejus, venerunt, dicentes: se etiam visionem Angelorum vidisse, qui dicunt eum vivere.

Vers 24. Et abierunt quidam ex nostris ad monumentum, & ita invenerunt sicut mulieres dixerunt, ipsum vero non invenerunt.

§. III. Correptio & informatio eorum.

Vers. 25. Et ipse dixit ad eos: O stulti & tardi corde ad credendum in omnibus quæ locuti sunt Prophetæ!

Vers. 26. Nonne hæc oportuit pati CHRISTUM, & ita intrare in gloriam suam?

§. IV. Interpretatio Scripturæ Mosis & Prophetarum.

Vers. 27. Et incipiens à Moyse & omnibus Prophetis interpretabatur illis in omnibus Scripturis, quæ de ipso erant.

§. V. Rogatus Jesus ut maneat penes discipulos.

Vers. 28. Et appropinquaverunt castello quo ibant: & ipse se finxit longius ire.

Vers. 29. Et coëgerunt illum, dicentes: Mane nobiscum: quoniam advesperascit, & inclinata est jam dies. Et intravit cum illis.

§. VI. Dignoscitur cum panem benediceret & frangeret: & evanescit.

Vers. 30. Et factum est dum recumberet cum eis, accepit panem & benedixit ac fregit, & porrigebat illis.

Vers. 31. Et aperti sunt oculi eorum, & cognoverunt eum: & ipse evanuit ex oculis eorum.

§. VII. Discipuli illi ad Apostolos properant, ibique audiunt Dominum Simoni apparuisse.

Vers. 32. Et dixerunt ad invicem: Nonne cor nostrum ardens erat in nobis, dum loqueretur in via, & aperiret nobis Scripturas?

Vers. 33. Et surgentes eadem hora, regressi sunt in Jerusalem: & invenerunt congregatos undecim, & eos qui cum illis erant,

Vers. 34. Dicentes: Quod surrexit Dominus vere, & apparuit Simoni.

[Prior ergo apparitio fuit quæ Simoni facta: utpote quæ jam cæteris Apostolis relata erat: tametsi ea ἀξιωματικῶς descripta haud extet, solum hic & 1. Cor. xv. 4. verbo indicata.]

§. VIII. Et sibi factam apparitionem referunt. Luc. xxiv. 35. Marc. xvi. 13.

Luc. XXIV. Vers. 35. Et ipsi narrabant quæ gesta erant in via: & quomodo cognoverunt eum in fractione panis.

Marc. XVI. Vers. 13. Et illi euntes nuntiaverunt cæteris: nec illis crediderunt.

[Quamvis ergo professi sint: Surrexit Dominus vere, & Simoni apparuit. id tamen plena fide amplexi non sunt, sed vel historice retulerunt, vel admodum dubii erant, atque hesitabant: quia hic aperte dicitur, eos non credidisse, & paulo post corripiuntur ob incredulitatem. Marc. XVI. 1.

CAPUT X.

Apparitio IESU discipulis, absente Thoma, facta.

§. I. Ultimo (illo resurrectionis die) foribus clausis apparuit JESUS discipulis Hierosolymis congregatis. Marc. xvi. 14. Luc. xxiv. 36. Joh. xx. 19.

Marc. XVI. Vers. 14. Novissime, recumbentibus illis undecim apparuit,

Luc. XXIV. Vers. 36. Dum autem hæc loquuntur, stetit JESUS in medio eorum, & dixit eis: Pax vobis: ego sum, nolite timere.

Johan. XX. Vers. 19. Quum ergo sero esset die illo, una Sabbatorum, & fores essent clausæ, ubi erant discipuli congregati propter metum Judæorum, venit JESUS, & stetit in medio, & dicit eis: Pax vobis.

§. II. Quum spectrum crederetur, ostendit illis manus & pedes, exprobrans ipsis incredulitatem eorum. Luc. xxiv. 37. 38. 39. 40. Marc. xvi. 14. Joh. xx. 20.

Luc. XXIV. Vers. 37. Conturbati vero & conterriti existimabant se spiritum videre.

Vers. 38. Et dicit eis: Quid turbati estis, & cogitationes afcendunt in corda vestra.

Vers. 39. Videte manus meas & pedes: quia ego ipse sum: palpate & videte: quia spiritus carnem & ossa non habet, sicut me videtis habe- re.

Vers. 40. Et quum hoc dixisset, ostendit eis manus & pedes.

Marc. XVI. Vers. 14. Et exprobravit incredu- litatem eorum, & duritiam cordis: quia iis qui viderant eum resurrexisse, non crediderunt.

Joh. XX. Vers. 20. Et quum hoc dixisset, osten- dit eis manus & latus.

[Apparet hinc, quod quæ retulêre mulieres, Simon & Emauntici discipuli, non aliter inter- pretati sint, quam quod ipsis spectrum aliquod, vel spiritus apparuerit.

§. III. Ut titubantes confirmaret, cibum coram eis sumfsit.

Luc. XXIV. Vers. 41. Adhuc autem illis non credentibus præ gaudio, dixit: Habetis hic ali- quid quod manducetur?

Vers. 42. At illi obtulerunt ei partem piscis assi, & favum mellis.

Vers. 43. Et quum manducasset coram eis, su- mens reliquias dedit eis.

§. IV. Aperuit illis sensum Scripturæ, unde or- tum gaudium. Luc. XXIV. 44-48. Johan. XX. 20.

Luc. XXIV. Vers. 44. Et dixit ad eos: Hæc sunt verba quæ locutus sum ad vos quum adhuc essem vobiscum, quoniam necesse est impleri o- mnia quæ scripta sunt in lege Moysi; & Prophe- tis, & Psalmis de me.

Vers. 45. Tunc aperuit illis sensum, ut intel- ligerent Scripturas,

Vers. 46. Et dixit eis: Quoniam sic scriptum est, & sic oportebat Christum pati & resurgere à mortuis tertia die:

Vers. 47. Et prædicari in nomine ejus pœni- tentiam & remissionem peccatorum in omnes gentes, incipientibus Jerosolyma.

Vers. 48. Vos autem testes estis horum.

Joh. XX. Vers. 20. Gavisi sunt ergo discipuli vi- so Domino.

§. V. Missio Apostolorum.

Vers. 21. Dixit ergo eis JESUS iterum Pax vobis: sicut misit me Pater, & ego mitto vos.

§. VI. Spiritus S. insufflatio & potestatis remit- tendi & retinendi peccata, concessio.

Vers. 22. Et hoc quum dixisset, insufflavit: & dicit eis: Accipite Spiritum Sanctum.

Vers. 23. Quorum remiseritis peccata, remit- tuntur eis: & quorum retinueritis, retenta sunt.

CAPUT XL

Apparitio Iesu præsente Thoma.

§. I. Thomæ incredulitas.

Vers. 24. Thomas autem unus ex duodecim, qui dicitur Didymus, non erat cum eis, quando venit Jesus.

Vers. 25. Dixerunt ergo ei alii discipuli: Vi- dimus Dominum. Ille autem dixit eis: Nisi vi- dero in manibus ejus figuram clavorum, & mit- tam digitum meum in locum clavorum, & mittam manum meam in latus ejus, non cre- dam.

§. II. Thomæ conversio, & confessio.

Vers. 26. Et post dies octo, iterum erant di- scipuli ejus intus, & Thomas cum eis. Venit Jesus januis clausis, & stetit in medio, & dixit: Pax vobis.

Vers. 27. Deinde dicit Thomæ: Infer digitum tuum huc, & vide manus meas, & affer manum tuam, & mitte in latus meum: & noli esse incre- dulus, sed fidelis.

Vers. 28. Respondit Thomas, & dixit ei: Do- minus meus, & Deus meus.

Vers. 29. Dicit ei Jesus: Quia vidisti me Tho- ma, credidisti: beati qui non viderunt, & credi- derunt.

§. III. Finis signorum Christi. Joh. XX. 30. 31. Act. I. 3.

Joh. XX. Vers. 30. Multa quidem & alia signa fecit Jesus in conspectu Discipulorum suorum, quæ non sunt scripta in libro hoc.

Vers. 31. Hæc autem scripta sunt, ut credatis quia Jesus est Christus Filius Dei, & ut credentes, vitam habeatis in nomine ejus.

Act. I. Vers. 3. Quibus & præbuit seipsum vi- vum post passionem suam in multis argumentis, per dies quadraginta apparens eis, & loquens de regno Dei. [Sed imprimis tertia vice discipulis quibus- dam è Galilæa sese manifestavit, de quo jam se- quitur.]

CAPUT XII.

Manifestatio Iesu admare Tiberiadis.

§. I. Jesus piscantibus discipulis apparet.

Joh. XXI. Vers. 1. Postea manifestavit se ite- rum Jesus discipulis ad mare Tiberiadis: manife- stavit autem sic:

Vers. 2. Erant simul Simon Petrus & Thomas. qui dicitur Didymus, & Nathanael, qui erat à Ca- na Galilææ, & filii Zebedæi, & alii ex discipulis e- jus duo.

Vers. 3. Dicit eis Simon Petrus: Vado piscari. Dicunt ei: Venimus & nos tecum. Et exierunt & ascenderunt in navim: & illa nocte nihil pren- diderunt.

Vers. 4. Mane autem jam facto, stetit Jesus in littore: non tamen cognoverunt discipuli quia Jesus est.

§. II. Miraculo captorum piscotum agnosci- tur.

Vers. 5. Dicit ergo eis Jesus: Pueri, nunquid pulmentarium habetis? Responderunt ei: Non.

Vers. 6. Dicit eis: Mittite in dexteram navi- gii rete, & invenietis. Miserunt ergo, & jam non valebant illud trahere præ multitudine pisci- um.

Vers. 7. Dicit ergo discipulus ille, quem dili- gebat JESUS, Petro: DOMINUS est. Si- mon autem Petrus quum audivisset quia DOMI- NUS est, tunica succinxit se (erat enim nudus) & misit se in mare.

Vers. 8. Alii autem discipuli navigio venerunt (non enim longe erant à terra, sed quasi cubitis ducentis) trahentes rete piscium.

§. III. Novum miraculum piscis prunis impo- siti, & panis inventi.

Vers. 9. Ut ergo descenderunt in terram, vide- runt prunas positas, & piscem superpositum, & pa- nem.

§. IV. Numerus piscium captorum.

Vers. 10. Dicit eis Jesus: Afferte de piscibus quos prendidistis nunc.

Vers. 11. Ascendit Simon Petrus, & traxit rete in terram, plenum piscibus centum quinquagin- ta tribus: & quum tanti essent, non est scissum rete.

§. V. Piscem & panem distribuit discipulis. Quæ tertia ejus manifestatio fuit.

Vers. 12. Dicit eis Jesus: Venite, prandete. Et nemo audebat discumbentium interrogare eum: Tu quis es? Scientes quia DOMINUS est.

Vers. 13. Et venit Jesus, & accepit panem, & dat eis, & piscem similiter.

Vers. 14. Hoc jam tertio manifestatus est Jesus discipulis suis quum resurrexisset à mortuis.

CAPUT XIII.

Colloquium Iesu cum Petro, quem in Aposto- latu suo constituit, & de martyrii genere informat.

§. I. Petro committuntur oves pascendæ, idque terna vice.

Vers. 15. Quum ergo prandissent, dicit Simo- ni Petro JESUS: Simon Joannis, diligis me plus his? Dicit ei: Etiam DOMINE: tu scis quia amo te. Dicit ei: Pasce agnos meos.

Vers. 16. Dicit ei iterum: Simon Joannis dili- gis me? Ait illi: Etiam DOMINE: tu scis quia amo te. Dicit ei: Pasce agnos meos.

Vers. 17. Dicit ei tertio: Simon Joannis a- mas me? Contristatus est, Petrus, quia dixit ei tertio: Amas me? & dixit ei: DOMINE, tu omnia scis, tu scis quia amo te. Dicit ei JESUS: Pasce oves meas.

§. II. Prædictio martyrii Petri.

Vers. 18. Amen, Amen dico tibi, quum esses ju- nior cingebas te & ambulabas ubi volebas: quum autem senueris, extendes manus tuas, & alius te cinget, & ducet quo non vis.

Vers. 19. Hoc autem dixit, significans qua morte clarificaturus esset Deum.

CAPUT XIV.

Colloquium Christi cum Petro de Johanne.

§. I. Petrus jussit Christum sequi, quum se- quebatur etiam Johannes, de eo quærit.

Vers. 19. Et quum hoc dixisset, dicit ei: Seque- re me.

Vers. 20. Conversus Petrus, vidit illum di- scipulum, quem diligebat Jesus, sequentem, qui & recubuit in cœna super pectus ejus, & dixit: Domine, quis est qui tradette?

Vers. 21. Hunc ergo quum vidisset Petrus, di- cit JESU: DOMINE, hic autem quid?

§. II. Responsum Christi male à discipulis in- tellectum vindicatur.

Vers. 22. Dicit ei Jesus: Si eum volo manere donec veniam, quid ad te? tu me sequere.

Vers. 23. Exivit ergo sermo iste inter fratres, quia discipulus ille non moritur. Et non dixit dixit ei Jesus: Non moritur: sed: Si eum volo manere donec veniam, quid ad te?

Vers. 24. Hic est discipulus ille qui testimo- nium perhibet de his, & scripsit hæc, & scimus quia verùm est testimonium ejus.

CAPUT XV. Apparitio Jesu in Galilæa cum solemni confir- matione Apostolatus, & institutione mi- nisterii.

§. I. Profectio discipulorum in Galilæam.

Matth. XXVIII. Vers. 16. Undecim autem disci- puli abierunt in Galilæam, in montem ubi con- stituerat illis Jesus.

§. II. Adoratus Jesus à quibusdam, dubitan- tibus de eo aliis.

Vers. 17. Et videntes eum, adoraverunt: qui- dam autem dubitaverunt.

[Non ex undecim discipulis, quibus jam Spiri- tum S. insufflando communicarat, Joh. XX. 22. Sed è numero illorum 500. quos Apostolus indigita- vit I. Cor. XV. Philippus Lansbergius Chronol. S. l. III. c. 20. observat, primum Apostolis Christum se patefecisse die resurrectionis: octiduo post iisdem præsente Thoma: altero octiduo itidem die domini- ca discipulis ad mare Tiberiadis sese stitisse: tertio octiduo post resurrectionem pariter die Dominico ap- paruisse fratribus illis plusquam quingentis. Quarto octiduo post visum esse peculiariter Jacobo. Quinto octiduo à resurrectione undecim Apostolis, cum venissent in Galilæam, sese manifestasse: cum con- firmaret eosdem in ministerio: ac novissime sexto octiduo à resurrectione Hierosolymis die ascensionis discipulis apparuisse: ac Sabbatho sequenti Pente- costen fuisse impletam, qua missus est Spiritus S. Sed quum prætermissam omnino ab Evangelistis tam frequentem Synodum, & apparitionem in ea factam verisimile non sit: præstat statue- re, illos quingentos fratres una adfuisse huic mani- festationi Apostolis factæ, quæ etiam Cornelii Jansenii, & B. Gerhardi est sententia. Neque constat, omnes apparitiones diebus Dominicis fa- ctas: illa certe novissima, die quadragesimo, non uti Lansbergius vult, quadragesimo primo à resur- rectione facta, non incidere potuit in diem Dominicum, quem quadragesimum tertium à resurrectionis die fuisse, extra controversiam est. Quanquam vero notante Jansenio sint, qui dicant, illam quingentis fratribus factam appari- tionem evenisse demum post ascensionem, recla- mat tamen aperte Paulina enumeratio, 1. Cor. XV. 6. post apparitionem duodecim Apostolis primo resurrectionis die factam quingentis fratribus, tum Jacobo, demum omnibus Apostolis apparuis- se dicitur Dominus: quum ergo indubie ante ascensionem omnibus Apostolis apparuerit, idq; in ipso die ascensionis; illam sane, qua visus est quingentis fratribus ante ascensionem contigisse, negari non potest.]

§. III. Professio JESU de potestate sibi da- ta.

Vers. 18. Et accedens Jesus, loquutus est eis, dicens: Data est mihi omnis potestas in cœlo & in terra.

§. IV. Emissio Apostolorum ad prædicandum Evangelium, & baptizandum: Matth. XXVIII. 19. 20. Marc. XIV. 15. 16.

Vers. 19. Euntes ergo' docete omnes gentes: baptizantes eos in nomine Patris & Filii & Spiri- tus Sancti.

Vers. 20. Docentes eos servare omnia quæ- cunque mandavi vobis:

Marc. XVI. Vers. 15. Et dixit eis: Euntes in mundum universum, prædicate Evangelium o- mni creaturæ.

Vers. 16. Qui crediderit, & baptizatus fuerit, salvus erit: qui vero non crediderit, condemna- bitur.

§. V. Signa promissa confirmandi Evangelii gratia.

Vers. 17. Signa autem eos qui crediderint, hæc sequentur: In nomine meo dæmonia ejicient: linguis loquentur novis:

Vers. 18. Serpentes tollent: & si mortiferum quid biberint, non eis nocebit: super ægros ma- nus imponent, & bene habebunt.

§. VI. Promissio præsentiæ JESU perpe- tuæ.

Vers. 20. Et ecce ego vobiscum sum omni- bus diebus usque ad consummationem secu- li.

CAPUT XVI. Ultima apparitio Jesu Apostolis facta, ipso Ascensionis Domini die.

§. I. Apostoli congregati jubentur Hieroso- lymis expectare promissionem Patris. Act. I. 4. 5. Luc. XXIV. 49.

Actor. I. Vers. 4. Et converscens, præcepit eis ab Jerosolymis ne discederent, sed expectarent promissionem Patris: Quam audistis (inquit) per os meum:

Vers. 5. Quia Johannes quidem baptizavit a- qua, vos autem baptizabimini Spiritu S. non post multos hos dies.

Luc. XXIV. Vers. 49. Et ecce ego mittam pro- missum Patris mei in vos: vos autem sedete in civitate, quoad usque induamini virtute ex alto.

[Perperam Vulgatus illud συναλιζόμενος Act. I. 4. transtulit Convescens: unde colligi possit, præceptum illud in prima Hierosolymis post re- surrectionem Apostolis facta apparitione à Lucæ c. XXIV. a vers. 36. usque 48. descripta, ubi con- vesci voluit Dominus cum Apostolis traditum es- se, ne Jerosolyma discederent: nam deinceps non legitur amplius cum Apostolis comedisse, neque id in ultima hac apparitione factum. Beza ergo verbum Græcum reddidit: Et cum illis conveniens, & exponi debere, congregans (Apo- stolos) docet Camerarius in notis ad h. l. Congre- gasse autem dicitur Apostolos, quia per Spiritus S. instinctum eos convenire fecit, ac congrega- tis apparens, præceptum illud dedit. Hoc enim datum non esse in ultima illa apparitione, etsi immediate à Luca in Historia Evangelica ei subjurgatur, ex hisce patet: (1.) Quod adhuc in Galilæam eos ire jusserit, ibique manifesta- tionem singularem Apostolis & fratribus suis promiserit; non ergo ex eo sedere in Jerusa- lem debuêre, ut hic præcipitur. (2.) Quod etiam intervenerit apparitio Apostolis, præsen- te Thoma, facta. (3.) Quod Jacobo peculiari- ter apparuerit Dominus post illam manifestatio- nem, quæ Apostolis Hierosolymis ipso die Re- surrectionis Dominicæ facta, teste Apostolo I. Cor. XV. 7. (4.) Quod non ipsa illa die quod ad præsentem manifestationem, sed δὶ ἡμερῶν τεσσαράκοντα ipsis apparuerit, teste ipsomet S. Luc Actor. I. 3. Quemadmodum etiam (5.) appa- ruisse legitur quibusdam Apostolis ad mare

Tiberiade, antequam adhuc folemni illa manife- statione in Galilæa omnibus Apostolis, aliisque ibi congregatis sefe stiterit: quæ prior fuit in Ga- lilæa apparitio, facta postquam duabus vicibus jam Apostolis Hierofolymis se visendum præbuerat: dicitur enim à Johanne tertia manifestatio quæ di- scipulis facta, cap. XXI. 14. Hæc ergo quarta A- postolis facta, & ultima apparitio Christi est.

§. II. Colloquium discipulorum cum Jesu de tempore restitutionis regni Israel.

Vers. 6. Igitur qui convenerant, interrogabant eum, dicentes Domine, si in tempore hoc resti- tues regnum Israel?

Vers. 7. Dixit autem eis: Non est vestrum nos- se tempora vel momenta quæ pater posuit in sua potestate.

Vers. 8. Sed accipietis virtutem supervenien- tis Spiritus Sancti in vos, & eritis mihi testes in Jerusalem, & in omni Judæa, & Samaria, & usque ad ultimum terræ.

[De tempore restitutionis regni Israel etsi directe non respondeat, præcise tempus definiendo, quod id ipsorum non sit, momenta nosse, quæ Pa- ter posuit in sua potestate: Non tamen sine re- sponso ad quæstionem propositam dimittuntur: siquidem in Jerusalem, omnique Judæa primum, deinde in Samaria ipsos testaturos, atque peracto ibidem Evangelii præconio in toto orbe, usque ad ultimos terræ fines ipsos prædicaturos; idque omne juxta directionem Spiritus S. quo induen- di sunt, doceat; quæ utique universa faciunt ad restitutionem regni Israel.]

CAPUT XVII. Ascensio Jesu in cælum.

§. I. Ubi & quando ascenderit in cælum. Marc. XVI. 19. Luc. XXIV. 50. 51. Actor. I. 9.

Marc. XVI. Vers. 19. Et Dominus quidem Je- sus postquam locutus est eis, assumtus est in cœ- lum, & sedit à dextris Dei.

Luc. XXIV. v. 50. Eduxit autem eos foràs in Bethaniam: & elevatis manibus suis, benedixit eis.

Vers. 51. Et factum est, dum benediceret illis, recessit ab eis, & ferebatur in cælum.

Actor. I. Vers. 9. Et quum hæc dixisset, viden- tibus illis, elevatus est: & nubes suscepit eum ab oculis eorum.

[Id factum esse in monte Oliveti, ex Actor. 1. 12. discimus.]

§. II. Concio Angelica de ascensu in cœlum, & reditu.

Vers. 10. Quumque intuerentur in cœlum euntem illum, ecce duo viri adstiterunt juxta illos in vestibus albis.

Vers. 11. Qui & dixerunt: Viri Galilæi, quid statis aspicientes in cœlum? hic Jesus qui assum- ptus est à vobis in cœlum, sic veniet quemadmo- dum vidistis eum euntem in cœlum.

CAPUT XIIX. Reversio discipulorum in Jerusalem.

§. I. Quomodo Hierosolymam reversi sint. Luc. XXIV. 52. Actor. I. 12.

Luc. XXIV. Vers. 52. Et ipsi adorantes regressi sunt in Jerusalem cum gaudio magno.

Act. I. v. 12. Tunc reversi sunt Jerosolymam à monte, qui vocatur Oliveti, qui est juxta Jerusa- lem, Sabbathi habens iter.

§. II. Quid reversi ibi egerint.

Luc. XXIV. v. 53. Et erant semper in templo, laudantes & benedicentes Deum, Amen.

CAPUT XIX. Universale præconium Apostolorum.

§. I. Egressus Apostolorum in orbem, ad præ- dicandum Evangelium.

Marc. XVI. Vers. 20. Illi autem profecti præ- dicaverunt ubique.

[Non id factum immediate post Ascensionem Christi: nam primum induendi erant virtute ex al- to: & præterea in Judæa sola sub initium prædi- care debebant, antequam augentes in totum or- bem se converterent. Summatim ergo rem com- plexus est S. Marcus.]

§. II. Cooperatio Domini.

Vers. ult. Domino cooperante, & sermonem confirmante sequentibus signis.

§. III. Conclusio Historiæ Evangelicæ.

Joh. XXI. Vers. ult. Sunt autem & alia multa, quæ fecit Jesus: quæ si scribantur per singula, nec ipsum arbitror mundum capere posse eos, qui scribendi sunt, libros.

JESU, TIBI SIT GLORIA, IN SECULORUM SECULA! AMEN.

## 1:1 Introduction: I. N. D. Abraham Annotations on the Gospel According to
I. N. D. ABRAHAM ANNOTATIONS ON THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO

Latin:

I. N D. ABRAHA ANNOT A AD EVANGELIU KATA M

## 1:1 Introduction: Preface on the Inscription
PREFACE ON THE INSCRIPTION

The ancient inscription does not have the nu- of εὐαγγέλιον, but εὐαγγέλιον Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ, as it is at the beginning of Mark: because, of course, the subject matter of the book was, as we have already said, the preaching of Christ: therefore the name of the writer could not be placed in the genitive case: just as we do not say the life of Caesar of Plutarch, but written by Plutarch. I judge this to be the reason why these books were not inscribed Matthew & Mark and so on, but according to Matthew, according to Mark, when otherwise that which is written by Matthew could be called the Gospel of Matthew no less correctly, just as Paul, dealing with the doctrine of Christ preached by himself, said, my gospel Rom. XVI. 25. comparing the passage I.9. Therefore, the gospel of Jesus Christ according to Matthew is nothing other than the doctrine delivered by Jesus Christ, as it is written down by Matthew: for that is what the Greek word according to signifies: and since this cannot be equally expressed by a Latin word, it is less to be wondered at if certain Latins, in citing these books, have kept the Greek expression.

It is handed down by the great consensus of the ancients that Matthew remained in the region of Palestine for some years after Christ's bodily sojourn (at least eight, as the Greeks and other writers have noted at the end of the book). Wherefore it is reasonable to believe that the evangelical history was written by him in the language which was common in that region. For as to the fact that some go about proving with great effort that the Greek which we have is the original of Matthew himself, in that I reject the great consensus of pious antiquity for no just reasons. For Papias, Irenaeus, Origen, and others, to whom it was easier to seek out the truth of that matter than it is for us, have handed down as a certainty that Matthew wrote in Hebrew. Eusebius adds from Pantaenus that the same Gospel, written in Hebrew letters, was preserved among the Indians, to whom Bartholomew had preached. Nor does Jerome seem ever to have doubted that matter, although he leaves in doubt whether that Hebrew Gospel of Matthew was the very one which the Nazarenes used in his time, and which he mentions existed in his age both in the Caesarean library and at Beroea, and elsewhere. Jerome adds in his third book against the Pelagians that it was written in the Chaldean and Syrian language, but in Hebrew letters, where by the Chaldean and Syrian language I understand the Jerusalem idiom, the language of that time. But the argument which they bring forward from the true Hebrew words which we see expressed in the Greek context, with interpretations added, has no weight with me. For it is customary for all writers, even translators, to keep the more notable foreign words intact, but with an interpretation added, which we see has also been done sometimes by the seventy elders. That Hebrew Gospel, indeed, which was edited by the Son, and the other which was edited by Münster, is so certainly not Matthew's that it needs no arguments: but that ancient one of the Nazarenes living at Beroea, which Jerome narrates he consulted and translated into other languages, I judge entirely to have flowed from the very codex of Matthew: which the same Jerome hands down to have been most constantly asserted by them: Epiphanius adds, though it appears he did not examine it, that the Nazarenes possessed a most complete Gospel of Matthew. Certainly those Beroean Nazarenes were the genuine offspring of those who were the first in Palestine to have embraced the faith of Christ. For it appears that this name was originally given to them from the name of our Lord, who was commonly called a Nazarene, Acts XXV. 5. just as those who embraced Christ in the Greek language were called Christians, Acts XI. 26. Add that, as Epiphanius also testifies, these very Nazarenes were a branch of those who, divinely warned, departed from Jerusalem to Pella at the time of the siege. Nevertheless, some narratives not written down by Matthew, but perceived by hearsay, seem to have been added little by little by the Nazarenes to the copies which they had, whence arose the diversity between their Hebrew one and the Greek one which we have. For the history of the adulteress, which we have handed down by John, was read in their Gospel. Such is that in chapter XII: namely, that he with the withered hand was a mason, who in miserable words begged to be spared from impending beggary, which Jerome reports: And this passage after the history of the resurrection: But the Lord, when he had given the linen cloth to the servant of the priest, went to James, and appeared to him. For James had sworn that he would not eat bread from that hour in which he had drunk the cup of the Lord, until he saw him rising from the dead. Soon after: Bring, says the Lord, bread and a table. He took bread and blessed and broke it, and gave it to James the Just, and said to him: my brother, eat your bread, because the son of man has risen from those who sleep. But also that which we read in Ignatius in the Epistle to the Smyrnaeans, that Christ said to Peter after the resurrection: Behold, touch me and see, because I am not a bodiless demon, and that he immediately touched him and believed, existed in that same Gospel according to the Hebrews. And that passage about the rich man in chapter XIX had it otherwise, as we shall say when we come to it. It was narrated in the same Gospel that the lintel of the temple had been broken and divided when Christ died. There is also another passage from the same Hebrew Gospel in the third dialogue of Jerome against the Pelagians: Behold, the mother of the Lord and his brothers said to him: John the Baptist baptizes for the remission of sins. Let us go and be baptized by him. But he said to them: what have I sinned, that I should go and be baptized by him? Add to these the passage which is below XVIII. 22. But also certain sayings of Christ, which are not written down in our books, were related in that book by report: such as that which Clement of Alexandria praises: he who has wondered shall reign, and he who has reigned shall rest: and another in Jerome: never be joyful, except when you have seen your brother in charity. It is credible that there were many more sayings of this kind handed down by hand, but consistent in meaning with those written down. For even in the Acts, that is cited as a saying of Christ which is not written down in those words, it is more blessed to give than to receive. XX. 35. I think, however, that Tatian, when he was weaving one [Gospel] out of four, followed in the words of Matthew not only the Greek but also the Hebrew codices, whence that Gospel of Tatian, which was commonly called διὰ τεσσάρων, was by others called κατὰ ἑβραίους, as Epiphanius narrates. And from this I also think it came about that others call that Gospel not διὰ τεσσάρων, but διὰ πέντε, as Victor of Capua does. Nor should that seem wonderful to you, since Ignatius, who is so much older, recites that story about the words after the resurrection, and Justin another about the Baptism of Christ, in such a way as it was read in the Gospel of the Nazarenes. I see there are those who think that the Gospel of the Nazarenes was not only augmented from traditions, but also mutilated, for which thing I find no suitable witness anywhere. For Epiphanius says the contrary, ἔχουσι δὲ τὸ κατὰ ματθαῖον εὐαγγέλιον πληρέστατον ἑβραϊστί. Nor can I agree with those who insert a negative into Epiphanius's words: although I know it is said by the same Epiphanius concerning the Ebionites, that they used the Gospel of Matthew, not whole and most complete, but corrupted and mutilated: nor am I ignorant that Jerome cites the Hebrew exemplar of Matthew in such a way that he seems to make it common to the Nazarenes and Ebionites. But I think the Gospel of Matthew was common to them, just as the Gospel of Luke was once common to the Catholics and Marcion, with a few things changed, of course, which displeased Marcion. Thus also the Ebionites deleted the entire genealogy and what follows, to that place where Christ was baptized by John, just as Marcion introduced the first chapters of Luke. The Ebionites did this, however, according to their own principle, as those who wished the Lord Jesus to be believed to have been born from the intercourse of Joseph, and to have obtained the grace of anointing by the merit of his mighty works, as we shall say elsewhere. But there was no reason why the Nazarenes should do this, who are not proven to have differed from other Christians in the matter of faith, although they observed Jewish rites by a custom handed down from their ancestors, the Apostles not forbidding it. For Sulpitius well notes that in Palestine almost all Christians until the times of Hadrian believed that Christ was God under the observance of the law. And since Epiphanius doubts whether these also called Christ a mere man, or whether they confessed with us that he was born of the Holy Spirit from Mary, but also says he does not know whether they cut off the genealogies from Abraham to Christ; while others who write about them attribute nothing at all to them as peculiar except the observation of Hebrew rites: and since Irenaeus makes no mention of them in his list of heresies, one must judge them in a better light, and all the more so, because Augustine, who consulted older writers, expressly affirms that the Nazarenes confess that Christ is the Son of God: and Origen, when he makes a twofold division of the Ebionites in his Disputation against Celsus, either confessing Jesus to be born of a virgin like us, or not born in that way, but as other men, abusing the name of Ebionites more loosely, describes the Nazarenes, as is credible, by that former note of his. Wherefore that Hebrew Gospel of the Nazarenes which Jerome often praises is indeed the same as the Gospel of Ebion, but as Gelasius rightly judged, stained by Ebion. And just as Mark used the Hebrew codex of Matthew, if I am not mistaken, so it seems to me that whoever that Greek interpreter of Matthew was, he used the Greek book of Mark: for what Mark had taken from Matthew, this same person placed here in almost the same words, except that he softened certain things expressed by Mark in a Hebrew or Chaldean manner of speaking, closer to the norm of the Greek language. I consider it a sin to doubt the authority and trustworthiness of this version, which was received by the Churches from the very beginning of Christianity.

INDEX.

Grotius reveals to us his mere conjectures and speculations. For what is certain and indubitable in these? If one is to indulge in divinations and conjectures in such matters, which concern a thing of such importance, the original text and the archetype of the book, what certainty will finally be left? He says that one must not doubt the authority and trustworthiness of the Greek version of Matthew: but if we do not have the prototype itself preserved by divine providence, which was divinely destined for the canonical use of the Church, how shall we be able to be certain, whether about the faith and authority of the translation, or about its perennial and unblemished preservation? We believe that the Word of God will not perish, and we securely place our faith in the word of Christ that not a jot or a tittle of it can perish, but we have no promise concerning the preservation of translations. Nor indeed can anyone say that the interpreter was an Apostle or a divinely inspired man: about whom they vary greatly: Athanasius says he is James the brother of the Lord, Jerome and Eusebius say Mark, Theophylact says John, Anastasius in Genesis sermon VIII says Luke and Paul, others say someone else: whence Baronius even went so far as to say that it can only be affirmed by comparing it with the Hebrew original, of what trustworthiness the Greek text is, concerning which see Casaubon, Exercit. XV. 12. But the Jesuit Bailius says in Catech. centur. tract. I. §. 14. and Conzenius quæst. V. proœm. that the true Hebrew text of Matthew no longer exists.

Furthermore, since the whole New Testament,

was written by holy men of God in the Greek language, which was known throughout the whole world, just as the Old Testament was consigned to the people of God in the Hebrew and related language by the amanuenses of the Holy Spirit, it is not likely that this principal part of the New Testament, the Gospel according to Matthew, was adorned in the archetype and original text in the Hebrew language. We have brought forward other reasons elsewhere, namely in the Critico Sacro, and T. 1. syst. Theolog. Now only concerning the Grotian speculations. It is credible, according to Grotius, that the evangelical history was written by Matthew, who remained in the region of Palestine, in the language which was frequented in that region. But Dorotheus in his synopsis teaches that Matthew preached the Gospel in Hieropolis in Parthia, and there met his end: nor was the language in Judea the Hebrew speech, such as is used in the Old Testament codex, but Syriac, which Widmanstadius, and Guido Fabricius, Bellarmine, as also Adam Conzenius, make the original idiom for Matthew, and Greek was then in common use: nor was this Gospel written only, or even chiefly, for the Hebrews, but Christ had predicted that it would be delivered primarily to the Greeks and Gentiles, Matt. 21.43. But Grotius rashly claims a very great consensus of antiquity. For Papias, a hearer not of John the Evangelist, but of Aristion and John the Elder, endowed with very little judgment, from whom he begins the tradition, is of no authority in antiquity, whom the Ebionites could easily deceive, as they did in other matters: what wonder is it, therefore, if Irenaeus and Origen accepted that from him with simple credulity, whom other traditions of Papias also swept into error? They certainly did not hand it down as a known fact that Matthew wrote in Hebrew. For no one of them saw a Hebrew copy. Nor could Eusebius cite any witness other than Pantaenus concerning the Gospel written in Hebrew letters: who, however, says only that he found the Hebrew Gospel of Matthew, brought by Bartholomew, among the Indians, not in Jerusalem or in Judea, but he did not claim that it was the original and primitive one. But Grotius himself admits that he did not examine the codex which Epiphanius praises: yet, more rash than he, he thinks that the Gospel of the Nazarenes living in Beroea, which Jerome narrates he consulted, flowed entirely from the very codex of Matthew, which he not only never saw, but concerning which he also had no witness from antiquity to produce. For by whose faith or authority does he think so? And what certainty Grotius had in that judgment, he himself testifies, when he admits that certain narratives, and also sayings of Christ not written in Matthew, were gradually stitched on by the Nazarenes, and he adduces some of them from Jerome and Clement of Alexandria. Furthermore, he calls those Nazarenes who used that Gospel, the Beroeans, the genuine offspring of those who first embraced the faith of Christ in Palestine. But if you listen to Jerome, they were Ebionites rather than believers, nor does their Gospel deserve the praise of authenticity. Thus, therefore, Grotius is more certain about the Gospel of the Beroeans after so many centuries than Jerome, who examined and consulted it. For he says that he left it in doubt whether that Hebrew Gospel was Matthew's? And is it the mark of believers to stitch something onto the authentic text of a canonical book, which is prohibited by the Holy Spirit under the most grave interdiction, Rev. 22.19. Now if Jerome himself makes the Gospel of Matthew, which they were using then, common to the Nazarenes and Ebionites, as Grotius says, how does Grotius dare to approve the Gospel of the Nazarenes as authentic, if indeed the Ebionites used the Gospel of Matthew not in its entirety and fullness but

As being adulterated and mutilated, according to Epiphanius, and by the admission of Grotius himself, their Gospel had been mutilated, and the γενεαλογία of Christ and what follows had been deleted, up to that place where Christ is baptized by John, as they wished the Lord to be believed to have been born from the coitus of Joseph and to have obtained the grace of anointing by the merit of his virtues. For Jerome did not hand down that distinction, that the Ebionites had a mutilated and corrupt Gospel, while the Beroeans and Nazarenes had another more sincere and incorrupt one—which are Grotian inventions—but he makes mention of only one Gospel. Regarding Tatian, who followed the Hebrew Codices of the faithful Nazarenes distinct from the codices of the Hebrews, Grotius narrates only his own conjectures: nor could he conceal that Epiphanius himself had been ambiguous as to whether the Nazarenes called Christ a ψιλὸν ἄνθρωπον. And they are nothing but mere divinations that Origen, while making the Ebionites twofold and abusing the name of the Ebionites more broadly, described the faithful Nazarenes under the former designation. Finally, whence will he provide us with proof that Mark used Matthew's Hebrew Codex? Or that, conversely, Matthew's Greek interpreter used Mark's Greek book? Should it not rather be concluded from the fact that what Mark had taken from Matthew, the latter placed here in almost the same words, that both Evangelists used the same language and wrote their Gospel? How much, indeed, Chrysostom attributed to the Hebrew Gospel of Matthew, these words of his in Matt. teach: 'They say,' he says, 'I, however, would prefer it to exist than to be established.' But about these things, it has already been said elsewhere. We add, however, what Jacobus Capellus discusses in book 2 of the Vindiciae of Isaac Casaubon against Andr. Eudæmon Joh. ch. VIII, concerning the opinions of the ancients on this cause, p. 43. “Three or perhaps four ancients said that the Gospel of Matthew was first written in Hebrew. But that Hebrew αὐτόγραφον, or authentic copy, not even one affirms to have been read by himself. Against the Gospel of Matthew which was displayed by the Ebionites as written in Hebrew, Epiphanius, Jerome, and others did not allow themselves to be pressed by its authority. Therefore, they did not hold that edition to be authentic. But that which was called authentic, who ever affirmed that he had seen it, what Orthodox person used its authority? The Fathers did not deny that some authentic Hebrew exemplar perhaps existed somewhere: For why was it necessary for that to be denied by them? What if it received it from nowhere else than from the Ebionites, which the first orthodox writer, Irenaeus, narrates in book 3, chapter 1.” What if those more recent than Father Irenaeus borrowed that report about the Gospel of Matthew being first written in Hebrew from nowhere else than from Irenaeus? How much more consistent with reason is it that we believe a few Doctors were too credulous in this part, than that we believe that sacrosanct deposit was held so negligently by all the Churches that not even one appears which can be called that divine κειμήλιον, and that they preserved neither an αὐτόγραφον, I say, nor any Hebrew ἀπόγραφον of it for even one year, or commended it to be kept for posterity?

Joh. Henricus Hottingerus, Syst. Theol. book 1, loc. 3, urges this: If Matthew had wished his Gospel to exist in Hebrew for the use of the Hebrews, he would have written it in the Jerusalem dialect rather than in pure Hebrew: he also urges this: that nowhere does an authentic Hebrew Gospel exist. But that the original text itself should have perished would be repugnant to divine providence. It is also helpful to hear Erasmus: who, at Matt. ch. VIII, says: 'It does not seem likely to me that Matthew wrote in Hebrew, since no one testifies that he saw any trace of that Hebrew volume: provided that that which they call the Nazarenes' is counted among the Apocrypha.' Sixtus of Siena, however, deserves no credit here, who in book IV of the Bibl. S. under the title of Joseph, p. m. 338, reports the following about Joseph, a Jew by nation, from the city of Tiberias, a Count by rank: This man, therefore, as Epiphanius testifies (but where in his works?), first brought to light the Hebrew Gospel of Matthew, written by the very hand of Matthew, which he found in a hidden treasury of the Jews near Scythopolis, together with the Gospel of John and the Acts of the Apostles translated from the Greek language into Hebrew. Let him who can reconcile these things with those which the same Sixtus has about Pantaenus on p. 359: 'When Pantaenus had preached the Gospel according to Matthew in Hebrew letters among the Indians, he brought it back with him returning to Alexandria.' For Sixtus of Siena affirms that Pantaenus flourished in the year of the Lord 200, but the aforementioned Joseph in the year of the Lord 370.

The argument which those who maintain that the Greek text of Matthew is the primitive one take from the Hebrew words added in the Greek context with explicit interpretations, does not lack its own weight. For even if foreign words are sometimes perhaps preserved by interpreters, with an interpretation added, that was not appropriate for the authentic Codices of Canonical Writers; namely, that something should be added and inserted beyond the original text. For thus the translation does not fully harmonize with the primitive text, in which such interpretations do not occur: provided that these interpretations also ought to be of Canonical authority, so that there is nothing in Scripture which is not Canonical and authentic. See examples in ch. I. 23 and ch. XXVII. 46 and 33. And therefore Cajetan urges that argument: to which, indeed, Maldonatus and Conzenius reply that those interpretations are not the author's, but the interpreter's. But in this way something would have been added to the sacred text of the Canonical book, which must not be said. Compare on this question, besides those whom we have already praised, Whitaker against Rainolds, ch. 12; Chamier, Panstratia, Vol. I, bk. XI, ch. 8; Flacius, preface to the N.T.; Rivetus, in Isagoge to Holy Scripture, ch. IX; Gomarus, in his dissertation on the Gospel of Matthew in Hebrew; Grotius, in Anti-Becanus, p. 27. Nor indeed is what Grotius assumes regarding the time of the writing of St. Matthew certain, namely that it came into existence in the eighth year after the Ascension of Christ: which Theophylact asserted, following Eusebius in his Chronicle. For Nicephorus, in Ecclesiastical History, bk. II, ch. 45, maintains that Matthew wrote only in the fifteenth year after the Ascension; Irenaeus determines that it was done at that time, bk. III, ch. 1, when Peter and Paul were evangelizing at Rome, which they refer to the 21st year after the Ascension of Christ. Baronius, however, draws it to the 12th year after the Ascension. And these things [pertain] to the Grotius Preface to the Gospel. of St. Matthew.

ON THE COMMENTATORS OF ST. MATTHEW.

Furthermore, besides the interpreters of the Bibles, whether of the whole or of the New Testament, and of the Quadriga, and of the Evangelical Harmony, the following authors have illustrated the Gospel of St. Matthew with commentaries. Hilary of Poitiers, in the year 370, Canons on Matthew; John Mair the Scot, three books of commentaries on Matthew, in the year 1392; Claudius the Scot, a disciple of the Venerable Bede, in the year 1300, adorned a commentary on Matthew; as did John the Scot, who was also a hearer of Bede, at the same time; Remigius of Auxerre, in the year 880; John of Regino, a Frenchman, wrote one book on the Gospel of Matthew in the year 1448. John Dominici, Cardinal

In the year of our Lord 1500. John Ferus, preacher of Mainz, published sermons on Matthew and John in the year 1535. Johannes Hofmeister wrote on Matthew, Mark, and Luke in the year 1546. Friedrich Nausea prepared a paraphrase on Matthew and John in the year 1540. Friedrich Titelmann published a paraphrastic elucidation on Matthew and John in the year 1530. Matthäus Bredenbach wrote on Matthew in the year 1550. Johannes Soarezius, Bishop of Coimbra and Count of Arganil in Spain, published commentaries on Matthew in the year 1560. At which time also Tilmann of Aachen, a German Carmelite and lecturer at the Academy of Cologne, wrote one book on the Gospel of Matthew in scholastic style; and Johannes Hesselius of Louvain commented on Matthew. And Sixtus of Siena reviewed these in his Bibliotheca Sancta, Book IV. Bellarmine, On Ecclesiastical Writers. mentions also Christian Dithmar in the year 1530. Antonio Possevino reported more in alphabetical order in his Apparatus under the word Matthew, namely these: Alfonso Tostado, Anselm of Canterbury, Antipater of Bostra, Antonio Pucci, Arnold, Athanasius, Aurelius, Augustine, Basil, Bonaventure, Claudius the Monk, Clement of Alexandria, Christian Druthmar, Chromatius, Cyprian of Carthage, Cyprian the Monk, Didymus, Domingo de Soto, Eccard, François Titelmann, Friedrich Nausea, Gregory of Antioch, Gregory of Nazianzus, Gregory of Nyssa, William of Auvergne, William Ludov. Langion, William Pelum, Guerric, John Chrysostom, John Dolea, John Dominici, John Hofmeister, John Ludovicus, John Mæstrosius, John Maldonado, John Maria, John Regino, John of the Holy Faith, John Scotus the Monk, John Soarez the Lusitanian, Jodocus, Joseph Tiberinus, Julius Africanus, Pope Leo, Leonitus, Matthew of the Royal Court, Matthew Bredenbach, Methodius, Michael Angrianus, Nicolaus Dintelspul, Pantaleon, Pantaenus, Paul of the Palace, Peter of Ailly, Remigius, Rodulphus Languis, Severianus, Symmachus, Theodore of Heraclea, Theodoret Herxen, Theodore of Ancyra, Theognostus, Tilmann of Aachen. Others also list Benedict, Pope, published at Venice in the year 1663 in folio, Porreda, printed at Venice in the year 1602, Alfonso de Avendaño at Madrid in folio 1593, Cass. Melo in folio at Pintza 1594. Claude Guilliaud of Billiac, who flourished in the year 1540, from whom, however, besides commentaries on the Epistles, Sixtus of Siena reports only that John was illustrated, Stanisław Sokołowski, Canon of Kraków, à Ponte, Lelio Pisciola the Jesuit, etc. From the ancient Greeks there exists a Catena of the Fathers, namely of 21 Greeks, under the title of 'Tomus prior' of Symbols on Matthew by Peter Possinus, and it exhibits the symbols of Athanasius, Antiochus of Ptolemais, Apollinaris, Basil, Chrysostom, Cyril of Alexandria, Eusebius of Caesarea, Gregory the Theologian, Gregory of Nyssa, Hesychius, Irenaeus of Lyons, Isidore of Pelusium, Origen, Peter of Laodicea, Photius, Severus of Antioch, Theodoret, Bishop of Cyrrhus, Theodore of Antioch, Theodore of Heraclea, Theodore the Monk, and Theodore of Mopsuestia. Furthermore, there is also another of 30 Greek Fathers Catena, compiled by Nicetas, Bishop of Serres, which Balthasar Corderius translated, published under this title: 'Tomus alter' of Symbols on Matthew: in which the following authors are contained: Ammianus, Ammonius, Anepigraphus, Anonymus, Athanasius, Basil, Chrysostom, Clement of Alexandria, Cyril, Damascenus, Dionysius, Dorotheus, Epiphanius, Ephrem, Irenaeus, Isaac, Isaiah the Ascetic, Isidore, Macarius, Marcus the Ascetic and Monk, Maximus, Nazianzen, Nicetas, Nilus, Nyssen, Severus, Thaumaturgus, Theodore of Heraclea, Titus. Like the Catena on Matthew, Mark, and Luke is the one which Marloratus compiled: but from more recent writers (as also in the remaining writings of the New Testament) whom he employed on those Evangelists, the following: Erasmus, Philipp Melanchthon, Brentius, Sacerrius, Vitus Theodorus: Zwingli, likewise, Bullinger, Bucer, Calvin, and Musculus. Moreover, there are read besides these, commentaries on Matthew from the Reformed: Oecolampadius, Lambert Daneau, Sebastian Münster, Tossanus, François Junius, David Pareus, and Christoph Pelargus, as also Abraham Scultetus: and not least the 'Horae Hebraicae' on Matthew by John Lightfoot: From our own, after those which were handed down in the 'Harmonia Exegetica' illustrated by the blessed Chemnitz, the blessed Polycarp Lyser, and the blessed Gerhard, the commentaries on Matthew by Caspar Cruciger, David Chytraeus, the blessed Aegidius Hunnius, and D. Caspar Bertram. The blessed John Gerhard left some things recorded on St. Matthew, which his blessed son, D. John Ernest, enriched with prolix and learned additions. Peter Winstrup compiled a quite dense volume on only the first five chapters of Matthew: just as Friedrich Spanheim, from the Reformed, in three parts of his Evangelical doubts, did not even fully explain those five chapters of St. Matthew, being more successful in gathering doubts than in solving them, rendering not a few things more doubtful, and disputing about them in a merely Pyrrhonian manner. John Jacob Grynæus wrote on the first ten chapters of Matthew.

THE ECONOMY OF ST. MATTHEW.

But leaving these aside, we proceed to the Economy of St. Matthew, who describes the genealogy and birth of Jesus in chapter I, the arrival of the Magi from the East to the manger of Jesus, and their departure, as well as the flight of Jesus into Egypt on account of the Herodian infanticide, and the recall from Egypt, and the dwelling of Joseph with the little Jesus in Nazareth, in chapter II. But thirdly, after the aforementioned proclamation and baptism of St. John, he deals with the baptism received by Jesus. And these are the things that happened before the public ministry of Jesus; to which, just as he was inaugurated by baptism and the illustrious theophany that occurred in it, so he can be said to have been prepared for it by the temptation endured in the desert: although that was also the first struggle in his holy ministry with the greatest of his antagonists and their leader. Concerning which, chapter IV treats, and in that way, there is an approach to the acts of the public ministry. Which, for the sake of the harmony of the Evangelical history, can be distributed according to the Passovers. Moreover, those things which pertain to the acts from the first Passover of the ministry of Jesus to the second are not recounted here, except for the arrival of Christ in Galilee after John was delivered up, and the summary of his sermons, as well as the calling of Simon Peter and Andrew, and also of James and John, in the same fourth chapter. To those things, however, which were done from the second Passover to the third, pertain the sermons in Galilee, and the miraculous healings commemorated in the final verses 23, 24, 25 of the same chapter, and the lengthy sermon of Christ described in chapters V, VI, and VII, as well as the miracles of the leper, and the Centurion's servant, and others healed, the calming of the storm at sea, the liberation of the two possessed men in chapter VIII, the paralytic cured, with the repeated calling of Matthew; the daughter of Jairus raised, the woman with the issue of blood restored, sight restored to two blind men, the mute and demoniac healed in chapter IX. There follows furthermore the sending 12. The mission of the Apostles with instruction and promises made to them c. X. John's embassy to Christ from prison, and Christ's complaint about the people, the preaching of God the Father, and the most sweet invitation of all who labor c. XI. the defense of the disciples rubbing grain on the Sabbath, the healing of the blind and mute with an apology against blasphemy c. XII. Many parables of Christ, and his new contempt in Nazareth c. XIII. and the feeding of five thousand men in the desert, and the walking on the sea c. XIV.

From the third to the fourth Passover the healing of the sick in the region of Gennesaret is commemorated, the traditions and hypocrisy of the Pharisees are refuted, the faith of the Canaanite woman is celebrated, many are healed, and four thousand men are fed c. XV. A sign of Jonah is presented to the Pharisees, and they are ordered to beware of their leaven, a confession is issued by Peter, Jesus predicts his passion, and commands his followers c. XVI. The transfiguration of Jesus, the healing of the lunatic son, and a discourse about the passion and resurrection, and the payment of the stater c. XVII. The contention about primacy, the warning about scandal, and about forgiving one's neighbor with the parable of the King demanding an account from his servants c. XVIII. Fuller information about divorce, the admission of little children, the testing of the youth seeking salvation through works, and at Peter's insistence the promised reward for the renunciation of all things c. XIX. The parable of the laborers in the vineyard, c. XX.

To the fourth Passover pertains the History of the Passion, death, and resurrection of the Lord, where occur 1. Acts on the journey to Jerusalem c. XX. in the second part, such as the prediction of the passion, death, and resurrection of Christ, the petition of the sons of Zebedee, and the healing of two blind men. 2. The solemn entry into Jerusalem, and what was done concerning it, where primarily the reformation of the temple is designated, the departure into Bethany, and upon the entry of the following day the cursing of the fig tree: Then Christ's sermon on the power of faith, and further what was done with the Priests and elders; where the question is about the authority of teaching, and about the origin of John's baptism; the parable of the two sons destined for the vineyard, with a warning about publicans and harlots entering heaven before the Pharisees: the parable of the servants and the son of the Lord of the vineyard with the application concerning the stone rejected by the Architects c. XXI. The parable of the wedding, the temptation about the census, about the woman with seven husbands, about the greatest commandment, with the question about the son and Lord of David c. XXII. And these things Christ did with his adversaries: Now the τὰ λεχθέντα (things said) to the disciples follow: such as the warnings about the Pharisees, and the manifold woe spoken to them, with the prediction of the devastation of Jerusalem c. XXIII. The signs of the destruction of the temple, and the coming of the son of man, with an exhortation to vigilance c. XXIV. the parables of the ten virgins, some foolish, others prudent, of the talents entrusted: and also the process of the final judgment c. XXV. All of which pertain to the τὰ προηγούμενα (things preceding), or the antecedents of the passion of Christ. There follows further the history of the passion of Christ described in c. XXVI. and XXVII., and finally the history of the resurrection c. XXVIII. Regarding those things in chapter 26, after the repeated prediction of the passion and the consultation of the priests, the previously mentioned anointing done in the house of Simon is commemorated, the pact of Judas the traitor, the celebration of the Passover and the Holy Supper, the predicted denial of the Lord's disciples and of Peter himself, the passion of Christ in Gethsemane, and the arrest made by betrayal, and the abduction to Caiaphas, the examination in the Council, and the triple denial of Peter with the tears that followed are contained. Furthermore, in chapter 27, the abduction of Jesus to Pilate, the despair of Judas, the examination of Pilate, and his wife warning in vain about the innocence of Jesus, his condemnation: the agitation of Jesus in the praetorium, his leading out, and crucifixion, the slanders poured out upon the crucified one, and his exclamation and death: and the consequences of the death, the miracles and the opening primarily of the tombs of the saints, the conversion of the centurion, and the burial done by Joseph of Arimathea: as well as the guarding and sealing of the sepulcher. Regarding the history of the manifested resurrection in chapter 28, the arrival of the women at the sepulcher, the angelic rolling away of the stone, and the discourse held concerning the resurrection of Jesus, and the future appearance in Galilee to be announced to the disciples, as well as the appearance of Jesus with the manifestation of himself, and a similar command: the report of the guards, who, having been corrupted by the priests, spread very discordant lies: the manifestation made to the Apostles in Galilee, and the sending into the world to teach and baptize, with the promise of his presence. The blessed D. Johann Gerhard handed down this economy of St. Matthew in his posthumous Annotations, p. 39. Matthew explains 1. The Person, 2. The Office of Christ. To the Person belongs the enumeration of ancestors, the description of his birth and upbringing. To the office belongs 1. The solemn preparation for it, 2. The public administration of the same, and indeed 1. of the Prophetic office through the preaching of the Gospel and the operation of miracles, completed in three years and a half of ministry. 2. Of the Priestly office through passion and death. 3. Of the Kingly office through resurrection and ascension.

PART I. OF THE GOSPEL OF ST. MATTHEW. Preparation for the description of the public ministry of Jesus.

Latin:

PRÆLOQUIUM DE INSCR

VEtus inscriptio non habet nu- de ἐυαγγέλιον, sed ἐυαγγέλιον Ἰη- σῦ Χριστῦ, ut est initio Marci : quia nimirum argumentum li- bri erat,ut jam diximus,κήρυγμα Christi : Ideo non potuit Scri- ptoris nomen poni patrio casu : sicuti non dicimus vita Cæsaris Plutarchi, sed scripta à Plutarcho. Hanc causam esse ar- bitror cur non Ματθαίου & Μάρκου atque ita deinceps, sed κατὰ Ματθαῖον, κατὰ Μάρκον hi libri inscripti fuerint, cum alioquin non minus recte id quod scriptum est à Matthæo Evangelium Matthæi possit dici, quam Paulus de doctrina Christi à se prædicata agens dixit, ἐυαγγέλιόν με Rom. XVI. 25. collato loco I.9. Est ergo ἐυαγγέλιον Ἰησῦ Χρισῦ κατὰ Ματθαῖον nihil aliud, quam doctrina à Jesu Christo tradita, prout ea à Matthæo præscripta est : id enim signifi- cat Græcum κατὰ : quod cum Latina voce haud æque possit exprimi, minus mirandum est si Latini quidam in citandis his libris Græcam dictionem servaverunt.

Matthæum in Palæstina regione mansisse annos ali- quam multos post Christi ἔνσαρκον ἐνδημίαν (octo mini- mum ut Græci aliiique exscriptores fine libri annotarunt) magno antiquorum consensu traditur. Quare par credi est scriptam ab eo Evangelicam historiam eo sermone, qui ea in regione frequentabatur. Nam quod quidam magno co- natu probatum eunt Græcum id quod habemus esse ipsius Matthæi primitivum, in eo nullis justis de causis maximam piæ antiquitatis consensionem repudiani. Nam Papias, Irenæus, Origenes atque alii quibus ejus rei veritatem quam nobis exquirere promtius fuit, pro comperto tradi- derunt, scripsisse Matthæum Hebraice. Addit ex Pantæno Eusebius, idipsum Evangelium Hebraicis literis scriptum, apud Indos servatum fuisse, quibus tradiderat Bartholo- mæus. Neque unquam ea de re dubitasse videtur Hiero- nymus, quanquam an illud Hebræum Matthæi esset illud ipsum, quo suo tempore utebantur Nazaræi, quodque tum in Bibliotheca Cæsareensi, tum Berææ, atque alibi ex- stitisse sua ætate memorat, in dubio relinquit. Addit Hie- ronymus tertio contra Pelagium scriptum fuisse Chaldai- co Syroque sermone, sed Hebraicis literis, ubi Chaldaicum Syrumque sermonem intelligo idioma Hierosolymita- num, linguam ejus temporis. Quod autem illi adferunt argumentum ex veris Hebraicis quæ in Græco contextu videmus expressa, additis interpretationibus pondus apud me non habet. Solenne enim est omnibus scriptoribus, etiam interpretibus, vocabula peregrina notabiliora ser- vare integra, sed addito interpretamento, quod aliquoties etiam factum videmus à senibus septuaginta. Illud quidem Hebraicum Evangelium, quod à Filio, & alterum, quod à Münstero est editum, non esse Matthæi adeo certum est, ut nullis indigeat argumentis : sed Vetus illud Nazaræorum Berææ habitantium, quod à se consultum, translatumque in linguas alias narrat Hieronymus, omnino arbitror, ex ipso Matthæi Codice fluxisse: quod ab illis quidem con- stantissime asseveratum fuisse, tradit idem Hieronymus : addit Epiphanius, sed quem non inspexisse, apparet, fuisse penes ipsos Evangelium Matthæi plenissimum. Certe Na- zaræi illi Berenses genuina erant progenies eorum, qui primi in palæstina Christi fidem erant amplexi. Nam id illis nomen primitus fuisse inditum, ex Domini nostri no- mine, qui vulgo Nazaræus vocabatur, apparet Act. XXV. 5. plane sicut illi, qui lingua Græca Christum sunt ample- xi, dicti sunt χριστιανοὶ Act. XI. 26. Adde, quod & Epipha- nius testatur, hos ipsos Nazaræos fuisse propaginem eo- rum, qui divinitus admoniti Hierosolymis Pellam disces- serunt, obsidii tempore. Attamen, narrationes non quæ- dam non perscriptæ à Matthæo, sed auditu perceptæ, vi- dentur paulatim à Nazaræis affutæ iis, quæ penes ipsos e- rant exemplaribus, unde nata diversitas inter ipsorum He- braicum, & quod nos habemus Græcum. Nam historia de adultera, quam nos à Johanne proditam habemus, in il- lorum Evangelio, legebatur. Tale est illud cap. XII. illum nempe, cum arida manu fuisse cæmentarium, qui misera- bilibus verbis imminentem mendicitatem deprecaretur, quod refert Hieronymus: Et hic locus post resurrectionis historiam: Dominus autem cum dedisset Sindonem servo sa- cerdotis, ivit ad Iacobum, & apparuit ei. Iuraverat enim Iaco- bus, se non comesturum panem ab illa hora, qua biberat calicem Domini, donec videret eum resurgentem à mortuis. Mox: Af- ferte, ait Dominus, panem & mensam. Tulit panem & benedi- xit ac fregit, & dedit Iacobo justo, & dixit ei: frater mi, come- de panem tuum, quia resurrexit filius hominis à dormientibus. Sed & id, quod apud Ignatium in Epistola ad Smyrnæos legimus, Christum Petro dixisse post resurrectionem: Ecce palpate me & videte, quia non sum dæmonium corporale, & sta- tim tetigisse eum & credidisse, exstabat in eodem illo se- cundum Hebræos Evangelio. Et locus ille de divite cap. XIX. aliter habebat, ut dicemus cum eo ventum erit. Nar- rabatur in eodem Evangelio fractum atque divisum fuisse limen superum templi, cum Christus mortem obiret. Est & aliud ex eodem Hebræo Evangelio locus in Dialogo Hieronymi tertio adversus Pelagianos: Ecce mater Domi- ni & fratres ejus dicebant ei: Iohannes Baptista baptizat in re- missionem peccatorum. Eamus & baptizemur ab eo. Dixit autem eis: quid peccavi, ut vadam & baptizer ab eo? Adde his locum, qui est infra XVIII. 22. Sed & sententiæ quæ- dam Christi, quæ in nostris libris perscriptæ non sunt, ex fama, in eum librum sunt relatæ: ut illa, quam laudat Cle- mens Alexandrinus: ὁ θαυμάσας βασιλεύσει, καὶ ὁ βασιλεύ- σας ἀναπαύσεται: & apud Hieronymum altera: nunquam læti sitis, nisi cum fratrem vestrum videritis in caritate. Cujus generis plures quoque fuisse sententias per manum tradi- tas, sed cum perscriptis sensu congruentes credibile est. Nam & in Actis ut Christi dictum citatur, quod illis ver- bis perscriptum non exstat, μακάριόν ἐστι διδόναι μᾶλλον ἢ λαμβάνειν. XX. 35. Puto autem Tatianum cum ex quatuor Evangeliis unum concinnaret, secutum in Matthæi verbis, non Græcos tantum, sed & Hebræos Codices, unde Evan- gelium illud Tatiani, quod vulgo vocabatur διὰ τεσσάρων, ab aliis dictum κατὰ ἑβραίους, narrat Epiphanius. Atque hinc etiam factum arbitror, ut istud Evangelium alii vo- cent, non διὰ τεσσάρων, sed διὰ πέντε, ut Victor Capuanus. Neque id mirum vobis videri debet, cum Ignatius tanto antiquior illam historiam de verbis post resurrectionem, Justinus alteram de Baptismo Christi recitet, ita, ut legeba- tur in Evangelio Nazaræorum. Video esse, qui putent non auctum tantum ex traditionibus, sed & mutilatum fuisse Evangelium Nazaræorum, cujus rei nusquam idoneum reperio testem. Nam Epiphanius contrarium dicit, ἔχουσι δὲ τὸ κατὰ ματθαῖον εὐαγγέλιον πληρέστατον ἑβραϊστί. Nec assen- tiri possum iis, qui Epiphani verbis negationem interfe- runt: quanquam scio ab eodem Epiphanio de Ebionæis dici, usos eos Matthæi Evangelio οὐχ ὅλῳ δὲ πληρεστάτῳ ἀλ- λὰ νενοθευμένῳ κὴ ἠκρωτηριασμένῳ : neque ignoro Hierony- mum ita Hebræum Matthæi exemplar citare, ut id com- mune videatur facere Nazaræis & Ebionitis. Sed com- mune illis arbitror fuisse Evangelium Matthæi, sicut olim Catholicis commune fuit cum Marcione Evangelium Lucæ, paucis scilicet mutatis, quæ Marcioni displicebant. Ita & Ebionitæ deleverunt totam γενεαλογίαν & quæ se- quantur, ad eum locum ubi Christus à Johanne baptiza- tus, plane sicut Marcio primo Lucæ capita induxit. Fece- runt autem hoc Ebionitæ pro suo instituto, ut qui Domi- num Jesum credi vellent natum ex Josephi concubitu, & virtutum merito consecutum unctionis gratiam, ut alibi dicemus. Hoc autem cur Nazaræi facerent, nihil erat causæ, qui non probantur in fidei negotio à cæteris Chri- stianis discrepasse, quanquam ritus Judaicos tradita à ma- joribus consuetudine observabant, Apostolis non prohi- bentibus. Bene enim notat Sulpitius, in Palæstina Christia- nos pene omnes ad Adriani usque tempora, Christum Deum sub legis observatione credidisse. Et cum dubitet Epiphanius, an hi quoque ψιλὸν ἄνθρωπον Christum dice- rent, an vero nobiscum faterentur ipsum διὰ πνεύματος ἁ- γίου γεγεννῆσθαι ἐκ Μαρίας, sed & nescire se dicat, an abscin- dant τὰς γενεαλογίας τὰς ἀπὸ τοῦ Ἀβραὰμ ἄχρι χριστοῦ; alii ve- ro qui de iis scribunt, nihil plane illis tribuant proprium præter Hebræorum rituum observationem: Irenæus vero nullam eorum mentionem faciat in recensu hæreseon, in partem meliorem de illis judicandum est, eoque magis, quod Augustinus, qui vetustiores scriptores consuluit, di- serte affirmet, confiteri Nazaræos, Christum esse Dei fi- lium: & Origenes, cum duplices facit Ebionæos in Dif- putatione contra Celsum ἤτοι ἐκ παρθένου ὁμολογοῦντας ὁ- μοίως ἡμῖν τὸν Ἰησοῦν ἢ οὐχ οὕτω γεγεννῆσθαι, ἀλλ' ὡς τοὺς λοιποὺς ἀν- θρώπους, Ebionæorum nomine laxius abutens, sua priore illa nota Nazaræos, ut credibile est, describat. Quare He- bræum illud Nazaræorum Evangelium quod sæpe laudat Hieronymus, est quidem idem ac Ebionis Evangelium, sed ut recte judicavit Gelasius, ab Ebione maculatum. Sic- ut autem Marcus usus est Matthæi Hebræo, ni fallor, codi- ce, ita Marci libro Græco usus mihi videtur quisquis is fuit Matthæi Græcus Interpres: nam quæ Marcus ex Matthæo desumserat, idem hic iisdem prope verbis posuit, nisi quod quædam à Marco, Hebraico aut Chaldaico loquendi ge- nere expressa, propius ad Græci sermonis normam emol- livit. De cujus versionis ab ipso Christianismi initio per Ecclesias receptæ autoritate ac fide dubitare, nefas arbi- tror.

ELENCHUS.

Meras conjecturas & ςοχασμὸς suos nobis pandit Grotius. Quid enim in his certi atque in- dubii est? Si divinationibus & conjecturis in tali- bus indulgendum, quæ rem tanti momenti tex- tum originalem, & ἀρχέτυπον libri concernunt, quænam relinquetur denique certitudo? Non du- bitandum esse dicit, de versionis Græcæ Matthæi auctoritate ac fide: sed si non habemus ipsum πρω- τότυπον divina providentia conservatum, quod in usum Canonicum Ecclesiæ destinatum erat di- vinitus, quomodo certi esse poterimus, sive de fi- de & autoritate translationis, sive de conservatio- ne ejusdem perenni & intemerata? Verbum Dei non periturum credimus, ac ne Jota, vel apicem ejus interire posse, verbo Christi securi fidem ad- hibemus, sed de translationum conservatione, nullam habemus promissionem. Nec vero quis- quam dicere potest, interpretem fuisse Aposto- lum vel virum θεόπνευςον: de quo admodum va- riant: Athanasius eum dicit fratrem Domini Jaco- bum, Hieronymus & Eusebius Marcum, Theophyla- ctus Johannem, Anastasius in Genes. serm. VIII. Lucam & Paulum, alii alium: unde Baronius eo etiam abiit, quod non nisi collato cum Ebræo origina- li affirmari possit, cujus fidei sit textus Græcus, quo de vid. Casaubonus Exercit. XV. 12. At verum tex- tum Matthæi Ebræum non amplius extare ait Bailius Jesuita in Catech. centur. tract. I. §. 14. & Conze- nius quæst. V. proœm.

Porro, quum totum Novum Testamentum,
