Græco sermone, qui per universum orbem notus erat, à sanctis Dei viris conscriptum sit, perinde uti Vetus Testamentum Ebræo, & cognato sermo- ne, populo Dei familiari consignatum est à Spiri- tus Sancti amanuensibus, non sit verisimile Ebræo sermone partem hunc præcipuam Novi Testa- menti, Evangelium κατὰ Ματθαῖον adornatum fuisse in archetypo, atque originali textu. Rationes alias alibi adduximus, utpote in Critico sacro, & T. 1. syst. Theolog. Nunc de ςοχασμοῖς solum Grotia- nis. Par credi est, secundum Grotium à Matthæo, qui in Palæstina Regione mansit, scriptam Evangeli- cam historiam eo sermone, qui in ea regione frequen- tabatur. At Dorotheus in synopsi Matthæum Hie- ropoli in Parthia Evangelium prædicasse, docet, ibique diem suum obiisse: nec in Judæa Ebræus sermo, qualis in Veteri Testamento Codice adhi- bitus, sed Syriacus, quod Idioma originale Mat- thæo faciunt Widmanstadius, & Guido Fabricius, Bellarminus, ut & Adam Conzenius & Græcus usita- tus tum erat: neque Ebræis solum, aut præcipue etiam scriptum est hoc Evangelium, sed imprimis Græcis & gentilibus traditum iri, Christus præ- dixerat Matth. XXI. 43. Maximam vero antiquita- tis consensionem temere prætendit Grotius. Nam Papias, non Johannis Evangelistæ, sed Aristionis, & Senioris Johannis auditor, modico admodum præ- ditus judicio, à quo traditionem auspicatur, fidei nullius est in antiquitate, cui imponi, ut in aliis, facile ab Ebionæis potuit: quid mirum ergo, si ab illo simplici credulitate accepit illud Irenæus & O- rigenes, quos traditiones etiam aliæ Papiæ in erro- rem abripuerunt? Non certe pro comperto id tra- diderunt, scripsisse Matthæum Ebraice. Nemo enim eorum vidit Ebræum exemplar. Neque Eu- sebius alium, quam Pantænum, testem laudare po- tuit de Evangelio Ebraicis literis scripto: qui vero se non Hierosolymis, vel in Judæa, sed apud Indos Evangelium Ebraicum Matthæi, à Bartholomeo il- latum invenisse solum, ait, non autem illud origi- narium esse, & primitivum perhibuit. Epiphanius vero Codicem, quem laudat, non inspexisse, fate- tur ipse Grotius: at illo magis temerarius, arbitra- tur, omnino Nazaræorum Berrææ habitantium Evan- gelium, quod à se consultum Hieronymus narrat, ex ipso Matthæi Codice fluxisse, quod non modo haud vidit unquam, sed de quo etiam testem ex antiquitate nullum producere habuit. Cujus enim fide vel autoritate ita arbitratur? Et qualem in ea κρίσει habuerit Grotius certitudinem, testatur ipse, cum narrationes quasdam, nec non sententias Chri- sti è Matthæo non perscriptas, paulatim à Naza- ræis assutas fatetur, earumque nonnullas ex Hiero- nymo & Clem. Alexandrino adducit. Porro Naza- ræos illos, qui Evangelio illo usi sunt, Berroënses ge- nuinam, dicit, progeniem eorum, qui primi in Palæ- stina Christi fidem amplexi erant. At si Hieronymum audias, Ebionitæ potius fuere, quam fideles, neque ἀυθεντίας laudem meretur eorum Evangelium. Sic ergo certior est Grotius de Evangelio Berroën- sium post tot secula, quam Hieronymus, qui il- lud aspexit & consuluit. Illum enim in dubio re- liquisse, ait, an illud Ebræum esset Matthæi Evan- gelium? Et num fidelium est assuere aliquid textui authentico canonici libri, quod sub gravissima in- terminatione à Spiritu Sancto prohibitum Apoc. XXII. 19. Jam si Hieronymus ipse commune facit Nazaræis & Ebionitis, quod dicit Grotius, Evange- lium Matthæi, quo tum utebantur, quomodo audet Grotius probare Nazaræorum Evangelium tanquam authenticum, siquidem Ebionitæ usi sint Matthæi Evangelio ἐκ ὅλῳ δὲ πληρεσάτῳ ἀλλὰ

νενοθευμένῳ καὶ ἠκρωτηριασμένῳ teste Epiphanio, ac fatente ipsomet Grotio, mutilatum fuerit eo- rum Evangelium, ac deleta tum γενεαλογία Christi, & quæ sequuntur, usque ad eum locum, ubi Christus à Johanne baptizatur, utpote qui Dominum credi vel- lent natum ex Josephi concubitu & virtutum merito consecutum unctionis gratiam. Non enim Hiero- nymus discrimen illud tradidit, quod Ebionitæ Evangelium mutilatum habuerint & corruptum, Beroënses & Nazareni aliud sincerius & incor- ruptius, quæ commenta sunt Grotiana: sed u- nius tantum Evangelii mentionem facit. De Tatiano sequuto Hebræos Codices Nazarenorum fi- delium distinctos ab Ebræorum codicibus, suas tantum conjecturas narrat Grotius: nec dissimu- lare potuit, Epiphanium ipsum ambiguum fuis- se, anne Nazaræi ψιλὸν ἄνθρωπον Christum dixe- rint. Nec nisi meræ divinationes sunt, quod Origenes, dum duplices Ebionæos facit, Ebionæo- rum nomine latius abutens, sub priore nota Naza- ræos fideles descripserit. Denique unde nobis fidem faciet, quod Marcus usus sit Matthæi Ebræo Codice? aut quod vicissim Marci libro Græco usus fuerit Matthæi Græcus Interpres? annon potius ex eo, quod quæ Marcus ex Matthæo desumse- rat, idem hic iisdem prope verbis posuerit, con- cludendum eodem utrumque Evangelistam ser- mone usum esse, ac Evangelium suum conscripsis- se. Quantum vero Chrysostomus Evangelio Mat- thæi Ebræo tribuerit, hæc ejus in Matth. verba do- cent: Ajunt, inquit, ego tamen malim extare, quam constare. Sed de his alias jam dictum. Addimus ta- men, quæ Jacobus Capellus l. 2. Vindiciar. Isaaci Casauboni adversus Andr. Eudæmon. Joh. c. VIII. de Veterum sententiis de hac causa disputat p. 43. „Evangelium Matthæi tres forte quatuorve vete- „res dixerunt Hebraice primum fuisse conscri- „ptum. Cæterum Hebraicum illud αὐτόγραφον, „vel authenticum, ne unus quidem à se lectum af- „firmat. Contra quod ab Ebionitis ostentabatur „Evangelium Matthæi scriptum Hebraice, hujus „autoritate urgeri se non patiebantur Epiphani?, „Hieronymus, alii. Non habebant igitur editio- „nem illam pro authentica. Illam vero quæ dice- „batur authentica, quis unquam à se conspectam „affirmavit, quis Orthodoxus illius usus est au- „thoritate? Hebraicum aliquod exemplar au- „thenticum alicubi forsan extare, non negabant „Patres: Quid enim id ab illis negari necesse erat? „Quid si non aliunde, quam ab Ebionitis accepit, „quod primus orthodoxus narrat Irenæus lib. 3. „cap. 1. Quid si Patre Irenæo recentiores non „aliunde, quam ab Irenæo mutuati sunt relatio- „nem illam de Matthæi Evangelio Hebraice pri- „mum scripto? Quanto rationi convenientius „est, ut credamus pauculos aliquot Doctores hac „in parte nimis credulos fuisse, quam ut credamus „sacrosanctum illud depositum ab omnibus Ec- „clesiis tam negligenter habitum, ut ne una qui- „dem compareat, quæ dici possit divinum illud „κειμήλιον, nec αὐτόγραφον, inquam, nec ullum e- „jus ἀπόγραφον Hebraicum vel ad annum unum „asservasse, posteris servandum commendasse?

Joh. Henricus Hottingerus Syst. Theol. l. 1. loc. 3. hoc urget: Si Matthæus Evangelium suum in u- sum Hebræorum Hebraice voluisset extare, Hierosoly- mitana potius, quam pure Hebraica dialecto illud ex- arasset: urget & hoc: quod nuspiam extet Hebrai- cum Evangelium authenticum. Periisse autem ipsum textum originalem providentiæ divinæ re- pugnet. Erasmum etiam audire juvat: qui ad Matt. c. VIII. Non mihi, inquit, sit verisimile Mat- thæum Ebraice scripsisse, cum nemo testetur, se vi- disse ullum illius Ebraici voluminis vestigium: siqui- dem illud, quod Nazaræorum vocant, inter Apocry- pha censetur. Sixtus vero Senensis fidem nullam hic meretur, qui lib. IV. Bibl. S. sub tit. Josephi p. m. 338. de Josepho natione Judæo, Patria Tyberinen- si, dignitate Comite refert, quæ sequuntur: Hic itaq;, ut Epiphanius testatur (at ubi locorum?) primus emisit in lucem Evangelium Matthæi Hebraicum, ipsa Matthæi manu conscriptum, quod in occulto Ga- zophylacio Judæorum apud Scythopolim una cum Evangelio Johannis, & Actibus Apostolicis de Græca lingua in Hebraicam translatis adinvenit. Quæ qui potest, conciliet cum illis quæ idem Sixtus de Pan- tæno p. 359. habet: Pantænus quum apud Indos Ev- angelium secundum Matthæum Hebraicis literis scriptum prædicasset, ipsum revertens Alexandriam secum retulit. Claruisse enim Pantænum Anno Domini 200. Josephum vero dictum anno Domi- ni 370. Sixtus Senensis affirmat.

Argumentum, quod ex verbis Ebraicis, in Græco contextu additis interpretationibus expressis desu- munt, qui Græcum Matthæi textum primitivum esse tuentur, non caret pondere suo. Nam etsi pe- regrina vocabula nonnunquam serventur forte ab interpretibus, addito interpretamento, id tamen authenticis Codicib. Canonicorum Scriptorum non conveniebat; addi nempe aliquid, & inferi præter originalem textum. Nam sic ex asse non consonat translatio cum textu primitivo, in quo talia inter- pretamenta non occurrunt: siquidem & inter- pretamenta ista authoritatis Canonicæ esse de- beant, ne in Scriptura quicquam sit, quod non sit Canonicum, atque authenticum. Exempla vide c. I. 23. & c. XXVII. 46. & 33. Ideoque Cajetanus argumentum illud urget: ad quod quidem Mal- donatus & Conzenius regerunt, interpretationes il- las non esse autoris, sed interpretis: Sed ita aliquid accessisset textui sacro libri Canonici, quod non dicendum. Conf. de hac quæstione præter eos quos jam laudavimus, Whitakerus c. Rainold. c. 12. Chamierus Panstrat. T. I. l. XI. c. 8. Flacius præf. in N. T. Rivetus in Isagog. ad Script. S. c. IX. Go- marus in dissert. de Evang. Matth. Ebr. Joh. Grotius in Anti-Bec. p. 27. Nec vero de tempore scriptionis S. Matthæi certum est quod assumit Grotius, octa- vo nimirum anno post Ascensionem Christi in ador- tum esse: quod Theophylactus, præeunte Eusebio in Chronico asseruit. Nicephorus enim l. II. Histor. Eccl. c. 45. decimo quinto demum post ascensionem anno Matthæum scripsisse vult: Irenæus id eo tem- pore factum statuit l. III. c. 1. quo Petrus & Paulus Romæ evangelizarint, quod referunt ad XXI. an- num post ascensionem Christi. Baronius vero trahit ad annum XII. post ascensionem. Atq; hæc ad Præloquium Grotianum in Evang. S. Matthæi.

DE COMMENTATORIBUS S. MATTHÆI.

CÆterum Commentariis illustrarunt Evan- gelium S. Matthæi præter Bibliorum, seu uni- versorum, seu N. Testamenti, & Quadrigæ, atque Harmoniæ Evangelicæ Interpretes, sequentes au- tores. Hilarius Pictaviensis An. CCCLXX. Canones in Matthæum: Joh. Maisrosius Scotus tres libros Commentariorū in Matth. An. IƆCCCXCII. Claudius Scotus Venerabilis Bedæ discipulus Anno IƆ ccc. comment. in Matt. adornavit: ut & Joh. Scotus, qui etiam Bedæ auditor fuit, eodem tempore: Remi- gius Antisiodorensis An. IƆCCCXXC. Johan. de Regino, Gallus librum unum in Evangel. Matthæi Anno clƆCCCCXLIIX. conscripsit. Joh. Dominici Cardinalis

Anno Domini cIɔ cccc. Joh: Ferus Concionator Moguntinus in Matthæum & Johannem concio- nes edidit, Anno cIɔ Iɔ xxxv. Johannes Hofmei- sterus in Matthæum, Marcum & Lucam scripsit An- no cIɔ Iɔ XLVI. Fridericus Nausea Anno cIɔ Iɔ XL. in Matthæum, & Johannem Paraphrasin adorna- vit. Fridericus Titelmannus Anno cIɔ Iɔ xxx in Matthæum & Johannem paraphrasticam diluci- dationem edidit. Matth. Bredenbachius scripsit in Matthæum Ann. cIɔ IɔL. Johannes Soarezius Epi- scopus Conimbricensis, & Arganisi in Hispania Comes edidit Commentarios in Matthæum Anno cIɔ Iɔ LX. Quo tempore etiam Tilmannus Aquensis Germanus Carmelita lector Academiæ Colonien- sis in Evang. Matthæi Scholastica dictione librum unum scripsit ; & Joh. Hesselius de Lovanio in Mat- thæum commentatus est. Atq; hos recensuit Six- tus Senensis, in Biblioth. S. libr. IV. Bellarminus de Script. Eccles. commemorat & Christianum Dith- marum Anno 1530. Antonius Possevinus plures retulit ordine Alphabetico in Apparatu ad vocem Matthæi, nempe hosce: Alphonsum Tostatum, Anshelmum Cantuariensem, Antipatrurn Bossien- sem, Antonium Puccium, Arnoldum Athanasium, Aurelium, Augustinum, Basilium, Bonaventuram, Claudium Monachum, Clementem Alexandrinum, Christianum Drutamarum, Chromatium, Cypria- num Carthaginensem, Cyprianum Monachum, Didymum, Dominicum Soto, Eccardium, Franc. Titelmannum, Fridericum Nauseam, Gregorium Antiochiæ, Gregorium Nazianzenum, Gregorium Nyssæ, Guilielmum Arvernum, Guilielmum Lu- dov. Langion. Guilielmum Pelum, Guerricum, Joh. Chrysostomum, Johannem Doleam, Johannem Do- minici, Johannem Hofmeisterum, Johannem Lu- dovicum, Johannem Mæstrosium, Johannem Mal- donatum, Johannem Mariam, Johannem Regino, Johannem Sanctæ fidei, Johannem Scotum Mona- chum, Johannem Soarez Lusitanum, Jodocum, Jo- sephum Tiberinum, Julium Africanum, Leonem Papam, Leonitum, Matthæum Aulæ Regiæ, Mat- thæum Bredembachium, Methodium, Michaelem Angrianum, Nicolaum Dintelspulum, Pantalio- nem, Pantænum, Paulum à Palatio, Petrum Alia- cum, Remigium, Rodulphum Languis, Severianum, Symmachum, Theodorum Heracleotem, Theodore- tum Herxen, Theodorum Ancyræ, Theognostum, Tilmannum Aquensem. Alii recensent insuper Be- nedictum Papam Venetiis Anno 1663. in fol. edi- tum, Porredam excusum Venetiis Anno 1602. Alphonsum ab Avendano Madriti in fol. 1593. Cass. Melo in fol. Pintzæ 1594. Claudium Guillandum Billiacensem, qui anno 1540. claruit, à quo ta- men, præter commentarios in Epistolas, solum Johannem illustratum esse refert Sixtus Senensis, Stanislaum Socolovium Canonicum Cracovien- sem, à Ponte, Lælium Pisciolam Jesuitam &c. Catena, collectore Niceta E- piscopo Serrarum contexta, quam interpretatus est Balthasar Corderius, edita sub hoc titulo : Sym- bolarum in Matthæum Tomus alter : in qua sequen- tur tes autores continentur: Ammianus, Ammonius, Anepigraphus, Anonymus, Athanasius, Basil. T.) quos in illos Evangelistas adhibuit se- quentes, Erasmum, Philippum Melanchthon. Bren- tium, Sacerrium, Vitum Theodorum: Zvvinglium, item, Bullingerum, Bucerum, Calvinum & Muscu- lum. Jacobus Grynæus in X. priora Mat- thæi capita scripsit.

OECONOMIA S. MATTHÆI.

SEd his relictis ad Oeconomiam S. Matthæi ac- cedimus, qui Genealogiam & Nativitatem Je- su cap. I. adventum Magorum ex Oriente ad præ- sepe Jesu, & discessum, nec non fugam Jesu, ob He- rodianum infanticidium, in Ægyptum, & revoca- tionem ex Ægypto, ac habitationem Josephi cum Jesulo in Nazareth, cap. II. describit: Tertio vero post commemoratum præconium & baptismum S. Johannis, de baptismo à Jesu suscepto agit. Atq; hæc ægny siueva sunt, ante ministerium Jesu publi- cum; ad quod uti inauguratus est Baptismo, & θεοφανείᾳ illustri in eodem facta, ita ad illud præ- paratus dici potest tentatione in deserto exantlata: quanquam ea etiam prima jam in S. Ministerio lu- cta fuerit cum antagonistarum maximo, & cory- phæo. Quo de cap. IV. tractatur, eaque ratione accessus sit ad acta ministerii publici. Quæ ob con- cinnitatem Harmoniæ Evangelicæ juxta Paschata distribui possunt. Cæterum quæ ad acta à primo ministerii Jesu Paschate ad secundum pertinent, hic nulla recensentur, nisi adventus Christi in Ga- lilæam post traditum Johannem, ac concionum ejus summa, nec non vocatio Simonis Petri, & Andreæ, ut & Jacobi & Johannis, cap. eodem quar- to. Ad ea vero quæ à Paschate secundo ad tertium gesta sunt, pertinent conciones in Galilæa, & mi- raculosæ sanationes ejusdem capitis versibus ultimis 23. 24. 25. commemoratæ, & concio Christi prolixa cap. V. VI. VII. descripta, nec non miracula le- prosi, & servi Centurionis, aliorumque sanatorum, tempestatis maris sedatæ, liberationis duorum ob- sessorum c. VIII. Paralytici curati, cum iterata vo- catione Matthæi; filia Jairirefiscitatæ, hæmor- rhoufe restitutæ, visus duobus cæcis redditi, muti & dæmoniaci sanati c. IX. Sequitur porro emissio 12. Apostolorum cum instructione, & promissis ipsis factis c. X. legatio Johannis ad Christum e carcere, & querela Christi de populo, prædicatio Dei Patris, & laborantium omnium suavissima in- vitatio c. XI. discipulorum sata in sabbato frican- tium defensio, cæci & muti sanatio cum apologia adversus blasphemiam c. XII. Parabolæ multæ Christi, ejusque in Nazareth novus contemtus c. XIII. ac cibatio quinque millium virorum in de- serto, & inambulatio in mari cap. XIV.

A Paschate tertio ad quartum sanatio ægroto- rum in regione Genezareth commemoratur, tra- ditiones & hypocrisis Pharisæorum redarguun- tur, fides Cananææ celebratur, sanantur plurimi, & cibantur quatuor millia virorum c. XV. Phari- sæis signum Jonæ sistitur, & fermentum eorum ca- veri jubetur, a Petro confessio editur, passionem suam prædicit Jesus, & sequelam suam præcipit c. XVI. Transfiguratio Jesu, filii lunatici curatio, & concio de passione & resurrectione, ac stateris so- lutio c. XVII. contentio de primatu, monitio de scandalo, & de condonando proximo cum para- bola de Rege rationem a servis exigente c. XVIII. informatio plenior de divortio, parvulorum ad- missio, probatio juvenis per opera salutem affe- ctantis, & ad instantiam Petri de omnium reli- ctione promissa remuneratio c. XIX. Parabola de operariis in vinea, c. XX.

Ad Quartum Pascha pertinet Historia Passio- nis, mortis & resurrectionis Dominicæ, ubi oc- currunt 1. Acta in itinere Hierosolymitano c. XX. parte altera, utpote passionis, mortis & resurre- ctionis Christi prædictio, filiorum Zebedæi peti- tio, ac duorum cæcorum sanatio. 2. Ingressus in Hierosolymam solemnis, & quæ circa illum gesta, ubi imprimis designatur templi reformatio, egres- sus in Bethaniam, & sub ingressum sequentis diei fici maledictio: Dehinc sermo Christi de fidei vir- tute, ac porro quæ cum Sacerdotibus & senioribus acta; ubi quæstio de potestate docendi, & de ori- gine baptismi Johannei; parabola de duobus filiis in vineam destinatis, cum monitu de publicanis & scortis præ Pharisæis cælum ingressuris: parabola de servis & filio Domini vineæ cum applicatione de lapide ab Architectis reprobato c. XXI. Parabo- la de nuptiis, tentatio de censu, de muliere septem- vira, de maximo præcepto, cum quæstione de filio & Domino Davidis c. XXII. Atq; hæc cum adver- sariis suis egit Christus: Nunc τὰ λεχθέντα ad disci- pulos succedunt: utpote monita de Pharisæis, & væ multiplex ipsis dictum, cum prædictione vastatio- nis Hierosolymæ c. XXIII. Signa destructionis tem- pli, & adventus filii hominis, cum adhortatione ad vigilantiam c. XXIV. parabolæ de decem virgini- bus aliis fatuis, aliis prudentibus, de talentis elo- catis: nec non processus extremi judicii c. XXV. Quæ omnia pertinent ad τὰ προηγούμενα, vel an- tecedentia passionis Christi. Sequitur porro passio- nis Christi historia c. XXVI. & XXVII. descripta, ac demum historia resurrectionis c. XXVIII. Circa illa c. XXVI. post repetitam prædictionem passionis, & consultationem Sacerdotum, commemorata præ- cedanea unctione in domo Simonis facta, Judæ proditoris pactum, Paschatos & S. Cœnæ celebra- tionem, prædictam discipulorum Domini ipsius- que Petri abnegationem, passio Christi in Geth- semane, & proditione facta apprehensio, & ad Cajapham abductio, Examen in Concilio, & tri- na Petri abnegatio cum lacrymis sequutis habe- tur. Porro c. XXVII. abductio Jesu ad Pilatum, Ju- dæ desperatio, Pilati examen, & nequicquam mo- nente de Jesu innocentia conjuge, ejusdem con- demnatio: Jesu in prætorio exagitatio, eductio, & crucifixio, in crucifixum effusæ calumniæ, ejus- demque exclamatio & mors: ac consequentia mor- tis, miracula & apertio imprimis monumento- rum sanctorum,conversio centurionis, & sepul- tura à Josepho Arimathæo facta: nec non sepul- cri custoditio, & obsignatio. Circa historiam resur- rectionis manifestatæ c. XXVIII. mulierum ad se- pulcrum adventus, angelica saxi revolutio, & con- cio habita de resurrectione Jesu, ac futura in Ga- lilæa apparitione discipulis nuncianda, nec non apparitio Jesu cum sui manifestatione, similique mandato: Custodum relatio, qui vero corrupti à Sacerdotibus mendacia valde dissona sparsere: Apostolis in Galilæa facta manifestatio, & ad do- cendum & baptizandum, cum promissione præ- sentiæ,in orbem emissio B. D. Job. Gerhardus hanc tradidit S. Matthæi οἰκονομίαν in Annot. posthum. p. 39. Explicat Matthæus 1. Personam, 2. Officium Christi. Ad Personam pertinet enumeratio majo- rum, descriptio nativitatis & educationis. Ad offi- cium pertinet 1. Solennis ad illud præparatio, 2. Pu- blicæ ejusdem administratio, & quidem 1. officii Pro- phetici per Evangelii prædicationem & miraculorum operationem, tribus ministerii annis ac semestri ab- solutam. 2. Officii Sacerdotalis per passionem & mortem. 3. Officii Regii per resurrectionem & a- scensionem.

PARS I. EVANGELII S. MATTHÆI. παρασκευὴ ad descriptionem Mini- sterii Jesu publici.

## 1:1 Argument
CHAPTER I. Argument and partition.

The catalog of the generation of Jesus, according to three sets of fourteen to David, to the Babylonian captivity, and to Jesus, to which is subjoined the suspicion and counsel of Joseph concerning Mary being pregnant with the angelic warning and information: and the Isaianic prophecy (c. VII. 14.) as well as the procreation and naming of Jesus. There are two parts: I. The genealogy of Jesus, to verse 18. II. The nativity of Jesus with the preceding angelic warning to Joseph to verse 25. Or as the blessed Gerhard has it: 1. The genesis or genealogy of Christ. 2. The gennesis or generation of Christ.

PART I. The genealogy of JESUS.

Verse 1. Βίβλος γενέσεως.] This is not an inscription of the whole book, as some have thought, but of the first particle, which stands out as if outside the body of the history. Such as there are many partial inscriptions in Moses and the Prophets. What the Greeks would say in one word as genealogy, the Hebrews cannot express except in two words. Moreover, the interpreters of the Hebrew codices are accustomed to render word for word: therefore they rarely use compound words. Βίβλος from the Hebrew usage of the word ספר, signifies a writing, however brief, which the Syrian rightly notes, who put כתבא in its place: γένεσις in Latin is origin. For thus Cicero translated it from Plato in the book on the universe. It is therefore βίβλος γενέσεως, just as the LXX also translated ספר תולדות Genesis V. 1. In Latin, description of origin. Nor is there any need for it to be supplemented, no more than in rubrics, which parts of books bear, or as often as NOMOS, MARTYRIA, PSEPHISMA are placed in orations.

We do not disapprove of this translation. Description of origin, which pleased the Syrian, כתבא description of generation, or of his kind and birth, and the Ethiopian, description of generation, as well as the one rendering it to Dio, enunciation of kind or family. Which Beza and Spanheim also approve. Regarding which, those things which we have said in the commentary on Gen. V. 1 may be compared. Yet the opinion of those who make this the inscription of the whole book does not seem to be much disparaged; to which also the translation of B. Luther tends, diß ist das Buch von der Geburt JEsu Christi. With which the Arabic, Persian, French, Italian, Spanish, and other translations agree. And Camerarius and Maldonatus favor that opinion. And it makes for this, that γένεσις by Hebraism sometimes connotes also a description of those things which follow a generation, that is, the acts of a whole life, and deeds performed: see Gen. XXXVII. 2. Furthermore, Grotius falsely supposes that the book of Matthew was translated from Hebrew into Greek. There is no need for this hypothesis, even if you prefer to render it a description of origin, rather than a book of generation. Which we also prefer. Because it is known that the Greek writers of the New Testament are not devoid of Hebraisms, and follow the Hellenists, the LXX Interpreters, in particular. Which Grotius also acknowledges. But that Dn. D. Peter Winstrupius seeks an emphasis in Pandect. sac. p. 31 in the singular number γενέσεως, because it is implied that not the whole generation of Christ is designated, but only the other, which pertains to him κατὰ σάρκα or according to human nature, rests on no foundation, because in Gen. V. 1 the singular number also occurs concerning Adam, apart from the mystery of different natures: nor does it suit his opinion, by which he determines that not generation, or birth, which is called γέννησις in verse 18, but progeny and the genus of Christ is called γένεσις, and distinguishes those words with Erasmus: because according to the divine nature Christ has no progeny.

υἱὲ Δαβὶδ, υἱὲ Ἀβραάμ] that is, who was of the descendants of David and Abraham: for בֵּן in Hebrew (which οἱ ἑρμηνευταὶ follow) extends as widely as τέκνον among the Greeks, and the appellation of child among the Latins: whereas otherwise among the Greeks υἱὸς, and among the Latins filius, denotes primarily only the first degree. But Matthew makes special mention of Abraham and David because of the promises made to them, to Abraham concerning a populous progeny: but to David concerning the stability of the kingdom, both of which were eminently fulfilled in Christ. Wherefore also those who had conceived something greater of Jesus than others call him the son of David, as appears in many places of the Gospels. But whoever was the interpreter of Matthew, a man undoubtedly of Apostolic gravity, brought forth the Hebrew names in Greek sound to which the Hellenists had long since adhered through the Septuagint and other versions: so that the minds of the readers might not be disturbed by any unnecessary novelty.

Latin:

CAPUT I. Argumentum & partitio.

CAtalogus generationis Jesu, secundum tres tessaradecadas ad Davidem, ad Babyloni- cam captivitatem, & ad Jesum, cui subjungitur suspicio & consilium Josephi ob Mariam gravi- dam cum monitione, & informatione Angelica: & vaticinio Esaiano (c. VII. 14.) nec non procrea- tio & denominatio Jesu. Partes duæ sunt: I. Genealogia Jesu, ad v. 18. II. Nativitas Jesu cum antecedanea monitione Josephi Angelica ad v. 25. vel ut B. Gerhardus ha- bet: 1. Christi γένεσις sive genealogia. 2. Chri- sti γέννησις sive generatio.

PARS I. Genealogia IESU.

Vers. 1. Βίβλος γενέσεως.] Non est hæc inscriptio totius libri, ut quidam putarunt, sed particulæ primæ, quæ velut extra corpus historiæ prominet. Qualis ἐπιγραφαὶ μερικαὶ multæ sunt in Mose, & Prophetis. Quod Græci uno ver- bo dicerent γενεαλογίαν, id Hebræi non possunt nisi duabus vocibus exprimere. Solent autem Græci Hebræorum co- dicum interpretes verbum verbo reddere: Ideo raro com- positis vocibus utuntur. Βίβλος ex Hebræo usu vocis ספר, scriptum quamvis breve significat, quod recte animadver- tit Syrus, qui ejus loco posuit כתבא: γένεσις Latine est origo. Ita enim ex Platone Cicero transtulit in lib. de u- niversitate. Est ergo βίβλος γενέσεως, quomodo & LXX. verterunt ספר תולדות Genes. V. 1. Latine descriptio originis. Nec quicquam opus suppleri, non magis quam in rubricis, quas partes librorum præferunt, aut quoties in o- rationibus ponitur ΝΟΜΟΣ, ΜΑΡΤΥΡΙΑ, ΨΗΦΙΣΜΑ.

Non improbamus hanc translationem. De- scriptio originis, quæ Syro placuit, כתבא descriptio generationis, seu generis & ortus ejus, & Æthiopi, descriptio generationis, nec non Dioni, enunciatio generis seu familiæ reddenti. Quam Beza & Spanh. quoque quoque probant. Qua de conferri poterunt, quæ in commentario ad Genes. V. 1. diximus. Non tamen multum vellicanda videtur eorum sententia, qui inscriptionem totius libri hanc fa- ciunt; Quo etiam abit translatio B. Lutheri, diß ist das Buch von der Geburt JEsu Christi. Cui consonant Arabica, Persica, Gallica, Italica, Hispani- ca, & aliæ translationes. Et favent illi sententiæ Ca- merarius ac Maldonatus. Atque eo facit, quod γέ- νεσις per Ebraismum interdum connotet quoque eorum, quæ generationem consequuntur, descri- ptionem, id est, vitæ totius acta, ac res gestas: vid. Gen. XXXVII. 2. Cæterum falso supponit Grotius librum Matth. ex Ebræo in Græc. translatum esse. Qua hypothesi opus non est, etiamsi malis redde- re descriptionem originis, quam librum de genera- tione. Quod nos etiam præferimus. Quia notum est, Græcos scriptores Novi Testamenti Ebrais- mis non destitui, & Hellenistas LXX. Interpp. im- primis sequi. Quod agnoscit etiam Grotius. Quod autem Emphasin quærit Dn. D. Peter Winstrupius in Pandect. sac. p. 31. in singulari numero γενέσεως, quia innuatur, non omnem generationem Christi, sed alteram tantum, quæ ipsi κατὰ σάρκα vel secundum humanam naturam convenit, designari, nullo fun- damento nititur, quia Genes. V. 1. etiam singularis occurrit numerus de Adamo, citra naturarum di- versarum mysterium: neque sententiæ ejus con- venit, qua non generationem, vel nativitatem, quæ γέννησις dicitur vers. 18. sed progeniem, & genus Christi, γένεσιν dici statuit, easque voces cum Eras- mo distinguit: quia secundum divinam naturam nullam Christus progeniem habet.

υἱὲ Δαβὶδ, υἱὲ Ἀβραάμ] hoc est, qui esset e posteris Davi- dis atque Abrahami: nam בֵּן in Hebræi sino (quem se- quuntur οἱ ἑρμηνευταὶ) tam late patet quam apud Græcos τέκνον, apud Latinos liberum appellatio: cum alioquin Græcis υἱὸς, & filius Latinis primum duntaxat gradum no- tet. Facit autem Matthæus Abrahami & Davidis specia- liter mentionem ob promissa illis facta, Abrahamo de populosa propagine: Davidi autem de regni stabilitate, quorum utrumque in Christo eminenter impletum est. Quare & qui de Jesu majus aliquid quam cæteri conce- perant, filium eum Davidis vocant, ut in multis Evange- liorum locis apparet. Quisquis autem fuit Matthæi inter- pres, vir haud dubie Apostolicæ gravitatis, nomina Hebræa Græco sono extulit cui Hellenistæ per septuaginta alio- rumque versiones jampridem affeverant: ne qua scilicet novitate non necessaria turbarentur legentium animi.

## 1:2
Vers. 2. Τὸν Ἰούδαν κὴ τὲς ἀδελφὸς ἀυτᾶ] By the way, Matthew commends Christ as a kinsman to all Israelites.

Vers. 2. Τὸν Ἰούδαν κὴ τὲς ἀδελφὸς ἀυτᾶ] Obiter Mat- thæus Christum ut cognatum omnibus Israelitis com- mendat.

## 1:3
Vers. 3. Καὶ τὸν Ζαρὰ] He added this name to renew the memory of the illustrious event which happened at their birth, a future step toward believing in the birth from a virgin.

Latin:

Vers. 3. Καὶ τὸν Ζαρὰ] Hoc nomen addidit, ad memo- riam innovandam illustris rei quæ in horum partu evenit, gradus futurus ad credendum partum è virgine.

## 1:5
Vers. 5. Ἐκ τῆς ῥαχὰβ] This is from the tradition of the Jews.

The sacred writers had no need of traditions, because they wrote φερόμενοι ὑπὸ πνεύματος ἁγίε 2. Pet. I. 21. Therefore we shall more correctly say that this proceeded from divine inspiration than from tradition. Although a tradition could have agreed with these, there was no certainty of it, unless the suggestion of the Holy Spirit was added.

Latin:

Vers. 5. Ἐκ τῆς ῥαχὰβ] Hoc ex traditione Judæorum.

Non opus habebant traditionibus scriptores sacri, quia scripsere φερόμενοι ὑπὸ πνεύματος ἁγίε 2. Petr. I. 21. Ideo rectius dicemus, profectum hoc esse ex inspiratione divina, quam ex traditio- ne. Quanquam consonare his potuerit traditio, ejus tamen nulla erat certitudo, nisi accedente Spiritus S. suggestione.

## 1:6
Vers. 6. Δαβὶδ τ̀ βασιλέα] The Hebrews were accustomed for the sake of honor to name David with this title added. דָוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ see the book of Kings I. ch. I. Matthew seems to have followed that. The letter B here takes the place of the digamma which had ceased to be written, and so the Greeks themselves expressed the sixth letter, which now keeps its order in numbers, but formerly was also seen in the Alphabet in the same place as among the Hebrews, in this way βαῦ, as Cornutus, Marius Victorinus, Priscianus, and Donatus reported from Varro and Didymus.

Ἐκ τῆς τῦ ὐρίε] A similar locution is found in Virgil: Hectoris Andromache Pyrrhin' connubia servas? For both wife and formerly are missing so that the speech may be complete. Few women are mentioned by the way in this census, noble by foreign origin or by crimes, whose history preludes to the calling of idolaters and criminals through the Gospel of Christ.

Latin:

Vers. 6. Δαβὶδ τ̀ βασιλέα] Solebant Hebræi honoris cau- sa Davidem ferine addito hoc titulo nominare. דָוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ vide librum Regum I. cap. I. Id secutus videtur Matthæus. B. litera hic locum obtinet τ̃υ δίγαμμα quod jam scribi de- sierat, itaque Græci ipsi litteram sextam quæ nunc in nu- meris ordinem suum servat, at olim in Alphabeto quoque eodem quo apud Hebræos loco conspiciebatur, exprime- bant hoc modo βαῦ ut ex Varrone & Didymo tradiderunt Cornutus, Marius Victorinus, Priscianus & Donatus.

Ἐκ τῆς τῦ ὐρίε] Similis locutio apud Virgilium: Hectoris Andromache Pyrrhin' connubia servas? Nam & uxor & quondam deest ut plenus fiat sermo. Mu- lieres in hoc censu obiter paucæ nominantur, extraneo or- tu aut criminibus nobiles, quarum historia ad vocatio- ne.n idololatrarum & criminosorum per Christi Evange- lium præludit.

## 1:11
Vers 11. Ἰωσίας δὲ ἐγέννησε τὸν Ἰεχονίαν, καὶ τὺς ἀδελ- φὺς αὐτῦ] All noble by their calamity: nor is that alien to this place, lest anyone wonder that the royal stock was reduced to a humble fortune.

Ἐπὶ τῆς μετοικεσίας] A looser designation of time. See Luke III. 23.

A doubt arises here concerning Jehoiakim, whom some assert to have been omitted through the error of scribes, on the authority of certain codices. For that codex which Robert and Henri Estienne used, as well as that ancient one which Stapulensis mentioned in v. 11, read thus: Ἰωσίας δὲ ἐγέννησε τὸν Ἰωακεὶμ. Ἰωακεὶμ δὲ ἐγέννησε τὸν Ἰεχονίαν καὶ τὺς ἀδελφὺς αὐτῦ ἐπὶ τῆς μετοικεσίας Βαβυλῶνος. The Spanish, French, and Danish versions, the 1607 edition, Piscator, and Beza in his earlier editions, retain Estienne's reading. In the MS of Lincoln College, Oxford, for τὸν ἰεχονίαν is read τὸν ἰωακεὶμ. But in the Bodleian MS 1, likewise in the old codex of Montfaucon and in the most ancient codex of the Wechel Library, it is read τὸν ἰωακεὶμ, ἰωακεὶμ δὲ ἐγένησε τὸν ἰεχονίαν. Nor does B. Chemnitius, whom Pareus and others follow, doubt that the generation of Jehoiakim was omitted in the common codices. But that codex of the Estiennes is without doubt false. For the ancient Epiphanius, Ambrose, Jerome, Augustine, Chrysostom, and others agree with the common reading, and Jeconiah, the son of Jehoiakim, had no brothers. But if, with Chemnitius, Brochmann in his System of Theology, Gerhard in this place, Svaningius on Daniel 1.1, Pareus, and Maldonado, the passage is restored thus: Josiah begat Jehoiakim and his brothers, Jehoiakim begat Jeconiah, the restoration will be purely arbitrary; for no Greek codex that reads thus can be produced. And it is held thus from Solomon to Jeconiah in the place of the second set of fourteen generations, but in the third set of fourteen, one generation will be missing. Wherefore it must be said that the Jeconiah in v. 11 is another person. begotten at the time of the deportation, who had brothers, namely Jehoiakim, who may have been known by two names, or may have been called Jeconiah by Matthew for the sake of euphony, and that the Jeconiah in the following verse, 12, who after the deportation begat Shealtiel, who had no brothers, is a different person. For thus the second set of fourteen will correctly end in Jehoiakim, whose brothers, it is established from 1 Chronicles 3:15, were Jehoahaz, Zedekiah, and Shallum: (of whom Cajetan and the Ambrosian commentator observe that mention is made here because they were all raised to royal dignity; others, because they experienced the same fate as Jehoiakim, namely, tragic ends:) Nor will anything be missing from the third set of fourteen beginning with Jeconiah, the son of Jehoiakim, and how it could otherwise be supplied does not appear at all. For the fact that Ludov. de Dieu, with Antonio Thysius as well as Petrus Possinus, refers Jeconiah (omitting Jehoiakim) to the second set of fourteen, and begins the third from Shealtiel, and for the sake of completing it inserts Mary into the generations, is foreign and inconvenient, since the genealogy of Joseph is being woven here, and Mary does not make a separate generation, but is joined to Joseph at least because she was his wife; furthermore, Jehoiakim is omitted without cause, and finally, it is against the clear letter of the text that Jeconiah should be excluded from the third set of fourteen, of which he is established as the head in v. 12. Thus Ambrose on Luke ch. 3: History indicates that there were two Jehoiakims, that is, two Jeconiahs, one before the transmigration, the other begotten in the transmigration itself, that is, Father and Son. Therefore the Father is counted among the earlier generations, who succeeded Josiah; the Son among the later, who succeeded the Father, that is, the grandson of Josiah. Therefore the Evangelist did not suppress one, but marked both, because both were called Jeconiah. Similarly, Epiphanius and also Jerome in this place: Let us know that the former Jeconiah is the same person, whom also Joakim, but the second son, not the Father, of whom the former is written with K. & M. and the following with H. & N. Which, through the fault of scribes and the length of time, has been confused among the Greeks and Latins. Whence the German version of B. Luther, as well as the Belgian version, and also the Danish edition of 1523, 1550, 1647, as also the Italian, etc., deservedly retain the ancient version.

If any scruple should arise from this, that Jechonias the Father (or Jojakim) is not said to have begotten Jechonias, as happens in the other generations, it can be answered that perhaps for the sake of avoiding polyodoria it was not said 'Jechonias begat Jechonias,' meanwhile by the very distinction of 'at the time of the transmigration' and 'after the transmigration' Matthew sufficiently indicated that they are different persons designated by this name, namely Father and Son, whence Cajetan rightly says: nor did the Evangelist omit this generation, but sufficiently signified it by saying: 'and after the transmigration Jechonias begat.' For it is clear enough from the History of the book of Kings and Chronicles that this one begetting after the transmigration is not that son of Josiah, but his grandson, though under other names, because both are called Jojakim. For only the Son Jechonias was led away to Babylon, but to Jojakim the Father an ignominious death was denounced outside the gates of Jerusalem in Judea, Jerem. XXX. 18, 19. The particle therefore 'epi' is not to be taken strictly, but with latitude, or to be translated not 'in the transportation,' but 'about the transportation,' or 'at the times of the transportation,' as it is taken in Mark II. 26, Luke III. 2, Acts XI. 28, whence B. Luther rendered it, 'umb die Zeit der Babylonischen Gefängniß' [about the time of the Babylonian captivity], whom the Belgian Interpreters follow, along with the Danish interpreters, who assign an Ellipsis: so that, namely, 'epi tes metoikesias' is said for 'tous epi tes metoikesias ontas' or 'gegonotas,' those who were in the transportation of Babylon. Others observe that the particle 'epi' with the second case is sometimes put for 'eis' with the fourth case, so that this may be the sense, that Josiah begat Jechonias or Jojakim and his brothers 'eis ten metoikesian,' into or to the Babylonian transportation, as for instance Spanheim and Winftrupius. But the first interpretation is simpler, which also solidly establishes the 'antithesis' in the following verse, 'meta de ten metoikesian.' But after the same transportation, so that 'metoikesia' is taken for 'metoikismo' or the act of transportation: because Salathiel was begotten by Jechonias in the Babylonian captivity, while the exile still lasted, 1 Par. III. 17. But we shall perhaps have Grotius agreeing here: who adds these things in this place: 'The sum will not consist in its number, unless we posit two Jechonias, one Joacim, which name, as Jerome rightly notes, could easily be confused with the nearby name Jechonias, (for even in the first Apocryphal Esdras in Latin copies this Joakim is called Jechonias) the other his son Jechonias: whom yet even the Hebrew compilers of times call 'Jojakim': whom Clement of Alexandria follows in Strom. I. and Josephus calls 'Joakim': who yet are distinguished as if namesakes by the very interval of such a long exile, and unless we count Christ himself as the final person of the third class.'

Which enumeration of the Tesseradecads [groups of fourteen] Jacob Faber Stapulensis proposed from ancient copies, in his introductory Commentaries on the Gospel of Matthew c. I. in this way: as it is cited by the Jesuit Petrus Possinus in his Dialectico Theo-genealogico page 505, 14, where however he observes that the tesseradecads are not of generations, but of persons who begat and were begotten, counted by the Evangelist: whence Abraham is counted in the first tesseradecad, who was begotten from Thare, even if his generation is not commemorated: otherwise up to David there were not fourteen but only thirteen generations. For that David begat Solomon belongs to the second tesseradecad: just as the generation or procreation of Jechonias by Jojakim is referred to the third tesseradecad, so that the fourteenth generation is the same, by which Jesus was born from Mary betrothed to Joseph. Thus therefore Faber has and counts: Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Judas, Phares, Efron, Aram, Aminadab, Naasson, Salmon, Booz, Obed, Jesse, David, 14. Salomon, Roboam, Abia, Asa, Josaphat, Joram, Ozias, Joatham, Achaz, Ezechias, Manasses, Amon, Josias, Joacim. 14. Salathiel, Zorobabel, Abiud, Eliacim, Azor, Sadoc, Acim, Eliud, Eleazar, Matthan, Jacob, Joseph, JESUS. St. Jerome also seems to have spoken of this. And the number of all is 42. This also is held from an ancient Greek Archetype, where Joacim, who is missing for us (why then did you substitute him in the above description of your own for Jechonias?) is placed in the twenty-eighth position: and this arrangement of the Tesseradecads, taken both from the ancients and from the first chapter of the first book of Chronicles, seems to approach more closely to the truth and the mind of the Evangelist. So far Faber, whom Possinus attacks undeservedly, because in these he recognizes Faber rather than Jacob: for these things agree entirely with the very 'autopsia' [eyewitness] of the Evangelist; but he himself is very inept, if not even profane, while besides Joseph he mixes Mary into this Tesseradecad, to complete the number, rendering this reason for it, that her male parts also were in the generation of Christ, if indeed Christ by reason of his human nature is 'apator' [fatherless], nor did Mary substitute for anything but the mother's role, and conceived Christ from the Holy Spirit, in which admirable act male parts were supplied by no one.

Latin:

Vers 11. Ἰωσίας δὲ ἐγέννησε τὸν Ἰεχονίαν, καὶ τὺς ἀδελ- φὺς αὐτῦ] Omnes calamitate sua nobiles: neque id ab hoc loco alienum, ne quis miretur regiam stirpem ad hu- milem fortunam detrudi.

Ἐπὶ τῆς μετοικεσίας] Temporis laxior designatio. Vide Luc. III. 23.

Dubium hic occurrit de Jojakimo, quem non- nulli errore librariorum omissum, codicum quo- rundam fide asserunt. Codex enim ille, quo Rober- tus & Henr. Stephani usi sunt, ut & antiquus ille, cu- jus mentionem fecit Stapulensis v. 11. sic legerunt: Ἰωσίας δὲ ἐγέννησε τὸν Ἰωακεὶμ. Ἰωακεὶμ δὲ ἐγέννησε τὸν Ἰεχο- νίαν καὶ τὺς ἀδελφὺς αὐτῦ ἐπὶ τῆς μετοικεσίας Βαβυλῶνος. Stephani lectionem retinent versiones Hispanica, Gallica, Danica, edit. 1607. Piscatoris, Bezæ, in prioribus editionibus. In MS. Collegii Lincoln. Oxon. pro τὸν ἰεχονίαν legitur τὸν ἰωακεὶμ. Sed in MS. Bodlejan. 1. item in vet. cod. Montf. & in cod. vetustiss. Bibl. Wechl. τὸν ἰωακεὶμ, ἰωακεὶμ δὲ ἐγένη- σε τὸν ἰεχονίαν. Neque dubitat, omissam in vulga- tis Codicib9 esse Jojacimi generationem B.Chem- nitius, quem Pareus, & alii sequuntur. Sed ille Ste- phanorum Codex sine dubio falsus est. Nam vul- gatæ lectioni consonant veteres Epiphanius, Am- brosius, Hieronymus, Augustinus, Chrysostom. alii, neque Jechonias Joachimi filius fratres habuit. Si vero cum Chemnitio, Brochmanno in System. Theol. Gerhardo in h. l. Svaningio in Daniel. I. 1. Pareo & Maldonato locus ita restituatur, Josias ge- nuit Joakim & fratres ejus, Joakim genuit Jecho- niam, mere arbitraria erit restitutio; nullus enim Codex Græcus, qui ita legat, proferri poterit. Et habetur ita a Salomone ad Jechoniam loco tessera- decadis pentadecas generationum, in tertia vero tesseradecade deficiet una generatio. Quapropter dicendum, alium esse Jechoniam v. 11. ἐπὶ τῆς μετοι- κεσίας genitū, qui fratres habuit nempe יהויקים Jehojakimum qui vel binomius fuerit, vel Jechonias à Matthæo euphoniæ causa vocatus sit, alium esse Jechoniam versu sequente 12. qui μετὰ τὴν μετοι- κεσίαν Salatheelem genuit, qui fratres non habuit. Ita enim recte se habebit altera tesseradecas desi- nens in Jojakim, cujus fratres fuisse Joachaz, Se- dekiam & Salum è 1. Paral. III. 15. constat: (quo- rum hic mentionem factam esse Cajetanus & Am- brosiensis observant, ideo quod omnes ad regiam dignitatem evecti fuerint; alii quod eandem cum Jojakimo sortem, tragicos nimirum exitus exper- ti sint:) Neque deerit quicquam tertiæ tesserade- cadi incipienti à Jechonia Joakimi filio, quæ quo- modo suppleri alias possit, neutiquam apparet. Nam quod Ludov. de Dieu cum Antonio Thysio, ut & Petro Possino Jechoniam (prætermisso Jojaki- mo) ad secundam tesseradecadem referunt, ac tertiam à Salathiele inchoant, ejusque complen- dæ gratia Mariam generationibus immiscent ἀλ- λότριον, & inconveniens est, cum Josephi genea- logia hic texatur, nec Maria peculiarem γενεὰν faciat, sed Josepho saltim, quod is vir ejus fue- rit, jungatur, adhæc præter causam Jojakim præter- mittatur, ac denique contra apertam textus lite- ram Jechonias è tertia tesseradecade, cujus caput constituitur. v. 12. excludatur. Sic Ambrosius in Luc. c. III. Duos Joachim, b. e. duos Jechonias fuisse Historia indicat, unum ante transmigrationem, al- terum in ipsa transmigratione generatum, id est, Patrem & Filium. Ergo Pater inter superiores generationes est computatus, qui successit Josiæ, Filius inter posteriores, qui successit Patri, id est, nepos Josiæ. Non igitur suppressit alterum Evan- gelista, sed utrumque signavit, quod uterque Je- chonias dictus sit. Similiter Epiphanius nec non Hieronymus h. l. Sciamus Jechoniam priorem ipsum esse, quem & Joakim, secundum autem filium, non Patrem, quorum prior per K. & M. sequens au- tem per H. & N. scribitur. Quod scriptorum vitio & longitudine temporum apud Græcos, Latinosque confusum est. Unde merito antiquam versionem retinent versio Germanica B. Lutheri, versio item Belgica, nec non Danica edit. 1523. 1550. 1647. ut & Italica &c.

Si cui scrupulus inde oriatur, quod Jechonias Pater (vel Jojakim) non dicatur genuisse Jechoniam, quemadmodum fit in cæteris generationibus, re- sponderi potest πολυδωρίας fortassis evitandæ causa non dictum esse Jechonias genuit Jechoniam, interim per ipsam distinctionem ἐπὶ τῆς μετοικε- σίας & μετὰ τὴν μετοικεσίαν satis indicasse Mat- thæum, diversas esse personas isto nomine indigita- tas, Patrem nempe & Filium, unde recte Cajetanus: nec Evangelista omisit hanc generationem, sed suf- ficienter significavit dicendo: & post transmigratio- nem Jechonias genuit. Satis enim clare constat ex Historia libri Regum & Paralipom. quod iste generans post transmigrationem non est ille filius Josiæ, sed nepos, sub aliis tamen nominibus, quia uterque appellatur Jojakim. Solus enim Filius Jechonias Babylonem abductus fuit, Jojaki- mo autem Patri mors ignominiosa denunciata ex- tra portas Hierosolymæ in Judæa Jerem. XXX. 18. 19. Particula ergo ἐπὶ non stricte accipienda, sed cum latitudine, vel vertenda non in transpor- tatione, sed circa transportationem, vel sub tempo- ra transportationis, uti Marc. II. 26. Luc. III. 2. Actor. XI. 28. accipitur, unde B. Luther. reddidit, umb die Zeit der Babylonischen Gefängniß. quem sequuntur Interpr. Belgici, cum interpp. Danico, qui Ellipsin assignant: ut nempe ἐπὶ τῆς μετοικεσίας dicatur pro τοὺς ἐπὶ τῆς μετοικεσίας ὄντας vel γεγονότας illos, qui erant in transporta- tione Babylonis. Alii particulam ἐπὶ cum secun- do casu poni quandoque pro εἰς cum quarto casu observant, ut hic sit sensus, Josiam genuisse Jecho- niam vel Jojakimum & fratres ejus εἰς τὴν μετοικε- σίαν in vel ad transportationem Babylonicam, utpote Spanhemius & Winftrupius. Sed simplicior est prima interpretatio, quæ statuminat etiam solide ἀντίθεσιν vers. sequ. μετὰ δὲ τὴν μετοικεσίαν. Post eandem vero transportationem, ut μετοικεσία pro μετοικισμῷ seu actu transportationis accipiatur: quia genitus à Jechonia Salathiel fuit in captivita- te Babylonica, durante adhuc exilio 1. Par. III. 17. Sed habebimus hic fortassis Grotium consentien- tem: qui h. l. ista addit: Non constabit autem nume- ro suo summa, nisi Jechonias ponamus duos, alterum Joacim, quod nomen, ut recte Hieronymus notat, fa- cile cum vicino Jechonia nomine confundi potuit, (nam & in Apocrypho Esdræ priore in latinis Ex- emplaribus hic Joakim dicitur Jechonias) alterum ejus filium Jechoniam: quem tamen & ipsum Hebræi temporum digestores יויכין Joacim vocant: quos sequitur Alexandrinus Clemens Strom. I. & Ἰωάχι- μον Josephus: qui tamen quasi cognomines distin- guuntur ipso tam longi exsilii intervallo, ac nisi Chri- stum ipsum annumeremus ut personam ultimam ter- tiæ classis.

Quam ἐξαρίθμησιν Tesseradecadum ex anti- quis exemplaribus proposuit Jacobus Faber Stapu- lensis, suis initiatorijs Commentariis in Evangel. Matthæi c. I. hoc modo: uti adducitur à Petro Pos- sino Jesuita in Dialectico Theo-genealogico pag. 505. 14. ubi tamen observa tesseradecadas non gene- rationum, sed personarum, quæ generarunt, & genitæ sunt, numeratas esse ab Evangelista: un- de Abraham annumeratur in prima tesseradeca- de, qui genitus è Thare, etsi hujus generatio non commemoretur: alias usque ad Davidem non quatuordecim sed tredecim tantum erant γενεαί. Nam quod David Salomonem genuerit, ad secun- dam pertinet tesseradecadem: quemadmodum ad tertiam tesseradecadem generatio vel procrea- tio Jechoniae à Jojakimo refertur, ut decima quar- ta generatio ejusdem sit, qua Jesus è Maria Jose- pho desponsata natus est. Sic ergo habet & nume- rat Faber: Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Judas, Phares, Efron, Aram, Aminadab, Naasson, Salmon, Booz, Obed, Jesse, David, 14. Salomon, Roboam, Abia, Asa, Josaphat, Joram, Ozias, Joatham, Achaz, E- zechias, Manasses, Amon, Josias, Joacim. 14. Sa- lathiel, Zorobabel, Abiud, Eliacim, Azor, Sa- doc, Acim, Eliud, Eleazar, Matthan, Jacob, Jo- seph, JESUS. De hac locutus videtur & S. Hiero- nymus. Estque omnium numerus 42. Hac quoque habetur ex vetusto Archetypo Graeco, ubi Joacim, qui nobis deest (cur tu illum igitur in superiori descriptio- ne de tuo pro Jechonia supposuisli? vicesimo octavo lo- co ponitur: & haec Tesseradecadum ordinatio cum ex antiquis, tum ex primi Paralipomenon cap. I. desumpta, magis veritati & menti Evangelistae ac- cedere videtur. Hactenus Faber, quem immeri- to exagitat Possinus, quod in his Fabrum potius agnoscat quam Jacobum: Haec enim ex asse con- gruere Evangelistae αὐτοψίᾳ ipsa docet; perquam vero ineptus, si non prophanus etiam, ipse est, dum praeter Josephum Mariam immiscet huic Tes- seradecadi, ut numerum compleat, hanc ejus reddens rationem, quod ejus viriles quoque partes fuerint in Christi generatione, siquidem Christus ratione humanae naturae ἀπάτωρ sit, nec nisi ma- tris vicem Maria subierit, Christumque è Spiritu S. conceperit, in quo admirando actu viriles par- tes à nullo suppletae fuêre.

## 1:16
Verse 16. [Jacob begat Joseph] That some think the lineage of Joseph is listed by Matthew, but that of Mary by Luke, does not seem at all probable to me. For since Luke in the same context says 'as was supposed the son of Joseph, of Heli,' and so on for the rest in succession, connecting the parts of that one in a continuous series, either to want Christ to be called the grandson of Heli with Joseph omitted, or Joseph to be not the son but the son-in-law of Heli himself, is altogether alien to correct speech. It must therefore be confessed that the lineage of the same Joseph is reckoned by one forward, by the other backward. Nor indeed is the origin of Joseph to be considered alien to Christ, since Christ was born from her whom Joseph retained in marriage. For if such is the force of the law, that the offspring of a widow conceived by the agnate of her deceased husband succeeds to every right of the deceased, no differently than if it had drawn its origin from his own procreation, why should that which is ratified without human effort from his legitimate spouse, as if instituted by God solely from him, not be considered his own? And hence it is, no doubt, that not only is Joseph called the father of Christ by the writers of the Gospel, marriage clearly demonstrating the father, but also Christ rendered to him all the obsequies and services which can be expected from a son established in the sacred paternal duties. But if everywhere among nations adopted children are reckoned from the nobility of that clan into which they are as it were grafted, how much more justly did all the gentile rights of Joseph and the divine promises made to his ancestors pertain to the Lord Jesus? But as for the fact that it is accepted that Mary's lineage can also be gathered from Joseph's lineage, I do not think it is sufficiently correctly built upon the foundations that are commonly posited. For the claim that those of the same tribe were required to marry those of the same tribe is neither perpetual, nor, if it were, can it have such force that it appears from that that Mary was born from the family of David. Wherefore it must be established that Mary could not marry not only outside the tribe, but not even outside the family: which is most true, since she had no brothers of the same blood. For Israelite girls who had no brothers are commanded by the law of Moses to marry their nearest agnates: and that is defined and stands in the last chapter of Numbers, from the specific case that had presented itself to Moses. For the word מטה which is found there several times, does not denote a tribe, if by the name of tribe the twelfth part of the Israelite people is understood, but in a looser sense it denotes a lineage, especially in this place, where another word is added, משפחה, which means the same as family to the Latins, so that משפחת מטה אביהם is properly the family of the paternal stock. Nor did the LXX understand it otherwise, who in this place call it now δῆμον, now φυλὴν. That Δῆμος among them is a part of the whole tribe, that is, the twelfth part, appears in several places in the book of Joshua. But Josephus also uses φυλὴν for family, as when he names the priestly tribes in book IV of the Jewish War. And in the same way both he and the LXX translated משפחת in I Samuel XX. 6, where it seems to be a matter of a family feast, not a tribal one. And conversely, πατριὰ is sometimes called what is properly a φυλὴ, whence "the twelve patriarchs" in the speech of Stephen, that is, φύλαρχοι or ἀρχίφυλοι, as others speak. Wherefore it is manifest that those words do not always signify the same thing, but are to be interpreted variously according to the diversity of the subject matter. But that in this place a family may be understood to be designated, the reason added to the law demands, which is this: that ancestral property may not pass to strangers by right of ownership, which can be understood to have been established for the sake of preserving not only tribes, but also clans and families, from a similar law which is about those who are to redeem. Hence it is that he who wrote the history of Tobias, not an unobservant observer of Jewish custom, introduces Sarah the virgin complaining that her father had no sons as heirs, nor indeed was there a brother to her, to whose son she might keep herself as a wife according to the law, chap. III. 18. Nor otherwise does he who wrote the history of Judith say that her husband was not only of her own tribe, but of her own family. Chrysostom also and Epiphanius, to whom the customs of the Jews could hardly have been unknown, living in those places where there was a very great multitude of Jews, interpret the law of Moses which I have mentioned in this way. In the Attic laws, indeed, whose most ancient ones it is very easy to prove were taken from the laws of Moses and all but copied, the same thing that we have said is found to be established. Such a girl, whether she were the sole heir to her father or had sisters but not brothers, was commonly called ἐπίκληρος, by Solon himself περικληρῖτις, and by others also πατρῶχος. He to whom her marriage belonged by law, namely the nearest agnate, was called ἐπιδικαζόμενος, in Hebrew הגואל, that is, he who inherits her, as it is in that history of Tobias which I mentioned, III. 25. From this law Apollodorus took the plot of the comedy to which he gave the name ἐπιδικαζόμενος, or as Donatus prefers, ἐπιδικαζομένη, from the person of the girl who seeks a husband by law. Terence translated it into Latin and inscribed it the Phormio: In which play these are the verses pertaining to that law:

The law is that orphans, who are nearest in kin, should marry them, and this same law commands them to take them.

In the same place Donatus: "Let orphans marry the nearest: let the nearest take the orphan," is an Attic law. The Greek words of the law exist in Sopater: "Let the nearest kinsman claim the heiress in court." But also in Diodorus Siculus, book XII, is the index taken from that Adelphi:

This friend of mine is nearest in kin to her: the laws compel him to marry her.

There is also frequent mention of this law in Demosthenes, Isaeus, and other Greek orators, as also in Aristophanes and Pollux. It appears, therefore, that what I said, that this right did not pertain to all girls, is true. For those who had brothers, since they saw no inheritance of land, were not bound by that law. Indeed, as Aristophanes says in jest, there cannot be any heiress while legitimate brothers exist, which sense Isaeus expressed thus in his oration on the inheritance of Philemon: "For surely, while legitimate sons exist, his daughter could not be an heiress." And the very same thing is proven by the history which is in the book of Judges XXI. 18, where the other tribes, in order not to give their daughters in marriage to the Benjaminites, show that they are prohibited not by divine law, but by the religious obligation of an oath. And David, descended from Judah, took Michal from the progeny of Benjamin as his wife: he was never reproached for that name: and we find it written among the Hebrews concerning Hillel the Pharisee that his father was from the tribe of Benjamin, his mother from the tribe of Judah. Which will also be confirmed by other examples at Luke chapter I. Josephus adds that any virgins could marry any Hebrew, if they renounced the inheritance brought to them. Wherefore not even the virgins of the Levitical clan were bound by that bond, as those who by law were not capable of land, and therefore could rightly marry anyone from the people. They err, therefore, who do not think it could have happened without prejudice to the law that Elizabeth, who was of the Aaronic family, was related to Mary. For nothing prevented Mary's father, grandfather, or some other ancestor, descended from David, from taking a Levitical virgin in marriage: for by that act the rights of inheritances were not harmed. Although Mary was in humble circumstances, which both the Bethlehem inn and the poor offering of turtledoves sufficiently show, nevertheless the right of heiresses must have been valid in her case, because of the divine promises made to the posterity of David, which was held in such high esteem among the Jews that even after Jerusalem was razed, in the seats of their exile they appointed patriarchs for themselves from none other than the stock of David, whom they obeyed almost as kings, just as Origen, Epiphanius, Theodoret, and Chrysostom teach us, and that mention of the crown gold which is in the Theodosian Code. Thus, when the Jews were in the Babylonian exile, and retained nothing of land beyond hope, the heiresses nevertheless married the nearest agnate, as appears from the history of Tobias. I am not unaware that in the Talmudic writings and the interpreters who followed after, it is handed down that that precept of Moses concerning marrying the nearest virgins was valid only in those times of the first division. But as in many other things, so in this too, the collectors of the Talmud seem to have reported only those from the various opinions of the jurists which had prevailed in customs at the time the collection was made, omitting others from which there had been a departure. For if that had been the perpetual consensus of the pious and the learned, how would either Josephus, the founder of history, have been ignorant of it, being instructed in the ancestral law, or how would it have come into the mind of the writer of Tobias to make mention of an unknown custom? Philo also reports this law as perpetual. The rest which pertains to reconciling the genealogy of Matthew with that of Luke, we shall treat at Luke.

Grotius describes the same genealogy of Joseph from Luke no less than from Matthew, thinking, as others do, that he followed Africanus. But it does not seem likely that both would have wanted to weave together the genealogy of one Joseph under different names, while remaining completely silent about the lineage of Mary, since only one of them, according to Grotius, scrupulously recounted the legal father of Joseph. Nor is that opinion free from significant difficulties, and you are forced to invent many people with two names in the genealogy of Christ, and it would be strange if Luke had called them by the name from which he had seen St. Matthew abstain, which in the judgment of Calixtus (who otherwise agrees here with Grotius) one might perhaps easily admit in one or two cases, but not so easily in so many. Therefore, not a few, with Galatinus and Dominicus à Soto, prefer that the genealogy of Joseph be described only by Matthew, and that the family of Mary be exhibited by Luke. Which Chemnitius, Bibliander, Lavaterus, Aretius, Paraeus, Gomarus, Fried. Spanheim, as well as Genebrardus, Jansenius, Didacus Stella, Baronius, Vincentius Regius, and others defend, that this reconciliation is not forced but easy, and that in this way the reason is easily consistent why another genealogy was added by Luke to the genealogical stem described by Matthew, so that, namely, a perfect and full genealogy of Christ might exist, and the maternal lineage not be neglected, concerning which let one read especially Gomarus in his examination of the controversy regarding the genealogy of Christ and Fridericus Spanheim in part 1 of the Evangelical Doubts, doubt XX. The reasoning of Grotius, that it is quite foreign to correct speech for Joseph to be called ἕ τοῦ ἡλὶ, who was not the son of Heli but his son-in-law, is not sufficiently solid. For since Luke does not use the word γεννᾶν as Matthew does, but the broader phrase τοῦ ἡλὶ, τοῦ Ματθὰτ, which can imply a varied σχέσιν, nothing prevents it from being expressed differently regarding Joseph in respect to Heli, and differently regarding the ancestors of Heli, just as it is acknowledged that in one sense Seth is called τοῦ Ἀδάμ, and in another Adam τοῦ Θεοῦ, and the same phrase implies a different σχέσιν elsewhere. 1 Corinthians III. 21, πάντα ἡμῶν ἐστιν, ἡμεῖς δὲ χριστοῦ, χριστὸς τοῦ Θεοῦ. Nor is the other solution, which Franc. Junius in his Notes, Diodati in his version of the Italian Bibles, and Fridericus Spanheim in his Evangelical Doubts adopt, inconsistent; namely, that these words (ὡς ἐνομίζετο υἱὸς Ἰωσὴφ) are parenthetical, so that the sense becomes: that Christ (as he was thought to be the son of Joseph) was the grandson of Heli through Mary his daughter. In this way B. Hülsemann also explains it in his annotations on Genesis 10:22.

Τὸν ἄνδρα] That it has been noted by learned men that husband and wife are also spoken of from the time of their betrothal is consistent with the customs not only of the Hebrews but also of other nations. For Servius the jurist (citing Pomponius) also rightly said that the title of father-in-law, mother-in-law, son-in-law, and daughter-in-law is acquired even from betrothal. Thus in the Epistles of the Heroines, Hermione betrothed to Orestes:

Husband, I pray, help your wife; brother, help your sister.

Servius on the eighth Eclogue: Of a spouse, he says, not who was, but who was hoped to be. See Deut. 22:23.

Μαρίας] It is the Hebrew name מִרְיָם, which is how the sister of Moses was called. But later Hebrews, in the Syrian manner, pronounced it מַרְיָם: that is, Mariam, which is how you may more often find that name in Matthew and Luke; and no differently in Ezekiel the Poet, who wrote Jewish tragedies in Greek. For the Greek language, being ignorant of the consonant Yod, forced it to be changed into a vowel; but since no Greek word ends in μ, and therefore all words ending in μ are indeclinable, they can receive the form of a Greek name and declension either by subtraction or addition. Josephus used addition, who pronounces this name as Mariamme; Luke and the interpreter of Matthew used subtraction, who, when they wish to vary this name in its cases, write Maria, Marias. Thus, since the Greek language similarly did not know the termination, Greeks either increased Punic names derived from Baal, as Philo of Byblos said Hierombalus, Asumbalus, or they diminished them, by adding a letter of Greek termination, such as Asdrubas, Annibas. Such also is Amilcar, Amilcas; Bogud, Bogos; and in Josephus, Cain, Kais. Thus for Abraham others said Abrames, as Artapanus in his Jewish works, others Abras, with the traces of both names remaining even in Latin usage. The same is Abramas in Nicolaus of Damascus. Similar is Ioses for Joseph, Matt. 27:56, Mark 6:3, 14:37, Acts 4:36, Luke 3:29, and Iosepos. So also from שַׁבָּת was made sabba, sabbatos, and sabbaton, sabbatou.

ὁ λεγόμενος χριστὸς] The participle must be referred to the time of the writer: for he indicates that he is dealing with that JESUS who had already become known to all by the surname of Christ. Thus also Josephus, writing about James, calls him the brother of Jesus who was called the Christ. Now, those are called Mashiachim in Hebrew who, by a singular benefit of divine providence, had been promoted to eminent dignities, such as Abraham and Isaac, Psalm 105:15. Thus, in the Old Testament, the priest who is the Christ is the high priest; the king who is the Christ is an eminent king, such as Cyrus, Isaiah 45:1; the King of Tyre, 24:14; the teacher who is the Christ is an eminent teacher, below 23:8. κατ' ἐξοχὴν, however, the Jews, stirred by the prophecies of the Prophets and especially of Daniel, called him by that name whom they expected from GOD as the supreme King and teacher, John 4:25. JESUS himself professed that he was that eminent Christ, and both he himself and his disciples provide the reason for the name: that he was equipped with a clearly incomparable power for bringing forth and confirming heavenly doctrine, as can be seen in Luke 4:18, Acts 4:27, 10:36, Heb. 1:9, John 3:34. In which sense, even while still leading his earthly life, he acknowledges himself as king, because, of course, through the truth testified by him, he already held a kingdom in the souls of his own, John 18:37. Although, in another sense, he is said to have been constituted Lord and Christ only after the resurrection, Acts 2:36. And this appellation of Christ prevailed to such an extent that among those outside, the name of Jesus being scarcely known, that surname passed into the use of a name. For thus Tacitus, Suetonius, and Pliny call him: whence it happened that the Jews, using the Greek language, who did not wish to acknowledge that Jesus was the Christ, began to call that one of theirs whom they were miserably expecting in vain, not Christos as before, but for the sake of distinction, Eleimmenos.

It is irrelevant what is brought forward concerning the Mashiachim. For when Jesus is called Mashiach, that word is not the same as eminent, but according to the proper force of the name, it denotes ANOINTED, which is evident from Psalm 45, Isaiah 61:1, Daniel 9:24. Nor do the examples adduced teach that the word Mashiach alone designates eminence, or eminent dignity apart from the anointing. Abraham and Isaac are so called because they were Prophets, who were accustomed to be anointed, as the exegesis added to Psalm 105:15 teaches, and because they were anointed with the gifts of the Holy Spirit above others, so that they could discharge this office. You see, says Eusebius, that in this place the ancients, the friends of God and the Prophets, David, and rather the divine spirit through him, called them Christs, though they were not anointed with any earthly ointment. Remigius, Bishop of Reims, explanation on the Epistle to the Hebrews, ch. 1:9. In the Old Testament, the patriarchs were participants of Christ in this anointing, because since they were not anointed with visible oil, but filled with the Holy Spirit, they are called Christs, that is, anointed (Psalm 105). Nor is Cyrus called Mashiach otherwise than that he was the anointed of the Lord, that is, a King constituted by the Lord: even though he was not anointed with external oil. For the Prophet calls the anointed of God in this way through a manner of speaking familiar to him, even though that custom of inaugurating Kings was proper to the Israelites, which even today the Poles and the French imitate: since all receive their authority from God, Proverbs 8, Daniel 2:21, ch. 4:2. The opinion of Adam Conzen the Jesuit concerning Cyrus, book 7 of Politics, ch. 3, book 1, that he was anointed in a peculiar way beyond the custom of his nation, and that by the counsel of Daniel and the Israelites, is peculiar. Let the same be the judgment concerning the King of Tyre, Isaiah 24. That this name is attributed to our Savior, because thus καθηγητὴς ὁ χριστός, that is, an excellent Teacher, Matth. XXIV. verse 8. is foreign to the text, for there χριστός is the subject, and ὁ καθηγητὴς holds the place of the predicate, and therefore it is wrongly taken as an epithet of the latter. Christ, he says, is one Master: In the same way King Cyrus is called anointed. Which cause of the name was brought forward by Christ himself & the Apostles in the places cited by Grotius, Luke IV. verse 18. Acts IV. verse 27. chap. X. verse 36. Heb. I. 9. John III. verse 34. not because he was only an excellent King or Doctor, but because he was anointed by God himself with immense gifts to perform the offices of Prophet, King & Priest. Therefore Cyril on the true faith to the Queens. When the word was made flesh, then we also say by nomination that he himself is Christ Jesus; for since he was anointed with the oil of gladness, that is, with the Holy Spirit by God the Father, therefore he was also named Christ. Chrysost. Sermon I. on the Epistle to the Romans. Christ is called so from anointing, which also pertains to the flesh itself. Nor can it be simply proven what Grotius says, that Christ professed himself to be King, while he was still leading an earthly life, in this sense only, that through the truth testified by him he already obtained a kingdom in the souls of his own: For although he is Messiah also on account of his Prophetic office, yet the Kingly office, to which he was also anointed, because he performed it while he was still living on earth, embraced more, and primarily brought with it the protection and defense of his own, whom no one could snatch from his hands. John X. verse 28. Whence he testified that he was present to those gathered in his name, Matth. XXVIII. verse 20. indeed he had all things in his hand, John III. verse 35. XIII. verse 2. although only after the resurrection was Christ of all

The Lord was established through exaltation at the right hand of God, as regards his incessant, universal, and plenary Dominion in heaven and on earth. Matt. XXVIII. ver. 19. Acts II. 36. Eph. I. 21. chap. IV. 10. Phil. II. 8.

Latin:

Vers. 16. [Ἰακὼβ δὲ ἐγέννησε τὸν Ἰωσήφ] Quod quidam ex- istiinanta Matthæo recenseri genus Josephi, à Luca au- tem Mariae, nequaquam probabile mihi videtur. Nam cum Lucas eodem contextu dicat ὡς ἐνομίζετο υἱὸς Ἰωσὴφ, τῦ Ἡ- λὶ, atque ita caetera deinceps, illius partibus continúa serie connectens, aut Josepho omisso velle Christum Heli ne- potem dici, aut Josephum ipsius Heli non filium sed gene- rum, à recto sermone usque alienum est. Fatendum igitur est ejusdem Josephi genus ab altero prorsum, ab altero re- trorsum censeri. Neque vero aliena à Christo existimanda est origo Josephi, cum natus sit Christus ex ea quam Jose- phus in matrimonio retinuerit. Nam si ea vis est legis, ut partus viduae ex agnato defuncti viri conceptus in omne jus defuncti succedat, non aliter quam si ex ipsius genitura ortum traxisset, quidni id quod sine humana opera ex legi- tima illius conjuge ratum est, quasi ipsius solo divinitus in- stitum, ipsius proprium censeatur? Atque hinc est nimirum quod non tantum ab Evangelii scriptoribus Josephus pa- ter Christi, nuptiis videlicet patrem demonstrantibus, no- minatur, sed & Christus omnia obsequia atque operas illi praestitit, quae expectari possunt à filio in sacris paternis con- stituto. Quod si ubique gentium adoptivi liberi ex ejus gen- tis, cui velut insiti sunt nobilitate, censentur, quanto ju- stius omnia jura gentilitia Josephi ac promissiones divinae ipsius majoribus factae ad Dominum Jesum pertinebant? Quod vero receptum est, etiam Mariae stemma posse ex Jo- sephi stemmate colligi, non arbitror satis recte superstrui iis quae vulgo ponuntur fundamentis. Nam quod ajunt tribules tribulibus nubere debuisse, neque perpetuum est, neque si sit eo usque valere potest, ut etiam ex Davidis fa- milia Mariam fuisse natà inde appareat. Quare statuendum non modo extra tribum, sed ne extra familiam quidem nubere Mariam potuisse: quod verissimum est, quando fratres consanguineos nullos habuit. Nam puellae Israëli- tides, quae fratres non haberent, lege Mosis jubentur nu- bere agnatis proximis: idque definitum exstat Numerorum capite ultimo, ex specie facti quae se Mosi obtulerat. Vo- cem enim מטה quae aliquoties ibi reperitur, non tribum, si inodo tribus nomine δωδεκατημόριον Israëlitici populi in- telligatur, sed laxiore significatu stirpem notat, praesertim hoc loco, ubi additur vox altera משפחה quae idem valet quod familia Latinis, ita ut משפחת מטה אביהם proprie sit familia stirpis paternæ. Neque aliter accepe- runt LXX. qui hoc loco modo δῆμον modo φυλὴν nominant. Δῆμος apud illos partem esse integræ tribus, id est, τὸ δω- δεκατημόριον ex Josuæ libro aliquot locis apparet. Sed & φυλὴν pro familia usurpat Josephus, ut cum φυλὰς ἀρχιερατικὰς nominat belli Judaici libro IV. Eodemque modo tum ipse tum LXX. verterunt משפחת I. Samuel. XX. 6. ubi de familiari, non tribuli convivio agi videtur. Et vicissim πατριὰ dicitur interdum quæ proprie est φυλὴ, unde οἱ δώδεκα πατριάρχαι in oratione Stephani, id est, φύλαρχοι aut ἀρχίφυλοι ut loquuntur alii. Quare mani- festum, voces illas non semper idem significare, sed pro materiæ diversitate varie interpretandas. Ut autem hoc lo- co familia designata intelligatur, exigit ratio legi addita, quæ hæc est: ne bona avita mancipii jure ad extraneos deveniant, quod non tribuum tantum, sed & gentium familiarumque conservandarum causa constitutum esse ex simili lege quæ est de redemturis, intelligi potest. Hinc est quod is qui Tobiæ historiam scripsit, moris Judaici non indiligens observator, Saram virginem conquerentem in- troducit, quod pater ipsius filios hæredes non haberet, neque vero esset frater ei, cujus filio se uxorem ex lege ser- varet cap. III. 18. Nec secus is qui Judithæ historiam scri- psit, maritum ejus ait fuisse non modo τῆς φυλῆς ἀυτῆς, sed τῆς πατριᾶς ἀυτῆς. Chrysostomus quoque & Epiphanius quibus mores Judæorum ignoti esse vix poterant iis in locis viventibus ubi maxima Judæorum erat multitudo, ita legem quam dixi Mosis interpretantur. Legibus sane Atticis, quarum antiquissimas ex Mosis legibus desumtas ac tantum non descriptas esse facillimum probatu est, idem quod diximus invenitur constitutum. Vocabatur autem puella talis sive sola ex asse heres esset patri, sive sorores, non etiam fratres haberet, vulgo ἐπίκληρος, ab ipso So- lone περικληρῖτις, ab aliis etiam πατρῶχος. Ad quem ejus nuptiæ lege pertinebant, agnatus nimirum proximus, is dicebatur ἐπιδικαζόμενος, Hebraice הגואל id est ὁ κλη- ρονομῶν αὐτὴν ut est in ea quam dixi Tobiæ historia III. 25. Ex hac lege argumentum Comœdiæ sumsit Apollodorus cui nomen fecit ἐπιδικαζόμενον, aut ut Donatus vult ἐπι- δικαζομένη ex puellæ persona quæ lege maritum petit. Eam Terentius Latine vertit inscripsitque Phormionem: In qua fabula hi sunt versus ad eam legem pertinen- tes:

Lex est ut orbæ, qui sint genere proximi Iis nubant & illos ducere eadem hæc lex jubet.

Ibidem Donatus: Orbæ proximo nubant: orbum proximus ducat, lex Attica est. Græca legis verba apud Sopatrum extant: τῇ ἐπικλήρῳ ἐπιδικαζέσθω ὁ ἀγχισεὺς. Sed & a- pud Diodorum Siculum lib. XII. indicem sumtum illud Adelphis:

Hic meus amicus illi genere est proximus: Huic leges cogunt nubere hanc.

Est & apud Demosthenem, Isæum aliosque oratores Græcos frequens ejus legis mentio, ut & apud Aristopha- nem & Pollucem. Apparet ergo quod dixi non ad omnes puellas hoc jus pertinuisse. Nam quæ fratres habebant, cum nullam rerum soli hæreditatem cernerent, ea lege non tenebantur. Quippe ut Aristophanes ludens ait, non potest ulla esse ἐπίκληρος ὄντων ἀδελφῶν γνησίων, quem sen- sum Isæus sic extulit in oratione de hæreditate Philemo- nis: ἡ γὰρ δήπου γνησίων ὄντων υἱέων συνυπάρχουσα ἐπίκληρος ἢν εἴη ἡ θυγάτηρ αὐτοῦ. Atque idipsum evincit historia quæ est in libro Judicum XXI. 18. ubi tribus cæteræ, quo mi- nus filias suas nuptum darent Benjaminittis, ostendunt se non lege divina, sed jurisjurandi religione prohiberi. Et David Juda profatus ex Benjaminis progenie Micho- lem duxit uxorem: nunquam eo nomine reprehensus: & de Hillele Pharisæo scriptum reperimus apud Hebræos patrem ei fuisse ex tribu Benjamin, matrem ex tribu Ju- da Quod & aliis exemplis confirmabitur ad Lucæ caput I. Adjicit Josephus potuisse quasvis virgines cuivis Hebræo nubere, si hæreditatem sibi delatam repudia- rent. Quare nec Leviticæ gentis virgines eo vinculo ob- stringebantur, ut quæ ex lege rerum soli capaces non es- sent, ideoque rite cuivis de populo nuberent. Errant igi- tur qui non putant salva lege fieri potuisse ut Elizabeth quæ Aaronicæ esset familiæ Mariam cognatione attingeret. Nam nihil obstabat, quo minus pater, avus aliusve quis majorum Mariæ Davide profatus Leviticam virginem in matrimonium duceret: neque enim eo facto jura hæredi- tatum lædebantur. Quanquam vero Maria in re tenui fuerit, quod & hospitium Bethlehemiticum & pauper- tina turturum oblatio satis ostendit, nihilominus valere in ipsa jus τῶν ἐπικλήρων debuit, ob divinas promissio- nes factas Davidis posteritati, quæ tanto in pretio erat apud Judæos, ut etiam post excisa Hierosolyma in exi- lii sui sedibus patriarchas sibi non aliunde quam ex Davidis stirpe præfecerint, quibus ferme ut regibus parebant, quemadmodum Origenes, Epiphanius, Theodoretus, Chrysostomus nos docent, & ea quæ in codice Theodosiano est coronarii auri mentio. Ita cum in Babylonico exsilio Judæi agerent, rerumque soli præ- ter spem nihil retinerent, virgines tamen μονοκληρόνομος agnato proximo nubebant, ut ex Tobiæ historia appa- ret. Non ignoro in Thalmudicis scriptis & post secutis interpretibus tradi præceptum illud Moysis de ducendis virginibus proximis tantum in illis divisionis primæ tem- poribus valuisse. Sed ut in aliis rebus non paucis, ita in hac quoque videntur Thalmudis collectores ex variis Jurisconsultorum sententiis eas tantum retulisse quæ tempore collectionis factæ moribus invaluerant, omis- sis aliis à quibus discessum erat. Nam si perpetuo is fuis- set piorum atque eruditorum consensus, quomodo aut Josephus historiæ conditor id ignorasset institutus in pa- trio jure, aut qui in mentem venisset scriptori Tobiæ mentionem facere moris incogniti?
