Philo quoque hanc legem ut perpetuam refert. Cætera quæ ad conciliandam cum Lucæ Matthæi γενεαλογίαν pertinent, ad Lucam tra- ctabimus.

Eandem Genealogiam Josephi à Luca non minus, quam à Matthæo describit Grotius, cum aliis Africanum sequutus existimat. At haut verisimile videtur utrumque unius Joseph genealogiam sub diversis nominibus pertexere, Mariæ autem genus prorsus reticere voluisse, quum unus tantum ex iis secundum Grotium le- galem Josephi patrem scrupulose recensuerit. Ne- que exiguis premitur scrupulis illa opinio, & necessum habes fingere multos binomines in ge- nealogia Christi, ac mirum fuerit, Lucam eos illos appellasse nomine, à quo S. Matthæum abstinuisse viderat, quod judicio Calixti, (qui hic alioquin cum Grotio facit) forte in uno aut al- tero facile quis admiserit, haud ita facile in tam multis. Ideo non pauci cum Galatino, & Do- minico à Soto malunt genealogiam Josephi tan- tum à Matthæo describi, à Luca vero Mariæ fa- miliam exhiberi. Quod Chemnitius, Biblian- der, Lavaterus, Aretius, Paræus, Gomarus, Fried. Spanhemius, nec non Genebrardus, Jan- senius, Didacus Stella, Baronius, Vincentius Re- gius & alii propugnant, quod hac conciliatio non contorta, sed facilis sit, quodque ita ratio facile constet, cur stemmati genealogico à Mat- thæo descripto, adhuc alia addita à Luca genea- logia, ut nempe perfecta, ac plena exstaret Christi genealogia, nec materna negligeretur prosapia, de quibus legatur cumprimis Goma- rus in examin. controvers. de Genealog. Christi & Fridericus Spanhemius part. 1. Dubior. Evangel. dub. XX. Ratio Grotii, quod à recto sermone us- que alienum sit Josephum dici ἕ τοῦ ἡλὶ, qui non filius Heli, sed gener ejus fuerit, non satis solida est, Nam cum Lucas non utatur verbo γεννᾶν uti Mat- thæus, sed phrasi latiori τοῦ ἡλὶ, τοῦ Ματθὰτ, quæ variam σχέσιν inferre potest, nihil obstat, quo minus aliter de Josepho respectu Heli, aliter de majoribus Heli efferatur, quem- admodum alio sensu Seth τοῦ Ἀδάμ, alio A- dam τοῦ Θεοῦ dici, in confesso est, eadem- que phrasis diversam σχέσιν alibi. 1. Corinth. III. 21. importat, πάντα ἡμῶν ἐστιν, ἡμεῖς δὲ χριστοῦ, χριστὸς τοῦ Θεοῦ. Neque inconcinna est altera solutio, quam Franc. Junius in Notis, Deo datus in versione Bibliorum Itali- corum, Fridericus Spanhemius in dubiis Ev- angelicis ineunt; verba nempe hæc (ὡς ἐνο- μίζετο υἱὸς Ἰωσὴφ) esse παρένθετα, ut sensus- fit: Christum (ut existimabatur filius Josephi) fuisse τοῦ Ἡλὶ nepotem ex Maria filia. Quo pacto explicat etiam B. Hülsemann. in annot. ad Genes. X. 22.

Τὸν ἄνδρα] Quod notatum est à viris doctis mari- tum atque uxorem etiam ex sponsalibus dici, non He- bræorum tantum, sed & aliarum gentium institutis con- venit. Nam & Servius jurisconsultus (citante Pompo- nio) recte dicebat Soceri & socrus & generi & nurus appellationem etiam ex sponsalibus acquiri. Ita in Epi- stolis Heroidum Hermione pacta Oresti:

Vir precor uxori, frater succurre sorori.

Servius ad Eclogam octavam: Conjugis, inquit, non quæ erat, sed quæ fore sperabatur. Vide Deut. XXII. vers. 23.

Μαρίας] Hebræum nomen est מִרְיָם quomodo appellata fuit soror Mosis. Sed posteriores Hebræi mo- re Syro מַרְיָם extulêre: id est μαριάμ, quomodo id nomen sæpius reperias apud Matthæum & Lucam: nec aliter apud Ezechielem Poëtam qui Judaicas tragœdias Græce scripsit. Nam ut Jod consonans in vocalem mu- taretur, extorsit Græca literatura eam consonantem igno- rans: cum vero nulla Græca vox in μ terminetur, eo- que omnia in μ sint ἄπτωτα, formam Græci nominis ac declinationis accipere possunt aut detractione aut ad- ditamento. Additamento usus est Josephus qui hoc no- men ita effert μαριάμμη: detractione Lucas & Matthæi interpres, qui ubi variare suis casibus hoc nomen volunt, scribunt Μαρία Μαρίας. Ita cum similiter à terminatio- nem Græca lingua nesciret, Punica nomina à Baal de- rivata Græci aut auxêre ut ἱερόμβαλος, ἀσύμβαλος dixit Philo Biblius, aut imminuerunt, apposita litera Græcæ terminationis ut ἀσδρούβας, ἀννίβας. Tale & Amilcar Ἀμίλκας, Bogud Βόγος: Et apud Josephum Cain, κάϊς. Ita pro Ἀβραὰμ alii dixêre Ἀβράμης ut Artapa- nus in Judaicis, alii Ἀβρᾶς, manentibus utriusque no- minis vestigiis etiam in usu Latino. Idem Nicolao Da- masceno est Ἀβράμας. Simile est pro Ἰωσὴφ ἰωσῆς Matth. XXVII. vers. 56. Marc. VI. vers. 3. XIV. vers. 37. Actor. IV. vers. 36. Luc. III. vers. 29. & ἰώσηπος. Sic etiam ex שַׁבָּת factum est σάββα σάββατος, & σάββατον σαββάτου.

ὁ λεγόμενος χριστὸς] Referendum est participium ad tempus scriptoris: indicat enim de illo JESU se age- re, qui jam omnibus Christi cognomento innotuisset. Sic & Josephus de Jacobo scribens ἀδελφὸν eum vocat ἰησοῦ τοῦ λεγομένου τοῦ χριστοῦ. Vocantur autem Hebraice מְשִׁיחִים qui singulari divinæ providentiæ benefi- cio ad eximias dignitates erant provecti, ut Abraham & Isaac Psalm CV. vers. 15. Ita ἱερεὺς ὁ χριστὸς in Veteri Te- stamento est ὁ ἀρχιερεὺς, βασιλεὺς ὁ χριστὸς Rex exi- mius, ut Cyrus Esai XLV. vers. 1. Rex Tyri XXIV. v. 14. καθηγητὴς ὁ χριστὸς Doctor eximius, infra XXIII. vers. 8. κατ' ἐξοχὴν vero Judæi, Prophetarum ac præ- sertim Danielis vaticiniis excitati, eo nomine illum ap- pellabant, quem à DEO expectabant Regem doctorem- que summum, Johan. IV. vers. 25. illum autem Chri- stum eximium se esse JESUS professus est, causamque no- minis reddit tum ipse, tum discipuli illius, quod ad pro- ferendam confirmandamque doctrinam cœlestem vi pla- ne incomparabili esset instructus, ut videre est Luc. IV. vers. 18. Actorum IV. v. 27. X. vers. 36. Hebr. I. vers. 9. Johan. III. vers. 34. Quo sensu etiam vitam adhuc agens terrenam, regem se agnoscit, quia nimirum per veritatem à se testatam jam regnum in suorum animis ob- tineret, Johan. XVIII. vers. 37. Cum alioqui sensu alio post resurrectionem demum dicatur esse constitutus Do- minus & Christus, Actorum II. vers. 36. Adeo au- tem invaluit hæc Christi appellatio, ut apud τοὺς ἔξω vix cognito Jesu nomine, agnomen illud in nominis usum transiret. Ita enim eum appellant Tacitus, Svetonius, Plinius: quo factum est, ut Judæi Græco utentes ser- mone, qui Jesum esse Christum agnoscere nolebant, suum illum quem frustra expectabant miseri, non ut ante χριστὸν, sed discriminis causa ἠλειμμένον vocare ince- perint.

Alienum est, quod de מְשִׁיחִים adfer- tur. Non enim cum Jesus dicitur מָשִׁיחַ vox il- la idem est quod eximius, sed juxta propriam no- minis vim UNCTUM notat, quod è Psalm XLV. Esai LXI. vers. 1. Daniel IX. vers. 24. constat. Neque exempla adducta docent, vo- cem משיח solam ἐξοχὴν designare, aut digni- tatem eximiam citra χίσιν ad unctionem. Ab- raham & Isaac ita dicuntur, quod Prophetæ es- sent, qui ungi consueverant, ut in ἐξηγήσει ad- dita Psalm CV. vers. 15. docet, & quod donis Spiritus Sancti essent præ aliis uncti, ut hoc mu- nere defungi possent. Vides, inquit Euse- bius, quod hoc loco veteres Dei amicos & Pro- phetas David, ac potius per illum divinus spiritus Christos appellaverit nullo terrestri unguento un- ctos. Remigius Episcop. Rhemens. explan. in Epist. ad Ebr. c. l. 9. In Veteri Testamento fue- runt patriarchæ participes Christi in hac unctione, quia cum non essent oleo visibili uncti, sed Spiri- tu Sancto repleti, appellantur Christi, hoc est, uncti (Psalm CV.) Neque Cyrus משיח di- citur aliter, quam quod unctus Domini fuerit, id est Rex à Domino constitutus: etsi externo o- leo unctus non fuerit. Nam vocat ita per ser- monem sibi familiarem Propheta unctum Dei, etsi mos ille inaugurandi Reges Israelitarum proprius fuerit, quem hodie etiam Poloni & Galli imitantur: Siquidem omnes imperium à Deo accipiant Proverb. VIII. Daniel II. vers. 21. cap. IV. vers. 2. Adami Conzenii Jesuitæ sententia de Cyro l. VII. Polit. cap. III. l. 1. quod præter morem gentis suæ peculiariter unctus sit, idque consilio Danielis & Israëlitarum peculia- ris est. Idem de Rege Tyri Esai XXIV. judi- cium esto. Salvatori nostro nomen hoc tribui, quod sic καθηγητὴς ὁ χριστός, id est, Doctor eximius, Matth. XXIV. vers. 8. à textu a- lienum est, nam ibi χριστός subjectum est, prædicati vero locum obtinet ὁ καθηγητὴς id- eoque perperam illud tanquam epitheton hujus accipitur. Christus, inquit, unus est Magister: Eodem modo Cyrus Rex unctus dicitur. Quæ causa nominis ab ipso Christo & Apostolis ad- ducta est locis à Grotio laudatis Luc. IV. vers. 18. Actor. IV. vers. 27. cap. X. vers. 36. Ebr. I. 9. Johan. III. vers. 34. non quod eximius tantum Rex aut Doctor, sed quod à Deo ipso donis im- mensis unctus esset ad obeunda officia Prophetæ, Re- gis & Sacerdotis. Ideo Cyrillus de recta fide ad Regin. Quando verbum caro factum est, tunc & nominatione dicimus ipsum esse Christum Jesum; nam quoniam unctus est oleo exultationis hoc est Spiritu Sancto à Deo Patre, idcirco & Christus nominatus est. Chrysost. Sermon. I. in Epist. ad Rom. Christus ab ungendo dicitur, quod & ipsum ad carnem pertinet. Nec probari simpliciter pot- est quod dicit Grotius, Christum Regem se professum esse, cum vitam adhuc terrenam age- ret, hoc solum sensu, quod per veritatem à se testatam jam regnum in suorum animis obtineret: Nam etsi Messias sit etiam ob Propheticum offi- cium, Regium tamen officium, ad quod unctus quoque fuit, quia fungebatur illo, dum adhuc in terris agebat, plura complectebatur, ac im- primis protectionem, ac defensionem etiam suorum inferebat, quos nemo è manibus ipsius eripere poterat. Johan. X. vers. 28. Unde se præsto esse congregatis in nomine suo testabatur Matth. XXVIII. vers. 20. imo omnia in ma- nu sua habebat Johan. III. vers. 35. XIII. vers. 2. etsi post resurrectionem demum Christus omnium

Dominus constitutus sit per exaltationem ad dex- tram Dei, quantum ad incessans, universale, ac plenarium Dominium in cœlo & in terra Matth. XXVIII. vers. 19. Actor. II. 36. Ephes. I. 21. cap. IV. 10. Phil. II. 8.

## 1:17
Ver. 17.

γενεαὶ] This word has various meanings, about which there will be a place to treat elsewhere. What is signified here seems to me not to be able to be expressed conveniently enough by one Latin word: therefore I interpret it as a generated person. For thus do the jurisconsults speak: a generated person always adds a degree. And I find this Greek word in this very sense in Isocrates in his Busiris, when he says that Hercules was τέτρασι γενεαῖς νεώτερον (four generations younger) than Perseus. But that Matthew omitted certain persons, that was done for the sake of rounding the number. For in order to consult the memory, he divided the whole pedigree into three times, to which he attributed clear epochs: before the kingdom, of the flourishing kingdom, and of the ceasing kingdom; and again he assigned to these three orders persons in equal number, as those are accustomed to do who arrange images in places for the sake of memory. In order to achieve this, he thought it of little importance to skip over certain less noble persons, which we see other historians also do when they summarize a matter, such as Solinus in the Kings of Macedonia; and among the Hebrews, Ezra in I Chron. IV. ver. 1, and the writer of the fourth book which is called Ezra, at the beginning, where a comparison of the Chronicles shows that six names are omitted. Also in I Chron. VI, in the census of the descendants of Aaron, it is easy to detect from Josephus that some were omitted. Especially since a father is said to have begotten not only a son, but also a grandfather his grandson, and a great-grandfather his great-grandson, without prejudice to the correctness of speech. However, the sum will not be consistent in number unless we posit two Jechoniahs, one being Joakim, which name, as Jerome rightly notes, could easily be confused with the neighboring name Jechoniah (for even in the first Apocryphal Ezra in Latin copies this Joakim is called Jechoniah), and the other his son Jechoniah: whom even the Hebrew chroniclers themselves call יויקם Joakim: whom Clement of Alexandria follows in Strom. I, and Josephus calls ἰωάχιμον: who nevertheless are distinguished as if they were namesakes by the very interval of such a long exile, and unless we count Christ himself as the final person of the third class. Although many things could be said subtly about the binary and septenary number, whose πολλαπλασιασμὸς (multiplication) among themselves makes fourteen, or even about the senary and septenary which likewise being multiplied together make up the whole pedigree, even from the discipline of the Hebrews, who note that there were XLII members in the golden candlestick, and as many columns in the three porticoes which surrounded the basilica of the temple, I nevertheless judge it better to abstain ταύτης τῆς περιεργείας (from this curiosity), since I persuade myself that this number was not affected by Matthew, but that the same number which the first and most well-known class offered was expressed in the following classes.

PART II. The Nativity of Jesus, with the preceding Angelic warning to Joseph.

Latin:

Vers. 17.

γενεαὶ] Varias significationes hæc vox habet, de quibus alias erit agendi locus. Quod hic significa- tur, videtur mihi non satis commode una Latina voce exprimi posse: itaque interpretor generata persona. Ita enim loquuntur jurisconsulti: semper generata persona gradum adjicit. Atque hoc ipso sensu Græcam hanc vo- cem reperio apud Isocratem Busiride, cum ait Hercu- lem fuisse Perseo τέτρασι γενεαῖς νεώτερον. Quod au- tem personas quasdam omiserit Matthæus, factum id est rotundandi numeri causa. Ut enim memoriæ consule- ret, primum stemma omne in tria tempora digessit, quibus dilucidas ἐποχὰς attribuit, ante regnum, regni florentis, & regni cessantis: rursumque ternis his or- dinibus personas pari numero adscripsit, ut solent qui memoriæ causa imagines locis disponunt. Quod ut consequeretur, parvi duxit personas quasdam minus nobiles transilire, quod & alios historicos ubi rem in summam conferunt facere videmus, ut Solinum in Ma- cedoniæ Regibus: & apud Hebræos Esdram I. Para- lip. IV. vers. 1. & scriptorem quarti qui dicitur Esdræ, initio, ubi sex nomina omitti collatio Paralipomenon docet. Etiam I. Paralip. VI. in censu posterorum Aa- ronis omissos quosdam facile ex Josepho deprehendere est. Præsertim cum genuisse non tantum pater filium sed & avus nepotem & pronepotem proavus salva recti sermonis ratione dicatur. Non constabit autem nume- ro sua summa, nisi Jechonias ponamus duos, alte- rum Joacim, quod nomen, ut recte Hieronymus notat, facile cum vicino Jechoniæ nomine confun- di potuit, (nam & in Apocrypho Esdræ priore in Latinis exemplaribus hic Joacim dicitur Jechonias) alterum ejus filium Jechoniam: quem tamen & ipsum Hebræi temporum digestores יויקם Joacin vocant: quos sequitur Alexandrinus Clemens Strom. I. & ἰω- άχιμον Josephus: qui tamen quasi cognomines di- stinguuntur ipso tam longi exsilii intervallo, ac ni- si Christum ipsum annumeremus ut personam ultimam tertiæ classis. Quanquam autem de binario & se- ptenario numero, quorum inter se πολλαπλασια- σμὸς efficit quatuordecim, aut etiam de senario & septenario qui itidem πολλαπλασιασθέντες totum stem- ma conficiunt, multa possint subtiliter dici, etiam ex Hebræorum disciplina, qui & in aureo candelabro membia notant fuisse XLII, & totidem columnas in tribus porticibus quæ templi Basilicam ambiebant, abstinere tamen ταύτης τῆς περιεργείας satius censeo, cum mihi persuadeam non affectatum hunc nume- rum Matthæo, sed quem obtulerat classis prima ea- que notissima, eundem in classibus sequentibus expres- sum.

PARS II. Nativitas Iesu, cum antecedanea monitio- ne Iosephi Angelica.

## 1:18
Ver. 18.

ἡ γέννησις] Formerly most codices had γένεσις. For whoever is the writer of the dialogue against the Macedonians, he not only cites it into the middle, but expressly adds, ἡ γένεσις εἶπεν, ὐχὶ ἡ γέννησις (it said genesis, not gennesis), and uses that argument to prove ὅτι τὸν ναὸν τοῦ σώματος τοῦ χριστοῦ, τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον ἔκτισε (that the Holy Spirit created the temple of the body of Christ). And soon again: πρῶτον γένεσιν ἄκουε τοῦ ναοῦ κᾀτότε γέννησιν (first hear the genesis of the temple and then the gennesis); it does not seem to me to matter much in which way we read it.

Μνηστευθείσης γὰρ] That γὰρ (for) is redundant here, as in Luke XII. 58 and elsewhere.

Πρὶν ἢ συνελθεῖν ἀυτοὺς] It does not seem to have been a perpetual rule that the bride would move from the day of the betrothal into the house of the bridegroom; although Chrysostom affirms it, I believe because he saw it happening at Antioch in his own age. When

the Jews themselves disagree, it is more credible that it was a matter of free law, and was practiced in one way or another for the convenience of both. For Rebecca was led to Isaac before the solemnities of the wedding, because it was inconvenient for Isaac to travel into Mesopotamia. Conversely, Samson's bride remained in her father's house. And that this was more customary is gathered quite probably from the passage in Deut. XX. ver. 6, which is also handed down in Roman customs by Modestinus, that she who is betrothed does not change her domicile before the marriage is contracted. Furthermore, it is certain that brides remained intact until the assembly was called and the marriage was initiated with solemn prayer: which, as I judge, was not so much commanded by law as handed down by the most ancient fathers, which the Jews observe now just as they did formerly, from whom this institution, most full of honor, flowed to the Christians, about which matter we shall treat below at chapter XXV. Therefore, even though the bridegroom had received into his care the custody of her virginal modesty, the bride nevertheless remained, until the day of the wedding, sequestered from the bridegroom ἐν τῇ γυναικωνίτιδι, just as if she were living in another house. For the words of Moses in Genesis 24:67 seem to signify this, where Isaac is narrated to have brought Rebecca into the tent which had been his mother's, and then to have taken her to himself as his wife. And upon this same custom, as one already received, that law concerning the captive woman, which exists in Deuteronomy chapter 21, verse 13, is built. Since these things are so, of the two meanings which the word τὸ παραλαβεῖν receives, namely that it signifies either the joining of a household or of a marriage bed, I shall prefer the former, because of what follows: μὴ φοβηθῇς παραλαβεῖν μαριάμ, and then, παρέλαβε τὴν γυναῖκα ἀυτοῦ. For that word, unless it refers to the mind, is accustomed to signify φορὰν τινα among the writers of the New Testament, and in this place it seems to me to differ in no way from that which John said in 19:27, λαμβάνειν εἰς τὰ ἴδια. Therefore, παράληψις, when there is talk of a bridegroom and a bride, is the very thing that the Romans call 'leading home.' The writer of Tobit said in its place κομίζεσθαι in 7:15, in which way Andocides also used that word, but with the addition of εἰς τὴν οἰκίαν. The ancient tradition of the Nazarenes, mentioned by Jerome in his Hebrew places, favors this interpretation of this passage.

Latin:

Vers. 18.

ἡ γέννησις] Olim plerique codices habuerunt γέ- νεσις. Nam quisquis est scriptor dialogi adversus Mace- donianos non tantum citat eum in medium, sed differte ad- jicit, ἡ γένεσις εἶπεν, ὐχὶ ἡ γέννησις, eoque argumento utitur ut probet ὅτι τὸν ναὸν τοῦ σώματος τοῦ χριστοῦ, τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον ἔκτισε. Et mox iterum: πρῶτον γένε- σιν ἄκουε τοῦ ναοῦ κᾀτότε γέννησιν, mihi non multum inter- esse videtur, utro legamus modo.

Μνηστευθείσης γὰρ] illud γὰρ hic abundat, ut Luc. XII. 58. & alibi.

Πρὶν ἢ συνελθεῖν ἀυτοὺς] Non videtur perpetuum fuisse, ut à sponsalium die sponsa in sponsi domum transiret: quanquam Chrysostomus id affirmat, cre- do quia Antiochiæ sua ætate id fieri videbat. Cum

Judæi ipfi diffentiant, credibilius est liberi juris id fuisse, aliterque atque aliter usurpatum pro utriusque com- modo. Nam Rebecca deducta est ad Isaacum ante nu- ptiarum solemnia, quia Isaaco incommodum erat in Mesopotamiam proficisci. Contra Samsonis sponsa mansit in domo paterna. Et id fuisse usitatius satis probabiliter colligitur ex loco Deuter. XX. vers. 6. quod & Romanis moribus proditum est a Modestino, eam quæ desponsa est ante contractas nuptias domicilium non mutare. Cæterum illud constat, sponsas intactas fuisse, donec convocato cœtu matrimonium solenni prece initiaretur: quod non tam lege præceptum, quam ab antiquissimis, ut arbitror, patribus traditum, Judæi ut olim ita nunc quoque observant, a quibus ad Christianos id institutum honestatis plenissimum ma- navit, qua de re agemus infra ad caput XXV. Ita- que etiamsi virginalis pudicitiæ custodiam in se spon- sus recepisset, manebat tamen sponsa ad nuptiarum diem ἐν τῇ γυναικωνίτιδι a sponso sequestrata, perinde quasi in alia domo ageret. Id enim significare vi- dentur Mosis verba Genes. XXIV. vers. 67. ubi Isaa- cus narratur Rebeccam ad se deductam in tentorium quod matris fuerat introduxisse, ac deinde eam sibi accepisse in uxorem. Atque eidem mori, ut jam recepto superstructa est lex illa de captiva muliere, quæ extat Deuteronom. cap. XXI. vers. 13. Quæ cum ita se habeant, ex duabus significationibus quas vox τὸ παραλαβεῖν recipit, ut nempe aut domicilii significet aut tori conjunctionem, priorem præferam, propter id quod sequitur, μὴ φοβηθῇς παραλαβεῖν μαριάμ, & deinde, παρέλαβε τὴν γυναῖκα ἀυτοῦ. Ea enim vox, nisi ubi ad animum refertur, φορὰν τινα significare solet apud Scriptores novi fœderis, atque hoc quidem loco nihil mihi videtur differre ab eo quod Joannes dixit XIX. vers. 27. λαμβάνειν εἰς τὰ ἴδια. Est ergo παράληψις, ubi de sponso sponsaque sermo est, id- issum quod Romani domum ductionem vocant. To- biæ scriptor ejus loco dixit κομίζεσθαι VII. vers. 15. quo modo eam vocem & Andocides usurpavit, sed addito εἰς τὴν οἰκίαν. Huic hujus loci interpretationi favet tradi- tio vetus Nazarethanorum memorata Hieronymo locis Hebraicis.

## 1:19
Vers. 19.

Δίκαιος] It does not seem to me that this signifies that general justice, by whose name Zacharias and Elizabeth are commended, and which is described in that Greek verse: ἐν δὲ δικαιοσύνῃ συλλήβδην πασ᾽ ἀρετή 'στι. But rather some special justice, and indeed not distributive or commutative, but that which we are accustomed to call goodness in a peculiar way: just as in Daniel and often elsewhere צדקה signifies kindness or mercy: whence it has come about that even benevolence toward the poor is signified by that name among the Hebrews. Nor would you wrongly refer here what is in the Epistle of John I, chapter 1, verse 9: ἐὰν ὁμολογῶμεν τὰς ἁμαρτίας ἡμῶν, πιστός ἐστι καὶ δίκαιος ἵνα ἀφῇ ἡμῖν τὰς ἁμαρτίας. The writer of Tobit also joined them as related things, ἐλεημοσύνην καὶ δικαιοσύνην, in 14:10. More closely, however, pertains here what Aristotle says, that τὸ ἐπιεικὲς is δίκαιον δικαίου τινὸς βέλτιον: and he describes τὸν ἐπιεικῆ as τὸν μὴ ἀκριβοδίκαιον, ἀλλ᾽ ἐλαττωτικόν. Donatus, regarding that passage of Terence's Andria, 'justa fuerit servitus,' says: 'justa,' that is, moderate. But this goodness shows itself especially whenever we do not rigidly exact the punishments prescribed by the laws: for as Sopater the philosopher says, τὸ ἐπὶ τοῖς ἐγκλήμασι κόπτον τῆς δίκης ὑπεξαιτεῖται τὸ πρᾶον καὶ φιλάνθρωπον τῶν χαρίτων πρόσωπον. Chrysostom well says in this place: Δίκαιος ὢν τοῦτ᾽ ἔστι χρηστὸς καὶ ἐπιεικής.

Παραδειγματίσαι] One may interpret it in Latin: since he did not want her to be an example; that is, as Hilary explains, since he did not want a legal decree to be made against her, κολάζεσθαι, Theophylact says, to be punished, Augustine says. Which is fair to be understood concerning the penalty of stoning established by the law of Moses for brides found to have committed fornication. For at that time the judgments of the law in Judea were being exercised by Herod, who wanted to appear studious of the law. And the word παραδειγματίζειν is used by Polybius regarding the death penalty: and therefore Demosthenes also said, διαιρετικῶς, ζῶντα παραδειγμα ποιῆσαι. Among the Hellenists, however, it appears that τὸ παραδειγματίζειν was used regarding the death penalty, both from the LXX interpretation of Numbers chapter 25, verse 4, and from the additions to Esther 14:9. But as for what learned men object, that it could have come into Joseph's mind that she was defiled before the betrothal the virgin, it seems more likely to me that the signs of the womb corresponded to the time of conception, which was later than the betrothal, Luke 1:26. Nor does Justin differ from us in his dialogue with Trypho, when he says that Joseph thought that Mary, his betrothed, was pregnant from the intercourse of a man, that is adultery in its scope, as appears in Matthew 5:32. And therefore Augustine was not afraid to say that he believed nothing other than that she was an adulteress. Nor indeed, if it were so, was it unworthy of a good man to spare a girl who was in danger of both her life and her reputation. For to omit what the law decrees concerning a vice committed in the city, Deut. 22:24, it is of the kind to which most laws belong, which so regard that which happens for the most part, that nevertheless there may occur cases of fact in which the law fails because of its generality and therefore needs correction; also, besides the force of law, many other things can happen which do not indeed remove the fault, but diminish it, in which direction goodness is always credulous. Add that the perceived character of the virgin gave Joseph cause to interpret everything more kindly. Furthermore, the law imposes a penalty on the accused and convicted, but it commands the accusation to no one. Indeed, if we believe Ambrose, the person of a just man is alien not only to the atrocity of vengeance, but also to the severity of accusation.

Λάθρα] Not indeed with no one knowing: for that could not happen, since it was the custom for Jews no less than for Romans that betrothals were neither contracted nor dissolved unless witnesses were employed: but privately, that is, without public judgment and without the cause being rendered. For that is what this word means here, opposed to 'to make an example of'.

Ἀπολῦσαι ἀυτήν] To send her a bill of divorce. The word is indeed common to repudiation and divorce, but for those speaking Latin, the interpretation must be varied.

Latin:

Vers. 19.

Δίκαιος] Non videtur hic mihi significari justitia illa generalis, cujus nomine Zacharias & Elizabeth com- mendantur, & quæ versu isto Græco describitur: ἐν δὲ δικαιοσύνῃ συλλήβδην πασ᾽ ἀρετή 'στι. Sed potius specialis aliqua, neque vero διανεμητικὴ aut συναλλακτική, sed illa quam peculiariter bonitatem vocare folemus: sicut apud Danielem & alibi sæpe צדקה χρηστότητα sive misericordiam significat: quo factum est, ut etiam benignitas erga pauperes eo no- mine Hebræis significetur. Neque male huc referas, quod est in Epistola Joannis I. cap. I. vers. 9. ἐὰν ὁμο- λογῶμεν τὰς ἁμαρτίας ἡμῶν, πιστός ἐστι καὶ δίκαιος ἵνα ἀφῇ ἡ- μῖν τὰς ἁμαρτίας. Tobiæ quoque scriptor conjunxit ut affinia ἐλεημοσύνην καὶ δικαιοσύνην XIV. vers. 10. Propius autem huc pertinet quod Aristoteles ait τὸ ἐπιεικὲς effe δίκαιον δικαίου τινὸς βέλτιον: & τὸν ἐπιεικῆ describit, τὸν μὴ ἀκριβοδίκαιον, ἀλλ᾽ ἐλαττωτικόν. Donatus ad illud Terentii Andria: justa fuerit servitus: justa, in- quit, moderata. Præcipue autem bonitas hæc se o- stendit quoties pœnas legibus præscriptas non rigide ex- igimus: nam ut ait Sopater Philosophus τὸ ἐπὶ τοῖς ἐγκλήμασι κόπτον τῆς δίκης ὑπεξαιτεῖται τὸ πρᾶον καὶ φιλ- άνθρωπον τῶν χαρίτων πρόσωπον. Chrysostomus be- ne hoc loco: Δίκαιος ἐν ὢν τοῦτ᾽ ἔστι χρηστὸς καὶ ἐπιει- κής.

Παραδειγματίσαι] Latine interpretari licet: cum cum re nollet ut ea exemplum esset: hoc est, ut explicat Hilarius, cum nollet in eam lege decerni, κολάζεσθαι Theophylactus, puniri Augustinus. Quod de lapida- tionis pœna lege Mosis statuta in sponsas stupri comper- tas par est intelligi. Nam ad id tempus judicia legis in Judæa per Herodem qui legis studiosus videri volebat, exercebantur. Et vox παραδειγματίζειν Polibio de mortis supplicio usurpatur: ideoque & Demosthenes διαιρετικῶς dixit ζῶντα παραδειγμα ποιῆσαι. Apud Hellenistas autem de mortis pœna usurpatum τὸ παρα- δειγματίζειν apparet tum ex LXX. interpretatione Num. cap. XXV. vers. 4. tum ex additamentis ad Estherem XIV. vers. 9. Quod autem objiciunt viri eruditi, po- tuisse Josepho in animum venire ante sponsalia vitiatam esse virginem, mihi verisimilius videtur uteri signa re- spondisse tempori conceptionis, quod sponsalibus po- sterius fuit, Luc. I. vers. 26. Neque dissentit hic a no- bis Justinus in colloquio cum Tryphone, cum dicit, pu- tasse Josephum τὴν μνηστὴν ἀυτῷ Μαρίαν ἐγκυμονεῖν ἀπὸ συνουσίας ἀνδρὸς τοῦτ᾽ ἔστιν ἀπὸ πορνείας. Nam vox πορ- νείας extra controversiam suo ambitu τὴν μοιχείαν com- prehendit, ut apparet Matth. V. vers. 32. Ideoque non veritus est Augustinus dicere, cum nihil aliud quam adulteram credidisset. Neque vero id si ita esset indignum fuit viro bono puellæ de vita famaque simul periclitanti parcere. Nam ut omittam quod de vitio in urbe ob- lato lex decernit Deut. XXII. vers. 24. ejus esse generis cujus sint pleraque legum, quæ ita respiciunt id quod ἐπὶ τὸ πλεῖστον accidit, ut tamen evenire possint facti spe- cies in quibus deficiat lex διὰ τὸ καθόλου eoque egeat ἐπανορθώματος, etiam præter vim multa alia possunt ac- cidere quæ culpam non tollant quidem, sed minuant, in quam partem semper credula est bonitas. Adde quod Josepho omnia benignius interpretandi causam præbue- runt perspecti virginis mores. Deinde accusatæ & con- victæ lex pœnam irrogat, accusationem autem nemini imperat. Quin si Ambrosio credimus non solum ab ultionis atrocitate, sed etiam accusationis severitate alie- na justi persona est.

Λάθρα] non quidem conscio nemine: id enim fieri non poterat, cum mos esset Judæis non minus quam Romanis, ut nec contraherentur, nec dirime- rentur sponsalia, nisi adhibitis testibus: sed privatim, id est, sine judicio publico & non reddita causa. Id e- nim hic valet vox ista, opposita τῷ παραδειγματίζειν.

Ἀπολῦσαι ἀυτήν] Repudium ei mittere. Vox quidem communis est repudio & divortio, sed Latine lo- quentibus varianda interpretatio.

## 1:20
Vers. 20.

Ἐνθυμηθέντος] When he was turning these things over in his mind: as this word is mostly taken among Greek writers and in Acts 9:19. For Joseph's mind seems indeed to have inclined toward repudiation, yet so that he had determined nothing certain as yet, but was distracted by various thoughts on this matter.

Ἄγγελος] The Hebrews call those spirits who are placed between God, the maker of things, and men, sometimes Elohim, sometimes Malachim, of which the former signifies God in Greek, the latter angel. And from there Pythagoras took those appellations, whom Numenius and other Pythagoreans professed to have drawn much from the Hebrews: and whose institutions were the same as the institutions of the Essenes, as Josephus revealed. But he also used those words with a distinction applied. For he called 'gods' the more sublime minds and those approaching more closely to the divine nature, which he established as 'unchangeable': but 'angels' those spirits who had obtained the place next to those first ones: 'as stepping in and announcing to us the rules for living well': as Hierocles speaks, who likewise teaches us that those commonly called angels are again distinguished into three classes, into angels properly and peculiarly so called, and into good demons and heroes. All of which were derived from the school of Pythagoras into the Platonic. The writer of those poems which were once considered even by the pagans themselves as Orphic, whom some say was Cecrops, others Onomacritus, a disciple of Pythagoras, mentions angels in these verses: 'And by the fiery throne stand the much-toiling Angels, to whom it is a care how all things are accomplished for mortals.' Which can be seen to have been taken from Hostanes the magus, if Cyprian had the verse correctly when he wrote on the vanity of idols. Aristides also uses the word 'angels' in this sense in his hymn to Minerva. Labeo the Roman had also used it, as we learn from Augustine in The City of God, book 9, chapter 19. Porphyry and Iamblichus use it everywhere, and Chalcidius in his Timaeus: But the Hellenistic Hebrews, dealing with the same spirits, did not willingly call them 'gods', because that name was already being used everywhere among all nations to the injury of the one supreme and creating God. But also with the word 'heroes' rejected and 'demons' relegated to malevolent spirits, the name 'angels' remained in use among them: which the Seventy also use very often, and following their example, the writers of the New Testament: indeed, even the Chaldean Paraphrasts of the Old Testament. Some Hellenists called angels 'watchers', which name is also read in Clement of Alexandria and other Christians from Daniel 4:10, where 'ir' is read, which Aquila and Symmachus translated as 'watchers'.

[Κατ' ὄναρ] The old interpreter is best with 'in dreams': for so Accius, Ennius, and Virgil speak when they deal with nocturnal visions. Cicero said 'during rest'. But generally in four ways, as the Hebrews rightly note, God is accustomed to reveal His will or future things to men: by daytime visions, by visions during rest, by voice, by inspiration; in Greek you would say it thus: by apparition, by dreams, by voice, by inspiration. Chalcidius divides 'apparition' into vision, which is from God, and spectacle, which is through angels. He calls the rest dream, admonition, revelation.

Latin:

Vers. 20.

Ἐνθυμηθέντος] Cum hæc animo agitaret: ut ple- rumque hæc vox sumitur apud Græcos scriptores & A- ctor. IX. 19. Videtur enim inclinasse quidem ad repudium Josephi animus, ita tamen ut nihil dum certi consti- tuisset, sed variis super hac re cogitationibus distrahe- retur.

Ἄγγελος] Hebræi spiritus istos qui inter Deum rerum opificem hominesque sunt interpositi modo אלהים, modo מלאכים vocant, quorum illud Græce θεὸς istud ἄγγελος significat. Atque inde eas appellationes sumsit Pythagoras, quem multa hausisse ab Hebræis Numenius aliique Pythagorici profitebantur: cujusque adeo instituta eadem esse cum Essenorum in- stitutis, Josephus prodidit. Sed & eas voces usurpavit adhibito discrimine. Nam θεοὺς vocabat mentes subli- miores & ad divinam naturam propius accedentes, quas statuebat ἀτρέπτους: ἀγγέλους autem eos spiritus, qui proximum primis illis locum essent sortiti: ὡς ἐπιβαίνον- τας καὶ διαγέλλοντας ἡμῖν τὰς πρὸς ἐνζωίαν κανόνας: ut loqui- tur Hierocles, qui itidem nos docet illos communiter dictos ἀγγέλους, iterum distinctos in classes tres, in ἀγ- γέλους proprie & peculiariter ita dictos, in δαίμονας ἀ- γαθοὺς καὶ ἥρωας. Quæ omnia ex Pythagoræ schola in Platonicam sunt derivata. Scriptor eorum carminum quæ olim ab ipsis etiam paganis pro Orphicis sunt ha- bita, quem alii Cecropem, alii Onomacritum Pythagoræ discipulum ajunt fuisse, Angelorum meminit istis versi- bus: Τῷ δὲ θρόνῳ πυρόεντι παρεστᾶσιν πολύμοχθοι Ἄγγελοι, οἶσι μέμηλεβροτοῖς ὡς πάντα τελεῖται. Quod ex Hostara mago sumtum videri potest, si eum recte versum habuit Cyprianus cum de Idolorum vani- tate scriberet. Usurpat vocem ἀγγέλων hoc sensu & Aristides hymno in Minervam. Usurpaverat & Labeo Romanus ut ex Augustino discimus de civitate Dei lib. IX. cap. XIX. Usurpant & Porphyrius & Jamblichus pas- sim, & Chalcidius in Timæum: At Hebræi Hellenistæ de iisdem spiritibus agentes θεοὺς non libenter eos vo- carunt, quia id nomen jam passim apud omnes gentes in unius summi atque opificis Dei injuriam usurpaba- tur. Sed & ἡρώων vocabulo repudiato & δαιμόνων ad maleficos spiritus relegato, in usu apud eos mansit no- men ἀγγέλων: quo & septuaginta utuntur sæpissime, & eorum exemplo novi fœderis scriptores: imo & Veteris Testamenti Chaldæi Paraphrastæ. Quidam Hel- lenistæ Angelos vocabant ἐγρηγόρους, quod nomen & a- pud Clementem Alexandrinum aliosque Christianos legitur ex Daniele IV. vers. 10. ubi עיר legitur, quod Aquila & Symmachus verterunt ἐγρηγόρους:

[Κατ' ὄναρ] Optime vetus interpres in somnis: ita enim loquuntur Accius, Ennius, Virgilius, cum de visis nocturnis agunt. Cicero secundum quietem dixit. Ferme autem quatuor modis, ut Hebræi recte notant, solet Deus hominibus voluntatem suam aut res futuras patefacere, visis diurnis, visis secundum quietem, voce afflatu, Græce ita dixeris δι' ὀπτασίας, δι' ἐνυπλίων, διὰ φωνῆς, δι' ἐπιπνοίας. Chalcidius ὀπτα- σίαν dividit in visum, quod à Deo, & spectaculum, quod per Angelos. Reliqua vocat somnium, admonitio- nem, revelationem.

## 1:21
Vers. 21.

[Ἰησῶν] That name which in the times of Moses was written Yehoshua, after the Babylonian exile began to be written Yeshua, with the vau and he, which usage had worn away, produced under the yod vowel. And thus we find it written in Ezra and Nehemiah, although Haggai and Zechariah retained the ancient spelling. This had undoubtedly come from the commerce of the Syrians, to whom it was accepted to omit letters of that kind. Wherefore the Syrian interpreter also writes this word in the same way. Thus from Caiphanta was made Caiphas. Thus the city Gaza is Aza in Chaldean, and in Greek Gaza: and Mashiach, Messias. To the Babylonians, Bel, who to others is Baal. Thus shicha is a pit for shichata, and many other similar things among the Hebrews of later times; and among the Chaldean interpreters. But also the last letter of the word was at first lightly pronounced, as appears from the Latin word Josue and the Greek Iesous, that is, Abishua, 1 Chronicles. VII. verse 3. to which is similar Ἀβιού from אֲבִיהוּ, and in a similar letter רְעוּ Ῥαῦ, it itself gradually vanished: which ease of sound the Hellenist Jews followed and wrote Ἰησοῦ with a circumflex on the last syllable, because almost all Hebrew names among the Greeks are written with an accent on the last syllable, as can be seen everywhere, which accent indeed, because the syllable is long by nature, has here become more produced, as also in Μωϋσῆς. But since such endings were unknown to the Greek language, and therefore did not suffer variation of cases, for the sake of easier construction two cases were fashioned in the Greek manner, the nominative by adding ς, and the accusative by adding ν. Thus it is said ὁ Μανασσῆς, τὸν Μανασσῆν (although we also read τὸν Μανασσῆ above in verse 10) and ὁ Ἰησοῦς τὸν Ἰησοῦν. Thus Ἡσαῦν in the accusative case in Josephus. Thus Ἐλιαῦς from Ἐλιαῦ among the Greek interpreters. Otherwise these words remain indeclinable. For we say τῷ Μανασσῆ, τῷ Μανασσῆ, ὦ Μανασσῆ, etc. τῷ Ἰησοῦ, τῷ Ἰησοῦ, ὦ Ἰησοῦ. And in this way this name is both written and declined, both among the LXX and the son of Sirach, concerning which the writers of the New Testament changed nothing, distinguishing by no difference of writing this proper name of Christ from the name of him who, succeeding Moses and leading the people into the promised lands, foreshadowed Christ, the giver of eternal rest, not only by the sound of the name, but also by his deeds: as can be seen in Acts VII. verse 45 and Heb. IV. verse 8. Nor is any other meaning of this word to be imagined than that which the Angel teaches us, ἀπὸ τοῦ σώζειν, which manifestly agrees with the Hebrew origin. Jesus is therefore in Greek σωτήρ: by which word Cicero says it is only signified, so that it cannot be expressed in Latin by one word. It does not seem to me that a Latin word of the same origin and efficacy is lacking, but it is older and received more in sacred contexts than in popular usage, namely Sospitator. Furthermore, that certain Christian writers, and indeed those not unskilled in the Hebrew language, derive this name ἀπὸ τοῦ ἰᾶσθαι, in that they do not seem to me to have looked to another Hebrew word, but to have sought a Greek word which would cohere with the Hebrew ישוע not only in meaning, but also in sound, in the manner of Philo, who loves to allude to Greek words in such a way that he departs as little as possible from the Hebrew notation. But it is certain that the Hebrew ישוע sometimes means the same as the Greek ἰᾶσθαι, and sometimes by a most accepted translation the meaning of giving salvation is expressed by that word, just as he who frees another from trouble is said in Latin to heal the evils of another. Whence also ἰᾶσθαι is put for σώζειν in Matt. XIII. verse 15, Luke IV. verse 18, and conversely σώζειν for ἰᾶσθαι as in Matt. IX. verse 21, Mark VI. 56. Acts IV. verse 9. Moreover, David Kimchi at Jerem. III. verse 28 explains 'to heal' as 'to forgive sins.' And from this I think it happened that certain Jews living among the Greeks and imbued with Greek literature, when they were called by this very Hebrew name, made for themselves the Greek name Jason, because that name of Greek custom would approach that Hebrew one most closely both in the proximity of sound and in the meaning of its origin. Among whom was that Cyrenaean The writer of the Maccabean history, of equal fate with Trogus Pompeius. But what is in Theodoret, ἰαὼ ἡ σωτηρία παρὰ τοῖς ἑβραίοις λέγεται, seems faulty to me, and it should be written ἰαοὺ so that it may be יְשׁוּעָה, for that the Greek ὼ should express the ע is not unusual.

He shall save his people from their sins] Although Christ can be said to free us from sins in a threefold way—first, because he seeks the remission of sins for us; second, because in this life he causes sin not to reign in us; finally, because through the other life he will utterly destroy both sin and death, the wages of sin—yet it seems to me that the Angel looked primarily to the remission of sins, because the Apostles also remembered that matter most when they explain the force of that word σωτῆρος in Acts 5:31 and chapter 13:23, joined with verses 32 and 38. And although by the word λαῷ all believers can be understood not inappropriately, yet since that word usually signifies the Israelite people even in the New Testament, to whom Christ was sent peculiarly, so that I judge these words should be taken in that first, at least most obvious, understanding, the passage I mentioned in Acts 5:31 and the one below in 15:21 support this.

Vers. 21.

[Ἰησῶν] Nomen illud quod Moysis temporibus יְהוֹשׁוּעַ scribebatur, post exilium Babylonicum cœ- pit scribi יֵשׁוּעַ in locum ו & ה quæ usus detriverat producta sub jod vocali. Atque ita scriptum reperimus apud Esdram & Nehemiam, quamquam Aggæus & Za- charias antiquam scripturam retinuerunt. Nimirum ve- nerat hoc ex Syrorum commercio, quibus receptum li- teras ejus generis prætermittere. Quare & Syrus inter- pres eodem modo scribit hanc vocem. Sic ex Caiphan- τα factum est Caiphas. Sic urbs עַזָה Chaldæo est עַזָא, Græcis Γάζα : & מָשִׁיחַ, μεσσίας. Babyloniis בֵּל qui aliis בַּעַל. Sic שִׁיחָא fovea pro שִׁיחָתָא, multa- que alia similia apud Hebræos posteriorum temporum; & apud Chaldæos interpretes. Sed & ultima vocis litera primum leviter pronunciata, ut apparet ex Latina voce Josue & Græca Ἰησοῦς id est אֲבִישׁוּעַ 1. Paralip. VII. vers. 3. cui simile est Ἀβιού 'ex אֲבִיהוּ, & in simili litera רְעוּ Ῥαῦ, paulatim & ipsa evanuit: quam foni fa- cilitatem secuti Hellenistæ Judæi Ἰησοῦ scripserunt cir- cumflexa ultima, quia nomina Hebræa ferme omnia apud Græcos scribuntur cum accentu in Syllaba ultima, ut passim videre est, qui quidem accentus ob syllabam natura longam factus hic est productior, ut & in Μω- ϋσῆς. Cum autem tales exitus ignoti essent Græco ser- moni, ideoque casuum variationem non paterentur, facilioris tamen constructionis gratia duo casus sunt effigiati in Græcum morem, rectus addito ς, & quartus casus addito ν. Itaque dicitur ὁ Μανασσῆς, τὸν Μανασσῆν (quanquam & τὸν Μανασσῆ legimus supra commate 10.) & ὁ Ἰησοῦς τὸν Ἰησοῦν. Sic Ἡσαῦν quarto casu apud Josephum. Sic Ἐλιαῦς ab Ἐλιαῦ apud Græcos interpretes. Cæteroqui manent hæ voces ἄπτωτοι. Dicimus enim τῶ Μανασσῆ, τῷ Μανασσῆ, ὦ Μανασσῆ, &c τῷ Ἰησοῦ, τῷ Ἰησοῦ, ὦ Ἰησοῦ. Atque hoc modo nomen istud & scribitur & declinatur, tum apud LXX. tum apud Sirachiden, de quo nihil immutarunt scripto- res novi fœderis, nulla scripturæ differentia distinguen- tes hoc Christi proprium nomen ab ejus nomine qui Mosi succedens populumque ducens in terras promissas Christum, æternæ quietis datorem, non tantum no- minis sono, sed & rebus gestis adumbravit: ut vide- re est Actorum VII. vers. 45. & Hebr. IV. vers. 8. Ne- que alia significatio hujus vocis comminiscenda est ab ea quam nos Angelus docet ἀπὸ τοῦ σώζειν, quæ cum Hebræa origine manifeste consentit. Est ergo Jesus Græce σωτήρ: qua voce tantum ait significari Cicero, ut id Latio uno verbo exprimi non possit. Mihi non videtur deesse vox Latina ejusdem originis utque effica- ciæ, sed antiquior & in sacris magis quam in usu popu- lari recepta, Sospitatoris. Cæterum quod Christiani quidam scriptores; & quidem Hebræi sermonis non im- periti nomen hoc ἀπὸ τοῦ ἰᾶσθαι deducunt, in eo mihi non videntur ad aliam vocem Hebræam respexisse, sed quæsivisse vocem Græcam, quæ Hebrææ ישוע non sola significatione, sed sono insuper cohæreret, Philo- nis more, qui ita ad Græcas voces amat alludere, ut ab Hebræa notatione quam minimum recedat. Cer- tum autem est Hebræum ישוע modo idem valere quod Græcum ἰᾶσθαι, modo per receptissimam translationem salutis dandæ significationem ea voce exprimi, sicut & Latinæ mederi alterius malis dicitur qui alterum ab incommodo liberat. Unde & ἰᾶσθαι pro σώζειν Matth. XIII. vers. 15. Luc. IV. vers. 18. & vicissim σώζειν pro ἰᾶσθαι ponitur ut Matth. IX. vers. 21. Marc. VI. 56. A- ctor. IV. vers. 9. Quin & David Kimchi apud Jerem. III. vers. 28. sanare explicat peccata condonare. Et hinc factum arbitror, ut Judæi quidam inter Græcos versan- tes & Græcanica literatura imbuti, cum hoc ipso no- mine Hebræo vocarentur, Græce sibi nomen Jasonis fecerint, quod id nomen Græcæ consuetudinis ad He- bræum illud & foni vicinitate & originis significatu proxime accederet. Quos inter fuit Cyrenæus ille Maccabaicæ historiæ scriptor, paris fati cum Trogo Pom- pejo. Quod vero apud Theodoretum est, ἰαὼ ἡ σωτη- ρία παρὰ τοῖς ἑβραίοις λέγεται, mendosum mihi videtur, scribendumque ἰαοὺ ut sit יְשׁוּעָה nam ut ע Græce, per ὼ exprimatur non est insolens.

Σώσει τὸν λαὸν ἀπὸ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν ἀυτῶν] Cum triplici modo dici nos possit Christus à peccatis libera- re, primum quia remissionem peccatorum nobis pe- petit, deinde quia in hac vita efficit ne peccatum in nobis regnet, postremo quia per vitam alteram dele- bit funditus & peccatum & mortem peccati stipendium, mihi tamen ad remissionem peccatorum præcipue vide- tur respexisse Angelus, quia & Apostoli ejus rei maxi- me meminerunt ubi vocis istius σωτῆρος vim explicant Actorum V. vers. 31. & cap. XIII. vers. 23. juncto com- mate 32. & 38. Quanquam autem voce λαῷ omnes credentes non incommode possint intelligi, cum tamen plerumque etiam in novo fœdere ea vox Israëliticum populum significet, ad quem peculiariter missus est Christus, ut de eo hæc verba primo saltem maxime- que obvio intellectu sumenda arbitrer, facit is quem dixi locus Actorum V. vers. 31. & qui infra est XV. vers. 21.

## 1:22
Vers. 22.

That it might be fulfilled] Whatever this word may be, it matters much that it be understood correctly. For Celsus and Julian, the ancient Jews of old, and now too, have been accustomed to object to Christians that the authority of the Prophets was brought forward by the Apostles and their followers less than faithfully. But it must be noted that the Apostles do not fight against the Jews with these as if they were testimonies to prove that Jesus is the promised Messiah: for there are few oracles which they use for this end, being content otherwise with the miracles and resurrection of Christ. For (as he once said) either these were enough, or nothing was enough. But to those who were already persuaded that JESUS was that Messiah, they wished to show at the same time how the whole divine διονομία of former times, having this very Christ and his deeds as a most beautiful and perfect model perpetually before its eyes, as it were, fashioned all other things to that likeness. To this point, besides many other things which will be explained in their proper places, pertains the fact that Christ is said to be προεγνωσμένθ πρὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου, 1 Peter 1:20. And this divine wisdom which shines forth in the sending of Christ is προωρισμένη πρὸ τῶν αἰώνων, 1 Corinthians 2:7. But most clear is that at 1 Corinthians 10:11: All these things happened to them (namely, those who were under the old covenant) ἐβενευαντ τυπικῶς: but they were written for our admonition εἰς ὃς τὰ τέλη τῶν αἰώνων κατήντησεν. Thus elsewhere the time of Christ is called the πλήρωμα of times, Galatians 4:4, Ephesians 1:10. Therefore, not only were the institutions of the law shadows of Christ, which is shown in Hebrews 8:5, chapter 10:1, and Colossians 2:17, but also his deeds, especially the more noble ones. Which Justin rightly warns against Trypho: ἔσθ' ὅτε γὰρ τὸ ἅγιον πνεῦμα καὶ ἐναργῶς πράττεσθαι τι, ὃ τύπθ τῷ μέλλοντι γίνεσθαι, ἦν ἐποίει. And afterwards he says that the deeds are προκηρύγματα τῶν κατὰ χρισῦ ἁπάντων. Tertullian on the Resurrection of the flesh: Such meanwhile are the lineaments of divine powers, with GOD working no less by parables than by speaking. Likewise: We know that the prophets spoke as much by things as by words. Chrysostom on Romans: For the prophets did not only speak, but also wrote what they spoke; and they did not only write, but also typified through deeds. And in the first to the Corinthians: Some things are set before them through words, others through types. And in the second sermon on fasting he says that one prophecy is through a type or deeds, another through speech or words. That which Paul says τυπικῶς is taken from painters and sculptors, or even from builders of edifices, who, planning some excellent work, first delineate it roughly, then gradually bring about what they had conceived in their mind. For those first lineaments are called τύποι: whence that Aristotelian ὡς ἐν τύπῳ, opposed to τῷ ἀκριβῶς. But that ἀκριβὲς is called by the Apostles τὸ πλήρωμα, in the manner of the Hebrews, who call it מילאת, and the τελειότητα of any thing, as Abenezra explains in Canticles 5:12, in which place the LXX have ἐπὶ πληρώματι. But if the things themselves look to Christ by divine counsel, surely the signs divinely instituted for things must also be referred to the same. Now there are two kinds of signs: visible and audible. And what are signified are past, present, and future. Christ, the Apostles, and other writers of the New Testament provide us with examples of all these kinds. Let us be content with a few, and none other than those in which this same word τοῦ πληροῦσθαι is found. A visible sign of a past thing, namely, the liberation from Egyptian slavery, was the Paschal lamb. But that liberation was a type of our liberation from sins. For this reason Christ is shown to have been foreshadowed in the Paschal lamb, 1 Corinthians 5:7. GOD providently permitted the impiety of the ancient Jews to act as a prelude to the supreme impiety which was exercised against Christ. But that old impiety, by the sign of coins of little value, for which GOD complained that he was valued, was attested by the command of GOD himself and the ministry of Zechariah, Zechariah 11:13; in that sign, therefore, is shown the delineation of the wicked pact between the Priests and Judas Iscariot, Matthew 27:9. To come to the audible signs, those, namely, which were pronounced by voice but as if they had been pronounced in writing (for letters are only secondary signs of voices, as voices are of things), the passage of Hosea 11:1 has a commemoration of a past benefit, namely, the liberation from Egypt, which, as we have already said, was a certain rudiment of the greater liberty obtained through Christ. The very History of Christ, however, admonishes us that the mind of the speaking Prophet was so directed by God, that what was said by him concerning the Israelite people might apply no less correctly, or even more correctly, to Christ, Matth. II. verse 15. Of the same argument is the song of Asaph, Psalm LXXVIII. verse 1, whose words are likewise such that they fit Christ most excellently, Matth. XIII. verse 35. Thus, the Paraphrasts in that place, and Solomon Jarchi, as also Saadia Gaon at Daniel VII. verse 14, refer Psalm LXXII, written in honor of Solomon, as the title indicates, to the Messiah. We have these examples of locutions which directly pertained to the instant time and yet, by divine counsel, were referred to Christ. Those things which Jeremiah had said concerning the slaughters committed in his own time in the Bethlehemite region, chapter XXXI. verse 15, so depict that which was perpetrated by Herod that the same thing could scarcely be expressed more signally in other words. That which is read in Isaiah LXI. at the very beginning, the Prophet indeed seems to speak of the duty imposed upon him of consoling the captive multitude with the hope of return: but those are words which, adapted to Christ, designate the thing itself most clearly, just as the return from Babylon itself prefigured the benefits of Christ. But since no one of the ancients was exercised by God with greater evils, and again affected with greater glory, than David, it clearly appears that this was done by God so that the things of Christ might be pre-signified in him more closely than in others. Therefore, the words with which he complains that he is undeservedly hated, nay, betrayed by him whom he had counted among his friends, are of such a kind that nothing could be said more accommodately to the things of Christ, which appears in Psalm XXXV. verse 19, John XV. verse 25, Psalm XLI. verse 10, John XIII. verse 15, Acts I. verse 17. What of the fact that David spoke certain things about himself in such a way that those things which suited him κατὰ λέξιν ἐσχηματισμένην, those pertained to Christ with the propriety of the words preserved? such as that concerning the division of garments and the casting of lots, Psalm XXII. verse 19, Matth. XXVII. verse 35, John XIX. verse 24, and concerning the bitter and sour drink, Psalm LXIX. verse 22, John XIX. verse 28. The same is to be observed in the presages of future things, except that we can say these are fulfilled twice: once when that thing occurs which is directly predicted, and again, and indeed more excellently, when that appears for the shadowing forth of which that very thing, and consequently also the words denoting it, served.

Grotius pursues these things for this reason, that he may maintain that most of the prophecies of Scripture which are brought forward concerning Christ in the New Testament do not treat of Christ, but of others of ancient times, and are not applied to Christ otherwise than as they exhibited something in the likeness of that which they prefigured. By which artifice he renders even illustrious oracles speaking openly of the Messiah doubtful in this place. Thus Psalm 72 he says was written in honor of Solomon, even though he is not unaware that it is referred to the Messiah by the Paraphrast, and Solomon Jarchi, as also Saadia Gaon at Daniel 7:14. What is read in Isaiah 61 concerning the Prophet's office of comforting the captive multitude with the hope of return, he accepts, even though the words could be adapted to Christ. Thus also Psalm 22, even though it is applied to Christ, and some things in it pertain to him by the propriety of the words confirmed in Matthew 27:35 and John 19:24, he says it must be understood of David. And no less those things concerning the bitter and sour drink in Psalm 69:12, notwithstanding the interpretation of the New Testament in John 19:28. Nor does he wish that to hold true only concerning expressions which he thinks pertained to the past or present time under the Old Testament. He observes the same thing also in the prophecies of future events, except that he wishes to say that these can be fulfilled twice: once when that event occurs which is directly predicted, and again, and more excellently, when that appears which that very thing, and consequently also the words denoting it, served to adumbrate. Let us add the examples which Grotius subjoins regarding this matter.

Thus in Isaiah 9:1, some light of Galilee seems to be announced which shone in the times of Hezekiah, but in such a way that that very light was a precursor to the light to be brought by Christ, and thus all the words of the Prophet are found to be most accommodated to the things of Christ. Thus, in the judgment of Grotius, what is said in Isaiah 42 can be referred to Zerubbabel, and what is read in Zechariah 9:9 to Judas Maccabeus, or to some other person, provided, however, that we admit, which is true, that Christ was also adumbrated by the deeds of these men, God even then wishing to accustom His people not to measure divine benefits by the pomp and noise of external things, and thus moving the minds of the Prophets so that their sayings would both respond to the first events and yet be more insignificantly performed through Christ. Grotius now concludes. All these things, therefore, and whatever others are of this kind, are to be examined in their own places; they are not properly used as the force of an argument, but for illustrating and confirming a matter already believed. Therefore, Paul, adapting the history of the old covenant to the times of the announced Gospel, adds, ἅτινα ἐστιν ἀλληγορούμενα. Which method of interpreting the scriptures, especially while the other, simpler, and less elaborate sense remains intact, cannot by any right be disapproved of by the Jews, as they count it among the types of explanations and highly value τὸ ἀλληγορούμενον, which the Hebraists call מדרש, and Philo, following Plato, calls ὑπόνοιαν. Indeed, the teachers of the Hebrews, both ancient and modern, assign two senses to the Prophets in many places, and David Kimchi himself explains Psalm 2 both of David and of the Messiah. What is more, even where some event occurs similar to an old one, they say מקיים המקרא or κατάληψιν, or 'this or that place of Scripture is confirmed.' But if the Apostles had felt that the entire divine dispensation concerning Christ had been openly revealed by the Prophets without any covering, they would by no means say that it is a mystery which, having been hidden from all ages, was finally revealed in that age (Colossians 1:26, 1 Corinthians 2:7, Ephesians 3:9). But whoever believes that JESUS is the CHRIST, which, as we have said, is abundantly proven even outside the faith of the prophecies by His miracles and resurrection, he indeed clearly perceives how divine providence most certainly directed both the things and the words of the ancient covenant to Christ as to the goal set before it. But those to whom their own obstinacy stands in the way of believing this, they have the eyes of their minds as if covered by a veil in the reading of that same covenant, nor is that veil taken away except for those who have already turned themselves to the Lord Jesus (2 Corinthians 3:14).

These are the words of Grotius, which tend toward the literal sense being snatched away to another in the prophecies of the Old Testament concerning Christ that deal with the interpretation of the New Testament and the συνάφειαν of the words, and that they are not accepted concerning Christ except in an allegorical and mystical sense. But we have noted that depravation of the most illustrious doctors of Scripture with just censure in our annotations on the Old Testament, and we have shown that only one sense, and that a literal one, obtains in those prophecies and others (which was also demonstrated in general concerning the whole of Scripture in the prolegomena of our commentary on Genesis), which oracles of the Old Testament are brought forward everywhere in the New Testament not only for the sake of illustration, but as the force of an argument, as the αὐτοψία itself testifies. Concerning the passage which he later brought forward, 2 Samuel 7:13, as if certain things are indicated concerning Solomon, so that they nevertheless look to Christ in a more eminent way, to whom those things which follow by no means pertain, we have spoken of that in our Annotations. Nor do those words of Paul in Galatians 4, ἅτινά ἐστιν ἀλληγορούμενα, contribute anything to the matter. For there the Apostle openly testifies that he is engaged in an allegorical exposition. But if faith is to be placed here in the teachers of the Jews, most of the prophecies will be significantly corrupted. Although Grotius surpasses those verpas in the craftiness and πανουργίᾳ of depraving, which we have observed more than once. But as for that mystery which the Apostles say was hidden from all ages, which was finally revealed in their own age (Colossians 1:26, 1 Corinthians 2:7, Ephesians 3:7), that is to be understood κατά τι, because it was not known IN THAT WAY, just as it is now revealed, as the Apostle explains himself, ὡς νῦν ἀπεκαλύφθη, as also by reason of the completion which was reserved for the fullness of times. For just as the event is the best interpreter of prophecies, so a far clearer and more perfect knowledge of all things is had under the New Testament, even of those things which were contained in the Old Testament in the predictions of the holy Prophets.

Now he applies this discovery of his in this way to the prophecy designated here. He twists it, of course, to the son of Isaiah, which the Evangelist interpreted as concerning the virgin's son Immanuel, our Jesus. But we have already discussed these Judaizing inventions in the annotations to Isaiah, therefore we do not wish to do what has already been done here. We only add what the force of truth here wrung from Grotius: 'That passage, "a virgin shall conceive," how much more excellent a sense does it have if it is referred to her who conceived in such a way that she remained a virgin after the conception, which happened to Mary alone?' Moreover, the name Immanuel, just as Jesus, may indeed have its restricted and limited signification in others, but in Christ it has another, infinitely more perfect, etc. But it is better to adduce the whole text: 'These things,' he says, 'I thought should be prefaced a little more fully at the very beginning of our commentary, because they seemed to me to be of no small moment, both for the explanation of some passages and for refuting those detractions in which our adversaries seem to place the greatest confidence. In order, therefore, that we may come to this passage which is in our hands, and in which Justin, Origen, and others have labored so much, it seems to me that nothing will be lost to the truth if we concede that one thing is indicated at first glance in Isaiah, but another is covered under a veil: and indeed in such a way that, as has just been shown to have happened in the Psalms, the very words of the Prophet, when related to that ultimate fulfillment, obtain a more proper and more excellent meaning.' But we must at the same time be warned that it often happens that not the individual words of the same περιτροπῆς (pericope) correspond to Christ, but certain principal ones: as, for example, in Nathan's prophecy those words: 'He shall build a house for my name, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever: I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son,' 2 Samuel VII, verse 13, are said of Solomon in such a way that they nevertheless look to Christ in a more eminent manner: but the things that follow do not pertain to Christ in any way. Let us now see what the words can be

The sense of the prophecies, offering itself at first glance, so that we may more correctly understand the other, then hidden ἐν μυστηρίῳ, but clearly revealed in the times of Christ. King Ahaz, terrified by the conspiracy of the Syrians and Israelites against him, and anxious not only about retaining his kingdom, but also fearing for his reputation and the other evils of a siege, conceived no hope of safety in his mind unless he gave himself into the faith and protection of the King of Assyria, the most powerful in those times. On the contrary, Isaiah urged him to abandon such plans and place his hope in God, affirming that not only would the attempts of the Kings of Syria and Israel be in vain, and the kingdom of Jerusalem remain with the descendants of David, but that the destruction of the kingdom of Israel was shortly imminent, and the power of Syria would remain within its own borders. When Ahaz did not put faith in these promises, Isaiah, by divine command, gives him the option of seeking some sign from God, by the testimony of which sign his faith might be convinced by words. But when Ahaz, with honest words but an impious mind—having, indeed, cast aside all trust in God—refused this very thing, Isaiah, after a serious rebuke of his impiety, says that God would nevertheless of His own accord shortly bring about that which was then least expected, and which would serve as a kind of pledge to seal the other promises. For both the forces of the Syrians and Israelites would depart from Judea with their attempt in vain, and in the meantime the Jews would suffer no shortage of necessary things, which was then most feared. The scope of that time is described by this interval, during which a girl, who was then still a virgin, would marry, conceive, give birth, and raise an infant, but within the years of infancy, or before the childish age reached the knowledge of good and evil: or, which amounts to the same thing, before that infant had learned to greet its parents. The abundance of food is expressed by this note, that it is said to that infant, until he grows up, neither honey nor butter will be lacking. For to the Hebrews, milk and honey συμβολικῶς designate an abundance not only of necessary things, but also of superfluous ones, as in Job XX, verse 17, and elsewhere. And just as by this reasoning it is shown to Ahaz how unjustly he acts in refusing to trust in God, so in the following words it is indicated how greatly the trust placed in the King of Assyria is going to deceive him. For from that source, evils more grievous than all the evils they feared were imminent for the Jews, and the exact opposite of the thing they so anxiously feared would happen: for Judea would not suffer from a shortage of food, but from cheapness due to the scarcity of inhabitants. The infant, however, to whom these things would apply, as far as can be gathered from what follows, does not seem to have been Hezekiah, as many of the Hebrews think, among whom is Trypho disputing against Justin, as he, if the times are correctly calculated, had already reached a certain age before the reign of Ahaz, as has been correctly noted by Rabbi Solomon, although what is said later in the ninth chapter seems to be able to be correctly referred to him; but rather this infant is the son of Isaiah himself, born of her who was still a virgin at the time the prophecy was issued, with Uriah and Zechariah called as witnesses, who married Isaiah, and who is herself indicated to have been a προφῆτις. And just as Isaiah had been ordered, when he approached the King, to take with him his son, upon whom the name Shear-jashub had been bestowed to stir up the hope of the Jews for every good thing, so two names were imposed upon this infant: first, indeed, Immanuel, by which it was shown that God was so present to Isaiah and his children that the things which had been foretold through them by words and signs would certainly come to pass; then, truly, Mahershalal-hash-baz, by which word it was signified that the arrival of the Assyrian to plunder Syria and Samaria was shortly imminent. And this is what Isaiah says, that he and his children were given by God as a sign and a document for the people: the certainty of his prophecy was not to be hindered by any human counsels, repeating the exclamation Immanuel as if sealing it. And this, indeed, seems to us to be the simple and first-obvious sense of the words of Isaiah, in which, however, it clearly appears to those who acknowledge Christ that there is a μυστήριον concerning Christ. For if all the liberations of the Jewish people were foreshadowings of that liberation which GOD was to effect through Christ, certainly that notable liberation from the hostile siege which the Prophet was promising also pertained to it. Gabriel himself taught Mary that the stability of the Davidic kingdom, also promised by the Prophet, had its true πλήρωμα in the eternal kingdom of Christ, Luke I, verse 32. But that 'a virgin shall conceive'—how much more excellent a sense does it have if it is referred to her who conceived in such a way that she remained a virgin after the conception, which happened to Mary alone? The name Immanuel, just as also Jesus, may indeed have its own meaning in others, restricted and limited, but in Christ it has another, perfect in infinite parts. For He is the one in whom all those glorious promises of God are ναὶ καὶ ἀμὴν, 1 Corinthians I, verse 20. He is the Word that became flesh and dwelt among us, John I, verse 14; finally, in Him dwells τὸ πλήρωμα τῆς θεότητος σωματικῶς, Colossians II, verse 9. For those who do not believe in Him, there awaits a φοβερὰ ἐκδοχὴ κρίσεως, Hebrews X, verse 27. The Jews object that our Lord was not called by that name Immanuel, to whom I reply with the words of Tertullian: 'The Hebrew sound which is Immanuel belongs to its own people: but the sense of it, which is God with us, is common by interpretation.' I ask, therefore, whether that word, God with us, which is Immanuel, is stirred up in Christ from the time that Christ shone forth: and I think you will not deny it at all. For those who believe in Christ from Judaism, from the time they believe in Him, when they wish to say Immanuel, they signify that God is with us. And thus it is established that He who was preached as Immanuel has already come, because that which Immanuel signifies has come, that is, God with us. Certainly, he who does not read the Prophets carelessly cannot be ignorant that it is said by them that he shall be called by some name, not that he should be called by that sound of voice, but that that word is appropriate for celebrating his deeds. The passages occur everywhere, Isaiah I, verse 26, IX, verse 6, LVI, verse 7, LX, verse 14, LXII, verse 4, Jeremiah III, verse 17, and XXIII, verse 6, Ezekiel XLVIII, verse 35, Zechariah VIII, verse 3. Therefore, where in Isaiah XIV, verse 20, there is יקרא, the Chaldean has יתקרי, it shall remain: and Luke, citing the said passage of Isaiah LVI, verse 7, translates יקרא as ἐστιν in XIX, verse 46. Such is below ξωροῦσι and κληθήσεται, and υἱοὶ θεοῦ κληθήσονται: where we shall also cite a similar expression of Philo. But if anyone attends rightly, there is the same force in the word Emmanuel and in the word Jesus. For to save is to show God propitious to us. But God is said by the Hebrews to be with us, as often as He looks upon us kindly and helps, Jos. I, verse 5, Jerem. I, verse 8. Acts XVIII, verse 10, although I would not deny that a certain more hidden meaning is present in that name. But also that other name, with which Isaiah is ordered to mark his infant as if with a more open (for that is what is meant by what is said therein in human style) [name], fits Christ most perfectly, who most swiftly conquered the devil and as victor divided the spoils for his own, as Chrysostom noted after Justin. See Luke XI, verse 22, and Ephesians IV, verse 8. And just as those names placed in Isaiah fit Christ most eminently, so the name προφῆτιδος which is found in the same oracle fits in a singular way Mary ever-virgin, who among women was εὐλογημένη καὶ κεχαριτωμένη Luke I, verse 28, and upon whom came the Holy Spirit Luke I, verse 35. Most truly, therefore, it was written by Matthew at the birth of Christ that the words of Isaiah were πληρωθῆναι, that is, fulfilled. For so I think that word is best rendered. But what Matthew says, that this was done so that what was predicted by Isaiah might be fulfilled, ought not to be understood as if God willed Christ to be born of a virgin for this purpose properly, that what Isaiah had said might come to pass, since rather because GOD willed that to be done, therefore He also willed it to be said through Isaiah. Either, therefore, Matthew means this, that these things happened because God wished to execute His decree, of which decree there was an indication in Isaiah, or the word ἵνα, as often, signifies not the end of the agent but only the consequence of the thing: as Psalm LI, 19, Rom. V, 20, Luke XIV, 10, and frequently elsewhere.

ὑπὸ τοῦ κυρίου] It is said everywhere that GOD said that which the Prophets said, first because God inserted the very meaning of the words into their minds: then, because He also moderated the words so that they would not stray from the meaning. For as it is not to be denied that even the words were dictated to them by God, as sometimes happened, so it does not seem to be perpetual. And hence it came about that according to the variety of times and speakers, the speech of the Prophets also differed.

‘Λέγοντος] To me it does not even seem doubtful that both here and in chapter II, verse 15, this genitive coheres with the word προφήτου. For the same words cohering in a similar way are found elsewhere in this writer, where no ambiguity can be feigned, as below II, 17, III, 3, IV, 14, VIII, 17, XIII, 35, XXI, 4, XXVII, 9.

We cannot prove this. For just as ALL Scripture is divinely inspired 2 Tim. III. ver. 16, so there is nothing in the sacred writings, whether you look at the words or the sense, which has not been implanted by God, and at his dictation consigned by his amanuenses to the very monuments of letters. Concerning which we have said more in Part I. Syst. Theol. pages 549, 561.

Latin:

Vers. 22.

Ἵνα πληρωθῇ] Quævis sit hujus vocis, multum refert recte intelligatur. Nam hunc similesque locos olim Celsus & Julianus, Judæi veteres olim, & nunc quoque soliti sunt Christianis objicere, tanquam mi- nus fideliter ab Apostolis, eorumque sectatoribus ad- ducta esset Prophetarum auctoritas. Sed notandum est, non pugnare Apostolos adversus Judæos his qua- si testimoniis, ut probent, Jesum esse promissum Mes- siam: pauca enim sunt oracula, quæ in hunc finem usurpant, contenti cæterum Christi miraculis, & re- surrectione. Nam (ut ille olim dicebat) aut hæc sa- tis erant, aut nihil erat satis. At quibus id jam per- suasum erat, JESUM esse illum Messiam, his simul ostensum voluerunt, quomodo tota divina διονομία priorum temporum hunc ipsum Christum, ejusque res gestas, ut pulcherrimam ac perfectissimam speciem perpetuo velut ante oculos habens cætera omnia ad illud instar effinxerit. Huc spectat præter alia multa quæ suis locis explicabuntur, quod Christus dicitur προεγνωσμένθ- πρὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου I. Petr. I. vers. 20. Et hæc sapientia divina quæ in Christo mittendo elu- cet προωρισμένη πρὸ τῶν αἰώνων I. Corinth. II. vers. 7. Sed maxime perspicuum illud ad Corinth. I, X. vers. 11. Hæc omnia illis (qui scilicet sub veteri fœdere fuerunt) ἐβενευαντ τυπικῶς: scripta autem sunt ad nostri admoni- tionem εἰς ὃς τὰ τέλη τῶν αἰώνων κατήντησεν. Sic alibi tempus Christi vocatur πλήρωμα temporum Galat. IV. v. 4. Ephes. I. v. 10. Non igitur instituta tantum legis umbra Christi fuêrunt, quod ostenditur Hebræor. VIII. vers. 5. cap. X. 1. & Coloss. II. vers. 17. sed & res gestæ, præsertim nobiliores. Quod recte mo- net Justinus adversus Tryphonem: ἔσθ' ὅτε γὰρ τὸ ἅγιον πνεῦμα καὶ ἐναργῶς πράττεσθαι τι, ὃ τύπθ- τῷ μέλ- λοντι- γίνεσθαι, ἦν ἐποίει. Et postea res gestas ait esse προκηρύγματα τῶν κατὰ χρισῦ ἁπάντων. Tertullianus de Resurrectione carnis: Talia interim divina- rum virium lineamenta, non minus parabolis operato DEO, quam locuto. Item: Scimus ut vocibus ita & rebus prophetarum. Chrysostomus ad Romanos: ὀ γὰρ ἔλεγον οἱ προφῆται μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἔγραφον ἅπερ ἔλεγον ἐκ ἔγραφον δὲ μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ διὰ πραγμάτων ἐτύπεν. Et in priorem ad Corinthios: τὰ μὲν διὰ ῥημάτων, τὰ δὲ διὰ τύπων ἐσιν ἀυτοῖς κείμενα. Et secundo sermone de jejunio ait aliam esse προφητείαν διὰ τύπω sive πραγμάτων, aliam διὰ λόγε, sive ῥημάτων. Illud au- tem quod Paulus dicit τυπικῶς, sumtum est à picto- ribus ac statuariis, aut etiam ab ædificiorum structo- ribus, qui egregium aliquod opus molientes primum crassius idipsum delineant, deinde paulatim id effi- ciunt quod animo conceperant. Nam prima illa li- neamenta τύποι dicuntur: unde illud Aristotelicum ὡς ἐν τύπῳ oppositum τῷ ἀκριβῶς. Illud autem ἀκρι- βὲς ab Apostolis vocatur τὸ πλήρωμα, more He- bræorum, qui מילאת vocant, cujusque rei τελειότητα ut Cantic. V. vers. 12. explicat Abenezra, quo loco LXX. habent ἐπὶ πληρώματι. Quod si res i- pse divino consilio Christum spectant, sane & signa rerum divinitus instituta eodem referenda sunt. Sunt autem signa duum generum ὁρατὰ καὶ ἀκουστὰ. Ec- quæ signantur sunt præterita, instantia, futura. O- mnium autem horum generum exempla nobis Chri- stus, Apostoli, aliique novi fœderis scriptores suppedi- tant. Contenti simus paucis, neque aliis quam in quibus hæc eadem vox τοῦ πληροῦσθαι reperitur. ὁρα- τὸν signum rei præteritæ, liberationis scilicet ex Æ- gyptiæ servitute, fuit agnus Paschalis. Liberatio au- tem illa typus liberationis nostræ à peccatis. Hac de causa Christus oftenditur in Paschali agno fuisse ad- umbratus 1. Corinth. V. vers. 7. Impietatem veterum Judæorum DEUS provide permisit summæ impietati quæ in Christum exercita est quasi præludere. Illa autem vetus impietas præsente signo nummorum haud magni pretii, quo se DEUS æstimatum querebatur, Dei ipsius jussu ac Zachariæ ministerio contestata est Zacharias XI. vers. 13. in eo igitur signo ostenditur de- lineatio fuisse sceleratæ pactionis inter Sacerdotes & Judam Iscariotem, Matth. XXVII. vers. 9. Ad ἀκουστὰ ut veniamus, ea nimirum, quæ voce sunt pronunciata at quasi pronunciata essent literis perscripta (nam literæ duntaxat secun- dariæ sunt notæ vocum, ut voces rerum, ) com- memorationem præteriti beneficii habet Oseæ locus XI. vers. 1. liberationis nimirum ex Ægypto, quæ, ut jam diximus, majoris libertatis per Christum partæ rudimentum quoddam fuit. Ipsa autem Historia Chri- sti nos admonet ita directam à Deo mentem Prophe- tæ loquentis, ut quod de populo Israëlítico ab ipso dicebatur, non minus recte aut etiam rectius in Chri- stum conveniret, Matth. II. vers. 15. Ejusdem argu- menti est carmen Asaphi Psalm. LXXVIII. vers. 1. cu- jus verba itidem sunt talia ut in Christum optime qua- drent, Matth. XIII. vers. 35. Sic Psalmum LXXII. scriptum honori Salomonis, ut titulus indicat, ad Messiam referunt Paraphrastes eo loco, & Salomon Jarchi, ut & Saadia Gaon ad Daniel. VII. vers. 14. Locutionum quæ ad instans tempus directe pertine- bant & tamen divino consilio ad Christum referre- bantur hæc habemus exempla. Ea quæ de stragibus suo tempore editis in Bethlehemica regione dixerat Jere- mias cap. XXXI. vers. 15. ita depingunt id quod ab Herode patratum est, ut vix aliis verbis possit idi- psum signatius exprimi. Quod legitur Esai. LXI. ipso initio, videtur quidem id Propheta dicere de munere sibi imposito consolandi captivam multitudinem spe reditus: at ea sunt verba quæ Christo aptata rem ipsam luculentissime designent, sicut & ipse reditus è Baby- lonia Christi beneficia figuravit. Cum vero veterum nullus majoribus malis à Deo exercitus, rursumque majore gloria adfectus fuerit, quam David plane ap- paret hoc à Deo actum, ut res Christi in illo propius quam in cæteris præsignarentur. Ideo & verba quibus conqueritur immerito se exosum, imo ab eo quem amicis accensuerat, proditum, ejusmodi sunt ut ad Christi res nihil possit accommodatius dici, quod apparet Psalm XXXV. vers. 19.
