Johan. XV. vers. 25. Psalm. XLI. vers. 10. Johan. XIII. vers. 15. Actorum I. vers. 17. Quid quod quædam ita de se elocutus est David, ut quæ ipsi conveniebant κατὰ λέξιν ἐσχημα- τισμένην, ea ad Christum servata verborum proprietate pertinerent? quale est illud de vestium divisione & sortibus jactis Psalm. XXII. vers. 19. Matth. XXVII. vers. 35. Joh. XIX. vers. 24. deque amaro atque aci- do potu Psalm. LXIX. vers. 22. Johan. XIX. vers. 28. Idem observare est in præsagiis futurorum, nisi quod hæc possumus dicere bis impleri, semel cum res illa e- venit quæ directe prædicitur, iterum vero, & quidem excellentius, cum id apparet cui adumbrando ipsa il- la res, ac proinde etiam verba eam notantia servie- bant.

Hæc ideo exequitur Grotius, ut Scri- pturæ vaticinia pleraque, quæ de Christo addu- cta sunt in Novo Testamento non de Christo, sed de aliis antiquorum temporum agere, nec aliter Christo applicari, quam quod instar ejus quoddam exhibuerint, obtineat. Quo artifi- cio illustria etiam oracula Messiam aperte lo- quentia dubia hoc loco porro reddit. Ita Psal- mum LXXII. honori Salomonis scriptum dicit, et- si ad Messiam referri à Paraphraste, & Salomone Jarchi, ut & Saadia Gaon ad Daniel VII. vers. 14. non nesciat. Quod legitur Esaiæ LXI. de Prophetæ munere consolandi captivam multitudi- nem spe reditus, accepit, etsi verba Christo apta- ri possint. Sic & Psalmum XXII. etsi Christo ap- plicetur, & ad eum firpata verborum proprie- tate nonnulla in ea pertineant Matth. XXVII. vers. 35. Johan. XIX. vers. 24. de Davide intelligendum esse ait. Nec minus illa de amaro atque acido potu Psalm. LXIX. vers. 12. haud obstante inter pre- tatione Novi Testamenti Johan. XIX. vers. 28. Neque solum de locutionibus, quæ ad præteri- tum vel instans tempus, sub Veteri Testamento pertinuisse censet, id obtinere vult. Idem ob- servat etiam in præsagiis futurorum, nisi quod hæc bis impleri dici posse, velit, semel cum res illa evenit, quæ directè prædicitur, iterum vero & excellentiùs, cum id apparet, cui adumbrando i- psa illa res, ac proinde etiam verba eam notantia serviebant. Addamus exempla quæ eam in rem subjicit Grotius.

Ita Esaiæ IX. vers. 1. videtur Galilææ lux aliqua annunciari, quæ Ezechiæ temporibus affulserit, sed ita ut ea ipsa lux prævia esset luci à Christo afferendæ, at- que adeo omnia Prophetæ verba reperiuntur ad res Chri- sti vel maxime accommodata. Ita possunt, judicio Grotii, quæ dicuntur Esaiæ XLII. ad Zorobabelem, & quæ leguntur Zachariæ IX. vers. 9. ad Judam Mac- cabæum, aut ad alium quempiam referri, dum tamen fateamur, quod verum est, horum quoque factis Chri- stum fuisse adumbratum, jam tum volente Deo popu- lum suum assuefacere, ne divina beneficia ex pompa strepituque rerum exteriorum metiretur, atque ita movente mentes Prophetarum, ut eorum dicta, & primis eventibus responderent, & per Christum tamen insignius præstarentur. Concludit jam Grotius. Hæc i- gitur omnia, & quæ alia sunt ejus generis, suis locis excutienda, non in vim argumenti proprie adhiben- tur; sed ad illustrandam atque confirmandam rem jam creditam. Ideo Paulus veteris fœderis historiam aptans ad annunciati Evangelii tempora addit, ἅτινα ἐστιν ἀλλη- γορούμενα. Quæ ratio scripturas interpretandi, præser- tim incolumi manente sensu altero simpliciori, mi- nusque elaborato, nullo jure à Judæis improbari pot- est, ut qui inter genera explicationum numerent, ma- ximique faciant τὸ ἀλληγορούμενον quod Hebraistæ מדרש, Philo autem Platonem secutus ὑπόνοιαν vocat. Imo He- bræorum Magistri & veteres & novi multis locis Pro- phetarum sensus duos assignant, atque ipse David Kim- chi Psalmum II, tum de Davide, tum de Messia expo- nit. Quod amplius est, etiam ubi factum aliquod veteri simile occurrit, dicunt מקיים המקרא sive κατάληψιν si- ve comprobatus est hic vel ille Scripturæ locus. Quod si sensissent Apostoli, omnem divinam de Christo dis- pensationem palam à Prophetis sine ullo involucro fuis- se proditam, neutiquam dicerent arcanum id esse, quod ab omni ævo absconditum, ista demum ætate patefie- ret Coloss. I. vers. 26. 1. Corinth. II. vers. 7. Ephes III. vers. 9. Quisquis vero credit JESUM esse CHRI- STUM, quod ut diximus, etiam extra vaticiniorum fidem miraculis ipsius ac resurrectione abunde pro- batur, is vero clare perspicit, quomodo divina pro- videntia & res & verba antiqui fœderis ad Christum, tan- quam ad scopum sibi præpositum, certissime direxerit. Quibus vero sua pertinacia obstat, quo minus id cre- dant, ii in lectione ejusdem fœderis, quasi velo obnu- ptos animi oculos habent, neque aufertur id velum, nisi his qui se jam ad Dominum Jesum converterint, 2. Corinth. III. vers. 14.

Hæc Grotius, quæ eo tendunt, ut in vati- ciniis Veteris Testamenti de Christo juxta in- terpretationem Novi Testamenti & verborum συνάφειαν agentibus, sensus literalis ad alium abripiatur, nec nisi allegorico, & mystico sensu de Christo ea accipiantur. Sed eam deprava- tionem luculentissimorum Scripturae doctorum in annotatis ad Vetus Testamentum justa censura notavimus, nec nisi unum tantum sensum, eumque literalem in vaticiniis istis aliisque obti- nere ostendimus (quod in genere quoque de u- niversa Scriptura prolegomenis commentarii Nostri in Genesin demonstratum) quae oracula Veteris Testamenti etiam non-illustrationis solum cau- sa, sed in vim argumenti passim in Novo Te- stamento adduci, αὐτοψία ipsa testatur. De loco, quem postea adduxit 2. Samuel. VII. vers. 13. ac si de Salomone quaedam indicantur, ut tamen Christum eminentiori quodam modo re- spiciant, ad quem neutiquam ea, quae sequuntur, pertineant, illic loci in Annotat. nostris dixi- mus. Neque quicquam ad rem faciunt illa Pauli Galat. IV. ἅτινά ἐστιν ἀλληγορούμενα. Nam ibi palam testatur Apostolus se versari in allegorica expositione. Judaeorum vero Magistris si hic fides adhibenda, pleraque vaticinia insi- gniter corrumpentur. Quanquam verpas il- los plurimum superet depravandi versutia & πανουργίᾳ Grotius, quod non semel obser- vavimus. Quod autem arcanum illud ab omni aevo absconditum Apostoli dicunt, quod sua de- mum aetate patefactum sit Coloss. I. vers. 26. 1. Corinth. II. vers. 7. Ephes. III. vers. 7. id κατά τι intelligendum, quod ITA notum haud fuerit, prout scilicet id nunc patefactum est, ut se explicat Apostolus, ὡς νῦν ἀπεκαλύφθη, ut & ratione complementi, quod reservatum e- rat plenitudini temporum. Nam uti even- tus optimus interpres vaticiniorum est, ita longe clarior ac perfectior notitia omnium ha- betur sub Novo Testamento, etiam eorum, quae in Veteri Testamento praedictionibus Sanctorum Prophetarum comprehensa fue- re.

Nunc hoc suum ἔυρημα ita applicat ad vatici- nium hic designatum. Nimirum ad Esaiae filium detor- quet, quod de virginis filio Immanuel, Jesu nostro, Ev- angelista interpretatus est. Quae vero commenta Ju- daizantia discussimus jam in annotatis ad Esaiam, ideo jam nolumus hic actum agere. Addimus solum, quae vis veritatis hic expressit Grotio: Illud autem virgo concipiet, quanto excellentiorem habet sensum, si refe- ratur ad eam, quae ita concepit, ut virgo post conceptum maneret, quod soli Mariae evenit? Nomen autem Imma- nuel, sicut & Jesu, habere quidem & in aliis suam pos- est significationem restrictam atque limitatam, at in Chri- sto aliam habet infinitis partibus perfectiorem &c. Sed praestat totum textum adducere: Haec, inquit, in ipso nostrae commentationis primordio uberius paulo praeloquenda censui, quia tum ad explicationem lo- corum aliquot, tum ad diluendas eas obtrectatio- nes quibus adversarii plurimum videntur confidere, non exigui momenti, mihi esse videbantur. Ut ergo veniamus ad hunc locum qui nobis in manu est, & in quo Justinus, Origenes aliique tantopere sudarunt, mi- hi nihil videtur periturum veritati, si concedamus aliud apud Esaiam prima fronte indicari, aliud autem sub involucro tegi: atque ita quidem ut quod in Psalmis evenisse modo ostensum est, verba ipsa Prophetae rela- ta ad ultimum illud complementum significatum ob- tineant magis proprium magisque excellentem. Sed illud simul admonendi sumus saepe fieri, ut ejusdem περιτροπῆς non verba singula in Christum congruant, sed praecipua quaedam: ut ecce in Nathanis vaticinio illa verba: Ipse aedificabit domum nomini meo, & firmabo solium regni ejus usque in seculum: Ego ero illi in patrem, & ipsi erit mihi in filium, 2. Samuel. VII. vers. 13. ita de Salomone dicuntur, ut ta- men Christum eminentiori quodam modo respiciant: quae autem sequuntur, ad Christum neutiquam per- tinent. Videamus nunc quis esse possit verboium

Propheticorum sensus primo intuitu se offerens, ut co- rectius alterum, tunc ἐν μυστηρίῳ absconditum, sed Christi temporibus plane revelatum intelligamus. Rex Achaz perterritus Syrorum & Israëlitarium in se con- spiratione, neque tantum de regno retinendo sollici- tus, sed & famam cæteraque obsidii mala metuens, nul- lam spem salutis animo concipiebat, nisi se in fidem & clientelam Regis Assyrii, illis temporibus poten- tissimi, daret. Contra Esaias hortabatur ipsum, ut omissis ejusmodi consiliis spem suam in Deo colloca- ret, adfirmans, non tantum irritos fore conatus Re- gum Syriæ atque Israëlis, regnumque Hierosolymo- tum mansurum penes Davidis posteros, sed brevi im- minere excidium Israëlis regno, Syri autem poten- tiam staturam intra suos limites. Quibus pollicitatio- nibus cum fidem Achaz non adhiberet, Esaias divi- no imperio dat illi optionem signi alicujus à Deo ex- petendi, cujus signi testimonio fides verbis fieret. Sed cum Achaz verbis honestis, animo autem impio, quippe abjecta omni in Deum fiducia, hoc ipsum re- cusaret, Esaias post seriam impietatis objurgationem, ait Deum tamen sponte sua brevi id effecturum, quod tum minime speraretur, quodque velut arrhabonis esset loco ad obsignandas promissiones cæteras. Nam & discessuras ex Judæa copias Syrorum & Israëlitarium conatu irrito, atque interea temporis Judæos nulla, quod tum maxime timebatur, laboraturos rerum ne- cessariarum penuria. Describitur autem temporis i- stius ambitus hoc spatio, quo puella, quæ tum virgo ad- huc erat, nuberet, conciperet, pareret & infantem educaret, sed intra infantiæ annos, sive priusquam puerilis ætas ad boni malique notitiam perveniret: aut quod eodem recidit, priusquam is infans parentes sa- lutare didicisset. Copia autem victus hac nota expri- mitur, quod dicatur ei infanti, donec adolescat, nec mel nec butyrum defore. Nam Hebræis lac & mel συμβολικῶς rerum non necessariarum tantum, sed & superfluentium copiam designant, ut Jobi XX. vers. 17. & alibi. Sicut autem hac ratione Achazo ostendi- tur, quam inique faciat, quod Deo recuset confi- dere, ita sequentibus verbis indicatur, quantopere ipsum sit deceptura fiducia in Rege Assyrio posita. Nam inde Judæis mala omnibus quæ metuerent malis gra- viora imminere, planeque contrarium ei rei, quam tam anxie metuerent, eventurum: non enim victus in- opia, sed vilitate laboraturam Judæam præ habitan- tium infrequentia. Infans autem in quem ista conve- nirent, quantum ex sequentibus colligere est, non videtur fuisse Ezechias, ut existimant Hebræorum multi, inter quos & Tryphon adversus Justinum dispu- tans, ut qui, si tempora recte supputentur, jam ante Achazi regnum ad ætatem aliquam pervenerat, quemadmodum à Rabbino Salomone recte est anno- tatum, quamquam quæ capite nono postea dicun- tur ad eum recte videantur posse referri, sed potius est is infans ipsius Esaiæ filius, natus ex ea quæ virgo adhuc editi vaticinii tempore, testibus Uria ac Zacha- ria adhibitis, Esaiz nupsit, quæ & ipsa προφῆτις fuis- se indicatur. Sicut autem cum Regem accederet Esaias jussus erat, secum ducere filium suum cui Sche- riasub boni omnis nomen ad spem Judæorum excitan- dam, inditum fuerat, ita huic infanti duo nomina sunt imposita, primum quidem Emmanuel, quo ostenderetur Deus ita adesse Esaiæ ejusque liberis, ut quæ verbis signisque per ipsos essent prænotata, eadem certo evenirent: deinde vero Maherschalal- hasbas, qua voce significabatur brevi imminere Assy- rii adventum ad spoliandam Syriam ac Samariam. Atque hoc est quod ait Esaias, se filiosque suos a Deo datos in signum & documentum populi: vatici- nii sui certitudinem nullis humanis consiliis impedien- dam, repetita exclamatione Emmanuel velut obsi- gnans. Atque hic quidem nobis videtur simplex pri- moque obvius esse sensum verborum Esaiæ, in qui- bus tamen inesse μυστήριον de Christo Christum agno- scentibus liquido apparet. Nam si omnes libera- tiones populi Judaici præfagia fuêre ejus liberationis quam DEUS per Christum erat effecturus, sane & illa insignis liberatio ab obsidione hostili quam Propheta promittebat, eo pertinuit. Stabilitatem regni Davi- dici, item à Propheta promissam, verum πλήρωμα in æterno Christi regno habuisse, Gabriel ipse Mariam docuit Luc. I. vers. 32. Illud autem virgo concipiet quanto excellentiorem habet sensum, si referatur ad eam, quæ ita concepit, ut virgo post conceptum mane- ret, quod soli Mariæ evenit? Nomen autem Imma- nuel, sicut & Jesu, habere quidem & in aliis suam potest significationem, restrictam atque limitatam, at in Christo aliam habet infinitis partibus perfectiorem. Nam is est in quo illa præclara Dei promissa omnia sunt ναὶ καὶ ἀμὴν, 1. Corinth. I. vers. 20. Is est verbum quod caro factum inter nos habitavit, Johan. I. vers. 14. in ipso denique habitat τὸ πλήρωμα τῆς θεότη- τος σωματικῶς, Coloff. II. vers. 9. In hunc qui non credunt, eos manet φοβερὰ ἐκδοχὴ κρίσεως, Hebr. X. vers. 27. Objiciunt Judæi, Dominum nostrum isto Emmanuelis nomine non appellatum, quibus Ter- tulliani verbis respondeo: Sonus Hebraicus quod est Emmanuel suæ gentis est: sensus autem ejus quod est Deus nobiscum, ex interpretatione communis est. Qua- ro ergo, an ista vox, nobiscum Deus, quod est Emma- nuel, exinde quo Christus illuxit, agitetur in Christo: & puto ex toto non negabis. Nam qui ex Judai- smo credunt Christo, ex quo in eum credunt, Emma- nuel cum volunt dicere, nobiscum Deum esse significant. Atque ita constat jam venisse illum qui prædicabatur Em- manuel, quia quod significat Emmanuel, venit, id est, nobiscum Deus. Certe qui Prophetas non supine legit, nescire non potest vocatum iri aliquo nomi- ne dici ab illis eum qui non eo vocis sono sit appel- landus, sed cujus rebus celebrandis vox ista conve- niat. Loca passim occurrunt, Esaiz I. vers. 26. IX. vers. 6. LVI. vers. 7. LX. vers. 14. LXII. vers. 4. Jerem. III. vers. 17. & XXIII. vers. 6. Ezech. XLVIII. vers. 35. Zachar. VIII. vers. 3. Ideo ubi Esaiz XIV. vers. 20. est יקרא Chaldæus habet יתקרי ma- nebit: & Lucas citans dictum locum Esaiz LVI. vers. 7. יקרא vertit ἐστιν XIX. vers. 46. Tale est infra ξωροῦσι & κληθήσεται, & υἱοὶ θεοῦ κληθήσονται: ubi & si- milem Philonis locutionem citabimus. Quod si quis recte attendat, eadem vis est in voce Emmanuel & in voce Jesu. Nam servare est Deum nobis præstare pro- pitium. Deus autem nobiscum esse Hebræis dicitur, quoties benignus non respicit, atque adjuvat, Jos. I. vers. 5. Jerem. I. vers. 8. Actor. XVIII. vers. 10, quam- quam & latentiorem quandam significationem isti nomini inesse non negaverim. Sed & alterum illud nomen, quo tanquam apertiore (id enim valet quod inibi di- citur stylo humano) infantem suum insignire Esaias ju- betur, perfectissime Christo congruit, qui celerrime diabolum devicit & victor suis spolia divisit, ut post Ju- stinum annotavit Chrysostomus. Vide Lucam XI, vers. 22. & Ephes. IV. vers. 8. Sicut autem Christo nomina ista apud Esaiam posita eminentissime conve- niunt, ita προφῆτιδος nomen quod in eodem oracu- lo reperitur singulariter convenit Mariæ semper virgi- ni, quæ inter fœminas fuit εὐλογημένη καὶ κεχαριτωμέ- νη Luc. I. vers. 28. & super quam venit Spiritus San- ctus Luc. I. vers. 35. Verissime ergo à Matthæo scri- ptum est in nativitate Christi verba Esaiæ πληρωθῆναι, id est, consummata esse. Ita enim puto id verbum o- ptime reddi. Quod autem dicit Matthæus factum hoc ut consummaretur quod prædictum erat per Esaiam, non ita intelligi debet quasi Deus Christum ex virgine na- sci voluerit, hoc proprie consilio, ut quod Esaias dixerat, fieret, cum potius quia id DEVS volue- rit fieri, ideo & voluerit per Esaiam dici. Aut ergo hoc vult Matthæus, eo hæc evenisse, quod Deus decretum suum vellet exsequi, cujus decreti in- dicium esset apud Esajam, aut vox ἵνα, ut sæpe, non finem agentis sed solam rei consequentiam significat: ut Psal. LI. 19. Rom. V. 20. Luc. XIV. 10. & alibi cre- bro.

ὑπὸ τοῦ κυρίου] Passim dicitur DEUS id dixisse, quod dixerunt Prophetæ, primum quia ipsam verbo- rum sententiam Deus menti illorum inseruit: deinde, quia & verba ita est moderatus ne à sententia aberrarent. Nam ut etiam verba à Deo illis dictata sint, ficuti in- terdum evenisse non est negandum, ita non videtur per- petuum. Atque hinc factum est ut pro temporum at- que loquentium varietate etiam sermo Prophetarum differret.

‘Λέγοντος] Mihi ne dubium quidem videtur quin & hic & cap. II. vers. 15. cohæreat iste genitivus cum voce προφήτου. Nam eædem voces simili modo cohæ- rentes alibi apud hunc Scriptorem reperiuntur, ubi nulla fingi potest ἀμφιβολία, ut infra II. 17. III. 3. IV. 14. VIII. 17. XIII. 35. XXI. 4. XXVII. 9.

Id probare non possumus. Nam ut O- MNIS Scriptura divinitus inspirata est 2. Tim. III. vers.16. ita nihil in sacris literis est, sive verba, sive sensum spectes, quod non à Deo sit inditum, eoque dictante ab amanuensibus ipsius literarum monumentis consignatum. De quo plura diximus Part. I. Syst. Theol. pag. 549. 561.

## 1:23
Ver. 23.

Παρθένος] The Jews deny in vain that the word עלמה, if the propriety of the word is considered, signifies one untouched by a man. For the origin is the best index of propriety, from עלם which is to hide: naturally because it was the custom among the Hebrews, no less than among the Greeks, to guard unmarried girls diligently ἐν τῷ παρθενῶνι. To this point refers that of Hesiod,

as she remains inside the house beside her dear mother, not yet knowing the works of golden Aphrodite.

And among Euripides, an old man addresses Antigone thus:

O child, go into the house, and remain within the rooms in your maiden chambers.

And Antigone herself, to her mother saying 'listen', replies 'whither, leaving the maiden chambers?' Which Seneca also imitated in the Agamemnon, saying, 'with what custom do you, a virgin, seek public gatherings?' Papinius concerning that same Antigone:

- - - not yet seen to be granted to the peoples, Antigone.

Usage, in which the norm of speaking resides, does not depart from this origin, as appears in Genesis XXIV. ver. 43, Exodus II. ver. 8, Deuteronomy XXII. ver. 23. In the Song of Solomon, however, chap. VI. ver. 7, the meaning of this word is even more open: for there the עלמות are clearly separated from wives and concubines. In the same Song I. ver. 3, עלמות is explained by Rabbi Solomon as בתולות. And the Seventy, both in Genesis chap. XXIV. ver. 43, and in this very place of Isaiah, translated it not as νεᾶνιν, as the later ones did, serving their own hypothesis, but as παρθένον: Aquila as ἀπόκρυφον. And Jerome notes that this use of the word remained until his own age among the Poeni, that is, the descendants of the Phoenicians, whose language, Syriac, is related to Hebrew. Nor is what the same Jerome brings forward concerning the Latin word 'alma' to be despised. For it can be demonstrated by so many arguments that the ancient words of Latium, especially those used in sacred matters, came from the East, that there is no room for the suspicion of a fortuitous συνερπτώσεως. 'Alma', however, does not come to the Latins from 'alendo' (nourishing), as some think, but it has the same value as 'sancta' (holy). That which is read in Proverbs XXX. ver. 19 does not prove the contrary. For it is common to all languages that words are transferred ἀπὸ τοῦ ὄντος πρὸς τὸ δοκεῖν. Indeed, even in Greek, παρθένος signifies both properly and customarily one untouched by a man. Nevertheless, among Aristophanes, as the Scholiast notes, it signifies 'her who is still considered a virgin', just as Musaeus also said

and going at dawn in a saffron robe, escaping her parents, a maiden in her garment, by night she goes.

And Homer had called Astyoche a παρθένον in the same sense. To omit now the bolder κατάχρησις of Virgil, who, as Servius notes, called Pasiphae, a mother of three children, a virgin. The writer of the Alexandrian history, to whom the name of the third book of Maccabees has been given, likewise the writer of the second book of Maccabees in chapter III. ver. 9, in order to avoid all ambiguity of the Greek word, said κατακλείτους παρθένους, a word used by Greek writers in this sense also, exactly expressing the Hebrew עלמות: because עלם, as we have said, is κατακλείειν. Philo in the book against Flaccus said in the same sense θαλαμευομένας παρθένους. Conversely, women of lost modesty are called by the Chaldeans those who go out into public. It appears, therefore, that עלמה is the same as what he placed here, בתולה.

ἕξει] This is more correct than ἔχει, which Jerome seems to read. For the Greek interpreter rightly translated that which is in the Hebrew here as a verb of uncertain future time, because the things which follow in the Prophet, being connected to this verb, are of future time.

καλέσουσι] I would not hesitate to follow the authority of the best codices and the Syriac interpreter, especially since Origen and Chrysostom have already read it this way. And in my judgment, the Greek interpreter of Matthew expressed it correctly in this manner.

The Hebrew וקרא, because the second person is placed here entirely indefinitely, as when it is said in Homer, φαίης ζάκοτον τινά έμμεναι. Thus Donatus on that passage of Terence, 'Quid facias?' for 'quid faciat,' that is, anyone. Servius on the fourth book of the Aeneid: 'Migrantes cernas.' It is an elegant figure if you refer a thing from the third person to the second: that is, if one should see. Afterwards: 'Mugire videbis.' One will see, as in 'Migrantes cernas.' In the sixth, 'nec dum poteris committere ferro.' One will be able. For he transferred the meaning of the third person to the second and speaks generally. In the eighth, 'credas innare revulsas Cycladas.' One would believe. In the eleventh, 'velis,' for 'si quis velis.' Thus Luke chapter 5, verse 34, μὴ δύνασθε ποιῆσαι νηστεύειν. Moreover, this very thing is expressed no less customarily by the third person of the plural number. For 'any men' is understood, as below in chapter 7, verse 16, Acts 13, verse 39, and in other places where we shall warn again. καλέσουσι, which indeed the codices and Eusebius follow, is from the Greek of the Seventy, who followed the Hebraism here. The Chaldean preferred to put 'he shall call,' that is, any man, with the sense resulting in the same thing. For in so many ways are impersonals accustomed to be expressed. But as for those who specifically wish this to be said of Mary, and that it is thereby indicated that Christ was ἀπάτορα, because otherwise the right of imposing the name would have belonged to the Father, what will they do with those words of the Angel to Joseph? καλέσεις τὸ ὄνομα αὐτῆ Ἰησῦν.

ὅ ἐστι μεθερμηνευόμενον] The excellent interpreter added similar interpretations of Hebrew names in some places for the use of those who did not know Hebrew, as can be seen in chapter 27, verses 33 and 46. Since the Syriac also has these, it is convinced from this also that Matthew's book was translated from the Greek, not from the Hebrew. The same appears regarding the Arabic.

Latin:

Vers. 23.

Παρθένος] Frustra negant Judæi vocem עלמה, si proprietas vocis spectetur, viro intactam significare. Nam origo optima proprietatis index est à עלם quod est abscondere: nimirum quia Hebræis, non mi- nus quam Græcis, in more positum fuit, innuptas puel- las diligenter asservare ἐν τῷ παρθενῶνι. Huc illud spe- ctat Hesiodi,

ἅτε δόμων ἔντοσθε φίλῃ παρὰ μητέρι μίμνει οὔπω ἔργ᾽ εἰδυῖα πολυχρύσου ἀφροδίτης.

Et apud Euripidem senex Antigonen ita alloquitur:

ὦ τέκνον ἔσβα δῶμα, κᾐ κατὰ στέγας ἐν παρθενῶσι μίμνε σοῖς.

Et ipsa Antigone matri dicenti ἤκου, respondet ποῖ, παρ- θενῶνας ἐκλιπῶ̃? Quod & Seneca imitatus in Agamemno- ne dixit, quo more caetus publicos virgo petis? Papinius de eadem illa Antigone:

- - - nondum concessa videri Antigone populis.

Ab hac origine non recedit usus quem penes loquendi norma est, ut apparet Genes. XXIV. vers. 43. Exod. II. vers. 8. Deuteronom. XXII. vers. 23. In Cantico autem Salomonis cap. VI. vers. 7. apertior; etiam est vo- cis hujus significatio: nam ab uxoribus & concubinis diferte ibi separantur עלמות. In eodem Cantico I. vers. 3. עלמות à Rabbino Salomone exponitur בתולות Et septuaginta tum Genes. cap. XXIV. vers. 43. tum hoc ipso Esaiæ loco non νεᾶνιν ut posteriores τῇ ὑποθέσει δουλεύοντες, sed παρθένον verterunt: Aquila ἀπό- κρυφον. Et notat Hieronymus mansisse hunc vocis usum ad suam ætatem apud Pœnos, traduces videlicet Phœni- cum, quorum lingua Syriaca cognata Hebrææ. Neque spernendum quod idem Hieronymus adfert de voce Lati- na alma. Nam priscas Latii voces, præsertim in sacris u- sitatas, ab Oriente venisse tam multis argumentis de- monstrari potest, ut suspicioni fortuitæ συνερπτώσεως non sit locus. Alma autem Latinis non ab alendo venit, ut quidam existimant, sed idem valet quod sancta. Non evincit contrarium id quod legitur Proverb. XXX. vers. 19. Commune enim est omnibus linguis, ut voces ἀπὸ τοῦ ὄντος πρὸς τὸ δοκεῖν transferantur. Quippe & Græce παρθένος & proprie & usitate viro intactam si- gnificat. Attamen apud Aristophanem ut notat Scho- liastes significat τὴν ἔτι παρθένον νομιζομένην, quomodo & Musæus dixit

ἠῶ δ᾽ ἐλευσίκπεπλον ἰὼς λήθουσα τοκῆας παρθένιος ἰματίῃ, νυχίη γονεῖ.

Et Homerus Astyochen παρθένον eodem sensu dixerat. Ut nunc omittam audaciorem Virgilii κατάχρησιν, qui ut Servius notat Pasiphaen trium liberum matrem virginem dixit. Scriptor historiæ Alexandrinæ, cui nomen fa- ctum est libri tertii Maccabæorum, item scriptor libri se- cundi Maccabæorum capite III. vers. 9. ut omnem vo- cis Græcæ ambiguitatem evitarent, dixerunt κατακλεί- τους παρθένους voce Græcis scriptoribus in hunc quoque sensum usitata, exacte exprimens Hebræum עלמות: quia עלם ut diximus est κατακλείειν Philo in libro adversus Flaccum eodem sensu dixit θαλαμευομένας παρ- θένους. Contra exuti pudoris feminæ Chaldæis vocan- tur in publicum prodeuntes. Apparet igitur idem esse עלמה & quod hic posuit בתולה.

ἕξει] ita rectius quam ἔχει quod legere videtur Hieronymus. Merito enim Græcus interpres id quod in Hebræo hic est temporis incerti futuri temporis verbo est interpretatus, quia & quæ sequuntur apud Pro- phetam huic verbo cohærentia, futuri sunt tempo- ris.

καλέσουσι] Non dubitem sequi optimorum codi- cum & Syri interpretis fidem, præsertim cum ita jam omnes legerint Origenes & Chrysostomus. Et recte me judice hoc modo expressit Græcus Matthæi interpres

Hebræum וקרא quia secunda persona omnino hic ponitur indefinite, ut cum dicitur apud Homerum φαίης ζάκοτον τινά έμμεναι. Sic Donatus ad illud Terentii, Quid facias? pro quid faciat, unusquisque scilicet. Ser- vius ad IV. Æneidos: Migrantes cernas Honesta figura si rem tertia persona in secundam referas: hoc est, si quis cernat. Postea: Mugire videbis. Videbit quis, ut Mi- grantes cernas. In VI. nec dum poteris committere ferro. Poterit quis. Tertis enim personæ significationem ad secun- dam transtulit & generaliter loquitur. In VIII credas in- nare revulsas Cycladas. Credas quis. In XI. velis, pro si quis velis. Ita Luc. cap. V. vers. 34 μὴ δύνασθε ποι- ῆσαι νηστεύειν. Hoc ipsum autem non minus usitate ex- primitur tertia persona numeri pluralis. Subauditur enim homines quilibet, ut infra VII. vers. 16. Actorum XIII. vers. 39. & aliis locis ubi iterum monebimus. καλέσουσι, quod quidem codices & Eusebius sequuntur, est à Græco LXX. senum, qui hic Hebraisinum secuti sunt. Chaldæus maluit ponere vocabit, nimirum quili- bet homo, sensu eodem recidente. Tot enim modis impersonalia exprimi solent. Qui vero speciatim ad Mariam hoc dici volunt, atque eo indicari, Christum fuisse ἀπάτορα, quia Patri alioqui jus imponendi nomi- nis fuerit competiturum, quid facient illis Angeli verbis ad Josephum ? καλέσεις τὸ ὄνομα αὐτῆ Ἰησῦν.

ὅ ἐστι μεθερμηνευόμενον] Similes interpretationes Hebræorum nominum in usum eorum qui Hebraice ne- sciebant addidit aliquot in locis optimus interpres, ut videre est cap. XXVII. vers. 33. & 46. Quas cum habeat & Syrus, convincitur hinc quoque Matthæi librum de Græco, non de Hebræo transtulisse. Idem de Arabe apparet.

## 1:25
Vers. 25.

ἐγίνωσκεν] A most ancient Hebrew idiom, as appears in Genesis 4, verse 1, and elsewhere: from there it was subsequently derived into other languages. And this is said not only of men, but also of women, as in Luke 1:34. Ovid in the epistle of Hypsipyle: 'Turpiter illa virum cognovit adultera virgo.'

ἕως ὗ] That this negation affirms nothing about the time before birth, but about the time after, has been demonstrated by many examples by others, to which I shall add the place which is below in chapter 12, verse 20. This manner of speaking is so known and customary to the Jews that the most learned among them attempt to interpret the prophecy of Jacob in Genesis 49, verse 10, in this way. Moreover, regarding the passage in Genesis 28, verse 15, no Jew ever doubted that it was to be understood in this way: nor can that which is in Psalm 123, verse 2, be explained otherwise. Then that which is in 1 Samuel 15, verse 25, cannot be explained otherwise. One may add Job 27, verse 5, Isaiah 22, verse 14, 2 Samuel 6, verse 23. Here, however, the very mind of the writer, who is doing this to show that it was most certain to Joseph that this birth was not conceived from himself, bids us to stop within that time which we have mentioned: for which matter the mention of a later time could have no weight.

Πρωτότοκον] Although there is no meaning of 'first' in the Hebrew words, yet this birth is rightly expressed by this Greek name, ὁ διανοίγων τὴν μήτραν, as Luke speaks after the Seventy in chapter 2, verse 23. For the word 'first' requires that no one precedes, not that someone follows, as has been noted by the grammarians on that passage of Virgil: 'Hic mihi responsum primus dedit ille petenti.' And on that of the Aeneid 1: '--- Trojæ qui primus ab oris.' Servius in the Fulda book: 'first, after whom there is no one.' And similarly in civil law, he is also called 'next' who is alone. And the matter itself speaks against Helvidius that this word is to be taken here in this way. For it looks to the dignity and the chief rights which were attributed in ancient times, even before the law of Moses, to sons, as much to those who were only children as to those who were firstborn. Nor do we speak otherwise today, as the laws of all nations concerning the succession of fiefs testify. There were, however, three πρωτοτόκια, as the Hebrews note in Genesis 49, verse 2: the principate, the priesthood, and the preeminence in the inheritance: all of which are indicated to belong to Christ by his birth. The Apocalypse often treats of the kingdom. The writer to the Hebrews treats of the kingdom and the priesthood: concerning the preeminence in the inheritance, see Romans 8, verse 17, Colossians 1, verse 15, Hebrews 1, verses 2 and 9.

ἐκάλεσε] Although the construction may seem ambiguous, you would nevertheless refer this more correctly to Joseph than to Mary: for that which the Angel had said above in verse 21 is fulfilled here. And the Syriac, which uses a verb of the masculine gender, understood it in this way. The Talmud in Pesachim and R. Nathan in Shemoth Rabba attribute the name of the firstborn to the Messiah.

Latin:

Vers. 25.

ἐγίνωσκεν] Antiquissima Hebræorum locutio ut ap- paret Genes. IV. vers. 1. & alibi: inde porro in cæteras linguas derivata. Neque tantum de viris hoc dicitur, sed & de feminis, ut Luc. I. 34. Ovidius in Hypsipylæ epistola: Turpiter illa virum cognovit adultera virgo.

ἕως ὗ] Negationem hanc de tempore ante partum nihil affirmare, sed de tempore posteriore, multis exem- plis ab aliis est demonstratum, quibus addam locum qui infra est XII. vers. 20. Judæis adeo notum atque usitatum est hoc loquendi genus ut doctissimi inter ipsos vaticinium Jacobi Genes. XLIX. vers. 10. ita conentur interpretari. De loco autem Genes. XXVIII. vers. 15. nemo unquam Judæorum dubitavit quin hoc modo es- set intelligendus: neque magis de illo qui est Psal. CXXIII. vers. 2. Tum qui est I. Samuel. XV. vers. 25. a- liter explicari nequit. Addi potest Job. XXVII. vers. 5. Esaias XXII. vers. 14. 2. Samuel. VI. vers. 23. Hic ve- ro intra id tempus quod diximus, consistere nos jubet ipsa mens Scriptoris, hoc agentis, ut ostendat compertis- simum Josepho fuisse, partum hunc non esse ex se conce- ptum: ad quam rem posterioris temporis mentio nullum habere poterat momentum.

Πρωτότοκον] Quamquam in Hebræis vocibus nulla est primi significatio, recte tamen hoc Græco nomine exprimutur partus ὁ διανοίγων τὴν μήτραν ut post LXX. Lucas loquitur II. vers. 23. Nam primi vox requirit ut nemo antecedat, non ut sequatur aliquis, quemadmodum à Grammaticis annotatum est ad illud Virgilii: Hic mihi responsum primus dedit ille petenti. Et ad illud Æneidos I. --- Trojæ qui primus ab oris. Servius in libro Fuldenfi: primus post quem nullus. Et si- militer in jure civili proximus dicitur etiam qui solus est. Et res ipsa contra Helvidium loquitur ita hic sumendam hanc vocem. Respicitur enim ad dignitatem & jura præ- cipua quæ antiquitus etiam ante Mosis legem tribuebantur filiis maritus tam unicis quam natu maximis. Nec ho- die aliter loquimur, ut testantur omnium gentium le- ges de feudorum successione. Erant autem πρωτοτόκια tria ut Hebræi notant Genes. XLIX. vers. 2. principatus, sacerdotium & prælatio in hæreditate: quæ omnia in Chri- stum competere nativitate ipsius indicatum est. De re- gno agit sæpe Apocalypsis. De regno & sacerdotio scri- ptor ad Hebræos: de prælatione in hæreditate vide Rom. VIII. vers. 17. Coloss. I. vers. 15. Hebr. I. vers. 2. & 9.

ἐκάλεσε] Quanquam ambigua videri potest con- structio, rectius tamen hoc ad Josephum quam ad Ma- riam referas: impletur enim hic quod Angelus supra dixe- rat vers. 21. Atque ita intellexit Syrus, qui verbum mas sculini generis usurpat. Nomen primogeniti Messiæ tri- buunt & Thalmud in Pefachim & R. Nathan in Sche- moth rabba.

## 2:1 Argument
CHAPTER II. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

The Magi arriving from the East inquire in Jerusalem about the recently born King of the Jews; a council is gathered, which teaches from Micah (ch. V. 2.) that the Messiah would come forth from Bethlehem. Herod sends the Magi to Bethlehem, ordering that when they have found the infant they should report it to him. The Magi are led by a star, find the infant, and adore him, offering gold, frankincense, and myrrh, but are warned by God to return home by another way: Joseph, however, is warned to flee with the infant into Egypt, whose death Herod seeks, which was done so that the prophecy might be fulfilled (Hos. XI. 1.). Herod, having sent out soldiers, kills all the male infants; thus the prophecy of Jeremiah (ch. XXXI. 15.) was fulfilled. But when he was dead, Joseph was recalled from Egypt, and when his son Archelaus was reigning, he withdrew into Nazareth, so that what was said by the Prophets might be fulfilled: He shall be called a Nazarene.

There are two parts: I. The history of the Magi, to verse 12. II. The history of the flight of Joseph into Egypt, and of his recall from Egypt to verse 23.

PART I. The history of the Magi.

Ver. 1.

Ἀπὸ ἀνατολῶν] The very ancient opinion of the Christians, and among them of Justin Martyr and Tertullian, which Epiphanius also follows, that these wise men came from Arabia, pleases me greatly. For the Jews commonly called it by this name, as being situated to their east, as can be seen in Genesis X. verse 30, XXV. verses 6, 18, Job I. verse 3, Judges VI. verse 3, 1 Kings IV. verse 30, Isaiah XI. verse 14, Jeremiah XLIX. verse 28. Tacitus in his description of Judea: The lands and borders which incline toward the East are bounded by Arabia. The Chaldeans were considered rather by the name of Northerners, Jeremiah XXV. verse 9. And the gifts which they brought are Arabian, not Persian, as we shall say below. Nor were only the wise men of the Persians called Magi by the Hebrews who used the Greek language, but others also, as can be seen in the Greek history of Daniel. But Arabia also had its wise men from antiquity, studious both of all nature and especially of the stars, as the dialogues of Job and his friends teach us. Nor is the fame otherwise, that Solomon is said to have excelled the wise men, such as those of Egypt and the East, that is, of Arabia, 1 Kings IV. verse 30. And it is written by Porphyry that the Arabs went to Pythagoras for the sake of wisdom, whose words on this matter exist in Cyril, tenth against Julian. Even the name ἐλύμας itself, which is translated by Luke as μάγος in Acts XIII. verse 8, comes from Arabia: and Pliny mentions the Magi of Arabia, and Ptolemy places the gulf of the Magi in Arabia. But what is said below about the two-year period does not prevent the Magi from having come from Arabia. For one could have come into Judea from Mesopotamia much more quickly. For Josephus says that it was a five-month journey to Jerusalem for those who lived above the Euphrates. Nor does it follow, if Herod, taking every precaution lest the boy escape, extended his cruelty more widely, no less in regard to age than to place, that therefore the star also appeared so long before. Although the star could have appeared some time before the journey was undertaken, so that by its very duration it might turn the minds of the wise men toward itself. It is a received opinion among almost all peoples that stars of such a kind (of which sort are those that are called comets) portend new empires. That line of Lucan is well known: And the Comet changing kingdoms for the lands. Vulcanius the augur, as Servius teaches us on the ninth eclogue, said that by a comet the end of an old age and the beginning of a new one is signified. And Chaeremon the Stoic had noted that sometimes a change for the better is also foretold by comets. The same Servius on that line of Georgics I, dire comets, because there are also good ones. And about that comet in Aeneid X, this one is said to be gentle. But it is credible that this star appeared in that part of the sky which, by the consensus of astrologers, pertained to Judea, as it is the custom for the regions of the earth to be assigned to certain spaces of the sky by the professors of that art: which I say, not because I wish to patronize superstitious divinations, but because I think that GOD disposes things in such a way that He sometimes draws those things which, whether rightly or wrongly, are held in high regard among men, into a testimony of the truth. That these Magi devoted effort to arts not entirely to be approved is the opinion of Origen, Ambrose, Basil, and Chrysostom: and the customs of those nations and those times make that highly probable. For if among the very people of God the Pharisees, the showmen of a certain singular holiness, sought signs of fate from the stars, what is it reasonable to believe was done by those who had even enslaved themselves to the worship of the stars? The Peripatetics and those who follow them hold it for certain that comets exist below the Moon, by which argument many assert that no new star has ever arisen in the starry region outside of this one, which Matthew treats: but whether both these assertions are sufficiently explored is doubted by others. Certainly, Origen posits that this star was a comet as if for certain in his book against Celsus VI. But whatever kind of star it was, that movement by which it is later narrated that Christ's lodging was shown was not only contrary to nature, but also without precedent: whence the Greeks think it was an angel rather than a star. Something similar is narrated in the martyrology to have happened in the times of Diocletian, when the Christians, seeking the bodies of the three martyrs, Tharacus, Probus, and Andronicus, suddenly saw as it were a splendid star sent from heaven resting over each of the bodies of the saints. Balaam's prophecy, by which many think the Magi were stirred—while I do not deny that it was drawn by certain Hebrews to the affairs of the Messiah (for Aquila also used this testimony to prove that Bar-Kochba was that promised Messiah)—is too obscure to have been able to impress upon any foreigner the comprehension of a certain time when read or heard: especially since it can conveniently, nay, as far as the primary sense is concerned, even ought to be referred to David, the conqueror of the Moabites. But also the oracles in Daniel which properly pertain to designating the times of Christ were not handed down to the Chaldeans, as some suspect, but to the Jews, to whom were entrusted the oracles of God, Rom. III. verse 2. Therefore, it is more relevant to the matter that others warn that the opinion was received among the Jews that the advent of the Messiah was imminent around those times, and that this was common among neighboring peoples. I say, however, regarding those times, that although the definite time was unknown, the conjecture did not stray far from the true time. For the Sibylline oracles, not those new ones which Christians cite, but the old ones preserved at Rome by the Quindecimviri, seem to me to have been nothing other than Greek verses of the Jews. From these, moreover, was drawn that which Cicero recites, that it was necessary, if they wished to be saved, that they acknowledge as King him who was King, and likewise Virgil's fourth Idyll containing the promise of a certain new kingdom, and indeed in almost the same words which the Hebrew Prophets use. From this also it came about that some interpreted Herod the Great to be the Messiah: soon Theudas, Judas the Gaulonite, and other impostors of that kind, that the minds of the Jews, while Jesus was on earth, were certainly aroused by the expectation of the Messiah, and that this rumor had even spread to the Samaritans, the history of the Gospel teaches us everywhere. Hence the Baptist is asked whether he himself is the Messiah: and the people, having seen the miracles of Jesus, immediately begin to doubt whether he is not that very one who was expected, and that fame endured and indeed spread through the whole East until the times of Vespasian, as Josephus, Tacitus, and Suetonius show: indeed even until the age of Hadrian: for that provided the occasion for Bar Kokhba to make his attempt. Moreover, leaders of note had aroused the Jews to the expectation of the Messiah around those times: the numbers of the years of Daniel: and the destruction of the Syrian and Egyptian kingdoms. This very fame, therefore, easily spread from the vicinity of the Jews through Arabia and gave authority to the unusual star.

This is the opinion of Justin Martyr and Tertullian, and also of Epiphanius, Hilary, and others among the more recent, Cornelius à Lapide, and Tirinus was approved by the first. Yet Clement, and Cyril of Alexandria, Basil the Great, Chrysostom likewise, and Theodoret, as also Leo the Great and Juvencus, preferred to summon them from the Persians. These are followed not only by distinguished men among the Papists and Reformed, Genebrard, Maldonatus, Petavius, Calvin, Bucer, Beza, Aretius, Beroaldus, Scaliger, Pareus, Casaubon, but also among our own by B. Chemnitius, B. Gerhard, and others. For no one doubts that the name of Magi was familiar among the Persians. Strabo, Cicero, Plato place the Magi in Persia. That this name was common among the Arabs will never be proven. Spanheim does not hesitate to declare that both the name of the Magi and the thing designated by the name were unheard of among the Arabs, so that to derive the Magi from Arabia is like summoning Druids from the Insubrians. Nor can it be doubted that Persia is east of Judea, and since Stapleton denies this, he is deservedly to be exploded by geographers. It is likely that the prophecies concerning the Messiah were known to the Persians from Daniel, among whom that custom of adoring and offering gifts was also accepted, and just as the Persians had gold from their own region, so they could easily have had frankincense and myrrh either from their own land or from neighboring Arabia. But whether ἰλύμας came from Arabia, Ludovicus de Dieu may be consulted on that, who, although he had previously thought so, judged otherwise on Acts 13.

Latin:

CAPUT II. ARGUMENTUM ET PAR- TITIO.

Magi advenientes ex Oriente Hierosolymam quærunt de recens nato Rege Iudæorum, congregatur concilium, quod e Michæa (cap. V. 2.) docet Messiam Bethlehemo proditurum. Herodes Magos Bethlehe- mum mittit, jubens, ut invento infante sibi id renuncient. Magi stella deducuntur, inveniunt infantem, eumque adorant, aurum thus & myrrham offerentes, sed jubentur a Deo alia via domum regredi: Iosephus vero monetur ut fugiat cum in- fante in Ægyptum, cujus mortem quærit Herodes, quod factum ut vaticinium im- pleretur (Hos. XI. 1.) Herodes satellitibus emissis infantes omnes masculos occidit; sic impleta Prophetia Ieremiæ (cap. XXXI. 15.) eo autem defuncto revocatus est Io- sephus ex Ægypto, & quum regnaret fi- lius Archelaus, in Nazareth secessit, ut impleretur, quod a Prophetis dictum: Nazaræus vocabitur.

Partes duæ sunt: I. Historia Magorum, ad vers. 12. II. Historia fugæ Iosephi in Ægyptum, & re- vocationis ex Ægypto ad vers. 23.

PARS I. Historia Magorum.

Vers. 1.

Ἀπὸ ἀνατολῶν] Perplacet mihi vetustissima Christia- norum, atque inter eos Justini Martyris, ac Tertulliani sententia, quam & Epiphanius sequitur ab Arabia venis- se hos sapientes. Eam enim Judæi, ut sibi ab ortu adsi- tam hoc nomine vulgo appellabant, ut videre est Genes. X. vers. 30. XXV. vers. 6. 18. Job. I. vers. 3. Jud. VI. vers. 3. I. Reg. IV. vers. 30. Esai XI. vers. 14. Ierem. XLIX. vers. 28. Tacitus in descriptione Judææ. Terræ finesque quæ ad Orientem vergunt, Arabia terminantur. Chaldæi Se- ptentrionalium potius nomine censebantur, Jerem. XXV. vers. 9. Et munera, quæ attulerunt, Arabica sunt, non Persica: ut infra dicemus. Neque vero soli Persarum sa- pientes Hebræis Græca lingua utentibus Magi vocabantur, sed & alii, ut videre est in Græca Danielis historia. Ha- buit autem & Arabia antiquitus sapientes suos, tum na- turæ omnis, tum astrorum imprimis studiosos, quod nos docent Jobi, ejusque amicorum Colloquia. Nec aliter famam, quod Salomon dicitur antecelluisse sapientibus ut Ægyptia & Orientis, id est, Arabiæ 1. Regum IV. vers. 30. Et Pythagoram sapientiæ causa Arabes adiisse scriptum Porphyrio, cujus in eam rem verba apud Cy- rillum exstant, decimo contra Julianum Quin ipsum nomen ἐλύμας quod à Luca μάγ☉ vertitur Actor. XIII. vers. 8. ab Arabia venit: & Plinius Magorum Arabiæ meminit & Ptolomæus in Arabia ponit Magorum si- num. Quod autem de biennio infra dicitur, non ob- stat quo minus ab Arabia Magi venerint. Quippe ex Mesopotamia quoque in Judæam veniri multo celerius potuit. Nam eos qui supra Euphratem habitabant, Hierosolyma Josephus venisse ait mensium quinque iti- nere. Neque vero sequitur, si Herodes omni modo cavens ne puer elaberetur, latius sævitiam extendit, non mi- nus in ætate quam loci ratione, ideo stellam quoque tanto ante apparuisse. Quanquam & stella aliquo tempore ante iter susceptum apparere potuit, ut ipsa sui diuturnitate sapientum animos in se adverteret. Stel- las certe ejusmodi (cujus sunt generis qui cometæ appellan- tur) nova imperia portendere apud omnes ferme gentes recepta sententia est. Notum est Lucani illud: Et terris mutantem regna Cometen. Vulcanius aruspex, ut nos Servius docet ad nonam eclo- c gam, dicebat cometa fignificari exitum veteris & ingref- sum novi sæculi. Et Chæremon Stoicus notaverat in- terdum per Cometas etiam in melius mutationem præ- notari. Idem ille Servius ad illud Georg. I. diri come- tæ, quia funt & boni. Et de illo Comete Æn. X. Hic blandus esse dicitur. Credibile autem est apparuisse hanc stellam in ea cæli parte quæ consensu Astrologorum ad Judæam pertinuerit, ut solent ab ejus artis professori- bus terrarum regiones certis cæli spatiis adscribi : quæ dico, non quod superstitiosis ariolationibus patrocinari cupiam, sed quod arbitrer DEUM ita res disponere, ut ea quæ sive jure sive injuria magni apud homines siunt, interdum trahat in veri testimonium. Artibus vero non usquequaque probandis operam dedisse hos Magos, O- rigeni, Ambrosio, Basilio & Chrysostomo placet: atque id perquam probabile faciunt istarum gentium, atque illorum temporum mores. Nam si in ipso Dei populo Pharisæi, singularis cujusdam sanctimoniæ ostentatores, fatorum indicia à sideribus petiverunt, quid par est credi factum ab iis qui etiam astrorum cultui se mancipave- rant? Peripatetici & qui eos sequuntur pro certo ha- bent, cometas infra Lunam existere, quo argumento multi asserunt nunquam novum sidus extra hoc, de quo agit Matthæus, in siderea regione exortum: sed utrum satis explorata sit utraque hæc assertio ab aliis dubi- tatur. Certe cometam fuisse hoc sidus Origenes qua- si pro certo ponit libro adversus Celsum VI. Cæte- rum qualecunque fuit sidus, motus ille quo postea narratur Christi hospitium fuisse monstratum, non mo- do præter naturam fuit, sed etiam citra exemplum: unde Græci Angelum potius quam stellam fuisse existi- mant. Simile aliquid in martyrologio narratur accidisse Diocletiani temporibus, cum Christiani quæ- rentes trium martyrum, Tharaci, Probi & Andronici corpora, viderunt subito velut stellam splendidam de cœlo missam super singula sanctorum corpora residen- tem. Balaami vaticinium, quo multi magos pu- tant excitatos, ut non nego ab Hebræis quibusdam tractum ad res Messiæ (nam & Aquila hoc testimonio usus est ut Barcho hebam probaret esse promissum il- lum Messiam) ita obscurius est, quam ut lectum au- ditumve certi temporis comprehensionem potuerit cui- quam externo insigere: præsertim cum commode possit, imo, quod sensum primum attinet, etiam debeat ad Davidem Moabitarum victorem referri. Sed & quæ apud Danielem oracula ad designanda Christi tempora proprie pertinent, non Chaldæis sunt tradi- ta, ut quidam suspicantur, sed Judæis οἷς ἐπιϛεύθησαν τὰ λόγια τῦ Θεῦ, Rom. III. vers. 2. Quare magis ad rem pertinet quod alii monent, receptam fuisse apud Judæos opinionem, circa illa tempora instare Messiæ adventum, idque vicinas apud gentes vulga- tum. Dico autem circa illa tempora, quia cum de- finitum tempus ignoraretur, non longe tamen à vero tempore aberravit conjectura. Nam Sybillina oracu- la, non nova illa quæ citant Christiani, sed vetera Romæ à XV. viris asservata nihil aliud mihi videntur fuisse, quam versus Græci Judæorum. Ex his autem depromptum illud, quod Cicero recitat, opus esse ut si salvi esse vellent, eum qui Rex esset Regem agno- scerent, itemque Virgilii Idyllium quartum novi cu- jusdam regni pollicitationem continens, & quidem serme verbis iisdem, quæ Prophetæ Hebræi usurpant. Hinc quoque factum ut Herodem Magnum quidam esse Messiam interpretarentur: mox Theudam, Judam Gauloniten aliosque id genus impostores, Judæorum certe animos, in terris agente Jesu, arrectos fuisse exspectatione Messiæ, eumque rumorem ad Samaritas etiam manasse, passim nos docet Evangelii histo- ria. Hinc Baptista interrogatur an ipse sit Messias: & populus conspectis Jesu miraculis statim dubitare inci- pit an non sit ille ipse qui exspectabatur, duravitque ea fama atque adeo Orientem totum pervagata est ad Ve- spasiani tempora, quod ostendunt Josephus, Taci- tus & Svetonius: imo ad Adriani usque ævum: nam id Barchochebæ audendi occasionem præbuit. Dux autem præcipuæ notæ in exspectationem Messiæ circa ea tempora Judæos erexerant: numeri annorum Da- nielis : & destructio regni Syriaci & Ægyptiaci. Hæc igitur ipsa fama ex Judæorum vicinia facile Ara- biam pervagata inusitato sideri auctoritatem adstru- xit.

Hæc Justini Martyris, & Tertulliani sen- tentia Epiphanio etiam Hilario, & aliis è re- centioribus, Cornelio à Lapide, ac Tirino im- primis probata fuit. E Persis tamen illos accer- sere maluere Clemens, & Cyrillus Alexandrinus, Basilius M. Chrysostomus item & Theodoretius, ut & Leo M. & Juveneus. Quos sequuntur non solum e Pontificiis & Reformatis viri præcipui, Genebrardus, Maldonatus, Petavius, Calvinus, Bucerus, Beza, Aretius, Beroaldus, Scaliger, Pareus, Casaubonus, sed e nostris etiam B. Che- mnitius, B. Gerhardus, & alii. Nam nomen Magorum apud Persas familiare fuisse, nemo am- bigit. Strabo, Cicero, Plato, Magos in Per- siam collocant. Apud Arabes nomen id pervul- gatum fuisse, nunquam docebitur. Spanhemius non dubitat pronunciare Magorum tum nomen, eum rem nomine designatam apud Arabes inauditum esse, ut Magos ex Arabia ducere, sit Druidas ex in- subribus arcessere. Neque dubitari potest, Per- siam Judææ orientalem esse, & cum Stapletonus id negat, explodendus merito a Geogra- phis. Persis autem nota fuisse vaticinia de Messia e Daniele verisimile est, penes quos et- iam receptus ille mos erat adorandi & munera offerendi, & uti habebant Persæ aurum ex sua re- gione, ita & thus, & myrrham vel ex sua terra vel e vicina Arabia, facile habere poterant. U- trum vero ἰλύμας ab Arabia venit, de eo con- suli poterit Ludovicus de Dieu, qui etsi antea ita censuerit, ad Actor. XIII. aliter judicavit.

## 2:2
Verse 2.

ἀυτοῦ τὸν ἀστέρα] So said as in Maro: Behold, the star of Dionean Caesar has risen: that is, a star dedicated to his honor.

Ἐν τῇ ἀνατολῇ] The land from which they had come, not a region of the sky, is denoted by this word, as also above and below in clause 9.

Προσκυνῆσαι ἀυτῷ] The Hellenists sometimes compose this word with the dative case as here and in the LXX, Genesis 37, verse 10, sometimes with the accusative as Greek writers do. It signifies, however, the gesture of a prostrate body for the sake of showing honor. The Greeks, accustomed to liberty, did not greet any human being in this way, as Herodotus and others teach us. Both sacred and profane history teach us that the peoples of the East showed this honor to kings. Josephus, concerning David venerating Saul: προσκυνῆσαι ἀυτὸν πεσὼν ἐπὶ πρόσωπον ὡς ἦθος. Livy, concerning the Carthaginian envoys: In the manner of those who adore (having received the rite, I believe, from that region from which they originated) they prostrated themselves. It signifies that this was the custom of the Phoenicians, whose neighbors the Hebrews were, as also Euripides, among whom the Phoenician women speak thus: Γονυπετεῖς ἕως προσκυνῶ σ’ ἄναξ, τὸν οἴκοθεν νόμον σέβων. The Latin writer of the life of Conon: for it is necessary, if you come into sight, to venerate you as king, which they call προσκυνεῖν. The Magi, therefore, who were persuaded that a kingdom was destined for this boy, venerate him in the manner of their own people. That προσκύνησις is described below in clause 11 by the verb πίπτειν, as also further down in 4, verse 9; 18, verse 26; Mark 5, verse 22; 9, verse 20. Luke said πίπτειν ἐπὶ πρόσωπον in 5, verse 12; Herodotus and other Greek writers said προσκύνησιν; Aeschylus said προσπίπτειν to the Persians: where there is a clear notation of that custom.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

ἀυτοῦ τὸν ἀστέρα] Ita dictum ut apud Maronem: Ecce Dionæi processit Cæsaris astrum: hoc est, astrum ejus honori dicatum.

Ἐν τῇ ἀνατολῇ] Terræ unde venerant, non cœli regio hac voce denotatur, ut & supra & infra comma- te 9.

Προσκυνῆσαι ἀυτῷ] Hellenistæ vocem hanc modo cum tertio casu componunt ut hic & LXX. Genes. XXXVII. vers. 10. modo cum quarto ut Græci scri- ptores. Significat autem procumbentis corporis gestum honoris habendi gratia. Græci affueti libertati hoc mo- do neminem hominum salutabant, ut nos docet Hero- dotus aliique. Orientis populos regibus eum honorem habuisse & sacra & profana historia nos docet. Jose- phus de Davide Saulem venerante προσκυνῆσαι ἀυτὸν πεσὼν ἐπὶ πρόσωπον ὡς ἦθος. Livius de Legatis Car- thaginensium: More adorantium (accepto credo ritu ex ea regione ex qua oriundi erant) procubuerunt. Signifi- cat Phœnicum, quorum vicini Hebræi, hunc morem fuisse ut & Euripides, apud quem sic Phœnissæ lo- quuntur: Γονυπετεῖς ἕως προσκυνῶ σ’ ἄναξ, τὸν οἴκο- θεν νόμον σέβων. Scriptor Latinus vitæ Cononis: neces- se est enim si in conspectum veneris, venerari te regem, quod προσκυνεῖν illi vocant. Magi igitur, quibus per- suasum erat huic puero regnum destinari, more suæ gentis eum venerantur. Describitur ista προσκύνησις in- fra commate 11. verbo πίπτειν, ut & inferius IV. vers. 9. XVIII. vers. 26. Marc. V. vers. 22. IX. vers. 20. πίπτειν ἐπὶ πρόσωπον dixit Lucas V. vers. 12. προσκύ- νησιν Herodotus atque alii scriptores Græci, προσπί- τνειν Æschylus Persis: ubi luculenta ejus moris nota- tio.

## 2:3
Verse 3.

Πᾶσα ἱεροσόλυμα] Both the accent and the ending teach that it is not a feminine singular word, but a plural of the neuter gender, as also above in clause 1 and elsewhere frequently, both in these books and among Greek and Latin writers. For as to the fact that Hierosolymam is read once in Cicero and once in Tacitus, I believe it to be an error created by the addition of one letter, since those very writers always call that city Hierosolyma elsewhere. Nor is it without precedent that πᾶσα is composed with it. For it refers to the thing, not to the form of the word. Thus above in chapter 1, clause 2, ἀυτῶν refers to τῶν λαῶν. Such is Præneste subipsa.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

Πᾶσα ἱεροσόλυμα] Et accentus & terminatio docent non vocem femininam singularem, sed pluralem esse neutrius generis, ut & supra commate 1. & alibi pas- sim tum in his libris, tum apud Græcos Latinosque scriptores. Nam quod apud Ciceronem semel, semel- que apud Tacitum Hierosolymam legitur, mendum es- se arbitror creatum unius literæ adjectione, cum illi ipsi scriptores alibi semper Hierosolyma eam urbem vocent. Neque tamen sine exemplo est quod ei componitur il- lud πᾶσα. Ad rem enim respicitur, non ad vocis for- nam. Ita supra cap. I. commate 2. ἀυτῶν refertur ad τῶν λαῶν. Tale est Præneste subipsa.

## 2:4
Verse 4.

Τοὺς ἀρχιερεῖς καὶ γραμματεῖς τοῦ λαοῦ] As to what some think, that there were two supreme senates of the Jews, one which presided over civil matters, the other over ecclesiastical, a more suitable place will be found elsewhere to discuss what we think about that. But in this place, since no public business was celebrated, but only the oracles of the Prophets were sought out by those who were believed to excel others in their knowledge, it does not seem to me that any certain and legitimate assembly should be understood; but a gathering of learned men convened out of order by the king. And therefore there is no mention here of the elders, who are usually named when there is a matter of judgment or public counsel. But since different duties are denoted by the name of scribes among the Hebrews, I think the office of assessor is understood here, by which those who are students of the law (as Paulus the Jurisconsult says) perform their parts. For just as Roman governors had legal experts as companions, whose counsel they used in pronouncing law, so also the Hebrew magistrates and likewise the priests, as the Jerusalem Talmud in Yoma and Maimonides in the title concerning the Day of Atonement teach, had their own assessors, chosen mostly from the Levitical tribe, which, being supported from the public treasury and not distracted by domestic business, abounded in leisure for the study of letters. And just as the law was the one teacher of all divine and human law, so among the Hebrews the interpretation of both laws rested with the same men. To this pertains that saying of Sirach: σοφία γραμματέως ἐν εὐκαιρίᾳ σχολῆς, Ecclesiasticus 38, verse 25. The Hebrews interpret סופר as רבנים. Our writers sometimes call them lawyers; Josephus calls them interpreters of the laws. Although it was indeed enjoined primarily upon the priests that they should devote themselves to the study of the law, yet since the honor, conferred by hereditary right, sometimes devolved upon less suitable talents, it happened that the priests themselves also stood in need of the counsel of others. Seraiah is certainly mentioned as a priestly scribe in the times of David, 2 Samuel VIII, verse 17. And the necessity of that office was undoubtedly increased by the sloth of the priests, and by the trafficking in honors which became established in the following centuries. By the name of Ἀρχιερέων, however, I think it should be understood here not only those who held or had held the high priesthood, and their deputies, but also the other princes of the XXIV priestly families, ἄρχοντας τῶν πατριῶν τῶν ἱερέων as the LXX speak in Paralipomenon XXIV. 6, which is made clear by the added word πάντων, which seems to me to designate a greater number than would be appropriate for those few. Nor does Josephus use this word otherwise in Antiquities XX, VII, where he narrates a sedition that arose between the Ἀρχιερέας and the ἱερέας, because the οἱ ἀρχιερεῖς were drawing all the tithes to themselves and allowing the other priests to be consumed by a lack of necessary things. Another passage of the same Josephus makes the matter very clear in the Jewish War, book IV, where he narrates that the Ἀρχιερέας were chosen by lot by the seditious from each family, whereas that honor was accustomed to be conferred by order of birth. But also 2 Chronicles XXXVI, 14, the Princes of the families are called שרי הכהנים.

As for Ἀρχιερεῖς, we agree with Grotius: but as for γραμματεῖς τὲ λαῶ, we judge that the ecclesiastical Doctors of the people, who interpreted τὰ ἱερὰ γράμματα, and were called νομοδιδάσκαλοι or νομικοὶ, experts in the law, from the divine law when they explained it, are denoted, and not indeed students of law, assessors of the Ἀρχιερέων chosen from the Levitical tribe. For that the scribes of the people are not political ones such as are commemorated in the Old Testament, Ex. V. 6, Jos. XXIII. 2, 1 Par. XXIII. 4, Esdr. IV. 8, but ecclesiastical ones, whose duty it was to unfold, search, and expound the sacred letters, is taught by a comparison of this passage with Matt. VII. 29, ch. XIII. 2, ch. XXIII. 2, 1 Cor. I. 20: such as are called νομικοὶ in Luke VII. 30. However, we do not deny that after the Babylonian captivity, when they were distracted by political government and neglected the office of teaching, scribes or experts in the law were joined to the princes of the Priests, just as today Professors of Theology perform that duty of lecturing on and interpreting Scripture, which was once imposed upon Canons. See B. Gerhard, Harm. Evang. part I, §. CLVI, p. 1276. B. Chemnitius, Harm. ch. X, distinguishes γραμματεῖς from νομικοῖς: as is clear from their distinction in Luke XI. 45. He says that the former were substituted after the gift of Prophecy had ceased, in the place of the Prophets, occupied in the reading and interpretation of Scripture, just as the profession of the Pharisees was concerned with traditions. That there was a peculiar college of these, whose duty it was to respond concerning doubtful cases from the law, i.e., concerning the law, just as they are also described as νομικοὶ by B. Polyc. Lyfer. Harm. c. CV. Ligthfoot in Hor. Ebr. in Matth. at this place makes the Scribes of the people Elders or assessors of the Sanhedrin, and distinguishes them from the Scribes of the clergy in the same Sanhedrin, because the latter were born of priestly or Levitical stock, but the former from other tribes. But they are not called scribes of the people by reason of birth and lineage, but by reason of their office, because they were in charge of instructing the people.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

Τοὺς ἀρχιερεῖς καὶ γραμματεῖς τοῦ λαοῦ] Quod qui- dam arbitrantur, duos fuisse senatus summos Judæorum, alterum qui civilibus, alterum qui Ecclesiasticis negotiis præeffet, de eo quid nobis videatur alibi aptior erit agen- di locus. Hoc vero loco, tum nihil celebratum sit negotii publici, sed dumtaxat exquifita Prophetarum oracula ab iis qui eorum scientia præstare cæteris crede- bantur, non videtur mihi certus aliquis atque legitimus consessus debere intelligi; sed doctorum hominum conventus extra ordinem à rege convocatus. Atque ideo nec πρεσβυτέρων hic sit mentio, qui plerumque no- minantur, ubi aut judicii aut consilii publici res est. γραμματέων autem nomine cum Hebræis diversa munia denotentur, hic officium assessoris puto intelligi, quo juris studiosi (ut inquit Paulus Jurisconsultus) parti- bus suis funguntur. Nam sicut Romani præsides ha- bebant comites jurisperitos, quorum consiliis in jure dicendo utebantur, ita & Hebræis magistratibus item- que sacerdotibus ut docet Thalmud Hierosolymitanum in Joma & Maimonides titulo de die propitiationis, sui aderant assessores delecti plerumque ex Levitica tri- bu quæ è publico sustentata, neque domesticis distrac- cta negotiis, ad literarum studia otio adundabat. Sic- ut autem lex erat una præceptrix divini omnis humani- que juris, ita apud Hebræos penes eosdem erat juris utriusque interpretatio. Ad hoc pertinet illud Siracidæ σοφία γραμματέως ἐν εὐκαιρίᾳ σχολῆς Eccles. XXXVIII. vers. 25. Sit Hebræi סופר interpretatur רבנים Nostri scriptores eos interdum νομικοὺς vocant: Jo- sephus ἐξηγητὰς νόμων. Quanquam vero sacerdoti- bus præcipue injunctum erat, ut legis studio vacarent, tamen cum honos successorio jure delatus interdum ad ingenia minus idonea delaberetur, factum est ut ipsi et- iam sacerdotes alieni consilii egerent. Seraja certe sacerdotalis scriba Davidis temporibus memoratur 2. Sa- muel. VIII. vers. 17. Auctaque procul dubio ejus mu- neris necessitas ignavia sacerdotum, & quæ sequentibus seculis inolevit, honorum nundinatione. Ἀρχιερέων autem nomine, ut hic intelligi putem non eos tantum qui maximo pontificatu aut fungebantur, aut functi erant, eorunque vicarios, sed alios quoque prin- cipes XXIV. sacerdotalium familiarum, ἄρχοντας τῶν πατριῶν τῶν ἱερέων ut loquuntur LXX. Paral. XXIV. 6. facit addita vox πάντων, quæ majorem numerum desi- gnare mihi videtur, quam ut paucis illis conveniat. Neque aliter utitur hac voce Josephus originum XX, VII. ubi seditionem narrat ortam inter ἀρχιερέας & ἱερέας, in- de quod οἱ ἀρχιερεῖς omnes decimas ad se pertraherent ac cæteros sacerdotes rerum necessariarum inopia consumi paterentur. Rem apertissimam facit alter ejusdem Jose- phi locus Belli Judaici lib. IV. ubi à seditiosis narrat forte lectos ἀρχιερέας ex quaque familia, cum is honos nafcen- di ordine deferri soleret. Sed & 2. Par. XXXVI, 14. fa- miliarum Principes vocantur שרי הכהנים.

Quod ἀρχιερεῖς adstipulamur Grotio: quod vero ad γραμματεῖς τὲ λαῶ, Doctores populi Ecclesiasticos, qui τὰ ἱερὰ γράμματα interpre- tabantur, & νομοδιδάσκαλοι vel νομικοὶ legisperiti, à lege divina vocabantur, quum explicabant, non ve- ro juris studiosos, assessores τ̃ ἀρχιερέων è Leviti- ca tribu delectos, denotari censemus. Scribas enim populi non politicos quales in Veteri Test. commemorantur, Ex. V. 6. Jos. XXIII. 2. 1. Par. XXIII. 4. Esdr. IV. 8. sed Ecclesiasticos, quorum fuerit sacras literas evolvere, scrutari atque expo- nere, designari, collatio hujus loci cum Matth. VII. 29. cap. XIII. 2. cap. XXIII. 2. 1. Cor. I. 20. do- cet: quales νομικοὶ dicti Luc. VII. 30. Conjunctos tamen fuisse principibus Sacerdotum post capti- vitatem Babylonicam, quam illi politica guberna- tione districti officium docendi negligerent, scri- bas vel legisperitos, non abnuimus, sicut hodie Professores Theologiæ funguntur illo munere Scri- pturam prælegendi, & interpretandi, quod olim Canonicis fuit impositum. Vid. B. Gerhard. Harm. Evang. part: I. §. CLVI. p. 1276. B. Che- mnitius Harm. cap. X. γραμματεῖς distinguit à νομικοῖς: uti Luc. XI. 45. apertum est eorum discri- men. Illos dicit suffectos fuisse postquam donum Prophetiæ desiisset, in locum Prophetarum, in lectione & interpretatione scripturæ occupa- tos, uti Pharisaeorum professio circa traditiones versata fuerit. Horum vero fuisse peculiare colle- gium, cui incubuerit de dubiis causis ex lege q. de jure respondere quomodo etiam νομικοὶ à B.Polyc. Lyfer. describuntur Harm. c.CV.Ligthfoot. in Hor. Ebr. in Matth. ad hunc locum Scribas populi Senio- res vel assessores Synedrii facit, eosque à Scribis cle- ri in eodem Synedrio discriminat, quod hi è Sa- cerdotali aut Levitica stirpe, isti vero ex aliis tribubus orti sint. At non dicuntur scribae populi ratione ortus & prosapiae, sed ratione officii, quod populo informando praefuerint.

## 2:6
Vers. 6. γῆ Ἰούδα] The Greek interpreter rightly expressed what was in the Hebrew as Bethlehem Ephrata, so that he might indicate the same place more certainly by a name better known in his own times. Demetrius the Historian concerning Jacob: ἔνθεν παραγίνεσθαι εἰς ἐφραθὰ, ἧν εἶναι Βηθλεὲμ. Τῇ Ἰούδα is a portion of land assigned to that tribe: just as γῆ Ζαβουλὼν καὶ γῆ Νεφθαλὶμ is said below IV. 15. By synecdoche, however, that name is attributed to towns, as γῆ Σοδόμων καὶ γομόṤῥων below X. 15, 24. Sophocles, citing Aristotle: καλεῖ δὲ μέν ἡδέ Γαῖα πελοπίαs χθονός. Servius on Aen. XI, where he says Ilia tellus for the city of Ilia. Moreover, the name of the region is added to Bethlehem, because there was another Bethlehem in Galilee, Jos. XIX. 15.

ὐδαμῶς] Since both the Prophet wrote in Hebrew and the experts in the Law reported the words of the Prophet himself, and it is not credible that Matthew departed from them, it is rightly asked whence the Greek interpreter took that ὐδαμῶς, especially since it does not exist among the LXX, which knot has greatly tormented Jerome and others. To me this answer seems most expeditious: it seemed to the interpreter that the words of the Prophet contained a question, which, after the manner of all nations, is worth just as much as a negation: in this way: Art thou, Bethlehem, the least in the census of the families of the tribe of Judah? Nay, truly, from thee shall the Messiah take his origin. Thus also the Chaldean Paraphrast reads that which is in Gen. IV. 24 with a question, and interprets it with a negation: and the Latin interpreter reads that which is in Deut. IX. 2, and the passage 2 Sam. XVI. 18, some with a negative particle, others without it, with the same sense. And the same thing happens in Job XIII. 15. & Esaiae XLIX. 7 The sense would be clearer if the interrogative ה were present, but it is often omitted, as in Job XL. 20, I. Reg. XXI. 7, Zach. VIII. 6. If it is not put for 'indeed', notes Servius on the XIth Aeneid.

What is to be thought of this allegation, we have said at Mich. V. 2.

ἐν τοῖς ἡγεμόσιν.] The Hebrew word אלף which sounds like 'thousand', designates a part of a tribe, that is, a family, as appears in Jud. VI. 15, not that this number corresponded to the families (for that could not happen) but that a certain number is put for an uncertain one; yet so that for the most part it would not depart far from the proportion. Wherefore also שרי אלפים Exod. XVIII. 25, they seem to me to be those whom Josephus calls patriarchs, in a more restricted sense than that in which that word is accustomed to be used in the New Testament. The same patriarchs, that is, princes of families, the Greek interpreter in this place calls ἡγεμόνας, designating the whole body by synecdoche with the name of the head: unless we prefer that he read in the Hebrew not אַלְפֵי but אַלֻּפֵי.

ἐκ σοῦ γὰρ] The Prophet seems properly to indicate the origin of the Messiah from the Bethlehemite family, namely, or the Davidic one, not numerous in itself, but to be heeded in every way by the Babylonians on account of the royal dignity which it had obtained. Yet God wished, by choosing this little town for the birth of Christ, to fulfill most fully what the Prophet had said, and at the same time to make the origin also attested by public records from the place of birth, as we are taught by Luke II, where πατριὰ Δαβὶδ is the same as אלף in the Prophet.

Latin:

Vers. 6. γῆ Ἰούδα] Recte interpres Graecus ita expressit quod in Hebraeo erat Bethlehem Ephrata, ut eundem lo- cum nomine suis temporibus notiore certius indicaret. Demetrius Historicus de Jacobo: ἔνθεν παραγίνεσθαι εἰς ἐφραθὰ, ἧν εἶναι Βηθλεὲμ. Τῇ Ἰούδα est terrae portio ei tri- bui asscripta: quomodo γῆ Ζαβουλὼν καὶ γῆ Νεφθαλὶμ dici- tur infra IV. 15. Per συνεκδοχὴν autem id nomen oppi- dis tribuitur, ut γῆ Σοδόμων καὶ γομόῤῥων infra X. 15 24. So- phocles citante Aristotele: καλεῖ δὲ μέν ἡδέ Γαῖα πελοπίαs χθονός. Servius ad AEn. XI. qua concidit Ilia tellus pro urbs Ilia. Regionis autem nomen Bethlehemo additur, quia alterum Bethlehemum erat in Galilaea Jos. XIX. 15.

ὐδαμῶς] Cum & Propheta Hebraice scripserit & ipsius Prophetae verba retulerint Legisperiti, neque credibile sit ab iis discessisse Matthaeum, quaeritur merito unde illud ὐδαμῶς sumserit Graecus interpres, praesertim cum non exstet apud LXX. qui nodus Hieronymum aliosque mul- tum torsit. Mihi expeditissima haec videtur responsio, visum interpreti verba Prophetae interrogationem conti- nere, quae more omnium gentium negationi tantundem valeat: hoc modo: Tune Bethlehem minima sis in censu familiarum tribus Judae? imo vero ex te originem sumtu- rus est Messias. Sic & Chaldaeus Paraphrastes id quod est Gen. IV. 24. legit cum interrogatione, interpretatur cum negatione: & Latinus interpres id quod est Deut. IX 2. & locum 2. Sam. XVI. 18. alii cum negativa particula, alii sine ea legunt sensu eodem. Idemque evenit Job. XIII, 15. & Esaiae XLIX. 7 Sensus esset apertior, si adesset ה inter- rogativum, sed id saepe omittitur, ut Job. XL. 20. I. Reg. XXI. 7. Zach. VIII. 6. Si non pro nempe poni notat Ser- vius ad XI. Aeneidos.

Quid de hac allegatione habendum sit, diximus ad Mich. V. 2.

ἐν τοῖς ἡγεμόσιν.] Vox Hebraea אלף quae χιλιάδα sonat, partem tribus, hoc familiam designat, ut apparet Jud. VI. 15. non quod familiis iste numerus responderet (id enim fieri non potuit) sed quod certus numerus positus est pro incerto; ita tamen ἐπὶ τὸ πλεῖστον à proportione non longe recederetur. Quare & שרי אלפים Exod. XVIII. 25. ii mihi esse videntur quos πατριάρχας vocat Jose- phus, sensu contractiore quam quo vox ea in novo fe- dere usurpari solet. Eosdem πατριάρχας, id est, fami- liarium principes, Graecus interpres hoc loco vocat ἡγε- μόνας, capitis appellatione totum corpus συνεκδοχικῶς de- signans: nisi malumus illum in Hebraeo legisse non אַלְפֵי sed אַלֻּפֵי

ἐκ σοῦ γὰρ] Videtur proprie Propheta originem Messiae indicare ex familia Bethlehemitica nimirum, sive Davidi- ca non numerosa per se, à Babyloniis autem, propter re- giam quam obtinuerat dignitatem, omnibus modis atte- renda. Voluit tamen Deus delecto ad Christi nativita- tem hoc oppidulo plenissime praestare quod Propheta di- xerat, & simul ex nascendi loco originem quoque actis publicis testatam facere ut docemur à Luca II. ubi πατριὰ Δαβὶδ est idem quod אלף apud Prophetam.

## 2:7
Vers. 7. Ἠκρίβωσε] The interpreter elegantly expressed in one word the same thing which he said a little later in two, ἀκριβῶς ἐξετάζειν. Thus in Isocrates, οἱ τὰ ἐκείνων ἀκριβοῦντες is ἀκριβῶς ἐξετάσοντες.

Φαινομένου] Φαινόμενα are called by the Greeks perpetual stars, especially the fixed ones. Nevertheless, the origin of the word extends more widely and is adapted by Aristotle himself to the halo, the parhelion, and even the comet. But you may rightly translate τὸν χρόνον τοῦ φαινομένου ἀστέρος, for how long a time the star was already appearing. For the participle of the present tense seems to have been chosen so that not the beginning, but the continuity might be denoted.

Latin:

Vers. 7. Ἠκρίβωσε] Eleganter expressit interpres una vo- ce idem quod paulo post dixit duabus ἀκριβῶς ἐξετάζειν. Ita apud Isocratem οἱ τὰ ἐκείνων ἀκριβοῦντες est ἀκριβῶς ἐξετά- σοντες.

Φαινομένου] Φαινόμενα Graecis dicuntur stellae perpetuae, praesertim αἱ ἀπλανεῖς. Attamen origo vocis latius patet & ab ipso Aristotele τῇ ἅλῳ, τῷ παρηλίῳ, τῷ κομήτῃ et- iam aptatur. Recte autem transferas τὸν χρόνον τοῦ φαινομέ- νου ἀστέρος, quanto jam tempore stella appareret. Videtur enim electum participium praesentis temporis, ut non ini- tium, sed continuitas denotaretur.

## 2:8
Vers. 8. πέμψας αὐτοὺς] πέμπειν in Homer is the same as what is more frequently called προπέμπειν: the Latins used to say 'prosequi'. For this also is properly to accompany someone departing for a distance for the sake of honor: whence it began to be transferred to other kinds of duties.

Latin:

Vers. 8. πέμψας αὐτοὺς] πέμπειν apud Homerum est i- dem quod frequentius dicitur προπέμπειν: Latini dicebant prosequi. Nam & hoc proprie est, abeuntem honoris causa aliquousque comitari: unde ad caetera officiorum genera transferri coepit.

## 2:9
Verf. 9. Ἔστη ἐπάνω ὗ ἦν τὸ παιδίον] That is: it ceased to proceed, and not long after, as it is credible, it vanished, when the Magi had arrived at the place in which the infant Jesus was. For otherwise, it is impossible for a celestial star to designate a place on earth so small with certainty. Therefore the Magi found the house not only by the leading of the star, but by having inquired diligently about the child, and perhaps also by the indication of the shepherds who were not far away living in the fields. Not unlike this is what Varro had written in the second book of divine affairs, as reported by Servius on the first Aeneid: from the time that Aeneas departed from Troy, he saw the star of Venus every day, until he came to the Laurentine field, in which he did not see it any further.

Verba textus clara sunt, The words of the text are clear, that the star stood over that house in which the infant was, which are rashly twisted; so that Ἔστη ἐπάνω ὗ ἦν τὸ παιδίον might mean it ceased to proceed, and they do not designate the place. And Grotius openly opposes the Evangelist here. For the latter testifies that the Magi found the house by the leading of the star, which Grotius denies. Nor is there anything in the text as to how the Magi found the house through inquiry: only Herod is mentioned as having ordered it, 'inquire diligently about the child'. They had no need of that investigation; nor could anyone easily have informed the Magi, for who would have taken account of that infant? And therefore the star led them into the house. And for that reason they rejoiced greatly when they saw the star. And they came thus into the house: as the Evangelist clearly says v. 10, 11. Grotius is mistaken in believing that the star remained in the ether, not in the air. For why could a star not point out a house situated in the air? Although Grotius was consistent with himself on that point. For he asserted the contrary at verse 1. Moreover, whatever sort of star it was, that motion by which it is later narrated that the lodging of Christ was pointed out, was not only contrary to nature, but also without precedent: whence the Greeks think it was an angel rather than a star. Something similar is narrated to have happened in the martyrology in the times of Diocletian, when Christians seeking the bodies of the three martyrs, Tharacus, Probus, and Andronicus, suddenly saw as it were a splendid star sent from heaven resting upon each of the bodies of the saints. So far Grotius. Certainly the star was extraordinary, which shone not only by night but also by day, and now appeared and now disappeared, and proceeded not by a circular but by a straight and level motion, and advanced with a slow motion adapted to the movement of the Magi, sometimes even rested and stood still; furthermore, it was low to the ground, and was employed only to provide service to the Magi, which being performed, it vanished, all of which are clear from the text.

Latin:
