Verf. 9. Ἔστη ἐπάνω ὗ ἦν τὸ παιδίον] Id est: defiit proce- dere, nec multo post, ut credi par est, evanuit, ubi Magi ad eum pervenerant locum in quo erat infans Jesus. Nam a- lioqui, ut locum in terris tam exiguum stella cœlestis cer- to designet, fieri non potest. Domum igitur invenerunt Magi non solo stellæ ductu, sed ἀκριβῶς ἐξετάσαντες περὶ τοῦ παιδίου, forte & pastorum non longe ἀγραυλούντων indi- cio. Non dissimile est quod Varro secundo rerum divi- narum scripserat, referente Servio ad primum Æneidos: ex quo de Troja egressus est Æneas, Veneris eum per diem quotidie stellam vidisse, donec ad agrum Laurentem ve- niret, in quo eam non vidit ulterius.

Verba textus clara sunt, quod steterit stella su- per domum illam, in qua erat infans, quæ temere torquentur; ut Ἔστη ἐπάνω ὗ ἦν τὸ παιδίον sit defiit procedere, neque designent locum. Et aperte ad- versatur hic Grotius Evangelistæ. Hic enim stel- læ ductu Magos domum invenisse testatur, quod negat Grotius. Neque quicquam in textu habe- tur, quomodo Magi per ἐξέτασιν invenerint do- mum: solum Herodes commemoratur id jussisse, ἀκριβῶς ἐξετάσετε περὶ τοῦ παιδίου. Non opus ha- bebant illa investigatione; neque quisquam facile informare potuisset Magos, ecquis enim infantis istius rationem habuisset? Ideoque stella eos dedu- xit in domum. Et ob id gavisi sunt valde, cum stellam viderant. Et venerunt ita in domum: ut σαφῶς Ev- angelista v. 10. 11. Fallitur Grotius, quod credit stellam in æthere hæsisse, non in aëre. Quidni enim Stella in aëre constitutam domum monstrare pos- sit? Quanquam sibi in eo nomine constitit Gro- tius. Contrarium enim ad v. 1. adseruit. Cæterum qualecunque fuit sidus, motus ille, quo postea narra- tur Hospitium Christi fuisse monstratum, non modo præter naturam fuit, sed etiam citra exemplum: unde Græci Angelum potius quam stellam fuisse exi- stimant. Simile aliquid in martyrologio narratur ac- cidisse Diocletiani temporibus, cum Christiani quæ- rentes trium martyrum, Tharaci, Probi & Androni- ci corpora, viderunt subito velut stellam splendidam de cælo missam super singula sanctorum corpora re- sidentem. Hactenus Grotius. Certe extraordi- narium fuit sidus, quod non tantum noctu sed & in- terdiu fulsit, & modo apparuit modo disparuit, nec circulari sed recto & plano motu processit, ac motu lento & accommodato ad motum Magorum se promo- vit, interdum etiam quievit, & substitit, adhæc hu- mile ad terram fuit, nec nisi ad ministerium Magis præstandum adhibitum, quo præstito evanuit, quæ o- mnia ex textu luculenta sunt.

## 2:11
Vers. 11. εἰς τὴν οἰκίαν) I cannot agree with Epiphanius, who thinks that a fixed domicile is understood here, to which Joseph and Mary with Jesus, now almost two years old, had immigrated after leaving Nazareth, although it seems to favor his opinion that below Joseph, returning from Egypt, is narrated to have been hindered by fear of Archelaus from going to Judea, and to have established his home in Nazareth, as if he had not lived there when departing into Egypt. But also what is said about the two-year age is weak: (as we said before.) And to that other point it can be answered that Joseph, when he had returned from Egypt, had domestic reasons which pertained to providing food or to the custom of his kinsmen (whom he had in those parts, as is clear from Luke II. 44) or finally to the upbringing of the child, why he might prefer to live in Judea, specifically in the way depicted, rather than in the parts of Galilee: but that he changed his plan out of fear of Archelaus. On the other hand, that I may believe the arrival of the Magi happened within that space of thirty-eight days which was prescribed by divine law for women after childbirth, I am moved by the words of Luke, who immediately after the καθαρισμὸν leads the child with his mother to Nazareth: I am moved also by those things set forth above: τοῦ δὲ Ἰησοῦ γεννηθέντος ἐν βηθλεὲμ τῆς ἰουδαίας ἐν ἡμέραις Ἡρώδου τοῦ βασιλέως, ἰδὺ μάγοι ἀπὸ ἀνατολῶν and what follows. For these words clearly denote a matter carried out shortly after Christ was born: just as in Heb. XI. 23, Μωσῆς γεννηθεὶς signifies shortly after he was born: and they do not deduce that Bethlehemite dwelling, in which the Magi greeted Jesus, from some new migration, which after the interval between the Jerusalemite and the restored

it happened that they lived in Nazareth, but they continue with the childbed itself. To which is added that the stay in Bethlehem was of such a short time that not even the slightest rumor of it reached the people, John I. 45, 46. Nor should the word παιδία cast doubt upon us as if it indicated someone older than a newborn. For Luke uses the word παιδία even of John, the son of Zechariah, not yet circumcised, I. 59, and speaking of Christ just born, he uses the names βρέφους and παιδίου interchangeably, II. 12, 16, 17, 21. But it is very credible that, the census being completed, an opportunity was given for slightly more relaxed lodging: and so from that cave, in which ancient writers record the manger to have been, Joseph and Mary moved into a house before the Magi arrived: although Justin seems to have thought otherwise.

τοὺς θησαυρούς) Thus the Greeks call not only, as the jurists do, that deposit of old money of which no memory exists, and which therefore has no owner, but absolutely all storehouses and repositories: just as Varro also says, Let there be no treasure, no breast loosened by gold. Servius on Georgics IV, on treasures, that is, repositories, as if he were saying storehouses. And perhaps the origin is not Greek but Oriental from תְּשׂוּרָה, which is a word in I Sam. IX. 7. The Greeks do not only speak this way, like Xenophon, Plutarch, and others, but Josephus does too. The Hebrew אֹוצָר has the same value, which I believe Matthew used. Some copies in the time of Epiphanius had in this place πήρας, which I judge happened from an interpretation.

Δῶρα) It was not only the custom for the Persians and their successors, the Parthians, to approach kings with gifts, but the whole East practiced the same. See Gen. XXXIII. 9, XLIII. 10 and 25, I Sam. XXV. 18, 27, I Kings X. 2, Ps. LXXII. 10. The Magi brought the most excellent gifts of their own region. For myrrh is born only in Arabia: nor is frankincense found except among the Sabaeans, a portion of the Arabs: but happy Arabia is also gold-bearing. And so the kings of the Arabs also brought gold as a gift to Solomon, I Chron. I. 4. Nor do I think the Magi had anything else in view, so perhaps there is no need here to allegorize. If, however, we wish to indicate something more mystical by divine counsel, it would not displease me that by these three signs those three things are noted which we now offer to God through Christ, the old sacrifices having been abolished: works of mercy, Phil. IV. 18, purity of bodies, Rom. XII. 1, and prayers, Ps. CXLI. 2 and Rev. V. 8. And that prayers can be understood by the likeness of incense, that very passage of the Psalms and the Apocalypse clearly teaches us; but gold is as it were the common measure of the goods of this world, by which we relieve the poverty of others: and there is hardly any other use for myrrh than to preserve bodies incorrupt, as Pliny teaches us, and John himself XIX. 39.

Latin:

Vers. 11. εἰς τὴν οἰκίαν) Non possum accedere Epiphanio existimanti fixum domicilium hic intelligi, quo Josephus & Maria cum Jesu jam ferme bimulo Nazareta relicta immi- graverint, quanquam favere ejus sententiæ videtur quod infra Josephus Ægypto rediens narratur metu Archelai im- peditus quo minus Judæam peteret, Nazaretæ larem po- suisse, quasi in Ægyptum discedens non habitasse. Sed & quod de bimatu dicitur infirmum est: (ut antea diximus.) Et ad alterum illud responderi potest, Josephum cum ab Ægypto revenisset causas habuisse domesticas quæ ad vi- ctum parandum aut ad consuetudinem cognatorum (quos habebat istis in partibus, ut patet Luc. III. 44.) aut ad pueri denique institutionem pertinebant, cur in Judæa peculiari- ter ita picta, quam in Galilææ partibus habitare mallet: sed metu Archelai consilium mutasse. Contra ut credam ma- gorum adventum accidisse intra spatium illud temporis triginta & octo dierum, quod erat puerperis à divina lege præstitutum, movent me verba Lucæ, qui statim post καθα- ρισμὸν puerum cum matre Nazaretam deducit: movent & illa superius posita: τοῦ δὲ Ἰησοῦ γεννηθέντος ἐν βηθλεὲμ τῆς ἰουδαίας ἐν ἡμέραις Ἡρώδου τοῦ βασιλέως, ἰδὺ μάγοι ἀπὸ ἀνατολῶν & quæ sequuntur. Plane enim verba hæc rem paulo post Christum natum gestam denotant: quomodo Hebr. XI. 23. Μωσῆς γεννηθεὶς significat, paulo postquam natus erat: & Bethlehemiticam illam mansionem, in qua Magi Jesum sa- lutaverunt, non dedocunt à nova aliqua migratione, quæ post interpositum inter Hierosolymitanum & repositam

Nazarætæ habitationem contigerit, sed cum ipso puerpe- rio continuant. Quibus accedit quod commoratio Beth- lehemitica tam exigui fuerit temporis, ut ne minima qui- dem ejus fama ad populum pervaserit, Joh. I. 45. 46. Ne- que scrupulum injicere nobis debet vox παιδία quasi pro- vechiorem recenter nato indicaret. Nam & de Johanne Za- chariæ filio necdum circumciso vocem παιδία Lucas usur- pat I. 59. & de Christo jamjam nato loquens promiscue u- titur nominibus βρέφους & παιδίου II. 12. 16. 17. 21. Illud vero perquam credibile est, peracto censu copiam datam paulo laxioris hospitii: atque adeo ex eo specu, in quo τὴν φάτνην fuisse antiqui scriptores memorant, Josephum & Ma- riam in domum transiisse antequam Magi adventarent: quanquam aliter sensisse videtur Justinus.

τοὺς θησαυρούς) Ita Græci vocant non tantum, ut Juris- consulti, depositionem illam veteris pecuniæ cujus non ex- stat memoria, & quæ proinde Dominum non habeat, sed o- mnes omnino ἀποθήκας & conditoria: quemodo & Varro, Non sit thesaurus, non auro pectus solutum. Servius ad IV. Georg. thesauris, id est repositoribus, quasi diceret apothecis. Et forte origo non est Græca sed Orientalis ex תְּשׂוּרָה quæ vox est I. Sam. IX. 7. Græce non tantum ita loquuntur Xenophon, Plutarchus, aliiqs, sed & Josephus Idem valet אֹוצָר Hebræum quo Matthæum usum existi- mo. Quædam exemplaria Epiphanii tempore habebant hoc loco πήρας quod ex interpretamento evenisse arbitror.

Δῶρα) Non Persis tantum & eorum successoribus Par- this in more positum fuit Reges cum donis adire, sed totus Oriens idem frequentavit. Vid. Gen. XXXIII. 9. XLIII. 10. & 25. I. Sam. XXV. 18. 27. I. Reg. X. 2. Psl. LXXII. 10. Attule runt autem Magi suæ regionis præstantissimas dotes. Nam myrrha non nisi in Arabia nascitur: nec thus nisi apud Sabæ- os Arabum portionem: sed & aurifera est felix Arabia. Itaqs & Salomoni Arabum reges aurum dono tulere, I. Par. L. I 4. Neq; aliud spectatum à Magis arbitror, ita hic forte nihil sit opus ἀλληγορεῖν. Si tamen μυστικώτερον aliquid divino con- silio volumus indicatum, mihi non displiceat his signis tri- bus tria illa notari, quæ nunc abrogatis veteribus sacrificiis, Deo per Christum offerimus: opera misericordiæ, Phil. IV. 18. corporum puritatem Rom. XII. 1. & preces Pf. CXLI 2. & Apoc. V. 8. Et thuris quidem similitudine preces intelligi posse ipse ille Psalmorum & Apocalypseos locus aperte nos docet; bonorum autem hujus sæculi, quibus aliorum ege- statem sublevamus, quasi communis mensura est aurum: & myrrhæ vix alius est usus, quam ut corpora incorrupta con- servet, ut nos Plinius docet, & ipse Joannes XIX. 39.

## 2:12
Vers. 12. χρηματισθέντες) A similar use of this word is in Luke II. 26, Acts X. 22, Heb. VIII. 5 and XI. 7. But χρηματισμός is a word of wider scope than the Latin 'oracle,' which I do not recall being said of visions by day or by night.

PART II. The history of the flight of Joseph into Egypt, and his recall from Egypt.

Latin:

Vers. 12. χρηματισθέντες) Similis hujus vocis usus Luc. II. 26. Act. X. 22. Heb. VIII. 5. & XI. 7. Est autem χρηματισ- μὸς vox latius patens, quam Latina oraculi, quod de visis diurnis nocturnisve dici non memini.

PARS II. Historia fugæ Josephi in Aegyptum, & revo- cationis ex Aegypto.

## 2:13
Vers. 13. ἀναχωρησάντων δὲ αὐτῶν) Since the place where this happened is not expressed, it can be understood that it happened either at Jerusalem, or even at Nazareth, to which Joseph and Mary returned after the purification of the mother, Luke II. 39, so that from there they proceeded further into Egypt.

Latin:

Vers. 13. ἀναχωρησάντων δὲ αὐτῶν) Cum non exprimatur locus ubi hoc factum sit, potest intelligi aut Hierosolymis id accidisse, aut etiam Nazareth, quo post lustrationem puer- peræ Josephus & Maria redierint, Luc. II. 39. ut inde porro in Ægyptum concesserint.

## 2:15
Vers. 15. Πληρωθῇ τὸ ῥηθὲν.) We have said above what τὸ πληρωθῆναι is here. God clearly wished, by the benefit of the old covenant and those things which He performed for us to Christ and through Christ (for that event also bore the image of our liberation from Egypt, of which we shall speak on Luke XXII. 16), that certain circumstances should be similar, so that it might be the more evident that these things were arranged by a certain peculiar counsel. Therefore, this passage was unjustly attacked long ago by Julian, and later also by the Jews.

Τὸν ὐιόν μου.) The Israelite people, peculiarly beloved by God, bore the image of Christ; and, if I am not mistaken, the people themselves, just as the Son of God is called the firstborn by God Himself, Exod. IV. 21 and Jer. XXXI. 9, are also called by the name of Christ, both in the prophet Habakkuk III. 13, and in the Epistle to the Hebrews XI. 25, 26, indeed in the same way that the Fathers, from whom the people drew their origin, are called anointed, or Christs, Ps. CV. 15.

Here Grotius retreats to his customary rule of falsehood: he says that prophecies about Christ are fulfilled in no other way in many oracles than that some similar circumstances happened in other persons who represented Christ: of which rule he makes not only this an example, but according to the same he interprets most of the prophecies of the Old Testament which are explained concerning Christ in the New Testament, and leaves almost no prophecies predicting Christ according to the literal sense. To which end he also invents that the people of God

were called by the name of Christ. Which does not appear from Hab. III. 13, as if they were called in the plural משיחיכם, perhaps looking to the version of the LXX Interpreters, which renders it, 'that you might save your Christs,' concerning which name Tostatus, Comment. on Matt. XIV. p. 39, not indeed because of that passage in Hab. III, but because of Ps. CV. 15. All the Jews were called CHRISTS, that is, ANOINTED: not that they were anointed corporally, but because in so far as they belonged to God, they seemed more visible than other nations to participate in a kingly rule, just as He Himself said in Exod. XIX that they were to Him a priestly kingdom, and a peculiar treasure from all nations, and therefore they were called CHRISTS. Furthermore, Jerome interpreted the passage of the Prophet with Aquila thus: 'You went forth with your Christ for the salvation of the people.' Which they commonly explain concerning David, the anointed Lord, with whom the Lord went forth for the salvation of the people. Conf. I Sam. XVI. 12, 13, II Sam. V. 3, 16, ch. XIX. 22, ch. XXII. 15, Ps. XX. 7.

As for the passage Heb. XI. 25. 26., there is a notable ψευδερμηνεία [false interpretation], because Grotius interprets the name of Christ, which in the New Testament is used of Jesus of Nazareth, as referring to the Israelites. For the Apostle celebrates the faith of Moses, because he held the reproach and cross of Christ in higher regard than the royal treasures of Egypt. But what should be thought of the passage in Hos. XI., we have stated in the annotations to the same. It is not an accommodation, or any kind of agreement of circumstances, but the fulfillment of a prophecy that is designated here: nor does that ἵνα πληρωθῇ τὸ ῥηθὲν [that it might be fulfilled which was spoken] occur anywhere solely regarding the analogy and agreement of certain circumstances; indeed, that phrase does not allow this gloss, inasmuch as it imports the fulfillment of a prophecy, or the real completion and performance of that which was predicted by the Prophet.

Latin:

Vers. 15. Πληρωθῇ τὸ ῥηθὲν.) Quid hic sit τὸ πληρωθῆναι supra diximus. Voluit plane Deus beneficio tum veteris fœ- deris & eorum quæ Christo & per Christum nobis præsti- tit (nam & nostræ ex Ægypto liberationis, de qua dicemus ad Luc. XXII. 16. ista res gessit imaginem) circumstantias, quasdam esse similes, ut eo magis constaret consilio quo- dam peculiari ista disponi. Immerito igitur vexatus est hic locus olim à Juliano, postea etiam à Judæis.

Τὸν ὐιόν μου.) Populus Israëliticus à Deo peculiariter dile- ctus Christi gessit imaginem; ac, ni fallor, ipse populus, quemadmodum filius Dei, primogenitus à Deo ipso vo- catur Exod. IV. 21. & Jer. XXXI. 9. ita & Christi appellatur nomine, tum apud Prophetam Abacucum III. 13. tum in Epistola ad Hebr. XI. 25. 26. nempe eodem modo quo Pa- tres, unde ortum ducebat populus, uncti, sive Christi vo- cantur Ps. CV. 15.

Recipit sese hic Grotius ad consuetam regulam falsi: non aliter impleri dicit de Christo Prophe- tias, in multis oraculis, quam quod similes aliquæ circumstantiæ in aliis personis, quæ Christum re- ræsentarint, acciderint: cujus regulæ non hoc tan- tum exemplum facit, sed juxta eandem pleraque vaticinia V. T. quæ de Christo explicantur in N. T. interpretatur, ac nullas fere prophetias secun- dum literalem sensum Christum prædicentes relin- quit. Quo fine etiam comminiscitur, populum Dei

Christi nomine appellatum esse. Quod ex Habac. III. 13. non apparet, quasi illi in plurali משיחיכם appellentur, forte LXX. Interpp. versionem respi- ciens, quæ reddit, ut salvares Christos tuos, de quo nomine Tostatus Comment. in Matth. XIV. p. 39. non quidem ob locum illum Habac. III. sed ob Ps. CV. 15. Omnes Judæi vocabantur CHRISTI, id est, UNCTI: non quod uncti essent corporaliter, sed quia in quantum pertinebant ad Deum, spectabiles, quam a- lia gentes, videbantur participare omnes principatu regnativo, sicut ipse dixit Exod. XIX. eos esse sibi re- gnum sacerdotale, & peculium de cunctis gentibus, & ideo vocabantur CHRISTI. Cæterum locum Pro- phetæ Hieronymus cum Aquila ita interpretatus est, exivisti cum Christo tuo ad salutem populi. Quod communiter explicant de Davide, uncto Domino, cum quo processit Dominus ad salutem populi. Conf. I. Sam. XVI. 12. 13. II. Sam. V. 3. 16. c. XIX. 22 c. XXII. 15. Ps. XX. 7.

Quod vero ad locum Ebr. XI. 25. 26. insignis ψευδερμηνεία est, quod Grotius nomen τοῦ χριστοῦ, quod in Novo Testamento de Jesu Nazareno usur- patur, de Israëlitis interpretatur. Nam celebrat A- post. Mosis fidem, quod opprobrium & crucem Chri- sti potiori loco habuerit, quam Regios Ægypti the- sauros. Quid autem de loco Hos. XI. habendum sit, in annot. ad eundem diximus. Non accommoda- tio, vel convenientia qualiscunque circumstantia- rum, sed complementum vaticinii hic designatur: neque uspiam illa ἵνα πληρωθῇ τὸ ῥηθὲν de analo- gia & convenientia solum quarundam circumstantia- rum occurrunt, imo non patitur illa phrasis hanc glossam: utpote quæ vaticinii complementum, vel ejus quod prædictum fuit à Propheta realem ad- impletionem & præstationem importat.

## 2:16
Vers. 16. Ἀποστείλας [having sent]) with soldiers sent: for this cruelty had no appearance of a public trial. Ἐν πᾶσι τοῖς ὁρίοις αὐτῆ [in all its borders]) That is, in all its territory. Cicero spoke of the territory of a colony in this way. Now territory, as defined by the Jurisconsult Pomponius, is the totality of fields within the boundaries of each city. Thus below, ὅρια μαγδαλὰ [borders of Magdala] xv. 39. Ἀπὸ διετοῦς καὶ κατωτέρω [from two years old and under]) This expression ἀπὸ διετοῦς is correct and appears in Pollux. Whoever it is from whom Macrobius described the sayings of Augustus, he says in Latin, quite correctly, intra bimatum [within two years]: unless we prefer to believe this was added by Macrobius himself, who lived in Theodosian times and held honors, and therefore was either a Christian or certainly read the books of the Apostles: which is the more credible because it cannot be said with sufficient correctness that Antipater, the son of Herod, already of advanced age, and who was not in Bethlehem, was killed among the Bethlehemite infants. Add that Antipater was killed five days before Herod's death, but this slaughter happened some time before, as those things which follow below in verse 19 teach. It seems, therefore, that Macrobius, by some error, mixed two histories of the same time. Certainly, that slaughter of the infants, either because of the scarcity of inhabitants in that tract, or because it was carried out under the pretext of a riot or sedition, with the King's command concealed, or finally because it was obscured by the greater crimes of Herod, was less noble than to reach the ears of Augustus; especially since Josephus, so diligent a writer, did not mention it. Furthermore, only the slaughter of the son pertains to the matter; but the cruelty εἰς τοὺς διετοῖς καὶ κάτω [to those two years old and under] could not cause Augustus to say that he would rather be Herod's pig than his son. Note, however, that what had been foreshadowed in the ancestors is fulfilled here in the descendants. Once Esau had lain in wait for Jacob: now the Idumean for Christ, who is also Jacob among the Prophets.

Latin:

Vers. 16. Ἀποστείλας) missis militibus: nam sævitia hæc nullam habuit speciem judicii publici. Ἐν πᾶσι τοῖς ὁρίοις αὐτῆ) Id est in omni territorio ejus. Ita territorium coloniæ dixit Cicero. Est autem territorium, definiente Pomponio Jurisconsulto, universitas agrorum intra fines cujusque civitatis. Sic infra ὅρια μαγδαλὰ xv. 39. Ἀπὸ διετοῦς καὶ κατωτέρω) Hæc locutio ἀπὸ διετοῦς proba est & apud Pollucem apparet. Latine admodum quisquis ille est ex quo Macrobius Augusti dicta descripsit intra bi- matum: nisi ab ipso Macrobio, qui Theodosianis tempori- bus vixit, honoresque gessit, ac proinde aut Christianus fuit, aut certe legit Apostolorum libros, hoc addictum malumus: quod eo est credibilius, quia non satis recte di- ci potest Antipater Herodis filius, jam provectæ ætatis, quique Bethlehemi non fuit, inter infantes Bethlehemiti- cos occisus. Adde quod Antipater occisus quinto ante mortis Herodem die, hæc autem laniena ante aliquanto contigit, ut docent quæ sequuntur infra commate 19. Vi- detur ergo Macrobius errore quodam historias duas ejus- dem temporis miscuisse. Certe laniena illa infantum, aut ob raritatem habitantium in eo tractu, aut quia tumul- tus seditionisve obtentu, dissimulato Regis imperio, fuit peracta, aut denique quod majoribus Herodis sceleribus obscuraretur, minus nobilis fuit, quam ut ad Augusti aures perveniret: quippe cum nec Josephus Scriptor tam diligens ejus meminerit. Deinde sola filii cædes ad rem pertinet: sævitia autem εἰς τοὺς διετοῖς καὶ κάτω efficere non potuit, ut diceret Augustus malfe se Herodis porcum esse quam filium. Nota autem hic impleri in posteris, quod in majoribus fuerat adumbratum. Olim infidiatus fuerat Esau Jacobo: nunc Idumæus Christo qui & Iacobus apud Prophetas.

## 2:18
V. 18. Ῥαμὰ [Rama]) The LXX translated it as a proper name even before this word, and so did the Chaldean interpreter: better, if I am not mistaken, than those who treat it as an appellative. Nor does it stand in the way that Rama is in the portion of Benjamin, but Bethlehem is in the part of Judah. For Bethlehem is in the furthest borders of Judah, and the very sepulcher of Rachel is in the Bethlehemite territory, but very close to the fields of Benjamin, Gen. XXXV. 16. 19. 20. But this is said ἐμφατικῶς [emphatically] so that the cry may be understood to have been heard far and wide. Although it is also clearly evident from the history which is in Jud. XIX. that Rama was not too far distant from Bethlehem. But I do not see why I should agree with Justin, who interprets Rama as a place in Arabia.

κλαυθμὸς κῂ ὀδυρμὸς πολὺς) What is said in Hebrew by way of construction בכי תמרורים, the interpreter rendered most excellently with joined words, and by adding πολὺς, he expressed the force of the plural number most fully.

Ῥαχὴλ κλαίουσα) It seems to me to be a prosopopoeia, a frequent ornament of poetic speech. Nor is that passage of Lucan much unlike it: Scipio deplores the ill-fated offspring destined to perish in Libyan lands; Cato, a greater enemy of Carthage, mourns the fates of a grandson who is not to be a slave.

Ὅτι ὀυκ εἰσὶ) So also the Greeks. In Hebrew, there is a singular for a plural in a distributive sense, and the existential verb is missing, which is most customary for that language as אינננו. To be, however, here signifies the same as to live, just as the dead are said by the Latins to have been, that is, to have lived. And Sophocles calls the dead ὡς ὄτ᾿ ὄντας: just as we say that has perished which has escaped sight or notice, to which that in Psalm 39:14 seems to look: before I go away and am no more. And Ps. 37:36, concerning the wicked, he was not, the Psalmist himself interprets, I sought him and he was not found. So also Gen. 5:24, concerning Enoch, he was not; the LXX translate ὀυχ᾽ εὑρίσκετο. So also Sirach 17:25, from the dead, as one who is not, thanksgiving perishes. Unless we prefer that 'not to be' is said of a man strictly, because neither the body separated from the soul, nor the soul from the body, is properly called a man. Josephus speaks in this manner also: For we have received from Him (God) our being, and we give back to Him our no longer being. Soon follows, the soul is always immortal. A similar passage is in Euripides in the tragedy Helena, where he denies that souls live, which he nevertheless acknowledges are punished after this life. For there is also retribution for these things to those below, and for all those above, the mind of the dead lives indeed, but it has no consciousness, having fallen into the immortal ether as an immortal thing.

Latin:

V. 18. Ῥαμὰ) Ita & ante hanc vocem LXX. proprio nomine transtulerunt, sed & Chaldæus interpres: melius ni fallor, quam qui appellativo. Nec obstat quod Ra- ma est in Benjaminis portione, Bethlehem autem in parte Judæ. Est enim Bethlehem in ultimis fi- nibus Judæ, ipsumque Rachelis sepulcrum in territorio Bethlehemitico, sed proxime agros Benjaminis, Gen. XXXV. 16. 19. 20. Dicitur autem hoc ἐμφατικῶς ut lon- ge lateque clamor exauditus intelligatur. Quanquam nec longe nimium Ramam à Bethlehemo distitisse liqui- do constat ex historia quæ est Iud. XIX. Iustino autem Ra- mam interpretanti Arabiæ locum non video cur assentiri debeam.

κλαυθμὸς κῂ ὀδυρμὸς πολὺς) Quod in Hebræo constructe di- citur בכי תמרורים, id copulatis vocibus optime reddi- dit interpres & pluralis numeri vim addito πολὺς plenissi- me expressit.

Ῥαχὴλ κλαίουσα) Videtur mihi esse προσωποποιΐα frequens Poetici sermonis ornamentum. Nec multum dissimile il- lud Lucani: Deplorat Libycis perituram Scipio terris Insaustam sobolem: major Carthaginis hostis Non servituri mæret Cato fata nepotis.

Ὅτι ὀυκ εἰσὶ) Sic & Græci. In Hebræo est singulare pro plurali sensu distributivo, & deest verbum ὑπαρκτικὸν, quæ אינננו ei linguæ usitatissima est. Esse autem, hic valet idem quod vivere, quomodo mortui Latinis fuisse, id est vixisse dicuntur. Et Sophocles mortuos dicit ὡς ὄτ᾿ ὄντας: sicut periisse dicimus id quod conspectum aut notitiam no- strant effugit, quo spectare videtur illud in Psalmo xxxix. 14. antequam abeo ut non sim amplius. Et Ps. xxxvii. 36. de impio non fuit, ipse Psalmographus interpretatur, quæ- sivi eum & non est inventus. Sic & Gen. V. 24. de Enocho, non erat LXX. vertunt ὀυχ᾽ εὑρίσκετο. Sic & Sirachides XVII. 25. ἀπὸ νεκρῦ, ὡς μηδὲ ὄντος, ἀπόλυται ἐξομολόγησις. Nisi malimus illud non esse κυριολεκτῶς dici de homine, quia nec corpus ab anima separatum, neque à corpore animus homo proprie dicitur. Loquitur hunc in modum & Jose- phus: κῂ γὰρ εἰλήφαμεν παῤ ἐκείνυ (τοῦ Θεοῦ) τὸ εἶναι κῂ τὸ μηκέτι εἶναι πάλιν ἐκείνῳ δίδομεν. Mox sequitur ψυχὴ ἀθάνατος ἀεὶ. Similis est apud Euripidem locus tragœdia Helena, ubi a- nimas negat vivere, quas tamen puniri post hanc vitam a- gnoscit. Καὶ γὰρ τίσις τῶν δ᾽ ἐστὶτοῖς τενεχτέροις, Καὶ τοῖς ἄνωθεν πᾶσιν ἀνθρώποις ὁ νῦς Τῶν κατθανόντων ζῇ μὲν ὀυ Γνώμην δ᾽ ἔχει Ἀθάνατον εἰς ἀθάνατον αἰθέρ᾽ ἐμπεσών.

## 2:19
Vers. 19. Τελευτήσαντος) That word is most customary to the Greeks, even without the word βιῦ or αἰῶν@ being added. Sophocles: before you see him having finished his life: and another: To him who has finished his life, each thing, even if one is a very great enemy, becomes a friend then. Nor do the jurists speak otherwise.

Latin:

Vers. 19. Τελευτήσαντος) usitatissima Græcis ea vox etiam non addita voce βιῦ aut αἰῶν@. Sophocles πρὶν τελευτή- σαντ᾿ ἰδῂς: & alius: Πρὸς τὸν τελευτήσανθ᾽ ἕκασθ᾽ κᾂν σφόδρα Ἂν ἐχθρὸς ᾖ τις, γίνεται φίλος τότε. Nec aliter jurisconsulti.

## 2:20
Vers. 20. Τεθνήκασι γὰρ οἱ ζητῦντες τὴν ψυχὴν τῦ παιδίυ) It is not without reason that the very words are used which exist in Exod. 4:19; for that is accustomed in the Holy Scriptures to denote a similarity of the event. Indeed, Josephus says that this was the cause of the infanticide for Pharaoh also, as for Herod, because he had understood from prophecies that a great leader would arise from the Hebrews.

Latin:

Vers. 20. Τεθνήκασι γὰρ οἱ ζητῦντες τὴν ψυχὴν τῦ παιδίυ) Non temere est quod ipsa verba usurpantur quæ exstant Exod. IV. 19. id enim solet in sacris literis rei gestæ simili- tudinem denotare. Sane Pharaoni quoque, ut Herodi, causam infanticidii Josephus hanc ait fuisse, quod ex vati- ciniis intellexisset magnum Ducem ex Hebræis exstiturum.

## 2:22
Vers. 22. ὅτι Ἀρχέλα@ βασιλεύει) Since he had rather hoped that Judea would be reduced to a province by the Roman Emperor, from whom he feared less for himself than from petty kings trembling at every suspicion, and therefore cruel: Archelaus was, moreover, more savage even than his brothers. Ἀντὶ) would have been in Hebrew חלף, as now in the Syriac, which little word sometimes indicates delegation, but here and in other places indicates succession. If you wish to speak Latin, βασιλέυειν ἀντὶ ἠρώδυ must be translated as to succeed Herod in the kingdom, or to reign in the place of Herod, as Martial: You write that you are heir and in your place, you madman. Thus 1 Macc. 13:32, it is said ἐβασίλευσεν ἀντ᾿ ἀυτοῦ.

Latin:

Vers. 22. ὅτι Ἀρχέλα@ βασιλεύει) Cum potius futurum sperasset ut Judæa in Provinciam redigeretur à Romano Imperatore, à quo minus sibi metuebat, quam a minutis regulis ad omnes suspiciones pavidis, eoque crudelibus: Erat autem etiam fratribus suis truculentior Archelaus. Ἀντὶ) fuerit in Hebræo חלף ut nunc in Syro quæ vocu- la interdum delegationem, hic vero aliusque locis succes- sionem indicat. Latine loqui si velis βασιλέυειν ἀντὶ ἠρώδυ vertendum erit, Herodi in regnum succedere, aut regnare lo- co Herodis, quomodo Martialis: Hæredem Scribis & esse tuo tu furiose loco. Sic I. Maccab. XIII. 32. dicitur ἐβασίλευσεν ἀντ᾿ ἀυτοῦ.

## 2:23
Vers. 23. Διὰ τῶν προφητῶν) The word for law and prophets are sometimes placed strictly, so that they constitute different parts of the divinely inspired scripture: sometimes more loosely, so that either of these words may comprehend the whole scripture of the Old Covenant: because, of course, Moses himself was a prophet and the other prophets were interpreters of the law given by Moses: but I will be content with one, Acts 3:21, 22, where Peter, having enumerated the prophets generally, subjoins: For Moses said. But why I think that this word should be taken in a looser sense here, will appear immediately.

Ὅτι Ναζωραῖ@ κληθήσεται) That 'that', even when testimonies of the Old Covenant are cited, often indicates a sense drawn from many places rather than the words of one place: as appears in Acts 10:43 and elsewhere. Although indeed this city, most known for the dwelling of Joseph and Mary, is written in Syriac with a צ, that does not seem to me sufficient cause to prevent us from believing that it was written in Hebrew in ancient times with a ז; for a change could easily have occurred between letters of such similar sound, so that both this and that are accustomed to be expressed by the same Greek letter. Thus also for צדק the Syrians write זרקיא and זרק are for them Sadducees: indeed, in the very codices of the Holy Scriptures, a commutation of these letters among themselves appears. Compare 1 Chron. 16:32 with Ps. 96:12, and 1 Chron. 13:9 with 2 Sam. 6; likewise Num. 26:12 with Gen. 46:10. So also Num. 26:14 with Gen. 46:16. And where there is now a ז, the Greeks read צ in Gen. 49:24. And where there is a צ, they read ז in Isa. 33:18. Thus Moses Gerundensis says that in Job 40:12 יחפץ is placed for יפח because these two letters are often interchanged, adding the examples זעקה and צעקה, likewise זרב and צרב.

Wherefore this seems to me to be the opinion of Matthew, that in the Old Covenant those who, above the common prescriptions of the law, dedicated not their possessions but themselves to God for a certain peculiar holiness, were called Nazarenes: that this, however, was eminently fulfilled in Christ, as one who devoted himself of his own accord not to abstinence from wine or other ceremonies of that kind, but to a bloody and ignominious death, to which the words of Christ in John 17:19 look, where there is the word ἁγιάζω, whence ἁγιασμέν@, which is placed among the LXX for a Nazarene. A passage of Philo concerning the Nazarites brings light to this interpretation: where he gives the reason why their vow was called μεγάλη εὐχὴ: when some offer first-fruits from every part of creation, of fire, barley, oil, wheat, the finest of the first-fruits, then the first-born of animals, consecrating those from the clean, and valuing those from the unclean according to their worth; and no longer having materials in which they might manifest their piety, they dedicate and consecrate themselves, showing an unspeakable holiness and a certain excess of a God-loving mind; wherefore it is rightly called a great vow; for a man is himself the greatest of possessions to himself, which he yields and gives up. If you compare these things with what the writer to the Hebrews treats in X. 5. 6. 7. 8. 9. 10. you will see most openly that the name of Nazarite belongs to Christ in the most perfect way. Matthew therefore says, things having been so disposed by God, that Joseph and Mary, having returned from Egypt, should fix their home in Nazareth, that this was done so that from that habitation that name might adhere to Christ, by which his most perfect holiness and the vow by which our salvation was undertaken might be noted. Nor indeed ought it to seem fortuitous that popular speech called our Lord Jesus a Nazarene, as if by a perpetual surname, as appears in Matt. XXVI. 7. Mark I. 24. X. 47. XIV. 67. XVI. 6. Luke IV. 34. XVIII. 37. XXIV. 19. John XVIII. 5. 7. XIX. 19. Acts II. 22. III. 6. IV. 10. VI. 14. XXII. 8. XXVI. 9. whence also those who had given their name to his most holy discipline were called Nazarenes XXIV. 5. Tertullian against Marcion IV. Christ was to be called a Nazarene according to the prophecy of the Creator: whence also by that very name the Jews call us Nazarenes through him: for we are also those of whom it is written, The Nazarenes were exalted above the snow. Nor would I omit that, since the name derived from the town has the ending Ναζαραῖος and Ναζαρηνὸς among the writers of the New Testament (which Stephanus in his work περὶ πόλεων teaches us comes into use in most gentile appellations of Oriental peoples), Matthew preferred to use the word Ναζωραῖος, as one that had been received in the meaning of votive holiness: for that which is Ναζιραῖος or Ναζιραῖος among the LXX and other Hellenists, Ναζιραῖος among Josephus and Greek Christian writers, but in the New Testament is written now Ναζωραῖος, now Ναζαρηνὸς, is a diversity of pronunciation, not of the word.

There are various opinions concerning this passage. First, that one is not inappropriate which wishes Christ to be called a Nazarene because it was predicted by the Prophets that he himself would be a Nazarene, since to be called the same is as much as to be in reality. For Christ would be a Nazarene, i.e., consecrated to God, not only shadowed forth by types, which excellently represented Christ, namely Joseph, who in Gen. XLIX. Deut. XXXIII. 16 is called the Nazarene of his brothers, Samson, who was a Nazarite to God from the womb Jud. XIII. 5. Samuel, who it is evident from the law of Nazariteship in 1 Sam. II. 28 was likewise devoted to God; but it was also predicted when the Prophets prophesied about the Messiah who would consecrate himself to God. See Ps. XL. 7 seqq. Ps. XXII. 23. Is. L. 4 seqq. ch. LII. 10. of whom Jerome in ch. II of Matthew interprets it as holy Nazarene, and all scripture commemorates that the Lord would be holy. And Theophylact on this passage. The word Nazarene signifies sanctified, and Jesus the Christ could reasonably be called a Nazarene, for the Lord is called the Holy One of Israel by many Prophets. For Christ was truly נצר separated from others, and holy Heb. VII. 26. Dan. IX. 24. and was formerly designated by Nazarites, both natural and votive, destined for a peculiar office, crowned with glory and honor. Concerning whom the Lord says in Ps. CXXXII. 17. 18. there I will make the horn of David to bud, where I have prepared a lamp for my anointed, I will clothe his enemies with shame, but upon him shall flourish the נצר his crown, or sanctification. It was done by the wonderful providence of God, as Spanheim says in Dub. Evang. XCIII., that Christ, on the occasion of his upbringing in Nazareth, should be called a Nazarene: by the Jews indeed in jest and contempt because of the abject condition of the city of Nazareth, but by God indeed from a most pious purpose as a testimony to that stubborn nation for a clearly different end, so that it might be designated that Christ is the true Nazarene, and indeed antonomastically such a true antitype and complement of the legal Nazarenes, both Kings and Priests and others consecrated to God in a special way. This opinion has approved itself to Tertullian, Book IV, ch. 8, against Marcion; Jerome and Theophylact (whom I praised earlier); Rupert of Deutz, John Ferus, B. Luther, B. Chemnitz, Calvin, Bucer, Toussain, Diodati in his notes on the Italian Bible, the Genevans in the marginal gloss, Scultetus, Spanheim, Heinsius in Aristarchus Sacrus, Exercitation IV; Nicolaus Collatus in a special treatise, and even F. Socinus in his sacred lectures, p. 76. B. Gerhard speaks thus of this opinion in his Commentary on Matthew, p. 138. Although Christ did not perform that vow which the Nazarenes were accustomed to perform (Num. 6:2), he was nevertheless a true Nazarene: that is, holy, innocent, undefiled, and separated from sinners (Heb. 7:24). It happened, therefore, by a wonderful disposition of God, that he dwelt for some time in Nazareth, and thus obtained that surname due to him for another reason. Nor does Erasmus's explanation in his annotations on this passage deny it: Nasir (נזיר) is called holy or consecrated by the Hebrews; now, indeed, in the Old Testament, he is not called holy in one place only, but everywhere, and in Daniel, the holy of holies.

Others, however, prefer a second opinion, namely that Matthew looked to those passages in which Christ is called נצר, a shoot, as for instance primarily in Isaiah 11:1: 'A rod shall come forth from the seed of Jesse, and a נצר, a shoot, from his roots.' They say the former designates Christ's origin from Bethlehem, the latter his habitation and upbringing in Nazareth. To this they also refer Isaiah 60:21, and indeed even Isaiah 53:2, Jeremiah 23:5, 33:15, Zechariah 3:8, 6:12, although in these places the name צמח occurs, which is a synonym for it. This opinion does not need the excuse of a change of letters, as if the city of Nazareth had been written with a ז in ancient times. For this is a mere conjecture. Certainly, that city is found everywhere expressed with a Zade, never with a Zain. And the same spelling is retained by the Syriac and Arabic interpreters. Thus, therefore, it happened by divine providence that Christ, that נצר predicted by the Prophets, inhabited that place, so that the prophecies of the Prophets might be fulfilled, to whom the name of the Messiah, נצר, from which Nazareth is also derived, was once attributed, and thus Jesus of Nazareth would be convinced to be the true Messiah even from the place of his upbringing. Added to this is the fact that David de Pomis, a Jewish lexicographer, observes that Nazareth itself was also called נצר, and with this observation admitted, Spanheim himself confesses that this opinion would be sufficiently probable: namely, that God, by a singular purpose, wished Joseph to inhabit such a city, which had the name נצר, so that the same name would cling to Christ while living there, and thus the truth would correspond to the predictions. Fr. Junius urges this, that it was fitting that just as Christ was described by the Prophets by his nation, mother, time and place of birth, doctrine, actions, and passions, as well as by his person and office; so also he should be described by the place of his habitation: and therefore the place of habitation is indicated by the Prophet Isaiah 11 through a ὑπαινιγμὸν (hint), consisting not in the meaning of the whole, but in the translation of a single word. Jerome supports this opinion in his Epistle to Pammachius on the best kind of interpreting, and in ch. 11: 'And now that which all the ecclesiastics seek in the Gospel of Matthew and do not find, where it is written: "And he shall be called a Nazarene," the LEARNED HEBREWS think it is taken from this passage.' Tremellius, Aretius, Piscator, Casaubon, Polanus, and Martinius also defend this along with Junius,

Ludovicus de Dieu, Constantinus l'Empereur in his annotations on Moses Kimchi's Hodoe poricon, pp. 94, 152. Likewise Lyranus, Tostatus, Salmero, Lucas Brugensis, Jansenius, Eman. Saa, Maldonatus, Barradas, Baronius, and from our own, B. Walther in his Harmony, B. Glassius in Philologia Sacra, as well as Schindler and others. Nor does B. Gerhard disapprove of that explanation in the aforementioned place.

Thirdly, Dr. Winstrupius in his Pandects on Matthew, p. 171, combines both of those opinions: that the sayings of the Prophets were fulfilled both properly and literally, namely those in which Christ is called נצר, a flower, shoot, or sprout (Isaiah 11:1, 4:2, 60:21), and allegorically, or typically and analogically, in which he himself was prefigured as נזר, a separated one, a Nazarene, of which types Joseph and Samson were examples. But those places and names are very different, nor if he is called a Nazarene from a shoot, could he be so denominated from the separation of the Nazarenes, for which reason those things are inconsistent: indeed, the Evangelist testifies that Christ was not called a Nazarene from either, neither from a shoot nor from a vow or order of Naziriteship, but from the city of Nazareth, which had been predicted by the Prophets. And therefore, the question is where it was predicted.

Fourthly, there are those who wish the name נצר to be looked to, which, being attributed to God, signifies a Savior (Job 7:20, Proverbs 24:12), insofar as it had been predicted everywhere through the Prophets that Christ is our Savior: which opinion B. Gerhard also brings up in the aforementioned place. And this especially pleased Socinus in his sacred lectures, p. 47, although he professes to have found it in no one.

Others, fifthly, have recourse here to lost books, such as Chrysostom, Tom. IX, on Matthew, and Ofterod in his Institutiones XXVI, which was also done by Socinus in the aforementioned place. Others, sixthly, to the Prophets so called in a secondary sense, namely the interpreters of the Prophets, with Jansenius and Andr. Osiander in his Harmony: but canonical writers are not accustomed to allege anything either from lost books or from those called Prophets in an improper sense under the title of Prophets, and it is not without danger to attribute such allegations to the Holy Spirit. Therefore, if anyone should still judge that the diversity of letters, which Grotius speciously excuses, stands in the way of the explanation, he will be able to prefer the second of those: for although Nezer and Nazarene are not the same, nothing prevents that in the denomination of a Nazarene, one could have looked to that prophecy concerning the shoot of the Davidic Nezer. If from a comparison of both places of Holy Scripture it be said that the Prophet hinted at the place of habitation in that appellation of the Messiah, whence the city of Nazareth had its name, and that the Evangelist explained more clearly that which was hinted at in the same place. There remains, however, lastly another and more convenient opinion, namely that, the tenor of the words of Matthew being observed, τὸ ῥηθὲν διὰ τῶν προφητῶν, that which was spoken through the Prophets, it may be said that some prophecy is referred to, handed down through one and another Prophet, which was known to the common people as, HE SHALL BE CALLED A NAZARENE, because the Evangelist does not say: that which IS WRITTEN in the Prophets, but that which WAS SPOKEN through the Prophets, just as he spoke the same in chapter XXVII. 9, when he attributed some prophecy that was unwritten, but not unknown to the people of God, handed down by Jeremiah, as then fulfilled: That which was spoken through Jeremiah the prophet. For since the Evangelist testifies that this was expressly predicted through the Prophets, not concerning some appellative name, nor concerning the state and condition of the Nazarite vow, but concerning a proper name, sought from the place of upbringing and a certain city, unless we wish to do violence to the same, what stands in the way of our believing that this was predicted long ago through the Prophets, or rather, who will be able to call this into doubt or derogate from the faith of the Evangelist who says that this was predicted? Nor in truth will anything accrue from this to the unwritten traditions of the Papists: because this prophecy, even if it was unwritten before the Canon of the New Testament, did not remain unwritten, but by Matthew here inserted into the Canon, it is now written. With the Papists, however, the dispute is about such traditions as remain in the Church after the Canon of Scripture has been established, and are not found in any part of the Canonical Scripture: just as the prophecy of Enoch was handed down for some centuries, indeed for some thousands of years, and perhaps propagated in the Church, yet afterwards it was brought into the Canonical Scripture by the Apostle Jude through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit and is no longer unwritten, and the saying of Christ, handed down unwritten and previously propagated or preserved, was recalled to memory by Paul to the Ephesians, and was brought into the Canonical Scripture by Luke in the Acts, recounting Paul's farewell address, Acts XX. 36. In which sense the opinion of Chrysostom, Euthymius, and Theophylact can be admitted, that this prophecy is held by tradition, and was of the Prophets, even if it does not exist in any prophetic writing. Nor can that argument move us, that the scribes were ignorant that the Messiah had to come from Galilee, John VII. 41, because there the discourse is about the place of birth, Bethlehem, and it is denied that Christ had to come from Galilee by reason of birth, not about the place of upbringing. And let us suppose that that prophetic oracle was unknown to the scribes, could it not therefore have been inspired by the Holy Spirit to Matthew? For the prophecy of Enoch could also have been unknown, which God truly suggested and inspired to Jude the Apostle, and through him brought into Scripture. It suffices that such oracles were once handed down by the Prophets (which Matthew and Jude openly testify) or were preserved and propagated in the Church up to that point, and thus were publicly known in their time, or less so, which can finally be left in the middle.

Naza- ræus vocari habebat secundum Prophetiam Christus creatoris: unde & ipso nomine nos Iudæi Nazaræos appellant per eum: nam & sumus de quibus scriptum est, Nazaræi exaltati sunt su- per nivem. Nec illud omiserim, cum nomen ab oppido de- ductum habeat exitum apud novi federis scriptores Ναζα- ραῖ@ & Ναζαρηνὸς (quod in plerisque appellationibus gen- tilitiis Orientalium populorum usu venire nos docet Ste- phanus περὶ πόλεων) maluisse Matthæum uti voce Ναζωραῖος, ut quæ recepta esset in significatu votivæ sanctimoniæ: nam quod apud LXX. & Hellenistas alios Ναζιραῖ@ vel Ναζι- ραῖ@, apud Josephum & Scriptores Christianos Græcos Να- ζιραῖ@, in novo autem federe modo Ναζωραῖ@, modo Να- ζαρην@ scribitur, pronunciationis est, non vocis diversitas.

Alii tamen secundo sententiam aliam præfe- runt, quod nempe ea loca respexerit Matthæus in quibus Christus vocatus est נצר surculus, utpote imprimis Es. XI. 1. Egredietur Virga de semine Isai, & נצר surculus de radicibus ejus. Priori dicant de- signatam esse Christi originem è Bethlehem, poste- riori habitationem & educationem ejus in Nazareth. Quo referunt quoque Es. LX. 21. imo etiam t. IV. 2 c. LIII. 2. Jer. XXIII. 1. c. XXXIII. 15. Zach. III. 8. c. VI. 12. quamvis in his locis nomen צמח occur- rat illi Synonymum. Quæ sententia opus non ha- bet excusatione commutationis literarum quasi antiquitus per ז scripta fuerit urbs Nazareth. Nam hæc mera est conjectura. Ubique certe reperitur urbs illa expressa per Zade, nusquam per Zain. Et retinetur eadem scriptio penes interpretes Sy- rum, & Arabem. Sic ergo divina providentia fa- ctum, ut eum inhabitaret locum Christus נצר ille prædictus à Prophetis, ut implerentur vaticinia Prophetarum, quibus nomen Messiæ נצר, unde Nazareth etiam derivatur, olim tributum, adeoque è loco etiam educationis Jesum Nazarenum ve- rum esse Messiam convinceretur. Accedit, quod David de Pomis Lexicographus Judæus observet, ipsam Nazareth quoque dictam נצר, qua observa- tione admissa fatetur ipse Spanhemius, probabi- lem satis futuram istam opinionem: Deum nempe sin- gulari consilio voluisse Josephum ejusmodi urbem in- colere, cui nomen נצר ut Christo ibidem agenti idem nomen hæreret, & sic veritas prædictionibus responde- ret. Fr. Junius id urget, conveniens fuisse, ut quem- admodum Christus à gente, matre, tempore & loco nativitatis, doctrina, actionibus & passionibus, per- sona simul & officio à Prophetis descriptus fuit; sic et- iam à loco habitationis describeretur: ideoque locum habitationis à Propheta Es. XI. per ὑπαινιγμὸν subindi- catum, consistentem non in sententia totius, sed in unius vocis translatione. Huic sententiæ patrocinatur Hieronym. in Epist. ad Pammach. de optim. inter- pret. genere & in c. XI. Et jam illud, quod in Evan- gelio Matthæi omnes quærunt Ecclesiastici, & non inveniunt, ubi scriptum sit: & Nazarenus vocabitur, ERUDITI HEBRÆI de hoc loco affumptum pu- tant. LX. tum allegori- ce, seu typice & analogice, in quibus ipse præti- guratus est ut נזר separatus, Nazaræus, cujus typi fuerint Josephus & Simson: Sed diversa maxime sunt illa loca & nomina, nec si à surculo Nazarenus dicitur, à separatione Nazaræorum sic denominari potuit, quapropter ἀσύςατα illa sunt: imo à neu- tro Christum Nazarenum vocari, neque à surculo, neque à voto aut ordine Nazaræatus, sed à civitate Na- zareth, prædictum fuisse à Prophetis testatur Ev- angelista. Ideoque ubi prædictum sit quæritur.

Quarto sunt, qui respici velint nomen נצר quod Deo tributum Servatorem significat Job. VII. 20. Prov. XXIV. 12. siquidem per Prophetas passim prædictum fuerit, Christum servatorem nostrum esse: quam sententiam adducit & B. Gerhardus l. c. Et imprimis ea placuit Socino lect. sacr. p. 47. etsi eam apud neminem se invenisse profiteatur.

Alii quinto recipiunt hic se ad libros deperditos, utpote Chrysost. Tom. IX. in Matth. Ofterod in in- stitut. XXVI. quod etiam à Socino factum l. c. Alii Sexto ad Prophetas sensu secundario ita dictos, in- terpretes nempe Prophetarum cum Jansenio & Andr. Osiandr. in Harmonia: sed neque è deper- ditis libris, neque ex Prophetis ἀκύρως ita dictis sub Prophetarum titulo allegare solent aliquid scri- ptores Canonici, & periculo non vacat, talia allega- ta Spiritui S. tribuere. Quapropter si literarum di- versitatem, quam speciose Grotius excusat, expli- cationi obstare quis adhuc judicaverit, secundam ex illis præferre poterit: Nam quamvis idem non sit Nezer & Nazaræus, nihil tamen obstat quo mi- nus in denominatione Nazareni ad vaticinium il- lud de surculo Davidici Nezer respici potuerit. Si ex collatione utriusque loci S. S. per Prophetam subinnuisse dicatur locum habitationis in illa appel- latione Messiæ, unde urbs Nazareth nomen ha- buit, & per Evangelistam, id quod ibidem subindi- catum fuit, clarius exposuisse. Restat tamen po- stremo alia adhuc, eademque convenientior sen- tentia, ut nempe observato tenore verborum Matthæi τὸ ῥηθὲν διὰ τῶν προφητῶν, quod dictum est per Prophetas, dicatur respici vaticinium aliquod traditum per unum atq; alterum Prophetam, quod dictum in Vulgus notum fuerit, NAZARENUS VOCABITUR, quia non ait Evangelista: quod SCRIPTUM EST in Prophetis, sed quod DI- CTUM EST per Prophetis, quemadmodum idem & c. XXVII. 9. loquutus est, cum vaticinium aliquod ἄγραφον, sed populo Dei non ignotum à Jeremia traditum alligavit tunc impletum: Τὸ ῥηθὲν διὰ ἰερεμίου τῦ προφήτε. Nam quum diserte id prædi- ctum fuisse testetur Evangelista per Prophetas, non de nomine quodam appellativo, nec de statu & conditione Nazaræatus, sed de nomine proprio, à lo- co educationis, & civitate certa petito, nisi vim ei- dem facere velimus, quid obstat, quo minus id prædictum olim per Prophetas credamus, imo qui vocari id in dubium aut fides dicenti Evangelistæ derogari poterit, hoc prædictum fuisse? Neque ve- ro inde traditionibus ἄγραφως Pontificiorum ac- cedet quicquam: quia vaticinium hoc, etsi ἄγρα- φον fuerit ante Canonem N. T. ἄγραφον non mansit, sed per Matthæum hic Canoni insertum ἔνγραφον, jam est. Cum Pontificiis v. disputatio de talibus est traditionibus, quæ post Scripturæ Canonem constitu- tum in Ecclesia superent, nec in ulla scripturæ Ca- nonicæ parte reperiantur: quemadmodum Eno- chi Vaticinium ante aliquot secula, imo millenarios aliquot annorum traditum & forsan in Ecclesia propagatum fuit, postea tamen in Scripturam Ca- nonicam per Apostolum Judam inspiratione S. S. relatum minime ἄγραφον amplius est, & dictum Christi ἄγραφως traditum, & prius propagatum vel conservatum, in memoriam revocatum à Paulo Ephesinis fuit, & à Luca in Actis recensente Pauli concionem valedictoriam in scripturam Canoni- cam relatum est Act. XX. 36. Quo sensu Chrysosto- mi, Euthymii & Theophylacti sententia admitti po- test, quod è traditione hæc Prophetia habeatur, & Prophetarum fuerit, etsi in nullo scripto Prophe- tico extet. Neque movere nos ratio illa potest, quod scribæ ignorarint, Messiam è Galilæa venire debuisse, Joh. VII. 41. quia ibi de loco nativitatis, Bethlehemo sermo est, & negatur Christum è Ga- lilæa ratione nativitatis prodire debuisse, non de loco educationis. Et ponamus, ignotum Oraculum illud Propheticum fuisse scribis, num ideo non po- tuit à S. S. Matthæo inspirari? Nam & vaticinium Enochi poterat ignotum fuisse, quod vero sugges- sit, & inspiravit DEUS Judæ Apostolo, & per eun- dem in Scripturam retulit. Sufficit, quod olim per Prophetas oracula talia tradita sint, (quod Mat- thæus æque, ac Judas palam testantur) seu conser- vata eo usque ac propagata in Ecclesia, adeoque nota, ipsorum tempore, publice fuerint, seu mi- nus, quod tandem in medio relinqui potest.

## 3:1 Argument
CHAPTER III. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

John the Baptist preaches in the desert, repent, the kingdom of heaven has drawn near, of which Isaiah prophesied (c. XL. 3.), his clothing and food, and the influx of the Jewish people to receive Baptism; he warns the Pharisees gravely about the fruits of repentance, lest they boast rashly of Abraham as their Father, and about the imminent coming of him who is to baptize with the Holy Spirit and is to purge his threshing floor. And when Jesus came from Galilee to be baptized, although the Baptist refused, yet with Jesus urging that all righteousness must be fulfilled, he himself was baptized, and heaven opened to him, and the Holy Spirit descended from heaven, and the voice of the Father was heard, testifying of the Son, in whom he was well pleased.

There are two parts: I. The sermon of John the Baptist, his baptism, and his prediction about Jesus, up to v. 12. II. The baptism of Jesus, after a conversation held with John, with a heavenly theophany. Up to the end of the chapter.

PART I. The sermon of John the Baptist, Baptism, and the prediction about Jesus.

Latin:

CAPUT III. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Johannes Baptista prædicat in deserto, agite pœnitentiam, appropinquavit regnum cœ- lorum, de quo vaticinatus est Esaias (c. XL. 3.) ejus amictus, & victus, ac con- fluxus populi Judaici ad Baptismum susci- piendum; qui Pharisæos graviter monet de fructibus pœnitentiæ, ne temere de Abrahamo Patre glorientur, & de immi- nente adventu ejus, qui Spiritu S. bapti- zaturus & aream suam purgaturus est. Et quum e Galilæa veniret Jesus, ut ba- ptizaretur, etsi renueret Baptista, urgen- te tamen Jesu, quod omnis implenda sit ju- stitia, baptizatus ipse est, cœlumque se aperuit, & descendit Spiritus S. de cœlo, vox autem Patris audita est, testans de Filio, in quo ipsi complacuit.

Partes sunt duæ: I. Johannis Baptistæ concio, ba- ptismus & de Jesu prædictio, ad v. 12. II. Jesu, collo- quio habito cum Johanne, baptizatio, cum Johanne, baptizatio, cum cælesti θεοφανεία. Usque ad finem capitis.

PARS I. Johannis Baptistæ concio, Baptismus, & de Jesu prædictio.

## 3:2
Vers. 2. Μετανοεῖτε) see Mark. Τῶν ὁρανῶν) The Hebrews indeed call heaven, even when it signifies the aerial or starry region, by a word of plural, or rather dual, number: and the Greeks do not do this: and therefore you will also find that region called in the singular number here and there in these writers. What then does this plural οὐρανῶν mean here and in many other places? It means the same thing that the Hebrews call שמי שמים, that is, the highest and invisible heaven: which for Chrysostom in the VIII chapter to the Romans is ὁ τῶν οὐρανῶν οὐρανός. For it is the custom of the Hebrews in such constructions sometimes to leave the first member unsaid: thus חכמות is said for חכמות חכמת, that is, most excellent wisdom: בהמות for בהמות בהמת, that is, the most excellent of beasts: אלהים for אלהים אלהה, that is, the highest God. In a clearly similar way the writer to the Hebrews, having first named ἅγια ἁγίων, soon calls them ἅγια by abbreviation in chapter IX. The kingdom of heaven among the Hebrews, whose speech Christ follows, sometimes signifies that most blessed state after the resurrection, when God will be all in all, sometimes those things that lead to it, that is, the law both old (for they also call this by that name) and new, that is, the kingdom of the Messiah, in which way the kingdom of heaven is taken here: for the prophecy of Daniel is looked to, the fulfillment of which was expected by the people around these times. All these things are also accustomed to be called the kingdom of God from Psalm XLVII. 9. For the kingdom of God and the kingdom of heaven are the same. For because that highest heaven is as it were the citadel and palace of God, it is therefore accustomed to be put for God. But since the Hebrews expected the greatest blessings in the times of the Messiah, they could sufficiently understand that to obtain them it was necessary for obstacles to be removed, that is, the crimes which would render them unworthy of such great benefits.

As there is no doubt that the kingdom of heaven often denotes the most blessed state in which God will be all in all, so Grotius rashly pronounces that the law, both old and new, which he asserts to be the Kingdom of the Messiah, is designated by the kingdom of God. He certainly had no passage to bring forward where the kingdom of heaven denotes the old law, none where it denotes the Gospel, nor any where the Gospel is the same as the Kingdom of the Messiah. But concerning the meaning of those words, the kingdom of heaven has drawn near, we have spoken above.

Grotius discourses about Baptism as if it were not a medium and Sacrament of regeneration and salvation, but merely an external economy, and one derived from both the Hebrews and the Gentiles. These things are unworthy of Christian minds and ears. For we know that Baptism was not derived from the Hebrews to the Christians, but is a Sacrament proper to the New Testament, instituted by Christ himself; that it is not an external rite indicating the idolatry and pollution of the Jews, but an effective medium ordained for the washing away of sins and for regeneration and eternal salvation. The traditions of the Hebrews are not of such antiquity that the baptism of John could have been derived from them, and they have little certainty; finally, they are clearly alien to this most holy institution. For it was not for the sake of superstitious rites or the will-worship of the Jews, which never pleased God and was gravely rebuked by Christ, Matt. XV. baptism was introduced, but that it pleased divine wisdom to ordain this means of regeneration and renewal in the time of the New Testament, and to substitute it in the place of circumcision, which because it was foretold by Zechariah ch. XIII, it also had to serve as a mark to designate the times and the coming of the Messiah, whence from this new and unusual Sacrament the Pharisees themselves and the experts in the Law [concluded] that John was either a unique Prophet or the Messiah himself, John I. But that the Gentiles also employed washings, that proceeded from emulation and the mockery of Satan, who as the perpetual ape of God introduced such rites among his own worshippers, which he was not ignorant had been prescribed for the worshippers of the true God, so that he might exalt the sacred rites of the Gentiles and obscure or harass the true worship of God. Whether, however, Baptism was always administered by immersion, which Grotius maintains, or also by pouring, we have spoken of that in the Appendix to the Examination of Doctrine and Syncretism. Ref. on the Perfection of Christ p. 490. Nor indeed even does the word βαπτισμῦ or the places chosen for that rite solidly prove immersion: nor is it indeed plausible that St. John immersed naked in the public sight of men and women whomever he was baptizing, or that such vessels were always at hand when those converted to Christ were baptized: for example, that jailer with his family in Acts 16:33, or where many thousands were baptized by the Apostles in one day, as we have here confessed by the Reformed scholar Ant. Walaeus in his Loca Communia, p. 937.

Latin:

Vers. 2. Μετανοεῖτε) vide Marcum. Τῶν ὁρανῶν) Hebræi quidem cœlum, etiam cum aërëam aut sideream regionem significat, appellant voce soni pluralis, aut potius binarii: ac Græci id non faciunt: ideoque etiam passim in his Scri- ptoribus utramvis illam regionem dictam invenies numero unitatis. Quid ergo & hic & aliis multis in locis sibi vult plurale hoc οὐρανῶν? Nimirum idem quod Hebræi dicunt שמי שמים, id est, cœlum supremum atque inaspe- ctabile: qui Chrysostomo in IIX. caput ad Romanos ὁ τῶν οὐρανῶν οὐρανός. Mos enim est Hebræis in ejusmodi constru- ctionibus interdum prius membrum subticere: ita חכמות dicitur pro חכמות חכמת, id est, excellen- tissima sapientia: בהמות pro בהמות בהמת, id est, eximia ferarum אלהים pro אלהים אלהה id est Deus summus. Simili plane modo Scriptor ad Hebræos, quæ primum nominârat ἅγια ἁγίων, mox per compen- dium ἅγια nominat cap. IX. Regnum autem cœli apud He- bræos, quorum sermonem Christus sequitur, interdum significat beatissimum illum statum post resurrectionem, cum Deus erit omnia in omnibus, interdum quæ eo du- cunt, id est legem tum veterem (nam hanc quoque eo no- mine appellant) tum novam, id est regnum Messiæ, quo- modo hic regnum cœli sumitur: Respicitur enim Danielis vaticinium, cujus implementum circa hæc tempora etiam à populo exspectabatur. Hæc omnia dici solent & re- gnum Dei ex Psalmo XLVII. 9. Idem enim est regnum Dei & regnum cœli. Nam quia summum illud cœlum velut arx & regia est Dei, ideo pro Deo poni solet. Ma- xima autem bona Messiæ temporibus cum exspectarent Hebræi, satis intelligere poterant, ad ea adipiscenda opus esse amoveri impedimenta, id est crimina, quæ ipsos indi- gnos tantis beneficiis essent redditura.

Regnum cœlorum uti beatissimum statum, quo Deus erit omnia in omnibus sæpe notare nullum est dubium, ita perperam legem tum veterem, tum novam, quam esse Regnum Messiæ ἅπερ γραφῆς as- serit, per regnum Dei designari temere pronunciat Grotius. Nullum certe locum proferre habuit, ubi Regnum cœli notet legem veterem, nullum ubi no- tet Evangelium, neque ullum, ubi Evangelium idem sit quod Regnum Messiæ. De sensu autem illorum verborum, appropinquavit regnum cœlorum, supra diximus.

De Baptismo ita disserit Grotius, ac si non me- dium & Sacramentum regenerationis & salutis illum haberet, sed pro mera Oeconomia externa, eaque tum ab Ebræis, tum à gentibus derivata. Quæ indigna sunt Christianis mentibus & auribus. No- vimus enim Baptismum non ab Ebræis ad Christia- nos derivatum, sed Novi Testamenti proprium Sa- cramentum esse ab ipso Christo institutum; non ri- tum esse externum, indicantem Judæorum Idolola- triam & pollutionem sed medium efficax ad abluen- dum peccata, & ad regenerationem ac salutem æter- nam ordinatum. Traditiones Ebræorum nec ejus antiquitatis sunt, ut inde βάπτισμα Johannis ac- cessi possit, & parum certitudinis habent; denique ab hoc sanctissimo etiam instituto plane alienæ sunt. Non enim in gratiam rituum superstitiosorum; vel ἐθελοθρησκείας Judæorum, quæ nunquam Deo placuit, & à Christo graviter reprehensa est Matt. XV. βά- πτισμα invectum est, sed quod divinæ sapientiæ placuerit, hocce medium regenerationis & reno- vationis ordinare tempore Novi Testamenti, illud- que in locum circumcisionis surrogare, quod quia prædictum erat à Zacharia c. XIII. characteris etiam vicem esse debebat ad designandum tempora, & adventum Messiæ, unde ex hoc novo & inusitato Sacramento ipsimet Pharisæi, & Legisperiti Johan- nem vel Prophetam singularem, vel ipsummet Mes- siam esse Joh. I. Quod vero gentes etiam lotiones adhibuêre, id ex κακοζηλίᾳ profectum, & ludibrio Satanæ, qui tanquam simia Dei perpetua tales ri- tus penes sui cultores invexit, quos veri Dei culto- ribus præscriptos non ignoravit, ut sacra gentilium extolleret, ac verum Dei cultum obscuraret, vel exagitaret. Utrum autem mersatione semper, quod Grotius vult, an perfusione etiam Baptisma admini- stratum sit, de eo diximus in App. ad Exam. Doctr. & Syncret. Ref. de Perf. Christi p. 490. Nec sane vel vox βαπτισμῦ vel loca ad eum ritum delecta so- lide mersionem probant: neque vero affine est S. Johannem nudos immersisse in conspectu pu- blico virorum, & mulierum quoscunque baptiza- bat, aut semper in promptu fuisse vasa talia, cum baptizati sunt conversi ad Christum: exempli gra- tia ille carceris præfectus, cum familia sua Act. XVI. 33. aut ubi multa millia uno die ab Apostolis ba- ptizata sunt, ut hic habemus confitentem è Refor- matis Ant. Walæum in LL. CC. p. 937.

## 3:3
Verse 3. ἑτοιμάσατε) The LXX rightly, and Matthew's interpreter following them, translates פנו as ἑτοιμάσατε. It is clear that this word is taken in this way in Gen. 24:31; regarding the meaning, see what is said on chapter 3 of Luke.

Latin:

Vers. 3. ἑτοιμάσατε) Recte LXX. & hos secutus Mat- thæi interpres פנו vertit ἑτοιμάσατε. Apertum est ita sumi hoc verbum Gen. XXIV. 31. de sensu vide quæ di- centur ad caput III. Lucæ.

## 3:4
Verse 4. ἀπὸ τριχῶν καμήλυ] A manner of life undoubtedly more severe, consistent with a frugal diet: such as Lucan ascribes to his Cato:

For him, hunger served as a feast, and his great household gods had banished winter from his roof, and he had donned a shaggy toga over his limbs in the manner of a Roman Quirite.

Previously he had said:

He had allowed his uncut gray hairs to descend onto his rigid brow, and a mournful beard to grow upon his cheeks. Among the Hebrews, it was the custom to be clothed in hair during mourning, as we learn from Josephus in book 16 of the Antiquities. Such were clearly the Nazarites of the Hebrews, whether temporary or perpetual. For they both let their hair and beard grow and were clothed in a shaggy toga, which toga had the name אדרת, as the Masters of the Hebrews teach us: Now John was a perpetual Nazarite, as Luke 1:15 teaches us. But since Elijah is also described to us with long hair in 2 Kings 1:8, and his own toga is called by that very name אדרת in 1 Kings 19:19, it follows that either he too was a Nazarite, or the habit of the Prophet and the Nazarite was the same. This is the more credible because Zechariah 13:4 calls the habit of a Prophet אדרת שער, a hairy toga, and the writer to the Hebrews, perhaps speaking of others as well, but especially of the Prophets, describes them to us ἐν μηλωταῖς, ἐν αἰγείοις δέρμασιν: Clement of Rome, however, who imitated the writer to the Hebrews in many things, as the ancients teach us, in his Epistle to the Corinthians, speaks thus of the Prophets, among whom he also names John the Baptist: ἐν δέρμασιν, αἰγέιοις τὲ μηλωταῖς, καὶ τριχῶν καμηλείων πλέγμασιν περιεπάτησαν. That is not unworthy of observation, brought about by divine providence, that he who came in the spirit of Elijah, and was therefore named Elijah by the Prophets, should also resemble Elijah in his outward habit.

Ζώνην δερματίνην) Matthew would have written אזור עור: which is said of Elijah in 2 Kings 1:8, where the LXX similarly translate it ζώνην δερματίνην. This also pertained to the profession of a more severe life, since other Jews had a belt of more exquisite material, and the wealthier ones even varied them with gold and jewels.

περὶ τὴν ὀσφὺν αὐτῦ) במתניו, as it is in the aforementioned place. It appears that the part of the body which is accustomed to be girded is called this. Luke 12:35, Eph. 6:14, 1 Pet. 1:13.

Ἀκρίδες) To those things which learned men have noted regarding the use of locusts for food, add what Leo Africanus has in book 9.

Latin:

Vers. 4. ἀπὸ τριχῶν καμήλυ] Habitus haud dubie seve- rior, victus parsimoniæ congruens: qualem Catoni suo Lucanus ascribit:

Huic epulæ fecisse famem, magnique penates Summovisse hiemem tecto, pretiosæque vestis Hirtam membra super Romani more Quiritis Induxisse togam.

Antea dixerat:

Intonsos rigidam in frontem descendere canos Passus erat, mæstamque genis increscere barbam. Apud Hebræos in luctu pilis vestiri mos erat, ut ex Josepho libro XVI. Antiquitatum discimus. Plane tales erant Hebræ- orum Nazaræi, sive temporarii sive perpetui. Nam & co- mam barbamque promittebant & hirta toga induebantur, cui togæ nomen erat אדרת ut nos docent Hebræorum Magistri: Fuit autem Johannes Nazaræus perpetuus quod nos docet Luc. I. 15. Cum vero & Elias describatur nobis coma promissa 2. Reg. I. 8. & toga ipsius illo ipso nomine אדרת vocetur 1. Reg. XIX. 19. sequitur aut hunc quoque fuisse Nazaræum, aut eundem fuisse habitum Prophetæ & Nazaræi. Quod eo magis credibile est, quia Zachar. XIII. 4. habitum Prophetæ vocat אדרת שער togam hirsu- tam, & Scriptor ad Hebræos, forte & de aliis, sed de Pro- phetis præcipue agens eos nobis describit ἐν μηλωταῖς, ἐν αἰγείοις δέρμασιν : Clemens autem Romanus Scriptorem ad Hebræos in multis imitatus, ut veteres nos docent, in Epistola ad Corinthios, de Prophetis, quos inter & Johan- nem Baptistam nominat, ita loquitur, ἐν δέρμασιν, αἰγέιοις τὲ μηλωταῖς, καὶ τριχῶν καμηλείων πλέγμασιν περιεπάτησαν. Illud observatu non indignum, factum divina providentia, ut qui veniebat in spiritu Eliæ, Elias propterea à Prophetis nominatus, etiam habitu exteriori Eliam referret.

Ζώνην δερματίνην) Scripserit Matthæus אזור עור: quod de Elia dicitur 2. Reg. I. 8. ubi LXX. similiter vertunt ζώνην δερ- ματίνην. Etiam hoc ad severioris vitæ professionem perti- nuit, cum Judæi cæteri cinctū haberent de materia exqui- sitiore, eumq; ditiores etiam auro & monilibus variarent.

περὶ τὴν ὀσφὺν αὐτῦ) במתניו ut est dicto loco. Appa- ret ita vocari partem corporis quæ cingi solet. Luc. XII. 35. Eph. VI. 14. 1. Pet. I. 13.

Ἀκρίδες) Ad ea quæ viri docti de locustarum usu ad ci- bum notarunt adde quæ habet Leo Afer lib. IX.

## 3:5
Verse 5. ἡ περίχωρος) It seems to me that the region which was of Judea across the Jordan is denoted. For it is certain that by this word not only the surrounding area, but also the adjacent area is signified.

Latin:

Vers. 5. ἡ περίχωρος) Denotari mihi videtur regio quæ Judææ erat trans Jordanem. Certum enim est hac voce non circumsita tantum, sed & adsita significari.

## 3:6
Verse 6. ἐβαπτίζοντο) This ceremony was not entirely new and it served as a prelude to the calling of the Gentiles. For the Hebrews report that sojourners who did not wish to obtain the right of Jewish citizenship did not necessarily have to be circumcised, but only had to be washed, so that in this way they might show that they were withdrawing from the worship of idols. And thus they narrate that many thousands of men were washed in the times of David and Solomon. But even now, those who come to Judaism from circumcised Gentiles, such as Ishmaelites, Persians, and Turks, are baptized by them. And the scholiast on Juvenal mentions this Jewish baptism, as does Arrian in Epictetus. They add that those who wished to be circumcised, if they came from idolatry, were washed in addition: but they also say that foreign women marrying Jews were washed, and that this very thing was done long ago by Sarah and Rebecca. There are also those who write that in the times of the Messiah there will be such a crowd of converts that they must be admitted through washing, not through circumcision. But when foreigners who were washed and not circumcised were held only by the laws which God had given to the whole human race, it is easy to understand that this washing was among the ancient institutions, having arisen, as I think, after the great flood in memory of the cleansed world, whence that famous saying among the Greeks: 'The sea washes away all the evils of men.' Certainly we read even in the Epistle of Peter that baptism is an antitype to the flood. And we shall show at the end of Matthew that washings were used by the Gentiles before their mysteries. But although baptism signifies many things which can be seen here and there among the Apostles, the primary reason for its institution seems to have properly looked to the sealing of a purpose and promise of a more amended life, in the way that Peter describes this washing in 1 Pet. 3:21, to which the remission of sins was then consequent. For John's baptism is everywhere called a baptism of repentance, with the addition sometimes of 'for the remission of sins'. It seems, therefore, that John wished to indicate by this sacred ceremony that the Jews, however much they were God's ancient confederates, had by now so far fallen away from true piety that they were to be reckoned among the worshippers of idols, and that they ought to change their whole way of life entirely by their example, if they wished to be saved. Josephus, in order to distinguish this washing of John from the lustrations of profane nations—who thought that faults themselves were washed away and souls purged of the consciousness of sins by sea water or even by a living stream, concerning which the poet says: 'O too easy ones, who think that the sad crimes of slaughter can be taken away by a river's water'—says that he taught that the mind must first be purged by a purpose of a just life, and only then was water used to wash the bodies. The words are: 'For thus he (John, of course, was teaching) taught that baptism would appear acceptable to Him (to God), not if they used it as a pretext for certain sins (to which they might still wish to indulge), but for the purity of the body, inasmuch as the soul had already been previously cleansed.' Similar is what Tertullian says in his book on repentance: 'We are not washed so that we may cease to sin, but because we have ceased; since we have already been washed in heart.' For this is the first intention of the hearer, a complete fear: [perhaps one should read 'a complete mind' or 'a complete motion']. So also Justin against Trypho says that the only baptism able to cleanse is repentance and the knowledge of God, adding also this sentiment, not unlike the saying of Josephus: 'For what is the benefit of that baptism which brightens the flesh and the body only? Be baptized in your flesh from anger, and from greed, from envy, from hatred, and behold, the body is clean.' Clement of Alexandria brings forward an old saying to the same effect: 'Know that you are clean not by a bath but by the mind'; then he adds: 'And I think that the cleansing which is directed toward the vain is sufficient, accurate, and firm, if, having condemned ourselves for the deeds that have gone before, we proceed forward after these things, having washed and cleansed the mind itself, and having felt pleasure in these things and in the former transgressions.' The propriety of the word, and the places chosen for that rite (John 3:23, Acts 8:38), and the many allusions of the Apostles which cannot be referred to sprinkling (Rom. 6:3-4, Col. 2:12), indicate that this rite was accustomed to be performed by immersion, not by pouring. The custom of pouring or sprinkling seems to have prevailed somewhat later, for the sake of those who, lying in serious illness, sought to give their name to Christ, whom others called 'clinics'. See the letter of Cyprian to Magnus. That the ancient Latins use 'tingere' (to dye/dip) for 'baptizare' (to baptize) should not seem strange, since the Latin word 'tingere' properly and for the most part means the same as to immerse.

ἐξομολογούμενοι τὰς ἁμαρτίας) It is true that by this manner of speaking nothing else is often indicated than the act, whether internal or external, of one professing himself guilty (1 John 1:9). Nevertheless, it is given to be understood from the passage in Acts 19:18, where 'and declaring their deeds' is added to the word 'confessing', that a special detestation of those sins which especially irritate God was also added. And it is credible that those who approached John did this, both so that they might be helped by his prayers to God (James 5:16) and so that they might be instructed by counsel accommodated to their special circumstances (Luke 3:12-14). The Septuagint interpreters use 'ἐξαγορεύειν'—which some think differs much from 'ἐξομολογεῖσθαι'—for the same thing in Lev. 5:5 and Num. 5:7. Nor were they deterred by the fact that that word was used in the sacred rites of the Gentiles, since otherwise one would have had to abstain from the words for altar and temple, and many other words as well.
