But as for the dispute among learned men whether by the stated laws of Leviticus and Numbers only confession before God and the one concerned is required, or indeed also before the Priest, the opinion of those who think that some particular confession of guilt was also made before the Priest seems most probable in those cases which, when known, did not bring the penalty of death, and that in others a general one sufficed: and it is credible that the same custom was observed even more religiously and freely than usual by the Jews who approached the Baptist, a man of the best faith, and not only a Priest, but also a Prophet.

Latin:

V. 6. ἐβαπτίζοντο) Cæremonia hæc neq; nova plane fuit & vocationi gentium prælusit. Tradunt enim Hebræi, in- quilinos, qui nollent jus civitatis Judaicæ adipisci, non ne- cesse habuisse circumcidi, sed ablutos dumtaxat fuisse, ut hoc modo ab idolorū cultu recedere se ostenderent. Atq; ita narrant multa hominum millia Davidis & Salomonis temporibus abluta. Sed & nunc qui ex gentibus circumci- sis, ut Ismaelitis, Persis, Turcis ad Judaismum veniunt ab i- psis baptizantur. Et hujus baptismi Judaici meminit Scho- liastes ad Juvenalem: & Arrianus Epicteto. Addunt eos etiam qui circumcidi vellent, si ab idolatria venirent in- super ablutos: sed & feminas extraneas Judæis nubentes ajunt ablutas, idque ipsum factum olim Saræ ac Rebeccæ. Sunt & qui scribant temporibus Messiæ tantam fore tur- bam conversorum, ut per lavacrum, non per circumcisio- nem sint admittendi. Cum vero peregrini abluti & non circumcisi solis legibus tenerentur quas Deus toti homi- num generi dederat, intellectu facile est, ablutionem hanc fuisse inter vetera instituta, orta, ut arbitror, post magnum diluvium in memoriam purgati mundi, unde illud celebre apud Græcos θάλασσα πλύζει πάντα τ’ ἀνθρώπων κακά. Cer- te baptisma ἀντίτυπον esse diluvio, etiam in Petri Epistola legimus. Et à gentibus ablutiones præmissas mysteriis o- stendemus ad finem Matthæi. Cum vero τὸ βάπτισμα mul- ta designet quæ passim apud Apostolos videre est, prima tamen ejus instituti ratio proprie spectasse videtur, ut obli- gnaret propositum & pollicitationem vitæ emendatioris, quomodo lavacrum hoc describit Pet. 1. III. 21. cui conse- quens deinde fuerit peccatorum remissio. Passim enim Jo- hannis βάπτισμα vocatur βάπτισμα μετανοίας additio inter- dum εἰς ἄφεσιν ἁμαρτιῶν. Videtur igitur Johannes hac sacra cæremonia indicare voluisse, Judæos, quantumvis Dei ve- teres fœderatos, in tantum jam à vera pietate descivisse, ut idolorum cultoribus accensendi essent, plæneque eorum exemplo totum vitæ genus mutare deberent, si vellentes- se salvi. Josephus, ut hanc Joannis lotionem discerneret à lustrationibus profanarum gentium, quæ aqua marina aut etiam vivo flumine culpas ipsas elui, animosq; purga- ri delictorum conscientia existimabant, de quibus Poeta: O nimium faciles, qui tristia crimina cædis Tollifluminea posse putatis aqua, ait ille auctore mentibus primum justæ vitæ proposito purgatis, usurpatam deinde aquam quæ corpora ablueret. Verba sunt: οὕτω γὰρ καὶ τὴν βάπτισιν ἀποδεκτὴν αὐτῷ (τῷ Θεῷ) φανεῖσθαι (docebat nimirum Johannes) μὴ ἐπί τινων ἁμαρτά- δων (quibus scilicet indulgere adhuc vellent) παραιτήσει χρωμένων, ἀλλ' ἐφ ἁγνείᾳ τοῦ σώματος, ἅτε δὴ καὶ τῆς ψυχῆς προεκκεκαθαρμένης. Simile est quod dicit Tertullianus libro de pœnitentia : non ideo abluimur ut delinquere desinamus, sed quia desiimus : quoniam jam corde loti sumus. Hæc enim prima audientis intentio est, metus integer : [legendum forte mens integra aut motus integer.] Sic & Justinus adversus Try- phonem: τὸ μόνον βάπτισμα καθαρίσαι δυνάμενον ait esse μετάνοιαν κὶ γνῶσιν τοῦ Θεοῦ, addens & hanc sententiam, Jose- phi dicto non dissimilem: τί γὰρ ὄφελος ἐκείνου τοῦ βαπτίσ- ματος, ὃ τὴν σάρκα κὶ μόνον τὸ σῶμα φαιδρύνει; βαπτίσθητε τὴν σάρκα ἀπὸ ὀργῆς, κὶ ἀπὸ πλεονεξίας, ἀπὸ φθόνου, ἀπὸ μί- σους, καὶ ἰδοὺ τὸ σῶμα καθαρόν ἐστι. Clemens Alexandrinus eun- dem in sensum adfert dictum vetus : ἴσθι μὴ λουτρῷ ἀλλὰ νόῳ καθαρὸς: deinde addit: ἱκανὴ δὲ οἶμαι κὶ ἡ ἐπὶ τὰ καθάρσιος, μα- ταίοις ἀκριβὴς καὶ βεβαία, εἴγε κατεγνωκότες ἑαυτῶν ἐπὶ τοῖς προγεγονόσι πραχθῆσι, προϊεμεν εἰς τὸ πρόσθεν μετὰ ταῦτα τού- σαντες κὶ τὸν νοῦν ἐξακαθύττες ταῦτα κατ' αἴσθησιν τερπόντων κὶ τῶν πρόσθεν πλημμελημάτων. Mersatione autem, non per- fusione agi solitum hunc ritum indicat & vocis proprietas, & loca ad eum ritum delecta, Joh. III. 23. Act. VIII. 38. & allusiones multæ Apostolorum quæ ad aspersionem refer- ri non possunt, Rom. VI. 3. 4. Col. II. 12. Sérius aliquanto videtur invaluisse mos perfundendi sive aspergendi, in eo- rum gratiam qui in gravi morbo cubantes nomen dare Christo expetebant, quos cæteri κλινικοὺς vocabant. Vide Epistolam Cypriani ad Magnum. Quod autem tingere pro baptizare usurpant Latini veteres, mirum videri non debet, cum Latine tingendi vox & proprie & plerumque idem valeat quod mersare.

ἐξομολογούμενοι τὰς ἁμαρτίας) Verum est hoc loquendi genere sæpe nihil aliud indicari quam actum sive internum sive externum sontem se profitentis, 1. Joh. I. 9. Attamen accessisse etiam specialem detestationem eorum peccato- rum quæ præcipue Deum irritant, ex loco Act. XIX. 18. intelligi datur, ubi voci ἐξομολογούμενοι additur κὶ ἀναγγέλ- λοντες τὰς πράξεις αὐτῶν. Hoc autem & eos, qui Johannem adibant fecisse credibile est, tum ut precibus ipsius apud Deum juvarentur, Jac. V. 16. tum ut instruerentur consilio ad speciales circumstantias accommodato, Luc. III. 12.14. ἐξαγορεύειν, quod sunt qui putant multum differre ab ἐξο- μολογεῖσθαι, pro eodem usurpant LXX. Interpretes Lev. V. 5. Num. V. 7. Neque eos terruit quod ea vox in sacris gentium usurpareturn, cum alioqui & altaris & templi, multisque a- liis vocibus abstinendum fuerit. Quod autem disputant viri eruditi an dictis legibus Levitici & Numerorum exi- gatur tantum confessio apud Deum & eum cujus interest, an vero etiam apud Sacerdotem, ea de re probabilis ma- xime videtur eorum sententia qui existimant etiam apud Sacerdotem factam aliquam particularem culpæ confes- sionem, in iis quæ cognita capitis pœnam non adferebant, in cæteris suffecisse generalem: eundemque morem etiam solito religiosius ac liberius observatum credibile est à Ju- dæis qui ad Baptistam optimæ fidei hominem, nec Sa- cerdotem tantum, sed & Prophetam accedebant.

## 3:7
V. 7. 'But seeing many of the Pharisees and Sadducees.' The Pharisees have their name not from the interpretation of the law, for so they would have to be called מְפָרְשִׁים, but from separation, because פְּרוּשִׁים are the separated, 'ἀφωρισμένοι', from the common custom of life, profession, morals, and dress, as R. Nathan in the 'Aruch', Elias in the 'Thisbi', and others have noted: and Josephus mentions them in Antiquities book 13, chapter 9, already in the time of Jonathan the Hasmonean, 140 years before Christ: who, besides the written law, urged the 'traditions of the elders', and by them either depraved the law or, contrary to divine prohibitions, were enriching it with various things: See Matt. V. & XXIII. Josephus b. XVII. ch. 3. b. XVIII. ch. 2. b. II. on the Jewish War ch. XII. Epiphanius heresy XVI. from which it may also be gathered that the Pharisees asserted fate, but at the same time attributed ἀδιαφορίαν (indifference) to human free will, and then indeed believed in the μετεμψύχωσιν (transmigration) of pious souls, (cf. Matt. XVII. 10.) or that resurrection which is to be for such a preservation as is in this life, such as even today the Jews dream of, as observed by the blessed Gerhard part I. Harm. Evang. ch. CLV. p. 1265. but they asserted that the souls of the impious were consigned to an eternal prison and tormented with eternal tortures, yet they denied the resurrection of their bodies, as Josephus reports in the cited book. Furthermore, they denied original sin, and did not consider concupiscence to be sin Rom. VII. 7. Matt. V, 21. 22. 28. they made some precepts of the law of the least account regarding guilt & condemnation, which, namely, do not exclude one from the kingdom of heaven, and others greater, Matt. V. 18. 19. they pretended that they could perfectly fulfill the law Luke X. 25. and setting up their own righteousness they did not submit themselves to the righteousness of faith, and they rejected it entirely, along with Christ himself, who alone is our righteousness: concerning which Paul writes in Rom. IX. & X. Content therefore with the external observance of the law, so that they might acquire for themselves the appearance of greater holiness, they [invented] traditions about the sanctification of the Sabbath Matt. XII. 2. Luke VI. 7. John IX. 6. as if it excluded works of necessity and charity, about various washings, and those superstitious ones, Matt. XV. 2. Mark VII. 3. 4. about the tithing even of trivial things Matt. XXIII. 22. Luke XII. 12. about avoiding association with sinners Matt. IX. 11. Luke VII. 39. about fasts, and long prayers Luke XII. 12. Matt. VI. 5. ch. XXIII. 14. and other things of that kind they vehemently urged: they extended their phylacteries and fringes Matt. XXIII. 5. they prayed at the corners of the streets, and publicly trumpeted their fasts, as also their alms, they adorned the sepulchers of the Prophets, and finally they claimed for themselves the key of knowledge. It would be easy to establish a parallelism between the Pharisees and the monks, Jesuits, and other Papists of today: if that had not already been done by many. See Pharisæism. by the blessed D. Henr. Eckard. Part. III. Dub. Spanhem. p. 107. Hotting. Th. Philol. p. 27. & Ligthforh. hor. Ebr. on this passage, where seven different kinds of Pharisees are both brought forward and compared with the institutions and orders of the Papists and monks.

The Sadducees have their origin and name from Zadok, who, with Baithos, from whom the Essenes arose, his fellow-soldier, [following] the saying of their teacher Antigonus, who lived 300 years before Christ, which is found in Pirke Aboth ch. 1., 'Be not like those who serve the Master for the sake of a reward,' falsely understood, concluded that if one is not to serve in the hope of retribution, there would be no resurrection of the dead, as Hottinger teaches from R. Sal. Jarchi, R. Maimon. and others in the cited book p. 34. Add Men. Ben. Israel on the Resurrection of the dead b. I. ch. 6. 7. and furthermore they denied the immortality of souls, positing that the soul is nothing other than the natural temperament of the elements, which perishes with the body. Whence Josephus b. XVIII. Antiq. ch. 2. [says] the opinion of the Sadducees extinguishes souls together with the body. Moreover, they denied divine providence, as witnessed by Josephus b. XIII. Antiq. ch. 9. b. II. on the Jewish War ch. 2. for which reason they are called Epicureans in the book Juchasin. They also denied angels Acts XXIII. 8. 9. Some say that they also rejected the writings of the Prophets, and admitted only the law of Moses: which, however, Drusius restricts in b. III. on the three Sects ch. 10. to the Sadducees of the Samaritans: but Scaliger in Elench. Trihæres. ch. 18., Spanhem. P. III. Dub. p. 111., Cunæus on the Hebrew Republic p. 476., and Hottinger in the cited book maintain that they accepted the whole Scripture. Genebrardus in b. II. Chronogr. p. 248. mentions that the sect of the Sadducees who deny the resurrection still flourishes today in Constantinople: they are said to still survive even in Italy: indeed, it is certain to Mr. D. Müller in Judaism p. 71. that Sadducees are still found among the Spanish Jews, who cites a certain Uriel, a Hebrew jurist, and his 'Examination of Philosophical Traditions regarding the written law' in the Spanish language, in which he defended the mortality of souls, who finally took his own life in the year 1640.

Same verse. Γεννήματα ἐχιδνῶν (Brood of vipers) Sophocles said 'offspring of a terrible viper.' And it is in the proverb 'a bad egg from a bad crow.' The poison of the viper is in the tongue; a specious plague. There is an allusion at the same time to the passage in Genesis, where the devil is the serpent.

Latin:

V. 7. Ἰδὼν δὲ πολλοὺς τῶν Φαρισαίων καὶ Σαδδουκαίων. Pharisæi nomen habent non ab interpretatione legis, nam ita dicendi forent מְפָרְשִׁים ,sed à separa- tione, quod פְּרוּשִׁים separati, ἀφωρισμένοι à communi vitæ consuetudine, professione, moribus, & amictu fuerint, ut R. Nathan in ערוך, Elias in Thisbi, aliiq; notarunt: meminitq; eorum Josephus l. XIII. Antiq. c. 9. jam tempore Jonathæ Assamonæi añis 140. ante Christum: qui præter legem scriptam παραδόσεις τῶν πρεσβυτέρων urgebant, iisq; vel depravabant le- gem, vel contra divina interdicta eam ἐπιβραβευόντων. variis variis locupletbant: Vid. Matth. V. & XXIII. Josephus l. XVII. c. 3. l. XVIII. c. 2. l. II. de Bell. Jud. c. XII. Epiphan. hær. XVI. e quibus etiam colligere est, quod fatum adstruxerint Pharisaei, at simul hu- mano arbitrio ἀδιαφορίαν tribuerint, tum vero με- τεμψύχωσιν animarum piarum crediderint, (conf. Matth. XVII. 10.) vel eam resurrectionem, quæ ad talem conservationem futura sit, qualis in hac vita est, qualem etiamnum hodie Judaei somniant, ut observatum B. Gerhardo part. I. Harm. Evang. c. CLV. p. 1265. impiorum vero animas æterno car- ceri mancipari, cruciatibus æternis torqueri asse- rebant quidem, at negabant corporum eorum re- suscitationem, ut Josephus l. c. tradit. De cætero peccatum originale inficiabantur, concupiscentiam non habebant pro peccato Rom. VII. 7. Matth. V, 21. 22. 28. præcepta legis alia ratione reatus & condemnationis minima, quæ sc. non excludant a regno cælorum, alia majora faciebant, Matth. V. 18. 19. legem se perfecte implere posse fingebant Luc. X. 25. & justitiam propriam erigentes justitia fidei sese non subjiciebant, eamque prorsus, cum ipso Christo, qui solus nostra est justitia, rejicie- bant: quo de Paulus Rom. IX. & X. Externa ergo legis observantia contenti, ut sanctitatis majoris speciem sibi conciliarent, traditiones de Sabbathi sanctificatione Matth. XII. 2. Luc. VI. 7. Joh. IX. 6. quasi ea necessitatis etiam atque charitatis opera excludat, de variis lotionibus, iisq; superstitiosis, Matth. XV. 2. Marc. VII. 3. 4. de decimatione etiam rerum vilium Matth. XXIII. 22. Luc. XII. 12. de vitanda conversatione cum peccatoribus Matth. IX. 11. Luc. VII. 39. de jejuniis, & prolixis precibus Luc. XII. 12. Matth. VI. 5. c. XXIII. 14. & id genus a- lia vehementer urgebant: phylacteria & fimbrias extendebant Matth. XXIII. 5. in angulis platearum orabant, & palam jejunia sua ebuccinabant, ut & e- leemosynas, sepulcra Prophetarum exornabant, clavem denique cognitionis sibi vendicabant. Pa- rallelismus hodiernorum Monachorum, Jesuitarum, aliorumque Pontificiorum in proclivi foret insti- tuere cum Pharisæis: nisi id factum a plurimis jam esset. Vid. Pharisæism. B. D. Henr. Eckard. Part. III. Dub. Spanhem. p. 107. Hotting. Th. Philol. p. 27. & Ligthforh. hor. Ebr. ad h. l. ubi VII. diversa genera Pharisæorum & adducuntur, & cum Papistarum & Monachorum institutis, & ordinibus conferuntur.

Sadducæi originem & nomen habent a Zadoco, qui cum Baithoso, a quo Essæi orti, commilitone, Antigoni præceptoris, qui 300. annis ante Christum vixit, dicto, quod in Pirke Aboth. c. 1. habetur, ne e- stote sicut qui serviunt Domino propter mercedem, falso intellecto concludebant, si non serviendum spe retributionis, nullam fore mortuorum resur- rectionem, ut e R. Sal. Jarchi, R. Maimon. aliisque docet Hottinger. l. c. p. 34. Adde Men. Ben. Israel de Resurr. mortuor. l. I. c. 6. 7. ac porro animarum immortalitatem negabant, animam statuentes ni- hil aliud esse, quam naturale temperamentum ele- mentorum, quod cum corpore intereat. Unde Josephus l. XIIX. Antiq. c. 2. Sadducæorum opinio cum corpo- re simul extinguit & animas. Inficiati adhæc sunt di- vinam providentiam, teste Josepho l. XIII. Antiq. c. 9. l. II. de Bell. Jud. c. 2. ideo Epicuræi dicti sunt in libro Juchasin. Negarunt etiam angelos Act. XXIII. 8. 9. Quidam eosdem quoq; Prophetarum scripta repudiasse, ac solam legem Mosis admisisse ajunt: quod tamen restringit Drusius l. III. de trib. Sect. c. 10. ad Sadducæos Samaritanorum: at Scaliger in Elench. Trihæres. c. 18. Spanhem. P. III. Dub. p. 111. Cunæus de Rep. Ebr. p. 476. Hotting. l. c. totam eos Scripturam recepisse statuunt. Sadducæorum resur- rectionem negantium sectam adhuc hodie Constanti- nopoli vigere Genebrardus l. II. Chronogr. p. 248. memorat: superesse adhuc etiam in Italia dicun- tur: id vero Dn. D. Müllero in Judaismo p. 71. certum est, inter Hispanicos Judæos adhuc reperiri Sadducæos, qui adducit quendam Urielem, Juri- stam Hebræum, ejusque in Hispanica lingua Ex- amen tradition. Philos. ad legem scriptam, in qua animarum mortalitatem propugnarit, qui tandem sibi mortem ipse Anno 1640. adsciverit.

Vers. eod. Γεννήματα ἐχιδνῶν) δεινῆς ἐχίδνης θρέμμα dixit Sophocles. Et in proverbio est κακῦ κόρακος κακὸν ὠόν. Viperæ venenum in lingua; pestis speciosa. Alluditur simul ad locum Geneseos, ubi diabolus serpens.

## 3:8
V. 8. καρπὸν ἄξιον τῆς μετανοίας (fruit worthy of repentance) is the same as Acts XXVI. 20. ἄξια τῆς μετανοίας ἔργα (works worthy of repentance). And everywhere works are called by the name of fruits. Luke said in the plural number καρποὺς ἀξίους (fruits worthy), which also persuaded some codices in this place, with the Syriac following. But the Latin and most codices prefer that reading.

Latin:

V. 8. καρπὸν ἄξιον τῆς μετανοίας) idem est quod Actor. XXVI. 20. ἄξια τῆς μετανοίας ἔργα. Et passim opera, fru- ctuum nomine appellantur. Lucas plurali numero dixit καρποὺς ἀξίους, quod & hoc loco in Codices quosdam per- suasit, sequente Syro. Sed illam lectionem Latinus & plurimi Codices præferunt.

## 3:9
V. 9. μὴ δόξητε λέγειν (do not think to say) do not be pleased to say, as Demosthenes [said] ὡκ ἐδόκει μ' ὁρᾶν ἔτι: it did not please them to see me any longer: nor is that far removed from οἱ δοκῦντες ἄρχειν τῶν ἐθνῶν (those who are accounted to rule over the Gentiles) Mark X. 42. who please themselves in that they rule over the nations. Similar to 1 Cor. XI. 16.

ἐκ τῶν λίθων τότων (from these stones) a figurative manner of speaking, although not exceeding the measure of divine power. Similar is Luke XIX. 40. οἱ λίθοι κεκράξονται (the stones will cry out). Nor is it absurd in both places to understand foreign nations as being obscurely indicated. For the Jews expected faith and piety from them no more than from stones. And the sacred scriptures are accustomed to compare those who worship stones to stones. But another allusion also seems to underlie it, as if Christ were saying: do not let it seem incredible to you if God makes children of Abraham from stones, since Isaac himself was born from Abraham who was already worn out. For the worn-out body of Abraham is compared to a stone Is. LI. 1.

to raise up children to Abraham) קום זרע לאברהם as Gen. xxxvIII. 8 which this Interpreter elsewhere translates ἀναστῆσαι in σπέρ- μα XXII. 24. For as children born from a surviving brother were children to the deceased brother not by nature but by law, so all believers are grafted into Abraham, and become not indeed children of the flesh, but children of the promise, Rom. IX. 8. Everywhere the Baptist, Christ, and the Apostles devote effort to take away from the Jews their pride and the hope of impunity conceived from the holiness of their parents, which was the greatest impediment to a good mind for them. See the Epistle to the Romans and Justin in his dialogue with Trypho,

Latin:

V. 9. μὴ δόξητε λέγειν) ne lubeat vobis dicere, ut Demosthe- nes ὡκ ἐδόκει μ' ὁρᾶν ἔτι: non lubebat ipsis amplius me videre: neque longe discedit illud οἱ δοκῦντες ἄρχειν τῶν ἐθνῶν Marc. X. 42. qui in eo sibi placent quod gentibus impe- rant. Simile 1. Cor. XI. 16.

ἐκ τῶν λίθων τότων) figuratum loquendi genus, quan- quam divinæ porentiæ mensuram non excedens. Simile est Luc. XIX. 40. οἱ λίθοι κεκράξονται. Nec absurdum utro- que loco gentes extraneas obscure indicatas intelligere. Nam ab his non magis quam à lapidibus fidem ac pieta- tem Judæi exspectabant. Et solent sacræ literæ lapidibus comparare eos qui lapides colunt. Sed & alia videtur al- lusio subesse, quasi dicat Christus: ne incredibile vobis videatur, si ex lapidibus faciat Deus liberos Abrahami, cum ipse Isaac ex Abrahamo jam effœto natus sit. Nam corpus effetum Abrahami lapidi comparatur Es. LI. 1.

ἐγῆραι τέκνα τῷ Ἀβραάμ) קום זרע לאברהם ut Gen. xxxvIII. 8 quod alias vertit hic Interpres ἀναστῆσαι in σπέρ- μα XXII. 24. Nam ut nati ex fratre superstite filii erant fra- tri defuncto non natura sed lege, ita credentes omnes Ab- rahamo inseruntur, fiuntq; non quidem τέκνα τῆς σαρκὸς, sed τέκνα τῆς ἐπαγγελίας, Rom. IX. 8. Passim Baptista, Chri- stus, Apostoli dant operam ut Judæis adimant superbiam & spem impunitatis de parentum sanctitate conceptam, quod illis maximum fuit bonæ mentis impedimentum. Vid. Ep. ad Rom. & Justinum in colloquio cum Tryphone,

## 3:10
V. 10. And now also the axe is laid to the root of the trees) Now God threatens you in your impenitence not with light evils, but with the abandonment of his covenant, which is as it were to cut down a tree by the roots.

Every tree not bringing forth good fruit is cut down) A symbolic explanation of that law which exists in Deut. xx. 20, which Philo interprets in a similar way in more than one place. See also Dan. IV. 11.

Latin:

V. 10. ἤδη δὲ κὶ ἀξίνη πρὸς τὴν ῥίζαν τ' δένδρων κεῖται) Jam De- us vobis in relipiscatis non levia mala minatur, sed fœderis sui derelictionē, quod est velut arborē radicit9 exscindere.

πᾶν ἐν δένδρον μὴ ποιῦν καρπὸν καλὸν ἐκκόπτεται) Explicatio symbolικὴ legis ejus quæ exstat Deut. xx. 20. quam simili modo Philo interpretatur non uno loco. Vid. & Dan. IV. 11.

## 3:11
V. 11. unto repentance) this can not inconveniently be explained in this way: I baptize you upon the profession of repentance, which you make.

But he who comes after me) He who a little later will begin his office. For that is what is signified by the word ἔρχεσθαι by the sacred writers.

sufficient) It has the same value as ἄξιος John I. 27. Acts XIII. 46. where to loose the thong of the sandal or the sandal itself denotes clearly the same ministry as here to bear the sandal, which was accustomed to be commanded to the vilest slaves: to which those things in the Comedies point: give now the sandals: and in Aeschylus in the Agamemnon: let someone quickly loose the sandals, the foot-covering of a slave. In Terence in the Heautontimorumenos: The slaves run up, they take off the slippers. In Tibullus: And he himself will take the bonds from the snowy foot. Therefore also David says he will cast his shoe over Edom Ps. CVIII. 10, namely that he may take them away when removed: for this is to bear. Thus also in the explanation of the precept forbidding CLXXVI. the Hebrews explain this vile ministry by an example, for instance, that he should loose the thong of the shoes, or that he should take them off.

with the Holy Spirit and with fire) It is treated here of that Spirit which Christ was about to give to those believing in him, yet so that not only his internal gifts of the spirit, but also external testimonies ought to be understood, I think he will easily see who has rightly attended to the passages Acts I. 5. and Acts XIX. 2. In the former passage Christ himself opposes the baptism of John which was done by water to the baptism by the spirit, which the Apostles were shortly to receive from him. In the latter passage it is shown that those who had been baptized by John or the disciples of John had received no gifts with the baptism such as those were receiving who had given their name to Christ having been baptized by the Apostles: To these add that passage which is John VII. 38. 39. where the Apostle John interpreted the words of Christ concerning rivers of living water as concerning the spirit which those believing in Christ were to receive. For at that time the Holy Spirit had not yet been given. What is said here and in Luke about baptizing with the Holy Spirit and fire, that in Mark I. 8. and John I.

33. They said simply to baptize with the Spirit: so that that word πυρὶ added exegetically may appear, clearly because, just as the nature of air, so the most subtle and most efficacious nature of fire best expresses that divine power which Christ was about to bestow upon those believing in Him, the intensity of grace, as Chrysostom speaks here, whence also the tongues sent over the Apostles with the sound of a wind bore the appearance of fire, Acts II. 2. 3. See the prophecy of El. IV. 4. 5. Moreover, the word for baptizing, used by metaphor for those gifts, signifies their abundance: as also that of Joel: I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh, Acts II. 17. But that the Ethiopians also use anointing alongside baptism, I judge to have been done after the custom of the ancient Christians, who added to the ceremonies handed down by Christ signs which might simultaneously call to memory the words of Scripture shadowing forth the same thing in one way or another. Such was the tasting of milk and honey, the signing of the cross, the adjuration of demons, the application of salt, anointing, and other things of that kind. That this custom is most ancient and not peculiar to the Ethiopian nation is taught to us by Heracleon, cited by Clement of Alexandria in his book on Prophecy; he says, some marked the ears of those being sealed with fire. Whether the Seleucians and Hermians, whom we read baptized with fire, observed this custom, I am uncertain, as also regarding Valentinus, of whom Tertullian says: He taught that one should be bathed twice, with the body passed through flame.

The custom of these, as it seems, gave cause to bolder scribes to delete the word πυρὶ in this place, which can be seen in certain codices. Furthermore, the more recondite sense here seems to be that it is not enough, in Christ's judgment, if we abstain from evil deeds, which the washing indicated; but that a power acting toward good things with a certain great impetus is required, which is shadowed forth by those conspicuous gifts.

Latin:

V. 11. εἰς μετάνοιαν) potest non incommode exponi hoc modo: Baptizo vos super professione pœnitentiæ, quem facitis.

ὁ δὲ ὀπίσω μ8 ἐρχόμεν@) Is qui paulo post me munus suū auspicabitur. Id enim voce ἔρχεσθ significari S. scriptores.

ἱκανός) Idem valet quod ἄξιος Joh. I. 27. Act. XIII. 46. ubi λύσαι τ ἱμάντα τῶ ὑποδήματος sive τὸ ὑπόδημα idem pla- ne ministerium denotat quod hic βαστάσαι τὸ ὑπόδημα, vilis- simis sc. servis mandari solitum: quo spectant illa in Comœ- diis: date jam soleas: & apud Æschylum Agamemnone: ὑπαί τις ἀρβύλας Λύοι τάχος, πρόδουλον ἔμβασιν ποδὸς. Apud Terentium Heautontimorumeno: Accurrunt servi, soccos detrahunt. Apud Tybullum: Vinclaq; de niveo detrahet ipse pede. Ideo & David aut Idumæo se objecturum soleas Ps. CVIII. 10. nimirum ut exutas auferat: hoc enim est βαστάζειν. Sic & in expositione præcepti vetantis CLXXVI. Hebræi vi- le ministerium hoc explicant exemplo, puta ut solvat cor- rigiam calceamentorum, aut ut extrahat ea.

ἐν πνεύματι ἁγίῳ κὶ πυρὶ) Agi hic de Spir. illo quem in se credentibus daturus erat Christus, ita tamen ut non interna tantum ejus spirit9 dona, sed & externa testimonia intelli- gi debeant, facile visurū puto qui recte attenderit ad loca Act. I. 5. & Act. xix. 2. Priore loco Christus ipse opponit Jo- hannis baptisma quod per aqua fiebat baptismo per spiritū, quē à se brevi accepturi erant Apostoli. Altero loco often- ditur eos qui à Johāne aut discipulis Johan. baptizati erant cum baptisino nulla accepisse dona qualia accipiebant hi qui ab Apostolis baptizati nomē Christo dederant: His ad- de locum eum qui est Joh VII. 38. 39. ubi verba Christi de fluminibus aquæ vivæ Apostolus Johannes interpretatus de spiritu quem accepturi essent credentes in Christum. Nam ad id tempus non fuisse Spir. S. Quod hic & apud Lu- cam dicitur baptizare Spir. S. & igne, id Marc. I. 8. & Joh. I.

33. dixerunt simpliciter baptizare spiritu: ut appareat illud πυρὶ adjectum ἐξηγητικῶς, nimirum quia ut aeris, ita ignis subtilissima atque efficacissima natura vim illam di- vinam quam in se credentibus Christus erat collaturus τὸ σφοδρὸν τῆς χάριτος, ut hic loquitur Chrysostomus, opti- me exprimit, unde & linguae super Apostolos missae cum venti sono ignis speciem praetulerunt, Act. II. 2. 3. Vide vaticinium El. IV. 4. 5. Vox autem baptizandi de donis illis per translationem usurpata eorundem ubertatem si- gnificat: ut & Joëlis illud: Effundam de Spiritu meo super omnem carnem, Actor. II. 17. Quod autem Aethiopes jux- ta baptismum unctionem quoque usurpant, factum arbitror more veterum Christianorum, qui traditis à Christo cere- moniis signa addebant, quae verba Scripturae eandem rem aliter atq; aliter adumbrantia simul in memoriam revoca- rent. Talis fuit lactis & mellis praegustatio, signatio crucis, daemonum adjuratio, salis admotio, unctio alíaq; ejusmo- di. Morem autem hunc vetustissimum esse neq; proprium gentis Aethiopicae docet nos Heracleon citatus a Clemen- te Alexandrino in libro de Prophetia, ἔνιοι, inquit, πυρὶ τὰ ὦ- τα τῶν σφραγιζομένων κατεσημήναντο. An Seleuciani & Her- miani, quos igne baptizasse legimus, hunc more observan- rint, incertu habeo, ut & de Valentino, de quo Tertullianus: Bis docuit tingi traducto corpore flamma.

Horum mos, ut videtur, librariis audacioribus causam de- dit delendi hoc loco vocabulum πυρὶ, quod in quibusdam codicibus videre est. Caeterum sensus magis reconditus hic videtur esse, non satis esse, Christo judice, si malis factis abstineamus, quod lutio indicabat; sed requiri vim ad bona agentem magno quodam impetu, quae donis illis conspicuis adumbrata est.

## 3:12
Vers. 12. ὗ τὸ πτύον ἐν τῇ χειρὶ αὐτᾶ] A Hebraism for ἐν ὗ χειρὶ τὸ πτύον. But just as the later words of this clause concerning the gathering of the fruits and the burning of the chaff pertain to the day of the last judgment, as appears from a comparison of the words of Christ below XIII. 30. & 49., of which judgment a certain shadowing forth is Psl. 4. Dan. II. 35., so the former can not inappropriately be referred to the very nature of the announced word, the purity of which is so great that in large part, even in this age, especially as often as the cross approaches, it separates the upright from the wicked. But also in individual men a similar kind of purgation is to be instituted, which Philo depicts by the very same similitude that the Baptist uses here in his book on Cain: Just as in the threshing floor wheat and barley and such things are separated by themselves, and the chaff and straw and whatever other light things are scattered elsewhere, so also among us, whatever things are best and useful and provide true nourishment, through which the upright life is completed, are as it were to be dedicated to God. But the other things which are not divine are to be left behind as refuse to the mortal. Servius on that line of Georgic I, the mystic winnowing-fan of Iacchus: because the rites of Father Liber pertained to the purgation of the soul: and thus men were purged by his mysteries just as grain is purged by winnowing-fans.

ἅλωνα] This word is found with a similar inflection in Dionysius of Halicarnassus.

Καὶ συνάξει τὸν σῖτον ἀυτᾶ] קבצם כעמיר he gathered them as sheaves of the threshing floor. Mich. IV. 12.

PART II. Jesus, having held a conversation with John, is baptized, with a heavenly theophany.

Latin:

Vers. 12. ὗ τὸ πτύον ἐν τῇ χειρὶ αὐτᾶ] Hebraismus pro ἐν ὗ χειρὶ τὸ πτύον. Sicut autem posteriora hujus commatis verba de colligendis frugibus & comburendis paleis ad ultimi judicii diem pertinent, ut apparet ex collatione verborum Christi infra XIII. 30. & 49. cujus judicii adumbratio qua- dam est Psl. 4. Dan. II. 35. ita priora ad ipsam verbi annun- ciati naturam non incommode possunt referri, cujus tan- ta est puritas, ut magna ex parte etiam in hoc aevo, prae- sertim quoties crux accedit, probos ab improbis segreget. Sed & in singulis hominibus similis quaedam purgatio in- stituenda, quam similitudine plane eadem, qua hic Ba- ptista utitur, Philo depingit libro de Caino: Καθάπερ ἓν ἐν τῇ ἅλῳ ὡσὶ πυροὶ κὶ κριθαὶ κὶ ὅσα τοιαῦτα καθ᾽ ἑαυτὰ χωρί- ζεται, ἀθέρες κὶ ἄχυρα κὶ ὅσες ἄλλα φορητὸς ἑτέρωσε σκίδνα- ται, ὕτω κὶ παῤ ἡμῖν, τὰ μὲν ὅσα ἄριστα κὶ ὠφέλιμα κὶ τὰς ἀ- ληθεῖς τροφὰς παρίσχοντα, δι ὧν ὁ ὀρθὸς ἀποτελεῖται βίος, ὥ- σπερ ἀναθετέον θεῷ. τὰ δ᾽ ἄλλα ὅσα μὴ θεῖα ὑπολειπτέον ὥσπερ σκύβαλα γίνεσ τῷ θνητῷ. Servius ad illud I. Georg. mystica vannus Iacchi: ideo quod liberi patris sacra ad purga- tionem animi pertinebant: & sic homines ejus mysteriis purga- bantur sicut vannis frumenta purgantur.

ἅλωνα] Haec vox simili flexione est apud Dionysium Halicarnassensem.

Καὶ συνάξει τὸν σῖτον ἀυτᾶ] קבצם כעמיר συνήγαγεν ἀυτοὺς ὡς δράγματα ἅλωνος. Mich. IV. 12.

PARS II. Jesu, colloquio cum Johanne habito, baptiza- tio, cum caelesti θεοφανείᾳ.

## 3:14
Vers. 14. Ἐγω χρείαν ἔχω ὑπὸ σᾶ βαπτισθῆναι] If one of us must be baptized at all, I rather ought to have sought baptism from you, as the most worthy.

Latin:

Vers. 14. Ἐγω χρείαν ἔχω ὑπὸ σᾶ βαπτισθῆναι] Si alter nostrum omnino baptizandus sit, ego potius abs te, ut di- gnissimo, baptismum petere debui.

## 3:15
ἄφες ἄρτι] ἀφιέναι here is to permit, as below VII. 4. 5. VIII. 12. But to permit is just as much as if he said, allow now what I ask.

Δικαιοσύνην] This word is taken most broadly in this very place, so that it signifies not only what is legal, but also whatever has any reason of equity and honesty. For the law of Moses had prescribed nothing concerning this Baptism, and the heavenly command which the Baptist had received pertained properly to repenting sinners. Yet since Christ was the exemplar of most perfect innocence, the ceremony, which sealed the purpose of innocence, was not empty even in Him. Nor could it be shown more efficaciously how great an honor was owed to rites instituted by God than if Christ Himself commended their use to us by His own example. Furthermore, through this ceremony, which inserts us into the people of God, He was as it were incorporated into the same people, and by His example made certain all those who, as is fitting, are baptized, of the opening of the heavenly kingdom to them, of the obtaining of the Spirit, and of the right of the sons of God. Thus δίκαιον is taken also in Phil. I. 7. & in some other places. In the so-called Constitutions of Clement we read in book VII. c. XXIII. And Jesus was baptized and prayed, not Himself having need of cleansing or fasting or purification, who was by nature pure and holy, but that He might both bear witness to the truth for John and provide a pattern for us.

This first conversation of Christ, instituted under the solemn inauguration of his office made both through Baptism and the Elogium of the heavenly voice, is described by Matthew alone. When John the πρωτοβαπτιςὴς (first-baptizer), the Μεσίτης (mediator) of the Old and New Testament, as he is called by Nazianzen, the boundary in which Judaism ceased and Christianity began, as he is called by Tertullian, was prohibiting Christ who was arriving for the sake of receiving Baptism, not by commanding, but by entreating, not out of error, but out of reverence and honor, ἵνα μὴ νομίσωσιν οἱ ὁρῶντες, τ᾽ αὑτὸν ὡς ἕνα τῶν πολλῶν εἰς μετάνοιαν βαπτιζόμενον (so that those who see him might not think that he himself is being baptized as one of the many unto repentance), as Theophylact rightly says, I have need, he says, to be baptized by you and you come to me. For he knew him not indeed ἐξ ἀνθρωπίνης φιλίας (out of human friendship), but ex ἀποκαλύψεως θείας (out of divine revelation) as Chrysostom distinguishes in homily 18 on John, not out of a familiarity previously contracted, but out of mere divine revelation. Christ responds: ἄφες ἄρτι· ὕτω γὰρ πρέπον ἐσὶν ἡμῖν πληρῶσαι πᾶσαν δικαιοσύνην (suffer it now: for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness). Which words of Christ present Christ's petition; ἄφες ἄρτι (suffer it now). Christ does not command by ordering out of authority, but asks that it be done, submitting himself, and that (1.) on account of the state of his Exinanition. (2.) as a document of Humility (3.) on account of the establishment of the authority of the divine ministry. He requests Baptism, he does not extort it, so that he may teach us to venerate ministers, and to approach the use of the Sacraments reverently and humbly. By the word ἄρτι (now) he distinguishes the times of that present and future state, of humiliation and glorification, of ministry and dominion, and at the same time adds a calculation to the Baptist's opinion, as if he were saying: It is indeed true that you rather have need to be baptized by me, as a servant by the Lord, but permit for now that I be baptized by you, who have come now, not that I might be ministered unto, but that I myself might minister to others. The ends of Baptism are to be distinguished here. John had need to be baptized by Christ because of the washing and remission of sins, which those baptized obtained only through Christ and in the name of Christ, Acts II. 38, c. XXII. 16. And thus Christ did not seek, nor had need to be baptized, being devoid of all sin. Heb. VII. 26. But he freely willed to be baptized, οἰκονομικῶς (economically), and for certain causes. (1.) on account of the approbation of the Johannine office, and so that he might show the conformity of his doctrine with the Johannine. (2.) on account of the commendation of this Sacrament made by his own example, lest men be burdened to come to Baptism, as Augustine says. (3.) on account of the sanctification of Baptism, which Christ sanctified by this act, so that it might be both the entrance or investiture of Christianity, as it is called by Bernard in his sermon on the Cana, just as this Baptism was the entry and inauguration of the office of Christ: and also the Gate of heaven, just as here in the Baptism of Christ heaven is opened, in which manner Blessed Augustine in book 2 of De Catechizandis Rudibus, chapter 2, elegantly called Baptism the gate of grace, and the first entrance of the Saints to the eternal custom of God and the Church, and also the Medium of participation in the merit of Christ and the fruit of the same, righteousness having been fulfilled, since indeed we put on Christ in Baptism Gal. III. 27. and also the Sacrament of Regeneration, through which God the Father regenerates us into sons of God in Christ his only-begotten son ἐν ᾧ εὐδόκησε (in whom he is well pleased) Gal. III. 26. Eph. I. 6. and also the Channel of the effusion of the Holy Spirit Tit. III. 5. since here it was signified that the Holy Spirit would be given to the baptized, as he descended here into Christ, although not in that manner, nor in that measure, and degree, in which he was given to Christ according to his human nature Acts II. 38. But that sanctification was not made by infusing some virtue or quality into the waters of the Jordan, which would subsequently spread from there to others, and sanctify all those dipped in Baptism ex opere operato (by the work performed), as the Papists wish, but he sanctified the waters by his will and his grace, nay even by consecrating them by the contact of his flesh, not so that some power might physically inhere in the water, but so that by a free divine economy the water thenceforth might serve as a sacrament and a means of salvation, which did not indeed operate by way of a physical cause, or exhibit grace like a box, but was an organic means of offering and dispensing grace. In which sense those words of Optatus of Milevis, book 1, p. 10, are to be accepted: The flesh of Christ is found to be holier than the Jordan itself, so that he rather cleansed the water itself by his descent, than was himself cleansed. And those of Jerome, against Lucifer, Vol. II, p. 138: Our Lord Jesus Christ was not so much cleansed in the bath, as he cleansed all waters by his own bath. In which manner also Hilary in Matthew, ch. II, says: That Christ was baptized in order to sanctify our bath in his own body, by way of likeness, because just as Christ received circumcision, so that by that sign he might be inscribed into the Church of the Jews; so also he wished to receive Baptism, that by this means he might be joined to the people of the Christians.

II. The reason for the petition, where it is necessary to weigh (1.) the argument expressed by the word γὰρ. But what are the consequences here? It rests upon that obedience, both active, by which he received Baptism according to the command of God, and passive, by which, receiving Baptism, he took upon himself the burden of our sins and the expiation of the same. For he is presented here in Baptism not laden with his own sins, but with ours, John I. 29, Heb. IX. 27. Not that he himself might be washed, but that he might merit washing for us. (2.) The manner ὕτω, which among other things is done by the reception of Baptism, which thus testifies to his humility as well as his readiness for the execution of his office. Therefore, the reason for the Baptism of Christ is one thing, and ours is another. We are baptized for the sake of regeneration, which he did not need; for us, Baptism is an instrument of obtaining salvation; his Baptism was a document of salvation to be acquired for the human race, and a certain pledge of satisfaction to be rendered. They agree, however, in that just as we are bound by this Sacrament to render obedience to God: so also Christ wished here to solemnly pledge his faith and obedience to God the Father. (3.) The duty of the office; πρέπον ἐςὶν ἡμῖν. Christ here includes both himself and John, because this is fitting for both according to the nature of the office of each: for John, that he might baptize the Savior of the world and inaugurate him into his office, for whom he had been required to prepare the way: for Christ, that he might receive Baptism so that he might enter upon his office, and fulfill this part of his duty as well. Meanwhile, Christ comes to John not by necessity, but freely; not by compulsion, but willingly; not by obligation, but by dispensation; not for his own sake, but for ours. He says, however, πρέπον ἐςὶ, not because he wishes here to perform or establish some work of supererogation, as Maldonatus thinks, but because this seemed ἀνάξιον & ἀπρεπὲς to John, for the Lord to be baptized by a servant, as Chrysostom hom. XII observes. To whom Christ responds with these words: that this is not to be forbidden, ὅτι & μάλιςα πρέπον ἐςί, because this is most fitting for the office of both: for John, that he might inaugurate the Messiah into his office; for the Messiah, that by this solemn ceremony he might both most perfectly bind and enslave himself to the execution of his duty. And those things are not called πρέποντα which are arbitrary, but also those which are ἀναγκαῖα necessary, which are δίκαια just, Eph. V. 3, Heb. II. 10, ch. VII. 26, just as Christ also teaches that this is δίκαιον in this place, while everyone is bound to execute with care those things which befit his office or his person. Cf. Vict. Antioch. in the Gospel of Mark, ch. I, Biblioth. Patr. T. 18, p. 296, as also Greg. Thaumaturg. sermon on the Holy Theophany, T. III, Bibl. Patr. p. 45. (4.) The office itself, which the words πληρῶσαι πᾶσαν δικαιοσύνην, to fulfill all righteousness, express, which, as far as John is concerned, are not to be extended further than the nature of his office allows, and therefore they are to be understood only secondarily with respect to him. But as for Christ, one must take them simply and in a universal sense, that is, that he had to ἀποτομίως fulfill all righteousness. Some indeed explain the word δικαιοσύνην not of legal, but of personal righteousness, as if the τὸ πρέπον of the person and the τὸ καθῆκον of the office were designated here, so that thus δικαιοσύνη in the Hellenistic style is the same as יָשָׁר right, ἔνδικον, and πληρῶσαι δικαιοσύνην (to fulfill righteousness) is to do ὡς καθήκει as is fitting and worthy: That whatever is pleasing to God is also called δικαιοσύνην, or finally that the sanction of the Lord is looked at at the same time by this word, because it was so constituted by God in a singular manner that Christ should receive Baptism, which Spanheim thinks is sufficient to explain this phrase, part 3, dub. Ev. dub. 43, p. 162. But one must not look only to this special act of received baptism, but to the entire force of the general statement, that it is altogether fitting for Christ to fulfill all righteousness. However, although the occasion was special, the statement itself is general, nor is there any reason why we should not understand δικαιοσύνην properly, of any legal righteousness whatsoever, especially since the word δικαιοσύνης commonly designates legal righteousness, and the universal particle is added here, so that it may be clear that the discourse is about all the righteousness of the law, which the rule of divine righteousness demands and prescribes, whatever and however much it may be. Add that πληρῶσαι is taken of fulfillment properly, which is done by performing the law, i.e., of the obedience and most perfect satisfaction rendered to the law by Christ, which similar passages confirm: Matt. V. 17, I have not come to destroy, but to πληρῶσαι fulfill the law. Rom. X. 4, Gal. IV. 4, see especially Greg. Neo-Caesar. in the elegant paraphrase of these words, T. III, Biblioth. Patr. 45. Concerning this colloquy of Christ, besides Vict. Antioch. praised above, one may compare Christian. Druthmannus, expos. in Matthew, T. IX, Bibl. Patr. p. 872, as also Paschasius Ratbertus in the Gospel of Matthew, book 2, T. IX, Bibl. Patr. part 3, p. 949.

Latin:

ἄφες ἄρτι] ἀφιέναι hic est sinere, ut infra VII. 4. 5. VIII. 12. Sinito autem tantundem est ac si diceret sias nunc quod solo.

Δικαιοσύνην] Vox haec hoc quidem loco latissime sumitur, ita ut significet non modo τὸ νόμιμον, sed & quicquid ullam aequi ac honesti habet rationem. Nam lex Mofis de hoc Baptismo nihil praescripserat, & caeleste mandatum quod Baptista acceperat, ad peccatores resipiscentes proprie per- tinebat. Attamen cum Christus perfectissimae innocen- tiae exemplar fuerit, ne in ipso quidem inanis erat cere- monia, quae innocentiae propositum obsignabat. Neque ef- ficacius ostendi potuit, quantus honos institutis à Deo riti- bus deberetur, quam si Christus ipse usum eorum nobis ex- emplo suo commendaret. Praeterea ipse per hanc ceremo- niam, quae nos populo Dei inserit, eidem populo velut concorporatus est, certosq; suo exemplo fecit omnes, qui, ut oportet, baptizantur, apertae ipsis regiae caelestis, conse- quendi spiritus, & juris filiorum Dei. Ita δίκαιον sumitur & Phil. I. 7. & alíis aliquot in locis. In Clementis, quae dicun- tur, constitutionibus legimus lib. VII. c. XXIII. Ἐβαπτίσθη δὲ κὶ ἐπίσινσεν (Jesus) ὐκ ἀυτὸς ἀπορυπάσεως ἢ νηστείας χρείαν ἔχων ἢ καθάρσεως ὃς ἦ φύσει καθαρὸς κὶ ἅγιος, ἀλλ᾽ ἵνα κὶ Ἰωάν- νῃ ἀληθεῖαν προσμαρτυρήσῃ κὶ ἡμῖν ὑπογραμμὸν παράσχηται.

Primum hoc Christi colloquium, sub inaugu- rationem muneris solennem tum per Baptismum tum per cœlestis vocis Elogium factam institutum à solo Matthæo describitur. Cum πρωτοβαπτιςὴς Johannes Μεσίτης Vet. & N. T. ut à Nazianzeno, limes in quo cessavit Judaismus & cœpit Christiani- smus, ut à Tertulliano vocatur Christum Baptismĩ suscipiendi causa adventantem prohiberet, non imperando,sed deprecando, non ex errore, sed reve- rentia & honore, ἵνα μὴ νομίσωσιν οἱ ὁρῶντες, τ᾽ αὑ- τὸν ὡς ἕνα τῶν πολλῶν εἰς μετάνοιαν βαπτιζόμε- νον, ut recte Theophylactus ego opus habeo,inquit is, ut baptizer à te & tu venis ad me. Noverat enim i- psum non quidem ἐξ ἀνθρωπίνης φιλίας, sed ex ἀποκαλύψεως θείας ut Chrysost.hom.18. in Johan. distinguit, non ex familiaritate antea contracta, sed ex mera revelatione divina. Respond. Christus : ἄ- φες ἄρτι· ὕτω γὰρ πρέπον ἐσὶν ἡμῖν πληρῶσαι πᾶσαν δικαιοσύνην. Quæ verba Christi sistunt n Christi petitionem; ἄφες ἄρτι.Non imperat Chri- stus ex autoritate præcipiendo, sed rogat, ut id siat, se submittens, idque (1.) ob Exinanitionis sta- tum. (2.) in Humilitatis documentum (3.) propter autoritatis divini ministerii stabilimentum. Petit Baptismum, non extorquet, ut nos venerari do- ceat ministros,& reverenter,ac humiliter accede- re ad usum Sacramentorum. Voce ἄρτι tempora distinguit status illius moderni & futuri,humiliatio- nis, & glorificationis,ministerii & dominii,simulque Baptistæ sententiæ calculum addit,q.dicat: Verum quidẽ est, quod tu potius opus habeas abs me ba- ptizari, ceu servus à Domino,sed permitte modo, ut abs te baptizer,qui veni nunc, non ut ministre- tur mihi,sed ut ipse aliis ministrem. Distinguendi hic sunt fines Baptismi. Opus habuit à Christo ba- ptizari Johannes quod peccatorum ablutionem, & remissionem,quam non nisi per Christum & in no- mine Christi baptizati consequebantur, Act. II. 38. c. XXII.16. Atq; ita non petebat,nec opus habebat baptizari Christus,expers omnis peccati.Ebr.VII. 26. Sed baptizari libere voluit, οἰκονομικῶς, & ob certas causas. (1.)ob officii Johannæi approbationem, & ut conformitatem doctrinæ suæ cum Johannæa ostenderet. (2.) ob Sacramenti hujus commendatio- nem exemplo suo factam, ne gravarentur homines venire ad Baptismum,dicente Augustino. (3.) ob Baptismi sanctificationem, quem hoc actu Christus sanctificavit, ut esset tum introitus vel investitura Christianismi, uti vocatur à Bernardo sermone de Cana, quemadmodum hic Baptismus ingressus e- rat & inauguratio muneris Christi: tum Janua cœ- li,prout hic in Baptismo Christi cœlum aperitur, quo pacto B.August. l. 2. de Catechism. rud. c.2.ele- ganter Baptismum portam gratiæ dixit, & primum introitum Sanctorum ad æternam Dei & Ecclesiæ con- suetudinem,tum Medium participationis meriti Chri- sti & fructus ejusdem,impleta scil. justitia,quando- quidem Christum induamus in Baptismo Gal. III. 27. tum Regenerationis Sacramentum,per quod in filios Dei regenerat nos Deus Pater in Christo fi- lio suo unigenito ἐν ᾧ εὐδόκησε Gal. III. 26. Eph.I. 6. tum Canalis effusionis Sp. S. Tit. III. 5. quum hic significatum fuerit baptisatis datum iriSpir.S.ut h. l. descendit in Christum,etsi non eo modo,nec ea mensura,& gradu, quo Christo secundum huma- nam naturam datus est Act. II. 38. Non autem san- ctificatio illa facta est virtutem vel qualitatem ali- quam aquis Jordanis infundendo,quæ se inde dis- sunderet postmodum ad alios, & sanctificaret o- mnes Baptismo tinctos ex opere operato, ut volunt Pontificii, sed sanctificavit aquas voluntate ac gra- tia sua, imo & contactu carnis suæ consecrando, non ut physice inhæreret aquæ vis aliqua, sed ut li- bera divina œconomia aqua deinceps in Sacra- mentum & medium salutis proficeret, quod non quidem per modum causæ physicæ, operaretur, vel pyxidis instar gratiam exhiberet, sed ὀργανικὸν esset offerendæ & dispensandæ gratiæ. In quam senten- tiam accipienda sunt illa Optati Milevitani l. 1. p. 10. Christi caro ipso Jordane sanctior reperitur, ut magis aquam ipsam descensu suo mundaverit, quam ipse mundatus sit. Et Hieronymi adv. Lucifer. T. II. p. 138. Dominus noster Jesus Christus non tam mundatus est in lavacro, quam lavacro suo universas aquas mun- davit. Quo pacto & Hilarius in Matth. c. II. ait: Christum baptizatum esse, ut lavacrum nostrum san- ctificaret in corpore suo, ob similitudinem, quod quemadmodum circumcisionem suscepit Christus, ut eo signo Judæorum Ecclesiæ adscriberetur; ita etiam Baptismum suscipere voluerit, ut hoc pacto jungeretur populo Christianorum.

II. Petitionis rationem, ubi expendere oportet (1.) argumentum voce γὰρ expressum. Quæ vero hic consequentiæ? Nititur illa obedientia tum a- ctiva qua secundum mandatum Dei suscipiebat Baptismum, tum passiva, qua suscipiens Bapti- smum peccatorum nostrorum onus in se suscepit, ac expiationem eorundem. Sistitur enim hic in Baptismo non suis, sed nostris onustus peccatis Joh. I. 29. Ebr. IX. 27. Non, ut abluatur ipse sed ut promereatur nobis ablutionem. (2.) Modum ὕτω, quod inter alia id fiat susceptione Baptismi, qui sic testatur suam tum Humilitatem, tum ad muneris sui executionem promptitudinem. Alia ergo ratio est Baptismi Christi, alia nostri. Nos baptizamur ob regenerationem, qua ille opus non habebat; nobis Baptismus est instrumentum salutis consequendæ, i- psius Baptismus erat documentum salutis generi hu- mano acquirendæ, & pignus quoddam satisfactionis præstandæ. Conveniunt tamen, quod uti nos hoc Sacramento ad obsequium Deo præstandum adstringimur: ita & Christus fidem atque obse- quium Deo Patri solenniter addicere hic volue- rit. (3.) Officii debitum; πρέπον ἐςὶν ἡμῖν. Com- plectitur hic Christus, se & Johannem, quod u- trumq; hoc deceat pro officii utriusq; ratione, Jo- hannem, quo baptisaret Salvatorem mundi & ad officium suum inauguraret, cui viam parare debu- erat: Christum, quo susciperet Baptismum ut offi- cium suum adiret, & hanc quoq; muneris sui par- tem impleret. Interim venit ad Johannem Christus non necessario, sed libere, non coacte, sed sponte, non ex obligatione, sed dispensatione, non sui, sed nostri causa. Dicit autem πρέπον ἐςὶ, non quod hic ali- quod opus supererogationis præstare vel stabilire velit, ut Maldonatus arbitratur, sed quod Johanni hoc ἀνάξιον & ἀπρεπὲς videretur, Dominum a servo baptizari, ut Chrysost. hom. XII. observ. Cui hisce respondet Christus: prohibendum id non esse, ὅτι & μάλιςα πρέπον ἐςί, quia conveniens maxime hoc sit officio utriusque Johanneo, ut Messiam ad offi- cium inauguraret; Messiæ, ut hac solemni ceremo- nia & perfectissime sese ad muneris sui executione obligaret, & manciparet. Nec ea tantum πρέποντα dicuntur, quæ arbitraria, sed etiam quæ ἀναγκαῖα necessaria, quæ δίκαια justa sunt, Eph. V 3. Ebr. II. 10. c. VII. 26.. prout etiam id hoc loco δίκαιον esse Christus docet, dum teneatur quisque cum cura exequi, quæ officio vel personæ suæ conveniunt. Conf. Vict. Antioch. in Evang Marc. c. I. Biblioth. Patr. T. 18. p. 296. ut & Greg. Thaumaturg. serm. in S. Theophania T. III. Bibl. Patr. p. 45. (4.) Ipsum- met officium, quod exprimunt verba πληρῶσαι πᾶσαν δικαιοσύνην complere omnem justitiam, quæ, quod ad Johannem quidem amplius extendenda non sunt, quam fert officii ejus ratio, ideoque solum secun- da dum quid ejus respectu intelligenda veniunt. Quod vero ad Christum de eo simpliciter sensuq; universali ea accipere oportet, quod sc. ἀποτομίως omnem justitiam implere debuerit. Vocem δικαιο- σύνην explicant quidem nonnulli de justitia non legali, sed personali, quasi τὸ πρέπον personæ & τὸ καθῆκον muneris hic designetur, ut ita δικαιοσύνη stylo Hellenistico idem sit quod יָשָׁר rectum, ἔνδικον, & πληρῶσαι δικαιοσύνην (implere justitiam) sit fa- cere ὡς καθήκει sicut conveniens & dignum est: Vo- cari etiam δικαιοσύνην quicquid Deo gratum est, vel denique respici simul hac voce sanctionem Do- mini, quod ita à Deo singulari ratione constitutum fuerit, ut Baptismum susciperet Christus, quæ Span- hem. isti phrasi explicandæ sufficere putat part. 3. dub. Ev. dub. 43. p. 162. At non respiciendum tantum ad hunc specialem actum suscepti baptismatos, sed ad vim universam generalis sententiæ, quod omnino deceat Christum implere omnem justitiam. Utut autem occasio specialis fuerit, sententia tamen ipsa generalis est, nec est causa ulla, cur δικαιοσύνην non intelligere debeamus proprie, de quacunque le- gali justitia, præsertim cum vox δικαιοσύνης com- muniter justitiam legalem designet, addaturq; hic universalis particula, ut de omni justitia legis, quamcunque & quantumcunque lex justitiæ di- vinæ Regula exigit ac præscribit, sermonem esse, liqueat. Adde quod πληρῶσαι de impletione pro- prie, quæ fit præstando legē, accipiatur h. e. de ob- edientia ac satisfactione perfectissima legi à Chri- sto præstita, quam comprobant loca similia Matth. V. 17. Non veni solvere, sed πληρῶσαι implere le- gem. Rom. X. 4. Gal. IV. 4. vid. imprimis Greg. Neo- Cæsar. in eleganti verborum horum παραφράσει T. III. Biblioth. Patr. 45. Conferri de hoc Colloquio Christi præter Vict. Antioch. supra laudatum pot- erit Christian. Druthmannus expos. in Matth. T. IX. Bibl. Patr. p. 872. ut & Paschasius Ratbertus in Ev- ang. Matth. l. 2. T. IX. Bibl. Patr. part. 3. p. 949.

## 3:16
Vers. 16. Ἀνέβη εὐθὺς] That is, he had scarcely ascended. For he does not mean that Christ ascended suddenly from the river, but that as he had ascended, what follows happened suddenly. In this manner almost, Mark uses εὐθέως, I. 29 & XI. 3. A not dissimilar kind of speaking is found in Aeschylus in Prometheus, ἐπεὶ τάχις ἤρξαντο, for τάχις ἐπεὶ ἤρξαντο. And in Aristotle, III. Polit. XIII, ἐπεὶ θᾶττον ἐγκρατῶς ἔχον τὴν ἀρχὴν for θᾶττον ἐπεὶ.

Ἀνεῴχθησαν αὐτῷ οἱ ὀρανοὶ] That is as a solemn sign preceding the visions. Ezek. I. 1. John I. 51. Acts VII. 56. I think, however, with Origen, Jerome, and others, that this is to be understood as a vision rather than in reality. Certain Hebrews wish it to be nothing other than a figure of speech, by which it is signified that something was done or shown by heavenly power. But even pagans believed that such a thing was sent before heavenly portents. Livy, book XXXII, at Falerii the sky seemed to be split as if by a great chasm: and where it opened, a huge light shone forth. Servius on that passage of the Aeneid IX: The sky parting: in the Augural books it is said that the sky also parted among the portents.

Καὶ εἶδε) I see no reason why we should not interpret this passage from the one that is in John I. 32, since it appears that the same event is being narrated, and it is not unusual for both profane and sacred writers that a verb is adapted to a person who is not immediately noted.

Τὸ πνεῦμα τῦ θεῦ καταβαῖνον ὡσεὶ περιστερὰν] It has been rightly noted long ago that the manner of speaking might seem ambiguous. For it can be understood either as the appearance of a dove being seen, or that what was seen descended in the way that doves are accustomed to. Moreover, since Luke says expressly that the Spirit descended σωματικῷ εἴδει III. 22, and Justin clearly expresses the appearance of a dove when he says ἐπελθόντος ἐν εἴδει περιστερᾶς πνέυματος, and no one among the ancients, as far as I know, thinks otherwise, I clearly believe that the appearance of a dove appeared, perhaps fiery, just as fiery tongues were seen above the Apostles: Origen called it φάσμα ὄρνιθος: although Tertullian affirms it was a real dove, lib. de carne Christi. But Justin expressly declares in his dialogue with Trypho that fire also appeared at this same time in the Jordan, undoubtedly from handed-down tradition. For also in the Gospel of the Ebionites, which was the same as that of the Nazarenes, except for whatever Ebion interpolated for the sake of his hypothesis, it was read thus: καὶ εὐθὺς περιέλαμψε τὸν τόπον φῶς μέγα.

And the same is found in the Liturgy of the Syrians in the narration of this history concerning baptism. I think, however, that the appearance of the dove pertained to this, because the spirit that was in Christ had already been described long ago by Isaiah XLII. 1, 2, 3, with a special mark of gentleness, as is explained below in XII, to which the words of Christ which are in Luke IX. 55 also seem to look. It is a known proverb, however, πραότερον περιστερᾶς, just as Christ also expresses the τὸ ἀκέραιον by the likeness of a dove below in X. 16. It is the more credible that that prophecy of Isaiah was particularly regarded here by God, because the voice that was uttered, which follows, also expressed almost the same words that exist in the same pericope of Isaiah. Philo, from the discipline of the Hebrews, says that wisdom is signified by the dove, not that φιλόκοσμον (such as the Baptist's was) but that which is ἡμερωτέρα τιθασεσὸς καὶ ἀγέλαιος. I would not, however, deny that there is a tacit reference to the ancient figure of the dove which, after the flood, brought signs of a renewed world to Noah. By its flight, however, is signified the divine influx noted also by Josephus Jacehai on Daniel IX.

Latin:

Vers. 16. Ἀνέβη εὐθὺς] Id est, vix ascenderat. Non enim vult subito ascendisse Christum ex amne, sed ut ascenderat subito factum quod sequitur. In hunc ferme modum εὐθέ- ως utitur Marcus I. 29. & XL 3. Non dissimile loquendi genus est apud Æschylum Prometheo, ἐπεὶ τάχις ἤρξαντο, pro τάχις ἐπεὶ ἤρξαντο. Et apud Aristotel. III. Polit. XIII. ἐπεὶ θᾶττον ἐγκρατῶς ἔχον τὴν ἀρχὴν pro θᾶττον ἐπεὶ.

Ἀνεῴχθησαν αὐτῷ οἱ ὀρανοὶ] Id velut solenne signum præ- vium ταῖς ὀπτασίαις. Ezech. I. 1. Joh. I. 51. Act. VII. 56. Puto autem cum Origene, Hieronymo & aliis intelligen- dum hoc κατὰ φάσιν potius quam reipsa. Hebræorum qui- dam nihil aliud esse volunt, quam figurarum loquendi ge- nus, quo significetur factum aliquid aut ostensum cœlesti virtute. Sed & pagani cœlestibus ostentis tale aliquid præ- mitti crediderunt. Livius libro XXXII Faleris cælum findi visum velut magno hiatu: quaq; patuerit, ingens lumen effulsis- se. Servius ad illud IX. Æneidos: Discedere cælum: in Au- guralibus libris inter ostenta etiam cælum discessisse dicitur.

Καὶ εἶδε) Ego nullam causam video, cur non hunc lo- cum interpretemur ex eo qui est Joh. I. 32. cum appareat rem eandem narrari, neque insolens sit tum profanis tum sacris scriptoribus, ut verbum aptetur personæ etiam quæ non proxime notata est.

Τὸ πνεῦμα τῦ θεῦ καταβαῖνον ὡσεὶ περιστερὰν] Recte anno- tatum est jam pridem ambiguum videri posse loquendi ge- nus. Potest enim intelligi aut species columbæ visa, aut quod visum est ita descendisse quomodo columbæ solent, Cæterum cum Lucas dicat diserte descendisse Spiritum σω- ματικῷ εἴδει III. 22. & Justinus aperte exprimat columbæ speciem, cum dicit ἐπελθόντος ἐν εἴδει περιστερᾶς πνέυματος, nec quisquam veterum, quod sciam, aliter sentiat, plane credo columbæ speciem apparuisse, igneam forte, quomo- do linguæ igneæ visæ sunt supra Apostolos: φάσμα ὄρνιθος dixit Origenes: quanquam veram fuisse columbam affir- mat Tertullian. lib. de carne Christi. Ignem autem eodem hoc tempore in Jordane apparuisse diferte prodit Justinus colloquio cum Tryphone, ex tradita haud dubie fama. Nam & in Ebionæorum Evangelio, quod idem erat cum Nazaræorum, præter si qua Ebion ὑποθέσεως χάριν interpo- lavit, ita legebatur: καὶ εὐθὺς περιέλαμψε τὸν τόπον φῶς μέγα.

Et idem reperitur in Liturgia Syrorum in hujus historiæ narratione circa baptismum. Columbæ autem speciem huc pertinuisse puto, quod is qui in Christo erat spiritus spe- ciali mansuetudinis nota jam olim descriptus esset ab Esaia XLII. 1. 2. 3. ut infra explicatur XII. quo respicere etiam videntur Christi verba quæ sunt apud Lucam IX. 55. No- tum est autem proverbium πραότερον περιστερᾶς, sicut & τὸ ἀκέραιον columbæ similitudine exprimit Christus infra X. 16. Eo autem credibilius est vaticinium illud Esaiæ à Deo hic peculiariter spectatum, quod & vox prolata, quæ sequitur, eadem prope verba, quæ in eadem Esaiæ peri- copa exstant, expresserit. Philo ex Hebræorum discipli- na per columbam significari ait sapientiam, non illam φιλό- κοσμον (qualis erat Baptistæ) sed eam quæ sit ἡμερωτέρα τιθασε- σὸς καὶ ἀγέλαιος. Negare tamen nolim tacitè respici ve- terem figuram columbæ quæ post diluvium signa renovati orbis ad Noam pertulit. Volatu autem significari influ- xum divinum notatum & Josepho Jacehai ad IX. Danielis.

## 3:17
Verse 17. Ἀγαπητὸς] That which is in Isaiah בחירי, ἐκλεκτός μου: for ἐκλεκτὸς and ἀγαπητὸς are accustomed to be used for the same thing. See Psalm II.

Ἐν ᾧ εὐδόκησα] This word, like the Latin 'placet', is referred sometimes to the decree of the will, sometimes to a propense affection. This is the difference: the Latin word is said of the object, the Greek of the subject. To signify affection, Greek writers say εὐδοκεῖν τινι. As for ἐνδοκεῖν ἔν τινι as here and below in XVII. 5, Mark I. 11, Luke III. 22, 1 Cor. X. 5, Heb. X. 38, or εἴς τινα as below in XII. 18, 2 Peter I. 17, the Hebraism חפץ בו is manifest, as in Gen. XXXIV. 14, or רצה בו as in 1 Chron. XXVIII. 4. What Jerome says, that this kind of speaking was invented by the LXX interpreters, is to be understood of this form of construction, and of the noun derived from it, εὐδοκία, which is not to be found except among the Hellenist Jews. Often, however, the LXX also translate רצה in this way, as in Ps. XL. 14 (in the Hebrew: for so I have decided to cite the Psalms), XLIV. 4, CXLVII. 10, CXLIX. 4, where רוצה בעמו is translated εὐδοκεῖ ἐν τῷ λαῷ. The sense is, however, clearly the same in these words ἐν ᾧ εὐδόκησα as in those of Isaiah רצתה נפשי, where also certain Greek interpreters have εἰς ὃν εὐδόκησεν ἡ ψυχή με. You will find εὐδοκεῖν with the Dative in the same sense, with the particle ἐν omitted. Thus the writer of the first book of Maccabees I. 45 said εὐδοκεῖν τῇ λατρείᾳ. The interpreter of Irenaeus translates this ἐν ᾧ εὐδόκησα as 'in whom I have been well pleased' in book III, chapter XL.

It is helpful here to add the observations proposed publicly here twenty-two years ago in lectures on the Utterances of the mouth of Christ: I. On the Reverence to be shown to the Ministry, which is gathered from the example of Christ. Here we are stirred (1.) By the authority of the divine command, 1 Cor. XVI. 15, 1 Tim. V. 17, Tit. II. 15, Heb. XIII. 17, especially 1 Thess. V. 17, to follow with double, that is, extraordinary honor, those who minister. (2.) By the sublimity of the office: They are servants and ambassadors of God, 2 Cor. VI. 4, 1 Thess. III. 2. They shine with the honor of the One sending: they are stewards, 1 Cor. IV. 1, they are ambassadors for Christ, 2 Cor. V. 20; the ignominy redounds to the principal, as Christ says in Matt. X. 40, Luke X. 16; they are fellow-workers of God, 1 Cor. III. 9, 2 Cor. V. 30. (3.) By the dignity of the names. They are called by the Holy Spirit. Men of God, 1 Sam. II. 27, 1 Tim. VI. 11, 2 Tim. III. 17. Angels of the Lord, Isa. XLII. 19, Mal. II. 7, ch. III. 1. Apoc. I. 30. They are to be received as Angels, Gal. III. 14. Pastors, Jerem. III. 15, Eph. IV. 1. Fathers, 2 Kings VI. 1, 1 Cor. IV. 15, Gal. IV. 9. Presbyters and Elders, Tit. I. 5, James V. 14. Doctors, Acts XIII. 1. Those who preside, 1 Tim. V. 17. Leaders, Acts XV. 22, Heb. XIII. 14. (4.) By the clarity of the examples, especially Gal. IV. 14, 1 Thess. II. 13. Finally, in this place, the example of Christ himself.

II. On the eminence of John, because Christ was baptized by him: he is 'greater' (περισσότερος), Matt. XI. 11, Luke VII. 28. See also Irenaeus, book 3 against heresies, ch. 11. John is at once a Prophet, who predicted that the Messiah would come; and at the same time an Apostle, because he also showed him present, indeed because he inaugurated the Messiah into his office: hence he is 'greater' than those born of women; but it is added, yet less than he who is least in the kingdom of heaven. Paschasius notes in book 2, T: 9 of the Bibliotheca, that this apparent contradiction can be removed in a twofold way.

PP. page 1044. (1.) That it is more intense, that this is still only something external, that he is called an Angel, and does not pertain to salvation, whence he who has that is happier. (2.) If the 'least in the kingdom of heaven' is understood to be Christ because of his extreme emptying and the setting aside of all glory, Isa. LIII. 5, he could appear less than John in the flesh, and therefore he judged it fitting that he should seek baptism, while in the meantime Christ was nevertheless greater because of the dignity of his office and person.

III. On the efficacy of the Baptism of John. Here one must dispute against the Calvinists, especially against Spanheim, Part 3, Dub. Evang., where he denies that our baptism was sanctified by the baptism undertaken by Christ, (1.) because the waters of the Jordan alone would have had that virtue, because they alone touched the flesh of Christ: (2.) That water was not capable of such a spiritual quality: (3.) That Sacraments are not boxes of grace, but seals (σφραγῖδες), nor do they act as physical causes, but as moral instruments: (4.) That the power of purging is proper to the Creator, incommunicable to a creature. I respond: 1. In general, all these things are rightly opposed to the Papists, insofar as they urge the 'work performed' (opus operatum) in the doctrine of the Sacraments, but not to the living efficacy of baptism. 2. In particular, as to the first, we deny (1.) that those waters were sanctified by material or bodily contact, and not rather by spiritual and virtual contact. (2.) The waters of the Jordan were not a Sacrament, as waters, but as waters consecrated by baptism, through the communication of divine grace, but which would agree with them only in the act of the dispensation of this Sacrament: let physical inherence be far from us. (3.) Just as Christ is said to have received our passions into Himself, and thus to have sanctified them, so also in this place the matter stands regarding baptism. Moreover, it must be added that the power of the Sacrament does not depend so much on this baptism of Christ, as on the institution of baptism made by Christ, and therefore these must be taken together. To the second I respond: Mere water and as such is not capable; but by divine institution and ordination it is rendered such: one must not look only at the earthly matter, but also at the heavenly, and the divine ordination: this supplies what is lacking in its nature. Furthermore to the third, (1.) we do not consider the Sacraments as boxes of grace, we confess them to be means and organs of grace, but not signifying it only or purely σημαντικὰ but προσφερόμενα. (2.) These means do not act only by way of a moral cause, but a physical one, because God willed these means to be so instituted, and the effect depends upon them, through a real influx, although they induce an effect superior to themselves, by divine ordination: for they act by an eminent power, not a natural one. To the fourth I respond: The power of cleansing in itself, from itself, and through itself is proper to God, but it can be communicated through the grace of God to a creature, as to the human nature of Christ. We distinguish, however, between communication by μετέκβασιν through transition, or transfusion, and by καθ' ἕνωσιν, through union, whether Sacramental or personal. See Mark 16:16, John 3:6, Galatians 3:27, 1 Peter 3:18. The error of the Donatists must also be observed here, who wished the power of baptism to be suspended from the dignity of the baptizer, when nevertheless the Lord here wished to be baptized by a servant. The Cathari and Anabaptists also err here, refusing to approach the Sacraments if wicked persons receive them at the same time. For Christ is baptized here with a promiscuous crowd, and with the same baptism as the hypocrites.

IV. Concerning the true Deity of Christ. The words of John the Baptist, I myself have need, etc., approved by Christ, affirm it. He by whom all have need to be baptized, not even the holiest men excepted, and from whom all baptism has its power, is not a mere man: but we all have a necessity to be baptized by Christ, and by him etc. For the sake of confirming this theme, these things can be observed (1) that baptism is to be received no less in the name of the Son of God than in the name of the Father and of the Holy Spirit, whence arises an ἀδιάλυτον argument against the enemies of Christ. For Christ in Matthew XXVIII. 19 commanded to baptize equally in his own name as in that of the Father and of the Holy Spirit, and indeed as in the name of one principal cause. But the argument shall be set forth in such a way that it is invincible: In whose name the Sacrament of regeneration ought to be received, he is the true God and the supreme cause of our regeneration. But in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit etc. (2.) The testimony of John the Baptist in John I. 27 confirms the Deity of Christ, who says that he himself is only a minister, but Christ is the primary baptizer, whom for that reason he calls ἰσχυρότερον than himself in Matthew III. 11. Add (3.) That John testifies that Christ will baptize with the Spirit and with fire, because it belongs not to a creature, but to God alone, the supreme, to send or pour out the Holy Spirit. (4.) That John shows religious honor to Christ, and calls himself unworthy to untie his sandals in Matthew III. 11, such honor as is shown to God in Exodus III. 5, Joshua V. 15. (5.) That John testifies that Christ was before him in John I. 27, from which we do not indeed argue thus, he who is before John is the true God, as the Photinians falsely attribute to us; nevertheless we can constrain them in this way: He who was before John, and yet not by reason of his human nature, he necessarily was before him according to another nature: But that nature is none other than the divine. (6.) That Christ is declared here by a solemn voice to be the Son of God from heaven, Matthew III. 17. But for him to be the Son of God in the proper sense, two things are required: 1. Generation from the Father: 2. Participation of the same essence: But Christ is not the improper, but the proper Son of God in Romans VIII. 32, just as his Father is ἴδιος God, in John V. 18.

V. Concerning the Most Holy Trinity. In this baptism a most illustrious θεοφάνεια occurred, concerning which we note a few things from this place. I. It is to be observed that since there are two things necessary to be believed concerning the Most Holy Trinity (1.) the plurality of persons, (2.) their ὁμοουσία, we prove from this illustrious θεοφανείᾳ that the former is primarily, and consequently the latter is evinced, with other documents applied at the same time: especially Matthew XXVIII. 19. For here the plurality of the divine persons could be perceived as if by the eyes and senses themselves, when he manifested himself.

By the voice the Father, the Son in body, the Spirit hail. Hence it was a solemn thing for the ancients to say to the Arians: Go to the Jordan, and you will see. For as many subjects as God manifested himself in here, so many are the divine persons. And since modern Anti-Trinitarians do not deny that the Father and the Son are distinct persons, only the personality of the Holy Spirit is to be proved. That is firmly concluded by this argument: Whoever assumed a substantial bodily form, appeared in it, was seen, descended visibly, he is an ὑφισάμενον and a subject, and since he is of an intellectual nature, he is truly a person: But the Holy Spirit etc. But those who cut every nerve of this argument are going to render an account to God, the innovators of Calixtus when they contend that the appearance of the dove-like body was not assumed by the Holy Spirit, but that he merely manifested himself in that appearance, it being said by the common mode of attribution, which they call appropriation. See Dreier in the Discussion, at length. The argument of the orthodox is certainly not saved in this way. It is said indeed that even that appropriation insinuates the distinction of persons: But could not the Photinian so easily object that one and the same person can appropriate different things to himself? Thus to appropriate to himself some divine attributes, for example divine justice and omniscience, the visitation of wrath, the inspection of hearts, etc., and yet not be persons. But with our explanation standing, the argument is unmoved, because this is not of a divine attribute, to assume a bodily form, and to appear in the same: But that is proper to subjects. Add that history clearly testifies in Luke III. 22 that the Holy Spirit descended in σωματικῷ εἴδει. See our Anti-Crellius. As regards the latter chapter, the ὁμοουσία is proved here secondarily, because these three are seen in the same light of divine majesty, 1. Timothy VI. 16, and that Christ is declared from heaven to be the Son of God, and thus ὁμοούσιος to the Father, but the Holy Spirit is so called the Spirit of God because he is in God, in whom no creature is, 1 Corinthians II. 11, just as neither could a creature send Christ into the desert, nor instruct him with gifts, which is attributed here to the Holy Spirit and in Matthew IV. 1. Compare Isaiah XI. 1.

VI. Concerning the satisfaction and merit of Christ: from Matthew III. 15. Let it be noted here (I.) the distinction between merit and satisfaction, which are indeed bound together with an adamantine bond, but are still formally distinct 1. in respect of the formal effect, 2. by reason of definition. For Christ, as regards the effects of his office and the θετικὰ and στερητικὰ benefits he prepared for us, the collation of goods and the removal of evils, so that we might not only be freed from due punishments, but also obtain undue rewards, satisfaction belongs to this class, merit to that. Thus St. Athanasius in his book on the incarnation of Christ: for this reason the Son of God assumed a body that could die, so that it, having been made a participant by reason of its parts, might suffice for all for a full satisfaction by death. Ambrose on the flight of the world, ch. 3. He undertook death so that the sentence might be fulfilled, and satisfaction might be made to the judgment through the curse of sinful flesh even unto death. Hence, therefore, Satisfaction is satisfaction for a debt, not properly the attainment of a reward. It is therefore another and distinct benefit, which also acquired eternal life. As to the definition: just as there is not one formal principle, so neither is there the same formal reason. Satisfaction consists in the translation of guilt and the enduring of punishment, merit in the vicarious fulfillment of the law; although indeed the active and passive obedience of Christ cohere greatly, it is nevertheless necessary to distinguish both: for passions are not formally actions, even if He acted in His passion, and in His action He suffered many things. In the Scriptures these do not seem to be so distinguished: for to the passion of Christ is attributed justification (Is. 53; 1 Pet. 2:24), righteousness (Rom. 5:9), the inheritance of eternal life (Heb. 5:8-9). But let this be in a double respect: 1. By an eminent reason, because by His passion the obedience of Christ was consummated (Phil. 2:8). 2. Mediately and consequently: because while He procured for us liberation from death, by that very fact He restored salvation, because He acquired the remission of sins, consequently He brought righteousness to us. For where sins are remitted, there also is righteousness, or innocence, and eternal salvation.

(II.) We prove the merit of Christ from these words: he who fulfilled all righteousness, he satisfied the law perfectly. Christ therefore did this either for Himself or for us: not the former, for He was Lord of the law (Matt. 12:8). If He is Lord of the Sabbath: therefore also of the law, if indeed He who instituted the Sabbath, He brought forth the law, and is Lord of the law. Where the Grotian depravation of the words of this passage comes to be observed, which he interprets in his usual manner, that is, he corrupts, explaining those words concerning a mere and naked man, because the Lord of the Sabbath is according to the rule of Rabbi Jonathan: The Sabbath was delivered into the hands of man: not man into the hand of the Sabbath: seeking nothing for reasons, (1.) that Christ professed himself subject to the law on earth: Resp. Both are true: he was a servant of the law by voluntary submission, but he was Lord by dignity of person, as true God, and man in the form of God. (2.) That from the parallel place Mark II. 24. it is manifest: Resp.
