That place favors Grotius in nothing: two causes are rendered by Christ, why he did not violate the Sabbath: 1. that the Sabbath was constituted for the sake of man; therefore for his sake man ought not to perish. 2. That Christ is more sublime than the Sabbath. This being observed, the whole mass of the Grotian argument collapses. (3.) That Christ at that time did not profess himself the Son of God. Resp. However that might not have been done by Christ directly, yet intellectually it was indicated not once, but also expressly signified in Matthew XI. 17, indeed in Matthew III. 17 God intimates it from heaven, and John had openly testified concerning him in John III. 35, 36, indeed the demons themselves had professed it in Matthew VIII. 29. We add, however, other parallel places (1.) Galatians IV. 4, where for our sake he is said to have been made under the law, where he is also distinguished from those being redeemed from the curse of the law, and those who were under the law by necessity; and he is said to have been made under the law not by birth, but after he was born, by voluntary subjection; not for his own sake but for ours, so that we might become sons of God, the Son of God was made under the law. (2.) Philippians II. 6 ff., where he is said to have submitted himself voluntarily, and it is referred to the form of a servant, which he freely and voluntarily assumed; therefore it is not to be referred to the property of nature; which is to be noted against those who say that Christ was a servant by property of nature, from which it would follow that Christ would be a servant of God even in the state of glory, which is absurd. Because glory does not take away nature, but only exalts it. Nor is there any reason for one to say: he is a servant in a more noble way now in the state of glory: for even so he would be our fellow-servant, and not to be worshipped, which conflicts with the passage Revelation XIX. 10. (3.) Romans X. 4, Christ is said to be the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes. Conf. 1 Corinthians I. 30, Romans V. 18, 19. The use of this doctrine is against Piscator and his followers, who contend that Christ was subject to the law in himself, and argue that his active obedience confers nothing upon men: likewise against Socinus, who assert that Christ fulfilled the law not for us, but for himself.

III. We prove the satisfaction of Christ also from this passage. We argue: If he had to fulfill all righteousness, it was necessary that he satisfy divine justice completely. The reason is clear: otherwise all righteousness would not have been fulfilled. It is confirmed from the end of the baptism undertaken, because by it he bound himself to his office: likewise from the attestation of the heavenly voice in Matthew III. 17. For how it pleased God in Christ, Colossians I. 19, 20, Paul explaining concerning the redemption made through him adds, that in him it pleased all the fullness to dwell, and through him to reconcile all things, which was done through his blood, and satisfactory death: Conf. Ephesians I. 6, Romans V. 8, 9. Nor is there any reason for one to object that Christ in these words includes John at the same time, who did not satisfy for men: For all things are to be understood according to the analogy of faith, and it is necessary to explain the predicates according to the diversity of the subject, according to the rule of the logicians: and therefore it is necessary to interpret from the Scriptures in what manner John, and in what manner Christ, is said to fulfill righteousness.

VII. Concerning modesty and humility. An example of which is provided both by John, refusing the office of baptizing Christ; and by Christ, seeking baptism from John, whom he could have commanded. Let us imitate them 1. so that we do not covet more serious offices, Sirach III. 18 ff., but wait for the calling of God, Job III. 27, Hebrews V. 4. 2. That we may strive for true humility, Philippians II. 3, Colossians III. 12. Conf. Philippians II. 5, John I. 81 ff.

VIII. Concerning the veneration of the Sacraments: that we may religiously venerate these divine means of salvation, the Sacraments. Christ, who did not need baptism, undertook it, lest we who do need it, reject baptism. Moreover, it warns and moves us 1. The dignity of the Sacraments, which shines forth especially from their names and titles, and from all the causes of the Sacraments. 2. The authority of the divine command, Matthew III. 8, chapter XXVIII. 19, 1 Corinthians XI. 23. 3. The gravity of the divine interdict. Matthew VII. 6, 1 Corinthians X. 14 ff. That which is holy is not to be given to dogs. Therefore let us not approach like dogs. Those who communicate with the body of Christ should flee idols, those who approach the table of the Lord should not communicate with the table of demons, much less with evil works. 1 John III. 8. 4. The atrocity of the punishment, Mark XVI. 16, 1 Corinthians XI. 29. 5. The clarity of examples: many baptized by John led by religion, and Christ himself, etc. Let this doctrine warn the ministers of the word to conduct themselves reverently in the dispensation, and not to admit the unworthy: and others also to prepare themselves for the Sacraments, not to extort them, not to despise them, Luke VII. 30.

Latin:

Vers. 17. Ἀγαπητὸς] Quod apud Esaiam est בחירי, ἐκλεκτός μου: nam ἐκλεκτὸς & ἀγαπητὸς pro eodem poni solent. Vid. Psal. II.

Ἐν ᾧ εὐδόκησα] Vox hæc, ut Latina, placet, modo ad voluntatis decretum, modo ad propensum affectum re- fertur. Hoc interest quod Latina vox de objecto, Græca de subjecto dicitur. Ad affectum significandum Græci scriptores dicunt εὐδοκεῖν τινι. Ad ἐνδοκεῖν ἔν τινι ut hic & infra XVII. 5. Marc. I. 11. Luc. III. 22. 1. Cor. X. 5. Hebr. X. 38. aut εἴς τινα ut infra XII. 18. 2. Petr. I. 17. manifestus est Hebraismus חפץ בו ut Gen. XXXIV. 14. aut רצה בו ut 1. Paral. XXVIII. 4. Quod Hieronymus dicit loquendi hoc genus à LXX. interpretibus esse confictum, intelli- gendum est de ista construendi forma, & de nomine inde derivato εὐδοκία, quod nisi apud Judæos Hellenistas non est invenire. Sæpe autem & רצה hoc modo vertunt LXX. ut Ps. XL. 14. (in Hebræo: ita enim Psalmos citare constitui) XLIV. 4. CXIVII. 10. CXLIX. 4. ubi רוצה בעמו vertitur εὐδοκεῖ ἐν τῷ λαῷ. Est autem plane sen- sus idem in his verbis ἐν ᾧ εὐδόκησα qui in illis Esaiæ רצתה נפשי ubi & Græci quidam interpretes habent εἰς ὃν εὐδό- κησεν ἡ ψυχή με. Invenies eodem sensu & εὐδοκεῖν cum Dativo, omissa ἐν particula. Sic εὐδοκεῖν τῇ λατρείᾳ dixit scriptor primi Maccabaici I. 45. Irenæi interpres hoc ἐν ᾧ εὐδόκησα vertit, in quo bene sensi libro III. cap. XL.

Addere hic juvat observationes in prælectioni- bus de Eloquiis oris Christi ante hos viginti duos annos publice hic propositas: I. De Reverentia Ministerio exhibenda, quæ colligitur ex exemplo Christi. Hic excitat nos (1.) Mandati divini au- toritas 1. Corinth. XVI. 15. 1. Tim. V. 17. Tit. II. 15. Ebr. XIII. 17. cumprimis 1. Thess. V. 17. dupli- ci, id est, eximio honore prosequendi qui mi- nistrant. (2.) Muneris sublimitas: Sunt servi & legati Dei 2. Corinth. VI. 4. 1. Thess. III. 2. Coru- scant honore Legantis: sunt œconomi 1. Corinth. IV. 1. sunt legati pro Christo 2. Corinth. V. 20. igno- minia redundat in principalem, ut ait Christus Matth. X. 40. Luc. X. 16. sunt συνεργοὶ Θεῦ 1. Cor. III. 9. 2. Corinth. V. 30. (3.) Nominum dignitas. Vocantur à Spiritu Sancto. Viri Dei 1. Sam. II. 27. 1. Tim. VI. 11. 2. Tim. III. 17. Angeli Domini Esa. XLII. 19. Mal. II. 7. c. III. 1. Apoc. I. 30. sunt excipiendi ut Angeli Gal. III. 14. Pastores, Jerem. III. 15. Ep. IV. 1. Patres, 2. Reg. VI. 1. Cor. IV. 15. Gal. IV. 9. Presbyteri ac Seniores Tit. I. 5. Jac. V. 14. Doctores Act. XIII. 1. Προεστῶτες 1. Tim. V. 17. Ἡγούμενοι Act. XV. 22. Ebr. XVII. 14. (4.) Exemplorum claritas, cumprimis Gal. IV. 14. 1. Thess. II. 13. Denique hoc loco Christi ipsius ex- emplum.

II. De Johannis eminentia, quod Christus ab eo baptizatus est: est περισσότερος Matth. XI. 11. Luc. VI. 28. Vid. & Irenæus l. 3. adv. hæreses c. 11. est Johannes simul Propheta, qui Messiam ventu- rum prædixit; simul Apostolus quia præsentem quoque ostendit, immo quia Messiam ad officium inauguravit: hinc est μείζων præ genitis è mulieri- bus; additur autem, minor tamen eo qui minimus in regno cœlorum. Ἐναντιοφανείαν hanc duplici modo posse tolli notat Paschasius l. 2. T: 9. Bibl.

PP. pag. 1044. (1.) quod firtentius, esse tantum hoc externum adhuc aliquid, quod Angelus dicatur, nec ad salutem spectare, unde qui illam habeat felicior sit. (2.) Si minimus in regno cælorum esse intelliga- tur Christus ob summam exinanitionem, & decus omne sepositum Esa. LIII. 5. minor Johanne in carne videri poterat, ideo decere censebat, ut ba- ptismum peteret, interim tamen major Christus e- rat ob muneris & personæ dignitatem.

III. De efficacia Baptismi Johannis. Hic con- tra Calvinianos disputandum, imprimis contra Spanhem. Part. 3. Dub. Evang. ubi inficiatur ba- ptismo a Christo suscepto nostrum esse sanctificatum, (1.) quia aquæ Jordanis solæ habituræ sic essent virtutem illam, quia ex solæ attigere Christi car- nem: (2.) Quod aqua capax ejusmodi qualitatis spiritualis non fuerit: (3.) Quod Sacramenta non sint pixides gratiæ, sed σφραγῖδες, nec agant ut cau- sæ physicæ, sed instrumenta moralia: (4.) Quod vis purgandi propria sit Creatori, incommunicabilis creaturæ. Respond. 1. in genere hæc omnia re- cte opponi Papistis, quatenus opus operatum in Sacramentorum doctrina urgent, sed non efficaciæ vivæ baptismi. 2. In specie, quod ad primum, negamus (1.) illas aquas per contactum materialem sive corporalem, & non potius spiritualem & virtualem sanctificatas esse. (2.) Aquæ Jordanis non fuere Sacramentum, qua aquæ, sed qua a- quæ baptismo consecratæ, per gratiæ divinæ communicationem, sed quæ conveniret ipsis tan- tum in actu dispensationis istius Sacramenti: absit inhærentia Physicæ. (3.) Uti Christus nostras pas- siones dicitur in se recepisse, & sic sanctificasse, ita & h. l. de baptismo res se habet. Addendum autem insuper, vim Sacramenti non tam depen- dere ab hoc Christi baptismo, quam a baptismi in- stitutione a Christo facta, ideoque hæc simul acci- pienda. Ad secundum resp. Aqua mera & qua talis non est capax; sed divina institutione & or- dinatione talis redditur: non respiciendum tan- tum ad materiam terrenam, sed & cælestem, ordi- nationemque divinam: supplet hæc quod naturæ ejus deest. Præterea ad tertium, (1.) non con- sideramus Sacramenta ut pyxides gratiæ, fatemur eadem esse media & organa gratiæ, eam autem non significantia tantum vel pure σημαντικὰ sed προσφερόμενα. (2.) Non agunt ea media tan- tum per modum causæ moralis, sed Physicæ, quia Deus hæc media voluit ita instituta, & effectus ab eis dependet, per realem influxum, licet inducant effectum se superiorem, ex ordinatione divina: agunt enim vi eminenti, non naturali. Ad quar- tum Respond. Vis purgandi in se, ex se, & per se Deo est propria, sed communicari per Dei gra- tiam creaturæ potest, uti humanæ naturæ Christi. Distinguimus autem inter communicationem μετέκβασιν per transitum, vel transfusionem, & καθ' ἕνωσιν, per unionem sive Sacramentalem sive personalem. Vid. Marc. XVI. 16. Johan. III. 6. Gal. III. 27. 1. Petr. III. 18. Observandus & hic Dona- tistarum error, qui suspensam voluerunt virtutem baptismi a dignitate baptizantis, cum tamen hic Dominus a servo voluerit baptizari. Cathari & Anabaptistæ hic quoque errant, renuentes ad Sa- cramenta accedere, si flagitiosi eadem simul ca- piant. Christus enim cum promiscua turba bapti- zatur hic, & eodem baptismo cum hypocritis.

IV. De vera Deitate Christi. Verba Johannis Baptistæ, ego ipse opus habeo &c. a Christo appro- bata eam affirmant. A quo baptizari omnes ne- cessum habent, ne sanctissimis quidem hominibus exceptis, & a quo omnis baptismus suam vim ha- bet, is non est homo merus: at à Christo baptiza- ri necessum habemus omnes, & ab eo &c. Ejus thematis confirmandi ergo observari hæc possunt (1) quod baptismus suscipiendus sit non minus in nomine Filii Dei, quam in nomine Patris & Spiri- tus Sancti, unde nascitur argumentum ἀδιάλυτον contra hostes Christi. Christus enim Matth. XXVIII. 19. æque in nomine suo ac Patris, & Spiri- tus Sancti jussit baptizare, & quidem ut in unius cause principalis nomine. Ita autem informabitur argumentum, ut invictum sit: In cujus nomine Sacramentum regenerationis suscipi debet, is est verus Deus & causa suprema nostræ regeneratio- nis. At in nomine Patris, Filii, & Spiritus San- cti &c. (2.) Testimonium Johannis Baptistæ Johan. I. 27. confirmat Christi Deitatem, qui ait se tantum esse ministrum, Christum autem ba- ptizatorem primarium, quem ideo sese ἰσχυρότε- ρον dicit Matth. III. 11. Adde (3.) Quod Jo- hannes Christum testetur baptizaturum Spiritu & igne, quia non creaturæ, sed solius Dei supre- mi est mittere vel effundere Spiritum Sanctum. (4.) Quod Johannes religiosum honorem Christo exhibeat, seque indignum dicat qui solvat calcea- menta ejus Matth. III. 11. qualis Deo honor ex- hibeatur Exod. III. 5. Jos. V. 15. (5.) Quod teste- tur Johannes Christum ante se fuisse Joh. I. 27. in- de non quidem ita argumentamur, qui est ante Johannem is est verus Deus, ut Photiniani nobis id affingunt; verumtamen eosdem hoc modo con- stringere possumus; Qui fuit ante Johannem, nec tamen ratione humanæ naturæ, is secundum a- liam naturam necessario ante eum fuit: Ea vero natura non alia, quam divina est. (6.) Quod Christus solenni voce hic Dei Filius de cœlo de- claretur, Matth. III. 17. Ut autem sit filius Dei sensu proprio, duo requiruntur: 1. E patre ge- neratio: 2. Participatio ejusdem essentiæ: Est autem Christus non improprius, sed proprius Dei Filius Rom. VIII. 32. uti Pater ejus ἴδιος est Deus, Joh. V. 18.

V. De Sacrosancta Trinitate. Hoc in ba- ptismo θεοφάνεια illustrissima facta est, de qua paucula notamus ex h. l. I. Observandum cum duo sint de Sacrosancta Trinitate creditu neces- saria (1.) personarum pluralitas, (2.) earum ὁ- μοουσία, probamus ex hac illustri θεοφανείᾳ pri- mario illam, consequenter hanc evinci, adhibitis simul aliis documentis: cumprimis Matth. XXVIII. 19. Hic enim quasi oculis & sensibus ipsis perci- pi potuit divinarum personarum pluralitas, cum se manifestavit.

Voce Pater, Natus corpore, Flamen ave. Veteribus hinc solenne Arianis dicere: Abi ad Jordanem, & videbis. Quot enim Deus se sup- positis hic manifestavit, tot sunt personæ divi- næ. Et quum moderni Anti-Trinitarii, Patrem & Filium esse distinctas personas non negent, pro- banda solum personalitas Spiritus Sancti. Ea firmiter hoc argumento concluditur: Quicunque formam corpoream substantialem assumsit, in ea apparuit, visus est, descendit visibiliter, is est ὑφισάμενον & suppositum, & cum sit intelle- ctualis naturæ, vere persona: At Spiritus San- ctus &c. Deo autem rationem reddituri sunt, qui Argumento huic omnem nervum incidunt, Calixti Novatores cum contendunt speciem co- lumbini corporis non esse assumtam à Spiritu Sancto, sed eum saltem ea specie se manifestasse, dici vulgari attributionis modo, quam appropriatio- nem vocant. Vid. Dreier in der Erört. prolixe. Orthodoxorum certe argumentum sic non salva- tur bitur. Dicit quidem, etiam appropriationem il- lam distinctionem personarum insinuare: Sed annon ita facile poterit excipere Photinianus, unam ean- demque personam posse sibi diversa appropriare? Ita attributa divina appropriare sibi nonnulla exem- pli gratia justitiam & omniscientiam divinam vi- sitationem iræ, inspectionem cordium, &c. & tamen non esse personas. Nostra autem stante explicatione argumentum immotum est, quia hoc attributi divini non est, assumere formam corporalem, inque eadem apparere: Sed pro- prium id est suppositorum. Adde quod historia clare testetur Luc. III. 22. quod σωματικῷ εἴδει descenderit Spiritus Sanctus. Vid. Anti-Crellius noster. Posteriùs caput quod attinet, ὁμοουσία hic δευτέρως probatur, quod hi tres aspiciantur in eadem luce, majestatis divinæ, 1. Tim. VI. 16. quodque Christus Filius Dei, adeoque ὁμοούσιος Patri declaretur è cœlo, Spiritus Sanctus autem ita Spiritus Dei dicatur quod in Deo sit, in quo creatura non est 1. Cor. II. 11. uti nec creatura Chri- stum in desertum mittere potuit, nec donis in- struere, quod tribuitur hic Spiritui S. & Matth. IV. 1. Conf. Esai XI. 1.

VI. De satisfactione & merito Christi: è Matt. III. 15. Notetur hic (I.) distinctio inter meritum & satisfactionem, quæ sane adamantino nexu de- vinctissima, sed formaliter tamen adhuc distincta 1. respectu formalis effectus, 2. ratione definitionis. Christus enim quod ad effecta muneris sui & be- neficia θετικὰ & στερητικὰ nobis paravit, bonorum collationem, & malorum ablationem, ut non tan- tum à pœnis debitis liberaremur, sed etiam præmia indebita consequeremur, ad hanc classem satisfa- ctio, ad illam meritum pertinet. Sic D. Athan. l. de incarnatione Christi: ideo corpus, quod mori posset, assumsit Dei Filius, ut illud ratione particeps factum pro omnibus morte ad plenam satisfactionem sufficeret. Ambros. de fuga seculi c. 3. Suscepit mortem ut impleretur sententia, satisfieret judicato per maledictum carnis peccatricis usque ad mortem. Hinc ergo Satisfactio est pro debito satisfactio, non proprie præmii adeptio. Alterum igitur & distinctum beneficium est, quod etiam ac- quisivit vitam æternam. Quod ad definitionem: ut formale principium unum non est, ita nec ea- dem ratio formalis. Satisfactio in culpæ transla- tione & pœnæ perpessione meritum in vicaria legis impletione consistit; quanquam vero activa & passi- va Christi obedientia cohæreant maxime, distin- guere tamen utramque necessum est: nec enim passiones formaliter actiones sunt, etsi in passione egerit, & in actione passus multa sit. In Scriptu- ris hæc non videntur adeo distingui: passioni enim Christi tribuitur justificatio Es. LIII. 41. 1. Pet. II. 24. justitia Rom. V. 9. hæreditas vitæ æternæ Ebr. V. 8. 9. Sed sit hoc duplici respectu: 1. Eminenti ra- tione, quia passione consummata est obedientia Christi Phil. II. 8. 2. Mediate & consequenter: quia dum nobis peperit liberationem à morte, eo ipso salutem reparavit, quia remissionem peccatorum acquisivit, consequenter nobis justi- tiam adduxit. Ubi enim remittuntur peccata, ibi & justitia est, vel innocentia, & salus æterna.

(II.) Probamus meritum Christi ex his verbis: qui omnem implevit justitiam, is legi satisfecit perfecte. Christus ergo id vel pro se, vel pro nobis fecit: non prius, nam erat Dominus legis Matth. XII. 8. Si Dominus Sabbati est: Ergo & legis, si- quidem qui Sabbatum instituit, is legem tulerit, legisque Dominus sit. Ubi observanda venit Grotiana depravatio verborum hujus loci, quem interpretatur pro more suo, h. e. corrumpit, ex- plicans ea verba de mero & nudo homine, quod Dominus Sabbathi sit juxta regulam Rabbi Jona- thanis: Sabbathum traditum est in manus hominis: non homo in manum Sabbathi: ne quicquam con- quirens rationes, (1.) quod Christus se subditum le- gis in terris professus est: Resp. utrumque verum est: legis servus erat voluntaria submissione, Do- minus autem fuit persona dignitate, qua verus De- us, & homo in forma Dei. (2.) Quod e loco pa- rall. Marc. II. 24. id manifestum sit: Resp. locus ille nil favet Grotio: duae causae a Christo reddun- tur, quod non violarit Sabbathum: 1. quod Sabbathum hominis gratia sit constitutum; ejus igitur causa hominem non debere perire. 2. Quod Christus sit sublimior Sabbatho. Hoc observa- to corruit omnis moles argumenti Grotiani. (3.) Quod Christus isto tempore se Filium DEI non professus fuerit. Resp. utut illud non fuisset fa- ctum a Christo directe, tamen διανοητικῶς id non semel indicatum, sed & expresse Matth. XI. 17. si- gnificatum, immo Matth. III. 17. Deus de coelo id intimatat, ac de eo Johan. III. 35. 36. palam Johan- nes testatus fuerat, imo ipsi daemones professi erant Matth. VIII. 29. Addimus autem alia loca pa- rallela (1.) Gal. IV. 4. ubi nostra causa dicitur factus sub lege, ubi & distinguitur a redimendis a maledi- ctione legis, illisque qui sub lege erant ἐξ ἀνάγκην; & sub lege factus dicitur non per nativitatem, sed postquam natus erat, per ultroneam subjectio- nem; non sui sed nostri causa, ut nos filii Dei fiere- mus, factus est sub lege Dei Filius. (2.) Phil. II. 6. seqq. ubi ultro dicitur se submississe, & refertur id ad formam servi, quam libere & voluntarie susce- pit; ergo non est referendum ad natura proprieta- tem; quod notandum contra eos qui Christum natura proprietate Dei fuisse servum dicunt, ex quo consequeretur, Christum etiam in statu glo- riae servum Dei esse, quod absurdum. Quia glo- ria naturam non tollit, sed tantum extollit. Nec est quod quis dicat: nobiliori modo eum esse servum nunc in statu gloriae: nam & sic esset conservus no- ster, nec adorandus, quod refragatur loco Apoc. XIX. 10. (3.) Rom. X. 4. τέλος νόμου ad justitiam omni credenti Christus dicitur. Conf. 1. Cor. I. 30. Rom. V. 18. 19. Usus hujus doctrinae est contra Pi- scatorem, & asseclas, qui Christum obnoxium fuisse legi per se contendunt, & obedientiam ejus activam hominibus nihil conferre pugnant: item contra Socin. qui non pro nobis, sed pro se legem implevisse Christum asserunt.

III. Probamus Satisfactionem Christi quoque ex h. l. Argumentamur: Si omnem justitiam im- plere debuit, necessum fuit ut justitiae divinae ex asse satisfaceret. Ratio patet: alias non fuisset omnis justitia impleta. Confirmatur e fine susce- pti baptismatis, quod eo se ad munus suum obstrin- xerit: item e vocis caelestis aetestatione Matth. III. 17. Quomodo enim complacitum sit Deo in Chri- sto, Coloss. I. 19. 20. Paulus explicans de redem- tione per ipsum facta addit, ὅτι ἐν αὐτῷ ἐυδόκησε πᾶν τὸ πλήρωμα κατοικῆσαι, καὶ δι αὐτοῦ ἀποκα- ταλλάξαι τὰ πάντα, quod factum per sanguinem ejus, & mortem satisfactoriam: Conf. Eph. I. 6. Rom. V. 8. 9. Nec est quod quis objiciat, Chri- stum in his verbis comprehendere simul Johannem, qui non satisfecit pro hominibus: Nam omnia intelli- genda secundum analogiam fidei, & pro diversita- te subjecti explicare oportet praedicata, juxta Re- gulam Logicorum: ideoque oportet e Scripturis interpretari, qua ratione Johannis, & qua Christus implere dicatur justitiam.

VII. De modestia & humilitate. Cujus exem- plum præbet tum Johannes, recusans munus ba- ptizandi Christum; tum Christus baptismum à Johanne petens, cui poterat imperare. Imite- mur eos 1. ne graviora munia ambiamus Syr. III. 18. seqq. sed vocationem Dei exspectemus Job. III. 27. Ebr. V. 4. 2. Ut humilitati veræ studea- mus, Phil. II. 3. Col. III. 12. Conf. Phil. II. 5. Joh. I. 81. seqq.

VIII. De Sacramentorum veneratione: ut hæc divina salutis media Sacramenta religiose vene- remur. Christus qui baptismo non eguit, susce- pit, ne nos qui egemus, baptismum respuamus. Monet autem & movet nos 1. Sacramentorum di- gnitas, quæ elucescit cumprimis è nominibus & e- logiis, & è causis omnibus Sacramentorum. 2. Divini mandati auctoritas, Matth. III. 8. cap. XXVIII. 19. 1. Cor. XI. 23. 3. Interdicti divini gravitas. Matth. VII. 6. 1. Cor. X. 14. seqq. San- ctum non est dandum canibus. Ne ergo acceda- mus tanquam canes. Qui communicant corpori Christi, idola fugiant, qui mensæ Domini acce- dunt, mensæ dæmoniorum ne communicent, ne- dum operibus malignis. 1. Joh. III. 8. 4. Supplicii atrocitas, Marc. XVI. 16. 1. Cor. XI. 29. 5. Exem- plorum perspicuitas: multi à Johanne baptizati reli- gione ducti, & ipse Christus, &c. Doctrina hæc mo- neat ministros verbi, ut se reverenter gerant in di- spensatione, nec indignos admittant: alios quoque ut ad Sacramenta se præparent, eadem non extor- queant, ne spernant, Luc. VII. 30.

## 4:1 Argument
CHAPTER IV.

ARGUMENT AND DIVISION.

Jesus, led away into the desert by the Spirit, after a fast of forty days being tempted that he might make stones into bread, repels the Devil with the word (Deut. VIII. 3.) Again, that he might cast himself down from the pinnacle, because custody was entrusted to the Angels, with Scripture as witness (Ps. XCI. 11.) he repels the same with the prohibition of tempting God, (Deut. VI. 16.) A third time tempted by the worship of the Devil, he defeats the same with the commandment concerning worshipping God alone (Deut. VI. 13.) whence the Devil left him, and Angels served him. Moreover, after the report concerning John being handed over, he came into Galilee, dwelling in Capernaum, that the prophecy of Isaiah might be fulfilled (c. IX. 1.) and he preached repentance and the coming of the kingdom of heaven. Furthermore, walking by the sea of Galilee, he saw two fishermen, Simon Peter and Andrew, and called them, they being about to become fishers of men: Soon he similarly called James and John, who, leaving their father Zebedee and their ships, likewise followed him. Thence, having traveled through Galilee, he taught here and there in the Synagogues, and cured various diseases, his fame being spread into Syria, and various sick people being brought to him from everywhere.

There are three parts: I. Preparation for public ministry made by a triple temptation in the desert, to v. 11. II. Certain things pertaining to deeds from the first Passover to the second, such as the arrival in Galilee, the dwelling in Capernaum, and the sermons of Jesus, as also the calling of the double pair of fisherman brothers, Simon Peter and Andrew, and also James and John, to v. 22. III. Some deeds from the second to the third Passover, such as sermons and the healings of various diseases in Galilee, to verse 25.

PART I. The temptations of Jesus in the desert.

Ver. 1. Ἀνήχθη] I think it is entirely true, both here and in other places of the sacred writers, that there is in this word the force of ἄνω, so that Christ is understood to have been led upward from the Jordan. Now, that is said to be upward which is closer to Jerusalem. John was indeed also in a desert place: but Christ was driven into a more horrific wilderness, in which wild beasts lived, as can be seen in Mark.

Εἰς τὴν ἔρημον] For the completion of the ancient figure. For the people of Israel were also led through the wilderness.

Ὑπὸ τοῦ πνεύματος] Luke teaches us that the Syrian interpreter and others do not err, who think that by that article a relation is indicated to that which immediately preceded; for because he had interposed a genealogy, he continues this history with the history of the Baptism and the Holy Spirit in this way: 'And Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan, and was led in the Spirit into the wilderness.' In which place it is briefly said ἐν πνεύματι, for which a fuller Hebraism would say ἐν χειρὶ τοῦ πνεύματος, for that has the same value as διὰ τοῦ πνεύματος, just as below v. 13, ἐν τίνι is διὰ τίνος. Luke expressed the same sense in IV. 14 with these words: ἐν τῇ δυνάμει πνεύματος; all of which I note the more willingly, lest anyone, with certain ancients and moderns, should think that what is narrated here happened to Christ not truly but κατὰ φαντασίαν. Moreover, we learn in this example of Christ that immediately after baptism, that is, the beginning of a sincere life, temptations loom. The wise Hebrew of Ecclesiasticus II. 1: 'My son, if you come to serve the Lord, prepare your soul for temptation.'

Διαβόλου] A word discovered by the Hellenists, by which they express the force of the Hebrew word Satan. For the general meaning of an adversary could suit no one more than a calumnious accuser. That it is written Zabulus by Hilary, Phoebadius, and other Doctors of the Latin Church is not to be sought from a true Greek dialect, but from the corrupted pronunciation of later times; for by two syllables coalescing into one, the same sound was made from dia that used to be expressed by za. Thus, in the writers of the Augustan history, we read zeta for dieta.

A struggle and fight immediately followed the inauguration of Christ to his office, and that by far the most serious, whether you look at the circumstance of place or time, or the mind, arts, and power of the enemy, or the frequency of the encounters, because for all those 40 days he was with the wild beasts and tempted by the devil, as the Holy Spirit testifies (Mark I. 13, Luke IV. 4). He was not, however, in heaven then, as the Socinians trifle; see Smalcius, De divinitate Christi, c. 4, p. 13. Yet Crellius contradicts this in his commentary on c. 4 of Matthew, p. 229, acknowledging that Christ was only there for those 40 days, although he wishes that Satan did not attack him so openly then, but rather sought him out as if from a distance with his darts, but after the fast began to fight with Christ at close quarters. But Spanheim (p. 3, Dub. Evang. 22, p. 302) denies in vain that other temptations preceded, since the phrase of Luke c. IV. 2 clearly implies it. ἡμέρας τεσσαράκοντα πειραζόμενος ὑπὸ τοῦ Διαβόλου, so that Spanheim had the necessity to invent an ellipsis and prefix the word ἦν; but who gave him the power to add anything to Scripture? There is no doubt that Satan wished to weary Christ first with various and exterior terrors and interior darts, so that, having (in his judgment) well exhausted him with those continuous temptations and long-lasting fasting, he might attack him with a more vehement assault and utterly overthrow him, whence, having placed a colophon only on the most serious temptations, he left the arena, routed by the word of the Lord.

Latin:

CAPUT IV.

ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Jesus in desertum abductus à Spiritu, post quadraginta dierum jejunium tentatus, ut lapides panes efficiat, repellit Diabolum verbo (Deut. VIII. 3.) Iterum ut se præcipi- tet de pinna, quia Angelis custodia deman- data est, teste Scriptura (Ps. XCI. 11.) re- pellit eundem interdicto tentationis Dei, (Deut. VI. 16.) Tertium tentatus Diaboli latria, profligat eundem mandato, de solo Deo adorando (Deut. VI. 13.) unde reliquit eum Diabolus, servieruntque ei Angeli. Post famam autem de tradito Johanne in Gali- læam venit, habitans in Capernaum, ut im- pleretur vaticinium Esaiæ (c. IX. 1.) & præ- dicavit pænitentiam & adventum regni cœ- lorum. Porro ad mare Galilææ ambulans, Piscatores duos, Simonem Petrum, & An- dream vidit, eosq̄ vocavit, facturos eos Pis- catores hominum: Mox similiter vocavit Jacobum & Johannem, qui Patrem Zebe- dæum & naves relinquentes itidem eum se- quuti sunt. Dehinc peragrata Galilæa in Sy- nagogis passim docuit, variosque morbos cu- ravit, fama ejus in Syriam divulgata, & un- diquaque adductis ipsi variis ægrotis.

Partes tres sunt: I. Præparatio ad ministerium pu- blicum trina tentatione in deserto facta ad v. 11. II. Quædam ad gesta à primo Paschate ad secun- dum pertinentia, utpote adventus in Galilæam, habitatio in Capernaum, & conciones Jesu ut & vocatio duplicis bigæ fratrum piscatorum, Simonis Petri & Andreæ, nec non Jacobi & Johannis, ad v. 22. III. Nonnulla gesta à secundo ad tertium Pascha, utpote conciones & variorum morborum sanationes in Galilæa, ad vers. 25.

PARS I. Tentatíones Iesu in deserto.

Vers. 1. Ἀνήχθη] Omnino verum puto tam hîc quam aliis sacrorum scriptorum locis huic voci inesse vim τοῦ ἄνω, ut scilicet à Jordane sursum ductus esse Christus intelliga- tur. Sursum autem dicitur quod propius abest ab Hieroso- lymis. Erat quidem & Johannes in loco deserto: sed Christus in horridiorem solitudinem actus est, in qua feræ degebant, ut apud Marcum videre est.

Εἰς τὴν ἔρημον] Ad complementum veteris figuræ. Nam & populus Israëlis per solitudinem ductus.

Ὑπὸ τοῦ πνεύματος] Non errare Syrum interpretem & a- lios, qui articulo isto indicari putant relationem ad id quod proxime antecessit, Lucas nos docet, qui quia gene- ris recensionem interposuerat, historiam hanc cum histo- ria Baptismi & Spiritus Sancti continuat hoc modo, Ἰησοῦς δὲ πνεύματος ἁγίου πλήρης ὑπέστρεψεν ἀπὸ τοῦ Ἰορδάνου, κᾀ ἤγε- το ἐν τῷ πνεύματι εἰς τὴν ἔρημον. Quo in loco breviter di- ctum est ἐν πνεύματι pro quo plenior Hebraismus diceret ἐν χειρὶ τοῦ πνεύματος, id enim idem valet quod διὰ τοῦ πνεύμα- τος, ut infra v. 13. ἐν τίνι est διὰ τίνος. Lucas eundem sensum extulit IV. 14. his verbis ἐν τῇ δυνάμει πνεύματος, quæ omnia eo libentius noto, ne quis cum veteribus qui- busdam novisque existimet, quæ hic narratur Christo non vere sed κατὰ φαντασίαν evenisse. Discimus autem in hoc Christi exemplo statim post baptismum, id est vitæ sinceræ profectionem, imminere tentamenta. Sapiens Hebræus Ecclesiastici II. 1. Τέκνον εἰ προσέρχῃ δουλεύειν τῷ κυρίῳ, ἑτοί- μασον τὴν ψυχήν σου εἰς πειρασμόν.

Διαβόλου] Vox ab Hellenistis reperta, qua vim vocis Hebrææ Satan exprimat. Generalis enim adversarii si- gnificatio nulli magis quam calumnioso accusatori conve- nire. Quod autem ab Hilario, Phœbadio aliisque Latinæ Ecclesiæ Doctoribus Zabulus scribitur non ex Græca vere- te dialecto petendum est, sed ex posteriorum temporum corrupta pronunciatione; duabus enim syllabis in unam coalescentibus factum est ex dia idem sonus qui per za ex- primi solebat. Ita in scriptoribus historiæ Augustæ zeta pro dieta legimus.

Inaugurationem Christi ad officium statim ex- cepit lucta & pugna, eaque longe gravissima, sive loci aut temporis circumstantiam spectes sive hostis animum, τέχνας & potentiam, sive congressuum fre- quentiam, quia per totos illos 40. dies cum feris fuit & tentatus à diabolo, teste Spiritu S. Marc. I. 13. Luc. IV. 4. Non vero in cælis tum fuit, uti nu- gantur Sociniani, vid. Smalc. de divin. Christ. c. 4. p. 13. Cui tamen contradicit Crellius comment. in c. 4. Matth. p. 229. agnoscens Christum per 40. illos dies tantum fuisse, licet velit Satanam eum non ita aperte tum aggressum, sed veluti eminus telis suis ipsum petiisse, post jejunium autem co- minus cæpisse cum Christo pugnare. Nequic- quam vero Spanhem. p. 3. dub. Evang. 22. p. 302. ne- gat, tentationes alias antegressas, cum id diserte fa- tis Lucæ phrasis innuat c. IV. 2. ἡμέρας τεσσαράκοντα πειραζόμενος ὑπὸ τοῦ Διαβόλου ut necessum ha- buerit Spanhemius Ellipsin fingere & præfigere verba ἦν; sed quis potestatem ei fecit Scripturæ aliquid adjiciendi. Nullum dubium est, Satanam Christum defatigare prius voluisse variis & exte- rioribus terriculamentis & interioribus telis, ut continuis illis tentationibus & diuturno jejunio (suo judicio) bene fessum, impetu aggrederetur ve- hementiori, penitusque prosterneret, unde nonni- si gravissimis tentationibus imposito colophone arenam deseruit verbo Domini profligatus.

## 4:2
Vers. 2. Νηστεύσας] Fasting kindles prayers. Therefore Christ, whose every action served our instruction, initiated the function of the office mandated to him with fasting. The ancient Christians imitated this, as appears in Acts XIII. 3, XIV. 22.

ἡμέρας τεσσαράκοντα] The solemn time of fasting, as appears from the history of Moses and Elijah; to which many think the forty days given to the Ninevites for repentance pertain, whence the custom seems to have been derived to the Christians. Certainly, in the Ethiopian and other Churches, the fast, which they exercise most rigidly, is even now called Ninevitic. But also the forty days during which the waters had risen for the cataclysm, and the same number of days during which Ezekiel was ordered to bear the sins of the people, are referred here by some not implausibly. These things are in favor of the Papistic, equivocally so-called, Lenten fast, which Alphonsus de Castro (lib. III, Advers. haeres., tit. Cibus haer. 2) urges, as defined by the Eighth Council of Toledo, c. IX; where he is judged guilty of the Lord's resurrection who has presumed to attempt the eating of meat during the days of Lent: such as Cardinal Bellarmine also asserts are not Christians (lib. II, De Bonis Operibus in partic., c. 9). But Cornelius Jansenius in his Concordance, c. 15, says: 'Who could imitate Christ, fasting for so many days without any food, and hungry?' For Christ, as Tirinus rightly says ad h. l., fasted like Moses and Elijah for 40 continuous days and nights, living without bodily food or drink.

Latin:

Vers. 2. Νηστεύσας] Preces accendit jejunium. Ideo Christus, cujus omnis actio nostræ serviebat institutioni, functionem mandati sibi muneris jejunio initiabat. Imitati hoc sunt Christiani veteres ut apparet Actor. XIII. 3. XIV. 22.

ἡμέρας τεσσαράκοντα] Solenne jejunii tempus, ut ex Mo- sis & Eliæ historia apparet; quo multi pertinere putant dies quadraginta Ninevitis ad pœnitentiam datos, unde mos ad Christianos videtur derivatus. Certe in Æthiopica aliis- que Ecclesiis etiam nunc jejunium, quod rigidissime exer- cent, Nineviticam apellatur. Sed & quadraginta dies, qui- bus aquæ creverant in cataclysmum, & dies totidem qui- bus peccata populi portare jussus est Ezechiel, sunt qui non improbabiliter huc referunt. Hæc in gratiam Papistici æquivoce ita dicti je- junii quadragesimalis, quod Concilio Toletano o- ctavo c. IX. definitum Alphonsus de Castro l. III. ad- vers. hæres. tit. cibus hær. 2. urget; ubi reus judi- catus est resurrectionis Dominicæ, qui esum carnium præsumserit diebus Quadragesimæ attentare: quales non esse Christianos asserit etiam Cardinalis Bellarm. lib. II. de Bon. oper. in partic. c. 9. Atqui Corne- lius Jansenius in Concord. c. 15. Christum, inquit, tot diebus sine omni cibo, atque esurie jejunantem quis i- mitari possit? Christum enim, ut recte Tirinus ad h. l. adinstar Mosis, & Eliæ jejunavit 40. diebus & noctibus continuis, sine cibo vel potu corporeo vi- vens.

## 4:3
Vers. 3. Ὁ πειράζων] The Hebrews, since they are destitute of verbals, use participles in their place: which the Hellenists often follow. And so ὁ πειράζων is ὁ πειραστὴς. That this word was used to signify Satan is shown by the passage of Paul, 1 Thess. III. 5. Moreover, πειράζειν, like 'explorare' in Latin, is a middle word: but according to the circumstances, it is taken sometimes in a good sense, sometimes in a bad one: in a bad one also not in one way only: for it is to entice to sin, as here, or to contrive a calumny, or even by provoking to put patience to the test. נסה among other things signifies to tempt: and thus Baldaeus translates: Gen. XXX, 27. Hence נחש, the serpent, which provided the figure and name to the devil, Gen. III, 1, Apoc. XII, 9, XX, 2.

The threefold temptations were recounted by Matthew the historian, in an arbitrary order by Luke, concerning which Augustine rightly says in his book On the Harmony of the Gospels, 2, ch. 16, that whether this was first and that afterwards is nothing to the point, provided it is manifest that all things were done. Namely: 1. The temptation of distrust. 2. Of presumption. 3. Of idolatry. The first solicited Christ's power, the second his wisdom, the third his piety and perseverance. But let us weigh the responses of Christ, by which he defeated the same, all taken from Holy Scripture as a most well-equipped armory against all temptations, by which he might establish and prove both the authority and sufficiency and perfection and validity and efficacy of the Scripture of the Old Testament. See the weapons of Christ, says Ambrose, with which he conquered for you, not for himself.

Εἰπὲ) can be understood as εἰπὲ τῷ Θεῷ, so that the sense here is, if you trust that you are dear to God, compel God that these stones may become bread for your sake. Certainly, ancient writers consistently deny, and not without great arguments, that the devil recognized anything greater than a man in Christ at this particular time. Nor did he say ὁ υἱὸς, as the Apostles often do, but υἱὸς. Every temptation of the devil tends toward sin. However, they sin who do not implore God's help in a general way, but also prescribe a method to him.

There is no need to posit an ellipsis here. For who would doubt that the Son of God can perform miracles by his own power, and produce bread from stones if he wishes! But it will not be taught that the Son of God is to be understood here in any way other than properly. There is no reason to depart from the literal meaning of the word. And the discourse is about such a Son as had recently been declared from heaven, Matthew 3:17. And therefore Grotius rashly seeks such an impropriety here in the omission of the article, as far as appears; for the article is not always prefixed when the Son of God, properly so called, is being discussed.

Latin:

Vers. 3. Ὁ πειράζων] Hebræi, cum verbalibus destituan- tur, vice eorum participia usurpant: quod sæpe sequuntur Hellenistæ. Itaque ὁ πειράζων est ὁ πειραστὴς. Usitatam fuis- se hanc vocem ad Satanam significandum ostendit Pauli locus 1. Thess. III. 5. est autem πειράζειν, ut explorare La- tine, vox media: sed pro circumstantiis modo in bonam, modo in malam partem sumitur: in malam quoque non uno modo: nam est illicere ad peccandum, ut hic, aut calumniam struere, aut etiam irritando patientiæ pericu- lum facere. נסה inter alia tentare significat: & sic vertit Baldæus: Gen. XXX, 27. Hinc נחש serpens qui diabolo figuram & nomen præbuit Gen. III, 1. Apoc. XII, 9. XX, 2.

Tentationes trinæ fuerunt à Matthæo recensi- tæ historico, à Luca arbitrario ordine, de quo re- cte August. l. de cons. Evang. 2. c. 16. An hoc prius & illud postea, nihil ad rem esse, dum omnia facta esse manifestum sit. Utpote 1. Tentatio diffidentiæ. 2. Præsidentiæ. 3. Idololatriæ. Prima sollicitavit Christi Potentiam, secunda ejus Sapientiam, tertia Pietatem & perseverantiam. Sed responsa Christi expendamus, quibus eundem profligavit omnia è S. Scriptura ceu armamentario instructissimo ad- versus omnes tentationes, desumta sunt, quo & autoritatem & sufficientiam ac perfectionem & vali- ditatem ac efficaciam Scripturæ V. T. stabiliret ac comprobaret. Vide arma Christi, inquit Am- brosius, quibus tibi, non sibi vicit.

Εἰπὲ) potest intelligi εἰπὲ τῷ Θεῷ, ut sensus hic sit, si te Deo carum esse confidis, compella Deum, ut hi lapides panes fiant tui causa. Sane diabolum majus aliquid ho- mine in Christo agnovisse hoc quidem tempore constan- ter, nec sine magnis argumentis, negant scriptores antiqui. Neque dixit ὁ υἱὸς, ut sæpe Apostoli, sed υἱὸς. Tentatio o- mnis diaboli ad peccatum tendit. Peccant autem qui non generaliter Dei auxilium implorant, sed & modum ei præscribunt.

Non opus est figere hic Ellipsin. Nam Filium Dei propria virtute posse miracula patrare, & è la- pidibus panes, si velit, producere, ecquis ambigat! Filium autem Dei aliter quam proprie hic intelli- gendum esse, non docebitur. Causa nulla est à proprietate vocis discedendi. Et de tali Filio ser- mo est, qualis declaratus nuper erat de cœlo, Matth. III, 17. Ideoque temere hic in articuli o- missione ejusmodi improprietatem, quantum ap- paret, quærit Grotius; Non enim semper articulus præfigitur, cum de Filio Dei proprie dicto agitur.

## 4:4
Vers. 4. ἐπὶ παντὶ ῥήματι] That is, in every divine command, whether general or special, there is contained either an express or a tacit promise of necessary things. The law is not to be excluded from the number of these commands, which among others also has this promise proposed to the obedient, 'Blessed shall be your basket and your kneading trough,' Deut. 28:5. Indeed, the very words of God in Deut. 8, from which Christ drew these, tend to the end that the Hebrews might be encouraged to obedience to the law, with the certain hope that God would supply them with what was necessary, either by the ministry of nature or by unusual and wonderful means: just as he had already done when, at his command, the people had gone out from Egypt into the vast wilderness; but Christ rightly adapts that which had been said universally on the occasion of the common law, even to the law peculiarly imposed upon himself for that time.

The first temptation, 'If you are the Son of God, say that these stones may become bread,' by which Satan was not so much intending to cause Christ to doubt himself and his own person, so that Christ would doubt whether he was the Son of God, as Crellius (l. d. p. 230) and Spanheim wish, as he was intending to cause doubt concerning divine Providence, whether God would sustain him, or even to solicit or test the power of Christ, whether he could provide for his own necessity; Christ defeats this with the words of Moses: 'It is written, Deut. VIII. 2, Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God.' For thus he also snatches the weapon from the tempter, that there is no need for him to produce bread from stones, or to doubt the Providence of God, even though he be destitute of bread to satisfy his hunger; by the example of the Israelites, who in the desert were sustained not for 40 days, but for as many years without ordinary bread, and he declares a trust which does not reject external means, even though it looks solely to the word of God, by which the faithful are sustained far more certainly than by any quantity of food whatsoever. Christ does not, however, deny that the Son of God could turn stones into bread, nor yet does he exert his power, partly so that he might not seem to gratify Satan's counsel, partly so that the victory might be more glorious, having been won by patience rather than by power, and partly because the demon was to be overcome not only by the virtue of the Deity, but also by the very humility of the flesh. The ancients add that Christ wished, by a modest concealment of his divinity, to wash away the affectation of divinity which precipitated our first parents into a grave fall, and that he had presented to Satan the infirmity of the assumed nature, so that this might be the bait, under which, like a hook, the hidden divine power might catch and overcome Satan.

Let us consider 1. Ἄρτησιν [The connection], 'Man shall not live by bread alone.' He does not deny that one lives by bread, lest ordinary means be excluded, but 'by bread alone,' lest we remain fixed solely on the means. By 'bread,' in the Hebrew phrase, he understands every kind of food, and whatever is required for the sustenance of life. Therefore, the discourse is not about the life of the soul, but about the life of the body. Meanwhile, Ambrose is not wrong on this passage: 'Whoever is fed by the word of Christ does not require earthly food, for he cannot desire the bread of the world who is refreshed by the bread of the Savior'; since Christ also intends this, that he has no need precisely of bodily sustenance, when he is both sustained and refreshed abundantly by the bread of divine grace. He teaches, says Cyprian in his sermon on the fasting of Christ, that the word of God is to be preferred to bodily foods, and that the mind is to be provided for sooner and more attentively than the belly. The former interpretation is simpler, for it wishes to teach that God can sustain the life of the body even without bread, as the manna shows.

2. Θεσιν [The thesis]. 'Man shall live by the word of God.' Ζήσεται is a potential mood among the Hebrews, 'shall live,' that is, 'will be able to live.' Moreover, 'by the word of God' is not added in Moses, but it is nevertheless contained virtually in those words: 'in everything that proceeds from the mouth of God,' by which the word of God is primarily understood. Heinsius observes that in the nourishment with which God fed his people in the desert, two things were to be looked at. The medium and the divine ordination or Word: because Manna by itself was not such as to nourish, but neither did Manna nourish, but the word of the Lord and the ordination through the Manna: and thus those who lived on Manna lived ἐπὶ ῥήματι θε̃ [by the word of God]. But this is more subtle than solid, for why could the Manna not have nourished! Just as that, too, which he thinks looks here to τὸν ὀυσιώδη λόγον [the essential Word], the Son of God, for he is not the Word proceeding from the mouth of God. Some explain it as everything that it pleases God to employ for the sustenance of man. But having followed Christ as the interpreter, we judge that the word of God is designated. Grotius interprets it as the Word of the command, which contains within itself either an express or a tacit promise of necessary things, which perhaps he drew from the Jews, who refer it to the precepts, by which man is sustained as if by food, but more correctly the Word of God is understood generally, by which man is said to live, not excluding bread or other ordinary means of sustenance, but including them, and that both because of the necessity of the divine blessing, without which even bread could not sustain them, which is obtained through the word (1 Tim. IV. 4). In which sense Jerome rightly infers that he does not live who does not feed on the word of God, and because of the promise of sustenance made in the word of God, which, when apprehended by faith, is by no means void. For the promise of God cannot be fallacious (Deut. XXVIII. 5; Ps. XXXVII. 25), provided we rely on the word of God in our calling. Beautifully, B. Chemnitius: 'Man shall not live by bread alone,' i.e., God is not bound to secondary causes in helping, 'but by every word,' i.e., when we have the word which proceeds from the mouth of God, whether in our calling or in the promise of grace, then there proceeds also from the mouth of the Lord a word of help, i.e., the efficacy of the word can provide for us without, besides, or even against the order of secondary causes, if God has willed it and has judged it salutary for us. He recalls [us] from the word of power, by which stones were to be turned into bread, to the word of grace, by adhering to which they will live even if they lack bread, or ordinary means of sustenance.

Latin:

Vers. 4. ἐπὶ παντὶ ῥήματι] Id est in omni mandato divi- no sive generali, sive speciali, inest aut expressa aut tacita promissio rerum necessariarum. Ex horum mandatorum numero lex non eximenda, quæ inter alias hanc quoque promissionem habet obedientibus propositam, Benedictus orbis tuus & mactra tua, Deut. XXVIII, 5. imo ipsa Dei verba Deut. VIII. unde hæc Christus depromsit, eo ten- dunt, ut ad legis obedientiam animarentur Hebræi, cum certa spe Deum quæ necessaria essent, ipsis suppeditatu- rum, sive naturæ ministerio, sive insolitis atque admiran- dis rationibus: sicut jam fecerat, cum ad ipsius imperium populus ex Ægypto in vastam solitudinem exiisset; Recte autem Christus id quod occasione legis communis dictum erat universaliter, etiam ad legem sibi pro eo tempore pe- culiariter impositum aptat.

Primam tentationem, Si Filius Dei es dic, ut lapi- des hi panes fiant, qua non tam intendebat Satanas diffidentiam Christi de se & persona sua, ut dubita- ret Christus, num sit Dei filius, uti vult Crellius l. d. p. 230. & Spanhemius, quam diffidentiam de Pro- videntia divina, utrum Deus ipsum sustentaturus sit vel etiam solicitationem aut explorationem po- tentiæ Christi, utrum suæ necessitati consulere pos- sit; profligat Christus verbis Mosis: Scriptum est Deut. VIII. 2. Non in solo pane vivet homo, sed in omni verbo, quod egredietur per os Dei. Sic enim & telum eripit tentatori, non opus esse, ut producat e lapidibus panes, aut de Providentia Dei diffidat, tameth pane ad famem sedandam destituatur; ex- emplo Israëlitarum, qui in deserto non 40. dies, sed totidem annos sine pane ordinario sustentati sunt, & fiduciam declarat, quæ non respuit externa me- dia, etsi unice verbum Dei intuetur, quo longe certius fideles sustentantur, quam quantacunque alimentorum copia. Non negat autem Christus Filium Dei posse lapides in panem convertere, nec tamen potentiam suam exserit, tum ne gratificari consilio Satanico videretur, tum ut gloriosior es- set victoria reportata potius per patientiam quam per potentiam, tum quod superandus dæmon non solum à Deitatis virtute, sed ab ipsa quoque car- nis humilitate. Addunt veteres, voluisse Christum modesta divinitatis occultatione divinitatis affecta- tionem eluere, quæ primos Parentes nostros in gravem lapsum præcipites dedit, ac infirmitatem assumtæ naturæ objecisse Satanæ, quo hæc q. esca foret, sub qua tanquam hamus latens divina vir- tus, Satanam caperet & superaret.

Consideremus 1. Ἄρτησιν, Non in solo pane vivit homo. Non negat pane vivere, ne media ordina- ria excludantur sed solo pane, ne unice mediis af- fixi hæreamus. Per panem Ebræa phrasi omne ci- borum genus intelligens, & quicquid ad sustentatio- nem vitæ requiritur. Non ergo de vita animæ, sed de vita corporis sermo est. Interim non male Ambrosius ad h. l. Quisquis verbo Christi pascitur, terrenum pabulum non requirit, neque enim potest panem seculi cupere, qui pane reficitur Salvatoris; quandoquidem Christus & id intendat, se non o- pus habere præcise sustentatione corporali, cum pane gratiæ divinæ & sustentetur & reficiatur ab- unde. Edocet, inquit Cyprianus serm. de je- jun. Christi, verbum Dei eduliis corporalibus præ- ponendum, & citius attentiusque menti providen- dum quam ventri. Prior interpretatio simplicior est, vult enim docere Deum posse etiam sine pane vitam corporis sustentare, sicut manna ostendit.

2. Θεσιν. Vivet homo Dei verbo. Ζήσεται mo- dus est potentialis apud Ebræos, vivet, id est, vi- vere poterit. Cæterum non habetur in Mose ad- ditum verbo Dei, sed virtualiter tamen contine- tur illis verbis: in omni quod egreditur ex ore Dei, quo vel imprimis Dei verbum comprehenditur. Heinsius observat, in nutrimento, quo Deus suos in deserto pavit, duo spectanda fuisse. Medium & or- dinationem divinam seu Verbum: quia Manna per se cavis non fuerit, ut aleret, sed neque Manna aluerit, sed verbum Domini & ordinatio per Man- na: atque ita qui vixerunt Manna, ἐπὶ ῥήματι θε̃ vixisse. Sed hoc argutius est, quam solidius, quid- ni enim Mannæ alere potuerit! Perinde uti & il- lud, quod respici censet hic τὸν ὀυσιώδη λόγον Fi- lium Dei, is enim non est Verbum egrediens ex ore Dei. Nonnulli explicant id de omni, quod placet Deo adhibere ad sustentationem hominis. Sed in- terpretem Christum secuti verbum Dei designari censemus. Grotius id interpretatur de Verbo mandati, quod eidem insit aut expreffa aut tacita promissio rerum necessariarum, quod forte à Ju- dæis hausit, ad præcepta id referentibus, quibus tanquam cibo sustentetur homo, sed rectius Ver- bum Deo generaliter intelligitur, quo vivere dici- tur homo non excluso pane, vel aliis sustentatio- nis mediis ordinariis, sed inclusis, idque tum ob necessitatem benedictionis divinæ, sine qua nec panis eos sustentare posset, quæ per verbum obtingit 1. Tim. IV. 4. Quo sensu Hieron. recte infert, illum non vivere, qui non vescitur verbo Dei, tum ob pro- missionem sustentationis in verbo Dei factam, quæ fide apprehensa minime sit irrita. Nec enim promissio Dei fallax esse potest Deut. XXVIII. 5. Psal. XXXVII. 25. dummodo verbo Dei nita- mur, in vocatione nostra. Pulchre B. Chemnitius: Non in solo pane vivet homo, h. e. Deus auxiliatu- rus non est alligatus causis secundis, sed in omni ver- bo h. e. quando verbum quod ex ore Dei egreditur sive in vocatione nostra sive in promissione gratiæ ha- bemus, tunc egreditur etiam ex ore Domini verbum auxilii, h. e. efficacia verbi potest sine, præter, imo contra ordinem causarum secundarum nobis consu- lere, si Deus voluerit, & nobis id salutare judicave- rit. Revocat à verbo potentiæ quo lapides erant in panem convertendi ad verbum gratiæ, cui ad- hærentes vivent etiamsi pane careant, seu ordi- nariis sustentationis mediis.

## 4:5
Verse 5. Παραλαμβάνει [He takes along] | As the Spirit of God [took] Philip (Acts VIII. 39).

Εἰς τὴν ἁγίαν πόλιν [Into the holy city] | Thus Matthew, writing to the Hebrews, called the city Jerusalem, and below XXVII. 53, just as John also does in the Apocalypse, indeed from a most accepted custom. See Dan. IX. 6. The inscription of the shekels was 'Holy Jerusalem.' And Christ himself calls it the city of the great King, that is, of God. The son of Sirach, praying for the same city to God: 'Have pity on the city of your sanctuary, Jerusalem, the place of your rest.' עיר הקדש (Isa. XLVIII. 2; Neh. XI. 1).

Ἐπὶ τὸ πτερύγιον τοῦ ἱεροῦ] Not on the ridge of the roof, which was not flat, as the Talmudists note, and bristled with golden spikes, as we learn from Josephus, but on that which Jerome called a little horn, and the LXX a crown in Deut. XXII. 8. For that which the law requires on flat roofs was added in the covered temple for the sake of ornament. Moreover, πτερύγιον is a Hellenistic word shadowed forth from the Hebrew כנף, which signifies an edge or margin. The Greeks call the same thing by a similar word περίπτερον, sometimes also περίδρομον, and the Latins a circuit.

Latin:

Vers. 5. Παραλαμβάνει] Ut Philippum Dei spiritus Act. VIII. 39.

Εἰς τὴν ἁγίαν πόλιν] Ita Matthæus Hebræis scribens urbem Hierosolyma appellavit & infra XXVII. 53. sicut & Johannes in Apocalypsi, nimirum ex receptissima con- suetudine. Vide Dan. IX. 6. Siclorum inscriptio erat Ie- rusalem sancta. Et Christus ipse eam vocat urbem magni Regis, Dei nimirum. Sirachides pro eadem urbe Deum orans: οἴκτειρον πόλιν ἁγιάσματός σου ἱερουσαλὴμ, τόπον κα- ταπαύσεως σου. עיר הקדש Efai. XLVIII. 2. Nehem. XI. 1.

Ἐπὶ τὸ πτερύγιον τοῦ ἱεροῦ] Non in columen tecti, quod neque planum erat, ut Thalmudistæ notant, & horrebat aureis verubus, ut ex Josepho discimus, sed in id quod Hieronymus dixit Coriculam, LXX. ςεφάνην Deut. XXII. 8. quod enim lex in planis tectis requirit id in templo te- cto ornatus causa erat additum. Est autem πτερύγιον vox Hellenistica adumbrata ex Hebræo כנף quod oram aut marginem significat. Græci idem simili voce περίπτερον vocant, interdum & περίδρομον, Latini circuitionem.

## 4:6
Vers. 6. Μήποτε] The Hebrew פן signifies 'lest', but in such a way that it generally shows that which follows to be not of things necessary, but of things possible; as below XXVII. 65. and elsewhere. From the same root is ואפונה 'I will doubt' in Psalm LXXXVIII. 16. The same value has μήποτε among the Greeks, which the LXX interpreters often use to express it. For πότε, when unaccented, as the Greek grammarians note, generally has the signification not of time, but of uncertainty: as appears in τίσποτε and other words of that kind, so that it is less to be wondered at if the old Latin interpreter, both here and in some other places, translated the Hebrew פן or the Greek μήποτε as 'lest perhaps'. It is found with an equal sense also as ἴσως in the Greek version, for the Hebrew אולי, as in Jerem. XXXVI. 3. Regarding which passage Chrysostom, in his discourse on why prophecies are obscure, says that this word was used 'so that His foreknowledge might not be thought to be some compelling force of disobedience'. The Psalmist signifies that God pursues those beloved to Him in a peculiar way, so that He preserves them from fortuitous evils by the ministry of angels. It is clear that fortuitous things are called in this place those which could happen either to those unaware or unwilling. The lying spirit therefore cavils in his usual manner when he wishes to transfer this to evils sought of one's own accord.

Προσκόψης πρὸς λίθον] A proverbial expression, used not only by the Hebrews but also by the Greeks for the signification of any harm whatsoever.

Latin:

Vers. 6. Μήποτε] Hebræum פן significat ne, sed ita ut plerumque ostendat id quod sequitur esse non τῶν ἀναγ- καίων sed τῶν ἐνδεχομένων; ut infra XXVII. 65. & alibi. Ab eadem radice est ואפונה dubitabo Psal. LXXXVIII. 16. Idem valet apud Græcos μήποτε quod ab exprimendum usurpant sæpe LXX. Interpretes. Nam πότε ἄτονον, ut Gram- matici Græci annotant plerumque non temporis, sed in- certitudinis habet significationem: ut apparet in τίσποτε & aliisque id genus vocibus, quo minus miranda est, si vetus Latinus interpres & hic & aliis aliquot in locis He- bræum פן aut Græcum μήποτε per ne forte transtulit. Re- peritur pari sensu & ἴσως in Græca versione, pro Hebræo אולי ut Jerem. XXXVI. 3. ad quem locum Chrysosto- mus in oratione cur obscura sint vaticinia, usurpatam eam vocem ait ἵνα μὴ ἡ πρόγνωσις ἀυτοῦ νομισθείη ἀναγκαστική τις εἶναι τῆς παρακοῆς. Significat Psalmographus Deum peculiari sibi dilectos prosequi, ita ut Angelorum mini- sterio ipsos à malis fortuitis servet. Palam est fortuita hoc loco dici ea quæ contingere poterant aut insciis aut in- vitis. Cavillatur igitur suo more spiritus mendax, cum hoc transferre vult ad mala sponte quæsita.

Προσκόψης πρὸς λίθον] παροιμιώδης locutio non Hebræis tantum, sed & Græcis usitata ad damni cujuslibet signifi- cationem.

## 4:7
Vers. 7. Ἐκπειράσεις] If you compare the passage of Deuteronomy with the preceding histories and with Psalm XXV. 8, it will appear that ἐκπειράζειν here is properly to wish to experience further the power or providence of God when sufficiently great proofs of it have already appeared. Thus Acts XV. 10.

Repelled by Christ, Satan, having been overcome in the first temptation, about to attack the second temptation, led Christ into the holy city, which translation was not imaginary, whether in a vision, as such things happened to the Prophets (Jer. 13:4; Ezek. 4:5), as Cyprian and others, Calvin in his Harmony of the Gospels (fol. 58), Bucer on Matthew 4 (fol. 78), and Scultetus in his Evangelical Exercises (book 2, ch. 3) think, or by objects presented to the eyes and mind of Christ by illusions, so that he believed in the desert; but it was true, real, and local, as the literal sense of the historical narrative implies, yet not forced, but voluntary, which the Papist Abulensis and the Photinian Crellius wish to have been done by way of carrying and snatching away, and Maldonatus attributes that opinion to Jerome and Gregory, nor does Spanheim entirely deny it, provided it is ascribed here not to the weakness of the Lord, but to the patience of him who humbled himself to that point, and not to the strength of the Tempter, but to his audacity, and indeed to his stupidity, because he believed that Christ was complying with him, while he was complying with the divine will. But it is more correctly said to have happened by leading than by snatching through the air, as the words παραλαμβάνειν, ἄγειν, and ἀνάγειν imply, which also better suits the dignity of the person and the voluntary following of the Lord, and is approved by Euthymius in chapter 4 of Luke.

He is said to have been led into the holy city, that is, Jerusalem, which is called such not only because of the common appellation (Matt. 27:53; Rev. 11:2), but also because of God's election and indwelling (2 Chron. 6; Ps. 134:21) and the new sanctification promised under the coming of Christ (Isa. 4:1; ch. 52:1; ch. 60:14; Zech. 8:3). However, not because of true holiness: it was holy by right, not in fact, because it was then profaned and polluted by many crimes. Ἐπὶ τὸ πτερύγιον, upon the pinnacle of the temple, that is, not the chair of the Rabbis, or the seat from which they taught, as some wish, but either that ἄκρον, which Josephus (Antiquities, book 15, ch. 14) says was a very high portico on the southern side, from which a view into the deep valley below could not be endured without dizziness (see Lud. Capell. in Compend. Hist. Jud.), or some extremity of the highest corners, on which no one could stand without danger of falling.

Satan used Holy Scripture as a pretext for the temptation: Ps. 91:12, 'He has given his angels charge over you, to keep you, and lest you dash your foot against a stone.' Crellius rashly pretends that these words are hyperbolic, since no reason for a hyperbole can be given. The temptation was directed toward Christ casting himself down from there, relying on angelic custody. Thus he wanted to precipitate the same person from one extreme of diffidence to the other of overconfidence; he who could not be subverted by gluttony, he strives to subvert by vainglory, says Cyprian. Being repelled, he brings forward Scripture and attacks the battle with it, but it is depraved not only in an alien sense, i.e. The promise of God's providence would have been made to rashness and excessive confidence, which, by tearing away what was given only to true and solid trust, thus separates the promise from the command of God, since it is annexed to the command, not absolute; but it was also mutilated and truncated (which Crellius here rejects in vain, and Scultetus attacks with Erasmus Rudinger in his Evangelical Exercises, book 2, ch. 4), since the omission of the principal part, 'in all your ways,' or of your calling, is clear, which Satan sophistically passed over. Whence Bernard, sermon 14 on Ps. 91: 'In all your ways: Is this a way, to throw oneself down from the pinnacle of the temple? This is not a way, but a ruin, and if it is a way, it is yours, not his.' Nor did Gregory Nazianzen and Jerome observe this without reason. that the victory of the faithful against Satan, which was immediately subjoined, had been neglected and passed over in silence, concerning which Bernard likewise says: 'But why do you remain silent about that which follows: You shall walk upon the asp and the basilisk, and you shall trample the lion and the dragon? He touches this with a parable!'

Christ's repelling response, from which the principle was taken again from Scripture, and indeed from the law and the divine command, by which Christ teaches that divine promises are to be understood under the hypothesis of observing the divine command, and protested that he neither could nor would do anything outside of and beyond, much less against, the command of God in the parts of his office. Πάλιν, 'again it is written.' That πάλιν is not antithetical, but explanatory, because he does not oppose Scripture to Scripture, but explains the same from Scripture, showing that it is to be understood as the analogy of faith permits, lest, for example, some contradiction be admitted (Rom. 12:6). But as for the momentum of the response itself from Deut. 6:16, 'You shall not tempt the Lord your God,' it is applied by some to the devil, because he is rebuked for having dared to tempt Christ, his God. But Christ testified not what he should do to the devil, but what he himself must do in the repelling of this triple temptation, and thus he implies that he would be tempting his God against the divine command if he were to cast himself down without reason, cause, or necessity, and he shows it to be forbidden by a general edict, as Cyprian says, 'It is not even clear in any distress whatsoever that any excess should tempt God by any presumption.' For the devil's temptation was one of seduction, by which he dared to solicit Christ to evil, not of exploration; but the words of Moses speak of the temptation of probation, or exploration, by which God is solicited by men either through diffidence, as in Exod. 16:2 and Num. 14:22. Whether from rashness and overconfidence, which Satan intended here, or from malice and stubbornness (Acts 5:9; 15:20), since it is a prohibited kind of thing to tempt the Lord apart from and against the word of the Lord, by soliciting his patience, grace, justice, and truth, even the species of temptation of grace made from rashness and overconfidence is prohibited; in Moses, indeed, the occasion of the prohibition was special through diffidence concerning divine providence (Exod. 17:2; Deut. 6:16). But the prohibition itself is general, by which every temptation undertaken against the word of God is prohibited, and the people are recalled solely to observing the word of God, whence Theodoret, question 5 on Deuteronomy, rightly describes the temptation: 'To tempt God is to do something recklessly without reason.'

Latin:

Vers. 7. Ἐκπειράσεις] Si locum Deuteronomii cum hi- storiis antecedentibus & cum Psal. XXV. 8. conferas, ap- parebit ἐκπειράζειν proprie hic esse Dei potentiam aut pro- videntiam velle amplius experiri cum satis magna jam ejus documenta apparuerint. Sic Act. XV. 10.

Depulsus à Christo, prima tentatione superata Satanas alteram tentationem aggressurus Chri- stum deduxit in civitatem sanctam, quæ translatio non imaginaria fuit sive in visione, ut Prophetis talia obtigere Jerem. XIII. 4. Ezech. IV. 5. ut Cyprianus, & alii, Calvinus in Harmon. Evangel. fol. 58. Bucerus in Matth. IV. fol. 78. Scultetus Exercit. Evangel. lib. II. cap. 3. censent sive obje- ctis oculis animoque Christi præstigiis, ut crederet se illuc deductum, etsi maneret in deserto, sed vera & realis ac localis, ut historicæ narrationis τὸ ῥητὸν infert, non tamen coacta, sed voluntaria, quam per modum gestationis ac raptationis Abu- lensis Papista & Crellius Photinianus factam vult, tribuitque eam sententiam Maldonatus Hierony- mo ac Gregorio, nec abnuit omnino Spanhemius, si modo non imbecillitati Domini, sed patientia se eousque demittenti nec Tentatoris robori, sed audaciæ, imo & stupori, quod crederet Christum sibi obsequi, dum obsequebatur voluntati divinæ, hic adscribatur. Sed ea rectius dicitur contigif- se deductione, quam raptatione per aërem, uti vo- ces παραλαμβάνειν, ἄγειν & ἀνάγειν innuunt, quæ etiam dignitati personæ voluntariæque Domini sequelæ magis convenit, & Euthymio in cap. IV. Lu- cæ probatur.

In civitatem autem sanctam deductus dicitur, h. e. Jerusalem, quæ talis nuncupatur, non tantum ob vulgarem appellationem Matth. XXVII. 53. Apoc. XI. 2. Sed & ob Dei electionem & inhabi- tationem 2. Paral. VI. Psal. CXXXIV. 21. novam- que sanctificationem sub adventum Christi promis- sam Esa. IV. 1. cap. LII. 1. cap. LX. 14. Zach. VIII. 3. Non autem ob veram sanctitatem: de jure sancta erat, non de facto: quia profanata tum & multis sceleribus polluta erat. Ἐπὶ τὸ πτερύγιον in pinnam templi, h. e. non Cathedram Rabbino- rum, vel sedem, ex qua illi docebant ut nonnulli volunt. Sed vel ἄκρον illud, de quo Josephus LXV. Antiquit. cap. 14. fuisse à parte australi præ- celsam quantam porticum unde prospectu in valle profunda fine vertigine baud patuerit. Vid. Lud. Capell. in Compend. Hist. Jud. vel extremitatem aliquam summorum angulorum, in qua fine pericu- lo lapsus nemo consistere poterat.

Tentationi prætexebat Satanas Scripturam S. Ps. XCI. 12. Angelis suis mandavit de te, ut custo- diant te, nec offendas ad lapidem pedem tuum. Quæ verba hyperbolica esse nonnisi temere fingit Crel- lius, cum nulla hyperboles ratio queat dari. Erat autem tentatio eo directa, quo se hinc præcipita- ret Christus deorsum, fretus Angelica custodia. Sic ab uno extremo diffidentiæ ad alterum præfi- dentiæ eundem præcipitare volebat, quem gula non potuit, vana gloria subvertere nititur, ait Cy- prianus. Depulsus S. Scriptura Scripturam ad- ducit, eaque pugnam aggreditur sed depravata non solum in sensum alienum, q. Providentiæ Dei promissio temeritati, nimiæque confidentiæ facta es- set, quæ solum veræ solidæque fiduciæ data divel- lens ita promissum à præcepto Dei, cum illud præ- cepto annexum sit, non absolute: sed & mutila- ta ac truncata (quod nequicquam hic reprobat Crellius, impugnat cum Erasmo Rudingero Schul- tetus l. 2. Exercit. Evangel. cap. 4.) cum omissio præcipuæ partis in viis tuis, vel vocationis tuæ luculenta sit, quam Sophistice prætermisit Sata- nas. Unde Bernhard. serm. 14. in Psal. XCI. in omnibus viis tuis : Nunquid in præcipitiis qualis via hæc de pinnaculo templi mittere se deorsum; non est via hæc, sed ruina, & si via est, tua est non illius. Nec abs re observarunt Gregor. Nazianzen. & Hie- ronym. neglectam tacitamque fuisse immediate subjunctam fidelium adversus Satanam victoriam, de qua itidem Bernhardus; Quid vero taces & il- lud quod sequitur: super aspidem & basiliscum ambulabis, & conculcabis Leonem & draconem? Tené hac parabola tangit!

Responsum Christi profligatorium, qua princi- pium desumptum est iterum è Scriptura, & qui- dem è lege, & mandato divino, quo docet Chri- stus promissiones divinas sub hypothesi observati præcepti divini esse intelligendas, ac protestatus, se neque posse, neque velle quicquam extra ac præter, nedum coutra mandatum Dei facere in partibus muneris sui. Πάλιν rursus scriptum est. Πάλιν illud non est ἀντιθετικὸν, sed ἐκτεθικὸν, quia non opponit Scripturæ Scripturam, sed exponit eandem è Scriptura, monstrans ita intelligendam esse, ut analogia fidei permittit, ne scil. ἀντιλογία quædam admittatur Rom. XII. 6. Quod vero ad ipsum responsum momentum è Deut. VI. 16. οὐκ ἐκπειράσης κύριον τὸν θεόν σε applicatur id à non- nullis diabolo, quod is redarguatur quod Christum Deum suum tentare ausus fuerit. Verum Chri- stum non quid diabolo, sed quid sibi faciendum sit in hac triplicis tentationis depulsione testatus est, adeoq; innuit se contra mandatum divinum Deum suum tentaturum, si præcipitem se daret sine ra- tione, causa, aut necessitate, ac generali edicto inter- dictum ostendit, dicente Cypriano nedum patet in quibuslibet angustiis quilibet excessus Deus ulla præ- sumtione tentetur. Diaboli enim tentatio sedu- ctionis erat, qua ad malum sollicitare Christum audebat, non explorationis: at verba Mosis lo- quuntur de tentatione probationis, seu exploratio- nis qua Deus ab hominibus sollicitatur sive dif- fidentia, ut Exod. XVI. 2. Num. XIV. 22. Sive è te- meritate ac perfidentia, quod hic intendebat Sata- nas, sive è malitia ac pervicacia Actor. V. 9. c. XV. 20. cum genus prohibitum sit, tentare Dominum citra & contra verbum Domini, sollicitando ejus pa- tientiam, gratiam, justitiam, veritatem, etiam species prohibita est tentationis gratiæ è temeritate ac præfidentia factæ: in Mose quidem occasio in- terdicti erat specialis per diffidentiam de divina providentia Exod. XVII. 2. Deut. VI. 16. Sed in- terdictum ipsum generale est, qua prohibetur o- mnis tentatio contra Dei verbum suscepta, po- pulusque revocatur unice ad observandum Dei verbum, unde recte Theodoretes, quæst. V. in Deut. tentationem describit: ἐκπειράζειν τὸν Θεὸν ὁ δίχα λογισμῦ ῥιψικινδύνως τι πράττων.

## 4:8
Ver. 8. He shows him] Doubtless as if placing in a picture all the apparatus of royal fortune that existed anywhere. For I do not think the eyes or the imaginative power of Christ were deluded, but rather certain images of things fashioned by the demon, which the Greeks call εἴδωλα and explain as, ἱστόμενα ἐν τῷ ἀέρι φαντάσματα ἄτατα ὄντα καὶ ἀβέβαια.

Latin:

Vers. 8. Δείκνυσιν αὐτῷ] Nimirum quasi in pictura po- nens omnem qui usquam esset regiæ fortunæ apparatum. Nam neque oculos neque vim imaginatricem Christi illu- sam puto, sed potius à dæmone effictas quasdam imagi- nes rerum, quæ εἴδωλα, Græci vocant & exponunt , ἱστόμενα ἐν τῷ ἀέρι φαντάσματα ἄτατα ὄντα καὶ ἀβέβαια.

## 4:9
Falling down you shall worship] We have treated above of this custom of worshipping by prostrating the body to the ground, when we said that this honor was shown to the kings of the East. But the Jews and other Oriental peoples also worshipped God in the same way, and indeed the Greeks, to which that remark of Herodotus refers when they deny that it was the custom for the Spartans to worship a man. But this honor was also paid to the Prophets, 1 Kings XVIII. 7, whence it may be asked whether kings paid this honor to prophets, or prophets to kings, or neither to the other. It seems to me that a distinction must be made as to whether the prophets approached the kings with a special mandate for them, or for other reasons. For Nathan, addressing David about public business without a special mandate, prostrates himself before David, 1 Kings I. 23; on the contrary, Nebuchadnezzar, as if to Daniel sent by God to him as an interpreter of mysteries, prostrates himself and worships, Dan. II. 46, 47, and Saul, whom he thought to be Samuel. Since, therefore, that very external sign of reverence was not proper to divine worship, as often as it was used outside of divine worship, whether it was done rightly or otherwise is to be judged from the intention of both the one demanding it and the one performing it. Therefore, in Sozomen, a man is praised

A Christian, who previously worshipped the King of the Persians according to the custom: but afterwards, being solicited to defect from Christ, refused to worship the King again in the same manner. And we read in Nazianzen that not only Roman emperors, but also their statues, were accustomed to be worshipped (προσκυνεῖσθαι) by Christians: but when Julian had ordered the gods of the Gentiles to be painted onto his own images, so that he might make a mixed worship (μικτὴν τὴν προσκύνησιν), the simpler ones were indeed deceived, but the more prudent ones underwent any punishments rather than offer the appearance of worshippers. They gave, he says, a penalty for their wisdom, pretending that they were refusing as if for the honor of the king, but in truth they were risking danger for the sake of the true King and the pious doctrine.

The second temptation of Satan having been routed, so that he had to be silent, he attacked Christ a third time by another way, leading him onto a very high mountain near Jerusalem, which was surrounded by mountains, Ps. 87:2, Ps. 124:1. and showing him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory: of which the former (the leading) could have happened by a true and real translation (a leading which is neither imaginary nor yet true and real, but intermediate, which Jansenius invents and Calixtus approves, because he made it seem to Christ sensibly that he was above the temple and the mountain through images of things, when he was not, is truly imaginary and nothing; but it is no wonder if Christ permitted himself to be led around by the devil, who permitted himself to be crucified by his members, as Gregory rightly says). This latter, however (the showing), did not happen by a real demonstration of the kingdoms themselves, but by an artificial representation of them, as Theophylact, Grotius, and others hold, that without illusion he represented their idols or images to his sight in a new way. For from a mountain, of whatever height it may be, to see all the kingdoms with their glory at one and the same time with the eyes in reality is among the impossibilities. Although it is better with Euthymius, the author of the Imperfect Work, and Thomas to understand these synecdochically, either that he only demonstrated all the regions and climates of the world, or that by all the kingdoms or by the word 'world' some parts of the world are designated. For the devil neither deceived the eyes of Christ with false appearances, nor could he act upon his imagination; indeed, he would not have had need to lead him onto a mountain to objectify some appearances to his internal and external senses. That 'in a moment of time' (c. 4:5) the Syrian explains as a short time, just as 'in an atom' or 'in the twinkling of an eye' seems to be taken in 1 Cor. 15:52; and who would doubt that the climates of the world could be shown even in a moment of time! But the most impudent Spirit boasts himself to be the absolute Lord of the world, and promises the concession of all the kingdoms of the world under the hypothesis of worship and adoration, which was the highest degree of diabolical impudence, to seek adoration from him whom he himself is bound to serve with terror, and whom the angels are bound to adore with dancing: therefore Christ rightly routed both the tempter and the temptation; these things pertain to the tempter: 'Get thee behind me, Satan,' which were also said to Peter in Matt. 16:23 when he was dissuading the passion, so that it may be clear that it is no less a Satanic abomination to resist the Counsel of God concerning the salvation of the human race than to commit idolatry; to designate another way of salvation than to adore the alien God. Rightly Theophylact: 'He calls Peter thus, since it was also against the will of Satan that Christ should suffer.'

Latin:

Πεσὼν προσκυνήσῃς] De more hoc venerandi prostrato in humum corpore egimus supra, cum diceremus regibus Orientis exhibitum id honoris. Sed & Deum eodem mo- do venerabantur Judæi, cæterique Orientalis populi, quin & Græci, quo illud spectat Herodoti cum negant, Spar- tiatiæ σφὶ ἐν νόμῳ εἶναι ἄνθρωπον προσκύνειν.
