Sed & Prophetis is honos habitus, 1. Reg. XVIII. 7. unde quæri potest Re- gesne Prophetis an Prophetæ Regibus, an neutri neutris id honoris detulerint. Mihi distinguendum videtur, an Prophetæ Reges accesserint cum speciali ad ipsos manda- to, an vero aliis de caussis. Nam Nathan de publica re Davidem alloquens citra mandatum speciale, coram Da- vide procumbit 1. Reg I. 23. contra Nabuchodonosor Da- nielem ut à Deo missum ad se arcanorum interpretem pro- cumbens veneratur Dan. III. 46. 47. & Saul quem putabat esse Samuelem. Cum ergo ipsum illud exter- num reverentiæ signum divini cultus proprium non fue- rit, quoties extra divinum cultum usurpatum est, rectene id an secus fieret, ex sensu tum exigentis, tum præstantis erit æstimandum. Ideo laudatur apud Sozomenum vir

Christianus, qui prius προσεκύνησε Regem Persarum κατὰ τὸ νενομισμένον: postea vero sollicitatus ad defectionem a Christo eodem modo iterum venerari Regem recusavit. Et apud Nazianzenum legimus non imperatores tantum Romanos, sed & eorum statuas etiam à Christianis ado- rari προσκυνεῖσθαι, solitas: sed cuin Julianus suis imaginibus Deos gentium appingi jussisset, ut faceret μικτὴν τὴν προ- σκύνησιν, deceptos quidem simpliciores, sed prudentiores quasvis potius pœnas subiisse, quam ut venerantium spe- cie:n præberent. Δίκην, inquit, ἔδοσαν τῆς συνέσεως πρόςχη- μα μὲν ὡς εἰς τιμὴν βασιλέως παραιτησάμενοι, τόδε ἀληθὲς ὑ- πὲρ τῦ ἀληθινῦ βασιλέως καὶ τῶ εὐσεβῶς δόγματος κινδυνεύ- σαντες.

Prosligata altera tentatione Satanæ, ut obmute- scere necessum haberet, alia via tertium adortus est Christum deducens eum in montem altissimum Hierosolymæ vicinum, quæ montibus circumdata erat, Psal. LXXXVII. 2. Psal. CXXIV.1. ac os- tendens ei omnia regna mundi & gloriam eo- rum: quorum illud (deductio) fieri potuit vera ac reali translatione, (deductio quæ neque imagi- naria sit neque tamen vera ac realis sed media, quam Jansenius comminiscitur, Calixtus appro- bat, quod per rerum imagines fecerit Christo vi- deri sensibiliter se esse supra templum & montem, cum non esset, vere imaginaria ac nulla est, nihil autem mirum est, si Christus se permisit à diabolo circumduci, qui à membris illius se permisit crucifi- gi, ut recte Gregorius) Hoc vero (ostensio) non reali contigerit ipsorummet regnorum omnium demonstratione, sed artificiosa eorundem repræ- sentatione, ut Theophylactus, Grotius, aliique vo- lunt citra illusionem obtutui novo modo repræ- sentarit εἴδωλα vel imagines eorum. E monte e- nim quantacunque altitudine sit regna omnia cum gloria eorum simul ac semel oculis reapse conspici ἐκ τῶν ἀδυνάτων est. Quanquam præ- stet cum Euthymio, Autore operis imperfecti & Thoma synecdochice hæc intelligere, sive quod plagas omnes & climata mundi tantum demon- stravit sive quod per omnia regna quædam sive per vocem mundi partes nonnullæ mundi designentur. Nec enim vel oculos Christi falsis speciebus delu- sit, vel in imaginationem ejus agere potuit diabo- lus, imo sic opus non habuisset in montem deduce- re, ut internis ac externis sensibus species aliquas objectaret. Illud ἐν στιγμῇ χρόνυ c. IV. 5. de par- vo tempore Syrus explicat uti etiam ἐν ἀτόμῳ, ἐν ῥυπῇ ὀφθαλμῦ videtur accipi 1. Corinth. XV. 52. & ostendi mundi climata etiam in momento tem- poris potuisse quis ambigat! Jactitat autem impu- dentissimus Spiritus sese mundi Dominum abso- lutum, ac promittit omnium regnoruin mundi concessionem sub hypothesi cultus & adorationis, qui summus diabolicæ impudentiæ gradus fuit, ab eo adorationem expetere, cui ipse cum terrore servire, quem Angeli cum tripudio adorare te- nentur : ideo & tentatorem & tentationem ex me- rito profligavit Christus; ad tentatorem hæc spectant: ὕπαγε Σατανᾶ: quæ etiam ad Petrum dicta Matth. XVI. 23. cum dissuaderet passionem, ut liqueat non minorem esse abominationem Sa- tanicam, Consilio Dei de salute generis humani resistere, quam idololatriam committere; alium salutis modum designare, quam alienum Dei ad- orare. Recte Theophylactus: καλεῖ δὲ ὕτως τὸν Πέτρον, ἐπεὶ κ͵ τῷ Σατανᾷ ἀθέλητον ἦν τὸ πα- θεῖν τὸν χρισόν.

## 4:9
Προσκυνήσης] In Hebrew it is השתחוה, which signifies internal reverence: in which way the Greek προσκυνεῖν is also often used. But the argumentation proceeds rightly from internal reverence to its external sign. For although no honor is owed to the devil, as a deserter of God—indeed, all honor is to be denied—it seemed sufficient to Christ to direct the response to that which was being sought. For the devil wanted honor to be shown to him as one having full power over all the kingdoms, which is of the one God. R. Judah was far from this piety of Christ, who says in the book Chasidim: 'If anyone sees the Devil, and fears for himself from him, let him prostrate himself before him.'

Αὐτῷ μόνῳ λατρεύσεις] In Hebrew it is תעבד, which word is also used concerning subjection owed or shown to men. But what it signifies here is shown by the preceding and following context, and especially by the added mention of an oath. That the Greek word λατρεύειν is not proper to divine worship, either by its origin or by the usage of those whom we hold as the best authors of the Greek language, has been rightly demonstrated by others. Indeed, the LXX, although more rarely, still use λατρεύειν more loosely in some places. But for the most part, λατρεία for them is עבודה, the worship which is shown to God by conspicuous signs. And it must be confessed that the writers of the New Testament hardly ever use that word except concerning worship which is shown to the true God, as is usually the case, or certainly concerning worship which is shown as if to God, as in Acts 7:42, 10:25. For the fact that the Levites are said to 'worship the tabernacle' (Heb. 13:10), likewise 'the example of heavenly things' (Heb. 13:5), can be conveniently referred to the place and manner of serving. Hence, therefore, was born that distinction between λατρεία and δουλεία, celebrated even by Augustine: not that δουλεία did not also pertain to God (for many places in Scripture prove the contrary), nor that the propriety of the word λατρεία had anything peculiar, but that the usage, first of the Hellenistic Jews, then of the Christians, had assigned the name λατρεία to divine worship, having abandoned the general and common meaning. The ancient pagan Greeks used to say θρησκείαν, which the Apostles did not shrink from, even though it is believed to have been derived from the Orphic mysteries, being so careless of words as long as they explained the mind conveniently. The same Greeks called the veneration next to this θεραπείαν. The author of the book De Mundo [writes]: sacrifices of gods and services of heroes. Following which distinction, Origen against Celsus, book VIII, dealing with demons [says]: towards those who do nothing to benefit us, but rather on the contrary, we do nothing ungrateful when we do not sacrifice to them, nor even serve them. But that the Seventy, whom the Greek interpreter of Matthew follows, should add that 'only' here, the very order of the Hebrew words also demanded: for it is not written והעבדו, which would have been 'and him you shall serve', but ואתו תעבד, which clearly contains an emphasis that cannot be understood in the Greek words except by living pronunciation: and therefore something had to be added, by which the reader might be reminded of that emphasis. For there is a tacit reference to that which had preceded in the same chapter, verse 4, that God is one. Wherefore Josephus also did not hesitate to add the same word in explaining this commandment, saying, 'that God is one, and him alone to be worshipped.' Add that in the passage of Deuteronomy it follows immediately: 'You shall not follow strange gods.' And Samuel, inculcating this same commandment to the people, had said expressly יעבדהו לבדו, 'and serve him alone', 1 Samuel VII. 3.

Latin:

Προσκυνήσης] In Hebræo est השתחוה quod internam re- verentiam significat: quomodo & προσκυνεῖν Græcum sæpe usurpatur. Recte autem ab interna reverentia ad sign um ejus externum procedit argumentatio. Quanquam enim diabolo, ut Dei perfugæ, nullus honos debetur, imo omnis honos negandus est, satis tamen Christo visum est responsum dirigere ad id quod petebatur. Volebat autem diabolus honorem sibi exhiberi tanquam plenam potestatem habenti in regna omnia, quod est unius Dei. Multum ab hac Christi pietate abfuit R. Juda, qui in libro Chasidim ait: Siquis Diabolum videat, sibique ab ipso metuat, procidat coram eo.

Αὐτῷ μόνῳ λατρεύσεις] In Hebræo est תעבד quæ vox etiam de debita aut exhibita hominibus subjectione usur- patur. At hic quid significet ostendunt præcedentia ac subsequentia, præcipue vero addita jurisjurandi mentio. Græcam quoque vocem λατρεύειν neque sui origine neque usu eorum quos optimos Græci sermonis auctores habe- mus propriam esse divino cultui recte ab aliis est demon- stratum. Quin & LXX. quanquam rarius, aliquot tamen locis λατρεύειν laxius usurpant. Sed plerumque λατρεία ipfis est עבודה cultus qui conspicuis signis Deo exhi- betur. Fatendumque est, scriptores novi fœderis eam vo- cem vix usquam usurpare, nisi de cultu qui Deo vero exhi- betur, ut plerumque, aut sane de cultu qui exhibetur tan- quam Deo ut Actor. VII. 42. X. 25. Nam quod Levitæ di- cuntur τῇ σκηνῇ λατρεύειν Hebr. XIII. 10. item ὑποδείγματι τῶν ἐπουρανίων, Hebr. XIII. 5. ad locum modumque serviendi commode referri potest. Hinc igitur nata est illa, Augustino etiam celebrata, λατρείας & δουλείας distinctio: non quod δουλεία non ad Deum quoque pertineret (contrarium enim multa Scripturæ loca evincunt) nec quod proprietas vocis λατρείας aliquid haberet peculiare, sed quod usus primum Judæorum Hellenistarum, deinde Christianorum, voci δουλείας, relicto significatu generali atque communi, λα- τρείας nomen divino cultui assignasset. Græci veteres pa- gani θρησκείαν dicebant, quod ipsum quanquam, ut credi- tur, ab Orphicis mysteriis ductum, Apostoli non reformi- darunt, adeo verborum incuriosi, dum mentem commo- de explicarent. Proximam huic venerationem iidem Græ- ci θεραπείαν vocabant. Scriptor libri de mundo θεῶν θυ- σίαι καὶ ἡρώων θεραπεῖαι. Quod discrimen secutus Origenes adversus Celsum lib. VIII. de Dæmonibus agens: πρὸς τοὺς μηδὲν εὐεργετοῦντας ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐκ τῶ ἐναντία ἰσαμένως μηδὲν ἀχάριτον ἡμᾶς ποιεῖν ὅταν αὐτοῖς μὴ θύωμεν, ἀλλὰ μηδὲ θε- ραπεύωμεν. Ut autem illud μόνῳ hic adjicerent LXX. quos sequitur interpres Græcus Matthæi, ipse etiam Hebræorum verborum ordo exigebat: neque enim scriptum est והעבדו quod fuisset καὶ αὐτῷ λατρεύσεις sed ואתו תעבד quod plane emphasim continet, quæ in Græcis verbis intelligi non poterit nisi viva pronunciatione: ideoque addendum aliquid fuit, quo lector ejus ἐμφάσεως admone- retur. Est enim tacita relatio ad id quod eodem capite commate 4. præcesserat, Deum unum esse. Quare nec Josephus dubitavit eandem vocem in præcepto hoc ex- plicando adjicere, ὅτι θεός ἐστι εἷς, inquiens, καὶ τοῦτον σέ- βεσθαι μόνον. Adde quod in Deuteronomi loco sequitur continuo: Non sectaberis Deos alienos. Et Samuel idem hoc præceptum populo inculcans diferte dixerat יעבדהו לבדו & ei soli servire 1. Samuel. VII. 3.

## 4:10
Verse 10. ὕπαγε] In Latin you would say 'be gone from here.' For it is a word of one opposing; that which is added in certain codices, 'behind me,' was stitched on from elsewhere, which the Syrian and the Greek writers on this passage show.

Latin:

Vers. 10. ὕπαγε] Latine dixeris facesse hinc. Est enim adversantis dictio; quod in quibusdam codicibus additur ὀπίσω μs aliunde assutum est, quod Syrus & Græci ad hunc locum Scriptores ostendunt.

## 4:11
Ver. 11. Then the devil leaves him] By a threefold temptation, as he was once the victor of our first parents and for a long time of the human race, so now he is conquered by Christ, and is to be conquered by Christians, 1 John V. 18. Now these temptations are from poverty, from confidence in predestination, and from the hope of human splendor.

The word Satan is explained by Theodoret in Sermon 3 on the Greek Affections, by Justin in his Dialogue with Trypho, and by Suidas by reason of its etymology as 'apostate': but the origin is the Hebrew שטן, which the Seventy render as 'to slander', Symmachus as 'to oppose', and it denotes an adversary. The formula 'get thee behind me' [ὕπαγε], when it is used because of the enormous indignity of a matter, indicates a more agitated mind, by which someone is reproved, Job XVI. 3, XX. 14, which is also done here, because blasphemous words are not to be heard with patience, but are to be rejected with indignation. And thus the Lord, as an example and prelude to the victory of the faithful, tramples not only the world and its glory, but also the prince of the world, and bids him keep his things to himself.

He repels the temptation again from Moses, Deuteronomy VI. 13, X. 20. It is written, 'You shall worship the Lord your God and him only shall you serve.' There it is held: 'You shall fear the Lord your God': here 'you shall worship', because worship is included under religious fear. If the fear due to God is to be attributed to no creature, then certainly neither should any species or sign of his adoration be attributed to any creature. There the word תעבד is used, which is δουλεύσεις; but here, λατρεύσεις. But even if προσκύνησις, taken generally, extends more widely than the worship of religion and religious adoration, yet for that reason προσκύνησις, specifically so called, is no less properly and religiously claimed for God alone than λατρεία, since the discourse is about adoration of such a kind as is owed to God as God, and is here opposed by Christ to Satan, who is demanding adoration. Unless, however, it were implying that προσκύνησις belongs to God alone, he would be repelling Satan less effectively. As for the word תעבד, it is rendered by the Hellenists sometimes by δουλεύειν, sometimes by λατρεύειν, and in Moses it is translated by the LXX Interpreters in this latter way, and for that reason it is repeated by Christ and Matthew. And certainly no distinction between δουλεία and λατρεία can be taught from the Scriptures, as the papizing Grotius admits in this place. Whatever, therefore, may be the case regarding the use of Ecclesiastical Writers, it has nothing to do with the matter when the issue is the Biblical meaning: indeed, Bellarmine is forced to acknowledge in Book 1 de Beat. Sanctor., chapter 12, that that distinction was devised by the School of Theologians.

The Papists say, of course, that λατρεία is worship owed to God alone: but that δουλεία is indeed a species of religious worship, but one that also belongs to the saints: and they claim ὑπερδουλεία for the human nature of Christ. But such a distinction cannot be taught from the Scriptures, as we have already pointed out: nor can Ecclesiastical Writers prejudice Scripture, or the sense and use of the Holy Spirit concerning phrases regarding religious worship, nor do they use these words in the same way. The Greeks certainly hold them as synonyms; whence Hesychius explains λατρεία by δουλεία, as does the Greek Glossary. But among profane authors, Bellarmine admits in Book 1 de Sanctior. beat., c. 14, that δουλεία and λατρεία signify exactly the same thing. Regarding the Sacred Writers, indeed, the same Bellarmine, c. 12, pronounces quite rashly that they never use the word λατρεία except for the worship of God; but he softens that later in c. 14, § 6, with the word 'almost' never. Moreover, it is manifest that it is used for official service among the LXX Interpreters from Deut. XXVIII. 48, Exod. XII. 16, Levit. XXIII. 3, 8, 21, 35, Num. XXXVIII. 18, 25, 26, XXIX. 1, 7, 12, 35. What is more, the word δουλεία is used elsewhere for truly divine worship, Galat. IV. 8, nor is δουλεία of the first table anything other than the λατρεία by which God is to be served, Matth. VI. 24, Acts XX. 18, 19, Rom. VII. 6, 25, XIV. 18, Col. III. 14. And in the Mosaic passage, the word תעבד removes from creatures δουλεία just as much as λατρεία: not to mention that, if that little distinction were admitted, Satan could have replied to Christ's response, along with the Papists, that it was not προσκύνησις of λατρεία that was being sought from him, but only of δουλεία.

Augustine, whom they cite for themselves, favors them little: he indeed dislikes worship, but taken generally into λατρεία and δουλεία, not indeed religious. Religious worship belongs to God alone, and is indivisible. There is indeed a twofold δουλεία in Scripture, but according to the different tables of the law, one is religious, the other official. If anyone wishes to add a memorial one regarding the deceased, we will not oppose him, but that differs from religious worship in its entire genus. The Papists do indeed distinguish between the term and the object of adoration, saying that the worship of saints tends toward God himself, and is not terminated in the Saints, and they say that in creatures only the gifts of God are adored: but these are only pretexts and fig leaves: Papistic idolatry cannot be excused or turned aside, because worship is attributed by them to Saints and Angels in the same way as to God: which public writings testify. Let even Costerus alone be compared in his Enchiridion. Therefore they are struck directly by this saying of Christ. Their definition of idolatry does not hold up legitimately. They define at least the most obvious species of idolatry; but this too is idolatry, when religious worship is attributed to a creature. The Israelites are certainly called idolaters who adored the calf, even if they did not terminate their worship in that image, but in God, etc. Which must also be held regarding the idolatry of Micah, Judges XVIII, who worshipped God in images, and of Jeroboam, 1 Kings XII. 8. The same is also clear from the worship of the gentiles, which is truly idolatrous, even if they did not adore those idols under the concept of the first principle, but with some subordination: Finally, idolatry is committed not only by reason of the object, but also by reason of the mode, but concerning these in the cited places. Finally, as for the exclusive 'only', Christ adds it here or rather repeats it from the version of the LXX Interpreters without any variation of sense: indeed, to express the very meaning of the divine law. For it is contained implicitly in the words of Moses, not only the word אֹתוֹ αὐτῷ, which is emphatic, implies it, namely to him alone: To him alone, as some observe the word אֹתוֹ in Ps. II. 7 excludes any others: But the thing itself also teaches it, whether you look at the subject, God, who, as he does not communicate his essence, so he does not communicate his glory to another outside himself, Is. XLII. 6, or the predicate, which is truly and merely divine and an incommunicable dignity, namely of adoration and religious worship, which by the force of the first table can belong to no one but God alone, and only to him; or the intention of the legislator, which was to bind the people to the fear and worship of one God. Add the explicit explanation of Scripture 1. Sam. VII. 3, where in the source itself the exclusive לְבַדּוֹ עִבְדוּ is added, serve him alone, which is also noted here by Grotius: and the perpetual harmony of Scripture, in which religious worship is claimed for one, and God alone.

PART II.

CHAPTER IV. Which also begins PART II of the HOLY GOSPEL OF MATTHEW. Narrative of the public ministry of Jesus.

SECTION I. From the first Passover to the second.

Latin:

Vers. 11. Τότε ἀφίησιν αὐτὸν ὁ διάβολος] Tergemina ten- tatione, ut olim primorum parentum, diuque humani ge- neris victor, ita nunc victus à Christo, & à Christianis vin- cendus, 1. Joh. V. 18. Tentationes autem istæ sunt ab egestate, à confidentia prædestinationis, & à spe splendo- ris humani.

Vox Satanas à Theodoreto sermon. 3. de Affect. Græc. Justino Dial. cum Tryph. & Suida ratione etymi explicatur per ἀποστάτην: sed origo est E- bræum שטן quod LXX. ἐνδιαβάλλειν, Symmachus ἀντικεῖσθαι reddunt, & adversarium notat. Formu- la ὕπαγε cum adhibetur propter enormem indignitatem rei, animum commotiorem, quo quis re- probatur, indicat, Job. XVI. 3. XX. 14. quod hic et- iam factum, quia blasphemæ voces non cum pa- tientia audiendæ, sed cum indignatione rejicien- dæ sunt. Atque ita Dominus in exemplum & præludium victoriæ fidelium non tantum mun- dum & gloriam ejus, sed & principem mundi cal- cat & res suas sibi habere jubet.

Tentationem repellit iterum ex Mose Deuter. VI. 13. X. 20. Scriptum est, Dominum Deum tuum ad- orabis & illi soli servies. Ibi habetur: Κύριον τὸν Θεόν σου Φοβηθήσῃ: hic προσκυνήσεις, quia sub ti- more religioso comprehenditur adoratio. Si creatu- ræ nulli timor Deo debitus tribuendus, utique nec species vel signum ejus adoratio ulli tribui de- bet. Ibi verbum תעבד adhibetur, quod est, δυ- λεύσεις; hic vero λατρεύσεις. Sed etsi προσκύ- νησις generaliter accepta latius pateat, quam cultus religionis & religiosæ adorationis, ideo tamen non minus προσκύνησις speciatim ita dicta propria & religiosa Deo soli vindicatur, quam λατρεία, quan- doquidem sermo sit de adoratione ejusmodi, quæ Deo ut Deo debetur, & à Christo Satanæ hic opponatur adorationem postulanti. Nisi au- tem soli Deo προσκύνησιν competere innueret, minus efficaciter Satanam repelleret. Quod ad verbum תעבד, redditur id ab Hellenistis modo per δουλεύειν, modo per λατρεύειν, & apud Mosem hoc posteriori modo à LXX. Interpp. translatum est, eaque ratione à Christo & Matthæo repetitur. Nec sane discrimen inter δουλείαν & λατρείαν è Scripturis doceri potest, ut fatetur h. l. papizans Grotius. Quicquid ergo sit de usu Scriptorum Ecclesiasticorum, is nihil ad rem facit, ubi de Bi- blica significatione res est: imo agnoscere cogitur Bellarminus l. 1. de Beat. Sanctor, cap. 12. distinctio- nem illam à Schola Theologorum excogitatam esse.

Nimirum λατρείαν cultum esse soli Deo debitum dicunt Pontificii: δουλείαν vero speciem quidem cul- tus religiosi, sed competere etiam sanctis: ὑπερ- δουλείαν naturæ humanæ Christi vindicant. At è Scripturis doceri tale discrimen non potest, uti jam monuimus: neque Scriptores Ecclesiastici præjudicare possunt Scripturæ, aut sensui, & usui Spiritus S. circa phrases cultum Religiosum con- cernentes, nec eodem modo utuntur illi his voci- bus. Græci utique eas pro Synonymis habent; unde Hesychius λατρείαν per δουλείαν exponit, ut & Glossarium Græcum. Apud profanos vero auto- res δουλείαν & λατρείαν prorsus idem significare fate- tur Bellarmin. l. 1. de Sanctior. beat. c. 14. De Sacris quidem Scriptoribus idem Bellarm. c. 12. satis te- mere pronunciat, eos nunquam vocem λατρείας usurpare nisi pro cultu Dei; sed emollit tamen post c. 14. §. 6. id per fere nunquam. Cæterum adhi- beri eam de servitute officiosa apud LXX. Interpp. è Deut. XXVIII. 48. Exod. XII. 16. Levit. XXIII. 3. 8. 21. 35. Num. XXXVIII. 18. 25. 26. XXIX. 1. 7. 12. 35. manifestum est. Quid quod & δουλείας vox alias de cultu vere divino adhibeatur, Galat. IV. 8. nec aliud sit δουλεία primæ tabulæ, quam λατρεία qua Deo est serviendum Matth. VI. 24. Actor. XX. 18. 19. Rom. VII. 6. 25. XIV. 18. Col. III. 14. Et in lo- co Mosaico vox תעבד à creaturis removeat æque δουλείαν ac λατρείαν: ut taceam, quod admissa il- la distinctiuncula Satanas ad elidendum Christi re- sponsum excipere potuerit cum Pontificiis, non peti à se προσκύνησιν τ̃ λατρείας, sed τῆς δουλείας solum.

Augustinus, quem citant pro se, ipsis parum fa- vet: displicet quidem cultum, sed generatim acce- ptum in λατρείαν & δουλείαν, non vero religiosum. Cultus religiosus soli Deo convenit, & insectilis est. Gemina sane δουλεία est in Scriptura, sed juxta diversas legis tabulas alia religiosa, alia officiosa. Si quis memorialem quoad defunctos addere voluerit, ei non repugnabimus, sed ea à cultu religioso, toto genere differt. Distinguunt quidem Pon- tificii inter terminum & objectum adorationis, quod cultus sanctorum tendat in Deum ipsum, non terminetur in Sanctis, & excellentia in creaturis Dei dona tantum adorari dicunt: sed προφάσεις hæ solum sunt, & ficus folia: non excusari potest vel declinari papistica idololatria, quia eodem modo cultus Sanctis & Angelis tribuitur ab ipsis, quo Deo: quod publica scripta testantur. Con- feratur vel solus Costerus in Enchiridio. Directe ergo ipsi feriuntur hoc Christo dicto. Ipsorum definitio idololatriæ non legitime se habet. Defi- niunt saltem liquidissimam idololatriæ speciem; At & hæc idololatria est, cum creaturæ cultus reli- giosus tribuitur. Postulantur utique Israelitæ ido- lolatrias, qui vitulum adorarunt, etsi non termi- narint cultum suum in imagine illa, sed in Deo, &c. Quod habendum etiam de Michæ idolola- tria Judic. XVIII. qui coluit in simulacris Deum, & Jeroboami; 1. Reg. XII. 8. Liquet etiam idem ex gentilium cultu, qui vere idololatricus, etsi ista idola non sub conceptu primi principii adorarint, sed cum subordinatione aliqua: Denique non tantum committitur idololatria ratione objecti, sed & ratione modi, sed de his in LL. CC. Tan- dem quod ad exclusivam μόνῳ, addit hic illam Christus vel repetit potius è versione LXX. Interpp. sine ulla sensus variatione: imo ad exprimendam ipsam divinæ legis sententiam. Contineri enim eam implicite in verbis Mosis, non solum vox אֹתוֹ αὐτῷ, quæ emphatica, innuit, ipsi scil. uni: Soli ipsi, uti observant nonnulli vocem אֹתוֹ tu Ps. II. 7. quosvis alios excludere: Sed & res ipsa docet, sive subjectum respicias Deum, qui ut essentiam, ita gloriam suam alteri extra sese non communi- cat, Es. XLII. 6. sive prædicatum, quod est vere & mere divinum & ἀκοινώνητον ἀξίωμα, adora- tionis sc. & cultus religiosi, quod vi tabulæ primæ non nisi Deo uni, ac soli competere potest; sive intentionem legislatoris, quæ erat ad unius Dei ti- morem & cultum adstringere populum. Adde disertam Scripturæ explicationem 1. Sam. VII. 3. ubi in fonte ipso additur exclusiva לְבַדּוֹ עִבְדוּ ser- vite ei soli, quæ etiam Grotio hic notata: & per- petuam Scripturæ harmoniam, in qua uni, ac soli Deo cultus religiosus vindicatur.

PARS II.

CAPUT IV. Quæ etiam inchoatur PARS II. EVANGELII S. MATTHÆI. Διήγησις Ministerii Jesu publici.

SECTIO I. A Paschate primo ad secundum.

## 4:12
Vers. 12. But when Jesus heard.

Walaeus noted these things from Calvin: John’s narrative does not seem to agree with these, who testifies that John and Christ performed the office of teaching at the same time. But it must be noted that the three other Evangelists pass over that brief space of time in silence for this reason, because John’s course was not yet finished, that is, the preparation for receiving the Gospel of Christ. And certainly, although Christ performed the office of Teacher within that time, he did not yet properly begin the preaching of the Gospel until he succeeded John.

ἀνεχώρησεν.

That is, he returned, or as in Luke 2:39, he went back. Above also in 2:12, the Magi are said to have withdrawn, that is, to have returned, so that ana here signifies the same as again. Others translate it as withdrew: which gave occasion in this place to discuss flight from persecution, as Beza has it here, and Walaeus following him.

Εἰς τὴν Γαλιλαίαν] Understand the Galilee not of Herod (whose cruelty he avoided with a certain plan and out of respect not for himself but for the men whom he had come to benefit), but of Philip: for the maritime part, in which Bethsaida and Capharnaum were, had fallen to him, as is clearly to be seen from Josephus, Antiquities XVIII. 3. Now Philip was of a nature not at all bloodthirsty.

In vain, therefore, does Beza here torment himself, and with him Walaeus, that he betook himself into Galilee to avoid the tyranny of Herod: let them be compared. This solution of Grotius is straightforward.

Latin:

Vers. 12. Ἀκούσας δὲ ὁ Ἰησοῦς.

E Calvino hæc notavit Walæus: Cum his non vi- detur congruere Johannis narratio, qui testatur eodem simul tempore Johannem & Christum obiisse docendi munus. Sed notandum est, tres alios Evangelistas breve illud temporis spatium ideo silentio transigere, quia nondum finitus erat Johannis cursus, hoc est, ad recipiendum Christi Evangelium præparatio. Et certe quamvis intra illud tempus Doctoris officio Christus functus sit; non tamen proprie exorsus est Evangelii prædicationem, donec Johanni succes- sit.

ἀνεχώρησεν.

Id est, ἐπανῆλθεν, vel ut Luc. II. 39. ὑπέστρεψεν. Supra etiam II. 12. dicuntur Magi ἀναχωρῆσαι, id est, ἐπαναστρέψαι, ut ἄνα idem hic valeat quod πά- λιν. Alii convertunt secessit: quod occasionem præ- buit hoc loco differendi de persecutionis fuga, ut hic ha- bet Beza, & ex eo Walæus.

Εἰς τὴν Γαλιλαίαν] Intellige Galilæam non Herodis, (cujus sævitiam certo consilio & non sui sed hominum qui- bus profuturus venerat respectu vitabat) sed Philippi: Nam huic pars maritima, in qua Bethsaida & Capharnaum, obvenerat, ut clare perspicere est ex Josepho originum XVIII. 3. Erat autem Philippus ingenii minime sanguina- rii.

Frustra ergo se hic macerat Beza, & cum eo Walæus, quod ut Herodis tyrannidem vitaret, in Galilæam se contulerit: qui conferantur. Expe- dita est hæc Grotii solutio.

## 4:14
Vers. 14. ἵνα πληρωθῇ] What we said before about the meaning of this word πληρῶσαι, we wish to be repeated here. For the words of Isaiah clearly seem to treat directly of some liberation that happened closer to those times: yet in such a way that there was an underlying ὑπόνοια of the times of Christ. Matthew cited word for word clause 2 of chapter IX of Isaiah. But because it could not be sufficiently understood from that of which people the Prophet was speaking, he therefore added from the preceding clause only those things which pertained to the designation of that people, omitting the rest, among which is the Hebrew word הקל which the seventy elders had translated ἐταχυποίει, a word newly coined by them, such as is also μοχοποιεῖν in Luke Acts VII. 41. For קל is properly ταχύς: and the form of the verb is hiphil, which is best expressed in Greek by words compounded with ποιῶ. But by the fault of the copyists, the newly compounded word split into two, and it became ταχὺ ποίει, then also more corruptly ταχὺ πίε: finally, both readings, the latter more faulty, the former referring more closely to the origin, were received into the context: and by the time of Tertullian that error had become established, as appears from his own Latin citation.

Although the words of Isaiah seem to treat of the liberation of those times specifically, we have taught, not only from this interpretation but also from the context of the Prophet in our Vindications of Isaiah, that they treat properly and according to the letter of the times of Christ. Which can be read there.

Latin:

Vers. 14. ἵνα πληρωθῇ] Quod ante diximus de sensu hu- jus vocis πληρῶσαι idem hic repetitum volumus. Plane e- nim videntur Esaiæ verba directe agere de liberatione ali- qua quæ propius illa tempora contigerit: ita tamen ut sub- esset ὑπόνοια temporum Christi. Citavit autem Matthæus κατὰ λέξιν comma 2. cap. IX. Esaiæ. Sed quia non satis inde intelligi poterat quo de populo ageret Propheta, id- eo ex antecedenti commate addidit ea duntaxat quæ ad populi illius designationem pertinebant, omissis cæteris, inter quæ est vox Hebræa הקל quam LXX. senes verte- rant ἐταχυποίει, voce ab ipsis noviter conficta, qualis est & μοχοποιεῖν apud Lucam Act. VII. 41. Nam קל proprie est ταχύς: & forma verbi est hiphil, quæ Græce vocibus ex ποιῶ compositis optime exprimitur. Sed descriptorum vitio vox noviter composita in duas dissiliit, factumque est ταχὺ ποίει, deinde etiam corruptius ταχὺ πίε: postremo le- ctio utraque, hæc mendosior, illa propius originem re- ferens, in contextum recepta est: jamque Tertulliani tempore id mendum inoleverat, ut apparet, ex Latina ipsius citatione.

Etsi videantur verba Esaiæ de liberatione isto- rum temporum proprio agere, proprie tamen, & quoad literam de temporibus Christi agere non ex hac solum interpretatione, sed e contextu etiam Prophetæ docuimus in vindiciis Esaiæ. Quæ illic legi poterunt.

## 4:15
V. 15. Ὁδὸν θαλάσσης] That is, καθ᾿ ὁδὸν. See Ezek. XLVII.

Πέραν τοῦ Ἰορδάνου] At the Jordan. For thus the word πέραν is taken both elsewhere and in John I. 28, and in the Greek of Num. XXXII. 19.

Τῶν ἐθνῶν] That is, the Galilee of the foreigners. For this tract of land had this name not from men of one nation, but inhabited by those gathered from everywhere because of the advantages of the adjacent sea, not from the pact of Solomon with Hiram, as some think, but from the most ancient times. For in Gen. XIV. 1, Tidhal is named מלך גוים βασιλεὺς τῶν ἐθνῶν, and in Jos. XII. 23, after many Kings of Syria-Palestine, ὁ βασιλεὺς τῶν ἐθνῶν is likewise listed, with לגלגל added, where Gilgal seems to be the same as גליל in the Prophet in this place and 1 Kings IX. 11, elsewhere גלילה or גלילות, the proper name of Galilee, to be sure, but coming from the common notion of a border. And Strabo notes that Galilee was inhabited by Egyptians, Arabs, and Phoenicians. Josephus says there were many Σύγκλυδας in Tiberias.

Latin:

V. 15. Ὁδὸν θαλάσσης] Id est, καθ᾿ ὁδὸν. Vide Ezech. XLVII.

Πέραν τοῦ Ἰορδάνου] Ad Jordanem. Sic enim vox πέραν sumitur & alibi & Johan. I. 28. & in Græco Num. XXXII. 19.

Τῶν ἐθνῶν] Id est Galilæa convenarum. Nam tractatus iste non unius nationis hominibus, sed undique collectis ob adjacentis maris commoda habitatus nomen hoc ha- buit, non ex Solomonis cum Hiromo pactione, ut qui- dam existimant, sed ab antiquissimis usque temporibus. Nam Gen. XIV. 1. nominatur Tidhal מלך גוים βασι- λεὺς τῶν ἐθνῶν, & Jos. XII. 23. post multos Reges Syriæ Pa- læstinæ itidem recensetur ὁ βασιλεὺς τῶν ἐθνῶν, addito לגלגל, ubi Gilgal idem esse videtur quod apud Pro- phetam hoc loco & 1. Reg. IX. 11. גליל alibi גלילה aut גלילות proprium nimirum Galilææ nomen, sed ex communi limitis notione veniens. Et Strabo notat Ga- lilæam habitatam ab Ægyptiis, Arabibus, Phœnicibus. Σύγκλυδας multos fuisse Tiberiade ait Josephus.

## 4:16
V. 16. Καθήμενος] The interpreter correctly translated two Hebrew words, ההולכים and ישבי, with one and the same Greek word: and no more subtle explanation is to be sought here. For καθήμενος is simply dwelling. Which the Hebrews express by the word for walking at one time, and for sitting at another. The same expression, and looking back to the same place of the Prophet, is in the song of Zechariah, Luke I. 79. Whence it appears that by these words are indicated not only the calamities of places, but of times.

Ἐν χώρᾳ καὶ σκιᾷ θανάτου] This is said in the same way as ἅμα φαίδην. Moreover, χώρᾳ καὶ σκιᾷ is said by way of ἓν διὰ δυοῖν for χώρᾳ σκιᾶς θανάτου. Thus 1 Maccab. XII. 17, περὶ τῆς ἀνανεώσεως καὶ ἀδελφότητος, that is, τῆς ἀδελφότητος.

Latin:

V. 16. Καθήμενος] Duas voces Hebræas ההולכים & ישבי recte una eademque voce Græca interpres transtulit: neque subtilior explicatio hic quærenda est. Nam καθήμενος simpliciter est degens. Quod Hebræi modo ambulandi, modo sedendi voce exprimunt. Eadem locutio & eun- dem Prophetæ locum respiciens, est in Zachariæ carmine Luc. I. 79. Unde apparet his vocibus non solum locorum, sed temporum calamitates indicari.

Ἐν χώρᾳ καὶ σκιᾷ θανάτου] Ita hoc dicitur quomo- do ἅμα φαίδην. Est autem χώρᾳ καὶ σκιᾷ dictum per ἓν διὰ δυοῖν pro χώρᾳ σκιᾶς θανάτου. Sic 1. Maccab. XII. 17. πε- ρὶ τῆς ἀνανεώσεως καὶ ἀδελφότητος, id est, τῆς ἀδελφότη- τος.

## 4:17
Vers. 17. Ἀπὸ τότε ἤρξατο ὁ Ἰησοῦς κηρύσσειν.] Spanheim, and from him Walaeus, have it thus here: The word ἄρχεσθαι denotes a present act among the Hellenists in such a way that it does not deny a preceding one, nor exclude a past one, nor necessarily posit something new that had not been said, done, or seen at all before. Nay, it often denotes that which was already done before, but either in another way, or at another time, or in another place, or among others. Mark VI. 34, ἤρξατο διδάσκειν αὐτοὺς πολλά, and yet he had already taught them before. Such are Mark VIII. 11, ἤρξαντο συζητεῖν αὐτῷ. XII. 1, ἤρξατο αὐτοῖς ἐν παραβολαῖς λέγειν. Thus for that which is in Matthew, μὴ δόξητε λέγειν ἐν ἑαυτοῖς, Luke has in chapter III. 8, Μὴ δόξητε λέγειν ἐν ἑαυτοῖς. In the first chapter of Acts, the first book is said to have been written by Luke about those things which ἤρξατο Jesus began both to do and to teach; which nevertheless embraces all those things which were done by him ἅ ἧς ἡμέρας ἀνελήφθη. It is known that the Hebrew התל is sometimes taken in the same sense. It is therefore said by Matthew that Christ began to preach, because after some interval he began to bring forth again those first things, which without doubt were also the words used by Christ at the beginning of his preaching.

Verse same. Repent. For the kingdom of heaven is at hand.

How Christ thereafter, having left Nazareth, dwelt in Capernaum, which is called as it were the propitiation of the penitent, in the borders of Zabulon and Naphtali, Matthew relates in chapter IV. 13, having adduced the prophecy of Isaiah chapter IX. verse 1. He teaches that this was then fulfilled, which Grotius and others, with the Rabbis, most perversely interpret concerning the light that arose in the slaughter of Sennacherib and concerning the birth of Hezekiah, whereas the Chaldean himself explains it concerning the Messiah; and at the same time he exhibits the summary of the sermons held in Galilee, of which there were three heads from the collation of Mark I.

15. it is manifest. Concerning the time of the New Testament, the time predicted, namely in the Old Testament, Gen. XLIX. 10, Dan. IX. 4, is fulfilled. Whence the fullness (τὸ πλήρωμα) to the Apostle in Galatians IV. 6. Compare John VI. 6, Hebrews I. 10. It designates therefore the consummation of the Old Testament and the beginning of the New Testament. Which was the first head of Christ's sermons, namely that the end of the Old Testament is at hand, and that the Messiah, who brings an end to it, has now arrived. Therefore he also testified: The Kingdom of God has approached, or as Matthew has it, the kingdom of heaven. By which words he looked, in the first place, to the prophecies concerning the kingdom of the Messiah, Gen. XLIX. 10, Ps. XLV. 7, Ps. XLVII. 9, Ps. XCVI. 10, Isa. IX. 7, chapter LII. 7, Jer. XXIII. 5, 6, XXXIII. 14, Dan. VII. 14, Micah IV. 7. Wherefore he teaches that the Kingdom of the Messiah, often promised by the Prophets, has now approached, or has drawn nearer, not that it did not obtain in the Old Testament, Hebrews XIII. 8. But that in the time of the New Testament it approached in a peculiar way (1.) By reason of the King Messiah coming into the flesh. By which name he was received thus, Mark XI. 10: Blessed be the Kingdom of David our father. (2.) By reason of the acquisition of the benefits in which the kingdom of God consists, Romans XIV. 7, as they were about to be acquired by the death of Christ. For the liberation from the power of Satan had been predicted everywhere, by which he was to acquire us for himself as his own people, as our Redeemer and King, by the ransom (λύτρῳ) of his blood, which was now imminent. (3.) By reason of the clearer, more frequent, and more diffuse announcement of the kingdom of God, which was most brilliantly preached by Christ himself, and was to be announced by the Apostles throughout the whole world. (4.) By reason of the translation into the Kingdom of God, because Christ was occupied in this, that he might transfer those whom he snatched from the kingdom of Satan by his death into his own kingdom, and propagate that kingdom of grace on all sides, in which God reigns, regenerating, justifying, and sanctifying for himself through the Word and Sacraments his own peculiar possession, which may serve him with true faith and holiness. The approach of the kingdom of grace is therefore understood, not indeed of the kingdom of glory, as Maldonatus in Matthew III. 2 and other Papists contend that the kingdom of heaven was closed before Christ, which they strive to prove perversely from Hebrews IX. 8, chapter 11. 39, 40, Luke XXII. 28, 6, XXIII. 42. It was indeed opened by the death of Christ, but by reason of merit and acquired opening, not by reason of the act or actual admission into the Kingdom. The heavenly gate was not closed until the times of Christ, but was opened by the Merit of Christ. But because that merit extends itself forward and backward, and the death of Christ was profitable before it was, Apoc. XIII. 8. therefore the Patriarchs, Prophets, and other faithful under the Old Testament did not lie hidden after their blessed ἀνάλυσιν in a certain limbo excluded from the Kingdom of Heaven until the coming of Christ, but the spirits of the perfect just were received into Heaven with Elijah, Moses, and Enoch, Heb. XII. 23. Moreover, the way to the Holy [place], Heb. IX. 8. is said not yet to have been made manifest by reason of actual merit, as Cornel. a Lapide explains with Salmeron, and also by reason of plenary manifestation, as Justinianus interprets, which was reserved for the time of the New Testament. Thomas understands Christ by the way, as does Dionysius the Carthusian; Estius interprets it concerning the Grace of the New Testament not yet manifested to the ancients. As for the passage Heb. XI. 39. They did not receive the promise, it is not to be taken concerning the promises of eternal life not yet made manifest to the ancients with the Remonstrants and Hugo Grotius: not concerning the vision of God of the blessed being deferred until the consummation of us all with the Greeks as also the Photinians and Innovators, but neither is it to be explained concerning the promise of eternal salvation not actually obtained before the coming of Christ with the Papists; But it ought to be understood either concerning the promise of consummated and perfect beatitude, which the faithful are to obtain in soul and body in the resurrection, with Augustine, Chrysostom, and others, as Alphonsus de Castro, Ribera, and Bellarmine agree: which sense Estius calls the more common one; Or concerning the promises about the Messiah, as Blasius de Viega and Salmero interpret: or that the ancients were not to be consummated without us by receiving the completions of the promises about the Messiah, because if the Messiah had come in the time of the ancients, since the times of the Messiah are the last, the consummation of the world would have followed before the pious of the New Testament were born, as B. Gerhardus explains with Primasius; or (which pleases us more) that something better was reserved for the men of the New Testament, lest the ancients should attain this τελείωσιν without them, which was reserved for them rather without the ancients, and before them, Luke X. 23. Or that the salvation of the ancients is suspended from our time, but our salvation is not suspended from the time of the ancients: as Flacius in his Gloss on this passage. That they might not be consummated without us, signifies that their salvation proceeded from this very Messiah exhibited to us, and finally in our time, his sacrifice having been performed, through whom we also together with them might be justified and saved. It is also probable to Flacius that some degree or accumulation of beatitude accrued to the holy souls when Christ came and fulfilled all things, just as the Evangelists testify that many rose again when he was buried, who without doubt ascended into heaven with him.

The second part of Christ's proclamation is μετανοεῖτε, repent, as the Old [Latin] translates in this passage. Mark I. 15. renders it 'do penance,' which solecism Maldonatus shamefully excuses, preferring to confess that he does not know why he rendered it so, rather than to accuse the ancient interpreter of ignorance or rashness. But what wonder that the Old [interpreter] slipped here, when far more of his ἁμαρτήματα occur, which have been observed in the Critici Sacri and Vol. I. in A. C. Moreover, John also preached repentance, as well as the nearness of the Kingdom of God, where as a Legate he usurped the words of him by whom he was sent; but he by no means inculcated a different repentance, as Theophylact opines. Which sermon was most necessary to the most corrupt state of the people at that time, indeed it ought never not to be prior to the proclamation of the Gospel, because without repentance men are not capable of the Gospel concerning the Kingdom of God.

The third part of Christ's proclamation is summarized in these words: Believe the Gospel. Matthew omits this in this passage because he had embraced the same with the word μετανοεῖτε. Mark, however, expressed it distinctly. For the word μετανοίας is taken either generally for the whole conversion, which embraces both contrition and faith, Wisd. II. 34. ch. XII. 10. Sir. XLIV. 16. or specifically concerning contrition, the other part of repentance, to which faith is contradistinguished. Adam Conzen asks in vain here: Why does repentance precede, when faith ought to precede! Since indeed repentance, or contrition, altogether precedes saving faith, just as the law is prior to the Gospel. But that 'to believe in the Gospel' is not to believe that Christ has already come, as Conzenius wishes, but it is to apply faith to the Gospel, as far as concerns the consummation of the Kingdom of God, and with the trust of the heart to truly embrace the Grace offered in the Gospel. It is known among the Hebrews that הֶאֱמִין with ל is to believe someone, 1 Kings X. 7. with ב is to place trust, Psalm CXIX. 66. and the Greeks are accustomed to use ἐν for εἰς in the Attic dialect, Luke I. verse 17. Romans I. 23, 24. 1 Thess. IV. 7. so that the sense may be: Believe ἐν τῷ εὐαγγελίῳ for εἰς τ᾿ εὐαγγέλιον, that is, embrace with true trust what the Gospel announces concerning me. From which discussion these LESSONS are noted. I. A certain time was defined in the Old Testament for the coming of Christ, which was fulfilled by the coming of JESUS of Nazareth. II. That JESUS is the promised Messiah is a proper dogma of the New Testament. III. The time of the Messiah exhibited is the completion of time, Galatians IV. 4. and the last hour, 1 John II. 18. IV. The Kingdom of Heaven is nearer to us than to the ancients, both on account of the richer grace under the New Testament, Romans XIII. 11. 2 Corinthians VI. 2. then on account of the imminent Glory of the Kingdom of Heaven at the final advent of Christ. V. The sum of all sermons is repentance and faith, to which two heads all the sermons of Christ are recalled. VI. The Gospel is not a sermon of repentance, because μετάνοια is opposed to faith in the Gospel. Repentance strictly so called is had from the Law. But the Gospel is opposed to the Law as a sermon of grace: Meanwhile if the Gospel be taken for the universal doctrine which was preached by Christ, repentance cannot be excluded, inasmuch as he inculcated it along with faith. VII. Repentance is not a Sacrament of the New Testament as Klingius concludes from this place, because John also preached thus, repent: nay, and the Prophets in the Old Testament. And neither the repentance which the Prophets preached, nor that which John preached, was a Sacrament, as the Papists admit. VIII. Repentance taken generally consists of two parts, contrition, which is had from the Law, and faith, which is to be placed in the Gospel.

Latin:

Vers. 17. Ἀπὸ τότε ἤρξατο ὁ Ἰησοῦς κηρύσσειν.] Spanhemius & ex eo Walæus ita hic habent: Ver- bum ἄρχεσθαι ita notat actum præsentem apud Helle- nistas, ut non neget antecedentem, nec excludat præte- ritum, nec ponat necessario aliquid novi, quod ante prorsus non fuerit vel dictum, vel factum, vel visum. I- mo sæpe id notat, quod jam ante factum, sed vel alio modo, vel alio tempore, vel alio loco, vel apud alios. Marc. VI. 34. ἤρξατο διδάσκειν αὐτοὺς πολλά, & jam tamen ante eosdem docuerat. Talia sunt Marc. VIII. 11. ἤρξαντο συζητεῖν αὐτῷ. XII. 1. ἤρξατο αὐτοῖς ἐν παραβολαῖς λέγειν. Sic pro eo quod apud Matthæum, μὴ δόξητε λέγειν ἐν ἑαυτοῖς, Lucas ha- bet cap. III. 8. Μὴ δόξητε λέγειν ἐν ἑαυτοῖς, Acto- rum capite I. 1. primus liber dicitur scriptus à Luca de illis quæ ἤρξατο cœpit Jesus & facere, & do- cere; qui tamen omnia illa complectitur quæ ab illo ge- sta ἅ ἧς ἡμέρας ἀνελήφθη. Eodem sensu התל Hebreorum quandoque sumi, notum. Dicitur ita- que à Matthæo, Christum cœpisse prædicare, quia post intervallum aliquod prima illa denuo profer- re cœpit, quæ dubio procul etiam fuere Christi ver- ba in principio prædicationis adhibita.

Vers. eodem. Μετανοεῖτε. ἤγγικε γὰρ ἡ βασι- λεία τῶν ὐρανῶν.

Quomodo dehinc Christus relicta Nazareth, in Capernaum, quæ dicitur quasi propitiatio pœ- nitentium, habitarit in finibus Zabulon & Na- phtali refert Matth. cap. IV. 13. adducto Esaiæ va- ticinio cap. IX. vers. 1. Quod tum completum do- cet, quod vero cum Rabbinis Grotius, & alii de luce in Sennacharib clade exorta, ac de nativita- te Ezechia perversissime interpretantur, quum Chaldæus ipse de Messia explicet; simulque ex- hibet Summam Concionum in Galilæa habitarum, quarum tria fuisse capita è collatione Marc. I.

15. manifestum est. De tempore Novi Testa- menti impletum est tempus prædictum scilicet in Veteri Testamento, Genes. XLIX. 10. Dan. IX. 4. Unde τὸ πλήρωμα plenitudo Apostolo Galat. IV. 6. Conf. Johan. VI. 6. Ebr. I. 10. Designat ergo Veteris Testamenti consummationem & Novi Testamenti inchoationem. Quod primum fuit Concionum Christi caput, quod nempe finis Ve- teris Testamenti adfit, quodque Messias, qui ei finem affert, jam advenerit. Ideo etiam testatus est: Appropinquavit Regnum Dei vel ut Matthæus habet regnum cælorum. Quibus verbis respexit, in primis vaticinia de regno Messiæ Gen. XLIX. 10. Psal. XLV. 7. Ps. XLVII. 9. Ps. XCVI. 10. Esa. IX. 7. cap. LII. 7. Jerem. XXIII. 5. 6. XXXIII. 14. Dan. VII. 14. Mich. IV. 7. Qua- propter docet Regnum Messiæ à Prophetis sæpe promissum nuuc appropinquasse, vel propius accesisse, non quod in Veteri Testamento non obtinuerit Ebr. XIII. 8. Sed quod Novi Testa- menti tempore peculiariter appropinquarit (1.) Ratione Regis Messiæ in carnem adventantis. Quo nomine exceptus ita fuit Marc. XI. 10. Benedi- ctum Regnum David Patris nostri (2.) Ratione ac- quisitionis beneficiorum, in quibus regnum DEI consistit Roman. XIV. 7. utpote quæ erant morte Christi jamjam acquirenda. Prædicta enim erat passim liberatio de potestate Satanæ, qua nos sibi acquirere debebat in proprium populum, ceu Redemptor, & Rex noster, λύτρῳ sanguinis, quæ jam imminebat. (3.) Ratione annuncia- tionis clarioris, frequentioris, & diffusioris regni Dei, quod à Christo ipso luculentissime prædi- catum fuit, & Apostolis annunciandum erat, per totum terrarum orbem. (4.) Ratione tra- ductionis in Regnum Dei, quia Christus in eo oc- cupabatur, ut quos morte sua è regno Satanæ e- ripuit, in regnum suum transferret, illudque re- gnum Gratiæ undiquaque propagaret, in qua regnat Deus, per Verbum & Sacramenta sibi re- generans, justificans atque sanctificans peculium proprium, quod vera fide, ac sanctitate sibi ser- viat. Intelligitur ergo appropinquatio regni gra- tiæ, non vero regni gloriæ, uti Maldonatus in Matth. III. 2. & alii Papistæ contendunt Regnum cælorum ante Christum clausum fuisse, quod per- peram ex Ebr. IX. 8. cap. 11. 39. 40. Luc. XXII. 28. 6. XXIII. 42. probare satagunt. Patefactum sane est morte Christi Regnum Cœlorum, sed ratio- ne meriti & acquisitæ reserationis, non ratione a- ctus sive actualis in Regnum immissionis. Porta cœlestis non usque ad tempora Christi clausa, sed Merito Christi aperta fuit. Verum quia meritum illud antrorsum & retrorsum se extendit, ac mors Christi profuit antequam fuit, Apoc. XIII. 8. id- eo Patriarchæ, Prophetæ, aliique fideles sub Ve- teri Testamento non delituêre post beatam avá- λυσιν in limbo quodam à Regno cœlorum exclusi usque ad Christi adventum, sed spiritus justorum perfectorum cum Elia, Mose & Enocho Cœlo re- cepti sunt Ebr. XII. 23. Via autem ad Sanctum Ebr. IX. 8. nondum patefacta dicitur ratione me- riti actualis, ut Cornel. a Lapide cum Salmerone explicat, nec non ratione plenariæ manifestatio- nis, uti Justinianus interpretatur, quæ tempo- ri Novi Testamenti reservata fuit. Thomas per viam Christum intelligit, ut & Dionysius Carthu- sianus, Estius de Gratia Novi Testamenti nondum manifestata veteribus interpretatur. Quod ad locum Ebr. XI. 39. Non acceperunt promissionem, is non de promissionibus vitæ æternæ Veteribus haud patefactis cum Remonstrantibus, & Hugone Gro- tio: non de visione Dei beatorum differenda us- que ad nostrum omnium consummationem cum Græ- cis ut & Photinianis ac Novatoribus accipiendus est, sed nec de promissione salutis æternæ actu haud impetrata ante adventum Christi explican- dus cum Papistis; Sed vel de promissione consum- matæ & perfectæ beatitudinis, quam fideles ani- ma & corpore consecuturi sunt in resurrectione, cum Augustino, Chrysostomo & aliis intelligi de- bet uti annuit Alphonsus de Castro, Riebera, Bel- larminus: Quem sensum communiorem dicit E- stius; Vel de promissionibus de Messia, ut inter- pretatur Blasius de Viega, & Salmero: sive quod non consummandi fuerint Veteres sine nobis acci- piendo complementa promissionum de Messia, quia si veterum tempore Messias venisset, cum tempora Messiæ novissima sint, consummatio mundi secuta fuisset, antequam pii Novi Testa- menti nati essent, uti cum Primasio exponit B. Gerhardus; sive (quod nobis magis placet) quod Hominibus Novi Testamenti melius quid re- servatum sit, ne Veteres sine illis hanc τελείωσιν consequerentur, quæ ipsis potius sine veteribus, & præ illis reservabatur Luc. X. 23. Vel quod salus veterum à tempore nostro, non autem salus nostra à tempore veterum suspendatur: u- ti Flacius in Glossa in h. l. Ut non sine nobis con- summarentur, significat ut eorum salus ex hoc ipso nobis exhibito Messia, nostroque demum tempore, peracto ipsius sacrificio prodiret, per quem & nos una cum ipsis justificaremur & salvaremur. Pro- babile etiam est Flacio, sanctis animabus aliquem quasi gradum cumulumve beatitatis, veniente o- mnia implente Christo, accessisse, sicut eo sepulto mul- tos resurrexisse Evangelistæ testantur, qui proculdu- bio cum ipso in cælum ascenderunt.

Altera pars præconii Christi est μετανοεῖτε, pæ- nitentiam agite, uti vertit h. l. Vetus. Marc. I. 15. reddit pœnitemini, quem Solœcismum turpiter excusat Maldonatus, malle se fateri quod nesciat cur ita reddiderit, quam ignorantiæ aut temerita- tis antiquum interpretem arguere. Sed quid mirum hic lapsum esse Veterem, cum longe plura ejus occurrant ἁμαρτήματα, quæ in Criti- co Sacro & Tom. I. in A. C. observata. Præ- dicavit autem Johannes quoque pœnitentiam, ut & propinquitatem Regni Dei, ubi ceu Lega- tus verba ejus à quo missus erat, usurpavit; Neu- tiquam vero diversam pœnitentiam, ut Theophy- lactus opinatur, inculcavit. Quæ concio statui corruptissimo populi tum maxime fuit necessa- ria, imo nunquam non prævia esse debet præco- nio Evangelii, quia sine pœnitentia homines ca- paces non sunt Evangelii de Regno Dei.

Tertia pars præconii Christi his summatim comprehenditur. Credite Evangelio. Hanc o- mittit Matthæus h. l. quia verbo μετανοεῖτε eandem complexus erat. Marcus autem distincte eam expreffit. Verbum enim μετανοίας accipitur vel generatim pro tota conversione, quæ & contri- tionem & fidem complectitur Sapient. II. 34. cap. XII. 10. Syr. XLIV. 16. vel speciatim de contri- tione, altera pœnitentiæ parte, cui contradistin- guitur fides. Frustra hic quærit Adam Conzen. Cur pœnitentia præcedat, cum fides præcedere de- beat! Siquidem omnino pœnitentia, seu con- tritio fidem salvificam antecedat, quemadmo- dum lex prior est Evangelio. Illud autem in Evangelium credere, non est credere Christum jam venisse, ut vult Conzenius, sed est fidem adhibe- re Evangelio, quantum ad consummationem de Regno Dei, & fiducia cordis vera amplecti Gra- tiam in Evangelio oblatam. Notum est apud Hebræos הֶאֱמִין cum ל esse credere alicui 1. Reg. X. 7. cum ב fiduciam ponere Psal. CXIX. 66. & solent Græci Dialectico Attica ἐν pro εἰς uti, Luc. I. vers. 17. Roman. I. 23. 24. 1. Thessal. IV. 7. ut sensus sit: Credite ἐν τῷ εὐαγγελίῳ pro εἰς τ᾿ εὐ- αγγέλιον, hoc est, vera fiducia amplectimini, quæ de me annunciat Evangelium. E qua συζητή- σει hæc notamur DOCUMENTA. I. Adven- tui Christi certum tempus in Veteri Testamento definitum fuit, quod per adventum JESU Na- zareni impletum est. II. JESUM esse promif- sum Messiam proprium est dogma Novi Testa- menti. III. Tempus Messiæ exhibiti est com- plementum temporis. Galat. IV. 4. & hora no- vissima 1. Johan. II .18. IV. Propinquius est nobis Regnum Cœlorum, quam veteri- bus, tum ob locupletiorem gratiam sub No- vo Testamento Roman. XIII. 11. 2. Corinth. VI. 2. tum ob imminentem Gloriam Regni Cælorum in novissimo adventu Christi. V. Summa omnium Concionum est pœnitentia & fides, ad quæ duo capita omnes Conciones Christi revocantur. VI. Evangelium non est concio pœnitentiæ, quia μετά- νοια opponitur fidei in Evangelium. Pœni- tentia stricte dicta è lege habetur. Evangelium autem legi opponitur ceu gratiæ Concio: Interim si Evangelium accipiatur pro doctrina universa, quæ à Christo prædicata est, pœnitentia ex- cludi nequit, utpote quam cum fide incul- cavit. VII. Pœnitentia non est Sacramentum Novi Testamenti ut ex h. l. concludit Klingius, quia etiam Johannes ita prædicavit, agite pœniten- tiam: imo & Prophetæ in Veteri Testamento. Atque neque pœnitentia quam Prophetæ prædi- carunt, neque quam Johannes, Sacramentum fuit, fatentibus Papistis. VIII. Pœnitentia γενι- κῶς accepta duabus constat partibus, contritione, quæ ex Lege habetur, & fide, quæ in Evangelium collocanda.

## 4:18
Vers. 18. ἀμφίβληστρον] Rightly, a casting-net. Virgil called it a fundam. The expression is taken from Isa. XIX. 8.

Consult here the annotations of Beza concerning this word. Ἀμφίβληστρον is a kind of net, named from ἀμφὶ and βάλλειν, because when it is cast, it expands from a narrow space into a wide one, and being curved into the shape of half an egg, it encompasses a huge space of water in a circle.

Latin:

Vers. 18. ἀμφίβληστρον] Recte, jaculum. Fandam dixit Virgilius. Locutio sumta est ex Esa. XIX. 8.

Cons. hic Bezæ annotationes de hac voce. Ἀμ- φίβληστρον est genus retis, dictum ab ἀμφὶ & βάλ- λειν, quod cum jacitur, ex angusto in latum ex- pandatur, & incurvatum in formam dimidiati ovi in orbem complectatur ingens aquæ spatium.

## 4:19
Verse 19. Come after me. John 1:35. Andrew and Peter are said to have already approached Christ before the imprisonment of John the Baptist; but in this passage, it is after Christ heard that John had been arrested. But one must distinguish the narrative of the voluntary approach of Andrew and Peter to Christ from the narrative of the calling of both: the former was met by a temporary following of Christ, the latter by a continuous one; the cause of the former was the preaching of John concerning Christ, the cause of the latter was the calling of the Lord; and in that place, it is not even indicated by a word from John that either Peter or Andrew were called by the Lord, but only that Andrew led his brother Simon to the Lord, and that either his name was changed by the Lord, or that the predicted change of name would follow. Add the distinction openly indicated by John in the immediately following verse between the spontaneous approach of Andrew and Peter to the Lord and the calling: there, they are not read to have been called by the Lord either before the approach or after the approach in that place, but Philip was called in the immediately following verse with 'follow me,' by which an open calling is meant; to this narrative of John must be postponed that which Matthew has, that Christ at another time called those very brothers to his discipleship and company, who had previously adhered to him for a time, whence they are also read to have followed him immediately as a Teacher already known, nay, as the Messiah designated by John; as Spanheim, and Bald. Walæus rightly [observe].

fishers of men] In a similar way Plato called 'man-hunting' the 'art of domesticating men.' See Ezekiel 47:10. Isaac Ben Aram says the truth of the prophecy was revealed to the fishermen. See Nebiensis on Psalm 117:11.

The reason why it was announced by the Lord to those disciples that they would be fishers of men is evident: namely, the condition of those disciples before the calling, to which it alludes, just as it is the Lord's custom to shadow forth spiritual things with carnal ones, and to seek figures and types from the matter at hand, which was done here, and elsewhere throughout, these similar things being used by the Lord rather than others, because objects of that kind offered themselves to the Lord as he spoke and could easily be grasped and understood by all, as Spanheim [says] again.

PART III. CHAPTER IV. In which SECTION II begins. Of the deeds from the second Passover to the third.

Latin:

Vers. 19. Δεῦτε ὀπίσω με. Joh. I. 35. dicuntur Andreas & Petrus jam acces- sisse ad Christum ante captivitatem Johannis Bapti- stæ; hoc autem loco postquam Christus audivit, Jo- hannem comprehensum. Sed distinguenda narra- tio de accessu ultroneo Andreæ, & Petri ad Chri- stum, à narratione de vocatione utriusque: illum excepit sequela Christi temporaria, istam continua; illius causa prædicatio Johannis de Christo, istius vo- catio Domini; & istic loci ne verbo quidem à Jo- hanne indicatum, sive Petrum sive Andream voca- tos à Domino, sed tantum Andream duxisse fra- trem Simonem ad Dominum, eique vel nomen mu- tatum à Domino, vel prædictam nominis mutatio- nem sequuturam. Adde versu immediate sequente discrimen à Johanne aperte indicatum, inter spon- taneam Andreæ & Petri accessum ad Dominum, & inter vocationem: illic nec ante acces- sum, nec post accessum istic loci à Domino vocati leguntur, vocatus vero Philippus versu immediate sequenti ἀκολύθει μοι, qua vocatio aperta, huic narrationi Johannis posponenda illa quam habet Matthæus, Christum alio tempore ad discipulatum & contubernium suum vocasse illos ipsos fratres, qui prius ei ad tempus adhæserant, unde etiam confe- stim illi ut Doctori jam noto, imo ut Messiæ à Jo- hanne designato, obsequuti leguntur; ut recte Spanhemius, & Bald. Walæus.

ἁλιεῖς ἀνθρώπων] Simili modo ἀνθρωποθηρίαν dixit Pla- to τέχνην τῶν ἀνθρώπων οἰκειωτικήν. Vide Ezechielem XLVII. 10. veritatem Prophetiæ piscatoribus patefactam ait Isaac Ben Aram. Vide Nebiensem ad Psalmum CXVII. 11.

Cur discipulis istis denunciatum fuerit à Domino, illos futuros piscatores hominum, ratio evidens: conditio nimirum discipulorum illorum, ante voca- tionem, ad quam alludit, prout solenne Domino spi- ritualia carnalibus adumbrare, & figuras ac typos è re nata petere, quod & hic factum, & passim alibi, his similibus à Domino potius adhibitis quam aliis, quia objecta ejusmodi sese Domino loquenti offere- bant, & facile ab omnibus capi poterant & intelli- gi, ut iterum Spanhemius.

PARS III. CAPUT IV. Qua inchoatur SECTIO II. Gestorum à Paschate secundo ad tertium.

## 4:23
Verse 23. in their synagogues] This word synagoge extends as widely as the Hebrew 'edah or the Latin conventus. For every assembly of men that is by institution, whether for judgments, or public council, or for the sake of sacred matters, is called by this name. But later it began to be transferred also to the places in which those assemblies were held, as Luke 7:5. Whether you understand here the assembly or the place in which the divine law was accustomed to be expounded, it makes no difference. It appears that not even Christians abhorred this word, James 2:2. Theophilus against the nations, book II: 'God still gives to the world, which is being ruined and tossed by sins, the synagogues, called holy churches.' Philo calls the same places sometimes didaskaleia, sometimes phrontisteria, elsewhere holy places: But they were also called Proseuchai from prayers, especially at Rome: which the Satires teach us: for it seems to me that a most learned man doubted in vain whether Proseuchai and Synagogues were the same, since, if I am not mistaken, Philo removes all hesitation in his embassy to Gaius with these words: 'He (Augustus) knew that they also had houses of prayer and assembled in them, and especially on the sacred seventh days, when they are publicly instructed in their ancestral philosophy. For what are the houses of prayer in the cities other than schools of prudence, and courage, and temperance, and justice, and piety, and holiness, and every virtue.' Nor should we wonder if Christ was permitted to speak to the people in the synagogues. For it was customary for the rulers of the synagogue to defer honor to grave and not unlearned men, as the history which is in Acts 13:15 teaches us. Which Tertullian rightly observes against Marcion, book IV. But even if the synagogue was frequented, it was not for teaching unless by one well known and explored and approved long since for this very purpose, or commended from elsewhere. That custom remained for some time in the Christian Church, that by the concession of the Bishops, not only presbyters or deacons, but also those who had obtained the grace of wisdom, interpreted the Scriptures. See Eusebius, who proves by the example of Origen and others that laymen may speak, not without permission, but by the authorization of the one presiding. To which also those things look that are read in 1 Corinthians 14:29.

The temple, that is, the place of sacrifice, was by God's command unique for the Jews, Deut. 12:13, and that finally at Jerusalem; but in the time of Christ, synagogues were more frequent through individual cities and villages, and indeed often several in one city, Acts 6:9. At Jerusalem, which were gathered from all provinces and regions, there are said to have been four hundred and eighty daily, in which they gathered not for sacrifice, but for the circumcision of infants, the reading and explanation of the Law and the Prophets, a sacred sermon, and finally for prayer, especially on the Sabbaths, Acts 15:21. Thus B. Joh. Gerhard in his Annotations on this passage, page 237.

Verse same. healing. Among physicians, therapeuein signifies properly to heal with medicines, by hand, or by a regimen of life, which they call to cure: whence therapeuteike, the art of healing, was named by Galen. But it is used improperly in this place: for Christ did not cure diseases by applying remedies, but healed them by a word. Thus Luke 9:1. The Apostles did not cure the sick by applying medicines; but they healed by commanding the diseases in the name of Christ to depart. See Walæus. Yet one should not say with Franc. Luc. Brugensis that the sacred writers abused this word: for the word therapeuein not only signifies to apply remedies to a sick person, but is also used of one who is present to a sick person, taking care of him, and performing necessary services for him. Wisdom 16:12. Neither herb, nor poultice healed them. B. Gerh. p. 240.

malakian] This word extends quite widely for those of the Jews speaking Greek, so that it includes every pain and evil, corresponding to the Hebrew words mak'ob as in Job 33:19 and choli as in Gen. 42:4; and here the promise of the law in Deut. 28 is fulfilled.

Thus also Scultetus in Walaeus: Suidas' μαλακία is ῥαθυμία, sloth and torpor. The LXX, although they denote infirmity and sickness by this word, Deut. VII. 15, 2 Chron. XXI. 12, Gen. XLI. 4 & 38. And just as the Evangelist couples πᾶσαν νόσον & πᾶσαν μαλακίαν; so in Moses, Deut. XXVIII. 61, πᾶσα μαλακία & πᾶσα πληγὴ are joined. I know there are those who define νόσον as a long-lasting perversion of the body's condition and μαλακίαν as the beginning of the body's dislocation: and therefore they translate νόσον as disease and μαλακίαν as languor, but what do they say when they read in the LXX, μαλακίας πονηρὰν 2 Chron. XXI. 15 & 19.

Latin:

Vers. 23. ἐν ταῖς συναγωγαῖς αὐτῶν] Vox hæc συναγωγὴ tam late patet quam Hebræa עדה aut Latina conventus. Omnis enim hominum cœtus qui ex instituto est sive ju- diciorum, sive publici consilii, sive rerum sacrarum gratia hoc nomine appellatur. Deinde vero cœpit & ad loca transferri, in quibus isti conventus habebantur, ut Luc. VII. 5. Hic sive cœtum, sive locum in quo lex divina expo- ni solebat intelligas, nihil refert. Ne Christianos qui- dem ab hoc vocabulo abhorruisse apparet, Jacob. II. 2. Theophylus adversus nationes libro II. ετι διδωκεν ὁ θεὸς τῷ κόσμῳ λυμαινομένῳ καὶ χειμαζομένῳ ὑπὸ τῶν ἁμαρτημάτων, τὰς συναγωγὰς, λεγομένας ἐκκλησίας ἁγίας. Eadem loca Phi- lo modo διδασκαλεῖα, modo φροντιστήρια appellat, alibi ἱεροὺς τόπους: Sed & à precibus Prosevchæ & vocabantur, Romæ præsertim: quod nos docent Satyræ: frustra enim dubitasse mihi videtur vir doctissimus an idem fuerint Pro- sevchæ & Synagogæ, cum omnem, ni fallor, hæsita- tionem eximat Philo legatione ad Cajum his verbis: ἐπί- στατο ὆ν (Augustus) καὶ προσευχὰς ἔχοντας καὶ συνιόντας εἰς αὐ- τὰς, καὶ μάλιστα ταῖς ἱεραῖς ἑβδόμαις, ὅτε δημοσίᾳ τὴν πάτρι- ον παιδεύονται φιλοσοφίαν. Τὰ γὰρ κατὰ πόλεις προσευκτήρια τὶ ἑτερόν ἐστιν ἡ διδασκαλεῖα φρονήσεως κὰι ἀνδρείας, κὰι σωφροσύ- νης κὰι δικαιοσύνης, ἐυσεβείας τε κὰι ὁσιότητος, κὰι συμπάσης ἀρετῆς. Neque mirari debemus si Christo permissum est in Synagogis verba ad populum facere. Solebat enim ab Archisynagogis in honos deferri viris gravibus & non ine- ruditis, ut nos docet historia quæ est Actor. XIII. 15. Quod recte adversus Marcionem observat Tertullianus lib. IV. Sed etsi passim Synagogæ adiretur, non tamen ad do- cendum nisi ab optime cognito & explorato & probato jam pridem in hoc ipsum, vel aliunde commendato. Mansit is mos aliquamdiu in Ecclesia Christiana, ut concessu Epi- scoporum Scripturas interpretarentur, non presbyteri tan- tum aut diaconi, sed & oi τῆς χρηστοτίας κ᾿ ἄϊτω τετυχη- κότες. Vide Eusebium qui Origenis aliorumque exemplo probat λαϊκοὺς ὁμιλεῖν ἐκ ἀπείθησιν, sed τῇ τῦ προεστῶτος ἐπι- τροπῇ. Quo & illa spectant quæ leguntur I. Cor. XIV. 29.

Templum h. e. sacrificii locus Judæis Dei man- dato erat unicum, Deut. XII. 13. idque tandem Hierosolymis; Synagogæ vero erant Christi tem- pore per singulas Civitates & vicos frequentiores, & quidem plures sæpe in una civitate, Actor. VI. vers. 9. Hierosolymis, quæ ex provinciis & regioni- bus omnibus confluebant, quotidie octuagintæ & quadringentæ fuisse narrantur, in quibus non ad sacrificium, sed ad infantulorum circumcisionem, le- gis ac Prophetarum lectionem, atque explanatio- nem, sacram concionem, denique ad orationem Sabbatis maxime conveniebatur, Actor. XV. 21. Ita B. Joh. Gerhardus in Annotatis ad h. l. pag. 237.

Vers. eod. θεραπεύων. Apud Medicos θεραπεύειν significat proprie, phar- macis, manu, aut victus ratione sanare, quod me- deri dicunt: unde dicta est à Galeno θεραπευτικὴ, Ars medendi. Improprie autem usurpatur hoc lo- co: Christus enim non curabat morbos adhibitis reme- diis, sed sanabat illos verbo. Sic Luc. IX. 1. Apo- stoli non curabant ægrotum adhibitis medicamentis; sed sanabant mandando morbis in nomine Christi, ut discederent. Vid. Walæus. Non tamen cum Franc. Luc. Brugensi dicendum, quod Scripto- res sacri abusi sint hac voce: nam vox θεραπεύειν non solum significat remedia ægroto adhibere, sed etiam usurpatur de eo, qui præsto est ægroto, curam ejus gerens, officiaque necessaria ei præstans. Sap. XVI. 12. Non herba, non malagma ἐθεράπευσεν ἀυτές. B. Gerh. p. 240.

μαλακίαν] Satis late patet hæc vox Judæorum Græce loquentibus, ita ut dolorem malumque omne includat, respondens Hebræis vocibus מכאוב ut Jobi XXXIII. 19. & חלי ut Gen. XLII. 4. impletur autem hic promis- sum legis Deut. XXVIII.

Sic etiam Scultetus apud Walæum: Suidæ μαλακία est ῥαθυμία sagnities ac torpor. LXX. hoc vocabulo quamvis infirmitatem & ægritudinem notant, Deut. VII. 15. 2. Par. XXI. 12. Gen. XLI. 4. & 38. Atque ut Evangelista πᾶσαν νόσον & πᾶ- σαν μαλακίαν copulat; ita apud Mosen Deuter. XXIIX. 61. πᾶσα μαλακία & πᾶσα πληγὴ conjun- guntur. Scio esse, qui voσον diuturnam perversio- nem habitudinis corporis μαλακίαν principium luxa- tionis corporis definiunt: & idcirco voσον morbum, μαλακίαν languorem vertunt, sed quid illi decent, ubi apud LXX. legerint, μαλακίας ποιηρὰν 2. Par. XXI. 15. & 19.

## 4:24
Verse 24. Βασάνοις. Vulgate: tormentis, that is, στρέβλαις, as the Attics call them. Erasmus translates it as torminibus (gripes), so that he might avoid the ambiguity, which nevertheless has a place even in the Greek; but it is easily removed by the preceding word: furthermore, by the name of tormina only a certain disease is contained, whereas the Evangelist now calls all severe diseases βασάνους, which torture the sick person with the sharpest pains, as if they were defendants placed on the rack and the wooden horse for the sake of extorting the truth. Thus Beza on this passage; Camerarius says that ἡ βάσανος properly is the touchstone by which gold is tested, which is Λυδίη πέτνη in the poem of Theocritus. It is transferred, however, to any questions whatsoever, even those of torture: and thus Aristophanes used the word βασανίζω in the Frogs. And now it signifies the torments and tortures of diseases.

Verse 24. δαιμονιζομένους] Among the Greeks the word δαίμων is neutral, and indeed, as I think, initially used in a better sense, not from a Greek origin as if they were demons, but rather from the Arabic ديمن. The Syrians use the Greek word slightly changed in the same sense: for they say דיומא. For from the East have almost all the most ancient words of sacred things come: just as that word of similar notion κάβειροι, which you can call divine in Latin, כבירים. But just as the Hebraist Jews did not wish to call God בעל, because that word had been occupied by profane nations, otherwise signifying nothing other than lord, so also the Hellenists did not wish to call the Angels of light by the name of Demons, but in detestation of pagan superstition they wished that name to be proper to harmful spirits, whom the Greeks for the sake of distinction called κακοδαίμονας, and the ancient Latins called Vejoves. But it appears that δαιμονιζομένους are not those who are insane in any way, but those seized and agitated by a greater force of impure spirits, such as those whom the Greeks called νυμφολήπτας, and the Latins called larvati, ceriti, or lymphatici. For a great abundance of those struggling with this evil was exhibited not only by the age of Christ and the Apostles, but also by a later age, as can be seen in Origen, Tertullian, and Cyprian.

σεληνιαζομένους] Although the Greeks sometimes call those suffering from the falling sickness σεληνιακοὺς; yet it seems that a more serious evil is indicated here, and one more remote from natural causes, to which however ἐπιληψης [is related]. For below in XVII. 15 and following, he who is called σεληνιαζόμενος is shown to have been both ἐπιληπτικὸς and δαιμονιζόμενος. Firmicus openly distinguishes Lunatics from those with the falling sickness; and Aegineta says that certain σεληνιακοὺς are ὡς ἐνθσιά- ζοντας. Nor do Basil or Jerome interpret σεληνιαζομένους otherwise.

Here can be compared what Balduinus Walæus has brought forward concerning these diseases from Johannes Walæus.

παραλυτικοὺς] struck by a star. Plautus: he is struck by a star, he cannot move. Scribonius Largus: it is useful for the tremulous and those struck by a star in either way, for one is seen from the contraction, the other with the relaxation of the nerves; they call both these defects παράλυσιν. The metaphor is drawn from trees which, struck by the dog-star, wither away. Celsus translates παράλυσιν as the resolution of the nerves.

Latin:

Vers. 24. Βασάνοις. Vulg. tormentis, id est, στρέβλαις, ut Attici vocant. Erasmus torminibus convertit, ut vita- ret amphibolian, quæ tamen etiam in Græco locum habet; sed facile vocabulo præcedente tollitur: deinde torminum appellatione certus tantum mor- bus continetur, cum & βασάνες jam vocet Evan- gelista sævos omnes morbos, qui ægrotum acer- rimis doloribus excruciant, quasi reos tormentis & equuleo veritatis extorquendæ causa impositos. Ita Beza in h. l. Camerarius, ἡ βάσαντος, inquit, proprie est coticula qua aurum exploratur, quæ est Λυδίη πέτνη in carmine Theocriteo. Transfertur autem ad quæscunque quæstiones, etiam tormento- rum: & ita verbo βασανίζω usus est Aristophanes Βατράχοις. Et nunc significantur cruciatus atque tormenta morborum.

Vers. 24. δαιμονιζομένους] Apud Græcos media est vox δαίμων, & quidem, ut arbitror, initio in partem meliorem usurpata, non ex Græca origine quod sint dæmones, sed ex Arabica potius ديمن . Græcam vocem leviter mu- tatam eodem sensu Syri usurpant: dicunt enim דיומא. Nam ab Oriente ferme venerunt antiquissimæ sacrorum voces: quomodo & illud similis notionis κάβειροι, di- vi potes Latine, כבירים. Sicut autem Hebræistæ Judæi Deum noluerunt appellare בעל, quod ea vox à profanis gentibus esset occupata, alioqui nihil aliud quam dominum significans, ita & Hellenistæ Angelos lucis no- luerunt appellare Dæmonum vocabulo, sed in detestatio- nem paganicæ superstitionis nomen id proprium esse vo- luerunt spiritibus noxiis, quos Græci discriminis causa κακοδαίμονας, veteres Latini Vejoves appellarunt. Δαι- μονιζομένους autem esse apparet non quovis modo insamien- tes, sed impurorum spirituum vi majore correptos atque agitatos, quales erant quos Græci νυμφολήπτας, Latini larvatos, ceritos, limphaticos vocabant. Cum hoc e- nim malo conflictantium copiam magnam exhibuit non Christi tantum Apostolorumque, sed & ferior ætas, ut videre est apud Origenem, Tertullianum, Cyprianum.

σεληνιαζομένους] Quanquam Græci morbo caduco labo- rantes σεληνιακοὺς interdum vocant; videtur tamen hic ma- lum gravius & à naturalibus causis remotius indicari, cui tamen ἐπιληψης. Nam infra XVII. 15. & deinceps, qui σεληνιαζόμενος vocatur, ostenditur fuisse & ἐπιληπτικὸς & δαιμονιζόμενος. Firmicus aperte distinguit Lunaticos à caducis; & Ægineta quosdam σεληνιακοὺς ait esse ὡς ἐνθσιά- ζοντας. Neque aliter interpretantur σεληνιαζομένους tum Basilius tum Hieronymus.

Conferri hic poterunt, quæ de his morbis è Joh. Walæo adduxit Balduinus Walæus.

παραλυτικοὺς] sideratos. Plautus: sideratus est, moveri non potest. Scribonius largus: facit ad tremulos & sidera- tione tentatos utralibet, una enim ex contrattione, altera cum remissione nervorum conspicitur, παράλυσιν hoc utrumq; vitium vocant. Tralatio ducta est ab arboribus quæ cani- culari sidere tactæ exarescunt. Celsus παράλυσιν transfert nervorum resolutionem.

## 4:25
Verse 25. δεκαπόλεως. Thus was the tract named from the ten cities situated there. It is handed down, however, to have been a small region, next to Galilee of the Gentiles. Furthermore, those ten cities, which are attributed to that region by Pliny in book V, chapter 18, do not comprise some small region, but a quite ample one: whence, having enumerated them, Pliny adds these words: The tetrarchies of the regions run between and surround these cities like individual ones, and are contributed into kingdoms, Trachonitis, Paneas, in which is Caesarea with the aforementioned spring, Abila, Arca, Ampelœssa, Gabe. Thus Piscator in this place.

Latin:

Vers. 25. δεκαπόλεως. Sic nominatus fuit tractus à decem urbibus ibi sitis. Traditur autem fuisse regiuncula, Gali- lææ Gentium proxima. Cæterum, decem illæ urbes, quæ isti regioni attribuuntur à Plinio lib. V. c. 18. non regiunculam aliquam, sed bene am- plam regionem comprehendunt: unde illis enu- meratis, Plinius subjungit hæc verba: Intercur- sant cinguntque has urbes tetrarchiæ regionum in- star singulæ, & in regna contribuuntur, Trachoni- tis, Paneas, in qua Cæsarea cum supradicto fonte, Abila, Arca, Ampelœssa, Gabe. Ita Piscator in h. l.

## 5:1 Argument
