CHAPTER V. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

Jesus on the mount explains who are blessed, namely the truly penitent, or those contrite and grieving for their sins, and those thirsting for true righteousness; the merciful, the pure in heart, the peacemakers, and those patiently enduring persecutions. He declares the office of the disciples by the similitude of salt and the light of the world, and teaches that the end of his coming is the fulfillment of the law, and requires a more abundant righteousness than the Pharisaical was for entry into the kingdom of heaven; he corrects the depravation of the precept concerning not killing, that homicide is committed not only by the hand or external work, bringing upon itself the guilt of eternal punishment, but also by the heart, gesture, and mouth; nor is any gift pleasing to God without reconciliation with one's neighbor: as also of the precept concerning not committing adultery; that adultery is committed by lust alone, and therefore the eye is to be plucked out, the hand is to be cut off, if they scandalize us, and that divorce, apart from the cause of adultery, is a cause of adultery, and he who marries a repudiated woman commits adultery: then also of the precept concerning not committing perjury, that any rash oath is to be avoided, and one must not swear by heaven, earth, or Jerusalem, or our own head: likewise of the precept concerning retaliation, that it leaves no place for private vengeance, but rather injury is to be borne, and indeed one must do good even to enemies, so that we may imitate God the Father.

The parts are V. I. Concerning the truly blessed, to verse 12. II. Concerning the office of the disciples of Christ, to verse 16. III. Concerning the end of the coming of Jesus, the fulfillment of the law, to verse 19. IV. Concerning true and saving righteousness, verse 20. V. Concerning the meaning of certain precepts of the divine law, to verse 48.

PART I. Concerning the truly blessed.

Vers. 1. εἰς τὸ ὄρος] Just as the old law was promulgated from a mountain, so also did Christ set forth the new one on a mountain. How, however, those things which Luke says in ch. VI agree with this narrative, we shall say when we come to Luke.

He reconciles them in this way: that Christ stood on a plain while he restored the sick to health, which Luke says, then sat down in the manner of a Teacher when he was beginning his precepts, as Matthew indicates: but that he betook himself from a higher retreat to a plain of the mountain capable of a larger crowd, so that the discourse was held ἐπὶ τόπου πεδινοῦ on a plain, and nevertheless on a mountain, which Matthew's narrative seems altogether to require. Which we entirely approve; for thus it is neither necessary to make two distinct histories with Ostandrus, which B. Chemnitius refutes, nor with others, that Christ spent the night on the mountain, and soon at daybreak designated the Apostles from the rest of the disciples, and immediately descended from the mountain with them into a level place to the rest of the crowd of people, and there held the sermon which is read here, so that Matthew omitted this calling of the Apostles and this descent of Christ.

καθίσαντος ἀυτᾶ] Not only the twelve or seventy, but all who followed his doctrine. Wherefore οἱ μαθηταὶ are the same who are called here and below VII. 28. ὄχλοι, and in Luke VI. 17. ὄχλος μαθητῶν. And thus we know the word μαθητῶν is used everywhere as below XII. 49, Luke VI. 13, Acts XI. 26, and in many other places. The precepts which are proper and peculiar to those separated for the preaching of the Gospel will follow below at the tenth chapter at last.

We admit that the precepts given and to be observed are common to all followers of Christ. The seventy, however, are rashly introduced here, who at that time had not yet been separated from the promiscuous assembly.

Latin:

CAPUT V. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Jesus in monte explicat, quinam beati sint, vere scil. pænitentes, vel contriti & do- lentes ob peccata, & veram justitiam si- tientes; misericordes, puricorde, paci- fici, & patienter persecutiones tolerantes. Officium discipulorum similitudine salis, & lucis mundi declarat, finemque adven- tus sui legis impletionem esse docet, ac ab- undantiorem justitiam, quam Pharisaica erat, ad ingressum in regnum cælorum re- quirit; depravationem præcepti de non occidendo emendat, quod non tantum ma- nu, vel externo opere homicidium, rea- tum pœna æterna inferens, committatur, sed etiam corde, gestu, & ore; nec sine re- conciliatione cum proximo Deo gratum sit ullum munus: ut & præcepti de non mœ- chando; quod sola concupiscentia adulte- rium committatur, ideoque oculus eruen- dus, manus abscindenda sit, scandali- zent nos, quodque divortium, citra adulte- rii causam, causa sit mœchationis, & qui repudiatam ducit, mœchetur: tum etiam præcepti de non committendo perjurio, quod quodlibet temerarium juramentum vitandum, neque per cœlum, terram, aut Hierosolymam, aut caput nostrum juran- dum sit: præcepti item de talione, quod non relinquat locum vindictæ privatæ, quin potius ferenda injuria sit, adeoque benefa- ciendum etiam inimicis, ut Deum Patrem imitemur.

Partes sunt V. I. De vere beatis, ad v. 12. II. de officio discipulorum Christi, ad v. 16. III. de fine adventus Jesu, impletione legis, ad v. 19. IV. de vera & salvifica justitia, v. 20. V. de sensu præceptorum quorundam legis divinæ, ad v. 48.

PARS I. De vere beatis.

Vers. 1. εἰς τὸ ὄρος] Sicut lex vetus de monte erat pro- mulgata, ita & novam Christus in monte proposuit. Quo- modo autem cum hac narratione conveniant ea quæ dicit Lucas c. VI. ad Lucam dicemus.

Conciliat ea hoc modo: quod steterit Christus in planitie dum ægrotos valetudini restituit, quod di- cit Lucas, deinde sederit Doctoris in morem, cum præ- cepta exordiretur, ut Matthæus indicat: de subli- miore autem secessu se contulerit in planitiem montis capacem majoris turbæ, ut sermo habitus sit ἐπὶ τό- πε πεδινᾶ in planitie, & nihilominus in monte, quod omnino exigere videtur Matthæi narratio. Quæ omnino probamus; ita enim nec cum Ostan- dro necesse est duas distinctas historias facere, quod refellit B. Chemnitius, nec cum aliis, Chri- stum in monte pernoctasse, & mox exorto die Apo- stolos ex reliquis discipulis designasse, & statim è monte cum iis in locum campestrem ad reliquam populi turbam descendisse, & ibi concionem, quæ hic legitur, habuisse, adeo ut Matthæus hanc Apo- stolorum vocationem, & hunc Christi descensum omiserit.

καθίσαντος ἀυτᾶ] Non duodecim aut septuaginta solum, sed omnes qui doctrinam ejus sectabantur. Quare οἱ μα- θηταὶ sunt iidem qui & hic & infra VII. 28. ὄχλοι, & Luc. VI. 17. ὄχλος μαθητῶν dicuntur. Atque ita vocem μαθητῶν scimus passim usurpari ut infra XII. 49. Luc. VI. 13. Actor. XI. 26. multisque aliis in locis. Præcepta quæ propria sunt ac peculiaria segregatorum ad prædicationem Evangelicam, infra sequentur capite demum decimo.

Admittimus communia esse præcepta omnibus Christi sectatoribus data & observanda. Septua- ginta vero hic temere ingeruntur, qui tum non- dum segregati erant è cœtu promiscuo.

## 5:2
Vers. 2. καὶ ἀνοίξας τὸ στόμα ἀυτοῦ. This phrase פתח פיו to open the mouth, among the Hebrews is to begin to speak, after some silence or interval, Job III. 1, and it is used κατ' ἔμφασιν, when it is a matter of some thing of singular importance, Psalm LXXVIII. verse 2, Matt. XIII. 35, Prov. VIII. 6, and this manner of teaching is noted at the same time

of Christ, because he taught with vehemence, ardor, and intensity, both of spirit and of voice, even on account of the numerous crowd present. Conf. Jud. XI. 35. Job. XXXIII. 2. Ps. XLIX. 4. Eph. VI. 19.

Latin:

Vers. 2. καὶ ἀνοίξας τὸ ςόμα ἀυτᾶ. Phrasis hæc פתח פיו aperire os, apud Ebræos est incipere loqui, post silentium aliquod vel intervallum Job. III. 1. & κατ' ἔμφασιν adhibe- tur, cum agitur de re aliqua singularis momen- ti, Psalm. LXXIIX. vers. 2. Matth. XIII. 35. Prov. IIX. 6. notaturque simul hic modus docendi

Christi, quod cum vehementia, ardore ac conten- tione tum animi tum vocis etiam ob turbam nu- merosam præsentem docuerit. Conf. Jud. XI. 35. Job. XXXIII. 2. Pf. XLIX. 4. Eph. VI. 19.

## 5:3
Vers. 3. μακάριοι] Christ imitates David, or certainly those who collected the ancient Psalms into one body. For what is placed before that book in the place of a prologue contains a description of a blessed man, with a similar beginning of words אַשְׁרֵי־הָאִישׁ. Nor is this without reason, for active disciplines must be started from the treatment of the end: from which depends the knowledge of goods and evils. For the highest good is the end itself, then also other things insofar as they lead to it: evils are those which lead away. Christ therefore shows that the end proposed to man ought to be another, better life: and in this life, the peace of conscience and what follows from it: consequently, other things are to be estimated from this, and so that he may render the listeners more attentive, he explains this very thing through certain paradoxical statements, pronouncing those blessed who are commonly called miserable.

οἱ πτωχοὶ πνεύματι] Since two explanations of these words are accustomed to be brought forward by the ancients, of which one pertains to the scarcity of means, the other to the humility of spirit, I have these reasons why I think the former should be preferred: first, because Luke writes simply μακάριοι οἱ πτωχοὶ Luc. VI. 20. and opposes the rich to them, without the added word of spirit: then, because I would scarcely think πτωχὸς is found in that other meaning. Christ therefore pronounces the poor blessed, in the same sense in which he also pronounces the mourning blessed in the following: because for the most part, the best and second-best things are the fuel of vices. Thus he said elsewhere, that it scarcely happens that a rich man arrives at the heavenly kingdom, XIX. 23. To which agrees that of Paul: Consider your calling, brothers: not many powerful, not many noble, 1. Cor. I. 26. And James II. 5. Did not God choose the poor of this world, rich in faith? For it is sufficient for the truth of a moral statement that it holds good for the most part: nor is precision to be demanded further than the nature of the thing allows, as it is in Aristotle at the beginning of the Nicomachean Ethics. Such also are these sentences of the Greeks:

Of Euripides, 'It is a terrible thing for the rich, and this is innate, to be boorish.'

Of the same: 'Wealth; and wealth is ignorance, and it is clear at the same time.'

And this: 'Wealth is unjust, and it does many things not rightly.'

Likewise: 'Prosperous; but wealth is cowardly and a vice that loves life.'

And this: 'For in wealth there is a certain baseness, but poverty has obtained wisdom because of its misfortune.'

Of Euphorion: 'Wealth is a bad teacher for men toward shamelessness, as are excessive luxuries.'

Of Antiphanes, 'But wealth, like a bad doctor, blind, having taken hold of those who see, makes everyone blind.'

Of Menander: 'The poor always think they are gods.'

Such is that Latin saying: poverty is the sister of a good mind. Diogenes used to say that poverty is a resource for self-taught wisdom, because it teaches by experience what others are scarcely taught by words. The philosopher Teles used to bring forward two reasons why poverty was more apt for wisdom than riches: the first, because it would less avoid labors; the second, because it would be less distracted by the cares of other things: which very thing Christ also signifies below VIII. 12. Lactantius discourses on this matter thus: It happens that the poor and humble believe in God more easily, who are unencumbered, than the rich who are entangled by very many impediments.

τῷ πνεύματι] This, which was passed over by Luke, Matthew expressed, in order to show that this beatitude pertains to those poor who would not have their bad fortune for a display, nor indeed would be fault-finding, but would acquiesce with a calm mind in their own modest circumstances, and would not covet riches. For spirit here signifies the mind, as in Isaiah LXVI. 2, below XXVI, John XI. 33 and XIII. 21, Romans I. 9, 1 Corinthians II. 13, VII. 34, Ephesians IV. 3. Thus to the Hebrews רוּחַ נְמוּכָה is a poor spirit, that is, patient. Therefore, they are poor in spirit who are not only poor in fortune, but also in mind: just as below, the pure in heart are those who are innocent not only in works, but also in mind.

ἀυτῶν ἐστιν ἡ βασιλεία τῶν ὀρανῶν) The same manner of speaking is below XIX. 14. Of such (namely, those who in their character reflect a childlike age) is the kingdom of heaven. The sense is, for to such are wont to happen heavenly riches, the knowledge of the truth, the remission of sins, the gift of the Spirit, and whatever other things come under the name of that kingdom. For there is an opposition in the word poor and in the word kingdom. The writer of Tobit IV. 22: Fear not, my child, that we have become poor; you have much if you fear God. For you should remember that where blessedness or eternal life is promised to one virtue, that is to be taken comparatively, in relation to those who lack such a virtue, and are therefore less fit to receive those benefits, or that it pertains to this, that a great power is understood to be situated in such a virtue, others however not being excluded.

Grotius seems to take these pronouncements as merely moral, and therefore illustrates the same from Gentile writers. But Christ does not act the part of a teacher of morals here when He explains the Beatitude; but He hands down the true reason of evangelical beatitude. He does not explain what kind of people, as regards the gifts of fortune, as they are called, those whom God has chosen or called are, whether rich or poor, but He instructs us who are the participants of true beatitude, and what are the things that accompany them. Therefore, Luke's simple denomination of the poor is to be explained from this addition of Matthew, that the poor in spirit are understood. The first four aphorisms make for the antecedents, as it were, to faith, or to repentance; the later ones make for the consequences of faith.

The first degree of penitents is not undeservedly exhibited in the poor in spirit. For it behooves us to be poor even in spirit, that is, to acknowledge our spiritual poverty: for these things are said as regards the perception and spiritual sense. Unless we feel our spiritual poverty, we will not desire, nor will we value, true riches. Because you say: that I am rich and have become wealthy and have need of nothing, and you do not know that you are wretched, and miserable, and poor, and blind, and naked, I advise you to buy from me gold refined by fire, that you may become rich, Revelation III. 17, 18.

Rightly, therefore, Spanheim says that to be poor in spirit is to be those who are humble in heart, weary, and burdened, who with a humble, contrite, and dejected mind feel humbly about themselves, acknowledge their spiritual poverty, deplore it, and groan daily on account of it, whether they abound in riches or are pressed by want. For they are extremely poor in spirit, since the word poor is derived from to tremble, which is to quake in fear, that which is wont to happen to the extremely poor: thus, therefore, the poor in spirit will be those who find no help or resource of salvation in themselves. Thus Augustine understands by the poor in spirit the humble and those who fear God, that is, those not having an inflated spirit. Similarly, Hilary and Jerome interpret it, as also Leo I in his homily on all the saints, and Gregory the Great, book XXXVI in Job, chapter XX, and from the Greeks, Athanasius, questions to Antioch, question XCI, Theodoret on Romans XII, and Chrysostom and Theophylact. in this place, he in homily XV: What are the poor in spirit? Those who are humble and contrite in mind. To this humility is laid as a foundation, which both those Greek Fathers treat more prolixly; the sum comes to this, that the poor in spirit are those who have a contrite spirit, a heart humbled and broken. Such poverty is certainly understood here, to which the added promise of the kingdom of heaven is appropriate, namely, the kingdom of grace in which true riches are dispensed, Matthew IV. 17, Mark I. 16, 1 Corinthians I. 5, Colossians II. 2, James II. 5, 1 Timothy VI. 18. Which sense the blessed Chemnitz also approves in his Harmony of the Gospels, chapter LI, page 531. Rightly also is the poverty of Spirit understood as spiritual poverty, concerning those who, by the acknowledgment of their sins and the sense of the wrath of God, are humbled, and despair of their own powers, virtues, and works, that is, of their own righteousness: and since they find nothing in themselves which they can oppose to the judgment of God, they are said to bear great and lofty

Spirit. To this effect it is said in Matt. XI. 5. the poor have the gospel preached to them. And Is. XVI. 2. To whom shall I look, but to the poor little one, and contrite of spirit and trembling at my words? Ps. XXXIV. 19. who are troubled in heart and humble in spirit: That poverty of Spirit therefore embraces many things, and extends itself widely, warning even the rich, that they should be poor in spirit, as James says: Let the rich man glory in his humility, Jas. I. 10. Nor is that opinion disapproved by the Blessed Gerhard, by which are understood those who acknowledge their spiritual poverty, because they are destitute of the righteousness by which they stand before God. Salmasius, in Balduinus and Walaeus, also prefers this sense to the interpretation approved by Grotius: It is more approved by me, that πτωχοὶ τῷ πνεύματι should be understood of the humble in spirit, and those who bear a humble spirit. It is certain that these words of Christ are not to be expounded of the poor, or beggars, who are destitute of everything, since it is possible to find many who are richer, and established in affluent circumstances, who are πτωχὸς τῷ πνεύματι, and upon whom that beatitude pronounced by Christ falls. On the contrary, one may see most who are in truth πτωχὸς τῷ ἀργυρίῳ and τῇ ὐσίᾳ, and needy of all things, who nevertheless are not πτωχοὶ τῷ πνεύματι, but puffed up and ὀργίλοι. Which explanation Corn. à Lap. also praised: Blessed are the poor in spirit, that is, blessed are they who do before God what beggars do before the rich, who, namely, with such humility of spirit confess their poverty, and with such affection beg for grace before God, as much as beggars demand a pittance from the rich. And Maldonatus acknowledges that by the poor in spirit the humble are understood by the greater part of the Fathers, bringing forward to that effect Hilary, Chrysostom, the author of the imperfect work, Ambrose, Augustine, Gregory of Nyssa, Epiphanius, Leo, Gregory. Nor indeed is merit to be placed in the poverty of Spirit: but only an order is indicated: that the spiritual sense of poverty precedes the desire for true righteousness: thus in salutary repentance, true contrition of spirit precedes saving faith. Grotius plays the Papist here, while by the poor in spirit he understands those who are not only poor in fortune, but also in mind, and who acquiesce with a placid mind in their own moderate circumstances, and do not covet riches, as if heavenly riches were promised to them, and he compares Tob. IV. 22. He adds, moreover, an observation pleasing and convenient to the Papists. Remember, he says, where beatitude or eternal life is promised to one virtue, that is to be taken comparatively in relation to those who lack such a virtue, and are therefore less fit to receive those benefits, or that it pertains to this, that a great power may be understood to be situated in such a virtue, others however not being excluded. That the Papists draw this to the vow of poverty from Franc. Lucas Brugensis on this passage, as also Corn. à Lap. and Maldon. here, and not least Bellarm. l. de Monach. c. 20, is well known. But neither are all who vow poverty poor in spirit, nor is the kingdom of heaven for all of them: and this spiritual poverty is not of counsel, but of precept.

Latin:

Vers. 3. μακάριοι] Imitatur Christus Davidem, aut certe eos qui Psalmos veteres in unum corpus collegerunt Nam quod ei libro προοιμίου vice præponitur, descriptionem ho- minis beati continet, simili verborum initio אַשְׁרֵי־הָאִישׁ Neque id ratione caret, nam disciplinæ activæ à finis tra- ctatione ordiendæ sunt: unde pendet bonorum malo- rumque notitia. Bonum enim summum finis ipse, dein- de & alia quatenus eo ducunt: mala quæ abducunt. Os- tendit igitur Christus finem homini propositum esse debe- re vitam alteram meliorem: & in hac vita pacem con- scientiæ & quæ eam consequuntur: proinde cætera hinc æstimanda, & quo attentiores reddat auditores explicat hoc ipsum per enuntiata quædam παράδοξα beatos pronun- tians eo, qui vulgo miseri vocentur.

οἱ πτωχοὶ πνεύματι] Cum duæ à veteribus afferri so- leant horum verborum explicationes, quarum altera ad tenuitatem facultatum, altera ad animi demissionem pertineat, cur priorem præferendam existimem, has habeo causas: primum quod Lucas simpliciter scribat μακάριοι οἱ πτωχοὶ Luc. VI. 20. eisque opponat divites, non addita spiritus voce: deinde quod πτωχὸς illo altero significatu vix existimem reperiri. Beatos ergo paupe- res Christus pronunciat, eodem sensu, quo & lugentes cominate sequenti: quia plerumque res optimæ & se- cundæ fomenta sunt vitiorum. Sic alibi dixit, vix eve- nire ut dives in regnum cœleste perveniat, XIX. 23. Cui convenit illud Pauli: Considerate vocationem vestram fratres: non multi potentes, non multi nobiles, 1. Cor. I. 26. Et Ja- cob. II. 5. Nonne elegit Deus pauperes mundi hujus divites in fide? Satis quippe est ad veritatem pronunciati moralis ut valeat ἐπὶ τὸ πολὺ: neque τ᾽ ἀκριβὲς ultra exigendum est quam rei fert natura, ut est apud Aristotelem initio ad Nicomachum. Tales sunt & istæ Græcorum senten- tiæ:

Euripidis, δεινόν γε τοῖς πλυτᾶσι τῦτο δ᾽ ἔμφυτον, σκαιοῖσιν εἶναι.

Ejusdem: πλῦτος; ὁ πλῦτος δ᾽ ἀμαθία, δῆλον δ᾽ ἅμα.

Et hoc: ἄδικον δ᾽ ὁ πλῦτος, πολλὰ δ᾽ ἐχ᾽ ὀρθῶς ποιεῖ.

Item: εὐσορῶς· δειλὸν δ᾽ ὁ πλῦτος κἀν φιλόψυχον κακόν.

Et hoc: ἐν τῷ γὰρ ὄλβῳ φαυλότης ἔνεστί τις, πενία δὲ σοφίαν ἔλαχε διὰ τὸ δυστυχές.

Euphorionis: κακὸν τὸ παίδευμ᾽ ἐστὶν εἰς ἀναιδείαν ὁ πλῦτος ἀνθρώποισιν, αἵτ᾽ ἄγαν τρυφαί.

Antiphanis, ὁ δὲ πλῦτος ἡμᾶς, καθάπερ ἰατρὸς κακὸς, τυφλὸς, βλέποντας παραλαβὼν, πάντας ποιεῖ.

Menandri: ἀεὶ νομίζονθ᾽ οἱ πένητες τῶν θεῶν.

Tale & Latinum illud: bonæ mentis soror paupertas. Dio- genes dicebat paupertatem subsidium esse ad sapientiam αὐτοδίδακτον, quia re doceat, quod alii verbis vix do- centur. Teles Philosophus duas adferebat causas cur aptior ad sapientiam esset paupertas divitiis, priorem quod labores minus subterfugeret: alteram quod alia- rum rerum curis minus distraheretur: quod ipsum Christus quoque significat infra VIII. 12. Lactantius hac de re sic disserit: Eo fit ut pauperes & humiles Deo credant facilius qui sunt expediti, quam divites qui sunt impedimentis plurimis implicati.

τῷ πνεύματι] Hoc quod à Luca prætermissum est, ex- pressit Matthæus, ut ostenderet μακαρισμὸν hunc ad eos pauperes pertinere qui malam fortunam non haberent ostentui, neque vero essent μεμψίμοιροι, sed animo placido in re sua modica acquiescerent, neque divitias appeterent. Πνεῦμα enim animum hic significat, ut Es. LXVI. 2. infra XXVI. Johan. XI. 33. & XIII. 21. Rom. I. 9. 1. Cor. II. 13. VII. 34. Ephes. IV. 3. Sic He- bræis רוּחַ נְמוּכָה spiritus pauper, id est, patiens. Sunt ergo πτωχοὶ πνεύματι hi qui non fortuna tantum, sed & animo sunt pauperes: sicut infra καθαροὶ καρδίᾳ qui non operibus tantum, sed & animo sunt innocen- tes.

ἀυτῶν ἐστιν ἡ βασιλεία τῶν ὀρανῶν) Idem loquendi ge- nus infra XIX. 14. Talium (nimirum qui moribus pueri- lem ætatem referunt) est regnum cælorum. Sensus est, ta- libus enim solent contingere divitiæ cœlestes, cognitio veritatis, remissio peccatorum, donum Spiritus, & quæ alia regni istius nomine veniunt. Est enim oppo- sitio in voce πτωχοὶ & in voce βασιλεία. Scriptor To- biæ IV. 22. μὴ φοβοῦ παιδίον ὅτι ἐπτωχεύσαμεν· ὑπάρχει σοι πολλὰ ἐὰν φοβῇ τὸν Θεὸν. Memineris enim ubi uni vir- tuti beatitudo, aut vita æterna promittitur, id sumendum comparate, ad eos qui tali careant virtute, eoque minus sint ad illa beneficia accipienda idonei, aut id eo perti- nere, ut vis magna in tali virtute sita intelligatur, aliis tamen non exclusis.

Pronunciata hæc pro mere moralibus habere videtur Grotius, ideoque è Scriptoribus gentili- bus eadem illustrat. At Christus hic non moralium Doctorem agit cum Beatitudinem explicat; sed Ev- angelicæ beatitudinis veram rationem tradit. Non quales, quoad fortunæ, ut vocantur, dona, sint, quos Deus elegit, vel vocavit, divites, an pauperes, exponit, sed quinam veræ beatitudinis participes sint, & quæ eorum sint προσκείμβα, nos erudit. Lucæ ergo simplex τῶν πτωχῶν denominatio ex hac Matthæi προσθήκῃ explicanda, quod οἱ πτωχοὶ πνεύματι intelligantur. Priores quatuor apho- rismi ad fidem quasi antecedentia, vel ad pœniten- tiam; posteriores ad consequentia fidei faciunt.

Primus gradus pœnitentium exhibetur non immerito in πτωχοῖς πνεύματι. Nam pauperes vel spiritu nos esse oportet, hoc est agnoscere nostram spiritualem paupertatem: hæc enim dicuntur quo- ad αἴσθησιν & sensum spiritualem. Nisi sentia- mus nostram paupertatem spiritualem, divitias veras non desiderabimus, neque æstimabimus. Quia tu dicis: quod dives sum & locupletatus & nullius egens, & nescis, quod tu es miser, & mi- serabilis, & pauper, & cæcus, & nudus, suadeo tibi emere à me aurum ignitum probatum, ut locu- ples fias Apoc. III. 17. 18.

Recte itaque Spanhe- mius, πτωχὺς πνεύματι esse, qui τάπεινοι τῇ καρδίᾳ κοπιῶντες, καὶ πεφορτισμένοι qui animo humili, contrito, demisso demisse de se sentiunt, paupertatem suam spiritualem agnoscunt, deplorant, ob eam quotidie gemunt sive affluant opibus, sive premantur egestate. Sunt enim πτωχοὶ πνεύ- ματι extreme pauperes spiritu, cum πτωχὸς de- ducatur à πτώσσειν, quod est in metu tre- pidare, id quod solet extreme pauperibus acci- dere: Sic ergo πτωχοὶ πνεύματι erunt, qui nihil auxilii vel subsidii salutis in seipsis inveniunt. Sic Augustinus per pauperes Spiritu intelligit hu- miles & timentes Deum, id est, non habentes spi- ritum inflatum. Similiter & interpretatur Hila- rius & Hieronymus, ut & Leo I. homil. de omnibus sanctis & Gregorius M. l. XXXVI. in Job. c. XX. & è Græcis Athanasius quæst. ad Antioch. q. XCI. Theodorelus in Rom. XII. & Chrysostom. ac Theo- phylact. in h. l. ille hom. XV. Τί ἐξιν οἱ πτωχοὶ τῷ πνεύμαλι, οἱ ταπεινοὶ καὶ συντετριμμένοι τὴν διάνοι- αν. Hὶς τὴν ταπεινόφροσύνην προκαταβάλλε- ται ὥσπερ θεμέλιον quæ prolixius utrique illi Græ- ci Patres exequuntur, summa huc redit, quod pau- peres spiritu sint, qui habent πνεῦμα συντετριμμέ- νον, καρδίαν τεταπεινωμένην, & συντεθραυσμένην. Talis certe hic paupertas intelligitur, cui promissio addita convenit regni cælorum, regni nempe gratiæ in quo veræ divitiæ dispensantur Matth. IV. 17. Marc. I. 16. 1. Cor. I. 5. Col. II. 2. Jac. II. 5. 1. Tim. VI. 18. Quem sensum probat etiam B. Chemnitius in Harm. Evang. c. LI. p. 531. Recte etiam paupertas Spiritus intelligitur spiritualis paupertas, de illis, qui agnitione peccatorum suorum, & sensu iræ Dei humi- liati, de suis viribus, virtutibus & operibus, hoc est, de propria justitia desperant: cumque nihil, quod judicio Dei opponere possint, in se inve- niant, dicuntur gerere magnos & excelsos

Spiritus. In hanc sententiam dicitur Matth. XI. 5. pauperes Evangelizantur. Et Es. XVI. 2. Ad quem respiciam nisi ad pauperculum, & contritum spiri- tu ac trementem sermones meos? Ps. XXXIV. 19. qui tribulati sunt corde & humiles spiritu: Pauper- tas igitur illa Spiritus multa complectitur, ac late se extendit monens etiam divites, ut sint pauperes in spi- ritu, sicut Jacobus inquit: Glorietur dives in humili- tate sua, Jac. I. 10. Nec improbatur ea sententia B. Gerhardo, qua intelliguntur, qui spiritualem suam paupertatem agnoscunt, quod destituti sint justitia, qua coram Deo consistunt. Præfert etiam hunc sensum interpretationi à Grotio probatæ Salmasius apud Balduinum, Walæum: Magis mihi probatur, ut πτωχοὶ τῷ πνεύματι intelligantur de humilibus spiritu, & qui humilem spiritum gerunt. Non de pau- peribus hunc locum, aut mendicis, qui omni re destitu- untur, illa Christi verba exponenda esse, certum est, cum multos ditiores, & in forte lautos constitutos re- periri sit, πτωχὸς τῷ πνεύματι, & in quos competat ille μακαρισμὸς à Christo proditus. E contrario ple- rosque licet videre revera πτωχὸς τῷ ἀργυρίῳ ac τῇ ὐσίᾳ, & omnium egenos, qui tamen non sint πτωχοὶ τῷ πνεύματι, sed magna flantes, & ὀργίλοι. Qualem ex- plicationem laudavit quoq; Corn. à Lap. Beati pau- peres spiritu, id est, beati qui faciunt apud Deum, quod faciunt mendici apud divites, qui sc. tanta humilitate spiritus confitentur suam paupertatem, tantoque affe- ctu mendicant gratiam apud Deum, quanto stipitem à divitibus flagitant mendici. Et agnoscit Maldona- tus, à majori parte Patrum per pauperes spiritu humi- les intelligi, adducens in eam sententiam Hilarium, Chrysostomum, autorem operis imperfecti, Ambro- sium, Augustinum, Gregorium Nyssenum, Epiphanium, Leonem, Gregorium. Neque vero meritum collo- candum in Spiritus paupertate: sed ordo tantum indicatur: quod antecedat sensus spiritualis pauper- tatis desiderium justitiæ veræ: ita in pœnitentia salutifera fidem salvificam antecedit vera spiritus contritio. Grotius papizat hic, dum per paupe- res spiritu intelligit, qui non fortuna tantum, sed & animo sunt pauperes, & animo placido in re sua modi- ca acquiescunt, neque divitias appetunt, quasi illis di- vitiæ cælestes promissæ sint, & confert Tob. IV. 22. Addit enim observationem Papistis gratam & commodam. Memineris, inquit, ubi uni virtuti be- atitudo, aut vita æterna promittitur, id sumendum comparate ad eos, qui tali carent virtute, eoque mi- nus sunt ad illa beneficia accipienda idonei, aut ideo pertinere, ut vis magna in tali virtute sita intelliga- tur, aliis tamen non exclusis. Ad votum pauperta- tis hæc Papistas trahere è Franc. Luca Brugensi in h. l. ut & Corn. à Lap. & Maldon. hic, nec non Bellarm. l. de Monach. c. 20. notum est. Sed nec o- mnes qui paupertatem vovent pauperes sunt spi- ritu, nec eorum omnium regnum cælorum est: & paupertas hæc spiritualis non est consilii, sed præcepti.

## 5:4
Vers. 4. ὁι πενθοῦντες) A sentiment similar to the previous one, which Paul explains as θλίψις, saying it works patience, and what follows in Rom. V. Doubtless patience rejoices in hardship: on the contrary, however, prosperous things are a hindrance to vices. Nor is it said in vain, you will be pious having lived through hardship, and in Pliny, that we are best when we are weak. But properly here those who mourn are understood with their quality: that is, those who patiently bear evils inflicted by men or by God.

παρακληθήσονται) Here in part, fully hereafter. See Paul I. Cor. I. 4. John XVI. 20. James I. 12. Rev. VII. 17.

This promise does not sound of the suffering or tolerance of the calamity or cross of evils, but of mourning for the evils of guilt: For it follows the sense of spiritual lack due to the defect of spiritual goods, in true contrition of the mourning of an afflicted heart, due to the sense of sins, since we do not labor only under the deprivation of spiritual goods and spiritual poverty, but we are also burdened with sins, as a most heavy load, for which we must grieve and mourn, by the example of David Ps. VI. and XXXIIX. And this is the second degree of repentance, our lamentation for evils committed, just as the former was the sorrow for goods lost. There is a good mourning, such as that for sin committed either by us or by others, there is a bad one, such as that of the impious for intercepted pleasures, there is a middle one, which of itself is neither good nor bad, such as that of those who suffer the loss of their property, which is bad when it is immoderate, there is the sorrow of the world and the sorrow according to God, the Apostle distinguishing in II. Cor. VII. 10. the one is of the miserable and unhappy, the other of the blessed, of this, and not of that, sounds the sentiment of Christ, by which they are pronounced blessed who mourn for sins committed by themselves, the sorrow according to God. Whence that word in spirit can here be repeated from the common. Such are the mourners whom Isaiah designates as to be raised up by the preaching of the Gospel, c. XXI. 2. to whom therefore consolation is promised here, for the sorrow according to God works repentance unto salvation 2. Cor. VII. 10. What that consolation is, we learn from Is. XL. 1. 2. Luke I. 47. Acts X. 47. Mourning penitents for sin committed: they rejoice for the comfort promised divinely: they mourn for the temptation of Satan: they rejoice for the divine liberation from evil John XVI. 32. II. Tim. IV. 18. Rom. V. 2. Furthermore, the Vulgate badly changed the order here, placing the meek in the second place, but the mourners in the third. The Greek Codices agree to one, all of them, and with them agree the Syriac, Arabic, Ethiopic, Titus, Chrysostom, the Author of the imperfect work, Euthymius, Theophylactus.

Latin:

Vers. 4. ὁι πενθοῦντες) γνώμη similis superiori, quam Pau- lus explicat θλίψις inquiens ὑπομονὴν κατεργάζεται & quæ sequuntur Rom. V. Nimirum gaudet patientia duru: contra autem res secundæ vitiis sunt obrentui. : Neque frustra di- ctum ὑπὲρ μαλέαν πελεύσας ἐυσεβὴς ἔση & Plinio Optimos es- se nos dum infirmi sumus. Sed proprie hic lugentes intelli- guntur cum sua qualitate: id est, qui mala ab hominibus aut à Deo inflicta patienter ferunt.

παρακληθήσονται) Hic pro parte, plene in posterum Vi- de Paulum I. Cor. I. 4. Joh. XVI. 20. Jacob. I. 12. Apoc. VII. 17.

Non de malorum calamitatis aut crucis perpes- sione aut tolerantia, sed de luctu ob mala culpæ, hæc promissio sonat: Nam sequitur sensum spi- ritualis carentiæ ob defectum bonorum spiritua- lium, in vera contritione luctus cordis afflicti, ob sensum peccatorum, siquidem non laboramus solum στερήσει bonorum spiritualium ac paupertate spiri- tuali, sed etiam peccatis onerati sumus, ceu sar- cina gravissima, ob quæ dolendum nobis lugen- dumq; est, exemplo Davidis Ps. VI. & XXXIIX. Atque hic est alter gradus pœnitentiæ planctus no- ster ob mala commissa, ficuti prior erat dolor ob bona amissa. Datur luctus bonus, qualis est ob peccatum sive à nobis sive ab aliis commissum, da- tur malus, qualis est impiorum ob interceptas vo- luptates, datur medius, qui ex se nec bonus nec malus est, qualis eorum est, qui rerum suarum jactu- ram faciunt, qui malus sit, cum immoderatus est, datur λύπη τῶ̄ κόσμι & λύπη κτ̄ὰ θεὸν distinguente Apostolo II. Cor. VII. 10. altera miserorum & in- felicium, altera beatorum est, de hac, non vero de illa Christi γνώμη sonat, qua beati pronunciantur, qui lugent peccata, à se commissa, λύπη κτ̄ θεὸν. Unde vox illa τῷ πνεύματι hic ἀπὸ κοινῦ repeti po- test. Tales sunt lugentes quos Esaias designat Ev- angelii concione erigendos, c. XXI. 2. quibus pro- inde hic promittitur παράκλησις consolatio, ἡ γὰρ κτ̄ θεὸν λύπη μετάνοιαν εἰς σωτηρίαν κατεργάζεται 2. Cor. VII. 10. Quæ illa consolatio sit, discimus Es. XL. 1. 2. Luc. I. 47. Act. X. 47. Lugentes pœnitentes ob peccatum commissum: gaudent ob solatium divi- nitus promissum: lugent ob Satanæ tentationem: gaudent ob divinam à malo liberationem Joh. XVI. 32. II. Tim. IV. 18. Rom. V 2. Cæterum male Vulgata ordinem hic immutavit, secundo loco mites, tertio autem lugentes collocans. Consonant Codices Græci ad unum omnes, & cum illis faciunt Syrus, Arabs, Æthiops, Titus, Chrysostomus, Autor imperfe- cti operis, Euthymius, Theophylactus.

## 5:5
Vers. 5. Πραεῖς) Those who bear with others calmly and instruct them gently. The πραεῖς or πραοῖ are properly opposed to the irascible, Arist. Magna Moralia, book I, 23. Plato, II De Republica: 'for gentle natures are, I suppose, the opposite of the spirited.' κληρονομήσουσι τὴν γῆν) From Ps. XXXVII. 11. The Hellenists use this word to express the Hebrew ירש, but that does not mean to acquire by title of inheritance: but to obtain or possess by right of ownership, because such things as these pass to heirs. And this is what is properly called κτᾶσθαι by the Greeks. For κτῆσις is usually opposed to χρῆσις, as mancipium is to use in Latin. But by 'the earth' he seems to mean firm and constant friendships, which is by far the best possession on earth. Those who are of a mild and calm spirit are most easily able to acquire these for themselves: although this virtue also avails much for protecting other lesser things. For θυμός, as it is in the Philosopher, is the cause of murders, an ally of misfortune, a partner of injury and dishonor, the loss of wealth, and furthermore the leader of madness. Add Ps. XLI. 1.

These things were not to be explained from the Philosopher, but from the style of Holy Scripture; for moral teachings are not being delivered, but supernatural ones; nor legal promises, but Evangelical ones. And what is this gloss to understand 'firm and constant friendships' by 'the earth'? Where in Holy Scripture does this word ever occur with that meaning? This must be understood of the new earth, which righteousness inhabits, 2 Pet. III. 17, and of the true κληρονομία prepared for us from the foundation of the world, Matt. XXV. Which things are promised to those who are truly πραεῖς.

πνέυματι & humble in spirit. Which is the third degree of true repentance, most rightly following the preceding ones. For such humility or humiliation cannot but follow the sense of spiritual poverty and the mourning conceived on account of sins. Christ has included meekness and moderation of anger in the fifth and seventh aphorisms: but in this aphorism, the discourse is about such πραότης as is prior to the desire for righteousness, which pertains to contrition, and still precedes faith, the other part of repentance. For thus the LXX use the word πραεῖς, from whose interpretation of Ps. XXXVII. 11 this sentiment is: not to denote the gentle and mild, but the humble and afflicted, see Ps. XXXIV. 3, Ps. LXXVII. 10. Ps. CXLVII. 6. Ps. CXLIX. 4. Zeph. II. 2. Thus the Psalmist declares himself, whom he understands by πραεῖς Ps. XXV. 8. 9. namely those who are afflicted in spirit and humbled on account of sin, as those who feel themselves cast away and rejected by sin from the face of God, and exiled from the land of the living, as the Hebrew word for exile implies. Which word is used of Moses, the most afflicted of all, Num. XII. 3. Which David also used Ps. XIIX. 36. And thy discipline itself shall teach me in the Hebrew: And while thou AFFLICTEST me, thou makest me great, and Solomon Prov. XV. 33. Before glory is HUMILITY. Thus also the afflicted are called πραεῖς Ps. X. 18. Thou hast heard the desire of the AFFLICTED O Lord and XLV. 5. Walk through the justice of the AFFLICTED. And Christ himself is called πραὸς Zach. IX. 9. Matt. XXI. 5. because for our sake he was humbled and afflicted Is. LIII. 5. Gal. III. 13. Whence the Syrian rendered πραεῖς as מכיכא humble, contrite, humbled, from מכך to be depressed, worn down, humbled. Therefore when we are afflicted in spirit, on account of our spiritual misery and the burden of sins, when we labor and are heavy laden, when we are humbled in the anguish of our heart, we are pronounced blessed, because he who is thus humbled with the publican, he is certainly exalted by God Luke XIIX. To such therefore is promised the possession of the earth, by which you may generally understand a blessing, but primarily the possession of the future heavenly inheritance, just as the blessing made to the Israelites included the inheritance of the promised land. This is the blessing in Christ, who for our sake willed to be afflicted and humbled, that we in him, and through faith in him, might be exalted. Whence Origen hom. XXVI. in Num. Basil. in Ps. XXXIII. Cyril in Is. LIIX. Nyssen on the beatitudes. Jerome in h. l. Damasc. l. II. de Orth. fid. c. 10. understand it of the new earth in the future life Is. LXVI. 22. 2. Pet. III. 13. Apoc. XXI. 2. Therefore they are pronounced blessed, who receive through faith the afflicted (Messiah, who was truly the most afflicted of all Is. LIII.) Ps. XLI. 1. for that prophetic Psalm treats of this, as is clear from the comparison of v. 10 with Job XIII. 18. Conf. Dn. D. Joh. Tarnovius in Ps. Prophet. who are so πραεῖς humble and afflicted, that they receive by faith Christ, who for our sake was made πραὸς, they are gloriously exalted by the Lord. Ps. CXLIX. 4.

Latin:

Vers. 5. Πραεῖς) Qui alios placide ferunt & blande insti- tuunt. Opponuntur πραεῖς sive πραοῖ proprie τοῖς ὀργίλοις Arist. magn. moralium l br. I. 23. Plato II. de republica: ἐνάντια γάρ που θυμοειδεῖ πραεία φύσεις. κληρονομήσουσι τὴν γῆν) Ex Ps. XXXVII. 11. Usurpant hoc verbum Hellenistæ, ut Hebræum ירש exprimant, id autem non significat titulo hæreditatis acquirere: sed jure mancipii adipisci aut possidere, quia talia quæ sunt, ad hære- des transeunt. Et hoc est quod proprie Græcis dicitur κτᾶσθαι. Opponi enim solet κτῆσις τῇ χρήσει ut Latinis man- cipium usui. Τὴν γῆν autem dicere videtur firmas atque constantes amicitias, quæ in terris longe optima est pos- sessio. Has autem comparare sibi facillime solent qui miti placidoque sunt animo: quanquam & ad alias res minores tuendas multum valet hæc virtus. Quippe ὁ θυ- μὸς ut est apud Philosophum φόνων αἴτιον συμφορᾶς σύμμα- χον, ἀλάβης σύνεργον κὰ ἀτιμίας, χρημάτων ἀπώλεια, ἔτι δὲ καὶ φορᾶς ἀρχηγόν. Adde Ps. XLI. 1.

Hæc non ex Philosopho, sed S. S. stylo expli- canda erant; Non enim moralia traduntur, sed su- pernaturalia; nec promissiones legales sed Evangeli- cæ. Et quæ hæc glossa per τὴν γῆν firmas & constantes amicitias intelligere? ubi uspiam in S. literis hæc vox isto significatu occurrit? De terra nova, quam justitia incolit 2. Pet. III. 17. de vera κληρονομίᾳ nobis in conditu mundi parata hæc accipienda Matth. XXVII. Quæ promissa illis, qui vere πραεῖς sunt

πνέυματι & humiles spiritu. Qui tertius gradus est veræ pœnitentiæ, rectissime excipiens præceden- tes. Nam spiritualis paupertatis sensum, & luctum ob peccata conceptum non potest non sequi ejusmodi humilitas seu humiliatio. Mansuetudinem & mode- rationem iræ quinto & septimo aphorismo com- plex9 est Christus: hoc vero aphorismo de tali πρα- ότητι quæ prævia est desiderio justitiæ, sermo est, quæ ad contritionem pertinet, & adhuc fidem antecedit, alteram pœnitentiæ partem. Sic enim LXX. voce πραεῖς utuntur, è quorum interpretatione Psal. XXXVII. 11. hæc sententia est: non ut mansuetos & mites notet, sed humiles atq; afflictos vid. Ps. XXXIV. 3. Ps. LXXVII. 10. Pf. CXLVII. 6. Pf. CXLIX. 4. Zeph. II. 2. Ita de- clarat sefe Hieropsaltes, quosnam πραεῖς intelligat Pf. XXV. 8. 9. qui nempe ob peccatum afflicti spiritu atque humiliati sunt, utpote qui sentiunt sese per peccatum abjectos & reprobatos esse à facie Dei, exulare à terra viventium, uti Ebræa vox exilium importat. Quod vocabulum de Mose omnium afflictissimo usurpatur Num. XII. 3. Quo etiam u- sus est David Pf. XIIX. 36. Et disciplina tua ipsa do- cebit me in Ebræo: Et dum AFFLIGIS me, magnum me facis, & Salomo Prov. XV. 33. Gloriam præcedit HUMILITAS. Sic etiam afflicti dicuntur πραεῖς Pf. X. 18. Desiderium AFFLICTORUM exaudisti Domine & XLV. 5. Incede per AFFLICTORUM justitiam. Et Christus ipse πραὸς dicitur Zach. IX. 9. Matth. XXI. 5. quod nostri causa humiliatus & afflictus sit Es. LIII. 5. Gal. III. 13. Unde Syrus πραεῖς reddidit מכיכא humiles, contritos, humi- liates, à מכך deprimi, atteri, humiliari. Quapro- pter cum affligimur spiritu, ob spiritualem no- stram miseriam & peccatorum sarcinam, cum la- boramus & onerati sumus, cum humiliamur in an- gustia cordis nostri, beati prædicamur, quia qui ita humiliatur cum publicano, ille certo exaltatur à Deo Luc. XIIX. Talibus ergo promittitur terræ possessio, per quam generatim benedictionem intel- ligere possis, imprimis autem hæreditatis futuræ cæ- lestis possessionem, quemadmodum benedictio Israe- litis facta terræ promissæ hæreditatem includebat. Hæc est benedictio in Christo, qui nostri causa affli- gi voluit, atq; humiliari, ut nos in ipso, & per fidem in ipsum exaltemur. Unde Origenes hom. XXVI. in Num. Basil. in Pf. XXXIII. Cyrillus in Es. LIIX. Nyf- senus de beatitud. Hieron. in h. l. Damasc. l. II. de Orth. fid. c. 10. intelligunt de terra nova in futura vita Es. LXVI. 22. 2. Pet. III. 13. Apoc. XXI. 2. Ideo beati prædicantur, qui afflictum (Messiam qui vere afflictissimus omnium fuit Es. LIII.) per fidem sus- cipiunt Pf. XLI. 1. de hoc enim agit Psalmus ille propheticus, ut è collatione v. 10. cum Job. XIII. 18. liquet. Conf. Dn. D. Joh. Tarnovius in Pf. Prophet. qui ita πραεῖς humiles ac afflicti sunt, ut Christum, qui nostri causa πραὸς factus est, fide suscipiant, illi gloriose à Domino exaltantur. Pf. CXLIX. 4.

## 5:6
Vers. 6. οἱ πεινῶντες κj διψῶντες τὴν δικαιοσύνην.] Hunger and thirst by a common metaphor signify a certain vehement appetite, as when it is said the sacred hunger for gold, and among Plutarch ὁ μὴ πεινῶν μηδὲ διψῶν τιμωρίας. And thus δίψος is taken in Is. XLI. 17. & LLI. Job VII. 37. and in some other places of these books. But the word δικαιοσύνης here signifies ὁδὸν δικαιοσύνης as this writer speaks below XXI. 32. that is, the doctrine of that obedience which God demands of us, which obedience is also noted below in verse 20 by the same word δικαιοσύνης. Philo also said λιμὸν ἀρετῆς in his book on Allegories. Furthermore, if anyone compares Luke with Matthew, he will see such a desire indicated here by which men, driven, willingly undergo other inconveniences, for instance hunger and thirst.

Hunger and thirst are rightly understood of a vehement appetite: but justice is not rightly explained as the way of justice or the obedience of it, which God demands of us. Since justice itself can be understood properly, nor is there need for a metonymy. But because justice is either imputed or inherent, some understand the one, others the other, others both. But imputed justice is most conveniently understood. For the hunger and thirst for this is excited primarily in those who are poor in spirit, mourning, and afflicted. Since that indigence, and the sense of the same, sharpen in us the appetite and desire for refreshment, the desire for true and perfect justice, which is nothing but the justice of Christ, nor can we be satisfied and refreshed except by the justice of Christ. It is a question of the thirst for such justice, by which the faithful are satisfied. But the justice which is inherent in us is by no means able to satisfy us. And the metaphor of food and drink leads us to the justice of Christ, and to the food and drink which Christ offers us for eternal life John VI. As in bodily hunger and thirst, so also in spiritual, the search for food and drink is outside the man who is hungering and thirsting, so that food and drink may be taken from elsewhere: which cannot be supplied to us for satisfaction from anywhere else than from Christ, who was made justice for us by God I Cor. I. 3. in whom alone we have both life and abundance John X. 10. And who would believe that in so many aphorisms about beatitude, no mention has been made of that justice, in which alone all our beatitude is situated? Nor is there any doubt that the invitation of Christ Is. LV. 13. and the prophecy c. LXV. 13. are being looked to. Which contain truly Evangelical promises. What of the fact that Christ designates a more abundant justice, by which it behooves us to enter the kingdom of heaven, which is none other than the imputed justice of Christ, by which alone all are justified, as many as are justified Rom. V. 19. in which the Kingdom of God consists Rom. XIV. 17. Which we enjoy through faith, nor can anyone enjoy it without faith, which is likewise described by Christ himself through eating and drinking, so that we neither hunger nor thirst ever, but are fully satisfied, Ps. XVII. 15. John IV. 14. c. VI. 35. Those who thus enjoy the justice of Christ through faith can boast: in the Lord we have justice Is. XLV. 24. And this is the justice, by which it is declared without the law (or works of the law) through the law and the Prophets, which through faith in Christ comes εἰς πάντας, καὶ ἐπὶ πάντας to all and upon all who believe Rom. III. 22. the justice, through which the justification of life is obtained for all who attain life. Rom. V. 18. Therefore they are pronounced blessed, who hunger and thirst for this justice: because the beatitude is of that one, as the Apostle teaches, to whom God imputes justice χωρὶς ἔργων Rom. IV. 6. where it is manifest that imputed justice alone is established as the cause of beatitude, with the exclusion of inherent justice, which pertains to works.

χορτασθήσονται) from Ps. 17:15. Indeed, all of God's benefits are accustomed to be described under the image of food and drink. Is. 65:13. Luke 1:53. But especially heavenly doctrine. For both the Hebrews call the law the food of the soul, and Christ calls his Gospel now by the name of bread, now by the name of water.

Not without serious cause does the Lord use the word χορτασθήσονται, they shall be satisfied, not they shall satisfy themselves: for this benefit is extrinsic from God, not from man, who alone fills the hungry with good things, Luke 1:53. By that very fact is also indicated not just any refreshment, but satiety, and a full satisfaction that will eventually follow: hence it is not said δοθήσεται αὐτοῖς φαγεῖν, they shall be given to eat, or ποτισθήσονται, they shall be given to drink, but χορτασθήσονται, with all hunger and all thirst excluded. That is also the opposite of all other carnal and worldly desires, to which a full satisfaction will never be obtained. See Walaeus.

Latin:

Vers. 6. οἱ πεινῶντες κj διψῶντες τὴν δικαιοσύνην.] Fames & sitis translatione usitata vehementem quandam appetitio- nem significant, ut cum dicitur auri sacra fames, & apud Plu- tarchum ὁ μὴ πεινῶν μηδὲ διψῶν τιμωρίας. Atque ita δίψος su- mitur Es. XLI. 17. & LLI. Iob. VII. 37. & aliis aliquot horum librorum locis. Δικαιοσύνης autem vox hic significat ὁδὸν δικαιοσύνης ut infra hic scriptor loquitur XXI. 32. id est do- ctrinam ejus obedientiæ quam à nobis Deus exigit, quæ obedientia & infra commate 20. voce eadem δικαιοσύνης notatur. Etiam Philo dixit λιμὸν ἀρετῆς libro de Allego- riis Cæterum si quis Lucam cum Matthæo conferat, vide- bit tale desiderium hic indicari quo acti homines alia in- commoda, puta famem sitimque, libenter subeant.

Recte fames & sitis de vehementi appetitione in- telligitur: sed justitia non recte explicatur de via justitiæ aut obedientia ejus, quam Deus à nobis exigit. Siquidem intelligi possit proprie ipsa justitia, nec opus sit metonymia. Quia vero justitia est vel imputata, vel inhærens, nonnulli illam, alii istam, alii utramque intelligunt. At commodissime intelligi- tur imputata justitia. Nam hujus esuries & sitis ex- citatur imprimis in illis, qui pauperes spiritu, lugen- tes, & afflicti sunt. Siquidem indigentia illa, & sen- sus ejusdem appetitum & desiderium refectionis, desiderium justitiæ veræ & perfectæ, quæ non est nisi Christi justitia, in nobis acuant, nec nisi justitia Christi saturari possimus ac refici. De talis justi- tiæ siti agitur, qua saturantur fideles. At justitia, quæ nobis inhæret, nos saturare minime valet. Et deducit nos Metaphora alimenti & potus ad justi- tiam Christi, & ad cibum, ac potum, quem Chri- stus nobis præbet ad vitam æternam Joh.VI. Uti in fame & siti corporali, sic & in spirituali inquisitio alimenti & potus extra hominem est esurientem & sitientem, ut aliunde assumatur cibus & potus: quæ nobis ad saturationem non possunt aliunde suppetere, quam à Christo, qui factus nobis à Deo est justitia I.Cor.I.3. in quo solo & ζωὴν habemus & περίσσειον Joh.X.10. Et quis credat in tam multis a- phorismis de beatitudine, nullam factam esse men- tionem illius justitiæ, in qua una omnis beatitudo nostra sita est? Neque dubium est, respici invita- tionem Christi Ef. LV. 13. & vaticinium c. LXV. 13. Quæ promissiones vere Evangelicas continent. Quid, quod justitiam abundantiorem Christus desi- gnet, qua ingredi nos oportet regnum cælorum, quæ nulla alia est, quam imputata Christi justitia, qua una justificantur, quotquot justificantur Rom. V.19. in qua Regnum Dei consistit Rom. XIV.17. Qua fruimur nos per fidem, nec quisquam sine fide frui potest, quæ ab ipso Christo per manducationem & bibitionem itidem describitur, ita ut nec esuriamus nec sitiamus unquam, sed plene saturemur, Psal. XVII.15. Joh. IV.14. c. VI.35. Qui ita per fidem fru- untur justitia Christi, gloriari possunt: in Domino justitiam habemus Ef. XLV. 24. Atque hæc est justi- tia, qua declarata est fine lege (vel operibus legis) per legem, & Prophetas, quæ per fidem in Christum εἰς πάντας, καὶ ἐπὶ πάντας in omnes & super omnes cre- dentes venit Rom. III. 22. justitia, per quam obtingit justificatio vitæ omnibus, qui vitam consequuntur. Rom. V.18. Ideo beati prædicantur, qui esuriunt & sitiunt hanc justitiam: quia beatitudo est illius, do- cente Apostolo, cui Deus justitiam imputat χωρὶς ἔργων Rom. IV. 6. ubi manifestum est, imputatam justitiam solum constitui beatitudinis causam, ex- clusa justitia inhærente, quæ ad ἔργα pertinet.

χορτασθήσονται) ex Ps. XVII.15. Omnia quidem Dei be- neficia sub imagine cibi ac potus describi solent. Ef. LXV. 13. Luc. II. 53. præcipue vero doctrina cœlestis. Nam & Hebræi legem cibum animæ vocant, & Christus Evangelium suum modo panis, modo aquæ nomine appellat.

Non sine gravi causa utitur Dominus verbo χορ- τασθήσονται saturabantur, non saturabant se: bene- ficium enim istud extrinsecum à Deo, non ab homine, qui solus implet bonis famelicos, Luc. II. 53. Eo ipso etiam indicata non refectio quævis, sed fatietas, & ple- na saturatio aliquando secutura: inde non dictum δοθήσεται αὐτοῖς φαγεῖν, ποτισθήσονται, sed χορ- τασθήσονται, exclusa fame omni, & potu omni. Op- positum id etiam desideriis omnibus aliis carnalibus & mundanis, quibus nunquam obtinget plena saturatio. Vid. Walæus.

## 5:7
Vers. 7. Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy] There is indeed in human usage that true saying of Publius: Mercy procures good defenses.

Likewise: He who lends aid in favorable times has help in adverse ones.

Furthermore, I think here that the Latin interpreter and other ancient writers rightly refer that ἐλεηθήσονται to divine mercy. For just as all these beatitudes, if you observe correctly, are explained in the tradition of the precepts, so what is said here sententiously is handed down exhortatorily below, ch. 5:44 and 6:14. The Stoics taught that it is the part of a wise man to succor, but not to pity: and they called mercy a vice of the mind. But Christ commands not only the works of mercy, but also commends the affection by his own example. For it is often read σπλαγχνισθῆναι, by which an affection, and indeed a vehement one, is denoted. Thus Paul wants the members to suffer together, 1 Cor. 12:26. Doubtless, as Lactantius rightly warns, Christian discipline neither extirpates the affections, nor commands mediocrity indiscriminately, but shows their right use, now more intense, now more relaxed according to the dignity of the matter. On which subject we shall treat more fully at Luke 19:41.

The promise is rightly understood concerning divine mercy: but whether all these beatitudes are found exhortatorily in this sermon is doubtful. Nor does it appear that this was Christ's purpose. He rather instituted to deliver the beatitudes here first; then also to vindicate the precepts of the law from the corruptions of the Pharisees. Moreover, this fifth aphorism embraces the fruit of justifying faith, along with the rest that follow. For after it had been treated of those things which precede faith, and the act of faith desiring the righteousness of Christ, then apprehending the same and feeding upon it, and satisfying miserable and famished hearts, described, now the fruits following faith: which is working through love are designated, from which mercy stands out. For when through faith we are made partakers of the mercy of God, we are kindled to mercy toward our neighbor Eph. V. 32. Col. III. 13. Mat. XVIII. 35. which consists in giving and forgiving, as Christ teaches Matth. VI. 12. just as God not only forgives us our sins, but also gives us the righteousness of Christ out of mere mercy. Since we are satisfied with the mercy of God, why should we not also show a certain mercy to our neighbor? But Christ declares the merciful blessed, not as if mercy or the remaining virtues contribute anything to blessedness, but because they are properties of the blessed and signs and proofs of true faith and blessedness Matth. XXV. 35. Whence divine mercy is again promised to them, just as on the contrary a grave judgment hangs over the unmerciful Jas. II. 13. Forgive, and it will be forgiven you, give and it will be given to you, says Christ Luke VI. 38. Be God to the wretched, advises Nazianzen, oration on the care of the poor, so that in turn God may be God to you in your calamity.

Latin:

Vers. 7. οἱ ἐλεήμονες ὅτι ἀυτοὶ ἐλεηθήσονται] Est quidem & in usu humano verum illud Publii: Bona comparat præsidia misericordia.

Item: Habet in adversis auxilia qui in secundis commodat.

Cæterum hic arbitror recte à Latino interprete aliisque scriptoribus antiquis illud ἐλεηθήσονται ad divinam miseri- cordiam referri. Nam sicut omnes hi μακαρισμοὶ, si recte ad- vertas, in præceptorum traditione explicantur, ita quod hic dicitur γνωμικῶς, infra traditur παραινετικῶς, c. V. 44. & VI. 14. Stoici docebant succurrere esse sapientis, misereri non esse: & misericordiam vitium vocabant animi. At Christus non opera tantum misericordiæ præcipit, sed & affectum suo exemplo commendat. Sæpe enim legitur σπλαγχνισθῆ- ναι, quo affectus & quidem vehemens denotatur. Sic Pau- lus vult τὰ μέλη συμπάσχειν I. Cor. XII. 26. Nimirum ut re- cte monet Lactantius, Christiana disciplina neque exfcin- dit affectus, neque mediocritatem indistincte præcipit, sed rectum eorum usum monstrat, modo intensiorem, modo remissiorem pro rei dignitate. Qua de re plenius agemus ad Lucam XIX. 41.

Recte de misericordia divina promissio accipi- tur: utrum vero omnes hi μακαρισμοὶ παραινετικῶς in hac concione reperiantur, dubium est. Neque id ap- paret Christo propositum fuisse. Instituit potius hic μακαρισμοὺς primum tradere; tum etiam præ- cepta legis à corruptelis Pharisæorum vindicare. Cæterum quintus hic aphorismus fructum fidei justi- ficantis, cum cæteris sequentibus complectitur. Postquam enim actum erat de iis, quæ antecedunt fi- dem, & actus fidei desiderantis justitiam Christi, tum eandem apprehendentis eademque pascentis, & exaturantis corda misera & famelica, descriptus, nunc fructus fidem consequentes: quæ per charita- tem est ἐνεργουμένη designantur, è quibus eminet mi- sericordia. Nam ubi per fidem participes reddimur misericordiæ Dei, ad misericordiam erga proxi- mum accendimur Eph.V.32. Col. III.13. Mat. XIIX. 35. quæ in donando, & condonando sita est docente Christo Matth. VI. 12. quemadmodum Deus nobis non tantum peccata condonat, sed etiam justitiam Christi donat ex mera misericordia. Quum satu- remur Dei misericordia, quidni etiam misericor- diam quandam proximo exhiberemus? Beatos au- tem prædicat misericordes Christus, non quasi mi- sericordia, aut reliquæ virtutes quicquam ad bea- titudinem conferant sed quod proprietates beato- rum ac signa, & τεκμήρια sint veræ fidei, ac beatitu- dinis Matth. XXV. 35. Unde illis iterum promitti- tur divina misericordia, quemadmodum ex adver- so immisericordibus grave judicium impendet Jac. II. 13. Remittite, & remittetur vobis, date & da- bitur vobis, inquit Christus Luc. VI. 38. Esto calami- toso Deus, monet Nazianz. orat. de cur. pauper. ut vicissim Deus in tua calamitate tibi sit Deus.

## 5:8
Ver. 8. the pure in heart) can be understood as upright, that is, those who are absent from all deceit and fallacies, whom the Latins call sincere. For the pure is wont to be joined with the unfeigned I Tim. I. 5. I Pet. I. 22. And thus the explanation of this maxim will have to be sought from those things which are discussed below in chapter VI. But it pleases me more that pure here be taken as one who is whole in life and pure from wickedness, whom Latin writers also call holy and chaste. The Greeks call those pure in hands who are not involved in homicide, and a woman is said to be pure who abstains from intercourse. Therefore Christ adds in heart, from Ps. LXXIII. 1, indeed also demanding the innocence of the mind, for by that censor [to use the words of Tacitus] those who deliberate have fallen away. But that I should interpret pure thus, what follows moves me: that they themselves shall see God. For also in John I Epist. III. 2, we read likewise: we shall see him as he is: then it is subjoined: and everyone who has this hope in him purifies himself, just as he is pure. For pure and clean are wont to be used for the same thing. Christ indeed sought attributes which would suit the subjects either from similarity or dissimilarity. Therefore to those who are of a pure heart (insofar as human frailty permits) he proposes the reward, that they shall see God, that is, the most pure mind. Wherefore the explanation of this maxim must be sought from those things which follow below, in the precepts, in verse 21, 27, and following of this chapter.

Unfeigned simplicity or unhypocritical can be joined with innocence of mind: for there is no true innocence of mind where hypocrisy underlies it, but as it ought to proceed from true faith I Tim. I. 5, so there is no purification of the heart without faith. For through faith our hearts are purified Acts XV. 9. And therefore also the pure in heart are declared blessed, because holiness, innocence, and sincerity of mind arise from faith, which is the cause of blessedness: since indeed our consciences are purified by the blood of Christ through faith, from dead works, to serve God Heb. IX. 14. This internal holiness of the heart, therefore, which the Holy Spirit works in us, although in many ways in this imperfection it is imperfect and contaminated because of the sin which so easily besets us, is called purity both because of the unfeigned sincerity of the heart, and free from hypocrisy, and simplicity lacking deceit and craftiness; and because of the holy purpose by which they desire to consecrate themselves wholly to God, as a holy and pure sacrifice Rom. XII. 1. II Cor. VII. 1. and especially because of the prior purification of faith, and the cleansing of the heart, through the blood of the Son of God, made cleansing us from all sins I John I. 7. But we are not blessed because of inherent holiness or purity of heart. For our righteousness, if it must be examined by the strict judgment of God, is so far from being pure in all ways and uncontaminated, that it labors under the greatest uncleanness, and should be considered like a menstrual cloth Is. LXIV. 6. and in the place of refuse Phil. III. 8. Moreover, those who have been justified by the holy obedience and innocence of Christ, and made partakers of true blessedness, in their hearts the Holy Spirit dwells through faith, through whom we are sanctified, whose fruits are in all goodness and righteousness and truth Eph. V. 9. Such as are noted I Cor. VII. 11. You were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, and in the Spirit of our God. To whom therefore the vision of God is promised, because with the eyes of the heart illuminated they see here, as in a riddle, and through a glass, one day to see him face to face John XIV. 21. I Cor. XIII. 12. The sophisms of the Papists, who strive to carve out from here the purity of heart and of just works in every way, and justification through inherent righteousness, or purity even through satisfactions, or finally the profession of celibacy, are refuted by Frid. Spanheim in Dub. Evangel. part III. Dubio LXXXVI. This is καθαρότης, simplicity, integrity, ἁπλότης opposed to διπλότητι, to craftiness, deceit, guile: Thus καθαρὸν τῇ καρδίᾳ are all those who are ἄδολοι, who are not δίψυχοι, Jas. iv. 8. who do not have לב & לב a heart and a heart, Ps. XII. 3. whose breast is open, in whom there is no divorce between heart and tongue, or between heart and heart; likewise those who are pure in heart, not in body, whose heart is washed, not their garments, not their hands, in contradistinction to legal and Pharisaical purifications, to the cleansing of the cup and the dish. Matt. XXIII. 25. Who also strive to flee all the pollutions of the world, and apply themselves to all purity not only as regards external acts, but as regards internal ones, and possess the seat of all those, namely the heart, as a vessel holy and sacred to God alone. And thus, they strive to have something other than ethical and philosophical cleanliness. But the heart, as is known, designates for the Hebrews all the faculties of the soul, and their habits, and thus purity of heart is purity of both judgment and will, and of the affections. Καθαρὸς ergo τῇ καρδίᾳ is therefore he who is called by the Hebrews תמים, הלך תמים, and also לבבו, ישר לבב. Thus for Augustine a clean heart here is a simple heart: as noted here by Walaeus.

Latin:

Vers. 8. οἱ καθαροὶ τῇ καρδίᾳ) intelligi possunt ἀκέραιοι, id est qui a fuco omni, & fallaciis absunt, quos sinceros vo- cant Latini. Solet enim τὸ καθαρὸν conjungi τῷ ἀνυποκρίτῳ I. Tim. I. 5. I. Petr. I. 22. Atque ita erit hujus γνώμης expli- catio παραυτικὰ petenda ex iis, quæ infra cap. VI. differun- tur. Sed magis mihi placet καθαρὸν hic accipi eum, qui sit integer vita scelerisq; purus, quem scriptores Latini etiam san- ctum, & castum vocant Græcis καθαροὶ τὰς χεῖρας dicuntur, qui homicidio affines non sunt, & fœmina καθαρεύειν quæ concubitu abstinet. Ideo addit Christus καρδίᾳ, ex Psal. LXXIII. 1. nimirum etiam exigens animi innocentiam, illo enim censore [ut Taciti utar verbis] qui deliberant, desciverunt. Ut autem καθαρὸν ita interpreter movet me quod sequitur ὅτι αὐτοὶ τὸν θεὸν ὄψονται. Nam & apud Johannem I Epist. III. 2. itidem legimus: ὀψόμεθα αὐτὸν καθώς ἐστι: deinde subjungitur: καὶ πᾶς ὁ ἔχων ἐλπίδα ταύτην ἐπʼ αὐτῷ ἁγνίζει ἑαυτὸν, καθὼς ἐκεῖνος ἁγνός ἐστι. Solent enim pro eodem usurpari ἁγνὸς & καθαρὸς. Quæsivit ni- mirum Christus attributa, quæ aut ex simili, aut ex dissi- mili, subjectis convenirent. Ideo his, qui puro sunt cor- de, (quatenus scilicet humana permittit fragilitas) præ- mium proponit, quod conspecturi sint Deum, purissimam scilicet mentem. Quare petenda est hujus γνώμης expli- catio ex his, quæ infra, in præceptis, sequuntur commate hujus capitis 21. 27. & deinceps.

Conjungi potest simplicitas infucata vel ἀνυπό- κριτος cum animi innocentia: nam non est vera in- nocentia animi, ubi subest ὑπόκρισις, sed ut eam ex fide vera proficisci oportet I. Tim. I. 5. ita nulla est cordis purificatio sine fide. Nam per fidem purifican- tur corda nostra Act. XV. 9. Atque ideo etiam beati prædicantur puri corde, quod sanctitas, inno- centia, & sinceritas animi è fide oriantur, quæ causa est beatitudinis: siquidem sanguine Christi per fidem purificantur conscientiæ nostræ, à mortuis operibus, ad serviendum Deo Ebr. IX. 14. Hæc ergo interna sanctitas cordis, quam operatur in nobis Spiritus S. etsi multis modis in hac imperfectione imperfe- cta est, & contaminata ob τὴν εὐπερίστατον ἁμαρ- τίαν, puritas vocatur tum ob sinceritatem cordis in- fucatam, & hypocrisæos expertem, & ἁπλότητα dolo, & versutia carentem; tum ob sanctum pro- positum, quo se consecratos cupiunt Deo totos, in hostiam sanctam & puram Rom. XII. 1. II. Cor. VII. 1. tum imprimis ob præviam fidei purificationem, & mundationem cordis, per sanguinem Filii Dei, mun- di dantem nos ab omnibus peccatis, factum I. Joh. I. 7. Non autem beati sumus ob inhærentem sanctitatem, vel puritatem cordis. Nostra enim justitia, si ad districtum judicii Dei examen sit exigenda, tan- tum abest, ut pura omnibus modis & incontamina- ta sit, ut immunditia maxima laboret, & instar panni menstruatæ sit Es. LXIV. 6. ac σκυβάλων loco haberi debeat. Phil. III. 8. Cæterum qui sancta Christi obedientia atque innocentia justificati, & beatitudinis veræ participes effecti sunt, in illorum cordibus habitat per fidem Sp. S. per quem sancti- ficamur, cujus fructus sunt ἐν πάσῃ ἀγαθωσύνῃ καὶ δικαιοσύνῃ καὶ ἀληθείᾳ Eph. V. 9. Quales notantur I. Cor. VII. 11. Abluti estis, sanctificati estis, justificati estis in nomine Domini Jesu Christi, & in Spiritu Dei nostri. Quibus proinde visio Dei promittitur, quia oculis cordis illuminatis vident hic, velut in enigmate, & per speculum, olim visuri ipsum de facie ad faciem Joh. XIV. 21. 1. Cor. XIII. 12. Ponti- ficiorum sophismata, qui puritatem cordis, & operum justorum omnimodam, ac justificationem per inhæ- rentem justitiam, vel puritatem etiam per satisfa- ctiones, vel denique professionem cælibatus hinc ex- sculpere satagunt, refellit Frid. Spanhemius Dub. Evangel. part. III. Dubio LXXXVI. Hæc καθαρό- της est, simplicitas, integritas, ἁπλότης opposita τῇ διπλοτητι, astutiæ, dolo, versutiæ: Sic καθαρὸν τῇ καρδίᾳ omnes illi qui ἄδολοι, qui non δίψυχοι, Jac. iv. 8. qui non habent לב & לב cor & cor, Psal. XII. 3. quorum pectus apertum, in quibus nullum divortium inter cor & linguam, vel inter cor & cor; item illi qui puri corde, non corpore, quorum cor lotum, non ve- stes, non manus, contradistincte ad purificationes le- gales & Pharisæicas, ad purgationem poculi & pati- næ. Matth. XXIII. 25. Qui etiam inquinamenta o- mnia mundi fugere conantur, & puritati omni non tantum quoad actus externos, sed quoad internos, student, & illorum omnium sedem, nimirum cor, ut: vas sanctum, & soli Deo sacrum possident. Adeoque, aliam à munditia Ethica & Philosophica habere sat- agunt. Cor vero, ut notum, Hebræis facultates ani- mæ omnes designat, & illarum habitus, adeoque puri- tas cordis, est puritas tum judicii tum voluntatis, tum affectuum. Καθαρὸς ergo τῇ καρδίᾳ est is qui He- bræis dicitur תמים, הלך תמים ,it. לבבו ,ישר לבב. Sic Augustino mundum cor hic est simplex cor: ut notatum hic Walæo.

## 5:9
Ver. 9. εἰρηνοποιοὶ] Properly, those are called peacemakers by the Greeks who interpose themselves as mediators for others who are at variance. But the Hebrew word, which the interpreter expressed with the Greek word שלמים, is clear to the Latins, and signifies those who are studious of peace, nor is that word to be taken otherwise in this place. For the explanation of this saying follows below in verse 23 and thereafter. υἱοὶ θεῦ κληθήσονται] God is called the God of peace Rom. VI. 20. I Cor. XIV. 33. II Cor. XIII. 11. Phil. IV. 9. I Thess. V. 23. II Thess. III. 16. The sense is that those who study peace will be most like God, and therefore also most beloved by God. Thus below ὅπως γέννησθε υἱοὶ τῦ πατρὸς ὑμῶν τῦ ἐν ὀρανοῖς in verse 45. The son of Sirach had once said: Γίνυ ὀρφανοῖς ὡς πατὴρ κὴ ἀντὶ ἀνδρὸς τῇ μητρὶ ἀυτῶν, κὴ ἔση ὡς υἱὸς ὑψίςῦ, κὴ ἀγαπήσῃ σε μᾶλλον ἢ μήτηρ σε IV. 10. Philo concerning those sacrificing: οἱ, σοὶ ἀρεστὸν τῇ φύσῃ δρῶντες κὴ τὸ καλὸν, υἱοί εἰσι τῦ θεῦ. Hierocles teaches us that the Pythagoreans also spoke in this way, undoubtedly having received the custom from the Hebrews: Τᾶνδε προεργᾶσθαι τὰ παιδὸς ἄξια τοῦ θεὸν πατέρα καλῶν. But καλεῖσθαι here is to obtain the thing indicated by that word I John III. 1. ἴδετε ποταπὴν ἀγάπην δέδωκεν ἡμῖν ὁ πατὴρ ἵνα τέκνα θεῦ κληθῶμεν, which he had said elsewhere ἔδωκεν ἀυτοῖς ἐξουσίαν τέκνα θεῦ γένεσθαι Gospel I. 12. Thus also Philo on the confusion of tongues: οἱ ἐπιστήμῃ κεχρημένοι τῷ ἑνὸς υἱοὶ θεῦ προσαγορέυονται δέοντως. From this true imitation of God there follows furthermore also a participation in divine glory, as John shows in the cited place of his Epistle, and Paul in Rom. VIII. 17.

Not obscurely does Grotius make the imitation of God and the study of peace the cause of the participation in divine glory, which we know to be done by the Papists, but although those who pursue peace are called blessed and are called children of God, yet the pursuit of peace is not established as the cause of that sonship or blessedness. The subject of blessedness is thus described only, namely that the blessed are not contentious, but are those who pursue peace 2 Tim. II. 22. Heb. XII. 14. but the cause of blessedness is not expressed: thus also his blessedness is said to be that of the one to whom God imputes righteousness without works Rom. IV. 6. The pursuit of peace is joined with purity of heart and mercy toward one's neighbor, because all these things cohere in a faithful heart by an indissoluble bond. For faith, just as it demands purity of heart unfeigned before God, so also it requires love unfeigned toward one's neighbor, and is working through love Gal. V. 6. and thus it both produces mercy and impels us to cultivate the pursuit of peace with all. Where there is true blessedness, there is peace with God Rom. V. 1. ch. XIV. 17. where there is a sense of peace and reconciliation with God, there cannot but be a pursuit of peace and concord with one's neighbor. To these, therefore, it is promised that they shall be called children of God: because God the Father Heb. XIII. 10. is the God of peace: God the Son is our peace and the prince of peace Eph. II. 14. Is. IX. 6. and he ratified peace between God and man through his blood Col. I. 12. Eph. II. 14. God the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of love 2 Tim. I. 1. and peace is the fruit of the Spirit Gal. V. 22. Therefore, as children of God, they enjoy divine love, providence, perfection, riches, and goods, and finally the eternal inheritance of the heavenly Father Rom. VIII. 17. but out of grace and the mere mercy of God, and on account of the reconciliation made by the blood of Christ, and not indeed because of the imitation of God, which is very imperfect and has no proportion with the glory of the heavenly inheritance, just as a son who emulates his father's virtue, since he is the heir of the Father, does not attribute this to his own virtue and imitation of the Father, but to his sonship. For he is the heir of the Father because he is a son, not because he emulates the father: thus if we are children, says Paul, we are heirs Rom. VIII. 17. but nowhere does he teach that we are heirs because we imitate the Father.

Latin:

Vers. 9. εἰρηνοποιοὶ] Proprie Græcis ita vocantur Pacifi- catores, qui aliis dissidentibus medios se interponunt. At Hebræa vox, quam Græca voce expressit interpres שלמים Latinis patet, pacisque studiosos significat, ne- que aliter hoc loco ea vox accipienda est. Sequitur enim hujus dicti explicatio infra commate 23. & deinceps. υἱοὶ θεῦ κληθήσονται] Deus vocatur Deus pacis Rom. VI. 20. I. Cor. XIV. 33. II. Cor. XIII. 11. Phil. IV. 9. I. Thess. V. 23. II. Thess. III. 16. Hebr. XIII, 20. Sensus est, eos, qui pa ci student, Deo simillimos, ac proinde etiam Deo dilectis- simos fore. Sic infra ὅπως γέννησθε υἱοὶ τῦ πατρὸς ὑμῶν τῦ ἐν ὀρανοῖς commate 45. Sirachides olim dixerat: Γίνυ ὀρφα- νοῖς ὡς πατὴρ κὴ ἀντὶ ἀνδρὸς τῇ μητρὶ ἀυτῶν, κὴ ἔση ὡς υἱὸς ὑ- ψίςῦ, κὴ ἀγαπήσῃ σε μᾶλλον ἢ μήτηρ σε IV. 10. Philo de sacrificantibus: οἱ, σοὶ ἀρεστὸν τῇ φύσῃ δρῶντες κὴ τὸ καλὸν, υἱοί εἰσι τῦ θεῦ. Hierocles docet nos, ita locutos & Pytha- goristas, haud dubie accepto ab Hebræis more: Τᾶνδε προεργᾶσθαι τὰ παιδὸς ἄξια τοῦ θεὸν πατέρα καλῶν. Est au- tem καλεῖσθαι hic rem ea voce indicatam consequi I. Joh. III. 1. ἴδετε ποταπὴν ἀγάπην δέδωκεν ἡμῖν ὁ πατὴρ ἵνα τέκνα θεῦ κληθῶμεν, quod alibi dixerat ἔδωκεν ἀυτοῖς ἐξουσίαν τέκ- να θεῦ γένεσθαι Evang. I. 12. Sic & Philo de linguarum con- fusione: οἱ ἐπιστήμῃ κεχρημένοι τῷ ἑνὸς υἱοὶ θεῦ προσαγορέυον- ται δέοντως. Ex hac vera Dei imitatione sequitur porro et- iam divinæ gloriæ participatio, ut ostendit Johannes dicto Epistolæ loco, & Paulus Rom. VIII. 17.

Haud obscure Grotius imitationem Dei, studi- umque pacis causam facit participationis divinæ gloriæ. Quod à Papistis fieri, novimus. Sed quanquam pacis studiosi beati prædicentur, & fi- lii Dei vocentur, non tamen studium pacis causa constituitur illius υἱότητος, vel μακαριότητος. Describitur ita solum subjectum beatitudinis, quod nempe beati sint non contentiosi, sed qui pacem per- sequuntur 2. Tim. II. 22. Ebr. XII. 14. non vero ex- primitur causa beatitudinis : Sic etiam μακαρι- σμὸς ejus esse dicitur, cui Deus imputat justitiam χωρὶς ἔργων, fine operibus Rom. IV. 6. Conjun- gitur pacis studium cum puritate cordis & misericor- dia, adversus proximum, quia insolubili vinculo hæc omnia cohærent, in fideli corde. Fides e- nim uti puritatem cordis exigit infucatam, coram Deo: ita & dilectionem requirit ἀνυπόκριτον ad- versus proximum, estque δι᾽ ἀγάπης ἐνεργουμένη Gal. V. 6. adeoque & misericordiam parit, & ad studium pacis colendum cum omnibus nos im- pellit. Ubi vera beatitudo, ibi pax est cum Deo Rom. V. 1. cap. XIV. 17. ubi pacis & reconcilia- tionis cum Deo sensus est, ibi non potest non esse studium pacis, & concordiæ cum proximo. His ergo promittitur quod υἱοὶ Θεῦ κληθήσονται: quia Deus Pater Ebr. XIII. 10. est Deus pacis : Deus Filius pax nostra & princeps pacis Eph. II. 14. Es. IX. 6. ac pacem sancivit inter Deum & homi- nem per sanguinem suum Col. I. 12. Ephes. II. 14. Deus Spiritus Sanct. est Spiritus dilectionis 2. Tim. I. 1. & pax est fructus Spiritus Galat. V. 22. Id- eo tanquam filii Dei, divina dilectione, provi- dentia, perfectione, divitiis ac bonis, denique patris cœlestis hæreditate sempiterna fruuntur Rom. VIII. 17. sed ex gratia, & mera Dei miseri- cordia, ac propter reconciliationem, sanguine Christi factam, non vero ob imitationem Dei, quæ valde imperfecta est, nec ullam proportio- nem habet cum gloria cœlestis hæreditatis, uti fi- lius, qui paternam virtutem æmulatur, cum hæ- res sit Patris, non id virtuti suæ, & imitationi Patris acceptum fert, sed τῇ υἱότητι. Nam hæres est Patris, quia Filius, non quia patrem æmulatur: ita si filii sumus, inquit Paulus, hæredes sumus Rom. VIII. 17. nuspiam autem hæredes nos esse docet ideo, quia Patrem imitamur.

## 5:10
Vers. 10.

Δεδιωγμένοι] To the Greeks, διώκειν is not only to accuse, but also to expel, as διώκειν ἐκ τῆς γῆς, διώκειν τῆς οἰκίας. But among the Hellenistic Jews, that word has a wider scope, so as to express the Hebrew רָדַף, which contains every kind of vexation, especially the more serious. In Latin, persequi, with nothing added, does not have this sense. Otherwise, persequi judicio, persequi bello, is correctly said. But Christians, imitating the Hebrews and Hellenists, said persequi, for which the ancient Romans would have said vexare or exagitare.

Ἕνεκεν δικαιοσύνης] This word hardly ever signifies an end in these books, but mostly the cause by which the agent is impelled. To the Latins, therefore, it has the same notion: as virtutis ergo. Δικαιοσύνη, however, here again signifies obedience to divine commands.

αὐτῶν ἐστιν ἡ βασιλεία τῶν οὐρανῶν] Since βασιλεία οὐρανῶν sometimes signifies heavenly doctrine and what follows from it in this life, and sometimes heavenly glory, as can be seen in many places, as the former sense above: so I feel that the latter is to be embraced here: both so that individual attributes may correspond to individual subjects, and because the very next clause seems to contain a particular explanation of this general statement, and there mention of the heavenly reward is expressed.
