And hence it happened that even in the times of Clement this passage was read in a different way. He himself cites ὅτι αὐτοὶ υἱοὶ κληθήσονται, which crept in from the following clause. He testifies that it is read by others as ὅτι αὐτοὶ ἔσονται τέλειοι: and also ὅτι ἕξουσι τόπον, ὅπου οὐ διωχθήσονται, all of which I judge to be glosses explaining what βασιλεία τῶν οὐρανῶν was in this place.

That the kingdom of heaven is taken for heavenly doctrine anywhere does not appear. You would therefore more correctly say that the kingdom of grace is noted in the first aphorism: but in this last, the kingdom of glory. However, the kingdom of grace, even if it is governed by the scepter of the Word, sent forth from Zion Ps. CX. 3. is not, however, the doctrine of the Word itself. Through the Word, the kingdom, or the people of the kingdom, is gathered for Christ: through the Word, the kingdom is likewise ruled and administered. But what the kingdom of God is, or in what it consists, the Apostle teaches Rom. XIV. 17. The kingdom of God is righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit. The kingdom of grace either denotes the government itself and the mode and form of the economy and administration, which is done through the Word and Sacraments, or it denotes those goods which the participants of the kingdom of Christ enjoy, which are righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit. In neither sense is the kingdom of grace the heavenly doctrine of Christ itself; nor is there a need to invent such a diverse signification of the kingdom of heaven on account of the diverse degrees of blessedness; since diverse respects are sufficient, v. 3 and 10. so that to those poor in spirit, true riches are promised in the kingdom of heaven, and to these pressed on account of righteousness, true liberty, dignity, and majesty are promised in the heavens; or there the kingdom of grace is assigned to them, in which they are rich in God Luke XII. 21. but here the kingdom of glory. Concerning righteousness, Gomarus notes in Walaeus: He does not understand the imputed righteousness of Christ, nor the virtue of inherent righteousness, because both are unknown to persecutors; but the works of this inherent righteousness: by a common metonymy, by which the names of virtues are very often used for their effects. These, moreover, are first the confession of true doctrine, and the refutation of false: and a manner of life in the true external worship of God, and in the performance of duties toward one's neighbor, consistent with the word of God. Which righteousness, that is, just works, of themselves indeed deserve the love and embrace of all; but by the fault of the enemies of the Church, or of imprudent zeal, or of impudent malice, it is seized upon as an occasion for persecution. Furthermore, patience is added here to the remaining virtues, because no one of the faithful is exempt from persecution and the cross, Acts 14:22, 2 Tim. 3:12, for the sustaining of which there is need of patience, and of perseverance in the true faith, which the Apostle calls ὑπομονήν in Heb. 10:36, so that doing the will of God, we may obtain the promise. This patience, however, is a mark and requirement of the blessed, not a cause or merit of blessedness, because there is no proportion between the sufferings of the present time and the future glory, as the Apostle testifies in Rom. 8:18.

Although indeed mention of a reward is made in v. 12, this reward is nevertheless not κατ᾽ ὀφέλημα or owed, but χάριν and unowed, Rom. 4:4, 5, not properly so called, but improperly, inasmuch as it is promised out of grace to those to whom grace has been granted, not only to believe in Christ, but also to suffer for Christ, Phil. 1:29. Those sufferings are due, not arbitrary, and therefore not meritorious. Since merit can only be found in an unowed work; and eternal life is obtained as an inheritance, as the portion of sons, not as the wages of hirelings. Add that the merits would not be ours, if there were any, but God's, who works all things in us; whence Augustine in Ps. 30: Your sins are yours, God's are the merits; punishment is owed to you, and when the reward comes, God will crown his own gifts, not your merits. What of the fact that those who suffer persecution are pronounced blessed here, so that in this passage, with mention made only of the persecution itself, and not of patience or tolerance, the state and condition sine qua non of the faithful is designated in this image of the blessed, rather than the fruit and effect of faith? Because the faithful cannot be without persecutions, which are their character and sign. John 15:19, Rom. 8:29. Spanheim rightly says: The reward, of which the Lord speaks in this place, is unowed, promised indeed out of grace, and to those to whom grace has been granted, not only of believing in Christ, but also of suffering for him, and of those whose sufferings do not approach the glory to be revealed, and therefore between which and the glory that is to follow there is no proportion. Add that those sufferings were due, not arbitrary, and therefore not meritorious. Since merit can only be found in an undue work. Moreover, the Apostle testifies at Rom. VIII. 18. 'the sufferings of the present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us.' Thus the Holy Spirit very aptly calls eternal life a 'recompense of the inheritance,' Col. III. 24, having regard both to the divine promise and to the order, because it is given from a promise, and after labor and struggle, but a 'recompense of the inheritance,' because it is obtained as an inheritance, as the portion of sons, not as the salary of mercenaries. For it is known that μισθὸς among the Hellenists is taken most broadly, with whom the writers of the New Testament for the most part speak. Thus מהיר to the Hellenists is not only ἀντάλλαγμα, but also μισθὸς and δῶρον. Thus אשכר is properly a gift, to the Hellenists a reward. Ezech. XXVII. 15. Thus they translate אתנן not only as μισθὸν, but simply as δῶμα. The word שכר also, meaning wages, is often taken broadly, and sometimes for a gift only: thus for example Psalm CXXVII, 3, נחלה and שכר, inheritance and reward, are equipollent: 'Lo, the inheritance of Jehovah are children, the reward, the fruit of the womb.' LXX: 'Lo, the inheritance of the Lord are sons, the reward of the fruit of the womb.' Thus what is μισθὸς in Matth. V. 46 is χάρις in Luc. VI. 33. Great reward is also blessedness itself, and heavenly glory, which is truly such then absolutely, because it consists both in perfect virtue and in the perfect happiness of the glorified; then comparatively in relation to the actions or sufferings of the children of God, which that heavenly prize infinitely exceeds, and therefore it is truly a great reward for a small labor. Therefore, a comparison of different things is instituted here, but of the same things, not of greater and lesser crowns or rewards, but of work and reward in relation to the same persons, who are to do or suffer little for the Lord, to be gifted at some time with a great and abundant reward, superior to all actions and sufferings. Vain, therefore, are the Papists here with their merits, vain also with their evangelical counsels of perfection, vain with the eight ways of salvation, which Petrus Bessaeus, Royal preacher, in his French Postil on this text, on the feast of All Saints, translated into the German language by the Jesuit Tympius, proposes, concerning which he himself exclaims: 'Do not complain any more about the narrowness or danger of the way which leads to heaven, for Christ sets before us eight ways, so that we should choose one of them and walk in it.' Besides, He promises us that we shall certainly come into the kingdom of heaven through one of them. Namely, according to that word of Christ in John XIV: 'I am the way, the truth and the life; no one comes to the Father except through me.' Likewise Matth. VII. 14: 'Narrow is the gate, and constricted is the way, which leads to life.' And these things concerning the eight beatitudes, which I explained in this way 18 years ago at Danzig, in a special sermon published under the title ICON BEATORUM: I see, however, that Flacius in his gloss especially agrees with our explanation; and that Mr. Dr. Winstrup favors it in his recent work of the Sacred Pandects on Matthew, p. 669, although in these, the 'meek' are not said to be in the same way, since he understands the meek to be those who are of a placid mind before God, by whom, as we have observed, the humble are rather denoted in the Hebrew phrase, as Flacius rightly explains: 'The afflicted and humiliated, and those prostrate in spirit, are here called meek.' He treats here of those afflicted spiritually by an evil conscience, the law, and the wrath of God, who are also contrite and humiliated, and seeking contrary remedies by faith. Thus also Jerome explains it. And thus all these things follow one another rightly and in order: First, contrition is inculcated, v. 3, 4, afterwards faith v. 6, finally new obedience v. 7, 8, 9, 10, to which order Winstrup also assents, that first the three degrees of contrition are described: spiritual poverty or the recognition of one's own injustice, spiritual mourning for sins and because of God offended by our sins, and spiritual humility, which arises from the recognition of spiritual poverty and the sorrow on account of it. Then faith is expressed by hunger and thirst for righteousness, finally the fruits of faith, mercy, purity of heart, the pursuit of peace and concord: to which he adds persecution adhering to faith accidentally and extrinsically, by which faith is tested, exercised, and thus increased.

Latin:

Vers. 10.

Δεδιωγμένοι] Græcis διώκειν est non tantum accusare, sed & expellere, ut διώκειν ἐκ τῆς γῆς διώκειν τῆς οἰκίας. Sed apud Hellenistas Judæos latius ea vox patet, ut exprimat Hebræum רָדַף, quod omne genus vexationis, præsertim gravioris continet. Latine persequi, nulla re adjecta, hunc sensum non habet. Alioqui persequi judicio, per- sequi bello, recte dicitur. Sed Christiani Hebræos & Hel- lenistas imitati dixerunt persequi, pro quo veteres Roma- ni dixissent, vexare aut exagitare.

Ἕνεκεν δικαιοσύνης] Vox hæc vix unquam in his libris finem, at plerumque causam significat, qua agens impel- litur. Latinis ergo eandem habet notionem : ut virtutis er- go. Δικαιοσύνη autem hic iterum obedientiam divinorum mandatorum significat.

αὐτῶν ἐστιν ἡ βασιλεία τῶν οὐρανῶν] Cum βασιλεία ὐ- ρανῶν modo doctrinam cœlestem, & quæ eam in hac vita consequuntur, modo gloriam cœlestem significet, ut multis in locis videre est, ut priorem sensum supra : ita posteriorem hic amplectendum sentio : tum ut singulis subjectis singu- la attributa respondeant, tum quod omnino proxime se- quens comma videatur dicti hujus generalis particularem ἐπεξήγησιν continere, ibi autem mercedis cœlestis expres- sa est mentio. Atque hinc factum est, ut jam Clementis temporibus diverso modo hic locus legeretur. Ipse citat ὅτι αὐτοὶ υἱοὶ κληθήσονται, quod ex sequenti Commate irre- psit. Ab aliis legi testatur, ὅτι αὐτοὶ ἔσονται τέλειοι: atque etiam ὅτι ἕξουσι τόπον, ὅπου ὐ διαχθήσονται, quæ omnia glos- semata esse arbitror explicantia quid esset βασιλεία τῶν ὀυρα- νῶν hoc loco.

Regnum cælorum pro doctrina cælesti uspiam accipi non apparet. Rectius ergo dixeris Regnum gratiæ aphorismo primo: hoc autem postremo re- gnum gloriæ notari. Regnum autem gratiæ, etsi geratur sceptro verbi, è Zione emisso Psal. CX. 3. non tamen est ipsa doctrina verbi. Per verbum colligitur Christo regnum, seu populus regni: per verbum regitur item, & administratur re- gnum. Quidnam autem sit regnum Dei, vel in quo consistat, docet Apostolus Rom. XIV. 17. Re- gnum Dei est justitia, pax & gaudium in Spiritu San- cto. Regnum gratiæ vel notat regimen ipsum mo- dumque & formam οἰκονομίας & administrationis, quæ fit per Verbum & Sacramenta, vel notat bo- na illa, quibus fruuntur consortes regni Christi, quæ sunt justitia, pax & gaudium in Spiritu San- cto. Neutro sensu regnum gratiæ est ipsa doctri- na Christi cœlestis; neque opus est fingere tam diversam significationem regni cœlorum, ob diver- sos beatitudinis gradus; quum diversi respectus suf- ficiant, v. 3. & 10. ita ut illis pauperibus spiritu, in regno cœlesti veræ divitiæ, his pressis propter ju- stitiam vera libertas, dignitas & majestas in cœlis promittatur; aut ibi etiam regnum gratiæ ipsis assignetur, in quo divites sunt in Deo Luc. XII. 21. hic vero regnum gloriæ. De justitia notat Goma- rus apud Walæum: Justitiam non intelligit impu- tatam Christi, nec virtutem justitiæ inhærentem, quia utraque persecutoribus est ignota; sed justitiæ hujus inhærentis opera: per Metonym. usitatam, quâ virtutum nomina pro effectis suis sæpissime u- surpantur. Ea autem sunt primum confessio veræ doctrinæ, & falsæ confutatio: & conversatio in vero cultu Dei externo, & officiis erga proximum præstantis, verbo Dei conveniens. Quæ justitia, hoc est, justa opera, per se quidem amorem & ample- xum omnium promerentur; sed hostium Ecclesiæ, vel zeli imprudentis, vel impudentis malitiæ vitio in occa- sionem persecutionis arripitur. Cæterum adjungi- tur hic virtutibus reliquis patientia, quia perse- quutionis & crucis expers nemo est fidelium Act. XIV. 22. 2. Tim. III. 12. ad quam sustinendam opus est patientia, & in vera fide perseverantia, quam ὑπομονὴν vocat Apostolus Ebr. X. 36. ut volunta- tem Dei facientes, promissionem consequamur. Hæc vero patientia nota & requisitum est beatorum, non causa vel meritum beatitudinis, quia nulla est proportio inter passiones præsentis temporis, & futuram gloriam, teste Apostolo Rom. VIII. 18.

Etsi vero mercedis mentio fiat v. 12. hæc tamen merces non est κατ᾽ ὀφέλημα vel debita, sed χάριν & indebita Rom. IV. 4. 5. non proprie ita di- cta, sed improprie, utpote ex gratia promissa illis, quibus facta gratia, non tantum credendi in Chri- stum, sed & patiendi pro Christo, Phil. I. 29. Pas- siones illæ debitæ sunt, non arbitrariæ, adeoque nec meritoriæ. Siquidem meritum non nisi in o- pere indebito reperiri possit; & vita æterna ob- tinetur ut hereditas, ut portio filiorum, non ut sa- larium mercenariorum. Adde quod merita non nostra forent, si quæ forent, sed Dei, qui omnia operatur in nobis; unde Augustinus in Psal. XXX. Tua peccata sunt, merita Dei sunt, supplicium ti- bi debetur, & cum præmium venerit, Deus sua do- na coronabit, non merita tua. Quid, quod bea- ti hic prædicentur, qui persequutionem patiuntur, ut hoc loco non patientiæ, aut tolerantiæ, sed ipsius solum persecutionis mentione facta status & condi- tio fine qua non potius fidelium in hoc icone beato- rum designetur, quam fructus & effectus fidei? quia fideles sine persecutionibus esse nequeunt, quæ character & signum eorum sunt. Johan. XV. 19. Rom. VIII. 29. Recte Spanhemius: Merces, de qua hoc loco Dominus, est indebita, promissa quippe ex gratia, & illis quibus gratia facta, non tantum credendi in Christum, sed & patiendi pro eo, & illis quorum passiones non accedunt ad gloriam re- velandam, adeoque inter quas & gloriam subsequu- turam nulla proportio. Adde, passiones illas debitas fuisse, non arbitrarias, adeoque nec meritorias. Quum meritum non nisi in opere indebito reperiri possit. Quin & Apostolus testatur ad Rom. VIII. 18. τὰ παθήματα τῦ νῦν καιρῦ ὐκ ἔναι ἄξια πρὸς τὴν μέλλυσαν δόξαν ἀποκαλυφθῆναι εἰς ἡμάς. Sic Spiritus S. vitam aternam apposite admodum vocat ἀνταπόδοσιν τῆς κληρονομίας, Col. III. 24. habita ra- tione & promissi divini, & ordinis, quia datur ex pro- misso, & post laborem & pugnam, ἀνταπόδοσιν vero κληρονομίας, quia obtinetur ut hareditas, ut portio filiorum, nonut salarium mercenariorum. Notum enim μισθὸς apud Hellenistas latissime sumi cum quibus Scriptores Novi Testamenti ut plurimum loquuntur. Sic מהיר Hellenistis non tantum ἀντάλλαγμα, sed & μισθὸς & δῶρον. Sic אשכר δῶρον proprie Helleni- stis μισθός. Ezech. XXVII. 15. Sic אתנן non tantum vertunt μισθὸν, sed simpliciter δῶμα. Vox etiam שכר merces late sape sumitur, & interdum pro dono tan- tum: sic verbi gratia Psalm. CXXVII, 3 נחלה & שכר hareditas & merces equipollent: Ecce hære- ditas Jehovæ filii, merces, fructus ventris. LXX. ἰδὺ ἡ κληρονομία Κυρίε υἱοί, ὁ μισθὸς τῦ καρπῦ τῆς γαστρός. Sic quod Matth. V. 46. μισθὸς, Luc. VI. 33. χάρις. Multa merces etiam est ipsa beatitudo, & gloria cœ- lestis, quæ revera talis tum absolute, quia consistit & in perfecta virtute, & in perfecta felicitate glo- rificatorum; tum comparate in ordine ad actiones vel passiones filiorum Dei, quas præmium illud cœleste infinite excedit, adeoque vere multa merces est pro parvo labore. Instituitur itaque hic comparatio diversorum, sed eorundem, nec coronarum vel præ- miorum majorum & minorum, sed operis & mer- cedis in ordine ad eosdem, parva vel facturos, vel passuros pro Domino multa & copiosa mercede, a- ctionibus & passionibus omnibus superiori aliquando donandos. Vani ergo sunt hic Papistæ cum meri- tis suis, vani etiam cum consiliis Evangelicis perfe- ctionis, vani cum octo viis salutis, quas Petrus Bes- sæus, Regius concionator, in Postill. Gallica super hunc textum, in festo omnium sanctorum, in lin- guam Germanicam à Tympio Jesuita translatis, proponit, de quibus ipse exclamat: Laß nicht mehr klagen über die Enge oder Gefährlichkeit des Weges / so zum Himmel leitet / denn Chri- stus stellet uns achterley Wege für / daß wir de- ren einen erwehlen sollen / und denselben gehen. Beynebenst verheisset Er uns / daß wir gewißlich durch deren einen in das Himmelreich werden kommen. Scilicet juxta illud Christi Joh. XIV. Ego sum via, veritas & vita, nemo venit ad Patrem, nisi per me. Item Matth. VII. 14. Angusta est porta, & arcta via, quæ ducit ad vitam. Atque hæc de octo beatitudinibus, quas ante hos 18. annos ita exposui Gedani, peculiari concione, sub titulo ICON BEATORUM, edita: Video autem nostræ ex- plicationi imprimis adstipulari Flacium in glossa; eique favere Dn. D. Winstrup. in nupero opere Pandectarum sacrorum in Matth. p. 669. etsi his ὁι πραεῖς non eodem modo dicantur, quum mansue- tos intelligat, qui placido animo sunt coram Deo, per quos potius, Ebræa phrasi, humiles notari ob- servavimus, ut recte explicat Flacius: Mites hic vo- cantur afflicti & humiliati, prostratique animo. A- git hic de afflictis spiritualiter à mala conscientia, le- ge, & ira Dei, qui etiam sunt contriti, & humilia- ti, contrariaque remedia fide quærentes. Sic & Hie- ronymus exponit. Atque ita recte & ordine se con- sequuntur hæc omnia: Primum inculcantur con- tritio, v. 3. 4. postea fides v. 6. postremo nova obe- dientia v. 7. 8. 9. 10. cui ordini annuit etiam Win- strupius, primum tres gradus contritionis describi, paupertatem spiritualem seu agnitionem propriæ inju- stitiæ, luctum spiritualem ob peccata & propter of- fensum per peccata nostra Deum: & humilitatem spi- ritualem: quæ ex agnitione paupertatis spiritualis & dolore propter eam oritur. Deinde fidem expri- mi per famem & sitim justitiæ, denique fructus fidei, misericordiam, munditiem cordis, pacis & concordiæ studium: quibus addit fidei accidentaliter & extrin- secus adhærentem persecutionem, qua fides probatur, exercetur, atque sic augetur.

## 5:11
Vers. 11.

Ὅταν ὀνειδίσωσιν] As was done formerly to Elisha, 2 Kings II. 23.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

Ὅταν ὀνειδίσωσιν] Ut olim Elisæo factum 2. Reg. II. 23.

## 5:12
Vers. 12.

Ὅτι ὁ μισθὸς ὑμῶν πολὺς] From Gen. XV. 1. Οὕτως ἐδίωξαν τοὺς προφήτας] Joseph, Moses, Samuel, David, Isaiah, Jeremiah, and others. See Nehemiah IX. 26, the speech of Stephen in the Acts, and what is said below XXIII. 31. Indeed, it is so, truth begets hatred: especially that which pertains to the amendment of morals. If this happened to Heraclitus, if to Democritus, if to Socrates, while they were shining a tiny torch, how much more is it to be expected for the disciples of Christ? Plato in the second book of the Republic says that for the testing of true virtue it is necessary that a good man, 'doing nothing unjust, should have the greatest reputation for injustice, so that he may be tested for justice by not being softened by ill-repute and the things arising from it, but let him be immovable until death.'

PART II. Concerning the office of the disciples of Christ, illustrated by the similitude of salt and light.

Latin:

Vers. 12.

Ὅτι ὁ μισθὸς ὑμῶν πολὺς] Ex Gen. XV. 1. Οὕτως ἐδίωξαν τοὺς προφήτας] Josephum, Mosem, Sa- muelem, Davidem, Esaiam, Jeremiam atque alios. Vide Nehemiam IX. 26. orationem Stephani in Actis, & quæ infra dicuntur XXIII. 31. Nimirum ita est, veritas odium pa- rit: præsertim ea quæ ad mores emendandos pertinet. Hoc si Heroclito, si Democrito, si Socrati evenit, tantillam faculam allucentibus, quanto magis Christi discipulis ex- spectandum est? Plato secundo de republica ait, ad explo- rationem veræ virtutis opus esse ut vir bonus μηδὲν ἀδικῶν, δόξαν ἔχῃ τὴν μεγίστην ἀδικίας, ἵνα ᾖ βεβασανισμένος εἰς δι- καιοσύνην τῷ μὴ τέγγεσθαι ὑπὸ κακοδοξίας καὶ τῶν ὑπ᾽ αὐτῆς γιγνομένων, ἀλλ᾽ ἤτω ἀμετάστατος μέχρι θανάτου.

PARS II. De officio discipulorum Christi, similitudine salis & luminis illustrato.

## 5:13
Vers. 13.

ὑμεῖς ἐστε τὸ ἅλας τῆς γῆς] As I began to say just now, I see no sufficient reason why these things should be restricted to the Apostles. For both the beatitudes are common to all: and the address which preceded the two preceding threats looks to all who endure injuries for the sake of the truth. Then indeed it is clear that the same persons are called the salt of the earth, and in the following verse the light of the world. But they are called luminaries in the world, not only Bishops, but all true Christians, as appears in Philippians II. 15. Similar to which is that saying in Justin: what the soul is in the body, that Christians are in the world. Now indeed this very thing which is said about salt, Luke says was spoken directly to the crowds in XIV. 25, 34. The sense therefore is that those who had received true and salutary doctrine from Christ himself ought not to seek an example of living from other men, but ought to be an example to others. Moreover, the chief power of salt is against putrefaction. Hence that saying of Varro, that the soul was given to swine instead of salt so that they would not putrefy, taken from Cleanthes, whose words were these: that they have a soul in place of salt so that the meat does not rot. Nor for any other reason did Homer call it salt-like. Hence wisdom began to be called salt, as is in the Comic poet: who has the salt that is in you. And Paul looks to the same thing when he wishes our speech to be so pleasant that it is nevertheless seasoned with salt, Colossians IV. 6. But closest to this manner of speaking approaches that which Livy calls Greece the salt of the nations. Therefore Christ shows that it is the duty of those who have drunk in the precepts of true wisdom to purge away the filth of others.

Τῆς γῆς] The word γῆς and the word κόσμου which is in the following verse, undoubtedly signify the universality of the human race, just as the words for lands and world are used by the Latins. Certainly those few instituted by Christ were the leaven for the whole lump that was leavened, below XIII. 34.

These things are not rightly restricted to those few instituted by Christ: for they pertain to all who are truly faithful, whether taught immediately by him or through the ministers of Christ, since all who are truly of Christ are luminaries in the world, Philippians II. 15, as Grotius himself admits, and therefore it is said of them that they are the salt of the earth, and that they ought to provide an example of living to others.

Μωρανθῇ] What the Greeks call ἄναλον, as also Mark IX. 50, is called in Hebrew תפל as in Job VI. 6, and the same word signifies foolish in Job XXIV. 12, Jeremiah XXIII. 13, Lamentations II. 14. Therefore the Greek interpreter expressed the Hebrew word as closely as he could.

Ἐν τίνι ἁλισθήσεται] Not to be taken absolutely, but as related. In what shall it be salted, says Mark, with all ambiguity removed. Salt ought to have in itself the power of seasoning. For if it has become putrid, there is nothing by which it may be corrected. Thus those who had drawn true doctrine from the Lord Jesus, they themselves ought to amend others, and not wait to be amended themselves by others. Similar to this proverb is that one used by the Greeks: when water chokes, what is there to drink?

to be trodden under foot by men] a proverbial expression concerning a thing of no value: But here one must understand at the same time a threat of punishment, which Luke explains in 21:24. שוּט for the Hebrews is what ἔσχατος is for those speaking Greek, as the LXX translate at the end of the book of Judges.

Latin:

Vers. 13.

ὑμεῖς ἐστε τὸ ἅλας τῆς γῆς] Ut modo dicere occæpi, ni- hil satis causæ video cur hæc ad Apostolos restringantur. Nam & μακαρισμοὶ communes sunt omnibus: & allocutio quæ præcessit cominatibus duobus antecedentibus, o- mnes spectat, qui pro veritate injurias sustinent. Tum verò clarum est eosdem dici ἅλας τῆς γῆς, & commate se- quenti φῶς τοῦ κόσμου. At φωστήρες ἐν κόσμῳ dicuntur non Episcopi tantum, sed omnes vere Christiani, ut apparet Phi- lipp. II. 15. Cui simile est illud apud Justinum: ὅπερ ἐστιν ἐν σώματι ψυχή, τοῦτ᾽ εἰσιν ἐν κόσμῳ χριστιανοί. Jam vero hoc ipsum quod de sale dicitur, Lucas directè dictum ait πρὸς τοὺς ὄχλους XIV. 25. 34. Sensus ergo est, eos, qui ab ipso Christo veram ac salutarem doctrinam percepissent, non exemplum vivendi ab hominibus aliis petere, sed aliis exemplo esse debere. Salis autem præcipua vis est adver- sus putredinem. Hinc illud Varronis, suillo pecori animam pro sale datam ne putisceret, ex Cleanthe desumtum, cu- jus hæc erant verba: τὰς ὗς ἀντ᾽ ἁλῶν ἔχειν τὴν ψυχὴν ἵνα μὴ σαπῇ τὰ κρέα. Neque alia de causa ἁλαῶτον dixit Ho- merus. Hinc sapientia, sal dici cœpit ut est apud Comicum: qui habet salem qui in te est. Atque eodem respicit Paulus, cum sermonem nostrum ita blandum vult esse, ut tamen sale condiatur, Coloss. IV. 6. Sed proxime ad hoc loquen- di genus accedit quod Livius Græciam sal gentium vocat. Ostendit ergo Christus officii esse eorum qui veræ sapien- tiæ præcepta hausissent, aliorum sordes expurgare.

Τῆς γῆς] Vox γῆς & quæ est commate sequenti vox κόσμου, haud dubie generis humani universitatem signifi- cant, quomodo & terrarum & mundi vox Latinis usurpan- tur. Nimirum pauci isti à Christo instituti fermentum fuêre pro tota farina fermentata est, infra XIII. 34.

Non recte ad paucos istos à Christo institutos hæc restringuntur: pertinent enim ad omnes sive immediate ab ipso, sive per ministros Christi edo- ctos, qui vere fideles sunt, quum omnes vere Christi Φωστήρες sint ἐν κόσμῳ Phil. II. 15. fatente ipsumet Grotio, de iisque dictum proinde sit quod sint ἅλας τῆς γῆς, quodque exemplum vi- vendi aliis præbere debeant.

Μωρανθῇ] Quod Græci dicunt ἄναλον, ut & Marcus IX. 50. id Hebræis dicitur תפל ut Jobi VI. 6. eademque vox τὸ μωρὸν significat Jobi XXIV. 12. Jerem. XXIII. 13. Thren. II. 14. Hebræam igitur vocem quam proxime po- tuit, expressit Græcus interpres.

Ἐν τίνι ἁλισθήσεται] Non absolute sumendum, sed relatæ. ἐν τίνι ἁλισθήσεται inquit Marcus omni ambigui- tate remota. Sal in se habere debet vim excoquendi. Nam si putruerit, non est quo corrigatur. Sic illi qui à Domino Jesu veram doctrinam hauserant, ipsi emendare alios de- bebant, non autem exspectare ut ab aliis ipsi emendaren- tur. Simile est huic proverbio illud Græcis usitatum ὅταν τὸ ὕδωρ πνίγῃ, ἐπὶ πίνειν τί δεῖ;

καταπατεῖσθαι ὑπὸ τῶν ἀνδρῶν] παροιμιῶδης locutio de re nihili: Sed intelligenda hic simul pœnæ commina- tio, quam explicat Lucas XXI. 24. שוּט Hebræis est quod ἔσχατος Græce loquentibus, ut fine libri Judicum vertunt LXX.

## 5:14
Verse 14.

a city to be hidden] Christ wishes the integrity of his hearers to be no less conspicuous than cities are accustomed to be, which are placed on the top of a mountain: such as was Jerusalem, a figure of the church. See Ezekiel at the end. That this does not treat directly of the assembly of the pious, which could be distinguished more easily while the Apostles lived than afterwards, both the preceding and following context show.

Latin:

Vers. 14.

πόλις κρυβῆναι] Vult Christus auditorum suorum in- tegritatem non minus esse conspicuam quam solent esse urbes, quæ in montis vertice sunt collocatæ: qualis erat Hierosolyma, ecclesiæ figura. Vide Ezechielem in fine. De cœtu autem piorum qui, dum vixerunt Apostoli faci- lius quam postea, dignosci potuit, hic directe non agi & præcedentia & sequentia ostendunt.

## 5:15
Verse 15.

A bushel] the word modis, although less used by the Greeks, nevertheless came from Greece into Latium. For Dinarchus also uses it. It is credible that it was written from Matthew as סְאָא, which the Syrian has here, since Jerome also translates modium as סְאָא in the Old Testament.

And it shines] a Hebraism for ἵνα λάμπῃ, correctly noted by the old Latin interpreter. Thus the lampstand shone in the middle of the tabernacle, and then in the middle of the temple building.

In the repetition of the similitude in Mark 4:21 concerning the bushel, it is added, under a bed, that is, a bench, because the Jews, when taking food, used little beds for benches. Some, however, explain the lamp as the word of God to be placed on a lampstand, or to be faithfully and assiduously proposed to the people, with the blessed Polycarp Lyser in Harm. Evang. CLXI. Others prefer to understand it of the teachers, under the person of the Apostles, in that they illuminate the world with the splendor of their doctrine and life, as lights divinely kindled, set upon the lampstand of the Church; just as Chrysostom explained concerning the Apostles: You will not only not be hidden, but you will illuminate the whole world, and therefore you will be clear and illustrious through it; I indeed have kindled the light, but that it may remain kindled, it is your concern, etc. Blessed Chemnitius in Harmon. c. LI. By the similitude of a lamp placed under a bushel, he teaches that, on account of the malice of the world, reproaches, and persecutions, the ministers of the word ought not to be wearied, or rendered more timid, so as to either hide or contract the rays of heavenly doctrine. Isidorus says, God kindles the lamp, that is, the Priest, and places it on a lampstand, that is, on a Chair bearing his light, so that it may bring to the Church, like lightning, the splendor of doctrines and actions free from all darkness, so that the people, beholding the rays of the life-giving brightness, may direct themselves to them, and glorify the Father of lights. Similarly Jerome, blessed Hunnius, Osiander, and others. Some wish these things to be said to all of Christ's hearers, to which Grotius accedes.

Since therefore these things were said to any of Christ's hearers, as Grotius admits, Papists rashly prove the perpetual visibility of the Church from this. It is to be observed, however, that the whole similitude is handed down here, and thus by the word ὕτω in verse 16, the apodosis is rendered in this way according to some: as a city placed on a mountain cannot be hidden or lie concealed, and as a candle is placed upon a lampstand, so that it may shine to all who are in the house: So the light, that is, the doctrine of Christ apprehended by true faith, and faith apprehending the doctrine of Christ, ought to shine before men, so that they may see your good works, etc. From which light not only are the Apostles called the light of the world, who, because they believed, were bound to hold a torch for others in that, and thus to shine before others equally by good works, but also all the faithful are called light, in the Lord, Ephesians 5:8. As light shines by its own nature, and cannot not shine, unless it is hindered (as when it is placed under a bushel), if faith is light, it never is, nor can it be, without the shining of good works, which can no more be absent from faith than splendor from light. Externally it can be hindered from shining before men, yet it shines in the heart of the faithful before God: and by the intention of God it ought to shine also before men, so that others may see our good works and glorify God. What has this to do with the perpetual visibility of the Church?

Latin:

Vers. 15.

Μόδιον] μοδίς vox quanquam Græcis minus usitata, ex Græcia tamen in Latium venit. Nam & Dinarchus ea utitur. Credibile est è Matthæo scriptum סְאָא quod hic habet Syrus, quando & Hieronymus in veteri fœdere סְאָא modium vertit.

Καὶ λάμπει] Hebraismus pro ἵνα λάμπῃ recte notatus à veteri latino interprete. Sic candelabrum in medio ta- bernaculo, deinde in media æde templi lucebat.

In repetitione similitudinis Marc. IV. 21. de modio additur, sub lecto, id est, scamno quia Judæi cibum capientes pro scamnis lectulis utebantur. Explicant autem nonnulli λύχνον de verbo DEI in candelabro locando vel fideliter, & assidue popu- lo proponendo, cum B. Polyc. Lyserο in Harm. Evang. CLXI. Alii de doctoribus malunt intellige- re, sub persona Apostolorum indigitatis quod illu- strent orbem doctrinæ, & vitæ splendore, ceu lumina divinitus accensa, in candelabro Ecclesiæ constituta; quemadmodum Chrysostomus de Apo- stolis exposuit: Non modo non latebitis, sed illustra- bitis totum orbem terrarum, ideoque clari per id eritis, atque illustres; Ego quidem lumen accendi, ut autem accensum permaneat, vestri sit studii &c. B. Chemnitius in Harmon. c. LI. Similitudine lu- cernæ sub modio posita docet, propter mundi mali- tiam, probra, & persecutiones ministros verbi non debere defatigari, aut timidiores reddi, ut radios doctrinæ cœlestis vel occultent, vel contrahant. Isi- dorus, DEUS, inquit, λύχνον lumen, id est, Sacerdotem accendit, & candelabro imponit, hoc est sua lucem ferenti Cathedræ, ut dogmatum, & actionum ab omni caligine liberarum splendorem Ec- clesiæ, fulguræ instar, afferat, ut plebs vivifici ful- goris radios spectans ad eos sese dirigat, patremque luminum glorificet. Similiter Hieronymus, B. Hun- nius, Osiander, alii. Nonnulli ad omnes Christi auditores hæc dicta volunt, quibus accedit Gro- tius.

Quum ergo hæc quibusvis Christi auditoribus di- cta sint fatente Grotio, Ecclesiæ visibilitatem per- petuam inde temere probant Papistæ. Obser- vandum autem integram hic traditam esse simili- tudinem, adeoque voce ὕτω v. 16. ἀπόδοσιν hoc modo juxta quosdam, reddi: ut urbs in monte posita non potest abscondi vel latere, & ut candela super candelabrum ponitur, ut omnibus luceat, qui in domo sunt: Sic lux, id est, doctrina Christi vera fide apprehensa, & fides doctrinam Christi ap- prehendens lucere debet coram hominibus, ut videant vestra bona opera &c. A qua luce non tantum Apostoli vocantur lux mundi, qui quod crede- bant ipsi in eo facem præferre aliis, & ita bonis operibus aliis pariter prælucere debebant, sed etiam fideles omnes lux dicuntur, in Domino Ephes. V. 8. Ut lux natura sua lucet, nec potest non lucere, nisi impediatur, (uti cum sub modio ponitur) si fides lux nunquam est, nec esse pot- est sine λάμψει bonorum operum, quæ à fide non magis abesse possunt quam splendor à luce. Ad extra impediri potest, ne luceat coram homi- nibus, lucet tamen in corde fidelium coram DEO: & intentione DEI lucere etiam coram homini- bus debet, ut alii bona opera nostra videant, & DEUM glorificent. Quid hæc ad Ecclesiæ visibi- litatem perpetuam?

## 5:16
Verse 16.

Let them see your good works and let them glorify] There is also here a Hebraism for 'having seen, let them glorify,' but in truth the notion of the word glorifying is not Greek but Hellenistic, according to the authors of the LXX, who thought that the Hebrew באר and כבד were best expressed in this way.

Your Father who is in heaven] Among the names of God which Hebrew commentators hand down is אבינו שבשמים. Although God, as the maker of all, may rightly be called Father for that reason, as 'father of men and gods,' it is apparent, however, from the fact that 'your' is added here, that Christ both here and in other places looked more to the peculiar and truly paternal love with which God pursues those who are studious of piety. Seneca's 'good man, true offspring of God,' in the book On Providence. Furthermore, we said above that the plural word 'heavens' in the speech of the Hellenists signifies that most blessed region which we embrace with the mind alone, the 'intelligible world.' Although God is often said to be 'in the heavens,' this is not to be understood as if God were bounded by any spaces outside himself. For Solomon truly said that God is not comprehended by the visible heaven nor by that supreme heaven, which he calls שמי שמים, I Kings VIII, verse 27. Before things were created, God undoubtedly sufficed for himself as a place; nor when he created things could his own nature be changed or limited by his own workmanship. Rightly, therefore, do the Hebrew masters attribute to God, among other names, מקום; because his immense nature is not held by any place outside himself, and thus he is to himself as it were a place infinitely greater than the things made by him, and containing them more excellently and effectively than a place is accustomed to contain located things: which opinion of the ancient Hebrews Philo explains in this manner: 'Since he is a place (that is, מקום) to himself and is himself full of himself, and is sufficient to fill and contain, but is himself contained by nothing else.' And the same is the opinion of the ancient Christians. 'God contains the whole by his will, greater than the whole, just as in essence, so also in dignity,' as the writer of the responses to the orthodox, question eleven, learnedly discusses. Theophilus in book II against the Gentiles: 'God is not contained, but he himself is the place of all things.' He is said, however, to be 'in the heavens' rather than elsewhere, because just as the majesty of God appears in that region in a singular and extraordinary way, so also we expect the highest rewards from him in that region, at the time when he is going to demonstrate himself to us most fully as both God and Father. But the Greeks also, as they had many things from the East, so they had this too. For they place the seat of the gods above the starry region. Aratus concerning our Eridanus.

--- is carried under the feet of the gods.

Which Callimachus imitated, and from Callimachus, Catullus in the Lock of Berenice:

But although the footprints of the Gods press upon me by night.

PART V. Concerning the purpose of the Lord's coming.

Latin:

Vers. 16.

Ἴδωσιν ὑμῶν τὰ καλὰ ἔργα κὴ δοξάσωσιν] Est & hic He- braismus pro ἰδόντες δοξάσωσι, tum vero vocis δοξάζειν no- tio non Græca est sed Hellenistica auctoribus LXX. qui ita optime putarunt exprimi Hebræum באר & כבד.

Τὸν πατέρα ὑμῶν τὸν ἐν ἐρανοῖς] Inter nomina Dei quæ commentatores Hebræi tradunt est אבינו שבשמים. Quanquam vero Deus omnium opifex, recte eam ob cau- sam pater dici possit, ut πατὴρ ἀνδρῶν τε θεῶντε, apparet tamen ex eo quod hic additur ὑμῶν, Christum & hic & a- liis in locis magis respexisse ad amorem peculiarem vere- que paternum, quo pietatis studiosos Deus prosequitur. Senecæ vir bonus, vera Dei progenies, libro de provi- dentia. Quin vox pluralis ἐρανῶν in Hellenistarum ser- mone significet, supra diximus, nimirum beatissimam illam regionem, quam sola mente complectimur, τὸν κό- σμον τὸν νοητόν. Quanquam autem Deus sæpe dicitur esse ἐν τοῖς ἐρανοῖς, non id tamen intelligendum est quasi DE- US ullis extra se spatiis terminetur. Vere enim dixit Salomo DEUM neque cælo aspectabili neque illo supre- mo cælo, quod שמי שמים vocat, comprehendi, I. Reg. VIII. vers. 27. Ante res conditas DEUS haud du- bie sibi suffecit pro loco: neque cum res condidit natura ipfius immutari aut à sui ipsius opificio limitari potuit. Re- cte ergo Hebræi magistri Deo inter alia nomen tribuunt מקום; quia ipsius immensa natura nullo extra se loco te- netur, atque adeo sibi est quasi locus rebus à se factis infini- to major, easque excellentius & efficacius continens quam locus soleat res locatas: quam Hebræorum veterum sen- tentiam hunc in modum exponit Philo: ἐπεὶ αὐτὸς ἑαυτῷ τόπος (hoc est מקום) κὴ αὐτὸς ἑαυτῦ πλήρης, κὴ ἱκανὰ ὄν- τα πληρῶν κὴ περιέχων, αὐτος δ᾽ ὑπ᾿ ἐδενὸς ἄλλε περιεχόμε- νον. Eademque veterum Christianorum sententia. Θεὸς περιέχει τῇ βελήσει τὸ πᾶν, μείζων τᾶ παντὸς, ὥσπερ τῇ ἐσίᾳ, ὕτως κὴ τῇ ἀξίᾳ, ut docte disserit scriptor responsio- num ad orthodoxos quæst. undecima. Theophilus li- bro II. adversus gentes: Θεὸς ὀ χωρεῖται ἀλλὰ αὐτός ἐστι τόπος τῶν ὅλων. Dicitur tamen ἐν ἐρανοῖς esse potius quam alibi, quia sicut in illa regione majestas Dei singulari & eximio modo apparet, ita & olim in ea regione summa ab ipso præmia expectamus, tunc cum se plenissime no- bis & Deum & Patrem est demonstraturus. Sed & Græci ut multa ex Oriente, ita hoc quoque habuerunt. Nam sedem Deorum ponunt supra sideream regionem. Ara- tus de Eridano nostro.

--- Θεῶν ὑπὸ ποσσὶ φορεῖται.

Quod imitatus est Callimachus & ex Callimacho Catullus in coma Berenices:

Sed quanquam me nocte premunt vestigia Divum.

PARS V. De fine adventus Domini.

## 5:17
Verse 17.

To abolish] What is here 'to abolish,' is called 'to loosen' below in the nineteenth verse. It is indeed true that 'to loosen the law' is often used by Demosthenes for 'to abrogate.' But here that word must be taken a little more loosely, for that which is to oppose the law by deeds or words. Such is that 'the scripture cannot be loosened' in John chapter ten, verse thirty-five, and that he is said 'to loosen the Sabbath' who acts against the Sabbath, chapter five, verse eighteen. Indeed, that very 'to loosen the law' is clearly taken in this way in John VII. 23, for which Paul also said 'to make void the law' in Romans III. 31. And that this is the true explanation of this passage is shown by what follows in the nineteenth verse, where 'to do and to teach' is opposed to 'to loosen.' But here the Jews rise up against us, crying out that that [was done] by the Apostles against this profession of the Master. But that they are mistaken through ignorance of our affairs may be evident from this, that the Apostles consecrated these very words of the Lord to memory, which they would never have done if their own teachings had disagreed with this teaching. Add that that very Apostle, than whom no one more constantly defended Christian liberty against the necessity of Hebrew rites, he says the same thing about himself that the master had said: do we then make void the law through faith? God forbid: yea, we establish the law. But he is the same person who says elsewhere that Christ abolished the law of commandments contained in ordinances, Ephes. II. 15. Again, what this Christ had said here, that he had come to fulfill the law, this also that preeminent one of the Apostles acknowledges more than once, as when he calls Christ the end of the law, Rom. X. 4, and the law a schoolmaster unto Christ, Galat. III. 25. Now indeed in the Apostolic writings it is where you may find the law called spiritual, Rom. VII. 14, and it is again where it is called the law of a carnal commandment, Hebr. VII. 13. Wherefore, since it can occur to no sane person that grave men, and so constant in the defense of their doctrine, wrote things contradictory not only to others but to themselves, it must be seen how those statements agree among themselves. First, therefore, it is most well known that one kind of law is natural, perpetual, and common to all, and another is constituted, which is usually peculiar and mutable: such is the law proper to each people which we call civil. Natural law, that is, the prescription of right reason, regards the mind chiefly, and estimates external actions from the mind. Civil law indeed tends to the same, but since it cannot obtain that through the depravity of men, it is content with exterior innocence: and, which is necessary to be done among men, it measures the mind from deeds. Therefore it is placed chiefly for the body, and deals with things insofar as they can be seen by the eyes and touched by the hands. It does not punish intentions and attempts, except in the most atrocious matters. Hence Seneca says that to be good according to the law is a small thing. And while that perpetual law strives to make men good through the love of virtue, this civil law restrains the bad through the fear of punishment, for which law there would have been no need if men had obeyed the sincere precepts of nature (that is, of reason illuminated and aided by God): But since parents were producing offspring daily more vicious, the rising malice had to be curbed, and the traces of knowledge, which corrupt custom had almost obliterated, had to be revived. Therefore, because of transgressions the law was added: that is, the law written on tablets was added to that law written in the minds, Galat. III. vers. 19. And indeed, what Paul said concerning the law of Moses, the law is not made for a righteous man, I. Tim. I. vers. 9, this Socrates had pronounced in general concerning civil law, that law was not made for the sake of good men. Nay, civil laws are even forced to connive at certain lesser external offenses, lest the edge of public authority grow dull with vain effort against grown vices. The law of Moses, therefore, since it was given to one Israelite people, no less than human civil laws, had to have certain things transferred from natural law, but certain things proper and accommodated to that people and those times. Josephus acknowledges this distinction in his ancestral law, discussing that matter accurately in Antiquities XVI. cap. X., where he calls that constituted law customs, but that perpetual law partly that which is common to all for the sake of virtue and alone sufficient to preserve the life of men, which law he says is especially regarded by the law. The teachers of the Hebrews wish these to be properly called commandments, but those statutes, as will be said in the beginning regarding Luke. Justin in his dialogue with Trypho clearly places the same distinction before the eyes of the Jew. when he says that some things are universally and by nature eternally good, which those who performed them of old will have brought back a glory common with Christians, but others were ordained because of the hardness of the heart of the people (he could have added and because of the occasions of times and places). Thus also in the constitutions which are called those of Clement, in many places the natural things of the law and the superadded things are distinguished. As therefore before the law was established, true piety, or trust in God effective through charity, was that which made a man most acceptable to GOD, so in the law itself GOD wished the traces of that approval to exist. Therefore he demands to be loved with an entire heart, he wants the heart to be circumcised, and whatever other things are of that form. But all this, as I said, is transferred, and is not properly a part of that law which was civil, but the scope and purpose, just as in the laws of Zaleucus and Charondas and the XII Tables certain things were inserted pertaining to the purity of the mind. This is apparent from the sanction of the law which was civil. For it threatened capital punishment to lawbreakers: but it is so far from the case that such punishment was inflicted on those sinning within the mind, that even certain external offenses were expiated by victims or scourging. But this that civil law had above human laws, that it provided not only impunity but also a long and prosperous life to those obeying, that is, living according to the norm of the law. But the law of Christ, as it has a graver threat, namely of perpetual punishment, Hebr. II. vers. 3, so it is also confirmed by better promises, Hebr. VII. vers. 10, namely of the heavenly kingdom. Let us see now what it is that Christ says he came to fulfill the law.

The scope of the law was to make men as good as possible, such as they become by the reverence of God and the mutual charity of men among themselves. These two greatest commandments of the law Christ calls Matth. XXII. vers. 37, 38, 39. Nay, he says that on these depend the whole law and the Prophets, 40. Paul says the law is fulfilled by loving another man, Rom. XIII. vers. 8, Gal. V. vers. 14. And James says the royal law is perfected by the same love, adding according to the scripture, understanding the books of the old covenant. But what was indeed shown by the law, yet in the time of the law was performed by few even in the Israelite people itself, that Christ brought about so that all believing in him could perform it, and that not by the force of the law (which restrained the bad more than it made them good), but by the peculiar aids of God, promising the remission of all preceding sins, making certain the faith of blessed immortality, and pouring out abundantly the fullness of his spirit. It appears, therefore, how Christ not only did not overturn that which was principal and immutable in the law, but also established and confirmed it. Moreover, the other law which we said was constituted pertains partly to divine worship, partly to civil society. Let us speak first of the law pertaining to divine worship, which it is permitted to call ritual or pontifical law. This law, therefore, Christ attacked neither by example nor by doctrine. For while He lived a mortal life on earth, He Himself obeyed the prescribed rites and was the author for other Hebrews to do likewise, as is to be seen below in chapter VIII, verse 4, and XXVI, verse 18. But that this law later vanished, happened from the very nature of the law itself. For it was not such that it pleased God in itself, but was adapted to the character of the people and to those times. For by those sacred rites and ceremonies, GOD wished to segregate the Israelite people, too prone to the contagions of superstition, from other nations, and to keep them occupied so that they would not lapse into the worship of false deities. Wherefore, when the time predicted by so many prophecies had come, in which other nations would coalesce with pious Jews into the worship of the one true God, with the promise of circumcision fulfilled and the cause of the law ceasing, it was right that the ritual law should also cease. For this law had been given until that Seed promised to Abraham should come, Galatians III, verse 16. And the Prophets had indicated this very thing not obscurely, foretelling a new covenant and sacrifices not restricted to any place, and to be performed with the mind; and Christ, agreeing with the Prophets, when He said that the time was imminent in which GOD would be worshipped no less elsewhere than in Jerusalem, in spirit and in truth. There was, therefore, no need for the law to be abrogated, which, having been constituted for a time, vanished with the maturity of time itself: just as laws proper to times of war fade away of their own accord once peace is made. There was only need for this peace of the Jews and the nations to be promulgated: which Christ did, both by His own voice, when He was about to depart from His disciples, and by signs sent from heaven, and openly by the spirit, the worker of miracles, given not only to the Jews but also to the foreigners who had believed in Him. Nothing, therefore, was done by Christ against the ritual law, just as he who sanctions and promulgates peace does not act against the laws pertaining to times of war. Indeed, this law also was ἐπληρώθη by Christ, first because He both obeyed it and commanded it to be obeyed, as long as the author of the law wished that law to be valid; then because He led men to the pure and pious veneration of God, which was the only thing that had been proposed principally to God, whereas the rites of sacrifices were instituted only on occasion. Moses Maimonides ingenuously confesses, and proves his opinion with these words of Jeremiah: I did not deal with your ancestors nor did I give them commandments concerning burnt offerings and victims on the day I led them out of Egypt, but this is what I commanded them, that they should listen to my voice and I would be their GOD and they would be my people, VII, verse 22, 23; in which very place Justin Martyr proves the same thing against Trypho. But in order that this πλήρωσις might be more conspicuous, the best and greatest GOD wished almost every circumstance of the Jewish rites to correspond to the affairs of Christ. And thus it is easy to demonstrate, as that same Martyr says, that πάντα τὰ ὑπὸ Μωσέως διαταχθέντα are types and symbols and announcements of the things that were to happen to Christ, and of those who were foreknown to believe in Him, and of those things that were likewise to happen to Christ Himself. Wherefore, what Christ says about the prophecies, that it was necessary for them to be fulfilled in Him, can also be referred in its own way to the ceremonies. But the Epistle to the Hebrews will provide the material for treating that matter more accurately. There remain the institutions pertaining to civil society. In these, however, the very necessity of the republic demands everywhere among nations that many things which are not approved in themselves by the authors of the laws should nevertheless be permitted, lest an occasion be given for greater evils, or even lest laws become cheapened without morals. For which reason Cicero holds the opinion that it should be said as in the dregs of Romulus, not as in Plato's Republic. But even Plato himself, when he had fashioned a certain commonwealth from his own genius, with no regard for men, subsequently described another in his laws which he calls hypothetical. Another man, when asked if he had set the most beautiful laws for the citizens, replied: Not the most beautiful absolutely, but the most beautiful of those he could. If, therefore, anyone does not use such institutions as necessity expressed to the author of the laws, or even renders others so good that they do not wish to use them, he certainly commits nothing either against the words of the law or against its intent: indeed, he is to be judged to be doing what is most pleasing to the author of the law. For, as it was most truly written by Aristotle, the purpose of all authors of laws is to make citizens good. But as for other institutions which could seem indifferent to true virtue, Christ nowhere opposed them: indeed, he himself obeyed them, and taught his disciples to obey the laws of any commonwealth whatsoever, however human they may be. The writer to Diognetus says well of the Christians: They obey the established laws, and by their own lives they surpass the laws. But if Christians are commanded to obey human laws of that kind, much more so those which had God as their author. Yet even this law died out, when, as a punishment for the stubbornness of the Jews, whatever remained of the commonwealth was extinguished: because once that which is principal is removed, it is necessary that the accessories also perish. Wherefore Christ did not oppose even this part of the law: indeed, since all institutions of that kind tend toward fostering concord among citizens, he himself, by turning the minds of men toward true peace, fulfilled the purpose of that part as well.

The obedience which the law required was not rendered by a few, but by none, nor can it even now be rendered, as the Apostle testifies in Rom. 8:3. And therefore there was need for the mission of Christ, that he himself might fulfill the law for us. Christ did not, therefore, perform it so that we might fulfill the law, but since this is impossible for us after the fall, he fulfilled the law in our place, and bestows his own righteousness upon us. For he himself is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes, Rom. 10:4. Nor did Christ promise only the remission of sins or immortal life: but he acquired the same for us, and because he acquired it, he makes us partakers of it, not only making us certain of it by the sealing of the Spirit, as many as believe in him. Because he is our savior both by merit and by efficacy. Grotius's explanation is too jejune and Pelagianizing and Socinianizing: which is also what he adds further on toward the end of this section, teaching: We see, he says, that the Apostles agree excellently with themselves and among themselves and with Christ. For those things which are in the law, as Justin speaks, natural according to the law, and just, the natural things of the law, as Irenaeus speaks in book IV, chapter XXVII, Christ perfected, explaining them more clearly than they had ever been explained before, and fortifying them with certain more exact precepts, and bringing minds into obedience to them by the magnitude and certainty of the promises, and the sealing of his own Spirit. And this is that perfect law, as James calls it, 1:25.

James says nothing about the more exact precepts of Christ, which is the gloss of Bellarmine, Lorinus, Justinianus, Guilbelmus Estius, Cornelius à Lapide, the Papists; Socinus, Ostorodius, Smalcius, and other Socinians: but it is clearly contrary to the perfection of the law, inasmuch as it was the most absolute form of all thoughts, words, and deeds, requiring not only the most perfect cleanliness of all external actions, but also of the internal affections and movements of any kind, Deut. 6:5, Rom. 7:14, admitting neither addition nor subtraction, Deut. 4 and 12. By the perfect law of liberty, the doctrine of the Gospel is understood, which is also called the law of the Spirit of life, Rom. 8:2, the law of faith, Rom. 3:27, just as the law of Moses is the law of fear and death, 2 Cor. 3:6, 7, the law of works, Rom. 3:27, the law of servitude, Gal. 4:24. Those two epithets teach this. For the law is called perfect because it renders a man perfect, but the law of works does not make anyone perfect, Heb. 7:19, but the doctrine of the Gospel, which both promises and effects perfection, Col. 1:28, Heb. 1:14. It is called the law of liberty because it fully and perfectly frees from the law of death, Rom. 9:2. Nor can what Grotius hands down concerning the end of the Ceremonial law be simply approved; that by those sacred rites and ceremonies God wished to segregate the Israelite people, too prone to the contagions of superstition, from other nations, and to keep them occupied, lest they should fall away to the worship of false gods. And that he says the rites of sacrifices were instituted merely from occasion: For the ceremonial law was not instituted primarily because God wished to accommodate himself to the character of the people and those times, lest they should deflect to superstitions and the worship of false gods, nor were those rites instituted merely from occasion: but by the singular economy of God it pleased him that his mysteries be dispensed to the people before the coming of Christ, and to exhibit in types and figures the substance which we have in Christ: which cause was more principal than that Grotian condescension. Which not even Grotius himself could deny, page 65, thus differing concerning the fulfillment of the ceremonial law after those things which he had warned a little earlier regarding the passage of James 1:25:

But Christ fulfilled and consummated the rites by exhibiting that for the sake of which the rites were devised, and which the rites themselves figured. But he abolished the same by that very fulfillment and consummation, not by removing the bond of the law, but by withdrawing the cause on account of which that law was born, and to which, as it was dying, it was destined to die together by the primordial decree.

And page 64. But in order that this πλήρωσις (fulfillment) might be more conspicuous, God, the best and greatest, willed that almost every single circumstance of the Jewish rites should correspond to the things of Christ. And thus it is easy to demonstrate, as that same martyr (Justin) says, πάντα τὰ ὑπὸ Μώσεως διαταχθέντα &c. (all things ordained by Moses, etc.). Wherefore, what Christ says concerning the prophecies, that it was necessary for them to be πληρωθῆναι (fulfilled) in him, the same can also be referred in its own way to the ceremonies. Finally, one must also observe that Grotian reconciliation, how the νόμος (law) is called πνευματικὸς (spiritual) in Rom. VII. 14, and yet is also called νόμος ἐντολῆς σαρκικῆς (law of a carnal commandment) in Heb. VII. 11.

νόμος πνευματικὸς (spiritual law), (thus he continues here) is so called because of that goal toward which it is directed. It is also called σαρκικὸς (carnal) because of the rites viewed in themselves, which protect the body from punishment, but do not perfect the spirit of man. Heb. VII. verse 11, IX. verse 9.

Grotius undoubtedly confuses the ἱερατικὴν (priestly) and ἠθικὴν (moral) law, the ceremonial and the moral: the Apostle treats of the moral in Rom. VII. v. 14, which is spiritual not only τελικῶς (finally) or by way of the goal toward which it is directed by itself, but also ὐσιωδῶς (essentially) or formally; because it is a certain ἀπεικόνισμα (image) of divine holiness: but the ceremonial is treated in Heb. VII. verse 16, which is called the law of a carnal commandment, not because it only protected the body from punishment—since the sacrifices also brought the remission of sins, by the virtue of the antitype, through faith, offered into the propitiatory sacrifice of Christ, even if, viewed in themselves, they could not, ex opere operato (by the work performed), as the scholastics barbarously speak, τῇ συνειδήσει τελειῶσαι τὸν λητρέυοντα (perfect the worshiper in conscience) Heb. IX. verse 9—but because the ἱερατικὴ (priestly) law was occupied with carnal rites, which were a shadow of spiritual things, Heb. X. 1.

[or the prophets] The prophets are viewed here not only as foretellers of future things, but also as interpreters of the law and daily reminders. In which sense the law and the Prophets are said to depend on the commandment of love, Matt. XXII. 40. The law and the Prophets are distinguished by Christ: and therefore they are not to be rashly confounded: and since Christ not only fulfilled the law by his coming, but also the Prophetic predictions, which sounded primarily of him, Acts X. v. 43, why should not the Prophets, as to their proper office, which was to prophesy, be understood here, by which they were distinguished from the law: since indeed Christ had to fulfill both the law by obedience both active and passive, in our place, and thus to provide the fulfillment for the predictions of the Prophets, who had borne witness of him. And therefore B. Chemnitius, Osiander, Hunnius, and others not undeservedly understand their predictions by the Prophets.

Latin:

Vers. 17.

Καταλῦσαι] Quod hic καταλύειν, infra λύειν dicitur commate decimo nono. Est quidem λύειν νόμον sæpe a- pud Demosthenem abrogare. Sed hic vox ista laxius pau- lo sumenda est, pro eo quod est legem oppugnare factis dictisve. Tale est illud ἐ δύναται λυθῆναι ἡ γραφὴ Joan- nis capite decimo, versu trigesimo quinto, & quod λύειν τὸ σάββατον dicitur qui contra Sabbatum facit, capite quin- to, versu decimo octavo. Imo illud ipsum λύειν τὸ νόμον apertum est ita sumi Johannis VII. 23. pro quo & καταρ- γεῖν τὸν νόμον dixit Paulus Rom. III. 31. Atque hanc ve- ram esse hujus loci explicationem, ostendit id quod sequi- tur commate decimo nono, ubi ποιεῖν κὴ διδάσκειν opponitur tur τῷ λύειν. Sed hic insurgunt in nos Judæi clamitantes istum ab Apostolis contra hanc magistri professionem. Sed labi illos rerum nostrarum ignorantia vel hinc pateat, quod hæc ipsa Domini verba Apostoli memoriæ consecra- runt, nunquam id facturi, si ipsorum documenta ab hoc documento discrepaffent. Adde quod ille ipse Apo- stolus, quo nemo constantius libertatem Christianam contra necessitatem Hebraicorum rituum defendit, idem de se dicit quod magister dixerat: νόμον ἐ͂ν καταργε͂μεν διὰ τῆς πίςεως; μὴ γένοιτο ἀλλὰ νόμον ἱςῶμεν. At idem est qui alibi dicit Christum νόμον τῶν ἐντολῶν ἐν δόγμασι καταργῆσαι Ephes. II. 15. Rursum quod hic Christus di- xerat venisse se πληρῶσαι τὸν νόμον, hoc & ille Apostolo- rum eximius non semel agnoscit, ut cum Christum vo- cat τέλος τε͂ νόμε Rom. X. 4. & νόμον παιδαγωγὸν εἰς χρι- ςόν, Galat. III. 25. Jam vero in scriptis Apostolicis est ubi invenias νόμον dici πνευματικὸν Rom. VII. 14. est ite- rum ubi vocatur νόμος ἐντολῆς σαρκικῆς Hebr. VII. 13. Quare cum sano nemini in mentem venire possit viros graves & in defensione doctrinae suae adeo constantes, non modo alios aliis, sed ipsos sibimet pugnantia scripsisse, vi- dendum est quomodo dicta ista inter se consentiant. Pri- mum igitur notissimum est jus aliud esse naturale, perpe- tuum, commune omnibus, aliud constitutum, quod ple- rumque solet esse peculiare ac mutabile: quale est jus po- puli cujusque proprium quod civile vocamus. Jus natu- rale, hoc est, rectae rationis praescriptum, animum praecipue respicit, & externas actiones ex animo aestimat. Jus civile eodem quidem tendit, sed cum id per homi- num pravitatem obtinere nequeat, contentum est ex- teriori innocentia: &, quod inter homines fieri necesse est, animum ex factis metitur. Itaque corpori praeci- pue ponitur, & de rebus agit quatenus cerni oculis ma- nibusque tangi possunt. Consilia conatumque non pu- nit, nisi in rebus atrocissimis. Hinc Seneca exiguam rem esse dicit ad legem bonum esse. Cumque perpetuum il- lud jus bonos certet efficere virtutis amore, hoc civile ma- los formidine poenae coercet, quo jure opus non fuisset, si homines sinceris naturae (id est rationis a Deo illuminatae atque adjutae) praeceptis obtemperassent: Sed cum paren- tes darent progeniem indies vitiosiorem, refraenanda fuit gliscens malitia, & resuscitanda notitiae vestigia, quae prava consuetudo paene obliteraverat. Ergo παραβάσεων χ́αριν νόμος προσετίθη: id est, addita est lex scripta in ta- bulis ad legem illam in mentibus scriptam Galat. III. vers. 19. Atque adeo quod de lege Mosis dixit Paulus δικαίω νόμος ȣ̓ κεῖται I. Tim. I. vers. 9. hoc in universum de lege civili Socrates pronuntiaverat νόμον ἕνεκα ἀγαθῶν ȣ̓ γενέ- σθαι. Quin ad minora etiam quaedam delicta externa connivere coguntur leges civiles, ne irrito adversum ad- ulta vitia nisu hebescat acies publicae auctoritatis. Lex igitur Mosis, cum data sit uni populo Israelitico, non minus quam leges civiles humanae, habere debuit quae- dam tralatitia ex jure naturali, quaedam vero propria isti populo istisque temporibus accommodata. Agnoscit hoc discrimen in lege patria Josephus accurate ea de re disserens Originum XVI. cap. X. ubi illud jus constitu- tum vocat τὰ ἔθη, illud autem perpetuum partim τὰ πρὸς καλοκαγαθίαν κοινὸν ἅπασι κ' μόνον ἱκανὸν διασώζειν τὸν τῶν ἀνθρώπων βίον, quod quidem jus potissimum a lege ait respici. Hebraeorum magistri haec proprie volunt di- ci מצות, illa vero חקים ut initio ad Lucam dicetur. Justinus in colloquio cum Tryphone idem discrimen cla- re Judaeo ob oculos ponit. cum alia ait esse καθόλȣ κ' φύ- σει αἰώνια καλὰ, quae qui olim praestiterunt, communem cum Christianis gloriam erunt reportaturi, alia vero πρὸς σκληροκαρδίαν τȣ͂ λαȣ͂ (addere poterat & ob occasio- nes temporum ac locorum) διαταχθέντα. Sic & in constitutionibus quae dicuntur Clementis plurimis locis distinguuntur τὰ φυσικὰ τȣ͂ νόμȣ & τὰ ἐπείσακτα. Sicut igitur ante legem conditam, vera pietas, sive fiducia in Deum per caritatem efficax, id fuit quod hominem DEO acceptissimum faceret, ita in ipsa lege voluit DEUS exstare ejus ἐυδοκίας vestigia. Itaque amari se integro corde postulat, cor vult circumcidi, & quae alia sunt ad eam formam. Sed hoc omne ut dixi trala- titium est, neque pars proprie legis ejus quae erat civilis, sed scopus atque propositum, quomodo & in Zaleuci & in Charondae legibus & XII. tabulis quaedam inferta erant ad animi castimoniam pertinentia. Apparet hoc ex sanctione legis quae erat civilis. Ea enim capita- le supplicium legirupis minabatur: tantum autem ab- est, ut intra animum peccantibus tale supplicium irro- gatum fuerit, ut etiam externa quaedam delicta victi- mis aut verberibus expiarentur. Hoc vero praeceptum habebat lex illa civilis supra humanas leges, quod obse- quentibus, hoc est, ad legis normam viventibus non tantum impunitatem sed & vitam longam atque prospe- ram praestabat. At Christi lex, ut comminationem graviorem habet, perpetui scilicet supplicii, Hebr. II. vers. 3. ita & melioribus promissis firmata est, Hebr. VII. vers. 10. nimirum regni coelestis. Videamus nunc quid sit quod Christus dicit se venisse νόμον πληρῶσαι.

Legis scopus erat homines quam optimos efficere, quales fiunt Dei reverentia & caritate mutua hominum inter se. Hæc duo maxima legis præcepta vocat Christus Matth. XXII. vers. 37. 38. 39. Imo ait hinc pendere le- gem totam & Prophetas, 40. Paulus diligendo homi- nem alterum legem ait πληρῦσθαι Rom. XIII. vers. 8. Gal. V. vers. 14. Et Jacobus legem regiam ait τελεῖσθαι ea- dem dilectione, addens κατὰ τὴν γραφὴν, veteris fe- deris libros intelligens. Sed quod lege monstrabatur quidem, legis tamen tempore à paucis in ipso etiam Is- raëlitico populo præstabatur, id ut omnes in se credentes præstare possent, Christus effecit, idque non vi legis (quæ malos coërcebat magis quam faciebat bonos,) sed pecu- liaribus Dei præsidiis, remissionem promittens antece- dentium peccatorum omnium, certam faciens fidem beatæ immortalitatis, & large effundens spiritus sui co- piam. Apparet igitur quomodo Christus id quod in lege erat præcipuum atque immutabile, non modo non e- verterit, sed & stabiliverit atque confirmaverit. Jus autem alterum quod constitutum diximus, partim ad cultum divinum, partim ad societatem civilem pertinet. Agamus primum de jure ad cultum divinum pertinen- te, quod rituale aut pontificium jus liceat vocare. Hoc igitur jus Christus neque exemplo neque doctrina oppugnavit. Nam dum in terris vitam vixit mortalem, & ipse præscriptis ritibus paruit & aliis Hebræis ut itidem facerent autor fuit, ut videre est infra cap. VIII. vers. 4. XXVI. vers. 18. Quod vero postea id jus evanuit, fa- ctum est ex ipsius juris natura. Neque enim tale erat ut Deo per se placeret, sed populi ingenio temporibus- que illis aptatum. Nam sacris illis cæremoniisque popu- lum Israëliticum, nimis patentem ad superstitionis con- tagia, DEUS ab aliis gentibus segregare voluit, & occupatum distinere ne ad falsorum numinum cultum deficeret. Quare cum venisset tempus tot vaticiniis prædictum, quo gentes aliæ cum piis Judæis in unius veri Dei cultum coalescerent, impleta circumcisionis promissione, legis causa cessante, æquum erat legem quoque ritualem cessare. Data enim hæc lex erat us- que dum veniret Semen illud Abrahamo promissum, Galat. III. vers 16. Et hoc ipsum non obscure in- dicaverant Prophetæ, novum fœdus, sacrificiaque nul- li loco adstricta, & animo peragenda prænuntiantes, & Prophetis consentiens Christus, cum diceret immi- nere tempus quo DEUS coleretur non alibi minus quam Hierosolymis, in spiritu & veritate. Nihil igitur o- pus fuit legem antiquari quæ ad tempus constituta ipsa temporis maturitate evanuit: sicut leges propriæ belli temporibus pace facta sponte sua exolescunt. Tan- tum opus erat pacem hanc Judæorum & gentium pro- mulgari: quod fecit Christus tum voce sua, jam à di- scipulis discessurus, tum visis cœlitus missis, tum palam spiritu miraculorum opifice dato non tantum Judæis, sed & alienigenis qui in ipsum crediderant. Nihil ergo à Christo factum est contra legem ritualem, sic- ut nec contra leges ad belli tempora pertinentes facit qui pacem sancit atque promulgat. Imo jus hoc quoque à Christo ἐπληρώθη, primum quia & paruit ei & pareri præcepit, quamdiu jus illud valere juris auctor voluit; deinde quia homines perduxit ad puram piamque Dei venerationem, quod solum principaliter Deo fuisse propositum, sacrificiorum autem ritus ex occasione dun- taxat institutos. Moses Maimonides ingenue fatetur, probatque sententiam suam his Jeremiæ verbis: Non egi cum majoribus vestris neque præcepta ipsis dedi de holo- caustis & victimis quo die eos ex Ægypto duxi, sed hoc est quod eis præcepi, ut voci meæ auscultarent egoque essem eis DEUS & ipsi essent mihi populus, VII. vers. 22. 23. quo ipso loco adversus Tryphonem idem probat Justinus martyr. Ut autem πλήρωσις ista magis esset conspicua, voluit DEUS optimus maximus singulas prope circum- stantias Judaicorum rituum congruere rebus Christi. Atque adeo demonstratu facile est ut inquit idem ille Martyr, πάντα τὰ ὑπὸ Μωσέως διαταχθέντα esse τύπυς καὶ σύμβολα καὶ καταγγελίας τῶν τῷ χριστῷ γίνεσθαι μελλόν- των, καὶ τῶν εἰς αὐτὸν πιστεύειν προεγνωσμένων καὶ τῶν ὑπ' αὐτῶ τῷ χριστῷ ὁμοίως γίνεσθαι μελλόντων. Quare quod de vaticiniis dicit Christus oportuisse ea in se πληρωθῆναι, idem ad ceremonias etiam suo modo referri potest. Sed ejus rei accuratius tractandæ materiam præbebit Episto- la ad Hebræos. Restant instituta ad societatem civi- lem pertinentia. In his autem exigit ubique gentium ipsa reipublicæ necessitas, ut multa quæ per se non probantur legum auctoribus, permittantur tamen ne majoribus malis detur occasio, aut etiam ne vilescant sine moribus leges. Quamobrem Cicero sententiam vult dici ut in fæce Romuli, non ut in Platonis Politia. Sed & ipse Plato cum finxisset quandam ex suo ingenio rempublicam, nullo ad homines respectu, aliam deinde descripsit in legibus quam vocat ἐξ ὑποθέσεως. Alius qui- dam interrogatus εἰ τοὺς καλλίστους ἔθετο τοῖς πολίταις νόμους re- spondit ὦ τοὺς καθάπαξ καλλίστους, ἀλλ᾽ ὧν ἐδυνάτο τοὺς καλλίστους. Talibus ergo institutis, quæ legum auctori expressit necessi- tas, si quis non utitur, aut alios etiam tam bonos red- dit, ut uti eis nolint, nihil profecto committit aut con- tra legis verba, aut contra sententiam: imo vero cen- sendus est id facere quod legis auctori maxime placet. Nam, ut ab Aristotele verissime scriptum est, omnibus legum auctoribus propositum est cives bonos efficere. Cætera vero instituta quæ ad veram virtutem videri pote- rant ἀδιάφορα, Christus nusquam oppugnavit: imo ipse eis paruit, & discipulos docuit cujusque reipublicæ legi- bus, quantum libet humanis, obedire. Bene de Christianis scriptor ad Diognetum: πείθονται τοῖς ὡρισ- μένοις νόμοις καὶ τοῖς ἰδίοις βίοις νικῶσι τοὺς νόμους. Quod si humanis ejus generis legibus parere jussi sunt Christiani, multo magis iis quæ Deum habebant auctorem. Atta- men hoc etiam jus emortuum est, cum in pœnam Iudæo- rum contumacis, extinctum est quicquid reipublicæ re- stabat: quia sublato eo quod principale est, necesse est et- iam accesiones corruere. Quare ne hanc quidem ju- ris partem Christus oppugnavit: imo cum omnia ejus generis instituta tendant ad alendam civium inter se con- cordiam, ipse ad veram pacem hominum animos flecten- do, propositum istius etiam partis implevit.

Quam lex requirebat obedientiam, ea non à paucis, sed à nullis præstita est, aut etiamnum præstari potest, teste Apostolo Rom. IIX. v. 3. Id- eoque opus fuit missione Christi, ut pro nobis i- pse legem impleret. Non ergo præstitit Chri- stus, ut nos legem impleamus, sed quum hoc ἀ- δυνάτον nobis sit post lapsum, legem nostri loco implevit, suamque justitiam nobis donat. Ipse enim est τὸ τέλος νόμου ad justitiam omni credenti Rom. X. vers. 4. Neque vero Christus solum remissionem peccatorum, aut vitam immortalem promisit: sed eandem acquisivit nobis, & quia ac- quisivit, participes nos reddit, non solum certos de ea facit, Spiritus obsignatione, quotquot in ipsum credimus. Quia servator noster est tum merito, tum efficacia. Jejuna nimis & Pela- gianizans atque Socinizans est explicatio Grotii: quod etiam quæ porro sub finem hujus commatis subjungit, docens: Videmus, inquit, optime consentire Apostolos secum & inter se & cum Christo. Nam illa, quæ in le- ge sunt, ut Iustinus loquitur, φύσει κατὰ νόμον ὄντα, καὶ δί- καια, naturalia legis, ut loquitur Irenæus libro IV. capite XXVII. perfecit Christus, explicans ea clarius, quam an- te unquam explicatæ fuerant, & præceptis quibusdam exactioribus muniens, & in eorum obsequium animos redigens, promissorum magnitudine & certitudine, spi- ritusque sui obsignatione. Atque hic est νόμος ille τέλειος, ut eum appellat Iacobus I. 25.

Nihil de exactioribus Christi præceptis Jaco- bus, quæ Bellarmini, Lorini, Justinianei, Guil- bel. Estii, Cornelii à Lapide, Papistarum; Soci- ni, Ostorodi, Smalcii aliorumque Socinistarum glossa est: sed perfectioni legis plane contraria, utpote quæ forma fuit omnium cogitationum, dictorum, & factorum, absolutissima, non tan- tum externam actionum omnium, sed internam etiam quorumvis affectuum, ac motuum mundi- tiem perfectissimam requirens Deut. VI. 5. Rom. VII. 14. nec προσθέσεως, nec ἀφαιρέσεως admittens Deuter. IV. & XII. Per legem libertatis perfectam doctrina Evangelii intelligitur, quæ etiam voca- tur lex Spiritus vitæ Rom. VIII. vers. 2. lex fidei Rom. III. vers. 27. quemadmodum lex Mosis est lex metus & mortis 2. Corinth. III. vers. 6. 7. lex operum Rom. III. vers. 2. lex servitutis Gal. IV. vers. 24. Docent id duo illa Epitheta. Lex e- nim perfecta dicitur, quod hominem perfectum reddat, at lex operum non præstat quenquam per- fectum Ebr. VII. 19. sed doctrina Evangelii, quæ & pollicerur & efficit perfectionem Col. I. vers. 28. Ebr. I. vers. 14. Vocatur eo lex libertatis quia à lege mortis plene & perfectè liberat Rom. IX. vers. 2. Neque simpliciter probari potest, quod de fine legis Ceremonialis tradit Grotius; quod sacris illis, ceremoniisque populum Israeliti- cum, nimis patentem ad superstitionis contagia, Deus ab aliis gentibus segregare voluerit, & occupa- tum destinere, ne ad falsorum numinum cultum deficeret. Quodque sacrificiorum ritus ex occasio- ne duntaxat institutos, ait: Nam neque ideo im- primis ceremonialis lex instituta, quod DEUS se ingenio populi, temporibusque illis accommo- dare voluerit, ne ad superstitiones & falsorum numinum cultum deflecterent, nec ex occasione tantum instituti ritus illi sunt: sed ex singulari Dei ὀικονομίᾳ ita placuit, mysteria sua populo dispensari, ante adventum Christi, & in typis ac figuris substantiam, quam in Christo habemus, exhibere: quæ causa magis præcipua erat, quam συγκατάβασις illa Grotiana. Quod nec ipse Grotius diffiteri potuit pag. 65. ita de imple- tione legis ceremonialis post illa, quæ paulo an- te circa locum Jacobi I. 25. monuerat differens:

Ritus autem implevit & consummavit Christus, id exhibendo, cujus causa ritus erant reperti, quodque ritus ipsi figurabant. Delevit autem eosdem eo ipso imple- mento ac consummatione, non tollendo legis vinculum, sed causam subtrahendo, propter quam lex ea nata, & cui morienti ex primævo decreto erat commoritura.

Et pag. 64. Ut autem πλήρωσις ista magis es- set conspicua, voluit Deus optimus maximus singulas prope circumstantias Judaicorum rituum congruere rebus Christi. Atque adeo demon- stratu facile est, ut inquit idem ille martyr, (Ju- stinus) πάντα τὰ ὑπὸ Μώσεως διαταχθέντα &c. Quare quod de vaticiniis dicit Christus, opor- tuisse ea in se πληρωθῆναι, idem ad ceremonias etiam suo modo referri potest. Observanda tan- dem etiam illa Grotiana conciliatio, quomodo νόμος dicatur πνευματικὸς Rom. VII. 14. & vo- cetur tamen etiam νόμος ἐντολῆς σαρκικῆς Ebr. VII. 11.

νόμος πνευματικὸς, (ita pergit hic) dicitur ob sco- pum illum, in quem dirigitur. Dicitur & σαρκικὸς ob ri- tus in se spectatos, qui corpus à pœna defendunt, cæ- terum spiritum hominis non perficiunt. Hebr. VII. vers. 11. IX. vers. 9.

Nimirum confundit Grotius legem ἱερατικὴν & ἠθικὴν, ceremonialem, & moralem: de morali agit Apostolus Rom.
