VII. v. 14. quæ non tantum τελικῶς s. finaliter ob scopum, quo per se dirigitur, spiritualis est, sed etiam ὐσιωδῶς vel formaliter; quia divinæ sanctitatis quoddam est ἀπεικόνισμα: de Ceremoniali vero agitur Ebr. VII. vers. 16. quæ lex mandati carnalis dicitur, non quod corpus tantum defenderit à pœna, quia remissionem etiam peccatorum adferebant sacrificia, virtute antity- pi, per fidem, in sacrificium Christi propitiato- rium oblata, etsi per se spectata non potuerint, ex opere sc. operato, ut barbare loquuntur scholastici, τῇ συνειδήσει τελειῶσαι τὸν λητρέυοντα Ebr. IX. vers. 9. sed quod circa carnales ritus occupata fue- rit lex ἱερατικὴ, qui umbra erant rerum spiritua- lium Ebr. X. 1.

[ἢ τὺς προφήτας] Spectantur hic Prophetæ non tan- tum ut futurorum præsagi, verum etiam ut legis inter- pretes, & quotidiani commemoratores. Quo sensu à præcepto dilectionis pendere dicuntur lex, & Prophetæ Matth. XXII. 40. Diftinguuntur à Christo lex, & Prophetæ : ideoque non temere confundendi sunt: & quum Christus non solum legem adventu suo impleve- rit, sed & vaticinia Prophetica, quæ de ipso im- primis sonabant Actor. X. v. 43. quidni Prophe- tæ, qua proprium munus, quod erat vaticinari, hic intelligendi, quo à lege distinguebantur: si- quidem Christus debuerit & legem implere obe- dientia cum activa tum passiva, nostri loco, & va- ticiniis ita Prophetarum, qui de eo testimonium perhibuerant, complementum præstare. Ideo- que per Prophetas vaticinia eorum non immerito intelligunt B. Chemnitius, Osiander, Hunnius, & alii.

## 5:18
Vers. 18.

Ἀμὴν] This Hebrew word, which is placed sometimes at the beginning, sometimes at the end of a discourse, has diverse meanings, which cannot be rendered by one Latin word. For if it be a declarative statement in which truth and falsehood exist, as Aristotle speaks, it has the same value as the Greek ἀληθῶς, and most learned men have long since noted that the Hebrew word is thus rendered both by the seventy elders and by Luke. But when joined to words of praying or wishing, it has the force that either 'I beseech' or 'would that' has among the Latins: in which sense it is rightly said by the LXX as γένοιτο. The Greek word ναὶ, however, embraces both meanings, as it sometimes asserts, and sometimes expresses the vehemence of desire. Wherefore Luke accurately translated Ἀμὴν with the word Ναὶ: but Paul and John placed ναὶ and ἀμὴν together, so that one word might receive light from the other. Moreover, this Hebrew word, as being very effective, was also preserved in the Greek language by the Hellenistic Jews: whom the Christians followed, retaining it not only in books, but also in popular usage, as can be seen in I. Cor. XIV. 16.

I am pleased with what Ludovicus de Dieu has to say about this word: I would not wish to oppose those who judge that there is not a simple assertion in the words of Christ, 'Amen Amen I say to you,' but one with an oath. For he cites the Truth itself as a witness, which is what but GOD himself, Christ himself, who for that reason is called 'the Amen' Apocal. III. 14, 'These things says the Amen, the witness, the faithful and true.' And the true GOD is called אֵל הֵי אָמֵן Esa. LXV. 16. So that ἀμὴν ἀμὴν λέγω ὑμῖν is the same as 'I, the Amen, the Amen, say to you.' Nor do I doubt that the great and most learned Father Jerome intended this, when he says that in the Old Testament the oath of God is, 'As I live, says the Lord,' but in the New, 'Amen amen I say to you.' Nor should anyone wonder that 'As I live' and 'amen amen,' when said by God, are taken for the same things. For wherever in the Hebrew there is חַי אָנִי, the Chaldean has קַיָּם אֲנָא, that is, properly, 'I am constant, stable, firm.' In Hebrew אָמֵן or נֶאֱמָן. For the life of God is the very truth, firmness, and stability of the divine essence. Wherefore in Psalm CII. verse 27, what the Psalmist says of God, תַּעֲמוֹד, designating the immutability of the life of God, the Apostle in Hebr. I. verse 11 translates as σὺ διαμένεις. When therefore God asserts by his Amen, he swears by himself, by his life, by the truth and stability of his essence. Nor does the adjective אֵיתָן denote anything else when it is joined to the substantive מַיִם, than a constant and perennial emanation, מַיִם חַיִּים, 'living waters,' incessantly gushing forth, מַיִן דְלָא פָסְקִין, as Jonathan translates, Jerem. II. verse 13. What is more? That קַיָּם is used among the Chaldeans everywhere for the Hebrew יִשָּׁבַע. קַיֵּים אֱלָהָא, 'God swore,' as if to say, he spoke a stable, certain, firm thing, he said amen. So that you may well translate 'amen amen I say to you' in Chaldean as מַקֵּים אֲנָא מַקֵּים אֲנָא לְכוֹן, 'I swear, I swear to you.' And hence I think it has come about that τὸ ἀμὴν is indeed used everywhere by the saints when they wish, but not when they assert. No one of the Prophets or

Apostles has said, 'Amen I say to you.' This is left only to God and Christ, because it belongs to him who asserts by himself.

Ἕως ἂν παρέλθῃ ὁ οὐρανὸς] παρίρχεσθαι indeed signifies to perish here, as also in Peter 2. ep. III. 10. Yet the time of the conflagration is not being looked to here as in Peter's epistle; but that it is a proverbial saying, as if you were to say in Latin, 'until the sky falls,' Luke teaches us, in whom this sentence is brought forth in this manner: 'It is easier for heaven and earth to pass away, than for one apex of the law to collapse.' In which manner of speaking, not the power of God, but the natural order is regarded. But according to nature, this seems to be of the impossible things, that heaven or earth should perish, both of which Hesiod called the 'ever-secure seat of the immortal Gods.' Similar things are to be found everywhere among the Greeks and Latins, 'while the earth shall stand,' 'while the stars shall run,' or in this manner.

Desinet esse prius contrarius ignibus humor.

And that very thing is to be seen more clearly below in XXIV. 35, Marc. XIII. 31, Luc. XXI. 33, where Christ speaks thus, dealing with his predictions: ὁ οὐρανὸς κὴ ἡ γῆ παρελεύσονται, οἱ δὲ λόγοι μᾶ ἐ μὴ παρέλθωσι. For the last word, which is of the potential mood, shows the sense to be, that it is possible for heaven and earth to perish sooner than that the things predicted should not be fulfilled. But that the former word is placed in those passages in the indicative mood, that comes from a Hebraism. Thus Esa. LIV. 10, כִּי הֶהָרִים יָמוּשׁוּ וְהַגְּבָעוֹת תְּמוּטֶינָה וְחַסְדִּי מֵאִתֵּךְ לֹא יָמוּשׁ וּבְרִית שְׁלוֹמִי לֹא תָמוּט. Word for word: 'For the mountains shall move themselves and the hills shall shake: And my mercy shall not depart from thee, and the covenant of my peace shall not move itself:' that is, the mountains would move themselves and the hills would shake sooner than this would happen. A most similar manner of speaking is LXXII. 7, עַד בְּלִי יָרֵחַ, in Greek ἕως ὗ ἀναιρεθῇ (it is commonly read wrongly as ἀνταναιρεθῇ) ἡ σελήνη. Add that which is in Jerem. XVIII. 8 & 10. XXXIII. 29. 21.

ἰῶτα ἓν ἢ μία κεραία] It is certain that this is also proverbial, like most things in the sermons of our Lord taken from common usage. And it is necessary that this adage took its origin from the method of writing which was then in force: from which it follows that even then in the Hebrew language the letter Jod occupied less space than the other letters, and consequently that those characters which the shekels display had already ceased to be used in the time of Christ, and that those which we have, the Assyrian ones, had begun to be written by the Hebrews from the times of Ezra, as is believed. The name κεραία, however, is derived by some from the vowel points: but it is the same as apex. In Latin, Gellius called the strokes of the letters themselves, or parts of them, the apices of letters, and from this the translation was born: to dispute about the technicalities of the law. Aristides also, dealing with the laws of the Greeks, said νόμων κεραίαυς. In the old glossaries, apex, κεραία γράμματος, ἄκρον. But the word κεραία also exists in that sense in Plutarch, Dio, Chrysostom, Philo Judaeus, Clement of Alexandria, and in the Pseudo-Sibyllines. Jerome said that the letter Resch differs from Daleth by an apex. And if I am not mistaken, the word خطة which the Arab placed here receives the same meaning. That old books, even after Ezra, were accustomed to be written without vowel points has been demonstrated by such clear arguments by men most learned in these matters, that to deny it further is only for the obstinate.

A wonderful confidence in asserting, but one which rests on no solid foundation. Both that opinion—concerning the old character of the Hebrews being different from the modern one, which idle men, born to devise anything, have feigned that we now possess as the Assyrian—and concerning the invention of the points, namely that they were by no means contemporary with the letters, but were added to the text only recently, many centuries later, which is diametrically opposed to the authority, perfection, perspicuity, and certainty of Holy Scripture, no less than to divine providence and truth, has been refuted by us elsewhere, especially in the Sacra Critica, where we have shown clearly and solidly, as we hope, that the arguments of Cappel, the author of the secret revelation of the points, which Grotius judges to be so brilliant, have nothing solid or of brilliant proof. If there are any who still wish to be blind in the clear midday, let them be blind. Nor indeed do I find a reason why, having disregarded the opinion of those who, with Chemnitz, think that the vowel points are designated by κεραίαν, we ought, with Grotius, to understand only the strokes and parts of the letters; even though the word κεραίας is accepted among foreigners in this sense. Because the whole body of the divine law is, without doubt, regarded, to which vowels pertain no less than letters; and thus it is said that not even the smallest of letters, namely the Yod, nor the smallest vowel point can perish from the law: whence that interpretation, as being more convenient to the original language, which is completed by consonants and points, is to be preferred. For what was the point of the strokes or tips of the letters being specifically designated, for the sake of the already named letters τῷ ἰῶτα, when with the strokes or tips and parts of the letters perishing, the letters themselves are immediately changed, and thus are no longer the same letters, but have perished with such κεραίαις perishing? Whence in the old Italic, and the new Diodati, and the French version, and also by Piscator, this word is taken concerning the points: and for that reason it is more aptly taught that nothing in the law will be rejected or void, not even the smallest point, but that all things will be fulfilled. To which the observation of the blessed Chemnitz contributes, that in the precepts of the first table the Yod is written more often than in the second, and that in the second the most severe prohibitions are marked by a most minute point in the word לֹא, even though the Yod is the most minute of all letters and the vowel points are even smaller. But Christ testifies that a single Yod and the most minute point in the law are held in such regard by God in that place, that heaven and earth will pass away more easily than it shall pass or fall without being fulfilled. Whence furthermore the blessed Chemnitz rightly expressed the sense of the words of Christ: The sense therefore is, that the Law is not satisfied by a particular and mutilated obedience, but it is necessary that all things be fulfilled most perfectly down to the smallest tip. That God would more easily admit the destruction of heaven and earth than that a single Yod or the most minute tip should fall away so that it is not fulfilled. And the same is the sentiment, just as Moses denounces a curse not only on those who have not remained in the great things, but who have not remained in all things which are written in the book of the law, and just as James says; Whoever shall have kept the whole law, but offends in one point, has become guilty of all. Therefore Christ adds: Whoever shall have kept the great (according to your opinion) commandments, but by transgressing shall have loosened even one of those which you deem least, with that persuasion as if God does not care, he shall not have a place in the kingdom of heaven.

ἓ μὴ παρέλθῃ ἀπὸ τῶ νόμυ ἕως ἂν πάντα γένηται] πα- ρερχεσθαι means to be made void, as below XXIV. 31. wherefore ἕως here has an adversative force: they will not perish, he says, but rather they will be thoroughly fulfilled. How this pertains also to the ceremonies, we have said above. But Christ treats that matter more obscurely on purpose, lest he should offend more tender minds. For this, as was prudently annotated by Origen in his second book against Celsus, was especially among those things which the Apostles themselves could not yet bear: and for which reason the Spirit had to come who would lead them into all truth, John XVI. 13.

That Christ treated the matter more obscurely on purpose is by no means to be conceded: nor is there any obscurity here, nor was it fitting for the heavenly Teacher, who spoke so that he might be heard and understood, to speak obscurely on purpose.

Latin:

Vers. 18.

Ἀμὴν] Vox hæc Hebræa, quæ modo in exordio, mo- do in clausula sermonis ponitur, diversas significationes habet, quæ una voce Latina reddi nequeunt. Nam si λόγος sit ἀποφαντικὸς ἐν ᾧ͂ τὸ ἀληθεύειν καὶ τὸ ψεύδεσθαι ὑπάρ- χει, ut Aristoteles loquitur, idem valet quod Græcum ἀληθῶς atque ita vocem Hebræam reddi tum à LXX. se- nibus, tum à Luca, viri doctissimi pridem annotarunt. At precandi optandive verbis adjunctum, eam vim habet quam apud Latinos aut quæso, aut utinam: quo sensu à LXX. recte dicitur γένοιτο. Utramque autem significatio- nem complectitur vox Græca ναὶ, ut quæ modo asseverat, modo desiderii vehementiam exprimit. Quare accurate Lucas Ἀμὴν voce Ναὶ transtulit: Paulus autem & Johan- nes ναὶ & ἀμὴν conjunctum posuerunt, ut altera vox ab altera lucem acciperet. Vox autem hæc Hebræa, ut valde efficax, etiam in Græca lingua ab Hellenistis Judæis servata est: quos secuti Christiani, non in libris duntaxat, sed in usu quoque populari eam retinuerunt, ut videre est I. Cor. XIV. 16.

Placent quæ Ludovicus de Dieu de hac vo- ce habet: Nolim refragari iis qui non simplicem, sed cum juramento asseverationem verbis Christi in- esse arbitrantur, Amen Amen dico vobis. Ipsam enim veritatem testem citat, quæ quid est nisi ipse DEUS, ipse Christus, qui propterea vocatur ὁ ἀ- μὴν Apocal. III. 14. τάδε λέγει ὁ ἀμὴν, ὁ μάρ- τυς, ὁ πιστὸς κὴ ἀληθινός. Et verus DEUS di- citur אֵל הֵי אָמֵן Esa. LXV. 16. Adeo ut ἀμὴν ἀ- μὴν λέγω ὑμῖν, idem sit atque ἐγὼ ὁ ἀμὴν ὁ ἀμὴν λέγω ὑμῖν. Nec dubito quin id voluerit magnus & eruditissimus Pater Hieronymus, quum ait in veteri Testamento Dei juramentum esse, Vivo ergo, dicit Dominus, in Novo autem, Amen amen dico vo- bis. Nec miretur quis, Vivo ego & amen amen, quum à Deo dicitur, ipsi pro iisdem sumi. Nam ubicunque in Hebræo est, חַי אָנִי ,Chaldæus habet קַיָּם אֲנָא id est proprie constans, stabilis, fir- mus ego. Hebraice אָמֵן vel נֶאֱמָן. Vita enim Dei est ipsa veritas, firmitas, stabilitas essentiæ di- vinæ. Quamobrem Psal. CII. vers. 27. quod Psal- mistes de Deo dicit תַּעֲמוֹד Vita Dei immuta- bilitatem designans, Apostolus Hebr. I. vers. 11. ver- tit σὺ διαμένεις. Quum ergo Deus asseverat per suum Amen, per se ipsum, per suam vitam, per essentiæ suæ veritatem & stabilitatem jurat. Nec aliud notat adjectivum אֵיתָן quum jungitur sub- stantivo מַיִם,quam constantem & perennem e- manationem, מַיִם חַיִּים aquæ perennes, in- desinenter scaturientes מַיִן דְלָא פָסְקִין ut Jona- than vertit, Jerem. II. vers. 13. Quid? quod קַיָּם apud Chaldæos pro Hebræor. יִשָּׁבַע passim pona- tur. קַיֵּים אֱלָהָא juravit Deus, quasi, rem stabilem, certam, firmam dixit, amen dixit. Ad- eo ut amen amen dico vobis, Chald. bene vertas מַקֵּים אֲנָא מַקֵּים אֲנָא לְכוֹן juro, juro vobis. Atque hinc factum arbitror, quod τὸ ἀμὴν passim quidem à sanctis usurpatur quum optant, sed non quum asseverant. Nemo unquam Prophetarum aut

Apostolorum dixit, Amen dico vobis. Soli Deo Christoque hoc relinquitur, quia ejus est qui per se ipsum asseverat.

Ἕως ἂν παρέλθῃ ὁ οὐρανὸς] παρίρχεσθαι quidem interire hic significat, ut & apud Petrum 2. ep. III. 10. Neque tamen hic respici tempus τῆς ἐκπυρώσεως ut in Petri episto- la; sed dictum esse παροιμιῶδες quasi Latine dicas, usque dum cælum ruat, Lucas nos docet, apud quem hæc sen- tentia hunc in modum effertur: Facilius sit cælum & ter- ram perire, quam uslum legis apicem collabi. In quo loquendi genere non Dei potentia, sed naturalis ordo re- spicitur. At secundum naturam videtur hoc esse τῶν ἀ- δυνάτων, ut cælum aut terra pereat, quorum utrumque Hesiodus dixit Deorum immortalium ἕδος ἀσφαλὲς αἰεὶ. Similia apud Græcos & Latinos passim reperire est, dum terra stabit, dum astra current, aut in hunc modum.

Desinet esse prius contrarius ignibus humor.

Atque id ipsum clarius conspicere est infra XXIV. 35. Marc. XIII. 31. Luc. XXI. 33. ubi ita loquitur Christus de suis prædictionibus agens : ὁ οὐρανὸς κὴ ἡ γῆ παρελεύσονται, οἱ δὲ λόγοι μᾶ ἐ μὴ παρέλθωσι. Nam postrema vox, quæ est mo- di potentialis, ostendit sensum esse, prius fieri posse, ut cælum ac terra pereant, quam ut prædicta non implean- tur. Quod autem prior vox istis locis posita est ὀρισ- τικῶς id ex Hebraismo venit. Sic Esa. LIV. 10. כִּי הֶהָרִים יָמוּשׁוּ וְהַגְּבָעוֹת תְּמוּטֶינָה וְחַסְדִּי מֵאִתֵּךְ לֹא יָמוּשׁ וּבְרִית שְׁלוֹמִי לֹא תָמוּט. Ad verbum: Nam montes movebunt se & colles nutabunt: Et misericordia mea non recedet, & fœdus pacis meæ non movebit se: id est, prius montes se moverent & colles nutarent quam hoc fieret. Si- millimum loquendi genus est LXXII. 7. עַד בְּלִי יָרֵחַ Græce ἕως ὗ ἀναιρεθῇ (male vulgo legitur ἀνταναιρεθῇ) ἡ σε- λήνη. Adde quod est Jerem. XVIII. 8 & 10. XXXIII. 29. 21.

ἰῶτα ἓν ἢ μία κεραία] Certum quidem est & hoc esse παροι- μιῶδες, qualia sunt pleraque in Domini nostri sermonibus de medio usu sumta. Atque necesse est id adagium ex scri- bendi ratione quæ tum vigebat originem duxisse: unde sequitur jam tum in Hebraica lingua Jod literam minus spatium occupasse, quam literas cæteras, ac proinde eos characteres quos sicli præferunt, jam Christi tempo- re usurpari desiisse, & in usu fuisse, quas habemus, As- syriacas ab Esdræ, ut creditur, temporibus scribi Hebræis cœptas. Κεραίας autem nomen ad puncta vocalia à quibus- dam trahitur: sed idem est, quod apex. Latine Apices Literarum ipsos literarum ductus, aut partes dixit Gellius, & hinc nata translatio: de juris apicibus disputare. Et- iam Aristides de Græcorum legibus agens dixit νόμων κεραίαυς. In glossis veteribus apex, κεραία γράμματος, ἄκρον. Sed & apud Plutarchum, Dionem, Chrysostomum, Philonem Judæum, Clementem Alexandrinum, & in Pseudo-Sy- billinis extat vox κεραία eo sensu. Apice literam Resch à Daleth differre dixit Hieronymus. Eundemque nisi fallor, sensum recipit خطة quod hic posuit Arabs. Libros veteres etiam post Esdram sine punctis vocalibus scribi so- litos adeo perspicuis argumentis à viris harum rerum do- ctissimis demonstratum est, ut id amplius inficiari non nisi pertinacium sit.

Mira asserendi confidentia, sed quæ nullo ni- titur solido fundamento. Utraque illa opinio & de charactere vetere Ebræorum à moderno diverso, quem nunc Assyriacum nos haberi commenti sunt otiosi homines, ad quævis excogitanda nati, fa- cti; & de invento punctorum, quod nempe ea- dem minime coæva literis fuerint, sed noviter demum, multis post seculis textui accesserint, Scripturæ S. autoritati, perfectioni, perspicuitati, certitudini non minus quam divina providentia & veritati καδδιάμετρον repugnans, profligata à nobis alias est in Critico imprimis sacro, ubi ar- gumenta Capelli, autoris arcani punctorum re- velationis, quæ tam luculenta esse judicat Gro- tius, nihil solidi aut luculentæ probationis habere, luculenter atque solide, uti speramus, ostendi- mus. Si qui adhuc in mero meridie cæcutire ve- lint, cæcutiant. Neque vero causam invenio, cur posthabita illorum sententia, qui cum Chemnitio per κεραίαν puncta vocalia designari censent, literarum ductus, & partes solum intelligere, cum Grotio, debeamus; etsi vox κεραίας apud exoti- cos hoc sensu accipiatur. Quia totum, sine du- bio, corpus legis divinæ respicitur, ad quod non minus vocales, quam literæ pertinent; adeoque nec minimam literarum, Jod nempe, neque pun- ctum vocale minimum de lege interire posse dice- tur: unde interpretatio ista, ceu convenientior linguæ originali, quæ consonantibus & punctis absolvitur, præferenda. Quid enim attinebat peculiariter ductus vel apices literarum designari, jam nominato literarum gratia τῷ ἰῶτα, quum pereuntibus ductibus vel apicibus, & partibus literarum ipsæ literæ actutum immutentur, adeo- que jam non amplius sint eædem literæ, sed per- ierint intereuntibus talibus κεραίαις? Unde in Italica veteri, & nova Diodati, & Gallica versio- ne, nec non à Piscatore de punctis hæc vox acci- pitur: eaque ratione aptius docetur, nihil in le- ge rejiculum, aut irritum fore, ne minimum qui- dem punctum, sed impletum iri omnia. Quo facit observatio B. Chemnitii, quod in præceptis tabulæ primæ Jod sæpius, quam in secunda scri- batur, & quod in secunda severissimæ prohibitiones per punctulum minutissimum in voce לֹא signen- tur, etsi Jod litera omnium minutissima & pun- cta vocalia adhuc minora sint. Christus vero te- stetur, unicum Jod, & minutissimum punctum in lege eo loco apud Deum haberi, ut priusquam præ- tereat, vel cadat, quin impleatur, facilius cælum & terram transiturum. Unde porro sensum ver- borum Christi recte expressit B. Chemnitius: Sensus igitur est, Legi non satisfieri particulari & mutila obedientia, sed necesse est, ut omnia usque ad minimum apicem perfectissime impleantur. Deum facilius destructionem cæli & terræ admissurum, quam ut unicum Jod, vel minutissimus apex inter- cidat, ut non impleatur. Et eadem est sententia, sicut Moses denunciat maledictionem non illis tantum, qui non in magnis, sed qui non in omnibus perman- serint, quæ scripta sunt in libro legis, & sicut Ja- cobus inquit; Quicunque totam legem servaverit, offendat autem in uno, factus est omnium reus. Ideo Christus addit: Quisquis magna (juxta ve- stram opinionem) mandata servaverit, ex illis vero, quæ vos minima reputatis, vel unicum transgredien- do solverit, illa persuasione, quasi Deus non curet, non habebit locum in regno cælorum.

ἓ μὴ παρέλθῃ ἀπὸ τῶ νόμυ ἕως ἂν πάντα γένηται] πα- ρερχεσθαι est irritum fieri ut infra XXIV. 31. quare ἕως hic vim habet adversativam: non peribunt inquit, quin imo penitus implebuntur. Quod quomodo ad cæremonias etiam pertineat, supra diximus. Sed de industria eam rem Christus obscurius tractat, ne teneriores animos offende- ret. Nam hoc vel præcipue, ut prudenter ab Origine est annotatum libro contra Celsum secundo, inter illa erat quæ ipsi Apostoli ferre nondum poterant: & quamobrem venire debebat Spiritus qui eos duceret in omnem verita- tem Joh. XVI. 13.

De industria rem obscurius tractare Chri- stum, minime concedendum: nec ulla hic obscu- ritas, nec de industria obscure loqui conveniebat cœlesti Doctori, qui loquebatur ut audiretur, & intelligeretur.

## 5:19
Vers. 19.

Τῶν ἐντολῶν τύτων] Jerome refers this to the words of the law. Others of the ancients better refer it to the commandments of the kingdom of heaven, which are τὸ πλήρωμα τῶ νόμυ. Therefore Christ does not say ἐκείνων, but τύτων, looking both to the preceding things in which a certain summary of those commandments was handed down under the description of blessedness, and to the following things, which contain a more extensive explanation of them. Moreover, such is the argumentation of Christ: if it is permitted to no one to break the law, much less will he carry it off with impunity who shall have broken those things to the preparation of which the law is a handmaid. See Heb. II. 2. But he shows that they are such in the following: λέγω γὰρ ὑμῖν and so forth. But the explanation of Jerome holds up far more correctly, as the συνάφεια of the preceding verse teaches. For he speaks of those commandments which he said were so constant that heaven and earth must perish before one iota or tip of them perishes. But he had spoken those things concerning the commandments of the law. Nothing is more evident. Whence the gloss of Grotius is deservedly rejected as alien. Nor did he name who those ancients are who hand it down. In the preceding he did not hand down commandments, but comprehended the blessedness of the truly faithful in certain aphorisms. But as for the following, that word τούτων is snatched away entirely against hermeneutical laws, although in those things which follow, Christ does not inculcate his own commandments, but exhibits his own vindications of the commandments of the law.

Τῶν ἐλαχίστων] κᾀν is understood. For the sense is, if anyone shall have despised even that which is least in these precepts. So below XXV. 40. ἑνὶ τούτων τῶν ἀδελφῶν μου τῶν ἐλα- χίστων, it is worth κᾀν ἐλαχίστων. Let Christians learn from this that there is no precept in the sermons of Christ so light that it is permitted to be spurned without detriment to salvation.

While Christ makes mention of τῶν ἐλαχίστων, he speaks by way of concession and κατ᾽ ἄνθρωπον, not by way of approval. For he acknowledges nothing as least in the law, just as there is no one in the kingdom of heaven who is called least in the kingdom of heaven here.

καὶ διδάξῃ ὕτω] This is, διδάξῃ λύειν. Moreover, καὶ is placed for ἤ. For both grammarians and jurists note that a conjunction is often taken for a disjunction. The sense is: whoever shall have done contrary or shall have taught to do contrary will be of the least value. The words which follow, directly opposed to these words, make this clear.

“He shall be called least in the kingdom of heaven.” We spoke above about the word καλεῖσθαι, but I consider that ἐν here is placed for the designation of time. Clearly as in Luke 14:14, “in the resurrection of the just.” For also in another place, the same Luke, what he had said in Luke 22:16, “in the kingdom of God,” he soon explains in verse 18, “until the kingdom of God shall come.” Nor do I judge that these things are to be interpreted concerning the Church, but concerning that supreme manifestation of divine majesty at the end of times, because of that which follows, “you shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven.” The writer of the Responses to the Orthodox says: “The divine Scripture knows how to call the kingdom of God not simply the resurrection, but the restoration after the resurrection, in which the separation of those being punished and those being glorified takes place.” The sense, therefore, of this passage is: he who shall have acted or taught against this will be held as least, when the consummation of the heavenly kingdom shall have arrived.

“Least and great,” as Walæus here rightly from Spanheim, “least and great,” do not here designate an opposition of degrees in the same species, but rather an opposition of genera, or conditions, or most diverse classes, nor do they note a comparison of the happy and the happy, but of the happy and the unhappy; for the least here are the unhappy, the great are the happy, the former excluded from all glory, the latter participants of it. Theophylact: “But he shall be called least in the kingdom of his, in the resurrection last and cast into hell, for he shall not even enter into the kingdom of heaven.” Although he adds certain things in the same place which do not well agree with that interpretation. Augustine, in book 1 of the Sermon of the Lord on the Mount: “He shall be called least in the kingdom of heaven, and perhaps for that reason he will not be in the kingdom of heaven, where none can be except the great.”

“But whoever shall do and teach.” Although these things especially look to the Apostles, they are not, however, to be so restricted to them that others are excluded. For it is the duty of all Christians not only to lead others by example, but also to admonish others with words. Romans 15:14; Colossians 1:28, where this very word διδάσκειν is found.

PART IV. Concerning true and saving righteousness.

Latin:

Vers. 19.

Τῶν ἐντολῶν τύτων] Hieronymus ad verba legis re- fert. Melius alii veterum ad mandata regni cælorum, quæ sunt τὸ πλήρωμα τῶ νόμυ. Ideo non dicit Christus ἐκείνων, sed τύτων, respiciens tum ad præcedentia in quibus sub bea- titudinis descriptione compendium quoddam eorum man- datorum erat traditum, tum ad sequentia, quæ fusiorem eorum explicationem continent. Est autem talis Christi argumentatio: si legem rumpere nulli licet, multo minus impune feret, qui ea ruperit, quibus præparandis lex an- cillatur. Vid. Hebr. II. 2. Sua autem esse talia ostendit in sequentibus: λέγω γὰρ ὑμῖν & deinceps. At rectius longe se habet Hieronymi expli- catio, quod versus præcedentis συνάφεια docet. Nam de illis mandatis loquitur, quæ adeo constan- tia dixit, ut cælum & terram prius interire oporteat, quam jota unum, vel apex de illis intereat. At |illa de mandatis legis dixerat. Nihil evidentius. Unde glossa Grotii ceu aliena merito reprobatur. Ne- que quinam illi veteres sint, qui eam tradant, no- minavit. In superioribus non mandata tradidit, sed beatitudinem vere fidelium certis aphorismis comprehendit. Ad sequentia vero prorsus contra leges herminevticas vox illa τούτων abripitur, quamvis in illis, quæ sequuntur, non mandata sua inculcet Christus, sed suas mandatorum legis vin- dicias exhibeat.

Τῶν ἐλαχίστων] Subauditur κᾀν. Sensus enim est, si quis vel id contemserit quod minimum est in his præceptio- nibus, Ita infra XXV. 40. ἑνὶ τούτων τῶν ἀδελφῶν μου τῶν ἐλα- χίστων, valet κᾀν ἐλαχίστων. Discant hinc Christiani, nul- lum esse in Christi sermonibus præceptum tam leve, quod sine salutis detrimento liceat aspernari.

Dum Christus τῶν ἐλαχίστων mentionem facit, loquitur per concessionem & κατ᾽ ἄνθρωπον, non per approbationem. Nihil enim minimi agno- scit in lege, uti nullus in regno cœlorum est, qui minimus in regno cœlorum hic dicitur.

καὶ διδάξῃ ὕτω] Hoc est, διδάξῃ λύειν. Positum est autem καὶ pro ἤ. Nam conjunctionem sæpe pro disjun- ctione accipi & Grammatici & jurisconsulti notant. Sensus est: qui contra fecerit quive contra facere docuerit mini- mi erit pretii. Clarum hoc faciunt quæ sequuntur verba his verbis directe opposita.

ἐλάχιστος κληθήσεται ἐν τῇ βασιλείᾳ τῶν ὐρανῶν] De verbo καλεῖσθαι diximus supra, illud autem ἐν hic posi- tum arbitror ad temporis designationem. Plane ut apud Lucam XIV. 14. ἐν τῇ ἀναστάσει τῶν δικαίων. Nam & alio loco, idem Lucas quod dixerat ἐν τῇ βασιλείᾳ τῦ Θεῦ XXII. 16. mox exponit ἕως ὅτε ἡ βασιλεία τῦ Θεῦ ἔλθῃ, 18. Neque de Ecclesia hæc interpretanda judico, sed de sum- ma illa patefactione divinæ majestatis in fine temporum, propter id quod sequitur non intrabitis in regnum cœlorum. Scriptor responsionum ad orthodoxos: βασιλείαν Θεῦ οἶ- δεν ἡ θεία γραφὴ λέγειν ἢ τὴν ἀνάστασιν ἁπλῶς, ἀλλὰ τὴν μετὰ τὴν ἀνάστασιν ἀποκατάστασιν, ἐν ᾗ γίνεται κολαζομένων τε καὶ δοξαζομένων ἡ διαίρεσις. Sensus ergo hujus loci est, cum qui contra fecerit docueritve minimi habitum iri, tunc cum regni cœlestis consummatio advenerit.

ἐλάχιστος & μέγας, ut recte è Spanhemio hic Walæus, minimus & magnus, hic non designant op- positionem graduum in eadem specie, sed potius oppo- sitionem generum, vel conditionum, vel classium diversissimarum, nec notant comparationem feli- cium & felicium, sed felicium & infelicium; mini- mi hic enim infelices, magni felices, illi à gloria omni exclusi, isti illius participes. Theophylactus: ἐλά- χιστος δὲ κληθήσεται ἐν τῇ βασιλείᾳ αὔτι τοῦ, ἐν τῇ ἀναστάσει ἔσχατος κᾀ ἀπεῤῥιμένος εἰς γέεναν, κᾀ γὰρ εἰς τὴν βασιλείαν τῶν ὐρανῶν εἰσελεύσεται. Etsi ibidem quædam attexat, quæ interpretationi illi pa- rum conveniunt. Augustinus libro 1. de sermone Domini in monte: Minimus vocabitur in regno cœ- lorum, & fortasse ideo non erit in regno cælorum, ubi nisi magni esse non possunt.

ὃς δ᾽ ἂν ποιήσῃ κᾀ διδάξῃ] Quanquam hæc præcipue Apostolos spectant, non ita tamen ad eos adstringenda sunt ut alii excludantur. Nam Christianorum omnium est non modo exemplo præire aliis, sed & alios verbis commone- facere. Rom. XV. 14. Col. I. 28. ubi hæc ipsa vox διδάσκειν reperitur.

PARS IV. De vera & salvifica justitia.

## 5:20
Verse 20.

“Unless your righteousness shall abound more.” We said above that by the word δικαιοσύνης, obedience is signified: that phrase, how- ever, περισσεύσῃ πλεῖον you can translate into Latin with one word: superaberit.

τῶν γραμματέων καὶ Φαρισαίων] Christ names the scribes as the most learned of the Jews; the Pharisees as noble for their reputation of peculiar holiness, and whose sect was the ἀκριβεστάτη in Judaism, Acts XXVI. verse 5. From this, however, it is given to be understood how necessary the promulgation of this new doctrine was, since those who were held to be the wisest and most religious among the Jews wandered so far from both wisdom and religion: and the sons of Levi themselves, the purifiers of others, stood in need of being purified. Malach. III. verse 3. Moreover, it contributes much to the understanding of these words and those which follow, to know correctly what the dogma of the legists and Pharisees was concerning the obedience to be rendered to God. But from whom shall we learn this rather than from the Apostle Paul, who had both drawn his Jewish doctrine from the chief legist Gamaliel, and had given his name to the Pharisaic sect? He therefore says that he lived at that time blameless, as far as concerned the righteousness which is in the law, Galatians III, verse 16. Where it is plain that the name of the law is used in the way we reported Seneca said, that it is a small thing to be good according to the law. Wherefore the same Apostle also calls this law here and there, for the sake of distinction, the law of works, indicating clearly that law which Hebrew judges were bound to follow in investigating cases: who could neither look into the mind, nor indeed had they received power to punish all things done otherwise, but only those which especially harmed civil society. In which sense Clement of Alexandria also calls the sin of the heart ἁμαρτίαν νόμῳ οὐχ̓ ὑποπίπτουσαν. But it is less surprising that pagans lived content with such a kind of innocence, of whom Tertullian, comparing them with Christians, speaks thus: Are we therefore the only innocent ones? What is the wonder, if it is necessary. Indeed it is necessary: we have been taught innocence by GOD and we know it perfectly as revealed by a perfect teacher, and we guard it faithfully as commanded by an incorruptible inspector. But to you, human estimation has handed down innocence; human authority likewise has commanded it, whence you have disciplines neither full nor so much to be feared for the truth of innocence. But concerning the Jews, that seems less credible, as those who knew the law was laid down by God, the inspector of minds, who both wished to be loved from the heart and forbade wicked desires. But the matter was undoubtedly so, because for such precepts no punishment was explicitly proposed, therefore they interpreted it more in the sense of counsel than in the necessity of law, or at least they thought those stains were so purged, partly by daily victims, partly by the annual expiatory sacrifice, that no memory of them remained before God. That what I say is true, that same Paul teaches us, who says that he learned only by attentive consideration of the law that wicked desires are in the category of sin, when otherwise he would have been ignorant of that very thing, hindered by Pharisaic prejudices, Romans VII, verse 7. Hence it is that Trypho the Jew, disputing against Justin, says that the τὰ ἐν τῷ εὐαγγελίῳ παραγγέλματα seem to him so great and so admirable that they clearly seem to be able to be performed by no one, understanding the mandates of interior innocence, and the avoidance of those vices which are accustomed to be held as small. But nothing could be said more openly than what the most learned of the Hebrews, David Kimchi, left written, who interprets those words of Psalm LXVI, verse 18, If I had seen iniquity in my heart, the Lord would not have heard, clearly against the writer's meaning, as follows: Even if I had seen iniquity in my heart, which I might even be prepared to carry into action, although it is before God as if I had uttered it with my lips, yet the Lord will not hear it, as if to say, He will not count it as a crime for me: GOD does not hold that wicked thought in place of a deed, unless it has been conceived in faith and religion toward God. See how manifestly he says that all decrees of the soul, even those which it did not rest with man to prevent from being fulfilled, with the sole exception of defection from Judaism, are not imputed by God, nor counted as sins. And Abenesdra notes on the Decalogue that this very opinion is approved by many Hebrews. Moreover, Josephus, as he himself confesses, having been accurately instructed in Pharisaism, criticizes Polybius, the most noble writer of histories, because he ascribes the death of Antiochus to a sacrilege that was indeed thought of, but not perpetrated, adding, τὸ γὰρ μηκέτι ποιῆσαι τὸ ἔργον βυλευσάμενον ὐκ ἦν τιμωρίας ἄξιον. This, therefore, is that Pharisaic innocence, which Christ declares does not suffice before God, contrary to the opinion accepted at that time. Clement of Alexandria explains Pharisaic and Christian righteousness in this way: ἐὰν μὴ πλειονάζῃ ὑμῶν ἡ δικαιοσύνη πλεῖον τῶν γραμματέων, καὶ Φαρισαίων, τῶν κατὰ ἀποχὴν κακῶν δικαιουμένων, σὺν τῷ

with the perfection in these things and with the ability to love and benefit one's neighbor, you will not be royal. Which comes to almost the same thing. For the law of love, although it is fulfilled by deeds, yet it does not come from a fixed prescription, but from the abundant goodness of the mind. But with the wisest counsel, Christ, about to instill the precepts of true holiness into his own, first removes the dogmas which prevented its necessity from being seen. For, as Seneca rightly says, certain decrees ought to be set before precepts, so that the precepts may adhere to the mind more deeply, as if fixed by those decrees.

The obedience which God demands from us, he had said was to be noted at verse 6: but although δικαιοσύνη sometimes denotes obedience: yet frequently δικαιοσύνη is one thing, righteousness, in the phrase of Scripture, especially in the New Testament, and obedience is another, which Grotius understands: and the righteousness by which we are constituted righteous before God when we are justified is clearly distinguished from the obedience which we render to the law of God. Christ explains it in John 16:8, 10, that it consists in his departure to the Father, or in the merit acquired for us by his death and resurrection, and Paul in Romans 1:17, that it comes to us ἐκ πίσεως εἰς πίσιν, Romans 3:21, 22, that it was manifested without the law, through faith in Jesus Christ, chapter 4:6, that it is imputed to us without works, chapter 9:3, that it is righteousness from faith, chapter 10:3, 4, that only those who believe in Christ, who is τὸ πλήρωμα τῶ νόμυ, are subject to the righteousness of God and possess that righteousness: but not those who seek to establish τὴν ἰδίαν δικαιοσύνην, their own righteousness. The Apostle contrasts this righteousness of God with the righteousness which is from the law in chapter 10:5, 6, as the righteousness which is from faith; and he teaches in verse 10 that when we believe that Jesus is Lord, and that God raised him from the dead, we believe εἰς δικαιοσύνην, unto righteousness; that is, when we believe, as Romans 4:25 has it, that he was delivered for our sins, and raised for our justification. He denies that this righteousness of God is from the law, for otherwise Christ would have died in vain, Galatians 2:21, and therefore he protests that, although he does not have his own righteousness which is from the law, he nevertheless has δικαιοσύνην ἐπὶ τῇ πίσει, righteousness through faith, Philippians 3:9. From this righteousness of God, every believer is called δίκαιος, righteous, of whom, with the Prophet Habakkuk 2:4, the Apostle says in Romans 1:17, Galatians 3:11, Hebrews 10:38, ὅτι ὁ δίκαιος ἐκ πίσεως ζήσεται, that the righteous shall live by faith. Moreover, the obedience which Grotius points out is a consequence and fruit of faith and of the righteousness of faith; nor can it have a place, or be conceived, without the law, which is the norm and rule of this obedience, or without works; because it consists in good works, or without one's own righteousness, since such obedience is our very own righteousness, and is as far removed from the righteousness of faith as the law is from the Gospel, indeed as far as the earth is from heaven. The righteousness dealt with here is that which is περισσεύεσα, abounding in praise, dignity, excellence, and fruit; just as the word περισσεύειν is taken in a good sense, either as abounding in praise, Luke 7:26, or in fruit, Matthew 13:12. But no man's own inherent righteousness is properly such; this belongs only to the righteousness of Christ; by which he was made under the law for us, Galatians 4:6. The righteousness dealt with here is that which is necessary for entry into heaven; or for eternal salvation. But it is not the obedience which God demands of us, or our own righteousness, but the righteousness which is from faith in Christ, who was made righteousness for us by God, 1 Corinthians 1:30, that is required for entry into heaven and for salvation: because justification, or even salvation and blessedness, does not come through works, nor are works required for justification or salvation, but to him who does not work but believes in Him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is counted as righteousness, and the blessedness, or his salvation, is of that man to whom God counts righteousness apart from works Rom. IV. 5. It treats of that righteousness which is more abundant than the righteousness of the Pharisees and Scribes, that is, legal, because Pharisaic righteousness is described in this way, that they sought a legal righteousness Rom. IX. 31. that they sought righteousness, not by faith, but by works of the law v. 32. that being ignorant of the righteousness of God, they attempted to set up their own righteousness, chap. X. 3. namely that righteousness which is from the law, of which Moses says, he who does these things shall live by them v. 5. But what is that more abundant righteousness than the legal righteousness of the Pharisees, by which we have work for entry into Heaven, what is that righteousness apart from works, a righteousness not from the works of the law, but from faith in Christ, who is the end of the law, if not the righteousness of God, or of Christ the God-man, through whose obedience alone we are constituted righteous by faith, through whose one act of righteousness, his satisfaction, justification of life comes to us Rom. X. 18. 19. It treats here of that righteousness which Christ, the Teacher of righteousness Is. LXIII. 1., both manifested to us and acquired for us, when He came not to abolish the law, but to FULFILL it v. 17. whom it behooved to fulfill all righteousness Matt. III. 15. and who is the end of the law, not by abolishing, but by fulfilling the law, for righteousness to everyone who believes Rom. X. 4. This passage is to be compared with Rom. III. 21. Do we then make the law void through faith? God forbid, rather we establish it. But this righteousness is not the obedience which GOD demands of us: for if we could perform that obedience, there would certainly have been no need for Christ to fulfill the law in our place, so that through faith in Him we might obtain righteousness. It treats in this place of that righteousness which those who feel spiritual poverty and mourn for their sins, in true humility and affliction or contrition, hunger and thirst for, so that they may be refreshed and satisfied Matt. V. 4. 5. 6. But our own righteousness, or the obedience which GOD demands of us, cannot refresh and satisfy such people; rather, those who have only that are forced to acknowledge their own destitution and poverty, and therefore have need to mourn, and are crushed, weary and heavy-laden Ap. III. 18. Matt. XI. 28. for whom, therefore, rest remains from Christ alone; in whom alone they find rest for their souls v. 29. Even if with the Apostle himself one is blameless according to the righteousness which is in the law Phil. III. 6. he will not yet have refreshment or rest in that righteousness, nor will his spiritual hunger and thirst be satisfied, much less will he enter the kingdom of heaven; rather, he will have need to count it, with the Apostle, as loss and dung, that he may be found in Christ, not having his own righteousness, which is from the law, but that which is through faith in Christ, or in Christ, the righteousness from God by faith, that righteousness from God which is through faith v. 7. 8. 9. Flacius is correct on v. 7 in the gloss on page 17. I certainly do not doubt here that Christ is resuming the beginning of His sermon, and as it were opening its sources, or the reason why. For from the true knowledge of the law, a true knowledge of oneself and one's own poverty is likewise received, just as a debtor recognizes his huge debt and poverty from a promissory note or the creditor's ledger. For since He had there exhorted all who were seeking blessedness or the highest good to acknowledge their own spiritual and shameful and clearly destructive nakedness or destitution, and to grieve over it, and to be humbled before God and to hunger and beg for His true righteousness, fullness, and kingdom, and lost riches: therefore, in order that He may now truly uncover this shameful nakedness of ours for us, and set it before our eyes to be looked upon, He brings the light and mirror of the law, and having wiped away the dust and stains from it, both of the Mosaic regime and of the Pharisaic glosses, He shows by its brightness what kind of being God is, and what kind of being He demands man to be, His image, and finally what a deformed image he bears on the face of his heart: so that men, hearing what exact righteousness the severe justice of God and the law demand of them, may also acknowledge the horrendous magnitude of their nakedness and the poverty of the once-implanted image of GOD, and thus may deplore that nakedness, and hunger and beg for the contrary riches and fullness. Thus, therefore, Christ here, by the explanation of the law, as if by a powerful machine of necessity, drives them to the point that they are forced to acknowledge their destructive nakedness of the image of God and of righteousness, and on the contrary to beg for gratuitous righteousness, to which He had only exhorted them at the beginning.

And therefore here the entry into the kingdom of heaven is denied to Pharisaic righteousness; and the more abundant righteousness is required, which is through faith in Christ: just as the Apostle in the cited passage, Phil. III. 5, said he was a Pharisee according to the law, by which he was blameless according to the righteousness which is in the law, but afterwards he counted that righteousness, or obedience, as loss, indeed as dung, so that he might gain Christ, and be found in Him through faith. Not that such obedience to the law is of its own fault, because the law is good, and just, and holy Rom. VII. 12. But it is our fault, who are carnal after the fall, while the law is spiritual v. 14. Therefore that Latin does not surpass the emphasis and force of the Greek phrase περισσεύσῃ πλεῖον; because it is not required that the justice be surpassing in any way whatsoever, or exceeding only by certain degrees, but much more abundant, indeed differing as much as the justice of God (of Christ the God-man, who is God blessed forever over all, and as man also ὅσιος, ἄκακος, ἀμίαντος, κεχωρισμένος ἀπὸ τῶν ἁμαρτωλῶν Heb. VII. 26. made for us by God justice 1 Cor. I. 30. Jehovah our justice Jer. XXIII. 5.) and our justice, who are carnal, sold under sin Rom. VII. 14. although now with Paul, being reborn, we delight in the law of God according to the inner man v. 22. and wish and strive to do τὸ καλόν. v. 21. Wherefore the interpretation of those who take that more abundant justice, which is necessary for those about to enter the kingdom of heaven, to be our incipient justice or obedience, which the reborn offer to divine precepts, does not deserve approval, nor is it consistent with the analogy of faith: which is done not only by the Papists, but also by the Calvinists and Calixtines, so that they may maintain that good works are necessary for salvation. Nor is it for anyone to object with Frid. Spanheim, part III, dub. Evangel. c. XXXVI. §. IV. p. 789, that the Lord's intention here is not to treat of the article of justification, and to show in what matter justice is to be sought before God, but only to impugn both false dogmas and the masked piety and justice of the Pharisees, and the restoration and corruption of the justice required by God in the law. For is not the discourse here about the entry into the kingdom of heaven? Is it not openly taught that, unless justice be more abundant, no one can enter the kingdom of heaven? But where there is a discussion of justice with respect to entry into the kingdom of heaven, there cannot be no respect to the article of justification. You say with Spanheim: indeed, not even a word here is concerning that which is necessary for justification, but concerning that which is necessary for entry into eternal life: But that which is necessary for the latter is not on that account necessary for the former. Resp. That, however, must be entirely inverted: because it is a question of that which is necessary for entry into eternal life; certainly, therefore, that which is necessary for justification can be concluded from this: since nothing can be necessary for obtaining eternal life which is not necessary for justification, and the reason is entirely the same regarding the condition on our part, which is thoroughly excluded from both justification and salvation, as the Apostle testifies Rom. IV. 5, 6, ch. VI, v. last, Eph. II. 8, Tit. III. 5, seqq. And indeed, salvation and blessedness are a gift of God equally gratuitous, obtained solely by the merit of Christ, to be apprehended and attained by us by faith alone, without the condition of works or of our obedience, so that he who believes in Christ is saved without work, by faith alone, says Ambrose: Blessed is that man to whom God imputes righteousness WITHOUT WORKS, he declares, and defines the Apostle from David, Ps. XXXII. 1, Rom. IV. 6. Nor does B. Luther inappropriately [say] in his disp. on justification, Anno 1536: To say that works are necessary for salvation is to say that Christ is a savior by initiation, not by perfection; likewise, it is to attribute to Christ and faith what is least, and to works what is greatest; to require Christ for justification as the least cause, but to require good works or new obedience for salvation as the greatest cause. Beware of these arguments: because this happens because Christ is no longer the savior; but he is despoiled of his honor, etc. And Spanheim had warned before, p. 788, that the mind of the Lord here is that, unless his disciples had and taught a more abundant righteousness, then considered objectively, i.e., a more perfect rule of righteousness, and unless they also studied it subjectively and had a more perfect one from elsewhere than the Scribes and Pharisees, they could not be saved. Although that [notion] concerning a more perfect rule of righteousness is indeed foreign to these words, yet how can the disciples have a MORE PERFECT righteousness FROM ELSEWHERE, unless it is that which is shown in the Gospel, which is the righteousness of Christ himself? Faith certainly does not seek, nor can it seek, from elsewhere than from Christ, since we can rely on our own faith. Spanheim also asked there whether the righteousness of the law and the righteousness of faith are opposed to each other? and he warned that it must be answered that both can be considered 1. in themselves and according to themselves; 2. in order to the same subject. In and according to themselves, they behave as disparate species under the same genus, for righteousness by the law is true righteousness where it is given, and righteousness by faith, as satisfaction either through one's own payment or through another's payment, is true satisfaction, both commanded by God, both pleasing to God, according to themselves; and either one or the other must be had, or man must perish, Lev. XVIII. 5, Rom. V. 1. Meanwhile, just as it is repugnant for two disparate things to belong to one and the same thing, insofar as they are disparate, and for the same person to be both a man and a brute, and to obtain something by the title of inheritance or donation, and at the same time by the title of mercenary labor and personal merit: so it is repugnant for the same person to attain eternal life by his own righteousness and by another's righteousness apprehended through faith. For he who attains it by his own righteousness has no need of another's; he who relies on another's is destitute of his own. Indeed, the lack of one's own righteousness makes room for both the seeking and the apprehension of another's righteousness, and leads to it as if by the hand. And thus the law was also a schoolmaster unto Christ. For he who feels himself destitute of his own righteousness, and yet knows that righteousness is necessarily required to appease God and obtain life, is by that very fact incited to flee to the righteousness of another, namely, the Mediator, by which he may be able to appear before the judgment of God. Thus far Spanheim, not badly. So therefore it is repugnant, in the judgment of the same, for the same person to attain eternal life by his own righteousness (which the Pharisees wanted, setting up their own righteousness) and by another's righteousness, apprehended through faith, which Christ so required against the Pharisees; so that unless his disciples have a more perfect one FROM ELSEWHERE, they cannot be saved. And that Christ was dealing entirely with justification here, from verse 6, namely that those who hunger and thirst for righteousness must be satisfied and refreshed, has already been established; and Spanheim himself acknowledged this at that place, Dub. LXXXIII, p. 401. Christ here seems to pronounce those blessed who with ardent desire seek both the righteousness that justifies before God and the righteousness that edifies before men: for both are connected, nor are those who do not study the latter held by the desire for the former, nor are those who are studious of the latter blessed without the study of the former. He rashly added the righteousness that edifies before men, which, even if it is connected to the former, cannot here be designated by the 'much more abundant righteousness'; since it is a question of such righteousness as is necessary for entry into the kingdom of heaven. Spanheim warned that those designated by the Lord with that phrase are those who, conscious of their own unrighteousness and indigence, ardently seek a remedy for the calming of their conscience before God, and who, when they do not find righteousness in themselves, seek it in him who was made righteousness for us by God, 1 Cor. I. 30, and desire to be found in him alone with Paul, Phil. III. 9. Who, therefore, denies now that it is the Lord's intention to deal here with the article of justification?

Meanwhile, Spanheim rightly denies against Maldonatus and other Papists that Christ calls the observance of the law righteousness, as if we were justified by the observance of God's commandments; nor was even that to be conceded to the modern Papist syncretists, that here legal righteousness or the observance of the law is established as necessary, as a condition without which there is no entry into the kingdom of heaven, even though he says that such a condition does not rely on a foolish cause, as the scholastics do: for this is also ἄγραφον, and ἀντίγραφον, nay, it is foolish, if we regard the wisdom of God as is fitting (who wills that we be saved by faith alone, that is, by the apprehension of the obedience of Christ), to add, forsooth, another condition of our own, namely, of our own righteousness and obedience, as if no one could enter heaven by that most abundant righteousness of Christ, unless under that condition that he be equipped with a more abundant observance of the law than the Pharisees, and with inherent righteousness: by which method legal promises are mixed with Evangelical ones, the law is confounded with the Gospel, the grace announced in the Gospel is suspended from the condition of the observance of the law, and a patch of our own menstrual righteousness is sewn onto the most holy righteousness of Christ, and that for the sake of entry into the kingdom of heaven; nor is there any reason for Spanheim to say that the Lord is not disputing against the righteousness of the law, but against the righteousness of the Scribes and Pharisees: because he is disputing against the righteousness of the law insofar as the Scribes and Pharisees judged that a man enters the kingdom of heaven through the observance of the law: since the Lord requires a far more abundant righteousness than the obedience to the law of either the Pharisees or any man is, or can be after the fall, and he acted concerning his office and the end of his coming for this reason, that he came to fulfill the law, that he might lead us to that more abundant righteousness. And here Spanheim prunes his own vineyards: while he immediately adds on page 790 that a more abundant righteousness is required: Therefore a greater righteousness than ours, which is not sufficient, less than abundant; such indeed is either legal only, exact obedience rendered to the whole law, or Evangelical, the fiducial application of the righteousness of the Mediator to whom alone there is place from when man began to be a sinner, and from when the Law ἠσθένησ' διὰ τῆς σαρκός [was weak through the flesh]. From which it is certainly evident that not legal, but Evangelical righteousness is urged by Christ.

Only for the sake of the Calixtines do we add that τὸ περισσεύειν πλεῖον [to abound more] does not always imply an intension of degree in the same species of righteousness, but that it can also signify the substitution of a completely different species, as in Matt. 11:9. The Baptist, who had denied himself to be a Prophet, is called πεῖσσότερον προφήτε [more than a prophet], more abundant, more excellent than a Prophet: Matt. 12:41, 42. Christ is πλεῖον [more] than Solomon and Jonah; ch. 6:3, the soul πλεῖον ἐςι τῆς τροφῆς [is more than food] is more than food. 2 Cor. 3:9, the διακονία [ministry] of the Gospel πολλῶ μᾶλλον περισσεύει ἐν δόξῃ [abounds much more in glory] than the διακονία [ministry] of condemnation, etc. Let us add also this, if anyone should interpret these things as being about legal righteousness, which interpretation, however, we by no means concede, there would be no consequence from a conditional negative to the opposite affirmative, just as it does not follow in John 4:48, Unless you see signs and wonders, you do not believe, therefore signs and wonders will be necessary for believing. Therefore, upon seeing signs and wonders, faith will follow! But much less is an absolute opposite affirmative to be inferred from a comparative conditional negative: just as it is not permitted to infer; if someone should say, unless you are chaster than Heliogabalus you will not enter into the kingdom of heaven, therefore you will enter the kingdom of heaven where you are like Socrates in chastity, therefore that greater chastity of Socrates was necessary for him for entry into the kingdom of heaven; the reason is, because such propositions say what will not follow from the present condition, not likewise what will follow from that one ceasing, or another quality being introduced. But Hornejus acknowledges in iterat. assert. contra D. Rothmaler. th. 57, that this Evangelical saying is not legal: and he proves it thus on p. 109. Christ explicitly begins that sermon from the 8 beatitudes: Then opening his mouth he said, saying: Blessed are the poor in Spirit, for theirs is the kingdom, Blessed are they that mourn, for they shall receive comfort, etc. But that eternal beatitude is primarily and in no way given through the law: but through the gospel. Whence also immediately before the words alleged he adds, lest they think that he came to dissolve the law and the Prophets, but that he himself might fulfill them for us and make us fulfill them in our way: for if anyone shall have broken and despised even the least, he is to be called the least in the kingdom of heaven: and he subjoins: for I say unto you, unless it shall have abounded, etc. Thus far Hornejus, the Majorist Julianus. For if this saying is Evangelical, how can it be explained concerning a legal condition, or concerning the observance of the commandments of God? since the Gospel is distinct from the law by the whole heaven. And given that explanation, which we do not deny is that of some orthodox, concerning legal righteousness which they understand as κατ' ἀκριβοδίκαιον [according to strict justice] perfect in all ways, the entry into the kingdom of heaven through one's own righteousness is not established, but removed: because there is no one who can fulfill the law according to that rigor, and therefore sayings of that legal kind only exhibit our ἀδυναμίαν [weakness] after the fall, and lead us to Christ, who fulfilled the law in our place. But it is better to understand it Evangelically, not indeed concerning our begun righteousness (for this contributes nothing to the Gospel, or Evangelical righteousness, since the Gospel is a sermon of grace concerning Christ, and his righteousness, the sum of which is the just shall live by his faith, and not a sermon of repentance, or concerning our obedience and righteousness, whose doctrine, and rule, and norm is the law, not the Gospel, but) concerning the righteousness of Christ, which is much more abundant than the Pharisaical, and through faith by apprehension is altogether necessary for entry into the kingdom of heaven. Which is gathered from the ἀντιθέσει [antithesis] of the doctrine of the Pharisees and of Christ. For they established that for righteousness and eternal life there is need of the fulfillment of the law, and when they understood that those things which are commanded concerning interior morals, in the mind and heart of man, concerning blemishes in gestures and words, and concerning love from the whole heart, the whole soul, and all one's strength, could by no means be fulfilled, they invented a distinction between commandments, that some are least, but some are great, and that the fulfillment of these is sufficient: which hypothesis Christ rejects, teaching that he who shall have broken one of the least (in their opinion) commandments, will be held as the least in the kingdom of heaven, that is, will have no place in it. In which way also the Papists and Innovators imagine that GOD under the new covenant does not require that all things be fulfilled according to the rigor of the law, provided that as much as is in us, we fulfill the law, and that that obedience can be opposed to the judgment of GOD for righteousness and eternal life, and they think this is required by Christ for entry into the kingdom of heaven. Christ therefore from the opposite teaches, with our B. Chemnitius rightly observing, that that Pharisaical righteousness, which does not most perfectly have the entire fulfillment of the law: but only a certain particle of the law, concerning certain external works somehow kept, cannot enter the kingdom of heaven. Christ therefore wishes the righteousness of his own to be more abundant or fuller, i.e., he wishes his own to bring to the judgment of GOD a most abundant, most full, and most perfect righteousness, so that through and because of it they may be able to enter into the kingdom of heaven. But because they do not find it in themselves, they seek it by faith, and apprehend it in the fulfillment of the law performed for us by Christ. Then there is, and ought to be, a righteousness of works in the regenerate, on account of the interior renewal of the Spirit, more abundant than the righteousness of the flesh in the Pharisees; but because even the regenerate, although they perceive the Law of God in their mind, yet in the flesh serve the Law of sin, Roman. VII. 25. Therefore by and because of their works; because they are imperfect and unclean, they cannot enter into the kingdom of heaven. But in this question, so that they may enter the kingdom of heaven, they do not flee to the righteousness of the flesh of the Pharisees, nor to their own spiritual imperfect obedience, but to the most perfect righteousness of Christ by faith. Concerning the works of the regenerate themselves, it will have to be spoken of in the following. But to the figment of the Pharisees concerning the least commandments, Christ opposes one iota and one tittle: so that he may deny as strongly as possible that there are certain commandments in the Law so minute that God does not care much about them, of which also, even if they are not fulfilled, there should be no account taken in establishing the righteousness of the Law before God. In this explanation of the blessed Chemnitz, as being derived from the inner depths of the text, we deservedly acquiesce: whom also Schlüffelburg follows in Catal: hær. l. VII. de Majorist. p. 463. B. Meisner, B. Hülsemann, B. Glass, with most other Doctors of our Church: concerning the sole imputed righteousness of Christ, necessary here for entry into the kingdom of heaven, brought forward.

But to return to Grotius: he repeats the Pharisaic innocence, which he judges Christ to assert against the opinion received at that time, from Paul, formerly addicted to the Pharisaic sect, who Gal. III. 16. (he meant to say, Phil. III. 6.) says that at that time he lived blameless, as far as pertains to that righteousness which is in the law: understanding by the law that which Hebrew judges were bound to follow in investigating cases, who could neither look into the mind, nor indeed received power to punish all things done otherwise, but only those which would especially harm civil society: which law of deeds he wishes to be called by the Apostle. Concerning which he discourses afterwards thus p: 73. let that innocence of deeds have δικαίωσιν, but among men: and it was profitable for temporal happiness. But the kingdom of heaven was destined by GOD to the spirit, not to that bodily innocence, but to spiritual righteousness, the source of which is true faith which is situated in the mind. For that law, viewed externally, could not τελειῶν τὴν συνείδησιν Hebr. IX. 9. But it was profitable πρὸς τὴν τῆς σαρκὸς καθαρότη- τα ibid. 13. From this pernicious error it also followed that, since they believed those external deeds were sufficient before God no less than before men, they were not solicitous about seriously seeking the remission of sins, nor did they devote effort to purging their souls and extirpating those vices which are wont to be dissimulated among men: nor did they think they had need of such a Messiah, who would bring medicine to that part which they did not feel to be ailing. And this is what Christ reproaches them with in many places, and Paul in his epistle to the Romans, clearly showing that this was fatal to them, that they did not submit themselves to the righteousness of GOD, which is spiritual, seeking to establish a certain righteousness of their own, that is, human righteousness. In this explanation of the Pharisaic opinion, we especially desire that he would not restrict the righteousness of their own, which the Jews wished to establish, to which Paul opposes the righteousness of God which is of faith, to the innocence of deeds: and that he would not explain the law of deeds as the judicial or forensic law, which Hebrew judges were bound to follow in hearing cases, and think that Paul testifies that he was ἄμεμπτον, blameless, Phil. III. 6, only in respect of it. Because the opposition of the righteousness of GOD and of faith and of one's own righteousness, and of the law, is adequate, and is so instituted by the Apostle that by the name of the latter he understands not only the external innocence of works or deeds, which are called into human judgment, but any observation of the law whatsoever, as much as can be performed by man after the fall. By the naming of the former, however, he designates the righteousness and obedience of Christ performed in our stead: concerning which, in the Vindications of the Pauline Epistles, with GOD. Nor is the matter for them only with the Pharisees; but also with the Pseudo-Apostles, who urged the righteousness of works, and he so asserts righteousness from faith, that he excludes from the cause of justification and salvation not only external works, but internal, and whatever pertains to the law. Grotius is also mistaken when he says that the law of deeds is called by the Apostle here and there for the sake of distinction, that which Hebrew judges were bound to follow in hearing cases: since he could not produce a single Apostolic passage where the law of deeds is so called; nor does that appellation occur in the Vulgate version, except only once Rom. III. 27, where in the Greek it is νόμου ἔργων, and it is manifest that the moral law is especially regarded, and that the law of works and the law of faith are immediately and adequately opposed: and so there, works of any kind, not only external but also internal, are understood, but here faith in Christ, to which justification is so ascribed that all works universally are excluded, and justification is attributed to faith alone. Nor indeed does the Apostle say that he was blameless only regarding cases pertaining to the forum and judgment; but generally, regarding the righteousness which is required in the law, embracing the moral law at the same time, which, however, hindered by Pharisaic prejudices, he did not believe prohibited wicked desires. Other things are also assumed precariously by Grotius, such as, that the law of love does not come from a certain prescription, but from the rich goodness of the mind (which openly contradicts the declaration of the lawyer handed down in Luke X. 24): that no penalty was clearly attached to such precepts about loving God from the heart and vexing wicked desires: (in which hypothesis Grotius was unmindful of the divine curse, pronounced upon all who do not remain in all things which are written in the book of the law, Deut. XXVII. 26.) Finally, that the Jews interpreted such precepts more as a matter of counsel than as a necessity of the law; or certainly that they thought those stains were so purged partly by daily sacrifices, partly by the annual expiatory rite, that no memory of them remained before GOD: in which latter point concerning expiation there is no error, as regards those who offered victims with true faith and instituted the annual expiation; since GOD has testified here and there that the remission of sins was made to them; when, however, God has forgiven sins, He does not wish to be mindful of them any longer. Is. XLIII. 25. XLVI. 23. Jerem. XXXI. 34. Matth. VII. 18. 19.

Vers. 20.

unless you enter into the kingdom of heaven] The kingdom of heaven, as we have already said, has diverse notions. Here, however, it is most equitable that these words be accepted not concerning doctrine or the assembly of the pious, but concerning eternal rewards: first, because almost wherever the kingdom of heaven is found in these books joined with the verb to enter, that heavenly glory is understood, Matth. VII. 21. XVIII. 3. XIX. 23. 24. Marc. X. 23. 24. Luc. XVIII. 24. 25. Johan. III. 5. Acts XIV. 22. In which places, as in this one of ours, there is a tacit allusion to those threats in the law: You shall not enter into the land. Num. XIV. 30. Ps. XCIV. 11. Then, because in the continuation of the discourse itself Christ opposed the kingdom of God to Gehenna, as is openly to be seen in Mark IX. 47. Jerome against Pelagius, who had said that it is clear that the kingdom of heaven is promised in the Old Testament, says that the kingdom of heaven is first preached in the Gospel, to which agrees that of Chrysostom. Reading the law, reading the Prophets, reading the Psalter, I never heard of the kingdom of heaven except in the Gospel. With whom Augustine agrees. Finally, that I may not have said it rashly, I do not know whether anyone has found in those books the name of the kingdom of heaven, which the Lord names so frequently. And this is indeed said as far as the word itself is concerned. But treating of the thing itself against Pelagius, Augustine in the book on the acts of the Synod of Palestine, distinguishes the name of the Old Testament: for he says that by it is understood either that covenant which was made on Mount Sinai; or all things which are contained in Moses and the Prophets. The covenant made on Mount Sinai, which they also often call the law, is said to have had earthly promises, and indeed earthly ones only, which he often proves with the words of Paul to the Galatians 3:12, 'he who does them (namely the works of the law) shall live in them,' that is, he shall have the reward so that he does not die on that mountain, so that he does not suffer stoning, the sword, or anything of this kind. Nevertheless, both Augustine and other Christian writers admit that even in the time of the law there were not lacking those who hoped for greater things than earthly goods. But they say this was drawn not from the law but from the fathers, to whom God had given hope of a greater good by many indications: in which class of indications not the least is that many exceptionally good men lived devoid of earthly happiness, an argument which the writer to the Hebrews pursues at length in chapter 11. The same writers add that those earthly promises given to the law of works were signs of those goods which followed the law of the Spirit, but this was understood by few: who, namely, although they lived in the time of the Old Testament, nevertheless belonged to the grace which was revealed in the times of the New Testament. Philo in the history of his embassy: 'The instruction, the interpretation of the holy scriptures is full of hopes for those who are truly noble. And the laws create good hopes for those who encounter them, not just with the tips of their lips.' Josephus Albo the Jew, disputing about this matter, says that spiritual happiness is indeed not promised expressly in the law of Moses, but that it is indicated by certain signs and wrappings: and that this was done because the law was not given only to the learned and wise, but to the whole people, in whom the uneducated were mixed with the more perceptive, wherefore in a common promulgation those things had to be set forth which could be perceived by all and could move the minds of all. Moreover, such sensible things are of value only among the wise, whereas to the judgment of the common people they do not even seem credible. For this reason, he says, the law set forth clearly bodily and conspicuous things that fall into the notice of the common people, but those things which are grasped by the intellect alone, it set forth under the wrappings of signs. Thus that Jew of very sharp judgment. Indeed, that which is perceived by the mind alone is such as Xenophanes said: 'It is no longer possible to approach it with the eyes, nor to grasp it with the hands, which is the greatest path of persuasion that falls into the human mind.'

That such are the goods of the other life, Paul openly declares in 1 Cor. 2:9. It is not to be wondered at, therefore, if to a coarse people, and one that, as appears from all history, was very σαρκικῷ (fleshly), God did not openly propose those things which would exceed their capacity. But, accommodating Himself to their nature, He wished to diminish the inveterate habit of sinning by the advantages and disadvantages of visible things: just as, indeed, parents do not entice children of tender age with the hope of an inheritance, which they do not understand, but partly deter them from delinquency by the fear of the rod, and partly, as that man says: -- Doctors coax boys with cookies, that they may wish to learn their first elements. Nor, however, was the way to better progress taken away through these rudiments. For there were Prophets present who would unfold what was covered, and would reveal to individuals as much as their capacity and the reason of utility allowed. But in public sermons, the Prophets and wise men spoke in such a way that they would neither bring the mysteries of the sanctioned discipline into contempt, and yet would excite the attentive listener to a concern for investigating. Justin says well: 'Whatever the prophets said and did, they covered with parables and places, so that most things might not be easily understood by all, hiding the truth in them, so that those who seek might find and learn.' Whom Origen follows against Celsus, VII. The prophets, therefore, spoke whatever was useful and contributed to the correction of morals, to be understood immediately by the hearers, without any concealment, according to the will of God; but whatever was more mystical and contemplative, and pertaining to a theory beyond the sensory hearing, these they declared by means of riddles and allegories and covered, dark sayings and so-called parables or proverbs, so that those who do not act carelessly, but undertake every labor for the sake of virtue and truth, might find them by examining, and having found them, as reason dictates, might manage them. And from this I think the distinction celebrated among the Jews in antiquity was born, as appears from Josephus, Philo, and others, between the written law and the oral law, תורה שעל פה, which they also call קבלה, that is, παράδοσιν (tradition): saying that both proceeded from Moses: not that there were other things in the tradition than in the written law, but that those things which were contained more occultly in the written law were unraveled for studious investigators by accurate interpretation. And this method of teaching seems to have prevailed among the coarser people, and a more refined one among τοὺς προκόψαντας (those who were advancing), up to the times that followed the Babylonian exile.

Whatever may be the case regarding the term 'kingdom of heaven,' the pious ancients do not deny that the thing itself is contained in the books of the Old Testament. Regarding the law, they deny it primarily, lest, namely, it be believed that anyone could have attained eternal life through the law: for they denied this against the Pelagians. Concerning which Primasius in chapter 2 to the Galatians: 'If the law could justify, Christ died in vain. Let them blush who say that the law sent [people] to the kingdom.' Likewise chapter 3: 'Hearing this, let them be silent who rave that the law by itself transmitted anyone to the kingdom of heaven.'
