For what Pelagius taught, that the kingdom of heaven was promised even in the Old Testament, is to be understood in the same way as Celestius handed down the same, whose opinion was this: 'The law sends to the kingdom of heaven just as the Gospel does.' Which St. Prosper expressed thus in his book against the ungrateful.

-- The same author also connects that, that the law sent the saints of old into the kingdom of heaven, just as grace sends them now.

Concerning which, Vossius is to be consulted, book III, part II, History of Pelagianism, thesis X. And Augustine speaks circumspectly about the Palestinian acts, chapter V: that earthly promises on Mount Sinai pertain PROPERLY TO THE OLD TESTAMENT. For heavenly promises pertain PROPERLY to the New Testament, because they are comprehended in such a way that the same grace of attaining them is promised to us at the same time, whereas in the OLD TESTAMENT, even if they were comprehended, that grace of attaining them was not promised. Furthermore, the law must be distinguished along with the promises which are comprehended by the law, when the discourse is about the moral law, by which they are viewed according to the use which they call Political or even moral and didactic, which is proper to it, and pertains properly to the Old Testament, in which respect earthly promises only fulfill the law, because those who keep it thus, so that the polity and external discipline are preserved, and life is instituted according to the same, as much as is allowed by this infirmity, for them no such political or temporal punishment is to be feared, and the reward of earthly happiness is promised. But when the law is viewed according to the pedagogical use, which is accidental to it, and at the same time involves a relation to the New Testament, then the law rigorously demands perfect holiness and obedience, not only external but internal, of all thoughts and movements of the heart, and when it does not find it in any of mortals, it condemns and concludes all under a curse, so that they are thus forced to seek Him through whom alone they are freed from the curse: to whom, therefore, it is a Pedagogue to Christ: there it is certain that the law promises eternal life itself, but to those who render such obedience to the law, not so that they may attain it through the law, but so that they may understand that they cannot attain it through the observance of the law; but attain it solely through the Gospel apprehended by faith. In which manner the promise of eternal life, viewed with effect, pertains properly to the New Covenant, not to the Old Testament, and in that sense the kingdom of heaven is not promised in the Old Testament. If the law is viewed absolutely, it does indeed of itself produce life, if it is kept; for it produces wrath and death only accidentally, not because it was given, but because it was not kept, not by its own fault, but by ours. This was the opinion of the ancients. For thus Augustine, book II, later against Julian, chapter XCVIII: Dare to say this, when the Apostle says that no one is justified by the law, when the Apostle says the law entered that the offense might abound, when the Apostle says if a law had been given which could give life, righteousness would have been altogether by the law, but the Scripture has concluded all under sin, that the promise by faith of Jesus Christ might be given to those who believe.

Furthermore, those who in the time of the law hoped for things greater than earthly goods did not conclude this merely from certain indications which could be understood by few, as if they had been proposed only under the wrappings of signs, but they held them from divine promises, and those asserted and sufficiently clear, which could not only be known by certain wise and perspicacious men, but were proposed clearly enough to all, to the end that they might be embraced by all. This is not the opinion of one or another Doctor; but it is the catholic opinion of the Fathers concerning the Evangelical promises in the Scriptures of the Old Testament, so that here we have no need to attend to the blind Jews, Joseph Albo, or the like, but to the Catholic Church, nay, to Scripture itself, which shines as a lamp in a dark place, as Peter testifies in his 2nd Epistle, I. 19, and is not obscure or dark in these things necessary for all for a saving end. For how could the Evangelical promises have been apprehended by faith by those to whom they were proposed as the cause of salvation to be believed, if they had been obscure? Therefore, when it was objected to Pelagius in the Council of Diospolis that he had said that the kingdom of heaven was promised even in the Old Testament (in the sense we have designated), and he defended himself thus: I indeed spoke following the authority of the Scriptures, since it is written in the Prophet Daniel, 'And the saints shall receive the kingdom of the Most High': having heard this, the Synod replied: Nor is this foreign to the ECCLESIASTICAL faith. And St. Augustine, concerning the Palestinian acts, chapter V, warned that this is not foreign to the catholic faith (that eternal life was promised in the Old Testament according to this custom of speaking), which the whole canonical Scripture before the incarnation of the Lord is considered to be, while the Old Testament administration is in force. Concerning which also Augustine, against the two Epistles of the Pelagians, book III, chapter IV. What CATHOLIC would say what the Pelagians boast that we say, That the Holy Spirit was not a helper in the Old Testament. But shall we deny that He pertains to the New Testament, who says: Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right Spirit within me, etc. "Whether therefore Abraham, or the just before him, or "after him up to Moses, or the other Proph- "ets after him, and the holy men of God up to John "the Baptist, are children of the promise of grace "according to Isaac, heirs of God not from the law, "but from the promise, co-heirs of Christ. For far "be it that we should deny that Noah the just and the just of the former time, "and whoever from him up to Abraham could be just, whether conspicuous "or hidden, pertain to the "supernal Jerusalem, which is our mother. Therefore in the time of the Old Testament We say that the Holy Spirit "in those who even then were children of the "promise according to Isaac, was not only a helper, which those "(Pelagians) think is sufficient for their dogma, "but also a bestower of virtue.

All these things are Augustine's, which are sufficiently bright and clear: With which Jerome entirely agrees, "book II. Comment. on Ep. Gal. VI. Just as all "die in the first-formed Adam not yet born, so "also all these, who were born before the coming of Christ, "are made alive in the second Adam. And thus it happens, that both we served the law in the Fathers, and they "are saved by grace in the sons. This understanding agrees with the Catholic Church, which asserts one providence for both the Old and New Testaments, nor does it distinguish in time those whom it joined in condition. These things also Jerome: thus therefore those things concerning eternal life were not set forth to a few only, nor was the Holy Spirit given to a few only extraordinarily, but the divine promises were openly proposed to all, which all were bound to receive by faith, and the gift of the Holy Spirit as the bestower of virtue was common to all the faithful. Nor indeed was it fitting for this office of the Prophets to hide these things from some, who rather made known the will of God to all, especially in the matter of eternal salvation Is. 45. Jer. 31. c. 32. & 33. & elsewhere passim.

But what Justin has concerning coverings and parables, not all being explained, does not concern the spiritual promises concerning the remission of sins and eternal life, but prophecies concerning the future state of the Church, proposed in various enigmas, types, figures, and parables, most of which, however, were explained clearly. But what Grotius inserts concerning the Cabala of the Jews for the sake, as it appears, of the Cabala, or the unwritten tradition of the Papists, does not pertain to the matter at all, and they are of doubtful and uncertain origin and truth. For others explain the Cabala of the Jews differently. The Cabala is either divine, such as was both the unwritten oral institution in the time of the Patriarchs received from God and propagated through πατροπαράδοτοι tradition, and the written, inasmuch as the Talmudists designate the prophetic writings by the name of Cabala; or human, fabricated by human genius, such as that which the Jews boast of, namely first the Talmudic, which the Jews pretend was handed down to Moses on Mount Sinai, and which they venerate greatly, having been redacted into one body under the title משנה, which constitutes a part of the Talmud, and concerns the ἁγραφον law (namely, not written in Moses, but handed down concerning the administration of Levitical worship, the government of the Republic, and a fuller explanation of the whole of Judaism). Then the Symbolic: which consists in a great part in a singular combination, numeration, and Alphabetical revelation, and is Theoretical but entirely vain and superstitious. Thirdly, the practical Cabala, which is joined with the horrible profanation of the word of God, and is occupied with exorcisms, amulets, and ἁμυντήρια, and is the origin of all Demonolatry, according to the judgment of Graserus Exerc. II. in cap. IX. Dan.

and Mr. Dr. Müller in Rabbinism p. 15. and finally, that which some Christians refer to as accepted by the Jews, namely a tradition concerning mysteries not expressly contained in the Scripture of the Old Testament nor openly proposed to all. Such as Grotius here attributes to the Jews, and thinks that the doctrine concerning the kingdom of heaven, or eternal life, pertained to the same. But that it was also among the hidden things, handed down not to the people, but only to the more perspicacious, is most false; nor does it consist with any document that such mysteries, which look to eternal life, were propagated orally up to Ezra, and were studiously hidden by the Prophets from the unlearned. That opinion draws its origin from a fabulous book, which is attributed to Ezra, and is called the fourth of Ezra; the primary champion of this fable, as is clear, was Pico della Mirandola in Apol. p. 82. But after they were restored from the Babylonian captivity by Cyrus under Zerubbabel, the temple having been restored, they applied their mind to repairing the law, Ezra then the prefect of the Church, after the book of Moses had been amended, since he clearly knew through the exiles, slaughters, flights, and captivity of the Israelite nation, that the custom instituted by the ancestors to be handed down by the hands of doctrine could not be preserved, and that it would happen that the secrets of heavenly doctrine divinely granted to them would perish, the memory of which could not last long without the intervention of commentaries, he decided, and having convened the wise men who then survived, that each one should bring into the midst what he held by memory concerning the mysteries of the law, and with scribes employed, they should be redacted into seventy volumes, for there were almost that many wise men in the sanhedrin. Concerning which matter those who do not believe me, let them hear Ezra himself speaking thus: When (4. Es. 14. 46.) 40. days had passed, the most high spoke, saying: The former things which you have written, put in the open, let the worthy and unworthy read: but the last seventy books you shall preserve, that you may hand them over to the wise men of your people: For in these is the vein of understanding, and the fountain of wisdom, and the river of knowledge and so I did. These things Ezra word for word. These are the books of the science of the Cabala, in which Ezra rightly pronounced with a clear voice that there was a vein of understanding, that is, an ineffable Theology concerning the supersubstantial Deity, a fountain of wisdom, that is, an exact Metaphysics concerning intelligible and Angelic forms, and a river of knowledge, that is, a most firm Philosophy concerning natural things. These books Sixtus the fourth, Pontiff. Max. who immediately preceded this Innocent VIII, under whom we live happily, took the greatest care and effort that they might be committed to Latin letters for the public utility of our faith, and already when he died, three of them had reached the Latins: these books, among the Hebrews, are cultivated at this time with such religious devotion that it is permitted to no one, unless born forty years, to touch them. Having procured these books for myself at no small expense, and having read them through with the greatest diligence and tireless labors, I saw in them (God is my witness) a religion not so much Mosaic as Christian; there the mystery of the Trinity, there the incarnation of the Word, there the divinity of the Messiah, there concerning original sin, concerning its expiation through Christ, concerning the heavenly Jerusalem, concerning the fall of the demons, concerning the orders of Angels, concerning the punishments of purgatory and of the infernal regions, I read the same things which we read daily in Paul and Dionysius, in Jerome and Augustine. But who will have faith in that rhapsody, stuffed with fables, which is sold under the holy name of Ezra? And who are those 70 books, which were to be commended only to the wise? Hottinger asks in Thesaur. Phil. lib. 1, cap. 3, where is the shadow? where is the apex, where is the conjecture of this Kabbalistic doctrine? The Pharisees, with whom was the key of knowledge, and who are called δευτερῴται for this reason, because they propagated the traditions of their ancestors with tireless zeal, themselves clinging to them tenaciously; no traces of this Kabbalistic doctrine do they show us. Indeed, for the New Testament and the coming of Christ, the true Kabbalah and the saving revelation of the mysteries was to be reserved. The eyes of the Apostles themselves were dimmed for some time. Paul, having followed the more accurate heresy of the Jews, and having been educated at the feet of Gamaliel, a man most polished in all Hebrew discipline, only then, taught by God, learned the true Kabbalah when he unlearned his own. And not without merit concerning these, Corn. Agrippa, De Vanit. scient. c. 47: But if this Kabbalah (which the Jews boast of) proceeded from God to lead to the perfection of life, to the salvation of men, to the worship of God, to the truth of intelligence, surely that Spirit of truth, who, having repudiated the synagogue, came to teach us all truth, would not have hidden this from his Church until these latter times, he who surely knows all things that are of God, whose blessing, baptism, and other sacraments of salvation have been revealed and perfected in every tongue. And how could the heavenly dogmas concerning eternal life and the resurrection of the dead have been hidden from the Jews, which are set forth clearly enough in the very Scriptures of the Old Testament, and are defended by the Jews themselves against the Sadducees from those same [Scriptures], as is known from the books of Menasseh Ben Israel on the resurrection of the dead.

But when Grotius, convinced by the evidence of the matter, could not deny that those things were set forth in the Prophets, he invented a distinction of times and of sacred writers before and after the Babylonian exile. For he confesses that those things were handed down in these later ones; but he denies that they were expressly promised in the former, and he fabricates this as the reason why they were handed down in the latter, that the people were then subject to more grievous persecutions.

Then indeed, he says, with grave danger impending, lest the people, accustomed to hear only those things which fell within the senses, with the splendor of the Jewish empire removed, groaning under foreign rule, anxious from the fear of loss, torture, and finally death, should fall away from Judaism, Daniel was the first of all to treat more openly of the resurrection, confirming the people with the hope of restoration to a better state, of the 'better resurrection,' as the writer to the Hebrews speaks. Ezekiel followed Daniel, to whom the writer of the exhortation to the Greeks looks back, among the works of Justin, which Plato holds concerning judgment after this life, he says were drawn from the Prophets. Hence begin the wise men, whom they call החכמים, who, educated by human means, not divinely, succeeded the Prophets, but with unequal authority. These also judged it necessary to fortify the people from Daniel against temptations, which could not be done sufficiently unless the cause of God was set before those dying with the hope of a better life. Therefore, that doctrine was then brought out as if from hiding and sealed with certain words. Hence that [remark] of Tacitus concerning the Jews: they think the souls of those killed in battle or by executions are eternal. Hence the contempt of dying. Numenius also, in the first book On the Good, placed the Brahmins, Jews, and Egyptians among the nations agreeing with the Platonic view on the immortality of souls. And indeed, that not only the immortality of souls, but also the resurrection, that is, a certain recovery of the body, was openly handed down and believed, appears most manifestly from that place which he cited from the writer to the Hebrews, and then from the other, which is Acts 23:8. To which are to be added two illustrious passages from the Maccabean history, book II, ch. VII, the former of which holds thus: 'The King of the world will raise us up, who have died for his laws, to an everlasting revival of life': the latter, however, thus: 'For our brothers now, having endured a short pain, have fallen under the covenant of God for everlasting life.' They called the state of pious souls after death, from that garden in which Adam was initially placed, in Hebrew גן עדן, in Greek παράδεισος, as can be seen also in Philo and Josephus: But they called the state after the resurrection by a more excellent term, in Hebrew מלכות שמים or מלכות אלהה, in Greek βασιλείαν τοῦ Θεοῦ, or βασιλείαν τῶν οὐρανῶν, to which pertains, among others, that passage of the son of Sirach: 'But the righteous live forever, and their reward is with the Lord, and the care of them is with the Most High. Therefore they shall receive the kingdom of glory and the crown of beauty from the hand of the Lord.' Animated by this dogma in the Maccabean times, very many endured most exquisite deaths for the sake of the law, as the annals of those times teach us, and as was wisely noted by the writer to the Hebrews. And the Chaldean Paraphrast on Genesis, who is believed to have been before Christ, makes open mention of judgment after this life, both elsewhere and in the history of Abel. Since these things are so, it is not without merit asked, in what sense then is Christ said to have brought life and immortality to light through the Gospel, 2 Tim. 1:10. These are the words of Grotius.

But he is entirely mistaken in believing that those heads of heavenly doctrine were manifested only because of the dangers and evils to be sustained, if indeed eternal life was promised even before the fall, when the first parents were exposed to no calamity in the state of integrity, if they had kept the law of the Lord, and they pertain to those things which are necessary for a man to believe if he wishes to be saved, whence they had to be believed by all who had to be repaired from the fall for salvation. For because they had to have faith in the Messiah, who had to deliver the human race from the death to which they were subject, and to restore eternal life, their faith could not in any way be consistent if they were completely ignorant of eternal life. Certainly, no Catholic in antiquity doubted that the article concerning eternal life pertained to the Catholic faith and that of all times. Furthermore, that it is false that Daniel was the first of all to treat openly of the resurrection of the dead, even the Jewish Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel has convinced Grotius: not to mention Christ convincing the Sadducees of the resurrection of the dead from the Pentateuch of Moses, Matthew 22. And how Grotius also did not leave this oracle of Daniel untouched, but most wretchedly corrupted it, we have said in its place. Which we have likewise observed concerning the prophecy of Ezekiel. These being weakened, no testimony will remain any longer in the canonical scriptures of the Old Testament concerning eternal life or the resurrection of the dead (according to the Grotian sense). Whence, therefore, did the author of the book of Wisdom, whence did the Maccabean martyrs have that faith, if it is not founded in the canonical Scriptures?

Now as to that catalogue of the Saints of the Old Testament in Hebrews 11, not only are the believers of later times celebrated, but also others from Abel onwards, because they believed God to be a μισθαποδότην (rewarder), which especially regards the gratuitous retribution of the other life, and by that faith the holy Patriarchs are commended, because they expected a remaining city. Nor is there any doubt that the holy Patriarchs inculcated saving faith and its chief heads to their families and to the universal Church entrusted to them, which the Lord Himself testified concerning Abraham in Gen. 18:19, not to mention that in the law itself eternal life was promised, albeit under the condition of perfect obedience, as interpreted by Christ Himself in Luke 10:28 and the holy Apostle in Gal. 3:12, of which we spoke at Lev. 18.

But as to the fact that Christ is said to have brought life and immortality to light through the Gospel, Grotius proceeds thus concerning it in this place on p. 73: 'Indeed, just as among the Greek philosophers some asserted the immortality of souls, while others denied it; Socrates, however, left it as it were in the middle, whom Aristotle seems to have followed, hesitating much here, as did the Latins Cicero and Seneca: so among the Jews a dogma of such moment for piety was among the things disputed. The Pharisees affirmed it, but the Sadducees denied it, since they accepted nothing unless they found it expressed in so many words in Moses. With the Pharisees on the other hand having almost nothing by which they could prove what they contended for except the authority of reason, the minds of many fluctuated between the struggles of the different schools. Concerning the end of the wicked, the matter was clearly uncertain, as it is even now among the Jews: for some believed they would rise again, while others contradicted it.' Christ brought the light of His definition to these so controversial and dark matters, and [declared] the punishments of the wicked and the rewards of the pious not only long-lasting, as many had thought, but also eternal, and indeed not of any kind, but such as would consist in the company of angels and in the conspicuous and singular presence of God Himself, announcing it publicly to all as a certain and by no means doubtful matter. To seal this doctrine, since He openly recalled the dead to life, showed Himself alive to many after death had been undergone, and even caused some to be restored to life through the Apostles, nothing more could now be desired by fair minds to give assurance of that fact. From these things which we have said, it appears that it is indeed true what the cited writers by us had said, that the term for the divine or heavenly kingdom is not used in this sense by Moses and the Prophets, yet that it was not originally invented by Christ, but taken from popular speech, from which it also received the names of Paradise and Gehenna. If to these we join those things which have just been said by us concerning the Pharisaic obedience to the law, it will now clearly appear what is the source of that error which is here and in every subsequent discourse so diligently refuted by Christ. For that innocence of deeds had its own δικαίωσιν, but among men: and it was profitable for temporal happiness. But the kingdom of heaven was destined by God for the spirit, not for that bodily innocence, but for spiritual justice, the source of which is true faith which is situated in the mind. For that law, viewed externally, could not τελειῶσαι τὴν συνείδησιν, Heb. IX. 9, but was profitable πρὸς τὴν τῆς σαρκὸς καθαρότητα, ibid. v. 13. From this pernicious error it also followed that, since they believed those external deeds were no less sufficient before God than before men, they were not solicitous about seriously seeking the remission of sins, nor did they devote effort to purifying their souls and extirpating those vices which are wont to be dissembled among men: nor did they think they had need of such a Messiah who would bring medicine to that part which they did not feel to be ailing. And this is what Christ reproaches them with in many places, and Paul in his epistle to the Romans, clearly showing that this was fatal to them, that they did not submit themselves to the justice of God, which is spiritual, seeking to establish a certain justice of their own, that is, a human one. There were also other errors of the Pharisees, such as that they equaled the constitutions of men to divine commands, and sometimes even preferred them, and that they often did not even perform that outward innocence, intent on certain cold ceremonies, by which they trusted that even grave offenses could be expiated, but Christ does not touch upon these in this place. For, benignly granting them that they performed that innocence which would escape the punishments expressed in the law, he shows that from this they falsely conceived the hope of obtaining the heavenly kingdom. For a far different obedience is required of those who would be candidates for such glory. Clement of Alexandria well says: To the perfect man, justice is not in political contracts, nor in the prohibition of the law, but from the performance of one's own duty, which is the love toward God. If anyone diligently considers these things, he will easily perceive that those things which Christ is about to say next in this discourse do not leave the freedom of counsel, but impose the necessity of a precept within certain bounds, and that they pertain not to the Apostles and Bishops alone, but truly to all those who seek to become participants in the heavenly kingdom.

But in truth, the matter concerning the immortality of the soul and the restriction of the wicked was not decided only by Christ; both were already handed down in the scriptures of the Old Testament, and indeed a demonstration concerning both the immortality of souls and the resurrection of bodies was brought forward by Christ himself from the scriptures of the Old Testament, by which the Sadducees were convinced, Matt. XXII, and Paul, asserting both, expressly protested that he taught nothing outside of Moses and the Prophets. Acts XXVI. 8, 22. But in what sense the saying of the Apostle concerning life brought to light through Christ is to be taken, the other member teaches, when it is said καταργήσας τὸν θάνατον. Namely, just as he destroyed death through his own death, so, having revived from death for the sake of our justice, he illuminated life and immortality through his Gospel, as if restored or acquired for the human race. The Gospel declares and testifies that the promise or promises which taught in the Old Testament that life would be restored, have in fact been restored through the death and resurrection of Christ, and in that way it illuminates life and immortality for us. Add that it did not shine with such light before the High Priest of the New Testament, entering the Holy of Holies, found eternal redemption and gave us παῥῥησίαν of entry in his blood, when he inaugurated for us a new and living way through the veil, that is, his flesh, Heb. X. 20. Wherefore, that eternal life is proposed by Christ and the Apostles more clearly in the New Testament, and in his glorious resuscitation shown as if before the eyes as a blessed resurrection, there is no doubt: it is not to be denied, however, that the same was proposed in the Old Testament in such a way that it could be grasped by the faithful, if indeed faith without the knowledge of eternal life is not faith.

PART V. Concerning the true sense of certain precepts of the law against Pharisaic depravations.

Latin:

Vers. 20.

ἐὰν μὴ περισσεύσῃ ἡ δικαιοσύνη ὑμῶν πλεῖον] δικαιο- σύνης voce obedientiam significari supra diximus: illud au- tem περισσεύσῃ πλεῖον Latiné uno verbo vertere possis supe- raberit.

τῶν γραμματέων καὶ Φαρισαίων] Legiperitos Christus no- minat ut Judæorum eruditissimos; Pharisæos ut peculia- ris sanctimoniæ fama nobiles, & quorum secta erat in Ju- daismo ἀκριβεστάτη, Actor. XXVI. vers. 5. Hinc autem in- telligi datur, quam necessaria esset novæ hujus doctrinæ promulgatio, cum qui sapientissimi ac religiosissimi inter Judæos habebantur, tum à sapientia tum à religione, tam longe aberrarent: ipsique filii Levi, aliorum purgatores, purgandi essent. Malach. III. vers. 3. Multum autem ad horum verborum & eorum quæ sequuntur intellectum refert, recte noscere quale fuerit de obedientia præstan- da Deo dogma legiprudentium & Pharisæorum. A quo autem potius hoc discemus, quam à Paulo Apostolo, qui & doctrinam Judaicam à summo legiperito Gamaliele hauserat, & Pharisaicæ sectæ nomen dederat? Is igitur eo tempore vixisse se ait inculpatum, quod justitiam attine- bat eam quæ est in lege, Galat. III. vers. 16. Ubi legis no- men palam est ita usurpari, quomodo retulimus à Sene- ca dictum, exiguum esse quiddam ad legem bonum es- se. Quare & legem hanc idem Apostolus passim discri- minis causa legem factorum vocat, eam nimirum legem indicans quam in cognoscendis causis Hebræi judices se- qui tenebantur: qui neque animum poterant introspice- re, neque vero ad punienda omnia secus facta, sed ea duntaxat quæ societatem civilem præcipue læderent, po- testatem acceperant. Quo sensu & Clemens Alexan- drinus cordis delictum vocat ἁμαρτίαν νόμῳ οὐχ̓ ὑποπίπτου- σαν. Sed paganos tali quadam innocentia contentos vixisse minus mirum est, quos cum Christianis compa- rans Tertullianus ita loquitur: Nos ergo soli innocentes? quid mirum, si necesse est. Enimvero necesse est: inno- centiam à DEO edocti & perfecte eam novimus ut à perfecto magistro revelatam, & fideliter custodimus ut ab incontemti- bili dispectore mandatam. Vobis autem humana æstimatio innocentiam tradidit: humana item dominatio imperavit, unde nec plenæ nec adeo timendæ estis disciplinæ ad inno- centiæ veritatem. At de Judæis minus id videtur credibi- le, ut qui scirent legem latam à Deo mentium inspecto- re, qui & ex animo se diligi vellet, & pravas cupiditates interdiceret. Sed nimirum ita res fuit, quia talibus præceptis pœna nulla diserte erat proposita, ideo eam in- terpretabantur in consilii magis partem, quam in legis necessitatem, aut certe partim quotidianis victimis, par- tim annuo sacro piaculari, ita putabant eas labes expur- gari ut nulla earum memoria apud Deum restaret. Ve- rum esse quod dico, docet nos idem ille Paulus, qui se attenta demum legis consideratione didicisse ait, pra- vas cupiditates in peccati esse censu, cum alioqui idipsum fuisset ignoraturus, Pharisaicis nimirum præjudiciis im- peditus, Roman. VII. vers. 7. Hinc est quod Try- phon Judæus adversus Justinum disputans, ait, tam ma- gna tamque admiranda sibi videri τὰ ἐν τῷ εὐαγγελίῳ πα- ραγγέλματα, ut plane videantur à nemine posse præsta- ri, interioris nimirum innocentiæ mandata, & eorum quæ pro parvis haberi solent, vitiorum fugam intelligens. Sed nihil apertius dici potuit eo quod scriptum reliquit Hebræorum doctissimus David Kimchi, qui verba ista Psalmi LXVI. vers 18. Iniquitatem si vidissem in corde meo, non exaudisset Dominus, plane contra scriptoris sen- tentiam ita interpretatur: Etiamsi viderim iniquitatem in corde meo, quam vel paratus essem in actum perducere, utut illa sit coram Deo ac si eam labiis protulissem, tamen non audiet eam Dominus, quasi dicas, non ducet mihi il- lam sceleri: cogitationem eam pravam DEVS non habet vice facti, nisi concepta fuerit in Dei fidem atque religionem. En quam manifeste omnia anima decreta, etiam quæ quo minus implerentur penes hominem non stetit, excepta so- la defectione à Judaismo, ait à Deo non imputari, neque pro peccatis duci. Et hanc ipsam sententiam à multis He- bræis probatam notat ad Decalogum Abenesdra. Quin & Josephus in Pharisaismo, ut ipse fatetur, accurate in- stitutus Polybium nobilissimum Historiarum scriptorem reprehendit, quod mortem Antiochi ascribat cogitato quidem, sed non perpetrato sacrilegio, subjiciens, τὸ γὰρ μηκέτι ποιῆσαι τὸ ἔργον βυλευσάμενον ὐκ ἦν τιμωρίας ἄξιον. Hæc igitur est illa innocentia Pharisaica, quam Christus contra receptam tunc sententiam apud Deum non sufficere pronuntiat. Clemens Alexandrinus Pha- risaicam & Christianam justitiam hoc modo explicat: ἐὰν μὴ πλειονάζῃ ὑμῶν ἡ δικαιοσύνη πλεῖον τῶν γραμματέων, καὶ Φαρισαίων, τῶν κατὰ ἀποχὴν κακῶν δικαιουμένων, σὺν τῷ

μετὰ τοῖς ἐν τύτοις τελειώσεως καὶ τῷ τὸν πλησίον ἀγαπᾷν καὶ εὐεργετεῖν δύνασθαι, ἐκ ἔσεσθε βασιλικοὶ. Quod eodem ferme recidit. Nam lex dilectionis, quanquam factis impletur, tamen non venit ex certo præscripto, sed ex ubere animi bonitate. Sapientissimo autem consilio Chri- stus veræ sanctimoniæ præcepta suis instullaturus primum amovet dogmata, quæ ejus necessitatem conspici vetabant. Nam, ut recte Seneca, præmitti debent præceptis decreta quædam, ut illis decretis præcepta velut infixa penitius ani- mo hæreant.

Obedientiam, quam à nobis Deus exigit, no- tari ad vers. 6. dixerat: sed quanquam δικαιοσύ- νη nonnunquam notet obedientiam: sæpicule ta- men aliud est δικαιοσύνη justitia, phrasi Scriptu- ræ, imprimis in Novo Testamento aliud vero o- bedientia, quam Grotius intelligit: & distingui- tur justitia, qua nos coram Deo justi constituimur, cum justificamur, aperte ab obedientia, quam legi Dei præstamus. Illam explicat Christus Io- han. XVI. vers. 8. 10. quod in abitu ad patrem, vel merito, morte & resurrectione nobis acquisito, consistat, & Paulus Roman. I. vers. 17. quod ob- tingat nobis ἐκ πίσεως εἰς πίσιν Roman. III. v. 21. 22. quod sine lege manifestata sit, per fidem JESU Christi cap. IV. vers. 6. quod imputetur no- bis sine operibus, cap. IX. vers. 3. quod sit ju- stitia ex fide, cap. X. vers. 3. 4. quod soli credentes in Christum, qui est τὸ πλήρωμα τῶ νόμυ, justitiæ Dei subjiciantur, eamque justitiam habeant: non vero qui τὴν ἰδίαν δικαιοσύνην propriam justi- tiam quærunt erigere. Quam justitiam Dei op- ponit Apostolus justitiæ, quæ est ex lege cap. X. vers. 5. 6. ceu justitiam, quæ ex fide est; & cum credimus, quod Jesus sit Dominus, & quod DEUS eum resuscitavit à mortuis, credere nos εἰς δικαιοσύνην ad justitiam, docet vers. 10. hoc est cum credimus, ut Rom. IV. 25. habet, quod tra- ditus sit ipse propter peccata nostra, & resuscitatus propter justificationem nostram. Quam justitiam Dei negat ex lege esse, alioquin enim Christum frustra mortuum fore Gal. II. vers. 21. ideoque protestatur, etsi non habeat justitiam suam, quæ ex lege est, habere tamen se δικαιοσύνην ἐπὶ τῇ πίσει justitiam per fidem Phil. III. vers. 9. A qua justitia Dei δίκαιος justus fidelium quisque dicitur, de quo cum Propheta Hab. II. vers. 4. Apostolus Rom. I. vers. 17. Galat. III. vers. 11. Ebr. X. v. 38. ὅτι ὁ δίκαιος ἐκ πίσεως ζήσεται, quod justus ex fi- de victurus sit. Obedientia autem, quam Grotius indigitat, fidei, & justitiæ fidei consequens & fru- ctus est; nec locum habere, aut concipi potest sine lege, quæ norma & regula est hujus obedien- tiæ, aut sine operibus; quia consistit in operibus bonis, aut sine justitia propria, quum talis obe- dientia sit ipsa propria nostra justitia, ac tantum distat à justitia fidei, quantum lex ab Evangelio, imo quantum terra à cœlo. De justitia ea hic a- gitur, quæ est, περισσεύεσα laude, dignitate, præ- stantia, & fructu abundat: quemadmodum ver- bum περισσεύειν in bonam partem sumtum est, vel laude Luc. VII. vers. 26. vel fructu abundare Matth. XIII. vers. 12. At nullius hominis ju- stitia propria & inhærens proprie talis est; so- li Christi justitiæ hoc convenit; qua sub lege factus est pro nobis Galat. IV. 6. De ea hic agi- tur justitia, quæ ad ingressum in cælum necessa- ria est; seu ad salutem æternam. At non obe- dientia, quam Deus à nobis exigit, vel propria nostra justitia, sed justitia, quæ est ex fide in Chri- stum, qui nobis à Deo factus est justitia 1. Cor. I. 30. ad ingressum in cœlum, & salutem requiritur: quia justificatio, aut etiam salus ac beatitudo non obtingit per opera, nec opera ad justificationem, vel salu- tem requiruntur, sed τῷ μὴ ἐργαζομένῳ πιστεύον- τι δὲ ἐπὶ τὸν δικαιοῦντα τὸν ἀσεβῆ λογίζεται ἡ πί- στις αὐτοῦ εἰς δικαιοσύνην, & μακαρισμὸς beatitu- do, vel salus ejus hominis est ᾧ ὁ Θεὸς λογίζεται δι- καιοσύνην χωρὶς ἔργων Rom. IV. 5. De ea agitur ju- stitia, quæ est περισσοτέρα abundantior Phari- sæorum & Scribarum justitia, hoc est, legalis, quia sic describitur Pharisaica justitia, quod quæsiverint justitiam legalem Rom. IX. 31. quod justitiam quæ- siverint, non ex fide, sed ex operibus legis v. 32. quod ignorantes justitiam Dei, τὴν ἰδίαν δικαιοσύ- νην, propriam justitiam erigere conati sint, cap. X. 3. illam nempe justitiam, quæ est ex lege, de qua Mo- ses, qui fecerit ea, vivet in eis v. 5. Quænam vero ab- undantior illa justitia legali Pharisæorum justitia est, qua opus nobis ad ingressum in Cœlum, quænam justitia illa χωρὶς ἔργων fine operibus, justitia quæ non ex operibus legis, sed ex fide in Christum, qui est τέ- λος νόμου, nisi justitia Dei, vel Christi θεανθρώπου, per cujus unius obedientiam nos justi per fidem con- stituimur, per cujus unius δικαίωμα satisfactionem, nobis δικαίωσις τῆς ζωῆς obtingit Rom. X. 18. 19. De ea agitur hic justitia, quam Christus Doctor justi- tiæ Es. LXIII. 1. nobis & manifestavit, & acquisi- vit, cum venit non solvere legem, sed IMPLERE verf. 17. quem decuit implere omnem justitiam Matth. III. 15. quique est τέλος τοῦ νόμου finis legis, non abolendo, sed implendo legem, ad ju- stitiam omni credenti Rom. X. 4. Conferendus hic locus Rom. III. 21. legem igitur inanem reddimus per fidem? Absit, imo stabilimus. At hæc justitia non est obedientia, quam à nobis DEUS exi- git: si enim eam obedientiam præstare possemus, utique opus non fuisset, ut Christus nostri loco impleret legem, ut per fidem in ipsum justitiam consequeremur. De ea agitur justitia hoc loco, quam qui sentiunt paupertatem spiritualem & lu- gent ob peccata, in vera humilitate & afflictione vel contritione esuriunt, ac sitiunt, ut reficiantur, & satientur Matth. V. 4. 5. 6. At propria nostra justitia, vel obedientia, quam DEUS à nobis exigit, tales refici, ac satiari adeo non possunt, ut eam solam habentes agnoscere cogantur suam e- gestatem ac pauperiem, atque ideo lugere neces- sum habeant, ac conterantur κοπιῶντες καὶ πε- φορτισμένοι Ap. III. 18. Matth. XI. 28. quibus pro- inde à solo Christo ἀνάπαυσις superest; in quo so- lo requiem inveniunt pro animabus suis vers. 29. Et- iamli cum ipso Apostolo quis κτὰ δικαιοσύνην τὴν ἐν νόμῳ ἄμεμπτος sit Phil. III. 6. non tamen in ea justitia vel ἀνάπαυσιν refectionem habebit aut esu- ries & sitis ejus spiritualis exatiabitur, nedum in- gredietur regnum cœlorum, imo ducere eam cum Apostolo necessum habebit ζημίαν καὶ σκύβαλα, ut inveniatur in Christo non habens suam justitiam, quæ est ex lege, sed eam, quæ est per fidem Christi, vel in Christum τὴν ἐκ θεοῦ δικαιοσύνην ἐπὶ τῇ πίστει illam ex Deo justitiam, quæ est per fidem v. 7. 8. 9. Recte Flacius ad v. 7. in glossa pag. 17. Non dubito certe hic, Christum resumere initium suæ con- cionis, ejusque quasi fontes, aut τὸ διότι aperire. Nam ex legis vera cognitione perinde vera sui, suæ- que paupertatis notitia accipitur, sicut debitor ex chirographo, aut libro rationali creditoris suum in- gens debitum, paupertatemque agnoscit. Quan- doquidem enim ibi hortatus fuerat omnes, beatitu- dinem summumve bonum appetentes, ut agno- scerent suam spiritualem pudendamque & plane exitialem nuditatem aut egestatem, eamque dole- rent, humiliarenturque coram Deo ac esurirent ac men- dicarent ipsius veram justitiam, faturitatem ac re- gnum, opesque amissas : ideo ut nunc istam nostram pudendam nuditatem nobis vere detegat, & ante oculos spectandam proponat: affert lucem ac specu- lum legis, detersoque ei pulvere & maculis tum Mosaici regiminis, tum & glossarum Pharisaica- rum, ostendit ejus fulgore, qualis sit Deus, & qua- lem flagitet esse hominem, suam imaginem, & de- nique quam deformem imaginem ille in facie cordis sui gerat: quo homines, audientes, quam exactam ju- stitiam severa Dei justitia, & lex ab ipsis exigat, a- gnoscant etiam horrendam magnitudinem suæ nudi- tatis, & paupertatis olim inditæ imaginis DEI at- que ita eam nuditatem deplorent, & contrarias di- vitias saturitatemque esuriant ac mendicent. Sic igitur eos hic Christus, explicatione legis, veluti præpotenti quadam necessitatis machina, eo adigit, ut cogantur suam exitialem nuditatem imaginis Dei ac justitiæ agnoscere, & contra gratuitam justi- tiam mendicare, ad quod eos initio tantum hortatus fuerat.

Atque ideo hic derogatur Pharisaicæ justitiæ ingressus in regnum cœlorum; ac requiritur δι- καιοσύνη ἡ περισσόyetρος, quæ est per fidem in Chri- stum : æque uti Apostolus loco laudato, Phil. III. 5. se κατὰ νόμον Φαρισαῖον dixit, qua erat κατὰ δικαιο- σύνην τὴν ἐν νόμῳ γινόμενος ἄμεμπτος, post au- tem pro damno, imo stercore eam justitiam, vel obe- dientiam habuit, ut Christum lucraret, & in eo inveniretur per fidem. Non quod sui vitio talis sit obedientia legis, quia lex bona est, & justa & sancta Rom. VII. 12. Sed nostra culpa, qui σαρκικοὶ carna- les sumus post lapsum, quum lex sit πνευματικὴ spi- ritualis v. 14. Non ergo Latinum illud superave- rit emphasin, ac vim Græcæ phraseos περισσεύσῃ πλεῖον exhaurit; quia non quocunque modo su- perans, vel gradibus tantum quibusdam excedens justitia requiritur, sed multum abundantior, imo tantum differens, quantum justitia Dei (Christi θεανθρώπου, qui Deus est benedictus in secula su- per omnia, & ut homo etiam ὅσιος, ἄκακος, ἀμίαν- τος, κεχωρισμένος ἀπὸ τῶν ἁμαρτωλῶν Ebr. VII. 26. factus nobis à Deo justitia 1. Cor. I. 30. Jeho- vah justitia nostra Jer. XXIII. 5.) & justitia nostra, qui carnales sumus, venundati sub peccatum Rom. VII. 14. etsi jam cum Paulo renati condelectemur le- gi Dei secundum interiorem hominem v. 22. & facere velimus ac studeamus τὸ καλόν. v. 21. Quapropter calculum non meretur, nec analogiæ fidei con- sentanea est eorum interpretatio, qui abundan- tiorem illam justitiam, quæ regnum cœlorum in- gressuris necessaria, de inchoata nostra justitia vel obedientia, quam præceptis divinis præstant renati, accipiunt: quod non à Pontificiis tantum, sed etiam Calvinianis, & Calixtinis fit, ut necessa- ria esse opera bona ad salutem obtineant. Neque est, ut quis cum Frid. Spanhem. part. III. dub. Evangel. c. XXXVI. §. IV. p. 789. obvertat, Domino hic non esse animum agere de articulo justificationis, & ostendere, qua in re justitia sit quærenda coram Deo, sed tantum impugnare tum dogmata falsa, tum lar- vatam pietatem & justitiam Pharisæorum, & resti- tutionem ac corruptionem justitiæ à Deo exactæ in le- ge. Annon enim de ingressu in regnum cælorum hic sermo est? Annon palam docetur, nisi abundantior sit justitia, non ingredi posse quenquam regnum cælo- rum? ubi vero de justitia cum respectu ad ingres- sum in regnum cœlorum agitur, non potest nul- lus respectus esse ad articulum justificationis. Di- cis cum Spanhemio: imo ne verbum quidem hic de eo quod necessarium ad justificationem, sed de eo quod necessarium ad introitum in vitam æternam: Quod vero necessarium ad posterius, non ob id neces- sarium ad prius. Resp. Id vero invertendum o- mnino: quia de eo, quod necessarium est ad introi- tum in vitam æternam, agitur; utique etiam de eo, quod ad justificationem necessarium est, hinc concludi potest: siquidem nihil ad æternam vitam consequendam necessarium sit, quod ad justifica- tionem non sit necessarium, eademque omnino sit ratio quoad conditionem ex parte nostri lega- lem penitus exclusam, & justificationis & salutis, teste Apostolo Rom. IV. 5. 6. c. VI. v. ult. Eph. II. 8. Tit. III. 5. seqq. Et profecto æque gratuitum Dei donum est solo Christi merito partum, sola fide a nobis apprehendendum, & consequendum, sine conditione operum, vel obedientiæ nostræ, salus ac beatitudo, ut qui credit in Christum salvus sit sine opere, sola fide, inquit Ambrosius: Beatitu- do est illius hominis, cui Deus imputat justitiam SI- NE OPERIBUS, pronunciat, & ex Davide Psal. XXXII. 1. definit Apostolus Rom. IV. 6. Ne- „que incommode B. Lutherus disp. de justific. „Anno 1536. Dicere opera necessaria ad salutem „est dicere, quod Christus sit salvator inchoatio- „ne non perfectione; item est tribuere Christo „& fidei, quod minimum est; operibus, quod „maximum est; Christum requirere ad justifica- „tionem, tanquam minimam causam; opera au- „tem bona aut novam obedientiam requirere ad „salutem, ut maximam causam. Cavete vobis ab „istis argumentis: quia hoc fit inde, quod Chri- „stus amplius non sit salvator; sed spoliatur ho- „nore suo, &c. Et monuerat ante Spanhemius „p. 788. Mentem Domini hic esse, nisi abundan- „tiorem justitiam tum objective consideratam h. „e. regulam perfectiorem justitiæ habuerint, & „docuerint discipuli sui, nisi etiam subjective, „perfectiori studuerint, & perfectiorem aliunde, habuerint, quam Scribæ & Pharisæi, illos salvari non posse. Quanquam vero illud de regula perfe- ctiori justitiæ ab his quidem verbis alienum sit, PERFECTIOREM tamen justitiam ALIUNDE quomodo habere possunt discipuli, nisi in Evan- gelio monstratam, quæ ipsius Christi justitia est? Aliunde certe quam a Christo non petit fides, nec petere potest, cum propria fide niti possumus. Quæsivit etiam illic Spanhemius, an justitia legis & justitia fidei sibi invicem opponantur? & respon- „dendum esse monuit, utramque 1. in se conside- „rari posse & secundum se; 2. in ordine ad idem „subjectum. In se & secundum se habent se ut „species disparatæ sub eodem genere, nam & ju- „stitia per legem est vera justitia ibi ubi datur, & „justitia per fidem, ut satisfactio sive per solutio- „nem propriam, sive per solutionem alienam „est vera satisfactio, utraque a Deo imperata, „utraque Deo grata, secundum se; & vel alterutra „habenda vel pereundum homini Lev. XVIII. 5. „Rom. V. 1. Interim ut repugnat, duo disparata u- „ni eidemque convenire, qua disparata sunt, & e- „undemque esse & hominem & brutum, & ti- „tulo hæreditatis aliquid obtinere vel donatio- „nis, & simul titulo mercenariæ operæ & proprii „meriti: sic repugnat, eundem vitam æternam asse- „qui justitia propria, & justitia aliena apprehensa „per fidem. Qui enim propria justitia eam assequi- „tur, non opus habet aliena; qui aliena nititur, „destituitur propria. Locum vero facit defectus „justitiæ propriæ tum inquisitioni, tum appre- „hensioni justitiæ alienæ & ad eam velut manu „ducit. Et sic etiam lex fuit pædagogus ad Chri- stum. Qui enim justitia propria se destitui sen-" tit, & tamen justitiam necessario exigi novit ad" placandum Deum, & obtinendam vitam, ille" eo ipso incitatur, ut confugiat ad justitiam alie-" nam, Mediatoris nimirum, qua coram judicio" Dei possit comparere. Hactenus Spanhemius non male. Sic ergo repugnat, ejusdem judicio, eundem æternam vitam assequi justitia propria (quod volebant Pharisæi, suam erigentes justi- tiam) & justitia aliena, apprehensa, per fidem, quam adeo requirebat contra Pharisæos Christus; ut nisi discipuli sui perfectiorem ALIUNDE ha- beant, salvari nequeant. Et quod egerit omnino hic Christus de justificatione, è versu 6. quod nempe esurientes & sitientes justitiam satiari & refici de- beant, jam constitit; idque agnovit ipse Spanhe- mius ad istum locum Dub. LXXXIII. p. 401. Chri- stus hic illos beatos pronunciare videtur, qui ardenti desiderio expetunt & justitiam justificantem coram Deo, & justitiam ædificantem coram hominibus: u- traque enim connexa nec illius desiderio tenentur, qui non student isti, nec posterioris studiosi beati, sine studio prioris. Temere addidit justitiam ædifican- tem coram hominibus, quæ etsi priori connexa sit, hic tamen per multo abundantiorem justitiam non potest designari; quum de tali justitia agatur quæ opus est ad introitum in regnum cœlorum. Monuit Spanhemius illos à Domino phrasi ista designatos, qui injustitiæ & indigentiæ suæ sibi conscii ardenter ex- petunt remedium tranquillandæ conscientiæ suæ coram Deo, & qui quum in se non inveniunt justitiam, quærunt in illo, qui nobis factus à Deo justitia. 1. Cor. I. 30. & in illo solo reperiri cupiunt cum Paulo Phil. III. 9. Qui ergo negat nunc, Domini ani- mum esse agere hic de articulo justificationis?

Interim recte contra Maldonatum & Papistas alios negat Spanhemius, Christum legis observa- tionem justitiam vocare, quasi observatione mandato- rum Dei justificemur, ita ne id quidem Pontificiis modernis syncretistis concedendum erat, quod hic justitia legalis, vel observatio legis necessaria constituatur ceu conditio sine qua non ad introitum in regnum cœlorum, etsi conditionem talem non niti causam fatuam cum scholasticis dicat: nam & hoc ἄγραφον, & ἀντίγραφον imo fatuum est, si sapientiam Dei ut par est, spectemus, (qui so- la fide nos salvari vult, hoc est, apprehensione obedientiæ Christi) adjungere nempe de nostro a- liam conditionem, utpote propriæ justitiæ & obe- dientiæ, ac si abundantissima illa Christi justitia in- gredi cœlum nemo posset, nisi sub ista conditione ut abundantiori quam Pharisæi legis observatione, ac inherente justitia instructus sit: quo pacto promis- siones legales, Evangelicis immiscœntur, lex cum Evangelio confunditur, gratia in Evangelio annun- ciata à conditione observantiæ legis suspenditur, ac justitiæ Christi sanctissimæ pannus menstruatæ justi- tiæ nostræ alluitur, idque ob ingressum in regnum cœlorum; Neque est quod dicat Spanhemius, Dominum non disputare contra justitiam legis, sed contra justitiam Scribarum & Pharisæorum: quia hactenus contra justitiam legis disputat, qua scribæ & Pharisæi per observantiam legis censebant hominem ingredi regnum cœlorum: quum longe abundantiorem justitiam requirat Dominus, quam seu Pharisæorum seu ullius hominis est le- gis obedientia, aut esse potest post lapsum, ac de officio suo & fine adventus sui ideo egerit, quod venerit ut legem impleret, ut nos ad abundantiorem illam justitiam deduceret. Et cædit hic propria vineta Spanhemius: dum statim addit pag. 790. requiri justitiam abundantem: Ergo majorem no- stra, quæ non sufficiens, minus abundans; talis vero vel legalis tantum, obedientia exacta præstita toti le- gi, vel Evangelica, applicatio fiducialis justitiæ Me- diatoris cui soli locus ex quo homo cœpit esse peccator, & ex quo Lex ἠσθένησ' διὰ τῆς σαρκός. Ex quibus uti- que constat non legalem, sed Evangelicam justitiam à Christo urgeri.

Solum in Calixtinorum gratiam addimus, τὸ περισσεύειν πλεῖον non inferre semper intensionem gradus in eadem specie justitiæ, quin significare etiam possit surrogationem plane alterius speciei, uti Matth. XI. 9. Baptista, qui se negaverat esse Prophetam, dicitur πεῖσσότερον προφήτε abundautior, præ- stantior Propheta: Matth. XII. 41. 42. Chri- stus πλεῖον Salomone & Jona est c. VI. 3. anima πλεῖον ἐςι τῆς τροφῆς plus est quam alimenta. 2. Cor. III. 9. διακονία Evangelii πολλῶ μᾶλλον περισσεύ- ει ἐν δόξῃ quam διακονία condemnationis &c. Adda- mus & hoc, si maxime de justitia legali hæc quis in- terpretetur, quam tamen interpretationem minime concedimus, nullam fore consequentiam à condi- tionali negativa ad oppositam affirmativam, uti non sequitur Joh. IV. 48. Nisi signa & prodigia vide- ritis, non creditis, E. signa & prodigia necessaria e- runt ad credendum. E. visis signis & prodigiis se- quutura fides! Multo vero minus ex conditionali negativa comparativa opposita affirmativa absoluta inferenda: quemadmodum inferre non licet; si quis dicat, nisi castior fueris Heliogabalo non introi- bis in regnum cælorum E. ingredieris regnum cæ- lorum ubi castitate Socrati similis fueris, E. Major illa Socratis castitas necessaria illi fuit ad introitum in regnum cælorum; ratio est, quia tales propo- sitiones dicunt, quid non sequuturum sit ad con- ditionem præsentem, non item, quid ad illam cessantem, seu introductam aliam qualitatem. Sed agnoscit Hornejus in iterat. assert. contra D. Rothmaler. th. LVII. dictum hoc Evangelicum esse non legale: idque ita probat p. 109. Diser- te concionem illam à beatitudinibus VIII. inchoat Christus: Tunc aperto ore suo dicebat, dicens: Beati pauperes Spiritu, quoniam ipsorum est re- gnum, Beati qui lugent, quoniam solamen reci- pient &c. Beatitudo autem illa æterna præcipue est & nullatenus datur per legem: sed per evangelium. Unde etiam proxime ante verba allegata addit, ne existiment, se venisse ut legem & Prophetas dis- solvat, sed ut impleat ipse pro nobis & nos implere nostro modo faciat: nam si quis etiam minimum solverit & contemserit, minimum in regno cælo- rum vocandum esse: & subjungit: dico enim vo- bis, nisi abundaverit &c. Hactenus Hornejus, Majo- rista Julianus. Nam si Evangelicum hoc dictum est, quomodo de legali conditione exponi potest, vel de observantia præceptorum Dei? quum Evan- gelium toto cœlo à lege distinctum sit. Et posita ex- plicatione illa, quam nonnullorum orthodoxo- rum esse non diffitemur, de justitia legali quam κατ' ἀκριβοδίκαιον omnibus modis perfectam intel- ligunt, non stabilitur, sed removetur ita introi- tus regni cælorum per justitiam propriam: quia nemo est qui legem secundum illum rigorem im- plere possit, ideoque dicta ejusmodi legalia solum ἀδυναμίαν nostram post lapsum exhibent, & ad Christum, qui nostri loco legem implevit, nos ma- nuducunt. Præstat autem Evangelice intelligere non quidem de justitia nostra inchoata, (hæc e- nim, nihil ad Evangelium, vel Evangelicam justi- tiam facit, quum Evangelium concio sit gratiæ de Christo, ejusque justitia, cujus summa est justus fide sua vivet, non vero concio pœnitentiæ, vel de obe- dientia, & justitia nostra, cujus doctrina, & regula, ac norma est lex, non Evangelium, sed) de justitia Christi, quæ multo abundatior, quam Pharisæica est, per fidem apprehensione ad introitum regni cæ- lorum omnino necessaria. Quæ ex ἀντιθέσει do- ctrinæ Pharisæicæ & Christi colligitur. Nam illi ad justitiam & vitam æternam opus esse impletione legis statuêre, ac quum intelligerent, ea, quæ de interioribus moribus, in mente, & corde ho- minis, de nævis in gestibus, & verbis, deque dile- ctione ex toto corde, tota anima, omnibusque viribus præcipiuntur, impleri haudquaquam pos- se, commenti sunt discrimen inter præcepta, quod quædam minima sint, quædam vero magna, quod- que horum sufficiat impletio: quam hypothesin reprobat Christus, docens, qui unum de minimis (opinione ipsorum) præceptis solverit, minimi ha- bitum iri in regno cælorum, hoc est, nullum in eo lo- cum habiturum. Quo pacto & Pontificii, ac Novato- res fingunt, DEUM sub novo fœdere non require- re, ut omnia secundum legis rigorem impleantur, dummodo quantum in nobis est, legem adimpleamus, eamque obedientiam opponi posse judicio DEI ad justitiam & vitam æternam, & hic à Christo re- quiri ad ingressum regni cælorum, censent. Chri- stus ergo ex adverso docet, recte observante B. Chemnitio nostro, Pharisæicam illam iustitiam, quæ non perfectissime habet integram legis impletio- nem: sed tantum particulam quandam legis, de quibusdam externis operibus utcunque servatis, non posse ingredi regnum cælorum. Suorum igitur justi- tiam Christus vult esse abundantiorem seu plenio- rem, h. e. suos vult ad judicium DEI adferre ab- undantissimam, plenissimam, & perfectissimam justitiam, ut per & propter eam possint ingredi in regnum cælorum. Eam vero quia in se non inve- niunt, fide quærunt, & apprehendunt in imple- tione legis à Christo pro nobis præstita. Deinde est & esse debet justitia operum in renatis, propter interiorem renovationem Spiritus abundantior, quam justitia carnis in Pharisæis; sed quia etiam renati, licet in mente sentiant Legem Dei, carne tamen serviunt Legi peccati Roman. VII. 25. Id- eo per & propter opera sua; quia imperfecta & im- munda sunt, non possunt ingredi in regnum cælo- rum. Sed in hac quæstione, ut ingredi possint re- gnum cælorum, non ad justitiam carnis Pharisæo- rum, nec ad spiritualem suam imperfectam obedien- tiam, sed ad perfectissimam justitiam Christi fide confugiunt. De ipsis vero renatorum operibus in sequentibus dicendum erit. Pharisæorum ve- ro figmento de mandatis minimis, Christus oppo- nit unum Jota & unum apicem: ut ita quam fortis- sime neget, esse quædam mandata in Lege ita mi- nuta, quæ DEUS non multum curet, quorum et- iam, quamvis non impleantur, non sit ratio ha- benda, in statuenda justitia Legis coram Deo. Huic B. Chemnitii explicationi, utpote è textus pene- tralibus derivatæ, merito acquiescimus: quem se- quitur etiam Schlüffelburgius Catal: hær. l. VII. de Majorist. p. 463. B. Meisner, B. Hülsemannus, B. Glassius, cum plerisque aliis Ecclesiæ nostræ Do- ctoribus: de sola imputata Christi justitia, ad introi- tum in regnum cælorum necessaria hic adferta.

Sed ut revertamur ad Grotium: innocentiam Pharisæicam, quam Christum contra receptam tunc sententiam adserere censet, è Paulo Pharisaï- cæ sectæ quondam addicto, qui Gal. III. 16. (dicere voluit, Phil. III. 6.) ait, eo tempore vixisse se inculpa- tum, quod justitiam eam attinet, quæ est in lege, re- petit: per legem intelligens eam, quam in cognoscen- dis causis Hebræi judices sequi tenebantur, qui neque animum poterant introspicere, neque vero ad pu- nienda omnia secus facta sed ea duntaxat, quæ societa- tem civilem præcipue læderent, potestatem accepe- runt : quam legem factorum ab Apostolo vult dici. De qua postea ita disserit p: 73. innocentia illa fa- ctorum habeat δικαίωσιν, sed apud homines : & proderat ad temporalem felicitatem. At regnum cælorum à DEO spiritu, non isti corporali innocentiæ, sed spirituali justitiæ erat destinatum, cujus fons est fides vera quæ in animo sita est. Nam lex illa exterius spectata non poterat τελειῶν τὴν συνείδησιν Hebr. IX. 9. Sed proderat πρὸς τὴν τῆς σαρκὸς καθαρότη- τα ibid. 13. Ex hoc pernicioso errore illud etiam se- quebatur, quod cum facta illa externa crederent non minus apud Deum, quam apud homines sufficere, de serio expetenda peccatorum remissione non erant solliciti, neque vero expurgandis animis, extirpan- disque vitiis illis, quæ inter homines dissimulari solent, operam navabant: neque Messia tali opus sibi pu- tabant, qui medicinam afferret ei parti quam ipsi æ- grotare non sentiebant. Et hoc est, quod multis locis Christus illis exprobrat, & Paulus ad Romanos epistola, dilucide ostendens hoc esse illis exitiale, quod DEI justitiæ, quæ est spiritualis, se non sub- jicerent, quærentes stabilire suam quandam, hoc est, humanam justitiam. In qua sententiæ Phari- saicæ explicatione id imprimis desideramus, quod justitiam suam, quam stabilire voluerunt Judæi, cui Paulus justitiam Dei, quæ ex fide est, opponit, restringat ad factorum innocentiam: & legem facto- rum de judiciali vel forensi lege, quam in cognoscen- dis causis Ebræi judices sequi tenebantur, explicet, ejusque solum respectu Paulus se ἄμεμπτον inculpa- tum fuisse Phil. III. 6. testari existimet. Quia op- positio justitiæ DEI & fidei ac justitiæ propriæ, & legis adæquata est, atque ita instituitur ab Apo- stolo, ut hujus nomine non solum externam ope- rum innocentiam aut factorum, quæ in judicium humanum vocantur, justitiam intelligat, sed quamcunque legis observationem, quanta ab homi- ne post lapsum præstari potest. Illius autem nun- cupatione justitiam & obedientiam Christi nostri vice præstitam designat: de quo in vindiciis Epi- stolarum Paulinarum, cum DEO. Neque cum Pharisæis ipsi tantum res est; sed etiam cum Pseu- do-Apostolis, qui justitiam operum urgebant, & ita adserit justitiam ex fide, ut à justificationis, & salu- tis causa opera non externa modo, sed interna, & quicquid ad legem pertinet, excludat. Fallitur et- iam Grotius, cum legem factorum passim Apostolum discriminis causa eam vocari dicit, quam in cogno- scendis causis Hebræi judices sequi tenebantur: si- quidem ne unicum proferre potuerit locum A- postolicum, ubi sic vocetur lex factorum; neque in vulgata versione appellatio illa occurrit, nisi se- mel tantum Rom. III. 27. ubi in Græco est νόμου ἔργων, & manifestum est imprimis respici legem moralem, atque immediate, & adæquate opponi legem operum, & legem fidei: adeoque illic opera quæcunque, non externa tantum, sed etiam inter- na, hic vero fidem in Christum intelligi, cui justifi- catio ita adscribitur, ut opera universim omnia ex- cludantur, solique fidei justificatio tribuatur. Nec vero tantum Apostolus inculpatum se fuisse, qua causas ad forum, & judicium pertinentes, ait; Sed generaliter, qua justitiam, quæ in lege requiritur, moralem simul legem complectens, qua tamen Pharisaicis prejudiciis impeditus pravas cupiditates prohiberi non credebat. Assumuntur & alia precario à Grotio, utpote, quod lex dilectionis non veniat ex certo præscripto, sed ex ubere animi bonita- te (quod aperte repugnat legisperiti declarationi Luc. X. 24. traditæ:) quod pœna nulla talibus præceptis de Deo ex animo diligendo & pravis cupidi- tatibus vexandis diferte apposita fuerit : (in qua hy- pothesi immemor fuit Grotius maledictionis divi- næ, omnibus indictæ, qui non permanent in o- mnibus, quæ scripta sunt in libro legis Deuter. XXVII. 26.) Denique quod præcepta talia Judæi in consilii magis partem, quam in legis necessitatem interpretati sint; aut certe partim quotidianis victi- mis, partim annuo sacro piaculari ita putarint eas labes expurgari, ut nulla earum memoria apud DEUM restaret: in quo posteriori de expiatio- ne nullus error, qua eos, qui vera fide offerebant victimas, & expiationem annuam instituebant; quum DEUS passim testatus sit, iisdem remissio- nem peccatorum factam; cum autem remisit Deus peccata, eorum memor amplius esse non vult. Es. XLIII. 25. XLVI. 23. Jerem. XXXI. 34. Matth. VII. 18. 19.

Vers. 20.

ἐ̔ μὴ ἐἰσέλθητε ἐἰς τὴν βασιλείαν τω̃ν ὐρανω̃ν] Βασιλείαν τω̃ν ὐρανω̃ν, ut jam diximus, diversas habet notiones. Hic tamen non de doctrina aut cœtu piorum, sed de præmiis æternis has voces accipi æquissimum est: primum quia ser- me ubicunque in his libris invenitur regnum cœleste jun- ctum intrandi verbo, gloria illa cœlestis intelligitur Matth. VII. 21. XVIII. 3. XIX. 23. 24. Marc. X. 23. 24. Luc. XVIII. 24. 25. Johan. III. 5. Actor. XIV. 22. In quibus locis ut in hoc nostro, tacita est allusio ad comminationes illas in lege: Non intrabitis in terram. Num. XIV. 30. Psal. XCIV. 11. Deinde quia in ipsius sermonis continuatione Christus τὴν βασιλείαν τε̃ θεε̃ opposuit Gehennæ, ut palam videre est apud Marcum IX. 47. Hieronymus adversus Pelagium, qui dixerat regnum cœlorum in Veteri Testamento repromitti perspicuum esse, inquit regnum cœlorum primum in Evan- gelio prædicari cui convenit illud Chrysostomi. Legens legem, legens Prophetas, legens Pfalterium, nunquam regnum cœlorum audivi nisi in Evangelio. Quibus consentit Augu- stinus. Denique quod non temere dixerim, nescio utrum quisquam in illis libris invenit nomen regni cœlorum, quod tam crebro nominat Dominus. Et hoc quidem dictum sic quod vocem ipsam attinet. De re vero ipsa agens adver- sus Pelagium Augustinus in libro de gestis Synodi Palæsti- næ, distinguit nomen veteris testamenti: nam eo intelligi ait aut pactum illud quod in monte Synai factum est; aut omnia quæ in Moyse & Prophetis continentur. Pactum in Sinai monte factum, quod & sæpe legem vocant, promis- sa dicit habuisse terrena, & quidem terrena tantum quod sæpe probat verbis Pauli ad Galatas III. 12. qui fecerit ea, (scilicet opera legis) vivet in eis, id est, habebit præmium ne ista monte moriatur, ne lapidationem, gladium, vel a- liquid hujusmodi patiatur. Nihilominus fatetur & Augu- stinus & Christiani scriptores alii, etiam legis tempore non defuisse qui majora terrenis bonis sperarent. Sed hoc hau- stum ajunt non ex lege sed ex patribus, quibus Deus mul- tis indiciis spem majoris bonis fecerat: in quo indiciorum genere non minimum est & illud, quod multi eximie boni terrestris felicitatis expertes vixerunt, quod argumentum late prosequitur scriptor ad Hebræos cap. XI. Addunt iidem scriptores terrena illa promissa data legi operum: signa fuisse eorum bonorum, quæ legem Spiritus sequebantur, sed hoc intellectum à paucis: qui scilicet, quanquam ve- teris testamenti tempore vixerunt, ad gratiam tamen per- tinebant eam quæ novi testamenti temporibus revelata est. Philo in historia legationis suæ: ἡ δὲ ἐνίσραφυς, ἱδ̓ ἐνποίη- sης τοι̃ς ἰεροι̃ς γράμμασιν ἐλπίδων ἐσι πλήρεις οἴ όντως εὐγενε̃ις. Καὶ οἰ νόμοι τοι̃ς εὐτυγχάνυσι μὴ χείλεσιν ἀκροι̃ς ἐλπίδας ἀγα- θὰς δημιυργου̃σιν. Josephus Albo Judæus hac de re dispu- tans ait, diserte quidem in Moysis lege non promitti spiri- tualem felicitatem: sed signis tamen quibusdam & invo- lucris eam indicari: idque factum quia lex non tantum data est doctis & sapientibus, sed universo populo, in quo rudes perspicatioribus erant permixti, quare in communi promulgatione ea poni debuisse, quæ ab omnibus percipi omniumque animos movere possent. Esse autem ejusmodi αἰσθητά cum τὰ νοητά apud sapientes tantum valeant, vul- gi autem judicio ne credibilia quidem videantur. Hac in- quit de causa lex res corporales atque conspicuas & in vul- gi notitiam cadentes explanate proposuit, ea vero quæ solo intellectu capiuntur, sub signorum involucris. Hæc ille acerrimi judicii Judæus. Nimirum id quod mente se- la percipitur, tale est quale dixit Xenophanes: Οὐκέτιν πελάσασθ̓ ἐδ̓ ὀφθαλμοι̃σιν ἔφικτὸν Ἡμετέροις, ἥχερσὶ λαβει̃ν. ἥπερτε μεγίςη Πειθε̃ς ἀνθρώποισιν ἁμαξιτὸς εἰς φρένα πίπτει.

Talia autem esse bona vitæ alterius aperte pronunciat Pau- lus 1. Cor. II. 9. Non mirandum igitur, si populo crasso, &, quod ex omni historia apparet, valde σαρκικῷ Deus non aperte proposuit ea quæ captum illorum excederent. Sed ipsorum ingenio se accommodans rerum aspectabi- lium commodis atque incommodis imminuere voluit adultam peccandi consuetudinem: sicut nimirum paren- tes primæ ætatis liberos non alliciunt spe hæreditatis, quam non intelligunt, sed partim verberum metu à de- linquendo absterrent, partim ut ait ille: -- Pueris dant crustula blandi Doctores, elementa velint ut discere prima. Neque tamen per hæc rudimenta exercitiis via erat adem- ta profectus melioris. Aderant quippe Prophetæ, qui obtecta evolverent, & singulis tantum aperirent quantum captus ipsorum & utilitatis ratio ferebat. In publicis au- tem concionibus Prophetæ ac sapientes ita loquebantur, ut nec in contemtum adducerent arcana sanctionis disci- plinæ, & tamen auditorem attentum ad investigandi sol- licitudinem excitarent. Bene Justinus: ὅσα εἶπον κᾀ ἐποίη- σαν οἱ προφῆται παραβολαῖς κᾀ τόποις ἐπεκάλυψαν, ὡς μὴ ῥᾳδίως τὰ πλεῖστα ὑπὸ πάντων νοηθῆναι, κρύπτοντες τὴν ἐν αὐτοῖς ἀλήθειαν, ὡς κᾀ ποιήσῃ τοὺς ζητῦντας εὑρεῖν κᾀ μαθεῖν. Quem sequitur Origenes contra Celsum VII. οἱ μὲν οὖν προφῆται ὅσα ἦν αὐτόθεν νοηθῆναι τοῖς ἀκούεσι χρήσιμα κᾀ συμβαλλόμενα τῇ τῶν ἠθῶν ἐπανορθώσει χωρὶς πάσης ἐπικρύψεως κατὰ τὸ βύ- λημα τῦ Θεῦ εἰρήκασιν· ὅσα δὲ μυστικώτερα ἦν κᾀ ἐποπτικώτε- ρα, καὶ ἐχόμενα θεωρίας τῆς ὑπὲρ τὴν καΐσθησιν ἀκοὴν, ταῦ- τα δὲ αἰνιγμάτων κᾀ ἀλληγοριῶν καὶ τῶν καλυμένων σκοτεινῶν λό- γων καὶ τῶν ὀνομαζομένων παραβολῶν ἢ παροιμιῶν ἀπεφήναν- το, ἵνα οἱ μὴ φυροποιοῦντες, ἀλλὰ πάντα πόνον ὑπὲρ ἀρετῆς κᾀ ἀληθείας ἀναδεχόμενοι, ἐξετάσαντες εὕρωσι κᾀ εὑρόντες, ὡς λόγος αἱρεῖ, οἰκονομήσωσιν. Atque hinc natum arbitror dis- crimen antiquitus inter Judæos celebratum, ut ex Jose- pho, Philone, aliisque apparet scriptæ legis & legis vo- calis תורה שעל פה quam & קבלה hoc est παράδο- σιν vocant: utramque dicentes à Mose profectam: non quod res aliæ fuerint in traditione quam in lege scripta, sed quod ea quæ lege scripta occultius continebantur, stu- diosis indagatoribus enodaret accurata interpretatio. Et hæc quidem docendi ratio apud populum crassior, lima- tior apud τοὺς προκόψαντας obtinuisse videtur ad ea tempo- ra quæ Babylonicum exilium sunt secuta.

Quicquid sit de voce regni cælorum, rem ipsam in Veteris Testamenti libris haberi, non negant pii veteres. De lege hactenus imprimis inficiantur, ne scil. per legem consequi aliquem potuisse æ- ternam vitam credatur: Hoc enim contra Pela- gianos negabant. De quo Primasius in cap. II. ad Gal. Si lex poterat justificare, superflue Christus mortuus est. Erubescant, qui dicunt, quod lex ad regnum miserit. Item cap. III. Hoc audientes conti- cescant, qui delirant, quod lex quenquam per se ad regnum cælorum transmiserit. Quod enim Pela- gius docuit regnum cœlorum etiam in Vet. Test. promissum fuisse, ita accipiendum, quemadmo- dum Cælestius idem tradidit, cujus hæc fuit sen- tentia: Legem sic mittere ad regnum cælorum quem- admodum Evangelium. Quod S. Prosper sic ex- pressit libr. ἀχαρίστων.

-- connectit & illud Idem auctor, quod lex ita sanctos miserit olim Cælorum in regnum, sicut nunc gratia mittit.

De quibus conferendus est Vossius l. III. part. II. Histor. Pelag. th. X. Et loquitur Augustinus cir- cumspecte de gestis Palæstinis cap. V. in monte Si- nai promissa terrena ad VETUS TESTAMEN- TUM PROPRIE pertinere. Pertinent enim promissa cælestia PROPRIE ad Novum Testa- mentum, quia ita comprehenduntur ut gratia ea- dem consequendi simul nobis promittatur, quum in VETERI TESTAMENTO, etiamsi compre- hensa eadem fuerint gratia illa consequendi pro- missa non sit. Distinguenda adhæc lex cum pro- missis, quæ lege comprehenduntur, cum de le- ge morali sermo est, qua spectantur secundum usum, quem vocant, Politicum vel etiam moralem & didacticum, qui ipsi proprius est, & proprie ad Vet. Test. pertinet, quo respectu legem tantum complent promissa terrena, quod qui eam hacte- nus custodiunt, ut politia, & disciplina externa conservetur, ac vita juxta eandem, quantum per hanc infirmitatem licet, instituatur, illis nec pœna ejusmodi politica, aut temporalis quæcunque me- tuenda sit, & præmium terrenæ felicitatis promit- tatur. Quando vero lex spectatur quoad usumpæ- dagogicum, qui ipsi accidentalis est, & χρέσιν simul involvit ad Nov. Testam. tum lex rigorose exigit perfectam sanctitatem & obedientiam, non externam modo sed internam omnium cogitationum & mo- tuum cordis, & quum eam non inveniat in ullo mortalium, condemnat & concludit omnes sub ma- ledicto, ut ita cogantur quærere illum per quem unice liberantur à maledicto: quibus proinde sit Pædagogus ad Christum: ibi certum est legem pro- mittere ipsummet æternam vitam, sed iis, qui legi talem obedientiam præstant, non ut per legem eam consequantur, sed ut intelligant, se per legis observantiam eam consequi non posse; sed unice per Evangelium fide apprehensum adipisci. Quo pacto ad Novum fœdus pertinet proprie vita æternæ promissio cum effectu scil. spectata, non ad Vet. Test. atque eo sensu regnum cœlorum in Vet. Test. re- promissum non est. Si absolute spectatur lex, per se quidem ea vitam operatur, si servetur, per acci- dens enim operatur iram & mortem, non quia data, sed quia non servata, non suo vitio, sed nostro. Quæ veterum fuit sententia. Ita enim August. l. II. po- ster. contra Jul. c. XCVIII. Aude (hoc) dicere, cum dicat Apostolus, quia in lege nemo justificatur, cum dicat Apostolus, lex subintravit, ut abundaret deli- ctum, cum dicat Apostolus, si data esset lex, quæ posset vivificare, omnino ex lege esset justitia, sed conclusit Scriptura omnia sub peccato, ut promis- sio ex fide Jesu Christi daretur credentibus.

Porro qui legis tempore majora terrenis bonis sperarunt, non ex indiciis tantum quibusdam ea concluserunt, quæ à paucis intelligi quiverint, quasi sub signorum involucris solum proposita fuerint, sed ex promissis divinis, iisq; assertis, & luculentis sa- tis habuere, quæ non solum sapientibus & perspi- cacibus quibusdam potuerint cognosci, sed o- mnibus satis luculenter proposita fuerint, ea fini, ut ab omnibus susciperentur. Hæc non unius aut alterius Doctoris; Sed catholica est Patrum sen- tentia de promissionibus Evangelicis in Scripturis Vet. Test. ut hic non opus habeamus attendere cæcis Judæis Josepho Albo, aut similibus, sed Ecclesiæ Catholicæ, imo scripturæ ipsi, quæ tanquam lucerna in loco caliginoso lucet, teste Petro 2. Epist. I. 19. non autem in hisce ad finem salvificam omnibus necessariis, obscura aut tenebricosa est. Quo- modo enim fide apprehendi potuissent ab iis, qui- bus salutis causa credendæ propositæ sunt promis- siones Evangelicæ, si tamen obscuræ fuissent? Ideo cum in Concilio Diospolitano Pelagio objicere- tur, quod dixerit, etiam in Vet. Testam. promissum fuisse regnum cælorum (eo quem designavimus sen- su) is vero ita sese defenderet: Ego vero Scriptu- rarum auctoritatem secutus dixi, quoniam in Pro- pheta Daniele scriptum est & accipient sancti re- gnum altissimi: eo audito respondit Synodus: Ne- que hoc alienum est à fide ECCLESIASTICA. Et S. August. de gestis Palæst. c. V. Non esse hoc alienum à fide catholica monuit (promissam esse vitam æter- nam in Vet. Test. secundum hanc loquendi con- suetudinem,) quæ universa Scriptura canonica ante incarnationem Domini ministrante Vet. Test. appella- tione censentur. De quo etiam Augustinus contra duas Epist. Pelag. l. III. cap. IV. Quis CATHO- LICUS dicat, quod nos dicere jactitant Pelagiani, Spiritum S. adjutorem in Vet. Test. non fuisse. An vero illum ad Testamentum novum negabimus perti- nere, qui dicit: Cor mundum crea in me Deus & Spiritum rectum innova in visceribus meis &c. „Sive igitur Abraham, sive ante illum justi, sive „post eum usque ad Mosen, sive cæteri Prophe- „tæ post eum, & sancti homines Dei usque ad Jo- „hannem Baptistam, filii sunt promissionis gratiæ „secundum Isaac filium non ex lege, sed ex pro- „missione hæredes Dei, cohæredes Christi. Absit „enim ut Noe justum & prioris temporis justos, „& quicunque ab illo usque ad Abraham justi esse „potuerunt vel conspicui, vel occulti, negemus ad „supernam Hierusalem, quæ mater nostra est, per- „tinere. Tempore igitur Vet. Test. Spiritum S. „in eis, qui etiam tunc secundum Isaac promissio- „nis filii erant, non solum adjutorem, quod isti „(Pelagiani) suo dogmati sufficere existimant, ve- „rum etiam largitorem dicimus fuisse virtutis.

Hæc omnia Augustinus, quæ luculenta satis, atq; perspicua sunt: Quibus omnino consonat Hieron. „lib. II. Comment. in Ep. Gal. VI. Quomodo omnes „in Protoplasto Adam necdum nati moriuntur, ita „& omnes etiam hi, qui ante adventum Christi na- „ti sunt, in secundo Adam vivificantur. Atque ita „fit, ut & nos legi servierimus in Patribus, & illi „gratia salventur in filiis. Iste intellectus Ecclesiæ „catholicæ convenit, quæ & Vet. & N. Test. unam „adserit providentiam, nec distinguit in tempore, „quos conditione sociavit. Hæc etiam Hierony- mus: sic ergo non paucis tantum nonnullis illa expo- sita fuêre de vita æterna, neque extraordinarie pau- cis solum Sp. S. datus, sed omnibus divinæ promis- siones fuêre palam propositæ, quas omnes fide sus- cipere tenebantur, donumque Sp. S. ceu largitoris virtutis omnibus fidelibus commune fuit. Neque vero. conveniebat hoc officio Prophetarum nonnul- lis hæc occultare, qui omnibus potius voluntatem Dei patefaciebant, imprimis in negotio æternæ sa- lutis Is. 45. Jer. 31. c. 32. & 33. & alibi passim.

Quod vero de involucris & parabolis Justinus habet, non omnibus expositis, non concernit pro- missiones spirituales de remissione peccatorum, & vita æterna, sed vaticinia de futuro Ecclesiæ statu, diversis ænigmatibus, typis, figuris, & parabolis pro- posita, quorum pleraque tamen exposita fuêre lu- culenter. Quæ vero de Cabala Judæorum inserit Grotius in gratiam, ut apparet, Cabalæ, vel traditio- nis non scriptæ Papistarum, neque ad rem facit quic- quam, & dubiæ ac incertæ sunt originis ac verita- tis. Nam Cabalam Judæorum alii aliter explicant. Cabala vel divina est, qualis fuit tum non scripta tempore Patriarcharam oralis institutio à Deo ac- cepta per πατροπαράδοτοι traditionem propa- gata, tum scripta, utpote cum Talmudistæ scripta pro- phetica Cabalæ nomine indigitant; vel humana, genio humano conficta, qualis est tum quam ja- ctant Judæi, utpote primo Talmudica, quam Mo- si traditam in monte Sinai fingunt Judæi, & in unum corpus sub titulo משנה, redactam maximopere venerantur, quæ partem Talmudis constituit, & legem ἁγραφον (in Mose scil. non scriptam, sed tra- ditam de cultus Levitici administratione, Reipubl. gubernatione, totiusque Judaismi pleniori explica- tione concernit. Deinde Symbolica: quæ magnam partem in singulari combinatione, numeratione & revelatione Alphabetaria sita est, & Theoretica sed vana prorsus est ac superstitiosa. Tertio Cabala practica, quæ cum horrenda profanatione verbi Dei conjuncta est, & occupatur circa exorcismos, a- muleta & ἁμυντήρια, & origo est omnis Dæmono- latriæ judice Grasero Exerc. II. in cap. IX. Dan.

& Dn. D. Müllero in Rabbinismo p. 15. tum deni- que, quam Judæis acceptam referunt nonnulli è Christianis, utpote traditio de mysteriis expresse in Scriptura Veteris Testam. non contentis neque omni- bus palam propositis. Qualem hic etiam Judæis tribuit Grotius, & ad eandem pertinuisse putat do- ctrinam de regno cælorum, vel vita æterna. Sed etiam inter occulta fuisse, non populo, sed perspicaciori- bus tantum tradita falsissimum est; neque ullo do- cumento constat, talia mysteria, quæ ad æternam vitam spectant, usque ad Esdram oretenus propa- gata, & studiose è rudibus à Prophetis occultata fuif- se. Originem illa opinio trahit è libro fabuloso, qui Esdræ affingitur, & quartus Esdræ dicitur; prima- rius hujus, ut patet, fabulæ propugnator fuit Picus Mirandulanus in Apol. p. 82. Verum postquam a Babylonica captivitate restituti per Cyrum sub Zoro- babele instaurato templo ad reparandam legem ani- mum appulerunt, Esdras tunc Ecclesiæ præfectus, post emendatum Moscos librum eum plane cognosceret per exilia, cædes, fugas, captivitatem gentis Israe- liticæ, institutum à majoribus morem tradendum per manus doctrinæ servari non posse, futurumque ut sibi divinitus indulta cælestis doctrinæ arcana perirent, quorum commentariis non intercedentibus, durare diu memoria non poterat, constituit, ac convocatis, qui tunc supererant, sapientibus, afferret unius cu- jusque in medium, quæ de mysteriis legis memoriter tenebat, adhibitisque notariis in septuaginta volumi- na, tot enim fere in synedrio sapientes, redigerentur. Quæ de re qui mihi non credunt, audiant Esdram i- psum sic loquentem: Exactis (4. Es. 14. 46.) 40. die- bus, locutus est altissimus, dicens: Priora quæ scri- psisti, in palam pone, legant digni & indigni: novis- simos autem septuaginta libros conservabis, ut tra- das eos sapientibus de populo tuo: In his enim est vena intellectus, & sapientiæ fons, & scientiæ flu- men atque ita feci. Hæc Esdras ad verbum. Hi sunt libri scientiæ Cabalæ, in quibus merito Esdras venam intellectus, id est, ineffabilem de supersstantiali Deitate Theologiam, sapientiæ fontem, id est, de intelligibili- bus, Angelicisque formis, exactam Metaphysicam scien- tiamque flumen, id est de rebus naturalibus firmissimam Philosophiam esse, clara imprimis voce pronunciavit. Hi libri Sixtus quartus, Pontif.
