Max. qui hunc, sub quo vivimus feliciter, Innocentium octavum, proxime antecessit, maxima cura studioque curavit, ut in pu- blicam fidei nostræ utilitatem Latinis literis manda- rentur, jamque cum ille decessit, tres ex illis perve- nerant ad Latinos: hi libri, apud Hebræos, hac tem- pestate tanta religione coluntur, ut nemini liceat, nisi annos quadraginta nato, illos attingere. Hos ego libros non mediocri impenso, mihi cüm comparassem, sum- ma diligentia indefessis laboribus cum perlegissem, vidi in illis (testis est Deus) religionem non tam Mosaicam quam Christianam, ibi Trinitatis mysterium, ibi verbi incarnatio, ibi Messiæ divinitas, ibi de peccato origina- li, de illius per Christum expiatione, de cælesti Hieru- salem, de casu dæmonum, de ordinibus Angelorum, de purgatorii, de inferorum pœnis, eadem legi, quæ apud Paulum & Dionysium, apud Hieronymum & Augusti- num quotidie legimus. Sed quis fidem habebit rhapsodiæ illi, fabulis refertissimæ, quæ sub Esdræ sancto nomine venditatur? Et quinam sunt illi LXX. libri, qui sapientibus tantum commendandi fuerint? Quærit Hottingerus in Thesaur. Phil. l. 1. c. 3. ubi umbra? ubi apex, ubi conjectura doctrinæ hujus Kabbalisticæ? Pharisæi, penes quos clavis e- rat scientiæ, quoque δευτερῴται propterea dicun- tur, quod Traditiones majorum suorum indeside studio propagarunt, ipsi illis mordicus adhærentes; nulla doctrinæ hujus Kabbalisticæ vestigia nobis oftendunt. Nempe Novo Test. & Christi adventui veraKabbala & salutaris mysteriorum ἀποκάλυψις erat reservanda. Ipsi Apostolorum caligabant ali- quamdiu oculi.Paulus ἀκριβεστέραν Judæorum se- cutus hæresin, & ad pedes Gamalielis, viri in omni disciplina Hebraica politissimi, educatus tum de- mum θεοδίδακτος, veram didicit Kabbalam cum suam dedidicit. Nec immerito de his. Corn. Agrip- pa de Vanit. scient. c.47. Quod si Kabbala hæc (quod Judæijactant) à Deo profecta ad vitæ perfectionem, ad hominum salutem, ad Dei cultum, ad intelligentiæ veritatem conduceret, profecto Spiritus ille veritatis, qui repudiata synagoga, venit nos docere omnem ve- ritatem, hanc usque in hæc postrema tempora suam non celasset Ecclesiam, qui profecto omnia novit, quæ sunt Dei, cujus benedictio, baptismus, cæteraque salu- tis sacramenta revelata & perfecta sunt in omni lin- gua. Et quomodo occulta esse potuêre Judæis do- gmata cælestia de vita æterna, & resurrectione mor- tuorum, quæ in ipsis Scripturis Vet. T. satis lucu- lenter exposita sunt, & à Judæis ipsis adversus Sad- ducæos ex iisdem defenduntur,ut ex libris Menassis Ben Israel de resurrectione mortuorum notum est.

Sed quum Grotius,rei evidentia convictus, ne- gare id nequiverit, in Prophetis illa exposita esse, discrimen commentus est temporum & Scriptorum sacrorum ante, & post Babylonicum exilium. In his enim posterioribus tradita illa esse fatetur; in prio- ribus autem expresse ea promissa esse, negat, ac causam, cur in istis tradita sint, hanc comminisci- tur, quod tum gravioribus persequutionibus ob- noxius fuerit populus.

Tum vero, inquit, gravi periculo imminente, ne populus solitus ea tantum audire, quæ in sensu caderent, ablato splendore Judaici imperii,gemens sub externo dominatu, damni,cruciatus, mortis deniq; metu sollicitus deficeret à Judaismo, primus omnium Daniel de resurrectione egit a- pertius, confirmans populum spe restitutionis in statum meliorem τῆς κρείττονος ἀναστάσεως, ut loquitur Scriptor ad Hebræos. Danielem secutus Ezechiel,ad quos respicens Scriptor paræneseos ad Græcos, inter opera Justini,quæ de judicio post hanc vitam habet Plato, ait e Prophetis hausta. Hinc incipiunt sapientes, quos החכמים vocant, qui humanitus,non divinitus eruditi, Prophetis, sed impari au ctoritate, successerunt. Hi quoque necessarium judicarunt, ex Daniele populum adversus tentamenta præmunire, quod fieri satis non poterat,nisi palamDei causa morientibus præ- posita spe vitæ melioris.Itaque ea tum doctrina velut è late- bris educta & certis vocibus obsignata est. Hinc illi Taciti de Judæis: animas prælio aut suppliciis peremptorum æter- nas putant. Hinc moriendi comtemtus. Numenius quoque libro primo de Bono, inter nationes Platonica de animarum immortalitate consentientes posuit Brachmonas, Judæos, Ægyptios. Neque vero animarum tantum immortalitatem, sed & resurrectionem, id est, quamdam corporis recupera- tionem palam traditam creditamque ruin ex eo, quem di- xit scriptoris ad Hebræos loco, tum ex altero,qui est Actor. XXIII.8. manifestissime apparet. Quibus addendi loci il- lustres duo ex historia Maccabaica lib. II. c. VII. quorum prior sic habet: ὁ τοῦ κόσμου βασιλεὺς ἀποθανόντας ἡμᾶς ὑπὲρ τῶν αὐτοῦ νόμων εἰς αἰώνιον ἀναβίωσιν ζωῆς ἡμᾶς ἀναστήσει: alter vero ita : οἱ μὲν γὰρ νῦν ἡμέτεροι ἀδελφοὶ βραχὺν ὑπενέγκαντες πόνον ἀενάς ζωῆς ὑπὸ διαθήκην Θεᾶ πεπτώκασιν.Statum piarum ani- marum post mortem,ab horto illo, in quo Adam initio con- stitutus fuerit גן עדן Hebraice, Græce παράδεισος appella- runt, ut apud Philonem etiam & Josephum videre est: At statum post resurrectionem excellentiori vocabulo dixe- runt Hebraice מלכות שמים aut מלכות אלהה Græce βασιλείαν τοῦ Θεᾶ, aut βασιλείαν τῶν ὀρανῶν, quo per- tinet inter cætera locus ille Sirachidæ; δίκαιοι δὲ εἰς τὸν αἰῶ- να ζῶσι, κὴ ἐν κυρίῳ ὁ μισθὸς ἀὐτῶν, κὴ ἡ φρόντισις ἀὐτῶν παρὰ ὑψίστῳ διὰ τοῦτο λήψονται τὸ βασίλειον τῆς ἐυπειπείας καὶ τὸ διάδημα τοῦ κάλλες ἐκ χειρὸς κυρίκ. Hoc dogmate animati Maccabaicis temporib plurimi præ legis studio exquisitis- simas mortes pertulerunt, ut illorum temporum annales nos docent, & à scriptore ad Hebræos sapienter annotatum est. Et Chaldæus Paraphrastes ad Genesin, qui ante Christum fuisse creditur, judicii post hanc vitam, tum alibi, tum Abelis historia apertam facit mentionem. Quæ cum ita sint, haut immerito quæritur, quo igitur sensu Christus vitam atque immortalitatem perEvangelium in lucem pro- duxisse dicatur, 2. Tim. I. 10. Hæc Grotius.

Sed fallitur in eo omnino quod credit, solum ob pericula & mala sustinenda manifestata illa cœ- lestis doctrinæ capita, siquidem vita æterna etiam ante lapsum, ubi in statu integritatis nulli expositi erant Protoplasti calamitati, promissa fuerit, si legem Domini servassent, & ad ea pertinent, quæ homini creditu necessaria sint, si salvus esse velit, unde ab omnibus credenda erant, qui à lapsu re- parari debuere, ad salutem. Nam quia fidem habere debebant in Messia, quod genus huma- num, à morte, cui obnoxii erant, liberare, vitam- que æternam reparare debuit, non poterat utique fides eorum sibi constare,si ignorarunt plane æter- nam vitam. Ad fidem certe catholicam omniumque temporum pertinuisse articulum de æterna vita, nemo Catholicorum in antiquitate dubitavit. Por- ro falsum esse, quod primus omnium de resurrectio- ne mortuorum Daniel aperte egerit vel Judaicus Rabbi Menasse Ben Israel convicerit Grotium: ne de Christo Sadducæos è Pentateucho Mosis de re- surrectione mortuorum convincente dicamus Matth. XXII. Et quomodo etiam hoc oraculum Danielis non intactum reliquerit, sed pessime de- pravarit Grotius, suo loco diximus. Quod de E- zechielis vaticinio pariter observavimus. Quibus enervatis, nullum amplius relinquetur in canonicis scripturis V. T. de æterna vita aut resurrectione mortuorum (juxta Grotianum sensum) testimo- nium. Unde ergo autor libri sapientiæ,unde mar- tyres Maccabæi fidem illam habuêre, si in Scriptu- ris canonicis eadem non fundata est?

Jam quod ad catalogum illum Sanctorum V. T. Ebr. XI. non posteriorum temporum fideles solum celebrantur, sed & alii inde ab Abele, quod credi- derint Deum μισθαποδότην, quod præcipue gra- tuitam retributionem alterius vitæ respicit, & ab illa fide S. Patriarchæ commendantur, quod ex- pectarint civitatem manentem. Neque dubium est S. Patriarchas fidem salvificam & capita ejusdem præcipua familiis suis & Ecclesiæ universæ sibi cre- ditæ inculcasse,quod de Abrahamo Dominus ipse testatus est Gen. XVIII. 19. ut taceam,quod in ipsa lege vita æterna promissa fuerit, etsi sub conditione perfectæ obedientiæ, interprete ipsomet Christo Luc. X. 28. Sanctoque Apostolo Gal. III. 12. de quo ad Lev. XVIII. diximus.

Quod vero Christus dicitur vitam atque immor- talitatem in lucem produxisse per Evangelium de eo ita pergit Grotius hoc loco p. 73. Nimirum, sicut inter Græcos Philosophos immortalitatem animarum alii asserebant, alii negabant; Socrates vero id tanquam in medio relinquebat,quem secutus videtur Ari- stoteles, multum hic hæsitans, ut & Latinorum Cicero & Seneca : ita apud Judæos δόγμα tanti ad pietatem momen- ti erat τῶν ἀμφισβητουμένων. Ajebant Pharisæi, sed nega- bant Sadducæi,quippe nihil recipientes, nisi quod totidem verbis in Mose expressum invenirent. Pharisæis contra ferme nihil habentibus quo probarent quod contenderent præter rationis auctoritatem, inter diversas scholæ certa- mina fluctuabant multorum animi. De impiorum exitu res erat plane incerta, ut & nunc est apud Judæos: Nam alii resurrecturos credebant, contradicentibus aliis. Chri- stus his tam controversis atque caliginosis attulit definitio- nis suæ lucem, & pœnas impiorum & piorum præmia non tantum diuturna, ut multi putaverant, sed & æterna, & quidem non qualiacunque, sed quæ in angelorum con- sortio & Dei ipsius conspicua ac singulari præsentia consi- sterent, ut rem certam minimeque dubiam publice omni- bus annuncians. Cui doctrinæ obsignandæ cum mortuos in vitam palam revocaverit, ipse se post mortem obitam vivum multis ostenderit, quosdam etiam per Apostolos vitæ reddi curaverit, nihil jam potuit ab æquis animis am plius ad fidem ei rei faciendam desiderari. Ex his quæ diximus, apparet verum quidem esse, quod dixerant citati à nobis Scriptores, vocem regni divini aut cœlestis hoc sen- su à Mose & Prophetis non usurpari, attamen eam à Chri- sto non primitus repertam, sed desumtam ex sermone po- pulari, unde & Paradisi & Gehennæ nomina accepit. His si jungamus ea quæ modo de Pharisaīca legis obedientia dicta à nobis sunt, jam clare apparebit fons ejus erroris, qui hic & omni consequenti sermone à Christo tam dili- genter refellitur. Innocentia enim illa factorum habebat suam δικαίωσιν, sed apud homines: & proderat ad tempo- ralem felicitatem. At regnum cœlorum à Deo spiritu, non isti corporali innocentiæ, sed spirituali justitiæ erat de- stinatum, cujus fons est fides vera quæ in animo sita est. Nam lex illa exterius spectata non poterat τελειῶσαι τὴν συνεί- δησιν, Hebr. IX. 9. sed proderat πρὸς τὴν τῆς σαρκὸς καθαρό- τητα ibid. v. 13. Ex hoc pernitioso errore illud etiam se- quebatur, quod cum facta illa externa crederent non mi- nus apud Deum quam apud homines sufficere, de serio expetenda peccatorum remissione non erant solliciti, ne- que vero expurgandis animis, extirpandisque vitiis illis quæ inter homines dissimulari solent, operam navabant: neque Messia tali opus sibi putabant qui medicinam affer- ret ei parti quam ipsi ægrotare non sentiebant. Et hoc est quod multis locis Christus illis exprobrat, & Paulus ad Romanos epistola, dilucide ostendens hoc esse illis exitia- le, quod Dei justitiæ, quæ est spiritualis, se non subjice- rent, quærentes stabilire suam quandam, hoc est, huma- nam, justitiam. Erant & alii errores Pharisæorum, ut quod hominum constitutiones divinis mandatis æquarent, interdum præferrent etiam, quod sæpe ne exteriorem quidem illam innocentiam præstarent, intenti frigidis qui- busdam ceremoniis, quibus etiam gravida delicta expia- ri posse confiderent, sed istos hoc loco Christus non attingit. Nam benigne illis largiens præstari ab ipsis eam innocen- tiam quæ pœnas in lege expressas effugeret, ostendit inde falso ab ipsis concipi spem adipiscendi regni cœlestis. A- liam enim longe obedientiam ab iis requiri, qui tantæ gloriæ essent candidati. Bene Clemens Alexandrinus: Τῷ τελείῳ οὐκ ἐν συμβολαίοις πολιτικοῖς, οὐδὲ ἐν ἀπογορεύσει νόμε, ἀλλ’ ἐξ ἰδιοπραγίας ἡ τῆς πρὸς θεὸν ἀγάπης ἡ δικαιοσύ- νη. Hæc si quis diligenter consideraverit, facile animad- vertet ea, quæ deinceps dicturus est Christus in hoc ser- mone, non relinquere consilii libertatem, sed intra certos fines imponere præcepti necessitatem, neque ad solos A- postolos & Episcopos, sed vero ad omnes eos qui regni cœlestis participes fieri expetunt pertinere.

Verum enim vero non à Christo demum res il- la decisa est de immortalitate animæ, & restrictio- ne impiorum: tradi jam in scripturis V. Test. u- traque imo & de animarum immortalitate & de cor- porum resurrectione è Scripturis V. T. à Christo i- pso adducta demonstratio, qua convicti Saddu- cæi Matth. XXII. & Paulus adserens utramque di- serte protestatus est se nihil extra Mosen & Pro- phetas docere. Act. XXVI. 8. 22. Dictum vero Apostoli de producta in lucem vita per Christum, quo sensu capiendum sit, alterum membrum do- cet, cum dicitur καταργήσας τὸν θάνατον. Nimi- rum ut destruxit mortem per mortem suam, ita re- divivus à morte propter justitiam nostram, illumi- navit vitam & immortalitatem per Evangelium suum, ceu reparatam vel acquisitam humano generi. Quam ἐπαγγελίας seu promissiones in Veteri Te- stamento reparatum iri docuêre, eam reapse esse reparatam per Christi mortem, & resurrectionem εὐαγγέλιον perhibet, ac testatur, eoque pacto vitam & immortalitatem nobis illuminat. Adde, quod illa tanto lumine non coruscarit, antequam ingrediens Sanctum Sanctorum Pontifex Novi Test. æternam redemptionem invenerit, ac παῥ- ῥησίαν nobis fecerit ingressus in sanguine suo, quum ἐνεκαίνισεν ἡμῖν ὁδον πρόσφατον, καὶ ζῶσαν διὰ τῦ καταπετάσματος τυτέσι τῆς σαρκὸς αὐτῦ Ebr. X. 20. Quapropter luculentius in Novo Te- stamento æternam vitam esse à Christo & Apostolis propositam, atq; in gloriosa resuscitatione ejus vel- ut πρὸς ὄμμα ostensam beatam resurrectionem, nullum est dubium: non negandum tamen, ean- dem in V. Test. ita, ut à fidelibus potuerit suscipi propositam esse, siquidem fides sine vitæ æternæ notitia non sit fides.

PARS V. De vero præceptorum quorundam legis sensu adversus Pharisæicas depravationes.

## 5:21
Vers. 21. It was said to the ancients. Interpreters also vary concerning the sense of these words, which contributes not a little to understanding the consequence. For some think τοῖς Ἀρχαίοις is put for ὑπὸ τῶν Ἀρχαίων, others for πρὸς τοὺς Ἀρχαίους: again, others refer Ἀρχαίους to the times of Moses, others to the age which intervened between the times of Ezra and Christ. I hold it for certain that by the dative case, not those who spoke the words, but those to whom the words were spoken, are indicated; for the opposition is evident. It was said to the ancients: but I say to you; for how this is to be taken for you, so also that must be taken for the ancients. And it is to be seen everywhere in these books that nouns of the dative case joined to verbs which have the notion of speaking are used in this sense: nor has any of the Greeks who wrote on this passage interpreted it otherwise. It remains that we see to what times this antiquity is to be referred, and why I accede to their opinion, because they trace this antiquity from the very time of Moses, I have these reasons. First, because that term ἀρχαῖος for the most part among the Greeks signifies a certain long-standing antiquity, and among the writers of the New Testament it has almost the same use. For except for that place which is Acts XXI. 16, elsewhere it is referred to the age of the Prophets or Moses, or even further, as can be seen in Luke IX. 8, 19, Acts XV. 7, 21, 2 Cor. V. 17, 2 Pet. II. 5, Rev. XII. 9, chap. XX. 2. Then, the words which Christ recites are the very ones which are found in the law, sometimes with no interpretation added, as below 27, 31, 33, 38. And that which is added here: shall be liable to judgment, and that which is added below in verse 45, you shall hate your enemy, will be explained below as not being outside the sense of the law. Add now, that for the most part the Apostles institute a comparison between those who had Moses as teacher and leader, and the followers of Christ, and indeed in such a way that they testify that a much greater light has shone upon the latter than upon the former, 1 Cor. 10, Heb. 2. Moreover, they show that this covenant of the new testament is in many parts superior to that covenant which was promulgated on Mount Sinai, Gal. 4:24, Heb. 8:6 and following. Wherefore it seems that Christ is here dealing with the Mosaic law in that sense in which the lawyers and Pharisees spoke of that law, and how that law flourished in forensic judgments, and that Christ is alluding to this is manifest from the immediately following verse. And indeed it is credible that even in the time of Moses many of that people, as they were σαρκικοὶ (fleshly), neither penetrated into those things which lay hidden under the shadow, nor paid much attention to those commandments which threatened no punishment to those acting against them. The sense therefore is, these things were indeed said to your ancestors, who, as they were σαρκικοὶ (fleshly), interpreted them only σαρκικῶς (fleshly). But I, who wish to gather a spiritual people, just as I clearly and without wrappings propose spiritual rewards to you, and denounce a punishment which is not of this life to the contumacious, so also I will dictate to you openly and explicitly the precepts, the force of which it is by no means obscure consists in the spirit itself.

For the sense of the whole discourse it matters little whether it is understood as said by the ancients or to the ancients, the former of which pleased Beza and Piscator, the latter the Syrian, Spanheim, and others. Nor shall we resist that this antiquity be traced back from the very time of Moses, provided that what Christ prefixes is not neglected, ἠκούσατε, you have heard, namely that these things are so often inculcated to you by the Pharisees and lawyers, that it was said to the ancients: you shall not kill, and whoever shall kill shall be liable to judgment, you shall not commit adultery, you shall not swear falsely, an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth, you shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy. For to all these is prefixed ἠκούσατε, because they heard these things thus handed down by the Pharisees, as if they had proceeded from the ancients and Moses himself, and were sold as divine laws, as if indeed nothing more had been prescribed to the ancients by God for true righteousness, except that they should abstain from external homicide, adultery, and perjury, should love only their neighbor, but hate their enemy, and should exercise or exact the punishment of retaliation, an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth. For the entire righteousness of the Pharisees and scribes (which the Lord here disapproves) consisted in the external obedience of the commandments, to which they themselves even added such accretions, and the sense they attributed to it, alien to reason and vengeance against one's neighbor. Whence it is still most clear that Christ is not opposing himself to the words and commands of Moses, but to the Pharisaic corruptions and additions by which the precepts of Moses were perverted under the pretext of antiquity and Mosaic authority: Grotius is therefore in vain while he here sails with the wind for the Socinians, who imagine that Christ here perfected the Mosaic law with his own additions. For even if they retained certain words from the law, they were not proposed in the sense intended by the legislator, but according to the Pharisaic depravation, nor were they left without human accretion, even such as was repugnant to the divine law, of which kind is that in verse 45: you shall hate your enemy. Furthermore, that a greater light has shone in the school of Christ than upon those who had Moses as their teacher does nothing for the Socinian heresy concerning the additions to the law made by Christ: for it was not so much the Evangelical Doctrine that brought light to the law against the dark glosses and corruptions of the Pharisees, which had been all but completely obscured. Nor does the excellence of the new covenant over the old pact consist in more perfect laws, but, as the Apostle himself explains in Heb. 8:6, because the new covenant has been established upon better promises: and Grotius himself acknowledges that Christ is here dealing with the Mosaic law in the sense in which the lawyers and Pharisees spoke of that law, and how that law was in force in forensic judgments; I add, how they themselves judged that they were performing and fulfilling all the justice of the law. Refer here to what is contained on page 77. The lawyers, says Christ, consider as offenses only those things which are accustomed to be restrained by legitimate punishments: and therefore they deter men from homicide because the law commands that murderers be struck with the sword. But I wish you to beware even of anger, being certainly persuaded that a punishment is also proposed for it in the other world, etc. However, although some perhaps among the ancestors, even in the very time of Moses, understood the commands of the law only carnally (which experience testifies is sometimes done even today in such great light of the New Testament), yet in that ancient time the true sense was not hidden from the people, or at least was not proposed under a shadow. Which can be taught from the elucidation of the individual precepts made in the Mosaic and Prophetic writings themselves.

Verse 21. Whoever shall kill shall be liable to the judgment] This does not indeed exist in so many words in the law, but the sense is open, that it is commanded by the law that a murderer be led to the judges and, condemned by their sentence, be subjected to capital punishment, Lev. 26:21, Num. 35:16, 17, 30. Whence it appears that, just as this, so also in the following clause the judgment which Matthew called דין is not the council of the Triumviri or the lower judges, but the auditorium of the judges who rendered justice on major cases at the gates of the city and were also accustomed to proceed by law against murderers, of whom it is treated in Deut. 16:18, 21:2. For although capital judgments had already been taken away from the Jews at the time when Christ said these things, yet that custom of the courts was known to all and in recent memory. But since all Hebrews say that the council of those judges was of twenty-three, it seems wonderful to many that Josephus, to whom nothing of his ancestral custom was hidden, seems to establish only seven, for thus he says in his description of the laws: let there be seven men appointed for each city, who have excelled in virtue and zeal for justice. But Josephus himself seems to me to solve this knot when he says in the following words, and let two servants be given to each authority from the tribe of the Levites. For by authority he understands those holding individual magistracies, to each of whom were added two assessors skilled in the law, whom Josephus calls servants, which is the Hebrew שוטרים; therefore there were seven municipal judges of the place, and besides them fourteen assessors, who were taken mostly from the Levites. To these, one or two supernumeraries seem to have been added.

Latin:

Vers. 21. Ὅτι ἐῤῥήθη τοῖς ἀρχαίοις] De horum quoque verborum sensu, qui non parum ad consequentiam intelli- gendam facit, variant interpretes. Alii enim τοῖς Ἀρχαί- οις positum putant pro ὑπὸ τῶν Ἀρχαίων, alii pro πρὸς τοὺς Ἀρχαίους: rursum Ἀρχαίους alii referunt ad Mosis tempora, a- lii ad ætatem, quæ Esdræ & Christi tempora intercessit. Ego pro comperto habeo, dandi casu non eos, qui verba fecerant, sed eos ad quos verba facta erant, indicari evidens enim est oppositio. Dictum est antiquis: Ego autem dico vobis quare quomodo hoc vobis, ita & illud antiquis su- mendum est. Ac passim videre est in his libris, nomina δοτικῆς πτώσεως adjuncta verbis, quæ dicendi habent notio- nem hoc sensu usurpari: nec Græcorum, qui in hunc lo- cum scripsere quisquam aliter est interpretatus. Superest videamus ad quæ tempora antiquitas hæc sit referenda, cur eorum accedam sententiæ, quia ab ipso Mosis tempore hanc antiquitatem repetunt, has causas habeo. Primum, quod vox illa ἀρχαῖος & plerumque apud Græcos longæ- vam quandam vetustatem significat, & apud Novi Testa- menti scriptores eundem ferme usum habet. Nam ex- cepto eo loco, qui est Act. XXI. 16. alibi ad Prophetarum aut Mosis ætatem, aut etiam, ulterius refertur, ut videre est Luc. IX. 8. 19. Actor. XV. 7. 21. 2. Cor. V. 17. 2. Petr. II. 5. Apoc. XII. 9. cap. XX. 2. Deinde verba quæ recitat Christus, ea ipsa sunt, quæ in lege reperiuntur, interdum nulla interpretatione adjecta ut infra 27. 31. 33. 38. Et quod hic adjicitur: obnoxius erit judicio, quodque infra ad- ditur commate 45. hostem odio habebis, non esse extra legis sententiam infra explanabitur. Adde jam, quod plerum- que Apostoli comparationem instituunt inter eos qui Mo- sem doctorem ducemque habuerunt, & Christi sectatores, & ita quidem ut his majorem multo, quam illis lucem af- fulsisse testentur, 1. Cor. X. Hebr. II. Quin & pactum hoc novi fœderis ostendunt multis partibus præstare ei pacto, quod in monte Sinai promulgatum est Gal. IV. 24. Hebr. VIII. 6. & deinceps. Quare videtur Christus de jure Mo- saico hic agere eo sensu, quo de eo jure loquebantur legis- periti & Pharisæi, & quomodo id jus in judiciis forensibus vigebat, & ad quæ Christum alludere ex commate proxi- me sequenti manifestum est. Et vero credibile est, etiam Mosis tempore multos de populo illo, ut erant σαρκικοὶ, nec penetrasse in ea, quæ sub umbra latebant, multum attendisse ad ea mandata quæ contra facientibus nullum supplicium minabantur. Sensus ergo est, majoribus qui- dem vestris ista dicta sunt, quæ illi ut erant σαρκικοὶ non nisi σαρκικῶς interpretabantur. At ego qui colligere volo populum spiritualem sicut clare & sine involucris præmia vobis propono spiritualia, & pœnam, quæ non sit hujus vitæ contumacibus denuncio, ita etiam aperte atque ex- plicate vobis dictabo præcepta, quorum vim potissimum in ipso spiritu consistere minime obscurum sit.

Ad sensum totius concionis parum interest, si- ve ab antiquis, sive ad antiquos dictum intelliga- tur, quorum prius Bezæ & Piscatori placuit, poste- rius Syro, Spanhemio, & aliis. Neque refraga- bimur, hanc antiquitatem ab ipso Mosis tempore repeti, modo non negligatur, quod præmittit Christus ἠκούσατε, audivistis, hæc scil. ita sæpe vobis à Pharisæis & legisperitis inculcari, quod dictum sit antiquis: non occides, qui autem occiderit, reus erit judicii, non mœchaberis, non pejerabis, oculum pro oculo, dentem pro dente, diliges proxi- mum tuum & odio habebis inimicum tuum. Nam hisce omnibus præmittitur ἠκούσατε quod audie- rint hæc ita à Pharisæis tradi, tanquam ab anti- quis, & Mose ipso profecta, & pro legibus divi- nis venditari, quasi nempe antiquis à Deo nihil amplius præscriptum sit ad veram justitiam, nisi ut externo homicidio, adulterio, & perjurio abs- tineant, proximum solum diligant, inimicum ve- ro odio habeant, ac pœnam talionis exerceant, aut exigant, oculum pro oculo, dentem pro den- te. Universa enim Pharisæorum & scribarum ju- stitia (quam hic improbat Dominus) in externa obedientia præceptorum consistebat, quibus ipsi etiam talia assumenta addebant, & sensum ejusmodi alienum de ratione & vindicta adversus proximum affricabant. Unde luculentiffi- mum adhuc est, non Mosis verbis, & mandatis sese opponere Christum, sed Pharisaicis corruptelis, & additamentis, quibus Mosis præcepta perverte- bantur, sub prætextu antiquitatis, & autoritatis Mosaica: frustra ergo est Grotius, dum Socinianis hic velificatur, qui hic Christum perfecisse addi- tamentis suis legem Mosaicam comminiscuntur. Nam etsi verba quædam ex lege retinuerint, non tamen illa sensu à legislatore intento, sed juxta de- pravationem Pharisaicam proposita erant, nec sine affumento humano relinquebantur, etiam tali, quod repugnabat legi divinæ, cujusmodi illud est vers. 45. hostem odio habebis. Porro, quod major lux affulserit in schola Christi, quam illis, qui Mosen Doctorem habuerunt, nihil facit pro hæresi Sociniana de additamentis legis à Christo ad- jectis: nam lucem adferebat non tam legi adver- sus caliginosas glossas & corruptelas Pharisæorum, quam Evangelica Doctrina, quæ tantum non pla- ne obtenebrata erat. Neque vero præstantia no- vi fœderis præ veteri pacto consistit in legibus perfectioribus, sed ut explicat ipse Apostolus Ebr. VIII. 6. quia novum fœdus ἐπὶ κρείττοσιν ἐπ- αγγελίαις νενομοθέτηται: & agnoscit Grotius i- pse, Christum de jure Mosaico hic eo agere sen- su, quo de eo jure loquebantur legisperiti & Pharisæi, & quomodo id jus in judiciis forensibus vigebat, ad- do, quomodo ipsi censebant, sese justitiam legis omnem præstare & adimplere. Huc refer, quæ habentur pag. 77. Legisperiti, inquit Chri- stus, ea tantum pro delictis habent, quæ solent legitimis pœnis coerceri: ideoque ab homicidio abster- rent homines, quia homicidas gladio feriri lex im- perat. At ego etiam iracundiam volo caveatis, cer- to persuasiei quoque propositam esse pœnam in seculo altero &c. Utut vero nonnulli forte è majori- bus, etiam ipso Mosis tempore, non nisi σαρκι- κῶς mandata legis intellexerint, (quod hodieque in tanta luce Novi Testamenti quandoque fieri experientia testatur,) non tamen antiquo illo tem- pore verus sensus populo dissimulabatur, aut sal- tim sub umbra proponebatur. Quod è singulo- rum præceptorum dilucidatione in ipsis scriptis Mosaicis & Propheticis facta, doceri potest.

Vers. 21. ὃς δ' ἂν φονεύσῃ ἔνοχος ἔσται τῇ κρίσει] Non exstat quidem hoc totidem verbis in lege, sed sensus est apertus, lege præcipi ut homicida deducatur ad judices & ex eorum sententia condemnatus capitali supplicio afficia- tur Lev. XXVI. 21. Num. XXXV. 16. 17. 30. Unde appa- ret ut hoc, ita & sequenti commate κρίσιν quod Matthæus dixit דין non esse confessum Triumvirorum sive pedaneo- rum judicum, sed auditorium judicum, qui in portis civitatis jus super causis majoribus reddebant & in homicidas etiam lege agere solebant, de quibus agitur Deut. XVI. 18. XXI. 2. Quanquam enim capitalia judicia jam eo tempore: quum Christus hæc diceret Judæis erant ademta, erat tamen mos ille judiciorum notus omnibus & recenti memoria. Cum autem confessum istorum judicum Hebræi omnes dicant viginti trium, mirum multis videtur, quod Josephus, quem patrii moris nihil latuit, septem solos statuere vide- tur, ita enim ait in legum descriptione: ἀρχέσθωσαν δὲ καθ' ἑκάστην πόλιν ἄνδρες ἑπτά, οἱ κᾀ τὴν ἀρετὴν καὶ τὴν περὶ τὸ δί- καιον σπουδὴν πρωτεύηκότες. Sed mihi ipse Josephus hunc nodum solvere videtur, cum verbis sequentibus dicit, ἑκάστῃ δὲ ἀρχῇ ἄνδρες δύο ὑπηρέται διδόσθωσαν ἐκ ῶ τῆς λευιτῶν φυ- λῆς. Nam ἀρχὴ intelligit singulos magistratum gerentes, quibus singulis bini erant additi assessores periti juris, quos Josephus ὑπηρέτας vocat, quod est Hebr. שוטרים septem ergo municipes loci erant judices, præterea asses- sores XIV. qui ex Levitis maxime sumebantur. His super- numerarii accessisse videntur unus & alter.

## 5:22
Verse 22. But I say to you] Most wisely Christ refers all offenses to precepts of the same kind. For because homicides are accustomed to be born from anger and insults, as we were just quoting from Aristotle, anger is the cause of all murder, therefore he refers anger and its offshoots to the precept concerning homicide.

Christ does not allege the law as it was handed down by Moses, or rather by God, but as it had been interpolated by the Pharisees and scribes: which the very words he uses teach. For when he cites the law or the scripture of the Old Testament, he is accustomed to bring it forward in the same words, or those which the LXX Interpreters used. Which was not done here. And that he opposes his own opinion to the corruptions of the Pharisees, not to the Mosaic opinion, is also clear from the fact that Moses, in prohibiting homicide, not only embraces external slaughter, but under the species of homicide, synecdochically, everything that in the phrase of scripture is homicide, and by that word teaches by emphasis that hatred, anger, strife, heat of passion, and other affects of that kind are in the eyes of God homicides; indeed, that everyone who does not love his neighbor is a murderer and remains in death, 1 John 2:14, 15. Indeed, he teaches this principally in vindicating the fifth precept, that inordinate anger is prohibited here. For if slaughter is separated from inordinate anger, it is not a sin, as we see in the Magistrate, when he inflicts deserved slaughter he does not sin against this precept, nor does he commit homicide. Whence Christ does not here add a new precept concerning anger, but shows the blindness of the Pharisees, because they do not understand that inordinate anger is primarily and in itself prohibited here, and consequently the slaughter of a man, and that not in itself, but insofar as it arises from inordinate anger: because such anger is prohibited, whether it proceeds as far as slaughter or not: and thus also that everything which arises from inordinate anger is entirely prohibited, whether it be a cursing word, or a hostile look, or homicide itself. To which contributes that in Matt. 15:19, Out of the heart come murders. Furthermore, we easily agree that he is called ἔνοχος τῇ κρίσει who is guilty of a capital punishment: and that by the Pharisees only he who had committed external murder was held both as a homicide and as guilty of the judgment, that is, worthy to be affected by capital punishment. But whether by κρίσιν that judgment of the twenty-three men is understood, seems doubtful to some. For some understand the judgment of three men, and think that not only the cognizance of pecuniary causes, but also of crimes and capital cases, belonged to it, inasmuch as the matter was not in the least doubtful. To whom B. Chemnitius adds in Harm. cap. LI. pericop. III. p. m. 563, thus differing concerning the three diverse judgments among the Jews: 1. In the judgment sat three men pronouncing on causes which were of manifest law: as on the punishment of homicide. 2. In every city of Israel there was a small Sanhedrin consisting of XXIII judges. They judged of causes which had something of controversy. 3. At Jerusalem there were LXXII judges, who took cognizance of the highest causes, Deut. XVII. 8. 9. Whom B. Gerhard followed in Homil. II. Domin. VI. post Trinit. pag. 334. But the opinion of those is more likely who think that capital judgments did not pertain to the inferior judges and the bench of three men in smaller towns, but to the judges in the gates of the cities, which had a number of citizens of at least CXX: just as the Jews also called that first and lowest judgment דיין ממונות judgment of a pecuniary cause, but the second and middle one דיין נפשות judgment of souls, besides which there was a third or supreme one in the metropolis called by the Jews בית דין house of judgment ἐξοχικῶς, and the great Sanhedrin, in distinction from the second, which was called the small Sanhedrin. Concerning which see Rambam or Maimonides, and R. Bechai, Buxtorf in his Hebrew abbreviations, page 17, Schindler in his Lexicon under the word שׁפט, to which Selneccer, Glaff, Winstrup, and others agree; Angelus Caninius in his Loca Novi Testamenti, page 62, reports from the Talmud, Massechet Sanhedrin, likewise three classes of judges by that method: the first, the house of judgment of three men, to which lesser cases, such as theft, private injuries, mistreatment, and finally dine Mamonoth (monetary laws) were referred; the house of judgment of twenty-three, or the small Sanhedrin, in which greater cases, namely capital ones, were heard; and the house of judgment of seventy-one, or the great Sanhedrin, in which the most serious cases, which pertained to the highest matters of the Republic, were accustomed to be treated, because it is written there thus: They do not pronounce judgment on a tribe, nor on a false prophet, nor on the high priest, except by the sentence of the court of seventy-one. And thus the gradation in the subsequent words of Christ holds itself more correctly, by which He defines the same punishment for rash anger, for gestures proceeding from anger, and finally for calumnious words or insults—namely, that of eternal death—and only designates different degrees of punishments: because in the krisis (judgment) of the twenty-three men, a capital punishment was dictated, and in the Sanhedrin, called by way of excellence, likewise, but a heavier one was dictated; but the most serious of all was that of the fire of Gehenna, in the valley of Ben Hinnom: so that here regard is had to the formula of Jewish judgments and capital punishments, but of a disparate degree. If a capital punishment was dictated in the judgment of the three men, what was that? And what was that heavier one to be dictated in the assembly of the twenty-three? Or was a heavier punishment defined for that reason, because the offense which was to be judged in this assembly was of less manifest law and more difficult cognition? And therefore Grotius observes not badly that in the judgment or small Sanhedrin, concerning which it is said here 'he shall be liable to the judgment,' the punishment of the sword was dictated for murderers, which was most customary there, but that crimes reserved for the great Sanhedrin were affected by a heavier punishment, which is that of stoning; finally, that the most serious punishment is designated by the words 'into the fire of Gehenna.'

Verse 22. ὁ ὀργιζόμενος (he who is angry)] In this treatment, one must diligently distinguish between to pathos (the passion), he horme (the impulse), and he synkatathesis (the assent). Pathos is like that faculty by which we are angered, to thymoeides (the spirited part), which, being implanted in us by nature, cannot be rooted out, and is among the indifferent things which one may use rightly or otherwise. But because that part of the soul in which the pathe (passions) reside is in itself alogos (irrational), it happens that the hormai (impulses) exert themselves without waiting for the judgment of reason: which, unless they are diligently restrained, are usually followed by synkatathesis, when, namely, that part which was given for moderating the affections allows itself to be drawn with the reins loosened. There is, therefore, as Gellius says, a voluntary synkatathesis, and it is at the discretion of man: but even those first movements, which philosophers compare to the blinking of the eyes, are usually overcome by diligent attention and exercise, and above all by the Spirit of God, lest they either last long or grow strong. It is necessary, therefore, as Plutarch speaks, to correct and drink down the angers that fall upon us from time to time. Then he adds: 'From diligence and practice, one must in some way [deal] with them.' Others call the hormai (impulses) propatheiai (pre-passions): but they call the same ones when adult pathe (passions). Jerome, in his letter to Demetrias: 'It is difficult, or rather impossible, for anyone to be free from the beginnings of perturbation, which the Greeks more significantly call propatheiai.' The same, to Eustochium on the custody of virginity: 'He is praised, he is proclaimed, who, as soon as he begins to think sordid things, immediately kills the thoughts and dashes them against the rock. And the rock is Christ.' The pathe themselves are also usually distinguished by certain degrees.

These things smell of the lamp of the Socinians and Papists. Forsooth, synkatathesis (assent) is held to be a sin, but the first movements, provided at least they do not last or grow strong, are not; and Grotius easily acquiesced in the judgment of Seneca, which he praises here as excellent from book II, chapter 4 of his work On Anger. 'And that you may know how the affections begin, or grow, or are carried away: the first movement is not voluntary, as it were a preparation of the affection, and a certain threat; the second is with a will not contumacious, as if I ought to be avenged, since I have been harmed: or he ought to pay the penalty, since he has committed a crime. The third movement is now impotent, which does not want to take revenge if it ought to, but rather [does so] because it has overcome reason.' We cannot escape that first strike of the soul by reason: just as we cannot escape those things which we said happen to bodies, lest the yawning of another provoke us, or the eyes be closed at the sudden movement of fingers. Reason cannot overcome that: custom perhaps and assiduous observation may attenuate it. That other movement, which is born from judgment, is removed by judgment. This warning is indeed excellent in a man not sufficiently imbued with Christian discipline; but we know, not only from this information of Christ, 'he who is angry eike (without cause),' but from the very law of the Decalogue, THOU SHALT NOT COVET, that even the first movements of anger themselves, when it creeps upon us eike, even if reason cannot overcome them, and those hormai (impulses) and propatheiai (pre-passions) as they call them exert themselves without waiting for the judgment of reason, and, as Jerome speaks in his Epistle to Demetrias, it is difficult, or rather impossible, for anyone to be free from the beginnings of perturbation, are sin in the true sense. For that impossibility is not from nature, such as it was instituted by God, but such as it is corrupted by the fault of man's sin, and therefore God, without injustice, demands from us that which is now impossible to us by our own fault, and can condemn us for sin if it is not performed. Nor is to hekousion (voluntariness) required for the form of sin: but every anomia (lawlessness) is hamartia (sin), whether it be voluntary or involuntary, 1 John 3:4, and therefore sin ought to be estimated and defined not by our will, but by anomia and repugnance against the law: according to which also the primary rash horme (impulse), as a wicked movement of the heart, is anomia, repugnant to the law, THOU SHALT NOT COVET, and a work of the flesh, Galatians 5:20, Colossians 3:8.

Τῷ ἀδελφῷ αὐτῦ (To his brother)] That is, to any other person. A Hebraism. For the Hebrews are accustomed to speak thus in Genesis 26:31, Joel 2:8, even concerning inanimate things, as Exodus 26:3, Ezekiel 1:9 and 23, 3:13. Here, therefore, brother is any man whatsoever. Thus below: Unless you forgive men.

Εἰκῆ] This is deservedly added. For not everyone who is accustomed to be angry is irascible, but he who is angry 'at what he ought not, and at what he ought not, and more than he ought,' as Aristotle speaks. Therefore, εἰκῆ is either without cause, or even without measure. That anger has the best cause which is conceived from the pain of a divine being offended, such as that of Christ was in Mark 3:5. But also in human affairs anger can be honorable, especially when it is not so much our own affair that is being conducted, as that of virtue itself, or even of other men: and when it is permitted to say that of Sosiphanes:

Now let your spirit be stirred before your eyes, old man, for now it is necessary to take up anger, when it is unjust.

But then also it behooves us, having received anger as an ally of virtue, to enjoy as much of it as is useful; but to cast out and expel the great and superficial part of it from the soul, as I use the words of Plutarch. In measure, however, it is included, both that we should not be angry more than is right, and that we should not be angry longer than is right. Against the former part of this caution offend those who are angry beyond measure at small sins, who, as the philosopher Apollonius used to say, do not allow those who have sinned to know when they have sinned more or less. Into the other part sin those who carry leaden, and what is commonly called immortal, angers, whom Arrian compares to those suffering from lingering fevers. This is undoubtedly that root of bitterness germinating in the heart, which the writer to the Hebrews 12:15 commands to be avoided, to which also that warning of Paul pertains, when he wishes us to be angry in such a way that we do not sin, that is, that we do not exceed the measure of what is right, which he himself explains thus, that we should not prolong anger until the setting of the sun, Ephesians 4:26. And let these things be said so that the force of the word εἰκῆ may be more correctly understood, which indeed the Syrian interpreter thought so proper and significant in this place that he preferred to retain it rather than translate it. Wherefore one should not agree with Jerome, who erases this word on the authority of certain copies, especially since it appears that the Greek interpreters also read it, and Justin himself brings forward this opinion in the epistle to Zenas and Serenus: then also Irenæus in two places, book II, chapter LVI, and book IV, chapter XXXI. It is much more credible that it was introduced by those who feared that all anger here, proceeding from some just cause, might seem to be approved, since the word εἰκῆ, as we have said, has a wider application.

ἔνοχος ἔσται τῇ κρίσει.] The experts in the law, says Christ, consider only those things to be offenses which are accustomed to be restrained by legal punishments: and therefore they deter men from homicide, because the law commands that murderers be struck with the sword. But I wish you to beware even of anger, being certainly persuaded that for it also a punishment is proposed in the other world, no less severe than that which murderers sustain here. But if anyone adds abusive language to anger, he will bear a punishment more severe than that, such as the punishment of stoning, or even, if the abuse is more atrocious, he will feel more exquisite tortures, such as are wont to be those of them who are burned with slow fires in the valley of Hinnom. This seems to me the simplest paraphrase of this passage, the reasons for which we will render part by part. Κρίσιν, as we learned in the preceding verse, is the council of twenty-three men, although the great senate, about which we are to speak later, was also called דין, whence he who was second to the prince of the senate was accustomed to be called אב בית דין: πατὴρ τοῦ οἴκου τῆς κρίσεως, just as in turn the council of twenty-three judges was called συνέδριον: But for the sake of distinction it seems to have been received by usage that that council of individual cities should be called κρίσις, but that supreme one should be called συνέδριον. Moreover, the most common punishment of the κρίσις was the sword, because cases of homicide were heard therein, as both Moses teaches us and Christ in the preceding verse. But wishing to indicate the degrees of future punishments in the other world for the degrees of offenses, Christ applied to that matter, beyond the similarity of the case, various deaths which were known to the people and differed in the magnitude of their torture.

ὃς δ' ἂν εἴπῃ] One must repeat from the common context what preceded, εἰκῆ ὀργιζόμενος. For he is dealing with one who, accustomed to indulge in rash anger, even breaks out into insults. For as Ariston said, τὴν κακολογίαν ἡ ὀργὴ φαίνεται ἀπογεννῶσα ὥςτε ἡ μήτηρ ἐκ ἀστῖα. The word Raca, which the Syrian language, with a changed vowel, pronounces raca, is something less than μωρέ. It has, however, the meaning of 'vain,' which is also used by the Latins in abuse: as 'vain Ligurian,' 'most vain elder.' But the crime is not placed in the word itself. For indeed James 3:20 knew the arguments, which is properly Rica (for certain Greek interpreters also translated what is in Judges 11:3 אנשים ריקים as ἄνδρες κενοὶ, and Hesychius as ῥακὰ κενός) and that which we said, μωροὶ, Christ brought against the Pharisees below in 23:17, 19, and Christ calls his own disciples ἀνοήτους, Luke 24:25. & the Galatians, Paul, Gal. 3:1, 3, to omit now those which are harsher, such as 'brood of vipers,' 'hypocrites,' and other things of that kind. But these were undoubtedly said by those upon whom the duty of chastising others rested, and who looked to nothing privately in it, from most grave causes, and with the purpose that the minds of others might be awakened from lethargy by such goads. But the Pharisees not only did not observe the measure, but attacked every most innocent person with insults with a malevolent mind, which Christ and his followers have very often experienced. This disease, too, had undoubtedly proceeded from the source of errors already indicated several times. For the law of Moses did not prosecute injuries of this kind, unless one had cursed either parents or a Prince.

Grotius rightly opposes the opinion of Christ in this paraphrase to the doctrine of the experts in the law. Therefore Christ does not, as a new legislator, perfect the divine law, which Grotius, with the Socinians and Papists, maintains, asserting on page 65 that Christ wished to fortify the law with certain more exact precepts; but he reproves the corruptions of the Pharisees and the experts in the law, and vindicates the sense of the law: the scope of which, Grotius professed above on page 63, was to make men as good as possible: which scope, however, would have been prefixed to the law by God in vain, if the law itself, by itself, without the more exact additions of Christ which he imagines, could not have made men as good as possible, as far as doctrine and instruction are concerned. But if, with Christ, the best interpreter of the law, teaching that the internal affection of rash anger itself deserves infernal punishment, just as gestures and abusive words do, there can be no doubt that in the law, along with gestures and abusive words resulting from rash anger, the affection of rash anger was also prohibited: for where there is no law, there is no transgression; where there is no transgression, there is no place for any punishment, much less an eternal and infernal one. But as for what Grotius says, that the law did not prosecute injuries of this kind, when one says 'Rica' to a brother, or 'fool,' unless one had cursed either parents or a Prince, he makes this only for impunity in the forum of the earth and divine judgment, and it does not procure immunity from guilt through the law of Moses, which brandishes the thunderbolt of a curse against all who do not keep all the words of the law.

Ἔνοχος ἔσται τῷ συνεδρίῳ] Because this word occurs here for the first time, although many things have been said sufficiently by others, I will nevertheless add what may bring some light to history. Just as in memory of the twelve male children of the first degree whom Jacob had begotten, twelve tribes and as many phylarchs were made, so in memory of those heads whom Jacob had brought into Egypt, the Israelites, as those who lived apart from the others, set over themselves seventy men [or rather seventy-two, about which matter we shall speak at Luke], who might care for and moderate their affairs as much as royal commands permitted. These, from the age at which they were chosen, were called elders, whence also among the Greeks the term γερουσία, and among the Romans the term Senate. But it is also in Homer: Βουλὴ δὲ πρῶτον μεγαθύμων ἷζε γερόντων.

Among these elders, before others, Moses is commanded to set forth the mandates which he had received from God, Exod. III. 16, which he also did, Exod. IV. 29. Of this number also seem to have been those from whom the Egyptian taskmasters demanded an account of daily labor, v. 14. Afterward, when by his father-in-law's counsel Moses had appointed judges who might decide lesser disputes, the cognizance of greater cases remained with Moses alone, to whom also more difficult controversies concerning lesser cases were referred, Exod. XVIII. 22. Therefore, up to that time, those seventy had no power of judging: an indication of which matter is that Moses, having been ordered to approach the mountain with Aaron, Nadab, Abihu, and those seventy (for that number is expressly stated), when he was then called alone by God to the summit of the mountain, ordered the seventy elders to remain below. There are, he says, with you Aaron and Hur; if anyone has any controversy, let him approach them, Exod. XXIV. 14, where Moses openly delegates his judicial duties for the time of his absence not to those seventy, but to Aaron and Hur. Finally, some time later, when Moses complained that he was not sufficient for this burden of supreme judgments and reports as well, God spoke to him thus: Num. XI. 16. Take to yourself seventy from the elders of the Israelites, whom you know to be senators and moderators of the people. They had, therefore, even then the care of the people's affairs: then God, instructing them with a new spirit, namely a judicial one, commands them to bear a part of the burden which Moses alone had hitherto sustained: that, however, is, as we have said, of supreme judgments and reports. Moreover, the meaning of those words which are read in Deuteronomy XVII. 8 seems to be this: since the Priests, enjoying abundant leisure, devoted effort to all branches of wisdom beyond the others, it was fair that a good many from their number be selected into that order to which we have said supreme judgments had already been entrusted: although Maimonides wrote that there was no one who could claim that place for himself by dignity of origin, and that not even the High Priest was elected to it unless it was well established concerning his wisdom: for which matter a δοκιμασία was instituted, which was sealed by the laying on of hands. But as I said, with the affairs of the Hebrews flourishing, it could not be otherwise than that in the class of Priests very many would be found worthy of that place. To these were added others who excelled in learning and holiness in other tribes. For thus the word ראשי seems to be understood in 2 Chron. XIX. 8. Wherefore Moses, in Deut. XIX. 17, dealing with the cognizance of false testimony and describing this senate, names the Priests and judges. Elsewhere, however, where it is a question of exploring the diligence of inferior judges in searching for a murderer, only the Priests, as the principal part of that Senate, are named: and it is added that all controversies and questions of wounds are to be defined according to their prescription. But as often as God had set someone over the people by heavenly indication, such as was Joshua, Gideon, Jephthah, Samson, Samuel, they had the right of judging even without the Senate, as appears in Jud. VIII. Such supreme magistrates of the free Republic and as it were Interreges were called שופטים, which name neighboring peoples also used. For among the Tyrians, too, Interreges were so called: from whose archives Josephus brings forward these things: [Greek text] where Josephus undoubtedly translates as [Greek text] those whom the Tyrians called [Hebrew text]. For the Carthaginians, colonists of the Tyrians, also retained the same name, which Roman writers pronounce as Suffete: with the letter Schin softened, just as the Ephraimites, inclining in that direction, used to pronounce it. Josephus also calls such a leader raised up by God a Prophet, because they were accustomed to shine forth by the gift of Prophecy, like Joshua or Samuel, or by another not dissimilar [gift] animating them and giving success, which Maimonides also notes in the Guide for the Perplexed, Book II, ch. 45. To them, although too strictly, because of their [Greek text] and irresponsible power, the name of kings is given, Jud. IX. 6 and XVIII. 1. But in those times when God had raised up no such person, it was necessary to have recourse entirely to the Senate, in which the High Priest almost always stood out. For Moses, too, as we just said, when he was forced to be away from the people, entrusted his duties to Aaron. By this right, Heli the High Priest held the leadership in the Republic, and the same was observed in the times of the Hasmoneans. God therefore wills that if anything more obscure should happen, which might require skill in more subtle law or even in medicine, the High Priest should be approached as one excelling in learning: or he who, raised up by God, held the dignity of Suffete. All, both lesser judges and private citizens, were ordered to obey their response, with the penalty of death proposed for the contumacious. Moreover, God indicates that the seat of his Senate would be in the place of public assemblies, which were first held at Shiloh, afterwards at Jerusalem. Therefore, what is said in verse 9, 'You shall approach the Levitical Priests and the Suffete,' is to be explained from that which follows in verse 12, 'to the Priest or the Suffete.' For in Hebraism, no less than in all languages, it is accepted that a conjunction may have the force of a disjunction. Nor, indeed, were there some judgments of the Priest and others of the Senate, for all Hebrew teachers constantly deny that. Josephus, who could not be ignorant of the custom of his own country, clearly shows that it was the same assembly, for he speaks thus in the second book against Apion: [Greek text]. Philo teaches us the same: 'The priests used to sit together,' in his book on the life of Moses. And in the book on the constitution of a prince: [Greek text]. Although all these ought to be considered rich witnesses in such a well-known history, yet it is not difficult to demonstrate the same to those desirous of learning the truth from the sacred code. For first, in this very place, the kinds of cases are not distinguished, nor are any cases named which could properly be seen as priestly, but if any controversy should happen to arise, concerning homicide, concerning a lawsuit, concerning a wound, they are ordered to approach the Priests, or him whom we said is called the Suffete. Again, without any distinction of cases, whatever they have pronounced, all are ordered to execute. The penalty for those who do not obey is the same. Furthermore, it is certain, both among the Hebrews and among more recent interpreters, that judgments were restored to the old pattern by King Jehoshaphat. Ezra, or whoever is the writer of Chronicles, first narrates that judges of the cities were appointed by the excellent King and admonished of their duty. Then continuing, 'But at Jerusalem,' he says, (namely in the city of public assemblies as the law commanded) 'Jehoshaphat appointed from the Levites and Priests (because among them, as we said, there was the greatest abundance of learned men to be found) and from the chief of the Israelite families for the judgments of God and for lawsuits, who returned to Jerusalem.' 'Judgments of God,' from a very well-known Hebraism, signifies judgments which are to be carried out not by human whim but by the command of the law. It follows in the history: 'The King commanded them in this manner: Do this, religiously, faithfully, and with a sincere mind: Whatever lawsuit shall have been brought to you by your countrymen who dwell in the cities, concerning the distinction of homicides, concerning the law, concerning the precept, concerning the statutes, concerning the order of judgments, admonish them lest they be held guilty before God, and the vehement wrath of God fall upon you and your countrymen. This, I say, do, lest you be guilty.' Behold how openly he wishes all those whom he had appointed at Jerusalem to take cognizance of every kind of case. Nor does what follows stand in the way of this. 'For indeed Amariah the Priest is your chief in every matter of God, and Zebadiah the son of Ishmael of the house of Judah in every matter of the King, and the Levitical masters are present with you. Be of good courage, and do this. God will be with the good.' For first, from this it also appears that the affairs of God, that is, of the law, and the affairs of the King were handled in the same Senate: and that both Amariah, whether he was High Priest or another priest, and Zebadiah were present in that Senate. And that 'matters of God' cannot be understood as affairs entrusted to priests alone is plain from another place in that history, where certain Hebronites are said to have been appointed by David over the parts of Reuben, Gad, and Manasseh, and placed over every matter both of God and of the King. Therefore, business of both kinds, both of judicial proceedings and of political deliberations, used to be handled by the Senate. But this is undoubtedly the παράφρασις (paraphrase) of the said passage: Do not lose heart as if you were not equal to such a great burden, for lack of the learning that might be desired for such great matters. You have excellent men who can shine before you with counsel: such is the prince of your Senate, Amariah the priest, a man most experienced in judicial matters; but if anything should arise pertaining more to civil prudence than to the knowledge of the law, Sabadias the Ishmaelite is present for you, who holds the first place in that kind of deliberation; then you have the Levite assessors, excellent in the skill of many arts. Only be of good courage and devote effort to what is fair and good, God will make the rest prosper. Sabadias seems entirely to have been the prince of the Senate. For the Hebrews explain the word נגיד by ראש. And it is established that the prince of the senate was called in this way. From these things which we have said, it also appears that once the kingdom was established, the authority of the Senate was great and as it were equal to the royal authority; for as the Hebrew teachers rightly note, the King himself did not judge in certain cases, and he did not execute his own judgments except by the sword. And what Sedecias says seems to pertain to this, when the Senators were demanding Jeremiah the Prophet for death: The King can do nothing against you. Indeed, the Hebrews note that the King did not even come into the Senate, so that he would not take away the freedom of others to give their opinion by his own judgment: except for David. What we have said with Josephus, Philo, and with the sacred scriptures themselves, that there were Priests in this supreme senate, is not refuted by the history of Jeremiah which is in chapter XXVI of his book, where the Priests seem to accuse Jeremiah, and the Senators to acquit him. For, not to mention that it could appear to be more of a dispute of colleagues among themselves, such as is described in John VII. 50. and Acts V. 35, rather than a legitimate accusation with others judging, it is certain that there were many Priests outside the Senate, and if any of them undertook the role of accuser, they had taken away from themselves the power of judging. There were indeed priestly duties: to teach the whole people and individuals seeking counsel, both about other matters and especially about all those things which pertained to sacred rites and ceremonies, Leviticus X. 10, 11; Ezekiel XLIV. 23; Haggai II. 12, 13. Furthermore, just as other tribes had their own moderators who looked after the common affairs of the tribes, so also in the Levitical tribe the most powerful of the Priests were in charge of the affairs of their tribe, through whom the collection and distribution of tithes and other revenues were managed, which were destined for the sustenance of the Priests and Levites and for the uses of the temple, as can be seen in 2 Kings XXII and 2 Chronicles XXXIV. and in many places in Josephus. But all these things pertained nothing to judicial power, which was not in the hands of some purely Priestly or Levitical college, but in the hands of the Senate which I mentioned, a good part of which consisted of Priests, as was proven above by some testimonies taken from Moses. Therefore, concerning the Priests, as being the chief ones in that Senate, it is said through Ezekiel: In judging cases let them observe the law, let them judge according to my laws and statutes, chapter XLIV. 24. But the same Ezekiel, describing the corrupt morals of the people somewhat earlier, had specifically mentioned the great Senate, naming seventy elders, and their prince Jaazaniah, VIII. 11. There is no doubt that these seventy retained their authority among the Jews in the Babylonian exile. Indeed, the Hebrews also report that capital judgments were exercised by this Senate with the consent of the Kings of Persia. But to those who had returned home, judicial power was granted by King Artaxerxes, Ezra VII. 25, 26. Afterwards, when liberty was restored by arms against Antiochus, the supreme power of affairs was in the hands of this senate, whence also the royal scepter was kept in the council chamber. The council chamber was in the temple itself in the southern part, and was called לשכת הגזית, the chamber of hewn stone. That order remained by continuous replacement, through the laying on of hands, as we have said, until Herod the Great, whose power and audacity rising more and more against the laws, when the Senators had not repressed them in time with severe judgments, as was fitting, God so disposing matters, they paid heavy penalties for their neglected duty, all being killed by Herod, except for one, Sameas, whom they had often despised when he warned of such things. In the place of those killed, Herod substituted others, undoubtedly his own faction, from those who had attained to priesthoods or other honors by his favor. But even before this, the authority of the Hierosolymitan Senate had been not a little diminished, when after Pompey's victory, Gabinius, the governor of Syria, had set up four other councils at Gadara, Amathus, Jericho, and Sepphoris, but not with equal right to the Hierosolymitan one. For Herod, not yet king, pleaded his case regarding matters done in Galilee before the Hierosolymitan Senate. Those councils, therefore, were for the purpose of managing instituted more for the sake of the republic than of the courts, or if for the sake of the courts, yet under the Jerusalem Senate. Indeed, even outside Palestine, the Jews had their own senates after the example of this Sanhedrin. Thus, there is mention of the γερουσίας of the Jews living in Alexandria in Philo. Josephus himself constituted a γερουσία in Galilee with a similar number of Senators when he had been appointed prefect there. But the power of the Jerusalem Senate became more restricted in the times of Augustus, when the better part of Judea had been reduced into a province, it being established, as in almost all provinces of the Roman empire, that the Senate should not subject anyone to the punishment of death without the consent of the Roman governor: the rest of its judicial power being preserved for it. And this is what the Talmudists say in the titles concerning the Sanhedrin and concerning the Sabbath, that judgments of souls, that is, capital ones, had been taken away from that Senate forty years before the destruction of the city. For when they were finally cut off by Titus at Jerusalem, that senate also perished entirely at the same time. The most common name of this Senate was συνέδριον, not because other assemblies of judges were not also called by that name, but because, on account of its excellence, that greatest council was properly honored with that name, which had also been used in Athens and in other Greek cities for the same name. After the Macedonians had become predominant in those parts, just as many other Greek words, so this one also migrated into the Hebrew language. And so, by the Talmudists, this senate is called now סנהדרין simply, now with the addition סנהדרין גדולה זו συνέδριον τό μέγα. This word συνέδριον is seen placed for the senate, or even for the senate-house, in many places in the Evangelical history and the Acts of the Apostles. It is also called γερουσία in the edict of Antiochus and elsewhere in Josephus, Judith XI. 11, I Maccab. XII. 6, 2 Maccab. and 3. Maccabees not long from the beginning, and likewise Acts V. 21, which name the Spartans also used. Likewise πρεσβυτέριον τῶ λαῶ Luke XXII. 66, so that it may be distinguished from the assemblies of the cities, which were likewise called πρεσβυτέρια. The Senators themselves are now commonly called πρεσβύτεροι or even άρχοντες τῶ λαῶ, by Josephus also γνώριμοι τῶ δήμῳ, now these who were Senators outside the Priests are called distinctly. Experts in the law sat beside these for the sake of counsel, as we said before, οἱ γραμματεῖς τῆς βυλῆς, as Josephus speaks, who designates a certain Aristaeus by that name of honor, whence we see him described everywhere as that Senate with these parts: the chief Priests, other elders, and experts in the law. These things having been explained, let us come to the words of Christ. If anyone rightly attends to those crimes which were reserved for the supreme sanhedrin alone, he will find that the punishment of stoning was established for the most serious of them, either by custom or by law: which pertained even to false Prophets themselves and those guilty of treason, Deuter. XVII. 5, 2 Kings XXI. 10. Wherefore I judge this punishment, as being more severe than the sword, to be placed in the second degree.

Εἰς τὴν γέενναν τῆ πυρός) Here now follows the third degree. But as the two former degrees were enunciated through a comparison of visible torments, so also this third one. But since there was no punishment in Jewish usage above stoning [for the punishment of fire was not the burning of a living person slowly, but the insertion of a glowing wick into the bowels], Christ sought from elsewhere the name of a horrendous torment, which would exceed both the sword and stoning. But it was a well-known thing to all Jews how, outside the city of Jerusalem, their ancestors, shamefully imitating the cruel superstition of the Phoenicians, had instituted the practice of torturing miserable infants to death with fires, while flutes and drums sounded around them in the meantime, so that the cry wrung out by pain might not be heard. The place dedicated to such a savage rite was called Tophet: the wider place of the place itself, the valley of the sons of Hinnom, גי הנום, which the pronunciation of later times brought out as γέενα. But that which is brought forward from the Hebrew teachers, that corpses were carried to the same place, agrees with the prophecy of Jeremiah VII. 32, and it began to be done in the times of Josiah, 2 Kings XXIII. 10. For he is read to have polluted that place: by the bringing in of corpses, of course. For it was the custom of the Jews to make places used for forbidden ceremonies impure and abominable in that way, as can be seen in the said chapter XXIII. 16. Thus Josephus narrates that the Samaritans, out of hatred for the Jewish temple, διάρῥιψιν ἀνθρωπείων ὀστῶν ἐν ταῖς στοαῖς ποῆσαι, Antiquities XXVIII. 3, but this does not pertain to the explanation of Christ's words. For it is apparent that a torment, and indeed a most severe one, is indicated by Christ. And just as here the more severe punishments of the future age are compared to the fires of Gehenna: so elsewhere, by a comparison migrating into custom, the punishments of the other age are signified by this very name. And in this sense this word is found in the Jerusalem paraphrase, Gen. III.

Plausible and not inelegant seems the explanation of Grotius concerning the different kinds of death, to which this especially favors, that the fire of Gehenna properly looks to that atrocious death in the valley of Hinnom rather than to the burning which was decreed in place of a punishment. Others, however, derive this third degree of capital punishment also from the sanhedrin, and repeat the preceding words ἀπὸ κοινοῦ: ἔνοχος ἔσται τῷ συνεδρίῳ εἰς τὴν γέενναν τοῦ πυρὸς: to which adds Mr. Winstrupius, along with Spanheim and others, teaching that the fire of Gehenna properly signifies nothing else in this place than שרפה, the burning alive, by which those to be burned were not cremated on a lit pyre, but were killed by molten metal poured into the mouth; to which opinion these things favor: (1.) That the discourse here is about punishments assigned in judgment, such as that roasting between the glowing arms of the statue of Moloch was not. Which was neither a punishment, nor was it decreed in Jewish courts: But it was a profane and idolatrous custom assumed by the Jews through κακοζηλίαν. (2.) That the most severe of punishments among the Jews was not stoning, but burning. To which point the observation of the blessed Glassius from Schikardus contributes, which he adduced in his treatise on royal law, chapter IV, from the Talmud: Besides beheading or the sword (by which alone it was permitted to the King to punish delinquents), the Sanhedrin had three kinds of punishments: strangulation, stoning, and burning. Those to be burned were not cremated on a lit pyre, as a witch is with us, but were killed by molten metal poured into the mouth, even in a foul swamp. These 4 types of punishments are usually otherwise enumerated in this order by the Hebrews: 1. הרג or הרג כסיף, the killing of the sword, or beheading. 2. חנק, strangulation. 3. סקילה, stoning, and 4. שרפה, burning: which four kinds of punishments are said to have been handed down לבית to the house of judgment. (3.) To this pertains what the blessed Chemnitius observes on p. 563: in the judicial system, certain punishments were determined and defined for certain offenses, as in the case of homicide; but in the councils, deliberations were held regarding the imposition of more severe and atrocious punishments according to the quality and enormity of the offenses. Gehenna, however, was a punishment in that polity joined with eternal abomination. For mention is made of Gehenna even among the degrees of political punishments. For the corpses of those who had been put to death on account of crimes were for the most part buried, as were those of Christ and Stephen, but the atrocity and abomination of the crime could be so great that even criminals were killed in the abominable place of Tophet, Jer. VII. 32, or their corpses were cast into that infamous place, either without burial or buried in a way peculiar to themselves. Such corpses, however, were cast or buried in the valley of the sons of Hinnom. For that place was in the lot of the tribe of Benjamin, Jos. XV. 8. § XIX. 16. On account of the immense idolatry which was practiced there by the burning of little children by fire in honor of Moloch, 2 Chron. 28:3, it had been rendered defiled, infamous, and abominable by King Josiah, and was called Tophet, 2 Kings 23:10, so that corpses and those things which were an utter abomination were cast out of Jerusalem into that place. And Jer. ch. 7:31, 32 and 19:6, 11, 12, 13, God himself describes his most atrocious punishments in this valley, saying: It shall no more be called the valley of slaughter, and they shall bury in Tophet, because there is no place, etc. Nor is there any doubt, according to Spanheim, Dub. 139, p. 802, that even those who were condemned to the fire in Jerusalem were burned in the valley of Hinnom, whence to be liable to the fire of Gehenna is, by the same author, to be liable to the fire kindled in the valley of Hinnom. (4.) B. Glassius observes that nothing more fitting could be brought forward by wisdom than that those who prevaricate with mouth and tongue are worthy of having molten metal poured into their mouths in return.

Moreover, the interpretation of Christ’s words by the Papists, whose cause this advocate willingly pleaded, may deservedly be opposed as a ψευδερμηνεία. For he acknowledges that different degrees of infernal punishment are designated by the similitude of different deaths, which were known to the people to differ in the magnitude of their torments. Bellarminus against the idea that a sin is given as venial by its own nature, twists these words of Christ, l. 1. de amiss. grat. & stat. pecc. c. IX. into his own mind: manifest abuse, in the judgment of Christ, makes one liable to the fire of Gehenna, and through this it is a mortal sin: Anger expressed by the sound of the voice, but not reaching the evil of abuse, makes one liable to the council, i.e., it is not certain whether it deserves Gehenna, but it is worthy of either that punishment or a lesser one. There are found, therefore, certain sins which are too light to deserve the fire of Gehenna. Yet Christ teaches that not only manifest abuse, but also anger expressed by the sound of the voice or by gesture, and rash anger itself, even if it does not break out externally, are homicides and make a man liable to eternal punishment by their own nature, even if He establishes degrees of eternal punishment under the likeness of different deaths. Therefore, by τὴν γεένναν τοῦ πυρὸς in these words, hellfire is not signified literally, but the punishment of death used among the Jews in the valley of Hinnom as the most grave and atrocious, although there should be no doubt that Christ wished to shadow forth by the same the most grave punishment in the other world. For it is gathered from the consequences that the sentiment of Christ tends to this, namely in verses 25 and 26, as also 30, where by the word Gehenna, hell itself is expressly signified. Since, therefore, the Scribes and Pharisees believed that in the fifth commandment only the external act of homicide was prohibited, and as for that alone a capital punishment was dictated in the judgment of the small sanhedrin, so they thought that in the divine judgment the liability to punishment in the other world was contracted by that alone: Christ, on the contrary, defines that besides external homicide, other homicides are comprehended and prohibited by the law of the fifth commandment; such as rash anger contained within, anger breaking out into injury or external contempt of a neighbor, and anger breaking out into grave abuse, and that the liability of all those before God is such that they all deserve the eternal punishment of the other world, only under different degrees of eternal punishment: just as there were different degrees of death, beheading in the small sanhedrin, stoning which was accustomed to be dictated in the great sanhedrin, and the fire of Gehenna. - Petitus observes that it is not said as in the preceding ἔνοχος ἔσται τῇ γεέννᾳ τοῦ πυρὸς, but with the manner of speaking changed ἔνοχος ἔσται εἰς τὴν γεένναν τοῦ πυρὸς, and from the words of David Kimchi on Ps. XXVII he gathers that these unburied corpses were cast into the valley of Hinnom at Jerusalem: then, when the corpses had rotted, their bones were burned by the fire which burned perpetually for this purpose in this valley. Whence we think it came about from this perpetual fire of the valley of Hinnom that Gehenna is called hell, in which there is perpetual fire, and not, as the learned wish, from the Topheth of that valley, where they burned children to Moloch. Hence, therefore, the words of Christ must be explained, ἔνοχος ἔσται εἰς τὴν γεένναν τοῦ πυρὸς, that is, he ought to be condemned εἰς τὴν γεένναν, just as it is said among Greek writers, εἰς κόρακας, among the Latins, ad Gemonias scalas, and if there are any such: he ought to be cast unburied into Gehenna, or the valley of Hinnom, which is by far the most grave and ignominious of all, and is most infamous, added to the capital punishment. Which opinion we leave in its place. The sense, therefore, is that such a distinction as was found among the Jews between being liable to judgment, council, and the fire of Gehenna, is found in the divine tribunal between these three kinds of homicides: which Vincent Regius the Jesuit acknowledges, part. II. diluc. Evang. l. IV. c.
