XXII. And this is the name by which Origen praises the exceptional purity of the Hebrew law: Θαυμαστὸν δὲ καὶ τὸ τῶν νεῶν ὑπεκκαύματα τὰς ἑταίρας ἀναιρεῖσθαι ἀπὸ τῆς πολιτείας ἀυτῶν. And Philo, whose passage on this matter regarding the life of Joseph is remarkable: Τοῖς δ' ἄλλοις ἐφεῖται μετὰ τὴν τεσσαρεσκαιδεκάτην ἡλικίαν πόρναις καὶ χαμαιτύποις καὶ ταῖς ὅσαι μισθαρνοῦσι ἐπὶ τῷ σώματι μετὰ πολλὰς ἀδείας χρῆσθαι· παρ' ἡμῖν δὲ κδ' ἑταίρα ἔξεστιν ἀλλὰ κατὰ τῆς ἑταιρευσης ὥρισαι δίκη θανάτου· πρὸ δὲ συνόδων νομίμων ὁμιλίαν ἑτέρας γυναικὸς οὐκ ἴσμεν, ἀλλ' ἁγνοὶ γάμων ἁγναῖς παρθένοις προσερχόμεθα, προτεθεικότες τέλΘ· οὐχ ἡδονὴν ἀλλὰ γνησίων παίδων σποράν. Nevertheless, the propriety of the word seems rather to be preserved, which is accustomed to distinguish μοιχεία from πορνεία, as appears below XV. 19, Gal. V. 19, Hebr. XIII. 4, just as the Hebrews also distinguish נאף and זנה, as can be seen in Hosea IV. 14. because not all offenses are included in the Decalogue, not even those which are punished by civil law, but only those which in any kind have the highest atrocity: for there is no mention of wounding, but of homicide, nor of every gain with the loss of another, but of theft, nor of every perfidy, but of false testimony. Added to this is that not a few of the Jews interpreted the law concerning harlotry in such a way that they judged that way of life forbidden to Hebrew girls, but not prohibited so that foreign women living among the people, but alien to Judaism, were allowed to make gain with their bodies: indeed, they even consider that the first intercourse with those captured in war was held with impunity, and that what is said about it in the law is to be understood of her who is retained for the sake of intercourse: nor did they think the law was set for the male sex, surely, as it is in the comedy, that it is no disgrace for a young man to visit a harlot, even according to the opinion of Cato: For as soon as dire lust has inflamed the loins, it is right for young men to descend hither. Since this opinion had prevailed even with customs [for we also read that women of that trade stood for judgment before Solomon], it happened from that that זונה, which signifies a foreign woman, was usurped to denote a harlot, as Prov. V. 3. Thus

And by the old Attic law, which we have said was derived from the Hebrew, it was permitted to no Attic citizen to prostitute himself: and if anyone had defiled an Attic virgin, he was compelled to marry her, as the Comedies also teach us. Nor, however, were harlots lacking, whom for that reason they called ξένας, just as the Hebrews did: which Terence also followed when he called the Andrian a foreigner. But what we have already said about other matters must be repeated here as well, that this laxity of the Jews in flattering themselves was not entirely to be excused. For it could be sufficiently clear to them that many things do not please God which nevertheless were outside the punishment of the laws. God had instituted marriage for the sake of seeking children and educating them honestly. Concubinage could not but conflict with that institution, which both keeps one from marriage and by its nature causes that either the offspring is of uncertain father, or certainly is not educated as is fitting with the common zeal of parents. For it appears that the cause of the prohibition was the very shamefulness of the act. Deservedly, therefore, the Apostle Paul reports that that slaughter of so many thousands, of which mention is made in Num. XXV, happened because of the crime of πορνείας, 1 Cor. X. 8, judging that this even alone, even if the worship of false gods had not been added, was a merit sufficiently worthy of that punishment. Nor indeed ought the Jews, aided by the law, to have been ignorant of what reason alone and right instruction had taught many among the Gentiles. Job proclaims his abstinence not only from married women, but from unmarried ones. Epictetus commands to καθαρεύειν τῶν ἀφροδισίων πρὶν τῶ γάμε, and Dion Chrysostom proves the same with several arguments. But especially excellent are those words of Musonius: ὅσαι συμπλοκαὶ μοιχείας ἐκτὸς ὖσαι πρὸς θηλείας ἐῖσιν, ἐστερημέναι τῶ γίνεσθαι κατὰ νόμον, καὶ ἀνται πᾶσαι αἰσχραὶ. For they are done out of intemperance, as one would not endure to approach a harlot with temperance, nor a free woman without marriage, nor indeed by his own handmaid. For that which is not lawful is neither becoming in these unions, but is a great shame and disgrace to those who pursue them. Porphyry, On Abstinence from Animal Food IV: ἐπεὶ κδ' ἑταίραις ὁμιλεῖν ἀπα- γορεύει τοῖς πολλοῖς (namely, the political law), but also considers the act of intercourse with harlots to be a reproach to such men and the intercourse with them shameful. This natural suggestion stood in the way of wandering Venus breaking through the barriers with one assault or even without distinction of modesty. For it is not unworthy of memory what Chrysippus has recorded about this matter: πρῶτον μὲν ἔξω πόλεως κἀι προσω- πεῖα περικείμεναι αἱ ἑταῖραι ἐξεμίσθεν ἑαυτάς τοῖν βυλομέ- νοις' ὑσ' ὕσερον καταφρονήσασαι ἀπέθεντο τὰ προσωπεῖα, κἀμὐπὸ τῶν νόμων μὴ ἐπιτρεπόμεναι ἐἰσιέναι ἐἰς τας πόλεις, ἔξω ἦσαν ἀυτῶν: which words I record the more willingly, because what he says, that in antiquity harlots did not prostitute themselves in cities but in the country (traces of which custom have been found even among the Peruvians and Tartars themselves) and not with an open but with a covered face, appears to be most true from the narrative of Moses himself, Gen. XXXIIX. 14. Among the Romans, whoever had defiled a free-born virgin was visited with capital punishment. Nor was a harlot's life permitted unless to those who had professed that life, who, as Tacitus says, were thought to be sufficiently tormented by the shame itself. Wherefore, as to what the Hebrews note regarding the history of Judah and Tamar, that the use of a harlot was permitted before the law, it can be conceded if the question is about impunity; not so if it is a question of that which could be done without shame. And indeed, Rabbi Johannes Maimonides, who is mentioned, even judged the first encounter with a captive in war to be illicit. But Gerundensis and others think it was rather dissembled than approved. In the book which is inscribed The Constitutions of Clement, an Apostolic decree is reported which exists in Acts XV in these words: ἐπιστεῖλαι ἀυτοῖς τῶ ἀπέχεσθαι ἀπὸ τῶν ἀλισγημάτων τῶν ἐθνῶν, ἐι- δωλοθύτω κὴ αἵματος κἀι πνικτῶ καὶ πορνέιας, ἅπερ κὴ τοῖς πάλαι τενομοθέτητο τοῖς πρὸς τῶ νόμω φυσικοῖς Ἐνῶς, Ἐνὼχ, Νῶε, Μελχισεδέκ, Ἰὼβ καὶ εἴτις τοιστ@ ἐγεγόνει. Add what will be said below XV. 19.

Grotius testifies that he agrees with the Hebrews, most of whom explain the divine law לֹא תִנְאַף as concerning concubinage with a married woman; because the propriety of the word seems to be preserved, which is accustomed to distinguish μοιχείαν from πορνείας, Matt. XV. 19, Gal. V. 19, Heb. XIII. 4, and because in the Decalogue not all offenses, not even those which are punished by civil law, are included, but only those which in each kind have the highest atrocity.

Thus, having abandoned Christ's explanation, Grotius follows not only the more recent Hebrews, but the Scribes and Pharisees, whom Christ refuted. For they understood the law as concerning only external adulteries. But although the words 8. μοιχεύσεις, as they are brought forward here from the mind of the Pharisees and Scribes, are taken according to the propriety of the word as concerning adultery, yet that not only adultery properly so called, and that external, was prohibited in the Decalogue, the vindications of the Mosaic precept against Pharisaic corruptions teach, which were instituted here by Christ; who defines not only external fornication but any carnal lust, even that which is by look alone, as adultery, and that it is prohibited under the interdict of adultery. Moreover, the word נאף is used by Moses, which is otherwise distinguished from זנה, which denotes fornication generally, or that of an unmarried person with an unmarried person, Jer. III. 9, Hos. IV. 3. distinguished, by synecdoche of the species, or rather by ἔκτασιν, so that it may be taught that whatever is committed against chastity out of lust is held as adultery before God, whether it is contained in the mind, or is brought forth by gesture or words, or is committed by an external act: whether regarding persons living in marriage, or regarding the unmarried. And thus the word is taken generally for fornication, Job XXIV. 15, and fornication is prohibited and disapproved in the O.T. both elsewhere and in the law itself, Lev. XIX. 29, ch. XXI. 7, Deut. XXII. 20, 21, XXIII. 2, 12, 13, 17, 18, Ez. XVI. 15, and indeed also the lustful look at another's wife, Job XXXI. 9, Prov. VI. 24, ch. XXIII. 33, Jer. V. 8, Ez. VI. 9, XXIII. 6, which is also interdicted in the Decalogue by the precept concerning not coveting, Ex. XX. 17, Deut. V. 21. confirms. The Pharisaical opinion of Grotius is therefore to be rejected, that not all offenses are included in the Decalogue, but only those which have the highest atrocity in each category: since the Decalogue is a perfect rule of every virtue and vice and sin. And Grotius himself acknowledges that it is not a new thing that μοιχείαv is spoken of, which would properly be called πορνεία, and that πορνείαv had been forbidden among the Jewish people up to that point, because girls were not permitted to lead a harlot's life, and he who had defiled an unmarried woman was compelled to marry her, or if the parents were unwilling, to provide a dowry, and she who had married with a defiled body, or who, while she was betrothed to another, had submitted herself to someone else, underwent the penalty of stoning. Deut. XXII. and for that reason he judged that Origen and Philo had judged the purity of the Hebrew law to be exceptional: nor does he deny that Aben-Ezra thought the word נאף in the law should be extended to all non-conjugal venery. Furthermore, since Grotius admits that such intercourse cannot but conflict with the institution and law of marriage, which God wished to fortify with this hedge of the sixth commandment in the Decalogue, which is both excluded from marriage and by its own nature causes either the offspring to be of uncertain father, or certainly not to be educated with the common care of parents as is proper: if indeed God instituted marriage for the sake of seeking and honestly educating children: and since he concedes that reason alone, and right instruction among the nations, prohibits fornication, how much more then is it to be believed that it is prohibited in the Decalogue? He alleges Job for this matter, whom he rashly assumes to have been devoid of divine laws: he alleges Epictetus, Dio Chrysostom, Musonius, Porphyry, and he praises the natural suggestion itself, by which who would call the Decalogue more imperfect? Job proclaims his abstinence not only from married women but also from unmarried ones, Epictetus commands καθαρεύειν τ̃ ἀφροδισίων πρὶν ἤ γάμɤ, and Dio Chrysostom proves the same with several arguments, etc. Among the Romans, whoever had defiled a free-born virgin was subjected to capital punishment. Nor was a harlot's life permitted except to those who had professed that life: which laws they thought, as Tacitus says, were sufficiently punished by the shame itself. Since these things are so, is it not the greatest injury to God the legislator, and to the Decalogue written by the hand of God himself, in that Decalogue, that mirror of virtues and vices, that most lucid image of divine holiness, that he contends such things, from which reason shrinks, and which it is agreed are base and vicious by natural suggestion itself, were not forbidden, after the manner of the Pharisees and Scribes? Is it not to be wondered at in a man who is very learned, and to be detested in a jurist, nay, a Christian Biblical commentator, that he should so adhere to that Pharisaic corruption that he almost casts his vote for those profane and most base opinions of the Jews as well; that for Hebrew girls prostitution was indeed forbidden, but not prohibited by divine law, so that foreign women living among the people, but alien to Judaism, were allowed to make gain of their bodies, and indeed that even when captured in war the first intercourse was had with impunity, and no law was laid down for the male sex; surely, as it is in the comedy, it is not (according to divine law) a disgrace for a young man to fornicate, and according to the opinion of Cato, For as soon as dire lust has swollen the veins, it is right for youths to descend hither. Which opinion he finally says has even prevailed in customs, and he is so far from declaring it contrary to the decalogue that he does not even think it was prohibited anywhere by any penal law of God: but he refers all these things among those which were outside the penalty of the laws, and at least he does not think this laziness of the Jews, flattering themselves, is entirely excusable. Behold a distinguished interpreter of divine laws and of the entire sacred code!

Latin:

Vers. 27. ὁ μοιχεύσεις) לא תנאף quod Hebræi ple- rique explicant de concubitu cum fœmina nupta, de quo agitur Deut. XXII. 22. Aben Ezra putat latius protenden- dam significationem ad omnem Venerem non conjuga- lem. Et sane sicut πορνεία interdum μοιχείαν significat, ut in- fra v. 32. c. XIX. 19. ita novum non est μοιχείαν dici quæ πορνεία proprie diceretur. Ita Danaen Juppiter dicitur μοι- χεῦσαι apud Lucianum, & Ovidius Medeam vocat adulte- ram virginem. Fuit autem in Judaico populo etiam πορ- νεία hactenus vetita, quod neque meretriciam vitam age- re puellæ permittebantur, & qui innuptam stupraverat, du- cere eam, aut si parentes nollent dotare cogebatur, & quæ polluto corpore nupserat, aut sponsa cum esset, alteri se subtraxerat, lapidationis pœnam subibat, quæ omnia vide- re est Deut. XXII. Et hoc est quo nomine legis Hebraicæ puritatem eximiam prædicat Origenes: Θαυμαστὸν δὲ καὶ τὸ τῶν νεῶν ὑπεκκαύματα τὰς ἑταίρας ἀναιρεῖσθαι ἀπὸ τῆς πολι- τείας ἀυτῶν. Et Philo, cujus ad hanc rem insignis est locus de vita Josephi: Τοῖς δ' ἄλλοις ἐφεῖται μετὰ τὴν τεσσαρεσκαι- δεκάτην ἡλικίαν πόρναις καὶ χαμαιτύποις καὶ ταῖς ὅσαι μισθαρνοῦσι ἐπὶ τῷ σώματι μετὰ πολλὰς ἀδείας χρῆσθαι· παρ' ἡμῖν δὲ κδ' ἑ- ταίρα ἔξεστιν ἀλλὰ κατὰ τῆς ἑταιρευσης ὥρισαι δίκη θανάτου· πρὸ δὲ συνόδων νομίμων ὁμιλίαν ἑτέρας γυναικὸς οὐκ ἴσμεν, ἀλλ' ἁγνοὶ γάμων ἁγναῖς παρθένοις προσερχόμεθα, προτεθεικότες τέλΘ· οὐχ ἡδονὴν ἀλλὰ γνησίων παίδων σποράν. Veruntamen servanda potius videtur vocis proprietas, quæ solet μοιχεί- av ἀπὸ τῆς πορνείας discernere, ut apparet infra XV. 19. Gal. V. 19. Hebr. XIII. 4. quomodo & Hebræi discernunt נאף & זנה, ut videre est Osee IV. 14. quia in Decalogo non omnia delicta, ne ea quidem quæ lege civili puniuntur, comprehensa sunt, sed ea duntaxat quæ in quoquo genere summam habent atrocitatem: neque enim vulnerationis sit mentio, sed homicidii, neque omnis lucri cum jactura alterius, sed furti, neque omnis perfidiæ, sed falsi testimonii. Accedit huc quod Judæorum haud pauci ita legem de meretricatu interpretabantur, ut censerent id vitæ genus puellis Hebræis interdictum, non etiam vetitum, ne peregrinæ in populo habitantes, sed à Judaismo alienæ, qæstum eorpore facere sinerentur: imo & cum bello ca- ptæ primum concubitum censent impune habitum, & quæ de eo in lege dicuntur intelligenda de ea quæ concubitus causa retineatur: neque vero virili sexui legem positam existimabant, nimirum, ut in comœdia est, non esse flagitium scortari hominem adolescentulum, ex Catonis etiam sententia: Nam simul ac senas inflavit dira libido Huc juvenes æquum est descendere. Hæc opinio cum moribus etiam invaluisset [nam & coram Salomone judicio se stitisse ejus quæstus feminas legimus] factum inde est ut זונה quod peregrinam significat, ad meretricem denotandum usurparetur, ut Prov. V. 3. Sic

& veteri jure Attico, quod ex Hebræo derivatum diximus, nulli civi Atticæ proftare licebat: & si quis virginem Atti- cam viciasset, ducere eam cogebatur, ut Comœdiæ et- iam nos docent. Neque tamen meretrices deerant, quas propterea similiter, ut Hebræi, appellabant ξένας: quod secutus est & Terentius, cum peregrinam Andriam dixit. Sed quod de aliis rebus jam ante diximus, etiam hic re- petendum est, non omnino fuisse excusandam hanc Ju- dæorum sibi blandientium supinitatem. Satis enim con- stare ipsis poterat, multa Deo non placere, quæ tamen erant extra legum pœnam. Instituerat Deus nuptias, liberûm quærendùm & honeste educandûm gratia. Non poterat cum eo instituto non pugnare concubitus, qui & à matrimonio arcet, & sui natura efficit, ut aut proles incerti sit patris, aut certe non ita uti par est communi parentum studio educetur. Apparet enim causam ve- tandi fuisse ipsam facti turpitudinem. Merito igitur A- postolus Paulus stragem illam tot millium, cujus mentio est Num. XXV. evenisse refert ob crimen πορνείας, 1. Cor. X. 8. scilicet id vel solum, etiamsi falsorum Deorum cul- tus non accessisset, satis dignum eo supplicio meritum existimans. Neque sane debebant Judæi lege adjuti ne- scire quod multos in gentibus sola ratio ac recta insti- tutio docuerat. Job suam non à nuptis tantum, sed ab innuptis abstinentiam prædicat. Epictetus jubet καθα- ρεύειν τῶν ἀφροδισίων πρὶν τῶ γάμε, idemque aliquot ar- gumentis probat Dion Chrysostomus. Sed imprimis præclara sunt ista Musonii: ὅσαι συμπλοκαὶ μοιχείας ἐκτὸς ὖσαι πρὸς θηλείας ἐῖσιν, ἐστερημέναι τῶ γίνεσθαι κατὰ νόμον, καὶ ἀνται πᾶσαι αἰσχραὶ. Πράττονται γὰρ δι' ἀκολασίαν, ὡς μετάγε σωφροσύνης ἐκ ἄν ἑταίρᾳ πλησιάζειν ὑπομείνειε τις ὔτ' ἄν ἐλευθέρᾳ γάμε χωρὶς, ὔτε μὰ διὰ θεραπαίνη τῇ ἑαυτῶ. Τὸ γὰρ μὴ νόμιμον μήτ' εὐπρεπὲς τῶν συνουσιῶν τετων, αἶσχος δὲ κὴ ὄνειδος μέγα τοῖς θηρωμένοις ἀυτὰς. Porphyrius de non esu animantium IV. ἐπεὶ κδ' ἑταίραις ὁμιλεῖν ἀπα- γορεύει τοῖς πολλοῖς (neinpe ὁ νόμος ὁ πολιτικὸς) ἀλλὰ κὰι πραττόμενον τοῖς ἑταίρας τὸ μίσωμα ἐπονειδισον ἡγεῖται τοῖς τετοίοις ἀνδράσι καὶ αἰσχρὰν τὴν πρὸς τάυτας ὁμιλίαν. Hæc naturalis suggestio obstitit quo minus vaga Venus u- no impetu aut etiam sine discrimine pudoris septa perrum- peret. Est enim memoria non indignum quod ea de re Chrysippus prodidit: πρῶτον μὲν ἔξω πόλεως κἀι προσω- πεῖα περικείμεναι αἱ ἑταῖραι ἐξεμίσθεν ἑαυτάς τοῖν βυλομέ- νοις' ὑσ' ὕσερον καταφρονήσασαι ἀπέθεντο τὰ προσωπεῖα, κἀμὐπὸ τῶν νόμων μὴ ἐπιτρεπόμεναι ἐἰσιέναι ἐἰς τας πόλεις, ἔξω ἦσαν ἀυτῶν: quæ verba eo libentius refero, quia quod dicit antiquitus meretrices non in urbibus sed in agro (moris cujus vestigia etiam apud ipsos Peruanos & Tartaros reperta sunt) neque aperto sed obtecto vultu prostitisse verissimum esse ex ipsius Mosis narratione ap- paret, Gen. XXXIIX. 14. Apud Romanos qui virgi- nem ingenuam struprasset pœna capitali afficiebatur. Ne- que meretricia vita permittebatur nisi eam vitam profes- sis, quas leges existimabant, ut inquit Tacitus, satis ipso pudore cruciari. Quare quod ad Judæ ac Thamaris historiam Hebræi notant, scorti usum ante legem permis- sum fuisse, concedi potest si de impunitate est quæstio; non item si de eo agitur quod sine turpitudine fieri po- tuit. Atque adeo etiam primum cum bello capta con- gressum illicitum censuit Rabbinus Johannes Maimoni- dæ memoratus. Gerundensis vero & alii censent, dissi- mulatum magis quam probatum. In libro qui inscribi- tur Constitutiones Clementis refertur decretum Aposto- licum quod exstat Actor. XV. hisce verbis: ἐπιστεῖλαι ἀυτοῖς τῶ ἀπέχεσθαι ἀπὸ τῶν ἀλισγημάτων τῶν ἐθνῶν, ἐι- δωλοθύτω κὴ αἵματος κἀι πνικτῶ καὶ πορνέιας, ἅπερ κὴ τοῖς πάλαι τενομοθέτητο τοῖς πρὸς τῶ νόμω φυσικοῖς Ἐνῶς, Ἐνὼχ, Νῶε, Μελχισεδέκ, Ἰὼβ καὶ εἴτις τοιστ@ ἐγεγόνει, Adde quæ dicentur infra XV. 19.

Facere sese testatur Grotius cum Hebræis, quo- rum plerosque de concubitu cum fœmina nupta legem divinam לֹא תִנְאַף explicent; quod servanda vi- deatur vocis proprietas, quæ solet μοιχείαν ἀπὸ τῆς πορνέιας discernere Matth. XV. 19, Gal. V. 19. Ebr. XIII. 4. quodque in Decalogo non omnia delicta, ne ea quidem quæ lege civili puniuntur, comprehensa sint, sed ea duntaxat, quæ in quoque genere summam habent atrocitatem.

Ita relicta Christi explicatione sequitur Grotius non Ebræos tantum recentiores, sed Scribas & Pharisæos, quos Christus refutavit. Hi enim sic accipiebant legem de solis adulteriis externis. At li- cet verba 8. μοιχεύσεις uti hic è mente Pharifæo- rum, & Scribarum adducuntur, secundum vocis proprietatem de adulterio accipiantur, non tamen in Decalogo solum adulterium prohibitum fuisse proprie ita dictum, idque externum, vindiciæ præ- cepti Mosaici à corruptelis Pharisæicis edocent, à Christo hic institutæ; qui non modo scortationem externam sed quamcunque libidinem carnalem et- iam eam, quæ aspectu solo sit, facit adulterium, ac sub interdicto adulterii prohibitam esse, defi- nit. Adhibetur autem à Mose verbum נאף, quod alias à זנה, scortationem generaliter, vel so- luti cum soluta,notante Jer. III.9. Os. IV.3. distin- guitur,per synecdochen speciei,vel potius per ἔκτα- σιν, ut doceatur,pro adulteris haberi coram Deo, quæcunque ex libidine contra castitatem designantur, seu animo contineantur, seu gestu, aut verbis sese proferant,seu opere externo committantur: seu quoad personas in matrimonio viventes, seu quoad solutas.Et accipitur ita verbum illud generaliter de scortatione Job. XXIV.15. ac prohibetur,atq; impro- batur in V.T. tum alias, tum in lege ipsa scortatio Lev.XIX.29. c. XXI.7. Deut. XXII. 20. 21. XXIII. 2. 12.13.17.18.Ez.XVI.15.imo & alienæ mulieris libidino- sus aspectus Job.XXXI.9. Prov. VI.24. c. XXIII.33. Jer. V. 8. Ez.VI.9. XXIII.6. quem decalogo quoq; interdictum esse, præceptum de non concupiscendo Ex.XX. 17.Deut.V.21. confirmat.Reprobanda itaq; Pharisaica Grotii opinio, quod in Decalogo non o- mnia delicta,sed ea tantum,quæ in quoque genere sum- mam habent atrocitatem comprehensa: quum deca- logus regula perfecta sit omnis virtutis & vitii ac peccati. Et agnoscit Grotius ipse novum non esse, μοιχείαv dici, quæ proprie πορνεία diceretur, ac fuisse in Judaico populo etiam πορνείαv hactenus vetitam, quod neque meretriciam vitam agere puellæ permitte- batur, & qui innuptam stupraverat ducere eam, aut si parentes nollent, dotare cogebatur, & quæ polluto corpore nupserat, aut sponsa cum esset alteri se sub- straxerat, lapidationis pœnam subibat. Deut. XXII. eoque nomine legis Hebraicæ puritatem eximiam judi- caffe Origenem & Philonem: neq; diffitetur Aben- Ezram vocem נאף in lege ad omnem venerem non conjugalem protendendam putasse. Accedit, quod cum instituto & lege conjugii, quam Deus hoc sepi- mento sexti præcepti in Decalogo munire voluit, talem concubitum non posse non pugnare largiatur Grotius, qui & à matrimonio arcetur, & sua natura efficit, ut aut proles incerti sit patris, aut certe non ita, uti par est,communi parentum studio educetur: siqui- dem nuptias instituerit Deus liberûm quærendûm & honeste educandûm gratia: quodque concedat so- lam rationem, ac rectam in gentibus institutionem scortationem prohibere, quanto ergo magis eam prohibitam in Decalogo esse credendum? Al- legat eam in rem Jobum, quem tamen expertem fuisse divinarum legum, temere assumit: alle- gat Epictetum, Dionem Chrysostomum, Musonium, Porphyrium ipsamque laudat naturalem suggestio- nem, qua imperfectiorem ecquis dicet decalo- gum? Job suam non à nuptis tantum sed & ab in- nuptis abstinentiam prædicat, Epictetus jubet καθα- ρεύειν τ̃ ἀφροδισίων πρὶν ἤ γάμɤ, idemque aliquot argumentis probat Dion Chrysostomus, &c. Apud Romanos qui virginem ingenuam stupraffet pœna ca- pitali afficiebatur.Neque meretricia vita permitteba- tur nisi eam vitam professis: quas leges existimabant, ut inquit Tacitus, satis ipso pudore cruciari. Quæ quum ita se habeant, annon summa in Deum le- gislatorem, & Decalogum Dei ipsius manu ex- aratum injuria in decalogo virtutum vitiorum- que speculo illo lucidissimo, divinæque sanctitatis imagine excellentissima talia, à quibus ratio ab- horret, quæque ipsa naturali suggestione turpia & vitiosa esse constat, haud interdicta fuisse, ad Pha- risæorum & Scribarum instar, contendit? Annon mirandum in viro longe doctissimo, & detestan- dum in JCto, imo commentatore Biblico Chri- stiano, quod adeo Pharisaicæ illi corruptelæ ad- hæreat, ut propemodum illis etiam Judæorum profanis, & turpissimis sententiis calculum adji- ciat; Ebræis quidem puellis meretricatum interdi- ctum, non autem vetitum lege divina fuisse, ne pere- grinæ in populo habitantes, sed à Judaismo alienæ, quræstum corpore facere sinerentur, imo & cum bello ca- ptæ primum concubitum impunè habitum, neque virili sexui legem positam; nimirum ut in comœdia est non esse (secundum legem divinam) flagitium scortari ho- minem adolescentulum, & ex Catonis sententia, Nam simul ac venas inflavit dira libido Huc juvenes æquum est descendere. Quam opinionem denique etiam moribus invaluiffe ait ac tantum abest ut decalogo eam adversam sta- tuat, ut ne quidem uspiam lege aliqua pœnali prohibitam à Deo censeat: sed hæc omnia inter ea referat, quæ fuerint extra legum pœnam ac saltim non omnino excusandam putet hanc Judæorum sibi blandientium supinitatem. Hem præclarum le- gum divinarum, totiusque sacri codicis interpre- tem!

## 5:28
Vers. 28. ὅτι πᾶς ὁ βλέπων] Because, to be sure, eyes are the leaders in love, as he says, or as Plato speaks ἀρχὴ τῶ ἐρω- τῶ ὄρασις: In another it is: ἡ ἐπιθυμία διὰ τῶν ὀφθαλ- μῶν ἕρχεται: which very thing Plutarch follows in Symposiacon III. 6, following Plato. Salvianus well said that the windows are in a way the light of our minds, and that all desires enter into the heart through the eyes, as if through natural tunnels. Hence eyes full of adultery at 2 Pet. II. 14.

γυναῖκα] It can be taken of any woman, so that what follows μοιχᾶται is taken more loosely: and thus the prelude to τῆς πορνείας is also forbidden here. It is simpler, however, that we understand γυναῖκα as τὴν γαμετὴν, in which way that word is often taken, as also the Latin mulieris, not because Christ does not also vehemently disapprove of τὴν πορνείαν, since it is also forbidden among the Jews themselves, but because he preferred to remain within the same kind of sinning between the same persons, so that the comparison of internal and external acts would be clearer.

Christ vehemently disapproves of τὴν πορνείαν, and he holds that not only is an immodest look a prelude to it, but he teaches that it is μοιχεία, which is clear from these vindications of the sixth commandment; how then in this proper place, when he explains by design in what ways fornication is committed, shall we think that he speaks only restrictively of a lustful look at τῆς γαμετῆς, and not truly of any woman whatsoever? The reasoning of Grotius rests upon a ψευδερμηνεία of the preceding words, as if, forsooth, Christ indicated that only the external act of fornication was prohibited by the law of the decalogue: whereas on the contrary Christ does not bring forward the divine law of the decalogue, handed down and understood according to the mind of the legislator, but marks with a black coal the Pharisaic depravation of the same, and vindicates the mind of the law. Which has been shown elsewhere against the Socinians, whom Grotius here assists. Rightly Lactantius l. VI. c. 73. God commands that not only adultery is to be avoided, but also the thought, lest anyone look upon another's wife and desire her in his mind. And nature itself in a way dictated this to healthy nations. Whence Quintilian the Father: You have looked upon another's matron otherwise than the laws permit. And Seneca the Father, it is incest even without defilement, which desires defilement. But Grotius also tries to corrupt the vindications of Christ, when he says that ἐπιθυμῆσαι here is to be explained as to solicit: although he himself observed that it is taken by the Fathers, Justin, Clement, Athenagoras, concerning lust alone and ἀναθυμιάσει τῆς ὀρέξεως, nor could he deny his vote to that interpretation. For thus he himself to the words

Πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτῆς] This is properly what Job XXXI. 4 says, if the mind has followed the eyes. Later Hebrews call it זן עינים והערוך to feed the eyes with an illicit spectacle: ὁρᾶν ἀκολάστως Chrysostom VIII. on Romans. It appears therefore that he is marked here by Christ who, enslaving his mind to impure love, fosters his wound by looking. Salvianus says that the wanton gazes of unchaste men are marked here. Tertullian on the veiling of virgins: A Christian sees a woman with safe eyes, he is blind in his mind toward lust. Quintilian the Father: You have looked upon another's matron otherwise than the laws permit. Lactantius book VI. c. 23. God commands that not only adultery is to be avoided, but also the thought, lest anyone look upon another's wife, and desire her in his mind. Although however τὸ ἐπιθυ- μεῖν is accustomed to be taken also in a good sense, here nevertheless, as in many other places, it is placed in a vice, as to desire in Afranius: The wise man will love, the others will desire. Justin explains τὸ ἐπιθυμεῖν as τῆς ὀρέξεως ἀναθυμίασιν. Clement a little more subtly: if anyone looks at the beauty of a body, the Word says, and the flesh seems beautiful to him according to desire, having looked carnally and sinfully, he who has admired is judged. Athenagoras: We are so far from being indifferent that it is not permitted for us even to look for the sake of desire. And ἐπιθυμῆσαι could be interpreted here as to solicit, in which way the Hebrew חמד is also accustomed to be taken. Thus in Canon IV of the Synod of Neocaesarea if anyone proposes to desire a woman, to sleep with her.

He has already committed adultery with her in his heart. Men, who cannot judge the mind except from outward signs, impose the name of the crime upon the final act. And yet the jurists themselves admit that the mind distinguishes crimes. Therefore, if a weapon escapes from the hand, he who kills a man is not a murderer: on the contrary, according to Roman laws, even he is a murderer who walked with a weapon for the purpose of killing a man, which Philo also draws to the law of Moses: 'Even if someone, having attempted to kill someone from an ambush, is unable to kill him, he is nonetheless subject to the penalty of murderers, as the law written concerning these things shows; for if, he says, someone attacks his neighbor to kill him by guile and flees to the altar, you shall take him to be put to death; and for the attacking alone, even if he does not die, he considered the planning of the murder an injustice equal to the killing.' The laws show, to be sure, what they desire: but what they desire they cannot fully provide. Tertullian well says: Human mediocrity judges only from deeds, because it is not equal to the hiding places of the will. He is a robber, says Seneca, even before he stains his hands. Wickedness is exercised and revealed by the deed, it does not begin with it. It is of the same author: everyone has done as much as he willed. Aristophanes: For thinking is equal to doing. Before God, the explorer of minds, he who has willed a crime has committed it. See the story of Glaucus in Herodotus, which also exists in Juvenal with this epiphonema: 'The mere will to sin suffers these punishments.' It is of the same author: 'For whoever thinks of any crime within himself, has the guilt of the deed.'

In this very crime of adultery, the master of wickedness saw that this is true, saying clearly the same thing about a woman that is said here about a man: 'If a woman is chaste because fear is removed, she is chaste at last. She who does not do it because it is not allowed, she does it.' So that now, even if your body is preserved, your mind is an adulteress: with all others excluded, the adulterer will be within.

Imitating this, Lactantius said that the mind becomes an adulteress if it has painted for itself even an image of pleasure. Seneca: 'Not undeservedly is he referred to the number of sinners who has offered his chastity to fear, not to himself.' Seneca the Elder: 'She is unchaste even without defilement, who desires defilement.' Especially, however, the author of the Responses to the Orthodox prudently saw that this saying of Christ has a place after the consent: whose words are these: 'So if knowledge awakens the passion of desire, even then he is a fornicator; but if the choice consents to the passion, then he is a fornicator either by the act or by the disposition.' Tertullian on repentance: The will is the origin of the deed, which is not freed even then, when some difficulty intercepts its perpetration: for it is cut off for itself, nor will it be able to be excused by that misfortune of carrying it out, working what was in its power. It is relevant here that the Jews once said, as witnessed by the book Alcath Rochel, that the Messiah would take away from man יצר הרע, the evil ferment, τὴν ἐπιθυμίαν (the desire). Naturally, in the manner of the Socinians, he attempts to see whether perhaps another meaning might underlie the words of Christ. And with the Moralists and other Papists—Toletus on ch. VII of the Epistle to the Romans, Coster in Enchiridion p. 394, Bellarmine book V on the loss of grace and the state of sin ch. 2, Corn. à Lapide on Matthew p. 140—he would willingly excuse the first movements of concupiscence and absolve them from sin. Which he also attempted regarding verse 22 concerning anger, as far as the impulses (ὁρμὰς) first creeping upon us without waiting for the judgment of reason, as if they were involuntary. However, one must distinguish between what is simply voluntary and what is deliberate: the latter proceeds from a preceding consultation of the matter; the former, however, from imagination alone, which represents the thing, toward which the will is immediately carried without prior investigation. For since those movements are inordinate and contrary to reason, the intellect and will cannot be free from blame if they do not prescribe a limit to the affections and movements of the heart; so far is it from being permissible to excuse concupiscence that is not indeed deliberate, yet still titillating. Indeed, when Christ prohibits the looking at a woman in order to lust, He condemned the very first movements of the heart that follow the looking, e.g., when concupiscence suggests it would be sweet to possess such a woman, even if one does not yet decide that he wills to possess her. And indeed, the natural law itself teaches that those who consent to sin by an internal movement sin, concerning which see the verses of Menander in Clement of Alexandria, Book V, Stromata, and of Philemon in Justin Martyr, book on Monarchy. can testify to this effect: That a good man, whom God loves, ought to look at or desire nothing alien, not a beautiful woman, not a house, not a possession, not a boy or a maidservant, not horses and oxen, not any of the beasts of burden, not even the thread of a needle. How much more, therefore, should it be believed that the first degree of concupiscence is disapproved by the law of God, if indeed Paul himself testifies that he would not have known concupiscence—that which is sin in the judgment of God—to be sin, before he was informed by the divine law. Concerning which Augustine is to be heard, Book I, On Marriage and Concupiscence, ch. LIX: 'He does much good who does what is written, "Go not after thy lusts," but he does not perfect it; because he does not fulfill what is written, "Thou shalt not covet." Therefore the law still says, 'Thou shalt not covet,' so that we, finding ourselves lying in this disease, might seek the medicine of grace and might know in what we ought to be crowned by progressing in that immortality, and by what precept it might be possible for us to arrive at most blessed immortality: for if it were not to be perfected at some time, it would never have to be commanded. And the Holy Scriptures reprove not only the desire that entices, conceives, or brings forth, but also that which tempts and draws away (James 1:14-15), even if concupiscence finally brings forth the sin of an external act by those distinct degrees. Therefore, it cannot be proven what Grotius says, that this saying of Christ, 'he has already committed adultery with her in his heart,' especially has a place after the consent (τὴν συγκατάθεσιν), because a lustful look alone, just as the very words of Christ testify, suffices for the guilt of adultery (τῆς μοιχείας): nor do the words of Christ teach what adultery is in particular, but what it is truly. Grotius says it is relevant here that the Jews once said, as witnessed by the book Alkath Rahel, that the Messiah would take away from man יצר הרע, the evil ferment (figment), τὴν ἐπιθυμίαν (the desire), but the Messiah ought to have taken away—not so much by a prohibition, which had already been made through Moses by the law of the Decalogue, 'Thou shalt not covet,' as by the power of His merit and expiation or satisfaction—just as all actual sins whatsoever, so also τὴν ἐπιθυμίαν, the wicked concupiscence, and that even original or connate: which the Jews once designated by that name.

Latin:

Vers. 28. ὅτι πᾶς ὁ βλέπων] Quia nimirum oculi sunt in amore duces, ut ille ait, aut ut Plato loquitur ἀρχὴ τῶ ἐρω- τῶ ὄρασις : Apud alium est: ἡ ἐπιθυμία διὰ τῶν ὀφθαλ- μῶν ἕρχεται: quod ipsum exsequitur Platonem sequens Plutarchus Symposiacon III. 6. Bene Salvianus dixit, se- nestras quodammodo esse nostrarum mentium lumen o- culorum, & omnes cupiditates in cor per oculos, quasi per naturales cuniculos intrare. Hinc oculi pleni adulte- rii apud 2. Pet. II. 14.

γυναῖκα] Potest de quavis muliere sumi, ita ut quod se- quitur μοιχᾶται sumatur laxius: atque adeo vetetur hic et- iam τῆς πορνείας prolusio. Simplicius tamen est, ut γυναῖκα intelligamus τὴν γαμετὴν, quomodo sæpe ea vox sumitur, ut & latina mulieris, non quod non etiam τὴν πορνείαν, quippe etiam Judæis inter se vetitam, vehementer im- probet Christus, sed quod in eodem peccandi genere in- traque easdem personas maluerit consistere, quo aper- tior esset actuum internorum & externorum comparatio.

Improbat Christus vehementer τὴν πορνείαν, ejusque non prolusionem habet tantum aspectum impudicum, sed μοιχείαν esse docet, quod ex hisce sexti præcepti vindiciis luculentum est; Quomodo ergo in hac sede propria, cum ex instituto expli- cat, quibus modis committatur fornicatio, restri- cte tantum loqui eum censebimus de aspectu libi- dinoso τῆς γαμετῆς, non vere cujuscunque mulie- ris? Ratio Grotii ψευδερμηνείας nititur verborum an- tecedentium, quasi scil. lege decalogi Christus pro- hibitum tantum esse fornicationis externum actum indicavit: quum contrà Christus non legem divi- nam decalogi adducat, ex mente legislatoris tradi- tam & intellectam, sed depravationem ejusdem Pha- risaicam atro carbone notet, legisque mentem vin- dicet. Quod contra Socinianos, quibus obstetrica- tur hic Grotius, alias ostensum. Recte Lactantius l. VI. c. 73. Non tantum adulterium esse vitandum, præcipit Deus, sed etiam cogitationem, ne quis adspi- ciat alienam & animo concupiscat. Et dictabat id quodammodo natura sanis gentibus. Unde Quin- tilianus Pater: Tu alienam matronam aliter quam le- ges permittunt, aspexisti. Et Seneca Pater, incesta est etiam sine stupro, quæ cupit stuprum. Corrumpere autem Christi etiam vindicias nititur Grotius, quando ἐπιθυμῆσαι hic esse explicari sollicitare, ait: etsi à Patribus, Justino, Clemente, Athenagora id de sola libidine & ἀναθυμιάσει τῆς ὀρέξεως accipi observarit ipse, nec illi interpretationi calculum denegare potuerit. Sic enim ipse ad verba

Πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτῆς] Hoc est proprie quod dicit Job. XXXI. 4. si animus oculos est insecutus. Hebræi posterio- res id vocant זן עינים והערוך pascere oculos il- licito spectaculo: ὁρᾶν ἀκολάστως Chrysostomus VIII. ad Rom. Apparet ergo à Christo eum hic notari, qui im- puro amori animum mancipans vulnus suum fovet aspe- ctu. Petulcos impudicorum hominum intuitus hic no- tari ait Salvianus. Tertullianus de velandis virginibus: Christianus salvis oculis fæminam videt, animo adver- sus libidinem cæcus est. Quintilianus Pater: Tu alienam ma- tronam aliter quam leges permittunt, aspexisti. Lactantius Ibro VI. c. 23. Non tantum adulterium esse vitandum præcipit Deus, sed etiam cogitationem, ne quis afficiat alie- nam, & animo concupiscat. Quamvis autem τὸ ἐπιθυ- μεῖν soleat & in bonam partem accipi, hic tamen ut mul- tis aliis in locis in vitio ponitur, ut cupere apud Afra- nium: Amabit sapiens, cupiens cæteri. Justinus τὸ ἐπι- θυμεῖν exponit τῆς ὀρέξεως ἀναθυμίασιν. Clemens paulo subtilius: ἐὰν εἰς κάλλος σώματος βλέψη τις, ὁ λόγος φησὶ, καὶ αὐτῷ ἡ σὰρξ εἶναι καθ᾽ ἐπιθυμίαν δόξῃ καλὴ σαρκικῶς ἰδὼν καὶ ἁμαρτικῶς, ὃς τεθαύμακεν, κρίνεται. Athena- goras: ἡμεῖς δὲ τοσοῦτον ἀδιάφοροι εἶναι ἀπέχομεν ὡς μηδὲ ἰδεῖν ἡμῖν πρὸς ἐπιθυμίαν ἐξεῖναι. Posset & ἐπιθυμῆσαι hic interpretari solicitare, quomodo & חמד Hebraicum su- mi solet. Sic in Canone IV. Synodi Neocæsariensis ἐὰν προθῆταί τις ἐπιθυμῆσαι γυναικὸς, συγκαθευδῆσαι μετ᾽ αὐ- τῆς.

ἤδη ἐμοίχευσεν αὐτὴν ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ αὑτῶ] Homines qui de animo nisi ex signis exterioribus judicare non possunt, delicti nomen actui ultimo imponunt. Et tamen ipsi jurisconsulti fatentur animum distinguere maleficia. Itaq; si telum manu fugit, qui hominem occidit homicida non est: contra Romanis legibus etiam is homicida est qui ho- minis occidendi causa cum telo ambulavit, quod & ad Mosis trahit legem Philo: κᾂν ἐξ ἐνέδρας μέν τοι τις ἐπι- χειρήσας ἀνελεῖν τινα, μὴ δυνηθῇ κτεῖναι, τῷ τῶν ἀνδροφόνων οὐδὲν ἧττον ὕποχος δίκῃ καθεστηκεν, ὡς ὁ γραφεὶς περὶ τούτων δηλοῖ νόμος· ἐὰν γάρ φησί τις ἐπιθῆται τῷ πλησίον, ἀπο- κτεῖναι αὐτὸν δόλῳ καὶ καταφύγῃ ἐπὶ τὸ θυσιαστήριον, λήψῃ αὐτὸν θανατῶσαι, καὶ τοῦ ἐπιτίθεσθαι μόνον, οὐκ ἀποθνήσκει, ἀλλ᾿ ἴσον ἡγήσατο ἀδίκημα τῷ κτεῖναι τὸ βουλεῦσαι τὸν φόνον. Os- tendunt nimirum leges quid cupiant: sed quod cupiunt plene præstare non possunt. Bene Tertullianus: Me- diocritas humana de factis solum judicat, quia voluntatis la- tebris par non est. Latro est, inquit Seneca, etiam ante- quam inquinet manus. Exercetur atque aperitur opere ne- quitia, non incipit. Ejusdem est: fecit quisque quan- tum voluit. Aristophanes: δύναται γὰρ ἶσον τῷ δρᾷν τὸ νοεῖν. Apud Deum mentium exploratorem, qui voluit scelus is fecit. Vide apud Herodotum de Glauco hi- storiam, quæ & apud Juvenalem exstat cum hoc epipho- nemate: Has patitur pœnas peccandi sola voluntas. Ejusdem est: Nam scelus intra se tantum qui cogitat ullum, Facti crimen habet.

In ipso hoc adulterii crimine verum hoc esse vidit magister nequitiæ, plane idem de muliere dicens, quod hic de viro dicitur: Si quæ metu demto casta est, ea denique casta est. Quæ quia non liceat non facit, illa facit. Ut jam servaris bene corpus adultera mens est: Omnibus exclusis intus adulter erit.

Quod imitatus Lactantius dixit, adulteram fieri mentem, si vel imaginem voluptatis sibi ipsa depinxerit. Sene- ca: Non immerito in numerum peccantium refertur quip- dicitiam timori præstitit, non sibi. Pater Seneca: Incesta est etiam sine stupro, quæ cupit stuprum. Præcipue autem hoc dictum Christi locum habere post τὴν συγ- κατάθεσιν prudenter vidit Scriptor responsionum ad Or- thodoxos, cujus hæc sunt verba: ὥστε εἰ ἡ γνῶσις ἐξυπνίσῃ τὸ τῆς ἐπιθυμίας πάθος κἂν οὕτως πόρνος ἐστιν, ἐὰν δὲ συγκατα- τίθηται τῷ πάθει ἡ προαίρεσις, τότε ἐστὶ πόρνος ἢ κατὰ τὴν πρᾶξιν ἢ κατὰ τὴν διάθεσιν. Tertullianus de pœnitentia: Volun- tas facti origo est, quæ ne tunc quidem liberatur, cume aliqua difficultas perpretationem ejus intercepit: ipsa enim sibi amputatur, nec excusari poterit per illam perficiendi in- felicitatem operans, quod suum fuerat. Pertinet huc quod Judæi olim dixerunt teste libro Alcath Rochel, Messiam ablaturum ab homine יצר הרע malum fomentum, τὴν ἐπιθυμίαν. Nimirum Socinianorum more tentat, num for- te alius sensus verbis Christi subesse possit. Et cum Moralistis aliisque Pontificiis Toleto ad c. VII. Ep. ad Rom. Coster. in Enchir. p. 394. Bellarm. l. V. de amiss. gratiæ & stat. peccat. c. 2. Corn. à Lap. in Matt. p. 140. primos motus concupiscentiæ libenter excusa- tos vellet, atque à peccato absolvere. Quod etiam ad v. 22. circa iram, quoad ὁρμὰς primum nobis ob- repentes non expectato rationis judicio se exerentes, ceu involuntarias tentavit. Distinguendum autem inter simpliciter voluntarium & deliberatum: Hoc ex præcedente rei consultatione procedit: illud vero ex sola imaginatione, quæ rem repræsentat, in quam illico voluntas fertur absque prævia disqui- sitione. Quum enim motus illi inordinati sint, & contra rationem, non potest intellectus, & voluntas culpa carere, si non præscribat modum affectibus, & motib⁹ cordis, tantum abest, ut concupiscentiam non deliberatam quidem titillantem tamen excusare liceat: imo cum Christus aspectum mulieris ad con- cupiscendum prohibet, ipsos primos motus cordis da- mnavit, qui aspectum sequuntur v. g. cum concu- piscentia suggerit suave fore, tali potiri muliere, utut nondum decernat quis, velle se eadem potiri. Et sane ipsa naturalis lex docet, peccare illos, qui in peccatum interno motu consentiunt, quo de versus Menandri apud Cl. Alex. L. V. Str. & Philemo- nis ap. J. Martyr. l. de Monarch. testari possunt hu- jus tenoris: Hominem bonum, quem Deus diligat, o- portere nihil alienum aspicere, aut concupiscere, non fa- minam præstantem, non domum, non possessionem, non puerum, aut ancillam, non equos & boves, non jumen- torum aliquid, ne filum acus quidem. Quanto ma- gis ergo concupiscentiæ primum gradum à lege Dei improbari credendum, siquidem Paulus ipse testetur, quod non noverit concupiscentiam eam, quæ peccatum in judicio Dei est, peccatum esse, antequam è lege informaretur divina. Quo de Au- gust. audiendus l. I. de nupt. & concup. c. LIX. Mul- tum boni facit, qui facit quod scriptum est, post con- cupiscentias tuas non eas, sed non perficit; quia non implet, quod scriptum est, non concupisces. Adhuc ergo dicit lex, non concupisces, ut nos in hoc morbo ja- cere invenientes medicinam gratiæ quæreremus & in eo quo debeamus in ista immortalitate proficiendo co- ronari, & quo possit à nobis præcepto sciremus, & im- mortalitate beatissima perveniri: nisi autem quando- que perficiendum esset, nunquam jubendum esset. Et re- probat S. S. non modo ἐπιθυμίαν τὴν δελεάζουσαν, συλλαβῦσαν, ἢ τικτῦσαν, sed etiam τὴν πειράζου- σαν καὶ ἐξελκῦσαν Jac. I. 14. 15. etsi peccatum exter- ni operis distinctis illis gradibus demum pariat con- cupiscentia. Non ergo probari potest, quod ait Grotius, præcipue hoc dictum Christi ἤδη ἐμοίχευ- σει αὐτὴν ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ αὑτῦ locum habere post τὴν συγκατάθεσιν, quia solus aspectus libidinosus, quemadmodum ipsa verba Christi testantur, suffi- cit ad reatum τῆς μοιχείας: nec quid præcipue μοι- χεία sit, sed quid vere, Christi verba docent. Perti- nere huc dicit Grotius, quod Judæi olim dixerunt, te- ste libro Alkath Rahel, Messiam ablaturum ab homine יצר הרע malum fermentum (figmentum) τὴν ἐπι- θυμίαν, sed Messias non tam prohibitione, quæ jam per Mosen facta, lege Decalogi, Non concupisces, quam meriti & expiationis sive satisfactionis suæ vir- tute auferre debuit ut peccata actualia quæcunque, ita quoque τὴν ἐπιθυμίαν pravam concupiscentiam, eamque etiam originalem vel connatam: quam o- lim isto nomine designarunt Judæi.

## 5:29
Verse 29. 'And if thy right eye'—In this passage also, if I am not very much mistaken in my judgment, many subtle things are gathered together than the popularity of speech allows. To me, both that fact, and the fact that these words do not follow a collection of precepts but are attached with inseparable continuity to that which was said concerning adulterous loves, and furthermore the repetition of the name of the eye which had preceded a little before, seem to make clear the meaning of this sentence, although its force extends more widely; the occasion arose from those things which had been said in the preceding verse, so that a reply might be made to a certain tacit objection, by an argument drawn from that which is greater, in this manner: Perhaps someone hearing these things might say, women, especially the more beautiful ones, are 'pains of the eyes,' as was accustomed to be said of the Persian women: and nature is so constituted that it is difficult not to love what is beautiful. Wherefore, let it be permitted to love with at least a harmless pleasure if it is not permitted to possess. The answer is that of two inconveniences, that which is the lesser must be chosen: namely, as the poet just cited, treating this argument from the prescription of prudence and not of piety, had said: 'If someone calls my precepts hard: we confess they are hard, but that you may be well, you will bear many things that are to be grieved.' If gangrene or a similar disease had occupied a part of the body, however dear, it would be right that you should suffer it to be cut off rather than that the spreading evil should create destruction for the whole body; as it is in Plutarch: 'The one who begat us made the foot and the hand, but when it rots, he gives a reward to the one who cuts it off,' how much more justly would that have to be done where the eternal destruction of soul and body is imminent unless you prevent it. In almost a similar way, that same person whom I mentioned argues: 'To redeem the body you will suffer iron and fires, nor will you relieve your dry mouth with water while thirsty. Will you refuse to endure anything for the sake of the health of your soul?' But that which can easily be supplied by the listener is left unsaid in this sense: And yet, since the danger I point out to you is greater than the loss of this mortal life, there is nevertheless less required to avoid that danger. You would owe it to yourself to pluck out your eye if you could not save yourself otherwise; but for me it is enough if you turn it away from a seductive face: you would owe it to yourself to cut off your hand; I ask for nothing more than that you keep it from unchaste caresses. We have examples of those who have allowed their foot to be cut off: for me it suffices that you direct your step elsewhere than where the fuel of evil is: Endure and force your unwilling feet to run. A not dissimilar saying is found in Seneca: Cast away whatever tears your heart, which, if they could not be extracted otherwise, the heart itself would have to be torn out with them. This very sense which we mention exists treated widely and at length in Porphyry, in the first book near the end, On Abstinence from Animal Food. For he also shows that, since we endure such harsh things for the sake of preserving the body, much greater things must be endured so that divine immortality may be prepared for our souls: and yet this usually costs less, namely, the cutting off of pleasures. In this circumlocution I also mention feet, because there is mention of them below in XVIII 8 and Mark X 45, in which places that which had been said here on the occasion of that affection, which is wont to be most uncontrollable, is applied generally to all vices. For the reason is the same. Here Job, in chapter XXXI, dealing with the flight from both injustice and obscene love, says that he had made a covenant with his eyes: that nothing unjust had clung to his hands: that his foot had not hastened to deceit. The sum, therefore, of this precept is that the nourishment of depraved desires must be avoided. For desire, giving birth to an act, if it is prevented from bringing it forth, causing an abortion, itself also perishes. Nor indeed do I doubt that Christ, who was not at all desirous of innovation, took this from the precepts of the ancient Hebrews, from where Philo also drew these things: διόπερ ἐλιέθαι ἂν μοι δοκοῦσιν οἱ μὴ τελείως ἀπαίδευτοι πεπηρῶσθαι μᾶλλον, ἢ τὰ μὴ προσήκοντ᾽ ὁρᾷν κεϰωφῶσθαι μᾶλλον ἢ βλα- βερῶν ἀϰύειν λόγων ϰὶ ἐκτετμῆσθαι γλῶτταν ὑπὲρ τῶ μηδὲν τῶν ἀῤῥήτων ἐκλαλῆσαι and what follows. Chrysostom, in his second sermon on fasting, says that this precept of Christ, which seems harsh, is most mild. It would have been harsh if he had ordered us to be present with women, to look at them, and to abstain. Add if he had commanded that which Valerius Maximus narrates that Xenocrates performed.

ὁ δεξιὸς] That is, κἂν ὁ δεξιὸς: which is said because, as Aristotle says, φύσῃ βέλτιον τὸ δεξιὸν τῶ ἀριστερῶ.

We add what Spanheim has here: By the right eye and the right hand are to be understood the most precious and dearest things, which are as dear to us as the right eye and the right hand, that is to say, the voluntary loss of such things is to be made, if they entice us to evil, rather than that by their occasion we be precipitated into sins and thus into destruction. The reason for the connection with the preceding is evident, if here are understood those things which are like eyes and hands to us which are most precious and dearest to us, and the sense of those words is conceived only as the loss of such things being preferable to that of salvation. Evils otherwise to be cast away by themselves, and others even if productive of no harm. Add that a hypothetical discourse is used here by the Lord, If thy eye, etc., if thy right hand, etc., and thus the consequent is not urged unless the antecedent is posited. The sense is clear, provided one attends to where the Lord draws the similitude, namely from those things which are wont to happen among men, for example, in bodily diseases. For it is known that if any part of the body is seized by gangrene and the whole body is endangered, and one or the other must be experienced, either the loss of one member or of the whole body, in such a case it is far better that the salvation of the whole be redeemed by the expenditure of one member, and to be deprived of an eye or hand than of life: Thus if allurements and conveniences of every kind are proposed to us, and we are moved in such things as tenderly as we are moved in the preservation of the right eye and right hand, it is nevertheless better that we be deprived of such things than to enjoy them with the loss of salvation: just as it would have been far better for the rich man to be deprived of all delights in this life than to be condemned to the fire of Gehenna in the future. Indeed, nothing prevents the words of the Lord from being taken hyperbolically, and by a certain exaggeration, even being explained literally, in this sense: If the eternal life were to be redeemed by the loss of either the right eye or the right hand, the deprivation of those members themselves, even with some inconvenience and pain, is to be chosen rather than that of life itself. By which very thing it is shown that those things which are less dear, or useful, or precious, or necessary to us are much more to be cast away and cut off; an ἐπίτασις therefore in the naming of the right eye and right hand. Whence Augustine: It was superfluous to speak of the left scandalizing, since not even the right is to be spared. Since the right parts seem to be prior, and more apt for work, being animated by a greater influx of spirits and heat, and endowed with greater strength and agility.

σκανδαλίζῃ σε] וקש לך as the Prophets speak. For what comes from there, מוֹקֵשׁ, the LXX translate as σκάνδαλον, Psalm LXIX. 23, whom Paul follows in Rom. XI. 9. And certainly the primitive meaning corresponds. For an interpreter explains σκάνδάληθρον among Aristophanes as τὸ ἐν τῇ παγίδι ἐπικαμπὲς ξύλον, Pollux as τὸ ἐν ταῖς μυάγραις ἐνισάμενον παττάλιον. Hesychius teaches us that σκάνδαλον is the same thing. But the same thing is also signified by the name σκώλον, which the LXX interpreters sometimes translate with the word מוֹקֵשׁ. By translation, this word designates everything that provides a cause of destruction, as Ps. CXL. 6, ἐχόμενα τρίβου σκάνδαλα ἔθεντό μοι, in which sense it is also found in the book of Judith V. 22 and XII. 2. And therefore also that by which one is incited to delinquency, as in Deut. VII. 16, and passim among the writers of the New Testament. The word מִכְשׁוֹל has a related sense, although the similitude is drawn from elsewhere, which is properly πρόσκομμα, by the addition of which word Paul interprets the word σκάνδαλον in Romans XIV. 13. Wherefore it is not a wonder that the Syrian here translates σκάνδαλον as מַכְשׁוּלָא, since the LXX also translated מִכְשׁוֹל as σκάνδαλον in Lev. XIX. 14. Seneca called this very thing an offense, saying, through such offenses this rugged journey must be traversed.

Pricæus warns that by that word are not designated the stumbling blocks that occasionally present themselves to the world, which, however, divinely aided, we repel or leap over: since without constant offenses, and indeed falls, no one reaches the goal of salvation; but those by whose magnitude and strength we allow ourselves to be overwhelmed, that is, affections so powerful that they hold us entirely enslaved, and act and behave as tyrants or imperious mistresses. Lest such things cut off our course entirely, they themselves must be cut off by us: namely εἰς ὄλεθρον σαρκὸς ἵνα σωθῇ τὸ πνεῦμα, 1 Cor. V. 5.

βάλε ἀπὸ σῦ] Projice: by which word the Latins also indicate contempt for a thing.

συμφέρει γὰρ σοι] ἀγαθὸν γὰρ ἀντὶ μείζονος κακᾶ ἐλάττονος λῆψις as Aristotle says in Rhet. book 1, chapter 6. καὶ μὴ] A Hebraism וְלֹא which means 'lest'. Wherefore you will translate it best thus: For it is expedient for you that one of your members perish, lest the whole body be cast into Gehenna.

γέενναν] That word which just now comparatively figured the punishments of the other age, now figuratively denotes the same. And Matthew indeed added nothing further, writing to the inhabitants of Palestine, among whom that word had long since received that sense: as appears from the books of the ancient Hebrews. Mark, however, so that those who were less accustomed to the word might understand its force, added πῦρ τὸ ἄσβεσον. It is placed in these books everywhere for the punishments after the resurrection: not for the state that intervenes between death and resurrection.

That had to be proved, not merely asserted. For the parable of the rich man teaches that immediately after death the souls of the impenitent are thrust into Gehenna, Luke XVI.

Latin:

Vers. 29. εἰ δὲ ὁ ὀφθαλμός σꙋ ὁ δεξιὸς] In hunc quoque locum ni valde animi fallor, multa congeruntur subtilia ra quam ferat sermonis popularitas. Mihi tum illud ᾤε tum quod hæc verba non præceptorum congeriem se- quuntur, sed indivulsa continentia annectuntur ei quod de adulteris amoribus dictum est, præterea vero repeti- tum oculi nomen quod paulo ante præcesserit, planum facere videntur hujus sententiæ, quamvis ejus vis latius se porrigat; occasionem natam ex his quæ dicta erant commate antecedente, ita ut ad tacitam quandam ob- jectionem responderetur, argumento ab eo quod ma- jus est ducto hunc in modum: Dicat forte aliquis hæc audiens, fœminæ præsertim formosiores sunt ἀλγηδόνες ὀφθαλμῶν, quod de Persicis dici solebat: & natura ita est comparatum ut difficile sit non amare quod pulchrum est. Quapropter Casso saltem delectamine Amare liceat si potiri non licet. Respondetur ex duobus incommodis eligendum esse id quod est minus: nempe ut modo citatus Poeta hoc argu- mentum ex prudentiæ non ex pietatis præscripto tractans dixerat: Dura aliquis præcepta vocet mea: dura fatemur Esse, sed ut valeas multa dolenda feres. Si gangræna aut morbus similis partem corporis quam- vis caram occupâsset, æquum esset ut patereris eam præ- cidi potius; quam proserpens malum toti corpori exi- tium crearet; ut apud Plutarchum est: Ὡς τὸν πόδα ϰὶ τὴν χεῖρα ὁ γεννήσας ἐποίησεν, ἀλλ᾽ ὅταν σαπῇ, μισθὸν δίδωσιν τῷ ἀποκόπτοντι, quanto justius id faciendum esset ubi æterna animi corporisque pernicies imin net ni antevertas. Si- mili ferme modo argumentatur idem ille quem dixi: Vt corpus redimas ferrum patieris & ignes, Arida nec sitiens ora levabis aqua. Vt valeas animo quicquam tolerare negabis? Subticetur autem id quod ab auditore facile suppleri pot- est in hunc sensum: Atqui cum majus sit periculum quod tibi monstro, quam hujus vitæ mortalis jactura, mi- nus tamen est quo vitari id periculum potest. Deberes si aliter te servare non posses vel oculum tibi eruere; at mihi satis est si eam a vultu illecebroso avertas: manum deberes tibi præcidere; ego nihil amplius postulo; quam ut eam arceas ab impudicis contrectationibus. Eorum qui pedem sibi abscindi passi sunt habemus exempla: mi- hi sufficit, ut alio, quam ubi mali fomenta sunt, gressum dirigas: Perfer & invitos currere coge pedes. Non dissimile est dictum apud Senecam: Projice quæcun- que cor tuum laniant, quæ si aliter extrahi nequirent, cor ipsum cum illis evellendum erat. Sensus hic ipse quem dici- mus late fuseque tractatus exstat apud Porphyrium libro primo circa finem de abstinentia ab animalibus. Osten- dit enim & ille, cum corporis servandi causa tam dura patiamur, multo majora patienda, ut divina inmortalitas animis paretur: & hanc tamen plerumque minoris consta- re, nempe voluptatum abscissione. In hac circumlocutio- ne pedum quoque memini, quia & eorum sit mentio infra XVIII 8. & Marc. X. 45. quibus in locis id quod hic occa- sione ejus affectus, qui solet esse impotentissimus, dictum erat, generaliter omnibus vitiis aptatur. Est enim eadem ratio. Hic Job. c. XXXI. de fuga tam injustitiæ quam ob- scœni amoris agens ait, fœdus se cum oculis pepigisse : manibus nihil adhæsisse iniqui: pedem suum non festi- ravisse ad dolum. Summa igitur hujus præcepti est, vitan- da pravarum cupiditatum alimenta. Cupiditas enim a- ctum parturiens, si eum eniti prohibeatur, abortum fa- ciens, ipsa quoque interit. Neque vero dubito quin & hoc Christus, minime novandi cupidus, sumserit ex veterum Hebræorum præceptis, unde & Philo hæc hausit: διόπερ ἐλιέθαι ἂν μοι δοκοῦσιν οἱ μὴ τελείως ἀπαίδευτοι πεπηρῶσθαι μᾶλλον, ἢ τὰ μὴ προσήκοντ᾽ ὁρᾷν κεϰωφῶσθαι μᾶλλον ἢ βλα- βερῶν ἀϰύειν λόγων ϰὶ ἐκτετμῆσθαι γλῶτταν ὑπὲρ τῶ μηδὲν τῶν ἀῤῥήτων ἐκλαλῆσαι & quæ sequuntur. Chrysostomus de jejunio sermone secundo, præceptum hoc Christi, quod durum videtur, ait esse mitissimum. Durum futurum fuisse, si jussisset nos adesse fœminis, eas aspectare & absti- nere. Adde si id præcipisset, quod Xenocratem præsti- tisse narrat Valerius Maximus.

ὁ δεξιὸς] Idest κἂν ὁ δεξιὸς: quod ideo dictum quia ut ait Aristoteles φύσῃ βέλτιον τὸ δεξιὸν τῶ ἀριστερῶ.

Addimus quæ habet hic Spanhemius: Per o- culum dextrum & manum dextram pretiosissima & charissima quæque intelligenda, quæ aque chara nobis ac oculus dexter, & manus dextra, talium vi- delicet jacturam voluntariam potius faciendam, si nos pelliciant ad malum, quam ut illorum occasione in peccata & sic in exitium præcipitemur. Ratio connexionis cum superioribus evidens, si hic intelli- gantur ea quæ oculorum instar & manuum nobis sunt, vel esse solent, adeoque quæ pretiosissima no- bis ac charissima, & is verborum istorum sensus tan- tum concipiatur, talium potius jacturam facien- dam quam salutis. Mala alias per se abjicienda, & quæ alia etsi nullius damni productiva. Adde, hypotheticam hic orationem adhiberi à Domino, Si oculus tuus, &c. si dextra tua manus, &c. adeoque consequens non urgeri, nisi posito antecedente. Sen- sus clarus, modo attendatur, unde Dominus du- cat similitudinem, ab iis nimirum quæ solent contin- gere inter homines, verbi gratia, in morbis corporeis. Notum enim si aliqua corporis parte correpta spha- celo periclitetur totum corpus, & alterutrum expe- riundum sit, vel membri unius, vel corporis totius jactura, in ejusmodi casu præstat longe membri u- nius dispendio redemptum iri salutem totius, & ocu- lo vel manu privari, quam vita: Sic si omnis generis illicia & commoda nobis proponantur, & nos in ta- lia affecti æque tenero feramur, quali ferimur in o- culi dextri, & manus dextræ conservationem, præ- stare tamen nos privari talibus, quam illis frui cum dispendio salutis: prout præstitisset longe Epulonem deliciis omnibus privari hac in vita, quam damnari ad ignem gehennæ in futura. Immo nihil obstat, quo minus hyperbolice acceptis verbis Domini, & per ex- aggerationem quandam, illa etiam ad literam ex- ponantur, hoc sensu: Si vel oculi dexteri, vel ma- nus dexteræ jactura redimenda foret vita æterna, il- lorum potius membrorum etiam cum incommodo & dolore aliquo, quam ipsius privationem eligendam. Quo ipso ostensum, multo magis abjicienda, & re- secanda esse illa, quæ minus nobis sive chara, sive uti- lia, sive pretiosa, sive necessaria; ἐπίτασις ergo in dexteri oculi & dexteræ manus nomenclatione. Unde Augustinus: De sinistro scandalizante superfluum erat dicere, quandoquidem nec dextero parcen- dum sit. Quum dexteræ partes priores esse videan- tur, & aptiores ad opus, majore quippe spirituum, & caloris influxu animatæ, & majori robore, & a- gilitate instructæ.

σκανδαλίζῃ σε] וקש לך ut loquuntur Prophetæ. Nam quod inde venit מוֹקֵשׁ σκάνδαλον vertunt LXX. Psal. LXIX. 23. quos sequitur Paulus Rom. XI. 9. Et certe respondet primitiva significatio. Nam σκανδάληθρον apud Aristopha- nem interpres exponit τὸ ἐν τῇ παγίδι ἐπικαμπὲς ξύλον, Pollux τὸ ἐν ταῖς μυάγραις ἐνισάμενον παττάλιον. Idem autem esse σκάνδαλον docet nos Hesychius. Sed & σκώλον nomine res eadem significatur, quam voce מוֹקֵשׁ inter- dum transferunt LXX. Interpretes. Per tralationem de- signat hæc vox omne id quod exitii causam præbet, ut Pf. CXL. 6. ἐχόμενα τρίβου σκάνδαλα ἔθεντό μοι quo sensu reperi- tur & in libro Judith. V. 22. & XII. 2. Ac proinde etiam id quo quis ad delinquendum incitatur, uti Deut. VII. 16. & passim apud novi fœderis Scriptores. Sensum affinem, quanquam aliunde ducta similitudine habet vox מִכְשׁוֹל quod proprie est πρόσκομμα, cujus vocis ad- ditamento vocem σκάνδαλον interpretatur Paulus Roman. XIV. 13. Quare mirum non est, quod Syrus hic σκάνδαλον vertit מַכְשׁוּלָא, cum & LXX. מִכְשׁוֹל verterint σκάν- δαλον Lev. XIX. 14. Id ipsum offensam dixit Seneca, per hujusmodi, inquiens, offensas emetiendum est confrago- sum hoc iter.

Pricæus monet, voce illa non designari offen- dicula subinde se objicientia orbis, quæ tamen di- vinitus adjuti repellimus vel transilimus: cum sine assiduis offensationibus, imo & lapsibus, nemo ad salutis metam pertingat; at ea quorum magni- tudine ac viribus nosmet obrui patimur, id est, affectus adeo potentes, ut totos nos mancipatos te- neant, tyrannorumque aut imperiosarum domina- rum vicem agunt feruntque. Ejusmodi ne penitus cursum præcidant, ipsa præcidenda nobis: ni- mirum εἰς ὄλεθρον σαρκὸς ἵνα σωθῇ τὸ πνεῦμα, 1. Cor. V. 5.

βάλε ἀπὸ σῦ] Projice: quo verbo Latini quoque rei contemtum indicant.

συμφέρει γὰρ σοι] ἀγαθὸν γὰρ ἀντὶ μείζονος κακᾶ ἐλάττο- νος λῆψις ut inquit Aristoteles Rhet. l. cap. 6. καὶ μὴ] Hebraismus וְלֹא quod valet ne. Quare ita optime verteris: Expedit enim tibi unum membrorum tibi perire ne totum corpus projiciatur in gehennam.

γέενναν] Vox ista quæ modo comparate supplicia alterius sæculi figurabat, nunc translate eadem notat. Et Mat- thæus quidem nihil ultra addidit, quippe Palæstinæ ha- bitatoribus scribens, apud quos pridem vox ista eum sen- sum acceperat: ut ex veterum Hebræorum libris appa- ret. Marcus vero, ut & qui ei vocabulo minus sueti e- rant, vim ejus intelligerent, apposuit πῦρ τὸ ἄσβεσον. Ponitur autem in his libris ubique pro suppliciis post re- surrectionem: non pro statu qui mortem & resurrectio- nem intercedit.

Probandum id erat, non nude asserendum. Nam statim post mortem in gehennam impœni- tentium animas detrudi, parabola de epulone docet Luc. XVI.

## 5:31
Vers. 31. Ἐῤῥέθη δὲ.] Namely by Moses by divine command: not by the private counsel of Moses, which Origen felt and Ambrose followed, which error Epiphanius gravely accuses in a certain Ptolemy, unless we think that Origen and Ambrose felt rather that these things, and certain others of this kind, were devised by Moses according to his prudence and referred to God, who then approved them as convenient for that people and those times. Certainly in Deut. I. 3, V. 1, VI. 1, it is openly said that Moses proposed to the people those things which God had commanded. From there, however, up to the chapter on divorce, it is one and continuous discourse. Nor is it credible that Moses, who did not wish to answer anything concerning a disputed case of inheritance without consulting God, would have established anything in a matter of much greater moment without God's command: Nor should it have moved anyone to the contrary opinion that Christ ascribes this act to Moses below in ch. XIX. 8. For everywhere even those things which no one doubts proceeded from God, Moses, being chosen for that matter as a minister by God, is recorded to have said and commanded, as below VIII. 4. Mark I. 44. VII. 10. Luke V. 14.

Here, however, neither the words of Moses nor the commands of God are being considered: but the mind and sense of the Pharisees. For Christ is engaged in refuting and correcting their false interpretation. What kind of interpretation that was is manifest, both from Christ's own declaration opposed to that ψευδερμηνείᾳ, and from the parallel passage in Matthew XIX, verse 7, and especially the question of the Pharisees εἰ ἔξεστιν ἀνθρώπῳ ἀπολῦσαι τὴν γυναῖκα αὑτᾶ κατὰ πᾶσαν αἰτίαν. However, even if we admit that the law concerning divorces proceeded from GOD himself, and was not sanctioned by the private counsel of Moses, Grotius rightly acknowledges that the right established in Deuteronomy chapter XXIV did not make it so that those things were done rightly, but only that they were done with impunity, because Christ taught that that permission was made on account of the hardness of the Jews, Matthew XIX, verse 8, namely, lest occasion be given for harsher treatment or even poisoning, for which end the mere concession of impunity suffices. And Selden observes that Christ changes his manner of speaking here: What he says was said, this in the verse Christ does not have expressed in the sacred law itself in such a way, just as the others which follow concerning retaliation and oaths. Namely, concerning those he says, it was said to the ancients; concerning this one only, it was said, as others also have observed; while others resist, and take it for what was said by Moses, by divine command. The sense seems to be, it was said, or the opinion that it was then on the lips of men, if anyone wished to dismiss a wife who displeased him, that this was done duly, without regard for any cause or reason, by giving her a bill of divorce. It is not unreasonable for us to suppose that this opinion concerning the total license to dissolve a marriage, without any cause at all, and at the husband's discretion, merely to dismiss a wife who displeased him on account of deformity, then flowed from that. This was the opinion of R. Akiba ben Joseph, a most famous Master born near the very birth of Christ, and so, with the Hillelians and Shammaeans disagreeing in that age, the latter permitting divorce only for the sake of indecency, the former even for food cooked with too much heat, that is, for any cause however slight, he adhered to the sect of the Hillelians, not without a more indulgent interpretation concerning the causes of divorce: which was afterwards embraced by the Masters. It must be observed, moreover, that it was not said that wives must be dismissed, but if anyone had decided to dismiss a wife, a bill of divorce must be given to her, to restrain the levity and petulance of husbands, whence Christ in Matt. XIX did not say Moses commanded, but permitted to you. Nor is there here any dissolution or correction of the law, but only an abuse of a custom not prescribed in the law, but tolerated for a time by the legislator, for the sake of a thick-headed and stiff-necked people, so that women would not be subject to perpetual slaughter; nor was that permission an approval of the deed of the Jews, but a non-prevention of it, nor was it without guilt in the forum of conscience, even if it were without penalty in the civil forum.

Vers. 31. Whoever shall put away his wife] This right was not granted to husbands, nor conversely to women, as among the Romans. For the first among the Jews, Salome, wife of Costobarus, usurped that license against ancient customs, as Josephus testifies. This difference had its origin from marital law. For wives under Hebrew law were in the hand of the spouse, as appears from many indications. You will rightly translate ἀπολύσῃ as 'shall have repudiated,' because it denotes most of all that act of the mind which the bill testifies, whence divorce follows. For usage, not even that of the Jurisconsults, has not received that divorce after nuptials be called 'repudium' and before nuptials 'divortium,' but the renunciation itself, whether before nuptials or after them, is accustomed to be so called. Gaius the Jurisconsult: In repudiations, that is, in renunciation, these words are approved: Keep your things to yourself; likewise these: Manage your things yourself. In the discussion of betrothals also, it was decided that a renunciation ought to intervene: in which matter these words were approved: I will not use your condition. Paulus: If a wife is sent away in a fit of heat and returns shortly, she does not seem to have been divorced. Justin Martyr to the Roman Senate: That which is called among you 'repudium,' dealing with the dissolving of marriage.

Let him give her a bill of divorce] Below, a book of divorce. By Josephus, a document of dismissal. Papinian said to give a bill of divorce, Emperor Diocletian to hand over a bill of repudiation. The origin of the name is from 'to depart,' which is to withdraw: but in the Latin language a wife who dissolves a marriage of her own accord is properly said to 'divortere' and 'discedere': which the Attics called 'to leave.' But to Jewish women, as we have said, that was not permitted. But it is properly the men's right 'to send away,' which word Josephus also uses: in Hebrew, 'to drive out.' But a bill of divorce or of separation is also rightly called that by which a husband orders his wife to divorce or depart from him. But it contained expressly, and the formula of the Jewish bill still contains today, which is as follows: OF MY OWN ACCORD, BY NO ONE'S COMPULSION, I HAVE DECIDED TO DISMISS, DESERT, AND REPUDIATE YOU, MY WIFE HITHERTO: AND NOW I THEREFORE DISMISS, DESERT, AND REPUDIATE YOU, AND CAST YOU OUT FROM ME, SO THAT YOU MAY BE OF YOUR OWN POWER AND AT YOUR OWN DISCRETION AND PLEASURE DEPART WHERE YOU WILL: AND MAY NO ONE AT ANY TIME PROHIBIT THIS. AND THUS BE DISMISSED, SO THAT IT MAY BE LAWFUL FOR YOU TO MARRY ANY MAN. Josephus teaches us that this formula is ancient when he says, 'It is not permitted for a woman who has been separated to marry on her own unless the former husband releases her.' And elsewhere: 'For thus she would receive the power'

to live with another. And hence it is that this act is called 'dismissal.' 'Ordered to leave the house,' says Quintilian. And Juvenal: 'The freedman will say, gather your little bundles and get out.' Martial: 'Wife, go outside.' Titinnius: 'Let her depart from the house.' Varro: 'He ordered her to go outside.' But the Latin language has also received the word for casting out, which the Jews use, in the same sense. Cicero: 'He drove out the mime.' If you translate the Hebrew word 'book of cutting off' literally, it will be a bill of abscission, that is, of separation. For Paul also said 'to be separated' for making a divorce, 1 Cor. VII. 10, 11, 15. Justin, 'to be separated from the union.' Latin Jurisconsults say to dissolve, separate, or break up a marriage. But those who think that it was not permitted for Jews to dismiss a wife unless the cause was proven before a judge are mistaken, as appears sufficiently from this passage. For Christ says that he who wishes to dismiss a wife, let him give a bill of divorce. Josephus removes every doubt for us, who, speaking of himself, says thus: 'At which time I also sent away my wife, not being pleased with her habits.' It is true, however, that this act, no less than the cession of an inheritance and other more solemn acts, was accustomed to be performed before judges, which the Talmudic digests teach us: but this was of voluntary, not contentious, jurisdiction, just as manumission before the Praetor in Roman law. Therefore, the judge did not interpose his cognizance unless a controversy had arisen concerning the dowry or a gift on account of marriage: clearly as also among the Romans. For in the old Roman law, an action concerning morals was instituted, by which a defeated woman lost her dowry or a part of it. But the woman could also demand, if she trusted in her innocence, that either the husband or the judges testify in writing that she was found guilty of no crime. Otherwise, as often as a divorce was made by mutual consent, as the Romans used to say, there was no need for a judicial inquiry. An illustrious example of this is in Josephus, Antiquities XVII. 1. 'In this matter, Herod sent away the daughter of King Aretas, who had been married to Alexander, to her father, having returned her dowry to him, so that there might be no dispute between them.' But it is also clear that those are mistaken who drag the phrase דבר ערות in Moses to the suspicion of adultery: although that is not a new but an old interpretation of Shammai, with Hillel, whom Josephus calls Pollio, dissenting. For if Moses had granted divorce only in that case in which Christ grants it, Christ would not say that this concession was made because of the hardness of the Jews, contrary to the original institution to which he himself recalls us: below XIX. 8, Mark X. 5. Nor would Moses have rightly said then, if it were not acceptable to him. For what need was there to say that about an adulteress? From the different authors of the School, therefore, arose that question, whether it was lawful for a husband to dismiss his wife for any cause, below XIX. 15. Today the Jews follow neither Shammai nor Hillel. For they approve of divorce not for any cause, as Hillel, but nevertheless for many causes besides fornication, which are enumerated in the Talmudic digests and are now also anxiously weighed by the Masters. But he followed the opinion of Shammai whose proverb exists concerning a wife: 'Gnaw the bone that has fallen to your lot.' To this question, which concerns the explanation of those words, adheres another much agitated among the interpreters of the sacred books, namely, whether that right established in Deuteronomy caused that which is in question to be done rightly, or whether it was merely done with impunity. That God could have relaxed the bond of matrimony introduced by Himself, if He wished; indeed, that He could have commanded the judges to overlook it while the bond remained, cannot be doubted: therefore, it is only a conjecture of the will. To me, that which I said last seems more likely to be true. First, because Christ teaches that this permission was made because of the hardness of the Jews, namely, so that occasion might not be given for harsher treatment or even for poisonings. But for such an end, the mere concession of impunity is sufficient: nor is the malice of men accustomed to be relieved by privileges. Added to this is the fact that the custom, the interpreter of the law, required no cause from the husband for the dissolution of the marriage. Otherwise, Joseph could not have dismissed Mary secretly. Therefore, the husband could say what Paulus Aemilius said at Rome, that it was best known to him where the shoe pinched.
