And yet, to dismiss a wife for no cause, or for the lightest of causes—to say nothing now of the primeval institution of God—the law of charity alone forbade, whether you consider the wife, who flees as a suppliant to the protection of her husband, or even the common children. Therefore, a divorce made for any cause could not be judged right and proper. Whence it follows that this permission, at least in some cases, freed from punishment, not from vice. Indeed, not even an example of any praised man who wished to claim that for himself is found. And the Romans, although no law forbade repudiation, nevertheless passed five hundred and twenty years without an example of repudiation. Nor is there almost any writer who does not gravely rebuke M. Tullius Cicero because he dismissed Terentia for light causes. God therefore wished by those words ערות דבר, which signify a shameful thing, or as the LXX translated it, ἄχημον πρᾶγμα, to warn the Hebrews not to dismiss their wives rashly: but that more serious evils might be avoided, he did not wish the truth and gravity of the cause to be referred to another's judgment: but permitted it to be estimated by the mind of the husband himself. Which is not surprising, since the laws of the ancient Gauls and other nations granted to husbands the power of life and death over their wives. But it is known that any judges, to whose supreme and most free power any matter is permitted, are not innocent if they depart from the rule of what is fair and good. It was therefore the law that a husband could expel a wife for any cause, but in that sense in which a Praetor is said to render justice even when he decrees unjustly, as Paulus the Jurisconsult speaks: who also said elsewhere, that not everything which is permitted is honorable. For something is said to be permitted in common usage, which is outside of punishment, and can be hindered by no one from being done. Thus it was permitted before the times of Antoninus for masters to kill slaves without a stated cause: but yet those who did so for causes not very grave, their inhumanity was hateful to good men, and Augustus is narrated to have been angry with a certain Senator on that account. Seneca well: In a slave one must consider not how much that can suffer UNPUNISHED, but how much the nature of WHAT IS FAIR AND GOOD permits to you. But the Jews, unmindful of both humanity and charity, what the law dissembled, they thought that in that nothing was sinned by them, or at least they admitted causes however futile into the patronage of their own moroseness. Concerning the passage Mal. II. 15, which is more obscure, I agree with those who interpret כי שנא שלח, because God hates τὸ ἀπολύειν. For the Hebrew construction bears this interpretation. Nor, however, do I think that this is to be understood of any divorce, but of that which was sent to women who were entirely innocent for the sole cause of a barren womb, which was also the first pretext for divorce at Rome, whence Aristotle in the fifth book of his Politics noted that the greatest discords in marriage arise. Concerning this hardness the Prophet says that women complain before God, and to show the iniquity of the deed, he uses the example of Abraham, a most wise man, who although he was held by a most just desire for offspring, yet retained his barren wife in marriage. For that Abraham is accustomed to be called אחד, the Jews have handed down with great consensus. But that name אחד seems to have adhered to Abraham from the fact that he was the one out of such a great number of men chosen by God to be the author of a holy and chosen race. This seems to be indicated at Hebrews XI. 12, διὸ κὶ ἀφ᾽ ἑνὸς ἐγεννήθησαν, where ἀφ᾽ ἑνὸς is מאחד: to which can be drawn that of the same Writer, ch. II. 11. For soon it follows: σπέρματος Ἀβραὰμ ἀντιλαμβάνεται. But just as Abraham was אחד, so his son Isaac was called by the cognomen יחיד, that is, μονογενὴς Gen. XXII. 2. Hebr. XI. 17. Sanchuniato in the Phoenician History: It was a custom among the ancients in the great crises of dangers, instead of the destruction of all, for those who held power over either city or nation to give up the beloved of their children to slaughter, a ransom to the avenging demons; and they were slaughtered as if given mystically; Cronus therefore, whom the Phoenicians call Israel, reigning over the country and later after the end of his life consecrated to the star of Cronus, having from a local bride named Anobret a son who was ONLY-BEGOTTEN, whom for this reason he called Ieoud, the only-begotten being still so called even now among the Phoenicians, when dangers from the greatest wars had overtaken the country, having adorned the son with royal attire, and having prepared an altar, he sacrificed him. In which words the Tyrian man, corrupting sacred history in many ways, which happened to almost all non-Jews who handed down Jewish matters, named Israel for Abraham, that is, the grandson for the grandfather, saying that he was the same as Saturn, doubtless because his descendants rested on the day of Saturn. But Anobret, that is, if I am not mistaken, הגברת, he called the chosen Sarah. For ἰεὺδ for יחיד is more a dialect than a corruption of the word. Thus also Orpheus placed μονογενῆ instead of the one יחיד for אחד, that is, Isaac for Abraham, when it is said to him that there was no one who rightly knew the true God,

If not some only-begotten one of the race from above of the Chaldeans. For he was knowledgeable of the course of the stars.

The Egyptians had these things ignorantly. For from the Chaldeans these things traveled to Egypt, from whence they came also to the Greeks. Orpheus therefore, whom Diodorus Siculus teaches us was in Egypt, understood there concerning Abraham and concerning Moses those things which were then either by him, or as is pleasing to Tatian, from his own books related into verse by Onomacritus. Let these things indeed be said thus probably concerning that passage of Philo of Byblos. For I am forced to doubt whether that ἰσραὴλ was not written by error in Eusebius for ἴλ, because by such a compendium ἲλ was noted by Greek Christians as ἰσραὴλ. But ἴλ in Philo of Byblos was the name of a king, whose word was given to the star of Saturn. For also elsewhere the same Philo of Byblos says that ἴλος is said by the Phoenicians, who is κρόν to the Greeks, namely אל, for which others אל.

Although wives were in the hand of the spouse by Hebrew law, indeed from the sentence promulgated after the fall Gen. III. as far as the power of the husband over the woman outside the marriage bed, yet divine law does not admit unequal power between spouses in the marriage bed, regarding conjugal faith and the conjugal debt, because neither the husband has power over his own body, nor the wife, without any inequality 1. Cor. VII. 9. whom the Apostle composes in an equal lot, not because of Roman laws, as Grotius p. 99. thinks, but by the force of the divine matrimonial law. And since the pact and connubial bond, by which spouses are one flesh, is no less violated if the husband consorts with a strange woman than if the wife has an affair with a strange man, why should it not be permitted for the woman to seek a divorce, which is permitted to the man on account of adultery? As divine law commands to punish no less the adulterer than the adulteress with death Lev. XX. 10. Deut. XXII. 22. Thus adultery, committed as much by the man as by the woman, is a cause for divorce. Mention is made here of the man dismissing his wife, not of the woman in the words of Christ, because wives more rarely dismiss their husbands: nor is it to be understood exclusively, but inclusively, on account of the equal and mutual obligation of the spouses, and their power over the marriage bed. However that forensic constitution of Deut. XXIV concerning the bill of divorce might have concerned husbands dismissing wives not on account of adultery—for that was to be punished by death—but on account of some indecency: Whence Josephus: That law permits the right of divorce to husbands alone: yet it did not depend on marital right, but was ordained on account of the σκληροκαρδίαν of the people, to avoid greater evils: and in correcting the abuse of the Pharisees, who granted dismissal for any cause whatsoever, Christ, defining divorce on account of fornication, admits no disparity between man and woman: and J. Martyr praises it in his Orat. ad Senat. Rom. the Christian woman, who sent a bill of divorce to one lusting beyond what is right, and divorced him. Whence furthermore Grotius is mistaken in this, that he thinks that by virtue of the constitution concerning the bill of divorce, it was permitted to dismiss a spouse FOR ANY CAUSE WHATSOEVER. It was a right, he says, that a husband could expel a wife for any cause, but in that sense in which a Praetor is said to render justice, even when he decrees unjustly, as Paulus the jurist speaks: who also said elsewhere, that not everything which is permitted is honorable. For something is said to be permitted in common usage which is outside of punishment, and which can be hindered by no one from being done. Thus, before the times of Antoninus, it was permitted for masters to kill slaves without a trial: but yet, those who did so for causes not very grave, their inhumanity was hateful to good men, and Augustus is narrated to have been angry with a certain Senator on that account. Seneca very well: In the case of a slave, one must consider not how much he can suffer WITH IMPUNITY, but how much the nature of WHAT IS FAIR AND GOOD permits you. But the Jews, unmindful of humanity and charity, thought that in what the law dissembled, nothing was sinned by them, or certainly they admitted causes however futile in defense of their own moroseness. But this παρερμηνεία leans rather toward the Pharisaic corruption than toward the meaning of the Mosaic constitution; in which we admit that by ערוח דבר [an indecent thing] fornication is not designated, which was the interpretation of Tertullian in his book against Marcion, ch. 34, and of Sameas, with Hillel—called Pollio by Josephus—dissenting, a point which Grotius rightly proves: For if Moses had granted divorce only in that case in which Christ grants it, Christ would not say that that concession was made because of the hardness of the Jews, contrary to the original institution, to which he himself recalls us: below XIX. 8, Mark X. 5. Nor would Moses have rightly said then, let her not be pleasing in his sight: For what need would there be to say that about an adulteress? Moreover, one must not yield to the false interpretation of the Pharisees and the opinion of Hillel, that it was permitted to expel a wife for any reason whatsoever with impunity: because the mention of an 'indecent thing' was not added in vain: by which Origen, Chrysostom, and others understand filthiness of body and mind, such as are, for example, in natural matters epilepsy, mania, sterility; in moral matters, stubbornness, disobedience, drunkenness, quarrelsomeness, etc. The Pharisees certainly understood the law in such a way that for any reason whatsoever, however slight, a husband could divorce his wife even with a clear conscience, and that both the one divorcing and the one divorced could enter into another marriage. But what Christ rejects, and censures and reproves that vague license of divorce, and does not teach that the divorce was granted as if it were lawful in itself, which, along with Scotus and Durandus, Paludanus, Tostatus, Cajetan, and Bellarmine wish, but as a lesser evil; because divorces were always illicit outside the case of adultery, as being contrary to the marriage law, and were tolerated only for the sake of avoiding a greater evil: which Thomas also acknowledges in IV Sententiarum, and Lyranus on Deut. XXIV. And Grotius himself observed that even the more recent Jews follow neither Sameas, as if it were permitted to give a bill of divorce only on suspicion of fornication, nor Hillel. For they prove, he says, that divorce is not κατὰ πᾶσαν αἰτίαν [for every cause], as Hillel held, but for many causes nevertheless ἐκτὸς τῆς πορνείας [outside of fornication], which are enumerated in the Talmudic digests; and are now also anxiously weighed by the Masters.

Latin:

Vers. 31. Ἐῤῥέθη δὲ.] Nimirum à Mose jussu divino: non privato Mosis consilio, quod sensit Origenes & eum secutus Ambrosius, quem errorem in Ptolomæo quo- dam graviter accusat Epiphanius, nisi hoc potius sensisse putemus Origenem, & Ambrosium, à Mose hæc, & a- lia quædam hujus generis, pro prudentia sua, excogitata & relata ad Deum, qui ea deince, ut isti populo & tem- poribus commoda probaverit. Certe Deut. L 3. V. 1. VI. 1. aperte dicitur Moses populo proposuisse ea, quæ Deus præceperat. Inde autem ad caput usque de divortio u- nus est atque continens sermo. Neque vero credibile est Mosem, qui de specie controversa juris hæreditarium respondere nihil voluit Deo inconsulto, in re momenti multo majoris quicquam constituisse Dei injussu: Neque movere quemquam in contrariam sententiam debuit, quod Mosi hoc factum adscribit Christus infra c. XIX. 8. Nam passim etiam ea quæ a Deo profecta nemo dubitat, Moses, quippe lectus in eam rem a Deo minister, dixisse ac præcepisse memoratur, ut infra VIII. 4. Marc. I. 44. VII. 10. Luc. V. 14.

Hic vero nec Mosis verba, nec jussus Dei respiciuntur: sed mens & sensus Pharisæorum. In eo enim est Christus, ut falsam eorum ex- plicationem redarguat, atque emendet. Quæ qualis fuerit, cum ex ipsa Christi declaratione illi ψευδερμηνείᾳ opposita, tum è loco parallelo Matth. XIX. vers. 7. & quæstione imprimis Pha- risæorum εἰ ἔξεστιν ἀνθρώπῳ ἀπολῦσαι τὴν γυ- ναῖκα αὑτᾶ κατὰ πᾶσαν αἰτίαν, manifestum. Utut autem admittamus, legem de divortiis à DEO ipso profectam, non privato Mosis consi- lio sancitam, merito tamen agnoscit Grotius, jus illud in Deuteronomio cap. XXIV. constitu- tum non effecisse, ut recte ea fierent, sed dunta- xat, ut impune fierent, quia Christus docuit per- missionem illam factam ob duritiem Judæorum, Matth. XIX. vers. 8. nimirum ne duriori tracta- tioni, aut etiam veneficiis daretur occasio, ad quem finem sufficit sola impunitatis concessio. Et observat Seldenus, quod sermonem hic mutet Christus: Quod dictum esse ait, hoc in versicu- lo Christus, in ipsa sacra lege non sic expressum habetur, quemadmodum cætera quæ de talio- ne ac juramento sequuntur. Scilicet, de illis ait, dictum est antiquis, de hoc tantummodo, dictum est, ut & alii observarunt; renitentibus aliis, & pro dicto à Mose, jussu divino, sumenti- bus. Sensus videtur, dictum esse, seu sententiam in ore hominum tunc volitasse, si quis uxorem sibi dis- plicentem velit dimittere, id rite fieri, nulla causa ratione habita, dato ei libello repudii. Quod de summa solvendi conjugii licentia, sine ulla omnino causa, ac pro viri arbitratu, tantummodo uxorem qua ob deformitatem displiceret dimittere fas esset, tum manasse absonum non est ut existimemus. Quae sententia fuit R. Aquiba Ben Joseph, celeberri- mi Magistri sub ipsis Christi natalibus nati, adeo- que dissentientibus eo in ævo Hillelianis & Sammea- nis, his non nisi ob rem turpitudinis, illis etiam ob cibum nimio ardore coctum, hoc est, causam quantu- lamcunque, divortium permittentibus, non sine in- dulgentiori de repudii causis interpretamento, Hil- lelianorum Sectæ adhæsit: quæ postmodum à Magi- stris fuit amplexata. Observandum præterea, quod non dictum fuerit, dimittendas esse uxores, sed si quis uxorem dimittere constituisset, dandum illi esse libellum repudii, ad coërcendam levitatem, & petulantiam maritorum, unde Christus Matth. XIX. non dixit ἐνετείλατο Moses, sed ἐπέ- τρεψεν ὑμῖν permisit vobis. Neque ulla hic legis solutio, vel correctio, sed abusus solum moris non præscripti in lege, sed tolerati ad tempus à legisla- tore, in gratiam populi crassi, & duræ cervicis, ne carnificinæ perpetuæ obnoxiæ essent mulieres; neque permissio ista approbatio fuit facti Judæo- rum, sed non impeditio illius, nec sine reatu in foro conscientiæ, etsi sine pœna esset in foro civi- li.

Vers. 31. Ὅς ἂν ἀπολύσῃ τὴν γυναῖκα ἀυτοῦ] Non mari- tis id jus concessum, non vicissim mulieribus, ut apud Romanos. Prima enim apud Judæos Salome Costobari uxor contra antiquos mores eam licentiam usurpavit, te- ste Josepho. Differentia hæc originem habuit ex jure maritali. Nam uxores jure Hebræo in manu erant con- jugis, ut multis indiciis apparet. Recte autem verteris ἀπολύσῃ repudiaverit, quia id actum animi maxime de- notat quem testatur libellus, unde sequitur divortium. Neque enim recepit usus, ne Jurisconsultorum quidem, ut divortium post nuptias, repudium ante nuptias dica- tur, sed ipsa renuntiatio sive ante nuptias sive post eas ita appellari solet. Cajus Jurisconsultus: In repudiis autem, id est, in renuntiatione comprobata hæc sunt verba: Tuas res tibi habeto; item hæc: Tuas res tibi agito. In spon- salibus quoque discutiendis placuit renuntiationem interve- nire oportere: in qua re hæc verba probata sunt: Condi- tione tua non utar. Paulus: Per calorem missio repudio si brevi reversa est uxor nec divortisse videtur. Justinus Mar- tyr ad Senatum Romanum: Τὸ καλούμενον παρ' ὑμῖν ῥεπού- διον, de matrimonio dirimendo agens.

Δότω ἀυτῇ ἀποστάσιον] Infra βιβλίον ἀποστασίου. Jose- pho γραμματεῖον ἀπολύσεως. Libellum divortii dare di- xit Papinianus, libellum repudii tradere Imperator Dio- cletianus. Origo nominis ab ἀφίστασθαι, quod est dis- cedere: divortere autem & discedere proprie in Latino sermone dicitur uxor, quæ sponte sua matrimonium diri- mit: Quod Attici vocabant ἀπολείπειν. At fœminis Ju- dæis ut diximus, id non licebat. Virorum autem pro- prie est τὸ ἀποπέμπεσθαι, qua voce & Josephus utitur: Hebræis גָּרֵשׁ. Recte autem libellus divortii aut disces- sionis dicitur etiam is, quo maritus jubet uxorem à se divortere aut discedere. Id autem continebat expres- se, continetque etiamnum hodie Judaici libelli formula, quæ talis est: MEA SPONTE, NULLIUS COA- CTU TE UXOREM HACTENUS MEAM DIMITTERE A ME, DESERERE AC RE- PUDIARE DECREVI: JAMQUE ADEO TE DIMITTO, DESERO AC REPUDIO, ATQUE A ME EJICIO, UT TUÆ SIS POTESTATIS TUOQUE ARBITRATU AC LUBITU QUO LIBET DISCEDAS: NEQUE ID QUISQUAM ULLO TEM- PORE PROHIBESSIT. ATQUE ITA DIMISSA ESTO, UT CUIVIS VIRO NUBERE TIBI LICEAT. Veterem esse hanc formulam Josephus nos docet cum ait, γυναικὶ οὐδι διαχωρισθείσῃ καθ' ἑαυτὴν ἔξεστι γαμηθῆναι μὴ τοῦ πρότερου ἀνδρὸς ἀφίεντος. Et alibi: λάβοι γὰρ ἂν ὕτως ἐξουσίαν

συνοικεῖν ἑτέρῳ. Et hinc est quod hic actus dicitur ἀπόλυσις. Domo egredi jussa inquit Quintilianus. Et Juvenalis: Collige sarcinulas dicet libertus & exi. Martialis: Vxor vade foras. Titinnius: ædibus facessat. Varro: foras betere jussit. Sed & ejiciendi verbum quod Judæi usurpant Latinus sermo eodem sensu recepit. Ci- cero: Mimam exegit. Hebræa vox ספר כריתת ad verbum si reddas, erit libellus abscissionis, id est χωρισμοῦ. Nam & χωρίζεσθαι pro divortium facere dixit Paulus 1. Cor. VII. 10. 11. 15. Justinus τῆς συζυγίας χωριζέσθαι. Dissolvere, separare, dirimere matrimonium dicunt Latini Jurisconsul- ti. Errare autem eos qui putant Judæis non licuisse uxorem dimittere nisi causa apud Judicem probata, satis ex hoc lo- co apparet. Dictum enim esse ait Christus, qui uxorem dimissam vult, libellum det repudii. Dubitationem o- mnem nobis Josephus eximit, qui de se agens ita ait: καθ᾽ ὃν δὴ καιρὸν κᾐ τὴν γυναῖκα μὴ ἀρεσκόμενος αὐτῆς τοῖς ἤθεσιν ἀπο- πεμψάμην. Verum tamen est hunc actum non minus, quam hæreditatis cessionem atque alios solenniores solitos coram judicibus peragi, quod nos digesta Thalmudica do- cent: sed erat hoc jurisdictionis voluntariæ, non con- tentiosæ, quomodo manumissio apud Prætorem jure Ro- mano. Cognitionem igitur suam judex non interponebat, nisi de dote aut donatione propter nuptias controversia inciderat: plane ut & apud Romanos. Nam Romano veteri jure instituta erat de moribus actio, qua victa mu- lier dotem aut totam aut partem ejus amittebat. Sed & postulare mulier poterat si innocentiæ suæ confideret, ut scripto testaretur aut maritus aut judices nullius se flagitii compertam. Alioqui quoties, ut Romani loquebantur, bona gratia fiebat divortium, nulla opus erat cognitione. Exemplum hujus illustre est apud Josephum Originum XVII. 1. Ἐν τούτῳ δὲ κᾐ τὴν ἀρχελάου θυγατέρα τοῦ βασιλέως ἡρώδης ὡς τὸν αὐτῆς πατέρα ἐξεπεμψεν ἀλεξάνδρῳ συνῳκηκυῖ- αν, ἐκ τῶν αὐτῷ τὴν προῖκα ἀποδοὺς, ὥστε ἀμφισβήτημα αὐ- τοῖς μηδὲν εἶναι. Sed & illos falli apertum est, qui apud Mo- sen דבר ערות ad stupri suspicionem trahunt: quam- quam ea non nova est sed vetus Samææ interpretatio, dissentiente Hillele quem Pollionem Josephus appellat. Nam si Moses in ea duntaxat specie divortium concessis- set in qua eam concedit Christus, non diceret Christus, eam concessionem factam ob duritiem Judæorum contra originale institutum ad quod ipse nos revocat: infra XIX. 8. Marc. X. 5. Neque recte tum dixisset Moses, si non sit gra- tiosa apud eum. Quid enim id opus dicere de adultera? Ex diversis igitur Scholæ autoribus nata illa quæstio, an liceret viro uxorem dimittere κατὰ πᾶσαν αἰτίαν infra XIX. 15. Ho- die Judæi neque Samæam sequuntur neque Hillelem. Pro- bant enim divortium non κατὰ πᾶσαν αἰτίαν ut Hillel, sed ob multas tamen causas ἐκτὸς τῆς πορνείας, quæ enumeran- tur in digestis Thalmudicis & nunc quoque à Magistris an- xie expenduntur. At Samææ sententiam ille sequebatur cujus hoc proverbium exstat de uxore: Os quod tibi con- tigit rode. Huic quæ de vocum istarum explicatione est quæstioni, adhæret altera inter sacrorum librorum inter- pretes multum agitata, an scilicet jus illud in Deutero- nomio constitutum effecerit, ut recte id de quo agitur, fieret, an duntaxat id fieret impune. Quin Deus potuerit intro- ductum à se matrimonii vinculum relaxare, si vellet: quin etiam potuerit manente vinculo judicibus dissimulationem imperare, dubitari non potest: sola ergo voluntatis conje- ctura est. Mihi id quod posterius dixi vero similius vide- tur. Primum quia ob duritiem Judæorum permissionem hanc factam Christus docet, nimirum ne duriori tractationi aut etiam veneficiis daretur occasio. Ad talem autem fi- nem sufficit sola impunitatis concessio: neque solet malitia hominum privilegiis sublevari. Accedit huc, quod con- suetudo legis interpres nullam à marito causam diremti matrimonii exegerit. Alioqui etiam non potuisset Jose- phus Mariam clam dimittere. Potuit igitur maritus dicere quod Romæ dixit Paulus Æmilius, sibi optime notum qua calceus urgeret. Atqui aut nulla, aut levissima de causa uxorem dimittere, ut jam de primæva Dei institutione ni- hil dicam, vel sola charitatis lex prohibebat, sive uxorem respicias, quæ veluti supplex ad mariti tutelam confugit, sive communes etiam liberos. Non potuit igitur factum quavis ex causa divortium rectum probumque censeri. Unde sequitur permissionem hanc, saltem in nonnullis ca- sibus, à pœna, non à vitio liberasse. Quin ne exemplum quidem ullius laudati viri, qui licere sibi id voluerit, inve- nitur. Et Romani, cum nulla lex repudium vetaret, annos tamen quingentos & vingenti sine exemplo repudii ege- runt. Ne quisquam ferme Scriptorum est, qui non gra- viter reprehendat M. Tullium Ciceronem quod levibus de causis Terentiam dimiserit. Voluit igitur Deus voci- bus illis ערות דבר quæ probrum, aut ut LXX. verte- runt ἄχημον πρᾶγμα significant, admonere Hebræos ne temere uxores dimitterent: cæterum ut graviora mala e- vitarentur & veritatem & gravitatem causæ noluit ad alie- num arbitrium referri: sed ipsius mariti animo id æsti- mandum permisit. Quod mirum non est, cum veterum Gallorum, aliarumque gentium leges jus vitæ ac necis in uxores maritis concesserint. At notum est quosvis ju- dices, quorum summæ ac liberrimæ potestati res aliqua permittitur, insontes non esse si ab æqui bonique regula discedant. Jus ergo fuit, ut quavis de causa uxorem maritus posset expellere, sed ea notione qua Prætor jus reddere dicitur etiam cum injuste decernit, ut Paulus Ju- risconsultus loquitur: qui & alibi dixit, non omne quod licet honestum esse. Licere enim in communi usu ali- quid dicitur, quod extra pœnam est, & quominus fiat a nemine impediri potest. Ita licebat ante Antonini tem- pora dominis servos occidere indicta causa: sed tamen qui id facerent ob causas non admodum graves eorum in- humanitas bonis odio erat, & Augustus narratur Sena- tori cuidam eo nomine succensuisse. Seneca optime: In mancipio cogitandum est non quantum illud IMPVNE pati possit, sed quantum tibi permittat ÆQVI BONIQVE natura. Sed Judæi & humanitatis & caritatis immemores, quod lex dissimulabat, in eo nihil a se peccari arbitra- bantur, aut certe causas quantumvis futiles admittebant in morositatis suæ patrocinium. De loco Mal. II. 15. qui est obscurior, illis assentior, qui כי שנא שלח interpre- tantur, quia odit Deus τὸ ἀπολύειν. Fert enim hanc in- terpretationem Hebræa constructio. Neque tamen arbitror id de quovis repudio intelligendum, sed de eo quod mit- tebatur fœminis plane innocentibus ex sola causa infœ- cundi uteri, qui & Romæ primus repudii obtentus fuit, unde & maximas in matrimonio discordias nasci notavit Aristo- teles de republica quinto. De hac duritie ait Propheta fœ- minas apud Deum conqueri, & ut ostendat facti iniquita- tem, exemplo utitur Abrahami, viri cordatissimi, qui cum justissimo teneretur desiderio prolis, tamen uxorem steri- lem in matrimonio retinuit. Nam אחד Abrahamum vo- cari solere, Judæi magno consensu tradidere. Videtur autem nomen illud אחד Abrahamo adhæsisse ex eo quod unus ex tanto hominum numero a Deo esset electus au- ctor sancti & immisi generis. Indicare hoc videtur ad Hebræos XI. 12. διὸ κὶ ἀφ᾽ ἑνὸς ἐγεννήθησαν, ubi ἀφ᾽ ἑνὸς est מאחד: quo trahi poteit illud ejusdem Scriptoris c. II. 11. ὅτε γὰρ ἁγιάζων κὲ οἱ ἁγιαζόμενοι ἐξ ἑνὸς πάντες. Nam mox sequitur: σπέρματος Ἀβραὰμ ἀντιλαμβάνεται. Sic- ut autem Abrahamus אחד, ita filius ejus Isaacus co- gnomento vocatus est יחיד, id est μονογενὴς Gen. XXII. 2. Hebr. XI. 17. Sanchuniato in Phœniciis: Ἔθος ἦν τοῖς πα- λαιοῖς ἐν ταῖς μεγάλαις συμφοραῖς τῶν κινδύνων ἀντὶ τῆς πάν- των φθορᾶς τὸ ἠγαπημένον τῶν τέκνων τές κρατῦντας ἢ πόλεως ἢ ἔθνους εἰς σφαγὴν ἐπιδιδόναι, λύτρον τοῖς τιμωροῖς δαίμοσι· κατεσφάττοντο δεοἱ διδόμενα μυστικῶς· Κρόνος τοίνυν, ὃν οἱ Φοίνικες Ἰσραὴλ προσαγορεύουσι βασιλεύων τῆς χώρας κέ ὕστερον μετὰ τὴν τῦ βίε τελευτὴν εἰς τὸν τῦ κρόνο ἀστέρα καθιερωθεὶς, ἐξ ἐπιχωρίας νύμφης Ἀνωβρὲτ λεγομένης υἱὸν ἔχων ΜΟΝΟΓΕΝΗ ὃν διὰ τῦτο Ἰεὲδ ἐκάλει, τῦ μονογενῦς ἔτως ἔτι κέ νῦν κα- λυμένε παρὰ τοῖς Φοίνιξι, κινδύνων ἐκ πολέμῧ μεγίσων κα- τειληφότων τὴν χώραν, βασιλικῷ κοσμήσας σχήματι τὸ ὑἹόν, βωμόν τε κατασκευασάμενος κατέθυσεν. Quibus verbis homo Tyrius multis modis sacram historiam depravans, quod fere omnibus contigit non Judæis qui res Judaicas tradiderunt, Israelem pro Abrahamo, hoc est, nepotem pro avo nominavit, eundem dicens esse Saturnum, nimirum quia posteri ejus Saturni die feriabantur. Ἀνωβρὲτ autem, id est ni fallor הגברת ἐκλεκτὴν vocavit Saram. Nam ἰεὺδ pro יחיד dialectus magis est quam corruptio vocabuli. Sic & Orpheus μονογενῆ posuit ἀντὶ τῦ ἑνὸς יחיד pro אחד id est Isaacum pro Abrahamo, cum ei dicitur nemo fuisse qui Deum verum recte cognosceret,

Εἰ μὴ μονογένης τις ἀπόῥῥοξ φύλε ἄνωθεν Χαλδαίων. ἴδρις γὰρ ἔην ἄστροιο πορείας.

νοσίας αἰγύπτιοι τέτων εἶχον ἀμαθῶς. ἐκ χαλδαίων γὰρ ταῦτ᾽ ἐφοίτησεν εἰς αἴγυπτον, ὅθεν ἦλθε καὶ εἰς τὸς ἕλληνας. Or- pheus igitur, quem in Ægypto fuisse docet nos Diodorus Siculus, ibi de Abrahamo, deque Mose ea intellexit, quæ deinde aut ab ipso, aut quod Tatiano placet ex ipsius li- bris ab Onomacrito in versus relata sunt. Hæc quidem ita probabiliter de illo Philonis Biblii loco dicta sunto. Du- bitare enim cogor an non illud ἰσραὴλ errore apud Euse- bium scriptum sit, pro ἴλ, quia tali compendio ἲλ Græ- cis Christianis ἰσραὴλ notabatur. ἴλ autem apud Philo- nem Biblium nomen fuerit regis, cujus vocabulum da- tum fuerit sideri Saturni. Nam & alibi idem Philo Biblius ἴλος ait Phœnicibus dici, qui κρόν est Græcis, אל scili- cet, pro quo alii אל.

Etsi uxores in manu conjugis fuerint jure E- bræo, imo ex sententia post lapsum promulgata Gen. III. quantum ad potestatem viri in mulierem ex- tra thorum, non tamen admittit jus divinum in- ter conjuges inæqualem potestatem in thoro, quoad fidem conjugalem & conjugale debitum, quia nec vir habet corporis sui potestatem, nec mulier, ci- tra ullam inæqualitatem 1. Cor. VII. 9. quos non ob leges Romanas, ut Grotius p. 99. autumat, sed vi legis divinæ matrimonialis pari sorte com- ponit Apostolus. Et quum pactum ac vinculum connubiale, quo conjuges sunt una caro, non minus violetur, si maritus cum aliena fœmina consue- scat, quam si uxor rem habeat cum viro alieno, quidni mulieri liceret divortium petere, quod li- cet viro propter adulterium? Ut non minus adul- terum, quam adulteram morte punire jubet lex divina Lev. XX. 10. Deut. XXII. 22. ita adulterium tam à viro, quam à muliere commissum, divortii est causa. Viri autem hic mentio fit, uxorem dimittentis, non mulieris in verbis Christi, quia rarius uxores dimittunt viros: nec exclusive id intelligendum, sed ob conjugum æqualem & mutu- am obligationem, & potestatem in thoro, inclusive. Utut ergo constitutio illa forensis Deut. XXIV. de libello repudii ad maritos, uxores dimittentes non ob adulterium, id enim morte plectendum erat, sed ob fœditatem aliquam, spectaret: Unde Jose- phus: Lex ista solis maritis jus repudii permittit: non tamen ea ex jure maritali dependebat, sed ob σκληροκαρδίαν populi, ad majora mala vitanda, sancta est: & in abusu Pharisæorum, qui ex qua- cunque caussa dimissionem concedebant, emendan- do, Christus divortium ob fornicationem defini- ens, nullam disparitatem viri & mulieris admittit: laudatq; J. Martyr Orat. ad Senat. Rom. fœminam Christianam, quæ ultra fas libidinanti repudium misit, & ab eo divortit. Unde porro fallitur in eo Grotius, quod vi constitutionis de libello repudii, licuisse QUA VIS DE CAUSA dimittere conju- gem, existimat. Jus fuit, inquit, ut quavis de causa uxorem maritus posset expellere, sed ea notione, qua Prætor jus reddere dicitur, etiam cum injuste decernit, ut Paulus, JCtus loquitur: qui & alibi dixit, non omne quod licet, honestum esse. Licere enim in communi usu aliquid dicitur, quod extra pœnam est, & quo minus fiat, à nemine impediri potest. Ita licebat ante Antonini tempora dominis servos occidere, indicta causa: sed tamen qui id facerent ob causas non admodum graves, eorum inhumani- tas bonis odio erat, & Augustus narratur Sena- tori cuidam eo nomine succensuisse. Seneca optime: In mancipio cogitandum est, non quantum illud IMPUNE pati possit, sed quantum tibi permit- tat ÆQUI BONIQUE natura. Sed Judæi hu- manitatis & charitatis immemores, quod lex dis- simulabat, in eo nihil à se peccari arbitrabantur, aut certe causas quantumvis futiles admittebant in morositasis suæ patrocinium. Sed hæc παρερμηνεία ad ad Pharisaicam corruptelam potius accedit, quam ad constitutionis Mosaicæ sententiam; in qua per ערוח דבר non designari fatemur stuprum, quæ Tertulliani libr. contr. Marc. c. 34. & Samææ inter- pretatio erat, dissentiente Hillele, à Josepho Pol- lione dicto, id quod recte probat Grotius: Nam si Moses in ea duntaxat specie divortium concessisset, in qua eam concedit Christus, non diceret Christus, eam concessionem factam, ob duritiem Judæorum contra originale institutum, ad quod ipse nos revocat: infra XIX. 8. Marc. X. 5. Neque recte tum dixisset Moses, non sit gratiosa apud eum: Quid enim id opus dicere de adultera? Cæterum nec id gratificandum Pha- risæorum ψευδερμηνείᾳ, Hillelisq; sententiæ, quod quavis de causa IMPUNE licuerit expellere conju- gem: quia non frustra addita fuit REI FOEDÆ mentio: per quam Origenes, Chrysostomus, aliiqve fœditates corporis, & animi intelligunt, quales sunt e. g. in naturalibus epilepsia, mania, sterili- tas, in moralibus pertinacia, inobedientia, ebrio- sitas, rixositas, &c. Pharisæi utique legem sic accipiebant, quod quacunque de causa, utut levissi- ma, etiam sana conscientia maritus potuerit uxo- rem repudiare, quodque cum repudians, tum re- pudiata aliud matrimonium inire potuerit. Quod vero Christus reprobat, & vagam illam divortii li- centiam taxat, ac reprehendit, neque concessum repudium docet, quasi per se licitum, quod cum Scoto & Durando, Paludanus, Tostatus, Cajetanus, Bellarm. volunt, sed ut minus malum; quia sem- per illicita fuêre divortia extra casum adulterii, ceu legi connubiali contraria, ac solum vitandi majoris mali causa tolerata: quod etiam agnoscit Thomas in IV. Sentent. & Lyran. ad Deut. XXIV. Et observavit ipse Grotius, Judæos etiam recentio- res, neque Samæam sequi, quasi tantum ob stupri su- spicionem licuerit libellum repudii dare, neque Hillelem. Probant enim, inquit, divortium non κατὰ πᾶσαν αἰτίαν, ut Hillel, sed ob multas tamen causas ἐκτὸς τ πορνείας, quæ enumerantur in digestis Thalmudt- cis; & nunc quoque à Magistris anxie expendun- tur.

## 5:32
Verse 32. But I say to you. That we said before that no part of the law promulgated by Moses is infringed by Christ, but that in the meantime better precepts are given than that law, especially insofar as it was observed in judgments, yet consistent with that divine will whose traces might appear in Moses and the Prophets, is to be recalled to memory here. For the sense is: The law of Moses, so that nothing more serious might happen, granted you judgment concerning your wife. You see to it that you use such great power humanely, certain that no divorces please God except those which extreme necessity has extorted. In the exposition of the sentences of Ben-Sira it is read: if anyone has a morose wife and does not divorce her, he does not come into judgment, that is, by that patience he obtains God as propitious.

Except for the cause of fornication. Unless for fornication, below XIX. 9. לבר מן מלתא דזנותא, the Syriac in this place: that is: outside the cause of fornication: in the other place דלא גיורח which is not an adulteress: Lactantius said 'besides the crime of adultery.' We have said before that by the name of fornication every manner of diminished modesty can be understood: just as Plautus and others have used 'stuprum' for adultery. But there are those who wish the word 'porneia' to be extended more broadly by imitation of a Hebraism, even to those offenses which do not pertain to the loss of modesty. They take an argument from the passage Judg. XIX. 2, where it is said of the Levite's concubine ותזנה עליו, by which it seems to be signified not that the concubine had intercourse with the Levite himself—for that is nothing new, nor was a concubine among the Hebrews held by law or infamy for fornication, since she differed from the mistress of the house only in dignity, and in the fact that children born from her did not have the right of succeeding their fathers in real estate (whence Josephus directly opposes 'pallakisi' [concubines] to 'eugeneis' [noblewomen] and elsewhere to 'tas episemon thugateras' [daughters of distinguished men])—but rather that she had been contumaciously disobedient to him, and finally, as follows, had deserted his company by flight. Which interpretation both the construction of the words seems to support, and the Chaldean interpreter clearly expresses. The LXX translated it 'she was angry with him.' Josephus 'she was alienated,' then 'having left her husband.' The other thing that is brought forward, concerning the worship of false gods which is accustomed to be indicated by the same name, is less firm, since in that metaphor the meaning of adultery remains, because, forsooth, the covenant entered into with God has a likeness to marriage. I, since the word 'porneia' and those which are derivatives of it have a perpetual meaning of unchastity, both among the Greeks and among the writers of these books, do not think that one should depart from the usage and propriety of the word even here. Meanwhile, so that the sense of this passage may be rightly grasped, it is to be observed that Christ in this whole discourse is not establishing civil laws, but giving precepts to the minds of individuals: and here specifically it is explained by him in what case a good man can use the benefit of the common law pertaining to divorces. Wherefore, since the law itself does not send the husband to a judge, Christ is not to be thought to do so either. And indeed if a husband were prepared to prove adultery to a judge, it would no longer be a matter of dissolving a marriage, but of punishing the adulteress. Therefore, that fornication is said to be a just cause for divorce must be referred either to lenient husbands who do not wish to demand the punishment of their wives, such as was Joseph, the husband of Mary, or to those who, because they believe or perhaps have even certainly discovered it, yet distrust their ability to prove it in court, to which that saying of Jerome pertains: wherever there is fornication and suspicion of fornication, the wife is freely dismissed. Which, however, is not to be taken in such a way that any movement of a suspicious mind should suffice for performing a divorce piously and holily: but so that the matter is not pressed to the subtlety of the laws. In that kind of question, however, nothing certain can be defined: but all this must be estimated by equity and fairness, a middle path between anxious credulity and gross negligence. Theodosius the Younger, a Christian and pious Emperor, and one who used the daily counsel of Bishops, in the question of divorce, tempering the conjectures of unchastity to the customs of his own age, judged it sufficient if a woman, without her husband's knowledge or against his will, sought out the banquets of strange men; if, against his wishes, without just and probable cause, she stayed out overnight except at her parents' house; or if she enjoyed herself at the Circus, theatrical games, or spectacles of the arena while he forbade it: To these, what did Justinian add? If a wife has intentionally caused an abortion; if she has shared a common bath with men; if, while she is in marriage, she has treated of marriage with another man. A difficult question remains, whether what is said here outside the cause of adultery is to be accepted so rigidly that no other cause can restore a tranquil mind. Those who insist on this single cause urge the words ἐκτὸς, εἰ μὴ, and what is commonly said, that it is the force of an exception to establish the generality of the definition set down. But on the contrary, Origen notes that these words are placed more by way of statement than by way of command. Nor is it rare that in such discourse what is said on occasion has the force of an example rather than of a restriction. For it is evident that not only in human laws, but also in the laws of God, some species of an act is often expressed more frequently, from which the rest ought then to be gathered, as in Exod. XXI. 18, 19, 20, 26, Deut. XIX. 5. And that interpretation will proceed much more easily if we interpret παρεκτὸς λόγου πορνείας here as when no cause of adultery underlies it: and if below in XIX. 9, with the Complutensian codex, we read not εἰ μὴ ἐπὶ πορνείᾳ but μὴ ἐπὶ πορνείᾳ, that is, not for the cause of adultery. For such locutions (which the Syriac seems to have expressed intentionally in both places) declare a species of act rather than a strict exception. But even if we suppose it to be an exception, the same opinion can remain. For in all laws, even those most odious, such as those which impose a penalty, it is accepted that where the reason is the same, the law should have the same force: but in more benign laws, interpretation proceeds even from like to like. But if we diligently attend to the nature of all of Christ's precepts, we will find that both their origin and their consummation consist in charity, which wishes us to consult for others in such a way that we are not cruel to ourselves, just as Paul teaches in 2 Cor. VIII. 13. To cast off a wife for any cause whatsoever is savage, it is inhuman. Antony reproached Cicero for casting off his wife whom he loved. It was prudently said by Varro: You must either remove your wife's fault, or bear it. He who removes the fault makes his wife more convenient for himself; he who bears it makes himself better. To which passage Gellius aptly says that a fault must be borne which can, of course, be borne honorably by a husband: for faults are lighter than crimes. How much more justly is this required of a Christian, who has professed the discipline of patience? He who is commanded to be kind even to his enemies, will he be implacably wrathful toward the partner of his life? Here it immediately occurs: is it therefore not permitted to dismiss her for any cause, not even if she has withdrawn herself to another's lust? Indeed, the same equity which had consulted for the wife here also consults for the husband, so that he is not forced to retain an unchaste woman. In the Constitutions of Clement it is read: He who keeps a woman who has been corrupted is contrary to the law of nature. Since he who keeps an adulteress is foolish and impious. In Canon VIII of the Synod of Neocaesarea: If after ordination she (someone's wife) commits adultery, he ought to put her away. Canon LXV of the Council of Elvira.

If the wife of any clergyman has committed adultery, and her husband knows that she is committing adultery, and does not immediately cast her out, let him not receive communion in the end: lest from those who ought to be an example of good conduct, there should seem to proceed a mastery of crimes. And this cause can be seen as the reason why Mark ch. X. 11 and Paul I Cor. VII. 10, commemorating this precept of Christ, use general words, with no exception appended: namely because such exceptions, coming from natural equity, are tacitly present in laws however generally pronounced. It must therefore be seen whether the same equity cannot also have a place in other cases, although less frequent, and therefore not equally necessary to be remembered. For what if a wife has plotted against the life of her husband with poison? What if, as Origen posits, she has killed their common pledges? Someone might perhaps say here that adultery conflicts with the end of marriage more than other crimes. But indeed, marriage was instituted not for the sake of offspring alone, but also for mutual aid: nor can anything be more adverse to the contract of such a close society than that by which one is committed against the life of the other. The ancient Romans distinguished in divorces between more serious and lighter morals, and perhaps someone might think that such a distinction is regarded by Christ and declared by a most well-known example. The Christian Emperors whom I mentioned enumerate some crimes outside of adultery, upon the proof of which a husband may repudiate his wife without any loss: and what is more, if he cannot prove them, they do not simply forbid the repudiation, but leave it to the husband's discretion whether he prefers to retain the wife, or to return the dowry and lose what he gave on account of the marriage. It was not permitted for Jewish women to divorce their husbands of their own accord. Nor does Christ pronounce anything about those, not even in the case of adultery. But by Roman laws the right of the husband and the woman was equal, whom the Apostle Paul therefore joins in an equal lot in I Cor. VII. 15. Justin Martyr, closest to the Apostolic times, in his oration to the Roman Senate praises a Christian woman who, using the benefit of Roman law, sent a repudiation to her husband who was lusting beyond what is right, and divorced him. "So that she might not become a partner in his injustices and impieties, by remaining in the marriage and becoming a table-companion and bed-companion." But it is added that she did this after she had achieved nothing with him by long warning and praying. That a wife of a whoring husband could not depart from the marriage for that reason, the Greeks note as having been observed perpetually among Christians in Canon XLVIII of the Apostles, and Basil in response IX. And that the same was observed in the West appears from the Eliberine Canon IX. A faithful woman who has left an adulterous husband who is faithful, and marries another, let her be prohibited from marrying: if she has married, let her not receive communion until he whom she left has first departed from the world. These and others of this kind are not unworthy of thought. But for me, weighing those things which Paul writes to the Corinthians, it is certain that these words of Christ are not to be extended further than to spouses both of whom profess the discipline of Christ. For Paul says that the Lord's precept exists concerning these: concerning others he denies that anything was expressly commanded by the Lord. Augustine, epistle LXXXIX: "For the Lord commanded both Christians that no one should dismiss his wife, except for the cause of fornication": which distinction is of the greatest moment. For among such, even if some more serious sin has been committed, reconciliation is not to be despaired of, as long as both remain in the same profession. For there are common monitors whose just counsels they ought to obey. Not any vice, but stubborn contumacy in vices, excludes one from this profession: for those who, as Tertullian speaks, depart from the rule of discipline, cease to be considered Christians. Which being rightly weighed, the principal difficulties we have raised seem to cease. For let it be that a spouse has offended against a spouse. There ought to be a place for repentance, there ought to be a place for pardon. Anger and the desire for revenge ought to be absent. What therefore prevents her whom he seriously repents of the deed from being retained in marriage, unless chastity has been diminished? In which very case many Christians abstained from another marriage, which Clement of Alexandria seems to approve of in such a way that he does not demand it as if it were necessary. Some also, like Hermes, thought that a woman touched by true repentance after one offense ought to be received again: and because of that hope, one should abstain from another marriage. That this opinion arose more from a peculiar goodness than from a common and received law appears from others and from Tertullian, who shows in more than one place that in his time those who had dismissed a wife on account of adultery were accustomed to be admitted to a second marriage. Origen narrates that the same was permitted by certain Bishops in his time: but also later it was decreed by the Eliberine, Aurelian, and first Arlesian councils that it is permitted: which the Greeks also observe now. See Chrysostom in his second oration on those who were fasting with the Jews, near the end. Lactantius also said: that he is an adulterer who has married one dismissed by her husband, and he who has dismissed his wife for a reason other than the crime of adultery, in order to marry another.

That exceptive sense is correct: but Grotius later diminishes its force, when he wishes these to be added more for the sake of example than for binding, or, having admitted the exceptive sense, he nevertheless extends divorces to other cases as well, outside of fornication, such as if a wife has plotted against the life of her husband with poison, or if she has killed their common pledges; furthermore, he determines with Origen that these are posited more by way of declaration than by command: Finally, he judges that these words of Christ are not to be extended further than to spouses, both of whom profess the discipline of Christ. But as to the first point, regarding the force of the exceptive particle, that it must be kept entirely intact is evidenced both by its proper meaning, from which we are scrupulous to depart, and by the scope and intention of Christ, and the ἀντίθεσις to the opinion of the Pharisees; because while they taught that divorce was lawful for any cause whatsoever, Christ, contradicting them, teaches that it is not lawful except for the cause of fornication, and that he who puts away his wife outside of that cause provides the occasion and cause for adultery: and finally by the parallel passage in Matt. XIX, where a clear decision of this matter is held. For when the Pharisees asked whether it is lawful to put away a wife for any cause, Christ answers that it is not lawful for any cause, except for fornication. Therefore, it is not merely an example that is brought forward, or a more frequent species of the act expressed, from which the rest ought then to be gathered, but a restriction to this single cause is expressed, and an exception of it alone: so that, indeed, all are guilty of adultery who put away their wives outside the case of fornication. Wherever, therefore, fornication does not intervene, there is no place for dismissal and divorce. And the cause of this definition of Christ shines forth from the law of matrimony; since the bond of marriage is removed by nothing else than by adultery, which fights against the very nature of marriage, by which two are one flesh, and overturns it. But the reason for other cases is different: they do not overturn the nature of marriage; whence, although divorce and separation as to bed and board may have a place on account of capital and irreconcilable enmities, cruelty, danger of poison, and other causes, yet the dissolution of the matrimonial bond does not.

Furthermore, it is manifest that we do not have here a bare statement apart from the law, but rather that what is agreeable to the divine law is being taught: namely, that divorces are not lawful outside the case of adultery, and that they are contrary to the law of marriage, are held in a similar passage in Matt. XIX, because what God has joined, let not man separate. Therefore, it is not only explained in what case a good man may use the benefit of the common law regarding divorces, but the cause is also defined, outside of which divorces are in no way lawful or legitimate. But Grotius objects in vain that adultery is not the dissolution of marriage, but that a capital punishment was sanctioned in the law. For where that execution has a place, there this question about divorce expires, nor is it to be referred, with Grotius, to old husbands who do not wish to demand their wives for punishment, or to those who, because they themselves believe, or perhaps even have discovered, yet distrust that they can prove it in court: because husbands cannot repudiate their spouses by their own will, and act as judges in their own cause, but the investigation of the cause, whether it be legitimate and just for divorce, pertains to others, to whom if the violation of matrimonial faith is proven, where the perfidious spouse cannot be seized for punishment due to absence, divorce has a place. But also where the political Magistrate is negligent or indulgent, so that he does not inflict capital punishment upon adulterers, divorce and the dissolution of marriage can be sought by the innocent party, and cannot by right be denied to them, see B. Luther, Vol. II, Jena, German, on the life of marriage, f. 151. The guilty can certainly be received back into favor, and reconciliation with them is deservedly attempted, contrary to what Jerome thought, whose opinion it was that an adulteress could not and should not be retained, in chapter XIX of Matthew. Yet a spouse is not bound to retain a perfidious partner, as seemed right to Augustine in his book on adulterous marriages to Pollentius, ch. VI, VII, and IX. For he uses his right by repudiating a perfidious spouse, by virtue of Christ's sentence. And Grotius observes that Tertullian shows in more than one place that it was customary in his time for those who had dismissed a wife for adultery to be admitted to another marriage: and that Origen reports the same was permitted by certain Bishops in his time: but also that it was later decided by the Councils of Elvira, Orange, and the first of Arles that this is lawful, which the Greeks also observe now.

Finally, as to the distinction, which Grotius warns is of the greatest importance here, between spouses, both of whom belong to the discipline of Christ, and infidels, it is of no importance here: because Christ pronounces absolutely, and without distinction or limitation, that no divorce is lawful outside of fornication, and he brings forward a universal cause, concerning everyone, without distinction, in Matthew XIX. Because those whom God has joined, man cannot separate. That reasoning, that among such who profess the doctrine of Christ, reconciliation is not to be despaired of, has nothing to do with the matter: because, as Christ defines it, separation is lawful not because of enmities, but for the sole cause of fornication. Reconciliation can certainly be attempted even in this case, as we have said, when modesty has been diminished, and Clement of Alexandria teaches that many Christians abstained from another marriage in that case, and he does not disapprove of it, yet in such a way that he does not demand it as necessary, as Grotius observes: Furthermore, the legitimate cause of divorce is fornication, and no other is recognized by Christ outside of it. Concerning which more can be read in B. Chemnitz, Mentzer, and Gerhard.

But as to the fact that some, even among the orthodox, add malicious desertion from 1 Corinthians VII. 15, which passage might seem contrary to this exceptive sense of Christ's words: it must be observed that it is one thing when the question is about the cause of a divorce to be justly made by the innocent party, which is only fornication, and another when it is about a divorce made rashly and unjustly by the guilty party, of which Paul is speaking: but if the infidel departs, let him depart: for the brother or sister is not subject to bondage in such cases. Doubtless the Apostle is explaining, not for what cause a husband may repudiate and dismiss his wife from himself, but if a spouse departs of their own accord out of malice and with the intention of deserting, what is lawful for the other spouse; and he teaches that it is not lawful for a spouse to depart from a spouse, whether faithful or infidel, provided the infidel wishes to cohabit as a spouse. Who, therefore, would approve of voluntary divorce outside the case of fornication? Add that malicious desertion is for the most part joined with adultery. But for a more accurate judgment of those things which Grotius has handed down here, one must by all means compare what we have said on Matthew XIX. 3, 4, and 9.

Ποιεῖ ἀυτὴν μοιχᾶσθαι] The law given through Moses grants a woman who has been dismissed the freedom to move on to another marriage: but after it is contracted, it forbids her to return to her former husband, lest, under the guise of divorce, men should give their wives to others for profit, which even profane writers criticize in the Spartans and Cato. And the document itself, as we have said, contains an express mention of that freedom. Nor can it be said here, as we were just saying about the husband, that the choice is indeed permitted to her, but that she ought to use it according to what is good and fair. For it is free for a husband to retain his wife: but it is not always free for a wife to return to her husband. Nor was it forbidden for anyone to marry a repudiated woman except for a Priest, whose wife, as he said, ought to be free not only from guilt but also from the suspicion of guilt. But Christ, what the law of Moses concealed for the sake of avoiding a greater evil, prohibits to those following his institutions out of natural equity. But let us see how he who dismisses an adulterous wife makes her commit adultery. Doubtless it could happen and often did happen among the Jews (whom Tacitus notes for their abandoned lust) that a woman, marked by the ignominy of divorce, and as Moses speaks, defiled, would not find another husband: and thus, cast down from the hope of marriage, would finally slip into promiscuous intercourse; for it has already been indicated that those are also accustomed to be indicated by the word μοιχέιας. But Christ deservedly cast the blame for that evil onto him who, for a light cause, had unkindly removed from himself one entrusted to his faith and protection, and not yet found guilty of any such crime. Moreover, even if it happened by chance that the woman's modesty remained intact, yet because it was not for lack of his effort that things turned out for the worst, what could have happened is deservedly imputed to him as if it had happened. It seems to me that Ambrose correctly grasped this sense: how dangerous, he says, if you offer the fragile age of a young girl to error.

Καὶ ὁς ἐὰν ἀπολελυμένην γαμήσῃ, μοιχᾶται] Augustine testifies that this clause was absent from certain copies. But now it is read in all: as also below in chapter XIX. But Christ seems to be dealing with one who marries a woman dismissed by a husband who nevertheless remains of the same discipline, and whose character therefore ought to be considered curable. For Paul teaches us, as has been said, that Christ is dealing with such marriages. Otherwise, while the law of Moses remained, as it certainly did at that time, it would have been harsh to condemn without distinction as adulterers those who had married a dismissed woman. For what if someone, moved by mercy, had taken into marriage a woman trampled by another's injury and in danger regarding her modesty? This must therefore be understood of those who received dismissed women without first having attempted all ways to reconcile the prior marriage, which Paul teaches must by all means be done, 1. 1 Cor. 7:11. Or, what is worse, gaping after other men's wives, they paved the way for themselves to marriages through divorces. Nor do the fuller words which we read below in 19:9 seem to me to point to anything else, where it is said that the former husband commits adultery, with this addition, if he marries another, and likewise that he who marries a divorced woman commits adultery: so that, namely, the crime of adultery falls back upon him who, by a new marriage, snatches away the hope of restoring harmony. Clement, Strom. 2: 'And not only does the one who puts her away become the cause at that time, but also the one who receives her, providing an occasion for the woman to sin; for if he did not receive her, she would return to her husband.' The tenth canon of the Council of Elvira holds as follows: 'But if a believer is taken by him who has left an innocent wife, and since he knew that he had a wife whom he left without cause, it has been decided that communion should not be given to her even at the end.' For this reason, it was established by the law of Theodosius that a woman who had sent a bill of divorce to her husband should not have the power of marrying within five years; and by the law of Anastasius, that not even if a divorce were made by mutual consent, should it be permitted for the woman to proceed to a second marriage within a year. And it is not far removed from this that at Athens, a woman wishing to divorce her husband had to bring the document to the magistrates not through another, but by herself, and summon her husband there, as Plutarch noted in his Alcibiades. All these things, just as they were prudently and wholesomely established to foster the hope of reconciliation, and so that adulteries might not be glued to marriages through the ease of divorces, so it seemed harsh to the Emperors that a woman who has been dismissed by her husband should at no time, and not even after all things that made for reconciliation had been attempted, and the husband's obstinacy, which was incurable and unworthy of a Christian man, had been explored, be admitted to second marriages: therefore, by the law of Constantine, the wife of an absent husband, after the intervention of four years, with no sign of his being alive having been received, is permitted to marry another: which, although it was abolished by the Emperor Justinian, another thing was nevertheless established by the same, in which there is much less equity, namely, that a marriage can be dissolved when a husband has been detained in captivity for some time. But what Paul says in 1 Cor. 7:39, that women remain bound to their husbands while they live, does not pertain to the question of divorces, since Paul intended to prove nothing else there than that the conjugal bond does not extend beyond the death of the husband, and therefore that second marriages are not rightly condemned. Indeed, the same Apostle elsewhere, although for a different purpose, using the same statement, cites the law of Moses as the author, Rom. 7:1. But there is no doubt that by the law of Moses, a marriage could be dissolved by divorce even before death. But let us return to the words of Christ; he says that he who takes a divorced woman is held by the crime of adultery, not only because marriages hastened after a divorce are wont to be suspected of past adultery: looking to which Martial said: She who marries so often is an adulteress by law, I am less offended by a simpler harlot. And the Mime: Frequent marriages have the place of a curse. But also because adultery before God is whatever is opposed to marriage the love owed to a spouse, which that it is adultery even if the act does not follow has already appeared before, or whether one interposes oneself so that love may not be renewed after a little cooling. But I have said these things about divorces with the intention of giving the pious and learned an opportunity to examine the matter more diligently. May that opinion prevail in doubt which wishes the faith of marriage to be as holy and unshaken as possible: lest we rashly break the bond instituted by God.

It seems to Grotius that Christ is dealing with one who marries a woman dismissed by her husband, who nevertheless remains of the same (Christian) discipline, and whose character therefore ought to be considered curable, so that the crime of adultery falls back upon him who by a new marriage has cut off the hope of restoring concord. But Christ added nothing about a believer or an unbeliever: nor does it make any difference to the law or substance of marriage whether one is a believer or an unbeliever. And therefore the true opinion of Christ remains, that he who marries a dismissed woman (outside the case of fornication) commits adultery, whether the husband who dismissed her is and remains a believer or not, because since such a repudiation is rash and illegitimate, done outside the cause of fornication, the matrimonial bond remains, and therefore he who marries a dismissed woman commits adultery. There is no reason, therefore, for Grotius to object that it would have been harsh, while the law of Moses remained, to condemn without distinction those who had married a dismissed woman as adulterers. They are indeed condemned, as adulterers not in the forum of the State, but of Conscience: because they marry her who was bound to her husband by the bond of marriage. But what if someone, moved by pity, had taken into marriage a woman trampled by another's injury and in danger regarding her chastity? Resp. If the bond of marriage remained safe, how could he take her into marriage without the crime of adultery? But the moral law pronounces the union to be indissoluble Gen. II. 24. Even if therefore in the forensic law repudiations were permitted, nevertheless what is or is not a sin before God is to be judged not from forensic laws, but from the moral law. And the opinion of Paul is clear 1. Corinthians VII. 39. that women remain bound to their husbands, while life remains; which Grotius rashly denies pertains to the question of divorces. For even if Paul intended to prove only that the conjugal bond does not extend beyond the death of the husband; and therefore that second marriages are not rightly condemned, yet that axiom is general: The woman is bound by the law as long as her husband lives. As long therefore as the husband has not yielded to fate, she remains, even if repudiated, bound to her husband. Which he also proves by the law of Moses Rom. VII. 1. where Grotius has denied in vain that it is doubtful by the law of Moses whether a marriage could be dissolved by divorce even before death. For this is entirely the κρινόμενον concerning the moral law, but the permission of the forensic law, made because of the σκληροκαρδίαν of the Jews, does not deserve to be attended to here, where it is being investigated what is a sin in the forum of conscience. And finally Grotius himself acknowledges that adultery before God is whatever is opposed to marriage, and therefore that he who seizes a dismissed woman is held by the crime of adultery: and he wishes that opinion to prevail which wishes the faith of marriage to be as holy and unshaken as possible, lest we rashly break the bond instituted by God.

Latin:

Vers. 32. Ἐγὼ δὲ λέγω ὑμῖν] Quod ante diximus nul- lam juris per Mosem promulgati partem à Christo infringi, at præcepta interim dari meliora quam lex illa, præsertim quatenus in judiciis observabatur, exigebat, ei tamen di- vinæ voluntati convenientia cujus vestigia, in Mose & Pro- phetis apparerent, hic in memoriam revocandum est. Sen- sus enim est: Lex Mosis ne quid gravius eveniret, tibi de uxore judicium indulsit. Tu vide ut tanta potestate hu- mane utaris, certus nulla Deo placere divortia, nisi quæ summa necessitas extorsit. In expositione sententiarum Ben-syræ legitur: si quis uxorem habeat morosam & eam non repudiet eum non venire in judicium, id est, ea pa- tientia Deum obtinere propitium.

Παρεκτὸς λόγου πορνείας] εἰ μὴ ἐπὶ πορνείᾳ infra XIX. 9. לבר מן מלתא דזנותא, Syrus hoc loco: id est: extra causam stupri: altero loco דלא גיורח que non sit adul- tera: præter crimen adulterii dixit Lactantius. Πορνείας nomi- ne omnem modum imminutæ pudicitiæ intelligi posse pri- dem diximus: quomodo & Plautus aliique stuprum pro a- dulterio posuerunt. At sunt qui πορνείας vocem imitatione Hebraïsmi latius porrigi velint, ad ea etiam delicta, quæ ad pudicitiæ damnum non pertinent. Argumentum sumunt ex loco Judic. XIX. 2. ubi de concubina Levitæ dicitur ותזנה עליו quo significari videtur non concubinam cum ipso Le- vita consuesse, id enim nihil novi, neq; concubina apud He- bræos stupti aut lege aut infamia tenebatur, cum à matrefa- milias tantum dignitate distaret, & eo quod liberis ex ea na- tis jus non esset succedendi patribus in rebus soli (unde Jo- sephus παλλακίσι directe opponit εὐγένεδας & alibi τὰς δια- σήμων θυγατέρας) sed potius eam ipsi contumaciter immo- rigeram fuisse, ac tandem quod sequitur fuga deseruisse ipsius contubernium. Quam interpretationem & constru- ctio vocum erigere videtur, & clare exprimit Chaldæus in- terpres. LXX. verterunt ὠργίσθη αὐτῷ. Josephus ἀλλοτρίως ἔσχε, deinde καταλιπῦσα τὸν ἄνδρα. Alterum quod affertur, de falsorum Deorum cultu qui eodem nomine indicari so- let, minus firmum est, cum in ea tralatione maneat adulterii significatus, quia nimirum fœdus cum Deo initum matrimonii habet similitudinem. Ego, cum vox πορνείας & quæ huic sunt παράγωγα tum apud Græcos, tum apud horum librorum Scriptores perpetuam impudicitiæ significationem habeat, ne hic quidem recedendum ab usu & proprietate vocis existimem. Interim ut hujus loci sensus recte accipiatur, observandum est, Christum toto hoc sermone non leges constituere civiles, sed animis singulorum dare præcepta: & hic nominatim ab eo exponi, quo casu vir bonus legis communis ad divortia spectantis beneficio uti possit. Quare cum lex ipsa maritum ad judicem non remittat, ne Christus quidem id facere censendus est. Et sane si maritus paratus esset probare adulterium judici, jam non de dirimendo matrimonio, sed de punienda adultera ageretur. Quod ergo stuprum justa esse divortii causa dicitur, id referri debet aut ad maritos lenes, qui ad pœnam deposeere uxores nolunt, qualis erat Josephus Mariæ conjux, aut ad eos qui quod ipsi credunt aut forte etiam certo con.pererunt probare tamen se in judicio posse diffidunt, quo illud Hieronymi pertinet: ubicunque est fornicatio & fornicationis suspicio, libere uxor dimittitur. Quod tamen non ita accipiendum est, ut quivis motus animi suspicacis ad pie sancteque faciendum divortium valere debeat: sed ne ad legum subtilitatem res exigatur. In isto autem quæstionum genere nihil certi definiri potest: sed omne hoc ex æquo bonoque æstimandum est, medio itinere inter anxiam credulitatem & crassain supinitatem. Theodosius junior, Imperator Christianus, & pius, & Episcoporum quotidiano usus consilio, in quæstione divortii impudicitiæ conjecturas ad sui sæculi mores temperans, sufficere judicavit si mulier viro ignorante vel nolente extraneorum virorum convivia appeteret; si ipso invito, sine justa & probabili causa, foris pernoctaret nisi apud suos parentes; vel si Circensibus theatralibus vel ludis aut arenarum spectaculis ipso prohibente gauderet: Quibus istas addidit Justinianus? Si uxor de industria abortum fecerit; si commune lavacrum cum viris habuerit; si dum est in matrimonio cum alio viro de matrimonio egerit. Restat difficilis quæstio, an quod hic dicitur extra adulterii causam, tam rigide sit accipiendum, ut nulla alia causa possit animum tranquillum reddere. Qui in hac sola causa consistunt, urgent verba ἐκτὸς, εἰ μὴ, & quod dici solet eam esse vim exceptionis, ut positæ definitionis generalitatem adstruat. Sed contra notat Origenes verba hæc poni magis enuntiando quam jubendo. Neque rarum est, ut in tali sermone id quod ex occasione dicitur exempli magis quam adstringendi vim habeat. Non enim in humanis tantum, sed & in Dei legibus palam est sæpe facti aliquam speciem frequentiusve exprimi, ex qua deinde cætera colligi debeant, ut Exod. XXI. 18. 19. 20. 26. Deut. XIX. 5. Atq; ea interpretatio multo facilius procedet si παρεκτὸς λόγου πορνείας hic interpretemur cum nulla subsit causa adulterii: & si infra XIX. 9. cum codice Complutensi legamus non εἰ μὴ ἐπὶ πορνείᾳ sed μὴ ἐπὶ πορνείᾳ, id est, non ob adulterii causam. Nam tales locutiones (quas utroque loco de industria Syrus videtur expressisse) speciem facti declarant magis, quam strictam exceptionem. Sed etsi ponamus esse exceptionem, potest eadem manere sententia. In omnibus enim legibus, etiam maxime odiosis, quales sunt quæ pœnam irrogant, receptum est, ut ubi eadem est ratio jus idem valeat: in benignioribus autem legibus etiam a paribus ad paria procedit interpretatio. Quod si diligenter advertamus ad naturam omnium Christi præceptorum, reperiemus & originem eorum & consummationem in charitate consistere, quæ ita nos vult aliis consulere, ut ne in nos ipsos crudeles simus, quemadmodum docet Paulus 2. Cor. VIII. 13. Quavis de causa uxorem protrudere, sævum est, inhumanum est. Ciceroni exprobrabat Antonius ἐκβαλὼν αὐτοῦ γυναῖκα παρ᾽ ἦν ἠγάπατο. Dictum prudenter a Varrone: Vxoris vitium tollas opus est, aut feras. Qui tollit vitium, uxorem commodiuseulam Sibi præstat; quifert, sese meliorem facit. Ad quem locum apposite Gellius vitium ait ferendum esse quod ferri scilicet a viro honeste potest: vitia enim flagitiis leviora esse. Quanto autem hoc justius a Christiano, patientiæ disciplinam professo, exigitur? qui in ipsos inimicos benignus esse jubetur, is in sociam vitæ erit implacabiliter iracundus? Hic statim succurrit: nulla ne igitur de causa dimittere licet, ne quidem si alienæ libidini se substraxerit? Imo vero eadem æquitas quæ uxori consuluerat, hic & viro consulit, ne retinere cogatur impudicam. In Clementis constitutionibus legitur: ὁ κατέχων τὴν παραφθαρεῖσαν, φύσεως θεσμοῦ παράνομος. ἐπείπερ ὁ κατέχων μοιχαλίδα ἄφρων κὴ ἀσεβής. In Canone VIII. Synodi Neocæsariensis: Ἐάν μετὰ τὴν χειροτονίαν μοιχευθῇ (γυνή τινος) ὀφείλει ἀπολῦσαι αυτήν. Eliberini Concilii canon LXV.

Si cujus Clerici uxor fuerit mœchata, & scierit eam maritus suus mœchari, & non statim eam projecerit, nec in fine acci- piat communionem: ne ab his qui exemplum bonæ conversatio- nis esse debent, ab eis videantur scelerum magisteria procedere. Et hæc causa videri potest, cur Marcus cap. X. 11 & Paulus I. Cor. VII. 10. hoc Christi præceptum commemorantes, ver- bis utantur generalibus, nulla exceptione apposita: nimi- rum quia tales exceptiones ex naturali æquitate venientes tacite insunt legibus quantumvis generaliter pronuntia- tis. Videndum ergo est an eadem æquitas non possit et- iam in aliis casibus, quanquam minus frequentibus, ideo- que memoratu haud æque necessariis, locum habere. Quid si enim uxor veneno vitæ mariti insidiata fuerit? quid si, quod ponit Origenes, communia pignora interfecerit? Di- cat hic forte aliquis adulterium magis quam cætera crimi- na pugnare cum fine matrimonii. At enim non prolis so- lius, sed & mutui auxilii causa conjugium est institutum: nec quicquam potest contractui tam arctæ societatis ma- gis esse adversum, quam quo in vitam committitur. Roma- ni veteres distinguebant in divortiis inter mores graviores & leviores, ac forte putet aliquis tale discrimen à Christo respici & notissimo exemplo declarari. Christiani quos dixi Imperatores extra adulterium aliquot scelera enume- rant, quibus probatis maritus sine ullo damno uxorem re- pudiet: & quod est amplius, ea si probare nequeat, non sim- pliciter repudium vetant, sed in arbitrio mariti relinquunt malitne uxorem retinere, an dotem reddere, & amittere quod propter nuptias donavit. Fœminis Judæis non licebat sponte sua à marito divortere. Neque Christus quicquan de illis pronuntiat, ne quidem in adulterii casu. At legibus Romanis par erat jus mariti & fœminæ, quos propterea pari sorte componit Paulus Apostolus I. Cor. VII. 15. Justi- nus Martyr Apostolicis temporibus proximus in oratione ad Senatum Romanum laudat fœminam Christianam quæ usa Romano legis beneficio marito ultra fas libidinanti re- pudium misit, & ab eo divortit. Ὅπως μὴ κοινωνὸς τῶν ἀδι- κημάτων καὶ ἀσεβημάτων γένηται, μένουσα ἐν τῇ συζυγίᾳ καὶ ὁ- μοδίαιτος καὶ ὁμόκοιτος γενομένη. Sed additur fecisse hoc il- lam, postquam diu monendo precandoque nihil apud eum profecerat. Viri autem scortantis uxorem eam ob causam discedere a matrimonio non potuisse, observatum perpe- tuo inter Christianos notant Græci ad Canon. Apostoli- cum XLVIII. & Basilius responso IX. Idemque in Occi- dente observatum apparet ex Eliberino Canone IX. Fœ- mina fidelis quæ adulterum maritum reliquerit fidelem, & al- terum ducit, prohibeatur ne ducat: si duxerit, non prius acci- piat communionem, nisi quem reliquerit, prius de sæculo exierit. Hæc aliaque hujus generis cogitatu sunt non indigna. At mihi expendenti ea quæ Paulus ad Corinthios scribit, cer- tum sit Christi hæc verba non ulterius extendenda, quam ad conjuges quorum uterque Christi disciplinam profite- tur. De his enim Paulus præceptum Dominicum ait ex- stare: de aliis diserte aliquid à Domino præceptum negat. Augustinus epistola LXXXIX. Ambobus quippe Christianis Dominus præcepit, ne quisquam dimittat uxorem, excepta cau- sa fornicationis: quæ distinctio maximi est momenti. Nam inter tales etiamsi quid peccatum sit gravius, non est despe- randa reconciliatio, quamdiu uterque manet in eadem pro- fessione. Sunt enim communes monitores quorum æquis consiliis parere debeant. Ab hac professione non vitium quodlibet sed præfracta in vitiis contumacia excludit: qui enim, ut Tertullianus loquitur, excedunt de regula disci- plinæ, desinunt haberi Christiani. Quo recte expenso ces- sare videntur præcipuæ quas movimus difficultates. Esto enim, deliquerit conjux in conjugem. Debet esse pœni- tentiæ, debet & veniæ locus. Iracundia & ultionis cupi- ditas abesse debent. Quid igitur obstat, quominus in ma- trimonio retineatur ea quam serio facti pœnitet, nisi pudi- citia sit imminuta? Quo tamen ipso casu multi Christiano- rum ab altero matrimonio abstinebant, quod ipsum ita pro- bare videtur Clemens Alexandrinus, ut tamen non exigat quasi necessarium. Quidam etiam, ut Hermes, putabant mulierem post unum delictum vera pœnitentia tactam recipi iterum debere: atque ob eam spem ab altero matri- monio abstinendum. Quam sententiam ex bonitate pe- culiari magis ortam, quam ex communi receptaque lege tum ex aliis tum ex Tertulliano apparet, qui non uno loco ostendit solitos suo tempore ad matrimonium alterum ad- mitti qui ob adulterium uxorem dimisissent. Idem suo tempore à quibusdam Episcopis permissum narrat Orige- nes: sed & serius conciliis Eliberino & Aurelianensi & Are- latensi primo decretum est id licere: quod nunc quoque Græci observant. Vide Chrysostomum oratione altera de his qui cum Judæis jejunabant circa finem. Etiam Lactan- tius dixit: adulterum esse qui à marito dimissam duxerit, & eum qui præter crimen adulterii uxorem dimiserit, ut alte- ram ducat.

Recte se habet ille sensus exceptivus: sed vim ejus imminuit postea Grotius, cum exempli ma- gis, quam adstringendi gratia hæc addi vult, aut ad- misso exceptivo sensu, extendit tamen divortia ad alios etiam casus, extra fornicationem, utpote si uxor veneno vitæ mariti insidiata fuerit, aut si com- munia pignora interfecerit; adhæc magis enuncian- do, quam jubendo hæc poni, cum Origene statuit: Denique hæc Christi verba non ulterius exten- denda censet, quam ad conjuges, quorum uterque Christi disciplinam profitetur. Verum quod pri- mo ad vim particulæ exceptivæ, omnino illam in- tegram servandam esse, tum propria ejus signifi- catio evincit, à qua discedere religio nobis est, tum scopus & intentio Christi, ac ἀντίθεσις ad Pha- risæorum sententiam, quia illis docentibus, ob quamcunque causam licita esse divortia, Christus contradicens, non nisi ob causam fornicationis ea licita esse, & qui extra eam causam eam dimittit uxorem, eum adulterio occasionem & causam præbere docet: tum denique locus parallelus Matth. XIX. ubi clara habetur hujus rei decisio. Quum enim quærerent Pharisæi, an liceat quavis ex causa dimittere uxorem, respondet Christus, non licere ulla ex causa, nisi ob fornicationem. Non ergo exemplum tantum adfertur, aut facti species frequentior exprimitur, ex qua deinde cætera colligi debeant, sed expressa est ad unicam hanc cau- sam restrictio, ejusque solius exceptio: ut nem- pe omnes adulterii rei sint, qui dimittunt uxo- res extra casum fornicationis. Ubicunque ergo non intervenit fornicatio, ibi nullum locum habet dimissio, & divortium. Et causa definitionis hu- jus Christi è lege matrimoniali elucescit; Siquidem vinculum matrimonii nulla alia re tollatur, quam per adulterium, quod cum ipsa conjugii natura pu- gnat, qua duo in unam carnem sunt, eamque e- vertit. Aliorum autem casuum alia est ratio: qui non evertunt naturam conjugii: unde tametsi ob inimicitias capitales & irreconciliabiles, sævitiam, periculum veneni, & alias causas divortium, & se- paratio quoad thorum & mensam locum habeat, non tamen solutio vinculi matrimonialis.

Porro non nudam enunciationem hic haberi ci- tra legem, sed potius quid consentaneum legi di- vinæ sit, doceri, in propatulo est: nimirum non licita esse divortia extra casum adulterii, eadem- que legi matrimonii contraria esse, in loco simi- li habentur Matth. XIX. quia quos Deus conjunxit, homo ne separet. Non ergo tantum exponitur quo casu vir bonus legis communis ad divortia spe- ctantis beneficio uti possit, sed definitur etiam cau- sa, extra quam nullo modo licita, aut legitima sunt divortia. Nequicquam vero regerit Gro- tius, adulterium non diremtionem matrimonii, sed pœnam capitalem sancitam esse in lege.
