Ubi e- nim ea exequutio locum habet, ibi exspirat hæc quæstio de divortio, nec cum Grotio ad maritos senes, qui ad pœnam deposcere uxores nolunt, aut ad eos, qui quod ipsi credunt, aut forte et- iam compererunt, probare tamen se in judicio pos- se diffidunt, hæc referenda: quia non possunt mariti conjuges repudiare, proprio arbitrio, & in causa propria arbitrari, sed causæ cognitio, an legitima & justa sit ad divortium, ad alios per- tinet, quibus si probetur violatio fidei matrimo- nialis, ubi conjux perfida ob absentiam, non rapi possit ad supplicium, divortium locum habet. Sed & ubi negligens aut indulgens Magi- stratus Politicus est, ut adulteris pœnam non ir- roget capitalem, divortium & solutio matri- monii à parte innocente peti potest, eique de- negari, jure non potest, vid. B. Luther. T. II. Jen. Germ. de vit. Conjug. f. 151. Recipi sane possunt in gratiam nocentes, & tentatur merito cum iis- dem reconciliatio, secus atque existimavit Hie- ronymus, cujus ea fuit sententia adulteram non posse, nec debere retineri, in cap. XIX. Matth. Non tamen tenetur retinere partem perfidam conjux, uti visum Augustino l. de adulter. Conjug. ad Pollent. c. VI. VII. & IX. Utitur enim jure suo repudiando perfidam conjugem, vi sententiæ Christi. Et observat Grotius, Tertullianum non uno loco ostendere, solitos suo tempore ad matrimo- nium alterum admitti, qui ob adulterium uxorem dimississent: idemque suo tempore à quibusdam Epi- scopis permissum referre Origenem: sed & serius Conciliis Eliberino, & Aureacensi, & Arelatensi pri- mo decertum esse, id licere, quod nunc quoque Græ- ci observent.

Quod denique ad distinctionem, quam maxi- mi momenti hic esse Grotius monet, inter conju- ges, quorum uterque ad Christi disciplinam pertinet, & infideles, ea hic nullius est momenti: quia Chri- stus absolute, & citro distinctionem, aut limita- tionem pronunciat, nullum divortium licitum es- se extra fornicationem, causamque adfert univer- salem, omnes attinentem, citra distinctionem Matth. XIX. Quia quos Deus conjunxit, homo se- parare non potest. Ratio illa, quod inter tales, qui doctrinam Christi profitentur, desperanda non sit reconciliatio, nihil ad rem facit: quia non ob inimicitias, sed ob solam fornicationis causam licita est, Christo definiente, separatio. Re- conciliatio sane etiam in hoc casu, ut diximus, tentari potest, cum imminuta est pudicitia, ac multos Christianorum ab altero matrimonio in eo casu abstinuisse, Clemens Alexandrin. docet, nec id improbat, sic tamen ut non exigat, quasi necessa- rium, observante Grotio: Cæterum causa di- vortii legitima est fornicatio, nec extra eam alia à Christo agnoscitur. De quo plura penes B. Chemnit. Mentzer. & Gerhardum legi pote- runt.

Quod vero nonnulli etiam ex orthodoxis ma- litiosam desertionem è 1. Corinth. VII. 15. addunt, qui locus huic exceptivo sensui verborum Christi contrarius videri possit: observandum, quod a- liud sit, cum de causa quæritur divortii à parte innocente juste faciendi, quæ tantum est fornicatio, aliud cum de divortio à parte nocente temere, at- que injuste facto agitur, de quo Paulo sermo est: quod si infidelis discedit, discedat: non enim servi- tuti subjectus est frater, aut soror hujusmodi. Ni- mirum explicat Apostolus, non qua de causa maritus uxorem repudiare, atque à se dimittere possit, sed si conjux sponte ex malitia, animoque deserendi discedat, quid alteri conjugi licitum sit; docetque non licere discedere conjugi à con- juge sive fideli, sive infideli, modo conjugiali- ter cohabitare velit infidelis. Qui ergo divor- tium voluntarium extra fornicationis casum proba- ret? Adde, quod malitiosa desertio cum adulterio plerumque conjuncta sit. Sed ad accuratiorem eorum quæ hic Grotius tradidit dijudicationem conferenda omnino quæ ad Matth. XIX. 3. 4. & 9. diximus.

Ποιεῖ ἀυτὴν μοιχᾶσθαι] Lex per Mosem data fœminæ dimissæ libertatem concedit migrandi ad alteras nuptias: sed post eas contractas, vetat eam ad priorem maritum redire, ne scilicet specie divortii alii aliis uxores darent usurarias, quod profani etiam Scriptores in Lacedæmo- niis & Catone reprehendunt. Et libellus ipse, ut dixi- mus, continet expressam ejus libertatis mentionem. Ne- que hic potest dici, quod modo de marito dicebamus, permitti quidem ipsi arbitrium, sed quo debeat ex bono & æquo uti. Nam marito liberum est uxorem retinere: uxori autem non semper liberum est ad maritum reverti. Nec cuiquam interdictum erat repudiatam ducere præterquam Sacerdoti, cujus uxor, ut ille dicebat, non culpa tantum, sed & culpæ suspicione vacare debebat, At Christus, quod majoris mali vitandi causa lex Mosis dissimulabat, ex naturali æquitate prohibet sua instituta sectantibus, Quomodo autem qui dimittit uxorem adulteram eam efficiat videamus. Nimirum fieri poterat fiebatque sæpe apud Judæos (quos projectæ libidinis Tacitus notat) ut mulier ignominia divortii notata, & ut Moses loquitur polluta, maritum alterum non inveniret: atque ita dejecta à spe nuptiarum tandem ad vagos concubitus delaberetur; nam eos quoque μοιχέιας voce indicari solere jam ante indicatum est. Ejus autem mali culpam merito Christus in eum rejecit, qui levi de causa suæ fidei tutelæque traditam, neque dum ullius talis flagitii compertam, à se inclementer amoverat. Quin etiamsi casu eveniret, ut illibata maneret mulieris pudicitia, tamen quia per illum non stetit, quo minus res pessime verteret, merito illi quod fieri potuit pro facto imputatur. Hunc sensum recte mihi videtur attigisse Ambrosius: quam periculosum, inquit, si fragilem adolescentulæ ætatem errori offeras.

Καὶ ὁς ἐὰν ἀπολελυμένην γαμήσῃ, μοιχᾶται] Abfuisse hanc particulam à quibusdam exemplaribus testatur Augustinus. At nunc in omnibus legitur: ut & infra cap. XIX. Videtur autem Christus agere de ducente dimissam à viro qui tamen disciplinæ ejusdem maneat, ac cujus proinde ingenium haberi debeat sanabile. Nam de talibus conjugiis à Christo agi Paulus ut dictum est nos docet. Alioqui manente Mosis lege, ut certe manebat eo tempore, durum fuisset sine discrimine tanquam adulteros damnari qui dimissam duxissent. Quid si enim fœminam aliena injuria proculcatam & de pudicitia periclitantem misericordia motus aliquis in matrimonium suscepisset? Intelligendum hoc ergo de illis, qui dimissas excipiebant, non tentatis prius omnibus viis ad reconciliandum prius matrimonium, quod omnino faciendum docet Paulus 1. Cor. VII. 11. aut quod pejus est, alienis uxoribus inhiantes per divortia sibi nuptiis sternebant viam. Neque alio mihi spectare videntur pleniora verba quæ infra legimus XIX. 9. ubi dicitur committere adulterium maritus prior, hoc addito si aliam duxerit, atque itidem committere adulterium qui dimissam ducit: ut scilicet in illum recidat adulterii crimen qui novo matrimonio spem restituendæ concordiæ abripit. Clemens Strom. II. οὐ μόνον δὲ ὁ ἀπολύσας αἴτιος γίνεται τότε, ἀλλὰ καὶ ὁ παραδεξάμενος αὐτὴν, ἀφορμὴν παρέχων τῷ ἁμαρτῆσαι τῇ γυναικί· εἰ γὰρ μὴ δέχοιτο, ἀνακάμψει πρὸς τὸν ἄνδρα. Canon decimus Concilii Eliberini sic habet: quod si fuerit fidelis quæ ducitur ab eo qui uxorem inculpatam reliquit, & cum scierit illum habere uxorem quam sine causa reliquit, placuit huic nec in fine dandam communionem. Hac scilicet de causa Theodosii lege constitutum fuit, ut mulier, quæ viro misisset repudium, intra quinquennium nubendi non haberet potestatem: & Anastasii lege, ne etiam bona gratia sive communi consensu facto divortio intra annum liceret mulieri ad secundas nuptias convolare. Nec longe abit quod Athenis mulier à viro divertere volens, non per aliam, sed per seipsa ferre libellum ad magistratus debuit, eoque virum vocare, ut Plutarchus Alcibiade notavit. Quæ omnia sicut prudenter ac salutariter sunt constituta ad fovendam spem reconciliationis, & ne per divortionum facilitatem adulteria nuptiis agglutinarentur, ita durum visum est Imperatoribus eam quæ à viro sit dimissa, nullo unquam tempore, ac ne quidem post tentata omnia quæ ad reconciliationem faciebant, exploratamque insanabilem & indignam Christiano homine mariti contumaciam, ad alteras nuptias admitti: itaque Constantini lege, uxor mariti absentis, post interventum annorum quatuor, nullo suspitatis ejus accepto indicio nubere alteri permittitur: quod quanquam sublatum est ab Imperatore Justiniano, aliud tamen ab eodem constitutum est in quo multo minus est æquitatis, nimirum ut marito aliquanto tempore in captivitate detento solvi possit matrimonium. Quod vero Paulus ait 1. Cor. VII. 39. manere fœminas maritis obnoxias vita manente, ad divortiorum quæstionem non pertinet, cum nihil aliud ibi probare instituerit Paulus, quam ultra mortem mariti conjugale vinculum non extendi, ac proinde secundas nuptias non recte damnari. Quin idem Apostolus alibi, quanquam diverso fine, idem enuntiatum usurpans legem Mosis citat autorem Rom. VII. 1. At lege Mosis dubium non est etiam ante mortem posse divortio connubium dirimi. Sed ad Christi verba redeamus; dicit is adulterii crimine teneri eum qui dimissam arripit, non modo qua festinatæ post divortium nuptiæ suspectæ esse solent retro adulterii: quo spectans Martialis dixit: toties quæ nubit adultera lege est: Offendor mœcha simpliciore minus. Et Mimus: Habent locum maledicti crebræ nuptiæ. Verum etiam quia adulterium est apud Deum quicquid matrimonio adversatur, neque multum refert amorem quis conjugi debitum in se derivet, quod adulterium esse et- iamsi actus non sequatur jam ante apparuit, an vero se- met interponat ne post frigusculum amor redintegretur. Sed hæc de divortiis dixi eo dixi animo ut piis & eruditis occasionem darem rei diligentius excutiendæ. Valeat in- dubio ea sententia quæ quam maxime sanctam & incon- cussam vult esse matrimonii fidem: ne temere rumpamus vinculum à Deo institutum.

"Videtur Grotio Christus agere de ducente dimissam a viro, qui tamen disciplinæ ejusdem (Christianæ) maneat, ac cujus proinde ingenium haberi debeat sanabile, ut in eum reci- dat adulterii crimen, qui novo matrimonio spem restituendæ concordiæ abrupit. Sed nihil Christus de fideli, vel infideli addidit: neque ad conjugii legem substantiam id facit, seu fidelis, quis sit, seu infidelis. Ideoque manet vera sen- tentia Christi, eum qui dimissam (extra casum fornicationis) ducit, mœchari, seu vir, qui dimisit fidelis sit & maneat, seu non, quia quum temerarium & illegitimum sit re- pudium ejusmodi, extra fornicationis causam factum, manet vinculum matrimoniale, ac proinde, qui dimis- fam ducit, adulterium committit. Non ergo est, quod excipiat Grotius, quod ita manente lege Mosis durum fuis- set, sine discrimine tanquam adulteros damnari, qui di- missam duxissent. Damnantur utique, ceu adulteri non in foro Politiæ, sed Conscientiæ: quia ducunt eam, quæ ma- trimonii vinculo obligata viro erat. Quid si vero fœminam aliena njuria proculcatam, & de pudicitia periclitantem misericordiæ motus aliquis in matrimonium suscepisset? Resp. si salvum mansit vinculum conjugii, quomodo absque adulterii crimine in matrimonium suscipere eandem po- tuit? Lex autem moralis pronunciat copulam indissolu- bilem esse Gen. II. 24. Etsi ergo in lege forensi permissa repudia fuerint, non tamen quid coram Deo peccatum sit, aut non sit, ex legibus forensibus, sed ex morali le- ge judicandum. Et aperta est Pauli sententia 1. Co- rinth. VII. 39. quod maritis obnoxiæ maneant fœminæ, manente vita; quam ad divortiorum quæstionem pertinere, temere negat Grotius. Nam etiamsi id solum probare insti- tuerit Paulus, ultra mortem mariti conjugale vinculum non extendi; ac proinde secundas nuptias non recte damnari, axioma tamen illud generale est? Mulier alligata est legi, quanto tempore vir ejus vivit. Quoad usque ergo vir fatis non concesserit, manet illa, etsi repudiata, viro alli- gata. Quod etiam lege Mosis probat Rom. VII. 1. ubi nequicquam negavit Grotius, lege Mosis dubium esse, et- iam ante mortem posse divortio conjugium dirimi. Hoc e- nim omnino est κρινόμενον de lege morali, Legis forensis autem permissio, ob σκληροκαρδίαν Iudæorum facta hic at- tendi non meretur, ubi, quid peccatum sit in foro con- scientiæ, disquiritur. Et agnoscit tandem ipse Grotius, adulterium esse apud Deum, quicquid matrimonio adversa- tur, atque ideo adulterii crimine teneri eum, qui amissam arripit: eamque valere vult sententiam, quæ quam maxime sanctam, & inconcussam vult esse matrimonii fidem, ne temere rumpamus vinculum à Deo institutum."

## 5:33
Vers. 33. ἐκ ἐπιορκήσεις] Philosophers have not thought the same thing about what τὸ ἐπιορκεῖν is: and among others two noble masters of the porch have handed down different things. It was the opinion of Cleanthes that he who swears is either keeping his oath or forswearing himself during the time in which he swears: for if he remains in what he said, so that he will perform the things according to the oath, he is keeping his oath; but if he has the intention not to perform it, he is forswearing himself. But Chrysippus thought far otherwise: for he said that τὸ ἀληθοορκεῖν is one thing, and τὸ ἐνόρκειν is another: likewise that τὸ ἐπιορκεῖν is one thing, and τὸ ψευδορκεῖν is another: which he explains thus, for I shall append the very words, because they contribute greatly to the understanding of these words: For he who swears at the time in which he swears is either swearing truly or swearing falsely. For what is sworn by him is either true or false, since it happens to be a proposition. But he who swears does not necessarily either keep his oath or forswear himself at the time in which he swears, when the time to which the reference of the oaths was made is not present. For in the same way that someone is said to be keeping or breaking a covenant, not when he makes the covenant, but when the times of the things according to the agreements arrive, so also someone will be said to be keeping his oath and forswearing himself, when the times arrive in which he agreed to perform the things according to the oaths. By which words Chrysippus signifies that the words of an oath promising for a future time have their truth or falsity not from an event which is uncertain, but from the mind of the one swearing; wherefore this word I will do is to be understood thus, I say that I will do it from the intention of my mind. For if a statement is brought forth in this way, it is already at this very time either true or false: because indeed through such a sworn utterance the will previously loose is so bound that it ought to persevere, it comes about that when one departs from that purpose, which appears when the time of fulfilling arrives, it is said that only then is perjury committed. And Cicero embraced this opinion in the third book of De Officiis. Moreover, common usage, not distinguishing these things so subtly, indiscriminately employs ἐπιορκεῖν and ψευδορκεῖν both regarding that oath which is committed with the intention of deceiving, and regarding the levity of one who does not fulfill promises. Wherefore, what is here ἐκ ἐπιορκήσεις, the Syrian translates דלא תרגל במומך, you shall not lie in an oath. But altogether in this place, the very words of the Decalogue are used by Christ: לא תשא את־שם יהוה אלהיך לשוא. For שוא, which Philo translates ἐπὶ ματαίῳ, as do the LXX, the most learned of the Hebrews, among whom is Abraham the Rabbi, interpret as falsely, so that, of course, every discrepancy of either mind or fact with an oath is properly and primarily forbidden. Indeed, that שוא and שקר, which denotes a lie, are used for the same thing appears from the Decalogue itself. For what is in Exodus לא־תענה ברעך עד־שקר, the very same is written in Deuteronomy לא־תענה ברעך עד שוא. In both places, however, the LXX translated ὀ ψευδομαρτυρήσεις κατὰ τὸν πλησίον σε μαρτυρίαν ψευδῆ. Thus Exod. XXIII. 1. לא תשא שמע שוא. The Jerusalem interpreter translates שקר, by which very word in that place the LXX, since they translate ἀκοὴν ματαίαν, sufficiently show that for them ματαῖον means the same as ψευδῆ. Thus also in Psalm XII. 3, שוא ידברו, μάταια ἐλάλησεν ἕκαστος, is undoubtedly they have lied: for it follows χείλη δόλια. In Zechariah X. 2, חלמות השוא, the same LXX translate ἐνύπνια ψευδῆ. Thus also Psalm XXIV, in the description of him who was to ascend into the mountain of the Lord, when it had said לא־נשא לשוא נפשי, ἐκ ἔλαβεν ἐπὶ ματαίῳ τὴν ψυχὴν ἀυτᾶ (the formula of an oath is referred to, 'as I live'), it immediately explains ולא נשבע למרמה, ὅ ἐκ ὤμοσεν ἐπὶ δόλῳ. Jerome also rendered the word שוא as a lie several times: whence it appears that the opinion of those is not sufficiently certain who think that by the said words of the Decalogue, oaths for causes not sufficiently grave are directly forbidden. For as I just said, the Decalogue names the greatest sins, and wishes the rest to be gathered from the mind of the author. These former words, according to Spanheim, correspond to the words of Moses in Leviticus XIX. 12, לא תשבע לשקר, which is ἐπιορκεῖν. Ἐπιορκία, Ψεῦμα according to Hesychius; Ἐπίορκος, ὅρκον μὴ φροντίζων. שוא also among the LXX in some places is ψευδὴς, more often μάταιος, ματαιότης, and adverbially ματαίως and μάτην, likewise κενός. Thus הבלי שוא, ματαιότητες διακενῆς, Psalm XXXI. 7. Rightly the LXX render the words of the law in Exodus XX. 7, ἐπὶ ματαίῳ. Aquila, εἰς εἰκῆ. The Targum, למגנא, which is the same as the חנם of the Hebrews, gratis, in vain, without cause. Whence the same word מגן in the Syrian interpreter corresponds to the word δωρεὰν in John XV. 25, with the words ἐμίσησάν με δωρεάν, they hated me without cause, just as also in Psalm XXXV. 19, the words שנאי חנם, those hating me without cause, the Targum renders by using the same word סנאי מגן. From Suidas it is also gathered that ἐπιορκεῖν is τὸ τελεῖν τὰ ὀμωμοσμένα, even if it is taken there for ὀμόσαι. Etymologicum magnum: ἐπιορκεῖν δηλοῖ τὸ ὑπὲρ ἄνω τῶν ὅρκων γίνεσθαι κὶ ὑπερβαίνειν ἀυτοῖς; it adds the reason, ἡ ἐπὶ πρόθεσις ἐν ταῦθ᾽ ἀντὶ τ᾽ ὑπὲρ κεῖται. The Glossary: ἐπιορκία, perjury; ἐπίορκος, perjured; ἐπιορκῶ, I abjure, I perjure. But a perjured person is not only he who swears with a perverse mind or against his own intention, but also he who neither cares for nor keeps the oath by which he has bound himself. To perjure, for Cicero in Book III of De Officiis, is not to swear falsely, but not to do what you swore according to the intention of your mind.

Ἀποδώσεις δὲ τῷ κυρίῳ τὰς ὅρκες σε] This is an exposition of what preceded: for he who does not wish to perjure himself, it behooves him to fulfill the faith of the oath. But also almost the same words exist in Numbers 30. 2. Aristides uses the word ἀποδιδόναι in the same sense regarding a vow, where he says, if the whole cannot be paid, at least a part must be paid: ὐ γὰρ ἐκλεπτέον ἐδὲν ἐυκταῖον φασὶν, ἀλλὰ πᾶν ἱστίον ἀποδιδόμενον κεῖσθαι ἢ καθάπαξ ἐκεῖ 9-εν. But that which is sworn is said to be paid to God, because even he who promises something to a man, invoking God as a witness and avenger of perfidy, at the same time binds himself to God: therefore, by the saying of Numbers In this place Moses joined a vow and an oath. It appears from this that Christ is properly dealing in this place with the oath which is called promissory. For concerning the testimonial oath, another precept of Moses exists: although it is true that what is said about the former can and ought to be applied to the latter also, by parity of reasoning, within certain limits. A good man in Psalm XV is depicted, among other things, by this mark: that he performs what he has sworn, even to his own detriment. It has been wisely noted by Seneca that certain things not rightly done ought to be placed outside the cognizance of the forum, so that the distinction between virtues and vices may shine forth more in voluntary actions: and for that reason, among most peoples, no action is brought against the ungrateful. Plato, in the eleventh book of the Laws, denies an action to a seller who has entered the price of a sold item into credit: which others have noted also pleased Charondas. But at Rome, an action was not granted from a pact unless either a συνάλλαγμα or a solemn stipulation had been added. Among the Jews, no pacts in judicial matters seem to have been valid unless they were confirmed by the religion of an oath, and indeed not just any oath, but such a one by which God was either expressly named or, by the interpretation of the wise, held to be named. But just as among the ancient Romans, as Polybius narrates, the use of an oath was rare, and indeed also of witnesses and signs in contracts, because one could hardly be found who would violate a given pledge in any way, so it is to be believed that among the Jews in the beginning the custom of swearing was not so frequent: or that it grew as perfidy grew.

These latter words, as Spanheim again holds, exist as to their substance in Deuteronomy XXIII. 23, Numbers XXX. 2, and in the words of the third commandment in Exodus XX. 7, and elsewhere throughout. The Lord neither disapproves of these, nor does He oppose His own words to them, but only to the corruptions added to those words, by which prohibited oaths were restricted only to those which were conceived directly in the name of God, and to perjuries. In that, therefore, fraud was admitted by the Jewish Doctors, because they did not hand down to their hearers the full breadth of the words and the sense of the law, such as it is in Exodus XX. 7. Indeed, profane men among the Jews played with oaths as boys do with knucklebones, holding oaths conceived by the temple as nothing, compared to oaths conceived by the gold of the temple. There was far greater religion among the pagans themselves regarding such things, by whom the θεοὶ ὅρκιοι were believed to preside over and be present at oaths, armed with thunderbolts for the punishment of the perjured. Hence ὅρκιος θεὸς, according to Suidas, is the president and arbiter of an oath. Thus, the Styx destined for the perjured was called ὕδωρ τὸ Διὸς ὅρκιον. Whence ἐνόρκιοι and ἴστοι are the same to the pagans.

Latin:

Vers. 33. ἐκ ἐπιορκήσεις] Quid sit τὸ ἐπιορκεῖν de eo non idem Philosophi existimarunt: atque inter alios duo nobiles magistri porticus diversa tradiderunt. Cleanthis erat sententia, τὸν ὀμνύοντα ἐνορκεῖν ἢ ἐπιορκεῖν καθ' ὃν ὄ- μνυσι χρόνον· ἐὰν μὲν γὰρ εἴτας ἐμμίνῃ, ὡς ἐπιτελέσει τὰ κα- τὰ τὸν ὅρκον ἐνορκεῖν· ἐὰν δὲ πρόθεσιν ἔχων μὴ ἐπιτελεῖν, ἐπιορ- κεῖν. At longe aliter sentiebat Chrysippus: aliud enim es- se τὸ ἀληθοορκεῖν, aliud τὸ ἐνόρκειν: item aliud τὸ ἐπιορκεῖν, aliud τὸ ψευδορκεῖν: quod ita explicat, verba enim ipsa ap- ponam, quia ad horum verborum intellectum apprime faciunt: Τὸν μὲν γὰρ ὀμνύντα καθ' ὃν ὀμνύῃ καιρὸν πάντας ἢ ἀ- ληθοορκεῖν ἢ ψευδορκεῖν. τὸ γὰρ ὀμνύμενον ὑπ' αὐτῦ ἢ ἀληθὲς εἶναι ἢ ψεῦδος, ἐπειδὴ ἀξίωμα τυγχάνει ὄν. τὸν δὲ ὀμνύϊα μὴ πάντως καθ' ὃν ὀμνύῃ χρόνον ἢ ἐνορκεῖν ἢ ἐπιορκεῖν, ὅτε μὴ πάρεστιν ὁ χρόνος εἰς ὃν ἡ ἀναφορὰ τῶν ὅρκων ἐγίγνετο. ὃν τρό- πον γὰρ λέγεταί τινα ἐυσωθετεῖν ἢ ἀσυνθετεῖν, ἐχ' ὅτε συντίθεται, ἀλλ' ὅτε οἱ χρόνοι ἐνίστανται τῶν κατὰ τὰς ὁμολογίας, ὕτω κὴ ἐνορκεῖν τις καὶ ἐπιορκεῖν ῥηθήσεται, ὅταν οἱ καιροὶ παραστῶσι καθ' ὃς ὁμολόγησεν ἐπιτελέσειν τὰ κατὰ τὲς ὅρκες. Quibus verbis significat Chrysippus verba juramenti promittentis in futurum tempus concepta veritatem suam aut falsitatem habere non ex eventu qui sit incertus, sed ex animo juran- tis; quare verbum hoc faciam ita accipiendum, dico ex a- nimi sententia me facturum. Nam ita si proferatur enun- tiatio, jam hoc ipso tempore aut vera est aut falsa: quia vero per talem prolationem juratam voluntas ante soluta ita colligatur ut perseverare debeat, eo fieri ut cum ab eo proposito disceditur, quod apparet ubi implendi tempus advenit, dicatur tum demum perjurium com- mitti. Et hanc sententiam amplexus est Cicero de offi- ciis tertio. Cæterum communior usus non tam subtiliter ista distinguens promiscue usurpat ἐπιορκεῖν & ψευδορκεῖν tam de eo juramento quod fallendi animo committitur, tum de levitate ejus qui promissa non implet. Quare quod hic est ἐκ ἐπιορκήσεις Syrus vertit דלא תרגל במומך non mentieris in jurejurando. Omnino autem h. l. a Christo usurpata ipsa Decalogi verba לא תשא את־שם יהוה אלהיך לשוא Nam שוא quod Philo vertit ἐπὶ ματαίῳ, quomodo & LXX. Hebræo- rum doctissimi, quos inter Rabbinos Abraham, interpre- tantur falso, ut nimirum proprie ac primario vetetur o- mnis disconvenientia aut animi aut facti cum jurejuran- do. Sane שוא & שקר quod mendacium denotat pro eodem poni ex ipso etiam Decalogo apparet. Nam quod in Exodo est לא־תענה ברעך עד־שקר idipsum in Deuteronomio scribitur לא־תענה ברעך עד שוא Utroque autem loco LXX. verterunt ὀ ψευδομαρτυρήσεις κατὰ τὸν πλησίον σε μαρτυρίαν ψευδῆ. Sic Exod. XXIII. 1. לא תשא שמע שוא Hierosolymitanus interpres vertit שקר quo ipso loco LXX. cum vertant ἀκοὴν μα- ταίαν, satis ostendunt sibi ματαῖον idem valere quod ψευ- δῆ. Sic & in Psal. XII. 3. שוא ידברו μάταια ἐλάλησεν ἕκαστος, haud dubie est mentiti sunt: sequitur enim χείλη δόλια. Zachariæ X. 2. חלמות השוא iidem LXX. vertunt ἐνύπνια ψευδῆ. Sic & Psalmus XXIV. in descriptione ejus, qui in Domini montem esset ascensu- rus, cum dixisset לא־נשא לשוא נפשי ἐκ ἔλαβεν ἐπὶ ματαίῳ τὴν ψυχὴν ἀυτᾶ (respicitur formula jurisjuran- di, ita vivam) statim explicat ולא נשבע למרמה ὅ ἐκ ὤμοσεν ἐπὶ δόλῳ. Hieronymus etiam שוא voce men- dacii aliquoties reddidit: unde apparet non satis certam esse eorum sententiam qui dictis decalogi verbis directe putant vetari juramenta ob causas non satis graves. Nam ut modo dixi, decalogus summa peccata nominat, cætera ex mente auctoris vult colligi. Verba hæc priora, juxta Spanhemium, respon- dent verbis Mosis Levit. XIX. 12. לא תשבע לשקר est ἐπιορκεῖν. Ἐπιορκία, Ψεῦμα Hesychio, Ἐπίορκος, ὅρ- κον μὴ φροντίζων. שוא etiam apud LXX. aliquot lo- cis est ψευδὴς, sæpius μάταιος, ματαιότης, & adver- bialiter ματαίως & μάτην, item κενός. Sic הבלי שוא ματαιότητες διακενῆς, Psal. XXXI. 7. Merito LXX. reddunt verba legis Exod. XX. 7. ἐπὶ ματαίῳ. A- quila εἰς εἰκῆ. Targum למגנא quod idem quod חנם Hebræorum gratis, frustra, sine causa. Unde ea- dem vox מגן apud Syrum interpretem respondet voci δωρεὰν Joh. XV. 25. verbis ἐμίσησάν με δωρεάν, ode- runt me immerito, prout & Psal. XXXV. 19. voces שנאי חנם odio me habentis gratis, reddit Tar- gum eandem vocem adhibendo סנאי מגן. Ex Suida etiam colligitur ἐπιορκεῖν esse τὸ τελεῖν τὰ ὀμωμοσ- μένα, cissilatius etiam ibidem sumatur pro ὀμόσαι. Etymologicum magnum, ἐπιορκεῖν δηλοῖ τὸ ὑπὲρ ἄ- νω τῶν ὅρκων γίνεσθαι κὶ ὑπερβαίνειν ἀυτοῖς, ratio- nem addit ἡ ἐπὶ πρόθεσις ἐν ταῦθ᾽ ἀντὶ τ᾽ ὑπὲρ κεῖται. Glossarium ἐπιορκία perjurium, ἐπίορκος perjurus, ἐπιορκῶ, abjuro, perjuro. Perjurus ve- ro non tantum qui perverso animo vel contra mentem suam jurat, sed & qui jusjurandum quo se obstrinxit, nec curat, nec servat. Pejerare Ciceroni lib. III. Of- fic. non est falsum jurare, sed, quod ex animi tui sen- tentia juraris, non facere.

Ἀποδώσεις δὲ τῷ κυρίῳ τὰς ὅρκες σε] Expositio est ejus quod præcessit: nam qui nolit pejerare, eum oportet im- plere fidem jurisjurandi. Sed & verba prope eadem exstant Num. 30. 2. Vocem ἀποδιδόναι eodem sensu de voto usur- pat Aristides ubi ait, si totum persolvi nequeat, certe partem persolvendam: ὐ γὰρ ἐκλεπτέον ἐδὲν ἐυκταῖον φασὶν, ἀλλὰ πᾶν ἱστίον ἀποδιδόμενον κεῖσθαι ἢ καθάπαξ ἐκεῖ 9-εν. Deo autem persolvi dicitur id quod juratum est, quia etiam qui homini aliquid promittit, Deum testem & perfidiæ ultorem in- vocans, simul Deo se obligat: ideo dicto Numerorum loco conjunxit Moses votum & jusjurandum. Apparet hinc proprie Christum hoc loco agere de juramento quod promissorium dicitur. Nam de jurejurando testimoniali extat alterum Mosis præceptum: quanquam verum est quæ de illo dicuntur etiam ad istud ex paritate rationis in- tra certos limites & posse & debere aptari. Vir bonus Psalmo XV. inter alia hac nota depingitur, quod juratus aliquid, etiam cum damno suo id præstet. Sapienter à Seneca notatum est quædam non recte facta extra fori cognitionem poni debere, quo magis in voluntariis a- ctionibus eluceat virtutum vitiorumque discrimen: at- que ideo in ingratos nullam apud plerosque populos prodi actionem. Plato de legibus undecimo, vendi- tori qui de rei venditæ pretio in creditum iverit actionem negat: quod & Charondæ placuisse notarunt alii. At Romæ ex pacto actio non dabatur, nisi aut συνάλλαγμα aut solennis stipulatio accessisset. Apud Judæos nulla pa- cta in judiciis valuisse videntur nisi quæ firmata essent reli- gione jurisjurandi, neque vero cujuslibet jurisjurandi, sed talis quo Deus aut expresse nominaretur aut ex sapientium interpretatione pro nominato haberetur. Quemadmo- dum vero apud Romanos veteres, narrante Polybio, ra- rus fuit usus jurisjurandi, imo & testium & signorum in contractibus, quia vix inveniebatur qui quovis modo da- tam fidem læderet, ita par credi est, & apud Judæos ini- tio non adeo frequentem fuisse jurisjurandi consuetudi- nem: seu crevisse eam crescente perfidia.

Posteriora hæc, ut iterum Spanhemius habet, verba quoad substantiam extant Deuter. XXIII. 23. Num. XXX. 2. & in verbis præcepti tertii Exod. XX. 2. & alibi passim. Ista nec improbat Domi- nus, nec iis verba sua opponit, sed corruptelas tan- tum verbis illis adfutas, quibus restringebantur ju- ramenta prohibita duntaxat ad illa quæ directa in Dei nomine concepta erant, & ad perjuria. In illo itaque fraus admissa à Doctoribus Judaicis, quod non totam latitudinem verborum & sensum legis, qua- lis Exod. XX. 7. auditoribus suis traderent. Immo homines profani inter Judæos juramentis ludebant, ut pueri astragalis, juramenta per templum concepta pro nihilo ducentes, præ juramentis per aurum tem- pli conceptis. Major longe religio ipsis paganis circa talia, à quibus θεοὶ ὅρκιοι præesse & adesse juramen- tis crediti, fulminibus armari in pœnam perjuro- rum. Hinc ὅρκιος θεὸς apud Suidam jurisjurandi præses, & arbiter. Sic Styx perjuris destinata vo- cabatur ὕδωρ τὸ Διὸς ὅρκιον. Unde ἐνόρκιοι & ἴ- στοι iidem paganis.

## 5:34
Vers. 34. Μὴ ὀμόσαι ὅλως] They are gravely mistaken who think that only the custom of swearing by things other than God is disapproved by Christ. For James, the best interpreter of Christ, says one must not swear, neither by heaven, nor by earth, nor by any other formula of swearing. Indeed, the sense of Christ is that one must not swear, not even by heaven, by earth, by Jerusalem, by one's head, which the opposite member shows. But let your speech be, yes, yes, no, no. The cause of this saying is undoubtedly this: that the more approved teachers of the Jews so deterred men from the facility of swearing that they nevertheless wished it to pertain only to those formulas by which God was directly named, such as that most holy one to the Jews, חי אלד, which Martial corruptly brought out as 'jura verpe per Anchialum.' But they did not intercede to prevent swearing by lesser things in daily use. Philo makes this most clear in his book περὶ τῶν ἐν εἴδει νόμων. For when he had said that it was indecorous for the sake of any things whatsoever ἐπὶ τὸ ποιητὴν καὶ πατέρα τῶν ὅλων διατρέχειν, he added that one could swear by parents, the earth, the sun, the stars, the universe. Clearly, as interpreters note regarding Homer, the most ancient of the Greeks were not accustomed προπετῶς κατὰ τῶν θεῶν ὀμνύειν, ἀλλὰ κατὰ τῶν προστυγχανόντων. But the best teacher of truth shows that these are miserable safeguards of evil custom, using this argument: that those formulas by things other than God were nevertheless tacitly referred to God, which he then explains one by one. Ulpian the Jurisconsult also saw that this was true: 'He who swears by his own safety,' he says, 'seems to swear by God: for he swears with respect to the divine majesty.' There was also another error of the Jews, that they thought some of those lesser formulas of swearing had the power of binding, and others did not; but because that does not properly pertain to the explanation of these words of Christ, it will be treated elsewhere. Let us see, therefore, what ὅλως means. Maimonides drew this opinion from the most ancient teachers of the Hebrews, that it is best for a man not to swear כלל, that is, at all. And a similar expression is found in Epictetus, παραιτήσῃ ὅρκον εἰς

ἅπαν. It appears that כּל־נִדְרֵי is the same as ὅλως τοὺς ὅρκους. Thus also Justin says that Christians μὴ ὀμνύναι ὅλως; and Chrysostom from this place of Matthew: ὦ θέμις ὅλως ὀμνύναι, ἐδὲ ἀνάγκην ἐπάγοντα ὅρκε, and the same in the seventh chapter to the Romans: κωλύων ὅρκος πλέον, ἀλλὰ τὸ ὀμνύναι καθόλες. And in the eighth book on the statues: καθόλες μὴ ὀμνύναι ὁ Θεὸς ἐκέλευσε. Similar things to which can be read in Hilary, Ambrose, Jerome, Chromatius, Theophylact, Oecumenius, Euthymius. Among Eusebius, a certain Basilides, contemporary with Origen, when required to take an oath, says μὴ ἐξεῖναι ἀυτῷ τὸ παράπαν ὀμνύναι· χριςιανὸν γὰρ ὑπάρχειν. But also among other writers, however pagan, there exist sayings of no less broadly reaching sound: such as that of Plato: ὅρκος περὶ παντὸς ἀπέστω. Of Choerilus: Ὅρκον τ’ οὔτ’ ἄδικον χρεὼν ἔμμεναι ὔτε δίκαιον. And of Menander: Ὅρκον δὲ φεῦγε κἂν δικαίως ὀμνύῃς. Therefore, τὸ ὅλως μὴ ὀμνύναι (not swearing at all) is opposed as something greater and holier to that which had preceded, that is, τῷ ἐυορκεῖν (to swearing truly), as if Christ were saying: although you have proposed that you will do what you promise, nevertheless do not swear. If this precept is explained compared with the precept of the old law in book VII of the constitutions which are called Clement's: ὃ ἐυορκεῖν νομοθετήσας, νῦν τὸ ἐπιεικὲς ἀπαγορεύσας τὸ μηδ’ ὀμνύναι παρήγγειλε (having legislated to swear truly, now having forbidden what is fair, he commanded not to swear at all). Here, however, again arises that question, whether therefore this interdiction bears no exception. The ancient Christians, some of whom we have already named, often seem to speak as if no exception should be admitted: but a benign interpretation ought to assist their sayings as well. For who would believe that Paul was unmindful of the Lord's precept? Yet his words are: God is my witness, in the first of the Romans, v. 9, and in the sight of God I do not lie, Gal. I, 28. God the Father of Christ knows that I do not lie, 2. Cor. XI, 17. It could not be sworn more expressly. For an oath is nothing other than a religious affirmation, as Cicero defines it, or as Clement of Alexandria says, ὁμολογία καθετηρικὴ μετὰ παραλήψεως θείας (a firm confession with the invocation of the divine), or as Philo defines it in two places, μαρτυρία θεᾶ περὶ πράγματος ἀμφισβητουμένου (a testimony of God concerning a disputed matter). Therefore, some tempering must be applied. For that reason, Epictetus added εἰ μὲν οἷόν τε (if it is possible). Quintilian: To swear at all, unless where it is necessary, is hardly suitable for a serious man. Augustine: Avoid an oath, he says, as much as you can: in another place he said, as much as is in you. Clement of Alexandria says it is for Christians ἐκ ἐυεπίφορον ἐπὶ τὸ ὀμνύνειν (not to be prone to swearing), which he interprets as σπανίως ἐπὶ τὸ ὀμνύναι ἐφικνέμενον (rarely reaching out to swearing). That first point is beyond controversy, that they act very badly τὲς ἔθει ποιητᾷ καταχῶς κὶ ἀνεξετάςως ὀμνύοντας ἐν τοῖς τυχεσιν (who by habit and improperly and unexaminedly swear on chance occasions), as Philo speaks, adding that perjury is born ἐκ πολυορκίας (from much swearing): just as Ulpian also said that some are easy to swear through contempt of religion. The wise Hebrew, Eccles. IX. 9: ὅρκῳ μὴ ἐθίσῃς τὸ ςόμα σε κὶ ὀνομασίᾳ τᾶ ἁγία μὴ συνεθιθῇς (do not accustom your mouth to an oath, and do not become accustomed to the naming of the Holy One). And soon after: ἀνὴρ πολύορκος πλησθήσεται ἀνομίας, κὶ ἐκ ἀποςήσεται ἀπὸ τᾶ οἴκε ἀυτᾶ μάςιξ (a man of many oaths shall be filled with iniquity, and the scourge shall not depart from his house). To which also that of Plato in the eleventh book of the Laws pertains: Θεῶν ὀνόματα μὴ χραίνειν ῥᾳδίως (do not defile the names of the gods lightly): and that of Hierocles: Μελέτη δὲ ἀρίςη τῆ τηρεῖν τὸ περὶ αὐτῶν σέβας, τὸ μὴ πυκνῶς μηδὲ ὡς ἔτυχε χρῆσθαι τῷ ὅρκῳ, μηδὲ ἐπὶ τοῖς παρατυχῦσι, μηδὲ ὡς ἀναπλήρωσι λόγε, μηδὲ εἰς πίςωσιν διηγήματος (the best practice for keeping reverence for them is not to use the oath frequently nor as it happens, nor on chance occasions, nor as a filler of speech, nor for the confirmation of a story): and afterwards: τὸ δὲ, σέβε ὅρκον, ὀ μόνον ἐυορκεῖν ἀλλὰ κὶ ἀπέχεσθαι ὅρκω παρεγγυᾷ ὕτω γὰρ ἂν τηρήσαιμεν τὸ ἀεὶ ἐνυρκκεῖν, εἰ μὴ καταχρησοίμεθα τοῖς ὅρκοις· κὶ γὰρ ἐν τῇ συνεχῶς [τῶ] ὀμνύειν ῥᾳδίως ἂν μεταπέσοι τις εἰς ἐπιορκίαν· φειδοῖ δὲ τήρησις ἕπεται· ἡ γὰρ ἐκ ὀμεῖται, ἢ ὅταν ὀμνύῃ ἐυορκήσει· κὶ ὔτε ἂν ὑπὸ συνηθείας προδραμῃ ἡ γλῶσσα, ὔτε ὑπὸ παθῶν ἀκρατείας ἡ διάνοια σφαλέιη· τῇ μὲν γὰρ ὁ τρόπος ὀρθῶς χρησοῦτᾶι, τὴν δὲ τὸ [ἐθ-] τῆς ἐποχῆς τᾶ ὀμνύνειν (but the command, 'revere the oath,' enjoins not only to swear truly but also to abstain from the oath; for thus we would keep the 'always swearing truly,' if we did not misuse oaths; for in the continuous [act of] swearing one might easily fall into perjury; but restraint follows sparing; for either he will not swear, or when he swears he will swear truly; and neither would the tongue run ahead through habit, nor would the mind stumble through lack of control of passions; for by the one the character is used rightly, and by the other the [habit] of refraining from swearing). Then again: Σέβε ὅρκον, τῷ μὴ προχείρως αυτῷ καταχρῆσθαι δι’ ὅ γ’ καθ’ ἕξ ἐυορκεῖν ἐκ τᾶ μὴ ἐθισθῆναι ὀμνύνειν (revere the oath, by not readily misusing it, through which one will habitually swear truly from not being accustomed to swear). Nor, however, does it seem that we should stop here, so that only ease and the assiduous habit of swearing are forbidden, so that, clearly, we might be safer from perjury. I am persuaded that not only by Christ, but also by those I have mentioned—the Jew Maimonides, the Greeks Choerilus, Menander, Epictetus—more is indicated. Paul swore, but not in his own affair, not in a trivial affair of another, but in matters of the greatest moment pertaining to God and the salvation of others. We today, if the situation demands it, swear over a small sum of money, and indeed even in our own affair, which Plato strongly disapproves of. And yet we want to be considered Christians, as if it were a sacrilege to risk the loss of a few coins for the reverence of the divine majesty. I wish that at least that religion of the oath held us which held not a few who were strangers to Christ. Let us hear Isocrates: Ὅρκον ἐπακτὸν χροσδέχε διὰ δύο προφάσεις, ἢ σαυτὸν ἀιτίας ἀισχρᾶς ἀπολύων, ἢ φίλως ἐκ μεγάλων κινδύνων διασώζων: ἕνεκα δὲ χρημάτων μηδένα θεὸν ὀμόσῃς, μηδ’ ἂν ἐυορκεῖν μέλλῃς. δόξεις γὰρ τοῖς μὲν ἐπιορκεῖν, τοῖς δὲ φιλοχρημάτως ἔχειν (accept an imposed oath for two reasons, either by absolving yourself of a shameful charge, or by saving friends from great dangers: but for the sake of money do not swear by any god, not even if you are about to swear truly. For you will seem to some to be perjuring yourself, and to others to be greedy). Behold, he admits only two causes for an oath, and indeed a judicial one, so that you may flee infamy, or so that you may save a friend from great danger: which example Simplicius also uses for Epictetus, adding: or so that you may render great service to your country. These, therefore, in a pecuniary matter, disapprove of any oath. When Clinias the Pythagorean could have escaped a fine of three talents by taking an oath, he preferred to suffer the loss of such a great sum of money rather than swear, an example which Basil holds up to the Christians of his own age. That Hierocles whom I mentioned similarly approves of no oath, except for necessary and noble matters, and those which cannot be obtained without an oath. His golden words on the golden poem of Pythagoras are these: 'Keep the use of it (the oath) in necessary and honorable matters, and only then when no other salvation for such things appears, unless it be through the truth of the oath alone.' And these things indeed he said concerning the oath which is taken for the sake of testifying to the truth. But in promises and agreements, with which Christ is properly dealing here, it is hardly possible for any cause so grave to be alleged, unless perhaps it be a matter in which the public safety is at stake, although even in such business a bare promise might perhaps achieve the same result if a penalty for perjury were added to secure the matter, which frightens most people more than the religious obligation of an oath: and those who promise something should be warned not to do anything unless it is deliberate and serious, and which among the Romans also fulfilled the role of an oath: 'FROM THE INTENTION OF HIS MIND.' To this kind of oath those words of Hierocles look: 'But he who reveres an oath, having in the beginning enjoined abstinence from swearing, adds further concerning those things which are possible and indefinite in their outcome. For these are small and changeable. Therefore they are not worthy to swear upon, when it is safe. For it is in our power to bring them to an end.' But concerning present matters that are necessarily connected and are of the greatest importance, it is safe and proper to swear. For neither does the changeability of things ever cause us to stumble, nor does their humble and groveling nature require divine testimony. Moreover, that even those who seem to reject every oath indiscriminately nevertheless admit some exceptions, especially those of great public utility, is apparent from many indications. Josephus said of the Essenes: 'Swearing is avoided by them,' which others also testify. And yet, that the same people were bound by an oath to the observance of their religion, the same Josephus makes clear: 'But before they touch the common food, they swear terrible oaths to them. First, that they will worship the Divine, then that they will keep justice toward men, and will neither harm anyone by their own will, nor by command. But that they will always hate the unjust and fight alongside the just. That they will always provide faithfulness to all, especially to those in authority.' And if he himself rules, never to abuse his authority, nor to outshine those who are subject to him with clothing or any greater finery. To love the truth always and to expose those who lie, to keep their hands clean from theft and their soul from unholy gain; and neither to hide anything from the members of the sect, nor to reveal anything of theirs to others, even if one is forced to the point of death. In addition to these, they swear that they will share the doctrines with no one otherwise than as they themselves received them; and that they will abstain from robbery and will preserve in like manner both the books of their sect and the names of the angels; with such oaths they secure those who join them.' Not far from this narrative departs what Pliny relates concerning the ancient Christians, whose institutions in many parts agreed with the Essenes, that they were accustomed to bind themselves by an oath, not to some crime, but not to commit thefts, not robberies, not adulteries, not to break their word, and not to deny a deposit when called upon. Tertullian records that Christians swore by the safety of the Caesars: and others, refusing an oath by the genius of Caesar, brought forward the reason that this genius was a demon, not that it was illicit to swear without that exception, as we shall soon see. Athanasius, who in his sermon on the passion and cross of the Lord seems to reject the oath indiscriminately, nevertheless, when accused by calumny, clears himself to Constantius in this manner: 'To your piety, with a loud and clear voice and outstretched hand, as I have learned from the Apostle, I call God to witness upon my own soul, and as it is written in the books of Kings, I take an oath: The Lord is witness and his Christ is witness, that I never mentioned you for evil before your brother Constans Augustus, nor did I incite him against you.' And soon after: 'I would wish this man, whoever he is, to be present here, so that with the oath offered under the attestation of truth I might inquire of him about these things, for those things which we are accustomed to say and hear as if in the presence of God, we Christian men are accustomed to conceive under this formula of an oath.' In the Synod of Ephesus, at which many were present whose writings seem likewise to oppose the custom of swearing, we see an oath imposed upon both Nestorius and Victor, so that it is not necessary to make mention of later times.

Grotius seems rather to err here by a fallacy of division: for those things which Christ joined together should have been joined, 'do not swear at all, neither by heaven'; which teach that Christ disapproves of oaths, not all in general, but those which are made by creatures. That 'at all' therefore is to be referred to all things which follow, not to all things absolutely, concerning which Heinsius is prolix here: which sense the words of James also exhibit, James 5:12. For the things that are added, 'nor any other oath,' look to a similar oath of that kind. Therefore the levity of the Pharisees is censured, who swore by creatures, and in light causes, and played with oaths, as boys with knucklebones. Meanwhile, we can admit that even those oaths which are made without a grave cause, by the name of the Lord, are prohibited, and we will not disagree with that explanation, 'do not swear, not even by heaven, by earth, by Jerusalem'; if these are taken in the sense in which oaths were also prohibited in the law, namely light and rash ones, and it is not imagined that something was added here to the law by Christ; to which Grotius inclines on page 104, when he says: that the opinion of those is not sufficiently certain who think that oaths for causes not sufficiently grave are directly forbidden in the decalogue: for it is certain that not only Christ, but even the law of Moses disapproves of all rash oaths: that Christ forbids oaths simply cannot be proven. And this same Grotius distinguishes here between a promissory and a testimonial oath, he acknowledges that the latter is not disapproved by Christ; but he confesses that even promissory oaths are not entirely prohibited. For if the public safety requires it, he does not deny that it can be performed. In promises, he says p. 107, and agreements, of which Christ is properly treating here, it is hardly possible that any cause so grave can be alleged, unless perhaps it be a matter in which the public safety is involved, although even in such business a bare promise might perhaps suffice, if the penalty of perjury were added to sanction it, which terrifies most people more than the religious obligation of an oath. But the same is the meaning of the words of the Decalogue about not taking the name of the Lord in vain, by which rash oaths are prohibited: but not those which are performed when the glory of the divine name, or the public safety, or some other grave cause demands it. Regarding that of Martial, 'jura verpe per Anchialum', one may see Selden at length in Prolegom. de succession. ad bona defunctor.

Nor is the argument of Grotius sufficiently firm, by which he proves here, and in book II of De Jure Belli ac Pacis, ch. XIII, n. XXI, that the discourse here and in James ch. V is properly about a promissory oath, namely that the former 'yea' and 'nay' signifies the promise, and the latter its fulfillment. Since those 'is is', 'not not', are doubled for the sake of asseveration and certainty, just as 'Amen' is accustomed to be doubled. However, those things with which Grotius concludes this passage on page 113 are correct: Christ does not forbid an oath as a thing evil in itself, but as a thing which it is not lawful to use except in matters of the greatest moment. But what such matters are cannot be comprehended so much by certain definitions as judged by the Spirit of charity. I shall conclude this treatment with the saying of Augustine: He who understands that swearing is to be held not among good things, but necessary ones, let him restrain himself as much as he can, so that he does not use it except by necessity, when he sees that men are slow to believe what it is useful for them to believe, unless it is confirmed by an oath.

Μήτε ἐν τῷ ὀρανῷ] That is, not even by heaven, as we have already said. Moreover, it is a Hebraism to say 'to swear in heaven' for which the Greeks would say 'to swear by heaven', or even 'by heaven'. We have already said that these modes of swearing are not specifically prohibited by Christ, but that not even these are excepted from the prohibition. By the law of Moses, it was forbidden to the Jews to swear by any god other than the God of Israel: therefore it was a crime for them to swear by Baal, Astarte, and other false deities of that kind. For which reason Tertullian also reproved the Christians of his time, who, either through ignorance or the vice of custom, would say 'Mehercule' and 'Medius fidius': which Jerome also did after him. For this same reason the Alexandrian Jews refused to make the name of Gaius Caesar an object of an oath, as Josephus narrates, because Gaius wanted his name to be used like God's in an oath. But to name certain things, as Philo speaks, as an effluence of the divine power,

corpses, in such a way, namely, that the religion of the soul might look to God, was not considered among forbidden things. Josephus swears in Gen. XLII. 14. As Pharaoh lives: in the manner of the Egyptians, indeed, as has been rightly noted by Abenezra: but a man of exceptional piety would not have been about to imitate it if he had thought there was anything irreligious in it. And what else is, as the King lives, than, may God keep the King safe? The prophet Elisha 2 Kings II. Elijah swears thus: As God lives and as your soul lives (or rather may live, for Hebraism does not distinguish those). Nor does Uriah otherwise 2 Sam. XI. 11. But also Paul seems to swear by the resurrection or by his own conscience, when he says by our boasting 1 Corinthians XV. 31. Tertullian relates in his Apologeticus that Christians did not swear as others did by the Genius of the prince, which the Greeks call the fortune of Caesar, which oath we read was offered to Polycarp and refused by him: deservedly, because there was in that word a sense of a false deity, which Origen explains thus: We do not swear by the fortune of the king, as neither by any other considered god. For whether (as some have named it) fortune is only an outflow, we do not swear by that which is in no way a being as a god; or if it is something entirely subsisting and able to do something. Or if we do not take the Homeric power into account. But also, as it seemed to some, those who swear by the demon (that is, the genius) of all the Roman kings, swearing by his fortune, the so-called fortune of the king is a demon, and thus it must be rejected rather than to swear by an evil demon and one often unfaithful, sinning together with the man to whom it has fallen, or sinning more than he. But Tertullian in the same place says that the same Christians swore by the safety of the Prince, which is more august than all the genii. But after the Emperors had given their name to Christ, this military oath was instituted, that they should swear by God and Christ and the Holy Spirit and by the majesty of the Emperor, which after God is to be loved and honored by the human race: which Vegetius teaches us. Thus Marcellinus in the conference at Carthage swears that he will judge according to the allegations of the parties by the safety of the princes: and the Greek interpreters note there that this is the very oath which the bishops were making, mentioned in the XXV canon of Chalcedon. Philo also mentions an oath by heaven. But also Origen against Celsus in the sixth book says that the Jews were accustomed to swear by heaven. But heaven here is rightly understood as the starry region.

It is the throne of God] From Isaiah LXVI. 1. These things are said for this purpose, that it may be shown that God is tacitly contained in all modes of swearing. That appears clearly below XXIII. 22. where Christ inserts it thus, he who swears by heaven swears at the same time by him who sits upon heaven as a throne. But it is called the throne of God, because in that work painted with most beautiful stars and by its perpetual and uniform motion, the divine majesty shines forth exceptionally, just as the glory of kings is then most conspicuous when they sit upon their throne. And the formula of this oath, and the cause of it, appears in that verse from Sophocles' Menalippa, I swear by the holy ether, the dwelling of Zeus. But also Julian against the Christians calls the sky the throne of God.

Latin:

Vers. 34. Μὴ ὀμόσαι ὅλως] Graviter falluntur qui solam à Christo improbari putant consuetudinem jurandi per res alias extra Deum. Nam Jacobus optimus Christi interpres ait non jurandum, neque per cœlum, neque per terram, ne- que alia quavis jurandi formula. Imo sensus Christi est, non jurandum ne quidem per cœlum, per terram, per Hieroso- lyma, per caput, quod ostendit membrum oppositum. Sit autem sermo vester est, est, non, non. Causa hujus dicti non dubie hæc est, quod Judæorum magistri probatiores ita abs- terrent homines à facilitate jurandi, ut id tamen vellent ad eas duntaxat formulas pertinere, quibus directo Deus no- minaretur, quale est illa Judæis sanctissima חי אלד quod corrupte Martialis extulit jura verpe per Anchialum. At quo minus in usu quotidiano per res minores juraretur non intercedebant. Apertissimum hoc facit Philo in libro περὶ τῶν ἐν εἴδει νόμων. Cum enim indecorum esse dixisset ob res quaslibet ἐπὶ τὸ ποιητὴν καὶ πατέρα τῶν ὅλων διατρέχειν, addidit jurari posse parentes, terram, solem, astra, universum. Pla- ne ut ad Homerum notant interpretes, Græcorum vetustissi- mos non esse solitos προπετῶς κατὰ τῶν θεῶν ὀμνύειν, ἀλλὰ κατὰ τῶν προστυγχανόντων. At optimus veri magister ostendit hæc misera esse mali moris præsidia, hoc usus argumento, quod illæ etiam formulæ per res alias, tacite tamen ad Deum referrentur, quod deinde singulatim explicat. Ve- rum hoc esse vidit & Ulpianus Jurisconsultus: Qui per sa- lutem, inquit, suam jurat Deum jurare videtur: respectu enim divini numinis jurat. Erat & alius Judæorum error, quod ex illis formulis minoribus jurandi alias putarent vim obli- gandi habere, alias non habere; sed istud quia ad horum Christi verborum explicationem proprie non pertinet alibi tractabitur. Videamus ergo quid sit ὅλως. Maimonides ex antiquissimis Hebræorum magistris hausit hanc sententiam, optimum esse homini non jurare כלל id est prorsus. Et similis est apud Epictetum locutio παραιτήσῃ ὅρκον εἰς

ἅπαν. Apparet idem esse כּל־נִדְרֵי, ὅλως τοὺς ὅρκους. Sic & Ju- stinus ait Christianos μὴ ὀμνύναι ὅλως· & Chrysostomus ex hoc Matthæi loco: ὦ θέμις ὅλως ὀμνύναι, ἐδὲ ἀνάγκην ἐπά- γονος ὅρκε, idemque VII. ad Romanos: κωλύων ὅρκος πλέον, ἀλλὰ τὸ ὀμνύναι καθόλες. Et de statuis octavo: καθό- λες μὴ ὀμνύναι ὁ Θεὸς ἐκέλευσε. Cui similia legere est apud Hilarium, Ambrosium, Hieronymum, Chromatium, Theophylactum, Oecumenium, Euthymium. Apud Eu- sebium Basilides quidam Origeni coævus jusjurandum ex- actus ait μὴ ἐξεῖναι ἀυτῷ τὸ παράπαν ὀμνύναι· χριςιανὸν γὰρ ὑ- πάρχειν. Sed & apud alios scriptores, quantumvis paganos, extitant dicta non minus late patentis soni: ut Platonis: ὅρ- κος περὶ παντὸς ἀπέςω. Chœrili: Ὅρκον τ’ οὔτ’ ἄδικον χρεὼν ἔμμεναι ὔτε δίκαιον. Et Menandri: Ὅρκον δὲ φεῦγε κἂν δικαίως ὀμνύῃς. Opponitur ergo τὸ ὅλως μὴ ὀμνύναι tanquam majus atque sanctius quiddam ei quod præcesserat, id est τῷ ἐυορκεῖν, quasi dicat Christus: quamvis proposueris facturum te quod promittis, tamen jurare noli. Si explicatur hoc præ- ceptum collatum cum præcepto legis veteris in libro VII. constitutionum quæ dicuntur Clementis: ὃ ἐυορκεῖν νομο- θετήσας, νῦν τὸ ἐπιεικὲς ἀπαγορεύσας τὸ μηδ’ ὀμνύναι παρήγγει- λε. Hic vero rursus illa exoritur quæstio, an igitur hæc in- terdictio nullam ferat exceptionem. Veteres Christiani, quorum aliquos jam nominavimus, sæpe ita loqui viden- tur quasi nulla admittenda esset exceptio: sed benigna interpretatio illorum quoque dictis debet succurrere. Quis enim credat Paulum præcepti dominici fuisse immemorem? At ejus sunt verba: Testis mihi est Deus, Romanorum pri- mo, v. 9. & in conspectu Dei non mentior, Gal. I, 28. Scit Deus Pater Christi me non mentiri, 2. Cor. XI, 17. Non potuit ju- rari expressius. Nihil enim aliud est jusjurandum quam religiosa affirmatio, ut Cicero definit, aut ut ait Clemens Alexandrinus ὁμολογία καθετηρικὴ μετὰ παραλήψεως θείας, aut ut Philo duobus locis definit μαρτυρία θεᾶ περὶ πράγ- ματος ἀμφισβητουμένου. Ergo aliquod adhibendum est tem- peramentum. Ideo Epictetus addidit εἰ μὲν οἷόν τε. Quinti- lianus: In totum jurare nisi ubi necesse est, gravi viro parum convenit. Augustinus: Juramentum cave, inquit, quan- tum potes: alio loco dixit, quantum in te est. Clemens Ale- xandrinus Christianorum ait esse ἐκ ἐυεπίφορον ἐπὶ τὸ ὀμνύ- νειν, quod interpretatur σπανίως ἐπὶ τὸ ὀμνύναι ἐφικνέμενον. Illud primum extra controversiam est, pessime facere τὲς ἔθει ποιητᾷ καταχῶς κὶ ἀνεξετάςως ὀμνύοντας ἐν τοῖς τυχεσιν, ut Philo loquitur, addens nasci ἐκ πολυορκίας ψευδορκίαν: sic- ut & Ulpianus dixit nonnullos esse faciles ad jurandum contemtu religionis. Sapiens Hebræus Eccles. IX. 9. ὅρκῳ μὴ ἐθίσῃς τὸ ςόμα σε κὶ ὀνομασίᾳ τᾶ ἁγία μὴ συνεθιθῇς. Et mox: ἀνὴρ πολύορκος πλησθήσεται ἀνομίας, κὶ ἐκ ἀποςήσεται ἀπὸ τᾶ οἴκε ἀυτᾶ μάςιξ. Quo & illud Platonis pertinet undecimo de legibus: Θεῶν ὀνόματα μὴ χραίνειν ῥᾳδίως: & Hieroclis istud: Μελέτη δὲ ἀρίςη τῆ τηρεῖν τὸ περὶ αὐτῶν σέβας, τὸ μὴ πυκνῶς μηδὲ ὡς ἔτυχε χρῆσθαι τῷ ὅρκῳ, μηδὲ ἐπὶ τοῖς παρατυ- χῦσι, μηδὲ ὡς ἀναπλήρωσι λόγε, μηδὲ εἰς πίςωσιν διηγήμα- τος: & postea: τὸ δὲ, σέβε ὅρκον, ὀ μόνον ἐυορκεῖν ἀλλὰ κὶ ἀπέχεσθαι ὅρκω παρεγγυᾷ ὕτω γὰρ ἂν τηρήσαιμεν τὸ ἀεὶ ἐνυρκ- κεῖν, εἰ μὴ καταχρησοίμεθα τοῖς ὅρκοις· κὶ γὰρ ἐν τῇ συνεχῶς [τῶ] ὀμνύειν ῥᾳδίως ἂν μεταπέσοι τις εἰς ἐπιορκίαν· φειδοῖ δὲ τήρησις ἕπεται· ἡ γὰρ ἐκ ὀμεῖται, ἢ ὅταν ὀμνύῃ ἐυορκήσει· κὶ ὔτε ἂν ὑπὸ συνηθείας προδραμῃ ἡ γλῶσσα, ὔτε ὑπὸ παθῶν ἀκρατείας ἡ διάνοια σφαλέιη· τῇ μὲν γὰρ ὁ τρόπος ὀρθῶς χρησοῦτᾶι, τὴν δὲ τὸ [ἐθ-] τῆς ἐποχῆς τᾶ ὀμνύνειν. Deinde iterum: Σέβε ὅρκον, τῷ μὴ προχείρως αυτῷ καταχρῆσθαι δι’ ὅ γ’ καθ’ ἕξ ἐυορκεῖν ἐκ τᾶ μὴ ἐθισθῆναι ὀμνύνειν. Neque tamen sic vide- tur constitendum ut facilitas duntaxat & assidua jurandi consuetudo vetetur, quo scilicet tutiores à perjurio simus. Mihi persuasum est, non tantum à Christo, sed & ab his quos dixi, Judæo Maimonide, Græcis Chœrilo, Menan- dro, Epicteto plus indicari. Juravit Paulus at non in re sua, non in re modica alterius, sed in negotiis maxi- mi momenti ad Deum & salutem aliorum pertinentibus. Nos hodie, si ita res ferat, de pecuniola juramus, & quidem in re etiam nostra, quod Plato valde improbat. Et tamen Christiani haberi volumus, quasi nefus sit reve- rentia divini numinis nummorum aliquot jacturam facere. Utinam ea saltem jurisjurandi religio nos teneret quæ non paucos à Christo alienos tenuit. Isocratem audiamus: Ὅρκον ἐπακτὸν χροσδέχε διὰ δύο προφάσεις, ἢ σαυτὸν ἀιτίας ἀισχρᾶς ἀπολύων, ἢ φίλως ἐκ μεγάλων κινδύνων διασώζων: ἕνεκα δὲ χρημάτων μηδένα θεὸν ὀμόσῃς, μηδ’ ἂν ἐυορκεῖν μέλ- λῃς. δόξεις γὰρ τοῖς μὲν ἐπιορκεῖν, τοῖς δὲ φιλοχρημάτως ἔχειν. Ecce duas tantum causas admittit jurisjurandi, & quidem judicialis, ut infamiam fugias, aut ut ami- cum è magno periculo serves: quo exemplo & Sim- plicius ad Epictetum utitur, adjiciens aut ut patriæ ma- gnam operam naves. Hi ergo de re pecuniaria jusjuran- dum omne improbat. Clinias Pythagoricus cum trium talentorum mulctam jurejurando effugere posset, maluit tantæ pecuniæ damnum facere, quam jurare, quod exem- plum sui sæculi Christianis exprobrat Basilius. Hierocles ille quem dixi similiter nullum probat jusjurandum, nisi ob res necessarias atque egregias, & quæ obtineri citra jusju- randum nequeant. Verba ejus aurea ad aureum Pytha- goræ carmen hæc sunt: Τηρεῖν ἀυτὸ (τὸ ὅρκῳ) τὴν χρείαν ἐν τοῖς ἀναγκαίοις ἅμα καὶ τιμίοις, καὶ τότε ὅτε ὀυδεμία ἄλλη ἳ τοιότων σωτηρία παραφαίνηται, ἐι μὴ διὰ μόνης ἐκ τὲ ὅρκυ ἀ- ληθείας. Et hæc quidem ille dixerunt de jurejurando quod præstatur testandæ veritatis ergo. In pollicitationibus au- tem & pactionibus, de quibus proprie hic agit Christus, vix est ut tam gravis aliqua causa possit obtendi, nisi forte ea res sit in qua salus publica vertatur, quanquam & in ejus- modi negotiis idem forte præstare posset nuda promissio si adjiceretur ad rem fanciendam pœna perjurii, quæ pleros- que plus terret quam jurisjurandi religio: & monerentur qui aliquid spondent ne quid agerent nisi deliberato serio- que & quod apud Romanos etiam vicem jurisjurandi im- plevit EX ANIMI SUI SENTENTIA. Ad hoc jurisjuran- di genus spectant ista Hieroclis. Ὁ δὲ σέβων ὅρκον ἐν ἀρχῇ πα- ραγγείλας τὴν ἀποχὴν τῶ ὀμνύναι προςέτιθ περὶ ἳ ἐνδεχομένων κὶ ἀορίστων τῆς ἐκβάσεως ἐχόντων τὸ πέρας. Ταῦτα γάρ τά μικρά κὶ μεταπίπτοντα. διόκτε ἄξιοι ἐπ' ἀυτοῖς ὀμνύναι, ὅτ᾽ ἀσφα- λές. ὃ γὰρ ἐφ' ἡμῖν ἐςὶ πέρας ἀυτὰ ἀγαγεῖν. περὶ δὲ τῶν παρόν των ἀναγκαίως τε συνημμένων κὶ μεγίςων ὅιλων ἀσφαλὲς τὸ ὀμνύ- ειν κὶ πρέπον. ὅτε γὰρ τὸ μεταπιπτει τῶν πραγμάτων ἡμᾶς ἄν πότε σφαλῇ. ὅτε τὸ ταπεινὸν ἀυτῶν κὶ χαμαιπετὲς τῇ θεία τήν ἐ- πιμαρτυρίαν ἀριῆται. Cæterum eos etiam qui indistincte vi- dentur omne jusjurandum rejicere, aliquas tamen admit- tere exceptiones, præsertim magnæ utilitatis publicæ, mul- tis indiciis apparet. De Essenis dixit Josephus τὸ ὀμνύειν ἀυτοῖς περιίσαται quod & alii testantur. Atqui eosdem jurejurando adactos ad observationem religionis, idem Josephus apertum facit: Πρίν δὲ τῆς κοινῆς ἅψασθ τροφῆς, ὅρ- κυς ἀυτοῖς ὄμνυσι φρικώδεις. πρῶτον μὲν ἐυσεβήσειν τὸ θεῖον, ἔπειτα τὰ πρὸς ἀνθρώπως δίκαια φυλάξειν, καὶ μήτε κατὰ γνώμην βλάψειν τινὰ, μήτε ἐξ ἐπιτάγματος. μισήσειν δὲ ἀεὶ τὲς ἀδίκυς κὶ συναγωνιεῖθ τοῖς δικαίοις. τὸ πιστὸν ἀεὶ παρέ- ξειν πᾶσι, μάλιστα δὲ τοῖς κρατᾶσιν. κἂν ἀυτὸς ἄρχῃ μηδέποτε ἐξυβρίσειν ἐις τὴν ἐξυσίαν, μηδὲ ἐσθῆτε ἤ τινι πλείονι κόσμῳ τὲς ὑποτεταγμένες ὑπερλαμπρυνεῖθ. τὴν ἀλήθειαν ἀγαπᾶν ἀεὶ κὶ τὲς ψευδομένως ἐλέγχειν προέλεαθ χεῖρας κλοπῆς κὶ ψυ- χὴν ἀνοσία κέρδος φυλάξειν· κὶ μήτε κρύψειν τι τὲς ἀιρετιςὰς, μήτε ἑτέροις ἀυτῶν τι μηνύσειν κἂν μέχρι θανάτε τις βιάζηται. πρὸς τύτοις ὀμνύωσι μηδενὶ μὲν μεταδῶσειν τῶν δογμάτων ἑτέ- ρως ἢ ἀυτὸς παρέλαβεν· ἀφέξεσθ δὲ λησείας κὶ συντηρήσειν ὁ- μοίως τάτε τῆς ἀιρέσεως ἀυτῶν βιδλία κὶ τὰ τῶν ἀγγέλων ὀνό- ματα· τοιύτοις μὲν ὅρκοις τὲς προςιοντας ἐξασφαλίζονται. A qua narratione non longe dilcedit quod de veteribus Christianis, quorum instituta multis partibus cum Essenis congruebant, narrat Plinius quod essent soliti se Sacramento non in scelus aliquod obstringere, sed ne furta, ne latrocinia, ne adulteria committerent, ne fidem fallerent, ne depositum appel- lati negarent. Jurasse Christianos per salutem Cæsarum memorat Tertullianus: & alii juramentum per genium Cæsaris detrectantes causam attulerunt, quod is genius es- set dæmon, non quod jurare sine illa exceptione esset illicitum, ut mox videbimus. Athanasius qui sermone de passione & cruce Domini jusjurandum videtur indif- criminate rejicere, ipse tamen per calumniam accusatus purgat se Constantio hunc in modum: Tuæ pietati magna & clara voce manuque extenta, quod ab Apostolo didici, Deum in meam if sius animam testor, & ut scribitur in libris Regum jusjurandum concipio, Testis sit Dominus & testis Christus ejus, quod nunquam in malum tui mentionem feci apud fra- trem tuum Constantem Augustum, neque illum adversum te irritabi. Et mox: Vellem hunc hominem quisquis is est hic in præsentia adesse, ut delato juramento sub attestatione veritatis hæc ab eo sciscitarer, quæ enim ita dici audirique so- lumus quasi Deo præsente, ea sub hac formula jurisjurandi NOS CHRISTIANI HOMINES CONCIPERE SOLE- MUS. In Synodo Ephesina, cui multi interfuerunt quo- rum scriptis itidem jurandi mos videtur oppugnari, & Nestorio & Victori impositum videmus jusjurandum, ita ut sequentium temporum mentionem facere nihil sit necesse.

Fallere potius hic Grotius videtur elencho divi- sionis: nam conjungenda erant, quæ Christus conjunxit μὴ ὀμόσαι ὅλως, μήτε ἐν τῷ ὀρανῷ; quæ docent, Christum improbare juramenta, non o- mnia in universum, sed quæ fiunt per creaturas. Illud ergo ὅλως ad omnia, quæ sequuntur, referen- dum, non ad universa absolute, quo de prolixus hic est Heinsius: quem sensum etiam exhibent verba Jacobi Jac. V. 12. Nam quæ adduntur μήτε ἄλλον τίνα ὅρκον, respiciunt simile ejusmodi jura- mentum. Taxatur ergo levitas Pharisæorum, qui per creaturas jurabant, & in causis levibus, ac ju- ramentis ludebant, ut pueri astragalis. Interim admittere possumus etiam ea juramenta, quæ citra causam gravem fiunt, per nomen Domini, prohi- beri, neque refragabimur illi explicationi, non ju- randum, ne quidem per cœlum, per terram, per Hierosolyma; si eo sensu hæc accipiantur, quo et- iam in lege prohibebantur juramenta, levia scilicet & temeraria, nec fingatur, hic aliquid legi adje- ctum à Christo; quo inclinat Grotius pag. 104. dum ait: non satis certam esse eorum sententiam, qui in decalogo directè putant vetari juramenta ob cau- sas non satis graves: certum enim est, non Chri- stum modo, sed etiam legem Mosis omnia temera- ria juramenta improbare: Simpliciter Christum interdicere juramentis, probari nequit. Et distin- guit hic ipse Grotius inter juramentum promisso- rium, & testimoniale, hoc à Christo non improbari agnoscit; sed neque promissoria juramenta omni- no prohibita esse, fatetur. Nam si salus publica ea requirat, præstari posse, non abnuit. In pollicita- tionibus, inquit p. 107. & pactionibus, de quibus pro- prie hic agit Christus, vix est, ut tam gravis aliqua causa possit obtendi, nisi forte ea res sit, in qua salus publica versetur, quanquam & in ejusmodi negotiis idem forte præstare posset nuda promissio, si adjiceretur ad eam sanciendam pœna perjurii, quæ plerosque plus terret, quam jurisjurandi religio. At eadem est mens verborum Decalogi de non assu- mendo in vanum nomine Domini, quibus juramen- menta temeraria prohibentur: non autem quæ gloria nominis divini, vel salute publica, aliaque gravi causa postulante, præstantur. De illo Mar- tialis, jura verpe per Anchialum, videri prolixe poterit Seldenus in Prolegom. de successsion. ad bona defunctor.

Neque firmum satis est argumentum Grotii, quo hic, & l. II. de Jur. bell. & pacis c. XIII. n. XXI. probat, de juramento promisssorio hic proprie ser- monem esse, & apud Jacobum c. V. quod nempe prius ναὶ, & sὶ promissum significet, posterius ejus im- plementum. Quum illa EST est, non non, gemi- nata dicantur asseverationis & certitudinis causa, ut geminari Amen solet. Recte autem se habent illa, quibus concludit hunc locum Grotius pag. 113. Non vetat Christus jusjurandum, ut rem per se malam: sed ut rem, quam nisi in negotiis maximi momenti usurpare non liceat. Quæ autem sint res ejusmodi, non tam certis definitionibus comprehen- di potest, quam Spiritu charitatis dijudicari. Con- cludam hanc tractationem dicto Augustini: Qui intelligit non in bonis, sed necessariis jurationem ha- bendam, refrenet se, quantum potest, ut non ea uta- tur nisi necessitate, cum videt pigros esse homines ad credendum, quod eis utile est credere, nisi juratione firmetur.

Μήτε ἐν τῷ ὀρανῷ] Id est, ne quidem per cœlum, ut jam diximus. Est autem Hebraismus ὀμνύειν ἐν τῷ ὀρανῷ pro quo Græci dicerent ὀμνύειν τὸν ὀρανὸν, aut etiam κατὰ τοῦ ὀρανοῦ. Jam diximus non hos modos jurandi à Christo specialiter prohiberi, sed ne hos quidem à prohibitione excipi. Ju- dæis lege Mosis vetitum erat Deum alium jurare præter Deum Israelis: itaque jurare illis nefas erat per Baalem, Astarten, aliaque id genus falsa numina. Quamobrem & Christianos sui temporis reprehendit Tertullianus, qui aut ignorantia aut consuetudinis vitio dicerent Mehercule, & Medius fidius: quod & post eum fecit Hieronymus. Ea- dem hac causa Judæi Alexandrini recusabant Caji Cæsaris ὄνομα ὅρκιον ποιεῖσθαι ut Josephus narrat, quia nomen suum ut Dei in jurejurando Cajus usurpari volebat. At nomi- nare quædam ut Philo loquitur τῆς θείας δυνάμεως ἀπο- κνίσμα,

πτώματα, ita scilicet ut animi religio Deum spectaret, in- ter vetita habitum non est. Jurat Josephus Gen. XLII. 14. Ita vivat Pharao: more quidem Ægyptiorum, ut recte ab Abenezra est annotatum: sed quem imitaturus non fuisset vir eximie pius si quid in eo irreligiosi esse existimasset. Et quid est aliud, ita vivat Rex, quam, ita Regem sospi- tem Deus præstet? Elisæus propheta 2. Reg. II. Elix ita jurat: Vivit Deus & vivit (aut vivat potius, nam Hebræi- smus ista non distinguit) anima tua. Nec aliter Urias 2. Sam. XI. 11. Sed & Paulus per resurrectionem aut per conscientiam suam jurare videtur, cum dicit νὴ τὴν ἡμετέ- ραν καύχησιν 1. Corinth. XV. 31. Narrat in Apologetico Tertullianus Christianos non jurasse ut cæteros per Ge- nium principis, quod Græci dicunt τὴν καίσαρος τύχην, quod jusjurandum Polycarpo delatum & ab eo recusa- tum legimus: merito, quia isti voci inerat falsi numinis sensus, quod ita explicat Origenes: Τύχην μέντοι βασιλέως οὐκ ὄμνυμεν, ὡς οὐδ᾽ ἄλλον νομιζόμενον θεὸν. εἴτε γὰρ (ὡς ὠνό- μασάν τινες) ἐκφορὰ μόνον ἐστὶν ἡ τύχη, οὐκ ὄμνυμεν τὸ μηδα- μῶς ὂν ὡς θεὸν; ἢ ὅλως ὑφεστηκὸς κὴ δυνάμενόν τι ποιῆσαι. ἤ τα μὴ τὴν ὁμητικὴν δύναμιν εἰς ἄμη δὲὶ παραλαμβάνειμεν. ἔθι καὶ, ὡς τίσιν ἔδοξεν, οἱ πᾶσι τῶ ῥωμαίων βασιλέων τὸν δαί- μονα (id est, genium) ὀμνύουσι τὴν τύχην ἀυτῶ ὀμνύον- τες, δαιμόνιον ἐστιν ἡ ὀνομαζομένη τύχη τῶ βασιλέως, κὴ ὕτως ἀποθετητέον ἐστι μᾶλλον ὑπὲρ τῶ μὴ ὀμόσαι μοχθηρὸν δαίμονα καὶ ἄπιστον πολλάκις συνιξαμαρτάνοντα ᾧ ἔλαχεν ἀνθρώπῳ ἢ πληέον αὐτῶ ἁμαρτάνοντα. Sed eosdem Christianos Tertullianus eodem loco jurasse ait per salutem Principis omnibus geniis augustiorem. Postquam vero Imperato- res Christo nomen dederant, institutum est hoc sacramen- tum militare, ut jurarent, per Deum & Christum & Spiri- tum Sanctum & per majestatem Imperatoris, quæ secundum Deum generi humano diligenda est & colenda: quod nos Vegetius docet. Sic Marcellinus in collatione Cartha- giniensi secundum allegationes partium se judicaturum per salutem principum jurat: & hoc ipsum esse juramen- tum quod episcopi faiebant, memoratum canone XXV. Chalcedonensi, notant ibi Græci interpretes. Jurisjurandi per cœlum etiam Philo meminit. Sed & Origenes adver- sus Celsum sexto, Judæos ait solitos, per cœlum jurare. Cœlum autem hic par est regionem sideream intelligi.

Θρόνὸς ἐστὶ τῶ Θεῶ] Ex Esaiæ LXVI. 1. Hæc eo dicta sunt, ut ostendatur omnibus jurandi modis tacite Deum contineri. Id clare apparet infra XXIII. 22. ubi ita in- sert Christus, qui per cœlum jurat simul jurat per eum qui cœlo tanquam solio insidet. Solium autem Dei dicitur, quod in eo opificio pulcherrimis astris picturato ejusque perpetuo & æquabili motu divina majestas eximie eluceat, quemadmodum regum gloria tunc maxime conspicua est cum solio suo insident. Et formula hujus juramenti, & cau- sa ejus apparet in versu isto ex Sophoclis Menalippa, ὄμνυμι δ᾽ ἱερὸν αἰθέρ᾽ οἴκησιν διὸς. Sed & Julianus contra Christia- nos κεατὸν vocat θεῶ θρόνον.

## 5:35
V. 35. It is the footstool of his feet] Isaiah has הדום, by which it seems to be signified in passing the vileness of the earth compared to heaven. For the Hebrews use הדום in that sense, which the LXX translate as footstool, as in Psalm CX. 2. Varro taught us that those which are of one scansion are called footstools, those of more, benches. But the Syrian translates כבש quite aptly, because mention of a throne preceded. For כבש is in 2 Chronicles IX. 18. the footstool of the royal throne, which the LXX themselves call a footstool from that place, such as can be seen painted under the bed of Cassiopeia in the book of Germanicus which we edited some time ago. Of another kind are the hollow benches which Ovid mentions, which the Greeks call authema. Pausanias mentions foot-rests under the royal throne in more than one place. But what is said here about the earth, Proclus in his Timaeus ascribes the same to the earth from Orpheus, who when he was describing God said: and the lowest base of the earth is the root. Macrobius cites from an Oracle: And you, Earth, are his feet. Among Clement of Alexandria and others we have this of Orpheus concerning God: For he himself is established toward the brazen heaven, on a golden throne. He has placed the earth upon his feet.

Neither by Jerusalem] The Hellenists use interchangeably for the Hebrew כ, now in, now into. Thus here the translator of Matthew said into Jerusalem, when before he had said in heaven, in earth. But the Jews swore by Jerusalem as the Romans by Rome. Ovid: By the divinity of the fatherland.

It is the city of the great king] In Psalm XLVIII. the city of the great king and the city of our God signify clearly the same thing. And among the son of Sirach, a place according to the whole of God. This therefore pertains to this, that he who swears by Jerusalem may be understood to swear by him who placed his kingdom in Jerusalem, just as he who swears by the temple, swears by the inhabitant of the temple, below XXIII. 21.

Latin:

V. 35. ὑποπόδιόν ἐστι τῶν ποδῶν ἀυτοῦ] הדום habet Esaias, quo obiter significari videtur vilitas terræ cœlo compara- tæ. Nam eo sensu הדום Hebræi usurpant, quod ὑποπό- διον vertunt LXX. ut Psal. CX. 2. Varro nos docuit quæ unius sunt scansionis, scabella, quæ plurium, scamna appellari. At Syrus vertit כבש fatis apposite, quia θρόνο mentio præcessit. Est enim כבש 2. Paralip. IX. 18. scabellum so- lii regalis, quo ipsum LXX. e loco ὑποπόδιον vocant, quale pictum videre est sub feliquastro Cassiopeæ in libro Germa- nici quem edidimus olim. Alterius generis sunt cava sca- mna quorum Ovidius meminit, quæ Græci αὔθεμα appel- lant. Suppedanei sub throno regali meminit Pausanias non uno in loco. Quod autem hic de terra dicitur, idem Pro- clus in Timæo terræ adscribit ex Orpheo, qui cum Deum describeret dixit: πυμάτη δὲ βάσις χθονὸς ἔτδαδε ῥί- ζημ. Macrobius ex Oraculo citat: Γαῖα δὲ σὺ πόδες εἰσὶ. Apud Clementem Alexandrinum & alios habemus hoc Orphei ac Deo Αὐτὸς γὰρ χάλκειον ἐς οὐρανὸν ἐστήρικται, Χρυσέῳ ἐνὶ θρόνῳ. Γαίησ᾽ ἐπὶ ποσσὶ τέθηκεν.

Μήτε εἰς ἱεροσόλυμα] Hellenistæ promiscue pro He- bræo כ modo ἰ, modo εἰς usurpant. Ita hic Matthæi inter- pres εἰς ἱεροσόλυμα dixit, cum ante ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ, ἐν τῇ γῇ di- xiffet. Jurarunt autem Judæi per Hierosolyma ut Roma- ni per Romam. Ovidius: Per patriæ numen.

Πόλις ἐστὶ τοῦ μεγάλου βασιλέως] In Psalmo XLVIII. plane idem significantia sunt קרית מלך רב & עיר אלהינו. Et apud Sirachiden τόπος κατὰ πάνσιαν Θεῶ. Hoc igi- tur eo pertinet, ut qui per Hierosolyma jurat intelligatur per eum jurare qui Hierosolymis regnum suum posuit, quem- admodum qui per templum jurat, jurat per habitatorem templi, infra XXIII. 21.

## 5:36
V. 36. Neither by your head shall you swear] Ulpian: But if I have offered that you should swear by God, you have sworn by your own head. Ovid: He himself accustomed to swear by his own head... Martial: You might swear by your sacred things and your head. It is a question here of that mode of swearing, not of that to which Juvenal alludes when he says: ... not yet prepared to swear by the head of another to the Greeks. Of which likewise examples exist everywhere: and jointly, by your head and ours: Among Synesius: By your sacred head and the safety of my children.

For you are not able] This pertains to this, that it may be proved that he who swears by his own head swears by God, no less than he who swears by his own safety, which oath Ulpian also said is made with respect to the divine divinity. The cause of both sayings is because a man is not the Lord of his own safety or of his own head. Thus Menander in the Dyscolus said that a man is the master of his own year.

To make one hair white or black] This is such as that which is said in the beginning, that one cannot add one cubit to his stature. But mention of a hair is made here rather, so that it may be shown that not even the least thing of nature can be changed by us. For the Hebrews, as also the Greeks and Latins, say a hair for the indication of the smallest thing.

Latin:

V. 36. Μήτε ἐν τῇ κεφαλῇ ὀμόσῃς] Ulpianus: Cæterum si ego detuli ut per Deum jurares, tu per caput tuum jurasti. Ovi- dius: Per caput ipse suum solitus jurare ... Martialis: Per tua jurares sacra tuumque caput. De eo jurandi modo hic agitur, non de eo ad quem alludit Juvenalis cum ait: ... nondum Græcis jurare paratis Per caput alterius. Cujus itidem passim extant exempla: & conjunctim, per- que tuum nostrumque caput: Apud Synesium: Nὴ τὴν ἱερὰν σὲ κεφαλὴν καὶ τὴν τῶν παίδων με σωτη- ρίαν.

Ὅτι ὀ δύνασαι] Hoc eo pertinet ut probetur per Deum jurare qui per caput suum jurat, non minus quam qui salutem suam jurat, quod jusjurandum respectu divi- ni numinis fieri Ulpianus etiam dixit. Causa utriusque dicti est, quia homo nec salutis nec capitis sui est Dominus. Sic Menander dyscolo dixit hominem κύριον ἐνιαυτὲ ἑαυτὲ.

Μίαν τρίχα λευκὴν ἤ μέλαιναν ποιῆσαι] Hoc tale est quale quod initia dicitur non posse cubitum unum ad sta- turam adjicere. Sed pili hic potius fit mentio, ut ne mi- nimum quidem naturæ à nobis posse immutari ostendatur. Num Hebræi ut & Græci & Latini pilum dicunt ad rei mi- nimæ indicationem.

## 5:37
Vers. 37.

Let your speech be, yea yea, nay nay] That is, as James explains, let your yea be yea, and your nay, nay. Both yea and nay in this place are formulas by which one responded to a stipulation. For Christ is continuing the discourse instituted, as we have said, concerning promises. And so the Syrian rightly placed אִין for yea, which is a particle of responding. The Roman language in responding repeats the verb of the interrogator: as, will you give? I will give: will you do? I will do. But also if someone asked, will you give? should answer, why not? Ulpian wrote that in that case he is bound: because the expression why not is accustomed to have the meaning of the Greek yea. But just as one responded to an interrogator affirming through yea, so one responded to a denier through nay. But what is said here and in James, that it is necessary that yea be yea and nay be nay, has this meaning: that deeds ought to correspond to words, or as Justin rightly explains in his Apology to Antoninus, that we ought to speak the truth always. For it is a figure which the Greeks call antanaklasis, and some also call ploke, where the same word is repeated continuously with the meaning slightly changed, as, From that time Corydon, Corydon is for us. To that day Memmius was Memmius, and similar things. For in the former place yea signifies what is said, in the latter the deed itself which is signified by the word. Thus Paul says that God's promises in Christ are yea, 2 Cor. 1:21, using this little word in the latter meaning I mentioned, to indicate that all promises are fulfilled through him. But what we have said about yea, the same is to be understood about the little word nay: namely, that it also is placed first for the sign of a denying promise, then for the effect. Moreover, this expression, like most others of Christ and the Apostles, is taken from the common usage of those times. For as has been noted by others, the maxim was very common: let the yea of the righteous be yea, and their nay be nay. On the contrary, of those whose deeds disagreed with their words, it was said among them that they had a yea and a nay, that is, their yea was said to be a nay, and their nay was said to be a yea; Paul uses this manner of speaking in the cited passage 2 Corinthians 1:18, 19, and explains that very thing when he denies that he used lightness.
