Festus at the word naucum: Some say that from the Greek, yea and nay, a fickle man is signified. Whence it is more manifest that in the same chapter, verse 17, in certain codices yea and nay are wrongly repeated, when they should have been placed only once: although it appears that this is an error of ancient scribes who imprudently looked back to the passages of Matthew and James from the Syrian and Arabic interpreters. But since yea, as both the coherence of this passage and the words of Paul show, pertains to promises, it will be translated more correctly in Latin by 'it shall be' than by 'it is'. The sense of Christ's words is: that faith ought to be performed by us in promises even without oaths, just as if an oath had been added: which sense is made more open by what follows in James, 'lest you fall into hypocrisy', that is, lest you be found deceitful, which least becomes Christians. Similar is that of Alexis: 'An oath is firm, if I only nod.' And what is in Philo: 'Let the word of the upright be a firm, unbending, most truthful oath.' And Hierocles said that nothing ought to be dearer to good men than truth, so that they are the same whether they are unsworn or swearing. Such ought a Christian to be, and, as Clement of Alexandria speaks, to show the trustworthiness of his confession in an unchangeable and firm life and word. But this coheres excellently with the preceding: because as Philo says, 'the most beautiful and most beneficial and most fitting thing for a rational nature is to be unsworn, having been taught to speak the truth on every occasion, so that words are considered to be oaths.' Josephus concerning the Essenes: 'Everything said by them is stronger than an oath; but swearing is avoided by them, as something worse than

Since, therefore, it appears that the performance of promises is here being dealt with by Christ, this passage requires that we see to what extent it pertains. There are those who think that promises do not have the power of binding by themselves, but receive it from civil law in a certain form and manner. But the consensus of the Gentiles opposes that opinion. It is indeed true that a simple assertion about what someone is going to do ought indeed to proceed from a mind that at that time wishes to do what he says he will do, but it does not follow that he who speaks is bound to persevere in his intention, because the human will has the right to change its decrees: nor can it take that right away from itself solely by its own regard. But in a promise there is more. For a promise has at the same time a transfer of right: for just as the owner of a corporeal thing can transfer it to another by some sign of his will, so also the right itself which someone has to his own acts or things can be transferred to another, in full or for a defined part. And because by such an act some right passes to another, therefore the will can no longer honestly change itself, because no one can honestly either wish or do anything against a right acquired by another. Hence the force of vows which are made to God and of promises among men arises. But for a promise to be valid by the law of nature, three things are necessary: namely, that he who promises be capable of promising, and that the thing itself be capable of being promised, and then that the thing can be performed by the promisor. The first condition is lacking in those who do not have the use of reason. For there can be no will without understanding: therefore the words of infants and the insane do not have the efficacy of a promise. The second is lacking in things which either cannot be done by the nature of things, such as touching the sky with a finger, or which are in themselves dishonest, such as it would have been to kill John the Baptist, an innocent man and a Prophet of God. For what it is not permitted to do, that cannot even be validly promised, since a promise tends toward an act. The third condition is required whenever the act which is promised is not in the right of the promisor, as if a slave were to promise the services of another to his master. For since a promise emanates from the right of the promisor, it can effect nothing beyond the amplitude of that right. And these things are indeed so clear by the very light of nature that they do not stand in need of proof. Nevertheless, often some law brings it about that promises rightly made are not performed: which seems strange to those who do not have a disciplined judgment in these matters. For they think that a law of this kind conflicts with natural law, which is immutable; but that is not so. For laws do not establish that promises which someone had the right to promise are not performed for another who has acquired a right from the promise: that would be against the law of nature: but the subject matter itself receives a change: which also happens without a law, whenever the stipulator releases the promisor: for here no one is going to say that the promisor is still bound, and that he would be acting against nature if he did not do what he said. For the right, the right to which it was promised, which was the foundation of the obligation, has perished, and consequently no obligation now remains. But the law is accustomed to bring it about that promises should not be brought to effect in two ways, either by forestalling an obligation that would otherwise arise, or by removing one that has arisen. The law can do both for a probable cause, as a certain higher right obtains over individuals and the rights of individuals for the public utility than that right which is in the possession of individuals. The obligation is forestalled, as when it is established that a wife's promise is not effective unless her husband has given his authority. For here, with the right to bind herself taken away from the wife, an obligation cannot be born. An obligation that has arisen is extinguished again in two ways, either because the law takes away the right that was acquired by someone, or because it does not only do this, but also takes away from him who promised the freedom of fulfilling it. In the former case it is permitted not to fulfill it, because the law has taken away the right acquired by another; in the latter case it is not permitted to fulfill it, because this right also has been removed by the authority of the law, which can and does prevail more than individuals. I will add that there are certain laws which neither prevent an obligation from arising nor rescind one that has arisen, but only forbid that a legal action be brought about it in court, such as the Roman laws concerning naked pacts. Charondas on credited things. In this case, the promisor sins against faith if he does not stand by his promise. For not all the right of the stipulator has been taken away, but only the coercion is denied to him. Which is to be diligently noted by religious minds, lest they use wicked teachers and seek a hiding place for perfidy.

Τὸ δὲ περισσὸν τούτων] That which is beyond yea, yea, nay, nay. ἐκ τοῦ πονηροῦ ἐστι] Some think that this πονηροῦ is from the nominative ὁ πονηρὸς, by which word the Devil is indicated. It pleases me more, both here and in several other places, that it be taken from the nominative which is τὸ πονηρὸν: just as John said that the world lies ἐν τῷ πονηρῷ, chapter V.19. I understand here by τὸ πονηρὸν the custom of not standing by promises. For as we were saying from Polybius, the custom of swearing has been most frequented from the time when the faith of words began to totter. For he who is asked for an oath, as Philo notes, ἤδη εἰς ἀπιστίαν ὑπονοεῖται. Thus also the Essenes ἤδη καταγινώσεσθαι φασι τὸν ἀπιστούμενον δίχα Θεοῦ as it is in Josephus. In Sophocles, that Oedipus in Colonus to

Theseus: ὅτω σ' ὑφ' ἕξομκγ' ὡς κακὸν πεπώσομαι. The levity and inconstancy of men has begotten distrust, for which a remedy has been sought in the taking of an oath. But this saying has this connection with the preceding ones: Do not think that you are excluded from the commerce of men if you abstain from taking an oath as religiously as possible. For since the custom of swearing has arisen from vices, it will be easy, once these have been removed, to remove the necessity of an oath. But that will happen if, as I have said, you fulfill any words and promises so constantly that you are believed when you are not swearing rather than others when they are swearing. Isocrates said: δεῖ γὰρ τὰς ἀγαθὲς ἄνδρας τρόπον ὅρκε πισότερον φαίνεσθαι παρε- χομένως. Therefore, the precept of Christ does not pertain only to this, that Christians should not demand an oath from Christians: but also that Christians should not swear, by whomever it may be demanded. For as Clement rightly explains, it befits a Christian even πρὸς τὸς ἔξω to have a life worthy of belief, so as not even to require an oath. But, as I have said before, all these precepts are to be measured not so much by the niceties of words as by the nature of the thing itself. Christ does not forbid an oath as a thing evil in itself: but as a thing which it is not lawful to use except in matters of the greatest importance. But what things are of such a kind can be judged not so much by certain definitions as by the spirit of charity. I shall conclude this discussion with the saying of Augustine: He who understands that swearing is to be held not among good things but necessary ones, let him restrain himself as much as he can, so as not to use it except by necessity, when he sees that men are slow to believe what it is useful for them to believe, unless it is confirmed by an oath.

Pricaeus rightly notes that the exposition concerning Satan is supported not so much by the proposed article (for John also in Epist. I, verse 19, said that the world ἐν τῷ πονηρῷ κεῖσθαι: where, however, a thing, not a person, is to be understood) as by another passage of the same writer, in the same Epistle, chap. III, verse 12, καθὼς Καῒν τέ πονηρᾶ ἦν: which in turn seem to be taken not of a thing, but of a person. To me, however, the conjecture of those who think that in this passage of Matthew τὸ πονηρᾶ is to be derived not from the nominative πονηρός, but πονηρὸν, has seemed more probable. Thus Rom. XIV. 23, ἐκ πίσεως: and 1 John III. 19, ἐκ τῆς ἀληθείας εἶναι. It is therefore here ἐκ τᾶ πονηρᾶ, from evil custom, from evil habit.

Latin:

Vers. 37.

Ἔστω δὲ ὁ λόγος ὑμῶν, ναὶ ναὶ, ὀ ὀ] Id est ut Jacobus explicat ἤτω δὲ ὑμῶν τὸ ναὶ, ναὶ, καὶ τὸ ὀ, ὀ. Tam ναὶ quam ὀ hoc loco formulæ sunt quibus ad stipulationem respon- debatur. Nam de promissionibus, ut diximus institutum sermonem Christus prosequitur. Ita que Syrus recte pro ναὶ posuit אִין quæ respondendi particula est. Romana lingua in respondendo verbum interrogantis repetit: ut, dabis? dabo: facies? faciam. Sed & si quis interrogatus dabis, re- sponderit quid ni? in ea causa esse ut obligetur scripsit Ul- pianus: quia vox quid ni, solet habere significationem Græ- ci ναὶ. Sicut autem ad interrogationem ajentem per ναὶ, ita ad negantem per ὀ respondebatur. Quod vero hic & apud Jacobum dicitur oportere ut ναὶ sit ναὶ & ὀ sit ὀ, eum sen- sum habet, debere facta dictis congruere, aut ut Justinus recte explicat Apologetico ad Antonium, debere nos τ᾽ ἀ- ληθῆ λέγειν ἀεὶ Est enim figura quam Græci ἀντανάκλασιν, quidam & πλοκὴν vocant, ubi vox eadem continuo repe- titur significatu paulolum mutato ut, Ex illo Corydon, Corydon est tempore nobis. Ad illum diem Memmius erat Memmius, & similia. Nam priore loco ναὶ dictum significat, posteriore factum ipsum quod dicto significatur. Ita Paulus Dei promissa in Chri- sto ait esse ναὶ 2. Cor. I. 21. voculam hanc posteriore quem dixi significatu usurpans, ut indicaret omnia promissa per i- psum impleri. Quod autem de ναὶ diximus, i. em de ὀ vocu- la intelligendum est: nempe eam quoque primum pro no- ta promissi negantis, deinde pro effectu poni. Est autem locutio hæc ut pleræque aliæ Christi & Apostolorum sum- ta ex medio usu illorum temporum. Nam ut ab aliis nota- tum est, γνώμη erat tritiffima: τῶν δικαίωνταὶ ἔσιν ναὶ, καὶ τὰ ὀ- σιν ὀ. Contra quorum facta dictis discrepabant, apud hos dicebatur esse ναὶ κὶ ὀ, id est ναὶ ipsorum dicebatur esse ὀ, & ὀ dicebatur esse ναὶ, pro loquendi genere Paulus utitur di- cto loco 2. Corinth. 1. 18. 19. idque ipsum explicat, cum ne- gat se χρήσασθαι ἐλαφρίᾳ levitate usum. Festus ad vocem naucum: Quidam ex Græco, ναὶ κὶ ὀχὶ levem hominem signi- ficari. Quo manifestius est ibidem commate 17. in qui- busdam codicibus male repeti ναὶ & ὀ, cum semel dunta- xat ponenda fuerint: quanquam veterum esse errorem li- brariorum ad Matthæi & Jacobi loca imprudenter respi- cientium ex Syro & Arabe interpretibus apparet. Cum ve- ro ναὶ, ut & hujus loci cohærentia & Pauli verba osten- dunt, ad ἐπαγγελίας pertineat, rectius Latine per fiet quam per est transferetur. Sensus verborum Christi est: fidem à nobis præstari debere in promissis etiam injuratis, perinde quasi jusjurandum accessisset: quem sensum apertiorem facit quod apud Jacobum sequitur μὴ εἰς ὑπόκρισιν πέσητε id est, ne fallaces inveniamini, quod Christianos minime de- cet Simile est illud Alexidis: Ὅρκον βέβαιός ἐστι, ἂν νεύσω μόνον. Et quod apud Philonem est: ὀ τῷ σπεδαίε λόγος ὅρκον ἔστω βέβαιον ἀκλινὴς ἀψευδέστατον. Et Herocles dixit, nihil vi- ris bonis veritate carius esse debere, ὥστε κἀνωμότοις εἶτε καὶ ὀμνύεσι. Talis esse debet Christianus, &, ut Clemens A- lexandrinus loquitur, τὸ πισὸν τῆς ὁμολογίας ἐν ἀμεταπτώτῳ κὶ ἑδραίῳ δεικνύειν βίῳ τε καὶ λόγῳ. Optime autem hoc cohæret cum præcedentibus: quia ut inquit Philo κάλλι- τον κὶ βιωφελέςατον κὶ ἄρμοττον λογικῇ φύσει τὸ ἀνώμοτον, ὕ- τως ἀληθεύειν ἐφ᾽ ἑκάςε δεδιδαγμένη, ὡς τὲς λόγες ὄρκες εἶ- ναι νομίζεσθαι. Josephus de Essenis: πᾶν τὸ ῥηθὲν ὑπ᾿ αὐτῶν ἰσχυρότερον ὅρκο· τὸ δὲ ὀμνύειν αὐτοῖς περιΐσταται, χεῖρον τι

Quoniam igitur apparet de promissorum præstatione hic agi à Christo, exigit hic locus videamus id quousque pertineat. Sunt qui existi- mant promissa per se vim obligandi non habere, sed eam accipere à lege civili certa forma, modoque. Sed ei sen- tentiæ consensus Gentium repugnat. Verum sane est, sim- plicem asseverationem de eo quod quis facturus sit, debere quidem ex eo animo proficisci qui tum temporis id velit facere quod se facturum dicat, at non item ex eo teneri eum, qui dicit, in proposito perseverare, quia voluntas hu- mana habet jus sua decreta mutandi: neque id jus solo sui respectu sibi potest auferre. At in promissione plus est. Ha- bet enim promissio simul juris translationem: Sicut enim Dominus rei corporalis eam potest in alium transferre si- gno aliquo voluntatis: ita etiam jus ipsum quod quis ha- bet ad suos actus aut res, potest in alterum transferri, in solidum aut pro parte definita. Et quia tali facto jus ali- quod in alterum transit, ideo voluntas jam ultra se ho- neste mutare non potest, quia nemo honeste potest aut velle aut facere contra jus alteri quæsitum. Hinc voto- rum quæ Deo fiunt & promissorum inter homines vis ori- tur. Sed ut jure naturæ valet promissio tria sunt neces- saria: nempe ut qui promittit ad promittendum sit ido- neus, & ut res ipsa promissi sit capax, deinde ut res possit præstari à promittente. Prima conditio deficit in his qui ra- tionis usum non habent. Nullum enim velle esse potest sine intellectu: ideo infantium & furiosorum verba non habent promissi efficaciam. Secunda deficit in rebus quæ aut per rerum naturam fieri non possunt, ut cælum digito attingere, aut quæ per se sunt inhonesta, quale erat Johan- nem Baptistam innocentem & Dei Prophetam occidere. Quod enim facere non licet, id ne promitti quidem valide potest cum promissio ad factum tendat. Tertia conditio de- sideratur quoties actus qui promittitur non est in jure pro- mittentis, ut si servus non domino operas promittat. Nam cum promissum emanet è jure promittentis nihil potest efficere ultra juris illius amplitudinem. Et hæc quidem ipso naturæ lumine ita sunt clara, ut probationis non indigeant. Veruntamen sæpe lex aliqua efficit ut recte promissa non præstentur: quod mirum videtur his qui judicium in istis rebus subactum non habent. Putant enim legem ejusmodi pugnare cum jure naturali, quod sit immutabile; id vero non ita est. Neque enim constituunt leges ne promissa quæ quis promittendi jus habuit alteri jus ex promissione nacto non præstentur: quod esset contra jus naturæ: sed ipsa ma- teria mutationem accipit: quod etiam citra legem fit, quo- ties stipulator promissorem liberat: hic enim nemo dictu- rus est promissorem adhuc teneri, & contra naturam factu- rum ni faciat quod dixerit. Jus enim, jus cui promissum est, quod fundamentum erat obligationis, interiit, ac proinde nulla jam restat obligatio. Solet autem lex efficere ne pro- missa ad effectum perduci debeant duobus modis, aut an- tevertendo orituram alioqui obligationem, aut ortam tol- lendo. Utrumque ex probabili causa facere lex potest, ut quæ in singulos atque jura singulorum ad utilitatem publi- cam jus quoddam superius obtineat eo jure quod est penes singulos. Antevertitur obligatio, ut cum constituitur ne ef- ficax sit promissum uxoris nisi maritus auctor accesserit. Hic enim jure ad obligandum se uxori ademto nasci obli- gatio non potest. Orta exstinguitur duobus iterum modis, aut quia lex jus quod alicui quæsitum est aufert, aut quia non hoc tantum facit, sed etiam ei qui promisit aufert im- plendi libertatem. Illo casu licet non implere, quia lex jus alteri quæsitum abstulit; hoc casu non licet implere, quia hoc quoque jus sublatum est imperio legis, quæ plus singulis potest polletque. Illud addam, esse leges quas- dam quæ obligationem nec oriri impediant nec ortam re- scindant, sed tantum in foro de eo jus dici vetent ut le- ges Romanæ de pactis nudis. Charondas de rebus credi- tis. Hoc casu promissor adversus fidem delinquit si non stet promisso. Non enim jus omne stipulatoris sublatum est, sed sola coactio ei denegatur. Quod religiosis animis di- ligenter est annotandum, ne pravis magistris usi latebram perfidiæ quærant.

Τὸ δὲ περισσὸν τούτων] Id quod est ultra ναὶ ναὶ, καὶ οὔ. ἐκ τοῦ πονηροῦ ἐστι] Quidam istud πονηρῦ putant esse à recto ὁ πονηρὸς, qua voce Diabolus indicatur. Mihi ma- gis placet & hic & aliis aliquot in locis sumi à recto quod est τὸ πονηρὸν: quomodo Johannes dixit mundum jace- re ἐν τῷ πονηρῷ, cap. V.19. Intelligo hic τὸ πονηρὸν morem non standi promissis. Nam ut ex Polybio dicebamus, mos jurandi ex eo maxime est frequentatus, ex quo laba- re cœpit dictorum fides. Qui enim juramentum poscitur ut Philo notat, ἤδη εἰς ἀπιστίαν ὑπονοεῖται. Sic & Esseni ἤδη καταγινώσεσθαι φασι τὸν ἀπιστούμενον δίχα Θεοῦ ut est apud Jo- sephum. Apud Sophoclem ille in Colono Oedipus ad p

Thesea: ὅτω σ' ὑφ' ἕξομκγ' ὡς κακὸν πεπώσομαι. Levitas hominum & inconstantia diffidentiam genuit, cui reme- dium quæsitum est jurejurando. Est autem hujus dicti cum superioribus hæc connexio: Ne putate vos ab hominum commercio excludi si jurejurando quam religiosissime abs- tineatis. Nam cum de vitiis ortus sit jurandi mos, faci- le erit iisdem sublatis tollere jurisjurandi necessitatem. Id autem fiet, si, quemadmodum dixi, tam constanter quævis dicta ac promissa impleatis, ut injuratis vobis po- tius quam juratis aliis credatur. Isocrates dixit: δεῖ γὰρ τὰς ἀγαθὲς ἄνδρας τρόπον ὅρκε πισότερον φαίνεσθαι παρε- χομένως. Non igitur eo tantum pertinet Christi præce- ptum, ne Christiani à Christianis exigant jusjurandum: verum etiam ne jurent Christiani à quocunque tandem exigatur. Nam ut recte explicat Clemens, decet Chri- stianum etiam πρὸς τὸς ἔξω τὸ βίον ἔχειν ἀξιόπιστον, ὡς μή- δε ὄρκον αἰτεῖσθαι. Sed, ut ante etiam dixi, omnia hæc præcepta non tam ex verborum apicibus quam ex rei i- psius natura metienda sunt. Non vetat Christus jusju- randum ut rem per se malam: sed ut rem quam nisi in negotiis maximi momenti usurpare non liceat. Quæ au- tem sint res ejusmodi non tam certis definitionibus com- prehendi potest quam spiritu charitatis dijudicari. Con- cludam hanc tractationem dicto Augustini: Qui intelligit non in bonis sed necessariis jurationem habendam, refrenet se quantum potest, ut non ea utatur nisi necessitate, cum videt pigros esse homines ad credendum quod eis utile est crede- re, nisi juratione firmetur.

Expositionem de Satana valide notat Pricæus fulcire non tam articulum præpositum (nam & Jo- hannes Epist. I. vers. 19. mundum ἐν τῷ πονηρῷ κεῖσθαι dixit: ubi tamen non persona, sed res in- telligenda est) quam alium ejusdem Scriptoris lo- cum, cap. ejusd. Epist. III. com. 12. 8 καθὼς Καῒν τέ πονηρᾶ ἦν: quæ vicissim non de re, sed persona capienda videntur. Mihi tamen probabilior visa est conjectura eorum, qui hoc Matthæi loco τὸ πονηρᾶ à recto non πονηρός, sed πονηρὸν deducendum putant. Sic Rom. XIV. 23. ἐκ πίσεως: & 1. Johan. III. 19. ἐκ τῆς ἀληθείας εἶναι. Est ergo heic ἐκ τᾶ πονηρᾶ, ex malo more, mala consuetudine.

## 5:38
Vers. 38.

ἠκέσατε ὅτι ἐῤῥέθη] You have understood that it was said, namely to your ancestors. He shows, moreover, that this ἐῤῥέθη also refers to an ancient time, the fame of which has reached posterity.

ὀφθαλμὸν ἀντὶ ὀφθαλμᾶ, κὶ ὀδόντα ἀντὶ ὀδόντῷ] You will conveniently supply the elliptical sentence if you add, he who did the injury shall pay. This is, moreover, a most ancient law among almost all nations. Aristotle calls it τὸ ἀντιπεπονθὸς and says that the law of Rhadamanthus is described by this verse: εἴκε πάθοι τὰ κ' ἔρεξε δίκη κ' ἰθεῖα γένοιτο. From Greece this also passed to Rome: whence in the XII Tables: If he has broken a limb, let there be retaliation. It appears, however, from the law of Moses, especially from the words which are in Deut. XIV. 21, that there was no exact retaliation except by the decree of a judge. Indeed, as Lucretius rightly said: Because each man wished to avenge himself more from anger than is now permitted by equitable laws, for that reason men grew weary of living a life of violence.

Which opinion the Emperors Honorius and Theodosius expressed thus: For this reason the vigor of judgments and the protection of public law seem to have been established in the midst, so that no one may be able to permit himself vengeance. It is indeed true that in certain cases the laws have indulged something to just grief, just as Roman laws permit a father to kill an adulterous daughter, or the ravisher of a daughter: just as also among the Hebrews the nearest kinsman could avenge a homicide by private hand: yet so, as I think it is rightly to be noted by the teachers of the Hebrews, that if that homicide had been committed beforehand without evil intent, the avenger himself would undergo the penalty of death. But in offenses which are less than homicide, nothing more is granted to the injured than to approach a judge, and to demand vengeance from him, as if by their own right. And this is the kind of punishment which Plato, Aristotle, and the philosopher mentioned by Gellius properly call τιμωρίαν, which Clement of Alexandria defines as κακᾶ ἀνταπόδοσι εἰς τὸ τᾶ τιμωρᾶντα σύμφερον ἀναφερομένη. Where τὸ σύμφερον is taken a little more loosely, as also in Aristotle, κέρδος in this very argument. For because for most people—vengeance is sweeter than life itself; therefore what harms the adversary is understood to be, as it were, profitable to them themselves, which the Mime expressed thus: The remedy for the pain of the injured is the pain of the enemy. Aristotle in his Art of Rhetoric says that τιμωρίαν (retribution) is for the sake of the one acting, so that he may be satisfied, where ὁ ποιῶν (the one acting) is he who exacts vengeance. For we are considered to do even that which we do through a judge. I do not doubt, however, that if we look to strict law, it was permitted to the injured party to demand precisely from the judge that a wound also be inflicted upon the adversary, just as Bathos taught: and Josephus explicitly testifies. But that among the Hebrews, as their teachers and the same Josephus note, and among the Romans, as Gellius testifies, money was usually paid for a limb, that arose from the equity of the injured, which through many examples passed into custom. But this very money, insofar as it exceeded the estimation of the damage given and the expenses, was vengeance: not commanded to the Hebrews but conceded: of which kind also among the Romans were both the accusations of public trials and the penal actions from private delicts, for double, triple, or quadruple.

Latin:

Vers. 38.

ἠκέσατε ὅτι ἐῤῥέθη] Intellexistis dictum esse, majo- ribus nimirum vestris. Ostendit autem hoc quoque illud ἐῤῥέθη ad antiquum tempus referri, cujus ad posteros fama pervenerit.

ὀφθαλμὸν ἀντὶ ὀφθαλμᾶ, κὶ ὀδόντα ἀντὶ ὀδόντῷ] De- fectivam orationem commode supplebis si addas, red- det qui injuriam fecit. Est autem hoc jus vetustissimum apud omnes prope gentes. Aristoteles τὸ ἀντιπεπον- θὸς vocat & dictum ait jus Radamanti isto versu descri- ptum: εἴκε πάθοι τὰ κ' ἔρεξε δίκη κ' ἰθεῖα γένοιτο. Ex Græcia & hoc Romam transiit: unde in XII. tabulis: Si membrum rupit, talio esto. Apparet autem ex lege Mosis, præcipue ex verbis quæ sunt Deut. XIV. 21. non exactam talionem nisi judicis decreto. Nimirum, ut recte Lucre- tius dixit: Amplius ex ira quod enim se quisque volebat Vlcisci, quam nunc concessum est legibus æquis, Idcirco est homines pertæsum vi colere ævum.

Quam sententiam Honorius & Theodosius Imperatores ita expresserunt: Iccirco judiciorum vigor jurisque publici tu- tela videtur in medio constituta, ne quisquam sibi ipsi permit- tere valeat ultionem. Verum quidem est, in quibusdam casibus leges aliquid indulsisse justo dolori, sicut jura Romana permittunt Patri adulteram filiam, aut filiæ ra- ptorem occidere: Quomodo & apud Hebræos homici- dium vindicare manu privata proximus agnatus potuit: ita tamen, quemadmodum ab Hebræorum magistris re- cte notandum arbitror, ut si prius illud homicidium sine dolo malo patratum esset, ipse ultor capitis pœnam subiret. Sed in delictis quæ infra homicidium sunt, ni- hil ultra concessum læsis, quam adire judicem, & ab eo ul- tionem, tanquam jure suo, exposcere. Et hoc pœnæ ge- nus est quod τιμωρίαν proprie vocant Plato, Aristoteles & rus Philosophus apud Gellium, quam definit Clemens A- lexandrinus κακᾶ ἀνταπόδοσι εἰς τὸ τᾶ τιμωρᾶντα σύμφερον ἀναφερομένη. Ubi τὸ σύμφερον paulo laxius sumitur, ut & apud Aristotelem κέρδος in hoc ipso argumento. Quia enim plerisque -- vindicta bonum vita jucundius ipsa; ideo quod adversario nocet, ipsis quasi prodesse intelligitur, quod ita Mimus extulit: Læso dolory remedium inimici dolor. Aristoteles in arte Oratoria τιμωρίαν esse dicit τῦ ποιε͂ντος ἕνεκα ἵνα ἀποπληρωθῆ, ubi ὁ ποιῶν est is qui ultionem exigit. Facere enim censemur etiam quod per judicem facimus. Non dubito autem, quin si jus strictum respicimus, licue- rit vulnerato à judice præcise exigere, ut adversario quo- que vulnus infligeretur, quemadmodum Bathos doce- bat: & Josephus diserte testatur. Quod autem apud He- bræos, ut notant eorum magistri atque idem Josephus, & apud Romanos teste Gellio, pro membro pecunia sol- vi solebat, id natum ex læsorum æquitate, quæ multis ex- emplis in morem transierit. Sed hæc ipsa pecunia quate- nus damni dati æstimationem & impendia excedebat, ul- tio erat: non imperata Hebræis sed concessa: cujus gene- ris & apud Romanos erant tum accusationes publicorum judiciorum, tum ex privatis delictis actiones pœnales, in duplum, triplum, quadruplum.

## 5:39
Verse 39.

I say to you, do not resist the evil one] I think those judge correctly who interpret that πονηρῷ (evil one) as a man, and that it is the very thing which Moses said in Hebrew in Exodus 22:13, לָרָשָׁע, which the LXX translate as τῷ ἀδικε͂ντι (the one doing wrong): by which example it may be permitted to translate τῷ πονηρῷ thus: to him who has done an injury. And it is manifest that τὸ ἀντιστῆναι (to resist) cannot be taken universally. For he also resists who testifies to his innocence with words, which Christ did, and after him the Apostles. But since the preceding words, to which this sentence is opposed, deal περὶ τῆς τιμωρίας (concerning retribution), τὸ ἀντιστῆναι must entirely be referred to the same thing, which Paul also teaches us, explaining this precept with these words, 'repaying no one evil for evil,' Rom. 12:17, which is, as we have said, a clear description of retribution: from which it also appears what is meant in the same passage of Paul by 'not avenging yourselves'. For since ἐκδικεῖν (to avenge) signifies now to take vengeance, now to defend, it must necessarily be taken there for vengeance: for he who only defends himself does not return evil for evil, but only he who takes vengeance: which the following words of Paul also declare, 'but giving place to wrath,' that is, to divine vengeance, as is to be seen in the same place. Aristotle everywhere places τὸ ἀμύνειν (to ward off/defend) in the part of virtue, whom Cicero followed, referring vindication to the law of nature, through which, he says, force and injury are repelled by defending or by taking vengeance. Of the same is that in his Offices: 'The first duty of justice is that it harms no one, unless provoked by injury.' 'O how he corrupted a simple and true sentiment,' says Lactantius, 'by the addition of two words.' For one must harm no one, not even him who has harmed first. Which Plato perceived more closely than the others. For it is his in the Crito: 'one must not return wrong for wrong': likewise: 'therefore one must neither return wrong nor do evil to any man, not even if one suffers anything whatsoever from them': which Maximus Tyrius, a follower of the dogmas of Plato, explains widely in the diatribe to which he gave the title 'Whether one who has done wrong should be wronged in return,' having demonstrated the inconveniences which usually follow vengeance. But Hierocles also said: 'to return wrong is to be carried into the same wickedness as those who do wrong.' The Lacedaemonians used to add to their prayers 'to be able to be wronged.' Worthy of memory also is that of Menander: 'This man is the most excellent, O Gorgias, who knows how to be wronged the most of mortals.' Among the tenets of Pythagoras, Iamblichus records: 'neither to initiate abuse nor to take vengeance on those who abuse.' The same: 'He commanded that it is much better to be wronged than to kill a man. For in the afterlife lies the judgment.' Metellus Numidicus in his speech to the people: 'Good men accept injury more easily than they inflict it on another.' Seneca is in the same parts: 'Vengeance,' he says, 'is an immense word, and distant from injury only by order: he who takes vengeance sins only more excusably.' But even this very 'sinning more excusably' he who repays injury does not grant, he whom I mentioned, Maximus, in whose judgment 'the one who takes vengeance is more unjust than the one who preceded.' I will add to these Musonius: 'To look at how one might retaliate against the one who bites and to do evil in return to the one who started it, is of some beast, not of a man.' And these things indeed can seem to pertain closely to that vengeance where one decides either by hand 'to ward off a man who first causes trouble.' Or also: 'to play the fox to another fox.' But Christ's precept openly looks to that kind of vengeance which is accustomed to seem less immodest: certainly it is not equally dangerous publicly, when an action instituted for vengeance is exercised before a Magistrate. For He forbids this very thing which God through Moses had not indeed approved indiscriminately (for leniency always pleased Him more than wrath) but which He had allowed to happen and about which He had wished judgment to be rendered, so that the occasion of a greater evil might be avoided. For otherwise the law itself was doing this, that if it were possible it might draw men back from the desire for vengeance: which Philo acknowledges, among whom the Alexandrian Jews address God thus: 'We are terrified, O Master, having been taught by the holy law to suffer fourfold the hatred of the enemy.' But what the scope of the law given through Moses was, and how it does not fight with this precept of Christ which agrees with the warnings of the Prophets, seems to me to have been explained quite clearly by Tertullian against Marcion, IV. Christ clearly teaches a new patience, prohibiting even the return of injury permitted by the Creator, demanding an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth: instead, He Himself commands that the other cheek be offered, and that the cloak also be yielded over the tunic. Clearly Christ added these things as supplements consistent with the discipline of the Creator. And so it must be immediately renounced whether the discipline of patience is preached under the Creator. Thus through Zechariah He commanded that no one should remember the malice of his brother, nor even of his neighbor. For again, 'Let no one,' He says, 'reconsider the malice of his neighbor.' Much more did He enjoin patience for injury, who enjoined oblivion. But also when He says: 'Vengeance is mine and I will repay,' He likewise teaches patience that waits for vengeance. Insofar, therefore, as it does not follow that the same person should be seen to demand tooth for tooth and eye for eye in return for an injury—he who prohibits not only retaliation but also vengeance, and even the recollection and reflection upon an injury—to that extent it is opened up to us how he judged 'eye for eye and tooth for tooth,' not to permit a second injury of retaliation (understand that it might be demanded rightly and piously), which he had prohibited by forbidding vengeance, but to restrain the first, which he had prohibited by the opposing retaliation, so that everyone, looking at the license (that is, that permission of the deed with the authority of civil law) of a second injury, might restrain himself from the first. For he knows that violence is more easily compressed by the representation of retaliation than by the promise of vengeance. But both had to be established according to the nature and faith of men, so that he who believed in God would expect vengeance from God; he who trusted less would fear the laws of retaliation. This will of the law, struggling with its interpretation, Christ, the Lord of the Sabbath and of the law and of all the Father's dispositions, both revealed and made competent, commanding the offering of the other cheek also, so that he might all the more extinguish the retaliation for an injury, which the law also had wished to prevent through retaliation, certainly which it had manifestly restrained through the Prophets, both prohibiting the memory of an injury and directing vengeance to God. Thus, if Christ introduced anything, it was not as an adversary but as a helper of the precept; he did not destroy the disciplines of the Creator. Finally, if I should consider the very reason for the patience to be commanded, and indeed so fully and perfectly, it will not stand if it is not of the Creator who promises vengeance, who provides the judge. Otherwise, if he who is not going to defend me imposes upon me such a weight of patience—not only of not striking back but also of offering the other cheek, and not only of not returning curses but even of blessing, and not only of not retaining the tunic but of granting the cloak as well—he commands patience in vain, not showing me the reward of the precept, I mean the fruit of patience, which is vengeance, which he ought to have permitted me if he himself does not provide it, or if he did not permit it to me, he himself should provide it. Since it is also in the interest of discipline that an injury be avenged. For by the fear of vengeance all iniquity is restrained. Otherwise, with liberty let loose everywhere, it will hold sway, digging out both eyes and cutting out every tooth because of the security of impunity. I have transcribed this passage, not unworthy of being read and considered, all the more willingly because from it one can understand why and to what extent such laws can be retained even in Christian lands, which restrain by the fear of retaliation or punishment those who have not yet learned to do right of their own accord: while the rule of patience remains intact for all the pious, which nature obscurely insinuates, not only the Prophets but also the Philosophers commend, and Christ explicitly commands. Mindful of this precept, those Christians of better ages did not hesitate to appeal to the testimony of their very enemies. Justin in his Apology: 'For we can demonstrate that many among us, having been changed from violent men and tyrants, either having been overcome by observing the endurance of life in their neighbors, or having noticed the strange patience of fellow-travelers who had been cheated, or having had experience of business partners.' Athenagoras: 'They are so purified in their souls that instead of hating their enemies they love them, and instead of—to say the least—speaking ill of those who have initiated insults, they bless them, and pray for those who plot against their lives.' Justin himself speaks thus about the accusers of the Christians: 'For we shall not deem it worthy to punish those who accuse you. For it is enough for them to have their own wickedness and ignorance of what is good.' It is pleasing, for the shame of those who now wish to be called Christians, to bring forward the words of Musonius pertaining properly to this judicial vengeance. He says: 'Neither would he himself ever bring a charge of insult, nor would he advise another to do so.' And we read in Lysias: 'It is unfree to be very litigious about slander.' And explaining the reason for his opinion, he says it is not shameful for a wise man to be mocked, spat upon, or finally beaten; but to mock, to spit upon, to beat [is shameful]. Soon, having brought forward examples of those who had overlooked injuries inflicted upon them, he concludes thus: 'How much better it is for the philosopher to appear in such a state that he deems anyone who might offend against him worthy of forgiveness, rather than to seem to be defending himself by going to law and making accusations, while in truth he is behaving unseemly, acting inconsistently with his own words.' To Zeno, who said, 'May I perish if I do not punish you,' he replied, 'And I, may I perish if I do not make you my friend.'

But whoever shall strike you on your right cheek, turn to him the other also] It often happens in Hebraisms that an adversative includes a comparison within itself: which being added, this sentence will be most plain in this manner: Do not, if someone has done you evil, repay him evil in turn or harbor hatred for him: but rather, to one striking one of your cheeks, turn the other also to be struck: rather, that is, than that you should take revenge. Furthermore, it is taken from a proverb to turn the cheek to one striking, for that which is to bear something patiently, as can be seen in Lamentations 3:30. And here, too, as several times above, there is a resolution of a tacit objection. For he who is commanded to abstain from all revenge, immediately there comes to his mind that saying of the Mime: By bearing an old injury, you invite a new one. Christ, therefore, lest anyone flatter himself with this pretext, says it is much better that a second injury be received than that revenge be taken. And this is what Plato said, that an injury is not to be returned, 'even if we must suffer things even more grievous than these.' The same objection is also found in Maximus of Tyre: 'For this reason, one might say, the just man is insulted, and slandered, and prosecuted, and deprived of his wealth, and cast into prison, and exiled, and dishonored, and dies.' He answers that it is no wonder such things happen to a good man, because there is little protection in naked innocence before wicked judges: that it is permitted to him meanwhile to exclaim with great confidence of spirit that Homeric line: 'I think I am honored by the will of Zeus.'

Grotius rashly opposes Christ to Moses. Christ's precept openly regards that kind of revenge which is wont to seem less immoderate: certainly, it is not equally dangerous in public, when an action instituted for vengeance is exercised before a Magistrate. For it forbids this very thing, which God through Moses had not indeed approved indiscriminately—for lenity always pleased Him more than wrath—but which He had allowed to happen, and concerning which He had willed that judgment be rendered, so that an occasion for a greater evil might be avoided. For otherwise, the law itself was striving for this, that if it were possible, it might draw men back from the desire for vengeance. Thus Grotius. Christ did not prohibit public vengeance, or retribution instituted for an injury, but [prohibited] that we should take revenge out of private affection. Nor do the Mosaic laws hold otherwise concerning it. For that 'an eye for an eye' looked to forensic laws, and was a prescription for the Magistrate, as in Deuteronomy 19:18-19. Nor, however, was that law abolished by this, as Faustus the Manichaean caviled, but the corruption of the Pharisees and the wicked custom of the Jews were corrected and amended, as if by the law of retaliation license were given to private individuals to provoke to vengeance and to solicit the Magistrate out of a spirit and affection of private revenge. Christ, however, deals here not with the right or duty of the Magistrate, but with the duty of a Christian man in private life, to whom He prescribes patience and meekness. Which Moses also prescribed in Leviticus 19:18: 'You shall not take vengeance, nor shall you reserve hatred against the children of your people,' and Solomon in Proverbs 24:29: 'Do not say, as he has done to me, so I will do to him; I will render to that man according to his work.' The whole law of Moses remained besides, which Christ professes in this very discourse is in no part infringed by Him. Christ could, however, with the law intact, command the injured party not to demand retaliation: because the law did not command him to do this, but granted it, and he does nothing against the law who does not use what is granted. But to forbid a judge from judging according to the law, with the law intact, He could not, because the law did not permit this to the judge's discretion, but distinctly and with a threat added, it commanded this to him, as can be seen both elsewhere and especially in Deuteronomy 19:11.

Latin:

Vers. 39.

ἐγὼ δὲ λέγω ὑμῖν, μὴ ἀντιστῆναι τῷ πονηρῷ] Recte eos sentire arbitror, qui illud πονηρῷ de homine interpretantur, & esse id ipsum quod Hebraice Moses dixit Exodi II. 13. לָרָשָׁע, quod LXX. vertunt τῷ ἀδικε͂ντι: quo exemplo τῷ πονηρῷ vertere sic liceat: ei qui injuriam fecit. Et mani- festum est non posse τὸ ἀντιστῆναι universe sumi. Nam re- sistit & qui innocentiæ suæ verbis testatur, quod fecit Christus, & post eum Apostoli. Sed cum præcedentia verba, quibus hæc sententia opponitur, agant περὶ τῆς τιμωρίας, omnino τὸ ἀντιστῆναι eodem referri debet, quod & Paulus nos docet, hoc præceptum his verbis explicans, μηδὲν κακὸν ἀντὶ κακῦ ἀποδιδόντες, Rom. XII. 17. quæ est ut diximus τῆς τιμωρίας perspicua descriptio: ex quo etiam apparet quid sit eodem Pauli loco μὴ ἑαυτὸς ἐκδικῦντες. Nam ἐκδικεῖν cum modo ulcisci significet, modo defende- re, necesse est ibi pro ultione accipiatur: qui enim se de- fendit tantum, is non reddit malum pro malo, sed is de- mum qui se ulciscitur: quod & sequentia Pauli verba de- clarant, sed dantes locum iræ, id est, divinæ ultioni, ut ibi- dem videre est. Aristoteles passim τὸ ἀμύνειν ponit in vir- tutis parte, quem secutus Cicero vindicationem ad jus na- turæ refert, per quam, inquit, vis & injuria defendendo aut ulciscendo propulsatur. Ejusdem est in officiis illud: Iu- stitiæ primum munus est ut necui noceat, nisi lacessitus injuria. O quam simplicem veramque sententiam, inquit Lactantius, duorum verborum adjectione corrupit. Nocendum enim nemini, ne ei quidem qui prior nocuerit. Quod Pla- to propius cæteris perspexit. Ejus enim est in Critone: ἐδὲ ἀδικύμενον δε͂ ἀνταδικε͂ν: item: οὔτε ἄρα ἀνταδικεῖν δεῖ οὔτε κακῶς ποιεῖν οὐδένα ἀνθρώπων, οὐδ᾽ ἂν ὁτιοῦν πάσχῃ ὑπ᾽ αὐτῶν: quod late explicat demonstratis incommodis quæ ultionem sequi solent sectator dogmatum Platonis Maxi- mus Tyrius diatriba cui titulum fecit εἰ τὸν ἀδικήσαντα ἀν- ταδικητέον. Sed & Hierocles dixit: τῷ ἀνταδικεῖν ἡμᾶς εἰς τὴν ἴσην τοῖς ἀδικοῦσι καχίξιαν ὔχεσθαι. Lacedæmonii preci- bus addere solebant τὸ ἀδικεῖσθαι δύνασθαι. Dignum memoria & Menandri illud: οὗτος κράτιστός ἐς᾽ ἀνὴρ, ὦ γοργία, ὅστις ἀδικεῖσθαι πλεῖστ᾽ ἐπίσταται βροτῶν. Inter Pythagoræ scita refert Jamblichus, μήτε ἄρχειν λοιδο- ρίαν μήτε ἀμύνεσθαιτὸς λοιδοροῦντας. Idem: Πολλῷ μᾶλ- λον ἀδικεῖσθαι δεῖν παρήγγειλεν ἤ κτείνειν ἄνθρωπον. ἐν ᾅδε γὰρ κεῖσθαι τὴν κρίσιν. Metellus Numidicus in oratione ad populum: Probi injuriam facilius accipiunt, quam alteri tradunt. Est in iisdem partibus Seneca: Immane, in- quit, verbum est ultio, & ab injuria tantum distans ordine: qui ulciscitur non nisi excusatius peccat. Sed & hoc ipsum excusatius peccare qui rependit injuriam, non concedit is quem dixi Maximus, quo judice ὁ τιμωρῶν τοῦ προϋ- πάρξαντος ἀδικώτερος. Addam his Musonium; τὸ σκο- πεῖν ὅπως ἀντιδήξηταί τις τὸν δάκνοντα καὶ ἀντικακώσῃ κακῶς τὸν ὑπάρξοντα, θηρίου τινὸς, οὐκ ἀνθρώπυ ἐστιν. Et hæc quidem videri possunt propne ad ultionem eam pertinere ubi quis aut manu statuit ἄνδρ᾽ ἀπαμύνασθαι ὅτις πρότερος χαλεπήνῃ. Aut etiam: ἀλωπεκίζειν πρὸς ἑτέραν ἀλώπεκα. At Christi præceptum aperte illud ultionis genus respicit quod minus immodestum videri solet: certe publice non æque periculosum est, cum apud Magistratum exerce- tur actio ad vindictam instituta. Nam hoc ipsum vetat quod Deus per Mosem non quidem indistincte probave- rat (semper enim ei lenitas præ iracundia placuit) sed quod fieri erat passus & de quo judicium reddi voluerat, ut majoris mali vitaretur occasio. Nam alioqui lex ipsa hoc agebat, ut si fieri posset homines à vindictæ cupiditate re- traheret: quod agnoscit Philo, apud quem Judæi Alexan- drini Deum ita alloquuntur: ἐκεφεδόμεθα ὦ δέσποτα τετ- ραμέρως ἐχθρᾶ δεδιδαγμένοι πρὸς τὸν ἱερὸν νόμον αἰδέσωπον παθεῖν. Sed quis scopus fuerit legis per Mosen latæ, ac quomodo ea non pugnet cum præcepto hoc Christi con- gruente cum Prophetarum monitis, videtur mihi sat s perspicue exposuisse Tertullianus adversus Marcionem IV. Novam plane patientiam docet Christus, etiam vicem inju- riæ prohibens permissam à creatore, oculum exigentem pro oculo & dentem pro dente: contra ipse alteram ampliùs ma- xillam offerri jubens, & super tunicam pallio quoque cedi. Plane hæc Christus adjecerit, ut supplementa consentanea disciplinæ creatoris. Atque adeo hoc statim renuntiandum est, an disciplina patientiæ prædicatur penes creatorem. Sic per Zachariam præcepit, ne unusquisque malitiæ fratris sui meminerit, sed nec proximi. Nam & rursus, Malitiam, inquit, proximi sui unusquisque ne recogitet. Multo magis pa- tientiam indixit injuriæ, qui indixit oblivionem. Sed & quum dicit: mihi vindictam & ego vindicabo, proinde patien- tiam docet vindictæ exspectatricem. In quantum ergo non capit, ut idem videatur, & dentem pro dente, oculum pro oculo in vicem injuriæ exigere, qui non modo vicem, sed etiam ultionem, etiam recordationem & recogitationem inju- riæ prohibet, in tantum aperitur nobis, quomodo oculum pro oculo & dentem pro dente censuerit, non ad secundam in- juriam talionis permittendam (intellige ut recte ac pie exi- geretur) quam prohibuerat interdicta ultione, sed ad pri- mam coërcendam quam prohibuerat talione opposita, ut unus- quisque respiciens licentiam (id est permissionem illam facti cum auctoritate juris civilis) secundæ injuriæ à primæ semetipsum contineret. Facilius enim vim comprimi scit re- presentatione talionis, quam repromissione ultionis. Utrumque autem constituendum fuit pro natura & fide hominum, ut qui Deo crederet, ultionem à Deo exspectaret: qui minus fideret,le- ges talionis timeret. Hanc legis voluntatem de intellectu laboran- tem, Dominus & Sabbati & legis & omnium paternarum dispo- sitionum Christus & revelavit & competem fecit, mandans al- teriàs quoque maxillæ oblationem, ut tanto magis vicem injuriæ extingueret, quam & lex per talionem voluerat impedisse, cer- te quam Prophetis manifestè coërcuerat, & memoriam inju- riæ prohibens, & ultionem ad Deum redigens. Ita si quid Christus intulit, non adversario sed adjutore præcepto, non destruxit disciplinas creatoris. Denique si in ipsam rationem patientiæ præcipiendæ & quidem tam plenè atque perfectè con- siderem, non consistet, si non est creatoris qui vindictam repromittit, qui judicem præstat. Alioquin si tantum patien- tiæ pondus non modo non repercutiendi sed & aliam ma- xillam præbendi, & non modo non remaledicendi sed etiam benedicendi, & non modo non retinendi tunicam, sed ampliùs & pallium concedendi is mihiimponit qui non sit me defensu- rus, in vacuum patientiam præcepit, non exhibens mihi mercedem præcepti, patientiæ dico fructum, quod est ultio, quam mihi permisisset debuerat si ipse non præstat, aut si mihi non permittebat, ipse præstaret. Quoniam & disciplinæ in- terest injuriam vindicari. Metu enim ultionis omnis iniqui- tas refrenatur. Cæterum passim emissâ libertate domina- bitur, utrumque oculum effossura, & omnem dentem ex- cisura præ impunitatis securitate. Locum hunc lectu & consideratu non indignum transcripsi eo libentius quod inde intelligi possit cur & quatenus etiam in Christiano- rum terris retineri possent ejusmodi leges, quæ talionis aut pœnæ formidine eos coërcent qui sponte recte face- re nondum didicerunt: incolumi interim piis omnibus manente patientiæ regula, quam obscure natura insi- nuat, commendant non Prophetæ tantum sed & Philo- sophi, præcepit autem diserte Christus. Hujus præce- pti memores Christiani illi meliorum sæculorum non dubitabant ad ipsorum hostium testimonium provocare. Justinus in Apologetico: ὃ γὰρ κὰν ἐπὶ πολλῶν τῶν παρ᾽ ἡ- μῖν, γεγενημένων ἀποδεῖξαι ἔχομεν, ἐκ βιαίων καὶ τυράννων μεταβαλὸν ἡττηθέντες ἢ γειτόνων καρτερίαν βίε παρακολυ- θήσαντες, ἢ συνοδιοπόρων πλεονεκτημένων ὑπομονὴν ξένην κα- τανοήσαντες, ἢ συμπραγματευομένων πειραθέντες. Athe- nagoras: οὕτως ἐκκεκαθαρμένοι εἰσὶ τὰς ψυχὰς, ὡς ἀντὶ τῶ μισεῖν τὺς ἐχθρὺς ἀγαπᾷν, κ᾽ ἀντὶ τῶ τὸ μετριώτατον, κα- κῶς ἀγορεύειν τὺς προκατάρξαντας λοιδορίας, εὐλογεῖν, κ᾽ ὑπὲρ τῶν ἐπιβουλευόντων σφι τὸ ζῆν, προσεύχεσθαι. Ipse Justinus de accusatoribus Christianorum ita loquitur: ἁ γὰρ τὺς κα- τηγορῦντας κολάζειν ὑμᾶς ἀξιώσομεν. ἀρκεῖτω γὰρ τῇ προ- σύσῃ πονηρίᾳ κὰι τῇ τῶν καλῶν ἀγνοίᾳ. Lubet in pudorem eorum qui se nunc Christianos dici volunt verba adferre Musonii proprie ad hanc judicialem vindictam perti- nentia. Ait is: ὕβρεως γραφὴν ἐτ᾽ ἂν αὐτός γράψασθαί τινα ποτὲ, ὔτ᾽ ἀνετέρωσυμβυλεύσαι: & apud Lysiam legi- mus: ἀνελεύθερον τὸ πάνυ φιλόδικον κακηγορίας δικάζε- σθαι: causamque sententiæ suæ explicans, irrideri, con- spui, verberari denique non est, turpe ait sapienti; sed irri- dere, conspuere, verberare. Mox prolatis exemplis eorum qui illatas injurias dissimulaverant, ita concludit: πόσῳ δὲ κρεῖττον οὕτως ἔχοντα φαίνεσθαι τὸν φιλόσοφον, ὥστε συγγνώμης ἀξιοῦν εἴτις πλημμελήσειεν εἰς αὐτὸν, ἢ δοκεῖν μὲν ἀμύνεσθαι ἑαυτῷ δικαζόμενον καὶ ἐγκαλοῦντα, τῇ δὲ ἀληθείᾳ ἀσχημονεῖν, ἀπακόλουθα τοῖς ἑαυτοῦ λόγοις πράττοντα. Zenon dicenti ἀπολοίμην ἐὰν μή σε τιμωρήσωμαι respondit ἐγὼ μὲν ἐὰν μή σε φίλον κτήσωμαι.

Ἀλλ' ὅστις σε ῥαπίσει ἐπὶ τὴν δεξιάν σου σιαγόνα τρέψον αὐτῷ καὶ τὴν ἄλλην] Sæpe in Hebraismo accidit ut adversativa comparationem in se includat: qua addita sententia hæc erit planissima hunc in modum: Noli si quis te malo affecit, ei vicissim malum rependere aut odium ejus induere: quin potius ferienti maxillarum unam, alteram quoque cædendam obverte: Potius scilicet quam te ulciscaris. Deinde ex proverbio petitum est maxillam obvertere cædenti, pro eo quod est patienter aliquid ferre, ut videre est Thren. III. 30. Est autem & hic ut supra aliquoties solutio tacitæ objectionis. Nam qui jubetur ab ultione omni abstinere, ei statim in mentem venit Mimi illud: Veterem ferendo injuriam invitas novam. Christus igitur, ne quis hoc obtentu sibi blandiatur, multo ait potius esse ut altera injuria accipiatur, quam ut sumatur ultio. Et hoc est quod Plato dixit non referendam injuriam, εἴτε δεῖ ἡμᾶς ἔτι τῶν δε χαλεπώτερα πάσχειν. Est eadem objectio & apud Maximum Tyrium: διὰ τοῦτο φαίη ἄν τις ὁ δίκαιος ἀνὴρ προσηλακίζεται, καὶ συκοφαντεῖται, καὶ διώκεται, καὶ χρήματα ἀφαιρεῖται, καὶ εἰς δεσμωτήριον ἐμβάλλεται, καὶ φεύγει, καὶ ἀτιμᾶται, καὶ ἀποθνήσκει. Respondet nihil mirum talia viro bono evenire, quia parum præsidii sit in nuda innocentia apud pravos judices: licere illi interim cum magna animi fiducia exclamare Achilleum illud: Φρονέω δὲ τετιμῆσθαι διὸς αἴσῃ.

Temere opponit Grotius Mosi Christum p. Christi præceptum aperte illud ultionis genus respicit, quod minus immodestum videri solet: certe publice non æque periculosum est, cum apud Magistratum exercetur actio ad vindictam instituta. Nam hoc ipsum vetat, quod Deus per Mosem non quidem indistincte probaverat, semper enim ei lenitas præ iracundia placuit, sed quod fieri erat passus, & de quo judicium reddi voluerat, ut majoris mali vitaretur occasio. Nam alioqui lex ipsa hoc agebat, ut si fieri posset, homines à vindictæ cupiditate retraheret. Hæc Grotius. Non prohibuit Christus vindictam publicam, aut ultionem ob injuriam institutam, sed ne ex privato affectu nos vindicemus. Neque aliter de eo habent leges Mosaicæ. Nam illud ὀφθαλμὸς ἀντὶ ὀφθαλμοῦ ad leges forenses spectabat, & Magistratus præscriptum erat Deut. XIX. 18.19. Neque tamen lex illa hac sublata, uti cavillabatur Faustus Manichæus, sed correcta & emendata corruptela Pharisæorum, & prava consuetudo Judæorum, quasi lege talionis privatis licentia daretur ad vindictam provocandi, & Magistratum solicitandi ex animo & affectu vindictæ privatæ. Christus vero hic agit non de jure, vel officio Magistratus, sed de officio hominis Christiani in vita privata, cui patientiam, & mansuetudinem præscribit. Quam etiam præscripsit Moyses Levit. XIX. 18. Non ulcisceris te, neque reservabis odium contra filios populi tui: & Salomo Proverb. XXIV. 29. Ne dicito, quemadmodum fecit mihi, ita faciam ei, reddam isti viro secundum opus ipsius: Manebat adhæc Mosis lex tota, quam Christus profitetur hoc ipso sermone, à se nulla in parte infringi. Poterat autem Christus salva lege imperare læso, ne talionem postularet: quia hoc lex illi non imperabat, sed concedebat, nihil autem contra legem facit, qui concesso non utitur. At judici interdicere, ne secundum legem judicaret, incolumi lege non poterat, quia non permittebat hoc lex judicis arbitrio, sed distincte & addita comminatione hoc ei imperabat, ut videre est tum alibi, tum præsertim Deuteron. XIX. v. 11.

## 5:40
Verse 40.

and to him who wishes to go to law with you] The Latin interpreter translates it 'to contend in judgment.' And there is no doubt that many in the past understood it in this way. And the word κρίνεσθαι has that meaning among the Greek interpreters, as in Job 9:3, Ecclesiasticus 6:10, Joel 3:2, Hosea 2:2. Salvian says that in this place we are commanded to relinquish those very things about which there is a dispute, while we are being stripped of our lawsuits. Others, however, prefer to explain κριθῆναι as 'to quarrel': and that מדין is indeed used for contention has been demonstrated by several examples. It must be added, however, that κρίνεσθαι here properly corresponds to the Hebrew דון, and that signifies 'to contend': as can be seen in 2 Samuel 19:9, where the Greeks have, some 'was contending,' others 'was disputing.' In which sense the Greeks also used ἄνδρα διακρινόμενον in Jeremiah 15:10 for the Hebrew איש מדין, which they translate elsewhere as 'a man of war.' But the Syriac placed that דון here: whence it could seem that κριθῆναι here is 'to fight': and all the more so because Luke, for what is κρίνεσθαι here, said 'to take away,' by force, that is, not by judgment. Christ, from one kind of injury which pertains to the body or even to dignity, passes to another by which fortunes are harmed, which the very conjunction that connects the preceding clause with this one shows. Wherefore, here too, in an equal manner, the sense seems to be able to be supplied by adding a sign of comparison. If anyone desires to take a tunic from you by force, rather permit him the cloak also than that you should harm him or conceive hatred for him in your mind. And this is what Luke said, 'do not hinder.' For κωλύειν there is not to admonish the robber with words, or even to retain what is one's own, but to deter or drive away by harming. But if we nevertheless grant that κρίνεσθαι signifies in this place to move a lawsuit, this also could be understood in a certain sense in this matter, namely that it is not permitted to undergo a lawsuit for the sake of any thing whatsoever, and such as a cloak or a tunic is. For those things which are accustomed to be said in this place by commentators against lawsuits, seem to me to regard the circumstances of lawsuits, which are frequent enough, rather than the judgments themselves. Paul indeed said that this very thing was ἥττημα, that the Corinthian Christians had lawsuits among themselves, and he adds, why do you not rather suffer wrong, why do you not rather suffer yourselves to be defrauded? But he said ἥττημα, not ἁμάρτημα: because, clearly, just as it is of a noble and lofty spirit to lose one's own rather than to pursue it by judgment, so there existed no universal precept of Christ at all concerning that matter. Otherwise, he would not have referred lawsuits to the arbitration of pious men. For how does a pious judge, especially when approached with the good will of the parties, differ from an arbitrator, except that he is a publicly elected minister of the law? Wherefore, if they are long uncertain about their right and approach a judge, or if someone defends a widow or an orphan, or consults for his own household, or so that he may have something to distribute to the poor, and trusting in his right, he challenges to judgment for a matter of the greatest moment, meanwhile burning with no hatred, but prepared to bear with an even mind whatever shall have been judged, I do not know whether he is to be said to sin against charity. But if those things which are usually accustomed to accompany lawsuits are looked at—an ulcerated mind, crafty arts, endless prolongation, expenses, distraction from better business, and finally hatreds—there is no doubt that a good and prudent man, if he could, would much more willingly go to an arbitrator, or even redeem so many troubles with any tolerable agreement. The Praetor does not disapprove (says Ulpian) of the act of him who valued it so much to be without the thing, so that he might not litigate about it more often: For this modest thought of him who execrates lawsuits is not to be blamed. Isocrates says thus of himself in his oration περὶ ἀντιδόσεως: 'I knew that I myself committed no wrong against others; but when wronged, I did not seek to exact penalties through a court, but to settle disputes among friends.' Aristides: 'You praise those private citizens who are reasonable and choose to be wronged rather than to contend with others.' Cicero in De Officiis II praises one who shrinks from lawsuits as much as is permitted, and even a little more than is permitted. Certainly, concerning the ancient Christians, who did not distinguish counsels from precepts as subtly as is usually done now, but in all things followed that which was best, Athenagoras said: 'They do not go to law against those who rob them.' A second, more difficult question arises from this passage: whether that which the laws permit, to repel force with force, is also consistent with Christian discipline. For there is no doubt that many things are conceded by the laws which do not befit the goodness and patience of a Christian man. And I think there are certain such things in this category as well, such as that which the law of Moses sometimes concedes, to kill a nocturnal thief, and that which the Roman law added, even a diurnal one, if he defends himself with a weapon: and much more that which the interpreters of Roman law added, that any invader of our goods may rightly be killed if the possession cannot otherwise be saved. Nor did the indulgence of the jurisconsults stop here, which is dangerous not only to souls, but also, if I am not mistaken, to the republic.

If they say this is permitted for the sake of goods, why not for the sake of preserving one's reputation? But it is shameful to flee; therefore it is permitted to commit homicide even if flight is possible. Likewise, it is shameful to suffer an insult, especially for a noble man: therefore, even for that reason, homicide committed is free from blame. Furthermore, even single combats have their patrons, and a matter to be forbidden by all laws is even regulated by laws. It has come to this, that among Christians, candidates of the cross, what the laws of profane nations would have severely punished is done openly and publicly every day. To such an extent is suffering an injury considered a disgrace: to kill a man, praise. But I truly think that neither that which they call honor, which is not honor but the foolish persuasion of vain men, nor any possessions are to be compared with the life of even the vilest man. And what charity, pray, ends by not valuing these things of ours more than what this world holds most worthy, human life, to which all created things serve? But the laws permit it. Nay, the laws disapprove of most of these things: but those are the inventions of jurists flattering their own age. Ulpian was once of a far different opinion: If anyone kills a nocturnal thief, he shall carry it off with impunity only if he could not spare him without his own danger. What if they were to permit it, however? They do not approve, they do not praise: they only grant impunity. But is there anyone who thinks it sufficient for a Christian if he escapes the penalties of the laws, not also those established for vices in the divine judgment? But let us also see how much it is permitted for a man to do for the sake of protecting his life. There are also jurists here who think that even an innocent person who intervenes to break up a brawl can be killed if there is no other way of securing safety, which I trust will please few: and a religious mind does not even accept that which has been put forward by some, that one should not wait until present danger is imminent, but that he who is believed to be about to do harm should be removed in time. For one should not indulge in fear to that extent. Cicero is more correct: Who ever established this, or to whom has it been granted without the greatest danger to all, that he could rightfully kill one from whom he says he feared that he himself might later be killed? And there is the same discussion of this matter in Gellius, book VIII, chapter 3. There are again others who think that not even an aggressor can be killed, even if life must be lost entirely unless that is done. This opinion had many authors in the first centuries of Christianity, at which time fervent piety easily embraced all honorable things as precepts. Origen, responding to Celsus who called Christians seditious, says: And yet if the cause of the sedition among the Christians was the faction, having taken its origin from the Jews, to whom it was permitted to take up arms for their own people and to kill their enemies, the lawgiver of the Christians would not have forbidden the killing of men entirely, lest he teach that the daring act of his own disciples against them was just, even if that were most unjust; for he did not think it fitting for his own divine legislation to permit any killing of a man whatsoever. For my part, if there is anyone of such a strong spirit that he would rather suffer his life to be taken than redeem it by the death of another, however hostile, I would deem him worthy of praise or even admiration. It is a rare love to die for enemies and the wicked, says Paul, Rom. 5:6, 7, 8. But whether this is required of Christians by the right of a precept must be seen further. For these words of Christ seem to deal properly with revenge, or even with force to ward off an evil that is easily reparable. But here the matter of life turns on both sides: so that either he dies who brought this evil upon himself, or he who is unwillingly pushed into that necessity. Now, indeed, not even in the goods serving this life, not even among friends, is it required of us by way of a precept that we should wish to provide relief to others and affliction to ourselves, as Paul speaks, 2 Corinthians 8:13. Why, therefore, should we say otherwise about life? For if you say that the life of another is more worthy than goods, surely our life is also more worthy than goods. Therefore, the same analogy remains. There are those who urge the precept given to Noah and his children, by which the shedding of human blood is forbidden. But nature itself commands this same thing: yet all natural precepts, however universally stated, have their exceptions based on equity and fairness. And we see all peoples, whose consenting judgment should not be rashly spurned (for as Heraclitus said, the common reason is a trustworthy proof), interpret that law of nature in such a way that they pronounce innocent him who, when he could not otherwise protect his life, killed one who was using force against him. Concerning which Cicero says there exists a law not written but born, which we have not learned, received, or read, but have snatched, drawn, and expressed from nature itself. However, it seems that the law of God, dictating the same thing as nature, should be accepted in the way that nature itself shows it should be accepted, unless something more express is added. There is one cause that seems to be equal to the danger of life: if someone is preparing to inflict rape upon the body and cannot be warded off otherwise than by killing. For not only do the laws permit this, but such deeds are accustomed to be celebrated with great praise among all peoples, and examples of this exist even in ancient Christianity. However, what has been said about protecting life with arms, if necessity urges, I would not dare to apply to warding off force which is inflicted by public authority. For the laws do not indulge in that, and if they did, it would be dangerous to the republic. The reason we brought forward also ceases. For the goods are not equal among themselves: public tranquility and the life of even an innocent person. Therefore, Peter, in a cause that could have seemed the most just of all, initiating armed force, was rebuked by Christ, and he himself, mindful of the Lord's precept, prescribes the laws of patience to those placed in a similar necessity, 1 Peter 4:15, 16. And the Christians observed this most religiously, to such an extent that if any resistance had been made by force to rampant cruelty, the body of them publicly disapproved of it. There seems, however, to be a different reason for those who resist their inferiors by the decree of higher powers. For inferiors, insofar as they exceed the mandates of their superiors, are to be reckoned as private individuals. To this must be referred the deed of Nehemiah and his associates, whom the authority of a royal edict armed against the neighboring governors. Having finished the question concerning self-defense, let us come to the other, which is about public trials, especially capital ones. For there are those who think that these too are forbidden by Christ in these words. But we have already shown that Christ is dealing with revenge, whether it is exacted in law or outside of law. But revenge is one thing, and punishment, which laws exact without anyone demanding it, is quite another. Revenge is demanded out of anger. But a judge, as Seneca truly said, is never less angry than when he punishes. Revenge is exacted because something was done that ought not to have been; but the punishment of public trials is exacted so that there may be no sin in the future. For it is either admonition or an example, as philosophers rightly distinguish. Admonition wishes to make him who has sinned better, as paternal chastisement does a child, which I understand is also practiced at home by those who criticize it in the republic. An example, however, deters others from delinquency by a sadder instance. Often, however, chastisement is joined with an example. And that both differ very greatly from revenge appears both from their origin and their end. How, therefore, will what was said by Christ about revenge be applied to a matter so different? I will say something further. As for that very punishment of revenge, or of retribution, the person who has been harmed is forbidden by Christ's precept to exact it for the sake of requiting pain, but the judge is not forbidden to act according to law if they are exacted. For the whole law of Moses still remained, which Christ professes in this very discourse is not infringed by him in any part. But Christ could, with the law intact, command the injured party not to demand retaliation: because the law did not command this to him, but conceded it; and he does nothing against the law who does not use what is conceded. But to forbid a judge not to judge according to the law, with the law intact, he could not: because the law did not permit this to the judge's discretion, but strictly and with an added threat commanded it to him, as can be seen both elsewhere and especially in Deuteronomy 19, verse 11. This argument also pertains to capital trials. For the law obligated the judge to those as well, unless insofar as he is prohibited by a greater force, such as the power of the Romans. Wherefore, since the law of Christ obligated its hearers as soon as it was promulgated, and the law of Moses had not been abolished at that time, it follows that both could be obeyed at the same time. But if at the time of the promulgation the words of Christ did not stand in the way of public trials, they cannot stand in the way even now. For that meaning of the words which had been at the beginning remains. Nor is there any reason for anyone to retort that the laws of Moses perished with the destruction of the Jewish republic; for the question is not whether one ought to be judged by the laws of Moses among those peoples whom the law of Moses did not bind even then when it was published, but whether it conflicts with Christ's precept to establish either the same or similar laws. That, indeed, is certain, that it is superfluous for such laws to be enacted for those who live by the discipline of Christ. For those who do right of their own accord have no need to be restrained by the fear of evil. But prophecies teach us, and the outcome of events teaches us, that the world is not Christian, but that truly Christians are the smallest portion of the world; laws, however, look to that which happens for the most part. Wherefore, since the greater part of the human race is now no less carnal than the Jewish nation was in the age of Moses, similar remedies must be applied to a similar disease. For innocence cannot be safer now without public trials than it was then. And although the Hebrew law, as we have said, was given by God to the Hebrew people alone, yet there is no doubt that other nations could rightly imitate it. Nothing, therefore, has been brought forward to show that these public trials displease God. Indeed, Paul teaches the contrary when he says that public authority is ordained by God and is the minister of God. For this cannot be understood only of providential permission and direction, in the way that God also permits robberies and makes use of them. For from that ordination or institution Paul concludes that honor and obedience are owed to them even from the heart: which cannot be said of robberies and other things permitted by God. He feels, therefore, that public governments are pleasing and acceptable to God. Moreover, whatever it is in which God ἐυδοκεῖ (is well-pleased), that is rightly performed. But Paul is so far from excluding capital judgments that he treats of that part of public government especially. For he says that the public power is a minister of God for wrath (that is, for punishment, for that word generally has that meaning) against evildoers: and what is more, he says that the sword is not borne by it in vain, for that ministry, of course, as the context of the words teaches. But by the name of the sword, public judgments are designated as if by the most noble part of themselves; whence also in law the right of the sword is the right of public punishments. It is gathered from this that the very use of the sword against evildoers is approved by God. But since GOD does not have decrees contrary to Himself, it can by no means be sin in that which GOD approves, unless a vice enters from elsewhere. But lest anyone think that this power is approved by God, but not approved so that it may be in the hands of Christians, let him note first that the precepts which exist here have a threat of the loss of the kingdom of heaven and of severe punishment. Therefore they pertain to all. Next, Paul openly testifies that he wants GOD to have all men saved and to come to the knowledge of the Evangelical truth, even kings 1. Timoth. II. vers. 2. 3. 4. Therefore Kings can also be saved through the Gospel, which the preceding words show must be understood even without laying aside royal dignity: for he wants prayer to be made for kings, that we may lead a quiet and tranquil life: but kings cannot provide this except as they are kings. He wants, therefore, for prayer to be made for kings also, as they are such, with the cause added, because God wants them to be saved, even as such, of course, so that the argumentation may proceed rightly. But how do kings provide a tranquil and quiet life? By praising the good, by punishing the bad, even by the right of the sword as the same Apostle explains Romans XIII. vers. 3. 4. God therefore wants kings, as they are kings, and as they use the right of the sword, to be able to be saved through the Gospel. Nor did the ancient Christians accept the words of the Apostle otherwise, ἐυχόμενοι (praying), as Justin speaks in his second Apology, that the kings and rulers might be found having royal power and a sound mind. But those prayers of the Christians, and the most ancient prophecies about kings who would serve Christ, beyond controversy had their outcome in Constantine and his successors. By these, however, the doctrine of Christ was so received that they neither exceeded their authority nor abolished public judgments. Nor indeed in such a great multitude of Bishops was there anyone who urged them to do so: which seems to me a most certain indication that it was constantly believed by all that there is nothing in those judgments contrary to the precepts of Christ and the salvation of Emperors, since otherwise there exist illustrious examples of the liberty of Bishops against sinning kings. Doubtless they remembered that Sergius the Proconsul was once converted to the faith of Christ by Paul, and yet it was not required of him that he should resign his proconsulship, in which was contained also the right of the sword. It will perhaps seem to some that Tertullian thought otherwise when he says: But even the Caesars would have believed in Christ, if either Caesars were not necessary to the world, or if Christians could also have been Caesars. But perhaps Tertullian meant this, since such was the state of the Roman empire that it could not bear a Christian Emperor, that in the meantime divine providence had so governed affairs that through pagan Emperors the public tranquility was in some measure provided for. For that same Writer already in his own time says that the tribes, the decuries, the palace, the senate, the forum had been filled with Christians. Other passages of the ancients also which seem to oppose public judgments receive a far more convenient interpretation. For either this is said, that the precepts of Christ have no sanctions of visible punishments, such as the law of Moses had, and that discipline is preserved among the people of Christ without such punishments: in which sense it was said by the same Tertullian: The new law does not avenge itself by the vengeance of the sword: or they dissuade from undertaking the magistracy, not as an illicit thing, but as one exposed to many dangers of sinning. In this sense Tatian says from the person of a Christian, σρατηγίαν παρῇτημαι (I have declined military command). A Christian does not even aspire to a lawsuit, says Tertullian, and he considers it much more just to abstain from judgments concerning life and modesty. And yet it is of the same man: No one denies that it is a good thing when the guilty are punished. And elsewhere he calls justice the avenger of violence. Origen, however, against Celsus, who objected to Christians that they avoided praetorships and other magistracies, answers thus: It is not that Christians flee the more common duties of life that they avoid such things, but that they keep themselves for a more divine and necessary service. Clement, however, older than both, speaking of a Christian who has already reached the highest degree of probity, says, even if he should ever be placed in authority, like Moses, he will lead for the salvation of those who are ruled and will tame the wild and the unbelieving, by honoring those who are worthy, and by punishing the wicked, which is inscribed for instruction according to reason; for a soul of a just man is especially a divine image and similar to God, in which through obedience to the commandments the ruler of all, both of mortals and immortals, the king and generator of good things, is enshrined and established, being truly law and ordinance, and eternal reason, being one savior privately to each and publicly to all. Nevertheless, I see that there is need of many cautions, which are everywhere neglected, so that that power of public judgments may be exercised without the expense of Christian gentleness. To use the most well-known examples, I am surprised that the law concerning the killing of farmers for catching game is defended with such diligence by jurists, when they would have devoted their efforts much better to the serious dissuasion of such things. It is also of this kind that thieves are ordered to be killed, and indeed in those places where adultery, a crime so much more serious beyond controversy, is barely touched by a censor's mark. I certainly do not see what compels us to be more harsh than the Hebrew law. In cases of homicide itself, it seems to me that one should not look so much at the bare act as at what the previous life of the killer was, whether he came to this crime by impulse or by deliberation, and, what is most important, whether his character is curable. For Seneca also teaches this, that no one should perish unless it is in the interest of the one perishing that he perish: which itself, however, seems to be able to have a place either never or very rarely. For when will it be established that all hope of repentance is cut off? It would be much better for these distinctions to be weighed by judges than for some to be dragged to death based solely on the name of the act heard, while others who are strong in favor and friends obtain full impunity through princely indulgence, no matter how atrocious their crimes.
