For as to the fact that some think the penalty of death naturally corresponds to homicide, they are mistaken in that. For the penalties for crimes are not established by the very law of nature or by any perpetual law of God, but are accustomed to be increased or relaxed according to the measure of the imminent danger. The history of Cain teaches us that in that first age of the world, the penalty for homicide was exile, to which was added that pious and pure men would avoid the sight and touch of those so contaminated. Euripides also mentions this most ancient institution: 'The ancients of old established these things well. They did not allow anyone who had blood on his hands to pass into the sight of their eyes, nor to meet them, but they did allow exile for the holy, though not to kill in return.' Which custom Plato wished to be restored. The savagery which had invaded human morals before the flood gave occasion for a new law, namely that the blood of a homicide should be shed, which law, as it was adapted to those times, was promulgated by God at the very restoration of the human race after the flood. But God, the best interpreter of His own law, refers that to a killing which is done deliberately and with traps laid, Exod. XXI. verse 14. The Roman Republic stood and flourished for a long time when the cognizance of the magistrates did not exceed deportation. Later also, when laws had already been passed about punishing with death those convicted of homicide and other crimes, usage nevertheless found many exceptions, so that severity often stopped at relegation. It is difficult to maintain an exact mean: but if one must err, it is better to err on that side of leniency. Perhaps condemnation to labor would deter no fewer people from committing crimes than death itself: and at the same time, which should be especially regarded by Christian love, space would be given for performing repentance, which is now sometimes cut short by the precipitation of the punishment. Certainly Constantine, when he first approved the Christian religion, prohibited capital punishments in most types of crimes, which were soon brought back 'on account of the license of the wicked,' as the histories teach us. And so, what we read about adulterers being punished with the sword in the constitution of Constantine, which is inserted into the Justinian Code, is missing in the older Theodosian Code. There remains the controversy about war, which is likewise accustomed to be treated by most people in this place. If the words of Christ do not prohibit moderate self-defense for individuals, they will be even less of an obstacle to those arms which are taken up by public authority for the necessary defense of the whole people. For by how much the safety of many is worth more than that of one, by so much more justly is it defended. Again, if it is permitted for pious kings to use the right of the sword against one robber, why should it not be permitted against many, who, in order to be defeated, must be overcome in battle? Nor is the authority of the sacred scriptures, even of the New Testament, lacking to us here, although the burden of proof rests more justly upon those who affirm it is forbidden. For to omit the words of the Baptist, about which we shall speak elsewhere, and the faith of that Centurion praised by Christ, and the effort devoted by Paul so that he might be preserved by military guard against the plots of the Jews, it seems to me that one thing alone suffices, that Cornelius, without laying down his centurionship, received both baptism from Peter and the Holy Spirit from God, with Luke by no means remaining silent if Cornelius had abandoned the profession of his former life, since he is never accustomed to omit signs of repentance, and this would have pertained most especially to teaching posterity. Nor do I find that the ancient Christians thought otherwise: for it is established that Christians served in the army under Marcus, and Tertullian not only mentions Christian soldiers, but indicates that their number was so great that they nearly filled the camps. Origen also says that bees were given to us by God as a lesson πρὸς τὸ δικαίως κὲ̓ τεταγμένως πολέμως εἴποτε δέοι γίνεσθαι ἐν ἀνθρώ- ποις.

But the fact that we sometimes read that Christians refused military service happened because the Emperors of those times demanded from the soldiers either an express departure from Christ, or a tacit one, namely by the oath taken through the gods, or through the Emperor as a god, or also because, with edicts proposed against the Christians, they used military force daily to carry them out. For in such times Christians were advised to avoid military service, and if any did serve, they were barred from pious assemblies. Nor does it pertain to anything else that it was decreed in the Nicene Synod against those who, having once laid down their military service under Licinius, had resumed the belt, namely under the same Licinius, who, as Eusebius teaches us, τὺς στρατιώτας ἐκέλευε ἀποβάλλεσθαι τὺ ἀξιώματα, εἰ μὴ τοῖς δαίμοσι θύειν αἰρέοιντο. For that this Canon should be understood generally about all military service is repugnant to the history of the times. Indeed, the greater part of Constantine's army was made up of Christians. And if any Christians had omitted military service under Licinius, Constantine made it free for them whether they wished to resume military service or to be exempt from it. But the fact that writers sometimes dissuade from military service is similar to what we were saying about the flight from honors: it also partly has causes proper to those times, as we shall show at Luke chapter III. Nor do I doubt that they would have dissuaded much more intensely if they had seen the madness of the wars of our time and the camps, polluted by perjuries, rapes, robberies, and finally by every confluence of vices. It has come to this, that a Christian soldier seems to perform a great thing if he does not surpass the soldier of ancient and pagan Rome, and finally the Turks themselves, in shameful morals. There must be far different soldiers with whom we deal according to the Gospel: for those are sufficiently condemned by both common sense and a comparison with ancient discipline. But to embrace in a few words what has been treated more extensively by many concerning war, and if anything is approved by them that is alien to piety, to refute it in passing: it is agreed that there are three parts of war, the beginning, the progress, the end. In the beginning itself, the laws of justice, prudence, and charity ought to be considered. I do not consider this to be a just cause for undertaking war, that another people abhors true piety. For who gave that judgment to one people or king over that other people? Σπάρταν ἐ̓λαχες τάυτην κόσμει. And it was rightly said by Plutarch πρόφασιν ἐῖναι πλεονεξίας ἡμερῶσαι τὰ βαρ- βαρικά. But if another people has also harmed us, nevertheless one must not have recourse to force as long as the matter can be debated with words. Hence the custom of demanding restitution before war is declared among the Hebrews, Greeks, and Romans. If he with whom we are dealing is prepared to go to arbitrators regarding the controversial matters, one must still abstain from war, ἐ γὰρ νόμιμον ἐπὶ τὸν δίκας διδόντα ὡς ἐπ̓ ἀδικοῦντα ἰέναι, as Archidamus says in Thucydides. But in no way is it to be accepted what some have handed down, that a war can be just on both sides: for that cannot happen even in a lawsuit: unless we wish 'just' to be understood as that which has rights of captivity, booty, and postliminy from accepted customs. But those things which are called just in this sense are for the most part nothing other than great robberies. Let us even hear Seneca: We restrain homicides and individual murders. What of wars and the glorious crime of slaughtered nations? Neither avarice nor cruelty knows a limit. Cruel things are practiced by decrees of the senate and plebiscites: and things forbidden privately are ordered publicly. We praise those things which, if committed, would be punished by death, when men in military cloaks have done them. Are men, the mildest species, not ashamed to rejoice in mutual blood, to wage wars, and to hand them down to their children to be waged, when there is peace even among the mute and wild beasts? Truly, if we look at the law of nature, what difference does it make whether a pirate holds the sea infested with one small boat, or Alexander with an army and fleet? Nor are those to be refuted with many words who teach that just wars are undertaken by those who, having been expelled from their own homes or having left, wish to be received into the possession of the homes of others: or who fear that a growing power might someday cause them danger. But even when the cause for waging war is just, prudence and laws will often stand in the way, and on both sides the sword and

human bodies: nor is the beginning and end of war in the power of the same person. Euripides well says: Ὅταν γὰρ ἔλθῃ πόλεμος εἰς ψῆφον λεὼ Οὐδεὶς ἔτ' αὐτῷ θάνατον ἐκλογίζεται Τὸ δυςυχὲς δὲ τοῦτ' ἐς ἄλλον ἐκτρέπει Εἰ δ' ἦν παρ' ὄμμα θάνατον ψῆφο φερᾶ Οὐκ ἄν ποθ' ἑλλὰς δοριμανὴς ἀπώλετο.

But above all, a Christian must consider what charity demands. For if Paul, dissuading from lawsuits, said, why do you not rather suffer injuries, how much more is it right for us to suffer as much as possible, rather than to come to that contention which involves the good and the bad in the same evils? Private defense brings only the invader into danger. Capital punishments are established for criminals. But in war, the innocent no less than the guilty perish and are plundered on both sides. Seneca prescribes to a prince that he should spare the blood of others as if it were his own, and know that a man should not be used prodigally by a man: what do we believe he demands of us who so solicitously commended peace to us with all men as much as can be done? Doubtless, if all these things are weighed as they ought to be, we shall see that it is not in vain that they can be applied also to external wars and other causes of wars, which Favonius had said: that civil war is worse than a lawless monarchy: and that those arms are truly pious which are necessary, that is, which are undertaken to avoid evils more cruel than arms. To the progress of war these laws pertain: that pacts be kept as religiously as possible, that no one who is peaceful be harmed, that it be decided with as little bloodshed as possible, that there be no cruelty toward captives, toward those who have surrendered, toward children, toward women, toward farmers, and the rest of the crowd of non-combatants. Finally, regarding the end of the war, it must be seen to that the war is not dragged out by anger and the desire for revenge: but that it may appear that nothing other than peace was sought by the war: which will be done if one departs from arms by any tolerable pact, or even after victory nothing is taken from the conquered except the license for injury. The noble ends of wars, he says, are where one settles by forgiving. And these things indeed pertain especially to those in whose power lies the right of undertaking, directing, and ending a war. Regarding allies, this must be added: that those treaties are contrary not only to charity but also to justice which promise aid to those either initiating or even repelling a war without distinction of causes. But those who merely provide service in war ought to know, if they are subjects, that subjects also do not owe obedience to kings without exception. And as some probable cause excuses the necessity of obeying, certainly those who serve as soldiers for pay, and much more so foreigners, have nothing by which they can defend their cause, unless it is clearly established to them that the war to which they pledge their effort was undertaken justly and piously. And even if this is established, they sin gravely, whoever, enticed not by charity for a people in danger, but by pay or plunder, treat war as a kind of business. Many laugh at these things, and deny that a republic can be managed without injury; they say it is the praise of a royal house to retain its own, but to contend for the property of others: that he who can destroy others ought to be destroyed in time: that there is nothing unjust against him who refuses what is just: and whatever other things are in that form. Let them say what they wish, and where they make a solitude, let them call it peace. By their decrees, which are truly written in human blood, that King of peace will not judge the human race. Nay, I rather fear this, that in this treatment I have been too prone to the side that indulges too much in war. Wherefore let the reader know that these things were said by me not with the intention of defining, but so that the truth might be inquired into more diligently; meanwhile I advise all to bear injuries rather than shed human blood, even that of the guilty, and to remember that saying often: what you doubt, do not do.

Latin:

Vers. 40.

καὶ τῷ θέλοντί σοι κριθῆναι] Latinus interpres vertit judicio contendere. Nec dubium est quin olim ita intelle- xerint plerique. Et habet eum sensum vox κρίνεσθαι apud Græcos interpretes, ut Jobi IX. vers. 3. Ecclesiastici VI. vers. 10. Joël. III. 2. Os. II. 2. Salvianus hoc loco juberi ait ut ea ipsa de quibus lis est relinquamus dum li- tibus exuamur. Alii vero κριθῆναι rixari malunt expo- nere: & מדין quidem pro contentione poni aliquot exem- plis demonstratum est. Addendum vero quod hic est κρίνεσθαι proprie respondere Hebræo כרן id autem con- tendere significat: ut videre est 2. Sam. XIX. 9. ubi Græci habent alii ἦν κρινόμενος, alii ἦν διακρινόμενος. Quo sensu & ἄνδρα διακρινόμενον posuere Græci Jerem. XV. vers. 10. pro Hebræo איש מדין quod alibi vertunt μάχιμον. Illud autem כרן hic posuit Syrus: unde vide- ri posset κριθῆναι hic esse μάχεσθαι: eoque magis quia Lu- cas quod hic est κρίνεσθαι dixit αἴρειν vi scilicet non judi- cio. Christus ab uno injuriæ genere quod ad corpus aut etiam ad dignitatem pertinet, transit ad alterum quo fortunæ læduntur, quod ostendit ipsa copula quæ præ- cedens comma cum isto connectat. Quare & hic pari modo sensus videtur suppleri posse addito comparandi si- gno. Si quis vi cupiat à te tunicam auferre, etiam pal- lium potius illi permitte quam illi noceas aut odium ejus animo concipias. Et hoc est quod Lucas dixit μὴ κωλύ- σῃς. Nam κωλύειν ibi est non verbis raptorem commo- nefacere, aut etiam quod suum est retinere, sed nocendo absterrere aut abspellere. Quod si tamen demus κρίνε- σθαι significari hoc loco litem movere, poterie & hoc in ea certum modum intelligi, nimirum ne causa rei cujus- vis, & talis qualis est pallium aut tunica, litem subire liceat. Nam quæ adversus lites hoc loco dici à tracta- toribus solent, ea mihi videntur circumstantias satis fre- quentes litium magis quam ipsa judicia respicere. Dixit quidem Paulus hoc ipsum esse ἥττημα quod Corinthii Christiani lites inter se haberent, additque cur non po- tius perfertis injuriam, cur non potius patimini vos despo- liari? sed ἥττημα dixit, non ἁμάρτημα: quia scilicet sicut præclari atque excelsi est animi suum amittere po- tius quam judicio persequi, ita nullum de ea re præceptum Christi omnino universale exstabat. Alioqui non reje- cisset lites ad arbitria piorum hominum. Quid enim dif- fert pius judex, præsertim cum bona partium gratia aditus, ab arbitro, nisi quod publice est lectus juris minister? quare si diu de jure suo incerti judicem adeant, aut aliquis ut viduam aut pupillum defendat, aut domui suæ consulat, aut ut habeat quod pauperibus largiatur, juri suo confisus ob rem momenti maximi ad judicium provo- cet, nullo interim odio oagrans, sed æquo animo la- turus quicquid judicatum fuerit, nescio an in charitatem peccare sit dicendus. Verum si spectentur quæ plerum- que litibus solent accedere, animus exulceratus, vafræ ar- tes, sine fine ampliatio, impendia, avocatio à negotiis me- lioribus, odia denique; non dubium est quin vir bonus & prudens multo si posset libentius sit iturus ad arbitrum, aut etiam quavis tolerabili pactione tot molestias redemtu- rus. Non improbat Prætor (inquit Ulpianus) factum e- jus qui tanti habuit re carere, ne propter eam sæpius litiga- ret: Hæc enim verecunda cogitatio ejus qui lites exsecratur, non est vituperanda. Isocrates de se oratione περὶ ἀντιδόσεως sic ait: ἠπιστάμην αὐτὸς μὲν εἰς τοὺς ἄλλως μηδὲν ἐξαμαρτά- νων' ἀδικούμενος δὲ μὴ μετὰ δικαστηρίου ποιεῖσθαι τὰς τιμω- ρίας, ἀλλ' ἐν τοῖς φίλοις τῶν ἐκείνων διαλύεσθαι περὶ τῶν ἀμ- φισβητημάτων. Aristides: τῶν ἰδιωτῶν ἐπαινεῖτε ἐυγνώμο- νας κᾀ ἐλαφθῆναι τινα μᾶλλον αἱρουμένως ἢ διαφέρεσθαι πρὸς τι- νας. Cicero de officiis II. laudat à litibus quantum li- ceat, ut etiam paulo plusquam liceat, abhorrentem. Cer- te de veteribus Christianis, qui non tam subtiliter quam fieri nunc solet consilia à præceptis distingvebant, sed in omnibus rebus id sectabantur quod erat optimum, dixit A- thenagoras κ' δικάζονται τοῖς ἁρπάζουσι. Altera ex hoc lo- co difficilior oritur quæstio, an quod leges permittunt vim vi repellere, id Christianæ etiam disciplinæ conveniat. Nam quin legibus multa concedantur quæ bonitatem ac patien- tiam hominis Christiani non decent, dubitandum non est. Et esse quædam talia in hoc etiam genere existimo, quale interdum esse potest quod lex Mosis concedit furem no- cturnum occidere, & quod lex Romana addidit etiam diur- num, si se telo defendat: multoque magis quod interpre- tes juris Romani addiderunt quemlibet bonorum nostro- rum invasorem recte necari si aliter servari posseffio ne- queat. Neque hac stetit Jurisconsultorum indulgentia, non animis tantum, sed & reipublicæ, ni fallor, periculosa.

Si ob bona hoc licet quid ni servandæ existimationis cau- sa, inquiunt. Est autem turpe fugere; licet igitur ho- micidium facere etiam si fuga pateat. Item turpe est con- vitium pati, præsertim viro nobili: ergo etiam ea de cau- sa homicidium patratum culpa vacat. Quin & singula- res dimicationes habent suos patronos, & res omnibus le- gibus vetanda, etiam legibus ordinatur. Eo ventum est, ut inter Christianos, crucis candidatos, quotidie pa- lam publice fiat, quod profanarum gentium leges severe puniissent. Adeo pati injuriam dedecus putatur: laus hominem occidere, Ego vero neque illud quod hono- rem vocant, qui non est honor, sed vanorum homi- num stulta persuasio, neque possessiones ullas cum vita hominis etiam vilissimi comparandas puto. Et quæ tan- dem charitas finit, non istas recolas nostras pluris facere, quam quod hic orbis digniffimum habet, vitam huma- nam, cui res conditæ omnes famulantur? At leges per- mittunt. Imo horum pleraque leges improbat: sed sunt ista Jurisconsultorum sæculo suo blandientium com- menta. Longe aliter olim Ulpianus: Furem nocturnum si quis occiderit, ita demum impune feret, si parcere ei sine periculo suo non potuit. Quid si tamen permitterent? Non probant, non laudant: tantum præstant impunitatem. Est- ne autem qui Christiano existimet sufficere, si pœnas le- gum effugiat, in scelere ratuin non etiam in vitia consti- tutas? Sed illud etiam videamus quantum liceat homini pro vita tuenda facere. Sunt & hic Jurisconsulti qui existiment, etiam innocentem qui dirimendæ rixæ se interponit, interfici posse, si alia ratio nulla sit expe- diendæ salutis, quod confido paucis placiturum: & ne illud quidem recipit religiosus animus quod à nonnullis est proditum, non esse exspectandum dum præsens immi- neat periculum, sed tollendum in tempore qui credatur nociturus. Non enim eousque timori indulgendum est. Rectius Cicero: Quis hoc statuit unquam, aut cui concessit sine summo omnium periculo pot st, ut eum jure po- tuerit occidere, à quo metuisse se dicat ne ipse posterius occi- deretur. Estque in ea idem rem apud Gellium dissertatio lib. VIII. cap. 3. Sunt rursum alii qui ne aggressorem qui- dem occidi posse arbitrantur, etiamsi vita, ni id fiat, o- mnino sit amittenda. Quæ sententia multos habuit au- ctores in primis Christianismi seculis, quo tempore fer- vida pietas facile honesta omnia pro præceptis amplecteba- tur. Origenes Celfo Christianos seoitiosos appellanti, ita respondet: καὶ τοιγε εἰς ὅσις ἦν τῆς συσάσεως τοῖς χρι- sιανοῖς ἡ αἰτία, τὴν ἀρχὴν ἀπὸ Ἰεδαιων εἰληφόσιν, οἷς ἐξῆν κὶ ὅπλα ὑπὲρ τῶν οἰκείων ἀναλαβεῖν, καὶ πολεμίως ἀναιρεῖν, ἐκ ἂν ὁ νομοθέτης Χρισιανῶν πάντη ἀναίρεσιν ἀνθρώπων ἀπηγό- ρευε, μήποτε δίκαιον εἶναι διδάσκων τὸ κατ' αὐτῶν τόλμη- μα τῶν ἑαυτῦ μαθητῶν, κἂν ἀδικώτατον ἐκεῖνο ᾖ· ὦ γὰρ πρέπειν ἡγεῖτο τῇ ἐνθέῳ ἑαυτῦ νομοθεσίᾳ τὸ συγχωρεῖν ὁ- ποίαν δήποτε ἀνθρώπε ἀναίρεσιν. Ego si quis sit tam forti animo, ut vitam eripi sive patiatur potius, quam alterius quantumvis infesti morte eam redimat, laude aut etiam admiratione dignum censeam. Rara dilectio est pro ini- micis atque improbis mortem oppetere, inquit Paulus Rom. V. 6. 7. 8. Sed an præcepti jure à Christianis hoc e- xigatur, videndum est amplius. Nam Christi hæc verba pro- prie de ultione agere videntur, aut etiam de vi ad arcendum malum quod facile sit reparabile. At hinc utrinque vitæ res vertitur: ut aut inde moriatur, qui hoc malum in se accessit, aut hinc qui invitus eo necessitatis detruditur. Jam vero ne in bonis quidem vitæ huic servientibus, ne in- ter amicos quidem per præcepti modum à nobis exigitur, ut aliis effe velimus ἄνεσιν, nobis θλίψιν, ut Paulus loqui- tur 2. Corinth. VIII. 13. Cur igitur de vita aliud dicamus? Nam si dicas, vitam alterius bonis esse digniorem, sane tan- to & vita nostra bonis est dignior. Itaque manet eadem ἀναλογία. Sunt qui præceptum Noe ejusque liberis datum urgent, quo vetatur fundi sanguis humanus. Verum idem hoc natura præcipit: at omnia præcepta naturalia, quan- tumvis universaliter enuntiata, habent suas ex æquo & bo- no exceptiones. Et videmus populos omnes quorum consentiens judicium non temere sperni debet nam ut He- raclitus dicebat ὁ ξυνὸς λόγος πισὸν τεκμήριον) ita jus illud naturæ interpretari, ut innocentem pronuncient, qui cum aliter vita n tueri nequiret, vim sibi inferentem oc- ciderit. De quo Cicero dicit non scriptam exstare sed na- tam legem, quam non didicimus, accepimus, legimus, verum ex ipsa natura arripuimus, hausimus, expressimus. Videtur autem debere lex Dei idem dictans quod natura, ita accipi, quomodo ipsa natura accipiendum monstrat, nisi addatur aliquid expressius. Una caussa est quæ vitæ pe- riculo æquanda videatur, si quis stuprum corpori parans inferre, aliter quam occidendo arceri nequeat. Neque e- nim leges tantum hoc permittunt, sed solent facta ejusmo- di apud omnes populos magnis laudibus celebrari, exstant- que etiam in veteri Christianismo ejus exempla. Quod tamen de vita armis, si necessitas urgeat, tuenda dictum est, id non audeam proferre ad arcendam vim, quæ in- fertur à publica potestate. Nam id neque leges indul- gent, & si indulgerent, reipublicæ sic periculosum. Cessat & ratio quam attulimus. Non enim æqualia inter se sunt bona, tranquillitas publica, & vita quantumvis innocentis. Itaque Petrus in causa, quæ omnium ju- stissima videri poterat, armatam vim incæptans, à Christo reprehensus est, & ipse Dominici præcepti me- moraliis in simili positis necessitate præscribit patientiæ leges Epist. I. cap. IV. 15. 16. Et hoc Christianæ religio- sissime observarunt, adeo ut si quam per vim obstitum es- set grassanti sævitiæ, id publice ipsorum universitas im- probaret. Videtur tamen alia esse causa eorum qui de- creto superiorum potestatum inferioribus resistunt. In- feriores enim quatenus superiorum mandata egrediun- tur, privatis sunt accensendi. Quo referendum est factum Nehemiæ & sociorum, quos contra vicinos præsides ar- mabat regii edicti auctoritas. Absoluta quæstione de sui tutela, veniamus ad alteram quæ est de judiciis publicis, præsertim capitalibus. Nam ea quoque à Christo his ver- bis prohiberi, sunt qui existimant. At jam ostendimus de ultione Christum agere sive ea in jure, sive extra jus exigatur. Longe autem aliud est ultio, aliud pœna, quam nullo postulante leges exigunt. Ultio ex ira po- stulatur. Judex vero, ut Seneca vere dixit, nunquam minus irascitur, quam cum punit. Exigitur ultio, quia factum est quod non oportebat: pœna vero publicorum judiciorum ideo exigitur, ne peccetur in posterum. Est enim aut νοθεσία, aut παράδειγμα, ut philosophi recte di- stinguunt. νοθεσία vult eum qui peccavit meliorem fa- cere, ut paterna castigatio liberum, quam ab iis quoque usurpari intelligo domi qui eam in republica reprehen- dunt. παράδειγμα autem exemplo tristiore alios à de- linquendo absterret. Sæpe autem conjungitur castiga- tio cum exemplo. Utrunque autem ab ultione longissi- me differre tuin ex origine tum ex fine apparet. Quomo- do igitur quæ de ultione dicta sunt à Christo ad rem adeo diversam producentur? Dicam aliquid amplius. Ipsa illa supplicia ultionis sive τῆς τιμωρίας quod attinet, Chri- sti præcepto is qui læsus est ea exigere doloris reponendi caua prohibetur, non prohibetur judex si exigantur lege agere. Nam manebat adhuc Mosis lex tota, quam Chri- stus profitetur hoc ipso sermone à se nulla in parte infringi. Poterat autem Christus salva lege imperare læso ne talio- nem postularet: quia hoc lex illi non imperabat, sed con- cedebat: nihil autem contra legem facit qui concesso non utitur. At judici interdicere ne secundum legem judi- caret, incolumi lege non poterat: quia non permitte- bat hoc lex judicis arbitrio, sed districte & addita com- minatione hoc ei imperabat, ut videre est tum alibi, tum præsertim Deuter. XIX. vers. 11. Pertinet autem hoc ar- gumentum etiam ad capitis judicia. Nam ad ea quoque judicem lex obligabat, nisi quatenus vi majore, ut pu- ta potestate Romanorum, prohibeatur. Quare cum & lex Christi statim ut promulgata erat auditores obligave- rit, & lex Mosis eo tempore non fuerit antiquata sequi- tur ut utrique simul pareri potuerit. Quod si tempore promulgationis verba Christi non obstiterunt publicis ju- diciis, ne nunc quidem obstare possunt. Manet enim ea quæ initio fuerat verborum sententia. Nec est quod quisquam regerat excidio Judaicæ reipublicæ leges Moy- sis concidisse: neque enim id quæritur an ex legibus Moy- sis judicari debeat in illis populis quos lex Moysis ne tunc quidem obstrinxit cum publicaretur, sed an cum Christi præcepto pugnet aut easdem aut similes leges figere. Il- lud quidem certum est, supervacuum esse ut tales leges ferantur in eos qui ex Christi vivunt disciplina. Nam qui sponte sua recte faciunt, eos nihil opus est coërceri mali formidine. Verum docent nos vaticinia, docet re- rum eventus mundum non esse Christianum, sed vere Christianos minimam esse mundi portionem: leges au- tem respiciunt id quod plerunque accidit. Quare cum humani generis pars major nunc sit non minus σαρκικὴ quam erat Moysis ætate gens Judæorum, simili morbo si- milia sunt adhibenda remedia. Neque enim sine publi- cis judiciis nunc tutior esse potest innocentia quam tum fuit. Quanquam vero lex Hebræa, ut diximus, à Deo data sit soli populo Hebræo, tamen dubium non est, quin eam recte imitari potuerint gentes cæteræ. Nihil igitur allatum quo constet hæc publica judicia Deo dis- plicere. Imo contrarium Paulus docet, cum dicit pu- blicam potestatem à Deo ordinatam, & Dei ministram esse. Neque enim intelligi id potest de sola provida per- missione & directione, quomodo etiam latrocinia Deus permittit eisque utitur. Nam ex ea ordinatione sive institutione Paulus colligit honorem eis & obedientiam etiam ex animo deberi : quod de latrociniis rebusque aliis a Deo permissis dici non potest. Sentit ergo Deo grata esse ac placere publica imperia. Quicquid autem est in quo Deus ἐυδοκεῖ, id recte praestatur. Capitalia au- tem judicia adeo non excludit Paulus, ut de ea par- te imperii publici praecipue agat. Ait enim publicam potestatem Dei esse ministram ad iram (id est, ad poenam, nam eum sensum plerunque ea vox habet) adversum maleficos : & quod amplius est, ait non fru- stra ab ea gladium ferri, ad istud scilicet ministerium, ut contextus verborum docet. Gladii autem nomine publica judicia tanquam a nobilissima sui parte nuncu- pantur; . unde & in jure jus gladii est jus publicarum animadversionum. Colligitur hinc probari a Deo ipsum etiam gladii usum adversum maleficos. Cum ve- ro DEUS non habeat decreta sibi contraria, neutiquam potest peccatum esse in eo quod DEUS probet, nisi aliunde vitium accedat. At ne quis putet probari a Deo hanc potestatem, sed non probari ut ea sit penes Chri- stianos, notet primum ea quae hic exstant praecepta comminationem habere jacturae regni coelorum & gra- vis supplicii. Ad omnes igitur pertinent. Deinde a- perte testatur Paulus velle DEUM omnes homines sal- vos fieri & ad cognitionem veritatis Evangelicae venire, etiam reges 1. Timoth. II. vers. 2. 3. 4. Possunt igitur & Reges per Evangelium servari, quod intelligendum etiam non exuta regia dignitate ostendunt verba prae- cedentia: vult enim pro regibus orari, ut quietam & tranquillam vitam agamus : at hoc praestare reges non possunt nisi qua reges sunt. Vult ergo orari pro regi- bus etiam, qua tales sunt, addita causa, quia vult eos Deus servari, etiam qua tales scilicet, ut recte procedat argumentatio. Tranquillam autem & quietam vitam quomodo reges praestant ? Laudando bonos, malos pu- niendo, etiam gladii jure ut idem Apostolus explicat Ro- man. XIII. vers. 3. 4. Vult ergo Deus reges, qua re- ges sunt, & qua utuntur gladii jure, posse per Evange- lium servari. Neque aliter verba Apostoli acceperunt Christiani veteres, ἐυχόμενοι ut Justinus loquitur Apolo- getico secundo τὺς βασιλεῖς καὶ ἄρχοντας μετὰ τῆς βασι- λικῆς δυνάμεως καὶ σώφρονα τὸν λογισμὸν ἔχοντας ἐυρέθηναι. Preces autem illae Christianorum, & antiquissima vatici- nia de regibus Christo famulaturis, extra controversiam in Constantino ejusque successoribus eventum habue- runt. Ab his autem ita recepta est Christi doctrina, ut nec imperio excederent, neque publica judicia abo- lerent. Neque vero in tanta Episcoporum multitudine quisquam fuit, qui eos ut id facerent hortaretur: quod mihi certissimum esse videtur indicium, constanter ab omnibus creditum, nihil esse in istis judiciis Christi prae- ceptis & Imperatorum saluti contrarium, cum alioqui libertatis Episcoporum adversus reges peccantes illustria extent exempla. Nimirum meminerant & Sergium Pro- praetorem olim a Paulo ad Christi fidem conversum, ne- que tamen ab eo exactum, ut se propraetura, in qua continebatur & jus gladii, abdicaret. Videbitur forte qui- busdam aliter sensisse Tertullianum cum dicit: Sed & Caesares credidissent super Christo, si aut Caesares non essent seculo necessarii, aut si & Christiani potuissent esse Cae- sares. Sed forte hoc voluit Tertullianus, cum is esset Ro- mani imperii status, ut Christianum Imperatorem ferre non posset, divino interim numine ita res gubernatas, ut per paganos Imperatores aliquatenus publicae tranquillitati consuleretur. Nam idem ille Scriptor jam suo tempore dicit tribus, decurias, palatium, senatum, forum imple- ta fuisse Christianis. Alia etiam veterum loca quae obsta- re publicis judiciis videntur, commodiorem longe inter- pretationem recipiunt. Nam aut hoc dicitur, Christi prae- cepta nullas habere sanctiones aspectabilium poenarum, quales lex Moysis habuit, & sine ejusmodi suppliciis in Christi populo servari disciplinam : quo sensu ab eodem Tertulliano dictum est: Nova lex se non vindicat ultio- ne gladii: aut magistratum suscipere dissuadent, non ut rem illicitam, sed ut multis delinquendi periculis ex- positam. Hoc sensu Tatianus ex Christiani persona di- cit, σρατηγίαν παρῇτημαι. Christianus nec ad litem af- fectat, inquit Tertullianus, multoque justius aestimat abstinendum judiciis de capite & pudore. Et tamen e- jusdem est: Bonum esse cum puniantur nocentes nemo ne- gat. Et alibi justitiam vocat violentiae vindicem. Ori- genes vero adversus Celsum objicientem Christianis quod praeturas aliosque magistratus defugerent, ita re- spondet. ἐ φεύγοντές γε τὰς κοινοτέρας τῶ βιῶ λειτυργίας χρισιανοὶ τὰ τοιαῦτα περιῑσανται, ἀλλὰ τηρῦντες ἑαυτὺς θειο- τέρᾳ κέ ἀναγκαιοτέρᾳ λειτυργίᾳ. Clemens autem, utro- que antiquior, loquens de Christiano qui jam ad summum probitatis gradum pervenerit, κᾂν εἰς ἀρχὴν, inquit, κα- ταστῆν ποτε, καθάπερ ὁ μωσῆς, ἐπὶ τῇ σωτηρίᾳ τῶν ἀρ- χομένων ἡγήσεται καὶ τὸ ἄγριον καὶ τὸ ἄπιστον ἐξημερώσεται, τιμῇ μὲν τῶν ἀξίων, κολάσει δὲ τῶν μοχθηρῶν, τῇ κατὰ λό- γον εἰς παιδείαν ἐγγραφομένῃ· μάλιστα γὰρ ἄγαλμα θεῖον καὶ θεῷ προσεμφερὲς ἀνθρώπῳ δικαίου ψυχή, ἐν ᾗ διὰ τῆς τῶν παραγγελμάτων ὑπακοῆς τεμενίζεται καὶ ἐνιδρύεται ὁ πάντων ἡγεμὼν θνητῶν τε καὶ ἀθανάτων βασιλεύς τε καὶ γεννήτωρ τῶν καλῶν, νόμος ὢν ὄντως καὶ θεσμὸς, καὶ λόγος αἰώνιος ἰδίᾳ τε ἑκάστοις καὶ κοινῇ πᾶσιν εἷς ὢν σωτήρ. Veruntamen ut illa publicorum judiciorum potestas exerceatur citra dispendium Christianæ lenitatis, multis cautionibus o- pus esse video, quæ passim negligantur. Ut notissimis utar exemplis, legem de necandis ob captam feram a- gricolis, miror tanta diligentia à Jurisconsultis defendi: cum multo meliorem posituri essent operam in seria ta- lium dissuasione. Tale etiam est quod necari fures jubentur, & quidem iis in locis ubi adulterium, tanto extra contro- versiam gravius delictum, vix censoria nota perstringi- tur. Ego sane non video quid nos cogat lege Hebræa esse immitiores. In ipsis homicidiis, non tam factum nudum spectandum mihi videtur, quam quæ anteacta vita occisoris fuerit, veneritne ad hoc facinus impetu, an deliberatione, & quod præcipuum est sitne ingenium sanabile. Nam hoc & Seneca præcipit, ne quis pe- reat nisi quem perire etiam pereuntis intersit: quod ipsum tamen videtur aut nunquam aut rarissime locum habere posse. Quando enim constabit spem omnem pœniten- tiæ præcisam? Hæc discrimina à judicibus expendi mul- to esset satius, quam alios ex solo facti nomine audito ad mortem rapi, aliis qui gratia & amicis valent per indul- gentiam principalem plenam contingere, quantumvis a- trocium facinorum, impunitatem. Nam quod quidam existimant homicidio naturaliter respondere capitis pœ- nam, in eo falluntur. Pœnæ enim delictorum non sunt ipso naturæ jure aut ulla Dei perpetua lege constitutæ, sed pro modo imminentis periculi intendi ac remitti so- lent. Docet nos Caini historia prima illa mundi ætate pœnam homicidii fuisse latam fugam, cujus accessio erat quod pii purique homines ita contaminatorum aspectum contactumque declinabant. Cujus antiquissimi instituti & Euripides meminit: Καλῶς ἔθεντο ταῦτα πατέρες οἱ πάλαι. Εἰς ὀμμάτων μὲν ὄψιν ἐκ εἴων περᾶν Οὐδ᾽ εἰς ἀπάντημ᾽ ὅστις αἷμ᾽ ἔχων κυροῖ, Φυγαῖσι δ᾽ ὁσίων, ἀνταποκτεῖναι δὲ μὴ· Quem morem reduci volebat Plato. Feritas quæ ante diluvium humanos mores invaserat, occasionem novæ legi dedit, ut nimirum homicidæ sanguis effunderetur, quæ lex ut illis temporibus acceommodata à Deo in ipsa humani generis post diluvium instauratione promulga- ta est. Sed optimus suæ legis interpres Deus id refert ad cædem quæ sit deliberato, structisque insidiis, Exod. XXI. vers. 14. Diu stetit & floruit Romana respublica, cum magistratuum cognitio deportationem non excede- ret. Postea quoque cum jam leges latæ essent de morte puniendis homicidis aliorumque criminum convictis, multas tamen exceptiones usus reperiit, ita ut sæpe intra relegationem severitas consisteret. Difficile est exactam servare mediocritatem: at si quid peccandum est, in istam lenitatis partem potius peccandum est. Forte non pauciores à delinquendo absterreret ad opus damnatio, quam mors ipsa: & simul, quod præcipue spectandum est Christianæ dilectioni, daretur spatium agendæ pœ- nitentiæ, quæ nunc interdum supplicii præcipitatione præciditur. Certe & Constantinus, cum primum Chri- stianam probavit religionem, in plerisque delictorum generibus supplicia capitalia inhibuit, quæ mox reducta sunt διὰ τὴν τῶν μοχθηρῶν ἄδειαν ut nos docent historiæ. Itaque & quod de puniendis gladio adulteris legimus Constantini constitutione, quæ inserta est codici Justi- nianeo deest in antiquiori codice Theodosiano. Re- stat controversia de bello, quæ itidem à plerisque ad hunc locum tractari solet. Si Christi verba moderatam sui defensionem singulis non prohibent, minus obsta- bunt iis armis quæ publica auctoritate pro necessaria to- tius populi defensione suscipiuntur. Nam quanto pluris est multorum quam unius salus, tanto etiam justius pro- pugnatur. Rursus si piis regibus licet uti jure gladii in latronem unum, quid ni liceat in plures, qui, ut rei fiant, acie vincendi sunt? Neque sacrarum literarum, etiam novi fœderis auctoritas hic nobis deest, quan- quam vetitum affirmantibus justius incumbit onus pro- bandi. Ut enim omittam Baptistæ verba de quibus a- gemus alias, & Centurionis illius fidem à Christo præ- dicatam, & operam à Paulo datam ut contra Judæorum infidias præsidio militari servaretur, vel unum illud suf- ficere mihi videtur, quod Cornelius non deposito centu- rionatu & baptisinum à Petro acceperit, & à Deo Spiri- tum Sanctum, neutiquam tacituro Luca, si Cornelius vi- tæ prioris professionem deseruisset, cum nunquam soleat omittere signa resipiscentiæ, & hoc vel maxime ad do- cendam posteritatem pertineret. Neque aliter sensisse reperio Christianos veteres: nam & sub Marco constat Christianos militasse, & Tertullianus non solum militum Christianorum meminit, sed tantum eorum indicat fuisse numerum, ut castra prope implerent. Origenes quoque apes ait nobis documentum à Deo datas πρὸς τὸ δικαίως κὲ̓ τεταγμένως πολέμως εἴποτε δέοι γίνεσθαι ἐν ἀνθρώ- ποις.

Quod autem interdum Christianos militiam de- trectasse legimus, ideo evenit, quod illorum temporum Imperatores à militibus exigerent aut expressam à Chri- sto discessionem, aut tacitam dicto scilicet sacramento per Deos, vel per Imperatorem ut Deum, aut etiam quod propositis contra Christianos edictis quotidie ad ea exercenda manu militari uterentur. Talibus enim temporibus Christiani monebantur defugere militiam, & si qui militarent, à piis cœtibus arcebantur. Neque a- lio pertinet, quod in Nicena Synodo constitutum est ad- versus eos qui semel deposita sub Licinio militia cin- gulum resumsissent, nempe sub eodem Licinio, qui ut nos Eusebius docet τὺς στρατιώτας ἐκέλευε ἀποβάλλεσθαι τὺ ἀξιώματα, εἰ μὴ τοῖς δαίμοσι θύειν αἰρέοιντο. Nam ut gene- raliter de omni militia is Canon intelligatur, historiæ tem- porum repugnat. Quippe major pars exercitus Con- stantini ex Christianis erat. Et si qui Christiani sub Lici- nio militiam omiserant, iis liberum fecit Constantinus an militiam resumere vellent, an à militia vacare. Quod autem militiam interdum dissuadent Scriptores, simile est ei quod de honorum fuga dicebamus: partim etiam causas habet temporum illorum proprias, ut ad Lucæ cap. III. ostendemus. Neque vero dubito quin multo im- pensius dissuasuri fuerint, si bellorum nostri temporis ra- biem & castra, perjuriis, stupris, latrociniis, omni de- nique vitiorum confluxu inquinata vidissent. Eo ventum est, ut rem magnam præstare videatur miles Christia- nus, si non veteris & paganæ Romæ militem, ipsos de- nique Turcas flagitiosis moribus vincat. Longe alii mi- lites sint oportet, cum quibus ex Evangelio agamus: nam istos & sensus communis & comparatio veteris di- sciplinæ satis condemnant. Ut vero quæ fusius à multis de bello tractata sunt, paucis complectar, & si quid à pietate alienum illis probatur, obiter refellam: constat tres esse belli partes, initium, progressum, exitum. In ipso initio spectari debent leges justitiæ, prudentiæ, ca- ritatis. Justam causam belli suscipiendi esse non arbitror hoc unum, quod populus alter à recta pietate abhorreat. Quis enim in illum populum alteri populo aut regi id judicium dedit? Σπάρταν ἐ̓λαχες τάυτην κόσμει. Et recte à Plutarcho dictum πρόφασιν ἐῖναι πλεονεξίας ἡμερῶσαι τὰ βαρ- βαρικά. Quod si etiam populus alter nos læserit, tamen ad vim confugiendum non est, quamdiu res potest verbis disceptari. Hinc mos res repetendi, antequam bellum in- dicatur apud Hebræos, Græcos, Romanos. Si is qui cum agimus paratus sit de rebus controversis ad arbitros ire, abstinendum adhuc bello est, ἐ γὰρ νόμιμον ἐπὶ τὸν δίκας διδόντα ὡς ἐπ̓ ἀδικοῦντα ἰέναι, ut ait apud Thucydidem Archidamus. Nullo autem modo recipiendum est, quod quidam tradiderunt justum utrinque esse bellum posse: nam id ne in lite quidem potest contingere: ni- si justum intelligi volumus, id quod ex moribus rece- ptis jura habet captivitatis, prædæ, postliminii. Sed quæ hoc sensu justa dicuntur, plerumque nihil sunt aliud, quam magna latrocinia. Vel Senecam audiamus: Ho- micidia compescimus & singulas cædes. Quid bella & occi- sarum gentium gloriosum scelus? Non avaritia, non cru- delitas modum novit. Ex senatusconsultis plebisque sci- tis sæva exercentur: & publice jubentur vetita privatim. Quæ commissa capite luerent, tum quis paludati fecerunt laudamus. Non pudet homines, mitissimum genus, gau- dere sanguine alterno, bella gerere, gerendaque liberis tra- dere, cum inter se etiam mutis & feris pax sit? Sane si jus naturæ respicimus, quid interest uno myoparone pirata mare infestum habeat, an Asiam cum exercitu & classe Alexander: Nec multis refutandi sunt, qui justa bella suscipi docent ab his qui sedibus suis expulsi aut egressi in alienarum sedium possessionem recipi volunt: aut qui metuunt ne crescens potentia aliquando ipsis pe- riculum faciat. Verum etiam cum justa est causa bellan- di, sæpe obstabunt prudentiæ, leges, Utrimque ferrum &

corpora humana: nec in ejusdem potestate est initium belli & finis. Bene Euripides: Ὅταν γὰρ ἔλθῃ πόλεμος εἰς ψῆφον λεὼ Οὐδεὶς ἔτ' αὐτῷ θάνατον ἐκλογίζεται Τὸ δυςυχὲς δὲ τοῦτ' ἐς ἄλλον ἐκτρέπει Εἰ δ' ἦν παρ' ὄμμα θάνατον ψῆφο φερᾶ Οὐκ ἄν ποθ' ἑλλὰς δοριμανὴς ἀπώλετο.

Sed imprimis Christiano spectandum est, quid charitas exigit. Nam si lites vitari dissuadens Paulus dixit, cur non potius injurias sustinetis, quanto magis æquum est quantumvis cura nos pati, quam ad eam venire disce- ptationem, quæ bonos malosque iisdem malis invol- vit? Privata defensio in periculum adducit solum inva- sorem. Supplicia capitalia in facinorosos sunt constituta. At in bello innocentes non minus quam nocentes utrim- que pereunt & spoliantur. Principi Seneca præscribit, ut alieno sanguini tanquam suo parcat, sciatque homi- ni non esse homine prodige utendum: quid illum exige- re credimus qui pacem nobis cum omnibus quantum fie- ri potest tam sollicite commendavit? Nimirum ista o- mnia, si quo modo debent, expendantur, videbimus non frustra ad externa quoque bella & alias bellorum causas aptari posse, quod Favonius dixerat χεῖρον εἶναι μο- ναρχίας παρανόμῳ πόλεμον ἐμφύλιον: & pia arma ea de- mum esse, quæ sunt necessaria, hoc est quæ suscipiuntur ad evitanda mala armis sæviora. Ad belli progressum leges istæ pertinent, ut pacta serventur quam religiosis- sime, ut pacato noceatur nemini, ut quam minimo san- guine decernatur, ne sæviatur in captos, in deditos, in pueros, in fœminas, in agricolas, & cæteram imbellium turbam. Postremo circa exitum belli videndum est, ne ira & ultionis cupiditate bellum trahatur: sed appareat nihil aliud bello quam pacem quæsitum: quod fiet, si quavis tolerabili pactione ab armis discedatur, aut etiam post victoriam nihil victis dematur præter injuriæ licen- tiam. Bellorum inquit ille egregii fines, ubi ignoscendo transigitur. Et hæc quidem ad eos præcipue pertinent, quos penes belli suspiciendi, regendi finiendique jus est. De sociis illud addendum est, non caritati tantum, sed & justitiæ adversari ea fœdera, quæ aut inferentibus aut etiam propulsantibus bellum auxilia pollicentur sine cau- sarum discrimine. Hi vero qui bello ministerium dunta- xat exhibent, scire debent, si subditi sunt, subditos quo- que regibus obsequium non sine exceptione debere. Et ut probabilis aliqua causa excusat parendi necessitatem, certe qui mercede conducti militant cives, multoque ma- gis externi,nihil habent,quo causam suam possint tueri, nisi plane ipsis constet juste pieque susceptum esse bellum cui o- peram addicunt. Et ut hoc constet,tamen graviter peccant, quicunque non caritate populi periclitantis, sed mercede aut præda illecti bellum in genere quæstus habent. Rident hæc multi, & negant rempublicam sine injuria geri pos- se, sua retinere privatæ domus: de alienis certare re- giam ajunt esse laudem: qui alios perdere possit eum per- dendum in tempore: nihil injusti in eum qui quod ju- sturn est recusat: quæque alia sunt in eam formam. Di- cant quod velint, & ubi solitudinem faciunt pacem ap- pellent. Ex illorum scitis, quæ vere scripta sunt huma- no sanguine, rex ilie pacis de genere humano non judi- cabit. Imo vero id potius vereor, ne in hac tractatione in eam partem quæ bello nimium indulget fuerim æquo pronior. Quare sciat lector non definiendi animo hæc à me dicta, sed ut verum diligentius inquiratur, interim sua- deo omnibus injurias ferant potius, quam humanum san- guinem quamvis nocentium fundant, & illius dicti sæpe meminerint: quod dubitas ne feceris.

## 5:41
Vers. 41.

And whoever shall compel you to go one mile: Christ sets forth three kinds of injuries: the first which is committed against the body: the second which is against the right of ownership: the third which is against liberty. The Hebrews, from the time when the power of the Persians had invaded the Orient, had been compelled, among other inconveniences of that servitude, to bear also the burden of the Angaria, the immunity from which was granted to them by Demetrius: as can be seen in Josephus, Antiq. XIII. Hence it happened that they vehemently hated the thing, and extended the name even to private vexations, as appears below XXVII. 32. and from many places of the Hebrew interpreters of Scripture. And in that sense Christ uses this word.

Mile: This is one of those words which, with human empire, came not only into Greece, but also into Palestine, which the Syrian also uses here: and the teachers of the Hebrews everywhere.

ὕπαγε μετ’ ἀυτῶ δύο] And here the sentence must be supplied, with the addition of μᾶλλον. For just as it is not better to be beaten again and to receive greater harm, so too it is not better to provide double the service that is demanded than to exact vengeance either by ourselves or through judges, or in any other way to sin against the law of loving: or at least this is what Christ wills, that those things which can be performed by us without great inconvenience, such as the walking of one mile, are not to be refused even if they are demanded through injury. However, these things do not stand in the way of our warding off a heavy yoke from ourselves by peaceful and calm methods. If you can be free, says Paul, use it rather: and do not become the servants of men, 1 Corinthians VII, verses 21, 23. For liberty is an instrument partly useful, partly necessary for doing many things: so that not without merit has the old poet said: Ἥμισυ τῆς ἀρετῆς ἀποαίρει δύλιον ἦμαρ:

Latin:

Vers. 41.

Καὶ ὅςις σε ἀγγαρεύσει μίλιον ἓν ] Tria injuriarum gene- ra Christus ponit: primum quod in corpus committitur: alterum quod contra jus dominii: tertium quod contra libertatem, Hebræi, ex quo Persarum potentia Orientem invaserat, coacti fuerant inter cætera ejus servitii incom- moda, etiam onus Angariæ ferre, cujus immunitas ipsis à Demetrio concessa est: ut apud Josephum videre est O- rig. XIII. inde factum ut rei vehementer exosænomen etiam ad privatas vexationes producerent, ut apparet in- fra XXVII. 32. & ex multis Hebræorum Scripturæ inter- pretum locis. Atque in eum sensum vocem hanc Chri- stus usurpat.

Μίλιον ] Hæc una est earum vocum quæ cum hu- mano imperio non in Græciam tantum, sed & in Palæsti- nam pervenerunt, quam & Syrus hic usurpat: & passim Hebræorum magistri.

ὕπαγε μετ’ ἀυτῶ δύο] Et hic supplenda sententia, ad- dito μᾶλλον. Ut enim iterum vapulare, majusque da- mnum accipere, ita & duplum operæ jus quæ exigatur præstare non satius est, quam ultionem aut per nos ipsos, aut per judices exigere, aut alio quovis modo peccare in diligendi legem: aut certe hoc vult Christus, quæ præ- stari à nobis sine magno incommodo possunt, qualis est miliaris unius deambulatio, ea non recusanda etiamfi per injuriam exigantur. Nihil autem hæc obstant, quo minus placidis atque sedatis rationibus jugum grave a no- bis arceamus. Si liber esse potes, inquit Paulus, eo po- tius utitor: & nolite fieri servi hominum, 1. Corinth. VII. vers. 21. 23. Est enim ad res multas agendas instru- mentum partim utile, partim necessarium libertas: ut non immerito vetus Poëta dixerit: Ἥμισυ τῆς ἀρετῆς ἀποαίρει δύλιον ἦμαρ:

## 5:42
Vers. 42.

Τῷ αἰτῦντί σε δίδε] Christ ordains another part of morals, namely that which pertains to benefits: as Tertullian rightly explains against Marcion IV. But the most necessary benefit is to relieve the needy: who are accustomed to be of two kinds, for they are either πτωχοὶ who have no hope of returning what is received, or they are ἐπαιτῶν who, afflicted by temporary fortune, ask for money not as a gift but as a loan. Therefore, from these benefits which are performed not so much to a man as to humanity, Christ wishes no one to be excluded: which must undoubtedly be understood from the rule of equity and goodness, insofar as both our means allow and their necessity demands, as Paul teaches the Corinthians. But if we are not equal to relieving everyone, it is fair that those be preferred whom the profession of piety joins to us.

Δανείσασθαι] This word is accustomed to be used by the Greeks, sometimes to signify to borrow money, sometimes to be to take at interest. But since usury was forbidden among the Jews themselves, and those whose affairs are in a tight spot are strangled rather than helped by usury, the word must be drawn here entirely to the former meaning. For usury does not even have the appearance of a benefit.

Grotius discusses here whether that which the laws permit, to repel force with force, befits even Christian discipline, inasmuch as the law of Moses grants the right to kill a nocturnal thief; he judges that it does not befit it. And what, he says, does charity finally allow us to value these rules of ours more than that which this world holds most worthy, human life, to which all created things are subservient? But the cause of that divine permission in Exodus XXII. 2 concerning killing a nocturnal burglar should have been attended to: namely, that in such a case the intent to kill is presumed, and that security at night ought to be certain for everyone. If this were contrary to love, certainly GOD, who is love itself, would not have permitted it in the law, who permits nothing contrary to love. Furthermore, Grotius also inquires about this, how much is it permitted for a man to do for the sake of protecting his life? Nor is he alien to the opinion of those who think that not even an aggressor can be killed, even if life must be entirely lost so that this does not happen? I, he says, if there be anyone of such a brave spirit that he suffers his life to be taken from him rather than redeem it by the death of another, however hostile, I would judge him worthy of praise or even admiration: But we are indeed commanded to love our neighbor as ourselves, yet we are not bound to love our neighbor more than ourselves; Grotius acknowledges that the law of nature and of nations itself suggests otherwise. We see, he says, all peoples, whose consenting judgment ought not to be rashly spurned (for as Heraclitus used to say ὀξυνὸς λόγος τεκμήριον) interpret that law of nature in such a way that they pronounce innocent the man who, when he could not otherwise protect his life, has killed one offering him violence. Concerning which Cicero says, there exists not a written but a born law, which we have not learned, received, read, but have snatched, drawn, and expressed from nature itself.

Latin:

Vers. 42.

Τῷ αἰτῦντί σε δίδε] Aliam morum partem Christus ordinat, eam scilicet quæ ad beneficia pertinet: ut recte explicat Tertullianus adversus Marcionem IV. Beneficium autem maxime necessarium est sublevare egentes: qui so- lent duorum esse generum, aut enim sunt πτωχοὶ qui nullam spem habent reddendi quod accipitur, aut sunt ἐπαιτῶν qui temporaria fortuna afflicti pecuniam non do- natam sed mutuam postulant. Ab his igitur beneficiis quæ non tam homini præstantur quam humanitati, nemi- nem vult Christus excludi: quod haud dubie ex æqui bo- nique regula intelligendum est, quatenus & nostræ facul- tates ferunt, & ipsorum necessitas postulat, ut Paulus ad Corinthios docet. Quod si omnibus sublevandis pa- res non simus, æquum est eos præferri quos pietatis pro- fessio nobis conjungit.

Δανείσασθαι] Solet ista vox Græcis usurpari, modo ut significet pecuniam sumere mutuam, modo ut sit fœ- neri sumere. Sed cum fœnus Judæis inter se interdi- ctum fuerit, & quorum in arcto res sunt fœnore jugulentur magis quam adjuventur, omnino ad significationem prio- rem vox hic trahenda est. Nam fœnus ne speciem quidem habet beneficii.

Disputat hic Grotius, an quod leges permit- tunt vim vi repellere, id Christianæ etiam disciplinæ conveniat, utpote quod lex Mosis concedit furem nocturnum occidere; non convenire arbitratur. Et quæ tandem, inquit, charitas finit nos istas regulas nostras pluris facere, quam quod hic orbis dignis- simum habet, vitam humanam, cui res conditæ o- mnes famulantur? Sed attendenda erat causa istius permissionis divinæ Exod. XXII. 2. de fure effra- ctore nocturno occidendo: quod nempe in tali a- nimus occidendi præsumatur, quodque securitas noctu cuivis constare debeat. Dilectioni si hoc contrarium foret, certe DEUS, qui ipsa cha- ritas est, in lege id minime permisisset, qui nihil dilectioni contrarium permittit. Porro disquirit etiam de eó Grotius, quantum liceat homini pro vita tuenda facere? Nec alienus est ab eorum sen- tentia, qui ne aggressorem quidem occidi pos- se arbitrantur, etsi vita, ne id fiat, omnino sit a- mittenda? Ego, inquit, si quis sit tam forti ani- mo, ut vitam eripi sibi patiatur potius, quam alte- rius, quantumvis infesti morte eam redimat, lau- de aut etiam admiratione dignum censeam: Sed jubemur quidem proximum diligere, sicut nos i- psos, non tamen proximum magis, quam nos i- psos diligere tenemur; agnoscit Grotius ipsum jus naturæ, & gentium aliud suadere. Videmus, inquit, populos omnes, quorum consentiens judi- cium non temere sperni debet (nam ut Heraclitus di- cebat ὀξυνὸς λόγος τεκμήριον) ita jus illud na- turæ interpretari, ut innocentem pronuncient, qui cum aliter vitam tueri nequiret, vim sibi inferen- tem occiderit. De quo Cicero dicit, non scriptam extare sed natam legem, quam non didicimus, acce- pimus, legimus, verum ex ipsa natura arripuimus, hausimus, expressimus.

## 5:43
Ἀγαπήσεις τὸν πλησίον σου] רע to the Hebrews and Greeks: πλησίον for the most part does not signify simply another, but one who is joined to us by the bond of blood, neighborhood, or friendship. And indeed among Moses Leviticus XIX. v. 18, which passage Christ here respects, רע is that very person who is said in the same place to be בן עמו that is, a fellow countryman. The Jews, seizing upon this, so warded off their liberality from foreigners that they would not even perform for them the common duties of humanity, such as showing the way kindly: which he who would not do was cursed with imprecations among the Athenians, as Diphylus teaches us: ἀγνοεῖς ἐν ταῖς ἀραῖς Ὅτι ἐστιν, ὅστις μὴ φράση ὀρθὴν ὁδὸν, Ἢ πῦρ ἐνάυση, ἢ διαφθείρη ὕδωρ. Of this kind also are those things which Cicero says are to be granted even to a stranger. Not to forbid flowing water, to allow fire to be taken from fire, to give faithful counsel to one deliberating. But that these very things were not accustomed to be performed by the Jews to extraneous men is testified by the verse of Juvenal: Not to show the way except to one who worships the same rites: To lead only the circumcised to the sought-for fountain. But also Tacitus: Among themselves faith is obstinate, mercy is ready, against all others there is hostile hatred. But undoubtedly this inhuman error of the Jews also arose from the source already often indicated, that they believed they had abundantly fulfilled all parts of their duties if they had obeyed those precepts by which their own civil society was contained: But certainly neither did the Jewish law abolish the natural one, nor did that closer society abolish the older society of the human race, to which he looked who called himself a cosmopolite, and the Florentine jurist when he says that a certain kinship was instituted among men by nature. Hence that: I am a man, I think nothing human is alien to me. And what are elsewhere to the same effect. This is the very thing which Christ taught by the parable of the Samaritan helping the wounded Jew, whom the Priest and Levite had passed by. He does not deny that a Jew is τὸν πλησίον to a Jew, by the closer bond of consanguinity and the tie of their own law. But he shows that this does not prevent common origin and the very law of nature from making every man τὸν πλησίον to every man, that is, not a stranger, but one connected by a certain relationship, and therefore that there is no one to whom we ought not to do good when the occasion is given. It must indeed be admitted that when God prescribed a peculiar manner of life for the Israelites, by this very thing it was signified that a very familiar association with foreign nations, as being most corrupt, was to be avoided by them: which was accommodated to the circumstances of those times. And hence it is that we read everywhere in these books that the Jews were not accustomed συγχρᾶσθαι, συνεσθίειν, κολλᾶσθαι, προσέρχεσθαι to foreigners. And this very thing Apollonius Molo, the teacher of M. Tullius Cicero, invidiously objected to the Jews: ὅτι μὴ παρεδέχοντο τὲς ἄλλαις προκατειλημμένως δόξαις περὶ θεῶν, μηδὲ κοινωνεῖν ἤθελον τοῖς καθ' ἑτέραν συνήθειαν βίε ζῆν προαιρουμένοις: which Josephus does not deny, but attempts to defend by the example of the Laconian ξενηλασίας. And everywhere in Josephus, enemies object to the Jews τὸ ἄμικτον, τὸ ἀσύμβυλον, which in another place he calls τὴν δίαιταν ἀμιξίαν. But those who are wise easily see that the Jews went beyond the prescriptions and meaning of the law, since certain common duties are owed even to those whom either the law or reason excludes from the bond of closer relationship. In the law of Moses, God, to speak with Tertullian, was gradually shaping the faith of some toward the brightness of Christian discipline, while it was still stammering at the very first precepts of kindness. Wherefore, since they could not yet provide that indefinite love, nor could their infirmity bear promiscuous association, especially in such a great kingdom of vices and impious superstitions, God willed that all offices of benevolence should at least be shown to those who were partners in blood and religion, and that very thing, beyond the common rules of nature, He sanctioned by a promulgated law. As long as, to return to the words of Tertullian, the sacrament was within Israel, He rightly commanded mercy only toward brothers: (namely in the formula of the covenant) But when He gave the nations to Christ as an inheritance and the ends of the earth as a possession, and that which was said through Hosea began to be blotted out: Not my people, my people, and not having obtained mercy, having obtained mercy: A nation, namely, from then on Christ extended the law of paternal kindness to all, excluding no one from compassion, just as in the calling.

Grotius very poorly restricts 'neighbor' according to the meaning of the law to fellow countrymen. For that word רע is common, and denotes any neighbor whatsoever.

what other thing the second table brings, the sum of which is handed down in these words: you shall love your neighbor as yourself. For who a neighbor may be, the precepts of the second table themselves concerning the love of a neighbor teach. For when we are forbidden to kill a neighbor, are we only prohibited from plundering his goods, and so on in other matters? Furthermore, that a neighbor is also an enemy, we are clearly taught in Exod. 23:4, and that we ought to pursue with love even an enemy by whom we have been harmed, we are warned in Lev. 19:17 and Prov. 25:21. But especially clear is Christ's explanation in Luke 10:30. For a Jew was not a fellow-countryman to a Samaritan. Nor does he explain the law of nature there (although Grotius rashly opposes the law of nature to the law of Moses in these matters), but he is engaged in expounding the Mosaic law, concerning which the matter was with the lawyer. Wherefore, the opinion of Augustine in Epistle 52 to Macedonius is entirely to be approved. A neighbor in this place is to be weighed not by the closeness of blood, but by the society of reason, in which all men are partners. For if the account of money makes men partners, how much more does the account of nature, common by the law of birth, not of trading? In which he has not only almost all Christians, but also the Rabbis in agreement. Grotius, however, preferred to follow the Socinians here, nay, even to adorn the cause of the Pharisees thus far, who restricted the word 'neighbor' here. Tertullian, to whom Grotius appeals, does not deserve to be heard here when he says, The old law teaches love toward neighbors, the new toward strangers.

And you shall hate your enemy] Here many think they have a firm argument by which they prove that all things which Christ says were said to the ancients are to be referred not to the law of Moses, but to the interpretation of the lawyers. But we, who with most of the ancients think that the words of Moses are being looked at, but in such a way that at the same time the perverse interpretation of those is refuted who, from the obedience of that law, because it was proper to the Jews, promised themselves not only the comforts of this life but also the heavenly kingdom, with the laws of nature and charity neglected, we do not doubt that the sense of these words also exists in the law of Moses. Indeed, in that law, the Jews are commanded to perform certain common benefits even to enemies, Exod. 23:4. But to fellow-countrymen, of course, which the compared passage, which is Deut. 22:1, makes clear. But again, Exod. 34:11. and Deut. 7:1, the Hebrews are forbidden to join in affinity, to make a treaty, or even to have pity on those seven nations: the Hittite, the Girgashite, the Amorite, the Canaanite, the Perizzite, the Hivite, and the Jebusite. We have, therefore, enemies; we have also hatred, yet not beastly, but circumscribed by certain limits. For conditions of peace had to be offered to these very nations, so that if they wished, they might redeem the impending destruction with servitude: just as has been rightly noted by the Hebrews on the passage Deut. 20:10. And that they are commanded to be destroyed by slaughter without any pardon after peace was rejected, pertains to the men of that age, not also to their descendants: for Solomon received them into servitude in the most praised times of his reign, 1 Kings 9:20. To these seven nations can be ascribed the Amalekites, against whom the Hebrews are commanded to have an unceasing war and to blot out their memory entirely, Exod. 17:16. Deut. 25:19, which I think is likewise to be understood so that they were either destroyed by slaughter or were in the number of those who surrendered. The case of the Ammonites and Moabites seems to be a little different. For what is said about them in Deut. 23:6, I would not want to be taken with certain Hebrews as if arms could be brought against them before they were invited to peace. For God had not granted the Hebrews any right into the lands of those nations, as is clear from Deut. 1:19. But neither did Jephthah bring war upon the Ammonites until after the ways of a just peace were attempted, Judg. 11:16, and David kept peace with them until he was provoked by the most atrocious injuries, 2 Sam. 10. Wherefore I think that by those words of Deuteronomy only treaties of alliance are forbidden. We see, therefore, how far the Hebrews could hate those nations, or even, as Moses speaks in the mentioned passage of Deuteronomy, abhor them. Nor indeed do those precepts conflict with the law of nature: for that the wicked should be punished with a just penalty does not conflict with the law of nature, but rather it is very much in agreement with it. But just as any public power has that right over the subjects of its own empire, so does God, the supreme king of all, over kings and peoples; who, in this execution of punishment, which he could have done by himself, preferred that the Hebrews impute the malice to the nations. Certainly, this was the opinion of the fathers of no low time, while it had reached the point that sacred rites were sacrificed to sacrilegious rites of the age, and the innocent were slaughtered by the savagery of the slaughter: as appears from Lev. 18:24, as it is explained in the book of Wisdom, chapters 12 and 14. This right had emanated from a special decree of God, not from any common and therefore eternal obligation. Whence it was permitted: which, so that it may be perceived more rightly, must be distinguished into the kinds of foreigners. For other nations, when they receive the religion of Judaism, brought in by the aid of trade: therefore they were of equal right with the Hebrews, concerning those excepted who had been made freedmen from the Ammonites and Moabites, and honors were not admitted. Justin Martyr, Dialogue: 'He who is circumcised, not approaching the people, is just like the Jew.' There were others who abstained from the worship of false gods and obeyed the rest which were in the granted laws: or which were commanded to posterity, and the liberty of keeping the institutions of the Hebrews. To these also it was permitted to live among the Hebrews: which the law of Lev. 17:20 clearly shows, where Moses thus commands concerning the carcass of a beast that died by its own fate: 'To the sojourner who is within your gates you shall give it, that he may eat, or you shall sell it to a foreigner.' Where the sojourner is a foreigner living with the Jews but not having the right of citizenship: the foreigner, however, is one who had his domicile outside the borders of the Jews. The Jews, therefore, did not harm those inhabitants who did not profess Judaism, but were nevertheless pious, whom they called חסידי אומות, nor did they assist them with any benefits, but they only had such dealings with them as common necessity indicated. Otherwise, they neither approached nor spoke to them, as appears in Acts 10:28. For whatever is in the law that commands foreigners to be loved and assisted, as in Deut. 10:19, the Hebrew teachers refer that only to the proselytes: nor is there any doubt that they held in the same regard foreign men if any lived outside the Jewish borders in the same manner as those inhabitants. Moreover, whoever defiled themselves with the worship of false gods, the Jews without distinction held them as enemies, and it was not a matter of religion for them either to kill or despoil them, if they were able: which Joseph Albo admits and even defends in his disputation against the Christians, bringing forward this reason, that he who lives without the law is deservedly held to be the common enemy of all, and therefore nothing is illicit against him. Truly, therefore, Tacitus had said that the Jews had hostile hatred against all others (for all peoples had fallen away from the true God). He whom I mentioned, Joseph Albo, adds that the same pleased the philosophers. And indeed there are certain such things among the philosophers. For Democritus plainly compared any wicked men to wild beasts and serpents, and therefore he pronounced him innocent who had killed them, whether he had done it by private hand or by public command. Nor does Aristotle go far from this, who says that the art of war is by nature an art of acquisition, and with Euripides that the Greeks were born to rule over the barbarians, in which matter he is believed to have gratified Philip and Alexander beyond what was fair as they were planning war in Asia. Nor were the Jews alone such toward outsiders: but the Greeks also, as Thucydides proves from Homer: indeed, even in the law of the Romans, traces of that inhumanity exist: for they judged that what had come to them from a non-allied people became their own: nor did any treaty avail against this right, but only that in which something had been agreed upon concerning friendship: just as if nature had established no friendship among men. But the light of the arts and disciplines gradually revived the law of nature, which had been buried under depraved customs. But to return to the Hebrews, many of their writings show that the opinion was accepted among them that those who had fallen away from the worship of the true God were rightly killed and despoiled. And yet, in the law of Moses, God, by designating certain peoples to be punished by name, sufficiently shows that the same right does not exist against others, even if they are entangled in false worship, especially since He wished the maturity of the time to be of His own judgment. For although the customs of those nations were already very corrupt in the times of Abraham, yet they had not yet filled that measure which it had seemed good to divine leniency to await, as Moses teaches us in Genesis 15:16. Now, indeed, to say nothing of the Idumeans, it is certain that the Egyptians, before the departure of the Hebrews, worshipped the image of an ox: for from there the example of foul superstition flowed to the Hebrews. Nor, however, does the law permit the Hebrews to harm the Egyptians. But also the custom of better times, as an interpreter of the law, opposes the Jews: for neither the Hebrew people nor good princes ever moved war against peoples, however superstitious, unless provoked by new causes. The Jews, therefore, wrongly drew what had been established by God against specific peoples in another direction. But it will also be convenient to note that not all the precepts of the divine law were for all times. For they were established concerning landed estates, it is certain that they could not be observed in the Babylonian exile when the victor held the estates. Thus also after the supreme power was transferred to the Romans, although some traces of the old republic remained, the laws concerning declaring and waging war were nevertheless silent, because that more eminent power, which embraces in itself the right of moving arms, had passed to the Romans. There was therefore no reason why in the time of Christ the Jews should allege laws of that kind for their hatred against other nations. Those exceptions, therefore, which GOD had prescribed for certain causes being removed, the law of nature remained intact, which commends all men to men, ὠδιὸς ἐχθρὸς τῷ ἰσποδαίῳ, which Hierocles says the ancient wise men were accustomed to say. Drawing the Jews back to this, Christ commands something greater than the Jewish civil law. Therefore Tertullian not badly: The old law teaches love toward neighbors, the new toward strangers. Nor, however, did what Christ taught conflict with the law of Moses; indeed, even among Moses there existed not obscure traces of this perpetual law. For Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph had lived by that law, men born to deserve well of men; who placed every opportunity of bestowing a benefit in gain: although the love of those times was not such and so great as that which Christ commanded and showed by his own example.

This gloss seems to have been devised for the sake of the Socinian error, for which the authority of certain ancients is used as a pretext, but this cannot prejudice the truth. Grotius is certainly mistaken when he says these things are consistent with the law of Moses concerning the hatred of enemies. For where does the law command such a thing? For those things which are brought forward concerning the seven nations not being tolerated do not pertain to the moral law, with which we are occupied, but are to be referred to the peculiar judgment of God. Therefore, those things which are extraordinary do not make a rule. Grotius himself acknowledged here the peculiar judgment of God. Nor indeed do those precepts, he says, p. 123, conflict with the law of nature, for that the wicked should be punished with a just penalty does not conflict with the law of nature, but rather is very consistent with it: but just as any public power has that right over the subjects of its own empire, so does God, the supreme King of all, over kings and peoples: who preferred to command this execution of punishment, which he could have done by himself, to the Hebrew people, and that after the patience of a very long time, when the sacrilegious rites, bestial cruelty, and incestuous lust of those very nations had reached the highest point, as can be read in Lev. XVIII. 24, and is eloquently explained in the book which is called Wisdom, ch. XII and XIII. Wherefore this right came from a special sentence of God, not from any common law. Thus Grotius. And what is to be said of others? Were all the remaining peoples, who were not the neighbors of the Jews, i.e., fellow countrymen, to be hated by the Jews? This gloss certainly demands that. But Grotius does not dare to assert that. For it is too false. But the things which he brings forward from Joseph Albo concerning idolatrous Gentiles are more worthy of Jews than of Christians, to whom those things will never be able to be approved: namely, that that Jew in a disputation against Christians defends that whoever defiled themselves with the worship of false gods, the Jews deservedly held them as enemies without any distinction, and that it was no matter of religion for them either to kill or to despoil them, if they could, for which he gives this (certainly remarkable) reason, that he who lives without law is deservedly held as the common enemy of all, and therefore nothing is illicit against him. But Grotius himself acknowledges that those hatreds were illicit, page 133. But to return to the Hebrews, many of their writings show that the opinion was accepted among them that those who had fallen away from the worship of the true God were rightly killed and despoiled. And yet in the law of Moses, God, by delegating certain peoples to be punished by name, sufficiently shows that the same right does not exist against others, even if they were involved in false cults, especially since he willed the maturity of the time to be of his own judgment. For although the morals of those nations were very corrupt, already

in the times of Abraham, yet they had not yet filled the measure which it had seemed good to divine leniency to await, as Moses teaches us in Gen. XV. verse 16. Now indeed, to say nothing of the Idumeans, it is certain that the Egyptians before the exodus of the Hebrews worshipped the image of an ox: for from there the example of foul superstition flowed to the Hebrews. Nor, however, does the law permit the Hebrews to harm the Egyptians, but even the custom of better times, as an interpreter of the law, opposes the Jews: for never did either the Hebrew people or good Princes move war against peoples, however superstitious, unless provoked by new causes. The Jews therefore wrongly drew what had been established by God against defined peoples in another direction. Finally, he concludes in this way: There was therefore no reason why in the time of Christ the Jews should allege laws of that kind for their hatred against other nations. Those exceptions, therefore, which God had prescribed for certain causes being removed, the law of nature remained intact, which commends men to all men, ὐδεὶς ἐχθρὸς τῷ σπυδαίῳ, which Hierocles says the ancient wise men were accustomed to say. Drawing the Jews back to this, Christ commands something greater than the Jewish civil law. Nor, however, did what Christ taught conflict with the law of Moses; indeed, even among Moses there existed not obscure traces of this perpetual law. For Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph had lived by that law, men born to deserve well of men; who placed every opportunity of bestowing a benefit in gain, although the love of those times was not such and so great as that which Christ commanded and showed by his own example. How will this last point be proved, namely, that the love of the holy Patriarchs, who were called friends of God, was not such and so great as that of the Christians? Certainly no one either then had, or today has, as much as Christ commanded, and by his own example demonstrated, because that is devoid of every defect. To us, however, just as to all the saints, defects always adhere: no one is found who loves his neighbor with that love, in perfection of parts and degrees, which not only Christ, but the law itself demands; and Christ alone repeats this commandment of his from the law in Matt. XXII, which commands and requires: You shall love your neighbor as yourself. Furthermore, if even today GOD should order someone to execute his extraordinary judgments against some peoples, who would say that such things are contrary to this commandment of Christ? Special precepts are exceptions to a common rule rather than commandments opposed to it. The passage Deut. XX. verse 10. has been weighed in its proper place. It is not a question there of the Canaanite nations, which were devoted to destruction, but of other enemies, to whom peace was to be offered first, by divine command.

Latin:

Ἀγαπήσεις τὸν πλησίον σου] רע Hebræis & Græcis: πλησίον plerumque non simpliciter alterum significat, sed cum qui conjunctus nobis sit sanguinis, vicinitatis aut amicitiæ vinculo. Et quidem apud Moysen Levit. XIX. v. 18. quem locum hic respicit Christus, רע est is ipse qui ibidem dicitur בן עמו id est popularis. Judæi hoc arripientes ab alienigenis adeo liberalitatem suam arce- bant, ut ne communia quidem humanitatis officia illis præstarent, quale est viam monstrare comiter: quod qui non faceret is apud Athenienses diris devovebatur, ut nos Diphylus docet: ἀγνοεῖς ἐν ταῖς ἀραῖς Ὅτι ἐστιν, ὅστις μὴ φράση ὀρθὴν ὁδὸν, Ἢ πῦρ ἐνάυση, ἢ διαφθείρη ὕδωρ. Hujus generis & illa sunt quæ Cicero dicit tribuenda vel ignoto. Non prohibere aquam profluentem, pati ab igne ignem capere, consilium fidele deliberanti dare. Hæc ipsa autem non solita esse à Judæis præstari hominibus ex- traneis testatur versus Juvenalis: Non monstrare vias eadem nisi sacra colenti: Quæsitum ad fontem solos deducere verpos. Sed & Tacitus: Apud ipsos fides obstinata, misericordia in promptu, adversus omnes alios hostile odium. Sed nimi- rum hic quoque error inhumanus Judæorum ex sæpe jam indicato fonte oriebatur, quod abunde se omnes officio- rum partes implesse crederent, si iis præceptis paruissent quibus ipsorum civilis societas continebatur: At certe neque lex Judaica naturalem tollebat, neque societas il- la proprior antiquiorem generis humani societatem, ad quam ille respexit qui se κοσμοπολίτην dixit, & Floren- tinus Jurisconsultus cum à natura cognationem quandam inter homines ait institutam. Inde illud: Homo sum, humani nihil à me alienum puto. Et quæ sunt alibi in eandem sententiam. Hoc ipsum est, quod apologo Samaritani Judæo vulnerato succurrentis, quem Sacerdos & Levita præterierant, Christus docuit. Non negat Judæum Judæo esse τὸν πλησίον, arctiore nexu consanguinitatis & propriæ ipsorum legis vinculo. Sed ostendit id non obstare, quo minus communis ortus & lex ipsa naturæ omnem hominem omni homini faciat esse τὸν πλησίον, id est non alienum, sed necessitudine quadam cohærentem, ac propterea neminem esse cui non data occasione benefacere debeamus.
