Illud qui- dem fatendum est, cum victus rationem peculiarem Deus Israelitis præscripsit, hoc ipso significatum consue- tudinem admodum familiarem externarum gentium, ut- pote corruptissimarum, ipsis esse defugiendam: quod ad illorum temporum rationem erat accommodatum. Atque hinc est quod passim legimus in his libris Judæos non solitos συγχρᾶσθαι, συνεσθίειν, κολλᾶσθαι, προσέρ- χεσθαι alienigenis. Et hoc ipsum Apollonius Molo M. Tullii Ciceronis præceptor invidiose objiciebat Judæis: ὅτι μὴ παρεδέχοντο τὲς ἄλλαις προκατειλημμένως δόξαις περὶ θεῶν, μηδὲ κοινωνεῖν ἤθελον τοῖς καθ' ἑτέραν συνήθειαν βίε ζῆν προαιρουμένοις: quod Josephus non negat, sed ex- emplo Laconicæ ξενηλασίας defendere conatur. Et pas- sim apud Josephum inimici Judæis objiciunt τὸ ἄμικτον, τὸ ἀσύμβυλον, quod alio loco vocat τὴν δίαιταν ἀμιξίαν. Sed qui sapiunt, facile vident extra legis præscripta & sen- tentiam à Judæis itum, cum communia quædam officia et- iam iis debeantur quos à propioris necessitudinis vinculo aut lex arcet aut ratio. In lege Moysis Deus, ut cum Ter- tulliano loquar, quorundam fidem paulatim ad disciplinæ Christianæ nitorem, primis quibusque præceptis balbutien- tis adhuc benignitatis informabat. Quare cum illam inde- finitam dilectionem illi præstare nondum possent, neque promiscuam consuetudinem ferret ipsorum infirmitas, in tanto præsertim vitiorum atque impiarum superstitionum regno, saltem in consortes sanguinis ac religionis omnia benevolentiæ officia exhiberi Deus voluit, idque ipsum, præter communes naturæ regulas, lege promulgata san- xit. Quamdiu, ut ad Tertulliani verba redeam, intra Is- raëlem erat sacramentum, merito in solos fratres misericor- diam mandabat: (nempe in fœderis formula) At ubi Chri- sto dedit gentes hæreditatem & possessionem terminos terræ, & cœpit expungi quod dictum est per Osee: Non populus meus, populus meus, & non misericordiam consecuta, mise- ricordiam consecuta: Natio scilicet, exinde Christus in omnes legem paternæ benignitatis extendit, neminem excludens im- miseratione, sicut in vocatione.

Pessime Grotius proximum de sententia le- gis restringit ad populares. Nam vox illa רע com- munis est, & quemvis proximum notat.

que aliud fert tabula secunda ratio, cujus sum- ma tradita est his verbis: diliges proximum tuum sicut teipsum. Nam quis proximus sit, ipsa secun- dæ tabulæ præcepta de dilectione proximi docent. Num enim cum proximum vetamur occidere, so- lum prohibemur populari bona sua sumri, atque ita in aliis? Porro quod proximus etiam inimicus sit, Exod. XIII. 4. clare docemur, & quod inimicum etiam amore prosequi debeamus, à quo læsi sumus Lev. XIX. 17. Proverb. XXV. 21. monemur. Sed imprimis luculenta est Christi explicatio Luc. X. 30. Nam Judæus Samaritano non erat popularis. Neq; enim ibi legem naturæ explicat (quamvis te- mere Grotius legem naturæ legi Mosis in hisce opponat) sed versatur in exponenda lege Mosai- ca, de qua res erat cum Legisperito. Qua- propter omnino probanda est Augustini sententia Epist. LII. ad Macedon. Proximus hoc loco non sanguinis propinquitate, sed rationis societate pen- sandus est, in qua socii sunt omnes homines. Nam si pecuniæ ratio socios sunt facit, quanto magis ratio naturæ non negotiandi, sed nascendi lege communis? In quo non tantum Christianos plerosque omnes, sed etiam Rabbinos habet consentientes. Grotius autem maluit Socinianos hic sequi, imo Pharisæo- rum causam hactenus ornare, qui proximi vo- cem hic restringebant. Tertullianus, ad quem provocat Grotius, hic audiri non meretur, cum ait, Lex vetus amorem docet in proximos, nova in extraneos.

Και μισήσεις τὸν ἐχθρόν σου] Hic multi putant, fir- mum se habere argumentum, quo probent, omnia quæ Christus antiquis ait dicta, non ad Mosis legem, sed ad in- terpretationem legisperitorum referenda. Nos autem, qui cum veteribus plerisque arbitramur, Mosis verba re- spici, sed ita, ut simul refellatur prava interpretatio eo- rum, qui ex obedientia legis illius, quia propria erat Ju- dæorum, non tantum vitæ hujus commoda, sed & re- gnum cœleste sibi spondebant, neglectis naturæ & chari- tatis legibus, etiam horum verborum sensum in Mosis le- ge exstare non dubitamus. Jubentur quidem in ea lege Judæi beneficia quædam vulgaria præstare etiam inimi- cis Exod. XXIII. 4. Sed popularibus scilicet, quod col- latus locus, qui est Deuteronomii XXII. 1. apertum facit. Rursum vero Exod. XXXIV. 11. & Deut. VII. 1. vetantur Hebrei cum septem illis populis Chittæo, Girgesæo, E- morræo, Cananæo, Perizzæo, Chivæo & Jebusæo, affini- tatem jungere, fœdus facere, aut etiam eorum misereri. Habemus ergo hostes, habemus & odium, non tamen ferinum, sed certis limitibus circumscriptum. Nam his ipsis populis pacis conditiones offerri debuerunt, ut si vel- lent, exitium imminens servitute redimerent: quemad- modum recte ab Hebræis annotatum est ad locum Deut. XX. 10. Et quod post pacem repudiatam sine ulla venia jubentur internecione deleri, ad ejus ætatis homines, non etiam ad eorum posteros pertinet: nam eos in servitutem Salomo recepit, laudatissimis regni sui temporibus. I. Reg. IX. 20. His septem populis adscribi possunt Amale- citæ, in quos Hebræi jubentur habere πόλεμον ἄσπονδον, atque eorum memoriam delere funditus Exod. XVII. 16. Deut. XXV. 19. quod itidem intelligendum puto, ut aut occidione delerentur, aut deditiorum essent numero. Am- monitarum & Moabitarum paulo esse alia videtur ratio. Nam quod de illis dicitur Deut. XXIII. 6. nolim cum He- bræis quibusdam ita accipi quasi arma illis inferri possent priusquam ad pacem invitarentur. Neque enimjus ullum Hebræis Deus in illorum populorum terras concesserat, ut liquet Deuter. I. 19. Sed nec Jephthes Ammonitis bel- lum intulit, nisi post tentatas æquæ pacis vias Jud. XI. 16. & David pacem cum iis servavit usque dum atrocissimis in- juriis lacesseretur 2. Sam. X. Quare illis Deuteronomii ver- bis sola fœdera συμμαχίας vetari existimo. Videmus igi- tur quousque Hebræi illos populos odisse, aut etiam, ut Moses loquitur dicto Deuteronomii loco, abominari potue- rint. Neque vero ea præcepta cum lege naturæ pugnant: nam ut fontes justa pœna afficiantur cum jure naturæ non pugnat, quin potius ei valde est consentaneum. Sicut au- tem quælibet potestas publica in sui imperii subditos id jus habet, ita in reges ac populos summus omnium rex Deus; qui hanc pœnæ exsecutionem, quam per se facere potue- rat, malitiam Hebræos gentibus imputasse: Certe non infimi temporis patrum sententia, dum ad sacra seculo sacrilega sacra, feritasque cœdis innoxios mactata fuisse pervenerat: ut apparet ex Levit. XVIII. vers. 24. ut explicatur libro Sapientiæ cap. duodecimo & decimoquarto. Te hoc jus ex speciali Dei sententia emanaverat, non ex aliqua communi, ac propterea æterne obligatione. Unde licuit: quod ut rectius percipiatur, distinguendum est in ἀλλοφύλων genera. Aliæ enim gentes cum ad religionem Judaïsmum recipiunt, ope mercaturæ advectæ: proinde pari cum Hebræis jure erant, de exceptis iis, qui ex Ammonitis & Moabitis facti erant libertini, & honores non admittebantur. Justinus martyr dialog. ὁ περιτεμνόμενος, οὐ τῷ λαῷ προσερχόμενος, ἔστι καθάπερ ὁ Ἰουδαῖος. Erant alii qui à falsorum Deorum cultu abstinebant, & cæteris parebant quæ in concessa legum: Sive quæ posteris erant imperata, libertatemque servandi Hebræorum institutis. His quoque permissum est inter Hebræos vivere: quod ostendit aperte lex Levit. 17. 20. ubi de cadavere bestiæ suopte fato emortuæ ita præcipit Moses: Peregrino qui intra portas tuas est illud dabis, ut comedat, aut vendes extraneo. Ubi peregrinus est ἀνέφυλος cum Judæis habitans sed jus non habens civitatis: extraneus autem cui extra fines Judæorum domicilium erat. Judæi igitur incolas istos Judaïsmum non professos, sed pios tamen quos vocabant חסידי אומות non lædebant, ita nec beneficiis ullis sublevabant, sed ea tantum cum illis habebant commercia quæ communis necessitas indicabat. Alioqui eos nec accedebant nec alloquebantur, ut apparet Actor. X. 18. Nam quicquid est in lege quod peregrinos amari & sublevari jubet, ut Deut. X. 19. id Hebræorum magistri ad solos τοὺς προσηλύτους referunt: nec dubium est, quin eodem habuerint loco homines extraneos si qui extra fines Judaicos eodem quo incolæ isti more vivebant. Cæterum quicunque falsorum Deorum cultu se inquinabant, eos Judæi nullo discrimine pro hostibus habebant, neque eos aut necare aut spoliare, si qua possent, religio erat: quod fatetur atque etiam defendit Josephus Albo in disputatione adversus Christianos, hanc rationem adferens, quod qui sine lege vivat, is communis omnium hostis merito habeatur, ideoque in eum nihil sit illicitum. Vere igitur Tacitus dixerat esse Judæis adversus alios omnes (nam omnes populi à vero Deo desciverant) hostile odium. Addit is quem dixi Josephus Albo idem Philosophis placuisse. Et sane sunt quædam apud Philosophos talia. Nam Democritus plane maleficos homines quosvis feris & serpentibus comparabat, atque ideo qui eos occidisset, innocentem pronuntiabat, sive id fecisset privata manu, sive jussu publico. Neque longe hinc abit Aristoteles qui ait τὴν πολεμικὴν εἶναι φύσει κτητικὴν, & cum Euripide Græcos in id natos ut barbaris imperent, qua in re creditur Philippo & Alexandro bellum in Asiam molientibus ultra æquum gratificatus. Neque Judæi soli tales fuere in externos: sed & Græci, ut Thucydides ex Homero probat: quin & in Romanorum jure inhumanitatis istius exstant vestigia: censebant enim suum fieri quod ad se pervenisset ex populo non fœderato: nec quodvis fœdus adversus hoc jus proderat, sed id demum in quo de amicitia aliquid convenerat: plane quasi natura nullam inter homines amicitiam constituisset. Sed lux artium & disciplinarum legem naturæ sub pravis moribus sepultam paulatim resuscitavit. Verum ad Hebræos ut redeamus receptam fuisse apud ipsos sententiam, recte occidi ac spoliari eos qui à veri Dei cultu defecorant, multa ipsorum scripta ostendunt. Atqui in lege Mosis Deus certos populos nominatim puniendos delegans satis ostendit in alios quamvis falsis cultibus implicatos non idem juris esse, præsertim cum temporis maturitatem sui voluerit esse arbitrii. Quamquam enim valde corrupti erant istarum gentium mores jam Abrahami temporibus, tamen nondum eum impleverant modum, quem divinæ lenitati visum erat opperiri, ut Moses nos docet Genes. XV. vers. 16. Jam vero, ut de Idumæis taceam, Ægyptios constat ante Hebræorum exitum bovis simulacrum coluisse: nam inde exemplum fœdæ superstitionis ad Hebræos manavit. Neque tamen permittit lex Hebræos nocere Ægyptiis. Sed & meliorum temporum consuetudo legis interpres Judæis adversatur: nunquam enim aut populus Hebræus aut boni principes in populos, quantumvis superstitiosos, bellum moverunt, nisi novis causis provocati. Mendose igitur Judæi quod in populos definitos à Deo constitutum erat, aliovorsum traxere. Sed illud quoque notari convenerit, non omnia præcepta divinæ legis omnium fuisse temporum. Namque de prædiis erant constituta, ea certum est in exilio Babylonico non potuisse observari cum prædia victor obtineret. Sic etiam post translatam in Romanos summam imperii, etsi manebant aliqua veteris reipublicæ vestigia, leges tamen de bello indicendo gerendoque si- lebant, quia eminentior illa potestas, quæ armorum movendorum jus in se complectitur, ad Romanos trans- ierat. Non erat ergo quod Christi tempore Judæi leges ejus generis suo in alias gentes odio obtenderent. Sub- latis igitur illis exceptionibus, quas certis causis DEUS præscripserat, integrum manebat jus naturæ, quod ho- mines omnes hominibus commendat, ὠδιὸς ἐχθρὸς τῷ ἰσποδαίῳ veteres sapientes dicere solitos ait Hierocles. Huc Christus Judæos retrahens, præcipit aliquid majus, lege civili Judaica. Ideo non male Tertullianus: Lex vetus amorem docet in proximos, nova in extraneos. Neque ta- men quod Christus docuit cum lege Mosis pugnabat, imo & apud Mosem juris istius perpetui non obscura exsta- bant vestigia. Nam eo jure vixerant Abrahamus, Isaa- cus, Jacobus, Josephus, homines demerendis hominibus nati; qui omnem beneficii collocandi occasionem pone- bant in lucro: quamquam illorum temporum dilectio non talis ac tanta erat, quantam Christus præcepit, & exemplo suo monstravit.

Glossa hæc in gratiam Sociniani erroris excogi- tata videtur, quibus veterum quorundam autori- tas prætexitur, sed hæc veritati præjudicare non potest. Fallitur certe Grotius, dum hæc legi Mosis consentanea dicit, de odio habendis ini- micis. Nam ubi lex tale quid jubet? Quæ enim de septem populis non ferendis adducuntur, non ad legem moralem, in qua occupamur, pertinent, sed ad peculiare Dei judicium referenda sunt. Non ergo regulam faciunt, quæ extraordinaria sunt. Agnovit hic ipse Grotius Dei judicium peculiare. Neque vero ea præcepta, inquit, p. 123. cum lege naturæ pugnant, nam ut fontes justa pœna afficiantur, cum jure naturæ non pugnat, quin po- tius ei valde est consentaneum: sicut autem quali- bet potestas publica in sui imperii subditos id jus ha- bet, ita in reges ac populos summus omnium Rex Deus: qui hanc pœnæ exsequutionem, quam per se facere potuerat, maluit Hebræo populo manda- re, idque post longissimi temporis patientiam, cum jam ipsarum gentium sacrilega sacra, ferina cru- delitas, incesta libido ad summa pervenissent, ut le- gere est Lev. XVIII. 24. & facunde explicatur libro Sapientiæ, qui dicitur, cap. XII. & XIII. Qua- re hoc jus ex speciali Dei sententia venit, non ex lege aliqua communi. Hæc Grotius. Et quid de aliis dicendum! Num omnes reliqui populi, qui non erant Judæorum proximi, h. e. populares, o- dio habendi erant à Judæis? Id utique postulat hæc glossa. Sed non audet id asserere Grotius. Nimis enim falsum est. Quæ vero de gentilibus ido- lolatris è Josepho Albo affert, Judæis digniora sunt, quam Christianis, quibus nunquam illa probari poterunt: quod nempe Judæus ille disputatione ad- versus Christianos defendat, quicunque falsorum Deorum cultu se inquinabant, eos Judæos nullo discrimine merito pro hostibus habuisse, neque eos aut necare, aut spoliare, si qua possent, religio- nem fuisse ipsis, cujus hanc ille, (præclaram cer- te) rationem reddit, quod qui sine lege vivat, is communis omnium hostis merito habeatur, ideoque in eum nihil sit illicitum. Sed agnoscit Grotius ipse, illicita fuisse illa odia, pag. 133. Verum ut ad Hebræos redeamus, receptam fuisse apud ipsos sententiam, recte occidi, ac spoliari eos, qui a veri Dei cultu defecerant, multa ipsorum scripta o- stendunt. Atqui in lege Mosis Deus certos popu- los nominatim puniendos delegans, satis ostendit, in alios quamvis falsis cultibus implicatos, non idem juris esse, præsertim cum temporis maturi- tatem sui voluerit esse arbitrii. Quanquam enim valde corrupti erant istarum gentium mores, jam

Abrahami temporibus, tamen nondum eum imple- verant modum, quem divina lenitati visum erat operiri, ut Moses nos docet Genes. XV. vers. 16. Jam vero, ut de Idumæis taceam, Ægyptios con- stat ante Hebræorum exitum bovis simulachrum coluisse: nam inde exemplum fœdæ superstitionis ad Hebræos manavit. Neque tamen permittit lex Hebræos nocere Ægyptiis, sed & meliorum tempo- rum consuetudo legis interpres Judæis adversatur: nunquam enim aut populus Hebræus, aut boni Principes in populos, quantumvis superstitiosos, bellum moverunt, nisi novis causis provocati. Men- dose igitur Judæi, quod in populos definitos à Deo constitutum erat, aliovorsum traxere. Denique concludit hoc modo: Non ergo erat, quod Christi tempore Judæi leges ejus generis suo in alias gentes odio obtenderent. Sublatis igitur illis exceptionibus, quas certis causis Deus præscripserat, integrum ma- nebat jus naturæ, quod homines omnibus hominibus commendat, ὐδεὶς ἐχθρὸς τῷ σπυδαίῳ veteres sapientes dicere solitos, ait Hierocles. Huc Chri- stus Judæos retrahens, præcipit aliquid majus lege civili Judaica. Neque tamen quod Christus docuit, cum lege Mosis pugnabat, imo & apud Mosen juris istius perpetui non obscura extabant vestigia. Nam eo jure vixerant Abrahamus, Isaacus, Jacobus, Josephus, homines hominibus demerendis nati: qui omnem beneficii collocandi occasionem ponebant in lucro, quanquam illorum temporum dilectio non talis ac tanta erat, quantam Christus præcepit, & exemplo suo monstravit. Postremum hoc quo- modo probabitur, Sanctorum nempe Patriar- charum, qui amici Dei vocati sunt, dilectio- nem talem ac tantam non fuisse, qualis & quan- ta Christianorum est? Tantam certe nemo vel tunc habuit, vel hodie habet, quantam Christus præcepit, & exemplo suo monstravit, quia illa ex- pers est omnis defectus. Nobis autem, perinde ut omnibus sanctis, defectus semper adhærent: nemo reperitur, qui ea dilectione diligat, per- fectione partium & graduum, proximum, quam non Christus solum, sed lex ipsa poscit; & ex lege repetit solum Christus hoc mandatum suum Matth. XXII. quæ præcipit, & requirit: Di- liges proximum tuum sicut teipsum. De cætero, si hodieque extraordinaria judicia sua quempiam exequi jubeat DEUS adversus populos non- nullos, ecquis dixerit, Christi huic præcepto talia contrariari? Præcepta specialia exceptio- nes potius sunt regulæ communis, quam oppositæ eidem mandata. Locus Deut. XX. vers. 10. suo loco expensus est. Non ibi de gentibus Cana- næis agitur, quæ excidio devotæ erant, sed de aliis hostibus, quibus pax prius offerenda, divino jussu.

## 5:44
Vers. 44.

ἀγαπᾶτε τὺς ἐχθρὺς] He calls those same ones enemies whom he calls those who hate, who are of a hostile mind toward us: and this can be understood of whole peoples, so that what follows, those who hate, may pertain to individuals. Christ teaches that the nature of the other is not taken away by their offense, and therefore benevolence ought not to be closed to anyone. Nor indeed can there be any more glorious victory than if, when injury has begun from another, a benefit should begin from us. Plutarch in his book on the utility to be taken from enemies: It is equitable even to pass over vengeance when the opportunity is offered by an enemy. And whoever does not love the kindness of one who has sympathized with an enemy who has stumbled, and has assisted one who has begged, and has shown some zeal and readiness for the children of enemies and their household affairs when they have been in need, for him a black heart has been forged out of adamant or iron.

ἐυλογεῖτε τὺς καταρωμένυς] The discourse ascends by degrees from the effect to the words, from the words to the things about to come. But that τὸ εὐλογεῖν may differ from that which follows, προσεύχεσθαι, I would altogether think that εὐλογεῖν here is to address with kind words, in which sense also the Hebrew בָרַך is accustomed to be placed. For Paul also seems to use the word εὐλογίας in this way, Rom. XVI. 8. And κατάρα, which is directly opposed to τῇ εὐλογίᾳ, both here and Rom. XII. 14. and James III. 10. frequently has the same value as is expressed in Latin by the word maledicti. Certainly Paul also opposed εὐλογεῖν and λοιδορεῖν to each other, I. Corinth. XIV. 12. Rightly, therefore, would you translate, bless those who curse, not however from the common usage of those words, but how Plautus and Cicero speak.

Pray for those who despitefully use you, and persecute you] What Moses once did, afterwards Christ, and by his example Stephen, Paul, and others. For διώκειν and ἐπηρεάζειν differ almost as injury and contumely. What διώκειν is, we have said above. ὁ δὲ ἐπηρεάζων φαίνεται καταφρονεῖν, as Aristotle teaches us, Rhetor. II. cap. II. The old Glossary translates ἐπηρεάζειν as to calumniate. The Hebrews relate that among the institutions of the Hasideans it was to pray to God thus: Remit and forgive all who vex us. These Hasideans are the same as the Essenes to others, the most powerful seed of the Christians in Judea.

Theodorus Beza translates: Pray for those who are hostile to you; following Budaeus, who writes that Pliny, Celsus, Tranquillus, and others have said infestare for ἐπηρεάζειν. And indeed the Greek grammarians also wish for this word, derived from Ἄρης, to denote a hostile, and as it were warlike, insult. To Isaac Casaubon, however, the old interpretation, pray for those who calumniate you, is vehemently pleasing, and not without cause: for the word ἐπηρεάζειν is a forensic one, and often signifies to calumniate, as it is easy to demonstrate from the Glossary, and from Demosthenes, Thucydides, Aristotle, and other authors. Therefore the word ἐπήρεια is to the most learned Camerarius also a violent contumely: And what else is it in Peter 1. Epist. III. 16. ἐπηρεάζειν τὴν ἐν χριστῷ ἀναστροφήν, than, as the old interpreter very well says in the same place, To calumniate the good conversation in Christ? Most illustrious also Lud. de Dieu observes that ἐπηρεαζόντων ὑμᾶς is translated by the Syrian interpreter, who lead you in violence, that is, who treat you violently: and that coincides with that which the Arab has: who violently drag you. Hesychius, ἐπηρεάζει, does violence, ἐπήρεια, βία, force: as here Walaeus.

Latin:

Vers. 44.

ἀγαπᾶτε τὺς ἐχθρὺς] ἐχθρὺς vocat eosdem quos μισῦντας, qui hostili in nos sunt animo: potestque id de totis populis intelligi, ut quod sequitur μισῦντες ad singulos pertineat. Docet Christus delicto alterius non tolli naturam, & propterea benevolentiam in neminem debere claudi. Neque sane ulla potest esse præclarior victoria, quam si cum ab altero cœperit injuria, à no- bis beneficium incipiat. Plutarchus libro de utilitate ex inimicis capienda: ἐχθρῦ δὲ κὰι τὸ τιμωρίαν παραλι- πῖν ἐν καιρῷ παρασχόντι ἐπιεικές ἐστι. Τὸν δὲ κὰι πταίσαν- τι συμπαθήσαντα κὰι δεηθέντι συλλαβόμενον, κὰι παισὶν ἐχ- θρῶν κὰι οἰκείοις πράγμασιν ἐν χρείᾳ γενομένοις σπυδήν τινα κὰι προθυμίαν ἐνδειξάμενον, ὅστις ὐκ ἀγαπᾷ τῆς ἐυμενείας, ἐκεῖνῷ ἐξ ἀδάμαντος ἢ σιδήρε κεχάλκευται μέλαιναν καρ- δίαν.

ἐυλογεῖτε τὺς καταρωμένυς] Per gradus scandit oratio, ab effectu ad verba, à verbis ad res ventura. Ut autem dif- ferat τὸ εὐλογεῖν ab eo quod sequitur προσεύχεσθαι, omnino putem εὐλογεῖν hic esse benignis verbis compellare, quo sensu & Hebræum בָרַך poni solet. Nam & Paulus εὐλογίας vocem ita videtur usurpare Rom. XVI. 8. Et κατάρα quæ τῇ εὐλογίᾳ directe opponitur, tum hic tum Rom. XII. 14. & Jacob. III. 10. frequenter idem valet quod Latine male- dicti voce exprimitur. Certe Paulus quoque opposuit inter se εὐλογεῖν & λοιδορεῖν I. Corinth. XIV. 12. Recte ergo verteris, benedicite maledicentibus, non tamen ex vulga- ri usu earum vocum, sed quomodo Plautus & Cicero lo- quuntur.

Προσεύχεσθε ὑπὲρ τῶν ἐπηρεαζόντων ὑμᾶς, καὶ διωκόν- των ὑμᾶς] Quod olim Moses fecit, postea Christus, ejus- que exemplo Stephanus, Paulus, alii. Differunt enim διώκειν & ἐπηρεάζειν ferme quomodo injuria & contumelia. Quid sit διώκειν supra diximus. ὁ δὲ ἐπηρεάζων φαίνεται καταφρονεῖν ut Aristoteles nos docet Rhetor. II. cap. II. Ve- tus Glossarium ἐπηρεάζειν vertit calumniari. Narrant He- bræi inter Hasidæorum instituta fuisse ita precari Deum: Remitte & condona omnibus qui vexant nos. Hi Hasidæi iidem qui aliis Esseni, potissima sementis Christianorum in Judæa.

Theodorus Beza vertit: Orate pro iis qui vo- bis sunt infesti; sequutus Budæum, qui scribit, Pli- nium, Celsum, Tranquillum & alios dixisse infesta- re, pro ἐπηρεάζειν. Et sane Græci etiam Gram- matici hoc verbo, ab Ἄρης deducto, hostilem, ac vel- ut bellicum insultum notari volunt. Isaaco tamen Casaubono, vetus interpretatio, orate pro iis qui calumniantur vos, vehementer placet, nec sine cau- sa: nam ἐπηρεάζειν vocabulum esse forense, sæpe- que significare calumniari, ut ex Glossario, & ex Demosthene, Thucydide, Aristotele, aliisque auctori- bus facile est demonstrare. Idcirco vox ἐπήρεια do- ctissimo quoque Camerario est violenta contumelia: Et quid aliud est apud Petrum 1. Epist. III. 16. ἐ- πηρεάζειν τὴν ἐν χριστῷ ἀναστροφήν, quam, ut optime ibidem vetus interpres, Calumniari bonam in Christo conversationem? Clariss. etiam Lud. de Dieu observat ἐπηρεαζόντων ὑμᾶς, verti à Syro inter- prete, qui ducunt vos in violentia, id est, qui vio- lenter vos tractant: idque coincidit cum eo, quod Arabs habet: qui violenter trahunt vos. He- sychius, ἐπηρεάζει, vim facit, ἐπήρεια, βία, vis: ut hic Walæus.

## 5:45
Vers. 45.

that you may become sons of the Father] Sons of the Father, that is, like the Father, as we explained above in verse 5. which the comparison of the words that are within in verse 48 also shows. Whence it also happened that in certain codices for υἱοὶ was read ὅμοιοι, an interpretation received into the text, which appears from Chrysostom. Therefore that ὅπως γένησθε does not signify the end, but the connection: as if I should say to someone: show yourself a good citizen that you may imitate your father.

that he makes his sun rise upon the wicked] Seneca uses the same argument for the same matter: To the wicked, he says, the sun rises. And elsewhere: how many are unworthy of the light, and yet the day rises. Again in another place: Not even the immortal gods neglect the sacrilegious from this so poured-out kindness, which deters them: They use their nature and help all things, and among those, the very bad interpreters of their gifts. Pliny in the Panegyric: The sun and the day does not rise for one and another, but for all in common. Add also Job XXV. 2. ἀνατέλλειν however is also with Homer transitive. And otherwise the Hellenists are accustomed to use all verbs that are per se intransitive in that meaning, so that they may express the Hebrew Hiphil. And so also in Psalm CXLVIII. הַמַצְמִיחַ is translated by τῷ ἐξανατέλλοντι, so above 15. καίουσι is, they make to burn. Hierocles did not poorly express this sense concerning a good man speaking in this manner: imitating in the measures of friendship God, who hates no one of men, but embraces the good man differentially.

He rains] A most ancient custom of almost all nations to refer the effects of nature to the author of nature. Thus the old Romans used to say when Jove was thundering, Jove was lightning: nor is anything else understood when we say κατ' ὕδατος, it rains, it thunders.

upon the just and the unjust] It is therefore to be understood restrictively, what the writer of Wisdom says cap. XII. do not give to the ungodly and what he places twice do not take from the sinner: so that the sense may be, either if it is such a kind of liberality that it cannot be scattered upon many, that then the better man is preferred, or also that nothing be given to the bad, by which their malice might be more instructed. Hierocles: but in the proper order let us make the measures of friendship, embracing the good, as preserving the perfection of man both because of nature and because of judgment in every way; but the base, as offering nothing from judgment for the choice of friendship, but loving them because of common nature alone. There is a notable sentiment of Seneca on this matter.

Latin:

Vers. 45.

ὅπως γένησθε υἱοὶ τοῦ πατρὸς] Filii patris, id est, si- miles Patri, ut supra explicavimus commate 5. quod o- stendit & collatio verborum quæ intra sunt commate 48. Unde etiam factum ut in quibusdam codicibus pro υἱοὶ le- geretur ὅμοιοι, interpretamento in textum recepto, quod ex Chrysostomo apparet. Ergo illud ὅπως γένησθε, non finem, sed connexionem significat: ut si cui dicam: præ- sta te bonum civem ut patrem imiteris.

ὅτι τὸν ἥλιον αὑτοῦ ἀνατέλλει ἐπὶ τοὺς πονηροὺς] Seneca ad rem eandem eodem utitur argumento: Sceleratis, in- quiens, sol exoritur. Et alibi: quam multi indigni luce sunt, & tamen dies oritur. Rursus alio loco: Ne Deos quidem immortales ab hac tam effusa benignitate sacrilegi negligentes, quæ eorum deterrent: Vtuntur natura sua & cuncta, inter- que illa ipsos munerum suorum malos interpretes juvant. Plinius Panegyrico: Sol & dies non oritur uni & alteri, sed omnibus in commune. Adde & Jobum XXV. 2. ἀνα- τέλλειν autem etiam apud Homerum est μεταβατικόν. Et solent alioqui Hellenistæ omnia verba per se ἀμετάβατα eo significatu usurpare, ut exprimant Hebræum Hiphil. Itaque & in Psalmo CXLVIII. הַמַצְמִיחַ vertitur τῷ ἐ- ξανατέλλοντι, ita supra 15. καίουσι est, faciunt ut ardeat. Sen- sum hunc Hierocles non male expressit de viro bono in hunc modum loquens: μιμούμενος ἐν τοῖς τῆς φιλίας μέτροις τὸν Θεὸν, ὃς μισεῖ μὲν οὐδένα ἀνθρώπων, τὸν δὲ ἀγαθὸν δια- φερόντως ἀσπάζεται.

Βρέχει] Mos antiquissimus omnium prope gentium naturæ effectus referre ad naturæ auctorem. Ita Romani veteres Jove tonante, Jove fulgurante dicebant: nec aliud intelligitur cum κατ' ὕδατος dicimus, pluit, to- nat.

ἐπὶ δικαίους καὶ ἀδίκους] Restricte igitur intelligendum est, quod dicit scriptor Sapientiæ cap. XII. μὴ δῷς ἀσεβεῖ & quod bis ponit μὴ ἀντιλάβῃ ἁμαρτωλῷ: ut sensus sit, aut si tale sit liberalitatis genus quod in multos spargi nequeat, ut tum præferatur vir melior, aut etiam ne quid malis de- tur, quo instructior sit eorum malitia. Hierocles: ἐκ τά- ξει δὲ τῇ πρεπούσῃ τὰ τῆς φιλίας μέτρα ποιησώμεθα, τοὺς μὲν ἀγα- θοὺς, ὡς ἀποσώζοντας τὴν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου τελειότητα καὶ διὰ τὴν φύσιν, καὶ τὴν γνώμην παντοίως ἀσπαζόμενοι· τοὺς δὲ φαύλους, ὡς μηδὲν ἀπὸ γνώμης εἰς αἵρεσιν φιλίας ὑπέχοντας, διὰ δὲ μόνην τὴν κοινὴν φύσιν ἀγαπῶντες. Est in hanc rem notabilis Sene- cæ sententia.

## 5:46
Vers. 46.

what reward have you] Namely with God. For with men they have that reward. See what follows below c. VI.

οἱ τελῶναι] Tertullian wrongly denies that the publicans were Jews: which the example of both Matthew and Zacchaeus proves: although I think that even in Judea, as in other Roman provinces, the contractors were Roman knights. But because they could not exercise the public revenue themselves, they leased it to Jews, or at least admitted them to a share of the profit: which the Talmudic Gemara on damage given, Book I, chapter X, teaches us. How great, however, was the dishonesty of the publicans, is taught both by the Baptist's discourse to them, and by the jurists, in whose number is Ulpian: There is no one who does not know of what audacity, of what rashness the factions of the publicans are. There exists in Livy a narrative about Posthumius the publican who for many years had had no equal in fraud and avarice. Among Plutarch is this about the Greeks: they consider tax-collecting a disgrace. But the Jews execrated not only the dishonesty usually connected with profit, but the profit itself: because they believed it unworthy of a Jewish man to become an instrument of foreign servitude, which they themselves bore with great difficulty, so much so that many refused even the tributes and taxes themselves under the guise of piety, as Josephus teaches us and the history of the Gospel. For these reasons, publicans were held in clearly the same place as ἐθνικοὶ, that is, ἀλλόφυλοι, aliens from God, from which they were called by the teachers of the Hebrews ἁμαρτωλοὶ, that is, חט אים, lawless, disorderly, who had no regard for either the law or Jewish discipline. And for that reason publicans are sometimes joined with ἐθνικοῖς, sometimes with ἁμαρτωλοῖς, and specifically with ταῖς πόρναις, as can be seen in many places: and Justin, designating this very passage in his second Apology, puts πόρναι for what is here τελῶναι, because all those were held to be equally impure and infamous, and unworthy not only of sacred rites but also of common social intercourse, as will be made clear elsewhere. And it is written in the Talmudic Pandect that publicans were not even admitted to give testimony before Jewish judges. And hence I also think it happened that in the following verse, for οἱ τελῶναι, certain codices wrote οἱ ἐθνικοὶ, as if those things were worth just as much. But Christ shows very well how little virtue there is in doing good to those who deserve well, when not only the lawyers and Pharisees, whom he had said earlier must be far surpassed by us if we wished to enter into heaven, do the same, but even profane men who are unconcerned with the other life, such as the publicans were commonly thought to be. For such is their very maxim: Hate him who hates you, and love him who loves you. And whatever other things are to that standard.

Salmasius argues in Walaeus that those who are called τελῶναι here should be called toll-gatherers rather than publicans: let him be seen.

Latin:

Vers. 46.

τίνα μισθὸν ἔχετε] Nimirum apud Deum. Nam a- pud homines habent ista mercedem. Vide quæ sequuntur infra c. VI.

οἱ τελῶναι] Publicanos Judæos fuisse male negat Tertullianus: quem & Matthæi & Zacchæi exemplum e- vincit: quamquam existimo etiam in Judæa, ut in aliis pro- vinciis Romanis, mancipes fuisse equites Romanos. Sed quia illi per se exercere publicum non poterant, Judæis elo- casse, aut certe eos admisisse in partem quæstus: quod ipsum nos docet Gemara Thalmudica de damno dato libro I. cap. X. Quanta autem fuerit publicanorum improbitas, tum Baptistæ ad ipsos sermo docet, tum & Jurisconsulti, in quo- rum numero Ulpianus: Quantæ audaciæ, quantæ temeritatis sint publicanorum factiones, nemo est qui nesciat. Exstat apud Livium narratio de Posthumio publicano qui multis annis parem fraude avaritiaque neminem habuerat. Apud Plutar- chum est de Græcis: τὸ τελωνεῖν ὄνειδός ἡγοῦνται. Verum Ju- dæi non tantum improbitatem quæstui plerumque conne- xam, sed ipsum etiam quæstum exsecrabantur: nimirum quod indignum crederent Judæo homine, instrumentum fieri externæ servitutis quam ipsi ægerrime tolerabant, adeo ut multi ipsa etiam tributa & vectigalia specie pieta- tis abnuerent, ut Josephus nos docet & Evangelii historia. His de causis publicani plane eodem loco habebantur quo ἐθνικοὶ id est ἀλλόφυλοι à Deo alieni, ex quo ἁμαρτωλοὶ Hæbræorum magistris dicti חט אים hoc est παράνομοι, ἄτακτοι, qui neque legis neque disciplinæ Judaicæ ullam habebant rationem. Proptereaque publicani modo jun- guntur ἐθνικοῖς, modo ἁμαρτωλοῖς, ac nominatim ταῖς πόρ- ναις, ut multis in locis videre est: & hunc ipsum locum de- signans Justinus Apologetico secundo, pro eo quod hic est τελῶναι ponit πόρνοι, quia pariter isti omnes impuri atque intestabiles habebantur, neque sacris tantum, sed & com- muni convictu indigni, ut alibi apertum fiet. Ac ne ad testimonii quidem dictionem admissos fuisse publicanos a- pud Judæos judices in Pandecta Thalmudica perscriptum est. Atque hinc etiam factum reor, ut sequenti commate pro οἱ τελῶναι, quidem codices scriberent οἱ ἐθνικοὶ, tan- quam ista tantundem valerent. Optime autem Christus ostendit, quam exiguæ virtutis sit bene merentibus benefa- cere, quando idem faciant non modo legisperiti & Phari- sæi, quos longe superandos à nobis antea dixerat, si in cæ- lum ingredi vellemus, verum ipsi etiam profani & vitæ alterius securi homines, quales vulgo existimabantur esse publicani. Talium enim est ipsa sententia: Μισοῦντα μίσει κᾀ φιλοῦντ᾽ ὑπερφίλει. Et quæ alia sunt ad eam normam.

Salmasius disputat apud Walæum, portito- res potius dicendos esse, qui hic τελῶναι vocantur, quam publicanos: qui videatur.

## 5:47
Vers. 47.

ἀσπάσησθε τοὺς ἀδελφοὺς] The Syriac rightly interprets this as a bland greeting, such as this: how are you? is everything well? See 2 Kings IX. 17, 18, 19, 22. For that is properly what the Hebrews and Syrians say about asking after peace. But the Jews performed these duties only for their brothers, that is, the Jews, holding others unworthy to be greeted: which Christian discipline observed only against those who, having professed Christ, had afterwards defected from him, as we are taught in the Second Epistle of John, verse 10. That some codices here have φίλους is from an interpretation.

Περισσὸν] Namely, than the publicans: just as he used τὸ περισσότερον above in the comparison of the Pharisees.

Latin:

Vers. 47.

ἀσπάσησθε τοὺς ἀδελφοὺς] Recte interpretatur Syrus de blanda compellatione, qualis est ista, ut vales? re- ctene omnia? Vide 2. Reg. IX. 17. 18. 19. 22. Id enim pro- prie est quod Hebræi & Syri dicunt de pace interrogare. Hæ autem officia Judæi solis fratribus id est Judæis præ- stabant cæteros indignos habentes quos salutarent: quod Christiana disciplina adversus eos solos observavit qui Chri- stum professi postea ab eo defecerant, ut docemur Episto- la Johannis II. commate 10. Quod hic quidam codices habent φίλους ex interpretamento est.

Περισσὸν] Scilicet τῶν τελωνῶν: sicut in Pharisæorum comparatione τὸ περισσότερον supra usurpavit.

## 5:48
Vers. 48.

ἔσεσθε ὖν ὑμεῖς τέλειοι] Perhaps there was in the Hebrew of Matthew קדושים, so that the sentiment was taken from Leviticus XI. 44, XIX. 2, XX. 7, whence Peter also received it, as can be seen in his first Epistle I. 16, or תמימים, as in Deuteronomy XVIII. 12. ἅγιος and τέλειος are of very similar meaning, whence also τελειῶν is ἁγιάζειν to the Greeks and to the writer to the Hebrews. But Christ properly calls τὸ τέλειον, or holiness, here a true and sincere goodness which is in being, not in seeming. For the LXX sometimes translate תמים as τέλειος, as in Genesis VI. 9, sometimes as ἄπλαστος, as in Genesis XXV. 27. Josephus did not speak badly to this effect when dealing with Moses: our lawgiver, having shown that God possesses virtue that is by nature perfectly pure, thought that men ought to try to partake of that.

I shall explain the matter itself more correctly with the words of the most ancient writer to Diognetus than with my own: 'Whoever takes upon himself the burden of his neighbor, whoever, in that in which he is superior, is willing to benefit another who is inferior, whoever, having received from God what he has, bestows it upon those in need, becomes a God to those who receive, he is an imitator of God.' Thus this epiphonema coheres excellently with the preceding admonitions, and at the same time connects what follows. Luke confirms the same interpretation, who explains what is here 'perfect' as 'merciful,' which is 'beneficent': Thus also Justin Martyr, for what is written here as 'perfect,' put 'kind and merciful.' For thus the Hellenists use that word. Some of the philosophers also saw that the highest happiness of man is placed in the imitation of God. Plato said: 'The end of good things is to become like God as far as possible; and to become like [Him] is to become just and holy with wisdom.' And the same is the best worship of God, as the Pythagoreans said: 'You will honor God best if you make your mind like God.' Moreover, the Pythagoreans wished this imitation to be seen particularly in beneficence toward any men whatsoever. For a good man, says Hierocles, 'imitates God also in the measures of friendship, who hates no one among men, offering the good of philanthropy to the whole race.' But they err who conclude from this that the things said here by Christ are counsels, not precepts, or at least precepts peculiar to those aspiring to perfection. For the words are too clear for it to be denied that these things are commanded, and indeed to all who desire to enter into the heavenly kingdom. Thus also Paul wishes all Christians to be 'perfect' (1 Cor. 14:20, Jas. 1:4, 3:2, Col. 1:28, 4:12) and imitators of God (Eph. 5:1). Add Luke 6:36, 1 John 1:7, 3:3, 1 Pet. 1:15. But also Justin, in his dialogue with Trypho, interprets 'to become perfect' as 'to become a Christian.' Although I know that elsewhere the word 'perfect' is taken in the comparison of Christians among themselves: but here there is no place for that meaning.

A theological rule is to be observed here: the consequence does not hold from precept to effect, from right to fact, from what we ought to do to what we are able to do. And we are commanded to be perfect, just as our Father is perfect: that we ought to emulate that perfection, not that we can attain it here; that we ought to strive for true perfection—not only external, but also internal holiness—by loving not only friends but also enemies, and that we ought to contend to attain it, with the example of the heavenly Father set before us: by which the sincerity of the mind and effort is expressed, not indeed the possibility of the thing; finally, that 'as' (ὥσπερ) insinuates here only a likeness (ὁμοιότητα), not indeed an equality (ἰσότητα).

Latin:

Vers. 48.

ἔσεσθε ὖν ὑμεῖς τέλειοι] Fuerit forte in Hebræo Matthæi קדושים ut sumta sit sententia ex Levitico XI. 44. XIX. 2. XX. 7. unde etiam Petrus accepit, ut videre est priore Epist. I. 16. aut תמימים ut Deut. XVIII. 12. Valde affinis sunt significationis ἅγιος & τέλειος, unde & τελειῶν Græcis & scriptori ad Hebræos est ἁγιάζειν. Proprie autem τὸ τέλειον sive sanctitatem hic Christus vocat bonitatem ve- ram atque sinceram quæ sit ἐν τῷ εἶναι non ἐν τῷ δοκεῖν. Nam & תמים LXX. modo vertunt τέλειος ut Gen. VI. 9. mo- do ἄπλαστος ut Gen. XXV. 27. Josephus non male in hanc sententiam dixit de Mose agens: ὁ ἡμέτερος νομοθέτης ἄκραν φύσει καθαρὰν τὴν ἀρετὴν ἔχοντα τὸν θεὸν ἀποφήνας, ᾠήθη δεῖν τοὺς ἀνθρώπους ἐκείνης πειρᾶσθαι μεταλαμβάνειν.

Rem ipsam antiquissimi Scriptoris ad Diognetum verbis rectius quam meis explicabo: ὅςις τὸ τῦ πλησίον ἀναδέχε- ται βάρος, ὃς ἐν ᾧ κρείσσων ἐςὶν ἕτερον τὸν ἐλαττύμενον εὐ- εργετεῖν ἐθέλει, ὅσα παρὰ τῦ Θεῦ λαβὼν ἔχει ταῦτα τοῖς ἐπι- δεομένοις χορηγῶν, Θεὸς γίνεται τῶν λαμβανόντων, ὗτος μι- μητής ἐςι Θεῦ. Ita optime cohæret hæc ἐπιφώνημα monitis superioribus, simulque sequentia connectit. Confirmat eandem interpretationem Lucas, qui quod hic est τέλειοι exponit οἰκτίρμονες, quod est benefici: Sic & Justinus Martyr pro eo quod hic scribitur τέλειοι posuit χρησοὶ κὰι οἰκτίρμονες. Ita enim Hellenistæ eam vocem usurpant. In Dei imitatione summam hominis felicitatem esse posi- tam quidam etiam Philosophorum viderent. Plato dice- bat: τέλος τῶν ἀγαθῶν τὸ ὁμοιωθῆναι θεῷ κατὰ τὸ δυνατόν. ὁμοίωσιν δὲ, δίκαιον κὰι ὅσιον μετὰ φρονήσεως γενέσθαι. Idemque optimus est Dei cultus, ut Pythagorei dicebant: τιμήσεις τὸν θεὸν ἄρισα ἐὰν τῷ θεῷ τὴν διάνοιαν ὁμοιώσῃς. Hanc autem imitationem Pythagorei peculiariter etiam spectari volebant in beneficentia erga homines quosvis. Nam vir bonus, inquit Hierocles, μιμῆται κὰι ἐν τοῖς τῆς φιλίας μέτροις τὸν θεὸν, ὃν μισεῖ μὲν ὀδένα ἀνθρώπων, τὸ τῆς φιλανθρωπίας ἀγαθὸν κοινω τῷ γένει προτείνων. Errant autem qui hinc colligunt ea quæ in his sermonibus à Christo di- cuntur, consilia esse, non præcepta, aut certe præ- cepta peculiaria τοῖς τελειότητος ἐφιεμένοις. Verba enim apertiora sunt, quam ut negari possit præcipi hæc, & qui- dem omnibus qui intrare cupiant in regnum cœleste. I- ta & Paulus omnes Christianos vult esse τελείυς I. Co- rinth. XIV. 20. Jacob. I. 4. III. 2. Coloss. I. 28. IV. 12. & imitatores Dei Ephes. V. 1. Adde Luc. VI. 36. I. Johan. I. 7. III. 3. 1. Petr. I. 15. Sed & Justinus in dia- logo cum Tryphone τέλειον γενέσθαι ipse interpretatur Chri- stianum fieri. Quanquam scio alibi vocem τελέις Chri- stianorum inter se comparatione accipi: sed hic ei signifi- cationi locus non est.

Observanda hic Regula Theologica: à præce- pto ad effectum, à jure ad factum, ab eo quod debe- mus, ad id quod possumus, non valet consequentia. Et esse jubemur perfecti, sicut Pater noster perfectus est: quod æmulari eam perfectionem debeamus, non quod assequi eam hic possimus, quod veræ perfectioni, neque externæ tantum, sed internæ et- iam sanctitati, non amicos tantum, sed etiam inimi- cos diligendo studere, & ut ad eam adipisremus, contendere debeamus, exemplo Patris cœlestis nobis proposito: quo sinceritas animi & conatus, non vero possibilitas rei exprimitur: denique ὥ- σπερ illud similitudinem tantum, ὁμοιότητα, non vero ἰσότητα vel æqualitatem hic insinuat.

## 6:1 Argument
CHAPTER VI. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

Hypocrisy in giving alms is to be avoided, lest they be done with pomp, and in prayer, lest it be for ostentation, and with much speaking: therefore a formula of prayer is prescribed, by which, if the remission of sins is to be obtained, offenses must also be forgiven to one's neighbor: hypocrisy is also to be avoided in fasting; and likewise avarice in collecting treasures, and effort is to be given to collecting treasures in heaven, and to true simplicity: the servitude of Mammon is to be fled, and the rash care for food and clothing, which is joined with diffidence: for the sake of which matter we are referred to the birds and the flowers, and we are commanded first to seek the kingdom of God, and not to be tormented with excessive anxiety about the future.

There are two parts: I. On the flight from hypocrisy in alms, prayers, and fasts, to verse 18. II. On the flight from avarice and preposterous anxiety about food and clothing, to verse 35. The former is didactic; the latter is dissuasive.

PART I. The flight from hypocrisy in alms, prayers, and fasts.

Verse 1.

Τὴν δικαιοσύνην ὑμῶν] Since it appears that the Syriac and Arabic read it thus, and there is no lack of authority from books, I believe that what happened here is entirely what has happened elsewhere often in these books, that the other reading was born from an interpretation of a gloss. Because 'righteousness' (δικαιοσύνη) was a gloss in the sense of 'alms' (ἐλεημοσύνης), that is, a less used word, and better known to the Hellenistic Jews than to the Greeks: therefore the other word of more frequent use was added. Christ teaches here by examples of beneficence, prayer, and fasting, that those things which are done for the purpose of capturing either praise or favor cannot be approved by God. Which sentiment Philo often expressed, as he is wont, in these words in his book on Cain: 'You will find, therefore, if you examine everyone, that those who are called benefactors are selling rather than giving, and even though we think we are receiving favors, we are in truth buying them; for those who give, hunting for a reward of praise or honor, seeking a return of favor, under the fair name of a gift, are actually performing a sale,' and what follows. Thus also Abenesdra at the beginning of the Decalogue: 'If anyone,' he says, 'bestows something upon a poor man, let him not do it in the hope of obtaining glory from him, or to boast before men: for if he does that, he will consider the glory that is among men to be better than that which is from God, the giver of riches.' There is a remarkable passage to this effect in the second book of Plato's Republic, where he describes the just man as 'simple and noble, according to Aeschylus, wishing not to seem, but to be good.' For, he says, 'the seeming must be taken away; for if he shall seem to be just, there will be honors and gifts for him, because he seems to be such; it is therefore unclear whether he would be such for the sake of justice or for the sake of the gifts and honors. He must be stripped of everything except justice,' and what follows. The verses of Aeschylus to which he refers are well known, spoken indeed by the poet about Amphiaraus, but understood in Athens about Aristides: 'For he does not wish to seem the best, but to be, reaping a deep furrow through his mind, from which noble counsels sprout.' To which may be added these verses of Philemon: 'A man is just, not he who does not do wrong, but he who, being able to do wrong, does not wish to. Nor he who refrains from taking small things, but he who endures not taking great things, being able to have and to hold them without penalty; nor he who merely preserves all these things, but he who, having a guileless and genuine nature, wishes to be just and not to seem to be.' And those excellent words of Hierocles: For everything that makes the soul better, this is truly virtue and the law of philosophy. But those things which tend only toward human decorum are specious sophistries and a sketch of good things, hunting for praise from the many, and making the whole concern to be thought good only. But for most men, as that man said, the thirst for fame is greater than that for virtue. But that Christ consistently placed here the works of mercy, prayers, and fasting, He did this also not without example. For these things were everywhere accustomed to be joined as ὁμογενῆ. See Tob. XII.9. After He had purged the divine law from Pharisaic corruptions, He now further shows in what manner or with what spirit the good works prescribed in the divine law are to be done. But just as the doctrine of the Pharisees has been brought forward thus far, so those things which are handed down in the former part of this chapter are opposed to the lives of the Pharisees, because the Pharisees did all their works with this intention, that they might be seen by men, Matt. XXIII. v. 5, as the blessed Joh. Gerhard rightly observed here. But Grotius rashly emended the text here with Beza. For Beza himself confessed that most Greek codices read τὴν ἐλεεμοσύνην: nor did the Syriac or Arabic render it 'righteousness,' but the former 'alms,' the latter 'mercies,' as did the Ethiopic, as Dievius notes. Compare v. 2 & 4, concerning which what the blessed D. Joh. Ernest. Gerhard has, even against Grotius at this place, must be compared entirely. Furthermore, προσέχετε is properly 'to apply,' understand 'the mind': that is, 'attend diligently.'

Μισθὸν] The Hebrew words which often correspond to this Greek one, כרה & אתנה, have the meaning of both reward and gift indiscriminately: from which it appears all the more that it is not the force of this word to require equality between the deed and the thing. But neither does the Latin word require it. And indeed 'merces' (reward), as Varro wishes, comes from 'merendo' (earning): but 'merere' or 'mereri' (to earn or deserve)

For the ancient Latins it was to obtain. Terence: Shall I suffer her to be married to him for one day? nothing of merit has been earned. Cicero: for what would you earn to cease to be an Epicurean, and similar things. That reward which God repays to our obedience has its foundation in His own liberal and merciful promise. Otherwise, the things which we suffer here (patience, however, is the noblest part of our obedience) are not worthy of the glorious reward which is to come to us: Briefly and well Salvian: Every human work is unworthy in comparison to future glory. But more fully on these things in Luke chapter XVII.

Latin:

CAPUT VI. ARGUMENTUM ET PAR- TITIO.

Hypocrisis in dandis Eleemosynis vitanda,ne cum pompa fiant, & in oratione, ne ado- stentationem, & cum multiloquio: ideo præscripta orationis formula, qua si remis- sio peccatorum obtinenda, proximo etiam remittenda sunt delicta: Vitanda etiam in jejunio hypocrisis; nec non avaritia in colligendis thesauris, & opera danda the- sauris in cœlo colligendis, ac veræ simplici- tati: fugienda Mammonæ servitus, & cu- ra victus & amictus temeraria, & cum diffidentia conjuncta: cujus rei gratia re- mittimur ad volucres, & flores, jubemur- que imprimis quærere regnum Dei, nec de futuro nimia solicitudine angi.

PArtes sunt duæ: I. de fuga hypocriseos in Elee- mosynis, precibus, jejuniis, ad vers. 18. II. de fuga avaritiæ, & præposteræ circa victum & ami- ctum solicitudinis ad vers. 35. Prior est διδακτικὴ: posterior ἀποτρεπτικὴ.

PARS I. Fuga hypocriseos in Eleemosynis, precibus & jejuniis.

Vers. I.

Τὴν δικαιοσύνην ὑμῶν] Cum ita legisse Syrum & Ara- bem appareat, nec desit librorum auctoritas, omnino hic accidisse arbitror, quod alibi sæpe in his libris, ut alte- ra lectio ex interpretamento glossematis nata sit. Quia e- nim δικαιοσύνη in sensu ἐλεημοσύνης erat glossema, id est, vox minus usitata, & Judæis Hellenistis quam Græcis no- tior: ideo asscripta est vox altera usus frequentioris. Docet hic Christus exemplis beneficentiæ, precationis & jejunio- rum, non posse Deo probari quæ ideo fiunt ut aut laus ca- ptetur aut gratia. Quam sententiam Philo sæpe unde, ut so- let, his verbis expressit libro de Caino: εὑρήσεις τοίνυν σκο- πῶν ἅπαντας καὶ τὰς λεγομένας χαρίζεσθαι πιπράσκοντας μᾶλλον ἢ δωρεμένους, κᾂ ὣς οἰόμεθα λαμβάνειν χάριτας, πρὸς ἀ- λήθειαν ὠνουμένους· οἱ μὲν γὰρ διδόντες ἀμοιβὴν ἔπαινον ἢ τι- μὴν θηρώμενοι, ζητῶντες χάριτος ἀντίδοσιν, εὐπρεπεῖ δω- ρεᾶς ὀνόματι κυρίως πρᾶσιν ἐργάζονται, & quæ sequuntur. Sic & Abenesdra ad decalogi initium: Si quis, inquit, pauperi largiatur aliquid, ne id faciat spe gloriæ ab ipso con- sequendæ, aut ut hominibus se jactet: nam si id faciat potio- rem ducet gloriam quæ est apud homines, quam eam quæ à Deo est opum largitore. Est in hunc sensum insignis locus in secundo de Republica Platonis, ubi τὸν δίκαιον describit ἄνδρα ἁπλοῦν καὶ γενναῖον, κατ᾿ Αἰσχύλον, οὐ δοκεῖν ἀλλ᾿ εἶναι ἀγαθὸν ἐθέλοντα. Nam, inquit, ἀφαιρετέον τὸ δοκεῖν· εἰ γὰρ δόξει δίκαιος εἶναι, ἔσονται αὐτῷ τιμαὶ κᾂ δωρεαὶ, δοκοῦντι τοιούτῳ εἶναι· ἄδηλον οὖν εἴτε τοῦ δικαίου εἴτε τῶν δωρεῶν τε καὶ τιμῶν ἕνεκα τοιοῦτος εἴη. γυμνωτέος δὴ πάντων πλὴν δικαιο- σύνης, & quæ sequuntur. Æschyli versus quos respicit noti sunt, de Amphiarao quidem dicti à Poëta, at de Aristide Athenis intellecti: Οὐ γὰρ δοκεῖν ἄριστος ἀλλ᾿ εἶναι θέλει, Βαθεῖαν ἄλοκα διὰ φρενὸς καρπούμενος, Ἀφ᾽ ἧς τὰ κεδνὰ βλαστάνει βουλεύματα. Quibus addere liceat & hos Philemonis versus: Ἀνὴρ δίκαιός ἐστιν, οὐχ ὁ μὴ ἀδικῶν, Ἀλλ᾿ ὅστις ἀδικεῖν δυνάμενος μὴ βούλεται. Οὐδ᾽ ὃς τὰ μικρὰ λαμβάνειν ἀπέχεται, Ἀλλ᾿ ὃς τὰ μεγάλα καρτερεῖ μὴ λαμβάνων, Ἔχειν δυνάμενος καὶ κρατεῖν ἀζημίως, Οὐδ᾽ ὅς γε ταῦτα πάντα διατηρῶν μόνον, Ἀλλ᾿ ὅστις ἄδολον γνησίαν τ᾿ ἔχων φύσιν Εἶναι δίκαιος κ᾿ οὐ δοκεῖν εἶναι θέλει. Et illa egregia Hieroclis: Πᾶν γὰρ ὃ ἀμείνονα τὴν ψυχὴν ποιεῖ, τοῦτο ὄντως ἀρετὴ καὶ φιλοσοφίας νόμος. Τὰ δὲ μόνον πρὸς ἀνθρωπίνην εὐσχημοσύνην τείνοντα, δελοπρεπῆ ἐστι σοφί- σματα κᾂ σκιαγραφία τῶν καλῶν, τὸν παρὰ τῶν πολλῶν ἔπαι- νον θηρωμένη, καὶ τοῦ δοκεῖν μόνον αὐτὸν εἶναι ἀγαθὸν τὴν πᾶ- σαν ποιουμένη φροντίδα. At plerisque hominum, ut dice- bat ille, major famæ sitis est quam virtutis. Quod au- tem Christus. cohærenter hic posuit opera misericordiæ, preces & jejunium, fecit hoc quo que non sine exemplo.Pas- sim enim ista ut ὁμογενῆ jungi solebant. Vid. Tob. XII.9. Postquam legem divinam à Pharisaicis corruptelis reprugasset, jam porro ostendit, quo modo quove animo bona opera in lege divina præscripta sint fa- cienda. Ut autem hactenus prolata Pharisæorum do- ctrina, ita quæ in priore hujus capitis parte tradun- tur, Pharisæorum vitæ sunt opposita, quia Pharisæi omnia sua opera eo animo faciebant, ut ab homini- bus viderentur, Matth. XXIII. v. 5. ut hic recte observavit B. Joh. Gerhardus. Temere autem emendavit Grotius hic cum Beza textum. Nam τὴν ἐλεεμοσύνην legere plerosque Codices Græ- cos Beza ipse fassus est: neque justitiam reddidit Syrus aut Arabs, sed ille eleemosynam, hic mise- ricordias, uti Æthiops, notante Dievio. Conf. v.2.& 4. de quo hic omnino conferenda quæ habet B. D. Joh. Ernest. Gerhardus etiam contra Grotium ad h. l. Cæterum προσέχετε proprie est adhibere, subin- tellige animum: id est, diligenter attendite.

Μισθὸν] Voces Hebrææ quæ Græcæ huic sæpe re- spondent כרה & אתנה promiscue mercedis & doni ha- bent significationem: quo magis apparet non eam esse vim hujus vocis, ut æqualitatem inter factum & rem deside- ret. Sed neque Latina vox id exigit. Et quidem mer- ces, ut Varro vult, à merendo: at merere aut mereri

Latinis veteribus erat consequi. Terentius: Egone illam cum illo ut patiar nuptam unam diem? nil suabe meritum est. Cicero: quid enim mereas ut Epicureus esse desinas, & similia. Merces illa quam Deus rependit obe- dientiæ nostræ fundamentum habet in liberali ac miseri- cordi ipsius promissione. Alioqui non digna sunt quæ hic patimur (est autem patientia pars nobilissima obedien- tiæ nostræ) glorioso præmio quod nobis obventurum est: Breviter & bene Salvianus: Indignum est ad futuræ gloriæ comparationem omne opus humanum. Sed de his plenius ad Lucam capite XVII.

## 6:2
Vers. 2. μὴ σαλπίσῃς] Theophylact, after Chrysostom, rightly notes that this was not a custom among the Jews, but that it is a proverbial expression. For the Hebrews were accustomed to call the people together with a trumpet, as Moses teaches us: and from there the use of the trumpet reached the Tyrians, from the Tyrians to the Tyrrhenians, who themselves are also an offshoot of the Tyrians, as the trace of the name indicates, and from the Tyrrhenians to the Greeks. Moreover, to sound a trumpet is to seek a witness from the people. Basil said eloquently, as he is accustomed: there is no profit in charity being trumpeted.

But as the blessed John Gerhard rightly observes, the Pharisees, when about to distribute alms in the principal places of the city, caused a trumpet to be sounded, indeed under the pretext that the poor might be gathered from all sides, but in reality with the end that they might obtain the praise of beneficence from everyone. Nor is there any reason why we should depart here from the proper meaning: and therefore the Jesuit Conzenius, whom Grotius followed, refuted Maldonatus, but silently. Jerome, Strabus, Lyranus, and others understand it properly.

οἱ ὑποκριταὶ] Whose characters are, to speak with the poet, masked. It is an old saying: The whole world practices play-acting.

Hypocrites, that is, simulators; which word theologians have retained. It is said, however, properly of actors, sustaining some role in a play; and it agrees (as Erasmus notes) with what he had said a little before, that you may be seen, as if in a theater, which itself also resounded with trumpeters: so that this whole action could seem clearly theatrical, in which everything was done in a simulated manner, as Beza here.

ἐν ταῖς συναγωγαῖς] You may rightly translate it as in circles. For the use of the word extends very widely: nor should it be restricted here to Proseuchae, which the following also show: indeed, even now the Jews show their liberality most of all at the funerals of the dead.

ἀπέχουσι] So also in Latin we say 'let him have it for himself,' that is, let him expect nothing further. In Arrian's Epictetus: you have received everything. Plutarch in Solon: he who in his old age overlooks the good, not for the sake of children, it is clear, but led by pleasure takes a wife, he also receives his reward. This pronouncement of Christ is directly opposed to the opinion of the Hebrews who think that works of mercy which are done with God invoked, yet with the hope and regard for human praise, will have less reward with God, yet will not be without reward. But Christ teaches that they will have what they wanted, namely, empty glory and nothing besides.

Latin:

Vers. 2. μὴ σαλπίσῃς] Recte post Chrysostomum Theo- phylactus notat non moris id fuisse apud Judæos, sed locu- tionem esse παροιμιώδη. Nam tuba convocare populum Hebræi solebant, ut Moses nos docet: atque inde ad Tyrios, à Tyriis ad Tyrrhenos, qui & ipsi propago sunt Tyriorum, ut nominis vestigium indicat, à Tyrrhenis ad Græcos tu- bæ usus pervenit. Est autem σαλπίζειν populum testem quærere. Basilius facunde, dixit, ut solet: τῆς ἐυποιΐας σαλπιζομένης ὄφελος ὐδέν.

At quod recte observat B. Joh. Gerhardus Pha- risæi eleemosynas distributuri in præcipuis civita- tis locis buccina cani curabant, eo quidem prætex- tu, ut pauperes undique convocarentur, sed re- vera fine eo, ut laudem beneficentiæ apud omnes consequerentur. Neque causa est cur hic à pro- pria significatione discedamus: ideoque Maldena- tum, quem sequutus est Grotius, refutavit sed taci-, te Jesuita Conzenius. Proprie intelligunt Hierony- mus, Strabus, Lyranus, alii.

οἱ ὑποκριταὶ] Quorum sunt, ut cum Poëta loquar, mo- res personati. Vetus dictum est: Totus mundus exercet histrioniam.

Hypocritæ, id est, simulatores; quod vocabulum Theologi retinuerunt. Dicitur autem proprie de hi- strionibus, personam aliquam sustinentibus, in fabula; convenitque (ut annotat Erasmus) cum eo quod dixe- rat paulo ante, ut spectemini, tanquam in theatro scilicet, quod & ipsum tubicinibus perstrepebat: ut tota hæc actio plane histrionica videri posset, in qua simulatē cuncta agerentur, ut hic Beza.

ἐν ταῖς συναγωγαῖς] Recte transferas in circulis. Latissi- me enim patet vocis usus: neque hic restringi debet ad Prosevchas, quod & sequentia ostendunt: quin & nunc Judæi liberalitatem suam maximè ostentant in exequiis mortuorum.

ἀπέχουσι] Ita & Latine dicimus habeat sibi, id est, nihil ul- tra exspectet. Apud Arrianum Epicteto: ἀπέχεις πάν- τα. Plutarchus Solone: ὁ ἐν γάνῳ παρορῶν τὸ καλὸν ὐ τέκνων ἕνεκα δῆλόν ἐστιν, ἀλλ' ἡδονῆς ἀγόμενος γυναῖκα, τόν τε μισθὸν ἀπέχει. Directe opponitur hæc Christi enun- ciatum opinationi Hebræorum sentientium opera miseri- cordiæ quæ fiunt invocato Deo, spe tamen & respectu hu- manæ laudis, minus habitura mercedis apud Deum, ne- que tamen mercede caritura. At Christus docet habitu- ros eos quod voluerunt, inanem scilicet gloriam nec quic- quam præterea.

## 6:3
Vers. 3. μὴ γνώτω ἡ ἀρισερά συ] This also is taken from a proverb, not unlike that of the Emperor who, when asked when he would give the signal for the journey, said that he would cast off his tunic too if he thought it was aware of it. The meaning is, do good as secretly as you can.

Latin:

Vers. 3. μὴ γνώτω ἡ ἀρισερά συ] Est & hoc è proverbio sumtum, cui non dissimile illud Imperatoris, qui inter- rogatus quando signum itinerari daret, dixit se tunicam quoque abjecturum si consciam putaret. Sensus est, be- nefac quam potes occultissime.

## 6:4
Vers. 4. ὅπως ἦ συ ἡ ἐλεημοσύνη ἐν τῷ κρυπτῷ] ἦ that is γίνηται and ἐν τῷ κρυπτῷ is expressed from the Hebrew. For what the Greeks would say in one word κρύφα, the Hebrews say בלאט and so the others of the same form. Certain Greeks translate בלאט in Jud. IV. 21 as ἐν κρυφῇ.

ὁ βλέπων ἐν τῷ κρυπτῷ] The article is missing so that it might be ὁ βλέπων τὸ ἐν τῷ κρυπτῷ, which is as we have said τὸ κρύφα γινόμενον. Thus what is said below XXII, 30, ἐν ὀρανῷ, Mark explains with the article added, οἱ ἐν ὀρανῷ. Thus below X. 23, ἐν τῇ πόλει is placed for οἱ ἐν τῇ πόλει. Mark IIX. 26, ἐν τῇ κώμῃ for ὧ ἐν τῇ κώμῃ.

Latin:

Vers. 4. ὅπως ἦ συ ἡ ἐλεημοσύνη ἐν τῷ κρυπτῷ] ἦ id est γίνη- ται & ἐν τῷ κρυπτῷ expressum est ex Hebræo. Nam quod Græci uno verbo dicerent κρύφα id Hebræi dicunt בלאט atque ita cætera ejusdem formæ. Græci quidam Jud. IV. 21. בלאט vertunt ἐν κρυφῇ.

ὁ βλέπων ἐν τῷ κρυπτῷ] Deest articulus ut sit ὁ βλέπων τὸ ἐν τῷ κρυπτῷ, quod est ut diximus τὸ κρύφα γινόμενον. Sic quod infra XXII, 30. dicitur ἐν ὀρανῷ, Marcus addito ar- ticulo explicat,οἱ ἐν ὀρανῷ. Sic infra X. 23. ἐν τῇ πόλει po- situm est pro οἱ ἐν τῇ πόλει. Marc. IIX. 26. ἐν τῇ κώμῃ pro ὧ ἐν τῇ κώμῃ.

## 6:5
Vers. 5. ἐν ταῖς γωνίαις τῶν πλατειῶν] In Latin 'in the crossroads' as Cicero and others speak. In the same sense it is said 'in the streets.' Catullus:

In all the crossroads the story is bruited about everywhere.

Musaeus:

And in silence the work which one performs at the crossroads he hears.

For there used to be a gathering of the common people at the crossroads: hence the term trivial words.

The Ethiopian version translates it as 'in the corners of the streets.' For the situation among Orientals is such that neighborhoods and streets are closed off by many gates. See Ludov. de Dieu and Walæus on this passage. ἑστῶτες] The Jews used to pray standing, except in times of mourning: for then they prayed prostrate or on their knees. See Dan. IX. 20. For in Lent, which is a time dedicated to repentance, they prayed on their knees. On Sundays and at Pentecost, i.e., the entire forty days after Easter, they prayed only standing: as Tertullian teaches in 'De Corona Militis,' and the last canon of the great Council of Nicaea. And those who were performing penance for their sins were, within the appointed times, ὑποπίπτοντες (prostrate), and afterwards συνεστῶτες (standing with others). Therefore, 'station' among the ancients signifies not just any mode of prayer, but the most accepted one. Thus Mark XI. 25: 'When you stand praying.' Luke XVIII: The Pharisee stands and prays, and in Nehemiah IX. 5, the people are commanded to rise for prayers. And Genesis XVIII. 22, where in the Hebrew it is 'Abraham was standing before God,' the Chaldean translates it as 'he was praying.' Nor is the word for standing used otherwise in Jer. XV. 1, XVIII. 19, and Job XXX. 20. And thus both Jews and ancient Christians use the term 'station,' and sometimes synecdochically for the assembly of the pious. The passages are found everywhere in Hermas, Tertullian, and Cyprian; who says in his book 'On the Lord's Prayer': 'When we stand for prayer.' Verse 6. εἰς τὸ ταμιεῖόν σε] Christ is dealing here primarily with prayers that are not made in common, but for private needs. Otherwise, he does not forbid doxologies and prayers for the common good to be made openly in assemblies; indeed, he even commands it elsewhere, as below in XVIII. 19. Furthermore, all those things which are said about the inner room and closing the door are taken from common usage to denote those things which are done without noise. See Isaiah XXVI. 20. Christ is speaking here by way of comparison: so far is it from being the case that you should wish to pray in public to hunt for the glory of men in the manner of the hypocritical Pharisees, that you ought rather to close your chamber when you are about to offer your prayers. τῷ ἐν τῷ κρυπτῷ] This reading pleases me, which the Latin interpreter himself also follows below in verse 18: so that it may note that which Orpheus drew from the writings of the Hebrews, speaking thus of the one God: 'No mortal sees him, but he himself sees all.' But it is the same in Philemon: 'He who sees all and is himself unseen.' There is a passage not unlike this one in Arrian's Epictetus I. 14: 'When you close the doors and make darkness inside, remember never to say that you are alone; for you are not, but God is inside.' Verse 7. Do not babble, as the Gentiles do. We are not forbidden to continue prayer for some time, which Christ and the Apostles did, nor to repeat what we earnestly seek several times, which we see Christ likewise did, especially in that final prayer for the Apostles and believers, as did Paul: but we are forbidden to enumerate words to God, as if He measured prayers by the length and labor of that external work rather than by the inner affection of the mind, for the exciting of which—not the informing of which—words serve in prayers. The Jews, however, were less prone to this vice, as they taught that prayers ought to be concise; which exists to this day in Aben Ezra at the beginning of Ecclesiastes and in other books of theirs: and in the son of Sirach it is written: 'Do not repeat a word in your prayer.' Where 'repeating a word' is the same as 'babbling' here. Therefore Christ took the example of avoiding this custom from foreign nations, to whom it was very familiar. Hence that line in the Comedy: 'Ohe, stop now, wife, beating the gods with thanks that your daughter has been found: unless you judge them by your own nature, so that you believe they understand nothing unless the same thing is said a hundred times.' Contrary to that custom is that line of Plautus in the 'Poenulus': 'Perform the divine service in few words.' To say the same thing a hundred times is to babble. That what is said there about thanksgiving is also accustomed to be done in prayers is shown by the hymns of the Greeks, and by what Plato, Juvenal, and Persius discuss on that matter. The Hellenist Jews, however, called the 'Gentiles' τοὺς ἀλλοφύλους (those of other tribes): according to the stricter usage of that word. For although in a looser sense the Jews themselves are called 'nations' (ἔθνη) in John XI. 15, Acts X. 22, XXIV. 10, and elsewhere; it was nevertheless more accepted to call the Jews 'the people' (λαὸς) and the others 'nations' (ἔθνη), just as the former were called 'am' (עם) in Hebrew, and the latter 'goyim' (גוים). And thus they are found opposed to one another: 'the people and the nations' in Acts XXVI. 17, 23. The reason for this distinct appellation is that they called any multitude of men 'nations,' but an assembly joined by law and statutes 'the people,' which applied especially to the Jews. In which sense God, calling the profane nations to the Gospel, is said to have acquired for Himself 'a people from the nations' in Acts XV. 14. ἐν τῇ πολυλογίᾳ] That is, 'because of much speaking.' They hope, he says, that those profane nations will be heard because they weary themselves with the tedium of a long prayer. Those who are 'much-speaking' are usually the same as 'babblers,' because in order to say many things they find it necessary to repeat what has already been said. But a prayer which contains nothing except what is necessary cannot be called 'much-speaking.' Wittily, Philemon:

Consider him a long-winded speaker who says nothing of what is necessary, even if he speaks two syllables; but do not consider him long-winded who speaks well, not even if he says very many things and for a long time. Take Homer as proof of this; for he writes for us myriads of verses, but not one person has called Homer long-winded. There are also lengthy prayers in the Sacred Scriptures. Therefore, what Christ teaches here does not pertain to the prolixity of prayers, but to that superstition by which prayers are, as it were, enumerated to God, and trust or merit is placed in prolixity, as it is among the Papists. Let much speaking be absent from prayer, says Augustine, Epist. 121, ch. 10, but let not much praying be absent, if the fervent intention persists.

Latin:

Vers. 5. ἐν ταῖς γωνίαις τῶν πλατειῶν] Latinæ in compitis ut Cicero atque alii loquuntur. Eodem sensu dicitur in triviis. Catullus:

Omnibus in triviis bulgatur fabula passim.

Musæus:

ἐν δὲ σιωπῇ Ἔργον ὅπερ τελέῃ τις ἐπὶ τριόδοισιν ἀκύει.

Solebat enim plebis concursus esse in triviis: inde verba trivialia.

Æthiops vertit, in angulis platearum portæ. Ita enim se res habet apud Orientales, ut vici & plateæ multis portis claudantur. Vid. Ludov. de Dieu & eo Walæus h. l. ἑστῶτες] Stantes orabant Judæi nisi luctus tempore: tunc enim orabant proni aut in genibus. Vide Dan. IX. 20. Nam in quadragesima, quod tempus pœnitentiæ dicatum, ora- bant in genibus. Diebus Dominicis & in Pentecoste, i. e. totis quadraginta diebus post Pascha, non nisi stantes: ut docet Tertullianus de corona militis, & canon ultimus Sy- nodi magnæ Nicæensis. Et qui pœnitentiam agebant deli- ctorum intra præstituta tempora erant ὑποπίπτοντες, postea συνεστῶτες. Statio igitur apud Veteres non quemvis, sed receptissimum orandi modum significat. Ita Marc. XI. 25. ὅταν στήκητε προσευχόμενοι. Luc. XIIX. Pharisæus stans orat, & apud Nehemiam IX. 5. populus ad preces jubetur con- surgere. Et Genes. XIIX. 22. ubi in Hebræo est Abraham stabat coram Deo Chaldæus vertit orabat. Neque aliter ver- bum standi usurpatur Jer. XV. 1. XIIX. 19. & Job. XXX. 20. Atque ita vocem stationis usurpant tum Judæi tum Chri- stiani veteres, interdum & συνεκδοχικῶς pro piorum conven- tu. Loca passim obvia apud Hermiam, Tertullianum, Cypri- anum; qui libro de Oratione: Quando stamus ad Orationem. Vers. 6. εἰς τὸ ταμιεῖόν σε] Agit hic Christus maxime de precibus quæ non in commune fiunt: sed in usus peculiares. Alioqui δοξολογίας & preces pro bono communi, non vetat palam in conventibus fieri, imo alibi etiam jubet, ut infra XIIX. 19. Præterea omnia ista quæ de conclavi & obseran- do ostio dicuntur sunt desumta ex communi usu ad ea de- notanda quæ sine strepitu fiunt. Vide Esaiam XXVI. 20. Nimirum comparate hic loquitur Christus: tan- tum abest ut in publico ad aucupandam hominum gloriam orare velis Pharisæorum hypocritarum more, ut cubiculum potius claudere debeas, pre- ces tuas oblaturus. τῷ ἐν τῷ κρυπτῷ] Placet hæc lectio quam & infra com- mate 18. ipse Latinus interpres sequitur: ut id notet quod ex Hebræorum literis hausit Orpheus ita de Deo unico lo- quens: οὐδέ τις αὐτὸν Εἰσοράᾳ θνητῶν· αὐτὸς γέ δε πάντας ὁρᾶται. Sed & Philemoni idem est: Ὁ πάνθ᾽ ὁρῶν τε κἀυτὸς οὐχ᾽ ὁρώμενος. Est locus huic loco non dissimilis in Epicteto Arriani I. 14. ὅταν κλείσητε τὰς θύρας κὴ σκότος ἔνδον ποιήσητε μέμνησθε μηδέποτε λέγειν ὅτι μόνοι ἐστέ· οὐδ᾽ ἐστέ, ἀλλ᾽ ὁ θεὸς ἔνδον ἐστὶ. Vers. 7. μὴ βαττολογήσητε, ὥσπερ οἱ ἐθνικοὶ] Non veta- mur aliquandiu continuare orationem, quod fecit Christus & Apostoli, neque id quod sollicite expetimus repetere a- liquoties, quod itidem Christum fecisse videmus, præsertim in suprema illa pro Apostolis & credentibus precatione, ut & Paulum: sed prohibemur Deo verba annumerare, quasi ille preces ex prolixitate potius & labore externi istius o- peris, quam ex intimo animi affectu, cui excitando, non in- dicando in precibus verba inserviunt, metiretur. Erant au- tem huic vitio minus obnoxii Judæi, ut qui potius docerent, preces concisas esse debere; quod hodieque exstat apud AbeneSdram initio ad Ecclesiasten & in aliis ipsorum libris: & apud Sirachiden est: μὴ δευτερώσῃς λόγον ἐν προσευχῇ σου. Ubi δευτερῶν τὸν λόγον idem est, quod hic βαττολογεῖν. Ideo Christus exemplum vitandi moris ab exteris gentibus petiit, quibus id erat perquam familiare. Unde illud in Comœdia: Ohe jam desine Deos uxor gratulando obtundere, Tuam esse inventam gnatam: nisi illos tuo ex ingenio judicas, Ut nil credas intelligere nisi idem dictum est centies. Contra eum morem est illud Plauti in Pœnulo: Paucis verbis rem divinam facito. Centies idem dicere est βαττολογεῖν. Quod vero ibi de gratiarum actione dicitur, idem in precibus fieri consueffe ostendunt hymni Græcorum, & quæ in eam rem differunt Plato, Juvenalis, Persius. ἐθνικοὺς autem Judæi Hellenistæ vocabant τοὺς ἀλλοφύλους: ex strictiore usu ejus vocis. Quan- quam enim significatu laxiore etiam Judæi ἔθνη vocantur Joh. XI. 15. Act. X. 22. XXIV. 10. & alibi; receptius tamen erat ut Judæos vocarent λαὸς, cæteros ἔθνη, quomodo He- braici illi עם, isti גוים vocabantur. Atque ita op- posita inter se inveniuntur λαὸς κὴ ἔθνη Actor. XXVI. 17. 23. Causa distinctæ appellationis hæc, quod ἔθνη vocarent quamvis hominum multitudinem, λαὸν autem cœtum jure & legibus sociatum, quod in Judæos eximie comperebat. Quo sensu Deus gentes profanas ad Evangelium vocans dicitur sibi comparasse λαὸν ἐξ ἐθνῶν Act. XV. 14. ἐν τῇ πολυλογίᾳ] Id est, πολυλογίας ἕνεκα. Sperant, inquit, profanæ illæ gentes ideo se exauditum iri, quia lon- gæ orationis tædio se defatigant. Πολύλογοι autem solent indem esse βαττολόγοι, quia ut multa dicant necesse habent sæpe jam dicta repetant. At quæ nihil nisi quod opus est complectitur oratio, non potest πολύλογος dici Facete Phi- lemon:

Τὸν μὴ λέγοντα τῶν δεόντων μηδὲ ἓν Μακρὸν νόμιζε, κᾂν δύ᾽ εἴπῃ συλλαβάς· Τὸν δ' εὖ λέγοντα, μὴ νόμιζ' εἶναι μακρὸν, Μηδ' ἂν σφόδρ' εἴπῃ πολλὰ καὶ πολὺν χρόνον. Τεκμήριον δὲ τῶδε τὸν Ὅμηρον λάβε Οὗτος γὰρ ἡμῖν μυριάδας ἐπῶν γράφει, Ἀλλ' οὐδὲ εἷς Ὅμηρον εἴρηκεν μακρὸν. Habentur & in Sacris prolixæ preces. Quod ergo hic Christus docet, non pertinet ad precum pro- lixitatem, sed ad illam superstitionem, qua pre- ces quasi annumerantur Deo, & in prolixitate fi- ducia, aut meritum, ut apud Papistas sit, colloca- tur. Absit ab oratione, ait Augustinus Epist. CXXI. c. 10. multa locutio, sed non desit multa precatio, si fervens perseveret intentio.

## 6:8
Verse 8. [For your Father knows what things you have need of] The Greeks and Romans were accustomed to ask even wicked and dishonest things from their gods, with vows conceived in secret, as we are taught everywhere. Christ, however, does not look to that, but to the fact that, not content with having commended themselves and their own in general, they would express with a long circuit of words what goods they wanted to be given to them—long life, strength of body, beauty, victory, eloquence, the favor of the powerful—all of which Juvenal treats at length. But Plato says one should rather pray as a certain poet had prescribed: 'King Zeus, give us good things both when we pray for them and when we do not, but ward off terrible things even when we pray for them.' Or as the Lacedaemonians: 'that the gods give good things for good deeds,' and nothing more should be added. An ancient poet, whose verse this is, agrees with Plato: 'May there not be for me what I want, but what is beneficial.' Following whom, Juvenal, when he had said, 'The gods, easily moved, have overturned entire houses by the very efforts of those praying.' And having proven this with many examples, he finally concludes thus: If you want advice, you will allow the deities themselves to weigh what is suitable for our affairs and useful to us; for the gods will give the most appropriate things instead of pleasant ones. Man is dearer to them than to himself; we, led by the impulse of our minds and by a blind and great desire, seek marriage and the birth of a wife's child, but it is known to them what kind of boy and what kind of wife she will be. He also adds a formula for praying: One must pray that there be a sound mind in a sound body. From which I think it is sufficiently apparent how these words of Christ cohere with the preceding. Why, he says, is there need of many words to commemorate those things which pertain to the use of this life? Let it be enough to desire in a general way that which is expedient. For what is expedient for each person, men themselves for the most part do not know; but God knows. Add what is below in verse 32. From this passage Julian took what he says: 'The gods anticipate prayers,' just as that which follows in the same author, 'and having given the divine things themselves first, they were not deprived of human things,' is from that which is below in verse 33. For he was doing this, but with a vain design, to transfer the well-spoken words and deeds of Christians to the Pagans.

What that much-speaking is, Salmasius explains thus in his work on Walaeus: While they were asking God for very many things in their prayers which they deemed necessary for themselves—a chaste wife, beautiful children, riches, estates, houses, faithful friends, faithful servants, dignities, honors, and other things—since they were asking for and requiring so many things, their prayers could not be concluded briefly. Hence, 'polylogia' and 'battologia' in praying. For they were not asking for few things, nor with few words. Because of the eagerness to obtain what they were asking from God, they repeated the same things more often. Which is 'battologia,' i.e., 'tautologia.' 'Battos,' indeed, is properly one who cannot clearly speak what he wants, such as those who are called 'mogilaloi' (speech-impaired). For they often repeat one syllable with many sounds before they can complete one syllable. Hence also those who repeat the same things more often in speaking are called 'battologein'. Therefore, Christ does not want his disciples to be assimilated to the Gentiles in pouring out prayers to God, nor to imitate their 'polylogia' and 'battologia' in asking for those things which are of use to them. But that 'for he knows' is to be noted: as if he were to say: If it is not undeservedly considered a fault to want to teach a man who already knows with many words, how much more, in the presence of God, to whom all things present, past, and future are known most exactly, ought we not to be long-winded. The word 'Father' is also emphatic: for lest anyone think that, although he knows my necessity well, he must nevertheless be moved to pity with many words, Christ comes to the rescue; he is of a fatherly mind toward you, therefore there is no need for 'polylogia'.

Latin:

Vers. 8. [Οἶδε γὰρ ὁ πατὴρ ὑμῶν ὧν χρείαν ἔχετε] Solebant Græci Romanique etiam scelerata & inhonesta à Diis suis petere, votis clam conceptis, ut passim docemur. Chri- stus tamen eo non respicit, sed quod non contenti in genere se suaque commendasse, longo verborum ambitu expri- merent quæ bona sibi vellent dari, vitam longam, robur corporis, formam, victoriam, eloquentiam, gratiam poten- tum, quæ omnia late exequitur Juvenalis. At Plato potius ita orandum ait ut Poëta quidam præscripserat: Ζεῦ βασιλεῦ, τὰ μὲν ἐσθλὰ καὶ εὐχομένοις καὶ ἀνεύκτοις Ἄμμι δίδου, τὰ δὲ δεινὰ καὶ εὐχομένοις ἀπαλέξοι. Aut ut Lacedæmonii, τὰ καλὰ ἐπὶ τοῖς ἀγαθοῖς τοὺς θεοὺς δι- δόναι. nec quicquam addendum ultra. Consentit Platoni vetus Poëta cujus hic est versus: Μή μοι γένοιθ' ἃ βούλομ' ἀλλ' ἃ συμφέρει.
