Quos secutus Juvenalis cum dixisset. Evertêre domos totas operantibus ipsis Di faciles. Idque multis comprobasset exemplis, tandem ita concludit: Si consilium vis, Permittes ipsis expendere numinibus, quid Conveniat no is rebusque sit utile nostris: Nam pro jucundis aptissima quæque dabunt Di Carior est illis homo quam sibi; nos animorum Impulsu & cæca magnaque cupidine ducti Conjugium petimus, partumque uxoris, at illis Notum qui pueri qualisque futura sit uxor. Addit & formulam precandi: Orandum est, ut sit mens sana in corpore sano. Ex quibus satis apparere arbitror, quomodo hæc Christi verba cum superiorib9 cohæreant. Quid, inquit, multis ver- bis opus est ea commemorare quæ ad vitæ hujus usum per- tinent? satis sit generaliter optare, id quod expedit. Nam quid cuique expediat, plerumque ipsi homines nesciunt: at scit Deus. Adde quod infra est commate 32. Ex hoc loco sumsit Julianus quod dicit: φθάνουσιν οἱ θεοὶ τὰς εὐχὰς, ut il- lud quod apud eundem sequitur καὶ αὐτὰ πρότερον τὰ θεῖα δόντες οὐδὲ τῶν ἀνθρωπίνων ἐστέρησαν, est ex eo quod infra est commate 33. Hoc enim ille agebat, sed irrito consilio, ut Christianorum bene dicta factaque ad Paganos transferret.

Quod illud multiloquium sit, ita explicat Salma- sius apud Walæum: Dum plurima nimirum in preci- bus suis à Deo peterent quæ sibi necessaria existima- rent, castam uxorem, pulchros liberos, divitias, fundos, ædes, amicos fidos, servos fideles, dignitates, hono- res & alia, cum tam multa peterent ac requirerent, non poterant breviter concludi eorum preces. Hinc πολυλογία & βαττολογία in orando. Non enim illi pauca poscebant, nec paucis. Præ cupiditate impetran- di quæ à Deo peterent, sæpius eadem repetebant. Quæ βαττολογία est, i. e. ταυτολογία. Βάττος quidem proprie qui non potest plane eloqui quod vult, uti sunt qui dicuntur μογίλαλοι. Sæpe enim unam syllabam multis vocibus iterant, priusquam unam syllabam queant integrare. Inde & βαττολογεῖν etiam dicun- tur, qui eadem sæpius repetunt in loquendo. Non igi- tur vult assimilari gentibus in precibus Deo funden- dis Christus suos discipulos, nec eorum πολυλογίαν & βαττολογίαν imitari in iis poscendis, quæ sibi usui sunt. Notandum autem illud οἶδε γὰρ: quasi dicat: Si vitio alicui haud immerito vertitur multis verbis hominem scientem docere velle, quanto magis co- ram Deo, cui omnia præsentia, præterita & futura sunt exactissime cognita, non debemus esse multi- loqui. Vox etiam πατρὸς est emphatica: Ne quis e- nim cogitet, quamvis necessitatem meam probe cognitam habeat, multis tamen verbis ad commise- rationem flectendus est, fuccurrit Christus, pater- no erga te est animo, non ergo opus est πολυλογία.

## 6:9
Verse 9. 'Thus'] In this sense. For Christ does not command the words to be recited, which we do not read that the Apostles did, although that too can be done with profit, but to draw the matter of prayers from here. And indeed there is nothing worthy of being prayed for that cannot be rightly arranged into the parts of this formula as into its own places. For this prayer, as Tertullian speaks, is as much diffused in its meanings as it is restricted in its words. Moreover, those things which have been cited by others from the books of the Hebrews teach us that this was not so much a formula conceived by Christ in his own words, as it was a gathering into it of whatever was praiseworthy in the prayers of the Hebrews: just as he also uses proverbs known in that age in his admonitions everywhere. So far was the Lord of the Church himself from all affectation of unnecessary novelty.

That 'thus' expresses not only the sense but also the manner: he intended not only to designate the matter of what is to be asked, but also to prescribe a certain formula which should be used. For just as he had previously prohibited 'battologia' and 'polylogia' in verse 7, so he now dictates a short prayer which ought to be employed in prayers. Which is testified to both by the very structure of the prayer and by its clause with the word of sealing, 'Amen.' Add that, when the Lord was asked to hand down a form of prayer, he prescribed a formula of this kind, as Luke testifies in ch. 11:1, 2: 'When you pray, say.' But that Christ, the hypostatic wisdom of God, drew this from the prayers of the Hebrews is asserted without foundation, just as that also about the admonitions and proverbs taken from common usage. For what prayers, admonitions, and proverbs existed then is not at all clear due to the lack of ancient Hebrew books; for the books that are cited do not reach that age, and it is more likely that such things flowed from the sermons of Christ to the Jews than that they were taken by Christ from the books, traditions, and customs of the Jews. Let it suffice to have observed this once here. For that hypothesis or persuasion has betrayed itself throughout these annotations of Grotius: whence he has compiled in vain many things from the commentaries of the Rabbis (which it is certain are truly more recent), being ensnared, no doubt, by Rabbinical trifles; we know that Christ warned about avoiding blind guides, and avoiding the leaven of the Pharisees, and about fleeing their traditions, and that he gravely rebuked their rites, superstitions, and ἐντάλματα. But we do not know that Christ sought exhortations, rites, formulas, prayers, and other things of that kind from them. Moreover, in the Seder Thephilloth of the Portuguese Jews, these things analogous to our prayer occur. Our Father who art in heaven, show us grace. Likewise: Thy name, O Lord our God, be sanctified, and thy memory be glorified. Our King in heaven above, and upon the earth below. Likewise: Because thine is the kingdom, and thou shalt reign gloriously for ever and ever. Ludovicus Capellus produced them in his Spicilegium.

Although Christ here prescribes a certain form and norm of prayer, to which all others may be referred, and which is to be used for the sake of avoiding πολυλογία (much speaking), he does not, however, mean by this that we should use this formula alone and never any other. For the delivery of one formula is not the exclusion of another. In this sense Tertullian, in his book on prayer, chapter IX, calls it the discipline of praying. And Chrysostom, homily XIV on Matthew, beautifully says: He who does not pray thus, as Christ taught, is not a disciple of Christ, because the Father does not willingly hear a prayer which the Son did not dictate. For the Father recognizes the thoughts of his Son, and does not receive words which human usurpation has devised, but those which the wisdom of Christ has set forth. And Cyprian, Sermon VI on the Lord's Prayer: Let the Father recognize the words of the Son when we make a prayer. Let him who dwells within in the heart be the mouth in the voice. And since we have him as an advocate with the Father for our sins, when we as sinners ask for our offenses, Let us bring forward the words of our advocate. For since he says, that whatsoever you shall ask the Father in my name, he will give you, how much more effectively do we obtain what we ask in Christ's name, if we ask by his own prayer?

Our Father who art in heaven] See what has been said by us above.

Rightly the Blessed Gerhard the Elder: In this preface we proclaim the kindness of God, in the words, Our Father; and his immense power, in the words, who art in heaven. These are the two pillars of our confidence, by which we can be confirmed concerning being heard. Aug. lib. 2. de serm. Dom. in monte c. 1. Cyprian. serm. de Or. Dom. No one of us would dare to touch this name (Father) in prayer, unless the abundance of his dignity and goodness had permitted it. Bernh. serm. de Natali B. Mariæ: These words remind us of divine adoption, while we say, Our Father: and of earthly pilgrimage, while we add, who art in heaven, so that we may simultaneously understand that we need help, because we are pilgrims, and conceive the confidence of asking, because we are children of God. Those words excite in us the fear and love of God: they insinuate the reason why God ought to and can hear us. Hugo the Cardinal: The Lord places PATER at the beginning of his prayer, not DOMINUS, because he desires to be loved, not feared, namely with a servile fear, but only with a filial one. Moreover, the name of Father is accepted not ὑποςατικῶς (hypostatically), as Gomarus wishes in Walaeus, but Ὀσιωδῶς (essentially), because all petitions and clauses apply to all three persons of the Deity: and God the Triune is our Father by reason of creation or formation in the womb, of preservation and sustenance, of regeneration and paternal love, and of introduction into the heavenly inheritance. The Jesuits Maldonado, Barradius, and Corn. à Lapide acknowledge this meaning in this place. Moreover, God is not said to be in heaven for that reason, so that he may be understood as enclosed by heaven, but partly on account of his heavenly, divine, and omnipresent rule, which is above all things in majesty, power, rule, and operation, so that he cannot be hindered by anyone on earth in any matter, so that it may be insinuated that he presides over all created things, rules all things, and holds all things in his hand. Ps. CXIII. v. 11. Our God is in heaven, he has done whatsoever he willed. Partly on account of manifestation. Alcuin l. II. de Trinit. c. 5. Therefore God is said to dwell in the heavens, because there is a greater knowledge of that supreme Majesty and essence in the Angels, or in the holy souls of the saints, than in the saints dwelling on earth, on account of the heaviness of carnal habitation. And therefore God is said to be in heaven, not because he is not everywhere, but because he manifests the glory of his presence most of all in heaven. It is thus insinuated that the one praying ought to be carried up into heaven, as Theophylact warns, and be withdrawn from the earth, so that he may think of and seek those things which are above, that is, spiritual and eternal things, and by no means earthly or perishable ones. I add: Let us not conceive or think in our mind anything humble or earthly, much less carnal, about God, but all things heavenly and Divine.

Hallowed be thy name] The teachers of the Hebrews rightly refer the hallowing of the name of God to works of piety. See what we had above on Matt. V. 16. 2. Pet. II. 12. But the ancients well note that in these first three members pious desires are expressed rather than petitions: nor is there any need for us to assign proper and distinct meanings to each. For Luke also seems to have omitted the third, as being included in the former.

But why should we believe that only desires, and not petitions, are comprised in these three members, when Christ himself says 'pray thus' and all the petitions sound with the same reason! And who would doubt, in a prayer free from all tautology, which Christ prescribed for the sake of avoiding it, that the individual members have a proper and distinct meaning? Indeed, it is manifest that the first member concerns the highest end, which is the glory of God, the second the subordinated one, which is our salvation, and the third pertains to the means, which are comprised in the performance of the divine will. And this is the first table of the Lord's Prayer concerning eternal goods; the second is that by which we ask for those things which are necessary on account of the misery of this life of ours, both in the fourth petition concerning earthly things, and in spiritual things, by which sins and past things, the remission of which must be asked, and future things, the temptation of which must be avoided, are sought, as well as all evils from which we desire and seek liberation in the last petition. As far as Luke is concerned, some, with Rupert, think that the formula which Luke recounts was delivered on a different occasion, namely when the Lord was asked to teach a form of prayer c. XI. 2, which occasion did not exist for him here in Matthew. As we judge that this must be said entirely, so nevertheless St. Luke did not omit the third member, as Grotius conjectures, even if some Latin Codices, and perhaps even Greek ones, do not read it; for these are to be corrected from the rest, since it is contained in almost all the rest of the Greek, Syriac, Arabic, and Ethiopic ones. Bellarmine himself (the defender of the authenticity of the Vulgate version) acknowledges that it could have happened that it is in the Latin, Greek, and Syriac Codices, and is explained by Euthymius and Theophylact in their commentary on Luke. See l. 1. de bonis operibus in particular. c. V. Moreover, the name of God is hallowed, not in an absolute sense, as if God in himself and by reason of himself were hallowed by us, but in a relative sense, because God, being holy, is acknowledged as such by us. This is done in three ways: (1.) dogmatically through sound doctrine. (2.) actively through a holy life. (3.) passively through sufferings endured for the confession of the Gospel. In prayer we ought not first of all to be solicitous about ourselves, but about the glory of God, to which as to the ultimate end all things ought to be referred. The name of God is God himself, as he is named among men, i.e., acknowledged & celebrated. This name of God is sanctified, that is, held and proclaimed holy: 1. Through the conversion of infidels & heretics. 2. Through the holy conduct of the faithful. 3. Through the glorification of the divine name. Is. VIII. 13. Matt. V. 16. 1 Pet. II. 12. chap. III. 15.

Latin:

Vers. 9. ὕτως] In hunc sensum. Non enim præcipit Chri- stus verba recitari, quod nec legimus Apostolos fecisse, quanquam id quoque fieri cum fructu potest, sed materiam precum hinc promere. Et sane nihil est dignum oratu, quod non in partes hujus formulę tanquam in locos suos recte di- geri possit. Oratio enim hæc, ut Tertullianus loquitur, quan- tum substringitur verbis, tantum diffunditur sensibus. Docent autem nos ea, quæ ex Hebræorum libris ab aliis sunt citata, non tam formulam hanc à Christo suis verbis conceptam, quam in eam congestum quicquid in Hebræorum precibus erat laudabile: sicut & in admonitionibus passim utitur no- tis eo seculo proverbiis. Tam longe abfuit ipse Dominus Ecclesiæ ab omni affectatione non necessariæ novitatis.

Illud ὕτως non tantum sensum, sed etiam modum exprimit: non materiam solum petendorum desi- gnare voluit, sed formulam etiam certam præscri- bere, qua utendum sit. Nam ut βαττολογίαν, & πο- λυλογίαν antea v. 7. prohibuerat, ita brevem nunc orationem dictat, quæ adhiberi debeat in precibus. Quod tum ipsa orationis structura, tum clausula e- jusdem cum voce obsignationis Amen testatur. Adde, quod rogatus Dominus ut orationis formam traderet, hujusmodi formulam præscripserit teste Luca c. XI. 1. 2. ὅταν προσεύχησθε, λέγετε. Quod au- tem ex Hebræorum precationibus hæc depromserit Christus sapientia Dei hypostatica, citra funda- mentum asseritur, quemadmodum etiam illud de admonitionibus & proverbiis ex usu communi desum- tis. Nam quæ tunc fuerint preces, admonitiones, & proverbia, ob defectum librorum veterum Ebræo- rum minime liquet; qui enim adducuntur libri, æ- tatem illam non assequuntur, & verisimilius est, ex Christi sermonibus talia ad Judæos redundasse, quam à Christo è Judæorum libris, aut traditioni- bus, & consuetudinibus transumta esse. Quod se- mel hic observasse sufficiat. Nam passim illa hypo- thesis vel persuasio se prodidit in hisce Grotii an- notationibus: Unde multa è Rabbinorum Commen- tis (quæ vero recentiora esse constat) frustra com- pilavit, nimirum inescatus Rabbinicis næniis, mo- nuisse novimus Christum de cavendis cæcis ductori- bus, & vitando Pharisæorum fermento, de traditioni- bus eorum fugiendis, & reprehendisse graviter eo- rum ritus, superstitiones, & ἐντάλματα. Ab illis vero paræneses, ritus, formulas, preces, & id genus alia Christum petiisse, haud novimus. Cæterum in Se- der Thephilloth Judæorum Lusitanorum hæc no- stæ precationi analoga occurrunt. Pater noster qui es in cælis, fac nobis gratiam. Item: Nomen tuum Do- mine Deus noster sanctificetur, & memoria tua glori- ficetur. Rex noster in cælo desuper, & super terram in- ferne. Item: Quia tuum est regnum, & in secula secu- lorum regnabis gloriose. Produxit ea in Spicileg. Lud. Capellus.

Quamvis vero Christus hic certam precationis formam & normam, ad quam reliquæ omnes revo- cari possint, quæq; vitandæ πολυλογίας causa ad- hibenda sit, præscribat, non tamen hoc vult, ut hac unice formula, & non alia unquam utamur. Unius enim formulæ traditio, non est alterius exclusio. Hoc sensu vocat eam Tertul. l. de orat. c. IX. Orandi disciplinam. Et Chrys. hom. XIV. in Matt. pulcre. Qui non sic orat, inquit, quemadmodum docuit Christus, non est Christi discipulus, quia nec Pater libenter ex- audit orationem, quam Filius non dictavit. Cognoscit e- nim Pater Filii sui sensus, & verba nec suscipit, quæ u- surpatio humana excogitavit, sed quæ sapientia Chri- sti exposuit. Et Cypr. Serm. VI. in Orat. Dom. Agnoscat Pater Filii verba cum precem facimus. Qui habitat intus in pectore ipse sit os in voce. Et cum ipsum habeamus apud Patrem advocatum pro peccatis no- stris, quando peccatores pro delictis nostris petimus, advocati nostri verba promamus. Nam cum dicat, quia quodcunq; petieritis à Patre in nomine meo, dabit vobis, quanto efficacius impetramus, quod peti- mus in Christi nomine, si petamus ipsius oratione?

Πάτερ ἡμῶν ὁ ἐν τοῖς Ὁρανοῖς] Vide quæ supra à nobis dicta sunt.

Recte B.Gerhardus Senior : In hoc proœmio præ- dicamus Dei benignitatem, in verbis, Pater noster; & ejusdem immensam potestatem, in verbis, qui es in cœlis. Hæc sunt duo fiduciæ nostræ fulcra, quibus de exauditione confirmari possumus. Aug. lib. 2. de serm. Dom. in monte c. 1. Cyprian. serm. de Or. Dom. Hoc nominis (Patris) nemo nostrûm in oratione au- deret attingere, nisi dignationis ejus & bonitatis uber- tas id permisisset. Bernh. serm. de Natali B. Mariæ: Admonent nos hæc verba adoptionis divinæ, dum dicimus, Pater noster : & peregrinationis ter- renæ, dum addimus, qui es in cœlis, ut simul intelli- gamus, nos egere auxilio, quia peregrini sumus,& fiduciam petendi concipiamus, quia filii Dei su- mus. Excitant illa verba in nobis Dei timorem & a- more m : insinuant rationem cur Deus debeat & pos- sit nos audire. Hugo Cardinalis: Ponit Dominus in principio orationis suæ PATER, non DOMI- NUS, quod amari appetit, non timeri, scilicet ser- vili timore, sed solum filiali. Patris autem nomen accipitur non ὑποςατικῶς, ut Gomarus vult apud Walæum, sed Ὀσιωδῶς, quia omnes petitiones & clausulæ conveniunt omnibus tribus personis Dei- tatis: estq; Deus Triunus Pater noster ratione crea- tionis seu formationis in utero, conservationis & sustentationis, regenerationis & dilectionis paternæ, & introductionis in cœlestem hæreditatem. Agno- scunt hanc significationem h. l. Jesuitæ Maldona- tus, Barradius, Corn. à Lapide. Cæterum non pro- pterea Deus in cœlo esse dicitur, ut cœlo inclusus in- telligatur, sed partim ob cœleste, divinum, & omni- præsens regimen, quod supra omnia sit majestate, potentia, regimine ac operatione, ut à nemine in terra impediri ulla in re possit, ut omnibus rebus creatis præesse, omnia regere, omnia in manu sua continere, insinuetur. Ps. CXIII. v. 11. Deus noster in cœlo, omnia quæcunq; voluit fecit. Partim ob manifestationem. Alcuinus l. II. de Trinit. c. 5. Ideo dicitur Deus habitare in cœlis, quia major cognitio est in cœlis illius summæ Majestatis & essentiæ in Ange- lis, vel in sanctis animabus sanctorum, quam in ter- ra habitantibus sanctis propter gravitatem carnalis habitationis. Ideoque dicitur Deus esse in cœlo, non quod ubique non sit, sed quoniam in cœlo gloriam præsentiæ suæ maximè manifestat. Innuitur autem ita, quod orator in cœlum subrehi debeat, monente Theophylacto & à terris subtrahi, ut scilicet quæ sur- sum sunt, hoc est spiritualia & æterna cogitet & quæ- rat, nequaquam vero terrestria vel caduca. Addo: Ne quicquam humile aut terrenum, nedum car- nale de Deo mente concipiamus aut cogitemus, sed omnia cœlestia & Divina.

ἁγιασθήτω τὸ ὄνομά σε] Recte Hebræorum magistri τὸν ἁγιασμὸν τῦ ὀνόματος Θεῦ ad pietatis opera referunt. Vide quæ habuimus supra Matth. V. 16. 2. Petr. II. 12. Bene au- tè notant veteres primis his tribus membris pia desideria po- tius exprimi, quam petitiones:neque vero opus est ut singu- lis sensus proprios, atq; distinctos assignemus. Nam & Lu- cas videtur tertium omisisse, ut prioribus comprehensum.

Cur vero desideria tantum, & non petitiones tri- bus hisce membris comprehendi credamus, quum Christus ipse dicat ὕτως προσέυχεσθε & eadem ra- tione sonent omnes petitiones! Et quis ambiget, in oratione omnis ταυτολογίας experte, quam vi- tandæ illius causâ præscripsit Christus, singula membra sensum proprium, atque distinctum habe- re? imo manifestum est, primum membrum finem fummum, qui est gloria Dei, secundum fubordina- tum, qui est salus nostra, concernere, tertium ad media pertinere, quæ comprehenduntur voluntatis divinæ præstatione. Atque hæc est prima q. ora- tionis Dominicæ tabula de bonis æternis, fecunda est, qua petimus ea, quæ ob vitæ hujus nostræ mise- riam necessaria sunt, cum in terrenis petitione quarta, tum in spiritalibus, qua peccata & præteri- ta, quorum remissio petenda, & futura, quorum tentatio declinanda, nec non qua mala omnia, à quibus liberationem desideramus, & expetimus petitione ultima. Quod ad Lucam attinet, existi- mant nonnulli, cum Ruperto, diversa occasione eam formulam, quam Lucas recenset, traditam quum nempe Dominus rogaretur, ut doceret o- randi formam c. XI. 2. quæ occasio hic apud Mat- thæum ipsi non fuit. Quod uti omnino dicendum censemus, ita tamen non omisit S. Lucas mem- brum tertium, uti conjectat Grotius, etsi nonnulli Codices Latini, forte etiam Græci id non legant; hi enim è reliquis corrigendi sunt, quum in Græcis plerisque omnibus, Syriacis, Arabicis, & Æthiopicis habeatur. Agnoscit ipse Bellarminus (authentias Vulgatæ versionis defensor) fieri potuisse, ut in Lat. Codd. Græcis & Syriacis, & exponatur ab Euthy- mio & Theophyl. in comm. in Luc. vid. l. 1. de bonis operibus in particular. c. V. Cæterum nomen Dei sanctificatur, non in sensu absoluto, quasi Deus in se & ratione sui à nobis sanctificetur, sed in sensu re- lativo, quod Deus sanctus existens à nobis talis agno- scatur. Id fit tripliciter: (1.) δογματικῶς per sanam doctrinam. (2.) ἐνεργητικῶς per sanctam vitam. (3.) παθητικῶς per passiones, ob Evangelii confessionem toleratas. In precatione non debemus primum o- mnium de nobis esse solliciti, sed de gloria Dei, ad quam tanquam ad finem ultimum omnia referri de- bent. Nomen Dei est Deus ipse, ut inter homines no- minatur, h. e. agnoscitur & celebratur. Hoc no- men Dei sanctificatur, id est sanctum habetur & præ- dicatur: 1. Per infidelium & hæreticorum conversio- nem. 2. Per sanctam fidelium conversationem. 3. Per nominis divini glorificationem. Es. IIX. 13. Matth. V. 16. 1. Petr. II. 12. cap. III. 15.

## 6:10
V. 10. ἐλθέτω ἡ βασιλεία σου] I do not think this is the meaning, which some have supposed, as if we are commanded to ask that the glory of the other life may arrive as quickly as possible. For rather the ancient Christians were accustomed to pray for the delay of the end. Wherefore it is more the case that this pertains to the propagation of that doctrine, which then was sounding only through Judea, through all lands: See Luke IX. 77.

Not only the propagation of doctrine through all lands, but whatever pertains to the increase of the kingdom of God, & the attainment of our salvation, is comprehended in this petition, so that primarily the kingdom of God may also reach us. For if the propagation of that doctrine, which then was sounding only through Judea, were signified only to other lands, that prayer was suitable only for that time. But Christ prescribed a form which might be suitable for every time. Well, however, as Lyranus notes, it is said ADVENIAT (let it come), because we cannot come to him through grace & glory, unless he himself first comes to us.

Γενηθήτω τὸ θέλημά σου.] In this saying we admonish ourselves to endurance, says Tertullian: Nor is this manner of speaking used otherwise below XXVI. 42. Luke XXI. 42. Acts XXII. 14. But the comparison which follows seems to pertain rather to divine commands, not excluding, however, the sense I mentioned. For this also is commanded in the meantime, that whatever divine providence shall have determined concerning us, we may bear with an equal mind: to which pertains that well-understood saying of Cleanthes: Ἄγε δή με ὦ Ζεῦ κᾀ σύ γ᾽ ἡ πεπρωμένη Ὅποι ποθ᾽ ὑμῖν εἰμι διατεταγμένος. Ὡς ἕψομαί γ᾽ ἄοκνος· ἦν δὲ γε μὴ θέλω, Κακὸς γενόμενος, ὀὐδὲν ἧττον ἕψομαι.

And an old epigram: If that which carries you carries you, carry and be carried; but if you are indignant and grieve yourself, that which carries you carries you. From the maxim of Pythagoras which is in Iamblichus: this is observant and sensible, not to resist and be indignant at divine providence. See if you like Hierocles on those lines of the golden poem: Whatever pains mortals have by divine fortunes, whatever share you have, bear it gently, and do not be indignant. Which sentiment Clement of Alexandria explains in a very Christian manner in this way: this would be perfect peacemaking, keeping the peaceful state unchanged in everything that happens, calling the administration holy and good, established in the knowledge of divine and human things, through which he considers the contrarieties in the world to be the most beautiful harmony of creation. ἐν ἐρατῷ κ᾽ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς] Hence κὶ has the force of a conclusion. Plutarch similarly: for as bodies appear larger in fog, so do matters appear larger through anger. You could interpret that 'in heaven' as referring to the course of the stars. 'In heaven nothing happens by chance,' says Aristotle. Thus also Lucan says that the mind of a wise man is so disposed: ---Just as the celestial stars are always rolled along, unshaken in their own motion. But it is more probable that Christ was thinking of the Angels, and that the place in Psalm 103:21 was looked to by him: Praise the Lord, all his hosts, ministers who do his will. In the Constitutions of Clement, book II, ch. 56: 'Just as all the heavenly natures of the incorporeal powers praise God in harmony, so also may all the people of the earth in one body and with one disposition praise the only God.'

This petition is rightly understood concerning the will of God, which we are bound to do, about which see John 6:40, Rom. 12:2, 1 Thess. 4:3, Heb. 10:36; yet it should not be denied that the will of divine good pleasure is simultaneously included, so that we may indeed pray that God may do whatever pleases Him, which He knows will contribute to the sanctification of His name and the coming of His kingdom, and at the same time that He may grant that we strive to do the divine will and what He has prescribed for us to do, so that the will of the Lord may be done everywhere, on earth just as in heaven, by men as by the Holy Angels. Blessed Luther has encompassed this beautifully and forcefully in his Small Catechism: God's good and gracious will is done also without our prayer, but we ask in this petition that it may be done among us also. In what way is that? When God breaks and hinders every evil counsel, will, and effort that stands in the way of our sanctifying the name of God and of His kingdom being able to come to us, such as the will of the devil, the world, and our own flesh. Then when He strengthens and preserves us firmly in His word and faith, until the end of our life. This is His gracious and good will. But the gloss of Grotius on 'in heaven' is new and unheard of, by which he thinks it can be understood as referring to the course of the stars: because, namely, 'in heaven nothing happens by chance,' as Aristotle says. Which interpretation needs no refutation. For the prayer speaks of those things which are done by will, not by the necessity of nature. Therefore he adds: But it is more probable that Christ was thinking of the Angels, and that the place in Psalm 103:21 was looked to by him: Praise the Lord, all his hosts, ministers who do his will. In the Constitutions of Clement, book II, ch. 56. 'Just as all the heavenly natures of the incorporeal powers praise God in harmony, so also may all the people of the earth in one body and with one disposition praise the only God.' Nor, however, are only the angels understood, but also the other blessed inhabitants of heaven, the spirits of the perfect saints (Heb. 12:23), by whom the will of God is also fulfilled. The author of the Opus Imperfectum rightly says on this passage: He commands those living here to have a common conversation with the inhabitants of heaven, and before that heavenly dwelling is provided, he wants heaven to be made from earth in a certain way. Scultetus, in his work against Walaeus, refutes Beza here: The learned Beza explains these words thus: let it be done, which you decree to be done. He seems to take the word 'will' for that hidden and secret decree of God concerning us being introduced into the kingdom of God through many tribulations; but that word, as everywhere else (Matt. 7:21, John 9:31, 1 Thess. 4:3

Rom. 12:2, is also used in this place without doubt for the will of God revealed in the Decalogue, the norm, namely, of all justice and holiness, which God demands from us who have been adopted into the number of His children, and which He finds pleasing. There, God's action and disposition is looked at; here, ours, that is, the action and obedience of the faithful elect. He uses the imperative 'genēthētō' instead of the optative 'genētheiē', just as 'elthetō' instead of 'elthoi': because, as Basil notes on Psalm 44, this is the custom of Scripture, to figure in this way those things which are wished for. We do not pray here, says St. Cyprian, that God may do what He wills to do, but that we may do what He wills us to do.

Latin:

V. 10. ἐλθέτω ἡ βασιλεία σου] Non puto eum esse sen- sum, quem nonnulli arbitrati sunt, quasi rogare jubeamur, ut gloria vitæ alterius quam celerrime adveniat. Potius enim orare folebant Christiani Veteres pro mora finis. Quare magis est ut hoc pertineat ad ejus doctrinæ, quæ tum Ju- dæam duntaxat personabat, propagationem per omnes ter- ras: Vide Luc. IX. 77.

Non solum propagatio doctrinæ per omnes ter- ras, sed quicquid ad regni Dei incrementum, & sa- lutis nostræ consecutionem pertinet, hac petitione comprehenditur, ut imprimis ad nos etiam regnum Dei perveniat. Nam si propagatio ejus doctrinæ, quæ tum Judæam duntaxat personabat, ad alias terras solum significaretur, tempori isti solum con- veniebat ea precatio. At Christus præscripsit for- mam, quæ omni tempori conveniat. Bene au- tem, notante Lyrano dicitur ADVENIAT, quod non possimus ad eum venire per gratiam, & gloriam, nisi ipse primum veniat ad nos.

Γενηθήτω τὸ θέλημά σου.] In hoc dicto ad sufferentiam nos ipsos admonemus, inquit Tertullianus: Neque aliter hoc loquendi genus usurpatur infra XXVI. 42. Luc. XXI. 42. Act. XXII. 14. Sed quæ sequitur comparatio videtur ad imperia potius divina pertinere, non excluso tamen eo, quem dixi, sensu. Nam & hoc interimperata est, ut quic- quid de nobis statuerit divina providentia æquo feramus a- nimo: quo pertinet Cleanthis illud sane intellectum: Ἄγε δή με ὦ Ζεῦ κᾀ σύ γ᾽ ἡ πεπρωμένη Ὅποι ποθ᾽ ὑμῖν εἰμι διατεταγμένος. Ὡς ἕψομαί γ᾽ ἄοκνος· ἦν δὲ γε μὴ θέλω, Κακὸς γενόμενος, ὀὐδὲν ἧττον ἕψομαι.

Et vetus Epigramma: Εἰ τὸ φέρον σε φέρει, φέρε καὶ φέρου· εἰ δ᾽ ἀγανακτεῖς Καὶ σαυτὸν λυπεῖς, καὶ τὸ φέρον σε φέρει. Ex Pythagoræ scito quod apud Jamblichum: ἐπισκοπητικὸν τοῦτο καὶ ἔνγνωμον, τὸ μὴ ἀντιτείνειν καὶ προσαγανακτεῖν τῇ θείᾳ προνοίᾳ. Vide si lubet Hieroclem ad illa aurei carminis: Ὅσσα τε δαιμονίῃσι τύχαις βροτοὶ ἄλγε᾽ ἔχουσιν, Ἣν ἂν μοῖραν ἔχῃς πρᾴως φέρε, μηδ᾽ ἀγανάκτει. Quam sententiam Christiane admodum hunc in modum explicat Clemens Alexandrinus: αὕτη δ᾽ ἂν εἴη τελεία εἰρηνο- ποίησις, ἡ ἐπὶ παντὶ τῷ συμβαίνοντι ἄτρεπτον φυλάσσουσα τὸ εἰρηνικὸν, ἁγίαν τε καὶ καλὴν τὴν διοίκησιν λέγουσα, ἐν ἐπιστήμῃ θείων καὶ ἀνθρωπίνων πραγμάτων καθεστῶσα, δι᾽ ἧς τὰς ἐν τῷ κόσ- μῳ ἐναντιότητας, ἁρμονίαν κτίσεως καλλίστην λογίζεται. ἐν ἐρατῷ κ᾽ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς] Hinc κὶ vim habet ἀποδόσεως. Plu- tarchus similiter: ὡς γὰρ οἱ ὀμίχλης τὰ σώματα κᾀ δι᾽ ὀργῆς τὰ πράγματα μείζονα φαίνεται. Illud ἐν ὐρανῷ possis de a- strorum cursu interpretari. ἐν ὐρανῷ ὐδὲν ἀπὸ ἀυτομάτε γίνεται inquit Aristoteles. Sic & Lucanus sapientis ani- mum ita se habere ait: ---Sicut cælestia semper Inconcussa suo volvuntur sidera motu. Sed probabilius est de Angelis sensisse Christum, & specta- tum ab eo Psalmi locum CIII. 21. Laudate Dominum omnes exercitus ejus, ministri facientes voluntatem ejus. In Clemen- tis constitutionibus lib. II. c. 56. ὅπως ὡς αἱ ἐπυράνιοι Φύσεις τῶν ἀσωμάτων δυνάμεων πᾶσαι δοξάζεσι τὸν Θεὸν συμφώνως, ὕτως κὶ τῆς γῆς πάντες οἱ ἄνθρωποι ἐν ἑνὶ σόματι κὶ μιᾷ διαθέσε δοξάσωσι τὸν μόνον Θεὸν.

Recte de voluntate Dei, quam nos facere tene- mur, hæc petitio intelligitur, de qua Job. VI. 40. Rom. XII. 2. 1. Thess. IV 3. Ebr. X. 36. neque tamen negari debet, voluntatem beneplaciti divini simul comprehendi, ut nempe petamus, faciat Deus quic- quid ipsi placuerit, quod ad nominis sui sanctificatio- nem, & regni sui adventum facere noverit, simul- que præstet, ut nos voluntatem divinam, & quæ no- bis facienda præscripsit, facere annitamur, ut un- diquaque fiat voluntas Domini, in terra pariter, ut in cælis, ab hominibus, uti à S. Angelis. Pul- cre & nervose hæc complexus est B. Lutherus in minori Catechesi: Bona ac misericors Dei voluntas fit quoque sine nostra oratione, sed rogamus hac peti- tione ut etiam apud nos fiat. Qua ratione sit istud? Cum Deus frangit ac impedit omne malum consilium, voluntatem, & conatus, qui obstant, quo minus nomen Dei sanctificemus, regnum ejus ad nos pervenire possit, ut est diaboli, mundi, & carnis nostræ voluntas. Deinde cum confortat & conservat nos firmiter in suo verbo ac fide, usque ad finem vitæ nostræ. Hæc est miseri- cors, ac bona ipsius voluntas. Nova autem & inaudita est glossa Grotii τῶ ἐν ὐρανῷ, qua ea de astrorum cursu intelligi posse arbitratur: quia scil. ἐν ὐρανῷ ὐ- δὲν ἀπὸ ἀυτομάτε γίνεται, dicente Aristotele. Quæ interpretatio nulla indiget confutatione. Nam de iis, quæ voluntate, non quæ necessitate naturæ fiunt, oratio sonat. Ideo addit: Sed probabilius est de Ange- lis sensisse Christum, & spectatum ab eo Psalmi locum CIII. 21. Laudate Dominum omnes exercitus ejus, ministri facientes voluntatem ejus. In Clementis consti- tutionibus lib. II. c. 56. ὅπως ὡς αἱ ἐπυράνιοι Φύσεις τ̄ ἀσωμάτων δυνάμεων πᾶσαι δοξάζεσι τὸν Θεὸν συμφώνως, ὕτως & τ̄ γῆς πάντες οἱ ἄνθρωποι ἐν ἑνὶ σόματι, κὶ μιᾷ διαθέσᾒ δοξάσωσι τ̄ μόνον Θεὸν. Neque tamen angeli solum intelliguntur, sed etiam cæteri beati cælytes, Spiritus Sanctorum perfecti Ebr. XII. 23. à quibus etiam impletur voluntas Dei. Re- cte Autor operis imperf. in h. l. Jubet hic degentes conversationem cum cæli habitatoribus communem, & antequam superna illa præstetur habitatio, cælum quodammodo vult fieri è terra. Bezam hic refel- lit Scultetus apud Walæum: Hæc verba Cl. Beza ita exponit: fiat, quod tu decernis ut fiat. Vide- tur voluntatis vocem accipere pro recondito illo & ar- cano Dei decreto, de nobis per multas tribulationes in regnum Dei introducendis; Verum vox ista, ut passim alibi (Matth. VII. 21. Joh. IX. 31. 1. Thess. IV. 3.

Rom. XII. 2. ita & hoc loco usurpatur proculdubio pro voluntate Dei decalogo revelata, norma scilicet omnis justitiæ & sanctitatis, quam Deus à nobis in filiorum numerum adoptatis postulat & gratam ha- bet. Illic spectatur Dei actio & dispositio, hic nostra, hoc est fidelium electorum actio & obsequium. Uti- tur autem imperativo γενηθήτω pro optativo γενη- θείη, sicut ἐλθέτω ἀντὶ τῶν ἔλθοι: quia, ut Basilius in Ps. XLIV. annotat, hic mos est Scripturæ, hoc mo- do figurare ea quæ optantur. Non petimus hic, in- quit S. Cyprianus, ut Deus faciat, quod vult facere, sed ut nos faciamus, quod ipse nos vult facere.

## 6:11
Verse 11. 'Our daily bread' [ton arton hēmōn ton epiousion] 'Periousios' is far different, which the LXX use to signify 'that which is exceptional', from 'epiousios', which in that sense is neither found, nor can it be reduced to the origin of that meaning. But if the writer had wished to say 'supersubstantial', he would have had to say 'hyperousiōdē'. For 'epi' in compounds does not have that meaning. Add that 'epi' in composition before the vowel letter 'i' is accustomed to lose it. And so the Platonists call 'epiousiōdes' that which is added to substance, which meaning, moreover, has no place here. Finally, the laws of grammar do not allow 'epiousios' to be derived from anywhere else than from the noun 'epiousia', which signifies the following day, as Ambrose warned. Although this ought indeed to have sufficed by itself, there is added, however, an argument of the greatest weight from the testimony of Jerome, who writes that he consulted the Hebrew codex of the Gospel which the Nazarenes, that is, the Christians ἑβραΐζονtes, used, and that he found there מחר, which is 'tomorrow'. Wherefore περὶ τῆς λέξεως one ought not to inquire further; it only remains that we see what the meaning of τῆς λέξεως is. For it seems strange, since Christ forbids us to be anxious for the morrow, that it is nevertheless commanded here by him that we pray for tomorrow's bread to be given to us. But it must be known, as has also been noted by Jerome, that מחר does not strictly signify to the Hebrews the day immediately following, but whatever future time is imminent, as in Exodus 13:14, where the LXX have μετὰ ταῦτα, Ex. 19:10, Josh. 4:6, Prov. 27:1, in which places the LXX preserved the word ἄυριον, in which sense Luke also uses ἄυριον in 13:33. Just as also the exact time is called by the Hebrews תמול, that is, yesterday. Therefore ἐπιοῦσα is that whole span of life which remains for us to traverse, unknown to us, known to God: ἐπιούσιον is that which suffices for that span. Many men, uncertain how long they are to live, use the expectation of old age as a pretext for avarice: and often, the less of the journey there is, the more of the travel-allowance is sought. Christ wants us to entrust this care to God, so that He may supply us with as much food as remains of our life: yet not in such a way that we ask for all of it to be presented to us. For it is a very ignoble mind that does not trust God unless under a pledge. Just as, therefore, those who are under the power of a head of a household, both good and wise and rich, will not demand that they be allowed to store up food for many years in their storerooms, but will be content with a daily ration: so also Christ wishes both diffidence and greed to be absent from our prayers. Therefore, σήμερον is placed here for that which would be said in a fuller Hebraism as σήμερον σήμερον. That is, with Luke as interpreter, τὸ καθ' ἡμέραν: whence in Greek καθημερόβιοι are called in Latin 'living for the day', who are content with present things and are not anxious for the long term. Thus also Alexis and Antiphanes said τροφὴν καθ' ἡμέραν. Which the Greek interpreters in Dan. 1:5 [rendered as] τὸ τῆς ἡμέρας καθ' ἡμέραν. Thus the precept of Christ which is below in verse 34 agrees very well with this prayer. And it signifies to us openly the same thing that was once foreshadowed by the daily distribution of Manna, which history Philo explains in such a way that he acts as an interpreter for these words of Christ: 'Good is that which is seasonable and measured, and not to take more than we need is greed; let the soul gather this, that of the day for the day, so that it may show itself not as a guardian of goods, but God as the bountiful giver.' He said Ἄρτον, however, as interpreter, to express the Hebrew לחם, or the Syriac לחמא, which signifies food, and is used particularly for bread as the chief of foods: indeed, if we believe Athenaeus, the Syrians called not mere bread, but bread with milk, oil, and salt, λάχμαν. Thus also in the writer of Tobit ch. 11, ἄρτοι τῶν ἐθνῶν are the victuals of the nations, which will be clear if you compare the passage of Daniel ch. 8. A broader usage extended to all those things

which human nature grieves to be denied, namely διατροφὰς and σκεπάσματα, as Paul speaks in 1 Tim. 6:8, or as Philo [says] in the passage which we shall cite below, τροφὴν κὶ σκέπην. The term 'sustenance' extends just as widely in Roman law, for it comprises those things which are for eating, drinking, and clothing the body, and those things which are necessary for men to live, as Ulpian has handed down. These alone God promises us in the new covenant, these alone He wishes to be asked for by us: and not in advance, but as much as is enough for the present: whereas, on the contrary, the Jews from

had learned from their masters to pray for great wealth for themselves. The meaning therefore of these words is: Give us, O God, sustenance which may suffice for the age to be spent hereafter, and if it does not please you to give it by the year, give it by the month, give it at least by the day; whatever is given beyond that will be adventitious.

The Vulgate version, which rendered it SUPERSUBSTANTIAL bread, is rightly refuted. The terms πειούσιος and ἐπιούσιος are also rightly distinguished. But it does not appear why the new Grotius version should be preferred to the ancient Latin version, received before Jerome, which rendered ἐπιούσιον as daily. Grotius prefers that it be rendered as tomorrow's bread. But in the first place, there is no reason for his interpretation. For even if ἡμέρα ἐπιοῦσα denotes the day of tomorrow in Acts 7:26, which Erasmus urges, here however it is simply called ἐπιούσιος, not bread of the coming day; and the Greeks say ἐπιόντα for things that are to be, and ἐπιοῦσαν for the day that is to come in Deut. 32:7. Prov. 27, from ἕπειμι, to arrive, whence, as the blessed Chemnitz observes in Harm. c. 51, p. 614, thus the bread ἐπιούσιος will be arriving or adventitious, which it is not enough to have received or taken once, but which in this vicissitude of changing times, it is necessary for us to have arrive continuously and always, every day, or daily. Thus in Luke 11:4, he calls the bread ἐπιούσιον καθ’ ἡμέραν, coming from the hand of God, passing by, circulating, or arriving every day: or if that explanation does not please, let it be called adventitious, by the same etymology, because it arrives or is added to the other primary gifts of God, necessary for the soul, so that there is no need for that unusual explanation of 'tomorrow's'. Nor does the Hebrew Gospel of the Nazarenes, of which mention was made above, have much weight, and therefore there is nothing solid in what Grotius brings forward for that opinion regarding the word. Furthermore, that interpretation does not sufficiently agree with Christ's dissuasion from anxiety about the morrow, whether we understand the day immediately following, or that whole span of life which remains for us to traverse. For how can we be asked to pray today for those things which suffice for the whole span of life, if we ought not to be anxious about the sustenance of the morrow? Rightly Chrysostom in the Catena of Greek Fathers: God wishes us to be in no way anxious about the morrow, nor to divide our mind and attention, drawn away from the thought or care of divine things, into these provisions for the future. Wherefore he also teaches us to ask for bread which suffices only for the urgent necessity of sustaining the body, and is enough merely for the use of this present day. Therefore Nyssenus rightly said τῆς ἐφημερινῆς χρείας, of daily necessity: and the Anonymous author in the catena. of Nicetas, we are commanded to seek bread, not for a number of many years, ἀλλὰ τὸν σήμερον ἡμῖν ἀρκοῦντα, but that which is sufficient for us today. Nor is there any reason why we should interpret that σήμερον otherwise than it is commonly, and according to the trite meaning of TODAY, which sense Luke's τὸ καθ’ ἡμέραν also bears: indeed we are warned so that we may repeat this prayer daily, give us our daily bread today. And since Cyprian, Ambrose, and also Augustine here agree with the ancient Latin version, as does Jerome himself in c. 2 to Titus and the Vulgate version in the parallel passage Luke 11:4, it does not seem that it should be rashly abandoned. Maldonatus notes that all ancient Latin authors read it so. Nor are the Greeks very different, Basil the Great in the Shorter Rules, q. 252, Gregory Nyssen, Orat. 4 on the Lord's Prayer, Chrysostom, Theophylact, Euthymius in c. 6. of Matthew, who explain ἄρτον ἐπιούσιον as that which is useful to our substance for daily life; that which suffices for our substance and is self-sufficient for our substance and constitution, bread accommodated to nourishing our substance, suitable and sufficient for sustaining us: Suidas interprets ἄρτος ἐπὶ τῇ ὀυσίᾳ ἡμῶν ἁρμοζὼν, ἢ καθημερινός, bread fitting for our nature, or daily. For thus we ask for what suffices for the present day, turning our anxiety away from the morrow. Tò ἐπιούσιος signifies what is more than enough in Gellius, book 1, c. 13, and therefore τὸ ἐπιούσιον could mean what is enough. Thus also the Syrian rendered it as bread of our indigence or sufficiency, as also the Arab as bread of our sufficiency. The Ethiopian and the Persian interpreter approach the ancient version even more, bread which is for each of our days, give us today. Whence St. Cyprian warns that by this added particle (today) anxious solicitude is removed, so that we do not extend the desires of our petition into the long term. According to these, therefore, ἐπιούσιος is derived from ἐπὶ and οὐσία. But the derivation and interpretation of the word which we gave in the Critici Sacri, p. 596, is still more convenient: that bread is called ἐπιούσιος from ἔπειμι, I arrive, as if to say bread arriving, i.e., which is as it were added to our spiritual necessity, and arrives, which the blessed Chemnitz also handed down: It can also be understood that it is called not 'sought-for' bread, but ἐπιούσιος, i.e., as Varinus interprets, ἐπερχόμενος, arriving, so that we do not attribute it to our industry, but to God's donation. Or: that bread is not the principal thing which is to be asked of God in prayer, but ἐπιούσιον, adventitious, accessory, additional. Matt. 6:33: Seek first the kingdom of God, and the rest shall be added unto you. These are the words of the blessed Chemnitz. Nor, as far as the origin of the word is concerned, does Claudius Salmasius, easily the foremost of the critics of our century, differ in Trapez. fœn. p. 813. Ἐπιούσιος is from ἐπιὼν, which is from ἐπιέναι, to arrive or to supervene, although he interprets it wrongly regarding Christ who is to come in the final judgment. For this petition pertains to those things which pertain to this life. For by the name of bread he includes all things necessary for the body, as Gregory Nyssen observes in his Orat. Dom.: which are added to those things which are necessary for the soul. Chrysostom also refers this part of the Lord's Prayer to τὰ βιωτικὰ (the things of life), hom. 54 in Gen., as also in his homily on the Lord's Prayer, as well as Basil the Great in his shorter rules, Theophylact in this place, and others, although we do not deny that Athanasius in de assumt. hum. nat. and Damascene, book 4, O. F. c. 24, also refer it to the future age; who nevertheless agree with us regarding the etymon, and derive the word from ἐπιέναι. Regarding the matter itself, we have Grotius agreeing, who understands the word bread not as spiritual bread, with Jerome, or spiritual and corporal together with Bellarmine (Book I, On Particular Works, ch. 6), nor as Sacramental with Gregory of Valencia (Vol. III, disp. VI, q. 2) and Barradius (Vol. II, Gospel Harmonies, Book VII, ch. 24), whom Leonard Lessius (Book II, On Justice and Law, ch. 37) and Cornelius Jansen (Gospel Harmonies, ch. XLI) refute, because the Apostles could not yet have understood what the Lord meant by those words, the Eucharist not yet having been instituted, but he understands the word bread as referring to those things which are necessary for the sustenance of our life. Compare Proverbs 30:7, 1 Timothy 6:18, and regarding the word bread, Genesis 29:20, Exodus 18:12, 2 Kings 6:32, Luke 14:1, Proverbs 31:14. Those who deny that corporal necessity is designated by this part of the prayer cannot acknowledge, with Cyprian, that the Lord's Prayer is the foundation of all our prayers. But it cannot be understood as both corporal and spiritual bread with Bellarmine: because the sense of one and the same word cannot be both literal and figurative at the same time. And therefore Toletus and Tirinus take it only as corporal bread, and the Roman Catechism acknowledges that this is the sense of the Fathers.

Latin:

Vers. 11. Τὸν ἄρτον ἡμῶν τὸν ἐπιούσιον] Longe aliud περιού- σιος, quod LXX. usurpant, ut significent τὸ ἐξαίρετον, aliud ἐπιούσιος, quod eo sensu nec invenitur, neque reduci potest ad ejus significationis originem. Quod si voluisset Scriptor dicere supersubstantialem, dicendum fuerat ὑπερουσιώδη. Nam ἐπὶ in compositionibus eam significationem non ha- bet. Adde quod ἐπὶ in compositione ante vocalem literam i. solet amittere. Itaque Platonici ἐπουσιῶδες vocant, quod substantiæ accedit, quæ significatio præterea hic locum non habet: Denique non patiuntur Grammaticæ leges ἐπιούσιος aliunde deduci, quam à nomine ἐπιούσια, quod diem poste- rum significat, ut monuit Ambrosius. Hoc vero quanquam per se sufficere debebat, accedit tamen maximi ponderis ar- gumentum ab Hieronymi testimonio, qui consultum à se scribit Hebræum Evangelii codicem quo Nazareni hoc est Christiani ἑβραΐζοντες utebantur, atque ibi reperisse מחר, id autem est crastinum. Quare περὶ τῆς λέξεως amplius quæri non debet, tantum restat videamus quæ sit τῆς λέξεως signi- ficatio. Mirum enim videtur, cum Christus vetet nos esse solicitos pro crastino die, hic tamen ab eo præcipi, ut ore- mus dari nobis panem crastinum. Sed sciendum est, quod & ab Hieronymo est annotatum, מחר Hebræis non signifi- care stricte diem proxime sequentem, sed quicquid futurum imminet, ut Exod. XIII. 14. ubi LXX. habent μετὰ ταῦτα Ex. XIX. 10. Jos. IV. 6. Prov. XXVII. 1. quibus locis servarunt LXX. vocem ἄυριον, quo sensu & ἄυριον usurpat Lucas XIII. 33. Sicut & exactum tempus Hebræis dicitur תמול, id est, heri. Est ergo ἐπιοῦσα omne id spatium vitæ, quod no- bis emetiendum restat, incognitum nobis, Deo cognitum: ἐπιούσιον, id quod ei spatio sufficit. Multi homines incerti quamdiu sint victuri senectutis expectationem avaritiæ prætendunt: & sæpe quo minus est viæ, eo plus quæritur viatici. Vult Christus nos Deo hanc curam committere, ut quantum vitæ superest, tantum nobis suppeditet alimento- rum: neque ita tamen, ut poscamus id omne nobis repræ- sentari. Est enim valde illiberalis animi non credere Deo, nisi sub pignore. Quemadmodum igitur hi qui in potestate sunt Patrisfamilias, & boni, & sapientis, & divitis, non po- stulabunt, ut alimenta in multos annos sibi in cellis recon- dere liceat, sed contenti erunt dimenso diurno: ita & Christus abesse vult à nostris precibus tum diffidentiam, tum aviditatem. Est ergo hic σήμερον positum pro eo quod pleniore Hebraismo diceretur σήμερον σήμερον. Id est, Luca in- terprete τὸ καθ' ἡμέραν: unde Græce καθημερόβιοι Latine in diem viventes dicuntur, qui contenti sunt præsentibus, ne- que in longum sunt solliciti. Sic & τροφὴν καθ' ἡμέραν di- xerunt Alexis & Antiphanes. Quod Græci interpretes Dan. I. 5. τὸ τῆς ἡμέρας καθ' ἡμέραν. Ita optime cum hac prece consentit præceptum Christi quod infra est commate 34. Omninoque idem nobis aperte significat, quod quo- tidiana Mannæ largitione olim adumbrabatur, quam histo- riam ita explicat Philo, ut vice interpretis sit ad hæc Christi verba: καλὸν τὸ ἐναίσιμον κὶ μεμετρημένον, κὶ μητὸ ὑπὲρ ἡμᾶς λαμβάνειν πλεονεξία τοῦτο γε τὸ τῆς ἡμέρας εἰς ἡμέραν συναγαγέτω ἡ ψυχὴ ἵνα μὴ ἑαυτὴν φύλακα τῶν ἀγαθῶν, ἀλ- λὰ τὸν φιλόδωρον Θεὸν ἀποφήνῃ. Ἄρτον autem dixit inter- pret, ut exprimeret Hebræum לחם, aut Syriacum לחמא, quod cibum significat, & peculiariter pro ciborum præci- puo pane usurpatur: imo si Athenæo credimus, Syri pa- nem non merum, sed cum lacte, oleo & sale λάχμαν voca- bant. Sic & apud scriptorem Tobiæ c. 11. ἄρτοι τῶν ἐθνῶν sunt edulia gentium, quod patebit si conferas locum Da- nielis cap. 8. Laxior usus ad ea omnia protulit

Queis humana sibi doleat natura negatis διατροφὰς scilicet, κὶ σκεπάσματα, ut Paulus loquitur 1. Tim. VI. 8. aut ut Philo loco, quem infra adducemus, τροφὴν κὶ σκέπην. Æque late patet in jure Romano victus appel- atio, comprehendit enim ea quæ esui, potui, cultuiq; cor- poris, quæque ad vivendum hominibus sunt necessaria, ut tradidit Ulpianus. Hæc sola nobis in novo fœdere Deus promittit, hæc sola vult à nobis postulari: neque in anteces- sum, sed quantum in præsens sat est: cum contra Judæi à

Magistris suis didicissent magnam sibi opulentiam precari. Sensus ergo horum verborum est: Da nobis Deus victum qui ætati in posterum agendæ sufficiat, & si non placet da- re annua, da menstrua, da saltem diurna, quicquid ultra da- bitur, id erit adventitium.

Recte refutatur vulgata versio, quæ reddidit SUPERSUBSTANTIALEM panem. Recte et- iam distinguuntur voces πειούσιος & ἐπιούσιος. Sed non apparet, cur antiquæ Latinæ versioni, ante Hieronymum receptæ, quæ ἐπιούσιον reddidit quo- tidianum, nova Grotiana præferenda sit. Panem crastinum reddi mavult Grotius. At primum nul- la est ejus interpretationis ratio. Etiamsi enim ἡμέ- ρα ἐπιοῦσα diem crastinum notet Act.VII.26. quod urget Erasmus, hic tamen ἐπιούσιος simpliciter dici- tur, non panis τῆς ἐπιούσης ἡμέρας; & dicunt Græci ἐπιόντα quæ futura sunt, ἐπιοῦσαν superventurum diem Deut. XXXII. 7. Prov. XXVII. ab ἕπειμι ad- ventare, unde observante B. Chemnitio, Harm. c. LI. p. 614. ita panis ἐπιούσιος erit adventans seu ad- ventitius, quem non sufficit semel accepisse, aut sum- psisse, sed quem in hac vertentium temporum vicissitu- dine, subinde & semper, singulis diebus, seu quotidie necesse est nobis advenire. Ita Luc. XI. v. 4. vocat ἐ- πιούσιον καθ’ ἡμέραν panem ex manu Dei, singulis diebus abeuntem, circumeuntem, aut adventantem: aut si non placeat illa explicatio, adventitius, di- catur, eàdem Etymologia, quod adveniat, vel acce- dat cæteris Dei donis primariis, animæ necessariis, ut non opus sit inusitata illa crastini explicatione. Neque multum momenti habet Evangelium E- bræum Nazarenorum, de quo supra dictum, ideo- que περὶ τῆς λέξεως nihil solidi est, quod in istam sententiam adfert Grotius. Porro non satis conve- nit illa interpretatio dehortationi Christi à solicitu- dine de crastino, sive diem proxime sequentem intel- ligamus, sive omne illud spatium vitæ, quod nobis emetiendum restat. Quomodo enim hodie ea dari petendum quæ ad totum vitæ spatium sufficiant, si de crastini diei victu soliciti esse non debemus? Recte Chrysost. in Caten. Græc. Patrum: Vult Deus nos ne- quaquam de die crastina solicitos esse, neque animum & attentionem nostram ex rerum divinarum cogita- tione aut cura revulsam in istas futuro provisiones dividere. Quare & panem petere nos docet, qui ad necessitatem urgentem sustentandi corporis suffi- ciat solum, & ad præsentem duntaxat diei hujus u- sum satis sit. Ideo Nyssenus jure dixit τῆς ἐφημερινῆς χρείας hodiernæ necessitatis: & Anonymus in caten. Nicetæ, panem quærere jussi sumus, non in multorum annorum numerum, ἀλλὰ τὸν σήμερον ἡμῖν ἀρκοῦντα, sed hodie nobis sufficientem. Neque causa est, cur σή- μερον illud aliter interpretemur, quam vulgo sit, & juxta tritam significationem HODIE, quem sensum etiam fert Lucæ τὸ καθ’ ἡμέραν: imo monemur ita, ut quotidie hanc orationem repetamus, panem no- strum quotidianum da nobis hodie. Et quum conso- nent Latinæ antiquæ versioni hic Cyprianus Ambros. nec non August. ut & Hieron. ipse in c.II. ad Tit. ac vulgata versio in loco parallelo Luc. XI. 4. non vi- detur ea temere deserenda. Maldonatus notat, quod omnes veteres Autores Latini ita legant. Neque alie- ni admodum sunt Græci, Basilius M. in quæstionibus breviorib. q. 252. Gregor. Nyssen. Orat. IV. de O- rat. Dom. Chrysostomus, Theophylactus, Euthymius in c. VI. Matth. qui explicant ἄρτον ἐπιούσιον τὸν πρὸς ἐφήμερον ζωὴν τῇ ὀυσίᾳ ἡμῖν χρήσιμον ὄντα; ἐπὶ τὴν ἡμῶν ὀυσίαν ἡ τροφὴν ἐπαρκῶντα τ’ ἐπὶ τῇ ὀυσίᾳ & συςάσει ἡμῶν αυτάρκη, substantiæ nostræ alendæ accommodatum panem, ad sustentandos nos idoneum & sufficientem: Suidas interpretatur ἄρ- τος ἐπὶ τῇ ὀυσίᾳ ἡμῶν ἁρμοζὼν, ἢ καθημερινὸς panis naturæ nostræ conveniens, aut quotidianus. Sic enim petimus, quod ad hodiernum diem suf- ficiat, de crastino solicitudinem nostram a ver- tes. Tò ἐπιούσιος significat quod plus satis apud Gellium l. 1. c. XIII. ideoque τὸ ἐπιούσιον poterat quod satis est. Ita etiam Syrus reddidit panem in- digentiæ, vel sufficientiæ nostræ, ut & Arabs panem sufficientiæ nostræ. Magis adhuc antiquæ versioni accedit Æthiops, & Persa interpres, panem, qui sin- gula diei nostræ, da nobis hodie. Unde S. Cyprianus monet, hac adjecta particula (hodie) anxiam solici- tudinem eximi, ut ne in longum desideria nostræ peti- tionis extendamus. Juxta hos ergo ἐπιούσιος ab ἐπὶ, & οὐσία derivatur. Sed commodior adhuc est vocis derivatio & interpretatio, quam in Critico Sacro dedimus p. 596. quod ἐπιούσιος dictus sit panis ab ἔπειμι supervenio, q. d. panis superveniens, h. e. qui spirituali nostræ necessitati velut adjicitur, & su- pervenit quam tradidit quoq; B. Chemnitius: Pot- est etiam intelligi, quod appelletur non quæsitus panis, sed ἐπιούσιος, h. e. sicut Varinus interpretatur, ἐπερχό- μενος superveniens, ne nostræ industriæ, sed Dei do- nationi illum tribuamus. Vel: panem non esse princi- pale, quod in oratione à Deo petendum est, sed ἐπιούσιον, adventitium, accessorium, adjectitium. Matth. VI. 33. Quærite primum regnum Dei, & cætera adjicien- tur vobis. Hæc B. Chemnitius. Neque quantum ad vocis originem, discrepat Criticorum seculi nostri facile præcipuus Claud. Salmas. Trapez. fœn. p. 813. Ἐπιούσιος est ab ἐπιὼν, quod est ab ἐπιέναι adve- nire, vel supervenire, etsi id perperam de Christo in extremo judicio venturo interpretetur. Nam ad ea pertinet hæc petitio, quæ ad hanc vitam. Panis enim nomine omnia ad corpus neceffaria complectitur, ut Greg. Nyssen. Orat. Dom. observat: quæ adjiciuntur illis, quæ animæ necessaria sunt. Ad τὰ βιωτικὰ re- fert hanc orationis Dominicæ partem etiam Chry- sost. hom. LIV. in Gen. ut & hom. in Or. Dom. nec non Basil. M. in regul. brev. Theoph. in h. l. aliique etsi non diffiteamur Athanas. de assumt. hum. nat. & Damasc. l. IV. O. F. c. 24. etiam ad futurum secu- lum referre; qui tamen quoad Etymon pariter no- biscum conveniunt, & ab ἐπιέναι vocem deducunt. De reipsa habemus Grotium annuentem, qui non de pane spirituali, cum Hieronymo, aut spirituali ac corporali simul cum Bellarm. l. I. de oper. in partic. c. 6. neque de Sacramentali cum Greg. de Val. T. III. disp. VI. q. 2. Barradio T. II. Conc. Evang. l. VII. l. 24. quos Leonh. Lessius l. II. de just. & jur. c. 37. Cornel. Jans. Conc. Evang. c. XLI. refellunt, quia Apostoli tum nondum intelligere potuerint, quid Dominus sibi istis verbis vellet, Eucharistia non- dum instituta, sed de iis, quæ ad vitæ nostræ susten- tationem necessaria sunt, vocem panis intelligit. Conf. Prov. XXX. 7. 1. Tim. VI. 18. & de voce panis Gen. XXIX. 20. Exod. XIIX. 12. 2. Reg. VI. 32. Luc. XIV. 1. Prov. XXXI. 14. Qui necessitatem corpora- lem hac orationis parte designari negant, non a- gnoscere possunt, cum Cypriano, orationem Domini- cam omnium nostrarum orationum fundamentum. Non vero cum Bellarmino & corporalis & spiritualis panis intelligi potest: quia unius ejusdemq; vocis sensus non potest simul esse & proprius & impro- prius. Ideoque Toletus & Tirinus de pane corpo- rali tantum accipiunt, eumque Patrum esse sensum Catechismus Roman. agnoscit.

## 6:12
Verse 12. Ἄφες ἡμῖν τὰ ὀφειλήματα ἡμῶν] Just as the Greeks say ὀφείλειν δίκην, and the Latins say to owe penalties, so among the Hebrews the word חוב, which signifies a debtor, is also accustomed to be used of those who are bound by a penalty, as in Daniel 1:10. Tertullian: Debt in the Scriptures is a figure of a transgression, because it is owed to judgment and is exacted by it. Therefore, what this interpreter expressed literally, Luke rendered equivalently when he used ἁμαρτίας: Thus the same Luke in the same sense, when he had previously said ἁμαρτία-

He soon placed ὀφειλέτας for Ὀφέλεταιs, XIII, 2. 4. But ἀφιέναι ἁμαρτίας is opposed to τῷ κρατεῖν. Moreover, both are said of God anthropopathically, because men, when they forgive things in good faith, cast them away as it were from their mind: what they are unwilling to forgive, they keep. Similar are not remembering sins, Jerem. XXXI. 34, and casting sins into the sea, Mich. VII. 19. Thus also χαρίζεųαι and λογίζεųαι are opposed to each other, but with the metaphor drawn more openly from monetary debts. Servius on the XIth Aeneid: Luitis supplicium. He used a legal term: for a debtor is said to pay (luere) who pays money: which is here used for capital punishment. That which is used, Servius signifies as λελεγμένον καταχρηųικῶς. But that those who thought this prayer pertains only to a few, or that indeed all ought to pray thus, yet not for themselves, or that by some this is pronounced even for themselves humbly not truthfully, is taught to us by the best interpreter of Christ, John, in his first epistle, ch. I. 8. 9. 10. From which we understand at the same time that this prayer is not to be bound to only those sins which are committed after the name of Christ has been given, whether they be ἁμαρτίαι strictly so named, of which John proceeds to treat in ch. II. 1, or πταίσματα of which James treats in III. 2, and which Augustine thinks are especially looked to here, but it must be referred in addition to the sins which preceded the Christian profession. For although by the stroke of the new covenant God promised forgiveness of antecedent sins to all who would believe in Christ, and seals it even in the souls of believers, He nevertheless did not wish the effect of that right, that is, liberation from death, to which eternal glory is connected, to reach us except on this condition: that while we are in this life, we always humbly acknowledge before God the guilt even of past time, and persevere in seeking forgiveness in that name also. See Paul, 1 Cor. XV. 9 and 1 Tim. I. 15, where he calls himself τῶν ἁμαρτωλῶν πρῶτον, which is a pious hyperbole, such as that also in the epistle of Barnabas: that Jesus chose his own apostles, being more lawless than all lawlessness. Chrysostom has useful things on this matter in his twelfth homily on the statues.

ὡς ὴ ἡμεῖς] The sense is, we do not hope for this indulgence from you in vain, since we, your children, follow your example by showing similar indulgence to other men, that is, we do not seek vengeance for being harmed, either in deed or in wish. Luke clearly intended the same when he said, 'for we also forgive everyone who is indebted to us.' Now ὀφειλέται or οἱ ὀφείλοντες are those who have sinned against us. The same sense is found in the wise Hebrew, Eccles. XXIX. 2: 'Forgive the injustice to your neighbor, and then when you pray, your sins will be forgiven,' where see also what follows.

Gomarus also explains the word ὡς in a causal sense: he does not, however, insist that we retain it as the proper meaning, and he warns that by that method a similarity is indicated, but not an equality of our remission. Compare Matt. XIII. 35. Now the forgiveness of injuries is not the meritorious cause of the remission of sins (otherwise it would not be properly remission, compare Matt. XIII. 23, Luke VII. 41), but it is a sign and effect of the remission of sins: because it is a work of love, which is the fruit of saving faith, Galat. V. 6. See the parable in Matt. XIII. 27, and non-forgiveness is an obstacle to the remission of sins: and therefore it ought to be removed. The connection is indicated by the fact that our forgiveness toward our neighbor and God's forgiveness toward us are joined, and ought to be, nor does one have a place without the other, not because our forgiveness is the cause of the divine, but because the former is a necessary and inseparable consequence of the latter. The divine remission of our debts is not suspended from the remission of debts which is done by us to our neighbor, because our mercy toward our neighbor is not either a cause or an antecedent condition, or the exemplar of divine mercy, but divine mercy is the cause, and reason, and exemplar of ours: Luke VI. 36, 'Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful'; Ephes. IV. 32, 'Be kind to one another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, just as God in Christ FORGAVE you'; Col. III. 13, 'Bearing with one another, and forgiving one another: just as Christ FORGAVE you, so also you.' The prior is the forgiveness of God and Christ, in the order of nature; the posterior is fraternal forgiveness. For we are not brothers to one another, or able to forgive one another as brothers, before we are received into favor by God, and having obtained the remission of sins through faith, have the same Father and are his children. And that was taught by

Christ in the double parable, both of the servant to whom all debts, however countless, were forgiven out of grace, who then ought to have forgiven his fellow servant his debts, which were by comparison with those very small, Matt. XVIII. 23 seqq., and of the debtor to whom more was given, who therefore loves his creditor more, or certainly is bound to love him, Luke VII. 42, 43. And it is to be observed that that ἀφίεμεν is to be understood primarily of purpose and readiness of mind, and the affection of forgiveness, just as we are prepared to forgive our neighbor: and that the pledge is made in this way, concerning forgiveness, when our debts have been forgiven to us: nor is only the wish for mercy toward our neighbor and fraternal reconciliation thus performed, but under this special promise we pledge in general any debts of love, not only toward our neighbor, but also toward God, Luke VII. 42, because charity toward our neighbor flows from charity and love of God, nor does it have a place without the love of God. Therefore, as our blessed Chemnitius well says in Harm. ch. LI, p. m. 618, Christ, by adding this clause, binds the purpose of those praying as by a public and solemn condition and pledge, that they wish in the future to avoid sins, to amend their life, and to strive for piety. It is therefore a most grave reminder under the formula of a pledge in the sight of the heavenly Father, that we do not abuse the paternal clemency and readiness of forgiveness for a license to sin, but that we pledge and as it were vow amendment. That general doctrine, however, concerning conceiving a good purpose of amendment, he proposes by a special example, congruent to the words of the petition, concerning mutual fraternal forgiveness, just as we said in Matt. V. v. 39 concerning turning the other cheek. Christ willed to insert this promise into the prayer prescribed to us daily and to be repeated frequently, both so that we may be mindful of our debt often and continually, as often as we repeat the Lord's Prayer in praying or recall it in our minds, and just as we have need to pray daily, 'give us this day our daily bread,' so we ought also daily not only to seek the remission of sins from God, but also to forgive offenses to our brothers, even if he should sin against us seven times in a day, Luke 17:4; and also so that we may know that this is not of our own strength, but must be obtained from God by prayers, that He may grant us a mind prompt and intent toward fraternal forgiveness and the duty of true piety, and may effect in us that which we promise to God for the sake of gratitude, on account of the gracious remission of sins. Concerning which the blessed Chemnitz likewise excellently warned: 'But because the flesh, corrupted by the root of bitterness, Heb. 12:15, is of itself full of impatience, desirous of vengeance, tenacious of anger, and most alien to fraternal reconciliation and forgiveness; therefore we simultaneously ask that that root of bitterness be mitigated, repressed, and mortified in us by the Holy Spirit, and that a zeal for concord, reconciliation, and forgiveness be kindled in us, and that it may not be imputed to us that the forgiveness is not done from the whole heart, but with our flesh resisting.' Since, therefore, our life on this earth is not spent without many sins against the Lord, nor is conversation among brothers without various mutual offenses: therefore He joined both in this fifth petition, so that in this way both the peace of conscience toward God may be preserved by the daily remission of sins, and fraternal charity, in which God especially delights, may be preserved among men by continuous mutual reconciliation and forgiveness. Finally, neither is this to be neglected, that the Lord's Prayer is prescribed to those who acknowledge God as Father in heaven, who therefore are already justified by faith and have received the remission of sins: who, since they stumble daily in many things, James 3:2, so that with whatever holiness they are endowed, they [need] the remission of sins not only [of that] which formerly they committed, but also of daily incursion, as Tertullian speaks, they have a necessity to seek, Psalm 32:6, so that they may still be justified according to that saying Revelation 22:11, ὁ δίκαιος δικαιωθήτω ἔτι, they pray, and beseech: For unless God forgives without intermission, it is all over for us, as B. Luther rightly says in the Larger Catechism. Such as are justified by faith in Christ can altogether profess of themselves, ἐ γὰρ αὐτοὶ ἀφίεμεν παντὶ ὀφείλοντι ἡμῖν, as Luc. XI. 4. these things they have. Who also, because they forgive offenses to their brothers, are thereby made more certain of the remission of sins before God: Because that fraternal forgiveness is a work of love; love is the fruit of faith Gal. V. 6. faith in Christ seeks and finds the remission of sins. Those who have true charity, and out of charity forgive offenses to their neighbor, are already justified by faith, and their sins are covered before God. And to these it is also said Luc. VI. 37. Forgive, and it shall be forgiven you: in which respect it can be admitted concerning the justified, that the remission of offenses is required, so that they themselves may be further justified, and not fall away from the remission of sins by the example of that unmerciful servant Matth. XVIII.: just as they are therefore warned after the Lord's Prayer, by Epanaphora: If you forgive men their errors, your heavenly Father will also forgive you. Thus, therefore, our forgiveness can be said to precede not indeed justification, but the continuation of justification; yet not as a cause or merit, but as a quality or requirement of the subject, lest by denying forgiveness to our neighbor, we fall away from divine grace and the gratuitous remission of sins. For the remission of sins is always gratuitous, yet not promised to the impenitent, the implacable, and the secure, but to those who acknowledge their sins, embrace Christ by faith, and working well from faith, forgive injuries to their neighbor. But he who retains an evil purpose of vengeance against his neighbor prays without true repentance, because he does not forgive his neighbor. Nor is it true faith which, in impenitence and an evil purpose of continuing in sins, feigns for itself remission and impunity in Christ, as if He were the patron of our impenitence. Therefore Mark c. XI. 25. 26. warns: When you shall stand to pray, consider, and inquire what purpose you find in your heart, and because you are about to pray that your heavenly Father, whom you have offended immensely by your sins, may remit your infinite debts to you, especially consider how your mind is affected toward your neighbor who has offended you. Conf. Syr. XXVIII. 1. seqq. B. Schilterus rightly says in his Catechism on the Lord's Prayer, p. 392. The adverb of likeness AS by no means denotes a perfect equality or similarity of divine and fraternal forgiveness, much less does it indicate the cause or merit of divine remission, of which our forgiveness might be the reason, but it signifies a most increased new obligation, and that a spontaneous one, to join fraternal reconciliation with one's neighbor with the divine remission of sins, and that as a gratuitous fruit of the same; or rather it denotes a liberal pledge, or a devout vow of fraternal forgiveness, in place of filial gratitude, owed to God the heavenly Father for the supreme benefit of the forgiveness of our debts; lest we abuse the ineffable indulgence and immense clemency of the heavenly Father who forgives our offenses, like degenerate children, for an infinite license to offend our neighbor and a perpetual hope of impunity, which is the greatest enticement to sin, under the hope of easily obtained pardon, through the highest and most detestable ingratitude. B. Luther in the Larger Catechism has it thus: If you do not have the grace to forgive your neighbor, there is no reason for you to promise yourself or think that God will forgive you your sins. But if you have kindly forgiven others, that consolation and security is proposed to you, that in heaven also it is certainly forgiven you. And this indeed not because of your forgiveness or pardon, which you bestow upon your neighbor: for He does it freely, and gratuitously out of mere grace, since He has received that He would do it, as the Gospel teaches: but so that He may make us certain and secure, as if by a symbol, or a certain sign proposed together with the promise, which accords with this prayer in Luc. VI. Forgive, and it shall be forgiven you. Therefore B. Luther beautifully warned that this addition appended to this prayer is not only necessary, but also full of consolation.

Latin:

Vers. 12. Ἄφες ἡμῖν τὰ ὀφειλήματα ἡμῶν] Sicut Græci di- cunt ὀφείλειν δίκην, Latini pœnas debere, ita Hebræis חוב quod debitorem significat, etiam de his qui pœnæ obstricti sunt usurpari solet, ut Dan. I. 10. Tertullianus: Debitum in Scripturis delicti figura est, quod perinde judicio debeatur & ab eo exigatur. Quod ergo hic interpres κατὰ λέξιν expres- sit, id ἰσοδυναμούσως reddidit Lucas, cum posuit ἁμαρτίας: Sic idem Lucas in eodem sensu, cum prius dixisset ἁμαρτία-

Ὀφέλεταιs mox posuit ὀφειλέτας XIII, 2. 4. ἀφιέναι autem ἁμαρτίας opponitur τῷ κρατεῖν. Est autem utrumque dictum de Deo ἀνθρωποπαθῶς, quia homines ea, quæ bona fide condonant, quasi ex animo projiciunt: quæ condonare nolunt, asservant. Similia sunt non meminisse delictorum Jerem. XXXI. 34. & in mare delicta projicere Mich. VII. 19. Sic et am inter se opponuntur χαρίζεųαι & λογίζεųαι, sed apertius ducta tralatione à debitis pecuniariis. Servius ad XI. Æneidos: Luitisi supplicium. Iuris verbo usus est: Luere enim debitor dicitur, qui pecuniam solvit: quod hic usurpatum est in capitalem pœnam. Illud usurpatum est, Servio significat λελεγμένον καταχρηųικῶς. Errasse autem eos qui putarunt hanc precationem ad paucos duntaxat pertinere, aut debere quidem omnes ita precari, non tamen pro se, aut à quibusdam hoc pronunciari etiam pro se humiliter non veraciter, docet nos optimus Christi interpres Johannes epistola I. cap. I. 8. 9. 10. Ex quo simul intelligimus hanc orationem non esse alligandam ad sola peccata, quæ siunt post datum nomen Christo, sive illa sint ἁμαρτίαι stricte nominatæ, de quibus Johannes pergit agere c. II. 1. sive πταίσματα de quibus agit Jacobus III. 2. & quæ potissimum hic respici putat Augustinus, sed referendum insuper ad delicta quæ Christianam professionem antecesserunt. Quanquam enim novi fœderis ictu promisit Deus veniam antecedentium delictorum omnibus in Christum credituris, eamque etiam in animis credentium obsignat, noluit tamen ejus juris effectum, id est liberationem à morte, cui connexa est gloria æterna, nobis contingere, nisi hac lege ut dum in hac vita sumus demisse semper coram Deo agnoscamus etiam exacti temporis culpam, & in petenda eo quoq; nomine venia persevemus. Vide Paulum 1. Cor. XV. 9. & 1. Tim. I. 15. ubi se vocat τῶν ἁμαρτωλῶν πρῶτον, quæ pia est ὑπερβολὴ, qualis & illa in epistola Barnabæ ὅτι ἐξελέξατο τὺς ἰδίυς ἀποσόλυς Ἰησῦς ὄντας ὑπὲρ πᾶσαν ἀνομίαν ἀνομωτέρυς. Utilia ad hanc rem habet Chrysostomus oratione de statuis duodecima.

ὡς ὴ ἡμεῖς] Sensus est, non frustra hanc indulgentiam à te speramus cum nos filii tui tuo exemplo simili indulgentia homines alios prosequamur, id est læsi vindictam nec facto nec voto experamus. Idem plane Lucas voluit cum dixit, καὶ γὰρ αὐτοὶ ἀφίεμεν παντὶ ὀφείλοντι ἡμῖν. Sunt autem ὀφειλέται sive οἱ ὀφείλοντες qui in nos deliquerunt. Sensus idem apud sapientem Hebræum Eccles. XXIX. 2. ἄφες τὸ ἀδίκημα τῷ πλησίον κὰ τότε δεηθέντος σου αἱ ἁμαρτίαι σου λυθήσονται ubi & quæ sequuntur vide.

Vocem ὡς sensu causali pronam explicat & Gomarus: non ebnuit tamen ut propriam significationem retineamus, eoque pacto similitudinem, non autem paritatem indicari remissionis nostræ monet. Conf. Matth. XIII. 35. Condonatio autem injuriarum non est causa meritoria remissionis peccatorum (alias non esset illa proprie remissio, conf. Matth. XIII. 23. Luc. VII. 41.) sed est signum & effectus remissionis peccatorum: quia est opus dilectionis, quæ est fructus fidei salvificæ Galat. V. 6. Vid. parabola Matth. XIII. 27. & non-condonatio est obstaculum remissionis peccatorum: ideoque removeri debet. Connexio indicatur, quod nostra condonatio erga proximum, & condonatio Dei, quoad nos conjuncta sint, & esse debeant, nec una sine altera locum habeat, non quod nostra condonatio causa divinæ, sed quod illa hujus consequens necessarium, & inseparabile sit. Non suspenditur divina debitorum nostrorum remissio à remissione debitorum, quæ sit à nobis proximo, quia non nostra erga proximum misericordia est vel causa aut conditio antecedanea, vel exemplar divinæ misericordiæ, sed divina misericordia causa est, & ratio, & exemplar nostræ: Luc. VI. 36. Estote misericordes, sicut & Pater vester misericors est; Ephes. IV. 32. Sitis alius in alium benigni, misericordes condonantes vobis invicem, sicut & Deus in Christo DONAVIT vobis: Col. III. 13. Sufferentes vos invicem, & condonantes vobis mutuo: sicut & Christus CONDONAVIT vobis, ita & vos. Prior est condonatio Dei & Christi, naturæ ordine; posterior fraterna condonatio. Non enim prius fratres sumus mutuo, aut ut fratres condonare mutuo possumus, quam à Deo in gratiam recipiamur, & remissionem peccatorum per fidem adepti eundem Patrem habeamus, ejusque filii simus. Idque docuit

Christus parabola gemina tum servi, cui ex gratia remissa omnia debita utut innumera qui porro conservo suo etiam debita sua remittere debuit, comparatione illorum valde exigua Matth. XIIX. 23. seqq. tum debitoris, cui plus donatum est, qui ideo plus etiam creditorem suum diligit certe de- ligere tenetur, Luc. VII. 42. 43. Et observandum illud ἀφίεμεν de proposito & animi promtitudine, ac condonationis affectu imprimis intelligendum esse, sicut & nos parati sumus proximo condonare: & sponsionem ita fieri, de condonatione, cum nobis do- nata fuerint debita nostra: neq; tantum misericor- diæ erga proximum & fraternæ reconciliationis votum ita præstari, sed sub hac speciali pollicita- tione in genere nos spondere quævis dilectionis de- bita, non solum erga proximum, sed etiam erga Deum, Luc.
