VII. 42. quia charitas erga proximum è charitate & amore Dei fluit, nec sine amore Dei locum habet. Ideo, ut præclare B. Chemnitius no- ster Harm. c. LI. p. m. 618. Christus adjecta hac clau- sula orantium propositum, tanquam publica & solenni conditione & sponsione obstringit, quod velint in poste- rum peccata cavere, vitam emendare, ac pietati studere. Est igitur gravissima commonefactio sub for- mula sponsionis in conspectu Patris cælestis, ne paterna condonationis clementia & promtitudine ad peccan- di licentiam abutamur, sed spondeamus & quasi vo- veamus emendationem. Illam vero generalem do- ctrinam, de bono proposito emendationis concipien- do, exemplo speciali, congruente ad verba petitio- nis, de mutua fraterna condonatione proponit, sicut Matth. V. v. 39. de obvertenda altera maxilla dixi- mus. Orationi autem nobis præscriptæ quotidie, ac frequenter repetendæ inferere hanc sponsio- nem voluit Christus, tum ut crebro, & jugiter de- biti nostri memores simus, quoties sc. orationem Dominicam precando repetimus, aut mente reco- limus, & quemadmodum quotidie precari neces- sum habemus, panem nostrum quotidianum da nobis hodie, ita & quotidie non solum remissio- nem peccatorum expetere à Deo, sed etiam fratri- bus condonare offensas debeamus, si vel septies in die erga nos deliquerit Luc. XVII. 4. tum ut nostra- rum id non esse virium, sed à Deo precibus impe- trandum esse, ut animum nobis ad fraternam con- donationem, veræque pietatis debitum promtum, & intentum donet, idq; in nobis efficiat, quod Deo gratitudinis causa, ob gratiosam peccatorum re- missionem spondemus. Quo de itidem eximie monuit B. Chemnitius: Quia vero caro, radice ama- ritudinis, Hebr. XII. v. 15. corrupta, per se impatien- tiæ plena, vindictæ cupida, iræ tenax, à fraterna reconciliatione & condonatione alienissima est; ideo simul petimus, ut radix illa amaritudinis per Spir. S. in nobis mitigetur, reprimatur & mortificetur, ac accendatur in nobis studium concordiæ, reconcilia- tionis, condonationis, nec imputetur nobis, quod non ex toto corde, sed reluctante carnis nostræ condonatio fiat. Quia igitur vita nostra in his terris non degitur sine multis peccatis contra Dominum, nec conversatio inter fratres sine mutuis variis offensionibus: ideo utrumque in hac quinta petitione conjunxit, ut ita si- mul conscientiæ pax erga Deum, quotidiana remis- sione peccatorum, & fraterna charitas, qua Deus præcipue delectatur, inter homines continua mutua reconciliatione & condonatione conservetur. Deni- que nec id negligendum, orationem Dominicam præscribi illis, qui Deum Patrem agnoscunt in cœ- lis, qui proinde justificati per fidem jam sunt, ac re- missionem peccatorum acceperunt: qui quum quotidie in multis labantur Jac. III. 2. adeo ut quantacunq; sanctitate etiam præditi sunt, remif- sionem peccatorum non tantum quæ olim com- misère, sed quotidiana etiam incursationis, ut Ter- tullianus loquitur, expetere necessum habeant Psal. XXXII. 6. ut adhuc justificentur juxta illud Apoc. XXII. 11. ὁ δίκαιος δικαιωθήτω ἔτι, orant, & precantur: Nisi enim citra intermissionem remittat Deus, actum est de nobis, ut rectè in Catechesi majo- ri B. Lutherus. Quales justificati per fidem in Christum omnino de se profiteri possunt, ἐ γὰρ αὐ- τοὶ ἀφίεμεν παντὶ ὀφείλοντι ἡμῖν, ut Luc. XI. 4. hæc habent. Qui etiam, quia fratribus offensas remit- tunt, ex eo certiores redduntur de remissione pec- catorum coram Deo: Quia fraterna illa condona- tio est opus dilectionis; dilectio est fructus fidei Gal. V. 6. fides in Christo remissionem peccato- rum quærit & invenit. Qui veram charitatem habent, & ex charitate offensas proximo condo- nant, jam sunt fide justificati, & peccata ipsorum coram Deo tecta. Atque his etiam dicitur Luc. VI. 37. Remittite, & remittetur vobis: quo respectu de justificatis admitti potest, quod remissio offen- sarum requiratur, ut porro ipsi justificentur, nec remissione peccatorum exemplo servi istius im- misericordis Matth. XVIII. excidant: quemad- modum ideo monentur post orationem Domini- cam, per Epanaphoram: Si remiseritis hominibus errata sua, remittet & vobis Pater vester cælestis. Sic ergo præcedere nostra condonatio dici pot- est non quidem justificationem, sed justificationis continuationem; non tamen ut causa, vel meri- tum, sed ut qualitas, vel requisitum subjecti, ne denegata proximo condonatione, divina gratia & gratuita peccatorum remissione excidamus. Re- missio enim peccatorum semper est gratuita, non tamen promissa impœnitentibus, implacabilibus & securis, sed illis, qui peccata agnoscunt, fide Christum amplectuntur, & ex fide bene operan- tes proximo injurias condonant. Retinens au- tem malum propositum vindictæ contra proxi- mum absque vera pœnitentia orat, quia proximo non dimittit. Nec vera fides est, quæ in impœ- nitentia, & malo proposito pergendi in peccatis fingit sibi remissionem & impunitatem in Christo, quasi is patronus sit impœnitentiæ nostræ. Ideo Marcus c. XI. 25. 26. monet: Quando stabis ad precandum, considera, & inquire, quale propo- situm in corde tuo invenias, & quia oraturus es, ut Pater tuus cœlestis, quem peccatis tuis in im- mensum offendisti, infinita tua debita tibi remit- tat, præcipue considera, quomodo erga proxi- mum, qui te offendit, animus tuus affectus sit. Conf. Syr. XXVIII. 1. seqq. Rectè B. Schilterus Catech. de Orat. Dom. p. 392. Adverbium simi- litudinis SICUT nequaquam denotat perfectam æqualitatem, aut similitudinem condonationis divina, & fraterna, multo minus causam aut meritum re- missionis divinæ indicat, cujus rationem habeat no- stra condonatio, sed significat auctissimam obligatio- nem novam, eamque spontaneam, ad conjungen- dam fraternam reconciliationem cum proximo, cum remissione peccatorum divina, eaque gratuita tanquam ejusdem fructum; vel potius sponsionem denotat liberalem, aut votum devotum condonatio- nis fraterna, loco filialis gratitudinis, Deo Patri cœ- lesti, pro summo condonationis debitorum nostrorum beneficio debita; ne cælestia Patris delictis nostris i- gnoscentis, indulgentia inenarrabili & clementia immensa, degenerum liberorum instar, ad infini- tam offendendi proximum licentiam & perpetuam spem impunitatis, quæ peccandi maxima illecebra est, sub spe veniæ facile impetrandæ, abutamur, per summam maximeque detestandam ingratitudinem. B. Lutherus in Catech. Major. ita habet: Si gra- tia paris ignoscere proximo, non est, quod tibi polli- cearis aut cogites Deum tibi tua peccata condona- turum. Sin autem benigne ignoveris aliis, ea tibi consolatio & securitas proposita est, ut in cælo quo- que tibi certo ignoscatur. Et hoc quidem non pro- pter tuam ignoscentiam aut veniam, quam largiris proximo: libere enim facit, & gratuito ex mera gratia, cum illud se facturum receperit, quemad- modum docet Evangelium: verum ut nos certos ac securos faciat, tanquam Symbolo, seu certo signo una cum promissione proposito, quæ huic orationi consonat Luc. VI. Remittite, & remittetur vobis. Ideo pulchre monuit B. Lutherus hoc auctarium huic pre- cationi adjectum non modo necessarium, sed etiam consolationis plenum esse.

## 6:13
Vers. 13. Do not lead us into temptation.] Frequent among the Hebrews is אל תביאנו ליד נסיון. The sense here is not that God should not permit us to fall into temptations, which is the common lot of all Christians, and especially of those who have progressed most in the doctrine of Christ Jac. I. 2. 3. but that He should not let us succumb to the burden. For בא במסא— to enter into temptation, signifies to be so entangled by enticements or dangers that you cannot extricate yourself, below XXVI. 41. Mark XIV. 38. Luc. XXII. 40. 46. Sometimes the Hebrews say more fully, to enter into the hand of temptation, that is, into its power and dominion. Hence in the Hiphil form it is said in Hebrew הביא, in Syriac (for to them בוא is equivalent to על) העל, which is also repeated here and in Daniel for destruction. To cause to enter, which the Hellenists translate as to lead into. But it is certain, and handed down by the Hebrews, that words of that form which they call Hiphil do not always signify an affirmative act, but often only a negative one, and often also that not the cause, but the occasion is indicated by that inflection. God not only leaves impious men to their vices, giving them up in the lusts of their hearts, as Paul speaks Rom. I. 24. but He also, for a time, as it were, abandons those who trust in their own strength more than is right. We are commanded to forestall this by the acknowledgment of our weakness and by assiduous prayers, as appears in the places we have already cited. Cyprian shows that in the old Latin version it was, unless perhaps he himself translated it so, do not suffer us to be led.

But deliver us from the evil one. The Hebrews say הצלינו מכל רע. This clause is opposed to the former; thus Peter said to deliver out of temptation, and John to keep from the hour of temptation, Apoc. III. 10. God does this, however, either by mercifully tempering the exploration to the strengths we have received, or by even increasing our strengths with secret and ineffable aids. For in both ways is provided the ability for us to bear it, as Paul speaks, 1 Cor. X. 13. Which one it is, however, is rather to be left to the paternal providence of God. Although indeed many temptations are from desire, James I. 14, and many also from the enemies of our profession, Luke VIII. 13, yet both kinds are accustomed to be ascribed to the evil one, that is to say, the devil, because he, by wondrous arts, both inflames desires and instigates enemies, whence he is called the tempter. Thus 1 Cor. VII. 5, the temptation from incontinence is referred to the devil: and no less the striking of a more serious fear, Luke XXII. 31. Although these things are true, nevertheless I do not oppose the desire to take that of the evil one a little more generally, from that which is the evil thing: in this sense, namely, that we are commanded to pray not for immunity from all inconveniences, but for an unconquered spirit against temptations. For the Hebrews also were accustomed to say thus: Do not lead us into the hand of temptation, but deliver us from the encounter with evil, as has been observed by others.

The meaning of the Lord's Prayer is rashly sought from the Hebrews. Nor is tautology, or the repeated petition of the same thing, to be conceded in this so succinct a prayer. This clause, therefore, is more correctly accepted as peculiar, and is distinguished from the preceding, so that there we pray against seduction to sin, that God may not suffer us to be led into temptation, and here we seek liberation from every evil, of body and soul, as Blessed Luther correctly explains. Therefore, liberation from temptation is not specifically sought here, or keeping from the hour of temptation, nor an unconquered spirit against temptations; for these look to the sixth petition. For there are not only six petitions of the Lord's Prayer, as with Calvin, Inst. Book III, ch. XX, 35, the Heidelberg Catechism, Piscator, Ursinus, and the remaining Reformed desire, with the Socinians not denying it in their Catechism.

Racovian Arminians in Confession ch. XIV. But just as those benefits are entirely distinct, preservation from temptations, and in the same, and deliverance from every evil: so our churches not undeservedly, with St. Augustine Enchirid. ch. CXV. and book II. on the Sermon of the Lord on the mount ch. 16, count seven petitions. Nor does that explanation, by which the devil is understood through τò πονηρòν, although it finds favor with Chrysostom, Beza, Piscator, Alsted, and other Calvinists, rest on a solid foundation, namely that the article is prefixed, since τò πονηρòν with the article denotes an evil thing also, not a person, or the devil, that Prince of evils, somewhere in Matt. V. 37, Rom. XII. 9. Nor do Calvin and Bullinger disagree here with Blessed Luther and Chemnitz in this place.

For thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory for ever. Amen. What follows, for thine is the kingdom, power and glory for ever and ever, since it did not exist in the most ancient Greek copies, but does exist in the Syriac, and in the Latin context, and in the Arabic, provides us with an argument from which we may learn that not only the Arabic and Latin version, but also the Syriac was made after the liturgy of the churches had received a certain form. For it was taken from the custom of the Greeks to be ascribed as a doxology rather than a part of the prayer, unknown to all the Latins. But also Amen appears not to have been added by Christ, but from the custom of the ancient Church approving the public recitation of voices with that word. For we are taught that the ancient Christians did that 1 Cor. XIV. 16. And that, like many things, by the example of the Hebrews Deut. XXVII. 15. and following. Thus also in Latin codices many things adhered from the Latin ritual, as below XXI. 17. these words: and he was teaching them about the kingdom of God. Luke XVIII. 13. Amen, in certain copies.

Grotius says these things for the sake of the Papists, who, so that they may defend their Vulgate Version and Liturgy, contend that that clause is an interpolation; Erasmus, Bellarmine book I. on Good Works ch. VI, Cornelius Jansenius in the Harmony of the Gospels, Maldonado in this place, Grefferus in Defense of Bellarmine, Cornelius à Lapide in this place. To whom they join efforts from the Calvinists Bullinger and Scultetus; and also the Arminians in Confession ch. XIV. But the arguments by which Grotius denies authority to this clause are nothing. What he says first, that it is not read in the most ancient Greek copies, does not hold. Because it could have been omitted by the fault and negligence of scribes, when they saw that it was not added in the Gospel of Luke. On the contrary, however, Greek codices of proven faith are found which do not omit the same in this place; Henry Stephens found it in an ancient Greek Codex, which besides one was the most ancient, and Erasmus himself testifies that it is read in all Greek Codices, nor does Bellarmine deny this in book II. on the word of God ch. II. Lucas Burgensis is a witness that he found it in all Codices, with one exception, which he judges to have been corrected according to Latin copies. It is read also in the Syriac and Arabic Codices, as Grotius admits, and in the Ethiopic and Persian. Vain is the suspicion of Grotius, as if it were brought into the Syriac and Arabic Codices from the liturgy of the Greeks, no less than that conjecture which he deduces from a false hypothesis, that these versions are more recent than the Liturgies. Whatever, however, may be the case regarding the antiquity of these versions, it is certainly not likely that the clause was brought into the Codices from the Liturgies, but it should rather be established thus, because it is found added to the Lord's Prayer in the liturgies, that it was also read in the presence of the Evangelist, from whom the Lord's Prayer was taken. For it is easily presumed that the authors of the liturgies did not add anything of their own to this prayer of prayers: much less is it to be believed that it later crept into the sacred, original, and authentic text, whose authority has always been sacrosanct, from the liturgies, contrary to the faith of the ancient Codices: whatever may be the case regarding certain formulas in the Codices

Latin ones, for whom that did not have authority in the Church, perhaps brought in.

But what Grotius judges secondly, that this is a doxology rather than a part of the prayer, he is mistaken in that refutation of opposites. For a confirmation also pertains to prayer, by which arguments for being heard are proposed, so that the heart of God may be moved, such as are exhibited in this confirmatory clause, three in number, very conformable to the prayer, for because the kingdom is the Lord's, therefore he alone will be able to grant that the kingdom of grace and glory may come to us; because the power is his, therefore he will be able to relieve our daily needs, and grant the good of indigence, and avert the evil of guilt and punishment without difficulty; because the glory is the Lord's, therefore he will bring it about that his name may be hallowed, and his will be done no less on earth than in heaven, and whatever he does for the illustration of the glory of the divine name, may happen to us. Chrysostom in this place: The Savior gives us courage against the Devil, by inspiring in us a great and generous hope. For if we have God, he says, as king, and a king powerful and glorious for ever, it cannot be that we are overcome by evil.

Although this conclusion was indeed unknown to the Latins for a third time, that cannot prejudice the Greek Codices, which are authentic; for since it was omitted in the Latin version, by error, as it appears, because it is not held in Luke, it is no wonder that the Latin Fathers do not recite or expound upon it. Whom, however, Grotius here also deserts, since in most Latin Codices, and in Jerome, the particle Amen is held, which Grotius wishes to be expunged. Furthermore, the Greek Fathers did not neglect the δοξολογίαν, such as Chrysostom, Theophylact, and Euthymius, whose authority is stronger for us here, since they agree with the Greek codices and other ancient versions. Whence Laurentius Valla, in his exposition of the Lord's Prayer, departs here from the common opinion of the Papists, warning that nothing was added here by the Greeks to the Canonical Scripture, but rather it was subtracted by the Latins. Add that this δοξολογία is consistent with Scripture, and especially with the Davidic thanksgiving in 1 Chron. XXIX. 11, and that Paul, following the example of Christ, after reciting the final petition concerning deliverance from all evil, adds a similar clause, to whom be glory forever, 2 Tim. IV. 18. All of which without doubt moved Chamier (Tom. I. Panstrat. Cathol. l. XII. c. XIII. §. 26) and Wendelin (Syst. Theol.) to abandon the opinion of Bullinger and the Socinians and to acknowledge this δοξολογίαν as authentic, which was also done by the Heidelberg Catechism.

Finally, since the comparison of Rabbinical formulas in the Lord's Prayer pleases Grotius here, he should have the less reproved this δοξολογίαν, because he was not ignorant of a similar one produced by his Capellus from the Seder Tehilloth, which we previously cited from the same.

What Grotius suspects regarding the word Amen being added by someone according to the custom of the ancient Church is entirely frivolous, and enjoys no semblance of truth. It is one thing to confirm vows with the word Amen in an assembly, but quite another to add that word to Holy Scripture. The former was by no means illicit, and was pious; the latter, however, is by no means permitted, and is alien to piety, Rev. XXII. 18.

Latin:

Vers. 13. Μὴ εἰσενέγκῃς ἡμᾶς εἰς πειρασμόν.] Frequens He- bræis אל תביאנו ליד נסיון. non hic sensus est, ne Deus nos permittat πειρασμοῖς περιπίπτειν, quæ commu- nis sors est Christianorum omnium, ac maxime eorum, qui plurimum in Christi doctrina profecerunt Jac. I. 2. 3. sed ne nos sinat oneri succumbere. Nam בא במסא— εἰσέρχεσθαι εἰς πειρασμόν, significat, ita involvi illecebris aut periculis, ut non extriceris, infra XXVI. 41. Marc. XIV. 38. Luc. XXII. 40. 46. Plenius interdum dicunt Hebræi, intrare in manum tentationis, hoc est, in potestatem ejus, ac dominium. Hinc in forma Hiphil dicitur Hebraice הביא, Syris (nam illis בוא valet על) העל, quod & hic repetitur & apud Danielem εἰς ἐκποίησιν. הבער facere intrare, quod Hellenistæ vertunt εἰσφέ- ρειν. Certum autem est, & ab Hebræis traditum, verba ejus formæ, quam Hiphil vocant, non semper significare actum καταφατικὸν, sed sæpe ἀποφατικὸν duntaxat, sæpe et- iam non causam, sed occasionem ea flexione indicari. Deus non tantum homines impios vitiis suis relinquit, παραδιδὺς ἐν ταῖς ἐπιθυμίαις τῶν καρδιῶν ἀυτῶν, ut loquitur Paulus Rom. I. 24. sed eos etiam, qui viribus suis plus æquo con- fidunt, ad tempus velut abdicat. Hoc jubemur agnitio- ne infirmitatis nostræ, & assiduis precibus antevertere, ut apparet iis quos jam adduximus locis. Cyprianus osten- dit in veteri Latina versione fuisse, nisi forte ipse ita vertit, ne nos patiaris induci.

Ἀλλὰ ῥῦσαι ἡμᾶς ἀπὸ τῶ πονηρᾶ] Hebræi dicunt הצלינו מכל רע. Membrum hoc priori opponitur; ita Petrus dixit ῥύειν ἐκ πειρασμᾶ, & Johannes τηρεῖν ἐκ τῆς ὥρας τῶ πειρασμᾶ Apoc. III. 10. Facit autem hoc Deus, aut explorationem clementer temperando ad eas, quas acce- pimus vires, aut vires etiam augendo arcanis & ineffabili- bus auxiliis. Nam utroque modo præstatur τὸ δυνάσθαι ἡμᾶς ὑπενεγκεῖν, ut loquitur Paulus 1. Cor. X. 13. Utrum autem sit potius, paternæ Dei providentiæ permittendum est. Quanquam vero multi πειρασμοὶ sint ἐκ τῆς ἐπιθυμίας Jac. I. 14. multi etiam ab hostibus nostræ professionis Lu- cæ VIII. 13. solet tamen utrumque genus τῷ πονηρῷ, diabo- lo scilicet ascribi, quia ille miris artibus & cupiditates in- flammat, & hostes instigat, unde ὁ πειράζων dicitur. Ita 1. Cor. VII. 5. ὁ πειρασμὸς ἐξ ἀκρασίας ad Diabolum refertur: neque minus gravioris metus incussio Luc. XXII. 31. Hæc quanquam vera sunt, tamen non refrager istud τοῦ πονηροῦ νο- lenti sumere paulo generalius, ab eo, quod est τὸ πονηρόν: hoc sensu nimirum, ut jubeamur precari non immunitatem ab incommodis omnibus, sed animum invictum adversus ten- tamenta. Nam & Hebræi ita dicere solebant: Ne nos in- ducas in manum tentationis, sed nos libera ab occursu ma- li, ut ab aliis observatum est.

Ab Ebræis temere petitur sensus orationis Do- minicæ. Neque in hac tam succincta precatio- ne concedenda est ταυτολογία, vel ejusdem rei iterata petitio. Membrum itaque hoc rectius tan- quam peculiare accipitur, & à præcedente distin- guitur, ita ut ibi deprecemur seductionem ad pec- catum, ne patiatur nos induci Deus in tentatio- nem, hic petamus liberationem ab omni malo, corporis & animæ, uti B. Lutherus recte explicat. Non ergo hic specialiter liberatio ἐκ πειρασμῦ ex- petitur, aut τήρησις ἐκ  ὥρας τῶ πειρασμᾶ, nec animus adversus tentamenta invictus; hæc enim ad sextam petitionem spectat. Neque enim sex tantum petitiones sunt Orationis Dominicæ, uti cum Calvino lib. III. Instit. c. XX. 35. Cateches. Heidelberg. Piscator, Ursinus, & reliqui Reforma- ti volunt, non abnuentibus Socinianis in Catech.

Racov. Arminianis in Confessione cap. XIV. Sed uti omnino illa distincta sunt beneficia, conservatio à tentationibus, & in iisdem, & liberatio ab omni malo: ita Ecclesiae nostrae non immerito cum S. August. Enchirid. c. CXV. & libr. II. de Sermon. Domini in monte c. 16. septem numerant petitio- nes. Neque explicatio illa, qua per τò πονηρòν in- telligitur Diabolus, etsi Chrysostomo, Beza, Piscatori, Alstedio, & aliis Calvinianis sese probet, solido in- pititur fundamento, quod nempe articulus præ- fixus sit, siquidem τò πονηρòν cum articulo rem malam etiam, non personam, vel Diabolum, illum malorum Principem, notet alicubi Matth. V. 37. Rom. XII. 9. Neque abnuunt hic B. Luthero, & Chemnitio, Calvinus & Bullingerus in h. l.

Ὅτι σῦ ἐστὶν ἡ βασιλεία, κὴ ἡ δύναμις, κὴ ἡ δόξα εἰς τὲς αἰῶνας. Ἀμήν. Quod sequitur, quoniam tuum est regnum, pote- stas & gloria in secula seculorum, cum in vetustissimis ex- emplaribus Græcis non exstiterit, exstet autem & in Syria- co, & in Latino contextu, & in Arabico, argumentum no- bis exhibet, unde discamus non Arabicam tantum & Lati- nam versionem, sed & Syriacam factam, postquam Eccle- siarum λειτουργία formam certam acceperat. Nam ex Græ- ciæ consuetudine capta est adscribi hæc δοξολογία magis quam pars precationis, Latinis omnibus ignota. Sed & Amen apparet non à Christo additum, sed ex more veteris Ecclesiæ publicam vocum recitationem ea voce approban- tis. Id enim factitasse Christianos veteres docemur 1. Cor. XIV. 16. Idque, ut multa, exemplo Hebræorum Deut. XXVII. 15. & deinceps. Sic & in Latinis codicibus ex rituali Latino multa adhæserunt, ut infra XXI. 17. hæc ver- ba: & docebat eos de regno Dei. Lucæ XVIII. 13. Amen, in quibusdam exemplaribus.

Hæc in gratiam Pontificiorum Grotius, qui ut Vulgatam suam Versionem & Liturgiam tueantur, clausulam illam ἐμβολιμαῖον esse contendunt Era- smus, Bellarmin. lib. I. de Bonis Oper. cap. VI. Cornel. Jansenius in Concord. Evangel. Maldona- tus in h. l. Grefferus in Defens. Bell. Cornel. à Lap. in h. l. Quibus operas jungunt è Calvinianis Bullin- gerus, & Scultetus; nec non Arminiani in Confess. c. XIV. sed argumenta, quibus αὐθεντίαν huic clausulæ denegat Grotius, nulla sunt. Quod pri- mo dicit in vetustissimis exemplaribus Græcis non le- gi, haud stringit. Quia omitti potuit librariorum culpa & incuria, cum viderint, non additam esse in Evangelio Lucæ. Ex adverso vero repe- riuntur Græci codices probatæ fidei, qui ean- dem non omittunt hoc loco; invenit eam in vetu- sto Codice Græco, qui præter unum antiquissimus fuit, Henricus Stephani, & testatur Erasmus ipse in omnibus Codicibus Græcis eam legi, nec id dissi- tetur Bellarmin. libro II. de verbo Dei cap. II. Lu- cas Burgensis testis est, se in omnibus Codicibus in- venisse, uno excepto, quem ad Latina exemplaria ca- stigatum censet. Legitur etiam ea in Codicibus Sy- riacis, & Arabicis, fatente Grotio, & in Æthiopi- cis, & Persicis. Vana est suspicio Grotii, quasi è λειτουργίᾳ Græcorum invecta sit in Syros & Arabi- cos Codices, non minus, atque conjectura illa, quam ex hypothesi falsa deducit, quod recentiores sint hæ versiones Liturgias. Quicquid vero sit de antiquitate harum versionum, non sit certe verosi- mile, è Liturgiis in Codices invectam esse clausu- lam, sed ita potius statuendum, quia in litur- giis reperitur addita orationi Dominicæ, ean- dem etiam penes Evangelistam lectam fuisse, un- de Oratio Dominica depromta fuit. Non enim huic orationi orationum aliquid de suo adjecisse li- turgiarum Autores, facile præsumendum est: multo minus credere licet, postmodum è litur- giis, præter Veterum Codicum fidem, in tex- tum sacrum Originalem & authenticum, cujus autoritas sacrosancta semper fuit, irrepsisse: quicquid sit de formulis quibusdam in Codices

Latinos, quorum ea non fuit in Ecclesia autoritas, fortassis invectis.

Quæ vero secundo Grotius censet δοξολογίαν hanc potius esse, quam partem orationis, in eo fal- litur elencho oppositorum. Nam ad orationem et- iam pertinet confirmatio, qua argumenta exaudi- tionis proponuntur, ut flectatur cor Dei, qualia in hac clausula βεβαιωτικῇ tria exhibentur, pre- cationi perquam conformia, nam quia Domini est regnum, ideo ipse solus præstare poterit, ut ad nos adveniat regnum gratiæ, & gloriæ; quia ipsius est potentia, idcirco nostris necessitatibus quotidianis subvenire, ac bonum indigentiæ concedere, & malum culpæ ac pœnæ avertere poterit citra ne- gotium; quia Domini est gloria, ideo efficiet, ut nomen suum sanctificetur, fiatque voluntas non mi- nus in terris, quam in cælis, & quicquid ad glo- riæ nominis divini illustrationem fecerit, nobis eveniat. Chrysostom. in h. l. Facit nobis animos contra Diabolum Salvator, magna nobis & gene- rosa inspirandi spe. Si enim Deum, inquit, ha- bemus regem, & regem potentem ac gloriosum in sæcula, fieri non potest, ut vincamur à malo.

Etsi vero tertio Latinis ignota fuerit hæc con- clusio, id tamen Græcis Codicibus, qui authen- tici sunt, præjudicare nequit; nam quum omissa fuerit in Latina versione, ex errore, ut apparet, quia penes Lucam non habetur, non mirum, quod Latini Patres eandem non recitent, aut ex- ponant. Quos tamen hic etiam deserit Grotius, siquidem in plerisque Latinis Codicibus, & apud Hieronymum particula Amen habeatur, quam ex- punctam vult Grotius. Porro, Græci Patres non neglexêre δοξολογίαν, ut Chrysostomus, Theophy- lactus, Euthymius, quorum hic nobis potior au- toritas, siquidem Græcis codicibus, & aliis anti- quis versionibus consonent. Unde Laurentius Valla in expositione Orat. Dom. hoc loco abit à communi Pontificiorum sententia, monens nihil hic à Græcis Scripturæ Canonicæ additum, sed à La- tinis detractum esse. Adde, quod congruat illa δοξολογία Scripturæ, & cumprimis gratiarum a- ctioni Davidicæ 1. Par. XXIX. 11. quodque Paulus exemplo Christi ultima petitione de liberatione ab omni malo recitata similem clausulam adjiciat, cui gloria in secula 2. Tim. IV. 28. Quæ omnia si- ne dubio moverunt Chamierum Tom. I. Panstrat. Cathol. l. XII. c. XIII. §. 26. Wendelin. Syst. Theol. ut relicta Bullingeri, & Socinnorum sententia δοξολογίαν hanc pro authentica agnoverint, quod etiam à Catechesi Heidelbergensi factum.

Denique quum placeat hic Grotio in Oratione Dominica collatio formularum Rabbinicarum, eo minus reprobare debuit hanc δοξολογίαν, quod similem è Seder Tehilloth à Capello suo productam, non ignorarit, quam antea ex eodem allegavi- mus.

Quod de voce Amen ex more veteris Ecclesiæ ab aliquo adjecta suspicatur Grotius, prorsus frivo- lum est, nec ulla veri gaudet similitudine. Aliud est, in congressu firmare vota voce Amen, aliud vero Scripturæ S. eam vocem adjicere. Illud mi- nime illicitum erat, & pium: hoc vero neutiquam concessum, & à pietate alienum, Apocal. XXII. 18.

## 6:14
Vers. 14. For if you forgive men their trespasses] There is indeed a place where παράπτωμα, when opposed to ἁμαρτία, may signify lesser offenses, as in Eph. II. 1. But also in this place, which the preceding words also prove, and elsewhere, as in Rom. IV. 25 and Col. II. 13, it embraces all kinds of offenses. Christ teaches here that just as the heavenly kingdom, so also that indulgence of sins which precedes the kingdom, is not open to us, unless under the condition of a new obedience, of which a great part consists in gentleness in forgiving injuries. Christ does not forbid παιδείαν καὶ νουθεσίαν [discipline and instruction] which parents owe to their children, and indeed to others: nor, as we showed above, does he abolish the laws of the courts, although it is certain that clemency is required even in the exercise of them: but he wishes us to be of a mind averse to revenge, so that we neither exact it ourselves, nor demand it from a judge, nor indeed even from God, but that, as he was just saying, we do good to those who have harmed us. Moreover, it is a benefit even to help them with prayers before God. Nor indeed, as some think, is this to be performed only to those who testify to their repentance by their deeds, but even to those who rage against us through some error, by the example of Christ in Luke 23:34. But those who sin inexcusably with a malicious purpose of mind are to be left to God, Romans 12:19. Effort must be made, however, that we interpret the faults of others as kindly as possible, especially those committed against us, since otherwise a grieving mind naturally inclines toward the harsher side. This is also the sentiment of Christ derived from the tenets of the ancient Hebrews: which is read both among the Talmudists and in the wise Hebrew, Ecclesiasticus 28:3: 'Man cherishes anger against man, and does he seek healing from the Lord? And he has no mercy on a man like himself, and he prays for his own sins; he himself being flesh cherishes wrath, and who will atone for his sins?' Where it is tacitly understood from the name of man and 'like' and 'flesh' that God is so much greater: just as here, from the word of the heavenly Father, the opposite of the earthly and heavenly brother is understood. It is from Seneca: 'That you may be absolved, forgive': and in the tragedy: 'Let him grant pardon easily, who has need of pardon.'

St. Augustine speaks beautifully of these things in Sermon 29 on the words of the Apostle, explaining the words 'As we also forgive our debtors.' This pledge with God is a true pledge and a fixed condition. You are a man, and you have a debtor, and you are also a debtor. You approach God, who has debtors and is not a debtor, to ask that your debts be released. But he says this to you: I have no debts, you have debts; for you owe me. But your brother also owes you. You are my debtor, and you also have a debtor. You are my debtor because you have sinned against me; you have a debtor in your brother because he has sinned against you. What you do with your debtor, I also do with him; that is, if you forgive, I forgive; if you hold, I hold. You hold against yourself if you do not forgive another.

These things, however, are not to be taken as Grotius takes them: as if the indulgence of sins were promised only under the condition of new obedience, of which gentleness in forgiving injuries is a part. For the remission of sins comes to us through faith, χωρὶς ἔργων [without works], as the Apostle testifies; therefore it is not right to introduce any condition here, since the Holy Spirit promises us the grace of God without condition. Nor does new obedience, or the purpose of it, precede justification or the remission of sins, but follows it, as the fruit of repentance and justice; and although it is required for continuing justification or not losing the remission of sins, it is not, however, the cause of the remission of sins or of our justification, lest that not be free and uncertain if it were suspended upon our forgiveness. Concerning which we spoke at verse 12. We are taught, therefore, that it is only our duty to forgive the τὰ παραπτώματα [trespasses] to our neighbor, just as God forgives our faults, so that we may imitate the heavenly Father in this, lest by our lack of mercy toward our neighbor we again fall from the mercy of God with that wicked servant: but the remission of sins is not suspended upon our gentleness or new obedience.

Latin:

Vers. 14. Ἐὰν γὰρ ἀφῆτε τοῖς ἀνθρώποις τὰ παραπτώματα αὐτῶν] Est quidem ubi παράπτωμα oppositum τῇ ἁμαρτίᾳ significet delicta minora, ut Eph. II. 1. Sed & hoc loco, quod præcedentia quoque evincunt, & alibi, ut Rom. IV. 25. Col. II. 13. omnia delictorum genera complectitur. Docet hic Christus, sicut regnum cœleste, ita eam quæ regnum præce- dit peccatorum indulgentiam, non patere nobis, nisi sub- conditione novæ obedientiæ, cujus pars magna fit lenitas in condonandis injuriis. Non vetat Christus παιδείαν καὶ νο- θεσίαν quam parentes liberis, imo & aliis debent: neque, ut supra ostendimus, judiciorum leges tollit, quamquam cer- tum est in illis etiam exercendis clementiam requiri: sed vult nos ab ultione animo esse alieno, ita ut eam nec exiga- mus ipsi, nec à judice, imo ne à Deo quidem postulemus, sed ut modo dicebat, benefaciamus iis qui nos læserunt. Beneficium autem est etiam precibus ipsos apud Deum ad- juvare. Neque vero, ut quidam putant, præstandum hoc est iis solis qui pœnitentiam factis testantur, sed illis etiam qui errore quodam in nos sæviunt, Christi exemplo Luc. XXIII. 34. Illi vero qui maligno animi proposito inexcuta- biliter peccant, Deo permittendi sunt Rom. XII.19. Dan- da autem est opera ut delicta aliorum quam benignissime interpretemur, præsertim quæ in nos sunt commissa, cum alioqui in partem sequiorem nimirum sua sponte provergat dolens animus. Est autem hæc etiam Christi sententia ex veterum Hebræorum placitis: quod & apud Thalmudicos legitur & apud sapientem Hebræum Ecclef. XXVIII. 3. ἄν- θρωπος ἀνθρώπῳ συντηρεῖ ὀργὴν κὶ παρὰ κυρίυ ζητεῖ ἴασιν· κὶ ἐπ ἀνθρωπον ὅμοιον αὐτῷ οὐκ ἔχει ἔλεον, κὶ περὶ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν αὑτῶ δεῖται· αὐτὸς σάρξ ὢν διατηρεῖ μῶνιν κὶ τίς ἐξιλάσεται τὰς ἁμαρτίας ἀυτῦ; Ubi tacite ex nomine hominis & simi- lis & carnis datur intelligi, Deus tanto major: sicut hic ex voce Patris cœlestis, intelligitur oppositum terrestris & fratris cœlestis, intelligitur oppositum terrestris & fratris. Senecæ est: Ut absolvaris, ignosce: & in tragœdia: Det il- le veniam facile, cui venia est opus.

Pulchre de his S. Augustinus sermon. XXIX. de verb. Apost. explicans verba Sicut & nos remit- timus debitoribus nostris. Sponsio hæc cum Deo ve- ra sponsio, & fixa conditio est. Tu homo es, & habes debitorem, & debitor etiam tu es. Accedis ad Deum, qui habet debitores, & debitor non est, ut postulet sibi debita relaxari. Sed hoc tibi dicit. Ego debita non habeo, tu habes debita; debes enim mihi. Sed etiam frater tuus debet tibi. Debitor meus es, habes & tu debitorem. Debitor meus es, quia peccasti in me, habes debitorem fratrem, quia peccavit in te. Quod feceris cum debitore tuo, facio & ego cum eo, id est, si dimittis, dimitto, si tenes, teneo. Tu contra te tenes qui alteri non dimittis.

Non tamen ita hæc accipienda, quemadmo- dum Grotius accipit: quasi peccatorum indulgentia sub conditione novæ obedientiæ, cujus pars est lenitas in condonandis injuriis, solum promittatur. Nam remissio peccatorum nobis obtingit per fidem, χωρὶς ἔργων, teste Apostolo; nullam ergo conditionem hic ingerere fas est, ut citra condi- tionem nobis gratiam Dei promittit Spiritus S. Neque novæ obedientiæ, aut propositum ejusdem antecedit justificationem, vel remissionem peccato- rum, sed consequitur eam, ceu fructus pœnitentiæ & justitiæ, & quanquam requiratur ad justificatio- nem continuandam vel peccatorum remissionem non perdendam, non tamen causa est remissionis pec- catorum, vel justificationis nostræ, ne illa non fit gratuita & incerta, si suspenderatur à nostra con- donatione. Quo de ad v. 12. diximus. Doce- mur ergo solum opus esse ut condonemus τὰ πα- ραπτώματα proximo, quemadmodum condonat nobis delicta nostra Deus, ut Patrem cœlestem in eo imitemur, ne immisericordia nostra adversus proximum cum servo illo nequam iterum Dei misericordia excidamus: non autem suspendi- tur remissio peccatorum à lenitate nostra, aut no- va obedientia.

## 6:16
Verse 16. Ὅταν δὲ νηστεύητε [But when you fast]. Christ is not dealing here properly with the common fasts of the people, such as the one solemn fast commanded by God regarding the days of the day of atonement, and three others added in the times of the restoration of the temple, but with those which each person imposed upon himself privately, whether for several continuous days out of order, or by some perpetual custom on set days, namely Monday and Thursday, as most Pharisees did, of whom those who wished to appear more religious added also the day of Tuesday and Friday. The ἀσκησις [asceticism] of the Pharisees was very severe; for they took absolutely no food before sunset, and even then they ate nothing but herbs or eggs. But they were also harder on themselves in their sleeping, for they not only separated themselves from their wives, but some observed χαμευνίαν [sleeping on the ground], and others, as Epiphanius testifies, even spread thorns under themselves so that they would not rest. As Christ does not disapprove of the exercise of fasting, so he here marks those who sought a reputation for holiness through such things. This applies especially to the Pharisees, who had even received their name from the fact that, not content with fulfilling the rites commanded by the law, they were distinguished from the rest of the people by other more severe institutions. See Luke 18:12.

Σκυθρωποὶ [Gloomy]: Sad: the Vulgate version is good. See Luke 24:17. Add the Greek interpreters Genesis 40:7, Daniel 1:10.

Σκυθρωπὸς [Gloomy] is said as if ὁ σκυθρὸς τὰς ὦπας [he who is gloomy in his looks], i.e., bearing an angry and sad countenance.

Ἀφανίζουσι γὰρ τὰ πρόσωπα [For they disfigure their faces]: They deform, just as Ovid said that a neglected face perishes. These verses are cited from the Eupla of Antiphanes in Stobaeus: Ὥσπερ ποιητῷ ζωγράφῳ τὰ χρώματα Πρώτιστον ἀφανίζουσιν ἐκ τῶ σώματος. But it should be read πόνῳ δ᾽ ὥσπερ ζωγράφου. The sense is: But adverse circumstances, as a painter is wont to do, first wash away the color from the body.

Moreover, Christ here is not dealing so much with leanness and pallor, which naturally accompany starvation, as with a certain affected sadness of countenance and gestures, such as Jeremiah 58:5 describes graphically.

Latin:

Vers. 16. Ὅταν δὲ νηστεύητε] Proprie agit hic Christus non de communibus populi jejuniis, quale erat à Deo præceptum solenne unum circa dies sacri piacularis, & tria alia addita instaurati templi temporibus, sed de his quæ privatim sibi quisque indicebat, sive per continuos aliquot extra ordinem, sive perpetuo quodam mo- re statis diebus, nimirum Lunæ & Jovis, ut plerique Pharisæi, quorum qui videri volebant religiosiores etiam Martis & Veneris diem adjungebant. Erat autem severa admodum Pharisæorum ἀσκησις; nam c bum plane nullum sumebant ante solem occasum, & tunc quoque non nisi oleribus aut ovis vescebantur. Sed & in cubitu erant in se duriores, neque enim tantum ab uxoribus se- cubabant, sed alii servabant χαμευνίαν, alii, Epiphanio te- ste, etiam spinas sibi substernebant quominus conqui- scerent. Christus ut non improbat jejunii exercitatio- nem, ita eos hic notat, qui per talia famam sanctimoniæ aucupabantur. Quod præcipue in Pharisæos convenit, qui nomen etiam inde acceperant, quod non contenti implere ritus lege præceptos, aliis severioribus institu- tis à reliqua plebe discernerentur. Vide Luc. XVIII. 12.

Σκυθρωποὶ] Tristes: bene vulgata versio. Vide Lucæ XXIV. 17. Adde Græcos interpretes Gen. XL. 7. Dan. I. 10.

Σκυθρωπὸς dicitur quasi ὁ σκυθρὸς τὰς ὦπας, h. e. iratum tristemque gerens vultum.

Ἀφανίζουσι γὰρ τὰ πρόσωπα] Deformant, quomodo fa- ciem neglectam perire dixit Ovidius. Citantur ex Euplæ Antiphanis apud Stobæum hi versus: Ὥσπερ ποιητῷ ζωγράφῳ τὰ χρώματα Πρώτιστον ἀφανίζουσιν ἐκ τῶ σώματος. Sed legi debet πόνῳ δ᾽ ὥσπερ ζωγράφου. Sensus est: At res adversæ, quomodo pictor solet, Primum colorem delinunt de corpore.

Cæterum Christus hic non tam agit de macie & pallore, quæ inediam naturaliter comitantur, quam de affectata quadam vultus tristitia & gestibus, quales describit graphi- ce Jerem. LVIII. 5.

## 6:17
Vers. 17. Anoint your head and wash your face] That is, show your daily countenance and habit: for both the Jews and their neighbors were accustomed to wash and be anointed outside of times of mourning: but especially as often as they were more joyful than usual, as on feast days, Ruth III. 3. 2 Sam. XII. 20. XIV. 2. 2 Kings IV. 2. Esther II. 12. Moreover, most used oil for anointing, Ps. CIV. 15. Thus in Homer, Odyss. 2. Χρῶν ἀποviπτεσϑ, καὶ ἀποχρίεσϑαι ἀλοιφῇ. The Scholiast interprets ἀλοιφῇ as oil. They were also more elegant with other ointments. See the history of Judith X. 3. & XVI. 9. The ancient Christians also did not abstain entirely from ointments: on which matter see Clement, Paedagogus, book [3], chapter XVIII, where he disapproves of the use of perfumes, but shows that anointing with ointment sometimes has honest uses, even citing that noble saying of Aristippus: let the catamites perish who have brought such a good thing into disrepute. But the honesty or baseness of such things is to be estimated not so much from their own nature as from the customs of nations. Let this saying hold here: It is good to follow the laws of the land. Justin, or whoever is the very ancient writer to Diognetus, says that Christians live everywhere in the world, among Greeks and Barbarians, following the local customs in clothing and diet and the rest of their life.

Latin:

Vers. 17. Ἄλειψαί σου τὴν κεφαλὴν κὶ τὸ πρόσωπόν σου νίψαι] Hoc est, præfer vultum & habitum quotidianum: nam & lavati & ungi solebant Judæi eorumque vicini extra luctus tempora: præcipue vero quoties solito erant lætio- res, ut diebus festis, Ruth. III. 3. 2. Sam. XII. 20. XIV. 2. 2. Reg. IV. 2. Esther. II. 12. ad unctionem autem pleri- que utebantur oleo, Ps. CXIV. 15. Sic apud Homerum Odyss. 2. Χρῶν ἀποviπτεσϑ, καὶ ἀποχρίεσϑαι ἀλοιφῇ. Scholiastes ἀλοιφῇ interpretatur ἐλαίῳ. nitidiores aliis et- iam unguentis. Vide Judithæ historiam X. 3. & XVI. 9. Christiani quoque veteres unguentis non in totum absti- nuerunt: qua de re videndus Clemens Pædagog. lib. cap. XVIII. ubi τὸ μυραλοιφεῖν improbat, τὸ δὲ χρίεσϑαι τῷ μύρῳ o- stendit usus honestos interdum habere, etiam nobile illud Aristippi dictum referens: pereant cinædi qui rem tam bo- nam infamarunt. Sed rerum ejusmodi honestas aut tur- pitudo non tam ex ipsarum natura quam ex gentium mori- bus æstimanda est. Valeat hic illud: Νόμοις ἕπεσϑαι τοῖσιν ἐγχώροις καλόν. Justinus, aut quisquis est scriptor vetustissimus ad Diogne- tum, Christianos ait vivere ubique terrarum, inter Græcos & Barbaros, τοῖς ἐγχωρίοις ἤθεσιν ἀκολουϑοῦντας ἐν τῇ ἐσθῆτι κὶ διαίτῃ κὶ τῷ λοιπῷ βίῳ.

## 6:18
Vers. 18. He will reward you] Fasting therefore has its own reward, not indeed viewed in isolation (for bodily exercise has little use in itself) but insofar as it serves piety, which has promises of the present life and the future, 1 Tim. IV. 8. Salvian, in book I of On Divine Providence, explains the use of fasting not badly: Someone not imprudently said in this place that if, because the body resists, we cannot do the things we desire, we must weaken the flesh so that we may do what we desire. For the weakness of the flesh, he says, sharpens the vigor of the mind, so that with the limbs affected, the strength of the bodies is transferred into the virtues of the souls, the marrow does not flow with base flames, hidden incentives do not kindle an evil mind, wandering senses do not grow wanton through various delights: but the soul alone exults, joyful because the body is affected, as if the adversary were subjugated. In public, which fewer manuscripts add here, is repeated from the preceding passages.

Spanheim more correctly observes that ἀποδιδόναι, both among the LXX and among the Hellenists who imitate them, is the same as διδόναι, and the word נתן is rendered indiscriminately by both, as it is also sometimes by δωρεῖσθαι. Hence both the simple and the compound are in indiscriminate use among the writers of the New Testament.

PART II. On the flight from avarice and worldly care.

Latin:

Vers. 18. ἀποδώσει σοι] Habet ergo jejunium suam quo- que mercedem, nimirum non seorsim spectatum (nam σω- ματικὴ γυμνασία exiguum per se usum habet) sed quate- nus pietati inservit, quæ promissiones habet vitæ præsentis & futuræ 1. Tim. IV. 8. Usum jejunii non male explicat Salvianus lib. I. de divina providentia: Non imprudenter quidam hoc loco dixit, quod si repugnante corpore is fortitudine quæ optamus facere non possumus, infirmandum nobis sit car- ne ut optata faciamus. Infirmitas enim carnis, inquit, vigorem mentis exacuit, ut affectis artubus vires corporum in virtutes transferantur animorum, non turpibus flammis medulla æ- fluent, non malefanam mentem latentia incentiva succendant, non vagi sensus per varia oblectamenta lasciviant: sed sola ex- sultet anima, læta corpore affecto, quasi adversario subjugato. Ἐν φανερῷ, quod pauciores codices hic addunt, ex locis superioribus repetitum est.

Rectius Spanhemius observat τὸ ἀποδιδόναι & apud LXX. & apud Hellenistas illorum imitatores, i- dem quod διδόναι, & verbum נתן promiscue per u- trumque redditum, ut & per δωρεῖσθαι quandoque. Hinc utrumque, & simplex, & compositum, in usu promiscuo apud Scriptores Novi Testamenti.

PARS II. De fuga avaritiæ & curæ Ethnicæ.

## 6:19
Vers. 19. Do not store up for yourselves treasures] Coelestius thought that in this and other places of the Gospel all possession of things not necessary, which we call riches, is forbidden. This is validly refuted by the words of Paul in 1 Tim. VI. 17. But one can also err in the other direction, as if we should suppose that here either only those are censured who, defrauding their own genius, brood over buried gold, or those who pursue gain through force and wicked deceit, the former of which vices the Greeks distinctly call φειδωλίαν, the latter πλεονεξίαν; whereas here is rather censured the vice of φιλαργυρία, the love of money, as Sallust expresses it, which the connection of verse 25 and ones with these preceding ones makes manifest. These are they whom Paul in the already mentioned Epistle VI, 8 calls τοὺς βουλομένους πλουτεῖν (those who desire to be rich), and whom he says are ensnared by many enticements, and at length are accustomed to be plunged into destruction: where βούλεσθαι (to desire) is taken almost in the same way as those who think their own thoughts are said βούλεσθαι τὰ τῶν συμμάχων (to desire the things of the allies). The word θησαυρίζειν (to treasure up) is indeed of itself neutral, so that it is used also of praiseworthy deeds in 1 Corinthians XVI. 2 and others not placed in the category of vice, 2 Corinthians XII. 14. But it happens to that word as to many others, that sometimes it signifies πρᾶξιν (the act), but sometimes, as here, τὴν ἕξιν (the habit), to which is usually joined a tenacity in spending money for the uses of others. For those who do this, that they may have as much as possible, either do it so that they themselves may live more sumptuously, more softly, and more proudly, or they are delighted by mere possession. But both are an obstacle to beneficence. In the same sense τὸ θησαυρίζειν (the treasuring up) is taken in Luke XII. 21 and James V. 3.

Ὅπου σὴς καὶ βρῶσις ἀφανίζει (Where moth and rust consume): The Hebrews use אכל, which corresponds to the Greek βρώσεως (of rust/consumption), of any consumption whatsoever, even by fire or sword. Hence it came about that that which specifically consumes a thing from within was called אכלת, which the Syrian here has placed, that is βρῶσις (rust/consumption), whence σητόβρωτα (moth-eaten) are those things which are consumed by moths, James V. 3. But in this place, since σὴς (moth) is specifically named, the word of the genus is to be referred to all other species of the same genus, such as that which the Greeks call ἰὸν (rust), and the Latins, according to the diversity of the material, call ærugo (copper rust) or ferrugo (iron rust). For what σὴς (moth) is in garments, this ἰὸς (rust) or βρῶσις (consumption) is in metals: whence those things are frequently wont to be joined, as in Menander?

And all things that damage are within. For instance, if you look at rust on iron, moths on a garment, and the woodworm on wood.

Moreover, the Apostle James himself, undoubtedly looking back at these words of Christ, says: τὰ ἱμάτια ὑμῶν σητόβρωτα γέγονεν. ὁ χρυσὸς ὑμῶν καὶ ὁ ἄργυρος κατίωται (your garments have become moth-eaten. Your gold and silver have rusted) in the mentioned chapter V. 2, 3. ἀφανίζειν (to consume) here is what is λυμαίνεσθαι (to damage) in Menander, and διαφθείρειν (to destroy) in Luke.

Καὶ ὅπου κλέπται διορύσσουσι καὶ κλέπτουσι (And where thieves break through and steal): With a similar argument Martial invites men to liberality: for when he had enumerated the cases to which the things we possess are wont to be subject, and among other things had said what fits this place especially well:

A cunning thief will carry off your coins from a broken chest:

at length he concludes:

The wealth you have given away is the only wealth you will always have. In Menander's Dyscolus also, a son exhorts his father to beneficence from the same instability of possessions:

You speak of money, an uncertain thing. For if you know that these things remain with you for all time, keep them, sharing them with no one else, and being yourself the master. If you do not even have them for yourself, but all things belong to fortune, why, father, would you begrudge them to anyone? For she, having taken them away from you, will perhaps add them all again to some other unworthy person; wherefore I say that you ought, as long as you are the master, to use them nobly, father, to help everyone yourself, and to make as many of your friends as you can prosperous through yourself.

Add what we shall now bring forward from Xenophon. Rabirius said: I have what I have given.

Latin:

Vers. 19. Μὴ θησαυρίζετε ὑμῖν θησαυροὺς] Putavit Cœle- stius hoc & aliis Evangelii locis omnem rerum non neces- sarium possessionem, quas divitias vocamus, prohiberi. Quod valide refutatur Pauli verbis 1. Tim. VI. 17. Sed in alteram quoque partem errari potest, ut si hic aut eos tantum- putemus notari qui genium suum fraudantes auro defos- so incubant, aut qui per vim dolumque malum lucra se- ctantur, quorum illud vitium φειδωλίαν, hoc πλεονε- ξίαν distincte Græci vocant: cum hic potius notetur vi- tium τῆς φιλαργυρίας, pecuniæ studium ut Sallustius lo- quitur, quod commatis 25. & sequentium cum his ante- cedentibus connexio manifestum facit. Hi sunt quos Paulus jam dicta Epistola VI, 8. vocat τοὺς βουλομένους πλου- τεῖν, quosque ait illaqueari multis irritamentis, ac tan- dem in exitium solere demergi: ubi βούλεσθαι ita ferme sumitur quomodo βούλεσθαι τὰ τῶν συμμάχων dicuntur οἱ τὰ αὐτῶν φρονοῦντες. Est quidem vox θησαυρίζειν per se media, ita ut & de factis laudabilibus I. Corinth. XVI. 2. aliisque non in vitio positis usurpetur, 2. Corinth. XII. 14. Sed ei voci accidit quod aliis pluribus, ut interdum πρᾶξιν, in- terdum vero ut hic τὴν ἕξιν significet, cui conjuncta es- se solet tenacitas erogandæ in alienos usus pecuniæ. Nam qui hoc agunt ut quamplurimum habeant, aut id faciunt ut ipsi lautius, mollius ac superbius vivant, aut nuda pos- sessione delectantur. Utrumque autem obstat beneficen- tiæ. Eodem sensu sumitur τὸ θησαυρίζειν Luc. XII. 21. & Jacob. V. 3.

Ὅπου σὴς καὶ βρῶσις ἀφανίζει] Hebræi אכל quod Græ- co βρώσεως respondet usurpant de quavis consumtione, et- iam per ignem aut gladium. Hinc factum, ut id præci- pue quod rem intus depascitur, diceretur אכלת quod hic posuit Syrus id est βρῶσις, unde σητόβρωτα quæ à tineis depascuntur Jac. V. 2. Hoc vero loco cum σὴς specialiter nominetur, generis vox ad omnes alias ejusdem generis species referenda est, ut id quod Græci ἰὸν, Latini pro ma- teriæ diversitate æruginem aut ferruginem vocant. Nam quod σὴς est in vestibus, hoc ἰὸς sive βρῶσις est in metallis: unde ista frequenter conjungi solent, ut apud Menan- drum?

Καὶ πάντα τὰ λυμαινόμεν' ἔνεστιν ἔνδοθεν. Οἷον ὁ μὲν ἰὸς τὸν σίδηρον ἂν σκοπῇς, Τὸ δ' ἱμάτιον οἱ σῆτες, ἡ δὲ θρὶψ ξύλον.

Quin & ipse Jacobus Apostolus haud dubie hæc Christi verba respiciens τὰ ἱμάτια ὑμῶν σητόβρωτα γέγονεν. ὁ χρυ- σὸς ὑμῶν καὶ ὁ ἄργυρος κατίωται dicto capite V. 2. 3. ἀφανίζειν hic est quod Menandro λυμαίνεσθαι, Lucæ διαφθείρειν.

Καὶ ὅπου κλέπται διορύσσουσι καὶ κλέπτουσι] Simili argu- mento Martialis homines ad liberalitatem invitat: nam cum enumerasset casus quibus subjecta esse solent quæ possideinus, atque inter cætera dixisset quod huic loco ap- prime convenit:

Callidus effracta nummos fur auferet arca:

tandem concludit:

Quas dederis, solas semper habebis opes. In Menandri etiam Dyscolo filius patrem ad beneficentiam hortatur ex eadem possessionum instabilitate:

Περὶ χρημάτων λαλεῖς ἀβεβαίου πράγματος. Εἰ μὲν γὰρ οἶσθα ταῦτα παραμένοντά σοι Εἰς πάντα τὸν χρόνον, φύλαττε μηδενὶ Ἄλλῳ μεταδιδοὺς· αὐτὸς ὢν δὲ κύριος. Εἰ μηδ' ἑαυτῦ, τῆς τυχῆς ἅπαντ' ἔχεις, Τί ἂν φθονοίης ὦ πάτερ τούτων τινί; Αὐτὴ γὰρ ἄλλῳ τυχὸν ἀναξίῳ τινὶ Παρελομένη σου πάντα προσθήσει πάλιν· Διόπερ ἐγώ σε φημὶ δεῖν, ὅσον χρόνον Εἶ κύριος, χρῆσθαί σε γενναίως, πάτερ, Αὐτὸν ἐπικουρεῖν πᾶσιν, εὐπόρους ποιεῖν Ὡς ἂν δύνῃ πλείστους διὰ σαυτῦ τῶν φίλων.

Adde quæ jam ex Xenophonte adferemus. Rabirius dixit: Hoc habeo, quodcunque dedi.

## 6:20
V. 20. Θησαυρίζετε δὲ ὑμῖν θησαυροὺς ἐν ὀρανῷ (But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven): He said ὀρανὸν (heaven) here and in some other places, which is more frequently ὀρανός. The meaning is with God, just as the baptism of John is said to have been ἐξ ὀρανῦ (from heaven), that is, from God, Luke XX. 4. But that storehouse which Christ commands to be filled are good works, as Paul interprets in 1 Timothy VI, 17, 18, as things which God preserves in His memory to profit us one day, as it is explained there by Paul. Among these good works, however, deeds of kindness to the poor hold a certain preeminent place, which Christ specifically calls θησαυρὸν ἐν ὀρανῷ (treasure in heaven) in Luke XIX. 21. But also the writer of Tobias, so that it may appear that this also is from the ancient sayings of the Hebrews. There is, however, a passage clearly similar to this in Xenophon, in the last book of the Cyropaedia, where Cyrus says that treasures are being gathered by him far different from those of other kings, namely such as do not decay, except that he refers these to the safeguards of this life, not to a better life. The words are: ὁρᾶς, ὦ κροῖσε, ὡς εἰσὶ κἀμοὶ θησαυροί. ἀλλὰ σύ μὲν κελεύεις με παρ' ἐμοὶ αὐτοὺς συλλέγοντα φθονεῖσθαί τε δι' αὐτοὺς κὴ μισεῖσθαι

and setting mercenary guards over them, to trust in these; but I, by making my friends rich, consider them my treasures, and believe them to be more faithful guardians of both myself and my possessions than if I had set mercenary sentinels over them. Soon after: but I serve the gods and always reach out for more; and whenever I acquire what I see is surplus to what is sufficient for me, with these I satisfy the needs of my friends, and by enriching and benefiting men I gain from them goodwill and friendship, and from these I reap security and good repute, which neither rot away nor cause harm when they are in excess. A locution not unlike ours is found in Philostratus concerning Herodes the Sophist: he was treasuring up his wealth in the minds of those who shared his views.

He wishes the meaning to be that a treasure, i.e., good works, ought to be stored up before God, so that God may observe them in His memory to be of profit to us one day, 1 Tim. VI. 17, 18, from which good deeds toward the poor are specifically called θησαυροὶ ἐν ὀυρανῷ, Luke XIX. 21. But the treasure in heaven is not good works or our good deeds, for they are in many ways too imperfect, nor can they be held as a treasure in heaven: but the treasure of divine grace and mercy, Eph. II. 4, Rom. XI. 33, ch. II. 4, especially because our heart ought to be fixed not on our works, but on the grace of God, as Christ says, where your treasure is, there your heart is. God Himself is called the treasure of Jacob, i.e., of the faithful, which treasure cannot be consumed or taken from us. But for this, that we may gather for ourselves this treasure in heaven and enjoy the grace of God, there is need above all of faith, because God has chosen the rich in faith, James II. 5, who are rich in God, Luke XII. 21, who, with Christ providing, acquire for themselves gold purified by fire, so that they may become rich; which is the counsel of Christ Himself, Rev. III. 18, who are rich through Christ in all doctrine and in all knowledge, 1 Cor. I. 5. For Christ was made poor for our sake, that we might become rich through His poverty, 2 Cor. VIII. 9. But those who are rich in faith also strive to be rich in good works, 1 Tim. VI. 18, but they do not place their trust in them; nay, they count all things as loss and as σκυβάλοις in comparison to the knowledge of Christ, with the holy Apostle, Phil. III. 8. The art of acquiring and gathering heavenly treasures, or of preparing purses that do not grow old, is handed down from the Scriptures by the blessed Chemnitius: there is no doubt that his explanation is to be preferred to this gloss of Grotius. But you see it in the author himself in his Harmonia Evangelica on this passage.

Latin:

V. 20. Θησαυρίζετε δὲ ὑμῖν θησαυροὺς ἐν ὀρανῷ] ὀρανὸν hic & a- liis aliquot in locis dixit quod frequentius ὀρανός. Sensus est apud Deum, quomodo baptisma Johannis dicitur fuisse ἐξ ὀρανῦ, id est a Deo Luc. XX. 4. Penu autem istud quod Christus recondi jubet, sunt opera bona ut Paulus inter- pretatur 1. Tim. VI, 17. 18. ut quæ Deus in memoria sua asservet olim nobis profutura, ut ibidem à Paulo exponi- tur. Inter hæc autem bona opera eximium quendam lo- cum obtinent benefacta in pauperes, quæ peculiariter θη- σαυρὸν ἐν ὀρανῷ Christus vocat Luc. XIX. 21. Sed & Tobiæ scriptor, ut appareat & hoc ex veteribus esse dictis Hebræo- rum. Est autem locus plane huic similis apud Xenophon- tem de Cyri institutione libro ultimo, ubi Cyrus ait longe alios à se thesauros comparari quam à cæteris regibus, ta- les nempe qui non marcescant, nisi quod ille hæc ad hujus vitæ præsidia, non ad vitam meliorem refert. Verba sunt: ὁρᾶς, ὦ κροῖσε, ὡς εἰσὶ κἀμοὶ θησαυροί. ἀλλὰ σύ μὲν κελεύεις με παρ' ἐμοὶ αὐτοὺς συλλέγοντα φθονεῖσθαί τε δι' αὐτοὺς κὴ μισεῖσθαι

κὴ φύλακας αὐτοῖς ἐφισᾶντα μισθοφόρους, τούτοις πιστεύειν· ἐγὼ δὲ τοὺς φίλους πλουσίους ποιῶν, τούτους μοι νομίζω θησαύρους, καὶ φύλακας ἅμα ἐμοῦ τε καὶ τῶν ἡμετέρων ἀγαθῶν πιστοτέρους εἶναι, ἢ εἰ φρουροὺς μισθοφόρους ἐπεστησάμην. Mox: ἐγὼ δὲ ὑπηρετῶ μὲν τοῖς θεοῖς κὴ ὀρέγομαι αἰεὶ πλειόνων· ἐπειδὰν δὲ κτήσωμαι ἃ ἂν ἴ- δω περιττὰ ὄντα τῶν ἐμοὶ ἀρκούντων, τούτοις τάς τ' ἐνδείας τῶν φί- λων ἐξαρκοῦμαι, κὴ πλουτίζων καὶ εὐεργετῶν ἀνθρώπους εὔνοιαν ἐξ αὐτῶν κτῶμαι κὴ φιλίαν, κὴ ἐκ τούτων καρποῦμαι ἀσφάλειαν κὴ εὔ- κλειαν, ἃ οὔτε κατασήπεται οὔτε ὑπερπληθοῦντα λυμαίνεται. Locutio huic nostræ non dissimilis apud Philostratum de Herode Sophista: ἐθησαύριζε τὸν πλοῦτον ἐν ταῖς ὃ μετεχόν- των αὐτῷ γνώμαις.

Sensum esse vult, apud Deum thesaurum h. e. bona opera recondi debere, ut quæ Deus in memoria sua observet olim nobis profutura 1. Tim. VI. 17. 18. è quibus benefacta in pauperes peculiariter vocentur θησαυροὶ ἐν ὀυρανῷ Luc. XIX. 21. At Thesaurus in cœlo non sunt bona opera, aut benefacta nostra, nam & multis modis imperfectiora sunt, neque pro thesauro in cœlis haberi possunt: Sed the- saurus gratiæ & misericordiæ divinæ Eph. II. 4, Rom. XI. 33. c. II. 4. imprimis, quia cor nostrum fixum es- se debet non in operibus nostris, sed in gratia Dei, uti Christus ait, ubi thesaurus vester, ibi cor vestrum. Deus ipse dicitur thesaurus Jacobi, h. e. fidelium, qui thesaurus non consumi, aut eripi nobis potest. Ad id autem, ut colligamus nobis hunc thesaurum in cœlis, & gratia Dei fruamur, opus imprimis est fide, quia Deus elegit divites in fide Jac. III. 5. qui divites sunt in Deo Luc. XII. 21. qui præbente Christi comparant sibi aurum igne purga- tum, ut divites evadant; quod Christi ipsius est consilium Apoc. III. 18. qui divites sunt per Chri- stum in omni doctrina, & in omni cognitione 1. Cor. I. 5. Christus enim factus est pauper propter nos, ut nos paupertate illius ditesceremus 2. Cor. VIII. 9. Qui vero in fide divites sunt, divites etiam in bonis ope- ribus esse student 1. Tim. VI. 18. sed in illis fiduciam suam non collocant, imo pro damno, & pro σκυ- βάλοις habent omnia in συγκρίσει ad agnitionem Christi, cum S. Apostolo Phil. III. 8. Artem ac- quirendi & colligendi cœlestes thesauros, seu comparandi sacculos, qui non veterascunt, è Scri- pturis tradit B. Chemnitius: cujus explicatio quin præferenda huic glossæ Grotianæ sit, nullum est du- bium. Sed videtis illam penes ipsum autorem in Harmon. Evang. in h. l.

## 6:21
Vers. 21. Ὅπου γάρ ἐστιν ὁ θησαυρὸς, ὑμῶν ἐκεῖ ἔσται, καὶ ἡ καρδία ὑμῶν] καρδία, that is, νοῦς, as Justin presents this passage in his second Apology. The Aulularia of Plautus shows this sentiment to be most true. We are accustomed to guard diligently only those things which we value highly. This, therefore, is what Christ means: according to how we judge things, so are we affected toward them: if we believe happiness is placed in riches, it will happen that we will neglect nothing in our zeal to acquire money: but if we believe true virtue is the solid good, we will devote all our effort to it. And indeed it is true, as the philosophers also teach, that from the decrees conceived in the mind follow τὰς ὁρμὰς κὴ τὰς ἐκκλίσεις. Epictetus, as is his custom, says forcefully: ὅπου τὸ συμφέρον ἐκεῖ κὴ τὸ εὐσεβές. Whence they also warn that we ought to be solicitous to learn to value each thing at its own price. Well, therefore, Horace:

what pertains more to us, and which it is a misfortune not to know, we discuss: whether men are made happy by riches or by virtue.

And elsewhere he brings forward this cause for the avarice of Staberius: as long as he lived, he believed poverty to be a huge vice, and he guarded against nothing more keenly, so that if by chance he perished less wealthy by a single farthing, he seemed to himself more wicked.

Nor, however, are vices to be excused because they are born from corrupt judgments, for as Hierocles rightly says: Τὰ δεικνύμενα ὑπὸ τοῦ Θεοῦ οἱ πολλοὶ οὐχ ὁρῶσι, διὰ τὸ μὴ ὀρθῶς χρῆσθαι ταῖς κοι- ναῖς ἐννοίαις ἂς προσέφυσεν ὁ δημιουργὸς τῷ λογικῷ γένει πρὸς ἐπίγνωσιν ἑαυτοῦ. It is therefore our duty τὸ νῶι προσέχειν and either not to admit those perverse judgments, or to cast them out once admitted, for which purpose those κοιναὶ ἔννοιαι or preconceptions have been given to us, so that we may examine the weights of our opinions by their infallible balance, to which Christ here appeals.

The opinion of Chrysostom is relevant here: Those who are about to move their dwelling to another place are accustomed to send their treasures ahead there: what folly is it, therefore, to store up treasures there from which one must soon depart, and not rather to send them ahead to the place where you are about to migrate, and where you are to remain forever?

Latin:

Vers. 21. Ὅπου γάρ ἐστιν ὁ θησαυρὸς, ὑμῶν ἐκεῖ ἔσται, καὶ ἡ καρδία ὑμῶν] καρδία id est νοῦς ut Justinus hunc locum pro- fert Apologetico II. Verissimam esse hanc sententiam o- stendit Aulularia Plauti. Diligenter asservare ea demum solemus quæ magni facimus. Hoc ergo vult Christus, prout de rebus judicamus, ita nos erga eas affici: Si in divi- tiis positam credimus felicitatem, futurum ut nihil præver- tamus conquirendæ pecuniæ studio: sin veram virtutem so- lidum credimus bonum, ei nos omnem daturos operam. Et sane verum est, quod Philosophi etiam docent, ex decre- tis in animo conceptis sequi τὰς ὁρμὰς κὴ τὰς ἐκκλίσεις. Epi- ctetus, ut solet, nervose: ὅπου τὸ συμφέρον ἐκεῖ κὴ τὸ εὐσε- βές. Unde etiam monent sollicitos nos esse debere ut di- scamus rem quamque suo pretio æstimare. Bene ergo Ho- ratius:

quod magis ad nos Pertinet, & nescire malum est agitamus, utrumne Divitiis homines, an sint virtute beati.

Atque alibi avaritiæ Staberii hanc causam adfert: quoad vixit credidit ingens Pauperiem vitium, & cavit nihil acrius, ut si Forte minus locuples uno quadrante periret, Ipse videretur sibi nequior.

Neque tamen excusanda sunt vitia, quia ex corruptis judi- ciis nascuntur, nam ut recte dicit Hierocles:Τὰ δεικνύμενα ὑπὸ τοῦ Θεοῦ οἱ πολλοὶ οὐχ ὁρῶσι, διὰ τὸ μὴ ὀρθῶς χρῆσθαι ταῖς κοι- ναῖς ἐννοίαις ἂς προσέφυσεν ὁ δημιουργὸς τῷ λογικῷ γένει πρὸς ἐπίγνωσιν ἑαυτοῦ. Est ergo nostri officii τὸ νῶι προσέχειν & pravas illas judicationes, aut non admittere, aut admis- sas ejicere, quam ad rem datæ nobis sunt illæ κοιναὶ ἔννοιαι sive προλήψεις, ut ad earum trutinam minime fallacem o- pinationum pondera examinemus, ad quas Christus hic provocat,

Facit huc Chrysostomi sententia: Illi qui habita- tionem in alium locum translaturi sunt, thesauros suos eo solent præmittere: quæ igitur stultitia est ibi reponere thesauros, unde mox sibi exeundum sit, ac non potius illuc præmittere, quo migraturus, & ubi perpetuo mansurus es?

## 6:22
Ver. 22. The lamp of the body is the eye] Hence the eyes are called φάεα by the Greeks, and lumina by the Latins. Christ compares judgment to the eyes, and the mind to the body, by a similitude also used among the philosophers. Aristotle Top. I, 14. As sight is in the eye, so is the mind in the soul. Aristides: For because the mind has something similar to sight. For as the latter, when corrupted, sees nothing, not even the nearest things, but when healthy reaches as far as it can reach and discerns, so this very thing: the mind of the prudent man is capable of managing all men; but that of the foolish man can guard neither his own body nor one house. Plutarch in the Roman Questions: For the soul within is light. Jamblichus in the Pythagorean Symbols: That which according to prudence is like the light of the soul, and being indefinite, it defines it, and leads it around as if from darkness into light. Proclus, in his commentary on Plato's books on the Republic, compares the eye of the soul, by which it thinks, to the eyes. Galen similarly: As the eye is to the body, such is the mind in the soul. M. Antoninus lib. XII. The light of the lamp shines until it is extinguished and does not lose its brightness. Shall the truth and justice and temperance within you be extinguished first? Thus also Ovid, dealing with Pythagoras: And what nature denied to human vision, he drew into the eyes of his heart. But also among the Jews. Philo on the creation of the world: For what the mind is in the soul, that the eye is in the body. Afterwards: To man, to whom (God) granted as a special gift a certain soul, just like the pupil in the eye. Chrysostom in chapter IV of the first epistle to the Corinthians compares the foresight of the mind to an eye.

Ἁπλοῦς] Ἁπλοῦς is an eye that does not deceive, to which is opposed πονηρός, a deceitful eye. To the Hebrews the former is תם, the latter רע.

Φωτεινὸν ἔσται] Φωτεινὸν here means πεφωτισμένον, illuminated, just as σκοτεινὸν means ἐσκοτισμένον, wrapped in darkness. Most of the body's actions are directed by the guidance of the eyes: therefore the body is said to be illuminated when the eyes are in a right state, and to be wrapped in darkness when they are ailing. Hierocles: For just as it is not possible for an eye that is bleary and not cleansed to see things that are very bright, so it is not possible for a soul that has not acquired virtue to mirror the beauty of truth.

Latin:

Vers. 22. ὁ λύχνος τῦ σώματός ἐστιν ὁ ὀφθαλμὸς] Hinc o- culi φάεα Græcis, Latinis lumina. Comparat autem Chri- stus judicium oculis, animum corpori, similitudine etiam apud Philosophos usitata. Aristoteles Top. I, 14. Ὡς ὄψις ἐν ὀφθαλμῷ, νῦς ἐν ψυχῇ. Aristides: Καὶ γὰρ ὅτι ἔχοι τι πα- ραπλήσιον ὁ νῦς τῇ ὄψει. ὡς γὰρ ἐκείνη διεφθαρμένη μὲν ὠδὲν, ὠδὲ τῶν πλησιαιτάτων ὁρᾷ, ὑγιὴς δὲ ὅσα μέχρις ἐφικνεῖται κὴ ἀπό- φωσιν ἐξικνεῖται, ταυτὸ δὴ τῦτο ἡ μὲν τῦ φρονίμυ διάνοια κὴ πάν- τας ἀνθρώπυς ἱκανὴ γίνεται διοικεῖν· ἡ δὲ τῦ ἄφρονος ὠδὲ ἐν σῶμα τὸ ἐκείνε δύναται φυλάττειν, ὠδὶ ἕνα οἶκον. Plutarchus quæstionibus Romanis: Φῶς γάρ ἐστιν ἡ ἐντὸς ψυχή. Jam- blichus in Symbolis Pythagoricis: ὃ κατὰ φρόνησιν τῆς τῶ φωτὶ ἔοικε τῆς ψυχῆς, κὴ ἀόριστον ὖσαν αὐτὴν ὁρίζει, περιάγει τε ὥσπερ ἐκ σκότω εἰς φῶς. Proclus ad libros Platonis de repu- blica comparat oculis τὸ ὄμμα τῆς ψυχῆς, ᾧ δὴ νοεῖν. Gale- nus similiter: ὥσπερ ὀφθαλμὸς τῷ σώματι τοιῦτον ἐν τῇ ψυ- χῇ νῦς. M. Antoninus lib. XII. ἡ τὸ μὲν τῦ λύχνυ φῶς μέχρι σβε- σθῇ φαίνει κὴ τὴν αὐγὴν ἐκ ἀποβάλλει. ἡ δὲ ἐν σοὶ ἀλήθεια κὴ δι- καιοσύνη κὴ σωφροσύνη προαποσβήσεται; Sic & de Pythagora agens Ovidius: Et quæ natura negavit Visibus humanis oculis ea pectoris hausit. Sed & apud Judæos. Philo de mundi conditura: ὅπερ γὰρ νῦς ἐν ψυχῇ τοῦτ' ὀφθαλμὸς ἐν σώματι. Postea: τὸν ἄνθρωπον ᾧ τῶν ἐξαίρετον ἐδωρεῖτο (ὁ θεὸς) ψυχῇ τινα ψυχὴν, καθάπερ κό- ρην ἐν ὀφθαλμῷ. Chrysostomus in prioris ad Corinthios cap. IV. oculo comparat τὸ τῆς διανοίας προορατικόν.

Ἁπλοῦς] ἁπλοῦς est oculus qui non fallit, cui oppo- nitur πονηρός, oculus fallax. Hebræis ille תם, hic רע.

Φωτεινὸν ἔσται] Φωτεινὸν hic valet πεφωτισμένον illustratum, ut σκοτεινὸν, ἐσκοτισμένον tenebris involutum. Pleræque cor- poris actiones ductu oculorum diriguntur: ideo corpus dicitur oculis recte se habentibus illustrari: ægrotantibus tenebris involvi. Hierocles: ὥσπερ γὰρ ὀφθαλμῷ λημῶντι κὴ οὐ κεκαθαρμένῳ τὰ σφόδρα φωτεινὰ ἰδεῖν οὐχ' οἷόν τε, οὕτως κὴ τῇ ψυχῇ μὴ ἀρετὴν κεκτημένῃ τὸ τῆς ἀληθείας ἐνοπτρίσασθαι κάλλος.

## 6:23
Ver. 23. If therefore the light that is in you is darkness] Judgment, as we have said, is the sight of the mind to Socrates in the Symposium: the eye of the soul to Hierocles: the eyes of the mind to Paul in Ephesians I. 18. But darkness is put for dark, in the Hebrew manner.

Τὸ σκότος πόσον] How blind must the affections necessarily be when the judgment of the mind is corrupted? Excellently Hierocles: Since therefore the act of showing reveals the activities of two persons running toward it; (for how could you show to a blind man, even if you offered a thousand times what he wishes to be shown, or how could you show to a lover without bringing anything forward?) both therefore must be present, both the good proposed by the one showing, and the discerning eye of the one to whom it is shown, so that from the one the visible object, and from the other the vision, may run together toward the completion of the showing.

Since the eyes are the chief indicators of the mind, the eye is used among the Hebrews for the whole character of a man. And so the indicator of the mind itself is signified here, to which we ought to have applied ourselves rather than to the accumulating of wealth: so that just as the body is ruled by the eyes, so also our whole life might be ruled, being illuminated by right reason (that is, by the Spirit of God). He understands, therefore, a simple eye or countenance, which testifies to those who look upon it a pure and integral mind, that is to say, pure and integral: to which is opposed the wicked one, that is, a witness of an ill-affected mind, that is, defiled by some vice: which we also call in the vernacular tongue un mauvais œil. He calls the body lucid, however, which is illuminated by the light of the eyes, that is, by the right judgment of one who sees clearly: to which is opposed the dark one, that is, that which is placed in darkness, because the lights of the mind are hindered by vicious affections: as here Walaeus with Beza. We add what B. Gerhard has: If your eye is simple, that is, if you look upon the goods of your neighbor with a simple and fair mind, so that you do not envy him; for thus ἁπλότης is used in Rom. XII. 8, 2 Cor. VIII. 2, chap. IX. 11, then the whole body will be lucid, that is, cheerful, you will be entirely filled with cheerfulness.

Πονηρὸς is used for envious in Matt. XX. 15, just as also in Prov. XXIII. 6, chap. XXVIII. 22, the envious man is called evil of eye. He commands that the heart be kindled by the divine light of true doctrine, by the study of God, of true piety, and of heavenly things, and not be obscured by errors, ignorance of God, and distrust, otherwise all actions will be depraved. Bellarmine, 4 de Justif. cap. 15. Christ wishes to teach by metaphorical speech that men often stumble because they do not act by the preceding light of the divine word, but that they act rightly when they follow the light of the divine word and the lamp of faith shining before them. — As the eye is the light of the body, and directs it: if the mind is the light of man and rules all actions. If the eye is dark, the body is ruled badly: thus if the mind is occupied by depraved desires, avarice, or care for sustenance, destruction threatens man.

Latin:

Vers. 23. Εἰοὖν τὸ φῶς τὸ ἐν σοὶ, σκότος ἐστὶ] Judicium ut diximus, ὄψις τῆς διανοίας Socrati in Symposio: ὄμμα τῆς ψυχῆς Hierocli: ὀφθαλμοὶ τῆς διανοίας Paulo Ephes. I. 18. σκότος autem positum est pro σκοτεινὸν more Hebræo.

Τὸ σκότος πόσον] Quam cæcos affectus necesse est se- qui judicio mentis corrupto? Præclare Hierocles: ἐπεὶ οὖν τὸ δόξαι ἐστιῶν δύο προσώπων ἐνεργείας εἰς αὐτὸ δραμούσας ἐμ- φαίνει· (πῶς γὰρ ἂν δόξαις τυφλᾷ κἂν μυριάκις προσφέρῃς ὃ θέ- λῃ δόξαι, ἢ πῶς ἂν τῷ ἐρῶντι δόξαις μηδὲν προάγων; ) ἀμφό- τερα οὖν παρεῖναι δεῖ, τότε παρὰ τῦ δεικνύντος προταγόμενον ἀγαθὸν, κὴ τὸ παρὰ τῦ ᾧ δείκνυται διορατικὸν ὄμμα, ἵνα ἐ- κεῖθεν μὲν τὸ ὁρατὸν, ἐντεῦθεν δὲ ἡ ὅρασις συνδράμῃ πρὸς τὴν τῆς δόξεως συμπλήρωσιν.

Quoniam oculi sunt præcipui mentis indices, ideo pro toto hominis ingenio apud Hebræos oculus ponitur. Itaque mentis ipsius indicium hic signifi- catur, cui comparando potius, quam accumulan- dis opibus incumbere nos oportuit: ut sicut oculis corpus, ita quoque recta ratione (id est, Spiritu Dei) illustrata tota vita nostra regeretur. Simpli- cem igitur intelligit oculum seu vultum, qui pu- rum & integrum animum intuentibus testetur, ni- mirum purum & integrum: Cui opponitur impro- bus, id est male affectæ mentis testis, id est, aliquo vi- tio inquinatus: quem etiam in vernaculo sermone vo- camus un mauvais œil. Lucidum autem corpus vocat, quod luce oculorum, id est recto cernentis ju- dicio, illustratur: cui opponitur tenebrosum, id est, quod in tenebris positum est, vitiosis videlicet affecti- bus luminibus mentis officientibus: ut hic cum Beza Walæus. Addimus quæ habet B. Gerhardus: Si oculus tuus fuerit simplex, id est, si proximi bona animo simplici & æquo aspexeris, ut ipsi non invi- deas; ita enim usurpatur ἁπλότης Rom. XII. 8. 2. Cor. VIII. 2. cap. IX. 11. tunc totum corpus erit lucidum, id est, hilare, totus eris hilaritate repletus.

Πονηρὸς pro invido usurpatur Matth. XX. 15. sicut & Prov. XXIII. 6. cap. XXVIII. 22. invidus vocatur malus oculo. Præcipit ut cor sit divino lumine veræ doctrinæ accensum, studio Dei, veræ pietatis ac re- rum cælestium, non erroribus, ignorantia Dei ac diffidentia obscuratum, alioqui omnes actiones fore pravas. Bellarm. 4. de Justif. cap. 15. Christus meta- phorico sermone docere vult, homines sæpe im- pingere, quia non agunt prævia luce verbi divini, tunc vero recte agere, quando lumen verbi di- vini & fidei lampadam prælucentem sequun- tur. — Ut oculus est lumen corporis, illudque diri- git: si animus est lumen hominis & regit omnes a- ctiones. Si oculus est tenebricosus, male regitur corpus: sic si animus occupatus est pravis cupidita- tibus, avaritia, cura victus, imminet homini exi- tium.

## 6:24
Ver. 24. No one can serve two masters] Christ meets, as is his custom, a tacit objection. For the lover of money easily defends himself in this manner because of his vice: I confess that my mind is intent on acquiring riches; but in the meantime I will not omit those things which are of divine worship. Christ answers that no one can serve two masters: for it will happen that he will either love the one and hate the other, or certainly care for the one while neglecting the other. This proverb is to be understood of masters in full, just as the jurists also say that there cannot be two masters of the same thing. Such masters, however, are piety and the love of money. For each demands the whole man for itself. For if the study of letters and the desire for wealth cannot come together in one seat, as Juvenal contends,

What place for talent; unless when they vex themselves with song alone and your breasts are carried by the masters of Cyrrha and Nysa, not admitting two cares, a great work of the mind, nor are they worried about providing a blanket,

And Quintilian: For the mind cannot in good faith apply itself wholly to many things at once, and wherever it looks, it ceases to contemplate what had been proposed. And elsewhere: It is necessary that a mind intent upon such a great matter be free from all other faults, even those that are blameless: How much less will one and the same man be able both to devote himself to piety as much as is necessary, and at the same time be distracted by perpetual anxiety about seeking and keeping riches? Aelian, book II, ch. 27. It is impossible for one who bestows so much care upon small and worthless things to be zealous for great ones. For it is necessary that his whole mind, being set upon those things, should neglect what is truly worthy of admiration. Epictetus: Being concerned for the one, it is necessary [to neglect] the other. Persius: You are split in opposite directions by a double hook. Whether you follow this one or that one: you must submit to masters with ambiguous obedience. Arrian on Epictetus IV. 2. For no one who wavers between two can make progress.

Therefore, Bellarmine wrongly concludes from this passage, lib. III. de Bon. Oper. cap. 7, that one cannot retain superfluous wealth without sin: which is the heresy of the Socinians, and was formerly that of the Manichaeans and Pelagians. He does not say, says Cornel. à Lap., you cannot have wealth and God, but, you cannot serve God and Mammon. Lorinus on Psalm LXI. v. 11.
