It is an error, he says, that riches are in themselves evil and illicit, which the Council of Gangra condemned in Eustathius.

Μαμμωνᾷ] All testify that this word is Syriac, and the Syriac interpretation shows this in this passage as well. But if it is Syriac, it is also Punic, as Augustine teaches us in sermon XXXV on the word of the Lord, where he interprets it as gain: for the Carthaginians originated from the Syrians. See also the Chaldean interpreter of Psalm XLIV. 13. Some also think it is Hebrew, but corrupted from ממון which is treasure. If that is true, these things cohere very well with the preceding, concerning not storing up treasure. Hesychius certainly interprets μαμωνᾶν as treasure. This word often occurs among the Talmudists. For to them דיני ממונות are judgments of money. The Chaldean word מכמני does not differ much, for Daniel uses it for treasures in XI. 43.

Latin:

Vers. 24. οὐδεὶς δύναται δυσὶ κυρίοις δουλεύειν] Occurrit Christus, ut mos est ipsius, objectioni tacitæ. Facile enim ὁ φιλάργυρος vitio suo hunc in modum patrocinetur: Fa- teor intendi à me animum ad divitias parandas; verum in- terim nec omittam ea quæ divini sunt cultus. Respondet Christus, non posse quenquam duobus dominis servire: futurum enim ut aut hunc amet, illum oderit, aut certe al- terum curet neglecto altero. Intelligendum est hoc pro- verbium de dominis in solidum, quomodo & Juriscon- sulti dicunt non posse duos esse dominos ejusdem rei. Sunt autem tales domini, pietas & φιλοχρηματία. Utraque e- nim totum sibi hominem postulat. Nam si studia lite- rarum & opum cupiditas in unam sedem convenire non possunt, ut Juvenalis contendit,

Quis locus ingenio; nisi cum se carmine solo Vexant & dominis Cyrrhæ Nisaque feruntur Pectora vestra, duas non admittentia curas, Magna mentis opus, nec de lodice paranda Attonitæ,

Et Quintilianus: Neque enim se bona fide in multa simul in- tendere animus totum potest, & quocunque respexerit, desi- nit intueri quod propositum fuerat. Et alibi: Mentem tantæ rei intentam vacare omnibus aliis etiam culpa carentibus vitiis oportet: Quanto minus unus idemque homo poterit, & pietati se quantum opus est impendere, & simul cir- ca divitias quærendas servandasque perpetua sollicitudine distrahi? Ælianus libro II. cap. 27. Ἀδύνατόν ἐστι, τὸν εἰς μικρὰ ἄττα, κᾀ οὐδενὸς ἄξια τοσαύτην φροντίδα κατατιθέμενον, ὑπὲρ μεγάλων τινῶν σπουδάσαι. πᾶσαν γὰρ αὐτῷ τὴν διάνοιαν εἰς ἐκεῖνα ἀποτεθεῖσαν ἀνάγκη ὀλιγωρεῖν ὧς ὄντως θαυμαζο δικαίων. Epictetus: Τῷ ἑτέρῳ ἐπιμελούμενον τῷ ἑτέρῳ ἀ- νάγκη. Persius: duplici in diversum scinderis hamo. Hunccine, an hunc sequeris: subeas alternum oportet Ancipiti obsequio dominos. Arrianus Epicteto IV. 2. οὐδεὶς γὰρ ἐπαμφοτερίζων δύναται προκόψαι.

Perperam ergo ex hoc loco colligit Bellarmi- nus lib. III. de Bon. Oper. cap. 7. superfluas opes si- ne peccato retinere non posse: quæ Socinianorum est, & olim Manichæorum & Pelagianorum fuit hære- sis. Non dicit, inquit Cornel. à Lap. non potestis opes habere, & Deum, sed, non potestis Deo servia re, & Mammonæ. Lorinus in Psal. LXI. v. 11. Er- ror est, inquit, per se malas & illicitas esse divitias, quem damnavit in Eustathio Concilium Gangren- se.

Μαμμωνᾷ] Vocem hanc Syriacam esse omnes testantur, & ostendit hoc etiam loco Syriaca interpretatio. Quod si Syriaca est, etiam Punica, ut nos Augustinus docet ser- mone XXXV. de verbo Domini, ubi lucrum interpretatur: nam Pœni Sarra oriundi. Vide & Chaldæum interpre- tem Psalm. XLIV. 13. Quidam & Hebræam arbitrantur, sed corruptam ex ממון quod est thesaurus. Id si verum est, optime hæc cohærent cum superioribus, περὶ τοῦ μὴ θη- σαυρίζειν. Hesychius certe μαμωνᾶν θησαυρὸν interpreta- tur. Apud Thalmudistas sæpe vox hæc occurrit. Nam illis דיני ממונות sunt judicia pecuniarum. Non longe abit vox Chaldæa מכמני nam pro thesauris usur- pat Daniel XI. 43.

## 6:25
Vers. 25. διὰ τοῦτο] Because, clearly, the mind cannot be intent upon the pursuits of piety and riches at the same time.

Μὴ μεριμνᾶτε] The word μεριμνᾷ, and the noun μέριμνα are undoubtedly of middle signification, 1 Cor. 7:32, 33, 34; 2 Cor. 11:28; Phil. 2:28. Nor does it seem to be used here by itself in a negative sense, because it follows below, 'the morrow will be anxious for itself.' But the added circumstances denote a fault. For those phrases, 'what you shall eat, what you shall drink, what you shall wear,' are to be referred to future time. Whence it also appears that in this verse and in verse 31 below, a solicitude that knows no measure or end is described: in which sense the same word is used in Phil. 4:6 and 1 Pet. 5:7. Luke calls the same thing μετεωρίζεσθαι, that is, to be of a suspended mind. For the matter to be understood, it must be known that here too Christ, according to his custom, is answering a tacit objection. For suppose someone says, so that one need not labor for superfluous things, 'since what is sufficient is enough for the wise.' But of those things which nature desires, I do not have such an abundance as could suffice for my whole life; when I am about to have that, I will put an end to the effort of acquiring. Christ shows that this objection proceeds 'from little faith' in verse 30 below, because we think less magnificently than we ought of the divine goodness and power. For God is both able and willing to provide for us regarding necessary things, even if we, caring only in passing for those things which present use requires, direct all the strength of our mind to the study of piety: which he supports with illustrious arguments. Seneca praises somewhere a mind curious about things pertaining to the body, yet not anxiously.

Τί φάγητε καὶ τί πίητε] I agree with the codices that write it thus. The Greek poet: 'For what do mortals need except two things only, the grain of Demeter and a drink of water?' And the Latin: 'The river and Ceres are enough for the people.' Nor does the fact that mention is made of food alone stand in the way. For by that name, as also by the Latin 'cibaria' (provisions), drink is also included.

The Vulgate is deservedly abandoned here: which Beza rightly criticizes; namely, because it does not have that particle 'and what you shall drink': since he found it in all the Greek copies.

ἐχὶ ἡ ψυχὴ πλεῖόν ἐστι τῆς τροφῆς, καὶ τὸ σῶμα τοῦ ἐνδύματος;] Aristotle rightly says, 'That which is desirable for its own sake is better than that which is for the sake of another': and the rule is trite: he who wills the end, also wills the things necessary for the end. Πλεῖον, that is, 'more,' to be valued more. By the name of 'soul' here it is clear that life is understood, and by the word 'body' the body itself. For sustaining life, food is needed. But clothing is needed to defend the body against the injuries of the weather. Now it is God who gave us life and body. Why then should he not be both able and willing to give the good things that are necessary for protecting both? Compare the passage of Philo on rewards: 'Except that the food and shelter of nature are inexpensive. Food is bread and water, which are poured out everywhere in the world, and shelter is of a double kind, one is clothing, the other is a house, because of the damages that follow from cold and heat.' ὧν ἑκάτερα ὅστις ἐθελήσειε τὴν περίεργον καὶ περιττὴν ἀφελεῖν πολυτέλειαν, εὐπορίσατον. Aristides: 'For I think we need clothing and shelter and food.'

He who has care of you before you existed, how shall He not have care when you now exist, He who willed that you should exist? says Augustine in Ps. XXXIX.

Latin:

Vers. 25. διὰ τοῦτο] Quia scilicet non potest animus si- mul in pietatis & divitiarum studia intendi.

Μὴ μεριμνᾶτε] Vox μεριμνᾷ, & nomen μέριμνα haud du- bie mediæ sunt fignificationis, 1. Corinth. VII. 32. 33. 34. 2. Cor. XI. 28. Phil. II. 28. Neque hic per se videtur po- ni in partem fequiorem, quia infra sequitur ἡ ἄυριον μεριμνή- σει τὰ ἑαυτῆς. Sed additæ circumstantiæ vitium denotant. Nam ista τί φάγητε, τί πίητε, τί ἐνδύσησθε, ad tempus fu- turum referenda sunt. Unde & apparet hoc commate & in- fra commate 31. sollicitudinem, quæ modum finemque nesciat, describi : quo sensu eadem vox usurpatur Phil. IV. 6. & 1. Petr. V. 7. Lucas idem vocat μετεωρίζεσθαι, hoc est, suspenso esse animo. Res ut intelligatur, sciendum & hic Christum suo more objectionem tacitam solvere. Esto e- nim dicat aliquis, ut de supervacuis non sit laborandum, ἐπεὶ τά γ' ἀρκοῦντ' ἱκανὰ τοῖσι σώφροσι. At eorum quæ na- tura desiderat non eam habeo copiam quæ in vitam o- mnem possit sufficere; quam ubi sum habiturus, finem fa- ciam studio habendi. Christus hanc objectionem ostendit procedere ἐξ ὀλιγοπιστίας infra commate 30. quia de boni- tate ac potentia divina minus quam oportet, magnifice sentiamus. Nam Deum nobis & posse & velle prospicere de necessariis, etiamli nos, obiter tantum curantes ea quæ præ- sens usus requirit, omnem animi vim intendamus in stu- dium pietatis : quod illustribus argumentis fulcit. Lau- dat alicubi Seneca animum curiosum ad corpus pertinen- tium, non anxie tamen.

Τί φάγητε καὶ τί πίητε] Assentior codicibus ita scribenti- bus. Græcus Poëta: Ἐπεὶ τί δεῖ βροτοῖσι πλὴν δυοῖν μόνον, Δήμητρος ἀκτῆς πώματός τ' ὑδρηχόυ; Et Latinus : Satis est populis fluviusque Ceresque. Neque obstat quod sequitur τροφῆς solius mentio. Nam eo nomine, ut & latino cibariorum, potus etiam compre- henditur.

Merito hic deseritur Vulgatus: quem jure re- prehendit Beza; quod nempe particulam illam & τί πίητε non habeat : siquidem eam repererit in o- mnibus exemplaribus Græcis.

ἐχὶ ἡ ψυχὴ πλεῖόν ἐστι τῆς τροφῆς, καὶ τὸ σῶμα τοῦ ἐνδύμα- τος;] Recte Aristoteles κρεῖττον τὸ δι' ἑαυτὸ αἱρετὸν τοῦ διὰ θά- τερον : & trita est regula : qui finem vult, idem vult & neces- saria ad finem. Πλεῖον, hoc est, יותר pluris faciendum. Ψυχῆς nomine hic perspicuum est vitam intelligi, σώματος voce corpus ipsum. Ad vitam sustentandam cibariis o- pus est. Vestitu autem ad defendendum corpus contra cœli injurias. Deus autem est qui vitam & corpus nobis dedit. Quidni igitur dare & possit & velit bonis quæ ad u- trumque tuendum sunt necessaria? Confer Philonis locum de præmiis: Πλῆν ὅτι δὲ ὁ μὲν τῆς φύσεως ἐυτελής ἐσι τροφὴ καὶ σκέπη. Τροφὴ μὲν δι ἄρτος, καὶ ἰαματιαῖον ὕδωρ, ἃ πανταχοῦ τῆς ὀικυμένης ἀνακέχυται, σκέπης δὲ διττὸν εἶδος, τὸ μὲν ἀμπεχόνη, τὸ δ' ὀικία, διὰ τὰς ἀπὸ κρυοῦ καὶ θάλπους παρακολουθύσας ζη- μίας. ὧν ἑκάτερα ὅστις ἐθελήσειε τὴν περίεργον καὶ περιττὴν ἀφελεῖν πολυτέλειαν, εὐπορίσατον. Aristides : ἐσθῆτος γὰρ ὀῖμαι καὶ σκέπης καὶ τροφῆς δεόμεθα.

Qui tui curam habet antequam esses, quomodo non habebit curam cum jam es, qui voluit ut esses? ait Augustinus in Psal. XXXIX.

## 6:26
Vers. 26. Τὰ πετεινὰ τοῦ ὀυρανοῦ] From the Hebrew עוף השמים Psalm 104:12. Luke put a species, 'ravens,' undoubtedly because that animal is the most greedy for food among the genus of birds.

ὀυδὲ συνάγουσιν ἐις ἀποθήκας] Christ does not here condemn all gathering, any more than sowing and reaping, but the argument is from the greater. If God provides for birds against hunger, which do not have the industry that humans have, how much more will he provide for humans? A similar argument is in verse 28 below. In the Talmudic book Kiddushin, the saying of Simeon son of Eleazar is recited: 'Have you ever seen a beast or a bird that held some craft, and yet they are fed, and without difficulty.'

Μᾶλλον διαφέρετε] Μᾶλλον is redundant here as also in Mark 7:36, 2 Cor. 7:13. Aristotle said 'more preferable' and 'more beautiful.' But you may also find similar things in Demosthenes and Plato.

Latin:

Vers. 26. Τὰ πετεινὰ τοῦ ὀυρανοῦ] Ex Hebræo עוף השמים Psal. CIV. 12. Lucas speciem posuit κόρακας, nimirum quod id animal in volucrium genere cibi sit avidissimum.

ὀυδὲ συνάγουσιν ἐις ἀποθήκας] Non reprehendit hic Chri- stus omnem συγκομιδὴν, non magis quam sementem & messem, sed argumentum est à majori. Si Deus volucri- bus prospicit adversus inediam, quibus non est ea industria quæ est hominibus, quanto magis hominibus prospiciet? Simile est argumentum infra commate 28. In Thalmudı- co libro Kidduschim recitatur dictum Simeonis Eleazari- dæ: Vidistine unquam bestiam vel avem quæ tenuerit arti- ficium aliquod, & tamen aluntur, neque difficulter.

Μᾶλλον διαφέρετε] Μᾶλλον hic παρέλκει ut & Marc. VII. 36. 2. Cor. VII. 13. Aristoteles αἱρετώτερον μᾶλλον & μᾶλ- λον κάλλιον dixit. Sed & apud Demosthenem & Platonem similia reperias.

## 6:27
Vers. 27. Τίς δὲ ἐξ ὑμῶν μεριμνῶν δύναται προσθεῖναι ἐπὶ τὴν ἡλικίαν ἀυτοῦ πῆχυν ἕνα] It is an argument from the lesser to the greater, which Luke 12:25-26 teaches us. Christ returns to that which he had said 'about the soul and the body.' These are beyond controversy worth more than the measure of the body: it also matters little of what stature one is. But if God accomplishes this which is less without our effort, how much more will he preserve those more important things in us without our anxious solicitude, and consequently grant what is necessary for their preservation? You will find the word ἡλικία for stature in Aristotle, 'On Plants' 1.4, and Plutarch, 'On the Education of Children,' in Lucian, 'A True Story' and 'On the Syrian Goddess,' and in Constantine Porphyrogenitus in the chapter on the castle of Cherson. So also Luke 2:52.

Vulgata μεριμνῶν non satis efficaciter reddidit cogitans: because it is more to be anxious than to think: therefore they derive μεριμνᾶν from 'dividing the mind,' because solicitude as it were distracts the mind into various parts.

Latin:

Vers. 27. Τίς δὲ ἐξ ὑμῶν μεριμνῶν δύναται προσθεῖναι ἐπὶ τὴν ἡλικίαν ἀυτοῦ πῆχυν ἕνα] Argumentum est à minori ad majus, quod nos docet Lucas XII. 25. 26. Redit Christus ad id quod dixerat περὶ ψυχῆς καὶ σώματος. Hæc extra con- troversiam pluris sunt quam mensura corporis: parum etim refert qua quis sit statura. Quod si hoc quod minus est Deus efficit citra studium nostrum, quanto magis citra anxiam nostram sollicitudinem illa potiora in nobis con- servabit, ac proinde largietur quæ ad conservationem eo- rum sunt necessaria? Vocem ἡλικίας pro statura reperies apud Aristotele.n de Plantis I. 4. & Plutarchum de pueris instituendis, apud Lucianum de Vera narratione & de Dea Syria, apud Constantinum Porphyrogennetam capite de castro Chersonis. Sic & Lucæ II. 52.

Vulgata μεριμνῶν non satis efficaciter reddidit cogitans: quia plus est solicitum esse, quam cogita- re: ideo μεριμνᾶν deducunt παρὰ τὸ μερίζειν ἕ νῶν, quod solicitudo animum quasi distrahat in va- rias partes.

## 6:28
Vers. 28. The lilies of the field. It is well known, says Scultetus, that both κρίνα and λείρια generally denote the flowers of the field. Such is the dignity of the lily flower, says Pollux, that Homer called all flowers λείρια. The scholiast of Apollonius Rhodius says, that in general, all flowers are called λείρια. And Lucian says, if I remember correctly, that flowers are called λείρια: Lilies are called, if I remember, flowers. This is the reason why, although it is commonly read in Exodus 25:34, "and its lilies," Symmachus translated it, "and its flowers." And in Psalm 45:1, the same interpreter translates the Hebrew word as "concerning the flowers," which Aquila and Theodotion translate as "concerning the lilies." Thus here, κρίνα are what "the flowers" are in general. For it is not likely that the valleys or fields, upon which the Lord cast his eyes, were crowned with no flowers other than lilies: and the beauty of many flowers is such that they can contend with the glorious attire of Solomon.

Consider the lilies of the field] Transitionally: as the Syriac and Latin interpreters rightly translated: thus Plutarch said that to consider the nature of things is καταμανθάνειν τὴν φύσιν.

Latin:

Vers. 28. Τὰ κρίνα τοῦ ἀγρῦ. Notum est, ait Scultetus, & κρίνα & λείρια ge- neratim flores campi denotare. Tanta est floris lilii di- gnitas, inquit Pollux, ut Homerus omnes flores voca- verit λείρια. Scholiastes Apollonii Rhodii, καθ' ὅλα, inquit, τὰ ἄνθη λείρια λέγεται. Et Lucia- nus λείρια καλεῖται, εἴγε μέμνημαι, τὰ ἄνθη: Li- lia vocantur, siquidem memini, flores. Hæc cau- sa est, cur cum vulgo legatur Exodi XXV. 34. καὶ τὰ κρίνα ἀυτῆς, Symmachus verterit, καὶ τὰ ἄνθη ἀυτῆς. Et Psalm. XLV. 1. τὸ אל ששכים idem interpre- tetur ὑπὲρ τῶν ἀνθῶν, quod Aquila & Theodotio ὑ- πὲρ τῶν κρίνων. Sic hic κρίνα sunt quod τὰ ἄνθη in genere. Neque enim verisimile est, valles vel cam- pos, in quos Dominus oculos conjecit, nullis nisi li- liorum floribus fuisse coronatos: & est plurium florum ea pulchritudo, ut cum glorioso Salomonis amictu pos- sint contendere.

Καταμάθετε τὰ κρίνα τῦ ἀγρῦ] Μεταβατικῶς: ut recte verterunt Syrus & Latinus interpres: ita καταμανθάνειν τὴν φύσιν naturam rerum considerare dixit Plutarchus.

## 6:29
Vers. 29. Solomon] He names Solomon, because in his times, on account of long peace and navigation to gold-bearing lands, the affairs of the Jews were most flourishing.

In all his glory] That is, when sitting with august appearance on an ivory, gilded throne (concerning which see 2 Chronicles 9:7) he gave laws to citizens, or responses to foreigners. For that throne is called the throne of glory, to which allusion is made below in 19:28, 25:31, or also the throne of judgment. It was the custom among almost all peoples that a King sitting on a throne should shine with a gilded robe. But Christ says that even that robe is surpassed by the beauty of the lilies, because, indeed, no art can contend with nature. Very similar to this saying of Christ is that of Solon, who, when he was asked, having seen King Croesus sitting on his throne, whether he had seen any more beautiful spectacle, "I have seen," he said, "namely, cocks, peacocks, and pheasants: for they are adorned with a natural flower and one a thousand times more beautiful": which Chrysostom and Jerome explain eloquently regarding this passage.

Chrysostom among other things: As much as a lie differs from the truth, so much difference lies between the attire of Kings and the colors of flowers. Jerome: What silk, what purple of kings, what texture of weavers can be compared to flowers? What is so red as a rose? What is so white as a lily? Indeed, that violets are surpassed by no purple dye is a judgment of the eyes rather than of speech.

Περιεβάλετο] Thus the Hebrew word לבש is usually translated.

Latin:

Vers. 29. Σολομὼν] Salomonem nominat, quia ejus temporibus ob longam pacem & navigationem in terras auriferas res Judæorum fuerunt florentissimæ.

Ἐν πάσῃ τῇ δόξῃ ἀυτῦ] Id est, cum augusta specie in so- lio eburneo aurato sedens (de quo vide 2. Par. IX. 7.) jura daret civibus, aut responsa externis. Vocatur enim illud solium, θρόνος δόξης, quo alluditur infra XIX. 28. XXV. 31. aut etiam כסא דין id est, solium judicii. Moris autem erat apud omnes ferme populos, ut Rex solio insidens tra- bea aurata fulgeret. Sed illam quoque trabeam' Christus ait pulchritudine liliorum superari, quia nimirum ars nulla potest cum natura contendere. Simillimum huic Christi dicto est Solonis illud, qui cum regem Cræsum in throno sedentem conspicatus interrogaretur, num pulchrius ul- lum vidisset spectaculum, vidi, inquit, gallos scilicet, pavo- nes & phasianos: φυσικῷ γὰρ ἄνθει κεκοσμήνται κὶ μυρίῳ καλ- λίονι: quod ipsum facunde ad hunc locum explicant Chry- sostomus & Hieronymus.

Chrysostomus inter alia: Quantum distat à ve- ritate mendacium, tantum inter Regum amictus & florum colores discrimen interjacet. Hieronymus: Quod sericum, quæ regum purpura, quæ textricum textura potest floribus comparari? quid ita rubet ut rosa? quid ita candet ut lilium? violæ vero purpu- ram nullo superari murice, oculorum magis quam sermonis judicium est.

Περιεβάλετο] Ita verti solet Hebræum לבש.

## 6:30
Vers. 30. Grass] Thus he calls the lily itself. For the Hebrews divide plants into two kinds, herb and tree, as can be seen in Genesis 1:11. The Hellenists, since they did not have Greek words of equally wide application, translated tree as wood, by which trees, shrubs, and similar things are contained. But herb or also grass, which the Talmudists write as a word from which in that kind are grains, herbs, flowers. In this sense, trees and grass placed together comprehend all those things which are born from the earth, Revelation 8:7. And in James, the same is called flower and grass, and together, the flower of the grass, 1:10, 11, which is also in Peter, 1 Epistle 1:24. Which passages are taken from that which is in Isaiah 40:6, where in the Greek it is grass, in the Hebrew it is grass, which, as I said, the Talmudists interpret by a word received from the Greeks.

Being today] A short duration is indicated, as in Psalm 90:5, 6.

Oven] The Syriac well uses the word for oven, as in Genesis 15:17, Exodus 8:3, Leviticus 2:4, 26:26, Psalm 21:10. And it has been rightly noted by others that a hearth and an oven are not always accustomed to be distinguished subtly. Indeed, some Greeks explain oven as furnace, as the scholiast of Aristophanes' Acharnians, and some Hebrews explain the word for oven as a furnace, although Kimchi distinguishes that. Moreover, ovens were accustomed to be kindled not only with the branches of trees, but also with flowers after they had withered, just as also with chaff and tares. Ulpian: By the term 'wood' in certain regions, as in Egypt, where they use reeds instead of wood, both reeds and papyrus are burned, and certain small herbs or thorns or hedges will be included. L. LV. D. de leg. III. exists, where also vine-cuttings and the remnants of materials and vine-stocks are said to come under the name of wood if the intention does not contradict it.

Ὀλιγόπιστοι] They are also called קטני אמנה by the Hebrews, those who, while they have enough for the present, are tormented by the uncertainty of the future. Moreover, the word נאמן, which the word πίστεως expresses, especially in the usage of the Hellenists, does not always signify the persuasion by which we believe that what is said is true, but often the trust which we place in someone's goodness and power, even if no words have intervened: which meaning seems to be embraced in this place. For although promises exist in the law pertaining to this matter, Christ does not draw an argument from them, but from manifest testimonies of divine goodness and power.

But what kind of faith in God is it, what trust in the grace and kindness of God is certain, indubitable, and firm without a word of divine promise? Testimonies of divine goodness and power which are read in the book of nature do not beget divine faith, which is not had except from the book of Scripture. Therefore, instead of ευδοκείσθω, it is held by the Apostle to have trust in God, which the Holy Spirit requires, without the word of God and divine promise: How shall they believe in whom they have not heard? How shall they hear without a preacher? Faith therefore is from preaching, but preaching is from the word of God, Rom. X. 14. 17.

Latin:

Vers. 30. Χόρτον] Ita vocat ipsum lilium. Nam Hebræi τὰ φυτὰ distrbuunt in duo genera עשב & עץ ut videre est Gen. I. 11. Hellenistæ cum voces Græcas non haberent æque late patentes עץ verterunt ξύλον, quo continentur ar- bores, frutices & similia. עשב autem aut etiam חציר χόρ- τον, quod Thalmudinstæ scribunt כרתי, in quo genere sunt farra, herbæ, flores. Hoc sensu ita δένδρη & χόρτον pariter posita comprehendunt omnia ea quæ terra nascuntur A- poc. VIII. 7. Et apud Jacobum idem vocatur ἄνθος & χόρ- τος, & conjunctim ἄνθος χόρτου I. 10. 11. quod & apud Petrum est 1. Epist. I. 24. Qui loci desumti sunt ex eo quod est apud Esaiam XL. 6. ubi in Græco est χόρτος in Hebræo חציר, quod ut dixi Thalmudinstæ voce à Græcis accepta כרתי interpretantur.

Σήμερον ὄντα] Brevis duratio indicatur, ut Psalm. XC. 5. 6.

Κλίβανον] Bene Syrus תנורא ut Gen. XV. 17. Exod. VIII. 3. 1. Levit. II. 4. XXVI. 26. Psal. XXI. 10. Neque enim solere semper distingui subtiliter ἰπνὸν κὶ κλίβανον recte ab aliis est annotatum. Quin & Græci quidam κλίβανον exponunt κάμινον ut Scholiastes Acharnensium Aristopha- nis, & Hebræi quidam תנור exponunt פורנו id est furnum, quamquam Kimchi istud distinguit. Solebant autem furni incendi non tantum ramalibus arborum, sed & floribus postquam exaruerant, quemadmodum & paleis & lolio. Ulpianus: Lignorum appellatione in quibusdam regionibus ut in Ægypto, ubi arundine pro ligno utuntur, & a- rundines & papyrum comburitur, & herbula quædam vel spina vel sepres continebuntur. Exstat L. LV. D. de leg. III. ubi & sarmenta & superamenta materiarum & vitium stirpes dicuntur venire ligni nomine si voluntas non refragatur.

Ὀλιγόπιστοι] קטני אמנה Hebræis etiam vocantur hi qui cum in præsens habeant satis, futuri incertitudine cruciantur. Vox autem נאמן quam exprimit vox πί- στεως præsertim in usu Hellenistarum, non semper significat persuasionem qua credimus vera esse quæ dicuntur, sed sæ- pe fiduciam quam in alicujus bonitate ac potentia poni- mus, etiamsi verba nulla intercesserint: quæ significatio hoc loco videtur amplectenda. Quanquam enim promif- siones exstant in lege ad hanc rem pertinentes, non tamen inde argumentum ducit Christus, sed à manifestis bonita- tis potentiæque divinæ testimoniis.

At quænam est fides in Deum, quæ fiducia in gratiam & benignitatem Dei certa, indubitata & firma sine verbo promissionis divinæ? Testimo- nia bonitatis & potentiæ divinæ quæ in libro na- turæ leguntur, non gignunt fidem divinam, quæ non nisi è libro Scripturæ habetur. Ideo pro ευδο- κείσθω habetur ab Apostolo fiduciam habere in Deum, quam Spiritus S. requirit, sine verbo Dei ac promissionis divinæ: Quomodo credent de quo non audierunt? Quomodo audient sine præcone? Fides ergo è præconio, præconium autem ex verbo Dei, Rom. X. 14. 17.

## 6:32
Vers. 32. Πάντα γὰρ ταῦτα τὰ ἔθνη ἐπιζητεῖ] πάντα signifies a sufficient abundance for all time, and ἐπιζητεῖν designates a certain vehement zeal.

Ὅτι χρήζετε] That you have need of those things for maintaining life and health. For these are in the category of τῶν πρὸς ἀναγκαίων, as the philosophers love to speak.

Chrysostom excellently: One approaching a fountain is not anxious about drinking: so foolish is he who has God the Father with him, and is anxious about future things, because the heavenly Father flows more than any fountain.

Latin:

Vers. 32. Πάντα γὰρ ταῦτα τὰ ἔθνη ἐπιζητεῖ] πάντα signifi- cat copiam sufficientem in omne tempus, & ἐπιζητεῖν vehe- mens quoddam studium designat.

Ὅτι χρήζετε] Opus esse vobis illis rebus ad vitam & va- letudinem tuendam. Sunt enim hæc in genere τῶν πρὸς ἀναγ- καίων, ut loqui amant Philosophi.

Præclare Chrysostomus: Accedens ad fontem non solicitatur de bibendo: sic stultus est qui secum habet Deum Patrem, & solicitatur de futuris, quia Pater cælestis omni fonte magis manat.

## 6:33
Ζητεῖτε δὲ πρῶτον] Do this, as it was accustomed to be said in sacred rites. For God is not content with either perfunctory or halved works: but He wants us to be occupied primarily in His worship. For most men treat the secondary work as the primary, and the primary as the secondary. But it was excellently said by the Poet: Nor for the sake of life, to lose the causes of living. By Plato, however: one must take care of the body for the sake of the soul's abundance. For certainly, as another poet sang: This part has a value greater than the body. There is an obscure reference to that which is in the history of Solomon, to whom, as he sought wisdom, both wisdom was given, and those things which he had not sought, 1. Reg. III. 11.

Τὴν βασιλείαν τοῦ θεοῦ κὶ τὴν δικαιοσύνην ἀυτοῦ] The kingdom of God or the heavenly kingdom as the goal: Righteousness, that is, the way by which one may arrive at the kingdom, just as these words are placed above in chap. V. 20.

That righteousness is not the way, but the cause of entry into the kingdom of heaven. But the righteousness of God is designated, not our own righteousness. See Rom. III. 22. 1. Cor. I. 30. Phil. III. 9. Compare on this saying B. Fevorborn. Synt. Theol. II. p. 209. seqq. two dissertations.

Προστεθήσεται ὑμῖν] Very significantly: for the Greeks call that προσθήκην which is also ἐπίδοσιν, πρόσδομα, ἐπίμετρον; the Latins call it a corollary, an accession, an augmentation, a makeweight. Piety indeed has promises of both lives, I. Tim. IV. 8. Marc. X. 30. But the principal thing is the glory of the other life: those things which are desired for this life have the role of an accession, which for that reason are also accustomed to happen more sparingly to the pious, so that more honor and value may be taken away from those things. And thus even in the time of the old law itself, just as God constantly provided that abundance which the law promised to those working for the sake of temporal reward, so to those who, under the guidance of the Spirit, panted for the heavenly fatherland, He exhibited internal comforts rather than an affluence of external things, without any loss to them, since they received better things for viler ones, as can be seen in Hebr. XI. And thus in those few, that dispensation was anticipated which was most widely diffused after the coming of Christ. Plato saw something of this when he said: διπλᾶ δὲ ἀγαθά ἐστι, τὰ μὲν ἀνθρώπινα, τὰ δὲ θεῖα, καὶ μὲν δεξατοις τὰ μείζονα, κτᾶται κὶ τὰ

ἰλατότα. It is a proverb of the Hebrews: כל המקבל עליו תורה ומעבירים ממנו עול מלכות ועול דרך ארץ He who takes upon himself the yoke of the law, the yoke of public burdens and the trouble of seeking a living is removed from him.

Latin:

Ζητεῖτε δὲ πρῶτον] Hoc agite, ut in sacris dici solebat. Neque enim contentus est Deus aut perfunctoria, aut di- midiata opera: sed vult in sui cultu præcipue nos esse oc- cupatos. Nam plerique hominum Τὸ μὲν πάρεργον ἔργον ὡς ποιούμεθας Τὸ δ' ἔργον ὡς πάρεργον ἐκποιούμεθα. Atqui egregie dictum est à Poëta: Nec propter vitam, vivendi perdere causas. A Platone autem ἐπιμελεῖσθαι χρὴ τοῦ σώματος ψυχῆς ἕνεκα περιουσίας. Nam certe, ut alter Poëta cecinit: Pars hæc pretium corpore majus habet. Respicitur non obscure id quod est in historia Salomonis, cui sapientiam optanti, & sapientia data est, & ea quæ non optaverat, 1. Reg. III. 11.

Τὴν βασιλείαν τοῦ θεοῦ κὶ τὴν δικαιοσύνην ἀυτοῦ] Regnum Dei sive regnum cœleste ut metam: Justitiam, id est viam qua ad regnum perveniatur, quomodo hæ voces supra ponuntur cap. V. 20.

Justitia illa non via est, sed causa ingressus in regnum cœlorum. Justitia autem Dei designa- tur, non nostra ipsorummet justitia. Vid. Rom. III. 22. 1. Cor. I. 30. Phil. III. 9. Conf. de hoc dicto B. Fevorborn. Synt. Theol. II. p. 209. seqq. binas dissertationes.

Προστεθήσεται ὑμῖν] Significanter admodum: nam προσ- θήκην Græci vocant quod & ἐπίδοσιν, πρόσδομα, ἐπίμετρον; Latini corollarium, accessionem, auctarium, mantissam. Habet quidem pietas promissa utriusque vitæ I. Tim. IV. 8. Marc. X. 30. Sed principale est gloria vitæ alterius: quæ ad hanc vitam desiderantur accessionis habent vicem, quæ propter etiam parcius solent piis contingere, quo magis il- lis rebus honos & pretium detrahatur. Atque adeo ipso et- iam veteris legis tempore, sicut mercedis temporariæ gra- tia operantibus constanter Deus præstitit eam ubertatem quam lex pollicebatur, ita his qui spiritus ductu ad cœle- stem patriam anhelabant, interna magis solatia exhibuit, quam rerum exteriorum affluentiam, sine ullo ipsorum damno, cum pro vilioribus meliora acciperent, ut videre est Hebr. XI. Ac sic in illis paucis anticipata est ea dispensa- tio, quæ post Christi adventum latissime diffusa. Vidit hic nonnihil Plato cum dixit: διπλᾶ δὲ ἀγαθά ἐστι, τὰ μὲν ἀνθρώ- πινα, τὰ δὲ θεῖα, καὶ μὲν δεξατοις τὰ μείζονα, κτᾶται κὶ τὰ

ἰλατότα. Hebræorum est proverbium: כל המקבל עליו תורה ומעבירים ממנו עול מלכות ועול דרך ארץ Qui suscipit in se jugum legis, tollitur ab eo jugum one- rum publicorum & molestia quærenda vitæ.

## 6:34
Vers. 34. For the morrow ] That is, do not promise care for a long time. For by the appellation of tomorrow, as we have said, the future is contained for the Hebrews. A very similar kind of speaking, although in a different sense, is found in Phileterus the comic poet: Εἰς ἄυριον δὲ μηδὲ φροντίζειν.

Moreover, here the expression (ἡ λῆξις) alludes to that which we read concerning Manna, a noble pledge of divine providence, in Exodus XVI. 20.

Kακία ] It had been well translated long ago, as Tertullian cites, 'vexation': for in the Hebrew proverb which Christ uses, there is צרה which the LXX are accustomed to translate θλίψιν. Thus also Plutarch, in his book on how to read poets, teaches that κακότητα is taken for vexation. Greek interpreters often use the word κακίας in such a way as to express the Hebrew רעה as in Amos III. 6. See, if you please, Chrysostom in his oration against those who ascribe the governance of human affairs to demons.

What the sense of this prohibition is, must be sought from the context: namely, it is not solicitude about the future that is simply prohibited, Prov. VI, 6. chap. XXX. 25. but that which hinders us from seeking the kingdom of God, that which precedes the solicitude for the kingdom of God, not that which follows it, that which is born from diffidence in divine providence, by which we wish to provide for ourselves concerning the future without God, and we sacrifice to our own care and solicitude, to our own net, and place our trust in it, which is not to serve one Lord, v. 24. Chrysostom in h. l. Let not the care of a further day wear you out: for since you do not know the span of the day you will see, for what reason are you tormented by the solicitude of that one?

Latin:

Vers. 34. Εἰς τὴν αὔριον ] Id est nolite curam in lon- gum promittere. Nam crastini appellatione, ut diximus, futurum Hebræis continetur. Simillimum loquendi ge- nus, quanquam in sensum alium, est apud Phileterum co- micum: Εἰς ἄυριον δὲ μηδὲ φροντίζειν.

Alludit autem hic ἡ λῆξις ad id quod de Manna, nobili pi- gnore divinæ providentiæ, legimus Exodi XVI. 20.

Kακία ] Bene olim versum fuerat, citante Tertulliano, ve- xationem: nam in Hebræo proverbio quo Christus utitur, est צרה quod LXX. θλίψιν solent vertere. Sic & κακό- τητα pro vexatione sumi docet Plutarchus libro de legen- dis Poëtis. Græci interpretes sæpe ita usurpant vocem κακίας, ut exprimant Hebræum רעה ut Amosi III. 6. Vide si placet Chrysostomum oratione adversus eos qui dæmonibus asscribunt rerum humanarum regimen.

Quis sensus hujus prohibitionis sit, e contextu petendum: nimirum non prohibetur simpliciter sollicitudo de futuro, Prov. VI, 6. cap. XXX. 25. sed quæ impedit, ne quæramus regnum Dei, quæ so- licitudinem regni Dei præcedit, non quæ sequitur, quæ nascitur ex diffidentia providentiæ divinæ, qua nobis ipsis de futuris sine Deo prospicere vo- lumus, nostræque curæ, & sollicitudini, nostro re- ti sacrificamus, & fiduciam in eum locamus, quod est non uni Domino servire, v. 24. Chrysostomus in h. l. Nequaquam ulterioris diei cura te conterat: cujus enim diei spatiam te visurum nescis, quam ob causam illius sollicitudine torqueris?

## 7:1 Argument
CHAPTER VII. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

We are recalled from rash judgment of our neighbor to judging ourselves, and from the profanation of the holy: we are stirred to prayers, and that we should show to our neighbor those things which we would wish to be done to us: and that we should strive to enter through the narrow gate, and therefore also that we should beware of false doctrine, and false Prophets, and of an impious and hypocritical life, and that we should perform the word of the Lord, which is to build upon the rock; just as those who do not perform it, build upon the sand. The people admire the doctrine of Jesus.

There are six parts: I. The avoidance of rash judgment to v. 5. II. A caution about not profaning the holy v. 6. III. An admonition concerning prayers to v. 11. IV. The sum of the doctrine of the law and the Prophets v. 12. V. An exhortation to the effort of entering through the narrow gate, and for that reason to avoid false doctrine and a hypocritical life, to v. 23. VI. The concluding exhortatory part of Christ's sermon on keeping the word of the Lord, with the judgment of the hearers concerning the doctrine of the Lord, to v. 29.

PART I. On avoiding rash judgment.

Vers. 1. Do not judge ] It is better translated 'judge' than 'condemn', because Luke, when he had said 'do not judge', adds 'do not condemn'. However, it is apparent from what follows that Christ is not dealing with judgments of any kind whatsoever, but with those which are exercised rigidly, just as James also opposes mercy to judgment. II. 13. The Hebrews say הויו ראת כל האדם וכף לכות. Judge every man to the scale of innocence. And concerning the Hasidim, that they were solicitous to judge everyone by the scale of innocence, even if they saw someone sinning.

Augustine, in his work on the harmony of the Gospels. In this place, he says, I believe nothing else is commanded, except that we interpret in the better part those deeds which are doubtful as to the spirit in which they are done. For concerning intermediate deeds, which can be done with a good or an evil spirit, it is rash to judge, especially so that we condemn. But wrongly in the vulgate is added here: do not condemn, and you shall not be condemned, which is not to be read in the Greek Codices, nor among the Syrian, Arab, or Ethiopian: nor is it held by Chrysostom, the Author of the imperfect work, Euthymius, Theophylact among the Greeks, or Tertullian in his book on patience, Ambrose in his book on the sermon of the Lord, Hilary, Jerome, Bede Latins, whence Cornelius a Lapide, Barradius, and Tirinus consider these as interpolations, here departing from their Maldonado.

Latin:

CAPUT VII. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Revocamur à temerario de proximo judicio ad nos ipsos dijudicandos, & à prophana- tione sancti: excitamur ad preces, & ut proximo ea exhibeamus, quæ nobis fieri vellemus: utq; ingredi satagamus per an- gustam portam, atque ideo & à falsa do- ctrina, falsisque Prophetis, & à vita impia & hypocritica caveamus, verbumque Do- mini præstemus, quod est super petram æ- dificare; uti qui non præstant illud, super arenam exstruunt. Populus admiratur doctrinam Jesu.

Partes sunt sex: I. Fuga temerarii judicii ad v. 5. II. Cautela de non prophanando sancto v. 6. III. Commonitio de precibus ad v. 11. IV. Summa do- ctrinæ legis & Prophetarum v. 12. V. Adhortatio ad studium ingrediendi per angustam portam, ejus- que causa fugiendam falsam doctrinam, & vitam hypocriticam, ad v. 23. VI. Conclusio concionis Christi exhortatoria ad servandum verbum Do- mini, cum judicio auditorum de doctrina Domini, ad v. 29.

PARS I. De vitando judicio temerario.

Vers. 1. Μὴ κρίνετε ] Melius transfertur judicate quàm condemnate, quia Lucas cum dixisset μὴ κρίνετε addit μὴ κα- ταδικάζετε. Apparet autem ex sequentibus, non de qualis burcunque judiciis Christum agere, sed de iis quæ rigide ex- ercentur, quomodo & Jacobus ἔλεος opponit τῇ κρίσει. II. 13. Hebræi dicunt הויו ראת כל האדם וכף לכות. Judica omnem hominem ad lanceam innotentiæ. Et de Ha- sidæis, sollicitos fuisse ut judicarent unumquemque lance innocentiæ, etiamsi quem viderent peccare.

August. de consens. Evang. Hoc loco, inquit, ni- hil aliud præcipi existimo, nisi ut ea facta quæ dubium est quo animo fiant, in meliorem partem interprete- mur. De factis enim mediis, quæ possunt bono & malo animo fieri, temerarium est judicare, maxi- me ut condemnemus. Perperam autem in vulgata hic additur: nolite condemnare, & non condemne- mini, quod nec in Codd. Graecis, neq; apud Syrum, Arabem aut Aethiopem legere est: nec habetur a- pud Chrysostomum, Autorem imperf. oper. Euthymi- um, Theophylactum e Graecis, aut Tertull. l. patient. Ambrof. l. de serm. Dom. Hilarium, Hieronym. Be- dam, Strab. Rupert. in h. l. e Latinis, unde pro em- bolimaeis ea habent Cornel. a Lapide, Barradius & Tirinus hic a Maldonato suo discedentes.

## 7:2
Verse 2. αντιμετρηθησεται υμιν] It shall be measured back to you. Now this was a proverb which Christ uses for diverse matters, common among the Hebrews, which they were accustomed to enunciate as במדה מדה כנגד מדה or the short הארס מודד בה ליורו לו. There are also those who say במדה שמדדת ליאמרר לך. The Arabs also use it. An old scholiast on that of Horace, Satire III, In trutina: The same judgment will be for him, and the same estimation. Αναλογικως. For he who forgives the sins of another will soon obtain the same pardon. Polybius, where he treats of the historian Timaeus in the fragments edited by Valesius: πικρος γαρ γεγονως κ' απαραιτητος επιτιμητης τοις πελας, εικοτως αν και υπο τ' πλησιον αυτος απαραιτητε τυγχανοι τιμωριας. I clearly conclude that the judgment of God is treated here, no less than in James when he says η κρισις ανιλεως τω μη ποιησαντι ελ: θ c. II. 13. It was certainly the custom of Christ to transfer sayings accustomed to be used about human affairs to divine ones.

Latin:

Vers. 2. αντιμετρηθησεται υμιν] Remensum vobis ibitur. Erat autem proverbium hoc quo Christus ad res diversas utitur, tritum usi Hebraeorum quod enunciare solebant במדה מדה כנגד מדה aut brevis הארס מודד בה ליורו לו Sunt & qui dicant במדה שמדדת ליאמרר לך Utun- tur & Arabes. Scholiastes vetus ad illud Horat. Sat. III. In trutina : Idem judicium de ipso erit, & eadem aestimatio. Ανα- λογικως. Nam qui ignoscit peccatis alterius, mox eandem ve- niam consequetur. Polybius ubi de Timaeo agit historico in fragmentis a Valesio editis : πικρος γαρ γεγονως κ' απαραιτη- τος επιτιμητης τοις πελας, εικοτως αν και υπο τ' πλησιον αυτος απα- ραιτητε τυγχανοι τιμωριας. Plane autem statuo de Dei judicio hic agi, non minus quam apud Jacobum cum dicit η κρισις ανιλεως τω μη ποιησαντι ελ: θ c. II. 13. Mos nimirum erat Christo dicta de rebus humanis usurpari solita ad divinas transferre.

## 7:3
Verse 3. Τι δε βλεπεις το καρφος] It seems to me well explained in Hesychius as καρφος, a small splinter of wood. The seventy elders translate שרף Gen. 8,11 as καρφος. What Christ explains here by a proverb frequent among the Jews (as appears also from their own books) the fabulist Phryxille also nearly intended to be understood by a little story about two wallets, of which one, laden with the vices of others, hangs before our eyes, while the other, bearing our own vices, hangs behind us: whence that saying: But we do not see the part of the wallet that is on our back. It is pleasing to illustrate this with verses of the Greek poets. It is of Menander: Απαντες εσμεν εις το νουθετειν σοφοι Αυτοι δ' αμαρτανοντες ε γινωσκεμεν. Of the same: Ουδεις εφ' αυτω τα κακα συνορα, παμφιλε, Σαφως ετερε δ' ατρεμιεντος οψεται. Of another unknown: Το μεν αλλοτριον ανθρωπε βασκανωτατε Κακον οξυδερκως. το δ' ιδιον παρεβλεπης. Cicero, Tusculan Disputations, book three: It is characteristic of folly to discern the vices of others, to forget one's own. And these things indeed pertain properly to the vices which we have in common with others, and which we severely notice in others, while we forgive ourselves, as in Horace, Manius. Certainly, as that same one sings, Stultus & improbus hic amor est dignusq; notari. But the malignity of some proceeds further, so that they even take what they receive in a good interpretation and twist it into the worst part. But we invert the virtues themselves, and Sincerum cupimus vas incrustare. Examples of whose κακοηθες can be seen in the same Satire, book I, 3. Or even, which ulcer Christ touches here properly, they are sharp-sighted toward the lesser vices of others, but wink at their own far greater ones: such as he whom Flaccus thus rebukes: Cum tua pervideas oculis mala lippus inunctis, Cur in amicorum vitiis tam cernis acutum. Quam aut aquila aut serpens Epidaurius? And then he admonishes thus: --- finally, examine yourself; whether nature or even bad habit has ever implanted any vices in you. For when this is done, it will appear how much that rigid persona of the Censor misbecomes us: He who demands that he not offend a friend with his own humps, should forgive his warts: it is fair that he who asks pardon for his sins, should render it in return. Those who do otherwise, he teaches, are establishing an unjust law against themselves. Indeed, as Seneca said, it is fair that he who needs pardon should easily grant it. Furthermore, from the Latin verses which we have cited, it appears that this βλεπειν, and συνοραν in Menander, can rightly be translated as to see or to discern.

Latin:

Vers. 3. Τι δε βλεπεις το καρφος] Bene videtur mihi apud Hesychium exponi καρφος, κεραια ξυλε λεπτη. Septuagin- ta senes שרף Gen. 8,11. vertunt καρφος. Quod aute Chri- stus hic explicat proverbio inter Judaeos frequentato (ut ex ipsorum quoque libris apparet) idem ferme t hryxille fabu- lator intellectum voluit narratiuncula de duabus manticis, quarum altera alienis vitiis onusta ante oculos, altera vero nostra ferens vit a retro nos pendeat: unde illud dictum est: Sed non videmus manticae quod in tergo est. Libet hoc illustrare Graecorum poetarum versibus. Me- nandri est: Απαντες εσμεν εις το νουθετειν σοφοι Αυτοι δ' αμαρτανοντες ε γινωσκομεν. Ejusdem: Ουδεις εφ' αυτω τα κακα συνορα, παμφιλε, Σαφως ετερε δ' ατρεμιεντος οψεται. Alterius ignoti: Το μεν αλλοτριον ανθρωπε βασκανωτατε Κακον οξυδερκως. το δ' ιδιον παρεβλεπης. Cicero Tusculanorum tertio : Stultitiae proprium est aliorum vitia cernere, oblivisci suorum. Et haec quidem proprie per- tinent ad vitia quae nos cum aliis habemus communia, quae que in aliis severe advertimus, cum ignoscamus nobis, ut apud Horatium Manius. Certe, ut idem ille canit, Stultus & improbus hic amor est dignusq; notari. At quorundam malignitas ultra progreditur, ut etiam qua bonam capiunt interpretationem in pessimam parte rapiat. At nos virtutes ipsas invertimus, atque Sincerum cupimus vas incrustare. Cujus κακοηθες exempla videre est in eadem Satyra lib. I. 3. Aut etiam, quod ulcus hic proprie tangit Christus, ad mi- nora aliorum vitia perspicaces, ad sua longe majora conni- vent: qualis ille quem Flaccus ita objurgat: Cum tua pervideas oculis mala lippus inunctis, Cur in amicorum vitiis tam cernis acutum. Quam aut aquila aut serpens Epidaurius ? Et deinde ita admonet: --- deniq; te ipsum Concute; num qua tibi vitiorum inseferit olim Natura aut etiam consuetudo mala. Hoc enim facto appariturum quam nos dedeceat rigida il- la Censoris persona: Qui ne tuberibus propriis offendat amicum Postulat, ignoscat verrucis illius: aequum est Peccatis veniam poscentem, reddere rursus. Aliter qui faciunt eos docet legem in se iniquam sancire. Nempe ut Seneca dixit aequum est, Det ille veniam facile cui venia est opus. Porro ex Latinis quos citavimus versiculis apparet quod hic est βλεπειν, & apud Menandrum συνοραν, recte posse verti, videre aut cernere.

## 7:4
Verse 4. ω κατανοεις] ω γινωσκεις as Menander speaks: παραβλεπεις as another Comic poet: you foresee, that is, you overlook, Horace.

Latin:

Vers. 4. ω κατανοεις] ω γινωσκεις ut Menander loquitur: παραβλεπεις ut alter Comicus: prævides, id est, prætervi- des Horatius.

## 7:5
Verse 5. υποκριτα] חנף Job VIII. 13. Εκβαλε πρωτον] It is an old proverb which is referred to in Zemach David under the name of R. Tarphon by the authority of Tryphon.

Και τοτε διαβλεψεις εκβαλειν] Not only because he who is prepared to speak against another must be free from fault, but because those severe chastisers usually have an ulcer lurking in their soul, which prevents them from examining the deeds of others with an equal balance, namely pride, with contempt or even hatred of others. When they have expelled this disease, then at last they will be fit to pass judgment on others.

To this contributes that of Justin Martyr to Zenas and Serenus: That which one instructs another in, he himself ought first to practice: lest, imprudent, he bring judgment upon himself through his neighbor. Therefore, a sensible man, when he turns his mind to the sins of some, says to himself, am I not also of this kind? But wrongly Becanus, book I, Man. c. 14, with his predecessor Bellarmine, book I, de amiss. grace, c. 9, says that venial sin is compared to a splinter, mortal to a beam, and since the former does not extinguish the eye, but injures it slightly, while the latter does extinguish the eye, he asserts that there is a sin which is venial by its nature: because neither is parabolic theology argumentative, nor is this parable directed to that: only a graver sin is compared to a beam, a lighter one to a splinter: however, graver sins can obtain forgiveness if repentance is present, just as lighter ones without repentance bring about guilt and condemnation: just as it can happen that a splinter also extinguishes the eye, if it is not removed: and therefore this happens to any sin whatsoever, that it is forgiven, but by its nature any sin whatsoever is mortal. If a sin is compared with another, one is greater than the other: if sins are compared with the divine law, any one brings about guilt and a curse, unless it is remitted, Deut. XXVII. 26. James II. 10.

PART II.

A caution concerning not profaning the holy.

Latin:

Vers. 5. υποκριτα] חנף Jobi VIII. 13. Εκβαλε πρωτον] Vetus est proverbium quod in Zemach David refertur sub nomine R. Tarphon fide Tryphonis.

Και τοτε διαβλεψεις εκβαλειν] Non tantum quia culpa careat oportet, qui paratus est in alterum dicere, sed quia se- veri isti castigatores plerumque habent ulcus in animo la- tens, quod obstat quo minus æqua lance aliorum facta exa- minent, superbiam scilicet, cum contemtu aut etiam odio aliorum. Hunc morbum ubi expulerint, tum demum ido- nei erunt qui de aliis judicium ferant.

Quo facit illud Justini Martyr. ad Zenam & Se- renum: Quod alium quis instituit, id prius ipse præ- stare debet: ne imprudens per proximum contra se- ipsum ferat sententiam. Dicit igitur sibi ipse, cum ad aliquorum peccata animum advertit vir cordatus, nunquid & ipse sum hujusmodi? Perperam vero Becanus l. I. Man. c. 14. præeunte suo Bellarm. lib. I. de amiss. grat. c. 9. peccatum veniale cum festuca, mortale cum trabe comparari ait, & quum illa ocu- lum non extinguat, sed leviter lædat, hæc vero o- culum extinguat, asserit dari peccatum, quod natu- ra sua veniale sit: quia neque Theologia parabo- lica argumentativa est, neque eo hæc directa est parabola: solum gravius peccatum trabi, levius festucæ comparatur: possunt autem graviora pec- cata condonationem si pœnitentia adsit consequi, ut leviora sine pœnitentia subsequa rea- tum & condemnationem adferunt: uti contingere potest, ut festuca etiam oculum extinguat, si non eximatur: ideoque accidit hoc peccato cuicunque, quod condonetur, natura sua autem peccatum quodcunque mortale est. Peccatum si compare- tur cum alio, majus unum est altero: si cum lege divina conferantur peccata, quodlibet reatum & maledictionem infert, nisi remittatur, Deut. XXVII. 26. Jac. II. 10.

PARS II.

Cautela de non prophanando sancto.

## 7:6
Vers. 6. Μὴ δῶτε τὸ ἅγιον τοῖς κυσί] The Chaldeans, Hebrews, and Egyptians, the most ancient professors of wisdom, used to deliver their precepts ἐν συμβόλοις (in symbols), as Clement of Alexandria teaches. Pythagoras brought this custom into Greece, whether from Egypt where he lived for some time, or from Syria, whence his teacher Pherecydes came, and as some think, Pythagoras himself. For many have reported that he was a Tyrrhenian: others, a Tyrian. But the Tyrrhenians, as we have said, were Tyrians by origin: but he had also approached the Jews, as many writers have reported concerning him. Nor did Pythagoras receive from the barbarian philosophers only the custom of teaching, but the very words of the precepts themselves, a great argument for which is that that saying, τὸ πῦρ μαχαίρᾳ μὴ σκαλεύειν (do not stir the fire with a sword), which Plutarch mentions in Numa as a Pythagorean precept, is found in the same words in the Gnomology of the Arabs. Such also are those: χελιδόνα ἐν οἰκίᾳ μὴ ἔχειν (do not keep a swallow in the house), τῆς χύτρας ἀρθείσης ἀπὸ τοῦ πυρὸς ἐν τῇ σποδᾷ τύπον μὴ ἀπολιπεῖν (when the pot is lifted from the fire, do not leave a mark in the ashes), ἀναστάς ἐξ εὐνῆς συνέχει τὰ στρώματα (having risen from bed, smooth the bedclothes), ἐπὶ γῆς μὴ πλεῖν (do not travel by land), κυάμων ἀπέχειν (abstain from beans). Of the same kind is this: μὴ δῶτε τὸ ἅγιον τοῖς κυσί, μηδὲ βάλητε τοὺς μαργαρίτας ὑμῶν ἔμπροσθεν τῶν χοίρων (do not give what is holy to the dogs, nor cast your pearls before the swine): which meaning the Pythagoreans expressed with this saying: σίτιον εἰς ἀμίδα μὴ ἐμβάλειν (do not cast food into a chamber pot). Christ had been dealing with rash and uncharitable judgment; lest anyone should suspect from this that all freedom of judging even about the most manifest matters was being taken away, he subjoins a precept pertaining to that prudence which he elsewhere wishes to be joined with simplicity. In the Law, the dog was an animal so detestable that it was not even lawful to consecrate the price obtained from it: and things that were most profane were given to dogs. Exod. XXII. 31. That the eating of swine was forbidden by the law of Moses was known to the Greeks and Romans as well. Peter also joined these two animals, 2 Epist. II. 21. & he teaches in what they most agree, namely, in the most extreme filthiness. But what was wont to be said in general among the Hebrews about all precepts of wisdom, that Christ applied to the precepts of his own wisdom, especially the interior ones, teaching with what caution they are to be imparted to others, which was the duty not only of the Apostles, but of all pious men as well, though not with equal right and degree. The meaning, therefore, is that prudence must be applied: and these things are not to be pressed upon those who, having been admonished about open and manifest wickedness, would nevertheless continue to wallow in the old mire of foul pleasures. For Christ also had willed that the preaching of repentance should precede the preaching of the heavenly kingdom. And when he sent the Apostles to teach, he ordered them to explore in every city or village who there was worthy of the word: below X. 14. Plato’s caution has a not dissimilar meaning: εὐλαβῶ μέν τοι μήποτε ἐκπέσῃ ταῦτα εἰς ἀνθρώπους ἀπαιδεύτους˙ σχεδὸν γάρ, ὡς ἐμοὶ δοκεῖ, οὐκ ἔστι τούτων πρὸς τοὺς πολλοὺς γελοιότερα ἀκούσματα (I am cautious, however, lest these things should fall into the hands of uneducated men; for almost, as it seems to me, there are no things more ridiculous than these to the many). And that of Heraclitus: τὰ τῆς γνώσεως βάθη κρύπτειν, ἀπιστίη ἀγαθή (to hide the depths of knowledge is a good distrust). And that of Lysis the Pythagorean in his Epistle to Hipparchus: μὴ κοινὰ ποιεῖσθαι τὰ-

Good things of wisdom for those who have purified their soul. Concerning those who act against this, Lysis pronounces the same thus: pouring into disturbed and flourishing dispositions, theorems and divine words, is just as if someone were to pour pure and clear water into a deep well full of mud. For then he stirred up the mud and destroyed the water. But if one wishes to distinguish more accurately between dogs and pigs, we shall be able to understand with Clement of Alexandria those who shamelessly bark at warnings, such as those Jews of Antioch who were contradicting and blaspheming, Acts XIII. 46, who are therefore said to have judged themselves unworthy of eternal life: which kind of Jews Paul also explicitly calls dogs, Phil. III. 2, and perhaps they are the same as those who are called dogs by John, Rev. XXII. 15. For also Psalm XXII, verse 17, interprets those whom it had called dogs as the assembly of the wicked. But pigs can be understood as those who do not indeed contradict, but by the impurity of their life show how much they hold warnings in contempt. For it will become clear at the end of chapter XIV that these were properly understood by the Jews under the image of pigs. And this distinction is followed here by Chrysostom. And indeed, the following words seem to require this distinction: for it is one thing to trample what is given, which is the way of pigs; another to attack with bites the one offering it, which is the way of dogs.

There is therefore no observation here by Pricaeus, and it is a vain quibble against Scripture: that both 'trample' and 'tear' are said here of pigs, and what he has besides about the two words applied to one genus of animals, even though mention has been made not only of pigs but also of dogs.

And having turned, they tear you] It usually happens that obstinate contemners of divine truth conceive immense hatred against its professors, as being opposed to their own advantages or glory, and as reproaching their own shameful deeds by the diversity of their morals, and they incite the common people and the authorities against them: which Christ and his Apostles experienced especially among the Jews. Justin knew such a one, Crescens the Cynic philosopher, and from him, not a vain prophet, he expected the causes of his own death. But just as Christ does not want sacred doctrine to be proposed for the sake of these alone, so neither does he want it to be withheld for their sake. But 'having turned' here means 'having been moved,' as we shall explain below at chapter XVI.

Dogs and pigs, says Euthymius, he named those who are held by immedicable impiety: dogs indeed as barking at Christ, but pigs as if wrapped in the mud of perturbations. To such, therefore, let it be a sacrilege to cast what is holy, or to admit them to the holy Supper. But the Papists are unjust toward the laity, even Princes and Kings, when they say that allowing them the reading of Holy Scripture is to give what is holy to dogs, and to cast pearls before pigs: for they value their own supreme heads so highly, holding them without distinction as dogs and pigs: to whom you would rather compare most of the purple-clad and the priests or the cowled ones.

PART III. Admonition concerning prayers.

Latin:

Vers. 6. Μὴ δῶτε τὸ ἅγιον τοῖς κυσί] Chaldæi, Hebræi, Ægyptii vetustissimi sapientiæ professores præcepta sua tra- debant ἐν συμβόλοις, ut docet Clemens Alexandrinus. Py- thagoras hunc morem in Græciam attulit, sive ex Ægypto ubi vixit aliquamdiu, sive ex Syria, unde erat magister ipsius Pherecydes, & ut quidam existimant ipse Pythagoras. Nam Tyrrhenum fuisse multi prodiderunt: alii Tyrium. Sed & Tyrrheni origine ut diximus Tyrii erant: sed & Judæos ad- ierat, ut complures de eo Scriptores prodiderunt. Neque vero morem tantum præcipiendi, sed & ipsa præceptorum verba à barbaris Philosophis accepit Pythagoras, cujus rei magnum est argumentum, quod illud τὸ πῦρ μαχαίρᾳ μὴ σκαλεύειν, cujus ut Pythagorici præcepti in Numa Plutar- chus meminit, totidem verbis reperitur in Gnomologico Arabum. Talia sunt & illa: χελιδόνα ἐν οἰκίᾳ μὴ ἔχειν, τῆς χύτρας ἀρθείσης ἀπὸ τοῦ πυρὸς ἐν τῇ σποδᾷ τύπον μὴ ἀπολιπεῖν, ἀναστάς ἐξ εὐνῆς συνέχει τὰ στρώματα. ἐπὶ γῆς μὴ πλεῖν, κυά- μων ἀπέχειν. Ejusdem generis & hoc est: μὴ δῶτε τὸ ἅγιον τοῖς κυσί, μηδὲ βάλητε τοὺς μαργαρίτας ὑμῶν ἔμπροσθεν τῶν χοίρων: quem sensum Pythagorici hoc dicto exprimebant: σίτιον εἰς ἀμίδα μὴ ἐμβάλειν. Egerat Christus de temerario atq; inclemente judicio, ne quis hinc suspicaretur omnem etiam de rebus manifestissimis judicandi libertatem tolli, subjungit præceptum ad eam prudentiam pertinens, quam alibi vult cum simplicitate conjungi. Canis in lege animal erat adeo exsecrandum, ut ne pretium quidem inde reda- ctum consecrare fas esset: & quæ erant profanissima cani- bus darentur. Exod. XXII. 31. Suem edi vetitum Mosis lege Græcis quoque & Romanis notum erat. Conjunxit hæc duo animalia etiam Petrus 2. Epist. II. 21. & in quo maxime conveniant docet, nempe in projectissima immunditie. Quod autem in universum de omnibus sapientiæ præceptis dici solebat apud Hebræos, id Christus suæ sapientiæ præ- ceptis, præsertim interioribus applicavit, docens qua cau- tione ea aliis sint impertienda, quod erat non Apostolorum duntaxat, sed piorum quoque omnium officium, etsi non æquali jure ac gradu. Sensus ergo est, prudentiam adhi- bendam: neque hæc inculcanda iis qui admoniti de apertis manifestisque flagitiis in veteri tamen luto fœdarum vo- luptatum pergerent volutari. Nam & Christus pœniten- tiæ prædicationem prædicationi cœlestis regni voluerat antecedere. Et cum Apostolos ad docendum mitteret, ex- plorare eos jussit in quaq; urbe aut vico, ecquis ibi esset di- gnus sermone: infra X. 14. Non dissimilem sensum habet Platonis illi cautio: εὐλαβῶ μέν τοι μήποτε ἐκπέσῃ ταῦτα εἰς ἀνθρώπους ἀπαιδεύτους˙ σχεδὸν γάρ, ὡς ἐμοὶ δοκεῖ, οὐκ ἔστι τούτων πρὸς τοὺς πολλοὺς γελοιότερα ἀκούσματα. Et illud Heracliti: τὰ τῆς γνώσεως βάθη κρύπτειν, ἀπιστίη ἀγαθή. Et Lysidis Py- thagorici in Epistola ad Hipparchum: μὴ κοινὰ ποιεῖσθαι τὰ-

σοφίας ἀγαθὰ τοῖς ὀδ' ὄνας τὰν ψυχὰν κεκαθαρμένοις. De his qui contra faciunt, idem Lysis sic pronuntiat: ἐγχέοντι ἤθεσι τεταραγμένοις τε κᾀ θαλεροῖς, θεωρήματα κᾀ λόγως θείως, καθάπερ εἴ τις εἰς φρέαρ βαθὺ βορβόρω πλῆρες ἐγχέοι καθαρὸν κᾀ διειδὲς ὕδωρ. τότε γὰρ βόρβορον ἀνετάραξε κᾀ τὸ ὕδωρ ἠφά- νισεν. Quod si accuratius libet distinguere inter canes & por- cos, canes cum Clemente Alexandrino poterimus intelli- gere eos qui monitis impudenter oblatrant, quales erant Judæi illi Antiocheni ἀντιλέγοντες κᾀ βλασφημῶντες, Act. XIII. 46. qui propterea dicuntur semet indignos judicasse vita æterna: cujus ingenii Judæos etiam Paulus diserte ca- nes vocat Phil. III. 2. ac forte iidem sunt qui canes appel- lantur à Johanne Apoc. XXII. 15. Nam & Psalmus XXII. commate 17. quos canes vocarat, interpretatur συναγωγὴν τῶν πονηρευομένων. Porci autem intelligi poterunt, qui non contradicunt quidem, sed vitæ impuritate ostendunt quan- to contemtui monita habeant. Nam hos proprie sub por- corum imagine à Judæis intellectos apertum fiet ad caput XIV. sub finem. Idque discrimen hic sequitur Chrysosto- mus. Et sane videntur hoc discrimen requirere quæ sequun- tur: nam aliud est datum proculcare, quod porcorum est: aliud porrigentem morsibus petere, quod canum.

Nulla ergo hic observatio est Pricæi & vana in Scripturam cavillatio: de porcis & τὸ καταπατή- σωσιν & τὸ ῥήξωσιν hic dici, & quæ ille habet præ- terea de duabus vocibus ad unum animalium ge- nus applicatis, etsi non porcorum tantum, sed etiam canum mentio facta sit.

κᾀ στραφέντες ῥήξωσιν ὑμᾶς] Plerumque fit ut obstinati contemtores divinæ veritatis in ejus professores, ut com- modis aut gloriæ suæ adversos, & diversitate morum sua ipsis flagitia exprobrantes, immane odium concipiant, plebemque & potestates in ipsos concitent: quod in Ju- dæis præsertim Christus ejusque Apostoli experti sunt. Talem Crescentem Cynicum Philosophum noverat Ju- stinus, & ab eo non vanus vates mortis suæ causas exspe- ctabat. Sicut autem Christus horum solorum causa non vult proponi sacram doctrinam, ita neque illorum causa eam vult reticeri. στραφέντες autem hic est commoti, ut explicabimus infra ad caput XVI.

Canes & porcos, inquit Euthymius, nominavit. qui immedicabili tenentur impietate: Canes qui- dem tanquam Christo oblatrantes, porcos vero quasi perturbationum luto obvolutos. Talibus ergo religio sit sacra projicere, aut eos ad sacram Cœnam admittere. Iniqui autem Papistæ sunt in Laicos, etiam Principes & Reges, cum illis lectio- nem Scripturæ S. permittere dicunt esse sanctum dare canibus, & margaritas porcis projicere: Tan- ti scilicet faciunt ipsi summa capita, habentes ea sine discrimine pro canibus & porcis: quibus po- tius plerosque purpuratos & sacrificulos vel cu- cullatos comparaveris.

PARS III. Commonitio de precibus.

## 7:7
Ver. 7. Ask and it shall be given to you] These are accustomed to be connected with the preceding in various ways. To me, it seems that certain general precepts are being added to many special ones; and here is handed down the method of how we can obtain those gifts which are necessary for persisting constantly in this path shown by Christ. For that this concerns obtaining the Holy Spirit is rightly proved by Maximus from Luke in his dialogue against the 'otomoious': James seems to call this same gift by the name of wisdom, I. 5. Paul joined both, when he says that he prays for the Ephesians that God may give them the spirit of wisdom and revelation, for the knowledge of him, the eyes of their mind enlightened to know what is that hope of his calling and what the wealth of his glory which is given to the saints by hereditary right, Eph. I. 17, 18. Surely Christ had said above that for the affections to be rightly directed, it is necessary that the eyes of the mind shine. For this matter, he wants celestial light to be obtained from us, and that by earnest prayers.

It is not only about obtaining the gift of the Holy Spirit, but about any goods and gifts whatsoever, which Christ had comprised in the formula of prayer in chapter VI, that this is concerned.

Latin:

Vers. 7. Αἰτεῖτε κᾀ δοθήσεται ὑμῖν] Diversis modis hæc solent cum superioribus connecti. Mihi videntur multis specialibus præceptis generalia quædam subjungi; atque hic tradi ratio, quomodo consequi possimus dona illa quæ ad insistendum constanter hoc iter à Christo monstra- tum sunt necessaria. Nam de impetrando Spiritu S. hic a- gi, recte ex Luca probat Maximus dialogo contra ὠτομοίους: Idem hoc donum sapientiæ nomine videtur Jacobus ap- pellare I. 5. Paulus utrumque conjunxit, cum pro Ephe- sis orare se ait ut Deus ipsis det spiritum sapientiæ, & re- velationis, ad cognitionem ipsius, mentis oculos illustra- tos ad cognoscendum quæ sit illa spes vocationis & quæ o- pulentia gloriæ eius quæ hæreditario jure sanctis datur Ephes. I. 17. 18. Nimirum supra dixerat Christus ad affe- ctus recte dirigendos opus esse ut mentis oculi luceant. Ad hanc rem impetrari vult à nobis lumen cœleste idque contentis precibus.

Non tantum de Spiritus S. dono impetrando, sed de quibusvis bonis & donis, quæ cap. VI. orationis complexus erat formula Christus, agi- tur.

## 7:8
Ver. 8. He who seeks finds] Sophocles: That which is sought is capturable. But that which is neglected escapes.

But here by the words to ask, to seek, to knock, the same thing is denoted, namely, the zeal of praying. Not badly Hierocles: Prayer is the boundary between our seeking and God's giving, holding onto the cause of us which leads us into being and perfects us toward well-being.

There is a gradation in the words ask, seek, knock. Augustine says that one asks by faith, seeks by hope, but knocks by charity. Others say that by the word 'ask' it is indicated that necessary things are to be sought, by the word 'seek' that one is to pray diligently, by the word 'knock' that one is to pray constantly and perseveringly.

Latin:

Vers. 8. Ὁ ζητῶν εὑρίσκει] Sophocles: τὸ δὲ ζητύμενον Ἁλωτὸν. ἐκ φεύγει δὲ τ' ἀμελούμενον.

Sed hic verbis αἰτεῖν, ζητεῖν, κρούειν idem denotatur, studium scilicet precandi. Non male Hierocles : εὐχὴ μεθόριον τῆς παρ᾽ ἡμῖν ζητήσεως κὰι τῆς παρὰ τῶ θεῶ δόσεως, ἐχομένη τῆς αἰ- τίας ἡμῶν τῆς εἰς τό εἶναι προαγούσης ἡμᾶς κὰι πρὸς τὸ εὖ ἐπαγ τελειούσης.

Gradatio est in verbis petite, quærite, pulsate. Augustinus ait fide peti, spe quæri, charitate vero pulfari. Alii verbo petere indicari necessaria esse expetenda, verbo quærite diligenter, verbo pulsare constanter & perseveranter esse oran- dum.

## 7:9
Vers. 9. ἡ τίς ἐστιν ἐξ ὑμῶν ἄνθρωπος] It may seem strange that the interrogative μὴ is subjoined to another interrogative, τίς. But it should be noted that among the Hebrews, quis is often used not so much interrogatively as hypothetically for si quis, as also below XII. 11. and XXIV. 45. Luke XI. 5, and 11. James III, 13. So also in Ps. CVII. 43. and Deut. XX. 8. Nor is that passage in Haggai II. 4 to be interpreted otherwise: Who among you is left, who saw this house in its former glory? For no one seems to have been among the companions of Zerubbabel who could have seen the temple built by Solomon: but the Prophet means this: if there were any of you now who had seen the former temple, how much this temple would appear base in comparison with that one. The sense of this passage, therefore, is: if there is anyone among you whose son asks for bread, will he give him a stone? for τὸ ἐὰν placed after ὅς is accustomed to be redundant, as above chapter V, verse 19, below chapter X, verse 14, 42, XI. 27, XII. 36, XV. 5, XVI. 19, XVIII. 5, 19, XX. 4, 7, 26, 27, and elsewhere. But also after ὅσον, ὧ, ὅπου and others of relative notation, as can be seen throughout these books. Μὴ, however, is interrogative here: in which sense also the Jewish word שם coming from the Greek language אם in the Gemara and elsewhere. Moreover, this adage about bread and stone passed from the Hebrews to other nations as well, as appears from Plautus:

In one hand he carries a stone, in the other he shows bread.

Latin:

Vers. 9. ἡ τίς ἐστιν ἐξ ὑμῶν ἄνθρωπος] Mirum videri pot- est quod interrogativo τίς alterum interrogativum μὴ subjungitur. Sed notandum est apud Hebræos quis sæpe poni non tam πνευματικῶς, quam ὑποθετικῶς pro si quis, ut & infra XII. 11. & XXIV. 45. Luc. XI. 5, & 11. Jac. III, 13. Sic & in Ps. CVII. 43. & Deut. XX. 8. Neque aliter inter- pretandum illud apud Aggæum II. 4. Quis ex vobis reliquus, qui viderit istam domum in gloria sua priore? Nemo enim videtur Zorobabelis comitum fuisse qui templum à Salo- mone conditum videri potuisset: sed hoc vult Propheta : si quis nunc vestrum esset qui prius templum vidisset, quam valde hoc templum præ illo sorderet. Hujus igitur loci sensus est: si quis inter vos est quem filius panem poscit, an lapidem ei dabit? nam τὸ ἐὰν post ὅς positum solet πα- ρέλκειν, vt supra cap. V. commate 19. infra cap. X. com. 14. 42. XI. 27. XII. 36. XV. 5. XVI. 19. XVIII. 5. 19. XX. 4. 7. 26. 27. & alibi. Sed & post ὅσον, ὧ, ὅπου aliaque rela- tivæ notationis, ut passim in his libris videre est. Μὴ autem interrogativum hic est: quo sensu & vox Judaica שם ex Græco sermone veniens אם in Gemara & alibi. Adagium autem hoc de pane & lapide ab Hebræis ad alias etiam gentes transiit, ut ex Plauto apparet:

Altera manu fert lapidem, panem oftendit altera.

## 7:11
Vers. 11. Πονηροὶ ὄντες] That is, compared to God. See Job XV. 14, 15.

Ἀγαθὰ δόματα] Gifts of the Holy Spirit, as we said above. See James I, verse 17, and compare with verse 5 in the same chapter. But the old interpreter translated δόματα as data. For that word is also a substantive for the Latins. An old glossary says δόσις is datum. Ausonius spoke of God as full of gifts.

PART IV.

The sum of the doctrine of the law and the Prophets.

Latin:

Vers. 11. Πονηροὶ ὄντες] Deo scilicet comparati. Vide Jobum XV. 14. 15.

Ἀγαθὰ δόματα] Dona Spiritus S. ut supra diximus. Vi- de Jacobi I. commate 17. & confer cum commate 5. eodem capite. Ben: autem vetus interpres δόματα data transtulit. Est enim ea vox Latinis etiam substantiva. Glossarium ve- tus δόσις datum. Plenus datorum de Deo dixit Ausonius.

PARS IV.

Summa doctrinæ legis & Prophetarum.

## 7:12
Vers. 12. Ὄσα ἂν θέλητε] When Christ had spoken about prayers, he now adds those things which might excite our efforts. For it is necessary that these things be joined, ὅπως τ᾽ ἐργαζόμεθα κὰι εὐχόμεθα, κὰι τ᾽ εὐχόμεθα ἐνεργῶμεν, as Hierocles hands down from the discipline of Pythagoras. Christ commands us, however, to take pains to perform for others those things which reason dictates we would not unjustly ask of others: but this is said because we usually see more correctly what is fair when nothing is lost to us. Laberius meant this:

Man always carries one thing in himself, and thinks another for his neighbor. But this happens from an excessive love of ourselves. Euripides:

Ὢς πᾶς τις αὑτὸν τῶ πέλας μᾶλλον φιλεῖ. Whence that saying of Sallust: To no one do their own injuries seem light. And yet it is most fair, that which that Mime said: Expect from another what you have done to another.

The Emperor Severus is said to have had on his lips this noble sentiment received from the Christians or from the Jews: What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another. The same sense is in the oration of Appius Caecus in Halicarnassensis. Nor does the historian add 'or from the Jews' in vain: for this saying was also on their lips: ὃ μισεῖς μηδενὶ ποιήσεις as is evident in Tob. IV. 16. Therefore, so that we may judge rightly, the person must be changed: and the same must be determined for another as we would judge to be fair for ourselves.

Rightly Prosper, book III, de vit. contempl. cap. 15. This is the whole love of one's neighbor, that whatever good you wish to be conferred upon you, you should wish also for your neighbor: and the evil which you would not wish to happen to you, you should not wish for your neighbor either. Hence Nazianzenus: οἷα πρὸς ἄλλον μὴ παθεῖν ὅλως θέλεις, τοιαῦτα καὶ σὺ μὴ δὲ δρᾶν ἄλλω θέλε. Such things as you do not wish to suffer at all from another: such things you also should not do to another. This is what Alexander Severus, as Aelius Lampridius testifies, claimed for himself in particular: What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another.

For this is the law and the prophets] That is, hence the law and the prophets depend, as is held below XVII. 30. Through this the law is fulfilled, as Paul speaks Rom. XII. 8. Gal. V. 14. This is indeed the scope which the law proposes to itself: for the sentence which preceded has the same meaning as that sentence, love your neighbor as you love yourself. But what is said both here and by Paul, that the sum of the law and the prophets consists in this one precept, is to be understood concerning the law and the admonitions regarding the mutual duties of men toward one another. For those things which pertain to the worship of God are comprehended in the other precept, as will appear below. But when he had spoken of prayers, Christ rightly subjoined those things which would excite our diligence, for this reason also, that we might not idly await divine aid. For God also helps the one who labors. Which he also pursues in the following exhortation. These things are altogether commonly accepted as such, because in them consists either the foundation or the sum of the moral doctrine of the law and the prophets concerning the love of the neighbor, Rom. XIII. 8. Gal. V. 14. Yet it could seem not inappropriate if these words were referred not only to the immediately preceding rule, but to the whole doctrine of Christ handed down thus far, because he did not only inculcate those things which pertain to the second table, nor merely legal matters alone, but almost the whole heavenly doctrine, or at least those heads to which the rest can be referred: as Blessed Gerhard explained in this place; unless the fact that that sentence is repeated elsewhere would demand the former sense; namely, Matt. XXII. 40, where the subject of the proposition, from which the law and the prophets depend, is constituted by the two precepts of the law. Therefore Clem. Alex. calls this rule an admonition pertaining to life, embracing all things.

PART V. Exhortation to the study of entering through the narrow gate.

Latin:

Vers. 12. Ὄσα ἂν θέλητε] Cum de precibus dixisset Chri- stus, jam ea addit quæ conatus nostros excitent. Opor- tet enim ista conjungi, ὅπως τ᾽ ἐργαζόμεθα κὰι εὐχόμεθα, κὰι τ᾽ εὐχόμεθα ἐνεργῶμεν, ut ex Pythagoræ disciplina tradit Hiero- cles. Jubet autem Christus operam nos dare, ut aliis præ- stemus ea quæ ratio dictat non inique nos ab aliis postu- laturus: hoc autem ideo dicitur, quia plerumque rectius videmus quid æquum sit, ubi nobis nihil decedit. La- berius hoc voluit:

Homo semper in se aliud fert, in alterum aliud cogitat. Contingit autem hoc ex nimio nostri amore. Euripi- des :

Ὢς πᾶς τις αὑτὸν τῶ πέλας μᾶλλον φιλεῖ. Unde illud Sallustii: Nemini sua injuriæ leves videntur. At- qui æquissimum est id, quod ille Mimus dixit: Ab alio exspectes alteri quod feceris.

Severus Imperator narratur in ore habuisse nobilem hanc sententiam à Christianis aut à Judæis acceptam : Quod ti- bi non vis fieri alteri ne feceris. Sensus idem in Appii Cœ- ci oratione apud Halicarnassensem. Non frustra autem adjicit Historicus aut à Judæis: nam & illis in ore fuit hoc dictum : ὃ μισεῖς μηδενὶ ποιήσεις ut patet Tob. IV. 16. Er- go ut recte judicemus, persona mutanda est: idemque statuendum in altero quod in nobis æquum simus existi- maturi.

Recte Prosper lib. III. de vit. contempl. cap. 15. Hæc est proximi tota dilectio, ut bonum quid tibi conferri vis, velis & proximo: & malum quod tibi accidere nolis, nolis & proximo. Inde Na- zianzenus : οἷα πρὸς ἄλλον μὴ παθεῖν ὅλως θέλεις, τοιαῦτα καὶ σὺ μὴ δὲ δρᾶν ἄλλω θέλε. Qualia ab altero omnino non vis pati: talia & tu alterine feceris. Hoc est quod Alexander Severus, teste Æ- lio Lampridio, peculiariter sibi vindicavit : Quod tibi non vis fieri, alteri ne feceris.

ὗτος γάρ ἐστιν ὁ νόμος καὶ οἱ προφῆται] Hoc est, hinc pen- det lex & Prophetæ, ut infra habetur XVII. 30. Per hoc lex πληρῦται, ut Paulus loquitur Rom. XII. 8. Gal. V. 14. Hic ni- mirum scopus est quem sibi lex proponit: nam quæ præcef- sit sententia idem plane valet illi sententiæ, dilige alterum quemadmodum te diligis. Quod autem dicitur & hic, & apud Paulum in hoc uno præcepto legis & Prophetarum summa consistere, intelligendum est de lege & monitis spectantibus mutua inter se hominum officia. Nam quæ ad Dei cultum pertinent, altero præcepto comprehenduntur, ut infra apparebit. Cum autem de precibus dixisset, re- cte subjunxit Christus ea quæ diligentiam nostram exci- tarent ob hoc quoque ne otiosi divinam opem exspecta- remus. Τῷ γὰρ πονῦντι καὶ θεὸς ξυναμβάνει. Quod & sequente adhortatione prosequitur. Hæc omnino ita accipiuntur communiter, quod in eis seu fundamentum seu summa doctri- næ moralis legis & Prophetarum de dilectione proximi consistat, Rom. XIII. 8. Gal. V. 14. videri tamen posset non inconcinnum, si verba hæc non tantum ad proxime præcedentem regulam, sed ad totam Christi doctrinam hactenus traditam refe- rantur, quia non tantum ea, quæ ad tabulam se- cundam pertinent, inculcavit, nec mere solum legalia, sed totam pene doctrinam cœlestem, aut certe ea capita, ad quæ referri cætera queant: uti B. Gerhardus in h. l. exposuit; nisi alibi ea senten- tia repetita priorem sensum postularet; Matth. nempe XXII. 40. ubi subjectum propositionis a quo scilicet pendeant lex & Prophetæ, consti- tuuntur duo præcepta legis. Ideo Clem. Alex. Re- gulam hanc vocat παραίνεσιν πάντα περιέχουσαν, admonitionem ad vitam pertinentem, omnia com- plectentem.

PARS V. Adhortatio ad studium ingrediendi per angu- stam portam.

## 7:13
Vers. 13. Narrow gate] Just as דֶּרֶך is for the most part among the Hebrews and ὁδὸς among the Hellenists, so also here gate signifies a way of life. For the gate is wide and the way is broad] If you compare it with the word of the opposite member, it will seem that the broad is opposed to the narrow, but the spacious to the afflicted. A way can be wide which is not spacious, that is, level, but rugged, for that is what afflicted means. I think, therefore, that the way of piety is called narrow because by its own nature it displeases the flesh: but rugged, because it is strewn with external impediments as if with certain thorns: but custom, the help of the spirit (John epistle I. ch. V. 4), and the hope of reward overcome these troubles. Concerning custom is the sentiment of Hesiod: The immortals have placed sweat before virtue; and the path to it is long and steep, and rough at first. But when one reaches the summit, it is easy then, though it was difficult. Which Silius imitates, introducing virtue speaking according to the example of Prodicus: An arduous path leads through the rocky cliff, rough at the beginning (for it is not my custom to deceive) it follows: labor is for the one wishing to enter to strive.
