Nor should those things be considered good which fickle fortune has given. And the same has the power to snatch them away, soon you will see from on high the race of men below you. Verses exist to the same effect in the catalects which are accustomed to be joined to Virgil concerning the letter of Pythagoras. Not alien to this sense is that one in Plutarch concerning the demon of Socrates: for the paths of life are wide, but few are those through which the demons lead men. Many are those who enter through it] Bias truly said that the majority are evil. Nor is that a wonder. For the noble are simple, but the evil are manifold. Vices lie wide open, and serve any passions whatsoever. The way of piety is unique, not indulging our desires, but surrounded on all sides by divine precepts. Vers. 14. How narrow] 'Ti' for 'hos' is of the Hellenists. For in Psalm VIII. 1, where the LXX have 'how wonderful is your name', other Greek interpreters have 'how great is your name'. Psalm XXXI. 20, where the LXX have 'how great is the multitude of your goodness', Symmachus placed 'how great is your good'. Thus, however, it appears that the Greeks read in this place, thus the Syrian, thus the Latin interpreter. Nothing, therefore, is to be changed.

Latin:

Vers. 13. Στενῆς πύλης] Sicut דֶּרֶך plerumque apud He- bræos & ὁδὸς apud Hellenistas, ita & hic πύλη vitæ institu- tum significat. Ὅτι πλατεῖα πύλη καὶ εὐρύχωρος ἡ ὁδὸς] Si compares verbo membri oppositi, videbitur τὸ πλατὺ opponi τῷ στενῷ, at τὸ εὐρύχωρον τεθλιμμένῳ. Potest via aliqua lata esse quæ non sit εὐρύχωρος, hoc est campestris, sed confratosa, nam id valet τεθλιμμένη. Puto igitur viam pietatis angustam di- ci, quia suapte natura displicet carni: confragosam vero, quia externis impedimentis quasi muricibus quibusdam strata est: sed has molestias vincit consuetudo, auxilium spiritus (Joh. epistola I. c. V. 4) & spes præmii. De con- suetudine est Hesiodi sententia: Τῆς δ' ἀρετῆς ἱδρῶτα θεοὶ προπάροιθεν ἔθηκαν Ἀθάνατοι· μακρὸς δὲ καὶ ὄρθιος οἶμος ἐπ' αὐτὴν, Καὶ τρηχὺς τὸ πρῶτον. ἐπὴν δ' εἰς ἄκρον ἵκηται, Ῥηϊδίη δ' ἔπειτα πέλει χαλεπήπερ ἐοῦσα. Quam Silius imitatur, virtutem Prodici exemplo ita lo- quentem inducens: Ardua saxoso per ducit semita clivo, Aspera principio (nec enim mihi fallere mos est) Prosequitur: labor ad nitendum intrare volenti. Nec bona censendum quæ fors infida dedisset. Atq; eadem rapuisse valet, mox celsus ab alto Infra te cernes hominum genus. Exstant in eandem sententiam versus in catalectis quæ Virgilio subjungi solent de litera Pythagoræ. Non alie- nus ab hoc sensu est ille apud Plutarchum de Socratis Dæ- mone: εὐρεῖαι μὲν γὰρ ἀτραποὶ βίων' ὀλίγαι δὲ δὶ ὃς δαίμο- νες ἀνθρώπως ἄγωσιν. Πόλλοι εἰσιν οἱ εἰσερχόμενοι δι' αὐτῆς] Bias vere πλείους κα- κὼς ἔφη. Neque id mirum. Ἐσθλοὶ μὲν γὰρ ἁπλῶς, παντοδαπῶς δὲ κακοὶ. Vitia late patent, & quibusvis affectibus famulantur. Pie- tatis unica via est, non cupiditatibus nostris indulgens, sed divinis præceptis undique circumsepta. Vers. 14. Τὶ στενὴ] τὶ pro ὡς Hellenistarum est. Nam in Psalmo VIII. 1. ubi LXX. ὡς θαυμαστὸν τὸ ὄνομά σου alii Græ- ci interpretes habent τὶ μέγα τὸ ὄνομά σꙋ. Pfalm XXXI. 20. ubi LXX. ὡς πολὺ τὸ πλῆθος τῆς χρηστότητός σꙋ, Symmachus pofuit τὶ πολὺ τὸ ἀγαθόν σꙋ. Ita autem hoc loco legisse Græ- cos apparet, ita Syrum, ita Latinum interpretem. Nihil i- gitur mutandum.

## 7:14
Those who find it] who attain it: as below XI. 29. Luke I. 30. and elsewhere. But why do they not attain it? Because they do not judge rightly concerning the ends of things and the ways to the end, nor do they devote effort so that they might be able to judge rightly.

The mind wanders uncertainly: life is lived by the way. But the great blame for this thing lies with the bad teachers with whom Christ deals consequently. Ulpian on the oration of Demosthenes against Ceptinen: the good are necessarily few. For the many are evil. But this saying is opposed, as is also chapter VII of the Apocalypse, to the false opinion of the Jews concerning the universal piety of men in the times of the Messiah.

Gate does not denote the way, but the door toward which we tend, which is opened at the end of the way, that is, of life, and is either of heaven or of hell. For the gate is distinguished from the way. But by the way is understood life, or the passage and journey through this age; which way is twofold, either of the children of the age, that is, of the unfaithful and the impious, or of the children of God, that is, of the faithful. That way is spacious because of the proclivity of the flesh, the ease of erring, the craftiness of Satan, the variety of seducers, and the sweetness of the pleasures of this age. But this way of the faithful, life, is Christ himself, but insofar as we live in him through faith, and walk through faith. John XIV. 6. because Christ is the unique way to the harbor of heaven by reason of merit: since no one comes to the Father except through him. Then indeed he is also set before us as an example, that we might walk in his footsteps, unless we wish to be carried away to the spacious way, not that we might penetrate into heaven through virtues, but that we ought to insist upon the holy footsteps of Christ, lest we be seduced from the way of true faith and piety to the devious paths of errors and vices, fall from faith and salvation, and be cast headlong into eternal destruction. For few find this way, with Augustine saying on this place, because there is no diligence in seeking, because in those who seek there is blindness of reason, perversity of the concupiscible, subtlety of the deceiving Devil, in us a proneness to falling, difficulty in rising, weakness in resisting, and a multiplicity of those drawing us away from the way. The word narrow denotes narrowness and compression, because of which we groan, because there is need of difficulty, agony, groans, and sighs, so that we may enter through the narrow gate, Luke XIII. 24. & τεθλημμένη is afflicted or beset by various afflictions, the way by which we enter, 2 Cor. IV. 8. Acts XIV. 22. Macarius in the Greek Catena of Nicetas: But if you wish to find the way that leads to life, seek it in the way that says: I am the way, the truth, and the life; and there you will find it: yet seek it with vehement labor, because few are they who find it, lest you also, being excluded by the few, be found with the many.

Latin:

Οἱ εὑρίσκοντες αὐτὴν] qui eam afsequuntur: ut infra XI. 29. Luc. I. 30. & alibi. Quare autem non afsequuntur? Quia de rerum finibus viisque ad finem non recte judi- cant, neque ut recte judicare possint operam ponunt.

Incerte errat animus: præter propter vitam vivitur. Magna autem hujus rei culpa est penes malos magistros de quibus consequenter agit Christus. Ulpianus ad Demosthe- nis orationem in Ceptinen: οἱ ἀγαθοὶ, ὀλίγοι ἀναγκαίως. κακοὶ γὰρ οἱ πολλοὶ. Opponitur autem hoc dictum, ut & ca- put VII. Apocalyseos falsæ Judæorum opinioni, de uni- versali hominum pietate temporibus Messiæ.

Non viam notat πύλη, sed portam ad quam tendimus, quæ sub exitum viæ, h. e. vitæ pandi- tur, & vel cæli est, vel inferni. Nam porta à via di- stinguitur. Per viam autem vita intelligitur, vel transitus & iter per hoc seculum; quæ via gemi na est, vel filiorum seculi, seu infidelium & im- piorum, vel filiorum Dei seu fidelium. Illa via εὐρύχωρος spatiofa est ob carnis proclivitatem, errandi facilitatem, Satanæ calliditatem, seducen- tium varietatem, ac voluptatum hujus seculi sua- vitatem. Hæc autem via fidelium vita Christus ipse est, sed quatenus in ipso per fidem vivimus, & per fidem ambulamus. Joh. XIV. 6. quia Christus unica via est ad portum cæli ratione meriti: quum nemo veniat ad Patrem nisi per ipsum. Tum ve- ro in exemplum nobis etiam sistitur, ut inceda- mus in vestigiis ejus, nisi abripi ad viam spa- tiosam velimus, non quod per virtutes in cæ- lum penetremus, sed quod insistere sanctis Chri- sti vestigiis debeamus, ne à via veræ fidei & pieta- tis ad devia seducti errorum & vitiorum à fide ac salute excidamus, & in æternum exitium præcipi- temur. Pauci enim inveniunt hanc viam, Au- gustino in hunc locum dicente, quia non est in quærendo sedulitas, quia in quærentibus est rationis cæcitas, concupiscibilis perversitas, Diaboli fallen- tis subtilitas, in nobis cadendi pronitas, resurgendi difficultas, resistendi debilitas, retrahentium à via multiplicitas. Vox στενὴ angustam, & com- pressionem notat, ob quam στενάζομεν, quia diffi- cultate, ἀγωνίᾳ, gemitibus & suspiriis opus est, ut per angustam portam ingrediamur, Luc. XIII. 24. & τεθλημμένη afflicta vel variis afflictionibus obsessa est via, qua ingredimur, 2. Corinth. IV. 8. Actor. XIV. 22. Macarius in Catena Græca Nice- tæ: Tu vero si viam invenire vis, qua ducit ad vi- tam, in via illam quære, qua dicit: Ego sum via, veritas & vita; ibique illam invenies: vehementi tamen labore quære, quia pauci sunt qui inveniant eam, ne etiam à paucis exceptus cum multis inve- niaris.

## 7:15
Vers. 15. ἀπὸ τῶν ψευδοπροφητῶν] That is, false teachers, as Peter interprets in chapter II. 1. For among the Hebrews, they were called prophets, not only those who foretold the future, but also others who came forward to teach the people, especially if they claimed to bear commands given from heaven. Such was Simon and Bar-Jesus, whom Luke calls a false prophet in Acts XIII. 6. Christ distinguishes these false prophets from the false Christs below in XXIV. 5, 11, 24, such as was Bar Kokhba. Yet I do not think that any false prophets whatsoever are meant here, but those who professed themselves to be followers of Christ: because of those things which cohere below in verse 21. He calls them false, however, not by reason of their mission, as is proven from the same verse 21, but because of their false and destructive doctrine. See Peter in the aforementioned place.

Ἐν ἐνδύμασι προβάτων] in sheepskins, as the writer to the Hebrews speaks in XI. 37. For that was almost the habit of the prophets: but Christ, as is clear from the opposite member, wishes under the name of habit to be understood every outward appearance of innocence in countenance, words, and laborious rites: especially indeed those smooth words and fair speeches of which Paul speaks in Rom. XVI. 17, and that by the example of Zechariah XIV. 4.

Ravenous wolves ] For they do not serve Christ, but their own belly Rom. XVI. 18. and they hold piety for gain 1. Tim. VI. 5. Thus also in Aesop's Fables the wolf is introduced covered in a sheep's skin.

These are the marks of false prophets: (I.) The manner of their arrival: that they come of their own accord ἄκλητοι, uncalled, unsent, Jerem. XXIII. 21. (II.) Their habit, or outward appearance, which is a double of the true Prophets: Sheep's skins, such as are 1. the specious titles of Catholic, Reformed, and illuminated Prophets. What are these sheep's skins, if not the outward surface of the Christian name; says Tertullian in his Prescription against Heretics, ch. 4. 2. Χρηστολογία, sweetness of words, Rom. XVI. 18. and ὁμοιότης: because ὅμοια μὲν λαλῦσιν, ἀνόμοια δὲ φρονῦσιν, they speak things similar to us, but think things dissimilar, as Irenaeus says. They disguise their appearance, says Athanasius in his second oration against the Arians, and they clothe themselves with the voices of the sacred scriptures as if with an honorable garment. 3. The appearance of a holy conversation, 2. Tim. III. 5. Col. II. 18. Cf. 1. Kings XVIII. 28. Matth. XXIII. 27. Theophylact in this place. they cast about a sweet-talking manner, and feign a solemn life. Heresy is said to lie not only with the tongue, but also with the life: if you question their faith, nothing is more Christian: if their conversation, nothing is more irreproachable, and what it speaks it proves by deeds, as Bernard says in sermon LXV. on the Song of Songs. 4. Boasting of truth. Which, if not by the name itself, they nevertheless trumpet forth by various other kinds of glorification. And this, says Augustine in tractate XLV. on John, has always been the one intention for all heretics, to capture glory from the singularity of Scripture. Such as the Calixtines are today, encrusting and instilling heretical opinions under the specious scheme of singular accuracy. Some explain the sheep's skin not as the habit received by the Prophets, but as the imitation of any true sheep of Christ: but the former interpretation seems more fitting, since false prophets do not so much simulate the sheep of Christ indiscriminately as they do the true Prophets, who were accustomed to wear sheepskins, as in Heb. XI. 37. (III.) A lupine spirit: which, even if it lies hidden most deeply within, it cannot be but that it sometimes betrays itself outwardly. For wolves are not only crafty and deceitful while they secretly lie in wait for the sheep, whence the wolf is called by Aristotle in book 1 of the History of Animals, ch. 1, θήριον ἐπίβουλον, an insidious animal, which creeps along on its belly and approaches the sheep: whose tail, as Pliny notes in book VIII. Natural History, ch. 22, is commonly believed to contain a love-inducing poison, by which sheep are attracted, and whose gaze is believed to be harmful, and to take away the human voice for the present from those whom it first contemplates: but they are also bold, when they rush into the fold and attack the sheep, and dare to leap upon the shepherd himself; and they are rapacious, when they do not spare the sheep, because they seize and tear them to pieces: to which, therefore, false prophets and heretics are compared, John X. 12. Acts XX. 24. They are also insatiable, like wolves, and stiff-necked and stubborn, as the Philosopher writes about wolves in book IV of the History of Animals, ch. 10: ὁ δὲ λυχην τοῖς μὲν ἄλλοις ἐπικαμπτὸς, καὶ σπονδύλες ἔχων: οἱ δὲ λύκοι (καὶ λέοντες) μόνοσον τὸν αὐχένα ἔχου- σι; whence they are called grievous wolves, Acts XX. 29. (IV.) A harmful and pernicious fruit: by which the false prophet is primarily distinguished, of which it is spoken in verses 16 and 20. To Chrysostom, indeed, it seems that by false prophets here are insinuated not only heretics, but also those who, while being of a corrupt life, put on the face of virtue, whom people commonly call impostors, and therefore it is added: by their fruits you shall know them: for among heretics often even an honest life is found; but among us, by no means: and Maximus, in the same place, says: everyone who feigns friendship for the harm of his neighbor is a wolf, hiding his malice in a sheep's skin: why also false prophets are thoughts which extenuate our sins and prophesy their remission: yet others more correctly accept these things as referring to heretics, of whom Chrysostom also interprets in the Chain of Greek Fathers edited by Peter Possinus: The Savior took wolves and sheep as an example in this place, from the ferocity of the former and the gentleness of the latter, completing the description of Heretics and False Prophets. For those men, hiding the lupine importunity and cruelty deeply fixed and founded in their heart, show outwardly a sheep-like gentleness; wherefore He warns us to take heed lest by chance they hunt our simplicity with that hook of a plausible appearance; for the use of which caution He suggests a certain mark for discerning hypocrites from the truly holy, when He adds: by their fruits you shall know them. For if that honest life which they put forward, with the leanness of fasting and the pallor of the face for the mere appearance of simulation, presents a void image of the thing, they will not long contain their lupine claws under that sheep's skin which they have put on for a time for the use of their snares and the opportunity of preying; but that being quickly shaken off, they will openly betray themselves to men by their rapines and their evil deeds.

Latin:

Vers. 15. ἀπὸ τῶν ψευδοπροφητῶν] Id est ψευδοδιδασκά- λων ut interpretatur Petrus II. cap. II. 1. Nam Hebræis Pro- phetæ dicebantur, non tantum præsagi futurorum, sed, & alii qui ad populum docendum procedebant, præsertim si mandata cœlitus data præ se ferrent. Qualis erat Simon & Barjesus quem ψευδοπροφήτην Lucas vocat Act. XIII. 6. Hos Pseudoprophetas Christus distinguit à Pseudochristis infra XXIV. 5. 11. 24. qualis erat Barchochebas. Neque tamen hic de quibusvis Pseudoprophetis agi arbitror, sed de iis qui se Christi sectatores profiterentur: ob ea quæ co- hærent infra commate 21. Falsos autem vocat non ratione missionis, ut ex eodem commate 21. convincitur, sed ob doctrinam falsam atque exitialem. Vide Petrum di- cto loco.

Ἐν ἐνδύμασι προβάτων] ἐν μηλωταῖς ut loquitur Scri- ptor ad Hebræos XI. 37. Namque is ferme habitus erat Prophetarum: at Christus, ut ex opposito membro liquet, sub habitus nomine omnem exteriorem innocentiæ spe- ciem in vultu, verbis, & operosis ritibus vult intelli- gi: præsertim vero illas χρηστολογίας καὶ εὐλογίας de qui- bus agit Paulus Rom. XVI. 17. idque exemplo Zacha- riæ XIV. 4.

Λύκοι ἅρπαγες ] Non enim Christo serviunt, sed ven- tri Rom. XVI. 18. & pietatem quæstui habent 1. Tim. VI. 5. Sic & in Æsopi Fabulis lupus inducitur ovina pelle obte- ctus.

Pseudoprophetarum γνωρίσματα hæc sunt: (I.) Modus adventus: quod veniant suapte spon- te ἄκλητοι, non vocati, non missi, Jerem. XXIII. 21. (II.) Habitus, vel vestitus speciosus, geminus ve- rorum Prophetarum: Pelles ovinæ, quales sunt 1. speciosi tituli Prophetarum Catholicorum, Re- formatorum illuminatorum. Quenam sunt istæ pelles ovinæ, nisi nominis Christiani extrinsecus su- perficies; ait Tertullianus de præscript. advers. hær. cap. 4. 2. Χρηστολογία, verborum suavi- tas, Rom. XVI. 18. & ὁμοιότης: quia ὅμοια μὲν λαλῦσιν, ἀνόμοια δὲ φρονῦσιν similia quidem no- bis loquuntur, dissimilia autem sentiunt, dicen- te Irenæo. Speciem suam dissimulant, ait Atha- nasius orat. II. contr. Arian. & literarum sacra- rum vocibus quasi honesto cultu induuntur. 3. Species sanctæ conversationis, 2. Tim. III. 5. Col. II. 18. Conf. 1. Reg. XVIII. 28. Matth. XXIII. 27. Theophyl. in h. l. χρηστολογίαν παραβάλλον- ται, & βίον ὑποκρίνοντα σεμνὸν. Hæresis dicta est mentiri non lingua tantum, sed & vita: si fidem in- terroges, nihil Christianius: si conversationem nihil irreprehensibilius, & quæ loquitur factis probat, dicente Bernhardo sermon. LXV. in Cantic. 4. Jactantia veritatis. Quam si non ipso nomi- ne, varia tamen gloriatione alioquin ebucci- nant. Et hæc omnibus, ait Augustinus tractat. XLV. in Joh. una intentio hæreticis semper fuit, captare gloriam de singularitate Scripturæ. Qua- les hodie Calixtini sunt, sub specioso ἀκριβείας singularis schemate hæreticas incrustantes & in- stillantes sententias. Nonnulli ovinam pellem non de habitu Prophetis recepto, sed de imita- tione quarumvis verarum ovium Christi expli- cant: sed prior interpretatio videtur concin- nior, quum non tam oves Christi promiscue, quam veros Prophetas simulent Pseudoprophetæ, qui μηλωτάς sive ovillas gestare solebant Ebr. XI. 37. (III.) Animus lupinus: qui etsi intrin- secus maxime latitet, fieri tamen non potest quin prodat etiam sese quandoque extrinsecus. Lu- pi enim non sunt tantum subdoli & fallaces, dum occulte insidiantur ovibus, unde lupus Aristoteli lib. 1. Histor. animal. cap. 1. θήριον ἐπί- βουλον animal insidiosum dicitur, quod ventre irrepens ovibus appropinquat: cujus caudæ Plinio notante lib. VIII. Histor. nat. cap. 22. vul- go creditur inesse amatorium virus, quo attrahan- tur oves, & cujus visus creditur esse noxius, vo- cemque humanam adimere ad præsens, quos prio- res contemplatur: sed etiam sunt audaces, cum in ovile ingruunt & oves aggrediuntur, & pa- storem ipsum insilire audent; nec non rapaces, quum ovibus non parcant, quia eas rapiunt & diripiunt: quibus ideo comparantur falsi Pro- phetæ & hæretici Johan. X. 12. Actor. XX. 24. sunt etiam insatiabiles, ut lupi, & duræ cervi- cis, ac pertinaces, uti Philosophus de lupis lib. IV. de animal. cap. 10. scribit: ὁ δὲ λυχην τοῖς μὲν ἄλλοις ἐπικαμπτὸς, καὶ σπονδύλες ἔχων: οἱ δὲ λύκοι (καὶ λέοντες) μόνοσον τὸν αὐχένα ἔχου- σι; unde βαρεῖς λύκοι dicuntur Actor. XX. 29. (IV.) Fructus noxius, & pernitiosus: ex quo im- primis dignoscitur Pseudopropheta, de quo vers. 16. & 20. Chrysostomo equidem videtur Pseu- doprophetas hic non tantum hæreticos insinuari, sed eos etiam qui cum sint vitæ corruptæ vul- tum virtutis induunt, quos vulgo impostores vo- care solent, ideoque subjungi, à fructibus eorum dignoscetis eos: apud hæreticos enim sæpenume- ro etiam vitam honestam inveniri; apud nos vero nequaquam: & Maximus u. f. omnis, in- quit, qui ad damnum proximi amicitiam simulat lupus est, ovina pelle occultans suam malitiam: cur etiam Pseudoprophetæ sunt cogitationes, quæ pecca- ta nostra extenuant, ac remissionem eorum vati- cinantur: rectius tamen alii hæc de hæreticis ac- cipiunt, de quibus etiam interpretatur Chry- sostomus in Catenâ Patrum Græcorum à Petro Possino edita: Lupos & oves in exemplum assum- psit Salvator hoc loco, ex illorum feritate & ha- rum mansuetudine, Hæreticorum ac Pseudopro- phetarum descriptionem absolvens. Isti enim lu- pinam importunitatem ac sævitiam in corde peni- tus fixam fundatamque occultantes, mansuetudi- nem exterius ovinam ostentant; quare animadver- tere nos admonet ne forte hamo isto speciei proba- bilis simplicitatem nostram venentur; cujus in usum cautionis certam notam suggerit ad discernendos à vere sanctis Hypocritas, dum addit: à fructibus eorum cognoscetis eos. Si enim vita ista hone- sta quam præferunt, jejunii macie & pallore faciei ad solum obventum simulationis, speciem objicit rei vacuam, non diu continebunt lupinos ungues sub i- sta, quam ad insidiarum usum, captandæque opportunitatem grassandi, ad tempus induerunt, ovina pelle; verum illa cito excussa, rapinis se ac maleficiis suis, hominibus palam prodent.

## 7:16
Verse 16. By their fruits you shall know them] From the works of iniquity, as is said below in VII. 23. But, someone might say, it has already been said that piety is most of all simulated by these people. Indeed: but that saying of the Mime is true: Things feigned quickly returned to their own nature. Lysias: a man can feign his character for only a short time. Sometimes some delay, sometimes only attention is needed. A flattering friend, says Cicero, can be separated and distinguished from a true one by applying diligence, just as all things faked and simulated can be from those that are sincere and true. They will not progress for long, says Paul, for their folly will be manifest. For they have the appearance of piety, but they overturn the power of it, 2. Tim. III. 5. 9. and thus in reality they repudiate their Lord and Redeemer, 2. Petr. II. 1. These are wont to be their fruits: that they flee from sufferings, they entice those who are stuck in vices, especially the wealthier ones, they stir up questions that contribute nothing to the progress of piety, they gladly disparage others, especially those placed in positions of dignity, so that under that guise of liberty they may boast before the people, and they adapt their dogmas to these matters, as can be seen in both epistles to Timothy, in the epistle of Jude, and in the second of Peter: and thus they show themselves to be such as they truly are, arrogant, full of hatred and envy, slanderous, greedy, and not as averse to pleasures as they wish to be thought, as can be seen in the same places. If anyone diligently compares these things with what is read in ecclesiastical writers concerning Cerinthus and Nicolaus, or, if we believe Clement, concerning the Gnostics who falsely used the name of Nicolaus, and other adulterers of the primitive truth, he will easily find that by almost all of them the sum of religion was established either in the gnosis or in ceremonies, while many things conflicting with the precepts of Christ were placed in the number of indifferent things, or certainly the necessity of the precepts was diminished by various pretexts.

Concerning the fruits of life and morals, as they call them, or evil works, some of the Papists indeed explain them, not as the fruits of doctrine, and Maldonatus affirms quite confidently that all the ancient authors understand by fruits the works which follow a doctrine that is by nature evil with evil, and good with good. But it is primarily the doctrine that must be understood. For just as the fruits of a Christian, in so far as he is a Christian, are good works, so the fruit of a teacher, in so far as he is a teacher, is the form or quality of the doctrine, and just as from works, as if from fruits, it is known who is truly a Christian or a hypocrite, so from the fruits, that is, from the quality of the doctrine, one must judge concerning true and false prophets. For such as the Spirit is that a Prophet has, such is his doctrine. But we cannot see the Spirit, and therefore we must judge him by his doctrine. Which explanation the blessed Chemnitius approves from the parallel words of Luke, chap. VI. 45. A good man out of the good treasure of his heart brings forth good, and an evil man out of the evil treasure of his heart brings forth evil. For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks. From that, therefore, which a Prophet brings forth and speaks, it must be judged what kind of treasure is in the heart of the Prophet, that is, whether he is a true or a Pseudoprophet. Nor are the Ancients alien to this explanation. Jerome on this passage, from the fruits of the soul, by which they draw the innocent to ruin, compares them to ravenous wolves. Similarly, the author of the imperfect work attributed to Chrysostom, homily XIX. By their fruits you shall know them. For the fruit of a man is the confession of his faith and the works of his conduct. If, therefore, you see a Christian man, immediately consider: If his confession agrees with the Scriptures, he is a true Christian: but if it is not as Christ commanded, he is a false one. For thus also John, when he had written an epistle about heretics, did not say, If anyone comes to you not having the name of Christ, do not even say greeting to him: but if anyone does not bring this doctrine. He did not refer the proof of Christianity to the name of Christ, but to the Confession, because not the name of Christ alone makes one a Christian, but also the truth of Christ: because many walk in the name of Christ, but few in his truth. Which Barradius also acknowledges: and Thomas Stapleton confesses in book X of the principles of doctrinal faith. chap. 1. that most of the fathers explain this passage, namely, that we ought to make a judgment about them from the doctrine which the Pseudoprophets propose. See Theodoret, book III of heretical fables, and Theophylact on this passage. Such harmful and pernicious fruits of heretics are the fruits of heretical doctrines, by which the glory of God is obscured, the pursuit of piety is undermined, and the foundations of true and life-giving consolation are subverted, which Gerhard the Elder, of blessed memory, shows in his learned Disputations regarding the false dogmas of the Photinians, Papists, and Calvinists.

Do men gather? ] And here the active personal is used for the passive impersonal, as is often the case.

Latin:

Vers. 16. Ἀπὸ τῶν καρπῶν ἐπιγνώσεσθε αὐτὸς] Ex operi- bus iniquitatis, ut infra dicitur VII. 23. Atqui, dicat a- liquis, jam dictum est pieratem ab istis vel maxime si- mulari. Sane: sed verum est illud Mimi: Cito ad naturam ficta reciderunt suam. Lysias: ὀλίγον χρόνον δύναιτ' ἄν τις πλάσασθαι τὸν τρόπον τὸν ἑαυτῦ. Interdum mora aliqua, interdum attentione so- la opus est. Secerni, inquit Cicero, blandus amicus à ve- ro & internosci tam potest adhibita diligentia, quam omnia fucata & simulata à sinceris & veris. Non diu proficient, inquit Paulus, nam insipientia illorum manifesta sit. Ha- bent enim speciem pietatis, sed vim ipsam evertunt, 2. Tim. III. 5. 9. atque ita revera repudiant Dominum ac Redemtorem suum, 2. Petr. II. 1. Fructus eorum hi esse solent, quod perpeffiones defugiunt, allectant eos qui in vitiis hærent, præsertim opulentiores, quæstiones movent nihil facientes ad profectum pietatis, libenter obtrectant aliis, præsertim in dignitate positis, ut ea libertatis specie se apud populum jactent, & ad istas res dogmata sua ac- commodant, ut videre est in utraque ad Timotheum, in Judæ epistola & Petri secunda: atque ita ostendunt se ta- les esse quales revera sunt, fastuosos, odii & invidentiæ plenos, maledicos, avaros, neque tam alienos à volupta- tibus quam existimari volunt, ut iisdem locis videre est. Quæ si quis diligenter conferat cum iis quæ de Cerintho deque Nicolao, aut si Clementi credimus, Nicolai nomen falso obtendentibus Gnosticis, aliisque primævæ verita- tis adulteris apud Ecclesiasticos scriptores leguntur, facile inveniet ab illis ferme omnibus summam religionis con- stitutam aut ἐν τῇ γνώσει aut in cæremoniis, multa autem cum Christi præceptis pugnantia posita in numero ἀδια- φόρων, aut certe necessitatem præceptorum variis obten- tibus imminutam.

De fructibus vitæ & morum, quos vocant, vel operibus malis explicant quidem nonnulli è Pontificiis, non de fructibus Doctrinæ, & confiden- ter satis Maldonatus affirmat, veteres autores omnes per fructus opera intelligere, quæ doctrinam natura malam mala, bonam bona sequuntur. Sed intelli- genda imprimis est doctrina. Sicut enim fructus Christiani, in quantum Christianus est, sunt bona opera, ita Doctoris in quantum doctoris fructus est forma, seu qualitas doctrinæ, & sicut ex ope- ribus tanquam ex fructibus cognoscitur quis, an sit vere Christianus, vel hypocrita, ita ex fru- ctibus, hoc est, ex qualitate doctrinæ, judican- dum est de veris & falsis prophetis. Qualem e- nim Spiritum Propheta habet, talis est doctri- na. Sed Spiritum videre non possumus, ideo- que e doctrina dijudicare eum oportet. Quam explicationem probat B. Chemnitius e verbis Lu- cae parallelis cap. VI. 45. Bonus homo ex bono the- sauro cordis sui profert bonum, & malus homo malo ex cordis sui thesauro profert malum. Ex abundantia enim cordis os loquitur. Ex eo igi- tur, quod Propheta profert, & loquitur, judi- candum est, qualis sit thesaurus in corde Pro- phetae, hoc est, an sit verus, seu Pseudopro- pheta. Neque alieni sunt ab hac explicatione Veteres. Hieronymus ad h. l. ex fructibus ani- mae, quibus innocentem ad ruinam trahunt, lupis rapacibus comparantur. Similiter autor operis imperfecti apud Chrysostomum homil. XIX. Ex fructibus eorum cognoscetis eos. Fructus enim ho- minis est confessio fidei ejus, & opera conversationis ipsius. Si ergo videris hominem Christianum, sta- tim considera: Si confessio ejus conveniat cum Scri- pturis, verus est Christianus: si autem non est, quem- admodum Christus mandavit, falsus est. Sic enim & Johannes, cum de hereticis scripsisset epistolam, non dixit, Si quis venerit ad vos, non habens no- men Christi, nec ave ei dixeritis: sed si quis non attulerit istam doctrinam. Indicium Christiani- tatis non ad nomen Christi retulit, sed ad Confes- sionem, quia non nomen solum Christi Christia num facit, sed etiam veritas Christi: quia in no- mine Christi multi ambulant, in veritate autem ejus pauci. Quod etiam agnoscit Barradius: & Tho- mas Stapleton. fatetur l. X. de princip. fid. doctrin. cap. 1. plerosque ex patribus locum hunc expo- nere, quod scilicet ex doctrina, quam Pseudo- prophetae proponunt, de iis facere judicium de- beamus. Vid. Theodoret. lib. III. haeres. fabul. & Theophyl. in h. l. Tales fructus noxii & perniciosi haereticorum sunt fructus doctrinarum haeretica- rum, quibus gloria Dei obscuratur, studium pie- tatis labefactatur, & consolationis verae & vivificae fundamenta subruuntur, quod de Photiniano- rum, Pontificiorum & Calvinianorum dogmatibus falsis, eruditis Disputationibus ostendit Gerhard. Senior ὁ μακαρίτης.

Μή τι συλλέγυσι ] Et hic activum personale pro passivo impersonali est positum ut saepe.

## 7:17
But the corrupt tree ] corrupt is bad, which the Greeks translate sometimes thus, sometimes as wicked.

Latin:

Τὸ δὲ σαπρὸν δένδρον ] σαπρὸν est באש, quod interdum sic, interdum πονηρὸν vertunt Graeci.

## 7:18
Verse 18. A good tree cannot bring forth evil fruit] Such also is that saying of Menander: No one who is good does a wicked thing. That of M. Antoninus also comes closer: He who does not wish the base man to sin is like him who does not wish a fig tree to produce sap in its figs. Christ gives the reason below in XII. 35, because out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks, which by similar reasoning ought to be extended to deeds. Philosophers say that actions are similar to qualities: all of which, as in moral matters, are to be understood for the most part. This, therefore, is what Christ means: if these men were truly lovers of piety as they wish to be considered, they would not admit such things. However, this is not to be carried to the point of saying that qualities cannot be changed, which Tertullian rightly defends against the sectarians of his own time, whose words I shall transcribe from his book on the soul: A bad tree will not give good fruits if it is not grafted, and a good one will not give bad ones if it is not cultivated. And stones will become children of Abraham, if they are formed into the faith of Abraham: And the offspring of vipers will produce the fruit of repentance, if they have spat out the poisons of malice. This will be the power of divine grace, more powerful indeed than nature, having within us the power of free will subject to it, which is called self-determination: which, since it is itself also natural and mutable, is converted by nature in whatever direction it is turned. Chrysostom, VII on Romans: As he says in the Gospel, a corrupt tree cannot bring forth fruit, not forbidding the change from vice to virtue, but the persistence in vice, saying that it cannot bring forth good fruits; for he did not say a wicked tree cannot become good, but that it cannot bring forth good fruits while remaining wicked.

who

Since Christ uses a general axiom, such as the tree such is the fruit, a bad tree cannot bear good fruits, from this he concludes that good fruits cannot be expected from Pseudoprophets, since they are imbued with false doctrines: therefore the general axiom is rightly applied to the man to the regenerate, that a work spiritually good cannot proceed from him, to overthrow the heterodoxy of the Pelagians, Socinians, and Papists concerning the powers of free will. But it is not rightly inferred, since regenerate men are good trees, Psalm CXII. 13, that they cannot bear bad fruits, unless under the reduplication, by which they are indeed regenerate and good trees: for the regenerate, as they are not entirely regenerate and spiritual, but still partly carnal, so they cannot be considered as perfectly good trees in this imperfection of life. See Rom. VII. 21. They do not indeed bring forth bad fruits, insofar as they are regenerate, yet they do bring them forth, insofar as the root of sin still clings in their flesh.

Latin:

Vers. 18 ὐ δύναται δένδρον ἀγαθὸν καρπὺς πονηρὺς ποιεῖν] Tale est & Menandri illud: Οὐδεὶς πονηρὸν πρᾶγμα χρηστὸς ὢν ποιεῖ. Propius etiam accedit illud M. Antonii: ὁ μὴ θέλων τὸν φαῦ- λον ἁμαρτάνειν, ὅμοιος τῷ μὴ θέλοντι συκῆν ὀπὸν ἐν τοῖς σύκοις φέρειν. Causam reddit Christus infra XII. 35. quia ex uber- tate cordis os loquatur, quod simili ratione ad facta pro- tendi debet. Philosophi dicunt actiones similes esse qua- litatibus: quae omnia ut in moralibus intelligenda sunt ἐπὶ τὸ πολὺ. Hoc ergo vult Christus, si vere essent isti amantes pietatis quales haberi volunt, non talia admitterent. Hoc autem non eo perducendum ut dicantur qualitates muta- ri non posse, recte adversus sui temporis sectarios defen- dit Tertullianus, cujus verba adscribam ex libro de anima: Non dabit arbor mala fructus bonos: si non inseratur, & bona malos dabit, si non colatur. Et lapides filii Abrahae fient, si in fidem Abrahae formentur: Et genimina viperarum fructum poenitentiae facient, si venena malignitatis expuerint. Haec erit vis divinae gratiae, potentior utique natura, habens in nobis sub- jacentem sibi liberi arbitrii potestatem, quod αὐτεξύσιον dici- tur: quae cum sit & ipsa naturalis atque mutabilis, quoquo vertitur, natura convertitur. Chrysostomus VII. ad Roma- nos: ὥσπερ ἐν ἐν τῷ ἐυαγγελίῳ φήσιν, ἐ δύναται δένδρον σα- πρὸν καρπὺς ποιεῖν, ἐτὴν ἀπὸ κακίας εἰς ἀρετὴν μεταβολὴν κωλύων, ἀλλὰ τὴν ἐν τῇ κακίᾳ διατριβὴν, λέγων μὴ δύνασθαι φέρειν καρπὺς καλὺς· ὐ γὰρ εἶπεν ὐ δύναται δένδρον πονηρὸν καλὸν γένεσθαι, ἀλλ᾽ ὅτι φέρειν καρπὺς καλὺς ὐ δύναται μένον πονηρόν.

qui

Quum generali axiomate utatur Christus, qua- lis arbor talis fructus, mala arbor non potest fru- ctus bonos ferre, exinde concludit à Pseudo-pro- phetis non posse expectari fructus bonos, quum falsis doctrinis imbuti sint: ideo recte applicatur generale axioma ad hominem ad renatum, quod ab eo non possit prodire opus spiritualiter bo- num, ad profligandam Pelagianorum, Socinia- norum, & Papistarum de viribus liberi arbitrii ἑτεροδοξίαν. Non recte autem infertur, quum renati arbores bonæ sint Psal. CXII. 13. eos non posse fructus malos ferre, nisi sub reduplicatione, qua nempe renati sunt, arboresque bonæ: nam re- nati uti non sunt ex asse renati & spirituales, sed ex parte adhuc carnales, ita pro arboribus perfecte bonis in hac vitæ imperfectione haberi non pos- sunt. Vid. Rom. VII. 21. Non proferunt quidem malos fructus, quatenus renati sunt, proferunt tamen, quatenus in ipsorum carne adhuc radix peccati hæret.

## 7:19
Verse 19. Every tree that does not bring forth good fruit is cut down] The Baptist proves the sentiment taken from Daniel. See above III. 10.

Vers. 19. Πᾶν δένδρον μὴ ποιοῦν καρπὸν καλὸν ἐκκόπτε- ται] Probat Baptistes sententiam ex Daniele desumtam. Vide supra III. 10.

## 7:20
Verse 20. By their fruits you shall know them] Since men willingly teach things consistent with their own morals, hold them themselves as suspects from such deeds before they instill their dogmas in you. For such as the masters are, such are they going to make the disciples.

Latin:

Vers. 20. Ἀπό τῶν καρπῶν ἀυτῶν ἐπιγνώσεσθε ἀυτοὺς] Cum libenter homines moribus suis convenientia doce- ant, ex factis istiusmodi suspectos ipsos habere priusquam dogmata sua vobis instillent. Quales enim magistri sunt, tales facturi sunt & discipulos.

## 7:21
Vers. 21. ὁ πᾶς ὁ λέγων μοι κύριε κύριε] Although this expression denies universally among the Hebrews, here however it is manifest that the negation is particular; for even those who obey God are included in that universality of those saying to Christ: Lord, Lord, that is, of those who profess themselves followers of Christ, John XIII. 13. The profession of Christianity is common to both, according to which they are called ἀκροαταὶ τοῦ λογοῦ, James I. 22. But obedience distinguishes them.

Ποιῶν] They are said ποιεῖν τὸ θέλημα τοῦ πατρὸς who have a serious purpose of obeying, namely οἱ πίσιν ἔχοντες ὀ νεκρὰν, ἀλλὰ δι᾽ ἀγάπης ἐνεργουμένην. For it is not rare that a study is signified by words of acting, but such a one as is active when the occasion is given. Justin explains this passage in his Apology thus: οἱ δ᾽ ἂν μὴ ἐυρίσκονται βιοῦντες, ὡς ἐδίδαξε, γνωριζέσθωσαν μὴ ὄντες χρισιανοὶ κ᾿ ἂν λέγωσι δια γλώττης τὰ τοῦ χριστοῦ διδάγματα. ὀυ γὰρ τοὺς μόνον λέγοντας, ἀλλὰ τοὺς κ᾿ τὰ ἔργα πράττοντας σωθήσεσθ᾽ ἔφη. The same man in his Dialogue with Trypho refutes the harmful opinion not only of the Jews, but also of certain ones who were called Christians, οἱ λέγουσι ὅτι κἂν ἁμαρτωλοὶ ὦσι θεὸν δὲ γινώσκωσιν, ὀυ μὴ λογίσηται ἀυτοῖς κύριος ἁμαρτίαν. Well to the same effect the Writer of the responses to the Orthodox: τὸ ἀγαθὰ ἡμᾶς εἶναι ἤ κακοὺς ὁ θεὸς ὀυκ᾿ ἐν τῇ γνώσει ἔθηκε τῶν γινωσκομένων, ἀλλὰ ἐν τῇ αἱρέσει τῶν αἱρεμένων. Older than these is Ignatius in his Epistle to the Magnesians: πρέπον ἐστὶ μὴ μόνον καλεῖσθαι χρισιανοὺς, ἀλλὰ κ᾿ εἶναι. ὀυ γὰρ τὸ λέγεσθ', ἀλλὰ τὸ εἶναι μακάριον ποιεῖ. Basil to Amphilochius: ἐάν τις τὸ ὀνομα λαβὼν τοῦ χρισιανισμοῦ, ἐνυβρίζῃ τὸν Χριστὸν, ὀυδὲν ὄφελος ἀυτῷ ἀπὸ τῆς προσηγορίας. Salvian explains and confirms the same sentiment in this manner: It all revolves into this, that he who does not perform the work of the Christian name, does not seem to be a Christian. For a name without its act and duty is nothing. For as someone says in his writings: what else is leadership without the sublimity of merits, but a title of honor without a man, or what is dignity in an unworthy person but an ornament in the mud? Therefore, that we also may use the same words, what else is a holy word without merit, but an ornament in the mud? and what follows further at the beginning of book IV of On Providence. All these interpret that εἰσελεύσεται εἰς βασιλείαν τῶν ὀυρανῶν concerning eternal happiness. And we observed above in chapter V. 20 that that expression is not accustomed to be taken otherwise by our writers.

Not only the purpose of obeying, nor primarily that, but especially faith in Christ pertains to this ποιεῖν τὸ θέλημα τοῦ πατρὸς. For Christ said that in verse 24, ποιεῖν τοὺς λόγους τούτους. But he was looking toward those words, to seek first the kingdom of GOD and his righteousness, Matthew VI. 33, which cannot be done without faith: and in the beginnings, and the sum of Christ's sermons was, believe in the Gospel, Mark 1:15. And for that reason those who hunger and thirst for righteousness are called blessed by Christ, Matthew 5:5, and a more abundant righteousness is required of those entering the kingdom, which is the very righteousness of faith, Matthew 5:20. And what is that will of the Father which Christ commanded to be done? Is not faith most required for it? This is the will of him who sent me, that everyone who sees the Son and believes in him may have eternal life, says Christ, John 6:40. And when it was asked, 'What must we do to perform the works of God?' he answered, 'This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he has sent,' v. 28, 29. There is indeed no doubt that he who does the will of the Father has a serious purpose of obeying, but above all it is required that he have faith in Christ, by which hearts are purified, Acts 15:10. and from which charity pleasing to God ought to arise: because faith is active and effective through charity, Galatians 5:6. Faith is the mother of every good action, as Ambrose says: and 'the goal of the commandment is love from a pure heart, and a good conscience, and sincere faith,' 1 Timothy 1:5. And this is his commandment, that we believe in the name of his Son Jesus Christ, and love one another, 1 John 3:23. Yet one must be careful not to attribute entry into the kingdom of heaven to love, or to the purpose of obeying; because Scripture attributes salvation solely to faith, as the cause, on our part, as we call it, organic. Blessed is he to whom God imputes righteousness without works, Romans 4:6. By grace you have been saved through faith, Ephesians 2:8, not from works, so that no one may boast, v. 9. But because true faith is not without works, even though it apprehends grace and salvation without works, and is the only receptive medium by which we take hold of and apply to ourselves those things which are offered in the Gospel; therefore those who only boast of faith and say, 'Lord, Lord,' are not said to do the will of the Father, but those who are devoted to true holiness by a living faith in Christ. In this sense, the opinions of the Fathers, which are praised here by Grotius, are correct.

Latin:

Vers. 21. ὁ πᾶς ὁ λέγων μοι κύριε κύριε] Quanquam i- sta locutio Hebræis universaliter negat, hic tamen mani- festum est negationem esse particularem; nam & qui o- bediunt Deo comprehenduntur in ista universalitate di- centium Christo: Domine, Domine, id est eorum qui se Christi sectatores profitentur, Johann. XIII. 13. Com- munis utrisque est professio Christianismi, secundum quam ἀκροαταὶ τοῦ λογοῦ dicuntur Jac. I. 22. At obedien- tia eos distinguit.

Ποιῶν] ποιεῖν τὸ θέλημα τοῦ πατρὸς dicuntur qui serium habent obediendi propositum, nimirum οἱ πίσιν ἔχοντες ὀ νεκρὰν, ἀλλὰ δι᾽ ἀγάπης ἐνεργουμένην. Neque enim ra- rum est, ut agendi verbis significetur studium, sed tale quod data occasione actuosum est. Hunc locum in Apo- logetico ita explicat Justinus: οἱ δ᾽ ἂν μὴ ἐυρίσκονται βιοῦντες, ὡς ἐδίδαξε, γνωριζέσθωσαν μὴ ὄντες χρισιανοὶ κ᾿ ἂν λέγωσι δια γλώττης τὰ τοῦ χριστοῦ διδάγματα. ὀυ γὰρ τοὺς μόνον λέγοντας, ἀλλὰ τοὺς κ᾿ τὰ ἔργα πράττοντας σωθήσεσθ᾽ ἔφη. Idem in Col- loquio cum Tryphone refutat noxiam opinionem non Ju- dæorum tantum, sed & quorundam qui Christiani dice- rentur, οἱ λέγουσι ὅτι κἂν ἁμαρτωλοὶ ὦσι θεὸν δὲ γινώσκωσιν, ὀυ μὴ λογίσηται ἀυτοῖς κύριος ἁμαρτίαν. Bene in eandem sen- tentiam Scriptor responsionum ad Orthodoxos: τὸ ἀγα- θὰ ἡμᾶς εἶναι ἤ κακοὺς ὁ θεὸς ὀυκ᾿ ἐν τῇ γνώσει ἔθηκε τῶν γινω- σκομένων, ἀλλὰ ἐν τῇ αἱρέσει τῶν αἱρεμένων. Vetustior his Ignatius in Epistola ad Magnesios: πρέπον ἐστὶ μὴ μόνον καλεῖσθαι χρισιανοὺς, ἀλλὰ κ᾿ εἶναι. ὀυ γὰρ τὸ λέγεσθ', ἀλλὰ τὸ εἶναι μακάριον ποιεῖ. Basilius ad Amphilochium: ἐάν τις τὸ ὀνομα λαβὼν τοῦ χρισιανισμοῦ, ἐνυβρίζῃ τὸν Χριστὸν, ὀυδὲν ὄφελος ἀυτῷ ἀπὸ τῆς προσηγορίας. Eandem sententiam hunc in modum explicat & confirmat Salvianus: Totum in id revolvitur, ut qui Christiani nominis opus non agit, Christianus non esse videatur. Nomen enim sine actu atque officio suo nihil est. Nam sicut ait quidam in scriptis suis: quid est aliud principatus sine meritorum sublimitate, nisi honoris titulus sine homine, aut quid est dignitas in indigno nisi ornamentum in luto? Itaque ut iisdem verbis etiam nos utamur, quid est aliud sanctum vocabulum sine merito, nisi ornamentum in luto? & quæ porro sequuntur initio libri IV. de providentia. Hi omnes illud εἰσελεύσεται εἰς βα- σιλείαν τῶν ὀυρανῶν de æterna felicitate interpretantur. Ne- que vero aliter eam locutionem sumi solere à Scriptori- bus nostris, supra observavimus cap. V. 20.

Non solum obediendi propositum, nec πρῶτως illud, sed maxime fides in Christum ad hoc ποιεῖν τὸ θέλημα τοῦ πατρὸς pertinet. Nam id dixit Chri- stus vers. 24. ποιεῖν τοὺς λόγους τούτους. Ad sermo- nes autem illos spectabat, quærere primum re- gnum DEI & justitiam ejus Matth. VI. 33. quod sine fide fieri nequit: & in primordiis, ac summa concionum Christi erat, credere Evangelio Marc. I. 15. Atque ideo beati dicti sunt à Christo esurientes & sitientes justitiam Matth. V. 5. & ab in- gredientibus in regnum abundatior requisita ju- stitia, quæ est ipsa Justitia fidei Matth. V. 20. Et quænam est illa voluntas Patris, quam facere jus- sit Christus? Nonne ad eam maxime requiritur fi- des? Hæc est voluntas ejus, qui misit me, ut omnis qui videt Filium, & credit in eum, vitam æternam habeat, ait Christus Joh. VI. 40. & cum quæreretur Τί ποιῶμεν, ἵνα ἐργαζώμεθα τὰ ἔργα τ̃ Θεῦ; re- spondit, Τῦτό ἐσιν τὸ ἔργον τ̃ Θεῦ, ἵνα πιςεύσητε εἰς ὃν ἀπέσειλεν ἐκεῖνος, v. 28. 29. Non equidem du- bium est, facientem voluntatem Patris serium ha- bere obediendi propositum, sed imprimis requiritur, ut fidem habeat in Christum, qua purificantur cor- da Act. XV. 10. & ex qua charitatem Deo placen- tem oriri oportet: quia fides per charitatem est ope- rosa & efficax Gal. V. 6. Fides est omnis bonæ actio- nis genetrix, dicente Ambrosio: & τὸ τέλος τ̃ πα- ραγγελίας ἐστὶν ἀγάπη ἐκ καθαρᾶς καρδίας, κὴ συνειδήσεως ἀγαθῆς, κὴ πίσεως ἀνυποκρίτε, 1. Tim. I. 5. Atque hoc est mandatum ejus, ut credamus nomini Filii ejus Jesu Christi, & diligamus nos invi- cem, 1. Joh. III. 23. Id tamen cavendum, ne ingres- sum in regnum cœlorum tribuamus dilectioni, vel proposito obediendi; quia salutem unice fidei tribuit Scriptura, ceu causæ, ex parte nostri, ut vocamus, organicæ. Beatitudo est ejus, cui Deus imputat ju- stitiam sine operibus Rom. IV. 6. Ex gratia salvi facti estis per fidem Eph. II. 8. non ex operibus, ne quis glorietur v. 9. Quia vero fides vera non est sine operibus, etsi sine operibus gratiam & salutem ap- prehendat, unicumque medium sit ἀντιληπτικὸν, quo scilicet ea, quæ offerentur in Evangelio, susci- pimus, nobisque applicamus; ideo facere volunta- tem Patris non dicuntur, qui solum jactant fi- dem, & dicunt, Domine, Domine, sed qui viva in Christum fide veræ sanctitati dediti sunt. Quo sensu recte se habent, quæ hic à Grot. laudantur, Patrum sententiæ.

## 7:22
Verse 22. In that day) Refer to the preceding. In that day in which one will enter into the heavenly kingdom, the Hebrews say ביום ההוא.

In your name) That is, by professing that we do this to testify to your power. For thus in these books these terms are used throughout, 'in the name,' 'by the name,' 'upon the name,' the explanation of which words must be sought from the passages in Acts 16:18, 19:13. I am surprised that Origen, such a philosopher, relies on this argument to prove against Aristotle that names are not by convention, as if the mere utterance of syllables, and not rather the will of God desiring to make the truth manifest, expressed in syllables, were effective for a miracle, especially since he himself also relates that according to the name of Jesus, the principal deeds of Jesus were also accustomed to be recounted in exorcisms. But since, as I said, miracles were given in testimony of the truth, it is not surprising that they were also performed by those who openly acknowledged the truth, although they had not composed their minds to its obedience. For generally they were employed not so much to commend those through whom they were done, as to convince the spectators: although the very promise of Christ, which exists in Mark 16:17, especially looked to those who believe, that is, those led to repentance, trusting in Christ and obedient to him, as Peter testifies in Acts 2:38 and chapter 5:32. Justin Martyr, Apology 2: 'Believing, or rather being convinced, that each one will pay the penalty through eternal fire according to the worth of his deeds, and will be required to give an account of the word according to the measure of the powers he received from God.' Origen: 'For these things, when spoken, have often caused demons to depart from men, and most of all when those who speak them say them from a healthy and genuinely believing disposition. So great, however, is the power of the name of Jesus against demons, that sometimes it is effective even when named by the wicked.' Similar things to these are found in the writer of the Responses to the Orthodox, question. 5. And in what are called the Constitutions of Clement, book 8, chapter 2.

we prophesied] Since this concerns deeds worthy of admiration, I believe that here we must understand predictions of future events.

It is not only about prophecies, but also about true miracles that are treated here: which, even though Julius Caesar Cœcurius, Epitome of Controversies, chapter 4, page 36, denies can be performed by false teachers, so that he may obtain the claim that the glory of miracles is the proper mark of the true Church, yet the contrary is evident both from this passage and from Matthew 24:24, 2 Thessalonians 2:9, and other Papists admit that true miracles can be performed by false teachers, not indeed by the authority of God, but in the name of God, and by his permission, Fr. Toletus on Luke, page 621, Costerus in Enchiridion of Controversies on the Church, chapter 2, page 99, Maldonatus on this passage, citing to that effect Chrysostom, Jerome, Euthymius, Theophylact, as also Cornelius à Lapide, and Tirinus on this passage. Add also Thomas 2.2, question 172, article 6, and the Questions and Answers to the Orthodox, question 5, in the works of Justin.

Latin:

Vers. 22. ἐν ἐκείνῃ τῇ ἡμέρᾳ) Refer ad præcedentia. In illa die qua intrabitur in regnum cœleste ביום ההוא dicunt Hæbræi.

Τῷ σῷ ὀνόματι) Hoc est, profitendo nos id facere ad te- standam potentiam tuam. Ita enim in his libris passim su- muntur ista, τῷ ὀνόματι, ἐν ὀνόματι, ἐπὶ τῷ ὀνόματι, quo- rum verborum explicatio petenda est ex Actorum locis XVI. 18. XIX. 13. Miror Originem tantum Philosophum hoc argumento niti, ut contra Aristotelem probet nomina non esse ex instituto, quasi ipsa syllabarum prolatio, & non potius Dei voluntas testatum facere cupientis veritatem syllabis expressam, ad miraculum valeret, præsertim cum ipse etiam narret juxta nomen Jesu in exorcismis solitas etiam referri res gestas Jesu præcipuas. Cum vero ut dixi miracula in testimonium veritatis data sint, mirum non est, etiam per eos fuisse edita, qui veritatem palam agno- scebant, quanquam animum ad eius obedientiam non composuissent. Plerumque enim non tam ad commenden- dos eos per quos fiebant, quam ad convincendos spectato- res adhibebantur: quanquam ipsa Christi promissio, quæ extat Marc. XVI. 17. præcipue credens, hoc est pœnitentia ductos in Christum confisos eique obedientes respiciebat. teste Petro Act. II. 38. & cap. V. 32. Justinus Martyr Apol. II. πισένουτες, μᾶλλον δὲ κὴ πεπεισμένοι, κατ' ἀξίαν τῶν πρά- ξεων ἕκαστον τίσειν διὰ πυρὸς αἰωνίε δίκας, κὴ πρὸς ἀναλο- γίαν ὧν ἔλαβε δυνάμεων παρὰ Θεῦ, τὸν λόγον ἀπαιτηθήσε- σθαι. Origenes: Ταῦτα γὰρ λεγόμενα πολλάκις ἰὺς δαίμονας πεποίηκεν ἀνθρώπων χωρισθῆναι, κὴ μάλισθ' ὅταν οἱ λέγοντες ἀπὸ διαθέσεως ὑγιῶς καὶ πεπιστευκυίας γνησίως αὐτὰ λέγωσι Τοσῦτον μέντοι δύναται τὸ ὄνομα τῦ Ἰησῦ κατὰ τῶν δαιμόνων, ὡς ἔσθ' ὅτε κὴ ὑπὸ φαύλων ὀνομαζόμενον ἀνύειν. Quibus si- milia sunt apud Scriptorem responsionum ad Orthodo- xos quæst. V. & in Clementis quæ dicuntur constitutio- nibus lib. VIII. c. II.

προεφητεύσαμεν] Cum hic de factis admiratione dignis agatur, plane hic futurorum præsagia intelligenda arbi- tror.

Non tantum de vaticiniis, sed etiam de mi- raculis veris hic agitur: quæ etsi à falsis Docto- ribus edi posse Julius Cæsar Cœcurius Epit. Con- trov. cap. 4. pag. 36. neget, ut gloriam miracu- lorum Ecclesiæ veræ [notam propriam esse obtineat, contrarium tamen patet tum ex hoc loco, tum è Matth. XXIV. vers. 24. 2. Thess. II. vers. 9. & admittunt alii Papistæ, miracula vera à falsis Doctoribus, non quidem autore, sed in nomine Dei, ejusque permissione edi posse, Fr. Toletus in Luc. pag. 621. Costerus in Enchirid. Controv. de Eccl. cap. 2. pag. 99. Maldonat. in h. l. adducens in eam sententiam Chrysostomum, Hieronymum, Euthymium, Theophylactum, ut & Cornelius à Lapide, ac Tirinus in h. l. Adde & Thomam 2. 2. q. 172. art. 6. & quæst. & respons. & Orthod. qv. V. in operib. Justini.

## 7:23
Verse 23. I will confess to them) The Greeks do not use this word in this sense. But because the Hebrew word 'yada', which often means to confess, has a wider range, and signifies a public profession, therefore the Hellenistic usage extends 'to confess' to that extent.

I never knew you] I never held you as my own, as in Galatians 4:9, in the Hebrew manner among whom 'yada' is accustomed to be taken in this way. Psalm 1:6, 2 Timothy 2:19, 1 Corinthians 8:3.

ἐργαζόμενοι τὴν ἀνομίαν] Thus the LXX translated in Psalm 5:6. פעל אן Luke correctly translated the force of the participle with the verbal noun ἐργάται τῆς ἀδικίας. Moreover, he uses this saying of Christ already in the passage to Timothy, from the opposite in this way: ἔγνω κύριος τῆς ὄντας αὐτῷ. κὴ ἀποστήτω ἀπὸ ἀδικίας πᾶς ὁ ὀνομάζων τὸ ὄνομα κυρίου.

Latin:

Vers. 23. ὁμολογήσω αὐτοῖς] Græci hanc vocem isto sensu non usurpant. Sed quia Hebræum ידע quod sæ- pe vult confiteri latius patet, & quamvis publicam profes- sionem significat, ideo & τὸ ὁμολογεῖν Hellenisticus usus eousque extendit.

οὐδέποτε ἔγνων ὑμᾶς] Nunquam vos pro meis habui, ut Gal. IV. 9. more Hebræo apud quos ידע ita sumi solet. Pf. I. 6. 2. Tim. II. 19. 1. Cor. 11x. 3.

ἐργαζόμενοι τὴν ἀνομίαν] Ita LXX. verterunt in Psalmo V. 6. פעל אן Lucas vim participii recte vertit per ver- bale ἐργάται τῆς ἀδικίας. Utitur autem hoc Christi dicto jam ad Timotheum loco, ex opposito hoc modo: ἔγνω κύριος τῆς ὄντας αὐτῷ. κὴ ἀποστήτω ἀπὸ ἀδικίας πᾶς ὁ ὀνο- μάζων τὸ ὄνομα κυρίου.

## 7:24
Vers. 24. ὅτις ἀκούει με τὰς λόγες τέτως) Just as we were just showing from James that those who profess Christianity are called hearers, so here by the verb ἀκούειν the entire profession is designated.

PART VI.

Exhortatory conclusion of the Sermon on the Mount.

κὴ ποιεῖ αὐτὲς] ποιεῖν, as we just said, signifies a purpose of acting. And here the distinction between merely contemplative assent and active assent is to be noted; for in order for assent to become active, these three things are required: first, that it be diligently considered what the way prescribed by Christ is, and what internal and external difficulties accompany it: then, that the magnitude of that eternal glory which Christ promises be likewise attentively weighed: thirdly, that the certain connection of that way with the goal, and of the goal with the way, be well fixed in the mind, namely, that it be established that it is impossible that one should not arrive there by this path, nor arrive at the same place by going another way. These things being well perceived and meditated upon, the will is bent into obedience to the understood truth, from which arises in the mind love, which takes the place of root and foundation. Eph. 3:17. Compare what is below in chapter 13 and Luke 14:28. This is what, against the blandishments of pleasures, the fear of pain, poverty, exile, ignominy, and finally death, and the new discipline of false teaching, retains that former and contemplative assent and its profession unshaken. On the contrary, those who, with things not well weighed and such a foundation not laid, approve of the true doctrine equally in understanding and in profession, are easily led by the enticements of sinning, the fear of imminent evil, and the allure of novelty, to prefer that what opposes their lust not be true, and seeking an escape in any way, they first doubt, gradually waver, and fall away from their profession. For it is a consequence, as Paul teaches in 1 Tim. 1:19, that those who either do not acquire or do not preserve a good conscience, also make shipwreck of the faith. But he had already given love of a sincere heart as a companion of a good conscience in verse 5. There is, however, a similar comparison of a building in Philo, in his book on Cain: οἶκος μὲν ἐν ὀλίγοις τὴν ἀόρατον ψυχὴν τῷ ἀοράτῳ Θεῷ λόγοις ἐσ ἐνδίκους κὴ κατὰ νόμον φέρομεν. ἵνα δὲ βέβαιον κὴ περιπαπέσατον εἴη ὁ οἶκος, θεμέλιοι μὲν ὑποβεβλήσθωσαν εὐφυΐα κὴ διδασκαλία

and may virtues with good deeds build him up. The sense is almost the same in the saying of the Hebrews: he whose knowledge is greater than his works is like a tree whose branches are many, but roots are few: into which a wind rushing, tears it up by the roots and overturns it. That saying of Plutarch happened to Sertorius: pure virtue and that which is constituted according to reason, no fortune could ever seem to shake into the opposite. These things concerning the way prescribed by Christ, concerning the goal, and its connection with the way would be correct, if that way were explained rightly and according to the mind of Christ, who does not call our love the way to life, but defines it far otherwise in John XIV. 6. I am the way: no one comes to the Father, except through me: and that faith is the obedience of truth, when indeed we receive Christ proposed in the Gospel by faith, and believe in him, is inculcated everywhere John I. 12. c. III. 16. c. IV. 29. Rom. I. 5. 2. Thess. II. 13. 1. Petr. I. 21. For there is salvation in no other name than in the name of Jesus Acts IV. 12. nor do we obtain the remission of sins and salvation, except through faith Acts X. 43. Rom. III. 28. Gal. I. 16. Eph. II. 8. Our love has no part here, which is nowhere established as a cause of salvation, nay, it is excluded from the class of causes of salvation, since we obtain salvation without works Rom. III. 28. not of works Eph. II. 9. Therefore, however much an active assent is required, not merely a contemplative one, yet that which is necessary for salvation is by no means to be described in this way, when the will is bent toward obedience, as far as the precept concerning love is concerned, but as far as the precept concerning faith is concerned: lest that be attributed to our obedience, and love of God, and neighbor, which consists in the reception of Christ through faith, and which ought to be claimed entirely for the justice, or obedience of Christ, by which it is necessary that we be justified and saved Rom. V. 18. 19. Acts IV. 12. with our love or our purpose of obeying the precepts concerning our love contributing or conferring nothing to that Eph. III. 17. as Grotius wishes with Calvin and Bullinger; but in the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus, by which God loved us, not by which we love God: because the love of God is the foundation and root of our life and salvation John III. 16. 1. John III. 16. c. IV. 10. therefore they are said to be rooted in Christ and built up, and confirmed in faith Col. II. 7. who believe in Christ, the Apostle asks, that we may be rooted and founded in the Love of God, that we may experience it more and more, and be made more certain of it, and so feel in our heart that we are loved by God in Christ, and place firm confidence and immovable hope of salvation in this love. Our love cannot be understood here: for this is not the foundation and root of our salvation, but is the fruit of saving faith and justice: but the name of root and foundation is wrongly attributed to fruits: Which has also been observed by Beza, who disagrees here with Calvin. The Apostle had previously desired the indwelling of Christ in our hearts through faith: now he prays: that rooted in the love of God we may be able to comprehend with all the saints the magnitude of the love of God: which we do not apprehend by our love, but in the sense of the love of God toward us. And Chrysostom notes that the same thing is now said as before (may he give you the Spirit of Wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him, that you may know what is the excellent magnitude of his power toward us who believe) that you may be able to comprehend what is the breadth, and length, etc. that is, that you may know the mystery which has been diligently dispensed for us: what is the magnitude of the love of God, how it has extended itself everywhere. Chrysostom adds that Christ dwells in the hearts of the faithful, who are rooted in his love, not wavering. Furthermore, that Rock to Peter, upon which he wishes us to be founded in this place Matt. VII. 24.

CHRIST, so that we may not be moved and overturned by any storms, is not our contrition, not our love, not our works, because no one can lay another foundation, besides that which is laid, which is Jesus Christ 1. Cor. III. 11. 1. Petr. II. 4. seqq. who is the only Rock of the Church, against which the gates of hell cannot prevail Matt. XVI. 17. who must be apprehended by true faith, since we ought to be founded in him, and through him, in the love of God. Finally, from the antithesis of hypocrisy, the blessed Chemnitz rightly teaches what it is to do the word of Christ: whose explanation it is helpful to append: But what it is to do the word of Christ, the antithesis of hypocrisy recited above shows most simply, namely that it should not stick in the ears, not float on the tongue, nor be shown only in external deeds, but should lay a foundation in the heart and take root there, as the parable says Luke XII. 15. and Paul Eph. III. 17. Col. II. 7. by the mention of rooting and foundation seems to allude to this. And Christ speaks of his whole doctrine. Of which there are three principal parts 1. Repentance, 2. Faith for the remission of sins, 3. Fruits of Repentance, or good works. Therefore, to do that which is preached about in this place must be deduced through those three heads, so that it may be opposed to those who hear and do nothing, or do something else and otherwise than the word of God prescribes. And those who hear and do are the true and genuine disciples and hearers of Christ.

Latin:

Vers. 24. ὅτις ἀκούει με τὰς λόγες τέτως) Sicut modo ostendebamus ex Jacobo ἀκροατὰς dici eos qui Christia- nismum profiterentur, ita hic verbo ἀκούειν tota professio designatur.

PARS VI.

Conclusio concionis montanæ exhortatoria.

κὴ ποιεῖ αὐτὲς] ποιεῖν ut modo diximus propositum a- gendi significat. Atque hic notandum est discrimen as- sensionis contemplativæ tantum, & assensionis activæ; Nam at assensio fiat activa, hæc tria requiruntur: primum ut diligenter consideretur, quæ sit via à Christo præscripta, quæque difficultates internæ atque externæ eam comiten- tur: deinde ut attente itidem expendatur magnitudo æter- næ ejus gloriæ quam Christus promittit: tertio ut bene in- figatur animo certa connexio vix istius cum meta & metæ cum via, nempe ut constet fieri non posse quin isthac eo ve- niatur, nec alia eundo eodem esse pervenire. His bene perceptis atq; meditatis, flectitur voluntas in obedientiam intellectæ veritatis, unde insurgit in animo dilectio, quæ radicis & fundamenti vicem præstat. Ephes. III, 17. Confer quæ infra sunt capite XIII. & Lucæ XIV. 28. Hæc est quæ adversus blanditias voluptatum, formidinem doloris; pau- pertatis, exsilii, ignominiæ, mortis denique, & novam falsi magisterii disciplinam, assensionem illam priorem & con- templativam, ejusque professionem inconcussam retinet. Contra qui rebus non bene expensis, neque jacto tali fun- damento veracem doctrinam intellectu æque etiam pro- fessione approbant, peccandi illecebris, metu imminentis mali, novitatis lenocinio facile eo adducuntur, ut quod lubidini suæ adversatur, malint non esse verum, & quovis modo quærentes effugium dubitent primum, paulatim la- bascant & à professione deficiant. Consequens enim est, docente Paulo 1. Tim. I. 19. ut qui bonam conscientiam aut non acquirunt aut non conservant, etiam fidei naufragium faciant. Bonæ autem conscientiæ comitem ante de- dederat dilectionem sinceri cordis commate 5. Est autem similis ædificii comparatio apud Philonem libro de Caino: οἶκος μὲν ἐν ὀλίγοις τὴν ἀόρατον ψυχὴν τῷ ἀοράτῳ Θεῷ λόγοις ἐσ ἐνδίκους κὴ κατὰ νόμον φέρομεν. ἵνα δὲ βέβαιον κὴ περιπαπέσατον εἴη ὁ οἶκος, θεμέλιοι μὲν ὑποβεβλήσθωσαν εὐφυΐα κὴ διδασκαλία

ἀρεταὶ δὲ μετὰ καλῶν πράξεων ἐποικοδομήσωσιν ἀυτῷ. Sensus ferme idem in dicto Hebræorum: cujus scientia major est quam opera, similis est arbori cujus rami multi sunt, radices paucæ: in quam irruens ventus, avellit eam ra- dicitus & subvertit. Accidit illud Plutarchi Sertorio: ἀρετὴν εἰλικρινῆ κᾀ κατὰ λόγον συνεστῶσαν; ἐκ ἄν ποτε δοκῇ τύχη τις ἐκσεῖσαι πρὸς τὀναντίον. Hæc de via à Christo præscripta, de meta, & connexione ejus cum via recte se haberent, si via illa dextre & ex sententia Christi explicaretur, qui viam ad vitam non dicit dilectionem nostram, sed longe aliter eam definit Joh. XIV. 6. Ego sum via: nemo venit ad Patrem, nisi per me: & obedientiam veritatis fidem esse, cum nempe Christum in Evan- gelio propositum fide recipimus, & in ipsum cre- dimus, passim inculcatur Joh. I. 12. c. III. 16. c. IV. 29. Rom. I. 5. 2. Thess. II. 13. 1. Petr. I. 21. Non enim in alio nomine est salus, quam in nomine Jesu Actor. IV. 22. nec remissionem peccatorum & salutem consequimur, nisi per fidem Act. X. 43. Rom. III. 28. Gal. I. 16. Eph. II. 8. Dilectioni nostræ hic nullæ sunt partes, quæ nuspiam causa salutis constitui- tur, imo à causarum salutis classe excluditur, siquidem χωρὶς ἔργων salutem consequamur Rom. III. 28. ἐκ ἐξ ἔργων Eph. II. 9. Utut ergo assensio activa requiratur, non contemplativa tantum, ea tamen, qua ad salutem opus est, neutiquam ita describenda est, cum flectitur voluntas ad obedi- entiam, quantum ad præceptum de dilectione, sed quantum ad præceptum de fide: ne id tribua- tur obedientiæ nostræ, & dilectioni Dei, & pro- ximi, quod obedientiæ est in susceptione Christi per fidem consistenti, & justitiæ, vel obedientiæ Christi in solidum vindicari debet, qua justificari nos, ac salvari oportet Rom. V. 18. 19. Actor. IV. 12. nihil ad id faciente, aut conferente nostra dilectione vel proposito nostro obediendi præceptis, de di- lectione nostra Eph. III. 17. uti cum Calvino, Bul- lingero, Grotius vult; sed in charitate Dei, quæ est in Christo Jesu, qua dilexit nos Deus, non qua diligamus nos Deum: quia Dei dilectio fundamen- tum & radix est vitæ & salutis nostræ Joh. III. 16. 1. Joh. III. 16. c. IV. 10. ideo in Christo radici di- cuntur & ædificati, & firmati in fide Col. II. 7. qui credunt in Christum, Petit Apostolus, ut radi- cemur, & fundemur in Charitate Dei, ut magis magisque eam experiamur, ac de ea certiores red- damur, adeoque in corde nostro sentiamus, nos in Christo à Deo diligi, & in hac dilectione firmam fiduciam, & spem salutis immotam collocemus. Nostra dilectio hic intelligi nequit: hæc enim non est fundamentum & radix salutis nostræ, sed est fructus fidei salvificæ & justitiæ: at fructibus male tribuitur nomen radicis & fundamenti: Quod observatum etiam Bezæ est, hic à Calvino dissen- tienti. Optarat antea Apostolus inhabitationem Christi in cordibus nostris per fidem: jam precatur: ut radicati in dilectione Dei valeamus καταλαβέσθαι cum omnibus sanctis magnitudinem dilectionis Dei: quam non charitate nostra apprehendimus, sed in sensu charitatis Dei erga nos. Et notat Chry- sostomus, idem nunc dici, quod antea (det vobis Spiritum Sapientiæ, ac revelationis in cognitione ipsius, ut sciatis, quæ sit excellens magnitudo po- tentiæ ipsius in nos, qui credimus) ut possitis com- prehendere, quæ sit latitudo, quæ longitudo &c. hoc est, ut cognoscatis mysterium, quod pro nobis diligenter dispensatum est: quæ sit magnitudo dile- ctionis Dei, quomodo illa nuspiam non se extenderit. Addit Chrysostomus, habitare Christum in cor- dibus fidelibus, in dilectione ipsius radicatis, non circumfluctuantibus. Porro Petro illa, supra quam nos fundari vult hoc loco Matth. VII. 24.

CHRISTUS, ut nullis procellis commoveamur, & evertamur, non est contritio nostra, non dile- ctio, non opera nostra, quia fundamentum aliud nemo ponere potest, præter id, quod positum est, quod est Jesus Christus 1. Cor. III. 11. 1. Petr. II. 4. seqq. qui unica Petræ Ecclesiæ est, adversus quam portæ inferorum prævalere non possunt Matt. XVI. 17. qui vera fide apprehendendus est, cum fundari in ipso, & per ipsum, in dilectione Dei debemus. De- nique ex antithesi hypocriseos recte docet B. Che- mnitius, quid sit facere verbum Christi: cujus explicationem subjungere juvat: Quid autem facere verbum Christi, antithesis hypocriseos supra recitata simplicissime ostendit, ut scilicet non hæreat in auribus, non natet in lingua, nec in externis tantum factis ostentetur, sed fundamentum ponat in corde & ibi radices agat, sicut inquit parabola Luc. XII. 15. & Paulus Eph. III. 17. Col. II. 7. mentione radicationis & fundamenti videtur huc alludere. Et de tota sua doctrina Christus loquitur. Cujus tres principales sunt partes 1. Pœnitentia, 2. Fides ad re- missionem peccatorum, 3. Fructus Pœnitentiæ, seu bona opera. Facere ergo illud, de quo hoc lo- co concionatur, deducendum est per tria illa capita, ita, ut opponatur illis, qui audiunt, & nihil faciunt, vel aliud & aliter faciunt, quam verbum Dei præ- scribit. Et qui audiunt & faciunt, sunt veri & genuini discipuli, & auditores Christi.

## 7:25
Vers. 25. τεθεμελίωτο) Thus this word stands in all the codices, when usage would demand ἐνετεθεμελίωτο. So also you will find πεποιηκό sometimes in Josephus.

ἐπὶ τὴν πέτραν) With a rocky ground laid underneath upon which the surface rests. For that we may understand fortresses placed on rocks, that which follows concerning the force of the river does not sufficiently allow. To build on sand is also a common Latin proverb.

Latin:

Vers. 25. τεθεμελίωτο) Ita hæc vox exstat in omnibus codicibus, cum usus postularet ἐνετεθεμελίωτο. Sic & apud Josephum aliquoties invenies πεποιηκό.

ἐπὶ τὴν πέτραν) Substrato solo saxeo cui superficies in- cumbat. Nam ut arces intelligamus in rupibus positas, non satis patitur id quod sequitur de fluminis impetu. Op- positum est in arena ædificare etiam Latino proverbio tri- tum.

## 7:27
Vers. 27. ἦλθον οἱ ποταμοὶ) An inundation in the Psalms often signifies adverse things: which is also called baptism below XX. 22. So also in Isaiah LIX. 19. a hostile arrival is compared to a river. And God is said to be a protection against an inundation to the same XXV. 4.

καὶ ἔπνευσαν οἱ ἄνεμοι) Compare Daniel VII. 2. Christ is a firm protection against rivers and winds. Isaiah XXXII, 2.

Latin:

Vers. 27. ἦλθον οἱ ποταμοὶ) Inundatio in Psalmis sæpe res adversas significat: quod & βάπτισμα infra vocatur XX. 22. Sic & Esaiæ LIX. 19. hostilis adventus fluvio compa- ratur. Et eidem Deus dicitur protectio contra inunda- tionem XXV. 4.

καὶ ἔπνευσαν οἱ ἄνεμοι) Compara Danielem VII. 2. Christus contra fluvios & ventos firmum præsidium. E- saias XXXII, 2.

## 7:29
Vers. 29. ὡς ἐξουσίαν ἔχων) It is manifest from what follows that Christ is not being compared to the ancient Prophets, whom that populace had never heard speaking, but to the experts in the law whom they heard daily interpreting the law. The experts in the law, destitute of all efficacy of miracles, did not even themselves put forward anything other than the doctrine of human institution, praising the authors of their opinions, some Sameas, others Hellel, others others. Christ, on the contrary, spoke with that majesty with which those who had received commands predetermined by God were accustomed to speak, ἐν ἀποδείξει πνεύματος καὶ δυνάμεως, as Paul says. And this very thing was now new and unusual, since for some centuries prophecy, certainly that which was ordinary and as it were public, had ceased. The Jews are accustomed to note [this] at the times of Ezra. Thus far the Prophets: thereafter the learned men החכמים. For this was in place of an epoch. Hence 1 Maccab. IX. 28. καὶ ἐγένετο θλίψις μεγάλη ἐν τῷ Ἰσραὴλ ἥτις οὐκ ἐγένετο ἀφ᾽ ἧς ἡμέρας οὐκ ὤφθη προφήτης αὐτοῖς. And if there was anything of a more difficult controversy, they left it indefinite μέχρι τοῦ παραγενηθῆναι προφήτην, as can be seen in 1 Maccab. IV. 46, which in the same book XIV. 41 is called ἕως τοῦ ἀναστῆναι προφήτην πιστόν. This, therefore, is what Luke VII. 16 narrates the people said, a great Prophet has been raised up among us, and God has visited his people. And hence it appears that ἐξουσίαν here signifies extraordinary right and power. See below XX. 23. Mark XI. 28. Luke XX. 22. To this ἐξουσίᾳ, however, δύναμις is aptly added in some places as a mark τῆς ἐξουσίας Luke IV. 36. IX. 1. Justin Martyr in his Second Apology concerning Christ: οὐ γὰρ σοφιστὴς ὑπῆρχεν, ἀλλὰ δύναμις Θεοῦ ὁ λόγος αὐτοῦ ἦν. This is an explanation of the passage Ps. XLV. 4.

Latin:

Vers. 29. ὡς ἐξουσίαν ἔχων) Manifestum est ex eo quod sequitur, non Prophetis vetustis Christum comparari, quos plebs illa nunquam loquentes audierat, sed legis pe- ritis quos quotidie audiebant legem interpretantes. Le- gis periti omni efficacia miraculorum destituti, ne ipsi qui- dem aliud quam doctrinam humanæ institutionis præ se ferebant, laudantes sententiarum suarum auctores alii Sa- meam, alii Hellelem, alii alios. Christus contra ea ma- jestate loquebatur, qua solebant qui à Deo præfinita man- data acceperant, ἐν ἀποδείξει πνεύματος καὶ δυνάμεως, ut lo- quitur Paulus. Atque hoc ipsum novum jam & insolitum erat, quando jam aliquot à sæculis Prophetia, certe illa quæ erat ordinaria & quasi publica, desierat. Solent an- notare Judæi ad Esdræ tempora. Hactenus Prophetæ: deinceps viri eruditi החכמים. Nam hoc erat vice ἐ- ποχῆς. Hinc 1. Maccab. IX. 28. καὶ ἐγένετο θλίψις μεγάλη ἐν τῷ Ἰσραὴλ ἥτις οὐκ ἐγένετο ἀφ᾽ ἧς ἡμέρας οὐκ ὤφθη προφή- της αὐτοῖς. Et si quid erat difficilioris controversiæ id in- definitum relinquebant μέχρι τοῦ παραγενηθῆναι προφήτην, ut videre est 1. Maccab. IV. 46. quod eodem libro XIV. 41. dicitur ἕως τοῦ ἀναστῆναι προφήτην πιστόν. Hoc igitur est quod narrat Lucas VII. 16. dixisse populum, magnus Propheta inter nos excitatus est, & invisit Deus populum suum. Atque hinc apparet ἐξουσίαν hic significare jus ac potesta- tem extraordinariam. Vide infra XX. 23. Marc. XI. 28. Luc. XX. 22. Huic autem ἐξουσίᾳ apposite aliquot locis ad- ditur δύναμις tanquam nota τῆς ἐξουσίας Luc. IV. 36. IX. 1. Justinus Martyr Apologetico II. de Christo: οὐ γὰρ σοφιστὴς ὑπῆρχεν, ἀλλὰ δύναμις Θεοῦ ὁ λόγος αὐτοῦ ἦν. Hæc expli- catio loci Ps. XLV. 4.

## 8:1 Argument
CHAPTER VIII. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

A leper meets Christ as he is descending from the mountain, who is healed and sent to the Priests: as he is coming into Capernaum, a Centurion prays for his servant, with this confidence, that he can restore him with a single word: admiring this faith, Christ predicts the calling of the Gentiles and the ejection of the children of the kingdom: entering the house of Peter, he heals his mother-in-law who is suffering from a fever, and many who are possessed and sick, so that what was said through the Prophet (Is. LIII. 4) might be fulfilled, and he testifies to a scribe wishing to follow him that he does not have where to lay his head, and he rightly instructs another who was going to attend to his father's burial first: and boarding a boat, he calms a storm that had been stirred up: but in the territory of the Gergesenes he frees two who are possessed, and permits the devils to invade a herd of swine, which, when they had thrown themselves into the sea, he is asked by the whole city to depart from those territories. There are three parts: I. The acts of Christ upon entering Capernaum, namely miracles in the healing of the leper, to v. 4, of the Centurion's servant to v. 13, of Peter's mother-in-law and other sick people to v. 17, and the things said to two who wished to follow him, to v. 22. II. The calming of the storm on the sea, to v. 27. III. The liberation of the two possessed men in the territory of the Gergesenes, to v. 34.

PART I. The acts of Christ upon entering Capernaum.

Latin:

CAPUT IIX. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Christo de monte descendenti occurrit lepro- sus, qui sanatur, & ad Sacerdotes remitti- tur: venientem in Capernaum orat Centu- rio pro servo suo, cum ea fiducia, quod uno verbo ipsum restituere possit: quam fidem admiratus Christus gentium vocationem & filiorum regni ejectionem prædicit: in- grediens vero ædes Petri socrum ejus febri- citantem, multosq́; obsessos & ægrotos sa- nat, ut impleatur quod per Prophetam di- ctum (Es. LIII. 4) & legisperito sequi ipsum volenti testatur, se non habere ubi caput re- clinet, aliumque sepulturam Patris prius curaturum rectius informat: ac navim conscendens, excitatam tempestatem compe- scit: in finibus autem Gergesenorum duos obsessos liberat, & diabolis permittit, ut gregem porcorum invadant, qui ubi se in mare præcipitarant, à tota civitate roga- tur, ut è finibus istis egrediatur. Partes tres sunt: I. Acta Christi sub ingressum in Capernaum, utpote miracula in sanatione le- prosi, ad v. 4. servi Centurionis ad v. 13. socrus Pe- tri & aliorum ægrotorum ad v. 17. & τὰ λεχθέντα ad duos ipsum sequi volentes, ad v. 22. II. Sedatio tempestatis in mari, ad v. 27. III. Liberatio duorum obsessorum in finibus Gergesenis, ad v. 34.

PARS I. Acta Christi sub ingressum in Capernaum.

## 8:2
Vers. 2. προσκύνει αὐτῷ] With his body cast upon the ground, as Luke explains in chapter V. 12. And he fell forward in such a way that he touched the knees of Christ, which is γονυπετεῖν in Mark, but not with bent knees, as some interpret, which was a lesser form of veneration. Thus also what the interpreter of Matthew said below, προσκυνεῖν IX. 18, Mark and Luke said πίπτειν πρὸς πόδας. Elsewhere, what our author here called προσκυνεῖν, Luke explains as πίπτειν ἐπὶ πρόσωπον. It seems entirely that this leper had conceived something great and extraordinary in his mind about Jesus, namely, a most free power of healing.
