But whether he believed this to be the promised Messiah can be doubted, since Jesus himself had not yet openly professed it, nor had that rumor spread among the common people.

The leper attributes to Christ not only a most free power of healing, which might depend on the divine and be inferior to it, but divine omnipotence, because it is a work of divine infinite virtue and power to free from leprosy, 2 Kings V. 7. Nor can it be doubted that he believed Jesus to be the promised Messiah, without whom faith in him, through which he obtained health, could not have had a place. And to whom else would he have claimed the divine power of cleansing from leprosy, if indeed this was a mark of the Messiah, Matt. XI. 5, and it did not befit any of the prophets to free from leprosy αὐτεξουσίως, as the leper professed of Christ, if you will, you can cleanse me. But it was not unknown that Jesus was the Messiah: because God the Father had proclaimed it from heaven in Matt. III., and John had openly testified about him in John I., and Christ had taken on disciples, by whom he was recognized and preached: whence the fame about him was spread to others. Nor did the other proclamation about the coming of the kingdom of God in Matt. IV. 17, and the public announcement of the Gospel made in the Jewish Synagogues in v. 23, combined with illustrious miracles, testify otherwise; and Matthew in the same chapter IV. 24 reports that the fame about him had gone out into all Syria, and that sick people of every kind were therefore brought to him. Finally, did not Christ declare those blessed who suffer persecution for his sake and his name? Did he not preach on the mountain, before a great crowd, about those who would perform miracles in his name, to be concluded by himself on the day of the Almighty, Matt. VII. 22, 28? From all of which it could sufficiently be established that he was the promised Messiah.

κύριε) It was the custom of the Jews to address anyone, even a stranger, in this way. John XX. 15.

ἐὰν θέλῃς δύνασαί με καθαρίσαι.] A persuasion of the power of God is usually the beginning of piety. For from this it happens that we approach God, Heb. XI. 6, and if he has promised anything, we have faith in him, however difficult that which the promise contains may seem, Rom. IV. 21, Heb. XI. 19. Thus also the principle of the Christian religion is to trust in the power of God in Christ, through which our bodies also are to rise again, which, so that it might be shadowed forth by a visible sign, Christ wished to confer the health of the body, an image of another greater health, only upon those who trusted that he could do it. See what is below in IX. 28. At the same time, the modesty of the man is to be noted, who, humbly acknowledging himself to be struck by God (for it was usually sent by God as a punishment for some crime, especially of evil-speaking, as in Num. XII.), dares not ask for anything openly: having only testified what he believes Christ can do. Καθαρίζειν, moreover, is properly said of leprosy, טהר.

Not only a persuasion of the power of God, but faith or trust in divine grace no less than power, that God not only can, but also wills to succor our misery and necessity, is the beginning and root of true piety: because Charity toward God and neighbor, by which true piety is comprised, and which is called by the Apostle the end of the commandment, ought to redound from a pure heart and a good conscience and faith unfeigned, 1 Tim. I. 5. But the heart is purified by faith, Acts XV. 9, and through the sprinkling of the blood of Jesus Christ in obedience to the truth, or faith through the Spirit, 1 Pet. I. 2, 22, Heb. IX. 14, 1 John I. 7, 1 Pet. I. 2, 19. The object of faith, however, is not so much the power of God as his grace and mercy, since the former is rather a presupposition of faith; inasmuch as it is directed straight toward divine grace, and apprehends it. Nor is it Heb. XI. 6. a persuasion concerning the power of God, but faith in God that is designated, by which we may please God: and that approach to God is not the beginning of piety, but rather it is the enjoyment of God, which is promised to those who believe, not only that God exists, or that He is omnipotent, but also that He is a μισθαποδότης of those who seek Him; for by this faith we approach God, by this we arrive at God; by this we possess God, and enjoy His grace and salvation: since indeed by true confidence we apply to ourselves this, that He Himself wishes to be our reward, and retribution, as He promised to Abraham the Father of believers, I am thy reward exceeding great Gen. XV. 1. Which promise ought to be apprehended by a special and applicatory faith; nor does a general faith of such a kind suffice, by which we believe those things which God has promised, even if the things which the promise contains are most difficult: because even the devils believe that God is omnipotent, nay, and that He is truthful, Jac. II. 19. yet they do not please God, nor do they approach to GOD, but are eternally excluded from GOD. Nor is it the beginning of the Christian religion, but the soul and form of the same, to trust in Divine grace in Christ Jesus, so that we believe we shall obtain the salvation of the soul, and the glorious resurrection of the body, through the same: just as the leper trusted that he would obtain through the grace of Christ both the health of the body, if the LORD wills, and primarily the salvation of the soul, provided he asks hypothetically, and commits to the Lord's will with humble devotion cleansing from bodily leprosy: although he was secure concerning His power, 'Lord, if You will, You can make me clean': but he sought and desired the cleansing from spiritual leprosy, of which that was an image, and the remission of sin, not only with a condition, but simply without hesitation, concerning the gracious will of God, which God deigned to confirm to all by an oath. Ezek. 18 & 33, and which Christ openly preached and announced to all, Matt. 4:17, ch. 5:6, ch. 7:7 ff., Mark 1:15, Luke 4:18, which also the forerunner of Christ, St. John, had already testified with a resounding voice, John 1:8, 16, 17, 29, not to mention the consenting testimony of the Prophets, that all who believe in Him obtain the remission of sins through faith in Christ, Acts 10:43, which could not have been unknown among those who had Moses and the Prophets. But to trust in the power of God in Christ, or rather in the divine power of Christ, because Christ is God over all blessed forever, Rom. 9:5, by which our bodies also are to live again, is understood either of faith in general, by which we believe that it can be done by the power of Christ, or we apply it to ourselves specifically, and we trust that that glorious and blessed resurrection will happen in OUR body, whoever we are that are faithful, i.e., that we ourselves shall be participants and sharers in it, of which the former pertains to the antecedents, but the latter to the very substance of faith. Chrysostom notes that the leper certainly showed great faith, συνετώτατος γὰρ ἦν ὁ τοιοῦτος, καὶ θεοφορούμενος, for such a one was most prudent and inspired by God, εἰδὼς ὡς ἀληθῶς, ὅτι θεός ἐστι, καὶ πάντα δυνάμενος ποιῆσαι, knowing most truly that He was God and could do all things, whom he was addressing.

Latin:

Vers. 2. προσκύνει αὐτῷ] Projecto in terram corpore, ut Lucas explicat cap. V. 12. Ita autem procidit ut genua Christi contingeret, quod est γονυπετεῖν apud Marcum, non autem flexis genibus, ut quidam interpretantur, quæ minor erat venerandi species. Sic & quod infra Matthæi interpres dixit προσκυνεῖν IX. 18. Marcus & Lucas dixerunt πίπτειν πρὸς πόδας. Alibi quod hic noster προσκυνεῖν di- xit, Lucas exponit πίπτειν ἐπὶ πρόσωπον. Videtur omnino vitiliginosus iste magnum aliquid & eximium de Jesu ani- mo concepisse, nimirum liberrimam sanandi potestatem. Sed an hunc esse promissum Messiam crediderit, dubitari potest, cum ipse Jesus id nondum palam esset professus, neque is rumor in vulgus manasset.

Non tantum liberrimam sanandi potestatem, Christo tribuit leprosus, quæ à divina dependeat, eaque inferior sit, sed divinam omnipotentiam, quia à lepra liberare opus est divinæ infinitæ virtutis & potentiæ 2. Reg. V. 7. Neque dubitari potest, ipsum credidisse Jesum esse promissum Messiam, sine quo fides in ipsum, per quam sanitatem conse- quutus est, locum habere non potuit. Et cui alii divinam potestatem mundandi à lepra vindicasset, siquidem hæc nota fuerit Messiæ, Matth. XI. 5. nec ulli prophetarum convenerit, αὐτεξουσίως, liberare à lepra, quemadmodum de Christo pro- fessus leprosus est, si vis, potes me mundare. Non autem ignotum erat, Jesum esse Messiam: quia & de cœlo proclamaverat id Deus Pater Matth. III. & Johannes testificatus palam erat de ipso Joh. I. & Christus discipulos assumserat, à quibus agni- tus & prædicatus fuit: unde fama de ipso ad alios divulgata. Neque aliud præconium de adventu regni Dei Matth. IV. 17, & annunciatio publica Evangelii in Synagogis Judaicis facta v. 23. cum miraculis illustribus conjuncta, testabatur; & in totam Syriam famam de ipso exiisse, atque omnis generis ægrotos ideo ad ipsum adductos perhibet Matthæus ibidem cap. IV. 24. Denique annon Christus beatos prædicavit, qui propter i- psum & nomen ipsius persequutionem patiuntur? annon de illis: qui in nomine suo miracula patratu- ri sint, in die παντοκρατικῷ abs se concludendis, concionatus in monte, coram magna turba erat Matth. VII. 22. 28. è quibus omnibus satis consta- re poterat, eum esse promissium Messiam.

κύριε) Moris erat Judæis hoc modo quemvis etiam i- gnotum appellare. Joh. XX. 15.

ἐὰν θέλῃς δύνασαί με καθαρίσαι.] Persuasio de potentia Dei initium solet esse pietatis. Nam hinc sit, ut ad Deum accedamus Hebr. XI. 6. & si quid promisit, ei habeamus fidem, quantumvis difficillimum videatur id, quod pro- missio continet Rom. IV. 21. Hebr. XI. 19. Sic etiam Christianæ religionis principium est, confidere Dei po- tentiæ in Christo, per quam etiam corpora nostra sint re- victura, quod ut signo visibili adumbraretur, sanitatem corporis, alterius majoris sanitatis imaginem iis demum Christus conferre voluit, qui ipsum id posse confiderent. Vide quod infra est IX. 28. Simul notanda hominis mo- destia, qui à Deo correptum se humiliter agnoscens (mo- ribus enim ille plerumque à Deo in pœnam criminis a- licujus, maledicentiæ præsertim, ut Num. XII. immitte- batur) nihil postulare aperte audet: tantum quid Christum posse credat, testatus. Καθαρίζειν autem טהר propriè di- citur lepra.

Non tantum persuasio de potentia Dei, sed fides vel fiducia in divinam gratiam non minus quam potentiam, quod Deus non modo possit, sed etiam velit nostræ miseriæ, & necessitati succur- rere, veræ pietatis initium, & radix est: quia Charitas in Deum & proximum, qua compre- henditur vera pietas, quæque τὸ τέλος τῆς παραγ- γελίας Apostolo dicitur, ex corde puro & conscien- tia bona & fide ἀνυποκρίτῳ redundare debet 1. Tim. I. 5. Cor autem purificatur fide Act. XV. 9. ac per aspersionem sanguinis Jesu Christi in obedientia veritatis, vel fide per Spiritum 1. Petr. I. 2. 22. Ebr. IX. 14. 1. Joh. I. 7. 1. Petr. I. 2. 19. Fidei vero objectum non tam est potentia Dei, quam gratia & misericordia, quum illa potius sit præsuppositum fidei; utpote quæ directè fertur in divinam gra- tiam, eamque apprehendit. Neque Ebr. XI. 6. persuasio de potentia Dei, sed fides in Deum defi- gnatur, qua Deo placeamus: & accessus ille ad Deum non est pietatis exordium, sed potius frui- tio Dei est, quæ promittitur illis, qui credunt, non tantum quod Deus sit, aut quod omnipotens sit, sed etiam quod μισθαποδότης sit eorum, qui requirunt eum; hac enim fide ad Deum accedi- mus, hac ad Deum pervenimus; hac Deo poti- mur, ejusque gratia & salute fruimur: cum nempe vera fiducia hoc nobis applicamus, quod ipse nostra velit esse merces, & retributio, uti A- brahamo Patri credentium promisit, Ego sum merces tua magna nimis Gen. XV. 1. Quæ promif- sio fide apprehendi debet speciali, & applicatoria; neque sufficit generalis ejusmodi fides, qua cre- dimushis, quæ promisit Deus, etsi difficillima sint, quæ promissio continet: quia & diaboli cre- dunt Deum omnipotentem, imo & veracem esse, Jac. II. 19. nec tamen Deo placent, aut ad DEUM accedunt, sed æternum à DEO exclusi sunt. Neque religionis Christianæ principium, sed anima ejusdem ac forma est, confidere Di- vinæ gratiæ in Christo Jesu, ita, ut salutem animæ, & gloriosam resurrectionem corporis, per ean- dem nos consequuturos credamus: quemad- modum leprosus confidebat, se per gratiam Chri- sti tum sanitatem corporis, si velit DOMI- NUS, tum imprimis animæ salutem conse- quuturum, siquidem hypothetice petat, ac Domini voluntati humili devotione committat purga- tionem a lepra corporis: etsi de potentia ejusdem se- curus esset, Domine, si vis potes me mundare: purga- tionem autem a lepra spirituali, cujus illa imago fuit, ac remissionem peccati non cum conditione so- lum petiit, ac desiderarit, sed simpliciter sine hesi- tatione, de gratiosa Dei voluntate, quam Deus o- mnibus jurejurando confirmare dignatus est. E- zech. XIIX. & XXXIII. quamque Christus omni- bus palam prædicavit, & annunciavit Math. IV. 17. c. V. 6. c. VII. 7. seqq. Marc. I. 15. Luc. IV. 18. quam etiam Prodromus Christi S. Johannes jam testatus erat sonora voce Joh. I. 8. 16. 17. 29. ut non dicam de consentienti Prophetarum testimo- nio, quod remissionem peccatorum per fidem in Chri- stum consequantur omnes, qui in ipsum credunt Act. X. 43. quod inter eos, qui Mosen & Prophetas ha- bebant, non poterat ignotum esse. To confidere autem potentiæ Dei in Christo, vel potius potentiæ Christi divinæ, quia Christus Deus est super omnia benedictus in secula Rom. IX. 5. qua etiam corpora nostra sint revictura, vel intelligitur de fide gene- ratim, qua credimus, in fieri virtute Christi posse, vel ad nos id applicamus sigillatim, illamque glo- riosam & beatam resuscitationem in corpore NO- STRO futuram confidimus, quicunque fideles sumus, h. e. nos ipsos ejusdem participes & con- sortes fore, quorum prius ad antecedentia, alterum vero adipsam substantiam fidei pertinet. Fidem sane multam ostendisse leprosum notat Chrysosto- mus, συνετώτατος γὰρ ἦν ὁ τοιοῦτος, καὶ θεο- φορούμενος Prudentissimus quippe erat, & a Deo in- stinctus εἰδὼς ὡς ἀληθῶς, ὅτι θεός ἐστι, καὶ πάντα δυνάμενος ποιῆσαι, sciens quam verissime Deum esse utique & omnia posse, quem alloquebatur.

## 8:3
Verse 3. He touched him.) From this history, as well as from two others in which Christ is said to have touched dead bodies, Greek interpreters draw an argument to teach that Christ was not subject to the law. And Paul expressly says, γε- νέσθαι ὑπὸ νόμον, to have been made under the law, Gal. 4:14, and Christ Himself, as we have already said, denied that He had come to earth to commit anything against the law, or to be the author of committing it. But besides the fact that by these deeds some uncleanness was indeed contracted, but one did not properly sin against the law (for otherwise it would not have been permitted to prepare for burial, nor to bury bodies, nor to heal scabies), it is furthermore certain that all works performed by divine power were always exempt from ritual precepts, just as we shall say below concerning the law of the Sabbath. For Elisha also lay upon the dead boy, so that he might restore life to him, 2 Kings 4:34, and by that act he did not commit anything contrary to the law. But this context was of the greatest use, so that it might appear that the health was neither restored by chance, nor did that power proceed from anywhere else than from Jesus Himself.

Concerning Christ, whether He was subject to the law or not? One must answer distinctly. For Christ is considered (1.) by reason of His Person, in which He consisted of a divine and human nature. By reason of neither was He subject to the law καθ' ἑαυτὸ and in Himself: for as GOD He had been the founder of the law, Exod. 20:1, Acts 7:38, but as man, since He was made a participant of the divine majesty, John 1:14, Col. 2:9, He is also Lord of the law, by virtue of the union and hypostatic communication, since He Himself is the only Lord, namely God and man: and the Son of Man is also Lord of the Sabbath, Matt. 12:8. But he who is Lord of the law, he as such is not liable or subject to the law. (2.) By reason of His office. In which manner, as mediator of God and men, He was made under the law of His own accord and willingly, Gal. 4:4, and when He was in the form of God, He willed to become a servant for us, and obedient to God the Father, even unto death, Phil. 2:6, 7, 8. and to fulfill all righteousness, Matt. 3:15: and therefore He observed not only the moral law, but also the ritual law holily. For He also underwent circumcision according to the law, Luke 2:21, but he who is circumcised is a debtor to the whole law

Therefore, as for the contact with the leper, which is attributed to Christ, it was not such a contact by which uncleanness, even only ceremonial, was contracted, because thus there would have been need of Levitical cleansing: or an unlawful one, by which one could sin at least against the ceremonial law, but it was a healing contact, to which the leprosy had to yield immediately, by which He touching the leper did not contract, but drew away and took away from the leper all uncleanness; it was not a forbidden contact, but one enjoined upon the Messiah, pertaining to His office, not foreign to the Messiah's office; as one who had to come also for that end, that He might heal lepers and take away every sickness of the body. Matt. 19:17, ch. 11:5, which He could perform whether by virtual contact alone, or even with bodily contact intervening, as a physician sent divinely. Chrysostom beautifully says of this contact: He takes hold of his hand, and touches the leper, showing thus that He observes the law, yet so that He is not liable to the law, but is the Lord of the law; at the same time indicating that nothing is unclean to the world: and that His flesh not only is holy, but also has the power of propagating holiness into all whom He might touch. Therefore, His work should not be compared with others, as this contact, proper to Him by virtue of His office, nor was His work liable to ritual precepts in the common manner of other men of God, but as He Himself willed, and the reason of His office required, who had this authority ἀφ' ἑαυτῦ, from Himself. John 10:29, just as divine power did not belong to Him in the common manner, but ἐξαιρέτως, and μονοτρόπως, not by extension or assistance, but καθ' ὑπόστασιν and hypostatic appropriation, Col. 2:9. Which is testified, even with Grotius himself as interpreter, by the imperative word of Christ, by which he himself, with independent authority and sovereign power, immediately put the leprosy to flight and cleansed the leper; for thus he comments on the words of verse 3, 'I will, be thou clean': Actions, says Grotius, men are also accustomed to command, but to produce things by command alone is truly divine. Therefore Christ often used passive words of commanding for miracles: For Moses also had described creation in this way: And God said: let there be light, and there was light: in which words a pagan man, the rhetorician Longinus, rightly observed that there is a wonderful majesty and σεμνότητα τῦ λόγυ, whose words are these: 'In this way also the lawgiver of the Jews, no ordinary man, since he recognized and revealed the power of God according to its worth, immediately at the beginning of his laws wrote: God said, he says, what? Let there be light, and it was. Let there be earth, and it was.' Whence Cyril most rightly: The Savior healed the leper by touching him, showing that the spirit dwelling within him heals diseases, but his body itself communicates sanctification by its contact.

Latin:

Vers. 3. ἥψατο ἀυτοῦ.) Ex hac historia, tum ex duabus aliis, in quibus mortua corpora Christus contigisse dicitur, argumentum trahunt Græci interpretes, ut doceant, Chri- stumnon fuisse legi subditum, Atq; Paulus diserte dicit, γε- νέσθαι ὑπὸ νόμον Gal. IV. 14. & Christus ipse, ut jam diximus, negavit venisse se in terras, ut quicquam contra legem cominitteret, committendive auct. esset. Sed præterquam quod istis factis immunditia quidem aliqua contraheba- tur, non autem proprie peccabatur in legem (nam alio- quin nec pollincire, nec condere corpora, nec scabiem sa- nare licuisset) certum insuper est, omnia opera patrata virtute divina semper exemta fuisse præceptis ritualibus, quemadmodum de lege Sabbati infra dicemus. Nam & Elisæus puero mortuo incubuit, ut vitam ei restitueret 2. Reg. IV. 34. neque eo facto quicquam admisit legi contra- rium. Contextus autem iste maximi erat usus, ut appa- reret, neque fortuito redditam sanitatem, neque virtutem eam aliunde, quam ab ipso Jesu, profectam.

De Christo, an lege fuerit subjectus nec ne? distincte respondendum. Nam consideratur Christus (1.) ratione Personæ, qua divina consta- bat natura & humana. Neutrius ratione καθ' ἑαυτὸ & per se legi subjectus fuit: nam ut DEUS conditor legis fuerat Exod. XX. 1. Act. VII. 38. ut homo vero quum particeps factus sit divinæ maje- statis Joh. I. 14. Col. II. 9. Dominus etiam legis est, vi unionis, & communicationis hypostaticæ, quum unus tantum ipse Dominus sit, nempe Deus & homo: & filius hominis etiam Sabbati Dominus sit Matth. XII. 8. Qui vero Dominus est legis, is qua talis, legi obnoxius, & subjectus non est (2.) ratione officiisui. Quo pacto ceu mediator Dei & homi- num ultro, & sponte sua factus est sub lege Gal. IV. 4. ac quum in forma Dei esset, servus fieri voluit pro nobis, & obediens Deo Patri, usque ad mortem Phil. II. 6. 7. 8. & implere omnem justitiam Matth. III. 15: ideoque non tantum legem moralem, sed etiam ritualem sancte observabat. Nam & cir- cumcisionem suscepit secundum legem Luc. II. 21. qui autem circumcisus est, debitor totius legis est

Quod itaque ad contactum leprosi, qui Christo tribuitur, non erat talis contactus, quo immunditia, etiam ceremonialis solum, contra- heretur, quia sic purgatione etiam Levitica opus fuiffet: aut ἄνομος, quo in legem saltem ceremo- nialem peccari poffet, sed erat contactus Sana- torius, cui lepra confestim cedere debebat, qua attingens leprosum non contrahebat, sed abstra- hebat, & tollebat à leproso omnem immundi- tiem; non erat contactus prohibitus, sed injun- ctus Messiæ, ad officium ejus pertinens, non alie- nus à Messiæ officio; utpote, qui venire debuit etiam ea fini, ut leprosos curaret, omnemque cor- poris ægritudinem tolleret. Matth. XIX. 17. c. XI. 5. quod sive solo virtuali, seu corporali etiam con- tactu interveniente, ceu medicus divinitus mis- sus, præstare poterat. Pulcre Chrysostomus de hoc contactu: Apprehendit ejus manum, ac lepro- sum tangit, ostendens ita, se observare legem, ut tamen obnoxius legi non sit, sed legis Dominus; simul indicans, mundo nihil immundum esse: car- nemque ejus non modo esse sanctam, sed vim etiam habere sanctitatis propagandæ in omnes, quos tan- geret. Non ergo cum aliis componi debet, qua hunc contactum, sibi vi officii proprium, ne- que communi aliorum virorum Dei more, opera ejus obnoxia erat præceptis ritualibus, sed qua volebat ipse, & officii ratio ferebat, qui ἀφ' ἑαυτῦ hanc ἐξουσίαν habebat. Joh. X. 29. quemadmodum nec communi more virtus divina ipsi convenie- bat, sed ἐξαιρέτως, & μονοτρόπως, non per παρέκ- τασιν aut assistentiam, sed καθ' ὑπόστασιν & οἰκείω- σιν hypostaticam Col. II. 9. Quod testatur, vel ipso Grotio interprete, verbum Christi imperativum, quo αὐτεξουσίως & αὐτοκρατορικῶς ipse statim lepram fugavit, & leprosum mundavit; ita enim ad verba vers. 3. θέλω, καθαρίσθητι commentatur: Actiones, inquit Grotius, imperare etiam homines solent, at res solo imperio effectas dare vere divinum est. Ideo Christus ad miracula usus sæpe est vocibus imperandi passivis: Nam & Moses creationem ita descripserat: Et dixit Deus: fiat lux, & facta est lux: quibus in verbis majestatem esse miram, & σεμνότητα τῦ λόγυ, recte anim- advertit paganus homo Longinus rhetor, cujus hæc sunt verba: ταύτῃ δὲ καὶ ὁ Ἰουδαίων θεσμοθέτης ὀυχ ὁ τυχὼν ἀ- νὴρ, ἐπειδὴ τὴν τῦ Θεῖυ δύναμιν κατ' ἀξίαν ἐγνώρισε κἀξέ- φηνεν, ἐυθὺς ἐν τῇ ἐισβολῇ γράψας τῶν νόμων. Εἶπεν ὁ Θεὸς, φησὶ, τί; γενέσθω φῶς, καὶ ἐγένετο. Γενέσθω γῆ, καὶ ἐγένετο. Unde rectissime Cyrillus: Contingens leprosum Sal- vator curavit, illum, ostendens: spiritum in se in- habitantem curare morbos, corpus vero ipsum ejus contactu suo sanctificationem communicare.

## 8:4
Verse 4. 'See thou tell no man' Diverse causes are brought forward for the commanded silence. Elsewhere I do not deny that an example of modesty was given to us by CHRIST. But in this place it seems to me that CHRIST did not command silence for longer than until he had presented himself to the priest to be examined, lest if the rumor that this had been done by JESUS reached the priests before he arrived, the priests, whose duty that was, touched by the poison of envy, might pronounce the man cleansed of the scab still unclean. For it must be noted that this miracle happened in Galilee, which the preceding and following context indicate, and most clearly Mark 1:39. But the priests were in Jerusalem: wherefore this man healed by CHRIST was ordered to hasten as much as he could: For those words in Mark, 'immediately he sent him away,' note that: namely, lest the report outrun him. Moreover, the priest was to be called out outside the gate, so that he might judge the disease there.

Although these things may have a place regarding the prohibition of the divulging of the miracle to be taken in a qualified sense, before the leper showed himself to the priest: because, however, the divulging of miracles is also prohibited elsewhere, Matt. 9:30, ch. 12:13, therefore the blessed Gerhard brings forward three causes for this prohibition of Christ: 1. He did not want men to stick at the miracles, but that they ought to regard doctrine above all. 2. He wished to show by the very fact that He was not seeking His own glory, John 8:50, and to stifle the vice of arrogance in us. 3. He was still in the state of humiliation, and the time had not yet arrived when miracles were to be divulged. Grotius notes that this miracle happened in Galilee most openly, Mark 1:39, but that is less clear. For that the healing of the same leper is described by Mark is assumed precariously, even if the circumstances are in almost the same manner. Since it is not new that some similar circumstances recur in different histories. But that these are different histories, time and place, and the antecedents and consequents teach not obscurely. For after the leper healed by Mark was introduced, He did not enter into Capernaum, but withdrew into the desert, and only after some days did He betake Himself to Capernaum, Mark 1:15, ch. 2:1. Matthew's leper was healed of leprosy when Christ had descended from the mountain and was heading toward Capernaum, Matt. 8:1. The miracle of the healed leper in Mark happened in a certain city, as is clear from the parallel passage Luke 5:12. The mountain sermon of Christ immediately preceded the present healing, but the healing in Mark was done after He had traversed Galilee, and had preached in the synagogues of the Jews throughout all Galilee, and had cast out demons. Finally, the healing of the present leper was immediately followed by the healing of the centurion's servant in Capernaum, not likewise the healing of the leper in Mark, to which many other things intervened, as is clear from a comparison of Mark 5:12. and 7:10 is clear, whence with the blessed Chemnitz, Molinaeus, and others, we conclude that these are distinct histories.

to the priest) To any one from the number of the priests to whom the others had delegated that province, Lev. 13:22. Now the Hebrew priests, no less than the Egyptian keepers of sacred animals, devoted effort to all parts of wisdom: and among them also to the knowledge of the nature of things and the affections of bodies: in which part he who had progressed the most was entrusted with the inspection of the sick.

The gift] But a double gift was owed by one cleansed of the scab, first two little birds with cedar, scarlet, and hyssop, then also two lambs, or if he were poorer, one lamb with a pair of turtledoves or pigeons, with fine flour and oil added. But since Mark and Luke expressly state the gift for the cleansing, it is better to understand here that first gift which was given on the day of his cleansing, Lev. 14:1, 7, since that latter one was given on the eighth day after, and that partly for a sacrifice of atonement, partly for a burnt offering.

For a testimony to them) So that, of course, after that gift is accepted, they must acknowledge that you are clean. For the gift was not received except after the health was diligently examined. Thus that 'for a testimony to them' is taken as an argument by which someone can be convinced, below 10:18, Mark 6:11, 9, James 5:3.

The Fathers, and among them Jerome, explain the testimony not only concerning the cleansing, but also concerning the author of the cleansing. And deservedly: because the priests ought not only to understand that the leper was truly cleansed, but also to learn, being convinced by this argument, that Jesus was the promised Messiah, who could cleanse lepers according to His own good pleasure, and put leprosy to flight by His command alone. For that 'for a testimony' is so accepted among the LXX Interpreters, Deut. 31:19, Matt. 24:14, Luke 9:5.

Latin:

Verf. 4. ὅρα μηδενὶ εἴπῃς] Diversæ causæ afferuntur indicti silentii. Alibi non nego modestiæ exemplum nobis à CHRISTO datum. Sed hoc loco videtur mihi CHRISTUS non diutius silentium imperasse, quam dum se ille stitisset sacerdoti explorandum, ne si ante ad Sacerdotes pervenisset rumor ab JESU hoc es- se factum, Sacerdotes, quorum ea notio erat, invidiæ veneno tacti, hominem à scabie mundatum adhuc im- mundum pronuntiarent. Notandum enim est hoc mi- raculum in Galilæa accidisse, quod priora ac posteriora indicant, & apertissime Marcus I. 39. Sacerdotes autem Hierosolymis erant: quare sanatus iste à CHRISTO jussus est quantum poterat properare: Id enim notant il- la apud Marcum εὐθέως ἐξέβαλε: scilicet ne fama ipsum anteverteret. Evocandus autem erat extra portam sacer- dos, ut ibi de morbo judicaret.

Quanquam hæc locum habere possint de pro- hibitione divulgationis miraculi secundum quid accipienda, antequam se leprosus ostenderet Sa- cerdoti: quia tamen alibi etiam prohibita est mira- culorum divulgatio, Matt. IX. 30. c. XII. 13. ideo tres causas hujus prohibitionis Christi adfert B. Ger- hardus: 1. Noluit, homines in miraculis hærere, sed doctrinam cumprimis respicere debere. 2. Ostendere voluit ipso facto, se non quærere suam gloriam, Joh. IIX. 50. ac vitium ἀλαζονίας in nobis suffocare. 3. E- rat adhuc in statu, exinanitionis, nec dum advenerat tempus, quo miracula debebant diuulgari. Notat Grotius, hoc miraculum in Galilæa accidisse, idque priora, ac posteriora apertissime indicare, Marc. I. 39. sed id minus apertum est. Nam à Marco ejus- dem leprosi fanationem describi, precario affumi- tur, etsi circumstantiæ propemodum eadem ratio- ne sese habeant. Siquidem non novum sit, simi- les nonnullas περιστάσεις in diversis historiis recur- rere. Quod autem diversæ hic sint historiæ, tem- pus & locus, & antecedentia & consequentia non ob- scure docent. Post fanatum enim leprosum à Mar- co introductum, non in Capernaum ingressus est, sed in desertum secessit, ac post aliquot demum dies in Capernaum se contulit, Marc. I. 15. c. II. 1. Mat- thæi leprosus à lepra sanatus est, cum à monte de- scendisset, & versus Capernaum tenderet Christus Matth. IIX. 1. Miraculum vero sanati leprosi apud Marcum in civitate quadam contigit, ut è loco parallelo Luc. V. 12. liquet. Præsentem sanationem concio montana Christi immediate antecessit, at sa- natio apud Marcum facta est, postquam peragras- set Galilæam, & in Judæorum Synagogis per to- tam Galilæam concionatus esset, ac dæmonia eje- cisset. Denique fanationem præsentis leprosi excepit statim sanatio famuli centurionis in Caper- naum, non item fanationem leprosi apud Mar- cum, cui alia multa intercessisse è collatione Marc. V. 12. & VII. 10. luculentum est, unde cum B. Che- mnitio, Molinæo & aliis distinctas has esse historias statuimus.

τῷ ἱερεῖ) Cuivis è Sacerdotum numero, cui cæteri eam provinciam delegaverant, Levit. XIII. 22. Sacerdotes autem Hebræi non minus quam Ægyptiorum πτωροφόροι o- mnibus sapientiæ partibus operam dabant: atque inter eas etiam cognoscendæ rerum naturæ corporumque affe ctionibus: in qua parte qui plurimum profecisset, ei mor- bidorum inspectio mandabatur.

Τὸ δῶρον] At duplex munus debebat scabie purgatus, primum passercuios duos cum cedro, cocco, & hyssopo, deinde & agnos duos, aut si pauperior esset, agnum unum cum pari turturum aut columbarum, addita simila & o- leo. Sed cum Marcus & Lucas diferte exprimant τὸ δῶ- ρον περὶ τοῦ καθαρισμοῦ prius illud munus hic intelligi satius est quod dabatur ביום טהרתו id est αὐτῇ τῇ ἡμέ- ρᾳ τοῦ καθαρισμοῦ, Levit. XIV. 1. 7. cum posterius illud da- retur octavo post die, idque partim in sacrificium ἱλασ- μοῦ partim in holocaustum.

Εἰς μαρτύριον αὐτοῖς) Ut nimirum post id munus acce- ptum fateri debeant, mundum te esse. Neque enim recipie- batur munus, nisi post valetudinem diligenter exploratam. Ita illud μαρτύριον αὐτοῖς pro argumento, quo quis con- vinci possit, sumitur infra X. 18. Marc. VI. 11. 9. Jac. V. 3.

Testimonium non tantum de mundatione, sed etiam de autore mundationis explicant Patres, & inter hos Hieronymus. Et merito: quia non tan- tum intelligere sacerdotes debebant vere munda- tum esse leprosum, sed etiam discere, hoc argu- mento convicti, Jesum esse promissum Messiam, qui leprosos mundare pro beneplacito suo, solo- que imperio lepram fugare posset. Nam ita ac- cipitur illud εἰς μαρτύριον apud LXX. Interpp. Deut. XXXI. 19, Matth. XXIV. 14. Luc. IX. 5.

## 8:5
Verse 5. He came to Him) Just as we are said in Latin to meet someone even by letter, so also in Greek 'to come to' is used without the presence of the body. Thus also we are said to come to God, Heb. 4:16, 7:25, 10:22, 11:6. And 'approach' is taken for a petitionary document. Although even if the propriety of the word did not support it in this part, that which is most accepted in law ought to suffice: that we do what we do through another. Thus also below 11:4, John is said to have said what he announced through his disciples. And thus these

and the following I do not doubt must be explained. For that we should believe another history is being narrated by Luke, such a sameness of circumstances does not allow: nor is it more likely that after the elder Jews and other acquaintances were sent to Christ, the centurion himself came to the conversation of Christ, since Luke narrates in exactly the same words through friends what are here ascribed to the centurion, and adds that when the friends had returned to report the outcome of their embassy, the servant had already recovered. Add to these that Luke uses the word 'saying,' which exists here, concerning the centurion, recounting those things which were said in his own words through others. And he attributes the 'beseeching' to the centurion himself, which is here attributed to the centurion. This is therefore one of those things which, having been handed down more broadly by Matthew, Luke wished to execute more accurately.

This is the reconciliation of St. Augustine, book 2, On the Harmony of the Gospels, ch. 20, that Matthew studied brevity, but Luke described it more fully and with all circumstances applied, how the centurion approached, namely through envoys. And indeed, that the centurion did not meet Christ himself in person, the words of Luke 7:7 expressly testify: I did not judge myself worthy to come into your sight. And similar examples are brought forward, Matt. 11:2, 3, Luke 7:19, Matt. 26:18, Mark 12:14, Luke 22:11. Which opinion of Augustine also pleased Bede and Leontius in this place, the blessed D. Aegidius Hunnius, the blessed D. Johann Gerhard, and the blessed D. Johann Ernst Gerhard, Fr. Lucas, Maldonado, and others. And not without merit, because of those things which we have brought forward from Luke, it is preferred to the reconciliation of Chrysostom, Euthymius, Theophylact, Gerson, the Weimar Paraphrase, and the blessed Walther, that the centurion first addressed Christ through envoys, and afterwards met Him himself.

Latin:

Vers. 5. προσῆλθεν αὐτῷ) Sicut Latine convenire ali- quem dicimur etiam per epistolam, ita & προσέρχεσθαι Græ- ce usurpatur citra præsentiam corporis. Sic & Deo προσ- έρχεσθαι dicimur Hebr. IV. 16. VII. 25. X. 22. XI. 6. Et προσέλευσις pro libello supplice sumitur. Quamquam etiamsi proprietas vocis hac in parte non suffragaretur, sufficere deberet illud in jure receptissimum facere nos & quod per alium facimus. Ita & infra XI. 4. Johannes di- xisse dicitur quæ per discipulos nuntiabat. Atque ita hæc

& sequentia exponenda esse non dubito. Nam ut aliam credamus historiam à Luca narrari, tanta circumstantiarum ταυτότης non patitur: neque magis vero simile est post ablegatos ad Christum seniores Judæos & familiares alios, ipsum centurionem venisse ad colloquium Christi, cum eadem plane κατὰ λέξιν Lucas narret per amicos dicta quæ hic adscribuntur centurioni, additque cum rediissent amici, ut legationis suæ eventum renuntiarent jam revaluisse servum. His adde quod Lucas vocem λέγων eandem quæ hic exstat, usurpat de centurione ea commemorans quæ verbis ipsius per alios dicebantur. Et τὸ παρακαλῶν ipse à Centurione allegatis tribuit, quod hic tribuitur centurioni. Est ergo hoc unum ex iis quæ à Matthæo παχύτερον tradita Lucas ἀκριβέστερον exsequi voluit.

Est hæc S. Augustini conciliatio l. II. de Consens. Evang. c. 20. Matthæum brevitati studuisse, Lucam vero plenius & omnibus adhibitis circumstantiis eam descripsisse, quomodo Centurio accesserit, videlicet per Legatos. Et sane non convenisse Centurionem ipsummet αὐτοπροσώπως Christum, verba Luc. VII. 7. diferte perhibent: Non judicavi me dignum, ut in conspectum tuum prodirem. Et adferuntur similia exempla Matth. XI. 2. 3. Luc. VII. 19. Matth. XXVI. 18. Marc. XII. 14. Luc. XXII. 11. Quæ Augustini sententia placuit quoque Bedæ & Leontio in h. l. B. D. Æg. Hunnio, B. D. Joh. Gerhardo, & B. D. Joh. Ern. Gerhardo, Fr. Lucæ, Maldonado & aliis. Nec immerito ob illa, quæ ex Luca adduximus, præsertur Chrysostomi, Euthymii, Theophylacti, Gersonis, Paraphrast Vinariens. & B. Waltheri conciliationi, quod Centurio prius per legatos Christum compellarit, postmodum ipse eum convenerit.

## 8:6
Vers. 6. παῖς us) The custom of the ancients of expressing harsh things softly: Nor do the Hebrews only speak thus, as can be seen in 1 Sam. XXI. 2, 5, 1 Kings XX. 15, Esther II. 2, but also in Aristophanes παῖς and in Terence, Cicero, and Horace, puer signifies a slave. Thus also a master was called the father of the family. Macrobius: Our ancestors, removing all odium from masters and all insult from slaves, called the master the father of the family and the slaves members of the family. See, if you like, Servius on that line of Maro, 'Close the streams now, boys': and Pliny in his letters. Tertullian: The name of piety is more pleasing than that of power: even in a family they are called fathers rather than masters.

βέβληται ἐν τῇ οἰκίᾳ) I interpret βεβλῆσθαι as 'to lie down,' as below concerning the fever-stricken in verse 14, and concerning another whose nerves were likewise relaxed at the beginning of the following chapter. He was lying down, therefore, and as Luke added in this account, with danger of death: wherefore it is credible that παράλυσιν is said here not of a part but of the resolution of the whole body, namely, apoplexy. For Celsus teaches that in his time this was also called παράλυσιν. It is added that physicians call a more vehement apoplexy incurable: which increases the cause for praying and the magnitude of the benefit.

βασανιζόμενος] This word is, like many others, Hellenistic in that sense, which for that reason, as being less Greek, Lucian the Pseudophist blames: but that word does not signify the pain which those struck by the stars lack, but a miserable constitution of the body.

That it cannot be understood as that, but that it was a παράλυσιν properly so called, our blessed Johann Gerhard warns; since that takes away both sense and motion at the same time, whereas this sick man is said to have felt most bitter pains. For that word always implies pains, and those most grave, as is evident from an induction of passages: Mark V. 7, Luke VIII. 28, ch. XVI. 23, 28, 2 Peter II. 8, Rev. IX. 5, ch. XI. 10, ch. XII. 2, ch. XIV. 10, 11, ch. XVIII. 10, 15, ch. XX. But when it occurs concerning an inanimate thing not feeling pain, it nevertheless imports a most grave concussion, such as is altogether that of the waves of the sea, Matthew XIV. 24, Mark VI. 48.

Latin:

Vers. 6. παῖς us) Mos veterum dura molliuer efferendi: Nec Hebræi tantum ita loquuntur, ut videre est 1. Sam. XXI. 2. 5. 1. Reg. xx. 15. Esther. II. 2. sed & Aristophani παῖς & Terentio, Ciceroni, Horatio puer servum significat. Sic & dominus paterfamilias dicebatur. Macrobius: Nostri majores omnem dominis invidiam, omnem servis contumeliam detrahentes, dominum patremfamilias, servos familiares appellaverunt. Vide si libet Servium ad illud Maronis, Claudite jam rivos pueri: & Plinium in epistolis. Tertullianus: Gratius est pietatis nomen quam potestatis: etiam familiæ magis patres quam domini vocantur.

βέβληται ἐν τῇ οἰκίᾳ) βεβλῆσθαι decumbere interpretor, ut infra de febricitante commate 14. & de alio cui nervi itidem resoluti initio capitis sequentis. Decumbebat ergo iste, & quod Lucas in hac historia addidit, cum mortis periculo: quare credibile est παράλυσιν hic dici non partis sed totius corporis resolutionem, ἀποπληξίαν scilicet. Nam suo tempore hanc etiam παράλυσιν dictam docet Celsus. Accedit quod Medici ἀποπληξίαν vehementiorem dicunt insanabilem: quod auget orandi causam, & magnitudinem beneficii.

βασανιζόμενος] Vox hæc est, ut multæ aliæ, isto sensu Hellenistica, quam propterea, ut minus Græcam, culpat Lucianus Pseudopophista: non autem dolorem vox ista significat, quo carent siderari, sed miseram corporis constitutionem.

Non posse eam intelligi, sed παράλυσιν proprie dictam fuisse, B. Joh. Gerhardus noster monet; siquidem illa auferat simul sensum & motum, ægrotus vero hic dicatur, acerbissimos dolores sensisse. Vox enim illa semper dolores, eosque gravissimos infert, ut ex inductione locorum constat Marc. V. 7. Luc. IIX. 28. c. XVI. 23. 28. 2. Petr. II. 8. Apoc. IX. 5. c. XI. 10. c. XII. 2. c. XIV. 10. 11. c. XIIX. 10. 15. c. XX. Cum vero de re inanimata dolores non sentiente occurrit, gravissimam tamen concussionem importat, qualis omnino est fluctuum maris Matth. XIV. 24. Marc. VI. 48.

## 8:8
Vers. 8. ἀποκριθεὶς) By a second embassy, which went out to meet Christ as He was now approaching.

ἑκατόνταρχος) The Romans in Judea, no less than through other parts of their empire in the most important cities, had soldiers for keeping the provincials in their duty. Josephus on Vespasian: 'installing centurions in cities.' In Jerusalem the number was greater under a Tribune and Centurions. In Caesarea, Capharnaum, and other places there were fewer under Centurions, which Roman term the Syrian kept as being commonly very well known.

ὐκ εἰμὶ ἱκανὸς) He knew that he had spent a great part of his life in the worship of false gods and other pollutions of the world. He saw that the Jews, for whose sake he had even taken care to have a synagogue built, abhorred closer contact with him. Moved by these things, he thought of himself as humbly as possible.

εἰπὲ λόγον) The centurion was stirred up by the fame both of those things which were narrated at the end of the fifth chapter, and of the recently healed leprosy: for he had not kept the law of silence, as appears from Mark and Luke. But no one gives credence to such narrations, even if they lean upon valid testimonies, unless he thinks rightly concerning the power of God.

Latin:

Vers. 8. ἀποκριθεὶς) Secunda legatione, quæ Christo jam adventanti obviam procellit.

ἑκατόνταρχος) Romani in Judæa non minus, quam per alias imperii sui partes in potissimis urbibus milites habebant ad continendos in officio provinciales. Jose- phus de Vespasiano: ἐγκαθιστὰς ἑκατοντάρχας πόλεσι. Hie- rosolymis major erat numerus sub Tribuno & Centurio- nibus. Caesareae, Capharnaumi atque aliis in locis pau- ciores erant sub Centurionibus, quam Romanam vocem ut vulgo notissimam Syrus servavit.

ὐκ εἰμὶ ἱκανὸς) Sciebat se magnam vitae partem exegis- se in cultu falsorum deorum & aliis mundi inquinamentis. Videbat Judaeos, in quorum gratiam etiam Synagogam ex- strui curaverat, convictum ipsius propiorem abhorrere. His motus de se quam humillime sentiebat.

εἰπὲ λόγον) Excitavit centurionem fama tum eorum quae fine capitis quinti narrata sunt, tum proxime sanatae viti- liginis: neque enim ille servaverat reticentiae legem ut ex Marco & Luca apparet. Sed talibus narrationibus, etiam- si testimoniis validis nitantur, fidem nemo adhibet, nisi qui de Dei potentia recte sentit.

## 8:9
Vers. 9. καὶ γὰρ ἐγὼ ἄνθρωπός εἰμὶ ὑπὸ ἐξουσίαν, ἔχων ὑπ᾽ ἐμαυτὸν στρατιώτας καὶ λέγω τούτῳ) A Hebraism: 'I am and I say' for 'being, I say.' For the sense is: 'For I also, being a man under authority, having soldiers under me, say to this one.' For I, too, although I am subject to another's power, nevertheless command the soldiers over whom I have power as to what I wish to be done by a word. Similar is that of Paul in Rom. VI. 17: 'But thanks be to God, that you were the slaves of sin, but you obeyed from the heart the form of doctrine to which you were delivered,' for 'that you who were formerly slaves of sin have obeyed.' And not otherwise below XI. 25 and XVIII. 21, as we shall say there. And not far otherwise below XXIII. 15. For it is not blamed in the Pharisees that they make proselytes, but that they corrupt those who are made. The centurion, therefore, silently compares himself, being subject to another's command and endowed with no power except that which is subordinate, to Christ, whom he acknowledges to be endowed with a clearly supreme and most celebrated power. He says, however, that he is 'under authority,' meaning not only of the emperor and the procurator, but also of the tribune. And the word 'authority' is properly taken here, in the way those are called 'those in authority' who command others, and 'authority' is defined as 'power over a free head.' But as for the fact that the centurion here says he is established under command, and in turn has command over others, there is a passage on that matter worthy to be read in the Silvae of Papinius: 'All things are governed by turns, and they press upon one another in turn.' Where he also adds examples, having imitated, as it seems, Philiscus, who, having likewise brought forward examples, had concluded his thought thus: 'But if you look at all things entirely, they are by nature smaller than other greater things; it is necessary for these to serve those always.'

πορευθέντι, καὶ πορεύεται) Without exception, as is the custom of military discipline, which consists not in questioning commands, but in obeying. Therefore, in Tacitus, the soldier is blamed who would rather interpret the commands of leaders than execute them.

Latin:

Vers. 9. καὶ γὰρ ἐγὼ ἄνθρωπός εἰμὶ ὑπὸ ἐξουσίαν, ἔχων ὑπ᾽ ἐμαυτὸν στρατιώτας καὶ λέγω τούτῳ) Hebraismus: εἰμὶ καὶ λέγω pro ὢν λέγω. Sensus enim est: καὶ γὰρ ἐγὼ ἄνθρωπός ὢν ὑπ᾽ ἐξουσίαν, ἔχων δι ὑπ᾽ ἐμαυτὸν στρατιώτας, λέγω τούτῳ. Nam & ego cum sim alienae subditus potestati, tamen militibus, in quos potestatem habeo, verbo quid fieri velim edico. Simile est illud Pauli Rom. VI. 17. χάρις δὲ τῷ Θεῷ, ὅτι ἦτε δῦλοι τῆς ἁμαρτίας, ὑπηκούσατε δὲ ἐκ καρδίας εἰς ὃν παρεδόθητε τύπον δι- δαχῆς pro ὅτι οἱ πρὶν ὄντες δῦλοι τῆς ἁμαρτίας ὑπηκούσατε. Nec aliter infra XI. 25. & XIIX 21, ut ibi dicemus. Nec longe aliter infra XXIII. 15. Neque enim reprehenditur in Pharisaeis quod proselytos faciant, sed quod factos cor- rumpant. Centurio igitur tacite se alieno imperio subdi- tum, nec potestate praeditum, nisi quae esset ὑπάλληλος, Christo comparat, quem plane sumina ac celeberrima po- testate praeditum agnoscit. Ait autem se esse ὑπὸ ἐξουσίαν, ni- mirum non imperatoris tantum & procuratoris, sed & tri- buni. Et proprie hic sumitur vox ἐξουσίας, quomodo οἱ ἐν ἐξουσίαις dicuntur qui aliis imperant, & tutela definitur ἐξυ- σία κατ᾽ ἐλευθέρας κεφαλῆς. Quod autem hic ait Centurio se sub imperio constitutum, in alios vicissim imperium ha- bere, ea de re locus est dignus legi in Papinii silvis: Vice cuncta reguntur Alternisque premunt. Ubi & exempla subjicit, imitatus ut videtur Philiscum, qui allatis itidem exemplis ita concluserat sententiam: Πάντα δ᾽ ἂν σκοπῆς ὅλως Ἑτέρων πέφυκε μειζόνων ἐλάττονα Τέτοις ἀνάγκη Ταῦτα δελεύειν ἀεί.

πορευθέντι, καὶ πορεύεται) Citra exceptionem, ut mos habet disciplinae militaris, quae non sciscitando imperia, sed pa- rendo constat. Ideo apud Tacitum reprehenditur miles qui imperia ducum interpretari mallet quam exsequi.

## 8:10
Vers. 10. Οὐδὲ ἐν τῷ Ἰσραὴλ τοσαύτην πίσιν εὗρον.) 'Faith' in this place signifies a firm persuasion of mind concerning the divine power in Jesus. This, however, was greater in the Roman man than in the Israelites healed before this, because he believed the divine power was sufficiently effective without any contact. See the history which is in 2 Kings IV. 30.

The word 'faith' does not only denote a persuasion concerning divine power, but it involves trust at the same time: just as the centurion did not acknowledge only the power of Christ, but also placed his trust in his favor. Nor indeed do we obtain divine benefits by the mere acknowledgment of divine power, but trust is necessary, without which it is impossible to please God (Heb. XI. 6). Whence Chrysostom joins both here: 'He proceeds, he says, from this induction to weave the supplication of a faithful soul. You therefore, he says, who are the true God, and always possess full authority over your soldiers, use that, I ask, for a little while, and command this disease, by which my boy is detained, that it may leave him and leave him healthy.' Nor is this error of Grotius light indeed: if he thinks so not only concerning the faith of the centurion, by which he obtained health for the boy, but concerning saving faith, by which we obtain the remission of sins and life, and makes it a mere persuasion concerning divine power, as is clear from v. 11, of which he renders this sense: 'just as this foreigner, being persuaded of the divine power in me above the Jews, obtained health for an afflicted body, so many from the Gentiles, fleeing to me with a similar persuasion, will obtain eternal salvation.' But that justifying and saving faith is described far otherwise by Paul, from Rom. III, IV, Gal. II, III, Heb. XI.

and other places of Scripture it is known, for which, besides assent or persuasion, a trustful apprehension of the grace of God exhibited in Christ is altogether necessary. But the discourse here is about such faith, by which the Gentiles obtain salvation, by the interpretation of Grotius himself. Let us hear the Papists themselves, who are sounder here than Grotius. Georgius Cassander in Consult. Art. IV. p. 30: 'For obtaining justification, such faith is required by which a man, after the example of Abraham, does not hesitate at the promise of God through diffidence, but believes against hope in hope: namely, that to him who believes in Him who raised Jesus Christ from the dead, who was delivered for our offenses and rose again for our justification, God will impute this faith for justification, and will not impute sins, and will vivify through the Holy Spirit him who was dead to sin.' An example of this thing is in the healing of bodily diseases, which bears the image of internal healing; for there faith is required by Christ, not by which a man believes that he is already healed, but by which he believes that Christ is endowed with such power that he can heal, and trusts that his goodness is such that he wishes to heal, by which faith they obtained health, but they perceived the health itself already given to them by sense, wherefore for knowing it there was no need of faith. But in internal healing, which is hidden and is known only by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, there is need of faith, by which we assent to this testimony of the Spirit. Ludov. Granat. on the 18th Sunday after Trinity on this text of ours, and from him Cornel. Jansenius in his Commentary on the Concordance. Evang. ch. XXXII. p. 177. it reads thus: When the Savior commends faith, the name faith, which has a varied use and meaning, ought not to be taken simply for credulity and the firm assent to those things which are to be believed concerning God and Christ, such faith as even the demons have. Therefore, it will be said most correctly, as it appears, that the name of faith in the Gospels, when salvation or the attainment of all things that we desire is attributed to it, embraces both, namely, both that firm assent in believing concerning God and Christ, and the confidence conceived from His omnipotent goodness, although in certain places regard seems to be had more to credulity and that assent of the mind, and in others truly to confidence itself. For these two so cohere with one another that neither can confidence exist without credulity, nor can credulity without confidence obtain anything from God.

Latin:

Vers. 10. Οὐδὲ ἐν τῷ Ἰσραὴλ τοσαύτην πίσιν εὗρον.) Πίσις hoc loco firmam de divina in Jesu potentia animi persua- sionem significat. Haec autem in Romano homine major fuit, quam in Israelitis antehac sanatis, quia vim divinam credebat efficacem satis esse sine ullo contactu. Vide hi- storiam quae est 2. Reg. IV. 30.

Non tantum persuasionem de divina potentia notat, sed fiduciam simul involvit vox πίσεως: quemadmodum nec solam potentiam agnovit Christi Centurio, sed etiam in gratiam ejus suam collocavit fiduciam. Neque vero sola divinae potentiae agnitione beneficia divina impetramus, sed opus est fiducia, sine quaDeo placere impossi- bile est Ebr. XI. 6. Unde conjungit utrumque hic Chrysostomus: Pergit autem, inquit, ex hac indu- ctione fidelis animi supplicationem pertexere. Tu ergo, inquiens, qui Deus verus es, plenamque semper in Tuos milites auctoritatem obtines, utere illa rogo tantisper, & praecipe morbo isti, quo puer meus deti- netur, ut illum deserens sanum relinquat. Neq; sane levis hic error est Grotii: siquidem non solum de fide Centurionis, qua sanitatem puero impetravit, sed de fide salvifica, qua nos remissionem peccato- rum & vitam consequimur, ita sentiat, eamque meram persuasionem de divina potentia faciat, ut e v. 11. liquet, cujus hunc reddit sensum: quemad- modum hic ἀλλόφυλος de divina in me potentia su- pra Judaeos persuasus sanitatem corpori afflicto im- petravit, ita ex gentibus plurimi simili persuasione ad me confugientes aeternam salutem consequentur. At longe aliter fidem justificantem & salvificam describi a Paulo, è Rom. III, IV. Gal. II. III. Ebr. XI.

aliisq; Scripturæ locis notum est, ad quam præter affensum, vel persuasionem, fiduciali apprehensione gratiæ Dei in Christo exhibitæ omnino opus est. De tali autem fide hic sermo est, qua gentes salu- tem consequuntur, interprete ipsomet Grotio. Audiamus ipsos Pontificios hic Grotio saniores. Georg. Cassander in Consult. Art. IV. p. 30. Ad ju- stificationem consequendam requiritur talis fides, qua homo exemplo Abrahæ ad promissionem Dei non hæsitet per diffidentiam, sed præter spem in spem credat: Deum videlicet credenti in eum, qui susci- tavit Jesum Christum à mortuis, qui traditus est propter delicta nostra, & resurrexit propter justifi- cationem nostram, imputaturum hanc fidem ad ju- stificationem, & peccata non imputaturum, & eum, qui mortuus erat peccato, per Spiritum S. vivificatu- rum. Hujus rei exemplum est in sanatione corpora- lium morborum, quæ interna sanationis imaginem gerit, ibi enim à Christo requiritur fides, non qua homo credat se jam sanatum, sed qua credat Chri- stum ea potentia præditum, ut sanare possit, & confi- dat eum ejus esse bonitatem, ut sanare velit, qua fide sanitatem consequuti sunt, ipsam vero sanitatem jam sibi donatam sensu perceperunt, quare ad eam cognoscendam fide opus non erat. In sanatione vero interiori, quæ occulta est, solaq; Spiritus S. inspiratio- ne cognoscitur, fide opus est, qua huic Spiritus testi- monio assentiamur. Ludov. Granat. Dominica XIIX. post Trin. in hunc textum nostrum, & ex eo Cornel. Jansenius Comment. in Concord. Evang. c. XXXII. p. 177. ita habent: Cum Salvator fidem commendat, non debet nomen fides, quod varium habet usum & significationem, accipi simpliciter pro credulitate, firmoque assensu eorum, quæ de Deo & Christo credenda sunt, qualem fidem etiam Dæmo- nes habent. Proinde rectissime, ut apparet, dicetur, nomine fidei in Evangeliis, cum ei tribuitur salus aut consecutio omnium, quæ volumus, complecti u- trumque, nempe & assensum illum firmum in cre- dendis de Deo ac Christo, & fiduciam ex illius omni- potente bonitate conceptam, quamvis in quibusdam locis magis videatur haberi respectus ad credulita- tem, & assensum illum mentis, in quibusdam vero ad ipsam fiduciam. Ita enim duo hæc ad invicem co- hærent, ut nec fiducia esse possit sine credulitate, nec credulitas sine fiducia quicquam impetret à Deo.

## 8:11
Vers. 11. πολλοὶ ἀπὸ ἀνατολῶν κὴ δυσμῶν ἥξουσι) The sense is: just as this foreigner, persuaded of the divine power in me above the Jews, obtained health for his afflicted body, so very many from the nations, fleeing to me with a similar persuasion, will attain eternal salvation. In Luke it is fuller: ἀπὸ ἀνατολῶν κὴ δυσμῶν κὴ ἀπὸ βοῤῥᾶ κὴ νότου, in which way the Greeks and Latins also are accustomed to speak whenever they wish to signify all regions of the world: but also the Hebrews, as is evident in Isaiah XLIII. 5, ch. XI. 12, and elsewhere. Moreover, Christ openly looks back to the promise made to Jacob in Genesis XXVIII. 14.

ἀνακλιθήσονται μετὰ Ἀβραὰμ κὴ Ἰσαὰκ κὴ Ἰακὼβ) Intelligible things are accustomed to be described by images of sensible things: thus divine powers are expressed by human limbs: heavenly joy is depicted by the appearance of a banquet. This custom, derived from the most ancient age, provided rich material for storytelling to the Poets, the Talmudists, and Mahomet: we will treat of the custom of reclining below at XXVI. 21. Moreover, the emphasis in this word ἀνακλιθήσονται is to be noted, as if it were said: all the Jews think themselves so holy that they do not wish to take food with a foreigner: but many foreigners will take food with their ancestors, whose names the Jews are accustomed to boast of, with the Jews themselves excluded.

Latin:

Vers. 11. πολλοὶ ἀπὸ ἀνατολῶν κὴ δυσμῶν ἥξουσι) Sensus est: quemadmodum hic ἀλλόφυλος de divina in me po- tentia supra Judæos persuasus sanitatem corpori afflicto impetravit, ita ex gentibus plurimi simili persuasione ad me confugientes æternam salutem consequentur. Apud Lucam est plenius: ἀπὸ ἀνατολῶν κὴ δυσμῶν κὴ ἀπὸ βοῤῥᾶ κὴ νότου, quo modo Græci quoque & Latini loqui solent quo- ties significare volunt omnes orbis regiones: sed & He- bræi ut patet Esaiz XLIII. 5. c. XI. 12. & alibi. Aperte autem respicit Christus promissionem Jacobo factam Ge- nes. XXI X. 14.

ἀνακλιθήσονται μετὰ Ἀβραὰμ κὴ Ἰσαὰκ κὴ Ἰακὼβ) τὰ νοητὰ describi solent imaginibus τῶν αἰσθητῶν: ita virtutes divinæ humanis membris exprimuntur: cœleste gaudium convivii specie depingitur. Qui mos à vetustissima ætate deductus Poëtis & Thalmudistis & Mahumeti uberem fabulandi ma- teriam præbuit: de more discumbendi agemus infra XXVI. 21. Est autem notanda ἔμφασις in hoc verbo ἀνακλιθήσον- ται quasi diceretur: omnes Judæi tam sanctos se existi- mant, ut cum extraneo nolint cibum capere: at multi ex- tranei cum ipsorum majoribus, quorum nomina Judæi so- lent jactare, cibum capient, ipsis Judæis exclusis.

## 8:12
Vers. 12. ὑὸς τῆς βασιλείας) Just as בן מור is for the Hebrews a man of death, ὑὸς θαλάμου he who is admitted into the bridal chamber, so the sons of the kingdom are those to whom, by the privilege of the covenant, the kingdom was destined above others, had they not stood in their own way. See Rom. IX. 4.

Τὸ ἐξώτερον) We have said before that the state of the other life is expressed by the names of places: wherefore τὸ ἐξώτερον σκότος, both here and below at XXII. 13 and XXV. 30, signifies punishments, not just any, but more severe ones, to which, for a fuller designation, weeping and gnashing of teeth is added in all those same places. Moreover, it is a matter in all those places of those by whom the will of GOD was most testified, which kind of men Christ elsewhere declares must be punished with double punishments. Therefore, the status of outer darkness is that which is most remote from heavenly joy, which is accustomed to be called by the name of light. This status is mystically noted in Psalm 49:20. Josephus called it a darker Hades in book III of the Jewish War, just as Aeschylus and other Greeks called it Tartarus beneath Hades: and Statius: Those who hold the undiscovered Tartarus for us, of whom you are the superiors.

The gloom of darkness] Peter and Jude. Thus Salvian somewhere warns certain people that if they despair of being able to become blessed, they should at least devote effort so that they are not burned, so that they are not tortured, and certainly so that they are not cast into the outer darkness. Theophylact follows the same interpretation here.

He takes the phrase concerning the more intense degree of infernal punishment, which is rather to be understood of the punishment of hell itself. This is taught by the parallel passages which are compared by Grotius himself. For in chapter 22:13, concerning the one destitute of a wedding garment, and in chapter 25:30, concerning the lazy servant who had gained nothing from the talent entrusted to him, it is equally applied, whose fault was not as great (in comparison) as that of the Jews who rejected, persecuted, and crucified Christ. Nor does Psalm 49 designate only a more intense degree of punishment, but the infernal punishment itself with the privation of light or joy, v. 20, which they call the punishment of loss as well as gnawing and affliction, and the punishment of sense, v. 15; which sense there is not mystical, but literal. Nor does Peter 2 Ep. 3:12. or Jude verse 13, hint through the gloom of darkness at an accident of infernal punishment, but at the infernal punishment itself, which is described there by different phrases: provided that no sufficient reason for that restriction to more intense degrees of punishment is discovered in the phrase or in the continuity of the text, and that outer darkness is said to be so because they are outside the heavenly light, and as remote as possible from it, and because they are the Lord's horrible and most grave darkness, such as are in no world, and are infernal, even when viewed essentially. For since by outer darkness not only the privation of natural light in that place of darkness (Job 39:19) is designated, but also spiritual gloom, blindness of mind (Eccles. 5:8), and perversity of will, which come to all the damned, why should it be admitted that only the punishments of certain damned ones are indicated here? Wicked men, says Dionysius the Carthusian on 2. Peter 3, walk in this life in the darkness of sins, from there they are precipitated from the darkness of vices into the darkness of torments. And Grotius fosters a certain suspicion here when he praises Salvian, who warns certain people somewhere that if they despair of being able to become blessed, they should at least devote effort so that they are not burned, so that they are not tortured, and certainly so that they are not cast into the outer darkness. For these things, recommended by one who otherwise strenuously acts like a Papist, easily imply that the punishment of loss can have a place without the punishment of sense, and that they are suitable for inducing despair. For if even one person must despair of blessedness, who could be certain of the grace of GOD and heavenly blessedness? On the contrary, GOD does not want anyone, however great his sins may be, to despair, but that the wicked man should turn and live.

Weeping] Isaiah 65:14. Gnashing of teeth] from Psalm 112:10. Go] The Hebrews, when they grant what is requested, are accustomed to say 'go', as in 1 Samuel 17:37, where the LXX have 'go': 2 Samuel 14:8, where others likewise have 'go', they themselves have 'walk'. Thus 'go' is used below in Mark 5:34, 7:29, 10:52; 'go' in Luke 7:50, 8:48, John 4:50 and 8:11. We have said elsewhere that 'go' is sometimes that of one turning away. It is also that of one commanding, as below in 21:28, Mark 6:38, 16:7. Pronunciation distinguished these meanings. Sometimes in that first notion, 'in peace' or something similar was added, as can be seen in some of the places already cited: Nor is there any doubt that the Syrians, whose word the interpreter has here, used it in a similar way, so that it had the force not so much of a verb as of an interjection. The same word is in Ezra 5:15. 'You have believed' that you believed I was able, have the effect. 'In that hour'] Thus the LXX translate 'in that very hour'. Daniel 4:30, where in the Chaldean it is 'at that moment' in that very moment of time: it also occurs below 'from that hour' in the same sense in chapter 15:28, 17:18.

Latin:

Vers. 12. ὑὸς τῆς βασιλείας) Sicut בן מור Hebræis est mortis damnus, ὑὸς θαλάμυ is qui in thalamum admit- titur, ita filii regni sunt quibus ex fœderis privilegio re- gnum præ cæteris destinabatur, nisi ipsi sibi obstitissent. Vide Rom. IX. 4.

Τὸ ἐξώτερον) Locorum nominibus statum vita alterius ex- primi ante diximus: quare τὸ ἐξώτερον σκότος & hic & infra XXII. 13. & XXV. 30. pœnas significat non quaslibet, sed graviores, quibus ad pleniorem notationem omnibus iisdem locis additur fletus & dentium stridor. Agitur autem omnibus istis locis de iis, quibus maxime testata fuit DEI voluntas, quod genus hominum duplis suppliciis puni- endum alibi Christus pronuntiat. Est ergo σκότὸς ἐξώτε- ρος status, qui longissime remotus est a cœlesti gaudio, quod lucis nomine solet appellari. Hunc statum mystice notat Psalmus XLIX. 20. Josephus ᾅδην σκοτιώτερον dixit belli Judaici lib. III. quomodo Æschylo & Græcorum aliis τάρ- ταρος νέρθεν ᾅδου : & Statius: Indeprensa tenent nobis qui tartara, quorum Vos estis superi.

Ζόφον σκότους] Petrus & Judas. Ita Salvianus alicubi monet quosdam, ut si beati fieri posse desperent, certe o- peram dent, ne urantur, ne torqueantur, certe ne in te- nebras exteriores injiciantur. Eandem interpretationem hic sequitur Theophylactus.

De gradu pœnæ infernalis intensiori phrasin ac- cipit, quæ potius de ipsa pœna inferni est intelli- genda. Quod loca parallela, quæ ab ipso Gro- tio conferuntur, docent. Nam cap. XXII. 13. de veste nuptiali destituto, & cap. XXV. 30. de servo pigro, qui talento sibi credito nil lucratus erat, æ- que adhibetur, quorum culpa tanta non fuit (ἐν συγκρίσει) quanta Judæorum Christum rejicien- tium, persequentium, in crucem agentium. Neq; Ps.XLIX. solum gradus intensior supplicii, sed sup- pliciam ipsum infernale designatur cum privatione lucis vel gaudii v.20. qua pœnam damni tam rosio- ne & afflictione, mortis v.15.quam pœnam sensus vo- cant; qui sensus illic non mysticus est, sed literalis. Neque vel Petrus 2. Ep. III. vers.12. vel Judas vers. 13. per ξόφον σκότους accidens infernalis pœnæ, sed pœnam infernalem, quæ illic diversis phrasibus describitur, innuit: siquidem nulla restrictionis istius ad intensiores pœnæ gradus in phrasi, sive in συνεχείᾳ textus ratio sufficiens deprehendatur, & exteriores tenebræ dicantur tam quod extra lucem cœlestem sint, & quam remotissimæ ab ea- dem, Domini quod horrendæ, & gravissimæ te- nebræ, quales nullo in orbe, infernales sint, et- iam ὀυσιωδῶς spectatæ. Quum enim per tene- bras exteriores non privatio solum lucis naturalis in loco illo tenebrarum Job. XXXIX. 19. sed ca- ligo spiritualis, cæcitas mentis Eccles. V. 8. ac per- versitas voluntatis designentur, quæ omnibus damnatis veniunt, cur solum certa damnatorum quorundam supplicia hic indicari,admittendum? Homines flagitiosi, inquit Dionyf. Carthuf. in 2. Petr. III. in hac vita ambulant in tenebris peccato- rum, inde de tenebris vitiorum præcipitantur in tenebras tormentorum. Et fovet hic ὑπόλόν τι Gro- tius, cum Salvianum laudat, alicubi quosdam monentem ut si beati fieri posse desperent, certe ope- ram dent, ne urantur, ne torqueantur, certe ne in exteriores tenebras rejiciantur. Hæc enim ab eo, qui strenue alias Papizat, commendata faci- le id inferunt, quod pœna damni sine pœna sensus locum habere possit, & ad inducendam despera- tionem idonea sint. Si enim vel uni desperan- dum de beatitudine, ecquis de gratia DEI, & beatitudine cœlesti certus esse possit? Ex adverso non vult DEUS, ut ullus, quantacunque ejus sint peccata, desperet, sed ut convertatur impius, & vivat.

κλαυθμὸς] Esaiæ LXV. 14. βρυγμὸς τῶν ὀδόντων} ex Psal. CXII. 10. ὕπαγε] Hebræi cum quod petitur concedunt solent dicere לֶךְ ut 1.Samuel. XVII.37. ubi LXX. habent πορεύου: 2. Samuel. XIV. 8. ubi alii itidem habent πορεύου, ipsi βά- διζε. Sic ὕπαγε usurpatur infra Marci V. 34. VII. 29. X. 52. πορεύου apud Lucam VII. 50. VIII. 48. Johan. IV. 50. & VIII. 11. Diximus alibi ὕπαγε nonnunquam aversantis esse. Est & imperantis, ut infra XXI. 28. Marci VI. 38. XVI. 7. Has significationes destinguebat pronuntiatio. In- terdum in prima illa notione addebatur ἐν εἰρήνῃ vel simi- le aliquid, ut aliquot locis jam citatis videre est: Neque dubium quin Syri זיל quod hic habet interpres, simili modo usurpaverint, ut non tam verbi quam interjectionis vim haberet. Est eadem vox Esdræ V. 15. ἐπίστευσας quod me posse credidisti, effectum habe. ἐν τῇ ὥρᾳ ἐκείνῃ ] Sic αὐτῇ τῇ ὥρᾳ vertunt LXX. Dan. IV. 30. ubi in Chaldaico est בה־ שעתא ipso illo temporis momento: occurrit & infra ἀπὸ τῆς ὥρας ἐκείνης sensu eodem c. XV. 28. XVII. 18.

## 8:14
Verse 14.

Into the house of Peter] Into which Peter and Andrew were accustomed to betake themselves as often as they were in Capernaum. For it is credible that it was the mother-in-law's house, since Peter and Andrew had had a home in Bethsaida before they followed Christ.

Latin:

Vers. 14.

εἰς τὴν οἰκίαν Πέτρου ] In quam Petrus & Andreas quo- ties erant Capharnaumi recipere se solebant. Credibile enim est socrus domum fuisse, cum Petrus & Andreas Bethsaidæ habuissent larem antequam Christum secta- rentur.

## 8:17
Verse 17.

That it might be fulfilled] Just as the deeds of the ancients had the figure of the things of Christ, so also the actions of Christ himself served to denote some things by others. For that the benefit of health restored to bodies bore the figure of the remission of sins and of healed minds cannot be doubted: Therefore the prophecy was fulfilled twice: first when Christ, exhausting himself until evening, labored to relieve the diseases of others, as Matthew shows here: later when, enduring the punishment of the cross, he obtained for us the remission of sins, as Peter teaches in 2 Ep. 2:24. For a comparison of the LXX version, which Peter follows almost step by step, shows that the same passage of Isaiah is looked to by Peter. 'Infirmities'] 'our diseases' quite properly the LXX and Peter 'sins', looking to the second and fuller sense. 'He bore'] Tertullian interprets 'he took away'. But there is in this word, as also in the Hebrew 'to bear' and the similar 'to lift' which the Syrian has placed here, a certain signification of a burden, that is, of trouble: just as what preceded 'he took up' is as if you were to say, he lifted onto his shoulders. The sense is therefore that Christ, in order to remove diseases from men, avoided no labors, however untimely: For that the time is expressed here, and no less in Mark and Luke, as being after the sun had set, has its emphasis, not badly noted by Theophylact. But neither should the other circumstance be omitted, that Christ was almost crushed among these things by the crowd of people coming together, which Mark and Luke thought should be noted when they were relating the history of the healed paralytic. Isaiah also describes, besides death, the many troubles and hardships of Christ in fulfilling his duty. Paul expressed the same force of the word 'to bear' when he said in Romans 15:1, 'To bear the infirmities of the weak', and Galatians 6:2, 'Bear one another's burdens'. This is what it wants, that others should be relieved even with some inconvenience to ourselves. Twice, therefore, was the prophecy of Isaiah fulfilled: first in the healing of diseases, not without trouble to Christ, then much more perfectly in his very death, which took away the diseases of the soul.

Grotius makes a twofold sense of the prophecy of Is. LIII: the first, namely, the more imperfect, and the second or fuller; he wishes חליינו in the second and fuller sense to denote ἁμαρτίας: and he says the prophecy was fulfilled twice, first when Christ, wearying himself, devoted his time until evening to relieving the diseases of others, as he thinks Matthew showed here: later when, enduring the punishment of the cross, he obtained for us the remission of sins, as Peter teaches in 2 Ep. II. 24. But that there can be only one sense of a single passage is a most certain axiom. Which we have sufficiently asserted in the Prolegomena to Genesis. And what is this more imperfect sense? Is it that concerning the relieving of diseases by Christ? Or indeed another, namely, concerning the afflictions to be endured by Jeremiah? Which sense Grotius made of the saying in his annotations on Is. LIII. But just as it was shown in our Vindications that Grotius, Judaizing, very badly twisted the prophecy there to another subject, so he wrongly carves out a peculiar sense here from the word πληρωθῇ, because the fulfillment of some prophecy can be shown in various ways, but different senses are not therefore to be attached to the same one. For it is evident from the result that the prophecy was fulfilled, inasmuch as sins were expiated when the penalty was taken away: in which way Chrysostom understands this passage. To confirm faith in the Evangelical narrative, the Evangelist adds the testimony of the prophetic oracle, citing the passage of Isaiah: which passage, however, where it mentions diseases, designates by that name sins rather than bodily sicknesses. Moreover, because most bodily diseases happen to men as a punishment for sins, Matthew rightly referred the Prophet's saying even to bodily diseases. The interpretation of Apollinarius also went in this direction. Isaiah referred that saying of his to the cross. Matthew, however, referred it to the healings of diseases. He did this, however, because the very passion of the Savior and healing for men. And it is sufficiently certain that by his death life was bought and prepared for us. Which are far more suitable than if, with Grotius, one were to drag Isaiah's saying to labors and to the troubles in overcoming diseases, and imagine a twofold fulfillment, first in the healing of diseases not without Christ's trouble, then much more perfectly in his very death, by which he took away the diseases of the soul: for those troubles were neither untimely for Christ, nor ever unwelcome or even burdensome, because a great number of sick people flocked to him to be healed, even though he was almost crushed by the crowd of people coming together, but we have spoken more fully about the sense of the prophecy in the place cited.

Latin:

Vers. 17.

ὅπως πληρωθῇ ] Sicut veterum res gestæ rerum Christi figuram habuerunt, ita & ipsius Christi actiones aliæ aliis denotandis inservierunt. Nam beneficium corporibus redditæ sanitatis quin figuram remissionis peccatorum & sanatarum mentium tulerit, dubitari non potest: Bis ergo impletum est vaticinium: prius cum Christus semet defa- tigans ad vesperam usque aliorum morbis levandis va a- vit, ut hic ostendit Matthæus: posterius cum crucis sup- plicium perferens remissionem peccatorum nobis impe- travit, ut docet Petrus 2. Ep. II. 24. Nam eundem locum Esaiæ à Petro respici docet collatio versionis LXX. quam ferme κατὰ πόδας Petrus sequitur. ἀσθενείας ] חליינו proprie admodum LXX. & Petrus ἁμαρτίας, respicientes sensum secundum ac pleniorem. ἐβάστασεν ] Abstulit interpretatur Tertullianus. Sed est in hac voce ut & in Hebræa סבל & ei simili נשא quam hic Syrus posuit oneris quædam, id est molestiæ, signifi- catio: sicut & quod præcessit ἀνέλαβε est quasi dicas, in humeros sustulit. Sensus est ergo, Christum ut morbos hominibus demeret, nullos labores quantumvis intempe- stivos defugisse: Nam quod hic, neque minus apud Mar- cum & Lucam, tempus exprimitur post Solem occasum ha- bere suam ἔμφασιν non male à Theophylacto notatum est. Sed neque altera circumstantia omittenda est quod Chri- stus inter hæc pene oblisus sit hominum concurrentium turba, quod Marcus & Lucas annotandum putaverunt, cum paralytici sanati historiam referrent. Sa e Esa as etiam præter mortem, molestias ærumnasque multas Christi in obeundo munere describit. Eandem vim ver- bi סבל Paulus expressit cum dixit Rom. XV. 1. Τὰ ἀσθενήματα τῶν ἀδυνάτων βαστάζειν, & Gal. VI. 2. Ἀλλή- λων βάρη βαστάζετε. Hoc e um vult, sublevandos alios etiam cum nostro aliquo incommodo. Bis igitur imple- tum est Esaiæ vaticinium, primum in morborum sanatio- ne, non sine Christi molestia, deinde multo perfectius in ipsa morte, quæ animi morbos sustulit.

Geminum facit Grotius Vaticinii Es. LIII. sensum: primum, nempe ac imperfectiorem, &; secundum vel pleniorem, חליינו sensu secundo & pleniori ἁμαρτίας notare vult: ac bis impletum va- ticinium ait, prius cum Christus semet defatigans ad vesperam usque aliorum morbis levandis vaca- rit, ut hic ostendisse Matthæum putat: posterius cum crucis supplicium perferens remissionem pec- catorum nobis impetravit, ut docet Petrus 2. Ep. II. 24. Ast unius loci non posse nisi unicum esse sensum, ἀξίωμα est certissimum. Quod in Pro- legomen. ad Genes. affatim asseruimus. Et quis hic sensus imperfectior? An ille de levandis morbis per Christum? An vero alius, de afflictionibus nempe à Jeremia exantlandis? quem sensum fe- cit dicti Grotius in annot. ad Es. LIII. sed uti pessime ad aliud subjectum ibi detorsisse vatici- nium Judaizantem Grotium ostensum in vindi- ciis nostris fuit, sic perperam sensum peculiarem exsculpit h. l. è verbo πληρωθῇ, quia comple- mentum alicujus vaticinii potest variis modis do- ceri, non autem ideo varii eidem affingendi sen- sus sunt. Nam impletum esse vaticinium etiam à posteriori constat, utpote expiata esse peccata, cum pœna aufertur: quo pacto intelligit Chrysost. hunc locum. Ad confirmandam fidem narrationi Evan- gelicæ prophetici oraculi testimonium adjungit Ev- angelista, Esaiæ locum adducens: qui tamen locus ubi morborum meminit, isto nomine peccata potius, quam corporis ægritudines designat. Cæterum quia plerique morborum corporis in pœnam peccatorum hominibus contingunt, merito Prophetæ dictum etiam ad corporeos morbos Matthæus retulit. Quo etiam abiit interpretatio Apollinarii. Efaias ad crucem dictum istud suum retulit. Matthæus vero ad morbo- rum curationes. Hoc autem fecit, quia ipsa passio Salvatoris nihil fuit aliud, nisi medicina, ac curatio hominum. Ac satis constat ejus morte nobis emptam & paratam esse vitam.
