Quæ longe convenientio- ra sunt, quam si cum Grotio ad labores dictum E- saiæ trahatur, & ad molestias in morbis profligan- dis, geminumque fingatur complementum, primum in morborum sanatione non sine Christi molestia, deinde multo perfectius in ipsa morte, qua animi morbos sustulit: illæ enim molestiæ nec intempe- stivæ fuêre Christo, nec ingratæ unquam aut et- iam graves, quod magno numero ad ipsum con- fluxerint ægroti, ut sanarentur, etsi pene oblisus hominum concurrentium turba fuerit, sed de sen- su vaticinii diximus uberius l. c.

## 8:18
Verse 18.

He commanded to depart to the other side] There is an ellipsis for he commanded to prepare everything for the departure. For when he was in the boat, only then did he command himself to be carried across.

Latin:

Vers. 18.

Ἐκέλευσε ἀπελθεῖν εἰς τὸ πέραν] Est ἔλλειψις pro ἐκέ- λευσε πάντα ἑτοιμάσαι εἰς τὸ ἀπελθεῖν. Nam in navi cum esset, tum demum jussit se transvehi.

## 8:19
Verse 19.

I will follow you wherever you go] This man was a lawyer, such as most of that age were, eager for honors and gain: wherefore, since he thought that great power would soon be present to Christ, who was performing so many miracles, he wished to profess his sect. But Christ, professing his own poverty, touched the very sore of the man.

Latin:

Vers. 19.

ἀκολουθήσω σοι ὅπου ἐὰν ἀπέρχῃ] Erat hic legisperitus, quales plerique ejus ævi, honorum & lucri studiosus: qua- re cum magnam Christo tot miracula edenti potentiam brevi adfuturam opinaretur, sectam ejus profiteri voluit. Sed Christus paupertatem suam profitens, ipsum homi- nis ulcus tetigit.

## 8:20
Verse 20.

Foxes have holes] There is in this comparison a sharpness which Plutarch observes in that similar one of Tiberius Gracchus: The wild beasts roaming Italy have a hole, and each of them has a lair and hiding places, but those who fight and die for Italy have a share of air and light, and nothing else, but wander homeless and unsettled with their children.

Nests] I do not think anyone who has inspected the passages below at XIII. 32, Mark IV. 32, and Luke XIII. 19 will doubt that this word pertains to the branches of trees.

And the Son of man] Pagans and sectarians have objected to Christians this title, as if it were contrary to the virginal birth: how the ancients solved this can be seen in the author of the responses to the Orthodox. But it was most simple to say what Justin said to Trypho: We know the fathers of children born to their daughters to be the progenitors of the females. But since Christ is never called by this name except by himself, another reason for this word must be sought. It must be known, therefore, that בן אדם and בן אנוש most often designate for the Hebrews a man of despised status. It is clear that בן אדם is taken in this way in Judges XVI. 7, 11 and Psalm XXII. 7, nor do the ancient Hebrews interpret בנות האדם in Genesis VI. 2 otherwise, to which are opposed בני האלהים, that is, בני הארי תנים, sons of heroes, or as the Greeks after the LXX translated, of the powerful, as the Chaldean also translates, in the way the Hebrews were accustomed to call those ten pious fathers of the first age. Thus also in Psalm XLIX. 3, בני אדם are opposed to those who are called there בני איש, where the LXX translated בני אדם as earth-born, that is, ignoble, whom the Latins also called sons of the Earth. Thus Ezekiel, Daniel, and Zechariah, when dealing with Angels, are reminded of their fragility by the title Son of man: that this signifies vileness has been noted also by Jacchiades on Daniel X. 16. Nor is אנוש to be taken otherwise in Daniel VII. 13, where it treats of the Messiah. For he says that to him who seemed the son of man, that is, of despised status, royal power was given. Christ therefore described with this word that emptying of his which is treated in Philippians II. 7. Nor is this ὁ ὑὸς τῶ ἀνθρώπω anything other than what is in Isaiah LIII. 3: נבזה וחדל אישים.

He has not where to lay his head] Christ shows himself so removed from a wealthier fortune that he does not even have a house of his own. He lived, therefore, in Capharnaum in a rented place, or stayed with his disciples. See above at verse 14.

Grotius does not poorly render Justin’s response from the Dialogue with Trypho to Pagans and Sectarians who object to this title of 'son of man' as if it were contrary to a virginal birth: Καὶ γὰρ πατέρας τῶν γενομένων, ταῖς θυγατράσιν ἀυτῶν τέκνων, τὰς τῶν θηλειῶν γεννήτορας ἐπιγινώμεθα. For we acknowledge the fathers of those born to their daughters to be the progenitors of the females. That he believed another reason for this oracle should be sought, however, because Christ is never called this way except by himself, and made this the reason, that the Hebrews very often designate a man of despised status in this way, in that he does not deserve assent. For it is not simply true that he alone calls himself so, because he is also so called by John in Apocalypse ch. 1 and 14, and by Daniel ch. 7:14. He is so called: and those passages in which he is called by this name sufficiently show that his kenosis is not being referred to, since it is not a matter of his despised status, but rather of his glory: and he is said to be like the son of man, as he was seen in divine majesty, Apoc. 1:13, ch. 14:14. The same must be held regarding the passage in Dan. 7, where the son of man, whom Grotius here acknowledges as Christ—though in his annotations on Daniel he dreamed it was the Roman people—certainly does not appear before the Ancient of Days in the clouds of heaven in a servile or perhaps despised form. Add also the passage in Ezek. 1:26, and likewise Ps. 8:6, where 'son of man' and 'man' are taken as equivalent. Finally, not all the examples that Grotius brought forward for this meaning are sufficiently consistent. For in Judg. 17:7, 11, it is by no means clear that איש־אחד denotes a man of despised status, since any man is indicated, not one endowed with an extraordinary gift of heroic fortitude. In Gen. 6:2, the 'sons of men' are not contrasted with the sons of commoners as sons of heroes, but the descendants of Cain with the sons of the holy Patriarchs. See what we have said on that passage. We do not deny that the expression is used that way in some places, especially Ps. 49:3, but we do not admit that Christ used it of himself in that sense: since by common Hebraism 'son of man' is the same as 'man,' just as 'sons of the Greeks' are Greeks in Joel 3:6, and παῖδες ἰατρῶν 'sons of physicians' are called physicians, etc., with the agreement of the blessed Glassius, book 3, Phil. 8, p. 137. Furthermore, Clichtoveus, Rosfensis, and Bundlerus only wrongly prove monastic poverty from this passage: because Christ willed to be poor for our sake, that he might enrich us, 2 Cor. 8:9, which does not befit monks. Nor does John XXII in Extravag. de Verb. signif. admit that Christ imposed poverty on the Apostles, or that it was accepted by them under a vow; indeed, he calls that doctrine pestiferous, erroneous, and condemned, condemning Nicholas himself, the Roman Pontiff, for it. Naturally, because it does not accord with the Patrimony of Peter, the palaces, and the riches of the Roman Pontiff: to whom you may not undeservedly sing that line of Jerome, Epist. 1 to Heliodorus: 'The Son of man has nowhere to lay his head, and you measure out ample porticoes and huge spaces of buildings!' Expecting the inheritance of the world, he will not be able to be a co-heir of Christ.

Latin:

Vers. 20.

αἱ ἀλώπεκες φωλεὺς ἔχουσι] Est in hac comparatione δεινότης quam Plutarchus observat in simili illa Tiberii Gracchi: τὰ μὲν θηρία τὴν Ἰταλίαν νεμόμενα κὴ φωλεὸν ἔχει, καὶ κοιταῖόν ἐσιν ἀυτῶν ἑκάστῳ κὴ καταδύσεις τοῖς δὲ ὑπὲρ τῆς Ἰταλίας μαχομένοις κὴ ἀποθνήσκουσιν ἀέρος καὶ φωτὸς, ἄλλου δὲ ὐδενὸς μέτεστιν, ἀλλ᾽ ἄοικοι καὶ ἀνίδρυτοι μετὰ τέκνων πλα- νῶνται.

κατασκηνώσεις] Quin vox hæc ad arborum ramos per- tineat dubitaturum non puto qui loca infra XIII. 32. Marc. IV. 32. & Lucæ XIII. 19 inspexerit.

ὁ δὲ ὑὸς τῶ ἀνθρώπω] Objecerunt Christianis pagani & sectarii hanc appellationem, quasi virginali partui contra- riam: quod quomodo solverint veteres videre est apud Scriptorem responsionum ad Orthodoxos. Simplicissimum autem erat id dicere quod Tryphoni dixit Justinus: πατέ- ρας τῶν γενομένων ταῖς θυγατράσιν ἀυτῶν τέκνων τὰς τῶν θη- λειῶν γεννήτορας ἐπισάμεθα. Sed cum Christus nunquam hoc modo nisi a seipso appelletur, quærenda est alia vocabuli hujus ratio. Sciendum igitur בן אדם & בן אנוש He- bræis sæpissime designare hominem contemtæ fortis. Palam est בן אדם ita sumi Jud. XVI. 7. 11. & Psal. XXII. 7. nec ali- ter בנות האדם Gen. VI. 2. veteres Hebræi inter- pretantur, quibus opponuntur בני האלהים id est בני הארי תנים υἱοὶ τῶν ἡρώων, aut ut Græci post LXX. ver- terunt τῶν δυνασευόντων, ut & Chaldæus vertit, quomodo decem illos primæ ætatis pios patres appellare solebant He- bræi. Sic & in Psalmo XLIX. 3. opponuntur בני אדם iis qui ibidem dicuntur בני איש ubi בני אדם LXX. ver- terunt γηγενεῖς id est ignobiles, quos & Latini Terræ filios vocabant. Sic Ezechiel, Daniel, Zacharias cum Angelis versantes appellatione filii hominis suæ fragilitatis admo- nentur: quo significari vilitatem notatum & Jacchiadæ ad Dan. X. 16. Neque aliter אנוש accipiendum apud Danie- lem VII. 13. ubi de Messia agitur. Dicit enim ei qui filius hominis, hoc est contemtæ fortis videbatur, datam esse regiam potestatem. Descripsit ergo hac voce Christus suam illam κένωσιν de qua agitur Philipp. II. 7. Nec aliud est hic ὁ ὑὸς τῶ ἀνθρώπω, quam apud Esaiam LIII. 3. נבזה וחדל אישים:

ἐκ ἔχει πῶ τὴν κεφαλὴν κλίνῃ] Adeo se remotum a di- vitiore fortuna Christus ostendit, ut ne domum quidem habeat propriam. Habitavit ergo Capharnaumi in condu- cto, aut divertit apud discipulos. Vide supra commate 14.

Non male Grotius Paganis & Sectariis, hanc fi- lii hominis appellationem quasi partui virginali contrariam objicientibus, Justini responsum e Dia- logo cum Tryph. reddit: Καὶ γὰρ πατέρας τῶν γενομένων, ταῖς θυγατράσιν ἀυτῶν τέκνων, τὰς τῶν θηλειῶν γεννήτορας ἐπιγινώμεθα. Eorum siquidem qui filiabus gignuntur liberorum, Patres fæmina- rum genitores novimus. Quod autem oraculi hu- jus rationem aliam ideo quærendam credidit, quia Christus nunquam hoc modo nisi à seipso appellatur, eamque hanc fecit, quod Hebræi sapif- sime ita designent hominem contemtæ fortis, in eo assensum non meretur. Nam neque id verum sim- pliciter est, quod solum ipse se ita appellet, quia & à Johanne in Apocalypsic. I. & XIV. & à Daniele cap. VII. 14. Sic vocatus est: & κένωσιν ejus hoc vo- cabulo non respici, ea loca satis docent, in quibus isto nomine vocatur, cum non de contemtæ e- jusdem sorte, sed potius de gloria ejus agitur: ac similis filio hominum dicitur, uti in divina majestate conspectus est, Apoc. I. 13. cap. XIV. 14. Quod de loco Dan. VII. pariter habendum, ubi filius hominis, quem hic agnoscit Grotius Chri- stum; in annot. vero ad Daniel. populum Romanum esse somniavit, certe non apparet coram antiquo dierum in nubibus cœli in forma servili, vel forte contemta. Adde etiam locum Ezech. I. 26. nec non Psal. VIII. 6. ubi filius hominis, & homo κατ’ ἰσοδυναμίαν accipiuntur. Denique nec satis con- veniunt exempla omnia, quæ adduxit Grotius huic significationi. Nam Jud. XVII. 7. 11. minime palam est איש־אחד hominem contemtæ fortis notare, quum quilibet homo indicetur, non præditus ex- traordinario fortitudinis heroicæ dono Gen. VI. 2. non filii hominum vulgarium filiis heroum op- ponuntur, sed posteri Caini filiis sanctorum Patri- archarum. Vid. quæ ad illum locum diximus. Non negamus, alicubi eam loquutionem ita usur- pari, inprimis Psal. XLIX: 3. sed Christum eo sen- su de se adhibuisse, non admittimus: quum usitato Hebraïsmo potius filius hominis idem sit, quod ho- mo, quemadmodum filii Græcorum Græci Joel. III. 6. παῖδες ἰατρῶν filii medicorum medici dicuntur &c. annuente B. Glassio l. III. Phil. 8. p. 137. Cæ- terum non nisi perperam Cblichtoveus, Rosfensis & Bundlerus ex h. l. Monasticam paupertatem pro- bant: quia Christus nostri causa pauper esse vo- luit, ut nos ditaret, 2. Corinth. VIII. 9. quod Mo- nachis non convenit. Neque admittit Johannes XXII. Extravag. de Verb. signif. Christum pauper- tatem imposuisse Apostolis, aut sub voto eam ipsis fuisse receptam, imo doctrinam eam pestiferam, erroneam, & damnatam dicit, Nicolaum ipsum P. R. ideo damnans. Nimirum quia non convenit ea cum Patrimonio Petri, Palatiis & divitiis Pon- tificis Romani: Cui illud Hieronymi Epist. I. ad Heliodor. non immerito occinas: Filius hominis non habet ubi caput reclinet, & tu amplas porticus, & ingentia tectorum spatia metiris! Hæreditatem expectans seculi, Christi cohæres esse non poterit.

## 8:21
Verse 21.

Τῶν μαθητῶν] Clement of Alexandria teaches us from ancient tradition that this was Philip. Θάψαι] That is, to be present with my father until I perform the final duty for him. See Tobit 8:14. He thought that after his father's death he would be a follower of Christ and would drink in his precepts soon enough. Christ shows that nothing is to be preferred to the hearing of his sermons, but that the opportunity for learning is to be seized with both hands. For the greatest matter is at stake, the attainment or loss of eternal life. 'Even to bury a father was slow for faith,' says Tertullian in his book On Idolatry.

Latin:

Vers. 21.

Τῶν μαθητῶν] Philippum hunc fuisse docet nos Cle- mens Alexandrinus ex antiqua traditione. Θάψαι] Id est eousque patri adesse donec ei faciam supremum officium. Vide Tobiæ VIII. 14. Satis mature post patris mortem putabat se Christi sectatorem fore, & præcepta ejus hausurum. Christus ostendit auditioni ser- monum suorum nihil esse antehabendum, sed rapiendam ambabus manibus discendi occasionem. Agi enim rem maximam, consecutionem aut jacturam vitæ æternæ. Etiam sepelire patrem tardum erat fidei, ait Tertullianus libro de Idololatria.

## 8:22
Verse 22.

Ἄφες τὺς νεκρὺς θάψαι τὺς ἑαυτῶν νεκρὺς] Christ was accustomed to take the occasion for his maxims from obvious things. Thus, when the man called by him had excused himself with the duty of burial, Christ recalled to him and to others both the law and the spiritual sense of the law. The law had been prescribed to the High Priest, and then to the Nazirite, in Lev. 20 and Num. 6, not to attend the funerals of even the closest relatives. For a body bereft of soul, as Philo explains, without the τῶν ἐν ἡμῖν ὄν-

world, signifies all those things which are corporeal and pertain in no way to the soul. Those who serve God ought to withdraw themselves from the care of these things. Now, indeed, Christian priests are called Nazarites: to them, therefore, and among them particularly to the heralds of the Gospel, that precept understood spiritually especially pertains. Philo on the Priest: 'For which reason let him remain undefiled, not touching a dead body, so that he may be ready to perform the prayers and sacrifices on behalf of the world at the proper times without hindrance; for it is otherwise a reproach to God, and one who has become a leader of the sacred order ought to be alienated from all things in generation, not being so overcome by the thoughts of parents, children, or brothers as to pass over or postpone (this is properly what is at issue here) any of the things that exist, which it is better to do immediately.' There is, however, in this saying of Christ a learned allusion to the double meaning of the word dead. For the dead are properly called corpses themselves, as in the latter part of the saying, through which, however, as we have said, all things not pertaining to the soul must be understood: but improperly, men alienated from true discipline, which is the life of the soul. 'For in the barbarian philosophy,' says Clement, 'they call those dead who have fallen away from the doctrines and have subjected the mind to psychic passions.' Philo defines death as a punishment, 'when the soul dies the life of virtue, but lives that of vice.' And elsewhere: 'The wretched are dead in their souls'; and many things to that effect occur among Hebrew and Arabian writers. Pythagoras drew this also, as other things, from the philosophy of the East: 'imitating the opinions of the Jews,' as Hermippus wrote about him; since indeed 'he also arrived at the Hebrews,' as Malchus writes about him from Diogenes: whence the custom arose that for those who were cast out of the assembly of the Pythagoreans, cenotaphs were built, which we read was done for a certain Hipparchus. Arrian to Epictetus: IV. 5. 'Then the modest part is deadened.' The sense, therefore, of Christ's words is: that the care of corporeal things should be put before the cultivation of the soul by those for whom the soul would become dull and sluggish. There are also two other laws among Moses which have a somewhat similar meaning: for those who were neither priests nor bound by a vow were not forbidden to touch a corpse, but if they had touched one, they were for some time impure and to be purified with water. Then all Jews were forbidden to eat the flesh of an animal that had died by its own fate: such institutions are to be observed even outside the Jewish commonwealth. For mention of the former is in Euripides: 'But I blame the sophistries of the goddess, who, if any of mortals touches slaughter, or childbirth, or touches a corpse with their hands, bars them from the altars.' In the books of Chrysippus it was: 'To proceed from a bed or death to a temple is irrationally forbidden.' In the sentences of Calpurnius: 'Religion is more polluted by a priest who is funereal than by a dead one.' Among Tacitus: 'Nor ought an Emperor, endowed with the augurate and most ancient ceremonies, to have handled funeral rites.' In which places it can be seen that men were also defiled by the contact of women in childbirth: which the law of Moses also prescribes, it being uncertain whether, like certain other things, it was also used in customs before, so that these things might seem to have proceeded from the children of Noah. We have Hierocles as a witness for the other, who among the precepts of Pythagoras includes 'abstaining from things that died,' by which he says his disciples were called away from the care of mortal things. Porphyry also mentions this custom in his Epistle to Anebo: and Aelian in book IV.

St. Ambrose, book VII on Luke, ch. 9, says very well: 'The burial of a paternal funeral is forbidden, so that you may understand that human things are to be postponed to divine ones. A good study, but a greater impediment. For he who divides his study, weakens his affection: he who divides his care, delays his progress.' But above all, Blessed Gerhard interprets these things concerning those who are dead in sins, Book on Death §. 19.

## 8:26
Vers. 26.

ὀλιγόπιστοι] They ought to have trusted that they, while they were accompanying Christ, were under the special protection of God: because that was consistent with divine goodness. Christ therefore shows that δειλία, that is, that trembling fear which moved the soul from its seat, is the offspring of τῆς ὀλιγοπιστίας. Indeed, as Varro once said, God is revered by the religious, but feared by the superstitious, namely with an anxious fear, a noble example of which we have in that man who sought the most hidden shelters at any sound of thunder. On the contrary, it is true what Aristotle, among others, had said, that those who judge rightly about divine things have a brave and lofty spirit.

ὀλιγόπιστοι] Confidere debuerant, se, dum Christum comitabantur, in peculiari esse Dei tutela: quia id divinæ bonitati erat consentaneum. Ostendit ergo Christus δειλίαν, hoc est, trepidam illam formidinem, quæ de sede sua ani- mum dimovebat, prolem esse τῆς ὀλιγοπιστίας. Nimirum, ut Varro olim dicebat, Deus à religioso veretur, à superstitio- so timetur, anxio scilicet metu, cujus exemplum nobile habemus in illo, qui ad quemvis tonitrus sonum abditissi- mas latebras quærebat. Contra verum est quod Aristote- les aliorumsum tamen dixerat, habere cur forti celsóque sint animo qui de rebus divinis recte judicant.

## 8:27
Vers. 27.

Ὅτι κὶ οἱ ἄνεμοι κὶ ἡ θάλασσα ὑπακύουσιν αὐτῷ ] They begin to suspect something greater than human magnitude in Christ. For it is an epithet of God in Psalm LXV. 8, משביח שאון ימים, stilling the roaring of the seas. Add Psalm CVII. 25. Not only something greater than human magnitude, but a truly divine and infinite power, since this is proper to divine power, and an epithet of GOD, as Grotius does not deny here on Psalm LXV. 8 and CVII. 25. Nor do they only begin to suspect, but they testify and profess that they believe, even if they are carried away into wonder that such power has been granted to a man; because they did not yet sufficiently understand the article concerning the God-man Messiah: they did not yet know the power of the Savior, as Jerome says, as was indeed fitting. Eleganter Chrysostomus: just as in Christ there was a twofold nature, one showing itself outwardly as human, the other divine lying hidden within, but occasionally flashing forth through the performance of miracles, so the minds of the disciples were tossed, fluctuating between alternating turns of faith and infidelity, and the one whom they felt by the judgments of their senses to be only a man, they soon acknowledged by the obedience of the elements to be greater than a man.

## 8:28
Vers. 28.

Τῶν γεργεσηνῶν] From the remnants of the Canaanites. ἐκ τῶν μνημείων ] Theophylact thinks that the dogma prevailed at that time that the souls of dead men become demons. But to me it is more likely that it was believed by many that the souls of the dead linger around corpses and are in the power of demons. For even now the Jews hand down such things, and formerly they relied on the story of the Pythoness raising Samuel for Saul to prove it: which opinion also flowed to the Christians, as can be seen in the dialogue of Justin with Trypho. Therefore, so that the devils might foster this opinion and necromancy in the minds of men, they spent much time in the tombs and fashioned many phantoms in the likeness of dead men.

Mihi vero similius est creditum a multis animas mortuo- rum circa cadavera hærere, & in dæmonum esse potestate. Nam & nunc Judæi talia tradunt, & olim ei probando his- storia Pythonissæ Samuelem Sauli excitantis adutebantur: quæ opinio ad Christianos etiam manavit, ut videre est in colloquio Justini cum Tryphone. Hanc ergo opinionem κὶ τὴν νεκρομαντείαν ut in animis hominum foverent diaboli, multum in sepulchretis versati sunt, ac pleraque φάσματα ad hominum mortuorum instar effinxerunt.

## 8:29
Vers. 29.

Τί ἡμῖν κὶ σοὶ] If you interpret this according to the usage of the Latin language, it seems to introduce contempt. For thus the Latins say: What is it to you with me? But to the Hebrews it means something else: namely, why do you cause me trouble? Which clearly appears in 2 Samuel XVI. 10 and 2 Chronicles XXXV. 21. Nor do I take what is in Joel III. 4 otherwise. For God denies that He gave the Tyrians or Sidonians any reason why they should be hostile to His people. And in almost the same sense the Scythians use this form of speech in Curtius: What is it to us with you? We have never touched your land. Πρὸ καιρῦ] Before that day of judgment for which the impure spirits know they are being kept, 2 Peter II. 4, Jude verse 6. Βασανίσαι] When the wicked are not allowed to do injury, they think they are receiving an injury. This is to be sent into the abyss. See what is said on Luke. Quanquam enim Torturæ expertes jam non sint: yet a more severe judgment is still to be expected by them, and they not only know this, but they testify here that they know Christ is the judge. For this prayer of the demons, as Apollinarius holds, is by no means that of ignorant prophetic oracles. From that, indeed, they had a clear view that Christ was to come into the world through the incarnation; and would return again at the consummation of all things, at which final time alone He was to judge them.

## 8:31
Verse 31.

permit us] So also Mark: Jesus immediately permitted them. Luke also uses the same word twice, both in expressing the request of the demons, and in narrating

by Christ's deed. Wherefore, since Mark also calls this very thing πέμπειν εἰς τοὺς χοίρους [to send into the swine], it appears most true that by active verbs often nothing else is indicated than a permission, especially one that is wise and provident. See the passages Gen. XX. 6. XXXI. 7. Exod. III. 19. XII. 29. Ps. XVI. 10. Act. II. 27. To cast the devil out of a man was Christ's action; for them to go into the swine, there was no need of any action by Christ; for the devils themselves desired this, and they were able to effect that very thing by their own native powers, provided they were not hindered by a greater force. Therefore, Christ did not exert an acting force in this matter, but withheld a force capable of hindering: for reasons undoubtedly great. As appears from Josephus, Jewish men mixed with Greeks lived in those places; it was the custom of the Greeks to mock Jewish institutions, and especially abstinence from swine's flesh, as an empty figment of human superstition. That saying of Juvenal is well known: 'Nor do they think swine's flesh differs from human flesh.' But long before, the comic poet Anaxandrides had said: 'You do not eat swine, but I delight in them.' And Plato the comic poet likewise: 'For of the four-footed beasts, we ought to kill none henceforth except swine; for their meat is most sweet, and nothing comes from a pig except bristles and mud and noise.' Nor is the sentiment of a certain person in Plutarch different, who said that the Jews abstain from that food which was the most just of all. And for the same reason, Aesop said that of every kind of living creature, swine utter the greatest cry when dragged, because they know they are of no use except when dying. Thus also Caligula, with a sneer, asked the Alexandrian Jews: 'Why do you abstain from swine's flesh?' And when they mentioned the various institutions of various nations, and that among others there were those who did not even eat lamb, 'Deservedly,' he said, 'for it is not so sweet.' Some also, as the same Plutarch notes, thought that the Jews were held by a certain veneration for that animal, which Persius also seems to have intended when he says: 'And ancient clemency indulges the old pigs.' Others conjectured other causes, like those from whom Tacitus drew this: 'They abstain from swine in memory of the plague, because scabies had once defiled them, to which that animal is prone.' Christ, therefore, by permitting the demons to rush into the swine, showed the Greeks that the religion of the Jews was by God's precept, and at the same time warned the Jews, who were adapting themselves too much to the customs of the Greeks, against the constitution made by their ancestors in the times of Hyrcanus as a hedge for the law, that it should be lawful for no one to raise a pig, concerning the mystical sense of the law: signifying that men who wallow in foul pleasures after the manner of swine are most displeasing to God and are slaves of the devil. Barnabas the Apostle: 'Do not be like those who, while appearing to fear the Lord, sin like the swine; for when hungry it cries out; but when full, it does not recognize its master.' Philo: 'The lawgiver very beautifully compares those who live in this way to the race of swine, not because of any clean or pure life, but because of a muddy and pit-like life, and one that wallows in the foulest things.' The same author elsewhere says that those who abandon themselves to gluttony and drink 'rejoice in wallowing in the mire after the manner of a swine': to which should be compared what we read in 2 Pet. II. 22. The same mystical interpretation of the law concerning not eating swine's flesh, received either from Philo or from the tradition of the Apostles, is beautifully explained by Lactantius in book IV of his Institutions, chapter XVII. The prohibition of swine's flesh also looks to the same end, from which, when God ordered them to abstain, he especially wished it to be understood that they should abstain from sins and impurities. For this animal is muddy and unclean, and never looks up to heaven, but is cast down upon the earth with both body and mouth, and always serves its belly and its fodder, nor can it provide any other use while it lives, like other animals which either provide a vehicle for riding, or help in the cultivation of fields, or pull wagons by the neck, or carry burdens on their backs, or provide clothing from their skins, or abound in a supply of milk, or keep watch for the guarding of houses. Did He therefore forbid them to eat swine's flesh, that is, that they should not imitate the life of swine, which are nourished only for death: so that, serving their belly and pleasures, they might not be useless for doing justice and be visited with death? To these things, therefore, Christ points His finger at the law of Moses, as He did to other things in words, so now by a deed. At the same time, however, He wished it to be shown how the most wise God circumscribes the power of the devil with certain limits, as can be seen in the history of Job: which, if it were not so, the devil would undoubtedly deal with men as he was dealing with those swine.

Isaac Casaubon, in Exercitation XIII on the Annals of Baronius, teaches that the Gadarenes were Greek, not Jewish, from Josephus, who in book XVII, chapter 13, in describing the affairs of Pompey, says that he took away from the Jews the ἑλληνάδας πόλεις [Greek cities] which were in Coele-Syria, and among these he names Gadara: as also from Strabo, who writes that the Jews 'made it their own' (by force), Gadara also, when, to wit, it was Greek: finally, from the abundance of philosophers, philologists, and orators born in Gadara.

Vers. 31.

ἐπέτρεψον ἡμῖν] Ita & Marcus ἐπέτρεψεν αὐτοῖς ἐνθέως ὁ Ἰησοῦς. Lucas quoque eandem vocem bis usurpat, tum in ex- primenda postulatione dæmoniorum, tum in narrando

Christi facto. Quare cum hoc ipsum Marcus etiam πέμπειν εἰς τοὺς χοίρους vocet, apparet verissimum esse vocibus activis sæpe nihil aliud quam permissionem præsertim sapien- tem ac providam indicari. Vide loca Gen. XX. 6. XXXI. 7. Exod. III. 19. XII. 29. Ps. XVI. 10. Act. II. 27. Ejicere dia- bolum ex homine, Christi fuit actio, in porcos ut irent nul- la actione Christi erat opus; hoc enim optabant ipsi diabo- li & viribus nativis id ipsum efficere poterant, dum ne vi majore impedirentur. Non ergo Christus in hac re vim a- gentem exseruit, sed vim impedire valentem sustinuit: ma- gnis haud dubie de causis. Habitabant illis in locis ut ex Jo- sepho apparet homines Judæi Græcis permixti: Græcis in more erat positum ridere Judaica instituta, præsertim vero abstinentiam à suillis carnibus; tanquam humanæ super- stitionis inane commentum. Notum est illud Juvenalis: Nec distare putant humana carne suillam. Sed jampridem Anaxandrides Comicus dixerat: ἐκ ἐσθίεις ὗα, ἐγὼ δὲ γ' ἥδομαι. Et Plato itidem Comicus: Τῶν γὰρ τετραπόδων ἐδὲν ἀποκτείνειν ἔδει Ημᾶς τὸ λοιπὸν πλὴν ὑῶν. τὰ γὰρ κρέα Ηδιστ' ἔχεσι, κ' ἐδὲν ἀφ' ὑὸς γίνεται Πλὴν ὕστριχες ἡμῖν καὶ πηλός τε κὶ βοή. Neque alia sententia cujusdam apud Plutarchum, qui Ju- dæos dicebat abstinere eo cibo qui omnium esset justissi- mus. Eandemque ob causam dicebat Æsopus ex omni ani- mantum genere sues maximum clamorem tractas edere, quia scirent se nisi morientes nulli esse usui. Sic & Caligula Judæos Alexandrinos cum irrisu interrogabat διὰ τί χοιρεί- ων κρεῶν ἀπέχεσθε; cumque illi varia variarum gentium in- stituta memorarent, atque inter cætera esse, qui ne agnina quidem vescerentur, merito, inquit, ne que enim tam suavis est. Quidam etiam, ut idem Plutarchus notat, existima- bant Judæos veneratione quadam ejus animalis teneri, quod & Persius voluisse videtur cum ait: Et vetus indulget senibus clementia porcis. Alii alias causas conjectabant, ut illi ex quibus hoc hausit Tacitus: Sue abstinent, memoria cladis quod ipsos scabies quon- dam turpaverat, cui id animal obnoxium. Christus igitur per- mittens dæmonibus in sues irruere, ostendit Græcis Judæo- rum religionem ex Dei esse præcepto, simulque Judæos qui se Græcorum moribus nimium aptabant, contra majo- rum constitutionem factam Hyrcani temporibus in sepi- mentum legis, ne cui porcum alere liceret, admonuit de mystico legis sensu: significans homines qui se in fædis vo- luptatibus suum more volutarent, Deo quam maxime dis- plicere & diaboli esse mancipia. Barnabas Apostolus: ὧδε ἐν ὁδῷ ἁμαρτωλῶν ἴση, καθὼς οἱ δοκῶντες φοβεῖσθαι τὸν κύριον ἁμαρτάνεσιν ὡς ὁ χοῖρος· πεινῶν γὰρ κραυγάσει· πληρωθεὶς δὲ τὸν δεσπότην ἐ γνωρίζει. Philo: παγκαλως τὲς ὕτω βιῶντας τῶν σοφιστῶν ὁ νομοθέτης τῷ σύων παραβάλλει γένει. διαυγῆ μὲν ἐδενικῇ καθαρῷ, θολερῷ δὲ καὶ βαραθρώδει βίῳ κὶ τοῖς αἰ- χίστοις ἐμφερομένῳ. Idem alibi eos qui se saginæ & potui mancipant ait συὸς τρόπον ἐν βορβόρῳ διαστομένως χαίρειν: quibus conferenda quæ legimus 2. Petr. II. 22. Eandem interpretationem mysticam legis de suilla carne non eden- da, aut ex Philone aut ex Apostolorum traditione acce- ptam pulchre explicat Lactantius lib. IV. Institutionum cap. XVII. Eodem spectat etiam suillæ carnis interdictio, à qua cum eos abstinere Deus jussit, id potissimum voluit intelligi, ut se à peccatis atque immunditiis abstinerent. Est enim lutulen- tum hoc animal atque immundum, nec unquam cælum aspi- cit, sed in terra toto & corpore & ore projectum ventri semper & pabulo servit, nec ullum alium, dum vivit, præstare usum potest, sicut cætera animantes, quæ vel sedendi vehiculum præ- bent, vel in cultibus agrorum juvant, vel plaustra collo tra- hunt, vel onera tergo gestant, vel indumentum exuviis suis exhibent, vel copia lactis exuberant, vel custodiendis domibus invigilant. Interdixit ergone procina carne vescerentur, id est, ne vitam porcorum imitarentur, qui ad solam mortem nutri- untur: ne ventri ac voluptatibus servientes ad faciendam justi- tiam inutiles essent ac morte afficerentur. Ad hæc ergo Mosis legem Christus ut verbis alias, ita nunc facto digitum inten- dit. Simul autem ostensum voluit, quomodo Deus sapien- tissimus vim diaboli limitibus quibusdam circumscribat, ut in Jobi historia videre est: quod ni esset, haud dubie acturum cum hominibus diabolum, quemadmodum cum porcis istis agebat.

Isaacus Casaubonus Exercit. XIII. ad Annal. Ba- ron. Gadarenos Græcanicos, non Judæos fuisse docet ex Josepho qui lib. XVII. c. 13. in rebus Pompeji de- scribendis ait, ademisse illum Judæis ἑλληνάδας πό- λεις urbes Græcanicas, quæ erant in Cœle-Syria, atq; inter has nominat Gadaram: ut & è Strabone, qui scribit καὶ ἀυτὴν ἐξιδιάσαντο ἰεδᾶιοι, Gadaram quoq; (per vim) Judæi suam fecerunt, quum sc. es- set Græcanica: denique ex copia Philosophorum, Philologorum & Oratorum Gadaris ortorum.

## 8:34
Ver. 34.

ὅπως μεταβῇ ἀπὸ τῶν ὁρίων ἀυτῶν [that he might depart from their borders]: Out of fear, as Luke explains. Doubtless, conscious of their sins, they feared the divine power in Christ. Compare the passage 1 Kings XVII. 18. And the words of Job concerning the men of the age of the flood, ch. XXII. 17.

Latin:

Vers. 34.

ὅπως μεταβῇ ἀπὸ τῶν ὁρίων ἀυτῶν] Præ metu, ut Lucas explicat. Nimirum peccatorum sibi conscii vim in Christo divinam metuebant. Confer locum 1. Reg. XVII. 18. Et verba Jobi de hominibus ætate diluvii c. XXII. 17.

## 9:1 Argument
CHAPTER IX. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

When Christ has returned to Capernaum, a paralytic is brought to Him, to whom, having forgiven his sins, He restores health: He calls Matthew from the tax office and takes food with the publicans, and defends this: He instructs the disciples of John why His own do not fast, He raises the daughter of a certain ruler, and heals the woman with the issue of blood, opens the eyes of two blind men, frees a mute and possessed man, being on that account subject to the calumnies of the Pharisees: and He preaches the Gospel everywhere, and heals the sick: He warns them to pray for laborers to be thrust out into the harvest.

There are six parts: I. The healing of the paralytic, to v. 8. II. The calling of Matthew, to v. 13. III. The instruction of the disciples of John concerning fasting, to v. 17. IV. The restoration of the daughter of the ruler and the woman with the issue of blood, the former to life, the latter to health, to v. 26. V. The healing of two blind men and other sick people, to v. 35. VI. The admonition to pray for laborers to be sent into the harvest, to v. 38.

PART I. The healing of the paralytic.

Verse 1.

εἰς τὴν ἰδίαν πόλιν] Even in Roman law our city is said to be where we have fixed our hearth. That Christ had moved to Capernaum had already been reported before by Matthew. Wherefore I am surprised that some of the ancients and moderns interpret Nazareth here, since it seems sufficiently certain to me that these things were done at Capernaum by the testimony of Mark ch. II. 1.

That cannot indeed be proven from that testimony: for we have shown in the Harmony that the same paralytic is not described by Mark as the one Matthew presents here. Nevertheless, there is no doubt for us that by his own city Capernaum is understood here: which is called the city of the Lord not because of his birth, which was Bethlehem, not because of his upbringing, which was Nazareth, but because of his residence, which he transferred there at the beginning of his ministry, John II. 12, Luke IV. 31, and there he had a rented house, or was received in the house of another, from which he even paid the tax, Matt. XVII. 24, and he held many sermons there, and performed many miracles, Matt. XI. 23. And thus Chrysostom, Theophylact, Euthymius, B. Chemnitius, the Weimar Paraphrase, Maldonatus, Jansenius, Conzenius, Cornelius à Lapide, Tirinus, and others understand the city of the Lord here.

Latin:

CAPUT IX. ARGUMENTUM ET PAR- TITIO.

Christo reverso in Capernaum adfertur Para- lyticus, cui remissis peccatis sanitatem re- stituit: vocat Matthæum è telonio & cum publicanis cibum capit, idque defendit: di- scipulos Iohannis, cur sui non jejunent, in- format, filiam Principis alicujus resusci- tat, & hæmorrhousam sanat, duobus cæcis oculos aperit, mutum & obsessum liberat, calumniis Pharisæorum idco obnoxius: ác passim prædicat Evangelium, & ægrotos curat: monet ut orent pro laborantibus in messem extrudendis.

Partes sex sunt I. Paralytici sanatio ad v. 8. II. Matthæi vocatio ad v. 13. III. Discipulorum Johannis de jejunio informatio, ad v. 17. IV. Filiæ Principis, & mulieris hæmorrhousæ, illius in vitam, hujus in sa- nitatem restitutio, ad v. 26. V. Cæcorum duorum & aliorum ægrotorum curatio, ad v. 35. VI. Ob exoran- dos laboraturos in messe admonitio, ad v. 38.

PARS I. Paralytici sanatio.

Vers. 1.

εἰς τὴν ἰδίαν πόλιν] Etiam in Romano jure civitas no- stra dicitur, ubi larem fiximus. Capharnaumum autem Christum immigrasse jam ante à Matthæo erat proditum. Quare miror veterum & recentium quosdam Nazarethum hic interpretari, cum Capharnaumi hæc esse acta mihi satis certum videatur Marci testimonio c. II. 1.

Id ex illo quidem testimonio probari nequit: Non enim eundem à Marco describi Paralyti- cum, quem hic sistit Matthæus, in Harmonia o- stendimus. Nullum tamen nobis dubjum est, per propriam civitatem hic Capernaum intelligi: quæ civitas Domini dicitur non ob nativitatem quæ Bethlehem, non ob educationem, quæ Nazareth, sed ob habitationem, quam sub initium ministerii eo transtulit, Joh. II. 12. Luc. IV. 31. ibique domum conductitiam habuit, vel domo alterius receptus fuit, unde censum etiam solvit Matth. XVII. 24. & plures illic conciones habuit, pluraque miracula fecit Matth. XI. 23. Atque ita civitatem Domini hic intelligunt Chrysostom. Theophyl. Euthymius, B. Chemnit. Paraphr. Vinar. Maldonat. Jansen. Con- zen. Cornel. à Lap. Tirinus, alii.

## 9:2
Verse 2. Τὴν πίσιν ἀυτῶν] Just as the faith of the master had benefited the centurion's servant; so the faith of his friends benefits this sick man: although it is credible that confidence was not lacking in him either.

That pronoun ἀυτῶν refers not only to the bearers, but also to the paralytic himself, which Lyranus, Albertus Magnus, and the Carthusian acknowledge, as does Castrius, part 1, Conc. 524. Note, he says, that Christ did not attend only to the faith of those carrying him, but also to that of the infirm man himself, who had allowed himself to be carried and to be lowered with such danger. That faithful intercession for others conduces to them, whether for bodily health, or for conversion and spiritual health, so that one may be led to faith, there is no doubt, James V. 15, 16, 1 Tim. II, Eph. I. 17, 18, but one must be careful not to think that anyone obtains salvation by another's faith: for the just shall live by his own faith, Hab. II. 4. Therefore, when Christ announces the remission of sins to the sick man, he says, Take heart,

Child, take heart, son, your sins are forgiven you. Since they are not forgiven except to those who believe: nor is justifying faith anything other than trust or confidence, which is the soul and form of the same. Θάρσει is not just 'be of good courage,' but 'take heart' μετὰ παῥῥησίας and have firm confidence, just as faith is described elsewhere through παῥῥησίαν. And he calls him son, so that he might place confidence in him as a Father; he called him Son, says Cyril, because he had believed in him, and had acknowledged him as Lord and creator. We note here the confession of the Jesuit Costerus, part 1, Concion. p. 521. 'Note,' he says, 'that no mention is made of their charity, which nevertheless was great, but of faith.' Furthermore, for this faith it is not enough to believe that those things which GOD said in the scriptures are true: for even Catholic sinners do this, but it is necessary to lean upon his promises, and to believe firmly that you will receive what he has promised in general. & p. 525. HE WAS TAKING HEART (the Paralytic), but Christ exhorts him to greater confidence, because we cannot trust GOD too much. Cassander also praises here the opinion of Hilary concerning the Paralytic in Consult. p. 35. 'From Christ,' he says, 'there is remission through faith, which the law could not release. For faith alone justifies.'

Take heart, child, your sins are forgiven you] The consciousness of graver crimes was undoubtedly striking him, which he feared would stand in his way of receiving health. For because not all offenses against the law reached the cognizance of judges, therefore God had sanctioned the law with threats of untimely death and even of diseases, as can be seen in Deut. XXVIII. 22 & 27. There are indeed sometimes natural causes of diseases or bodily defects, God permitting, as we shall see at John V. 14. But here this disease undoubtedly drew its cause from the man's own fault. Which we are taught often happens, John V. 14, I Cor. XI. 30. Which Christ, in order to raise him to the hope of health, testifies that forgiveness of sins has been granted to him. Θάρσει must entirely be translated 'be of good courage,' just as the Syrian also translates it: both here and below IX. 22. For this word has this meaning where it is placed intransitively. Hence to bid to be of good courage, to add heart. Then 'child' is a friendly and gentle form of address, as in Mark X. 24. It is not entirely foreign to this place what Plato reports to have been said by Zamolxis: 'that just as one ought not to attempt to cure the eyes without the head, nor the head without the body, so neither the body without the soul.'

Latin:

Vers. 2. Τὴν πίσιν ἀυτῶν] Sicut centurionis servo pro- fuerat domini fides; ita prodest huic ægroto fides amico- rum: quanquam & ipsi fiduciam non defuisse credibile est.

Pronomen illud ἀυτῶν non bajulos tantum, sed ipsum etiam paralyticum respicit, quod agnoscunt Lyranus, Albertus M. Carthusianus, ut & Castrius part. 1. Conc. 524. Notæ, inquit, Christum non atten- disse solam portantium fidem, sed ipsius infirmi quoq;, qui portari se permiserat & cum tanto periculo de- mitti. Fidelis intercessio pro aliis quin ipsis condu- cat, seu ad salutem corporalem, seu ad conversio- nem & sanitatem spiritualem, ut ad fidem perdu- catur nullum est dubium Jacob. V. 15. 16. 1. Tim. II. Eph. I. 17. 18. sed cavendum, ne fide aliena quem- piam salutem adipisci censeamus: Justus enim fide sua vivet Hab. II. 4. Ideo cum peccatorum remis- sionem ægroto annunciat Christus, Θάρσει, inquit,

τέκνον, Confide fili, remissa tibi sunt peccata tua. Quia non remittuntur, nisi credentibus : nec fides justi- ficans aliud est, quam fiducia vel confidentia, quæ ejusdem anima & forma est. Θάρσει non est tantum bono esto animo, sed confide μετὰ παῥῥησίας fir- mamque habe fiduciam, quemadmodum alias per παῥῥησίαν describitur fides. Et filium vocat, ut con- fidentiam in ipsum ceu Patrem collocet; Filium vo- cavit, inquit Cyrillus, quia crediderat in ipsum, eum- que ut Dominum ac creatorem agnoverat. Nota- mus hic confessionem Jesuitæ Costeri part. 1. Con- cion. p. 521. Nota, inquit, nullam fieri mentionem charitatis illorum, quæ tamen magna fuit, sed fidei: Porro ad fidem hanc non sufficit credere, quod veræ sint, quæ in scripturis DEUS dixit: hoc enim & peccatores Catholici faciunt, sed oportet promissioni- bus ejus inniti, & quod promisit generatim, firmi- ter credere te accepturum. & p. 525. CONFIDE- BAT (Paralyticus) sed ad majorem fiduciam eum hortatur Christus, quia DEO non possumus nimium fidere. Laudat & hic Cassander sententiam Hilarii de Paralytico in Consult. p. 35. A Christo, inquien- tis, per fidem remissio est, quod lex laxare non pote- rat. Fides enim sola justificat.

Θάρσει τέκνον, ἀφέωνταί σοι αἱ ἁμαρτίαι συ] Percellebat ipsum haud dubie facinorum graviœrum conscientia, quæ timebat obstitura sibi, quominus sanitatem reciperet. Nam quia non omnia contra legem delicta ad judicum co- gnitionem perveniebant, ideo Deus mortis intempestivæ, atque etiam morborum comminationibus legem sanxerat, ut videre est Deut. XXVIII. 22. & 27. Sunt quidem & na- turales interdum morborum aut vitiorum corporalium causæ, Deo permittente, ut videbimus apud Joh. V. 14. Se l hic morbus haud dubie causam trahebat ex ipsius hominis culpa. Quod sæpe contingere docemur Joh. V. 14. I. Cor. XI. 30. Quæ e Christus, ut eum in spein sanitatis erigat, testatur veniain ipsi factam peccatorum. Θάρσει omnino vertendum est bono esto animo sicut etiam vertit Syrus: & hic & infra IX. 22. Hanc enim significationem habet vox ista ubi ponitur ἀμεταβατικῶς. Hinc Sappœ̃ν κελέυειν, ani- mum addere. Deinde τέκνον amica & blanda est compel- latio, ut Marci X. 24. Non omnino alienum est ab hoc lo- co quod Plato à Zamolxi dictum refert: ὅτι ὥσπερ ὀφθαλμὺς ἄνευ κεφαλῆς ὐ δεῖ ἐπιχειρεῖν ἰᾶσθαι, ὐδὲ κεφαλὴν ἄνευ σώμα- τος, ὕτως ὐδὲ σῶμα ἄνευ ψυχῆς.

## 9:3
Vers. 3. He blasphemes] We are taught that this word in the Greek language also refers properly to injury against God, besides other things, by these verses of Menander: 'He who reviles his father speaks impiously. And he practices blasphemy against the divine.' There is also a frequent use of this word among the Pythagoreans. Hierocles explains 'to blaspheme' as 'impiety against God.' But he is said here to 'blaspheme' not who curses God, but who arrogates to himself what belongs to God. See below XXVI. 65 and what is said on Mark in this place.

Latin:

Vers. 3. βλασφημεῖ ] Vocem hanc in Græco etiam ser- mone propriè referri ad Dei injuriam præter cætera istis Menandri versibus docemur: ὁ λοιδορῶν τὸν πατέρα δυσφημεῖ λόγῳ. Τὴν εἰς τὸ θεῖον δὲ μελετᾷ βλασφημίαν. Est & apud Pythagoricos frequens ejus vocis usus. Hiero- cles τὸ βλασφημεῖν exponit ἀσέβεια κατὰ Θεῦ ἀνόσια. Dici- tur autem hic βλασφημεῖν non qui Deo maledicit, sed qui quod Dei est sibi arrogat. Vide infra XXVI. 65. & quæ ad Marcum hoc loco.

## 9:4
Vers. 4. And Jesus seeing their thoughts] That was among the signs of the Messiah, as the Talmudists observe against Bar Kokhba, in the title concerning the Sanhedrin.

Since the Messiah is true God, whose property it is to see the thoughts of the heart, this is not to be accepted only with the Jews, as a sign of some Prophet, who, even if he is a 'mere man' as to his nature, recognizes the thoughts of men by the dictation of the spirit, but it is to be held as a criterion and most certain argument of the divine nature. Rightly Chrysostom: 'Because Christ perceives the secret thoughts of hearts, and although secretly, under the silent veil of conscience, he openly convinces and refutes those sinning, by that fact he undoubtedly testifies that he is not only a perfect man, but also a perfect and true GOD.'

Latin:

Vers. 4. Καὶ ἰδὼν ὁ Ἰησῦς τὰς ἐνθυμήσεις αὐτῶν ] Erat id in- ter notas Messiæ, ut contra Barchochebam observant Thal- mudici, titulo de Synedrio.

Quum Messias verus Deus sit, cujus proprium est videre cogitationes cordis, non id cum Judæis tantum, ceu nota Prophetæ alicujus, qui etsi ψιλὸς ἄνθρωπος quantum ad naturam, cogitata homi- num, dictante spiritu, agnoscat, accipiendum, sed ceu κριτήριον & argumentum certissimum divinæ naturæ habendum. Recte Chrysost: Quod Christus arcanas cogitationes perspicit cordium, & clam licet, sub tacita conscientiæ velo, peccantes palam convin- cit ac coarguit, eo facto baud dubie testatur, esse se non tantum perfectum hominem, sed perfectum item, ac verum DEUM.

## 9:5
Vers. 5. Is it easier] It is more to forgive sin than to heal a disease. But he who promises an invisible thing is not as easily convicted of vanity as he who pledges that he will do that which falls under sight.

Latin:

Vers. 5. ἐυκοπώτερον ] Plus est condonare peccatum quam sanare morbum. Sed non æque facile vanitatis con- vincitur qui rem inconspicuam pollicetur, quam qui id se facturum spondet quod sub aspectum cadit.

## 9:6
Vers. 6. But that you may know] A visible miracle specially applied to prove another thing which cannot be seen gives firm assurance of it. Nor does he use any prayers here, but a bare command. And the sick man recovers not gradually, but suddenly and completely.

on earth to forgive] That 'on earth' with the verb 'to forgive'

Mark teaches us must be joined: and a similar construction 'shall be loosed on earth,' although not in the same sense of forgiving, is found below XVIII. 18. But it was significantly said by Christ, that to him, although living a mortal life among men, such right had been granted. Therefore Christ is not speaking about the announcement of forgiveness, which had been entrusted even to Nathan to David and to other Prophets, but about the power of forgiving sins by his own authority. However, the power given to Christ as a man acting on earth must be distinguished from that which he professes was given to him after the resurrection. That power extended to those things which pertained to the function of the ministry then undertaken according to the reason of places and times; the other, circumscribed by no limits of places, embraced all things celestial and terrestrial.

Latin:

Vers. 6. ἵνα δὲ εἰδῆτε ] Miraculum aspectabile speciali- ter adhibitum ad probandam rem alteram quæ spectari non potest firmam ejus fidem facit. Neque ullas hic preces ad- hibet, sed imperium nudum. Et æger non sensim, sed su- bito totusque revalefcit.

ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς ἀφιέναι ] Illud ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς cum verbo ἀφιέναι

conjungendum Marcus nos docet: ac similis constructio λύσει ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς, quanquam non eodem remittendi sensu invenitur infra XVIII. 18. Significanter autem à Christo di- ctum est, sibi, quanquam inter homines vitam agenti mor- talem, tantum jus esse concessum. Non igitur agit Christus de annuntiatione veniæ, quæ Nathani etiam ad Davidem & Prophetis aliis mandata fuerat, sed de potestate peccata suo arbitrio remittendi. Distinguenda tamen est potestas Christo ut homini in terris agenti data, ab ea quam post re- surrectionem sibi datam profitetur. Illa potestas ad ea ex- tendebatur quæ ad ministerii tum suscepti functionem pro locorum ac temporum ratione pertinebant; altera nullis locorum limitibus circumscripta, cœlestia omnia ac ter- restria complectebatur.

## 9:8
Vers. 8. To men] The change of number is familiar to almost all languages, as often as we wish to say something indefinite about the whole. Such is 'he was buried in the cities of Gilead': 'he went down into the sides of the ship.' And those things which we will note below XXI. 7, XXVII. 44. For the crowd was not admiring this, that to that Jesus of Nazareth specifically this right had been granted, but it understood with amazement that such right had been given to any of men. For no example of such a thing existed in all antiquity. But all these things tended to this, that men might more willingly and with greater confidence surrender themselves to the discipline of Christ, trusting that they would obtain the forgiveness of sins not only through him, but also from him.

Grotius distinguishes the power given to Christ as a man acting on earth, and that which he professes was given to him after the resurrection: That power, he says, extended to those things which pertained to the function of the ministry then undertaken according to the circumstances of places and times; the other, circumscribed by no limits of places, embraced all things celestial and terrestrial. But there was one and the same power: because the power of remitting sins according to his own will is proper to GOD alone, and therefore it is unique, nor can it be doubled. Grotius ought to have distinguished between the power itself and the exercise of the power: or the κτῆσιν and χρῆσιν of the same. Christ had infinite power as a man, when he acted on earth, over all things in heaven and on earth, as regards the κτῆσιν, even if he is said to have received it as regards the plenary and incessant χρῆσιν of that power over all things after the resurrection, Matt. XXVIII. 18. Grotius seems here to approach the error of the Socinians who limit the very power of Christ acting on earth to certain objects, and do not admit that he had the same authority over all things. See Socinismum Proflig.

PART II. The calling of Matthew.

Latin:

Vers. 8. Τοῖς ἀνθρώποις] ἐναλλαγὴ numeri familiaris o- mnibus prope linguis, quoties aliquid ἀόριστον de toto vo- lumus. Tale est sepultus in urbibus Galaad: descendit in latera navis. Et quæ notabimus infra XXI. 7. XXVII 44 Non enim hoc plebs admirabatur, isti potissimum Jesu Nazare- no hoc jus esse concessum, sed ulli hominum tantum juris datum esse cum stupore intelligebat. Nullum enim talis rei exemplum in omni vetustate extabat. Hæc autem omnia eo tendebant, ut libentius majoreque cum fiducia homines se in Christi traderent disciplinam, confisi se veniam pecca- torum non tantum per ipsum, sed & ab ipso consecuturos.

Distinguit Grotius potestatem, Christo ut ho- mini in terris agenti datam, & eam, quam post re- surrectionem sibi datam profitetur: Illa, inquit, po- testas ad ea extendebatur, quæ ad ministerii tum sus- cepti functionem pro locorum ac temporum ratione pertinebant; altera nullis locorum limitibus circum- scripta, cælestia omnia ac terrestria complectebatur. Ast una fuit eademque potestas: quia potestas pro arbitrio suo peccata remittendi uni DEO propria, ideoque unica est, nec geminari potest. Distin- guere debebat Grotius inter potestatem ipsam & exercitium potestatis: seu κτῆσιν, & χρῆσιν ejus- dem. Infinitam potestatem habebat Christus ut homo, cum in terris ageret, super omnia in cælo & in terra, quantum ad κτῆσιν, etsi quoad plenariam, & incessanten χρησιν illius potestatis super omnia accepisse eam dicatur post resurrectionem Matth. XXVIII. 18. Accedere hic videtur Grotius ad er- rorem Socinianorum qui limitant ipsam potesta- tem Christi in terra agentis ad certa objecta, nec im- perium eundem in res omnes habuisse admittunt. Vid. Socinismum Proflig.

PARS II. Matthæi vocatio.

## 9:9
Vers. 9. Τελώνιον] The place in which the public tax was exacted is so called: wherefore what is in the old Glossary, τελώνιον vectigalium, telonatum, mancipatum, should be written vectigalarium, telonarium, manciparium, in that form, of course, in which spoliarium is said. The contractors themselves were called the redeemers of the public revenues.

Ματθαῖον λεγόμενον] Namely him who was afterwards made an Apostle, as appears below X. 3. and who wrote this book in the Hebrew language. I see that all today think this is the same person whom Mark and Luke call Levi: and indeed the circumstances of the narratives agree. Yet neither does Matthew ever call himself Levi, nor do they call Matthew Levi, nor in the list of the Apostles do they call Matthew by any other name than Matthew, although they designate others by their surnames. But it moves me more that Heracleon, who was close to those times, reciting those to whom the opportunity of bearing public witness to Christ before the powers was denied, names Matthew, Philip, Thomas, Levi: and that Clement of Alexandria cites those words in such a way that he does not obscurely approve what is said. But also Origen, disputing against Celsus, when he had said that Matthew had been a publican, adds then, ἴσα δὲ κὶ Λευῒς τελώνης ἀκολουθήσας τῷ Ἰησοῦ, ἀλλ᾽ ὗτοι γε τῷ ἀριθμῷ, ἐξ ἀποστόλων ἀυτὸς ἦν, εἰ μὴ κατὰ τινα τῶν ἀντιγράφων τῶ κατὰ Μάρκον ἐυαγγελία. Behold, he openly denies that Levi was an Apostle, although, as he says, certain copies of Mark seem to prefer that: whence it may be conjectured that in the list of the Apostles certain books of Mark had the name Levi separately from the name of Matthew. Perhaps this Levi, called at the same time as Matthew, was a brother of James, since Alphaeus is ascribed as father to both; and one not of those twelve, but of the other followers of Christ: if we accept this, we shall say that the banquet was held in his house, not in Matthew's house, as one who had then left all his possessions: for

Others call Levi the master of the house: Matthew, however, spoke of the house, without naming the master: perhaps Levi was an ἀρχιτελώνης like Zacchaeus, in whose service Matthew had been.

Grotius acknowledges that ALL today think this way, that this is the same person whom Mark and Luke call Levi, and that the circumstances of the narratives agree. And yet one rises up against ALL; but with what arguments? Very trivial ones. That Matthew nowhere calls himself Levi, nor do those men call Levi Matthew, nor in the list of the Apostles do they call Matthew by any other name than Matthew, when they designate him with his surnames. But although Matthew does not call himself Levi, is it not sufficiently evident from Mark and Luke, who, describing the same history, with all circumstances testifying, called that publican summoned by Christ, whom he himself designated by the name of Matthew, Levi, that Matthew is Levi? And what kind of consequence is that: He is not called by the name Levi in the list of the Apostles. Therefore he did not have the name Levi? The Fathers acknowledge here in Matthew true repentance, because he himself did not hide the filth and vice of his former life, in which Matthew was called, when other Evangelists concealed that name and called him Levi: such as Chrysostom, Jerome, and even Origen. But that Heracleon, who was close to those times, designates Matthew and Levi as distinct persons is not of such weight that it should be opposed to the most evident circumstances of the Evangelists' narratives: even if Clement of Alexandria were to approve of it, which in truth does not appear in Clement. For who would prefer human testimonies to a report of divine authority? Not to mention that another person named Levi could still have been a disciple of Christ, whom Heracleon might have indicated, even if Matthew also possessed this name. But the fact that Origen, arguing against Celsus, denies that Levi was an Apostle, although certain copies of Mark seem to prefer that, from which Grotius conjectures that some books of Mark in the list of the Apostles had the name Levi separately from the name of Matthew, and that that Levi was called at the same time as Matthew, who perhaps was the brother of James, because Alphaeus is ascribed as father to both, and one not of those twelve, but of other followers of Christ—these things, as uncertain and consisting of mere divinations, have no power to move us from the common consensus of all others, especially because it cannot be persuaded by any document from the Scriptures that Matthew is different from Levi, nor is Levi introduced anywhere else who was outside the choir of the Apostles, nor is it likely that Mark and Luke would have omitted the calling of the Apostle Matthew, but would have commemorated that of some Levi who was not an Apostle. Nor did Origen, whatever he may hand down against Celsus—whether κατ᾽ ἄνθρωπον or from his own opinion—concerning a certain Levi who was not an Apostle but followed Christ when he was previously a publican, deny that the Levi of Mark II and Luke V, called from the tax office, was the Apostle Matthew himself: nay, he even provided the reason why Mark and Luke conceal the former name of Matthew, while Matthew himself openly expresses it: he saw Matthew the publican: ταῦτα δὲ λέγει ἵνα ἡμεῖς θαυμάσαντες τὴν τέχνην τῦ ἰατρέυσαντος αὐτὸν θεῦ πισεύωμεν εἰς αὐτὸν ἀκροβαέσατα. He says these things, however, so that from the knowledge to be drawn from here of the deplorable state of the Physician who cured him, namely, we may recognize the art and extraordinary power of GOD, and from that be strengthened in faith. Finally, when Grotius thinks that the banquet was not celebrated in Matthew's house, as one who had then left all his possessions, but in the house of Levi, who perhaps was an ἀρχιτελώνης like Zacchaeus, in whose service Matthew had been, he assumes these things without authority and merely precariously: for even if Matthew does not add that the banquet was celebrated in his house, but simply says ἐν τῇ οἰκίᾳ, that house could nevertheless be his, as the Arab according to the London edition explicitly adds, in the house of Matthew, and Erasmus in the house of him. Nor indeed, when Matthew is called in this place, is he said to have left everything, as is expressly added in the history described by Luke, when he names Levi as being called, and he left everything, and rising followed him v. 27, who nevertheless immediately adds in v. 29 that a great banquet was prepared by him, and in his own house: whence it is clear that it does not conflict with that leaving of everything that he prepared a banquet in his house.

Latin:

Vers. 9. Τελώνιον] Ita dictus locus in quo publicum exi- gebatur: quare quod in veteri est Glossario, τελώνιον vecti- galium, telonatum, mancipatum scribendum est vectigala- rium, telonarium, manciparium, ea nimirum forma qua spoliarium dicitur. Mancipes vocabantur ipsi publico- rum redemtores.

Ματθαῖον λεγόμενον] Eum nimirum qui Apostolus po- stca est factus, ut apparet infra X. 3. quique hunc librum scripsit sermone Hebræo. Video omnes hodie ita existimare hunc eundem esse quem Marcus & Lucas Levin nominant: & sane congruunt narrationum circumstantiæ. Tamen ne- que Matthæus usquam se Levin vocat, neque isti Levin Matthæum nominant, neque in recensione Apostolorum Matthæum alio quam Matthæi vocant nomine, cum alios cognomentis suis incigitent. Sed magis me movet quod Heracleon illis temporibus proximus recitans eos quibus publicum testimonium apud potestates Christo exhibendi negata est occasio nominat Matthæum, Philippum, Tho- mam, Levin: quodque ea verba ita citat Clemens Alexan- drinus, ut quod dicitur non obscure approbet Sed & Orige- nes adversus Celsum disputans, cum dixisset Matthæum publicanum fuisse, addit deinde, ἴσα δὲ κὶ Λευῒς τελώνης ἀκο- λουθήσας τῷ Ἰησοῦ, ἀλλ᾽ ὗτοι γε τῷ ἀριθμῷ, ἐξ ἀποστόλων ἀυτὸς ἦν, εἰ μὴ κατὰ τινα τῶν ἀντιγράφων τῶ κατὰ Μάρκον ἐυαγγελία. Ecce aperte negat Levin Apostolum fuisse, quanquam, ut ait, Marci quædam exemplaria id videantur præferre: unde conjectare licet in recensu Apostolorum libros quosdam Marci nomen Levi seorsim à nomine Matthæi habuisse. For- te is Levis simul cum Matthæo vocatus frater fuerit Jacobi, quando utrique pater Alphæus adscribitur; unusq; non il- lorum duodecim, sed aliorum Christi sectatorum: quod si recipimus, in hujus domo, non in Matthæi domo, ut qui tum omnia sua reliquerat, dicemus celebratum convivium:nam

Levin dominū domus nominant alii: Matthæus autem nu- de domum dixit,domino non nominato:forte Levis fuit ἀρ- χιτελώνης ut Zachæus,in cujus ministerio fuerit Matthæus.

Agnoscit Grotius OMNES hodie ita existimare, hunc eundem esse, quem Marcus & Lucas Levin no- minant, & congruere narrationum circumstantias. Et insurgit tamen unus contra OMNES; sed quibus rationibus? Admodum leviculis. Quod neq; Mat- thæus usquam se Levin vocet, neque isti Levin Mat- thæum nominent, neque in recensione Apostolorum Matthæum alio, quam Matthæi vocant nomine, cum cognomentis suis indigitent. Sed quanquam Mat- thæus se non vocet Levin, annon satis id è Marco & Luca constat, qui eandem describentes histori- am, testibus omnibus circumstantiis, publicanum illum à Christo vocatum, quem ipse Matthæi no- mine indigitavit, Levin appellarunt, Matthæum esse Levin? & quænam illa consequentia est: Non vocatur nomine Levi in recensione Apostolorum. Ideo nec habuit nomen Levi? Agnoscunt hic in Matthæo Patres veram pœnitentiam, quod non dissimula- vit ipse sordes & vitium vitæ prioris, in qua Mat- thæus vocatus est, quum alii Evangelistæ nomen illud occultarint, eumq; Levi vocarint: utpote Chrysostomus, Hieronymus, etiam Origenes. Quod autem Heracleon illis temporibus proximus Mat- thæum & Levin ceu distinctas personas designat, tanti non est, ut evidentissimis narrationumEvan- gelistarum circumstantiis opponi debeat: etiamsi id approbaret Clemens Alexandrinus, quod vero in Clemente non apparet. Ecquis enim humana testimonia relationi divinæ autoritatis præferret? ut taceam quod adhuc alius Levi nomine insigni- tus Christi discipulus esse potuerit, quem Heracle- on indigitàrit, etsi & Matthæus hoc nomen obti- nuerit. Quod vero Origenes adversus Celsum di- sputans,Levin Apostolum fuisse negat, quanquam id Marci quædam Exemplaria præferre videantur, ex quo conjecsat Grotius in recensu Apostolorum libros quosdam Marci nomen Levi scorsim à Matthæi no- mine habuisse, ac Levin illum simul cum Matthæo vo- catum, qui forte Jacobi frater fuerit, quia utrique Pater Alphæus asscribitur, & unus non illorum duo- decim, sed aliorum Christi Sectatorum,ea ut incerta, & meris divinationibus constantia dimovere nos minime valent à communi Omnium aliorum con- sensu, imprimis quia nullo è Scripturis documen- to suaderi potest,diversum à Levi esse Matthæum,nec uspiam alias Levi introducitur, qui extra chorum Apostolorum fuerit, neq; verisimile est, Marcum & Lucam prætermissuros fuisse Matthæi Apostoli, commemoraturos vero Levi alicujus, qui non Apo- stolus fuerit, vocationem. Neque Origenes, quic- quid de Levi quodam non Apostolo Christum se- ctato, quum prius publicanus esset, contra Cel- sum, seu κατ᾽ ἄνθρωπον, seu ex propria sententia, tradat, inficiatus est, Levin Marc. II. & Luc. V.è telonio vocatum esse ipsum Matthæum Apostolum: quin imo causam reddidit, cur Marcus ac Lucas nomen prius Matthæi occultent,Matthæus vero il- lud aperte exprimat: vidit Matthæum publicanum: ταῦτα δὲ λέγει ἵνα ἡμεῖς θαυμάσαντες τὴν τέχνην τῦ ἰατρέυσαντος αὐτὸν θεῦ πισεύωμεν εἰς αὐτὸν ἀκροβαέσατα. Hæc autem ita dicit, ut ex notitia hinc haurienda deplorati ejusstatus Medici, qui i- psium curavit, nempe DEI artem ac vim eximiam agnoscamus, indeq; in fide corroboremur. Cum de- nique non in Matthæi domo, ut qui tum omnia sua reliquerat, convivium celebratum censet Grotius, sed in domo Levi,qui forte ἀρχιτελώνης fuerit,ut Za- chæus, in cujus ministerio fuerit Matthæus, sine auto- ritate, ac mere precario ista assumit: Etsi enim Matthæus non addat in domo sua celebratum con- 'vivium, sed simpliciter dicat ἐν τῇ οἰκίᾳ, domus ta- men illa ipsius esse poterat, uti Arabs secundum e- ditionem Londinensem diserte addit, in domo Matthæi, & Erasmus in Domo illius. Neque vero cum Matthæus vocatur hoc loco, omnia reliquisse dicitur, uti expresse in historia à Luca descripta, cum Levin nominat vocatum, additur, & relin- quebat omnia, & surgens sequebatur eum v. 27. qui tamen confestim subjungit v. 29. ab ipso, & in i- psius domo adornatum esse magnum convivium: un- de luculentum est, cum ista relictione omnium no pugnare, quod in domo sua convivium instruxerit.

## 9:10
Vers. 10. κὶ ἁμαρτωλοὶ] Above we said that those were so called by the Jews whom they detested no less than profane ἀλλοφύλες because of their way of life or impurity of morals.

Latin:

Vers. 10. κὶ ἁμαρτωλοὶ] Supra diximus ita Judæis voca- tos esse eos quos ipsi ob vitæ institutum aut morum impuri- tatem non minus quam profanos ἀλλοφύλες detestabantur.

## 9:11
Vers. 11. ἰδόντες] That is, when they noticed. For they do not seem to have been present. In the same sense this word is not rarely found both in these and in other books.

ἐσθίει] Contrary to what the experts of the law taught should be done. But they held publicans and men of similar life in the same place as τὲς ἀλλοφύλες: whence they are accustomed to be joined as τελῶναι κὶ ἐθνικοὶ.

Latin:

Vers. 11. ἰδόντες] Id est, cum animadverterent. Neque enim præsentes fuisse videntur. Eodem sensu vox ista tum in his tum in aliis libris non raro invenitur.

ἐσθίει] Contra quam fieri oportere legisperiti docebant. Publicanos autẽ & similis vitæ homines eodẽ habebãt loco quo τὲς ἀλλοφύλες: unde conjungi solent τελῶναι κὶ ἐθνικοὶ.

## 9:12
Vers. 12. ὐ χρείαν ἔχεσιν οἱ ἰσχύοντες ἰατρῦ] Christ speaks from a supposition. If you are such as you seem to yourselves, you certainly do not need my work. Thus Antisthenes, when it was objected to him that he associated with men of disapproved life: Even physicians, he said, [are] with the sick. Pausanias: ἐπεὶ ἰατρὸς παρὰ τοῖς ὑγιαίνεσι, ὅπα δὲ οἱ νοσῦντες διατρίβειν εἰώθασι. Ovid, Book II of the Pontic Epistles, IV: 'The healthy are strong by themselves, and seek no Machaon; the doubtful sick man flees to medical aid.' And Diogenes, when asked why, while praising the institutions of the Lacedaemonians, he did not live among them? ἐδὲ γὰρ ἰατρὸς εἶπεν ὑγείας ὢν ποιητικὸς ἐν τοῖς ὑγιαίνεσι τὴν διατριβὴν ποιεῖται. The Pharisees were such excellent pretenders of piety that they imposed not only on others, but also on themselves. See Luke XVIII. 11. Meanwhile, the mind was full of hatred, envy, pride, avarice, cruelty. So true it is that it is easier to heal the diseases of the body than of the mind: because when the body is sick, the mind, understanding the disease, consults for the body: but for the mind that is sick, the body, being a brute, cannot consult, and the mind itself is hindered by the disease from understanding the disease, to feel which is a part of health. See what [is written] on Mark chapter II.

Latin:

Vers. 12. ὐ χρείαν ἔχεσιν οἱ ἰσχύοντες ἰατρῦ] Loquitur Christus ex suppositione. Si vos tales estis, quales vobis vi- demini, sane meæ operæ non indigeris. Sic Antisthenes cum objectum illi esset quod cum improbatæ vitæ hominibus versaretur: Etiam medici, inquit, cum ægrotis. Pausanias: ἐπεὶ ἰατρὸς παρὰ τοῖς ὑγιαίνεσι, ὅπα δὲ οἱ νοσῦντες διατρίβειν εἰώθασι Ovidius l. ii. de Ponto elegia IV. Firma valent per se, nullumque Machaona quærunt: Ad medicam dubius confugit æger opem. Et Diogenes rogatus cum Lacedæmoniorum laudaret in- stituta cur non apud eos viveret? ἐδὲ γὰρ ἰατρὸς εἶπεν ὑγείας ὢν ποιητικὸς ἐν τοῖς ὑγιαίνεσι τὴν διατριβὴν ποιεῖται. Pha- risæi tam egregii erant pietatis simulatores ut non aliis tan- tum, sed & sibi imponerent. Vide Luc. XVIII. 11. Interea animus erat plenus odii, invidiæ, fastus, avaritiæ, crude- litatis. Adeo verum est facilius sanari corporis quam ani- mi morbos: quia cum corpus ægrotat, animus morbum intelligens corpori consulit: at animo ægrotanti corpus, quippe brutum, consulere non potest, & animus ipse mor- bo impeditur quo minus morbum intelligat, quem sentire pars aliqua est sanitatis. Vide quæ ad Marcum cap. II.

## 9:13
Vers. 13. ἔλεον θέλω κὶ ὐ θυσίαν] חפד in Hosea is what is here ἔλεος. In Latin you would correctly render it as beneficence. Opposed to this is זבח θυσία, which word here synecdochically signifies every observation of rites, because in that kind of work sacrifices excelled. Under the former member is included recalling a sinning man to a good harvest, under the latter, abstaining from the company of wicked men. Although this latter was not expressly commanded in the law of Moses, yet since experience teaches that many are defiled by the company of the depraved, and grave men cannot show more openly how much a base life displeases them than if they avoid the meeting and sight of such men, which custom, derived from the most ancient ages, had pervaded almost all nations, Christ does not disapprove of such an institution: as will be shown more openly elsewhere. But with the two laws compared with one another, the one naturally honest which demands from us love and beneficence toward any men, the other ritual, which commands that the guilty be avoided, he teaches from Hosea which ought to outweigh the other. For that ולא which is translated here does not designate a simple but a comparative negation, which the following words in Hosea make most manifest: ודעת אלהים מעלות that is, and religion instead of burnt offering. Known among rhetoricians is the topic concerning laws that conflict with one another not from the intention of the authors, but by some chance; the Greeks call this species of antinomy τὴν ἐκ περιστάσεως μάχην. For the adjudication of such a controversy certain rules are accustomed to be handed down, the chief of which I will explain in the words of Cicero: who says thus in the second book of De Inventione: First, therefore, it is necessary to compare the laws by considering which law pertains to greater, that is, to more useful, more honorable, and more necessary things. From which it is concluded that if two laws, or if more, or however many there may be, cannot be reconciled because they disagree among themselves, that one is thought to be most preserved which seems to pertain to the greatest things. Now Hosea teaches us, in the name of God himself, that piety placed in the mind and the duties of humanity are of much greater moment before God than the observation of rites and ceremonies. The reason is at hand, because reverence for God and integrity of life and beneficence are approved by God per se and primarily: but ritual works only secondarily, insofar as they testify to piety by institution, not naturally: whence it follows that the former never fail to please God; but the latter do not please otherwise than if the former have preceded. We brought forward above at chapter V some things from Plato and Seneca to this effect: but below an opportunity will be given to treat of this matter more fully. Rightly, therefore, Christ concludes that the instruction concerning the avoidance of familiar association with the τῶν ἀτάκτων [disorderly] must be observed in such a way that opportunities for leading them back to the right path are not meanwhile neglected: for which reason, since it clearly appears that he was called to come to those who might provide hope of a better life, and with no other intention than to draw back to God those who were fugitives from God, it is most unjust that this be turned to his discredit. Following this lesson, Paul warns the Christian Thessalonians μὴ συναναμιγνύεσθαι [not to associate] with those who would not obey the word of the Gospel: but lest anyone should think that all access to them was indiscriminately forbidden, he added that they were not to be treated as enemies (which the Jews were accustomed to do) but to be admonished as brothers. Indeed, with that closer bond dissolved which unites those who are zealous for piety among themselves, the common tie of human nature and the memory of former friendship remain. Hierocles rightly advises, when he had said that a friend must be separated from us διὰ τὴν πρὸς τὸ χεῖρον μεταβολὴν [on account of a change for the worse], he added ἡ δὲ ἀπόθεσις φυλαττέτω τὸ μὴ εἰς ἔχθραν μεταπεσεῖν· δῖον γάρ, εἰ κἀκεῖνος τῆς Φιλίας ἑαυτὸν ὑπεξήγαγε, ἡμᾶς γε πλείστη ἐ- πιμέλεια ποιεῖσθαι ὅπως ἐπανακληθείη πρὸς τὸ δέον, ἠκἀγα- πῶντας τὴν ἀπόπτωσιν τῶ Φίλω, ὀ δὲ ὑπερφρονῆσαι τὸ καταδε- ὲς ἀυτῶ τῆς γνώμης [but let the putting away guard against falling into enmity; for it is divine, even if he has withdrawn himself from the friendship, that we at least should take the greatest care that he might be recalled to what is right, loving the falling away of the friend, but not despising the inferiority of his judgment].

ὀ γὰρ ἦλθον [For I did not come] See the commentary on Mark.

PART III. The information of John's disciples concerning fasting.

Latin:

Vers. 13. ἔλεον θέλω κὶ ὐ θυσίαν] חפד apud Oseam est quod hic ἔλεος. Latine recte reddideris beneficentiam. Huic opponitur זבח θυσία, quæ vox hic συνεκδοχικῶς omnem rituum observationem significat, quia in eo operum gene- re sacrificia excellebant. Sub priori membro comprehendi- tur peccantem hominem ad bonam frugem revocare, sub altero, abstinere a convictu hominum flagitiosorum. Quan- quam autem posterius hoc non erat diserte præceptum in lege Mosis, tamen cum experientia doceat multos inquina- ri pravorum consuetudine, neque possint viri graves aper- tius ostendere quantum sibi displiceat vita turpis, quam si talium hominum congressum conspectumque defugiant, qui mos ab antiquissimis sæculis deductus omnes prope gentes pervaserat, non improbat tale institutum Christus: ut alibi apertius demonstrabitur: Sed comparatis inter se duabus legibus, altera naturaliter honesta quæ dilectio- nem & beneficentiam erga quosvis homines à nobis exigit, altera rituali, quæ vitari nocentes præcipit, ex Osea docet utra utri præponderare debeat. Nam illud ולא quod hic transferturl non simplicem sed comparatam negatio- nem designat, quod sequentia apud Osean verba manife- stissimum faciunt: ודעת אלהים מעלות id est, & religionem pro holocausto. Notus est apud Rhetores locus de legibus non ex auctorum proposito, sed casu ali- quo inter se pugnantibus Græci hanc ἀντινομίας speciem vo- cant τὴν ἐκ περιστάσεως μάχην. Ad talis controversiæ dijudi- cationem regulæ quædam tradi solent, quarum præcipuam Ciceronis verbis explicabo: qui sic ait de Inventione secun- da: Primum igitur leges oportet contendere considerando ultra lex ad majores hoc est ad utiliores, ad honestiores ac magis neces- sarias res pertineat: ex quo conficitur ut si leges duæ, aut si plures, aut quotquot erunt, confer sari non possint, quia discrepent inter se, ea maxime conservãda putetur quæ ad maximas res pertine- re videatur. Jam docet nos Oseas, Dei ipsius nomine, pieta- tem in animo positam & humanitatis officia apud Deum multo majoris esse momenti, quam rituum cæremoniarũ- que observationem. Causa in promtu est, quia Dei reveren- tia & vitæ integritas ac beneficentia per se κὶ προηγουμένως Deo probantur: ritualia autem opera ἑπομένως duntaxat, qua- tenus ex instituto, non naturaliter pietatem testantur: un- de sequitur illa Deo nunquam non placere; hæc vero non aliter, nisi illa præcesserint. Adduximus supra ad caput V. ex Platone & Seneca quædam in hanc sententiam: sed infra plenius hac de re agendi se dabit locus.
