Recte igitur Christus colligit ita observandum illud institutum de vitanda fami- liari consuetudine τῶν ἀτάκτων, ut non negligantur interim occasiones eos reducendi in rectam viam: quamobrem cum palam appareat se vocatum ad eos venire qui spem melioris vitæ facerent, neq; alio animo quam ut Dei fugitivos ad De- um retraheret, iniquissime id sibi vitio verti. Hoc documen- tum sequens Paulus Thessalonicenses Christianos monet, μὴ συναναμιγνύεσθαι iis qui verbo Evangelii non obedirent: sed ne quis omnem ad eos aditum indiscriminatim vetitum putaret, adjecit non pro hostibus ducendos (quod facere so- lebant Judæi) sed fraterne admonendos. Nimirum resoluto illo nexu propiore qui pietatis studiosos inter se colligat, manet commune humanæ naturæ vinculum & prioris ami- citiæ memoria. Bene monet Hierocles cum dixisset amicum à nobis separandum διὰ τὴν πρὸς τὸ χεῖρον μεταβολὴν, addidit ἡ δὲ ἀπόθεσις φυλαττέτω τὸ μὴ εἰς ἔχθραν μεταπεσεῖν· δῖον γάρ, εἰ κἀκεῖνος τῆς Φιλίας ἑαυτὸν ὑπεξήγαγε, ἡμᾶς γε πλείστη ἐ- πιμέλεια ποιεῖσθαι ὅπως ἐπανακληθείη πρὸς τὸ δέον, ἠκἀγα- πῶντας τὴν ἀπόπτωσιν τῶ Φίλω, ὀ δὲ ὑπερφρονῆσαι τὸ καταδε- ὲς ἀυτῶ τῆς γνώμης.

ὀ γὰρ ἦλθον] Vide ad Marcum.

PARS III. Discipulorum Iohannis de jejunio informatio.

## 9:14
V. 14. οἱ μαθηταὶ Ἰωάννυ [The disciples of John] Luke and Mark also teach that the same controversy was raised by the Pharisees against the Apostles: whether at the same time is uncertain: although Mark connects these things.

Νηστεύομεν πολλὰ [We fast much] It is discussed here also, as above, not concerning public fasts but those which were undertaken privately: which was done by the Pharisees indeed for the sake of hunting for fame, but by the disciples of the Baptist on account of the imprisonment of their master, for whom they were pouring out prayers before God. For both the reason of the times and the mention of δεήσεων [supplications] which is in Luke seem to show this.

ὀ νηστεύουσι [they do not fast] That is, they are not accustomed to fast: for this verb, as elsewhere, signifies the frequency of an act. Thus in Mark 14:12, ὅτε τὸ πάσχα ἔθυον [when they were accustomed to sacrifice the Passover], and 15:6, ἀπέλυε [he was accustomed to release]. Luke for the same thing said: ἐσθίουσι κὶ πίνουσι [they eat and drink]: that is, they live in the popular manner, in which sense it is also said below that the Baptist came μήτε ἐσθίων μήτε πίνων [neither eating nor drinking], but Christ ἐσθίων κὶ πίνων [eating and drinking], chapter 11:18, 19.

Latin:

V. 14. οἱ μαθηταὶ Ἰωάννυ] Eandem controversiam mo- tam Apostolis etiam à Pharisæis Lucas & Marcus docent: an eodē tempore incertum: quanquam Marcus ista connectit.

Νηστεύομεν πολλὰ] Agitur & hic ut supra non de publi- cis jejuniis sed de iis quæ privatim suscipiebantur: quod fie- bat a Pharisæis quidem ad aucupium famæ, à Baptistæ au- tem discipulis ob captivitatem magistri pro quo preces a- pud Deum fundebant. Hoc enim ostendere videtur & ra- tio temporum, & quæ apud Lucam est δεήσεων mentio.

ὀ νηστεύουσι] Id est, non solent jejunare: nam verbum hoc ut & alibi frequentiam actus significat. Ita Marci XIV. 12. ὅτε τὸ πάσχα ἔθυον quo tempore Pascha imaclare solebant, & XV. 6. ἀπέλυε solebat dimittere. Lucas pro eodem di- exit: ἐσθίουσι κὶ πίνουσι: id est, vivunt populariter, quo sensu & infra dicitur Baptista venisse μήτε ἐσθίων μήτε πίνων, Chri- stus autem ἐσθίων κὶ πίνων, cap. XI. 18. 19.

## 9:15
Vers. 15. οἱ ἱοὶ τὲ νυμφῶνος [the sons of the bridechamber] מרעים in the history of Judges where the LXX translated νυμφαγωγὸς [bridesman]. But νυμφαγωγος is properly an auspex: to which corresponds the pronuba: here it is better that they be understood as πα- ρανυμφίοι [groomsmen], ὁμήλικες [peers] to the Greeks, equals also to the Latins; to the later Hebrews שושבני. The Apostle John for the same thing said τὸν Φίλον τῶ νυμφίο [the friend of the bridegroom] ch. 3:29, just as also αἱ παρανυμφῖοι [the bridesmaids] are called רעות that is αἱ φίλαι [the friends]. Ps. 45:14, and רעות in the same verse 15, where the LXX translate αἱ πλησίον [the neighbors]. Moreover, it is a Hebraism, ὑοὶ τῶ νυμφῶνος [sons of the bridechamber], signifying those who were admitted within the bridal chamber, namely with the bridegroom just as the virgins with the bride. Thus in Hosea בני מים are those of the sea: in the First Book of Maccabees 4:2, ὑοὶ τῆς ἄκρας [sons of the citadel] are the guards of the Acra. Among the Greeks, the new husband went to bed first, to whom the new bride was then led, as the Epithalamium of Helen in Theocritus teaches us; on the contrary, we learn from Catullus that it was done at Rome: Now you may come, husband: The wife is in the chamber for you.

Whether this was observed among the Hebrews, I could not easily say. The Jews relate that when new spouses were placed in the bed, these companions stood outside the chamber, and then returned into the chamber to recognize those signs which are discussed in Deut. 22:17. In Pollux I find καλᾶτῳ δὲ τις τῶν νυμφίε Φίλων κὶ θυρωρός, ὁ ταῖς θύραις ἐφεστηκὼς κὶ ἔιργων τὰς γυναῖκας βοηθεῖν τῇ νύμφῃ βοώσῃ [and let one of the bridegroom's friends be a doorkeeper, who stands at the doors and prevents the women from helping the bride who is crying out]. By this comparison, however, Christ, having omitted the Pharisaic fasts, about which he had dealt before, properly answers the disciples of the Baptist, showing that the reason for which they themselves were fasting did not now apply to his own disciples: but that times were coming when they themselves, also deprived of their master, would endure not only fasts, that is to say, signs of mourning, but even heavier things. It was therefore fair that those for whom such things were in store should meanwhile enjoy the brief interval of joy. Thus, in passing, the saying of the Baptist himself is recalled to the minds of his disciples, who had designated Jesus by the name of bridegroom: and the passage in Hosea 2:16.

Πενθεῖν [To mourn] Fasts are signs of mourning, or of great danger, 1 Macc. 3:17, ch. 4:47, 2 Macc. 13:12, 1 Sam. 14:24, whence it was a religious duty for the Jews to fast on the Sabbath, because the Sabbath was dedicated to joy. Wherefore it is a fault of the Roman writers, through ignorance of Jewish custom, or certainly, the word Sabbath is taken by abuse for any religious day when Martial writes thus: And the fasts of the sabbatarians.

Persius, however: Where kings practice the sabbaths with a festive foot. For it is certain that barefoot days are days of fasting. Christians, following the example of the Jews, abstained from fasts on Sundays and throughout Pentecost, because that whole period of fifty days after Easter, no less than the Lord's days, had been consecrated to the memory of the resurrection. κᾀ τότε νηςεύσουσι] They will very often be in mourning, and among many hardships they will also be tormented by hunger and thirst, 1 Cor. 4:11, 2 Cor. 6:5, ch. 11:27. But they shall also appoint fasts for themselves, Acts 10:30, 13:2, ch. 14:22, 1 Cor. 7:5. Christ, however, shows in what follows that it was by the kindness of God that such great labors did not yet overtake his disciples, who were still weak. Rupert: They will clearly fast in those days soon to come, when the Bridegroom has been taken away, when he has suffered, died, and having been buried, has risen and ascended into heaven, no longer to dwell with them bodily in this world. B. Lyserus, Harm. ch. 66, col. 950, says the sense is most simple: that Christ wishes the pious to rejoice when God grants weddings, that is, happy times, according to that saying: Whatever hour God has made fortunate for you, take with a grateful hand. Later, when the bridegroom is taken away, that is, when adversities are presented, then let them be patient, let them pray, let them call upon God, and let them add fasts so that their prayers may be more ardent. But this is a special prediction: a time will come when the bridegroom will be taken away from the disciples, the children of the bridechamber or wedding guests, through death, and then it will be necessary for them to mourn and fast: which Christ explains in John 16:20, as he had come into the world through his departure from the Father, but by the assumption of our flesh, John 1:14, ch. 16:18. Heb. 2:14, 16. He was present with the disciples through his pleasant conversation, salutary instruction, and the illustrious manifestation of divine glory, John 1:14, 2:11; thus he was to be taken away from them through his departure from the world and return to the Father, ch. 16:18. When this was said to his disciples, sadness filled their hearts, v. 6. And this is hinted at here: but the days are coming, that is, there will be a time, when the bridegroom will be taken away from the children of the bridechamber, then they will fast, that is, they will mourn. By the children of the bridechamber, says Chrysostom in Corderius's Catena, he understands all those who had believed in him, but especially his divine disciples and Apostles. And he says: as long as I am with the disciples, it is necessary for them to rejoice and exult in the present fruit of my sight and company, for I am the bridegroom. But when the time of the passion and my being taken from them has come, then indeed they will fast and be afflicted by hunger and thirst, rejected and cast about by the hatred of all. The same in Nicetas's Catena: He prefaces the discourse on the passion, instructing the disciples in their mutual contradictions, and training them to meditate on those things which seemed more bitter. For it was too grave and burdensome to say that to them from that moment: since even much later it troubled them when it was said to them; it was said therefore to others, and thus it was made easier for them to bear: but since it was likely that they would grow insolent because of the passion of John, he suppresses their fear from that source. He does not say, when he has departed from them, nor when he has died, but when he has been taken away, signifying that he was to be removed from the midst of those very Pharisees with whom he was speaking, as Maldonatus notes here. Who, however, is mistaken in that he thinks Christ spoke with the Pharisees here. This is indeed certain regarding the former question: but Matthew is the witness that the disciples of John proposed this doubt about fasting to Christ, not the Pharisees: which Maldonatus indeed explains from a comparison of the passage in Luke 5:33, that the disciples of John approached Christ at the instigation of the Pharisees, and that is why Luke says the Pharisees approached: but St. Augustine, in book 2, De consensu Evangelistarum, ch. 27, reconciles it by saying that both approached, but that Luke named only the Pharisees, and Matthew only the disciples of John. But in truth, we have shown in our Evangelical Harmony, from the circumstance of time, that the histories of Matthew and Luke are different, even if they are very similar.

Latin:

Vers. 15. οἱ ἱοὶ τὲ νυμφῶνος] מרעים in Judicum hi- storia ubi νυμφαγωγὸς verterunt LXX. Sed νυμφαγωγος pro- prie est auspex: cui respondet pronuba: hic magis est ut πα- ρανυμφίοι intelligantur, ὁμήλικες Græcis, æquales etiam Lati- nis? Hebræis posterioribus שושבני. Johannes Apostolus pro eodem dixit τὸν Φίλον τῶ νυμφίο c. III. 29. quomodo & αἱ παρανυμφῖοι virgines vocantur רעות id est αἱ φίλαι. Ps. XLV. 1. & רעות ibidem commate 15. ubi LXX. ver- tunt αἱ πλησίον. Est autem Hebraismus ὑοὶ τῶ νυμφῶνος, si- gnificans eos qui intra thalamum admittebantur, nempe cum sponso sicut cum sponsa virgines. Sic apud Oseam בני מים sunt maritimi: Primo Maccabaico IV. 2. ὑοὶ τῆς ἄκρας Acræ custodes. Apud Græcos prior cubitum ibat novus maritus, ad quem deinde nova nupta deduceba- tur, ut nos docet Epithalamium Helenæ apud Theocritum, Contra Romæ factum ex Catullo discimus: Iam licet venias marite: Vxor in thalamo est tibi.

Utrum apud Hebræos observatum sit haud facile dixerim. Narrant Judæi collocaris in cubili novis conjugibus hos so- dales extra thalamum stetisse, ac deinde in thalamum re- gressos ad cognoscenda signa illa de quibus agitur Deut. XXII, 17. Apud Pollucem invenio καλᾶτῳ δὲ τις τῶν νυμφίε Φίλων κὶ θυρωρός, ὁ ταῖς θύραις ἐφεστηκὼς κὶ ἔιργων τὰς γυναῖκας βοηθεῖν τῇ νύμφῃ βοώσῃ. Hac autem comparatione Christus, omissis jejuniis Pharisæicis, de quibus egerat antehac, pro- prie respondet Baptistæ discipulis, ostendens causam pro- pter quam ipsi jejunarent in suos discipulos nunc quidem non congruere: sed ventura tempora, cum ipsi quoq; magi- stro orbati, non jejunia tantum, luctus scilicet signa, sed graviora etiam tolerarent. Æquum igitur esse, quos tam a- certa manerent, eos interim frui brevis gaudii interusurio. Sic obiter Bapistæ discipulis in mentem revocatur ipsius Ba- pistæ dictum qui Jesum νυμφίε nomine designaverat: & lo- cus Oseæ II. 16.

Πενθεῖν] Jejunia luctus signa, aut magni periculi 1. Macc. III. 17. c. IV. 47. 2. Maccab. XIII, 12. 1. Sam. XIV. 12. un- de Sabbato jejunare religio erat Judæis, quia sabbatum læti- tiæ dicatum. Quare peccatum est à Romanis Scriptoribus i- gnorantia moris Judaici, aut certe, vox Sabbati per abusionē sumta pro quovis religioso die cum ita scribit Martialis: Et jejunia sabbatariorum.

Persius autem: Exercent ubi festamero pede sabbata reges. Nam nudipedalia certum est dies esse jejuniorum. Christia- ni Judæorum exemplo à jejuniis abstinuerunt diebus Do- minicis & tota Pentecoste, quia totum illud tempus quin- quaginta dierum post Pascha, non minus quam Domi- nici dies, consecrati erant memoriæ resurrectionis. κᾀ τότε νηςεύσουσι] Sæpissime in luctu erunt, interque multa incommoda etiam fame & siti torquebuntur, 1. Cor. IV. 11. 2. Cor. VI. 5. c. XI, 27. Sed & jejunia sibi indicent Act. X. 30. XIII. 2. a. XIV. 22. 1. Cor. VII. 5, Ostendit autem in sequentibus Christus factum Dei benignitate ne tanti la- bores discipulos suos exciperent adhuc infirmos. Rupertus: Plane jejunabunt in illis proxime venturis diebus, cum ablatus fuerit Sponsus, cum passus, mortuus, & sepultus resurrexerit & in cælum ascenderit, jam non ultra cum eis in hoc mundo cor- poraliter conversurus. B. Lyserus Harm. c. LXVI. col. 950. sensum dicit simplicissimum. Christum velle, ut pii lætentur, quando DEUS concedit nuptias, hoc est, læta tempora, juxta illud: Tu quamcunque DEUS tibi fortunaverit horam, grata sume manu. Postea quando aufertur sponsus, hoc est, quando objiciuntur adversitates, tum sint patientes, orent, Deum invo- cent, & ut preces sint ardentiores jejunia adjungant. Sed specialis hic prædictio est, tempus venturum, cum sponsus à discipulis thalami filiis vel ministris nuptialibus per mortem auferetur, & tunc lugen- dum & jejunandum fore iisdem: quod explicat Christus Joh. XVI. 20. ut in mundum venerat per exitum à Patre, at carnis nostræ assumtionem Joh. I. 14. c. XVI. 18. Ebr. II. 14. 16. discipulis aderat per sua- vem conversationem, salutarem informationem, & illustrem divinæ gloriæ manifestationem Joh. I. 14. II. 11. ita auferendus erat ab iisdem per mundi relictio- nem, & regressum ad Patrem, Cap. XVI: 18. quod ubi discipulis suis diceretur, tristitia cor ipsorum reple- vit v. 6. Idq; hic innuitur: veniunt autem dies, id est tempus erit, cum auferetur a filiis sponsi sponsus, tunc jejunabunt, id est, lugebunt. Filios vero thalami, in- quit Chrys. in Cat. Corderi, omnes quidem eos in- telligit, qui in ipsum crediderant, præcipue vero divi- nos ejus discipulos atque Apostolos. Ait atq; : quamdiu cum discipulis sum necesse est gaudere ipsos & exulta- re præsenti fructu conspectus convictusq; mei, qui sci- licet sponsus sum. Cum verò tempus passionis venerit assumtionisque ex ipsis mea, tunc sane jejunabunt fa- meq; ac siti conflictabuntur omnium odiis repulsi ja- ctatiq; Idem in Nicetæ Catena: Sermonem passionis præmittit, in mutuis eorum contradictionibus erudi- ens discipulos, exercensq; eos ad ea, quæ acerbiora vi- debantur, meditanda. Illud etenim ex nunc ad eos di- cere grave erat nimium ac onerosum: quandoquidem etiam multo post eis dictu illos turbavit, ad alios igitur dictum est, atq; ita toleratu levius illis factu: verum quonia verosimile erat ob passione Joannis eos insole- scere, inde hanc illorum timorē deprimit. Non dicit, cum ab illis discesserit, nec cum mortuus fuerit, sed cū ablatus fuerit significans de illis ipsis Pharisæis, qui- buscum loquebatur de medio tollendū, ut hic notat Maldonatus. Qui tamē in eo fallitur, quod cū Pha- risæis hic Christū loquutum putat. Quod de priori qæstione quidem constat: hic autem discipulos Jo- hannis hoc dubium de jejunio Christo proposuisse testis est Matthæus, non Pharisæos: quod Maldena- tus quidem ita è collatione loci Luc. V. 33. explicat, quod discipuli Iohannis instigantibus Pharisæis Chri- stum accesserint, atq; ideo Lucas Pharisæos accessisse dicat: S. Augustinus vero l. II. de consens. Ev. c. 27. ita conciliat, utrosq; accessisse, sed Lucam solos Phari- sæos, Mattheum solos discipulos Johannis nominasse. Verum enim vero diversas esse, etsi maxime similes historias, Matthæi & Lucæ, è circumstantia tempo- ris in Harmonia Evangelica ostendimus.

## 9:16
Verse 16. No one puts a piece of unshrunk cloth on an old garment. The old Latin interpreter of Mark expressed this passage excellently and in the best Latin: No one sews a patch of raw cloth onto an old garment. For Horace also said to sew on a patch. And raw cloth, ἄγραφος, is never fulled, for the jurists also contrast new garments with fulled ones: and what is here ῥάκος ἄγραφος, Luke called ἱμάτιον και-

τὸν: just as the Syrian also translates this here: Tertullian, book III against Marcion, ἐπίβλημα is a patch, συμβολὴ Exodus chapters XXVI, XXVIII, & XXXVI. For it takes away the fullness from the garment] πλήρωμα is the nominative, for αὐτῶ understand τῶ ῥάκες. αἴρει ἀπὸ τῶ ἱματίε is said elliptically for τί ἀπὸ τῶ ἱματίω: just as elsewhere we shall show below in chapter XXVII. 9 that τινὲς, when ἀπὸ follows, is accustomed to be understood. And thus the Syrian understood all these things. But here πλήρωμα signifies the seam or joining of a raw cloth with an old garment, after the example of the Hebrews, among whom מלאים or מלאות are called seams, and מלא to join, as in Exodus XXV. 7 and XXVIII. 17, from which origin the Syrian placed the name both here and in Mark. The teachers of the Hebrews say that everything which fills a concavity is called מלאת or מלאו or מלאים. With the word מלאו, although in a slightly different sense, the LXX also translated πλήρωμα in Canticles V. 12. That seam is therefore said to tear away a part of the garment, that is, to give cause for a rupture. A not dissimilar sentiment exists in Philo where he explains the law which forbids wool and linen to be woven together: for even in these, not only is some corruption incompatible, but also the mastery of the one, when it is drawn through, will produce a tearing rather than a union.

Latin:

Vers. 16. ὐδεὶς δὲ ἐπιβάλλει ἐπίβλημα ῥάκυς ἀγνάφου ἐπὶ ἱματίῳ παλαιῷ] Optime & Latinissime hunc locū expressit vetus Marci inte pre. Latinus: Nemo assumentum panni rudis assuit vestimento veteri, Nam pannum assuere etiam Hora- tius dixit. Et rudis pannus ἄγραφος nunquam interpo'a- tus, nam & jurisconsulti nova vestimenta opponunt inter- polis: & Lucas quod hic est ῥάκος ἄγραφος dixit ἱμάτιον και-

τὸν: quomodo & Syrus hic vertit: Tertullianus plagulam III. in Marcionem ἐπίβλημα est συμβολὴ מחברו Exo- di capp XXVI. XXVIII. & XXXVI. αἴρει γὰρ τὸ πλήρωμα αὐτῶ ἀπὸ τῶ ἱματίω] πλήρωμα est no- minativus, αὐτῶ intellige τῶ ῥάκες. αἴρει ἀπὸ τῶ ἱματίε dictũ ἐλλειπτικῶς pro τί ἀπὸ τῶ ἱματίω : sicut & alibi τινὲς, cu:n ἀπὸ sequitur, subaudiri solere infra ostendemus cap. XXVII. 9. Atq; ita hæc omnia accepit Syrus. Significat autem hic πλή- ρωμα commissuram sive juncturam rudis panni cum veste vetere Hebræorum exemplo, apud quos מלאים sive מלאות dicuntur commissuræ & מלא committere ut Exodi XXV. 7. & XXVIII. 17. cujus originis nomen etiam Syrus tum hic, tum apud Marcum posuit. Hebræorum ma- gistri omne id quod concavitatem implet vocari ajunt מלאת aut מלאו aut מלאים. Voce מלאו, quanquam sensu paulum diverso πλήρωμα verterunt etiam LXX. Cant. V. 12. Dicitur igitur illa commissura partem ve- stis abrumpere, id est causam rupturæ dare. Exstat non dissimilis sententia apud Philonem ubi exponit legem quæ ἕρια κ̓ λινᾶ συνφαίνεσθαι vetat: κὲ γὰρ ἐπὶ τύτων ὐ μόνον ἡ διαφθορά τις ἀκοινώνητον, ἀλλὰ κὲ ἡ ἐπικράτεια θατέρυ, ῥῆξιν ἀπεργασομένη μᾶλλον ἡ ἕνωσιν ὅταν διηχέηται.

## 9:17
Verse 17. into old wineskins] Let us consider whether in Job XXXII. 19 new wineskins are said to be those in which there is new wine, the container for the content.

But these things are opposed to the Pharisees, who were laboring with untimely zeal in saving the traditions of the ancients, and it is taught that these are not to be joined with the new doctrine of the Gospel.

Grotius here, having followed Maldonatus, who renders this meaning: it is not fitting that a more difficult and entirely dissimilar way of life be suddenly prescribed to disciples accustomed to an easier way of living, lest they succumb to the difficulty and desist from a well-begun institute of life. For as yet, like a worn garment and old wineskins not yet stripped of the old custom of living, they were weak and could not contain new wine. Chrysostom preceded both in the Catena of Possinus on Peter: It is not necessary, he says, to burden the disciples with fasts and sleeping on the ground. For every excess has the power to corrupt. But there is a need to accustom them little by little, until they have progressed to perfection. Whence also that advantage will follow, that they may learn to use moderation themselves in teaching the nations and in performing the public office of preaching; and not terrify men at their very first entry, and overwhelm them, as if struck by a superimposed mass, with a multitude of sad admonitions importunately heaped together. Therefore, he called the seam of raw cloth and the new wine, fasting: but the old garment and the old wineskins, the infirmity and imperfection of the disciples. But Photius in the same Catena favors our explanation: He calls old wineskins men established in the state of the old law. But the new wine, the grace of Christ given to us later, or the new testament: Nyssenus also favors this in the Catena of Nicetas: It is fitting for the Gospel to put new wine into old wineskins: for wine recently pressed, by the fervor of the liquid implanted by nature, is full of spirit, and by natural motion boils up the dreggy impurities; that, however, in my judgment, is nothing else but the doctrine of the Holy Spirit (just as the Apostle says, fervent in spirit), which putrid and leaking wineskins, and those corrupted by infidelity, do not contain: but they are burst by the exuberance of the doctrine; therefore, if some more sublime sense of doctrine is put into them, they are burst by the gravity of the dogma, and they themselves perish through the disruption, and allow the grace of the spirit to flow away rashly. Basil the Great also favors this in the same place. Those who have been renewed by the spirit, and have drawn new wine from the true vine, are said to be new wineskins: but those who have not yet put off the old man are old wineskins, to whom the reception of new wine cannot be entrusted. And before them Tertullian, book III against Marcion, calling the old garment and old wineskins the law, and the new wine the Gospel. But B. Lyserus explains this most conveniently concerning traditions in the Harmony of the Gospels, chapter LXVI, column 951. Christ therefore wishes to say: as a new and raw patch does not fit a worn old garment,

for these two cannot bear each other, and a greater and worse tear is made, so the traditions of the fathers and your ancient superstitions do not fit my Evangelical doctrine, which two doctrines if anyone wishes to join, he will accomplish nothing but to introduce a shameful and laughable confusion of different religions. Which the blessed one excellently executes against Syncretistic confessions. And Maldonatus acknowledges that the discourse here is not about fasts which were both commanded in the old law and observed by all: But about the fasts of the Pharisees and the disciples of John, which were not commanded, nor common, but voluntary, and proper to them, by which they boasted themselves to be Pharisees, that is, singular, and holier than others, Luke XVIII. 11, 12.

PART IV. The resuscitation of the daughter of a certain Prince, and the healing of the woman with the issue of blood.

Latin:

Vers. 17. εἰς ἀσκὺς παλαιὺς] Cogitemus an apud Jobum XXXII. 19. utres novi dicantur hi in quibus est vinum no- vum, continens pro contento.

Opponuntur autem hæc Pharisæis, qui intem- pestivo zelo in salvandis veterum traditionibus la- borabant, easque cum nova Evangelii doctrina conjungendas non esse docetur.

Grotius hic Maldonatum sequutus, qui sensum hunc reddit, non convenire, ut discipulis faciliori vi- vendi rationi assuetis genus vitæ difficilius, prorfusq; dissimile subito præscribatur, ne difficultati succum- bant, & a bene cæpto vitæ instituto desistant. Adhuc enim sicut vestis attrita, & veteres utres vetere vi- vendi consuetudine nondum exutæ imbecilles erant, nec vinum novum capere poterant. Utrique autem præivit Chrysostomus in Caten. Petr. Possini: Non oportet, inquit, gravare discipulos jejuniis & humi- cubationibus. Excessus enim omnis corrumpendi vim habet. Sed opus est paulatim assuefacere ipsos, donec ad perfectum profecerint. Unde & illud conse- quetur commodum, ut congrua & ipsi moderatione uti discant in gentibus docendis, & fungendo publice prædicationis munere; neq; homines primo statim in- gressu terreant, multitudineque importune congesta tristium monitorum, quasi mole superjecta perculsos obruant. Commissuram ergo panni rudis, & novum vinum, jejunium appellavit: vetus autem vestimen- tum & utres veteres, infirmitatem imperfectionemq; discipulorum. Sed nostræ explicationi favet Pho- tius in eadem Catena: Utres veteres homines in sta- tu legis veteris constitutos, dicit. Vinum vero novum, Christi gratiam nobis posterius datam, aut novum testamentum: Favet & Nyssenus in Catena Nicetæ: Fetat Evangelium veteribus utribus novum vinum immittere: vinum enim recens expressum insito à na- tura liquoris fervore, spiritus plenum est, motuq; na- turali fæculentas sordes ebullit; illud vero, meo quidē judicio, nihil est aliud, nisi Sancti Spiritus doctrina, (quemadmodum ait Apostolus spiritu ferventes,) quam putridi diffluentesq; utres, & ab infidelitate corrupti non continent: sed doctrinæ exuberantia dis- rumpuntur; idcirco si sublimior aliquis ipsis inditur doctrinæ sensus, ex dogmatis rumpuntur gravitate, ipsiq; per disruptionem pereunt, & spiritus gratiam temere diffluere sinunt. Favet ibidem quoq; Basilius M. Qui spiritu renovati sunt, ac novum vinum ex vera vite hauserunt, utres novi esse dicuntur: qui ve- ro nondum veterem hominem exuerunt, utres sunt veteres, quibus novi vini susceptio credi non potest. Et ante illos Tertullianus l. III. contr. Marc. vete- rem vestem & veteres utres legem, & vinum novũ Evangelium dicens. Convenientiffime autem ex- plicat B. Lyserus de traditionibus in Harm. Evang. c. LXVI. col. 951. Vult ergo Christus dicere: ut vesti- mento attrito veteri non convenit pannus novus &

sedi- rudis, hæc enim duo se mutuo ferre non possunt, & fit scissura major ac deterior, ita patrum traditiones & antiquæ vestræ superstitiones non conveniunt doctri- næ meæ Evangelicæ, quas duas doctrinas si quis con- jungere velit, nihil efficiet, quam ut turpem & deri- dendam diversarum religionum confusionem introdu- cat. Quæ ὁ μακαρίτης eximie contra Syncretisti- cas confessiones exequitur. Et agnoscit Maldona- tus, sermonem hic non esse de jejuniis quæ & in veteri lege præcepta erant, & ab omnibus servabantur: Sed de Pharisæorum & discipulorũ Johannis jejuniis, quæ præcepta non erant, neq; communia, sed voluntaria, & illis propria, quibus se Pharisæos, id est, singulares, cæ- terisque sanctiores esse gloriabantur Luc. XVIII. 11. 12.

PARS IV. Filia Principis cujusdam resuscitatio, & mu- lieris hæmorrhousæ sanatio.

## 9:18
Verse 18. ruler] Namely of the synagogue, which Luke VIII. 41 adds. It is to be noted that the overseers of the Jewish Synagogue were men of proven probity, who were called by the Chaldean word פרנסין, that is, the shepherds, which word is also read more than once in the itinerary of Benjamin, or also רבים as the Syrian placed in Mark, or כששיש which is gatherers or arbiters, which is read in the Acts in the Syrian. The Hellenists called these rulers of the synagogue, as we are taught in Acts XIII. 15, where mention is made of several rulers of the synagogue of one and the same assembly. But among them one excelled, preferred to the others by the name of erudition, whose proper office it was to interpret the law and to compose prayers, as Justin against Trypho teaches us. He was called by the Hebrews ממנה, or also רש הקהל, in Syriac ריש כנושתא, in Greek ruler of the synagogue, which word the Syrian retained here, and by way of eminence the ruler of the synagogue, Luke XIII. 14. For Philo, the president, sometimes also the elder, to whom he attributes the teaching of things not known in the books, likewise, the discussing and the singing of the hymn. Such was that Jairus of Capernaum, where I believe there was only one synagogue. Wherefore there is no need for 'tis' to be understood here, since there was only one ruler, although he was the same as, as Mark says, 'one of the rulers of the synagogue.' Moreover, these rulers of the synagogue were not priests; for the work of the priests was assigned to the temple: these dwelt in their own cities. Indeed, even with the temple destroyed, the distinction of orders remained. Constantine, in the law which exists in the Theodosian Code under the title concerning the Jews, [mentions] priests and rulers of the synagogue and fathers of the synagogues, where the fathers are those whom I have called Parnasim; Epiphanius names rulers of the synagogue, priests, elders, and those who will be spoken of below, the Chazzanim. The same Epiphanius says elsewhere that the Ebionites had their own elders and rulers of the synagogue. And we read that the Emperor Severus, because he was believed to favor Judaism, was called by the reproachful name of ruler of the synagogue and high priest.

ἄρτι ἐτελεύτησεν] That is, she is now dead: for 'arti' does not always signify an exact time, but often the present, 'at the present time,' as the Greek scholiasts interpret, just as in Sophocles: 'for the man happens to be inside just now.' In Philostratus: 'just now about the time of the words.' And so it is mostly taken in these books, as above III. 15, XXVI. 53, John IX. 19, 25, XIII. 7, 33, 38, XVI. 12, and hence 'ap' arti' henceforth, and 'heos arti' hitherto, occur everywhere. Nor is this word to be interpreted otherwise here. For Jairus does not mean by this that much or little time had elapsed since his daughter died, but that at this very moment when he was addressing Christ, he did not doubt that she had expired, and that for the reason that she had already left her soul behind. For this is what Luke says, 'she was dying': to which corresponds the fact that while he was speaking with Christ, a messenger arrived affirming for certain what he had said by conjecture, namely that his daughter had expired: as the same Luke teaches us.

Ἐπίθες τὴν χεῖρά σου] It was known to the Jews that God was accustomed to show this honor to the prophets, so that He might confer His gifts upon others at the prayers of the prophets, the symbol of which was the laying on of hands. Thus Moses was commanded to lay hands upon Joshua, so that he might in that way receive the increases of the divine Spirit at the prayers of Moses, Num. XXVII. 18, 20. And Naaman the Syrian joins the invocation of God with the laying on of hands, 2 Kings V. 11. Closely, the laying on of hands designates the efficacy of divine power. For 'to stretch out the hand' is used of God in that sense in Acts IV. 30. Therefore, because divine power was invoked for another through prayers, the laying on of hands was customary with prayers. See what is below XIX. 13. However, Jairus seems to have thought less highly of Christ than others, who hoped for healing from Christ by touch alone, which Jairus, as is credible, thought could not be provided by Jesus except by prayers.

Jairus did not seek this laying on of hands, as if he thought less nobly of Christ than others, who hoped for health from Christ by mere touch, which he himself thought, as is credible to Grotius, could be provided by Jesus only through prayers. For why should he not have thought most nobly of Christ, since he acknowledged that he could overcome not only diseases, which had been believed by others until now, but even death itself; nor does there appear in the text any sign or trace that he believed there was need for the laying on of hands, as if he had thought that it could be provided only by prayers. For although it was known to the Jews concerning the Prophets that they were accustomed to confer their gifts upon others at their prayers: and it may be admitted that, because the divine power was invoked for another through prayers, the laying on of hands was customary along with prayers: yet Christ had already performed far greater things, and had shown himself by invincible proofs not merely a Prophet, but true GOD, and was known as the Son of GOD: nor did Jairus betake himself to him for the sake of his daughter being raised from the dead as to some Prophet, but because he believed him to be the Messiah himself, such as he had been publicly declared by John the Forerunner, and by God from heaven in the Jordan, and whom he could understand from his sermons, and miracles, and other γνωρίσματα [signs of recognition]: whom this Ruler of the Synagogue, without doubt, acknowledged from the Prophetic scriptures to be not a mere man, but true GOD. More frequent, says Grotius himself at v. 25. and greater miracles than the ancient examples had already caused Jesus to be believed by some to be not just a Prophet, but that promised Messiah. See John VII. 31. Therefore, that healing by the laying on of hands which was done by the Prophets, 2 Kings V. 11, was far different, not by their own power, but by divine efficacy obtained through prayers, than the restoration to life which he expected here, which he desired from Christ as the Messiah. Nor was that laying on of hands a symbol of prayers, but such a concurrence of the divine hand as that of a primary cause with a secondary, or a principal with an instrumental: because, as Grotius himself admits, the laying on of hands properly designates the efficacy of divine power, Acts IV. 30. And thus also Christ laid hands on children, Matthew XIX. 13, so as to designate divine power, not which he would summon from elsewhere through prayers, but which he himself would exercise for their blessing.

Latin:

Vers. 18. ἄρχων] Nimirum τῆς συναγωγῆς quod addit Lu- cas VIII. 41. Notandum est Synagogæ Judaicæ præpositos fuissse viros spectatæ probitatis, qui vocabantur Chaldaico vocabulo פרנסין id est οἱ ποιμαίνοντες, quæ vox & in itinerario Benjamini non semel legitur, aut etiam רבים ut Syrus apud Marcum posuit, aut כששיש quod est congregatores aut disceptatores, quod in Actis apud Syrum legitur. Hellenistæ hos vocabant ἀρχισυναγώγους ut doce- mur Act. XIII. 15. ubi plurium ἀρχισυναγώγων unius ejus- demq; cœtus fit mentio. Sed inter eos unus eminebat eru- ditionis nomine prælatus cæteris, cujus proprium erat mu- nus legem interpretari & preces concipere, ut Justinus ad- versus Tryphonem nos docet. Is Hebræis vocabatur ממנה, aut etiam רש הקהל, Syriace ריש כנושתא Græce ἄρχων τῆς συναγωγῆς, quam vocem hic Syrus reti- nuit, & καθ' ἐξοχὴν ὁ ἀρχισυνάγωγος Luc. XIII. 14. Philoni ὁ πρόεδρος, interdum etiam ὁ πρεσβύτατος, cui tribuit τὰ μὴ γνώριμα ἐν ταῖς βίβλοις ἀναδιδάσκειν, item, τὸ διαλέγεσθαι κὴ τὸν ὕμνον ἄδειν. talis fuit Jairus iste Capharnnumi, ubi unam duntaxat Synagogam fuisse arbitror. Quare ni- hil necesse est hic τὶς subaudiri, cum unus duntaxat ἄρχων fuerit, quamvis ille idem esset ut Marcus loquitur εἷς τῶν ἀρχισυναγώγων. Non erant autem isti archisynagogi sacer- dotes; nam sacerdotum opera templo erat assignata: isti in suis urbibus morabantur. Quin & diruto templo mansit ordinum discrimen. Constantinus in lege quæ extat Codi- cis Theodosiani titulo de Judæis Hiereos & Archisynagogos & patres synagogarum, ubi patres sunt quos dixi פרנסים, Epiphanius nominat ἀρχισυναγώγους, ἱερέας, πρεσβυτέρους, & de quibus infra dicetur ἀζανίτας. Idem Epiphanius alibi ait Ebionitis suos fuisse πρεσβυτέρους κὴ ἀρχισυναγώγους. Et Severum Imperatorem, quod Judaismo favere crederetur, legimus convitio archisynagogum & archierea fuisse ap- pellatum.

ἄρτι ἐτελεύτησεν] Id est, jam mortua est: Neque enim ἄρτι semper exactum tempus, sed sæpe præsens significat εἰς τὸ παρόν, ut interpretantur Græci Scholiastæ, quemad- modum apud Sophoclem: ἔνδον γὰρ ἀνὴρ ἄρτι τυγχάνει. Apud Philostratum: ἄρτι περὶ τὸν καιρὸν ῦ ῥημάτων. Atq; ita plerumq; in his libris sumitur, ut supra III. 15. XXVI. 53. Joh IX. 19. 25. XIII. 7. 33. 38. XVI. 12. & hinc ἀπ' ἄρτι de- inceps, & ἕως ἄρτι hactenus, passim occurrunt. Neq; aliter hic ea vox interpretanda est. Non enim hoc significat Jai- rus, multum parumve temporis effluxisse ex quo mortua sit filia, sed hoc ipso tempore cum Christum compellaret, non dubitare se quin exspirasset, idq; ideo quia jam animam a- gentem reliquerat. Hoc enim est quod ait Lucas, αὕτη ἀπέ- θνησκεν: cui convenit quod colloquenti cum Christo super- venit nuntius pro certo affirmans, quod ille ex conjectura dixerat, filiam scilicet exspirasse: ut nos idem Lucas docet.

Ἐπίθες τὴν χεῖρά σου] Notum erat Judæis, solere Deum pro- phetis hunc exhibere honorem, ut in alios dona sua con- ferret ad Prophetarum preces, quarum Symbolum erat ma- nuum impositio. Ita Moses Josuæ jussus erat manus impo- nere, ut ille ea ratione ad Mosis preces divini Spiritus aug- menta acciperet, Num. XXVII. 18. 20. Et Naaman Syrus invocationem DEI conjungit cum manuum impositione 2. Reg. V. 2. Proxime manuum impositio designat efficaciam divinæ potentiæ. Nam χεῖρα ἐκτεῖναι de Deo eum in sensum usurpatur Act. IV. 30. Ideo quia per preces divina potentia pro altero invocabatur, usitata erat cum precibus manuum impositio. Vide quæ infra XIX. 13. Videtur autem Jairus mi- nus præclare de Christo sensisse, quam alii, qui solo contactu sanitatem à Christo sperabant, quam Jairus, ut credibile est, arbitrabatur ab Jesu non nisi precibus posse præstari.

Non expetiit Jairus hanc χειροθεσίαν, quasi minus præclare de Christo senserit, quam alii, qui so- lo contactu sanitatem à Christo sperabant, quam ipse arbitraretur, ut credibile est Grotio, ab Jesu non nisi precibus posse præstari. Quidni enim præcla- rissime de Christo senserit, cum non morbos solum eum profligare posse, quod ab aliis hactenus cre- ditum, sed mortem etiam ipsam, agnoverit; neque de eo in textu vel vola vel vestigium apparet, quod manuum impositione ideo opus esse, credi- derit, quasi arbitratus fuerit, non nisi precibus id præstari posse. Etsi enim de Prophetis notum Judæis erat, quod ad eorum preces in alios dona sua con- ferre consueverint: atque admitti possit, ideo quia per preces divina potentia pro altero invocata fuit, usitatam fuisse, cum precibus, manuum impositionem: tamen longe majora jam patrârat Christus, ac se non Prophetam modo, sed verum DEUM docu- mentis invictis ostenderat, cognitusque DEI Fi- lius erat: nec Jairus ad eum se recepit filiæ resusci- tandæ à mortuis causa, ut Prophetam quendam, sed quod ipsum Messiam, qualis à Johanne Proto- baptista publice, & à Deo de cœlo declaratus in Jordane erat, & quem è concionibus, & miracu- lis, aliisque γνωρίσμασι intelligere poterant, esse crederet: quem non merum hominem, sed verum DEUM fore è Propheticis scripturis hic Archi- Synagogus, sine dubio, agnovit. Frequentiora, in- quid Grotius ipse ad v. 25. & majora veteribus ex- emplis miracula jam effecerant, ut à quibusdam Jesus non Propheta tantum, sed promissus ille Mes- sias crederetur. Vid. Joan. VII. 31. Longe ergo alia erat illa per impositionem manuum curatio, quæ à Prophetis fiebat 2.Reg. V. 11. non propria virtute, sed impetrata per preces divina efficacia, alia, quam hic expectabat, in vitam revocatio, quam à Chri- sto, ceu Messia, desiderabat. Neque illa manuum impositio precum Symbolum erat, sed concursus manus divinæ talis, qualis est causæ primæ cum me- dia, vel principalis cum instrumentali: quia, faten- te Grotio ipso, manuum impositio proprie designat divinæ potentiæ efficaciam, Act. IV. 30. Atque ita etiam Christus manus imponebat pueris Matth. XIX. 13. ut divinam potentiam, non quam aliun- de per preces accerseret, sed quam ipse ad benedi- ctionem ipsorum exerceret, designaret.

## 9:20
Vers. 20.

τẽ κρασπέδε τẽ ἱματίε ἀυτẽ] It may seem that what Malachi IV. 2 says about the Messiah is also looked to here: מרפא בכנפיו healing in his fringes. For in Deuteronomy XXII. 13, what is in Hebrew כנפות is in the LXX version κρασπέδων. And the Syriac below XIV. 36 translates the word κρασπέδε as כנפא. Moreover, it seems that both here and in the aforementioned place XIV. 26, and below XIII. 5, by the name κρασπέδων are understood συνεκδοχικῶς [by synecdoche] those filaments in the fringes which the Hebrews call ציצית: as also in Zechariah VIII. 23, where likewise in Hebrew it is כנף and in Greek κρασπέδε. Thus in the aforementioned place in Deuteronomy, for the Hebrew גדילים which signifies filaments, the Chaldean has placed כרוספדין which word is the very Greek κράσπεδον. This was, however, a peculiar mark of Israelite holiness.

What he compares here from Malachi IV. 2 is so far irrelevant; because it does not treat there of the fringes of the Messiah's garment, but of the wings of his grace, under which there is healing for us. But regarding the place itself, let those things be compared which we have said in the Annotations Anti-Grotianae on that passage.

Latin:

Vers. 20.

τẽ κρασπέδε τẽ ἱματίε ἀυτẽ] Videri potest & huc spectari quod de Messia dicit Malachias IV. 2. מרפא בכנפיו sanatio in fimbriis ejus. Nam Deut. XXII. 13. quod in Hebræo est כנפות in versione LXX. est κρασπέδων. Et Syrus infra XIV. 36. vocem κρασπέδε vertit כנפא. Videntur autem & hic & dicto loco XIV. 26. & infra XIII. 5. κρασπέδων nomi- ne συνεκδοχικῶς intelligi filamenta illa ἐν τοῖς κρασπέδοις quæ ציצית Hebræi vocant: ut & Zach. VIII. 23. ubi iti- dem in Hebræo est כנף in Græco κρασπέδε. Sic dicto Deu- teronomii loco pro Hebræo גדילים quod filamenta si- gnificat, Chaldæus posuit כרוספדין quæ vox est ipsa Græca κράσπεδον. Erat autem hæc peculiaris nota sancti- moniæ Israëliticæ.

Quod hic confert è Mal. IV, 2. hactenus alie- num est; quia ibi non de vestis Messiæ fimbriis, sed de alis gratiæ ejusdem, sub quibus sanatio nobis est, agitur. De loco vero ipso conferantur, quæ in Annot. Anti-Grot. ad illum diximus.

## 9:21
Vers. 21.

ἐὰν μόνον ἅψωμαι τẽ ἱματίε ἀυτẽ σωθήσομαι] This woman seems to have thought partly correctly, partly incorrectly about Christ: Correctly, because she understood that Christ, as much as he was, was full of divine power, and just as the ointment poured upon the head of the Priest flowed down to the very lowest edges of his garment, so from him a healing force emanated on all sides. Incorrectly, because she thought this emanation to be natural rather than of the will and dispensation of Christ himself, just as many philosophers said that God does all things φύσει [by nature] and not βυλήσει [by will], whom the writer of the responses to the Greeks solidly refutes. Hence she had conceived some hope that she could steal health from him secretly. But that Christ allowed himself to be touched by this woman, he did nothing in that matter against the law, as was said above concerning similar deeds: although that also can be added which Tertullian observes against Marcion, that the solemn flow from the duty of nature, not from the vice of infirmity, is contained in the prohibition of the law. Grotius thinks the woman thought incorrectly about Christ in that she believed a certain natural emanation rather than one of his own will and dispensation, and from there conceived some hope that she could steal health from him secretly. But whence is it certain that she believed this? For she did not attribute health to the bare touch, but was certain that her faith would not be ineffectual, given her earnest desire for his help. Therefore he also honors her with that eulogy, the Knower of Hearts, to whom without doubt more must be attributed than to the Grotian suspicion: by which a philosophical [notion] is attached to this remarkable faith, and the same vain persuasion, namely that God does all things by nature and not by will, which had never entered the mind of this woman. Take heart, daughter, he says, your faith has saved you. For he knew that the eyes of the Lord look upon faith, Jer. V. 3, and that without faith it is impossible to please GOD, Heb. XI. 6. Nor did he merely understand that a bodily touch could provide anything, since even the impious touched Christ in the days of his flesh; but she trusted solely in his grace, and hoped that her faith would not be rejected in the least. Therefore she did not want to steal health from Christ, because she firmly believed that Christ would acknowledge that touch, because it proceeded from true faith, and she piously resolved with herself that she would obtain bodily health from this, unless the concession were contrary to her eternal salvation. For who will persuade their own mind that they can steal anything from the Lord, whom they do not doubt knows even the secrets of the heart?

Latin:

Vers. 21.

ἐὰν μόνον ἅψωμαι τẽ ἱματίε ἀυτẽ σωθήσομαι] Videtur hæc fœmina partim recte, partim non recte de Christo sensisse: Recte, quod Christum totum quantus erat plenum esse in- telligeret divinæ virtutis, & quemadmodum unguentum fusum in caput Sacerdotis ad imas usque vestimenti oras defluebat, ita ab ipso undique vim mitificam emanare. Non recte, quod hanc emanationẽ putaret naturalem magis esse quam arbitrii ac dispensationis Christi ipsius, sicut Philoso- phi multi dicebant Deum agere omnia φύσει ὲ βυλήσει, quos solide refutat scriptor responsionum ad Græcos. Hinc spem aliquam conceperat sanitatem se posse ab ipso furtim subducere. Quod autem Christus ab hac fœmina se passus est contingi, nihil ea in re fecit contra legem, ut supra de fa- ctis similibus dictum est: quanquam & illud addi potest quod adversus Marcionem Tertullianus observat, legis in- terdicto contineri profluvium solenne ex officio naturæ, non ex vitio valetudinis. Non recte sensisse fœminam de Christo Grotius in eo putat, quod emanationem quandam naturalem potius, quam arbitrii ac dispensationis ipsius credide- rit, atque inde spem aliquam conceperit, sanitatem se posse ab ipso furtim subducere. Sed unde id constat, ipsam ita credidisse? Neque enim contactui nudo salutem tribuebat, sed quod fidem suam ab anim- adverso desiderio opitulationis ejusdem, non irri- tam fore, certa esset. Ideo etiam elogio illo conde- corat eam ὁ καρδιογνώστης, cui sine dubio plus tri- buendum, quam Grotianæ suspicioni: qua Philo- sophica fidei huic insigni affingitur, eademque vana persuasio, Deum nempe agere omnia Φύσει, & θε- λήσει, quæ nunquam huic fœminæ in mentem ve- nerat. Confide, inquit filia, fides tua te servavit. No- verat enim oculos Domini respicere fidem Jer. V. 3. ac sine fide impossibile esse placere DEO, Ebr. XI.6. Neque contactum solum corporalem præstare quic- quam posse, quam etiam impii in diebus carnis Christum attigerint, probe intelligebat; sed con- fidebat unice in gratia ejus, ac fidem suam minime reprobatum iri sperabat. Non ergo furtim à Chri- sto sanitatem subducere volebat, quia Christum il- lum contactum, quod ex vera fide proficiscatur, a- gniturum firmiter credebat, & hinc sanitatem cor- poralem, nisi æternæ saluti ejus concessio adversa fuerit, sese consecuturam, pie secum statuebat. Quis enim furtim Domino, quem etiam occulta cordis novisse haud dubitat, se aliquid subducere posse, animo persuadebit suo?

## 9:22
Vers. 22.

Θάρσει θύγατερ, ἡ πίστις σου σέσωκέ σε] Θάρσει, as above, means 'be of good courage.' For those who act secretly are accustomed to tremble, fearing lest they be caught, just like this woman, who feared that Christ might shun her touch as unclean. But Christ, while correcting her error and yet showing what was to be commended in her, signifies that it was not the touch, but that remarkable persuasion concerning divine power that would profit her for health: which was a presage, as we have already said several times, of the forgiveness of sins and of obtaining eternal salvation through obedient trust in God and His Christ: whence it also came about that this saying of Christ was frequent in the mouths of Christians, which Celsus even cast at the Christians, as if it were a sign of a mind not supported by reasons, but occupied by a certain blind assent. Responding to this in two places, Origen confesses that the doctrine of Christ was delivered simply, as it ought to be salutary not only for men who have leisure for the study of letters, but for anyone from the common people, even those most occupied, from whom it would be unfair to demand subtlety of disputation: meanwhile, however, that this συγκατάθεσιν or κατάληψιν rests upon the most certain arguments, on one hand the power of God, on the other the consenting testimony of the best of men. Clement, however, explaining the same saying, rightly warns: οὐχ’ ἁπλῶς τοὺς ὁτωσῦν πιστεύσαντας σωθήσεσθαι, but only those who have added pious works (given the opportunity, of course) to their faith: that is, those who have had a living and efficacious faith. Concerning Pythagoras, Iamblichus says: ὑπῆρχε δὲ αὐτῶ ὑπὸ τῆς εὐσεβείας κὶ ἡ περὶ τῶν Θεῶν πίστις. Παρῆγγελλε γὰρ περὶ Θεῶν μηδὲν θαυμαστὸν ἀπισεῖν, μηδὲ περὶ θείων δογμάτων ὡς πάντα τῶν Θεῶν δυναμένων. See also Dan. VI. 23. Although the word θάρσει implies this at the same time: 'be of good courage,' it nevertheless primarily commands trust, and not merely a persuasion concerning divine power, which without trust profits nothing, since even demons are most persuaded of the power of GOD: by which, therefore, it is rashly asserted that Daniel was delivered from the lions' den, Dan. VI. 23. For Daniel trusted in his GOD firmly, which the emphasis of the words imports: הֵימִן בֵאלָהֵהּ, which word implies trust, by which the mind is nourished, and which is firm and certain, whence also the particle אָמֵן of one affirming and swearing by the truth is derived, and it is applied to the trust of Abraham which was imputed to him for righteousness, Gen. XV. 6. the explanation of this Mosaic saying, Cajetan on Gen. XV. Moses does not say that Abraham believed GOD, but in GOD: for this is more. For to believe GOD is to have faith in His words as truthful: but to believe in GOD adds, moreover, trust in GOD. Without trust, no one can be of good courage, and from trust alone flows tranquility of mind and conscience Rom. V. 1. The woman with the issue of blood did not tremble, like those who act secretly, who, because they do what is not permitted, fear lest they be caught: for she was attempting nothing illicit; and who would have feared that Christ would decline her touch as impious, whom she knew had come for the sake of cleansing our impurity? But that is now clearly contrary to Evangelical and Apostolic doctrine, that we obtain the forgiveness of sins and eternal salvation through obedience to GOD and trust in His Christ, i.e., through a persuasion concerning the power of GOD and Christ, and the obedience which is rendered to the precepts of GOD and Christ: because that persuasion is not the trust which, as the whole Scripture testifies, is necessary for justification and salvation: for that is in the intellect, this in the will; that has for its object the power of GOD, this the grace of GOD founded upon the merit of Christ; that of itself does not bring about application; this consists properly in the very apprehension of the grace of GOD and the merit of Christ: Nor does our obedience, or the pursuit of good works, contribute any ἐπιβάλλον μέρος [contributing part] to our justification or salvation, or in any way effect its attainment: because we are both justified and saved χωρὶς ἔργων [without works], by mere grace, and through the sole obedience of Christ apprehended by faith, as the Apostle testifies Rom. III. IV. V. Eph. II. III. Gal. II. III. Tit. III. &c. So that that philosophical συγκατάθεσις [assent], which is supported by reasons, has no place here, where one must believe the word of GOD solely on account of the authority of GOD who speaks, not indeed with a blind, but with a most sighted assent, because the eyes of the mind illuminated by GOD Himself are needed for that faith which rests ἀμεταπτώτως [unwaveringly] upon the word of GOD, and beholds His power, grace, and truth with an unswerving, if I may say so, eye, believing in hope against hope, and is the ἔλεγχος [conviction] τῶν μὴ βλεπομένων [of things not seen]: so for obtaining justification and eternal salvation, mere συγκατάθεσις [assent] or κατάληψις [apprehension], however much it may rely on the most certain arguments superior to any exception—which indeed can by no means be had in divine matters—and the consenting testimony of the best men, since even the best men, although they may affirm something consistently, can be subject to error and have no privilege of infallibility, is by no means sufficient. For first of all, there is need of that which Christ demands here, Θάρσει [Take courage], CONFIDE [TRUST], or trust, which is the ὑπόστασις [assurance] τῶν ἐλπιζομένων [of things hoped for], and according to him is required for the definition of faith as the ἔλεγχος [conviction] τῶν μὴ βλεπομένων [of things not seen]: without which it is impossible to please GOD, Heb. XI. 1. 6. For what kind of faith is justifying faith must be learned not from the School of Pythagoras, or from Iamblichus, but solely from the School of the Holy Spirit and the Prophetic and Apostolic doctrine: which does not confuse faith with obedience, but distinguishes it from it; nay, the Apostle excludes obedience and pious works from justification, when he teaches that GOD justifies the ungodly, τῷ μὴ ἐργαζομένῳ πιστεύοντι δὲ [to him who does not work but believes], by imputing faith to him for righteousness Rom. IV. 5. although in the meantime he does not separate good works from justifying faith, as they do not indeed precede the one to be justified, yet they altogether follow the one who is justified. Which was also the admonition of Clement. But these things [are] for another time against the Socinians, Arminians, Papists, and the Calixtine innovators, and Grotius himself, who complies with them, expressly: Cons. Exegem. Aug. Confess. art. IV. Christ was here requiring faith alone, Θάῤῥει [Take courage], trust, daughter; He was looking solely to faith in the woman with the issue of blood; He was proclaiming faith alone as the reconciler of health, which were meant to be not omens, but proofs, that we obtain the salvation of the soul by faith alone, if indeed we obtain even the health of the body itself through faith. Take courage, He says, daughter, your faith has made you whole. Feeling the approach of the woman suffering from the flow of blood, Christ did not disdain her, but healed her and called her daughter, since she is faithful, says Cyril. He wished to persuade others also who were standing around, as Chrysostom [says] here, of what it was in their interest to know, ὅτι δυνάτός ἐστι πάντα ποιεῖν ἀναλόγως τῇ πίστει τῶν προσερχομένων αὐτῷ [that He is able to do all things in proportion to the faith of those coming to Him], that there was in Him the power of the trust which each one had conceived concerning Him: and to which, being animated, he would approach Him, responding exactly. Jerome says, He did not say, your faith is going to make you whole, but has made you whole: In that you believed, you are already made whole. Cons. what was said to v. 2. That Christ looked only to faith is confirmed for Jairus immediately after the said command in Mark V. 30. μόνον πίστευε [only believe], and Luke VIII. 50. μόνον πίστευε, καὶ σωθήσεται [only believe, and she shall be saved]. Which is therefore rightly urged by our Theologians also for the justification of faith alone. Which consequence Bellarmine himself admits in his book on Justification, ch. X. In Matt. XV. and Mark VII. the efficacy of obtaining health is openly attributed to faith. Nor should one respond that it is one thing to speak of justification, another of the curing of a bodily disease. For the Lord attributes both kinds of health to faith in exactly the same words: for to the sinful woman He said: your faith has made you whole, Luke VII. and to the woman cured of the flow of blood He similarly said: your faith has made you whole. This is Bellarmine.

Latin:

Vers. 22.

Θάρσει θύγατερ, ἡ πίστις σου σέσωκέ σε] Θάρσει ut supra si- gnificat, bono esto animo. Solent enim trepidare, qui clam aliquid agunt, timentes, ne deprehendantur, sicut hæc mu- lier, quæ verebatur, ne Christus contactum suum ut impu- rum declinaret. At Christus simul errorem ipsius corrigens, & tamen quid in ea probandum esset ostendens, significat, non contactum, sed insignem illam de divina potentia per- suasionem ipsi ad sanitatem profuturam: quod præsagium fuit, ut aliquoties jam diximus, veniæ delictorum & salutis æternæ consequendæ per obedientem in Deum & Chri- stum ejus fiduciam: unde etiam factum est, ut hoc Christi effatum frequens esset in ore Christianorum, quod etiam Celsus Christianis objecit, quasi signum animi non rationi- bus fulti, sed cæco quodam assensu occupati. Huic duobus locis respondens Origenes fatetur, doctrinam Christi sim- pliciter traditam, ut quæ salutifera esse deberet non homi- nibus tantum studio literarum vacantibus, sed quibusvis de plebe, etiam maxime occupatis, à quibus iniquum esset exigere disputandi subtilitatem: Interim vero istam συγκα- τάθεσιν sive κατάληψιν niti certissimis argumentis, hinc Dei potentia, inde virorum optimorum consentiente testimo- nio. Clemens autem idem dictum explicans recte monet: οὐχ’ ἁπλῶς τὸς ὁτωσῦν πισεύσαντας σωθήσεσθαι, sed eos de- mum, qui pia opera (data scilicet occasione) fidei adjunxe- rint: hoc est, eos, qui fidem habuerint vivam atque efficacē. De Pythagora Jamblichus ὑπῆρχε δὲ αὐτῶ ὑπὸ τῆς εὐσεβείας κὶ ἡ περὶ τῶν Θεῶν πίστις Παρῆγγελλε γὰρ περὶ Θεῶν μηδὲν θαυμαστὸν ἀπισεῖν, μηδὲ περὶ θείων δογμάτων ὡς πάντα τῶν Θεῶν δυναμένων, Vide & Dan. VI. 23. Quanquam verbum θάρσει id simul inferat: bono esto animo, id tamen imprimis fiduciam impe- rat, non autem solum de divina potentia persuasio- nem, quæ sine fiducia nihil prodest, quum & dæmo- nes de potentia DEI quam persuasissimi sint: qua proinde temere asseritur, Danielem è lacu leonum liberatum esse, Dan. VI.23. Confidebat enim Da- niel DEO suo firmiter, quod emphasīs verborum importat: הֵימִן בֵאלָהֵהּ quod verbum fiduciam, quæ animus nutritur, quesq; firma est & certa, unde etiam אָמֵן particula affirmantis & jurantis per ve- ritatem est, infert, & de Abrahami fiducia quæ in justitiam ipsi imputata Gen. XV. 6. adhibetur. In cujus dicti Mosaici enarratione Cajetan. ad Gen. XV. Moses non dicit Abrahamum credidisse DEO, sed in DEO: hoc enim plus est. Nam credere DEO est fidem habere illius verbis ut veracibus: credere autem in DEO insuper addit fiduciam in DEO. Sine fiducia bono animo nemo esse potest, & ex sola fiducia tranquillitas animi & conscientiæ re- dundat Rom. V. 1. Non trepidavit hæmorrhousa, ceu illi, qui clam agunt, quod non licet, timentes ne deprehendantur: nihil enim illiciti tentabat; & qui verita fuisset, ne Christus contactum suum ut impium declinaret, quem impuritatis nostræ mun- dandæ causa venisse non nesciebat? Id vero do- ctrinæ Evangelicæ & Apostolicæ plane adversum jam est, quod veniam delictorum & salutem æter- nam consequamur per obedientiam in DEUM & Christum ejus fiduciam h. e. per persuasionem de DEI & Christi potentia, & obedientiam, quæ præ- ceptis DEI & Christi præstatur: quia illa persua- sio non est fiducia, qua ad justificationem & sa- lutem, teste universa Scriptura, opus est: illa e- nim in intellectu, hæc in voluntate est, illa pro objecto habet DEI potentiam, hæc DEI gratiam in Christi merito fundatam; illa per se non infert applicationem; hæc in ipsa apprehensione gratiæ DEI & meriti Christi proprie consistit: Neque obedientia nostra, vel studium bonorum operum aliquod ἐπιβάλλον μέρος confert ad nostri seu justificationem, seu salutem, aut ullo modo ad eam consequendam facit: quia & justificamur & salva- mur χωρὶς ἔργων, ex mera gratia, & per unicam Christi obedientiam fide apprehensam, teste Apo- stolo Rom. III. IV. V. Eph. II. III. Gal. II. III. Tit. III. &c. Ut philosophica illa συγκατάθεσις, quæ rationibus fulcitur, hic locum nullum habeat, u- bi verbo DEI solum propter auctoritatem dicentis DEI credendum, non sane cæco, sed maxime o- culato assensu, quia oculis animi à DEO ipso illu- minatis opus est ad eam fidem, quæ verbo DEI ἀμεταπτώτως innititur, ac potentiam, gratiam, & veritatem irretorto, ut ita dicam, oculo intue- tur, credens in spem contra spem, & τῶν μὴ βλεπο- μένων ἔλεγχος est: ita ad justificationem ac salu- tem æternam consequendam sola συγκατάθεσις aut κατάληψις quantumvis argumentis nitatur certissimis omni exceptione superioribus, quale profecto haberi minime potest in rebus divinis, & ad fidem ingenerandam consentiens optimorum virorum testimonium, quum optimi etiam viri, et- si consentienter aliquid affirment, errori obnoxii esse possint, nec infallibilitatis ullum habeant pri- vilegium, neutiquam sufficit. Nam imprimis opus est eo, quod hic exigit Christus, Θάρσει CONFI- DE, seu fiducia, quæ ὑπόστασις est τῶν ἐλπιζομέ- νων, & juxta eum ἐλέγχῳ τῶν μὴ βλεπομένων ad fidei definitionem requiritur: sine qua DEO pla- cere impossibile est, Ebr. XI. 1. 6. Qualis enim fides justificans sit, non è Pythagoræ Schola, aut è Jamblicho, sed unice è Schola Spiritus S. & doctrina Prophetica, & Apostolica discendum est: quam non cum obedientia confundit, sed ab eadem distin- guit, imo obedientiam & opera pia à justificatione excludit Apostolus, cum DEUM justificare impium docet, τῷ μὴ ἐργαζομένῳ πιστεύοντι δὲ non operanti, credenti autem fidem imputando ad ju- stitiam Rom. IV. 5. etsi interim bona opera à fide justificante non separet, utpote quæ non quidem justificandum antecedunt, omnino ta- men justificatum sequuntur. Quod Clementis etiam monitum fuit. Sed hæc alias contra Soci- nianos, Arminianos, Pontificios, & Novatores Calixtinos, ipsumque etiam Grotium illis obste- qui- trteantem ex professo: Cons. Exegem. Aug. Confess. artic. IV. Fidem unice hic Christus re- quirebat, Θάῤῥει conside filia; fidem unice respi- ciebat in muliere hæmorrhousa: fidem unice ceu sanitatis conciliatricem deprædicabat, quæ non præsagia, sed documenta esse debebant, fide sola nos salutem animæ consequi, siquidem ipsam et- iam sanitatem corporis per fidem consequimur. Confide, inquit, filia, fides tua te salvam fecit Mu- lieris sanguinis fluxu laborantis accessum Christus sentiens, non est eam dedignatus, sed curavit & siliam vocavit, quippe quæ fidelis est, ait Cyrillus. Persuadere aliis quoque circumstantibus, ut hic Chrysostomus, voluit, quod scire intererat ipsorum, ὅτι δυνάτός ἐστι πάντα ποιεῖν ἀναλόγως τῇ πί- στει τῶν προσερχομένων αὐτῷ inesse in se potentiam fiduciæ, quam quisque de eo præcepisset: quaque a- nimatus ad eum accederet exacte respondentem. Hiesonymus, Non dixit, inquit, fides tua te sal- va factura est, sed salvam te fecit: In eo, quod credidisti jam salva facta. Cons. quæ ad v. 2. di- cta. Solam fidem Christum respexisse etiam Jai- ro immediate post dictum mandatum confirmat Marc. V. 30. μόνον πίστευε, & Luc. VIII. 50. μόνον πίστευε, καὶ σωθήσεται. Quod proinde recte à no- stris Theologis etiam urgetur pro justificatione solius fidei. Quam consequentiam Bellarm. ipse admittit lib. de Justif. c. X. Matth. XV. & Marc. VII. aperte tribuitur fidei efficacia impetrandæ sa- nitatis. Neque respondere debet, aliud esse loqui de justificatione, aliud de curatione morbi corpo- ralis. Nam Dominus iisdem plane verbis tribuit fi- dei utramque sanitatem: peccatrici enim dixit: fi- des tua te salvam fecit, Luc. VII. & mulieri cura- tæ à fluxu sanguinis similiter dixit: fides tua te sal- vam fecit. Hæc Bellarminus.

## 9:23
Verse 23.

Τοὺς αὐλητὰς [The flute players] Josephus also teaches us in book III of the Jewish War that flutes were customary in mourning among the Jews. But I think those are mistaken who think this custom was derived by the Hebrews from profane nations. For it has been rightly demonstrated by others that traces of this custom exist in the most ancient writings of the Hebrews: just as there is also mention of mourning women in Jeremiah IX. 17. nor indeed is any prohibition of this matter found in the law. Finally, the whole funeral procession was not a novel invention, but relied on the example of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph: by which is refuted the error of Tacitus, who thought that the care of the body and the custom of burying rather than burning came to the Jews from the Egyptians. For it appears from sacred history that long before the Hebrews had immigrated into Egypt, the same custom was practiced by their own ancestors. But it is likely that funeral rites, and especially the custom of burying bodies (which among all nations is more ancient than cremation), have their origin in the first times after the flood, for the detestation of τῆς ἀνθρωποφαγίας, which among other crimes of extreme savagery had invaded the primeval world. For the verses of Moschion show that the report of that matter also reached the Greeks:

And they led the life of the leaders to a gentle way of living; and from this he ordained by law to cover the dead with tombs, and to distribute dust upon the unburied corpses, and not to leave in sight the impious reminder of the former feast.

Thus also the seven-day mourning, mention of which is in the history of the burial of Jacob, Gen. 50 verse 10, and in Josephus at the end of the sixth and in book XVII of the Antiquities, remained among the Jews, not from any law, but from an ancient and not forbidden custom. Hence the son of Sirach [says] πένθος νέκρου ἑπτὰ ἡμέραι c. XXII. 13. Moreover, there is a record in Josephus of the same custom being observed even to the latest times: and in Clement, Stromata book four. But we learn from Marcellinus, book XIX, that not even this was peculiar to the Jews, but was used by other nations as well; the words are thus: For a space of seven days, the men all indulged in feasts by messes and companies, dancing and singing a certain sad kind of dirge, lamenting the royal youth: but the women with miserable wailing bewailed with accustomed tears the hope of the nation cut down in its prime. Add to these what will be said below XI. 17. Plutarch, however, in his book περὶ τῶ EI, notes that the flute was not used at funerals in the most ancient times, but later. But the same author, or whoever is the author of the book on Music, says that Olympus played a funeral dirge for Python in the Lydian mode.

Latin:

Vers 23.

Τοὺς αὐλητὰς] Tibias in luctu usitatas apud Judæos et- iam Josephus belli Judaici libro III. nos docet. Puto au- tem falli eos qui à profanis gentibus morem hunc ad Hebræos putant deductum. Recte enim ab aliis demon- stratum est, existare in antiquissimis Hebræorum scriptis ejus moris vestigia: sicut & præficarum mentio est apud Jeremiam IX. 17. neque vero in lege ulla ejus rei inter- dictio invenitur. Denique tota pompa funeralis, non novitium erat inventum, sed Abrahami, Isaaci, Jacobi, Josephi exemplo nitebatur: quo convincitur Taciti error putantis curam corporis, moremque condendi magis quam cremandi, ab Ægyptiis ad Judæos pervenisse. Ap- paret enim ex sacra historia multo ante quam Hebræi in Ægyptum immigrassent, eundem morem ab ipsorum ma- joribus usurpatum. Vero autem simile est ritus funerales, præsertim vero humandorum corporum morem (qui a- pud omnes gentes crematione est antiquior) originem habere à primis post diluvium temporibus, ad detestatio- nem τῆς ἀνθρωποφαγίας, quæ inter cætera extremæ feri- tatis scelera pristinum orbem invaserat. Nam & ejus rei famam ad Græcos imanasse ostendunt versus Moschio- nis:

Καὶ τὸν ἡγεμώματον Εἰς ἥμερον δίαιταν ἤγαγον βίον˙ Κἀκ τοῦδε τοὺς θανόντας ὥρισεν νόμῳ. Τύμβοις καλύπτειν, κἀπιμοιρασθαι κόνιν Νεκροῖς ἀθάπτοις, μηδ᾽ ἐν ὀφθαλμοῖς ἐᾶν Τῆς πρόσθε θοινῆς μνημόνευμα δυσσεβές.

Sic & luctus septemdialis, cujus mentio est in historia se- pulturæ Jacobi, Genes. L. vers. 10. & apud Josephum fi- ne sexti & libro XVII. Originum apud Judæos mansit, non ex lege ulla, sed ex antiqua & lege non vetita consuetu- dine. Hinc Syrachides πένθος νέκρου ἑπτὰ ἡμέραι c. XXII. 13. Quin & apud Josephum ejusdem moris ad ultima usque tempora servati memoria est: & apud Clementem stroma- teon quarto. Sed ne hoc quidem peculiare fuisse Judæis, sed aliis quoque gentibus usurpatum ex Marcellino discimg, li- bro ejus XIX. verba sic habent: Per dierũ spatium septem, viri quidem omnes per contubernia & manipulos epulis indulgebant, saltando & cantando trist a quadã genera næniarum, regium ju- venem lamentantes: femina vero miserabili planctu in primævo flore succisam spem gentis solitis fletibus conclamabant. His adde quæ infra dicentur XI. 17. Tibiam tamen non antiquis- simis temporibus, sed serius adhibitam funeribus notat Plutarchus libro περὶ τῶ EI. At idem aut quisquis est au- ctor libri de Musica ait, ὄλυμπον ἐπὶ τῷ Πύθωνι ἐπικήδειον αὐλῆσαι λυδιστί.

## 9:24
Verse 24.

For the girl is dead] a euphemism: such as that in Antiphanes: For they are not dead, but have gone before on the same road which it is necessary for all to travel.

but she is sleeping] Menander says of the dead, 'He has fallen into a happy sleep.' These expressions, as well as the fact that they called the dead 'blessed' or 'the blessed ones,' and what Tertullian writes was used among the Romans of old, 'he has departed and must return,' seem to be traces of a most ancient tradition, opposed to the Sadducees, to whose opinions the house of Jairus seems to have been favorable.

Whence is it gathered that the house of Jairus was addicted to the sect of the Sadducees? This presumption is rash regarding a man so distinguished, a director of the School, whose faith shone forth here clearly, in that he would not have instructed his family more correctly in those things which pertained to the first principles of the oracles of God, and to the very foundation of religion, by the judgment of the Hebrews themselves, such as was the head of the doctrine concerning the resurrection of the dead, Heb. 5:12, 6:1. Even if, therefore, there were those present who mocked Christ saying, 'The girl is not dead, but sleeps,' it is not to be presumed of the house and family of Jairus itself that it denied the resurrection of the dead in the manner of the Sadducees. And they mocked him because they thought they knew more correctly that she was truly dead, not merely sleeping: not because they judged that she would never be resurrected, to remain eternally in death. And for that reason Christ wished those mockers to be his witnesses, as Chrysostom notes, to prove that the girl had truly been dead: so that they could not, under any pretext, object to the miracle about to be performed: that the virgin, having been placed in a syncope or some greater swoon, had appeared to die, but had not truly been dead. Nor is it unlikely that Christ himself used this formula in a singular sense regarding those whom he was about to raise, namely, that they were sleeping FOR HIM, to be awakened immediately by his voice or call alone. For although our death is truly nothing other than ὕπνος τότω ἗ ἐν συνηθείᾳ μακρότερος, a sleep longer than this customary one, as Chrysostom teaches here (see 1 Cor. 11:20, 15:20), nothing prevents something peculiar from being hinted at here. For as their resurrection was singular, because this girl was not being raised to glory, nor to incorruptibility, but to another death, as Tertullian says, 1. On the Resurrection of the Flesh, so it was said in a peculiar way of the death of such persons who were to be raised shortly, that it is not death, but sleep. Other believers sleep as far as the body alone is concerned, because their souls enjoy the blessed vision of God in heaven (Rev. 14:13), and they are to be considered as watching more than they ever watched in the body, for they have no rest from the celebration of God, neither by night nor by day (Rev. 4:8). And it is by no means likely that these, as regards the soul, perceived the blessed vision of God and heavenly happiness and pleasure, for they could by no means have been cast down from that blessedness and thrust again into earthly misery, saving the justice of God. And therefore, the souls deprived of the divine vision were in a certain extraordinary state; after, that is, that natural bond and union with the body, having been dissolved by death, ceased for a time. Therefore, there was no need for the glorification of the body for the fellowship of the soul enlightened by the beatific vision of God, but the soul, such as it had been in the flesh when the union with the body was dissolved, concerning which vivification made by the contact and voice of Christ, Chrysostom speaks beautifully. Namely, by the contact of his hand he imparted power to the lifeless body to receive life: but by his words he truly restored life and spirit to the dead.

Latin:

Vers. 24.

ὁ γὰρ ἀπέθανε τὸ κοράσιον] ἐυφημισμὸς: qualis ille apud Antiphanem: Οὐ γὰρ τεθνᾶσιν, ἀλλὰ τὴν αὐτὴν ὁδὸν ἧν πᾶσιν ἐλθεῖν ἔσθ' ἀναγκαίως ἔχον, Προεληλύθασιν.

ἀλλὰ καθεύδει] Κατέδαρθεν ἐυδαίμων inquit Menander de mortuo. Hæ autem locutiones, ut & quod mortuos μά- καρας aut μακαρίτας vocabant, & quod Tertullianus apud Romanos antiquitus usurpatum scribit, abiit & reverti de- bet, vestigia esse videntur antiquissimæ traditionis, oppo- sita Sadducæis, quorum sententiæ favisse videtur Jairido- mus.

Unde hoc colligitur, quod Sadducæorum sectæ addicta domus Jairi fuerit? Temeraria est hæc præsumtio de viro tam insigni, Scholæ directo- re, cujus fides hic præclare eluxit, quod non re- ctius familiam suam informarir in his, quæ ad τὰ στοιχεῖα τῆς ἀρχῆς τῶν λογίων Θεοῦ, & ad ipsum θεμέλιον religionis, proprio Ebræorum judicio, spectabant, quale erat caput doctrinæ de resurre- ctione mortuorum Ebr. V.12. c. VI. 12. Etsi ergo ad- essent, qui Christum dicentem: non est mortua puella, sed dormit, irriderent, non tamen id de ipsa domo & familia Jairi præsumendum, quod Sadducæorum more negarit resuscitationem mor- tuorum. Et deridebant illi eum, quod putarent, se rectius scire, ipsam vere mortuam esse, non so- lum dormire: non quod censerent, nunquam re- suscitatum iri, æternum in morte mansuram. Id- eoque derisores illos testes suos esse, notante Chry- sostomo, volebat Christus, qui probarent, vere defunctam puellam fuisse: ne quicquam, tum præ- textu, excipere contra miraculum mox edendum possent: in Syncope aut deliquio majori quodam con- stitutam virginem obiisse visam, mortuam autem vere non fuisse. Neq; vero est absimile singulari sensu de iis, quos mox excitaturus Christus erat, hac for- mula usum ipsum esse, nempe quod dormirent SI- BI, statim à se sola voce vel acclamatione excitan- di. Etsi enim vere mors nostra nihil aliud sit quam ὕπνος τότω ἗ ἐν συνηθείᾳ μακρότερος somnus hoc usitato longior, docente hic Chrysostomo vid. 1. Cor. XI. 20. c. XV. 20. nihil tamen obstat, quo mi- nus hic peculiare quid innuatur. Nam uti singula- ris eorum fuit resuscitatio, quia non in gloriam, nec incorruptibilitatem, sed in mortem aliam suscitaba- tur hæc puella, dicente Tertull. 1. de resurr. carn. sic de morte etiam talium brevi resuscitandorum peculiari modo dicebatur, quod non mors sit, sed somnus. Alii fideles dormiunt, quoad corpus so- lum, quia animæ eorum beatâ visione DEI in cælis fruuntur Apoc. XIV. 13. magisque vigilare censen- dæ sunt, quam unquam in corpore vigilarunt, non enim requiem à celebratione DEI habent, nec nocte, nec die, Ap. IV. 8. & hos quoad animam beatam visionem DEI ac felicitatem ac voluptatem cœle- stem percepisse minime verisimile est, ab ea enim beatitudine deturbari, & denuo in terrenam mi- seriam, salva DEI justitia, detrudi minime po- tuissent. Ideoque in statu quodam extraordinario e- gêre animæ visionis divinæ expertes; postquam sc. naturale illud vinculum ac unio cum corpore, fa- cta per mortem solutione, ad tempus cessavit. Proinde non opus erat corporis glorificatione, ad animæ visione DEI beatifica collustratæ con- sortium, sed anima, qualis fuerat in carne, cum solveretur unio cum corpore, de qua vivificatio- ne Christi contactu & voce facta pulchre Chryso- stom. Nimirum contactu manus vim impertivit st exanimato corpori vita recipienda: verbis suis ve- ro vitam vere ac spiritum reddidit mortuæ.

## 9:25
Verse 25.

He took her by the hand] just as we are accustomed to do when we wake someone from sleep: so Christ demonstrated that it is no less easy for God to recall the dead to life than to awaken those who are sleeping, which was of the greatest importance for confirming our faith: Otherwise, to take by the hand is also to lead or support, as in the LXX, Isaiah 41:13 and 45:1. But it appears from what has been said on chapter 8 that Christ did not offend against the law by this contact.

PART V. The healing of two blind men and other sick persons.

Latin:

Vers. 25.

ἐκράτησε τῆς χειρὸς ἀυτῆς] sicut solemus facere cum aliquem ex somno excitamus: ita demonstravit Christus non minus Deo in proclivi esse mortuos in vitam revoca- re, quam expergefacere dormientes, quod ad fidem no- stram confirmandam maximi erat momenti: Alioqui κρατεῖν τῆς χειρὸς est etiam manuducere aut sustentare, ut apud LXX. Esaiz XLI. 13. & XLV. 1. Nihil autem hac contactione Christum in legem deliquisse apparet ex iis quæ dicta sunt ad caput VIII.

PARS V. Cæcorum duorum & aliorum ægrotorum sanatio.

## 9:27
Verse 27.

υἱὲ Δαβὶδ] More frequent and greater miracles than the examples of the ancients had now brought it about that by some Jesus was believed to be not only a Prophet, but that promised Messiah. See John VII. 31. Moreover, ὁ υἱὸς Δαβὶδ and ὁ Χριστὸς mean the same thing, as appears below XII. 23.

Latin:

Vers. 27.

υἱὲ Δαβὶδ] Frequentiora & majora veteribus exemplis miracula jam hoc effecerant, vt à quibusdam Jesus non Propheta tantum, sed promissus ille Messias crederetur. Vide Johan. VII. 31. Idem autem valet ὁ υἱὸς Δαβὶδ & ὁ Χριστὸς ut apparet infra XII. 23.

## 9:28
Vers. 28.

οἰκίαν] Roman jurists note that a person's house is spoken of even if one lives in another's house, whether rented or free of charge. See what was said above on chapter VIII.

ὅτι δύναμαι] See what was said on chapter VIII.

Latin:

Vers. 28.

οἰκίαν] Notant Jurisconsulti Romani domum alicu- jus dici etsi quis in aliena domo habitet sive in conducto, sive gratuito. Vide quæ supra ad caput VIII.

ὅτι δύναμαι] Vide quæ dicta sunt ad caput VIII.

## 9:29
Vers. 29.

κατὰ τὴν πίστιν ὑμῶν] See the same place.

Latin:

Vers. 29.

κατὰ τὴν πίστιν ὑμῶν] Vide ibidem.

## 9:30
Vers. 30.
