Ανεῴχθησαν] A Hebraism signifying the ability to use the instrument of sense: See Mark VII. 34, where it is said of ears, as in this place and elsewhere of eyes. See Psalm CXLVII, of which this is the fulfillment.

Latin:

Vers. 30.

Ανεῴχθησαν] Hebraismus significans facultatem uten- di instrumento sensus: Vide Marci VII. 34. ubi de auri- bus dicitur, ut hoc loco & alibi de oculis. Vide, Pl. CXLVII. cujus hic complementum.

## 9:33
Vers. 33.

καὶ ἐκβληθέντος τοῦ δαιμονίου] This is to loose the bound in the cited Psalm passage.

Οὐδέποτε ἐφάνη ὕτω] Something is understood, as also above, and besides that, 'having happened'. Thus also Mark II. 12. The sense is, so many signs so admirable, so quickly, and not by touch only, but also by word, and in every kind of disease, were produced by no one before this, not even by Moses. The same expression is in Judges XIX. 30.

These do not refer to all miracles in general, but they treat specifically of the mute and demoniac, for whom Christ had loosened the bond of the tongue, and from whom He had cast out the demon: such a judgment as was passed concerning the paralytic himself when he was healed, Mark II. 12.

Latin:

Vers. 33.

καὶ ἐκβληθέντος τοῦ δαιμονίου] Hoc est solvere vinctos dicto Psalmi loco.

Οὐδέποτε ἐφάνη ὕτω] Subauditur τι, ut supra quoque, ac præterea γενόμενον Sic & Marci II. 12. sensus est, tot signa tam admirabilia, tam celeriter, neque contactu tantum, sed & verbo, & in omni morborum genere, à nemine ante- hac edita, ne à Mose quidem. Locutio eadem Jud. XIX. 30.

Non omnia miracula universim hæc respiciunt, sed speciatim de muto & dæmoniaco, cui Chri- stus linguæ vinculum solverat, & è quo dæmoni- um ejecerat, agunt: quale judicium cum paraly- ticus sanaretur, de ipso latum Marc. II. 12.

## 9:34
Verse 34.

ἐν τῷ ἄρχοντι τῶν δαιμονίων] We shall discuss the meaning of this passage below in chapter XII. 2. But here is used for ἐν χειρὶ, as we have also warned above. ὁ ἄρχων τῶν δαιμονίων is ὁ ἄρχων τοῦ κόσμου, John XII. 13.

Latin:

Vers. 34.

ἐν τῷ ἄρχοντι τῶν δαιμονίων] De hujus loci sensu age- mus infra cap. XII. 2. autem hic est positum pro ἐν χειρὶ, ut supra quoque admonuimus. ὁ ἄρχων τῶν δαιμονίων est ὁ ἄρχων τοῦ κόσμου, Joh. XII. 13.

## 9:35
Verse 35.

καὶ τὰς κώμας, διδάσκων ἐν ταῖς συναγωγαῖς] Synagogues were indeed for the most part only in cities, to which all who were in the territory of those cities, those of the parish, used to gather. Moreover, it seems possible to gather from this passage that some were also established in larger and more populous villages. This was also the custom in the first times of Christianity, a gathering of all staying in cities or the countryside in one place. And at Cenchreae, which was the port of the Corinthians, there was a Church already in Paul's time, of which Phoebe was a deaconess.

PART VI. An exhortation concerning the need to pray for those who are to labor in the harvest.

Latin:

Vers. 35.

καὶ τὰς κώμας, διδάσκων ἐν ταῖς συναγωγαῖς] Erant qui- dem plerumque in urbibus tantum Synagogæ, ad quas conveniebant omnes qui in earum urbium erant territorio, οἱ τῆς παροικίας. Cæterum in vicis quoque majoribus ac fre- quentioribus aliquas constitutas ex hoc loco videtur posse colligi. Sic etiam primis Christianismi temporibus fieri so- lebat, πάντων κατὰ πόλεις ἢ ἀγρὸς μενόντων συνέλευσις ἐπὶ τὸ ἀυτό. Et Cenchreis, qui portus erat Corinthiorum, Ecclesia fuit jam Pauli tempore, cujus diaconissa erat Phœbe.

PARS VI. Ob exorandos laboraturos in messe exhortatio.

## 9:36
Verse 36.

ἐσκυλμένοι] It appears that not only the old Latin interpreter read it this way, but also the Syrian, who used דלאין. Christ saw the Israelite people being treated very badly by those who ought to have fed them, the priests and the experts in the law, as they were people who pursued their own advantages, hypocritical (as Salvian speaks) and bringing the name of religion to the most wicked gains and the title of holiness to the most sordid dealings. He saw, moreover, the miserable people being pulled in different directions, on one side by the Pharisees, on the other by the Sadducees, so that it was not sufficiently clear to them what they should follow and what they should flee. Thus ἐσκυλμένοι pertained to ill-treatment, ἐῤῥιμμένοι to the pursuit of sects. Compare Isaiah 50:6. And a figure of this matter in Esther 3:8.

Erasmus also thinks it should be read thus, appealing to Chrysostom, Jerome, Hilary, and Theophylact. Nor does B. Gerhard dissent, nor Beza. But it is commonly read ἐκλελυμένοι; and one should not rashly depart from the received reading, for why should they not be said to be exhausted, drained of strength, and as Luther says, verschmachtet: cf. Matt. 15:32, Mark 8:3, Gal. 6:9, Heb. 12:3, 6. And thus one must look not to weariness or exhaustion on the way, to which Beza also draws the word τὸ σκύλλεσθαι, because most were weary from the journey, but rather to the weakening, and the defect, and the languor of the soul, as in Heb. 12:3, 5, where the word τὸ ἐκλύεσθαι is also used: in which way the sense comes back to the same thing, with the interpretation of Grotius, and the cause of that defect and spiritual languor will still be rightly deduced from those wicked Doctors, from whom little or no vigor, spiritual virtue, or recreation and consolation of the soul could be expected, such as Christ promised only to those in Matt. 11:28 who were spiritually fatigued and burdened.

Μὴ ἔχοντα ποιμένα] Who, of course, might care for the flock with a pastoral spirit, studying the advantage of the flock, not his own, which is the duty of καλῶς ποιμένειν, as Christ teaches in John 10:11. Homer on sheep: 'They were scattered on the mountains through the folly of the shepherd.' This expression is taken from Num. 27:17 and 1 Kings 22:17.

Latin:

Vers. 36.

ἐσκυλμένοι] Apparet ita legisse non veterem tantum Latinum interpretem sed & Syrum, qui posuit דלאין. Vi- debat Christus plebem Israëliticam pessime haberi ab iis, qui pascere ipsos debebant, sacerdotibus & legisperitis, ut qui suis studerent commodis, simulatrices (quemadmodum loquitur Salvianus) improbissimis quæstibus nomen religionis & proferentes ad sordidissimas negotiationes titulum san- ctitatis. Videbat præterea miseros homines hinc à Pha- risæis, inde à Sadducæis in partes diversas trahi, ita ut quid sequerentur, quid fugerent, non satis esset ipsis ex- ploratum. Ita ἐσκυλμένοι ad malam tractationem, ἐῤῥιμ- μένοι ad sectarum studia pertinebat, Confer. Jes. L, 6. Et figuram hujus rei Esth. III. 8.

Sic & Erasmus legendum censet ad Chrysosto- mum, Hieronymum, Hilarium, & Theophylact. provocans. Nec abnuit B. Gerhardus, neque Beza. At communiter legitur ἐκλελυμένοι; ne- que temere à recepta lectione discedendum est, cur enim non dicerentur defatigati, viribus ex- haufti, & ut Luther. verschmachtet : Conf. Matth. XV. 32. Marc. VIII. 3. Gal. VI. 9. Ebr. XII. 3. 6. Et sic respiciendum non ad laffitudinem, vel de- fatigationem ἐν via, quo etiam τὸ σκύλλεσθαι Beza trahit, quod de via plerique defessi essent, sed potius ad debilitationem, & defectum, ac languorem ani- mi, uti Ebr. XII. 3. 5. etiam adhibetur τὸ ἐκλύ- εσθαι: quo pacto sensus eodem recidit, cum in- terpretamento Grotiano, & causa istius defectus ac languoris spiritualis recte adhuc deducetur ab illis pravis Doctoribus, à quibus parum, aut nihil vigoris, virtutis spiritualis, aut recreationis & con- solationis animæ expectari poterat qualem solis promittebat Christus Matth. XI. 28. qui spiritua- liter fatigati, & onerati erant.

Μὴ ἔχοντα ποιμένα] Qui nimirum pastorali animo gregem curet, gregis commodo non suo studens, quod est καλῶς ποιμένειν officium, ut Christus docet Joh. X. 11. Homerus de ovibus: Αἰγ᾽ ἐν ὄρεσσι Ποιμένος ἀφραδίῃσι διέτμαγον. Locutio hæc sumta ex Num. XXVII 17. & 1. Reg. XXII. 17.

## 9:37
Vers. 37. ὁ μὲν θερισμὸς πολὺς] This is what is said in John 4:35, that the fields are white for the harvest: that is, the minds of many are sufficiently raised by the expectation of sounder doctrine ἐνθέτως πρὸς τὴν βασιλείαν τοῦ Θεοῦ. λαὸς πολύς, Acts 18:10. A figure of this matter is in the history of Ruth, chapter 2.

Latin:

Vers. 37. ὁ μὲν θερισμὸς πολὺς] Hoc est quod apud Johannem IV. 35. dicitur, agros albos esse ad messem : id est animos multorum satis erectos exspectatione sanioris doctrinæ ἐνθέτως πρὸς τὴν βασιλείαν τοῦ Θεοῦ. λαὸς πολύς, Act. XVIII. 10. Figura hujus rei in Ruthis historia cap. II.

## 9:38
Vers. 38. ἐκβάλη ἐργάτας] ἐκβάλλειν is often nothing other than ἐξάγειν, John 10:4, or προσφέρειν below 12:35; here it is the same as ἀποστέλλειν in Paul, Rom. 10:15. By both is signified not only the dispensation of divine providence, but the conferring of special power, with peculiar mandates and gifts. Thus, of old, Moses, Elijah, Jeremiah, and others were sent. The following history concerning the mission of the Apostles coheres excellently with these words, by which began to be fulfilled that which Christ had said was to be prayed for.

ἐργάτας] The Greeks call a laborer of the earth an agricolam, as Plutarch does. Here it appears that reapers are meant, so that the simile may be consistent in its parts.

Latin:

Vers. 38. ἐκβάλη ἐργάτας] ἐκβάλλειν sæpe non est aliud quam ἐξάγειν, Johan. X. 4. aut προσφέρειν infra XII. 35. hic idem quod ἀποστέλλειν Paulo Rom. X 15. Utroque significatur non sola divinæ providentiæ dispensatio, sed collatio spe- cialis potestatis, cum peculiaribus mandatis donisque. Ita olim missus Moses, Elias, Jeremias, atque alii. Optime autem cum his verbis cohæret sequens historia de missio- ne Apostolorum, quo cœpit impleri id quod Christus o- ptandum dixerat.

ἐργάτας] ἐργάτην γῆς agricolam vocant Græci ut Plu- tarchus. Hic apparet messores intelligi, ut similitudo su is partibus constet.

## 10:1 Argument
CHAPTER X. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

Jesus, having called the Apostles to himself, grants them wonder-working power; they are named and sent out to the lost sheep of Israel, that they may preach the kingdom of heaven, nor should they be anxious about their sustenance; they should leave the ungrateful, who will experience a heavier destruction in the final judgment than the Sodomites: they should be prudent, and not fear persecutors, for the Holy Spirit will stand by them, and those who persevere to the end will obtain salvation: nor is a disciple above his Master: but He is to be feared who can destroy both body and soul. Furthermore, that their hairs are also numbered: and whoever shall have confessed Jesus before men, Jesus will confess him before his heavenly Father. Moreover, that love of necessary things is not to be preferred to love of the Lord, nor even love of life: finally, to those who receive the disciples of Christ, a reward is promised.

These parts are: I. The mission and instruction of the Apostles, to v. 15. II. The prediction of persecutions, and the forewarning against them, to v. 26. III. The incitement to intrepid confession, to v. 39. IV. The admonition concerning the reception of the disciples of Jesus, to v. 42.

PART I. The mission and instruction of the Apostles.

Vers. 1.

Τὸς δώδεκα μαθητὰς] Those familiar to the others and daily companions selected by him some time before, as appears from Luke. Of old, twelve parts were made for dividing by Ahijah the Shilonite: now, twelve for gathering by Christ. Concerning the number twelve, Tertullian, book IV against Marcion. From this I can interpret Christ as having been predicted not only by the voices of the Prophets, but also by the arguments of things. For I discover figures of this number in the Creator. The twelve springs of Elim. The twelve gems in the priestly tunic of Aaron. The twelve stones chosen by Joshua from the Jordan and placed into the ark of the Testament. For just as many Apostles were foreshadowed, therefore, as springs, they were to irrigate the arid world: as gems, they were to illuminate the sacred garment of the Church, which Christ the Pontiff of the Father put on: as stones solid in faith, which Christ the true one chose from the washing of the Jordan, and received into the sanctuary of his Testament. To this are also referred the twelve oxen, the brazen sea, built by Solomon, supporting and carrying: of which three looked to the north, three to the south, three to the west, three to the east. As if they were destined for all the regions of the world: and to carry the baptistery into them. Others add the twelve spies sent from the desert into the land of Canaan: the twelve stones on the Throne of Solomon. Also the twelve prophets. But they usually omit that which is the most important, the twelve Patriarchs, the sons of Jacob, who is also Israel, who propagated that elect people, and it is all the more surprising that they omitted it, because, as Chemnitius observes, Christ himself seemed to allude to it, Matt. 19:28: You shall sit upon twelve seats, judging the twelve tribes of Israel. These men, however, traversed the world, not moving shields, not bending bows, not shooting arrows, not distributing money, not relying on eloquence, Chrysostom says.

ἔδωκεν αὐτοῖς ἐξουσίαν] Here the divine power of Christ shines forth more clearly than ever before: the Prophets also had performed miracles, but they had granted the power to perform miracles to no one by their own will: not even Moses to Joshua, nor Elijah to Elisha. Thus was Psalm 92:12 fulfilled.

Latin:

CAPUT X. ARGUMENTUM ET PAR- TITIO.

Jesus Apostolis ad se vocatis potestatem θαυ- ματουργικὴν concedit, qui nominantur, & emittuntur ad oves perditas Israelis, ut prædicent regnum cælorum, nec soliciti de sustentatione sint, ingratos relinquant, gravius exitium in novissimo judicio præ Sodomitis experturos: Prudentes sint, nec timeant persequutores, adstiturum enim i- psis Spiritum Sanctum & perseverantes ad finem salutem adepturos: Neque vero discipulum esse supra Magistrum: Illum autem timendum, qui corpus & animam perdere potest. De cætero numeratos et- iam esse capillos ipsorum: & qui confessus fuerit Jesum coram hominibus, illum con- fessurum esse Jesum coram Patre suo cæle- sti. Non esse autem præferendum amorem necessariorum amori Domini, ac ne amo- rem quidem vitæ: denique illis qui Chri- sti discipulos suscipiunt, promittitur re- muneratio.

Partes hæ sunt: I. Apostolorum missio & in- structio, ad v. 15. II. Persequutionum prædictio, & adversus eas premunitio, ad v. 26. III. Ad con- fessionem intrepidam excitatio, ad v. 39. IV. De susceptione discipulorum Jesu, commonitio, ad v. 42.

PARS I. Apostolorum missio & instructio.

Vers. 1.

Τὸς δώδεκα μαθητὰς] Familiares cæteris & convi- ctores quotidianos aliquanto prius à se selectos, ut ex Lu- ca apparet. Olim ad dividendum duodecim factæ partes per Achiam Siloniten: nunc ad colligendum duodecim per Christum. De numero duodenario Tertullianus l. IV. contra Marc. Ex hoc Christum interpretari possum, non tantum vocibus Prophetarum, sed & argumen- tis rerum prædicatum. Hujus enim numeri figu- ras apud creatorem deprehendo. Duodecim fontes Elim. Duodecim gemmas in tunica Sacerdotali Aa- ron. Duodecim lapides à Josua de Jordane electos, & in arcam Testamenti conditos. Totidem enim Apo- stoli prætendebantur, proinde ut fontes, irrigaturi aridum orbem: ut gemmæ, illuminaturi sacram Ec- clesiæ vestem, quam induit Christus Pontifex patris: ut lapides solidi fide, quos de lavacro Jordanis Chri- stus verus elegit, & in sacrarium Testamenti sui recepit. Huc etiam referuntur duodecim boves, mare æneum, à Salomone ædificatum, sustentantes & portantes: è quibus tres aquilonem respiciebant, tres meridiem, occidentem tres, orientem tres. Quasi in omnes mundi plagas essent destinati: & baptiste- rium in illas deportare. Addunt alii duodecim explo- ratores è deserto missæ in terram Canaan: Lapides duodecim in Throno Salomonis. Prophetas etiam duodecim. Sed omittunt plerumque, quod est κο- ρυφαιότατον, duodecim Patriarchas, filios Jacobi, qui & Israel, qui populum illum electum prose- minarunt, eoque magis mirum omisisse, quod, quemadmodum Chemnitius observat, Christus ipse videbatur eo alludere, Matth. XIX. 28. Sede- bitis super duodecim sedes, judicantes duodecim tri- bus Israël. Peragrarunt autem isti orbem terrarum, non scuta moventes: non arcus tendentes: non sagit- tas mittentes: non pecunias largientes: non eloquen- tiæ confidentes, Chrysost. ait.

ἔδωκεν αὐτοῖς ἐξουσίαν] Hic Christi divina vis manife- stius quam unquam antea elucet: fecerant mira etiam Pro- phetæ, sed mira facie di potestate nemini suopte arbi- trio concesserant: ne Moses quidem Josuæ, nec Elias Eli- sæo. Sic impletus Psalmus XCII. 12.

## 10:2
Vers. 2. Ὀνόματα] It was of great importance to know the names of these men, from whose consenting testimony the truth was to be estimated. For there were not lacking those who would falsely claim that name.

Πρῶτος Σίμων ὁ λεγόμενος πέτρος] Without doubt the prince of the college designated by Christ, to maintain the cohesion of the body. Nor should it offend anyone that in Galatians II. 9, Cephas is read as being between James and John. For in a most ancient manuscript, which came from Greece to England, that name is absent there. Later Greeks added it.

Grotius wished to gratify the Papists with these things, who use this argument, that Peter is placed in the first position, Bellarmine, lib. 1, de R. P. cap. 18, Torniel, Tirin in their Commentaries. But we will not say that the word πρῶτος is an interpolation, which Beza affirms against the authority of the Greek Codices, the Syriac interpreter, and the Fathers, Chrysostom, Jerome, and others. We note only this: that the Evangelist designates not a primacy of dignity or jurisdiction, which makes for maintaining the cohesion of the body, but a primacy of order. For the other Apostles were certainly what Peter also was, endowed with an equal partnership of both honor and power, says St. Cyprian, and from him the Canon Law speaks, Caus. 24, q. 1. And Anacletus admits in c. in Novo dist. XXI that the other Apostles received honor and power with Peter in equal partnership, and Clement denies the contrary in L. VI, Constit., in Eusebius, lib. II, Histor. Eccl. c. 1. that Peter claimed this dignity for himself: Peter, James, and John, after the assumption of the Savior, although they were preferred by Him to almost everyone, yet did not claim for themselves the glory of the primacy, but they established James, who was called the Just, as the Bishop of the Apostles. Nor does Erasmus observe without reason regarding this list in this place, page 38, that St. Jerome indicates that the Apostles are not listed in the same order by other Evangelists as they are by Matthew, lest anyone on this account make Peter the first of all because he is placed in the first position here. For the others attribute the first place to Matthew, the next to Thomas. And Tostatus himself acknowledges and proves, q. XXVII in chapter X of Matthew, that there was no order of degrees of dignity instituted among the Apostles by Christ: because they themselves sometimes contended among themselves as to which of them seemed to be the greater, Luke XXII, and they even asked this of Christ, Matthew XVIII. Christ, however, did not wish to tell them who was the greater, Mark IX. And this doubt always remained with them, as long as they were with Christ, even on the day of the Lord's Supper, Luke XXII. Therefore Christ did not establish this order. Furthermore, the Bishop of Avila also gave a poor reason why Peter is listed in the first place, namely, that the order of time was observed. Theophylact, along with Chrysostom, also gives this reason. He places Peter and Andrew first, since they were also called first. Nor does Scripture always observe this order elsewhere; indeed, James is placed before Peter in Gal. II. 9. Although the Papists have tried to counter this argument in various ways, Hector Pintus, in ch. 1 of Daniel, by denying that the Apostle Peter is understood by Cephas, Bellarmine in the same place, that James is placed before Peter because James was the Bishop of Jerusalem, where the Apostles were at that time; Estius, by referring it to the honor of the Lord, whose brother James was; yet no one was of such audacity as to call the authentic text into doubt, no one of such impudence as to affirm that the name of Cephas had crept in from elsewhere, as does Grotius, this parasite of the Papal Chair. For with great consensus all editions have the name of Cephas, and that it is not an interpolation, but belongs to the text, both the preceding verses 7 and 8, and the following verses 11 and onwards, teach: and not even the Papists themselves will allow Cephas to be expunged here, even though placed in the middle position, because of the title of COLUMNS added, lest others be seen and considered columns of the Church without PETER, by whom the building of the Church would be sustained, as Estius explains the columns. More easily in one M.S. No one will doubt that that name could have slipped out of the codex rather than have crept into all other things. Add that Grotius himself acknowledges below that the name of Cephas is by no means corrupted in them, in the annotations on chapter 16 of Matthew.

Latin:

Vers. 2. Ὀνόματα] Magni retulit scire horum nomina, ex quorum consentiente testimonio veritas erat æstiman- da. Non defuerunt enim, qui id nomen ementirentur.

Πρῶτος Σίμων ὁ λεγόμενος πέτρος] Princeps haud du- bie collegii à Christo designatus, ad retinendam corporis compagem. Nec offendat quenquam, quod Gal. II. 9. Cephas medius inter Jacobum, & Joannem legitur. In manuscripto enim antiquissimo, qui ex Græcia in Angliam devenit, abest ibi id nomen. Græci posteriores appo- suere.

Pontificiis hæc gratificari voluit Grotius, qui hoc argumento utuntur, quod Petrus primo loco ponatur Bellarmin. lib. 1. de R. P. cap. 18. Torniel. Tirin. in Commentar. At non dice- mus, vocem πρῶτος esse irreptitiam, quod Be- za contra Codd. Græcorum, Syri interpretis ac Patrum, Chrysostomi, Hieronymi, & aliorum autoritatem affirmat. Id solum notamus: non principatum dignitatis, aut Jurisdictionis, qua ad retinendum corporis compagem facit, sed principatum ordinis designare Evangelistam. Hoc enim erant utique & cæteri Apostoli, quod fuit & Petrus, pari consortio præditi & honoris & pote- statis, ait S. Cyprianus, & ex eo jus Canoni- cum C. loquitur Caus. 24. q. 1. Et fatetur Anacle- tus c. in Novo dist. XXI. cæteros Apostolos cum Petro pari consortio honorem & potestatem acce- pisse, negatque ex adverso Clemens L. VI. Con- stit. apud Euseb. lib. II. Histor. Eccl. c. 1. Petrum sibi hanc dignitatem vendicasse: Petrus, Jacobus & Jobannes post assumptionem salvatoris, quamvis ab ipso fuerint omnibus pene prælati, tamen non sibi vendicabant primatus gloriam, sed Jacobum, qui dicebatur Justus, Apostolorum Episcopum statuunt. Neque præter rem observat de hac recensione Erasmus in h. l. pag. 38. indicare D. Hieronymum, non eodem ordine recenseri Apostolos ab aliis Evan- gelistis, quo à Matthæo, ne quis ob hoc omnium primum faciat Petrum, quod hic primo loco pona- tur. Nam cæteri primum locum tribuunt Mat- thæo, proximum Thomæ. Et agnoscit, probat- que Tostatus ipse q. XXVII. in cap. X. Matth. non fuisse inter Apostolos progradibus dignitatis à Chri- sto institutum ordinem: quia ipsi aliquando con- tendebant inter se, quis eorum major videretur Luc. XXII. & etiam hoc quærebant à Christo Matth. XVIII. Christus autem noluit eis dicere, quis esset major Marc. IX. & semper duravit eis hoc dubium, quamdiu fuerunt cum Christo etiam in die Cœnæ Domini Luc. XXII. Non ergo posuit Christus i- stum ordinem. Porro causam etiam malam, cur Petrus recenseatur primo loco, reddidit Abulen- sis Episcopus, nimirum, quod temporis ratio ob- servata fuerit. Quam rationem etiam reddit cum Chrysostomo Theophyl. Præponit Petrum & An- dream, quoniam & primum vocati. Nec sem- per observat ordinem istum Scriptura alibi; si- quidem Jacobus Petro præponatur Gal. II. 9. Cui argumento etsi Papistæ variis modis occurrere conati sint, Hector Pintus, in c. 1. Daniel. ne- gando, quod per Cepham Apostolus Petrus in- telligatur, Bellarmin. l. c. præponi Jacobum Pe- tro, quia Jacobus erat Episcopus Hierosolymita- nus, ubi tunc erant Apostoli; Estius id referendo ad honorem Domini, cujus Jacobus frater erat; nemo tamen ejus audaciæ fuit, ut textum Au- thenticum in dubium vocaret, nemo ejus im- pudentiæ, ut nomen Cephæ aliunde irrepsisse af- firmaret, quemadmodum hic Papalis Cathedræ parasitus Grotius. Magno enim consensu edi- tiones omnes nomen Cephæ habent, nec id irrep- titium esse, sed ad textum pertinere, cum antece- dentia v. 7. 8. tum consequentia v. 11. seqq. docent: & nec ipsi Papistæ expungi hic Cepham, etsi me- dio loco positum, patientur, ob elogium CO- LUMNARUM adjectum, ne alii sine PETRO COLUMNÆ Ecclesiæ visi & habiti censeantur, quibus ædificium Ecclesiæ sustentaretur, ut co- lumnas explicat Estius. Facilius in uno M. S. Codice excidere, quam in alia omnia irrepere nomen illud potuisse, nemo ambiget. Adde, quod infra Grotius ipse agnoscat, Cephæ nomen illis minime νοθεύεσθαι, in annotatis ad caput Matth. XVI.

## 10:3
Verse 3. Bartholomew. Lightfoot thinks this is Nathanael. Calculate the order, he says, in which the disciples were called in John 1, with the order in which they are for the most part listed, and you will find Bartholomew coinciding in the same place as Nathanael, so that you might think him to be the same as him: Nathanael called by his proper name, and Bartholomew by his paternal one. Bar-Talmai, that is, Son of Talmai. For the Greek interpreters render Talmai as Tholmi, 2 Samuel 13:37. And Tholomaios occurs in Josephus, Antiquities, book 20, chapter 1.

He who is called Thaddaeus] I think it is the same name that Luke anciently set forth as Judas: from the pronunciation of which name some Jews, it seems, abstained because of the concurrence of the letters of the Tetragrammaton. The origin, if I am not mistaken, is the same but the inflection is different. Nor is it new that a doubling of a consonant is put for a long vowel. Moreover, Jerome interprets the other name of this Apostle, Lebbaeus, as 'heart,' by which name P. Nasica was called at Rome. Pliny reports that those who excelled in wisdom were called 'corculi' with a masculine ending. But others prefer it to be 'lebi,' because the Hebrews called those who had the name of Judah 'lions' from the prophecy of Jacob. Nor is it a wonder that 'to be called' is used here for a most proper name. For Appian also said 'Crassus the Marcus by surname.' And another John, different from the Apostle, is called 'called Marcus,' Acts 12:25.

But why are Judas and Thaddaeus not left as distinct names, as they are commonly held, so that there is no need for that transformation of letters? For even if they are perhaps of the same etymology and meaning, and both names denote a confessor (which Ludovicus de Dieu denies regarding the name of Thaddaeus, observing that in the Syriac language it denotes a spring herb), yet the superstition of the Jews concerning the concurrence of the letters of the Tetragrammaton was not even then in force, or here in the name of Jude or Thaddaeus can it provide an argument for being noted. And when it is added that he was 'called' (which word 'called' the Vulgate wrongly omits, contrary to the faith of the Greek codices and other versions, such as the Syriac, Arabic, Ethiopic, Persian, etc.), and that the name of Jude was not a surname, but should rather be considered his proper name, by which he is commonly and absolutely designated, it is more likely that it is distinct from the name of Judas. Compare. Drusius, Scultetus, Caninius.

Latin:

Vers. 3. Βαρθολομαῖος. Hunc Lightfoothus putat esse Nathanaëlem. Computa ordinem, inquit, quo vocati sunt discipuli Joan. I. cum ordine quo ut plurimum recensentur, & Bartholomæum in eundem locum cum Natha- naele coincidentem comperies, ita ut eundem cum eo esse opineris: Nathanaëlem nomine proprio di- ctum, & Bartholomæum paterno. בר תלמי id est, Filium Talmai. Nam Græci interpretes Talmai reddunt Θολμὶ, 2. Sam. XIII. 37. Atque occurrit Θολομαῖος apud Josephum Antiquit. lib. XX. cap. I.

Ὁ ἐπικληθεὶς Θαδδαῖος] Puto idem esse nomen quod vetuste Lucas extulit Ἰούδας: cujus nominis pronunciatione quidam Judæi ut videtur abstinebant ob concursum litera- rum τῶν τετραγραμμάτων. Origo ni fallor eadem est sed alia flexio. Neque novum ut pro vocali longa ponatur gemi- natio consonantis. Nomen autem hujus Apostoli alterum Λεββαῖος Hieronymus corculum interpretatur, quo no- mine Romæ P. Nasica fuit appellatus. Plinius masculina terminatione corculos nominatos refert qui sapientia præ- stabant. Sed malunt alii esse לבי, quia Hebræi eos qui nomen habebant Judæ leones vocabant ex Jacobi vatici- nio. Neque mirum est τὸ ἐπικαλεῖν hic usurpari de no- mine maxime proprio. Nam & Appianus dixit κράσσος ὁ μάρκος ἐπίκλην. Et Johannes alius ab Apostolo dicitur ἐπικαλούμενος μάρκος, Act. II. 12. 25.

Cur vero non Judas & Thaddæus relinquuntur distincta nomina, uti communiter habentur: ne opus sit illa literarum μεταμορφώσει? Etsi enim ejusdem forsan etymi, & significationis sint, & confessorem notet utrumque nomen, (quod ve- ro de nomine Thaddæi negat Lud. de Dieu, id in lingua Syra herbam vernam notare observans) non tamen superstitio Judæorum de concursu li- terarum τετραγράμματο vel tum in vigore jam fuit, vel hic in Jude, aut Thaddæi nomine conno- tando argumentum præbere potest. Et quum ad- datur quod Ἐπικληθεὶς cognominatus ita fuerit (quam vocem Ἐπικληθεὶς vulgata contra fidem Codd. Græcorum & versionum aliarum perperam omittit, utpote Syri, Arabis, Æthiopis, Persæ &c. nomen autem Jude non fuerit cognomen, sed pro- prium potius ejus nomen censendum sit, quo communiter & absolute designatur, vero magis si- mile est, id à Judæ nomine distinctum esse. Conf. Drusius, Scultetus, Caninius.

## 10:4
Verse 4.

Ἀποστόλων] What is שְׁלוּחַ in Hebrew, the Septuagint translates as ἀπόστολον, as in 1 Kings 14:6. Properly, however, those were called שְׁלִיחִין in Talmudic books who collected tithes and other things and brought them to the Levites: those who bring up the sacrifices, as Philo calls them in his embassy to Gaius. Augustus in an edict to the cities of Asia calls the same men ἀποδοχέας. Philo also calls them ἱεροπόμπους τῶν χρημάτων ἀρισίνδην ἐπικριθέντας: Julian in his letter to the Jews, and Epiphanius, call their function ἀποστολὴν. This name remained among the Jews even after the destruction of the city, for the assessors of the patriarchs were called Apostles, as attested by Epiphanius, and by Honorius and Arcadius in the law which is in the Theodosian Code, under the title concerning the Jews: It is unworthy of the superstition that the archisynagogues or elders of the Jews, or those whom they themselves call Apostles, who are sent by the Patriarch at a certain time to exact gold and silver, should carry back to him the exact sum collected from each synagogue. Following this example, even in the first age of Christians, those who were sent by the churches to carry the gifts of the churches back and forth were called the apostles of those by whom they were sent, as can be seen in 2 Cor. 8:23 and Phil. 2:25. Ignatius calls the same men sometimes θεοδρόμους, sometimes θεοπρεσβευτὰς. Although the word ἀποστόλων in itself is very broad (for Christ himself is also called by that name in Heb. 3:1 & in Justin Martyr and others), it is nevertheless credible that Christ, in using this title, was alluding to the custom of the Hebrews, and at the same time to the history of Moses who had sent twelve scouts into the same land, where in Hebrew there is the word שְׁלַח and in Greek the word ἀποστέλλειν, and wished to signify that he also had ministers whom he would send with commands, but of a far different kind, who would bring back to him the desired fruits. This title, however, was given peculiarly to those who were sent with extraordinary power, twelve in number, witnesses of all the things of Christ while he lived on earth, as we are taught in Acts 1:21.

After Christ's resurrection, the same honor is given to Matthias, Paul, Barnabas, and perhaps also to other founders of Churches, about whom there will be a place to speak in due time.

Regarding the name 'Αποστόλων, Lightfoot writes thus in Horae Hebraicae on Matthew, p. 144: These twelve were called Apostles שלוחי, or שליחי, a title with which Moses and Aaron were distinguished by the Chaldean Paraphrast on Jeremiah II. 1. It does not merely mean a messenger, but a messenger bearing the authority of the one who sends him. For, שלוחו של אדם כמותו, an apostle of any man is as he himself is, by whom he is deputed. Bab. Beracoth, fol. 34. 2. See the fortieth verse of this chapter. If you read through the treatise of Maimonides here, which is titled שלוחין ושותפין, you will perhaps not entirely waste your oil and labor. He adds: The seven shepherds and eight princes in Micah V. 5, according to Kimchi, are the disciples of the Messiah.

Benedict Aretius in Romans I. 1 provides another derivation and explanation of the word. Στόλος, he says, is a fleet, and the commander of it is an Ἀπόστολος, who was also another type of magistrate. Thus, the legates of Christ are called Apostles, as if they were governors of the Church of Christ in this world, seeking hospitality. If you ask, who governs the ship of Christ? I answer, Christ primarily, after whom the doctrine of the Apostles ought to govern it, not the voice of another. The same author in 2 Corinthians I. 1 says that the word Apostle in the Greek language signifies a civil magistrate, but when the name of Christ is added, this office is distinguished from political functions. Although, indeed, the adjective 'Απόστολα (πλοῖα) is used for ships that are accustomed to be sent now here, now there, by the commanders of naval affairs, Plato, Epist. 7. And the noun ἀπόστολος, according to Hesychius, denotes the commander of an army who is placed in charge of a naval expedition: yet that meaning is special and foreign here. In general, ἀποστέλλειν is to send, which sometimes specifically means to send someone with mandates, to send a legate, as in Thucydides: Μαλήσιππον ἀποστέλλᾳ εἰς τὰς Ἀθήνας; ἀποστολὴ is a mission, dismissal, or remission, whence among the jurists, ἀπόστολοι are called letters of dismissal, l. 106, de V.S., which are given by the one from whom an appeal is made to the one who is to take cognizance of the appeal, for the sake of testifying to the appeal, as Brisson defines it. Therefore, the legates of Christ, whom He sent into the whole world to announce the Gospel, were called Apostles. That this Greek name was accepted from the Jews rather than from the Greeks is not as certain as it is impossible to prove, since those Talmudic books already existed in the age of the Apostles. The LXX, who used this word in 1 Kings XIV. 6. Ἐγώ εἰμι Ἀπόστολος πρός σε σκληρός, and they were known to the ancient writers and, without ambiguity, to the sacred writers of the New Testament: from them, therefore, this word seems to have been more accepted; for they used it for the word שׁלוּחַ regarding the Prophet Ahijah, sent by the Lord with a certain mandate, or a legate of the Lord. But that the same honor was given to Barnabas or others as to the XII Apostles is by no means to be admitted. For they alone were constituted by Christ immediately as teachers of the whole world and were adorned with the privilege of infallibility, not Barnabas, not others.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

Ἀποστόλων] Quod Hebraice est שְׁלוּחַ id LXX. vertunt ἀπόστολον, ut 1. Reg. XIV. 6. Proprie autem vocabantur in Talmudicis libris שְׁלִיחִין qui decimas atque alia per- cipiebant & ad Levitas deferebant: οἱ τὰς θυσίας ἀνάγοντες ut eos vocat Philo legatione ad Cajum. Augustus in edicto ad Asiæ civitates eosdem vocat ἀποδοχέας. Philo etiam ἱερο- πόμπους τῶν χρημάτων ἀρισίνδην ἐπικριθέντας: functionem eorum ἀποστολὴν Julianus in Epistola ad Judæos, & Epipha- nius. Mansit hoc nomen inter Judæos etiam post urbis ex- cidium, nam patriarchartum assessores vocabantur Ἀπό- στολοι teste Epiphanio, Honorius & Arcadius in lege quæ est Codice Theodosiano, titulo de Judæis: Superstitionis indigna est, ut archisynagogi sive presbyteri, Judæorum, vel quos ipsi Apostolos vocant, qui ad exigendum aurum atque argentum à Patriarcha certo tempore diriguntur à singulis Sy- nagogis exactam summam atque susceptam ad eundem repor- tent. Ad quod exemplum etiam prima Christianorum æ- tate qui ad perferenda ultro citroque ecclesiarum munera ab ecclesiis mittebantur dicti sunt ἀπόστολοι eorum à quibus mittebantur, ut videre est 2. Cor. VIII. 23. Philipp. II. 25. Ignatius eosdem modo θεοδρόμους, modo θεοπρεσβευτὰς ap- pellat. Quanquam autem vox ἀποστόλων per se latissime pa- tet (nam & Christus ipse eo nomine appellatur Hebr. III. 1. & apud Justinum Martyrem atque alios) credibile tamen est Christum hac appellatione alludentem ad usum Hebræo- rum, simulque ad Mosis historiam qui duodecim explora- tores in eandem terram dimiserat, ubi in Hebræo est vox שְׁלַח in Græco vox ἀποστέλλειν, significatum voluisse & se habere ministros quos cum mandatis sed longe aliis mitteret, qui sibi fructus optatos reportarent. Data au- tem hæc appellatio peculiariter illis, qui cum eximia potestate mittebantur, numero duodecim, testes omnium rerum Christi dum in terris vixit, ut docemur Actor. I. 21.

Post Christi resurrectionem idem honos datur Matthiæ, Paulo, Barnabæ, forte etiam aliis Ecclesiarum fundatori- bus, de quibus suo tempore erit agendi locus.

De 'Αποστόλων nomine ita Lightfootus in Ho- ris Hebraic. in Matth. p. 144. Vocati sunt hi, duode- cim Apostoli שלוחי, vel שליחי, quo titulo insigniti sunt Moses & Aaron à Chaldæo Paraphr. Hierem. II. 1. Non nude Nuntium sonat, sed nuntium vices mit- tentis gerentem. Nam, שלוחו sel אדם כמותו A- postolus cujusvis est sicut ipse, à quo deputatur. Bab. Beracoth. fol. 34. 2. Vide versum hujus capitis quadragesimum. Si tractatum Maimonidis hic perle- geris cui titulus שלוחין ושותפין oleum forsan & o- peram non omnino perdes. Addit; Septem Pastores atque octo Primates Mich. V. 5. apud Kimchium sunt discipuli Messiæ.

Aliam & derivationem & explicationem vocis tradit Benedictus Aretius in Rom. I. 1. Στόλος, in- quit, est classis, & præfectus illius est Ἀπόστολος, qui alius quoque fuit Magistratus. Ita Christi le- gati Apostoli dicuntur, tanquam gubernatores Eccle- siæ Christi in hoc mundo quærendis hos pitiis. Si roges, navcm Christi qui regat? Respondeo, Christum im- primis, post quem Apostolorum doctrina eam debet regere, non alterius vox. Idem in 2. Cor. I. 1. Apo- stoli vocem in Græca lingua Magistratum civilem si- gnificare ait, dum autem Christi nomen additur, distingui munus hoc à politicis functionibus. Quan- quam vero Adjectivum 'Απόστολα (πλοῖα) di- cantur, quæ modo huc modo illuc dimitti solent à rei navalis præfectis, Plat. Epist. 7. Et substantivum ἀπόστολος, Hesychio Autore, notet Imperatorem exercitus, qui expeditioni navali præficitur: ea ta- men significatio specialis, & hic aliena est. In ge- nere ἀποstέλλειν est mittere, quod interdum pe- culiariter mittere aliquem cum mandatis mittere le- gatum significat, ut apud Thucyd: Μαλήσιππον ἀποστέλλᾳ εἰς τὰς Ἀθήνας, ἀποστολὴ missio, dimissio, vel remissio est, unde apud JCros ἀπόστολοι literæ dimissoriæ dicuntur l. 106. de V.S. quæ ab eo, à quo appellatur, ad eum, qui de appellatione cogniturus est, dantur, testandæ appellationis causa, definiente Brisson. Ideo legati Christi quos in totum terra- rum orbem misit, ad annuntiandum Evangelium, Apostoli dicti. A Judæis potius, quam à Græcis nomen istud Græcum acceptum esse tam non constat, quam non potest probari, Apostolorum ætate jam Thalmudicos illos libros extitisse. LXX. qui hac voce usi sunt 1. Reg. XIV. 6. Ἐγώ εἰμι Ἀπόστολος πρός σε σκληρός, & antiquiores, & citra ambiguum scriptoribus sacris Novi Te- stamenti cogniti fuere: Ab illis ergo hæc vox ma- gis accepta videtur: nam illi pro voce שׁלוּחַ eam adhibuerunt de Propheta Ahia à Domino cum certo mandato misso seu legato Domini. Barnabæ autem vel aliis etiam eundem honorem datum, qui XII. Apostolis, minime admittendum. Illi enim totius orbis doctores à Christo immediate constituti, & privilegio infallibilitatis ornati soli sunt, non Barnabas, non alii.

## 10:4
Verse 4. Cananaean] It does not signify origin, in the way Uriah is called a Hittite, but it is the surname 'Qanan,' which Luke properly rendered as 'Zealot,' just as the Septuagint had rendered that word in Exodus 20:5 and elsewhere. Wherefore the Syrian expressed this name with a 'q' and not with a 'k'. The Greek interpreter of Matthew added a Greek ending to the name, by repeating the 'k' letter and interposing a vowel, so that this word might approach more closely to a Greek form; just as they called Athenodorus the philosopher 'Kakaniten,' but Strabo says it was from a certain village. Thus Josephus calls 'Annas' 'Ananos,' with a similar repetition of the same letter.

There does not appear to be a solid reason why one should depart from the received opinion that Simon was a Cananaean by country, even though Toussain criticizes B. Luther's version on this account here. For the fact that he is called a Zealot in Luke 6:15 does not stand in the way of this, since he could be called a Cananaean by reason of his origin from the city of Cana, and have the surname of Zealot, of which Matthew indicated one, and Luke the other. But this matter is not of such importance that we think it should be contended over. Lightfoot surmises that this Simon was from the sect of the Zealots, which Josephus noted, before his conversion.

Iscariot] It seems to be contracted from 'Ish Issachar'

which exists in Judges 10:1, but with the addition of an ending familiar to the Greeks.

Others think he was so called from the village of Iscarioth in the tribe of Ephraim, with Chrysostom, Jerome, and Cornelius à Lapide; others, with Caninius, Beza, and Toussain, think he was called 'Ish Kerioth,' a man of Kerioth from the city of the tribe of Judah, Joshua 12:24. The Syrian derived it from 'sakar' (reward) and 'nata' (he failed), whence he deduced 'yosa' as the future passive of the third conjugation: as if he were called: he is led by a reward to defection. The Londoners in the Interpretation of Hebrew, Chaldean, and Greek Names explain it as a man of slaughter or extermination. By Lightfoot, it is believed to be from 'corium' (leather), either because he was a tanner like that Simon in Acts 9:43, or because Judas, the bearer of the money-bag, wore a leather garment or belt, i.e., Judas with a belt: in which belts purses for money were sewn; or even from 'aschara' or strangulation, because he was strangled by the Devil. But we leave those trifles to be weighed by others. He certainly had the name before the money-bag was entrusted to him, and thus also long before his death; which, moreover, when it is ascribed to the strangulation of the Devil, should deservedly be considered fabulous, as being assumed without Scripture and merely fictitious. And Ludovicus de Dieu admits that 'mascera' for strangulation cannot be found in any lexicons; he wishes, however, for Judas to be named from 'sakar' (he closed, he obstructed): that he was seized by some disease, by which the mouth of the fistula that is in the neck is accustomed to be obstructed, which was sent by God, and was thus suffocated.

Latin:

Vers. 4. Κανανίτης] Non originem significat, quomo- do Urias Chittæus dicitur, sed est cognomen קנאן quod Lucas proprie reddidit ζηλωτὴς, quomodo & LXX. eam vocem reddiderant Exod. XX. 5. & alibi. Quare Syrus per ק non per כ hoc nomen expressit. Græcanicam termina- tionem nomini addidit Græcus Matthæi interpres: repeti- ta כ litera & interposita vocali; ut magis ad Græcam for- mam vox hæc accederet: quomodo Athenodorum Philo- sophum κακανίτην vocabant, sed à pago quodam ait Stra- bo. Sic Ἄνναν Josephus Ἄνανον vocat, simili literæ ejus- dem repetitione.

Non apparet ratio solida, cur à recepta senten- tia, quod patria Cananæus fuerit Simon, receden- dum sit, etsi Tossanus eapropter B. Lutheri versio- nem hic redarguat. Nam quod Luc. VI. 15. voca- tur Zelotes, eidem non obstat: quum & Cananæus originis ratione è Civitate Cana dici potuit, & co- gnomen habere Zelotis, quorum alterum Mat- thæus indigitarit, Lucas alterum. Sed hæc res tanti non est, ut de ea contendendum ducamus. Lightfoothus è Secta Zelotarum, quam Josephus notavit, ante conversionem hunc Simonem fuisse autumat.

Ἰσκαριώτης] Videtur esse contractum ex איש יששכר

quod exstat Jud. X. 1. sed addita terminatione Græcis familiari.

Alii ex vico Ischarioth in tribu Ephraim cum Chrysostomo, Hieronymo, Corn. à Lapid. alii cum Caninio, Beza, Tossano quasi איש קריות virum Kariotharim è civitate tribus Juda Jos. XII. 24. dictum putant. Syrus à סכר merces & נטא defecit, unde יוסא futurum passivum tertiæ conjugationis deduxit: quasi dictus sit: mercede inducitur ad defectionem. Londinenses in Interpret. Nomin. Ebr. Chald. & Græc. exponunt virum occisionis, vel exterminationis. Lightfootho à corio dicto creditur, sive quod Coriarius fuerit ut Simon ille Act. 9. 43. sive quod coriaceum vestimentū aut cinctorium gesserit Judas portitor glossocomi, q. d. Judas cum cinctorio: in qualibus cinctoriis consutæ fuerint crumenæ pro nummis: vel etiam ab אשכרא seu strangulatione, quod à Diabolo strangulatus sit. Sed illa τερετίσματα aliis expendenda relinquimus. Nomen certe habuit antequam crumena eidem credita, adeoque longe etiam ante interitum: qui præterea cum Diaboli strangulationi adscribitur, merito fabulosus censendus, utpote ἄτερ γραφῆς assumtus, mereque fictitius. Neque Mascera pro strangulatione in ullis Lexicis reperiri, admittit Lud. de Dieu: vult tamen à סכר clausit, obstruxit, Judam denominari: quod morbo aliquo, quo os fistulæ, quæ in collo est, obturari solet, divinitus immisso correptus fuerit, & ita suffocatus.

## 10:5
Δώδεκα] Christ, about to build a spiritual kingdom, expresses the image of the Jewish Republic, so that it might appear more clearly that the promises of the eternal kingdom were solidly fulfilled in Him. For just as there were twelve tribes, so there were twelve tribal leaders of eminent dignity, to which the words of Christ allude below in XIX. 28 and Luke XXII. 30. See Revelation XXI. 12 and 14.

Latin:

Δώδεκα] Christus spirituale regnum extructurus expri- mit Judæicæ Reipublicæ imaginem, quo clarius appareat, regni æterni promissiones in ipso solide impletas. Sicut enim tribus duodecim, ita duodecim erant φυλαρχοὶ exi- mia dignitate, ad quam alludunt verba Christi infra XIX. 28. Luc. XXII. 30. Vide Apoc. XXI. 12. & 14.

## 10:5
Vers. 5. Do not go into the way of the Gentiles, and do not enter into a city of the Samaritans] 'Into the way of the Gentiles' is towards the nations, as Jer. II. 18. For 'into a city' one must supply 'any', as 'a bone that shall not be broken', John XIX. 36, is 'any bone'. Christ forbids his envoys to go beyond the borders of Palestine. He does not forbid passing through the territory of the Samaritans (for that transit was convenient for those traveling from Galilee to the Jerusalem region), but he prohibits entering their towns, so that it might appear that this mission was not instituted for the sake of the Samaritans. For the Samaritans were partly themselves of foreign origin, not associated with the Jews in the fellowship of religion, and partly they were Jews who, having abandoned their ancestral rites, had defected to them. Did Christ therefore wish the privilege of their nobility to be preserved for the Jews? Which was neither as great as they themselves supposed, secure in this almost sole confidence, nor yet was it of such small moment as Paul teaches to the Romans and elsewhere. Therefore, an illustrious sign of this preference is that Christ wished the primary care to be placed in establishing them: which was also diligently observed by the Apostles after Christ's resurrection, as is clear from Acts II. 39, ch. XIII. 46.

Latin:

Vers. 5. Εἰς ὁδὸν ἐθνῶν μὴ ἀπέλθητε, κὴ εἰς πόλιν Σαμαρειτῶν μὴ εἰσέλθητε] εἰς ὁδὸν ἐθνῶν est versus gentes, ut Jer. II. 18. εἰς πόλιν subaudiendum τινα, ut ὀςᾶν ὀ συντριβήσεται ἀυτᾶ, Joh. XIX. 36. est ὀςᾶν τι. Vetat Christus legatos suos egredi fines Palæstinæ. Per agrum Samaritanorum transiri non vetat (erat enim is transitus opportunus ex Galilæa tractum Hierosolymitanum petentibus) sed prohibet oppida intrari, ut appareat Samaritanorum causam non institutam hanc legationem. Nam Samaritani partim erant & ipsi externæ originis, non consociati cum Judæis consortio religionis, partim erant Judæi qui relictis patriis ritibus ad illos defecerant. Voluit igitur Christus servari Judæis nobilitatis suæ privilegium? quod neque tantum erat quantum ipsi existimabant, hac prope sola fiducia securi, neq; tamen momenti erat exigui ut Paulus ad Romanos & alibi docet. Hujus igitur prælationis illustre signum hoc est, quod Christus in ipsis instituendis primam curam poni voluit: quod etiam post Christi resurrectionem ab Apostolis diligenter servatum est, ut liquet Act. II. 39. c. XIII. 46.

## 10:6
Vers. 6. To the lost sheep of the house of Israel] For the saving of whom Christ himself professes that he was properly sent, below XV. 24. For so that faith in the promises which God had made to the ancestors of the Jews might be fully established, Christ himself showed himself to be a 'minister of the circumcision', Rom. XV. 8, Luke I. 54, 55. To outsiders, however, he performed no benefits except incidentally, waiting most patiently for the conversion of the Jews to himself, so that then, through them, with their own highest glory, other nations might be converted.

The expression concerning lost sheep is taken from Isa. LIII. 6, Jer. L. 8, Ezech. XXXIV. 5.

Latin:

Vers. 6. Πρὸς τὰ πρόβατα τὰ ἀπολωλότα οἴκε Ἰσραὴλ] Quibus servandis Christus ipse proprie se missum profitetur infra XV. 24. Nam ut plena constaret fides promissis quæ Deus Judæorum majoribus fecerat, ipse Christus se exhibuit διάκονον περιτομῆς, Rom. XV. 8. Luc. I. 54. 55. Externis autem nulla nisi obiter beneficia præstitit, exspectans patientissime Judæorum ad se conversionem, ut deinde per ipsos cum summa ipsorum gloria gentes aliæ converterentur.

Loquutio de ovibus perditis desumta ex Esa. LIII. 6. Jer. L. 8. Ezech. XXXIV. 5.

## 10:7
Vers. 7. The kingdom of heaven is at hand] If anyone compares this with the proclamation of the Baptist and the beginning of Christ's sermons, he will find that nothing more was commanded to the Apostles now than that they should exhort the Jews to a better life and draw them to listen to Christ, from whom they were to receive the rest of the things that were necessary for them for salvation.

He seems to mean the same thing that John Camero does in Myroth. Evangel. on Matt. XVI. 20, that Christ did not send out the Apostles to preach the Gospel, since he reserved this for himself, but that they should only prepare hearers and disciples for him. But because Christ preached the Gospel in the same words that he enjoined upon the Apostles, how can it be denied that they preached the Gospel? For the kingdom of heaven having approached, according to the interpretation of Hunnius, is that the long-desired kingdom of the Messiah, expected for many centuries, which God promised through the mouth of the holy Prophets from the beginning of the world, has come. The interpretation of others, Jerome and Chrysostom, is concerning eternal life proposed and promised by Christ and the Apostles. It is not to be understood as if it were not proposed in the Old Testament, but that now, without figures and the wrapping of earthly goods, it is offered openly to all in the Gospel.

Latin:

Vers. 7. Ἤγγικεν ἡ βασιλεία τῶν ὀρανῶν] Si quis hoc conferat cum proclamatione Baptistæ, & exordio sermonum Christi, reperiet nihil nunc quidem ultra mandatum Apostolis, quam ut Judæos ad vitam meliorem hortarentur, & ad Christum audiendum pertraherent, à quo accepturi essent cætera, quæ ad salutem ipsis essent necessaria.

Videtur idem velle, quod Joh. Camero in Myroth. Evangel. ad Matt. XVI. 20. quod Christus non emiserit Apostolos ad prædicandum Evangelium, quum ipse sibi hoc reservarit: sed ut auditores solum & discipulos sibi pararent. At quia iisdem verbis Evangelium prædicavit Christus, quæ Apostolis injunxit, qui negari potest, hos Evangelium prædicasse? Appropinquasse enim regnum cælorum, interprete Hunnio, est venisse optatum illud multisque seculis expectatum regnum Messiæ, quod Deus per os S. Prophetarum inde ab exordio Mundi pollicitus est. Aliorum interpretatio Hieron. Chrysost. de vita æterna à Christo & Apostolis proposita & promissa non ita est accipienda, quasi in V. Test. proposita non sit, sed quod nunc sine figuram, & bono- rum terrenorum involucro palam omnibus in Ev- angelio offeratur.

## 10:8
Verse 8. Καθαρίζετε] I do not wonder that what some here ascribe, νεκροὺς ἐγείρετε, is absent from the most ancient copies, nor that it is not acknowledged by the Greeks who expound this passage. For we do not read of any dead person being restored to life by the Apostles before the resurrection of Christ. It is the more credible that it was added from other places, because the Syriac and Latin do not place this member in the same position.

Grotius wishes these words to be considered spurious, as does Franc. Lucas. But the reasoning of Grotius is not compelling: the consequence from the negation or omitted commemoration of a secondary act to the negation of the primary act is not valid. Therefore, the reliability of the Greek Codices, most of which have those words, should not be called into question, with the principal Syriac editions agreeing, even if it is not read that the Apostles raised anyone from the dead before the resurrection of Christ. For they are not read to have cleansed lepers either. But are those words therefore also to be judged as having crept in?

Δωρεὰν ἐλάβετε δωρεὰν δότε] This is a saying not unusual among the Hebrews. For in Deut. IV. 5 and 14, where Moses says that he had delivered the law just as he had received it, the interpreters explain it: מה אני בחנם אף אתם כמי בחנם, 'As I did it freely, so you also ought to do it freely.' So also here Christ says, 'You have received freely,' namely, this power of healing. Since the students of physicians do not receive any skill in healing diseases, such as it is, except with great expenditure of time and great payment made to their masters, you have received this most full faculty in one moment, without any cost to yourselves. Hence these δυνάμεις are accustomed to be called χαρίσματα. Christ shows from this that what he commands is neither burdensome nor unjust, that the acts of these powers should also be exercised freely. And indeed, to bargain for a price for such an act, which is directly ordered toward the glory of God, undoubtedly opposes the glory of God: which natural reason itself dictates, by which Peter sharply convicts Simon Magus, who was otherwise ignorant of this precept. For if Ulpian said that civil knowledge is not to be considered as something to be valued for money, nor to be honored, how much more justly is that said of a virtue gifted divinely? Furthermore, to receive gifts offered spontaneously without a contract for such an act does not have a natural baseness. For some things, as the same Ulpian says, although they are received honestly, are nevertheless sought dishonestly. Indeed, as Jerome notes regarding Micah, those who used to consult the Prophets were accustomed to give them some small gifts, signs of which custom we have in 1 Sam. 9. 7, 8 and 1 Kings 14. 9. Thus also the philosophers of the Greeks, as Origen notes against Celsus, ἀπὸ τ̄ γνωρίμων ἐλάμβανον τὰ πρὸς τὰς χρείας. Nor, however, did the Prophets always receive them, but they judged what needed to be done from the circumstances of the times and persons. Therefore, Elisha did not want to receive anything at all from Naaman the Syrian, lest the grace of the benefit received should become cheap in the eyes of an outsider. Hence the Prophet says to his servant, 'Was it now the time to receive silver or garments?' and what follows in 2 Kings 5. 26. And Daniel refused to receive gifts from King Belshazzar, Dan. 5. 17. With similar prudence, Abraham, living among men alien to the worship of the true God, did not want anything from the spoils taken from the enemies to come to him, Gen. 14. 22. Christ, who saw that much would be lost to the authority of the Evangelical doctrine, and indeed that his disciples would not be beyond calumny if they received any reward for acts that ought to have pertained only to testifying to the truth, prohibited not only foul bargains, but all gain whatsoever from such things, or even from the very work of teaching: which has been most holily observed by the true Apostles and their successors, among whom, as Tertullian speaks, 'no thing of God cost a price.' Tatian in his oration against the Greeks: Φιλοσοφοῦσι τε ὦ μόνον οἱ πλεῦντες, ἀλλὰ κὶ οἱ πένητες τῆς διδασκαλίας ἀπολαύουσι· τὰ γὰρ παρὰ θεῦ τῆς ἐν κόσμω δωρεᾶς ὑπερεπαίρει τὴν ἀμοιβήν. Meanwhile, both Christ and the Apostles taught by words and example that it is just that those who, neglecting their own affairs, were occupied with providing for the salvation of others, should in turn be honestly supported by them: just as it was noted by Quintilian, and attributed to Socrates for his sustenance, and the wise, if their family circumstances required it, allowed gratitude to be returned to them. They received sustenance for necessity, as Augustine speaks, but the reward of their stewardship from the Lord: although the Apostles, and Paul especially, very often yielded even this right of theirs, seeking their own livelihood with their own hands, rather than being a burden to the poor or lying open to the calumnies of the malevolent. By these arts the Evangelical truth was propagated throughout the whole world, from which how greatly the customs of later times have departed is as superfluous to say as it is sad to contemplate.

Blessed Gerhard says, Christ does not prohibit receiving the necessary sustenance of life, as is evident from the verse immediately following, 10, and 1 Cor. 9. 14, but [he prohibits] making gain from the preaching of the Gospel and miracles, and seeking one's own advantage, which is to be noted against the Anabaptists. Cf. Luke 10. 7, Rom. 15. 27, Gal. 6. 6, Phil. 4. 15. One must also distinguish here between the sale of spiritual benefits, which is prohibited in 1 Tim. 6. 5, Acts 8. 20, 2 Kings 5. 23, and the remuneration of labors, Luke 8. 3.

Latin:

Vers. 8. Καθαρίζετε] Quod hic quidam adscribunt νεκροὺς ἐγείρετε, id non miror abesse a vetustissimis exemplaribus: neque agnosci a Graecis hunc locum exponentibus. Nul- lum enim mortuum ab Apostolis vitae redditum legimus, ante Christi resurrectionem. Adjectum ex aliis locis eo est credibilius, quia Syrus & Latinus non eodem loco ponunt hoc membrum.

Verba haec νοθεύεσθαι vult Grotius, ut & Franc. Lucas. Sed ratio Grotii non est stringens: a nega- tione vel praetermissa commemoratione actus se- cundi ad negationem actus primi non valet conse- quentia. Non ergo solicitanda fides Codicum Grae- corum, qui plerique verba illa habent, annuenti- bus editionibus Syriacis praecipuis, etiamsi non legantur Apostoli ante resurrectionem Christi quenquam a morte resuscitasse. Nam nec leprosos mundasse leguntur. Num vero ideo etiam illa verba irreptitia censenda?

Δωρεὰν ἐλάβετε δωρεὰν δότε] Dictum est non inusitatum apud Hebraeos. Nam Deut. IV. 5. & 14. ubi Moses dicit se ita tradidisse legem sicut acceperat, explicant interpretes מה אני בחנם אף אתם כמי בחנם Quod ego gratis feci, & vos gratis facere oportet. Ita & hic Christus, gratis accepistis, inquit, nempe potestatem hanc sanandi. Cum medicorum discipuli non nisi magno temporis im- pendio, & magna magistris mercede soluta qualemcunque morborum medendorum peritiam accipiant, vos hanc ple- nissimam facultatem uno momento, sine ullo sumtu vestro accepistis. Hinc χαρίσματα dici solent ista δυνάμεις. Osten- dit hinc Christus nec grave nec iniquum esse quod impe- rat, ut earum potestatum actus gratis quoq; exerceantur. Et quidem mercede pacifci pro actu tali, qui directe ordinatur ad Dei gloriam, haud dubie Dei gloriae adversatur: quod ipsa dictat ratio naturalis, ex qua Simonem magum, hujus a- lioquin praecepti ignarum, acriter convincit Petrus. Nam si civilem scientiam pretio nummario no esse existimandam nec de honestanda dixit Ulpianus, quanto id justius de do- nata divinitus virtute dicitur? Caeterum citra pactione pro actu ejusmodi dona sponte oblata recipere non habet na- turalem turpitudinem. Quaedam enim, ut idem ait Ulpian9, tametsi honeste accipiantur, inhoneste tamen petuntur. I- mo ut ad Micheam notat Hieronymus, qui Prophetas con- sulebant solebant iis munuscula aliqua donare, cujus moris indicia habemus 1. Sam. 9. 7. 8. & 1. Reg. 14. 9. Sic & Graeco- rum Philosophi, ut Origenes adversus Celsum notat, ἀπὸ τ̄ γνωρίμων ἐλάμβανον τὰ πρὸς τὰς χρείας. Neq; tame ea semper recipiebant Prophetae, sed ex temporum ac personaru cir- cumstantiis quid opus factu esset aestimabant. Ideo a Saara- pa Syro nihil omnino accipere voluit Elisaeus, ne apud ho- minem externum vilesceret accepti beneficii gratia. Hinc ad puerum suu inquit Propheta, Eratne nunc tempus acci- piendi argentum aut vestes? & quae sequuntur 2. Reg. 6, 26. Et a rege Baltasare dona accipere abnuit Daniel 6, 17. Si- mili olim prudentia Abraham9 vivens inter homines a veri Dei cultu alienos, nihil de praeda ab hostibus parta ad se pervenire voluit, Gen 14. 22. Christus qui videret multum decessurum auctoritati doctrinae Evangelicae, quin neq; ex- tra calumniam futuros discipulos suos, si pro actibus qui ad testandam duntaxat veritatem pertinere debebant, aliquid acciperent praemii, non foedas tantum pactiones, sed o- mnem omnino ex rebus ejusmodi, aut etiam ex ipsa do- cendi opera quaestum prohibuit: quod a veris Apostolis eorumque successoribus sanctissime est observatum, apud quos, ut Tertullian. loquitur, nulla res Dei pretio consta- bat. Tatianus oratione contra Graecos: Φιλοσοφοῦσι τε ὦ μό- νον οἱ πλεῦντες, ἀλλὰ κὶ οἱ πένητες τῆς διδασκαλίας ἀπολαύουσι· τὰ γὰρ παρὰ θεῦ τῆς ἐν κόσμω δωρεᾶς ὑπερεπαίρει τὴν ἀμοιβήν. Interim & Christ9 & Apostoli tum verbis tum exemplo do- cuerunt aequum esse, ut qui reb. neglectis, procurandae alio- rum saluti vacarent, ab ipsis vicissim honeste alerentur: quo- modo a Quintiliano notatum est, & Socrati collatum ad vi- ctum, & sapientes, si res familiaris id exigeret, passos sibi gratiam referri. Sustentatione necessitatis, ut Augustinus lo- quitur, recipiebant a populo, mercedem dispensationis a Domino: quanquam huic quoq; juri suo Apostoli & Paulus praesertim saepissime cesserunt, manib9 suis victura sibi po- tius quaerentes, quam aut pauperculis oneri essent, aut ad malevolorum calumnias paterent. His artibus Evangelica veritas per orbem totum propagata est, a quibus quantope- re recesserint posteriorum temporum mores, tam dictu su- pervacuum est, quam triste cogitatu.

B. Gerhardus, non prohibet, inquit, Christus ne- cessariam vitæ sustentationem accipere, ceu patet ex versu statim sequente 10. ac 1. Cor. IV. 14. sed ex Ev- angelii prædicatione, & miraculis quæstum facere, & proprium commodum quærere, quod contra A- nabaptistas notandum. Conf. Luc. X. 7. Rom. XV. 27. Gal. VI. 6. Phil. IV. 15. Distinguendum etiam hic inter beneficiorum spiritualium venditionem, quæ prohibita 1. Tim. III. 5. Act. VIII. 20. 2. Reg. V. 23. & laborum renumerationem, Luc. VIII. 3.

## 10:9
Verse 9. Μὴ κτήσησθε] When he had forbidden receiving a reward for healing, he did not doubt that it would immediately come into the minds of the Apostles, 'We must therefore not begin this journey unless we are well-equipped with provisions for all things.' Encountering this thought, Christ affirms that God, whose business they are conducting, will provide for them regarding necessary things: and so that they might have a more certain proof, he orders them to set out without any provisions. This symbol was a precept for that time, by which the experience of divine providence would be more certain for them: as Chrysostom rightly noted in his sermon: ὅτι κ' χρὴ διαβλέπειν τὰς ἱερεῖς. The thing noted through the symbol was to be valid for security of trust forever. Therefore, κτᾶσθαι here is to acquire in advance; which Menander called σκέπτεσθαι and περιποιεῖσθαι: Ἂν μὲν πλέωμεν ἡμερῶν πω τεττάρων Σκεπτόμεθα τ' ἀναγκαι᾽ ἑκάστης ἡμέρας. But if there is any sparing for the sake of old age, shall we not say that we are providing provisions? In Hebrew, there will undoubtedly have been קָנָה, which is well known to be used in that sense.

Since this command was given to the Apostles for this journey and was temporary, the Papists foolishly extract a vow of poverty from it: Alphonsus de Castro, Clichtoveus, Bellarmine—from whom, however, these men depart: John of Torquemada, Arboreus, Barradius, Jansenius, Corn. à Lapide, Tirinus.

Εἰς τὰς ζώνας] Luke 10:4, 22:35 rightly called the belt a purse. C. Gracchus in Gellius: 'The belts which I carried out full of silver, I brought back from the province empty.' Others have noted the same use of the word in Horace, the authors of the law, Suetonius, Spartianus, and Lampridius: from which it appears that not only copper, but also gold and silver coins were accustomed to be carried in the belt.

Latin:

Vers. 9. Μὴ κτήσησθε] Cum vetuissfet mercedem pro sana- tione accipi, non dubitabat quin statim in mentem venturu esset Apostolis, oportet nos igitur hoc iter non incipere nisi rerum omnium commeatu pulchre instructos. Huic cogi- tationi occurrens Christus affirmat, Deum, cujus res gerant, prospecturum ipsis de rebus necessariis: quo autem certius habeant documentum, jubet illos sine ullo commeatu pro- ficisci. Hoc σύμβολον pro illo tempore præceptum, quo cer- tior ipsis esset divinæ providentiæ experientia: ut recte no- tavit Chrysostomus in sermone: ὅτι κ' χρὴ διαβλέπειν τὰς ἱερεῖς. Res notata διὰ συμβόλου, fiduciæ securitatis in perpetuum e- rat valitura. Est ergo hic κτᾶσθαι in antecessum comparare; quod σκέπτεσθαι & περιποιεῖσθαι dixit Menander: Ἂν μὲν πλέωμεν ἡμερῶν πω τεττάρων Σκεπτόμεθα τ' ἀναγκαι᾽ ἑκάστης ἡμέρας. Ἂν ᾗ δὲ φείσασθαί τι τῇ γήρως χάριν, Οὐ φησομενδ' ἐφόδια περιποιούμενοι; In Hebræo haud dubie fuerit קָנָה quod eo significatu usur- pari notissimum est.

Quum præceptum hoc Apostolis, pro hac pro- fectione, datum, & temporarium fuerit, inepte Pontificii hinc votum paupertatis exsculpunt: Al- phonsus de Castro, Clichtoveus, Bellarm. à quibus tamen hic abeunt, Johan. de Turre cremata, Arbo- reus, Barradius, Jansenius, Corn. à Lapide, Tirinus.

Εἰς τὰς ζώνας] ζώνην recte βαλάντιον dixit Luc. X. 4. XXII. 35. C. Gra. chus apud Gellium: Zonas quas plenas argenti extuli, eas ex provincia inanes retuli. Eundem vocis usum apud Horatium; juris auctores; Suetonium, Spartianum, Lam- pridium alii annotarunt: ex quibus apparet non æra tan- tum, sed & aureos & argenteos nummos in zona portari solitos.

## 10:10
Vers. 10. Πήραν] A wallet in Latin, into which travelers were accustomed to store bread and some small provisions. Martial also called it a 'pera' in Latin.

Μηδὲ δύο χιτῶνας] A custom almost of those who think themselves content with the minimum. Galen, in his book on correcting the passions of the soul: 'And so also to have double clothing is sufficient!' To have one garment is very poor, such as the swineherds in Homer; who speak thus in Odyssey 14: 'For there are not many cloaks and tunics for you to wear, but one for each man.' The same author, when he describes the luxury of the Phaeacians, names 'garments for changing, and warm baths, and beds.' See 2 Kings 5:2. Among the institutions of the Essenes, from whom many Christians came, Josephus records: 'They do not change their garments or shoes until they are torn or completely worn out by time.'

Μηδὲ ὑποδήματα μηδὲ ῥάβδον] The Syriac and Latin read ῥάβδον, not ῥάβδους. Understand a staff other than the one you carry in your hand, or sandals other than those you are now wearing, for that this is the meaning is shown both by what precedes, 'two tunics,' that is, a garment other than that which you are wearing, and by what is in Mark, where the staff they were carrying and the sandals they were wearing are explicitly permitted. Doubtless, because those sandals were worn out by those making a journey, and it not infrequently happened that a staff was broken or left somewhere, they were accustomed to put other sandals and other staffs in their baggage. Christ wishes his Apostles to abstain from this precaution: wherever they were to travel, they would find things necessary for food and the journey. And for that reason, Luke used the plural number ῥάβδους, to signify that it was not forbidden to have one staff, but rather more than one, which must be understood by the same right regarding the pair of sandals. See also what will be said regarding Mark.

The explanation of B. Hunnius on page 328 also has it this way, who repeats the word 'two' from the preceding: but he does not grant them shoes, that is, double or spare ones. He does not forbid in general to protect the feet with shoes, since suitable shoes do not hinder the speed of the journey, but rather promote it. Therefore, Mark, reporting these same commands, writes that it was permitted to them to be shod with sandals, which were a certain kind of lighter footwear suitable for those traveling to hasten their journey. This was also the interpretation of the blessed Lyser in his Harm. Evang. ch. LXXII, as well as that of Thomas, Cajetan, and others, regarding ὑποδήματα; Corn. à Lapide’s distinction between sandals, which protect only the sole of the foot, which were permitted, and shoes covering the whole foot, is to be preferred as more subtle than solid. Besides this, Lightfoot has brought forward another point from the Rabbis, that shoes were for more delicate use, sandals for harder use, the sole or lower part of which was of wood, the upper of leather; so that two tunics and shoes are forbidden, not that they might overcome pride, worldly vanity, or a more delicate custom entirely, but rather that they might carry about a habit and demeanor that was most humble. Regarding the staves, however, the reconciliation is more apt, which has pleased most of our own, as well as Cajetan, Franc. Luke, Jansenius, Cornelius, and also Beza, Gualter, and others, than the Grotian one. The blessed Hunnius explains it thus: that the Lord does not grant the Apostles staves of such a kind that they might use them in place of weapons, and either inflict force upon others or repel force brought from elsewhere. For He wishes to send them out plainly unarmed, so that regarding necessary defense they might depend entirely upon divine protection. He does, however, grant staves or lighter rods, with which they might steady their step while walking. Although Andr. Osiander also suggested this explanation in his Annot. on Harm. Evangel. bk. II, ch. XIX, he himself preferred, though wrongly, to say the passage in Luke was corrupt, and to posit that instead of εἰ μὴ, it had been written μήτε by a drowsy or even bold scribe, rather than that a rod signifies one thing in Luke, which is forbidden, namely that which is carried for the sake of taking vengeance: and another in Mark, which is permitted for the sake of supporting a weary journey. But the corruption of the text is not to be conceded: nor is there any necessity for it, since another most convenient method of reconciliation is available.

Vers. 10. ἄξιος] This word in Greek, and those which correspond to it in Hebrew and Latin, does not always denote equality, but any kind of suitability of a thing, as is clear from Eph. IV. 1, Phil. I. 27, Col. I. 10, 1 Thess. II. 12, John Epist. III. 6.

Τροφῆς] The name τροφῆς is taken here more generally, in the way that jurists declare that when food is bequeathed, provisions, clothing, and housing are owed, because without these the body of another cannot exist. Although this sentiment, that he who performs services is worthy of food, or as Luke and Paul say, of wages, could be referred to the estimation of divine kindness, yet since Luke and Paul openly place this ἄξιον not between God and the heralds of the Gospel, but between those same heralds and those who are taught by their proclamation, I think that here too the meaning of the same pronouncement is the same, so that Christ says this: with God providing, you will receive food from those very people to whose teaching and healing you will devote effort: and that by most just right. For what is more just than that those who sow spiritual things should reap carnal things, 1 Cor. IX. 1? How little is a meager living, if it is compared with such great benefits? And here it appears again that wages are spoken of without a ratio of equality: and not only where the reward exceeds the work, which we have shown elsewhere, but even where the reward is unworthy to be compared to the work. For even concerning the teachings of human opinion, Aristotle did not fear to say: that worth is measured by money, but honor is not an equivalent; it cannot be; but perhaps it is sufficient, just as it is toward gods and toward parents, as far as is possible.

Latin:

Vers. 10. Πήραν] Manticam Latine, in quam viatores condere panem & obsonioli aliquid solebant. Peram La- tine dixit etiam Martialis.

Μηδὲ δύο χιτῶνας] Qui mos ferme eorum etiam qui mini- mo contentos se putant. Galenus libro de corrigendis ani- mi passionibus: ὥτω δὲ κὶ τὴν ἐσθῆτα διπλῆν ἔχειν ἀυτάρκες! Unam vestem habere valde pauperum, quales subulci apud Homerum; qui sic loquuntur Odyssea ξ: Οὐ γὰρ πολλαὶ χλαῖναι ἐπίμοι σοί τε χιτῶνες Εὐλάδε ἰσνυαδ, μία δ' οἴη φωτὶ ἑκάστῳ. Idem contra ubi luxum Phæacum describit, nominat Εἵματα τ' ἐξημοιβὰ, λοέτρα τε θερμὰ κὶ ἐνυνάς; Vide 2. Reg. V. 2. Inter Essænorum unde plurimi Christia- ni, instituta Josephus memorat: κδὲ ἐσθῆτας κδὲ ὑποδήμα- τα ἀμείβωσι, πρὶν ἢ διαῤῥαγῆναι τὸ πρότερον, ἢ παντάπασι δια- πατηθῆναι χρόνῳ.

Μηδὲ ὑποδήματα μηδὲ ῥάβδον] ῥάβδον non ῥάβδως legere Syrus & Latinus. Intellige baculum alium quam quem manu geritis, aut soleas alias quam quibus nunc induti e- stis, nam hunc esse sensum oftendit tum quod præcetlit, δύο χιτῶνας, hoc est, vestem alteram ab ea qua vestimini: tum quod apud Marcum est, ubi diferte permittitur bacu- lus quem gerebant, & soleæ illæ quibus erant induti. Ni- mirum quia iter facientibus soleæ illæ atterebantur, neq; raro fiebat ut baculus frangeretur, aut alicubi adhæresceret, ideo in sarcinulis solebant ponere alias soleas aliosque baculos. Hac cautione Christus Apostolos suos vult absti- nere: quocunque iter facturi essent reperturos & victui & itineri necessaria. Atque ideo multitudinis numero ῥάβδως dixit Lucas, ut significaret non interdici, quo minus bacu- lum unum haberent, sed quo minus plures, quod æquo jure de paribus soleatum debet intelligi. Vide etiam quæ ad Marcum dicentur.

Ita etiam habet B. Hunnii explicatio p. 328. qui vocem δύο è præcedentibus repetit: sed nec calcea- menta concedit illis, nimirum duplicia seu mutato- ria. Non in universum prohibet calceis muniri pe- des, siquidem celeritatem itineris non impediunt, sed potius promovent idonea calceamenta. Ideo Marcus eadem hac præcepta referens scribit, concessum esse illis, ut calcearentur sandaliis, quæ erant genus quod- dam calceamenti levioris ad maturandum cursum itinerantibus accommodum. Quæ etiam B. Lyseri fuit Harm. Evang. c. LXXII. ut & Thomæ, ac Caje- tani aliorumque interpretatio, quoad ὑποδήματα, Corn. à Lapide distinctioni, inter sandalia, plantam pedis duntaxat munientia, quæ concessa, & calceos totum pedem contegentes, subtiliori, quam solidiori præferenda. Præter quam aliam adhuc è Rabbinis attulit Lightfooth, quod usus delicatioris fuerint calcei, durioris sandalia, quorum solea vel pars in- ferior è ligno, superior è corio erat; ut ita inter- dicantur duæ tunicæ & calcei, ne superbiam, mun- danumve fastum, aut morem delicatiorem omni- no superent, sed ut potius habitum gestumq; cir- cumferrent quam humillimum. De baculis tamen conciliatio aptior est, quæ nostris placuit plerisque, ut & Cajetano, Franc. Lucæ, Jansenio, Cornelio, nec non Bezæ, Gualtero, aliis, quam Grotiana. Expli- cat eam ita B. Hunnius: Dominum non concedere Apostolis hujusmodi baculos, quibus armorum vice uterentur, & vel vim inferrent aliis, vel illatam a- liunde propulsarent. Vult enim plane inermes eos emittere, ut quoad defensionem necessariam toti à di- vino præsidio penderent. Concedit autem baculos seu virgas leviores, quibus in eundo gressum firmare possent. Quam explicationem etsi Andr. Osiander etiam suggesserit in Annot. ad Harm. Evangel. l. II. c. XIX. maluit tamen ipse, sed perperam, locum a- pud Lucam corruptum dicere, & pro εἰ μὴ ab osci- tante vel etiam audace librario μήτε fuisse scriptū statuere, quam quod virga aliud significet apud Lucam, quæ prohibeatur, quæ scilicet vindicandi causa geritur: aliud apud Marcum, quæ permittti- tur sustentandi lassi cursus gratia. Sed non con- cedenda est textus corruptela: nec ulla ejus neces- sitas est, quum alia suppetat convenientissima conciliandi ratio.

Vers. 10. ἄξιος] Vox ista Græcis, & quæ huic respon- dent Hebræis & Latinis, non semper τὸ ἴσον sed qualem- cunque rei convenientiam notat, ut liquet Ephes. IV. 1. Phil. I. 27. Col. I. 10. 1. Thess. II. 12. Joh. Epist. III. 6.

Τροφῆς] Sumitur hic τροφῆς nomen generalius, quomodo Jurisconsulti pronuntiant legatis alimentis, cibaria & vesti- tus & habitationem deberi, quia sine his alii corpus non po- test. Quanquam autem sententia hæc, eum qui operas præ- stet, victu, aut ut Lucas & Paulus loquuntur, mercede di- gnum esse, referri possit ad divinæ benignitatis æstimatio- nem, tamen cum Lucas & Paulus aperte hanc ἄξιον ponant, non inter Deum & Evangelii præcones, sed inter eosdem præcones, & qui eorum præconio edocentur, putem hic quoque ejusdem pronuntiati eandem esse sententiam, ut hoc dicat Christus: Deo providente victum accipietis ab il- lis ipsis, quibus docendis sanandisque operam navabitis: id- que jure æquissimo. Quid enim justius, quam τὰς τὰ πνευ- ματικὰ σπείροντας τὰ σαρκικὰ θερίζειν, 1. Cor. IX. 1. quantil- lum est tenuis victus, si cum tantis beneficiis comparetur? Atque hic iterum apparet μισθὸν dici citra æqualitatis ratio- nem: neque tantum ubi merces operam excedit, quod alibi ostendimus, verum etiam ubi indigna est merces quæ ad o- peram comparetur. Nam & de humanæ sententiæ docu- mentis non est veritus dicere Aristoteles ἡ πρὸς χρήμαθ' ἡ ἀξία μετρεῖται, τιμὴ δ' ἰσόῤῥοπον· ἐκ ἂν γένοιτο· ἀλλ' ἴσως ἰ- κανόν, καθάπερ κὴ πρὸς θεὺς κὴ πρὸς γονεῖς τὸ ἐνδεχόμενον.

## 10:11
Vers. 11. κἀκεῖ μείνατε] Let him double the fickleness for Christ: He wishes nothing to be changed rashly. He who has learned to live on little will neither seek out more sumptuous dinners, nor will he fear that he might exhaust his host with expense. Therefore κἀκεῖ pertains to the house, which follows ἕως ἂν ἐξέλθητε to the city or village. See Luke ch. X. 7.

Latin:

Vers. 11. κἀκεῖ μείνατε] Duplicet Christo levitas desulto- ria: nihil vult temere mutari. Qui parvo didicit vivere, is neque cænas lautiores captabit, neq; timebit, ne hospitem sumtu exhauriat. Ergo κἀκεῖ ad domum pertinet, quod se- quitur ἕως ἂν ἐξέλθητε ad urbem aut pagum. Vid. Luc. c. X. 7.

## 10:12
