Vers. 12. Ἀσπάσασθε αὐτήν.] I believe it most true that in the Hebrew it was שׁאלוּ שׁלוֹם, as it is in the Syriac. Thus the mention of peace followed appropriately in the following verse. But the Greek interpreter did not render word for word, but expressed the force of the Hebrew expression with a very well-known Greek word. Others later, when they did not think that what follows, ἡ εἰρήνη ὑμῶν, cohered sufficiently, stuffed a few words from Luke in here. And yet the very force of the word εἰρήνης, that is, of safety or security, was sufficiently comprehended in that ἀσπάζεσθαι.

Grotius supposes that the original text was Hebrew. But that hypothesis is precarious, nay, false. Meanwhile, he rightly acknowledges that in that ἀσπάζεσθαι is comprehended the force of the word εἰρήνης, of safety and security. Which was expressed by the word of greeting familiar to the Hebrews, or at least was included in it, because שׁלום comprehended not only peace, but safety and every kind of happiness. But those words which some stuff in: λέγοντες εἰρήνη τῷ οἴκῳ τούτῳ, most codices omit, as do the Syriac, Arabic, Ethiopic, and Persian versions.

Latin:

Vers. 12. Ἀσπάσασθε αὐτήν.] Verissimum arbitror in He- bræo fuisse שׁאלוּ שׁלוֹם quomodo est in Syriaco. Ita ap- posita est secuta mentio pacis commate sequenti. At Græcus interpres non verbum verbo reddidit, sed vim Hebraicæ lo- cutionis Græca notissima voce expressit. Alii postea cum non putarent sat cohærere quod sequitur ἡ εἰρήνη ὑμῶν vo- ces aliquot ex Luca huc infarserunt. Atqui vis ipsa vocis εἰρήνης, hoc est, salutis sive incolumitatis in illo ἀσπάζεσθαι satis comprehendebatur.

Supponit Grotius textum originalem Ebræum fuisse. Sed ea hypothesis precaria, imo falsa est. Interim recte agnoscit in illo ἀσπάζεσθαι compre- hendi vim vocis εἰρήνης salutis, & incolumitatis. Quæ voce salutationis Ebræis familiari exprime- batur, aut certe eidem includebatur, quia שׁלום non tantum pacem, sed salutem & felicitatem omni- genam comprehendebat. Verba autem illa quæ infarciunt nonnulli : λέγοντες εἰρήνη τῷ οἴκῳ τούτῳ, plerique codices omittunt, ut & Syriaca, Arabica, Æthiop. & Persic. versio.

## 10:13
Vers. 13. ἡ οἰκία ἀξία] Xenophon also used οἰκία for family, when he said οἰκίαν διατρέφειν. Nor is it used otherwise in John IV. 53, 1 Cor. XVI. 15, Phil. IV. 22. But in those places the family is distinguished from the head himself, whereas here it comprehends the father of the family himself at the same time: just as Ulpian noted that family is used in Roman usage. A family is called ἀξία in this place, which is of a teachable mind, not averse to piety, and which therefore is hoped to respond to the calling: just as, in the contrary way, those who are affected are said ἐκ ἀξίως κρίνειν ἑαυτὸς τῆς αἰωνίε ζωῆς, Acts XIII. 46. Pothinus, Bishop of Lyons, when asked by the governor who the God of the Christians was, replied: if you are worthy, you will know.

Ἡ εἰρήνη ὑμῶν] The Hellenists, in imitation of the Hebrews, call by this word whatever is held in the census of goods, that is, whatever is wont to be sought and desired. ὑμῶν, that is, which you yourselves have prayed for.

Πρὸς ὑμᾶς ἐπιστραφήτω] A Hebraism. A word is said to return to the one who utters it when it lacks the desired outcome: as can be seen in Isaiah LV. 11 and Psalm XXXV. 13.

Latin:

Vers. 13. ἡ οἰκία ἀξία] οἰκίαν pro familia etiam Xenophon posuit, cum dixit οἰκίαν διατρέφειν. Neque aliter usurpatur Joh. IV. 53. 1. Cor. XVI. 15. Phil. IV. 22. Sed istis in locis familia ab ipso capite distinguitur, hic vero ipsum Patrem familias simul comprehendit: quomodo & in usu Roma- no familiam dici Ulpianus notavit. Ἀξία hoc loco voca- tur familia, quæ animo est docili, non à pietate averso, ac quæ proinde speretur responsura vocationi: sicut contra- rio modo qui sunt affecti, dicuntur ἐκ ἀξίως κρίνειν ἑαυτὸς τῆς αἰωνίε ζωῆς, Actor. XIII. 46. Pothinus Lugdunensis E- piscopus interrogatus à præside, quis esset Christianorum Deus, respondit ἐὰν ἧς ἄξιος, γνώσῃ.

Ἡ εἰρήνη ὑμῶν] Hellenistæ Hebræorum imitatu, hac vo- ce appellant quicquid in bonorum censu habetur, hoc est quicquid expeti atque optari solet. ὑμῶν id est, quam vos ipsis precati fueritis.

Πρὸς ὑμᾶς ἐπιστραφήτω] Hebraïsmus. Reverti verbum ad proferentem dicitur quod eventu optato caret: ut vide- re est Esaiæ LV. 11. & Psal. XXXV. 13.

## 10:14
Vers. 14. Shake off the dust] It does not seem to me that this rite, directly at least, contains a denunciation of divine judgment, such as Nehemiah intended to be understood by shaking his garment, and the Romans by throwing a stone, but that it meant as much as if the Apostles were saying: we came here not for our own advantage, but for the sake of your salvation: now since you do not wish to listen to our warnings, keep your affairs to yourselves: we have no further dealings with you, and indeed we do not seek even the slightest thing of yours. As Tertullian explains: He commands the dust to be shaken off against them, in testimony, and to the horror of their land, much less any remaining communion. For this sense seems to be required by the fact that Luke in one place put it imperatively, 'and shake off the dust from your feet' IX. 5, but in another place enunciatively in the words of the Apostles themselves: 'and the dust which has clung to us from your city we wipe off against you,' X. 11, clearly contrary to what Naaman had done, who had carried away with him some of the Jewish soil, for the sake of reverence, 2 Kings V. 17. Moreover, Mark and Luke rightly add 'for a testimony to them,' because by the same rite it was simultaneously testified that teachers of truth had come to them. Thus God to Ezekiel ch. II. 5: That they may know that a Prophet has been in their midst.

Blessed Gerhard has explained the causes more fully, whose opinion we approve: That Christ commands them to shake off the dust signifies the innocence of the Apostles, who do not take even a speck of dust from the impious. Augustine, q. 7 on Matthew. Next, the magnitude of the punishment, which will be so great that the pious will not wish to have even the communion of dust with the impious. Thirdly, it is a testimony of despised grace, which those who rejected the offered salvation would be execrating. It was also a prelude that He would shake off or pour out His wrath upon them. It was customary among the Jews to join external symbols to words to strike more deeply. Not unlike this is what is read in Nehemiah V. 13, that Nehemiah shook out the fold of his garment in testimony against those who violated the faith given. Lightfoot observes that the Schools of the Scribes taught that the dust of Gentile land defiles by contact; and therefore this is the meaning: Wherever an Israelite city does not receive you, when you depart, shake the dust from your feet, that is, demonstrate that you consider that city, however Israelite it may be, as Gentile, profane, and impure, and that you abhor it. Regarding the passage 2 Kings V. 17, see the Annotations on the Old Testament.

Latin:

Vers. 14. Ἐκτινάξατε τὸν κονιορτὸν] Non videtur mihi ritus iste, directe quidem, denuntiatione divini judicii contine- re, qualem Nehemias excusso brachio, & Romani projecto lapide volebant intelligi, sed tantundem valuisse quasi di- cerent Apostoli: veneramus huc non nostri commodi, sed salutis vestræ causa: nunc quando monitis nostris auscul- tare non vultis, res vestras vobis habete: nihil nobis vo- biscum ultra commercii est, quin adeo ne tantillum qui- dem vestri expetimus. Quomodo Tertullian. explicat: Pulverem jubet excuti in illos, in testificationem, & ad horren- tiam terræ eorum, nedum communicationis reliquæ. Hunc e- nim sensum postulare videtur id quod Lucas uno loco im- perative posuit καὶ τὸν κονιορτὸν ἀπὸ τῶν ποδῶν ὑμῶν ἐκτινάξατε IX. 5. altero vero enunciative ipsorum Apostolorum ver- bis: καὶ τὸν κονιορτὸν τὸν κολληθέντα ἡμῖν ἐκ τῆς πόλεως ὑμῶν ἀ- πομασσόμεθα ὑμῖν, X. 11. contra scilicet quam fecerat Nee- man, qui de humo Judaica secum asportaverat, reverentiæ causa, 2. Reg. V. 17. Bene autem addunt Marcus & Lucas εἰς μαρτύριον αὐτοῖς, quia eodem ritu simul testatum sit ve- nisse ad ipsas doctores veritatis. Ita ad Ezechielem De- us c. II. 5. Vt sciant Prophetam fuisse in medio sui.

Plenius exposuit causas B. Gerhardus, cujus sen- tentiam probamus: Quod Christus jubet excutere pulverem, significat innocentiam Apostolorum, ne pulvisculum quidem ab impiis auferentium. Augu- stin. q. 7. in Matthæum. Deinde pœnæ magnitudi- nem, quæ tanta futura, ut ne quidem pulveris com- munionem pii cum impiis habere velint. Tertio est testimonium contemtæ gratiæ, quam essent execran- di, qui oblatam salutem respuerent. Fuit quoq; præ- ludium, quod iram suam in illos excussurus seu ef- fusurus sit. Usitatum erat apud Judæos verbis ad- jungere externa symbola ad magis percellendum. Non absimile est quod Nehemiæ V. 13. legitur, Nehe- miam excussisse oram vestimenti sui in testimonium contra eos, qui fidem datam violarent. Lightfooth observat Scholas Scribarum docuisse, pulverem terræ Ethnicæ ex contactu inquinare; ideoq; hunc sensum esse: Ubicunque vos non exceperit urbs Israelitica, cum discedatis excutite pulverem à pe- dibus vestris, id est, demonstrare vos urbem istam utcunque Israeliticam pro Ethnica, profana, im- pura reputare, atque abominari. De loco 2. Reg. V. 17. Vid. Annot. ad Vet. Test.

## 10:15
Vers. 15. In the day of judgment] Christ does not refer to the past time when those cities burned with heavenly fire, but to the future, as the word ἔσται shows. For even this day which Matthew calls 'the day of judgment,' Luke called with a mark of eminence, 'that day,' as Jude 'the judgment of the great day,' for which Peter had said, as Matthew here, 'the day of judgment.' Elsewhere 'the judgment' signifies the same thing: namely, the day destined for universal judgment. Concerning the Sodomites, therefore, it was not so much judged long ago as prejudged: nor indeed ought it to seem unjust to us if a heavier punishment threatens the despisers of the Gospel than those who were most foul with filthy lust and every kind of vice. For sins are to be estimated not precisely only from their own nature, but also from other circumstances of things and persons. The Sodomites had natural knowledge and the tradition of their parents: the Jews, the law of Moses, which is much clearer. The Sodomites had Lot as a monitor: and the Jews, the Apostles, bringing such great promises, remarkable for such great miracles. And from this also, no less than from many other places, it appears that the contempt of the Gospel is not a necessary effect of any vice that is common to the human race: but is either a peculiar fault, and one which could have been avoided, or certainly a certain testimony of such a fault. For that which flows necessarily from some fault cannot, above the lot common to that fault, aggravate the punishment of anyone.

Moreover, it is evident from this that there will be degrees of punishments in hell. Conf. c. XI. 21. Luke X. 12. c. XII. 47. 48. Rom. II. 9.

PART II. The prediction of persecutions, and the forewarning against them.

Latin:

Vers. 15. Ἐν ἡμέρᾳ κρίσεως] Non respicit Christus tempus præteritum quo urbes istæ cœlesti incendio conflagrarunt, sed futurum, ut ostendit verbum ἔσαι. Nam & diem hanc quam Matthæus vocat ἡμέραν κρίσεως, Lucas cum nota emi- nentiæ dixit, ἡμέραν ἐκείνην, ut Judas κρίσιν μεγάλης ἡμέρας, pro quo Petrus dixerat, ut hic Matthæus, ἡμέρας κρίσεως. Alibi ἡ κρίσις idem significat: nimirum diem universali judi- tio destinatum. De Sodomis ergo non tam judicatum est olim quam præjudicatum: neq; vero iniquum nobis videri debet, si gravior pœna imminet Evangelii contemptoribus, quam illis fœdissima libidine & omni vitiorum genere in- quinatissimis. Peccata enim non præcise tantum ex suapte natura, verum etiam ex aliis circumstantiis rerum & perso- narum æstimanda sunt. Habuerunt Sodomi notitias natu- rales & parentum traditionem: Judæi legem Mosis multo clariorem. Habuerunt Sodomi monitorem Lotum: ac Ju- dæi Apostolos tanta adferentes promissa, tantis miraculis spectabiles. Atque hinc quoq; non minus quam ex aliis lo- cis plurimis apparet, contemtum Evangelii non esse effectū necessarium alicujus vitii, quod sit commune humano ge- neri: sed aut culpam esse peculiarem, & quæ vitari potuit, aut certe culpæ talis certum testimonium. Quod enim ex culpa aliqua necessario fluit, id supra sortem ei culpæ com- munem, pœnam alicujus gravare non potest.

Patet autem hinc gradus fore suppliciorum in inferno. Conf. c. XI. 21. Luc. X. 12. c. XII. 47. 48. Rom. II. 9.

PARS II. Persecutionum prædictio, & adversus eas- dem præmunitio.

## 10:16
Vers. 16. I send you] By a verb of the present tense, he embraces the future at the same time. For the things which follow do not pertain so much to this mission as to those which Christ was afterwards about to entrust to the Apostles.

As sheep in the midst of wolves] Sophocles: [Greek text].

Wise as serpents.] I do not know whether Christ looked to that which has been handed down not only by many profane writers, but by David, that snakes most diligently stop up their ears against magical whispers, Ps. LVIII. 5, but also that they most diligently watch the feet of men so that they may not be crushed by them; it is simplest to say that reference is made to the keen-sightedness which is proper to serpents: for you see as sharply as an eagle, or an Epidaurian serpent.

Not only serpentine perspicacity, but also prudence, which the word itself implies, is referred to, to which also pertains the fact that they stop their ears, and that they watch and avoid dangers, because Scripture itself testifies of that in Ps. LVIII. 5; but that this is a part of prudence, such as falls to serpents, no one doubts. Concerning that, Bede on this place, with Augustine preceding in Ps. LVII: The prudence of the serpent is that it applies one ear to the rock and closes the other with its tail, so that it may not hear the enchanters. Concerning this, Ambrose, book VI, Ep. 42: In this let us follow the cunning of the serpent, that we do not cast our head into dangers, but guard it whole above all others. But our head is Christ; let this remain unharmed so that the poisons of the serpent cannot harm us. Isidore of Pelusium, book I, Ep. 16: The Lord commands us to be prudent as serpents. Namely, so that we may preserve our head, i.e., faith in Christ, in every temptation. Jerome, Vol. 1. Ep. 13 to Paulinus: Have the simplicity of the dove, so that you may not plot deceits against anyone, and the cunning of the serpent, so that you may not be tripped up by the snares of the wicked. Let the cunning of the serpent sharpen the simplicity of the dove, as Gregory the Great warns, book IV, Ep. 31 to Maurice, and let the simplicity of the dove temper the cunning of the serpent.

And harmless as doves] Cicero well advises in II De Officiis that there are many who, admiring versatile and crafty men, judge malice to be wisdom; therefore Christ, separating the recommendation of prudence from all fraud and deceit, joins innocence or simplicity to it as a companion. Even for Martial, among those things which make life happier, is prudent simplicity.

Latin:

Vers. 16. Ἀποστέλλω ὑμᾶς] Præsentis temporis verbo fu- turum simul complectitur. Quæ enim sequuntur non tam ab hanc legationem pertinent quam ad eas quas Chri- stus postea Apostolis erat mandaturus.

Ὡς πρόβατα ἐν μέσῳ λύκων] Sophocles: σπανῖσι ποθοῖς ἐκ σόφων διόλλυται.

Φρόνιμοι ὡς οἱ ὄφεις.] Nescio an id spectaverit Christus, quod non à profanis tantū scriptoribus plurimis, sed à Da- vide proditum est, angues diligentissime aures sibi obtura- re, adversus susurros magicos Ps. LVIII. 5. sed & pedes ho- minum ne ab iis obterantur, diligentissime observant, sim- plicissimum est ut dicamus respici τὸ ὀξυδερκὲς quod serpen- tibus est proprium: nam cernis acutum Quam aut aquila, aut serpens Epidaurius.

Non tantum perspicacitas serpentina, sed etiam prudentia, quod ipsa vox infert, respicitur, ad quā etiam pertinet, quod aures obturent, quodque ob- servent ac declinent pericula, quia de illo scriptura ipsa testatur Ps. LVIII. 5. hoc vero partem pruden- tiæ, qualis in serpentes cadit, esse nemo ambigit. De illo Beda in hunc locum præeunte August. in Ps. LVII. Prudentia serpentis est, quod unam aurem pe- træ apponit, alteram cauda claudit, ne audiat incan- tantes. De hoc Ambros. l. VI. Ep. 42. In eo astutiam serpentis sequamur, ut caput nostrum non projiciamus in pericula, sed præ cæteris integrum custodiamus. Caput autem nostrum Christus est, hoc maneat inco- lume ut serpentis venena nobis non possint nocere. Isi- dor. Pelusiot. l. 1. Ep. 16. Dominus nos prudentes ut serpentes esse jubet. Sic nempe ut caput nostrum h. e. fidem in Christum in omni tentatione conservemus. Hieronym. T. 1. Ep. 13. ad Paulin. Habeto simplicita- tem columbæ, ne cuiquam machineris dolos, & ser- pentis astutiam, ne à malorum supplanteris insidiis. Serpentis astutia columbæ simplicitatem, monente Gregorio M. l. IV. Ep. 31. ad Maurit. acuat, & co- lumbæ simplicitas serpentis astutiam temperet.

Καὶ ἀκέραιοι ὡς αἱ περιστεραί] Bene monet Cicero II. de of- fic. multos esse qui versutos homines & callidos admiran- tes, malitiam sapientiam judicent, Ideo Christus commen- dationem prudentiæ ab omni fraude doloque segregans, comitem ei adjungit innocentiam sive simplicitatem. Etiam Martiali inter ea quæ beatiorem vitam efficiunt, est pru- dens simplicitas.

## 10:17
Vers. 17. But beware of men] It was said elegantly by the old comic poet: How graceful a thing is man, if he be a man. But on the contrary, nothing is more savage than this living creature, when once it has fallen away from humanity, as a Greek rightly began a certain epigram: O man, more untamed than wild beasts.

And Ovid in his Epistle: I have found every kind of wild beast milder than you.

The Apostles are therefore commanded to be on their guard, i.e., not to contend with others about the conveniences and honors of this age, to avoid offenses as much as possible while keeping the truth uncorrupted; not to waste the very words of truth upon those whose wickedness is beyond hope.

Eis συνέδρια] Above we saw that the Sanhedrin is properly called by Christ the great Sanhedrin. Now Gabinius had instituted five such in Judea, as we said above: some of which (for I do not think all) could have survived in the time of Christ. But if one chooses to understand the lesser assemblies of XXIII judges, not even that will conflict with the usage of the word.

Και ἐν ταῖς συναγωγαῖς] This passage has seemed so obscure to most learned men that they held the reading, fortified by the faith of all the codices, to be suspect. But undoubtedly they were misled because they understood Proseuchae by the name of Synagogues. And yet it is certain that συναγωγὰς is also used for civil and judicial assemblies. 1 Macc. VII. 12. Additions to Daniel XIII. 14. Nor do I doubt that here the discourse ascends from Sanhedrins to Synagogues: for this to be understood, it must be noted that the Jews were accustomed at times, in matters pertaining to the height of religion or the state, to summon to the Sanhedrin as many of the tribal leaders or others endowed with honors as they could have, so that what they might decree would have the authority of a law approved by the people rather than of a senatus consultum. Such an assembly was called by the Hebrews קהל, in Greek sometimes ἐκκλησία, sometimes συναγωγὴ μεγάλη. Of such a kind was that assembly by whose decree King Josiah proclaimed the Passover 2 Par. XXX, 2. But elsewhere Josephus also relates that the γερουσίαν σὺν τοῖς φυλάρχοις (senate with the tribal leaders) had convened, among other times in the days of Joshua. Regarding the anathema by which the Hebrews relate that the contumacious were punished in the time of Ezra, it was done by the greater and lesser Sanhedrin. L. 1 Macc. XIV, 28. A certain Ψήφισμα (decree) is found in this form: on the eighteenth of Elul, in the one hundred and seventy-second year, and this is the third year under Simon the high priest in Saramel, in the great assembly of the priests and the people and the rulers of the nation and the elders of the country. Thus the teachers of the Hebrews call the great assembly כנסת הגדולה that gathering of, as they say, one hundred and twenty men around the times of the building of the second temple, in which gathering, besides the τοὺς συνέδρους (members of the Sanhedrin), there were also prophets and other leaders; Josephus calls such a gathering an ἐκκλησίαν πάνδημον (a public assembly of all the people), such as he says was gathered by Herod the Great, having summoned many, not only from the city but also ἐκ τῆς χώρας (from the country). Thus Gorionides says that the same Herod, not yet King, was accused for the killing of Hezekiah before the greater and lesser Sanhedrin. The outcome will show that what I say is most true, responding exactly to the words of Christ. Acts 4, Peter and John are brought before the high priests, elders, and scribes, whose assembly is called a συνέδριον (Sanhedrin) in that same place, as also elsewhere in verse 15. Soon in Acts V, it is related that the High Priest had summoned not only the συνέδριον, but also πᾶσαν τὴν γερουσίαν τῶν υἱῶν Ἰσραὴλ (all the senate of the children of Israel) in verse 21, because, clearly, with the people flowing together to the Apostles from all the towns (as is related in verse 16), this matter seemed to pertain to the danger of the highest state, so that it was worth the effort to seek the votes of all the honored men: or at least, as in the two examples already brought forward above, to join the senate of the city of Jerusalem with the senate of the people. This, therefore, was the συναγωγὴ μεγάλη; and the sense of the words of Christ is: you will be brought not only before ordinary consistories, but also for my sake you will be held in extraordinary assemblies. And it is apparent from the cited chapter of Acts, verse 40, that the Apostles were beaten with rods before such an extraordinary assembly. Synagogues can also be understood in the common meaning of a place of assembly, especially outside the Roman empire. For often by the favor of Kings, the power of punishment over their own people was granted to the Jews in those parts, the αἰχμαλωτάρχαις (exilarchs), which it is not incredible was accustomed to be exercised in the Synagogues: for Epiphanius also relates that a certain Jew, when he wished to defect to the Christians, was beaten with scourges in the synagogue. See what is in Acts XXII. 19 and XXVI. 11. And in Eusebius, a book written against the Montanists during the reign of Commodus is cited, where he says that no one of their flock was ἐν συναγωγαῖς ἰουδαίων μαστιγωθῆναι ἢ λιθοβοληθῆναι (scourged or stoned in the synagogues of the Jews).

Latin:

Vers. 17. Προσέχετε δὲ ἀπὸ τῶν ἀνθρώπων] Dictum est ele- ganter à Comico vetere. Ὡς χάριεν ἐς᾽ ἄνθρωπος ἂν ἄνθρωπος ᾖ. Sed contra nihil hoc animante sævius, ubi semel ab huma- nitate defcivit, ut recte Græcus epigramma quoddam ita inceperit, Εἶ θηρῶν βροτὲ μᾶλλον ἀνήμερος

Et Epistolam Ovidius: Mitius inveni quam te genus omne ferarum.

Cavere ergo homines jubentur Apostoli, i. e. de commo- dis & honoribus hujus ævi cum aliis non contendere, vita- re offensas quantum fieri potest incorrupta veritate; ipsa veritatis verba non perdere apud eos quorum deplorata est improbitas.

Eis συνέδρια] Supra vidimus à Christo Synedrium dici proprie synedrium magnum. Talia autem Gabinius quinq; instituerat in Judæa, ut supra diximus: quorum aliqua (Nam de omnibus non arbitror) superesse potuerunt Christi tempore. Quod si placet intelligere consessus minores XXIII. Judicum, ne id quidem cum vocis usu pugnabit.

Και ἐν ταῖς συναγωγαῖς] Tam obscurus viris doctissimis hic locus visus est, ut suspestam haberent lectionem omniũ codicum fide munitam. Sed nimirum imposuit illis quod Synagogarum nomine Proseuchas intelligerent. Atqui certum est συναγωγὰς dici etiam civiles & juridicos convent9. 1. Macc. VII. 12. Additamentis ad Danielem XIII.14. neque dubito quin hic scandat oratio à Synedriis ad Synagogas: quod ut intelligatur notandum est solitos fuisse interdum Judæos in rebus ad summam religionis aut imperii spectantibus advocare ad synedrium quotquot habere poterant tribuum primores aliúsve honoribus præditos, ut quod constituerent legis potius à populo probatæ, quam senatus consulti haberet auctoritate. Talis convent9 vocabatur Hebræis קהל Græce interdum ἐκκλησία, interdum συναγωγὴ μεγάλη. Ejusmodi fuit is conventus ex cujus decreto Pascha indixit rex Josias 2. Par. XXX, 2. Sed & alibi Josephus narrat convenisse γερουσίαν σὺν τοῖς φυλάρχοις, inter cætera Josuæ temporibus. De anathemate quo Esdræ tempore puniti contumaces narrant Hebræi factum à synedrio majore & minore. L. 1. Macc. XIV, 28. Ψήφισμα quoddam invenitur in hanc formam: ὀκτωκαιδεκάτῃ ἐλοὺλ, ἔτους δευτέρου κὴ ἑβδομηκοστοῦ κὴ ἑκατοστοῦ, κὴ τοῦτο τρίτον ἔτ᾽ ἐπὶ σίμωνος ἀρχιερέως ἐν Σαραμελ, ἐπὶ συναγωγῆς μεγάλης ἱερέων κὴ λαοῦ κὴ ἀρχόντων ἔθνους κὴ τῶν πρεσβυτέρων τῆς χώρας. Ita Hebræorum magistri μεγάλην συναγωγὴν כנסת הגדולה vocant cœtum illum centum, ut ajunt, & viginti virorũ circa tempora ædificationis templi secundi, in quo cœtu præter τοὺς συνέδρους & Prophetæ fuerunt & primores alii; Josephus talem cœtum vocat ἐκκλησίαν πάνδημον, qualem coactum ait ab Herode magno convocatis multis, non ex urbe tantum sed & ἐκ τῆς χώρας. Sic Herodem eundem, nondum Regem, ob interfectum Ezechiam accusatum ait Gorionides coram synedrio majore & minore. Verissimum esse quod dico ostendet eventus, Christi verbis ad amussim respondens. Act. 4. sistuntur Petrus & Johannes pontificibus, seniorib. & legisperitis, quorum confessus ibidem, ut & alibi συνέδριον vocatur commate 15. Mox Act. V. narratur Pontifex convocasse non tantũ συνέδριον, sed & πᾶσαν τὴν γερουσίαν τῶν υἱῶν Ἰσραὴλ commate 21. quia scilicet populis ex omnibus oppidis ad Apostolos confluentibus (ut narratur commate 16) res hæc ad summæ reipublicæ periculum spectare videbatur, ita ut operæ pretium esset omniũ honoratorum suffragia exquirere: aut saltem, ut in duobus exemplis supra jam adductis, senatũ urbis Hierosolymitanæ, cum senatu populi conjungere. Hæc ergo fuit συναγωγὴ μεγάλη; sensusq; verborũ Christi est: non tantum ordinariis consistoriis sistemini, sed & conventus extraordinarii vestri causa habebuntur. Coram tali autẽ conventu extraordinario cæsos virgis Apostolos apparet dicto Actorum capite commate 40. Possunt etiam synagogæ intelligi vulgari significatu loci conventuum, præsertim extra Romanum imperium. Sæpe enim Regum beneficio illis in partibus Judæis αἰχμαλωτάρχαις concessa est animadversio in populares, quam in Synagogis solitam exerceri non incredibile est: nam & Epiphanius narrat Judæum quemdam cum ad Christianos deficere vellet in synagoga flagris cæsum. Vide quæ Act. XXII. 19. & XXVI. 11. Et apud Eusebium citatur liber imperante Commodo adversus Montanistas scriptus, ubi ait eorum gregis neminem ἐν συναγωγαῖς ἰουδαίων μαστιγωθῆναι ἢ λιθοβοληθῆναι.

## 10:18
Vers. 18. Καὶ βασιλεῖς] Although those who have vicarious or delegated power are sometimes called מלכים by the Hebrews, in which sense that name also seems to be applied to Pontius Pilate in Acts IV. 26, 27, yet since the mention of ἡγεμόνων (governors) has preceded, it is necessary that the word be taken more strictly here. The same opposition of ἡγεμόνων and βασιλέων is also found in Peter 1 Ep. II. 13, εἴτε βασιλεῖ ὡς ὑπερέχοντι, εἴτε ἡγεμόσιν ὡς δι' αὐτοῦ πεμπομένοις (whether to the king as supreme, or to governors as sent by him). This oracle therefore maintained its own truth, when Peter spoke his defense before Nero, John before Domitian, and others before the kings of the Parthians, Scythians, and Indians.

Εἰς μαρτύριον αὐτοῖς κὴ τοῖς ἔθνεσι] See chapter VIII for the force of this expression. By this act, says Christ, the governors and Kings and peoples who will stand before their tribunals will be convinced of the truth they have heard.

Latin:

Vers. 18. Καὶ βασιλεῖς] Quanquam Hebræis מלכים dicuntur interdum qui vicariam aut mandatam habent potestatem, quo sensu nomen illud etiam Pontio Pilato videtur aptari Act. IV. 26. 27. cum tamen ἡγεμόνων mentio præcesserit, necesse est vocem illam hic strictius accipi. Eadem oppositio ἡγεμόνων & βασιλέων est & apud Petrum 1. Ep. II. 13. εἴτε βασιλεῖ ὡς ὑπερέχοντι, εἴτε ἡγεμόσιν ὡς δι' αὐτοῦ πεμπομένοις. Constitit igitur huic oraculo sua fides, cum Petrus apud Neronem, Johannes apud Domitianum, alii apud Parthorum, Scytharum, Indorum reges causam dixere.

Εἰς μαρτύριον αὐτοῖς κὴ τοῖς ἔθνεσι] Quæ sit vis hujus locutionis vide cap. VIII. Hoc facto convincentur, inquit Christus, præsides & Reges & populi, qui illorum tribunalibus astabunt, auditæ veritatis.

## 10:19
Vers. 19. Μὴ μεριμνήσητε] The word μεριμνᾶν does not signify just any meditation, but anxiety of mind and laborious preparation such as is customary for orators. See what we said at chapter 7. Mark said προμεριμνᾷν; Luke said προμελετᾷν.

Δοθήσεται γὰρ ὑμῖν ἐν ἐκείνῃ τῇ ὥρᾳ τὶ λαλήσετε] There is a reference to the passage in Exodus III. 11. Even if anything is lacking to you beforehand, at that very time it will be supplied by heavenly aid, with the divine Spirit providing both wisdom to the mind and, to the mouth, eloquence that is not artificial but by a simple gravity reflecting the very nature of naked truth. We see the fulfillment of this promise in Peter and Stephen: indeed, in all the martyrologies. Christ demands of the Apostles that they be willing to bear witness to his doctrine; that they may do this rightly, he himself will provide, in that hour, as was said above VIII. 13. IX. 22.

Latin:

Vers. 19. Μὴ μεριμνήσητε] Vox μεριμνᾶν non qualemcunq; meditationem, sed animi anxietatem significat & laboriosam præparationem qualis esse oratorum solet. Vide quæ diximus ad c. 7. προμεριμνᾷν dixit Marcus: προμελετᾷν Lucas.

Δοθήσεται γὰρ ὑμῖν ἐν ἐκείνῃ τῇ ὥρᾳ τὶ λαλήσετε] Respicitur locus Exod. III. 11. Etiamsi quid vobis antea desit, eo ipso tempore ope cœlesti supplebitur, Spiritu divino suppeditante & animo sapientiam, & ori eloquium non calamistratũ, sed simplici gravitate ipsam nudæ veritatis naturam refe- rens. Hujus promissionis complementum in Petro & Ste- phano videmus: imo in omnibus martyrologiis. Ab Apo- stolis exigit Christus ut suæ doctrinæ velint præbere testi- monium; ut recte id faciant ipse præstiturus, ἐν ἐκείνῃ τῇ ὥρᾳ dictum ut supra VIII. 13. IX. 22.

## 10:20
Verse 20. For it is not you who are speaking. Note again that the negation is to be interpreted not absolutely but comparatively. It will not be so much you who will speak, as the Holy Spirit through you. See the histories already named in the Acts of the Apostles, with the addition of the passage 2 Sam. XXIII. 2. Lest the Apostles be dismayed by such great dangers, Christ promises them great help, not angels, but the Spirit of God himself, than which nothing greater could be promised.

Latin:

Vers. 20. ὀ γὰρ ὑμεῖς ἐστε οἱ λαλοῦντες] Nota iterum negatio- nem non absolute sed comparate interpretandam. Non tam vos eritis qui loquemini, quam per vos Spiritus S. Vide jam nominatas historias in actis Apostolicis, addito loco 2. Sam. XXIII. 2. Ne consternarentur tantis periculis Apostoli, ma- gnum illis auxilium Christus promittit, non Angelos, sed ipsum Dei Spiritum, quo nihil majus promitti potuit.

## 10:21
Verse 21. And he will deliver up. The Hebrews bring these signs of the times of the Messiah in the Talmud under the titles Sanhedrin and Ketubath.

Latin:

V. 21. Παραδώσει δὲ] Hæc signa temporum Messiæ afferunt Hebæi in Thalmude titulis Sanhedrin & Ketubath.

## 10:22
Verse 22. Being hated by all. That is, by most men. For thus the particles of universality are accustomed to be taken. Petronius Arbiter: If anyone, an enemy of all vices, begins to insist upon the straight path of life, he first has hatred because of the difference in morals. For who can approve of things that are different? Athenagoras: From whence it follows how, and not only among you, according to some divine law and reason, it has followed that vice should war against virtue.

My name. For this reason, because you profess yourselves to be my disciples. For this is the meaning of 'name': because it was the custom for disciples to be called by the name of their masters. Peter explains this when he says that thanks and praises are to be given to God when we suffer as Christians, 1 Pet. IV. 15, to which passage add that which is in Acts V. 41.

But he who has endured to the end, he shall be saved. Virgil expressed the force of the word 'endure' very well in that verse: Endure and save yourselves for favorable things. For it signifies patience with the expectation of some good, 'Blessed is he who waits,' Dan. XII. 12. Irenaeus rightly warns that patience is twofold, one from the beginning, the other from repentance. Christ exhorts the Apostles to the former, yet so that he does not meanwhile exclude the latter from the hope of salvation.

Latin:

Vers. 22. Μισούμενοι ὑπὸ πάντων] Id est à plerisque homi- nibus. Ita enim sumi solent particulæ universitatis. Petro- nius arbiter: Si quis vitiorum omnium inimicus rectum iter bi- læ cœpit insistere, primum propter morum differentiam odium habet. Quis enim potest probare diversa? Athenagoras: ἀνα- θεν πῶς ἐθῶν, ϰὴ ὀκ ἐφ' ὑμῶν μόνον, κατά τινα θεῖον νόμον ϰὴ λόγον παρηκολούθηκε προσπολεμεῖν τὴν κακίαν τῇ ἀρετῇ.

Τὸ ὄνομά με] Eam ob causam, quod vos discipulos meos profitemini. Hæc enim est significatio ὀνόματος: quia moris erat discipulos vocari ex magistrorum nomine. Explicat Pe- trus, cum dicit gratias laudesque agendas Deo cum patimur ut Christiani 1. Pet. IV. 15. cui loco adjunge eū qui est Act. V. 41.

Ὁ δὲ ὑπομείνας εἰς τέλος, ὗτος σωθήσεται] Vim vocis ὑ- πομένειν optime Virgilius illo versu expressit: Durate & rebus vosmet servate secundis. Patientiam enim cum exspectatione boni alicujus signifi- cat, אשרי המחכה Dan. XII. 12. Bene autem monet Irenæus ὑπομονὴν esse duplicem, aliam ἐξ ἀρχῆς, aliam ἐκ μετανοίας. Ad illam Apostolos hortatur Christus, ita tamen ut hanc interim à spe salutis non excludat.

## 10:23
Verse 23. They persecute. Since 'flee' follows, I clearly think 'to persecute' here should be taken strictly, for 'to cast out.' Thus 'in this city' is placed for 'from this city,' as we said above VI. 6, which, because it was more obscure, an interpretation 'they persecute from this city' was once added, which then, as is wont to happen, was admitted into the text of some codices. The meaning is: Being cast out of one city by force, do not desist from the duty imposed upon you. Therefore flee, not into some wilderness where you might be safer, but into another city, there also to experience the fruit of your instruction. It appears, therefore, that an argument for the question of voluntary flight solely for the sake of avoiding danger is not rightly drawn from this place: however, it is not easy to define anything universally about flight, since it must be decided differently according to the circumstances of times and places. Cyprian, who otherwise held the authority of Tertullian in high regard, disapproved by his own example the opinion of him who condemned all flight. Clement in Stromata IV and VII very well left it to be estimated from the glory of God and the utility of men, which dangers are to be undergone and which are to be avoided, by a mind that neither desires nor fears death. 'Even if a Christian flees,' says Origen against Celsus, 'and flees because of cowardice, but keeping the commandment of the Teacher and keeping himself pure, others will be benefited by his salvation.' Nor should what the same Origen wrote on this matter to John, and after him Athanasius in his book on that subject, and Augustine in his letter to Honoratus, be despised.

You shall not have finished the cities of Israel until the Son of Man comes. 'Finish the cities,' i. e., 'finish teaching the cities,' such an ellipsis of the infinitive we have also noted above and will note elsewhere. And 'until' is placed in place of 'before,' as we said also above V. 18. But interpreters disagree as to what advent is to be understood here. It is certain to me that the advent of Christ in these books is said in many ways, and often by it is understood not the presence of the body, but proofs of power, in which kind that most abundant mission of the grace of the Holy Spirit excels, not only upon the Apostles but upon other believers, by which most certain sign it is established that that long-expected kingdom had now arrived, and Christ had been constituted its king with most full power by the Father. Founding this opinion of mine on John the Apostle, in whose work Christ, explaining now somewhat more clearly what he had said more obscurely here, consoles his disciples against all the force of impending dangers by saying that he will send them that Spirit of truth, and immediately adds: 'I will not leave you as orphans bereft of a parent: I am coming to you' XIV. 18, where I think it is most clear that by the advent of Christ the mission of the Spirit is signified. Add those words of Peter, Acts II. 33: 'Exalted to the sublime by the right hand of God and having obtained from the Father that long-promised Spirit, he poured out this which you yourselves see and hear.' Therefore, this is the paraphrase of Christ's words: I have said what evils were impending over you: I have said nevertheless that it is your duty to hold your ground: but do not lose heart: my great and royal power is at the doors, which is about to appear shortly, indeed before you have finished teaching the Jews within the borders of Palestine: By these words Christ shows that the grace

of the Spirit would anticipate their long journeys. For even afterwards, when he was now about to depart from the Apostles, he gave them the command to instruct all nations, but yet so that they should make their beginning from Jerusalem: and there they should remain, until that promised Spirit had come upon them, Luke XXIV. 47, 48, 49. Acts I. 4, 5, 8. Therefore, what follows coheres very well. If Christ could not arrive at that glory except through the most grievous calamities, the followers of Christ ought not to shun the same lot.

Grotius is correct and concise here. Τελει̃ν τὰς πό- λεις concerns that completion which is done by traversing the world, for the execution of which the Apostles had been sent into the cities of Judea. Cf. 1 Sam. 16:12. The explanation of Cameron in Myroth. Evang. and others is less suitable, as if Christ here promises the Apostles his presence in the function of teaching, insofar as he himself was about to teach publicly in Judea and Galilee and to give assurance to the Apostles' mission by stupendous miracles. For the words of the promise do not sound of assistance in the present, but of the future coming of the Son of Man. Heinsius takes these words to refer to the final coming of Christ, but very awkwardly. These things were said to the Apostles, which indeed regarding τὸ τελει̃ν τὰς πόλεις, cannot be drawn to all ministers of the word, the successors of the Apostles. Beza wishes Christ to have signified that he would be present again with the disciples before they had traveled through the whole region: lest, clearly, thinking themselves sent away by their Master, they should lose heart. Which is also the interpretation of Theophylact. Others refer these things to the final and most famous entry into Jerusalem. Which seems clever to Beza. But, as I have said, the Grotian explanation is most convenient. Not inconvenient, however, is the ἐξήγησις of B. Ægidius Hunnius: It is an anticipation, by which the Lord forestalls the objection of his disciples. For they could have objected that by this reasoning, very little fruit would follow from the preaching of the Gospel, if persecutions are immediately stirred up, and they themselves, driven and expelled now from this city, now from that, have need to seek hiding places continually. Therefore, in place of consolation, the Lord adds this promise, confirmed by his oath, that their preaching will not be idle or vain. For if the Gospel should be rejected even in one city, nevertheless it would find a place in another, nor would they have traveled through all the cities of Judea before they manifestly perceived that the Son of Man had come, that is, that Christ by his divine grace, power, and blessing had given increase to their labors. For he discourses in this place about this coming of the Son of Man, by means of which, clearly, Christ is carried into the world in the chariot of his Gospel, and insinuates himself into the hearts of men by his power.

Latin:

Vers. 23. Διώκωσιν] Cum sequatur φεύγετε, plane arbitror διώκειν hic stricte sumendum, pro ἐκβάλλειν. Ita 15 ἐν τῇ πόλει ταύτῃ positum est pro δι ἐν τῇ πόλει ταύτῃ ut diximus supra VI. 6. quod quia erat obscurius ideo adjecta est olim inter- pretatio διώκωσιν ἐκ τῆς πόλεως ταύτης, quæ deinde ut fieri so- let in aliquorum codicum textum admissa est. Sensus est: Ex una urbe per vim ejecti, ne destitite ab imposito vobis mu- nere. Iccirco fugite non in solitudinem aliquam ubi sitis tu- tiores, sed in urbem aliam, ibi quoque experturi proventū vestræ institutionis. Apparet igitur non recte ex hoc loco peti argumentum ad quæstionem de fuga voluntaria solo vitandi periculi respectu:non est autem facile de fuga quic- quam universim definire, cum pro circumstantia temporum ac locorum aliter atq; aliter sit statuendum. Tertulliani sen- tentiam qui fugam omnem damnabat, Cyprianus, alioqui magni ejus auctoritatem faciens, exemplo suo improbavit. Optime Clemens Stromateon IV. & VII. quæ pericula sub- eunda, quæ vitanda sint, animo mortem neq; optanti,neq; metuenti, ex Dei gloria & hominum usu æstimandum reli- quit. Κἂν φύγῃ ὁ χρισιανὸς, inquit adversus Celsum Orige- nes, & διὰ δειλίαν φέυγη, ἀλλὰ τηρῶν ἐντολὴν τῷ διδασκάλυ ϰ ἑαυτὸν φυλάττων καθαρὸν, ἑτέρων ὠφεληθησομένων σωτηρίας. Ne- que contemnenda quæ hac de re idem Origenes ad Joan- nem & post eum Athanasius libro ejus argumenti, & Au- gustinus in Epistola ad Honoratum scripsere.

ὑμὴτελέσητε τὰς πόλεις τῶ Ἰσραὴλ, ἕως ἂν ἔλθῃ ὁ ὑὸς ἀνθρώπε] τελέσητε τὰς πόλεις, i. e. τελέσητε διδάξαι τὰς πόλεις, qualem infinitivi ἔκλειψιν suprà quoque annotavimus & annotabi- mus alibi. Et ἕως ἂν positum est vice τῶ πρὶν, ut dixim9 etiam supra V. 18. Quis autem hic adventus intelligendus sit, di- screpant interpretes. Mihi constat adventum Christi in hisce libris multis modis dici, & sæpe eo non corporis præsenti- am, sed virtutis documenta intelligi, in quo genere excellit missio illa copiosissima gratiæ Spiritus S. nec in Apostolos tantum, sed in credentes alios, quo certissimo indicio con- stitit regnum illud diu exspectatum jam advenisse, & Chri- stum ejus regem cum plenissima potestate à patre constitu- tum. Fundūdo huic sententiæ meæ Johannem Apostolum, apud quem Christus jam clarius aliquanto explicans quod hic obscurius dixerat, adversus omnem vim ingruentium periculorum discipulos suos eo solatur, quod missurum se dicat ipsis Spiritum illum veracem, statimq; addit: non re- linquam vos velut pupillos parente orbos: venturus sum ad vos XIV. 18. ubi apertissimum puto Christi adventu missionē Spi- ritus significari. Adde illa Petri verba Act. II. 33. Dextra Dei in sublime evectus & à Patre nactus Spiritum illum diu promis- sum, effudit hoc quod ipsi aspicitis atq; auditis. Est ergo verborū Christi hæc paraphrasis: Dixi quæ mala vobis imminerent: dixi nihilominus vestrum esse inflare capro: sed nolite animum despondere:præ foribus est mea magna & regia potestas, quæ ap- paritura est brevi, imo antequam finem feceritis docendis Judæis intra fines Palestinæ: His verbis ostendit Christus gratiam

Spiritus anticipaturam ipsorum longinquas profectiones. Nam & postea, jam jamque ab Apostolis discessurus, man- datum, ipsis dedit omnes gentes instituendi, sed ita tamen, ut ab Hierosolymis exordium facerent: ibique subsiste- rent, donec promissus ille Spiritus ipsis supervenisset, Luc. XXIV. 47. 48. 49. Act. I. 4. 5. 8. Optime ergo cohærent quæ sequuntur. Non si Christus ad istam gloriam perve- nire, nisi per gravissimas calamitates non potuit, non de- bent Christi sectatores eandem sortem defugere.

Recte hæc & concinne Grotius. Τελει̃ν τὰς πό- λεις concernit illud perficere, quod fit mundo obe- undo, ad quod exequendū in civitates Judææ missi erant Apostoli. Conf. 1. Sam. XVI. 12. Minus conve- niens est Cameronis in Myroth. Evang. & aliorum explicatio, quasi promittat hic Christus Apostolis suam in docendi functione præsentiam, quatenus & ipse publice in Judæa & Galilæa docturus, & mi- raculis stupendis Apostolorum legationi fidem fa- cturus erat. Nam non de assistentia in præsenti, sed de futuro adventu filii hominis promissionis verba sonant. De adventu ultimo Christi, sed admo- dum incommode accipit Heinsius. Dicta hæc ad Apostolos, quod quidem ad τὸ τελει̃ν τὰς πόλεις, non possunt trahi ad omnes verbi ministros, Apo- stolorum successores. Beza vult Christum signifi- casse se rursus affuturum discipulis, priusquam to- tam regionem peragrāssent: ne videlicet sese à Ma- gistro ablegari existimantes animum desponde- rent. Quæ etiam Theophylacti est interpretatio. Alii hæc ad ingressum ultimum & celeberrimum in Hierusalem referunt. Quod Bezæ argutum vi- detur. Sed, ut dixi, convenientissima est Grotiana explicatio. Non incommoda tamen B. Ægid. Hun- nii ἐξήγησις: Occupatio est, qua discipulorum suo- rum objectionem antevertit Dominus. Etenim po- tuissent illi obtendere hac ratione, perexiguum secu- turum fructum ex prædicatione Evangelii, si sub- inde moveantur persecutiones, atque ipsi nunc hac, nunc alia civitate excussi & expulsi latibula subinde quærere necesse habeant. Ideo Dominus solatii vice hanc promissionem suo juramento confir- matam subjicit, quod prædicatio illorum otiosa aut inanis futura non sit. Si enim maxime in una ci- vitate repellatur Evangelium, tamen locum esse in- venturum in alia, neque ipsos perambulatusos esse civitates omnes Judææ, quin manifeste sentiant venisse filium hominis, id est, Christum divina sua gratia, virtute & benedictione laboribus illorum dedisse incrementum. De hoc enim adventu filii hominis isto loco disserit, quo scilicet mediante, Chri- stus Evangelii sui curru in mundum invehitur, & in hominum pectora virtute sua se insinuat.

## 10:24
Verse 24. οὐκ ἔστι μαθητὴς ὑπὲρ τὸν διδάσκαλον] This proverb, most accepted by the Hebrews, seems to conflict with this Greek proverb: Πολλοὶ μαθηταὶ κρείσσονες διδασκάλων. But the Greek verse deals with those who have been disciples: the Hebrew sentiment with those who remain disciples, just as Christ's disciples must never cease to be his disciples. However, Christ does not always use this proverb, as also the other not dissimilar one, by which a servant is denied to be greater than his Lord, in the same sense, as can be seen in Luke 6:40, John 13:16, chapter 15:20, which also occurs in other proverbs. Here an equal outcome is signified because of the nature of the same doctrine.

Latin:

Vers. 24. οὐκ ἔστι μαθητὴς ὑπὲρ τὸν διδάσκαλον] Videtur pugnare hoc adagium Hebræis receptissimum isti ada- gio Græco: Πολλοὶ μαθηταὶ κρείσσονες διδασκάλων. Sed Græcus versus agit de iis qui discipuli fuere: Hebræa sententia de iis qui discipuli manent, sicut Christi discipuli nunquam debent desinere ejus esse discipuli. Hoc autem proverbium, ut & alterum non dissimile, quo servus nega- tur esse Domino major, Christis non eodem semper sensu usurpat, ut videre est Luc. VI. 40. Joh. XIII. 16. cap. XV. 20. quod & in aliis proverbiis occurrit. Hic par eventus significatur ob doctrinæ ejusdem ingenium.

## 10:25
Verse 25. Ἀρκετὸν τῳ̃ μαθητῃ̃ ἵνα γένηται ὡς ὁ διδάσκαλος αὐτου̃] רב לעבד להיות כרבו Midrash on Ps. 10. Βεελζεβὺλ] Thus the Syriac: thus the ancient Latins: thus the Hebrew language. That others write βεελζεβοὺλ is a corruption either of the writer or of the pronunciation, which often happens to the final letters. Thus ἄβακοὺμ is read for ἄβακοὺκ in the LXX version. And συνυχαρίη for συνυαχρείθ. Thus for Manaen in Acts 13:1, the Syriac has מנאיל, and for בליעל we read βελιάρ everywhere. But since this was the name of him who was believed to excel among the gods of the nations, it is hardly credible that it was called Beelzebub, that is, lord of flies, by the Accaronites themselves and their neighbors. For μύαγρος, σμίνθευς and similar are names of minor deities.

It pleases me greatly that it has been noted by men who have deserved very well of sacred history that the gods of the nations were accustomed to be called by the Hebrews by names changed in contempt, just as they called Bethlehem, that is, the house of God, Bethaven, that is, the house of vanity. Thus that deity which the Accaronites, as other Phoenicians, called βεελσαμᾶν, that is, Δία ὐράνιον, or Δία ὀλύμπιον as Dius wrote in the history of the Phoenicians, the Jews called βεελζεβούβ, that is, the fly-Jupiter. But that Beelsamen was called the god of those nations, Augustine teaches us besides Philo of Byblos at Judges chapter II. But it can still be asked, whence the origin of the contemptuous name? I will say what seems likely. The ancient Jews relate with great consensus that among other privileges which God had granted to the Jerusalem temple, this was also one, that, although such a great number of victims was slaughtered daily, yet no fly was ever seen in the temple, which, since that most celebrated among profane nations Ζεὺς ὐράνιον could not provide, but his temple was perpetually swarming with flocks of flies, therefore he was called by the Jews the Jupiter of flies. Moreover, the Phoenicians and their colonists the Carthaginians worshipped a celestial god, who is בעלת שמין & בעל שמין and a celestial goddess who is Esaix, מלכת השימם, Juno Maroni. But it is not to be doubted that by the former word they indicated the Sun, by the latter the moon, the most ancient deities of almost all nations. In the old Epistle of Nebuchadnezzar which Abydenus the Assyrian historiographer described, בעל is Βῆλος, כמלת ἐστι Βᾶλτις. Moreover, the Jews, taught by the Prophets that the gods of the nations are demons, that is, that the oracles which were uttered from such statues of gods were not uttered by the power of those stars, which the nations thought, but by the work of impure spirits, to whom therefore in reality all the honor of that worship would redound, called the prince of evil demons by that name by which the prince of the falsely believed-in gods was called. See below XII. 24. Now indeed, since the Pharisees wished to persuade the common people that the miracles which were performed by Christ were performed by the power of that prince of demons, therefore they also called Christ himself, through the greatest wickedness, as if he were the agent and vicar of that demon, Beelzebub.

Grotius does not want the name Beelzebub to have originated from the Accaronites. He prefers that it was so called by the Hebrews in contempt of their deity. But if the deity of the Accaronites had been so called by the Hebrews out of contempt, Ahaziah would not have called it so; when he ordered to consult it 2 Kings I. 2. Nor is it credible that the deity was called the Lord of flies from an inability to drive away flies, and it is very akin to a fable what the Jews relate about the privilege of the Jerusalem temple, which Grotius believed too easily, namely that no fly was ever seen in it; but it is more likely that he was called the lord and driver-away of flies, just as he was called ἀπόμυιον by the Gentiles themselves as Jupiter, because the Accaronites believed that they could be freed from the flies, by which they were gravely afflicted, through this deity of theirs, just as it is read that when the Cyrenians were sacrificing to that deity all the flies flew away; and that he exhibited their deity in the form of a Fly as if he were the prince of flies, whence others prefer to render the God Fly as Beelzebub, rather than of Flies, just as on Phoenician coins a Fly was therefore accustomed to be represented as an image. See Selden, book II, de DIS Syr. c. 6, and B. Job. Ern. Gerh. in analect. ad Matth. XII. 24.

Πόσῳ μᾶλλον τὺς οἰκιακὺς αὐτῦ] The outcome responds to the words: Celsus calls the apostles γόητας (sorcerers). Ulpian the jurist calls Christians who performed exorcisms impostors: Tacitus says they were convicted of hatred of the human race. Everywhere Christians and ἀθεοι (atheists) were placed in the same category. This is the thanks that incorrupt teachers of truth receive from the world.

Latin:

Vers. 25. Ἀρκετὸν τῳ̃ μαθητῃ̃ ἵνα γένηται ὡς ὁ διδάσκαλος αὐτου̃] רב לעבד להיות כרבו Midrasch in Ps. X. Βεελζεβὺλ] Ita Syrus: ita Latini veteres: ita Hebræus sermo. Quod alii scribunt βεελζεβοὺλ, aut scriptoris aut pro- nuntiationis est corruptio, quæ in postremas literas sæpe incidit. Ita ἄβακοὺμ pro ἄβακοὺκ legitur in versione LXX. Et συνυχαρίη pro συνυαχρείθ. Sic pro Maran Act. XIII. 1. Sy- rus habet מנאיל, & pro בליעל passim legimus βελιάρ. Cum vero hoc fuerit nomen ejus qui inter deos gentium excellere crederetur, vix credibile est ab ipsis Accaro- nitis eorumque vicinis dictum fuisse Beelzebub, id est muscarum dominum. Nam μύαγρος, σμίνθευς & simi- lia minorum numinum sunt vocabula.

Mihi valde placet quod a viris optime de sacra historia meritis est annotatum, solitos gentium Deos ab Hebræis appellari nominibus in contumeliam mutatis, sicut & Bethlehem, hoc est, domum Dei, Bethaven, id est, va- nitatis domum dixere. Sic illud numen quod Accaronitæ, ut Phœnices alii vocabant βεελσαμᾶν, hoc est, Δία ὐράνιον, aut Δία ὀλύμπιον ut Dius scribebat in Phœnicum historia, Judæi vocarunt βεελζεβούβ, hoc est, Jovem muscarium. Beelsamen autem vocatum fuisse Deum istarum nationum, præter Philonem Byblium Augustinus nos docet ad Judi- cum cap. II. Sed quæri adhuc potest, unde origo contu- meliosi nominis? Dicam quod videtur. Narrant magno consensu Judæi veteres inter alia privilegia quæ Deus templo Hierosolymitano concesserat, hoc etiam fuisse, quod, cum tantus quotidie victimarum numerus cæde- retur, nulla tamen unquam in templo musca conspecta sit, quod cum præstare non posset ille celeberrimus inter profanas gentes Ζεὺς ὐράνιος, sed perpetuo templum ipsius muscarum gregibus scateret, ideo à Judæis muscarum Ju- piter appellatus est. Coluerunt autem Phœnices & eo- rum coloni Carthaginenses Deum cœlestem, qui est בעלת שמין & בעל שמין & Deam cœlestem quæ est Esaix, מלכת השימם, Juno Maroni. Sed dubitandum non est quin illo vocabulo Solem, isto lunam indicaverint, antiquissima omnium prope gentium numina. In veteri Epistola Nabuchodonosoris quam descripsit Abydenus As- syriorum historiographus בעל est Βῆλος, כמלת ἐστι Βᾶλτις. Cæterum Judæi ex Prophetis edocti Deos gen- tium dæmonia esse, hoc est oracula quæ ab ejusmodi deo- rum statuis edebantur, non vi istorum siderum edi, quod putabant gentes, sed opera impurorum spirituum, ad quos proinde revera omnis cultus illius honos redundaret, ma- lorum dæmonum principem eo appellarunt nomine, quo creditorum falso Deorum princeps appellabatur. Vide infra XII. 24. Jam vero cum plebi persuasum vellent Pharisæi quæ à Christo ederentur miracula edi virtute il- lius principis dæmonum, ideo ipsum quoque Christum per summum scelus tanquam dæmonis istius procurato- rem ac vicarium Beelzebub appellarunt.

Non vult Grotius nomen Beelzebub ab Accaro- nitis profectum. Placet magis ab Ebræis in con- temtum numinis ipsorum ita vocatum. Sed si ab Ebræis per contemtum ita vocatum Numen Ac- caronitarum esset, non ita vocasset illud Acha- zias; cum illud consulere jussit 2. Reg. I. 2. Ne- que ab impotentia agendi muscas, credibile est muscarum Dominum vocatum numen, & fabulæ affine valde est, quod de privilegio templi Hiero- solymitani Judæi tradunt quibus facile nimis cre- didit Grotius, quod nempe in eo nulla unquam musca conspecta sit; Vero autem similius est, muscarum dominum dictum & abactorem uti ἀπό- μυιον ab Ethnicis ipsis dictus est Jupiter, quod se à muscis, à quibus graviter afflicti sunt liberari pos- se, per hoc numen suum, crederent Accaronitæ, quemadmodum Cyreneis numini illi sacrificantibo muscæ omnes evolasse leguntur; quodque nu- men eorum sub Muscæ forma sese ceu musca prin- ceps, unde Deum Muscam alii Beelzebub reddere malunt, quam Muscarum, exhibuerit, quemad- modum in Phœnicum nummis ideo Musca effi- gies olim repræsentari consuevit. Vid. Selden. l. II. de DIS Syr. c. 6. & B. Job. Ern. Gerh. in ana- lect. ad Matth. XII. 24.

Πόσῳ μᾶλλον τὺς οἰκιακὺς αὐτῦ] Dictis respondet e- ventus: Apostolos γόητας vocat Celsus. Ulpianus Ju- risconsultus Christianos qui exorcizabant, impostores ap- pellat: Tacitus eos dicit convictos in odio humani ge- neris. Passim Christiani & ἀθεοι pari loco ponebantur. Hanc gratiam à mundo ineunt incorrupti veritatis docto- res.

## 10:26
Vers. 26. οὐδὲν γάρ ἐστι κεκαλυμμένον, ὀ̗ ὐκ ἀποκαλυφθή- σεται] Sophocles: All things long and numberless time brings forth from obscurity. The same elsewhere: Therefore hide nothing, for time, which sees all and hears all, reveals all.

Euripides: And time will show, having learned from Ismenius, whether I shall know you to be good or evil. Menander: Time brings truth to light. And it happens no differently. For time has refuted both the calumnies of the Jews concerning the magical arts and impostures of Christ and the Apostles, and the most wicked lies of the pagans concerning incestuous meetings and the drinking of human blood. Add Deut. XXXII. 33.

PART III. An exhortation concerning fearless confession.

Latin:

Vers. 26. οὐδὲν γάρ ἐστι κεκαλυμμένον, ὀ̗ ὐκ ἀποκαλυφθή- σεται] Sophocles: Ἀπαντ̓ ὁ μακρὸς κἀναρίθμητος χρόνος Φύει τ̓ ἄδηλα. Idem alibi: Πρὸς ταὐτα κρύπτε μηδὲν. ὡς ὁ πάντ̓ ὁρῶν Καὶ πάντ̓ ἀκούων πάντ̓ ἀναπτύσσει χρόνος.

Euripides: Χρόνος δὲ δείξει τῷ Ἰσμηνίου μαθὼν Η χρηστὸν ὄντα γνώσομαί σε ἢ κακόν. Menander: Ἄγει δὲ πρὸς φῶς τὴν ἀλήθειαν χρόνος. Neque aliter accidit. Nam & Judæorum calumnias de magicis artibus & imposturis Christi atque Apostolorum, & paganorum improbissima mendacia de incestis con- gressibus, & sanguinis humani potatione, dies revicit. Adde Deut. XXXII. 33.

PARS III. De confessione intrepida adbortatio.

## 10:27
Vers. 27. ὃ εἰς τὸ ὖς ἀκούετε, κηρύξατε ἐπὶ τῶν δωμάτων] Not only those things which I now speak to the people, but also those which I shall hereafter explain to you alone familiarly, and afterwards explain more clearly through the Spirit, as concerning the promiscuous calling of the Gentiles and the expiration of Jewish rites, proclaim openly to all. Δώματα, however, are properly, as has been noted by others, flat roofs, but it appears that those projecting platforms from which heralds, or even the magistrates themselves, were accustomed to address the people, began to be called by their likeness. Both, however, are proverbial, both to speak into the ear, and to proclaim from a projection. There is also a proverb among the Latins, to read acts into the ear, by which those are noted who sell things known to all as secrets.

Latin:

Vers. 27. ὃ εἰς τὸ ὖς ἀκούετε, κηρύξατε ἐπὶ τῶν δωμάτων] Non ea tantum quæ ego nunc ad populum loquor, sed & quæ posthac vobis solis familiariter edisseram, & postea per Spiritum clarius explicabo, ut de promiscua gentium vocatione & exspiratione Judaicorum rituum, palam o- mnibus enunciate. Δώματα autem proprie quidem sunt, ut ab aliis annotatum est, solaria, sed apparet ad eorum similitudinem ita vocari cœpisse podia illa proje- cta de quibus præcones, aut etiam ipsi magistratus popu- lum solebant alloqui. Utrumque autem proverbiale est, & in aurem dicere, & de projecto promulgare. Latinis quoque proverbium est, acta in aurem legere, quo no- tantur qui res omnibus notas pro arcanis venditant.

## 10:28
Vers. 28. μὴ φοβηθῆτε ἀπὸ τῶν ἀποκτεινόντων τὸ σῶμα, τὴν δὲ ψυχὴν μὴ δυναμένων ἀποκτεῖναι ] A sentiment undoubtedly famous among the Jews from the times of Ezra. The writer of the book περὶ ἀυτοκράτορος λογισμῦ (concerning the sovereignty of reason), which is ascribed to Josephus, makes one of the sons of Eleazar speak thus: Let us not fear him who seems to kill the body, for there is great danger of the soul lying in eternal torment for those who transgress the commandment of God. The writer of Wisdom XVI. 13: For you have power over life and death, and you lead down to the gates of Hades and lead up. But man kills indeed by his malice, but the spirit having gone out will not return, nor does he release a soul that has been taken. But it is impossible to flee from your hand. In which place I have substituted ἀνατρέψει for ἀναστρέψει, which some translate as 'he will return', others as 'he will lead back', with no convenient sense: But with one letter removed, the sense will be the same as in these words of Christ: You, O GOD, have the highest power of life and death: you lead to the underworld and lead back. A man indeed by his malice kills another: but only the body: for he cannot overturn the soul that has departed from the body, nor dissolve the spirit received by you. But neither soul nor body can escape your power. It must be known, however, that the words of this first sentence are taken from the book of 1 Samuel II. 6. With a similar argument Hierocles proves that one must not obey parents if they command anything unjust, because their cruelty cannot extend beyond the body. I shall set down his own clear words indeed: εἰ γὰρ προτείνοιεν θάνατον μὴ πειθομένοις ἡ βία ἀποστερήσειν, ἐδὲν ἐκφοβητέον διὰ τοὺς ἰσχυροὺς, ἀλλ᾽ ἐν οὐδότῳ τὸ ταῦτα πεισόμενον, καὶ ὅτι ᾧ ἐγέννησαν ἀπαλλάσιμόν τὸ δὲ ἀπαθὲς Τύτων ἐλεύθερον, προσήκει τηρεῖν κὶ μόνῳ Θεῷ ἐνπειθές. Arrian, book I, chapter 9 of Epictetus: οἱ τύραννοι δοκοῦντες ἔχειν τινα ἐφ᾽ ἡμῖν ἐξουσίαν διὰ τὸ σωμάτιον. Compare Isaiah LI. 7.

Τὸν δυνάμενον κὶ ψυχὴν καὶ σῶμα ἀπολέσαι ἐν γεέννῃ ] Above in chapter V, Christ dealt with the punishment of the body in Gehenna: now he adds that it is God who can also destroy the soul, not understanding by the name of soul the life of the whole man, which anyone can snatch away from a man, but that nobler substance which together with the body constitutes a man: which in other places is called πνεῦμα. Thus Rabbi Israel concerning the soul, chapter VIII, says that of the Israelites who have sinned in the body, both body and soul are burned. How, however, the soul perishes, Hierocles explains thus: ὡς οἷον τε ἀθανάτῳ οὐσίᾳ θανάτου μοίρας μεταλαχεῖν, ὦ τῷ εἰς τὸ μὴ εἶναι ἐκβᾶσαι, ἀλλὰ τῷ τῶ εὖ εἶναι ἀποπεσᾶσαν. But Christ seems deliberately not to have repeated here the word for killing, which was in the former member, but to have used the word for destroying, which has the meaning of torment, as in the letter of Tiberius to the Senate: 'What I should write to you, Conscript Fathers, or what I should not write at all at this time, may all the gods and goddesses destroy me worse than I feel I am perishing daily, if I know': to which words Tacitus adds from Plato: 'To such an extent had their own crimes and outrages turned into punishment for them.' Nor in vain was the most excellent of wisdom accustomed to affirm that if the minds of tyrants were laid open, their lacerations and blows could be seen; since just as bodies are torn by lashes, so the mind is torn by cruelty, lust, and evil counsels: for neither fortune nor solitude protected Tiberius from confessing the torments of his breast and his own punishments. Which I add the more willingly, because they seem to me to present a not obscure image of the most sorrowful punishment which threatens the souls of the impious, at which time, with all secrets unfolded, their own conscience to each one with deadly torches as if armed. That the teachers of the Hebrews did not think the same concerning the souls of the impious, I have also touched upon above; David Kimchi, on the first Psalm and on Ps. CIV. 30, according to the more accepted opinion of the Talmudists, hands down that they are extinguished together with the body, just as Seneca said: Death is indivisible, harmful to the body, nor sparing the soul. And the same is the opinion of Rabbi Bechai regarding the ἀλλοφύλες: for he wishes the resurrection to be proper to the Israelites. But he thinks that those Israelites who have fallen away from the law will rise again and experience eternal punishments of soul and body. But those who have not fallen away, yet have not lived according to the rule of the law, will pass into nothingness after the torment of a predetermined time. But Rabbi Haggaon, Rabbi Saadia, and Abenezra say that all Israelites who are not to rise again to eternal life will remain in a state of ignominy that will have no end. That the same was the opinion of Eliezer elsewhere, that Kimchi seems to hand down at 1. Sam. XXV. 29. Tacitus says that the Jews had the same persuasion concerning the underworld as the Egyptians had. Now the Egyptians believed in the grave and eternal punishments of certain most wicked people, and the temporary ones of others. Hence Homer drew his νεκυίαν, who it is certain was in Egypt, in whose work Tantalus and Tityus are perpetually tormented, just as in Virgil: Unhappy Phlegyas sits and will sit eternally. Whom Plato followed in his book on the soul, saying of the supremely wicked: The appropriate fate casts these into Tartarus, from whence they never emerge. But he thinks the less wicked are tormented for a time. I cannot omit adding here an excellent passage of Hierocles against him who, by the persuasion that the soul will perish, flatters his own crimes, whom he says finds the only cure to be the flight into non-existence, from whence it occurs to him to cure evil with evil, by soothing wickedness with the destruction of the soul, and by voting for himself non-existence after death, a flight from the pains of judgment; for the wicked man wishes his own soul to be mortal, so that he may not endure being punished, and he anticipates the judge there by voting for his own death, as if it were fitting that the wicked soul should not even exist. But neither does he who has been led into wickedness through lack of judgment reasonably pass sentence upon himself out of negligence. But the judges in Hades, since they make their judgment according to the rule of truth, also judge that the soul ought not to be. A similar opinion is found in Justin's second Apology: For he had been released toward the end of each of the kings who had been born: that they died a common death to all. If it had gone into insensibility, it would have been a godsend to all the unjust. Philo wisely says in his book on rewards and punishments: For men think that death is an end of punishments. But in the divine court, this is scarcely the beginning. Since, therefore, the deed is new, it is fitting that the punishment for it should also be found to be new. What then is this? To live while always dying, and in a way to endure an endless death. For there is a twofold kind of death: the one according to being dead, which is good or indifferent, and the other according to dying, which is entirely evil, and the longer it lasts, the heavier it is. Which sense Tatian briefly expressed: But it (the soul) rises again later at the end of the world with the body, receiving death through punishment in immortality. But a more favorable opportunity for discussing the immortality of souls will present itself hereafter.

Grotius says that the opinion concerning the immortality of the soul was famous among the Jews from the times of Ezra, but it was famous in the Church from the very cradle of the world. For if the immortality of the soul had been unknown, what hope could the Patriarchs and other Saints have had? Furthermore, above in ch. V, Grotius says that Christ dealt with the punishment of the body in Gehenna, now he adds, that it is God who can also destroy the soul: but how will it be taught that Christ indicated only the punishment of the body in Gehenna in ch. V, when he dealt with the punishment not only of the body, but of the man, to whose integrity both body and soul belong, and the soul is the first thing capable of the sins for which he indicates the punishment of Gehenna. But Grotius rightly observes that Christ here does not repeat the word for killing, but for destroying, if indeed that has the meaning of torment: and against the Jews, since, as noted on Ps. I and CIV. 30, R. D. Kimchi, according to the more accepted opinion of the Talmudists, thinks that souls are extinguished together with the body, which opinion he warns is also R. Bechai's regarding the ἀλλοφύλες, inasmuch as he makes the resurrection

proper to the Israelites, but in such a way that he teaches that apostates will experience eternal punishments, but those who have not fallen away, yet have not lived according to the rule of the law, will pass into nothingness after the torment of a predetermined time, whereas on the contrary R. Haggaon, R. Saadia, and Aben Ezra say that all Israelites who are not to rise again to eternal life will remain in a state of ignominy that will have no end. Whatever, however, may be the case regarding them, Christ here teaches that God can destroy both the soul immediately after death (as Luke has it, after he kills) and the body with the soul after the resurrection in Gehenna, which must be understood as perdition or a state worse than the death of the body, as the words of Christ demand: and thus it cannot be understood as mere abolition. Cf. Mark I. 24.

Latin:

Vers. 28. μὴ φοβηθῆτε ἀπὸ τῶν ἀποκτεινόντων τὸ σῶμα, τὴν δὲ ψυχὴν μὴ δυναμένων ἀποκτεῖναι ] Sententia haud du- bie celebris inter Judæos ab Esdræ temporibus. Scriptor libri περὶ ἀυτοκράτορος λογισμῦ qui Josepho adscribitur, ita loquentem facit unum ex Eleazari filiis, μὴ φοβηθῶμεν τὸν δοκῦντα ἀποκτείνειν τὸ σῶμα, μέγας γὰρ τῆς ψυχῆς κίνδυνος ἐν αἰωνίῳ βασανισμῷ κείμενος τοῖς παραβαίνουσι τὴν ἐντολὴν τῦ Θεῦ. Scriptor Sapientiæ XVI. 13. Σὺ γὰρ ζωῆς καὶ θα- νάτου ἐξουσίαν ἔχεις, κὶ κατάγεις πύλας ἅδε κὶ ἀνάγεις. ἄνθρω- πος δὲ ἀποκτείνει μὲν τῇ κακίᾳ ἀυτῦ, ἐξελθὸν δὲ πνεῦμα ἐκ ἀναστρέψει ἐδὲ ἀναλύει ψυχὴν παραληφθεῖσαν. τὴν δὲ σὴν χεῖρα φυγεῖν ἀδυνατόν ἐστι. In quo loco reposui ἀνατρέ- ψει pro ἀναστρέψει, quod alii vertunt revertetur, alii reducet, nullo sensu commodo: At una litera demta i- dem erit sensus qui in his Christi verbis: Tu o DEVS vitæ necisque summam habes potestatem: tu ad inferos du- cis ac reducis. Homo quidem malitia sua alius interficit: sed corpus tantum: nam egressam è corpore animam ever- tere non potest, neque dissolvere spiritum à te susceptum. Tuam autem vim nec anima nec corpus possunt effugere. Sciendum autem est, primæ hujus sententiæ verba de- promta esse ex libro 1. Samuelis II. 6. Simili argumen- to probat Hierocles parentibus non esse obtemperandum, si quid injusti præcipiant, quia sævitia illorum ultra cor- pus extendi non potest. Verba ipsius luculenta sane apponam: εἰ γὰρ προτείνοιεν θάνατον μὴ πειθομένοις ἡ βία ἀποστερήσειν, ἐδὲν ἐκφοβητέον διὰ τοὺς ἰσχυροὺς, ἀλλ᾽ ἐν οὐδό- τω[?] τὸ ταῦτα πεισόμενον, καὶ ὅτι ᾧ ἐγέννησαν ἀπαλλάσιμόν τὸ δὲ ἀπαθὲς Τύτων ἐλεύθερον, προσήκει τηρεῖν κὶ μόνῳ Θεῷ ἐν- πειθές. Arrianus Epicteti libro I. cap. 9. οἱ τύραννοι δοκοῦντες ἔχειν τινα ἐφ᾽ ἡμῖν ἐξουσίαν διὰ τὸ σωμάτιον. Confer Es. LI. 7.

Τὸν δυνάμενον κὶ ψυχὴν καὶ σῶμα ἀπολέσαι ἐν γεέννῃ ] Supra capite V. egit Christus de corporis supplicio in Gehenna: nunc addit Deum esse qui & animam possit perdere, a- nimæ nomine non vitam intelligens totius hominis, quam nemo non homini potest eripere, sed substantiam illam no- biliorem quæ simul cum corpore hominem constituit: quæ aliis in locis πνεῦμα appellatur. Sic Rabbi Israel de anima c. IIX. ait Israëlltarum qui in corpore peccarint & corpus & a- nimum comburi. Quomodo autem pereat anima ita Hie- rocles explicat ὡς οἷον τε ἀθανάτῳ οὐσίᾳ θανάτου μοίρας μετα- λαχεῖν, ὦ τῷ εἰς τὸ μὴ εἶναι ἐκβᾶσαι, ἀλλὰ τῷ τῶ εὖ εἶναι ἀποπεσᾶσαν. Videtur autem Christus de industria non repetiisse hic ver- bum occidendi, quod erat in membro priore, sed posuisse verbum perdendi, quod cruciatus habet significationem, ut in Tiberii Epistola ad Senatum: Quid scribam vobis Patres conscripti, aut quid omnino non scribam hoc tempore di me deæque omnes pejus perdant quam perire quotidie sentio, si scio: ad quæ verba ita Tacitus ex Platone: Adeo facinora atque flagitia sua ipsi quoque in supplicium verterant. Neq; frustra præstantissimus sapientiæ firmare solitus est, si recludantur ty- rannorum mentes posse aspici laniatus & ictus; quando ut cor- pora verberibus, ita sævitia, libidine, malis consiliis ani- mus dilaceretur: quippe Tiberium non fortuna, non solitudines protegebant, quin tormenta pectoris suasque ipse pœnas fatere- tur. Quæ eo libentius adscribo, quia non obscuram mi- hi videntur præferre imaginem tristissimi supplicii, quod impiorum animis imminet, quo tempore omnibus arcanis evolutis sua in quemque conscientia feralibus quasi facibus armabitur. De impiorum autem animis non idem sensisse Hebræorum magistros, supra quoq; attigi, David Kimchi ad primum Psalmum & ad Ps. CIV. 30. ex receptiore Thalmudistarum sententia tradit eos extingui una cum corpore, sicut Seneca dixit: Mors individua est noxia corpori, Nec parcens animæ. Eademq; est sententia Rabbi Bechai quod ἀλλοφύλες atti- net : nam resurrectionem propriam vult esse Israelitarum. At Israëlitas qui à lege defecgrunt, arbitratur resurrecturos & æterna sensuros supplicia animorum & corporum. Eos vero qui non defecerunt, neque tamen vixerunt ex legis regula, post præfiniti temporis cruciatum in nihilum a- bituros. At Rabbi Haggaon, Rabbi Saadia, & Abenezra o- mnes Israëlitas qui non resurrecturi sunt ad vitam æternam, mansuros ajunt in statu ignominiæ finem non habituræ. Eandem fuisse alibi Eliezeri sententiam, tradere videtur ille Kimchi ad 1. Sam. XXV. 29. Tacitus Judæis ait ean- dem fuisse de inferis persuasionem quæ esset Ægyptiis. Cre- diderunt autem Ægyptii quorundam sceleratiffimorum gravia & æterna supplicia, aliorum temporaria. Hinc su- am νεκυίαν hausit Homerus, quem in Ægypto fuisse con- stat, apud quem Tantalus & Tityus perpetuo cruciantur, sicut apud Virgilium: Sedet æternumque sedebit Infelix Phlegyas. Quos secutus Plato in libro de anima de summe facinorosis ait : Τούτους ἡ προσήκουσα μοῖρα ῥίπτει εἰς τὸν τάρταρον ὅθεν ὕποτε ἐκβαίνουσι. Minus autem sceleratos ad tempus torqueri ex- istimat. Non possum omittere quin hic addam egregium Hieroclis locum adversus eum qui persuasione interituræ animæ sceleribus suis blanditur, quem ait μόνην ἴασιν εὐ ρίσκειν τὴν εἰς τὸ μὴ εἶναι καταφυγὴν ὅθεν αὐτῷ παρίσαται κα κῷ τὸ κακὸν ἰᾶσθαι, φθορᾷ τῆς ψυχῆς τὴν κακίαν παραμυ- θουμένῳ, καὶ τὴν μετὰ θάνατον ἐδένειαν ἑαυτῷ καταψηφιζο- μένῳ, φυγὴν, τῶν τῆς κρίσεως πόνων ἢ βούλεται γὰρ ὁ κακὸς ἀ- θάνατον εἶναι τὴν αὑτοῦ ψυχὴν, ἵνα μὴ ὑπομείνῃ τιμωρούμε νος, καὶ φθάνει τὸν ἐκεῖ δικαστὴν θανάτῳ ἑαυτοῦ καταψηφιζό- μενος, ὡς πρέπον τὴν πονηρὰν ψυχὴν μηδὲ εἶναι. ἀλλ᾿ οὔτε μὲν ὡς ἀβουλία πρὸς κακίαν ὑπενεχθεὶς εἰκότως ἀμελείᾳ τὴν καθ᾽ ἑαυτοῦ ψῆφον ἐκφέρει. οἱ δὲ ἐν ᾅδου δικασταὶ ἅτε πρὸς τὸν τῆς ἀληθείας κανόνα τὴν κρίσιν ποιούμενοι & κρίνουσι μὴ εἶναι δεῖν τὴν ψυχήν. Similis sententiæ eit apud Justinum Apo- logia secunda: Ἀπολελύψατο γὰρ πρὸς τὸ τέλος ἑκάστῳ τῶν γενομένων βασιλέων: ὅτι τοι κοινὸν πᾶσι θάνατον ἀπέθανον. ὁ περ εἰς εἰς ἀναισθησίαν ἐχώρει, ἕρμαιον ἂν ἦν τοῖς ἀδίκοις πᾶ- σιν Sapienter Philo libro de præmiis & pœnis: ἄνθρω- ποι μὲν γὰρ πέρας τιμωριῶν εἶναι νομίζουσι θάνατον. ἐν δὲ τῷ θείῳ δικαστηρίῳ, μόγις ἐστὶν οὗτος ἀρχὴ. ἐπεὶ τοίνυν καινὸν τὸ ἔργον, ἰδέᾳ καὶ τὴν ἐπ᾿ αὐτῷ τιμωρίαν καινὴν εὑρεθῆναι. Τίς ὖν ἐστιν αὕτη; ζῆν ἀποθνήσκοντα ἀεὶ, καὶ τρόπον τινὰ θάνατον ὑπο- μένειν ἀτελεύτητον. θανάτε γὰρ διττὸν εἶδος, τὸ μὲν κατὰ τὸ τεθνάναι, ὅπερ ἀγαθόν ἐστιν ἢ ἀδιάφορον, τὸ δὲ κατὰ τὸ ἀποθνή- σκειν, ὃ δὴ κακὸν πάντως κᾀ ὅσῳ χρονιώτερον, βαρύτερον. Quem sensum breviter expressit Tatianus: ἀνίσταται δὲ εἰς ὕστερον (ἡ ψυχὴ) ἐπὶ συντελείᾳ τῷ κόσμου σὺν τῷ σώματι θά- νατον διὰ τιμωρίας ἐν ἀθανασίᾳ λαμβάνουσα. Sed de animo- rum immortalitate differendi posthac se dabit benignior occasio.

Sententiam de immortalitate animæ celebrem inter Judæos ab Esdræ temporibus dicit Grotius, sed illa inde ab incunabulis mundi in Ecclesia ce- lebris fuit. Si enim ignota fuisset animæ im- mortalitas, quamnam spem habere potuissent Pa- triarchæ, aliiq; Sancti. Porro supra c. V. dicit Grotius egisse Christum de corporis supplicio in ge- henna, nunc addere, Deum esse, qui & animam perdere possit: sed quomodo docebitur tantum corporis supplicium in gehenna Christum indigi- tasse c. V. quum de pœna non corporis tantum, sed hominis, ad cujus integritatem corpus & anima pertinet, egerit, ac peccatorum quibus indicit pœ- nam gehennæ πρῶτον δεκτικὸν anima sit. Chri- stum autem de industria hic non repetere verbum occidendi, sed perdendi recte Grotius observat, siquidem id cruciatus habeat significationem : & contra Judæos, quum notante ad Ps.I. & CIV. 30. R. D. Kimchio ex receptiore Thalmudistarum sen- tentia, censeant, animas una cum corpore extingui quam etiam R. Bechai quoad ἀλλοφύλες senten- tiam esse monet, utpote qui resurrectionem te

Israëlitarum propriam faciat, sed ita ut aposta- tas æterna sensuros supplicia, eos autem qui non defecerunt, neque tamen vixerant è legis Regula post præfiniti temporis cruciatum in nihilum abituros doceat, quum contra R. Higgaon R. Saa- dia, & Aben Ezra omnes Israëlitas, qui non re- surrecturi sunt ad vitam æternam mansuros ajant in statu ignominiæ finem non habituræ. Quic- quid vero de iis sit, Christus hic docet, Deum posse & animam post mortem statim (ut Lucas habet, postquam occidit) & corpus cum anima post resurrectionem perdere in gehenna, quod accipiendum de perditione vel statu deteriori, quam sit mors corporis, ut verba Christi po- scunt: adeoque non potest de sola abolitione intelligi. Conf. Marc. I. 24.

## 10:29
Vers. 29. στροθία] Moschopulus says that all small birds are so called. Ἀσσαρίῳ] איסר or אשׁר is a coin worth half of a λεπτόν. Ἄνευ τῦ πατρὸς] This is, as Cyprian interprets, without God knowing or permitting. Oppian said not dissimilarly: For what is possible for mortals without the gods, not even to lift a footprint from the ground, nor to open the surrounding circles of the eyelids.

Epicurus denies providence entirely: Aristotle confines it to the heavens: some Arabs wish it to be occupied with universals, not with particulars: which opinion Justin notes even among the Greek philosophers and rebukes as impious at the beginning of his dialogue with Trypho. Some Hebrews [limit it] to humans, not to beasts: which Pythagoras can also be seen to have learned from the Hebrews and to have taught the Greeks. For Hierocles says thus: "But let not the fact that the same irregularity appears in irrational animals and plants and inanimate things themselves as in humans disturb us. For it is not because of this that our affairs are unprovided for, if these things happen to them as they may." Jerome does not seem to abhor this opinion in his exposition on Habakkuk, unless one chooses to interpret his words more kindly. Moreover, what Christ teaches here, right reason also shows, which I shall explain in the words of Athenagoras: "For it is necessary for one who has accepted that God is the maker of this universe to attribute the guardianship and providence of all things that have come into being to His wisdom and justice, if they wish to remain consistent with their own principles.
