And holding these views about these things, one must consider nothing, whether on earth or in heaven, to be without a governor or without providence, but to know that the care from the Maker extends to every hidden and visible thing alike, both small and great." It is indeed true that providence does not behave in the same way regarding all things, but this very fact, as Chrysostom rightly said, is the greatest form of providence. For since God's knowledge and power are infinite, and it is certain that He acts in many things beyond the order implanted in nature, sometimes more openly, sometimes more secretly, it follows that the things He permits to the natural order, He permits by a certain and wise counsel, inasmuch as He would have hindered them if it had seemed otherwise to Him. He cares for man as an animal closest to God and created for the sake of enjoying its own happiness: but for beasts as ordered for the use of humans. And so we see the very species of beasts preserved, which cannot happen without the sustenance of individuals, since the universality of each species consists in individual things. Plato, in the tenth book of the Laws, excellently demonstrates by the example of physicians and sailors that the whole does not consist without the care of even the smallest parts, whence he infers that it is not at all worthy of belief that "God, being most wise, and wishing and being able to take care, should in no way take care of small things, for which it was easier to take care, like some lazy or cowardly person shirking because of the labor, while taking care of the great." Wherefore, the statements that seem to deny God's care for beasts are to be understood comparatively, which appears even from Paul asking whether God takes care of oxen, 1 Cor. 9:9. For he himself had cited the law of Moses which forbids muzzling the ox that treads the grain. It cannot be denied that He who commanded that law also took care of oxen: but not primarily, nor as much for the sake of the oxen as for the sake of humans, as the following verses in the Apostle explain. Plutarch proves from Homer that it was the opinion of the ancient wise men that not only oxen [for these are his words] but also all other animals are cared for by the divine power, as participating in vital nature. But there are also certain degrees of providence regarding humans themselves: The Psalmist says of God, He knows the way of the righteous, that is, He cares for and cherishes it in a peculiar way. See Jacchiades on Dan. 7:3. Salvianus, book 2. Although God is the governor of all, yet it is said that the government is peculiarly provided by God for those who deserve to be ruled peculiarly by the divinity. Thus, the providence of God regards kings and kingdoms in one way, and private individuals in another, to use the words of Plato again: 'For him who cares for the whole, all things are ordered for the salvation and virtue of the whole, of which each part, according to its capacity, suffers and does what is appropriate.' Wherefore, when the Hebrew sage says of God in 6:8, 'he cares equally for all,' that 'equally' is to be understood as 'without partiality': for it preceded: 'he will not be moved by greatness.'

That in Luke 12:6 five sparrows are said to be sold for two assaria agrees well with this passage. Because when only two sparrows were bought, they were sold for an assarion, but when two assaria were being sold, a fifth sparrow was accustomed to be added, just as sellers are accustomed, when more are bought, to add something in abundance. Furthermore, Heinsius thinks that for 'on the earth' Chrysostom, Epiphanius, and Jerome read 'into a trap.' But that cannot be proven from the interpretation that they read it that way, since interpreters often render not the words themselves, but only the sense.

Latin:

Vers. 29. στροθία] Moschopulus ait ita vocari πάντα τὰ μικρὰ τῶν ὀρνίθων. Ἀσσαρίῳ] איסר vel אשׁר nummus est valens dimi- um τῦ λεπτοῦ. Ἄνευ τῦ πατρὸς] Hoc est, ut Cyprianus interpretatur, non sciente, aut non permittente Deo. Oppianus non dis- similiter dixit: Τὶ γὰρ μερόπεσσιν ἀνυστόν Νόσφι θεῶν, ὐδ᾽ ὅσσον ὑπ᾽ ἐκ ποδὸς ἴχνος ἀεῖραι, Οὐδ᾽ ὅτον ἀμπετάσαι βλεφάρων περιφαῖα κύκλα.

Epicurus providentiam omnino negat: Aristoteles eam cœlo includit: Arabes nonnulli circa universalia eam vo- lunt occupari, non circa singularia: quam sententiam in Græcis etiam Philosophis notat & ut impiam reprehendit Justinus initio colloquii cum Tryphone. Hebræorum a- liqui circa homines, non circa bestias: quod & didicisse ab Hebræis & Græcos docuisse videri potest Pythagoras. Ita enim Hierocles: μὴ ταραττέτω δὲ ἡμᾶς τὸ κὴ ἐπὶ τῶν ζώων ἀ- λόγων κὴ φυτῶν κὴ ἀυτῶν τῶν ἀψύχων τὴν αυτὴν ἀνωμαλίαν ἐπιφαίνεσθαι ἣν κὴ ἐπ᾽ ἀνθρώπων. ἰ γὰρ διὰ τῦτο τὰ καθ᾽ ἡμᾶς ἀπρονόητα ἕιγε ἐκείνοις ταῦτα ὡς ἔτυχε συμβαίνει: A qua sen- tentia non abhorrere videtur Hieronymus expositione ad Abacucum, nisi verba ejus benignius libeat interpretari. Cæterum quod Christus hic docet, idem monstrat recta ratio, quod explicabo Athenagoræ verbis: Διῖ γὰρ ποιητὴν τὸν Θεὸν τῶδε τῶ παντὸς παραδεξαμένως τῇ τότε σοφίᾳ κὴ δι- καιοσύνῃ τὴν τῶν γενομένων ἁπάντων ἀνατιθέναι φυλακήν τε κὴ πρόνοιαν, ἕιγε ταῖς ἰδίαις ἀρχαῖς παραμένειν ἐθέλοιεν. ταῦτα δὲ περὶ τότων φρονῶντας, μηδὲν ἡγεῖσθαι μήτε τῶν κατὰ γῆν μήτε τῶν κατ᾽ ἐρανὸν ἀνεπιτρόπευτον μηδ᾽ ἀπρονόητον, ἀλλ᾽ ἐπὶ πᾶν ἀφανὲς ὁμοίως κὴ φαινόμενον μικρότα κὴ μεῖζον διήκουσαν γινώσκειν τὴν παρὰ τῶ ποιήσαντος ἐπιμέλειαν. Verum qui- dem est non circa omnia uno modo se habere providenti- am, sed hoc ipsum, ut recte dixit Chrysostomus, προνοίας μέ- γισον εἶδός ἐςι. Nam cum Dei infinita sit & scientia & po- tentia constetque eum in multis agere præter naturæ ordi- nem rebus insitum, modo apertius, modo vero occultius, se- quitur, ut quæ naturali ordini permittit, eadem certo ac sa- piente consilio permittat, quippe impediturus si aliter ipsi visum esset. Hominem curat, ut animal Deo proximum & propriæ felicitatis fruendæ causa conditum: bestias vero ut in usum hominum ordinatos. Itaque genera ipsa be- stiarum conservari videmus, quod sine singularium susten- tatione fieri non potest, cum in singulis rebus consistat generis cujusque universitas. Egregie Plato de legibus de- cimo medici & nautæ exemplo demonstrat totius partem non consistere sine partium etiam minimarum cura, unde infert minime dignum esse creditu τὸν θεὸν ὄντα σοφώτατον, βυλόμενον τε ἐπιμελεῖσθαι κὴ δυνάμενον, ὧν μὲν ῥᾷον ἦν ἐπιμεληθῆ- ναι, σμικρῶν ὄντων μηδαμῆ ἐπιμελεῖσθαι καθάπερ ἀργὸν ἢ δειλόν τινα διὰ πόνες ῥαθυμῦντα, τῶν δὲ μεγάλων. Quare quæ effata negare videntur Dei curam circa bestias, com- parate sunt intelligenda, quod vel ex Paulo apparet quærente an Deus boum gerat curam I. Cor. IX. 9. Nam ipse legem Mosis citaverat quæ bovi trituranti os vetat obligari. Negari non potest, quin qui eam legem jus- sit, gesserit & boum curam: sed non præcipue, neque tam boum quam hominum causa, ut sequentia apud Apostolum explanant. Plutarchus ex Homero probat antiquorum fuisse sapientum sententiam curari divino numine ἐ μόνον βόας [hæc enim illius verba sunt] ἀλλὰ κὴ πάντα τὰ ἀλλὰ ζῶα. ὡς τῆς φύσεως ζωτικῆς μετέχον- τα. Sed & circa homines ipsos sunt certi providentiæ gradus: Novit viam justorum, inquit de Deo Psal- tes, idest, peculiariter eam curat ac fovet. Vide Jacchiadem ad Dan. VII. 3. Salvianus libro II. Licet gubernator omnium Deus sit, illis tamen peculiariter regimen præstari à Deo dici- tur, qui regi peculiariter à divinitate mereantur. Sic aliter reges ac regna respicit Dei providentia, aliter privatos, ut Platonis iterum verbis utar: τῷ τοῦ παντὸς ἐπιμελουμένῳ πρὸς τὴν σωτηρίαν καὶ ἀρετὴν τοῦ ὅλου πάντ' ἐστὶ συντεταγ- μένα ὧν καὶ τὸ μέρος εἰς δύναμιν ἕκαστον τὸ προσῆκον πάσχει καὶ ποιεῖ. Quare ubi dicit sapiens Hebræus de Deo VI. 8. ὁμοίως προνοεῖται περὶ πάντων illud ὁμοίως intelligen- dum ἀπροσωπολήπτως: præcessit enim: οὐκ ἐντραπήσεται μέγεθος.

Quod Luc. XII. 6. quinque passeres duobus assa- riis venire dicuntur, cum hoc loco probe con- venit. Quia cum duo tantum emebantur passe- res, assario veniebant, sed cum duo assaria ven- debantur, solebat quintus passer adjici, ut so- lent, quum plura emuntur, vendentes ex abun- danti aliquid adjicere. Cæterum pro ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς Chrysostomum, Epiphanium, & Hierony- mum legisse εἰς παγίδα Heinsius putat. Sed id non probari potest ex interpretatione, quod ita legerint, quum non verba ipsa, sed tantum sensum sæpe reddant Interpp.

## 10:30
Verse 30. 'But even the hairs of your head are all numbered.'] Of you, he says, who are not only men, but also messengers of divine truth, whom therefore God takes into special protection as His ministers. It is, however, a proverbial expression: for we are accustomed to count those things which we value, just as we are said to count those things which we despise as being in no place or to hold them outside of the count. Then, a hair signifies a very small thing, even to the Greeks and Latins. Hence the Hebrew idiom, 'not even a hair of his will perish,' that is, he will not feel even the slightest damage, 1 Sam. 14:45, Luke 21:18, Acts 25:11, 34. Seneca, Epistle 29: 'And the unborn infant already has the law of a beard and gray hairs.' The sense, therefore, is: However much men may rage against you, be certain that no harm will happen to you, except what will be for your own and others' benefit; otherwise, God, who loves you and who is able and powerful above all, would not permit it at all.

The proverbial expression can be admitted: but so that the force of the gradation may remain; not only will a single sparrow not perish without the Father's will, but not even a single hair of our head: not as if God's providence does not extend itself to the hairs or feathers of birds as it does to the hairs of a human head, but by which the more special care for men is designated. Moreover, that the designation of hairs, with which they are endowed as men, not as disciples or believers, teaches that the disciples of Christ are to be considered not as disciples, but as men. In Phesichta, fol. 18, it is held: 'Do I not count all the hairs of every creature?'

Latin:

Vers. 30. ὑμῶν δὲ καὶ αἱ τρίχες τῆς κεφαλῆς πᾶσαι ἠριθμημέ- ναι εἰσί.] Vestrum, inquit, qui non tantum estis homines, verum etiam nuncii divinæ veritatis, quos proinde Deus ut ministros suos, in tutelam specialem suscipit. Est au- tem dictum παροιμιῶδες: numerare enim solemus ea, quæ habemus in pretio, sicut ea quæ contemnimus dicimur nullo loco numerare vel extra numerum habere. Dein- de pilus significat rem minimam, etiam Græcis & Latinis. Hinc Hebræa locutio, ne pilus quidem ejus peribit, id est ne minimum quidem damnum sentiet, 1. Sam. XIV. 45. Luc. XXI. 18. Actor. XXV. II. 34. Seneca epistola XXIX. Et legem barbæ & canorum nondum natus infans habet. Sensus ergo est: Utcunque in vos sæviant homines, certi estote nihil damni vobis eventurum, nisi quod futurum sit in vestram aliorumque utilitatem, alioquin minime id Deum permissurum qui vos amat, quique plus omni- bus potest polletque.

Admitti potest Proverbialis locutio: sed ut maneat vis gradationi; non modo se passerem u- num periturum, citra Patris voluntatem, sed nec unicum pilum capitis nostri: non quasi ad pilos aut pennas avium Dei sese haud extendat Provi- dentia ut ad pilos humani capitis, sed quo spe- cialior cura hominum designatur. Considerari autem discipulos Christi non ut discipulos, sed ut homines vel designatio pilorum, quibus ut ho- mines, non ut discipuli vel fideles præditi sunt, docet. In Phesichta f. 18. habetur: Nonne omnes capillos omnis creaturæ ego numero?

## 10:31
Verse 31. 'You are of more value'] I think it is best translated 'you are worth more,' because a little before Christ had said that two little birds were valued at one as.

Latin:

Vers. 31. διαφέρετε] Optime puto verti pluris estis, quia paulo ante dixerat Christus duas aviculas unius assis æsti- mari.

## 10:32
Verse 32. 'Shall confess in me'] יודה לי. For the Hellenists everywhere translate the particle ל in this construction by ἐν, just as the Syrian also placed here רנודא בי.

Latin:

Vers. 32. ὁμολογήσῃ ἐν ἐμοὶ] יודה לי. Nam ל parti- culam in hac constructione passim Hellenistæ per ἐν ver- tunt, quomodo & Syrus hic posuit רנודא בי.

## 10:33
Verse 33. 'I also will deny him'] Christ demands not only the faith of the heart but also the confession of the mouth, Rom. 10:10. And just as the preceding promise of perseverance includes a condition, so this threat is to be understood as having a tacit condition within itself, unless serious repentance has followed, as happened to Peter, but before he received the spirit of fortitude.

Latin:

V. 33. ἀρνήσομαι αὐτὸν κἀγὼ] Non cordis tantum fidem sed & oris confessionem Christus exigit Rom. X. 10. Sicut autem antecedens promissio perseverantiæ includit condi- tionem, ita hæc comminatio intelligenda est, tacitam in se habere conditionem, nisi subsecuta sit seria pœnitentia, ut Petro evenit, sed ante acceptum fortitudinis spiritum.

## 10:34
Verse 34. 'Do not think that I came to bring peace on the earth'] as many then supposed from Isaiah ch. 11, which was poorly understood.

A sword] By the word 'sword' here, war should not be understood (for there is no war where one strikes and the other only takes the blows, as was done in those pure times of Christian innocence) but dissension: which is most clear from Luke, who for the same thing placed 'division' in ch. 12:51, in which very place, however, some copies formerly had 'sword,' and the following words here declare the same. The translation is taken from there because it is the proper office, as it were, of a sword to divide, to which the writer to the Hebrews 4:12 also alludes. But that which is most manifest here by the words 'I came to bring a sword, I came to divide' is not the purpose, at least not the primary intention of Christ, whose every counsel and wish looked toward peace and concord, but rather the event is to be understood; we ought to remember this for the explanation of other passages as well. Similar things occur among all writers, as in the old epigram:

These I brought forth by flames, the rest he said by waters. Except that here, besides the event, the foreknowledge of the event must be understood, and the firm counsel of sowing the truth notwithstanding that. The Greeks, even the Christians, call such a sense 'ecbatic': such is that 'I will destroy the wisdom of the wise' 1 Cor. 1:19.

Latin:

Vers. 34. μὴ νομίσητε ὅτι ἦλθον βαλεῖν εἰρήνην ἐπὶ τὴν γῆν] ut multi tum existimabant ex Esaiæ c. XI. male intellecto.

Μάχαιραν] μαχαίρας voce hic non bellum (neque enim bellum est ubi alter cædit, alter vapulat tantum, quemad- modum factum est puris illis Christianæ innocentiæ tem- poribus) sed dissidium debet intelligi: quod ex Luca aper- tissimum est, qui pro eodem posuit διαμερισμὸν cap. XII. 51. quo tamen ipso loco quædam exemplaria olim habuerunt μάχαιραν, idemque hic sequentia declarant. Tralatio inde sumta quia μαχαίρας proprium quasi officium est μερίζειν, quo alludit etiam Scriptor ad Hebræos IV. 12. Quod au- tem hic manifestissimum est verbis ἦλθον βαλεῖν μάχαιραν, ἦλθον διχάσαι non propositum, saltem τὸ προηγούμενον Chri- sti, cujus omnia consilia & vota ad pacem atque concor- diam spectabant, sed eventum potius intelligi, ejus me- minisse ad aliorum quoque locorum explicationem de- bemus. Similia apud omnes Scriptores occurrunt, ut in veteri Epigrammate:

Hæc peperi flammis, cætera dixit aquis. Nisi quod hic præter eventum præcognitio eventus, & ea non obstante seminandæ veritatis firmum consilium in- telligi debet. Sensum talem ἐκβατικὸν vocant Græci, et- iam Christiani: Tale illud ἀπολῶ τὴν σοφίαν τῶν σοφῶν I. Cor. I, v. 19.

## 10:35
Verse 35. 'Against his father'] He shows that the coming times were no less dangerous than those which Micah 7:6 had lamented; therefore he repeats his words.

Latin:

Vers. 35. κατὰ τοῦ πατρὸς αὐτοῦ] Ostendit ventura tem- pora non minus periculosa quam ea fuerant, quæ deplan- xerat Micheas VII. 6. ideo verba ejus repetit.

## 10:37
Vers. 37. He who loves father or mother more than me, is not worthy of me] that is, it does not suit my discipline. For so Luke interprets in XIV. 26. Therefore Paul, commanding not to cultivate peace with all, providedly added, as much as is possible, and as much as is in you. For truth and the study of salutary wisdom ought always to be more friendly. See the example of Abraham Gen. XII. Must I call Hierocles here again? If the choice of parents is obedient to divine laws, what must one do when they have fallen into such lawlessness, which it is better to keep from command when many duties have come to an end, for when greater and lesser goods are set before one, one must choose the greater before the lesser, when it is not possible to preserve both. For example, it is good to obey God, and it is good also to obey parents; but if the persuasion of the latter should lead to these, it would be a godsend and irresistible. But if the law of God should lead to one thing, and parents to another, the choice being in conflict, one must follow the better, disobeying parents only in those things in which they themselves disobey divine laws; for it is not possible for one who wishes to keep the canons of virtue to agree with those who transgress them. And to those verses: 'Do not hate your friend for a small fault if you can. For the power of necessity dwells nearby,' the same excellent interpreter says: 'In all things we yield to our friends, as if pressed by the greatest necessity of friendly disposition, except for one thing, for we will yield to them even when they are carried away toward the worse, nor will we follow them when they change from the study of philosophy to some other purpose of life, nor will we ourselves be carried away with those who fall from the goal of virtue that is proper.'

Latin:

Vers. 37. ὁ φιλῶν πατέρα ἢ μητέρα ὑπὲρ ἐμὲ, οὐκ ἔστι μου ἄ- ξιος] id est, non convenit meæ disciplinæ. la enim Lucas interpretatur XIV. 26. Ideo Paulus jubens non pacem co- lere cum omnibus, provide adjecit, quoad fieri potest, & quantum in vobis. Semper enim amicior esse debet veritas & salutaris sapientiæ studium. Vide exemplum Abrahami Gen. XII. Vocandus hic iterum mihi Hierocles? εἰ δὲ οἵτε τῶν θείων νόμων εὐήκοοι ἐσιν ἡ τῶν γονέων προαίρεσις, τί δεῖ ποιεῖν εἰς ἀτινομίαν ἐμπεσόντας τοιαύτην, ἧ τέτος κῤῥεῖτ πολ- λῶν καθηκόντων ἐκ προστάσεως εἰς ἐναλίωσιν ἐλθόντων προστακῆ φυλάττειν, μειζόνων γὰρ κὶ ἐλαττόνων προκειμένων καλῶν, τὰ μείζονα πρὸ τῶν ἐλαττόνων ποιεῖσθαι δεῖ, ὅταν μὴ ἀμφότερα ἐξῆ διασώζειν. οἷον καλὸν μὲν τῷ Θεῷ πείθεσθαι, καλὸν δὲ καὶ τοῖς γονεῦσιν· εἰ δὲ ἡ πρὸς ταῦτα ἡ ἀφετέρων ἄγοι πειθὼ, ἑρ- μαιον ἂν εἴη κὶ ἄμαχον. εἰ δὲ πρὸς ἄλλο μεν ὁ Θεοῦ νόμος, πρὸς ἄλλο δὲ οἱ γονεῖς φέροιεν, μαχομένης τῆς αἱρέσεως, τοῖς ἀμείνο- σιν ἑπέσθαι δεῖ, πρὸς ταῦτα μόνον ἀπειθοῦντας γονεῦσι, πρὸς ἃ κὶ αὐτοὶ τοῖς θείοις νόμοις ἀπείθονται· τὸν γὰρ φυλάττειν βε- λόμενον τὰς τῆς ἀρετῆς κακόνας, ὐχ οἷόν τε τοῖς τάτας πα- ραβαίνεσι συμφωνεῖν. Et ad illa carmina: Μηδ' ἔχθαιρε φίλον σὸν ἁμαρτάδος ἕνεκα μικρῆς Ὄφρα δύνῃ. δύναμις γὰρ ἀνάγκης ἐγγύθι ναίει, idem ille optimus interpres: εἰς παντα ὧν τὲς φίλες ἀπεξό- μεθα, ὡς ἀπὸ μεγίσης ἀνάγκης τῆς φιλικῆς διαθέσεως πιεζό- μενοι, πλὴν ἑνὸς, ὃ γὰρ δὴ καὶ πρὸς τὸ χεῖρον ὑποφερομέ- νοις αὐτοῖς εἴξομεν, ὐδὲ μεταβαλλομένοις ἐκ τῆς πρὸς φιλοσο- φίαν σπεδῆς εἰς ἑτέραν τινα τῦ βίε πρόθεσιν ἐπακολυθήσομεν κἀγαὶ αὐτοὶ συνεκφερόμενοι τοῖς ἀποπίπτεσιν ἀπὸ τῶ πρεσήκοντος ἀρετὴ σκοπῦ.

## 10:38
Vers. 38. His cross] This way of speaking is found also among the Rabbis: as in Aram in Genesis in the history of Isaac. The cross is the most atrocious and most full of ignominy punishment, most customary among the Romans, among whom that word began to be transferred to all kinds of inconveniences: as, go to the bad cross: the highest law is the highest cross: to torture. To the Jews, therefore, for whom that kind of punishment was not ancestral (for the Jewish hanging was of a different kind), this expression came either from the Romans, whose empire they had already borne for some years, or even from the Persians: for it is certain from Josephus, as well as many other authors, as learned men warn, that these also used the punishment of the cross, even if perhaps somewhat different from the Roman cross. To which, among other things, pertains that passage in the decree of Darius Ezra VI. 11. where there is the Chaldean word זקיף which the Syrian also placed here. Moreover, Christ used the general word in such a way that he nevertheless pointed a finger also to its proper notion, signifying that not even that infamous and atrocious punishment should be avoided for the sake of professing the truth. This exhortation of Christ, besides its general use in all Christians, also had a peculiar event in Peter and the other Apostles and Martyrs who most bravely endured that very punishment of the cross, dedicated by the example of Christ: which when I think of, it seems to me not without the instinct of divine providence that Plato once said in Republic II concerning the true worshipper of justice: 'having suffered all evils, he will be impaled.' For Greek interpreters explain ἀναχινδιλέυειν by ἀνασκολοπίζειν. But what is said here as 'taking up the cross,' below in XVI. 24. and Mark VIII. 34. and X. 21. and Luke IX. 23. is said as 'lifting up the cross,' but in Luke XIV. 27. bearing the cross: which passages if you compare with the history of the passion of Christ in which likewise there is the word 'lifting up' below in XXVII. 32. and Mark XV. 21. and 'bearing' in John XIX. 17. it will most openly be evident that these ways of speaking look back to that custom by which 'each of those being punished carried out his own cross,' as Plutarch speaks. And so I would translate 'takes up' here. For Cicero said 'to take up' a burden, dangers, labors, pain in the same sense. The Hebrews say 'to lift a burden onto the shoulders' נשא: which the Hellenists sometimes translate as 'to carry' as in Isaiah LIII. sometimes 'to take up,' as the interpreter of Matthew translated the same passage of Isaiah above in VIII. 17. sometimes 'to take' as in Leviticus XVII. 16. and elsewhere.

Follow behind me] A pure and unmixed Hebraism. For the Hebrews subjoin the particle אחרי to the verbs of following by way of pleonasm, as in Judges IV. 16. Psalm CXLIII. 3. and elsewhere: the same interpreter here below expressed the same sense by a Greek phrase 'let him lift up his cross and follow me,' XVI. 24. which Mark and Luke also speak in one place: for in another he said 'he comes behind me,' which is likewise a Hebrew periphrasis for 'following': so that it is superfluous to invent a more subtle interpretation. But he follows Christ who [leads] his life his own, as far as it can be done, he conforms to his own words and deeds.

Latin:

Vers. 38. τὸν σαυρὸν αὐτοῦ] Reperitur hoc loquendi genus etiam apud Rabbinos: ut in Aramo in Genesin in Isaaci hi- storia. Crux atrocissimum & plenissimum ignominiæ sup- plicium Romanis usitatissimum, apud quos ea vox transfer- ri ad omnia incommodorum genera cæpit: ut, i in malam crucem: summum jus summa crux: cruciare. Ad Judæos i- gitur quibus non erat avitum id supplicii genus (nam Ju- daica suspensio alterius erat modi) locutio ista venit aut à Romanis, quorum imperium jam per aliquot annos pertu- lerant, aut etiam à Persis: nam hos quoque usos crucis sup- plicio, etsi forte à Romana cruce aliquatenus diversæ, ut vi- ri docti monent, tum ex Josepho, tum aliis multis aucto- ribus constat. Quo inter cætera pertinet locus ille in de- creto Darii Esdræ VI. 11. ubi est זקיף vox Chaldæa quam hic etiam posuit Syrus. Cæterum Christus ita vocem gene- ralem usurpavit, ut tamen ad propriam quoque notionem digitum intenderet, significans ne illud quidem infame & attrox supplicium defugiendum esse veritatis profitendæ causa. Hæc autem Christi adhortatio præter generalem sui usum in Christianis omnibus, etiam peculiarem eventum habuit in Petro aliisque Apostolis & Martyribus qui illam ipsam pœnam crucis, Christi exemplo dedicatam, fortissi- me pertulerunt: quæ cum cogito, videtur mihi non sine divinæ providentiæ instinctu olim Plato dixisse de republi- ca II. de vero justitiæ cultore: πάντα κακὰ παθὼν ἀναχινδυ- λευθήσεται. Nam ἀναχινδιλέυειν per ἀνασκολοπίζειν exponunt Græci interpretes. Quod autem hic dicitur λαμβάνειν τὸν ταυρὸν, infra XVI. 24. & Marc. IIX. 34. & X. 21. & Luc. IX. 23. dicitur αἴρειν τὸν σαυρὸν, Lucæ autem XIV, 27. βασάζειν τὸν ταυρὸν: quæ loca si conferas cum historia passionis Christi in qua itidem est vox αἴρειν infra XXVII, 32. & Marci XV. 21. & βασάζειν Joh. XIX. 17. apertissime constabit hæc lo- quendi genera morem illum respicere quo τῷ σώματι τῶν κολαζομένων ἕκαστος ἐξέφερε τὸν ἑαυτῦ σαυρὸν ut Plutarchus loquitur. Itaque λαμβάνειν hic verterim suscipit. Nam eo- dem sensu suscipere onus, pericula, labores, dolorem di- xit Cicero. Hebræi onus in humeros tollere נשא di- cunt: quod Hellenistæ modo vertunt φέρειν ut Esaiæ LIII. modo ἀναλαμβάνειν, ut eundem Esaiæ locum supra vertit Matthæi interpres IIX. 17. modo λαμβάνειν ut Levit. XVII. 16. & alibi.

Ακολουθεῖ ὀπίσω με] Purus putus Hebraïsmus, Nam He- bræi verbis sequendi subjungunt κατὰ πλεονασμὸν particu- lam אחרי ut Jud. IV. 16. Psal. CXLIII. 3. & alibi: idem hic interpres infra eundem sensum locutione Græcanica extulit ἀράτω τὸν σαυρὸν αὐτε κὶ ἀκολυθείτω μοι, XVI. 24. quos modo etiam loquitur Marcus & Lucas uno loco: nam altero dixit ἔρχεται ὀπίσω μᾶ, quæ itidē est Hebraïca περίφρασις τῦ ἀκολυθεῖν: ita ut subtiliorem interpretationem conminisci sit supervacuum. Sectatur autem Christum qui vitam suam quatenus fieri potest ad dicta ipsius ac facta compo- nit.

## 10:39
Verse 39. ὁ εὑρὼν ] εὑρίσκειν here is σώζειν, which word this same Writer uses below XVI. 25, Mark VIII. 35, and Luke IX. 24 in this same sense. Nor does that word signify anything else in Luke XV. 24, 32. Similar is Prov. XXIV. 10, יבקשו נפשו ἐκζητήσουσι ψυχὴν αὐτῦ they will seek his life, that is, they will strive to save it.

ψυχὴν αὑτῦ] That is, himself, by a manner of speaking familiar to the Hebrews and Syrians. I prefer to explain it thus rather than 'life,' because of the passage John XV. 25. Indeed, Luke himself interprets it so. For what is in Matthew XVI. 26 as ψυχὴν ἑαυτῦ, he said as ἑαυτὸν. Moreover, they are said to gain themselves by their own opinion, who by the denial of the truth escape danger.

ἀπολέσῃ αὐτὴν] ζημιωθήσεται αὐτὴν as within XVI. 26, he will suffer the loss of himself.

PART IV. An admonition concerning the reception of the disciples of Jesus.

Latin:

Vers. 39. ὁ εὑρὼν ] εὑρίσκειν hic est σώζειν, qua voce idem hic Scriptor utitur infra XVI. 25. Marc. IIX. 35. & Luc. IX. 24. in eodem hoc sensu. Neqs aliud vox ista significat Luc. XV. 24. 32. Simile est Prov. XXIV. 10. יבקשו נפשו ἐκ- ζητήσουσι ψυχὴν αὐτῦ quærent vitam ejus, id est, servare stu- debunt.

ψυχὴν αὑτῦ] Id est, semetipsum, genere loquendi Hebræ- is & Syris familiari. Ita exponere malo quam vitam, ob lo- cum Joh. XV. 25. Quin & ipse Lucas ita interpretatur. Nam quod apud Matthæum est XVI. 26. ψυχὴν ἑαυτῦ, ille dixit ἑαυτὸν. Dicuntur autem semet lucrari ex sua ipsorum opinione, qui abnegatione veri periculum effugiunt.

ἀπολέσῃ αὐτὴν] ζημιωθήσεται αὐτὴν ut intra XVI. 26. sui ipsius damnum faciet.

PARS IV. De susceptione discipulorum Iesu commonitio.

## 10:40
Verse 40. ὁ δεχόμενꭢ] Christ comforts the disciples again, showing that among so many hostile things, comforts will not be lacking to them from pious men, whom God stirs up for that very purpose, with a great reward proposed: thus it was said to Abraham of old, I will bless those who bless you, Gen. XII. 3.

Latin:

Vers. 40. ὁ δεχόμενꭢ] Solatur iterum discipulos Chri- stus, ostendens inter tot infesta non defore ipsis solatia à piis hominibus, quos Deus in id ipsum excitet magna pro- posita mercede : ita Abrahamo olim dictum fuit, benefa- ciam tibi benefacientibus, Gen. XI. 35.

## 10:41
Verse 41. προφήτην ] If anyone observes correctly, he will see three degrees of Christ's disciples being posited: the lowest is of the lowest, who are called μικροὶ here, as also below XVIII. 6, Mark IX. 42, Luke XVII. 2, or ἐλάχιστοι as below XXV. 40, 45, and νήπιοι in Christ 1 Cor. III. 1, Τεκνία and παιδία 1 John II. 12, 14, who are still occupied in the first rudiments of Christianity, and therefore are more easily offended: the second degree is of those of moderate standing, who are called δίκαιοι here and below XIII. 17, elsewhere νεανίσκοι 1 John II. 13: the third is of those who have already received the greatest gifts of the spirit, who are called προφῆται here and in the cited place XIII. 17, ἀνδρες τέλειοι Eph. IV. 13, πατέρες 1 John II. 13, 14. Thus also Clement of Alexandria posits three degrees of Christians: in the first he has ὁ ἐξ ἐθνῶν ἐπιστρέφων; in the second, ὁ εἰς γνῶσιν ἀναβαίνων; in the third, ὁ κορυφαιότερος γνωστικός. Elsewhere he said κλητὸς, ἐκλεκτὸς, τέλειος. Origen: the simpler ones, those who have ascended to a certain extent, the perfect ones.

εἰς ὄνομα προφήτη] This is what is commonly said in the vernacular, in the quality of a Prophet.

Εἰς ὄνομα, that is, literally, 'into the name.' Εἰς put for ἐν. That is, as a Prophet, and because he is a Prophet, as is explained in Mark IX. verse 41. For we ought to worship Christ in his servants: otherwise we perform nothing that even profane nations do not perform in abundance, as Beza and Walaeus here.

Μισθὸν προφήτε λήψεται. Here the reward of a Prophet is that blessing which is called εὐλογία ἐπὶ τῷ ποδὶ, Gen. XXX. 30: 'for little was what you had before me, and it has increased into a multitude, and the Lord has blessed you at my foot,' that is, לרגלי, Jacob says to Laban: which Laban himself said a little before, 'God has blessed me at your coming,' at your arrival. For the foot even of a poor man accepted by God, to whom good is done, is followed by the blessing of God, who repays that good: although in that place it concerns a temporal blessing or happiness, as Walaeus here from Heinsius.

Latin:

Vers. 41. προφήτην ] Si quis recte advertat videbit tres poni discipulorum Christi gradus : infimus est infimorum qui hic μικροὶ vocantur, ut & infra XIIX. 6. Marci IX. 42. Luc. εἰς ὄνομα προφήτη] Hoc est quod barbare vulgo dicitur, in qualitate Prophetæ.

Εἰς ὄνομα, id est ad verbum, in nomen. Εἰς pro ἐν posito. Id est, ut Prophetam, & eo quod est Propheta, sicut explicatur Marc. IX. vers. 41. Debemus enim Christum colere in ipsius servis: alioqui nihil præstamus quod profanæ quoque gen- tes cumulate non præstent, ut hic Beza & Wa- læus.

## 10:42
Verse 42. ποτήριον ψυχρᾶ μόνον] A proverbial manner of speaking which we use even today in many languages, as often as we wish to signify some very small benefit. We are taught here that deeds are estimated by God from the mind, not the mind from the deeds.

Latin:

Vers. 42. ποτήριον ψυχρᾶ μόνον] Proverbiale loquendi genus quo hodieque in multis linguis utimur, quoties mi- nimum aliquod beneficium significatum volumus. Do- cemur hic facta ex animo, non animum ex factis apud Deum æstimari.

## 11:1 Argument
CHAPTER XI. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

JESUS, after having sent out the Apostles, teaching here and there, John sends his disciples to him, that they may ask whether he is the ὁ ἐρχόμενος [the one who is to come], whom he sends back to those things which they were hearing and seeing: but before the people he bears testimony concerning John, that he is more than a Prophet, namely that Angel who according to Scripture (Mal. 3:1) was to prepare the way for the Lord, and the greatest among those born of women, and also the Elijah who was to come. He complains of this generation, that it has slandered both John and the Son of man, and he predicts that the judgment of the citizens of Chorazin and Bethsaida will be more severe on the last day than that of the Tyrians and Sidonians, and that of the Capernaites than that of the Sodomites. He celebrates God the Father for the manifestation made to infants, and calls all who labor and are burdened to himself, with a promise of refreshment and an exhortation to take up the sweet yoke of Christ.

These are the parts: I. The embassy of the disciples of John to Christ, to verse 6. II. The testimony of Christ concerning John, to verse 15. III. The most grave rebuke of the Jews, and especially of certain cities, to verse 24. IV. The most ardent doxology of the Father for the revelation of the Gospel to verse 27. V. The most sweet invitation of all who are burdened, to verse 30.

PART I. The embassy of the disciples of John to Christ.

Vers. 1. ἐν ταῖς πόλεσιν ἀυτῶν [in their cities] That is, of the Jews: thus the Hebrews are accustomed, and our writers following them, to place relative pronouns, even when no noun has preceded, provided it is such that it can easily be understood. It will occur below in Luke several times: thus in Psalm 99:8. So below 12:9 ἦλθεν ἐις τὴν συναγωγὴν ἀυτῶν [he came into their synagogue]. Similarly in Luke 4:15 it is placed ἐν ταῖς συναγωγαῖς ἀυτῶν [in their synagogues]. See also Luke 5:17.

Our blessed Gerhardus [says] in their cities, that is, of the Apostles, namely Galilee, which were their homeland, or which they had traversed while preaching. Blessed Chemnitius [says], to which the Apostles had been sent in chapter 10:6.

Latin:

CAPUT XI. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

IESV post emissos Apostolos passim docente, Iohannes discipulos ad eum ablegat, ut quærant an ipse sit ὁ ἐρχόμενος, qui eos ad ea quæ audiebant, & videbant, re- mittit: penes populum vero testimo- nium de Iohanne perhibet, quod plus quam Propheta sit, Angelus nempe ille qui juxta Scripturam (Mal. III. 1.) viam Domino præparaturus erat, & maxi- mus inter natos è mulieribus, nec non Elias qui venturus erat. Queritur de generatione ista, quod & Iohannem, & Filium hominis calumniata sit, & præ- dicit, gravius futurum in novissimo die civium Chorazin & Bethsaida judi- cium, quam Tyriorum & Sidoniorum, & Capernaitarum, quam Sodomitarum. Celebrat Deum Patrem ob manifestatio- nem infantibus factam, omnesque labo- rantes, & oneratos ad se vocat, cum promissione recreationis, & adhortatione ad suscipiendum suave Christi jugum.

Partes sunt hæ: I. Legatio Discipulorum Jo- hannis ad Christum, ad vers. 6. II. Testificatio Christi de Johanne, ad vers. 15. III. Gravissi- ma increpatio Judæorum, & imprimis civitatum quarundam, ad vers. 24. IV. Ardentissima do- ξολογία Patris pro revelatione Evangelii ad vers. 27. V. Suavissima invitatio omnium oneratorum, ad v. 30.

PARS I. Legatio discipulorum Iohannis ad Christum.

Vers. 1. ἐν ταῖς πόλεσιν ἀυτῶν] Id est, Judæorum: ita so- lent Hebræi & nostri Scriptores eos secuti relativos pone- re, etiam cum nomen nullum antecessit, dum tale sit quod facile possit subintelligi. Occurret infra in Luca aliquo- ties: ita in Psal. XCIX. 8. Sic infra XII. 9. ἦλθεν ἐις τὴν συ- ναγωγὴν ἀυτῶν. Similiter Lucæ IV. 15. positum est ἐν ταῖς συναγωγαῖς ἀυτῶν. Vide & Lucæ V. 17.

B. Gerhardus noster in civitatibus ipsorum, id est Apostolorum, Galilææ scilicet, quæ erant ipsorum patria, vel quas prædicando peragra- rant. B. Chemnitius, ad quas Apostoli erant missi c. X. 6.

## 11:2
Vers. 2. Τὰ ἔργα τῶ χριστ̃ [The works of Christ] Deeds, indeed, most openly agreeing with the ancient oracles concerning Christ, of which he wanted his disciples to be eyewitnesses, so that even while bound, as far as he could, he might discharge the duty of the index [pointer/witness] imposed upon him.

Ε’ν δεσμωτηρίῳ [In prison] The Syrian rendered it in the house of the bound. It is called a prison (desmoterion), because captives are accustomed to be held bound in a prison. Clement of Alexandria names the disciples who were sent as Silas and Carpus: by whose authority, it is not certain.

Latin:

Vers. 2. Τὰ ἔργα τῶ χριστ̃] Facta nimirum cum veteri- bus de Christo oraculis apertissime congruentia, quorum testes oculatos volebat esse discipulos suos, ut etiam vin- ctus quatenus poterat, defungeretur mandato sibi indicis munere.

Ε’ν δεσμωτηρίῳ Syrus reddidit in domo vincto- rum. Carcer dicitur δεσμωτήριον, quia in carce- re vincti detineri solent captivi. Missos disci- pulos nominat Clemens Alex. quod Silas fuerint & Carpus: quo autore, non constat.

## 11:3
Vers. 3. ὁ ἐρχόμενος [the one who is to come] He of whom that word of coming was used by Jacob in Genesis 49:10 and Isaiah 35:4.

Therefore the passage of Isaiah is to be understood concerning Christ, in the days of his flesh: and concerning the advent of the incarnation, otherwise than Grotius in his Annotations on that passage judged: where he drew the oracle to ancient times, and to the help of God against the King of Ethiopia. See our animadversions on those annotations. And concerning that name ὁ ἐρχόμενος, what the blessed Lyserus has in Harm. Evang. c. 55. See also Deut. 18:15, Psalm 40:8, Hagg. 2:8, Mal. 3:1, John 3:31, c. 6:14, c. 11:27, 2 John v. 7. ὁ ἐρχόμενος according to Camerarius in Myrothecium is ὁ ἔμελλε ἔρχεσθαι [he who was about to come], just as in Matthew 17:11 ἔρχεται [he comes] is used for ἔμελλε ἔρχεσθαι. But John did not send for his own sake, who had heard the voice of the heavenly Father, and had already testified concerning Jesus, but for the sake of his disciples, ἵνα πληροφορηθῶσιν οἱ μαθηταὶ [that the disciples might be fully persuaded], as Theophylact has it. Therefore, what Lightfoot has here on p. 158 is not to be approved. A scruple, it seems, stuck in the good man here, why all from

obtain benefit and comfort from Christ, except for me? Perhaps she was suffering from the eye disease with which the whole generation of Christ's disciples was suffering, regarding his kingdom, victories, and earthly triumphs: from which, alas, how far removed was this, that his forerunner and chief minister should lie bound in chains. If you are that one, of whom the Prophets predict such triumphant things; why am I in prison for so long? Are you that one? Or is another to be expected, from whom these things are to be expected?

Latin:

Vers. 3. ὁ ἐρχόμεν@@] Ille de quo verbum illud veni- endi usurpavit Jacobus Genes. XLIX. 10. & Esaias xxxv. vers. 4.

De Christo ergo accipiendus locus Esaiæ, in diebus carnis ejus: & de adventu incarnationi, se- cus atque Grotius in Annot. ad illum locum cen- suit: ubi ad tempora antiqua oraculum traxit, & ad auxilium Dei adversus Regem Æthiopiæ. Vid. animadversiones nostræ ad ista annotata. Et de nomine illo ὁ ἐρχόμεν@, quæ habet B. Lyserus Harm. Evang. c. LV. Vid. & Deut. XIIX. 15. Psal. XL. 8. Hagg. II. 8. Mal. III. 1. Joh. III. 31. c. VI. 14. c. XI. 27. 2. Joh. v. 7. ὁ ἐρχόμεν@ juxta Camer. in Myroth. ὁ ἔμελλε ἔρχεσθαι, uti Matth. XVII. 11. ἔρχεται pro ἔμελλε ἔρχεσθαι. Non autem sui causa mittebat Johannes, qui vo- cem cœlestis Patris audierat, & de Jesu jam testi- ficatus fuerat, sed ob discipulos suos, π πληροφορη- θωσιν lές μαθητὰς, ut Theophylactus habet. Non er- go probanda quæ hic habet Lightfooth. p. 158. Hæsit, ut videtur, viro bono hic scrupulus, quare omnes à

Christo beneficium ac solatium obtinent, me exce- pto? Ea forte laborabat lippitudine, qua cum tota gente discipuli Christi, de ejus regno, victoriis & triumphis terrenis: à quibus, heu quantum! hoc abfuit, quod catenis vinctus jaceret præcursor ejus, ac præcipuus minister. Si tu ille, de quo trium- phante tanta prædicant Prophetæ; quare ego tam- diu in carcere? Tune ille es? an alius exspectandus, à quo ista expectanda?

## 11:4
Ver. 4. Report to John] So that he himself, in whom you place your trust, may tell you what the Prophets said about him who is to do these things: thus the proposition will be most certain, resting on divine authority: the assumption also is undoubted, since it consists of eyewitness testimony. Whence, by the necessity of the consequence, the inference defining the question will follow.

Latin:

Vers. 4. ἀπαγγείλατε Ἰωάννῃ] Ut ipse, cui vos fidem adhibetis, dicat vobis, quid de eo qui ista sit facturus Prophetæ dixerint: ita propositio erit certissima, nixa divina auctoritate: assumtio quoque indubitata, quippe constans oculata fide. Unde consecutionis necessitate sequetur illatio quæstionem definiens.

## 11:5
V. 5. The dead are raised] It is true what the Jews celebrate in a proverb, that God, not content with performing promised benefits, adds something to the heap. Isaiah had prophesied about the healing of the blind, deaf, and lame, and the Psalmist in Ps. CXLVI. 8. God added, which is more, the resuscitation of the dead.

The passage Ps. CXLVI. 8. does not present a prophecy about Christ, but generally proclaims the benefits of God: nor by the prisoners, whom God releases, does it understand those who are held by diseases, as Grotius wished there by comparing Luke XIII. 16. but those who are held captive; and similarly by the bowed down or curved whom God raises up, he does not designate paralytics, as Grotius contends, or such as was the woman who was bent over in Luke XIII. 11. but those who are bowed down or prostrated by enemies: just as also in that place the Lord is said to succor those who suffer injury, and to execute judgment, to love the righteous, to protect strangers, to receive the orphan and the widow, and to despise the ways of sinners, which were not proper works or characteristics of the Messiah when he came in the flesh. It is strange that Grotius should look for such things there, where no one has sought or found them, yet he has not feared to corrupt and twist into a foreign sense the illustrious prophecies which all interpret as being about Christ, because they speak clearly of him. Although the Old Testament Scripture did not openly predict the resuscitation of the dead concerning the Messiah acting in these lands, it nevertheless attributes to him liberation from death, and victory over death, and the vivification of men, Ps. XLIX, Ps. LXIIX. 21, Is. XXV. 8, Hos. XIII. 14. And since it is read of the Prophets in the O.T. that they raised the dead, was it not easy to gather from the same that the great Prophet Messiah, whom the Prophets describe as God, and whom the O.T. taught clearly enough would expiate sins and take away all the punishments of sins, would be much more conspicuous in this kind of benefit and miraculous power, as one whose types only the Prophets were!

The poor have the gospel preached to them] ענו, which is of the same origin as עני, does not always signify one meek in spirit, but often perhaps one humble and abject: especially in Isaiah. For also in ch. XI. 4. the poor of the earth are the same as those he calls דלים, that is, the poor. Not badly, therefore, did the LXX translate that of Isaiah LXI. 1. to preach good tidings to the poor, whom the interpreter of Matthew and Luke IV. 18 follow here. From the same words of Isaiah it is certain that the word are preached to is to be taken passively here: as the Greeks are accustomed to form passives even from actives governing the dative, since the word to preach the gospel is also found with the accusative. Thus below is placed to be served XX. 28. But especially Christ seems to use this prophecy to show how much his method of teaching differs from the customs of the teachers of his age. For the lawyers would scarcely teach anyone except for a great price, they despised the common people, whom they called the people of the land, indeed they had found a proverb both foolish and proud, that the Spirit does not rest except upon the rich. Formerly the Prophets were sent primarily to Kings, CHRIST first revealed himself to fishermen.

Grotius understands it of the poor and perhaps humble and abject: which is also the explanation of the Papists Corn. à Lap., Barradius, Conzenius, and Tirinus, from which they seek in vain some support for the Monastic vow of voluntary poverty: for certainly the Gospel was not preached by Christ to Monks, not to those who had chosen poverty by a vow, let alone those who were poor without lack, as the Monks of today, mixed into the very bowels of the world, call themselves, and while affecting royal luxury, they feign mendicancy, as Erasmus speaks in Method. Stud. Theol. p. 139. And the Poor are understood here not corporally, but spiritually, and not such in reality, but in the sense and conscience of their own mind, that is, those who acknowledge their own misery, and see that there is nothing in themselves by which they can be freed from the judgment of God, and so are of a contrite, humiliated, and abject spirit, as John. Ferus explains the parallel passage of Matt. V. 3: Blessed are the poor in spirit, with Leo the Great, Bishop of Rome, leading the way, as those whom humility of mind commends more than the lack of resources. Corn. à Lap. certainly admits that by the poor he understands those who are impoverished because of sins, that is, destitute of grace and salvation, especially those who acknowledge themselves to be such, Tertullian, book IV against Marcion, ch. 11, Origen, Eusebius, book III of the demonstration, ch. I, Jerome, Ambrose, Theophylact: and Dionysius the Carthusian explains it in the same way, as does Franc. Lucas. Compare Is. LVII. 15, Matt. V. 3, Rev. III. 17. Furthermore, we do not deny to Grotius that the word are preached to is taken passively, even if Theophylact, as well as the Etymologicum, as well as our Franzius on the interpretation of scripture oracle CXV, explain it actively. For it is certain from the words of Isaiah ch. LXI. 1 that that word is taken passively here.

Latin:

V. 5. νεκροὶ ἐγείρονται] Verum est quod Judæi Proverbio celebrant, Deum promissa beneficia præstare non conten- tum, aliquid ad cumulum addere. De cæcis, surdis, claudis sanandis, vaticinatus erat Esaias, & Psalmogra- phus Ps. CXLVI. 8. Addidit Deus, quod amplius est, mor- tuorum resuscitationem.

Locus Ps. CXLVI. 8. non exhibet vaticinium de Christo, sed generaliter Dei beneficia depræ- dicat: nec per compeditos, quos Deus solvit, intel- ligit eos, qui morbis tenentur, ut illic voluit Gro- tius conferens Luc. XIII. 16. sed qui captivi deti- nentur; ac similiter per elisos vel curvatos quos eri- git Deus, non Paralyticos, quemadmodum con- tendit Grotius, vel tales, qualis erat ἡ συγκύπτουσα Luc. XIII. 11. sed qui ab hostibus curvantur, aut pro- sternuntur, designat: uti etiam istic generatim eis, qui injuriam patiuntur, succurrere, ac judicium facere, justos diligere, advenas custodire, pupillum & viduam suscipere, & vias peccatorum despicere Dominus dicitur, quæ non erant propria ἔργα aut characteres Messiæ, cum in carne veniret. Mi- rum, quod illic quærat talia Grotius, ubi nemo ea inquisivit, aut invenit, vaticinia autem illustria quæ de Christo omnes interpretantur, quia luculenter de eo agunt, depravare, & in alienum sensum de- torquere veritus non sit. Mortuorum resuscitatio- nem etsi de Messia in his terris agente non prædi- xerit aperte Scriptura Vet. Test. eidem tamen tri- buit liberationem à morte, & victoriam de morte hominumque vivificationem Ps. XLIX. Ps. LXIIX. 21. Es. XXV. 8. Hos. XIII. 14. cumque de Prophetis in V. T. legatur, quod mortuos resuscitarint, annon de magno illo Propheta Messia, quem ceu Deum Prophetæ describunt, ac peccata per ipsum expia- tum, omnesque peccatorum pœnas ablatum iri V. T. luculenter satis docuit, colligere ex eodem pronum erat, eum multo magis hoc beneficii & miraculosæ virtutis genere conspicuum fore, ut- pote cujus typi solum fuêre Prophetæ!

πτωχοὶ εὐαγγελίζονται] ענו quod ejusdem est originis cum עני non semper animo mitem, sed sæpe forte humi- lem atque abjectum significat: præsertim apud Esaiam. Nam & cap. XI. 4. ענוי ארץ sunt iidem quos דלים vocat, id est pauperes. Non male igitur LXX. illud Esaiæ LXI. 1. לבשר ענוים verterunt εὐαγγελίσασθαι πτωχοῖς, quos hic sequitur Matthæi interpres & Lucas IV. 18. Ex eisdem Esaiæ verbis certum est εὐαγγελίζονται hic sumen- dum passive: ut solent Græci passiva formare etiam ab a- ctivis dativum regentibus, cum εὐαγγελίζω etiam cum ac- cusativo reperiatur. Sic infra ponitur διακονηθῆναι XX. 28. Sed præcipue videtur Christus hoc vaticinio uti, ut osten- dat quantum sua docendi ratio distet à moribus docto- rum sui sæculi. Nam legisperiti vix quemquam nisi ma- gno pretio docebant, contemnebant plebem, quam vocabant populum terræ, imo proverbium repérerant & stultum & superbum, Spiritum non requiescere nisi super divitem. Olim Prophetæ ad Reges potissimum mitte- bantur, CHRISTUS piscatoribus se primum patefe- cit.

De pauperibus & forte humilibus atque abjectis intelligit Grotius: Quæ etiam Pontificiorum Corn. à Lap. Barradii, Conzenii, Tirini est explicatio, inde pro voto Monastico paupertatis spontaneæ ali- quid subsidii nequicquam expectantium: non e- nim certe Monachis prædicatum à Christo Evan- gelium, non illis qui voto paupertatem elegerant. nedum qui pauperes fuerint sine defectu, ut ipsis mundi visceribus immixti hodie Monachi se vo- cant, & regium luxum affectantes, mendicitatem prætexunt, ut Erasm. in Method. Stud. Theol. p. 139. loquitur. Et intelliguntur hic Pauperes non corporaliter, sed spiritualiter, nec re ipsa tales, sed mentis suæ sensu & conscientia, hoc est qui mi- seriam suam agnoscunt, videntque nihil in seipsis esse, quo à judicio Dei liberari possint, adeoque spiri- tu sunt contrito, humiliato & abjecto, ut Joh. Ferus locum Matth. V. 3. hujus parallelum: Beati paupe- tes spiritu explicat, præeunte Leone M. Rom. Episc. quos humilitas commendat animorum magis, quam indigentia facultatum. Fatetur utique Corn. à Lap. per pauperes eos, qui ob peccata depauperati, id est gratia & salute destituti sunt, præsertim qui se ta- les agnoscunt intelligere Tertul. l. IV. contra Mar- cion. c. 11. Origenem, Eusebium, l. III. demonstr. c. I. Hieron. Ambros. Theophylactum: atque ita ex- ponit etiam Dionysius Carthusian. ut & Franc. Lu- cas. Confer Es. LVII. 15. Matth. V. 3. Apoc. III. 17. Cæterum non abnuimus Grotio verbum εὐαγγε- λίζονται passive accipi, etsi active Theophyl. ut & Ethym. ut & Franzius noster de interpretatione scripturæ orac. CXV. explicent. Id enim ex ver- bis Esaiæ c. LXI. 1. certum est, quod passive hic verbum illud accipiatur.

## 11:6
Ver. 6. shall be offended in me.] Shall not have been offended by my humble and poor state, and the vexations impending upon me. See below XXVI. 31, 1 Cor. I. 2, 3.

PART II. The testimony of Christ concerning John.

Latin:

Vers. 6. σκανδαλισθῇ ἐν ἐμοὶ.] Non offensus fuerit statu meo humili ac paupere, & imminentibus mihi vexationi- bus. Vide infra XXVI. 31. 1. Cor. I. 2. 3.

PARS II. Testificatio Christi de Iohanne.

## 11:7
Vers. 7. A reed shaken by the wind.] The meaning is: you had, I think, some reason for which you ran with such zeal into those desert places. For it is not credible that you gathered together to see reeds shaken by the wind. This is because, apart from John, there was almost nothing else to see in those places.

Latin:

Vers. 7. Κάλαμον ὑπὸ ἀνέμου σαλευόμενον.] Sensus est:ha- buistis puto causam aliquam, ob quam tanto studio in loca illa deserta cucurristis. Neq; enim credibile est vos coivisse ut arundines vento agitatas videretis. Hoc ideo, quia ex- tra Johannem nihil ferme aliud istis in locis erat spectare.

## 11:8
Vers. 8. In soft clothing] In silk: for Virgil also called silk soft wools. Moreover, the dearness of silks was so great that they were weighed against gold.

are in kings' houses] Not in desert places: wherefore not even this could have been the cause of your gathering.

The discourse is not about a reed properly so called to be seen in the desert, but it comes under the name of a reed metaphorically; one who allows himself to be moved here and there by any wind in doctrine, and John is denied to be such a one. By a reed, Scripture designates lightness and inconstancy of mind, 1 Kings 14:15, Isaiah 36:6. Therefore Chrysostom says thus in Homily 38 on Matthew, that John is commended here because he was not easily swayed and fickle, but firm and steadfast: and Eusebius Emissenus, Sermon 3 on Advent. John, he says, is not a reed, but a pillar; he similarly proclaims John because he is not like those who are in courts wearing soft clothing: he removes from him the pursuit of flattery, luxury, and pride, and attributes to him temperance of food and clothing, and true humility: or, as Blessed Hunn says, that he is not such a one who, by a certain softness of mind, would compose the office entrusted to him to the pleasure of men, just as courtiers wearing soft and splendid garments are for the most part endowed with a soft disposition, not proud in sumptuous clothes, who would wish both to be called soft themselves, and in turn speak soft things to others: Chrysostom wishes this to be said for the clearing of John, as if Christ were meeting the objection of those saying: that John might not seem unacquainted with courtly arts, which are contained by mutability and the fiction of themselves at another's nod, especially as one who in

had been for a long time in Herod's palace, and had tasted the delicacies of which there is an abundance there. Christ refuted and dissolved this foundation of suspicion by mentioning the austere lifestyle and diet of John, who certainly, if he had fashioned himself for favor, would be living comfortably in royal halls, not as he was then, in prison; if he loved delicacies, he would be clothed in soft garments, not a rough and uncomfortable tunic. Grotius's explanation is too meager, as if it were only a matter of clothes: what use are silk garments in desert places? which he understands by the words μαλακοῖς ἱματίοις, because Virgil also called silk 'soft wools'.

Latin:

Vers. 8. Μαλακοῖς ἱματίοις] Sericis: nam serica molles lanas etiam Virgilius dixit. Sericorum autem tanta erat caritas ut auro contra pensarentur.

ἐν τοῖς οἴκοις τῶν βασιλέων εἰσὶν] Non in locis desertis: qua- re ne ista quidem concursus vestri causa esse potuit.

Non de calamo proprie dicto in deserto spe- ctando sermo est, sed metaphorice calami nomine venit; qui à quovis vento hinc inde se in doctrina moveri patitur, ac talis Johannes esse negatur. Per arundinem Scriptura levitatem & inconstantiam animi designat 1. Reg. XIV. 15. Es. XXXVI. 6. Ideo Chrysostomus ita hom. XXXIIX. in Matth. Johannem hic commendari ait, quod non fuerit εὔκολος, & εὐ- ριπτος, sed πεπηγὸς, & βέβαιος: & Euseb. Emiss. Serm. III. Advent. Johannes, inquit, non est arundo, sed columna, similiter Johannem prædicat quod non similis sit iis, qui in aulis sunt τὰ μαλακὰ φέροντες ἱ- μάτια: removet ab eo adulationis studium, luxum & fastum, tribuit ei victus & amictus temperantiam, veramq; humilitatem: vel, ut B. Hunn. quod non ta- lis sit, qui quadam animi mollitie munus sibi concredi- tum ad hominum placita componeret, uti aulici mol- lia splendidaque vestimenta gerentes plerumque molli etiam sunt ingenio præditi, non sumtuosis vestibus su- perbiens, qui & sibi mollia dici exoptet, & mollia vi- cissim dicat aliis: Chrys. hoc ad purgationem Johan- nis dictum vult, quasi occurrat Christus exceptioni dicentium: posse Joannem non rudem videri aulica- rum artium, quæ mutabilitate, ac fictione sui ad nu- tum alienum continentur maxime, utpote qui in

Palatio Herodis diu fuerit, & delicias quarum illic affluit copia, gustaverit. Hoc firmamentum su- spicionis modo refutata diluit Christus, commemora- tione austeri cultus, victusque Joannis, qui utique si ad gratiam se finxisset, in Regiis ædibus commode habitaret, non ut tunc erat, in carcere; si delicias a- maret, mollibus vestiretur, non hirta molestaque tu- nica. Nimis jejuna est Grotii explicatio, quasi solum de vestibus agatur: quid in locis desertis se- ricæ vestes? quas intelligit per voces μαλακοῖς ἱ- ματίοις, quia etiam Virgilius serica molles lanas dixit.

## 11:9
Vers. 9. Προφήτην] Gorionides also calls this John a Prophet.

Latin:

Vers. 9. Προφήτην] Etiam Gorionides Johannem hunc Prophetam vocat.

## 11:10
Vers. 10. Ἀγγελόν με] מלאכים or ἄγγελοι were called not just any Prophets, but those who were sent by God to the people regarding a great matter, such as Moses in Numbers xx. 16, Haggai I. 33, and he from whom this prophecy is taken, Malachi, whose very name signifies ἄγγελον: whence it happened that the ancient Christians often called him by the Greek ἄγγελον as if it were a proper name. The same word was used for the ὁ τῆς πρεσβυτερίας προστώς in the Christian Church, as one who was accustomed to speak words to the people in God's name, because he would occupy the same place in the Church that the High Priest occupied in the temple, who is himself also called מלאך, that is, ἄγγελος. Mal. II. 7. Diodorus Siculus, cited by Photius, says of the Jews: 'They call the High Priest and consider him to be an Angel to them of God's commandments.'

Πρὸ προσώπε σε] It appears from this also that the words of the Prophets are not cited by Christ word for word, but in such a way that the words are sometimes changed while the meaning remains: just as Homer's verses are very often cited among the Greeks with the person or the mode of the verb changed. For in the Prophet the speech is directed to the people: here to the Messiah himself: and what is here ἔμπροσθέν σε, is in the Prophet ἔμπροσθέν με.

ὃς κατασκευάσει τὴν ὁδόν σε] The office of a quartermaster is described: which Roman word Suidas explains thus: 'a quartermaster is one sent ahead before the leader.' Compare what was said above III. 3. from Isaiah.

Latin:

Vers. 10. Ἀγγελόν με] מלאכים sive ἄγγελοι diceban- tur non quivis Prophetæ, sed qui de re magna à Deo ad po- pulum erant legati, ut Moses Numer. xx. 16. Aggæus I. 33. & ille unde hoc vaticinium sumtum est, Malachias, cujus nomen ipsum ἄγγελον significat: unde factum est ut Chri- stiani veteres sæpe eum Græce ἄγγελον quasi proprio nomi- ne appellent. Dictus est eodem vocabulo in Ecclesiæ Christianæ ὁ τῆς πρεσβυτερίας προστώς ut qui Dei nomine ver- ba ad populum facere solerent quod scilicet eundem lo- cum in Ecclesia obtineret, quem in templo magnus Sacer- dos qui & ipse מלאך id est ἄγγελος dicitur. Mal. II. 7. Diodorus Siculus de Judæis citatus Photio: Ἀρχιερέα δὲ τὸν προσαγορεύουσι κὶ νομίζουσιν αὐτοῖς Ἄγγελον γενέσθαι τῶν τοῦ Θεῦ προταγμάτων.

Πρὸ προσώπε σε] Apparet hinc etiam verba Propheta- rum non citari à Christo κατὰ λέξιν : sed ita ut voces inter- dum mutentur manente sententia: quomodo & apud Græ- cos sæpissime citantur Homeri versus mutata à persona aut modo verbi. Nam apud Prophetam dictio ad populum di- rigitur: hic ad ipsum Messiam: & quod hic est ἔμπροσθέν σε, apud Prophetam ἔμπροσθέν με.

ὃς κατασκευάσει τὴν ὁδόν σε] Describitur officium meta- toris: quam vocem Romanam ita exponit Suidas: μετά- τωρ ὁ προαποστελλόμενος πρὸ τῶ ἄρχοντος. Confer quæ su- pra III. 3. ex Esaia.

## 11:11
Vers. 11. ἐγήγερται] The propriety of the speech is to be noted. For Prophets are properly said to be ἐγείρεσθαι (raised up), Luke VII. 16, John VII. 52.

ἐν γεννητοῖς γυναικῶν] The meaning is: no prophet greater than John appeared to the human race before him: thus in Luke at the cited place: 'a great prophet has been raised up among us': that is, has appeared in our midst. Nor is 'to be among those born of women' in this same narrative in Luke anything other than to be in human affairs, or to be seen by men. Thus in Job XIV. 1, XV. 14, XXV. 4, a man is called ילוד אשה, γεννητὸς γυναικὸς, and in Sirach X. 17, γέννημα γυναικός.

Ὁ δὲ μικότερος ἐν τῇ βασιλείᾳ τῶν ἐρανῶν] That is, in the preaching of the heavenly kingdom: which had been foreshadowed before this, but not openly proclaimed by the Prophets. The entire comparison is in the gift of the Prophet itself, which Luke expressed more openly. Therefore, by as much as John excelled all the Prophets before him, by so much will the prophets of the new covenant, even the lowest, excel John, namely in the magnitude of their knowledge concerning the liberation of the human race: for that was a mystery before John, it began to shine forth in John's time, and after Christ's passion and resurrection and the sending of the Holy Spirit, it appeared clearer than the midday light. Thus below in XIII. 17, Christ says that many Prophets desired to be able to see the things that were given to his Disciples to see. Μικρότερος here is ἐλάχιστος, as also in Luke IX. 48. Therefore, no necessity compels us to restrict this comparison to two, so that we might further conclude from it that Christ is speaking here about himself. Nam quod affirmat vir ha- rum rerum peritissimus, for as to what a man most skilled in these matters affirms, that μείζων and μικρότερος are always said of two unless an explicit noun of the plural number is present, we are taught that he is mistaken in that very point by the words of Luke IX. 48, where there is a plural end: 'who then is greater in the kingdom of heaven,' and yet it is not so obvious that a comparison of two is set forth there that it stands in need of proof.

There are two principal interpretations of this passage. The former is that a comparison is instituted between John and Christ, and that by μικρότερον is understood Christ, who was indeed lesser than John in respect to the state of κενώσεως and ταπεινώσεως: the other is that John is compared with the disciples of Christ and the ministers of the Word in the New Testament, and that the least of them after the passion and resurrection of Christ and the mission of the Holy Spirit is said to be greater than the Proto-Baptist in respect to a more abundant knowledge of Christ: which Grotius prefers. Each has its own advocates. For the latter is approved not only by the Reformed, Bucer, and Cameron, but also by our own B. Quistorp, as well as B. Gerhard: nor is it disapproved by B. Polyc. Lyser in his Harmony, although he leaves the option of choosing whichever one wishes: the former, however, is approved by most of the more excellent interpreters, not only recent ones, but also the ancient interpreter B. Chrysost. Euthymio, Theophylacto, B. Luthe- ro, Osiander, Hunnius, the Vinarie Paraphrast, and among the Papists, Salmeron, Franc. Lucas, Jansenius, Corn. a Lap., Tirinus, and others. Nor are there lacking reasons why it seems to be preferred: for in the preceding verses Christ had also compared himself with John, and had taught that he was the Messiah, the one who is to come, and that John was his forerunner: whose dignity he testified to, in that it is so great that no one born of women can be compared to him; but lest he seem to have preferred the same to himself, Christ adds that he who is least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than John, thus vindicating for himself the honor which his state of humiliation seemed to obscure, lest the estimators of John attribute more than is just to this man of God, to the detriment of the glory of the Messiah. Added to this is the fact that in the following verses the comparison is continued with John, v. 18 seqq., but nothing is insinuated by that word about other disciples of Christ. Furthermore, that comparison with the other disciples regarding doctrine does not hold up so conveniently: for although, with respect to certain wξιςασεις concerning the life and miracles of Christ, concerning his passion, death, and resurrection, there was a more illustrious knowledge and more abundant information after those things were accomplished than in the time of John the forerunner, yet the doctrine itself concerning Christ, regarding his person, office, and state, was not only handed down in the O.T., where also most of the peculiar circumstances are predicted in the Psalms and Prophets, to whose testimonies and prophecies Christ and the Evangelists frequently appealed, but it also happened to St. John, who was already filled with the Holy Spirit in his mother's womb, that he had such an ελλαμψις in these divine matters and in the understanding of the Holy Scriptures, that he cannot be so conveniently or truly placed after the least of the heralds after the resurrection of Christ; which the things concerning his office, as taught by the angel and his father Zacharias in Luke 1:15 ff., as also v. 76 ff., and his testimonies, as well as the sermons of John in Matthew 3, Luke 3, John 1 and 3, together with that remarkable Θεοφανεια made to him in Matthew 3, can teach. But that explanation of Grotius—that the kingdom of heaven was only foreshadowed, not openly announced by the Prophets, understood in the sense of Grotius, who is Socinianizing and Pelagianizing, namely that in the O.T. there were only some foreshadowings of eternal life, but the same was not openly proposed until finally by Christ—is to be utterly rejected: nor does it suit this passage, where the subject is John, who certainly announced eternal life openly (John 3:36), nor can he be placed as inferior in the gifts of prophecy to the least herald of the Gospel after the resurrection; and how could he, who, as the angel taught, had to turn the hearts of the fathers to the children and the disobedient to the wisdom of the just (Luke 1:16-17), yield in the magnitude of his knowledge concerning the liberation of the human race to the prophets or ministers of the word of the N.T.? and as his father Zacharias prophesied, to give knowledge of salvation to the people, which is in the remission of sins, through the tender mercies of God, through which the dayspring from on high has visited us (Luke 1:76-77). That the liberation of the human race was a mystery before John is a Socinian αιτημα, contrary to the testimony of Peter in Acts 10:43, that all the prophets testify concerning the remission of sins to be obtained through faith in Christ, and of Paul concerning the whole scripture in 2 Timothy 3:15, and thus contrary to the whole of scripture. However, that it shone more clearly in the time of John, and most clearly after the outpouring of the Holy Spirit, we admit only as regards the degrees of manifestation; for the rest, such and so great a clarity of manifestation in the Old Testament is not to be denied, as great and such as was necessary for them, so that through faith in the Messiah, outside of which no salvation ever occurred, the pious ancients might obtain salvation. Acts 15:11, ch. 4:12, Heb. 12:2, Rev. 13:8. And these are the primary interpretations of Christ's saying.

Furthermore, neither does Calixtus's explanation, which is the third, have any place, that by the least in the kingdom of heaven is understood here anyone who through faith has been made a participant of adoption and eternal inheritance, because such a one is greater than John, since an office, however great, is to no one a cause of salvation: for it is not causes of salvation that are being explained: nor does the dignity of an office come into contention with faith, as to which is greater; the least in the kingdom of heaven is the least in faith and in adoption, and John cannot be placed after such a one, whose faith was indeed great: and if he were to be placed after him by reason of office, the same must be said equally of others, whatever doctors, Moses, the Prophets, the Apostles: why therefore would this be asserted here of John alone? There remains the fourth explanation, which is Smalcius's in his Refutation. Franz, p. 395, is that any Christian in the New Testament designated here by the least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than John, provided that the Johannine doctrine is far too imperfect to be proposed to Christians as a rule of life, which is in some way akin to Grotius's interpretation: but it is to be rejected as false, and deservedly so. For as to the substance of religion, not only John, but also the chorus of Prophets in the Old Testament, handed down the same doctrine that was handed down by Christ, and which is for us Christians a rule of believing and living, we who can also be informed from the Old Testament concerning faith unto salvation, 2 Tim. 3:15, and to which we ought to attend as to a rule, 2 Pet. 1:19, and hear Moses and the Prophets as our teachers concerning avoiding eternal condemnation, Luke 16:29, and be built up upon the Scripture of the Prophets as well as the Apostles as a foundation, Eph. 2:20.

Latin:

Vers. 11. ἐγήγερται] Notanda sermonis proprietas. Nam Prophetæ proprie dicuntur ἐγείρεσθαι Luc. VII. 16. Joh. VII. 52.

ἐν γεννητοῖς γυναικῶν] Sensus est: major Johanne nullus ante ipsum Prophetæ humano generi apparuit: ita apud Lu- cam dicto loco: προφήτης μέγας ἐγήγερται ἐν ἡμῖν: id est apparuit in medio nostri. Neque aliud est apud Lucam in hac ipsa narratione εἶναι ἐν γεννητοῖς γυναικῶν quam in re- bus humanis esse, aut ab hominibus conspici. Sic Jobo XIV. 1. XV. 14. XXV. 4. homo dicitur ילוד אשה γεννητὸς γυναικὸς, apud Sirachidem X. 17. γέννημα γυναικός.

Ὁ δὲ μικότερος ἐν τῇ βασιλείᾳ τῶν ἐρανῶν] Id est in prædicatione regni cœlestis: quod antehac adumbratum non aperte pronuntiarum à Prophetis fuerat. Comparatio tota est in ipso dono Prophetæ, quod Lucas apertius expres- sit. Quanto ergo Johannes præstitit omnibus ante se Pro- phetis, tanto Prophetæ novi fœderis, etiam infimi, antcsta- bunt Johanni, nimirum magnitudine notitiæ de liberatione humani generis: namque id ante Johannem mysterium fuit, Johannis tempore cœpit illucescere, post Christi pas- sionem & resurrectionem & missum Spiritum S. meridiana luce clarius patuit. Sic infra XIII. 17. ait Christus multos Prophetas optasse ea posse videre, quæ videnda dabantur Discipulis suis. Μικρότερος, hic est ἐλάχιστος ut & apud Luc. IX. 48. Nulla igitur necessitas nos cogit ad duos hanc comparationem restringere, ut inde porro colligamus Christum de se ipso hic agere. Nam quod affirmat vir ha- rum rerum peritissimus, μείζων & μικρότερος nisi adsit ex- pressum nomen pluralis numeri semper de duobus dici, in eo ipso falli docemur verbis Lucæ XI IX. L ubi fine plu- rali est τίς ἄρα μείζων ἐν τῇ βασιλείᾳ τῶν ἐρανῶν, neque tamen ibi duos comparationem sisti apertius est quam ut proba- tionis indigeat.

Duæ sunt præcipuæ loci hujus interpretatio- nes. Prior est comparationem inter Johannem & Christum institui, & per μικρότερον intelligi Chri- stum, qui minor utique erat qua statum κενώσεως & ταπεινώσεως Johanne: Altera est, comparari Johannem cum discipulis Christi, ac ministris Ver- bi in N. T. ac minimum eorum post passionem, & resurrectionem Christi ac missionem Spiritus S. majorem dici Proto-Baptista, qua cognitionem uberio- rem de Christo: quam præfert Grotius. Utraque r suos habet assertores. Posterior enim probata non tantum Reformatis, Buccero, Cameroni, sed etiam e nostris B. Quistorpio, ut & B. Gerhardo: neque improbata B. Polyc. Lysero in Harmon. etsi optionem relinquat eligendi, utram quis velit: prior tamen plerisque præstantioribus est probata non recentioribus solum, sed etiam antiquis In- terp. B. Chrysost. Euthymio, Theophylacto, B. Luthe- ro, Osiandro, Hunnio, Paraphrast. Vinariens. & e Pontificiis Salmeroni, Franc. Lucæ, Jansenio, Corn. a Lap. Tirino, aliis. Neque desunt rationes cur ea præferenda videatur: nam in antecedentibus com- pararat etiam sese Christus cum Johanne, ac se Messiam τ' ερχομενον Johannem vero prodromum suum esse docuerat: cujus dignitatem testatus fuit, quod ea tanta sit, ut nemo e mulieribus natus ipsi componi queat, ne autem ideo sibi ipsi eun- dem prætulisse videretur, addit Christus, eum qui minimus in regno cælorum est, majorem Johanne esse, vindicans ita sibi honorem, quem status ελαττω- σεως obscurare videbatur, ne æstimatores Johan- nis plus justo huic viro Dei tribuant, cum detri- mento gloriæ Messiæ. Accedit, quod in conse- quentibus comparatio continuetur cum Johanne v. 18. seqq. nihil vero de aliis discipulis Christi illo verbo insinuetur. Adhæc non ita commode se habeat illa cum discipulis aliis ratione doctrinæ comparatio: nam etsi quoad wξιςασεις nonnullas circa vitam & miracula Christi, circa passionem, mortem & resurrectionem ejus illustrior cognitio fuerit, atque uberior informatio, postquam illa peracta sunt, quam Johannis protobaptistæ tem- pore doctrina tamen ipsa de Christo, quoad perso- nam, officium & statum ejusdem non in V. T. tan- tum tradita, ubi etiam peculiares circumstantiæ pleræque, in Psalmis & Prophetis sunt prædictæ, ad quorum testimonia & vaticinia Christus & Ev- angelistæ subinde provocarunt, sed ea etiam con- tigit S. Johanni, qui in utero materno Spiritu S. jam repletus fuit, in rebus istis divinis, & Scriptu- rarum S. intelligentia ελλαμψις, ut minimo præco- num post resurrectionem Christi non adeo conveni- enter aut vere postponi queat; quod de & officium ejus ab angelo & patre Zacharia Luc. I. 15. seqq. ut & v. 76. seqq. & testificationes, nec non conciones Johannes Matth. III. Luc. III. Joh. I. & III. cum in- signi illa Θεοφανεια ipsi facta Matth. III. docere possunt. Illa vero Grotii explicatio: quod regnum cæleste adumbratum tantum, non aperte annuncia- tum a Prophetis fuerit, sensu Grotii, Socinianizan- tis, & Pelagianizantis intellecta, quod nempe in V. T. adumbrationes tantum aliquæ fuerint æ- ternæ vitæ, non vero eadem aperte proposita fue- rit, nisi a Christo demum, prorsus reprobanda est: neque huic loco, ubi de Johanne agitur, convenit, qui certe vitam æternam palam annunciavit Joh. III. 36. neque in donis Prophetiæ inferior minimo post resurrectionem Evangelii præcone statui potest; & quomodo magnitudine notitiæ de liberatione generis humani cedere poterat prophetis seu mi- nistris verbi N. T. is, qui, docente angelo, conver- tere debuit corda Patrum ad filios, & infideles ad pru- dentiam justorum Luc. I. 16. 17. & vaticinante Pa- tre Zacharia, cognitionem salutis dare populo, quæ in remissione peccatorum est, per viscera misericordiæ Dei, per quæ visitavit nos oriens ex alto, Luc. I. 76. 77. Mysterium fuisse ante Johannem liberationem humani generis socinianum αιτημα est, contrarium testimonio Petri Act. X. 43. quod omnes Prophe- tæ de remissione peccatorum consequenda per fi- dem in Christum testificentur, & Pauli de tota scri- ptura 2. Tim. III. 15. totique adeo scripturæ adver- sum. Clarius autem id illuxisse tempore Johan- nis, & clarissime post effusionem Sp. S. non nisi quantum ad gradus manifestationis ultro admitti- mus, de cætero tanta & talis claritas manifestatio- nis in V. T. neganda non est, quanta & qualis opus ipsis fuit, ut per fidem in Messiam, extra quam nul- la unquam contigit salus, pii veteres salutem con- sequerentur. Act. XV. 11. cap. IV. 12. Ebr. XII. 2. Apoc. XIII. 8. Atque hæc de primariis dicti Chri- sti interpretationibus.

Porro neque Calixti, quæ tertia est, explicatio locum habet, per minimum in regno cælorum, in- telligi hic quemcunque qui per fidem particeps fa- ctus sit ὑιοθεσίας & hæreditatis æternæ, quod talis major sit Johanne, quoniam officium, quantumcun- que nemini salutis causa est: non enim salutis causæ explicantur: nec officii dignitas cum fide in conten- tionem venit, utra major sit; minimus in regno cæ- lorum minimus in fide, & ὑιοθεσίᾳ est, nec tali Jo- hannes postponi potest, cujus magna utique fides fuit: ac si postponi ratione officii idem de aliis pari- ter dicendum, quibuscunque doctoribus, Mose, Prophetis, Apostolis: cur ergo hic de solo Johanne id assereretur? Superest quarta explicatio, quæ Smal- cii in Refut. Franz. p. 395. est, quod quilibet Chri- stianus in N. T. per minimum in regno cælorum hic designatus major sit Johanne, siquidem imperfe- ctior longe sit Johannea doctrina, quam ut Christia- nis ceu vivendi regula proponi debeat, quæ affinis quodammodo est Grotianæ interpretationi: sed ceu falsa merito rejicienda. Nam quod ad reli- gionis substantiam, eandem doctrinam tradidit, non Johannes tantum, sed etiam in V. T. chorus Prophetarum, quæ à Christo est tradita, nobisque Christianis credendi, & vivendi regula est, qui è V. T. de fide informari etiam possumus ad salutem 2. Tim. III. 15. eique tanquam regalæ attendere de- bemus 2. Pet. I. 19. Mosenque & Prophetas ceu do- ctores nostros audire de evitanda æterna conde- mnatione Luc. XVI. 29. ac super Prophetarum æque ac Apostolorum Scriptura ceu fundamento super- strui Eph. II. 20.

## 11:12
Verse 12. βιάζεται] It is invaded by a great concourse of men. Formerly the people were forbidden βιάζεσθαι to climb Mount Sinai. For that word is in the Greek version of Exod. 19:24. Now that is permitted unto that most mystical mountain.

Βιασται] Christ shows that there is need of a great spirit for those who wish to obtain possession of that heavenly kingdom, which had been predicted more obscurely by the Prophets, indicated more closely by John, and most openly revealed by Christ himself; just as God commands Joshua to be of a strong and intrepid spirit to invade Canaan, the image of the heavenly kingdom, Josh. 1:6, 7, 9.

Lightfoot rightly [says] here, p. 159. And these things also contribute to the praises of John. That he was a most noble Prophet, and of no common mission and authority, these things prove, because the kingdom of heaven took its beginning from his preaching, and was so pushed into it in crowds and throngs by infinite multitudes, as if they were occupying that kingdom by violent seizure. The divine surge of the people, betaking themselves thither in such countless crowds and with such an overflowing fervor, sufficiently argues and teaches the dignity of both the teacher and the doctrine. Not concerning the kingdom of glory, which was not obscurely, but clearly enough, [revealed] by the Prophets, Lev. 18:5, Job 19:26, Ps. 16:last, Ps. 22:27, Ps. 36:8, Isa. 25:8, ch. 35:10, ch. 65:17, 18, ch. 66:22, 23, Ezek. 18:33, ch. 33:11, Dan. 2:44, ch. 7:26, ch. 12:2, Joel 2:32, Mal. 3:18, ch. 4:1, etc. handed down to be acquired by our studies and works; for it is that gift of God, Rom. 6:23. To which we aspire by faith alone, Rom. 4:5, 6, not by works, Eph. 2:8, 9, but concerning the kingdom of grace, which John was showing no less openly than Christ himself, Matt. 3:2, ch. 4:17, or that it must be seized violently, against the Pharisaical revocation from it, and the varied temptation of the Devil, the world, and the flesh, and that one must contend so that we are not led away from Christ, who calls all to himself and repels no one, Matt. 11:28, John 6:37, as Hilary, Chrysostom, Photius, and others explain.

Latin:

Vers. 12. βιάζεται] Magno concursu hominum invadi- tur. Olim populus vetitus βιάζεσθαι ad montem Sinæ scan- dendum. Est enim ea vox in versione Græca Exod. XIX. 24. Nunc id licet in montem illum μυσικώτατον.

Βιασται] Ostendit Christus magno opus esse animo his qui possessionem velint adipisci regni illius cælestis, quod à Prophetis obscurius prædictum, à Johanne propius indica- tum, ab ipso Christo apertissime erat revelatum, sic Josuam Deus ad invadendam Canaanæam, regni cælestis imaginem, forti & intrepido esse animo jubet, Jos. I. 6. 7. 9.

Recte hic Lightfoothus p. 159. Et hæc etiam fa- ciunt in Encomia Joannis. Nobilissimum illum fuis- se Prophetam, ac missionis atŕ autoritatis non vulga- ris fidem hæc faciunt, quod ab ejus prædicatione & i- nitium sumserit regnum cælorum, ac confertim ac catervatim adeo sit eo protrusum ab infinitis cæ- tibus, ac si violenter arreptum regnum illud occu- parent. Divinus populi æstus, catervis tam innume- ris ac fervore tam inundante eo se conferentis, divi- nam satis arguit & docentis & doctrinæ dignitatem. Non de regno gloriæ, quod non obscure, sed clare satis à Prophetis Lev. XIIX. 5. Job. XIX. 26. Ps. XVI. ult. Ps. XXII. 27. Ps. XXXVI. 8. Es. XXV. 8. c. XXXV. 10. c. LXV. 17. 18. c. LXVI. 22. 23. Ez. XIIX. 33. c. XXXIII 11. Dan. II. 44. c. VII. 26. c. XII. 2. Joel. II. 32. Mal. III. 18. c. IV. 1. seqq. &c. traditum studiis, & operibus nostris acquirendo; est enim id χάρισμα τῶ Θεῶ Rom. VI. 23.
