Ad quod fide solum aspiramus Rom. IV. 5. 6. non operibus Eph. II. 8. 9. sed de regno gra- tiæ, quod monstrabat Joannes haud minus aperte quam ipse Christus Matth. III. 2. c. IV. 17. vel vio- lenter, adversus Pharisaicam ab illo revocationem, variamque Diaboli mundi, & carnis tentationem, rapiendum id esse, adeoque contendendum, ut ne à Christo abducamur, omnes ad se vocante, nec quenquam repellente, Matth. XI. 28. Joh. VI. 37. ut Hilarius, Chrysostomus, Photius aliique exponunt.

## 11:13
Verse 13. ἕως Ἰωάννη] He does not mean by this that the law died with the coming of John: [for it was necessary that it should last until that solemn mission of the Holy Spirit] nor that any prophecies extend beyond John: (for there are those which pertain to the final destruction of the city of Jerusalem) but that the Messiah, that prince of the new kingdom, whom the ceremonies of the law had shadowed forth, the Prophets had predicted, and a more perfect doctrine, began to be known together with John and through John. See what [is said] on Luke.

Grotius renders this sense: The Messiah, that prince of the new kingdom, whom the ceremonies of the law had shadowed forth, the Prophets had predicted, and a more perfect doctrine, began to be known together with John, and through John. But although the Messiah began to be known, as regards the manifestation of this individual, that Jesus of Nazareth is that promised Messiah, of whom John testified, John 1:7, 8, 19, etc., yet that doctrine concerning the Messiah was not new, that he was to liberate the human race, and lead those who were to believe in him to eternal life: nor was the advent of the Messiah, who was to hand down these things, only shadowed forth and predicted, but his office also, that very liberation of the human race, and that the same must be received through faith if one wishes to obtain salvation, were already exhibited in the Old Testament and before John, both in the Prophetic oracles. Which has been asserted elsewhere against the Socinians and the Innovators. Neither did John, nor Christ, nor the Apostles hand down a doctrine more perfect in its parts than that which had been handed down by the Prophets, although the doctrine in the N.T. differed in degrees of clarity, inasmuch as it was set forth more clearly. Moreover, to those words: For all the prophets and the law prophesied until John, because it was a matter of the kingdom of heaven suffering violence and of Christ the Messiah, and of blessedness through faith in him, c. XI. 13. (cf. Matt. XI. 12, 13), this sense seems to agree best, which Peter rendered in Acts X. 43: To him all the prophets bear witness, that through his name all who believe in him receive forgiveness of sins. This is also taught by what follows concerning John, that he is the Elijah who was to come for the purpose that he might testify of him, so that through him all might believe in Christ, Matt. XI. John I. 7. For Christ does not say: The Law and the Prophets lasted until John, but they prophesied, namely concerning Christ, Ps. XL. 7, and all the prophets bear witness to him. Cf. John V. 39 ff. and v. 46, 47. Not unlike this is that interpretation, which the blessed Gerhard calls common, that all the prophets and the law until John prophesied concerning the coming of Christ, whom John indeed pointed out with his finger as present.

Latin:

Vers. 13. ἕως Ἰωάννη] Non hoc vult cum adventu Johan- nis emortuam legem: [debebat enim illa durare usque ad so- lemnem illam missionem Sp. S.] neque ulla vaticinia ultra Johannem extendi : (sunt enim quæ ad postremum urbis Hierosolymorum excidium pertinent) sed Messiam illum novi regni principem, quem legis ceremoniæ adumbrave- rant, Prophetæ prædixerant, & doctrinam perfectiorem simul cum Johanne & per Johannem cœpisse cognosci, Vide quæ ad Lucam.

Sensum hunc reddit Grotius: Messiam illum novi regni principem, quem legis cæremoniæ adum- braverant, Prophetæ prædixerant, ac doctrinam per- fectiorem simul cum Johanne, & per Johannem cœpis- se cognosci. Sed quamvis Messias cœperit cognosci, quoad hujus individuæ manifestationem, quod Jesus Nazarenus ille promissus Messias sit, de quo testa- tus Johannes est, Joh. I. 7. 8. 19. seqq. non tamen ea de Messia doctrina nova erat, quod is liberaturus sit genus humanum, ac eos, qui in ipsum credituri sunt, ad vitam æternam perducturus: nec tantum adumbratus & prædicatus fuit Messiæ adventus, qui hæc traditurus esset, sed officium etiam ejusdem, ipsa illa generis humani liberatio, & quod eadem per fidem suscipienda sit, si salutem quis consequi velit, in V. T. & ante Johannem tum in oraculis Pro- pheticis jam exhibita fuère. Quod contra Socinia- nos, & Novatores alibi assertum est. Neque doctri- nam partibus perfectiorem vel Johannes, vel Chri- stus vel Apostoli tradidère, quam tradita à Prophe- tis erat, etsi claritatis gradibus doctrina in N. T. dif- ferret utpote luculentius proposita. Cæterum ver- bis illis : Omnes enim Prophetæ, & lex usque ad Johan- nem prophetarunt, quia de regno cœlorum vim pa- tiente & Christo Messia, ac beatitudine per fidem in ipsum actum erat, c. IX. 6. 12. hic sensus optime convenire videtur, quem Petro reddidit Act. X. 43. Iluic omnes Prophetæ testimonium reddunt, quod in nomine ejus remissionem peccatorum consequantur omnes qui credunt in ipsum. Quod etiam docent, quæ sequuntur de Johanne, quod is Elias sit, qui venire debuit eo fine, ut testaretur de ipso, ut per i- psum crederent omnes in Christum Matth. XI. Joh. I. 7. Non enim dicit Christus: Lex & Prophetæ dura- runt usque ad Johannem, sed vaticinati sunt, nimi- rum de Christo Psal. XL. 7. & omnes Prophetæ ipsi te- stimonium perhibent. Conf. Joh. V. 39. seqq. & v. 46. 47. Non absimilis est illa interpretatio, quam communem B. Gerhardus dicit, omnes prophetæ & lex usque ad Johannem prophetarunt de adventu Chri- sti, quem vero Johannes digito præsentem ostendit.

## 11:14
Vers. 14. εἰ θέλετε δέξασθαι] If you can bear to be told the truth.

Ἠλίας] Elijah in the most corrupt times was deterred by no danger from setting their sins before the eyes of the King and all the people. The same Spirit and power, i.e., the same fortitude, appeared in John. Because of this eminence of zeal, the Jews fable that the soul of Phinehas came into Elijah. But I think it was said by the ancients that Elijah had come in the spirit of Phinehas, just as the Angel says John would come in the spirit of Elijah, Luke I. 17.

ὁ μέλλων ἔρχεσθαι] δεχόμενον, as just now concerning the Messiah in verse 3, or μέλλων ἔρχεσθαι as in this place, signifies an office predetermined by the certain decree of God.

Latin:

Vers. 14. εἰ θέλετε δέξασθαι] Si patiamini verum vobis dici.

Ἠλίας] Elias corruptissimis temporibus nullo periculo absterritus est, quominus Regi omnique populo peccata i- psorum ob oculos poneret. Idem Spiritus ac virtus, i. e. fortitudo eadem in Johanne apparuit. Ob hanc ζήλη emi- nentiam Judæi animam Phineæ in Eliam venisse fabulan- tur. Sed a vetustioribus dictum puto fuisse, Eliam venis- se in Spiritu Phineæ, quomodo Johannem venturum in spiritu Eliæ dicit Angelus Luc. I. 17.

ὁ μέλλων ἔρχεσθαι] δεχόμενον, ut modo de Messia com- mate 3. aut μέλλων ἐρχέσθαι ut hoc loco, significat of- ficium certo Dei decreto præfinitum.

## 11:15
Vers. 15. ὁ ἔχων ὦτα ἀκούειν, ἀκουέτω] An epiphonema with which Christ, and John following him in the Apocalypse, very often close their pronouncements on matters of great importance. Luke explains it elsewhere thus: Lay these words to your ears. Such are found among the poets: It is worth the effort to hear, and hear and turn your minds to these things. For ears here and in other places are used by metaphor to signify the intellectual faculty, just as we also speak of the eyes of the mind. Hierocles, dealing with evil affections: But the one solution for these is that which is toward God

There was a turning point for those who find the eye of the soul and are hastening toward the acquisition of good things. Moreover, the matter about which Christ is speaking was most noteworthy, if only because the whole prophecy had ended in those very words, and it had given an indication of when it was to be restored after a long interval of time. But the Jews, just as they boasted most of all in the privilege of prophecy, so they bore its loss heavily.

PART III. The rebuke of the Jews, and especially of certain cities illustrious for miracles.

Latin:

Vers. 15. ὁ ἔχων ὦτα ἀκύειν, ἀκυέτω] ἐπιφώνημα quo Chri- stus & eum secutus in Apocalypsi Johannes sæpissime clau- dunt pronuntiata sua de rebus magni momenti. Lucas alibi ita explicat: Θέσθε ὑμεῖς τὰ ὦτα ὑμῶν τὸς λόγυς τόυτυς. Talia apud Poetas: Audire est operæ pretium & audite atque animis advertite vestris. Aures enim hic alusque locis per trans- lationem positæ sunt ad significandum intellectivam facul- tatem, quomodo & mentis oculos dicimus. Hierocles a- gens de malis affectionibus: Τούτων δὲ λύσις μία ἡ πρὸς θεὸν

ἐπιστροφὴ ἦν ἐξευρίσκουσιν οἱ τὸ ὄμμα τῆς ψυχῆς κὴ τὸ ἐς πρὸς τὴν τῶν ἀγαθῶν ἀνάληψιν ἐπειγόμεντες. Erat autem res de qua agit Christus maxime notanda, vel ideo quod tota Pro- phetia in illis ipsis verbis desierat, & quando post longi temporis intermissionem instauranda esset, indicium fece- rat. Judæi autem sicut Prophetiæ privilegio maxime glo- riabantur, ita ejus jacturam graviter ferebant.

PARS III. Increpatio Judæorum, & imprimis civitatum quarundam miraculis illustrium.

## 11:16
Ver. 16. To what shall I liken] A beginning familiar to the Jews when starting a parable, as appears both from the Talmudic books and from Mark IV. 30, Luke XIII. 18, 20.

Generation] A race of men circumscribed by a certain time and place: thus Cicero spoke of the iron race in Aratus: But we are taught that it is spoken properly of the Pharisees and lawyers in Luke VII. 30.

—is like to children] It must be noted once, because it occurs often, that the force of that dative is not to denote the term of comparison itself, which for the most part is contained not in that immediate word but in the whole following narrative. For Christ does not compare the Jews to that childish song sung in the marketplace, but rather that that song fits them so well. Thus below in XIII. 24 it is said that the kingdom of heaven is like a sower, although Christ does not compare the sower to the kingdom, but says that the matter of the kingdom of heaven is such, as if someone were sowing and then what follows happens. Thus also elsewhere the same kingdom is said to be like a king.

Latin:

Vers. 16. Τίνι δὲ ὁμοιώσω] Exordium familiare Judæis pa- rabolam inceptantibus, ut apparet tum ex Talmudicis li- bris, tum Marci IV. 30. Lucæ XIII. 18. 20.

Γενεὰν] Hominum genus certo tempore ac loco circum- scriptum: ita ferream prolem in Arateis dixit Cicero: Proprie autem de Pharisæis & Legisperitis agi docemur Luc. VII. 30.

— ὁμοία ἐστὶ παιδίοις] Semel notandum est, quia sæpe occur- rit, vim istius dativi non esse ut denotet ipsum comparatio- nis terminum, qui plerumq; non illa proxima voce sed tota insequenti narratione continetur Neq; enim Judæos Chri- stus comparat illud puerile carmen in foro cantantibus, sed potius carmen illud in ipsos ita quadrare. Sic infra XIII. 24. dicitur regnum cœlorum simile esse satori, cum tamen non satorem regno comparet Christus, sed rem regni cœlestis ita se habere dicat, quasi aliquis serat & deinde quæ sequuntur eveniant. Sic & alibi idem regnum dicitur regi esse simile.

## 11:17
V. 17. We have piped] Aemilius Probus wisely prefaces his lives of illustrious men by saying that it will seem trivial to many that it is commemorated in the virtues of Epaminondas that he danced well. But he replies that he expects this only from those who, being ignorant of Greek literature, think nothing is right unless it conforms to their own customs. He adds that such things are not honorable or shameful for everyone, but are judged according to the institutions of their ancestors. The customs of the Jews in this regard were closer to the Greeks than to the Romans. For it did not seem shameful to them to attest to public or private joys as much by dancing as by singing, to which I refer the customary games at victories, the mention of which is in Josephus, Antiquities XII. 12. Indeed, even today the Jews, both in sacred assemblies and at weddings, use certain movements that are quite unrestrained, the memory of the old harmony having long since been abolished among them. Although, however, a grave character most becomes Christians, and therefore I do not doubt that even in matters of this kind Roman customs pleased the ancients more than Jewish or even Greek ones, yet it is not unworthy of note that what was established in ancient Synods regarding this matter pertains not so much to mere dancing as to soft and mimic gesticulations.

We have mourned unto you and ye have not lamented.] To mourn is to make a dirge or sing a lament, as the professional mourners used to do among the Romans, at whose signal the lamentation was made. The writer On the World: 'Just as in a chorus, when the leader begins, the whole chorus echoes.' Thus in Euripides and Seneca, Hecuba leads the lament, the Trojan women follow, whose beating of breasts Seneca describes in these verses: 'Our right hand strikes our arms for you: It strikes your bloody shoulders for you: Our right hand beats our head for you.' We learn that a similar custom clearly prevailed among the Jews both from this passage and from Josephus, who in the third book of the Jewish War says that hired flute players led the dirges. Eustathius on the last book of the Iliad: 'The leaders of dirges are barbarian singers.' Moreover, there is a saying similar to ours which is reported from R. Papa in the Gemara: 'I wept for you, but you did not pay attention: I laughed for you, but you did not care: woe to you who do not distinguish between good and evil.'

Latin:

V. 17. ἠὐλήσαμεν] Sapienter præfatur Æmilius Probus ad vi- tas virorum illustrium leve multis visum iri quod in Epami- nondæ virtutibus commemoretur saltasse eum commode. Sed respondet hoc se ab iis denum exspectare, qui expertes Græcarum literarum nihil rectum nisi quod moribus ipso- rum conveniat putent. Addit talia non omnibus honesta esse atq; turpia, sed ex majorum institutis judicari. Judæo- rum hac in parte mores Græcis quam Romanis propiores fuere. Neq; enim turpe illis visum fuit publica aut privata gaudia tam saltatione quam cantu testari, quo refero τὰς συν- ήθεις ἐν τοῖς ἐπινικίοις παιδιὰς quarum mentio apud Jose- phum Originum XI!. 12. Quin hodieque Judæi tum in con- ventibus sacris, tum in nuptiis usurpant motus quosdam satis inconcitos, abolita pridem apud ipsos veteris harmo- niæ memoria. Quanquam autem Christianos maxime de- ceat gravis persona, ac proinde non dubitem etiam in reb9 ejusmodi Romanos mores præ Judaicis ac Græcis ipsis an- tiquitus placuisse, tamen non indignum notatu est quæ in Synodis antiquis ea de re constituta sunt, non tam ad mera tripudia, quam ad molles mimicasque gesticulationes per- tinere.

Ἐθρηνήσαμεν ὑμῖν κὴ οὐκ ἐκόψασθε.] θρηνεῖν est les- sum facere aut næniam canere, ut solebant apud Romanos præficæ, ad quarum κέλευσμα plangebatur. Scriptor de mundo: καθάπερ ἐν χορῷ κορυφαίου κατάρξαντος συνεπηχεῖ πᾶς ὁ χορός. Ita apud Euripidem & Senecam lessu præit Hecuba, sequuntur Troades, quarum planctum his versi- bus Seneca describit: Tibi nostra ferit dextra lacertos: Humerosque ferit tibi sanguineos: Tibi nostra caput dextera pulsat. Plane morem apud Judæos similem obtinuisse tum ex hoc loco discimus, tum ex Josepho, qui belli Judaici tertio, mer- cede conductos ait ἀυλητὰς οἳ θρήνων ἐξῆρχον. Eustathius ad I- liados ultimum: Βαρβαρικὸν δὲ τῶν θρηνῶν ἔξαρχοι ἀοιδοί. Est autem dictum huic nostro simile quod ex R. Papa in Gema- ra refertur: Ploravi tibi, sed animum non advertisti: risi tibi, sed non curasti: væ tibi qui bonum malumq; non internoscis.

## 11:19
Ver. 19. Glutton] A reveller, a diner-out.

Wine-bibber] A heavy drinker. For in Hebrew it is said not of anyone who drinks wine, but of one who indulges in wine: as in Psalm LXIX. 13, Amos V. 1, 6, Prov. XXXI. 4.

But that 'we have piped,' thus Ludov. de Dieu: What our Savior reproaches the Jews with here in this elegant proverb is the very thing that Solomon says in Prov. XIX. 9: 'A wise man disputes with a fool, and is angry and laughs, and there is no rest.' That is, when a wise and good man has to do with a foolish and wicked man, he attempts to correct him in every way, now he is indignant, now he laughs, now he treats him rigidly, then gently; and yet he cannot cause him to rest and abstain from evil. On which passage of Solomon a commentary exists in the Gemara Sanhedrin chap. XI, which it seemed good to transcribe here, because it contains that very proverb which our Savior uses here. It is thus: God says, I was angry with Ahab and delivered him into the hands of the kings of Damascus.

But he sacrificed and offered incense to their gods. This is what is said in 2 Chron. XXVIII. 23, 'And he sacrificed to the gods of Damascus, which smote him, and said, The gods of the kings of Syria help them, I will sacrifice to them that they may help me, and they were the ruin of him and of all Israel.' But I played with Amaziah, and I gave the kings of Edom into his hand. But he brought their gods, and worshipped them. As it is said in 2 Chron. XXV. 14, 'And it came to pass after that Amaziah was come from the slaughter of the Edomites, that he brought the gods of the children of Seir, and set them up to be his gods, etc.' R. Papa says: This is what the common people say, 'I wept for a man, but he did not acknowledge it: I laughed for a man, but he did not acknowledge it. Woe to the man who does not discern between good and evil.'

And Wisdom is justified by her children.] It is true what the man who has deserved very well of very many passages warns, that κὶ here is taken for ἀλλὰ, indeed by the example of the Hebrews among whom it is very often placed thus. But also the most eloquent Theophrastus has said κὶ sometimes for consensus. I think, however, that what follows is a Jewish proverb, but accommodated to the present purpose. ἡ σοφία here is nothing other than what in Luke 7:30 is βουλὴ τοῦ Θεοῦ, the most wise counsel of God, namely, of recalling the Jews to repentance by both the severity of John and the gentleness of Christ, so that he might leave nothing unexpected and also so that they might have nothing to complain of. Many were pleased with themselves by the austerity of life; in this very thing John preceded them much. Others sought popularity: no one was ever more popular than Christ. Again, John as a herald of repentance was composed for severity, Luke 1:15, Matthew 3:4. Christ was gentle as a bestower of pardon. The former was commended by a rare and inimitable manner of living: the latter by the greatest power of miracles. Δικαιοῦν here, as in Psalm 51:6 and Romans 3:4 and among Greek writers, does not lack example. Thucydides said thus: ἀπὸ πολέμου ἐφθάρησαν. Nor did the Syrian render it otherwise here, who also rendered τέκνων αὐτῆς as עבדוהי, that is, his servants, not inappropriately. But the children or servants of wisdom are not to be understood as those who were already wise, as some think, but rather those who were held by a certain pious reverence for divine wisdom, such as were the publicans and some of the common people in the time of John and Christ, Luke 7:29, 30. In a similar way Luke 9:6 said ὑὸν εἰρήνης. Christ added this, however, so that it might be understood that the work of both John and himself had not been entirely sterile until then.

This Grotian explanation is added to the interpretation of those who likewise take it concerning the justification of approval, but do not understand it through τὴν σοφίαν as that counsel of God concerning recalling the Jews to repentance by the severity of John and the gentleness of Christ—which gloss is peculiar to Grotius—but explain it either concerning Christ, the hypostatic Wisdom of God, or concerning the doctrine and Gospel of Christ, which is the Wisdom of God, 1 Corinthians 1:24. Certainly, the wisdom of God is nowhere taken in that Grotian sense concerning that counsel of God: nor in Luke 7:30. βουλὴ τοῦ Θεοῦ has that sense, but it designates the counsel of God concerning salvation and its causes and means, not concerning a process in the recall to repentance; nor was this a new counsel, or one prescribed for those times, but in time God invited the Israelites to repentance now through the severity of the law and threatening, now through the sweetness of the Gospel and promise, and the servants of the Lord, the prophets, showed themselves now austere, now gentle, as reason and the direction of the Spirit dictated. Whence the gloss of Grotius is not to be rashly embraced, to which the paraphrase of Calixtus is a twin: Thus indeed many behaved themselves against John and Christ, and in that way in which it was said, but wisdom, i.e., the most wise counsel of God concerning attracting men to repentance and salvation by this way and that, has been justified, i.e., acknowledged and proclaimed by its children, or disciples of wisdom seeking and magnifying it. Nor does Grotius correctly explain the children of wisdom, for they were not held only by a certain reverence for divine wisdom, but the faithful were already truly wise, as those who adhered to Christ through faith and through faith obtained the remission of sins, which is true wisdom of the children of God, which John also ought to confer, Luke 1:76. Justification itself, or the approval of wisdom, is an argument that they were truly wise, not merely led by a certain reverence for wisdom, because no one justifies or approves unless he understands it; nor indeed did John or Christ propose heavenly doctrine obscurely, such that those attending to it could not understand the same. Most orthodox scholars more correctly understand by the voice of Wisdom the hypostatic Wisdom, the Son of God, or at least the wisdom of God in our justification through Christ: and by the children of wisdom or its hearers, who ought to receive his voice reverently, as children the admonitions of their Parents, Prov. 4:1 seqq. even if they are degenerate children Deut. 32:5, Isa. 1:4, or those whom he begat for himself through the word, whose [children] justified, that is, condemned wisdom, as Luther explains in Tom. 4 Lat. Jena, f. 320, and the German version aims at this, as do Osiander, and B. Aegidius Hunnius, B. Gerhard here, and Brentius in the Confessio Württembergica, as well as Scultetus. But these justified the same by approving and celebrating it: just as Chrysostom, Hilary, Jerome, Augustine, Theophylact, Euthymius interpret: Beza, Piscator, Tossanus, Thomas Gadaker; B. Quistorpius, Glassius in Gram. S. p. 605, Tarnov. in Exercit. Bibl. p. 147, and most Papists. We have embraced this sense in the Parascëve Anti-Crell. p. 87 seqq., and it is favored by 1. The appellation of the children of Christ, and of God, which properly befits the faithful; for these are τέκνα Σοφίας and children of Christ by reason of his doctrine, which they hear, and by reason of faith, by which they receive Christ, John 1:12, but nowhere are those who reject the wisdom of God or Christ called children of wisdom, or of Christ. 2. The word of justification: For this is constantly taken in a good sense, never in a worse one: whether it be applied in respect to God concerning our absolution from sins, Matt. 12:37, Luke 7:29, Acts 13:38, 39, Rom. 2:13, ch. 3:20, 26, 28, 30, ch. 4:5, ch. 5:1, 9, ch. 8:30, 1 Cor. 4:4, ch. 6:11, Gal. 2:16, 17, ch. 3:24, ch. 5:4, Tit. 3:7, or in respect to us, or others, when we absolve ourselves and hold ourselves as just, Luke 10:29, ch. 16:15, or when our justice is made manifest to others, who acknowledge and celebrate us as just, James 2:21, 24, 25. In which manner God also is said to be justified, when his justice, goodness, and faithfulness are made manifest, acknowledged, and celebrated, Rom. 3:4, Psalm 51:6, and Christ is said to be justified by the Spirit, 1 Tim. 3:16, that is, acknowledged and declared just and perfect through miracles done by the divine power of the Spirit. Thus also in the present passage the wisdom of God is justified, that is, it is acknowledged, declared, and celebrated as just. As B. Luther writes in the marginal notes: The Holy Spirit praises Christ in the Gospel and faith, whom otherwise all the people condemned and blasphemed. 3. The antecedents: which teach that an antithesis is instituted here, and therefore the particle καὶ is to be taken in an adversative sense, which is not infrequent. See Matt. 1:25, ch. 12:26, 39, ch. 13:22, John 5:40, Acts 10:28, 1 Cor. 5:10, 1 Thess. 2:18, Heb. 10:38, 1 John 2:20, just as the Hebrew Vav is accustomed to be taken, see Gen. 3:3, ch. 30:30, ch. 42:10, Exod. 14:8, Ps. 1:6, Ps. 2:6, 10, Ps. 4:4, Isa. 9:9, 10, ch. 29:3, ch. 53:5, Mal. 1:3. For Christ wishes to say this: Wisdom of God, the Pharisees rebuke me, but yet I am absolved, or I obtain testimony of justice from all my children: so that an opposition is made between the Pharisees rebuking Christ the Wisdom of God on one side, and all those who justify or absolve and celebrate Christ, and offer him testimony of justice, as his genuine children, on the other side. 4. The use of the universal particle: for it is said to be justified by all its children in Luke ch. 7:35, which certainly cannot be understood of reprobation. For not all his hearers rejected him. 5. The comparison of those things which preceded in Luke: All the people hearing, and the publicans, ἐδικαίωσαν τὸν θεὸν, justified God, having been baptized with the baptism of John, but the Pharisees and Lawyers rejected the counsel of God against themselves, not having been baptized by him. For as here the Pharisees and the whole people are opposed to one another, who rejected the counsel of God, and who justified God, so in our passage the Pharisees are noted as mockers, and all the children of wisdom are opposed to them, as those who justify wisdom. Let the persons, the predicates, the opposition, the connection, and the words themselves be considered accurately on both sides, and the sense which we have indicated will reveal itself clearly.

Latin:

Vers. 19. Φάγος] Comessator, cœnipeta.

οἰνοπότης] Bibaculus. Nam Hebræis שותה שכר aut שותה יין dicitur non quivis vinum bibens, sed qui vino indulget: ut Psal. LXIX. 13. Amos V. 1. 6. Prov. XXXI. 4.

At illa ἡυλήσαμεν ita Ludov. de Dieu: Quod Servator noster eleganti hoc proverbio Judæis hic ex- probrat, id ipsum est quod Salomon Prov. XIX. 9. di- cit: Vir sapiens disputat cum stulto, & irascitur & ridet, neq; est quies. Id est, quum viro sapienti ac probo res est cum stulto & improbo, quovis modo cor- rigere eum tentat, nunc indignatur, nunc ridet, jam rigide, deinde blande eum tractat; nec tamen efficere potest, ut à malo quiescat & obstineat. In quem Sa- lomonis locum commentarius exstat in Gemara San- hedrim cap. XI. quem hic adscribere visum est, quia ipsum illud proverbium continet, quo hic Servator noster utitur. Sic habet: Dicit Deus, succensui Achabo & tradidi eum in manus regum Damasci.

Ille vero facrificavit & fuffitum fecit Diis ipforum. Hoc est, quod dicitur 2. Chron. XXIII. 23. & sacri- ficavit Diis Damasci, qui cæciderant eum, ac di- xit, Dii regum Syriæ auxiliantur ipsis, iis sacrifi- cabo ut juvent me, fueruntque offendiculo ipsi & toti Israëli. Lusi autem cum Amasia, & dedi re- ges Edom in manum ejus. At ille deos eorum addu- -xit, eosque adoravit. Sicut dicitur 2. Chr. XXV. 14. Et fuit postquam venisset Amasia à cæde Edomæ- orum, adduxit Deos filiorum Seir, & constituit eos & sibi in Deos, &c. Ait R. Papa: Hoc est quod dicit vulgus, Flevi viro, at non agnovit: risi viro, at non agnovit. Væ viro qui non discernit inter bonum & malum.

κὶ ἐδικαιώθη ἡ Cοφία ἀπὸ τῶν τέκνων αὐτῆς.] Verum est quod monet vir de plurimis locis optime meritus, κὶ hîc sumi pro ἀλλὰ, nimirum Hebræorum exemplo apud quos sæpissime ita ponitur. Sed & ὁ ἀπλικώτατος Theophrastus κὶ aliquo- ties consensu dixit. Puto autem quod sequitur proverbium esse judaicum, sed præsenti instituto accommodatum. ἡ σο- φία hîc nihil aliud est, quam quod apud Lucam VII. 30. βουλὴ τοῦ Θεοῦ sapientissimum nimirum Dei consilium Ju- dæos & Johannis severitate, & Christi comitate ad pœni- tentiam revocantis, ne quid inexpectatum relinqueret at- que etiam ne quid illi causari possent. Placebant sibi multi vitæ austeritate, hac ipsa in re multum illos Johannes ante- cessit. Alii popularitatem requirebant: Christo nemo un- quam fuit popularior. Rursum Johannes ut pœnitentiæ præco ad severitatem compositus, Luc. I. 15. Matth. III. 4. Christus comis ut veniæ largitor. Illum rara neque imita- bilis vivendi ratio: hunc miraculorum vis maxima com- mendabat. Δικαιοῦν hîc ut in Psalmo LI. 6. & Rom. III. 4. & apud Græcos scriptores non caret exemplo. Thucydides i- ta dixit: ἀπὸ πολέμου ἐφθάρησαν. Neque aliter hic reddidit Syrus, qui & τέκνων αὐτῆς עבדוהי, id est, cultores ejus, non incommode. Filii autem sive cultores sapientiæ non sunt intelligendi, qui jam tum sapiebant, ut quidam pu- tant, sed illi potius, qui pia quadam divinæ sapientiæ re- verentia tenebantur, quales Johannis & Christi tempore erant publicani & de plebe aliqui Luc. VII. 29. 30. simili modo ὑὸν εἰρήνης dixit Lucas X. 6. Hoc autem ideo Christus addidit, ut intelligeretur non omnino sterilem hactenus fuisse operam tum Joannis tum suam.

Accedit hæc Grotiana explicatio eorum inter- pretationi, qui de justificatione approbationis iti- dem accipiunt, non autem per τὴν σοφίαν, consi- lium illud Dei de Judæis Johannis severitate & Chri- sti comitate ad pœnitentiam revocandis, quæ glossa Grotio propria est, intelligunt, sed vel de Christo hypostatica Dei sapientia, vel de doctrina, & Ev- angelio Christi, quod est Sapientia Dei 1. Cor. II. 6. eam explicant. Nuspiam certe ita sapientia Dei de consilio illo Dei sensu Grotiano, accipitur: neque Luc. VII. 30. βουλὴ τοῦ Θεοῦ eum sensum habet, sed consilium Dei de salute, ejusque causis, & mediis, non de processu in revocatione ad pœnitentiam di- verso designat: nec novum hoc erat, aut tempori- bus illis præscriptum consilium, sed in tempore Deus modo per severitatem legis & comminatio- nem, modo per suavitatem Evangelii, & promis- sionem, invitabat Israëlitas ad pœnitentiam, & jam austeros, jam comes se præbebant servi Domini Prophetæ, uti ferebat ratio & Spiritus directio. Unde temere non amplectenda Grotii glossa, cui gemella est Calixti paraphrasis: Ita quidem plerique adversus Johannem & Christum, eoque quo dictum fuit modo se gesserunt, sed sapientia h. e. sapientissi- mum Dei consilium de hominibus cum hac, tum il- la via ad resipiscentiam & salutem alliciendis, justi- ficatum est, h. e. agnitum & prædicatum est à filiis suis, sive discipulis sapientiæ eam quærentibus & ma- gnifacientibus. Neque filios sapientiæ recte expli- cat Grotius, nam non tenebantur solum qua- dam divinæ sapientiæ reverentia, sed revera jam tum sapiebant fideles, utpote qui per fidem Christo adhærebant, & per fidem remissionem peccato- rum consequebantur, quæ vera est sapientia filio- rum Dei, quam conferre etiam Johannes debuit, Luc. I. 76. Ipsa justificatio, vel approbatio sapien- tiæ argumentum est, vere eos sapuisse, non tan- tum reverentia quadam sapientiæ ductos fuisse, quia non justificat, vel approbat quis nisi id intel- ligat; neque sane obscure vel Johannes, vel Chri- stus doctrinam cœlestem proponebat, quin ean- dem intelligere possent eidem attendentes. Re- ctius per vocem Sapientiæ plerique orthodoxi Sa- pientiam hypostaticam, Filium Dei intelligunt, aut certe sapientiam Dei in nostri justificatione per Christum: & per filios sapientiæ seu auditores ejus, qui debebant vocem ejus reverenter suscipere, ut filii Parentum monita, Prov. IV. 1. seqq. etsi degene- res sint filii Deut. XXXII. 5. Es. I. 4. seu illos, quos sibi per verbum genuit, quorum illi justificarunt, hoc est, condemnarunt sapientiam, ut explicat Lutherus Tom. IV. Lat. Jen. f. 320. eoque collimat versio Germanica, nec non Osiander, & B. Ægydius Hunnius, B. Gerhardus hic, & Brentius in Con- fess. Würtenb. ut & Scultetus. Hi vero justifica- runt eandem approbando & celebrando: quemad- modum interpretantur Chrysostomus, Hilarius, Hieronymus, Augustinus, Theophylactus, Euthy- mius: Beza, Piscator, Tossanus, Thomas Gadake- rus; B. Quistorpius, Glassius in Gram. S. p. 605. Tarnov. in Exercit. Bibl. p. 147. & plerique Pontifi- cii. Quem sensum amplexi sumus in Parascëve Anti-Crell. p. 87. seqq. eique favent 1. Appellatio filiorum Christi, & Dei, quæ proprie fidelibus con- venit; hi enim τέκνα Σοφίας & filii Christi sunt ratione doctrinæ ejus, quam audiunt, & ratione fi- dei, qua recipiunt Christum, Joh. I. 12. nuspiam vero illi qui reprobant sapientiam Dei vel Chri- stum, filii sapientiæ dicuntur, aut Christi. 2. Ver- bum justificationis: Hoc enim constanter sumi- tur in bonam partem, nunquam in sequiorem: sive adhibeatur ratione Dei de nostra à peccatis abso- lutione Matth. XII. 37. Luc. XIIIX. 14. Act. XIII. 38. 39. Rom. II. 13. cap. III. 20. 26. 28. 30. cap. IV. 5. c. V. 1. 9. cap. IIX. 30. 1. Cor. IV. 4. cap. VI. 11. Gal. II. 16. 17. cap. III. 24. cap. V. 4. Tit. III. 7. sive ratione no- stri, aut aliorum, cum nosmetipsos absolvimus, & pro justis habemus Luc. X. 29. cap. XVI. 15. vel cum aliis justitia nostra patescit, qui nos justos agno- scunt & celebrant Jac. II. 21. 24. 25. Quo pacto etiam Deus justificari dicitur, quando justitia, bonitas, fidesque ejus patescit, agnoscitur & cele- bratur, Rom. III. 4. Psalm. L. 6. & Christus dici- tur justificatus Spiritu 1. Tim. III. 16. h. e. justus & perfectus, agnitus & declaratus per miracula divina virtute Spiritus facta. Sic & in præsenti loco ju- stificata est sapientia Dei h. e. justa agnita, decla- rata & celebrata est. Quomodo B. Luther. in no- tis margin. scribit; Der H. Geist preiset Christum im Evangelio und Glauben/welchen sonst alles Volck verdammte und lästerte. 3. Anteceden- tia: quæ docent hic ἀντίθεσιν institui, adeoque particulam καὶ sensu adversativo, accipiendam esse, qui non infrequens est. Vid. Matth. I. 25. cap. XII. 26. 39. cap. XIII. 22. Joh. V. 40. Actor. X. 28. 1. Cor. V. 10. 1. Thess. II. 18. Ebr. X. 38. 1. Joh. II. 20. quemadmodum & Vav Ebræorum accipi consuevit, Vid. Genes. III. 3. cap. XXX. 30. cap. XLII. 10. Exod. XIV. 8. Psal. I. 6. Psal. II. 6. 10. Psal. IV. 4. Es. IX. 9. 10. cap. XXIX. 3. cap. LIII. 5. Mal. I. 3. Id enim vult dicere Christus Sapien- tia Dei, Pharisæi me reprehendunt, sed tamen ab- solvor seu justitia testimonium consequor ab omni- bus filiis meis: ut oppositio fiat Pharisæorum reprehendentium Christum Sapientiam Dei ab una, & omnium eorum, qui justificant seu absol- vunt, celebrantque Christum, ac testimonium justitiæ ei præbent, ut genuini ipsius filii, ab alte- ra parte. 4. Particulæ universalis usus: justificari enim dicitur ab omnibus filiis suis Lucæ cap. VII, 35. quod certe intelligi non potest de reprobatio- ne. Nec enim omnes ejus auditores ipsum re- probarunt. 5. Collatio eorum, quæ apud Lu- cam præcesserunt: Omnis populus audiens, & publicani ἐδικαίωσαν τ θεὸν justificârunt Deum ba- ptizati baptismo Johannis, Pharisæi vero & Legis- periti Dei ἠθέτησαν rejecerunt adversus semetipsos, non baptizati ab eo. Nam ut hic sibi opponun- tur Pharisæi, & totus populus, qui rejecerunt con- silium Dei, & qui justificârunt Deum, ita in no- stro loco Pharisæi notantur ceu empæctæ, & op- ponuntur iis omnes filii sapientiæ, ut qui justifi- cans sapientiam. Considerentur accurate perso- næ, prædicata, oppositio, connexio, verba eadem u- trobique, & prodet sese γυμνῆ κεφαλῆ sensus, quem indicavimus.

## 11:20
Verse 20. ὀνειδίζειν τὰς πόλεις] Thus Plato ὀνειδίζειν ἵνα ἴκατω.

Latin:

Vers. 20. ὀνειδίζειν τὰς πόλεις] Ita Plato ὀνειδίζειν ἵνα ἴ- κατω.

## 11:21
Verse 21. εἰ ἐν Τύρῳ κὴ Σιδῶνι ἐγένοντο αἱ δυνάμεις] There is undoubtedly a great power in miracles for striking into men a reverence for the divine majesty, and for sealing promises and threats. If miracles, joined with those aids which are wont to accompany miracles, were not effective for correcting minds, Christ would not say that a peculiar and signal guilt is contracted by the contempt of such benefits. See John 15:24. Nor do the words of Abraham to the rich man in the parable, saying: If they do not listen to Moses and the Prophets, neither will they be persuaded if someone should rise from the dead, stand against this opinion, Luke 16:31. For he speaks of those who, while they were not ignorant that the law of Moses was confirmed by great miracles, nevertheless instituted a life which they knew to be directly contrary to the law of Moses. For such men showed by this very fact that they were so delighted by their vices that they would not wish to strip them off by any reverence for miracles. But the case is far different, both for those to whom the Law of Moses did not pertain, and for those to whom other things were announced than what they knew with sufficient certainty to be contained in the law of Moses. Christ deals here with both these kinds of men. Add what we shall say concerning Luke.

Πάλαι ἂν ἐν ζάκκῳ κὴ σποδῷ μετενόησαν] I refer that 'long ago' to ancient times, as at the beginning of the Epistle to the Hebrews. I think, however, that those times are designated in which Ezekiel lived, who gravely warned the Tyrians and Sidonians concerning their sins and the impending divine vengeance. Christ therefore says that if at that time they had received such and so great miracles at those sermons of Ezekiel, as Christ had performed in the Galilean cities, they would have done what the Ninevites did of old, namely, they would have performed penance for their transgressions, even with the greatest demonstration of mourning. Hence he gathers how great is the guilt of those who, warned by such great signs, had not received his divine and saving doctrine. These terms σάκκῳ & σποδὸς are joined also in Isaiah 58:5, Jeremiah 6:26, Daniel 9:3, and in the history of Judith 4:8. Nor is it true that 'saccus' signifies the same thing to the Hebrews as it does to the Latins, although I do not deny that there is something similar in both meanings. For in Latin it signifies a receptacle for either money or grain or some other thing; but to the Hebrews, haircloth, as the old Latin interpreter rightly translated in several places. That haircloths are one thing and sacks another appears also from the third Verrine oration, where we read of haircloths and sacks ordered from the cities. But the Hellenists used the Hebrew word in the Hebrew sense even in the Greek language, whom Josephus also follows, as in Antiquities book 20, chapter 5: 'Having put on sacks, having sprinkled their heads with ashes.' He himself elsewhere, where there is שק in the Hebrew, has placed now 'humble attire,' now 'mourning garment.' Indeed, other Greek writers also: Plutarch on superstition: 'He sits outside having a small sack, rolling in the mud.' Menander had said of the Syrians: 'Then they took a sack, and sat themselves in the road on dung.' The Christians also began to do the same, not only in Greek, but also in Latin. Thus in Tertullian we read of prayers made in sackcloth and ashes on account of the drought of the year. By the name of ashes, however, the Hebrews understand all filth. And so in Job 2:8, where in the Hebrew it is 'in ashes,' the Greeks have placed 'on the dunghill,' and the Latin 'in the dunghill.' Although however, the hardness of the Tyrians and Sidonians in the time of Ezekiel was not that which was of a great part of the Galileans in the age of Christ, this nevertheless does not free the Tyrians from blame. For the law inscribed on their minds sufficiently condemned them, demanding equity in commerce and mercy toward those whose affairs were afflicted: whereas they, on the contrary, mixed force and deceit with their trade, and from the sole hope of deriving gain for themselves, cruelly insulted the Jews, their old friends and allies, already conquered and prostrated by the Chaldean: all of which and other things besides can be seen in the Prophet. But Homer also bore witness against them: 'Then came a Phoenician man, skilled in deceit, a glutton, who indeed did many evils to men.' A glutton, that is, greedy, says Eustathius. To this points that which is in Philostratus' dialogue to the Phoenician: 'You have slandered trade as being money-loving and gluttonous.' To this was added that such great proximity of the Jews, a common language, and daily commerce did not allow them to be ignorant of the most certain arguments of the worship owed to the one God: especially when the Prophets sent by the same God addressed them by name, either by voice or by letters, quite often. These things, therefore, and others could either amend the Phoenicians if they wished, or if they did not wish, could convict them of contumacy: even if those miracles, so many and so great, which were reserved for the times of the Messiah by the most wise counsel of God, did not happen to them. It is our duty to receive with a grateful hand the gifts which God bestows, not to prescribe to Him what and how great He ought to give. But what Christ complains of here, God also complained of long ago, that if He had bestowed upon those peoples, whom the Jews despised as wild and barbarian, the effort which He bestowed upon the Jews, He would have accomplished somewhat more. Ezek. II, 16. Showing at the same time His unmerited kindness toward the Jews, the evil offspring of good parents, and paving the way for demonstrating His justice in that most abundant calling of the profane nations which was to come through Christ, of which grace those very Tyrians and Sidonians, so despised by the Jews, were partakers, and not without fruit, as appears in Acts XXI and XXVII. Although indeed there is no doubt for me that there was in Christ certain knowledge concerning those things which, a condition being posited, were about to happen, or had been, yet since those whom He was addressing at that time did not attribute so much to Christ, I think it better to explain these, like other sayings of Christ, popularly, so that He said what, by human judgment, things being well weighed, was quite probable. Looking to which, as it seems, the Latin interpreter translated what follows next, ἔμειναν ἂν, as 'perhaps they would have remained'.

But why would that be better? Did not the Son of God explain the rays of divine Majesty in His sermons just as much as in His miracles, even if the hearers did not perceive them, or did not attribute as much to Him as was proper? Nor indeed does Christ speak only doubtfully, but assertively, bearing an infallible judgment concerning them. Which strikes the hearers more than if He had added that 'perhaps,' which is rather excluded by the particle ἂν. For this signifies 'certainly' or 'indeed,' as the Arabic interpreter rendered it. For Christ teaches that that grace, which would have truly converted the Sidonians, was exhibited to the Chorazinites and neglected by them, and that this is the cause of their damnation and of a more severe judgment. Compare what the blessed Joh. Ernest. Gerhard has on this passage, and the Exercitations of Dr. D. Scherzer on Matt. XI. 21, who refuted the various exceptions of the Calvinists here, of Voetius, Spanheim, Arnold, and Maresius, §. 49 seqq. Gomarus' refuge, that the repentance of the Tyrians, the condition of those miracles being posited, would have been future, is to be understood as common to the elect and the reprobate, such as that of the Ninevites was: But Scripture is ignorant of such a common repentance of the faithful and the unfaithful, nor does Christ speak of it here, but of the true repentance of the faithful: nor is the repentance of the Ninevites to be held as common, but true, and such as is that of the faithful, as is clear from Matt. XII. 41. And Christ certainly required a saving repentance in these cities: and therefore He indicated that the same would have been in the Tyrians. Whence Episcopius, Tom. II. Oper. f. 63: 'Would not,' he says, 'the external repentance being posited, the same reason for rebuking the Tyrians and Sidonians have still remained, that they had not repented?' and consequently the same reason for redoubling the woe to the Tyrians and Sidonians, just as had been done to the Chorazinites and Bethsaidites? Certainly: and what then will be the force of this exclamation, 'Woe to you, Chorazin and Bethsaida, woe to you'? For it could be retorted, 'And woe to the Tyrians and Sidonians, if they repent only externally.' That is truly worthy of admiration, that some are sometimes carried away so far in the interpretation of the Scriptures, in order to defend and maintain their thesis, that they seize upon that which was brought in to increase the splendor of some thing, as in this place of repentance, no differently than if it had been produced to diminish it.

Latin:

Vers. 21. εἰ ἐν Τύρῳ κὴ Σιδῶνι ἐγένοντο αἱ δυνάμεις] Mira culorum haud dubie magna vis est ad incutiendam homi- nibus divini numinis reverentiam, & ad obsignandas promissiones ac minas. Quod nisi miracula conjuncta cum iis adminiculis quæ miracula comitari solent ad cor- rigendos animos valerent, non diceret Christus peculiarem atque insignem culpam talium beneficiorum contemtu contrahi. Vide Joh. XV. 24. Nec obstant huic sententiæ verba Abrahami ad Epulonem in parabola dicentis: Si Mosi & Prophetis non auscultant, nec siquis mortuorum re- surrexerit, persuadebuntur. Luc. XVI. 31. De iis enim loqui- tur, qui cum non ignorarent legem Mosis magnis miracu- lis esse comprobatam, tamen vitam institueient quam sci- rent legi Mosis directe adversari. Tales enim homines hoc ipso ostendebant ita se vitiis suis delectari, ut nulla miraculorum reverentia ea vellent exuere. Longe au- tem alia est ratio, tum eorum ad quos Lex Mosis non per- tinebat, tum eorum quibus alia annuntiabantur quam quæ satis certo scirent Mosis lege comprehendi. De u- troque hoc hominum genere hic agit Christus. Adde quæ ad Lucam dicemus.

Πάλαι ἂν ἐν ζάκκῳ κὴ σποδῷ μετενόησαν] πάλαι illud ad vetusta tempora refero, ut initio ad Hebræos. Puto au- tem designari ea tempora, quibus vixit Ezechiel, qui Tyrios & Sidonios de peccatis ipsorum & imminente di- vina ultione graviter admonuit. Dicit igitur Christus si eo tempore ad illas Ezechielis conciones miracula talia ac tanta accepissent, qualia Christus in Galilæis urbibus ediderat, facturos illos fuisse, quod olim Ninivitæ, pœ- nitentiam nimirum acturos delictorum, etiam cum ma- xima luctus testatione. Hinc colligit quanta sit illo- rum culpa, qui suam divinam ac salutarem doctrinam tantis signis admoniti non recepissent. Conjunguntur hæc σάκκ& & σποδὸς etiam apud Esaiam LIIX. 5. Jer. VI. 26. Dan. IX. 3. & in Judithæ historia IV. 8. Neque verum est, Hebræis saccum idem significare quod Latinis, quan- quam esse aliquid simile in utroque significatu non nego. Nam latinis receptaculum significat aut pecuniæ aut fru- menti aut alterius rei: Hebræis autem cilicium, ut recte transtulit aliquot in locis vetus Latinus interpres. Aliud autem esse cilicia, aliud saccos, etiam ex tertia Verrina apparet, ubi legimus imperata civitatibus cilicia & saccos. Sed Hellenistæ Hebræam vocem sensu Hebraico usurpa- runt etiam in Græco sermone, quos & Josephus sequitur, ut Orig. XX. cap. 5. Μετειδυσαμένοι ζάκκους, σποδῶ τὰς κε- φαλὰς ἀναπαλήσαντες. Qui ipse alibi, ubi in Hebræo est שק, posuit nunc σχῆμα ταπεινὸν, nunc πενθικὴν ἐσθῆτα. Imo & Græci Scriptores alii: Plutarchus de superstitione: ἔξω κάθηται σακκίον ἔχων ἐν πηλῷ καλινδόμενο. Menan- der de Syris dixerat: εἶτα ζακκίον ἔλαβον, εἰς δ' ὁδὸν Ἐκάθισαν αὐτοὶ ἐπὶ κοπρῶ. Idem & Christiani facere cœperunt, nec in Græco tan- tum, sed & in Latino. Ita in Tertulliano legimus pre- ces in sacco & cinere factas ob anni siccitatem. Cine- ris autem nomine Hebræi sordes omnes intelligunt. Itaque Jobi II. 8. ubi in Hebræo est, in cinere, Græci po- suerunt ἐπὶ τῆς κοπρίας, & Latinus in sterquilinio. Quan- quam autem non ea fuerit Tyriorum & Sidoniorum durities Ezechielis tempore, quæ fuit magnæ partis Ga- lilæorum ætate Christi, id tamen Tyrios à culpa non li- berat. Satis enim damnabat ipsos lex inscripta menti- bus, æquitatem in commerciis exigens, & misericor- diam adversus eos quorum res erant afflictæ : cum illi contra vim dolumque miscerent mercimoniis, & sola spe derivandi ad se quæstus, Judæis, amicis veteribus ac fœ- deratis suis, à Chaldæo victis jam atque prostratis cru- deliter insultarent: quæ omnia atque alia insuper videre est apud Prophetam. Sed & Homerus adversus eos te- stimonium dixit: Δὴ τότε Φοῖνιξ ἦλθεν ἀνὴρ ἀπατήλια εἰδὼς, Τρώκτης, ὃς δὴ πολλὰ κάκ’ ἀνθρώποισιν ἐώργει. Τρώκτης, id est, κερδαλέος, ait Eustathius. Huc spectat illud in Philostrati dialogo ad Phœnicem: τὰς ἐμπορίας δια- βέβλησθε ὡς φιλοχρήματοί τε κὶ τρῶκται. His accedebat quod tanta Judæorum propinquitas, communis lingua, quotidiana commercia, non patiebantur eos ignorare certissima argumenta cultus uni Deo debiti: præsertim cum ab eodem Deo missi Prophetæ ipsos nominatim aut voxe aut literis sæpius compellarent. Hæc igitur atque al a Phœnicas aut emendare si vellent, aut si nollent, contumaciæ convincere poterant: etiamsi miracula illa tot ac tanta, quæ sapientissimo Dei consilio Messiæ tem- poribus asservabantur, ipsis non contingerent. Nostrum est grata manu accipere dona quæ Deus largitur, non quæ ac quanta dare debeat ipsi præscribere. Quod au- tem hic Christus conqueritur, idem & olim conquestus est Deus, si eam quam Judæis impendebat operam, im- pendisset iis populis, quos Judæi ut feros ac barbaros contemnebant, aliquanto plus se profecturum fuisse Ezech. II, 16. Ostendens simul immeritam suam bonitatem erga Judæos, bonorum parentum malam progeniem, viamque sternens demonstrandæ justitiæ suæ in uberrima illa quæ per Christum ventura erat gentium profanarum vocatione, cujus gratiæ ipsi illi adeò despecti Judæis Tyrii & Sidonii participes fuére, nec sine fructu ut apparet A- ctor. XXI. & XXVII. Quanquam vero non dubium mihi est, fuisse in Christo certam cognitionem de rebus iis quæ posita aliqua conditione eventuræ erant, aut fuerant, tamen cum hi quos alloquebatur eo tempore, tantum Christo non tribuerint, satius arbitror hæc, ut alia Christi dicta, exponere populariter, ut dixerit, quod humano ju- dicio rebus bene expensis admodum erat probabile. Quo respiciens, ut videtur, Latinus interpres, quod mox se- quitur ἔμειναν ἂν vertit forte mansissent.

Cur vero id satius esset? Annon radios divinæ Majestatis in concionibus æque ac miraculis ex- plicuit Filius Dei, etsi auditores non perceperint, aut tantum ei non tribuerint, quantum par erat. Neque vero dubitative tantum loquitur Chri- stus, sed assertive, infallibile de illis judicium ferens. Quod magis percellit auditores, quam si illud fortassis adhibuisset, quod excluditur po- tius per particulam ἂν. Hæc enim utique vel profecto significat, uti interpres Arabs reddi- dit. Docet enim Christus eam gratiam, quæ Sidonios revera convertisset, Chorazitis exhibi- tam & ab iis neglectam fuisse, eamque causam esse damnationis, & judicii eorum severioris. Confer quæ habet B. Joh. Ernest. Gerhard. in h. l. & Dn. D. Scherzeri Exercitat. ad Matth. XI. 21. qui Calvinianorum varias exceptiones hic retudit, Voëtii, Spanhemii, Arnoldi, Maresii, §. 49. seqq. Gomari κρησφύγετον, quod Tyriorum pœ- nitentia, posita miraculorum illorum conditio- ne, futura, communis intelligenda sit electis & reprobis, qualis & Ninivitarum fuerit: Sed ta- lem communem pœnitentiam fidelium & infide- lium ignorat Scriptura, nec de ea hic loquitur Christus, sed de vera fidelium pœnitentia: neq; Ninevitarum pœnitentia communis habenda est, sed vera, & qualis est fidelium, ut è Matth. XII. 41. liquet. Et requisivit utique Christus in his civitatibus salutarem pœnitentiam: ideoque eandem in Tyriis futuram fuisse indicavit. Unde Episcopius Tomo II. Oper. f. 63. Annon, in- quit, posita resipiscentia externa, eadem adhuc mansisset ratio objurgandi Tyrios ac Sidonios, quod non resipuissent? ac proinde eadem ratio væ Ty- riis ac Sidoniis ingeminandi, sicut Chorazitis & Bethsaiditis factum erat? certe: & quæ tum vis hujus exclamationis erit, væ vobis Chorazin & Bethsaida, væ vobis? regeri enim posset, & væ Ty- riis ac Sidoniis, si externe tantum resipiscant. Illud profecto admiratione dignum est, eo usque aliquan- do abripi aliquos in Scripturarum interpretatione, quo thesin suam defendant ac tueantur, ut id quod ad augendum rei alicujus, uti hoc loco resipiscen- tiæ, splendorem allatum est, arripiant non aliter quam si ad imminuendum eam productum esset.

## 11:22
Vers. 22. πλὴν λέγω] In Latin you might say: 'Furthermore.' Elsewhere it is worth 'but,' or 'nevertheless,' as those particles are wont to have various meanings.

ἐν ἡμέρᾳ κρίσεως] Why we should not think that the day of special visitation is to be understood here, but the common judgment of the human race, we have rendered the reasons at the chapter immediately preceding.

Latin:

Vers. 22. πλὴν λέγω] Latine dicas: Hoc amplius. Alibi valet cæterum, aut veruntamen, ut solent particulæ illæ varias habere significationes.

ἐν ἡμέρᾳ κρίσεως] Cur non diem ἐπισκέψεως specialis, sed commune generis humani judicium hic intelligendum putemus, causas reddidimus ad caput proxime antecedens.

## 11:23
Vers. 23. ἡ ἕως τῦ ὀρανῦ ὑψωθεῖσα, ἕως ἅδε καταβιβασθήσῃ.] I do not doubt that this pertains to the affairs of this life, so that in these which follow in the next verse the discourse may rise. Capharnaum was flourishing in fishing, trade, and whatever other advantages there are wont to be for cities situated by the sea. For it is not in vain that it is called 'maritime' above in IV. 13, nor without cause did Christ transfer His dwelling here. Now Christ denounces the most grievous disasters to that city, persisting in incredulity, which we do not doubt happened in the war of Vespasian, and the commotions which then occurred in Galilee. But the expression is proverbial, even among the Greeks and Latins, 'to be lifted to the stars,' or 'to strike the stars with a lofty head,' for that which is to be in flourishing circumstances and an illustrious place. Contrary to this is 'to be cast down to Hades,' that is, to the lowest places, such as are tombs: by which the overturning of fortunes is signified. Isaiah 14:15 concerning Babylon אֶל־שְׁאוֹל תּוּרַד εἰς ἅδε καταβήσῃ, and 57:2 הִשְׁפַּלְתְּ עַד שְׁאוֹל in Greek ἐταπεινώθης ἕως ᾅδε. And this is the simplest meaning of the words of Hannah in the Canticle: God makes descend to the underworld and ascend 1 Sam. 2:6, which is explained in Tobit thus, ὅτι αὐτὸς μασιγοῖ κὴ ἐλεεῖ, κατάγει εἰς ᾅδην κὴ ἀνάγει: Meanwhile it must be known that by the direction of divine providence it came to pass that such modes of speaking existed in the prophetic writings, which figuratively signified deliverance from disasters, yet by the very propriety of the words shadowed forth the mystery of the resurrection, just as we showed a little before that the writer of the book of Wisdom used that passage of Samuel. And the same is to be observed in some passages of the Psalms, Daniel, and Ezekiel.

Although we can easily acquiesce in the explanation concerning Capernaum: yet those things which are brought forward concerning the meaning of the words of Hannah are not to be simply approved: For not only is a vicissitude of fortune, or of calamity and bodily happiness, or deliverance from some disaster or affliction insinuated, nor is a shadowing forth of the mystery of the resurrection held here, which was not hidden in the O.T., as Grotius with Socinus wishes, but was made manifest. That sentence, God makes descend to the underworld, imputes a more serious temptation, and that a spiritual one, and deliverance from the same, when it is added and ascend. For those are said to descend into hell in a metaphorical sense who experience the most serious afflictions of the soul, and a sense of divine wrath, and some of the punishments of hell, concerning which see Ps. 88:4 ff., Ps. 69:1 ff. The sentence which precedes there would make more for the mystery of resuscitation: The Lord kills and makes alive: but other sentences in the canticle of Hannah speak of the vicissitude of status in bodily matters, and those things which pertain to this life. Which did not wish to pass over even those turns of more serious spiritual temptation, and of deliverance from the same: which the Psalmist, well exercised in that school, is accustomed to designate similarly. Our annotations opposed to the Grotian depravation of the passages in the Psalms, Daniel, and Ezekiel dealing with the resurrection of the dead may be seen.

PART IV. Doxology of the Father for the revelation of the Gospel.

Latin:

Vers. 23. ἡ ἕως τῦ ὀρανῦ ὑψωθεῖσα, ἕως ἅδε καταβιβασθήσῃ.] Hoc non dubito quin ad res hujus vitæ pertineat, ut in his quæ sequuntur commate proximo assurgat oratio. Flore- bat Capharnaum piscatu, mercatu & quæ alia esse solent commoda ad mare sitarum urbium. Neque enim frustra παραθαλασσία dicitur supra IV. 13. neque sine causa Chri- stus huc habitationem suam transtulit. Jam Christus ei ur- bi, perseveranti in incredulitate, gravissimas clades denun- ciat, quas non dubitamus evenisse bello Vespasiani, & motibus qui tum in Galilea acciderunt. Proverbialis au- tem est locutio, etiam Græcis & Latinis, ad astra tolli, aur sublimi vertice sidera ferire, pro eo, quod est rebus florentibus & illustri loco esse. Huic contrarium est εἰς ᾅδη, hoc est ad infima loca, qualia sunt sepulchra, demer- gi: quo fortunarum eversio significatur. Esaïæ XIV. 15. de Babylone אֶל־שְׁאוֹל תּוּרַד εἰς ἅδε καταβήσῃ, & LVII. 2. הִשְׁפַּלְתְּ עַד שְׁאוֹל Græce ἐταπεινώθης ἕως ᾅδε. Et hæc simplicissima est sententia verborum Annæ in Canti- co: Deus facit descendere ad inferos & afcendere 1. Sam. II. 6. quod in Tobia ita explicatur, ὅτι αὐτὸς μασιγοῖ κὴ ἐλεεῖ, κατάγει εἰς ᾅδην κὴ ἀνάγει: Interim sciendum est divina pro- videntia dirigente factum, ut talia loquendi genera in pro- pheticis scriptis extarent, quæ figurate significarent libe- rationem à cladibus, ipsa tamen vocum proprietate la- tens resurrectionis mysterium adumbrarent, quomodo il- to Samuelis loco uti scriptorem libri Sapientiæ paulo an- te oftendimus. Idemque in Psalmorum, Danielis & E- zechielis aliquot locis observare est.

Etsi facile acquiescere possimus explicationi de Capernaum: ea tamen quæ de sententia verborum Annæ adferuntur, non simpliciter probanda sunt: Nam non solum fortunæ, aut calamitatis, & felici- tatis corporalis vicissitudo, vel liberatio à clade vel afflictione aliqua insinuatur, neque adumbratio mysterii resurrectionis hic habetur, quod in V. T. non latuit, uti cum Socin. vult Grotius, sed pate- factum fuit. Graviorem tentationem, eamque spiritualem imputat illa sententia, Deus facit de- scendere ad inferos, & ex eadem liberationem, cum additur & afcendere. Nam in infernum descen- dere dicuntur sensu Metaphorico, qui gravissimas animi afflictiones, & sensum iræ divinæ, ac pœnarum infernalium aliquem experiuntur, quo de Psal. XXCIIX. 4. seqq. Ps. LXIX. 1. seqq. Ad mysterium resuscitationis magis faceret sententia, quæ illic an- tecedit: Dominus occidit & vivificat: de status au- tem vicissitudine in corporalibus, & iis, quæ ad hanc vitam pertinent aliæ sententiæ in cantico Annæ loquuntur. Quæ præterire noluit etiam illas gravioris spiritualis tentationis, & ab eadem liberationis vices: quas Hierophaltes in illa Scho- la probe exercitatus similiter designare solet. De depravatione locorum in Psalmis, Daniele, & Ezechiele de resurrectione mortuorum agentium Grotiana, annotata nostra eidem opposita videri poterunt.

PARS IV. Δοξολογία Patris pro revelatione Evangelii.

## 11:25
Verse 25. ὅτι ἀπέκρυψας ταῦτα (that you have hidden these things): This is a Hebraism, such as we observed above in chapter 11:9; for Christ is not giving thanks for concealment, but properly for revelation. A customary expression would be: that you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent, you have revealed them to babes. Those wise men, the whole house of Hillel and Shammai.

ἀπεκάλυψας ἀυτὰ νηπίοις (you have revealed them to babes): Here 'babes' appears to be opposed to 'prudent,' that is, to those who seemed to themselves to be very wise: 'judging by their own gray hairs,' to speak with Paul, 1 Cor. 2:3; therefore, these 'babes' are those who think humbly of themselves. Moreover, this sentiment was also celebrated of old among the Jews. Sirach 3:21: 'Many are high and honorable, but to the meek He reveals His mysteries. For great is the power of the Lord, and He is glorified by the humble.' Where 'meek' and 'humble' are placed together, as also in this chapter below in verse 29. The Psalmist had said: 'The mystery of the Lord is with those who fear Him,' chapter 25:13. And all the Hebrews note that Moses was no one more humble-minded, and to no one was more revealed by God. To these must be added what Christ says below: 'To you it is given to know the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven, but to them it is not given,' chapter 13:11. The Pythagoreans also, having been taught by the Hebrews in many other things, were taught this as well, saying that God does not reveal Himself to all, which Hierocles explains with a convenient distinction: 'He is not therefore the cause of not showing to all, but those who are near to good things are thus seeing, as they are hearing. And for this reason they are said to have self-chosen sufferings. The cause is of the one who chooses, but God is blameless of evils, always shining forth good things to all who are in His power, and always showing them to all, while the contemplative eye of the majority is closed to the good things set before them, and looks downward due to preoccupation with worse things.' To this order of divine dispensation being carried out within, the exterior dispensation was also accommodated. For the preaching of repentance is set before the kingdom of heaven: the Baptist before Christ: But then both the Baptist and Christ Himself shone with no apparatus of external things, and not even with the supports of eloquence or human wisdom, so that it might the more appear that no confidence should be placed in things of that kind, but that humble obedience should be rendered to a humble teacher. The things above look to this, as when Christ said of Himself: 'Blessed is he who shall not be offended in me,' and speaking of the Baptist, 'if you are willing to receive it.' But it is to be noted that, just as in the tenth chapter Christ dealt with the first mission of the Apostles in such a way that He added many things pertaining to later missions, so in this place also He deals with the things that had happened up to that point in such a way that He also secretly foreshadows things to come. For just as men puffed up with knowledge did not understand the prophecies about the sending of the Messiah, because of His despicable state, which was the beginning of His emptying Himself, so afterwards the cross of Christ and the fear of ignominy increased thereby hindered the same people from believing in Christ now more openly revealed: the Lord always tempering His dispensations so that the same path might admit the humble and exclude the proud.

Latin:

Vers. 25. ὅτι ἀπέκρυψας ταῦτα] Est Hebraismus, qualem suprà observavimus cap. IIX 9. neque enim pro occultatio- ne, sed pro revelatione proprie gratias agit Christus. Usi- tata locutio esset ὅτι ἀποκρύψας ταῦτα ἀπὸ σοφῶν κὴ συνε- τῶν, ἀπεκάλυψας ἀυτὰ νηπίοις. Sapientes illi, tota domus Hillelis & Sameæ.

ἀπεκάλυψας ἀυτὰ νηπίοις] νηπίως hic apparet opponi συνε- τοῖς, id est, iis, qui sibi multum sapere videbantur: κρίνοντες τῦ ἐιδίας πολιά, ut cum Paulo loquar 1. Cor. II. 2. 3. ut ergo νήπιοι hi qui de se humiliter sentiunt. Erat autem hæc quoque γνώμη antiquitus celebrata inter Judæos. Sira- chides III. 21. πολλοί εἰσιν ὑψηλοὶ, κὴ ἐπίδoξοι, ἀλλὰ πραέσιν ἀποκαλύπλεται μυσήρια. ὅτι μεγάλη ἡ δυνασεία κυρίυ κὴ ὑπὸ τῶν ταπεινῶν δοξάζεται. Ubi junctim ponuntur πρα- εῖς κὴ ταπεινοὶ ut & hoc capite infra commate 29. Psaltes dixerat: Mysterium Domini, timentibus ipsum cap. XXV. 13. Et Hebræi omnes notant Mose neminem fuisse τα- πεινοφρονέςερον, nemini plus à Deo revelatum. His adden- dum quod infra dicit Christus ὑμῖν δέδοται γνῶναι τὰ μυσή- ρια τῆς βασιλείας τῶν ὀυρανῶν, ἐκείνοις δὲ ὀυ δέδοται cap. XIII. 11. Etiam Pythagorici ab Hebræis in multa alia ita hoc quoque edocti, dicebant Deum se non omnibus patefacere, quod commoda distinctione ita explicat Hierocles: ὀυκ ἄρα ἀυτὸς ἄντιῷ τῷ μὴ πᾶσι δεῖξαι, ἀλλ᾽ οἱ τῶν ἀγαθῶν πέλας ὄντων ὕτω ἐσορῶντες, ὥτε κλύοντες. κἀγ διὰ τῦτ᾽ ἀυθαί- ρετα πήματ᾿ ἔχειν λέγονται. ἀιτία ἓν τῦ ἑλομένε, θεὸς δὲ κα- κῶν ἀναίτιῷ, προλάμπων μὲν ἀεὶ τὰ ἀγαθὰ πᾶσιν ὅσοι ἐφ᾽ ἑαυτῷ, κὴ δεικνὺς δὲ πᾶσιν ἀεὶ, τῷ τὸ θέωρον ὄμμα τῶν προτει- νομένων ἀγαθῶν ἐν τοῖς πλείσοις μεμυκέναι κἀι κάτω νένειν ἀσχολίᾳ τῇ πρὸς τὰ χείρονα. Huic ordini divinæ pa esa- ctionis intus peragendæ accommodata fuit etiam dispen- satio exterior. Nam regno cælorum præmittitur pœni- tentiæ κήρυγμα: Christo Baptista: Tum vero & Baptista & Christus ipse, nullo fulgebant rerum exteriorum appa- ratu, ac ne eloquentiæ quidem aut sapientiæ humanæ præsidiis, quo magis appareret nullam in rebus ejusmodi ponendam esse fiduciam, sed humilem obedientiam præ- standam humili magisteri). Huc spectant & superiora, ut cum de se dixit Christus: beatus qui in me non offendetut, & de Baptista loquens, si vultis accipere. Sed notandum est, sicut decimo capite de prima Apostolorum legatione ita e- git Christus, ut multa attexeret ad posteriores legationes pertinentia, ita hoc etiam loco de iis quæ contigerant ha- ctenus ita agere Christum, ut occulte etiam ventura præ- monstret. Nam sicut vaticinia de mittendo Messia non in- tellexerunt homines scientia inflati, ob statum ipsius de- spicabilem, quod principium erat τῆς ἀυτᾶ κενώσεως, ita po- stea crux Christi & auctus inde ignominiæ metus iisdem obstitit, quominus in Christum jam apertius revelatum crederent: ita semper dispensationes suas Domino tem- perante, ut idem iter admitteret humiles & excluderet su- perbos.

## 11:26
Verse 26. ἐυδοκία (good pleasure): A Hellenistic word, as we said at chapter 3, which elsewhere signifies a propense affection, but here and in other places signifies a divine decree. So also Paul: 'It pleased God through the foolishness of the preaching to save those who believe,' 1 Cor. 1:21. Similar is 2 Macc. 14:26: 'You, O Lord of all, being in need of nothing, were pleased that a temple of Your dwelling should be among us.' Nor is it shown by that word that there were no reasons why it seemed so: rather, on the contrary, Christ praises both the equity and the wisdom in this decree of God. And thus also in human affairs Paul used that word, Rom. 15:26.

Latin:

Vers. 26. ἐυδοκία] Vox Hellenistica ut ad caput III. di- ximus, quæ alibi propensum affectum, hic vero & aliis in locis decretum divinum significat. Ita & Paulus: ἐυδό- κησεν ὁ θεὸς διὰ τῆς μωρίας τῦ κηρύγματῷ ζῶσαι τὰς πι- τεύοντας 1. Cor. I. 2 1. Simile est 2. Macc. XIV. 26. Σὺ κύριε τῶν ὅλων ἀπροσδεὴς ὑπάρχων ἐυδόκησας ναὸν τῆς σῆς σκηνώ- σεως ἐν ἡμῖν γενέσθαι. Neque ea voce ostenditur causas nullas fuisse, cur ita visum fuerit: imo contra laudat Chri- stus in hoc decreto Dei & æquitatem & sapientiam. Et fic etiam in humanis negotiis eam vocem usurpavit Paulus Rom. XV. 26.

## 11:27
Verse 27. Πάντα μοι παρεδόθη ὑπὸ τῶ πατρός με (All things have been delivered to me by my Father): Christ continues to deal with the decrees of the divine dispensation, from which it follows that one does not come to the knowledge of the mysteries except through faith had in Him, nor to faith except through a sense of misery and repentance; the series of the discourse shows that it is dealing with mysteries pertaining to human salvation, the revelation of which has been entrusted to the Son.

This is an open distortion. Christ speaks universally: 'All things have been delivered to me by my Father.' 'In all things nothing has been subtracted,' says Irenaeus, book 4, chapter 37, with the Apostle preceding, Heb. 2:8. Grotius takes the word particularly concerning the mysteries pertaining to human salvation; Christ is dealing with supreme power over all things, as the words themselves teach. Grotius explains that delivery as the revelation entrusted to the Son. Christ is intent on asserting for Himself the majesty communicated to Him, and the consubstantiality

with the Father, and also the independent authority in the revelation of the Father: which the ancients believed with great consensus, and it has not been called into doubt by any Catholic, since the words are clear. 'As the Father,' says Chrysostom, 'revealed the mysteries to the babes: so I, knowing and recognizing the Father most perfectly, reveal Him to you.' As if He were saying: 'I and the Father are one: and he who knows me, knows my Father also.' For there is not one will of the Father and another of the Son, nor one power and another: but the will of the Trinity is one, as is the power, and the nature, and the form, and the substance; and to whom the Father reveals, to the same the Son and the Holy Spirit also reveal. Grotius goes into all other things and contends that the discourse is only about the decrees of the divine dispensation. Neither does the series of the discourse convince the Grotian sense, nor does it render ours doubtful. For to the part of the revealed things which had been manifested of knowledge, the knowledge of the person and office of Christ pertained entirely: to which contributed, as far as the person is concerned, the delivery of all things made to Christ, regarding His human nature, through the hypostatic communication of divine majesty: as well as the incomprehensible majesty of Christ, which the Father alone knows comprehensively, as also the full and comprehensive knowledge of the Father, which the Son alone (not excluding, however, the Holy Spirit, who searches even the depths of God, 1 Cor. 2:10) has. But as for the office, that He also reveals the Father, as much as we have need, as Prophet, and recreates us, and procures rest for our souls, who are weary and heavy-laden, as our Mediator and Redeemer. B. Hunnius renders the Συνέχειαν of the text thus: Just as all things have been delivered to me by my Father through eternal generation, as God, and through incarnation, as man: so among these things that also has been delivered to me, that no one can know either the Son without the kindness of the revealing Father, or the Father without the revelation of the Son, I mean with a saving knowledge, and one required for the attainment of a blessed life: But that those at last arrive at the knowledge of the Father, to whom the Son has willed to manifest it. Chrysostom has it thus: It seems indeed to the ignorant to be disconnected from the preceding, but it greatly agrees with them: for when he said: All things have been delivered to me by my Father, he adds, and what wonder, he says, if I am Lord of all, as I also possess something else greater, that I have known the Father, and am of the same substance with him? for he even secretly indicates this from the fact that he alone knows the Father in this way, for when he says: no one knows the Father except the Son, he does not say that all are ignorant of him, but that he is not known by another with that knowledge with which he himself knows. οὐδεὶς ἐπιγινώσκει τὸν υἱὸν, εἰ μὴ ὁ πατήρ] What the Son is about to do and suffer, and what glory awaits him, the Father alone knows, who predetermined it from eternity. οὐδὲ τὸν πατέρα τις ἐπιγινώσκει, εἰμὴ ὁ υἱὸς] How the Father wishes the calling of the Jews first, and then also of the Gentiles, to be dispensed, the Son alone is privy to it. For not even the Prophets saw those things which they predicted concerning these matters, except through a lattice, as it is said. See 1 Pet. 1. 10. It is not only a question of those things which the Son is about to do and suffer, and what glory awaits him, but of the full knowledge of the Son. For of him who does not have this, it cannot be said absolutely that he ἐπιγινώσκει τὸν υἱὸν; and the knowledge of the Father by which he ἐπιγινώσκει τὸν υἱὸν, is not particular, not imperfect, not merely apprehensive, but total, perfect, comprehensive; and conversely such is the Son's regarding the Father: because on account of the ταυτότητα or ὁμοουσίαν of essence, the Father and the Son know each other intimately and adequately, mutually and reciprocally: which other ancients, Athanasius especially, Hilary, and Augustine, asserted from this passage against the Arians. Nor indeed does the Father alone know the Son's passion and glory, for the Prophets had already handed down what the Son was to do and suffer, and what glory awaited him, as David did in the Prophetic Psalms, Isaiah throughout, and especially in chapter LIII, and others, because Christ himself taught that it was necessary for the Son to suffer and enter into his glory, as it is handed down in Moses, the Psalms, and the Prophets, Luke XXIV. 27. Furthermore, to know the Father is not to know how the Father wills to dispense the calling of the Jews first, and then of the Gentiles: nor did the Son alone know this, except regarding the particular moments of manner, time, and other circumstances: for the Prophets had already handed down that the Jews were to be called first, and then the Gentiles were to be converted, who had not only glimpsed these things through a lattice, but had known them by divine suggestion and inspiration, even if they anxiously searched into the articles of the times: which God reserves to his own authority. Acts I. 7. Incidentally and as if in passing, I observe here Chrysostom's response to the objection of the Calvinists: If anyone asks doubtingly: And how could the wise have known the mysteries, when God was hiding them from them, to this it must be answered: the cause of that matter is to be imputed to them, who showed themselves unworthy of the manifestation of the mysteries? For he did not hide them as if out of envy: but since they seemed wise to themselves, they became fools, for the reason that they placed their trust in their own wisdom, not in God. For they did not call upon God, nor did they take care to learn from him whence they might become wise; whence it happened that he did not give to them not asking, and he humbled those who exalted themselves. For he knew that if they knew the divine mysteries, they would despise them and reject them with insult.

And to whomsoever the Son wills to reveal] This is to be referred to both, both to that which is known about the Father, and to that which is known about the Son. For it was permitted to the wisdom of the Son both to whom and how much and when he wished to open them. Nor did he open the mysteries to all, but a certain part to those already believing in him, a part to the Apostles alone. See below XIII. 11. Mark XIV. 11. Luke VIII. 10. Rom. XVI. 25. 1 Cor. II. 7. Eph. III. 5. Col. I. 16. Clement of Alexandria, Stromata VI: 'it is more to know than to believe': but he also makes degrees of the gnostics: for he calls some perfect gnostics, Stromata VII and elsewhere. You may see similar things in Origen against Celsus, book three.

PART V. The sweetest invitation of all who are burdened.

Latin:

Vers. 27. Πάντα μοι παρεδόθη ὑπὸ τῶ πατρός με] Pergit Christus agere de decretis divinæ dispensationis, ex quibus consequens esse, ut nec ad cognitionem mysteriorum ve- niatur, nisi per fidem sibi habitam, neque ad fidem, nisi per sensum miseriæ & pœnitentiam, monstrat orationis se- ries agi de mysteriis ad salutem humanam pertinentibus, quorum revelatio Filio est credita.

Detorsio hæc est aperta. Christus loquitur universaliter: πάντα, omnia mihi data sunt à Patre meo: In omnibus nihil subtractum est, ait Iren. l. IV. c. 37. præeunte Apostolo Ebr. II. 8. Grotius accipit vocem particulariter de myste- riis ad salutem humanam pertinentibus, Chri- stus de potestate suprema in omnia agit, ut verba ipsa docent. Grotius de revelatione Filio credita eam παράδοσιν explicat. Christus in eo est, ut majestatem sibi communicatam, & ὁμουσίαν

cum Patre, nec non αὐτεξουσίαν in revelatione Pa- tris fibi adserat: quod magno consensu veteres credidêre, nec à quoquam catholico in dubium vocatum est, quum verba sint luculenta. Ut Pater, inquit Chrysost. revelavit parvulis myste- ria: sic ego Patrem, sciens & cognoscens perfectis- sime, revelo ipsum vobis. Quasi diceret: Ego & Pater unum sumus : & qui novit me, novit & Patrem meum. Non enim alia voluntas Patris, alia Filii, neque alia & alia potentia : sed una est voluntas, una potentia Trinitatis, sicuti & na- tura una, & forma & substantia, & cui revelat Pa- ter, eidem & Filius & Spiritus Sanctus revelat. Grotius in omnia alia it: & solum de decretis divinæ dispensationis sermonem esse contendit. Neque orationis series aut convincit Grotianum sensum, aut nostrum dubium reddit. Nam ad partem revelatorum quæ τῆς γνώσεως manife- stata erant, pertinebat omnino cognitio perso- næ, & officii Christi: ad quam faciebat, quantum ad personam, omnium παράδοσις Christo facta, quoad humanam naturam, per communicatio- nem divinæ majestatis hypostaticam : nec non in- comprehensibilis Christi majestas, quam solus Pater comprehensive novit, ut & plena & comprehensiva Patris cognitio, quam solus Filius (non excluso tamen Spiritu S. qui scrutatur etiam τὰ βάθη pro- funditates Dei 1. Cor. II. 10.) habet. Quod vero ad officium, quod & revelet Patrem, quantum no- bis opus est, ut Propheta, ac recreet nos, & requiem conciliet animabus nostris, qui laboramus, & o- nerati sumus, ut Mediator, & Redemptor noster. B. Hunnius ita reddit Συνέχειαν textus: Quemad- modum mihi per generationem æternam, ut Deo, & per incarnationem, ut homini, universa sunt tra- dita à Patre meo: sic inter hæc illud quoque mihi tra- ditum est, ut nec Filium sine Patris revelantis beni- gnitate, nec Patrem sine Filii revelatione quisquam noffe valeat, notitia, inquam, salutari, & ad vitæ beatæ consecutionem requisita: Sed ut hi demum in Patris notitiam perveniant, quibus manifestare vo- luerit Filius. Chrysostomus ita habet: Videtur quidem ignorantibus illud à superioribus esse disjun- ctum, magnopere vero cum eis consentit: cum enim dixit: Omnia mihi tradita sunt à Patre meo, sub- dit, & quid mirum, inquit, si omnium sim Domi- nus, uti & aliud quid majus possideo, quod Patrem noverim, & ejusdem sim cum illo substantiæ? hoc enim etiam occulte indicat ex eo, quod solus ipse ita Patrem norit, cum enim dicit: nemo novit Patrem nisi Filius, non omnes eum ignorare ait, sed non co- gnosci ea cognitione ab alio, qua ipse cognoscit. οὐδεὶς ἐπιγινώσκει τὸν υἱὸν, εἰ μὴ ὁ πατήρ] Quid Filius factu- rus passurusque sit, quæ ipsum maneat gloria, solus novit, quæ præfinivit ab æterno Pater. οὐδὲ τὸν πατέρα τις ἐπιγινώσκει, εἰμὴ ὁ υἱὸς] Quomodo Pa- ter dispensari velit vocationem Judæorum primum, deinde & gentium, & conscius ipsi solus est filius. Nam ne Pro- phetæ quidem ea quæ super istis rebus prædixerunt, vide- bant, nisi per transennam quod dicitur. Vide I. Petr. 1. 10. Non tantum de illis, quæ Filius facturus pas- surusque sit, quæque ipsum maneat gloria, sed de plena Filii cognitione agitur.
