Hanc enim qui non habet, de eo absolute dici nequit ἐπιγινώ- σκει τὸν υἱὸν; & Patris cognitio qua ἐπιγινώσκει τὸν υἱὸν, non est particularis, non imperfecta, non apprehensiva solum, sed totalis, perfecta, compre- hensiva; ac vicissim talis est Filii quoad Patrem: quia ob essentiæ ταυτότητα vel ὁμοουσίαν, intime & adæquate, mutuo ac reciproce se cognoscunt Pater & Filius: quam ex hoc loco alii veteres, Athanasius imprimis, Hilarius, & Augustinus, adversus Arianos asseruêre. Nec vero Filii pas- fionem & gloriam solus Pater novit, tradiderant e- nim jam Prophetæ, quid Filius facturus passurusq; sit, quæque ipsum maneat gloria, utpote David in Psalmis Propheticis, Esaias passim, & cap. imprimis LIII. & alii, quia sic oportuisse Filium pati & in gloriam intrare, uti in Mose, Psalmis & Prophetis traditum est, docuit Christus ipse, Luc. XXIV. 27. Porro nec Patrem cognoscere est no- visse, quomodo Pater dispensari velit vocationem Judæorum primum, deinde & gentium: nec id so- lus Filius noverat, nisi quoad particularem modi, temporis, & aliarum circumstantiarum momenta: nam de primum vocandis Judæis, deinde & genti- bus convertendis, Prophetæ jam tradiderant, qui ea non solum per transennam inspexerant, sed ex suggestione, & inspiratione divina cognoverant, etsi temporum articulos anxie scrutati sint: quos Deus potestati suæ reservat. Act. I. 7. Obiter & ὡς ἐν παρόδῳ observo hic responsionem Chry- sostomi ad Calvinianorum objectionem: Quod si quis dubitans quærat: Et quomodo poterant sapien- tes nosse mysteria, Deo ea ipsis occultante, huic re- spondendum est: ipsis ejus rei causam imputandam, qui se indignos præbuerint manifestatione mysterio- rum? Non enim quasi per invidiam occultavit ipsis: sed cum ipsi sibi sapientes viderentur, stulti facti sunt, idcirco quod in propria sapientia non in Deo fiduciam posuerunt. Non enim invocaverunt De- um, neque curaverunt ab eo discere unde sapien- tes fierent; unde contigit ut iis non postulantibus non daret, & sese efferentes deprimeret. Sciebat enim eos si divina mysteria cognoscerent, spreturos ipsa, & cum contumelia rejecturos.

κᾲ ᾧ ἐὰν βούληται ὁ ὑιὸς ἀποκαλύψαι] Hoc ad utrumque referendum, tum ad id quod de Patre, tum ad id quod de Filio noscitur. Filii enim sapientiæ permissum erat & qui- bus & quantum & quando vellet aperire. Neque ille a- peruit mysteria omnibus, sed partem aliquam jam in se credentibus, partem Apostolis solis. Vide infra XIII. II. Marci XIV. II. Luc. IIX. 10. Rom. XVI. 25. 1. Cor. II. 7. Ephes. III. 5. Coloss. I. 16. Clemens Alexandrinus Stro- mateon VI. πλέον δέ ἐσι τοῦ πιστεῦσαι τὸ γνῶναι: sed & γνω- τικῶν facit gradus: quosdam enim vocat γνωστικὸς τελείους Strom. VII. & alibi. Similia videas apud Origenem ad- versus Celsum tertio.

PARS V. Suavissima omnium oneratorum invitatio.

## 11:28
Verse 28. Come to me all you who labor and are burdened.] He had said that the revelation of the mysteries was not given to all. But he calls all to faith in himself, excluding no one, but in such a way that he wishes the preparation of repentance to go before. For faith is not of all. Therefore, there are those who labor and are burdened, who sigh under the burden of sin and aspire to freedom, whom Baruch, or whoever is the author of that book, does not poorly describe II. 18: The soul that is grieved at the greatness, which walks stooping and weak, and the eyes that fail, and the hungry soul, shall give you glory and righteousness, O Lord. Compare the passage John VII. 37: If any man thirst, let him come to me and drink. But there follows he who believes in me, etc., so that it may appear that to come is to believe, as also in John VI. 44.

I will give you rest] I will make you secure from sins committed heretofore, and free from the dominion of sin hereafter: finally also from death and miseries.

Augustine, book to Boniface, ch. 3. To come to Christ is to believe in Christ. But it cannot be inferred from that that a man can come to Christ by his own powers: because no one comes to him unless the Father draws him, John VI. 44. But that we can come to hear Christ, from which hearing is faith: and that we ought not to place an obstacle to grace willing to convert us and work faith in us. However, all are invited: because all are pressed by the burden of sins, even if all do not feel it.

Rom. II. 9, ch. V. 12, seqq., ch. XI. 32, Gal. III. 22, and thus that invitation, as being most universal, extends itself even to those who refuse to come, Matt. XXII. 5, 6, XXIII. 37, Acts VII. 51, ch. XIII. 46, ch. XVII. 30, Prov. I. 24, Is. LV. 1, seqq., ch. LXV. 2, Jer. VII. 14, Ez. XXXIII. 11. Although, therefore, only those who feel the burden of sins actually obtain refreshment, yet Christ testifies to a will so ready and beneficial to refresh all.

Latin:

Vers. 28. δεῦτε πρός με πάντες οἱ κοπιῶντες κᾲ πεφορτισμέ- νοι.] Revelationem mysteriorum dixerat non omnibus da- ti. Ad fidem vero in se omnes vocat, excluso nemine, sed ita ut præire velit pœnitentiæ præparationem. Non enim omnium est fides. Sunt igitur οἱ κοπιῶντες κᾲ πεφορτισμέ- νοι, qui peccati onere suspirant & ad libertatem aspirant, quos non male describit Baruch aut quisquis est libri illius auctor II. 18. ἡ ψυχὴ ἡ λυπουμένη ἐπὶ τὸ μέγεθος, ὃ βαδίζει κύπτον κᾲ ἀσθενῶν, κᾲ οἱ ὀφθαλμοὶ οἱ ἐκλείποντες, κᾲ ἡ ψυχὴ ἡ πεινῶσα δώσουσι σοι δόξαν κᾲ δικαιοσύνην κύριε. Confer locum Joh. VII. 27. ἐάν τις διψᾷ ἐρχέσθω πρός με καὶ πινέτω. Sequitur autem ὁ πιστεύων ἐἰς ἐμὲ &c. ut appareat venire esse credere, ut & Joh. VI. 44.

ἀναπαύσω ὑμᾶς] Securos vos præstabo à peccatis ante- hac commissis, & libros à dominio peccati in posterum: tandem etiam à morte & miseriis.

Augustin. l. ad Bonif. c. 3. Venire ad Christum est credere in Christum. Non autem inde inferri potest, hominem propriis viribus ad Christum ve- nire posse: quia nemo venit ad eum, nisi Pater tra- xerit eum, Joh. VI. 44. sed quod venire possimus ad audiendum Christum, ex quo auditu fides est: quodq; non debeamus gratiæ nos convertere & fidem in nobis operari volenti obicem ponere. Invitantur autem omnes: quia omnes onere pec- catorum pressi sunt, etsi omnes id non sentiant.

Rom. II. 9. cap. V. 12. seqq. cap. XI. 32. Gal. III. 22. adeoque extendit se illa invitatio ceu maxime u- niversalis etiam ad eos qui venire tenuunt Matth. XXII. 5. 6. XXIII. 37. Act. VII. 51. c. XIII. 46. 6. XVII. 30. Prov. I, 24. Es. LV. 1. seqq. c. LXV. 2. Jer. VII. 14. Ez. XXXIII. 11. Etsi ergo qui onus peccatorum sentiunt tantum refocillationem a- ctu consequantur, testatur tamen ita Christus promtam & beneficam omnes refocillandi vo- luntatem.

## 11:29
Verse 29. The yoke] signifies the commandments. Thus that word is taken in Acts XV. 10, and John, explaining this passage, said commandments for yoke, 1 Epist. ch. V. 3. Our countrymen more correctly say that both doctrine and punishments, which in the O.T. are also called a yoke, Lam. III. 9, are noted. Indeed, the yoke of the cross of Christ is also light, because whatever weight was in it on account of sin through tribulations, Christ took upon himself and carried, so that they are not a punishment to us, but a benefit, and do not lead to our destruction, but to our advantage and salvation, Rom. V. 3, ch. VIII. 28, Heb. XII. 11. It is therefore light because of Christ's taking it up, because whatever is heavy in that burden, he himself undertook to be carried, and carried it for us, Is. XLIII. 24, ch. LIII, and because of the divine moderation of the cross, 1 Cor. X. 13, and also because of the gracious direction toward a good end, Rom. VIII. 28. Beautifully, the blessed Hunnius: just as Christ will take away that intolerable burden of sins from them (sinners coming to him), and casts it upon his own shoulders, so by a most desirable exchange he imposes another yoke and burden, which is convenient and light. The blessed Luther, commentary later on the Epistle to the Galatians, Vol. IV, Jena, Lat. f. 37. The yoke, he says, which Christ imposes, is sweet, and his burden is light. For with sin remitted and the conscience liberated from the burden and sting of sin, a Christian can bear all things easily. Because within all things are sweet and pleasant, therefore he does and suffers all things willingly.

Learn from me] I think it is placed absolutely, without relation, as how to learn is used elsewhere, John VI. 45, 1 Cor. XIV. 31, 1 Tim. II. 11, so that the sense is, give yourselves to my discipline.

ὅτι πρᾶός εἰμι κὴ ταπεινὸς τῇ καρδίᾳ] There is no reason for you to fear me on account of the consciousness of your sins. I am not like those proud and unmerciful masters. I love the humble; I forgive those led by repentance. We said above that πρᾶον κὴ ταπεινὸν are accustomed to be joined, and not undeservedly: for pride is something morose and inhuman. The passage at Zech. IX, 9 is referred to.

κὴ εὑρήσετε ἀνάπαυσιν ταῖς ψυχαῖς ὑμῶν] Christ loves to speak in the words of the Prophets. These exist in Jeremiah VI. 16.

Latin:

Vers. 29. Τὸν ζυγὸν] Jugum mandata significat. Ita vox ista sumitur Actor. XV. 10. & Johannes hunc locum ex- plicans pro jugo ἐντολὰς dixit I. Epist. c. V. 3. Rectius nostrates tam doctrinam, quam casti- gationes, quæ in V. T. etiam jugum vocantur, Thr. III. 9. notari ajunt. Nimirum jugum etiam crucis Christi leve est, quia quicquid gravitatis ob pecca- tum tribulationibus inerat, Christus in se suscepit ac portavit, ut non supplicium illæ nobis, sed be- neficium sint, non exitio, sed commodo & saluti nostræ cedant, Rom. V. 3. c. IIX. 28. Ebr. XII. 11. Leve ergo est ob Christi susceptionem, quod quicquid in eo onere grave est, ipse portandum susceperit, & pro nobis portarit Es. XLIII. 24. c. LIII. & ob divi- nam crucis moderationem, 1. Cor. X. 13. nec non ob gratiosam ad finem bonum directionem, Rom. VIII. 28. Pulcre B. Hunnius: quemadmodum Christus ab illis (peccatoribus ad se venientibus) intolera- bilem illam sarcinam peccatorum auferet, & in suos humeros rejicit, ita exoptatissima permutatione ju- gum & onus aliud, quod commodum & leve sit, im- ponit. B. Lutherus commentar. post. in Epist. ad Gal. Tom. IV. Jen. Lat. f. 37. Jugum, inquit, quod Christus imponit, svave, & onus ipsius leve est. Re- misso enim peccato & conscientia liberata ab onere & morsu peccati, Christianus omnia facile ferre potest. Quia intus omnia sunt suavia & dulcia, ideo omnia volens facit, & patitur.

μάθετε ἀπ' ἐμᾶ] Puto absolute poni, sine relatione, ut quomodo μανθάνειν & alibi usurpatur, Joh. VI. 45. 1. Cor. XIV. 31. 1. Tim. II. 11. ut sensus sit, date vos in meam di- sciplinam.

ὅτι πρᾶός εἰμι κὴ ταπεινὸς τῇ καρδίᾳ] Non est quod me formidetis ob peccatorum conscientiam. Non sum, qua- les illi superbi atque inclementes magistri. Humilis hu- miles amo: clemens pœnitentia ductis ignosco. Supra diximus jungi solere πρᾶον κὴ ταπεινὸν, Neque id immeri- to: morosuin enim & inhumanum quiddam est super- bia. Respicitur locus Zach. IX, 9.

κὴ εὑρήσετε ἀνάπαυσιν ταῖς ψυχαῖς ὑμῶν] Amat Christus loqui Prophetarum verbis. Exstant hæc apud Jeremiam VI. 16.

## 11:30
Vers. 30. ὁ γὰρ ζυγός με χρησὸς, κὴ τὸν φορτίον με ἐλα- φρόν ἐσι] Doubtless on account of the help of the Spirit, and the magnitude and certainty of the proposed reward, as explained by John in 1 Epist. V. 4, concerning which matter we treated above at chapter VII. Add to these that the precepts of Christ are also in themselves such that they are suitable to human nature, since they are situated in loving God and men, so that if a comparison is made of the habit of one man living rightly and another living in wickedness, the life which is according to virtue will undoubtedly be much sweeter. For those who serve ambition, who serve avarice, who serve lust, pay most heavy taxes: Therefore the wise Hebrew says that those serving sins διοδεύειν ἐρήμους ἀβάτες. Philo: ἡ ἀρετὴ φαντασίᾳ μὲν ἥ τε τὴν πρόχειρον ἔντευξιν ἀργαλέον εἶναι δοκεῖ' μελέτῃ δὲ ἥδισον κὴ ἐξ ἐπιλογισμᾶ συμφέρον: in which sense that of Chrysostom is also true: δυσκολώτερον ἡ κακία τῆς ἀρετῆς. Salvianus: For what does He demand of us, what does He command to be offered to Him by us, except only faith, chastity, humility, sobriety, mercy, holiness, which indeed do not burden us, but adorn us?

The yoke of Christ is easy, and his burden light, because he does not impose the ἀβάσακτον yoke and burden of the law and of traditions, Act. XV. 10. Matth. XXIII. 4. but proposes His satisfaction and merit in the Gospel, and by its efficacy and the help of the Holy Spirit makes all things light for us, demanding only faith and a zeal for holiness, with repentance and the bearing of the cross: which He indeed demands in such a way that He also works effectively within us, granting both the will and the performance, Phil. II. 13. c. I. 29. and by the free promise of reward makes His yoke light and sweet for us, 2. Cor. IV. 17.

Latin:

Vers. 30. ὁ γὰρ ζυγός με χρησὸς, κὴ τὸν φορτίον με ἐλα- φρόν ἐσι] Nimirum ob Spiritus auxilium, & magnitudinem ac certitudinem propositi præmii, explicante Johanne 1. E- pist. V. 4. qua de re egimus supra ad caput VII. Adde his, quod præcepta Christi etiam per se talia sunt, ut naturæ hu- manæ conveniant, quippe indiligendo Deo & hominibus sita, ita ut si par ponatur consuetudo, unius hominis ad re- cte vivendum, alterius ad flagitia, non dubie multo dulcior sit futura vita quæ secundum virtutem est. Gravissima e- nim tributa pendunt qui ambitioni, qui avaritiæ, qui li- bidini serviunt: Ideo sapiens Hebræus peccatis servientes ait διοδεύειν ἐρήμους ἀβάτες. Philo: ἡ ἀρετὴ φαντασίᾳ μὲν ἥ τε τὴν πρόχειρον ἔντευξιν ἀργαλέον εἶναι δοκεῖ' μελέτῃ δὲ ἥδισον κὴ ἐξ ἐπιλογισμᾶ συμφέρον: quo sensu & illud Chrysostomi verum est: δυσκολώτερον ἡ κακία τῆς ἀρετῆς. Salvianus: Quid namque à nobis exigit, quid præstari sibi à nobis ju- bet, nisi solam tantummodo fidem, castitatem, humilita- tem, sobrietatem, misericordiam, sanctitatem, quæ utique o- mnia non onerant nos, sed ornant?

Facile est jugum Christi, & onus leve, quod non imponat jugum & onus ἀβάσακτον legis, & traditionum Act. XV. 10. Matth. XXIII. 4. sed satis- fatisfactionem & meritum suum proponat in Ev- angelio, ejusque efficacia & Spiritus S. auxilio no- bis omnia reddat levia, fidem solum poscens, & studium sanctitatis, cum pœnitentia, & crucis tole- rantia: quæ vero ita poscit, ut in nobis efficaci- ter etiam operetur, donans & velle & perficere, Phil. II. 13. c. I. 29. nobisque gratuita renumera- tionis promissione leve & suave jugum suum ef- ficiat, 2. Cor. IV. 17.

## 12:1 Argument
CHAPTER XII. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

Christ defends the disciples rubbing ears of corn on the Sabbath, by the example of David, who ate the showbread, and of the Priests, and by His own lordship over the Sabbath; and He defends the healing of the withered hand by the similar concession that a sheep may be pulled out of a pit on the Sabbath; and because of the snares of the Pharisees He withdraws, healing many, but with an interdict that they should not divulge it, according to the prophecy of Isaiah (c. XLII. 1. seqq.); He restores a blind and mute demoniac, and defeats the blasphemous thoughts of the Pharisees concerning Beelzebub, and warns about blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, teaching that a bad tree does not bear good fruit, and that evil comes out of an evil heart. He says that no sign is to be given to those demanding one, except the sign of Jonah, whom the Ninevites and the Queen of the South will one day condemn. He warns about the unclean spirit returning and about the true relatives of Christ.

These are the parts: I. Information concerning the Sabbath on account of the disciples rubbing ears of corn, and the healing of the withered hand, to v. 21. II. The deliverance of the mute and blind demoniac, and its defense with a grave exhortation, to v. 37. III. The denial of any sign other than that of Jonah, to v. 42. IV. Admonition concerning the returning unclean Spirit, to v. 45. V. Instruction concerning the mother and brothers of Christ, to v. 50.

PART I. Information concerning the Sabbath, on account of the disciples rubbing ears of corn, and the healing of the withered hand.

Vers. 1. Τοῖς σάββασι] We said above that Hebrew words are inflected to the Greek form of nouns by addition or diminution. Thus from the Hebrew שבת by adding, the word σάββατον was made, but by diminishing שבתא, σάββατο, whence the dative plural σάββασι. But the latter word ceased to be used in the singular number: and therefore it began to be counted among those which have a singular meaning with a plural sound, as appears here and below XXVIII. 1. Acts XIII. 14. and elsewhere. Thus in Horace: Today are the thirtieth sabbaths.

There is no reason why you should understand this as referring to the week. For Luke shows that it is the seventh day that is being dealt with here, and indeed a solemn one. Nor could this murmuring of the Jews have arisen on another day: since the disciples would not have violated the law. For what Erasmus says, that the individual days of the week were called sabbaths (which Theophylact also asserts below, c. XXVIII.), even if it were true, cannot fit the present passage. Thus Beza in this place.

Τίλλειν στάχυας] Luke interprets this τίλλειν as ψώχειν, to rub, in which sense the word τίλλειν is used both in Diodorus Siculus and in the glosses as τιλμός οσπρίων. It was permitted by the law (Deut. XXIII. 25) to pluck ears of corn in another's field, which grants not impunity but a right to the act. But whether it was permitted to pluck and rub on the Sabbath was another question. The law of Moses forbids doing מלאכת עבדה on the Sabbath, which the Hebrews rightly interpret as servile work. In Roman Pontifical law, a large part of which was from the Etruscans, and the Etruscans had received it from the Hebrews, where it dealt with feast days, there was the same manner of speaking, that maidservants should not perform works: for from there Cicero took in De Legibus II: On holidays remove strife, and hold them to the works performed by servants. But among the Romans, a more indulgent usage had found many exceptions for the works of servants. And so in Virgil these things are taken from Pontifical law, as Macrobius teaches us:

For even on feast days, the divine law and the statutes allow certain things to be practiced. No religion has forbidden the leading of streams, the placing of a hedge before the corn, the setting of snares for birds, the burning of thorns, or the immersing of a flock of bleating sheep in the wholesome river.

The Hebrews did not admit such exceptions, being aware of the decree of God that a man was stoned because he had gone to gather wood on the Sabbath. And specifically in their Pandects, rubbing ears of corn is numbered among servile works. Nor does Christ deny that it is a servile work, but from the circumstances He shows that this act of the disciples is not comprehended by the intent of the law. It is therefore a question of the letter and the intent, the status of the written word and the will, as Tertullian speaks when dealing with this very matter.

Latin:

CAPUT XII. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Discipulos Sabbato spinas fricantes defendit Christus, Davidis, qui panes propositionis comedit, & Sacerdotum exemplo, & suo in Sabbatum dominio, manusque aridæ sa- nationem simili ovis è fovea Sabbato ex- trahi concessæ tuetur & ob insidias Phari- sæorum secedit, plurimos curans, sed cum interdicto, ne divulgarent id, juxta vatici- nium Esaiæ (c. XLII. 1. seqq.) cæcum & mu- tum obsessum restituit, ac cogitationes bla- sphemas Pharisæorum de Beelzebub profli- gat deq́; blasphemia in Spiritum S. monet, arborem malam non ferre bonũ fructum, & ex corde malo malũ exire, docens. Si- gnum postulantibus aliud haud dandum, præterquam Ionæ signum ait, quos Ninivitæ & Regina Austri aliquando condemnabūt. De immundo spiritu iterum revertente: & de veris Christi necessariis, monet.

Partes hæ sunt: I. De Sabbato ob discipulos spicas fricantes, & sanationem manus aridæ infor- matio, ejusque consequens Christi secessus, ad v. 21. II. Obsessi muti & cæci liberatio, ejusque de- fensio cum gravi parænesi, ad v. 37. III. Signi al- terius, quam Ionæ denegatio, ad v. 42. IV. De Spi- ritu immundo redeunte commonitio, ad v. 45. V. De matre & fratribus Christi instructio, ad v. 50.

PARS I. De Sabbato, ob discipulos spicas fricantes, & sanationem manus aridæ informatio.

Vers. 1. Τοῖς σάββασι] Supra diximus voces Hebræas ad Græcam nominum figuram flecti additione aut immi- nutione. Ita ex Hebræo שבת addendo facta est vox σάββατον, diminuendo autem שבתא σάββατο, unde dati- vus pluralis σάββασι. Sed posterior vox in singulari nume- ro usurpari defiit: ideoque iis cœpit accenseri quæ plu- rali sono singularem habent significationem, ut hic appa- ret & infra XXVIII. 1. Act. XIII. 14. & alibi. Ita apud Horatium: Sunt hodie tricesima sabbata.

Nihil causæ est cur hoc de hebdomade intelligas. Nam de septimo demum die hic agi, & eo quidem so- lemni, Lucas ostendit. Neque hoc murmur Judæo- rum alio die exorire potuisset: siquidem non violas- sent legem discipuli. Nam quod Erasmus ait sin- gulos dies hebdomadis fuisse sabbata appellatos (quod etiam asserit Theophylactus infra, c. XXVIII. etiam- si verum esset, præsenti loco quadrare non potest. Ita Beza h. l.

Τίλλειν στάχυας] τίλλειν hoc Lucas interpretatur ψώχειν, fricare, quo sensu vox τίλλειν est & apud Diodorum Sicu- lum & in glossis τιλμός οσπρίων. Vellere spicas in agro alieno licebat per legem Deut. XXIII. 25. quæ non impu- nitatem sed jus ad factum concedit. Sed an sabbato vel- lere ac fricare liceret alia erat quæstio. Lex Mosis interdi- cit Sabbato facere מלאכת עבדה quod Hebræi recte inter- pretantur opus servile. In jure Pontificio Romano, cu- jus pars magna ab Ethruscis erat, Ethrusci autem ab He- bræis acceperant, quo loco de festis diebus agebatur, e- rat idem loquendi genus, ne famulæ opera patrantor: nam inde accepit Cicero de legibus II. Feriis jurgis amovento, easque in famulis operibus patratis habento. Sed apud Ro- manos usus indulgentior multas exceptiones famulorum operum invenerat. Itaque apud Virgilium hæc sunt ex ju- re Pontificio petita, ut nos Macrobius docet:

Quippe etiam festis quædam exercere diebus Fas & jura sinunt. Rivos deducere nulla Religio vetuit, segeti prætendere sepem, Insidias avibus moliri, incendere vepres, Balantumque gregem fluvio mersare salubri.

Hebræi tales exceptiones non admittebant, quippe gna- ri decreto Dei lapidatum hominem, quod lignatum ivis- set in Sabbato. Ac nominatim in Pandectis ipsorum spi- cas confricare numeratur inter famula opera. Neque ne- gat Christus opus esse famulum, sed ex circumstantiis ostendit factum hoc discipulorum legis sententia non comprehendi. Est ergo quæstio τοῦ ῥητοῦ καὶ τῆς διανοίας, sta- tus scripti & voluntatis, ut hac de ipsa re agens Tertullia- nus loquitur.

## 12:2
Vers. 2. ὅ οὐκ ἔξεστι ποιεῖν ἐν σαββάτῳ] They understand the plucking of the ears of corn, not walking. For Christ also walks: but the Pharisees note only the disciples: The Hebrews counted a longer journey among servile works: a shorter one not so, as it pertained more to refreshing the mind than to the appearance of labor. However, the distinction between a journey and walking is by nature indefinite, so that there might be something certain in judgments, it was defined by human law, by the space of two thousand cubits. Therefore, in this part, the Pharisees had nothing they could slander.

Latin:

Vers. 2. ὅ οὐκ ἔξεστι ποιεῖν ἐν σαββάτῳ] Vulsionem spi- carum intelligunt, non deambulationem. Nam ambulat & Christus: at Pharisæi solos discipulos notant: Iter ma- jus Hebræi famulis operibus accensebant: minus non i- tem, ut quod ad reficiendum animum magis quam ad la- boris speciem pertinebat. Discrimen autem inter iter & ambulationem natura indefinitum, ut certi aliquid esset in judiciis, lege humana definitum erat, spatio bis mille cubitorum. Hac igitur in parte nihil habebant Pharisæi quod calumniarentur.

## 12:3
Vers. 3. οὐκ ἀνέγνωτε τί ἐποίησε Δαβὶδ] To know the laws, say the Jurisconsults, is not to hold their words, but their force and power, because the mind of the speaker is prior and more powerful than the voice. Therefore, as often as the mind of him who wrote the law can be grasped by certain indications, the intent should be preferred to the letter. For it is true, as we read in Cicero in the second book of De Inventione, that no matter can be rightly administered, neither by laws nor by any writing, nor finally even in daily conversation and domestic commands, if everyone wishes to look at the words and not approach the will of him who spoke the words. But in prohibitive laws, the words generally extend more widely than the very mind of the law. For as it is in the same place in Cicero, not all things are provided for by writings, but certain things, which are clear, are provided for by tacit exceptions. Hence Aristotle says that it is the property of equity, which he calls ἐπιεικείαν, to be the correction of the law where it is deficient on account of its universality. Unless that is applied, that highest law, τὸ ἀκριβοδίκαιον, may be the highest cross and the highest injustice. Nor indeed do the things we have said have a place only in human laws, but also in divine ones, namely of that kind which is not just by nature, but by constitution. For God, speaking with men in the human manner, wishes to be understood in the way that a man saying the same thing would be understood. Among all the exceptions, however, which are tacitly contained in laws, there is none either more accepted or more just than that which flows from necessity. Seneca says well: Necessity is the great defense of human weakness: whatever it compels, it excuses. Nor indeed is that necessity to be understood only as that which consists, so to speak, in the extreme line: but it also has its own πλάτος, sometimes greater, sometimes lesser, according to the necessity or utility of the law itself. In every kind of law, however, the laws of sacred rites and civil institutions are of the least necessity and utility, which it is certain were devised not for the thing itself that is in the law, but for the sake of either εὐταξίας or some signification. In the interpretation of these laws, therefore, necessity is taken a little more loosely. Christ could have brought forward many things here from Jewish law pertaining to this. For in the Maccabean times it was decreed that it was permitted to fight against an enemy on the Sabbaths. But by the reception of opinions, public couriers and merchants setting out at fixed times ἐν συνοδίᾳ, which they now call a caravan, were exempted from the law of the Sabbath. But because these relied only on the authority of custom, nor were there wanting those who dissented, of which thing there is a great argument in that after the Maccabean times Jerusalem was twice taken on the Sabbath, Christ takes a most valid argument from the sacred letters themselves from a like cause, which is such: In a like cause the law ought to be the same. The law of the Sabbath and the law concerning the proposed loaves not being eaten except by the priests are both ritual. David and his companions, pressed by a like necessity to that by which my disciples are now pressed, acted against τὸ ῥητόν of the law concerning the loaves, and yet they are not considered to have acted against τὴν διάνοιαν. It follows therefore that my disciples also do not commit anything against the intent of the law by this deed.

Καὶ οἱ μετ' αὐτῦ] These words are too clear for it to be possible to deny that David had some companions in his flight. And even if these words could be evaded in some way, those in Mark certainly cannot: ἒδωκε καὶ τοῖς σὺν αὐτῷ ὖσι. Wherefore, the fact that the Pontiff wonders in the history of Samuel that David is alone ought to be understood in such a way that his companions had stopped elsewhere.

Latin:

Vers. 3. οὐκ ἀνέγνωτε τί ἐποίησε Δαβὶδ] Scire leges, in- quiunt Jurisconsulti, non est verba earum tenere, sed vim ac potestatem, quia prior atque potentior est quam vox, mens dicentis. Ideo quoties certis indiciis comprehendi potest mens ejus qui legem scripserit, præferri debet δια- νοια τῷ ῥητῷ. Verum enim est, quod apud Ciceronem libro de Inventione secundo legimus, nullam rem neque legibus neque Scriptura ulla, denique ne in sermone qui- dem quotidiano, atque imperiis domesticis, recte posse administrari, si unusquisque velit verba spectare, & non ad voluntatem ejus qui verba habuerit accedere. In le- gibus autem prohibitoriis plerumque verba latius patent, quam mens ipsa legis. Nam ut eodem loco apud Cice- ronem est, non omnis scriptis, sed quædam, quæ per- spicua sunt, tacitis exceptionibus caventur. Hinc æqui- tatis quam ἐπιεικείαν vocat proprium esse dicit Aristote- les ἐπανόρθωσιν τοῦ νόμου ᾗ ἐλλείπει διὰ τὸ καθόλου. Ea nisi ad- hibeatur, jus illud summum, τὸ ἀκριβοδίκαιον, sit summa crux, summaque injuria. Neque vero ea quæ diximus in humanis tantum legibus locum habent, sed & in di- vinis, ejus nempe generis quod non natura justum est, sed constitutione. Deus enim cum hominibus loquens humano more, ita vult intelligi, quomodo idem dicens homo intelligeretur. Inter omnes autem exceptiones, quæ tacite insunt legibus, nulla est aut receptior, aut justior, quam ea quæ fluit ex necessitate. Bene Seneca: Necessitas magnum humanæ imbecillitatis patrocinium: quic- quid cogit excusat. Neque vero ea necessitas demum intel- ligenda est, quæ in extrema ut ita dicam linea consistit: sed habet & illa suum πλάτος, modo majus, modo minus, pro necessitate aut utilitate legis ipsius. In omni autem legum genere minimæ necessitatis utilitatisque sunt leges sacro- rum rituum & institutorum civilium, quas certum est non ob idipsum quod in lege est, sed aut εὐταξίας aut significationis alicujus gratia repertas. In harum igitur legum interpretatione necessitas sumitur paulo laxius. Poterat hic Christus multa afferre ex Judaico jure huc pertinentia. Nam Maccabaicis temporibus decretum est, ut pugnare in hostem Sabbatis liceret. Sed ex sententis receptione cursores publici, & mercatores statis tempo- ribus proficiscentes ἐν συνοδίᾳ, quam nunc Carvanam vo- cant, lege Sabbati eximebantur. Sed quia hæ sola con- suetudinis nitebantur auctoritate, nec deerant qui dissen- tirent, cujus rei magnum est argumentum quod post Mac- cabaica tempora bis Hierosolyma sabbato sunt expugna- ta, Christus ex ipsis literis sacris validissimum à pari cau- sa sumit argumentum, quod tale est: In pari causa jus idem esse oportet. Lex Sabbati & lex de propositis pani- bus non edendis nisi à Sacerdotibus, ambæ sunt rituales. David ejusque comites pari necessitate pressi, qua nunc premuntur discipuli mei, fecerunt contra τὸ ῥητόν legis de panibus, neque tamen censentur fecisse contra τὴν διά- νοιαν. Sequitur ergo nec discipulos meos hoc facto quic- quam adversus legis sententiam committere.

Καὶ οἱ μετ' αὐτῦ] Nimis aperta sunt haec verba quam ut negari possit Davidem ejus fugae comites aliquos habuisse. Et ut haec verba aliqua ratione possent eludi, illa certe apud Marcum non possunt: ἒδωκε καὶ τοῖς σὺν αὐτῷ ὖσι. Quare quod Pontifex in Samuelis historia miratur Davi- dem esse solum, ita intelligi debet, comites alibi substi- tisse.

## 12:4
Vers. 4. Εἰς τὸν οἶκον τῦ θεῦ] That is, the place in which the tabernacle was. For as yet no temple existed.

Τὺς ἄρτυς τῆς προθέσεως] The LXX sometimes say ἐνωπίυς, sometimes προσώπυ, sometimes προκειμένυς: but very often, as here, ἄρτυς προθέσεως, which Philo also follows.

ὃς ὐκ ἐξὸν ἧν αὐτῷ φαγεῖν] Which it was not lawful for him to eat, taken strictly according to the letter: but it was lawful according to the sense, which appears from the fact that neither is David blamed on that account, nor would Achimelech the most religious priest have conceded it had he known it to be in conflict with the law.

Latin:

Vers. 4. Εἰς τὸν οἶκον τῦ θεῦ] Id est locum in quo erat ἡ σκηνὴ. Nam templum adhuc nullum exstabat.

Τὺς ἄρτυς τῆς προθέσεως] LXX. modo ἐνωπίυς, modo προσώπυ, modo προκειμένυς dicunt: saepissime vero ut hic ἄρτυς προθέσεως, quod & Philo sequitur.

ὃς ὐκ ἐξὸν ἧν αὐτῷ φαγεῖν] Quibus vesci ipsum fas non erat κατὰ τὸ ῥητὸν rigide sumtum: fas autem erat κατὰ διάνοιαν, quod inde apparet, quia neque David reprehenditur eo nomine, neque Achimelec sacerdos religiosissimus con- cessurus fuerat quod sciret cum lege pugnare.

## 12:5
Vers. 5. ἢ ὐκ ἀνέγνωτε ἐν τῷ νόμῳ] Christ's second argument from the lesser to the greater. The law of the Sabbath receives such an interpretation that it does not stand in the way of the works of the temple. Therefore, it ought not to stand in the way of prophetic works either. The antecedent is proven from the law in Num. XXVIII.9 and most well-known custom: whence there was a rule of Jewish law that there is no Sabbath in the temple. Christ proves the consequence in the following verse.

Βεβηλῦσι] The writer of the Maccabean History also said βεβηλῦν τὴν ἡμέραν τῶν σαββάτων, l. B. I. c. II. 34. But here it must be understood according to the letter. Therefore it follows καὶ ἀναίτιοί εἰσι, because, namely, they admit nothing against the sense of the law. And indeed, the ancient Hebrews use this very manner of speaking in the Talmudic Pandect, and David Kimchi after them, when they say that the Sabbath is sometimes rightly violated, and they prove it by the example of priestly works. They also add the history which Justin also uses against Trypho, of the ark being carried around Jericho on the Sabbath no less than on other days. Thus, by the Pontifical law of the ancient Romans, Umbro denied that one was polluted who had performed work pertaining to the gods or for the sake of sacred rites.

Latin:

Vers. 5. ἢ ὐκ ἀνέγνωτε ἐν τῷ νόμῳ] Alterum Christi argu- mentum a minori ad majus. Lex Sabbati eam recipit in- terpretationem, ut non obiter operibus templi. Ergo nec propheticis operibus obitare debet. Antecedens probatur ex lege Num. XXVIII.9. & notissima consuetudine: unde regula erat juris Judaici, in templo non esse Sabbatum. Consequentiam probat Christus commate sequente.

Βεβηλῦσι] βεβηλῦν τὴν ἡμέραν τῶν σαββάτων dixit etiam Scriptor Historiae Maccabaicae l. B. I. c. II. 34. Sed hic subin- telligi debet κατὰ τὸ ῥητὸν. Ideo sequitur καὶ ἀναίτιοί εἰσι, quia scilicet contra legis διάνοιαν nihil admittunt. Atque adeo hoc ipso loquendi genere utuntur Hebraei veteres in Pan- decte Thalmudico, & ex illis David Kimchi, cum dicunt recte interdum violari Sabbatum, idque probant exemplo operarum sacerdotalium. Addunt & historiam qua & Justinus adversus Tryphonem utitur, arcae circum Hieri- chuntem portatae Sabbato non minus quam diebus caete- ris. Sic ex jure Pontificio veterum Romanorum Umbro negabat pollui qui opus ad Deos pertinens sacrorumve causa fecisset.

## 12:6
Vers. 6. Τῦ ἱερῦ μεῖζόν ἐστιν ὧδε] Every Prophet was greater than the temple, whence it was permitted for Prophets to sacrifice outside the temple, as Elijah did: but Jesus is greater than a Prophet, as he will say below in verse 41. But you might say, the rites of the temple could not be observed unless some labor were expended on the Sabbath day: but what such connection is there between the prophetic office of Christ and his Apostles, and the plucking of the ears of grain? Doubtless this: that Christ and his Apostles had been so occupied in performing their office that they had no leisure to prepare food for themselves to eat on the Sabbath day. Either, therefore, they should have interrupted their Prophetic office, or acted against the letter of the law of the Sabbath. But the priestly office was not interrupted on account of the law of the Sabbath; therefore, neither should the Prophetic office, which was greater, be interrupted on that account.

Latin:

Vers. 6. Τῦ ἱερῦ μεῖζόν ἐστιν ὧδε] Plus templo erat omnis Propheta, unde Prophetis extra templum sacrificare licuit, ut Eliae: Jesus autem plusquam Propheta, ut infra dicet commate 41. Sed dicas aliquis, templi ritus observari non poterant nisi labor aliquis die Sabbati insumeretur: quae autem talis connexio est inter propheticum Christi ejusque Apostolorum munus, & inter spicarum vulsionem? Ni- mirum ista, quod Christus ejusque Apostoli ita occupati fuerant in obeundo suo munere, ut non vacaret ipsis ci- bum sibi parare quo Sabbati die vescerentur. Aut ergo intermittere debuerant munus Propheticum, aut facere contra τὸ ῥητὸν legis sabbati. Sacerdotale autem munus non intermittebatur ob legem Sabbati; igitur nec Prophe- ticum, quod majus erat, intermitti eo nomine debebat.

## 12:7
Vers. 7. Εἰ δὲ ἐγνώκειτε τί ἐστιν] Christ's third argument, taken from the topic of contrary laws. And it is the same prosyllogism as above in chapter IX. As often as laws collide due to circumstances, so that both cannot be kept at the same time, the better law must be kept: but the law that commands beneficence is better than that which pertains to rites: therefore it is to be preferred. The proposition is of most well-known law: the assumption is proven, as above, also by the words of Hosea. There remains the application of the general conclusion to this specific case. The fact that the law which commands us to be beneficent is ritual is taught by the thing itself, and is beyond controversy. Christ could not simultaneously devote effort to teaching, to preparing men for his doctrine, and to preparing those things which pertained to the rigid observation of the Sabbath, as we have also said before. Therefore, it followed from what had been concluded before that the law of the Sabbath had to yield to the precept of holy instruction. Moreover, that which is proved here from Hosea—that all laws of ritual are of much less value in the sight of God than laws of morals, and especially those of religion and beneficence—is a most conspicuous truth, which did not escape many even among the profane nations. I shall bring forward a few from many. Plato in Alcibiades II: κὴ γὰρ ἂν δεινὸν εἴη, εἰ πρὸς τὰ δῶρα καὶ τὰς θυσίας ἀποβλέπυσιν ἡμῶν οἱ θεοὶ, ἀλλὰ μὴ πρὸς τὴν ψυχὴν ἄν τις ὅσιός τε καὶ δίκαιος ὢν τυγχάνῃ. In which sentiment, and in his books on the Republic, many things are excellently said. The verses which I shall now adduce some ascribe to Menander, others to Philemon, and they are unworthy of neither. Referam autem ita ut emendandos censeo:

Εἰ θυσίαν τις προσφέρων ὦ πάμφιλε Ταύρων τε πλῆθος ἢ ἐρίφων ἢ νὴ Δία Ἑτέρων τοιύτων, ἢ κατασκευάσματα Χρυσᾶς ποιήσας χλαμύδας ἤτοι πορφυρᾶς,

He who thinks to establish God by images of ivory or emerald is deceived and has a dull mind. For a man must be naturally useful, not corrupting virgins, committing adultery, stealing, or murdering for the sake of money. Do not covet even the smallest trifle, my friend; for God sees you, being present at your side. Of the same author is also this: Sacrifice, and sacrifice continually, being righteous, not being brilliant in your robes, but in your heart. To these let Persius be added: Nay, let us offer to the gods that which the blear-eyed offspring of great Messala cannot offer from a large platter: a mind in which law and divine right are blended, the sacred recesses of the soul, and a breast imbued with noble honor. This I bring to the temples, and with a handful of meal I shall make my offering. Hierocles to the same effect: οἶδε τιμᾷν θεὸν ὁ προηγουμέ- νως ἱερεὺς ἑαυτὸν προσάγων καὶ ἄγαλμα θεῖον τεκταίνων τὴν ἑαυτοῦ ψυχὴν καὶ ναὸν εἰς ὑποδοχὴν τοῦ θείου φωτὸς τὸν ἑαυτοῦ παρασκευάζων νοῦν : For God, as he says in the same place, τὸ εὐτελέ- στατον προκρινεῖ τῆς πολυτελείας ὅταν θεοσεβείας γνώμῃ κοσ- μῆται· μετ' αὐτῆς γὰρ πάντα θεοφιλῆ, καὶ ἄνευ ταύτης οὐδὲν θεῷ φίλον ἂν ποτε γίνοιτο. Grotius mixes the law of GOD with the traditions of the Jews. Servile works were prohibited on the Sabbath in the divine law; but whether rubbing ears of grain should be referred to those works was not to be learned from the Jewish pandects, which do not have canonical authority. Although Christ does not expressly deny that the work is servile, he does not concede that it is such, and that it is prohibited in the law. It was enough to defend the deed of the disciples from the circumstances themselves. Although Grotius rightly [quotes] from Seneca, 'Necessity, the great defense of human weakness, excuses whatever it compels': yet it cannot be simply approved that the same person urges in this place, that the Law of the Sabbath and the law concerning the showbread not being eaten except by the Priests are not equally ritual. For the latter was clearly ritual. In the former, however, there was much of morality, concerning which in its proper place. But this is the reasoning of Christ's collection: If David in a case of necessity could eat the sacred loaves destined for God alone, much more could the Apostles rub ears of grain on the Sabbath to appease their hunger: because eating those was contrary to the law: but rubbing ears of grain is expressly prohibited by no law, whence Blessed Hunnius: And indeed the work itself, which they had done, was by no means of such a kind that by it the sanctification of the Sabbath would be diminished even in the slightest. For otherwise, by the same reasoning, it would not have been permitted to eat or drink on the Sabbath, which everyone understands to be false. Christ, however, ἐκ περιουσίας (abundantly) answers the Pharisees by a certain concession, but one which would have another defense joined to it, so that he might the more validly press and urge the Pharisaic adversaries, as if he were saying: Be it so, let this be such a work by which the Sabbath would otherwise be profaned (which, however, has not yet been proven by you), yet a case of necessity exempts from the law, or excuses my disciples, so that what they did cannot be held as a violation of the divine order. That those ceremonial laws can admit of such a dispensation, the Savior proves by the example of David. Chrysostom has it thus: where necessity is present, there a lapse is not liable to censure. Wherefore the Pharisees here ridiculously accuse an innocent nature. The Lord clears their accusation to the point, by the example of David, removing every shadow of doubt, with a defense even exceeding the use of the case. For indeed David had dared something greater, who, when hungry, ate the showbread, which it was unlawful for anyone, especially the Prophets and the Father of the Messiah of God, to eat, he himself and his companions, which it was not permitted to eat except by the Priests alone. In the other argument of Christ concerning the work of the Priests regarding sacrifices on the Sabbath, the annotations of Grotius are correct: But someone might say the rites of the temple could not be observed unless some labor were expended on the Sabbath day: but what such connection is there between the prophetic office of Christ and his Apostles, and the plucking of the ears of corn? Surely this, that Christ and his Apostles had been so occupied in performing their office, that they had no leisure to prepare food for themselves to eat on the Sabbath day. Either, therefore, they ought to have interrupted their prophetic office, or to have acted against the letter of the law of the Sabbath. But the priestly office was not interrupted because of the law of the Sabbath, therefore neither ought the prophetic, which was greater, to have been interrupted on that account. Chrysostom gives this reason for the consequence, that if the Priests do not violate the law concerning the Sabbath while they work in the temple before the Lord, much less do those who, in the presence of Christ, who is greater than the temple, rub the ears of corn, violate the law: How do the Priests, being certainly knowledgeable in what the observance of the law consists, and exact observers of it, cut wood and kindle fire on the Sabbath? What seems to you? Do the Priests then violate the Sabbath? By no means. But hold this: something greater than the temple is here, that is: I am greater than the temple, since I am the Lord of the temple and of the law; but I am with the disciples; whence they have full right, when use has demanded, to break the Sabbath, even somewhat more than the priests. But the argument of Christ is of this kind: When the Priests do the work of God on the Sabbath, they nevertheless do not violate the law: therefore not all works are prohibited by the law of the Sabbath without exception: but if the worship of the temple excused the Priests from resting on the Sabbath, much more was the Lord of the temple and of the Sabbath himself, doing the work of God, not bound by the law of the Sabbath. It appears, therefore, that Christ is recalling the proposed hypothesis; and deservedly so. For the disciples had been superstitiously reproved by the Pharisees, and therefore they were in need of no excuse; as Beza here.

Latin:

Vers. 7. Εἰ δὲ ἐγνώκειτε τί ἐστιν] Tertium Christi argu- mentum petitum ex loco de contrariis legibus. Estque idem προσυλλογισμὸς qui supra cap. IX. Quoties leges ex circumstantia colliduntur, ita ut simul utraque servari ne- queat, servanda est lex potior: Potior autem est lex quae beneficentiam praecipit, quam quae ad ritus pertinet: praeferenda igitur. Propositio notissimi est juris: affum- tio probatur ut supra quoque Oseae verbis. Restat com- plexionis generalis ad hanc speciem applicatio. Lex quae beneficos nos esse jubet, haud dubie ante omnia a nobis exigit, ut quantum in nobis est, aeternae aliorum saluti consulamus, & quidem quam celerrime, cum nemo sibi possit crastinum polliceri. Legem de Sabbato esse ritua- lem res ipsa docet, & extra controversiam est. Simul non poterant Christus docendis, Apostoli ad ejus doctri- nam praeparandis hominibus incumbere, & ea parare quae ad rigidam sabbati observationem pertinebant, ut ante etiam diximus. Debebat ergo ex eo quod ante conclu- sum erat, lex sabbati cedere praecepto sanctae institutio- nis. Quod autem hic ex Osea probatur, leges omnes ri- tuum multo minoris esse pretii apud Deum, quam leges morum, praesertim vero religionis ac beneficentiae, con- spectissimae est veritatis, quae multos etiam ex profanis gentibus non effugit. Ex multis pauca adferam. Plato Alcibiade II. κὴ γὰρ ἂν δεινὸν εἴη, εἰ πρὸς τὰ δῶρα καὶ τὰς θυ- σίας ἀποβλέπυσιν ἡμῶν οἱ θεοὶ, ἀλλὰ μὴ πρὸς τὴν ψυχὴν ἄν- τις ὅσιός τε καὶ δίκαιος ὢν τυγχάνῃ. In quam sententiam & in de republica libris multa praeclare sunt dicta. Versus quos jam adducam alii Menandro adscribunt, alii Philemoni, neutro indignos. Referam autem ita ut emendandos censeo:

Εἰ θυσίαν τις προσφέρων ὦ πάμφιλε Ταύρων τε πλῆθος ἢ ἐρίφων ἢ νὴ Δία Ἑτέρων τοιύτων, ἢ κατασκευάσματα Χρυσᾶς ποιήσας χλαμύδας ἤτοι πορφυρᾶς,

Ἤ δι' ἐλέφαντος ἢ σμαράγδυ ζώδια, Εὔνεν νομίζει τὸν θεὸν καθιστάναι, Πλανᾶτ' ἐκεῖνος καὶ φρένας κωφὰς ἔχει. Δεῖ γὰρ τὸν ἄνδρα χρήσιμον πεφυκέναι, Μὴ παρθένους φθείροντα καὶ μοιχώμενον, Κλέπτοντα καὶ σφάττοντα χρημάτων χάριν. Μηδὲ βελόνης ἔναμμ' ἐπιθυμῇς πάμφιλε. Ὁ γὰρ θεὸς βλέπει σε πλησίον παρών. Ejusdem auctoris est & hoc: Θύε͂ δὲ θύε διὰ τέλους δίκαιος ὢν, Μὴ λαμπρὸς ὢν ταῖς χλαμύσι ὡς τῇ καρδίᾳ : Accedat his Persius : Quin damus id superis! de magna quod dare lance Non possit magni Messalæ lippa propago : Compositum jus fasque animi, sanctosq; recessus Mentis & incoctum generoso pectus honesto. Hoc cedo ut admoveam templis & farre litabo. Hierocles in eundem sensum: οἶδε τιμᾷν θεὸν ὁ προηγουμέ- νως ἱερεὺς ἑαυτὸν προσάγων καὶ ἄγαλμα θεῖον τεκταίνων τὴν ἑαυτοῦ ψυχὴν καὶ ναὸν εἰς ὑποδοχὴν τοῦ θείου φωτὸς τὸν ἑαυτοῦ παρασκευάζων νοῦν : Nam Deus, ut ille ibidem ait, τὸ εὐτελέ- στατον προκρινεῖ τῆς πολυτελείας ὅταν θεοσεβείας γνώμῃ κοσ- μῆται· μετ' αὐτῆς γὰρ πάντα θεοφιλῆ, καὶ ἄνευ ταύτης οὐδὲν θεῷ φίλον ἂν ποτε γίνοιτο. Commiscet Grotius legem DEI cum traditio- nibus Judæorum. Opera servilia prohibita erant Sabbato in lege divina; sed num spicas confrica- re ad ea opera referendum sit, non erat e pandectis Judaicis discendum, quorum non est Canonica autoritas. Etsi vero Christus expresse non neget epus esse famulum, non tamen id concedit quod tale sit, ac prohibeatur in lege. Satis erat ex ipsas circumstantiis tueri factum discipulorum. Etsi recte Grotius e Seneca, Necessitas magnum humanæ imbecillitatis patrocinium, quicquid cogit, excusat : Non probari tamen simpliciter potest, quod hoc loco idem urget, Lex Sabbati & lex de propositis panibus non edendis nisi a Sacerdotibus, non æque sunt rituales. Hæc enim plane ritua- lis fuit. In illa vero multum erat moralitatis, de quo suo loco. Est autem collectionis Christi hæc ratio; Si David in casu necessitatis panibus sa- cris soli Deo destinatis vesci potuit, multo magis Apostoli potuere in Sabbato spicas fricare, ut famem sedarent : quia vesci illis legi refragabatur : Spicas autem fricare diserte nulla lege prohibitum est, unde B. Hunnius : Et sane opus ipsum, quod fece- rant, nequaquam erat ejus generis, ut per id Sabba- tismi sanctificationi vel tantillum decederet. Alias enim pari ratione non licuisset edere aut bibere Sab- bato, quod falsum esse quisque palam intelligit. Christus autem ἐκ περιουσίας respondet Pharisæis per quandam concessionem, sed quæ adjunctam ha- beret defensionem aliam, ut eo validius premeret, & urgeret adversarios Pharisæos, quasi dicat : Esto, sit hoc tale opus, quo alias Sabbatum profanaretur (quod tamen haud dum a vobis probatum est) ta- men casus necessitatis eximit a lege, vel excusat di- sipulos meos, ut quod egerunt, pro violatione ordi- nis divini haberi nequeat. Posse autem leges illas ceremoniales hujusmodi admittere dispensatio- nem, probat Salvator exemplo Davidis. Chryso- stomus ita habet : ubi necessitas adest, ibi lapsus repre- hensioni non est obnoxius. Quare hic ridicule Phari- sæi naturam innoxiam criminantur. Quorum ac- cusationem ad liquidum Dominus diluit exemplo Davidis, omnem dubitationis umbram ambigens, de- fensione etiam supra causæ usum abundante. Plus enim sane quiddam ausus erat David, qui quod Pro- phetæ præsertim & Dei Messiæ Patri nefas erat, pa- nes propositionis esuriens comedit, ipse & comites ejus, quos comedere non licebat, nisi solis Sacerdoti- bus. In altero argumento Christi de operis Sacerdo- tum circa sacrificia in Sabbato recte se habent Gro- tianæ annotationes : Sed dicas aliquis templi ritus observari non poterant nisi labor aliquis die Sabbati insumeretur: quæ autem talis connexio est inter pro- pheticum Christi ejusque Apostolorum munus, & inter spicarum vulsionem? Nimirum ista, quod Christus ejusq́; Apostoli ita occupati fuerant in ob- eundo suo munere, ut non vacaret ipsis cibum sibi pa- rare quo Sabbati die vescerentur. Aut ergo inter- mittere debuerant munus Propheticum, aut facere contra τὸ ῥητὸν legis Sabbati. Sacerdotale autem mu- nus non intermittebatur ob legem Sabbati, igitur nec propheticum, quod majus erat, intermitti eo nomine debebat. Chrysostomus hanc reddit consecutionis rationem, quod si non violant Sacerdotes legem de Sabbato, dum in templo coram Domino operantur, multo minus eos, qui in præsentia Christi, qui major templo est, spicas fricant, legem violare: Quomodo Sacerdotes, gnari utique in quo sita sit legis observa- tio, ejusq́; cultores exacti, Sabbatis ligna scindunt, & ignem accendunt? Quid vobis videtur? an Sa- cerdotes Sabbatum tunc violant? minime. Atqui sic habetote: majus hic quidpiam templo est, hoc est: major sum ego templo, cum sim Dominus templi & legis; sum autem cum discipulis; unde ipsis plenum jus est, cum usus poposcerit, Sabbato solvendi, plus etiam aliquanto, quam sacerdotibus. Argumen- tum autem Christi est ejusmodi: Sacerdotes cum Dei opus faciunt Sabbato, tamen legem non vio- lant: itaque Sabbati lege omnia opera non prohi- bentur sine exceptione: quod si Sacerdotes quo- minus sabbato quiescerent, excusabat templi cul- tus, multo magis ipse templi & Sabbati Dominus, Dei opus faciens, Sabbati lege non tenebatur. Apparet ergo Christum propositam hypothesin revocare; & merito quidem. Nam superstitiose reprehensi fuerant discipuli à Pharisæis, ac proin- de nulla excusatione egebant; ut hic Beza.

## 12:8
Ver. 8. For the Son of man is Lord even of the Sabbath.] They err who understand Christ specifically by the Son of man in this place. For Christ, acting on earth, professed himself subject to the law, and neither derogated from it, nor abrogated it, but interpreted it according to the Father's mind, and confirmed his interpretation both by the authority of the law and by arguments drawn from equity and goodness. Therefore, this Son of man is any man whatsoever, which Mark makes so plain that it cannot be contradicted. For thus Christ speaks in his account: The Sabbath is for the sake of man, not man for the sake of the Sabbath; wherefore the son of man is Lord also of the Sabbath. For these words do not cohere if you interpret the son of man as the Messiah, sent with the power of abolishing the law. Add now, that Jesus at that time neither preached himself to be Christ to the people or the Pharisees, nor wished it to be preached. See below XVI. 21. Mark VIII. 30. But, as I said, it is most well known to the Hebrews that ben adam signifies any man whatsoever, although sometimes, as we have said, it is restricted to the less illustrious: Nor is it said otherwise below 32. whoever shall speak a word against the Son of man: as we shall say therein. The sense, therefore, of the words of Christ, which are expressed somewhat more fully by Mark, is this: That which is provided for the sake of another thing, that ought to yield to him for whose sake it was provided. But the Sabbath was provided for the sake of man, therefore it ought to yield to man, surely where it is a matter of man's salvation, to be Lord is said in Greek as in Hebrew baal, who has the right of using some thing: Just as man, in such a case, has the right of turning even the Sabbath day to his own use. It is clearly the same as what Rabbi Jonathan said, that the Sabbath was delivered into the hand of men, and not men into the hand of the Sabbath. For to be delivered into the hand is the same as to be in dominion. Therefore, Christ here also used a rule well known among the Jews.

Grotius decides quite confidently that those who understand Christ here are in error. But with reasons not sufficiently firm. For that Christ first confessed himself subject to the law, this pertains to the form of a servant, and voluntary obedience to the law; nor should that which pertains to the form of God, in which he was when he emptied himself for the sake of our redemption, be opposed to it. For the Apostle joins these, but does not oppose them as inconsistent, Phil. II. 6. and such is that, that Christ was Lord of the Sabbath, and of the law itself. For this befits Christ both by reason of his divine nature in itself and by itself, and by reason of his human nature; on account of the hypostatic union, by which he was in the form of God. Because if he had been subject to the law by himself, as man, he would neither have voluntarily subjected himself to the law, nor could he have fulfilled the law in our place, as one who was himself obligated to perform the same for himself. But as for what then pertains to the passage of Mark, which he makes parallel to this in chap. II. v. last, but Flacius in his gloss contends that it is not parallel, and concerns a different history, that it is so plain, in favor of the Grotian opinion, as Grotius thinks, neither can we see, nor have others seen. For most have accepted this concerning Christ, that he is Lord of the Sabbath. Nor indeed is it necessary that the particle so be rendered in an illative sense, which it is known is also sometimes the same as and, or therefore. Which sense a comparison with our passage of Matthew, and Luke chap. VI. 5. confirms. For that a peculiar reason is completed by these words, is not at all obscure from them, since they add nothing more. And therefore that also is urged in Mark, that the Sabbath was instituted for the sake of man, namely for his good, and that, that Christ, who it is established is called the Son of man, is also Lord of the Sabbath, which reason the other Evangelists exhibited specifically. What furthermore Grotius urges thirdly, that Jesus had not yet preached himself as Christ to the people or the Pharisees then, nor wished it to be preached, does not bind. For it was arbitrary when, or where he wished himself to be so preached. And already proclaimed from heaven, nay, by John having been sent in the preceding chapter, he had not only testified that he was he, but had confirmed it also by works and the testimony of Scripture. Finally, when we teach that the Son of man is Lord of the Sabbath and of the law, in this place, we do not interpret it in such a way that the Messiah was sent with the power of abolishing the law. For this is opposed to the protestation of Christ himself, Matt. V. I came not to destroy the law, but to fulfill. And could He not Himself as Lord of the Sabbath be dispensed regarding the Sabbath, even if He did not antiquate nor abrogate the law of the Sabbath? That this is deservedly accepted concerning Christ, first that very name ὁ υἱὸς τ. ἀνθρώπε teaches, by which He perpetually designates Himself, and so that He may distinguish Himself from others He nowhere calls any man whatsoever the son of man, just as it cannot be taken of any other than Christ in v. 32. Next, the prefixed article ὁ, which insinuates a singular son of man definitely, but not just anyone indefinitely; Thirdly, if Mark understood any man whatsoever, without doubt he would repeat the word man, which he had used twice; but since he varies the discourse, and now speaks not of man, but of τῷ υἱῷ τ ἀνθρώπε, he sufficiently indicates that he understands not any man in general, but that very one who is peculiarly called the son of man. Fourthly, the predicate is too august for it to suit any man whatsoever. For no mortal is Lord of either the Sabbath or the law. This is proper to God alone: whose it is to bring forth law, his it is also to dispense regarding the law, and to be Lord of the law. And this eulogy is far too magnificent to be able to be compared with the Rabbinic dictum; that the Sabbath was delivered into the hands of men, who certainly cannot dispense regarding the Sabbath at their own discretion according to the opinion of the Rabbis: so far are they from being Lords of the Sabbath. And therefore that axiom must be accepted κατὰ τι: namely in that sense which the words of Christ bear, the Sabbath is for the sake of man, but not man for the sake of the Sabbath. Nor is the Son of man called κύριος τ. Σαββάτε for that reason alone, that whatever right he may have of using the Sabbath; something more is added to this dignity, namely that he can dispose of the Sabbath by his own authority. Otherwise he would not be called absolutely Lord of the Sabbath.

Latin:

Vers. 8. Κύριος γάρ ἐστι καὶ τοῦ σαββάτου ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου.] Errant qui υἱὸν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου hoc loco Christum peculiariter intelligunt. Christus enim in terris agens legi se subditum professus est, neque ei aut derogavit, aut abrogavit, sed ex Patris sententia eam est interpretatus, suamque interpre- tationem & legis auctoritate & ductis ex æquo bono q; ar- gumentis confirmavit. Est ergo hic υἱὸς ἀνθρώπου homo qui- vis, quod ita apertum facit Marcus, ut contradici nequeat. Ita enim apud illum loquitur Christus: Sabbatum est hominis causa, non homo Sabbati causa; quare filius hominis etiam Sab- bati est Dominus. Hæc enim verba non cohærent, si filium hominis interpreteris Messiam, missum cum potestate legis antiquandæ. Adde jam, quod Jesus eo tempore se esse Christum populo aut Pharisæis nec prædicaverit, nec præ- dicari voluerit. Vide infra XVI. 21. Marci VIII. 30. Sed, ut dixi, notissimum est Hebræis בן אדם hominem quemvis significare, quanquam interdum, ut diximus, ad minus illustres restringitur: Neque aliter dicitur infra 32. ὃς ἐὰν εἴπῃ λόγον κατὰ τοῦ υἱοῦ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου: ut inibi dicemus. Sensus igitur Christi verborum quæ plenius aliquanto sunt à Marco expressa hic est: Quod alterius rei causa compa- ratum est, id cedere debet ei cujus causa comparatum est. At Sabbatum comparatum est hominis causa, debet ergo homini cedere, nimirum ubi de hominis salute agitur, κύ- ριος εἶναι Græce ut Hebraice בעל dicitur, qui aliquâ re utendi jus habet: Sicut homo, in tali casu, jus habet vertendi in usum suum etiam Sabbati diem. Plane idem est quod dixit Rabbi Jonathan, Sabbatum traditum esse in manum hominum, & non homines in manum Sabbati. Nam tradi in manum, idem est quod esse in dominio. Er- go hic etiam notam inter Judæos regulam Christus usur- pavit.

Satis confidenter decernit Grotius, errare eos, qui Christum hic intelligunt. At rationibus non satis firmis. Nam quod primum Christus legi se subditum confessus est, hoc ad formam servi, & obedientiam legis voluntariam pertinet; nec op- poni ei debet, quod ad τὴν μορφὴν τοῦ θεοῦ spectat, in qua erat, cum se nostræ redemptionis causa exinanivit. Nam hæc conjungit, non autem ut ἀσύστατα opponit Apostolus Phil. II. 6. tale autem est illud, quod Christus Dominus Sabba- ti, ipsiusque legis, fuerit. Hoc enim Christo convenit tum ratione divinæ naturæ καθ᾽ αὑτὸ & per se, tum ratione humanæ naturæ; ob commu- nicationem hypostaticam, qua fuit in forma Dei. Quia si per se legi fuisset obnoxius, ut homo, ne- que ultro se legi subjecisset, neque nostri loco le- gem implere potuisset, utpote qui ipse pro se ean- dem præstare obligatus fuerit. Quod vero de- inde Marci locum attinet, quem parallelum huic facit cap. II. v. ult. sed parallelum esse negat, ac di- versam historiam concernere Flacius in gloss. contendit, eum ita apertum esse, pro Grotiana sententia, uti putat Grotius, neque nos videre possumus, neque viderunt alii. Plerique enim de Christo hoc acceperunt, quod Dominus Sabbati sit. Nec vero necessum est, ut sensu illativo red- datur particula ὥστε, quam etiam nonnunquam idem esse, quod καὶ, vel ἄρα, notum est. Quem sensum collatio cum nostro Matthæi, & Lucæ cap. VI. 5. loco comprobat. Nam quod peculiaris ratio his verbis absolvatur, ex iisdem minime ob- scurum est, quum nihil amplius addant. Ideo- que & illud apud Marcum urgetur, quod hominis causa Sabbatum institutum sit, ejus nempe bono, & illud, quod Christus quem constat vocari Fi- lius hominis, etiam Sabbati Dominus sit, quam rationem cæteri Evangelistæ peculiariter exhi- buere. Quod porro tertio urget Grotius, quod Jesus nondum se Christum populo aut Pharisæis tum prædicarit, nec prædicari voluerit, non stringit. Nam id arbitrarium erat quando, aut ubi se ita prædicari vellet. Et de cælo jam proclamatus, imo à Johanne missis cap. præced. se eum esse non testatus solum ipse fuerat, sed operibus quoque ac testimonio Scripturæ confirmarat. Denique cum Filium hominis Dominum Sabbati ac legis es- se, hoc loco docemus, non interpretamur id ita, quod Messias missus sit cum potestate legis antiquan- dæ. Hoc enim adversatur ipsius Christi prote- stationi Matth. V. Non veni solvere legem, sed im- plere. Et annon potuit ipse ut Dominus Sabba- ti dispensari circa Sabbatum, etiamsi legem Sab- bati non antiquaret, nec abrogaret? Quod autem de Christo hoc merito accipiatur, primo ipsum nomen illud ὁ υἱὸς τ. ἀνθρώπε, docet, quo perpe- tuo seipsum designat, atque ut se ab aliis discer- nat nusquam hominem quemvis filium hominis vocat, uti nec de alio quam Christo v. 32. accipi potest. Deinde articulus præfixus ὁ, qui singula- rem hominis filium definite, non vero quemvis indefinite insinuat; Tertio si hominem quemvis in- telligeret Marcus, sine dubio vocem hominis re- peteret, qua bis usus erat; quum vero sermonem variet, & jam non de homine, sed de τῷ υἱῷ τ ἀνθρώπε loquatur, non quemvis in genere homi- nem, sed ipsum illum, qui peculiariter filius ho- minis dicitur, se intelligere satis indicat. Quar- to nimis augustum est prædicatum, quam ut ho- mini cuivis conveniat. Nemo enim mortalium vel Sabbati vel legis Dominus est. Proprium est hoc uni Deo: cujus est legem ferre, ejus etiam est de lege dispensare, ac legis Dominum esse. Et longe magnificentiuseft hoc elogium, quam ut componi possit cum Rabbinico dicte- rio; Sabbatum traditum esse in manus hominum, qui certe non pro arbitrio de Sabbato dispensa- re possunt ex Rabbinorum sententia: tantum abest ut Sabbati Domini sint. Ideoque axioma il- lud κατὰ τι accipiendum: eo nempe sensu, quem verba Christi ferunt, Sabbatum est hominis causa, non vero homo Sabbati causa. Neque eo solum κύριος τ. Σαββάτε Filius hominis dicitur, quod jus qualecunque habeat utendi Sabbato; Insertur quid amplius hac dignitate, quod nempe αὐτεξό- σίως de Sabbato disponere possit. Alias absolute non diceretur κύριος τẽ Cαββάτε.

## 12:11
Verse 11. Who shall be of you] A mode of speaking by which the Jews formed their hypotheses, as we observed at chapter VII. The Essenes differed from the others in the explanation of the Sabbath law, scarcely admitting any excuse. But the more common interpretation admitted exceptions. By the most recent law of the Jews, which is some centuries later than the age of Christ, it is established that if a beast has fallen into a pit on the Sabbath, it should be fed, and if need be, propped up with straw placed underneath, so that it may last until the following day: provided that the pit is such that it would drown the beast unless it is immediately led out. I omit what the Jews might do now; certainly in the age of Christ the opinion was more accepted that the religion of the Sabbath does not prevent the life of a beast from being cared for. For this is what is read in the old Babylonian law of the Hebrews: the Sabbath is pushed aside by the danger to a life: which they themselves say, סעַת נֶפֶשׁ רחה שַׁבָּת. The words in the Mishnah are: Every work is prohibited on the Sabbath, unless it is done for a soul. And so accepted was that exception among the Jews, that in many codices it began to be written in as an interpretation: which I gather from Tertullian. For thus he says in the fourth book against Marcion: Just as also again in the law: You shall not do any work in it, except that which shall be done for every soul. And against the Jews he cites the law thus: You shall not do any servile work in it, except that which pertains to the soul. But also Jerome on Isaiah XXXVIII: It is commanded in the law that we should not do servile work on the Sabbath, that we should not light a fire, that we should sit in one place, that we should do only those things which pertain to the salvation of the soul. But by the name of soul, the ancient interpreters included the life of a beast. Wherefore that new, more rigid interpretation was devised out of hatred for Christians, just as that Dositheus, whom Origen and Epiphanius mention, immediately after the age of Christ, made the interpretation of the Sabbath law more severe. From this rule of law, therefore, Christ supports that argument which we have proposed above in the third place. It is not foreign to this place what Scaevola had noted from the Roman pontifical law, that if an ox had fallen into a pit, and the head of the household had freed it by applying labor, it was not seen to have polluted the holidays. Macrobius mentions this in Saturnalia, book 1, chapter 16.

Latin:

Vers. 11. Τίς ἔται ἐξ ὑμῶν] Modus loquendi quo Judæi formabant τὰς ὑποθέσεις, ut ad caput VII. observavimus. Dissentiebant in explicatione legis Sabbati Esseni à cæteris, vix ullam recipientes excusationem. At communior inter- pretatio exceptiones admittebat. Jure Judæorum novissi- mo, quod Christi ætate aliquot seculis est posterius, consti- tuitur ut pecus in fossam prolapsum in sabbato alatur, & si opus sit stramine subjecto fulciatur, ut duret in diem se- quentem : quod si talis sit fossa, quæ demersura sit pecudem ni continuo educatur. Quid nunc facturi sint Judæi omit- to, certe Christi ætate receptior erat sententia, non obstare Sabbati religionem quominus vitæ pecudis consulatur. Hoc enim est quod in veteri Babylonico Hebræorum ju- re legitur periculo animæ pelli sabbatum: quod ipsi dicunt, סעַת נֶפֶשׁ רחה שַׁבָּת. Verba in Misnajot sunt: O- mne opus prohibetur in Sabbato, nisi fit pro anima. Atque a- deo recepta erat apud Judæos ista exceptio, ut in multis co- dicibus legi vice interpretamenti ascribi cœperit: quod ex Tertulliano colligo. Ita enim is ait quarto adversus Mar- cionem : Sicut & rursus in lege : Non facies omne opus in eo, nisi quod fiet omni animæ. Et contra Judæos ita legem citat: Omne opus servile non facietis in eo, præterquam quod ad ani- mam pertinet. Sed & Hieronymus ad XXXVIII. Esaiæ: Le- ge præceptum est ne in Sabbato opus servile faciamus, ne accen- damus ignem, ut in uno sedeamus loco, ut illa tantum faciamus quæ ad animæ salutem pertinent. Animæ autem nomine an- tiqui interpretes pecudis vitam comprehendebant. Qua- re nova illa interpretatio rigidior odio Christianorum est excogitata, sicut & Dositheus ille, cujus Origenes & Epi- phanius meminerunt, statim post Christi ætatem exaspe- ravit interpretando legem sabbati. Ex hac ergo juris regu- la Christus fulcit argumentum illud, quod supra tertio lo- co propositum duximus. Non est ab hoc loco alienum quod ex Romanorum jure pontificio Scævola notaverat, si bos in specum decidisset, eumque paterfamilias adhibi- tis operis liberasset, non esse visum ferias polluisse. Me- minit Macrobius Saturn. l. c. 16.

## 12:12
Verse 12. How much then does a man differ from a sheep] Lest the Pharisees should object that in their law it is a matter of life, here of the integrity of a limb, Christ meets them, showing that a man is so much more valuable than a beast that the health of a man deservedly outweighs the life of a beast.

To do well] This is to do good, as Mark and Luke said in one word. But to do good in Luke VI. 9, Acts XIV. 17, as also to do good works in Paul 1 Tim. VI. 18, is the same as to do a kindness. What the opinion of Christ is, is more fully understood from Mark and Luke, where Christ asks whether it is lawful on the Sabbath to do good or indeed to do evil, where to do evil is to harm, but in that sense in which he is said to kill who denies food. For thus he harms who does not help a miserable person whom he can help, whether by divine aid or even by human skill. There is a charming story in Synesius about a Sabbatarian sailor, who, upon the arrival of the seventh day, would abandon the rudder, and for a long time could be compelled neither by force nor by threats to perform his duty: until, as the storm grew worse and the danger was now manifest, he rose of his own accord, saying that the matter had been brought to such a pass that it was lawful to work even on the Sabbath. Thus in Josephus, Jonathan, the brother of Judas Maccabeus, encourages his men to battle on the Sabbath, saying that the danger was for their lives. Where, therefore, some sick or weak person implores help that is in your power, it remains that you either kindly bring him aid, or cruelly deny it. But which, says Christ, seems to you to be more fitting for a festive and holy day? It must be recalled to memory what we said above, that for the exception of equity to have a place, the ultimate necessity is not required, but such a one as the nature of the law easily admits.

Latin:

Vers. 12. Πόσῳ ὖν διαφέρει ἄνθρωπος προβάτε] Ne ob- jicerent Pharisæi in suo jure agi de vita, hic de membri in- tegritate, occurrit Christus ostendens tanto hominem pecude esse potiorem, ut merito hominis sanitas pecudis vitæ præponderet.

Καλῶς ποιεῖν] Hoc est ἀγαθοποιῆσαι ut uno verbo dixe- runt Marcus & Lucas. ἀγαθοποιεῖν autem apud Lucam VI. 9. Actor. XIV. 17. ut & ἀγαθοεργεῖν apud Paulum 1. Tim. VI. 18. idem est quod εὐεργετεῖν. Quæ Christi sit sententia plenius intelligitur ex Marco & Luca, ubi Christus interro- gat, liceatne in Sabbato ἀγαθοποιῆσαι an vero κακοποιῆσαι, ubi κακοποιῆσαι est nocere, sed eo sensu quo necare dicitur qui alimentum negat. Nam sic nocet qui miserum non ju- vat quem potest juvare, sive divina ope sive etiam arte hu- mana. Lepida est apud Synesium narratio de nauta sabba- tario, qui die septimo adventante omittebat gubernacu- lum, ac diu neque vi neq; minis cogi poterat ut munere suo fungeretur: donec ingravescente tempestate & mani- festo jam periculo, ultro surrexit, dictitans rem in eum ca- sum perductam quo & sabbato opus facere liceret.Sic apud Josephum Jonathas Judæ Maccabæi frater suos sabbato in prælium animat dicens,περὶ τῶν ψυχῶν αὐτοῖς εἶναι τὸν κίν- δυνον. Ubi ergo ægrotus aliquis aut debilis auxilium quod in tua sit facultate implorat, restat aut opem ei benigne fe- ras, aut crudeliter deneges. Utrum vero, inquit Christus, vobis videtur diei festo ac sacro melius convenire? Repe- tendum memoria est, quod supra diximus, ut locum ha- beat æquitatis exceptio, non requiri ultimam necessita- tem, sed talem quam facile admittat legis natura.

## 12:13
Verse 13. He says to the man] The true doctrine concerning the Sabbath having now been set forth, he cuts off every handle for calumny. For without contact, by voice alone, he heals the man, which could not even have the appearance of a violated Sabbath.

And he stretched it out and it was restored whole, as the other] Here also the conjunction with the verb has the force of a participle. For the sense is, he stretched it out to be restored whole, as the other: for he could not have stretched out the hand unless it had been restored by divine power.

to hold a council, and in this place some codices have they held a council as an interpretation. In Hebrew it would have been they took counsel, which the LXX are accustomed to translate sometimes as they deliberated, sometimes as they took counsel. Having gone out] From the synagogue, namely, in which these things had been done, as appears above in verse 9. Verse 15. He withdrew] Athanasius is used in this place also, to prove that flight is lawful. Concerning which matter we have spoken above. All] Namely, those who desired to be healed by him: in which way universal particles are often to be interpreted. Verse 16. That they should not make him known] Before the time of the resurrection, namely. It does not seem to me that he has deserved a censorious note in this place, who thinks that the cause of the enjoined silence is the same as that of the withdrawal. For also what follows from the Prophet seems to demand that sense. Gregory Nazianzen does not poorly bring forward the flight from persecutors among the causes of a just flight, which Origen also illustrates with the example of Aristotle, who, departing from Athens, said that he did so, lest he should give the Athenians an occasion to commit another crime after the killing of Socrates and to sin a second time against philosophy. It seemed still excusable in some way, if not of all, at least of a great part of the Pharisees, the zeal for ancestral traditions. And so, by adding other miracles upon others, Christ wished to await their repentance, meanwhile restraining them from the atrocity of the crime, until, opposing their own conscience, as we shall soon see some of them did, they had more and more deserved to be stained with innocent blood, and by that crime to bring upon themselves the most serious punishments, which was not to happen unless the doctrine of Christ had already been completed, as Tertullian, otherwise an excessive accuser of flight, not poorly observes. Origen, to Celsus objecting this very thing, besides what we have said, replies in this manner: ὀυκ ἔτι δι᾽ ἀγεννέις, τὸ μετ᾿ οἰ- κονομίας περιΐσταμενοι τῆς κινδύνες, μὴ ὀμόσε ἀυτοῖς χωρεῖν· κὶ διὰ φόβον θανάτε, ἀλλּ ὑπὲρ τῶ χρησίμως ἀυτοῖς τῷ βίῳ ἐπιδη- μῆναι ἑτέρες ὠφελεῖν, ὅως ἐπιβῆ ὁ ἐπιτήδειος καιρὸς τῶ τὸν ἀ- νειληφότα τὴν ἀνθρωπίνην φύσιν ἀνθρώπῳ θάνατον ἀποθανεῖν ὑ- χοῦλα τι χρήσιμον τοῖς ἀνθρώποις. Vers. 18. ἰδὲ ὁ παῖς με] The Septuagint in many places added certain things of their own to explain the meaning of the Hebrew words: as in this place before ὁ παῖς με they placed Ἰακὼβ & before ὁ ἐκλεκτός με, Ἰσραήλ: and thus Justin twice cites it while disputing with Trypho the Jew. For what Eusebius says in the ninth book of the Evangelical Demonstration, παρὰ τοῖς ἑβδο- μήκοντα ὠβέλισται τὸ τῷ Ἰακώβ κὶ τὸ τῷ Ἰσραὴλ ὄνομα, is to be understood thus: that those words were marked by the critics with an obelus as having been added, since they did not exist in the Hebrew language. For Epiphanius, Jerome, and Augustine teach us that such was the use of the obelus in the editions of the Greek version of the Old Testament. Therefore, the man of highest learning errs, who for that reason denies that these words were written by the seventy interpreters. Nor do I doubt that this passage of the Prophet was understood by the same interpreters as if it were speaking of the Hebrew people, and that because of those things which precede in chapter XLI. 8. and those which follow in XLIII. 1. although they ought to have observed from other passages of Isaiah, and especially from those which are in the Prophet chapter XLIV. 6. that this treats of him who was to bring light both to the Jews and to the Gentiles: which the Chaldean paraphrast rightly saw, who added the name of Messiah here. Moreover, Justin, in order to win the authority of the seventy interpreters to his side, wishes Christ to be indicated by the name of Jacob and Israel, which to me, at least in this instance, does not seem probable.

Grotius rightly accepts the prophecy of Isaiah XLII. concerning Christ, and teaches that it must be accepted, because from other passages of Isaiah, especially from those which are in the Prophet c. XLIV. 6. it may be observed that this treats of him who was to bring light both to the Jews and to the Gentiles: which he observes the Chaldean also rightly saw, who added the name of Messiah here. These things, however, we deservedly oppose to the distortion of the Prophetic passage, which he snatched away in his Annotations on Isaiah. But that it treats not of Isaiah, but of the Messiah, we demonstrated in our vindication of that passage, where we also weighed the whole text brought here by Matthew with the Grotian notes on the present passage of Matthew. Therefore, the τὸ πραχθὲν πρᾶξαι does not please. Therefore, those things may be sought from there. But whether all the editions of the LXX interpreters placed Ἰακὼβ here before ὁ παῖς με, and Ἰσραήλ before ὁ ἐκλεκτός με, just as the allegation of Justin has it in the Dialogue with Trypho, the words of Eusebius in the IXth book of the Evangelical Demonstration, παρὰ τοῖς ἑβδομήκοντα, render doubtful, in our judgment.

The name Jacob and Israel has been obelized, which does not mean (as Grotius thinks) that those words were marked with an obelus by the Critics as if they were added, since they did not exist in the Hebrew language, but that they were omitted by the LXX Interpreters themselves in their genuine editions. For although that use of the obelus may have been common among the Critics in the editions of the Greek version of the Old Testament, which Grotius points out, as is evident from the example of Origen: Eusebius, however, does not speak of the obelus of the Critics, but says, 'it has been obelized among the Seventy,' because those names were omitted by the LXX themselves, and are deservedly marked with an obelus.

Latin:

Vers. 13. Λέγει τῷ ἀνθρώπῳ] Vera doctrina de Sabbato ex- posita jam omnein calumniæ ansam præcidit. Nam sine contactu sola voce hominem sanat, quod ne speciem qui- dem violati sabbati habere poterat.
