Καὶ ἐξέτεινε καὶ ἀποκατεςάθη ὑγιὴς, ὡς ἡ ἄλλη] Hic quoque conjunctio cum verbo vim participii habet. Sensus enim est, ἐξέτεινε ἀποκαταςαθῆναι ὑγιῆ, ὡς ἡ ἄλλη: neque enim extendere manum potuisset nisi divina virtute restitu- tam.

βούλιον ποιεῖν, & hoc loco quidam codices ex interpretamen- to habent συμβούλιον ἐποίησαν. In Hebræo fuerit נועצון quod LXX. modo ἐβουλεύσαντο, modo συνβουλεύσαντο ver- tere solent. ἐξελθόντες] Ex Synagoga scilicet, in qua hæc erant ge- sta ut apparet supra commate 9. Vers. 15. Ἀνεχώρησεν] Ucitur hoc quoque loco Atha- nasius, ut probet licitam esse fugam. Qua de re diximus supra. Πάντας] Nempe qui sanari ab ipso cuperent: quomodo sæpe interpretandæ sunt particulæ universales. Vers. 16. ἵνα μὴ φανερὸν αὐτὸν ποιήσωσι] Ante tempus re- surrectionis scilicet Non videtur mihi hoc loco notam cen- soriam meruisse, qui injuncti silentii causam eandem esse putat quæ secessus fuerat. Nam & quod ex Propheta sequi- tur, eum videtur sensum postulare. Gregorius Nazianze- nus non male inter causas justæ fugæ adfert τὴν φυγὴν τῶν διωκόντων, quod Origenes Aristotelis quoque exemplo illu- strat, qui Athenis discedens, dixerit id se facere, ne occasio- nem daret Atheniensibus alterum scelus admittendi post cædem Socratis κὶ δευτέραν ὀὺς τὴν φιλοσοφίαν ἀσεβεῖν. Vide- batur adhuc excusabile aliquo modo si non omnium, sal- tem magnæ partis Pharisæorum, studium pro avitis tradi- tionibus, Itaque additis aliis superalia miraculis opperiri il- lorum pœnitentiam Christus voluit, interim eos arcens ab atrocitate facinoris, donec suam ipsi conscientiam oppu- gnantes, ut mox quosdam ipsorum fecisse videbimus, ma- gis magisque meruissent innoxio sanguine inquinari, eoque scelere gravissimas in se pœnas accersere, quod fieri non o- portebat nisi consummata jam Christi doctrina, ut Tertul- lianus, nimius alioqui fugæ accusator, non male observat. Origenes Celso hoc ipsum objicienti, præter id quod dixi- mus, hunc in modum respondet: ὀυκ ἔτι δι᾽ ἀγεννέις, τὸ μετ᾿ οἰ- κονομίας περιΐσταμενοι τῆς κινδύνες, μὴ ὀμόσε ἀυτοῖς χωρεῖν· κὶ διὰ φόβον θανάτε, ἀλλ᾽ ὑπὲρ τῶ χρησίμως ἀυτοῖς τῷ βίῳ ἐπιδη- μῆναι ἑτέρες ὠφελεῖν, ὅως ἐπιβῆ ὁ ἐπιτήδειος καιρὸς τῶ τὸν ἀ- νειληφότα τὴν ἀνθρωπίνην φύσιν ἀνθρώπῳ θάνατον ἀποθανεῖν ὑ- χοῦλα τι χρήσιμον τοῖς ἀνθρώποις. Vers. 18. ἰδὲ ὁ παῖς με] Septuaginta multis in locis de suo quædam addiderunt ad explicandam Hebraicorũ ver- borum sententiam: ut hoc loco ante ὁ παῖς με posuerunt Ἰακὼβ & ante ὁ ἐκλεκτός με, Ἰσραήλ : atque ita bis citat cum Tryphone Judæo disputans Justinus. Quod enim ait Eu- sebius nono Evangelicæ demonstrationis, παρὰ τοῖς ἑβδο- μήκοντα ὠβέλισται τὸ τῷ Ἰακὼβ κὶ τὸ τῷ Ἰσραὴλ ὄνομα ita ac- cipiendum est, à Criticis ea verba obelo notata tanquam quæ adjecta sint, cum in Hebræo sermone non exstarent. Nam eum fuisse obeli usum in editionibus versionis Græcæ Veteris Testamenti docent nos Epiphanius, Hieronymus, Augustinus. Errat igitur vir summæ eruditionis, qui ideo negat hæc verba à septuaginta Interpretibus scripta esse. Neque dubito ab iisdem Interpretibus hunc Prophetæ lo- cum ita intellectum, quasi de Hebræo populo ageret, idque propter ea quæ præcedunt capite XLI. 8. & quæ sequuntur XLIII. 1. cum tamen ex aliis Esaiæ locis, præsertim vero ex iis quæ sunt apud Prophetam capite XLIV. 6. observare de- buissent agi hic de eo qui lucem allaturus sit tum Judæis tum gentibus: quod recte vidit Chaldæus paraphrastes, qui Messiæ nomen hic addidit. Cæterum Justinus, ut Septua- ginta interpretum auctoritatem in suas partes perduceret, Jacobi & Israelis nomine Christum vult indicatum, quod mihi hic quidem verisimile non videtur.

Recte vaticinium Esaiæ XLII. de Christo acci- pit Grotius, & accipiendum esse docet, quod ex aliis Esaiæ locis, præsertim vero ex iis, quæ sunt apud Prophetam c. XLIV. 6. observare liceat, agi hic de eo, qui lucem allaturus sit tum Judæis tum gentibus: quod recte etiam vidisse Chaldæum, qui Messiæ no- men hic addidit, observat. Hæc autem merito opponimus detorsioni Prophetici loci, quem in Annotatis ad Esaiam abripuit. Non autem de Esaia, sed de Messia eum agere, in vindiciis loci istius demonstravimus, ubi etiam totum hic à Mat- thæo adductum textum cum notis Grotianis ad præsentem Matthæi locum expendimus. Non pla- cet ergo τὸ πραχθὲν πρᾶξαι. Ideo illinc ea peti poterunt. Utrum autem LXX. interpretum edi- tiones omnes hic ante ὁ παῖς με posuerint, Ἰακὼβ, & ante ὁ ἐκλεκτός με, Ἰσραὴλ, quemadmodum al- legatio Justini habet in Dial. cum Tryphone, du- bium reddunt, nostro judicio, verba Eusebii IX. Evangel. demonstrat. παρὰ τοῖς ἑβδομήκοντα

ὠβέλισαι τὸ Ἰακὼβ καὶ τὸ Ἰσραὴλ ὄνομα, quæ non id volunt, (ut Grotius existimat) à Criti- cis ea verba obelo notata esse, tanquam quæ adjecta sint, cum in Hebræo sermone non extarent, sed quod ab ipsis Interpp. LXX in genuinis editionibus omissa sint. Etsi enim Criticis ille usus obeli fue- rit, in editionibus versionis Græcæ V. T. quem indigitat Grotius, ut exemplo Origenis constat: Eusebius tamen non de obelo Criticorum loqui- tur, sed παρὰ τοῖς ἑβδομήκοντα, inquit, ὠβέλισαι, quod ab ipsis LXX. nomina illa omissa sint, & me- rito obelo notentur.

## 12:18
ἡρέτισα] The Greek interpreter of Matthew has eruditely and effectively expressed the word אתמך: Nor less correctly did Jerome, when he translated it 'whom I have taken up.' For those are called αἱρετισαὶ by the Greeks who stand on someone's side, and if they are more powerful, they are called in Latin 'susceptores' (supporters). Hence the rubric in the Justinian Code that no one should take up rustics for his patronage: hence 'suscepti' (those taken up) in Salvian, Symmachus, and others. The same is meant by ἀντιλαμβάνεσθαι, which the Seventy placed here, a word which is found with the same meaning in Luke 1:54, where the Latin interpreter likewise rendered it 'suscepit' (he has taken up): which word should have been used here also to express the propriety of the Greek word, which corresponds best to the Hebrew.

Ἀγαπητὸς] It appears from this also that the force of the word ἀγαπητὸς and ἐκλεκτὸς is the same, as we said above. The LXX rendered word for word; our interpreter expressed the thing itself: just as, conversely, for what follows רצתה, our interpreter more properly, and as the LXX are accustomed to do elsewhere, expressed it by εὐδόκησε, whereas the LXX themselves placed προσεδέξατο in this passage. But we have dealt with the meaning of the word εὐδοκεῖν at chapter III, which is the same, although less effective, in the word προσδέχεσθαι.

Πνεῦμά μυ] The spirit properly of meekness and humility, designated by the visible sign of a dove: which sense is required both by what follows in the Prophet, and by the occasion which led Matthew to cite the Prophet. See what we said at chapter IV.

Κρίσιν τοῖς ἔθνεσιν ἀπαγγελεῖ] Following the origin of the word κατὰ τὸ λεπτότατον, the LXX had placed ἐξοίσει. Moreover, it appears that ἐξαγγέλλειν is properly signified by that word, in Deuteronomy 22:19 and many other places: whence it is also easy to gather which meaning of the polysemous word משפט, which the Hellenists translate as κρίσιν everywhere, fits best here: namely, that which indicates a law or norm of living, for it is most proper for a law to be published. But that this is true is shown by what follows immediately in the Hebrew: 'The far-off nations shall wait for his law.'

Latin:

ἡρέτισα] Erudite atque efficaciter expressit Matthæi Græcus interpres vocem אתמך: Neque minus recte Hie- ronymus, cum vertit quem suscepi. Nam αἱρετισαὶ Græcis di- cuntur, qui stant ab alicujus partibus, qui si potentiores sint vocantur Latine susceptores. Hinc rubrica in Codice Justinianeo ut nemo ad suum patrocinium suscipiat rusti- canos: hinc suscepti apud Salvianum, Symmachum atq; alios. Idem valet ἀντιλαμβάνεσθαι quod hic posuerunt septua- ginta, quæ vox eodem significatu reperitur Luc. I. 54. ubi Latinus interpres itidem reddidit suscepit: quo verbo hic quoque utendum fuit ad exprimendam Græcæ vocis pro- prietatem, quæ Hebrææ optime respondet.

Ἀγαπητὸς] Apparet hinc quoque eandem esse vim vo- cis ἀγαπητὸς & ἐκλεκτὸς quod supra diximus. Verbum verbo reddiderunt LXX. noster interpres rem ipsam expressit: sicut contra quod sequitur רצתה noster magis proprie, & ut alibi solent LXX. expressit per εὐδόκησε, cum ipsi LXX. hoc loco posuerint προσεδέξατο. Sed de vocis εὐδοκεῖν significatione egimus ad caput III. quæ eadem quoque est, etsi minus efficax, in verbo προσδέχεσθαι.

Πνεῦμά μυ] Spiritum proprie mansuetudinis & humi- litatis, designatum visibili columbæ signo: quem sensum exigunt tum quæ sequuntur apud Prophetam, tum occa- sio quæ Matthæum ad citandum Prophetam adduxit. Vi- de quæ diximus ad caput IV.

Κρίσιν τοῖς ἔθνεσιν ἀπαγγελεῖ] Originem vocis κατὰ τὸ λε- πτότατον secuti LXX. posuerant ἐξοίσει. Cæterum proprie ἐξαγγέλλειν ea voce significari apparet, Deut. XXII. 19. a- liisque multis in locis: unde etiam collectu facile est, quæ significatio vocis πολυσήμου משפט quam κρίσιν passim vertunt Hellenistæ, hic maxime quadret: ea nempe quæ legem sive normam vivendi indicat, legis enim maxime proprium est publicari. Verum hoc esse ostendit quod mox in Hebræo sequitur: Ad legem ejus longinqua gentes exspectabunt.

## 12:19
Vers. 19. ὐκ ἐρίσει, ὐδὲ κραυγάσει] Since in the Hebrew there are two words of the same meaning, denoting a clamor, our interpreter rightly substituted ἐρίζειν in place of the other, to show that the clamor in question here is one that is usually a sign of an angry mind. Hence Paul, when he had mentioned bitterness, wrath, and anger, adds 'clamor': and Quintilian called a clamorous person a 'clamosus altercator.' Justin to Zenas and Serenus: 'None of those who shout are of sound mind.' In the version of the seventy men it is ὐ κεκράξεται, ὐδὲ ἀνήσει, that is to say, his voice. Nevertheless, Justin in one place cites ὐκ ἐρίσει ὔτε κράξει, in another ὐ κεκράξεται only. The exemplar in which the apex ש̇ was wrongly marked gave Symmachus, who translated ישא as ἀπαληθήσεται, the cause for error, although even so he should have translated it ἀπαλήσει rather than ἀπαληθήσεται.

ὐδὲ ἀκύσει τις ἐν ταῖς πλατείαις τὴν φωνὴν ἀυτῦ] It means the same as what the LXX have, ὐδὲ ἀκυσθήσεται ἔξω ἡ φωνὴ ἀυτῦ, just as Justin also cites it in one place: but in another, ὔτε ἀκύσεταί τις ἐν ταῖς πλατείαις τὴν φωνὴν ἀυτῦ, I believe because he was citing the Prophet extemporaneously, almost as it is read here, and at another time having inspected the codex of the LXX interpreters. חוץ is literally ἔξω: but because a street is outside buildings, it is therefore most frequently called by that name. Mark elsewhere combined both, saying ἔξω ἐπὶ τὰ ἀμφόδα chapter 11:4. It is a sign of anger to shout outside the doors. Menander:

Τὸ δ᾽ ἐπιδιώκειν εἰς τε τὴν ὁδὸν τρέχειν Ἔτι λοιδορυμένη, κυνός ἐς ἔργον ρόδη.

Plautus said 'pipulo ante aedes differre' (to rail at someone with a clamor before the house). Without doubt, this proverbial locution shows that Christ was of such kindness that he did not want the vices of those in whom some good hope remained to be made public. This is what Justin expressed in the book addressed to Zenas with these words: 'One must admonish the sinner not in public, unless he needs it because of his arrogance.'

Latin:

Vers. 19. ὐκ ἐρίσει, ὐδὲ κραυγάσει] Cum in Hebræo duæ sint voces ejusdem significationis, clamorem denotantes, recte noster interpres alterius loco substituit ἐρίζειν, ut ostenderet de eo clamore hic agi qui signum esse solet ex- candescentis animi. Hinc Paulus cum cominasset πικρίαν, θυμὸν κὴ ὀργὴν addit κραυγὴν: & Quintilianus clamosum altercatorem dixit. Justinus ad Zenam & Serenum: τῶν δὲ κεκραγότων ὐδεὶς σώδρων ἐστι. In septuaginta virum versio- ne est ὐ κεκράξεται, ὐδὲ ἀνήσει scilicet φωνήν. Attamen Justi- nus altero loco citat ἐκ ἐρίσει ὔτε κράξει, altero ὐ κεκράξε- ται tantum. Symmacho qui ישא transtulit ἀπαληθήσεται, errandi causam præbuit exemplar in quo apex ש̇ perpe- ram fuit notatus, quamquam sic quoque ἀπαλήσει potius quam ἀπαληθήσεται transferre debuit.

ὐδὲ ἀκύσει τις ἐν ταῖς πλατείαις τὴν φωνὴν ἀυτῦ] Idem valet quod habent LXX. ὐδὲ ἀκυσθήσεται ἔξω ἡ φωνὴ ἀυτῦ, quomo- do & Justinus citat altero loco: altero vero ὔτε ἀκύσεταί τις ἐν ταῖς πλατείαις τὴν φωνὴν ἀυτῦ, credo quia nunc ex tem- pore citarat Prophetam ita ferme ut hic legitur, nunc inspe- cto codice LXX. interpretum, חוץ ad verbum est ἔξω: quia vero platea est extra ædificia, ideo eo nomine fre- quentissime appellatur. Marcus alibi utrumque conjun- xit dicens ἔξω ἐπὶ τὰ ἀμφόδα cap. XI. 4. Iracundiæ signum est extra fores clamitare. Menander:

Τὸ δ᾽ ἐπιδιώκειν εἰς τε τὴν ὁδὸν τρέχειν Ἔτι λοιδορυμένη, κυνός ἐς ἔργον ρόδη.

Plautus dixit pipulo ante ædes differre. Haud dubie o- stendit proverbialis hæc locutio, Christum ea fuisse boni- tate, ut palam fieri nollet eorum vitia de quibus aliquid superesset bonæ spei. Hoc est quod dicto ad Zenam libro Justinus his verb s expressit, νυθετηθέον τὸν ἀμαρτάνοντα μὴ κατὰ κοινὸν, ἐκτὸς εἰ μὴ χρῄζει διὰ τὸ ὑπεροπτικόν.

## 12:20
Vers. 20. Κάλαμον συντετριμμένον ὐ κατεάξει] Thus Justin in one place: in another as the LXX have it, κάλαμον συντετρασμένον ὐ συντρίψει. The Syrian said συντετριμμένον, he will break רעועא

תבר. But just as the Hebrew רצץ and שבר do not differ much in meaning, because to the Hebrews it is to break, and תבר is placed in Syriac for שבר. Nor among the Greeks is there any exceptional difference between συντρίβειν, συνθλᾷν, and κατάγνυσθαι. For what is placed here in the first part by the Interpreter is placed by the LXX in the latter part, and soon after in the Prophet לא ירוץ is said for ישבר: wherefore the sense is, he will not further break a reed already somewhat broken: that is, he will not precipitate into ruin those who have fallen through some weakness, such as most of the Pharisees could be seen to be up to that day; nay, on the contrary, they will soften τὸ συντετριμμένον, as it is in Ezekiel 34:16.

Τυφόμενον] Thus also some copies of the LXX Interpreters have it, and Justin cites it no differently, although in others it is καπνιζόμενον with the same sense. The Hebrew word signifies that which is near to being extinguished, such as lamp-wicks in which smoke recalls some trace of flame, which therefore catch the flame to themselves more easily than if they had gone out completely; τὸ ἀλεηγορούμενον appears to be the same as that in the previous member.

Ἕως ἂν ἐκβάλη εἰς νῖκος τὴν κρίσιν] I do not agree with Jerome, who suspects that something was omitted here through the fault of the scribes. But Matthew omitted words that are poetically redundant. For what is interposed in the Hebrew לא יכהה ולא ירוץ signifies nothing other than 'it shall not be extinguished,' namely, the work itself, the wick, more than it is extinguished, nor shall it be broken, namely, the reed, more than it is broken; for the words are repeated from the previous clause, from which it appears that what we have said is true, that the words placed there are not antithetical by their own force, but because the sense demands it. For the words used there regarding imperfect breaking and extinguishing are used here regarding perfect ones. But the LXX. Interpreters, as if it were not a matter of the reed and the wick, but of the servant of God himself, translated it as ἀναλάμψει καὶ οὐ θραυσθήσεται, thinking that 'it shall not grow dim' was said by litotes for 'it shall shine': hence the writing of Justin Martyr must be amended, in whom ἀναλήψει is placed twice for ἀναλάμψει, and with faulty punctuation as well. But also what Isaiah had said twice, 'he shall bring forth judgment to truth,' and 'until he set judgment in the earth,' Matthew rightly contracted, and retained 'until' from the latter member, but from the former he placed that which the Greek interpreter translated as εἰς νῖκος, expressing the sense most fully, which I prefer to say the interpreter missed through the ambiguity of the Syriac word: what the seventy had turned as εἰς ἀληθείαν ἐξοίσει κρίσιν (thus the version of the LXX is to be amended from Justin, in which εἰς ἀληθῆ is wrongly read), our interpreter said with the very same meaning, ἕως ἂν ἐκβάλλῃ εἰς νῖκος τὴν κρίσιν: nay, Justin also cites in another place ἕως ἂν νῖκος ἐξοίσει, likewise expressing the sense, not counting the words, interpreting משפט or κρίσιν in this place otherwise than above, as a cause which is called into dispute, a most accepted meaning. Therefore, he is said κρίσιν ἐκβάλλειν or ἐκφέρειν (for these differ in nothing) εἰς ἀληθείαν or εἰς νῖκος, or εἰς τέλος, as in Job 23:7, or even ἐκφέρειν νῖκος, who makes his own just claims so manifest that he can carry off the victory before any judge. See Psalm 51:6. But Christ did this when he bore the evil ways of the Jews with that utmost gentleness and patience, and spared no effort in recalling them to a better way of life: thus, in the same Prophet, God, recounting how many benefits he had bestowed upon his vineyard, and with how much patience he had awaited good grapes, challenges it to judgment, chapter 5, verse 3, which passage contributes wonderfully to explaining this.

By the name of judgment, the blessed Gerhard understands the right manner of divine worship: but that 'he shall announce' (Hebrew יוציא, he shall bring forth, he shall cause to go out) to the nations, concerns the preaching of the Gospel to the nations performed by the Apostles, Matt. 28:19, Mark 16:15. Regarding the words ἕως ἂν ἐκβάλῃ εἰς νῖκος τὴν κρίσιν, Lightfoot, Hor. Ebr. p. 167, has this: The words in both places (in Isaiah and Matthew) mean this: that Christ would not produce in the world any sound or noise of pomp, applause, or pride; but would conduct his affairs in humility, silence, poverty, and patience, both while he himself was on earth, and through the Apostles after his ascension, who were laboring under contempt, poverty, and persecution: but that at length he would bring forth judgment to victory, that is, he would break forth and exhibit himself as Judge, avenger, and victor against that most wicked nation of the Jews, from whom both he and his own suffered such things. But then also he brought forth judgment to truth, and asserted himself as the true Messiah and Son of God before the eyes of all, and confirmed the truth of the Gospel, by avenging his cause from his enemies, in a manner so conspicuous and tremendous. And hence it is that this proclamation and execution of judgment upon that nation is almost always called in the New Testament his Advent in glory. For when Christ and his kingdom had lain hidden for so long under the veil of humility and under the cloud of persecution, the avenger finally burst forth and cut off that persecuting nation, and showed himself a victor before the eyes of all, both Jews and Gentiles. B. Gerhard: It signifies to bring forth true judgment concerning enemies unto victory: Until he shall have brought forth judgment unto victory, with a certain power, while the world and Satan struggle in vain, he will bring forth sentence and judgment. Until he pronounces the sentence by which he declares himself the victor over all his enemies, which was done when the Gospel was promulgated throughout the whole world. Until he shall have executed his office in these lands, and shall have ascended gloriously and victoriously into heaven, then he will also call the nations to his kingdom. In Isaiah it is said: The isles. By this are understood the nations which dwell in the isles, that is, in remote and far-distant places.

Latin:

Vers. 20. Κάλαμον συντετριμμένον ὐ κατεάξει] Ita Justi- nus uno loco: altero ut habent LXX. κάλαμον συντετρασμέ- νον ὐ συντρίψει. Syrus συντετριμμένον dixit רעועא κατεάξει

תבר. Sicut autem Hebræa רצץ & שבר non multum differunt fignificatu quod & Hebræis est frangere & תבר Syriace pro שבר pofitum. Neque apud Græcos eximium aliquod discrimen est inter συντρίβειν, συνθλᾷν, κατάγνυσθαι. Nam & quod hic in priori parte pofitum est ub Interprete, à LXX. viris pofitum est in posteriori, & mox apud Pro- phetam לא ירוץ dicitur pro ישבר: quare fenfus est, arundinem aliquatenus jam fractam non ultra franget: id vero est, non præcipitabit in ruinam imbecillitate aliqua lapsos, quales ad istum diem videri poterant Pharisæorum plerique, imo contra τὸ συντετριμμένον μαλάξουσι, ut est apud Ezechielem XXXIV. 16.

Τυφόμενον] Ita habent & quædam exemplaria LXX. In- terpretum, neque aliter citat Justinus, quanquam in aliis est καπνιζόμενον sensu eodem. Verbum Hebræum signifi- cat id quod prope est ut extinguatur, qualia sont ellych- nia in quibus fumus aliquod flammæ vestigium refert, quæ proinde facilius flammam ad se rapiunt, quam si pla- ne refrixissent, τὸ ἀλεηγορούμενον apparet idem esse quod in membro fuperiore.

Ἕως ἂν ἐκβάλη εἰς νῖκος τὴν κρίσιν] Non assentior Hiero- nymo suspicanti omissum hic aliquid exscribentium vi- tio. Sed verba ποιητικῶς πλεονάζοντα omisit Matthæus. Nam quod in Hebræo interjicitur לא יכהה ולא ירוץ ni- hil aliud significat quam non extinguetur, scilicet ipsius opera, ellychnium amplius quam extinctum est, neque frangetur, scilicet arundo amplius quam fracta est; sunt e- nim voces repetitæ ex priori commate, unde apparet verum esse quod diximus, voces ibi positas non ἀντιδιαιρετικῶς suapte vi, sed ex eo quod fenfus exigit. Nam quæ ibi voces ufurpa- tæ funt de imperfecta fractione atque exstinctione, hic de perfecta ufurpantur. At LXX. Interpretes quasi non de a- rundine atque ellychnio, sed de ipso Dei servo ageretur, transtulerunt ἀναλάμψει καὶ 8 θραυσθήσεται, putantes non ca- ligabit dictum esse κατὰ λιτότητα pro splendebit: unde e- mendanda est scriptura Justini Martyris, apud quem bis positum est ἀναλήψει pro ἀναλάμψει, etiam distinctione vitiosa. Sed & quod bis dixerat Esaias, ad veritatem judicium educet, & donec ponat in terra judicium, recte contraxit Matthæus, & donec retinuit ex posteriori membro, ex prio- ri autem id posuit, quod Græcus interpres transtulit εἰς νῖ- κος, fenfum plenissime exprimens, quod malo quam am- biguitate vocabuli Syriaci, lapsum dicere interpretem: quod septuaginta verterant εἰς ἀληθείαν ἐξοίσει κρίσιν(ita ex Justi- no emendanda verfio LXX. in qua male legitur εἰς ἀληθῆ) interpres noster eadem plane sententia dixit, ἕως ἂν ἐκβάλ- λῃ εἰς νῖκος τὴν κρίσιν: imo & Justinus citat altero loco ἕως ὦ νῖκος ἐξοίσει itidem sensum exprimens, non verba annu- merans משפט five κρίσιν hoc loco aliter quam supra interpretor pro causa quæ in disceptationem vocatur, rece- pttissima significatione. Ergo κρίσιν ἐκβάλλειν aut ἐκφέρειν(hæc enim nihil differunt) εἰς ἀληθείαν five εἰς νῖκος, five εἰς τέ- λος, ut Jobi XXIII. 7. aut etiam ἐκφέρειν νῖκος is dicitur, qui justa sua ita manifesta facit, ut quovis judice victo- riam referre possit. Vide Pf. LI. 6. Hoc autem fecit Christus, cum summa illa lenitate ac patientia malos Judæorum mo- res pertulit, nihilq; operæ pepercit eis ad meliorem frugem revocandis: ita apud eundem Prophetam Deus referens quanta beneficia vineæ suæ præstitisset, quantaque cum pa- tientia probas uvas exspectasset, ad judicium provocat cap. V. commate 3. qui locus mire huic explicando facit.

Judicii nomine B. Gerhardus intelligit rectam cultus divini rationem: illud vero annunciabit Ebr. יוציא proferet, exire faciet gentib9, de præ- dicatione Evangelii gentibus per Apostolos facta Matt. XXVIII. 19. Marc. XVI. 15. De verbis ἕως ἂν ἐκβάλῃ εἰς νῖκος τὴν κρίσιν Lightfooth. Hor. Ebr. p. 167. i- ta habet: Verba utrobique (apud Esaiam & Mat- thæum) hæc volunt: Christum in mundo sonitum aut strepitum pompæ, plausus, aut fastus non editu- rum ullum; fed in humilitate, filentio, paupertate & patientia res fuas acturum, & dim ipse esset in terris, & per Apostolos post ejus ascensionem, con- temptu, paupertate & persecutione laborantes: tan- dem vero prolaturum eum Judicium ad victoriam, hoc est, Judicem, vindicem, victorem proruptu- rum ac se exhibiturum in gentem istam Judæo- rum nequissimam, à qua talia passi sunt &' ipse & sui. At tunc etiam Judicium protulit ad veritatem, & se verum Messiam, filiumque Dei, coram ocu- lis omnium asseruit, veritatemque Evangelii confir- mavit, causam suam ab inimicis suis ulciscendo, modo tam conspicuo, & tremendo. Atque hinc est, quod prolatio, atque executio ista Judicii in istam gentem in Novo Testamento semper fere vocetur Adventus ejus in gloria. Cum nempe tamdiu de- latuisset Christus, atque ejus regnum, sub velo humi- litatis, & sub persecutionis nube; prorupit tandem ultor, & gentem istam persecutricem excidit, vi- ctoremque se exhibuit præ oculis omnium, & Judæo- rum & Gentium. B. Gerhardus: Significat judi- cium verum proferre de hostibus ad victoriam: Us- que dum protulerit ad victoriam judicium, cum vi quadam frustra obnitente mundo & Satana, feret sententiam & judicium. Donec pronunciet senten- tiam, qua se victorem declaret omnium inimicorum suorum, id quod factum est, cum Evangelium pro- mulgaretur per universum orbem. Donec officium suum in his terris fuerit executus, & gloriose ac vi- ctoriose in cælum adscenderit, tunc etiam gentes ad suum regnum vocabit. Apud Esaiam dicitur In- sulæ. Intelliguntur vero gentes, quæ in Insulis, i.e. in remotis ac procul dissitis locis habitant.

## 12:21
Verse 21. And in his name shall the nations hope. It coheres excellently with the preceding: for the nations deservedly place their trust in the goodness of him who bore with the disobedient Jews with such leniency. אִיים, which is in Hebrew, does not always signify isles, but often any regions whatsoever, as in Gen. X. 5. Rightly, therefore, both the LXX and our interpreter have rendered the sense with the word nations. The same people render יוחילו as shall hope excellently: for so both the LXX and the Hebrews explain it elsewhere. But that for his law among the LXX men we have in his name, it is no error of the scribes: for Justin also cites it twice in this way: and our author here, who in this whole passage has not followed the LXX, has likewise rendered it in his name or in the name, as some codices have it. Doubtless, law frequently signifies to the Hebrews that which they otherwise call way, which the more elegant Greeks call heresy, but the Hellenists call the same thing name, because it is the custom for followers to be named after the author of their institution. Thus Paul denies that he baptized anyone in his own name, indicating that he is the author of no new institution. Therefore, the LXX, who interpreted this passage concerning the Israelite people, thought that the Prophet meant this, that foreign nations would place their trust in the profession of Judaism: whereas the sense is, as Matthew and the thing itself teaches us, that the nations would do this very thing in the profession of Christianity, which in itself contains the perfection of Judaism.

Excellently, says Junius, is this passage adapted by Matthew to that interdict of Christ, which he is said to have used in verse 16. He healed, says Matthew, them all, and charged them that they should not make him known. But why? That it might be fulfilled which was spoken by Isaiah, etc. The sense is that the sign which Isaiah predicted concerning the manner of Christ's administration, Christ performed in reality. For Isaiah had said that this would be the manner of his administration, that he would not act contentiously with anyone, but with the greatest humility, v. 2, nor would he provide an argument of offense to the weak who were coming to the Kingdom of God, but rather with the greatest leniency and prudence he would alleviate the present weakness of his own, and prevent the future, verse 3. This, therefore, Christ performed in reality, and indeed performed with such religious care that he preferred to instill the dignity of his person, the majesty of his calling, the amplitude of his benefits, and the truth of the salvation (which he exhibits to all) gradually into the minds of weak men, rather than to permit that, by untimely clamor and the preaching of his name, an occasion should be given to the weak to turn back from his school, or to adversaries to rush upon him. Or, to speak more briefly, pitying human weakness, he preferred to teach men himself gently from the effects, that is, from his works, and to lead them to himself by the infinity of his benefits, rather than to allow those who were to arrive at his kingdom to be untimely offended and struck down by the persecution of the former or the preaching of the latter. And to me, indeed, this passage of Isaiah seems to pertain to very many other passages which exist among the Evangelists, where

Christ forbade his name, word, or benefit to be preached, whether by the Devil or by men; but it seemed sufficient to Matthew to bring forward the words of Isaiah in this place only, which might be adapted by pious men to similar narratives.

PART II. The deliverance of the possessed mute and blind.

Latin:

Vers. 21. Καὶ ἐν τῷ ὀνόματι αὐτõ ἔθνη ἐλπιõσι] Optime cum præcedentibus cohæret: merito enim fiduciam gentes col- locant in ejus bonitate qui Judæos immorigeros tanta le- nitate pertulit. אִיים quod in Hebræo est non semper Insulas, sed sæpe regiones quasvis significat, ut Gen. X. 5. Recte igitur & LXX. & noster interpres sensum reddiderunt voce ἐθνῶν. Iidem יוחילו ἐλπιõσι optime: nam ita & alibi exponunt tum LXX tum Hebræi. Quod autē pro לתורתו apud LXX. viros habemus ἐπὶ τῷ ὀνόματι, nullum est ex- scriptorum vitium: nam & Justinus bis ita citat: & noster hic qui toto hoc loco LXX. non est secutus, itidem reddi- dit ἐν τῷ ὀνόματι aut τῷ ὀνόματι, ut quidam habent codices. Nimirum תורה Hebræis frequenter significat id quod ipsi alias דרך, Græci elegantiores dicunt ἄἵρεσιν, Hellenistæ autem idem vocant ὄνομα quia moris est sectatores ab insti- tuti sui auctore nominari. Ita Paulus negat se quenquam in suo nomine baptizasse, indicans nullius se novi instituti esse auctorem. Putarunt igitur LXX. qui locum hunc de populo Israelitico interpretabantur, hoc velle Prophetam, exteras gentes fiduciam collocaturas in professione Judai- smi: cum sensus sit ut Matthæus & res ipsa nos docet, id i- psum facturas gentes in professione Christianismi, qui in se Judaismi perfectionem continet.

Optime, inquit Junius, a Matthæo accommo- datur hic locus illi interdicto Christo, quo usus fuisse dicitur versu 16. Sanavit, inquit Matthæus, eos omnes, & interminatus est eis, ne ipsum palam fa- cerent. Cur autem? ut impleretur quod dictum erat per Esaiam, &c. Sensus est, quod signum E- saias prædixit de modo administrationis Christi, id Christus reipsa præstitit. Dixerat autem Esaias, hunc fore administrationis modum, ut neque conten- tiose cum ullo ageret, sed humilitate maxima, v. 2. neque infirmis ad Regnum Dei venturis offensionis præberet argumentum, sed potius lenitate, pruden- tiaque maxima infirmitatem suorum præsentem le- varet, futuramque præcaveret, versu 3. Hoc igi- tur Christus re ipsa præstitit, & tanta quidem reli- gione præstitit, ut dignitatem personæ suæ, majesta- tem vocationis, amplitudinem beneficiorum, & sa- lutis (quam omnibus exhibet) veritatem maluerit sensim instillare in mentes hominum infirmorum, quam permittere, ut intempestivo clamore ac præ- dicatione sui nominis, infirmis daretur occasio pe- dem referendi a schola ipsius, vel adversariis in ipsum irruendi. Sive, ut dicamus brevius, miser- tus infirmitatis humanæ, maluit ab effectis, id est, ab operibus suis, homines ipse docere leniter, & bene- ficiorum infinitate ad se perducere, quam sinere ut horum persecutione, aut illorum prædicatione in- tempestive offenderentur & percellerentur qui ad regnum ipsius erant perventuri. Ac mihi quidem videtur hic Esaiæ locus ad quam plurimos alios per- tinere locus, qui apud Evangelistas exstant, ubi

Christus vetuit suum nomen, sermonem, aut bene- ficium, sive à Diabolo, sive ab hominibus prædica- ri; sed id Matthæo visum fuit satis, sic hoc tantum loco Esaiæ verba adduceret, quæ à piis hominibus ad consimiles narrationes accommodarentur.

PARS II. Obsessi muti & cæci liberatio.

## 12:23
Verse 23. Is this the son of David? Because of the miracles with which the people expected the Messiah would come. For what is more just than that he who was to be the prince of the Prophets should also surpass the other Prophets in the magnitude of his miracles, so that the blindness of the Jews is wonderful who now, contrary to all the ancient authors, deny that the Messiah will perform miracles. Verse 24. If not by Beelzebub the prince of the demons. Both the writings of the Jews and of the Apostles teach us that among the impure spirits there is one who presides. He is the prince of the world, John XII. 31, XIV. 30, XVI. 11, the prince of this age, 1 Cor. II. 6, 8, the prince of the power of the air, Ephes. II. 2. We touched above on why he was called Beelzebub by the Jews. Moreover, it was the custom of enchanters, when they accomplished nothing by trying everything, to use at last against the demons the force and power of that prince of demons, whose secret name they also threatened they would pronounce. In Lucan, Erichtho: Or must he be addressed, at whose calling the earth never trembles without being shaken, who sees the Gorgon exposed, and chastises the trembling Fury with her own lashes, who holds the Tartarus for you, whose superiors you are, who swears by the Stygian waters? Tiresias in Papinius: Do not despise, I warn you, and we have the power to rage: for we know whatever you fear to be said and known, and to disturb Hecate, were I not to fear you, Thymbraean, and him whose name it is forbidden to know, the highest of the triple world, but I am silent. Porphyry wishes this prince of demons, the presiding power (as he himself speaks) of the evil demons, to be called Serapis, whose words are these: We do not suspect the evil demons to be under Serapis without reason, and elsewhere: But especially Serapis rules over such things, and the symbol of these is the three-headed dog; that is, the evil demon in the three elements, water, earth, and air: which passage, if I am not mistaken, illustrates that Statian passage concerning the triple world. The same Porphyry in another place which Theodoret cites in his discourse on the Angels: Βύλονται γὰρ εἶναι θεοὶ, κὶ ἡ προεςῶσα ἀυτῶν δύναμις δο- κεῖ θεὸς εἶναι μέγιςθ. To the same person belong those verses in the same Porphyry whom I mentioned: Δαίμων ἁλιτρονόων ψυχῶν διάδημα λελογχὼς Ἠερίων ὑπένερθε μυχῶν, χθονίων δ' ἐφύπερθεν, and the formulas of threats in Iamblichus, book VI, chapters 5, 6, and 7. These are the rites of secret arts, by which they address I know not what powers, as Arnobius says. Verse 25. Πᾶσα βασιλεία] A most well-known maxim among the Hebrews, such as that Sallustian one: By concord small things grow, by discord the greatest fall apart. Cicero used almost the very same words. For thus he says concerning friendship: What house is so stable, what state so firm, that it cannot be utterly overturned by hatreds and dissensions? Nor does that Sophoclean line depart far from this: Ἀναρχίας γὰρ μεῖζον ἐκ ἔσιν κακὸν Αὕτη πόλεις τ' ὄλλυσιν, ἥδ' ἀνασάτες Οἴκες τίθησιν. Moreover, this argument of Christ is most valid for accomplishing what he intends, namely, for overturning that hypothesis which the Pharisees borrowed from the Magi, namely that demons are compelled by the power of other demons to do certain things: which Porphyry also approved, with this oracle of Hecate: Ἤλυθον ἐσαίυσα τεῆς πολυφράδμονθ εὐχῆς Ἣν θνητῶν φύσις εὗρε, θεῶν ὑποθημοσύνῃσι. And with this one: τίνθ δὲ χαλίζων Σεῖο δόμης ἑκάτην με θεὴν ἐπέδησας ἀνάγκη. Clement of Alexandria: But the Magi already boast that the demons are servants of their own impiety, having registered them as their own household slaves, having made them slaves compelled by incantations. Christ refutes this thus: it is agreed that demons are intelligent; but those who are intelligent act to establish their own affairs, which cannot be done except by concord. Therefore, demons do not dissent, which nevertheless would be necessary if one compelled another, as you wish to persuade the people. Wherefore, the emphasis in the word ἐκβάλλει is to be noted. ὀ σταθήσεται] לא יקים.

Vers. 23. Μήτις ὗτός ἐσιν ὁ ὑιὸς Δαβὶδ] Ob miracula cum quibus venturum Messiam populus exspectabat. Quid enim justius quam eum qui princeps futurus erat Prophe- tarum, etiam miraculorum magnitudine anteire Prophe- tas cæteros, ut mira sit Judæorum cæcitas qui nunc con- tra veteres auctores omnes Messiam negant miracula fa- cturum. Vers. 24. Εἰ μὴ ἐν τῷ βεελζεβὲδ ἄρχοντι τῶν δαιμονίων] Inter impuros spiritus unum esse qui præsideat, & Judæo- rum &Apostolorum scripta nos docent. Is est ἄρχων κόσμγ, Joh. XII. 31. XIV. 30. XVI. 11. ἄρχων τᾶ αἰῶνθ τέτε. 1. Cor. II. 6. 8. ἄρχων ἐξεσίας τᾶ ἀέρος, Ephes. II.2. Hic cur Beelzebub à Judæis diceretur supra attigimus. Solebant autem incantatores ubi omnia tentando nihil proficerent, postremo adversus dæmones uti vi ac potestate illius dæ- monum principis, cujus etiam arcanum nomen enuntia- turos se minabantur. Apud Lucanum Erichtho: An ille Compellandus erit, quo nunquam terra vocato Non excussa tremit, qui Gorgona cernit apertam, Verberibusq; suis trepidam castigat Erynnin, Indepesta tenet vobis qui Tartara, cujus Vos estis superi, Stygias qui pejerat undas? Tiresias apud Papinium: Spernite ne, moneo, & nobis sævire potestas: Scimus enim & quicquid dici nosciq; timetis, Et turbare Hecaten, ni te Thymbræe vererer, Et triplicis mundi summum quem scire nefastum est Illum, sed taceo. Porphyrius hunc principem dæmonum τὴν προεςῶσαν (ut ipse loquitur) τῶν κακοδαιμόνων δύναμιν, vult dici Serapin, cujus hæc sunt verba: τὲς δὲ πονηρὲς δαίμονας ἐκ εἰκῆ ὑπὸ τὸν Σάραπιν ὑποπτεύομεν & alibi: μάλισα δὲ τοιοῖσιν ὢν ἄρχε ὁ Σάραπις κὶ τέτων σύμβολον ὁ τρικάρηνος κύων· τῦτ' ἔσιν, ὁ ἐν τοῖς τρισὶ τοιχείοις ὕδατι, γῇ, ἀέρι πονηρὸς δαίμων: qui locus Statiana illa de triplici mundo, ni fallor illustrat. Idem Por- phyrius alio loco quem citat Theodorethus sermone de An- gelis: Βύλονται γὰρ εἶναι θεοὶ, κὶ ἡ προεςῶσα ἀυτῶν δύναμις δο- κεῖ θεὸς εἶναι μέγιςθ. Ad eundem pertinetat versus illi apud eundem quem dixi Porphyrium: Δαίμων ἁλιτρονόων ψυχῶν διάδημα λελογχὼς Ἠερίων ὑπένερθε μυχῶν, χθονίων δ' ἐφύπερθεν, & minarum formulæ apud Jamblichum lib. VI. c. 5. & 6. & 7. Hi sunt secretarum artium ritus, quibus affantur nescio quas potestates, ut ait Arnobius. Vers. 25. Πᾶσα βασιλεία] Gnome notissima inter He- bræos, qualis illa Salustiana: Concordia res parvæ crescunt, discordia maximæ dilabuntur. Cicero ferme ipsa verba posuit. Ita enim ait de amicitia: Quæ domus tam stabilis, quæ tam firma civitas est, quæ non odiis atque dissidiis funditus possit everti? Nec longe abscedit illud Sophocleum: Ἀναρχίας γὰρ μεῖζον ἐκ ἔσιν κακὸν Αὕτη πόλεις τ' ὄλλυσιν, ἥδ' ἀνασάτες Οἴκες τίθησιν. Est autem hoc argumentum Christi validissimum ad id conficiendum quod vult, nempe ad evertendam ὑπόθεσιν il- lam quam à Magis Pharisæi mutuabantur, dæmones scilicet vi aliorum dæmonum coactos aliqua facere: quod & Por- phyrius probabat, hoc oraculo Hecates: Ἤλυθον ἐσαίυσα τεῆς πολυφράδμονθ εὐχῆς Ἣν θνητῶν φύσις εὗρε, θεῶν ὑποθημοσύνῃσι. Et isto: τίνθ δὲ χαλίζων Σεῖο δόμης ἑκάτην με θεὴν ἐπέδησας ἀνάγκη. Clemens Alexandrinus: Μάγοι δὲ ἤδη ἀσεβείας τῆς σφῶν ἀυ- τῶν ὑπηρέτας δαίμονας ἀυχᾶσιν οἰκέτας ἀυτὲς ἑαυτοῖς καταγρά- ψαντες, τὲς κατηναγκασμένως δέλες ταῖς ἐπῳδαῖς πεποιηκό- τες. Hoc ita convellit Christus: sapere dæmonas constat; at qui sapiunt hoc agunt ut res suas stabiliant, quod nisi concordia fieri non potest. Non dissident igitur dæmo- nes, quod tamen necesse esset si alter alterum cogeret, ut vos populo persuasum vultis. Quare notanda ἔμφασις in voce ἐκβάλλει. ὀ σταθήσεται] לא יקים.

## 12:26
Verse 26. ἐφ' ἑαυτὸν ἐμερίσθη] Doubtless ὁ σατανᾶς, that is, the Satanic totality. See Mark.

Latin:

Vers. 26. ἐφ' ἑαυτὸν ἐμερίσθη] Nimirum ὁ σατανᾶς id est universitas Satanica. Vide Marcum.

## 12:27
Verse 27. οἱ υἱοὶ ὑμῶν] Not the Apostles, who were being accused by the Pharisees together with Christ, but the common people and disciples of the Pharisees: nor among them those who used herbs, fumigations, and bonds against demons, which was not a practice of Jewish origin derived from Solomon, as Josephus claims, but taken from the Gentiles, as Justin rightly teaches Trypho, but those who cast out demons not indeed in the name of Jesus himself, which at that time no one did except those who followed Jesus, but by invoking the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob. For that these were the solemn formulas of incantation, which I would not deny flowed from Solomon, not only Jews but also Christian writers have clearly declared, whose testimonies it will be worth the effort to produce to bring light to this passage. Justin, disputing against Trypho: 'But if you exorcise by any name of those who have existed among you, whether kings, or righteous men, or prophets, or patriarchs, none of the demons will be subject to you; but if someone among you should exorcise by the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, perhaps he will be subject.' Irenaeus, Book II, ch. 5: 'All things are subject to the appellation of the Most High and Almighty: and by the invocation of this, even before the coming of our Lord, men were saved both from most wicked spirits and from all demons.' Shortly after: 'And for this reason the Jews even until now put demons to flight by this very invocation, since all things fear the invocation of him who made them.' Tertullian, treating the history which is now at hand from the Gospel of Luke against Marcion: 'If I,' he says, 'cast out demons by Beelzebub, by whom do your sons cast them out?' What does he portend more by this voice than that they cast them out in the same way as their sons? Namely, by the power of the Creator. For if you think it must be understood thus: 'If I cast out demons by Beelzebub, by whom do your sons [cast them out]?', as if he were reproaching those who cast them out by Beelzebub, the former sense will resist you, that Satan cannot be divided against himself. Thus, neither did they cast them out by Beelzebub, but as we have said, by the power of the Creator. Theophilus against the Nations: 'And even until now they are exorcised by the name of the truly God, and the wandering spirits themselves confess that they are demons.' Where what he says, 'the truly,' is undoubtedly not the tetragrammaton name: which both Philo and others interpret in that way. Origen, however, shows by the recitation of the names I have mentioned, that in his age not only Jews but also Egyptians used them in exorcisms. First against Celsus: 'Moses records the name of Abraham only, associating him with God.' But indeed many of those who cast out demons use in their words, 'the God of Abraham'; doing so because of the name and the intimacy with God which the righteous man had, for which reason they take up the phrase 'God of Abraham' not knowing who Abraham is; the same must be said also concerning Isaac and concerning Jacob and concerning Israel, which, being admittedly Hebrew names, have been scattered in many places into the teachings of the Egyptians who profess some efficacy. Book IV: 'It is clear that the Jews are genealogized from the three fathers, Abraham and Isaac and Jacob, whose names, when joined to the appellation of God, have such power that not only do those from the nation use them in prayers to God and in casting out demons, but almost all those who deal in incantations and magic; for such an invocation of God is found in many places in magical writings.' I remember catching a trace of what Origen says here in the interpreter of Papinius Statius. The same Origen in Book IV says that not only these names of God, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, but also Zebaoth and Adonai were used to put demons to flight. Iamblichus also mentions Assyrian names in Book VII, ch. 4, of his work on the mysteries. By Assyrian, however, he understands Hebrew, just as Themistius says that the saying, 'the heart of the King is in the hand of God,' is from Assyrian books. Photius from Isidore: 'But as the demon of the woman would not cease to depart, the most pious man compelled it by oath with gentler words, although he knew neither how to practice magic nor had studied theurgy; he adjured the rays of the sun and the God of the Hebrews.' From demons the custom passed also to diseases. Marcellus Empiricus in 'On Heart Pain': 'In the name of the God of Jacob, in the name of the God of Sabaoth.' See also Nicephorus on the book of Synesius on dreams. Exorcisms of this kind therefore often had their result, not because any power was situated in the pronunciation of the syllables, but because the true God wished to be known and called upon by those names in particular, and therefore exerted his power only when it was established by the most open speech that he himself, and not one of the gods of the Gentiles, was being invoked. Now, according to this, Christ's argument is as follows: In a like case, a like judgment ought to be made: you believe that your disciples cast out demons by divine power: why do you not believe the same of me? If they refer the glory of the work to your God, I do the same.

ὑμῶν ἔσονται κριταὶ] That is, their own deed will suffice for convicting and condemning you, as below in verses 42 and 43.

Many of the ancients, Athanasius, Hilary, Jerome, Theophylact, Chrysostom, Euthymius, understand only the Apostles and the 70 disciples by their sons, because they were sons of the Hebrews according to the flesh; but because they could not conveniently be called sons and disciples of the Pharisees, and at that time had not yet received the power of casting out demons, B. Chemnitius rightly rejects that opinion, which was not disapproved by Erasmus, Maldonado, Beza, or Calixtus. Regarding those among the Pharisaic disciples who used herbs and fumigations against demons, Delrio, Cornelius à Lapide, and other Papists understood that and derived that practice from Solomon, from whom Grotius here rightly departs. Only this remains: whether, besides those who followed Jesus, others also who had come from the discipline of the Pharisees cast out demons in the name of Jesus: which is doubtful. For although Grotius proves that this was done by the invocation of the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, as in Justin against Trypho, Irenaeus book II, chapter V, Theophilus against the Nations, Origen books I and IV against Celsus, and Tertullian against Marcion: could not some of them also have done this in the name of Jesus? Which the blessed Polycarp Lyserus judged in this passage: not to mention that he could also have spoken about the exorcists of the Jews, who cast out demons from collusion with Satan, just as he used that argument in an anthropopathic manner.

Latin:

Vers. 27. οἱ υἱοὶ ὑμῶν] Non Apostoli, qui a Pharisaeis u- na cum Christo accusabantur, sed populares Pharisaeorum atque discipuli: neque inter eos illi qui herbis, suffitibus, & vinculis adversus daemonas utebantur, quod non erat institutum origine Judaicum atque a Salomone deductum, quod vult Josephus, sed a gentibus desumtum, ut recte docet Tryphonem Justinus, sed ii qui daemonas ejiciebant non quidem ipsius Jesu nomine, quod tum nemo faciebat praeter eos qui Jesum sectabantur, sed invocantes Deum Abrahami, Deum Isaaci, Deum Jacobi. Nam has fuisse solennes carminis formulas, quas a Salomone manasse non negaverim, diferte prodiderunt non Judaei tantum, sed & Christiani scriptores, quorum testimonia ad lucem huic loco afferendam producere erit operae pretium. Justi- nus adversus Tryphonem disputans: ἐὰν δὲ κατὰ παντὸς ὀνό- ματος τῶν παρ' ὑμῖν γεγενημένων ἢ βασιλέων ἢ δικαίων, ἢ προφητῶν, ἢ πατριαρχῶν ἐξορκίζητε ὑμεῖς, οὐχ ὑποταγήσε- ται οὐδὲν τῶν δαιμονίων· ἀλλ' εἰ ἄρα ἐξορκίζοι τις ὑμῶν κατὰ τοῦ Θεοῦ Ἀβραὰμ, καὶ Θεοῦ Ἰσαὰκ, καὶ Θεοῦ Ἰακὼβ ἴσως ὑποταγή- σεται. Irenaeus libro II. cap. 5. Altissimi & omnipotentis ap- pellationi omnia subjecta sunt: & hujus invocatione etiam ante adventum Domini nostri salvabantur homines & a spiritibus nequissimis & a daemonis universis. Mox: Et propter hoc Ju- daei usque nunc hac ipsa advocatione daemonas effugant, quan- do omnia timent invocationem ejus qui fecit ea. Tertullia- nus historiam quae nunc est prae manibus ex Lucae Evange- lio tractans adversus Marcionem: Si ego, inquit, in Beel- zebule ejicio daemonia, filii vestri in quo ejiciunt? Hac voce quid magis portendit, quam in eo ejecere se in quo & filii eo- rum? In virtute scilicet creatoris. Nam si putas, sic accipien- dum. Si ego in Beelzebule ejicio daemonia, filii vestri in quo, quasi ille sugillaret in Beelzebule ejicientes, resistet tibi prior sensus, non posse Satanam dividi adversus seipsum. Adeo nec illi in Beelzebule ejiciebant, sed ut diximus in virtute crea- toris. Theophilus adversus Nationes: κᾀ μέχρι τοῦ δεῦρο ἐξορκίζονται κατὰ τοῦ ὀνόματος τοῦ ὄντως Θεοῦ καὶ ὁμολογεῖ αὐτὰ τὰ πλανὰ πνεύματα εἶναι δαίμονες. Ubi quod dicit, τοῦ ὄντως, haud dubie non est nomen tetragrammaton: quod & Philo & alii eo modo interpretantur. Origenes autem o- stendit recitatione eorum quae dixi nominum, suo aevo non Judaeos tantum, sed & Aegyptios in exorcismis usos. Primo adversus Celsum: Τῷ δ' Ἀβραὰμ τὸ ὄνομα ὁ Μωϋ- σῆς ἀναγράφει μόνον οἰκειῶν αὐτὸν Θεῷ. ἀλλὰ γὰρ κᾀ πολλοὶ τῶν ἐπᾳδόντων δαίμονας χρῶνται ἐν τοῖς λόγοις αὐτῶν τῷ, ὁ Θεὸς Ἀβραάμ· ποιοῦντες μὲν διὰ τὸ ὄνομα κᾀ τὴν πρὸς τὸν δίκαιον τῷ Θεῷ οἰκειότητα, διὸ παραλαμβάνουσι τὴν Θεὸς Ἀβραὰμ λέξιν ἐκ ἐπιστάμενοι δε τίς ἐστιν ὁ Ἀβραάμ· τὰ δ' αὐτὰ λεκτέον κᾀ περὶ τοῦ Ἰσαὰκ κᾀ περὶ τοῦ Ἰακὼβ κᾀ περὶ τοῦ Ἰσραὴλ, ἅτινα ὁμολο- γημένως Ἑβραῖα ὄντα ὀνόματα, πολλαχοῦ τοῖς αἰγυπτίοις ἐπαγγέλ- λομένοις ἐνεργεῖαν τινα ἐπισπαρθαι μαθήμασι. Libro IV. σα- φῶς δ' ὅτι γενεαλογοῦνται Ἰουδαῖοι ἀπὸ τῶν τριῶν πατέρων τοῦ Ἀβραὰμ καὶ τοῦ Ἰσαὰκ καὶ τοῦ Ἰακὼβ, ὧν τοσοῦτον δύναται τὰ ὀνόματα συναπτόμενα τῇ τοῦ Θεοῦ προσηγορίᾳ, ὡς ἐ μόνον τοὺς ἀπὸ τοῦ ἔθνες χρῆσθαι ἐν ταῖς πρὸς Θεὸν εὐχαῖς καὶ ἐν τῷ κατεπάδειν δαίμονας, ἀλλὰ γὰρ σχεδὸν κᾀ πάντας τοὺς τὰ τῶν ἐπῳδῶν κᾀ μαγειῶν πραγματευομένως· εὑρίσκεται γὰρ ἐν τοῖς μαγικοῖς συγγράμμασι πολλαχοῦ ἡ τοιαύτη τοῦ Θεοῦ ἐπίκλησις. Ejus quod Origenes hic dicit vestigium me deprehendere memini in Lactatio Papinii interprete. Idem Origenes li- bro IV. non ista tantum nomina Dei Abraham, Isaac & Ja- cob sed & Zebaoth & Adonai usurpata ait ad fugandos dae- monas. Assyriorum nominum meminit & Jamblichus libro VII. c. 4. de mysteriis. Per Assyria autem intelligit Hebraica, quomodo & Themistius illud, cor Regis in manu Dei, dicit esse ex libris Assyriis. Photius ex Isidoro: Ὡς δ' οὐκ ἐπαύετο τὸ δαιμόνιον τῆς γυναικὸς ἐξελθεῖν, λόγοις ἡμεροτέροις ὅρκῳ αὐτὸ ἐπηνάγκαζεν ὁ θεοσεβέστατος, καίτοι οὐδὲ μαγευειν εἰδὼς οὐδὲ θεουρ- γίας μελετήσας· ὥρκιζε τὰς τοῦ ἡλίου ἀκτῖνας καὶ τὸν ἑβραίων Θεόν. A daemonibus ad morbos quoque mos transiit. Mar- cellus Empiricus in Corci dolore, In nomine Dei Iacob, in nomine Dei Sabaoth. Vide & Nicephorum in Synesii li- brum de somniis. Ejusmodi ergo exorcismi eventum saepe suum habuerunt, non quod vis ulla in Syllabarum pronun- tiatione esset sita, sed quod verus Deus illis potissimum nominibus nosci appellarique vellet, atque ideo vim suam tum demum exsereret, cum apertissima locutione consta- ret ipsium, non aliquem gentium Deorum esse invocatum. Est autem secundum hoc Christi argumentum tale: In pa- ri causa par judicium fieri oportet: creditis vos discipulos vestros daemonia ejicere vi divina: cur de me idem non creditis? si illi gloriam operis ad Deum vestrum referunt, idem ego facio.

ὑμῶν ἔσονται κριταὶ] Hoc est, ipsorum factum suffi- ciet vobis convincendis atque condemnandis, ut infra vers. 42. & 43.

Apostolos tantum & LXX. discipulos per fi- lios ipsorum intelligunt, quia Ebræorum filii erant secundum carnem, multi veterum Athanas. Hi- larius, Hieron. Theophyl. Chrystost. Euthymius: sed quia illi commode Pharisæorum filii ac disci- puli dici non poterant, eoque tempore nondum potestatem dæmones ejiciendi acceperant, sen- tentiam illam Erasmo, Maldonato, Bezæ, Calix- to non improbatam merito improbat B. Chemni- tius. De illis vero inter discipulos Pharisæicos, qui herbis & suffitibus utebantur adversus dæmo- nas, intellexêre & institutum illud à Salomone deduxêre Delrio, Cornelius à Lapide, & alii Pon- tificii, à quibus hic recte discedit Grotius. Id tantum superest, anne præter eos, qui Jesum se- cuti sunt, alii etiam qui è Pharisæorum disciplina prodierant, in Jesu nomine dæmonas ejecerint: quod dubium est. Etsi enim id factum invocatio- ne Dei Abrahami, Dei Isaaci, & Dei Jacobi, ut è Justino advers. Tryph. Irenæo l. II. c. V. Theophilo adv. Nation. Origene l. I. & IV. contra Celsum, Tertul. contra Marc. Grotius probat: annon ali- qui etiam eorum id in nomine Jesu facere pote- rant: Quod B. Polycarp. Lyserus in h. l. censuit: ut taceam, quod etiam de exorcistis Judæorum, qui è collusione cum Satana ejecerunt Dæmones, loqui potuerit, sicut ἀνθρωποπαθῶς eo argumento usus fuerit.

## 12:28
Verse 28. ἐν πνεύματι Θεῦ (by the Spirit of God). Everywhere the Holy Scripture attributes the active power to the Spirit. Hence the Spirit is also called the power of the Most High, and in this place in Luke, by the example of Moses, the finger of God.

ἡ βασιλεία τῦ Θεῦ (the kingdom of God). Dan. IV. 29, VII. 14. The time of the Messiah is so called. But how does it follow, if that casting out of demons was done by divine power, that that time had arrived? Because Jesus expressly did these things and proclaimed that he was doing them to prove that he was sent by the true God: which divine providence would never have permitted, unless the thing itself had been true, for the attestation of which miracles were employed, as appears from that which we read in Deuteronomy XVII, that one who performs signs is not to be believed if he tries to lead the people to the worship of false gods: because, clearly, God, after so many and such excellent signs performed in the sight of the people, had made it so certain and established to all that He is the true and only God, that they ought not to depart from that faith induced by any prodigies: from which exception the Jews rightly gather the rule that one who performs miracles is to be believed, if he is not the author of the worship of idols. For unless God had established in His law some certain norm for judging miracles, all those portents by which the Prophets confirmed their mission would have been empty. But just as many and great miracles performed by Moses by the finger of God were a sign of the imminent liberation from Egypt, so the more and greater miracles of Jesus signified that that liberation was imminent which would overshadow the memory of that former benefit. See Psalm CXLVI. 7, 8.

Latin:

Vers. 28. ἐν πνεύματι Θεῦ] Passim sacra Scriptura Spi- ritui tribuit τὸ ἐνεργητικὸν. Hinc i. em Spiritus vocatur δύ- ναμις ὑψίστ & hoc loco apud Lucam Mosis exemplo, di- gitus Dei.

ἡ βασιλεία τῦ Θεῦ] Dan. IV. 29. VII. 14. ita vocatur tempus Messiæ. Quomodo autem sequitur, si ista dæmo- num ejectio fiebat divina virtute, tempus illud advenisse? Quia Jesus expresse ista faciebat ac se facere prædicabat, ut se à Deo vero missum probaret: quod providentia divi- na nunquam permisisset, nisi res ipsa vera fuisset, cui testan- dæ miracula adhibebantur, ut ex eo apparet quod legimus Deuter. XVII. signa facienti non esse credendum si popu- lum perducere conetur ad cultum falsorum deorum: quia scilicet Deus post tot, tamque eximia signa in conspectu populi patrata tam certum atque exploratum fecerat omni- bus se esse verum atque unicum Deum, ut nullis prodigiis inducti ab ea fide deberent discedere: ex qua exceptione recte Judæi regulam colligunt ei qui miracula faciat cre- dendum, si non sit auctor cultus idolorum. Nam nisi in lege sua certam aliquam normam judicandi de miraculis Deus statuisset, inania fuissent omnia illa ostenta quibus Prophetæ missionem suam confirmabant. Sicut autem multa ac magna miracula à Mose edita per Dei digitum si- gnum erant instantis liberationis ex Ægypto, ita Jesu mi- racula plura ac majora significabant eam liberationem in- stare quæ prioris illius beneficii memoriam esset obum- bratura. Vide Psal. CXLVI. 7. 8.

## 12:29
Verse 29. ἢ πῶς δύναται (or how can). The third argument of Christ, which does not serve, like the former ones, to refute only certain men, but confirms the matter itself clearly. He who brings the greatest loss to the affairs of another shows that he is not colluding with him, but is his enemy, and therefore a victor. But this I do: for my doctrine leads men from vices, in which the power of the devil is situated, to true holiness of life,

τῦ ἰσχυρῦ (of the strong man). Isaiah XLIX. 12. See John XVI. 11.

Latin:

Vers. 29. ἢ πῶς δύναται] Tertium Christi argumentum quod non ut priora certis duntaxat hominibus refellendis inservit, sed rem ipsam plane confirmat. Qui summum rebus alterius dispendium affert, is ostendit se cum eo non col- ludere, sed hostem esse ejus, atque adeo victorem. Hoc autem ego facio: doctrina enim mea homines à vitiis, in quibus sita est diaboli potentia, ad veram vitæ sanctimo- niam perducit,

τῦ ἰσχυρῦ] Esaiæ XLIX. 12. Vide Joh. XVI. 11.

## 12:30
Verse 30. ὁ μὴ ὢν μετ᾿ ἐμῦ κατ᾿ ἐμῦ ἐστι (he who is not with me is against me). A Jewish proverb used in both directions: for it was also accustomed to be said: He who is not against you is for you. Luke IX. 50. Thus the Pythagoreans would sometimes say to walk on the public road, and sometimes not to walk on the public road: and in the gnomes of Solomon, answer a fool and do not answer a fool: all of which have their truth according to the matter to which they are applied. But it seems to me that this proverb in this place proceeds from the lesser to the greater in this way: If in a war of extermination, such as is between the servants of God and demons, it is permitted to no one to be of neither party, but those in the middle are considered as enemies, how much more must I be considered an enemy of the devil, who not only do not profit him, but harm him as much as possible? Nor should it disturb anyone against this interpretation that Christ seems to speak about himself: for that is not necessary, since in sentences of this kind pronouns of the first, second, and third person are sometimes used indefinitely for any man; which must be kept in memory for the interpretation of many passages. Such is what we shall note below XXVI. 31. and not unlike that in Virgil: 'Nor let your vineyards go toward the setting sun, / Nor let it please me then to take soft slumbers under the sky, / Nor to have lain upon the grass along the ridge of the grove.' For he (as Quintilian explains) does not instruct some I-know-not-who first, nor afterwards himself alone, but everyone.

And he who does not gather with me, scatters] Not unlike that in Quintilian VIII. 6: 'Whatever does not help, hinders.'

Latin:

Vers. 30. ὁ μὴ ὢν μετ᾿ ἐμῦ κατ᾿ ἐμῦ ἐστι] Proverbium Ju- daicum in utramque partem usurpatum: nam & dici sole- bat: Qui non est contra vos pro vobis est. Luc. IX. 50. Sic Pythagorici modo dicebant λεωφόρῳ βαδίζειν modo λεω- φόρῳ μὴ βαδίζειν: & in gnomis Salomonis, respondeas stulto & ne respondeas stulto: quæ omnia veritatem suam habent pro materia cui aptantur. Videtur autem mihi pro- verbium istud hoc loco à minori ad majus hoc modo pro- cedere: Si in bello internecino, quale est inter Dei servos & dæmonas, nemini licet neutrarum esse partium, sed medii pro hostibus habentur, quanto magis ego hostis censendus sum diaboli, qui non modo illi non prosum, sed obsum quam maxime? Neque contra hanc interpretationem mo- vere quenquam debet, quod de se loqui videtur Christus: id enim non est necessarium, cum in sententiis ejusmodi modo primæ, modo secundæ, modo tertiæ personæ pro- nomina usurpentur ἀορίστως pro quovis homine; quod ad multorum locorum interpretationem memoria tenendum est. Tale est quod infra notabimus XXVI. 31. nec dissimi- le illud apud Virgilium. Neve tibi ad solem pergant vineta cadentem, Nec mihi tum molles sub divo capere somnos, Neu dorso nemoris libeat jacuisse per herbas. Non enim (ut Quintilianus explicat) nescio cui alii prius, nec postea sibi uni, sed omnibus præcipit.

Καὶ ὁ μὴ συνάγων μετ᾽ ἐμᾶ̃, σκορπίζει] Non dissimile est illud apud Quintilianum VIII. 6. Obstat quicquid non adjuvat.

## 12:31
Vers. 31. For this reason] This must be referred to the whole discourse which preceded, in this way: Since it is established by such manifest reasons that what I do is done not by the power of demons, but of God; see what a grave punishment you bring upon yourselves when you say that those things are effected by the power of demons. Mark teaches us this connection in chapter III. 30. Yet Christ did not say this relying only on his own arguments, but at the same time, as Matthew had just said, 'knowing their thoughts.' The inspector of minds saw, of course, that they themselves recognized the truly divine power, but were inventing anything at all rather than allow the common people to pass from their teaching to Christ.

Every sin and blasphemy shall be forgiven to men] Since it is most evident that Christ is not saying here that all other sins will be forgiven (for how many are there which are not forgiven!), this Hebraism must be noted by all means, such as we observed above at chapter V in those words of Luke: 'Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away,' which the same Luke expressed elsewhere thus: 'It is easier for heaven and earth to pass away than for one tittle of the law to fall.' And so the Hebrews very often say, 'this will happen, and that will not happen,' not because they affirm the first member, but because they wish to show that what is placed later is much more difficult, just as the Latins say: 'Before, an exile having wandered through the borders of both, / Either the Parthian will drink the Arar, or Germany the Tigris.' The sense therefore is, it is easier for whatever crimes can ever be committed, and indeed even all calumnies, which easily hold the first place among crimes, to be forgiven, than for that calumny which is committed against the Spirit of God to be forgiven. See a similar comparison in 1 Sam. II. 25.

That Hebraism is rashly attached to these passages. For neither here is it only a hypothesis, or are the words to be understood comparatively, that it is easier for all other crimes to be forgiven than the sin against the Holy Spirit, nor in the other cited sayings. Here certainly nothing prevents the words from being understood simply as they sound, that every other sin and every blasphemy is forgiven; but that the sin against the Holy Spirit can by no means be forgiven. But whence, I pray, is it most evident that Christ is not saying here that all other sins will be forgiven, when the text is most evident that Christ is saying this, which he pronounces here with a clear voice, and on the contrary it is most false that there are many sins which are not forgiven? For what are those? And where is such a thing handed down in the Scriptures? Is this not diametrically contrary to the most ample, inexhaustible mercy of God, to the most universal Satisfaction of Christ, to the most gracious Evangelical promises of the Holy Spirit? Nor is there anything in the words of Luke XXI. 33 that forces us to depart from that sense which those words bring of themselves; indeed, the antithesis between heaven and earth, as perishable things which are eventually to perish, and the word of God, which is plainly invariable, clearly confirms that opinion, since what is attributed to one of the opposites, namely perishing, is removed from the other of the opposites: nor is there any doubt that heaven and earth will eventually perish at the consummation of the age, if one weighs other places of Scripture which are parallel to this, especially Ps. CII. 27, 2 Pet. III. 10 ff., Rev. XXI. 1. Finally, there is nothing for that Grotian Hebraism in the passage 1 Sam. II. 25. For those words also can be taken simply as they sound, that what is committed against a man can be settled in human judgment; so that there is no need for a contrary sense,

Latin:

Vers. 31. διὰ τᾶ̃το] Referendum est hoc ad totam o- rationem, quæ præcessit, hoc modo: Cum tam manife- stis rationibus constet, quæ facio non dæmonum, sed Dei virtute fieri; videte quam gravem in vos pœnam accersatis, cum dicitis ista vi dæmonum effici. Hanc connexionem docet nos Marcus cap. III 30. Neque tamen solis argumen- tis suis confisus hoc Christus dicebat, sed simul, ut modo dixerat Matthæus, εἰδὼς πὰς ἐνθυμήσεις αὐτω̃ν. Videbat ni- mirum mentium inspector agnoscere ipsos virtutem vere divinam, sed quidvis potius comminisci, quam ut plebem paterentur à suo magisterio ad Christum transire.

Πᾶσα ἁμαρτία κ̀ βλασφημία ἀφεθήσεται τοῖς ἀνθρώποις] Cum apertissimum sit non hoc dicere Christum omnia alia peccata condonatum iri (quam multa enim sunt, quæ non condonantur!) notandus omnino hic est Hebraismus, qualem observavimus supra ad caput V. in illis verbis Lu- cæ: ὁ οὐρανὸς κ̀ ἡ γῆ παρελεύσεται εἰ δὲ λόγοι μᾶ̃ κ̀ μὴ παρέλ- θωσι, quod alibi idem Lucas ita extulit: ὡ κοπώτερον δὲ ἐστι τὸν οὐρανὸν κ̀γὶ τὴν γῆν παρελθεῖν ἠ̃ τᾶ̃ νόμα μίαν κεραίαν πεσεῖν. Et ita sæpissime Hebræi dicunt, hoc fiet, & istud non fiet, non quod prius membrum affirment, sed quod ostendere velint, quod posterius ponitur multo esse difficilius, quo- modo Latini dicunt: Ante pererratis amborum finibus exsul, Aut Ararim Parthus bibet, aut Germania Tigrin. Sensus ergo est, facilius est, quicquid criminum unquam patrari poterit, atque adeo calumnias etiam omnes, quæ in criminibus primum facile locum obtinent, remitti, quam ut remittatur ea calumnia quæ adversus Spiritum Dei committitur. Vide similem comparationem 1. Sam. II. 25.

Ebraismus ille temere his locis affingitur. Nam neque hic tantum hypothesis est, vel compa- rate verba intelligenda sunt, facilius esse, ut cri- mina omnia alia condonentur, quam peccatum in Spiritum Sanct. neque in aliis allegatis dictis. Hic sane nihil obstat, quo minus simpliciter intel- ligantur verba, ut sonant, omne peccatum aliud, & omnem blasphemiam remitti; peccatum au- tem in Spiritum Sanct. neutiquam remitti posse. Unde autem obsecro apertissimum est Christum hoc non dicere, omnia alia peccata condonatum iri, quum textus apertissimus sit hoc dicere Chri- stum, quod λευκάδι φωνῇ hic pronunciat, & con- tra falsissimum sit, multa esse peccata, quæ non condo- nentur. Quænam enim illa? & ubi tale quid in Scri- pturis traditum! Annon hoc amplissimæ, inex- haustæ & Dei misericordiæ, annon universalissi- mæ Christi Satisfactioni, annon gratiosissimis Spi- ritus Sancti promissionibus Evangelicis è diametro contrarium est? Nec in verbis Lucæ XXI. 33. est, quod discedere nos cogat ab eo sensu, quem per se illa inferunt; imo antithesis inter cælum & ter- ram, ceu res caducas, quæ tandem interituræ sint, & verbum Dei, quod plane est invariabile, confirmat luculenter eam sententiam, cum quod uni tribuitur oppositorum, interitus nempe, ab altero oppositorum removetur: neque dubium est, cælum, & terram tandem in consummatione seculi peritura, si quis alia Scripturæ loca perpen- dat, quæ huic parallela, inprimis Psal. CII. 27. 2. Petr. III. 10. seqq. Apoc. XXI. 1. Denique ni- hil pro illo Ebraismo Grotiano locus 1. Sam. II. 25. Nam & ista verba simpliciter ut sonant, accipi possunt, quod quæ adversus hominem committun- tur, in judicio humano componi possit; ut non opus sit sensu contrario,

## 12:32
Vers. 32. Against the Son of man] What we observed above at verse

8, I think the same must be observed here regarding 'the Son of man,' although with the article added, not only Christ is understood here, but any man whatsoever, not even excluding Christ. For the article is often a sign of generality, as 'the Gentile' below chapter XVIII. 17, 'the priest' Mark I. 44, 'the children' Rev. II. 23. The sense is: You know it is a grave crime to slander an innocent man: for by the law of Moses, the penalty of death is established for that crime as the most grave. Think therefore how much graver it is to oppose the works of God himself with calumnies: to sin 'with a high hand' (Num. XV. 30): which is explained as heaping reproaches upon God, Num. XIV. 29, as Korah and his followers did. This passage is illustrated by that in the Acts of the Apostles V. 4, where how grave the fault of Ananias is, is shown by Peter through a similar opposition: 'You have not lied to men, but to God.' But Peter had said before that it had been the intention of Ananias 'to lie to the Holy Spirit.' As therefore he is called a 'Lord-killer' who does not revere the present Spirit of God, so she [the calumny] now slanders not a man but God, who, although he recognizes the works of God within himself, nevertheless persists in calumny. How great a crime this is, and how much it surpasses all others, can be understood by three comparisons. First, by that example of Ananias, who, tempted by avarice, as we said, did not revere the Spirit of God present in the Apostles: then by the example of Simon Magus, who, when he had dishonored the gift of the Holy Spirit with the intention of trafficking, heard from Peter, 'May your money be to your destruction, because you thought the gift of God could be bought with money': and afterwards: 'Repent of this wickedness of yours, and pray to God if perhaps the thought of your heart may be forgiven you.' Behold, Peter weighs this fault so heavily that he almost despairs of pardon. Let the third example be that of Pharaoh, which it is manifest is here referred to by Christ from Luke, who, as we have said, uses the very words of Moses. Although, says Moses, the magicians said to Pharaoh that the finger of God was there, yet Pharaoh's heart hardened itself: after which time God so took away Pharaoh's mind that, warned by no portents, he would repent, but was carried headlong into ruin. Thus those who insult the Spirit of grace, as the divine writer to the Hebrews speaks, imitating the words of Moses in Num. XV. 30, fall into the hands of the living God: who also elsewhere argues thus: if contumacy against the precepts given through Angels was compensated with such great punishments, what is it right for those to expect who have neglected this salvation, which received testimony from God through so many signs and portents? But no insolence can be graver than that which adds calumny to contempt, such as this of the Pharisees was.

It shall be forgiven him] More easily, as we have already said.

neither in this world, nor in the world to come] The exposition of Chrysostom is simple according to litotes: he will be punished severely both in this and in the future world: to the strengthening of which it contributes that the Jews were accustomed to speak thus. For in the Misna we read: 'They are evil men in this world and have no part in the world to come.' And Eleazar in the Epitome of Jason of Cyrene says: if I pass as a foreigner, I shall not escape the hands of the Almighty, neither living nor dead 2 Macc. VI. 26. Nor does Maimonides otherwise in the rules of Repentance chap. VI say that there are certain sinners from whom punishment is exacted both in this world and in the future. It seems, however, that Christ deliberately named both worlds, so as to take away from the Jews that persuasion with which they flattered themselves against the gravest offenses. For they thought that sins committed by those who persevered in the profession of Judaism were remitted either through mere repentance, as those which were committed against mandatory precepts, or on the solemn day of reconciliation, as those which were committed against most prohibitive precepts, or through the chastisements of this life, as those which have the punishment of death or excision attached, or at least after death, whether immediately or after the delays of some time, as those which had been committed with contempt of the divine majesty. Hence that prayer of the dying: may my death be a remission of all my sins. Hence that formula of prayer for the dead, which they call Kaddish: hence that Talmudic statement: every Israelite has a part in the world to come. Therefore, on the contrary, Christ teaches that those sins which contain grave contempt of God are to be punished both here and hereafter without end or measure. In the Constitutions of Clement book VI. chap. XVIII. those who have blasphemed the Spirit of grace, and have rejected the gift from Him after the grace, to whom it shall not be forgiven neither in this world nor in the world to come, compare the passages of the Apocalypse XIV. 10. 11. & XX. 10. Tertullian in his book on Modesty calls blasphemy a crime irremissible both in this and in the future world. Which we have already indicated was believed by most Jews, that those who were oppressed by grave diseases or other inconveniences in this life were freed from the punishments of the other life; many traces of that opinion exist in the writings of the Hebrews and remain in their proverbs even today. Origen, citing the passage 3 Kings II concerning Joab, but in which he wrongly reads 'you shall bring down' instead of 'you shall not bring down', adduces this as rashly said by a Hebrew man, which he himself seized upon with excessive ease: it is clear that, as the Hebrew also reported to us, that he would be put to rest in peace through punishment, the punishment and torture being owed to him there because he had already been wiped out from here after his departure from here. Moreover, that the persuasion concerning the remission of certain sins after death is older than the times of Christ is most evident from that Jason of Cyrene whom I mentioned, who narrates that sacrifices were offered for the sin of those who had fallen. I cannot at all persuade myself that the judgment of the Christian Church is being dealt with here: for I believe our Lord spoke in the way He knew best that He would be understood by the Jews.

By the Son of man Grotius does not understand Christ alone, which is the common explanation of others, but any man whatsoever, not even excluding Christ. But if not even Christ is excluded, is not the slander cast against Christ imagined to be of the same kind as the slander cast against any other man? Yet there is no doubt that it is far more serious, by as much as Christ is greater than other men. And since Scripture is accustomed to understand Christ specifically by the Son of man, why should we posit here that unusual meaning concerning any man? Furthermore, there is no need for the force of the article to be diminished here, even if perhaps certain other passages exist in which the article is a sign of generality. Moreover, the discourse ascends: Every sin and every blasphemy will be forgiven, indeed even blasphemy cast against Christ as the Son of man. Finally, ςρεβλότης is that sense of easier and more difficult remission, as if it were only hinted that that crime is forgiven more easily when someone slanders an innocent man than the blasphemy of the Spirit: for Christ teaches that this is absolutely irremissible, not just forgiven with more difficulty, as Grotius wishes, following the Socinians—concerning whose opinion in the Profligated Socinianism—and certain Papists, Lyranus, Cornelius, Maldonado, and Bellarmine.

Furthermore, the things he sprinkles here concerning the passage in Acts 5:4, how Ananias lied to God when he did not revere the present Spirit of God, which are analogous to the glosses of the Socinians who infringe upon the Deity of the Holy Spirit, as well as concerning the words of Peter to Simon Magus in Acts 8:22, 'If perhaps it may be forgiven thee,' that he made so much of that fault that he almost despaired of pardon, which are twin to the same principles of the Socinians and Papists, will have their place elsewhere. However, we accept that which he posits in the words 'in this age, or in the age to come,' following Chrysostom, as a litotes, in this sense: he will be punished severely both in this and in the future age, so that no one may think that any remission of sins is brought about in the other age: even if it is as doubtful whether Christ had regard for that persuasion of the Jews—that sins which had been committed with contempt for the divine majesty were at least after death, whether immediately or after the delays of some time, [remitted]—as it is that the aforementioned persuasion flourished among the Jews at that time, whatever may be the case regarding the fact that in the Maccabean books sacrifices are read to have been offered for the sin of those who had fallen. Grotius himself therefore understood that the Papists find nothing in this passage for their purgatory, or purification after this life: whose confession it is helpful to note: for he is otherwise accustomed to gladly 'Papize'. 'I cannot,' he says, 'at all persuade myself that the judgment of the Christian Church is being dealt with here. For I believe our Lord spoke in the way He knew best that He would be understood by the Jews.' Grotius judges here that Christ did not approve, but rather disapproved of the persuasion of the Jews. Yet, he says, it seems that Christ deliberately named both ages, so that He might take away from the Jews that persuasion with which they flattered themselves against the most serious offenses. For they thought that sins committed by those who persevered in the profession of Judaism were remitted either through mere repentance, as those which were admitted against commanding precepts; or on the solemn day of reconciliation, as those which were admitted against most forbidding precepts; or through the chastisements of this life, as those which have the penalty of death or excision attached; or at least after death, whether immediately or after the delays of some time, as those which had been committed with contempt for the divine majesty. Hence that prayer of the dying: 'May my death be a remission of all my sins.' Hence that formula of praying for the dead which they call Kaddish: hence that Talmudic statement: 'Every Israelite has a share in the future age.' Therefore, Christ teaches the opposite, that those sins which contain grave contempt for God are to be punished both here and in the future without end or measure. These are the words of Grotius: which we deservedly oppose to his own annotations on Cassander, in the chapter on the sacrifice of the body and blood of Christ: where he strives to build up faith in purgatory from the inventions of the Hebrews. 'The Hebrews think,' he says, 'that after some time of perfection, that is, of purification, the spirit is received into heaven.' Thus speaks the Gemara Hagigah; thus Midrash Anatholam on the beginning of Genesis, R. Moses Barschem Tob in his notes to Rabbi Israel, Maimonides in several places, which opinion has also prevailed among Christians in the West. He adds indeed: 'These things, as in the great darkness of such matters, must be treated soberly and circumspectly.' But yet he employs them for strengthening the Papistic liturgies, which he falsely calls ancient (for they have been interpolated by the Papists); 'but,' he says, 'the ancient liturgies are not to be condemned, since not even Christ ever rebuked the prayers for the dead accustomed to be made among the Jews, of which a formula exists in the Talmudic writings, made, it is believed, in the Babylonian exile, and mention is made in the second book of Maccabees.' All of which sail for the Papistic cause. We know that the Papistic purgatory can be derived equally from the Jews, and the Heathens, and the Turks, for whom this fiction is common.
