But our only Rabbi is Christ, whom the blind Jews did not acknowledge; that Master did not teach us that all Israel would have a share in the future age. The ungodly also, who are said to be under no repentance and are pressed by no sorrow for their sins, will suffer in the underworld for twelve months, and only afterwards will obtain their portion in eternal life, but not as great a one as the just and pious. But those who utterly deny God and profane his holy name, such that, if they become Christians, their foreskin grows anew as if they had never been circumcised, those remain in the underworld forever. That supreme Rabbi did not teach that liberation from purgatory is effected by a certain prayer, which they call קדיש Kaddisch, through which a father might be liberated if a son recites it daily for an entire year, through which also a pious wife will be able to liberate her husband from the underworld. If Christ never expressly rebuked the prayers for the dead accustomed to be made among the Jews, the formula of which exists in the Talmud, it does not follow from that that he approved of them, or even that they were in use at the time when he was on earth. For it is assumed, not proven, that that formula was made during the Babylonian exile. If the prayers of the living had been useful or necessary for the deceased, Christ would not have said in Matthew VIII, p. 22, to the disciple asking permission to depart to bury his father, 'Let the dead bury their own dead': by which form of speech he wished to indicate that this care, although not to be neglected ceteris paribus, less concerns those who live for Christ: which he would not have said if, for the funerals of the dead, prayers and sacrifices had been necessary. How many trifles are there in the Talmud, of which Christ makes no mention? It is enough that He very often condemned the traditions of men and the leaven of the doctrine of the Pharisees. Which Paul warned us against, [referring to] Jewish fables. Nor does the Epitome of Jason of Cyrene contribute anything to this, in which mention is made of an offering for the dead, which has no foundation in the most exact ancient law. In the ancient sacred history, mention is often made of those who were gathered to their fathers in peace, [but] nowhere that prayers were poured out for them. These and other things, which Rivet set against Grotius, we do not undeservedly repeat here, because they strike at the throat of the causes, nor was Grotius able to dilute them in his amoebaean verses: so that here indeed Rivet had no need of an Apologetic, nor of vindications for an Apologetic.

However, he agrees with Grotius here, where he was still sounder than the later Grotius, when he had begun to attempt Syncretism (for the Annotations on the earlier Gospels were written to Callandrus and others born from that). Tostatus, Bishop of Avila, in this place, q. LXXIV on Matthew: Christ could say this, not supposing that another sin against the Son would be forgiven after death, but to remove the error of some who might think that sins are forgiven after death which were not forgiven to those living. And he approves the λιτότητα (litotes) of Chrysostom, as was also done by Ferus in this place: By saying less, he signifies more. For he means that such a sin is punished not only in the future, but also here. Which explanation of Chrysostom is praised both by the Jesuit Conzenius in this place and by Jansenius, the Bishop.

Finally, what will the Papists gain from these words, when we have an explicit interpretation of these words, superior to every exception, in the parallel passage Mark 3:29: 'hath not forgiveness forever, but will be guilty of eternal judgment,' which teaches nothing other than that some are not guilty of eternal judgment; which makes nothing at all for purgatory. And furthermore, Bellarmine himself confesses that this does not follow from the words of Christ, according to Dialectical rules: 'The sin against the Holy Spirit will not have forgiveness in the future age; therefore, there is given a certain sin which will have forgiveness in the future age.' He adds, indeed, that it follows according to the rules of prudence, but this is just as inept as if you were to say that Syntactical rules are not from Grammar, but from Politics; that rules about tropes are to be drawn not from Rhetoric, but from Ethics; or that the addition of numbers is done not according to Arithmetic, but according to Statics.

Latin:

Vers. 32. κατὰ τᾶ̃ ὑᾶ̃ ἀνθρώπɤ] Quod supra ad comma

8. observavimus, idem hic observandum puto per υἱὸν ἀν- θρώπου quamvis addito articulo non hic Christum solum intelligi, sed hominem quemvis, ne Christo quidem exce- pto. Est enim sæpe articulus fignum generalitatis, ut ὁ ἐθνι- κὸς infra cap. XVIII. 17. τῷ ἱερεῖ Marc. I. 44. τὰ τέκνα Apoc. II. 23. Sensus est: Scitis grave esse crimen innocentem hominem calumniari: nam lege Mosis in id crimen tan- quam gravissimum, capitis pœna est constituta. Cogitate ergo quando gravius sit Dei ipsius opera calumniis oppu-, gnare: peccare ביד רמה manu elata: quod exponitur Deum probris afficere Num. XIV. 29. ut Core cum suis. Illustrat hunc locum illud in Actis Apostolicis V. 4. ubi quam gravis sit culpa Ananiæ simili oppositione à Petro o- stenditur: ὀυκ ἐψεύσω ἀνθρώποις, ἀλλὰ τῷ Θεῷ. Ante au- tem dixerat Petrus propositum fuisse Ananiæ ψεύσασθαι τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον. Sicut ergo ille κυριοκτόνος dicitur Deo mentiri, qui præsentem Spiritum Dei non reveretur, ita il- la jam non hominem sed Deum calumniatur, qui cum in- tra se Dei opera agnoscat, tamen perstat in calumnia. Quan- tum autem hoc sit crimen quantoq; aliis omnibus antistet, tribus comparationibus intelligi potest. Primum isto A- naniæ exemplo, qui avaritia tentatus, ut diximus, præsen- tem in Apostolis Dei Spiritum non reverebatur: deinde exemplo Simonis Magi, qui cum donum Spiritus Sancti nundinationis proposito dehonestasset, audiit à Petro, Pecunia tua tibi in perniciem sit, quia donum Dei existimasti pecunia posse comparari: & postea: pœnitentiam age hujus malitiæ, & Deum precare si forte condonetur tibi cogitatio cor- dis tui. Ecce tanti pendit hanc culpam Petrus, ut de venia pene desperet. Tertium exemplum esto Pharaonis, quod hic respici à Christo ex Luca, qui ipsa, ut diximus, Mosis verba usurpat, manifestum est. Quamvis, inquit Moses, magi dicerent Pharaoni, digitum Dei ibi esse, tamen Pharao- nis cor semet obstinavit: post quod tempus Deus ita mentem ademit Pharaoni, ut nullis ostentis monitus resipisceret, sed præceps ferretur in ruinam. Ita οἱ ἐνυβρίζοντες τὸ πνεῦ- μα τῆς χάριτος, ut loquitur divinus ad Hebræos scriptor, verba Mosis imitans Num. XV. 30. incidunt in manus Dei viventis: qui & alibi ita argumentatur: si contumacia ad- versus præcepta per Angelos data tantis suppliciis compen- sata est, quid æquum est eos exspectare, qui hanc salutem neglexerint, quæ à Deo per tot signa atque ostenta testimo- nium accepit? At nulla ὕβρις esse potest gravior, quam quæ contemtui calumniam adjungit, qualis erat hæc Phariseo- rum.

Ἀφεθήσεται αὐτῷ] Facilius, ut jam diximus.

ὔτε ἐν τούτῳ τῷ αἰῶνι, ὔτε ἐν τῷ μέλλοντι] Simplex est Chry- sostomi expositio κατὰ λιτότητα: punietur graviter & in hoc & in futuro sæculo: cui firmandæ facit quod sic loqui solebant Judæi. Nam in Misnaqth legimus הבאנם רעין מן האדם בעלם הזה ואין לא חלק לעולם. Et Eleazarus in Epitome Jasonis Cyrenæi, fi, inquit, transeam ὡς ἀλ- λοφυλισμὸν, omnipotentis manus non effugiam, neque vi- vus neque mortuus 2. Macc. VI. 26. Nec aliter Maimoni- des in regulis Pœnitentiæ cap. VI. quosdam ait peccatores esse de quibus pœna exigatur & in hoc sæculo & in futu- ro. Videtur tamen Christus de industria utrumque secu- lum nominasse, ut Judæis auferret eam qua sibi blandie- bantur adversus gravissima delicta persuasionem. Existi- mabant enim peccata commissa ab his qui in Judaismi pro- feffione perseverarent remitti aut per meram pœnitentiam, ut quæ admitterentur contra præcepta jubentia, aut in die solenni reconciliationis ut quæ admitterentur contra ple- raque præcepta vetantia, aut per hujus vitæ castigationes, ut quæ mortis aut excidii pœnam adjunctam habent, aut saltem post mortem, sive statim sive post temporis alicujus moras, ut quæ cum contemtu facta essent divini numinis. Hinc illa precatio morientium: sit mors mea remissio pecca- torum meorum omnium. Hinc illa precandi formula pro mortuo, quam קדיש vocant: hinc Thalmudicum illud enunciatum: omnis Israelita partem habet sæculi futuri. Contra ergo Christus docet, ea peccata quæ gravem Dei contemtum continent, & hic & in posterum sine fine mo- doque plectenda. In Clementis constitutionibus libro VI. cap. XVIII. οἱ βλασφημήσαντες τὸ πνεῦμα τῆς χάριτος, καὶ ἀποποιήσαντες τὴν παρ᾽ αὐτῷ δωρεὰν μετὰ τὴν χάριν, οἷς ὐκ ἀφεθήσεται ὔτε ἐν τῷ αἰῶνι τὐτῳ ὔτε ἐν τῷ μέλλοντι, con- fer loca Apocalypseos XIV. 10. 11. & XX. 10. Tertullia- nus libro de Pudicitia blasphemiam vocat crimen & in hoc & in futuro sæculo irremissibile. Quod jam indicavimus creditum à Judæis plerisque eos qui gravibus morbis aut aliis incommodis in hac vita premerentur liberari à pœnis vitæ alterius, ejus opinionis multa exstant in Hebræorum Scriptis & Proverbiis hodieque manentibus vestigia. Ori- genes citans locum 3. Reg. II. de Joabo, sed in quo per- peram legit κατάξεις pro ὐ κατάξεις, adfert hoc ab Hebræo homine temere dictum, quod ipse nimia facilitate arripuit: δῆλοι δὲ ὅτι, ὡς καὶ ὁ ἑβραῖος ἡμῖν ἀπήγγειλε, τὸ διὰ τῆς κολάσεως αὐτὸν ἐν εἰρήνῃ κοιμηθήσεσθαι, ἐκεῖσε ὀφειλομένης αὐτῷ κολάσεως, καὶ βασάνου διὰ τὸ ἐ̓ντεῦθεν ἤδη ἀπαληφίναι αὐτὸν μετὰ τὴν ἐ̓ντεῦθεν ἀπαλλαγήν. Antiquiorem autem Christi temporibus esse persuasionem de peccatis quibusdam post mortem remittendis apertissimum est ex eo quem dixi Jasone Cyraeneo, qui oblata narrat sacrificia περὶ ἁμαρτίας τῶν προπεπτωκότων. De Ecclesiae Christianae judicio hic agi plane persuadere mihi non possum: ita enim locutum credo Dominum nostrum, quomodo loquentem se sciebat optime a Judaeis intelligi.

Per υἱὸν τῆ ἀνθρώπου Grotius non Christum solum intelligit, quae communis aliorum explicatio est, sed hominem quemvis, ne Christo quidem excepto. Sed si ne Christus quidem excipitur, annon calumnia in Christum vibrata ejusdem commatis esse fingitur cum calumnia in quemvis alium hominem jactata? Quam vero longe graviorem esse dubitandum non est, quanto nempe major est Christus aliis hominibus. Et quum Scriptura per Filium hominis intelligere soleat peculiariter Christum, cur hic insolitam illam significationem de quovis homine statuamus? Adhec non opus est, ut articuli vis hic imminuatur, etsi forte loca quaedam alias suppetant, in quibus articulus signum generalitatis sit. Porro scandit oratio: Omne peccatum, & omnis blasphemia remittetur, imo etiam blasphemia in Christum ut Filium hominis jactata. Denique ςρεβλότης est ille facilioris & difficilioris remissionis sensus, quasi tantum innuatur, facilius remitti crimen illud, cum innocentem hominem quis calumniatur, quam blasphemiam Spiritus: hanc enim prorsus esse irremissibilem Christus docet, non tantum difficilius remitti, uti cum Socinianis, de quorum sententia in Socianismo profligato, & Papistis quibusdam, Lyrano, Cornelio, Maldonato, Bellarm. Grotius vult.

Quae porro hic inspergit de loco Actor V. 4. quomodo Ananias Deo mentitus sit, cum praesentem Spiritum Dei non revereretur, Socinianorum argumentum Deitatis Spiritus Sancti infringentium glossae analoga, nec non de verbis Petri ad Simonem Magum Act. VIII. 22. Si forte condonetur tibi, quod tanti fecerit eam culpam, ut de venia pene desperarit, quae iisdem Socinianorum, & Pontificiorum principiis gemina sunt, alias suam habebunt sedem. Id autem acceptamus, quod in verbis ἄτε ἐν τῷ νῦν αἰῶνι, ὄτε ἐν τῷ μέλλοντι, praeeunte Chrysostomo, λιτότητα statuat, hoc sensu: punietur graviter & in hoc & in futuro seculo, ne quis remissionem aliquam peccatorum in altero seculo inferri censeat: etsi Christum respexisse illam Judaeorum persuasionem, quod peccata quae cum contemtu numinis divini facta essent, saltim post mortem sive statim, sive post temporis alicujus moras, aeque, si non magis dubium sit, quam quod isto tempore penes Judaeos viguerit praedicta persuasio, quicquid de eo sit, quod in Maccabaicis oblata legantur sacrificia περὶ ἁμαρτίας τῶν πεπτωκότων. Intellexit ergo Grotius ipse, hoc in loco nihil invenire Pontificios pro purgatorio suo, vel purgatione post hanc vitam: cujus confessionem notare juvat: Solet enim alias lubenter Papizare. De Ecclesiae, inquit, Christianae judicio hic agi plane persuadere mihi non possum. Ita enim locutum credo Dominum nostrum, quomodo loquentem se sciebat optime a Judaeis intelligi. Non autem approbasse, sed improbasse potius Christum Judaeorum persuasionem hic censet Grotius. Videtur tamen, inquit, Christus de industria utrumque seculum nominasse, ut Judaeis auferret eam, qua sibi blandiebantur adversus gravissima delicta per- suasionem. Existimabant enim peccata commissa ab his qui in Iudaismi professione perseverarent re- mitti aut per meram pœnitentiam, ut quæ admitte- rentur contr.a præcepta jubentia; aut in die solenni reconciliationis, ut quæ admitterentur contra pleraq; præcepta vetantia; aut per hujus vitæ castigationes, ut quæ mortis aut excidii pœnam adjunctam habent; aut saltem post mortem, sive statim, sive post tempo- ris alicujus moras, ut quæ cum contemptu facta essent numinis divini. Hinc illa precatio morientium: Sit mors mea remissio peccatorum meorum o- mnium. Hinc illa precandi formula pro mortuo quam קדיש vocant: hinc Thalmudicum illud e- nunciatum: omnis Israëlita partem habet seculi futuri. Contra ergo Christus docet, ea peccata quæ gravem Dei contemptum continent & hæc & in po- sterum sine fine modoque plectenda. Hæc Grotius: quæ merito ipsius annotatis ad Cassandrum Cap. de sacrificio corporis & sanguinis Christi opponi- mus: ubi ex Ebræorum commentis purgatorio fi- dem adstruere satagit. Putant Ebræi, inquit, post tempus aliquod τελειώσεως id est purgationis Spiritus in cœlum recipi. Sic loquitur Gemara Hagita; Sic Midrasch Anatholam in capite Bereschit, R. Mo- ses Barschem Tob in notis ad Rabbiram Israëlem, Maimonidem compluribus locis, quæ sententia e- tiam apud Christianos in Occidente invaluit. Ad- dit quidem: Hæc ut in magna rerum istarum cali- gine sobrie, & circumspecte tractanda sunt: Sed adhibet tamen illa pro firmandis Papisticis, quas falso veterum dicit, (sunt enim à Papistis inter- polatæ) Liturgiis; non autem, inquit, damnan- dæ sunt veteres liturgiæ, cum ne Christus quidem orationes pro mortuis apud Judæos fieri solitas, qua- rum & formula exstat in Thalmudicis facta ut cre- ditur in Babylonico exsilio, & mentio est in Mac- cabaico secundo, unquam reprehenderit. Quæ o- mnia Papistico velificantur. Novimus à Judæis pa- riter, & Ethnicis & Turcis quorum commune est hoc figmentum, derivari posse Papisticum pur- gatorium. Sed unicus Rabbi noster est Christus, quem cæci Judæi non agnoverunt, Magister ille non docuit nos, totum Israëlem partem habitu- rum in futuro seculo. Impios etiam qui nulla dicun- tur pœnitentia, nulloque propter sua peccata mœ- rore premuntur per duodecim menses in inferis pas- suros, ac postea demum partem suam consequuturos in vita æterna, sed non adeo magnam quam ju- sti & pii. Iis vero qui Deum prorsus abnegant, & sanctum ejus nomen prophanant, ut qui fiant Chri- stiani, præputium de novo crescere, quasi nunquam circumcisi fuerint, illosque in æternum in inferis permanere. Non docuit summus ille Rabbi libe- rationem è purgatorio fieri precatione quadam, quam vocant קדיש Kaddisch, per quam liberetur pater, si eam filius recitet per integrum annum quo- tidie, per quam etiam pia uxor poterit maritum suum ab inferis liberare. Si Christus nunquam ex- presse reprehendit orationes pro mortuis apud Ju- dæos fieri solitas, quarum formula extat in Thal- mude, inde non sequitur, quod eas approbave- rit, vel etiam quod tempore, quo in terris versa- batur, in usu fuerint. Nam formulam illam fa- ctam fuisse in exilio Babylonico assumitur, non probatur. Si vivorum preces defunctis fuissent utiles aut necessariæ, non dixisset Christus Matth. VIII. p. 22. discipulo petenti veniam abeundi, ut sepeliret patrem suum, Sine mortuos sepelire mor- tuos suos: qua loquendi formula indicare voluit, curam hanc, quamvis non negligendam cæteris paribus, minus spectare eos, qui Christo vi- vunt: quod non dixisset, si ad mortuorum exe- quias preces & sacrificia fuissent necessaria. Quot sunt nugamenta in Thalmude, quorum Christus nusquam meminit? sufficit, quod sæpissime da- mnavit traditiones hominum, & fermentum doctri- næ Pharisæorum. Quod Paulus nos monuit contra fabulas Judaicas. Nec ad id quicquam facit Epi- tome Jasonis Cyrenai, in qua fit mentio oblationis pro mortuis, quæ in veteri lege exactissima nul- lum habet fundamentum. In historia sacra veteri sæpe fit mentio eorum qui collecti fuerunt ad patres suos in pace, nullibi quod pro eis fusæ fuerint preces. Hæc & alia, quæ reposuit Grotio Rivetus, non immerito hic repetimus, quia causæ jugulum pe- tunt, nec diluere ea valuit in amæbæis Grotius: ut hic quidem nec Apologetico, nec vindiciis pro Apologetico Rivetus opus habuerit.

Consentit autem Grotio, hic, qua sanior adhuc fuit posteriore Grotio, ubi Syncretismum tentare ceperat, (Annotata enim ad Evangelia priora sunt scripto ad Callandrum & inde enatis aliis.) Tostatus Episcopus Abulensis hoc loco q. LXXIV. in Matth. Poterat hoc Christus dicere, non supponendo, quod aliud peccatum in Filium di- mitteretur post mortem, sed ad tollendum errorem aliquorum, qui putarent dimitti peccata post mor- tem, quæ viventibus non fuerunt dimissa. Et λι- τότητα Chrysostomi approbat, uti quoque à Fero in h. l. factum: Minus dicendo plus significat. Vult enim quod non solum in futuro, sed etiam hic puni- tur tale peccatum. Quam Chrysostomi explica- tionem & Conzenius Jesuita h. l. & Jansenius Epi- scopus laudat.

Denique quid lucrabuntur ex his verbis Pa- pistæ, quum disertam, omnique exceptione su- periorem verborum horum interpretationem habeamus in loco parallelo Marc. III. 29. non ha- bet remissionem in æternum, sed reus erit æterni ju- dicii, quæ nihil aliud docet, quam quod nonnul- li non sint rei æterni judicii; quod nihil omnino facit pro purgatorio. Et fatetur præterea Bellar- minus ipse ex verbis Christi hoc non sequi, secun- dum regulas Dialecticas: peccatum in Spiritum Sanctum non habebit remissionem in futuro seculo E. datur peccatum quoddam quod habebit in futuro seculo remissionem; qui addit quidem, sequi secun- dum regulas prudentiæ, sed hoc ineptum æque est, ac si dicas, regulas Syntacticas non esse è Grammati- ca, sed ex Politica; regulas de tropis non ex Rhetori- ca, sed Ethica hauriendas esse; aut additionem nu- merorum fieri non secundum Arithmeticam, sed se- cundum Staticam.

## 12:33
Verse 33. ἢ ποιήσατε] Thus also the Latins say 'fac' (make), for which the Greeks would say τίθετε (set/place). But Christ's judgment is most true, that a judgment about the quality of the soul ought to be made from acts that are either perpetual or more frequent and long-lasting, a matter which we discussed at chapter VII. All the works of Christ were full of beneficence: all His doctrine looked toward piety: what cause, therefore, is there to suspect anything otherwise about Him?

Σαπρὸν] בּוּשׁ for the Hebrews, בּאִישׁ for the Syrians. Thus they call whatever is evil: which locution is also below in 13:48.

Moreover, the τὸ ἀυτεξέσιον (free will) is not attributed to man here, but the mask of hypocrisy is stripped from the Pharisees, so that if they wish to be good, they should not merely feign good things, but do them. Simulation is the leaves, works are the fruit. The tree is known not by its leaves, but by its fruits.

Latin:

Vers. 33. ἢ ποιήσατε] Ita & Latini dicunt fac, pro quo Græci dicerent τίθετε. Verissima autem est Christi senten- tia, ex actibus aut perpetuis aut frequentioribus ac diutur- nis de animi qualitate judicium fieri debere, qua de re egi- mus ad cap. VII. Opera Christi omnia plena erant benefi- centiæ: doctrina omnis ad pietatem spectabat: quæ igitur causa sequius de ipso aliquid suspicandi?

Σαπρὸν] בּוּשׁ Hebræis בּאִישׁ Syris. Ita illi quic- quid malum est vocant: quæ locutio & infra XIII. 48.

Cæterum non τὸ ἀυτεξέσιον homini hic tri- buitur, sed Pharisæis larva hypocriseos detrahi- tur, ut si boni esse velint, non simulent tantum, bona, sed faciant. Simulatio folia sunt, opera fructus. Non ex foliis sed fructibus arbor cogno- scitur.

## 12:34
Verse 34. πῶς δύνασθε] Take a proof from yourselves, says Christ, how true that sentence is. For since you are evil within, we see that the things you speak are also evil: nor can it be otherwise. For however much a dissimulated character may be, it very easily leaps out. Christ is not dealing here with the common weakness of men, but with the most serious vices of hatred, envy, and arrogance, which the Pharisees had contracted of their own accord. And according to the nature of the subject matter, τὸ δύνασθαι (the 'being able') is to be understood.

is to be understood, not κατὰ τὴν φυσικὴν ἀκρίβειαν (according to physical precision), but κατὰ τὴν ἠθικὴν πλατύτητα (according to moral breadth): and ἀγαθὰ λαλεῖν (to speak good things) not about one or another act, but about that which happens ἐπὶ πολὺ (for the most part), which the subject matter also most clearly shows. Thus Jeremiah 13:23, 1 Corinthians 2:14, John 8:45, and chapter 12:39. See what [we wrote] on Mark 6:5.

ἐκ γὰρ τοῦ περισσεύματος τῆς καρδίας τὸ στόμα λαλεῖ] Just as the stomach vomits what abounds in it, so also does the heart. He calls the πε- ρίσσευμα καρδίας (abundance of the heart) and later the θησαυρὸν (treasure) the ἕξιν (habit) itself, and what he had said about works in general, he here adapts to words. Menander says the same: ᾿Ανδρὸς χαρακτὴρ ἐκ λόγου γνωρίζεται (A man's character is known from his speech). And Aristides: οἷος ὁ τρόπος τοιοῦτος κἀ ὁ λόγος (As is the manner, so is the speech). Quintilian in book XI. 1: 'For speech generally brings forth character, and uncovers the secrets of the soul.' Nor without cause have the Greeks handed down that as a man lives, so also he speaks.

Latin:

Vers. 34. πῶς δύνασθε] A vobis, inquit Christus, do- cumentum sumite quam vera sit illa sententia. Nam cum intus mali sitis, videmus etiam mala esse quæ profamini: ne- que aliter fieri potest. Nam quantumvis dissimulatum in- genium facillime prosilit. Non agit hic Christus de com- muni hominum imbecillitate: sed de gravissimis vitiis odii, invidiæ atque arrogantiæ, quæ Pharisæi sua sponte contraxerant. Et pro subjectæ materiæ ratione τὸ δύνασθαι

intelligendum, non κατὰ τὴν φυσικὴν ἀκρίβειαν, sed κατὰ τὴν ἠθικὴν πλατύτητα : & ἀγαθὰ λαλεῖν non de uno aut altero actu, sed de eo quod ἐπὶ πολὺ accidit, quod etiam subjecta ratio apertissime ostendit. Sic Jerem. XIII. 23. 1. Cor. II. 14. Johan. VIII. 45. & cap. XII. 39. Vide quæ ad Mar- cum VI. 5.

ἐκ γὰρ τοῦ περισσεύματος τῆς καρδίας τὸ στόμα λαλεῖ ] Sicut ventriculus quod in se abundat evomit, ita & cor. πε- ρίσσευμα καρδίας & postea θησαυρὸν vocat ἕξιν ipsam, & quod de operibus in universum dixerat, hic ad sermones aptat. Idem dicit Menander. ᾿Ανδρὸς χαρακτὴρ ἐκ λόγου γνωρίζεται. Et Aristides : οἷος ὁ τρόπος τοιοῦτος κἀ ὁ λόγος. Quintilia- nus libro XI. 1. Profert enim mores plerumque oratio, & ani- mi secreta detegit. Nec sine causa Græci prodiderunt, ut vivat quemque etiam dicere.

## 12:36
Verse 36. ῥῆμα ἀργὸν] Κενὸν λόγον (empty word), as Paul speaks in Ephesians 5:6. In Latin, I would call it 'sermonem vanum' (vain speech). I think, however, that the speech noted here is not that which is in any way useless, but that which lacks the solidity of truth: in the way we said above that the Hebrew שוא is used. There is, however, a tacit argument from the greater: If every lie will be brought into judgment, how much more so calumny.

Jerome more correctly: 'An idle word is that which is brought forth without the utility of the speaker or the hearer, if, omitting serious matters, we speak of frivolous things and tell ancient fables.' Moreover, he who explains scurrilous things and dissolves his mouth in laughter, and brings forth something of filth, he will be held guilty not of an idle word, but of a criminal one. And Gregory the Great in his Morals: 'An idle word is that which lacks either the reason of just necessity or the intention of pious utility.'

᾿Αποδώσουσι περὶ αὐτοῦ λόγον] This locution, which Paul also uses in Romans 14:12, is transferred from stewards who are called to account. It signifies in this place to undergo an examination, just as, conversely, in civil law those are called ἀνυπεύθυνοι (unaccountable) to whom the burden of rendering accounts has been remitted.

Hence Bernard suggests in his sermon on the triple custody: If for every idle word that men shall have spoken, they shall render an account to God on the day of judgment, how much more strictly shall they be judged for a lying, biting, and injurious word, for an arrogant or lascivious one, for a flattering or detracting one.

Latin:

Vers. 36. ῥῆμα ἀργὸν ] Κενὸν λόγον ut Paulus loquitur Eph. V. 6. Latine sermonem vanum dixerim. Puto autem non eum sermonem hic notari, qui quoquo modo sit in- utilis, sed eum, qui veri soliditate careat: quomodo שוא Hebræum usurpari supra diximus. Inest autem tacita à majori argumentatio : Si quodvis mendacium in judicium deducetur, quanto magis calumnia.

Rectius Hieronym. Verbum otiosum est, quod sine utilitate loquentis vel audientis profertur, si omissis seriis, de rebus frivolis loquamur & fabu- las narramus antiquas. Cæterum qui scurrilia ex- plicat & cachinnis ora dissolvit, & aliquid profert turpitudinis, hic non otiosi verbi, sed criminosi te- nebitur reus. Et Gregorius M. in moral. otiosum verbum est, quod aut ratione justæ necessitatis, aut intentione piæ utilitatis caret.

᾿Αποδώσουσι περὶ αὐτοῦ λόγον ] Locutio hæc qua & Paulus utitur Rom. XIV. 12. translata est à dispensatori- bus qui ad calculum vocantur. Significat autem hoc lo- co examen subire, sicut vicissim in jure civili ἀνυπεύθυνοι vocantur quibus remissum est onus reddendarum ratio- num.

Suggerit hinc Bernhardus serm. de triplici custodia : Quod si de omni vel otioso verbo, quod- cunque loquuti fuerint homines, Deo sunt redditu- ri rationem in die judicii, quanto districtius de ver- bo mendaci, mordaci & injurioso, de elato vel la- scivo, de adulatorio aut detractorio judicabun- tur.

## 12:37
Vers. 37. ἐκ γὰρ τῶν λόγων σου δικαιωθήσῃ] Christ refers this proverb, which is frequent in human judgments, to the divine judgment, which is accustomed to be described to us under the form of human judgment, as if he were to say: even if other deeds did not exist, it will easily be established from words alone whether you are upright or wicked. And so the καὶ which follows has a disjunctive force, as in Exod. XXI. 15. 17. Num. XXX. 4. 5. 6.

This, therefore, is noted, not that speech will be the cause of our righteousness, that pious speech offering no scandal will absolve us, that we have not been slanderous, blasphemous, or scandalous with our tongue. Conversely, from their own words, the slanderous, blasphemous, and those who have wickedly abused their tongue will be condemned: Cf. Eph. IV. 29. c. V. 4. Jac. III. 6. seqq. But from words, what kind of faith and piety lies hidden in the breast, as well as unbelief and impiety, a judgment can be brought, and will be brought, whether absolutory or condemnatory. For what else are holy words than faith sounding forth? Nor can unbelief and wickedness in the breast remain entirely hidden, without betraying itself at some time in speech: which is the character and index of both the upright and the wicked mind.

PART III. The denial of a sign other than Jonah's.

Latin:

Vers. 37. ἐκ γὰρ τῶν λόγων σου δικαιωθήσῃ] Proverbium hoc in judiciis humanis frequentatum, ad divinum judi- cium, quod sub humani judicii forma describi nobis solet, Christus refert, quasi dicat : etiamsi facta alia non exstarent, ex solis sermonibus facile constabit probi an improbi sitis. Itaque καὶ quod sequitur vim habet disjunctivam, ut Exod. XXI. 15. 17. Num. XXX. 4. 5. 6.

Id ergo notatur, non quod sermo futurus sit justitiæ nostræ causa, quod sermo pius nullum præ- bens scandalum nos absoluturus sit, quod non fuerimus maledici, blasphemi aut scandalosi lin- gua nostra. Ex adverso è dictis suis condemna- buntur maledici, blasphemi, & improbe lingua sua abusi : Conf. Eph. IV. 29. c. V. 4. Jac. III. 6. seqq. sed è sermonibus, qualis fides & pietas in pecto- re lateat, nec non incredulitas & impietas, judi- cium ferri potest, & feretur sive absolutoriurn si- ve condemnatorium. Quid enim aliud sermones sancti, quam fides sonans ? Nec latere prorsus potest incredulitas & improbitas in pectore, quin se prodat aliquando sermone: qui character & in- dex animi & probi est & improbi.

PARS III. Signi alterius quam Ionæ denegatio.

## 12:38
Vers. 38. Τότε ἀπεκρίθησάν τινες] ἀποκρίνεσθαι here, as often, is only to address. He added τινες, however, so that they would not be thought to be the same ones who had accused Christ of the magic art. For these presented the appearance not of accusers, but of doubters. Therefore Luke expressed it ἕτεροι δὲ πειράζοντες. Σημεῖον ] They are accustomed sometimes among the Hellenists indiscriminately to use σημεῖον, τέρας, δύναμιν: but you may often find σημεῖον & δύναμιν distinguished from one another, and often also those three δύναμιν, τέρας, σημεῖον, namely with the word σημεῖον used sometimes more loosely, sometimes more strictly. Here σημεῖον is opposed to δυνάμει. For the power which is shown in healing men and casting out demons is properly and strictly called δύναμις. Although quite many prodigies of this kind had been performed by Christ, those Pharisees and lawyers did not allow themselves to be satisfied by them, but, as if that matter were not of divine but of their own judgment, they demanded not δύναμις but σημεῖον, and not just any σημεῖον, but as Luke and in another place Matthew explains, σημεῖον ἀπ' ὀυρανῦ: importunately and impudently, when the very method of healing which Christ used, either by mere touch or by voice alone, and likewise his doctrine, contrary to the desires of demons, openly showed divine power. But God, who in the business of piety deals with men in such a way that he may most fully overcome malice, not that he may serve the immoderate desires of men, knew that those things which had been performed were abundantly sufficient, unless they themselves, as hunters of honors or advantages, had sought a cloak for their own incredulity from every side. Add that terrible signs had been appropriate to the severity of the law, and beneficial signs to the person of the Savior.

Erasmus rightly observed here that because they demanded a sign, tempting the Lord, they would have believed no more even if he had done what was demanded, but whether he had done it or not, they would have had a calumny ready. Therefore they were called a wicked and adulterous or filthy generation, because they had degenerated too much from the holy Fathers, so much so that they deserved to be held not as legitimate sons but as adulterous sons.

Latin:

Vers. 38. Τότε ἀπεκρίθησάν τινες] ἀποκρίνεσθαι hic ut sæpe est al- loqui tantum. Ideo autem addidit τινες, ne putarentur eidem esse qui Christum magicæ artis accusaverant. Nam hi non accusantium, sed dubitantium speciem præfere- bant. Ideo Lucas expressit ἕτεροι δὲ πειράζοντες. Σημεῖον ] Solent interdum apud Hellenistas promiscue usurpari σημεῖον, τέρας, δύναμιν: sed saepe inter se distincta invenias σημεῖον & δύναμιν, saepe etiam tria ista δύναμιν, τέρας, σημεῖον, nempe voce σημεῖον modo laxius, modo an- gustius usurpata. Hic σημεῖον opponitur δυνάμει. Nam vis quae in sanandis hominibus expellendisque daemonibus ostenditur, proprie & stricte vocatur δύναμις. Hujus ge- neris prodigia cum satis multa essent a Christo edita, iis ta- men satisfieri sibi Pharisaei isti & legisperiti non patieban- tur, sed, quasi ista res non divini, sed sui esset arbitratûs, exigebant non δύναμιν sed σημεῖον, nec qualecunque ση- μεῖον, sed ut Lucas & alio loco Matthaeus exponit σημεῖον ἀπ' ὀυρανῦ: importune atquePct verecunde, cum ipsa sa- nandi ratio, qua Christus utebatur, aut nudo contactu aut voce sola, itemque doctrina, daemonum votis con- traria, divinam virtutem aperte ostenderent. Sed Deus, qui in negotio pietatis ita cum hominibus agit, ut malitiam revincat plenissime, non ut immoderatis hominum cupi- ditatibus inserviat, sciebat ea quae erant praestita abunde sufficere, nisi ipsi honorum aut commodorum aucupes un- dique incredulitati suae mantellum quaesissent. Adde quod legis severitati convenerant signa terribilia, Servatoris per- sonae signa benefica.

Recte hic observavit Erasmus, quia signum postularunt, tentantes Dominum, nihilo magis credituros illos, etiamsi quod postulabatur fecis- set, sed sive fecisset, sive non habituros paratam calumniam. Ideo generatio prava & adultera seu spurca dicebantur, quia nimium à sanctis Pa- tribus degeneraverant, adeo ut merito non pro legitimis filiis sed adulterinis filiis habendi fue- rint.

## 12:39
Vers. 39. Μοιχαλὶς] Literally adulteress, but it is more likely that adulterous offspring is signified here, as if you were to say supposititious, which falsely boasts of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob as parents. The Syrian understood it thus, who puts גיירתא. And that I should take it so is supported by that passage in John VIII. 39, where when Christ had denied that those Jews were the offspring of Abraham, they respond ἡμεῖς ἐκ πορνείας ἐγεννήθημεν. They were indeed from Abraham according to the flesh, but in spirit no less alien to him than those whom a mother conceives from adultery.

σημεῖον ὀυ δοθήσεται ἀυτῇ] Σημεῖον, as I said, is opposed to δυνάμεσιν, as if it were something greater and more excellent. The sense therefore is, as if Christ were saying: No portent will be given to them greater and more excellent than that which will be given not from heaven, as they fastidiously demand, but on the contrary from the very bowels of the earth, not so much to convert them, who after so many δυνάμεις did not wish to be converted, as to testify to my innocence, and at the same time to their own inhumanity, as those who extended their hatreds against me, an innocent man, even unto death. See John II. 8 & XVI. 10 & Luke XI. 29, 30. But because this sign, by reason of the greater part of the Pharisees and lawyers, was more refutatory than instructive, therefore Christ, having risen from the dead, appeared to none of them. For enough had been given to their contumacy.

But did they sin by seeking a sign, which Gideon sought without sin, Jud. VI. 17, and Hezekiah 2 Kings XX. 8, whereas Ahaz did not wish to seek it without sin, Is. VII. 12? I answer: They sought a sign for the sake of faith, so that they might be confirmed in it; the Pharisees out of infidelity; they without temptation, these tempting, Mark VIII. 11, and insidiously: for they did not seek it so that they might believe, but were investigating an opportunity for criticizing, as Chrysostom says: It is certain that Ahaz sinned, not because he did not want to seek a sign, but because he did not want to receive the one offered out of diffidence, and despaired utterly of the outcome. Beautifully on the sign of Jonah, Justin in Questions and Answers, no. 64. Just as Jonah obtained a three-day restoration from the whale as a sign of the faith to be held in him, that he had been sent by God as a herald of the destruction of the Ninevites: in the same way also the Savior obtained a three-day resurrection from the sepulcher as a sign of the faith to be held in him, that he had been sent by God as a herald of the kingdom of heaven.

Latin:

Vers. 39. Μοιχαλὶς] Ad verbum adultera, sed magis est ut adulterina soboles hic significetur, quasi dicas sup- posititia, quae falso parentes jactat Abrahamum, Isaacum, Jacobum. Ita intellexit Syrus, qui ponit גיירתא. Atque ut ita accipiam facit illud apud Johannem VIII. 39. ubi cum Christus negasset Judaeos istos Abrahami esse sobolem, respondent ἡμεῖς ἐκ πορνείας ἐγεννήθημεν. Erant quidem ex Abrahamo κατὰ σάρκα sed spiritu non minus ab illo alieni, quam quos mater ex adulterio concipit.

σημεῖον ὀυ δοθήσεται ἀυτῇ] Σημεῖον ut dixi opponitur δυνάμεσιν, quasi majus aliquod atque excellentius. Sensus ergo est, quasi dicat Christus: Nullum ostentum illis dabi- tur majus atque excellentius, quam id quod dabitur non ex coelo, ut ipsi fastidiose postulant, sed contra ex ipsis ter- rae visceribus, non tam illis convertendis qui post tot δυνά- μεις converti noluerunt, quam testandae innocentiae meae, simulque ipsorum immanitati, ut qui in me innocentem odia sua ad mortem usque extenderint. Vide Joh. II. 8. & XVI. 10. & Lucam XI. 29. 30. Quia autem signum hoc ratione majoris partis Pharisaeorum & legisprudentium ἐλεγκτικὸν magis erat quam νυθετητικὸν, ideo nulli eorum Christus post mortem redivivus apparuit. Satis enim da- tum erat illorum contumaciae.

Sed num peccarunt illi signum expetendo, quod sine peccato expetiit Gedeon. Jud. VI. 17. Ezechias 2. Reg. XX. 8. non sine peccato petere voluit Achaz, Es. VII. 12? Resp. Illi ob fidem pe- tiere signum, ut in ea confirmarentur, Pharisaei ex infidelitate; illi citra tentationem, hi πειράζον τες, Marc. VIII. 11. & insidiose: non enim ut cre- derent, quaerebant, sed facultatem reprehendendi investigabant dicente Chrysostomo: Achazum ve- ro peccasse constat, non quod signum petere, sed quod oblatum ex diffidentia recipere nollet, & de eventu penitus desperaret. Pulchre de signo Jo- nae Justinus in quaest. & respons. n. 64. Quemad- modum Jonas signum fidei sibi habenda, quod à Deo missus esset Ninevitarum eversionis praeco, tridua- nam ex ceto obtinuit restitutionem: Ad eundem mo- dum & Salvator signum fidei habenda, quod à Deo missus esset Praeco regni caelorum, triduanam ex se- pulchro obtinuit resurrectionem.

## 12:40
Vers. 40. ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ τῆς γῆς] Christ alludes to the words of Jonah who says he was cast בלבב ימים, into the heart of the sea, as the LXX translate. But just as Jonah was not precisely in the middle of the sea, so neither was Christ in the middle of the earth: for it suffices for the truth of this expression that Christ was hidden within the earth in a cave. For Paul also, Eph. IV. 9, called this very thing the lower parts of the

earth, opposite, of course, to that which is accustomed to be called פני ארץ, the face of the earth. τρεις ἡμέρας καὶ τρεῖς νύκτας] Because the Hebrew language does not indulge them the freedom of compounding words, they are forced to use circumlocutions, which the Hellenists follow. Thus what Moses said, And there was evening and there was morning, one day, Gen. I. 5, the Greeks would say, and the first day-night occurred. Daniel VIII. 14, without a conjunction, said until evening and morning two thousand three hundred, that is, until two thousand three hundred day-nights. Thus Paul, when he said he had been in the deep a day-night, 2 Cor. XI. 25, expressed in Greek the Hebrew evening-morning. Thus here nothing else is signified than that Christ would be in the sepulcher for three day-nights, to the fulfillment of which sense it suffices that he was buried for a time whose parts reached to three day-nights. For in the designation of time, the Greeks do not strictly observe the distinction between the fourth and third case. But it seems to me that the old Latin translator did not imprudently choose the sixth case. Nor should it be omitted here, where the law of Moses expresses a number of days, as in circumcision, it is accepted among interpreters that even the hour of one day-night makes a day: because, they say, the legal day is not computed from time to time. See Aben Ezra on Levit. XII. 3. Similar to this is that expression of Roman law, about which Paul the Jurisconsult speaks in L. Mores D. de Feriis: whatever is done in these twenty-four hours is just as if it had been done in any hour of light.

Regarding the computation of this three-day period, and regarding the phrase itself, see what is said in our sacred Chronicle, last section, question XIII.

Latin:

Vers. 40. ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ τῆς γῆς] Aludit Christus adver- ba Jonae qui se projectum dicit בלבב ימים, εἰς καρδίας θαλάσσης ut transferunt LXX. Sicut autem Jonas non fuit in meditullio maris praecise, ita nec Christus in meditullio terrae: sufficit enim ad hujus locutionis veritatem quod Christus intra terram in specu abditus fuerit. Nam & Pau- lus Ephes. IV. 9. hoc ipsum vocavit τὰ κατώτερα μέρη τῆς

γῆς, opposite nimirum ad id quod פני ארץ πρόσωπον τῆς γῆς vocari solet. τρεις ἡμέρας καὶ τρεῖς νύκτας ] Hebræi quia voces compo- nendi libertatem sua ipsis lingua non indulget, coguntur u- ti circumlocutionibus, quas sequunturHellenistæ. Ita quod Moses dixit ויהי ערב ויהי בקר יום אחד Gen. I. 5. Græci dicerent καὶ ἐγένετο τὸ νυχθήμερον πρῶτον. Daniel VIII. 14. sine conjunctione dixit עד ערב בקר אלפים ושׁלשׁ מאות id est ἕως νυχθημέρων διχιλίων καὶ τριακοσίων. Sic Paulus cum dixit se fuisse in profundo νυχθήμερον 2. Cor. XI. 25. Græce expressit Hebræum ערב בקר. Ita hic nihil aliud significatur, quam futurum Christum in sepulchro τρισὶ νυχθημέροις, cui sensui implen- do sufficit eum sepultum fuisse tempore eo cujus partes ad τρία νυχθήμερα pertingerent. Nam in temporis designa- tione Græci discrimen quarti & tertii casus non regiè ob- servant. Videtur autem mihi Latinus interpres vetus non imprudenter sextum casum elegisse. Neque omittendum hic, ubi lex Mosis dierum numerum exprimit, ut in circum- cisione, receptum apud interpretes etiam sensthoram uni- us νυχθημέρα diem facere: quia dies legalis ajunt, non com- putatur de tempore ad tempus. Vide Aben Esdram ad Levit. XII. 3. Cui similis est illa Romani juris locutio, de quâ Paulus Jurisconsultus in L. Mores D. de Feriis: quic- quid in his viginti quatuor horis actum est, perinde est quasi quavis bora lucis actum esset.

De computo tridui hujus, deque phrasi ipsa vide quæ dicta in Chronico nostro sacro sectione ult. quæst. XIII.

## 12:41
Vers. 41. ἀναστήσονται] Again the divine judgment is described according to the form of human judgment, in which witnesses are accustomed to rise from their seats when they are about to give testimony, which Mark XIV. 57 shows to have been the custom among the Jews just as it was among the Romans. Add Acts VI. 13. The Ninevites perform the role of witnesses, because they show that much smaller benefits were sufficient to convert souls. For they were both barbarians and had seen no miracles of Jonah, and had heard only a few words, when they composed themselves for repentance.

μετὰ τῆς γενεᾶς ταύτης ] For they were also standing as defendants. κατακρινοῦσιν ἀυτὴν] That is, they will cause it to be condemned, just as he also said above, they will be your judges. Thus Cicero says that Verres was condemned by him, and Tacitus says that Claudia was condemned by the accuser Domitius.

Μετανόησαν ] Without waiting for the end of the forty days they did what these men do not do even now, nor will they do even if waited for for forty years.

Πλεῖον] יותר More has been provided for you than for them in Jonah. For not only is person compared to person, but the benefits provided through them are compared with one another.

But why should persons not be compared? The words certainly carry that meaning, and the sense is appropriate, and the συνέχεια holds correctly. Concerning which the blessed Hunnius says thus: by the word PLUS the Savior understands that infinite difference and immense interval by which he himself transcends the dignity of Jonah and the excellence of all the prophets. Wherefore Christ teaches that those Ninevites, in the council of the world and in the final judgment, will publicly condemn by their example that treacherous faction and crowd of unbelieving Jews. Finally, this is the common interpretation. But it pleased Grotius, both here and often elsewhere, to be singular. Which it is also permitted to observe at v. 42; for he added there to the word πλεῖον this gloss: The fullness of divine wisdom offering itself freely for the eternal salvation of men. It is better, however, that person be compared to person at C. XIII 34, where he annotates these things to the words, ἐλάλησεν ἐν παραβολαῖς, Greater than Solomon. above XII. 42.

Latin:

Vers. 41. ἀναστήσονται] Rursus judicium divinum ad humani judicii formam describitur, in quo testes cum te- stimonium sunt dicturi surgere solent ex subselliis, quod ut apud Romanos ita & apud Judæos moris fuisse ostendit Marcus XIV. 57. Adde Actor. VI. 13. Præstant autem vi- cem testium Ninevitæ, quia ostendunt suffecisse ad conver- tendos animos multo minora beneficia. Nam & barbari erant & nulla Jonæ miracula conspexerant, & pauca dur- taxat verba audierant, cum se ad pœnitentiam composue- runt.

μετὰ τῆς γενεᾶς ταύτης ] Nam & rei stabant. κατακρινοῦσιν ἀυτὴν] Id est, efforient ut condemnetur, quomodo & supra dixit, judices vestri erunt. Ita Cice- ro à se Verrem, Tacitus à Domitio accusatore condemna- tam ait Claudiam.

Μετανόησαν ] Non exspectato fine dierum quadraginta fecerunt quod isti neque nunc faciunt, neque facient ex- spectati per annos quadraginta.

Πλεῖον] יותר Plus vobis præstitum est quam illis in Jona. Non enim persona tantum personæ, sed beneficia per eos præstita inter se comparantur.

Sed cur non comparentur personæ? verba cer- te id præ se ferunt, Et sensus est conveniens, ac συνέχεια recte se habet. De quo ita B. Hunnius: per vocabulum PLUS intelligit Salvator infinitum illud discrimen & immensum intervallum, quo ipse dignitatem Jonæ, omniumque Prophetarum ex- cellentiam transcendit. Quamobrem docet Chri stus, illos Ninivitas in concilio orbis terrarum, ju dicioque extremo publice condemnaturos esse exem plo suo perfidam illam incredulorum Judæorum fa Etionem & turbam. Denique communis hac est interpretatio. Sed placuit Grotio tum hic, tum alias sæpe singulari esse. Quod etiam ad v. 42. ob- servare licet; addidit enim illic ad vocem πλεῖον hanc glossam: Plenitudo divinæ sapientiæ ad æter- nam hominum salutem ultro se offerens. Personam tamen personæ comparari satius est ad C.XIII 34. ubi hæc annotat ad verba, ἐλάλησεν ἐν παραβο- λαῖς, Major Salomone. supra XII. 42.

## 12:42
Vers. 42. ἐκ τῶν περάτων τῆς γῆς] A hyperbole for that which is from a far-off region. This has force in the comparison, because Christ himself came to the Jews, so that no journey was necessary to be undertaken for his sake: which she had done, having left her kingdom.

Concerning the region from which the Queen came, we spoke at c. X of the first book of Kings: that she did not come from Ethiopia, but from Arabia Felix, which is to the south of Jerusalem, and is called a far-off land in Jerem. VI. 20, concerning which Herodotus l. III says: To the south of the furthest regions which are inhabited is Arabia, in which alone of all lands are born frankincense, myrrh, cassia, and cinnamon.

to hear the wisdom of Solomon.] by means of riddles, which is a most ancient custom among kings. Now this wisdom consisted partly in natural history, of which subject we read many books written by Solomon; partly in the doctrine of duties, of which his books, or rather selections from his books, exist even now.

Not only on account of natural history and moral doctrine concerning duties; but primarily for the sake of knowing the true religion, the Queen of the South came to Solomon, stirred by the fame of Jehovah, as is contained in 1 Kings 10:1 et seq.

more] The fullness of divine wisdom offering itself freely for the eternal salvation of men.

Simplicius the Syrian. And behold, something greater than Solomon is in this place. Thus also Blessed Luther and other interpreters.

PART IV. A warning concerning the returning unclean Spirit.

Latin:

Vers. 42. ἐκ τῶν περάτων τῆς γῆς] ὑπερβολικὸν pro eo, quod est è longinqua regione. Habet autem hoc vim in comparatione, quia Christus ipse ad Judæos venit, ita ut nullum iter ipsius causa necesse esset suscipi: quod illa fe- cerat regno relicto.

De Regione, unde venerit Regina ad c. X. prio- ris Regum diximus: Non ex Æthiopia, sed Arabia Felice eam venisse, quæ Australis Hierofolymæ est, & terra longinqua vocatur Jerem. VI. 20. de qua He- rodotus l. III. Ad meridiem ultimai regionibus, quæ habitantur, Arabia est, in qua sola omnium nascun- tur thus, myrrha, Casia, cinnamomum.

ἀκῦσαι τὴν σοφίαν Σολομῶντος.] διὰ προβλημάτων, qui regum inter se mos antiquissimus. Hæc autem σοφία par- tim in historia naturali consistebat, cujus argumenti mul- tos libros à Salomone scriptos legimus; partim in do- ctrina de officiis, de qua libri ejus aut potius librorum ἐκλογαὶ etiam nunc exstant.

Non tantum ob naturalem historiam & Mora- lem doctrinam de officiis; sed imprimis ob reli- gionem veram cognoscendam ad Salomonem ve- nit Regina Austri, fama de Jehova percita ut ha- betur 1. Reg. X. 1. seq.

πλεῖον ] Plenitudo divinæ sapientiæ ad æternam homi- num salutem ultro se offerens.

Simplicius Syrus. Et ecce præstantior quam Sa- lomon est hoc loco. Sic & B. Lutherus aliique In- terpp.

PARS IV. De redeunte immundo Spiritu commonitio.

## 12:43
Verse 43. when the unclean] It seems to me that this is not a parable but a common statement illustrated by many lights of translation, which is then applied specifically to the Jews. I believe, however, that the sense of this universal statement is that those who, when they have once escaped the pollutions of the world, are again entangled in the same, fall more grievously than before, with God avenging the contempt of His grace. I give the foundation of this interpretation to Peter, who also uses the very words of Christ, that their last condition is worse than the first, in this sense in 2 Epistle, chapter 2, verse 20. The difference is that Peter, having regard to his own time, speaks of those who have professed Christianity: whereas the statement of Christ extends to all times. Nor does that saying of Christ to the paralytic tend elsewhere: You are healed, see that you do not sin, lest something worse happen to you. John 5:14. That those who serve this world are said everywhere to be possessed by an evil Spirit is so obvious that it does not need proof. A very similar sense is found in Dio Chrysostom in Oration 5: 'One of the many might attempt to cleanse his own soul, as if it were a place inaccessible and full of savage beasts, and having cast out and destroyed the race of desires, then hoping to have been delivered and to have escaped, not having bound them strongly, a little later he is destroyed and corrupted by the remaining desires.'

Therefore, Christ begins here another admonitory discourse against the security of those who believed themselves to be freed from the power of Satan, by predicting to them the most sad punishments of hardening, with the Demon about to occupy them more powerfully: For relapse in bodily diseases is dangerous: but much more so in spiritual ones. And therefore some warn that the discourse is continued concerning the sin against the Holy Spirit, which Christ had said was irremissible. The Spirit is called unclean, both because of the internal uncleanness contracted through apostasy from God, and because He is the Author of all uncleanness, and delights in it supremely. Which name occurs also in Matthew 10:1, Mark 1:26, chapter 3:11, chapter 5:2, chapter 7:25, Luke 11:24, Acts 5:16, Revelation 18:2. Compare concerning this discourse of Christ, Blessed Franzius, On the Interpretation of Scriptural Oracles, 8.

from the man] From any man whatsoever: which by equal reasoning is also applied to a people, who through a continued succession over many ages is reckoned in the place of one man. See the breviary of Florus and the authors of Roman law.

waterless places] That is, places in which no one would willingly dwell, such as the squalid sands of Libya celebrated in the verses of the poets in this sense. But all places outside of man are such for demons, as he alone is capable of vice. Christ applies to a moral sense what was accepted among the Hebrews, that demons delight in desert places and for that reason are called se'irim. That is indeed said for the reason that those spirits are enemies of human gatherings and cities, unapproachable, lawless, homeless.

rest] That is, a place of dwelling: for so the Hebrews use menuchah.

There are those who understand arid places as the breasts of the faithful, scorched and arid as if by the flame of the Holy Spirit and the heat of love and faith, as Dr. Caspar Bertram with Lambert of Avignon in chapter 11 of Luke, who says, 'He walks through parched places, that is, those truly acknowledging themselves as humble sinners and most miserable, and seeking rest in them.' But Theophylact understands it more correctly concerning the unfaithful, and so also Blessed Lyserus: 'He seeks whether he may have a place there, where the seed of the word is not sown; where the streams of God do not flow, which make glad His city, Psalm 46:5.' Those places do not please Satan, he does not find rest there. For he himself takes no pleasure unless he inflicts harm on the human race. This is his rest, these are his delights, if he can find new prey daily. The Carthusian also understands hearts not having the dew of divine grace. Calixtus, like Grotius, accepts [the interpretation] concerning desert places and those most remote from habitation. But this may be admitted in the protasis, or in the parable, not in the apodosis or the application of the parable, in the husk, not in the marrow.

Latin:

Vers. 43. ὅταν δὲ τὸ ἀκάθαρτον ] Mihi videtur hæc non esse παραβολὴ sed commune enuntiatum pictum multis translationum luminibus, quod deinde peculiariter Judæis applicatur. Universalis autem hujus enuntiati, hunc sen- sum esse arbitror, eos qui cum inquinamenta mundi semel effugerint, iisdem rursus implicantur, gravius quam ante ruere, contemtum gratiæ suæ Deo ulciscenfe. Cujus inter- pretationis fundum do Petro, qui & ipsa Christi verba, sit nobissima eorum conditio pejor priore, in hunc sensum usur- pat Epist. II. cap. II. com. 20. Illud interest quod Petrus sui temporis habens rationem agit de his qui Christiani- smum sunt professi: cum Christi enuntiatum ad omnia se tempora extendat. Nec alio tendit illud à Christo dictum paralytico: Sanatus es, vide ne pecces, ne quid pejus tibi eve- niat. Johan. V. 14. Dici autem passim à Spiritu maligno possideri eos qui mundo huic serviunt, adeo obvium est ut probationis non egeat. Sensus est huic persimilis apud Dionem Prusæensem Oratione V. τῶν πολλῶν μέν εἴη τίς ἀπεχείρησε καθᾶραι τὴν αὑτῶν ψυχὴν, ὧσπερ ἄβατόν καὶ με- σόν τινα θηρίων χαλεπῶν τόπον, ἐξελῶν δε κὰ ἀπολέσας τὸ τῶν ἐπιθυμιῶν γένος, εἶτ' ἐλπίσας ἀπηλλάχθαι κὰι διαπεφευ- γέναι; ἐκ ἰσχυρῶς ἀποεδήσας, ὀλίγον ὕστερον ὑπὸ τῶν λειπο- μένων ἐπιθυμιῶν ἀπολέσθαι κὰι διαφθαρῆναι.

Alium itaque orditur hic Christus sermonem monitorium adversus securitatem eorum, qui se à potestate Satanæ liberatos credebant, prædi- cendo iis longe tristissimas indurationis pœnas Dæmonio potentius eos occupaturo: Nam re- cidiva in morbis corporalibus periculosa est: at multo magis in spiritualibus. Ideoque monent nonnulli, continuari sermonem de peccato in Spiritum Sanctum, quod irremissibile Christus dixerat. Dicitur autem Spiritus immundus, tum ob internam immunditiem per apostasiam à Deo contractam, tum quia omnis immunditiei Autor est, eaque summe delectatur. Quod nomen oc- currit etiam Matth. X. 1. Marc. I. 26. cap. III. 11. cap. V. 2. c. VII. 25. Luc. XI. 24. Actor. V. 16. Apoc. XVIII. 2. Conf. de hoc sermone Christi B. Fran- zius de interpret. script. orac. VIII.

ἀπὸ τῦ ἀνθρώπε] Ex homine quovis: quod pari ratio- ne etiam ad populum applicatur, qui per multas quamvis ætates continuata successione unius hominis vice cense- tur. Vide Flori breviarium & juris Romani auctores.

ἀνύδρων τόπων] Id est loca in quibus nemo libenter habitet, quales sunt Libyæ squallentis arenæ Poetarum ver- sibus in hunc sensum celebratæ. Talia autem sunt dæmo- ni loca omnia extra hominem, ut qui solus vitii sit capax. Applicat ad sensum moralem Christus, quod apud He- bræos receptum erat, dæmonas locis desertis gaudere & ob id dici שעירים. Id vero ideo dictum, quod illi spi- ritus inimici sunt humanorum cœtuum ac civitatum ἀφή- τορες, ἀθέμιστοι, ἀνέστιοι.

ἀνάπαυσιν] Id est, habitandi locum: ita enim Hebræi usurpant מנוח.

Sunt qui arida loca intelligant de pectoribus fidelium, flamma Spiritus Sancti & æstu amoris ac fidei quasi tostis & aridis, uti D. Caspar Bertram cum Lamberto Avenionensi in c. XI. Luc. qui, am- bulat, inquit, per loca arentia, hoc est, vere hu- miles se peccatores & miserrimos agnoscentes, & in eis quærens requiem. Sed rectius Theophyla- ctus de infidelibus accipit, atque ita etiam B. Ly- serus: Quærit an ibi locum habeat, ubi semen ver- bi non spargitur; ubi non fluunt fluenta Dei, quæ læ- tificant ipsius civitatem, Psal. XLVI. 5. Illa loca Satanæ non arrident, non invenit ibi requiem. Ne- que enim ullam ipse capit voluptatem, nisi damnum inferat mortalium generi. Hæc autem ipsius quies, hæ delitiæ, si indies novam prædam invenire possit. Corda gratiæ divinæ rorem non habentia etiam in- telligit Carthusianus. De locis desertis, & ab in- colatu remotissimis Calixtus uti Grotius accipit. Sed hoc in προτάσει admitti queat, vel in parabo- la, non in ἀποδόσει vel parabolæ applicatione, in cortice, non in medulla.

## 12:44
Vers. 44. Σχολάζοντα, σεσαρωμένον καὶ κεκοσμημένον] That is, a possession not only empty, but also prepared. Because man is here called a house, therefore the rest of the translation is taken from a house. Such are men to the Devil, who do not attend to their own ways. Such were the Hebrews under the Kings and after the return from Babylon.

Latin:

Vers. 44. Σχολάζοντα, σεσαρωμένον καὶ κεκοσμημένον] Id est possessiorem non vacuam tantum, sed & paratam. Quia homo domus hic dicitur, ideo à domo sumitur reli- quum translationis. Tales Diabolo sunt homines, qui ad vias suas non attendunt. Tales Ebræi sub Regibus & post reditum è Babylone.

## 12:45
Vers. 45. ἑπτὰ ἕτερα πνεύματα] Just as John spoke of the Spirit of God as ἑπτὰ πνεύματα, Apoc. I. 4. It is called ἑβδομὰς τελεσφόρος, as Philo notes. Therefore, whatever in its own kind reaches a full measure is signified by that number, as I Sam. II. 5, Eccl. IV. 1.

Καὶ γίνεται τὰ ἔσχατα τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ἐκείνου χείρονα τῶν πρώτων) A triple reason is usually given: 1. In the Devil, who takes more anxious care of such men, turning away the minds of those he has blinded from all means of obtaining salvation, 2 Cor. IV. 24. 2. In the sinners themselves, who by their relapse double the evil (α) by so enervating the powers of the mind and will, with the Holy Spirit expelled along with grace, that they can rise again only with the greatest difficulty (β) by so delighting themselves in the sweetness of iniquity that they persist in it most pleasantly without any fear of the Divine. 3. In God, who as a just Judge delivers them to Satan. Cyril gives these causes: Therefore he said, he finds no rest, to show that such a man must necessarily be captured by the snares of demons. For he had two incentives to good here: the experience of the former evil and the benefit of liberation; indeed, a third is added, the threat of suffering worse things. Johannes Huss in his commentary on 2 Pet. II. 20 alleges these reasons: The first is the weakness for rising again in the one who relapses, the second is the breaking of the covenant initiated with the Lord, the third is a more grievous subjection to enemies, the fourth is the mocking of divine mercy, the fifth is the injury brought upon one's own soul, the sixth is the grieving of the Holy Spirit and the heavenly court, and the rejoicing of the demons, the seventh is the ingratitude for the pardon and grace already given, and the glory promised, the eighth is because the one who relapses, as much as in him lies, repeats the passion of Christ. Therefore Chrysostom warned gravely concerning the fall of the first man: Do not sin after pardon, do not be wounded after being cured, do not be defiled after grace. Wherefore he is an ungrateful person who sins after pardon, he is unworthy of health who wounds himself after he has been cured: nor does he deserve to be cleansed who defiles himself after grace (of abolition or cleansing).

κῇ τῇ γενεᾷ ταύτῃ τῇ πονηρᾷ] It seems to me that Christ is looking at the Hebrew people from the time they were brought into Babylon until the destruction by Titus. Before the deportation, the crimes of the people were grave, which can be seen in the Prophets; in the exile itself, most began to amend themselves, and thus, with God disposing the occasions, they returned to their homeland. But in the times of the Hasmoneans, they fell again into vices shameful even to Barbarians, and to all these they added the contempt of the Messiah, who was sent with such great miracles and such great clemency. By which act, being abandoned by God, they became the most wicked of all men, such as Josephus describes them in his history of the last times.

Chrysostom in the Catena of the Greek Fathers by Possinus. He shows that the Jews had fallen into extreme destruction, for the reason that they did not accept Christ. For just as those who have been freed from demons, if they make a place for them again by a remission of diligence, suffer worse things from them, as the occasion is given to those who avenge their ejection: so the nation of the Jews, having been previously seized as if by a certain demon by the pursuit of idolatry; but having been freed from it through the preaching of the Prophets, with Christ finally coming to lay the final hand upon their salvation and perfection, they were miserably rolled back again into evils worse than the former; not only not receiving the Messiah sent by God, but slaughtering him with the most cruel punishments.

PART V. Instruction concerning the mother and brothers of Christ.

Latin:

Vers. 45. ἑπτὰ ἕτερα πνεύματα] Sicut ἑπτὰ πνεύματα de Dei Spiritu dixit Johannes, Apoc. I. 4. Vocatur ἑβδο- μὰς τελεσφόρος, ut notat Philo. Ideo quicquid in suo ge- nere ad plenam mensuram pervenit, eo numero significa- tur, ut I. Sam. II. 5. Eccl. IV. 1,

Καὶ γίνεται τὰ ἔσχατα τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ἐκείνου χεί- ρονα τῶν πρώτων) Ratio solet dari triplex 1. in Dia- bolo, qui magis anxiam talium hominum gerit cu- ram ab omnibus salutis consequendæ mediis ani- mos eorum, quos excæcavit, avertens, 2. Cor. IV. 24. 2. In ipsis peccatoribus, qui suo relapsu malum conduplicant (α) vires mentis & volun- tatis, Spiritu Sancto cum gratia expulso, ita ener- vando, ut difficillime resurgere valeant (β) Ini- quitatis dulcedine se ita oblectando, ut in ea sua- vissime absque omni Numinis timore perseve- rent. 3. In Deo, qui tanquam justus Judex eos Satanæ tradit. Cyrillus has causas reddit: Idcir- co dixit, non invenit requiem, ut ostendat hujus- modi hominem necessario dæmonum insidiis capien- dum. Duo enim hic ad bonum incitamenta ha- buit, experientiam prioris mali & liberationis be- neficium: imo vero & tertium accedit, pejora pa- tiendi comminatio. Johannes Huss in comment. ad 2. Petr. II. 20. has allegat rationes: Prima est debilitas ad resurgendum in recidivante, secunda ruptio fœderis initi cum Domino, tertia, inimicis subjectio gravior, quarta, divinæ misericordiæ subsannatio, quinta, credulitas animæ propriæ il- lata, sexta, Spiritus Sancti & cælestis curiæ con- tristatio, ac dæmonum lætificatio, septima, ingra- titudo veniæ & gratiæ jam datæ, & gloriæ promif- sæ, octava, quia recidivans, quantum in eo est, Christi iterat passionem. Ideo graviter monuit Chrysostomus: de lapsu primi hominis: Noli pec- care post veniam, noli vulnerari post curam, no- li sordidari post gratiam. Quare indulgentia in- gratus est, qui post veniam peccat, sanitate indi- gnus est, qui semetipsum, postquam curatus est, vulnerat: nec mundari meretur, qui semetipsum post gratiam (abolitionis vel mundationis) sordi- dat.

κῇ τῇ γενεᾷ ταύτῃ τῇ πονηρᾷ] Videtur mihi Christus po- pulum Hebræum intueri ab eo tempore quo in Babyloni- am adductus est ad Titi excidium. Ante deportationem gravia erant populi flagitia, quæ videre est apud Prophe- tas, in ipso exilio cœperunt se emendare plerique: at- que ita Deo occasiones disponente, in patriam redierunt. Sed Asmonæorum temporibus rursum in vitia vel Barba- ris pudenda prolapsi, adjecerunt his omnibus contem- ptum Messiæ tantis cum miraculis, tantaque cum clemen- tia missi. Quo facto, à Deo derelicti, evaserunt homines omnium sceleratissimi, quales eos Josephus in ultimorum temporum historia describit.

Chrysostomus in Catena Græcor. Patr. Possin. Ostendit in extremam perniciem Judæos devenisse, idcirco quod Christum non acceperint. Ut enim qui liberati à Dæmonibus sunt, si locum eis iterum remissione diligentiæ fecerint, graviora patiuntur ab iis, occasione data ejectionem ulciscentibus: sic Judæorum natio quasi quodam antea dæmone corre- pta idololatriæ studio; sed eo liberata, per prædica- tionem Prophetarum, Christo ad extremum ve- niente, ut saluti ac perfectioni eorum manum ulti- mam imponeret, rursus miseri revoluti sunt in ma- la prioribus pejora; non solùm non excipientes à Deo missum Messiam, sed crudelissimis ipsum sup- pliciis mactantes.

PARS V. De matre & fratribus Christi instructio.

## 12:46
Verse 46. Ζητοῦντες ἀυτῷ λαλῆσαι] In Latin, wishing to speak with him: undoubtedly because, having understood the conspiracies of the Pharisees against him, they were striving to withdraw him from danger by any means. For the series of the history and those things which are in Mark seem to me to indicate this.

Latin:

Vers. 46. Ζητοῦντες ἀυτῷ λαλῆσαι] Latine conventum ipsum volen- tes: nimirum quia intellectis Pharisæorum adversus i- psum conspirationibus eum quovis modo periculo stude- bant subtrahere. Hoc enim series historiæ & ea quæ apud Marcum sunt, indicare mihi videntur.

## 12:48
Verse 48. Τίς ἐστιν ἡ μήτηρ μου] Showing that in the duty committed to him he follows neither the affections nor the counsels of the flesh. Compare Luke II. 49, John II. 4. Thus he answers Peter, who is anxious about the life of the Lord, ὀυ φρονεῖς τὰ τοῦ Θεοῦ, ἀλλὰ τὰ τῶν ἀνθρώπων. Below XVII. 23.

Latin:

Vers. 48. Τίς ἐστιν ἡ μήτηρ μου] Ostendens se in manda- to sibi officio neque affectus neque consilia carnis sequi. Conjunge Luc. II. 49. Johan. II. 4. Ita Petro de vita Do- mini sollicito respondet, ὀυ φρονεῖς τὰ τοῦ Θεοῦ, ἀλλὰ τὰ τῶν ἀνθρώπων. infra XVII. 23.

## 12:49
Verse 49. ἐκτείνας τὴν χεῖρα ἀυτοῦ] This is δακτυλοδεικτικῶς, as the Greeks say.

ἰδοὺ ἡ μητήρ με καὶ οἱ ἀδελφοί μου] Thus Andromache to Hector in Homer.

σύ μοι ἐσσὶ πατὴρ κὴ πότνια μήτηρ, Ἠδὲ κασίγνητος.

With which compare that of the Song of Songs VIII. 1. Christ signifies that the more obedient anyone is to God, the more he is also near to Him: which is the mystical sense of the Song of Songs. Nor are these words to be drawn in any way to the injury of the most holy mother.

Therefore, as Ambrose rightly says, parents are not rejected injuriously, but the bonds of minds are taught to be more religious than those of bodies.

Latin:

Vers. 49. ἐκτείνας τὴν χεῖρα ἀυτοῦ] Hoc est δακτυλοδεικ- τικῶς ut Græci loquuntur.

ἰδοὺ ἡ μητήρ με καὶ οἱ ἀδελφοί μου] Ita Andromache Hestori apud Homerum.

σύ μοι ἐσσὶ πατὴρ κὴ πότνια μήτηρ, Ἠδὲ κασίγνητος.

Quicum confer illud Cantici VIII. 1. Significat Christus, quoquis Deo est obsequentior, ita & sibi esse propiorem: qui mysticus est sensus Cantici Canticorum. Neque ullo modo trahenda hæc verba sunt ad sanctissimæ matris in- juriam.

Non ergo ut recte Ambrosius, injuriose refu- tantur Parentes, sed religiosiores copulæ mentium docentur esse, quam corporum.

## 13:1 Argument
CHAPTER XIII. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

Jesus, with a great crowd gathered at the sea, proposes from a boat the parable concerning the seed and the different field, and gives the reason for the parabolic discourse to the people, and why it is given to the disciples to know the mysteries, but not to others, according to the prophecy of Isaiah (chap. VI. 10). Furthermore, the blessedness of the disciples is proclaimed above the Prophets and the righteous of the Old Testament: and the parable is explained: and another is handed down concerning the good seed, and concerning the tares, and also another concerning the grain of mustard seed, likewise concerning the leaven: so that what was said through the Prophet might be fulfilled (Psalm LXXVIII. 2). The people having been dismissed, the explanation of the tares is handed down to the disciples who ask for it, and another parable again concerning the treasure hidden in a field, and concerning the precious pearl, and an admonition is subjoined concerning the scribe instructed for the kingdom of God. Thence he taught in his own country with the contempt of his citizens, to whom he brings forward the proverb concerning a Prophet despised in his own country: performing no miracles there on account of their unbelief.

There are two parts: I. Various parables proposed partly to the people, partly to the disciples and explained to them, up to verse 52. II. The preaching and consensus of Christ in his own country, up to verse 58.

PART I. Various parables proposed to the people and to the disciples, with their cause and exposition.

Ver. 1. ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ ἐκείνῃ. See what we have said in the Harmony of the Gospels, Sect. II. Art. II. chap. XVII.

Ver. same. ἀπὸ τῆς οἰκίας] Which was too narrow to be able to contain the hearers, as appears above XII. 46.

ἐκάθητο] In the manner of those teaching, as above V. 1.

Latin:

CAPUT XIII. ARGUMENTUM ET PAR- TITIO.

Jesus ad mare congregata multa turba è na- vigio de semine, & diverso agro parabolam proponit, ac parabolici sermonis ad popu- lum causam reddit, & cur discipulis de- tur cognoscere mysteria, aliis non item, juxta Esaiæ vaticinium (cap. VI. 10.) Por- ro beatitudo discipulorum præ Prophetis & justis Vet. Testam. prædicatur: atque ex- ponitur parabola: aliaque traditur de se- mine bono, & de zizaniis, nec non alia de grano sinapis, item de fermento: ut im- pleretur quod dictum est per Prophetam (Psal. LXXVIII. 2.) Dimisso populo disci- pulis petentibus explicatio zizaniis tra- ditur, & alia iterum parabola de thesau- ro abscondito agri, deque pretiosa mar- garita, & de scriba ad regnum Dei erudi- to monitio subjungitur. Dehinc in Patria sua docuit cum contemtu civium suorum, quibus adagium de Propheta in Patria contemto oggerit: nulla ibi ob increduli- tatem signa edens.

Partes duæ sunt: I. Parabolæ variæ partim ad populum, partim ad discipulos propositæ & his expositæ, ad vers. 52. II. Concio & consensus Chri- sti in patria, ad v. 58.

PARS I. Parabolæ variæ ad populum, & ad discipulos propositæ, cum earum causa, & expositione.

Vers. 1. ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ ἐκείνῃ. Vide quæ in Harmon. Evangel. Sect. II. Ar- tic. II. cap. XVII. diximus.

Vers. eod. ἀπὸ τῆς οἰκίας] Quæ angustior erat, quam ut auditores capere posset, ut apparet supra XII. 46.

ἐκάθητο] Docentium more, ut supra V. 1.

## 13:2
Ver. 2. εἰς τὸ πλοῖον] Which served in place of a pulpit, as a small hill often does.

Latin:

Vers. 2. εἰς τὸ πλοῖον] Quod vice suggesti, ut sæpe col- liculus.

## 13:3
Ver. 3. ἐν παραβολαῖς] παραβολὴ, to which the Hebrew מָשָׁל corresponds in a broader sense (for rhetoricians define it more narrowly), is a comparison of things differing among themselves, which is wont to be employed for the sake of either amplification, or efficacy, or even clarity, as we read among the masters of speech: Cicero called it a collation. Of this there are two parts: παράθεσις and ἀνταπόδοσις. παράθεσις is sought either from true things or from fictitious ones. To fictitious παράθεσις belong the little fables which the Greeks call αἴνους: such as that one in Hesiod about the hawk and the nightingale: and one much older in the history of Judges IX. 18. Such also is that little fable by which Menenius reconciled the Roman plebs to the senate, and by which Demosthenes escaped being handed over to Alexander, and by which Themistocles dissuaded the change of magistrates. A later age began to call these ἀπολόγους, in which genre that Phrygian fabulist attained the greatest name. But often the ἀνταπόδοσις is suppressed, for which custom Phaedrus brings forward this reason in his fables: 'Servitus obnoxia Quia quod solebat non audebat dicere, Affectus proprios in fabellas transtulit, Calumniamque fictis elusit jocis.' But it is credible that the majesty of speech was also consulted by the wise, and at the same time the diligence of the hearers was aroused ὥσ- however, a concise one is called a proverb, such as that which we had, that pearls are not to be cast before swine; therefore Quintilian calls a shorter fable a proverb. But the Hebrews called both παραβολὴν and αἶνον, מָשָׁל, and more broadly, as is wont to happen, in a transferred sense, they called by the same word every figurative speech, as is to be seen both elsewhere and in Ezek. XX. 49. Furthermore, however, because maxims were wont to be uttered in such speech, therefore all maxims, even those which did not contain a figure, received the same name, as is to be seen 1 Sam. XXIV. 14. and in the title of the book of Solomon which contains many non-figurative maxims. Thus also the Latins called any sentences whatsoever proverbs. The Hellenist Jews, who, in order to express the force of Hebrew words as closely as possible, are less wont to attend to the propriety of the Greek language, translate מָשָׁל now as a proverb, now as a parable. And thus the Christians did these; (for there are few full parables) the other writers said parables, John said proverbs: just as conversely a maxim is called a parable, below XV. 15. Jerome, who lived in those places, teaches us below at chapter XVIII that it is familiar to the Syrians and especially to the Palestinians to teach by parables.

The Greeks define a parable as being a comparative placing of a thing before the subjects for a more effective manifestation. Likewise: a parable is a speech representing through other things those things which are properly said with efficacy. According to Varinus, a parable is a comparative placing for the clarity of the subjects. Therefore, parables are not obscure in themselves, nor are they proposed for the sake of obscurity, so that the sense might not be perceived, but so that the sense might be imprinted more effectively and cling to the minds. Chrysostom, hom. XLV. in Matt., teaches that Christ used parables in order that he might make the speech more emphatic, and might instill greater memory, and might bring the things under view, that is, so that he might render the speech more effective and instill greater memory, and as it were place the things themselves under view. Therefore Varinus teaches that parables are employed for the sake of amplification, efficacy, and perspicuity. Which is to be noted on account of the Papists arguing that the scriptures are obscure because of the parables. Seneca says: Among the ancients, he says, plausible speech was not yet sought; those who spoke simply and for the sake of demonstrating a thing were filled with parables, which I consider necessary not for the same reason as the poets, but so that they may be supports for our weakness, and may bring the speaker and the listener to the present matter. We add what Walaeus has on the word παραβολὴ from Gomarus on Matt. XXII. 1. The origin of this word is from the verb παραβάλλω: which, as I add and call Acts XX. 15, denotes: thus to compare and to liken, because when we are about to compare something with something else, we are usually accustomed to bring it near to that thing, as Henricus Steph. rightly observed in his Thesaurus of the Greek language: from which the name παραβολὴ is derived, just as in Mark IV. 30, Τίνι ὁμοιώσομεν τὴν βασιλείαν τοῦ Θεοῦ, ἐν ποίᾳ παραβολῇ παραβάλωμεν αὐτήν; To what shall we liken the kingdom of God, or by what comparison shall we compare it, as Lord Beza rightly translates, following Cicero. Just as Quintilian says in Institut. Orat. book V. chap. II. For παραβολὴ (which Cicero calls a comparison) is accustomed to trace back the things that are being compared from further away. From this origin of the word παραβολῆς, its proper meaning is a discourse which embraces the likeness of some thing to be compared, consisting of diverse members. In which sense it is said in Matt. XIII. 10, Why do you speak in parables? and verse 24, 31, he proposed another parable. But the improper meaning is that which has been derived from the proper one through some trope. For first (which is less commonly observed) through a metonymy of the adjunct sign for the subject matter signified, it denotes the meaning of a parable, as in Matt. XIII. 18, But you hear the parable of him who sows, that is, the meaning and exposition of the parable: just as the following things demonstrate this manifestly. Then, through a metaphor, it is accepted in two ways. For as in a Parable there is both a likeness, and from that arises the resulting elegance of the discourse: so sometimes, by reason of the former, that word signifies a likeness generally, Heb. XI. 19, or specifically it signifies a Prophetic likeness or type and exemplar, divinely destined for the designating of some similar thing: just as in Heb. IX. 9 the tabernacle is called παραβολὴ, that is, a type, namely of heaven, shadowed forth by it: as he declares in verses 8 and 11. For which word, ὑπόδειγμα, a sign or exemplar, and ἀντίτυπος, an exemplar responding from the opposite side, is substituted in the same sense ibid. verses 23, 24. But from the latter, or from the elegance which is in parables, the other meaning has arisen: not indeed in the New Testament, but frequent in the version of the LXX Interpreters, namely to designate a maxim, or a brief and wise saying, or generally anything: or specifically something commonly worn out, or a proverb. These are Gomarus's words.

Vers. 3. ὁ σπείρων] The Sower. For the poverty of the Hebrew language compelled them to place participles for verbal nouns. Moreover, to compare God to a sower is frequent among the Hebrews. Philo on the Allegory of the Laws: 'the seed which the Creator sowed in the virtuous soil of the rational soul.' The same in the book on Colonies: 'for they bring forth even before some notions of men enter into us, without those things which are customary working together, God sowing and begetting noble offspring.' And often elsewhere.

Latin:

Vers. 3. ἐν παραβολαῖς] παραβολὴ cui respondet מָשָׁל Hebræum latiore significatu (nam arctius definiunt Rhe- tores) est rerum differentium inter se comparatio, quæ ad- hiberi solet ἢ αὐξήσεως ἢ ἐνεργείας ἢ καὶ σαφηνείας χάριν, ut apud loquendi magistros legimus: Cicero collationem dixit. Hujus duæ sunt partes παράθεσις καὶ ἀνταπόδοσις. πα- ράθεσις aut à rebus veris aut à fictis petitur. Ad fictam πα- ράθεσιν pertinent fabellæ quas Græci αἴνους vocant: qualis est illa apud Hesiodum de accipitre & lusciniæ: multoque antiquior in Judicum historia IX. 18. Talis & illa fabella qua Menenius plebem Romanam senatui reconciliavit, & qua Demosthenes evasit ne Alexandro dederetur, & qua Themistocles magistratuum mutationem dissuasit. Poste- rior ætas hos ἀπολόγους vocare cœpit, in quo genere maxi- mum nomen consecutus est Phryx ille fabulator.
