Sæpe au- tem subticetur ἀνταπόδοσις, cujus moris hanc causam ad- fert Phædrus in fabellis: Servitus obnoxia Quia quod solebat non audebat dicere, 'Affectus proprios in fabellas transtulit, Calumniamque fictis elusit jocis. Sed credibile est etiam majestati orationis consultum à sa- pientibus, & simul excitatam auditorum diligentiam ὥσ- autem concisus vocatur παροιμία, quale illud quod habui- mus, margaritas porcis non objiciendas; ideo fabellam breviorem Quintilianus vocat. Sed Hebræi & παραβολὴν & αἶνον, מָשָׁל dixere, & latius, ut fieri solet, potefcto significatu, eadem voce appellarunt πάντα λόγον ἐσχηματι- σμένον, ut videre est tum alibi tum apud Ezech. XX. 49. Porro autem quia γνῶμαι solebant efferri tali sermone, ideo omnes γνῶμαι etiam quæ figuram non continebant idem nomen acceperunt, ut videre est 1. Sam XXIV. 14. & in titulo libri Salomonis qui multas continet γνώμας ἀσχημα- τίστους. Sic & Latini quasvis sententias proverbia dixere. Judæi Hellenistæ, qui ut vim Hebraicarum vocum quam proxime effingant, ad Græci sermonis proprietatem minus solent attendere, מָשָׁל modo παροιμίαν, modo παρα- βολὴν vertunt. Atque ita hos Christiani; (nam paucæ sunt plenæ παραβολαὶ) cæteri scriptores παραβολὰς, Johannes παροιμίας dixit: sicut vicissim γνώμη vocatur παραβολὴ, in- fra XV. 15. Familiare esse Syris & maxime Palæstinis τὰ parabolis docet nos qui in illis locis vixit Hieronymus infra ad cap. XVIII.

Græci definiunt parabolam, quod sit ὁμοίωμα- τικὴ πράγματος τοῖς ὑποκειμένοις παράθεσις πρὸς δήλωσιν ἐνεργεστέραν. Item: παραβολή ἐστι λέξις δι' ἑτέρων τὰ κυρίως λεγόμενα μετ' ἐνεργείας παριστάνουσα. Varino παραβολὴ παράθεσις ἐστιν ὁμοιωματικὴ ἐπὶ σαφηνείᾳ τῶν ὑποκειμένων. Non ergo parabolæ per se obscuræ sunt, aut obscurita- tis causa, ne sensus percipiatur, proponuntur, sed ut eo efficacius sensus imprimatur, mentibusque hæreat Chrysostomus hom. XLV. in Matth. Chri- stum parabolis usum esse docet ἵνα καὶ ἐμφατι- κώτερον τὸν λόγον ποιήσει, καὶ πλείονα τὴν μνή- μην ἐνθῇ, κ᾿ ὑπ' ὄψιν ἀγάγῃ τὰ πράγματα, hoc est, ut efficaciorem redderet sermonem & majorem in- deret memoriam, & q. sub aspectum res ipsas poneret. Ideo Varinus parabolas adhiberi docet αὐξήσεως, ἐνεργείας κ᾿ σαφηνείας, amplificationis, efficaciæ & perspicuitatis gratia. Quod ob Pontificios scriptu- ras ob parabolas obscuritatis arguentes notan- dum. Seneca: Apud antiquos, inquit, nondum captabatur plausibilis oratio, illi qui simpliciter & demonstranda rei causa loquebantur, pa- rabulis referti erant, quas existimo necessarias non ex eadem causa, qua Poetis, sed ut imbecillita- tis nostræ adminicula sint, & differentem & au- dientem in rem præsentem adducant. Addimus quæ de voce παραβολὴ habet e Gomaro Walæus ad Matth. XXII. 1. Origo hujus vocis est a verbo παρα- βάλλω: quod ut adjicio & appello Act. XX. 15. no- tat: sic inde translata significatione, per metaph. pro conferre ac comparare usurpatur, quod aliquid cum aliquo collaturi, id illi admovere plerumque soleamus, ut recte Henricus Steph. in Græc. ling. thesauro observavit: unde nomen παραβολὴ deriva- tur, quemadmodum Marc. IV. 30. Τίνι ὁμοιώσομεν τὴν βασιλείαν τοῦ Θεοῦ, ἐν ποίᾳ παραβολῇ παραβάλω- μεν αὐτήν; Cui assimilabimus regnum Dei, aut qua collatione conferemus illud, ut Dominus Beza recte transfert, Ciceronem secutus. Quemadmodum Quin- tilianus Instit. Orat. lib. V. cap. II. ait. Nam παρα- βολὴ (quam Cicero collationem vocat) longius res quæ comparantur repetere solet. Ex qua vocis παραβολῆς origine, propria illius significatio est ora- tio, quæ rei alicujus conferendæ similitudinem, di- versis membris constantem complectitur. Quo sen- su dicitur Matth. XIII. 10. Quare per parabolas loqueris? & vers. 24. 31. aliam proposuit para- bolam. Impropria vero significatio est, quæ a pro- pria, per tropum aliquem, deducta est. Primum enim (quod minus vulgo observatum est) per Me- ton. adjuncti signi pro subjecta re significata, notat parabolæ significationem, ut Matth. XIII. 18. Vos autem audite parabolam ejus qui seminat, hoc est, parabolæ significationem & expositionem: quem- admodum sequentia hoc manifeste demonstrant. Deinde per Metaph. bifariam accipitur. Nam ut in Parabola & similitudo est, & inde consequens orationis elegantia existit: sic interdum, prioris ratione, ea vox generatim similitudinem significat, Hebr. XI. 19. vel speciatim simile Propheticum seu typum atque exemplar, rei alicui simili designandæ divinitus destinatum significat: quemadmodum Hebr. IX. 9 tabernaculum vocatum παραβολὴ, hoc est, typus nempe cæli, eo adumbrati: ut vers. 8. & 11. declarat. Pro qua voce, ὑπόδειγμα signum seu exemplar, & ἀντίτυπος exemplar ex adver- so respondens, eodem sensu substituitur ibid. vers. 23. 24. A posteriori vero, sive ab elegantia quæ parabolis inest, orta est altera significatio: non qui- dem in Novo Testamento, sed in LXX. Interpre- tum versione frequens, nimirum ut sententiam, seu breve ac sapiens dictum, vel generatim quodvis: vel speciatim vulgo tritum, seu proverbium desi- gnet. Hæc Gomarus.

Vers. 3. ὁ σπείρων] Sator. Nam Hebræos linguæ penu- ria coëgit pro verbalibus participia ponere. Deum autem satori comparare frequens Hebræis. Philo de legum Alle- goria: σπορὰν ἣν ὁ ποιητὴς ἐν ἀρετώσῃ χώρᾳ κατέσπειρε λο- γικῇ ψυχῇ. Idem libro de Coloniis: τίκτουσι γὰρ κὶ πρὶν εἰ- σελθεῖν τινας ἐπινοίας ἀνθρώπων πρὸς ἡμᾶς, ἄνευ τῶν ἐξ ἔθους συνεργόντων, σπείροντος κὶ γεννῶντος Θεοῦ τὰ ἀστεῖα γεννή- ματα. Et alibi sæpe.

## 13:5
Vers. 5. διὰ τὸ μὴ ἔχειν βάθος γῆς] Because it cannot penetrate downwards, it directs its force upwards, and because it is not far from the surface of the earth, it immediately shows itself. For this passage, and no less for the one which is below in v. 21, this remark of Quintilian is not useless for understanding: 'For as earth poured out more deeply is more fertile for generating and nourishing seeds: so progress not sought from the surface pours out the fruits of studies more abundantly and holds them more faithfully. For without this consciousness, that very faculty of speaking extemporaneously will give only empty loquacity, and words born on the lips. There are the roots, there are the foundations: there are the riches as if stored in a holier treasury, from where they may be brought forth even for sudden contingencies, when the matter demands it.' Nor should that be omitted from the declaration on the corpses of cattle, which exists under the same name of Quintilian: 'Either the seeds, tightened without effort, had their roots under the very furrows, or the root, called forth by a light dew, ran into dust, or the dying crop grew pale, scorched by the burning sun with herbs.'

These things are said according to the reason and nature of the Israelite land, as Lightfoot observes, which is quite rocky, and yet those places are not entirely unsuitable for cultivation.

Latin:

Vers. 5. διὰ τὸ μὴ ἔχειν βάθος γῆς] Quia deorsum pe- netrare non potest, vim sursum erigit, & quia a terræ su- perficie non longe abest, statim se ostentat. Huic loco, nec minus ei qui infra est v. 21. intelligendo non inutilis hic Quintiliani: Nam ut terra altius effusa generandis alendisque seminibus fœcundior est: sic profectus non a summo petitus, studiorum fructus effundit uberius & fidelius continet. Nam sine hac quidem conscientia illa ipsa ex tempore dicendi facul- tas, inanem modo loquacitatem dabit, & verba in labris nascentia. Illic radices, illic fundamenta sunt: illic opes velut sanctiore ærario reconditæ, unde ad subitos quoque casus, cum res exiget, proferantur. Nec illud omittendum ex decla- ratione Pasti cadaveribus, quæ sub eodem Quintiliani ex- tat nomine: Aut adstricta citra conatum sata sub ipsis ha- buere sulcis, aut levi rore evocata radix in pulverem incurrit, aut perustus torrido sole herbis moribunda seges palluit.

Dici hæc pro ratione & natura terræ Israëlitic- ex observat Lightfootus, quæ saxola admodum, & tamen ista loca non omnino culturæ inidonea.

## 13:6
Vers. 6. ἀνατείλαντ@@] With the sun shining, as the Hebrew חרח is sometimes accepted.

ἐκαυματίσθη] They were scorched, as Columella speaks: which things are such as Aristotle calls ἡλιώμενα. Ovid: 'And there is less weight in you than in the top of the ear of corn, which, light, stiffens, scorched by the constant suns.' This heat is an image of heavy vexation, as is explained below and in Apocal. XVI. 8.

διὰ τὸ μὴ ἔχειν ῥίζαν, ἐξηράνθη] 'Roots are analogous to plants, and what is called the mouth to animals, through which the former take nourishment from the earth, and the latter through themselves,' says Aristotle. These seeds, therefore, because they could not turn downwards, were lacking a root, and therefore also the moisture which is drunk from the earth through the root. Moreover, the poverty of moisture, with external heat approaching, causes them to dry up. Aratus on the Syrian: 'No longer do the plantations deceive with the sun rising, flourishing tenderly; for he rushed sharply through the rows, and some he strengthened, but of others he destroyed all the bark.' Which Marcus Tullius paraphrases thus: 'Here, when it has raised itself equally with the sun into the lights of heaven, it does not suffer the trees, adorned with foliage, to hold their suspended spirits in vain. For those whose roots the earth has embraced and holds, these it increases and soothes with vital breath; but those whose roots cannot cleave the lands, it strips of leaves on the branches and of bark on the trunks.' Seneca Epistola LXXXVI. And for this reason it allows the nascent roots to come forth, and to grasp the soil, which it is necessary to hold still and clinging precariously, a light agitation also tears away.

Latin:

Vers. 6. ἀνατείλαντ@@] Fulgente sole, ut חרח Hebræ- um interdum accipitur.

ἐκαυματίσθη] Torresacta sunt, ut Columella loquitur: quæ talia sunt ἡλιώμενα vocat Aristoteles. Ovidius: Et minus est in te quam summa pondus arista, Quæ levis assiduis solibus usta riget. Æstus hic imago gravis vexationis, ut infra exponitur & Apocal XVI. 8.

διὰ τὸ μὴ ἔχειν ῥίζαν, ἐξηράνθη] ἀνάλογον αἱ ῥίζαι τοῖς φύτοις καὶ τὸ καλέμενον ςόμα τοῖς ζώοις, δι᾽ ὗ τὴν τροφὴν, τὰ μὲν ἐκ τῆς γῆς λαμβάνει, τὰ δὲ δι᾽ ἁυτῶν inquit Aristo- teles. Hæc ergo semina quia deorsum vergere non po- tuerunt, defeccta sunt radice, ac propterea etiam humore qui ex terra per radicem bibitur. Humoris autem penu- ria, accedente calore externo, efficit ut exarescant. Ara- tus de Syrio: Οὐκ ἕτι κᾶνον ἅμ᾽ ἠελίῳ ἀνίοντι Φυταλιαὶ ψεύδονται, ἀταλδία φυλλιόωσαι Ῥεῖα γὰρ ἐν ἔκρινε διὰ ςίχας ὀξὺς ἀίξας, Καὶ τὰ μὲν ἐῤῥωσεν, τῶν δὲ φλοὸν ὤλεσε πάντα. Quæ Marcus Tullius ita παραφράζει: Hic ubi se pariter cum sole in lumina cæli Extulit, haud patitur foliorum tegmine frustra Suspensos animos arbusta ornata tenere. Nam quorum stirpes tellus amplexa prehendit, Hæc augens anima vitali flamine mulcet: At quorum nequeunt radices sindere terras, Denudat foliis ramos & cortice truncos. Seneca Epistola LXXXVI. Et ob hoc nascentes radices pro- dire patitur, & solum apprehendere, quas necesse est tenere adhuc & precario hærentes, levis quoque revellat agitatio.

## 13:7
Vers. 7. ἀνέβησαν αἱ ἄκανθαι] Virgil: 'The thistle and the paliurus rises with sharp thorns.'

Latin:

Vers. 7. ἀνέβησαν αἱ ἄκανθαι] Virgilius: Carduus & spinis surgit paliurus acutis.

## 13:8
Vers. 8. τὴν καλὴν] cultivated, plowed, weeded.

ὃ μὲν] with the accent: for so the best codices have it. The discourse continues in the neuter gender, and no masculine noun is to be understood here.

ἑκατὸν] That which is reported by Varro concerning the Sybarite field, regarding agriculture: by Pliny concerning the Byzacian and Babylonian [fields].

B. Joh. Ernest. Gerhardus refers here to what is read in the Jerusalem Talmud concerning a certain man who sowed one seah, which produced or brought forth three hundred seahs: Buxtorf, Lexicon Talmudicum, under the word חרד. Lightfoot, however, noted here the hyperbolic nature of the Talmudic accounts concerning the fertility of the land of Israel. Regarding the hundredfold harvest, see Genesis XXVI. 12.

Latin:

Vers. 8. τὴν καλὴν] cultam, aratam, sartam.

ὃ μὲν] cum accentu: ita enim optimi codices. Per- severat oratio in neutro genere, neque masculinum ali- quod nomen hic subintelligendum est.

ἑκατὸν] Quod de Sybaritano agro à Varrone prodi- tum, de re rustica: à Plinio de Byzacico & Babylonia.

B. Joh. Ernest. Gerhardus huc refert, quod in Thalmud Hierosolymitano legitur, de quodam qui sevit satum unum, quod fecit seu protulit sata trecenta: Buxtorf. Lexic. Talmud. voce חרד. Hyperbolica tamen in Talmudicis de terræ Israë- liticæ fertilitate hic notavit Lightfootus. De messe autem centupla vid. Genes. XXVI. 12.

## 13:9
V. 9. ὁ ἔχων ὦτα ἀκέειν, ἀκουέτω] See what we said at chapter XI.

Latin:

V. 9. ὁ ἔχων ὦτα ἀκέειν, ἀκουέτω] Vid. quæ diximus ad c. XI.

## 13:10
Vers. 10. αὐτοῖς] That is, as Mark explains in chapter IV. 34, you teach us many things clearly in private, but you speak to the crowd in parables, which, because no moral application follows, have something enigmatic about them. And this is what Josephus Albo especially objects to the Christian religion, that it was delivered in parables when the law ought to be clear: but what he assumes for himself departs far from the truth. For Christ had already delivered the very precepts of believing, hoping, and living in the most open words, as appears in chapters V, VI, and VII of this book, and in the other writers of the New Testament. But those are what properly have the nature of law. Those things, however, which he explains in parables are of another kind, which Christ himself calls the mysteries of the kingdom: in which is partly explained the admirable divine dispensation, and partly it is predicted what the outcome of the Evangelical institution will be, both among the Jews and among the Gentiles. Prophecies are usually proposed in more obscure words, the Jews admit. For the chief end is that afterwards, when the event occurs, the certainty of divine foreknowledge may appear. Hence prophecy is often called a sealed book.

It is rash to distinguish the mysteries of the kingdom from things to be believed, since they are entirely included under them. Nor do parables, as was noted before, bring about obscurity by themselves: and if they were not explained then, they were at other times to the people: furthermore, the mysteries of the heavenly kingdom were proposed by Christ not only in parabolic words, but also in simple and literal ones: finally, the other hearers could equally have asked, indeed they ought to have asked, for the meaning of the parables, just as the disciples of Christ did. Nor can you object, says Chrysostom, Homily XLVI on Matthew, that these things were said to them obscurely: for they could have approached and asked at an opportune time, just as the disciples did: but corrupted by sloth and negligence, they did not want to. Why did I say did they not want to? Nay, they even zealously strove against him: for they not only did not believe, or did not listen, but they even attacked and persecuted him as he preached. Verse 11. ὑμῖν δίδοται] to the humble, to the lowly, as was explained above in chapter XI: to you who have received those precepts, proposed in the clearest words, with a humble and teachable mind. Δίδοται, however, is from the Father, to whom Christ is accustomed to refer all his own things. Διδόναι γνῶναι is for the one Hebrew word הוֹדִיעַ. ἐκείνοις δὲ ὀὐ δίδοται] Who seem to themselves to be wise and prudent: and thus they fastidiously reject those precepts leading to humility and gentleness, which are the elements of all piety. Since, however, there were many such in the crowd, this reason was sufficient for why those things which were more useful than necessary for salvation were proposed more obscurely. If there were any who were desirous of learning, they could approach Christ privately outside the crowd and ask for an explanation of those things which they did not sufficiently grasp by themselves: which we have said elsewhere was done also in the times of the Prophets. Justin: 'Whatever the prophets said and did, they revealed in parables and types, so that most things were not easily understood by all, hiding the truth within them, so that those seeking to find and learn might labor.' Similar is that of Iamblichus concerning Pythagoras: 'He himself concealed much of what was said, so that those who were being purely educated might clearly partake of them; but others, just as Homer says of Tantalus, are pained by the things being in the midst of their hearing, while enjoying nothing.' The Jews heard Christ teaching in parables here indeed, but they did not ask him about the meaning of the parables, as was done by the disciples. Therefore Theophylactus rightly explained that 'to you': to those seeking to learn, for 'everyone who asks receives,' those seeking to learn, for everyone who asks receives. Whence St. Chrysostom, loc. cit.: 'He said this, not showing any necessity, nor a rash attribution of doctrine to some by chance, and as it happens, but so that he might signify that the cause of all evils is in themselves.' Verse 12. ὅστις γὰρ ἔχει, δοθήσεται ἀυτῷ] He proves the equity of the divine counsel, the rule of which he himself follows, from a most trite maxim among them, which he also uses elsewhere for a slightly different matter, as is accustomed to be done in maxims. It is frequent, however, that in such maxims the same word is used now in one sense, now in another, as a little later 'seeing they do not see, and hearing they do not hear.' Thus in this place 'to have' is now to use, now simply to have received. Augustine on Christian Doctrine I: 'For he says: he who has, to him it shall be given.' He will therefore give to those who have, that is, to those using with kindness what they have received, he will fulfill and increase what he has given. Such is that of the Mime: 'The miser lacks what he has just as much as what he does not have.' He lacks because he does not use it. Thus, he who had buried his talent under the ground is said below not to have had it: he who had put his money at interest is said to have had it. And to Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics VII. 5, he whose mind is disturbed is said to have the knowledge of the right in a way and not to have it. Columella from Xenophon: 'Poverty is most certain when you need something of someone, and cannot use it.' But it will be given, says Tertullian, an increase of faith or intellect or salvation itself. κᾲ περισσευθήσεται] he will be enriched by what is given. They are opposed in Paul: 'to abound and to lack.' Similar is that of the Mime: 'He receives more benefits who knows how to return them.' ὃ ἔχει] Which he has already received, and is said to have to that extent: although in another sense in Luke he is said to seem rather to have. To have, says Ulpian, is accepted in two ways: for we say he has who is the owner of the thing: and he who is not indeed the owner but holds it: finally, we are accustomed to say we have a thing deposited with us. Therefore, if something has been given to anyone under a condition, he has it, because he holds it, he does not have it but seems to have it, insofar as he does not have full right. Gaius the Jurisconsult: 'He does not seem to have perfected that it is his own which can be taken away by chance.' ἀρθήσεται ἀπ᾽ ἀυτῦ] An argument from the greater. From the ungrateful or those who do not use what is given, what has been given, if it can be justly taken away, either by common law or by pact, is accustomed to be taken away: so far is it from the case that they receive more. It is not fair, therefore, that I should heap other things upon those who have long since fastidiously rejected what was given and is necessary for salvation. Nay, it is tacitly hinted that it will come to pass that eventually even human prudence, by which the Jews were proud, would be taken away from them, which also happened. 'Whoever has, to him it shall be given.' Sirach XXXIII. 2. He who seeks the word of God will find this abundantly. That is: Those who hear the word more often and attentively, to them

God will bestow increases of faith. But those who think they have learned everything, and fastidiously reject the word, just as most of the listeners departing from Christ were doing then, in them the persuasion of divine regeneration will vanish. Cf. Camero in Myrothecium on this passage. Luke VIII. 18, that which he has, is explained as that which he seems to have; one must be careful, however, not to gratify the Arminians, Socinians, and Papists by saying that God here promises supernatural illumination to one who uses the light of nature well. For it appears from the context that by 'the one who has' is understood he who has already been illuminated from the hearing of the word; nor can 'not having' be taken concerning the light of nature. For there is no one who does not have that. Furthermore, one must also be careful that 'to have' is not claimed for the elect alone with the Calvinists, as if to say: To the elect person having some grace, more will be given. If indeed it is taught here that grace can be taken away, which happens in those who are temporary, and that the word has a certain natural power to produce a salutary effect, which is evident from the intrinsic faculty of the seed which falls to the way, into the rock and thorns, which is not only of the same species as that seed which falls into good ground, but also of its juice and goodness, which by nature it could generate, just as the same food is prepared for those appearing and not appearing, for the worthy and the unworthy, Matt. XXII. 4 seqq., and that the divine intention is present with every preached word, so that it might exert its natural power and that a salutary one even in those in whom God foresaw from eternity that it would be hindered, is manifest from Is. V. 4, Ezek. XXIV. 13, Matt. XXIII. 37, John XV. 22, 24. But rightly from this saying, and the parallels Mark IV. 25, Luke 8:18. It is concluded that every motion of converting grace is ordinarily and regularly successive, progressing from lesser degrees of grace to greater ones. But similar sayings in Matthew 25:29 and Luke 19:26 must be distinguished from these; for these sayings do not deal with the grace of conversion and regeneration, which we commonly call sanctifying grace, but deal with the talents of ecclesiastical ministry, or graces freely given, in such a way that the good use of those talents obtains an increase of the degrees of grace and glory, not essential glory itself. The former testimonies, however, deal with the first effect of the preaching of the Gospel and the beginning of regeneration brought about through the preaching of the word. For after the Savior had dealt with the fourfold kind of hearers under the fourfold difference of the field into which the seed is sown, he immediately adds: Take heed how you hear; for to everyone who has, it will be given, etc. And it is thus evident from the scope that this discourse is about the increments and degrees of divine grace, which begins from the preaching of the word, and because the Savior describes there the ordinary way of converting men through the sowing of the word, it is rightly inferred, especially from the declaration which exists in Mark 4:28, 'The earth sown with the seed of the divine word first produces the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear,' that every conversion, that is, the illumination of the mind, the renewal of the will and affections, and finally the progress both in faith and in piety, happens successively, not in an instant, nor irresistibly.

Latin:

Vers. 10. αὐτοῖς] Hoc est ut Marcus explicat cap. IV. 34. nos quidem seorsim multa perspicue doces, apud turbam autem loqueris δι αἰνιων, qui, quia ἐπιμύθιον non accedit, habent aliquid αἰνιγματῶδες. Et hoc est quod Josephus Albo imprimis legi Christianæ objicit, quod tradita sit δι αἰνιων cum lex debeat esse perspicua: sed quod sibi sumit longe a vero recedit. Nam ipsa credendi, sperandi, viven- dique præcepta jam ante Christus tradiderat apertissimis verbis, ut apparet capp. V. VI. & VII. hujus libri, & apud cæteros novi fœderis Scriptores. At illa sunt quæ proprie le- gis habent rationem. Quæ vero δι αἰνιων explicat sunt alte- rius generis, quæ Christus ipse appellat μυστήρια τῆς βασι- λείας: In quibus partim explicatur dispensatio divina admi- rabilis, partim quis futurus sit Evangelicæ institutionis e- ventus, tum in Judæis tum in gentibus prædicitur. Solent autem vaticinia proponi verbis obscurioribus fatentur Ju- dæi. Finis enim præcipuus est, ut postea cum res evenit, divinæ præscientiæ certitudo appareat. Hinc προφητεία sæ- pe vocatur liber signatus.

Temere mysteria regni à credendis discrimi- nantur, quum sub illis comprehensa omnino sint. Neque vero parabolæ, ut antea monitum, per se obscuritatem important: & explicatæ si non tunc, alias fuêre populo: adhæc non solum parabolicis verbis, sed etiam simplicibus & pro- priis à Christo regni cælestis mysteria propo- sita sunt: denique auditores cæteri æque roga- re poterant, imo debebant sensum parabolarum, ac discipuli Christi. Nec objicere potes, inquit Chrysost. hom. XLVI. in Matth. obscure illis hæc dicta fuisse: potuissent enim opportune accedere & interrogare, sicut & discipuli fecerunt: sed torpo- re atque negligêntia corrupti noluerunt. Cur dixi- noluerunt? imo etiam adversus eum studiose nite- bantur: nec enim non solum non credebant, vel non audiebant, verum etiam impugnabant & perseque- bantur prædicantem. Vers. 11. ὑμῖν δίδοται] τοῖς ταπίοις, τοῖς ταπεινοῖς ut supra cap. XI. explicatum est: vobis qui præcepta illa aper- tissimis verbis proposita humili ac docili accepistis animo. Δίδοται autem, a patre scilicet ad quem sua omnia Christus solet referre. Διδόναι γνῶναι est pro una voce Hebræa הוֹדִיעַ. ἐκείνοις δὲ ὀὐ δίδοται] Qui sibi videntur σοφοὶ κᾲ συνετοὶ: atque adeo præcepta illa ad humilitatem & mansuetudi- nem ducentia, quæ omnis pietatis elementa sunt fastidiose respuunt. Cum autem tales multi essent in turba, sufficie- bat hæc ratio, cur ea quæ utilia magis erant quam ad salu- tem necessaria obscurius proponerentur. Si qui erant di- scendi cupidi, poterant extra turbam Christum privatim accedere, & explicationem petere eorum quæ per se non satis assequebantur: quod & Prophetarum temporibus fa- ctitatum alibi diximus. Justinus: ὅσα εἶπον κᾲ ἐποίησαν οἱ προφῆται παραβολαῖς κᾲ τύποις ἀπεκάλυψαν, ὡς μὴ ῥᾳδίως τὰ πλεῖστα ὑπὸ πάντων νοηθῆναι, κρύπτοντες τὴν ἐν αὐτοῖς ἀλή- θειαν, ὡς καὶ πονῆσαι τοὺς ζητῶντας εὑρεῖν καὶ μαθεῖν. Simile est illud Jamblichi de Pythagora: συνεπικρύπτεσθαι αὐτὸν πολὺ τῶν λεγομένων, ὅπως οἱ μὲν καθαρῶς παιδευόμενοι σαφῶς ἀυτῶν μεταλαμβάνωσιν· οἱ δὲ, ὥσπερ ὅμηρος φησὶ τὸν τάν- ταλον, λυπῶνται παρόντων αὐτοῖς ἐν μέσῳ τῶν ἀκουσμάτων, μηδὲν ἀπολαύοντες. Judæi Christum in parabolis docentem au- dierunt hic quidem, sed de sensu parabolarum non interrogarunt ipsum, ut à discipulis factum. Ideo Theophylactus recte illud ὑμῖν vobis exposuit: τοῖς ζητᾶσι μαθεῖν, πᾶς ὁ γὰρ αἰτῶν λαμβάνει, quæ- rentibus discere, nam omnis qui postulat accipit. Un- de S. Chrysost. l.c. Hoc dixit, non necessitatem quam- piam ostendens, nec temerariam ad aliquos doctri- næ attributionem à casu, & ut contingit, illatam, sed ut in ipsis omnium causam esse malorum signif- caret. Vers. 12. ὅστις γὰρ ἔχει, δοθήσεται ἀυτῷ] Æquitatem divini consilii cujus ipse præscriptum sequatur, ex tritissi- ma inter ipsos sententia probat, qua & alibi in rem paulo diversam utitur, ut ἐν γνώμαις fieri solet. Frequens autem est, ut in sententiis ejusmodi vox eadem modo hoc, mo- do alio sensu usurpetur, ut paulo post βλέποντες ὀυ βλέπουσι, κᾲ ἀκούοντες ὀυκ ἀκούουσι. Sic hoc loco ἔχειν modo est ut, mo- do simpliciter accepisse. Augustinus de doctrina Christi- ana I. Ille enim ait: qui habet, dabitur ei. Dabit ergo ha- bentibus, id est cum benignitate utentibus eo quod acceperunt, adimplebit atque cumulabit quod dedit. Tale est illud Mimi: Tam deest avaro quod habet quam quod non habet. Deest quia non utitur. Sic non habuisse talentum infra di- citur, qui sub terram defoderat: Habuisse, qui in fœnore nummos posuerat. Et Aristoteli Nicomacheorum VII. 5. dicitur is cui perturbatus animus, notitiam recti ἔχειν πῶς κᾲ μὴ ἔχειν. Columella ex Xenophonte: paupertatem cer- tissimam esse cum alicujus indigeas, uti eo non posse. Dabitur autem, inquit Tertullianus, adauctio fidei vel intellectus vel salus ipsa. κᾲ περισσευθήσεται] ditescet datis. Opponuntur apud Paulum περισσεύειν κᾲ ὑστερεῖσθαι. Simile est illud Mimi: Beneficia plura recipit qui scit reddere. ὃ ἔχει] Quod jam accepit, atque eatenus habere di- citur: quanquam alio sensu apud Lucam dicitur videri potius habere. Habere, inquit Ulpianus, dupliciter accipi- tur: nam & eum habere dicimus qui rei dominus est: & eum qui dominus quidem non est sed tenet: denique habere rem apud nos depositam solemus dicere. Itaque si cui aliquid datum est sub conditione, is habet, quia tenet, non ha- bet sed habere videtur, quatenus non habet jus plenum. Cajus Jurisconsultus: Non videtur perfecisse cujusque id esse quod ex casu auferri potest. ἀρθήσεται ἀπ᾽ ἀυτῦ] A majori argumentum. Ingra- tis aut qui non utuntur datis, quod datum est si juste au- ferri potest, aut ex lege communi, aut ex pacto, auferri solet: tantum abest ut plura accipiant. Æquum igitur non est ut istis, quamdiu pridem data & ad salutem necessaria fastidiose respuunt, alia ingeram. Quin tacite innuitur fore, ut tandem etiam humana prudentia, qua superbie- bant Judæi, ipsis auferretur, quod & contigit. Quisquis habet dabitur illi. Syr. XXXIII. 2. Qui quærit verbum Dei, opulenter hoc nanciscetur. Id est: Qui verbum sæpius & attente audiunt, illis

Deus incrementa fidei largietur. Qui vero pu- tant, se omnia didicisse, ac verbum fastidiunt, sic- ut tum faciebant plerique auditores à Christo dis- cedentes, in illis persuasio divinæ regeneratio- nis evanescet. Conf. Camero in Myroth. ad h. l. Luc. VIII. 18. illud, quod habet, exponitur, quod videtur habere; Cavendum tamen, ne cum Armi- nianis, Socinianis, & Papistis id gratificemur, bene utenti naturæ lumine DEUM supernatura- lem illuminationem hic promittere. Nam per ha- bentem intelligi, qui ex auditu verbi jam illumi- natus est ἐ συνεχείᾳ apparet; nec τὸ non habere de lumine naturæ accipi potest. Nemo enim non habet illud. Porro & id cavendum ne τὸ habere solis electis vindicetur cum Calvinianis, q. d. E- lecto habenti aliquam gratiam dabitur major. Si- quidem hic doceatur gratiam posse auferri, quod in προσκάιροις fit, ac verbo naturalem quandam vim inesse ad producendum salutarem effectum, quod patet ex intrinseca facultate seminis quod ad viam, in petram & spinas cadit, quod non so- lum ejusdem speciei cum illo semine, quod in terram bonam cadit, sed ejus etiam succi, & bo- nitatis, quæ per naturam possit generare, quem- admodum idem cibus animarum comparenti- bus, & non comparentibus, dignis, & indignis paratus est Matth. XXII. 4. seqq. omnique ver- bo prædicato adesse divinam intentionem, ut na- turalem suam vim eamque salutiferam exerat etiam in iis, in quibus DEUS impeditum ean- dem iri ab æterno prævidit, manifestum est ex Es. V. 4. Ezech. XXIV. 13. Matth. XXIII. 37. Joh. XV. 22. 24. Recte autem ex hoc dicto, & parallelis Marc. IV. 25. Luc. VIII. 18. concluditur omnem motum gratiæ convertentis ordinarie & regulari- ter esse successivum progredientem à minoribus gratiæ gradibus ad majores. Sed distinguenda sunt ab his dictis similia Matth. XXV. 29. Luc. XIX. 26. sono quidem eadem sed objectis diversa; His enim dictis non agitur de gratia conversionis & regene- rationis, quam communiter vocamus gratiam gra- tum facientem, sed agitur te talentis ministerii Ec- clesiastici, seu gratiis gratis datis, quomodo illorum Talentorum bonus usus augmentum graduum gratiæ & gloriæ non ipsam essentialem gloriam con- sequatur. Priora autem testimonia agunt te primo effectu prædicationis Evangelicæ & initio regenera- tionis per prædicationem verbi facto. Postquam enim Salvator de quadruplici genere auditorum sub quadruplici differentia agri, in quem semen spargitur, egisset, è vestigio addit: Videte quomodo audiatis; omni enim habenti dabitur &c. Patetque adeo ex scopo de incrementis & gradibus gratiæ di- vinæ, quæ à prædicatione verbi incipit hic sermo- nem esse, & quia salvator modum ordinarium con- vertendi homines per seminationem verbi illic describit, recte infertur, præsertim ex declaratio- ne, quæ apud Marcum extat c. IV. 28. Terra semine verbi divini consita primum producit herbam, dein- de spicam, postea plenum frumentum in spica, o- mnem conversionem, id est, illuminationem men- tis, renovationem voluntatis & affectuum, pro- gressus denique tum in fide, tum in pietate fieri successive, non in instatne, neque irresistibiliter.

## 13:13
Verse 13. ὅτι βλέποντες οὐ βλέπουσι] And yet Mark says that Christ brought forward this reason why he proposed the mysteries of the kingdom more obscurely to them, ἵνα βλέποντες βλέπωσι καὶ μὴ ἴδωσι, καὶ ἀκούοντες ἀκούωσι καὶ μὴ συνιῶσι, which is also in Luke. But the one coheres with the other most excellently: therefore, says Christ, I speak more obscurely to them, lest they understand the later things, who were unwilling to admit into their minds the earlier things clearly proposed. In the Constitutions of Clement: Διὸ ᾐρθη ἀπ᾽ αὐτῶν ἡ γνῶσις ὅτι ἰδόντες παρεῖδον.

ἀκούοντες οὐκ ἀκέσι] Heraclitus: The unintelligent, when they hear, are like the deaf. Fame bears witness to them that they are absent while present. Which meaning those ancient verses also express: When the mind is not settled in someone, it is not possible for him to hear anything because of his passion. Aristides: As in a fable, some secret word is spoken to those who are able to hear, but to you no more so. But Christ here speaks properly of the assenting intellect.

Latin:

Vers. 13. ὅτι βλέποντες οὐ βλέπουσι] Atqui Marcus Chri- stum dicit hanc attulisse causam cur arcanaregni obscurius illis proponeret ἵνα βλέποντες βλέπωσι καὶ μὴ ἴδωσι, καὶ ἀκούον- τες ἀκύωσι καὶ μὴ συνιῶσι, quod & apud Lucam est. Sed o- ptime alterum alteri cohæret: ideo, inquit Christus, ob- scurius ad illos loquor, ne posteriora intelligant, qui prio- ra clare proposita in animum admittere noluerunt. In Clementis constitutionibus: Διὸ ᾐρθη ἀπ᾽ αὐτῶν ἡ γνῶσις ὅτι ἰδόντες παρεῖδον.

ἀκούοντες οὐκ ἀκέσι] Heraclitus : ἀξύνετοι ἀκούσαντες κωφοῖς ἐοίκασι. Φάτις αὐτοῖσι μαρτυρεῖ παρεόντας ἀπεῖναι. quem sensum & veteres illi versus exprimunt : Όταν δ' ὁ νῦς ἧ μὴ καθεστηκώς τινι Οὐκ ἔς' ἀκύειν ὀδὲν αὐτῷ δι' ἐρᾶν. Aristides : ὧσπερ ἐν μύθῳ τις ἀπόῥῥητον λόγον τοῖς μὲν ἀκό- ειν δυνατοῖς εἴρηται, σοὶ δὲ ὀδὲν μᾶλλον. Sed Christus proprie hic agit de intellectu assentiente.

## 13:14
Vers. 14. ἀναπληρῦται ἐπ' αὐτοῖς] A saying indeed among Isaiah concerning the men of his own time, as the passage also shows, and Paul explains in Acts XXVIII. 25, but in such a way that they bore the image of these, and in these many, the same words were fulfilled even more fully than in those. See what has been said elsewhere about the word πληρῦσθαι. However, it seems that Christ said ἀναπληρῦται deliberately, not ἀναπεπλήρωται: because the completion of that saying in the Jews had a duration of time, from the advent of Christ until the destruction of the temple, with the malice of the Jews growing more and more and breaking out more openly. See the place I mentioned in the Acts.

ἀκοῇ ἀκύσετε] Because both the most holy interpreter of Matthew, whoever he was, and Paul, or at least Luke in the Acts in this place—which they do not always do elsewhere—follow the LXX Interpreters, I therefore do not doubt that they judged the Hebrew meaning to be best expressed by the same LXX, which also seems so to me. But just as we have already seen in the preceding discourse of Christ, which is confirmed by this prophecy, that the guilt of the Jews is expressed by Matthew as the impelling cause, but by Mark the end itself, why Christ spoke more obscurely to the crowd, namely the punishment, so I think both of these appear in the words of Isaiah, but the punishment first, then the cause of the punishment, αἰτιολογικῶς. In the former member, Isaiah uses imperative words, but the LXX partly the indicative, partly the subjunctive: but if anyone pays attention, the matter comes to the same thing: for that part which has the future indicative in Greek signifies a concession: that which has the subjunctive, a commination. But both are also accustomed to be signified by the imperative mood. But the LXX interpreters avoided τὸ ἀμφίβολον: so that if I say: Hear with your ears as much as you like, you will understand nothing: and strain the sight of your eyes: yet you will perceive nothing: it will be worth the same as if I say: You will indeed hear, but in such a way that you understand nothing: you will strain the sight of your eyes, but in such a way that you perceive nothing.

The saying of Isaiah VI. 9. does not only concern the men of that age, but the Jewish nation from that time until the final destruction. The men who lived at that time, to whom the Prophets were sent, are not excluded, but are designated there; but we deny that the men of subsequent times are excluded, since the same sentiment is explained concerning them both by Christ here, and by John ch. XII. 38, and by Luke in Acts XXVIII. 25, who, although he teaches that these things were said to the Fathers, yet not about the Fathers alone; and by Paul in Rom. XI. 8. Nor indeed did this pertain only to the latest times of the Jews, in that the men of the earlier times of Isaiah bore their image, but for the same reason it deals with these and those in the literal sense: because the Jews were always of the same character and disposition, and it was the same people: for just as the river is the same, even if other and other water flows and succeeds, so, as Basil says, the Jewish people were always the same, even if silently other and other men succeeded one another in it. Nor indeed do the things which are had in v. 11 c. VI of Isaiah, until the cities are desolate without an inhabitant, look to the devastation made by the Chaldeans, as Vatablus, or by Sennacherib, as Grotius wishes: But they deal with the latest destruction, which is to be by the Romans, as Jerome, Basil, Cyril, Haymo, Rupert, and others have interpreted, and that from the cited places of the N.T., especially Acts XXVIII. & Rom. XI. is very clear: nor could Grotius deny it entirely, therefore he added what follows: It seems that Christ said ἀναπληρῦται deliberately, not ἀναπεπλήρωται, because the completion of that saying in the Jews had a duration of time, from the advent of Christ until the destruction of the temple, with the malice of the Jews growing more and more and breaking out more openly. See the place I mentioned in the Acts.

For the rest, the Prophetic words, and the various allegations made in the New Testament, which the Calvinists abuse so that they may make God the author of sin, Grotius has not poorly explained: As we have already seen in the preceding discourse of Christ, etc. To which must also be added what the same observed regarding the following verse, as they pertain to the same argument.

Latin:

Vers. 14. ἀναπληρῦται ἐπ' αὐτοῖς ] Dictum quidem a- pud Esaiam de hominibus sui temporis, ut & locus osten- dit, & Paulus explicat Actor. XXVIII. 25. sed ita ut illi ho- rum gererent imaginem, atque in his multis etiam plenius, quam in illis eadem verba implerentur. Vide quæ de voce πληρῦσθαι dicta sunt alibi. Videtur autem Christus de in- dustria dixisse ἀναπληρῦται, non ἀναπεπλήρωται : quia istius dicti completio in Judæis tractum temporis habuit, ad adventu Christi usque excidium templi, magis magis- que crescente & apertius erumpente Judæorum malitia. Vide quem dixi in Actis locum.

ἀκοῇ ἀκύσετε ] Quia & Matthæi, quisquis fuit, san- ctissimus interpres, & Paulus, aut certe Lucas in Actis hoc in loco, quod alibi non semper faciunt, sequuntur LXX. Interpretes, ideo non dubito quin judicarint ab iis- dem LXX. sensum Hebraicum optime expressum, quod & mihi videtur. Sicut autem jam vidimus in antecedenti ora- tione Christi, quæ hoc vaticinio confirmatur, à Matthæo culpam Judæorum exprimi ut causam impellentem, a Mar- co autem finem ipsum, cur Christus apud turbam obscu- rius loqueretur, pœnam scilicet, ita utrumque horum in Esaiæ verbis arbitror apparere, sed pœnam prius, deinde causam pœnæ, αἰτιολογικῶς. In membro priore Esaias uti- tur verbis imperativis, LXX. autem partim indicativo, par- tim subjunctivo : sed si quis animum advertat eodem res recidit: ea enim pars quæ Græce indicativum futurum ha- bet, concessionem significat : quæ subjunctivum, commi- nationem. Utrumque autem solet etiam imperandi mo- do significari. Sed interpretes LXX. vitarunt τὸ ἀμφίβολον : ut si dicam: Audite auribus quantum lubet, nihil intellige- tis: & intendite oculorum aciem : nihil conspicietis tamen : idem valebit ac si dicam : Audietis quidem, sed ita ut nihil intelligatis: intendetis aciem oculorum, sed ita ut conspiciatis nihil.

Dictum Esaiæ VI. 9. non solum homines istius ætatis concernit, sed gentem Judaicam ex eo tem- pore usque ad excidium finale. Non excluduntur, sed designantur illic homines, qui illo vixêre tem- pore, ad quos mittebantur Prophetæ, excludi autem temporum sequentium homines negamus, quin de illis etiam explicatur eadem sententia tum à Christo hic, tum à Johanne cap. XII. 38. tum à Luca Actor XXVIII. 25. qui etsi ad Patres, non tamen de Patribus solis ea dicta docet; à Paulo Rom. XI. 8. Nec vero ita tantum ad tempora Ju- dæorum novissima hoc pertinebat, qua tempo- rum priorum Esaiæ homines eorum imaginem gerebant, sed eadem ratione sensu literali de his, & de illis agit: quia ejusdem fuêre semper Judæi ingenii, atque indolis, idemque fuit populus: si- cut enim idem est fluvius, etsi alia & alia affluat & succedat aqua, ita dicente Basilio, idem sem- per fuit Judæorum populus, etsi tacite alii, & alii homines in eo invicem sibi successerint. Nec vero quæ v. 11. c. VI. Esaiæ habentur, donec desolentur civitates absque habitatore, respiciunt vastationem per Chaldæos factam, ut Vatablus, aut per Sen- nacheribum, uti vult Grotius: Sed de excidio novissimo, per Romanos futuro agunt, ut Hiero- nymus, Basilius, Cyrillus, Haymo, Rupertus, alii- que interpretati sunt, idque ex locis allegatis N. T. imprimis Actor. XXVIII. & Rom. XI. valde luculentum est: neque diffiteri potuit prorsus Grotius, ideo addidit, quæ sequuntur: Videtur Christus de industria dixisse ἀναπληρῦται, non ἀ- ναπεπλήρωται, quia istius dicti completio in Judæis tractum temporis habuit, ab adventu Christi usque ad excidium templi, magis magisque crescente & apertius erumpente Judæorum malitia. Vide quem dixi in actis locum.

De cætero verba Prophetica, & allegationes diversas in Nov. Test. factas, quibus abutuntur Calviniani, ut Deum autorem peccati faciant, non male exposuit Grotius: Sicut jam vidimus in antecedenti oratione Christi, &c. Quibus ad- denda etiam quæ idem ad versum sequentem ob- servavit utpote ad idem argumentum facientia.

## 13:15
Vers. 15. ἐπαχύνθη γὰρ] There follows the cause which moved God, why He wished them to be addressed in such a way, both in the times of Isaiah and of Christ, because, forsooth, they had not wished to see what they could and ought to have seen. It stands against this interpretation among many, that God in the Prophet seems to use imperative words, just as if He were commanding the Prophet to make the heart fat and to make the eyes dull and the ears heavy, in the way that Abraham the Rabbi also explained among the Jews, which, although it can receive a certain figurative meaning and one that is not inconvenient, namely that the Prophet is commanded to do that which he predicts will happen, as in the same Jeremiah I. 10, yet since the Hebrew words can be referred no less to the infinitive mood than to the imperative, I prefer to agree with Joseph Kimchi and most other masters of the Hebrews who refer them to the infinitive, so that, namely, the particle על or מן or some similar one is understood, as if you were to say διὰ τὸ παχῦναι τὴν καρδίαν τῦ λαῦ τότε: for it is known that in such usage transitive and passive verbs are used indiscriminately: as presently ἐπιστρέψωσι. Thus the sense will be the same, which is in the Greek of the LXX interpreters, and which fits the purpose of both Christ and Paul in the Acts of the Apostles much better than that other thing which I mentioned. For what is in John, τετύφλωκεν ἀυτῶν τὰς ὀφθαλμὸς κὴ πεπώ- ρωκεν ἀυτῶν τὴν καρδίαν, and in Paul to the Romans ἔδωκεν ἀυτοῖς ὁ Θεὸς πνεῦμα κατανύξεως, ὀφθαλμὸς τῦ μὴ βλέ- πειν κὴ ὦτα τῦ μὴ ἀκέειν, I think is properly a circumlocution not of this clause but of that which preceded, ἀκοῇ ἀ- κέσετε: although John, as also Mark, wove that former part together with the latter member of this clause, since the sense was rendered more universally than by individual words, whereas it was the purpose of Matthew and Paul in the Acts, as is openly to be seen, to read the very traces of the words. But that παχύνεσθαι καρδίαν does not signify any inattention, but that which is born from prosperous circumstances, as is to be seen in Deut. XXXII. 15. Thus the Greeks say, a fat belly does not beget a subtle mind. The Jews were indeed under the Roman empire, but in such a way that they were governed moderately and gently enough, retaining many traces of autonomy, with only the license of rebelling taken away.

ἐκάμμυσαν] They closed their eyes to themselves or bruised them, they winked, for Priscian approves of that past tense in the Latin language. By the preaching of two whole years they had become nothing the better.

μήποτε ἴδωσι] It coheres in the Prophet and his interpreters with the latter sense, which does not threaten, but renders the cause of the threat: as if you were to say, they did this, so that they might not understand anything: nor do Mark and John refer these same things badly to punishment: because both God in the Prophet and Christ in this place show that the punishment will be similar to the fault. Thus we read in Moses, Pharaoh hardened his heart, and God hardened the heart of Pharaoh.

ἰάσωμαι ἀυτὲς] In the Hebrew word for word, and let him be healed, or and let health come to him, from me of course: for God is speaking. Therefore the LXX rightly translated ἰάσομαι. But this medicine, as David Kimchi also explains, is the forgiveness of sins. Therefore Mark for the same thing put κὴ ἀφεθῇ ἀυτοῖς τὰ ἁ- μαρτήματα. But that Mark refers that very thing, as also what preceded, to punishment, can, as it seemed to Chrysostom, signify either the greatest difficulty of obtaining forgiveness, or also a divine severity that will last for some time. For even in Isaiah the threat does not extend beyond the Babylonian destruction: and it is credible that some of those with whom Christ is dealing, after Christ was cruelly slaughtered, turned to repentance with the sharpest bite of heart. For such is the human disposition, to spurn obvious goods, and to desire forbidden things more ardently: We hate virtue when it is safe, we seek it when it is taken from our eyes, being envious. But also dealing with the Jews of his own time. Paul, when he had said that they were hardened and held by a blinding spirit, added until this very day. Nor was it badly noted by the ancients that it is often in the interest of the men themselves that remedies be deferred, so that whatever is impure within may show itself more. For wounds that are covered over quickly easily break out again. Not badly in this sense does Origen in On First Principles III: sometimes to be healed more quickly does not turn out for the good of those being healed, if, having fallen into difficult things, they might easily be freed from those things into which they have fallen; for despising the evil as incurable, and not guarding against falling into it a second time, they will be in it. Wherefore in the case of those

The eternal God, the knower of hidden things, who knows all things before their creation, according to his goodness, surpasses the swifter help toward them, and, in such a way, helping them, he helps.

Latin:

Vers. 15. ἐπαχύνθη γὰρ] Sequitur causa quæ Deum mo- vit, cur eos ita compellari vellet, tum Esaiæ, tum Christi temporibus, quia nimirum quæ videre poterant & debeant, videre noluerant. Obstat huic interpretationi apud mul- tos, quod Deus apud Prophetam verbis videtur uti impe- rativis, perinde quasi præcipiat Prophetæ, ut ipse cor ob- limet & oculos hebetes & aures aggravet, quomodo ex- posuit etiam apud Judæos Abrahamus Rabbinus quod quanquam accipere sensum quendam figuratum eumque non incommodum potest, nempe ut jubeatur Propheta facere, id quod futurum prædicit, ut apud eundem Jere- miam I. 10. tamen cum Hebraicæ voces non minus ad in- finitivum modum, quam ad imperativum referri pos- sint, Josepho Kimchi & plerisque aliis Hebræorum ma- gistris assentiri malo ad infinitivum referentibus, ita scili- cet ut subaudiatur particula על vel מן vel aliqua similis quasi dicas διὰ τὸ παχῦναι τὴν καρδίαν τῦ λαῦ τότε : no- tum enim est in ejusmodi usu verba transitiva & passiva promiscue usurpari: ut mox ἐπιστρέψωσι. Ita erit idem sen- sus, qui est in Græco LXX. interpretum, quique tum Chri- sti, tum Pauli in actis Apostolicis proposito multo melius convenit, quam alterum illud quod dixi. Nam quod apud Johannem est, τετύφλωκεν ἀυτῶν τὰς ὀφθαλμὸς κὴ πεπώ- ρωκεν ἀυτῶν τὴν καρδίαν, & apud Paulum ad Romanos ἔδωκεν ἀυτοῖς ὁ Θεὸς πνεῦμα κατανύξεως, ὀφθαλμὸς τῦ μὴ βλέ- πειν κὴ ὦτα τῦ μὴ ἀκέειν, puto proprie circumlocutionem esse non hujus commatis sed ejus quod præcessit ἀκοῇ ἀ- κέσετε: quanquam Johannes ut & Marcus, partem istam priorem cum hujus commatis posteriori membro conte- xuit, quippe reddito magis universo sensu quam verbis sin- gulis, cum Matthæo Pauloque in actis propositum fuerit, ut palam videre est, ipsa verborum vestigia legere. Illud au- tem παχύνεσθαι καρδίαν non quamvis ἀπροσεξίαν significat, sed eam quæ ex rebus fecundis nascitur, ut videre est Deut. XXXII. 15. Sic Græci dicunt παχεῖα γαστὴρ λέπτον ὐ τίκτει νόον. Erant quidem Judæi sub Romano imperio, sed ita ut moderate ac clementer satis regerentur, multa retinentes vestigia ἀυτονομίας, deinta tantum rebellandi licentia.

ἐκάμμυσαν] Oculos sibi occlusere aut sugillavêre, cœniverunt, nam id præteritum in Latino sermone probat Priscianus. Totius biennii prædicatione nihilo facti erant meliores.

μήποτε ἴδωσι] Cohæret apud Prophetam & ejus inter- pretes cum posteriori sensu, qui non comminatur, sed comminationis causam reddit: quasi dicas, hoc egerunt, ne quid intelligerent: neque male Marcus & Johannes ea- dem ad pœnam referunt: quia & Deus apud Prophetam & Christus hoc loco ostendunt pœnam fore culpæ simi- lem. Ita apud Mosem legimus, induravit Pharao cor suum, & induravit Deus cor Pharaonis.

ἰάσωμαι ἀυτὲς] In Hebræo ad verbum & medicetur ei, aut & sanitas ei adveniat, à me scilicet: nam Deus lo- quitur. Ideo recte verterunt LXX. ἰάσομαι. Hæc autem medicina, ut & David Kimchi exponit, est peccatorum venia. Ideo Marcus pro eodem posuit κὴ ἀφεθῇ ἀυτοῖς τὰ ἁ- μαρτήματα. Quod autem Marcus id ipsum, ut & quod præ- cessit ad pœnam refert, potest ut Chrysostomo visum est aut maximam difficultatem significare impetrandæ veniæ, aut etiam severitatem divinam ad tempus aliquod duraturam. Nam & apud Esaiam comminatio non ultrà Babylonicum excidium extenditur: & eorum de quibus agit Christus nonnullos post Christum crudeliter trucidatum cum acer- rimo cordis morsu ad pœnitentiam versos credibile est. Ita enim humanum est ingenium, bona obvia spernere, ne- gata ardentius concupiscere: Virtutem incolumem odimus Sublatam ex oculis quærimus invidi. Sed & de sui temporis Judæis agens. Paulus cum dixisset eos πωρωθῆναι & cæcutiente spiritu teneri, addidit ἕως τῆς σήμερον ἡμέρας. Neque male à veteribus annotatum est sæpe ipsorum hominum interesse ut differantur remedia, quo magis quicquid intus impuri est se promat. Facile e- nim recrudescunt cito obducta vulnera. Non male in hanc sententiam Origenes περὶ ἀρχῶν III. ἐνίοτε τάχιον θεραπευθῆ- ναι ὐ πρὸς καλῦ γίνεται τοῖς θεραπευομένοις, εἴπερ ἑαυτές χαλε- ποῖς περιπεσόντες ἐυχερῶς ἀπαλλαγεῖεν τέτων οἷς περιπεπτώ- κασι· καταφρονῦντες γαρ ὡς ἐνιάτω τῦ κακῦ δεύτερον κ᾿ φυ- λαττόμενοι περιπεσῦν ἀυτῷ, ἐν ἀυτῷ ἔσονται. διόπερ ἐπὶ τῶν-

τοιῆται ὁ Θεὸς δ᾽ αἰώνι[ος], ὁ τῶν κρύπτων γνώστης, ὁ εἰδὼς τὰ πάντα πρὶν γενέσεως ἀυτῶν, κατὰ τὴν χρηστότητα ἀυτοῦ ὑπερβίθεται τὴν ταχοτέραν πρὸς ἀυτὸς βοήθειαν κὴ, ἐν᾿ ὕτως ἅπω, βοηθῶν ἀυτοῖς ὐ βοηθεῖ.

## 13:16
V. 16. 'your eyes, because they see, and your ears, because they hear.' I have no doubt that this deals with the eyes and ears of the mind. For the same thing had been dealt with in the preceding verse. Therefore, in other words, the same thing is said here that had been said above in verse 11. Which the connection of verse 18 also makes clear.

To illustrate the whole passage, so that it may not be distorted by the Calvinists, the observation of B. Luther is especially useful. This whole passage is to be read copulatively, so that it depends in this way, as if by a chain. This people has a hardened heart and closed eyes, etc., whereby it happens that they cannot be converted and healed; i.e., the hardening of their heart stands in the way, so that they do not see and I do not heal them. I would wish, he says, to heal, therefore I send the Son, but the hardening of the heart stands in the way of my will and their salvation. Thus it is said more briefly and clearly than what Lyra is accustomed to say: to accept the particles 'lest' or 'that' in this place consecutively, not effectively. For if you arrange the text thus: 'The heart of this people is hardened lest they see, and I heal them,' the sense is clear: that they cannot be healed is caused by the fact that they do not see; that they do not see is caused by the fact that the heart is hardened. Thus it is evident that the will to heal is preached in God, but the obstacle of the heart in man is reproved.

Latin:

V. 16. οἱ ὀφθαλμοὶ, ὅτι βλέπυσι καὶ τὰ ὦτα ὑμῶν, ὅτι ἀκύει] De oculis auribusque mentis hic agi, non dubito. Nam de iisdem actum erat præcedenti commate. Itaque aliis verbis idem hic dicitur quod dictum erat supra commate 11. Quod & connexio commatis 18. apertum facit.

Ad illustrandum totum locum, ne à Calvi- nianis detorqueatur, apprime facit B. Lutheri ob- servatio. Totus hic locus copulative legendus est, ut dependeat hoc modo quasi & catena. Populus iste habet cor induratum & oculos clausos &c. quo fit, ut non possint converti & sanari, q. d. indu- ratio cordis eorum obstat, ne videant & sanem eos. vellem, inquit sanare, ideo mitto Filium, sed meæ voluntati, & eorum saluti obstat induratio cor- dis. Sic brevius & clarius dicitur, quam quod Ly- ra solet dicere: accipi hoc loco particulas ne, vel, ut, consecutivè, non effectivè. Nam si textum sic or- dines. Cor populi hujus est induratum ne vide- ant, & sanem eos, clarus est sensus: Ipsos non posse sanari, facit, qui non videant: Quod autem non vident, facit, quia induratum est cor: Sic patet, quod voluntas sanandi prædicatur in Deo, sed ob- staculum cordis in homine reprehenditur.

## 13:17
Vers. 17. 'For truly I say to you, that many prophets.' He gives the reason why the Apostles ought to esteem themselves blessed by that name, that is, affected by a peculiar grace from God: because that honor had not fallen to many prophets and other holy men, namely, of learning so many mysteries of the divine dispensation, which God had reserved for the times of the Messiah, as has been said by us elsewhere. Thus he recalls the Apostles from submission of mind, who might otherwise easily think, when that revelation was denied to other Jews because of their crimes, that it was attributed to themselves by merit of their virtues. Christ, countering this error, says: 'Nay, you are not better than Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Isaiah, Jeremiah, and other prophets, to whom that happiness was not granted.' See Isaiah 64:4. Therefore, that it is denied to other Jews is of justice; that it is attributed to you is of divine dispensation and grace.

and did not see. They did not see all those things, nor did they understand them as clearly as the writer to the Hebrews teaches in 11:13 and Peter in his first epistle 1:10-11; indeed, not even the angels, as seems to be signified by Peter in the same place.

Latin:

Vers. 17. ἀμὴν γὰρ λέγω ὑμῖν, ὅτι πολλοὶ προφῆται] Cau- sam reddit cur Apostoli beatus se ea nomine, hoc est pe- culiari à Deo gratia affectos, æstimare deberent: quia multis Prophetis aliisque viris sanctis is honos non con- tigisset, nempe discendi tam multa arcana divinæ dispen- sationis, quæ in Messiæ tempora Deus servaverat, ut ali- bi à nobis dictum est. Ita ab submissionem animi Apo- stolos revocat, facile alioqui cogitatuos, quando ista pa- tefactio Judæis aliis ob crimina denegaretur, sibi eam vir- tutum merito tribui. Huic errori Christus occurrens, imo inquit, meliores non estis Abrahamo, Isaaco, Jacobo, Esaia, Jeremia aliisque Prophetis: quibus ea felicitas do- nata non est. Vide Esaiam LXIV. 4. Ergo quod Judæis aliis negatur, justitiæ est, quod vobis tribuitur, divinæ dispensationis & gratiæ.

καὶ ἐκ εἶδον] Non ista omnia, neque tam clare intel- lexerunt ut docet Scriptor ad Hebræos XI. 13. & Petrus I Ep. I. 10. 11. imo ne angeli quidem, ut à Petro ibidem si- gnificari videtur.

## 13:19
Vers. 19. The word. The word is very well compared to seed. For in Latin also, 'sermo' (speech) is believed to be said from 'serendo' (sowing), and the Greeks said 'pseudos katabolen' (a false sowing). Aristotle, in the tenth book of the Nicomachean Ethics: 'It is necessary for the soul of the listener to have been prepared beforehand by habits to rejoice rightly and to hate, just as the earth is to nourish the seed.' Cicero, Tusculan Disputations II: 'Philosophy prepares minds to receive seeds and entrusts to them and, if I may say so, sows those things which, when grown, bear the richest fruits.' Plutarch also calls the word seed.

not understanding. That is, not paying attention, as it is explained in Homer: 'he understood him in silence.' So in Psalm 41:1, 'he who understands concerning the poor.' It was not without reason that it was once proclaimed in the sacred rites: 'Attend to this.'

In the word 'synienai' there is an emphasis, 'to send together,' when, namely, he who hears sends his mind together with the speech which he hears, so that he may attend; whence the phrase of the Latins, 'I do not follow what you mean.'

the evil one comes and snatches. The negligence of men, as we saw above, gives power to the devil over them. Therefore, what men despise to wait for when they hear, he even deletes from their memory: thus it happens as Luke teaches, that they do not believe; whence we learn that the most frequent cause of incredulity is inattention. That which corresponds to the birds in the parable is the evil demon in the explanation, which was not new among the Jews, who were accustomed to call demons birds. It is evident in the book Zohar and concerning the death of Moses. That statement of Philo in the book 'On the Giants' pertains to this sense: 'But indeed, even upon the holy ones, the appearance of the good often flies suddenly, but they are unable to grasp it and keep it with themselves.'

this is he who was sown by the wayside. That is, he who is such can be said metaphorically to be sown by the wayside. In these comparisons, the whole corresponds to the whole, as they say; not the smallest particles to particles. Therefore Luke compares men to seed synecdochically, denoting the whole from a part.

Latin:

Vers. 19. Τὸν λόγον] Optime λόγος semini comparatur. Nam & Latine sermo à serendo dici creditur, & Græci di- xerunt ψεῦδος καταβολὴν. Aristoteles Nicomachiorum de- cimo: δεῖ προδιειργάσθαι τοῖς ἤθεσι τὴν τὲ ἀκροατῶ ψυχὴν πρὸς τὸ καλῶ χαίρειν, κὴ μισεῖν ὥσπερ τὴν γῆν θρέψεσαν τὸ σπέρ- μα. Cicero Tusculanarum II. Philosophia præparat animos ad satus accipiendos eaque mandat his &, ut ita dicam, serit, quæ adulta fructus uberrimos ferant. Etiam Plutarchus τὸν λόγον vocat semen.

μὴ συνιέντ] Id est, μὴ προσέχοντΘ, ut exponitur apud Homerum σιγῇ τὸν ξυνίει. Ita in Psal. XLI. 1. ὁ συνιὼν ἐπὶ πτωχὸν. Non temere olim in sacris acclamatum: Hoc age.

In verbo συνιέναι emphasis est, simul mittere, cum scilicet is qui audit mentem suam simul mit- tit cum sermone, quem audit, ut attendat: unde phrasis Latinorum, non adsequor, quid velis.

ἔρχεται ὁ πονηρὸς κὶ ἁρπάζει] Hominum negligentia, ut supra vidimus, potestatem diabolo in ipsos facit. Quod ergo homines cum audiunt contemnunt expectare, id il- le etiam è memoria delet: ita sit quemadmodum Lucas docet ut non credant: unde discimus incredulitatis causam frequentissimam esse τὴν ἀπροσεξίαν. Quod autem avibus in parabola respondet in explicatione malus dæmon, apud Judæos novum non erat, qui soliti dæmonas aves appel- lare, Patet in libro Zoar & de morte Mosis. Pertinet ad hunc sensum Philonis illud libro de Gigantibus: ἀλλὰ γὰρ κὴ τοῖς ἐξαγίοις ἐπιποτᾶται πολλάκις αἰφνίδιον ἡ τῶ καλῶ φαντα- σία, συλλαβεῖν δ᾽ ἀυτὴν καὶ φυλάξαι παρ᾽ ἑαυτοῖς ἀδυνα- τῦσιν.

ὗτός ἐστι ὁ παρὰ τὴν ὁδὸν σπαρεὶς] Id est; qui talis est, μεταφορικῶς dici potest juxta viam consitus. In his com- parationibus totum complexum; quod vocant, complexo respondet: non minimæ particulæ particulis. Ideo Lucas homines semini comparat συνεκδοχικῶς ex parte comple- xum denotans.

## 13:20
Vers. 20. 'But he who was sown on the rocky ground.' That is, he who can be said metaphorically to be sown on stony ground. 'Immediately with joy receiving it.' 'With joy' is 'willingly,' as in Hebrews 10:34, 'to receive' or 'to accept.' But since here it is opposed to 'not understanding,' and below 'understanding' is placed for that which here is 'receiving with joy,' we see from this that it can hardly happen that he who diligently turns his mind to the word of God does not apply assent to it. Tertullian in the Apology: 'He who has heard will find God; he who has also studied to understand will be compelled also to believe.' This joy is not only the earthly joy of worldly conveniences, as Tossanus wishes, or that which arises from a craving for novelty (Acts 17:21), but also spiritual, of which we know from Hebrews 4:4 that even the 'temporary' are participants.

Latin:

Vers. 20. ὁ δὲ ἐπὶ τὰ πετρώδη σπαρείς] Id est qui μετα- φορικῶς dici potest super saxofa consitus. εὐθὺς μετὰ χαρᾶς λαμβάνων αὐτὸν] μετὰ χαρᾶς est liben- ter ut Hebr. X. 34. λαμβάνειν seu δέχεσθαι acceptare. Cum vero hic opponatur τῷ μὴ συνίεντι & infra positum sit συνιὼν pro eo quod hic est μετὰ χαρᾶς λαμβάνων, videmus hinc fie- ri vix posse, ut qui ad verbum Dei animum diligenter ad- vertat, eidem non adhibeat assensum Tertullianus Apolo- getico : qui audierit, inueniet Deum: qui etiam studuerit in- telligere, cogetur & credere. Gaudium hoc non tantum terrenum est mun- danorum commodorum ut Tossanus vult, vel quod ex novitatis aviditate oritur Act. XVII. 21. Sed etiam spirituale, cujus participes etiam προσ- καίρους esse ex Ebr. IV. 4. novimus.

## 13:21
Vers. 21. 'But he has no root in himself.' It coheres very well with what he had said, 'immediately.' Thus Quintilian said of a precocious talent, which is what Christ says here of a precocious and poorly cooked affection: 'It does not provide much, but quickly; there is no true strength underneath, nor does it rely on deeply cast roots.' Similar is that comparison of Callidorus in Plautus's Pseudolus: 'I was like a solstice herb for a little while: suddenly I sprang up, suddenly I perished.' The root here, therefore, is a well-meditated purpose of obtaining the good, with all things weighed, having spurned other things. Paul seems to call this very thing the 'firmness of faith' in Colossians 2:5, and those who have attained it 'rooted in love' in Ephesians 3:18. Cicero used the same simile, saying that virtue is fixed with the deepest roots. 'He is temporary.' Just as Paul opposes 'temporary' things to 'eternal' things in 2 Corinthians 4:18. Thus here πρόσκαιρος is opposed to the stable ὴ ἐῤῥιζωμένῳ, that is, to him who contains within himself a solid and durable strength. He is consistent with himself while things are sufficiently prosperous, as the Syrian explains in Luke.

The root is not the purpose of attaining the highest good, but faith well-founded in the word of GOD: which root is the mother of every good purpose and of every good action; nor is the root understood otherwise in Col. II. 5. We are said to be rooted in charity in Eph. III. 17, not our own, but GOD's, which likewise happens through faith. For the charity of GOD towards us must be apprehended by faith, in which we are founded and rooted, so that we may persist unmoved. Deprived of this root are the πρόσκαιροι, that is, those who, even if they have faith, because they are not properly rooted in it, or faith has not taken root in them, nor is it solidly founded, easily fall away from the faith. Therefore, it is not the nullity of faith, but its instability and amissibility that is noted in them.

Θλίψεως ἢ διωγμᾶ] The word διώκειν is taken generally as we have said elsewhere, and θλῖψις for that which we more frequently call διωγμὸς, as in Acts XI. 19. Otherwise, in this place, I think θλῖψις should be taken for private vexation, and διωγμὸς for public vexation. Thus Paul distinguished διωγμὸς and παθήματα in 2 Tim. III.

Εὐθὺς σκανδαλίζεται] נִכְשָׁל suddenly, just as he had suddenly received the word. There is here, however, a μετάληψις which signifies the consequence from the antecedent. For from ἐκ τᾶ σκανδαλίζεσθαι he wishes to be understood τὸ ἀφίςασθαι, which Luke expressed, just as one who is offended by the ruts of a road chooses another path for himself. The cause of the defection is referred to the instability of the mind, which is born from security, and security almost always from excessive self-confidence. Hence Christ so often warns his own to watch and pray in time, and before danger encroaches.

Latin:

Vers. 21. οὐκ ἔχει δὲ ῥίζαν ἐν ἑαυτῷ] Optime cohæret cum eo quod dixerat εὐθὺς. Ita de præcoci ingenio dixit Quin- tilianus, quod de præcoci & male cocto affectu Christus hic dicit: Non multum præstat, sed cito; non subest veræ vir, nec penitus immissis radicibus innititur. Similis est illæ Callidori comparatio in Pseudolo Plautinæ : Quasi solstitialis herba paulisper fui: Repente exortus sum, repentino occidi. Radix igitur hic est bene meditatum rebus omnibus ex- pensis propositum boni adipiscendi spretis rebus aliis. Hoc ipsum τὸ ςερέωμα τῆς πίςεως Paulus vocare videtur Coloss. II. 5. & qui id consecuti sunt ἐῤῥιζωμένους ἐν ἀγάπῃ, Ephes. III. 18. Eadem similitudine usus Cicero virtutem dixit al- tissimis defixam radicibus. πρόσκαιρός ἐστι] Sicut Paulus πρόσκαιρα opponit αἰω- νίοις 2. Cor. IV. 18. ita hic πρόσκαιρος opponitur stabili ὴ ἐῤῥιζωμένῳ, id est, ei qui vim solidam atque durabilem in se continet. Constat is sibi, dum res sunt satis prosperæ, ut ad Lucam exponit Syrus.

Radix non est propositum adipiscendi summi boni, sed fides bene fundata in verbo DEI: quæ radix & mater est omnis boni propositi, omnisque bonæ actionis; nec aliter radix intelligitur Col. II. 5. Radicati in charitate dicimur Ephes. III. 17. non nostra, sed DEI, quod pariter sit per fidem. Nam charitas DEI erga nos fide apprehendenda est, in qua nos fundamur & radicamur, ut immoti per- sistamus. Qua radice destituti πρόσκαιροι sunt, hoc est, qui etsi fidem habeant, quia tamen in ea radicati probe non sunt, aut fides in ipsis radicem non egit, nec fundata solide est, facile fide exci- dunt. Non ergo fidei nullitas, sed instabilitas, & a- missibilitas in iis notatur.

Θλίψεως ἢ διωγμᾶ] Sumitur & vox διώκειν generaliter ut alibi diximus, & θλῖψις pro eo quod frequentius διωγμὸς dicimus, ut Actor. XI. 19. Alioqui hoc in loco θλῖψις pro privata, διωγμὸς pro publica vexatione acci- piendum arbitror. Sic Paulus distinxit διωγμὸς & παθήματα 2. Tim. III.

Εὐθὺς σκανδαλίζεται] נִכְשָׁל repente, ut repente ver- bum admiserat. Est autem hic μετάληψις quæ ex antece- denti consequens significat. Nam ἐκ τᾶ σκανδαλίζεσθαι vult intelligi τὸ ἀφίςασθαι quod Lucas expressit, sicut qui viæ salebris offenditur, aliam sibi viam eligit. Causa defe- ctionis ad instabilitatem animi refertur, quæ ex securitate nascitur, securitas ferme ex nimia sui fiducia. Hinc Chri- stus toties suos monet, ut in tempore, & antequam peri- culum ingruat, vigilent ac precentur.

## 13:22
Vers. 22. ὁτῶν ἐστιν ὁ τὸν λόγον ἀκέων] Repeat ἐκ ποινᾶ τὸ μετὰ χαρᾶς λαμβάνων: or as is said above and below, συνιὼν. That which follows, however, is placed in the Hebrew manner in place of a relative. For the sense is: This is he who hears and receives with joy, but in whom the cares and anxieties of this age suffocate the word.

ἡ μέριμνα τῶ αἰῶνῶ τᾶτε, κὴ ἡ ἀπάτη τῶ πλᾶτε] μέριμνα τῶ αἰῶνῶ τᾶτε seems to be said here as that which is in John in the Epistle, ἀλαζονεία τᾶ βίs, 1 Epist. cap. II. com. 16, namely, the pursuit of those things which seem most splendid in this life, in which class the desire for honors and glory excels, which is finally cast off even by the wise. But for riches, Matthew wisely placed here ἀπάτην τῶ πλέτε, showing that while riches are indeed in the number of intermediate things, men are for the most part ensnared by their sweetness, concerning which matter we have cited the notable sayings of the ancients. Most relevant here is that saying of Menander:

ὁ δὲ πλᾶτῶν τυφλός, Τυφλὼς δ᾽ ἐς αὑτὸν ἐμβλέποντας δεικνύει.

Imitating this, Cicero said: Not only is fortune herself blind, but she also usually makes those blind whom she has embraced. But the mime says: Fortune makes those whom she favors too foolish. There is also another from the same Menander: Excessive luxury becomes arrogant when it has driven the possessor of wealth into a different character than that in which he was before. This is John's 'lust of the eyes.' But as to why Matthew omitted the third cause, which likewise is accustomed to stifle the pursuit of piety—namely, the pleasures of the body, which John called 'the lust of the flesh,' Mark in this place 'the desires concerning the rest,' and Luke 'the pleasures of life'—I suspect that this was the reason: because by naming riches, he thought they were sufficiently understood, since riches are generally sought for the sake of the pleasures of the body.

On the anxiety of life, Augustine, Sermon 42 on the Saints: What is worse than the anxiety of life, which does not allow one to arrive at life? What is more miserable than to lose life by caring for life? What is more unhappy than to fall into death by fearing death? Let the thorns be rooted out, let the field be prepared, let the seeds be received, let one arrive at the harvest, let the granary be desired, let not the fire be feared. On the thorns of riches, Chrysostom, Homily 13 on John: Just as thorns are sterile, so are riches; just as those thorns lacerate those who touch them, so does the desire for these; just as they are easily caught by fire and are hated by farmers, so are the affairs of this age. Finally, just as wild beasts, vipers, and scorpions hide among thorns, so they do in the frauds of riches. Theophylact on this passage: Just as a sharp thorn penetrates into the body and is with difficulty eradicated, so also do growing delights enter into the soul and are with difficulty eradicated. Cf. Matt. 19:23, Luke 16:9, 1. 1 Tim. 6:9-10. Although the Holy Spirit, the author of Scripture, did not add the pleasure of the flesh to these, He did not, however, omit it in the Gospels of Mark and Luke, but rather suggested the same to His own amanuenses.

it chokes the word and it becomes unfruitful] Since the comparison proceeds by degrees, it seems that this concerns those who had made greater progress in piety than those second ones, and thus, having struck roots, had begun to bring forth fruit not unworthy of praise, but, overwhelmed by various desires which they had neglected to purge, they lose that fruit-bearing power; for this is what 'it becomes unfruitful' means: for which Luke said 'and they do not bring to maturity,' that is, they do not carry the fruit through to the harvest. We have an example of this kind in Demas, of whom Paul says: 'Demas has forsaken me, having loved this present world,' 2 Tim. 4:10.

Latin:

Vers. 22. ὁτῶν ἐστιν ὁ τὸν λόγον ἀκέων] Repete ἐκ ποινᾶ τὸ μετὰ χαρᾶς λαμβάνων: aut ut supra infraque dicitur συνιὼν Quod autem tequitur, Hebræo more positum est vice re- lativi. Sensus enim est: Hic est qui audit & cum gaudio recipit, sed in quo curæ ac sollicitudines hujus ævi ver- bum suffocant.

ἡ μέριμνα τῶ αἰῶνῶ τᾶτε, κὴ ἡ ἀπάτη τῶ πλᾶτε] μέριμνα τῶ αἰῶνῶ τᾶτε dici hic videtur id quod Johanni in Epistola est ἀλαζονεία τᾶ βίs epist. I. cap. II. com. 16. studium scilicet earum rerum quæ in hac vita splendidissima videntur, in quo genere excellit honorum & gloriæ cupido, quæ sa- pientibus etiam novissime exuitur. Pro divitiis autem sa- pienter hic posuit Matthæus ἀπάτην τῶ πλέτε, oftendens esse quidem divitias in rerum mediatum numero, sed plerumque inescari earum dulcedine homines, qua de re insignia veterum dicta citavimus. Maxime huc pertinet Menandri illud:

ὁ δὲ πλᾶτῶν τυφλός, Τυφλὼς δ᾽ ἐς αὑτὸν ἐμβλέποντας δεικνύει.

Quod imitatus Cicero dixit: Non solum ipsa fortuna cæca est, sed eos etiam plerumque efficit cæcos, quos ipsa complexa est. Mimus autem: Fortuna nimium quos fovet stultos facit. Est & ejusdem Menandri alterum: Ὑπερήφανον πυ γίνεθ' ἡ λίαν τρυφὴ. Ὅτε πλῦτον ἐξώκειλε τὸν κεκτημένον. Εἰς ἕτερον ἦθον, ἐκ ἐν ᾧ τὸ πρόσθεν ἦν. Hæc est Johanni ἐπιθυμία τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν. Cæterum cur ter- tiam causam quæ itidem suffocare solet pietatis studium, voluptates scilicet corporis, quas Johannes dixit ἐπιθυμίαν σαρκὸς, Marcus hoc loco τὰς περὶ τὰ λοιπὰ ἐπιθυμίας, Lucas ἡδονὰς τᾶ βίυ, Matthæus omiserit, causam hanc fuisse suspi- cor, quod divitiis nominatis eas satis putaret intelligi, quia ferme propter voluptates corporis divitiæ expetuntur.

De Solicitudine vitæ Augustinus serm. XLII. de Sanctis. Quid pejus solicitudine vitæ, quæ per- venire non permittit ad vitam, quid miserius, quam curando vitam amittere vitam? quid infeli- cius, quam timendo mortem cadere in mortem? Exstirpentur spinæ, paretur ager, suscipiantur se- mina, perveniatur ad messem, horreum desidere- tur, non timeatur ignis. De divitiarum spinis Chrysost. homil. XIII. in Johan. Quemadmodum spinæ steriles sunt, ita & divitiæ, quemadmodum illæ eos, qui tangunt, lacerant, ita harum cupidi- tas: quemadmodum facile igni comprehenduntur, & odio habentur agricolis, ita hujus seculi negotia. Postremo ut inter spinas, feræ, viperæ, scorpii de- litescunt, ita in fraudibus divitiarum. Theophyl. in hoc loco Sicut spina acuta in corpus penetrat & vix eradicatur: Sic & delitiæ invalescentes in animam ingrediuntur & vix eradicantur. Conf. Matth. XIX. 23. Luc. XVI. 9. 1. Tim. VI. 9. 10. Voluptatem carnis etsi his non addiderit Spiritus Sanctus, autor scripturæ, non tamen eam præter- misit in Marco, & Lucæ Evangeliis, quin suis eandem suggereret amanuensibus.

συμπνίγει τὸν λόγον καὶ ἄκαρπον γίνεται] Cum per gradus procedat comparatio, videtur hic de iis agi, qui majores quam secundi illi profectus in pietate fecerant, atque ad- eo actis radicibus cœperant fructum non illaudabilem pro- ferre, sed variis cupiditatibus, quas purgare neglexerant, obruti vim illam frugiferam perdunt, hoc enim est ἄκαρπον γίνεται: pro quo Lucas dixit & τελεσφορῦσι, hoc est ad mes- sem usque frugem non perferunt: Hujus generis exem- plum habemus in Dema, de quo Paulus: δημᾶς με ἐγκατέ- λιπεν, ἀγαπήσας τὸν νῦν αἰῶνα, 2. Tim. IV. 10.

## 13:23
Verse 23. on the good ground] In a clearly similar way, Philo, in his book on rewards, calls the rational soul, which is planted by God, 'a land flourishing with virtue.' But also in his book on Allegories, he interprets the words of Jacob to Rachel mystically in this way: 'For I am in the place of God, who alone is able to open the wombs of souls (the edition incorrectly has 'the measures of souls') and to sow virtues in them and to make them pregnant and bringing forth good things.' Again, in his book on Cain: 'But it is not right for a mortal man to obtain a share in virtues that are many and perfect and bringing forth; but if they have not received offspring from some other, they will never conceive from themselves alone. Who then is the one sowing good things upon them, except the Father of all? The unbegotten God, who begets all things. He indeed sows, but the offspring which He sowed He grants as His own; for God begets, needing nothing for Himself, as He is the one who lacks nothing, but all things need Him to receive.'

which indeed brings forth fruit] That is, 'brings to maturity,' as the reason for the opposition shows. This is what Luke says here: 'they bring forth fruit with patience.' It is known that in the Apostolic writings the word 'patience' usually signifies perseverance, and not just any, but that which endures to the very end, according to that saying of Christ: 'He who endures to the end, this one shall be saved.' From the collation of which passages we learn that here, by the name of fruits, not the rewards of works, but the works themselves are designated.

some a hundred, some sixty, some thirty] It can be understood simply as the diversity of fruits signified according to the varied nature of the soil and the industry of cultivation. Nor, however, would you inappropriately refer the triple fruit to the triple Christians, as we have said elsewhere: children, young men, fathers. The hundredfold fruit, moreover, is set as the measure of the highest abundance, Gen. 26:12. But also among the poets. Pliny also mentions the hundredth yield.

Latin:

Vers. 23. ἐπὶ τὴν γῆν τὴν καλὴν] Plane simili modo Phi- lo libro de præmiis ἀρετώσαν χώραν vocat τὴν λογικὴν ψυ- χὴν, quæ a Deo sit consita. Sed & libro de Allegoriis ver- ba Jacobi ad Rachelem mystice ita interpretatur: ὗ γὰρ ἀντὶ Θεῦ ἐγώ εἰμι τῶ μόνυ δυναμένε τὰς ψυχῶν μήτρας (male edi- tus τὰ ψυχῶν μέτρα) ἀνοίγνυναι καὶ σπείρειν ἐν ἀυταῖς ἀρε- τὰς καὶ ποιεῖν ἐγκύμονας καὶ τικτούσας τὰ καλά. Rursus libro de Caino: ἀρεταῖς δὲ πολλα καὶ τέλειαι τικτούσαις θέμις ἐκ ἐσιν ἀνδρὸς ἐπιλαχεῖν θνητῦ. μὴ δεξαμέναις δὲ παρά τινΘ ἑτέρα ἐ- πιγονὴν ἐξ ἑαυτῶν μὲν μόνον ἐδέποτε κυήσυσι. τίς ὖν ὁ σπείρων ἐπ' ἀυταῖς τὰ καλά, πλὴν ὁ τῶν ὅλων πατήρ; ὁ ἀγέννητος Θεὸς κὶ τὰ σύμπαντα γεννῶν· σπείρει μὲν ἓν ὗτος τὸ δὲ γέννημα τὸ ἴδιον ὃ ἔσπειρε δωρεῖται, γεννᾷ γὰρ ὁ Θεὸς ἐδὲν ἀυτῷ χρειῶν ἅτε ὐδενὸς πάντα δὲ τῷ λαβεῖν δεομένῳ.

ὃς δὴ καρποφορεῖ] Id est τελεσφορεῖ ut oppositionis ra- tio monstrat. Hoc est quod Lucas hic dicit καρποφορῦσιν ἐν ὑπομονῇ. Notum est in Apostolicis scriptis ὑπομονῆς voce plerumque significari perseverantiam, nec quamlibet, sed eam quæ ad finem usque perdurat juxta illud Christi; ὁ ὑπομείνας εἰς τέλος ὗτος σωθήσεται. Ex quorum locorum collatione discimus hic fructuum nomine non præmia o- perum, sed opera designari.

ὃ μὲν ἑκατὸν, ὃ δὲ ἑξήκοντα, ὃ δὲ τριάκοντα] Potest simpli- citer intelligi significata fructuum diversitas pro vario so- li ingenio & culturæ industria. Neque tamen inepte fru- ctum triplicem referas ad triplices, ut alibi diximus, Chri- stianos, παῖδας, νέυς, πατέρας. Centuplus autem fructus pro summa ubertatis mensura ponitur Gen. XXVI. 12. Sed & apud Poëtas. Meminit & Plinius centesimæ frugis.

## 13:24
Verse 24. another parable he set before them] A parable of a parable, as Ezekiel 12:23 speaks.
