the kingdom of heaven is like a man sowing] The whole narrative is compared to the whole meaning. Both, however, as we have said, are indicated synecdochically by certain particles that often do not directly correspond: as if you were to say: 'The matter of the Gospel is thus, as if someone goes to sow, etc.,' which Mark expresses more clearly. For 'a man' here is 'someone,' in the Hebrew manner.

And yet we have observed in the Harmony that the parable described by Mark in chapter 4 was at another time, namely, before the calming of the sea storm and the liberation of the possessed men of Gadara.

Latin:

Vers. 24. ἄλλην παραβολὴν παρέθηκεν ἀυτοῖς] משל המשל ut loquitur Ezechiel XII. 23.

ἡ βασιλεία τῶν ἐρανῶν ἀνθρώπῳ σπείροντι] Tota narratio toti significato comparatur. Utrumque autem ut dixi- mus συνεκδοχικῶς indicatur particulis quibusdam sæpe non directe respondentibus: quasi dicas: Ita se habet res Evan- gelii ac si quis eat satum &c. quod clarius exprimit Marcus. ἀνθρώπῳ enim hic est alicui, more Hebræo.

Atqui parabolam à Marco c. IV. descriptam alio tempore nempe ante tempestatem maris se- datam, & liberatos obsessos Gadarenos in Har- monia observavimus.

## 13:25
Verse 25. but while men were sleeping] 'Men' here is indefinite, not universal: as if you were to say, 'while there was sleeping.' This, however, is nothing other than a description of opportunity.

Men snoring and sleeping in sins are being looked at. Jerome understands the ministers of the Church, through whose negligence the Devil oversows the tares, that is, the dogmas of heretics.

Latin:

Vers. 25. ἐν δὲ τῷ καθεύδειν τοὺς ἀνθρώπους] ἀνθρώπους hic indefinitum est, non universale: quasi dicas, cum dormi- retur. Hoc autem nihil est aliud quam descriptio oportu- nitatis.

Respiciuntur homines in peccatis stertentes & dormientes. Ministros Ecclesiæ intelligit Hie- ronymus, per quorum negligentiam Zizania, h. e. hæreticorum dogmata superseminat Diabolus.

## 13:26
Vers. 26. ὁ χόρτος] Regarding how widely this word extends among the Hellenists, see what has been said above at chapter VI.

καὶ καρπὸν ἐποίησεν] A description not of the harvest, but of that time when the crops begin to appear. Mark: ὅταν δὲ παραδῷ ὁ χόρτος, that is, חנט, Cant. II. 13.

Latin:

Vers. 26. ὁ χόρτος] Quam late hæc vox apud Helle- nistas pateat, vide quæ supra dicta sunt ad cap. VI.

καὶ καρπὸν ἐποίησεν] Descriptio non messis, sed ejus tem- poris, quo apparere sata incipiunt. Marcus ὅταν δὲ παραδῷ ὁ χόρτος, id est חנט Cant. II. 13.

## 13:27
Vers. 27. προσελθόντες δὲ οἱ δοῦλοι] This address does not have any special ἀνταπόδοσιν (correspondence) in Christ's explanation. And there are many such things in these and other parables which are not to be cut to the quick. For they are employed for the context of the narrative.

οὐχὶ καλὸν σπέρμα ἔσπειρας ἐν τῷ ἀγρῷ] A Hebraism for which the Latins would say: Surely you had sown good seed in the field.

Latin:

Vers. 27. προσελθόντες δὲ οἱ δοῦλοι] Hæc allocutio non habet in Christi explicatione ullam specialem ἀνταπόδοσιν. Et multa sunt talia in istis aliisque apologis, quæ non sunt ad vivum resecanda. Adhibentur enim ad contextum narrationis.

οὐχὶ καλὸν σπέρμα ἔσπειρας ἐν τῷ ἀγρῷ] Hebraismus pro quo Latini dicerent: Certe tu probum semen in agro severas.

## 13:28
Vers. 28. ἀπελθόντες] It is redundant: like πορευόμενοι in Luke VIII. 14. And because it preceded here just now: καὶ ἀπῆλθεν, there is no reason why what has been said once should be repeated often.

Latin:

Vers. 28. ἀπελθόντες] παρέλκει: ut πορευόμενοι apud Lu- cam VIII. 14. Et quod hic modo præcessit: καὶ ἀπῆλθεν quod semel dictum non est cur sæpe repetatur.

## 13:29
Vers. 29. ἐκριζώσητε ἅμα αὐτοῖς τὸν σῖτον] For there is a kind of darnel which can hardly be distinguished from wheat by sight.

Latin:

Vers. 29. ἐκριζώσητε ἅμα αὐτοῖς τὸν σῖτον] Est enim lolii genus quod à tritico visu discerni vix potest.

## 13:30
Vers. 30. ἄφετε συναυξάνεσθαι] A similar passage in Bereshit Rabba.

If it can even be distinguished, the servants are nevertheless commanded to let the tares grow together, either because it is noted only that GOD will permit them, but not remove them, except at the time of the harvest or the end of the age, so that Divine permission is properly designated, and not the duty of the servants, and thus the power of excommunicating or punishing heretics and evildoers is not taken away, but it is hinted that, just as tares grow among the seeds until the harvest, so also vices and heresies are to remain until the end of the world: Or because if the tares were eradicated there would be no Church left, or because the Church (by the hypothesis of the necessity of scandals) would have to be removed if scandals were removed, as Blessed Luther explains: If we were unwilling to suffer any scandals, there would also be no Church: Because since the Church cannot exist without tares, then to eradicate the tares would be the same as to eradicate the Church: Or because that which is now a tare can become wheat by divine grace, as Augustine says in this place: In the field there are tares, and it is possible that those who are tares today may be wheat tomorrow. Therefore Theophylact: If Matthew, Paul, the thief, each of whom was a tare, had perished in that way, the wheat that sprouted later would have been cut down at the same time: Which sense Blessed Luther also praises, that some good people, who are among them and are yet to be converted, would be damned and lost at the same time if the Church and the fellowship of the wheat were denied to them; which must by no means be done because the throne of grace must be open to the penitent. For to be eradicated is to be simply repelled from the Church and society: Which reasoning Isidore of Pelusium extends further in Book I, Epistle 195: lest the wheat also be uprooted, that is, lest one be snatched away who is looking toward the amendment of life, lest innocent children be cut down together with their wicked parents, who are indeed often still in their fathers' loins, but already exist before God, as He who sees hidden things. For He did not harvest Esau while he was sinning, before his offspring were born, lest He also uproot Job, who traced his lineage from him: nor did He likewise inflict death upon Matthew while he was devoting effort to collecting taxes, lest He hinder the preaching of the Gospel; nor did he oppress harlots who were devoted to lust and unchastity, so that examples of repentance might not be lacking, nor is there any [example] of Peter's abjuration, since he was looking upon his own hot tears. Add from B. Luther, what he has in Tom. IV. Jen. Germ. fol. 252. Christ has no friends, for those whom He makes from His enemies, and where He should kill His enemies, He would also have to make no more Christians, and would thus pull up the wheat with the weeds. Where would St. Paul be, if he were to have been strangled when he was an enemy? Moreover, we judge that all these things can be comprehended here at the same time, as being subordinate: that servants indeed ought not to eradicate the weeds: both because they cannot be sufficiently distinguished from the wheat, and because GOD gathers the Church among the weeds, and permits the weeds in the Church, so that the good may be exercised and proved by the bad, and the bad may be edified by the good: nor does He want the weeds to be removed, because either the bad themselves can be converted and changed into wheat, or good can arise from them; and whatever other causes of the Divine economy there are: yet the proper and literal sense is, suffer the weeds to grow, that is, the sons of the evil one, lest you eradicate the wheat together with them, that is, not those who can be made wheat from the darnel, but, as Christ interprets in v. 38, the sons of the kingdom, who are already such. Which expression is not one of approval of the malice of the weeds, but of exhortation to patience, i.e., because you are compelled to bear the bad, and you do not have a Church without the bad, therefore be patient. B. Luther acknowledges this as the simplest sense. Compare B. Lyserus in this place.

Latin:

Vers. 30. ἄφετε συναυξάνεσθαι] Similis locus in Bere- schit Rabba.

Si etiam discerni possit, jubentur tamen servi sinere simul crescere zizania, sive quod note- tur solum, ea DEUM permissurum, non vero sublaturum, nisi messis vel consummationis se- culi tempore, ut Divina permissio, non vero of- ficium servorum proprie designetur, adeoque non adimatur potestas excommunicandi vel pu- niendi hæreticos & facinorosos, sed innuatur, quod sicut zizania usque ad messem inter semina cre- scunt: ita & vitia atque hæreses usque ad finem mundi mansuræ sint: Sive quod zizaniis eradica- tis nulla amplius futura Ecclesia sit, vel quod Ecclesiam (ex hypothesi necessitatis scandalo- rum) tolli oporteat, si tollantur scandala, ut B. Lutherus explicat: Si nulla pati vellemus scandala, nullam etiam fore Ecclesiam: Quia cum Ecclesia sine zizaniis esse non possit, tunc eradicari zizania idem esset, ac Ecclesiam eradicari: Sive quod tri- ticum fieri possit divina gratia, quod jam est zi- zanium, ut Augustinus in h. l. In agro sunt ziza- nia, & fieri potest, ut qui hodie sunt zizania, cras sint frumentum. Ideo Theophylactus. Si Mat- thæus, Paulus, latro, quorum unusquisque erat zizanium, ita periissent, simul excisum fuisset triticum postea enatum: Quem sensum laudat e- tiam B. Lutherus, quod simul aliquot boni, qui sunt inter eos adhuc convertendi, damnarentur & perderentur, si negaretur eis Ecclesia, & tritici socie- tas; quod nullo modo sit faciendum quia pænitentibus debet patere thronus gratiæ. Eradicari enim est ab Ecclesia & societate simpliciter repelli: Quam ratio- nem amplius extendit Isidorus Pelusiota l. I. Epist. 195. ne evellatur & triticum, hoc est, ne rapiatur ad vitæ emendationem spectans, ne una cum improbis pa- rentibus infontes liberi simul exscindantur, qui ad- huc sæpe quidem in paternis lumbis sunt, verum apud Deum, utpote occulta cernentem jam existunt. Neq; enim Esau peccantem nondum edita prole demessuit, ne unaquoque Jobum evelleret, qui ex eo genus du- xit: nec item Matthæum portoriis exigendis operam dantem morte affecit, ne Evangelii prædicationem impediret; nec libidini atque impudicitiæ studen- tes meretrices oppressit, ne pœnitentiæ exempla de- essent, nec Petri abjurationem ullus est, quoni- am calentes ipsius lacrymas prospiciebat. Adde à B. Luthero, quæ habet Tom. IV. Jen. Germ. fol. 252. Christus hat keine Freunde / denn die Er aus seinen Feinden machet / und wo Er solte seine Feinde umbbringen / muste Er auch keine Christen mehr machen/und würde also den Weis zen mit dem Unkraut aufrauffen. Wo wäre S. Paulus/wann er solte erwürget seyn/da er Feind war? Cæterum hæc omnia hic simul comprehen- di posse, ceu subordinata, censemus: quod servi quidem non debeant eradicare zizania: tum quia illa à tritico non satis discerni possint, tum quia DEUS Ecclesiam inter zizania colligit, & zi- zania in Ecclesia permittit, ut boni per malos exerceantur & probentur, mali per bonos ædi- ficentur: nec tolli zizania vult, quod seu mali i- psi converti possint, & in triticum commutari, seu ex illis boni oriri queant; & quæ aliæ Divinæ οἰκονομίας sunt causæ: Sensus tamen proprius & literalis est, sinite crescere zizania, hoc est, fili- os τοῦ πονηροῦ, ne eradicetis simul cum illis & tri- ticum, hoc est, non qui ex lolio triticum fieri possunt, sed interprete Christo v. 38. filios re- gni, qui jam sunt tales. Quæ vox est non ap- probationis malitiæ zizaniorum, sed exhorta- tionis ad patientiam, q. d. quia ferre cogimini malos, & sine malis Ecclesiam non habetis, ideo estote patientes. Quem sensum simplicissi- mum agnoscit B. Lutherus. Conf. B. Lyserus in h. l.

## 13:31
Vers. 31. another parable] I think that by the two following comparisons is indicated the small number of Jews who were about to believe in Christ, and the incredible multitude which, through their work, was to be led from the Gentiles to the true religion. For how widely, and in how short a time, the word of salvation was spread, and what progress it made without any human supports, we learn from the Acts of the Apostles and the Epistles of Paul; to which can be added the illustrious passages of writers of the following age. Tertullian enumerates those nations whose names exist in the Apostolic writings, as already subject to Christ in his own age: the varieties of the Getuli, many borders of the Moors, all the ends of the Spains, the diverse nations of the Gauls, and the places of the Britons inaccessible to the Romans, and of the Sarmatians and Dacians and Germans and Scythians and many hidden nations and provinces and many islands unknown to the Romans. Now Tertullian was writing about the two-hundredth year from the Lord's birth. Even older than him is Irenæus, Lib. I. c. 3, who names the churches of the Germans, Gauls, Spains, the East, Egypt, Libya, and the South. Add Origen, Homily IV on Ezekiel, Arnobius in book II, Athanasius in his Synodical Epistle, which is in Theodoret's Ecclesiastical History IV. 3, Jerome in his Epistle to Evagrius, Chrysostom in his sermon on Pentecost, and Theodoret in his Therapeutic.

Latin:

Vers. 31. ἄλλην παραβολὴν] Duabus sequentibus compa- rationibus indicari puto exiguum numerum Judæorum qui in Christum erant credituri, & incredibilem multitudinem, quæ istorum opera ex gentibus ad veram religionem esset perducenda. Quam latè enim, quamq; brevi tempore spar- sum sit verbum salutare, quantosq; sine ullis humanis præ- sidiis profectus fecerit, discimus ex Actis Apostolicis & E- pistolis Pauli; quibus addi possunt illustria Scriptorum se- quentis ævi loca. Tertullianus iis nationibus quarum no- mina in Scriptis Apostolicis exstant annumerat, ut jam sua ætate Christo subditas, Getulorum varietates, Maurorum multos fines, Hispaniarum omnes terminos, Galliarum diversas nationes, & Britannorum inaccessa Romanis loca, & Sarmatarum & Dacorum & Germanorum & Scytharum & abditarum multarum gentium & provinciarum & insu- larum multarum Romanis ignotarum. Scribebat autem Tertullianus circa annum à Dominico natali ducentesi- mum. Eo etiam vetustior Irenæus Lib. I. c. 3. ecclesias no- mit at Germaniarum, Galliarum, Hispaniarum, Orientis, Æ- gypti, Lybiæ, Meridiei. Adde Originem Homilia IV. in E- zechielem, Arnobium libro II. Athanasium Epistola Syno- dica, quæ apud Theodoretum Historiarum IV. 3. Hiero- nymum Epistola ad Evagrium, Chrysostomum sermone de Pentecoste, Theodoretum Therapeutico.

## 13:32
V. 32. which is smaller than all] See what has been said on chapter XI, verse 11. Now the comparison is made to those herbs which were better known in Judea. Thus below XVII. 20, a grain of mustard seed is spoken of for the smallest thing. It becomes a tree] It grows up to the size of a tree. nesting] That is, so that they may as it were dwell in its branches. Ps. CIV. 12. For it is not only a matter of nests. These words look back to Nebuchadnezzar's dream in Daniel IV. 9, where there is [Hebrew word]. See also what was said above on chapter IIX. Tertullian also compares Christ's kingdom, among other things, to Nebuchadnezzar's kingdom in the aforementioned place.

Latin:

V. 32. ὃ μικρότερον μὲν ἐστι πάντων] Vide quæ ad capitis XI. com. 11. dicta sunt. Fit autem comparatio ad eas herbas quæ in Judæa erant notiores. Ita infra XVII. 20. κόκκος ζινάπεως pro re minima dicitur. Γίνεται δένδρον] In arboris magnitudinem excrescit. κατασκηνῶν] Id est ut quasi habitent in ramis ejus. Pf. CIV. 12. Neque enim de nidis tantum agitur. Respiciunt hæc ver- ba Nabuchodonosoris somnium apud Danielem IV. 9. ubi est ידרן. Vide & quod supra dictum est ad caput IIX. Christi regnum inter cætera Nabuchodonosoris regno comparat etiam Tertullianus dicto loco.

## 13:33
Vers. 33. three measures] For only so much was accustomed to be mixed at once: as appears in Gen. XVIII. 6, Jud. VI. 19, 1 Sam. I. 24.

Latin:

Vers. 33. ζάτα τρία] Tantum enim simul misceri sole- bat: ut apparet Gen. XIIX. 6. Jud. VI. 19. 1. Sam. I. 24.

## 13:34
Vers. 34. he spoke in parables] Greater than Solomon. Above XII. 42.

Latin:

Vers. 34. ἐλάλησεν ἐν παραβολαῖς] Major Salomone. Supra XII. 42.

## 13:35
Vers. 35. that it might be fulfilled which was spoken by the prophet] 'that' does not signify the purpose of Asaph [who is called a prophet here in a more general sense], but such an event to which those words would more excellently, nay even more properly, correspond. For Asaph said [Hebrew words] for a sententious narrative figuratively, which narrative itself nevertheless contained hidden figures of the things of the Messiah. But here by that name are indicated the riddles which are properly [Hebrew word], and if an interpretation is added, [Hebrew word]. Tom. I.

Asaph's [Hebrew word] is from ancient time, when it properly signifies, as the LXX also translated, from the beginning, which is said here not so much by explaining as by applying from the foundation of the world. Thus Paul calls this very thing, which Christ is dealing with here, a mystery kept secret for eternal times, Rom. XVI. 25, and elsewhere a mystery hidden from the ages, Col. I. 26, elsewhere wisdom in a mystery hidden, 1 Cor. II. 7. Now the participle 'hidden' is placed here in place of the noun 'riddles', or as the LXX have 'problems', because what follows 'from the foundation of the world' coheres more correctly with the participle. Often, however, when it is a matter of the doctrine of the Gospel and God's dispensation concerning it, mention is made of the creation of the world, so that it may be shown that this had already been agitated in God's counsel at that time, and all things directed toward it. See the aforementioned passage 1 Cor. II. 7. Now the writers of the Gospels, but also Paul to the Ephesians, Peter also, and the writer to the Hebrews, and John in the Apocalypse, use 'foundation of the world' for the creation of the world, a manner of speaking transferred from buildings, so that it may appear that it was a most accepted phrase of those times.

Grotius supposes that in Ps. LXXVIII. 1, 2, Asaph is speaking in his own person and intimating his own purpose. Yet he acknowledges that those words correspond more excellently, nay even more properly, to Christ. Why then does he not leave the same to Christ? For the words of Scripture should be understood rather of him to whom they correspond MORE PROPERLY. Why should we descend to a figurative sense, when a proper sense can have a place? Why should we not understand [Hebrew words] properly? And since [Hebrew word] properly signifies, as the LXX translated, from the beginning, and as the Evangelist rendered, from the foundation of the world, which Grotius admits, why should we interpret it otherwise than its proper signification bears, and understand it only of ancient time? Since here riddles are explained through the hidden things, and the things hidden from the foundation of the world are taught, which are secret from the origin of the world, to be designated in the Psalm: why should we explain them otherwise, having abandoned the infallible interpretation of Holy Scripture? For this is not a bare application here, as Grotius wishes, but an explanation, since that same thing is said to be fulfilled, with JESUS speaking in parables. Grotius understands the completion of the doctrine of the Gospel delivered by Christ to be designated by the Evangelist: who therefore denies that the prediction is to be understood in like manner? For predictions are not understood more correctly than from their fulfillment. Furthermore, it appears from the Psalm itself that those things were not said in the person of Asaph. For Asaph was neither King, nor did he have a people. But he who speaks there addresses the Israelites, as a King his people, Attend, O my people. Which fits Christ, whose peculiar possession the Israelite people was. Nor was the law Asaph's, but the Lord's, which the people ought to observe: Attend to my law. And therefore these things are more correctly accepted concerning Christ, who is the Lord of the law, if the law is to be understood in the common sense; and no less so, if by the law the evangelical doctrine of Christ is understood, which he deservedly calls his law, or rather his doctrine, as the Hebrew word is accustomed to be understood. This word, as Coccejus rightly observes, from its etymology signifies doctrine, which shows the end, or goal and way: whether it be speech indicating to man his duty, by doing which they may attain life; or whether it be speech showing the sinner the way and method of also receiving the granted righteousness, which is the righteousness of God, and with righteousness, life. And just as תורה is said of both kinds of speech, so also is νόμος, law. For the Apostle does not fear to say the law of works and the law of faith, Rom. III. 27. To him we are particularly commanded to incline the ear to the words of his mouth, as Ps. LXXVIII. 1 warns, speaking, Him you shall hear Deut. XVIII. 16. Hear him, Matth. XVII. 5. Wherefore it has always seemed to me that Asaph introduced the Son of God speaking, especially because the interpretation of the Holy Spirit delivered through Matthew is clear, and it is certain that not only the Spirit of Christ spoke in the Prophets 1 Pet. II, but also that the Son of God is often introduced by the Prophets as speaking. Therefore, the Συμφωνία (harmony) which I discovered in the recent commentaries of Cocceius occurred more gratefully: who interprets verses 1 and 2 of this Psalm likewise concerning Christ: the things which he has concerning Him are worthy to be brought forward here: It easily appears, he says, that he who is introduced speaking in the Psalm is not David. Wherefore it is worthy of consideration who may seem suitable, so that Asaph the Prophet in the Holy Spirit may represent his discourse to the people of God before that time in which it was to be heard, and commend it to the Church, and insinuate that it should be repeated for all time. I certainly find no one else except Christ the Son of David, that great Prophet whom GOD once foretold at Mount Sinai that He would speak His words. Deut. XVIII, 15. And the words are as of a King to the people: and as of a Prophet professing to explain the enigmas of preceding times, although not without a parable. When the Lord JESUS did this, the Apostle Matthew, chapter XIII. 35, rightly affirms that what is written here in the second verse was predicted concerning Christ. For he says that when Christ spoke in parables, that which is read here was fulfilled. I was once so foolishly credulous that I would say with others that it seemed that what was said to have been fulfilled in Christ could be said of Christ just as it is written. I repent of this credulity. I have learned that one must think far otherwise. The words of the Holy Spirit are not to be taken in a common way, but as the analogy of the promise in the Old Testament and of the Gospel in the New persuades. It does not happen outside the intention of the Holy Spirit that that which fulfills the measure of what He Himself dictated to the Prophets is preached and done. Finally, this discourse under the Old Testament, as long as the Law and the Prophets were prophesying, could be said by no one as a proper and congruent discourse. Which will appear in the treatment itself. The doctrine of this Psalm is clearly explained in 1 Cor. X from v. 1 up to v. 12. For the Israelites are warned to obey their king, whom GOD had granted them out of grace, speaking the words of God, and copiously explaining all the enigmas, mysteries, and shadows of the former time, and, so as not to offend the ears of the people, addressing him in parables, lest they provoke Him with incredulity, diffidence, petulance, concupiscence, and other sins of theirs, just as the Fathers had done, and be rejected by God, just as the tribe of Ephraim had been rejected. These are the words of Cocceius, who learnedly observes that this Psalm is διαλογισικὸν (dialogical) after the manner of Psalm LXXV, and that the King speaks to the people, v. 1, 2, and the people concerning their duty and concerning the King. And further: the King, he says, calls his people. These are correlates. It is not fitting that someone from the people should say, My people. Just as no one would say of the Church, My Church. The members of the people call each other brothers: he who is the Lord of the people rightly and aptly says my people. Whom, namely, I bought and enslaved to myself, whom I separated for myself from all nations, when I left the rest of men as not-peoples without God in the world. He came to i- δίυς (his own) John I. 2, who speaks thus. And to verse 2, in the explanation of the reason for the precept concerning attending to the manner and certainty of the doctrine. In the reason, he says, is the manner of teaching 1. ἐν ἀνοίξῃ στόματος (in the opening of the mouth), with the opening of the mouth. 2. ἐν παραβολαῖς (in parables). Christ spoke freely indeed and fully concerning our salvation and the will of the Father; but yet not without parables, and that on account of σκληροκαρδίαν (hardness of heart), the hardness of the heart, partly that He might allure them to Himself; Mark IV. 33, partly that He might punish. Matt. XIII. 11. 3. And therefore there is need of obedience, attention, and faith. John VII. 17, as also Mark IV. 23, 24. If anyone has ears to hear, let him hear. See what you hear. 3. In clarity and richness worthy of the Gospel, such as has not existed before this. I will utter, I will gush forth enigmas. Rom. XVI. 25, with certainty: that it is nothing new but he utters ancient enigmas. The Apostle says (σεσιγημένον μυστήριον (a mystery kept silent), which has never been narrated, as it has been done, so that it could be recited as it is seen and heard; of which indeed certain parts have not been spoken, and the whole order and καιροὶ (times) remained stored in the power of God. Rom. XVI. 25, Ephes. III. 5, 1 Pet. I. 10, 11, 12. It is added that God willed most parts to be proposed and inculcated to the people through the catechesis of the fathers and elders according to the institution of Moses, with the demonstration of the scriptures. When they neglected to do this, God repeatedly sent Prophets who would bring them to the knowledge of the truth. Who had few disciples, with more people, as happens even now, opposing the truth. With the Babylonian captivity impending and in it itself, these Prophets were more frequent. After that, the school of the Pharisees prevailed, which devoted effort more to tradition than to demonstration. Whence it happened that many things were kept silent, and not a few were distorted into false senses. Therefore, this mystery escaped the common knowledge of men for most times, and, even things clearly said were to them obscure αἰνίγματα (enigmas). Besides all these things there was a veil, etc., where he further learnedly declares that there were enigmas even in the letter of the law, adding what we have judged should also be added here: There were therefore in the discourse, which the Fathers heard from all time, enigmas. But they were awaiting the solution of the enigmas and the illustration of the shadows through the very image of things. Which Christ, exhibiting and proposing in few words, became a fountain gushing forth living water and bringing enigmas into the open. Some understand enigmas concerning the things narrated in this Psalm thereafter: but it is fitting to take it more generally concerning everything that received light through Christ and the Gospel. The doctrine concerning Christ was in the O.T. חִידָה (chidah) αἴνιγμα (enigma), a more obscure discourse, not only not known to carnal men, but also not sufficiently perceived by the wise; but in the New it is מְלִיצָה (melitsah) ἑρμηνεία (interpretation), explanation, ἐξήγησις (exegesis). John I. 18. Even children in Christ know toward what all things tend, which in the O.T. were said and instituted and done with such effort, such apparatus, in so many ways, and in so many parts. For they do not have need to seek the key of knowledge from some corner or from a Prophet, or from a college of elders or Doctors. Meanwhile Christ, the ἐξηγητὴς and יָפֵחַ, the interpreter of Hab. II. 3, did not speak only plainly and simply (for he did speak thus, and yet he was seen to speak ἐν παροιμίαις), but he also for the most part taught the people through various parables. Which, as I have said, pertained both to his clemency and to the richness of his teaching. Ezech. XXI. 5. מַשִׁיל מְשָׁלִים Joh. XVI. 25. ἐν παροιμίαις λαλεῖν and ἐν παῤῥησίᾳ ἀναγγέλλειν are contrasted. These things I have spoken to you in parables, but the hour comes when I will no longer speak to you in parables, but I will announce to you plainly about my Father, i.e., Now indeed I seem to have been speaking to you figuratively and obscurely; but then it will appear that I have announced all things clearly and openly. In which sense this verse also can be conveniently understood, in this way: I open indeed my mouth in parables; but I belch forth or, like a bubbling fountain, I pour out riddles from of old. All these things Coccejus, who also deserves to be consulted in his ἐξηγήσει of v. 3, 4, 5, 6, and 7. Which are much more correct than those which Spanheim has in his Dubia Evangelica, dub. LXXII, rashly asserting that Asaph says the former things about himself, from an inspection of Psalm II, IT BEING CLEAR, meanwhile, that they are also APPLIED to himself by Christ; and he says ignorantly that little depends on it, whether this be said to be fulfilled (perhaps he meant to say signified) in Asaph only, or in Christ (fulfilled) mystically, or whether they are posited by Christ as applied to himself only by accommodation, or transference, not noting that a third option is given, since the Evangelist explains these things about him neither merely mystically, nor by this fictitious transference, but in the literal sense. Wherefore also the opinion of Heinsius falls, who says that τὸ ἵνα πληρωθῇ is an elegant formula of applying from time to time, when it is sometimes a matter of words which are only applied and not explained, but he does not prove it: the opinion of Franciscus v. Junius, parall. l. 1. n. 26., who posits the figure not in the word πληρωθῇ, but in the other τὸ ῥηθὲν, i.e., that it might be fulfilled by Christ, which the Prophet had once fulfilled by a similar example, is more subtle than solid, nor does it remove the doubt, or satisfy the words of the Evangelist. Nor is there need for it; since the Prophet is not speaking of himself, but introduces Christ speaking.

Latin:

Vers. 35. ὅπως πληρωθῇ τὸ ῥηθὲν διὰ τοῦ προφήτου] ὅπως non significat propositum Asaphi [qui hic προφήτης generalio- ri notione dicitur] Sed eventum talem cui verba illa excel- lentius, imo etiam magis proprie, congruerent. Nam Asa- phus משל & חידות dixit pro narratione sententiosa κα- ταχρηστικῶς quæ tamen ipsa narratio latentes rerum Messiæ figuras continebat. Hic vero eo nomine indicantur aἶνοι qui proprie sunt חידות & si addatur ἀπόδοσις, משלים. Tom. I.

Asaphi מני קדם est ab antiquo tempore, cum proprie si- gnificet, ut & LXX. transtulerunt ἀπ' ἀρχῆς, quod hic non tam explicando quam applicando dicitur ἀπὸ καταβολῆς κό- σμου. Ita Paulus hoc ipsum de quo hic agit Christus, vocat μυστήριον χρόνοις αἰωνίοις σεσιγημένον, Rom. XVI. 25. & a- libi μυστήριον ἀποκεκρυμμένον ἀπὸ τῶν αἰώνων. Col. I. 26. a- libi σοφίαν ἐν μυστηρίῳ ἀποκεκρυμμένην 1. Cor. II, 7. Parti- cipium autem κεχρυμμένα positum hic est vice nominis αἰ- νίγματα, aut ut LXX. habent προβλήματα, quia quod se- quitur ἀπὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου cum participio rectius cohæ- ret. Sæpe autem, ubi de Evangelii doctrina, Deique cir- catam di pensatione agitur, mentio fit creationis mundi, ut ostendatur jam tum hoc in Dei consilio fuisse agitatum, atque eo directa omnia. Vide dictum locum 1. Cor. II. 7. καταβολὴν autem κόσμου pro mundi creatione, translatum ab ædificiis loquendi genus passim Evangeliorum scripto- res, sed & Paulus ad Ephesios, Petrus quoque, & scriptor ad Hebræos usurpant, & in Apocalypsi Johannes, ut ap- pareat receptissimam eorum temporum φράσιν fuisse.

Supponit Grotius Ps. LXXIIX. 1. 2. Asaphum ex persona propria loqui, suumque propositum in- timare. Agnoscit tamen verba illa excellentius, imo etiam magis proprie congruere Christo. Cur ergo non Christo eadem relinquit? De eo enim intelli- genda potius scripturæ verba, cui MAGIS PRO- PRIE ea congruunt. Cur ad κατά χρησιν descen- damus, cum proprius sensus locum habere potest? Cur non proprie משלים & חידות intelligamus? Et quum מני קדם proprie significet, ut LXX. tran- stulerunt ἀπ' ἀρχῆς, & uti Evangelista reddidit ἀπὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου, quod fatetur Grotius, cur id aliter interpretemur, quam fert propria signi- ficatio, & intelligamus solum de antiquo tempore? Quum hic αἰνίγματα explicentur per τὰ κε- κρυμμένα, ac doceantur τὰ κεκρυμμένα ἀπὸ κα- ταβολῆς κόσμου, quæ occulta sunt ab origine mundi, designari in Psalmo: cur secus illa explicemus, re- licta infallibili Scripturæ sacræ interpretatione? Non enim nuda hic est applicatio, ut Grotius vult, sed explicatio, quum idem illud impletum dicatur, JESU ἐν παραβολαῖς loquente. De Doctrina Ev- angelii a Christo tradita complementum ab Evan- gelista designatum intelligit Grotius: Qui ergo negat prædictionem pariter intelligendam? Non enim rectius prædictionis intelliguntur, quam e complemento. Porro e Psalmo ipso apparet, ea non ex Asaphi persona dicta esse. Nam As- saph nec Rex fuit, nec populum habuit. Is autem qui ibi loquitur compellat Israëlitas, ceu Rex po- pulum suum, Attendite populus meus. Quod Chri- sto congruit, cujus peculium erat populus Israëli- ticus. Neq; Assaphi erat lex, sed Domini, quam observare populus debeat: Attendite legem meam. Ideoq; de Christo, qui Dominus legis, hæc rectius accipiuntur, si lex intelligenda communi sensu; nec minus, si per legem doctrina Christi Evangeli- ca, quam merito vocat legem suam, vel potius do- ctrinam suam, uti Ebræa vox accipi consuevit, in- telligatur. Hæc vox, ut recte observat Coccejus, ex Etymo significat doctrinam, quæ monstrat finem, sive metam & viam: sive sit sermo indicans homini debitum suum quid faciens vitam consequantur? sive sit sermo monstrans peccatori viam & rationem ac accipiendi justitiam donatam, quæ est justitia Dei, & cum justitia vitam. Et quemadmodum תורה de utroque sermone dicitur, ita etiam νόμος lex. Nam Apostolus non veretur νόμον ἔργων legem operum & νόμον πίστεως legem fidei dicere, Rom. III. 27. Huic peculiariter jussi sumus inclinare aurem in verba oris ipsius, uti monet Ps. LXXIIX. 1. loquens, Ipsum audies Deut. XIIX. 16. Ipsum audite, Matth. XVII. 5. Quapropter semper visus mihi est Assaph introduxisse loquentem Filium Dei, imprimis quia luculenta est interpretatio Spiritus Sancti per Matthæum tradita, & constat non modo Spiritum Christi loquutum esse in Prophetis 1. Petr. II. sed etiam Filius Dei saepe loquens introducitur a Prophetis. Ideo gratior accidit Συμφωνία, quam in nuperis Cocceji com- mentariis deprehendi: qui pariter de Chri- sto vers. 1. & 2. Psalmi hujus interpretatur: digna sunt quae de eo habet; quae hic adducantur: Faci- le, inquit, apparet, eum, qui in Psalmo introdu- citur loquens, non esse Davidem. Quare dignum consideratione est, quis videatur idoneus, ut As- saph Propheta in Spiritu S. ejus sermonem ad popu- lum Dei ante id tempus, quo is audiendus erat, re- praesentet, & Ecclesiae commendet, & in omne ae- vum repetendum insinuet. Ego certe nullum alium reperio, nisi Christum Filium Davidis, magnum illam Prophetam, quem DEUS ad montem Si- nai verba sua olim locuturum esse prenunciavit. Deut. XVIII, 15. Et sunt verba tanquam Regis ad populum: & tanquam Prophetae enigmata prae- cedentium temporum se enarrare, quanquam non sine parabola, profitentis. Quod cum faceret D. JESUS, recte Apostolus Matthaeus cap. XIII. 35. id quod hic versu secundo scriptum est, de Christo praedictum esse, affirmat. Nam Christo lo- quente in parabolis, dicit, impletum esse, quod hic legitur. Fui aliquando tam stolide credulus, ut cum aliis dicerem, videri id dictum impletum fuisse in Christo, quod similiter atque scriptum est, de Christo dici potuit. Poenitet me hujus credulitatis. Longe aliter sentiendum esse didici. Non vulgariter sunt verba Spiritus S. accipienda, sed ut suadet in Vet. Test. analogia promissionis, in Novo Evangelii. Non fit praeter intentionem Spi- ritus S. ut id praedicetur & geratur, quod expleat mensuram ejus quod ipse dictavit Prophetis. De- nique sermo hic sub Veteri Testamento, quamdiu Lex & Prophetae prophetabant, a nemine, ut pro- prius & congruens sermo, dici potuit. Quod in ipsa tractatione apparebit. Doctrina hujus Psal- mi plane explicatur 1. Cor. X. a v. 1. usque ad v. 12. Monentur enim Israëlitae, ut obediant regi suo, quem DEUS ipsis ex gratia concesserat, verba Dei loquenti, & omnia enigmata, mysteria & um- bras anterioris temporis copiose exponenti, &, ad non offendendas aures populi, in parabolis eum al- loquenti ne incredulitate, diffidentia, petulantia, concupiscentia aliisque peccatis suis ipsum irrita- rent, quemadmodum Patres fecerant, & a Deo re- jicerentur, quemadmodum tribus Ephraim rejecta erat. Haec Coccejus, qui erudite observat, Psalmum hunc διαλογισικὸν esse ad instar Psalmi LXXV. & loqui I. Regem ad populum, vers. 1. 2. II. Populum de officio suo & de Rege. Et porro: populum suum, inquit, Rex compellat. Sunt ea correlata. Non convenit, ut aliquis de populo di- cat, Popule mi. Quemadmodum nemo de Ec- clesia dixerit, Ecclesia mea. Membra populi se invicem fratres compellant: is qui est populi Domi- nus, recte & apte dicit popule mi. Quem scil. ego emi, & mihi mancipavi, quem separavi mihi ab omnibus gentibus, quum reliquos homines pro non populis sine Deo in mundo omisi. Venit ad i- δίυς proprios suos Joh. I. 2. qui ita loquitur. Et ad versum 2. in explicatione rationis praecepti de at- tendendo a modo & certitudine doctrinae. In ra- tione, inquit, est modus docendi 1. ἐν ἀνοίξῃ στόμα- τος, cum apertione oris. 2. ἐν παραβολαῖς. Libere quidem & plene de salute nostra & voluntate Patris elocutus est Christus; sed tamen non sine parabolis, id- que propter σκληροκαρδίαν, cordis duritiem, partim ut alliceret ad se; Marci IV. 33. partim ut puniret. Matt. XIII. 11. 3. Ideoq; obedientia, attentione & fide opus est. Joh. VII. 17. ut & Marc. IV. 23. 24. Si quis habet aures ad audiendum, audiat. Videte, quid audiatis. 3. In claritate & ubertate Evangelio digna, quanta non extitit ante hac. Eructabo, scaturiam enigmata. Rom. XVI. 25. cum certitudine: quod nihil novum sed eructat antiqua enigmata. Apostolus dicit (σεσιγημέ- νον μυστήριον, quod nunquam narratum est, ut fa- ctum est, ut potuerit sic recitari, ut videtur & auditur; cujus adeo partes quædam non sunt dictæ, & totus or- do & καιροὶ tempora in Dei potestate reposita manse- runt. Rom. XVI. 25. Ephes. III. 5. 1. Petr. I. 10. 11. 12. Accedit, quod Deus plerasq́; partes per catechesin pa- trum & seniorum juxta institutionem Mosis voluit populo proponi atq́; inculcari, cum demonstratione scripturarum. Quod cum ii negligerent facere, Deus identidem misit Prophetas, qui eas adducerent ad co- gnitionem veritatis. Qui paucos habuerunt discipu- los, pluribus, ut nunc etiam fit veritatem oppugnanti- bus. Captivitate Babylonica imminente & in ea ipsa hi Prophetæ fuerunt crebriores. Post illam obtinuit Pharisæorum schola, quæ magis traditioni quam de- monstrationi operam dedit. Quo factum, ut multa si- lerentur, non pauca in falsos sensus detorquerentur. Ergo mysterium hoc plerisq́; temporibus fugit vulga- rem hominum notitiam, &, etiam clarè dicta, fue- runt ipsis αἰνίγματα obscura. Præter hæc omnia fuit velum, &c. ubi porro doctè declarat, quod in legis litera etiam fuerint ænigmata, addens, quæ hic etiam addenda censuimus: Erant igitur in sermo- ne, quem audiverunt Patres ab omni tempore, æni- gmata. Expectabant autem illi ænigmatum solutio- nem, umbrarumq́; illustrationem per ipsam imagi- nem rerum. Quam exhibens Christus & paucis ver- bis proponens factus est fons scaturiēns aqua viva & ænigmata in apertum producens. Quidam ænigmatæ intelligunt de rebus in hoc Psalmo deinceps enarratis: sed convenit generalius capere de omni eo, quod per Christum & Evangelium lucem accepit. Doctrina de Christo erat in V. Test. חִידָה αἴνιγμα sermo ob- scurior, non tantum carnalibus hominibq non cognitq, sed etiam sapientibus non satis perspectus; at in Novo est מְלִיצָה ἑρμηνεία explanatio, ἐξήγησις. Joh. I. 18. Etiam pueri in Christo sciunt, quo tendant omnia, quæ in V. T. tanto molimine, tanto apparatu, tot mo- dis, tot partibus dicta, & instituta & gesta sunt. Ne- que enim opus habent, ut clavem cognitionis ex an- gulo aliquo vel à Propheta, vel à collegio seniorum aut Doctorum petant. Interim Christus ἐξηγητὴς & יָפֵחַ index Hab. II. 3. non tantum planè & simpliciter locutus est (nam & sic locutus est, & tamen visus est ἐν παροιμίαις loqui) sed & populum plerumq; per varias parabolas docuit. Quod ut dixi, & ad cle- mentiam pertinuit, & ad ubertatem docendi. Ezech. XXI. 5. מַשִׁיל מְשָׁלִים Joh. XVI. 25. ἐν παροιμίαις λαλεῖν & ἐν παῤῥησίᾳ ἀναγγέλλειν opponuntur. Hæc in parabolis locutus sum vobis, sed venit hora, quum non amplius in parabolis loquar vobis, sed palam de Patre meo renuntiabo vobis, h. e. Nunc quidem videor fuisse locutq vobis figuratè & obscurè; sed tunc appa- rebit, me omnia clarè & apertè enuntiasse. In quam mentem hic etiam versus commodè accipi potest, hoc modo: Aperio quidem os meum in parabolis; sed eru- cto vel ut fons scaturiēns effundo ænigmata ab anti- quo. Hæc omnia Coccejus, qui etiam consuli mere- tur in ἐξηγήσει v. 3. 4. 5. & 6. & 7. Quæ multo rectio- ra sunt iis, quæ habet Spanhemius dub. Evangelic. dub. LXXII. temerè asserens, priora Assaphum de seipso dicere, ex inspectione Psalmi II. LIQUERE, interim à Christo sibi quoque APPLICARI; & parum in eo situm esse imperitè ait, sive hoc typicè in Assapho duntaxat adimpletum (significatum dicere fortassis voluit) dicatur in Christo (adim- pletum) mystice, sive statuantur à Christo sibi appli- catum tantum per accommodationem, vel trans- sumtionem, non attendens, quod detur tertium, quum neque mystice tantum, neque per ficti- tiam istam transsumtionem, sed sensu literali hæc Evangelista de illo explicet. Quare & Heinsii sententia cadit, qui τὸ ἵνα πληρωθῇ elegantem ap- plicandi subinde formulam esse, cum de verbis nonnunquam agitur, quæ solum applicantur & non explicantur, dicit, sed non probat: Francisci v. Junii parall. l. 1. n. 26. figuram statuentis non in voce πληρωθῇ, sed in altera τὸ ῥηθὲν q. d. ut im- pleretur à Christo, quod simili olim exemplo imple- verat Propheta, sententia subtilior, quam solidior est, nec dubium tollit, aut Evangelistæ verbis sa- tisfacit. Neque ea opus est; quum non de se lo- quatur Propheta, sed Christum loquentem intro- ducat.

## 13:38
Vers. 38. ὁ δὲ ἀγρός ἐστιν, ὁ κόσμος. ] Lest the disciples might think that this seed was to be scattered only in Judea, as hitherto. Τὸ δὲ καλὸν σπέρμα, ὗτοί εἰσιν οἱ υἱοὶ τῆς βασιλείας] What we observed above from Luke in the first parable comes into use here. For as he had said there τὸ εἰς τὰς ἀκάνθας πεσὸν ὗτοι εἰσιν οἱ ἀκούσαντες, for that which Matthew had more properly said, ὁ εἰς τὰς ἀκάνθας σπαρεὶς ὗτός ἐστιν ὁ τὸν λόγον ἀκούων, so here τὸ καλὸν σπέρμα is put for the whole complex, when otherwise it should have been said οἱ τῷ καλῷ σπέρματι σπαρέντες. The Manichaeans therefore crudely gathered from these and the following words that the very natures, good and evil, are sown by God and the devil. The seed is considered either as it is scattered, and it is the very word of God: or as it fructifies, and regenerates: in which way the children of the kingdom are the seed, by metonymy. Isidorus in the Catena of Viceta translated by Corderius on this passage notes that the word is both the seed, and he who received it, and because of the connection with it, and in a way the transformation. For Christ is formed in us through the word, but we are conformed to Christ. For this reason the seed is also cast, so that it may assimilate man to itself; those therefore who have received the heavenly seed, having been fattened by the virtue of the word, have themselves also become heavenly seed: And therefore it is said, but the good seed are these children of the kingdom: Similarly also the seed of the wicked, injected into the minds of men in atheistic dogmas, has made them wicked children, for the tares have also rendered them evil seed. οἱ υἱοὶ τῶ πονηρᾶ] Not just any evil men are denoted by the tares, but those who profess Christianity. This is what had been said, that the tares are sown among the wheat, and below ἐκ τῆς βασιλείας ἀυτῶ. And soon at the end, by a comparison of those senses, τὰ καλὰ καὶ τὰ σαπρὰ are in the same dragnet. But just as those are called children of God who imitate divine goodness, as above V. 9. & 45., so those are children of the Devil who imitate the malice of the devil, John VIII. 44. That heretics are specifically designated is gathered from the fact that the seed is the word of God, and as the tare is similar to the wheat, so heresies imitate the sincere doctrine in the sound of the words, even if they differ greatly in the tenor of their meanings, and indeed the magistrate is not ordered to permit the wicked, but is forbidden to kill heretics, according to B. Gerhard, L. de Magistr. §. 322. They explain it concerning heretics with Chrysostom: Lyranus, Stapleton, Becanus in his disputation on the faith of heretics to be kept, B. Balduinus, and B. Affelmannus on the toleration of heretics. nonetheless they are not excluded as criminals, but are included under the tares, as being also children τοῦ πονηροῦ, just as wickedness and the wicked, as well as heresies and heretics, are opposed to the seed of the Word of God and to the children of the kingdom who are born from it, and the Ministers of the Word, who come under the name of servants, are admonished concerning the toleration of both, but not their killing, and thus it is taught that it is not fitting to remove the disobedient in the Church by force and the sword, as far as pertains to Ecclesiastical power or jurisdiction, which only argues with men by the Word without the sword, which is proper to the civil power, as Selneccerus rightly says. Christ wishes to restrain, according to B. Lyserus, the untimely zeal which he perceived in the minds of the Apostles. They wished to exercise a very sharp reformation and excommunication in the Church, Luke IX. 54.

Latin:

Vers. 38. ὁ δὲ ἀγρός ἐστιν, ὁ κόσμος. ] Ne putarent discipu- li in sola Judæa, ut hactenus spargendum id semen. Τὸ δὲ καλὸν σπέρμα, ὗτοί εἰσιν οἱ υἱοὶ τῆς βασιλείας] Usu hic ve- nit quod supra ex Luca observavimus in prima parabola. Nam ut ibi ille dixerat τὸ εἰς τὰς ἀκάνθας πεσὸν ὗτοι εἰσιν οἱ ἀκού- σαντες, pro eo quod proprie magis Matthæus dixerat, ὁ εἰς τὰς ἀκάνθας σπαρεὶς ὗτός ἐστιν ὁ τὸν λόγον ἀκούων, ita hic τὸ κα- λὸν σπέρμα pro toto complexo ponitur, cum alioqui dicen- dum fuisset οἱ τῷ καλῷ σπέρματι σπαρέντες. Crasse igitur Manichæi ex his & sequentibus verbis colligebant naturas ipsas bonas malasque à Deo & diabolo seri. Semen consideratur vel ut spargitur, estque i- psum Dei verbum: vel prout fructificat, & regene- rat: quo pacto filii regni semen sunt, per metony- miam. Isidorus in Catena Vicetæ à Corderio transla- ta ad h. l. notat, & verbum semen esse, & eum, qui excepit, & ob connexionem cum eo, ac quodammodo transformationem. Per sermonem enim in nobis for- matus Christus, nos autem Christo conformamur. Ob hanc enim causam semen quoque jacitur, ut ho- minem sibi assimilet, pinguefacti igitur, qui semen cæleste susceperunt ex sermonis virtute, facti sunt etiam ipsi cæleste semen: Ideoque dictum est. bonum autem semen hi sunt filii regni: Similiter etiam ma- ligni semen in atheis dogmatibus hominum animis injectum filios nequam effecit, zizanium enim eos etiam semen malum reddidit. οἱ υἱοὶ τῶ πονηρᾶ] Non qualescunque mali homines per lo- lium denotantur, sed hi qui Christianismum profitentur. Hoc est quod dictum erat lolium seri inter triticum, & in- fra ἐκ τῆς βασιλείας ἀυτῶ. Et mox in fin. illis sensus compara- tione τὰ καλὰ καὶ τὰ σαπρὰ sunt in eodem everriculo. Sicut autem filii Dei dicuntur, qui divinam imitantur bonitatem, ut supra V. 9. & 45. ita filii Diaboli qui diaboli imitantur malitiam, Joh. IIX. 44. Hæreticos speciatim designari colligitur inde, quia semen est verbum Dei, & ut zizanium tritico simile est, sic hæreses sinceram imitantur doctri- nam verborum sono, etsi maxime distent senten- tiarum tenore, neque vero sceleratos permittere jubetur magistratus, sed prohibetur hæreticos in- terficere, juxta B. Gerhard. L. de Magistr. §. 322. De hæreticis explicant cum Chrysostomo Lyranus, Stapletonus, Becanus disp. de fide hær. serv. B. Bal- duinus, & B. Affelmannus de hæret. ferend. non ta- men facinoroso excluduntur, sed comprehendun- tur sub zizaniis, utpote etiam filii τοῦ πονηροῦ, quemadmodum Verbi Dei semini, &, qui inde nascuntur, filiis regni adversantur improbitas & improbi pariter atque hæreses & hæretici, & de utrisque tolerandis non vero interficiendis, Verbi Ministri, qui servorum nomine veniunt, com- monefiunt, adeoque docetur, non decere in Ec- clesia vi & gladio tollere inobedientes, quantum at- tinet ad potestatem sive jurisdictionem Ecclesiasti- cam, quæ tantum Verbo arguit homines sine gladio, qui est proprius civilis potestatis, ut recte Selnecce- rus. Christus frenare vult, juxta B. Lyserum, in- tempestivum zelum, quem deprehendebat in animis Apostolorum. Hi valde acrem volebant exercere re- formationem & excommunicationem in Ecclesia, Luc. IX.54.

## 13:39
Vers. 39. σπείρας αὐτὰ] A great crop of vices springs up from the sleepiness of men, the craftiness of the devil, and the wise and just permission of God.

συντέλεια τῦ αἰῶνῶ-] To the writer to the Hebrews συντέλεια τῶν αἰώνων is the time destined for the advent of the Messiah: to Matthew, the time of the universal judgment. Thus to the Hebrews the future age; sometimes it is the time of the Messiah, sometimes of the resurrection. And the kingdom of God or the heavenly kingdom signifies now this, now that.

Latin:

Vers. 39. σπείρας αὐτὰ] Magna vitiorum seges enascitur hominum somnolentia, diaboli astu, Dei sapiente ac justa permissioue.

συντέλεια τῦ αἰῶνῶ-] Sscriptori ad Hebræos συντέλεια τῶν αἰ- ώνων est tempus destinatum Messiæ adventui: Matthæo tempus judicii universalis. Ita Hebræis seculum futurum; modo est tempus Messiæ, modo resurrectionis. Et regnum Dei sive regnum cœleste, modo hoc, modo illud significat.

## 13:41
Vers. 41. πάντα τὰ σκάνδαλα κὶ τὲς ποιῦντας τὴν ἀνομίαν] In this is the whole force of the comparison. In the beginning the Christian Church was of admirable purity, consisting of men full of the Holy Spirit, or at least already expecting that Spirit. But when that first love had grown cold, already in the very times of the Apostles and much more afterwards, two kinds of vicious men began to mix themselves with Christians, some teaching perverse things, others disgracing their pure profession with a shameful life. Men of the former kind are called scandals here. For that word is not attributed only to deeds, but also to men, as below XVI. 23. But just as Paul elsewhere joined διχοστασίας κὶ τὰ σκάνδαλα παρὰ τὴν διδαχὴν Rom. XVI. 17., so here the scandals are οἱ διχοστατῶντες, those departing separately from the doctrine of true piety. For also what Christ had said ἀνάγκη ἐστιν ἐλθεῖν τὰ σκάνδαλα, Paul expressed thus δεῖ αἱρέσεις ἐν ὑμῖν εἶναι, 1. Cor. XI.19. And thus the ancient Christians were accustomed to use this term frequently. Origen, in the fifth book against Celsus: ἀληθῶς δὲ τὸ τῶν σκανδάλων ὄνομα πολὺ ἐν ταῖς γράμμασι ταύταις ἐστίν· ὅπερ εἰώθαμεν λέγειν περὶ τῶν διαστρεφόντων ἀπὸ τῆς ὑγιαινούσης διδασκαλίας τὰς ἁπλουστέρας καὶ ἐνεξαπατήτους. Such especially had been the Nicolaitans and Gnostics, specifically noted in the Epistles of Peter and Jude, who under the guise of Christian liberty taught that those things which are repugnant to natural decency are ἀδιάφορα. The other class of men are those who indeed teach nothing depraved, but do not order their lives according to the Christian rule, ἀδελφοὶ ἀτάκτως περιπατοῦντες, as Paul speaks in 2 Thessalonians III. With both of these classes of men the Apostles and their successors had much business; nor is there any doubt that if such men had remained as they were when Christ spoke these things, the Apostles would often have wished that fire from heaven might consume such men: which Luke teaches us in 9:54, that they judged to be most just in the case of the villagers of Samaria who did not receive Christ. Against this vehemence, not tempered by the lenity that is required, Christ fortifies them, showing this to be his counsel: to allow the good to live mixed with the wicked, and those who teach depraved things with those who teach right things, in Christianity until the time of the universal judgment had matured. Tertullian: He who has once destined an eternal judgment does not precipitate the separation, which is a condition of judgment, before the end. But why it seems so to him, Christ does not explain the causes here, except that he may seem to have obscurely hinted at them when he said that one must take care lest the wheat be pulled up together with the tares. But it is not altogether difficult to gather them from other places of the sacred scriptures. For first, as regards general punishments, such as floods, fires, and other plagues of that kind, since they cannot be inflicted in such a way that they touch only the wicked, for the sake of even a few good men God either abstains from them or at least tempers them. See Genesis 18:32 and that which is below in 24:22. Next, among those who teach depraved things or live outside the rule, some are more curable than others, whose repentance God patiently awaits. For this reason Peter says that the last day of judgment is deferred, because God deals patiently with men, not wishing anyone to perish, but rather wishing all to come to repentance, 2 Ep. chap. 3, verse 9. Furthermore, however, depraved teachers, and those who are of unamended life, provide material for the good and upright in which they may exercise their constancy and lenity; constancy, while they do not allow themselves to be carried away by evil examples; lenity, while they strive in any way to draw them back to a better life. This is what Paul says, ἵνα οἱ δόκιμοι φανεροὶ γίνωνται ἐν ὑμῖν, 1 Cor. 11:19, which the author of the Responses to the Orthodox explains not inappropriately in question 22. Although it is most certain that by this saying of Christ, neither are public judgments taken away from magistrates, which restrain the wicked by the fear of punishment, nor is the right of the Church to separate from its assemblies those who either adulterate doctrine or stain the Christian name with the baseness of their life, yet that lenity and divine patience are proposed to be imitated by all men, and among others also by magistrates and those set over the church, at least in some way, there is no room for doubt. For even in lenity towards the wicked, we are commanded to express the goodness of our Father above at V. 45. And indeed, concerning the clemency to be employed in public judgments, we have said something above: which certainly ought to have a place especially when either it appears that the character is curable, or because of the multitude of offenders punishment cannot be exercised otherwise than by involving the innocent with the guilty, which especially has a place as often as wars are undertaken for the sake of a crime. But we are also taught everywhere that the judgments of the Church must be exercised with great temperance and leniency. For there are also errors in dogmas of such a kind, in which there ought to be a place for τὸ ἀσθενοῦντα τῇ πίστει προσλαμβάνεσθαι, μὴ εἰς διακρίσεις διαλογισμῶν. And Paul indeed wishes that one abstain from too familiar association with τῶν ἀτάκτων, yet in such a way that they are not held as explored, but are admonished fraternally. Now indeed, as often as the number of offenders was great, and among them, as happens, many had fallen excusably, it can be proven by many examples that something was relaxed from the rigor of discipline. And Augustine's opinions on this matter are well known. The writer of the questions to the Orthodox, and likewise Chrysostom and Jerome, interpret this parable of Christ concerning heretics: not badly, since from the comparison of other passages, as we have already said, it appears that the word σκάνδαλον pertains especially to this. Augustine, having followed the same interpretation, was for a long time of the opinion that no punishments at all should be used against those who are called heretics. But after many struggles with the Donatists, men sufficiently stubborn, he changed his opinion to this extent, that he did not disapprove of those punishments which left time for repentance: but he very often interceded against capital punishments. If we seek the opinion of older Christianity, we shall certainly find arguments which they themselves twist as most valid against the pagans, that it includes what could be no less rightly used against the punishments of heretics. For they are not content to defend the truth of their faith, they prove that, even if they erred gravely, nevertheless for that reason punishments should not be exercised upon them. Emperor Constantine, when with his first edicts he had professed that the worship of God should be free for all according to the sentiment of their own mind, afterwards, whether because he thought it would be conducive to the empire, or because the Bishops avoided the labor of daily disputation, he established punishments against those who had separated themselves from the communion τῆς μεγάλης ἐκκλησίας, but especially pecuniary ones. Among those separated ones were also the Novatians, men as it appears by no means evil (I do not speak of the founders of the sect, but of their descendants) and in dogmas sufficiently in agreement with the others, only desirous of a certain more rigid discipline. The succeeding Emperors, as they judged it expedient for their affairs, so they coerced or ignored the separate assemblies, which grew up new and new every day, so that it is a very difficult thing to enter into the number of Christian sects.

Grotius rightly observes that τὰ σκάνδαλα are called men teaching perverse things, from the comparison of Matt. XVI. 23, Rom. XVI. 17, 1 Cor. XI. 19, and that the writer of the questions to the Orthodox, and likewise Chrysostom, Jerome, and Augustine interpret this parable concerning heretics: to whom must be added Cyprian, book III, Ep. 3. For as the word of God is designated by seed, so they judge that heresies are peculiarly noted by tares: which, as tares are twin to wheat before they reach maturity, they report are ὅμοια to the word of God, even if they think ἀνόμοια. Add that for some, tares do not denote darnel, but that species of wheat which they call scorched, which can be distinguished from wheat with difficulty, and is pulled up with difficulty without the wheat being pulled up at the same time. But the Anabaptists wrongly conclude from this parable that criminals are not to be subjected to capital punishment: which according to most refers not to criminals, but to heretics, and pertains not to Magistrates, but to ministers of the word, contra Rom. XIII. 3. That heretics are by no means to be punished with death, Grotius acknowledges with us, departing in that part from the truculence of the Papists, and tacitly criticizing it, which from

He teaches that it first had its origin with the Arians. Capital punishments, he says, were so hated by all, I believe because of the memory of pagan cruelty, that in Gaul the Bishops, who had been the authors to the authorities that the Priscillianists, authors of most perverse dogmas and men of iniquitous life, should be punished with the sword, were for that reason removed from the communion of the Churches: and in the East the Synod was condemned which had consented to the burning of the Bogomils. Certainly, for Arius, Macedonius, Nestorius, Eutyches, the leaders of new sects, nothing harsher than relegation happened. The Arian Emperors and the kings of the same sect in Africa seem to have been the first to institute more severe punishments, and then also to have stained their hands with the blood of those who disagreed. What times followed afterwards, there is no need to relate. No death seemed sufficient: but cruelty exercised its own genius in seeking out punishments. Anathemas were pronounced not against men, but against peoples, and lest these be brute thunderbolts, kings were incited to destroy provinces with iron and flame, with no discrimination of age or sex. Thus, where they had made a solitude, they called it peace. And to all these things, zeal for the divine name is usually pretended, but for the most part it is only pretended. For God disdains forced services, nor can that please Him which is extorted by human force. In reality, those who do this are accustomed to consult not the divine name, but their own honors, their own advantages and tranquility, which He knows, who looks into minds. And thus it happens that the tares are pulled up with the wheat, the innocent with the guilty: indeed, the wheat is often taken for the tares: for it does not go so well with human affairs that better things always please more people or stronger ones. But as the bull in the herd, so among men he who is stronger in force strikes the weaker: And the same people often dare to do to others what they complained was being done to them. But if it is right to act thus everywhere, I do not see why it is not permitted for us to say that the weapons of our warfare are carnal, which Paul denies: I do not see what the examination of Christian wisdom will be, or why what was said, ὁ κατὰ σάρκα γεννηθεὶς τὸν κατὰ πνεῦμα, Gal. IV. 29, cannot be inverted to the other side. There are those who defend the most savage things by the example of the Jewish law. To say nothing now of the different spirit of the old and new law, whom does that law finally strike? Doubtless those who were doing this with the most malicious intent, so that they might lead men away from the one true God, from that God, I say, whom both nature taught and so many miracles most openly testified. But most things of the Christian religion are not known to us by nature, but by heavenly revelation: and the miracles by which that religion was once sealed pertained to the sum of the doctrine, not to the individual points which come into controversy. Indeed, the ancients admit that even among those whom they called heretics or schismatics (the name being often too loosely applied, as is especially to be seen in Epiphanius) miracles occur, God of course seeing to it, not for the confirmation of error, but as a testimony to that doctrine which was common to the different assemblies. However, I do not say these things with the intention that I wish to exempt from judgment the Gaulonites and Theudas, who under a feigned name of religion stir up wars or shake the state of the empire, or the Circumcellions in Africa who go about in robbery, or if there is anything similar to these. For crimes remain crimes by whatever name they are commended; indeed, they are the more execrable the more specious a title they put on themselves: but I would wish deeds to be distinguished from opinions, as things which are not equally ἐφ' ἡμῖν. Moreover, by the scope of opinion I simultaneously include those things which follow almost necessarily from opinions. But also that a distinction of opinions be observed, both from their own nature according as they lead more or less away from true piety, and from the cause which lured men into error: in doubtful matters, however, that which is milder and more lenient should always be chosen, lest He whom we profess as our Lord have need to say to us, 'You know not what spirit you are of.'

These things [are from] Grotius, no common friend of the Jesuits, [and] otherwise a notable advocate of the Roman Pontiff.

Verse 41. Ἀποστελεῖ ὁ ὑἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου τοὺς Ἀγγέλους αὐτοῦ] Some understand this of good angels, because they are called the angels of Christ, and the gathering of the elect from the four winds is attributed to good angels, Matt. XXIV. 31, and because also the devils will be thrust into hell by good angels, Apoc. XX. 3. But the angels of Christ can also be called evil angels, as they are sent by Christ, who are also called angels absolutely, Rom. VIII. 38, 1 Cor. VI. 3, nor is the gathering of the elect from the four winds designated here, but the collection of the wicked and the segregation from the elect, and the casting into the furnace of fire: as therefore that is of good angels, so this seems to be of evil angels, who are the lictors to whom the wicked are handed over, so that they may be cast into prison, Matt. V. 25, where the name ὑπηρέτης is found, [and] Luke XII. 58, where the name πράκτωρ is found. Ὑπηρέτης for an apparitor, a lictor, Acts V. 22, 25, as Schmidius observes on Matt. V.: O' πράκτωρ, according to the same author, is an exactor, whether of debts or of punishments, who compels the condemned to obey the sentence of the judges. B. Luther rendered it Stockmeister. That the devil will be thrust into hell by good angels is nowhere taught in Scripture. Apoc. XX. 3. it should be understood not as a created Angel but as the Son of God, as we taught in Tom. IV. Syst. Theol. p. 269. However, it seems consistent that the name of Angels of Christ is used here in a general sense, so that both evil and good Angels are sent forth at the time of the harvest, or at the end of the world, signified by the name of reapers: so that the former may gather the scandals, that is, the workers of iniquity, and cast them into the furnace of fire, figured by the tares, the sons of the evil one, the sons of malice or of that evil Devil, who comes by this name κατ᾽ ἐξοχὴν: but the latter may gather the wheat, that is, the sons of the kingdom, into the barns of the Lord. But whether the reapers are said to be both good and evil Angels, because in death the former are ordinarily employed by God for reaping the good, and the latter for the evil, just as such things are read in 2 Sam. XXIV. 16, 2 Kings XIX. 35, I would not rashly say. Some things are accustomed to be used in a parable for the sake of ornament, which should not be cut to the quick in the application. Every simile is dissimilar.

ποιῦντες τὴν ἀνομίαν] It is to be understood as above XIII. 41. V. 42. ἐις τὴν κάμινον τῦ πυρὸς] לגוא־אתון נורא as it is in Daniel III. 6, which the Syriac followed here. That darnel and other things of that kind are accustomed to be cast into the fire is clear from those things which are above III. 2, VI. 30, and elsewhere. Plutarch says that a caution was interposed at certain buildings so that bath-house keepers would not use darnel for the fire. At the same time, there is an allusion to the punishment of burning alive, which was customary in the East. He does not say into the fire, but into the furnace of fire, so that he may express the inevitable and perpetual nature of that heat. For just as those who are thrown into a burning furnace cannot escape the punishment of the fire, but are enclosed on all sides by the fire as well as the furnace: so for the impious, there will never be an opening for exit or liberation from the torments of that eternal fire. B. Gerhard in h. l. ἐκεῖ ἔσαι ὁ κλαυθμὸς] See above IIX. 12. Vers. 43. τότε οι δίκαιοι ἐκλάμψυσιν.] Christ interprets Daniel very well. For the Hebrews call those משכילים who order their lives wisely. But true piety is true wisdom. Again, Christ said well τότε, as if he were saying, then when the Church shall have been purged from all contagion of evil men. The writer of Wisdom, speaking of the just: ὡς χρυσὸν ἐν χωνευτηρίῳ ἐδοκίμασεν αὐτὸς: and then κὴ ἐν καιρῷ ἐπισκοπῆς αὐτῶν, ἐκλάμψυσι. He refers to the passage in Dan. XII. 1, which he admits treats of the splendor of the just in the other life. Ad most basely corrupted in Annot. ad Dan. XII. 1, having followed the impious scoffer Porphyry, as we said there in our Anti-Grotiana. Since he acknowledges that Christ here interpreted Daniel very well, who explained it concerning the glory of the other age, Grotius's interpretation in his annotations on Daniel is undoubtedly the worst, when he interpreted Daniel concerning the fame of a name in this age. Nor does Grotius agree with himself regarding the word משכילים; for here he wishes it to denote those who order their lives wisely. But there, those who instructed others in dangers, when Lysias, bearing the person of Antiochus, exercised all the most cruel things against the Jews, etc. Ὡς ὁ ἥλιος] Hence we see that the brightness of the heaven in Daniel is a periphrasis for the sun: as the radiance is often used among the Latins. But Paul also seems to compare the glory of those who excel most among the just to the sun, 1 Cor. XV. 24 and following. Grotius wrongly confuses the brightness of the heaven in Daniel with the splendor of the sun, or the sun itself. For the Prophet distinguishes between the splendor of the stars, to which the sun belongs, and the brightness of the firmament. And he designates a gradual difference of glory for those who are learned in righteousness, and who have instructed others in it. But here it is not a question of different degrees of glory, but of heavenly glory viewed essentially, which will be common to all the just: which was also observed by Augustine, l. de cognitione verae vit. c. 46. Compare what we observed there concerning the passage of Daniel.

Latin:

Vers. 41. πάντα τὰ σκάνδαλα κὶ τὲς ποιῦντας τὴν ἀνομίαν] In hoc tota vis est comparationis. Initio Christiana Eccle- sia erat admirandæ puritatis, ex hominibus constans plenis Spiritu Sancto, aut certe Spiritum illum jamjam axspectan- tibus. Sed ubi prima illa dilectio refrixerat, jam ipsis Apo- stolorum temporibus multoq; magis postea immiscere se Christianis cœperunt duo hominum vitiosorum genera, alii prava docentes, alii puram professionem vita turpi de- honestantes. Prioris generis homines σκάνδαλα hic vo- cantur. Neque enim ea vox factis tantum, sed & homini- bus tribuitur, ut infra XVI. 23. Sicut autem Paulus alibi conjunxit διχοστασίας κὶ τὰ σκάνδαλα παρὰ τὴν διδαχὴν Rom. XVI.17.ita hic scandala sunt οἱ διχοσατῶντες, seorsim abeun- tes à veræ pietatis doctrina. Nam & quod Christus dixe- rat ἀνάγκη ἐστιν ἐλθεῖν τὰ σκάνδαλα, Paulus ita extulit δεῖ αἱρέ- σεις ἐν ὑμῖν εἶναι, 1. Cor. XI.19. Atque ita hanc vocem usur- pare frequenter solebant Christiani veteres. Origenes quin- to adversus Celsum: ἀληθῶς δὲ τὸ τῶν σκανδάλων ὄνομα πολὺ ἐν ταῖς γράμμασι τετοις ἐστιν· ὅπερ εἰώθαμεν λέγειν περὶ τῶν διαστρο φόντων ἀπὸ τῆς ὑγιᾶς διδασκαλίας τὰς ἁπλυστέρας κὶ ἐνεξαπατητως. Tales præcipue fuerant Nicolaitæ & Gnostici specialiter notati in Epistolis Petri & Judæ, qui sub specie libertatis Christianæ docebant ἀδιάφορα esse ea quæ naturali hone- stati repugnant. Alterum genus hominum sunt qui nihil quidem pravi docent, sed non ex regula Christiana vitam instituunt, ἀδελφοὶ ἀτάκτως περιπατῦντες ut loquitur Pau- lus 2. ad Thessalonicenses III. Cum utroq; hoc hominum genere Apostolis eorumque successoribus multum fuit ne- gotii: neqs dubium est quin si tales, quales erant cum Chri- stus hæc loqueretur, mansissent, Apostoli optaturi sæpius fuerint, ut ignis de cœlo tales homines consumeret:quod il- los æquissimum arbitratos in Samariæ vicanis Christum non recipientibus Lucas nos docet IX. 54. Adversus hanc vehe- mentiam non qua oportet lenitate temperatam munit eos Christus, ostendens hoc suum consilium, pati in Christia- nismo probos improbis, prava docentes recta docentibus permixtos vivere usque dum maturuisset universalis judicii tempus. Tertullianus: Qui semel æternum judicium destina- vit, non præcipitat discretionem, quæ est conditio judicii, ante fi- nem. Cur autem sibi ita videatur, causas Christus hic non expunit, nisi quod obscure innuisse eas videri potest, cũ di- xit, cavendum ne cum lolio simul evellatur triticum. Sed ex aliis sacrarum literarum locis eas colligere non usque- quaque difficile est. Nam primum quod pœnas generales attinet, quales sunt diluvia, incendia, aliæque id genus pe- stes, cum non possint ita infligi ut solos improbos contin- gant, proborum etiam paucorum causa Deus aut iis abstinet aut certe eas temperat. Vide Gen. XIIX. 32. & id quod infra est xxiv. 22. Deinde inter prava docentes, aut extra regulam viventes sunt alii aliis sanabiliores, quorum pœnitentiam Deus patienter opperitur. Ob hanc causam dicit Petrus ul- timum judicii diem differri, quiaDeus patienter cum homi- nibus agat, nolens quemquam perire, sed omnes potius vo- lens pervenire ad pœnitentiam 2. Ep. cap. III. com. 9. Præ- terea vero pravi doctores, & qui vitæ sunt inemendatæ, bo- nis ac probis materiam præbent in qua constantiam suam & lenitatem exerceant; constantiam dum malis exemplis non patiuntur se abripi: lenitatem dum eos quovis modo stu- dent ad meliorem vitam retrahere. Hoc est quod Paulus dicit ἵνα οἱ δόκιμοι φανεροὶ γίνωνται ἐν ὑμῖν 1. Cor. XI. 19. quod non incommode explicat Scriptor responsionum ad Ortho- doxos quæstione XXII. Quanquam vero certissimum est, hoc Christi dicto neque magistratibus publica judicia adimi quæ malos formidine pœnæ coërceant, neque Ecclesiæ jus segregandi à suis cœtib9 eos qui aut doctrinam adulterant, aut vitæ turpitudine maculant nomen Christianum, tamen quin lenitas ac patientia divira aliqua salté ratione, homi- nib9 omnibus, atq; inter cæteros etiam magistratibus & ec- clesiæ præpositis imitanda proponatur, minime est dubiran- dum. Nam etiam in lenitate advers9 malos patris nostri bo- nitatem jubemur exprimere supra V. 45. Et de clementia quidem in publicis judiciis adhibenda, supra aliquid diximus: quæ sane tum præcipue locum habere debet, cum aut appa- ret ingenium esse sanabile, aut propter multitudinem pec- cantium exerceri pœna aliter nequit, nisi ut fontibus infon- tes involvat, quod præcipue locum habet quoties delicti causa bella suscipiuntur. Sed & Ecclesiæ judicia magno cum temperamento ac lenitate exercenda esse passim docemur. Sunt enim & in dogmatibus errores ejusmodi, in quibus locum habere debeat, τὸ ἀσθενοῦντα τῇ πίστει προσλαμβάνεσθαι, μὴ εἰς διακρίσεις διαλογισμῶν. Et abstineri quidem a familia- ri nimium convictu τῶν ἀτάκτων vult Paulus, ita tamen ut non habeantur pro exploratis, sed fraternæ admoneantur. Jam vero quoties magnus erat peccantium numerus, atque inter eos, ut fit, multi excusabiliter prolapsi, remissum ali- quid de rigore disciplinæ multis exemplis probari potest. Et notæ sunt Augustini in eam rem sententiæ. Scriptor quæstionum ad Orthodoxos, itemque Chrysost. & Hierony- mus hanc Christi parabolam de hæreticis interpretantur: non male, cum ex collatione aliorum locorum, ut jam dixi- mus appareat σκάνδαλον vocem huc potissimum per- tinere. Augustinus eandem secutus interpretationem diu ejus fuit sententiæ ut existimaret nullas omnino pœnas u- surpandas in eos qui vocantur hæretici. Sed post multa cum Donatistis, hominibus satis pertinacibus, certamina haste- nus sententiam mutavit, ut eas pœnas non improbaret quæ pœnitentiæ tempus relinquerent: capitalibus autem suppli- ciis intercessit sæpissime. Si vetustioris Christianismi exqui- ramus sententiam, inveniemus sane argumenta quæ ipsi ut validissima torquent adversus paganos, id comprehendere quod adversus hæreticorum supplicia non minus recte pos- sit usurpari. Neque enim contenti veritatem fidei suæ de- fendere, probant, etiamsi graviter errarent, tamen ejus cau- sa pœnas in se non esse exercendas. Constantinus Impera- tor cum primis edictis liberum debere esse omnibus ex a- nimi sui sententia Dei cultum professus esset, postea seu quod imperio ita conducere arbitraretur, seu quod Episco- pi laborem quotidianæ disputationis subterfugerent, pœnas constituit in eos qui se a communione τῆς μεγάλης ἐκκλησίας separaverant, sed maxime pecuniarias. Inter segreges istos erant & Novatiani, homines ut apparet minime mali (non de sectæ institutoribus, sed de eorum posteris loquor) & in dogmatibus satis consentientes cum cæteris, cupidi tan- tum rigidioris cujusdam disciplinæ. Secuti Imperatores, ut expedire rebus suis judicabant, ita ut coërcuerunt, aut dis- simularunt conventus segreges, qui indies novi novique succrescebant, ita ut Christianarum sectarum inire nume- rum res sit difficillima.

Recte observat Grotius, τὰ σκάνδαλα dici ho- mines prava docentes, è collatione Matth. XVI. 23. Rom. XVI. 17. 1. Cor. XI. 19. & quod scriptor quæ- stionum ad Orthodoxos, itemque Chrysostomus, Hiero- nymus, & Augustinus hanc parabolam de hæreticis interpretentur: Quibus addendus Cyprian. l. III. Ep. 3. Ut enim per semen verbum Dei designatur, sic per zizania hæreses peculiariter notari censent: quæ, ut zizania tritico antequam ad maturitatem perveni- unt, gemina sunt, verbo Dei ὅμοια tradunt, etiamsi ἀνόμοια sentiant. Adde quod nonnullis zizania non lolium, sed illam tritici speciem, quam adustam vocant, notent, quæ à tritico ægre discerni potest, ac difficulter evellitur, quin simul evellatur triti- cum. Perperam autem ex hac parabola Anaba- ptistæ colligunt, facinorosos non esse capitali afficien- dos supplicio: qui juxta plerosque non facinorosos, sed hæreticos respicit, nec ad Magistratus, sed ver- bi ministros pertinet, contr. Rom. XIII. 3. Hæreti- cos v. minime esse capite plectendos, agnoscit no- biscum Grotius, discedens ea parte à Papistarum truculentia, eamque tacite perstringens, quam ab

Arianis primum originem habere docet. Pœnæ, inquit, capitales adeo omnibus invisæ erant, credo ob memoriam paganæ sævitiæ, ut in Gallia Episcopi, qui auctores pote- statibus fuerant, ut in Priscillianistas pravissimorum dogma- tum auctores, & vitæ iniquitatæ homines gladio animad- verteretur, eam ob causam ab Ecclesiarum amoti sunt communione: & in Oriente damnata Synodus quæ in Bo- gomili exustionem consenserat. Certe Ario, Macedo- nio, Nestorio, Eutycheti, novarum sectarum principibus nihil durius relegatione evenit. Videntur Ariani Impe- ratores & ejusdem sectæ in Africa reges primi graviora supplicia instituisse, deinde etiam imbuisse manus diffiden- tium sanguine. Quæ postea secuta sint tempora, nihil opus est referre. Non quævis mors visa sufficere: sed in exquirendis suppliciis ingenium suum sævitia exercuit. Anathemata non in homines, sed in populos pronuncia- ta, & ne bruta hæc essent fulmina, accensi reges, ut ferro flammaque provincias exscinderent, nullo ætatis, nullo sexus discrimine. Ita ubi solitudinem fecerant, pacem ap- pellabant. Et his omnibus obtendi solet studium divini nominis, sed plerumque obtendi tantum. Nam Deus de- dignatur coacta servitia, nec placere illi potest quod vi humana exprimitur. Reipsa solent qui id faciunt, non nomini divino, sed suis honoribus, suis commodis & tran- quillitati consulere, quod scit iste, qui mentes introspicit. Atque ita fit, ut lolium evellatur cum tritico, innocentes cum nocentibus: imo triticum sæpe sumatur pro lolio: non enim tam bene agitur cum rebus humanis ut semper me- liora pluribus aut validioribus placeant.
