Sed ut in grege taurus, ita inter homines qui viribus est editior imbecillio- rem cædit: & iidem sæpe quæ pati se querebantur, mox in alios audent. At ita passim agere si fas est, non video cur nobis dicere non liceat, militiæ nostræ arma carnalia esse, quod negat Paulus: non video, quæ futura sit Christianæ sapientiæ exploratio, aut cur non inverti in partem alteram possit, quod dictum est ὁ κατὰ σάρκα γεννηθεὶς τὸν κατὰ πνεῦ- μα, Gal. IV. 29. Sunt qui sævissima quæq; defendunt Judai- cæ legis exemplo. Ut jam nihil dicam de legis veteris novæ- que diverso spiritu, quos tandem ferit illa lex? nimirum eos qui malignissimo proposito hoc agebant, ut homines ab u- no vero Deo abducerent, ab eo inquam Deo quem & na- tura docebat, & tot miracula apertissime testabantur. At Christianæ religionis pleraq; non natura nobis nota sunt, sed cælesti patefactione: & miracula quibus olim ea reli- gio obsignata est ad summam doctrinæ pertinebant, non ad singula capita quæ in controversiam veniunt. Imo fatentur veteres etiam apud eos, quos vocabant hæreticos aut schis- maticos (sæpe laxato nimium nomine, ut apud Epiphanium imprimis videre est) fieri miracula, Deo scilicet id curan- te, non in erroris confirmationem, sed in testimonium e- jus doctrinæ quæ diversis cœtibus erat communis. His autem non eo dico animo, quod judicio eximere velim Gaulonitas & Theudas, qui mentito religionis nomine bella excitant, aut imperii statum concutiunt, aut circum- celliones in Africa latrocinio grassantes, aut si quid est ho- rum simile. Scelera enim manent scelera quocunque no- mine commendentur, imo eo sunt exsecrabiliora, quo spe- ciosiorem sibi titulum induunt: sed facta velim discerni ab opinatoribus, ut quæ non æque sint ἐφ' ἡμῖν. Opinationem autem ambitu simul ea comprehendo, quæ opinationes quasi necessario sequuntur. Sed & opinationum observa- ri discrimen, tum ex ipsarum natura prout à vera pietate plus minusve abducunt, tum ex causâ quæ homines in er- rorem pellexit: in dubiis autem rebus semper eligi id quod est mitius leniusque, ne ille quem Dominum no- strum profitemur necesse habeat nobis dicere, nescitis quo spiritu ducamini.

Hæc Grotius Jesuitarum non vulgaris amicus, Pontificis Romani advocatus cæteroquin insignis.

Vers. 41. Ἀποστελεῖ ὁ ὑἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου τοὺς Ἀγγέλους αὐτοῦ] De Angelis bonis intelligunt non- nulli, quia Angeli Christi dicuntur, & Angelis bo- nis congregatio electorum à quatuor ventis tribui- tur, Matth. XXIV. 31. & quia etiam Diaboli de- trudentur in infernum ab Angelis bonis, Apoc. XX. 3. Sed Angeli Christi dici etiam possunt mali Angeli, qua mittuntur à Christo, qui & ab- solute Angeli vocantur, Rom. VIII. 38. 1. Cor. VI. 3. neque hic congregatio electorum à quatuor ventis, sed collectio impiorum & segregatio ab electis, & projectio in caminum ignis designa- tur: uti ergo illa est bonorum, ita hæc malo- rum Angelorum esse videtur, qui hi sunt licto- res, quibus traduntur impii, ut in carcerem conjiciantur, Matth. V. 25. ubi nomen ὑπηρέτης, Luc. XII. 58. ubi nomen πράκτωρ habetur. Ὑπηρέτης pro apparitore, lictore, Actor. V. 22. 25. ut ad Matth. V. observat Schmidius: O' πράκτωρ, eodem Autore, exactor est sive debitorum, sive pœnarum, qui damnatos cogit judicum senten- tiæ parere. B. Lutherus reddidit Stockmeister. Diabolum à bonis Angelis in infernum detru- sum iri, nuspiam docetur in scriptura. Apoc. XX. 3. non Angelus creatus sed Filius Dei intelligatur, ut Tom. IV. Syst. Theol. p. 269. docuimus. Consentaneum autem videtur, hic generaliter nomen Angelorum Christi adhiberi, ut cum mali tum boni Angeli emittantur tempore messis, vel in fine mundi, nomine messorum significati: ut illi quidem scandala, hoc est, iniquitatum o- perarios colligant, & in caminum ignis proji- ciant, zizaniis figuratos t8s ὑιὲς τῦ πονηρῦ, filios malitiae vel mali illius Diaboli, qui κατ᾽ ἐξοχὴν isto nomine venit: Hi vero triticum, id est fi- lios regni colligant in horrea Domini. Num vero messores & boni & mali Angeli dicantur, quod in morte illi bonis hi malis demetendis ordinarie a Deo adhibeantur, quemadmodum talia leguntur 2. Sam. XXIV. 16. 2. Reg. XIX. 35. non temere dixerim. Solent in parabola non- nulla ornatus causa adhiberi, quae in applicatio- ne ad vivum resecanda non sint. Omne simile est dissimile.

ποιῦντες τὴν ἀνομίαν] Intelligendum ut supra XIII. 41. V. 42. ἐις τὴν κάμινον τῦ πυρὸς] לגוא־אתון נורא ut est in Daniele III. 6. quod hic secutus est Syrus. Loli- um atque alia id genus in ignem conjici solere patet ex i- is quae supra III. 2. VI. 30. & alibi. Plutarchus ad aedi- bus quibusdam ait cautionem interpositam ne balneo- rum conductores ad ignem lolio uterentur. Simul au- tem alluditur ad supplicium vivicomburii quod in Ori- ente erat usitatum. Non dicit in ignem, sed in caminum ignis, ut ardoris illius vehementiam inevitabilem & perpe- tuam exprimat. Ut enim illi, qui in fornacem ardentem injecti sunt, non possunt ignis supplicium effugere, sed undique tam igne, quam fornace con- clusi sunt: sic impiis nunquam ex inferno patebit e- gressus aut liberatio ex cruciatibus ignis illius aeter- ni. B. Gerhard. in h. l. ἐκεῖ ἔσαι ὁ κλαυθμὸς] Vide supra IIX. 12. Vers. 43. τότε οι δίκαιοι ἐκλάμψυσιν.] Optime Danielem interpretatur Christus. Nam משכילים Hebraeis di- cuntur qui sapienter vitam instituunt. Vera autem pie- tas vera est sapientia. Rursum bene dixit Christus τότε, quasi dicat, tunc cum Ecclesia ab omni malorum homi- num contagio erit purgata. Scriptor sapientiae loquens de justis: ὡς χρυσὸν ἐν χωνευτηρίῳ ἐδοκίμασεν αὐτὸς: dein- de κὴ ἐν καιρῷ ἐπισκοπῆς αὐτῶν, ἐκλάμψυσι. Respicit locum Dan. XII. 1. quem fatetur de splendore justorum in altera vita agere. Ad pessime depravavit in Annot. ad Dan. XII. 1. Porphyrium Empaectam impium sequutus, ut in Anti-Grotia- nis nostris illic diximus. Quum agnoscat Christum hic interpretatum esse optime Danielem, qui de glo- ria alterius seculi exposuit, pessima sine dubio est Grotii interpretatio in annot. ad Daniel. cum de fama nominis in hoc seculo, Danielem interpreta- tus est. Neque in voce משכילים secum conve- nit Grotius; Hic enim eos qui sapienter vitam insti- tuunt eam notare vult. At illic eos, qui alios insti- tuerunt in periculis, cum Lysias Antiochi personam gerens omnia crudelissima in Judaeos exercuit &c. Ὡς ὁ ἥλιος] Hinc videmus fulgorem coeli apud Danie- lem esse solis περίφρασιν: ut saepe jubar apud Latinos. Sed & Paulus gloriam eorum qui inter justos maxime excellunt soli comparare videtur, 1. Cor. XV. 24. & sequentibus. Fulgorem caeli apud Danielem perperam con- fundit Grotius cum splendore solis, aut sole ipso. Pro- pheta enim distinguit inter splendorem stellarum, ad quas sol pertinet, & fulgorem firmamenti. Et gradualem gloriae differentiam designat eorum, qui docti sunt ad justitiam, & qui alios de ea erudierunt. Hic vero non de gradibus gloriae diversis, sed de gloria caelesti οὐσιωδῶς spectata, quae omnibus justis communis erit, agitur: quod etiam Augustino ob- servatum l. de cognitione verae vit. c. 46. Confer. de loco Danielis, quae illic observavimus.

## 13:43
ὁ ἔχων ὦτα ἀκούειν ἀκουέτω] I think this clause refers to the preceding rather than to the following. For we have had a similar use of the same epiphonema in this chapter. Therefore Christ says this: Turn your mind to the end to which the pious and the impious are destined: that will be a comfort to you against the troubles of the present age and the prosperity of the impious.

Latin:

ὁ ἔχων ὦτα ἀκούειν ἀκουέτω] Puto clausulam hanc ad præ- cedentia potius quam ad sequentia referri. Nam similem u- sum ejusdem ἐπιφωνήματος habuimus hoc capite. Hoc ergo dicit Christus: Advertite animum ad exitum cui pii atque impii destinantur: id vobis adversus præsentis ævi molestias & impiorum prospera erit solatium.

## 13:44
Vers. 44. πάλιν ὁμοία ἐστὶν] These parables, whether proposed to the Apostles alone or before the crowd, receive an explanation from the former, and so the Apostles do not desire the first two of these to be explained to them specifically, although they do not have an epimythium, as they are sufficiently understood, as appears below 51. κεκρυμμένῳ] Above, the words of the Gospel were said to be κεκρυμμένα com. 35. Therefore the treasure is ὁ λόγος.

πάντα ὅσα ἔχει πωλεῖ] It signifies that the pursuit of glory, riches, and pleasure must be cast away, and, if pressure should arise, everything, even life itself, must be renounced, so that the word of salvation may be ours not by temporary use only, but by right of possession, that is, so that one may persevere in the obedience of that word to the end. Therefore, seek the explanation from those things which were said in verse 20, 21, 22. It seems that by Hebrew law the ownership of the treasure followed the owner of the field.

ἀγοράζει ⁊ ἄγει τὸν ἐκεῖνον] That is, he strives in every way to make his faith firm and stable, so that it may be not only his own, but as Clement of Alexandria speaks, ἰδίᾳ πεφυσιωμένη, turned into nature. For he uses that word in that way several times.

Latin:

Vers. 44. πάλιν ὁμοία ἐστὶν] Hæ fabellæ, sive Apostolis solis, sive coram turba propositæ ex prioribus explicatio- nem accipiunt, itaque duas harum priores, quanquam ἐπιμύθιον non habent, ut satis intellectas, peculiariter sibi explicari non desiderant Apostoli, ut apparet infra 51. κεκρυμμένῳ] Supra verba Evangelii dicta erant κεκρυμμέ- να com. 35. Est ergo thesaurus ὁ λόγος.

πάντα ὅσα ἔχει πωλεῖ] Significat studium gloriæ, divitia- rum & voluptatis abjiciendum, &, si pressura ingruat, o- mnia etiam vitam ipsam abdicandam, ut verbum salutare sit non usu tantum temporario, sed jure mancupii no- strum, hoc est, ut in ejus verbi obedientia ad finem per- severetur. Pete da ergo explicatio ex iis quæ dicta sunt commate 20. 21. 22. Videtur jure Hebræo thesauri pro- prietas agri dominum secuta.

ἀγοράζει ⁊ ἄγει τὸν ἐκεῖνον] Id est omnimodo nititur fidem suam firmam ac stabilem reddere, ut sit non ἰδίᾳ tantum, sed ut Clemens Alexandrinus loquitur, ἰδίᾳ πεφυσιωμένη, in naturam versa. Ita enim illa eo verbo aliquoties utitur.

## 13:45
Vers. 45. ζητοῦντι καλοὺς μαργαρίτας] The Evangelical doctrine shone upon some who were thinking neither of God, nor of amending their life, nor of the hope of another life, such as were most of the people among the external nations to whom Paul adapts that prophecy, I was found by those who did not seek me. There were also those studious of wisdom among the Jews and elsewhere who were touched by a certain desire of knowing the truth, or who were awaiting with eager souls some Prophet, or even the Messiah himself: the comparison of the treasure looks to the former; these things about the pearl look to the latter.

Latin:

Vers. 45. ζητοῦντι καλοὺς μαργαρίτας] Doctrina Evange- lica quibusdam affulsit, neque de Deo, neq; de vita emen- danda, neque de spe vitæ alterius quicquam cogitantibus, quales erant plerique in gentibus externis quibus illud va- ticinium Paulus aptat, inventus sum non quærentibus me. Erant & sapientiæ studiosi inter Judæos atque alibi qui ve- ritatis cognoscendæ desiderio quodam tangebantut, quive Prophetam aliquem, aut ipsum etiam Messiam avidis a- nimis exspectabant: Priores respicit thesauri compara- tio: posteriores ista de unione.

## 13:46
Vers. 46. πολύτιμον μαργαρίτην] A commodity known to the Jews from the proximity of the Red Sea. The beginning, says Pliny, and the summit of all things in value are held by pearls. Therefore, just as he is said to have found a treasure who has obtained a huge good, so a thing of the greatest price is best compared to a pearl. Moreover, Christ had regard for an opinion known among the Jews, which teaches that wisdom is to be preferred both to gold and to pearls, which exists in the Gnomology of Solomon 8:9, 10, to which you will find similar things also in the Psalms.

Isidore of Pelusium, book 1, epistle 183, explains the parable of the pearl and applies it to Christ. Ambrose, sermon 6, vol. 3, f. 230, explains it in the same way. Ephrem the Syrian on the precious pearl, f. 667. Cyprian on Works and Alms, chapter 8, f. 352, understands it as eternal life. Nazianzen, oration 12, f. 193, and Luther in the margin, as the word of the Gospel. Augustine on Matthew 9:13, vol. 4, f. 367 (and also tractate 5 on John), Bede, vol. 5, f. 46, Anselm, f. 66, understand it as charity, which is the most excellent of all virtues. (Athanasius, Disputation in the Council of Nicaea against Arius, vol. 1, page 82, as piety.) These interpretations are not contrary, but subordinate. The properties of pearls can be beautifully compared with Christ and the Gospel. 1. Pliny, book 9, chapter 35. They report that shells, when the genial hour of the year has stimulated them, opening themselves with a certain yawning, are filled with a dewy conception, and afterwards, being pregnant, bring forth, and that the offspring of the shells are pearls according to the quality of the dew received. Ephrem, in the aforementioned work on the Pearl: It is not the conjunction of shells that forms the pearl, but the mixture of lightning and water. Elias of Crete proves the same in his commentary on Nazianzen. 2. Pearls are bitter and are extracted from the shells with danger. 3. Pearls are rendered the more beautiful the more severe the storms and waves are. Isidore of Charax in Athenaeus, book 3, f. 93. 4. Although it is small, it is powerful, says Ephrem: for it is useful against vertigo, palpitation of the heart, and dimness of the eyes. Concerning the price of pearls, see Pliny, book 9, chapter 35. It pleased me to repeat these from Blessed Gerhard, as they seemed worthy to be read here.

Latin:

Vers. 46. πολύτιμον μαργαρίτην] Notum Judæis merci- monium maris rubri vicinitate. Principium, inquit Plinius, culmenque omnium rerum pretiis margaritæ tenent. Sicut ergo thesaurum invenisse dicitur qui ingens bonum est a- deptus, ita res pretii maximi unioni optime comparatur. Respexit autem Christus notam inter Judæos γνώμην, quæ docet sapientiam præferendam & auro & margaritis, quæ extat in Gnomologico Salomonis IIX. 9. 10. cui similia invenies & in Psalmis.

Parabolam de margarita exponit Isidorus Pe- lusiota lib. 1. epist. 183. & ad Christum accommo- dat. Eodem modo exponit Ambrosius serm. 6. tom. 3. f. 230. Ephrem Syrus de Marg. prec. f. 667. Cyprianus de Op. & Eleemos. cap. 8. f. 352. intel- ligit de vita æterna. Nazianz. orat. 12. f. 193. & Lutherus in marg. de verbo Evangelii. August. in Matth. IX. 13. t. 4. f. 367. (nec non tr. 5. in Job.) Beda tom. 5. f. 46. Anshelmus f. 66. intelligunt de caritate, quæ est virtutum omnium præstantissima. (Athanas. Disp. in Conc. Nic. contra Arium t. 1. pag. 82. de pietate.) Hæ interpretationes non sunt contrariæ, sed subordinatæ. Possunt proprietates margaritarum cum Christo & Evangelio pulcre comparari. 1. Plinius lib. 9. cap. 35. Conchas, ubi genialis anni stimulaverit hora, pandentes sese quadam oscitatione impleri roscido conceptu tra- dunt, gravidas postea eniti, partumq; concharum esse margaritas pro qualitate roris accepti. E- phrem l. d. Margaritam non concharum conjun- ctio format, sed fulguris & aquæ commixtio. Idem probat Elias Cretensis ad Nazianz. 2. Mar- garitæ sunt amaræ & cum periculo è conchis exi- muntur. 3. Margaritæ eo redduntur pulchriores, quo graviores sunt tempestates & fluctus. Isido- rus Characenus apud Athen. lib. 3. f. 93. 4. Par- va cum sit, magna potest, inquit Ephrem: prod- est enim contra vertiginem, palpitationem cordis & caliginem oculorum. De pretio margaritarum vid. Plinius lib. 9. cap. 35. Hæc è B. Gerhardo re- petere placuit, digna visa quæ hic legerentur.

## 13:47
Verf. 47. σαγήνῃ] A dragnet. Ulpian the Jurist: 'If anyone prevents me from fishing in the sea or from drawing a dragnet, which in Greek is called σαγήνη.' And he called it thus. Varro, On Agriculture: 'The nature of a dragnet, as the word itself shows, is such that it drags with it whatever is in its way.' Hence Cicero calls a judgment for fraud a 'dragnet' of malice, because no kind of malice can escape the formula of that judgment. Homer called this very kind of net πανάγρων, as has been noted by Plutarch in the book where he disputes about the cleverness of land and sea animals. Hence we see why Christ chose to name this particular kind of net here.

ἐκ παντὸς γένους] Although other things are also accustomed to come into a dragnet, I think, however, that 'fish' are rightly understood here by the Latin interpreter: for we are accustomed to embrace something common but definite in our mind when we say 'every kind.' Therefore, σαπρὰ are the refuse and dregs of the fish, which kind we see being thrown away by fishermen as unworthy of being kept.

Latin:

Verf. 47. σαγήνῃ] Everriculo. Ulpianus Jurisconsultus. Si quis me prohibet in mari piscari vel everriculum quod Græce σαγήνη dicitur ducere. Et ita appellavit. Varro de re rusti- ca. Est autem everriculi ea natura, quemadmodum vox ipsa ostendit, ut quicquid obvium est secum trahat. Hinc Cicero de dolo malo judicium everriculum vocat malitia- rum, quia nullum genus malitiæ ejus judicii formulam, potest effugere. Homerus hoc ipsum retis genus πανάγρων vocavit, ut à Plutarcho annotatum est libro quo de soler- tia terrestrium & marinorum animantium disputat. Hinc videmus, cur hoc potissimum retis genus hic Christus no- minaverit.

ἐκ παντὸς γένους] Quanquam solent & alia venire in ever- riculum, puto tamen recte hic à Latino interprete pisces in- telligi: Solemus enim quidquam commune sed definitum animo complecti, cum omne genus dicimus. Ergo σα- πρὰ sunt nugamenta & quisquiliæ piscium, quod genus ut servatu indignum videmus à piscatoribus abjici.

## 13:48
Vers. 48. ἀναβιϐάσαντες] This is what the Roman jurists call drawing nets up from the sea.

Latin:

Vers. 48. ἀναβιϐάσαντες] Hoc est quod Romani Juris- prudentes vocant retia è mari subducere.

## 13:49
Vers. 49. ὕτως ἔσαι] The same moral as in the comparison of the tares and the wheat. Therefore, these are 'the wicked,' as above 'the sons of the wicked,' those who, having been drawn to the profession of Christianity in the preaching of the Gospel, are found to be evil at the time of the selection. For the comparison ought not to be extended further, nor does the nature of similarities allow that every little detail should be in the same way. Tertullian expresses the sentiment indicated by this parable in his Apology thus: 'He who has once destined an eternal judgment after the end of the age does not precipitate the separation, which is a condition of judgment, before the end of the age.'

Latin:

Vers. 49. ὕτως ἔσαι] Idem ἐπιμύθιον quod in compara- tione lolii & frumenti. Sunt ergo hic οἱ πονηροὶ, ut supra οἱ ὑοὶ τ̃ πονηρᾶ, illi qui in prædicatione Evangelica pertracti ad Christianismi professionem, delectus tempore mali compe- riuntur. Ultra enim extendi comparatio non debet, neq; similium natura patitur ut minima quæque eodem modo se habeant. Sententiam hac fabella indicatam exprimit ita Tertullianus Apologetico: Qui semel æternum judicium destinavit post sæculi finem, non præcipitat discretionem quæ est conditio judicii ante sæculi finem.

## 13:52
Vers. 52. πᾶς γραμματεὺς.] γραμματεῖς were properly called assessors of magistrates, as we saw at the second chapter, but because they were the same as those learned in the law (just as among the Romans it was the duty of jurists to sit with magistrates), therefore those who are otherwise called νομοδιδάσκαλοι or νομικοὶ are called γραμματεῖς. Thus Ezra is called סופר by Artaxerxes. It is the custom of Christ and the Prophets to signify by names accepted among the Jews both the gifts and the offices that were to be in the Christian Church. See Joel 2:28, Acts 2:17, Isaiah 66:21. Properly, however, those who in the Christian Church are called διδάσκαλοι correspond to the γραμματεῦσιν, which name is read several times in the Acts and in the epistles of Paul.

They were instructed concerning the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven and appointed as teachers and stewards of the right doctrine; therefore Christ exhorts them to store all these things in the inner chambers of their hearts, following the example of a prudent steward, and to bring them forth at some time for the use of the Church. Accordingly, even if assessors of magistrates were called γραμματεῖς, they did not, however, have this name more than others, or claim it for themselves more properly, since others were rather called γραμματεῖς by the Holy Spirit, who were also called νομικοὶ from νόμος, because they were learned in the scripture or law, which kind of skill was required in assessors: as Flacius observes, he was once called a scribe whom we now call a theologian. For they derived the name ἀπὸ τ̃ γραμμάτων, i.e., the sacred ones (2 Tim. 3:15), which are the proper object of scribes. Which meaning is almost perpetual in the Old Testament among the Septuagint. Interpreters, however, encounter γραμματεῖς regarding political scribes, whether they be of a higher or lower order, Ezra 6:8, Esther 3:12, 8:2, as also Acts 19:35. And therefore it seems to be a general name by itself, even if in the New Testament it is used particularly of those learned in the law and teachers; whence, the word having been transferred from the Synagogue to the Christians, the same were noted as Doctors, called διδάσκαλοι in Ps. 23:34, as rightly observed here by Grotius, see Acts 13:1, 1 Cor. 12:29, Eph. 4:11. Add what he has at Matt. 15:1, where these things occur concerning the use of the word among the Jews: 'There was a private investigation, but instituted by those who had the leadership of the Schools. For all the most learned, as we have said, were called γραμματεῖς. The family of the Pharisees followed the authority of these, distinguished from the rest only by the fact that, over and above the common precepts, it had enjoined upon itself peculiar acts of will-worship.'

Μαθητευθεὶς] מחוכם in Psalm 58:6 and Proverbs 30:24.

Εἰς τὴν βασιλείαν τοῦ Θεοῦ] A doctor, he says, well prepared and learned for delivering the precepts of the kingdom of heaven. Thus Luke said 'fit for the kingdom of God.' Wherefore it does not seem that in this place εἰς is put for ἐν.

Θησαυροῦ] ἀποθήκης, as we said at chapter 2. But it seems to me well explained by others, that which follows, 'old and new,' so that it signifies every kind of food, both that which is accustomed to be kept and that which cannot be kept by storing. By this similitude, the Apostles are warned that, following the example given by Christ, they should strive to store up the dogmas of piety with a certain variety of delivery. For 'He has carried every point who has mixed the useful with the sweet.' Ennius, describing the wise man Catus Aelius Sextus, had said: 'Holding many things, old, buried, and ancient, which make customs and hold the one who is old.'

Most think that by 'old and new' in the protasis different kinds of foods and drinks are understood, that is, aged and fresh, which are brought forth opportunely by the steward as the occasion arises: but in the apodosis, most interpreters understand the Old and New Testament with great consensus: Irenaeus, Origen, Chrysostom, Jerome, Hilary, Augustine, Theodoret, Beza, Theophylact, Euthymius, B. Luther, Brentius, Hunnius, Lyserus, likewise Lyranus, Salmero, Barradius, Jansenius, Maldonatus, Cornelius à Lapide, and even among the Reformed, with Calvin and Bucer not denying it in vain, Diodati, Piscator, Pareus, Rivetus, Heinsius. The Apostles, says Jerome in book II of his commentary on Matthew at this place, were bringing forth from the treasury of doctrines new and old: so that whatever they preached in the Gospel, they might confirm by the testimony of the King and the Prophets: whence the bride says in the Song of Songs, 'new and old, my kinsman, I have kept for you.' St. Irenaeus, book IV, 21, calls this explanation free from all contradiction: He calls the things which they bring forth from the treasury, old and new, without contradiction, the two Testaments. Which is to be opposed to Tostatus and Calvin, who alike impugn that explanation.

PART II. The preaching, and the contempt of Christ in his own country.

Latin:

Vers. 52. πᾶς γραμματεὺς.] γραμματεῖς proprie diceban- tur assessores magistratuum, ut ad secundum caput vidi- mus, sed quia iidem erant legisperiti (ut & apud Romanos jurisconsultorum erat adsidere magistratibus) ideo γραμ- ματεῖς dicuntur qui alias νομοδιδάσκαλοι aut νομικοὶ. Ita Esdras vocatur סופר ab Artaxerxe. Mos autem est Christo & Prophetis, nominibus apud Judæos receptis significare tum dona, tum munia, quæ futura erant in Ecclesia Chri- stiana. Vide Ioel II. 28. Actor. II. 17. Esaias LXVI. 21. Proprie autem τοῖς γραμματεῦσιν respondet ii qui in Eccle- sia Christiana dicti sunt διδάσκαλοι, quod nomen in Actis & in epistolis Pauli aliquoties legitur.

Instituti erant de mysteriis regni cælestis, & constituti rectæ doctores & œconomi, ideo Chri- stus eos hortatur, ut exemplo prudentis œconomi hæc omnia in penetralia cordis sui reponant, & ad Ecclesiæ usum aliquando depromant. Proinde etsi Assessores Magistratuum γραμματεῖς dicti fuerint; non tamen præ aliis illi hoc nomem habuerunt, aut magis proprie sibi vendicarunt, quoniam alii po- tius à Spiritu S. γραμματεῖς dicti fuerint, qui & νομικοὶ à νόμῳ, quod in scriptura vel lege periti es- sent, qualis peritia in assessoribus requirebatur: uti Flacius observat, eum olim scribam appellatum esse, quem nunc dicimus Theologum. Deduxerunt e- nim nomen ἀπὸ τ̃ γραμμάτων sc. ἱερῶν 2. Tim. HI. 15. quæ proprium scribarum objectum sunt. Quæ significatio fere perpetua est in V. T. Apud LXX. Interpretes tamen γραμματεῖς de politicis scribis, seu superioris illi sint, seu inferioris ordinis, occur- rit, Esdr. VI. 8. Esth. III. 12. c. IIX. 2. ut & Act. XIX. 35. Ideoq; generale nomen per se videtur, etsi pecu- liariter in N. T. imprimis de legisperitis & doctori- bus adhibeatur; unde voce à Synagoga ad Christia- nos translata Doctores eadem notati sunt Ps. XXIII. 34. διδάσκαλοι dicti, ut recte hic observatum Gro- tio v. Actor. XIII. 1. Cor. XII. 29. Eph. IV. 11. Adde quæ habet ad Matth. XV. 1. ubi de usu vocis a- pud Judæos hæc occurrunt: Fuit privata explo- ratio, sed ab illis instituta qui Scholarum habe- bant principatum. Nam doctissimi quique ut di- ximus γραμματεῖς vocabantur. Horum autem auctoritatem sequebatur Pharisæorum familia, hoc tantum distincta à cæteris, quod super commu- nia præcepta peculiares sibi ἐθελοθρησκείας injun- xerat.

Μαθητευθεὶς] מחוכם Psalmo LVIII. 6. & Proverb. XXX. 24.

Εἰς τὴν βασιλείαν τοῦ Θεοῦ] Doctor, inquit, bene paratus atque eruditus ad tradenda præcepta regni cœlestis. Sic Lucas dixit εὔθετον εἰς τὴν βασιλείαν τοῦ Θεοῦ. Quare non vi- detur hoc quidem loco εἰς pro ἐν positum.

Θησαυροῦ] ἀποθήκης ut diximus ad caput II. Bene autem ab aliis explicatum mihi videtur, quod, sequitur vetera & nova, ut significet omne genus edulia, tam quæ servari so- lent, quam quæ servando servari non possunt. Hac autem similitudine monentur Apostoli, ut ad exemplum à Christo datum studeant pietatis dogmata condire quadam traden- di varietate. Nam Omne tulit punctum qui miscuit utile dulci. Ennius virum sapientem Catum Ælium Sextum describens dixerat: Multa tenens antiqua, sepulta, senusta, Quæ faciunt mores veteresque tenentem.

Per vetera & nova in προτάσει diversa ciborum & potuum genera intelligi plerique censent, vetusta pu- ta & recentia, quæ pro re nata ab Oeconomo depo- nuntur opportune: in ἀποδόσει vero Vetus & N. T. plerique Interpretes magno consensu intelligunt, Ireneus, Origenes, Chrysostomus, Hieronymus, Hila- rius, Augustinus, Theodoretus, Beza, Theophylact9, Euthymius, B. Lutherus, Brentius, Hunnius, Lyse- rus, Lyranus item, Salmero, Barradius, Jansenius, Maldonatus, Cornelius à Lapide, etiam è Reforma- tis nequicquam renuente Calvino & Bucero, Deo- datus, Piscator, Pareus, Rivetus, Heinsius. Apostoli, inquit Hieronymus l. II. comm. in Matth. h. l. erant ejicientes de thesauro doctrinarum nova & vetera: ut quicquid in Evangelio prædicabant, Regis & Pro- phetarum testimonio comprobarent: unde sponsa di- cit in Cantico Cantic. nova & vetera fratruelis meus servavit tibi. D. Ireneus l. IV. 21. hanc expli- cationem omnis contradictionis expertem dicit: Ea, quæ de thesauro proferunt vetera & nova sine con- tradictione duo Testamenta dicit. Quæ Tostato pariter, & Calvino explicationem illam impu- gnantibus, opponenda.

PARS II. Concio, & contemtus Christi in Patria.

## 13:53
Verse 53. μετῆρεν] וישא רגליו as in Gen. XXIX. 1.

Latin:

Vers. 53. μετῆρεν] וישא רגליו ut Gen. XXIX. 1.

## 13:54
Verse 54. πατρίδα] That Nazareth is to be understood there is not even a doubt. But it is rightly called his country from the long residence of his parents. For it is credible that from the time when the posterity of David began to become vile, and indeed even suspected by those in power, the ancestors of Mary and likewise of Joseph fixed their domicile in a more obscure place. Hence Christ is called 'from Nazareth,' John I. 46, Acts X. 38. And we learn from what follows that their kinsmen dwelt in the same place.

Chrysostom, Euthymius, Theophylact, Jerome, and others interpret it thus.

ἐν τῇ συναγωγῇ] I think that is more correct than what the Syriac and Latin versions have placed, 'in the synagogues.' For Nazareth, not being a large city, was easily satisfied with one synagogue.

Latin:

Vers. 54. πατρίδα] Nazaretham intelligi ne dubium qui- dem est. Patria autem recte vocatur ex longo parentum incolatu. Credibile enim est ex quo vilescere, imo & su- specta esse imperantibus Davidis posteritas cœperat, Mariæ eœsdemque Josephi majores domicilium fixisse in loco ob- scuriore. Hinc Christus dicitur, ἀπὸ Ναζαρὲτ, Joh. I. 46. Act. X. 38. Et discimus ex sequentibus cognatos eorum ibidem habitasse.

Ita interpretantur Chrysostomus, Euthymius, Theophylactus, Hieronymus, alii.

ἐν τῇ συναγωγῇ] Id rectius puto quam quod Syrus & La- tinus posuerunt in synagogis. Nam Nazaret urbs haud am- pla facile contenta fuit una synagoga.

## 13:55
Verse 55. ὁ τοῦ τέκτονος υἱός] Since the very ancient writer Justin records that Joseph was a carpenter, I would not doubt that the word τέκτων is to be taken in this way here. Nor does it appear that the ancient Christians thought otherwise, from the saying of him who, when insultingly asked by a pagan what the son of the carpenter was doing, replied that he was making a coffin for Julian. Indeed, since Christ himself is also called a carpenter by the Nazarene populace, in whose sight he had grown up, in Mark, I would not dare to contradict those who record that Christ assisted Joseph in the carpenter's trade, and, as Justin says, made plows and yokes. Nor is that unworthy of the state which he had assumed, emptying himself. For besides the fact that 'work is no disgrace,' as was said by Hesiod, it was certainly a praiseworthy custom among the Hebrews that even those who were in more affluent circumstances should learn some craft against all the accidents of fortune: and even those who devoted their efforts to the study of wisdom, of whom we read that some were cobblers, some bakers, some tanners. Either memory failed Origen, or the copies of Mark at that time had a different reading. For he says expressly: 'Nowhere in the Gospels current in the churches is Jesus himself written as a carpenter.'

Is not his mother called Mariam] They were offended even in his mother, whom Celsus objects to the Christians as having been a hand-worker, that is, either a nurse or one preparing a living by other manual labor. Tertullian, in his book on Spectacles, speaking of Christ: This is that son of a carpenter or a harlot, that is, a hand-worker. Thus is fulfilled what Isaiah said XLIX. 7.

And his brothers James and Joses and Simon and Judas] Epiphanius, whom the Greeks follow, posits for certain that these were all sons of Joseph from a former marriage. But Origen teaches us that this rumor took its beginning from books which falsely prefixed the name of Peter and James. Wherefore we shall more rightly side with Jerome, who thinks that all these were our Lord's cousins. For it seems impossible to deny that the same Mary who is called below in Matthew and similarly in Mark the mother of James and Joses, is called in John the sister of the Lord's mother, as one who stood by the cross of Christ with the Lord's mother and with the Magdalene. But if she is the mother of James and Joses, she will certainly also be the mother of Simon and Judas, namely of him who in his epistle calls himself the brother of James, and who in the list of the Apostles makes a pair with the same Judas. But that James, to distinguish him from the other who had for a brother John and for a father Zebedee, is called the less, by reason of age, I think, and the son of Alphaeus: whence it may be gathered that Clopas or Cleopas, from whom this Mary is named, was the father of the same Mary, and Alphaeus her husband. This, therefore, is the James whom not only Paul, but also Josephus in his Jewish annals, calls the brother of Jesus, that is, by a manner of speaking known also to the Greeks and Romans, a cousin: concerning whom, what Hegesippus has fabled is not worth the effort to recite or refute: the same Josephus teaches us that he was stoned by the people under the high priest Ananus. But what John narrates in the Gospel that not even the brothers of Jesus believed in him VII. 5, I think is to be understood of more distant kinsmen, not of these cousins, and certainly not of all. But that those whom we just read came to Jesus with his mother were these very cousins, is very likely, as they were the ones who, with Joseph now dead (for there is no mention of him in the history of the passion, and if he had not been dead, John would not have taken the Lord's mother into his own home), managed Mary's affairs. The name Joses, however, as others have noted, is the same as the name Joseph, but with the last letter dropped, as is also wont to be done by the Hebrews themselves, and then a Greek termination added. Therefore, both concerning him and concerning Barnabas, who had the same name, the Syrian and Latin versions use the name sometimes Jose, sometimes Joseph. Indeed, some codices here have Ἰωσὴφ, undoubtedly from an old interpretation.

Latin:

Vers. 55. ὁ τοῦ τέκτονος υἱός] Fabrum fuisse lignarium Jo- sephum cum Scriptor vetustissimus Justinus tradat, ego non dubitem vocem τέκτων ita hic accipiendam. Neque aliter sensisse Christianos veteres apparet ex dicto illius qui contumeliose à pagano interrogatus, quid faceret ὁ τοῦ τέκτονος υἱὸς respondit eum feretrum Juliano fabricare. Quin cum ipse etiam Christus à plebe Nazaretana, in cujus conspectu adoleverat, τέκτων vocetur apud Marcum, non audeam eis refragari qui Christum Josepho adfuisse in fa- brili opere tradunt, & ut Justinus ait, aratra fecisse & juga. Neque id indignum eo statu quem assumserat, ἑαυτὸν κενῶν. Nam præterquam quod ἔργον οὐδὲν ὄνειδος, ut ab Hesiodo dictum est, mos sane laudabilis inter Hebræos fuit, ut etiam quibus res esset lautior adversus omnes fortunæ ca- sus opificium aliquod addiscerent: atque illi etiam qui sapientiæ studiis operam dabant, quorum alios sutores, alios pistores, alios pelliones fuisse legimus. Aut memo- ria fefellit Origenem, aut Marci exemplaria eo tempore aliam habuerunt scripturam. Diserte enim dicit: οὐδαμοῦ τῶν ἐν ταῖς ἐκκλησίαις φερομένων εὐαγγελίων τέκτων αὐτός ὁ Ἰησοῦς ἀναγέγραπται.

οὐχὶ ἡ μήτηρ αὐτοῦ λέγεται Μαρὶαμ] Etiam in matre offen- debantur, quam χερνῆτιδα fuisse, id est, aut nutricem, aut alio manuum labore victum parantem, Christianis Celsus objicit. Tertullian. libro de Spectaculis de Christo loquens: Hic est ille fabri aut quæstuariæ filius, id est, χερνῆτιδος. Sic impletur quod dixit Esaias XLIX. 7.

Καὶ οἱ ἀδελφοὶ αὐτοῦ Ἰάκωβος καὶ Ἰωσῆς καὶ Σίμων καὶ Ἰούδας] Pro certo ponit Epiphanius, quem Græci sequuntur, fuisse hos omnes filios Josephi ex priori matrimonio. Sed docet nos Origenes famam hanc initium sumsisse ex libris qui fal- so Petri & Jacobi nomen præferebant. Quare rectius Hie- ronymo accedemus arbitranti hos omnes Domini nostri fuisse consobrinos. Negari enim videtur non posse quin ea- dem quæ infra Matthæo & similiter Marco dicitur Maria mater Jacobi & Jose, Johanni dicatur Maria soror matris Domini, ut quæ cum Domini matre & cum Magdalena cru- ci Christi adstiterit. Quod si ea est mater Jacobi & Jose, erit sane & Simonis & Judæ, ejus nempe, qui in epistola se fra- trem Jacobi nominat, quique in Apostolorum recensu cum eodem Juda par unum facit. Is autem Jacobus ad discrimen alterius, qui fratrem Johannem, patrem habebat Zebedæ- um, minor vocatur, ætatis, ut puto, ratione, & Alphæi fili- us: unde colligere liceat Clopan sive Cleopan à quo Maria ista denominatur patrem ejusdem Mariæ fuisse, Alphæum autem conjugem. Hic ergo est Jacobus quem Jesu fratrem, id est consobrinum loquendi genere etiam Græcis & Roma- nis noto, vocat non Paulus tantum, sed & Josephus in Ju- daicis annalibus: de quo quæ fabulatus est Hegesippus neq; recitare neque refutare est operæ pretium: lapidatum à po- pulo fuisse Anano Pontifice idem Josephus nos docet. Quod autem Johannes in Evangelio narrat ne ipsos quidem fratres Jesu in ipsum credidisse VII. 5. de remotioribus con- sanguineis, non de consobrinis istis, certe non de omnib9 intelligendum puto. Eos autem quos modo cum matre ad Jesum venisse legimus, hos ipsos fuisse consobrinos, ve- ro persimile est, ut qui Josepho jam mortuo (neq; enim in passionis historia ulla illius est mentio, & nisi mortuus is fuisset non transtulisse Johannes Domini matrem in domi- cilium suum) Mariæ rerum curam gerebant. Ioses autem nomen, ut alii annotarunt, idem est cum nomine Joseph, sed abjecta, ut fieri etiam solet ab Hebræis ipsis, litera ulti- ma, deinde apposita terminatione Græcanica. Itaq; tum de isto, tum de Barnaba, cui idem fuit nominis, Syrus & Latinus modo Jose, modo Joseph nomen usurpant. Imo & hic quidam codices habent Ἰωσὴφ ex vetere haud dubie interpretamento.

## 13:56
Vers. 56. And his sisters are they not all with us] Epiphanius, and Theophylact following him, call these sisters Mary and Salome. Theophylact also agrees with Epiphanius in this, that he makes Clopas the brother of Joseph: but Theophylact adds that the wife of the deceased Clopas married Joseph, and from that union were born Mary, called Clopas's by law, and Salome. But as I have said, I think all these things are from apocryphal books, and from a not sufficiently understood meaning of the word brothers and sisters. Moreover, it appears that these sisters, that is, cousins or otherwise near kinswomen, were also poor: for that too offended the Nazarenes. What is to be held concerning these, we have said at Matt. XXVII. 55.

Whence then to him all these things] Since he had not been away from Nazareth before this, nor could he have learned these things at home, as none of them were imbued with learning above the common people.

Latin:

Vers. 56. Καὶ αἱ ἀδελφαὶ αὐτοῦ οὐχὶ πᾶσαι πρὸς ἡμᾶς εἰσι] Has sorores Epiphanius & eum secutus Theophylactus Ma- riam & Salomen vocant. Consentit & in hoc cum Epipha- nio Theophylactus quod Clopam facit Josephi fratrem: sed addit Theophylactus Clopæ mortui uxorem nupsisse Jose- pho, atque inde natam Mariam, dictam Clopæ ex lege, & Salomen. Sed ut dixi puto hæc omnia esse ἐκ βιβλίων ψευδε- πιγράφων, & ex non satis intellecta significatione vocis fra- trum & sororum. Cæterum & has sorores, id est consobri- nas aut alioqui cognatas proximas pauperculas fuisse ap- paret: nam id quoque offendebat Nazarenos. Quid de his habendum, diximus ad Matth. XXVII. 55.

Πόθεν οὖν τούτῳ ταῦτα πάντα] Cum neque antehac Nazare- tha abfuerit, neque domi à suis potuerit ista discere, ut quo- rum nemo sit literis supra plebem imbutus.

## 13:57
Vers. 57. And they were offended in him] I do not think they were of such malice as to ascribe these works of Christ to the devil: for Christ does not reproach them with any such thing. But the lot of his birth, known to them, stood in the way of their wonder turning into reverence. See above XI. 6. But this was a sign of a mind neither sufficiently fair nor thinking sufficiently magnificently of divine power. And yet they had on their lips maxims which say that from the dust God raises up those whom he places on the throne of princes, and that he is happy who judges rightly of a man of despised lot.

A prophet is not without honor, except in his own country and in his own house] A famous proverb among the Jews, which, as we have said of other maxims, is to be understood with comparison: as if you were to say: nowhere are eminent men, such as especially Prophets are, more despised than among their own countrymen. Indeed: Whatever is sought, seems best. And it is a vice common to great and small cities, envy over the ignorance of what is right. There is a very similar sentiment in Aristides: to all philosophers it seemed that life is difficult in one's own country. Nor is that different which Philostratus records the Sophist Scopelianus to have said, when asked to declaim in his own country: that the nightingale should not sing in a small cage. Pliny on Protogenes: He was held in low esteem by his own, as domestic things usually are. Thus David was despised by his own house, 1 Sam. XVI. 11, XVII. 28.

are despised, because we admire external things, and usually we judge men from their humble origin, not from their divinely given gifts, and thus we despise the glory of God in him to our own great harm. Prophets and Teachers are therefore despised in their own country where they ought to have been held and heard in so much higher esteem. The Prophets of the Old Testament were nowhere in less value than in Judea. The causes of the contempt of great men in their own country are an innate envy as it were among fellow citizens, familiarity from tender years, and the nature of the human mind, which admires foreign things more than domestic: everything rare is precious.

Latin:

Vers. 57. Καὶ ἐσκανδαλίζοντο ἐν αὐτῷ] Non puto eos tantæ fuisse malitiæ, ut hæc Christi opera diabolo ascriberent: ne- que enim tale quid illis exprobrat Christus. Sed quominus admiratio in reverentiam transiret, obstabat natalium sors illis cognita. Vide supra XI. 6. Erat autem hoc signum ne- que satis æqui neq; de potentia divina satis magnifice sen- tientis animi. Atqui erant in ore ipsis sententiæ, quæ di- cunt ex pulvere à Deo suscitari, quos in procerum solio collocet, & felicem eum esse qui de homine contemtæ sortis æque judicet.

Οὐκ ἔστι προφήτης ἄτιμος, εἰμὴ ἐν τῇ πατρίδι αὐτοῦ καὶ ἐν τῇ οἰκίᾳ αὐτοῦ] Adagium celebre inter Judæos, quod, ut de aliis sententiis diximus, cum comparatione intelli- gendum est: quasi dicas: nusquam magis quam inter po- pulares suos contemni viros eximios, quales imprimis sunt Prophetæ. Nimirum: Quicquid quæritur, optimum videtur. Et vitium est magnis parvisque civitatibus commune super ignorantiam recti invidia. Sententia est huic persimilis a- pud Aristidem : πᾶσι τοῖς φιλοσόφοις ἔδοξε χαλεπὸς ἐν τῇ πα- τρίδι ὁ βίος. Nec abit illud quod Scopelianum Sophistam dixisse Philostratus memorat, cum rogaretur, ut in patria de- clamaret: τὴν ἀηδόνα ἐν οἰκίσκῳ μὴ ᾄδειν. Plinius de Protoge- ne: Sordebat illi suis, ut plerumque domestica. Sic David à sua domo contemtus, 1. Sam. XVI. 11. XVII. 28.

mnuntur, quia externa miramur, & plerumque ho- mines ex humilitate ortus, non ex Divinitus datis donis censemus, atque ita gloriam Dei in illius magno nostro malo contemnimus. Prophetæ ergo & Doctores in patria contemnuntur ubi tanto pluris fieri, audi- rique debuissent magis. Prophetæ Vet. Testamenti nullibi in minori fuere pretio, quam in Judæa. Causæ contemptus virorum magnorum in patria sunt ingenita quasi inter concives invidia, familia- ritas à teneris, & humani ingenii indoles, quod magis peregrina admiratur, quam domestica: παν το σπανιον, τίμιον.

## 13:58
Vers. 58. because of their unbelief] And yet Paul said of the gift of tongues that it was given to be a sign, not to those who believe, but to those who do not believe. It is to be noted therefore that it is not said here that Christ did no miracles in Nazareth, but that he did not do many, which Mark also says. Christ did miracles everywhere, so that those to whom nothing was known about him might believe in him: to those beginning to believe he added other things, by which they might be confirmed in the faith already begun. To those who spurned the first, he did not press more, lest divine liberality should become cheap. Thus God is accustomed to bestow benefits and demand duties by turns.

Latin:

Vers. 58. διὰ τὴν ἀπιστίαν αὐτῶν] Atqui de linguarum do- no dixit Paulus datum esse ut signum sit, ἐ τοῖς πιςεύουσιν, ἀλλὰ τοῖς ἀπίστοις. Notandum igitur non dici hic, nulla fe- cisse Christum miracula Nazarethæ, sed fecisse non multa, quod & Marcus dicit. Fecit passim Christus miracula, ut hi quibus de ipso nihil constabat, in ipsum crederent: Credere incipientibus alia addidit, quibus in fide jam in- choata confirmarentur. Prima spernentibus plura non ingessit, ne vilesceret divina liberalitas. Ita solet Deus al- ternis beneficia præstare & oficia exigere.

## 14:1 Argument
CHAPTER XIV.

ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

Herod, hearing about Jesus, suspects that John has been raised from the dead, whom he had thrown into prison because he had censured his marriage with his brother's wife, and on his birthday, at the solicitation of the dancing daughter who pleased him, he had caused John's head to be cut off. Therefore Jesus withdrew into the desert, followed by a great crowd, which he fed with five loaves and two small fish, with 12 baskets of leftovers remaining after 5000 men had been satisfied. To the disciples in danger in a boat, Jesus, walking on the sea, comes to their aid with comfort. He bids Peter, who wishes to come to him on the water, to do so, and catches him as he trembles and begins to sink, and having entered the boat with him, he is acknowledged as the Son of God, and is carried to the land of Gennesaret, and heals those coming to him there.

There are three parts: I. The history of the beheading of John, to v. 12. II. The history of the feeding of the five thousand men in the desert, to v. 21. III. Of the walking of Jesus and Peter on the sea: with the subsequent journey into Gennesaret and the healing of the sick, to v. 36.

PART I.

The history of the beheading of John.

Vers. 1. Ἐν ἐκείνῳ τῷ καιρῷ] How did Jesus become known to Herod so late? Naturally, things that do not please tyrants to hear are rarely told to them. But I believe most of Christ's miracles occurred while Herod was on a Roman journey. Soon the affairs of the Arabian war occupied him.

Casaubon refutes this reason: Some wish to say that Herod was absent from Judea during the previous years of our Lord's preaching, occupied in an Arabian expedition against King Aretas. But I ask, whence do they have it that Herod managed the war in person, and not while absent through his legates? For Josephus, from whom alone they learned the history, recorded the contrary in express words; for in book XVIII he writes thus concerning both of these kings: Ἐ δυνάμεως ἑκατέρω συλλεγείσης, εἰς πόλεμον καθίσαντο, ςρατηγὸς ἀπεσταλκότες ἀνθ' ἑαυτῶν. After forces had been gathered on both sides, war was kindled between the kings; who sent their own legates in their stead. Therefore, the absence of Herod because of the Arabian war, is not history, but rather their conjecture, fighting diametrically against historical truth. But then, what they say, that this war was drawn out for many years, because Josephus makes mention of Vitellius, the Governor of Syria, in his explanation of it; this also shows their wonderful Chronology. death of Philip the Tetrarch, as is clear from the history of Josephus. Who writes that Philip had fulfilled his fate in the twentieth year of Tiberius, as the Greek edition has it; or even the twenty-second, as the version of Rufinus has it, and Scaliger defends. But even if the former number is retained, the war nevertheless could not have been waged before the following year, because of Herod's journey to Rome: whence, before he had returned, and the controversy of the Kings had erupted into open war, a space of less than a year cannot have passed. Let us suppose, therefore, that this war was waged at the end of the twenty-first year of Tiberius, for it could certainly not have been sooner: that is the year in which Vitellius was sent into Syria to succeed Pilate. Wherefore it is false that, because mention of Vitellius occurs in the narrative of that war, it must have been drawn out for many years. But since they refer the Lord's passion to the eighteenth year of Tiberius, which was at least the third year before the aforementioned war was waged; it appears with what judgment they maintain that the reason why Herod was ignorant of the first years of Christ's preaching was that, being occupied with waging war, he was away from home: for thus an anachronism of five or six years, or more, is committed.

Ὁ τετράρχης] Kings are sometimes distinguished from Tetrarchs, as in Horace: 'sometimes kings and tetrarchs, speaking of all great things': sometimes the tetrarchs themselves, as Dejotarus to Cicero, are called kings. The origin of the name is from Galatia, whose three parts each had four princes. Thence the name passed to others ruling over a part of some nation.

Τὴν ἀκοὴν] Thus the Hellenists translate the Hebrew שׁמע which signifies fame, as appears in Exodus 23:1. Nor is that word adapted only to the one hearing, but also to the one spreading the fame, as in Isaiah 53:1. In a similar way Tacitus said 'auditionem' for fame.

Latin:

CAPUT XIV.

ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Herodes audiens de Jesu suspicatur Iohannem esse resuscitatum, quem in carcerem conje- cerat, quod ejus conjugium cum fratris u- xore taxarat, & natali suo filia saltatri- ce, qua delectabatur, caput Johannis sol- licitante, decollari fecerat. Ideo secessit Jesus in desertum, sequente multa turba, quam panibus quinq; & duobus pisciculis cibavit, reliquiis manentibus 12. cophino- rum, postquam 5000. virorum saturata essent. Navigio periclitantibus discipulis Jesus mari inambulans solatio succurrit. Petrum volentem ad se in aqua venire ju- bet trepidantem, & submergi incipientem apprehendit, & cum eo navem ingressus, Filius Dei agnoscitur, & in terram Ge- nezareth provehitur, eoque venientes sa- nat.

Partes tres sunt: I. Historia Johannis decollati, ad v. 12. II. Historia cibationis quinque millium virorum in deserto, ad v. 21. III. Ambulationis Jesu & Petri in mari: cum consequentibus prove- ctione in Genezareth & ægrotorum sanatione, ad v. 36.

PARS I.

Historia decollationis Iohannis.

Vers. 1. Ἐν ἐκείνῳ τῷ καιρῷ] Qui tam sero Herodi Iesus innotuit? Nimirum raro Tyrannis dicuntur quæ audire eos non juvat. Sed credo pleraque Christi miracula con- tigisse dum Herodes in Romano est itinere. Mox Arabici belli negotia illum distinuere.

Hanc causam diluit Casaubonus: Volunt qui- dam Herodem superioribus annis prædicationis Domi- ni nostri è Judæa abfuisse, occupatum in expeditione Arabica contra Regem Aretam. Obsecro vero, unde habent illi Herodem per se bellum administrasse, non absentem per legatos suos? Josephus enim à quo so- lo historiam didicêre, contrarium verbis conceptis me- moriæ prodidit; nam lib. XVIII. de utroque horum Regũ ita scribit: Ἐ δυνάμεως ἑκατέρω συλλεγείσης, εἰς πόλεμον καθίσαντο, ςρατηγὸς ἀπεσταλκότες ἀνθ' ἑαυτῶν. Postquam utrimq; erant copiæ con- scriptæ, bellum inter Reges conflatũ est; qui vicẽ suam Legatos suos miserunt. Absentia igitur Herodis propter bellum Arabicum, historia non est, verum conjectura illorum, pugnans è diametro cum histo- rica veritate. Tum autem quod ajunt, bellum hoc multos annos fuisse tractum, quia in ejus explicatio- ne Vitellii Praesidis Syriae mentionem facit Josephus; mirificam eorum Chronologiam etiam hic ostendit. Res ita habet : Belli hujus causa contracta est post Philippi Tetrarchae mortem, ut clarum est ex histo- ria Josephi. Qui fato functum esse Philippum scribit, anno Tiberii vigesimo, ut habet Graeca edi- tio; vel etiam vigesimo secundo, ut habet Rufini versio, & defendit Scaliger. Sed etsi prior nume- rus retineatur, bellum tamen ante proximum an- num geri non potuit, propter Herodis profectionem Romam: unde priusquam rediisset, & controversia Regum in bellum apertum erupisset, annuo minus spatium praeteriisse non potest. Ponamus igitur anno Tiberii XXI. exeunte bellum istud esse gestum, citius enim profecto non potuit: is est annus, quo Vitellius missus est in Syriam, ut Pilato succederet. Quare falsum est, oportere, quia in ejus belli nar- ratione Vitellii incidat mentio, ut id multos annos fuerit tractum. Quum autem Dominicam passio- nem referant ad annum Tiberii XVIII. qui fuit ter- tius minimum annus ante gestum superius bellum; apparet quo judicio statuant, causam cur praedica- tionis Christi primos annos ignoraverit Herodes, fuisse, quod bello gerendo occupatus, domo abesset: nam sic anachronismus committitur, annorum quinque vel sex, aut plurium.

Ὁ τετράρχης] Distinguuntur interdum reges à Tetrar- chis ut Horatio, modo reges atque tetrarchas omnia magna lo- quens: modo tetrarchae ipsi, ut Dejotarus Ciceroni, reges appellantur. Origo nominis ex Galatia cujus tres partes singulae quatuor habebant principes. Inde ad alios gentis alicujus parti imperantes nomen transiit.

Τὴν ἀκοὴν] Ita Hellenistae transferunt Hebræum שׁמע quod famam significat, ut apparet Exod. XXIII. 1. Neque tantum audienti sed & famam vulganti ea vox aptatur, ut Esaiae LIII. 1. Simili serme modo auditionem pro fama di- xit Tacitus.

## 14:2
Vers. 2. Τοῖς παισὶν ἀυτᾶ] He said this to the servants of the court more freely, not asserting it, but doubting whether what some were saying, that John had come back to life, was true. That saying of Virgil is not spoken rashly: 'I will be present as a shade in all places: you, wicked one, shall pay the penalty.' And in Euripides, Orestes exclaims: 'O mother, I beseech you, do not set upon me the blood-eyed and serpent-like maidens.' It should not be doubted that the image of a most holy and innocent man, slaughtered by crime, hovered in Herod's mind by night and by day: to the stings of conscience was added the inseparable companion of tyrants, fear. At that time too, says Seneca, 'when they are not being sought, they judge themselves to be sought, and have no moment immune from fear': The wise Hebrew joins both in 17:11: 'for wickedness is a cowardly thing, condemned by its own witness; and it always takes on hardships, being constrained by conscience.'

Ὁ βαπτιςὴς] So also Josephus: 'John who is called the Baptist.' כהן מטבל to the Hebrews: for it should not be doubted that the Niphal is there placed for the Piel, as is often done by the Rabbis: thus in Zechariah 9:9, the LXX translate נושע as σώζων. The teachers of the Hebrews call the same John כהן הגרר whence it may be allowed to think that Zechariah was the prince of his own family: but since sacred history never says this, and indeed indicates the contrary when it says that the λειτεργίαν (ministry) fell to Zechariah by lot, I am led to believe that John was called כהן, that is, a priest, κατ᾿ ἐξοχην ἰκῶς (by way of excellence), so that he might be understood as an excellent minister of God, just as Moses is also called כהן in the Psalm. For the Chaldean Paraphrast also, without doubt from the custom of the Jews, calls Elijah and Jeremiah great Priests. Elijah indeed in the paraphrase of the Song of Solomon: Jeremiah, however, in the title of Lamentations.

Αὐτὸς ἠγέρθη ἀπὸ τῶν νεκρῶν] Among the various opinions of the Hebrews concerning the soul, I believe there were some in ancient times (for it is not doubted that it is now defended by many Kabbalists) who taught the transition into other bodies, whence the Pythagorean dogma of palingenesis was drawn. For the fact that some thought John, who was well known to them (for he was of the priestly race), was Elijah while he was still living, others Jeremiah, cannot, in my judgment, be referred to the ἀνάςασιν (resurrection) or even to a similarity of spirit, but it shows that the transmigration of souls was believed. Indeed, some of the Hebrews have handed down that Phinehas and Elijah had the same soul: others that Adam, David, and the Messiah had the same. And that which the Greeks call transmigration of souls, they themselves call גלגול נפשות. I do not, however, think that the passage of Josephus should be drawn into this: for he is speaking not of any Jews from the common people, but of the Pharisees, who, as we are taught elsewhere in the Apostolic Writings, believed not in παλιγγενεσίαν but in ἀνάστασιν. Josephus himself elsewhere expresses their dogma thus: ἀθάνατόν τε ἰσχὺν ταῖς ψυχαῖς πίστις αὐτοῖς εἶναι, καὶ ὑπὸ χθονὸς δικαιώσεις τε καὶ τιμὰς οἷς ἀρετῆς ἢ κακίας ἐπιτήδευσις ἐν τῷ βίῳ γέγονε· καὶ ταῖς μὲν εἱργμὸν ἀΐδιον προστίθεσθαι, ταῖς δὲ ῥαστώνην τοῦ ἀναβιοῦν. Josephus therefore seems to have understood the mind of the Pharisees in this way, that souls are not returned to the same bodies, but are clothed by God with another body: not that they may live here, but in places that escape our knowledge. And this is what he says: ψυχὴν δὲ πᾶσαν μὲν ἄφθαρτον, μεταβαίνειν δὲ εἰς ἕτερον σῶμα τὴν τῶν ἀγαθῶν μόνην: which he also makes clearer in Book III of the Jewish War, where, arguing περὶ τῆς αὐτοχειρίας, he addresses his countrymen thus: ἆρα οὐκ ἴστε ὅτι τῶν μὲν ἐξιόντων τοῦ βίου χρέος ἐκλιπόντων, ὅταν ὁ θεὸς κομίσασθαι θέλῃ, κλέος μὲν αἰώνιον, οἶκοι δὲ καὶ γενεαὶ βέβαιοι, καθαραὶ δὲ ὑπακούουσιν αἱ ψυχαὶ χῶρον οὐρανοῦ λαχοῦσαι τὸν ἁγιώτατον, ἔνθεν ἐκ περιτροπῆς αἰώνων ἁγίοις πάλιν ἀντενοικίζονται σώμασιν. And in the second book against Apion: ὅτι τοῖς τοὺς νόμους διαφυλάξασι, κ᾿ ἂν εἰ δέοι θνήσκειν ὑπὲρ αὐτῶν, προθύμως ἀποθανοῦσιν, ἔδωκεν ὁ θεὸς γενέσθαι τε πάλιν, καὶ βίον ἀμείνω λαβεῖν ἐκ περιτροπῆς. Thus, according to his own opinion and that of certain others, David Kimchi says on Malachi IV that Elijah will come in a new body, the old one having long since been dissolved. Moreover, that opinion of Herod and also of others from the common people (for Luke teaches us that it arose from others) cannot pertain to παλιγγενεσίαν, because according to that view, souls are insinuated not into adults, but into those being born. It follows, therefore, that they believed the soul of John had either assumed a new body, or had even returned into that body which had been buried by the disciples. Nor ought that to seem so new, since the ancient histories of bodies resuscitated by Elijah and Elisha were extant. This suspicion was increased because it was heard that the κήρυγμα of Jesus was the same as that of John had been, concerning repentance and the heavenly kingdom.

Διὰ τοῦτο] Namely, because God wished in that way to testify to the innocence of John and the wicked crime of Herod.

Αἱ δυνάμεις] Thus are called here not the miracles themselves, as often, but the gifts that produce miracles.

Ἐνεργοῦσιν] They exert their power. For thus this word is used intransitively in Gal. II. 8, Eph. II. 2.

Latin:

Vers. 2. Τοῖς παισὶν ἀυτᾶ] Aulae mancipiis haec dixit li- berius, neque asseverans, sed dubitans an quod quidam dicebant, Johannem revixisse, verum esset. Non temere dictum illud a Virgilio: Omnibus umbra locis adero: dabis improbe poenas. Et apud Euripidem Orestes exclamat: Ὦ μῆτερ, ἱκετέυω σε, μὴ πίσειέ μοι Τὰς αἱματωπὸς κᾀ δρακοντώδεις κόρας. Dubitari non debet quin sanctissimi & innocentissimi viri per scelus trucidati imago noctu diuque Herodis animo oberraverit: Conscientiae stimulis accessit comes individ- sus tyrannorum metus. Eo quoque tempore, inquit Seneca, quo non captantur peti se judicant, nullumque momentum immune à metu habent: Utrumque conjungit sapiens He- braeus XVII. 11. δειλὸν γὰρ ἰδίᾳ πονηρία μάρτυρι καταδικαζο- μένη· ἀεὶ δὲ προσείληφε τὰ χαλεπὰ συνεχομένη τῇ συνειδήσει.

Ὁ βαπτιςὴς] Ita & Josephus Ἰωάννη τῷ ἐπικαλυμένῳ βα- πτιςῇ. כהן מטבל Hebraeis: nam quin ibi Niphal sit positum pro Piel, ut à Rabbinis saepe, dubitari non debet: ita apud Zachariam IX. 9. נושע LXX. vertunt σώζων. Vocant eun- dem Johannem Hebræorum magistri כהן הגרר unde arbitrari liceat Zachariam fuisse familiae suae principem: sed cum nunquam id dicat sacra historia, imo contrarium potius indicet cum sortito Zachariae λειτεργίαν dicit obti- gisse, inducor ut credam Johannem כהן id est sacerdotem dictum κατ᾿ ἐξοχην ἰκῶς, ut intelligeretur excellens Dei mini- ster, quomodo & Moses in Psalmo כהן vocatur. Nam & Chaldaeus Paraphrastes haud dubie ex Judaeorum consue- tudine Eliam & Jeremiam vocat Sacerdotes magnos. E- liam quidem in paraphrasi Cantici Solomonis: Jeremiam autem in titulo Threnorum.

Αὐτὸς ἠγέρθη ἀπὸ τῶν νεκρῶν] Inter varias Hebræorum de anima sententias credo antiquitus fuisse (nam nunc à multis Cabalistis id defendi non dubium est) qui transitio- nem in alia corpora docerent, unde inde haustum Pytha- goricum δόγμα παλιγγενεσίας. Nam quod quidam Johan- nem satis sibi notum (erat enim e gente Sacerdotali) cum adhuc viveret esset putarunt Eliam, alii Jeremiam, non po- test, me judice, ad ἀνάςασιν aut etiam ad spiritus similitudi- nem referri, sed oftendit creditam animarum μετενσωμά- τωσιν. Quin & Hebræorum nonnulli tradiderunt Phineæ & Eliæ eandem fuisse animam: alii eandem Adami, Davi- dis & Messiæ. Atque eam quam Græci vocant μετενσωμά- τωσιν ipsi appellant גלגול נפשות. Josephi tamen lo- cum eo trahendum non arbitror: agit enim non de quibus- vis ex plebe Judæis, sed de Pharisæis, qui ut & Scriptis A- postolicis alibi docemur, crediderunt non παλιγγενεσίαν sed ἀνάστασιν. Ipse Josephus alibi ita eorum dogma exprimit: ἀθάνατόν τε ἰσχὺν ταῖς ψυχαῖς πίστις αὐτοῖς εἶναι, καὶ ὑπὸ χθονὸς δικαιώσεις τε καὶ τιμὰς οἷς ἀρετῆς ἢ κακίας ἐπιτήδευσις ἐν τῷ βίῳ γέγονε· καὶ ταῖς μὲν εἱργμὸν ἀΐδιον προστίθεσθαι, ταῖς δὲ ῥαστώνην τοῦ ἀναβιοῦν. Videtur igitur Josephus ita accepisse mentem Phari- sæorum, non eadem corpora animus reddi, sed alio eas cor- pore à Deo vestiri: non ut hic vivant, sed in locis nostram notitiam fugientibus. Et hoc esse quod dicit: ψυχὴν δὲ πᾶσαν μὲν ἄφθαρτον, μεταβαίνειν δὲ εἰς ἕτερον σῶμα τὴν τῶν ἀ- γαθῶν μόνην: quod etiam manifestius facit belli Judaici lib. III. ubi περὶ τῆς αὐτοχειρίας disputans ita populares suos al- loquitur: ἆρα οὐκ ἴστε ὅτι τῶν μὲν ἐξιόντων τοῦ βίου χρέος ἐκλιπόν- των, ὅταν ὁ θεὸς κομίσασθαι θέλῃ, κλέος μὲν αἰώνιον, οἶκοι δὲ καὶ γενεαὶ βέβαιοι, καθαραὶ δὲ ὑπακούουσιν αἱ ψυχαὶ χῶρον οὐρα- νοῦ λαχοῦσαι τὸν ἁγιώτατον, ἔνθεν ἐκ περιτροπῆς αἰώνων ἁγίοις πάλιν ἀντενοικίζονται σώμασιν. Et libro altero adversus A- pionem: ὅτι τοῖς τοὺς νόμους διαφυλάξασι, κ᾿ ἂν εἰ δέοι θνήσκειν ὑπὲρ αὐτῶν, προθύμως ἀποθανοῦσιν, ἔδωκεν ὁ θεὸς γενέσθαι τε πά- λιν, καὶ βίον ἀμείνω λαβεῖν ἐκ περιτροπῆς. Sic ex sua & alio- rum quorundam sententia David Kimchi ad IV. Malachiæ Eliam ait venturum in novo corpore, vetere pridem resolu- to. Cæterum illa Herodis atque etiam aliorum è vulgo opinio (nam ab aliis ortam docet nos Lucas) ad παλιγγενε- σίαν pertinere non potest, quia ex illa sententia animæ non jam adultis sed nascentibus insinuantur. Sequitur igitur, ut crediderint Johannis animam aut novum assumsisse cor- pus, aut etiam rediisse in corpus illud quod à discipulis erat sepultum. Neque id novum adeo videri debet, cum resusci- tatorum ab Elia & Elisæo corporum veteres historiæ exsta- rent. Suspicionem hanc auxit quod audiretur idem esse κήρυγμα Jesu quod Johannis fuerat, de pœnitentia & re- gno cœlesti.

Διὰ τοῦτο] Scilicet quia Deus eo modo testatam velit Johannis innocentiam & Herodis sceleratum facinus.

Αἱ δυνάμεις] Ita vocantur hic non ipse miracula, ut sæ- pe, sed dona miraculorum effectricia.

Ἐνεργοῦσιν] Vim suam exserunt. Ita enim ἀμεταβατικῶς hæc vox usurpatur Gal. II. 8. Eph. II. 2.

## 14:3
Vers. 3. ὁ γὰρ Ἡρώδης] It is a parenthesis, narrating by occasion what had been done before, ὕστερον πρότερον in the Homeric manner, as Cicero says, which figure rhetoricians also unanimously call πρωθύστερον. Nor is there any doubt that there are many such things here and there in the scripture of the Old and New Testament, although not everywhere so conspicuous: so that the Jews have not undeservedly said that in the sacred letters there is no τὸ πρότερον καὶ τὸ ὕστερον, that is, that the order of times is not exactly observed; but many things are narrated as the occasion presented itself. However, there would be less obscurity in such figures if the Hebrews had distinctions of past time, as the Greeks and Latins have the imperfect, perfect, and pluperfect. Now all those have the same sound among them. Here also our interpreter has placed an aorist in place of the pluperfect. Thus Gen. XII. ויאמר he had said was to be translated, it is apparent from that which had preceded in chapter XI. 31, and from the passage in Acts VII. 5.

We have observed that these things are recounted in their proper place in the Harmony of the Evangelists. There is therefore no such πρωθύστερον here, at least as much as is posited by Grotius: which is rather to be posited in Luke VII. Meanwhile, we do not deny with Beza that the beheading of John had already happened before, and is mentioned by occasion. Concerning the time of the beheading of John, Lightfoot in Hor. Ebr. page 182. We elicit the time of his beheading from those words of the Evangelist John, chapter VI. 4. 'And the Passover was now near,' by this reasoning. It can be concluded without controversy that the disciples, as soon as they heard of the death of their master and buried him, betook themselves to Christ, narrating the same things about their Master, and providing him with a warning by that example so that he might consult for his own safety. He, the matter having been heard, crosses into the desert of Bethsaida, and there feeds five thousand men miraculously, when the Passover was already near, as John reports, recognizing that history with the remaining Evangelists. Therefore, we think the decapitation of the Baptist was a little before the Passover, when he had already suffered imprisonment for a year and a half, just as he had preached freely for a year and a half before his incarceration.

Διὰ Ἡρωδιάδα] For her sake, although Josephus reports another cause, that Herod feared a defection of the people, I do not think so, because he believed John to be a seditious man, whose whole life was composed toward piety; but because the wicked hate and fear whatever is hostile to their vices in a prince. The good, he says, are always more suspect than the bad, and another's virtue is always fearsome. Thus we see Jews, Christians, and even professors of wisdom driven from the city by the worst of the Emperors, so that nothing honorable might ever meet their eyes. For even if good men remain as silent as possible, which is not always right, their very life reproaches tyrants for their shameful deeds. For which matter they find no other remedy than to suppress great hatreds with great fear.

Φιλίππꙋ.

The Vulgate omitted this name by a manifest error, since it is read consistently here, as well as in Mark 6:17 and John 3:19, not only in all Greek Codices and versions—Syriac, Arabic, Ethiopic, Persian—but also in the Latin interpreter: whence the Jesuit Conzenius was too bold in asserting that it is sufficiently certain that that name was added here from a gloss. We have here Grotius agreeing, whom we deservedly oppose as a patron of the Papists to the patrons of the Vulgate; his words are these: Since this name exists in all copies of Mark, and even in the most ancient ones of Matthew and Luke, and in all those places in the Syriac and Latin interpreters, the reading should not be disturbed. Nor could those writers have easily erred here, as I think, I would have proven even from a non-Christian. For first, three writers agree, who in those very times, or certainly closer to those times than anyone else, committed to memory that matter which was neither obscure nor ignoble, but, as the affairs of kings are, most well-known to all. Add that more than one of the Jews names Philip as the husband of this woman. Moreover, the supreme trustworthiness and diligence of Josephus, and the intimate knowledge of the affairs of that family which appears everywhere in him, deserves that we do not pronounce anything rashly against him. Wherefore I believe it most true that among the sons of Herod the Great, who were nine, two were named Philip; but that the latter of these, who was born from the daughter of Simon the High Priest, was called Philip Herod, just as this one, about whom this history is told, was called Antipater or Antipas Herod: and by this addition this younger Philip was distinguished from the other older one, who was Tetrarch of Trachonitis. Nor should it seem more wonderful that two were called Philip in such a number of children than that two were likewise called Antipater in the same number. For Antipater and Antipas are the same name. Nor do I doubt that there was some Philip among the progenitors of Herod the Great, from whom that name was propagated into many of his offspring.

Latin:

Vers. 3. ὁ γὰρ Ἡρώδης] Est Παρεμβολὴ ex occasione nar- rans quod ante erat gestum, ὕστερον πρότερον ὁμηρικῶς, ut in- quit Cicero, quam figuram Rhetores etiam una voce πρω- θύστερον vocant. Neque dubium est quin multa passim sint talia in veteris & novi fœderis scriptura, etsi non ubique tam conspicua: ut non immerito dixerint Judæi in sacris literis non esse τὸ πρότερον καὶ τὸ ὕστερον, hoc est ordinem illum tem- porum non exacte observari; sed multa narrari ut se tulit occasio. Minus autem obscuritatis inesset figuris talibus, si haberent Hebræi discrimina transacti temporis, ut habent Græci & Latini imperfectum, perfectum & plusquamperfe- ctum. Nunc illa omnia apud ipsos habent eundem sonum. Hic etiam noster interpres vice plusquamperfecti posuit ἀέ- ριστον. Sic Gen. XII. ויאמר vertendum dixerat, apparet ex eo quod præcesserat cap. XI. 31. & ex loco Act. VII. 5.

Hæc vero in propria sede recenseri in Har- monia Evangelistarum observavimus. Nullum ergo hic tantum πρωθύστερον, quantum quidem à Grotio constituitur: quod potius Luc. VII. con- stituendum. Interim decollationem Johannis antea jam contigisse, & ex occasione commemora- ri Bezæ non obnuimus. De tempore decolla- tionis Joh. Lightfooth in hor. Ebr. pag. 182. Tem- pus decollationis ejus elicimus ex verbis istis Joannis Evangelistæ, cap. VI. 4. Aderat jam autem Pascha, hac ratiocinatione. Absque controversia concludi potest, Discipulos, quamprimum de morte magi- stri audientes, eumque sepelientes, ad Christum se contulisse, eadem Magistri narrantes, eique cautio- nem isto exemplo præbentes ut sibi consuleret de salute sua. Is, re audita, transit in desertum Bethsaida, atqs illic quinq; hominum millia pascit miraculose, cum adeffet jam Pascha, ut refert Johannes historiam istam recognoscens cum reliquis Evangelistis. Decapita- tionem ergo Baptistæ arbitramur fuisse paulo ante Pascha, cum carcerem jam passus fuerat per ses- quiannum, prout per sesquiannum libere prædicasset ante incarcerationem.

Διὰ Ἡρωδιάδα] In ejus gratiam, quanquam Josephus al- teram causam refert, quod metuerit Herodes defectionem populi, non arbitror, quod Johannem hominem seditio- sum crederet, cujus tota vita ad pietatem erat composita; sed quia oderunt & metuunt mali principis quicquid vi- tiisinimicum est. Boni, inquit ille, quam mali suspectiores sunt semperque aliena virtus formidolosa est. Ita videmus à pessimis quibusq; Imperatorum pulsos urbe Judæos, chri- stianos, etiamque sapientiæ professores, ne quid usquam honestum oculis occurreret. Nam ut viri boni quam maxi- me taceant, quod tamen non semper fas est, tamen ipsa il- lorum vita tyrannis sua flagitia exprobrat. Cui rei non aliud inveniunt remedium, quam ut magna odia magno metu compescant.

Φιλίππꙋ.

Nomen hoc prætermisit Vulgatus errore ma- nifesto, quum non tantum in omnibus Codicibus Græcis & versionibus, Syra, Arabica, Æthiopica, Persica, hic, sed & Marci VI. 17. Joh. III. 19. con- stanter legatur: unde audaculus nimis Conzenius Jesuita fuit, asserendo, satis constare nomen illud bic additum ex glossa. Habemus hic consitentem Grotium, quem ceu Papistarum Patronum Vul- gatæ Patronis merito opponimus; cujus hæc sunt: Cum nomen hoc exstet in Marci exemplaribus omnibus, in antiquissimis etiam Matthæi, & Lucæ, atque omnibus i- stis locis apud Syrum & Latinum interpretes, sollicitanda le- ctio non est. Neque errare hic potuisse eos scriptores facile, ut arbitror, vel à non Christiano evicerim.. Primum enim consentiunt tres scriptores, qui illis ipsis temporibus, aut certe propius ea tempora, quam quisquam alius, rem istam non obscuram neque ignobilem, sed ut res sunt regum, o- mnibus notissimam memoriæ mandarunt. Adde quod Ju- dæorum non unus hujus fœminæ maritum Philippum no- minat. Josephi autem summa fides & diligentia, & quæ passim in eo apparet intima cognitio rerum familiæ istius meretur, ne quid temere contra eum pronunciemus. Qua- re verissimum credo inter Herodis magni filios, qui no- vem fuere, duos appellatos fuisse Philippos; sed horum alterum qui natus erat ex Simonis Pontificis filia, dictum fuisse Philippum Herodem, quomodo & iste de quo hæc narratur historia, Antipater aut Antipas Herodes diceba- tur: atque isto additamento Philippum hunc minorem di- stinctum ab altero majore, qui Trachonitidis fuit Tetrar- cha. Neque duos in tot liberum numero dictos fuisse Philippos magis mirum videri debet, quam duos itidem eodem in numero dictos Antipatros. Nam Antipatri & Antipæ idem est nomen. Neque dubito quin inter He- rodis magni progenitores Philippus aliquis fuerit, unde id nomen in multos ejus genitis propagatum est.

## 14:4
Vers. 4. ἔκ ἐξεςί σοι] It is unlawful for you, as one circumcised and therefore bound to the observance of the law given through Moses. Roman law pronounces the prince exempt from the laws. But the law of Moses grants no favor to a king any more than to a private citizen: although that shameful act of Herod, certainly at the time when it began to be committed, was opposed not only to the laws of Moses but also to the laws of nature, which bind all nations and the kings of nations in any case. Euripides says well: 'Those who rule should not rule where they ought not.' ἔχειν αὐτήν] ἔχειν here signifies to have in marriage, which the Syriac expressed, not like ἔχειν παῖδα, and 'who had Chrysis yesterday?' For Herod calls it a marriage: he uses this name to cloak his guilt. For both Josephus and Mark openly signify this. The writer of the work 'On those things after the accusations' among the works of Aristotle says: 'A man is said to have a wife, and a woman a husband. But the way just mentioned seems most alien. For we signify nothing else by "to have" than to live together.' And yet it is a lesser abuse when a man is said to have a woman than when a woman is said to have a man. For by the laws and customs of most nations, a wife is in the hand of her husband: certainly by the law of the Hebrews, who for that reason call a husband בעל: just as the Attics call him κύριον. Mark explains the reason why it was unlawful for Herod, when he makes John speak thus: 'It is not lawful for you to have your brother's wife,' by which words, since the Baptist seems to point his finger at that law which exists in Leviticus chapter 18, verse 6, which the LXX translated in this manner, 'You shall not uncover the nakedness of your brother's wife,' I am easily led to believe that the husband of Herodias was dead when John said these things to her. For we see that even in the law, she is called a wife who is no longer under a husband, by a relation made to that which she had been. In taking away Herodias, the transgression of Herod the Tetrarch was twofold. For to take away a wife from a living husband, not dismissed by him, was abduction and adultery, with this more notable injury, that it was committed against a brother. To the adultery was added the crime of incest according to the law of Moses which we mentioned. For that law had only one exception, if the husband had died childless. But the husband of Herodias was both living at that time and had a daughter by her, Salome, who is mentioned here. Josephus briefly touched upon both offenses when he said: 'With whom (Salome) Herodias, having thought of the offspring in confusion of the ancestral customs (he indicates the law of Leviticus), is married to Herod, having separated from her husband while he was living, who was his brother by the same father.' It appears from this passage that Tertullian and those who followed him are mistaken when they think that Herodias married Herod the Tetrarch only after the death of her former husband. Furthermore, those words 'having separated while he was living' seem to hint that the former husband did not survive that divorce for long. And indeed John does not accuse the beginning, but the very τὸ ἔχειν (having). David, contrary to the law, had usurped the wife of Uriah: but when Uriah was dead, he had her as his wife by the best of rights: because the former marriage being dissolved, there was no other law that would impede the marriage. But here, even with the former husband dead, or even while he was alive, having testified that he did not wish her to be his wife, another law stood in the way, namely that which forbids ἔχειν τὴν γυναῖκα τοῦ ἀδελφοῦ (to have the wife of one's brother). To act against this law was συγχέειν τὰ πάτρια (to confound ancestral customs), which was not permitted even to a king, as we have already said. Josephus notes the same crime in Archelaus, who married Glaphyra, the wife of his dead brother Alexander, who had children, ἀπώμοτον ὃν Ἰουδαίοις γαμετὰς ἀδελφῶν ἄγεσθαι (a thing forbidden to the Jews to take the wives of brothers). Luke adds that the Tetrarch was reproved by the Baptist not only on account of this offense, but περὶ πάντων ὧν ἐποίησε πονηρῶν (concerning all the evil things which he had done).

These Grotian points are to be opposed to Bellarmine, book 1, on matrimony, chapter 17, and to Conzenius on this passage, the Jesuits. For they contend that John reproved the deed of Herod for the reason that Philip was still among the living. Although indeed Augustine, On Faith and Works, chapter 19, says that this is ambiguous, and it seems that he joined his brother's wife to himself with a certain appearance of honesty, because, as Mark testifies, ἐγάμησεν αὐτὴν (he married her), veiling the incest with the honor of marriage: yet from the correction itself, 'it is not lawful for you to have her as a wife,' it is evident that John disapproved of that marriage on account of the degree of kinship: and not because he had taken the wife of his brother while he was alive. And our countrymen rightly conclude that the laws of Leviticus 18 were not merely forensic, which do not bind in the New Testament, but pertain to the law of nature: against which Herod had offended, and was therefore reproved by John; just as Bellarmine calls this marriage incestuous, which certainly is repugnant to the law of nature.

Latin:

Vers. 4. ἔκ ἐξεςί σοι] Nefas est tibi, utpote circumciso ac proinde obligato ad observationem legis, per Mosem datæ. Jus Romanum Principem legibus solutum pronun- tiat. At Mosis lex regi non magis quam privato sui gra- tiam facit: quanquam illud Herodis flagitium, tunc cer- te cum patrari cœpit, non Mosis tantum, sed & naturæ le- gibus adversabatur, quæ omnes utique gentes & gentium reges tenent.
