Bene Euripides: Οὐ τὰς κρατῶντας χρὴ κρατεῖν ἃ μὴ χρεών. ἔχειν αὐτήν] ἔχειν significat hic habere in matri- monio, quod expressit Syrus, non ut ἔχειν παῖδα, & quis heri Chrysidem habuit? Nam Herodes Conjugium vocat: hoc prætexit nomine culpam. Id enim & aperte Josephus & Marcus significant. Scriptor τῶν μετὰ τὰς κατηγορίας inter opera Aristotelis: λέγεται κὴ ὁ ἀνὴρ γυναῖκα ἔχειν, καὶ ἡ γυνὴ ἄνδρα. ἔοικε δὲ ἀλλοτριωτάτῳ ὁ νῦν ῥηθεὶς τρόπῳ. ὐδὲν γὰρ ἄλλο τῷ ἔχειν σημαίνομεν ἢ ὅτι συνοι- κεῖν. Atqui minor est abusio cum vir dicitur mulierem ha- bere, quam cum mulier virum. Nam plerarumque gen- tium legibus atque institutis uxor in manu est mariti: certe Hebræorum jure qui propterea maritum בעל vocant: ut κύριον Attici. Causam cur nefas Herodi fuerit, Marcus explicat, cum ita Johannem loquentem facit: ὐκ ἐξεςί σοι ἔχειν τὴν γυναῖκα τῶ ἀδελφῶ τꙋ, quibus verbis cum digitum intendere videatur Baptista in legem eam, quæ exstat Levi- tici capite XVIII. commate 6. quam LXX. hunc in modum verterunt, ἀχημοσύνην γυναικὸς ἀδελφῶ ὐκ ἀποκαλύψεις, facile adducor, ut credam maritum Herodiadis cum ista Johannes diceret defunctum fuisse. Videmus enim etiam in lege γυναῖκα dici eam quæ non amplius sit ὕπανδρος, rela- tione facta ad id quod fuerat. In abducenda Herodiade du- plex fuit Herodis Tetrarchæ παρανομία. Nam viventi mari- to uxorem, non ab ipso dimissam, abducere, raptus atque adulterium erat, hoc infigniore injuria, quod in fratrem committebatur. Accedebat adulterio crimen incesti ex le- ge Mofis quam diximus. Nam ea lex unam duntaxat habe- bat exceptionem, si maritus mortuus esset illiberis. Hero- diadis autem maritus & vivebat eo tempore, & filiam ex i- psa habebat Salomen, cujus hic fit mentio. Breviter u- trumque delictum perstrinxit Josephus cum dixit: μεθ᾽ ἧς (Σαλώμης) τὰς γονὰς ἡ Ἡρωδιὰς ἐπὶ συγχύσει φρονήσασα τῶν πατρί- ων (legem Levitici indicat) Ἡρώδῃ γαμεῖται τῷ ἀνδρὸς τῷ ὁμο- πατρίῳ ἀδελφῷ διαστᾶσα ζῶντος. Apparet hoc ex loco fal- li Tertullianum & qui eum sunt secuti, cum existimant, Herodiadem Tetrarchæ Herodi nupsisse post mortem de- mum mariti prioris. Videntur præterea illa verba διαστᾶσα ζῶντος hoc innuere, maritum priorem non diu supervixis- se isto divortio. Et sane Johannes non initium accusat, sed ipsum τὸ ἔχειν. David contra legem uxorem Uriæ usurpa- verat: at mortuo Uria uxorem eam habuit optimo jure: quia soluto matrimonio priore nulla lex erat alia quæ nu- ptias impediret. At hic etiam mortuo marito priore, aut etiam dum viveret testato se eam uxorem sibi esse nolle, obstabat lex alia, ea nempe quæ vetat ἔχειν τὴν γυναῖκα τοῦ ἀδελφοῦ. Adversus hanc legem facere erat συγχέειν τὰ πά- τρια, quod nec regi licebat, ut jam diximus. Notat idem crimen in Archelao Josephus qui fratris Alexandri mortui uxorem duxit Glaphyram liberos habentem, ἀπώμοτον ὃν Ἰουδαίοις γαμετὰς ἀδελφῶν ἄγεσθαι. Addit Lucas reprehen- sum fuisse Tetrarcham à Baptista non hujus tantum delicti nomine, sed περὶ πάντων ὧν ἐποίησε πονηρῶν.

Hæc Grotiana Bellarmino l. 1. de matrim. c. 17. & Conzenio in hunc locum, Jesuitis opponenda. Hi enim contendunt, Johannem factum Herodis ideo reprehendisse, quod adhuc Philippus in vivis fuerit. Quanquam vero hoc ambiguum esse Au- gust. de fide & operibus c. XIX. dicat, & videatur specie quadam honestatis fratriam suam sibi con- junxisse, quia Marco teste ἐγάμησεν αὐτὴν conjugii honore obvelans incestum: ex ipsa tamen ἐπανορθώ- σει, non licet tibi eam habere in uxorem, constat, quod conjugium illud ob propinquitatis gradum improbarit Johannes: non vero quod vivente fra- tre uxorem ejus acceperit: Recteque nostrates colligunt, Leges Lev. XVIII. non fuisse forenses tantum, quæ in N.T. haud obligent, sed pertinere ad legem naturæ: contra quam deliquerat Hero- des, propterea à Johanne reprehensus: quemád- modum incestum vocat hoc conjugium Bellarmi- nus; qui utique legi naturæ repugnat.

## 14:5
Verse 5. Θέλων αὐτὸν ἀποκτεῖναι (Wishing to kill him)] Not with a definite will, but with an ambiguous mind. He hated the free reprover, for as Josephus most truly said, Βαρὺ τοῖς ἀδικεῖν ἰθύλεσι τὸ συνειχῶς νουθετεῖν (It is burdensome to those who intend to do wrong to be constantly admonished). Furthermore, he envied his reputation. But he had not yet reached the final line of wickedness which places pleasure in the magnitude of infamy. He feared the judgments of the people concerning himself if he were to kill such a man: he also feared his own conscience, having been accustomed formerly to listen to his warnings, before illicit love drove his mind astray: anger pushed his mind, fluctuating in doubt, by a slight momentum toward the worse side.

Ὡς προφήτην αὐτὸν εἶχον (They held him as a prophet)] As a man sent by God: for thus this word is explained below in chapter 21:25, 26.

Latin:

Vers. 5. Θέλων αὐτὸν ἀποκτεῖναι] Non definita voluntate, sed ambiguus animi. Oderat liberum castigatorem, nam ut verissime dixit Josephus Βαρὺ τοῖς ἀδικεῖν ἰθύλεσι τὸ συνει- χῶς νουθετεῖν. Præterea famæ ipsius invidebat. Sed nondum pervenerat ad ultimam improbitatis lineam quæ volupta- tem ponit in magnitudine infamiæ. Reverebatur populi de se judicia, si talem virum occideret: reverebatur suam quoque conscientiam, solitus olim ipsius monitis auscul- tare, antequam illicitus amor mentem transversam ageret: ira in dubio fluctuantem animum leve momentum in par- tem pejorem impulit.

Ὡς προφήτην αὐτὸν εἶχον] Ut hominem à Deo missum: ita enim hæc vox infra explicatur cap. XXI. 25. 26.

## 14:6
Verse 6. Γενεσίων δὲ ἀγομένων τοῦ Ἡρώδου (And when Herod's birthday was kept)] After the manner of the kings of the East. Herodotus: 'This dinner is prepared once a year on the day on which the king was born.' We have a very ancient example of this custom in Egypt, Genesis 40:20. Josephus concerning King Agrippa: 'Celebrating the day of his birth, when he set out festivities for all over whom he ruled.' The writer of the second book of Maccabees seems to say that the birthday was celebrated by Antiochus not every year, as was the custom for others, but every month.

Others more correctly interpret it not of the birthday of the reign, but of the birthday of Herod's life, Chrysostom, Lyser, Hunnius, and the passage in Genesis 40:20 is also to be understood in this way.

ὠρχήσατο (She danced)] With Ionic movements, as Horace says: not with that crude and uncomposed type of dancing which we have said was used in ancient times by Jewish matrons and virgins during public rejoicings. From neighboring kingdoms, that custom had spread into the Jewish court. Thus Josephus, in Antiquities II, narrates that a beautiful dancing girl was introduced into the banquet of the King of Egypt. Dio, concerning the King of Edessa in the times of Trajan: 'And he entertained him at dinner, and brought forward his own child dancing in a barbaric manner.'

Ἐν τῷ μέσῳ (In the midst)] With the guests looking on, as the Syriac rightly interprets.

Latin:

Vers. 6. Γενεσίων δὲ ἀγομένων τοῦ Ἡρώδου] More regum Ori- entis. Herodotus: τοῦτο δὲ τὸ δεῖπνον παρασκευάζεται ἅπαξ τοῦ ἐνιαυτοῦ ἡμέρῃ τῇ ἐγένετο βασιλεύς. Antiquissimum exem- plum ejus moris in Ægypto habemus, Gen. XL. 20. Josephus de rege Agrippa, ἡμέραν ὧν ἑορτάζων αὐτῷ γενέθλιον ὅτε πᾶσιν ὧν ἦρχεν ἐνφροσύνας καθίσαντο θάλειαι. Videtur Scriptor se- cundi Maccabæorum dicere ab Antiocho actum natalem non quotannis, ut mos erat aliis, sed quot mensibus.

Rectius alii non de die natali regni, sed natali vitæ Herodis interpretantur, Chrysost. Lyser. Hun- nius, ac de eo etiam accipiendus est locus Gen. XL. 10.

ὠρχήσατο] Motibus Jonicis, ut inquit Horatius: non rudi illo atque incomposito saltandi genere, quod in publi- cis gaudiis matronis virginibusq; Judæis antiquitus usurpa- tum diximus. A finitimis regnis mos iste in aulam Judæi- cam pervaserat. Sic in Ægypti Regis convivium introdu- ctam ὀρχηστρίδα ἐνπρεπῆ narrat Josephus originum II. Dion de rege Edessæ Trajani temporibus: κᾀκεῖνος εἰστίασεν αὐτὸν ἔν τε τῷ δείπνῳ παῖδα ἑαυτῦ ὀρχησάμενον βαρβαρικῶς πῶς παρήγαγεν.

Ἐν τῷ μέσῳ] Inspectantibus conviviis, ut recte interpreta- tur Syrus.

## 14:7
Vers. 7. He promised with an oath.] He promised under oath. See to what point the ease of swearing has finally come, I do not say now among profane nations, but among those very people who professed themselves to be bound by the laws of Moses. Philo in his book On the Special Laws: 'For there are some who swear, if it happens, that they have committed thefts and sacrileges, or adulteries, or corruptions, or wounds and slaughters, or any of the like evils, and they do them without delay, making the oath a pretext.' Where he also adds the example of a rich young man who had sworn that he would do no good to anyone from his own resources. Such also were those in Acts 23:12 who had bound themselves with curses unless they killed Paul.

Whatever he might ask.] Thus Philip of Macedon assured the actor Satyrus that he would grant whatever he might ask, according to Diodorus Siculus in book 16. Mark expresses the very words, 'Whatever you ask of me I will give you, up to half of my kingdom.' It should be known that this manner of speaking is proverbial and customary among kings, when they grant anyone the most free power of choosing. See the history of Esther 5:3, where the Septuagint has the same words: 'up to half of my kingdom.'

Latin:

Vers. 7. Μεθ' ὅρκου ὡμολόγησεν] Jurato promisit. Vide quo tandem jurandi facilitas evaserit, non jam apud profa- nas dico gentes, sed apud eos ipsos qui Mosis legibus teneri se profitebantur. Philo libro περὶ τῶν ἐν ἔδει νόμων: εἰσὶ γὰρ οἳ ὀμνύουσι ἐὰν τύχη κλοπὰς καὶ ἱεροσυλίας, ἢ μοιχείας, ἢ φθοράς, ἢ τραύματα καὶ σφαγὰς ἤ τι τῶν ὁμοιοτρόπων κακῶν ἐργάσασθαι, καὶ ἀνυπερθέτως αὐτὰ δρῶσι, ποιέμενοι πρόφασιν τὰ ἐνόρκον. Ubi etiam exemplum addit divitis adolescentis, qui jurave- rat, se de facultatibus suis nemini quicquam benefacturum. Tales & illi erant Act. XXIII. 12. qui diris se obstrinxerant ni Paulum interficerent.

Ὃ ἐὰν αἰτήσηται] Sic Philippus Macedo Satyro historioni διεβεβαιώσατο πᾶν ὅτι ἂν αἰτήση χαρίσασθαι apud Diodor. Si- culum libro XVI. Marcus ipsa verba exprimit, ὃ ἐάν με αἰτή- σῃς δώσω σοι, ἕως ἡμίσους τῆς βασιλείας με. Quod loquendi genus sciendum est esse proverbiale regibus usitatum, ubi liberrimam optandi facultatem cuiquam faciunt. Vide E- steris historiam V. 3. ubi LXX. eadem habent verba: ἕως ἡμίσους τῆς βασιλείας με.

## 14:9
Vers. 9. He was grieved.] An example of lack of self-control. Reason dictates that an innocent man should not be killed. On the other side, the memory of a free promise stirs up anger: love is added, all the more fervent because it is forbidden: the one commands to avenge an enemy; the other commands to gratify a wife. An indefinite promise and shame, lest he seem to fear the crowd, add some appearance of honor to a dishonorable matter. Thus the mind, long accustomed to follow worse things, having cast off the bridle of reason, allowed itself to be dragged along by excited passions. The ancient Christians noted the descriptions of these movements in the poets very diligently. Famous above others is that of Medea: 'And I know indeed what evils I am about to do. But passion is stronger than my counsels.' Which Ovid expressed thus: 'I see the better things and approve them, I follow the worse.' Of the same is: 'I hate, and yet I cannot help but be what I hate: Alas, how heavy it is to bear what you strive to put away.' For strength is lacking to me for myself, and the power of ruling: I am carried away like a ship driven by a rapid stream. But Seneca, from the persona of Phaedra: 'What you mention, nurse, I know to be true: but madness compels me to follow the worse: the mind goes headlong, knowing it, and returns, seeking healthy counsels in vain. Just as when a sailor pushes a ship burdened by an adverse wind, the labor yields in vain, and the ship, overcome, is carried away by the rushing current.' Men are accustomed to use many pretexts to excuse crimes of this kind, sometimes God, as that one: 'Alas, this is already a divine evil for men, when someone knows the good, but does not do it.' Sometimes nature, as another: 'Nothing of these things which you advise me has escaped my notice; but nature, having taken hold of me, forces me.' But Clement of Alexandria wishes no other cause to be acknowledged than that we ourselves betray ourselves, 'willingly giving ourselves over to passion and desire.' Moreover, how reason and passion alternately pull a man this way and that, the tragic poet Neophron seems to me to have described best in the persona of the Medea I mentioned. 'Well then, what will you do, my heart? Take counsel well before you sin, and make your most beloved things most hateful. Where, where have you rushed, wretch? Restrain your spirit and your god-hated strength. And why do I lament these things, seeing my soul desolate and neglected by those by whom it least should be? But we become soft when suffering such evils. You will not betray yourself, my heart, in evils. Alas, it is decided; the children are out of sight. For already a murderous madness has entered my heart. O hands, hands, to what a deed are we arming ourselves? Woe, wretched for my daring, which I am coming to destroy my long labor in a short time.' Compare this with those things which are in Seneca's Medea, act five: so that you may rightly understand what kind of 'grieved' this is, which is being dealt with here. But there is often even in men not so much a conflict of reason with passions as a conflict of passions among themselves, such as Josephus prudently notes in Herod the Great concerning Mariamne.

Because of the oaths.] There were, as I said, ancient causes: but this pretext also was seized upon: otherwise very weak in itself. For what is easier to say than that the words of an oath pronounced in a general way are to be interpreted in such a way that they comprehend nothing of that sort? Nor do I doubt that Jephthah interpreted his vow in this way, and did not sacrifice his daughter as some wish, but as a sacred thing dedicated to God, he set her apart from human commerce: Then, however, what if Herod had promised in express terms the slaughter of an innocent person? Should he not have thought that what is illicit in itself cannot become licit by the interposition of an oath? I cannot pass over, but that I should here append a notable passage of the most eloquent writer Philo concerning oaths of this kind: 'Let everyone who does unjust things under oath know that he will indeed keep his oath, but he overturns the oath which is worthy of much guarding and care, by which good and just things are sealed; for he adds causes of blame to causes of blame, in oaths made at an improper time, in which it would have been much better to be silent; but abstaining from doing injustice, let him persuade God, so that He may share His merciful power with him, forgiving him for the things he swore having used poor judgment; for it is more desirable to choose the lesser of two evils, being able to cast off half of them, than madness and mental blindness which is hard to cure.' Nor can it come into my mind that this was unknown to that most wise man Joshua, although I see that Augustine and certain others think so, that he was moved by the religion of an oath to act against the divine law, which devoted the possessors of Canaan to destruction: For I think it is clearly most true, what I said at chapter 5, that that law, by comparison with another law which is in Deuteronomy, is to be tempered in such a way that it would apply only to those who, after war was duly declared, had refused to surrender themselves to the Hebrews into servitude.

And those reclining with him.] Who, as is the custom of the court, fawning upon the favor of Herodias, were pushing the wavering mind of Herod. A similar story is in Herodotus, where Amestris, the wife of Xerxes, at a banquet asks of her husband the wife of Masistes. The writer adds that the king desired 'to fail the one asking, when it was possible for him at a royal banquet set before them.'

Latin:

Vers. 9. Ἐλυπήθη] Exemplum ἀκρασίας. Dictat ratio non occidendum innocentem. Ab altera parte memoria liberæ castigationis iram instigat: accedit amor hoc fervidior quod vetitus: illa inimicum ulcisci; hic uxori morem gerere im- perat. Rei inhonestæ speciem aliquam honesti addit indefi- nita pollicitatio & pudor ne metuere plebem videretur. Ita animus dudum assuetus sequi pejora, ejecto rationis fræno, permisit se raptandum concitatis affectibus. Notarunt Chri- stiani veteres admodum diligenter in Poëtis horum mo- tuum descriptiones. Celebre præ cæteris illud Medeæ: Καὶ μανθάνω μὲν οἷα δρᾶν μέλλω κακά. Θυμὸς δὲ κρείσσων τῶν ἐμῶν βουλευμάτων. Quod ita expressit Ovidius: Video meliora proboque, Deteriora sequor. Ejusdem est: Odi, nec possum cupiens non esse quod odi: Heu quam quod studeas ponere, ferre grave est. Nam desunt vires ad me mihi, jusq; regendi: Auferor ut rapida concita puppis aqua. Senecæ autem ex Phædræ persona: quæ memoras scio, Vera esse nutrix: sed furor cogit sequi Pejora: vadit animus in præceps sciens, Remeatque, frustra sana consilia appetens. Sic cum gravatam navita adversa ratem Propellit nuda, cedit insanum labor Et victa prono puppis aufertur vado. Solent ad excusanda facinora ejusmodi multa homines prætexere, modo Deum, ut ille Αἲ αἲ τόδ' ἤδη θεῖον ἀνθρώποις κακὸν Ὅταν τις εἰδῇ τ' ἀγαθὸν, δράσῃ δὲ μὴ. modo naturam, ut alter Λεληθεν ὐδὲν τῶν δέ μ' ὧν σὺ νεθετεῖς· Γνώμη δ' ἐχούσα μ' ἡ φύσις βιάζεται. Sed causam non aliam vult agnosci Clemens Alexandrinus quam quod ipsi nos prodimus ἑκόντες σφᾶς αὐτὸς ἐπιδόντες θυμῷ τε καὶ ἐπιθυμίᾳ. Cæterum quomodo alternis ratio & affectus huc atque illuc hominem trahunt, optime mihi in ejus quam dixi Medeæ persona descripsisse videtur Tragicus Neophron. Εἶεν τί δράσεις θυμέ; βύλευσαι καλῶς Πρὶν ἢ 'ξαμαρτεῖν, καὶ τὰ προσφιλέστατα Ἔχθιστα θέσθαι. ποῖ ποῖ' ἐξῆξαι τάλας; Κάτισχε λῆμα καὶ σθένος θεοστυγές. Καὶ πρὸς τί ταῦτ᾽ ὀδύρομαι, ψυχὴν ἐμὴν Ὁρῶσ᾽ ἔρημον, καὶ παρημελημένην, Πρὸς ὧν ἐχρῆν ἥκιστα; μαλθακοὶ δὲ δὴ Τοιαῦτα γιγνόμεθα πάσχοντες κακά. Οὐ μὴ προδώσεις θυμὲ σαυτὸν ἐν κακοῖς. Οἴμοι, δέδοκται· παῖδες ἐκτὸς ὀμμάτων. Ἀπίλθετ' ἤδη γάρ με φοινία μίγαν Δέδυκε λύσσα θυμόν. ὦ χέρες, χέρες, Πρὸς οἷον ἔργον ἐξοπλιζόμεσθα; Φεῦ Τάλαινα τόλμης, ἣ πολὺν πόνον βραχεῖ Διαφθεροῦσα τὸν ἐμὸν ἔρχομαι χρόνον. Confer cum iis quæ sunt apud Senecam Medeæ actu quin- to: ut recte intelligas quale sit hoc λυπηθεὶς quo de hic agi- tur. Est autem sæpe etiam in hominibus non tam rationis cum affectibus quam affectuum inter se pugna qualem in Herode magno circa Mariammen prudenter notat Jose- phus.

Διὰ δὲ τὰς ὅρκες] Erant, ut dixi, causæ veteres: sed hæc quoque species arrepta est: infirmissima alioqui per se. Nam quid facilius dictu quam juramenti verba generaliter enun- tiata ita esse interpretanda, ut illi isti nihil comprehendant. Neque dubito quin ita votum suum interpretatus sit Jeph- thes, euque filiam non mactaverit ut quidam volunt, sed ut rem sacram Deoque dictam ab hominum commercio sepo- suerit: Deinde vero quid si διαῤῥήδην pollicitus esset Hero- des insontis cædem? nonne cogitare debuit id quod per se illicitum est, interposito jurejurando licitum fieri non posse? Prætermittere non possum, quin hic apponam disertissimi Scriptoris Philonis locum insignem de id genus juramentis: Ἴσω δὲ πᾶς ἐνωμότως ἄδικα δρῶν, ὅτι εὐορκήσεῖ μὲν ἧ, τὸν δὲ πολ- λῆς φυλακῆς κᾑ ἐπιμελείας ἄξιον ὅρκον ἀνατρέπς, ᾧ τὰ καλά κᾑ δίκαια ἐπισφραγίζεται· προστίθεται γὰρ ὑπαίτια ὑπαιτίοις, ἐν ὀ δέοντι γινομένοις ὅρκοις, οἷς πολὺ βέλτιον ἦν ἡσυχάζεσθαι πράξεις παρανόμους· ἀπεχόμενον δὲ τῆς ἀδικοπραγαῖν πείλιά- θω τὸν θεὸν, ἵνα μεταδῶ τῆς ἴλεω δυνάμεως αὐτῷ συγγνῶς ἐφ' οἷς ἀβουλία χρησάμενοθ ὤμοσεν· διπλασία γὰρ αἱρετώτερα κακά, δυνά- μενον τὴν ἡμίσιαν αὐτῶν ἀποφορλίσασθαι, μανία κᾑ φρενοβλά- βεια δυσίατον. Neque hoc ignoratum viro sapientissimo Josuæ in mentem mihi potest venire, quanquam video Au- gustinum atque alios quosdam ita existimare, permotum jurisjurandi religione fecisse eum contra legem divinam, quæ Cananææ possessores internecioni devovebat: Plane enim verissimum puto, quod dixi ad caput V. legem illam collatione legis alterius quæ in Deuteronomio est, ita tem- perandam, ut in eos demum valeret, qui de bello rite de- nuntiato dedere se Hebræis in servitutem recusassent.

Καὶ τὸς συνανακειμένως] Qui, ut mos est aulæ, captantes Herodiadis gratiam labantem Herodis animum impellebant. Similis historia apud Herodotum, ubi Amistus Xerxis uxor in convivio petit à marito Masistis uxorem. Addit Scriptor concupiisse regem ὅτι ἀτυχῆσαι τὸν χρήζοντα ᾦ σφι δυνατὸν ἐςι βασιληίῳ δείπνῳ προκειμένῳ.

## 14:10
Vers. 10. Πέμψας ἀπεκεφάλισε] He sent through whom he might behead. For thus I think the force of the Hebraism is rightly expressed. So above II. 16. ἀποςείλας ἀνεῖλε, he sent through whom he might kill. Below XXVII. 19. ἀπέςειλε λέγουσα, she sent through whom she might say. Theophanes in the life of Emperor Justin: πέμψας ἀπεκεφάλισεν αὐτὸν. But in the Hebrew there was undoubtedly, he sent and beheaded, he sent and killed: he sent and said. For thus the Hebrews speak, the LXX also following, as Psalm LVII. 4. ἐξαπέςειλεν ἐξ ὐρανῶ καὶ ἔσωσέ με, that is, he sent from heaven who might deliver me. Psalm CV. 20. ἀπέςειλεν βασιλεὺς κᾑ ἔλυσεν ἀυτὸν, he sent through whom he might free him from chains. Arrian in Epictetus IV. 10. ὦ πέμπεις, κᾑ ἄλλων καινὴν ἀ- γοράζεις.

Ἐν τῇ φυλακῇ] It appears that this banquet was celebrated at Machaerus. The holy man is slaughtered without even the order of trials being observed. For the law of Moses commands that the guilty be punished with all the people watching. At Rome, Flaminius was accused of the crime of diminished magistracy, because he had ordered a man, undoubtedly guilty, to be killed not according to the custom of the ancestors, but at a banquet.

Dubium tamen de loco movet Lightfoot. Josephus reports that John was imprisoned by Herod at Machaerus, Ὑποψίᾳ τῇ ἡρώδε δέσμιο- εἰς τὸν Μαχαιρῶτα πεμφθεὶς. Antiquities book XVIII. c. 7. Machaerus was, however, the extreme border of Peraea, towards the South. Id. on the war book 3. cap. 4. And Peraea was within the dominion of Herod. Id. on the war book 2. cap. 2. Now indeed if John lay bound there, when it was being decided concerning his life, there was need of a very long journey for the executioner, and which could scarcely be accomplished within two days from Tiberias, where the palace of the tyrant was, to execute that cruel mandate. So that not until after several days, from the celebrated birthday, was the girl presented with that horrible dish, the venerable head of the Prophet.

PARS II. The history of the feeding of the five thousand in the desert.

Latin:

Vers. 10. Πέμψας ἀπεκεφάλισε] Misit per quem decolla- ret. Ita enim Hebraismi vim recte exprimi puto. Ita supra II. 16. ἀποςείλας ἀνεῖλε, misit per quos occideret. Infra XXVII. 19. ἀπέςειλε λέγουσα, misit per quem diceret. Theophanes in vita Justini Imperatoris: πέμψας ἀπεκεφάλισεν αὐτὸν. Sed in Hebræo haud dubie fuit, misit & decollavit, misit & occidit: misit & dixit. Nam ita Hebræi loquuntur, sequentibus et- iam LXX. ut Psal. LVII. 4. ἐξαπέςειλεν ἐξ ὐρανῶ καὶ ἔσωσέ με, id est, misit è cælo qui me liberaret. Psal. CV. 20. ἀπέςειλεν βασιλεὺς κᾑ ἔλυσεν ἀυτὸν, misit per quem eum eximeret vincu- lis. Arrianus Epicteto IV. 10. ὦ πέμπεις, κᾑ ἄλλων καινὴν ἀ- γοράζεις.

Ἐν τῇ φυλακῇ] Apparet Machaunte celebratum hoc con- vivium. Trucidatur vir sanctus ne judiciorum quidem or- dine servato. Nam sontes populo omni inspectante plecti lex Mosis jubet. Romæ Flaminius accusatus est imminuti magistratus crimine, quod hominem haud dubie nocen- tem, non more majorum, sed in convivio jussisset interfici.

Dubium tamen de loco movet Lightfoot. Re- fert Josephus Joannem ab Herode incarceratum fuisse Machærunte, Ὑποψίᾳ τῇ ἡρώδε δέσμιο- εἰς τὸν Μαχαιρῶτα πεμφθεὶς. Antiquit. lib. XVIII. c. 7. Erat autem Macherus extremus Peræa limes, versus Austrum. Id. de bell. lib. 3. cap. 4. Eratque Pe- ræa intra ditionem Herodis. Id. de bell. lib. 2. cap. 2. Jam vero si vinctus illic jaceret Joannes, cum de ca- pite ejus decerneretur, longissimo itinere opus fuit carnifici, & quod vix intra biduum confici posset à Tiberiade, ubi regia tyranni, ad crudele illud man- datum exsequendum. Ita ut non nisi post dies ali- quot, à celebratis natalitiis, puella præsentaretur, horrendum istud ferculum, caput venerandum Pro- phetæ.

PARS II. Historia cibationis quinque millium in de- serto.

## 14:13
Vers. 13. Ἀκούσας ὁ Ἰησοῦς] He returns from his retreat to where he had gone. He heard, he says, what discourses were being held about himself in the court.

Ἐκεῖθεν] He withdraws from the more frequented places of Galilee into the wilderness, so that without any loss of his mandated duty he might avoid Herod who was threatening him. See what has been said above on chapter XIII.

Casaubonus has it thus: ἀνεχώρησεν ἐκεῖθεν: From where? Or from his own country to which he is said to have gone above XIII. 54. Mark VI. 1. Or rather ἐκεῖθεν, that is, from that place where he was when the death of John the Baptist was announced to him? Furthermore, the desert into which he is said to have withdrawn was in the territory of Bethsaida, as Luke notes: to the west of the city of Bethsaida, as it seems can be conjectured from that which a little later Christ, departing from the desert and making for Capernaum, commands the disciples to go ahead by ship προάγειν εἰς Βηθσαϊδὰν, Mark VI. 45. Lightfoot p. 183. From Capernaum, that is, into the desert of Bethsaida, Luke IX. 10. which is rendered by John, he departed across the sea, John VI. 1. which is to be understood properly: from Galilee, that is, into Peraea.

Latin:

Vers. 13. Ἀκούσας ὁ Ἰησοῦς] Ex divorticulo redit unde abierat. Audivit, inquit, Jesus qui de se sermones in aula haberentur.

Ἐκεῖθεν] Ex locis Galilææ frequentioribus in solitudi- nem secedit, ut sine ullo dispendio mandati muneris immi- nentem sibi Herodem evitaret. Vide quæ supra dicta sunt ad caput XIII.

Casaubonus ita habet: ἀνεχώρησεν ἐκεῖθεν: Un- de? an è Patria sua ad quam ille dicitur supra XIII. 54. Marc. VI. 1. An potius ἐκεῖθεν, id est, ex illo loco quo erat quando mors Johannis Baptistæ ei est annun- ciata? Eremus porro in quâ secessisse dicitur, fuit in a- gro Bethsaidan, ut annotat Lucas: urbi Bethsaida πρὸς δύσιν, ut videtur ex eo posse conjici, quod paulo post Christus ex eremo discedens & Capernaum petens, jubet discipulos navibus προάγειν εἰς Βηθσαϊδὰν, Marc. VII. 45. Lighthooth p. 183. A Capernaumo scilicet in desertum Bethsaide, Luc. IX. 10. quod à Johanne redditur, ἀπῆλθεν πέραν τῆς θαλάσσης, Joh. VI. 1. quod proprie intelligendum est: à Galilæa scilicet, in Peræam.

## 14:14
Vers. 14. ἐσπλαγχνίσθη.] The Hellenists love to use this word: to explain the Hebrew verb רחם, whose origin is from the noun רחם which signifies bowels, although it is mostly used for the womb. Luke I. 78 said σπλάγχνα ἐλέους, following Isaiah, in whom מעיך, that is, literally thy bowels, signifies mercies, as the LXX translate it. And there is the same use of the word σπλάγχνα in Euripides and in the Aesopic fables. But ἐσπλαγχνίσθη is added here because Christ neglected the rest of refreshing his body for their sake.

Latin:

Vers. 14. ἐσπλαγχνίσθη.] Amant uti Hellenistæ hac voce: ut exponant Hebræum verbum רחם cujus origo est à nomine רחם quod σπλάγχνα significat, quanquam plerumque pro utero ponitur. Lucas I. 78. σπλάγχνα ἐλέυς dixit, Esaiam secutus apud quem מעיך, id est ad verbum τὰ σπλάγχνα σου, significat οἰκτιρμὺς, ut vertunt LXX. Estque idem usus vocis σπλάγχνα apud Euripidem & in fabulis Æsopeis. ἐσπλαγχνίσθη autem ideo hic est additum quia Christus quietem refovendo corpori quæsitum illorum causa neglexit.

## 14:15
Vers. 15. Ὀψίας δὲ γενομένης] Since we read below, after the food was taken and Christ had withdrawn, ὀψίας δὲ γενομένης, it cannot be denied that there were two evenings for the Hebrews, that is ערבים, between which two evenings the Passover had to be eaten, as we read in Exodus and Leviticus. Moreover, that those two evenings should not be defined by the space of twilight seems to me most evident from this passage. For the things that are narrated here as having been done after the former and before the latter evening require a space of several hours. Wherefore I think it most certain that the former evening begins as soon as the sun, the greater part of the day having passed, begins to decline from noon toward the setting: but the latter from the setting of the sun. Thus the Rabbis Sadaias, Simeon son of Johai, and Solomon interpret that בין הערבים. Indeed, we also read in the Mechilta that this is a most ancient tradition from which I do not think one should depart. Therefore, the time for evening prayer was roughly midway between the beginning of the former evening and the latter evening.

Ἡ ὥρα ἤδη παρῆλθεν] The time for lunch, that is.

Latin:

Vers. 15. Ὀψίας δὲ γενομένης] Cum infra post cibum sumtum & secessum Christi iterum legamus ὀψίας δὲ γενομένης, negari non potest duas fuisse ὀψίας Hebræis, hoc est ערבים, inter quas duas ὀψίας edi debuit Pascha, ut in Exodo & Levitico legimus. Cæterum non debere duas istas ὀψίας crepusculi spatio definiri ex hoc loco mihi videtur apertissimum. Nam quæ narrantur hic facta post priorem & ante posteriorem ὀψίαν aliquot horarum spatium exigunt. Quare certissimum puto ὀψίαν priorem incipere simul atque sol a meridie ad occasum cœpit vergere majore diei parte exacta: posteriorem autem à sole occaso. Ita illud בין הערבים interpretantur Rabbini Sadaias, Simeon filius johai & Salomo. Quin & in Mechilta legimus hanc esse παράδοσιν antiquissimam à qua recedendum non puto. Precandi igitur tempus vespertinum medium serme fuit inter initium prioris vesperæ & vesperam posteriorem.

Ἡ ὥρα ἤδη παρῆλθεν] Prandii tempus scilicet.

## 14:19
Vers. 19. Ἐπὶ τὺς χόρτυς] Upon the grass, as poets often say. For that also is signified by the word χόρτου, as has been noted elsewhere. And Mark explains it by saying green grass.

Εὐλόγησε] John says εὐχαρίsτησε. Christ approves of this custom of blessing food, just as he does other Jewish rites introduced by the wise. See what must be said below on chapter XXVI.

Latin:

Vers. 19. Ἐπὶ τὺς χόρτυς] Per herbam, ut sæpe Poëtæ, Nam id quoque χόρτου voce significatur, ut alibi annotatum est. Et Marcus explicat dicens χλωρὸν χόρτον.

Εὐλόγησε] εὐχαρίsτησε inquit Johannes. Probat Christus ut alios ritus Judaicos à sapientibus introductos, ita & hunc benedicendi cibis. Vide quæ dicenda sunt infra ad caput XXVI.

## 14:20
Vers 20. ἔφαγον πάντες] So that it might be shown by a conspicuous sign that the time had now arrived when that which is in Isaiah LV. 1 would be fulfilled.

Τὸ περισσεῦον] הותר 2 Chronicles XXXII. 10. This is more than either Moses had obtained in the manna, or Elijah in the flour.

Δώδεκα κοφίνυς] Each of the Apostles, it seems, had brought a basket, according to the custom usual for Jews whenever they made a journey far from towns. Thus, Jews used to go with a basket from Rome to the proseuchae which were in the Arician grove at the tenth milestone, and indeed with hay which served in place of a bed. See Juvenal's third satire. In these baskets or even hampers they were accustomed to carry bread with them, as appears below XVI. 7, Mark VIII. 14. The LXX interpreters translated the Hebrew דוד, which they translate as basket elsewhere, as κόφινον in Psalm LXXXI. 7.

Heinsius understands τὸ περισσῦον τῶν κλασμάτων as that which was kept for the poor according to the custom of the Jews. But his solid proof is deservedly lacking. How κλάσματα and ψιχία, about which see chapter XV. 17, are distinguished, see B. D. Franzius and B. D. Joh. Ern. Gerhard on this passage.

PART III.

Jesus' walking on the sea.

Latin:

Vers 20. ἔφαγον πάντες] Ut ostenderetur signo conspicuo adesse jam tempus quo impleretur illud Esaias LV. 1.

In his cophinis aut etiam sportulis ferre secum panem solebant, ut apparet infra XVI. 7. Marci VIII. 14. LXX. Interpretes דוד Hebræum quod alibi κάλαθον vertunt, in Psalmo LXXXI.7. verterunt κόφινον.

Heinsius τὸ περισσῦον τῶν κλασμάτων intelligit id quod pauperibus ex usu Judæorum servatum erat. Sed solidior ejus probatio merito desideratur. Quomodo κλάσματα & ψιχία de quibus cap. XV. 17. distinguantur, vid. B. D. Franzius, & B. D. Joh. Ern. Gerhard. h. l.

PARS III.

Jesu ambulatio in mari.

## 14:22
Vers. 22. Ἠνάγκασεν] Regarding what he said elsewhere, he ordered them to depart, chap. VIII. 18. Christ did not want his disciples to take part in that scheme by which the crowd intended to make him king.

Εἰς τὸ πέραν. Mark specifies the place to which Christ ordered the disciples to go before him, namely the city of Bethsaida. From this it is understood how τὸ πέραν should be taken here. For it does not mean what it meant above in chapter VIII. 28; for there it is understood as the other bank of the Lake of Gennesaret, but here it is not to be taken as the other bank, but as the same one, since the wilderness and Bethsaida and Capernaum are situated on the same side of the lake. Casaubon in his notes. Therefore, τὸ πέραν here is τὸ πρόσω. Thus the Hebrew עבר sometimes means on this side, sometimes across, and the meaning cannot be established unless the location of the speaker or the listener is considered: as here B. Gerhard. Lightfoot has it thus here: The Chorographic tables placed Bethsaida in Galilee, on the same shore as Capernaum: thus also the commentators imagine only a bay of the sea lying between those two cities: which we also once opined with them; but we have been taught. finally by Josephus, that Bethsaida was ἐν τῇ ἄνω Γαυλανιτικῇ, in Lower Gaulanitis (which we observe elsewhere), from the eastern shore of the Sea of Gennesaret, in Perea. Ἠκολύθησαν αὐτῷ πεζῇ. From this, interpreters argue that Capernaum and Bethsaida were not on different shores of the sea, but on the same one: for how else, they say, could the crowd follow him on foot? Very well, I say; having crossed the Jordan near Tiberias, the location of which we have demonstrated elsewhere at the outflow of the Jordan from the Sea of Galilee. They followed him on foot ἀπὸ τῶν πόλεων, says our Evangelist. Now, the cities of any note closest to Capernaum were Tarichaea on one side, and Tiberias on the other. Let it be granted that the crowd made the journey after Christ from these cities: the road by which they proceeded on foot was to the bridge of the Jordan at Chamnath: that place was a mile or less from Tiberias; and about three miles or so from Capernaum. Having crossed the Jordan, they proceeded through the field of Magdala, and after that through the territory of Hippos: now Magdala was one mile from the Jordan, Hippos two: and after Hippos was Bethsaida, on the eastern shore of the sea; and after Bethsaida a bay of the sea protruding somewhat into the land, and from there the wilderness of Bethsaida. When, therefore, he had returned from there, having compelled the disciples into the boat, he orders them to proceed to Bethsaida, while he himself dismissed the crowd, after which he himself would finally follow them on foot, and from there sail with them to Capernaum.

Latin:

Vers. 22. Ἠνάγκασεν] Quod alibi dixit ἐκέλευσεν ἀπελθεῖν, cap. VIII. 18. Noluit Christus discipulos suos in partem venire ejus molitionis qua plebs regnum ipsi destinabat.

Εἰς τὸ πέραν. Marcus exprimit locum, quo Christus jussit discipulos sibi præire, nempe Bethsaidam urbem. Ex quo intelligitur, quomodo τὸ πέραν hic accipi debeat. Non enim id significat, quod supra cap. VIII. 28. ibi enim de altera lacus Genesaretici ripa intelligitur, hic vero non de altera ripa, sed de eadem est accipiendum, tum eremus & Bethsaida atque Capernaum ad idem lacus sint sitæ. Casaub. in notis. Τὸ πέραν igitur hic est τὸ πρόs- σω. Sic Ebræum עבר significat interdum cis, in- terdum trans, nec nisi considerato dicentis aut audientis loco constitui significatio potest: ut hic B. Gerhardus. Lightfooth ita hic habet: Ta- bulæ Chorographicæ Bethsaidam disposuerunt in Galilæa, in eodem littore, quo & Capernaumum: sic & commentatores sinum maris tantum inter- jacentem sibi fingunt inter duas istas urbes: quod & nos aliquando sumus cum iis opinati; at docti sumus. tandem à Josepho, Bethsaidam fuisse ἐν τῇ ἄνω Γαυλανιτικῇ, In inferiori Gaulanitide (quod observamus alibi) ab ora maris Gennefari- tici Orientali, in Peræa. Ἠκολύθησαν αὐτῷ πε- ζῇ. Hinc arguitur ab interpretibus, Caper- naumum & Bethsaidam non in diversis maris lit- toribus fuisse, sed in eodem: nam quomodo ali- ter, inquiunt, potuit turba eum pedibus sequi? Optime, inquam ego; transito Jordane prope Ti- beriada, cujus situm demonstravimus alibi ad ef- fluxum Jordanis è mari Galilææ. Secuti sunt eum pedibus ἀπὸ τῶν πόλεων, inquit Evangelista noster. Civitates autem, alicujus nominis, Ca- pernaumo vicinissimæ erant, hinc Tarichææ, il- lim Tiberias. Detur, turbam ex his urbibus iter post Christum carpisse: via, per quam itinere pedestri perrectum est, erat ad pontem Jordanis in Chamnath: distabat locus iste à Tiberiade millia- ri, aut minus; à Capernaumo milliaribus tribus aut circiter. Transito Jordane perrectum est per agrum Magdalensem, & post eum per Hippo- nensem: distabat autem Magdala à Jordane mil- liari uno, Hippo duobus: & post Hippon erat Bethsaida, ad littus maris Orientale; & post Bethsaidam sinus maris aliquantum se in terram protrudens, atque exinde desertum Bethsaidæ. Cum igitur inde reversum foret, Discipulis in na- vim coactis imperat, ut Bethsaidam pergant, dum ipse turbam dimiserit, quo eos tandem ipse secutu- rus esset pedes, atque inde cum iis navigaturus Capernaumum.

## 14:24
Vers. 24. Μέσον τῆς θαλάσσης ἦν, βασανιζόμενον] He was tossed in the deep, so that we may transfer to the lake what is usually said about the sea.

Latin:

Vers. 24. Μέσον τῆς θαλάσσης ἦν, βασανιζόμενον] In alto jactabatur, ut ad lacum transferamus quod dici de mari solet.

## 14:25
Vers. 25. Τετάρτῃ δὲ φυλακῇ τῆς νυκτὸς] The ancient Jews, while the right of arms was in their own hands, divided the night into three watches, which has been correctly noted by David Kimchi and others. The Romans into four: to which custom the Jews had already become accustomed since the times of Pompey, following the older example of the Greeks: for Euripides called it a four-part night watch. Wherefore what is said here must be interpreted according to the Roman, not the Jewish custom.

Περιπατῶν ἐπὶ τὴν θάλασσαν] Whether by divine power inhibiting the weight of the body, or by the surface of the water being solidified, or by some inconspicuous nature interposed between the body and the water, even the ancients show that they are not in agreement. And it seems to me that conjecture on such matters is free, but definition is rash. Moreover, by this act also, Christ remarkably showed his divine power. For it is said of God in Job IX: he who walks, as if on solid ground, upon the sea. And indeed, most things said about God in the books of the Prophets, Christ visibly fulfilled.

What was the point of solidifying the surface of the water, or interposing some nature, if the weight of the body was inhibited by divine power, or the first act was restrained so that it would not exert itself, and the second act was thus checked. Nor was there need for a miracle either in the water or in the Body of Christ, nor for the interposition of an inconspicuous substance; since the body of Christ, by the power communicated to it through personal union, could have been where it wanted, and how it wanted. And Grotius admits that by this act also Christ remarkably showed his divine power. And he adds: for it is said of God in Job IX: he who walks, as if on solid ground,

on the sea. And indeed, Christ visibly fulfilled most of the things said about God in the books of the Prophets.

Latin:

Vers. 25. Τετάρτῃ δὲ φυλακῇ τῆς νυκτὸς] Judæi veteres dum penes ipsos jus armorum fuit noctem in ternas vigi- lias diviserunt, quod à Davide Kimchi, aliisque recte est notatum. Romani in quaternas: cui mori jam à Pom- peji temporibus Judæi assueverant, Græcorum vetustiore exemplo: nam τετράμοιρον νυκτὸς φρουρὰν Euripides dixit. Quare quod hic dicitur, ex Romano non ex Judaico mo- re interpretandum.

Περιπατῶν ἐπὶ τὴν θάλασσαν] Gravitatem corporis inhi- bente vi divina, an solidato aquæ summo, an natura quadam inconspicua inter corpus aquamque interposita, etiam veteres oftendunt sibi non constare. Videturque mihi rerum ejusmodi libera esse conjectura, definitio au- tem temeraria. Cæterum hoc quoque facto insigniter Christus divinam suam potentiam ostendit. Nam de Deo dictum est apud Jobum IX. ὁ περιπατῶν, ὡς ἐπὶ ἐδάφους, ἐπὶ θαλάσσης. Et sane pleraque de Deo dicta in libris Prophe- tarum, Christus visibiliter implevit.

Quid attinebat solidare aquæ summum, aut naturam aliquam interponere, si gravitas cor- poris inhibita vi divina, vel actus primus co- hibitus ne se exereret, & actus secundus ita suf- flaminatus. Nec miraculo opus fuit seu in a- qua, seu in Corpore Christi, neque interjectio- ne materiæ inconspicuæ; siquidem corpus Christi virtute sibi per unionem personalem communi- cata potuerit esse ubi vellet, & quomodo vel- let. Ac fatetur Grotius, hoc quoque facto Christum insigniter divinam suam potentiam ostendisse. Additque: nam de Deo dictum est apud Jobum IX. ὁ περιπατῶν, ὡς ἐπὶ ἐδάφους,

ἐπὶ θαλάσσης. Et sane pleraque de Deo dicta in libris Prophetarum Christus visibiliter implevit.

## 14:26
Verse 26. It is a ghost] an idol, as others called it. See Cicero's letter to Cassius, book V. This opinion comes from the discipline of the Pharisees, who thought that spirits, just as they exist by themselves, also appear to men clothed in human form. But because evil spirits are believed to show themselves at night rather than by day, the Apostles were afraid for themselves. In Hebrew, a nocturnal specter is called לִילִית: about which they invent stories no less monstrous than the ancient Latins did about the screech-owl.

Beza is correct: This word in this place signifies not some image conceived merely in the mind, or of the kind we seem to see whether we are awake or asleep; but something beyond the order of nature, presenting itself to be seen in a visible form: in which way not only have Angels often appeared, but also demons, especially representing the form of dead men, if they were summoned, as by that witch who is mentioned in 1 Sam. XXVIII, or if they were of their own accord thus deluding men: in which way they undoubtedly attacked Christ himself in the desert. Therefore, in a similar matter, Luke XXIV. 37 uses the name of a spirit.

Latin:

Vers. 26. Φάντασμά ἐστιν] ἔιδωλον ut alii appellabant. Vi- de Ciceronis Epistolam ad Cassium libro V. Opinio hæc ex Pharisæorum disciplina, qui spiritus ut existere per se putabant, ita & indutos humana figura hominibus appa- rere. Quia autem mali spiritus noctu potius quam in- terdiu ostentare se creduntur, inde sibi metuebant Apo- stoli. Hebræis spectrum nocturnum לִילִית dicitur: de quo non minus portentosa fabulantur quam de strige Latini veteres.

Recte Beza: Significat hæc vox hoc loco non imaginem aliquam animo duntaxat conceptam, aut cujusmodi nobis videmur seu vigilantes seu dormi- entes videre; sed quippiam præter naturæ ordinem, forma visibili se conspiciendum præbens: quo mo- do non tantum Angeli sæpe apparuerunt, sed etiam dæmones, mortuorum præsertim hominum formam repræsentantes, si e eliciti, ut ab illa venefica cujus fit mentio 1. Sam. XXVIII. sive ultro sic homi- nibus illudentes: quomodo proculdubio Christum ipsum est in deserto aggressus. Idio in re simili Lucas XXIV. 37. utitur nomine πνεύματος.

## 14:30
Verse 30. To be sunk] Thus the Greeks translate טבע in Exodus XV. 4.

Latin:

Vers. 30. Καταποντίζεσθαι] Sic Græci vertunt טבע Ex- od. XV. 4.

## 14:31
Verse 31. O you of little faith, why did you doubt] Here doubting is opposed to believing, just as in James I. 6 and below in XXI. 22, faith is opposed to wavering. This is the very thing that the Rabbis call הרהרת after the Chaldean paraphrast in Num. XVI. 39. Thus also Philo in his book on the heir of divine things says: 'For to be in doubt is the work of one who is wavering, but to no longer seek is the work of one who has believed.' The same author in 'On Flight' says thus: 'These are not the doctrines of those who are double-minded, but the firm faith of those who have taken hold.' From this we understand that to believe here is nothing other than to trust in the power of God in Christ: the reason why Christ usually demanded this before his benefits began to be discussed at chapter VIII. Peter had given a notable proof of his confidence when he showed that he believed that what could not be done by nature could be done by the word of Christ alone: but that prompt and ardent spirit of his did not know about itself that it still lacked something for the full strength of faith, and Christ wanted him to learn this by experience: so that he might strive to obtain by humble prayer and effort what was lacking. Christ objects to this little-faith in many places to his disciples, which, when compared to solid faith, is even called unbelief, as by him who said, 'I believe, Lord; help my unbelief' (Mark IX. 24). In the book which is called Ecclesiasticus, and which contains the sentiments of the ancient Hebrews expressed in Greek, we read thus in I. 34: 'Do not be disobedient to the fear of the Lord when you are in need, and do not approach him with a double heart': where a double heart is a doubting heart, fluctuating between faith and diffidence. In the Constitutions of Clement, book VII, chapter XII. Do not be double-minded in your prayer; it will be, or it will not.

Latin:

Vers. 31. ὀλιγόπιστε, εἰς τί ἐδίστασας] Opponitur hic δισά- ζειν τῷ πιστεύειν quomodo apud Jacobum I. 6. & infra XXI. 22. πίστις opponitur τῷ διακρίνεσθαι. Id ipsum quod Rabbini dicunt הרהרת post Chaldæum paraphrasten Num. XVI. 39. Sic & Philo libro de hærede rerum divinarum τὸ μὲν γὰρ ἀπορεῖν ἐνδοιάζοντός, τὸ δὲ μηκέτι ζητεῖν πεπιστευκότος ἔργον εἶ- ναι. Idem περὶ Φυγαργίας fic ait: τὰ δὲ δόγματα ἐκ ἐπαμ- φοτεριζόντων ταῦτ᾽ ἐστὶν, ἀλλὰ βεβαία πίσις καλεχημένων. Unde intelligimus, credere nihil hic esse aliud, quam potentiæ Dei in Christo confidere: quod cur Christus plerunque an- te beneficia sua exegerit, cœptum est dici ad caput VIII. Insigne fiduciæ suæ argumentum Petrus dederat, cum o- stendit credere se, solo Christi verbo fieri posse, quod per naturam fieri non poterat: sed quod de se nesciebat prom- tus ille semper & calens animus, non partum adhuc sibi de- esse ad plenum fidei robur, id Christus ipsum experimen- to discere voluit: ut quod deerat, supplici prece ac nisu impetrare contenderet. Hanc ὀλιγοπιστίαν multis in locis discipulis suis Christus objicit, quæ comparata ad solidam fidem ἀπιστία etiam nominatur, ut ab illo qui dicebat πιστεύω κύριε, βοήθει με τῇ ἀπιστίᾳ Marci IX. 24. In libro qui Ec- clesiasticus dicitur, & Hebræorum veterum sententias Græ- ce expressas continet, ita legimus I. 34. Μὴ ἀπειθήσῃς φόβῳ κυρίου ἐνδεὴς ὢν, καὶ μὴ προσέλθῃς ἀυτῷ ἐν καρδίᾳ δισσῇ: ubi καρδία δισσὴ est καρδία δισάζουσα inter fidem ac diffidentiam fluctuans. In Clementis constitutionibus lib. VII. c. XII. Μὴ γίνου δίψυχος, ἐν προσευχῇ σου· ἔται, ἢ ὔ.

## 14:32
Verse 32. It ceased] Either שכך as others have noted, or also שקע. For thus what is in Numbers XI. 2, 'and the fire was quenched,' was translated by the LXX, 'the fire ceased.' The author of the Problems which exist under the name of Aristotle uses this verb regarding a lake in XXIII. 34.

Beza: it ceased: As if, clearly, exhausted by blowing. For since 'kopos' declares heavy labor, it seems that 'to cease' is properly said only of that rest which follows some very vehement motion: and the most learned Camerarius observed that Herodotus uses this verb similarly in Polymnia, likewise dealing with a storm calmed by the Magi (as indeed he reports). Vulgate: It ceased. Erasmus: It quieted down. The Syriac interpreter, however, more properly: שלית.

Latin:

Vers. 32. Ἐκόπασε] Aut שכך ut alii notarunt, aut etiam שקע. Nam ita quod in Numeris est XI. 2. ותשקע האש versum est à LXX. ἐκόπασε τὸ πῦρ. Verbum hoc de lacu usurpat Scriptor problematum quæ exstant sub Aristotelis nomine XXIII. 34.

Beza: ἐκόπασεν: Quasi videlicet flando delas- satus. Cum enim κόπος gravem laborem declarat, videtur τὸ κοπάζειν proprie de ea demum quiete dici, quæ vehementissimam aliquam motionem consequa- tur: & hoc verbo similiter uti Herodotum in Poly- mnia observavit doctissimus Camerarius, itidem a- gentem de tempestate à Magis (ut quidem tradit) se- data. Vulg. Cessavit. Erasmus, Conquievit, Sy- rus autem interpres magis proprie, שלית.

## 14:33
Verse 33. But those in the boat] The sailors themselves.

You are the Son of God] It appears that this surname was commonly given to the Messiah. For Nathanael says in John I. 49, 'Rabbi, you are the Son of God, you are that King of Israel.' Doubtless from the second Psalm, which the ancient Hebrews interpreted in a more mystical sense concerning the Messiah. And so, below, where Jesus is called by Peter in Matthew the Christ, the Son of the living God, Mark and Luke were content with the word Christ. Add what is below in XXVI. 63 and Heb. V. 4, 5.

It would be a wonder if Grotius did not want to gratify the Socinians here, who contend that the name of the Son of God is interchangeable with the name of the Messiah, and does not denote anything essential, but is rather a kind of surname for the Messiah, so that they may deny that the eternal generation and the consubstantiality can be built upon it. This we have expressly refuted in our Anti-Crellius in Natural and Revealed Theology, p. ff. Moreover, our Anti-Grotian vindications on the same Psalm in the Annotations on the Old Testament have long since taught that the second Psalm deals with Christ not only in a mystical sense, but in a literal one.

Latin:

Vers. 33. Οἱ δὲ ἐν τῷ πλοίῳ] Nautæ ipsi.

Θεῦ ὑὸς εἶ] Apparet hoc cognomen vulgo Messiæ da- tum. Nam Nathanaël Joh. I. 49. Rabbi, inquit, tu es Fi- lius Dei, tu es Rex ille Israel. Nimirum ex Psalmo secundo quem Hebræi veteres κατὰ τὸ μυσικώτερον de Messia inter- pretabantur. Itaque infra ubi apud Matthæum Jesus à Petro dicitur esse Christus filius Dei viventis, Marcus & Lucas contenti fuerunt Christi vocabulo. Adde quæ infra XXVI. 63. & Hebr. V. 4. 5.

Mirum ni gratificari voluerit Socinianis hic Grotius, qui Filii Dei nomen cum Messiæ nomi- ne permutari, nec aliquid essentiale denotare, sed quoddam cognomen Messiæ potius esse, conten- dunt, ut ex eo generationem æternam & τὸ ὁμού- σιον exstrui posse inficientur. Quod ex professo in Anti-Crellio nostro profligavimus in Theol. naturali & revelata p. feqq. Psalmum autem secundum non tantum sensu mystico, sed literali de Christo agere, vindiciæ nostræ Anti-Grotianæ ad eundem in Annot. ad Vet. Testam. jam pridem docuêre.

## 14:34
Vers. 34. Gennesaret] Origen on this passage: They arrived at the land of Gennesaret, the interpretation of which if we knew, we might be helped somewhat toward the interpretation of this passage. Namely, for finding allegories, of which he is exceedingly fruitful. I think Jerome meant this very thing when he said: If we knew what Gennesaret sounded like in our language, we would understand how Jesus, through the type of the Apostles and the ship, brings the Church, delivered from the shipwreck of persecutions, onto the shore. That is, if the etymon were known so that we could interpret it in Latin. He confesses, therefore, that he is ignorant of the origin of that word. Nor is that a wonder, for it is not a Hebrew word, but corrupted by faulty pronunciation from the Hebrew כנרת, which name many think was given to the lake from the fact that it resembled the image of a lyre, as if the land then received the name from the lake, though Josephus thinks otherwise, who says thus: The lake of Gennesar is named from the adjacent region. But it is most probable that the name was given to both the lake and the region from a very ancient city, which in the book of Joshua is called sometimes in the plural number כנרות, as in chapter XI, and sometimes כנרת in chapter XIX. A later age, softening the name of the lake, preferred to say Ginofar, which occurs several times in the Chaldean interpreter of the Old Testament for the Hebrew כנרת; the author of the first book of Maccabees writes Gennesar.

Latin:

Vers. 34. Γεννησαρέτ] Origenes adhunc locum: Pervenerunt ad terram Gennesaret, cujus interpretationem si cognosceremus, & hinc nonnihil juvaremur ad hujus interpretationem loci. Ad inveniendas scilicet ἀλληγορίας quarum supra modum fœcundus est. Hoc ipsum puto voluisse Hieronymum cum dixit: Si sciremus quid in nostra lingua sonaret Gennesareth, intelligeremus quomodo Jesus per typum Apostolorum & navis, Ecclesiam de persecutionum naufragio liberatam transducat in littus. Hoc est, si notum esset τὸ ἔτυμον ita ut id Latine possimus interpretari. Fatetur igitur ignorare se vocis istius originem, Neque id mirum, non est enim Hebræum vocabulum, sed prava pronuntiatione corruptum ex Hebræo כנרת quod nomen multi inditum lacui putant ex eo quod citharæ imaginem referret, quasi ex lacu terra deinde nomen acceperit, contra sentiente Josepho qui ita ait: ἡ δὲ λίμνη γεννησὰρ μὲν ἀπὸ τῆς προσεχοῦς χώρας καλεῖται. Sed maxime probabile est tum lacui tum regioni nomen factum ab antiquissima urbe, quæ in Josuæ libro modo plurali numero כנרות vocatur, ut cap. XI. modo כנרת cap. XIX. Lacus vocabulum postera ætas emolliens Ginofar maluit dicere, quod apud Chaldæum interpretem veteris instrumenti aliquoties occurrit pro Hebræo כנרת γεννησὰρ scribit auctor primi Maccabaici.

## 15:1 Argument
SECTION III. OF THE ACTS ACCORDING TO THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW FROM THE THIRD PASSOVER OF CHRIST TO THE FOURTH. CHAPTER XV. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

The Pharisees, expostulating with Christ because his disciples did not observe the traditions concerning the washing of hands, are rebuked for violating the commandments of God regarding the honoring of parents on account of human traditions, with Isaiah alleging a prophecy concerning them (c. XXIX. 13) and informing the people that it is not something entering the mouth, but something coming out of the mouth, that renders a man unclean, and that plants not planted by the Father are to be rooted up. He further warns that the Pharisees, as blind guides, are to be left alone; and he interprets those things which come out of the mouth, namely, sins overflowing from the heart. Moreover, in the borders of Tyre and Sidon, to a woman asking about her daughter afflicted by a demon, he at first answers nothing, then says that he was sent only to the lost sheep of Israel, and that bread is not to be snatched from the children and thrown to the dogs; finally, when she herself asks only for the crumbs falling from the table, he celebrates her faith and grants her request. Then, having proceeded to the Sea of Galilee, he heals various sick people brought to him—the blind, the mute, the lame—and, having compassion on the people, he feeds four thousand men with seven loaves and a few fish, with seven baskets of fragments remaining, and is carried by boat into the borders of Magadan.

These are the parts: I. A comparison and information concerning traditions, to v. 21. II. The healing of the Canaanite daughter, to v. 28. III. The restoration of many sick people, with the miraculous feeding of the present crowd of four thousand, to v. 39.

PART I. A comparison and information concerning the traditions of the Pharisees.

Vers. 1. The scribes and Pharisees from Jerusalem] Not sent by the Sanhedrin: just as those disciples of the Pharisees and Herodians, whose mention is made below at XXII. 10, were not sent by the Sanhedrin. For we nowhere read that there were Herodians in the Sanhedrin: and even if there were, it is certain that the authority of the Sadducees was greater than theirs. But no one is sent by the Sadducees. It was therefore a private investigation, but instituted by those who held the leadership of the schools. For the most learned men, as we have said, were called scribes. Now the family of the Pharisees followed the authority of these men, distinguished from the rest only by the fact that, over and above the common precepts, they had imposed upon themselves peculiar self-willed worships. And they came from Jerusalem because the most noble of the masters and the leaders of these parties lived in the primary city.

Latin:

SECTIO III. ACTORUM JUXTA EVANGELIUM MATTHÆI à PASCHATE TERTIO CHRISTI AD QUARTUM. CAPUT XV. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Pharisæi expostulantes cum Christo, ob discipulos traditiones non observantes, de lotione manuum, redarguuntur ob violata mandata Dei, de honorandis parentibus, propter traditiones humanas, allegante Esais de ipsis vaticinium (c. XXIX. 13.) & informante populum, quod non aliquid ingrediens os, sed egrediens ex ore hominem immundum reddat, ac de plantis à Patre non plantatis eradicandis. Qui porro Pharisæos cæcos Ductores relinquendos esse, monet; atque interpretatur ea, quæ ex ore egrediuntur, è corde nempe redundantia peccata. In finibus autem Tyri & Sidonis mulieri quærenti de filia à dæmone afflicta primum quidem nil respondet, deinde ait, se missum tantum ad oves perditas Israel, nec eripiendum panem esse filiis, ac projiciendum canibus, denique ipsa micas tantum de mensa decidentes petente, fidem ejus celebrat, & petito ejus gratificatur. Dehinc ad mare Galilææ progressus ægrotos varios allatos, cæcos, mutos, claudos sanat, populique misertus cibat quatuor millia virorum, septem panibus & paucis piscibus, remanentibus septem sportis reliquiarum, & remigio provehitur in fines Magedan.

Partes sunt hæ: I. De traditionibus collatio & informatio ad v. 21. II. Filia Cananæa sanatio, ad v. 28. III. Multorum ægrotorum restitutio, cum turbæ præsentis quatuor millium miraculosa ci- batione, ad v. 39.

PARS I. De traditionibus Pharisæorum collatio, & informatio.

Vers. 1. Οἱ ἀπὸ ἱεροσολύμων γραμματεῖς κὶ φαρισαῖοι] Non missi à Synedrio: sicut nec discipuli illi Pharisæorum & He- rodianorum, quorum infra sit mentio XXII. 10. à Synedrio erant missi. Nusquam enim legimus in Synedrio fuisse He- rodianos: & ut fuerint, constat majorem fuisse Sadducæo- rum quam illorum auctoritatem. Atqui à Sadducæis nemo mittitur. Fuit igitur privata exploratio, sed ab illis instituta qui scholarum habebant principatum. Nam doctissimi qui- que ut diximus γραμματεῖς vocabantur. Horum autem au- ctoritatem sequebatur Pharisæorum familia, hoc tantum distincta à cæteris, quod super communia præcepta peculia- res sibi ἐθελοθρησκείας injunxerat. Ideo autem ab Hierosoly- mis venerunt, quia in primaria urbe habitabant nobilissimi magistrorum & partium istarum duces.

## 15:2
Vers. 2. The tradition] παράδοσις is nothing other than what the Greek philosophers call a dogma. Christ himself below at XVI. 11 calls it teaching, for to hand down is to teach, just as it is to tradere for the Latins: as when Caesar says that the Druids taught the youth much about the power and influence of the gods, from which Gellius also fashioned the word tradition after the example of the Greek noun παράδοσις. Thus Paul uses both the verb παραδιδόναι and the noun παράδοσις when dealing with the dogmas of Christianity, 1 Cor. XI. 2, 17, ch. XV. 3, which he explains elsewhere by saying traditions which you were taught, 2 Thess. II. 15. He said handed down in Rom. VII. 17. Thus the faith handed down to the Jews. And the counterpart to this is לקח, a receiving, for a dogma insofar as it is accepted. Thus Ovid: Antiquity is believed as a great witness: spare to disturb the accepted faith.

When I say dogmas, I do not take the word as strictly as it is usually taken when it is opposed to exhortations, but in such a way that it also includes them. For both what must be done and what must be believed are prescribed under that name, as appears from the cited passages, with the addition of the one which is 2 Thess. III. 6. Therefore, this word does not of itself signify merely human inventions, but the breadth of that word, as also of dogmas, extends to that as well. Therefore, something is usually added, as when they are called traditions of men, Col. II. 8, or of the elders, as here and elsewhere. But the later Hebrews said Qabbalah, not for any tradition, but for an unwritten one. Now, however, not even every unwritten tradition is called by this word, but only that which is more mystical. Otherwise, the origin of the word is broader, for it is from Qabal, that is, to receive, which is the counterpart to handing down, as appears in 1 Cor. XI. 23, XV. 1, 3, Gal. I. 12, Phil. IV. 2, Col. II. 6. Thess. II. 13, ch. IV. 1, 2 Thess. III. 6. But the ancient Christians also use it more loosely, as Cyprian: Whence is this tradition? Does it descend from the authority of the Lord and the Gospel, or does it come from the commands and epistles of the Apostles? For God testifies that those things which are written must be done. Shortly after: If therefore it is commanded in the Gospel, or is contained in the epistles or acts of the Apostles, let this holy tradition also be observed.

Concerning παράδοσις or tradition, because of the Papists, who take the word tradition, if it occurs anywhere in the Scriptures, for their own unwritten traditions, I would wish these things to be well observed: to which our Grotius, with more willingness than the willingness itself, sometimes gratifies them; but the Papists, while they receive traditions with the same affection of piety as Holy Scripture, and sometimes even prefer them to Scripture, are not unlike the Pharisees and the Rabbis: concerning whom Lightfoot [writes] in this place. How highly they valued their traditions, even above the divine Word, is sufficiently clear from this very passage, verse six. From the infinite examples that occur in their own writings, we shall bring forward only one passage. Hieros. Beracoth, fol. 3. 2. The words of the Scribes are more amiable than the words of the Law: for the words of the Law are heavy and light; but the words of the Scribes are all light, etc.

The elders] The reason why I do not think that the senators of the great Sanhedrin are meant here is that it was the duty of the Sanhedrin to preside over judgments, not to teach the people or even to establish laws. For laws, at the time when they were ruled by the He- manuscripts of the same Writer under the title περὶ γραμμάτων where ἀνδῶν is written for Ἀδδῶν, & against Marcion, where it is written corruptly τῶν μὲν Δαειδ for τῶ μὲν Ἀδδᾶ: from which passage we also learn that that Akiba was older than the Babylonian exile: but I shall add that he existed after the times of the postliminium.

What Grotius notes here, as to who were called πρεσβύτεροι, are not of the same stamp. He says that the Senators of the great Sanhedrin are not called πρεσβύτεροι here, because it was the function of the Sanhedrin to preside over judgments, not to teach the people or even to establish laws. That there were no Senators among the presbyters is doubtful, and Grotius himself did not dare to say that none taught the people. To teach the people, he says later, was not the function of the whole Sanhedrin, or of any one from the senate, but of those who had obtained an outstanding reputation for learning among the people, whether they were Senators or private individuals. For just as at Rome formerly, to give legal advice was not sought as a favor, but it was permitted to those who had confidence in themselves to profess that art, so also among the Jews. These were called החכמים. But they are also not wrongly called πρεσβύτεροι, either because that name was accustomed to be given to all who were eminent either by dignity or even by authority alone, just as the name πατέρων, or because in ancient times the wise, especially some time after their death, were called among the Hebrews הקר מינים. Where, however, it is not easily to be conceded that they permitted anyone to teach the people without a calling. For from that, mere confusion would have arisen. And Christ himself said that the Scribes and Pharisees sit in the Chair of Moses, whom they could hear, Matt. XXIII. 2. 3. Who certainly were not lacking a calling: for no one snatched a Chair for himself at will, or if he had dared to do so, would he be said to sit in it and be heard as a legitimate Doctor. Nor is it simply to be approved that it was not the function of the Sanhedrin to establish laws, even if at the time when the Hebrews were ruled by Kings, they were accustomed to be established by the Kings, 1. Sam. XXX. 25. but in a free Republic παρὰ τῆς ἐκκλησίας, by the assembly of the people. For the great Sanhedrin also took that power to itself and ought not to have ceased to be מחקק until Shiloh should come. And Grotius admits that the συναγωγὴν μεγάλην, as a compendium of the people, filled the place of the assembly, especially following the approval of the whole people. Finally, since he admits that the decrees and traditions of the elders had the force of laws, was not the authority of the great Sanhedrin greater than that of presbyters who held no dignity of office? But he says that these were first considered as counsels, and after the usage of the people and long time were added to the authority of the hearers, they began to be turned into precepts, and not only into such precepts by which external society was contained, but which also bound the mind when no one was looking. Whence did that come about? Certainly not without the authority and consent of the great Sanhedrin, either express or tacit and interpretative.

Νίπτονται] Properly. For as Pollux teaches, νίπτεσθαι is before food: ἀπονίπτεσθαι after food. But this Jewish washing, which Mark accurately describes, was not opposed to rusticity, a not insignificant part of which is ἡ ἁλυσία, but was done with definite gestures, τῇ ὁσίας χάριν. The cause of this was that the teachers of the Hebrews (blind, indeed, leaders of the blind, as Christ will soon teach us) thought that if anyone were ἀκάθαρτος or otherwise impure according to the law, or had touched food or drink itself, or anything that touched food or drink, for instance their own hands, with which they were about to take food, which part of the body is most exposed to contact, or the vessels in which food was to be cooked, or the cups from which they were about to drink, that such a contagion of defilement would transmit that food or drink first to their own body, then to their mind: for which reason they had discovered a καθαρισμὸν (as John calls it), by accurate washing, namely an empty remedy for the fear of hands, as Menander wittily said, whose verses I cannot but append, a little more corrected than they are wont to be read: εἰ μέν τι ἀληθὲς κακὸν Εἶχες Φίλ’ ἀληθὲς φάρμακον τούτου σ’ ἐδει. Νῦν δ’ οὐκ ἔχεις. εὕρηκα κενὸν τὸ φάρμακον Πρὸς τὸ κενόν. οἰήσει δ’ ὠφελῶν τίσει. Let the women wipe you around in a circle And let them sprinkle water from three springs.

With this he is sprinkled, having cast in salt, and lentils. Everyone is pure who knows no evil in himself. Of this Pharisaic opinion there is no slight trace in the Apostles, when they interpret Christ's saying about leaven as if it were a sin to procure food either from the Pharisees or from the Sadducees. And the teachers of the Hebrews note that the Jews proclaimed to the Samaritans, and the Samaritans to the Jews, when they met, do not touch. Josephus notes concerning the Essenes that the more advanced are accustomed to wash themselves from contact with the less advanced as if from contact with foreigners. They undoubtedly wanted this opinion of theirs to be supported by the authority of the divine law, which willed that bodies be considered impure by the contact of certain bodies, so that even if that were later discovered, some purgation was to be applied, just as the Essenes, according to Josephus, believed they were defiled by a bowel movement, even though the discharge is natural, but were purified by taking water. But not even by those things which the law of God calls impure did the mind contract guilt, unless after the neglect of a divine command. Nor had God commanded these things primarily, but so that He might restrain a people too fond of ceremonies with those rites, by which even better things were signified. But that dogma, which the legates of the lawyers and the Pharisaic sect here object to the Apostles of Christ, rested on a clearly false persuasion. For they thought first that some contacts were impure by their nature, concerning which no law of God existed: then also that the mind of the ignorant is affected by that impurity: finally, however, that a stain unpunished in the mind could be washed away by a rite which God had not commanded, but which they themselves had invented. From a similar foolishness arose the superstition of the Hemerobaptists, which Mahomet, like many other things scraped together from everywhere, transferred into his own law.

Grotius could have added the Papistic sprinklings and washings, which are either not unlike Jewish and Mahometan superstition, or certainly owe their origin to it, as Marsilius Columna in Hydragius, book 1, section II, chapter 2, number 2, derived holy water from Judaism and Gentilism. Holy water, which was surely proposed by the Church with decency and the greatest reason. For if water was in use among the Gentiles for the expiation of men, as they themselves believed, as Tertullian testifies in chapter 5 of De Baptismo, and Lylius Gyraldus, History of the Gods, Syntagma 17. If likewise the priests of the Hebrews used it, it was certainly more consistent that it should also be instituted among the Christian Church and be holier and have greater efficacy. Meanwhile, Grotius does not rashly conclude that the error of the Pharisees clung to the Apostles from Matthew 16:7. Of this Pharisaic opinion, he says, there is no slight trace in the Apostles when they interpret Christ's saying about leaven as if it were a sin to procure food from either the Pharisees or the Sadducees. Which our own interpreters had already indicated. For since the Jews did not have common meals with the Samaritans, because they were excommunicated, the Apostles thought Christ meant the same thing regarding the Pharisees, Sadducees, and Herod, namely that they should regard them as excommunicated, from whose food they should abstain in all things, as the blessed Lyserus observed in Harmony, chapter 83. Concerning Pharisaic traditions and the washing of hands, Lightfoot is prolix here, noting among other things the gloss in the Babylonian Taanith: Shibta is one of the demons who harm those who do not wash their hands before food.

Latin:

Vers. 2. Τὴν παράδοσιν] παράδοσις nihil aliud est, quam quod Græci Philosophi vocant δόγμα. Christus ipse infra XVI. 11. διδαχὴν nam παραδιδόναι est διδάσκειν, ut & Latinis tradere: velut cum Cæsar ait Druides multa de deorum vi ac potestate juventuti traderetunde & traditionjs vocem effin- xit Gellius ad exemplum Græci va. abuli παραδόσεως. Ita Paulus & verbum παραδιδόναι & nomen παραδόσεως usurpat agens de dogmatis Christianismi 1. Cor XI. 2. 17. cap. XV. 3. quod alibi explicat dicens παραδόσεις ἃς ἐδιδάχθητε 2. Thess. II. 15. παραδοθεῖς dixit Rom. VII. 17. Sic Judæ πα- ραδοθεῖσα πίστις. Et ἀντίστροφον huic est לקח λῆψις, pro dog- mate quatenus admittitur. Sic Ovidius: pro magno teste vetustas Creditur: acceptam parce movere fidem.

Δόγματα cum dico non ita stricte accipio vocem quomodo sumi solet cum opponitur ταῖς παρανέσισιν, sed ita ut eas quoque comprehendat. Tam enim quæ agenda quam quæ credenda præscribuntur eo nomine veniunt, ut apparet di- ctis locis, addito eo qui est 2. Thess. III. 6. Commenta ergo mere humana vox ista per se non significat, sed eo quoque vocis istius ut & δογμάτων, latitudo se extendit. Ideo addi plerunque aliquid solet, ut cum dicuntur παράδοσεις ἀνθρώ- πων Col. II. 8. aut τῶν πρεσβυτέρων, ut hic atque alibi. At He- bræi posteriores קבלה dixerunt non quamvis παράδοσιν, sed ἄγραφον. Nunc autem ne omnis quidé ἄγραφος παράδο- σις sed ea demum quæ est μυσικώτερος hoc vocabulo appel- latur. Alioquin origo vocis latius patet, est enim à קבל id est, παραλαμβάνω, quod est ἀντιστρέφον τῷ παραδιδόναι, ut apparet 1. Cor. XI. 23. XV. I. 3. Gal. I. 12. Phil. IV. 2. Col. II, 6. 1. Thess. II. 13. cap. IV. 1. 2. Thess. III. 6 Sed & veteres Christiani laxius usurpant, ut Cyprianus: Vnde est ista tradi- tio, utrumne de dominica & evangelica auctoritate descendens, an de Apostolorum mandatis atque epistolis veniens? Ea enim facienda esse quæ scripta sunt Deus testatur Mox: Si ergo aut in Evangelio præcipitur, aut in Apostolorum epistolis aut acti- bus continetur, observetur etiam & hæc sancta traditio.

De παράδοσις vel traditione, ob Pontificios, vo- cem traditionis, si qua in Scripturis occurrit, pro suis non-scriptis traditionibus accipientes, ista probe observari velim: quibus alias lubentia ipsa lubentius Grotius noster gratificatur, Pontifi- cii autem dum pari pietatis affectu cum Scriptura S. traditiones suscipiunt, nonnunquam etiam eas- dem Scripturæ præferunt, Pharisæis non absimi- les sunt, & Rabbinis: de quibus Lightfooth in h. l. Quanto pretio traditiones suas æstimarint, etiam præ Verbo divino, satis patet ex hoc ipso loco, versu sexto. Ex infinitis exemplis, quæ in ipsorum scriptis occur- runt, nos unum tantum locum proferemus. Hieros. Beracoth. fol. 3. 2. חביבים דברי כופרים מדברי תורה Amabilia sunt verba Scribarum præ verbis Legis: nam verba Legis sunt gravia & levia; at verba Scribarum sunt omnia levia, &c.

Τῶν πρεσβυτέρων] πρεσβυτέρος cur hic non arbitrer dici Senatores magni Synedrii hæc causa est, quod Synedrii erat judiciis præsidere, non docere populum aut leges etiam constituere. Leges enim, quo tempore regnabantur He- codices ejusdem Scriptoris titulo περὶ γραμμάτων ubi ἀνδῶν scriptum est pro Ἀδδῶν, & adversus Marcionem, ubi corru- pte scribitur τῶν μὲν Δαειδ pro τῶ μὲν Ἀδδᾶ: ex quo loco etiam discimus Akibam illum fuisse antiquiorem exsilio Babylo- nico: Addam autem post tempora postliminii exstitisse.

Quae hic notat Grotius, quinam πρεσβύτεροι dicti fuerint, non ejusdem commatis sunt. Ait, non dici hic πρεσβυτέρους Senatores magni Synedrii, quod Synedrii fuerit judiciis praesidere, non docere popu- lum aut leges etiam constituere. Nullos Senatores inter presbyteros fuisse dubium est, nullos populos docuisse, nec ipse Grotius ausus est dicere. Docere, inquit postea, populum non erat aut Synedrii totius, aut cujuslibet e senatu, sed eorum qui eximium eru- ditionis nomen apud populum erant consecuti, sive Senatores essent, sive privati. Nam sicut Romae olim de jure respondere non pro beneficio impetrabatur, sed licebat eis qui fiduciam sui habebant eam artem profiteri, ita & apud Judaeos. Hi dicebantur החכמים Sed & πρεσβύτεροι non male vocantur, seu quia id nomen omnibus aut dignitate aut etiam sola aucto- ritate eminentibus dari solebat, quomodo & nomen πατέρων, sive quia antiquitus sapientes, praesertim a- liquo post mortem tempore apud Hebraeos vocabantur הקר מינים. Ubi tamen non facile conceden- dum, quod docere populum cuilibet, sine vocatio- ne, permiserint. Inde enim mera orta fuisset con- fusio. Et in Cathedra Mosis sedere Scribas & Pha- risaeos Christus ipse dixit, quos audire possint Matth. XXIII. 2. 3. Qui utique vocatione non de- stituebantur: nec enim quisquam pro lubitu sibi Cathedram rapiebat, aut si id ausus fuisset, in ea se- dere, & audiendus esse ceu legitimus Doctor, di- ceretur. Neq; simpliciter probandum, quod Syne- drii non fuerit leges constituere, etsi quo tempore re- gnabantur Ebraei constitui a Regibus consueverint, 1. Sam. XXX. 25. libera autem Republica παρὰ τῆς ἐκκλησίας, a populi conventu. Nam & Synedrium magnum eam sibi sumpsit potestatem neque desine- re debuit מחקק donec veniret שילה. Et fatetur Grotius, συναγωγὴν μεγάλην quasi compendium populi locum impleffe conventus, praesertim subsecuta populi totius approbatione. Deniq; quum τῶν πρεσ- βυτέρων δόγματα, & παραδόσεις admittat legum vim habuisse, annon major autoritas fuit Synedrii magni, quam presbyterorum nulla officii dignita- te fungentium? Sed haec pro consiliis primum habita postquam ad autoritatem auditorum usus populi & longa dies accessit, in praecepta verti cepisse, dicit, neq; in talia tantum praecepta, quibus externa societas con- tineretur, sed quae etiam nemine inspectante animum obstringerent.. Unde id factum? Certe non sine au- ctoritate & consensu Synedrii magni seu expresso seu tacito & interpretativo.

Νίπτονται] Proprie. Nam ut Pollux docet, νίπτεσθαι est an- te cibum: ἀπονίπτεσθαι post cibum. Haec autem lotio Judaica, quam Marcus accurate describit, non erat rusticitati oppo- sita, cujus non exigua pars est ἡ ἁλυσία, sed fiebat definitis gestibus, τῇ ὁσίας χάριν. Causa haec erat, quod arbitrarentur Hebraeorum magistri (caeci nimirum, caecorum duces, ut nos mox docebit Christus) si quis ἀκάθαρτος aut alioqui juxta legem impurus, aut cibum ipsum potumve attigisset, aut quicquam, quod cibu potumve contingeret, puta ipso- rum manus, quibus cibum sumturi erant, quae pars corporis maxime ad contactum patet, aut vasa in quibus obsonium coqueretur, aut pocula e quibus erant potaturi, eum cibum potumve, talis inquinamenti contagium ad corpus primum suum, deinde ad animum immittere: quapropter καθα- ρισμὸν (ut Johannes vocat) repererant, accurate lotione, nimirum manis metus inane remedium, ut lepide dixit Me- nander, cujus versus non possum non apponere paulo quam legi solent emendatiores: εἰ μέν τι ἀληθὲς κακὸν Εἶχες Φίλ’ ἀληθὲς φάρμακον τούτου σ’ ἐδει. Νῦν δ’ οὐκ ἔχεις. εὕρηκα κενὸν τὸ φάρμακον Πρὸς τὸ κενόν. οἰήσει δ’ ὠφελῶν τίσει. Περιμαξάτωσαν σ’ αἱ γυναῖκες ἐν κύκλῳ Καὶ περιλιτωσαν ἀπὸ τριῶν κρηνῶν ὕδωρ.

Τούτω̣ περιῤῥαίνεται, ἐμβαλὼν ἅλας, κᾀ Φακούς. Πᾶς ἁγνὸς ἔσθ᾽ ὁ μηδὲν οἱ συνειδὼς κακόν. Hujus Pharisaicæ opinionis non leve vestigium est in Apo- stolis, cum Christi dictum de fermento ita interpretantur, quasi nefas esset vel à Pharisæis vel à Sadducæis cibum com- parare. Et notant Hebræorum magistri Judæos Samaritis, Samaritas Judæis obviis proclamasse, noli attingere. Jose- phus de Essenis notat, provectiores à minus provectis con- tactus abluere se solere quasi à contactu ἀλλοφύλων. Vola- runt haud dubie hanc suam sententiam divinæ legis aucto- ritate, quæ quorundam corporum contactu corpora impu- tari voluit, ita ut etiamsi id postea rescisceretur, purgamen- tum aliquod esset adhibendum, quomodo & Esseni Josepho teste crediderunt pollui se levata alvo καίπερ φυσικῆς ὔσης τῆς ἐκκρίσεως, sed aqua sumta purgari. At ne illis quidem rebus, quas lex Dei impuras vocat, culpam contrahebat animus, nisi post neglectum divinæ jussionis. Neque ista Deus προη- γουμένως præceperat, sed ut populum nimis amantem cere- moniarum istis ritibus distineret, quibus res etiam meliores signabantur. Dogma autem illud, quod hic Apostolis Chri- sti objiciunt, legisperitorum & Pharisaicæ sectæ legati, pla- ne falsa nitebatur persuasione. Existimabant enim primum aliquos contactus immundos esse sui natura, de quibus lex Dei nulla exstabat: deinde etiam ignorantis animum affici ea impuritate: postremo autem elui posse maculam animo inultam ritu, quem Deus non imperaverat, sed ipsi erant commenti. Ex simili stultitia ortum habuit ἡ ἡμεροβαπτιστῶν superstitio, quam Mahumetus, ut multa alia undique cor- rasa, in legem suam transtulit.
