Addere potuisset Grotius aspersiones, & lotiones Papisticas, quæ superstitioni Judaicæ & Mahome- tanæ, aut non absimiles sunt, aut certe originem suam debent, uti Marsilius Columna in Hydragio l. sect. II. c. 2. n. 2. aquam benedictam è Judaismo & Gentilismo deduxit. Aqua benedicta quam decenti sane ac maxima cum ratione ab Ecclesia proposita fuit. Nam si aqua apud Gentiles expiandis, ut ipsi credebant, hominibus in usu erat, ut Tertullianus te- statur c. V. de Baptismo, & Lylius Gyrald. Hist. Deor. Syntagm. 17. Si item illa utebantur Hebræorum Sa- cerdotes, magis certe consentaneum fuit, ut & illa a- pud Ecclesiam Christianam institueretur sanctiorque esset & majorem illa efficaciam haberet. Interim Apostolis hæsisse errorem Pharisæorum è Matth. XVI. 7. non temere colligit Grotius. Hujus Phari- saicæ opinionis, inquit, non leve vestigium est in Apo- stolis cum Christi dictum de fermento ita interpre- tantur, quasi nefas esset vel à Pharisæis vel à Saddu- cæis cibum comparare. Quæ nostrates Interpp. jam indicarant. Nam quoniam Judæi non habebant com- munem victum cum Samaritanis, eo quod hi excom- municati essent, putabant Apostoli Christum, quoad Pharisæos, Sadducæos & Herodem idem velle, ut ha- berent nimirum eos pro excommunicatis à quorum victu per omnia abstineant, ut observavit B. Lyse- rus in Harm. c. LXXXIII. De Pharisaicis traditio- nibus, de lotionibus manuum prolixus hic est Lightfooth, notans inter alia glossam in Bab. Taa- nith: Shibta ex dæmonibus est, qui iis nocent, qui non lavant manus ante cibum.

## 15:3
V. 3. διὰ τὶ κᾀ ὑμεῖς παραβαίνετε] Before Christ disputes about that tradition which they were objecting to, he tears down the very foundation upon which their entire reasoning rested. For they assumed as certain that one must stand without any exception by the received opinions of the Sages, in whose consensus there was ἀναμάρτητος: which Christ shows to be false by a most evident example of a received dogma, which fought implacably with the divine law.

Latin:

V. 3. διὰ τὶ κᾀ ὑμεῖς παραβαίνετε] Christus antequam de illa quam objiciebant traditione disputet, convellit funda- mentum ipsum cui tota illorum ratiocinatio innitebatur. Pro certo enim ponebant, standum sine ulla exceptione receptis Sapientum sententiis, in quorum consensio esset ἀναμάρτη- τος: quod falsu esse Christus ostendit exemplo evidentissimo recepti dogmatis, quod cum lege divina ἀσπόνδως pugnabat.

## 15:4
V. 4. Τίμα] It is the Hebrew word כבד by which is also included the dutiful honesty of supporting parents. In which sense the word τιμῆς is also used by Paul; and the verb τιμᾶν in 1 Timothy 5:3, 17. Therefore, that which follows here κᾀ ὀ μὴ τιμήσῃ τ πᾱτέρα, Mark explains as ἐκ ἔτι ἀφίετε ἀυτὸν ἐδὲν ποιῆσαι τῷ πᾱτρί, where ποιεῖν is ἀγαθοποιεῖν. Nor do the most learned of the Hebrews explain it otherwise in Numbers 24:11, and those who explain this very commandment of theirs say that the provision of food, drink, and clothing is contained therein. Therefore, there was no need for Christ to labor in proving it. Indeed, the laws of the Greeks and Romans also command the same. And Hierocles also explains the verb τιμᾶν in this way: 'But in all other things let us honor our parents exceedingly, offering them service of the body and provision of money as most readily as possible.' ὁ κακολογῶν] The Hebrew word קלל, which is found in Exodus and Leviticus, is directly opposed to the word כבד. For just as כבד in its origin is to add weight, so קלל is to subtract weight. But the LXX interpreters, whom our author here follows word for word, declaring the matter with a most well-known example, said ὁ κακολογῶν: in which sense it is certain that the Hebrew word, although it extends more broadly, is very often taken. Nor did Christ add this in vain. For it is agreed that among the precepts of God those are to be considered of the greatest importance which are sanctioned by a capital penalty. Christ therefore shows that not just any precept is violated by the authority of the lawyers, but such a one as God himself testified was to be held among the principal ones.

Latin:

V. 4. Τίμα] Vox Hebræa est כבד qua comprehenditur etia officiosa honestie alendi parentes. In quem sensum vox τιμῆς etiam à Paulo usurpatur; & verbum τιμᾶν 1. Tim. V. 3. 17. Itaque id quod hic sequitur κᾀ ὀ μὴ τιμήσῃ τ πᾱτέρα, Mar- cus exponit ἐκ ἔτι ἀφίετε ἀυτὸν ἐδὲν ποιῆσαι τῷ πᾱτρί, ubi ποιεῖν est ἀγαθοποιεῖν. Neq; aliter exponunt Hebræorum eruditis- simi Num. XXIV. 11. & qui eorum hoc ipsum præceptum ex- plicant, ajunt cibi, potus & vestimenti præbitionem eo con- tineri. Itaq; non erat quod in eo probando Christus labora- ret. Quin Græcorum quoque & Romanorum leges idem præcipiunt. Et verbum τιμᾶν ita explicat etiam Hierocles: εἰς δὲ τὰ ἀλλὰ πάντα γονέας τιμήσωμεν ὑπερβαλλόντως, σώματος ὑ- πηρεσίαν καὶ χρημάτων χορηγίαν ἀυτοῖς ὑπέχοντες ὅτι μάλιςα προθυμοτάτην. ὁ κακολογῶν] Verbum Hebr. קלל quod in Exodo &amp; Levitico reperitur directe opponitur verbo כבד. Nam ut כבד sua origine est pondus addere, ita קלל est pon- dus detrahere. At LXX. interpretes, quos noster hic verbo- tenus sequitur, notissimo exemplo rem declarantes dixe- runt ὁ κακολογῶν: in quem sensum certum est vocem He- bræam, quanquam latius patentem, sæpissime accipi. Non frustra autem &amp; hoc Christus adjecit. Constat enim inter Dei præcepta ea esse maximi ducenda quæ capitali pœna sanciuntur. Ostendit ergo Christus non quodlibet præce- ptum legisperitorum auctoritate violari, sed tale quod in- ter præcipua habendum Deus ipse testaretur.

## 15:5
Vers. 5. ὃς ἂν εἴπῃ] I do not think there is an ἀποσιώπησις here, as many suppose, but rather that the ὃς is redundant in the Hebrew manner, as below xxviii. 9, Mark xiii. 34, Luke II. 15, & 21, & 27, 28, likewise Luke V. 35, c. IX. 51, c. XIII. 25, c. XIV. 1, which I say once, so that I may not be forced to repeat the testimonies. Therefore I interpret it thus: But you teach: whoever shall say to his father or his mother δῶρον ὃ ἐὰν ἐξ ἐμοῦ ὠφεληθῇς, let him not support his father or his mother. And in Mark, But you teach in this manner: If anyone shall say to father or mother, κορβᾶν ὃ ἐξ ἐμοῦ ὠφεληθῇς, you do not permit him to provide anything further to father or mother. Λέγειν in both places is to teach. For thus it is accustomed to be used in the Hebrew Schools, אמר, that is, ἔφη.

Δῶρον] Mark placed the word itself κορβᾶν and the Syrian here קרבני, from which we learn that not just any δῶρον is signified here, but that which is consecrated to God, in the way we saw the word δῶρα used also in the fifth chapter. And hence it is that some of the ancients, citing this passage, do not place δῶρον nakedly, but δῶρον τῷ θεῷ. This formula is cited from the Hebrew masters in this manner קָרְבָּן שֶׁאַתָּה נֶהֱנֶה לִי and thus also מַה דְתִתְהַנֵּא מִנִּי: קָרְבַּן, from which the Syrian does not depart far, who in this place placed it thus: קָרְבָּנִי דְתִתְהַנֵּא מִנִּי. Let us see what ὃ ἐὰν ἐξ ἐμοῦ ὠφεληθῇς is, then what κορβᾶν ὃ ἐξ ἐμοῦ ὠφεληθῇς means here: the interpreters express the formula I mentioned in almost as many words as מַה שֶׁאַתָּה נֶהֱנֶה מִמֶּנִּי, and they say that the noun הֲנָאָה extends so widely that it comprehends both food and everything by which a man can be helped by a man. That force could not be expressed better than by the Greek verb ὠφελεῖσθαι. Est autem illud ὠφεληθῇς here is an ἀπολετικὸν: wherefore it is permitted to express it in Latin thus: whatever it is by which you can be helped by me. In the Nehardin Codex is found: קוֹנָם שֶׁאֲנִי עָנְשֶׁה עַל פִּי אַבָּא וְכֵיוּ יָכוֹל לְהָפֵר שְׁכָל מַה: Which Maimonides interprets thus: אֵינָם שֶׁאעַ שהלא יֹאכַל מִמֶּנּוּ אַבָּה מַאַנְמָה כָּל שֶׁלֹא יֵהָנֶה בּוֹ. That whatever I shall have prepared, my father shall not eat anything from it, i.e., that he will not perceive utility from it. But as far as the other word קָרְבָּן is concerned, it is accustomed among the Hebrews, like חרם, as often as it is placed alone, to include the force of a substantive verb: wherefore κορβᾶν is worth κορβᾶν ἔστω, i.e., let it be dedicated to God. But what was thus dedicated to God, that was believed to be entirely outside the power and commerce of men: Hence that קָרְבָּן in this formula the Hebrew interpreters do not badly explain as אָסוּר עָלֶיךָ i.e., let it be prohibited or closed off to you. Liber Caph Nical thus explains this kind of vow: הֶקְדֵשׁ יְהֵא כָּל מַה שֶׁאֲנִי עוֹשֶׂה מִלְבוֹ מִלְבוֹ עַל פִּי אבּא Let it be sacred, whatever I shall prepare in the future for the mouth of my father. The Rabbis in this way: כָּל שֶׁאֲנִי עוֹשֶׂה לְפִי אַבּא קוֹנָם אֵינוֹ יָכוֹל לְהָפֵר Whatever I shall prepare for my Father, let it be sacred. He who has vowed thus cannot make the vow void. And because in the name κορβᾶν the mention of God was included (for קָרְבָּן is, as we have said, a thing sacred to God, whence Josephus, concerning those who devote themselves to God, οἱ κορβᾶν ἑαυτὸς ὀνομάζοντες), therefore this vow was believed not to be naked but to comprise the religion of an oath. Hence the Tyrians, when they forbade τοὺς ξενικοὺς ὅρκους, specifically named τὸν ὅρκον καλούμενον κορβᾶν, on the authority of Theophrastus in his book on laws, the mention of which oath Matthew also makes below XXIII.18. Plane frequens fuisse Judæis that it was common for the Jews to bind themselves not only by a vow but also by an oath not to benefit this or that person, we learn both from the Hebrew masters and from Philo, whose words are worthy of note for this matter: εἰσὶ δ' οἳ τὴν φύσιν ἀμίκτοι κᾀκοινώνητοι δι' ὑπερβολὴν μισανθρωπίας γεγονότες, ἤ κᾀ ὑπ' ὀργῆς οἷα χαλεπῆς δεσποίνης ἐκβιασθέντες, ὅρκῳ τὴν ἀγριότητα πισοῦνται τῶν ἠθῶν, οἵ τινες ὥσφασιν ὁμοτράπεζον ἤ ὁμορόφιον ἕξειν τὸν δεῖνα ἤ πάλιν ΤΩ ΔΕΙΝΙ ΜΗ ΡΕΞΕΙΝ ΩΦΕΛΕΙΑΝ ΤΙΝΑ ἤ παρ' ἐκείνῳ ἵνα λήψεσθαι κᾀμέχρι τελευτᾶς: where he openly describes that vow which the Hebrews call נֶדֶר הֲנָאָה, i.e., εὐχὴν τῆς ὠφελείας. But this vow, so that it might be firmer and holier, was accustomed, as we learn from Matthew and Mark, to have added the consecration of the thing in that case if ever anything were given to τῷ δεῖνι. Quod si is qui votum tale nuncupasset, postea immutata voluntate largiri aliquid vellet τῷ δεῖνι, the priests, of whom the Pharisees were a great part, claimed the matter for the sacred treasury by the law of the vow. But the revenues of that treasury were dispensed partly for the works of the temple, partly for the uses of the poor, partly for the Priests and Levites themselves. Wherefore it is more credible that the Pharisees, who were Φιλάργυροι as Luke teaches us XVI.14, stubbornly stood by the utilities of the treasury against the just rights of any men. For vows even under Roman law bound men in such a way that they were forced to fulfill the vow. Furthermore, what Origen narrates here, that he learned from a Hebrew that creditors often transferred names to the treasury, so that they might thrust a harsher adversary upon their debtors, as I believe it to be true, so it does not properly pertain to this.

These things have been observed not inappropriately. Yet those things which have been adduced by him from the Hebrews, although they may contribute to illustration, are not of such antiquity or authority that they deserve to be reckoned. Many such things are wont to be brought forward from the formulas and rites of the Hebrews. But we do not easily esteem those blind guides so highly that we should bring them into the dust and the sun. Not rarely do they intermix their own novel παραδόσεις, so that it is difficult to discern what they have had from the ancients. And such things often make more for display than for illustrating the meaning of the sacred writers. Furthermore, others explain that saying differently, namely: This Corban which I offer to God is a profit to me and mine: because by this compact they thought themselves rendered free from charity toward parents. Others, that a gift offered to God would be of benefit to parents, whence there is no need to help them otherwise, as Tremellius. He rendered the Syriac text: it is an oblation, that from which you will take utility from me, which sense Ludovicus de Dieu extracted from the Greek text, because the particle ἤ often abounds and not rarely serves for an interrogation, thus: But you say, Whoever shall have said to father or mother, It is a gift that you will gain from me, has he not honored his father or his mother? That is, You say: Has he not affected his parents with enough honor, who has said to them that he has offered a gift to God, from which they also might take utility? No, says Christ, this is not to honor the father enough, but this is ἀκυρῶν τὴν ἐντολὴν τοῦ θεοῦ. However, he does not wish to urge this explanation strongly, because in Mark 7:11 the sentence is abrupt and imperfect, κορβᾶν, ὅ ἐστι, δῶρον ὃ ἐὰν ἐξ ἐμοῦ, ὠφεληθῇς, which, with the verb rendered by the imperfect subjunctive, Dievius interprets thus: it is a gift (consecrated to God) whatever you might gain from me, or of utility you might take; in the same sense which Grotius delivered; the words, he says, are of a son rejecting the petition of a father, and that by this argument, because all my faculties are Corban, are a gift and offering consecrated to God, nor is it permitted for you therefore to ask that you might take any utility from them, nor for me to grant it; for you would take utility from divine things, which is repugnant to my vow, by which I have bound all my things to God. And this is what Mark adds, κ’ ἐκέτι ἀφίετε αὐτὸν ὐδὲν ποιῆσαι τῷ πατρὶ αὐτοῦ, ἢ τῇ μητρί αὐτοῦ. That is, after his faculties have once been made corban, you no longer permit him from that time to expend anything of it upon his parents. He adds: just as in the Papacy children sometimes, without the knowledge and against the will of their parents, bind themselves by a vow of monasticism, and by that are emancipated from the right and power of their parents, so also were the children of the Jews taught by the Pharisees to vow their faculties to God; whereby it happened that when parents were to be honored, that is, to be helped, they would hold out corban or a vow of oblation, and by that excuse themselves. This is that Ludovicus. Akin to these are the things which Lightfoot has at length here: where among other things: The words are introduced, he says, as if uttered with indignation: as if, when a needy father asked for sustenance from his son, that angry one should reply, and with contempt: As if it were a sacred thing, whatever of mine might be of use to you. But sacred things were not to be expended for common uses. And: The words of the verse therefore can be rendered thus, without any interjected addition, which most interpreters append: Whoever shall have said to father or mother, Let it be a gift (consecrated), by whatever you might be helped by me: then he by no means honors his father or his mother. Compare also the dissertation on these things published by Ludov. Capellus, and what Walaeus has adduced here from Selden.

Latin:

Vers. 5. ὃς ἂν εἴπῃ] Non puto esse hic ἀποσιώπησιν, ut multi arbitrantur, sed potius redundare Hebræo more ὃς, ut infra xxviii. 9. Marc. xiii. 34. Luc. II. 15. &amp; 21. &amp; 27. 28. i- tem Luc. V. 35. c. IX. 51. c. XIII. 25. c. XIV. 1. quod semel di- co, ne testimonia repetere cogar. Itaq; sic interpreter: Vos autem docetis: qui dixerit patri suo aut matri suæ δῶρον ὃ ἐὰν ἐξ ἐμοῦ ὠφεληθῇς, ne alat patrẽ aut matrem suam. Et apud Mar- cum, Vos autem docetis hunc in modum: Si quis patri matri've dixerit, κορβᾶν ὃ ἐξ ἐμοῦ ὠφεληθῇς non permittitis eum quicquam ultra patri matri've præstare. Λέγειν utrobiq; est docere. Ita e- nim in Scholis Hebraicis usurpari solet אמר hoc est ἔφη.

Δῶρον] Vocem ipsam posuit Marcus κορβᾶν &amp; Syrus hic קרבני, unde discimus nõ quodvis δῶρον hic significari, sed id quod Deo sacratur, quomodo voce δῶρα usurpari vidim9 &amp; quinto capite. Atq; hinc est quod veterum quidam hunc locum citantes non δῶρον nude ponunt, sed δῶρον τῷ θεῷ. For- mula hæc ex Hebræis magistris citatur huc in modum קָרְבָּן שֶׁאַתָּה נֶהֱנֶה לִי &amp; sic etiã מַה דְתִתְהַנֵּא מִנִּי: קָרְבַּן unde nõ lõge abit Syr. qui hoc loco ita posuit: קָרְבָּנִי דְתִתְהַנֵּא מִנִּי. Videamus quid sit ὃ ἐὰν ἐξ ἐμοῦ ὠφεληθῇς, deinde quid hic velit κορβᾶν ὃ ἐξ ἐμοῦ ὠφεληθῇς: interpretes e- jus quã dixi formulæ totidem prope verbis exprimunt מַה שֶׁאַתָּה נֶהֱנֶה מִמֶּנִּי &amp; nomen הֲנָאָה ajunt tam late pa- tere, ut &amp; alimenta &amp; omne id quo homo ab homine juva- ri potest comprehendat. Ea vis melius exprimi non potuit quam Græco verbo ὠφελεῖσθαι. Est autem illud ὠφεληθῇς hic ἀπολετικὸν: quare Latine ita licet exprimere: quicquid est quo à me juvari possis. In Codice Nehardin invenitur: קוֹנָם שֶׁאֲנִי עָנְשֶׁה עַל פִּי אַבָּא וְכֵיוּ יָכוֹל לְהָפֵר שְׁכָל מַה : Quod ita interpretatur Maimonides: אֵינָם שֶׁאעַ שהלא יֹאכַל מִמֶּנּוּ אַבָּה מַאַנְמָה כָּל שֶׁלֹא יֵהָנֶה בּוֹ. Quod quicquid paravero, ex illo non comedet pater meus quicquam, i. e. quod utilitatem inde non per- cipiet. At alterã vocem קָרְבָּן quod attinet, solet ea apud Hebræos, ut חרם,quoties sola ponitur includere vim verbi substantivi: quare κορβᾶν valet κορβᾶν ἔστω, i. e. Deo di- catum esto. Quod autẽ ita Deo dicatum erat, id credebatur o- mnino esse extra hominũ potestatem atq; commercium: Hinc illud קָרְבָּן in hac formula nõ male Hebræi interpre- tes exponunt אָסוּר עָלֶיךָ i. e. prohibitum sive præclusum esto tibi. Liber Caph Nical ita explicat hoc genus voti: הֶקְדֵשׁ יְהֵא כָּל מַה שֶׁאֲנִי עוֹשֶׂה מִלְבוֹ מִלְבוֹ עַל פִּי אבּא Sacrũ erit quicquid paravero in futurũ ad os patris. Rab- binĩssim hoc modo:כָּל שֶׁאֲנִי עוֹשֶׂה לְפִי אַבּא קוֹנָם אֵינוֹ יָכוֹל לְהָפֵר Quicquid paravero Patri meo, sacra- tum esto. Qui sic vovit non potest irritum facere votum. Et quia in nomine κορβᾶν Dei mentio erat inclusa (nam קָרְבָּן est ut diximus res Deo sacra, unde Josephus de iis qui se Deo devovent, οἱ κορβᾶν ἑαυτὸς ὀνομάζοντες) ideo hoc votum non esse nudum sed jurisjurandi religionem complecti crede- batur. Hinc Tyrii cum vetarent τοὺς ξενικοὺς ὅρκους, specia- tim nominarunt τὸν ὅρκον καλούμενον κορβᾶν, auctore Theo- phrasto libro de legibus, cujus juramenti mentionem & Matthæus infra facit XXIII.18. Plane frequens fuisse Judæis ut non voto tantum sed &amp; jurejurando se obstringerent ne huic aut illi benefacerent, cum ex Hebræorum magistris di- scimus, tum ex Philone, cujus hæc verba sunt notatu ad hanc rem digna: εἰσὶ δ' οἳ τὴν φύσιν ἀμίκτοι κᾀκοινώνητοι δι' ὑ- περβολὴν μισανθρωπίας γεγονότες, ἤ κᾀ ὑπ' ὀργῆς οἷα χαλεπῆς δεσποίνης ἐκβιασθέντες, ὅρκῳ τὴν ἀγριότητα πισοῦνται τῶν ἠθῶν, οἵ τινες ὥσφασιν ὁμοτράπεζον ἤ ὁμορόφιον ἕξειν τὸν δεῖνα ἤ πάλιν ΤΩ ΔΕΙΝΙ ΜΗ ΡΕΞΕΙΝ ΩΦΕΛΕΙΑΝ ΤΙΝΑ ἤ παρ' ἐκείνῳ ἵνα λήψεσθαι κᾀμέχρι τελευτᾶς: ubi aperte describit id votũ quod Hebr. נֶדֶר הֲנָאָה h. e. εὐχὴν τῆς ὠφελείας vocant. Hoc autẽ votum quo firmius sanctiusq; esset, solebat ut ex Matthæo Marcoque discimus, adjici consecratio rei in eum casum si quando τῷ δεῖνι quicquam daretur. Quod si is qui votum ta- le nuncupasset, postea immutata voluntate largiri aliquid vellet τῷ δεῖνι, sacerdotes, quorũ pars magna erant Pharisæi, rem ex voti lege sacro ærario vindicabant. Ejus autem ærarii obventiones, partim in opera templi, partim in usus paupe- rũ, partim in ipsos Sacerdotes ac Levitas erogabantur. Quo magis credibile est Pharisæos qui erant Φιλάργυροι ut Lucas nos docet XVI.14. contumaciter adfuisse utilitatibus ærarii contra quorumvis hominũ justa. Nam vota etiam jure Ro- mano homines ita obligabant, ut votum implere coge- rentur. Cæterum quod Origenes hic narrat ab Hebræo se didicisse etiam creditores sæpe nomina transcripsisse gazo- phylacio, ut debitoribus suis duriorem adversarium ob- truderent, ut verum credo, ita huc proprie non pertinet.

Hæc non incommode observata. Quæ tamen ex Ebræis ab ipso adducta sunt, etsi ad illustrationẽ facere possint, ejus non sunt vel antiquitatis, vel auctoritatis, ut calculum mereantur. Solent multa talia ex Ebræorum formulis, & ritibus conferri. Sed cæcos illos duces non facile æstimamus tanti, ut in pulverem & solem producamus. Admiscent non raro novellas suas παραδόσεις, ut ægre quid ab antiquis habuerint, discernere liceat. Et ad pompam sæpe magis talia faciunt, quam ad illu- strandam sacrorum scriptorum sententiam. Cæte- terum aliter explicant alii dictum illud nempe. Hoc Corban quod ego Deo offero profit mihi & meis: quod hoc pacto putarint se liberos reddi à charitate in parentes. Alii, quod munus Deo oblatum parentibus profuturum sit, unde non opꝰ sit aliter eos juvare, uti Tremell. Syriacum textum reddidit: oblatio est id, unde utilitatem capies ex me, quem sensum è textu Græco, quia particula ἤ, sæpe πλεονάζῃ, ac non raro interrogationi inservit, ita eruit Ludovicus de Dieu: Vos autem dicitis, Quicunq; dixerit patri aut matri, Donum est quod ex me lucraberis, an non honoravit patrem suum aut matrem suam? Id est, Vos dicitis: An non is magno satis honore affecerit pa- rentes, qui dixerit ipsis, munus se Deo obtulisse, unde & ipsi utilitatem capere possint? non inquit Christus, hoc non est satis honorare patrem, sed hoc est ἀκυρῶν τὴν ἐντολὴν τοῦ θεοῦ. Quam tamen explicationem valde urgere non vult, quia Marc. VII, 11. abrupta & imperfecta est sententia, κορβᾶν, ὅ ἐστι, δῶρον ὃ ἐὰν ἐξ ἐμοῦ, ὠφεληθῇς, quæ verbo per imperfectum sub- junctivi reddito, sic interpretatur Dievius: donum est (Deo consecratũ) quicquid ex me lucrareris, vel u- tilitatis caperes; sensu eodem quem Grotius tradi- dit; verba, inquit, sunt filii aversantis petitionem pa- tris, idq́; hoc argumento, quia omnes mea facultates sunt Corban, sunt donum & munus Deo consecratum, nec tibi ergo petere licet, ut aliquam inde utilitatem ca- pias, nec mihi concedere; ex divinis enim utilitatem ca- peres, quod voto meo repugnat, quo omnia mea Deo obstrinxi. Atq́; hoc est quod Marcus subjicit, κ’ ἐκέτι ἀ- φίετε αὐτὸν ὐδὲν ποιῆσαι τῷ πατρὶ αὐτοῦ, ἢ τῇ μη- τρὶ αὐτοῦ. Id est, postquam ejus facultates semel factæ sunt corban, non amplius ab eo tempore permittis ut parentibus suis de eo quicquam eroget. Addit: sicut in Papatu insciiis nonnunquam invitisq́; parentibus libe- ri se Monachatus voto adstringunt, eoǵ; juri ac pote- stati parentum emancipantur, ita & à Pharisæis Ju- dæorum filii edocebantur facultates suas Deo vovere; quo fiebat ut quum honorandi, id est, juvandi essent parentes, obtenderent corban sive votum oblationis, eoǵ; sese excusarent. Hæc Ludovicus ille. Quibus affinia sunt quæ prolixe hic habet Lightfooth: ubi inter alia: Inducuntur, inquit, verba quasi prolata cum indignatione: ac si, cum à filio alimoniam posceret egenus pater, responderet ille iracundus, & cum con- temptu: Sicut res sacrata sit, quodcunq; meum tibi prodesse possit. Res autem sacratæ non erant in usus communes erogandæ. Et: Verba commatis ergo sic red- di possunt, absq́; ulla interjecta additione, quà apponũt interpretes pleriq́;: Quicũq; dixerit patri, aut matri, Donum (sacratum) sit, quocunq; possis à me juvari: tunc nequaquam honorat patrem suum aut ma- trem suam. Conf. & Ludov. Capellus dissert. de his edita, & quæ ex Seldeno hic adduxit Walæus.

## 15:6
Verse 6. ἠκυρώσατε τὴν ἐντολὴν τοῦ θεοῦ.] You have made void the Commandment of God, as far as is in you. Deservedly does the best defender of the divine law accuse this dogma of the lawyers. It relies they were moved by this argument, in which we have seen them lapse more broadly than is right and elsewhere, that precepts regarding God ought to be preferred to those which pertain to the utility of men. In the former category, however, they placed vows and oaths: in the latter, all duties of beneficence. But men, fascinated by a miserable superstition, did not notice that vows and oaths are modes by which we are obligated: yet all obligation must proceed from the right which pertains to us. Wherefore, the matter of an obligation cannot be that which is already beyond our liberty: as is, not to feed one's parents. For both natural equity and the law published through Moses ensured that this was not permitted. But the law which wishes vows and oaths to be kept must undoubtedly be understood concerning legitimate vows and oaths, that is, those by which that which is honest is vowed or sworn, and which is in the power of the one vowing or swearing. Wherefore in this case that law cannot be objected: therefore the other law, which commands piety toward parents, ought to prevail. The sixteenth canon of the Synod of Gangra pertains here: if any children of parents, especially believers, should withdraw under the pretext of piety and not render the due honor to their parents, piety being clearly preferred by them to their parents, let them be anathema. Indeed, as Philo rightly declares against certain of his countrymen, not even if such a vow has been conceived and consecrated by an oath against any other person, who is neither a parent nor a blood relative, ought it to prevail, since God and nature command one man to bring aid to another, especially indeed in whatever way he can relieve his poverty.

These things, as being solidly stated by Grotius, can equally be opposed to Papistic vows, of which he was a champion in his final years. For if the matter of an obligation cannot be that which is not in our power, what place will there be for a vow of perpetual monastic celibacy? What place for a vow of perpetual continence in married persons? What place for the vows of children vowing monastic life against the will of their parents?

Latin:

Vers. 6. ἠκυρώσατε τὴν ἐντολὴν τοῦ θεοῦ.] Irritum fecistis Dei Præceptum, quantum in vobis est. Merito accusat hoc le- gisperitorum dogma legis divinæ optimus vindex. Nite- bantur illi hoc argumento, in quo latius quam par est ex- tendendo & alibi eos lapsos vidimus, quod præcepta Deum spectantia iis essent anteferenda, quæ ad hominum utilita- tem pertinerent. In illo autem genere ponebant vota ac ju- ramenta: in hoc autem omnia beneficentiæ munia. Sed non animadvertebant homines misera superstitione fascinati, vota & juramenta modos esse quibus obligemur: omnem autem obligationem ex jure eo quod nobis competat de- bere proficisci. Quare materiam obligationis esse non pos- se id quod ante adeptum sit nostræ libertati: ut est, paren- tes non alere. Nam & naturalis æquitas & lex per Mosen e- dita efficiebant ne id liceret. Lex autem quæ vota & jura- menta servari vult, intelligenda haud dubie est de votis ac juramentis legitimis, hoc est, quibus id vovetur aut juratur quod honestum est, quodq; est in voventis aut jurantis po- testate. Quare hoc casu lex illa objici non potest: debet ergo valere lex altera, qua pietatem in parentes præcipit. Pertinet huc Gangrensis Synodi canon XVI. εἴ τινα τέκνα γονέων, μάλιστα πιστῶν, ἀναχωροίη προφάσει θεοσεβείας κᾖ μὴ τὴν καθήκουσαν τιμὴν τοῖς γονεῦσιν ἀπονέμοι, προτιμωμένης δηλονότι παῤ αὐτοῖς τῆς θεοσεβείας, ἀνάθεμα ἔστω. Imo, ut recte contra populares quosdam suos Philo pronunciat, nec si adversus alterum quemvis, qui neque parens sit, neque sanguine proximus, conceptum sittale votum & jurejurando con- secratum, valere debet, cum hominem alterum alteri o- pem ferre, præcipue vero qua potest egestatem ejus sub- levare, Deus & natura imperent.

Hæc utpote solide dicta à Grotio, votis Papisticis pariter opponi possunt, quorum ille propugnator postrema ætate fuit. Si enim obligationis mate- ria non potest esse id quod non est in nostra pote- state, ecquis locus erit voto cælibatus monastici perpetui? ecquis voto perpetuæ continentiæ in con- jugatis? ecquis votis filiorum invitis parentibus vitam monasticam voventibus?

## 15:7
V. 7. Προσφήτευσε] The words of Isaiah indeed seem to look first to those times which preceded the Babylonian siege, but in such a way that they would no less, nay even more, square with the times of Christ, which will be manifest if the whole pericope is inspected. For God says that He will bring it about that the Jews, and especially the Jerusalemites, reading the sacred utterances of the Prophets, will not understand: and this as a punishment for a corrupted religion, which they had diverted from true piety and love to empty and fictitious rites. And so it would come to pass that the very teachers who were considered the wisest of all would fall into foul errors. Could anything have been said more aptly about these men? It must be known, as has often been noted, that one and the same prophecy can be fulfilled more than once: so that it fits this and that time, not only by the event, but also by the divine direction of the words.

These former things are sounder than those which Grotius handed down on Isaiah XXIX. For he acknowledges that the things said in verse 11 concern the blindness of the Jews in the times of Christ; which he rashly strove to restrict there to the predictions concerning the expedition of Sennacherib and the liberation from the same, which were not understood. Let those things be read which we have commented upon there against Grotius regarding Isaiah. But what he warns here, and says has often been noted by himself, that one and the same prophecy can be fulfilled more than once; so that it fits both this and another time, not only by the event, but also by the divine direction of the words, that has also often been refuted by us already: Because if that was the divine direction of the words, that prophecies could be understood of different times and fit different events, not a little will be lost to both the perspicuity and the certainty of defined divine prophecies: and God will be considered to have directed the words on purpose so that they would be ambiguous, doubtful, and uncertain in some place. Which is by no means to be admitted.

Latin:

V. 7. Προσφήτευσε] Verba quidem Esaiæ primo spe- ctare videntur ea tempora, quæ Babylonicam obsidionem antecesserunt, sed ita ut non minus, imo etiam magis qua- drarent Christi temporibus, quod manifesto constabit, si inspiciatur tota περικοπὴ. Dicit enim Deus, effecturum se ut Judæi, præsertim vero Hierosolymitæ, sacra Propheta- rum effata legentes non intelligant: idque in pœnam cor- ruptæ religionis, quam à vera pietate ac dilectione ad in- anes & commentitios ritus traduxissent. Itaque futurum, ut ipsi Magistri qui omnium sapientissimi habebantur, in fœdos errores incidant. Ecquid potuit in istos homines aptius dici? Sciendum est quod sæpe notatum est, posse unum idemque vaticinium plus semel impleri: ita ut huic & illi tempori conveniat, non solu eventu, sed divina et- iam verborum directione.

Priora hæc saniora sunt iis, quæ tradidit Gro- tius ad Es. XXIX. Agnoscit enim quæ vers.11. dicta, cæcitatem Judæorum tempora Christi concernere; quæ ibi temere ad prædictiones de expeditione Sen- nacherib, & liberatione ab eodem non intellectas re- stringere sategit. Legantur quæ ad Esaiam ibi contra Grotium commentati sumus. Quod vero hic monet, ac sæpe à se notatum ait, posse u- num idemque vaticinium plus semel impleri; ita ut & huic, & alii tempori conveniat, non solo eventu, sed divina etiam verborum directione, id sæpe etiam à nobis jam profligatum est: Quia si ea fuit verbo- rum directio divina, ut de diversis temporibus va- ticinia intelligi, & diversis eventibus convenire possint, & perspicuitati, & certitudini vaticiniorum divinorum definitæ non parum decedet: ac data opera censebitur Deus ita direxisse verba, ut am- bigua, dubia, atque incerta alicubi essent. Quod minime admittendum.

## 15:8
V. 8. ἐγγίζει μοι] He shows himself a friend to me, James IV. 8. V. 9. Μάτην δὲ σεβονταί με] So also the LXX, who it appears read וַתָּהִי for וַתְּהִי which we now read, and took תֹּהוּ for that which is mostly said לְתֹהוּ, for that is μάτην, or εἰς μάταιον, as the same LXX translate Isaiah XLIX. 4. It appears, however, that not only this, but in many other places in the ancient Hebrew scripture, the letters Vau and Jod could scarcely be distinguished. But also this, that not all discrepant readings were annotated by the Masoretes, which is made most clear by the codex described in Samaritan character compared with the copies which the Jews use: likewise the two alphabetical Psalms XXXVII and CXLV, in the former of which the beginning of the verse starting with ע is missing, and in the latter the beginning of the verse with נ, in which place the Vulgate Latin version shows that fuller codices had them there indeed

עולים and some other vowels, but here indeed both the Greek and Latin show there was נאמן and something besides, although the diligence of the Masoretes is silent here. But whichever way you read it here, it matters nothing. For it is necessary that they worship God in vain, whose worship displeases God.

It is in vain that a different reading is imagined, since all codices consistently have ותהי in Isaiah XXIX. 11, and the sense of the words is plain, which Grotius rendered thus in his annotations on Isaiah: And the worship with which they worship me is a precept which men teach. The LXX are not necessarily to be considered to have had another reading in their codices, since they looked to the sense and did not recite the words. But that that worship was in vain according to the commandments of men is gathered from the Prophet, because it is joined with the most grave sin of hypocrisy, and is at the same time constituted as the cause of the most grave punishment of blinding, namely in divine matters. Grotius took this different reading from Morin, he certainly agrees with him: whom we are now refuting in the Critico Sacro p. 527 seqq., which is to be compared here. But whether the LXX Whether the elders were always able to distinguish or were not able to distinguish the similar letters and Jod, from that neither does prejudice accrue to the Hebrew truth, nor does a presumption of a different reading of the Hebrew source have a place. Concerning the Samaritan Codex, it has been spoken of elsewhere: and no less concerning those Alphabetic Psalms, in which an error is imagined in vain, since the Holy Scriptures could have had their own reasons for the omission of this or that letter, nor was it restricted to the number of letters of the Alphabet. Conf. what [is said] regarding Psalm XXV. Furthermore, by human dogmas Grotius wishes to understand Isaiah and Christ, not only those which fight directly with the divine law, nor all things which men teach should be done, for instance by a probable interpretation of that which is ambiguous, or by a fair definition of that which is left to discretion, or by faithful counsel concerning those things which pertain to piety or charity; but those which have a foundation in mere human persuasion, and are not divinely delivered. But in those things which concern divine worship, there is need not of probable interpretation, but of undoubted knowledge of the divine will, and not of arbitrary definition, but of the direction of the divine law: because if the Word of God is accepted by ἰδίᾳ ἐπιλύσει, or those things which pertain to divine worship are defined by human discretion, God is worshipped in vain by such things: and what else do they beget than mere persuasion, if they do not exhibit the sense divinely delivered? Nor indeed does Christ any less disapprove in divine worship those things which are brought to it besides the divine law, than those which are against it: because He rejects ἐθελοθρησκείας, and teaches with Isaiah that they are vain and provoke the judgment of God. Nor were some traditions of the Jews impious in themselves, against which Christ so decides: they are reprehended only because they were delivered as necessary for the worship of God, besides the law of God.

Latin:

V. 8. ἐγγίζει μοι] Amicum se mihi præbet, Iac. IV. 8. V. 9. Μάτην δὲ σεβονταί με ] Ita & LXX. quos apparet pro וַתְּהִי quod nunc legimus, legisse וַתָּהִי & accepisse תֹּהוּ pro eo quod plerumque dicitur לְתֹהוּ id enim est μάτην, aut εἰς μάταιον, ut iidem LXX. transferunt Esa. XLIX. 4. Appa- ret autem non hoc tantum, sed multis aliis ex locis in vete- ri scriptura Hebraica Vau & Jod literas vix potuisse discerni. Sed & hoc, non omnes discrepantes Lectiones à Masore- tis fuisse annotatas, quod apertissimum facit codex Samari- tano charactere descriptus collatus cum exemplaribus qui- bus Judæi utuntur: item Psalmi duo Alphabetici XXXVII. & CXLV. in quorum priore initium versûs incipientis ab ע in altero initium versûs à נ deest, quo loco vulgata Lati- na versio ostendit pleniores codices ibi quidem habuisse

עולים & aliquas vocales alias, hic vero & Græca & La- tina ostendit fuisse נאמן & aliquid præterea, quanquam tacente hic Masoretarum diligentia, Verum utro modo hic legas nihil refert, Necesse est enim frustra Deum colant, quorum cultus Deus displicet.

Frustra fingitur diversa lectio, quum Codices constanter omnes habeant, ותהי Esa. XXIX. 11. & sensus verborum planus sit, quem ita reddidit an- not. ad Ef. Grotius: Et cultus, quo me colunt, est præ- ceptum quod homines docent. LXX. non necessario censendi habuisse aliam lectonem in suis codici- bus, quũ sensum respexerint, non verba recitarint. Frustra autem fuisse illum cultum secundum man- data hominum, hinc colligitur è Propheta, quia conjungitur cum gravissimo hypocryseos pecca- to, & causa simul constituitur pœnæ gravissimæ excæcationis nempe in rebus divinis. Sumsit hanc diversam lectionem Grotius è Morino, certe con- sentit eidem: quem vero jam profligamus in Critico sacro p. 527. seqq. qui hic conferendus. Sive autem LXX. Senes discernere semper potuerint, seu non potuerint literas affines & Jod, inde nec præjudicium veritati Ebrææ accedit, aut præsum- tio locum habet diversæ lectionis fontis Ebræi. De Samaritano Codice alias dictum est: nec minus de Psalmis illis Alphabeticis, in quib. frustra error fingitur, quum suas habere potuerit S. S. rationes prætermittendæ hujus aut illius literæ, nec ad nu- merum literarum Alphabetici adstrictus sit. Conf. quæ ad Psal. XXV. Cæterum per humana dogmata Esaiam & Christum vult Grotius intelligere neque sola, quæ pugnant directe cum lege divina, neque o- mnia, quæ homines docent facienda, puta probabili interpretatione ejus quod ambiguum est, aut defini- tione æqua ejus, quod in arbitrio relictum est, aut fi- deli consilio circa ea, quæ ad pietatem, aut charitate pertinent; sed ea, quæ fundamentum habent in per- suasione mere humana, & non divinitus tradita. Sed in iis, quæ cultum divinum concernunt, neq; pro- babili interpretatione, sed indubitata voluntatis di- vinæ cognitione, neq; arbitraria definitione, sed le- gis divinæ directione op9 est quod si ἰδίᾳ ἐπιλύσει acceptetur Verbum Dei, aut humano arbitrio de- finiantur, quæ ad cultum faciunt divinum, frustra Deus talibus colitur: & quid ea gignunt aliud, quã meram persuasionem, si sensum divinitus traditum non exhibent? Nec vero minus improbat Chri- stus in culto divino ea, quæ præter legem divinam ad eundem conferuntur, quam quæ contra eun- dem: quia ἐθελοθρησκείας rejicit, ac frustraneas esse, Deiq; judicium provocare, cum Esaia docet. Neque impiæ erant per se traditiones nonnullæ Ju- dæorum, contra quas ita decernit Christus: re- prehenduntur tantum, quod ceu necessariæ ad cul- tum Dei, præter legem Dei, traderentur.

## 15:9
Σέβονταί με] In Hebrew יראתם אתי, that is, word for word τὸ σέβας αὐτῶν πρός με ἐσί.. For as often as יראת is referred to God, it is worship itself, divine. Therefore this has been translated very well.

Διδάσκοντες διδασκαλίας ἐντάλματα ἀνθρώπων] The LXX added the word διδάσκοντες so that the construction might be more convenient: and what is here προσθήκαις, διδασκαλίας ἐντάλματα ἀνθρώπων, there is συνθήκαις, ἐντάλματα καὶ διδασκαλίας. In the Hebrew it is מצות אנשים מלמדה, word for word ἐντολὴ παρ᾽ ἀνθρώπων δεδιδαγμένη: but this is dogmas which consist in doing. But human dogmas are called by Isaiah and Christ, not only those which fight directly with the divine law (for Christ does not use this oracle only for the confirmation of that which He had already said, but also to pave the way to the following things, by which He shows the Apostles were not rightly accused) nor all things which men teach should be done, for instance by a probable interpretation of that which is ambiguous, or by a fair definition of that which is left to discretion, or by faithful counsel concerning those things which pertain to piety or charity: but those which have a foundation in mere human persuasion, and are not divinely delivered: such as those about which it was now being treated, as is shown more explicitly presently.

Latin:

Σέβονταί με] Hebraice יראתם אתי hoc est ad verbum τὸ σέβας αὐτῶν πρός με ἐσί.. Nam יראת quoties ad Deũ re- fertur est ipse cultus, divinus Itaq; optime hoc versum est.

Διδάσκοντες διδασκαλίας ἐντάλματα ἀνθρώπων] Verbum δι- δάσχοντες adjecerunt LXX. ut commodior esset constructio: & quod hic est προσθήκαις, διδασκαλίας ἐντάλματα ἀνθρώπων, ibi est συνθήκαις, ἐντάλματα καὶ διδασκαλίας. In Hebræo est מצות אנשים מלמדה ad verbum ἐντολὴ παρ᾽ ἀν- θρώπων δεδιδαγμένη: hoc autem est dogmata quæ in facien- do consistunt. Humana autem dogmata dicuntur Esaiæ & Christo, neque sola quæ pugnant directe cum lege divina (neque enim hoc oraculo Christus utitur tantum ad confir- mationem ejus quod jam dixerat, sed etiam ut viam sternat ad sequentia, quibus Apostolos ostendit non recte accusa- tos) neque omnia quæ homines docent facienda, puta pro- babili interpretatione ejus quod ambiguum est, aut defini- tione æqua ejus quod in arbitrio relictum est, aut fideli con- silio circa ea quæ ad pietatem aut charitatem pertinent: sed ea quæ fundamentum habent in persuasione mere huma- na, & non divinitus tradita: qualia sunt illa de quibus nunc agebatur, ut mox explicatius ostenditur.

## 15:10
Vers. 10. τὸν ὄχλον] Concerning the common people, whom the experts in the law despised as unlearned, and the Pharisees as little religious, in comparison to themselves.

Hear and understand] Christ desires attention: because for the most part men are unwilling to admit that what they learned as youths must be discarded as old men.

Latin:

Vers. 10. τὸν ὄχλον] De plebe homines, quos legisperiti ut indoctos, Pharisæi ut parum religiosos, præ se fastidiebant.

Ἀκούετε κᾲ συνίετε] Attentionem desiderat Christus: quia plerumque homines nolunt, Quæ juvenes didicere, senes perdenda fateri.

## 15:11
Verse 11. Not that which enters into the mouth defiles the man] To defile (טמא) is opposed to to sanctify (ἁγιάζειν): and deservedly so, for those things which are holy are as it were separated for God. The rest are as if outside of God's property. When these are referred to the mind, as in this passage, to sanctify signifies immunity from guilt, to defile signifies contracted guilt. Porphyry used μιαίνειν for κοινοῦν, looking back to this passage or at least to this dogma of the Christians. For thus he says in his first book on abstinence from animals: for foods, they say, do not defile us. He adds, executing the same sense of the Christians: if we are cautious about eating, we have been deceived by the opinion of fear; but all things ought to be subject to us. The Pharisees thought, as we have said, that certain things were so unclean by their own nature that they polluted the mind by themselves, not by institution. Besides other Jews, the writer of the book on the sovereignty of reason, who is ascribed to Josephus, teaches this, where these are the words: the law itself permitted us to eat those things which would be appropriated to our souls, but forbade us to eat those which would be opposed to them. Christ denies this here. That which enters into the mouth, therefore, must here be understood from the subject matter, which enters in such a way that no vice is received from the human will. Therefore Mark said that which enters into him from outside the man. Christ therefore teaches nothing here against the law distinguishing foods, nor had the time arrived: although obliquely, while he shows that nothing is unclean by nature, contrary to what the Pharisees thought, he at the same time signifies that that law is not immutable. For Paul also uses the same argument that every creature of God is good, 1 Tim. IV. 4. Thus an equitable interpretation of the law concerning the distinction of foods, as also before concerning the Sabbath, softly prepared the way for the abrogation of those same laws. For it was very relevant to this that it be understood that the matter of those laws was in itself indifferent, and that what was commanded was not commanded primarily, but given on occasion or for the sake of another thing.

But that which proceeds out of the mouth] More generally in Mark, those things which proceed out of the man: that is, those things which proceed from the will. But because many of them are accustomed to be performed either by the mouth, such as evil thoughts, false testimonies, blasphemies, or at least not without the aid of the mouth, just as murders arise from quarrels, and adulteries, fornications, and thefts are born from shameless conversations and solicitations, and for the most part have a lie joined to them, therefore Christ added this by way of example, so that the antithesis might be more evident. The opposition of those things which enter through the mouth and go out is very similar in Plato in the Timaeus, perhaps from barbarian philosophy, from which there are many things in that book: the organizers arranged the power of our mouth for the tongue and lips for the sake of necessities and the best things, as it is now ordered, contriving the entrance for the sake of necessities. And the exit for the best things; for it is necessary that everything that enters provides food for the body, but the stream of words is the most beautiful and best of all streams, going out and serving the mind. Which passage the Jewish Plato, namely Philo, paraphrases thus: What is the mouth? Through which, as Plato said, there is an entrance for mortal things, but an exit for immortal things; for foods and drinks enter into it, corruptible foods for a corruptible body, but from an immortal soul go out immortal laws, through which the rational life is governed.

Latin:

Vers. 11. ὀὐ τὸ εἰσερχόμενον εἰς τὸ ςόμα κοινοῖ τὸν ἄνθρωπον] κοινοῦν טמא opponitur τῷ ἁγιάζειν: & merito nam quæ sancta sunt Deo quasi separantur. Cætera sunt velut extra Dei peculium. Hæc cum ad animum referuntur, ut hoc lo- co, τὸ ἁγιάζειν culpæ immunitatem, τὸ κοινοῦν culpam con- tractam significat. μιαίνειν pro κοινοῦν dixit Porphyrius, hunc locum aut certe hoc Christianorum dogma respiciens. Sic enim ait de abstinentia ab animalibus primo: ὀὐ γὰρ ἡμᾶς μολύνᾐ, φασὶ, τὰ βρώματα. Addit eundem Christianorum sensam exequens: ἐὰν ἐυλαβηθῶμεν βρῶσιν, ἐδολώθημεν τῷ τᾶ Φόβυ Φρονήματι· δεῖ δὲ πάνθ᾽ ἡμῖν ὑποτετάχθαι. Putabant, ut diximus, Pharisæi, ita immunda esse quædam natura sua, ut per se, non ex instituto animum polluerent. Docet hoc præter cæteros Judæos scriptor libri περὶ ἀυτοκράτορος λο- γισμᾶ, qui Josepho ascribitur, ubi hæc sunt verba: ὁ τε νόμος ἡπῖστος τὰ μὲν οἰκειωθησόμενα ἡμῶν ταῖς ψυχαῖς ἐπέτρεψεν ἐσθί- ειν, τὰ δὲ ἐναντιωσόμενα ἐκώλυσε σαρκοφαγεῖν. Id Christus hic negat. τὸ εἰσερχόμενον εἰς τὸ ςόμα igitur hic ex subjecta ma- teria intelligi debet, quod ita ingreditur ut nihil vitii acce- dat ab humana voluntate. Ideo Marcus dixit ἔξωθεν τᾶ ἀν- θρώπυ εἰσπορευόμενον εἰς ἀυτὸν. Nihil igitur hic Christus do- cet contra legem ciborum discriminatricem, neque enim tempus advenerat: quanquam oblique, dum ostendit nihil esse natura immundum, contra quam Pharisæi existima- bant, simul significat legem illam non esse immutabilem. Nam & Paulus eodem argumento utitur ὅτι πᾶν κτίσμα θεᾶ καλὸν 1. Tim. IV. 4. Ita æqua interpretatio legis de ciborum discrimine, ut & ante de Sabbato, earundem legum anti- quationi viam molliter præstruxit. Valde enim eo pertine- bat intelligi, materiam istarum legum per se esse ἀδιάφορον, & quod præceptum erat non esse præceptum προηγυμένως, sed data occasione ant alterius rei causa.

Ἀλλὰ τὸ ἐκπορευόμενον ἐκ τᾶ ςόματος] Generalius apud Marcum τὰ ἐκπορευόμενα ἐκ τᾶ ἀνθρώπυ: hoc est ea quæ ex voluntate procedunt. Sed quia eorum multa solent aut ore peragi, ut διαλογισμοὶ πονηροὶ, ψευδομαρτυρίαι, βλασφη- μίαι, aut certe non sine oris adminiculo, quemadmodum ex rixis φόνοι, ex impudicis colloquiis & lenociniis nascuntur μοιχείαι, πορνεῖαι, & κλοπαὶ plerumque conjunctum habent mendacium, ideo hoc exempli causa Christus addidit, quo evidentior esset ἀντίθεσις. Simillima est oppositio eorum quæ per os intrant atq; exeunt apud Platonem in Timæo, forte ex barbara Philosophia, unde multa in eo sunt libro: τὴν δὲ δὴ τᾶ ςόματος ἡμῶν δύναμιν ἐδόσις τῇ γλώττῃ κᾲ χείλεσιν ἕνεκα ἳ ἀναγκαίων κᾲ τῶν ἀρίςων διεκόσμησαν οἱ διακοσμῆντες, ᾗ νῦν διατέτακται, τὴν μὲν ἔσοδον ἳ ἀναγκαίων μηχανώμενοι χάριν. τὴν δὲ ἔξοδον τῶν ἀρίςων· ἀναγκαῖον μὲν γὰρ πᾶν ὅσον ἐσέρχεται τροφὴν διδὸν τῷ σώματι, τὸ δὲ λόγων νᾶμα ἔξω κᾲ ὑπηρετῶν φρο- νήσεϊ κάλλιςον κᾲ ἄριςον πάντων ναμάτων. Quem locum ita παραφράζει Plato Judæus, Philo scilicet: Στόμα τί. δι ὗ γίνε- ται θνητῶν μὲν ὡς ἔφη Πλάτων, εἴσοδος, ἔξοδος δ᾽ ἀφθάρτων· ἐπεισέρχεται μὲν γὰρ ἀυτῷ σιτία καὶ ποτὰ, Φθαρτῷ σώματι φθαρταὶ τροφαί λόγοι δ᾽ ἐξίασιν ἀθανάτε ψυχῆς ἀθάνατοι νό- μοι, δι ὧν ὁ λογικὸς βίος κυβερνᾶται.

## 15:12
Verse 12. They were offended] Because the Pharisees valued the traditions of the elders most highly, and in the observation of both those traditions and certain rites which they had imposed upon themselves, they constituted the greatest part of divine worship. For it is not credible that Christ's words were taken by them to refer to the promiscuous use of all foods, since, though they were searching for crimes everywhere, they never objected this to him.

Latin:

Vers. 12. Ἐσκανδαλίσθησαν] Quia Pharisæi maximi facie- bant traditiones sapientum, & in observatione tum earum traditionum tum rituum quorundam quos sibi ipsi impera- yerant, maximam divini cultus partem constituebant. Nam ad promiscuos ciborum omnium usus tracta ab ipsis Chri- sti verba credibile non est, cum omnia undique crimina conquirentes nunquam hoc illi objecerint.

## 15:13
Verse 13. Every plant] Christ shows that stumbling blocks are to be avoided in such a way (concerning which he had warned often before) that nevertheless those things which make for solid piety should be taught no less freely, even with the refutation of dogmas that would hinder the progress of piety. For dogmas are called a plant for the same reason that they are called seed. But those dogmas which do not have a foundation in divine revelation and the use of right reason are not from God. Ignatius transfers what he had said about the dogmas of Christ to the authors of dogmas, with the sense preserved, in his Epistle to the Trallians: these are not a plant of the Father, but cursed offspring; but every plant, says the Lord, which my heavenly Father has not planted, shall be rooted up; for if they were branches of the Father, they would not be enemies of the cross of Christ.

Some explain those plantations as human traditions, not instituted by God, Acts V. 38; others as the impious and hypocrites, who are found in the external society of the Church, which is the garden of God, but are not rooted by faith in Christ, Col. II. 7. But the former exposition is to be preferred. Hilary on this passage: He signifies that the tradition of men is to be rooted up, by whose favor they have transgressed the precepts of the law.

It shall be rooted up] That is, it must be torn out. Namely, by leading men to the knowledge of the truth, as appears from what follows.

Latin:

Vers. 13. Πᾶσα φυτεία] Ostendit Christus ita vitanda esse ossendicula (de quo monuerat antehac sæpius) ut tamen non eo minus libere docerentur, quæ ad solidam pietatem facerent, etiam cum refutatione dogmatum quæ pietatis profectui obstarent. Dogmata enim vocantur φυτεία eadem ratione qua appellantur semen. A Deo autem non sunt dogmata quæ fundamentum non habent in revelatione di- vina rectæq; rationis usu. Ignatius quod de dogmatis Chri- sti dixerat ad dogmatum auctores transfert sensu salvo Epi- stola ad Trallenses: ἔτωι ὀυκ εἰσὶ φυτεία πατρὸς, ἀλλ᾽ ἔγγονα καταραμένα· πᾶσα δὲ, φησὶν ὁ κύριος, φυτεία, ἣν ὀυκ ἐφύτευσεν ὁ πατήρ με ὁ ὀυράνιος, ἐκριζωθήτω· εἰ γὰρ ἦσαν τᾶ πατρὸς κλάδοι, ὀυκ ἂν ἦσαν ἐχθροὶ τᾶ ςαυρᾶ τᾶ Χριστᾶ.

Quidam plantationes istas exponunt de huma- nis traditionibus, à Deo non institutis, Actor. V. 38. alii de impiis & hypocritis, qui in Ecclesiæ, quæ est hortus Dei, externa societate inveniun- tur, sed non sunt fide in Christo radicati, Col. II. 7. Sed præferenda est prior expositio. Hilarius in h. l. Significat traditionem hominum eruendam, cu- jus favore transgressi sunt præcepta legis.

Ἐκριζωθήσεται] Id est, oportet eam evelli. Nempe ducendo homines ad veri cognitionem, ut ex sequentibus apparet.

## 15:14
Verse 14. Let them alone] As we say, you may bid a miserable man to be miserable willingly. Christ signifies that their offenses are not of such importance that the cause of truth making for salvation should be abandoned on their account.

They are blind leaders of the blind] The sense and connection seem to me to be this: If they do not want to be counseled, let us at least counsel the common people, who otherwise, using such blind leaders, will themselves also fall blindly into destruction. A similar comparison is in Sextus Empiricus, II. Against the Mathematicians: for it is like if someone were to say that the one who sees is led by the one who is blind. Horace said: As if a blind man would wish to point out the way. Moreover, there was an old tradition among the Hebrews which exists in Midrash Tehillim, Psalm CXLVI, that the teachers would be blind at the time when God was to have a tabernacle among them. See Isaiah XLII. 9 and below XXIII. 24.

Εἰς βόθυνον πεσῦνται] A reference is made to the passage in Isaiah 3:6, 8.

Latin:

Vers. 14. Ἄφετε αὐτὺς] Quomodo dicimus jubeas miserum esse lubenter. Significat Christus eorum offensas tanti non esse, ut propterea deserenda sit causa facientis ad salutem veritatis.

Ὁδηγοί εἰσὶ τυφλοὶ τυφλῶν] Videtur mihi hic esse sensus atque connexio: Si illi consuli sibi nolunt, at plebi consulamus, quæ alioqui tam cæcis ductoribus usa, ipsa quoque cæca in exitium ruet. Similis comparatio est apud Sextum, Empiricum II. adversus mathematicos, ὅμοιον γάρ ὡς εἴτις λέγοι, τὸν βλέποντα ὑπὸ τῦ πεπηρωμένυ ὁδηγεῖσθαι. Horatius dixit: Vt sicacusiter monstrare velit. Erat autem vetus traditio apud Hebræos quæ exstat in Midras Thillim Psalm. CXLVI. doctores cæcos fore quo tempore Deus inter ipsos habiturus esset tabernaculum. Vide Esaiam XLII. 9. & infra XXIII. 24.

Εἰς βόθυνον πεσῦνται] Respicitur locus Esa. III. 6. 8.

## 15:15
Vers. 15. τὴν παραβολὴν ταύτην] That is, a maxim, namely that concerning what enters into the mouth and what proceeds out of the mouth. For there is no need to take the word παραβολῆς otherwise here, since it has been shown above that the Hebrew משׁל is very often taken in this way.

Latin:

Vers. 15. τὴν παραβολὴν ταύτην] Id est γνώμην, illam scilicet deeo quod in os intrat, quodque ex ore proficiscitur. Nihil enim necesse est aliter hic accipere παραβολῆς vocem, cum sæpissime apud Hebræos ita sumi משׁל supra ostensum sit.

## 15:16
Vers. 16. ἀκμὴν κὶ ὑμεῖς] You, who ought long ago to have learned from me what those things are in which true piety consists.

᾿Ακμὴν is used adverbially, as if κατ᾽ ἀκμὴν, according to vigor, so that it may be signified that something is still vigorous and enduring. Justin uses it in the same way in his Dialogue with Trypho, as Casaubon notes. ἀκμὴν is equivalent to ἔτι ἰ̓ νῦν. Polybius, however, said ἀκμὴν ἔτι ἰ̓ νῦν in parallel, book 15. Mark interprets it as ὕτω, chapter 7:18, as does B. Gerhard here.

Latin:

Vers. 16. ἀκμὴν κὶ ὑμεῖς] Vos qui jamdudum à me discere debuistis quæ sint illa in quibus vera pietas consistit.

᾿Ακμὴν adverbialiter ponitur, quasi κατ᾽ ἀκμὴν, secundum vigorem, ut significetur, adhuc aliquid vigere ac durare. Eodem modo usurpat Justinus in Dialogo cum Tryph. Casaub. in not. ἀκμὴν valet ἔτι ἰ̓ νῦν. Polyb. autem ἐκ παραλλήλων dixit ἀκμὴν ἔτι ἰ̓ νῦν, lib. 15. Marcus interpretatur ὕτω, cap. VII. 18. ut hic B. Gerhardus.

## 15:17
Vers. 17. Εἰς τὴν κοιλίαν χωρεῖ ἰ̓ εἰς ἀφεδρῶνα ἐκβάλλεται] Christ clearly explains that there is no natural uncleanness in food that can penetrate to the soul; he assumes, however, that which was agreed upon among the Jews, that the heart is the seat of the soul, especially of that part by which we will, from which guilt is born. Whence it follows that if uncleanness does not reach the heart from food, it does not reach the soul either. But food, while it is still mixed with its dregs, is not carried to the heart, but εἰς κοιλίαν, into the lower part of the belly where the stomach is. Then the food is purged, and whatever is unclean by its own nature, and therefore not suitable for nourishing man, is cast out through the bowels. It appears, therefore, that neither before purging nor after purging does that which is naturally unclean in food reach the heart, and much less the soul. Mark teaches us this sense when he says καθαρίζον πάντα τὰ βρώματα. Therefore, what is said here, πᾶν τὸ εἰσπορευόμενον εἰς τὸ σόμα εἰς ἀφεδρῶνα ἐκβάλλεται, is to be understood according to the nature of the subject matter: namely, insofar as it could be said that there is anything unclean in it. Thus, that which Jerome and Zacharias relate was objected to Christ in this regard is most conveniently solved.

It is a synecdoche: everything, that is, of everything that enters into the mouth, something is cast out through the privy.

Latin:

Vers. 17. Εἰς τὴν κοιλίαν χωρεῖ ἰ̓ εἰς ἀφεδρῶνα ἐκβάλλεται] Nullam esse in cibo naturalem immunditiam, quæ ad animum possit penetrare, dilucide Christus explicat, ὑποτίθεται autem id quod constabat inter Judæos, cor sedem esse animi, ejus præsertim partis qua volumus, ex qua culpa nascitur. Unde sequitur si à cibo immunditia ad cor non pertingit, ne ad animum quidem pertingere. At cibus dum adhuc permixtus est suis fæcibus, non ad cor defertur, sed εἰς κοιλίαν, in partem ventris depressiorem in qua est ventriculus. Deinde purgatur cibus, & quicquid natura sua immundum est, ac proinde homini alendo non idoneum, id per alvum dejicitur. Apparet ergo nec ante purgationem nec post purgationem, quod in cibo est naturaliter immundum ad cor pervenire, multoque minus ad animum. Hunc sensum nos Marcus docet cum dicit καθαρίζον πάντα τὰ βρώματα. Ergo quod hic dicitur πᾶν τὸ εἰσπορευόμενον εἰς τὸ σόμα εἰς ἀφεδρῶνα ἐκβάλλεται, intelligendum est pro ratione subjectæ materiæ: nempe quatenus in eo dici posset aliquid esse immundi. Ita commodissime solvitur id quod Christo hac in parte objectum narrant Hieronymus & Zacharias.

Synecdoche est: omne, id est, de omni, quod in os intrat, aliquid per secessum ejicitur.

## 15:19
Vers. 19. διαλογισμοὶ πονηροὶ] Wicked thoughts, which, if the effect did not follow, the Jews did not think were to be counted as a crime even before God, as has been observed elsewhere. Dionysius of Halicarnassus also used διαλογισμὸς πονηρὸς in a similar sense.

Πορνεῖαι] Here Christ shows in passing that not only adultery, as the duller Jews thought, but also fornication is forbidden by divine law, and that perpetually: since he nowhere else demonstrates this expressly, because, forsooth, the better teachers of the Hebrews were not mistaken in that matter. Abraham Zachuth explains the continence of the Essenes praised by Josephus: they kept themselves from whoredom. Indeed, they consider intercourse with a harlot so impure that they use it as a proverb, as when they say: To eat bread with unwashed hands is the same as to lie with a harlot. Christ perhaps alluded to this sentiment here, to show that the things they were comparing differed greatly from one another. In what way these things are said to proceed from the mouth, we have said above.

Latin:

Vers. 19. διαλογισμοὶ πονηροὶ] Pravæ cogitationes quas effectu non secuto Judæi ne apud Deum quidem in crimine poni putabant, ut alibi observatum est. Dixit autem διαλογισμὸς πονηρὸς etiam Dionysius Halicarnassensis sensu simili.

Πορνεῖαι] Obiter hic Christus ostendit non μοιχείαν tantum, ut craffiores Judæi existimabant, sed & πορνείαν lege divina, eaque perpetua interdici: cum alioqui nusquam hoc ex professo demonstret, quia scilicet magistri Hebræorum meliores ea in re non hallucinabantur. Helsenorum ἐγκράτειαν à Josepho laudatam exponit Abraham Zachuth: custodiebant seipsos à scortatione. Imo congressum cum scorto ita impuru habent, ut proverbii loco usurpent, veluti cum dicunt: Panem edere illotis manibus, perinde est atq; cubare cum scorto. Ad quam sententiam forte hic Christus allusit, ut quæ illi comparabant ea multum inter se differre ostenderet. Quo modo autem hæc dicantur ex ore proficisci, supra diximus.

## 15:20
Vers. 20. Ἀνίπτοις χερσὶ φαγεῖν, ὐ κοινοῖ τὸν ἄνθρωπον] He wishes the antecedent to be understood from the consequent. For it contributed nothing to the purity of the soul whether they washed their hands or not, because that which they thought was cleansed by washing was not such that it could defile a soul that was well-conscious of itself.

He does not say with impure hands, but with unwashed hands: because, as Lightfoot noted, they were bound to wash, even if they were not conscious that their hands had been unclean. In Mark it is κοιναῖς χερσὶ, chapter 7:2, which seem to be called impure hands by the Talmudists, due to the mere absence of washing.

PART II.

The healing of the Canaanite daughter.

Latin:

Vers. 20. Ἀνίπτοις χερσὶ φαγεῖν, ὐ κοινοῖ τὸν ἄνθρωπον] Ex consequenti antecedens vult intelligi. Ideo enim ad puritatem animi nihil referebat, manus lavarent nec ne, quia id quod illi lavando putabant emundari, tale non erat ut animum bene sibi conscium posset inquinare.

Non dicit autem impuris manibus, sed illotis: quia, ut notavit Lightfooth, ad lavandum tenebantur, quamvis conscii non forent manus fuisse immundas. Marco est κοιναῖς χερσὶ cap. VII. 2. quæ Talmudicis videntur vocari impuræ manus, ob meram absentiam lotionis.

PARS II.

Filia Cananæa sanatio.

## 15:21
Ver. 21. Into the parts of Tyre and Sidon] such is the verse here as the Syrian translated it. For Mark says into the borders: that is, to the confines of Tyre and Sidon. For Christ does not seem to have gone out of the borders of the land of the Hebrews.

Walaeus has brought forward learned things here from Bochart concerning Sidon and Tyre: which should be compared.

Latin:

Vers. 21. Εἰς τὰ μέρη Τύρου καὶ Σιδῶνος] sic hic est versus ut transtulit Syrus. Nam εἰς τὰ μεθόρια inquit Marcus: id est ad confinia Tyri & Sidonis. Neque enim videtur exiisse Christus terræ Hebræorum fines.

De Sidone ac Tyro erudita hic è Bocharto Walæus attulit: quæ conferantur.

## 15:22
Ver. 22. Canaanite] That this is the same as Syrophoenician in Mark should not even be doubted. For the Canaanites were called by the Hebrews strictly and peculiarly those who inhabited Sidon and Tyre and what lies adjacent to the maritime coast. A Canaanite is one dwelling by the sea, says Moses, Num. XIII. 8. Again, the Sidonians are reckoned among the Canaanites, Jud. I. 31. And Procopius on Genesis explains Canaanites as Sidonians: and Stephanus says, Chna, thus is Phoenicia called, where Chna is Canaan with the letter Nun omitted: which the Hebrews acknowledge to be paragogic. Thus also Philo of Byblos from Sanchuniathon in Eusebius, book I, Praepar. c. X, says, brother of Chna, the first to be renamed Phoenix. These, however, are the Phoenicians likewise properly so called by Strabo, Pliny, and others: And as they are celebrated as Phoenicians by Homer and all who followed him because of navigation and trade, so they are called Canaanites by Solomon, Isaiah, Hosea, and Zechariah: Wherefore just as the LXX, which is in the Hebrew, Jos. V. 1. the kings of the Canaanite, they translated as kings of Phoenicia, and Job XL. 25, Canaanites as nations of Phoenicians, so in this place, what Matthew's interpreter had called Canaanite, Mark placed as Syrophoenician, in which word the addition of 'Syro', as often among the poets, signifies nothing other than to distinguish the indigenous Phoenicians of Asia from their own African Phoenician colonists, as has been rightly observed long ago. Hence the Syrian interpreter in the said place of Mark said distinctively the Punic of Syria. Nor is that passage of Horace to be interpreted otherwise:

---- and let both the Carthaginian serve one.

Namely, the Syrophoenicians and the Libyphoenicians. They themselves also in Africa called themselves Phoenicians, Canaanites. For Augustine in his book of expositions of the Epistle to the Romans says that the rustic Africans near Hippo, if asked who they were, answered in Punic, 'Canaani'. But learned men seek the origin of the word 'Phoenix' from the Syriac in vain. For they were not called so by themselves, but were Canaanites. But the Greeks called them Phoenicians, as Aristotle reports in his 'On Marvelous Narrations', because they killed men as they landed on any shore while plundering. For among the ancient Greeks, to slaughter was called 'phoenixai': which the interpreter of Aristophanes also noted in the Acharnians. And for the same reason, the Carians were also called Phoenicians by Bacchylides and Corinna. But that this woman is called a Greek by Mark signifies that she was neither Hebrew by race nor a Judaizer. Nor does it follow, however, that she was a worshiper of idols. For both in Judea and in the neighboring regions and elsewhere there were many men and women who were pious, fearing God, outside the profession of Judaism, such as Cornelius, Lydia, and others, about whom one may see Acts X. 2, c. XVII. 4, 17. And in this sense Paul often said 'Greek', dividing the whole human race into Greeks and Jews. But this woman came from the Sidonian or Tyrian borders to the fame of Christ. God so disposing the outcome that, just as the preceding discussion foreshadowed the abrogation of the ritual law, so this might foreshadow the adoption of the Gentiles.

Others wish her to be called so from the town of Cana on the borders of Phoenicia and Galilee, with Adrichomius and Arias Montanus. But the letters do not agree, because Cana is written not with a Kaph but with a Qoph, nor was this woman from the tribe of Asher, where they say Cana is situated, or from the Israelites, but she was Greek and Gentile as to her origin, Mark VII. 26, even if converted to the true God. Grotius's opinion about the Canaanite woman does not displease here. Which is illustrated by what Lightfoot has in this place, why some among the seven nations to be destroyed by the Israelites were specifically called Canaanites, namely because Canaan himself inhabited a peculiar part of that land (the northern, that is) with his firstborn sons Sidon and Heth. And from there the name of Canaanites was given to that special progeny, distinct from all his other sons; and that region was called by the peculiar name Canaan, distinctively from the rest of the land of Canaan. Hence Jabin, king of Hazor, is called king of Canaan, Jud. IV. 2, and the kings (unless he himself is mistaken) of Tyre and Sidon are called Kings of the Hittites, 1 Kings X. 29. But that this woman was Syro-Greek by race, which denomination is from the Syro-Greek kingdom, the memory of which had not yet vanished; Phoenician by habitation, and thence Canaanite by nomenclature. Bochart has written learnedly on the Canaanites, and Walaeus from him on this place. Anyone who has accurately weighed either the name and location of Phoenicia, or the language, institutions, customs, and arts of the ancient Phoenicians, will easily perceive that the Phoenicians were born from the Canaanites. Hence it is that the LXX translators use the names of Phoenicians and the land of Canaan, and likewise of Phoenicians and Canaanites, interchangeably. Thus the same Saul is called the son of the Phoenician woman, Exod. VI. 15, and of the Canaanitess, Gen. XLVI. 10, as in the Hebrew text. Likewise Exod. XVI. 35, they ate the manna until they came to a part of Phoenicia. And Jos. V. 12. they harvested the land of the Phoenicians. For Phoenicia and the region of the Phoenicians, in both places it is 'the land of Canaan' in the Hebrew. Again, in the same chapter, verse 1, the kings of Phoenicia, that is, the kings of Canaan or the Canaanites. For so Joshua. And Job XL. 25, others 30, where it is about Leviathan, the nations of the Phoenicians shall divide him; Heb. Canaanites or merchants. Prov. last chapter, verse 24, she made Sidonians and sold to the Phoenicians, girdles to the Canaanites; the words 'to the Phoenicians' are missing in most copies, and indeed they are a gloss, which crept into the text from the margin, where for 'to the Canaanites' someone had written 'to the Phoenicians' from another interpreter. By this example, whom Matthew had called a Canaanite, her faithful interpreter, the Evangelist Mark, names a Syrophoenician. And indeed, although mention of the Canaanites among the Greeks is very obscure, yet it did not entirely escape them that the Phoenicians took their origin from the descendants of Canaan. We have on this matter a notable passage of Eupolemus in his book on the Assyria of the Jews, although it is otherwise sprinkled with many fables. There, indeed, it is read that Belus was born from Saturn and Chanaan, τοῦτον δὲ τὸν Χαναὰν γεννῆσαι τὸν πατέρα τῶν Φοινίκων, that this Chanaan begat the father of the Phoenicians. Alexander Polyhistor cites this from Eupolemus, and Eusebius from Alexander. To this point pertains what is mentioned in Philo of Byblos, the interpreter of Sanchoniathon, a Phoenician writer by far the most ancient, of a certain ΧΝᾹ τοῦ πρώτου μετονομασθέντος Φοίνικος, CHNA who was the first to be distinguished by the surname of Phoenician. For there is no one who does not see that the name CHNA was born from the truncated Chanaan. And so, in Stephanus of Byzantium in his book on cities, Phoenicia is called CHNA and the Phoenicians CHNAI. The words are: ΧΝΑ͂, οὕτως ἡ Φοινίκη ἐκαλεῖτο. And a little later, τὸ ἐθνικὸν ταύτης χνάους. Now if you ask why the Phoenicians, if they are the descendants of Canaan, are nowhere called Canaanites in the monuments of the Greeks: I answer that the Canaanites were ashamed of their name, and ceased to be called so, on account of the curse cast upon their father Canaan: especially when they saw that they were being attacked by the Jews in a war of extermination, and were being afflicted with great disasters, for no other reason than that they were Canaanites: and so they preferred to be called Syrians, Assyrians, Sidonians, Phoenicians, and Syrophoenicians instead of Canaanites. And the name of the Syrians, indeed, which was common to them thereafter with the surrounding nations, I think was once their own, since it seems to be derived from the Phoenician metropolis, Tyre: for the Hebrews call it צור Tsor or Sur, and the inhabitants Sorim or Surim, who are the very same as Σύροι. Furthermore, because there was a contention between the Sidonians and the Tyrians for primacy, just as from Sur, which is Tyre, the Phoenicians were called Σύροι Syrians and Assyrians, so from Sidon they were called Sidonians. This did not escape Hesychius, who interprets Σιδονίους as Phoenicians. And so the seventy elders have Phoenicians for Sidonians in Deuteronomy 3:9, and Phoenicia for Sidon in Isaiah 23:2.

Latin:

Vers. 22. Χαναναῖα] Quin idem sit, quod apud Marcum Συροφοίνισσα ne dubitari quidem debet. Nam Χαναναῖοι He- bræis dicti stricte, ac peculiariter hi, qui Sidonem & Tyru & quod adjacet oræ maritimæ habitabant. Cananæus ha- bitans ad mare, inquit Moses Num. XIII. 8. Rursum Sido- nii accensentur Cananæis Jud. I. 31. & Procopius ad Gene- sin, Chananæos explicat Sidonios: & Stephanus Χνᾶ ὕτως ἡ Φοινίκη καλεῖται, ubi Χνᾶ est כנען omissa litera נ: quam παραγωγικὴν Hebræi fatentur. Sic & Philo Byblius ex San- choniathone apud Eusebium libro I. Præpar. c. X. ἀδελφὸς Χνᾶ τοῦ πρώτου μετονομασθέντος Φοίνικος. Hi autem sunt φοίνι- κες itidem proprie dicti Straboni, Plinio, aliis: Et ut φοίνι- κες Homero, omnibusque eum secutis celebrantur ex na- vigatu & mercatu, ita Solomoni, Esaiz, Oseæ, Zachariæ Cananæi: Quare sicut LXX. quod est in Hebræo Jos. V. 1. מלכי הכנעני verterunt βασιλεῖς τῆς Φοινίκης, & Jobi XL. 25. Cananæos φοινίκων ἔθνη, ita hoc loco quod Matthæi in- terpres dixerat Χαναναίαν, Marcus posuit Συροφοίνισσαν, qua in voce Syri adjectio, ut sæpe apud Poëtas, nihil aliud quam Phœnicas Asiæ αὐτόχθονας à colonis ipsorum Afri- canis Phœnicibus distinguit, ut pridem recte est observa- tum. Hinc Syrus interpres dicto Marci loco διακριτικῶς di- xit Punicam Syriæ. Nec aliter interpretandum Horatii il- lud:

---- & uterque Pœnus Serviat uni.

Syrophœnices scilicet & Libyphœnices. Ipsi quoq; in A- frica Phœnices Cananæos se vocabant. Nam Augustinus li- bro expositionum epistolæ ad Romanos ait rusticos Afros Hipponæ vicinos si interrogarentur qui essent, Punice re- spondiffe, Canaani. Vocis autem Phœnicis originem fru- stra viri eruditi ex Syriaco quærunt. Neq; enim à seipsis ita vocabantur, sed Cananæi. Phœnicas autem Græci dixere, ut Aristoteles refert de mirandis narrationibus, quod latro- cinantes ut in quamque oram appulerant homines occide- rent. Nam veteribus Græcis αἱμάξαι dicebatur φοινίξαι: quod & Aristophanis interpres ad Acharnenses notavit. Ea- demque de causa etiam Cares dicti φοίνικες Bacchilidæ & Corinnæ. Quod autem ἑλληνὶς hæc mulier Marco dicitur, significat nec Hebræam fuisse gente, nec ἰουδαΐζουσαν. Neque tamen sequitur fuisse idolorum cultricem. Nam & in Judæa & in vicinis regionibus & alibi multi erant viri fœminæque ὁνσιβείς σεβόμενοι τὸν θεὸν, extra professionem Judaismi, qualis Cornelius, Lydia, atque alii,, de quibus videre est A- ctor. X. 2. c. XVII. 4. 17. Atq; hoc sensu ἕλληνα sæpe dixit Paulus, omne humanum genus in Græcos & Judæos dis- pertiens. Hæc autem fœmina ex Sidoniis aut Tyriis fini- bus ad Christi famam processit. Deo eventus ita disponen- te, ut quomodo antecedens disputatio antiquationem le- gis ritualis, ita hæc adoptionem gentium adumbraret.

Alii à Cana oppido in finibus Phœniciæ, & Galilææ cum Adrichomio, & Ariæmontano eam dictam volunt. Sed nec literæ consonant, quia Cana non per כ sed per ק scribitur, neque è tri- bu Asser, ubi Canam sitam dicunt, aut ex Israë- litis erat hæc mulier, sed Græca & Ethnica quo- ad ortum erat, Marc. VII. 26. etsi ad verum Deum conversa. Non displicet hic Grotii de Cananæa muliere sententia. Quam illustrant quæ habet Lightfooth in h. l. cur speciatim nonnulli inter se- ptem gentes ab Israëlitis perdendas Cananæi dicti sint, quod nempe Canaan ipse peculiarem partem terræ istius (Septentrionalem scilicet) habitaverit cum primogenitis suis Sidone & Heth. Atque inde speciali isti progeniei nomen Cananæorum inditum fuisse, ab aliis omnibus filiis suis distinctum; regio- nemque istam peculiari nomine Canaan vocatam, distinctive à reliqua terra Canaanitide. Hinc Ja- bin regem Hazor vocari regem Canaan, Jud. IV. 2. & reges (ni, ut ait, ipse fallatur) Tyri & Sidonis vocari Reges Hittæorum 1. Reg. X. 29. Mulierem autem istam fuisse Syro-Græcam gente, quæ deno- minatio à regno Syro-Græco, cujus memoria non- dum evanuerat; Phœnissam habitatione, atque inde Canaanæam nomenclatura. De Cananæis e- rudite Bochartus & ex eo Walæus ad h. l. Ex Chananæis ortos esse Phœnices facile animadvertet quisquis aut Phœniciæ nomen & situm, aut prisco- rum Phœnicum linguam, instituta, mores & artes accurate perpenderit. Hinc est quod LXX. Interpre- tes Phœnices & terræ Chanaan, Phœnicum item & Chananæorum nomen promiscue usurpant. Sic i- dem Saul dicitur filius τῆς Φοινίσσης Exod. VI. 15. & τῆς χανανίτιδος Genes. XLVI. 10. ut in Hebræo textu. Item Exod. XVI. 35. ἔφαγον τὸ μὰν, ἕως πα- ραγένοντο εἰς μέρος τῆς φοινίκης. Et Jos. V. 12. ἐκαρπίσαντο δὲ τὴν χώραν τῶν Φοινίκων. Pro Phœ- nice & regione Phœnicum utrobiq; est in Hebræo terra Chanaan. Rursus ejusdem capitis vers. 1. οἱ βασι- λεῖς τῆς Φοινίκης, id est Reges Chanaan vel Cha- nanæorum. Ita enim Josue. Et Job. XL. 25. alii 30. ubi de Leviathan, μεριτεῦονται αὐτὸν Φοινίκων ἔ- θνη; Hebr. Chananæi vel mercatores Prov. cap. ult. vers. 24. Σιδόνας ἐποίησε κ’ ἀπέδοτο τοῖς Φοίνι- ξι, περιζώματα τοῖς Χανανίοις, voces τοῖς Φοίνιξι desunt in plerisque exemplaribus, & vero sunt glosse- ma, quod irrepsit in textum è margine, ubi pro τοῖς Χανανίοις aliquis ex alio interprete scripserat τοῖς Φοίνιξι. Hoc exemplo quam Chananæam Mat- thæus appellaverat, eam Matthæi fidus interpres Marcus Evangelista nominat Syrophœnissam. Et vero quamvis Chananæorum apud Græcos sit valde obscu- ra mentio, tamen eos id non latuit prorsus, Phœnicas ex posteris Chanaan ortum duxisse. Habemus ea de re insignem Eupolemi locum in libro de Judæorum Assyria, quamvis alioqui multis fabulis insperso. Ibi nempe legitur ex Saturno Belum ortum & Cha- naan, τοῦτον δὲ τὸν Χαναὰν γεννῆσαι τὸν πατέ- ρα τῶν Φοινίκων, hunc vero Chanaan genuisse Phœ- nicum Patrem. Ex Eupolemo citat Alexander polyhistor, ex Alexandro Eusebius. Huc facit quod in Philone Biblio Sanchoniathonis interprete, Phœnicii Scriptoris longe vetustissimi, mentio fit cujusdam ΧΝᾹ τοῦ πρώτου μετονομασθέντος Φοί- νικος, CHNA qui Phœnicis cognomine primus insignis fuerit. Nemo enim est qui non videat no- men CHNA natum esse ex decurtato Chanaan. I- taque apud Stephanum Byzantinum in libro de urbibus Phœnice vocatur CHNA & Phœnices CHNAI. Verba sunt: ΧΝΑ͂, οὕτως ἡ Φοινίκη ἐκαλεῖτο. Et paulo post, τὸ ἐθνικὸν ταύτης χνάους. Jam si roges cur Phœnices, si sint posteri Canaan, in Græcorum monumentis Chananæi nusquam vo- centur: Respondeo Chananæos puduisse sui nomi- nis, & desiisse sic appellari, propter anathema contortum in patrem suum Chanaan: Maxime cum viderent à Judæis se bello peti internecino, & magnis affligi cladibus, non alia de causa quam quod Chananæi essent: itaque pro Chananæis Syros, Assyrios, Sidonios, Phœnicas, Syrophœnicas ap- pellari se maluerunt. Et Syrorum quidem nomen illis commune deinceps cum circumfusis gentibus, puto olim fuisse proprium, cum deductum videatur à Phœnices metropoli Tyro: Eam enim צור Tsor vel Sur Hebræi nominant, & incolas Sorim vel Surim, qui ipsissimi Σύροι sunt. Porro quia Si- doni cum Tyro de primatu fuit contentio, ut à Sur qua Tyrus est, Phœnices Σύροι Syri dicti sunt & Assyrii, sic à Sidone Sidonii. Hesychium id non latuit, qui Σιδονίους interpretatur Φοινίκας. I- taque LXX. seniores Phœnicas pro Sidoniis Deut. III. 9. & pro Sidone Phœnicen habent, Esa. XXIII. 2.

## 15:23
Vers. 23. He answered her not a word. Thus Lucilius: he dares not say a muttum. For muttum is a word, as the Scholiast rightly says regarding Persius, which manner of speaking remains in the Romance language of the Franks.

ἀπόλυσον ἀυτήν ] I would translate it 'dismiss her': just as Terence and others use this word.

Latin:

Vers. 23. ἐκ ἀπεκρίθη ἀυτῇ λόγον ] Ita Lucilius : non au- det dicere muttum. Nam muttum est verbum, ut recte ad Persium Scholiastes, qui mos loquendi manet in lingua Romanensi Francorum.

ἀπόλυσον ἀυτήν ] Verterim absolve hanc: quomodo Te- rentius aliique hanc vocem usurpant.

## 15:24
Vers. 24. I was not sent. This mandate, he says, I received from the Father: as if sent by him, that I might propose to the Jews the words of saving doctrine and confirm them with miracles. For that numerous seed from the nations was promised to Christ only after his death, when he would no longer be a legate, but a king sitting at the right hand of the Father.
