Nor did this, however, prevent him from using his power indiscriminately within the borders of Judea and benefiting another. But Christ, stating part of the truth and keeping silent on part, wished to make the woman's persevering confidence manifest, to the reproach of the Jewish nation.

Τὰ πρόβατα τὰ ἀπολωλότα ] See above IX. 36.

Latin:

Vers. 24. ἐκ ἀπεsάλην ] Hoc mandatum, inquit, à patre accepi: tanquam ab eo missus, ut Judæis proponam verba salutaris doctrinæ & miraculis consignem. Nam semen illud numerosum ex gentibus Christo promissum erat de- mum post mortem, cum jam non amplius futurus esset le- gatus, sed rex assidens dextræ Patris. Neque tamen hoc obstabat, quominus intra Judææ fines ἀδιαφόρως uti atque alteri benefaceret. Sed Christus veri partem enuntians, partem reticens, perseverantem fœminæ fiduciam testatam facere voluit, in opprobrium Judaicæ gentis.

Τὰ πρόβατα τὰ ἀπολωλότα ] Vide supra IX. 36.

## 15:26
Vers. 26. οὐκ ἔστι καλόν ] That is, it is not becoming. The Syrian [version has] לא שפיר. Elsewhere it stands for it is expedient, as below XVIII. 8. 9. Mark XIV. 21. 1 Cor. VII. 1.

τοῖς κυναρίοις ] It is true that those whom we despise are accustomed to be called dogs by the Hebrews and ancient Greeks. But the word κυναρίων does not fit that meaning. For that was the common name for dogs that were kept as pets, such as Maltese dogs. Therefore, Christ only wished to indicate the distinction that existed at that time between the children of the promise and outsiders.

With this title, says Lightfoot on the word τοῖς κυναρίοις, the Jews, out of virulence and contempt, decorated the Gentiles, whom they held as nothing more than objects of hatred, mockery, and cursing, everyone except themselves. Midr. Till. fol. 6. 3. אומות עולם נמשלו ככלבים. The nations of the world (that is, the heathens) are likened to dogs. The Savior uses this phraseology from the common speech of the nation rather than from his own sentiment, for the Gentiles were not so hateful to him, and it was his custom to speak with the common people. This stone of an ignominious name, thrown at the heathens, finally falls back upon their own heads, and that by a guiding hand and divine justice. For although they, out of pride and contempt, cast that reproach upon the Gentiles, it was nevertheless rebounded upon them by the Holy Spirit to their own supreme demerit. See Ps. LIX. 6; Philipp. III. 2; Apoc. XXII. 15, etc. Furthermore, the word 'dog' figuratively denotes in almost all languages a most vile, impudent, and hateful person. Why the word Κυναρίε should not also be taken in that way does not appear. Chrysostom, certainly most learned in Greek, says: He calls the Gentiles dogs because of the impurity of their lives and the worship of idols, but the Jews children. And did not this woman, when she called herself by that name, voluntarily profess her own unworthiness? She persisted in asking, says Augustine in Sermon LXXIV de tempore: and by that very reproach she showed humility and obtained mercy. For she was not moved, nor did she grow angry, that she was called a dog while seeking a benefit and begging for mercy; but she says: 'Yes, Lord': You have called me a dog, I am clearly a dog: I acknowledge my name; and the truth speaks: But I am not therefore to be repelled from the benefit, etc.

Latin:

Vers. 26. ἐκ ἔsι καλόν ] Id est ἧ πρέπον. Syrus לא שפיר . Alibi pro συμφέρει ut infra XIIX. 8. 9. Marcus XIV. 21. 1. Cor. VII. 1.

τοῖς κυναρίοις ] Verum est canes Hebræis & Græcis vete- ribus dici solere eos quos contemnimus. Sed vox συναρίων ei significationi non convenit. Ita enim appellari vulgo solebant canes, qui in deliciis erant, quales Melitenses. Tantum ergo indicatum voluit Christus discrimen quod ad id tempus erat inter τὰ τέκνα τῆς ἐπαγγελίας & extra- neos.

Hoc titulo, inquit ad vocem τοῖς κυναρίοις Light- foot, ex virulentia & contemtu, Judæi Gentiles de- decorarunt, quibus nihil prius, quam omnes præter seipsos odio, ludibrio, maledictioni, habere. Midr. Till. fol. 6. 3. אומות עולם נמשלו ככלבים. Natio- nes mundi (id est, Ethnici) assimulantur canibus. Ex communi gentis loquela potius, quam ex sensu suo, Phraseologia hac utitur Salvator, cui Gentiles non tam exosi, & cui in more fuit loqui cum vulgo. Reci- dit tandem in propria capita saxum hoc nominis ignominiosi, in Ethnicos jactum, idque dirigente ma- nu, & justitia divina. Nam quamvis illi ex super- bia & contemptu opprobrium illud Gentilibus im- pegerint, summo tamen eorum demerito in ipsos re- ellisum est à Spiritu Sancto. Vide Ps. LIX. 6. Philipp. III. 2. Apoc. XXII. 15. &c. Cæterum canis vox figu- rate in omnibus fere linguis vilissimum, impuden- tem & exosum hominem denotat. Κυναρίε vox cur ita etiam accipi non debeat, non apparet. Chrysostomus certe Græce scientissimus, Canes, inquit, dicit gentiles propter impuritatem vitæ ipso- rum, & Idolorum cultum, filios autem Judæos. Et annon mulier hæc, cum se isto nomine vocavit, in- dignitatem suam ultro professa est! Institit petendo, inquit Augustinus Serm. LXXIV. de tempore: & eo ipso veluti convitio humilitatem ostendit, miseri- cordiam impetravit. Neque enim commota est, aut succensuit, quod canis appellata fuerit petens benefi- cium, rogans misericordiam; sed ait: Ita Domine: Dixisti me canem, plane sum canis: agnosco nomen meum; & veritas loquitur: Sed non ideo à beneficio repellenda sum. &c.

## 15:27
Vers. 27. Yes, Lord. Although I do not strongly disagree with the most learned man who thinks that ναὶ is a particle of one beseeching, yet the simplest meaning to me seems to be if we interpret it as a sign of assent, in this way: You speak the truth, Lord, that the children's bread should not be thrown to the little dogs; for I agree that the little dogs ought to be content with the crumbs falling from the table: as if she were to say: I do not ask for many or great benefits, but one, which can be granted incidentally and without detriment to others. For it is very easy to supply this from the similitude proposed by the Lord, which she pursues. It was accepted everywhere that leftovers were given to dogs. Euripides in the Cresphontes: 'and by custom he throws the scraps to the dogs.' Plutarch relates that it was the custom of the Persian kings to place even for the dogs what they were to eat at their own table. In Quintilian there is: 'He even feeds the dog.' Philostratus in the Life of Apollonius: 'to throw to the dogs nearby what falls from the feast of those eating.' Aristotle in the second book of the Generation of Animals, chapter 6: 'And in the management of the food that is produced, the best is set aside for the free, the worse and the remainder of that for the servants. And they give the worst to the animals that are fed with them.'

Latin:

Vers. 27. Ναὶ κύριε ] Quanquam non valde refrago: viro doctissimo, qui putat ναὶ esse obsecrantis particulam, tamen simplicissimus mihi sensus esse videtur si interpretemur pro nota assensus, hoc modo: Verum dicis Domine panes filiorum catellis non objici; consenti enim catelli esse debent micis de men- sa cadentibus: quasi dicat: & ego nec multa nec magnani- mium beneficia postulo, sed unum, quod obiter & sine a- liorum detrimento concedi mihi potest. Nam hoc supplere facillimum est, ex similitudine à Domino proposita quam persequitur. Reliquias canibus dari receptum ubiq;. Euri- pides Cressis: νόμῶ δὲ λείψαν' ἐκβάλλει κυσίν. Narrat Plu- tarchus Persarum regibus in more fuisse etiam canibus quod ederent in sua mensa ponere. Apud Quintilianum est: Etiam canem pascit: Philostratus vita Apollonii: πλησίον τοῖς κυσὶ πράττειν τοῖς σιτυμένοις τὰ ἐκπίπτοντα τῆς δαιτός. Aristo- teles secundo de Generatione animantium cap. 6. ἐν δὲ ταῖς οἰκονομίαις τῶν γενομένης τροφῆς ἡ μὲν βελτίση τέτακται τοῖς ἐλευθέροις ἡ δὲ χείρων καὶ τὸ περίττωμα ταύτης τοῖς έτ οἰκέ- ταις. τὰ δὲ χείρισα κὲ τοῖς συντρεφομένοις διδόασι ζώοις.

## 15:28
Vers. 28. Great is your faith. Faith truly Israelitic in a foreign woman. For to Jacob, when the name of Israel was given to him, it was said: כִּי שָׂרִיתָ עִם אֲנָשִׁים וַתֻכָל, which could be said with the best right to this woman. A notable presage of the calling of the nations. Origen on this passage: Nothing in the sight of God is wonderful, although it may be precious and great, except faith alone. The charity of the woman shone in the requested healing of her daughter and the preference for the Jews; piety in the seeking of the true God; humility in her prostration and confession of unworthiness; hope in her prayer; prudence in her responses; perseverance in her rebuffs. Christ, however, praises only her faith, 1. because it alone is the medium through which divine benefits are received. 2. because it is the reason for the other virtues: as here Blessed Gerhard.

PART III. The restoration of many sick people, and the miraculous feeding of 4000 men.

Latin:

Vers. 28. μεγάλη σε ἡ πίσις ] Fides vere Israelitica in ex- tranea muliere. Nam Jacobo, cum ei Israelis no..en in- deretur dictum est כִּי שָׂרִיתָ עִם אֲנָשִׁים וַתֻכָל quod optimo jure huic fœminæ dici pote- rat. Infigne præsagium τῆς ἐθνῶν κλήσεως. Origenes h. l. Nihil in conspectu Dei est mira- bile, quamvis pretiosum sit & magnum, nisi tan- tum fides. Caritas mulieris enituit in filiæ petita curatione, & Judæorum prælatione; pietas in veri Dei inquisitione; humilitas in prostratione & indi- gnitatis confessione; spes in oratione; prudentia in responsis; perseverantia in repulsis. Christus tamen solam fidem laudat, 1. quia sola est medium, per quod beneficia divina recipiuntur. 2. quia est ratio virtu- tum reliquarum: ut hic B. Gerhardus.

PARS III. Multorum ægrotorum restitutio, & 4000. virorum miraculosa cibatio.

## 15:30
Ver. 30. Κυλλοὺς] Since this word among the Greeks, and indeed most commonly, signifies one who is maimed, and is taken in that sense beyond controversy below and in Mark, and appears in no other meaning in these books, and the Syriac interprets it in that manner; I do not see what prevents us from believing that such bodily defects were also healed by Christ, although nothing of the sort is read elsewhere. Thus ὑγιεῖς below must be taken for ὑγιέσι. Arias Montanus translates it 'debiles' (weak): because the discourse is not about those whose limbs are maimed or missing, but have been rendered useless: who are not ἀσθενεῖς or infirm, but are hindered by some defect from being able to use all their members: which the Arab took specifically, substituting for it 'the deaf hear,' just as the Persian rendered it 'the lepers and elephantiasiacs are cleansed.' Moreover, the Syriac does not omit these words κυλλοὺς ὑγιεῖς, but reads them, and all of Beza's ancient codices read them, and therefore the Vulgate and the Ethiopic version incorrectly omit them.

Latin:

Vers. 30. Κυλλοὺς] Cum vox hæc Græcis, & quidem usi- tatissime mutilum significet, atque ita extra controversiam sumatur infra & apud Marcum, neque alio significatu in his libris appareat, & Syrus eum in modum interpretetur; non video, quid obstet, quo minus & talia corporis vitia à Christo sanata credamus, quanquam alibi nihil tale legittur. Ita ὑγιεῖς infra sumendum erit pro ὑγιέσι. Arias Montanus vertit debiles: quod sermo sit non de iis, quibus membra mutila sint, aut desint, sed ἄχρησα facta sint: qui non ἀσθενεῖς vel infir- mi sint, sed vitio aliquo impediantur, quo minus omnibus membris uti possint: quod specialiter ac- cepit Arabs pro eo substituens, surdos audire, uti Persa reddidit, leprosos & elephantiacos mundari. Cæterum non omittit hæc κυλλοὺς ὑγιεῖς, sed le- git Syrus, & legêrunt ea omnes Bezæ vetusti codi- ces, ideoque perperam ea prætermittit Vulgata & Æthiopica versio.

## 15:31
Ver. 31. ὥστε τοὺς ὄχλους θαυμάσαι βλέποντας, τοὺς κωφοὺς λαλοῦντας] Seeing the prophecy of Isaiah XXXV. 5 fulfilled.

Latin:

Vers. 31. ὥστε τοὺς ὄχλους θαυμάσαι βλέποντας, τοὺς κωφοὺς λαλοῦντας] Videntes impleri vaticinium Esaiæ XXXV. 5.

## 15:35
Ver. 35. ἀναπεσεῖν] Above, ἀνακλιθῆναι. There is absolutely no difference between ἀναπίπτειν, ἀνακλίνεσθαι, and ἀνακεῖσθαι, when it concerns banquets: nor does it matter whether one reclines on the ground or on couches: as has been noted by others. The fifth canon of the Synod of Ancyra, dealing with those who had dined in an idol temple: ὅσοι δὲ ἀνῆλθον μετὰ ἐνδύματος πενθικοῦς καὶ ἀναπεσόντες ἔφαγον, that is, ἀνακείμενοι: for it follows, μεταξὺ δ' ὅλης τῆς ἀνακλίσεως δακρύοντες.

Latin:

Vers. 35. ἀναπεσεῖν] Supra ἀνακλιθῆναι. Plane nihil dif- fert ἀναπίπτειν, ἀνακλίνεσθαι, & ἀνακεῖσθαι, ubi de conviviis a- gitur: neque refert humine an id lectis discumbatur: ut ab aliis notatum est. Canon Synodi Ancyranæ quintus de iis agens qui in idoleo cœnaverant: ὅσοι δὲ ἀνῆλθον μετὰ ἐνδύμα- τος πενθικοῦς καὶ ἀναπεσόντες ἔφαγον, id est, ἀνακείμενοι: sequitur enim μεταξὺ δ' ὅλης τῆς ἀνακλίσεως δακρύοντες.

## 15:36
Ver. 36. εὐχαριστήσας] It is the same as εὐλογήσας, as we saw above.

Latin:

Vers. 36. εὐχαριστήσας] Idem est quod εὐλογήσας ut su- pra vidimus.

## 15:37
Ver. 37. σπυρίδας] Below, a basket (sporta) is distinguished from hampers (cophini). Perhaps because they thought the journey would be longer, they had taken baskets rather than hampers.

Latin:

Vers. 37. σπυρίδας] Distinguitur infra sporta à cophinis. Forte ad iter quod diuturnius fore putabant sportas potius quam cophinos assumserant.

## 15:39
Ver. 39. Μαγαδὰν] The Greek reading formerly had it thus, as appears from Jerome and Augustine, and even now codices of the best quality do: so also the old Latin. Wherefore, since even now certain copies have μαγδαλὰν, that spelling seems to rest on more testimonies. Add that in Mark, instead of Δαλμανουθὰ, some codices have μαγεγαδὰ, and Augustine records that not a few codices formerly had μαγαδὰ in that same place: which, however, is not enough for me to disturb the reading that is in Mark: for from the map of Judea which the Jews provided, we learn that it is the same tract in which the villages of Magadan and Dalmanatha are, so that that tract could be named from either, just as the tract of Gadara and Gergesa is the same, as was said above: but since I judge that what is in some of Mark's codices is an interpretation taken from this passage of Matthew, it seems to me that this also adds to the other testimonies of the reading I mentioned, μαγαδὰν. And yet I do not deny that there was a place which was called Magdala, from which the name of the Magdalene came; indeed, I believe the error arose from the vicinity of that village. I advise that here and wherever readings differ, they consult the most ancient codices, if anyone has the means to obtain them.

Grotius is too bold in that he changes the text, and substitutes μαγαδὰν for μαγδαλὰ in the text itself. The reasons are quite weak. For it is not yet effectively proven that the Greek reading was once thus, because it had been written so before in Jerome's copy, since that could have been a scribal error, or a memory error, just as Jerome was also mistaken in that, in saying that Mark records the same name. But Grotius does not show which codices of the best quality read it thus. Without doubt, therefore, this is the man's conjecture.

For he is prepared and ready in conjectures of this kind concerning diverse readings. Among their sixteen Codices, the Parisians found only one, and that one adorned here and there to match the Vulgate version, which had μαγαδὼν, and neither Beza nor the Londoners, who with great care sought out and compared the most ancient Codices of the best quality, report more than one reading it so. But all the others had μαγδαλὰ, which reading the Arab and Ethiopian Interpreter also followed, as did the Syrian and Persian, as well as Chrysostom and Theophylact. And although we easily admit that Magdala, which is situated in the tribe of Judah, does not pertain to this, as it is too far distant from the Sea of Galilee, there is nevertheless another city on this side of the Sea of Galilee on the very shore, of a nearly similar name, called מגדליתא Magdalitha, or if that be foreign here, because the Lord seems to have traveled across the sea, μαγδαλὰ and μαγεδὰν are to be considered names of the same place, with only the letters of the same organ or linguals, Nun and Lamed, interchanged. Furthermore, that Dalmanutha and Magedan or Magdala were neighbors appears from the Map, where between the village of Dalmanutha and the city of Gerges or Gerasa there was Magedan across the Sea of Galilee in the half-tribe of Manasseh.

Latin:

Vers. 39. Μαγαδὰν] Ita olim habuit Græca lectio, ut ex Hieronymo, & Augustino apparet, atque etiam nunc opti- mæ notæ codices: ita & Latinus vetus. Quare cum etiam nunc exemplaria quædam μαγδαλὰν habeant, ea scriptura pluribus testimoniis niti videtur. Adde quod in Marco pro Δαλμανουθὰ quidam codices habent μαγεγαδὰ, & olim haud paucos codices ibidem habuisse μαγαδὰ commemorat Au- gustinus: quod mihi quidem non sufficit, ut lectionem quæ apud Marcum est sollicitem: nam ex tabula Judææ, quam Judæi dederunt, discimus eundem esse tractum, in quo vici Magadan & Dalmanatha, ita ut ab utrovis denominari is tractus potuerit, sicut idem est tractus Gadaræ & Gergesæ, ut supra dictum est: sed cum id quod in quibusdam est Mar- ci codicibus, interpretamentum esse arbitrer ex hoc Mat- thæi loco desumtum, videtur mihi hoc quoque ad cætera testimonia ejus quam dixi lectionis μαγαδὰν accedere. Ne- que tamen nego fuisse locum, qui μαγδαλὰ appellaretur, unde Magdalenæ nomen fuerit, imo ex ejus Neminis vici- nitate errorem natum arbitror. Suadeo & hic & ubicunque lectiones discrepant, vetustissimos codices consulant, si quibus nanciscendi est copia.

Nimis audax est Grotius, quod textum immu- tat, & pro μαγδαλὰ in ipso textu μαγαδὰν substi- tuit. Rationes satis leves sunt. Nam ita habuisse olim Græcam lectionem nondum efficaciter pro- batur, quod ante in Exemplari Hieronymi sic scri- ptum fuerit, quum id potuerit error esse γραφι- κὸς, aut μνημονευτικὸς, quemadmodum in eo et- iam falsus fuit Hieronymus, quod Marcum ejusdem nominis recordari dixit. Quinam vero opti- mæ notæ Codices sic legerint, non docet Gro- tius. Sine dubio ergo viri hæc conjectura est.

Nam pransus & paratus est in ejusmodi conjectu- ris de diversis lectionibus. Parisienses inter sedecim suos Codices non nisi unum invenêre, eumque ad vulgatam versionem passim adornatum, qui μαγα- δὼν habuerit, nec nisi unum Beza & Londinenses re- ferunt, qui magna cura vetustissimos & optimæ notæ Codices按钮conquisivêre & contulère, sic legen- tem. Cæteri autem omnes habuerunt μαγδαλὰ, quam lectionem etiam secutus est Arabs & Æ- thiopis Interpres, quam etiam Syrus & Persicus, ut & Chrysost. ac Theophylact. Et quanquam facile ad- mittamus Magdalam, quæ in tribu Judæ consti- tuitur, huc non pertinere, utpote quæ nimis pro- cul à mari Galilææ distat, est tamen alia urbs cis mare Galilæa in ipso littore, similis fere nominis, dicta מגדליתא Magdalitha, aut si ea hic aliena sit, quia Dominus ultra mare profectus videtur, μα- γδαλὰ, & μαγεδὰν ejusdem loci nomina censen- da, permutatis solum literis ejusdem organi seu lingualibus Nun & Lamed. De cætero vicina fu- isse Dalmanutha & Magedan vel Magdalam è Mappa apparet, ubi inter vicum Dalmenutha & urbem Gerges, vel Gerasavicuse rat Magedan ul- tra mareGalilææ in dimidia tribu Manassè.

## 16:1 Argument
CHAPTER XVI. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

The Pharisees and Sadducees, demanding a sign from heaven, are rebuked because, while they discern the signs of the weather, they do not judge the signs of the present time, and He denies that another sign will be given, except the sign of Jonah. The disciples are warned about the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees, and when they understood this as referring to bread not taken, they are reproved because they had not yet perceived its force from the five thousand men miraculously fed once, and the four thousand a second time. Questioned about the Son of Man, they give a confession through Peter as interpreter, upon which the Church is said to be founded, and the keys of the kingdom of heaven are committed to Peter, and the passion, death, and resurrection of Christ are predicted: when Peter resisted this, he is rebuked as scandalous: and the disciples are warned about following Christ, and about the most serious loss of the soul: and about the final coming of the Son of Man, as well as about the imminent coming of the kingdom of grace.

There are V. parts: I. The rebuke of those demanding a sign from heaven, to v. 4. II. The warning to beware of the leaven of the Pharisees, to v. 12. III. Peter's confession concerning Christ, and the promise made concerning the Church, to v. 20. IV. The prediction of the Passion and Resurrection of Christ, with the rebuke of Peter who contradicted it, to v. 23. V. Information concerning following Christ, to v. 28.

PART I. The rebuke of those demanding signs.

Vers. 1. πειράζοντες] Seeking an occasion for calumny. Thus the same word is used below in chap. XIX. 3, chap. XXII. 18, and elsewhere. Vers. 2. ὀψίας γενομένης · λέγετε, ἐυδία. Sc. ἔσαι. There is a certain emphasis in that aposiopesis: Behold serenity, i.e., it will be. Eὐδια signifies the goodness of the air, from the adverb ἐὺ and the accusative διὰ, of the name ζεύς. By the name of Jove, the heaven or air is understood metonymically. Vers. 3. συγνάζων ὁ ὐρανὸς. The heaven is said to συγνάζειν, to be sad, by an elegant metaphor. Concerning this prognosis, Aratus says:

Μήδ' ὅτε ἡ ὀλίγη νεφέλη πάρθ' ἀντέλλησι, Τὴν δὲ μετ' ἀκτίνων κεχρωσμέν' αὐτὸς ἀερθῆ Ἅμνησᾶν ὑετοῖο. He says that one should not be unmindful of rains if a thin cloud rises before the Sun, and the Sun itself, following it, rises in such a way that the rays are colored. And again: εἰ δ' ὁ μὲν ἀνέφελος βάπτοι ῥόον ἑσπερίοιο ] αἱ δὲ κατερχο- μένῳ νεφέλαι τε καὶ οἰχομένοιο πλησίον ἑστήκωσιν ἐ- ρευθέες, οὐ σὲ μάλα χρὴ ἄυριον οὐδ' ἐπὶ νύκτα πᾶ- τερχθέειν ὑετοῖο. If the Sun touches the evening waves without clouds, but with those following it standing very near and reddish, there is no need to fear rains then, nor on the following day. Morning redness generally denotes winds or rains, because the Sun draws a watery and red cloud toward us, which if it is dewy, rains fall: but if it is not dewy, yet better cooked, it provides material for winds. Evening redness is an index of serenity, because the Sun draws the watery cloud into another horizon, and by the cold of the night that watery cloud is meanwhile condensed, so that it cannot be resolved into rain. In the morning and evening, light is seen through vapors collected around the horizon. Whence the light turns purple; but at midday it becomes more yellowish, because it is seen through rarer vapors and those thinned by the excellence of the Sun. Just as fire also appears in different colors, according to the different media through which it is seen, although by its nature it is most luminous and imbued with no color. So also when many smokes and exhalations are gathered around the horizon, which the Sun cannot consume because of its oblique ray, the light seen through them appears purple. But why do purple clouds signify serenity in the evening, but rains in the morning? The cause is that the evening redness is more in a cloud dried by the daily heat of the Sun, into which the ray falling does not penetrate, but being reflected is doubled: or because these vapors are near the earth, and because of a lack of heat cannot be raised to the middle region of the air, whence they are converted into dew by the cold of the night; or because the air for the most part follows the motion snatched by the heaven. Whence perhaps rains exist at night in the other hemisphere, but in the morning serenity follows, the night rain having purged the air, which however we did not feel in our hemisphere. The opposite happens in morning redness. But in the morning the cloud is red because it is watery, which is raised by the heat of the Sun and easily dissolved into rain. Which it seemed good to repeat here from the blessed Gerhard. Conf. Gerhardus, Joh. Vossius l. III. de Theol. Gentil. p. 791. Succinctly Vallesius in Walaeus: The cause of this seems to me to be that dense clouds touched by an oblique sun, such as one that is already setting, present a blackness. Those therefore that are reddish are not so opaque and dense, but are penetrated by light, for which reason they indicate no preparation for a storm for the following day, and therefore promise serenity. But when, as the Sun rises, the heaven shows itself sad and cloudy here and there, clouds are usually dispersed at the first encounter of the rising Sun. Which, however, if they are dense, as when the heaven is sad, are not dissipated, but the rays of the Sun received through them seem to glow: but finally, in the evening, when the Sun, with which they have struggled all day, grows weak, they run together, thicken, and become rains.

Vers. eod. ὑποκριταὶ] He often addresses the Pharisees by this name. Why also the Sadducees, who by denying the afterlife were quite openly overturning the force of religion? Doubtless they wanted to appear φιλοπάτριδες, and the most zealous guardians of the public laws. Josephus says of the Sadducees that they are cruel in their judgments beyond all other Jews: and for this reason they obtained the highest honors, as he notes elsewhere.

Latin:

CAPUT XVI. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Pharisæis & Sadducæis signum de cœlo postu- lantib9 exprobratur, quod quum signa tem- pestatum dignoscant temporis præsentis si- gna non dijudicent, aliudq; signum datum iri negat, præterquam Ionæ signum. Disci- puli monentur de fermento Pharisæorum & Sadducæorum, quod quum illi de pane non assumto intelligerent, redarguuntur, quod nondum vim ejus perceperint è mi- raculose cibatis semel quinque, iterum quatuor millibus virorum. Quæsiti de filio hominis, interprete Petro confessionem e- dunt, super quam fundanda Ecclesia dici- tur, committunturque Petro claves regni cœlorum, & predicitur passio, mors & re- surrectio Christi : cui ubi reluctaretur Pe- trus, ceu scandalosus reprehenditur: mo- nenturque discipuli de Christi sequela, & de gravissimo animæ damno : deque ad- ventu Filii hominis novissimo, nec non de adventu regni gratiæ imminente.

Partes V. sunt: I. Signum de cœlo postulan- tium correptio, ad v. 4. II. De fermento Phari- sæorum cavendo monitio, ad v. 12. III. Petri de Christo confessio, & de Ecclesia facta promissio, ad v. 20. IV. Passionis & Resurrectionis Christi prædictio, cum Petri contradicentis reprehen- sione, ad v. 23. V. De Christi sequela informa- tio, ad v. 28.

PARS I. Signa postulantium correptio.

Vers. 1. πειράζοντες] Quærentes calumniæ occasionem. Ita vox eadem infra sumitur cap. XIX. 3. cap. XXII. 18. & alibi. Vers. 2. ὀψίας γενομένης · λέγετε, ἐυδία. Sc. ἔσαι. Est in illa aposiopesi emphasis quædam: Ecce serenitas, sc. erit. Eὐδια significat aëris bo- nitatem, ex Adverb. ἐὺ & accus. διὰ, nominis ζεύς. Jovis nomine metonymice intelligitur cœ- lum, seu aër. Vers. 3. συγνάζων ὁ ὐρανὸς. Cœlum dicitur συγνάζειν triste esse, per meta- phoram elegantem. De hoc prognostico Aratus:

Μήδ' ὅτε ἡ ὀλίγη νεφέλη πάρθ' ἀντέλλησι, Τὴν δὲ μετ' ἀκτίνων κεχρωσμέν' αὐτὸς ἀερθῆ Ἅμνησᾶν ὑετοῖο. Non esse, ait, imbrium obliviscendum, si tenuis nubes ante Solem oriatur, & ipse hanc sequens ita erumpat, ut radii colorentur. Et rursus: εἰ δ' ὁ μὲν ἀνέφελος βάπτοι ῥόον ἑσπερίοιο ] αἱ δὲ κατερχο- μένῳ νεφέλαι τε καὶ οἰχομένοιο πλησίον ἑστήκωσιν ἐ- ρευθέες, οὐ σὲ μάλα χρὴ ἄυριον οὐδ' ἐπὶ νύκτα πᾶ- τερχθέειν ὑετοῖο. Si tetigerit undas Sol vespertinas absque nubibus, sed cum his sequentibus se proxi- me rutilis non sunt, neque tunc, neque postridie metuendi imbres. Rubedo matutina plerumque, ven- tos aut pluvios notat, quia Sol attrahit nubem aquo- sam & rubram ad nos, quæ si rorulenta est, pluviæ de- cidunt: sin minus rorida, melius tamen percocta, ven- torum suppeditat materiam. Rubedo vespertina sere- nitatis index est, quia Sol aquosam nubem in alium horizontem detrahit, & frigiditate noctis aquea illa nubes interim condensatur, ne in pluviam resolvi pos- sit. Mane & vesperi conspicitur lumen per vapores circa horizontem collectos. Unde lumen purpurascit; in meridie vero magis flavescit, quia per vapores ra- riores & præstantia Solis subtiliatos conspicitur. Quemadmodum etiam ignis comparet diversis colori- bus, prout per diversa media conspicitur, cum tamen sua natura sit lucidissimus & nullo colore imbutus. Sic etiam quando circa horizontem congregantur multi fumi atque exhalationes, quas Sol propter obliquum radium absumere nequit, lumen per illas conspectum apparet purpureum. Cur autem nubes purpureæ se- renitatem vesperi significant, mane vero pluvias? Causa est quod vespertina rubedo magis est in nube siccata diurno æstu Solis, in quam radius incidens non penetrat, sed repercussus duplicatur: vel quia hi vapores sunt terræ vicini, & propter defectum caloris elevari non possunt ad mediam regionem aëris, unde frigore nocturno convertuntur in rorem; vel quia aër ut plurimum motum cæli raptum sequitur. Unde fortasse noctu existunt pluviæ in altero hemisphærio, mane vero subsequitur serenitas, purgato aëre pluvia nocturna, quam tamen nos in nostro hemisphærio non sensimus. Contrarium in rubedine matutina ac- cidit. Mane vero rubet nubes, quia est aquosa, quæ calore Solis elevatur ac facile in pluviam dissolvi- tur. Quæ è B. Gerhardo hic repetere visum fuit. Conf. Gerhardus, Joh. Vossius l. III. de Theol. Gentil. p. 791. Succincte Vallesius apud Walæum: Causa hujus mihi hæc esse videtur, quod nubes densæ tactæ sole obliquo, qualis est qui jam occidit, nigritiem præ se ferunt. Quæ ergo rubicundæ sunt, non sunt adeo opacæ & densæ, sed penetrantur lumine, quapropter in diem posterum nullum indicant tempestatis appa- ratum, serenitatem ergo promittunt. Cum vero orien- te Sole, triste hinc inde, & nubilosum se exhibet cœ- lum, plerumque solent ad primum orientis Solis occur- sum dispergi nubes. Quæ tamen si densæ sunt, quales cum triste cælum, non dissipantur, sed excepti per eas radii Solis videntur rutilare: postremo vero, vesperi, cum Sol, cum quo toto die sunt colluctatæ, languescit, concurrunt, densantur, fiuntque imbres.

Vers. eod. ὑποκριταὶ] Pharisæos sæpe hoc nomine com- pellat. Cur & Sadducæos qui negando vitam alteram vim religionis aperte satis evertebant? Nimirum videri volebant φιλοπάτριδες, & legum publicarum acerrimi custodes. Jose- phus de Sadducæis εἰσὶ περὶ τὰς κρίσεις ὠμοὶ παρὰ πάντας τοὺς Ἰουδαίους: atque hac ratione summos honores adipisceban- tur, ut alibi notat.

## 16:3
Διακρίνειν] That is, to discern in such a way that from it you may predict what storm is impending: and that you may arrange your affairs according to those omens, or as the Greeks call them, διοσημεῖα. Thus Aratus says that the stars were set apart by GOD for their significations:

For he himself says he fixed signs in the sky, having distinguished the stars. But you cannot [discern] the signs of the times] Rightly 'signs': for prognostics, which draw their causes from the quality of the sky, are referred to the class of signs, as Quintilian also noted, lib. V. 10. 'Of the times', of this time, as the Syrian translates, and Luke said in the singular 'the time'. The sense is this: If divine providence was so kind to men that it sent ahead certain signs of fair weather, winds, and rains, as that same Aratus says in his 'Diosemeia', 'Already all things are revealed from Zeus and lie everywhere', how much more reasonable is it to believe that signs of the imminent advent of the Messiah were given by that same providence: since that matter is of infinitely greater moment, pertaining not to the undertaking or delay of some journey, but to the ordering of one's whole life? but you are diligent enough in considering those signs, yet you demand signs concerning the advent of the Messiah, as if none had been given, when many and most certain ones have been given, but to which you either have no time or no desire to attend. For if you were to inspect the oracles of the Prophets as solicitously as you gaze upon the face of the sky when about to set out somewhere, you would undoubtedly recognize that the end of the weeks of Daniel is at hand, the glory of the kingdom taken away from Syria and Egypt, the most depraved morals of the people, the very leaders of the people, who are you, either extinguishing the fire of piety by taking away the hope of a better life, or converting all religion into cold ceremonies; on the other hand, that a doctrine of conspicuous purity is being proposed by me: that signs are being added, not such as are done for the sake of the soul, but by which men are helped; that sight is being restored to the blind, a gait to the lame, health to the sick: all of which are most certain signs of the kingdom of the Messiah. But what does Christ mean by 'you cannot'? the sense is: how does it happen that you cannot see, unless it is because you do not wish to see? 'Because you do not discern the time', as it is in Luke. There is, moreover, a not entirely dissimilar comparison in Plutarch: 'For it is absurd to pay careful attention to the throat-sounds of crows and the scratching of hens and the grunting of pigs when they are raging for food, as Democritus said, making them signs of winds and rains, but not to anticipate or guard against the movements and agitations and pre-affections of the body, nor to have within oneself signs of a winter that is about to happen and is coming.' The rest that pertains to this has been explained above at chapter XII. Let us note in the meantime that the same things were said and done by Christ more than once: which, since it often appears from the narrative of a single writer, the less we need to labor if, where different writers sometimes assign different places or times or circumstances to the same things.

PART II. A warning concerning avoiding the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees.

Latin:

Διακρίνειν] Id est, ita discernere ut inde prædicatis quæ immineat tempestas: atque ad ea præsagia, sive ut Græci vocant, διοσημεῖα componatis res vestras. Sic astra à DEO in suas significationes discreta dicit Aratus:

Αὐτὸς γὰρ λέγε σήματ᾽ ἐν ὀρανῷ ἐςήριξε ἄςρα διακρίνας. Τὰ δὲ σημεῖα τῶν καιρῶν ὀ δύνασθε] Recte σημεῖα: nam prognostica, quæ causas ex qualitate cœli trahunt, ad signo- rum genus referri, notavit & Quintilianus lib. V. 10. Τῶν καιρῶν, hujus temporis, ut vertit Syrus, & Lucas singula- riter dixit Τὸν καιρὸν. Sensus hic est: Si divina providentia tam benigna fuit in homines, ut sereni, venti, pluviæ signa quædam præmitteret, quomodo idem ille Aratus dicit ἐν διοσημείοις Ἐκ διὸς ἤδη πάντα πεφασμένα πάντοθι κεῖται, quanto æquius credi est ab eadem providentia data esse si- gna imminentis adventus Messiæ: cum ea res sit infinito ma- joris momenti, non ad susceptionem dilationemve itineris alicujus, sed ad vitam omnem instituendam pertinens? sed vos ad illa signa consideranda satis estis diligentes, de adven- tu autem Messiæ signa poscitis, quasi nulla sint data, cum data sint & multa & certissima, sed ad quæ vobis aut non vacat aut non lubet attendere. Nam si Prophetarum oracu- la tam sollicite inspiceretis, quam aliquo prosecturi cœli faciem intuemini, agnosceretis haud dubie instare finem hebdomadum Danielis ablatumSyriæ & Ægypto regni de- cus, populi mores depravatissimos, ipsos ductores populi, qui vos estis, aut extinguere pietatis ignem ademta spe vitæ melioris, aut omnem religionem in frigidas cæremonias convertere; contra à me proponi doctrinam conspicuæ pu- ritatis: accedere signa, non quæ animi gratia fiant, sed quibus homines juventur; cæcis reddi visum, claudis gressum, æ- grotis sanitatem: quæ omnia certissima sunt signa regni Messiæ. Quod autem dicit Christus ὀ δύνασθε? sensus est: qui fit, ut videre nequeatis, nisi quia videre non vultis? ὅτι ὀ δοκιμάζετε τὸν καιρὸν, ut est apud Lucam. Est autem comparatio non omnino dissimilis apud Plutarchum: Ἄτοπον γάρ ἐςι κοράκων μὲν λαρυγγισμοῖς κι κνωσμοῖς ἀλεκτορίδων κι συ- σιν ἐπὶ φαρυτῶ μαργαινόσαις, ὡς ἔφη Δημόκριτος, ἐπιμελῶς προσέχειν σημεῖα ποιεμένες πνευμάτων καὶ ὀμβρων, τὰ δὲ τῶ σώ- ματος κινήματα κι σάλες καὶ προπαθείας μὴ προλαμβάνειν μηδὲ προφυλάττειν, μηδὲ ἔχειν σημεῖα χειμῶνος ἐν ἑαυτῷ γενη- σομένε κι μέλλοντος. Cætera quæ huc pertinent explicata sunt supra ad caput XII. Notemus interim res easdem plus semel à Christo dictas factasque: quod cum sæpe ex unius Scri- ptoris narratione appareat, eo minus laborandum est nobis, sicubi scriptores diversi interdum rebus eisdem diversa lo- ca aut tempora aut circumstantias assignant.

PARS II. De cavendo Pharisæorum & Sadducæo- rum fermento monitio.

## 16:5
Verse 5. 'The disciples having come to the other side' That is, when they were setting out to the further bank. For often 'to come' in these books is not to come but to go, as twice again in this chapter and XVI. 24, but most openly in Luke XV. 20. But also Luke II. 44. For I agree with Jerome, who gathers from Mark that these discourses were held during the very journey and indeed in the boat. For I judge that the history which is in Luke chapter XII is different from this one. Here it is a matter of the leaven of both the Pharisees and the Sadducees: there, of the leaven of the Pharisees only: here Christ addresses the disciples alone, there the whole multitude of the people: not to mention that there it is rather a matter of evil examples, which Paul also calls 'leaven' 1 Cor. V. 6, here of the dogmas themselves. The nature of leaven is to spread its force widely: therefore above true doctrine was compared to leaven. Here, and in Paul to the Galatians, false dogmas are compared to leaven for the same reason, but also besides because of the bitterness of the taste: and because fermentation is a certain corruption. Elsewhere, as I said, evil examples, which themselves also harm by transmission: especially indeed those which are for the misleading of men. Plutarch in his Roman Questions: 'Leaven is made from corruption itself and corrupts the dough when mixed in. For it becomes inedible and fermentation is altogether like putrefaction.' The Rabbis call evil appetites leaven.

Latin:

Vers. 5. ἐλθόντες οἱ μαθηταὶ ἀυτῶ εἰς τὸ πέραν] Id est, cum in ulteriorem ripam proficiscerentur. Sæpe enim ἔρχεσθαι in his libris est non venire sed ire, ut bis iterum hoc capite & XVI. 24. apertiffime vero Lucæ XV. 20. Sed & Lucæ II. 44. Hieronymo enim assentior, qui ex Marco colligit hoc ser- mones in ipso itinere atq; adeo in navi habitos. Nam quæ apud Lucam est historia capite XII. ab hac diversam esse ar- bitror. Hic de fermento & Pharisæorum & Sadducæo- rum agitur: ibi de fermento Pharisæorum duntaxat: hic di- scipulos solos Christus alloquitur ibi totam populi multitu- dinem: ut jam taceam ibi potius de malis exemplis agi, quæ ζύμην etiam Paulus vocat 1. Cor. V. 6. hic de ipsis dogmati- bus. Natura fermenti eit vim suam late spargere: ideo su- pra vera doctrina fermento comparata est. Hic, & apud Paulum ad Galatas, falsa dogmata fermento comparantur eandem ob causam, sed & præterea ob saporis amaritiem: & quia fermentatio, corruptio quædam est. Alibi, ut dixi, mala exempla, quæ & ipsa nocent transitione: præsertim vero ea quæ sunt hominibus inslandis. Plutarchus quæstionibus Romanis: ἡ ζύμη γέγονεν ἐκ φθορᾶς ἀυτὴ καὶ φθείρει τὸ φύραμα μιγνυμένη. Γίνεται γὰρ ἄσιτον καὶ ὅλως ἔοικε σῆψις ἡ ζύμωσις εἶναι. Rabbini malos appetitus fermentum vocant.

## 16:6
Verse 6. 'Of the Sadducees' And yet Mark, omitting the Sadducees, names the 'leaven of Herod'. I believe it is because some of the Sadducees were at the same time Herodians, that is, they were saying that Herod the Great was the Shiloh promised by Jacob. That this was rightly reported by Tertullian to be about the Herodians can be taught to us also by Persius, and the old annotator on him, so that Jerome quite undeservedly denied it at chapter XXII of this writer, who nevertheless, writing against the Luciferians, had affirmed the same thing. Epiphanius hands down the same thing about the Herodians, except that he draws to Herod the executioner of the Baptist that which pertained to Herod the Great. But such an opinion was not alien to those who placed all their hopes in the happiness of this life and the flourishing state of the republic. For the glory of the kingdom, interrupted from the times of the Babylonian destruction, was at last restored to the Jews in Herod, who observed the Roman majesty so courteously that in the meantime he held the full rights of the kingdom. Wherefore it is no wonder if, while Herod was living and reigning, the Sadducees attained to the greatest dignities, which Josephus notes. Christ therefore teaches that two kinds of dogmas are to be solicitously avoided: those which place the chief part of piety in the external observation of rites, especially those invented by men, and those which transform religion into a kingdom of this world.

Latin:

Vers. 6. Σαδδεκαίων] Atqui Marcus Sadducæis præteritis nominat ζύμην Ἡρώδε. Credo, quod Sadducæorum non- nulli simul erant Herodiani, hoc est, Herodem Magnum esse dicebant Siloh à Jacobo promissum. Quod recte à Ter- tulliano de Herodianis esse proditum docere nos potest etiam Persius, & vetus ad eum annotator, ut plane immerito id negarit Hieronymus ad caput hujus Scriptoris XXII. qui tamen ipse contra Luciferianos scribens idem affirmaverat. Idem de Herodianis tradit Epiphanius, nisi quod ad He- rodem Baptistæ interiectorem trahit id quod ad Herodem Magnum pertinebat. Non erat autem talis opinio aliena ab illis qui in hujus vitæ felicitate & florenri reipublicæ statu spes omnes collocabant. Nam regni gloria intermissa ab excidii Babylonici temporibus in Herode demum Judæis erat restituta, qui ita comiter observabat Romanam ma- jestatem, ut interim plena haberet regni jura. Quare mirum non est, si vivente & regnante Herode Sadducæi ad dignita- tes maximas pervenerunt, quod Josephus notat. Duo igi- tur dogmatum genera sollicite vitanda Christus docet, ea quæ præcipuam pietatem ponunt in externa rituum, præser- tim ab hominibus repertorum, observatione, & ea quæ re- ligionem transformant in regnum hujus mundi.

## 16:7
Verse 7. 'Among themselves' That they not only thought silently, but spoke among themselves, is not only likely, but most certain from the words of Mark chapter VIII. 16. 'Because we have taken no bread' Understand: for that reason, clearly, he said this: such an ellipsis is also in the following verse, and most openly below XXV. 9. They were thinking that Jesus, since he knew that they lacked bread, was warning them in time not to procure for themselves bread from men of the Pharisaic or Sadducaic sect, just as if that bread were going to defile them. So quickly had the precepts of Christ slipped from them, by which he had taught that there was no force in things of that kind to defile the soul. At the same time, however, lest they suffer from a shortage of bread, they began to fear anxiously, especially since, as they thought, the freedom of buying was circumscribed and reduced to great straits.

Latin:

Vers. 7. ἐν ἑαυτοῖς] Non tacitos tantum cogitasse, sed in- ter se collocutos, non est verisimile tantum, sed certissimum ex Marci verbis cap. IIX. 16. Ὅτι ἄρτους οὐκ ἐλάβομεν] Subaudi ideo scilicet hoc dixit: qua- lis ἕλλειψις est & in sequenti commate, & apertissima infra XXV. 9. Existimabant Jesum cum sciret deesse illis panes, monere eos in tempore ne panem sibi ab hominibus Phari- saicæ aut Sadducaicæ sectæ compararent planè quasi is pa- nis ipsos esset inquinaturus. Tam cito illis Christi præce- pta exciderant, quibus docuerat nullam esse vim in rebus istiusmodi ad animum inquinandum. Simul autem ne pa- nis penuria laborarent, anxie metuere cœperunt, præser- tim circumscripta, ut existimabant, & in magnas angustias redacta emendi libertate.

## 16:8
Vers. 8. Because you took no bread] That is, why do you think this was said by me for the reason that you had no supply of bread, as if it were necessary for you either to perish from hunger or to receive bread from men, but that you must be entirely on your guard not to receive it from the Pharisees or Sadducees? Can I not feed you even if you procure bread from no man? Therefore, there was no reason for me to forbid you the dealings of the Sadducees and Pharisees so anxiously on that account.

Latin:

Vers. 8. Ὅτι ἄρτους οὐκ ἐλάβετε] Id est, quid existimatis hoc à me ea de causa dictum, quod panum copiam non ha- beatis, quasi scilicet necesse sit vobis aut fame perire, aut ab hominibus panes accipere, sed cavendum omnino ne à Pha- risæis aut Sadducæis eos accipiatis? An non ego vos pos- sum pascere etiamsi à nemine homine panem comparctis? Itaque non erat quod vobis eo nomine tam sollicite Sad- ducæorum & Pharisæorum commercia interdicerem.

## 16:11
Vers. 11. I told you to beware] Again an ellipsis for I told you when I said to beware. Those who did not understand this construction added 'but beware'.

PART III. Peter's confession concerning Christ, and the promise made by Christ to the Church.

Latin:

Vers. 11. εἶπον ὑμῖν προσέχειν] Iterum ἕλλειψις pro εἶπον ὑμῖν ὅτε εἶπον προσέχειν. Quam constructionem qui non intellexerunt addiderunt προσέχετε δέ.

PARS III. Petri de Christo confessio, & Christi Ecclesia facta promissio.

## 16:13
Vers. 13. And when Jesus had come] 'Having come' here again does not mean 'when he had arrived' [as if he were setting out]. For these conversations were held 'in the way,' as Mark says: by which it is not signified that they were held on a public road; for on the contrary, we learn from Luke that they were held in a certain retreat where Christ was praying: but before the end of the journey had been reached, 'of Caesarea Philippi'] That was added so that it would not be understood as the Caesarea which is usually called simply by that name in the Acts, founded by Herod, whose old name was Strato's Tower. 'The Son of man'] That is, me, I say, who in all outward preparation show nothing beyond a man from the common people.

Lightfoot is correct here: That phraseology, or title, Son of man, by which Christ most frequently designates himself, denotes neither his humanity alone, nor his humility (for see that in John V. 27: 'He gave him authority to execute judgment, because he is the Son of man'), but declares the seed promised to Adam, the second Adam; and it carried with it a tacit refutation of a twofold ignorance and error among the Jews. (1) They did not know what to determine concerning the origin of the Messiah, and in what manner he was to be born, whether he was to be from the living, as we noted before, in an unknown manner of origin, or from the dead. This phrase solves this knot and openly teaches that he, the seed promised to the first man, was to be born and to arise from the seed of the woman. (2) They dreamed of earthly victories for the Messiah, and that nations would be subjugated by him: but this title, Son of man, leads their minds back to the first promise, where the victory of the promised seed is the crushing of the serpent's head, not the subjugation of nations by some warlike and earthly triumph.

Latin:

Vers. 13. Ἐλθὼν δὲ Ἰησοῦς] Ἐλθὼν hic iterum non profi- cisceretur non cum venisset. Habiti enim sunt hi sermones ἐν ὁδῷ, ut ait Marcus: quo non significatur habitos in via publica: nam contra ex Luca discimus habitos in secessu quodam ubi Christus precabatur: sed antequam ad itine- ris finem perventum esset, Καισαρείας τῆς Φιλίππου] Id additum ne intelligeretur Cæ- sarea quæ ἁπλῶς sic dici in Actis solet, ab Herode condi- ta, cui nomen vetus Stratonis turris. Τὸν ὑὸν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου] Id est, me, inquam, qui omni paratu exteriore nihil præter de plebe hominem præfero.

Recte hic Lightfootus: Phrasiologia ista, vel ti- tulus, Filius hominis, quo seipsum frequentissime in- signit Christus, nec humanitatem ejus solùm denotat, nec humilitatem, (nam vide illud Joh. V. 27. Autori- tatem ei dedit judicium exequendi, quia est Filius hominis,) sed semen Adamo promissum enuntiat, Adamum secundum: duplicisque apud Judæos igno- rantiæ atque erroris confutationem tacitam secum portavit. (1) Non norunt quid de origine Messiæ sta- tuerent, & qualiter ille oriundus, an è vivis futurus, ut notavimus ante, ignoto originis modo, an è mor- tuis. Nodum hunc solvit hæc Phrasis palamq; docet, eum, semen bomini primo promissum, è mulieris se- mine oriundum, nascendumq;. (2) Victorias Messiæ terrestres, & subjugandas ab eo gentes somniabant: at mentes eorum reducit hic titulus Filius hominis ad primam promissionem, ubi victoria seminis promissi est contritio capitis serpentis, non subjugatio gen- tium triumpho aliquo bellico, & terreno.

## 16:14
Vers. 14. John the Baptist] We have said above why this cannot be referred to the opinion of reincarnation. Many of the Hebrews thought that only those who had suffered death for the divine law would rise again: as we have noted elsewhere from Tacitus, to which that passage in 2 Maccabees VII. 9 also seems to pertain: 'But the King of the world will raise us up, who have died for his laws, to an everlasting revival of life.' Certainly, the persuasion concerning these was firmer than concerning others. Wherefore some believed that the time of resurrection was represented even in this age.

Elijah] This is to be referred neither to reincarnation nor properly to the resurrection. For because it is read that Elijah was caught up in his body, he himself was thought to be about to return, and indeed before the times of the Messiah: that this was a received opinion of the masters, surely from a misunderstood prophecy of Malachi, we are taught below in chapter XVII. 10. Traces of this opinion exist in the books of the Hebrews: some of whom, however, wish him to come in another body, as David Kimchi noted on Malachi.

Jeremiah] This can be referred to the πάλιν] ἐνεσίαν. For the Hebrews were expecting the return of Jeremiah, as appears from Gorionides. Indeed, some thought the soul of Jeremiah was reborn in Zechariah: just as the soul of Phinehas in Elijah. But it can also be understood concerning the resurrection, as what follows.

Lightfoot notes that the Messiah would arise from the dead rather than from the living, perhaps having persuaded this reason among others, that such piety could by no means be expected at that time in any living person as had shone forth in those dead ones. He also notes that a certain one of the Babylonish Gemarists suspects that Daniel, resurrected from the dead, would be the Messiah. For the rest, the same Lightfoot conjectures at Matt. 27:9 that the memory of Jeremiah flourished above all other prophets, because Jeremiah had obtained the first place in the volume of the Prophets; which we leave in its place.

Or one of the prophets] Namely, one who has now risen, Luke 9:8. But it appears that those who opined these things had heard nothing of the birth of Jesus, and had received the first report about him from miracles, and indeed very recently. You could also interpret 'one of the prophets' as a new prophet, but equal to the old ones, of which opinion Mark makes mention in chapter 6:15.

Latin:

Vers. 14. Ἰωάννην τὸν βαπτιστήν] Cur hoc ad παλιγγενεσίας opinionem referri nequeat, supra diximus. Multi Hebræo- rum putabant eos demum resurgere qui ob legem divinam mortem oppetiissent: ut ex Tacito alibi notavimus, quo & illud pertinere videtur 2. Macc. VII. 9. ὁ δὲ τοῦ κόσμου βασιλεὺς ἀποθανόντας ἡμᾶς ὑπὲρ τῶν αὐτοῦ νόμων εἰς αἰώνιον ἀναβίωσιν ζωῆς ἡμᾶς ἀναστήσει. Certe de his firmior quam de cæteris fuit persuasio. Quare quibusdam etiam in hoc sæculo repræ- sentari resurrectionis tempus crediderunt.

Ἠλίαν] Hoc neque ad παλιγγενεσίαν, neque ad ἀνάστασιν proprie referendum. Nam quia Elias corpore sursum raptus legitur, ideo is ipse rediturus putabatur, & quidem ante Mef- siæ tempora: quam receptam fuisse magistrorum sententia, nimirum ex male intellecto Malachiæ vaticinio, infra doce- mur c. XVII. 10. Exstant ejus sententiæ vestigia in Hebræo- rum libris: quorum tamen nonnulli venturum eum volunt in alio corpore, ut David Kimchi notavit ad Malachiam.

Ἱερεμίας] Hoc potest ad πάλιν] ἐνεσίαν referri. Nam He- bræi exspectabant reditum Jeremiæ, ut ex Gorionide appa- ret. Imo quidam animam Jeremiæ renatam in Zacharia existimabant: quomodo animam Phineæ in Elia. Sed pot- est & de resurrectione accipi ut quod sequitur.

Notat Lightfoothus, è mortuis oriturum Messiam potius quam è vivis, forsan hanc inter alia ratio- nem suasisse, quod minime tunc dierum exspectari posset ea pietas in aliquo vivente, qualis eluxerat in istis mortuis. Notat etiam quendam è Gema- ristis Babylonis, Danielem è mortuis resuscita- tum Messiam futurum suspicari. De cætero conjectat idem Lightfoothus ad Matth. XXVII.9. memoriam Jeremiæ præ omnibus aliis Prophetis viguisse, quia Jeremias in volumine Prophetarum primum locum obtinuerit; quod nos suo loco re- linquimus.

Η ἕνα τῶν προφητῶν] Qui scilicet nunc resurrexerit Luc. IX. 8. Hæc autem qui opinabantur, eos apparet nihil audi- visse de natalibus Jesu, priinamq; de eo famam ex miracu- lis, & quidem nuper admodum, accepiffe. Possis etiam in- terpretari ἕνα τῶν προφητῶν Prophetam novum, sed veteri- bus parem, cujus opinionis Marcus meminit cap. VI. 15.

## 16:16
Verse 16. Simon Peter] Whom Chrysostom and Augustine do not wrongly call the mouth of the Apostles. See John 6:63. However, he seems to have seized the conversation more because of the eagerness which shines forth in him everywhere, than by right of leadership, because of those things which are narrated below in 18:1 and in other places. Wherefore, that the name of the first, that is, of the one who holds the first place, is added to him in the list of the Apostles, it is credible that it is a prolepsis: because when those things were written, he held that honor, which I think is so manifest from the passage in Acts 1:15 and others that it ought to be placed beyond controversy.

Grotius acknowledges that it cannot be concluded from the fact that Peter answers here in the name of others that he had authority and power over the others, which is accustomed to be done by Papists. He says, he seems to have seized the conversation more because of the eagerness which shines forth in him everywhere, than by right of leadership, because of those things which are narrated below in 18:1 and in other places. But as for the fact that Grotius nevertheless thinks that Peter had obtained power over the others, because the name of the first is attributed to him in the list of the Apostles in Matthew 10, and that he held that honor himself when those things were written, he thinks it so manifest that it ought to be placed beyond controversy, in that he is vehemently mistaken. For whence is that manifest? The contrary rather ought to have been called so manifest. Because just as that power over the other Apostles nowhere appears in the Scriptures, so on the contrary many things occur which clearly derogate the same from him. That name of 'first' is not the same as 'prōtos' at Matthew 10, as has already been noted, and thus it is said without proof, and therefore it is rejected with the same ease with which it is asserted. Acts 1:15, Peter holds a speech to the other disciples, and proposes the point about filling the place of Judas, or the election of a new Apostle, not as the head of the Apostles, of which dignity there is no trace there, but as the first by reason of order, or even the chief among them, yet outside of jurisdiction or oversight over them. For he does not conclude himself from the fullness of Pontifical power, nor does he ordain anyone at his own discretion into the vacant place; indeed, he does not even segregate or name those from whom the election ought to be made: for this is reported to have been done by a common voice, verse 23, just as they asked God by common prayer that He might deign to choose from those two who were segregated, the one who should receive the Apostleship, and the same one whom the lot divinely indicated, they added to the others. And therefore the Greek Fathers Chrysostom, Theophylact, and Oecumenius note there the prudent moderation of Peter, not claiming for himself authority and power, but wishing the deliberation to be common.

of the living] 'Chai', the most ancient surname of God, as we learn in Genesis 16:14, which it appears the Jews used frequently below in 26:63, Romans 9:26, 2 Corinthians 3:3, chapter 6:16, 1 Thessalonians 1:9, 1 Timothy 3:15, chapter 4:10, Hebrews 3:12, chapter 9:14, chapter 10:31.

chapter 12:22. But it seems that by that name the true God is distinguished from the gods of the Gentiles, who in reality did not live, but were the inventions of men. See Acts 14:15.

Latin:

Vers. 16. Σίμων Πέτρος] Quem os Apostolorum non male vocant Chrysostomus & Augustinus. Vide Joh. VI. 63. Videtur autem arripuisse sermonem magis διὰ τὸ πρό- θυμον quod in eo ubique elucet, quam jure προστασίας ob ea quæ narrantur infra XIIX. 1. atque aliis in locis. Quare quod in recensu Apostolorum additur illi nomen primi, hoc est πρωτεύοντος, credibile est esse πρόληψιν: quia cum ista scriberentur, eum honorem obtinebat, quod ex loco Act. I. 15. aliisque ita manifestum puto, ut extra con- troversiam poni debeat.

Agnoscit Grotius non posse ex eo, quod hic re- spondet aliorum nomine Petrus, super alios autorita- tem ac potestatem concludi, quod à Papistis fieri so- let. Videtur, inquit, arripuisse sermonem magis διὰ τὸ πρόθυμον, quod in eo ubiq; elucet, quam jure προστα- σίας ob ea quæ narrantur infra XVIII.1. atq; aliis in locis. Cæterum quod nihilominus censet Grotius, Petrum obtinuisset in alios potestatem, quia tribuitur illi nomen primi in recensu Apostolorum Matth. X. eumque honorem ipsum tunc habuisse cum ista scribe- rentur, ita manifestum putat, ut extra controver- siam poni debeat, in eo vehementer fallitur. Unde e- nim id manifestum? Contrarium potius ita mani- festum dici debebat. Quia uti nuspiam illa super a- lios Apostolos potestas in Scripturis comparet, ita contra occurrunt multa, quæ eandem luculenter ipsi derogant. Illud primi nomen non idem esse, quod πρῶτος ad Matth. X. jam monitum est, & fic sine probatione dicitur, ideoq; eadem facilitate rejicitur, qua asseritur. Act. I. 15. Petrus orationem habet ad alios discipulos, ac proponit punctum de supplendo loco Judæ, vel electione novi Apostoli, non ut caput Apostolorum, cujus dignitatis ibi nul- lum est vestigium, sed ut primus ratione ordinis, aut etiam præcipuus inter ipsos, extra tamen jurisdi- ctionem aut ἐπισκοπήν in ipsos. Non enim conclu- dit ipse ex plenitudine potestatis Pontificalis, nec or- dinat aliquem pro arbitrio in locum vacantem, i- mo nec segregat, aut denominat eos, è quibus ele- ctio fieri debeat: hoc enim commune voce factum refertur v. 23. quemadmodum communi prece Deum rogabant, ut è duobus illis segregatis elige- re dignetur, qui accipiat Apostolatum, eundem- que quem fors divinitus indicabat, cæteris ad- jungebant. Ideoque notant ibi Græci Patres Chrysostomus, Theophylactus, & Oecumenius pruden- tem Petri moderationem non vendicantis sibi autori- tatem & potestatem, sed volentis esse communem de- liberationem.

τῦ ζῶντος] חי cognomen Dei antiquissimum, ut discimo Gen. XVI. 14. quo Judæos frequenter usos apparet infra XXVI.63. Rom. IX. 26. 2. Cor. III. 3. c. VI. 16. 1. Thess. I. 9. 1. Tim. III.15. c. IV. 10. Hebr. III.12. c. IX.14. c. X.31.

c.XII.22. Videtur autem eo nomine Deus verus discerni à Diis gentium, qui revera non vivebant, sed hominum e- rant commenta. Vide Act. XIV. 15.

## 16:17
Verse 17. Simon Bar-Jona] Just as Simon is without doubt Simeon, as that name is still written in the second epistle of Peter, so 'Bariona', as has been rightly demonstrated by others from a comparison of other passages, is equivalent to 'Bariōana', with the guttural letter worn away in the manner of that age, there an 'ayin' here a 'cheth'. Thus in Luke 3:30, 'Iōnan' seems to be 'Jochanan'. But I think the name of Bar-Jona is added here for no other reason than that he was commonly called so before he gave himself to the discipline of Christ: for it was the custom among the Hebrews that a patronymic was added to a somewhat common name for the sake of distinction, as can be seen in the Old Testament in many places and in these books somewhere, as above 10:3, below 23:35, Mark 2:14, John 6:42. But as often as we read that a name was changed for someone, there we see mention made of both the former and the subsequently given name, so that the distinction may appear: as in Genesis 17:5 and 32:28. Following that example, when Christ first bestowed a new name upon Peter, He mentions the old one, as is in John 1:42, 'You are Simon the son of Jona, you shall be called Cephas.' Christ repeats this here, as He is about to give the reason for the changed name.

that flesh and blood has not revealed it to you] Flesh and blood, as often as they are opposed to God, signify man in Hebraism. Thus Paul, Galatians 1:16, after the revelation made to him by God, denies that he conferred with flesh and blood, that is, with any man. Christ shows by this opposition that the other things which the Apostles had said were commonly bruited about concerning Christ are the inventions of men: but that which the Apostles were professing through Peter is the very truth now revealed by God the Father as if in advance, to be revealed shortly through the Spirit.

By flesh and blood it is opposed to God or the Spirit, as here to the revelation of the Spirit; not so much man is signified simply, as the corrupt nature of man, or even human frailty. Which we also judge to be the case in this passage. For the natural man does not understand the things that are of the Spirit of God, I Cor. II, verse 14; it is not to be learned from flesh and blood or corrupt reason, but solely from divine revelation, what is to be believed concerning Christ. The revelation of flesh and blood is that which nature, left to itself without the dictation of the Spirit, attains. But the revelation of the heavenly Father, which we have through the Holy Spirit, which exceeds the grasp of carnal reason, and can neither be investigated by reason, nor apprehended, without the grace of the Holy Spirit. Moreover, that that truth was only now at last revealed, and indeed as it were in advance, that Jesus is the Christ the Son of God, unless it be restricted to the individual human nature of Christ, is openly false: For even in the Old Testament it had been made manifest concerning the Messiah, that he is the Son of God, and it was publicly proclaimed from Heaven, Matth. III. 16, and preached by John, and announced and confirmed by Jesus himself when he was asked, Matth. XI.

Latin:

Vers. 17. Σίμων βαριωνᾶ] Sicut Σίμων haud dubie est שמעון Συμεὼν, quomodo etiamnum id nomen scribitur in Petri secunda, ita βαριωνᾶ ut ex collatione aliorum loco- rum recte ab aliis est demonstratum, valet βαριωανᾶ detrita more ejus sæculi litera gutturis, ibi ע hic ח. Ita Lucæ III. 30. Ἰωνᾶν videtur esse יוחנן. Nomen autem Barionæ non alia de causa hic adjectum reor, quam quod ita vulgo appel- lari soleret antequam se in Christi disciplinam daret: moris enim erat apud Hebræos ut nomini paulo communiori dis- criminis gratia adderetur πατρωνυμικὸν, ut videre est in ve- teri fœdere multis locis & in his libris alicubi, ut supra X. 3. infra XXIII. 35. Marc. II. 14. Job. VI. 42. Quoties autem nomen alicui mutatum legimus, ibi videmus & prioris & postea dati nominis fieri mentionem, ut discrimen appare- at: ut Gen. XVII. 5. & XXXII. 28. Ad id exemplum Chri- stus cum primum novum nomen Petro inderet, meminit veteris, ut apud Johannem est I. 42. σὺ εἶ Σίμων ὁ υἱὸς Ἰωνᾶ, σὺ κληθήσῃ κηφᾶς. Id Christus hic repetit, quippe rationem redditurus mutati nominis.

ὅτι σὰρξ κῂ αἷμα ὐκ ἀπεκάλυψέ σοι] Caro & sanguis quoties Deo opponuntur, hominem significant in Hebræi- smo. Ita Paulus Gal. I. 16. post revelationem sibi à Deo fa- ctam negat se contulisse consilia cum carne & sanguine, id est, cum homine quoquam. Ostendit Christus hac opposi- tione, cætera quæ Apostoli dixerant vulgo de Christo ja- ctari, esse commenta hominum: illud vero quod Apostoli per Petrum profitebantur, esse ipsissimam veritatem nunc à Deo Patre velut in antecessum revelatam, brevi per spi- ritum revelandam.

Per carnem & sanguinem cum Deo vel Spiritui opponitur, ut hic revelationi spiritus, non tam ho- mo significatur simpliciter, quam hominis corrupta natura, aut etiam humana fragilitas. Quod hoc lo- co etiam censemus. Non enim intelligit animalis homo quæ sunt Spiritus Dei I. Cor. II. vers. 14. non à carne & sanguine vel corrupta ratione discendum, sed unice è divina revelatione, quid de Christo credendum. Carnis & sanguinis revelatio est ea, quam natura sibi relicta sine Spiritus dictamine as- sequitur. Patris autem cœlestis revelatio, quam per Sp. S. habemus, quæ rationis carnalis captum ex- cedit, nec indagari ratione potest, vel apprehen- di, citra Sp. S. gratiam. Cæterum revelatam nunc demum esse veritatem illam & quidem velut in an- tecessum, quod Jesus sit Christus Filius Dei, nisi re- stringatur ad humanæ naturæ Christi individuum, aperte falsum est: Nam & in V. T. de Messia patefa- ctum erat, quod Filius Dei sit, & de Cœlo publice id proclamatum Matth. III. 16. & à Johanne id præ- dicatum, & à Jesu ipso dum rogaretur, annuncia- tum & confirmatum Matth. XI.

## 16:18
Vers. 18. κἀγὼ δὲ] And I in turn, in return for that free confession of yours, reply this to you. A similar locution is in Luke XXII. 28, 29.

Ἐπὶ ταύτῃ τῇ πέτρᾳ] When Christ said this, he did not point to himself, but to Peter with his finger or a nod: for that was appropriate to the purpose of giving the reason for the name imposed. Thus it was said of Abraham: Your name shall be Abraham, because I have made you the father of many nations. To Jacob: Israel shall be your name: for you behave as a prince among angels and men. Thus Christ: You have been named Peter by me, because you will be as a Rock. See Philo on the change of names. But the translator of Matthew well changed the gender of the Hebrew word, because a man could not be called πέτρα without prejudice to the rule of the Greek language, nor did πέτρος customarily signify that which Christ wished to be indicated: namely, such a stone upon which something is accustomed to be built.

οἰκοδομήσω με τὴν ἐκκλησίαν] The word ἐκκλησία, so noble in Christianity, occurs for the first time in this place, which the Syrian very well translates עדה: which signifies, as the teachers of the Hebrews teach us, a gathering not of just anyone, but one that consists of a certain kind of people: whereas קהל denotes a gathering of any kind whatsoever. But these words are accustomed to be mixed in usage, nor did the LXX distinguish them. In Proverbs V, where there is בתוך קהל ועדה, the LXX have ἐν μέσῳ ἐκκλησίας κῂ συναγωγῆς. But in Psalm XXVI. 5, מריעם קהל they translate as ἐκκλησίαν τῶν πονηρευομένων, just as also I Chronicles XIII. 2, לכל קהל ישראל they interpret as τῇ πάσῃ ἐκκλησίᾳ Ἰσραήλ. Again, Leviticus IV. 13, 14, where in the Hebrew there is first עדה then קהל, the LXX in both places placed συναγωγὴ. And the writer of the book which

Ecclesiasticus is called a promiscuous collection, it calls the crowd ἐκκλησίαν ὄχλυ. But for the most part ἐκκλησία is nothing other than the people of Israel, in the way that עֵדָה is taken in the cited passage of Leviticus: thus Stephen uses the word ἐκκλησία in Acts VII. 38. Thus Caleb is said to have received an inheritance ἐν τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ, 1 Macc. II. 56. And in the writer of Ecclesiasticus, λαὸς and ἐκκλησία are placed for the same thing, ch. XXIV. 1 and ch. XLIV. 15; thus the same writer said πᾶσαν ἐκκλησίαν Ἰσραὴλ, ch. L. 15 and 20, and likewise the writer of the Maccabean history in book I, ch. IV. 59 and ch. III. 13; and the tables of the covenant are said to have been recited ἐνώπιον τῆς ἐκκλησίας, ch. XIV. 19, where presently ἐκκλησία is explained by the word δῆμε, v. 21, 85. Nor is there any doubt that this meaning fits this passage very well. For that Israelite people, living in one region, bore the image of the Christian multitude dispersed throughout the whole world. Therefore the Christian multitude is called by the name λαὸς everywhere, as can be seen in Acts XV. 14, Rom. IX. 25, 2 Cor. VI. 16, Tit. II. 14. But, as we have said, λαὸς and ἐκκλησία are the same. Paul, however, excellently illustrates this passage of Christ in 2 Cor. VI. 16: ὑμεῖς γὰρ ναὸς θεῦ ἐστε ζῶντος, καθὼς εἶπεν ὁ θεὸς ὅτι ἐνοικήσω ἐν αὐτοῖς κὶ ἐμπεριπατήσω κὶ ἔσομαι αὐτῶν θεὸς κὶ αὐτοὶ ἔσονταί μοι λαός. For what had been said about the Israelite people, he adapts to the multitude of Christians, and at the same time, by naming them the temple of God, he explains what ὀικοδομῶν is here. Nor do I doubt that he whom Christ addresses here, Peter, looked to these very words of Christ when he says in 1 Epist. II. 5: κὶ αὐτοὶ ὡς λίθοι ζῶντες ὀικοδομεῖσθε οἶκος πνευματικὸς, presently calling the same ones λαὸν εἰς περιποίησιν. Thus Paul calls believers Θεῦ οἰκοδομὴν, 1 Cor. III. 9. But how believers are built upon Peter is not obscure, since they are said by Paul to be ἐποικοδομηθέντες ἐπὶ τῷ θεμελίῳ τῶν ἀποστόλων κὶ τῶν προφητῶν, Eph. II. 20. And in the Apocalypse the city of God is said to have twelve foundations, on which are inscribed the names of the twelve Apostles. For it is no obstacle that elsewhere God is called a Rock, and Christ the only foundation, since it is not new that the same similitudes are accustomed to be used to signify different things in a different way. For Paul also calls himself an architect elsewhere, which office Christ claims for himself here. Nor indeed is the name of rock or foundation attributed to the Apostles otherwise than τὸ σώζειν, Rom. XI. 14. But when Christ says οἰκοδομήσω, he looks to that time when Peter, having obtained most solid faith with the help of the sent Spirit, was the first of all—which Tertullian rightly observes in his book De Pudicitia c. 21, and Basil in Contra Eunomium II—to announce to the Jews (Acts II. 14.) and then to the Gentiles (Acts X and XV. 7) that very thing which he was professing here, namely that Jesus is the Christ and the only-begotten Son of God, after, of course, God had declared this very thing most openly by raising this very Jesus to life: by which most invincible argument Peter proves the truth of this profession of his in the cited passages of Acts. Therefore Christ, shortly after these words were spoken, out of the whole number of the Apostles, wished Peter, with two others who together with Peter are called pillars of the Church in Gal. II. 9, to be a witness as he had been before of the raised daughter of Jairus, in his own resurrection as it were, so then of his own μεταμορφώσεως, which was a presage of future glory: and after the resurrection he commanded all the disciples and Peter by name to go into Galilee, there to see him. And Paul says that Christ appeared to Peter specially even outside the assembly of the Apostles, 1 Cor. XV. 5. Therefore, both Jews and Gentiles believed the resurrection of Jesus, to which it is consequent that he is the Christ and the Son of God, by the common testimony of the Apostles and also by the peculiar testimony of Peter, who confirmed this very testimony of his, scattered through all Judea and through all the διασπορὰν of the Jews, by the holiness of his life, by miracles, and finally even by endured death, and that in the capital city of the world. By this manner Peter was made the Rock or foundation of the Christian people: στερεὰ τῆς πίστεως πέτρα, as Chrysostom speaks. And at the same time it appears how the things that follow cohere with these.

These things are for the dictatorial authority of the Patron and Advocate of the Roman Chair: that when Christ said this, he did NOT designate HIMSELF, but Peter with his finger or a nod. Which is indeed a postulate of the Papists, but not of the Catholics, not of the ancient doctors of the Church. It is to be noted, however, that the question is not whether Peter can be called a foundation of the Church in respect of doctrine just as other Apostles can; but whether Peter, in respect of his person, is that Rock upon which the Church is built, and whether in these words he is constituted the foundation of the Church in place of Christ, and in respect of his office is the head and foundation of Christians, and indeed even of the remaining Apostles? Which the Papists contend and hold as a chief article of faith. But the reason which Grotius brings forward to confirm that is worth nothing, not even a hair. For, he says, it was fitting for the purpose of giving the reason for the name imposed: You are called Peter by me, because you will be as a Rock. He assumes, of course, as a conceded point what is here clearly a point in dispute. For that is in question: whether Christ wished to give the reason for the name in the way that Grotius gave it with the Papists? That, therefore, ought to have been proved most solidly, not simply assumed in that way. For is not the reason for the name given, why he called Simon Peter, namely because he had produced a confession worthy of Peter, and one upon which the whole Church was to be built, as upon an immovable Rock, or because he had confessed the Rock Christ, who is the foundation of the Church? For could not he who, before others and in the name of others, produced a confession about Christ, which was to be placed as a foundation upon which the Church was to be built (because of Christ, whom it embraces), and who had thus confessed Christ, who is the Rock or cornerstone and foundation of the Church, be judged worthy of the name of Peter? Thus indeed did the most ancient Fathers judge, whose judgment is far to be preferred to the κρίσις of this Advocate, or to the gloss of a Pope affecting supreme authority in the Church and desiring to extend his fringe. For they were established outside the partisanship of factions: of whom some say that Christ pointed out himself with his finger or a nod, whom Peter had confessed: some say, which amounts to the same thing, that he looked to the confession issued by Peter, but they do not think that Peter was designated by the Rock, nay, they deny it; or at least they deny that Peter by reason of his person is the Rock, or the foundation of the Church, nor do they make him a foundation, when they do make one, except by reason of his doctrine, as they do the other Apostles; so indeed, that not he, or another of the Apostles, but his Apostolic doctrine, which is common to all, is to be held as the foundation of the Church. All of which things tend to the same point, namely that Christ, whom Peter had confessed, preached in the Gospel, and apprehended by faith, or that doctrine concerning Christ and the confession of Christ, ought to be understood by the Rock, against which the gates of hell cannot prevail. Which Basil of Seleucia explains excellently above others in a sermon on this passage of Matthew: When Christ had named this confession the Rock, he calls him Peter, who was the first of them to confess, granting him this appellation as a badge and monument of his confession. For this is truly the Rock of salvation, this is the edge or base of salvation, this is the wall of faith, this is the foundation of truth; for no one can lay another foundation, etc. Furthermore, in the Papistic reasoning of the name Peter assumed by Grotius, it is supposed that Peter was called so simply from the Rock, which is false. For Peter's fortitude was not natural, but supernatural, and flowing from none but Christ the Rock, who can supply to a man powers above a man: Therefore the Fathers do not say that Simon Peter was called so simply from the Rock, but from Christ the Rock, as Casaubon observes in Exerc. XV. on Baronius's Ecclesiastical Annals, p. 341, whence those words, Thou art Peter, are to be accepted as if the Lord had said, Thou art he whom I have called Peter from the true Rock. But I am the true Rock, whom thou hast just confessed to be the Son of the living God, and upon this Rock, which thou hast confessed, I will build my Church. Which explanation rests upon immovable foundations. For that not Peter, but Christ, or the doctrine and Confession concerning Christ is to be understood, the variation of the name teaches first: for CHRIST does not say, Thou art Peter and upon thee Peter I will build my Church; but with the change name, You are Peter, and upon that rock. Therefore Peter is one thing, but the Rock is another. He does not say upon Peter, but upon the Rock I will build the Church: To which the observation of the Greek Grammarians, noted by Casaubon, contributes, that πέτραν is one thing, and πέτρον another. For πέτραν is a cliff or a huge stone: but πέτρον is a small stone, such as those which are called by the Greeks χερμάδες & χερμάδια, because they fill the hand, which he proves from Homer and Eustathius: of whom the latter notes that πέτραν is a mountain, and πέτρον or λίθον is τὸ τῆς πέτρας ἀποτμηθὲν, a particle cut off from the mountain. He teaches that this grammatical observation is especially appropriate to this passage. For, as Augustine says more than once, and Ambrose pursues in more detail elsewhere, just as a Christian is named from Christ, so Peter is named from the Rock, which is another name for that same Christ. Therefore, the Rock and Peter are not the same. Christ is the cliff, Peter is the stone cut from that cliff. Christ is strength itself and αὐτοδύναμις: Peter is δυνατὸς, strong, because he receives strength from the Rock.

But the evasion and invention of Grotius is vain. The reason, namely, that the interpreter of Matthew changed the gender of the Hebrew word; For it is also falsely assumed that Christ spoke in Hebrew, or that Matthew wrote in Hebrew, since Christ rather spoke in Syriac, and the Evangelist wrote in Greek. Moreover, in the Syriac idiom, which Casaubon notes in the same place, the same distinction holds, as far as the thing itself is concerned; Christ is כפא in the feminine gender: for that word among the Syrians for Rock is of the feminine gender: so that we may understand him to be τὴν αὐτοφυῆ πέτραν, or as the Platonists would say, τὴν αὐτόπετραν, the very origin, I say, of that strength and virtue, which is denoted by the appellation Cepha, and which contains the structure of the universal Church. Peter, with the gender changed, ὁ כפא Cephas, is named as if from Cepha, the Rock. That there is no diversity of gender in the termination is to be attributed to the Syriac language, which expresses the names of men of that form derived from other substantives homonymously, not paronymously, as Greek and Latin generally do.

But Grotius says, in the Greek language, a man could neither be called πέτραν according to the rule of Greek speech, nor did the word πέτρος usually signify what Christ wished to be indicated, namely such a stone upon which something is accustomed to be built. But why could a man not be called πέτρα, since Christ is called the Rock? Or why could the Syrian name Cepha not be retained, which is used elsewhere in the Gospel history? Or why could it not be added, so that it might be clear that the discourse was about Peter, 'upon You, as a rock, I will build the Church,' or some other indication by which it might be noted that the Church was to be built upon Peter! But we assume what Grotius admits, that the name πέτρος does not usually signify such a stone upon which something is accustomed to be built.
