But Christ called Simon Peter, not the Rock: not by giving a surname, nor by naming him metaphorically: what, therefore, is more certain than that Christ did not wish to call Simon such a stone upon which the Church could be built? Since Baronius understands this, he dares to correct the Latin version, which was pronounced authentic at Trent: In Latin, he says, the sentence should be said thus, you are the Rock, and upon this Rock. But he also dared to amend the Greek text of the Holy Spirit, and to describe it thus: You are Cephas and upon this Cephas I will build my Church. Which intolerable audacity of the Innovators, as was fitting, Casaubon chastised. How much more religious, however, was St. Augustine, Retr. lib. I. c. 21, who adhered to the letter of the authentic text: It was not said to Peter, you are the Rock, but you are Peter. But the Rock was Christ, whom Simon confessed, just as the whole Church confesses him, and was called Peter.

Then the force and proper meaning of the word Rock confirms our opinion. Which, placed simply, without doubt stands for the more famous analogate. But it belongs to Christ beyond controversy, in that he is called the Rock by reason of his nature or person, as God, to whom that name צור, which the Greek interpreters are accustomed to render as πέτραν in countless places of the O.T., is attributed, Deut. XXXIII. 3. 1 Sam. XXII. 3. Ps. XXXI. 3. Ps. LXXIII. 26. etc., on account of the immutability of his essence, and by reason of his office, with a relation made to the Church, to which he gives being and endurance, τὸ εἶναι ϰὴ τὸ μένειν ἀσάλευτον, not to denote his own rule, but rather τὸ πάγιον, the firmness of the Church founded in Christ as if on a cliff and Rock: whence he is named the Rock and the foundational stone of the building of the Church, Is. XXII. 16. Ps. CXVIII. Matt. XXI. 41. Luke XX. 17. Acts IV. 2. 1 Pet. II. 16. Eph. II. 20. as the author and preserver of the Church, so that the faithful may know that the Church is a work of unshaken firmness and eternal duration, which rests upon the foundation of the Rock Christ, let them also learn that faith in Christ ought to be firm and immovable, as Chrysostom warns: whence Eusebius, lib. I. Praepar. Evang. says that the Church stands and remains immovable, because Christ pronounced that it stands and is rooted upon the immovable Rock, by his own power. By which name Christ is also called the foundation of the Church, and indeed for that reason, that the Apostle asserts that no other foundation can be laid, 1 Cor. III. 11. because the foundation and the Rock are the same here, since the Church was to be built upon the Rock as a foundation, Matt. VII. Luke VI. However, therefore, Peter and the other Apostles, and indeed even the faithful, may be called rocks and stones on account of the immovable firmness which ought to be in them, and the foundation of the Prophets and Apostles may be called their doctrine, Eph. II. 20, Christ nevertheless is called the foundation and the Rock κατ᾽ ἀντονομασίαν and more principally, whom Augustine therefore called the foundation of foundations in Ps. LXXXI. And therefore he rightly understands here not Peter, but Christ, indicated absolutely by the Rock, from whom the Apostles and the faithful have the fact that they are rocks. Just as Basil the Great, homil. de poenit., warned: Christ is in truth the immovable Rock; but Peter is so on account of the Rock. For Jesus bestows his own dignities upon his own. And Ambrose, L. VI. in Evangel. Lucae: The Rock is Christ, who also did not deny the grace of this name to his disciple, so that he himself might also be Peter, because he has the solidity of constancy and the firmness of faith from the Rock. Strive therefore that you too may be a Rock. And so do not seek the Rock outside yourself, but within yourself. And thus also Leo the Great, Bishop of Rome, in his Epistle to Flavian, says that Peter drew both the solidity of his virtue and of his name from the Principal Rock. And Gregory the Great, likewise Bishop of Rome, in his Register, book VI, Epistle 37: He drew the firmness of his mind into his name, so that Peter might be called from the Rock. And in his explanation of the VII penitential Psalms: The Mediator of God and men himself says to the prince of the Apostles: You are Peter, and upon this Rock I will build my Church. For the Mediator of God and men himself is the Rock, from whom Peter also received his name, and upon whom he said he would build his Church. To this must be added the ordinary gloss on this passage: You are Peter, that is to say, a Rock from me, yet in such a way that I retain for myself the dignity of the foundation.

Thirdly, the demonstrative particle ἐπὶ ταύτῃ τῇ πέτρᾳ designates not Peter, who was never called by the name Rock; but him whom Peter had confessed, or that very confession which he had just then uttered; as Augustine in his 1st Epistle of John. What is, upon this rock I will build my Church? Upon this faith: upon that which was said: Thou art Christ the Son of God, upon this rock I will found my Church. For the pronoun ταύτῃ is either anaphoric and has the force of a relative, or deictic and demonstrative: If it is a relative, it is referred either to the preceding confession, or to the word Petra included in the preceding utterance Petrus; because those words, Thou art Peter, signify here, the name of Peter was given to you by the Rock Christ, as was done in John VIII. 44: If it is demonstrative, it is therefore rightly understood of Christ: since in all languages demonstrative pronouns are sometimes most elegantly understood of the person speaking, as we have an example in John II. 19. Thus, therefore, upon this rock it would not be absurd, but rather elegant, to have said it for upon me, as Augustine observed: Upon me, he says, I will build you, not me upon you, with our Lord assisting his voice with a gesture, which the Greeks call speaking deictically, and they call the habit of the speaker. And so also the gloss of the Canon law to the Canon, thus the Lord, distinct. XIX. Upon this Rock. By this expression I do not believe the Lord demonstrated anything other than these words, which Peter answered to Christ, when he said: Thou art Christ the Son of the living God, because upon that article of faith the Church is founded. Therefore, the Lord founded the Church upon himself.

Fourthly, such is the condition of the predicate that it by no means fits Peter, but ought to be claimed solely for Christ: He, therefore, is to be understood by the Rock, upon whom, as a foundation, like an immovable rock, the Church was to be built. But it was not upon Peter, but upon Christ as an immovable foundation like a rock that it was to be built. For Peter could by no means sustain the whole mass of the Church, nor could any mere man: and since it must be sustained until the end of the age, how will that fit Peter, or any one man? For what they say about the successors of Peter is a mere fiction, and does not fit the passage: If this was said to Peter for the reason of the changed name, which they themselves want, what is this to others, upon whom the name of Peter has not been imposed? And where is it handed down in the Scriptures that the same thing pertains to the successors of Peter? Will there not thus be many rocks, who therefore is called ἐπὶ ταύτῃ τῇ πέτρᾳ, and is expressly designated as the one rock in number? And whom does Peter have as successors, in that they sustain the Church like a rock? Christ designated none, the Apostles know of none, the whole of Scripture knows of none. It hands down that the Apostle Peter was like the rest: but in the Apostleship, neither he nor the other Apostles had successors. Concerning an ecumenical Pontificate, either entrusted to Peter or promised to the successors of Peter, there is not even a jot in the Scriptures. Let the vain fictions of men, therefore, depart in a matter of such great moment concerning the salvation of the Church.

Fifthly, the Church, which Christ calls his own, is not only that which was to be built in the New Testament, but that which has been built since the foundation of the world; the Church of Christ is the assembly of the faithful and the elect, as much triumphant in heaven as it is militant on earth. But it is very absurd that Peter should be the rock upon which the Church of the Old Testament and the assembly of the elect triumphant in heaven should lean: which is, however, most true of Christ. And therefore this cannot be understood of Peter, but must necessarily be understood of Christ.

Sixthly, he is understood by the Rock who, by the sustaining of the Church, ensures that the gates of hell cannot prevail against it. But Peter cannot ensure this, but Christ alone ensures it by the sustaining of the Church. Therefore, not Peter, but Christ alone is understood here by the rock. Seventhly, the passage 1 Cor. III. 11 is to be compared, from which it may be concluded: he is to be understood by the rock who is the foundation of the Church. But Peter is not the foundation of the Church, but Christ is, as the Apostle testifies, who acknowledged no other foundation besides that which is laid, which is Christ Jesus. Which St. Augustine urges in De fide et operibus c. XVI, and indeed the Roman Bishop Gregory the Great himself, l. XXVIII. moral. c. 6. When in sacred eloquence it is said not foundations, but in the singular number foundation, no one else but the Lord himself is designated, by whose divine power the hearts of our weakness are strengthened, of whom Paul says: no one can lay another foundation besides that which is laid, which is Christ Jesus. Eighthly, the Apostles built the Church upon Christ alone, not upon Peter, as ministerial Architects, 1 Corinth. III. 11. Peter himself built the faithful upon Christ alone, as a foundation, 1 Pet. II. 4. Ninthly, there is no medium given by which the Church is united with Peter, or Peter with each of the faithful in the Church, as a foundation and the building built upon it must be united. Tenthly, not without reason does Mr. Dr. Seb. Schmied in Colleg. Bibl. post. ad h. l. p. 291 note the connection of the words v. 17 and 18 and that the speech rises, nay rather I say to you: i.e. Nay rather, concerning that confession of yours, I not only say that flesh and blood did not reveal it to you, but my Father who is in heaven; but I also assert further that you are Peter through this, and that upon this rock, that is, upon that confession, I am about to build my Church, etc. Eleventhly, let the testimonies and suffrages of the ancient and more recent Church now be added, which, if you except the Roman Synagogue, and that a new one, not an ancient one, and one that sails for its own honor and advantage, with unanimous consent [speak] not of the dominion of Peter, or even of an ecumenical Pontificate, not of the universal Church to be built upon Peter the Pontiff, but of the doctrine and confession of Peter concerning Christ, and the object of the same, that Rock and cornerstone of the whole Church of the Old and New [Testament]. The Church, militant and now triumphant in heaven, has received and interpreted these words of Christ, who is the unique foundation upon which it leans, by whom it is sustained and cherished, not even the Roman Bishops themselves being excluded from this number of witnesses: which consensus is testified to from the Greek Fathers by Epiphanius, Gregory of Nyssa, Basil the Great, Chrysostom, Basil of Seleucia, Theodoret, Theophylact, Oecumenius, and from the Latins by Tertullian, Hilary, Ambrose, Jerome, Augustine, Paulinus, Victor of Antioch, Bede, and Hincmar, Bishop of Reims, in the year 800, Haymo, Bishop of Halberstadt, around the year of Christ 850, and others. But among the Roman Bishops, Eutychianus around the year of Christ 275, Leo the Great in the year 440, Felix III in the year 483, Felix IV in the year 526, Gregory the Great in the year 590, Leo II in the year 682, Adrian I around the year 772, Nicholas I in the year 858, Stephen VI in the year 886. Nicholas II in the year 1059, also Gregory VII, Hildebrand, the chief assertor of Pontifical Dominion in the year 1073, and those who followed him, Innocent II in the year 1130, Adrian IV in the year 1154, whom our blessed Gerhard produced in the Confessio Catholica, book 1, part 2, chapter 2. To these are added entire Councils, even of later times: such as the Council of Soissons in the year 909. Which Church genera- letter from one head, Christ, built upon the rock, that is, upon the confession of Peter: Trier, 1549. The foundation of true faith in Jesus Christ is that rock of which our Savior spoke, upon which the Church is to be built. Nor do the glosses of the Bibles received in the Papacy, whether ordinary or interlinear, or the approved Interpreters, Doctors, and Scholastics, or the glosses of Canon law deny this: one may see primarily Hugo de Caro in his postil on this passage, Albert the Great in his commentary on this passage, Thomas Aquinas 2. 2. q. 174. art. 6, Durand in his Rationale Divinorum Officiorum book I, chapter 7, Nicolaus Lyranus on this passage, Nicolaus Gorranus on this passage, Dionysius the Carthusian on this passage, Guilhelmus on this passage, Gabriel Biel in lecture 22 on the Canon, who flourished before Blessed Luther: to whom also those contemporary with Blessed Luther and those after him give their support, Erasmus, Ludovicus Vives, the author of the Oneris Ecclesiae, Johannes Ferus, Alfonsus Salmeron. Jacob Schopperus, and others likewise brought forward by Blessed Gerhard in the aforementioned place. Let us note at least two from those who wrote before Luther, and as many from those after, such as Antoninus, Archbishop of Florence, around the year of Christ 1459, part 1, History, title 5, chapter 1, on the words: 'You are Peter.' Not pointing to you, but to me, whom you have confessed, upon this confessed truth; and Alphonsus Tostatus, Bishop of Avila, around the year 1440, on this passage: 'It is not true that the Church is founded upon Peter, etc.' Johannes Arboreus, in his Theosophia, book V, chapter 5, argues at length that the Church is founded upon the Rock (Christ) and not upon Peter: Alphonsus à Castro, in the preface to his book on heresies: 'Faith is the basis and foundation of the whole Christian structure, and upon it, as upon a certain most firm Rock, God has founded His Church, etc.' Compare on this passage the 'Sheep's Skin' of Nicolaus Hunnius, § 541 and following. Furthermore, Casaubon reviews and reconciles the opinions of the Fathers regarding this passage thus: 'We shall briefly indicate,' he says, 'the principal opinions of the Fathers on this matter. Let the first be of those who wished every one of the faithful to be designated by the name of Rock: which is that of Origen in his tract on Matthew 1, Gregory of Nyssa in his book on Perfection, and Ambrose in book VI on Luke. Let the second opinion be of those Fathers who believed that by the appellation of Rock, the Lord understood Peter's faith, or the confession made here by Peter. Chrysostom expressly on this passage: ἐπὶ ταύτῃ τῇ πέτρᾳ, τουτέστι, τῇ πίστει τῆς ὁμολογίας. Theophylact likewise: αὕτη ἡ ὁμολογία ἣν ὡμολόγησας, θεμέλιον μέλλει εἶναι τῶν πιστευόντων. This confession which you have confessed will be the foundation of believers. In agreement with these are Augustine in his first tract on the Epistle of John, tract X, and Basil of Seleucia in his sermon on this pericope of Matthew. The third was the opinion of those who thought that by the Rock, Peter himself was to be understood properly, whose testimonies occur frequently in many places. The fourth was of those who wish the true Rock and the true foundation of the Church to be understood as Christ Himself: how the word 'Rock' is to be taken in this place is taught accurately and copiously by the great Augustine in many places, such as in his tract on John CXXIV, on the Trinity, book II, chapter XVII, and much more fully in his sermon XIII on the words of the Lord according to Matthew, and in his Retractations, book I, chapter 21. Many other Fathers feel the same as Augustine; but let Paul be the example of all the Fathers, than whom a more faithful interpreter of the mind and words of the Lord cannot even be imagined. Now the words of Paul are 1 Corinthians 3:11: 'No one can lay another foundation besides that which is laid, which is Jesus Christ.' Yet this oracle of Paul does not prevent the previous interpretations of the Fathers from being correct and orthodox. For these four opinions do not differ among themselves in the things themselves, but only in manner and reason. Christ is indeed the primary efficient cause of the building of the Church, from whom, as from a unique fountain, all power arises by which He institutes, protects, and makes the Church endure. While he lived, Peter was a secondary efficient cause, as an Apostle and the first of the Apostles: whom Paul says are in this work of Christ συνεργούς, and as it were, partners in the work: but after his death, the doctrine of Peter, which he had taught while alive by voice and writing, which is often called Peter metonymically in the writings of the Fathers, both was, and is today, and will always be, the most firm foundation of the Church. Faith is the instrumental cause: each one of the faithful is the material cause of the temple of God, which is built, says Augustine in his Enchiridion to Laurentius, from those whom God makes, not having been made. Who would deny that all these expositions of the pious fathers are pious and orthodox? For they all agree in one, and are so akin to one another, that one may observe everywhere that the same fathers now follow this, now that, of the aforementioned expositions, embrace it, and adapt it to their purpose.

Finally, the Papistic gloss can also be refuted from the confession of Grotius: for first, on page 292, he explains this οἰκοδομὴν: but how believers are built upon Peter is not obscure, since they are said by Paul to be ἐποικοδομηθέντες ἐπὶ τῷ θεμελίῳ τῶν Ἀποστόλων & τῶν προφητῶν, Ephesians 2:20. And in the Apocalypse, the city of God is said to have twelve foundations, on which are inscribed the names of the twelve Apostles. For if Peter is called the foundation of the Church in no other way than the rest of the Apostles, then certainly Peter is not the foundation of the Church in the sense that he is the unique vicar of Christ and the head of the rest of the Apostles. For thus there would be twelve vicars and as many heads: and he himself would be his own head. Secondly, the name of rock or foundation is attributed to Peter and the other Apostles in no other way than τὸ σώζειν, Romans 11:14, as Grotius admits. But this is not attributed to them because they are heads of the Church, but because ministerially and by the power of their doctrine, which they preach, they save others: which there is no doubt also pertains to other ministers of the word, 1 Timothy 4:16. Thirdly, Grotius admits here that other Apostles are called pillars of the Church with Peter, Galatians 2:9, which, contradicting himself, he had previously denied at Matthew 10:1, and again denies at Galatians 2:9. Since, therefore, those Apostles, James and John, are by no means established in the place of Christ as heads of the Church, neither is it to be attributed to Peter, who is not a pillar of the Church in any other sense. Fourthly, Grotius says that Peter was made a Rock or foundation of the people of Christ in this way, because, with the help of the Spirit sent, having obtained a most solid faith, he first announced to the Jews alone, Acts 2:14, and then also to the Gentiles, Acts 10 and 15:7, that very thing which he confessed here, namely that Jesus is the Christ and the only-begotten Son of God, and because both Jews and Gentiles believed both by the common testimony of the Apostles and also by the peculiar testimony of Peter, who confirmed this very testimony of his, scattered throughout all Judea and throughout all the διασπορὰν of the Jews, by the holiness of his life, by miracles, and finally even by the death he endured, and that indeed in the city that is the prince of the world. But the other Apostles obtained a faith no less solid than Peter, when the Holy Spirit was sent upon them, and they no less than others announced to the Jews and Gentiles, through the word, Jesus Christ the only-begotten Son of God. The Jews and Gentiles believed no less through others than through Peter, and others no less than Peter confirmed their doctrine by the holiness of their life and by miracles, and finally even by the death they endured. But what do those things contribute to that which is the point at issue here, namely that Peter was established in the place of Christ as the head and foundation of the Apostles and of the whole Church? Moreover, the fact that he himself was the first to preach to the Jews in Acts 2 and to the Gentiles in chapter 10, if it counts for anything for the prerogative of order, certainly contributes nothing to demonstrating an ecumenical Pontificate of Peter: nor does it contribute anything to that The martyrdom endured at Rome is sufficient for the moment; for it was not on that account that Rome was the head of the whole Church, because it underwent martyrdom at Rome. Indeed, Paul would also have been the head of the Church, who they say likewise underwent martyrdom at Rome. To say nothing of the fact that among the Papists it is not entirely beyond doubt whether Peter endured death at Rome: of whom William, the tutor of Wycliffe, taught that Peter had not even ever seen the city, while Michael Cesenas, Lyranus, and Mantuanus professed that he was not bishop there, according to Wolf, T. I. memor. p. 23, and Clement, L. VII. Constit. cap. XLV., handed down that Linus was appointed Bishop of the Roman Church not by Peter, but by Paul: Cf. Salmero in Epist. ad Tucc. tom. ult p. 413.

Πύλαι ἅδε ὀ κατισχύσωσιν ἀυτῆς] I am very surprised that this passage is explained with such consensus regarding the machinations of the Devil or even of the wicked. For I nowhere find the word ἅδε, neither among the Hellenists nor among the writers of the New Testament, in any other meaning than that of death, or the sepulcher, or the state after death, all of which are related to one another. It has been demonstrated by many interpreters, whom the Apostles follow in this part, that שאול is translated as ἅδης. ἅδης signifies death in Wisdom 1:4, Ecclesiasticus 9:17, and several times in the history of the Maccabees: where you may also find προπέμπειν ἐἰς τὸν ἅδην, which is familiar to Greek poets: just as the writer of Baruch also said καταβαίνειν ἐἰς ἅδε, which is likewise most customary among the Greeks. The same word designates the state of the dead rather than death itself in Ecclesiasticus 41:7. You may often find both θάνατον and ἅδην joined together, both in that former and in the latter meaning, as in Isaiah 28:15. Ecclesiasticus 48:5 and chapter 51:8, Wisdom 2:1, and no less in the Apostolic books, as 1 Cor. 15:55, Rev. 1:12, chapter 20:13, 14. Moreover, in the same Apocalypse 6:8, ἅδης is said to follow θάνατον, where θάνατος signifies the act of dying itself, and ἅδης the following state, which itself is also very often called θάνατος. It is well known that in Acts 2:27 and 31 the word ἅδε corresponds to the Hebrew שאול. But above, at 11:23 and Luke 10:15, we showed that it is a figurative expression, which denotes the greatest miseries by the name of death or the sepulcher: just as grave dangers are also called by the word ἅδε. There remains the single passage Luke 16:23, where he who is ἐν βασάνοις is said to be ἐν τῷ ἅδῃ. But not even there does ἅδης by itself signify τὸ βασανιστήριον, as we shall show when we come to it. However, I think there is no one who has read it who would think the word ἅδε is used for the seat or state of the fallen angels, or for the wicked leading this mortal life. Nor is it a difficult conjecture what πύλαι ἅδε signify here, since the same expression is found in the song of King Hezekiah which is in Isaiah, 38, where in the Hebrew it is אלכה בשערי שאול and in the Greek πορεύσομαι ἐν πύλαις ἅδε. Moreover, in the same place, ἡ γῆ ζώντων is opposed to τῷ ἅδῃ. Thus also Psalm 9:14 and 107:18, and Wisdom 16:13. πύλαι ἅδε are nothing other than what the writer of the book of Wisdom called βασίλειον ἅδε: κράτος θανάτε Heb. 2:14. Just as the Greeks used πέμπειν εἰς ἅδε, καταβαίνειν εἰς ἅδε, so too they said πύλας ἅδε, having been taught by the Syrians, whose expressions are everywhere expressed by Homer, as has been rightly noted by most learned men. To the most well-known passage of Homer can be added that of the old comic poet:

Χρυσὸς δ᾽ ἀνοίγει πάντα κ᾽ ἀἰδε πύλας.

Et ille incerti autoris:

Φύντα δ᾽ ὅπως ὤκιςα πύλας ἀίδαο περῆσαι.

You may find ἅδε πύλας both in the Alcestis of Euripides and in the Agamemnon of Aeschylus. Themistius, praising Theodosius because he had freed those who had offended against him from death, says ἐπαναγαγεῖν εἰς τὸν ἥλιον ἐκ τῶν πυλῶν τᾶ Ἀχέροντος: and afterwards: εἴδομεν ἀνθρώπες ἐν τῶν τῶ ἅδε προθύρων εἰς τὸ ζῇν ἐπανιόντας. Pythagoras also, as Laertius recounts, said that beans were like ἅδε πύλαις because they produce nothing from themselves. In Plutarch, On Superstition: ἅδε τινες ἀνοίγονται πύλαι βαθεῖαι. Lucian, in Menippus, says that the magi ἀνοίγειν τὲ ἁδὲ τὰς πύλας. Therefore, just as it was said by Paul concerning Christ the head, θάνατος ἀυτᾶ κ ἔτι κυριεύει Rom. 6:9, and by Peter, ἐκ ἦν δύνατον κρατεῖσθαι ἀυτὸν ὑπὸ τῶ θανάτε, Acts 2:24, so here it is promised to the body of Christ, that is, the people of believers, that death itself, whose kingdom is greatest and insatiable, will not have such strength that it can hold them under its law and power. For he who believes passes from death into life, John 5:24, chapter 11:25, 26, now indeed by hope and confidence, but in the event someday when the last enemy will be triumphed over, when it will be permitted to say πῶ σε ἅδη τὸ νῖκος 1 Cor. 15:55, when Christ shall πα- ραςήσῃ ἑαυτῷ ἔνδοξον this same Church of which we are treating here, Eph. 5:25. Unless perhaps the Church is treated here universally, not partially, and its perpetual duration is promised according to the saying of the Hebrews כל כנסיא שהי לשם שם יים סופה

להתקים Omnis Ecclesia quæ sit propter Deum, firma permanebit. Compare Acts 5:39. In this sense Chrysostom interprets ἅδε πύλας as dangers closest to destruction, in the oration ὅτι Θεὸς ὁ χρησὸς. Thus πρὸς πύλας ἅδε καθεςῶτας Macc. 3.

Grotius takes these things concerning liberation from the state of death; that death itself, whose kingdom is greatest and insatiable, will not have such strength that it could hold them under its law and power. Which gloss he borrowed from the Socinians and Arminians. For thus Ostorodus explained it in Instit. cap. XLII., with Socinus himself leading the way in the tract on the Church, p. 69, that by hell is designated the state of the dead: and that the meaning is that those who are Christ's cannot be held eternally in the state of the dead. The Arminians, Apol. c. XXII., wish that nothing is promised to the Church dwelling here on earth, but that something is promised after death to the Church which is on earth and remains until death, whose ςρεβλότης has been discussed in the refuted Socinianism and Arminianism. It is too manifest that this passage treats of the Church acting in these lands, built upon the immovable Rock, Christ, to whom the keys of binding and loosing have been granted: and therefore these things are wrongly snatched away to the state after this life, nor is it a matter of death, the state of death, or hell, but of the gates of hell, that is, of the kingdom, force, and strength, and of infernal tyranny and power, just as gates were once the place of judgments and the fortifications placed there: and thus it is hinted that no infernal force and power will prevail against the Church of Christ, and will storm it, as Origen, Epiphanius, Cyril, Jerome, Ambrose, Euthymius, and Isidore interpret. And Grotius acknowledges that this passage is explained by great consensus concerning the machinations of the Devil, or even of the wicked. He says that he is indeed very surprised, because he does not find the word ἅδε either among the Hellenists or among the writers of the N.T. in any other meaning than either death (Wisdom 1:4, Ecclesiasticus 9:17) or the sepulcher or the state after death (Ecclesiasticus 51:7); no one has ever read the word ἅδε concerning the seat or state of fallen angels, or concerning the wicked living this mortal life. But here it is not the word ἅδης that is being discussed, but what πύλαι ἅδε signify. And what is infernal power other than the power of the Devil, the prince of the infernal regions? Now, indeed, the ancients noted that by the word ἅδης or hell, the Devil is also signified by metonymy, as in Job 26:6, Proverbs 30:16, Revelation 1:18, chapter 20:14, where a comparison with verse 10 confirms that sense: hell, that is, the Devil, was cast into the lake of fire. Concerning the place of the Devils and the damned, various things are observed. Numbers 16:33, Deuteronomy 33:12, Psalm 49:15, Psalm 56:16. Proverbs 26:20, Isaiah 5:14, Hosea 13:14. That passage is certainly manifest in 16:23 ff. Compare Matthew 25:41, 2 Peter 2:4. But in the end, Grotius does not trust his gloss much, adding these words: Unless perhaps it is treated here of the Church universally, not partially, and its perpetual duration is promised according to the saying of the Hebrews: Every Church which is for the sake of God will remain firm. Compare Acts 5:39.

Latin:

Vers. 18. κἀγὼ δὲ] Ego vicissim pro illa tua libera confes- sione hoc tibi repono. Similis locutio Luc. XXII. 28. 29.

Ἐπὶ ταύτῃ τῇ πέτρᾳ] Christus cum hoc diceret, non se- metipsum, sed Petrum digito, aut nutu designavit: id enim conveniebat proposito reddendæ rationis impositi nomi- nis. Ita de Abrahamo dictum: Nomen tuum erit Abraham, quia patrem multarum gentium te constitui. Jacobo: Israelet- rit nomen tuum: nam ut principem te geris apud Angelos & homines. Ita Christus: Petrus à me nominatus es, quia eris quasi Petra. Vide Philonem de Nominum mutatione. Be- ne autem Matthæi interpres vocis Hebrææ genus mutavit, quia neque vir πέτρα dici salva Græci sermonis regula po- terat, neque πέτρος id usitate significabat, quod Christus volebat indicatum: nempe saxum tale super quo aliquid ædificari soleat.

οἰκοδομήσω με τὴν ἐκκλησίαν] ἐκκλησίας vox adeo nobi- lis in Christianismo hoc primum loco occurrit, quam Syrus optime vertit עדה: quod significat, ut nos docent Hebræo- rum magistri, cœtum ἐκ τῶν τυχόντων sed eum qui ex certo con- stet hominum genere: cum קהל cœtum qualemcunq; denotet. Sed solent istæ voces in usu permisceri, neq; LXX. distinxerunt. Proverbioū V. ubi est בתוך קהל ועדה, LXX. habent ἐν μέσῳ ἐκκλησίας κῂ συναγωγῆς. At in Psal. XXVI. 5. מריעם קהל vertunt ἐκκλησίαν τῶν πονηρευομένων, ut & I. Paral. XIII. 2. לכל קהל ישראל interpretan- tur τῇ πάσῃ ἐκκλησίᾳ Ἰσραήλ. Rursus Levit. IV. 13. 14. ubi in Hebræo est primum עדה deinde קהל LXX. utro- que loco posuerunt συναγωγὴ. Et Scriptor libri qui

Ecclesiasticus vocatur collectionem promiscuam turbæ vocat ἐκκλησίαν ὄχλυ. Sed plerumque ἐκκλησία nihil aliud est quàm populus Israël, quomodo עֵדָה sumitur di- cto Levitici loco: ita vocem ἐκκλησίας usurpat Stephanus Actor. VII. 38. Ita Caleb dicitur ἐν τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ accepisse hæreditatem, 1.Macc. II. 56. Et apud Ecclesiastici Scripto- rem pro eodem ponitur λαὸς & ἐκκλησία cap. XXIV. 1. & c. XLIV. 15. ita πᾶσαν ἐκκλησίαν Ἰσραὴλ dixit idem Scriptor cap. L. 15. & 20. itemque Scriptor Maccabaicæ historiæ libro I.c.IV.59. & cap.III.13. & tabulæ fœderis dicuntur re- citatæ ἐνώπιον τῆς ἐκκλησίας cap. XIV. 19. ubi mox ἐκκλησία explicatur voce δήμε v. 21. 85. Neque dubitandum est quin hæc significatio huic loco optime conveniat. Nam populus ille Israëliticus una in regione habitans multitudinis Chri- stianæ per totum orbem dispersæ gessit imaginem. Ideo multitudo Christiana passim λαῦ nomine appellatur, ut vi- dere est Actor.XV. 14. Rom.IX. 25. 2.Cor.VI. 16. Tit.II.14. Idem autem est, ut diximus, λαὸς & ἐκκλησία. Eximie au- tem hunc Christi locum illustrat Paulus 2.Cor. VI. 16.ὑμεῖς γὰρ ναὸς θεῦ ἐστε ζῶντος, καθὼς εἶπεν ὁ θεὸς ὅτι ἐνοικήσω ἐν αὐ- τοῖς κὶ ἐμπεριπατήσω κὶ ἔσομαι αὐτῶν θεὸς κὶ αὐτοὶ ἔσονταί μοι λαός. Nam quod de Israëlitico populo dictum fue- rat, aptat Christianorum multitudini, simulque templum Dei eos nominando explicat, quid hic sir ὀικοδομῶν. Nec dubito quin hæc ipsa Christi verba respexerit ille quem hic Christus alloquitur Petrus, cum dicit 1.Epist.II.5. κὶ αὐτοὶ ὡς λίθοι ζῶντες ὀικοδομεῖσθε οἶκος πνευματικὸς, eosdem mox vocans λαὸν εἰς περιποίησιν. Sic credentes, Θεῦ οἰκοδομὴν vocat Paulus 1.Cor.III.9. quomodo autem super Petro æ- dificentur credentes obscurum non est, cum Paulo iidem dicantur ἐποικοδομηθέντες ἐπὶ τῷ θεμελίῳ τῶν ἀποστόλων κὶ τῶν προφητῶν, Ephes. II.20. Et in Apocalypsi Dei civitas dica- tur habere duodecim fundamenta, in quibus inscripta sint nomina duodecim Apostolorum. Neque enim obstat, quod alibi Deus Petra dicitur, & Christus unicum funda- mentum, cum novum non sit easdem similitudines ad di- versas res diverso modo significandas solere adhiberi. Nam & alibi Paulus se architectum vocat, quod officium Christus hic sibi vindicat. Neque vero aliter petræ aut fundamenti nomen tribuitur Apostolis, quam τὸ σώζειν, Rom XI. 14. Cum autem dicit Christus οἰκοδομήσω, tempus illud respi- cit quo Petrus fidem nactus solidissimam missi Spiritus au- xilio, primus omnium, quod recte observat Tertullianus li- bro de Pudicitia c. 21. & Basilius contra Eunomium II. Ju- dæis (Act. II. 14.) deinde & alienigenis (Act. X. & XV. 7.) erat annuntiaturus id ipsum quod hic profitebatur, nempe Jesum esse Christum & unigenitum Dei filium, postquam ni- mirum Deus hoc ipsum apercissime declaræset hunc ipsum je um in vitam resuscutando: quo invictissimo argumento Petrus hujus suæ professionis veritatem probat dictis Acto- rum locis. Ideo Christus, paulo post hæc dicta, ex omni Apostolorum numero Perrum cum duobus alteris, qui una cum Petro columnæ Ecclesiæ vocantur Gal. II. 9. testem es- se voluit ut antehac excitatæ Jairī filiæ, in sua resurrectionis quasi arDefault, ita tunc suæ μεταμορφώσεως quæ futuræ gloriæ erat præsagium: & post resurrectionem discipulis u- niversis & nominatim Petro imperavit ut in Galilæam irent, ibi ipsum conspecturi. Et Paulus specialiter etiam extra cœtum Apostolorum Christum dicit Petro apparuisse 1. Cor. XV. 5. Resurrectionem igitur Jesu, cui consequens est eum esse Christum & Dei filium, crediderunt & Judæi & gentes tum communi Apostolorum tum peculiari etiam Petri testimonio, qui hoc ipsum suum testimonium sparsum per omnem Judæam, perque omnem Judæorum διασπο- ρὰν, confirmavit vitæ sanctimonia, miraculis, postremo etiam tolerata morte & quidem in urbe mundi principe. Per hunc modum Petrus factus est Petra sive fundamen- tum populi Christiani: στερεὰ τῆς πίστεως πέτρα, ut Chry- sostomus loquitur. Ac simul apparet quomodo quæ se- quuntur cum his cohæreant.

Hæc pro dictatoria autoritate Patronus & Ad- vocatus Romanæ Cathedræ: Christus cum hoc di- ceret NON SEMETIPSVM, sed Petrum digito aut nutu designavit. Quod Pontificiorum quidem αἴτημα est, non autem Catholicorum, non vete- rum Ecclesiæ doctorum. Notandum autem, quod non quæratur, an Petrus similiter ut alii Apostoli doctrinæ ratione fundamentum Ecclesiæ dici queat; sed an Petrus ratione personæ suæ Petrà illa sit, super quam exstructa est Ecclesia, & loco Christi funda- mentum Ecclesiæ his verbis constituatur, ac ra- tione officii, Christianorum, imo etiam Aposto- lorum reliquorum caput & fundamentum sit? quod contendunt & pro fidei articulo præcipuo habent Papistæ. Ratio autem quam illi firman- do Grotius adfert, nullius hili vel pili est. Id enim, inquit, conveniebat proposito reddendæ ra- tionis impositi nominis: Petrus a me nominatus es, quia eris quasi Petra. Nimirum assumit ceu ὁμολο- γούμενον quod hic plane est κρινόμενον. Id enim in quæstione est, anne ita rationem reddere volue- rit nominis Christus, ut cum Pontificiis eam red- didit Grotius? id ergo solidissime probandum e- rat, non simpliciter ita assumendum. Annon enim ratio nominis redditur, cur Petrum dixerit Simo- nem, quod nempe confessionem Petro dignam, eam- que ediderit, super quam ædificanda tota Ecclesia, ceu super immotam Petram, vel quod confessus est Petram Christum, qui fundamentum est Ec- clesiæ! Annon enim qui præ aliis, & aliorum no- mine confessionem de Christo edidit, quæ ceu Petra Ecclesiæ ædificandæ supponenda sit fundamenti loco (ob Christum, quem complectitur,) adeoque Christum, qui Petra vel lapis angularis est & funda- mentum Ecclesiæ, confessus erat, dignus judicari poterat Petri nomine? Ita vero judicarunt Patres antiquissimi, quorum judicium longe præferen- dum Advocati hujus κρίσει, aut Papæ auctoritatem summam in Ecclesia affectantis, & fimbriam suam extendere cupientis glossæ. Illi enim extra par- tium studia constituti fuere: è quibus aliqui Chri- stum semetipsum digito aut nutu demonstrasse, quem confessus erat Petrus: aliqui, quod eodem recidit, confessionem à Petro editam respexisse ajunt non vero Petrum per Petram designatum censent, imo negant; aut certe Petrum ratione personæ Pe- tram, vel fundamentum Ecclesiæ esse, inficiantur, nec nisi ratione doctrinæ suæ, uti reliquos Aposto- los, fundamentum faciunt, cum faciunt; ita nempe, ut non ipse, vel alius Apostolorum, sed ipsius, quæ communis omnium est, doctrina Apostolica habenda sit pro fundamento Ecclesiæ. Quæ omnia eodem tendunt, nimirum Christum, quem confessus erat Petrus, in Evangelio prædi- catum, & fide apprehensum, vel illam de Christo doctrinam & Christi confessionem per Petram in- telligi debere, adversus quam portæ inferorum prævalere non possint. Quod explicat præ aliis eximie Basilius Seleuciensis sermone in hanc Mat- thæi pericopam: Hanc confessionem quum nomi- nasset Christus Petram, Petrum nuncupat eum, qui primus illorum est confessus, donans illi hanc appel- lationem tanquam insigne & monumentum suæ con- fessionis. Hæc enim est revera salutis Petra, hæc salutis crepido sive basis, hic fidei murus, hoc ve- ritatis fundamentum; fundamentum enim aliud nemo potest ponere, &c. Porro in Papistica no- minis Petri ratione a Grotio assumta, Petrum à Petra simpliciter dictum supponitur, quod fal- sum est. Petri enim fortitudo non naturalis fuit, sed supernaturalis, nec nisi à Christo Petra manans, qui homini vires supra hominem suffice- re potest: Propterea Patres non dicunt simpliciter à Petra dictum esse Simonem Petrum, sed à Christo Petra, uti observat Casaub. Exerc. XV. ad annal. Ecclesiast. Baron. p. 341. unde illa verba, Tu es Pe- trus, sic accipienda, ac si dixisset Dominus, Tu is es, quem ego Petrum dixi à vera Petra. Petra au- tem vera ego sum, quem tu modo confessus es, Dei viventis esse Filium, & super hanc Petram, quam tu confessus es, ædificabo Ecclesiam meam. Quæ ex- plicatio immotis nititur fundamentis. Nam quod non Petrus, sed Christus, vel doctrina, & Confessio de Christo intelligatur, docet primum nominis varia- tio: non enim dicit CHRISTUS, Tu es Petrus & super te Petro ædificabo Ecclesiam; sed mutato nomine, Tu es Petrus, & super petram illam. Aliud ergo est Petrus, aliud vero Petra. Non dicit su- per Petrum, sed super Petram ædificabo Ecclesiam: Quo facit observatio Grammaticorum Græ- corum, notata Casaubono, aliud esse πέτραν, aliud πέτρον. Nam πέτραν esse rupem aut saxum ingens: πέτρον vero parvum lapidem, quales sunt qui Græ- cis χερμάδες & χερμάδια, quod manum impleant, dicuntur, quod ex Homero & Eustathio probat: quorum hic notat πέτραν esse montem, πέτρον vel λίθον τὸ τῆς πέτρας ἀποτμηθὲν particulam à monte re- scissam. Quam Grammaticam observationem huic loco apprime convenire docet. Nam, ut ait Augustinus non semel, & Ambrosius alicubi plu- ribus prosequitur, sicut à Christo dicitur Christia- nus, sic à Petra, quod est alterum ejusdem Christi nomen, dictus est Petrus. Non igitur idem est Petra, & Petrus. Christus est rupes, Petrus est la- pis ab illa rupe excisus. Christus est fortitudo ipsa & αὐτοδύναμις: Petrus est δυνατὸς, fortis, quia accipit vires à Petra.

Vanum autem effugium & commentum est Grotii. Causa nempe, quod Matthæi interpres vocis Hebrææ genus mutarit; Nam & falso as- sumitur Christum Ebraice locutum esse, aut Mat- thæum Ebraice scripsisse, quum Christus locutus potius Syriace sit, & Evangelista Græce scripserit. In idiomate autem Syriaco, quod ibidem notat Ca- saubonus, eadem distinctio locum habet, quod ad rem quidem ipsam attinet; Christus est כפא genere fœminino: nam ea vox Syris pro Petra est fœminini generis: ut intelligamus illum esse τὴν αὐτοφυῆ πέτραν, vel ut Platonici dicerent, τὴν αὐ- τόπετραν, ipsissimam, inquam, originem ejus fortitu- dinis & virtutis, quæ denotatur appellatione Cepha, quæque Ecclesiæ universæ compagem continet. Pe- trus mutato genere ὁ כפא Cephas, tanquam à Cepha Petra denominatur. Quod in termina- tione nulla est diversitas generis, Syriacæ linguæ est tribuendum, quæ virorum nomina istius for- mæ ab aliis substantivis derivatæ ὁμωνύμως effert, non παρωνύμως, ut fere Græca & Latina.

At dicit Grotius, in Græca lingua neque virum πέτραν dici salva Græci sermonis regula potuisse, neque vocem πέτρος id usitate significasse, quod Christus volebat indicatum, nempe saxum tale, su- per quo aliquid ædificari soleat. Quidni vero vir πέτρα dici potuerit, quum Christus Petra dica- tur? aut retineri nomen Syrum Cepha, quod ali- cubi in Evangelica historia adhibetur? aut addi, ut constaret de Petro sermonem esse, super Te, tanquam petram, ædificabo Ecclesiam, aut aliud quoddam indicium, quo notaretur super Petrum ædificandam esse Ecclesiam! Id autem assumimus, quod fateatur Grotius, nomen πέτρος non signifi- care usitate saxum tale super quo aliquid ædificari soleat. At Christus Simonem Petrum dixit, non Petram: non cognominando, neq; Metaphorice denominando: quid ergo certius, quam Christum Simonem noluisse dicere ejusmodi saxum, super quo ædificari possit Ecclesia? Quod cum intelligat Baronius, audet hic Latinam versionem, quæ Tri- denti authentica pronunciata est, corrigere: La- tine, inquit, sic dicenda sententia, tu es Petra, & su- per hanc Petram. Sed & ausus est Græcum tex- tum Spiritus S. emendare, atque ita describere: Tu es Cephas & super hanc Cepham ædificabo Eccle- siam meam. Quam intolerabilem Novatorum audaciam, ut par erat, castigavit Casaubonus. Quanto religiosior autem S. Augustinus Retr. l. I. c. 21. inhæsit textus authentici literæ: Non dictum est Petro, tu es Petra, sed tu es Petrus. Petra autem erat Christus quem confessus Simon, sicut eum tota Ecclesia confitetur, dictus est Petrus.

Deinde confirmat nostram sententiam vocis Petra vis, & propria significatio. Quæ simplici- ter posita sine dubio pro analogato stat famosiori. At ita Christo competit extra controversiam, quâ Petra dicitur ratione naturæ vel personæ, ut Deus, cui nomen illud צור quod πέτραν reddere solent Græci Interpretes innumeris in locis V. T. tribui- tur, Deut. XXXIII. 3. 1.Sam. XXII. 32. Ps.XXXI. 3. Ps. LXXIII. 26. &c. ob essentiæ immutabilitatem, & ratione officii relatione facta ad Ecclesiam, cui dat esse & durare, τὸ εἶναι ϰὴ τὸ μένειν ἀσάλευτον non ad notandum ipsius imperium, sed potius τὸ πάγι- ov firmitudinem Ecclesiæ in Christo veluti rupe & Pe- tra fundatæ: unde Petra & lapis fundamentalis nominatur ædificii Ecclesiæ Es. XXII. 16. Ps. CXIIX. Matth. XXI. 41. Luc. XX. 17. Act. IV. 2. 1. Petr. II. 16. Eph. II. 20. ceu auctor & conserva- tor Ecclesiæ, ut sciant fideles inconcussa firmitudi- nis & durationis æternæ opus esse Ecclesiam, quæ fun- damento nitatur Petra Christo, discant etiam fidem in Christum debere esse firmam atq; immotam, mo- nente Chrysostomo: unde Euseb. lib. I. præpar. Ev- ang. ait, Ecclesiam stare, & manere immotam, quia Christus pronunciavit eam stare, & radicatam esse super immota Petra, virtute sua. Quo no- mine etiam Christus dicitur fundamentum Ec- clesiæ, & quidem eâ ratione, ut asserat Apostolus aliud fundamentum poni nullum posse, 1. Cor. III. 11. quia fundamentum & Petra hic idem sunt, quum super Petram ceu fundamentum ædifican- da fuerit Ecclesiæ, Matth. VII. Luc. VI. Utut ergo Petrus & Apostoli alii, imo etiam fideles Pe- træ ac lapides dicantur ob firmitudinem immotam, quæ in ipsis esse debeat, fidei veræ, ac Prophetarum & Apostolorum fundamentum doctrina eorum di- catur, Eph. II, 20. Christus tamen ϰατ᾽ ἀντονομα- σίαν & principalius dicitur fundamentum & Petra, quem ideo fundamentum fundamentorum dixit Augustinus in Ps. XXCI. Ideoq; hic merito non Petrum, sed Christum per Petram absolute indi- gitatam intelligit, à quo habent Apostoli & fide- les, quod Petræ sint. Quemadmodum Basilius M. homil. de pœnit. monuit: Christus revera Pe- tra est inconcussa; at Petrus propter Petram. Je- sus enim dignitates suas largitur suis. Et Ambros. L. VI. in Evangel. Lucæ: Petra est Christus, qui etiam discipulo suo hujus vocabuli gratiam non ne- gavit, ut & ipse sit Petrus, quod de Petra habeat soli- ditatem constantiæ, fidei firmitatem. Enitere ergo ut & tu Petra sis. Itaque non extra te, sed intra te Pe- tram require. Atque ita etiam Leo M. Episco- pus Romanus Epist. ad Flavian. Petrum à Prin- cipali Petra soliditatem & virtutis traxisse & no- minis. Et Gregor. M. itidem Episcopus Rom. in Regist. lib. VI. Ep. 37. Firmitatem mentis tra- xit in nomine, ut Petrus à Petra vocaretur. Et ex- plic. VII. Psalm. pœnitent. Ipse Dei & hominum Mediator ad Apostolorum principem ait: Tu es Petra, & super hanc Petram ædificabo Ecclesiam meam. Ipse enim Dei & hominum mediator est Petra, à qua etiam Petrus nomen accepit, & super quam se ædificaturum Ecclesiam dixit. Addenda est & glossa ordinaria in hunc locum, Tu es Petrus, nimirum à me Petra, ita tamen, ut mihi ego retine- am fundamenti dignitatem.

Tertio demonstrativa particula ἐπὶ ταύτῃ τῇ πέτρᾳ designat non Petrum, qui nunquam Petra nomine nuncupatus est; sed illum, quem confes- sus erat Petrus, vel ipsam illam confessionem, quam de eo jamjam ediderat; ut August. in Epist. 1. Joh. Quid est, super hanc petram ædificabo Ecclesiam meam? super hanc fidem: super id quod dictum est: Tu es Christus Filius Dei, super hanc petram fundabo Ecclesiam meam. Pronomen enim ταύτῃ vel ἀναφορικὸν est & relativi vim habet, vel δεικτικὸν & demonstrativum: Si relativum, aut ad præcedentem confessionem refertur, aut ad vocem Petra in præcedente dictione Petrus inclusam; quia verba illa, Tu es Petrus, hic significant, ti- bi nomen Petri inditum est à Petra Christo, uti Jo- hann. VIII. 44. factum: Si demonstrativum est, recte itaque de Christo accipitur: siquidem in o- mnibus linguis pronomina demonstrativa elegan- tissime interdum accipiantur de loquentis perso- na, ut exemplum habemus Johan. II. 19. Sic igi- tur super hac petra non absurde, verum eleganter dictum fuerit pro super me, ut observavit Augu- stinus: Super me, inquit, ædificabo te, non me super te, Domino nostro vocem suam gestu adju- vante, quod Græci dicunt λέγειν δεικτικῶς, & συνήδειαν loquentis vocant. Atque ita etiam glossa juris Canonici ad Canon. ita Dominus distinct. XIX. Super hanc Petram. Per hanc dictionem non credo, Dominum aliud demonstrasse, quam hæc verba, quæ Petrus respondit Christo, cum dixit: Tu es Chri- stus Filius Dei vivi, quia super illo articulo fidei fun- data est Ecclesia. Ergo super seipso fundavit Domi- nus Ecclesiam.

Quarto ea est prædicati conditio, ut Petro mi- nime id conveniat, sed Christo unice vendicari de- beat: Is ergo per Petram intelligendus est, super quem ceu fundamentum, instar petræ, immo- tum, ædificanda erat Ecclesia. At non super Pe- trum, sed super Christum ceu fundamentum in- star petræ immotum ea ædificanda fuit. Petrus enim totam molem Ecclesiæ sustinere minime poterat, nec ullus homo merus: & quum ea susti- nenda sit usque ad consummationem seculi, quo- modo Petro id conveniet, aut ulli uni homini? Nam quod de successoribus Petri dicunt, merum commentum est, nec loco convenit: Si Petro hoc dictum ob rationem nominis mutatam, quod ipsi volunt, quid hoc ad alios, quibus nomen Petri non est impositum? Et ubi hoc in Scripturis tradi- tum, quod Petri successoribus idem competat? Annon ita plures erunt petræ, qui ergo dicitur ἐπὶ ταύτῃ τῇ πέτρᾳ, ac expresse designatur unica nu- mero petra? Et quosnam habet Petrus successo- res, in eo quod Petræ instar sustentent Ecclesiam? Nullum designavit Christus, nullum norunt Apo- stoli, nullum Scriptura universa. Petrum Aposto- lum reliquis similem tradit: sed in Apostolatu, nec ille, nec alii Apostoli successores habuêre. De cœ- cumenico Pontificatu & vel Petro commisso, vel successoribus Petri promisso ne gry quidem in Scripturis habetur. Facessant ergo in re tanti momenti salutem Ecclesiæ concernente vana ho- minum commenta.

Quinto Ecclesia, quam suam dicit Christus, non tantum est illa, quæ in Novo Testamento ex- truenda erat, sed quæ inde ab orbe condito extru- cta; Ecclesia Christi cœtus est fidelium & electo- rum tam triumphans in cœlis, quam militans in terris. Perquam autem absurdum est, Petrum esse petram, cui innitatur Ecclesia Veteris Test. cœtus- que electorum triumphans in cœlis: quod vero de Christo verissimum. Ideoque de Petro intel- ligi hoc non potest, sed de Christo intelligendum est necessario.

Sexto is per Petram intelligitur, qui sustenta- tione Ecclesiæ id præstat, ut portæ inferorum non prævalere possint adversus eam. At hoc Petrus præstare non potest, sed unice præstat Christus su- stentatione Ecclesiæ. Non ergo Petrus, sed uni- ce Christus per petram hic intelligitur. Septimo conferendus est locus 1. Cor. III. 11. unde concludere licet: is per petram intelligen- dus est, qui Ecclesiæ fundamentum est. Non au- tem Petrus, sed Christus Ecclesiæ fundamentum est, teste Apostolo, qui aliud non agnovit, fun- damentum, præter id quod positum est, quod est Christus Jesus. Quod urget S. Augustinus de fide & operibus c. XVI. imo ipse Romanus Episcopus Gregorius M. l. XXVIII. moral. c. 6. Cum in sa- cro eloquio non fundamenta, sed in singulari numero fundamentum dicitur, nullus alius nisi ipse Domi- nus designatur, per cujus divinitatis potentiam infir- mitatis nostræ corda solidantur, de quo Paulus: fun- damentum aliud nemo ponere potest, præter id quod positum est, quod est Christus Jesus. Octavo Apostoli super Christum solum, non super Petrum exstruxêre Ecclesiam ceu ministe- riales Architecti 1. Corinth. III. 11. Petrus ipse su- per Christum solum fideles exstruxit, ceu funda- mentum, 1. Pet. II. 4. Nono nullum datur medium, quo Ecclesia cum Petro uniatur, aut Petrus cum unoquoque fidelium in Ecclesia, uti fundamentum & ædifi- cium ei superstructum uniri oportet. Decimo non abs re notat Dn. D. Seb. Schmied in Colleg. Bibl. post. ad h. l. p. 291. συνέχειαν ver- borum v. 17. & 18. & quod assurgat oratio, quin imo dico tibi: q. d. Quin imo de tua ista confessione non tantum id dico, quod caro & sanguis non il- lam revelârit tibi, sed Pater meus, qui in cælis est; sed etiam amplius assero, quod tu per hanc sis Petrus, & quod super petram hanc, hoc est, su- per illam confessionem ædificaturus sim Eccle- siam meam, &c. Undecimo accedant nunc testimonia & suffra- gia veteris & recentioris Ecclesiæ, quæ, si Ro- manam excipias Synagogam, eamque novam, non antiquam, ac proprio honori & commodo velifi- cantem, unanimi consensu non de Petri dominatu, vel Pontificatu etiam æcumenico, non de Ecclesia universa super Petro Pontificatu exædificanda, sed de Petri doctrina & confessione de Christo, ejus- demque objecto, Petra illa & lapide angulari totius Ecclesiæ Vet. & Nov. Test. militantis, & jam trium- phantis in cælis, Christo Jesu, qui unicum est funda- mentum, cui innititur, à quo sustentatur & fove- tur Ecclesia, hæc Christi verba accepit, & inter- pretata est, ne quidem ipsis Romanis Episcopis ab hoc testium numero exclusis: Quem consen- sum è Patribus Græcis Epiphanius, Gregorius Nys- senus, Basilius M. Chrysostomus, Basilius Seleuciensis, Theodoretius, Theophylactus, Oecumenius, è Latinis Tertullianus, Hilarius, Ambrosius, Hieronymus, Augustinus, Paulinus, Victor Antiochenus, Beda, & Hincmarus Remensis Episcopus Anno 800. Haymo Episcopus Halberstadiensis circa ann. Christi 850. & alii testantur. Ex Episcopis vero Romanis Euty- chianus circa Annum Christi 275. Leo M. anno 440. Felix III. Anno 483. Felix IV. Anno 526. Gregorius M. anno 590. Leo II. Anno 682. Adrianus I. circa ann. 772. Nicolaus I. anno 858. Stepha- nus VI. anno 886. Nicolaus II. an. 1059. etiam Gre- gorius VII. Hildebrandus, præcipuus Dominatio- nis Pontificiæ assertor Anno 1073. & qui eum se- quuti sunt Innocentius II. Anno 1130. Adrianus IV. Anno 1154. quos produxit B. Gerhardus noster in Confess. Cathol. l. 1. part. II. c. II. Quibus Concilia integra, etiam sequiorum temporum accedunt: ut- pote Suessionense Anno 909. Quæ Ecclesia genera- liter ab uno capite Christo super petram, id est, super confessionem Petri ædificata: Trevirense Anno 1549. vera in Jesum Christum fidei fundamentum est, & petra illa, de qua Salvator noster dixit, super il- lam ædificandam esse Ecclesiam. Nec abnuunt glos- sæ Bibliorum in Papatu receptæ, sive ordinaria, sive interlinearis, aut probationes Interpretes, Doctores ac Scholastici, aut Glossæ juris Canonici: videri imprimis possunt Hugo de Caro in postill. ad h. l. Albert. M. in Commentar. ad h. l. Thomas de Aquino 2. 2. q. 174. art. 6. Durand. Ration. Di- vin. Offic. l. I. c. 7. Nicolaus Lyran. in h. l. Nicol. Gorranus in h. l. Dionys. Carthus. in h. l. Guilhelmus in h. l. Gabr. Biel. lect. 22. in Canon. qui ante B. Lutherum floruerunt: quibus suffragantur etiam B. Luthero coævi, eoque posteriores, Erasmus Ludov. Vives, Autor oneris Eccles. Joh. Ferus, Al- fons. Salmer. Jacob Schopperus, aliique itidem ad- ducti, à B. Gerh. l. c. Notamus saltem ex iis, qui ante Lutherum scripserunt binos, & totidem è posterioribus, utpote Antonin. Archi-Episcop. Florentin. circa Annum Christi 1459. part. 1. Hist. tit. 5. c. 1. super verba: Tu es Petrus. Non te demon- strando, sed me, quem confessus es, super hanc veri- tatem confessam; & Alphons. Tostatus, Abulens. Episc. circa annum 1440. in h. l. Non verum est, quod super Petrum fundata est Ecclesia &c. Johan. Arboreus L. V. Theosoph. c. 5. prolixe disputat, Ecclesiam fundatam esse super Petram (Christum) & non super Petrum: Alphonsus à Castro præfat. libr. de hæres. Fides est basis & fundamentum totius Christianæ structuræ, & super quam velut firmissi- mam quandam Petram Deus fundavit Ecclesiam suam &c. Conf. de hoc loco Nic. Hunnii pellis o- vina §. 541. seqq. De cætero Patrum sententias ita recenset, & conciliat circa hunc locum Casauto- nus: Præcipuas, inquit, Patrum sententias hac de re breviter indicabimus. Prima esto illorum, qui unumquemque fidelium Petræ nomine voluerunt de- signari: quæ est Origenis in Matth. tract. 1. Grego- rii Nysseni lib. de Perfectione; Ambros. lib. VI. in Luc. Secunda sententia esto illorum Patrum, qui ap- pellatione Petræ intellexisse Dominum crediderunt Petri fidem, sive confessionem à Petro hic editam. Chrysostomus diserte in hunc locum: ἐπὶ ταύτῃ τῇ πέτρᾳ, τουτέστι, τῇ πίστει τῆς ὁμολογίας. Theo- phylactus itidem: αὕτη ἡ ὁμολογία ἣν ὡμολόγη- σας, θεμέλιον μέλλει εἶναι τῶν πιστευόντων. Hæc confessio quam confessus es, fundamentum erit credentium. Cum his faciunt Augustinus in Epist. I. Johan. tract. X. & Basilius Seleucens. serm. in hanc Matth. pericopam. Tertia illorum fuit sententia, qui per Petram κυρίως Petrum putarunt intelligendum, quorum testimonia plura passim occurrunt. Quarta fuit eorum qui veram Petram, & verū Ecclesiæ fundamen- tum volunt intelligi, ipsum Christum: quomodo vocem Petræ esse isto loco accipiendam accurate & copiose do- cet magnus Augustinus pluribus locis, ut in Johan. tract. CXXIV. de Trinit. l. II. c. XVII. & multo uberius de verbis Domini secund. Matth. serm. XIII. & Re- tract. lib. I. cap. 21. Cum Augustino & Patres alii sen- tiunt plures; sed instar omnium Patrum Paulus esto, quo fidelior mentis verborumque Domini interpres ne fingi quidem potest. Sunt autem Pauli verba 1. Cor. III. 2. Fundamentum aliud nemo potest ponere, præter id quod positum est, quod est Christus Je- sus. Neque tamen obstat Paulinum hoc oraculum, quin & superiores Patrum interpretationes rectæ sint & orthodoxæ. Non enim rebus ipsis differunt inter se quatuor istæ sententiæ; sed modo tantum & ratione. Christus nempe ædificii Ecclesiæ prima causa effi- ciens, à quo ceu fonte unico, vis omnis oritur, qua lis- lis- clefiam instituit, tuetur, & facit durare. Petrus dum viveret, causa efficiens secundaria extitit, ut Aposto- lus & Apostolorum primus: quos ait Paulus esse in isto opere Christi συνεργούς, & quasi opera socios: post ejusdem vero obitum, Petri doctrina, quam vivus docuerat voce & scripto, quæ μετωνυμικῶς sæpe dici- tur Petrus in Scriptis Patrum, & fuit, & est hodie- que, & semper erit, Ecclesiæ firmissimum fundamen- tum. Fides causa est instrumentalis: unusquisque fi- delium, causa materialis templi Dei, quod ædifica- tur, ait Augustinus in Enchir. ad Laur. ex iis, quos facit non factus Deus. Quis neget omnes has piorum patrum expositiones pias esse & orthodoxas? Omnes enim in unum congruunt, adeoque sibi invicem sunt affines, ut passim observare liceat, eosdem patres mo- do hanc, modo illam ex superioribus expositionibus sequi, amplecti, & proposito suo accommodare.

Denique è Grotiana quoque confessione glos- sa Papistica infringi potest: primo enim pag. 292. explicat hanc οἰκοδομὴν: quomodo autem super Pe- tro ædificentur credentes, obscurum non est, cum Paulo iidem dicantur ἐποικοδομηθέντες ἐπὶ τῷ θεμε- λίῳ τῶν Ἀποστόλων & τῶν προφητῶν Eph. II. 20. Et in Apocalypsi Dei civitas dicatur habere duodecim fun- damenta, in quibus inscripta sint nomina duodecim Apostolorum. Si enim Petrus non aliter fundamen- tum Ecclesiæ dicitur, quam reliqui Apostoli, utique Petrus non est eo sensu fundamentum Ecclesiæ, quod unicus Christi vicarius, & caput reliquorum Apostolorum sit. Sic enim duodecim essent vicarii & totidem capita: idemque sui ipsius esset caput. Secundo non aliter petræ aut fundamenti nomen tri- buitur Petro, aliisq; Apostolis, quam τὸ σώζειν, Rom. XI. 14. fatente Grotio. At hoc non tribuitur eis, quod capita sint Ecclesiæ, sed quod ministerialiter & do- ctrinæ suæ, quam prædicant, virtute salvent alios: quod etiam aliis verbi ministris competere, dubi- um nullum est 1. Tim. IV. 16. Tertio fatetur hic Gro- tius, alios Apostolos cum Petro columnas Ecclesiæ dici, Gal. II. 9. quod sibi contradicens antea ad Matth. X. 1. negarat, & ad Gal. II. 9. iterum negat. Quum ergo Apostoli illi, Jacobus & Johannes neutiquam con- stituti loco Christi, capita Ecclesiæ sint, neque Petro, qui alio sensu Ecclesiæ columna non est, id tri- buendum est. Quarto Petrum per hunc modum fa- ctum esse Petram sive fundamentum populi Christi, ait Grotius, quia misso Spiritûs auxilio fidem nactus solidissimam primum solum Judæis, Act. II. 14. dein- de & alienigenis Act. X. & XV. 7. annunciavit id i- psum, quod hic confessus est, nempe Jesum esse Chri- stum, & unigenam Dei Filium, & quia crediderunt & Judæi & gentes tum communi Apostolorum, tum peculiari etiam Petri testimonio, qui hoc ipsum suum testimonium sparsum per omnem Judæam, perque o- mnem Judæorum διασπορὰν confirmavit vitæ sancti- monia, miraculis, postremo etiam tolerata morte, & quidem in urbe mundi principe. At non minus alii Apostoli, quam Petrus, fidem nacti solidissimam sunt, cum mitteretur in eos Spiritus Sanctus nec mi- nus alii Judæis & gentibus annunciarunt, per ver- bum, Jesum Christum Filium Dei unigenitum. Non minus per alios, quam per Petrum credidere Judæi & gentiles, non minus alii, quam Petrus do- ctrinam suam confirmarunt vitæ sanctimonia, & miraculis, postremo etiam tolerata morte. Quid vero illa ad id faciunt, quod hic est τὸ κρινόμενον, quod nempe Petrus constitutus sit loco Christi A- postolorum totiusque Ecclesiæ caput & fundamentum? Quod autem primus ipse prædicavit Judæis Act. II. & gentibus c. X. si quid pro ordinis prerogativa fa- cit, utique ad demonstrandum œcumenicum Petri Pontificatum nihil confert: nec quicquam ad id momenti fufficit martyrium Romæ toleratum; non enim ideo Romæ caput Ecclesiæ totius fuit, quia martyrium Romæ subiit. Ita sane & Paulus caput Ecclesiæ fuisset, quem itidem Romæ martyrium subiisse ajunt. Ut taceam, quod penes Papistas non omnino indubium sit, an Petrus Romæ mortem tolerarit: è quibus Guilhelmus Wiclefi præceptor docuit, Petrum ne vidisse quidem unquam urbem, E- piscopum vero illic non fuisse Michael Cesenas, Ly- ranus, Mantuanus professi sunt, apud Wolfium T. I. memor. p. 23. ac Clemens L. VII. Constit. cap. XLV. tradidit, Linum non à Petro, sed à Paulo Ro- manæ Ecclesiæ Episcopum constitutum esse: Conf. Salmero in Epist. ad Tucc. tom. ult p. 413.

Πύλαι ἅδε ὀ κατισχύσωσιν ἀυτῆς] De Diaboli aut et- iam de improborum molitionibus tanto consensu hunc lo- cum exponi valde miror. Nusquam enim reperio ἅδε vo- cem neque apud Hellenistas neque apud Novi fœderis Scri- ptores in alia significatione quam aut mortis, aut sepulcri, aut status post mortem, quæ omnia sunt inter se affinia. Ab interpretibus quos hac in parte sequuntur Apostoli, שאול verti ἅδης à multis demonstratum est. Mortem ἅδης significat Sapientiæ I. 4. Ecclef. IX. 17. & in historia Maccabæorum aliquoties: ubi & προπέμπειν ἐἰς τὸν ἅδην invenias quod Græcis poëtis familiare est: quomodo & Scriptor Baruchi dixit καταβαίνειν ἐἰς ἅδε quod itidem apud Græcos usitatissimum est. Statum potius mortuorum quam mortem ipsam designat eadem vox Ecclef. XLI. 7. Reperias sæpe & θάνατον & ἅδην inter se conjuncta, tum in priore illo, tum in posteriore significatu, ut Esaiæ XXVIII. 15. Ecclesia- stici XLVIII. 5. & cap. LI. 8. Sap. II. 1. nec minus in Apo- stolicis libris, ut 1. Cor. XV. 55. Apoc. I. 12. cap. XX. 13. 14. In eadem autem Apocalypsi VI. 8. dicitur ἅδης sequi θάνα- τον, ubi θάνατος ipsum moriendi actum significat, ἅδης sta- tum sequentem, qui & ipse alias sæpissime vocatur θάνατος. Actorum II. 27. & 31. vocem ἅδε respondere Hebraicæ שאול notissimum est. Supra autem XI, 23. & Lucæ X. 15. ostendimus figuratam esse locutionem, quæ mortis aut se- pulcri nomine maximas miserias denotat: sicut & pericula gravia ἅδε voce appellantur. Restat unicus locus Lucæ XVI. 23. ubi is qui est ἐν βασάνοις dicitur esse ἐν τῷ ἅδῃ. Sed ne ibi quidem ἅδας per se τὸ βασανιστήριον significat, ut ostende- mus cum eo ventum erit. Vocem autem ἅδε de Angelorum defectorum sede aut statu, aut de improbis mortalem hanc vitam agentibus usurpatam neminem esse puto qui legerit. Nec quid hic significent πύλαι ἅδε difficilis est conjectura, cum eadem locutio reperiatur in carmine regis Ezechiæ quod apud Esaiam est, XXXVIII. ubi in Hebræo est אלכה בשערי שאול in Græco πορεύσομαι ἐν πύλαις ἅδε. Opponitur autem ibidem τῷ ἅδῃ, ἡ γῆ ζώντων. Sic & Psal. IX. 14. & CVII. 18. & Sap. XVI. 13. Non sunt aliud πύ- λαι ἅδε quam quod βασίλειον ἅδε dixit Scriptor libri Sa- pientiæ: κράτος θανάτε Hebr. II. 14. Græci ut πέμπειν εἰς ἅ- δε, καταβαίνειν εἰς ἅδε, ita & πύλας ἅδε dixére à Syrus edocti, quorum locutiones passim ab Homero exprimi, à viris do- ctissimis recte est annotatum. Notissimo Homeri loco adjungi potest iste veteris Comici:

Χρυσὸς δ᾽ ἀνοίγει πάντα κ᾽ ἀἰδε πύλας.

Et ille incerti autoris:

Φύντα δ᾽ ὅπως ὤκιςα πύλας ἀίδαο περῆσαι.

Reperias ἅδε πύλας & in Euripidis Alcestide, & in Agame- mnone Æschyli. Themistius Theodosium laudans quod eos qui in eum deliquerant, à morte liberasset, ἐπαναγαγεῖν, ait εἰς τὸν ἥλιον ἐκ τῶν πυλῶν τᾶ Ἀχέροντος: & postea: εἴδομεν ἀνθρώπες ἐν τῶν τῶ ἅδε προθύρων εἰς τὸ ζῇν ἐπανιόντας. Etiam Pythagoras, recitante Laërtio, fabas eo quod nihil de se gi- gnant similes dicebat ἅδε πύλαις. Apud Plutarchum de su- perstitione: ἅδε τινες ἀνοίγονται πύλαι βαθεῖαι. Lucianus Me- nippo magos ait ἀνοίγειν τὲ ἁδὲ τὰς πύλας. Sicut ergo de Chri- sto capite dictum est à Paulo θάνατος ἀυτᾶ κ ἔτι κυριεύει Rom. VI. 9. & à Petro ἐκ ἦν δύνατον κρατεῖσθαι ἀυτὸν ὑπὸ τῶ θανάτε. Act. II. 24. ita hic Christi corpori, id est populo cre- dentium, promittitur fore ut mors ipsa, cujus maximum & insatiabile est regnum, non eas vires habeat, ut eos detinere possit sub suo jure ac potestate. Nam qui credit transit de morte in vitam Joh. V. 24. cap. XI. 25. 26. nunc quidem spe ac fiducia, eventu autem olim cum ultimus hostis trium- phabitur, cum dicere licebit πῶ σε ἅδη τὸ νῖκος 1. Cor. XV. 55. cum Christus eandem hanc ἐκκλησίαν de qua hic agitur πα- ραςήσῃ ἑαυτῷ ἔνδοξον, Ephes. V. 25. Nisi forte de Eccle- sia hic agitur universim, non partitim, & ejus perpe- tua duratio promittitur juxta dictum Hebræorum כל כנסיא שהי לשם שם יים סופה

להתקים Omnis Ecclesia quæ sit propter Deum, firma per- manebit. Confer Act. V. 39. Hunc in sensum Chrysostomus ἅδε πύλας interpretatur pericula exitio proxima, oratione ὅτι Θεὸς ὁ χρησὸς. Sic πρὸς πύλας ἅδε καθεςῶτας Macc. III.

Hæc accipit Grotius de liberatione è statu mortis; fore ut mors ipsa, cujus maximum & insatiabile est regnum, non eas vires habeat, ut eos detinere pos- set sub suo jure ac potestate. Quam glossam à So- cinianis & Arminianis mutuo sumsit. Sic enim exposuit Ostorodus in Instit. cap. XLII. præeunte Socino ipso tract. de Eccles. p. 69. per infernum designari statum mortuorum: ac sensum esse, illos qui Christi sunt, in statu mortuorum æternum deti- neri non posse. Arminiani Apol. c. XXII. volunt, Ecclesiæ his in terris versanti nihil promitti, sed Ec- clesiæ, quæ in terris est, & usque ad mortem manet, promitti aliquid post mortem, quorum ςρεβλότης in Socinianismo & Armidianismo profligato discussa est. De Ecclesia in his terris agente, superstructa Pe- træ immotæ, Christo, cui claves concessæ sunt li- gandi & solvendi, nimis manifestum est hic agi: ideoque perperam ad statum post hanc vitam hæc abripiuntur, nec de morte, statu mortis, aut infer- no, sed de portis inferorum, hoc est, de regno, vi, ac robore, & tyrannide ac potestate infernali agitur, uti portæ erant locus judiciorum & propugnacula illic collocata quondam sunt: adeoque id innui- tur, nullam infernalem vim ac potestatem præva- lituram adversus Ecclesiam Christi, eamque ex- pugnaturam, ut Origenes, Epiphan. Cyrillus, Hie- ronymus, Ambrosius, Euthym. Isidorus interpretan- tur. Et agnoscit Grotius de Diaboli, aut etiam im- proborum molitionibus magno consensu eum locum exponi. Quod valde quidem se mirari ait, eo quod non reperiat vocem ἅδε seu apud Hellenistas, seu a- pud N. T. scriptores in alia significatione, quam aut mortis Sap. I. 4. Eccles. IX. 17. aut sepulcri aut status post mortem, Eccles. LXI. 7. nunquam de Angelorum defectorum sede aut statu, aut improbis mortalem hanc vitam agentibus vocem ἅδε quis legerit. At hic non de voce ἅδης, sed quid πύλαι ἅδε signifi- cent, disquiritur. Et quid potentia infernalis a- liud est, quam potentia Diabolorum principis infe- rorum? Jam vero voce ἅδης vel inferni per meto- nymiam etiam Diabolum significari veteres nota- runt, utpote Job. XXVI. 6. Proverb. XXX. 16. Ap. I. 18. c. XX. 14. ubi collatio cum v. 10. illum sensum confirmat, infernum, id est, Diabolum in stagnum ignis missum est. De ־אש vero Diabolorum & da- mnatorum loca varia observantur. Num. XVI. 33. Deut. XXXIII. 12. Psal. XLIX. 15. Psal. LVI. 16. Prov. XXVI. 20. Es. V. 14. Os. XIII. 14. Locus certe ille manifestus est XVI. 23. seqq. Conf. Matth. XXV. 41. 2. Petri II. 4. Sed non multum fidit tandem Grotius glossæ suæ, hæc adjiciens: Nisi forte de Ec- clesia hic agitur universim, non partitim, & ejus perpetua duratio promittitur juxta dictum Hebræo- rum: Omnis Ecclesia quæ sit propter Deum, firma permanebit. Confer. Act. V. 39.

## 16:19
Verse 19.

τὰς κλεῖς] Not those prophetic ones, which the teachers of the Hebrews had hidden away, believing them to be entrusted to themselves, and as much as was in them, had closed off the approach to men to the heavenly kingdom, that is, to that eternal glory (see Luke 11:52), but the Apostolic ones, a great part of which consists in that which we have mentioned, the testimony concerning Christ's Resurrection, by which mark Peter himself describes the Apostolic office in Acts 1:22.

The keys of the kingdom of heaven are one thing, and the preaching and testimony concerning the resurrection of Christ, or the Gospel, is another. For by the keys, the power of both loosing and binding is designated: which everyone understands to differ from the testimony concerning Christ. Compare Matthew 18:18, John 20:20. Lightfoot interprets the keys of the kingdom of heaven in a new way: I will give to you the keys, that is, You shall be the first to open the door of faith to the Gentiles. He had said, he says, that he would build a Church that would endure forever, against which the gates of hell would never prevail, which had prevailed against the Jewish one; And to you, he says, O Peter, I will give the keys of the kingdom of heaven, so that you may open the door for the introduction of the Gospel to that Church. Which was performed by Peter in that memorable history concerning Cornelius, Acts X. And I have no doubt that Peter’s words in Acts XV. 7 looked back to these words of Christ: From ancient days God chose among us, that by my mouth the Gentiles should hear the word of the Gospel, and believe. This paraphrase, therefore, he renders on p. 202. I am about to build, says Christ, a Gentile Church, and to you, O Peter, I give the keys of the kingdom of heaven, so that you may be the first to open the door of faith to them: but if you ask by what rule that Church is to be regulated, since the Mosaic rule might seem to them quite alien, you are so led by the Holy Spirit that whatever of the Mosaic law you forbid them will be forbidden, and whatever you grant will be granted, and that under sanction in heaven. Hence, at that instant, when he was about to use his keys, that is, when he was now about to open the door of the Gospel to the Gentiles, Acts X, he is taught from heaven that the association of the Jew with the Gentile, which had previously been bound, was now dissolved, concerning the eating of any animal suitable for food: and he likewise dissolves these two things. Those words of the Savior, John XX. 23, Whose sins you remit are remitted to them, are for the most part forced into the same sense as these under consideration; although they carry with them a far different one. The matter here concerns doctrine only, not persons; there it concerns persons, not doctrine: here it concerns things lawful or not lawful in religion, to be determined by the Apostles; there it concerns obstinate or non-obstinate persons, to be punished or not punished by them. But this explanation does not deserve approval in our judgment.

And whatever you bind on earth] To bind is to restrain, to loose is to release, as appears in John XX. 23. Both are properly attributed to God the Father and Christ, as can be seen in Eph. IV. 32, Col. III. 13, Matt. IX. 6, Mark II. 10, Luke V. 24, and to the Apostles, in such a way as to save, namely because of the embassy they perform, which is the ministry of reconciliation, 2 Cor. V. 18, 19, 20, 21. In this way Peter remitted sins to those who believe, and retained them for those who stumble at the word, as he himself teaches us in his first Epistle II. 7, 8. See also Acts II. 38 and X. 43. This embassy is carried out on earth, that is, by men living a mortal life (in the way the same expression is used in the just-cited passages of Matthew, Mark, and Luke), but it is ratified in heaven, that is, before God. The Hebrews similarly attribute to the interpreters of the law asar, to bind, and hattir or patar, to loose: but they had performed this office so poorly that the Apostles had to loose many who had been bound by them, and bind those who had been loosed: because they had turned true religion into superstitious commendation.

Latin:

Vers. 19.

τὰς κλεῖς] Non illas Propheticas, quas sibi creditas Hebræorum magistri abdiderant, & quantum in ipsis erat, aditum hominibus præcluserant ad regnum cœleste, id est, ad gloriam illam æternam (vide Luc. XI. 52.) sed Apostoli- cas, quarum pars magna consistit in illo, quod diximus, te- stimonio de Christi Resurrectione, qua nota Apostolicum munus describit ipse Petrus Act. I. 22.

Aliud sunt claves regni cœlorum, aliud prædi- catio, ac testimonium de resurrectione Christi, vel Evangelium. Nam per claves potestas designatur tum solvendi tum ligandi: quam à testimonio de Christo differre nemo non intelligit. Confer Matth. XVIII. 18. Joh. XX. 20. Lightsootus nova ratione claves regni cœlorum interpretatur: Dabo tibi claves, id est, Tu primus aperies ostium fidei gentibus. Dixerat, inquit, ædificaturum se Ec- clesiam in æternum duraturam, in quam porta infe- rorum nunquam prævalituræ, quæ prævaluerant in Judaicam; Tibique, inquit, ô Petre, dabo claves regni cælorum, ut ostium aperias introductioni Ev- angelii ad istam Ecclesiam. Quod à Petro præstitum est in memorabili ista historia de Cornelio, Actor. X. Atque ad hæc verba Christi respexisse ita verba Petri minime dubito, Actor. XV. 7. Ἀφ᾽ ἡμερῶν ἀρ- χαίων ὁ Θεὸς ἐν ἡμῖν ἐξελέξατο, διὰ τῶ στόματός μυ ἀκῦσαι τὰ ἔθνη τὸν λόγον τῶ Εὐαγγελίκ, καὶ πιστεῦσαι. Hanc ergo paraphrasin reddit p. 202. Ædificaturus sum, inquit Christus, Ecclesiam Gen- tilitiam, tibique ô Petre, do claves regni cælorum, ut tu primus ostium fidei iis aperias: si autem quæ- ras, quanam norma regulanda sit ista Ecclesia, cum norma Mosaica isti videri possit admodum aliena, tu ita à Spiritu Sancto duceris, ut quodcunque legis Mosicæ illis prohibueris erit prohibitum, quodcun- que concesseris erit concessum, idque sub sanctione in cælo. Hinc in illo instante, cum clavibus suis usu- rus esset, id est, cum jam aperturus januam Evan- gelii Gentilibus, Act. X. edocetur cælitus solutam jam esse consociationem Judæi cum Gentili, quæ an- tea fuerat ligata, comestioneum animalis cujusvis, e- sui convenientis: atque is pariter hæc duo solvit. Verba ista Salvatoris, Joan. XX. 23. Quorum pec- cata remiseritis remittuntur iis, ut plurimum in eundem sensum cum his sub manibus coguntur; cum longe alium secum ferant. Agitur hic de doctrina solum, non de personis; illic de personis, non de doctrina: hic de rebus licitis, aut non licitis in reli- gione, determinandis ab Apostolis; illic de personis obstinatis, aut non obstinatis, per eos puniendis, aut non puniendis. Sed hæc explicatio calculum no- stro judicio non meretur.

κὶ ὃ ἐὰν δήσης ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς] Δεῖν est κρατεῖν, λύειν est ἀ- φιέναι, ut apparet Joh. XX. 23. Utrumque proprie tri- buitur Deo Patri & Christo, ut videre est Ephes. IV. 32. Col. III. 13. Matth. IX. 6. Marc. II. 10. Luc. V. 24. Apo- stolis, ita ut σῴζειν, nimirum ob eam qua funguntur legatio- nem quæ est διακονία τῆς καταλλαγῆς 2. Cor. V. 18. 19. 20. 21. Remisit hoc modo Petrus peccata τοῖς πιστεύουσι, retinuit τοῖς προσκόπτουσι τῷ λόγῳ, ut ipse nos docet Epistola prio. re II. 7. 8. Vide & Act. II. 38. & X. 43. Hæc legatio in ter- ris peragitur, id est per homines mortalem vitam viventes (quomodo eadem locutio usurpatur citatis modo Mat- thæi, Marci & Lucæ locis) rata autem est in cælo, id est apud Deum. Hebræi similiter legis interpretibus tribuunt אסר δέειν & התיר vel פטר λύειν: sed illi tam male erant functi hoc officio, ut multos ab illis ligatos solve- re debuerint Apostoli, & solutos ligare: quia religionem veram in superstitiosa commenda verterant.

## 16:20
Verse 20. That they should tell no one that he is the Christ] This is how it must be read entirely, as the Syriac has it; and the most ancient Greek and Latin copies. And it appears that neither Origen formerly, nor Ambrose later, nor Theophylact more recently, read it otherwise. Jesus is a proper name, by which he was known among all: Christ is a name of dignity: wherefore what some codices have here, Jesus, was undoubtedly an interpretation. It appears from this passage that the Apostles, in the embassy of which mention was made before, made known to all Jesus’ holiness and miracles, that repentance was to be practiced, and that the kingdom of heaven was not far off. But that Jesus is the Christ, that is, the King of that kingdom, that was not published by them: but the announcement of that matter was reserved for the Lord himself to be dispensed according to the circumstances of places and times. See John V. 18, ch. XIII. 58, ch. X. 30, ch. XI. 27, Mark XIV. 61. For that fame could be spread among all indiscriminately with much greater fruit after Christ had obtained possession of his kingdom, and had testified to that very fact by his resurrection, ascension into heaven, and the mission of the Holy Spirit, no longer subject to human infirmities, the regard for which could have drawn men away from the proper veneration of him. The same point is made by what is below in ch. XVII. 9.

Regarding this diverse reading, one may look at what the blessed Johannes Ernestus Gerhardus says here against Grotius: The received reading must be entirely retained, which rests upon many most ancient Greek codices, and Latin ones, as attested by Burgensis, Erasmus, Beza, and Walton, that he himself is Jesus the Christ. It was important to know both; and that he himself was Jesus, which name, although it was known among all as a proper name, the reason for the name, which the Angel had revealed, was not known to all: and that he himself was Christ. Nor is the latter an interpretation of the former: because the name Christ signifies anointed, but the name Jesus signifies Savior, which are most distinct. For the Anointed is the Son of God with immense gifts of the Spirit according to the flesh, which had been predicted concerning the Messiah, Ps. XLV, Dan. VII and IX, so that he might be the Savior. The end of the anointing, therefore, why he was so anointed, is this, that he himself might be our Savior, as Priest, Prophet, and King, who by his priestly offering would acquire salvation for us, by his prophetic office would announce it, and by his royal office would confer, defend, and preserve it.

But as for what Grotius further gathers from this passage, that the Apostles in their embassy made known to all Jesus’ holiness and miracles, that repentance was to be practiced, and that the kingdom of heaven was not far off, but that Jesus is the Christ, i.e., the King of that kingdom, was not published by them, but the announcement of that matter was reserved for the Lord himself, to be dispensed according to the circumstances of places and times, that cannot be admitted as simply stated in that way. For that announcement was not simply forbidden; on the contrary, since it was a clear sign among the signs and characteristics of the Messiah designated in the Old Testament, and confirmed by the testimonies of Mary, Elizabeth, and Zechariah, manifested by the announcement of the angels, the shepherds of Bethlehem, the Magi from the East, and likewise by the public preaching of Simeon and Anna, declared by the demonstration of John, the confession of Andrew, Philip, Nathanael, and others, and the same thing was spread everywhere by the testimony of the disciples themselves concerning Jesus, namely that he is the Christ, the Son of God: with the solemn proclamation from heaven also added: Who would presume that God did not wish for this to be publicly known? John was certainly sent by God to testify concerning that light illuminating all men, so that ALL might believe in it, John 1:7. Nor for any other purpose did Christ manifest his glory through miracles and signs than that all might believe in him, John 2:11.
