Therefore, what Christ forbade—that they should tell anyone that he himself was that Jesus Christ—is not only to be taken as a temporary prohibition, but also to be explained in a certain respect, namely concerning the full preaching of this doctrine, and so that they might not rashly invite danger through its indiscriminate announcement: since neither were they themselves sufficiently instructed for this proclamation before the Resurrection and Ascension of Christ and the mission of the Holy Spirit, because of their preconceived opinion about the earthly kingdom of the Messiah, nor was the people, on account of the scandal of the state of humiliation and especially the imminent death of Christ, suitable for receiving that doctrine with true and firm faith. Concerning which see Chrysostom, Homily 55. If the disciples, who saw many things and heard many mysteries, were scandalized by hearing alone, and not they alone, but even the head of all, Peter: consider now with yourself what the common people, who had inspected nothing higher in secret and were established by no grace of the Spirit, would have suffered if they had learned that he whom they had learned to be the Son of God was being crucified and seen to be agitated by every insult. Nor inappropriately does Basil say in his Apology to the Caesareans: He had not yet finished his course; he preferred, therefore, that it be known from the predictions of the Prophets rather than from the testimonies of his household.

to be acknowledged as the Messiah; concerning which the blessed Ægidius Hunnius in Matthew p. 550. This is admitted, that that prohibition does not look to the fact that he envied men the saving knowledge of himself: but as far as is gathered from the reason of those times and other circumstances, he therefore did not wish to become known to men, because he knew that both the disciples and also the remaining Jews did not yet understand the nature of the Messiah's kingdom, but were demanding for themselves such a Messiah, whom they might constitute as king for themselves by inciting a sedition, so that, relying on his protection, they might shake off the yoke of the Roman nation, which is what they had already attempted in John 6. Since, therefore, the Lord knew that the common people of the Jews would abuse this manifestation for the purpose of stirring up new things, at that very time, in that very place, and among those men, among whom he was then moving, he did not wish to manifest himself for some time. Consult the blessed Polycarp Lyser on this passage.

PART IV. The prediction of the passion and resurrection of Christ, and the rebuke of Peter who contradicted him.

Latin:

Vers. 20. ἵνα μηδενὶ εἴπωσιν, ὅτι ἀυτός ἐστιν ὁ χριστὸς] Ita omnino legendum, quomodo habet Syrus; vetustissima- que tum Græca tum Latina exemplaria. Et apparet non a- liter legisse aut olim Origenem, aut postea Ambrosium, aut serius Theophylactum. Jesus nomen est proprium, quo apud omnes noscebatur: Christus nomen est dignitatis: quare quod nonnulli codices hic habent Ἰησῦς haud dubie interpretamentum fuit. Apparet ex hoc loco Apostolos in legatione, cujus antehac facta est mentio, notam omni- bus fecisse Jesu sanctimoniam & miracula, agendam pœni- tentiam & non longe esse regnum cælorum. Jesum autem esse Christum, hoc est regni illius regem id non esse ab ipsis publicatum: sed ejus rei enuntiationem reservatam ipsi Domino pro ratione locorum & temporum dispensandam. Vide Johan. V. 18. cap. XIII. 58. cap. X. 30. cap. XI. 27. Marc. XIV. 61. Multo enim majore cum fructu promiscue ad omnes præferri ea fama potuit, postquam Christus pos- sessionem regni sui erat adeptus, idque ipsum testatus erat resurrectione, ascensu in cælum & missione Spiritus Sancti, non ultra obnoxius humanis infirmitatibus, quarum re- spectus à recta veneratione ipsius avellere homines pote- rat. Eodem facit quod infra est c. XVII. 9.

De hac diversa lectione videri poterunt, quæ B. Johannes Ernestus Gerhardus hic contra Gro- tium: Omnino retinenda est recepta lectio, quæ Codicibus pluribus antiquissimis Græcis, & Lati- nis teste Burgensi, Erasmo, Beza, Waltono, nititur, ὅτι ἀυτός ἐστιν Ἰησοῦς ὁ χριστὸς. Utrumque scire intererat; & quod Jesus ipse esset, quod nomen etsi ut proprium apud omnes noscebatur, ratio tamen nominis, quam Angelus aperuerat, non erat omnibus nota: & quod Christus ipse. Nec vero illud hujus interpretamentum est: quia Christi no- men unctum significat, Jesu vero nomen Salvato- rem, quæ maxime distincta sunt. Unctus nem- pe est Filius Dei immensis Spiritus donis secun- dum carnem, quod de Messia prædictum erat. Psal. XLV. Dan. VII & IX. ut esset Salvator. Un- ctionis ergo finis, cur ita unctus fuerit, hic est, ut noster Salvator ipse esset, ceu Sacerdos, Propheta & Rex, qui Sacerdotali oblatione nobis acquireret salutem, Prophetico munere eam annunciaret, Regali eam conferret, tueretur, ac conserva- ret.

Quod autem porro Grotius ex hoc loco col- ligit, Apostolos in legatione notum omnibus fecisse Jesu Sanctimoniam, & miracula, agendam pœni- tentiam, & non longe esse regnum cælorum, Jesum autem esse Christum, h. e. Regni illius Regem, id non esse ab ipsis publicatum, sed ejus rei annunciationem reservatam ipsi Domino, pro ratione locorum, & temporum dispensandam, id simpliciter ita dictum admitti non potest. Nam nec simpliciter interdi- cta fuit illa annunciatio, imo cum e signis & cha- racteribus Messiæ in V. T. designatis, luculen- tum illud fuerit, ac testimoniis Mariæ, Elisabe- thæ, Zachariæ confirmatum, annunciatione An- gelorum, Pastorum Bethlehemiticorum, Mago- rum ex Oriente, Simeonis item & Hannæ publi- ca deprædicatione manifestatum, Johannea de- monstratione, Andreæ, Philippi, Nathanaelis, aliorumque confessione declaratum, ac discipu- lorum ipsorummet testificatione passim idem de Jesu divulgatum, quod nempe Christus sit filius Dei: Accedente etiam solemni de cælo procla- matione: Ecquis præsumet Deum noluisse, ut hoc publice constaret? missus certe Johannes erat à Deo, ut testificaretur de luce illa omnes homines illuminante, ut OMNES crederent in eam Johan. I. 7. Nec alio fine per miracula & signa Christus gloriam suam manifestabat, quam ut omnes in i- psum crederent Johan. II. 11. Quod ergo Christus interdixit, ne hoc cuiquam dicerent, quod ipse Jesus Christus ille esset, id non tantum accipien- dum ceu interdictum temporarium, sed etiam se- cundum quid explicandum, de plena nempe hujus Doctrinæ prædicatione, ac ne temere promiscua e- jus annunciatione periculum accerserent: siqui- dem nec ipsi ante Resurrectionem & Ascensionem Christi, ac missionem Spiritus Sancti ad hoc præ- conium satis instructi essent, propter opinio- nem præconceptam de regno Messiæ terreno, nec populus ob scandalum status exinanitionis, & mortis imminentis Christi præcipue, idoneus ad doctrinam illam vera ac firma fide suscipiendam. De quo Chrysost. homil. LV. Si discipuli, qui pluri- ma viderunt multaque audierunt arcana, solo audi- tu scandalizati fuerunt, nec ipsi solum, verum etiam & vertex omnium Petrus: cogita nunc tecum, quod vulgus, quæ nihil altius secrete inspexerunt, nulla Spiritus gratia stabiliti fuére, perpessi fuissent, si quem Filium Dei esse didicissent, eum crucifigi, & omni contumelia exagitari viderent. Nec incommode Basilius in Apol. ad Cæsar. Nondum absolverat suum cursum, maluit igitur ex Prophetarum prædi- ctionibus, quam ex Domesticorum testimoniis pro

Messiæ agnosci; de quo B. Ægid. Hunnius in Matth. p. 550. Hoc in confesso est, non spectare inhibitio- nem illam, quod invideat salvificam sui notionem hominibus: sed quantum ex ratione illorum tempo- rum, aliarumque circumstantiarum colligitur, ideo noluit hominibus innotescere, quod nosset cum disci- pulos, tum etiam Judæos reliquos rationem regni Messiæ haud dum intelligere, sed omnino talem sibi ex- poscere Messiam, quem concitata seditione regem sibi constituant, ne freti præsidio ejus jugum Romanæ gentis excutiant, id quod Joh. 6. pridem tentaverant. Quoniam ergo scivit Dominus, vulgus Judæorum abusurum esse hac manifestatione ad moliendum res novas, eo sane tempore, eo etiam loco, iisque homi- nibus, inter quos tum versabatur, se aliquandiu ma- nifestare noluit. Cons. B. Polyc. Lyser. in h. l.

PARS IV. Passionis & resurrectionis Christi prædictio, & Petri contradicentis reprehensio.

## 16:21
Verse 21. that he must] I think the Syrian interprets it best as what was about to be: For here it is not a question of the predetermined counsel of God, or of the utility of the matter, as elsewhere, but a future event is predicted nakedly: and therefore Peter tries to persuade Christ to avoid this very thing, which it is hardly credible he would have done if at that very moment he had understood this to be the predetermined counsel of God. Whoever will have attended diligently to many places of the New Testament will find that δεῖ is not rarely placed in such a way that it signifies nothing other than a future event, as below XXIV. 6, Mark XIII. 7, Rev. I. 1, IV. 1, XXII. 6, Acts IV. 12, so below XVII. 11, Elias must come: which above XI. 14 was is about to come. There is no cause why one should depart from the customary and proper meaning of the word δεῖ: which Grotius also rashly abandons in those places Matthew XXIV. 6, Mark XIII. 7, Acts IV. 12. But that Peter nevertheless desires to persuade Christ to avoid this, indicates the force of a preconceived opinion, and of our nature's blindness in grasping spiritual things even if they are most clearly indicated, and of the reluctance against God, Rom. VIII. 6: which we cannot do unless by the grace of the divine Spirit, to take captive our reason under the obedience of faith, 2 Cor. X. 4. elders] elders here are senators, to the Hebrews זקנים whence the sanhedrin itself is not rarely called a presbytery, Acts XX. 5, Luke XXII. 66, as also elsewhere gerousia with the same meaning: thus the letter of the Spartans is inscribed to the elders and to the priests and to the rest of the people 1 Macc. XIV. 20. And Jonathan is said to have summoned the elders of the people to distinguish them from those who were elders of the cities, namely, judges of lesser causes, such as were not only in other towns, but also in the city of Jerusalem. Although, however, in the same senate there were for the most part also the chief priests, yet these are accustomed to be named specifically on account of their eminent authority. Scribes, however, were present to the senate as assessors. We see these three kinds of men named in a promiscuous order in these books as often as mention is made of the gathered Sanhedrin. and on the third day be raised] Namely, so that thus also it might be fulfilled in detail what had been said metaphorically by Hosea ch. VI. 2, and pre-signified in Isaac who on the third day was as it were restored to life Gen. XXII. Verse 22. taking him aside] Since to take aside in Greek signifies among other things to embrace, it seems to me that that meaning fits this place better than the other, of leading away separately, which pleases many. For by this gesture Peter wished to testify to his highest love for Christ. Nor does the translation, which appears in Rom. XV. 7 and other places, seem to be drawn from elsewhere. God be merciful to you Lord. 8 may this not be to you] To understand the word God, and that this place was not understood otherwise by the Syrian, is demonstrated by others with such clear testimonies that there is no room for doubting. Thus the LXX in Genesis XLIII. 23, God be merciful to you, do not fear: for what follows your God, pertains to the following sense, otherwise than the Vulgate punctuation has it. 1 Sam. XIV. 46, God lives and what follows. 2 Sam. XX. 20, God be merciful to me, God be merciful to me, if I shall drown and destroy. Where if is put for than or that. The writer of the first book of Maccabees ch. II. 21, God be merciful to us to abandon the law and the ordinances, where besides God is understood so that not: but what follows 8 may this not be to you

then is the explanatory part of this locution. For the future is placed in the Hebrew manner for the optative. Therefore this is just as much as if you were to say God forbid, which is how the LXX often translate חלילה which in the places already cited from Samuel and elsewhere they translated God be merciful; as 1 Sam. XXVI. 11, Josh. XXII. 19. For the same is placed by no means to me 1 Sam. XIV. 7. And where they have God be merciful, the versions of others in Greek have God forbid. Thus in Latin, God avert and far be it are worth just as much, which the Latin interpreter has not unlearnedly placed here. Josephus for the same says it is immovable by the word.

Thus rightly Grotius, with the most learned Fuller leading the way: who concerning the Syriac version says: The interpretation of the Syrians, he says, is to be translated entirely, not may you be propitious, or be, but propitious is (God) to you Lord: as if he were saying, he is more propitious to you than that this should happen to you. But Fuller rightly disapproves of those who, following the prejudice of Beza here, together with Erasmus, explain in this place God be merciful to you as may you be propitious to yourself, without any regard for the Syro-Greek idiom, observing especially those words of Josephus God be merciful to you, do not fear, in which it is certain beyond a doubt that no place at all is given to the second person, may you be propitious to yourselves, but the highest necessity compels one to employ the third person, and to understand God himself. Do not fear therefore, he says, the words of the Hebrew truth are peace to you, that is, peace to you: But indeed God be merciful to you is the very formula of the Syrians. He adds that from both joined together is composed that most significant Rabbinic form God be merciful and peace, that is, propitious is (God) and peace, and all things are safe.

Latin:

Vers. 21. ὅτι δεῖ ἀυτὸν] Puto optime interpretari Syrum quod fu- turum esset: Neque enim hic aut de præfinito Dei consilio, aut de utilitate rei agitur, ut alibi, sed res futura nude prædicitur: atque ideo Petrus Christ conatur persua 'ere, ut hoc ipsum evitet, quod vix credibile est facturum fuis- se, si eo ipso momento intellexisset hoc esse præfinitum Dei consilium. Qui diligenter attenderit ad multa loca Novi fœderis inveniet δεῖ ita non raro poni, ut nihil aliud quam rem futuram significet, ut infra XXIV. 6 Marc. XIII. 7. Apoc. I. 1. IV. 1. XXII. 6. Act. IV. 12 ita infra XVII. 11. δεῖ ἐλθεῖν σε Elia: quod supra XI. 14. erat μέλλει ἔρχεσθαι. Nulla est causa, aur ab usitata & propria vocis δεῖ significatione discedatur: quain etiam temere deserit Grotius in istis locis Matth. XXIV. 6. Mar- ci XIII. 7. Actor. IV. 12. Quod autem Petrus ni- hilominus persuadere Christo cupit, ut hoc evi- tet, vim præconceptæ opinionis, & naturæ nostræ cæcitatis in capiendis rebus spiritualibus etsi cla- rissime indicatis, ac reluctantiæ adversus Deum Rom. VIII. 6. indicat: quam non possimus nisi Spiritus divini gratia, captivare rationem nostram sub obsequium fidei, 2. Cor. X. 4. πρεσβυτέρων] πρεσβύτεροι hic sunt senatores, Hebræis זקנים unde συνέδριον ipsum non raro πρεσβυτέριον voca- tur, Actor. XX. 5. Luc. XXII. 66. ut & alibi γερουσία signi- ficatu eodem: ita epistola Spartiararum inscribitur τοῖς πρεσβυτέροις καὶ τοῖς ἱερεῦσι καὶ τῷ λοιπῷ δήμῳ 1 Marc XIV. 20. Et Jonathan dicitur convocasse τὲς πρεσβυτέρους τῶ λαῶ ad di- scrimen eorum qui erant πρεσβύτεροι τῶν πόλεων, judices sci- licet minorum causarum, quales erant non in aliis tantum oppidis, sed & in urbe Hierosolymorum. Quanquam a- tem in eodem senatu plerumque erant & Sacerdotum prin- cipes, tamen solent hi peculiariter nominari ob eminentem auctoritatem. Γραμματεῖς autem tanquam adsessores ad- erant Senatui. Tria hæc hominum genera videmus ordi- ne promiscuo in his libris nominari quoties Synedrii coacti fit mentio. κὶ τῇ τρίτῃ ἡμέρᾳ ἐγερθῆναι] Nimirum ut sic etiam κα- τὰ πόδας impleretur quod μεταφορικῶς dictum erat ab Osea cap. VI. 2. & præsignificatum in Isaaco qui die tertio quasi in vitam fuit restitutus Gen. XXII. Vers. 22. προσλαβόμενος] Cum προσλαμβάνεσθαι Græ- ce inter cætera complecti significet, videtur mihi ea signifi- catio huic loco melius convenire, quam altera, seorsim ab- ducendi, quæ multis placet. Hoc enim gestu summum suum amorem in Christum testari Petrus voluit. Neque a- liunde ducta videtur translatio, quæ Rom. XV. 7. aliisque in locis apparet. ἵλεώς σοι κύριε. 8 μὴ ἴσαι σοι τῦτο] Subaudiri vocem Θεὸς, neque aliter intellectum hunc locum a Syro, tam per- spicuis testimoniis ab aliis demonstratum ut nullus sit du- bitandi locus. Ita LXX. Genes. XLIII. 23. ἵλεως ὑμῖν, μὴ φοβεῖσθε: nam quod sequitur ὁ Θεὸς ὑμῶν, ad sequentem sen- sum pertinet secus quain habet vulgata distinctio. 1. Sam. XIV. 46. ἵλεως ζῇ κύριος & quæ sequuntur. 2. Sam. XX. 20. ἵλεως μοι, ἵλεως μοι, εἰ καταποντιῶ κὶ διαφθερῶ. ubi εἰ posi- tum est pro quam ut. Scriptor Maccabæorum primi cap. II. 21. ἵλεως ἡμῖν καταλιπεῖν νόμον καὶ δικαιώματα, ubi præter Θεὸς subauditur ὥσε μὴ: quod autem sequitur 8 μὴ ἴση σοι

τότε est hujus locutionis ἐξηγητικὸν. Futurum enim more Hebræo positum est pro optativo. Tantundem ergo hoc est quasi dicas μὴ γένοιτο, quomodo LXX. sæpe vertunt חלילה quod locis jam citatis è Samuele & alibi verte- runt ἵλεως; ut 1. Sam. XXVI. 11. Jos. XXII. 19. Pro eodem ponitur μηδαμῶς ἐμοί 1. Sam. XIV. 7. Et ubi illi habet ἵλεως, aliorum versiones Græce habent μὴ γένοιτο. Ita Latine, tantundem valent Avertat Deus, & absit, quod hic non inerudite posuit Latinus interpres. Josephus pro eodem dicit ἀκίνη παρὰ τῷ λόγῳ.

Ita rectè Grotius præeunte doctissimo Fullero: qui de Syriaca versione: Syri, inquit, interpre- tatio omnino transferenda, non propitius sis, vel esto, sed propitius est (Deus) tibi Domine: qua- si dicat, magis tibi propitius est, quam ut hoc ti- bi accidat. Improbat autem merito Fullerus eos qui præjudicium Bezæ hic sequuti una cum Era- smo exponunt hoc loco ἵλεώς σοι propitius tibi sis, absque ullo idiomatis Syro-Græci respectu, ob- servans imprimis verba illa Josephi ἵλεως ὑμῖν, μὴ φοβεῖσθε, in quibus certo certius est locum omni- no nullum dari secundæ personæ, propitii sitis vo- bis ipsis, sed summa necessitas cogit personam tertiam adhibere, & Deum ipsum subintelligere. Ne metuite igitur, inquit, verba Hebraicæ veri- tatis sunt שלום לכם id est pax vobis: At enim ἵλεως ὑμῖν ipsissima est formula Syrorum חסלכון. Addit ex utrisque conjunctis composi- tam esse formam illam Rabbinicam significantissi- mam חסי ושלום id est propitius est (Deus) & pax, & salva sunt omnia.

## 16:23
Vers. 23. Στραφεὶς] Here στραφεὶς seems to denote a countenance composed for greater severity. Thus in Luke IX. 55, τραφεὶς δὲ ἐπετίμησεν αὐτοῖς. For there too there were none others whom he was addressing than the disciples; as also here: nor indeed did Christ look upon Peter alone but upon all the disciples when he said these things, as we learn from Mark. Thus also in John XX. 16, στραφεῖσα indicates a change of mind or countenance. And in Acts XVI. 18, ἐπιστρέψας τῷ πνεύματι is more moved in spirit. And the same is the meaning of the word ἐπιστρέψαντα. Acts XXII. 40. See also above VII. 6. The Hebrew הפנה, which the Syriac translator has placed here, is accustomed to have the same meanings.

Ὕπαγε ὀπίσω μου] See above IV. 10. ὀπίσω μου, that is, out of my sight.

Σατανᾶ] It appears that this word שׂטנא was already pronounced in Christ's age. For the Hebrew is שטן, which the LXX rendered sometimes as ἐπίβουλον (as in 2 Sam. XIX. 22, 3 Kings V. 4), sometimes as διάβολον, as in Psalm CIX. 5. They retained the Hebrew word with the same meaning as it is placed here in 2 Kings XI. 14, καὶ ἐξήγειρε κύριος σατᾶν τῷ σολομῶντι τὸν Ἁδὲρ τὸν ἰδουμαῖον, which passage Tertullian, citing from the Greek in Against Marcion III, says: For he will raise up Satan, he says, that is, an enemy. Wherefore it is not surprising that the Hebrew word was retained by Matthew's interpreter, since it was in use among the Hellenists as well. Christ shows that Peter, under the guise of love, was in reality an adversary to him, and he gives the reason, ὅτι οὐ φρονεῖς τὰ τοῦ Θεοῦ ἀλλὰ τὰ τῶν ἀνθρώπων. For the mind of the flesh is enmity against God, Rom. VIII. 7.

Mira hic Hilarii, notante Heinsio, subtilitas, who, in order to remove the name of Satan from Peter along with St. Jerome and others, punctuates this passage thus: ἄπαγε ὀπίσω μου. Σατανᾶ, σκάνδαλόν μου εἶ, so that ἄπαγε ὀπίσω μου is said to Peter; the rest to the devil. But, he says, the Lord, knowing the instinct of the diabolical art, says to Peter, Go back behind me, that is, that he might follow him by the example of his passion. But turning to him through whom this opinion was suggested, he added, Satan, you are a scandal to me. For it is not fitting to think that both the name of Satan and the offense of scandal are attributed to Peter, after those great proclamations of granted blessedness and power: but because all infidelity is the work of the Devil, the Lord, offended by Peter's response, with the reproach of the name, detested the author of that infidelity. And in the same way Chrysologus, Homily XXVII. Unde Dominus servum post se mittit, scandalum remittit autori: dicendo ad Petrum, Vade post me; & Diabolo, Satana, scandalum mihi es. Simplicius Chrysostomus, qui & ita dici

He means Peter, and deservedly so, ὡς ἀθετοῦντα τὸ τοῦ σταυροῦ τὸ μυστήριον, because he either did not sufficiently value, or attempted to hinder, the mystery of the cross. And he speaks distinctly, ᾧ ἐπετίμησε τῷ Πέτρῳ κὶ Σατανᾶν ἐκάλεσεν, and he rebuked and called Peter Satan, who was so gravely לשטן, that is, an offense to the Lord. Yet one should not agree with Heinsius in the point that he thinks the word שטן denotes nothing other than scandal and offense here: for that Σατανᾶ and σκάνδαλον are openly distinguished, and שטן properly denotes an adversary: but σκάνδαλον an offense: and in that, Peter was truly an adversary to Christ, and at the same time, as much as in him lay, he wished to be an offense and a hindrance, so that what he had undertaken to perform might not be performed, since he was attempting to turn the Lord away from his passion.

Σκάνδαλόν μου εἶ] As much as in you lies, you cast upon me a horror of ignominy, of torments, and of death: which horror it appears was at times greater, at times lesser, in the flesh of Christ. See below XXVI. 38. Heb. II. 18. IV. 15. Moreover, this σκάνδαλόν μου εἶ is an explanation of the word σατανᾶ. For even thus those who led the Jews away from the observance of the law are said to have been made εἰς Διάβολον τῷ Ἰσραήλ 2 Macc. I. 37. which is explained in the same place as εἰς παγίδα, εἰς ἔνεδρον and V. 4. εἰς παγίδα καὶ εἰς σκάνδαλον.

Grotius attempts to soften τὰ σκληρὰ of Peter, and the things said against Peter: Christ did not mean that he himself was affected by a scandal, because Christ could not be scandalized, or that Peter cast upon him a horror of ignominy, of torments, and of death, but that he spoke those things which were by their nature apt to beget scandal, and that he opposed himself to his own calling and the divine decree, which is in truth a scandal given, and therefore a grave prevarication, worthy of being beaten back with such harshness. To this contributes the observation that scandals and seductions are not always to be estimated by their effect, but by their own nature and condition; what they are in themselves, and what they could effect, unless they are warded off or prevented from elsewhere. Therefore also the word Satan cannot be softened as Grotius thinks: for he calls Peter Satan because by his dissuasion, as much as in him lay, he stood in the way of and opposed that which had been decreed by the heavenly Father, and thus performed the part of Satan himself. Concerning which Chrysostom: for as Satan, which word sounds adversary, did not want Christ to suffer, so neither does Peter now: whence Christ called him Satan. And even from this fall of Peter, and this rebuke of Christ, it is evident that Peter is not the rock and foundation of the Church, against which the gates of hell cannot prevail: since he prevaricated so gravely that he was held worthy of the nomenclature of Satan. Shall we make Satan, who opposes himself to Christ, the vicar of Christ, the Oecumenical head of the whole Christian world in the place of Christ, and the foundation of the Church of Christ, which neither Satan nor any infernal power can overcome?

Ὅτι ὀ φρονεῖς τὰ τοῦ Θεοῦ, ἀλλὰ τὰ τῶν ἀνθρώπων] He now demonstrates to him, whom he had just before declared blessed, how infirm he still is, so that recognizing his disease he might seek a remedy from God. Moreover, φρονεῖν in this and other places signifies not arrogance but the inclination of the mind. Thus we say in Greek Φρονῶ σοι φίλα, Φρονῶ σοι κακά, Φρονεῖν τὰ δέοντα: nor do the Hellenists otherwise. Thus the writer of the first book of Maccabees X. 20 said φρονεῖν τὰ ἡμῶν, Josephus Φρονεῖν τὰ ῥωμαίων XIV. Origines X. Φρονεῖν τὰ τῶν ἀνθρώπων is what Paul said Φρονεῖν τὰ τῆς σαρκὸς, to care for and value highly those things which pertain to the comforts of this life, neglecting the business of God, which ought to be more important to us than all comforts, as Christ explains in the following words.

Concerning which Casaubon more fully: I do not see how arrogance and a false persuasion about himself can be gathered from the words of Peter: nor, I think, is Peter rebuked by our Lord on this account, which learned men conjecture from the word Φρονεῖν. And so I would also wish to avoid the word 'to be wise' in interpreting, since it is sufficiently known to those skilled in the Greek language that τὸ φρονεῖν is often translated quite incorrectly. Finally, I think that φρονεῖν τὰ τοῦ Θεοῦ is nothing other than to estimate things not by the will and decree of God, but by the sense of the flesh and the judgment of men: since it is certain that the ways of the Lord are not as the ways of men: which, however, that it was little known even to the Apostles themselves before the resurrection of Christ, almost infinite passages of these books teach. They seem to me to do an injury to Peter who gather his arrogance from the word φρονεῖν: which, as I think, was none: although ancient interpreters note in many places the highest θερμότητα in that holy man: but one most alien from all pride and arrogance. Theophylact feels no differently, whose words I am pleased to add: Τὰ τῶν ἀνθρώπων δὲ ἔφησε φρονεῖν τὸν Πέτρον, καθὸ ταπεινά τινα φρονῶν & σαρκικὰ ἤθελεν ἐν ἀνέσει εἶναι τὸν Κύριον, καὶ μὴ σταυρωθῆναι.

PART V. Information concerning the following of Christ.

Latin:

Vers. 23. Στραφεὶς] Videtur hic στραφεὶς denotare vul- tum ad majorem severitatem compositum. Ita Lucæ IX. 55. τραφεὶς δὲ ἐπετίμησεν αὐτοῖς. Nam ibi quoque nulli alii erant quos alloqueretur, quam discipuli; ut & hic: neque vero Petrum solum sed discipulos omnes intuitus est Christus, cum hæc diceret, ut ex Marco discimus. Ita & apud Johan- nem XX. 16. στραφεῖσα animi aut vultus immutationem in- dicat. Et Actorum XVI. 18. ἐπιστρέψας τῷ πνεύματι est animo commotior. Eademque significatio est vocis ἐπιστρέψαντα. Act. XXII. 40. Vide & supra VII. 6. Solet easdem significa- tiones habere Hebræum הפנה quod hic posuit Syrus.

Ὕπαγε ὀπίσω μου] Vide supra IV. 10. ὀπίσω μου id est extra conspectum meum.

Σατανᾶ] Apparet jam Christi sæculo enuntiatam hanc vocem שׂטנא. Nam Hebræum est שטן quod LXX. mo- do ἐπίβουλον (ut 2. Sam. XIX. 22. 3. Reg. V. 4.) modo διά- βολον reddiderunt, ut Psal. CIX 5. Hebræam vocem reti- nuerunt eodem quo hic ponitur significatu 2. Reg. XI. 14. καὶ ἐξήγειρε κύριος σατᾶν τῷ σολομῶντι τὸν Ἁδὲρ τὸν ἰδουμαῖον, quem locum ex Græco citans Tertullianus adversus Mar- cionem III. Suscitabit enim ille Satan, inquit, id est hostem. Quare mirum non est à Matthæi interprete retentam vo- cem Hebræam, cum esset ea & Hellenistis in usu. Ostendit Christus Petrum, amoris specie, reve a sibi esse adversato- rem, causamque reddit, ὅτι οὐ φρονεῖς τὰ τοῦ Θεοῦ ἀλλὰ τὰ τῶν ἀνθρώπων. Nam τὸ φρόνημα τῆς σαρκὸς ἔχθρα εἰς Θεὸν, Rom. VIII. 7.

Mira hic Hilarii, notante Heinsio, subtilitas, qui ut cum B. Hieronymo & aliis nomen Satanæ à Petro removeret, ita locum hunc distinguit, ἄπαγε ὀπίσω μου. Σατανᾶ, σκάνδαλόν μου εἶ, ut τὸ, ἄπαγε ὀπίσω μου Petro; cætera diabolo dicantur. Sed sciens, inquit, Dominus diabolicæ artis instinctum, Pe- tro ait, Vade retro post me, id est, ut exemplo se passionis sequatur. In eum vero per quem opinio hæc suggerebatur, conversus, adjecit, Satana, scan- dalum mihi es. Non enim convenit existimare, Pe- tro & Satanæ nomen & offensionem scandali de- putari, post illa indultæ & beatitudinis & potesta- tis tanta præconia: sed quia infidelitas omnis Dia- boli opus est, Petri responsione Dominus offen- sus, cum opprobrio nominis, infidelitatis istius est detestatus autorem. Eodemque modo Chrysologus, Homil. XXVII. Unde Dominus servum post se mit- tit, scandalum remittit autori: dicendo ad Petrum, Vade post me; & Diabolo, Satana, scandalum mi- hi es. Simplicius Chrysostomus, qui & ita dici

Petrum, & merito quidem, vult, ὡς ἀθετοῦντα τὸ τοῦ σταυ- ροῦ τὸ μυστήριον, quod vel non satis æstimaret, vel impedire crucis conaretur mysterium. Et difer- te, ᾧ ἐπετίμησε τῷ Πέτρῳ κὶ Σατανᾶν ἐκάλεσεν, & increpuit & Satanam vocavit Petrum, qui tam gra- viter לשטן, hoc est, offendiculo esset Domino. Nec tamen Heinsio assensus in eo præbendus, quod vo- cem שטן nihil aliud quam scandalum & offendi- culum hic notare censet: nam aperte distinguitur illud Σατανᾶ & σκάνδαλον, & proprie שטן adver- sarium notat: σκάνδαλον vero offendiculum: inque eo erat vere adversarius Christo Petrus, ac simul offendiculo & impedimento, quantum in ipso fuit, esse volebat, ne id quod susceperat exequen- dum exequeretur, quum convertere Dominum à passione conaretur.

Σκάνδαλόν μου εἶ] Quantum in te est, horrorem mi- hi ignominiæ, cruciatuum & mortis injicis: quem hor- rorem in Christi carne modo majorem, modo minorem fuisse apparet. Vide infra XXVI. 38. Hebr. II. 18. IV. 15. Est autem hoc σκάνδαλόν μου εἶ explicatio vocis σατανᾶ. Nam & sic qui Judæos à legis observatione abducebant dicuntur facti εἰς Διάβολον τῷ Ἰσραήλ 2. Macc. I. 37. quod ibidem exponitur εἰς παγίδα, εἰς ἔνεδρον & V. 4. εἰς παγίδα καὶ εἰς σκάνδαλον.

Emollire conatur Grotius τὰ σκληρὰ Petri, & adversus Petrum dicta: non id Christus volebat, quod se scandalo afficiat, quia Christus scandaliza- ri non poterat, vel quod sibi horrorem, ignomi- niæ, cruciatuum & mortis injiciat Petrus, sed quod ea loquatur, quæ apta nata per se erant scan- dalum gignere, & quod vocationi suæ & decreto divino se opponat, quod revera est scandalum da- tum, adeoque gravis prævaricatio, digna, quæ tanta asperitate retundatur. Quo facit observa- tio, quod scandala & seductiones non semper æsti- mentur ex effectu, sed ex natura & conditione pro- pria; qualia per se sint, & quid efficere possint, nisi aliunde depellantur, aut præpediantur. Ideo etiam verbum Satanæ ita emolliri nequit, uti censet Grotius: Satanam enim vocat Petrum, quod sua dehortatione, quantum in ipso erat, obstaret, & adversaretur illi, quod à cœlesti Patre decretum erat, atque sic ipsius Satanæ partes obiret. Quo de Chrystost. ut enim Satanas, quæ vox sonat adver- sarium, nolebat pati Christum, ita neque nunc Pe- trus: unde ipsum Satanam vocavit Christus. Et vel ex hoc Petri lapsu, & hac Christi reprehensione constat, Petrum non esse petram, & fundamen- tum Ecclesiæ, adversus quod nec portæ inferorum prævalere possint: siquidem tam graviter prævari- catus est, ut Satanæ nomenclatura dignus habere- tur. Num Satanam Christo se opponentem vica- rium Christi, Oecumenicum caput totius Chri- stiani orbis loco Christi, & Ecclesiæ Christi funda- mentum faciamus, quod nec Satanas, nec ulla in- fernalis potestas superare possit?

Ὅτι ὀ φρονεῖς τὰ τοῦ Θεοῦ, ἀλλὰ τὰ τῶν ἀνθρώπων] Quem jam modo beatum prædicaverat, ei nunc quam sit adhuc infirmus, demonstrat, ut morbum agnoscens à Deo reme- dium expeteret. Φρονεῖν autem & hoc & aliis in locis non ar- rogantiam sed animi studium significat. Ita Græce dicimus Φρονῶ σοι φίλα, Φρονῶ σοι κακά, Φρονεῖν τὰ δέοντα: neque ali- ter Hellenistæ. Ita φρονεῖν τὰ ἡμῶν dixit Scriptor Maccabæo- rum primi X. 20. Josephus Φρονεῖν τὰ ῥωμαίων XIV. Origi- num Χ. Φρονεῖν τὰ τῶν ἀνθρώπων est quod Paulus dixit Φρονεῖν τὰ τῆς σαρκὸς ea curare magnique facere quæ ad vitæ hujus commoda pertinent, posthabitis Dei negotiis, quæ nobis o- mnibus commodis esse debent potiora, ut sequentibus ver- bis Christus explicat.

Quo de uberius Casaubonus: Non video qua- nam ex verbis Petri arrogantia, & falsa de se per- suasio possit colligi: neque hoc, opinor, nomine repre- henditur à Domino nostro Petrus, quod docti viri conjiciunt ex verbo Φρονεῖν. Itaque etiam verbum sapere vitare interpretando velim, quum satis no- tum sit Græcæ linguæ peritis, ita sæpe parum recte ver- ti τὸ φρονεῖν. Denique e φρονεῖν τὰ τοῦ Θεοῦ, nihil puto esse aliud, quam res æstimare non ex voluntate & decreto Dei, sed ex sensu carnis & hominum judicio: quum certum sit vias Domini non esse, sicut sunt viæ hominum: quod tamen ante Christi resurrectionem, parum fuisse ne ipsis quidem Apostolis cognitum, infi- niti fere horum librorum loci docent. Omnino inju- riam Petro facere mihi videntur, qui ex verbo φρο- νεῖν ejus arrogantiam colligunt: quæ ut puto nulla fuit: quanquam θερμότητα summam in eo sancto viro multis locis notant veteres interpretes: sed ab omni fastu & arrogantia alienissimam. Theophylactus non aliter sentit, cujus verba placet adscribere: Τὰ τῶν ἀνθρώπων δὲ ἔφησε φρονεῖν τὸν Πέτρον, καθὸ ταπεινά τινα φρονῶν & σαρκικὰ ἤθελεν ἐν ἀνέσει εἶναι τὸν Κύριον, καὶ μὴ σταυρωθῆναι.

PARS V. De Christi sequela informatio.

## 16:24
Vers. 24. ὀπίσω μου ἐλθεῖν] That is, πορεύεσθαι; For the Hellenists say πορεύεσθαι for ἀκολουθεῖν, as Jerem. II. 25. and elsewhere passim. Wherefore in this clause the same thing is expressed by two locutions, one Hellenistic, the other Greek. For the sense is: He who wishes to follow me, let him renounce himself, and take up his cross upon his shoulders, so that he may truly be able to follow me.

ἀπαρνησάσθω ἑαυτὸν] A translation taken from those who desert the party of someone, and openly profess it. Thus ἀρνεῖσθαι is used figuratively of such desertion which is not indeed in words but in the thing itself, 2 Tim. II. 11. Tit. I. 16. Heb. XI. 24. 2 Pet. II. 1. Jude 4. This ἀπαρνεῖσθαι ἑαυτὸν is therefore כחש, which in Luke is μισεῖν τὴν ἑαυτοῦ ψυχὴν, chap. XIV. 26. Moreover, Christ speaks according to the opinion of the common people, which he then refutes. For he is commonly called a deserter of himself and a spendthrift of himself, who does not preserve the comforts of life, and life itself, with every effort. Φιλαύτους καλᾶσιν, says Aristotle in Ethics IX. chapter VIII. those who assign to themselves the greater share in money and honors and bodily pleasures; for the many desire these. But he himself argues on the contrary that that should be called τὸ κυριώτατον (the most authoritative) which is chief in man, and that he who loves this and favors this is most a lover of self, even if he must die for it. Whether this opinion can be rightly defended by a Philosopher who acknowledges no rewards or punishments after this life is not without reason doubted. Augustine certainly says that if those rewards and punishments were removed, the truth would stand on the side of Epicurus. The Apostle himself, after so many gifts received from God, says, if in this life only we have our hope placed in Christ, we are of all men most miserable. Many praise that saying of Antigonus, from which Sadduceeism is said to have arisen: nor do I deny that he could have thought more rightly than those who have abused this saying. But the merciful God, just as He says it is the mark of slaves to be deterred from evil only by the fear of present punishment, and of base minds to perform duty for the hope of perishable things, so He perpetually places before our eyes that true heavenly and eternal reward. Indeed, the divine Writer to the Hebrews places the very substance of religion in this, that we acknowledge ὅτι Θεός ἐστι καὶ ὅτι τοῖς ἐκζητοῦσιν αὐτὸν μισθαποδότης γίνεται (that God exists and that He becomes a rewarder to those who seek Him). Christ also in this passage invites us to make a loss of mortal things, and of life itself if need be, by this argument, that in that loss the greatest gain is situated.

ἀράτω τὸν σταυρὸν αὐτοῦ] Let him take up his cross: in which sense it was said above λαμβάνειν σταυρὸν (to take the cross), chap. X. 38, elsewhere βαστάζειν (to bear); this is, let him not refuse the evils which are brought upon him for the sake of piety. For it is of this kind of evils that we are properly treating here.

Latin:

Vers. 24. ὀπίσω μου ἐλθεῖν] Id est, πορεύεσθαι; Nam πορεύε- σθαι dicunt Hellenistæ pro ἀκολουθεῖν, ut Jerem. II. 25. & a- libi passim. Quare in hoc commate duabus locutionibus, altera Hellenistica, altera Græca res eadem exprimitur. Sen- sus enim est: Qui me sequi vult, se abdicet, crucemque in humeros suos tollat, ut vere sequi me possit.

ἀπαρνησάσθω ἑαυτὸν] Translatio sumta ab iis qui par- tes alicujus deserunt, idque palam profitentur. Ita ἀρνεῖ- σθαι de tali desertione quæ non verbis quidem sed re ipsa sit, figurate usurpatur, 2. Tim. II. 11. Tit. I. 16. Hebr. XI. 24. 2. Pet. II. 1. Judæ 4. Est ergo hic ἀπαρνεῖσθαι ἑαυτὸν כחש, quod apud Lucam μισεῖν τὴν ἑαυτοῦ ψυχὴν, cap. XIV. 26. Lo- quitur autem Christus ex vulgi opinione, quam deinde re- fellit. Nam is vulgo desertor sui suique prodigus dicitur, qui vitæ commoda, vitamque ipsam non omni studio conser- vat. Φιλαύτους καλᾶσιν, inquit Aristoteles de moribus IX. ca- pite VIII. τοὺς ἑαυτοῖς ἀπονέμοντας τὸ πλεῖον ἐν χρήμασι καὶ τι- μαῖς καὶ ἡδοναῖς ταῖς σωματικαῖς· τούτων γὰρ οἱ πολλοὶ ὀρέγονται. At ipse contra disputat hominem dici debere τὸ κυριώτατον quod in homine præcipuum est, κἀγὼ τοῦτο ἀγαπῶντα καὶ τοῦτο χαριζόμενον μάλισα φίλαυτον εἶναι, κἂν δέῃ ὑπεραποθνή- σκειν. Quæ sententia an recte defendi possit a Philosopho nulla agnoscente præmia pœnasve post hanc vitam, non immerito dubitatur. Augustinus certe, sublatis illis præ- miis pœnisque verum staturum ait à partibus Epicuri. Ipse Apostolus, post tot accepta à Deo dona, si in hac vita tan- tum, inquit, in Christo spem nostram habemus repositam, omnibus hominibus miseriores sumus. Laudant multi di- ctum illud Antigoni, unde ortus dicitur Saducæismus: ne- que nego potuisse illum rectius sentire, quam qui hoc dicto abusi sunt. At misericors Deus, sicut mancipiorum esse ait sola pœnæ præsentis formidine malis absterreri, & ingenio- rum fatis vilium, spe rerum caducarum officium facere, ita veram illam cœlestem atque æternam mercedem perpetuo nobis ob oculos ponit. Imo divinus ad Hebræos Scriptor religionis ipsam velut substantiam in eo locat ut agnosca- mus ὅτι Θεός ἐστι καὶ ὅτι τοῖς ἐκζητοῦσιν αὐτὸν μισθαποδότης γίνε- ται. Christus quoque hoc loco nos ad faciendam rerum mortalium, vitæque ipsius, si opus sit, jacturam hoc argumen- to invitat, quod in ea jactura maximum situm sit lucrum.

ἀράτω τὸν σταυρὸν αὐτοῦ] Suscipiat crucem suam: quo sensu supra dictum est λαμβάνειν σταυρὸν, cap. X. 38. alibi ba- στάζειν; hoc est ne detrectet mala quæ ipsi inferuntur ob cau- sam pietatis. Nam de hoc malorum genere proprie hic agitur.

## 16:25
Vers. 25. ψυχὴν (soul)] In what sense we think ψυχὴν should be taken here, we have said regarding the similar sentiment in chap. X. 38.

Latin:

Vers. 25. ψυχὴν] Qua notione ψυχὴν hic putemus acci- piendam diximus ad sententiam similem cap. X. 38.

## 16:26
Vers. 26. Τὴν δὲ ψυχὴν αὐτοῦ ζημιωθῇ (and lose his own soul)] When it is a matter of judgments, the Greeks say ζημιοῦν θανάτῳ (to punish with death), but not ζημιοῦν τὸν βίον (to punish the life). Nothing seems to me more certain than that ζημίαν (loss) is here simply opposed to τῷ κέρδει (gain), as in Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics V, chap. VII; it has the same value as הפסד (loss) in the Syriac. The old interpreter therefore translates it well.

Ἢ τί δώσει ἄνθρωπος ἀντάλλαγμα τῆς ψυχῆς αὐτοῦ (Or what shall a man give in exchange for his soul)] In Hebrew it would have been מחיר (price), or also כפר (ransom), for which the LXX is accustomed to put ἐξίλασμα (propitiation) or λύτρον (ransom). For just as the LXX sometimes say ἐξίλασμα for the price of redemption, so conversely the Writer of Ecclesiasticus XLIV. 17 said ἀντάλλαγμα (exchange), where it should properly have been said ἐξίλασμα. For these are of near meaning. It is without doubt a proverb worn out in that age, and as I think taken from that of Job, וכל אשר לאיש יתן בעד נפשו (and all that a man has he will give for his soul), where the LXX: καὶ πάντα ὅσα ὑπάρχει ἀνθρώπῳ ὑπὲρ τῆς ψυχῆς αὐτοῦ ἐκτίσει (and all that belongs to a man he will pay for his soul): where indeed they rightly expressed the force of τοῦ ἀνταλλάγματος (the exchange) by ἐκτίσει (he will pay). Note also the Hebraism in that τί δώσει (what shall he give), for it is taken in place of the potential, as in that passage of Job, and τί is an emphatic question, as when it is said מה־אדיר שמך where the LXX says: how wonderful is your name: others: how great is your name. Therefore, what will he give is how much would he gladly give, how many and how great things would a man give, placed in danger of death, for the sake of preserving himself? But Christ adapts this proverb most excellently to his own purpose, for he argues from this temporary life to that eternal life. For if we think that all things which we possess are rightly spent so that we may preserve ourselves in this life, certainly much more are all the same things, and this very mortal life itself, to be spent so that we may arrive at the immortal life, which surpasses this life infinitely more than this life surpasses all things which we possess. I do not think it is to be doubted that this is the truest interpretation of this passage, which shows most excellently the coherence of what follows. Similar to this maxim of the Hebrews are those existing among the Greeks, such as: For there is nothing more precious than the soul. And that of Sophocles: For living, O child, is the sweetest prize of all. And of Quintus Smyrnaeus: For there is nothing else dearer to men than the soul.

Latin:

Vers. 26. Τὴν δὲ ψυχὴν αὐτοῦ ζημιωθῇ] Cum de judiciis a- gitur, dicunt Græci ζημιοῦν θανάτῳ, non autem ζημιοῦν τὸν βίον. Nihil mihi videtur certius, quam ζημίαν hic simplici- te opponi τῷ κέρδει, ut apud Aristotelem de moribus V. cap. VII, idem valet הפסד apud Syrum. Bene ergo vertit vetus interpres.

Ἢ τί δώσει ἄνθρωπος ἀντάλλαγμα τῆς ψυχῆς αὐτοῦ] In Hebræo fuerit מחיר, aut etiam כפר, pro quo LXX. so- let ponere ἐξίλασμα aut λύτρον. Nam sicut LXX. pro pretio redemtionis dicunt interdum ἐξίλασμα, ita vicissim Scri- ptor Ecclesiastici XLIV. 17. ἀντάλλαγμα dixit, ubi proprie dicendum erat ἐξίλασμα. Sunt enim hæc vicinæ fignificatio- nis. Proverbium est haud dubie tritum eo sæculo, & ut puto sumtum ex illo Jobi וכל אשר לאיש יתן בעד נפשו ubi LXX. καὶ πάντα ὅσα ὑπάρχει ἀνθρώπῳ ὑπὲρ τῆς ψυχῆς αὐ- τοῦ ἐκτίσει: ubi vero ἐκτίσει recte expresserunt vim τοῦ ἀν- ταλλάγματος. Notandus & Hebraismus in illo τί δώσει, nam & sumtum est loco δυνητικῷ, ut in illo Jobi loco, & τί est ἐρώτημα ἀυξητικὸν, ut cum dicitur מה־אדיר שמך ubi LXX. ὡς θαυμαςὸν τὸ ὀνομά σου: alii τί μέγα τὸ ὄνομά σου. Ergo τί δώσει est πόσα ἂν δώῃ quam multa ac magna liben- ter daret homo in mortis periculo constitutus sui conser- vandi gratia? Optime autem Christus proverbium hoc suo instituto aptat, argumentatur enim à vita hac temporaria ad vitam illam æternam. Nam si omnia quæ possidemus arbitramur recte impendi ut nosmetipsos in hac vita serve- mus, certe multo magis eadem omnia, ipsaque hæc morta- lis vita impendenda sunt, ut ad vitam immortalem per- veniamus, quæ infinito amplius hanc vitam superat, quam vita hæc omnia quæ possidemus. Dubitandum non puto, quin hæc sit verissima hujus loci interpretatio, quæ optime monstrat sequentium cohærentiam. Huic Hebræorum γνώ- μῃ exstant similes apud Græcos, ut Ψυχῆς γὰρ ὀυδέν ἐστι τιμιώτερον. Et illud Sophoclis: Τὸ ζῇν γὰρ, ὦ παῖ, παντὸς ἥδισον γέρας. Et Quinti Smyrnæi: Οὐ γάρ τι ψυχῆς πέλει ἀνδράσι φίλτερον ἄλλο.

## 16:27
Verse 27. in the glory of his Father] The same glory is called both the glory of Christ, Matt. 25:30, and the glory of the Father, because it is from the Father, John 17:5. And thus perhaps that passage in John 1:14 is to be interpreted, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, so that 'given' is to be understood: We saw his glory such as parents are accustomed to give to only children. See what is there.

The glory of Christ is not called the glory of the Father only because it is from the Father by reason of origin, but because it is the very same glory which is proper to the Father by reason of essence: because it is not a finite glory, such as that of a man or of any angel, which is granted to them by God the Father; but truly immense and infinite, and therefore the very glory of God the Father itself, because the Son and the Father are one in essence and glory, John 10:30, and from eternity the Son of God had that glory, John 17:5. But from eternity there was nothing finite: but eternal glory is truly immense and infinite glory. That interpretation of the illustrious passage in John 1:14, 'we saw his glory such as parents are accustomed to give to only children,' is too meager. Nor does the preposition 'para' connect with the more remote noun 'glory,' but with the closer 'only-begotten,' because in truth that glory which Christ manifested was that which is of the only-begotten Son of God, who alone and uniquely is begotten from the Father and from the essence of the Father. For the particle 'as' is not of comparison in this place, but corresponds to the Hebrew 'kaph' or of truth. Therefore Chrysostom, homily 56 on Matthew: 'He saw how the glory is one of the Father and the Son: but if the glory is one, it is evident that the essence is also one.'

with his angels] The Hebrews were accustomed to describe God dealing with great matters after the example of a King sitting in an assembly of nobles: as in 1 Kings 22 and as can be seen in the Chaldean paraphrast on the first chapter of Job. And thus indeed they explain that anthropopathically: let us make man. See also Deut. 33:2 and Dan. 7:10.

according to his deed] as his work, Psalm 62:13, according to the works, Rom. 2:6, according to his own labor, 1 Cor. 3:8, according to what he has done, whether good or evil, 2 Cor. 5:10, which passages, and especially that one in 1 Cor. 3:8, seem to show not only a differing outcome for the good and the evil, but also degrees of rewards no less than of punishments. Concerning the degrees of punishments, the passages above, 11:22, 24, are illustrious. Concerning the degrees of rewards, that which is in Paul, 1 Cor. 15:41, is usually understood. Clement of Alexandria, Stromata 4: 'For there are with the Lord both rewards and many mansions according to the proportions of lives.' And there is no doubt that this was the constant opinion of all Christian writers. But we must understand 'deed' here as every act of man in which goodness or malice has a place: especially the internal: the external insofar as it corresponds to the internal.

Latin:

Vers. 27. ἐν τῇ δόξῃ τοῦ πατρὸς ἀυτοῦ] Eadem gloria voca- tur & Christi gloria, Matth. XXV. 30. & Patris gloria, quia est à Patre, Johan. XVII. 5. Atque ita forte interpretan- dum illud Joh. I. 19. δόξαν ὡς μονογενοῦς παρὰ πατρὸς, ut sub- audiatur δοθεῖσαν: Vidimus gloriam ejus talem, qualem pa- rentes dare solent filiis unicis. Vide quæ ibi.

Gloria Christi non tantum ideo gloria Patris dicitur, quod à Patre sit originis ratione, sed quod eadem ipsa sit gloria, quæ Patri propria est, ratio- ne quidditatis: quia non gloria est finita, qualis hominis, aut Angeli alicujus, quæ à Deo Patre ipsis concessa; sed vere immensa, & infinita, ad- eoque ipsissima Dei Patris gloria, quia Filius & Pater unum sunt essentia, & gloria Johan. X. 30. & ab æterno Filius Dei habuit eam gloriam Johann. XVII. 5. Ab æterno autem nihil finiti fuit: sed æterna gloria vere immensa, & infinita est glo- ria. Illud interpretamentum loci illustris Jo- han. I. 14. vidimus gloriam ejus talem, qualem pa- rentes dare solent filiis unicis, nimis exile est. Ne- que præpositio παρὰ patres cohæret cum nomi- ne remotiori δόξαν, sed cum propinquiori μονογενοῦς, quod revera gloria illa, quam manifestavit Chri- stus, ea fuerit, quæ est unigeniti Filii Dei, qui solus & unus à Patre & ex essentia Patris est genitus. Par- ticula enim ὡς non est similitudinis hoc loco, sed respondet כ vel veritatis Ebræo. Ideo Chrystost. hom. LVI. in Matth. εἶδεν πως δόξα μία πατρὸς καὶ υἱοῦ: εἰ δὲ δόξα μία, ἔυδηλον, ὅτι καὶ ὀυσία μία.

μετὰ τῶν ἀγγέλων ἀυτοῦ] Solebant Hebræi Deum de rebus magnis agentem describere ad exemplum Regis con- sidentis in cœtu procerum: ut I. Reg. XX. & apud Chal- dæum paraphrasten ad primum Jobi caput videre est. Et sic quidem ἀνθρωποπαθῶς explicant illud: faciamus hominem. Vide & Deut. XXXIII. 2. & Dan. VII. 10.

κατὰ τὴν πρᾶξιν ἀυτοῦ] כמעשהו Psal. LXII. 13. κα- τὰ τὰ ἔργα. Rom. II. 6. κατὰ τὸν ἴδιον κόπον I. Cor. III. 8. πρὸς ἃ ἔπραξεν εἴτε ἀγαθὸν εἴτε κακὸν 2. Cor. V. 10. qui loci, præ- sertim vero ille I. Cor. III. 8. non tantum differentem exi- tum bonorum malorumq; videntur ostendere, sed & gradus non minus præmiorum quam pœnarum. De pœnarū gradi- bus illustres sunt loci supra XI. 22. 24. De præmiorum gra- dibus intelligi solet quod est apud Paulum I. Corinth. XV. 41. Clem. Alexandrinus Strom. IV. εἰσὶ γὰρ παρὰ κυρίῳ κὶ μισθοὶ κὶ μοναὶ πλείονες ταῖα ἀναλογίαι βίων. Nec dubium est quin ea constans fuerit omnium verbum Christianorum sententia. πρᾶξιν autem hic intelligere debemus omnem hominis actum, in quo bonitas aut malitia locum habeat: internum præcipue: externum quatenus interno congruit.

## 16:28
Verse 28. unless they taste of death] That 'to taste of death' and 'to see death' are the same appears in John 8:52. Doubtless because 'ta'am' for the Hebrews is to experience, Ps. 34:9, Prov. 31:8. Add Heb. 2:9.

in his kingdom] Mark explains it as 'until they see the kingdom of God having come in power.' Which words quite clearly, if I am not mistaken, indicate that this concerns the resurrection, the ascension into heaven, the mission of the Holy Spirit, and the propagation of the Gospel through signs and miracles: by which most certain testimonies it was known that Christ was already reigning, and the kingdom of the Messiah is called the kingdom of God by the teachers of the Hebrews, and by our writers throughout. See Luke 22:18. And thus Peter refers what is said about the kingdom of the Messiah in Psalm 110 to the times I have mentioned, Acts 2:33, 34, 35, 36. Nor does this cohere badly with what precedes. For so that they might believe what he had said, that he would be the judge of the human race, he says that the conspicuous signs of his kingdom would soon be present: then, namely, especially when his scepter, the law of the New Covenant, would go forth from Zion. For although by the customs of certain peoples they are accustomed to be distinguished, yet by the very nature of things, kingdom, legislation, and judgment cohere with one another. See James 2:8, 4:12. Deservedly, therefore, they are commanded to believe in the judge whom they are about to see as the lawgiver.

Thus Gregory the Great, Bede, and others also explain the present passage: among our own, the Vinarian Paraphrasts, B. Glassius in his Sacred Grammar, as also B. Gerhard the Elder on this passage. The Savior had said that he would come in the glory of the Father, and would render to each according to his deeds. Hence it could be asked, are you then about to depart from this world into heavenly glory, so that you may return from there to judgment? That, indeed, Christ answers, is so certain that some of those standing by, namely the Apostles, are about to see it with their eyes: Compare Acts 1. However, not a few of the ancients—Chrysostom, Cyril, Maximus, Euthymius, Hilary, Ambrose, Jerome, and among our own B. Polyc. Lyser in his Harmony and B. Aeg. Hunnius in his Commentary on this passage, Francis Junius and others among the Reformed, as well as Lymnus, Thomas, Maldonatus, and Cornelius à Lapide among the Papists—explain it concerning the transfiguration of Christ. Whom he designates, says Chrysostom, those words, who shall not taste death, until they see the Son of man coming in his glory, they were Peter, and James and John, for these he took as witnesses of his transfiguration. Furthermore, he calls his transfiguration his kingdom. Because that was a tasted specimen and a delineation shadowed forth by purer rays of the magnificent coming, by which he is about to render to each according to his works. The former explanation, however, which Grotius makes his own, seems simpler, because he does not properly come ἐν τῇ βασιλείᾳ ἀυτõ, when he was transfigured: and his glory, which was then manifested, is one thing, and his kingdom, or as Mark and Luke have it, the kingdom of God, is another, which they saw coming ἐν δυνάμει, when Christ, having been raised into heaven, sent the Holy Spirit and propagated the kingdom of God throughout the world, and gathered the nations from everywhere to his kingdom. Nor do the words sound concerning that which was to be immediately after, or because of that particular manifestation made on the mountain and already imminent, did that assertion seem necessary, Amen I say to you. The things, however, which Grotius sprinkles here concerning the νομοθεσίᾳ, are to be received dexterously, lest a new lawgiver be formed from Christ with the Socinians and Papists. Finally, the things which he hands down here from Ps. 110 are to be compared with those which he commented on regarding the same Psalm in the Annotations to the Old Testament, and with our own Elenctic works in the same place. But a certain anonymous Arian in the Paradoxes of Sandius is most inept, saying that by the holy angels in this verse 27, the seven Spirits can be understood: concerning which Apoc. 1.4, and by the seven Spirits, the Holy Spirit himself. Which seems absurd to him to say that the Holy Spirit is omitted in this place. For nowhere is the Holy Spirit understood by the holy angels: and it is clearly asserted that the angels will come with the Son of man to judgment, Matt. 25.31, but the Holy Spirit is nowhere said to be about to come with the Son of man. But if even there, because the Holy Spirit is omitted, the Holy Spirit is to be understood by all the holy angels!

Latin:

Vers. 28. ἐ μὴ γέυσωνται θανάτου] Idem esse γεύεσθαι θα- νάτου & θάνατον θεωρεῖν apparet Joh. VIII. 52. Nimirum quia טעם Hebræis est experiri, Ps. XXXIV. 9. Prov. XXXI. 8. Adde Hebr. II. 9.

ἐν τῇ βασιλείᾳ ἀυτοῦ] Marcus exponit ἕως ἂν ἴδωσι τὴν βασιλείαν τοῦ Θεοῦ ἐληλυθυῖαν ἐν δυνάμει. Quæ verba satis cla- re, ni fallor, indicant, agi hic de resurrectione, ascensu in cœlum, missione Spiritus Sancti & propagatione Evange- lii per signa & miracula: quibus certissimis testimoniis co- gnoscebatur Christum jam regnare, Messiæ autem regnum & Hebræorum magistris regnum Dei dicitur, & nostris scriptoribus passim. Vide Lucam XXII. 18. Atque adeo quæ de regno Messiæ dicuntur in Psal. CX. ad ea quæ dixi tempora refert Petrus Act. II. 33. 34. 35. 36. Neque idsuspe- ctum rioribus male cohæret. Ut enim credant quod dixerat, se judicem humani generis fore, dicit propediem adfutura signa conspicua regni sui: tunc scilicet præcipue cum sce- ptrum ipsius, lex Novi fœderis, ex Sione esset exitura. Quanquam enim quorundam populorum institutis distin- gui solent, ipsa tamen rerum natura inter se cohærent βασι- λεία, νομοθεσία, κρίσις, Vide Jac. II. 8. IV. 12. Merito igitur ju- bentur judicem credere, quem visuri sunt legis conditorem.

Sic explicat etiam locum præsentem Grego- rius M. Beda, & alii: è nostris Paraphrast. Vina- rienses, B. Glassius in Gram. sacra, ut & B. Ger- hardus Senior in h. l. Dixerat Salvator, se ventu- rum in gloria Patris, redditurusque unicuique se- cundum facta. Hinc quæri poterat, tuné igitur ex hoc mundo discessurus es in gloriam cælestem, ut in- de ad judicium redeas. Id quidem, respondet Chri- stus, tam certum est, ut quidam ex astantibus, Aposto- li scilicet, oculis id sint visuri: Conf. Act. I. Veteres tamen non pauci Chrysost. Cyrillus, Maximus, Eu- thymius, Hilarius, Ambrosius, Hieronymus, & è nostris B. Polyc. Lyser. in Harm. & B. Æg. Hun- nius in Commentar. ad h. l. Franc. Junius & alii è Reformatis, Lymnus item, Thomas, Maldon. Cor- nelius à Lap. è Pontificiis de transfiguratione Christi exponunt. Quos designat, inquit Chrysost. illis verbis, qui non gustabunt mortem, donec videant Filium hominis venientem in gloria sua, ii fuerunt Pe- trus, & Jacobus & Johannes, hos enim adhibuit trans- figurationis suæ testes. Regnum porro suum transfigu- rationem vocat. Quod ea fuerit delibatum specimen & purioribus radiis adumbrata designatio magnifi- cenric adventus, quo redditurus est unicuique juxta opera sua. Prior tamen explicatio, quam Gro- tius suam facit, videtur simplicior, quia proprie non venit ἐν τῇ βασιλείᾳ ἀυτõ, cum transfigura- tus est: & aliud est gloria ejus, quæ tum manifesta- ta, aliud regnum ejus, vel ut Marcus & Lucas ha- bent, regnum Dei, quod viderunt venire ἐν δυνά- μει, cum evectus in cælum Christus misit Spiritum S. & regnum Dei per orbem terrarum propagavit, ac gentes undique ad regnum suum congregavit. Neque de eo verba sonant, quod immediate post futurum erat, aut ob particularem istam manife- stationem in monte factam eamq; jamjam immi- nentem, ista asseveratione opus videbatur, Amen dico vobis. Quæ tamen de νομοθεσίᾳ inspergit Grotius, dextre accipienda sunt, ne è Christo no- vus νομοθέτης cum Socinianis & Papistis formetur. Denique quæ è Ps. CX. hic tradit, componenda cum illis, quæ ad eundem Ps. in Annotatis ad V. T. commentatus est, nostrisque ibidem Elenchicis. In- eptissimus autem est in Paradoxis Sandii Anonymus quidam Arianus per sanctos angelos hoc v. 27. intel- ligi posse dicens septem Spiritus: de quibus Ap. I. 4. & per septem Spiritus ipsismet Spiritum S. Quod absurdum ipsi videatur dicere Spiritum S. hic loci omissum. Nuspiam enim per sanctos angelos Spiritus S. intelligitur: & angelos venturos cum Filio hominis ad judicium Matth. XXV. 31. lucu- lenter asseritur, nuspiam autem cum Filio hominis venturus dicitur Spiritus Sanctus. Num autem ibi etiam quia Spiritus Sanctus omissus per omnes san- ctos angelos intelligendus Spiritus Sanctus!

## 17:1 Argument
CHAPTER XVII. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

Christ, having taken Peter, James and John, is glorified before them on the mountain: Moses and Elijah appear to him talking with him, Peter wants three tabernacles to be built there: they are surrounded by a bright cloud, and this voice is heard from heaven, This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased, hear him. Jesus raises up the terrified disciples, and descending from the mountain, he warns them not to divulge this vision before his resurrection, and when they ask about the opinion of the Scribes concerning the coming of Elijah, he teaches that he has already come, so that they might understand that this was said about John the Baptist. But when the parent of the lunatic asks why a certain disciple of his could not heal him, he rebukes the faithless generation, and by rebuking the devil, he casts him out, and instructs the disciples concerning the power of faith, which is so great that it even moves mountains. He again predicts his passion, death, and resurrection, and pays the tax in Capernaum for himself and Peter, a stater extracted from a fish. These are the parts: I. The transfiguration of Christ on the mountain, with information about the coming of Elijah, to v. 13. II. The restoration of the lunatic, with information about the power of faith, to v. 21. III. The prediction of his passion, death, and resurrection, to v. 24. IV. The payment of the tax for himself and Peter extracted from a fish, to v. 27.

PART I. The transfiguration of Christ on the mountain.

Vers. 1.

Μεθ’ ἡμέρας ἓξ] Matthew set a designated time: Luke was content to speak παχυμερῶς (roughly), as we are accustomed to do when we are not far from some more celebrated measure, as if I should say 'it is a month,' one understands that I have spoken correctly even if there are a few days [remaining]. For what Luke says, ὡσεὶ ἡμέραι ὀκτὼ (about eight days), is such as when we commonly say 'a journey of a week.' For that the Jews called eight days that which is from one Sabbath to another, appears in John XX. 26. Josephus, Antiquities VII, ch. IX, when he had said ἐπὶ ἡμέρας ὀκτὼ (for eight days), immediately explains it as ἀπὸ σαββάτου ἐπὶ σάββατον (from Sabbath to Sabbath).

Beza explained these things more exquisitely, who on Mark IX. 2 has it thus: These things were done on the sixth day from that on which the Lord had held the preceding discourse: they were done, I say, on the very sixth day, and indeed towards evening. For this is what Luke says, that these things happened not on the eighth, but almost on the eighth day after: because, clearly, they were done while the seventh day was already declining. For Luke counts also that day on which Christ had held the former discourse, and furthermore observes the time when they ascended into the mountain; namely, at the approach of the night which was ushering in the eighth day, at which time the Lord ascended the mountain according to custom to pray, yet not alone, as he was usually wont, but having taken three disciples with him. That, however, is clear even from the fact that the same Luke narrates that the eyes of the disciples were weighed down with sleep, and that they descended from the mountain only on the following day, namely the eighth, on which they had spent the night. I know, however, that Chrysostom reconciles Luke with Matthew and Mark in another way; as if all those six days had intervened between the discourse held and the transformation of the Lord, because he refers the particle ὡσεὶ not to the beginning of the eighth day, as I do, but to the end. So much for him. However, most of our people follow the reconciliation of Chrysostom after the blessed Luther (T. IV. Lat. Jen. p. 368), that Matthew and Mark counted only the intermediate days, but Luke counted also the extremes, namely the one on which the prior discourse was held, and the one on which Christ was transfigured. Which is also the reconciliation of the blessed Jerome: The answer is easy, he says, because here (in Matthew and Mark) the middle days are placed, there (in Luke) the first and the last are added. Compare Bede and Theophylact. But Luke says 'about eight days': because the extremes were not whole.

Τὸν Πέτρον, καὶ Ἰάκωβον, καὶ Ἰωάννην] I do not doubt that these three gathered the most disciples for Christ out of the twelve Apostles: whence that name was given to Peter about which we spoke before, and the name of 'Sons of Thunder' to the other two. Christ therefore took these, so that such a great matter might be established not by the testimony of only two, but abundantly, namely by three: to which point the words of Peter in his second epistle, ch. 1. 16, 17, 18. And just as the future glory of Christ had to have three witnesses from heaven and as many from earth, 1 John V. 7, 8, so this rudiment of his glory had three witnesses as it were from heaven, God the Father, Moses, Elijah: and likewise three from the earth, Peter, John, and James: Peter, the προστάτην (leader) of the apostolic assembly; James, who was the first of the Apostles to seal his testimony with his blood; John, who surviving after all the Apostles was to transmit this testimony to the following age by word of mouth. But since it appears that this James was the son of Zebedee, they err who place this title before the Syriac Epistles of James, Peter, and John: 'Three Epistles of the three Apostles before whose eyes our Lord transfigured himself': unless perhaps they believed this epistle to be of James the Zebedaean, against which all the ancients feel, who assign it to James of Alphaeus or even to James the Bishop of Jerusalem (whom some make different from James of Alphaeus), undoubtedly more congruently with the account of the times. Similar is the forgetfulness of Augustine, who draws to this James, the witness τῆς μεταμορφώσεως (of the transfiguration), that which is in Galatians, and of Ambrose, who attributes the chair of Jerusalem to this same person.

Αναφέρει] The Greeks translate עלה as ἀνάγειν and ἀναφέρειν.

Εἰς ὄρος ὑψηλὸν] Undoubtedly Itabyrium, as ancient tradition also holds, and has been demonstrated by others, which mountain Peter calls holy, for no other reason than because the divine majesty of Christ showed itself there to be seen, just as God, showing his power to Moses in the bush, called Horeb holy by that name, Ex. III. 5. Nor will it become clear that the passage of Mark c. IX. 30 stands in the way of this opinion when one has arrived at it.

Most of our people also explain it as Mount Tabor, with Brentius in the preface to his Commentary on Exodus, and also the Papist interpreters: Tostatus, Toletus, Maldonado, Adrichomius as well, and others. Faber Stapulensis, however, and Fr. Lucas Burgensis prefer to understand it as Mount Lebanon. Ephrem thought it was Mount Sinai, which also seems to have been the opinion of Tertullian, lib. IV. against Marcion. But most of the ancients choose Mount Tabor: Cyril of Jerusalem, Catech. XII; Jerome, epistles XVII and XXVII; Philo Carpathius on the Canticles; Bede on the holy places, ch. 17; Euthymius on Psalm LXXXVIII; Damascenus, sermon on the transfiguration of the Lord. The text favors these, because Christ, immediately after his transfiguration, when he had descended from the mountain, was in Capernaum. For this city was near Mount Tabor, or Itabyrium. Nor does it stand in the way that in Mark IX. 30 it seems to be said that he had passed through Galilee. For τὸ παραπορεύεσθαι does not mean to pass by or to pass over, but to pass through, or as Grotius has it at the place cited, to go by a detour, not by the royal road.

Latin:

CAPUT XVII. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Christus assumtis Petro, Iacobo & Iohanne, in monte coram illis clarificatur: apparent ei Moses & Elias colloquentes cum eo, Petrus vult tria ibi tabernacula exstrui: circun- dantur nube lucida, & vox hac de cælo au- ditur, Hic est Filius meus dilectus, in quo mihi complacuit, hunc audite. Perterrefa- ctos discipulos erigit Jesus, ac descendens de monte monet ne hanc visionem ante suam resurrectionem divulgent, quærentesque de sententia Scribarum de Eliæ adventu, jam venisse docet, ut de Johanne Baptista id di- ctum intelligerent. Quærente autem Luna- tici parente, quod discipulus ejus quidam i- psum sanare nequiverit, redarguit incredu- lam generationem, & diabolum increpando ejicit, ac discipulos de fidei vi informat, quæ tanta ut etiam montes transferat. Prædicit iterum passionem, mortem & resurrectio- nem suam, & solvit in Capernaum censum pro se & Petro staterem e pisce extractum. Partes hæ sunt: I. Christi in monte transfigura- tio, cum informatione de Eliæ adventu, ad v. 13. II. Lunatici restitutio, cum informatione de fidei virtute, ad v. 21. III. Passionis, mortis & resurrectio- nis suæ prædictio, ad v. 24. IV. Census pro se & Pe- tro è pisce extracti persolutio, ad v. 27.

PARS I. Christi in monte transfiguratio.

Vers. 1.

Μεθ’ ἡμέρας ἓξ] Matthæus designatum tempus po- suit: Lucas satis habuit παχυμερῶς loqui, ut solemus cum à mensura aliqua celebriore non longe absumus, ut si di- cam mensis est, recte dixisse intelligat etiamsi sint dies ali- quot. Quod enim Lucas dicit, ὡσεὶ ἡμέραι ὀκτὼ, tale est quale cum vulgo dicimus post septimanam iter. Nam Judæos octo dies appellasse id quod ab uno Sabbato est ad alterum, apparet Joh. XX. 26. Josephus Antiquit. VII. cap. IX. cum dixisset ἐπὶ ἡμέρας ὀκτὼ statim explicat ἀπὸ σαββάτου ἐπὶ σάββατον.

Exquisitius hæc exposuit Beza, qui ad Marc. IX. 2. ita habet: Hæc gesta sunt sexto die ab eo quo Dominus sermonem præcedentem habuerat: gesta, inquam, sunt sexto ipso die, & quidem sub vesperam. Hoc enim est quod ait Lucas, non octavo, sed fere octavo post die ista evenisse: quia videlicet inclinan- te jam die septimo gesta sunt. Numerat enim Lu- cas eum etiam diem quo superiorem sermonem Chri- stus habuerat, & præterea tempus observat quo in montem ascenderunt; imminente nimirum nocte quæ octavum diem auspicabatur, quo tempore Dominus de more in montem conscendit ut oraret, non tamen solus, ut fere solebat, sed tribus assumtis discipulis. Id autem vel ex eo liquet, quod idem Lucas narrat discipulorum oculos somno fuisse gravatos, & poste- ro demum die, octavo videlicet, è monte descendisse, in quo nimirum pernoctarant. Scio tamen Chrysosto- mum alia ratione Lucam cum Matthæo & Marco conciliare; quasi toti sex isti dies inter sermonem ha- bitum & transformationem Domini intercesserint, quia particulam ὡσεὶ non ad initium octavi diei, ut ego, sed ad finem refert. Hæc ille. Chrysostomi ta- men conciliationem, quod Matthæus & Marcus tantum intermedios dies computarint, Lucas ve- ro etiam extremos annumeravit, eum nempe quo prior habitus est sermo, & eum quo transfiguratus est Christus, sequuntur post B. Lutherum T. IV. Lat. Jen. p. 368. plerique nostrates. Quæ etiam est B. Hieronymi conciliatio: Facilis, inquit, est re- sponsio, quia hic (apud Matth. & Marc.) medii po- nuntur dies, ibi (in Luca) primus additur & extre- mus. Conf. Beda ac Theophylactus. Dicit autem fe- re octo dies Lucas: quia extremi non erant integri.

Τὸν Πέτρον, καὶ Ἰάκωβον, καὶ Ἰωάννην] Non dubito, quin de duodecim Apostolis hi tres plurimos Christo discipulos collegerint: unde Petro vocabulum illud de quo ante egi- mus, datum est, & cæteris duobus Tonantium nomen. Hos ergo Christus assumsit, ut non duorum tantum, sed abundanter, trium scilicet, testimonio res tanta constaret: quo spectant Petri verba in epistola II. cap. 1. 16. 17. 18. Et ficut futura Christi gloria tres habere testes debebat de cœ- lo & de terra totidem, 1. Joh. V. 7. 8. ita hoc ejus gloriæ rudimentum tres quasi de cœlo testes habuit, Deum Pa- trem Mosen, Eliam: tres itidem de terra, Petrum, Johan- nem & Jacobum: Petrum Apostolici cœtus προστάτην : Ja- cobum qui primus Apostolorum sanguine testimonium erat obsignaturus: Johannem qui post omnes Apostolos superstes testimonium hoc ad sequentem ætatem viva voce transmissurus. Cum autem appareat Jacobum hunc Ze- bedæi fuisse filium, errant qui Syrorum Epistolis Jacobi, Pe- tri & Johannis hunc præfigunt titulum: Tres Epistola trium Apostolorum ante quorum oculos Dominus noster se transfigu- ravit: nisi istam forte epistolam Jacobi Zebedaidæ credi- derunt, contra quam veteres omnes sentiunt, qui Jacobo Alphæi aut etiam Jacobo Episcopo Hierosolymorum (quem nonnulli à Jacobo Alphæi diversum faciunt) eam assi- gnant, haud dubie temporum rationi congruentiùs, Similis est Augustini immemoria, qui ad hunc Jacobum, testem τῆς μεταμορφώσεως, trahit id quod est ad Galatas, & Ambro- sii qui huic eidem tribuit cathedram Hierosolymorum.

Αναφέρει] עלה ἀνάγειν & ἀναφέρειν vertunt Græci.

Εἰς ὄρος ὑψηλὸν] Itabyrium haud dubie ut & vetus tra- ditio habet, & ab aliis demonstratum est, quem montem sanctum Petrus vocat, non alia de causa quam quia divina Christi majestas ibi se videndam præbuit, quomodo Deus Mosi potentiam suam in rubo ostendens, Horebum eo no- mine sanctum appellabat Ex. III. 5. Neq; obstare huic senten- tiæ Marci locum c. IX. 30. apertum fiet cum eo erit ventum.

De monte Tabor etiam explicant plerique no- strates cum Brentio præf. Comment. super Exod. nec non Pontificiis Interpp: Tostato, Toleto, Maldonato, Adrichomio item, aliisque. Faber tamen Stapulensis, & Fr. Lucas Burgensis de monte Libano intelligere malunt. Ephrem puta- vit fuisse montem Sinai, quæ etiam videtur fuisse Tertulliani sententia lib. IV. advers. Marcion. Montem autem Tabor eligunt plerique veteres, Cyrillus Hierosol. Catech. XII. Hieronymus e- pist. XVII. & XXVII. Philo Carpathius in Cantic. Beda de locis sanct. cap. 17. Euthymius in Psalm. XXCVIII. Damascen. serm. de transfig. Dom. Quibus favet textus, quod Christus mox à trans- figuratione sua, cum è monte descenderat, in Ca- pernaum fuerit. Hæc enim urbs vicina erat monti Tabor, vel Itabyrico. Nec obstat quod Marc. IX. 30. videatur dici prætergressus esse Galilæam. Nam τὸ παραπορεύεσθαι non est prætergredi seu præterire, sed pertransire, vel ut Grotius ad l. c. ha- bet, diverticulo ire, non via regia.

## 17:2
Verse 2. μετεμορφώθη] μορφὴ is often for the Greeks ὄψις, θέαμα, the exterior appearance of a thing, which Luke called εἶδος. Thus Cicero: 'You see the form, as it were, and the very face of honesty.' And elsewhere, although grammarians distinguish them, he uses form and figure interchangeably.

ἔλαμψε τὸ πρόσωπον αὐτᾶ ὡς ὁ ἥλιος] As lightning, Daniel had said in X. 2. His splendor as light. Habakkuk III. 4.

Λευκὰ ὡς τὸ φῶς] That is, as the light of the Sun, not in the Sun but received in another body, just as the garments of Christ were receiving light from the very body of Christ. Such light, however, is accustomed to appear white. Thus also Angels are described to us throughout as having both white and glittering garments. Compare what is below in XXVIII. 3, Mark XVI. 5, and John XX. 12 with Luke XXIV. 4. This is what Herod Agrippa wished to imitate with that silver robe of which Josephus writes: 'where, upon the first strikes of the sun's rays, the silver, being illuminated, shone forth wonderfully, flashing something fearful and terrifying to those gazing upon him,' upon seeing which the people called him a God, that is, an Angel, κρείττονα θνητῆς φύσεως, as Josephus explains. Similar among the Greeks was the madness of Salmoneus, who simulated clouds and the inimitable lightning with bronze and the running of hoofed horses.

There also approaches more closely the deed of Clearchus, tyrant of the Heracleans, concerning whom the historian Memnon recorded these things: 'He would not endure for his face to be colored with natural dyes, but by being varied with different appearances, it would appear to those looking at him as shining and reddish; and he would also change his tunics to something more fearful and delicate.'

The transformation was not substantial, but accidental. Concerning which Theophylact says: By transformation, understand not a change of character and features, but that, while remaining as he was before, an ineffable increase of light took place, so that these white garments are spoken of as light, likewise according to Mark, as snow: for just as its own darkness belongs to shadows, so its own brightness belongs to light. Luke attributes both whiteness and a shining light to them.

Latin:

Vers. 2. μετεμορφώθη] μορφὴ sæpe Græcis est ὄψις, θέα- μα, facies rei exterior quam εἶδος vocavit Lucas. Ita Ci- cero: formam quasi ipsam & tanquam faciem honesti vides. Et alibi formam & figuram, quamquam distinguunt Gram- matici, promiscue usurpat.

ἔλαμψε τὸ πρόσωπον αὐτᾶ ὡς ὁ ἥλιος] tanquam fulgur di- xerat Daniel X. 2. Splendor ejus ut lux. Abacuc. III. 4.

Λευκὰ ὡς τὸ φῶς] Id est, ut lux Solis, non in Sole sed alio corpore excepta, sicut vestes Christi ex ipso Christi cor- pore lucem accipiebant. Talis autem lux solet candida ap- parere. Sic & Angeli passim nobis describuntur vestibus & candidis & coruscantibus. Confer quod infra XXVIII. 3. Marci XVI. 5. & Joh. XX. 12. cum Lu. XXIV. 4. Hoc est quod Herodes Agrippa imitari voluit veste illa argentea de qua Josephus : ἔνθα ταῖς πρώταις τῶν ἡλιακῶν ἀκτίνων ἐπιβολαῖς ὁ ἄργυρος καταυγασθεὶς θαυμασίως ἀπέστιλβε μαρμαίρων τι φο- βερὸν κὴ τοῖς εἰς αὐτὸν ἀτενίζουσι φρικῶδες, quo conspecto po- pulus illum Deum vocavit, id est Angelum, κρείττονα θνητῆς φύσεως, ut Josephus explicat. Similis apud Græcos Sal- monei dementia qui nimbos & non imitabile fulmen Ære & cornipedum cursu simulabat equorum.

Proprius etiam accedit factum Clearchi Heracleensium ty- ranni de quo Memnon historicus hæc prodidit. Τὸ πρόσωπον μὴ ἀνέχεσθαι ταῖς ἐκ φύσεως χρωματίζεσθαι βαφαῖς, ἄλλαις δὲ κὴ ἄλλαις ἰδέαις ποικιλλόμενον ἐπὶ τὸ σιλπνόν τε κὴ ἐρευθὲς τοῖς ὁρῶσιν ἐπιφαίνεσθαι· ἐξαλλάττειν δὲ κὴ τὰς χιτῶνας ἐπὶ τὸ φοβε- ρόν τε κὴ ἁβρότερον.

Non substantialis, sed accidentalis fuit transfor- matio. Quo de Theophylactus: Per transfor- mationem intellige non characteris & lineamen- torum immutationem, sed manente, qualis prius erat, ineffabilis lucis factum esse augmentum, ut hic candida vestimenta dicuntur sicut lux, item a- pud Marcum, sicut nix : ut enim sua caligo est te- nebris, ita luci suus candor. Lucas & albedinem & fulgidum lumen iis tribuit.

## 17:3
Vers. 3. Moses and Elijah] The one a promulgator of the law, the other the most noble of the Prophets, whom Christ had also expressed in his forty days' fast, are present here, so that they might show what Luke indicates, the sufferings of Christ, figured by the rites of the law, and then predicted by the oracles of the Prophets. That they appeared in their true and own body, for the assurance of the resurrection both of Christ and of our own, is the more credible, because these bodies can be seen to have been preserved by God for this use. For the body of Elijah was caught up into the heavens, but the body of Moses, not found and guarded by angelic ministry, lest it should fall into the power of the devil, the one having the power of death, as the writer to the Hebrews speaks in chapter II. 14, whom the Hebrews call the angel of death, and by whose command they say the body is dissolved into dust, which, as it is rightly understood, does not depart from the truth, so it is wrapped by them in a great heap of fables. But what I said, that the body of Moses was preserved from decay, that seems to be indicated in the epistle of Jude. Josephus, however, dealing with Moses, when he says he disappeared, speaks in the same way as he does of Enoch and of Elijah. Thus, therefore, they dealt with the sufferings of Christ, so that at the same time they might place before the eyes his own resurrection, prefigured in their own bodies. But the bodies of these also appeared in glory, but undoubtedly less than that which was Christ's, just as much as the stars yield to the sun, 1 Cor. XV. 41. And this glory was then given to them as if on loan, since they were to obtain their own solid right later. For they had not yet at that time received the perfection of the promise, as is easily gathered from the writer to the Hebrews, if you compare what is at the end of chapter XI with verses 23, 24, 25, 26, 27, 28, 35, 36, 37, 38 of the same chapter attentively.

Grotius deservedly acknowledges that they appeared in their true body, but that he deems it more credible because these bodies can be seen to have been preserved for that use, in that no consequence appears; nay, this is more obscure than that, and it is more credible that they truly appeared in the body than that their body had been preserved by God for this use: nor does it deserve assent; for whence, I pray, will it be taught that God wished to preserve those bodies for this use? And what is to be held concerning the body of Enoch, which was likewise received into heaven, which was certainly not preserved for such a use?
