What necessity, therefore, is there for us to say that bodies extraordinarily received into heaven were received by God for the purpose that they might be preserved for the use of illustrating the transfiguration of Christ? Which, as it is asserted rashly, without Scripture, is rejected with the same ease with which it is asserted. There are reasons for God's counsel, even if they are not obvious to us. That bodies which were received into heaven appeared from heaven in the transfiguration is certainly true, but that they were received into heaven of old for the reason that they might one day appear from there is pronounced without Scripture, nor can such a thing be shown concerning all who were received into heaven.

Furthermore, that Moses and Elijah appeared on this holy mountain for the assurance of the resurrection of Christ and our own is asserted equally rashly. For however much the faith of our resurrection may be strengthened by the example of Moses, yet that was not what was being done then, nor was that the end of that apparition, that our resurrection should be established, nor can Christ's resurrection be proved by a solid consequence from the appearance of Moses and Elijah in their own body, by whose virtue (we indicate the resurrection of Christ) both Moses and Elijah were rather received into the heavens, and the former was indeed carried up there alive, but the latter revived after death, concerning whom Grotius imagines that the body of Moses was guarded by angelic ministry, lest it should fall into the power of the Devil, or the angel of death, by whose command the Hebrews say the body is dissolved into dust, but where are such things handed down in the scriptures? Jude indeed testifies that an angel intervened so that the body of Moses would not come into the power of Satan, but most people think that this was done, and it is not improbable, so that there would not be an occasion for idolatry, to which the people could be seduced by the Devil, and to which they were very prone, not, however, so that it would not be reduced to dust; nor can it be pronounced with certainty concerning it that the body of Moses did not see corruption, which could be raised from the dust by divine power just as easily as it could be recalled to life after death, whole before its dissolution into dust: Nay, there does not appear a cause why God should have buried, and entrusted to the earth, the mother of us all, the body of Moses, Deut. XXXIV. 6, unless it had to return to dust by the common law of all, since otherwise Moses could have been transferred to heaven alive, like Enoch and Elijah, or the body could have been quickened and assumed without burial; unless perhaps it must be said that the body of Moses had to remain in the sepulcher for three days, so that it might come forth incorrupt as a type of Christ, of whom, however, the Lord established not Moses in the sepulcher, but Jonah in the belly of the whale, as a type, Matt. XVI. 4. Finally, as it was the property of that holy one alone not to see corruption, Ps. XVI. 10, so neither did the body of Elijah, nor of Enoch, entirely lack it, much less Moses, but in their very translation they experienced something analogous to corruption, through a change, such as those who survive will experience at the final coming of Christ, when they will be snatched up to meet the Lord; even if they were translated to heaven alive; which cannot be said of Moses. For what he brings forward from Josephus, that he used the word disappeared of him just as of Enoch and of Elijah, is not to be admitted otherwise than with the preservation of the burial of Moses, namely, that after death his body did not appear anymore, and not even his sepulcher was found by any mortal. But how can it be established with Grotius that the resurrection of Christ was prefigured in the body of Elijah while he appeared here with Christ, if indeed the body of Elijah neither saw death properly, nor was it resurrected into life, but was transformed in the ascension into heaven?

Let us therefore leave these and other inventions of this kind to Grotius, especially that the glory of Elijah and Moses, in which they appeared here, was only as it were given on loan. Which he wishes to prove by a misinterpretation of the Apostolic passage in Hebrews XI, in the last verses: but there the τελείωσις τῆς ἐπαγγελίας, which the faithful of the Old Testament are said not to have received, is not about the perfection of another life, for neither does the Apostle understand this by the promise, nor can Grotius understand it, because he denies, along with the Pelagians, Socinians, and Arminians, that the promise of another life was made to the saints in the Old Testament, but it is about that consummation of the promise which the Apostles and other faithful under the New Testament obtained through the coming of the Son of God in the flesh in the fullness of time, of which blessedness of theirs Christ speaks in Luke X. 23. And how could Moses and Elijah exist in heaven with bodies not glorified, when flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God, 1 Cor. XV. 50.

Latin:

Vers. 3. Μωσῆς κὴ Ἠλίας] Alter legis promulgator, alter Prophetarum nobilissimus, quos etiam in XL. dierum jeju- nio Christus expresserat, in hoc adsunt, ut ostendant quod Lucas indicat, perpessiones Christi, eum legis ri- tibus figuratas, tum Prophetarum oraculis prædictas. Vero autem ac suo corpore, in fidem resurrectionis & Chri- sti & nostræ, eos apparuisse, eo credibil us est, quia hæc cor- pora videri possunt à Deo in hunc usum asservata. Nam E- liæ corpus in superna raptum est, Mosis autem corpus non inventum & custoditum Angelico ministerio, ne perveniret in potestatem diaboli τῦ ἔχοντ@ τὸ κράτ@ τῦ θανάτυ, ut Scriptor ad Hebræos loquitur cap. II. 14. quem Angelum mortis Hebræi vocant, & cujus imperio ajunt corpus in pulverem dissolvi, quod ut recte intellectum à vero non abit, ita ab illis magno fabularum cumulo involvitur. Sed quod dixi à putredine asservatum Mosis corpus, id indicare videtur in epistola Judas. Josephus autē de Mose agens cum ait ἀφανισθῆναι, quomodo & de Enocho & de Elia loqui- tur. Ita ergo de perpessionibus Christi egerunt, ut simul resurrectionem ei suam in ipsorum corporibus præfigura- tam, ob oculos ponerent. Apparuerunt autem horum quo- que corpora ἐν δόξη, sed minore haud dubie quam illa erat Christi, quantum scilicet sidera soli cedunt 1. Cor. XV. 41. Atque hæc tum gloria illis quasi pro mutuo data est, pro- prium solidumque jus adepturis postea. Nondum enim eo tempore acceperant τὴν τελείωσιν τῆς ἐπαγγελίας, ut ex Scriptore ad Hebræos facile collectum est, si quæ sunt in fi- ne capitis XI. cum ejusdem capitis commate 23. 24. 25. 26. 27. 28. 35. 36. 37. 38. attenta conferas.

Vero corpore suo eos apparuisse merito agnoscit Grotius, quod autem ideo credibilius censet, quia hæc corpora videri possunt in eum usum esse asserva- ta, in eo nec consequentia apparet, imo hoc obscu- rius illo est, magisque credibile, ipsos vero ap- paruisse corpore, quam quod corpus ipsorum in hunc usum à Deo asservatum fuerit: nec assensum meretur; unde enim, obsecro, docebitur, quod corpora illa in hunc usum asservare Deus volue- rit? Et quid de Enochi corpore, quod itidem in cœlum receptum fuit, habendum, quod in talem usum utique asservatum non fuit? Quæ ergo ne- cessitas, ut dicamus, corpora in cœlum extraor- dinarie recepta, eo fine à Deo recepta fuisse, ut as- servarentur in usum illustrandæ transfigurationis Christi? Quod uti temere, sine Scriptura, afferi- tur, eadem facilitate rejicitur, qua asseritur. Sunt Deo consilii sui rationes, etsi nobis obviæ eædem non sint. Corpora quæ cœlo recepta, è cœlo ap- paruisse in transfiguratione certum sane est, sed ideo ea recepta olim in cœlum fuisse, ut inde ali- quando apparerent, ἄτερ γραφῆς pronunciatur, nec de omnibus cœlo receptis tale quid ostendi potest.

Porro in fidem resurrectionis Christi & nostræ Mosen, & Eliam in hoc sancto monte apparuisse, æ- que temere asseritur. Nam utut exemplo Mosis resurrectionis nostræ fides firmari queat, non ta- men id tunc agebatur, aut is finis erat istius appa- ritionis, ut adstrueretur nostra resurrectio, neque Christi resurrectio è Mosis & Eliæ in corpore pro- prio apparitione probari solida consequentia po- test, cujus virtute (resurrectionem Christi indigi- tamus) potius & Moses & Elias in cœlos recepti sunt, & ille quidem vivus eo evectus est, hic vero post mortem redivivus, de quo Grotius fingit, Mosis corpus custoditum Angelico ministerio, ne per- veniret in potestatem Diaboli, vel Angeli mortis, cu- jus imperio ajunt Ebræi corpus in pulverem dis- solvi, at ubi talia in scripturis tradita? Judas equi- dem testatur Angelum intercessisse, ne in Satanæ potestatem veniret corpus Mosis, sed id factum ple- rique censent, nec improbabile est, ne idolola- triæ, ad quam seduci à Diabolo poterat, valde- tur que pronus erat populus, extaret occasio, non ve- ro ut ne in pulverem redigeretur; nec de eo pro- nunciari certo potest corruptionem non vidisse cor- pus Mosis, quod tam facile divina virtute e pulve- re resuscitari, quam integrum ante dissolutionem in pulverem post mortem in vitam revocari po- tuit: Imo non apparet causa, cur Deus sepelisset, terræque omnium nostrum matri credidisset cor- pus Mosis Deut. XXXIV. 6. nisi communi omnium lege in pulverem reverti debuisset, quum alioquin vel vivus, ad instar Enochi & Eliæ, in cælum transferri Moses potuerit, vel Corpus extra se- pulturam vivificari, & assumi; nisi forte dicen- dum, quod Mosis corpus per triduum in sepul- chro manere debuerit, ut incorruptum prodiret in typum Christi, cujus vero typum non Mosen in se- pulchro, sed Jonam in utero ceti Dominus consti- tuit, Matth. XVI. 4. Denique ut solius sancti illius proprium fuit non videre corruptionem Psal. XVI. 10. ita ne Eliæ quidem, nec Enochi corpus e- jus plane expers fuit, nedum Mosis, quin in ipsa eorum translatione aliquid analogum corruptio- ni, per ἀναλλαγὴν, qualem superstites in adventu Christi novissimo sensuri sunt, cum in occursum Domino abripientur, experti sint; etsi vivi in cæ- lum sint translati; quod de Mose dici nequit. Nam quod e Josepho adfert, quod de ipso pariter ut de E- nocho & de Elia verbum ἀφανισθῆναι adhibuerit, non aliter admittendum, nisi salva Mosis sepultu- ra, quod scilicet post mortem non amplius appa- ruerit corpus ejus, ac ne sepulcrum quidem ejus a quoquam mortalium inventum sit. In corpore au- tem Eliæ dum hic apparuit cum Christo, resurre- ctionem Christi præfiguratam fuisse, quomodo cum Grotio statui potest, siquidem Eliæ corpus nec mortem viderit proprie, nec in vitam resuscita- tum, sed in ascensione in cælum transmutatum fuerit?

Hæc ergo & alia hujusmodi commenta Grotio relinquamus, imprimis, quod Eliæ & Mosis glo- ria, in qua hic apparuerunt sum quasi promutuo da- ta tantum fuerit. Quod ψευδερμηνεία loci Apo- stolici Hebræor. XI. vers. postremis probare vult: sed ibi τελείωσις τῆς ἐπαγγελίας, quam non accepisse fideles V. T. dicuntur, non de τελειώσει alterius vitæ, hanc enim per ἐπαγγελίαν nec Apostolus intelligit, nec intelligere potest Grotius, quia ἐπ- αγγελίαν alterius vitæ sanctis in V. T. factam esse, cum Pelagianis, Socinianis & Arminianis inficiatur, sed de illa consummatione promissionis, quam per adventum Filii Dei in carnem nacti sunt Apostoli, aliique fideles sub N. T. in plenitudine temporis, de qua beatitudine ipsorum Christus loquitur Luc. X. 23. Et quomodo in cælis cum corporibus non glorificatis agere possent Moses & Elias, quum caro & sanguis hæreditare non possint regnum Dei. 1. Cor. XV. 50.

## 17:4
Verse 4. καλόν ἐστιν ἡμᾶς ὧδε εἶναι] What is to be thought of the heavenly supper, the appetizer of which Peter so much enjoyed? All these things tended to this, that their minds might be fortified against future calamities by the hope of better things. For I think those are mistaken who draw Peter's words in another direction.

Latin:

Vers. 4. καλόν ἐστιν ἡμᾶς ὧδε εἶναι] Quid de cœna cœle- sti existimandum est, cujus promulsis adeo Petr allube- scebat? Hæc omnia eo pertinebant, ut adversus futuras calamitates spe meliorum animi munirentur. Nam falsi arbitror qui alioversum trahunt Petri verba.

## 17:5
Verse 5. νεφέλη φωτεινὴ] A cloud is a sign of divine presence: as in Exodus XL. 34, a bright one, to distinguish it from the old law which was given in a thick and dark cloud, by which the different economy of the times is given to be understood.

Οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ ὑός μου ὁ ἀγαπητὸς] The Son, not a servant, as Moses in Hebrews III. 5, 6, and the other Prophets in Hebrews I. 2. See also what is above at III. 17. Here Moses learns more than he had predicted in Deuteronomy XVIII. 17.

The circumstances teach that this voice was made from heaven after Moses and Elijah had already left the scene. Furthermore, Grotius acknowledges here that Moses in Deuteronomy XVIII. 17 spoke of Christ.

must be noted against his gloss on that Mosaic passage. For there he explained the words of Moses concerning other Prophets, with no mention of Christ made. Let those things be compared which we opposed to Grotius there. But that Moses had learned more here in the transfiguration of Christ than he had known before, even if this can be conceded in a sense, because he had not known Jesus according to the flesh, nor could it be established that this Jesus born of the Virgin Mary was the Messiah promised of old, Jesus not yet being born: It is evident, however, that a false dogma is hidden in these things, as if it were unknown to Moses that the Messiah would be the very Son of God. Which could not and ought not to have been ignored in the Old Testament, because in the knowledge of him is situated salvation and eternal life. John III. 16. chapter XX. 31.

Αὐτẽ ἀκύετε] emphatically hear him above Moses, above the Prophets, as the complement of Moses and the Prophets. But the very words of Moses are אליו תשמעון Deut. XVIII. 15. which were spoken so of Jesus the son of Nun, and perhaps also of the Prophets who followed him, that by divine direction they fit much more and more excellently this Jesus, the Lord and prince of the Prophets, just as Peter, the best interpreter of God's words, teaches us Acts III. 22. And those things which follow in Moses are to be noted: as if it were said, You yourselves asked that God should not deal with you with those signs that cause terror. God performs what you wished. The Word was made flesh: he emptied himself and took the form of a servant. Behold him who with the vehemence of zeal into the house of God, might surpass Elijah, at the same time he surpasses Moses in meekness. Not thunders, not darkness, not fire from heaven provide testimony to him: but the gentle light and kindness of the paternal voice.

If these are the very words of Moses, if Peter, the best interpreter of God's words, teaches that they were spoken by Moses concerning Jesus the Lord and prince of the Prophets, Acts III. 22. if they, the context, or what follows in Moses Deut. XVIII. demand this interpretation, all of which Grotius grants here for both, why does Grotius determine that they were spoken concerning Joshua the son of Nun, and perhaps others who followed him, against the Petrine interpretation, against the context of the words of Moses, and against the very declaration of the words of Moses made here from heaven? But the evasion which he employs concerning a less excellent, or more general sense, and concerning a more excellent sense, is a very vain one. Because the oracle of Deut. XVIII. designates some singular Prophet similar to Moses: it does not deal with many being raised up at different times: nor has it been explained otherwise than in the singular concerning the one Jesus in the New Testament, and that in an exclusive sense, so that it may be established that the oracle does not sound for others: and therefore it is rashly understood concerning Joshua, and those who followed him. Which we have executed more fully in the cited place. Nor can that opinion newly devised by Grotius concerning the Holy Scriptures be admitted, that some prophecies were spoken of others in such a way that by divine direction they fit Christ much more. The perspicuity of Scripture does not bear that. Nor does the manner of speaking, when the discourse is not ambiguous. Not the intention, or direction of God: who wished the Messiah to be separated very far from others, and not to be held in an equal place with others, and to differ from others only according to a degree of eminence; because one had to believe in the Messiah as God and Redeemer: which suited none of the Prophets, however eminent. And thus also the Messiah was presented in Deut. XVIII. which we show there. But if God, dealing with others, had directed his speech in such a way that it fit the Messiah more, and by the same speech had at the same time comprehended others and the Messiah, even if dealing with one definite subject by design and direct intention, however much more excellently the same things suited the Messiah, he would have hinted at it there, or it would be established from elsewhere, would it not have been permissible to conclude that the Messiah, just like others, was a mere man, however more excellent than others? would he not, by a speech so ambiguous and sounding of different things, have led the pious in the Old Testament into error, so that they would believe the Messiah would be only a mere man, and superior to others only by certain gifts or accidents?

Latin:

Vers. 5. νεφέλη φωτεινὴ] Nubes signum divinæ præsen- tiæ: ut Exodi XL. 34. lucida, ad discrimen legis veteris quæ data in nube densa ac caliginosa, quo diversa tem- porum οἰκονομία datur intelligi.

Οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ ὑός μου ὁ ἀγαπητὸς] Filius, non servus, ut Moses Hebr. III. 5. 6. & Prophetæ cæteri Hebr. I. 2. Vin de & quæ supra III. 17. Discit hic Moses plus quam præ- dixerat Deut. XVIII. 17.

Factam hanc vocem esse de cœlo postquam e scena jam exierant Moses & Elias, circumstan- tiæ docent. Cæterum agnoscit hic Grotius, quod Moses Deut. XVIII. 17. de Christo egerit.

observandum contra glossam ejus ad illum Mo- saicum locum. Ibi enim de aliis Prophetis verba Mosis exposuit, nulla Christi mentione facta. Conferantur, quæ illic Grotio opposuimus. Mo- sen autem plus hic in transfiguratione Christi didicis- se, quam antea noverit, etsi hoc sensu concedi queat, quia Jesum secundum carnem non noverat, neque hunc Jesum è Maria virgine natum Messiam esse olim promissum, Jesu nondum nato, con- stare poterat: Patet tamen in his falsum dogma occultari, quasi Mosi incognitum fuerit Messiam fore ipsummet Dei Filium. Quod ignorari in V. T. non potuit, nec debuit, quia in ejus cognitio- ne sita est salus & vita æterna. Johan. III. 16. cap. XX. 31.

Αὐτẽ ἀκύετε] ἐμφατικῶς hunc audite supra Mosen, supra Prophetas, ut complementum Mosis & Propheta- rum. Sunt autem ipsa Mosis verba אליו תשמעון Deut. XVIII. 15. quæ ita de Jesu filio Nun, forte etiam de Prophe- tis eum secutis dicta sunt, ut divna directione multo magis atque excellentius in hunc Jesum, Dominum ac princi- pein Prophetarum, quadrent, quemadmodum Petrus, optimus Dei verborum interpres, nos docet Actor. III. 22. Et notanda sunt quæ sequuntur apud Mosen: quasi dicatur, Postulatis ipsi, ne Deus vobiscum signis illis ad terrorem facientibus ageret. Præstat Deus quod voluistis. Verbum caro factum est: inanivit se & servi formam induit. En illum qui cum vehementia τẽ ζήλκ in domum Dei, E- liam vincat, simul mansuetudine Mosen superat. Non il- li tonitrua, non caligo, non ignis de cœlo testimonium præbent: sed blanda lux & comitas vocis paternæ.

Si Mosis verba ipsa hæc sunt, si Petrus optimus Dei verborum interpres ea à Mose dicta de Jesu Domino ac principe Prophetarum, docet Act. III. 22. si ea, contextus, vel quæ sequuntur apud Mo- sen Deut. XVIII. hanc interpretationem postu- lant, quæ omnia τῶν ἀμφοῖν hic largitur Gro- tius, cur ea de Josua filio Nun, & forte aliis eum secutis dicta statuit Grotius contra Petrinam inter- pretationem, contra verborum Mosis contex- tum, & contra ipsam verborum Mosis de cœlo hic factam declarationem? Quod autem adhibet de sensu minus excellenti, vel generaliori, & de sensu excellentiori, effugium perquam vanum est. Quia singularem aliquem Prophetam Mosi similem ora- culum Deut. XVIII. designat: non vero de pluri- bus diversis vicibus suscitandis agit: nec aliter, quam μοναδικῶς de uno Jesu in N. T. explicatum est, idque sensu exclusivo, ut nempe constet, de aliis oraculum non sonare: ideoque de Josua, eum- que secutis temere intelligitur. Quæ fusius loco citato exequuti sumus. Neque admitti potest illa de S. literis opinio à Grotio noviter excogitata, vaticinia nonnulla ita de aliis dicta esse, ut divina di- rectione multo magis in Christum quadrent. Non id fert Scripturæ perspicuitas. Non loquendi ratio, cum non ambigua est oratio. Non intentio, aut dire- ctio Dei: qui voluit Messiam longissime ab aliis separatum, non vero parili loco cum aliis haben- dum, ac secundum gradum solum eminentiæ ab a- liis differre; quia in Messiam ceu Deum ac Redem- ptorem credendum erat: quod nulli Prophetarum utut eminentissimo conveniebat. Atque ita etiam sistebatur Messias Deut. XVIII. quod illic oftendi- mus. Si autem Deus de aliis agens ita orationem suam direxisset, ut ea magis in Messiam quadraret, atque eadem oratione simul alios, simul Messiam, etsi de uno definito subjecto agens ex instituto, & directa intentione, comprehendisset, quan- tumvis excellentius Messiæ eadem convenire, ibi innuisset, aut aliunde id constaret, annon Messiam perinde ut alios, ψιλὸν. ἄνθρωπον esse, utut ex- cellentiorem aliis, colligere licuisset? annon ora- tione tam ambigua, & de diversis sonante in erro- rem induxisset pios in V. T. ut crederent Messiam merum tantum hominem, ac solum donis, aut ac- cidentibus quibusdam aliis superiorem fore?

## 17:6
Vers. 6. ἔπεσον ἐπὶ πρόσωπον αὐτῶν, καὶ ἐφοβήθησαν σφόδρα] This was not so much horror as it was stupor on account of the greatness of the miracle. Therefore Mark in a similar matter said, ἐξεθαμβήθησαν chapter XVI. 5. where Luke says ἐμφόβων δὲ γενομένων. But that which precedes ἔπεσον ἐπὶ πρόσωπον αὐτῶν is to be referred to this very stupor rather than to veneration. For the Apostles, struck and cast down from their state of mind, as other writers teach us, were neither saying nor doing anything by the judgment of their mind. But just as sudden light causes us to cast our eyes to the ground, of which thing there is an example in Luke XXIV. so it is not a wonder if greater consternation casts the bodies themselves to the ground. Thus Daniel says of himself in chapter VIII. 17, ואפלה על־פני where the LXX have the same phrase πίπτω ἐπὶ πρόσωπόν μου. But ἐθαμβήθη had preceded, which place clearly explains this. Nor do those things which follow here seem to me to allow another interpretation. Compare the place Num. XVI. 22.

Although there is no doubt that both horror and stupor on account of the greatness of the miracle are noted here, and that what is said ἔπεσον ἐπὶ πρόσωπον αὐτῶν is also referred to stupor, which was rightly observed by Grotius from Dan. VIII. 17 and those things which follow here, yet the sense of veneration, which the same phrase of falling on the face is accustomed to bring, is not to be excluded: nor were the Apostles so struck in mind and cast down from their state of mind that they could not even venerate such great majesty, which was revealing itself to them, or do anything by the judgment of their mind, even if they did not sufficiently understand what that manifestation meant, and believed themselves to be in that blessedness which was to remain, and thus were dealing with building tabernacles, thus far they knew not what they were saying: but not altogether, as it seems to Grotius, disturbed from their state of mind. Only carnal ignorance, from which these things proceeded, is noted, and Peter truly did not know what he was saying, because neither eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor has it ascended into the heart of man, the things which God has prepared for us, Is. LXIV. 4. 1 Cor. II. 9. of which these were the preludes and representation. Cyril of Alexandria says thus to these, they knew not what they were saying: For before the passion and resurrection of the Savior, and the destruction of death and the corruption of our bodies, it could not be that Peter should be with Christ, and enjoy the heavenly tabernacles.

Latin:

Vers. 6. ἔπεσον ἐπὶ πρόσωπον αὐτῶν, καὶ ἐφοβήθησαν σφόδρα] Non tam horror hic erat quam stupor ob magnitudinem miraculi. Ideo Marcus in re simili dixit, ἐξεθαμβήθησαν cap. XVI. 5. ubi Lucas ἐμφόβων δὲ γενομένων. Quod autem præce- dit ἔπεσον ἐπὶ πρόσωπον αὐτῶν ad hunc ipsum stuporem po- tius quam ad venerationem referendum est. Perculsi enim Apostoli & de statu mentis dejecti, ut alii Scriptores nos do- cent, nihil aut loquebantur aut faciebant animi judicio. Sicut autem lux subita efficit ut oculos in terram dejicia- mus, cujus rei exemplum est Luc. XXIV. ita mirum non est si major consternatio corpora ipsa in terram dejiciat. Ita de se Daniel cap. VIII. 17. inquit, ואפלה על־פני u- bi LXX. eadem locutione πίπτω ἐπὶ πρόσωπόν με. Præcef- ferat autem ἐθαμβήθη qui locus hunc manifeste explicat. Neque videntur mihi quæ hic sequuntur aliam interpreta- tionem pati. Confer locum Num. XVI. 22.

Etsi dubium non sit & horrorem & stuporem ob magnitudinem miraculi hic notari, & ad stupo- rem referri quoque quod dicitur ἔπεσον ἐπὶ πρό- σωπον αὐτῶν quod è Dan. VIII. 17. & iis, quæ hic sequuntur, recte observatum Grotio, non ex- cludendus tamen venerationis sensus, quem ea- dem phrasis procidendi in faciem, inferre solet: neque ita animo perculsi, & de statu mentis dejecti fuêre Apostoli, ut ne venerari quidem tantam majestatem, quæ ipsis sese patefaciebat, potue- rint, aut quicquam facere, animi judicio, etsi non intelligerent satis, quid sibi velit ea Φανέρωσις, ac se in ea esse beatitudine crederent, quæ perman- sura sit, adeoque de construendis tabernaculis a- gerent, hactenus quid loquerentur, nescuii: non vero omnino, ut Grotio videtur, de statu mentis deturbati. Inscitia solum carnalis, ex qua hæc pro- fecta, notatur, & vere non noverat, quid loque- retur Petrus, quia nec oculus vidit, nec auris audivit, nec in cor hominis ascendit, quæ præparavit nobis Deus, Es. LXIV. 4. 1. Cor. II. 9. quorum hæc fuêre præludia, & repræsentatio. Cyrillus Alex. ita ad hæc, nesciebant, quid dicerent: Ante passionem enim & resurrectionem Salvatoris, destructionemque mor- tis & corruptionem corporum nostrorum fieri non pot- erat, ut Petrus esset cum Christo, & tabernaculis cæ- lestibus frueretur.

## 17:9
Vers. 9. ὅραμα] It may be permitted to translate it as spectacle, because a vision is more of a φάντασμα, as Cicero and others teach us: which, however, is itself often ὅραμα to the sacred writers and interpreters. What is ὅραμα here, Luke sometimes called ὀπτασίαν: both words express the Hebrew מראה which is found among the Prophets and Daniel.

Latin:

Vers. 9. ὅραμα] Vertere liceat spectaculum, quia visum magis est φάντασμα, ut nos Cicero atque alii docent: quod tamen & ipsum ὅραμα sæpe sacris Scriptoribus interpreti- busque. Lucas quod hic est ὅραμα aliquoties dixit ὀπτασίαν: utraque vox exprimit Hebræum מראה quod est apud Prophetas & Danielem.

## 17:10
Vers. 10. Why then do the scribes say that Elijah must come first?] Add from the following verse κὶ ἀποκαθιστάναι πάντα. For the teachers of the Hebrews taught both that Elijah would come and that he would correct all crooked things. Indeed, they even said that it would be Elijah who would anoint the Messiah as king and make him known to the people, which Trypho affirms for certain in the Disputation against Justin. Indeed, even today the Jews are accustomed to refer all knots of questions to what the Samaritans say about the Messiah, 'When Elijah comes, he will announce all things to us.' The occasion for this statement of the Apostles is to be sought from nowhere else than that they had indeed seen Elijah, but in such a way that he had departed again from their sight. But, they say, according to the received opinion of the learned, he ought to have come not to depart, but to amend all things, to teach the people, to point out the Messiah. πρῶτον, however, here is before the manifestation of the Messiah. Trypho, in the aforementioned place, speaks thus about the Messiah: 'nor does he have any power until Elijah comes and anoints him.'

Latin:

Vers. 10. Τί ὖν οἱ γραμματεῖς λέγεσιν, ὅτι Ἠλίαν δεῖ ἐλθεῖν πρῶτον;] Adde ex sequenti commate κὶ ἀποκαθιστάναι πάντα. Nam utrumque tradebant magistri Hebræorum & ventu- rum Eliam & omnia curva correcturum. Imo & Eliam fore dicebant qui Messiam esset uncturus in regem, eumque po- pulo notum facturus, quod pro certo affirmat Tryphon in Disputatione contra Justinum. Quin hodieque Judæi ado- mnes quæstionum nodos solent dicere, quod de Messia Sa- maritis, ὅταν ἔλθῃ Ἠλίας ἀναγγελεῖ ἡμῖν πάντα. Occasio hujus dicti Apostolorum non aliunde petenda est, quam quod Eliam vidissent quidem sed ita ut iterum abiisset è conspe- ctu. Atqui, inquiunt, ex recepta eruditorum sententia, veni- re debebat non abiturus, sed omnia emendaturus, docturus populum, monstraturus Messiam. πρῶτον autem hic est an- te manifestationem Messiæ. Tryphon dicto loco de Messia ita loquitur: ὐδὲ ἔχει δύναμιν τινα μέχρις ἂν ἐλθὼν Ἠλίας χρίσῃ αὐτὸν.

## 17:11
V. 11. he comes first, and will restore all things] It seems clear to me that these words look to the same thing as those which follow, namely to John the Baptist. For when all this discourse was finished, it is added, 'then the disciples understood that he spoke to them about John the Baptist.' But that it is said in the future tense ἀποκαταστήσει (just as you may rightly explain ἔρχεται as ἐλεύσεται) is done because it is shown that that old tradition was true and rightly accepted concerning the coming Elijah: not that he was still to come when Christ was speaking. It is clearly similar to what Christ said in chapter XI about the same Baptist, 'he is Elijah who is about to come': for he was not then about to come; indeed, he had almost finished his course and was near to death. But ὁ μέλλων ἔρχεσθαι is ὃς ἔμελλεν ἔρχεσθαι. Thus here ἔρχεται

to the restoration, or as Mark says, coming he restores, is nothing else than coming he comes and restores, just as also above chapter II. 4. how shall it be, that is, it is about to be, and chapter XI. 3. he who comes; it is he who was about to come, Luke XXIV. 44. that it must be fulfilled for that it is to be fulfilled. This will appear most true if one is pleased to consider whence that word to restore was taken. To me it is certain it was taken from Malachi, whose last verse the LXX translated thus: who shall restore the heart of the father to the son, and the heart of a man to his neighbor: where it appears the Hebrew הֵשִׁיב was translated by restore the heart, not badly: for to restore among other things is to put back into a true and natural state. Thus the member is restored when it is healed, above c. XII. 13. and morals when they are amended. But the Angel interprets this very passage of Malachi in such a way as to show that it was to be fulfilled in John the Baptist: he says, he shall go before him in the spirit and power of Elijah, to turn the hearts of the fathers to the children: explaining, of course, the to restore by the verb to turn, and explaining more fully what is here all things from the Prophet. This restoration, therefore, was consummated when John published the doctrine of repentance and sealed it with baptism, guiding our feet into the way of peace, as his father speaks in the sacred song. For in words of this kind, often not so much the fruit of the work as the work itself is regarded, although the work of John also does not lack great fruit. Therefore, they contradict the Angel who deny that those words of Malachi can be applied to the Baptist. I confess and willingly grant that not only the teachers of the Hebrews who lived in the time of Christ, but also those who were some centuries before, took those words according to the letter. For the LXX also added Thesbite to the word הֵשִׁיב, and the writer of Ecclesiasticus refers those words of Malachi to turn the heart of the father to the son to the same Thesbite. But most prophecies are so conceived that they can hardly be understood before the event, so that it is no wonder that men both pious and learned slip in their explanation, which I think happens to many today also in explaining the Apocalypse. Nor should the mention made there of the great and terrible day before which Elijah is to come, and what is subjoined, lest I come and strike the earth with a curse, move us from this heavenly interpretation of the words of Malachi. For these are to be referred not to the common judgment of the world, as many think, but to those punishments which awaited the Jews who were not amended, which God exacted by the hand of Titus. See above chapter III. 10. and Acts II. 17. I know the old tradition about Elijah returning before the end of the world is objected. But not everything that Tertullian believed and persuaded others of is necessarily to be held as an Apostolic tradition. Irenæus says this tradition flowed from the disciples of the Apostles, that Enoch and Elijah were translated into Paradise; that they remain there until the consummation, initiating incorruption, that is, as I suspect it was in the Greek, beginning incorruption: just as he said elsewhere about Enoch, that he is preserved as a witness of the just judgment of God. About the return of either Enoch or Elijah, there is nothing even there where he treats of the signs of the coming of the Antichrist. If we wish to consult later writers, whose authority cannot be equal in evaluating traditions, Procopius disagrees, Primasius disagrees, Nazianzenus doubts: which is enough to make it clear that this was never believed as if it were a sin to disagree. I, however, think that this persuasion arose from the Hebrews, in whose books we find that Elijah will be hidden after the times of the Messiah, and will reveal himself again in the days of Gog and Magog. For because the Apocalypse also mentions Gog and Magog, therefore whatever has been said in the Prophets about Gog and Magog, or whatever Hebrew credulity has added to the Prophets, Christian writers are accustomed to refer to the times of the Antichrist, which could be proved by many examples, if that discussion were not more rightly reserved for another place. Nor, however, do I deny that there is also in the Apocalypse itself what seems to favor this opinion, namely where it deals with those two witnesses, whom some want to be understood as Enoch and Elijah, but Hilary, as it seems to me, more probably as Moses and Elijah, because just as that: Fire will go out of their mouth, seems to pertain to Elijah, so by that other: they have power over the waters to turn them into blood, Moses seems to be signified. But even if the names of Moses and Elijah themselves were present there, as the name of Elijah exists in Malachi, we could, with two greatest authorities, Christ and the Angel of God, interpret that prophecy as concerning true teachers who would come in the spirit of Moses and the spirit of Elijah.

That tradition of the Rabbis must have been notorious then, that Elijah is to come, and as appears from the following verse, to correct all crooked things, which is to restore all things which proceeded from a false interpretation of the prophetic oracle, Mal. IV: For the teachers of the Hebrews understood this first of Elijah the Thesbite who was to return into the world, as is clear from this passage and the question proposed to John the Baptist in John I. 21: that this was an ancient tradition, Grotius rightly observes, because the LXX added Thesbite to the word Elijah, and because the writer of Ecclesiasticus refers the words of Malachi to the same Thesbite. But the angel taught Zacharias the parent that the oracle was to be accepted concerning John the Baptist, who came in the spirit and power of Elijah, Luke I. and he explained the restoration, which word is used of limbs when they are healed in Matthew XIX. 13. and of morals when they are amended, just as to restore among other things is to put back into a true and natural state, by the verb to turn, to which corresponds in Malachi, because conversion is a spiritual restoration of the heart. Then the Rabbis, according to their custom, adorned their tradition with various schemes, and among other things with that fiction which Trypho asserted in the disputation held with him in Justin, that Elijah would anoint the Messiah as King and make him known to the people, who speaks thus of the Messiah in the place mentioned, ὧδὲ ἔχει δύναμιν τι- να μέχρις ἂν ἐλθὼν Ἠλίας χρίσῃ αὐτὸν: Which, however, in another sense, not that Rabbinical one, was true of John, who was to come in the Spirit of Elijah, not only because the Messiah was to be anointed by him, i.e., as it were introduced into the possession of his office, which was formerly done by anointing, as Grotius softens the Jewish tradition at ch. IV. Matt. V. 5, but also because, as he was about to baptize Christ, the Holy Spirit was to anoint him himself with His gifts by His descent upon him, Matt. III. 16. Add also that which even today the Jews are accustomed to say to all the knots of questions, which the Samaritan woman says of the Messiah ἕταν ἔλθῃ Ἠλίας ἀναγγελεῖ ὑμῖν πάντα. Nor does Grotius observe badly that the occasion of this saying of the Apostles is not to be sought from elsewhere than that they had seen Elijah, but in such a way that he had again departed from sight. But, they say, according to the received opinion of the more learned, he ought to have come not to depart, but to amend all things, to teach the people, to show the Messiah. And that πρῶτον here is before the manifestation of the Messiah.

Moreover, this especially deserves observation here, how Grotius cuts the nerves of the Papists' fable about the return of Elijah before the final advent of Christ, which they try to deduce from Scripture, and shows its true origin. For since the Papists urge that it is said in the future here, ἔρχεται πρῶτον ᾄ ἀποκαταστήσει πάντα, he not only acknowledges that these words look to the same thing as those which follow, namely to John the Baptist, because after all this speech is finished it is added τότε συνῆ- καν οἱ μαθηταὶ ὅτι περὶ Ἰωάννε τῦ Βαπτιστῦ εἶπεν αὐτοῖς: but he also gives the reason for the use of the future tense: That it is said in the future tense ἀποκαταστήσει (just as you may rightly explain ἔρχεται by ἐλεύσεται) is done because it is shown that that old tradition, rightly accepted concerning the coming Elijah, was true; not that he was still to come when Christ was speaking. It is clearly similar to what Christ said in chapter XI about the same Baptist αὐτός ἐstιν Ἠ- λίας ὁ μέλλων ἔρχεσθαι. For he was not then about to come; indeed, he had almost finished his course, being near to death. But ὁ μέλλων ἔρχεσθαι is ὃς ἔμελλεν ἔρχε- σθαι. So here ἔρχεται & ἀποκαταστήσει or as Mark speaks ἐλθὼν ἀποκαθισᾷ is nothing else than ἔμελλεν ἔρχεσθαι καὶ ἀποκαθισάναι, just as also above II.4. πῶ γεννᾷται that is μέλλει γεννᾶσθαι & XI. 3. ὁ ἐρχόμενος is ὇ς ἔμελλεν ἔρχεσθαι. Luc.XXIII. 44. ὅτι δεῖ πληρωθῆναι for ἔδει πληρωθῆναι, which he proves by comparing the other from Malachi ch. IV with Luke I. Concerning which he concludes: they contradict the angel who deny that those words of Malachi can be adapted to the Baptist. Which I would like the Pontificians to note, with Bellarmine lib. III. de Rom. Pontif. cap. 6. the present place Matt. cap. XVII. & Matt. cap. IV. interpreting [the passage] concerning Elijah the Tishbite: those who, although they otherwise lean toward Popery with Grotius, also oppose Arias Montanus in chapter IV of Malachi. Job Ferus on Matthew XI, Hentenius in his preface to the Commentaries, Aretius on the Apocalypse, inasmuch as they acknowledge that the passage of Malachi must be understood as referring to none other than the Baptist: which Cornelius Jansenius in his Commentary on Malachi observes that Burgensis and Clarius also admit, and he adds his own vote to theirs in chapter XLVIII of Sirach, nor does Alcafar deny it on Apocalypse XI.3 regarding the passage of Malachi. Whence Ribera in Malachi IV praises the opinion of Jerome and others, which is in agreement with us, regarding the present passage of Matthew XVII. The exception of Cornelius a Lapide, that Malachi IV speaks of Elijah as a type regarding the first advent and of the true Elijah regarding the second, is not worthy of being discussed: because it concerns no one but a single person who was to come at the first advent of Christ, both by the force of the letter of the text and according to the infallible [interpretation] of Christ in Matthew XI and in this place. and the interpretation of the Angel Gabriel in Luke I. 17. For if the Papists growl that Malachi spoke of the great and terrible day of the Lord and of the land that was to be struck with a curse, which have been returned to them by us in place of a response, we do not repeat them here, but we observe at least the discourse of Grotius against the Papists: 'Nor,' he says, 'should the mention made in the same place of the great and terrible day, before which Elijah is to come, move us from this heavenly interpretation of the words of Malachi, and what is added, lest I come and strike the land with a curse. For these things are to be referred not to the common judgment of the world, as many think, but to those punishments which awaited the unrepentant Jews, which he exacted by the hand of Titus.' See above III. (Matthew) v. 10 and Acts II. 17.

Furthermore, regarding the things which the Papists draw from Apocalypse XI. 3 concerning the return of Elijah, although Grotius admits that some wished to understand Elijah and Enoch as the two witnesses, but Hilary more probably Moses and Elijah, he nevertheless adds: 'Even if the very names of Moses and Elijah were present there, as the name of Elijah exists in Malachi, we could, with two greatest authorities, Christ and the Angel of God, interpret that prophecy as referring to true teachers who would come in the Spirit of Moses and the Spirit of Elijah': which sense regarding true teachers he holds in common with the orthodox: nor does Thomas Aquinas deny that by the two witnesses in his Commentary on Apocalypse XI all preachers are to be understood. But just as Grotius was ambiguous here, defining nothing certain, and bringing forward only the probable opinion of Hilary concerning Moses and Elijah (which Lorinus refutes in 2 Peter 1. 16.) and that it could be understood as referring to true teachers: so he invented a completely different and unheard-of gloss of the Apocalypse passage in his Annotations on the same; concerning two assemblies, or kinds of Christians when Elijah began to be established, namely those sprung from Judea and those from the Gentiles, which it is not relevant to refute here. Let it suffice to have pointed out the inconsistency and uncertainty of the man.

Grotius also replied concerning the tradition which the Papists object, and he derives it not from the Apostles, but from the Hebrews: 'I know that the ancient tradition is objected concerning Elijah who is to return before the end of the world, but not everything that Tertullian believed and persuaded others of is to be held as an APOSTOLIC tradition.' Irenaeus says that this tradition flowed from the disciples of the Apostles, that Enoch and Elijah were translated into Paradise. 'There they remain until the consummation, beginning the incorruption, that is, as I suspect it was in the Greek, προκαταρχομένους τῆς ἀφθαρσίας: just as he said elsewhere of Enoch, that he is preserved as a witness of the just judgment of God.' But concerning the return of either Enoch or Elijah, [he says] nothing, not even where he treats the judgments of the advent

of the Anti-Christ. If we wish to consult later writers, whose authority cannot be equal in evaluating traditions, Procopius dissents, Primasius dissents; Nazianzenus doubts: which is enough to make it clear that this was never believed as if it were a sin to dissent. (Rupertus says, 'Concerning the advent of Elijah, I would not dare to define anything, because some of the Doctors, with whom we generally agree, believe that he is to come literally, but others by no means, with whom the illustrious man, B. Jerome, seems to agree.') Joachim Abbas in chapter XI of the Apocalypse, fol. 146. Nor, he says, can it be proven by spiritual or historical understanding that those witnesses whom John writes of are Enoch and Elijah, especially since the words which seem to make some presumption in part do not seem to touch upon Enoch and Elijah.) 'But I,' (thus Grotius continues) 'think that this persuasion originated from the Hebrews, in whose books we find that Elijah will be hidden after the times of the Messiah, and will reveal himself again in the days of Gog and Magog. For because the Apocalypse also mentions τꭣ̃ γὼγ καὶ μαγὼγ, therefore whatever has been said either in the Prophets concerning Gog and Magog, or whatever has been added to the Prophets' Hebrew credulity, Christian writers are accustomed to refer to the times of the Anti-Christ.' Which is also the opinion approved by the Papists, that the Anti-Christ is to come at the end of the world, [and] is the opinion in the appendix to the interpretation of the New Testament passages concerning the Anti-Christ, almost at the end: 'The Jews learned nothing from the Christians in sacred matters, nor do they wish to learn: but not a few of the ancient Christians drew more from the Jews than was necessary. And so Armilus, who was to arise at the end of the world, and indeed at Rome (for so the Jews wish, and their Armilus is nothing other than Romulus with a prefix, in the Chaldean manner), produced for us the Anti-Christ who is to come at the end of the world, not the other way around.' Concerning which I wish Grotius had settled with his Jesuit brothers before he departed to the majority. But how the Jews trifle that Elijah will first appear at the resurrection of the dead to announce it, see John. Hornbeck de convinc. Jud. p. 559. But these things are by occasion of the discourse of Grotius on this place, yet not beside the point: since some of the Papists, Jansenius in Conc. Evang. c. LXVII., Gagnejus on this place, Catharinus in Gen. c. II., would have it that Moses and Elijah appeared in the transfiguration of Christ because they are to return into this world before the judgment: and Maldonatus on this place affirms that John in Apoc. XI. 3. 6. writes so openly that Moses and Elijah are to come, that no one can deny it not only without rashness, but not even without impudence, which Lorinus not only disapproves of in that very place, but Grotius also acknowledges, even if the passage of John were far more open, and expressly named Elijah and Moses, it would not yet be necessary that Moses and Elijah, who once lived in the O.T., be understood, since other witnesses twin in Spirit to Moses and Elijah can be understood.

Latin:

V. 11. ἔρχεται πρῶτον, κὶ ἀποκαταστήσει πάντα] Liquidum mi- hi videtur verba hæc eodem spectare quo ea quæ sequun- tur, ad Johannem Baptistam scilicet. Nam finita omni hac oratione subjicitur τότε συνῆκαν οἱ μαθηταὶ ὅτι περὶ Ἰωάννα τῦ βαπτιςᾶ εἶπεν αὐτοῖς. Quod autem futuro tempore dicitur ἀποκαταστήσει (quomodo & ἔρχεται recte explices per i- λίνσεται) eo factum est quia ostenditur veram fuisse vete- rem illam παράδοσιν recte acceptam de venturo Elia: non quod venturus adhuc esset cum Christus loqueretur. Pla- ne simile est quod cap. XI. dixit Christus de eodem Baptista, αὐτός ἐσιν Ἠλίας ὁ μέλλων ἔρχεσθαι: non enim tum erat ven- turus: imo cursum suum ferme absolverat morti vicinus. Sed ὁ μέλλων ἔρχεσθαι est ὃς ἔμελλεν ἔρχεσθαι. Ita hic ἔρχεται

τῇ ἀποκαταστάσει, aut ut Marcus loquitur ἐλθὼν ἀποκαθι- στᾷ, nihil est aliud quam ἐρχόμενος ἔρχεται καὶ ἀποκαθιστάνει, quo- modo & supra cap. II. 4. πῶ γεννᾶται, id est μέλλει γεννᾶσθαι, & cap. XI. 3. ὁ ἐρχόμενος· est ὃς ἔμελλεν ἔρχεσθαι, Luc. XXIV. 44. ὅτι δεῖ πληρωθῆναι pro ἰδεῖ πληρωθῆναι. Verissimum hoc esse apparebit si considerare libeat unde sumta sit vox ista ἀποκαθιστάναι. Mihi pro certo est sumtam ex Malachia cujus postremum comma ita verterunt LXX. ὃς ἀποκαταστήσει καρ- δίαν πατρὸς πρὸς ὑὸν, καὶ καρδίαν ἀνθρώπου πρὸς τὸν πλησίον αὐ- τοῦ: ubi apparet הֵשִׁיב Hebræum versum esse per ἀποκα- ταστήσει καρδίαν, non male: nam ἀποκαθιστάνειν inter cæte- ra est reponere in verum & naturæ congruentem statum. Ita membrum ἀποκαθίσταται cum sanatur, supra c. XII. 13. & mores cum emendantur. At hunc ipsum Malachiæ locum Angelus ita interpretatur, ut eum ostendat in Johanne Ba- ptista impletum iri: αὐτὸς, inquit, προελεύσεται ἐνώπιον αὐτοῦ ἐν πνεύματι καὶ δυνάμει Ἡλίου, ἐπιστρέψαι καρδίας πατέρων ἐπὶ τέκ- να: nimirum τὸ ἀποκαθιστάναι exponens per verbum ἐπιστρέ- ψαι, & quod hic est πάντα fusius ex Propheta explicans. Hæc ergo ἀποκατάστασις consummata est, cum doctrinam pœni- tentiæ publicavit Johannes & baptisino obsignavit, κατευ- θύνων τοὺς πόδας εἰς ὁδὸν εἰρήνης, ut pater ipsius in carmine sacro loquitur. Nam in verbis hujusmodi sæpe non tam fructus o- peræ quam opera ipsa respicitur, quanquam & opera Johan- nis fructu magno non caret. Angelo igitur contradicunt, qui negant ista Malachiæ verba Baptistæ posse aptari. Fateor ac do libenter, non solos magistros Hebræorum qui Christi vi- vebant tempore, sed & eos qui aliquot ante fuerunt seculis verba ista κατὰ τὸ ῥητὸν accepisse. Nam & LXX. ad vocem הֵשִׁיב addiderunt Θεσβίτην, & Ecclesiastici Scriptor verba illa Malachiæ ἐπιστρέψαι καρδίαν πατρὸς πρὸς ὑὸν ad eundem Thesbiten refert. Sed pleraque vaticinia ita sunt concepta, ut ante eventum intelligi vix queant, ita ut mirum non sit in eorum explicatione labi viros & pios & eruditos, quod hodie quoq; in explicanda Apocalypsi multis arbitror con- tingere. Neque dimovere nos ab hac verborum Malachiæ cælesti interpretatione debet mentio ibidein facta diei ma- gnæ & terribilis quam ante venturus sit Elias, & quod sub- jungitur, ne percutiens feriam terram anathemate. Hæc e- nim non ad commune de mundo judicium, ut multi pu- tant, sed ad eas pœnas referenda sunt quæ Judæos non e- mendatos manebant, quas Titi manu Deus exegit. Vide su- pra cap. III. 10. & Act. II. 17. Scio objici veterem παράδοσιν de redituro Elia ante mundi exitum. Sed non quicquid Ter- tullianus credidit, & aliis persuasit, utique Apostolica tradi- tio habenda est. Irenæus à discipulis Apostolorum manas- se ait hanc traditionem, Enochum & Eliam in Paradisum es- se translatos; ibi eos manere usque ad consummationem, coauspicantes incorruptelam, id est, ut in Græco fuisse suspi- cor, προκαταρχομένους τῆς ἀφθαρσίας: quomodo & alibi de E- nocho dixit, conservari eum testem justi judicii Dei. De re- ditu aut Enochi aut Eliæ nihil ne ibi quidem ubi tractat in- dicia adventus Antichristi. Si posteriores Scriptores consule- re volumus, quorum in æstimandis traditionibus non potest par esse auctoritas, dissentit Procopius, dissentit Primasius, dubitat Nazianzenus: quod satis est ut liqueat nunquam hoc ita creditum quasi dissentire nefas esset. Ego vero arbi- tror persuasionem istam ab Hebræis ortam, in quorum libris reperimus Eliam post tempora Messiæ occultatum iri, ite- rumq; se patefacturum in diebus Gog & Magog. Nam quia Apocalypsis quoque meminit τοῦ Γὼγ καὶ Μαγὼγ, ideo quic- quid aut in Prophetis dictum est de Gog & Magog, aut quicquid ad Prophetas adjecit Hebræa credulitas, solent Christiani Scriptores ad Antichristi tempora referre, quod multis exemplis probari posset, nisi ea tractatio rectius alii loco reservaretur. Neq; tamen nego esse & in ipsa Apocaly- psi, quod huic opinioni favere videatur, rubi nempe de duo- bus illis testibus agitur, quos alii Enochum & Eliam, Hila- rius, ut mihi videtur, probabilius Mosem & Eliam vult intel- ligi, quia sicut illud: Ignis exibit de ore eorum, ad Eliam vide- tur pertinere, ita altero illo: potestatem habent super aquas convertendi eas in sanguinem, Moses videtur significari. Sed etiamsi ipsa Mosis & Eliæ nomina ibi exstarent, ut apud Ma- lachiam exstat nomen Eliæ, possemus, duobus maximis au- ctoribus, Christo & Angelo Dei, vaticinium illud interpreta- ri de veri doctoribus venturis in spiritu Mosis & spiritu Eliæ.

Notoriam tum fuisse oportet illam Rabbino- rum traditionem, quod venturus Elias sit, & uti è sequenti commate apparet, curva omnia correctu- rus, quod est ἀποκαθιστάναι πάντα quæ è ψευδερμη- νείᾳ oraculi Prophetici, Mal. IV. profecta: Hoc enim primum de Elia Thesbite in mundum reditu- ro intelligebant Ebræorum Magistri, ut ex hoc lo- co, & quæstione Joh. I. 21. Johanni Baptistæ pro- posita liquet: quam παράδοσιν antiquam fuisse, re- &e observat Grotius, quod LXX. ad vocem Ἠλίαν addiderint θεσβίτην, quodque scriptor Ecclesiastici verba Malachiæ ad eundem Thesbitem referat. Quod vero oraculum de Johanne Baptista, qui in spiritu & virtute Eliæ venit, accipiendum esle, angelus Zachariam parentem docuit Luc. I. & ἀποκατάσα- σις, quæ vox de membris cum sanantur Matth. XIX. 13. de moribus, cum emendantur, adhibe- tur, uti ἀποκαθιstάναι inter cætera est reponere in verum, & naturæ congruentem statum, exposuit, per verbum ἐπιστρέψαι, cui apud Malachiam re- spondet השיב, quia conversio est spiritualis ἀποκατάsασις τῆς καρδίας. Deinde traditionem suam variis schematibus, pró more suo, exorna- runt Rabbini, & eo, inter cætera, commento, quod apud Justinum in disputatione cum eo habi- ta, asseruit Tryphon, Eliam uncturum Messiam in Regem, eumque populo notum facturum, qui de Messia ita loco dicto loquitur, ὧδὲ ἔχει δύναμιν τι- να μέχρις ἂν ἐλθὼν Ἠλίας χρίσῃ αὐτὸν: Quod ta- men alio sensu, non Rabbinico illo verum erat de Johanne, in Spiritu Eliæ venturo, non tantum, quod ab eo Messias ungi, h. e. quasi in possessionem muneris sui introduci, quod olim per unctionem fiebat, de- buerit, ut Grotius ad c. IV. Matth. V. 5. Judæo- rum traditionem emollit, sed quod etiam eo Chri- stum baptizaturo Spiritus Sanctus ipsum, descensu suo in eundem, donis suis uncturus sit, Matth. III. 16. Adde & illud, quod hodieque Judæi ad omnes quæ- stionum nodos solent dicere, quod de Messia Samari- tis ἕταν ἔλθῃ Ἠλίας ἀναγγελεῖ ὑμῖν πάντα. Ne- que male observat Grotius, occasionem hujusce di- sti Apostolorum non aliunde petendam esse, quam quod Eliam vidissent, sed ita ut iterum abiisset è conspectu. Atqui, inquiunt, ex recepta eruditiorum sententia, venire debebat non abiturus, sed omnia emendaturus, docturus populum, monstraturus Messiam. Et πρῶ- τον hic esse ante manifestationem Messiæ.

Cæterum id imprimis observationem hic me- retur, quomodo nervos incidat fabellæ Papicola- rum de reditu Eliæ ante adventum Christi novissi- mum, quam è Scriptura deducere conantur, e- jusque originem veram monstret Grotius. Nam quum urgeant Papistæ, quod in futuro hic dica- tur, ἔρχεται πρῶτον ᾄ ἀποκαταστήσει πάντα, non agnoscit tantum verba hæc eodem spectare, quo ea, quæ sequuntur, ad Johannem Baptistam scilicet, quia finita omni hac oratione subjicitur τότε συνῆ- καν οἱ μαθηταὶ ὅτι περὶ Ἰωάννε τῦ Βαπτιστῦ εἶπεν αὐτοῖς: seu rationem etiam reddit adhibitiæ in fu- turo loquutionis: Quod autem futuro tempore di- citur ἀποκαταστήσει (quomodo & ἔρχεται recte ex- plices per ἐλεύσεται) eo factum est, quia ostenditur veram fuisse veterem illam παράδοσιν recte acceptam de venturo Elia; non quod venturus adhuc esset cùm Christus loqueretur. Plane simile est quod capite XI. dixit Christus de eodem Baptista αὐτός ἐstιν Ἠ- λίας ὁ μέλλων ἔρχεσθαι. non enim tum erat ventu- rus, imo cursum suum ferme absolverat morti vici- nus. Sed ὁ μέλλων ἔρχεσθαι est, ὃς ἔμελλεν ἔρχε- σθαι. Ita hic ἔρχεται & ἀποκαταστήσει aut ut Mar- cus loquitur ἐλθὼν ἀποκαθισᾷ nihil est aliud quam ἔμελλεν ἔρχεσθαι καὶ ἀποκαθισάναι quomodo & su- pra II.4. πῶ γεννᾷται id est μέλλει γεννᾶσθαι & XI. 3. ὁ ἐρχόμενος est ὇ς ἔμελλεν ἔρχεσθαι. Luc.XXIII. 44. ὅτι δεῖ πληρωθῆναι prò ἔδει πληρωθῆναι, Quod alterius è Malachia cap. IV. cum Luc. I. colla- to probat. de quo concludit; angelo contradicunt, qui negant ista Malachiæ verba Baptistæ posse apta- ri. Quod Pontificii, velim, notent, cum Bel- larmino lib. III. de Rom. Pontif. cap. 6. locum præsentem Matth. cap. XVII. & Matth. cap. IV. de Elia Thesbite accipientes: quibus vero cum Grotio alias Papizante, adversantur etiam Arias Montan. in cap. IV. Malach. Job. Ferus in Matth. XI. Hentenius in præfat. ad Comment. Aret. in A- poc. utpote qui agnoscunt, non nisi de Baptista lo- cum Malachiæ accipiendum esse: quod etiam Bur- gensem, & Clarium fateri Corn. Jansenius in Com- ment. ad Malach. observat, iisque calculum adjicit in c. XLVIII. Syrac. neque abnuit Alcafar ad Ap. XI.3. de loco Malachiæ. Unde præsente loco Matth. XVII. laudat Ribera in Mal. IV. Hieronymi, & alio- rum nobis ὁμόψηφον sententiam. Cornelii Lapidei exceptio quod Mal. IV. & de Elia typico circa pri- mum, & de vero circa secundum adventum sermo sit, digna non est, quæ discutiatur: quia non nisi de una persona sub adventum primum Christi ven- tura agitur & vi literæ textus, & secundum infalli- bilem Christi Matth. XI. & h. l. & Angeli Gabrie- lis Luc. I. 17. interpretationem. Nam si Pontificii ogganniant, quod de die magno Domini & terribili ac de terra anathemate percutienda loquutus sit Malachias, quæ ipsis responsionis loco reddita sunt à nobis, hic non repetimus, Grotianum sal- tem adversus Pontificios discursum observamus: Neque dimovere, inquit, nos ab hac verborum Mala- chiæ cælesti interpretatione debet mentio ibidem facta diei magnæ, & terribilis, quam ante venturus sit Elias, & quod subjungitur, ne percutiens feriam terram anathemate. Hæc enim non ad commune de mundo judicium, ut multi putant, sed ad eas pœ- nas referenda sunt, quæ Judæos non emendatos ma- nebant, quas Titi manu exegit. Vide supra III. (Matth.) v. 10. & Act. II. 17.

Quæ porro ex Ap. XI. 3. de reditu Eliæ depro- munt Pontificii, etsi fateatur Grotius nonnullos per duos testes Eliam & Henochum, Hilarium vero pro- babilius Mosen, & Eliam voluisse intelligi, addit tamen: etiamsi ipsa Mosis, & Eliæ nomina ibi exstarent, ut apud Malachiam extat nomen Eliæ, possemus, duobus maximis auctoribus, Christo, & Angelo DEI, vaticinium illud interpretari de veris doctoribus venturis in Spiritu Mosis, & Spiritu E- liæ: quem sensum de veris doctoribus cum ortho- doxis communem habet: nec abnuit eidem Tho- mas de Aquino in Comment. Ap. XI. per duos testes intelligi omnes prædicatores. Ut autem hic ambigu- us fuit Grotius, nihil certi definiens, probabilem solum afferens Hilarii de Mose & Elia sententiam (quam non tantum in Joachimo Abbate, Jansenio, Gagnejo, Catharino, sed etiam in Maldonato so- cietatis suæ Patre, Lorinus refellit, in 2. Petr. 1. 16.) & quod possit de veris Doctoribus accipi: sic aliam plane, ac inauditam commentus loci Apocalypti- ci est glossam in Annotatis ad eundem; de duobus conventibus, seu Christianorum generibus cum condi Ælia cœpit, ex Judæa nempe, & ex gentibus ortis, quam hic non attinet refellere. Sufficiat incon- stiantiam, & incertitudinem hominis indicasse.

De traditione etiam respondit Grotius, quam obvertunt Papistæ, eamque non ab Apostolis, sed Ebræis derivant: scio objici veterem παράδοσιν de redituro Elia ante mundi exitum, sed non quicquid Tertullianus credidit, & aliis persuasit, utique A- POSTOLICA traditio habenda est. IRENEUS à discipulis Apostolorum manasse ait hanc traditio- nem, Enochum & Eliam in Paradisum esse transla- tos. Ibi eos manere usque ad consummationem coau- spicantes incorruptelam, id est, ut in Græco fuisse suspicor, προκαταρχομένους τῆς ἀφθαρσίας: quo- modo & alibi de Enocho dixit, conservari eum testem justi judicii DEI. De reditu aut Enochi, aut Eliæ nihil ne ibi quidem ubi tractat judicia adventus

Anti-Christi. Si posteriores scriptores consulere vo- lumus, quorum in æstimandis traditionibus non po- test par esse auctoritas, dissentit Procopius, dissentit Primasius; dubitat Nazianzenus: quod satis est, ut liqueat nunquam hoc ita creditum quasi dissentire nefas esset. (Rupertus, de adventu Eliæ, inquit, quicquam definire non ausim, quia Doctorum aliqui, quibus fere consentimus, credunt, eum ad literam esse venturum, alii vero nequaquam, quibus vir il- lustris, B. Hieronymus consentire videtur. Joachi- mus Abbas in cap. XI. Apoc. fol. 146. Neque ait, in- tellectu spirituali, neque Historico probari potest, eos testes, quos scribit Johannes esse Enochum & Eliam, maxime cum verba, quæ videantur ex parte ali- quantam facere præsumtionem non videantur tange- re Enoch & Eliam.) Ego vero arbitror (ita per-“ git Grotius) persuasionem istam ab Hebræis“ ortam, in quorum libris reperimus Eliam post“ tempora Messiæ occultatum iri, iterumque se“ patefacturum in diebus Gog & Magog. Nam“ quia Apocalypsis quoque meminit τꭣ̃ γὼγ καὶ“ μαγὼγ, ideo quicquid aut in Prophetis dictum“ est de Gog & Magog, aut quicquid ad Prophetas“ adject. Hebræa credulitas, soleant Christiani“ scriptores ad Anti-Christi tempora referre.“ Quæ etiam de opinione illa Pontificiis probata,“ quod Anti-Christus sub finem mundi venturus sit,“ in appendice ad interpretationem locorum N.“ T. de Anti-Christo fere sub finem est sententia:“ Judæi a Christianis in rebus sacris nihil didicere,“ nec volunt discere: Christianorum autem vete-“ rum non pauci plura ab Judæis hausêre, quam o-“ pus esset. Itaque ארמילוס sub finem mundi ex-“ titurus, & quidem Romæ (ita enim volunt Judæi,“ & ארמילוס ipsorum nihil aliud est, quam“ Romulus præposita voce, more Chaldaico) An-“ ti-Christum nobis sub finem mundi adventu-“ rum peperit, non contra. De quo vellem transe-“ gisset cum fratribus suis Jesuitis Grotius, ante- quam ad plures migraret. Quomodo autem Eliam primo appariturum justante mortuorum resurre- ctione: ut eam annunciet, Judæi nugentur, vid. Joh. Hornbeck de convinc. Jud. p. 559. Sed hæc oc- casione discursus Grotiani ad h. l. non tamen præ- ter rem: siquidem è Pontificiis nonnulli Jansenius in Conc. Evang. c. LXVII. Gagnejus in h. l. Catha- rinus in Gen. c. II. Mosen & Eliam ideo in transfi- guratione Christi apparuisse velint, quia ante ju- dicium redituri sint in hunc mundum: & Maldona- tus ad h. l. affirmet, Johannem in Apoc. XI. 3. 6. tam aperte scribere Mosen, & Eliam esse venturos, ut nemo non solum sine temeritate, sed nec sine impu- dentia negare possit, quod non improbat modo in ipso Lorinus, sed agnoscit quoque Grotius, etiamsi longe apertior esset locus Johannis, & diserte nomi- naret Eliam, ac Mosen, non tamen necessum fore, ut Moses & Elias, qui olim vixerunt in V. T. intelli- gantur, quum possint alii testes Spiritu Mosi, & Eliæ gemini intelligi.

## 17:12
Vers. 12. ὅσα ἠθέλησαν] Whatever pleased them, God not impelling, but wisely permitting. However, the nominative is missing, which can be supplied in various ways. To me it seems that 'the Jews' should be understood, which word comprehends as well Herod and the Galilean nobles, as the Chief Priests, Senators, and experts in the law, the former the slayers of the Baptist, the latter of Christ,

PART II. The restoration of the lunatic.

Latin:

Vers. 12. ὅσα ἠθέλησαν] Quicquid ipsis collibitum est, Deo non impellente, sed sapienter permittente. Deest au- tem nominativus, qui diversis modis suppleri potest. Mihi intelligendum videtur Judæi, quæ vox tam Herodem & Galilæos proceres, quam Pontifices, Senatores & legisperi- tos, illos Baptistæ, hos Christi interfectores comprehendit,

PARS II. Lunatici restitutio.

## 17:14
Vers. 14. Γονυπετῶν αὐτῷ] Thus γονυπετὴς in Euripides is one who falls upon his knees. In Aratus, ὁ ἐν γόνασι, in Latin, nixus. The LXX concerning Solomon 2 Paralip. VI. 13. ἔπεσεν ἐπὶ τὰ γόνατα αὑτοῦ. Γονυπετῶν is just to fall at the knees, which is called προσπίπτειν τοῖς γόνασι, as in Luke V. verse 8, concerning which matter we spoke above at the beginning of the eighth chapter:

merely to fall upon the knees, which gestures are various. Concerning falling upon the knees, there is much everywhere in Homer, Euripides, and the Latin poets as well as the historians. There is, says Pliny, a certain religion in the knees of man by the observation of nations: suppliants touch these. To the bending of the knees pertains that of the same writer: They adore the King, they submit their knees. And that of Ovid: And on bended knees as a suppliant and like one asking.

The Hellenists, however, say γονυπετεῖν τινι, as here, and γονυπετεῖν τινα, as in Mark 1:40, chapter 10:17, for that which is γονυπετεῖν ἔμπροσθέν τινος, as below in chapter 27:29. Luke also, instead of γονυπετεῖν, has sometimes said τιθέναι γόνατα, Mark τιθέντες τὰ γόνατα προσεκύνει αὐτῷ, and Paul γόνατα κάμπτειν. In this place, indeed, the Syriac and Latin interpreter take γονυπετεῖν in the latter sense.

Latin:

Vers. 14. Γονυπετῶν αὐτῷ] Ita γονυπετὴς Euripidi qui in genua procumbit. Arato ὁ ἐν γόνασι, Latinis nixus. LXX. de Solomone 2. Paralip. VI. 13. ἔπεσεν ἐπὶ τὰ γό- νατα αὑτꭣ̃. Γονυπετῶν modo est genibus advolvi, quod dicitur προσπίπτειν τοῖς γόνασι, ut Luc. V. vers. 8. qua de re diximus supra ad initium capitis octavi:

modo in genua procidere, qui gestus diversi sunt. De ad- volutione ad genua passim multa apud Homerum, Euri- pidem, Latinosque tum Poëtas tum historiarum Scripto- res. Hominis genibus, inquit Plinius, religio quædam inest observatione gentium: hæc supplices attingunt. Ad flexionem genuum pertinet illud ejusdem Scriptoris: Regem adorant, genua submittunt. Et Ovidii istud: Et genibus pronis supplex similisque roganti.

Dicunt autem Hellenistæ γονυπετεῖν τινι, ut hic, & γονυπε- τεῖν τινα, ut Marci I. 40. cap. X. 17. pro eo quod est γονυπε- τεῖν ἔμπροσθέν τινος, ut infra cap. XXVII. 29. Lucas quoque pro γονυπετεῖν aliquoties dixit τιθέναι γόνατα, Marcus τιθέν- τες τὰ γόνατα προσεκύνει αὐτῷ, & Paulus γόνατα κάμπτειν. Hoc quidem loco τὸ γονυπετεῖν posteriore significatu Syrus & Latinus interpres accipiunt.

## 17:15
Verse 15. σεληνιάζεται] See what was said above on chapter 4. That a demon was the cause of this disease appears below in verse 18. But demons, because they excel in knowledge, are accustomed to join natural causes to their own power. Thus here the demon was accustomed to occupy those times in which the brain is weaker, which is accustomed to happen at lunar intervals. This man was a lunatic not only from the opinion of the common people, which seemed so to Photius; but because his body labored altogether at the times of the moon with the comitial disease and other affections of such a kind: but that madness was also added to the diabolical disease, the history sufficiently testifies.

Latin:

Vers. 15. σεληνιάζεται] Vide quæ supra ad caput IV. Causam hujus morbi fuisse dæmonium, apparet infra commate 18. Solent autem dæmones, quia pollent scien- tia, etiam naturales causas ad suam vim adjungere. Ita hic dæmon ea tempora occupare solebat, quibus cerebrum est infirmivs, quod Lunaribus intervallis contingere solet. Lunaticus hic fuit non tantum ex vulgi opinio- ne, quod Photio visum; sed quod omnino corpus lunæ temporibus comitiali morbo, aliisque ta- lium affectibus laborârit: sed ad morbum Diabo- licum etiam furorem accessisse satis historia testa- tur.

## 17:17
Verse 17. Εἶπεν. ὦ γενεὰ ἄπιστος κῂ διεστραμμένη] These things were not said to the Apostles, whose little faith is nevertheless rebuked below, but to the father of the sick boy and his friends, as is clear from Mark, yet so that by their example the common vice of the Jewish nation was accused. These words are taken from Deuteronomy 32:20, where the LXX say, 'for it is a perverse generation, children in whom there is no faith.' Paul said γενεὰν διεστραμμένην in Philippians 2:15. We learn from these words and those which follow, that God, in order that he may perform miracles as benefits for men, for the most part requires two things: trust in him who is about to perform the sign, and trust in him to whom the sign is to be profitable: yet so that a great and excellent trust of one of these can supply what is lacking in the other. Nor is that a wonder, since all these things tended to this, that the power of true trust in God might be commended, through which eternal benefits are believed in, and by believing are obtained, as has been explained elsewhere.

ἕως πότε ἔσομαι μεθ' ὑμῶν; ἕως πότε ἀνέξομαι ὑμῶν] Christ shows that the final times of divine patience toward the Jews are now being spent: tacitly looking back at what follows in Deuteronomy concerning the provocation of the Gentiles.

Latin:

Vers. 17. Εἶπεν. ὦ γενεὰ ἄπιστος κῂ διεστραμμένη] Non in Apostolos hæc dicta sunt, quorum tamen ὀλιγοπισία in- fra reprehenditur, sed in Patrem ægroti ejusque amicos, ut ex Marco liquet, ita tamen ut ex eorum exemplo com- mune Judaicæ gentis vitium accusaretur. Sunt autem sumpta hæc verba ex Deuteronomio XXXII. 20. ubi LXX. ὅτι γενεὰ ἐξεστραμμένη ἐστὶ, υἱοὶ οἷς ὀυκ ἔστι πίστις ἐν ἀυ- τοῖς. Γενεὰν διεστραμμένην dixit Paulus Phil. II. 15. Disci- mus ex his verbis & quæ sequuntur, Deum ut miracula beneficia hominibus præstet, ἐπιτοπολὺ duo requirere, fiduciam in eo qui signum sit editurus, & fiduciam in eo cui signum sit profuturum: ita tamen ut magna atque excellens fiducia horum alterius supplere possit quod alte- ri deest. Neque id mirum, cum omnia hæc eo tende- rent, ut commendaretur vis veræ in Deum fiduciæ per quam beneficia æterna creduntur, & credendo impetran- tur, ut alibi explicatum est.

ἕως πότε ἔσομαι μεθ' ὑμῶν; ἕως πότε ἀνέξομαι ὑμῶν] O- stendit Christus ultima divinæ erga Judæos patientiæ tempora nunc agi: tacite respiciens quod in Deuterono- mio sequitur de gentium sugguratione.

## 17:20
Verse 20. Ἀπιστίαν] He calls ὀλιγοπιστίαν 'unbelief,' compared, of course, to the trust which they ought to have had in proportion to the reason of their long instruction and the duty imposed upon them. It is to be noted, however, that the words πισὸς and ἄπιστος are taken one way among Greek writers, and another way among Jewish Hellenists. To the Greeks, πισὸς is one who stands by his promises, and therefore worthy of being trusted: ἄπιστος is perfidious: in which meanings these words are also to be found in these books. But it is a property of the Hellenists to call him πιστὸν who believes in someone and trusts, and ἄπιστον him who is otherwise disposed. Clement of Alexandria conveniently defines ἀπιστίαν for this place: 'a weak and negative assumption of the opposite.'

Grotius rightly notes that ὀλιγοπιστίαν is called ἀπιστίαν here, compared, of course, to that which they ought to have had in proportion to the reason of their long instruction and the duty imposed upon them: And that the word πισὸν and ἄπιστον are taken one way among Greek writers, and another way among Jewish Hellenists: because to the Greeks, πισὸς is one who stands by his promises, and therefore worthy of being trusted: ἄπιστος is perfidious: But it is a property of the Hellenists to call him πιστὸν who believes in someone and trusts, and ἄπιστον him who is otherwise disposed. Which is to be opposed to the Papists, who deny that faith is trust: See Bellarmine, book 1 on justification, chapter 5, and Pistorius in his positions on justification, thesis 4, who boldly affirm that in the whole of Holy Scripture, especially in the New Testament and in the matter of justification, the word πίστις is distinct from the word for trust. If anyone should desire passages, these following ones out of many can be seen, in which πίστις cannot be taken otherwise than as trust. Matthew 9:22, chapter 15:28, Luke 5.

20. John 6, last verse. Acts 14:9. 1 John 5:13. Whence Jansenius in his Harmony of the Gospels, chapter 32, most rightly says that the name of faith in the Gospels, when salvation or the attainment of all things that we wish is attributed to it, embraces both, namely, both that firm assent in believing things about God and Christ, and the TRUST conceived from his omnipotent goodness. And Cajetan in his explanation of the said Mosaic passage, 'Abraham believed' (Gen. 15), Moses does not say that Abraham believed God, but in God, for this is more: For to believe God is to have faith in his words as truthful. But to believe in God adds, moreover, TRUST in God. Georgius Cassander in his Consultations, article 4, has it thus on page 12. To obtain justification, such faith is required as that by which a man, after the example of Abraham, does not hesitate at the promise of God through unbelief, but believes in hope against hope, namely that to him who believes in Him who raised Jesus Christ from the dead, God will impute this faith for justification, and will not impute sins. Grotius, although already leaning toward Popery in his annotations on Cassander, could not disapprove of this: since he approved the Ratisbon formula, that living faith APPREHENDS the mercy of God in Christ, and believes that the righteousness which is in Christ is freely imputed to him. See our Exegema on the Augustan Confession, art. IV, cap. VII, §. VI. Nor do the Waleburg brethren deny this, but concede that faith is taken for special faith, which applies general promises in particular with true confidence conjoined, as we observed in the same place, §. XVII.

But as for the fact that the Jesuit Julius Caesar Coturius, in Epit. Contr. demonstr. XI, cap. IV, p. 275, attempts to show an implication here from our own principles—as he barbarously speaks—because confidence is prior to justification in our opinion (in the order of nature, that is), whence he concludes: if the act of faith or confidence is prior to justification, then in that prior state, in which the sinner believes and is certain that he is just, he believes and trusts a falsehood: because in that prior state in which he thus believes and trusts, he is not yet just, but only becomes just afterwards: these are trifles, unworthy of Jesuitical acuteness. Because the confidence which is required by us antecedently to justification is not the act of trusting, or the confidence of a sinner by which he believes himself to be just—for this is a consequence of justification, not an antecedent—but that immovable confidence of the heart by which a sinner determines not only generally that Christ died, but also trusts in particular, and firmly believes, that God WILLS to be propitious to him in Christ, and for the sake of Christ's merits actually to remit all his sins, to impute righteousness, and to grant eternal life, as Coturius himself explained our opinion on page 278. Therefore, it is not that confidence by which we believe that our sins HAVE BEEN remitted, that righteousness HAS BEEN imputed to us, that eternal life HAS BEEN granted to us—as the Sophist subsequently perverts our opinion—but that by which we believe that God WILLS to remit our sins, that God WILLS to impute to us the righteousness of Christ, that God WILLS to grant us eternal life, which is that faith by which we are justified; by which, namely, we embrace with true confidence of heart this gracious WILL OF GOD declared in the word of promise, and lean upon the same, and thus we apprehend the PROMISE of the Gospel itself, and apply it to ourselves, and so we obtain the gracious remission of sins and the imputation of righteousness, and are justified: which justification is finally followed by that certainty of grace, righteousness, and our salvation. ὡς κόκκον σινάπεως] A proverb famous among the Hebrews requires that this be referred to quantity, not to quality, just as mention was made above of a grain of mustard as a very small thing. In Latin we would say demonstratively, if you had even a little bit of trust: when Christ says this, he does not deny that the Apostles have some trust, but as I have said, having regard for the time and the duty, he says that this trust is less than the least, that is, extremely small.

Ἐρεῖτε τῷ ὄρει τύτῳ, μετάβηθι ἐντεῦθεν ἐκεῖ] And this is also proverbial, as appears from Paul, 1 Cor. 13:2. The sense, therefore, is: you would perform the most difficult things. Nor do the words of Christ, who attributes the moving of mountains to small faith, conflict with those of Paul, who seems to refer this very thing to the greatest faith. For that small faith which Christ requires is of such a measure that it suffices for any miracles whatsoever: if anything is added beyond this, it cannot increase the efficacy of miracles brought to fullness. Furthermore, that Christ is not here dealing with the gift of signs is proven by the fact that to lack it is not among the things to be blamed, but rather to have it is of rare happiness. And so this faith is rather a condition required for the use of the gift. But this very faith, adapted to eternal benefits, is that which, with love preceding, profits for salvation, as Paul demonstrates in the cited passage. For unless love is added, that faith will indeed exist, but it will not be living or efficacious. It becomes living and efficacious, however, when we diligently weigh not only what God can do and what He promises, but also what He requires of us. Nor would I deny that what is said here is sometimes fulfilled κατὰ τὴν κυριολεξίαν, since the martyrologies report that through the prayers of Nonnosus a rock of immense size was moved to Soracte; and authors not to be despised testify that the same was performed by an Armenian Bishop at the insistence of the Babylonian Caliph in the year 1225. But the allegorical sense is that there will be nothing so lofty that it does not vanish at their prayers. See Apoc. VIII. 8.

That this is proverbial is entirely apparent from 1 Cor. XIII. 2, so that the sense is: you might perform the most difficult things; nor is the proverb celebrated among the Hebrews, ὡς κόκκον σινάπεως, poorly explained in Latin: we would say demonstratively: if you had even the slightest bit of confidence, in this sense indeed, that Christ does not deny that the Apostles had some confidence, but, having regard for the time and the office, says that that confidence was less than the least, that is, extremely small. Finally, although it must not be denied that what is said here was sometimes fulfilled even literally, since martyrologies report that a rock of huge mass was moved to Soracte by the prayers of Nonnosus; and the same was performed by an Armenian Bishop at the insistence of the Babylonian Caliph in the year 1225, such as are also [reported] concerning Gregory Thaumaturgus by Nyssen in his life of him, and by Eusebius, lib. VII. Histor. Eccles. chap. 25. Jerome in his life of Hilarion, and M. Paul the Venetian in Part 1, chap. XVIII of his History of the East, report concerning the Christians who, at the demand of a tyrant, moved a mountain in Tartary: which literal sense Chrysostom urges in homily LVIII. We readily concede, however, to Grotius that the sense here is allegorical, that there will be nothing so lofty that it does not vanish at the prayers of the Apostles, or rather that by this one named example it is implied that others are to be understood in like manner, so that the expression is proverbial: the moving of mountains is therefore not excluded, even if it is not the only thing designated.
