Furthermore, that this very faith, which Grotius not inappropriately maintains is not itself the χάρισμα τῶν σημείων, but rather a condition required for the use of the gift, is adapted to eternal benefits, and that it is this which, with love added, profits unto salvation, is perversely asserted for the sake of Syncretism: for love added to faith does not contribute anything to salvation, but when we have been justified and made safe through faith, faith also works love, Gal. V. 6. And therefore Holy Scripture ascribes neither justification nor salvation to our love or charity, inasmuch as it is both in many ways imperfect and unclean, and follows justification as a fruit, not preceding it as a cause, concerning which see what we have said at the loc. cit. in the Exeg. August. Confess. But as to what he says

Grotius, unless love is added, that faith will indeed exist, but it will not be living or efficacious; in this he is mistaken in two ways. First, because he believes that true confidence can exist without love, even if it is not living: for confidence that is not living is not true, but imaginary, just as a man who is not living, but feigned or painted, is not a true man; and confidence in God and Christ can no more exist without love than the sun can exist without rays, or life without motion. Secondly, because he thinks that love causes faith to be living and efficacious. For although there is no true and living faith without love, and love is a sign of life and of living faith, yet love itself does not bestow life upon faith, but rather obtains life from faith, because faith is δι᾿ ἀγάπης ἐνεργουμένη, and is the cause, mother, origin, and root of love. Who would say that the root has life from the fruit, and not rather that the fruit draws life, and all its sap, power, and vital vigor from the root? Can it indeed be denied that works, to which charity looks, are the fruits of faith? Or can it be affirmed to the contrary that faith is the fruit of works and charity? Nor does the passage in 1 Corinthians XIII. 2 help Grotius. For he falsely assumes that the Apostle is there dealing with justifying faith, and that he is comparing it with love, and contending that it does not avail for salvation without love. For the discussion there is not instituted concerning justification, or the manner of attaining eternal salvation: nor concerning the faith apprehending the merit of Christ, by which we are justified, just as Grotius, having already become closer to the Papists, nevertheless still explained justification, and justifying faith, namely that a living faith apprehends the mercy of God in Christ, and believes that the righteousness which is in Christ is freely imputed to itself, (which we observed a little before) and by Cassander: whom Grotius valued most highly, it is taught that a man is justified by faith alone, i.e., by the grace of God alone, not from works, and that faith indeed cannot be alone, yet it alone justifies; but the matter there concerns the faith, as they call it, of miracles: which whether you say the gift itself of performing miracles is so named, or the condition required for the use of the gift, which Grotius preferred more recently, is different, nay, it can even be separated from justifying faith, as is evident from the example of the false Prophets in Matt. VII. 22. Therefore this very faith of miracles is not the faith which profits for salvation, namely adapted to eternal benefits, which Grotius wanted before: but saving faith is other, and different from the faith of miracles, since that can exist without this, and usually does, and this is sometimes found without that. The Greeks, Theodoret, Chrysostom, Oecumenius, Theophylact, and among the Papists Salmero, interpret the Apostle as speaking not of faith in dogmas, but of signs, not of common, not of ordinary, but of miraculous faith. And those who extend the Apostle's statement to saving faith acknowledge that it is a hyperbolic expression, and that the argument is drawn from an impossible condition, with Bellarmine leading the way in book 1 de justific. cap. XV, or they affirm with Benedictus Justinianus that the Apostle spoke hypothetically, whether those things which the Apostle gathers here can be separated from charity, or otherwise.

ὀυδὲν ἀδυνατήσει ὑμῖν] In Greek ἀδυνατεῖν is taken actively as in Epicharmus, ἀδυνατεῖ δ᾽ ὀυδὲν θεὸς. But in our writers it is also passive, as also in Luke I. 37, ὀυκ ἀδυνατήσει παρὰ τῷ θεῷ πᾶν ῥῆμα. To which what is said here by the Apostle must be restricted to the subject matter: you will be able to do nothing that is impossible, namely of those things which will pertain to the testimony of the doctrine and to conciliating authority for your office.

Latin:

Vers. 20. Ἀπιστίαν] Ἀπιστίαν vocat τὴν ὀλιγοπιστίαν, com- parate scilicet ad eam quam pro ratione diuturnæ institu- tionis & impositi muneris habere debebant fiduciam. Notandum autem voces πισὸς & ἄπιστος aliter sumi apud Græcos Scriptores, aliter apud Judæos Hellenistas. Græ- cis πισὸς est qui stat promissis, ac proinde dignus cui fidem habeas: ἄπιστος perfidus: quibus significationibus eas voces & in his libris reperire est. At illud Hellenistarum proprium πιστὸν dicere eum qui credat alicui atque confi- dat, ἄπιστον qui aliter sit animatus. ἀπιστίαν convenienter huic loco definit Clemens Alexandrinus: ὑπόληψιν τῷ ἀν- τικειμένῳ ἀσθενῆ ἀποφατικήν.

Recte notat Grotius ἀπιστίαν vocari hic ὀλιγο- πιστίαν, comparate scilicet ad eam, quam pro ratio- ne diuturna institutionis, & impositi muneris ha- bere debebant fiduciam: Et vocem πισὸν & ἄπι- στον aliter sumi apud Græcos scriptores, aliter apud Judæos Hellenistas: quia Græcis πισὸς est, qui stat promissis, ac proinde dignus cui fidem habeas: ἄ- πιστος perfidus: At illud Hellenistarum proprium πιστὸν dicere eum qui credat alicui atque confidat, ἄπιστον qui aliter sit animatus. Quod opponen- dum Pontificiis: fidem esse fiduciam negantibus: Vid. Bellarmin. lib. 1. de just. cap. 5. & Pistorium in posit. de justific. th. 4. qui audacter affirmant, in tota Scriptura S. præsertim in Novo Testamento & in materia justificationis vocabulum πίστις à vo- cabulo fiduciæ distinctum esse. Si loca quis desi- deret, videri poterunt è multis hæc sequentia, in quibus aliter accipi πίστις nequit, quam de fiducia. Matth. IX. 22. cap. XV. 28. Luc. V.

20. Johan. VI. v. ult. Actor. XIV. 9. 1. Joh. V. 13. Unde Jansen. in Harmon. Evang. c. XXXII. Rectissime dicitur, nomen fidei in Evangeliis, cum ei tribuitur salus, aut consecutio omnium quæ vo- lumus, complecti utrumque, nempe & assensum illum firmum in credendis de Deo, & Christo, & FIDUCIAM ex illius omnipotente bonitate con- ceptam. Et Cajetanus in explicat: dicti Mosai- ci, credidit Abraham Gen. XV. Moses non dicit, Abrahamum credidisse Deo, sed in Deo, hoc enim plus est: Nam credere Deo est fidem habere illius verbis, ut veracibus. Credere autem in Deum insuper addit FIDUCIAM in Deo. Georg. Cas- sand. in Consult. artic. IV. ita habet p. 12. Ad ju- stificationem consequendam requiritur talis fides, quæ homo exemplo Abrahæ ad promissionem Dei non hæsitat per diffidentiam, sed præter spem in spem credat, Deum videlicèt credenti in eum qui suscita- vit Jesum Christum à mortuis, imputaturum hanc fidem ad justificationem, & peccata non imputatu- rum. Quæ Grotius, etsi jam Papizans in annot. ad Cassandrum improbare non potuit: siquidem approbavit formulam Ratisbonensem, quod fides viva APPREHENDAT misericordiam Dei in Christo, & credat justitiam, quæ est in Christo sibi gratis imputari. Vide Exegema nostrum in August. Confess. art. IV. cap. VII. §. VI. Ne- que fratres Waleburgici negant, sed concedunt, fidem sumi pro fide speciali, quæ promissiones ge- nerales in particulari applicat cum adjuncta ve- ra fiducia, ut ibidem §. XVII. observavi- mus.

Quod vero Julius Cæsar Coturius Jesuita in E- pit. Contr. demonstr. XI. cap. IV. pag. 275. è pro- priis nostris principiis hic implicantiam, ut barbare loquitur, ostendere conatur, quia fiducia prior ju- stificatione est nostra sententia (ordine scilicet natu- ræ) unde colligit: si actus fidei seu fiducia prior est justificatione, tunc in illo priori, quo credit & certo fidit peccator se justum esse, falsum credit, & fidit: quia in illo priori quo sic credit, & fidit non- dum justus est, sed tantum postea fit justus: nugæ sunt, acumine Jesuitico indignæ. Quia fiducia, quæ ad justificationem antecedenter requiritur à nobis, non est τὸ confidere, vel fiducia peccatoris, qua credit se justum esse, hoc enim consequens est justificationis, non antecedens: sed immota illa cordis fiducia, qua peccator statuit non solum gene- raliter mortuum esse Christum, sed etiam in parti- culari fidit, firmiterque credit, Deum VELLE sibi in Christo propitium esse, & propter merita Christi sibi actualiter peccata omnia remittere, justitiam im- putare, & vitam æternam donare, ut Coturius ipse pag. 278. nostram sententiam exposuit. Non ergo fiducia illa, qua credimus remissa nobis ES- SE peccata, justitiam nobis imputatam ESSE, vitam æternam nobis donatam ESSE, ut Sophi- sta nostram deinde pervertit sententiam, sed qua credimus Deum VELLE nobis peccata remitte- re, Deum VELLE nobis justitiam Christi imputa- re, Deum VELLE nobis vitam æternam dona- re, est fides illa qua justificamur; qua nempe hanc gratiosam DEI VOLUNTATEM in pro- missionis verbo declaratam vera cordis fiducia amplectimur, ac eidem innitimur, adeoque PRO- MISSIONEM ipsam Evangelii apprehendimus, nobisque applicamus, & ita gratiosam peccato- rum remissionem, justitiæque imputationem consequimur, ac justificamur: quam demum ju- stificationem consequitur certitudo illa gratiæ, ju- stitiæ & salutis nostræ. ὡς κόκκον σινάπεως] Proverbium inter Hebræos celebre exigit ut ad quantitatem hoc, non ad qualitatem referatur, quomodo & supra grani sinapis tanquam rei minimæ fa- cta est mentio. Latine diceremus δεικτικῶς, si vel tantillum haberetis fiducia: quod cum dicit Christus, non neget esse aliquam Apostolis fiduciam, sed ut dixi habita temporis & muneris ratione, dicit eam fiduciam esse minima minorem, hoc est, perquam exiguam.

Ἐρεῖτε τῷ ὄρει τύτῳ, μετάβηθι ἐντεῦθεν ἐκεῖ] Et hoc pro- verbiale est ut apparet ex Paulo 1. Cor. XIII. 2. Sensus ergo est, res difficillimas præstaretis. Neque pugnant verba Chri- sti, qui montes transferre exiguæ fidei attribuit, & Pauli, qui ad maximam fidem hoc ipsum videtur referre. Nam illa exigua fides quam Christus exigit ejus est mensuræ quæ miraculis quibusvis sufficiat: supra quam si quid accedat id miraculorum efficiendiam ad plenitudinem perductam au- gere non potest. Porro non agere hic Christum περὶ τῦ χα- ρίσματος τῶν σημείων, inde evincitur, quod eo carere ὐκ ἔσι τῶν ψεκτῶν, sed habere potius raræ est felicitatis. Itaque fides hæc potius conditio est requisita ad usum doni. Hæc autem ipsa fides aptata beneficiis æternis ea est quæ dile- ctione antecedente ad salutem proficit, ut dicto loco Pau- lus demonstrat. Nam nisi dilectio accedat, erit quidem illa fides, sed non viva, non efficax. Fit autem viva at- que efficax ubi diligenter expendimus non tantum quid Deus possit ac polliceatur, verum etiam quid à nobis exi- gat. Neque vero negarim etiam κατὰ τὴν κυριολεξίαν inter- dum impletum quod hic dicitur, cum Nonnosi precibus in- gentis molis saxum ad Soracte translatum martyrologia prodant: & idem ab Episcopo Armenio præstitum instante Calipha Babylonico, anno millesimo ducentesimo quinto & vicesimo, haud spernendi auctores sint. At sensus al- legoricus est, nihil fore tam excelsum quod non ad eorum preces evanescat. Vide Apoc. VIII. 8.

Proverbiale hoc esse omnino è 1. Cor. XIII. 2. ap- paret, ut sensus sit: res difficillimas præstaretis: neque male proverbium inter Ebræos celebre ὡς κόκκον σινάπεως Latine explicatur: diceremus δεικτικῶς: si vel tantillum haberetis fiduciæ, hoc nempe sensu, quod Christus non neget, esse ali- quam Apostolis fiduciam, sed habita temporis & muneris ratione, dicat eam fiduciam esse minima mi- norem, hoc est, perquam exiguam. Denique, etsi negandum non sit, etiam κτ᾽ τὴν κυριολεξίαν interdum impletum, quod hic dicitur, cum Nonno- si precibus ingentis molis saxum ad Soracte transla- tum martyrologia prodant; & idem ab Episcopo Ar- menio præstitum instante Calipha Babylonio anno 1225. qualia etiam de Gregorio Thaumaturgo Nys- sen. in vita ejus, & Euseb. lib. VII. Histor. Eccles. cap. 25. de Hilarione Hieronymus in ejus vita, de Christianis qui Tyranno id exigente, montem in Tartaria transtulerint, M. Paul. Venetus P. 1. Histor. Orient. cap. XVIII. referunt: quem proprium sensum urget Chrysostom. homil. LVIII. Concedimus tamen facile Grotio, sen- sum hic allegoricum esse, nihil fore tam excelsum, quod non ad Apostolorum preces evanescat, vel potius hoc uno nominato exemplo alia similiter intelligenda innui, ut proverbialis sit locutio: non excluditur ergo montium translatio, etsi so- la non designetur. Cæterum hanc ipsam fidem, quam non esse ipsam χάρισμα τῶν σημείων, sed conditionem potius requisitam ad usum doni, haud inconcinne statuit Grotius, aptatam beneficiis æ- ternis eam esse, quæ dilectione accedente ad salu- tem proficit, in gratiam Syncretismi perverse as- feritur: non enim accedens ad fidem dilectio ad salutem quicquam facit, sed cum per fidem justi- ficati & salvi facti sumus, dilectionem etiam o- peratur fides, Gal. V. 6. Ideoque nec justifica- tionem, nec salutem dilectioni vel charitati no- stræ adscribit Sacra Scriptura, utpote quæ & multis modis imperfecta, atque immunda est, & justificationem consequitur, ceu fructus, non antecedit ceu causa, de quo vid. quæ l. c. in Exeg. August. Confess. diximus. Quod vero ait

Grotius nisi dilectio accedat, erit quidem illa fides, sed non viva, non efficax, in eo duobus modis fallitur. Primum, quod credat fiduciam veram esse sine dilectione, etsi viva non sit: quia fidu- cia non viva non est vera, sed imaginaria, uti homo non vivus, sed fictus vel pictus verus non est homo, & tam non potest esse sine dilectione fiducia vera in Deum & Christum, quam non pot- est Sol esse sine radiis, vita sine motu. Deinde quod censeat dilectionem efficere, ut fides viva sit, atque efficax. Etsi enim sine dilectione fides vera ac viva nulla sit, ac dilectio signum sit vitæ, & vivæ fidei, non tamen vitam largiatur fidei ipsa dilectio, sed à fide potius vitam nanciscitur, quia fides est δι᾿ ἀγάπης ἐνεργουμένη, & dile- ctionis causa, genitrix, origo, & radix. Ec- quis dicat, radicem vitam habere à fructu, ac non potius fructum è radice vitam, & omnem succum, vim ac vigorem vitalem trahere? Num vero negari potest, opera, ad quæ charitas spe- ctat, fructus esse fidei? aut affirmari contra, fi- dem esse fructum operum ac charitatis? Nec ju- vat Grotium locus 1. Corinth. XIII. 2. Falso enim assumit, quod ibi Apostolus de fide justifican- te agat, eamque cum dilectione componat, nec sine dilectione ad salutem proficere contendat. Non enim ibi de justificatione, aut modo con- sequendi æternam salutem instituitur tractatio: nec de fide apprehendente meritum Christi, qua justificamur, quemadmodum propior jam Papi- stis factus Grotius justificationem tamen adhuc exposuit, & fidem justificantem, quod nempe fides viva apprehendat misericordiam Dei in Christo, & credat justitiam, quæ est in Christo, sibi gratis imputari, (quod paulo ante observavimus) & à Cassandro: quem maximi fecit Grotius, do- cetur, sola fide justificari hominem, h. e. sola Dei gratia, non ex operibus, ac fidem solam qui- dem esse non posse, solam tamen justificare; Agi- tur autem ibi de miraculosa, quam vocant, fide: quæ sive donum ipsum miracula patrandi sic nuncu- pari dicas, sive conditionem ad usum doni requisi- tam, quod proxime maluit Grotius, diversa est, imo sejuncta etiam esse potest à fide justificante, ut exemplo falsorum Prophetarum Matth. VII. 22. constat. Non ergo hæc ipsa fides miraculorum est fides, quæ ad salutem proficit, aptata nempe beneficiis æternis, quod volebat ante Grotius: sed fides salvifica alia est, & diversa à fide miracu- lorum, quum & illa sine hac esse possit, & ple- rumque sit, & hæc sine illa quandoque invenia- tur. De fide non δογμάτων, sed σημείων inter- pretantur Apostolum Græci, Theodor. Chryso- stom. Oecumen. Theophyl. & è Pontificiis Salmero, de fide non communi, non ordinaria, sed miraculo- sa. Et qui ad fidem salvificam extendunt Apo- stoli dictum, locutionem hyperbolicam esse, ac argu- mentum duci à conditione impossibili agnoscunt, præeunte Bellarmino lib. 1. de justific. cap. XV. aut hypothetice loquutum esse Apostolum, cum Benedict. Justin. affirmant, sive illa sejungi possint, quæ hic conge- rit Apostolus, à charitate, sive secus.

ὀυδὲν ἀδυνατήσει ὑμῖν] Græcis ἀδυνατεῖν sumitur active ut apud Epicharmum ἀδυνατεῖ δ᾽ ὀυδὲν θεὸς. At nostris Scri- ptoribus etiam passive, ut & Luc. I. 37. ὀυκ ἀδυνατήσει πα- ρὰ τῷ θεῷ πᾶν ῥῆμα. Ad quod hic Apostolis dicitur, restrin- gendum est ad subjectam materiam: nihil non poteritis, eorum scilicet quæ ad testimonium doctrinæ & concilian- dam muneri vestro auctoritatem pertinebunt.

## 17:21
Vers. 21. Τοῦτο δὲ τὸ γένος] This kind of evil spirits which is sent in as a punishment for crimes, and indeed more serious ones. For I do not doubt that this is the true interpretation of this passage. Nor does it stand in the way that in Mark it is said that this one was vexed by an evil spirit from childhood. Nor is it certain that it ought to be translated from infancy, since even those who have reached an age capable of vices are called παιδία by the Greeks. I therefore agree with the Syrian, who in this place has placed that word which a comparison of another passage, which is chapter V. 4, declares to be more suitable to adolescence than to infancy. Ἐν προσευχῇ ϰαὶ νηστείᾳ] Christ had said above that faith is necessary for these miracles of a greater mark in particular. Now he shows how they can be performed, namely by fervent prayers. He adds fasting for this reason, because a humble mind is required above all for prayers, a thing which fasting serves. Whence we see that νηστείαν & δέησιν or προσ- ευχὴν are usually joined, Luke II. 37, Acts X. 30, chapter XIV. 23, 1 Corinthians VII. 5. See, if you like, Jacchiades on Daniel X. 3. But I wish that even now among Christians fasts would neither become cheap, nor degenerate εἰς τὸ θεατρικὸν ϰαὶ παρὰ τραγῳδίαν. Certainly it appears everywhere that devils bear the image of vices. Wherefore the sentence which Christ uttered on this occasion, which is to be valid forever, signifies this: that there are some vices so grave or so mature that they cannot be overcome except by the great effort of humble prayer.

PART III. The prediction of the passion, death, and resurrection of Christ.

Latin:

Vers. 21. Τοῦτο δὲ τὸ γένος] Hoc genus malorum spiri- tuum quod in pœnam facinorum & quidem graviorum immittitur. Hanc enim veram esse hujus loci interpreta- tionem non dubito. Nec obstat quod apud Marcum est, vexatum hunc fuisse à malo spiritu παιδιόθεν. Neque enim certum est verti debere ab infantia, cum παιδία Græ- cis dicantur etiam qui ad ætatem vitiorum capacem perve- nerunt. Syro igitur assentior qui isto loco eam posuit vo- cem quam adolescentiæ potius quam infantiæ convenire collatio loci alterius, qui est cap. V. 4. declarat. Ἐν προσευχῇ ϰαὶ νηστείᾳ] Supra dixerat Christus fiducia opus esse ad hæc præsertim notæ majoris miracula. Nunc ostendit quomodo ea patrari possit, precibus nimirum fer- vidis. Jejunium ideo adjungit, quia ad preces imprimis requiritur animus demissus, cui rei inservit jejunium. Un- de plerumque conjungi videmus νηστείαν & δέησιν sive προσ- ευχὴν Luc. II. 37. Actor. X. 30. cap. XIV. 23. 1. Corinth. VII. 5. Vide si libet Jacchiaden ad Dan. X. 3. Utinam vero nunc quoque inter Christianos neque vilescant jeju- nia, neque εἰς τὸ θεατρικὸν ϰαὶ παρὰ τραγῳδίαν degenerent. Certe diabolos vitiorum gerere imaginem passim apparet. Quare sententia quam Christus hac occasione in perpe- tuum valituram est elocutus, hoc significat, esse quædam tam gravia aut tam adulta vitia, quæ nisi magno nisu hu- milis precationis nequeant expugnari.

PARS III. Passionis, mortis & resurrectionis Christi prædictio.

## 17:22
Verse 22. Ἀναστρεφομένων] While they were staying: for returning cannot have a place here, since it appears that what has been narrated so far was done in the descent from Mount Tabor, which is in Galilee. These things were done, therefore, on the journey from the parts near Nazareth towards the lake. See what is said on Mark.

From the series of the history it seems to be understood that these things were done after Christ's return from Caesarea Philippi into Galilee. And so in this place ἀναστρέφεσθαι can also signify a return: yet the other interpretation seems to be preferred, while they were staying in Galilee: which these words of Mark confirm: παρεπορεύοντο διὰ τῆς Γαλιλαίας: as Casaubon and B. Gerhard [think].

παραδίδοσθαι] The usage of this word is various in this matter. For the Father is said to have delivered the Son, because He permitted Him to the power of evil men, and the Son [is said to have delivered] Himself, because He willingly underwent death: and Judas [is said to have] delivered Him to the chief priests and the scribes, and the chief priests and scribes to Pilate, and Pilate to the soldiers. Since it is said here simply εἰς χεῖρας ἀνθρώπων, I think this should be understood of the Father, who so delivered the Son to men that they did to Him what was pleasing to them, as Christ was speaking above in verse 12. Nor perhaps would it be absurd if we interpret in the same way that which is above in chapter IV. 12, ὅτι Ἰωάννης παρεδόθη. For it is customary for the name of God to be understood in the words.

PART IV. The payment of the census for Christ and Peter.

Latin:

Vers. 22. Ἀναστρεφομένων] Versantibus: nam revertenti- bus hic locum habere non potest, cum quæ hactenus nar- rata sunt appareat gesta esse in descensu à monte Itabyrio qui est in Galilæa. Gesta hæc igitur in itinere à partibus Nazaretæ vicinis lacum versus. Vide quæ ad Mar- cum.

Ex Historiæ serie intelligi videtur, gesta esse hæc post reditum Christi è Cæsarea Philippi in Galilæam. Itaque potest etiam hoc loco ἀναστρέφεσθαι reditum significare: altera tamen interpretatio videtur præ- ferenda, versantibus ipsis in Galilæa: quam con- firmant hæc Marci verba: παρεπορεύοντο διὰ τῆς Γαλιλαίας: uti Casaubonus & B. Gerhar- dus.

παραδίδοσθαι] Varius in hac re usus est hujus vocabu- li. Nam & pater dicitur filium tradidisse, quia eum ma- lorum hominum potestati permisit, & filius sese, quia vo- lens mortem subiit: & Judas eum tradidisse pontificibus & legisperitis, & pontifices ac legisperiti Pilato, & Pilatus militibus. Ego cum hic simpliciter dicatur εἰς χεῖρας ἀνθρώ- πων, putem de Patre hæc intelligenda, qui filium ita ho- minibus tradiderit ut ei fecerint quod ipsis est collibitum, ut supra Christus loquebatur commate 12. Neque absur- dum forte sit, si eodem modo interpretemur id quod supra est cap. IV. 12. ὅτι Ἰωάννης παρεδόθη. Nam Dei nomen in verbis subintelligi usitatum est.

PARS IV. Census pro Christo & Petro persolutio.

## 17:24
Verse 24. Οἱ τὰ δίδραχμα λαμβάνοντες] Not the publicans of the Romans: for you will nowhere find the didrachm among the Roman tributes: but those sent by the priests, whom we have said elsewhere are called שליחים by the Hebrews, and ἀποστόλους or ἀποδοχέας by the Hellenists. For this didrachm was paid by the Jews for the use of the temple even to the times of Vespasian: concerning which I wonder that there is doubt, since the words of Josephus about Vespasian are clear: φόρον δὲ τοῖς ὅπου δήποτ’ ὖσιν Ἰουδαίοις ἐπέβαλε, ΔΥΟ ΔΡΑΧΜΑΣ ἕϰαστον ϰελεύσας ἀνὰ πᾶν ἔτος εἰς τὸ ϰαπετώλιον φέρειν, ὥσπερ πρότερον εἰς τὸν ἐν Ἱεροσολύμοις νεὼν συνετέλουν. Maimonides also noted this in the book which has the name Manus, reading 3, title 7, which is about the Shekel: Suetonius also [mentions it] regarding Domitian, and Dio Cassius. Appian in his Syriaca calls it φόρον σωμάτων. Thus, what the men of the Jewish religion used to pay voluntarily was turned into a necessity and into very different uses: just as Theodosius and Valentinian also ordered the crown gold, which the Jews were accustomed to give to their Patriarchs, to be exacted by compulsion and brought into their own treasuries. Nor is there any doubt that Martial is dealing with this Vespasianic didrachm when, speaking most obscenely of the circumcision of the Jews, he says it was condemned by a tribute. And this is, if I am not mistaken, the calumny of the Jewish fiscus, removed afterwards as ancient coins testify. For we do not read that any other burden was imposed specifically τοῖς Ἰουδαίζουσι. The didrachm had its origin from the very law of Moses. For God had ordered through Moses that for the use of the tabernacle there be paid per head σίκλου τὸ ἥμισυ, says Josephus, adding, ὁ δὲ σίκλος νόμισμα ἑβραίων ὢν δέχε- ται δραχμὰς τέσσαρας: namely Attic [drachmas], which he himself adds elsewhere. That which is δίκωνον among the LXX, τὸ ἥμισυ τοῦ διδράχμου κατὰ τὸ δίδραχμον τὸ ἅγιον, differs in words, but is the same in reality; for the LXX everywhere use double drachmas, that is, Alexandrian. Josephus, however, as also this Matthew here, deal with the Attic drachma. Although indeed most of the Hebrews think that that law of Moses was perpetual, yet the opinion of those who think it was temporary, but repeated as times demanded, pleases me more. For as often as the tithes and other Levitical revenues, with the addition also of the liberality of the kings (as can be seen in 1 Chronicles XXVI. 26, 27), sufficed for the needs of the temple, what need was there for the tribute of the didrachm? But after the defection of the ten tribes, with the revenues of the Levites much diminished, the didrachm began again to be commanded according to the example of the ancient law, 2 Chronicles X, chapter XIV. 6, 9. Nehemiah, however, having regard, as is credible, to the present poverty and the burdens by which the people were oppressed, commanded a third instead of a half-shekel, which the Greek interpreters call τρίτον τοῦ διδράχμου, namely Alexandrian. But afterwards we have seen from Josephus that there was a return to the common didrachm: and that was paid not only by those who lived under the power of the Sanhedrin, whatever it was, but also in Galilee, and indeed throughout the whole world, but by them voluntarily and by private religion. And at Jerusalem indeed the didrachm was collected in the temple itself on the 25th day of the month Adar by the money-changers set over that business. In other parts the same was done by others. There is a notable passage, and one very useful for the interpretation of these words, in Josephus, Ant. XVIII. 12, where, dealing with the Jews who were τῆς βαβυλωνικῆς διασπορᾶς, and with the city of Nisibis: The Jews, he says, τῇ φήσῃ τῶν χωρίων πε- πιστευκότες, τὸ δίδραχμον τῷ θεῷ καταβάλλειν ἑκάστοις πάτριον ταύτῃ κατετίθεντο. Maimonides records the same fact in the city of Nehardea. Wherefore it either pertains properly to the δίδραχμον, or at least it also includes the δίδραχμον, which Cicero in his speech for Flaccus says was accustomed to be exported annually in the name of the Jews from Italy and from all the Roman provinces: and what Tacitus says, that tributes and contributions were accustomed to be gathered at Jerusalem: and the passage of Philo, II. de Monarchia: σχεδὸν παρὰ πᾶ- σαν πόλιν ταμεῖον τῶν ἱερῶν χρημάτων ἐστιν, εἰς ὃ παραγενομέ- νοις εὐθὺς ἀπάρχεσθαι κᾐ χρόνοις ὡρισμένοις ἱεροπομποὶ τῶν χρημά- των εἰσιν ἀριστίνδην ἐπικριθέντες. Likewise those edicts, both of Augustus and of the Roman governors, of which there is frequent mention in Philo and Josephus, which permit the Jews to collect money and carry it to Jerusalem.

ἁ τελοῦντα δίδραχμα] They do not act by imperial authority, as the tax collectors of the Romans or of King Herod would, but they ask whether he is accustomed to pay. It is credible that many, because they were not compelled, had refused that burden. Norbanus, in an edict to the Sardians by the authority of Augustus, permits the Jews to collect those things which were contributed ἐκ τῆς ἰδίας προαιρέσεως, εὐσεβείας ἕνεκα τῆς πρὸς τὸ θεῖον. Among these was τὸ δίδραχμον, as we have already said.

Latin:

Vers. 24. Οἱ τὰ δίδραχμα λαμβάνοντες] Non publicani Romanorum: nusquam enim inter Romana tributa di- drachmum invenies: sed missi à sacerdotibus, quos שליחים Hebræis, Hellenistis ἀποστόλους aut ἀποδοχέας vo- cari alibi diximus. Nam δίδραχμον hoc à Judæis pensitatum est in usum templi ad ipsa Vespasiani tempora: de quo mi- ror dubitari, cum clara sint Josephi verba de Vespasiano: φόρον δὲ τοῖς ὅπου δήποτ’ ὖσιν Ἰουδαίοις ἐπέβαλε, ΔΥΟ ΔΡΑΧΜΑΣ ἕϰαστον ϰελεύσας ἀνὰ πᾶν ἔτος εἰς τὸ ϰαπετώλιον φέρειν, ὥσπερ πρότερον εἰς τὸν ἐν Ἱεροσολύμοις νεὼν συνετέλουν. Notaviti- dem Maimonides libro cui Manus nomen, lectione 3. ti- tulo 7. qui est de Siclo: Suetonius quoque Domitiano & Dion Coccejus. Appianus Syriacis φόρον σωμάτων vocat. Ita quod ultro pendebant Judaicæ religionis homines, in necessitatem ususque longe alios versum est: quomodo Theodosius quoque & Valentinianus aurum coronarium quod dare Judæi Patriarchis suis solebant, compulsu exigi & suis largitionibus inferri jusserunt. Neque dubium quin de didrachmo hoc Vespasianeo agat Martialis cum τὴν τῶν Ἰουδαίων περιτομὴν obscœnius eloquens damnatam ait tribu- to. Et hæc est, ni fallor, calumnia fisci Judaici sublata postea ut nummi veteres testantur. Nullum enim aliud onus impo- situm peculiariter τοῖς Ἰουδαίζουσι legimus. Ortum habuit τὸ δίδραχμον ex ipsa Mosis lege. Nam Deus per Mosen jusserat in usum tabernaculi capitatim pendi σίκλου τὸ ἥμισυ, inquit Josephus addens, ὁ δὲ σίκλος νόμισμα ἑβραίων ὢν δέχε- ται δραχμὰς τέσσαρας: nempe Atticas, quod ipse alibi adji- cit. Quod apud LXX. est δίκωνον, τὸ ἥμισυ τοῦ διδράχμου κατὰ τὸ δίδραχμον τὸ ἅγιον, verbis differt, re idem est; nam LXX. ubique drachmis utuntur duplaribus, id est, Alexan- drinis. Josephus autem, ut & hic Matthæus de drachmæ Atticæ agunt. Quanquam vero plerique Hebræorum pu- tant legem illam Mosis fuisse perpetuam, mihi tamen ma- gis placere eorum sententia qui temporariam fuisse existi- mant, sed temporibus ita exigentibus repetitam. Nam quoties decimæ cæteræque obventiones Leviticæ, acce- dente etiam regum liberalitate (ut videre est 1. Paral. XXVI. 26. 27.) ad templi necessitates sufficiebant, quid opus erat tributo didrachmi? At post defectionem decem tribuum multum imminutis reditibus Levitarum, cœpit iterum ad exemplum legis antiquæ didrachmum imperari, 2. Paral. X. cap. XIV. 6. 9. Nehemias vero rationem, ut credibile est, habens præsentis paupertatis, & onerum quibus populus premebatur, pro semisse sicli imperavit trientem, quod Græci interpretes vocant τρίτον τοῦ διδράχμου, nempe Ale- xandrini. Sed postea ad didrachmum commune reditum ex Josepho vidimus: atque id pensitatum non modo ab his qui sub Synedrii qualicunque potestate vivebant, sed etiam in Galilæa, imo & per totum terrarum orbem, sed ab his sponte ac religione privata. Et Hierosolymis quidem col- ligebatur dedrachmum in ipso templo 25. die mensis Adar à mensariis ei negotio præpositis. In aliis partibus idem fa- ctum per alios. Locus est insignis & ad horum verborum interpretationem perutilis apud Josephum Orig. XVIII. 12. ubi de Judæis agens qui erant τῆς βαβυλωνικῆς διασπορᾶς, & de urbe Nisibi: Ἰουδαῖοι, inquit, τῇ φήσῃ τῶν χωρίων πε- πιστευκότες, τὸ δίδραχμον τῷ θεῷ καταβάλλειν ἑκάστοις πάτριον ταύτῃ κατετίθεντο. Maimonides in urbe Nehardea idem factum memorat. Quare aut ad δίδραχμον proprie perti- net, aut certe δίδραχμον etiam comprehendit, quod Cicero pro Flacco ait aurum Judæorum nomine quotannis ex Ita- lia, & ex omnibus Romanis provinciis exportari solitum: & quod Tacitus ait tributa & stipes Hierosolyma congeri solita: & Philonis locus II. de Monarchia: σχεδὸν παρὰ πᾶ- σαν πόλιν ταμεῖον τῶν ἱερῶν χρημάτων ἐστιν, εἰς ὃ παραγενομέ- νοις εὐθὺς ἀπάρχεσθαι κᾐ χρόνοις ὡρισμένοις ἱεροπομποὶ τῶν χρημά- των εἰσιν ἀριστίνδην ἐπικριθέντες. Item edicta illa tum Augu- sti, tum præsidum Romanorum, quorum apud Philonem & Josephum frequens mentio, quæ Judæis permittunt col- ligere pecunias & Hierosolyma deferre.

ἁ τελοῦντα δίδραχμα] Non pro imperio agunt, ut aut Ro- manorum aut Regis Herodis publicani, sed quærunt an sol- vere soleat. Credibile est multos, quia non cogebantur, id onus detrectasse. Norbanus in edicto ad Sardianos ex Augusti imperio permittit Judæis ea colligere quæ tribue- bantur ἐκ τῆς ἰδίας προαιρέσεως, εὐσεβείας ἕνεκα τῆς πρὸς τὸ θεῖον. In his erat τὸ δίδραχμον, ut jam diximus.

## 17:25
Vers. 25. Οἱ βασιλεῖς τῆς γῆς ἀπὸ τίνων λαμβάνουσι τὰ τέλη] He draws a comparison from the kings of the earth to the King of heaven in this way: We see everywhere that those who are exempt from tributes are held by kings, if not others, certainly their own sons. Furthermore, the δίδραχμον is exacted in the name of God. Who, therefore, would doubt that God would wish me, His only Son, who is נגיד, that is, prince, to Daniel c. IX. 25, 26, to be relieved of this burden? Indeed, the Son is greater than the temple, above c. XII. 6, and it is not customary for the greater to pay tribute to the lesser. Therefore, from the mind of God Himself, whose business the priests said they were conducting, Christ proves Himself free. He uses the plural number not because He extends that freedom to others, but because the comparison required it, taken not from the custom and practice of one king, but of all. We have seen from Josephus that this tribute was exacted in the name of God, who says τὸ δίδραχμον τῷ Θεῷ καταβάλλειν. Then that point is most relevant here which Titus, in Josephus, mentions to the besieged: διασμολογεῖν ὑμῖν ἐπὶ τῷ θεῷ ἐπετρέψαμεν; Which itself evidently shows that this custom had remained until the times of the destruction. The tribute imposed by Augustus, which was not a burden peculiar to the Jews but common to all the provinces, as we have already begun to say, is not of this place, and much less that which Agrippa remitted not to the Jews but to the Jerusalemites: for that was a burden not of persons, but of houses.

Κῆνσον] A word frequent among later Hebrews, which began to be used by them from the times of Pompey. And thus any burdens whatsoever, whether of persons or of estates, are called, as appears from the title of the Digest concerning censuses.

Latin:

Vers. 25. Οἱ βασιλεῖς τῆς γῆς ἀπὸ τίνων λαμβάνουσι τὰ τέλη] Similitudinem à regibus terræ ad cœli regem deducit hoc modo: Videmus passim à regibus immunes tributorum haberi, si non & alios, certe filios suos. Adhoc δίδραχμον nomine Dei exigitur. Quis igitur dubitet, quin Deus me Filium suum unicum qui נגיד id est princeps Danieli c. IX. 25. 26. velit hoc onere sublevatum? imo filius major est templo, supra c. XII. 6. non solet autem major minori tri- butum pendere. Ex mente igitur ipsius Dei, cujus nego- tium se agere Sacerdotes dicebant, liberum se Christus probat. Plurali numero utitur non quod ad alios eam ex- tendat libertatem, sed quod comparatio id exigebat sumta non ab unius sed ab omnium regum more ac consuetudi- ne. Dei nomine exactum hoc tributum ex Josepho vidi- mus, qui dicit τὸ δίδραχμον τῷ Θεῷ καταβάλλειν. Tum illud huc potissimum pertinet quod Titus apud Josephum obses- sis commemorat διασμολογεῖν ὑμῖν ἐπὶ τῷ θεῷ ἐπετρέψαμεν; Quod ipsum evidenter ostendit mansisse hunc morem ad excidii tempora. Tributum ab Augusto indictum, quod non Judæorum erat proprium onus sed commune omnium provinciarum, ut jam dicere cœpimus, non est hujus loci, multoque minus id quod Agrippa remisit non Judæis sed Hierosolymitis: id enim non personarum, sed domum erat onus.

Κῆνσον] Vox apud Hebræos posteriores frequens, cœpta apud ipsos usurpari à Pompejanis temporibus. Ita autem vocantur onera quævis aut personarum aut prædiorum, ut ex titulo Digestorum de censibus apparet.

## 17:26
Vers. 26. Ἀλλοτρίων] ἀλλότριος here are opposed to the sons of the household. Thus in Roman law the word is taken for an extraneous heir.

Grotius understands that it was not the census of the Romans that was accustomed to be paid to the tax collectors, but that which was sent by the priests for the use of the temple: which also the Jesuits, and those Cardinals, Baronius, Vol. I. Ann. 33. num. 31, and Bellarmine, book on the Clergy, chap. XXVIII.

After Franciscus Lucas Burgensis, it pleased [me] that they should not infringe upon our argument concerning the non-exemption of the Clergy, and that not even the Roman Pontiff himself, who claims to be the successor of Peter, can withdraw himself from the jurisdiction of the civil Magistrate. Although indeed some of the ancients also understood these things concerning the sacred tribute, Hilary, Chrysostom, Theophylact, to whom are added Casaubon, Exerc. XV. S. XIX, Johan. Camero, Praelect. Theol. p. 106, Simon Episcopius T. 1. oper. p. 95, Wilh. Schickard, de jure Regio Ebraeor. p. 84, others nevertheless have interpreted it more correctly as concerning the tribute to be paid to the Magistrate, not only of our own [people] B. Lyserus in Harm., B. Hunnius, B. Waltherus Centur. Miscell. c. II, and among the Reformed, Buxtorf, Lex. Talm. p. 2020, Petitus, var. lect. l. II. But also from the Papists themselves: such as Salmero, Maldonatus, Barradius, Tirinus, Jansenius, and others, both because the Evangelist here uses the word κῆνσον, a Roman tribute, denoting that which was imposed by the Romans in Matt. XXII. 18, v. 25, and because Christ speaks openly about the kings of the earth, from whom they receive tribute: which question would be foreign if this discourse were about the shekel of the capitation tax to be brought to the temple: whence Jansenius says, it is evident that this didrachma was not exacted according to the law of Exod. XXX, but according to the prescription of the Romans, to whom the Jews had already become tributary: for the Lord asks, from whom do the kings of the earth receive tribute or tax? by which it is manifestly signified that these didrachmas were exacted for the tribute and tax owed to the Romans. For Matthew also uses the Roman term κῆνσον: and because tributes for the use of the temple were accustomed to be collected in the temple, and that from all who had exceeded the twentieth year of age: which was not done here: for Christ paid only for himself and Peter, for that reason, that Christ and Peter, but not the other Apostles, lived as inhabitants in Capernaum. Thus Salmero tom. VI. tract. XXXVII. p. 738. If this didrachma were collected for the uses of the tabernacle, it would be received not in Capernaum, but in the temple of Jerusalem, and not for two, Christ and Peter, but for all and each of the Apostles who exceeded the twentieth year. But although Grotius with Bellarm. and others objects that didrachmas were paid here, which were accustomed to be paid per head for the use of the tabernacle from the very law of Moses, which demanded a half-shekel, which Grotius teaches from Josephus was received up to the very times of Vespasian, others nevertheless respond: that the tribute to be paid to the emperor was also a δίδραχμον: even if only a denarius is brought forward in Matt. XXII, to which Barradius replied to Bellarmine: that the denarius is called the coin of the census in that place: because it was a part of the tribute. For two denarii were paid: or it can be said that the tribute indicted by the Romans was a denarius, therefore called the coin of the census: but the tribute of Herod, who ruled the city of Capernaum, was a didrachma. This is certainly no consequence: in the collection of tribute for the temple a δίδραχμον was accustomed to be paid: Therefore where a didrachma is paid, there the collection is instituted for the use of the temple. Let the argument be from the undistributed to the distributed. Add that even in the time of Nehemiah they paid for the half-shekel a third, τρίτον τῶ διδράχμα, only for the use of the temple, as was observed by Grotius himself, although he notes from Josephus that later they returned to the common didrachma: and he asserts that this was also paid in Galilee, voluntarily, and by private religion: which however does not fit this passage. For this was not a free payment, but was exacted, and indeed by the authority of the secular Magistrate: since there is open mention here of the kings of the earth. Grotius indeed tries to invert the argument from the words of Christ about the kings of the earth, in this way: We see everywhere that they are held immune from tributes by kings, if not others, certainly their sons. But this δίδραχμον is exacted in the name of GOD. Who therefore would doubt that God wishes me, his only son, who is נגיר that is, Prince to Daniel IX. 26, to be relieved of this burden? Nay, the Son is greater than the temple, Matt. XII. 6, and the greater is not accustomed to pay tribute to the lesser. But it is manifest that Christ does not construct his immunity from the contribution for the use of the temple by the argument from the sons of kings: which Grotius acknowledges was free for those living in Galilee, and proves it was paid ἐκ τῆς ἰδίας προαιρέσεως according to an edict to the Sardians; why therefore, when Christ was already immune and free by the force of edicts, would he have had need to bring forward his own immunity? That proof of Christ therefore rather means this: Since tributes are not imposed on the sons of kings, but on the subject by the kings of the earth, much less is the Son of the King of Kings subject to the contribution: just as Chrysostom observes, who concludes thus: If the kings of the earth do not receive from their sons, but from those whom they rule, how much more ought I to be free from this demand, the Son not of an earthly King, but of the heavenly, and the King of heavens?

Latin:

Vers. 26. Ἀλλοτρίων] ἀλλότριος hic opponuntur filiis fa- miliarum. Ita in jure Romano sumitur vox extranei hæ- redis.

Non censum Romanorum publicanis tribui soli- tum, sed in templi usum missis à Sacerdotibus exfol- vendum intelligit Grotius: quod etiam Jesui- tis, iisque Cardinalibus, Baronio, Tom. I. Ann. 33. num. 31. & Bellarmino l. de Cler. cap. XXVIII.

post Francisc. Lucam Burgens. placuit, ut argu- mentum nostrum de non exemptione Clericorum, & quod nec ipse Romanus Pontifex qui successo- rem se venditat Petri Magistratus civilis jurisdi- čioni se subducere possit, infringant. Quan- quam vero etiam è veteribus nonnulli de sacro tri- buto hæc acceperint, Hilarius, Chrysostomus, Theophylactus, quibus accedunt Casaubon. Exerc. XV. S. XIX. Johan. Camero prælection. Theol. pag. 106. Simon Episcopius T. 1. oper. p. 95. Wilh. Schickard. de jure Regio Ebræor. p. 84. rectius ta- men alii de tributo Magistratui exœlvendo inter- pretati sunt, non è nostris tantum B. Lyserus in Harm. B. Hunnius, B. Waltherus Centur. Miscell. c. II. & Reformatis Buxtorf. Lex. Talm. pag. 2020. Petitus var. lect. l. II. Sed etiam ex ipsis Pontificiis: utpote Salmero, Maldonatus, Barradius, Tirinus, Jansenius, alique, tum quod vocem κῆνσον Ro- manam tributum, à Romanis impositum notantem Matth. XXII. 18. hic adhibeat Evangelista v. 25. tum quod Christus palam agat de Regibus terræ, à quibusnam illi censum accipiant: quæ quæstio aliena foret si de capitationis siclo templo inferen- do hic sermo esset: unde Jansenius, patet, in- quit, didrachma hoc non exigi secundum legem Ex- od. XXX. sed secundum præscriptum Romanorum, quibus Judæi jam erant facti tributarii: quærit e- nim Dominus, à quibus Reges terræ acciperent tri- butum vel censum? quo manifeste significatur, Di- drachma hæc exacta fuisse pro tributo & censu Ro- manis debito. Nam & Matthæus utitur dictione Romana κῆνσον: tum quod tributa in usum tem- pli colligi consueverint in templo, idque ab omni- bus, qui annum ætatis vigesimum excesserant: quod hic factum non est: nam Christus solvit so- lum pro se & Petro, ex illa causa, quod Christus & Petrus, non item alii Apostoli, veluti incolæ in Ca- pernaum habitarent. Ita Salmero tom. VI. tract. XXXVII. p. 738. Si in usus tabernaculi colligeretur hoc didrachmum, non in Capernaum, sed in templo Hierosolymitano acciperetur, nec pro duobus, Chri- sto, & Petro: sed pro omnibus ac singulis Apostolis, qui excederent annum vigesimum. Etsi autem Gro- tius cum Bellarm. & aliis obvertat, quod hic di- drachma soluta sint, quæ solebant capitatim pen- di in usum tabernaculi ex ipsa Mosis lege, dimi- dium siclum exigente, quod usque ad ipsa Ve- spasiani tempora receptum fuisse è Josepho docet Grotius, respondent tamen alii: tributum impe- ratori solvendum etiam fuisse δίδραχμον: utut de- narius tantum proferatur Matth. XXII. de quo Bellarmino Barradius id reposuit: Denarium nu- misma census ibidem appellari: quod pars esset tri- buti. Duo enim denarii solvebantur: vel dici pos- se, tributum à Romanis indictum fuisse denarium, numisma census ob id dictum: tributum vero Hero- dis, qui civitati Capernaum imperabat, fuisse di- drachmum. Nulla certe hæc est consequentia: in collectione tributi pro templo solvi consuevit δίδραχμον: Ergo ubi didrachmon solvitur, ibi collectio est in usum templi instituta. Ar- gumentum sit à non distributo ad distributum. Adde quod etiam Nehemiæ tempore pro semissi sicli trientem, τρίτον τῶ διδράχμα solum in templi usum solverint, ut ipsi Grotio observatum, etsi postea ad didrachmum commune reditum è Josepho notet: idque etiam in Galilæa, sponte, ac religione priva- ta solutum fuisse asserat: quod vero huic loco non congruit. Non enim hæc libera erat solu- tio, sed exigebatur, & quidem autoritate Ma- gistratus secularis: quum Regum terræ hic aperta mentio fiat. Conatur quidem Grotius argumen- tum è verbis Christi de regibus terræ invertere, hoc modo: Videmus passim à regibus immunes tri- butorum haberi, si non & alios, certe filios suos, At hoc δίδραχμον nomine DEI exigitur. Quis igitur dubi- tet, quin Deus me filium suum unicum, qui נגיר id est, Princeps Danieli IX. 26. velit hoc onere subleva- tum? imo Filius major est templo Matth. XII. 6. non solet autem major minori tributum pendere. Sed manifestum est, non adstruere Christum argu- mento à regum filiis immunitatem suam à contri- butione ad usum templi: quam liberam fuisse in Galilæa agentibus, agnoscit Grotius, & ἐκ τῆς ἰδίας προαιρέσεως solutam ex edicto ad Sardia- nos probat; cur ergo quum vi edictorum jam im- munis, & liber fuerit Christus, opus habuisset adhuc suam adferre immunitatem? Id itaque po- tius hæc Christi probatio vult; Quum Regum filiis tributa non imperentur, sed subditus à Regibus ter- ræ, multo minus se Regum Regis filium obnoxium esse contributioni: quemadmodum observat Chry- sostomus, quod ita concludat: Si reges terræ à fi- liis suis non accipiunt, sed ab iis, quibus imperant, quanto magis me ab hac postulatione liberum esse oportet, non terreni Regis, sed cælestis Filium & cæ- lorum Regem?

## 17:27
Vers. 27. Σκανδαλίσωμεν] Lest they say that the temple is despised by me. Christ teaches us by his example to redeem sinister suspicions even with some expense, if there is need.

Εὑρήσεις] The words seem to imply more that it was known to Christ that a stater was in that fish, than that it was brought about that a stater should exist in the fish. But since a stater was worth a τετράδραχμον, this occasion was seized by Christ to relieve Peter at the same time. It is entirely credible that the δίδραχμον was exacted in the place where each person had his home. That Christ lived in Capernaum is beyond controversy. See above chapter IV. 16. Peter had formerly lived in Bethsaida: but from the time when, having left his affairs, he had clung to Christ as a constant companion, he was counted in his family.

Ἀντὶ ἐμοῦ καὶ σοῦ] That is, for me and for you. For this is ἀντὶ for the Greeks and חלף for the Syrians.

To Grotius, the words of Christ seem to imply rather that the stater was known to Christ to be in that fish, than that a miracle occurred so that the stater existed in the fish. But these are not opposites. For Christ could both bring it about that a stater existed there in the fish, and indicate by his omniscience that very fish in which the stater was. Severus notes on this passage: The Savior says to Peter, opening the mouth of the fish you will find a stater. He did not, however, say that the stater had been swallowed by the fish: indicating that it had been held in its mouth, prompt and ready, by the fish serving the divine ordinance in any case: Chrysostom: For it was no small thing, he says, to predict in those deep waves the first fish that was about to swallow the hook, which would pay the tribute. And so by his command, as if a net had been lowered into the sea, that fish was caught which would bring the stater; but that is a matter of divine and ineffable power, θείας δυνάμεως & ἀποῤῥήτου, to bring it about that the sea brings gifts and shows its subjection from every side, both while it is silent in its raging surge, and while it receives a fellow servant in its ferocity, and now again while it pays for him to the tax collectors. This is Chrysostom. But a stater was needed, that is, a whole shekel, which was called אש תירא, because Christ was paying for himself and for Peter. A stater is equivalent to half an imperial, a τετράδραχμον making two didrachms; and thus a drachma, or denarius, constitutes a fourth part of a Joachimic.

Latin:

Vers. 27. Σκανδαλίσωμεν] Ne dicant à me templum con- temni. Docet nos Christus exemplo suo etiam cum di- spendio aliquo, si ita opus sit, redimere sinistras suspicio- nes.

Εὑρήσεις] Videntur verba magis id innuere notum Chri- sto in eo pisce esse staterem, quam factum ut stater in pi- sce existeret. Cum autem stater valeret τετράδραχμον, ar- repta a Christo est hæc occasio Petrum simul sublevandi. Credibile omnino est exactum δίδραχμον eo loci ubi quis- que larem habebat. Christum Capharnaumi habitasse extra controversiam est. Vide supra cap. IV. 16. Petrus olim Bethsaidæ habitaverat: sed ex quo rebus relictis Chri- sto assiduus comes hæserat, in ipsius familia censebatur.

Ἀντὶ ἐμοῦ καὶ σοῦ] Id est, meam tuamque vicem. Nam hoc est Græcis ἀντὶ & Syris חלף.

Grotiο videntur verba Christi magis id innuere, notum Christo in eo pisce esse staterem, quam factum ut stater in pisce existeret. Sed hæc opposita non sunt. Nam & efficere potuit Christus, ut illic stater in pisce existeret, & indicare pro omniscien- tia sua illum ipsum piscem infallibiliter, in quo stater erat. Severus notat ad h. l. Ait Salvator Petro, aperiens os piscis invenies staterem. Non dixit autem deglutitum à pisce staterem: indicans detentum eum fuisse in ore promptum & paratum à pisce divina utique ordinationi serviente: Chryso- stomus: Neque enim, inquit, exiguum erat prædi- cere in profundis illis fluctibus primum piscem, qui hamum esse hausturus, tributum soluturum. Atque ita imperio ejus, quasi reticulo in mare demerso, il- le captus est piscis, qui staterem afferret; sed divi- næ illud ineffabilisque virtutis illud est θείας δυνά- μεως & ἀποῤῥήτου ita efficere, ut mare dona ferat & undequaque suam subjectionem ostendat, & dum in rabiem æstum tacet, & dum ferociens conservum su- scepit, & nunc rursus dum exactoribus pro eo solvit. Hæc Chrysostomus. Statere autem opus erat, h. e. siclo integro, qui אש תירא dicebatur, quia pro se Christus & pro Petro solvebat. Æqui- valet dimidio imperiali stater, τετράδραχμον duo didrachma efficiens; adeoque quartam partem Joachimici constituit drachma, vel denarius.

## 18:1 Argument
CHAPTER XVIII.

ARGUMENT AND DIVISION.

As the disciples were asking about the greatest in the kingdom of heaven, Christ sets a child before them, warning that those who wish to come into the kingdom of heaven must be like him, and that such as believe in him should not be scandalized, and woe is spoken to those who cause scandal, and they are commanded that those things which are the cause of scandal be cut off, because of the danger of hell: concerning the angels of children, and the cause of the coming of the Son of man: who seeks one lost sheep before ninety-nine wandering ones. Concerning fraternal correction, and the power of binding and loosing, and concerning the hearing of public prayers: and also an admonition concerning fraternal forgiveness, illustrated by the parable of the wicked servant.

These are the parts: I. Information for those inquiring about primacy in the kingdom of heaven, to v. 5. II. Concerning Scandal, to v. 10. III. Concerning the purpose of the coming of the Son of man, to v. 14. IV. Concerning fraternal correction, to v. 20. V. Concerning fraternal forgiveness, to v. 35.

PART I.

Information for those inquiring about primacy in the kingdom of heaven.

Vers. 1. At that time] Even at other times, as it seems to be gathered from a comparison of the Scriptures, they dealt with this matter, but especially then, having heard the mention of the resurrection so often, by the completion of which, as if the enemies were conquered, they thought that Christ's kingdom, not merely spiritual but also visible, such as all the Jews were hoping for, was about to begin. See Acts 1:6.

Who then is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven] Which of them, of course, as Luke indicates: and 'greater' is 'greatest', as has been noted elsewhere. 'In the kingdom of heaven' is the same as 'in the kingdom' or 'in the glory of Christ' below in chapter XX. 21, Mark X. 37. They do not doubt that the chief offices of the kingdom were about to come to them as the domestics of the king: but they were disputing among themselves, vying for who was to obtain the principal place. For what the wife of Zebedee demands a little later, that her sons should sit at the right and left of Christ, is nothing other than that the two first offices of the kingdom be given to them, such as were the offices in the Sanhedrin of him who was called Nasi and of him who was called Ab Beth Din.

Latin:

CAPUT XVIII.

ARGUMENTUM ET PAR- TITIO.

Quærentibus discipulis de maximo in regno cælo- cœlorum, infantem sistit Christus, monens ut illi similes sint, qui in regnum cœlorum venire volunt, ac ne scandalizentur tales in ipsum credentes, ac væ dicitur scandali- zantibus, jubenturque ea, quæ scandali causa sunt, amputari, ob gehennæ peri- culum: de puerorum angelis, & adventus Filii hominis causa: qui unam ovem per- ditam quærit præ nonaginta novem erran- tibus. De correptione fraterna, & po- testate ligandi ac solvendi, deque exaudi- tione precum publicarum: nec non de con- donatione fraterna admonitio, parabola de servo nequam illustrata.

Partes hæ sunt: I. Informatio quærentium de primatu in regno cœlorum, ad v. 5. II. De Scan- dalo, ad v. 10. III. De fine adventus filii hominis, ad v. 14. IV. De correptione fraterna, ad v. 20. V. De condonatione fraterna, ad v. 35.

PARS I.

Informatio quærentium de primatu in regno cœlorum.

Vers. 1. Ἐν ἐκείνῃ τῇ ὥρᾳ] Etiam alias, ut ex collatione Scriptorum videtur colligi, hac de re egerunt, sed tunc præcipue, audita toties resurrectionis mentione, qua per- acta, velut hostibus devictis, Christi regnum non mere spirituale, verum etiam aspectabile, quale Judæi omnes sperabant, inchoatum iri arbitrabantur. Vide Act. I. 6.

Τίς ἄρα μείζων ἐν τῇ βασιλείᾳ τῶν ὀυρανῶν] Quis ipsorum scilicet, ut Lucas indicat: & μείζων est maximus, ut alibi notatum est. ἐν βασιλείᾳ τῶν ὀυρανῶν idem est quod ἐν τῇ βασι- λείᾳ aut ἐν τῇ δόξᾳ τῶ χριστ̃ infra cap. XX. 21. Marc. X. 37. Non dubitant quin præcipua regni munia ad ipsos ut do- mesticos regis essent perventura: sed inter ipsos quis prin- cipem locum esset obtenturus æmulantes inter se disputa- bant. Nam quod paulo post exigit Zebedæi uxor ut sui liberi à dextra sinistraque Christo assideant, nihil est a- liud, quam ut duo prima regni munia ipsis dentur, qualia e- rant in Synedrio munia ejus qui נשיא & ejus qui אב בית דין vocabantur.

## 18:2
Vers. 2. Having called a child to him] That 'having called to him' shows that he was somewhat older, as one who could walk; it is 'talia' in the Syriac. Moreover, by using this conspicuous image, he imprints the following sentiment more deeply upon their minds and memory.

What Camero says about it is more correct: 'child' in this place is used in the same sense as in chapter II of Matthew, where the Angel commands Joseph to 'take the child'. For if it were a question of a boy here, there is almost no boy so ingenuous that, approaching that age which is called adolescence, he could be a suitable example of this humility and simplicity to which Christ exhorts his own. Nor does it stand in the way that Christ is said to have called a little boy, for in Mark chapter IX. 36, Christ is said to have 'taken' a little boy; and in Luke, much more emphatically, to have 'seized' a little boy by laying on a hand. 'To take hold of' in Greek. And it certainly pertained to that sweetness of Christ's affection to gently address a nursing child. Similar to this is the passage in the following chapter, verse 13. the children were brought to him, and 'suffer the children', where for the word 'children' Luke in chapter XVIII. 15 uses 'infants', which in Greek signifies nursing children, and says that Christ 'called to him' those infants, so that no one from this, because Christ is said to have called those little children to him here, can necessarily conclude that those children had the use of reason. And so the Evangelists do not contradict each other, when one of them says Christ 'called to him', but the others 'to take' or 'to seize' a child.

Latin:

Vers. 2. Προσκαλεσάμενος παιδίον] Illud προσκαλεσάμε- νος ostendit fuisse majusculum, ut qui ambulare posset, טליא est apud Syrum. Hanc autem adhibita conspicua imagine sententiam quæ sequitur altius imprimit animis ac memoriæ.

Rectius se habent quæ de eo Camero: παιδίον hoc loco eodem sensu usurpatur, quo cap. II. Mat- thæi, ubi jubet Angelus Josepho παραλαμβάνειν τὸ παιδίον. Nam si de puero hic agitur, nullus est fe- re adeo ingenuus puer, ut accedens ad ætatem illam quæ adolescentia dicitur, possit esse idoneum exem- plum hujus humilitatis & simplicitatis, ad quam Christus suos hortatur. Nec obstat quod dicitur Christus advocasse puerulum, nam apud Marcum cap. IX. 36. Christus dicitur λαβεῖν sumsisse pue- rulum; & apud Lucam multo ἐμφατικώτερον ap- prehendisse puerulum injecta manu. Ἐπιλαβέσθαι Græce. Et pertinebat sane ad suavitatem illam affe- ctus Christi, puerulum lactentem blande compella- re. Similis est isti locus cap. sequenti vers. 13. προσ- σενέχθη αὐτῷ τὰ παιδία, & ἄφετε τὰ παιδία, u- bi pro voce παιδία Lucas cap. XVIII. 15. usurpat βρέ- φη, quod Græce significat pueros lactentes, aitque Christum προσκαλέσασθαι, advocasse illa βρέφη, ut nemo hinc, quod Christus istos puerulos hic advo- casse ad se dicitur, possit colligere necessario pueru- los illos habuisse dum usum rationis. Itaque non pugnant inter se Evangelistæ, quum eorum unus ait Christum προσκαλέσασθαι, alii vero λαβεῖν vel ἐ- πιλάβεσθαι παιδίον.

## 18:3
Vers. 3. Unless you be converted and become as children] Christ commands the Apostles to cease this desire for eminence, to root it out from their minds. Aristotle counts 'magnanimity' among the virtues, with which he who is endowed, as he himself speaks, 'deems himself most worthy' of honor. He adds that 'powers are to be chosen for the sake of honor': he also denies that a man who is such would willingly go where others are preferred. But on the contrary, he places 'pusillanimity' as a vice, so that one deprives himself of a very good thing of which he is worthy. And it appears that almost all Greeks and Romans, even those who are most praised, lived according to this prescription. Plato is better in the first book of the Republic, saying that rule is the management of another's affair: but that there is no one who would strive to involve himself in the affairs of others except for the sake of a reward: and that the reward consists either in money or in honor. But when a good and wise man is neither a lover of money nor a lover of honor, it follows that he should not even desire public honors, unless perhaps for the sake of avoiding some greater evil, as if he were to see that otherwise the republic would fall into the power of evil men. 'If any man desires the episcopate,' says Paul, 'he desires a good work': but in those times, when the Ecclesiastical prefecture was a most heavy burden, exposed to a thousand dangers, and having a most frequent outcome of violent death. But if at that time no one had striven to render himself suitable for that office, a desolation of the Churches was about to follow with great loss to the truth. But those who in prosperous and peaceful times studiously affect civil or Ecclesiastical offices, it is hard for them to be free from this vice of 'love of rule', which we learn from Christ's words is how contrary it is to salvation. Indeed, often to the 'love of rule' there is also added 'love of money' and a desire for a life passed a little more softly. But that now conflicts not only with the rules of Christ, but also with natural equity, to claim for oneself the guardianship of another's affair, not with this primary wish that you may profit another, but that you may profit yourself: which, even if all other injury were absent, is in itself sufficiently unjust. But Christ wishes his followers to become like a child, because that age is furthest removed from that ambition, which is wont to be referred not even to youth but to virile and robust age: for as Horace says: 'With changed pursuits, virile age and mind / Seeks wealth and friendships, and serves honor.' Unless you enter into the kingdom of heaven] So far are you from being about to have the first seats, that you will not even have a part in the heavenly kingdom. By the phrase 'kingdom of heaven', the disciples, along with the other Hebrews, understood a visible kingdom, but one given from heaven. Christ, reserving the true nature of his kingdom to be explained at other times, speaks of the glory after the resurrection, which itself was also accustomed to be called the heavenly kingdom, and indeed most excellently. Thus he often recalls us from the bread of this life to the bread of the other life.

Grotius rightly observes that the βασιλείαν ὐρανῶν (kingdom of heaven) was understood in one sense by the disciples, and in another by Christ. The disciples, by the term heavenly kingdom, understood with the Hebrews a visible kingdom, but one given from heaven. Christ, reserving the true nature of his kingdom to be explained at other times, speaks of the glory after the resurrection, which itself was also accustomed to be called the heavenly kingdom, and indeed most excellently. Thus he often recalls us from the bread of this life to the bread of the other life. The disciples did not doubt that the chief offices of the kingdom would come to them, as members of the King's household; but they disputed among themselves, vying for who would obtain the first place, and who the second. In that, however, Grotius speaks too generally when he says that ALL Jews hoped for a visible kingdom of Christ. Luke testifies otherwise concerning Zechariah, Elizabeth, Mary, Simeon, Anna, and those who with them were awaiting the redemption of Israel, and their discourses and hymns in Luke 1 and 2 teach as much. Nor do those things deserve consideration which he hands down concerning the desire for the Episcopate or political office regarding the words of Christ ἐὰν μὴ τραφῆτε & γένησθε ὡς τὰ παιδία (unless you be converted and become as little children), which hardly differ from the vice of Φιλαρχίας (love of power), and which he argues against Aristotle, who counts μεγαλοψυχίαν (magnanimity) as a virtue. Certainly, the words of Paul, εἴ τις Ἐπισκοπῆς ὀρέγεται καλᾶ ἔργα ἐπιθυμεῖ (if any man desire the office of a bishop, he desireth a good work), 1 Tim. 3:1, are wrongly restricted to those times, when ecclesiastical leadership was a most heavy burden exposed to a thousand dangers, and having a very frequent outcome of violent death. Nor does the Apostle speak only of ecclesiastical leadership, but by the name of Bishop he understands pastors generally, as in Acts 20:28, nor does he look only to those times, which were such as they were when he wrote these things. But he prescribes common rules without distinction of times, just as he also designated the common requirements and duties of Pastors there. Verse 4. ὡς τὸ παιδίον τῦτο] ἑαυτὸν. For ταπεινόν ἐσι is understood. In Psalm 131, in which it is manifest that Christ is looking back, there is the same emphasis. The LXX have it thus: εἰ μὴ ἐ- ταπεινοφρόνεν ὡς τὸ ἀπογεγαλακτισμένον ἐπὶ τὴν μητέρα ἀυ- τῦ. For the infant does not practice humility; but it is humble. What kind of children they are by nature, namely alien to ambition, such we are commanded to be by our own choice. Similar is that which Paul says, he does not want us to be childish in malice 1 Cor. 14:20, that is, to be guileless as children are. Clement of Alexandria, Paedagogus book 1, chapter 5, whose title is this: that all who are occupied with the truth are children before God, has many things on this matter: this among others: children are rightly those who have known God alone as Father, guileless and infants and innocent. That well-known saying of Euripides: A new care is not accustomed to cause pain. And that of Menander: Anxieties, glories, ambitions, laws, all these things are evils added to nature. And Plato said of young men that they do not have in themselves examples similar to the wicked. Pythagoras taught, as witnessed by Iamblichus, that the class of strong desires, and likewise the very class of ambitions, and similarly the remaining impulses and dispositions, as many as happen to be of a harsh and tumultuous kind, arrive from the age of a man into that of young men. Chalcidius on the Timaeus: Avarice, lust, cruelty, and other plagues of this kind signify nothing great in childhood, but are harmful in a confirmed age. Verse 5. Δέξηται] δέχεσθαι which properly denotes hospitality, is here taken for every kind of benefit, as in Acts 21:17, which will appear if you compare the place in Mark chapter 9:41 with this. Such a child] The translation is made from a similitude, as is often the case. Therefore such a child is thus humble: he who is like this child, as the Syriac translates here. Christ shows how much he values this virtue, since he promises the first seats in the heavenly kingdom not only to those who are endowed with it, but also that benefits conferred upon them are imputed to himself.

PART II.

Admonition concerning scandal.

Latin:

Vers. 3. Ἐὰν μὴ στραφῆτε κὴ γένησθε ὡς τὰ παιδία] Destiti- esse satis Christus Apostolis imperat istud eminendi studium ex animo evellere. Aristoteles virtutibus annumerat τὴν μεγαλοψυχίαν, qua qui sit præditus τιμῆς ut ipse loquitur ἑαυτὸν μάλιςα ἀξιοῖ. Addit τὰς δυναςείας διὰ τὴν τιμὴν εἶναι αἱρετά: Negat etiam eum, talis qui sit, libenter iturum ὦ προςεύσι ἄλλοι. At contra μικροψυχίαν in vitio ponit, ut perquam bono quo quis dignus sit, ipse se privet. Et ex hoc præscripto vixisse apparet Græcos Romanosque pene omnes, etiam qui maxime laudantur. Melius Plato de re- publica primo, imperium ait esse procurationem rei alie- næ: neminem autem esse qui alienis negotiis immiscere se studeat nisi propter mercedem: mercedem autem aut in pe- cunia aut in honore consistere. Cum vero vir bonus ac sapiens neque φιλάργυρος sit, neque φιλότιμος, sequi ut pu- blicos honores ne cupiat quidem, nisi forte mali alicujus gravioris evitandi causa, utpote si alioqui videret in malo- rum hominum potestatem perventuram rempublicam. Εἴ τις ἐπισκοπῆς ὀρέγεται, inquit Paulus, καλᾶ ἔργα ἐπιθυμεῖ: sed iis temporibus, cum præfectura Ecclesiastica onus esset gravissimum, mille periculis expositum, & frequentissi- mum habens exitum mortis violentæ. Quod si tum nemo se studuisset ei munere reddere idoneum, secutura erat vastities Ecclesiarum cum magno dispendio veritatis. At qui rebus secundis ac placidis munera civilia aut Ecclesiastica studiose affectant, vix est ut absitit ab hoc φιλαρχίας vitio, quod quam saluti sit contrarium discimus ex Christi verbis. Imo sæpe ad φιλαρχίαν etiam φιλαργυρία accedit & cupido vitæ paulo mollius transigendæ. Id vero jam non cum Chri- sti tantum regulis, sed cum naturali etiam æquitate pugnat, tutelam alienæ rei sibi deposcere, non hoc maxime voto ut alteri prosis, sed ut tibi: quod ut alia omnis absit injuria, ipsum per se satis injustum est. Puero autem similes vult fieri Christus sectatores suos, quod ea ætas longissime absit ab isto studio, quod ne ad juventam quidem sed ad virilem & robustam ætatem referri solet: nam ut Horatius ait: Conversis studiis ætas animusque virilis Quærit opes & amicitias, inservit honori. Ἐὰν μὴ εἰσέλθητε εἰς τὴν βασιλείαν τῶν ὐρανῶν] Tantum ab- est ut primas sedes habituri sitis, ne partem quidem habe- bitis in regno cœlesti. Discipuli voce regni cœlestis intel- ligebant cum Hebræis cæteris regnum aspectabile, sed de cœlo datum. Christus veram regni sui naturam explican- dam aliis temporibus reservans, agit de gloria post resurre- ctionem, quæ & ipsa regnum cœleste & quidem excellentis- sime dici solebat. Ita sæpe à pane hujus vitæ ad panem vitæ alterius nos revocat.

Recte observat Grotius, alio sensu βασιλείαν ὐρανῶν intellectam à discipulis, alio à Christo. Di- scipuli voce regni cælestis intelligebant cum Hebræis regnum aspectabile, sed de cælo datum. Christus veram regni sui naturam explicandam aliis tempo- ribus reservans, agit de gloria post resurrectionem, quæ & ipsa regnum cæleste & quidem excellentissime dici solebat. Ita sæpe à pane hujus vitæ ad panem vitæ alterius nos revocat. Non dubitabant disci- puli, quin præcipua regni munia ad ipsos, ut domesticos Regis, essent perventura: sed inter ipsos quis principem, quis deincipem locum esset ob- tenturus, æmulantes inter se disputabant. In eo tamen nimis generaliter loquitur Grotius, quod ait, OMNES Judæos aspectabile regnum Christi sperasse. Aliud de Zacharia, de Elisabetha, de Maria, de Simeone, de Hanna, & qui cum iis re- demtionem Israelis expectabant, testatur Lucas, docentque sermones, & hymni eorum Luc. I. & II. Nec calculum merentur, quæ circa verba Christi ἐὰν μὴ τραφῆτε & γένησθε ὡς τὰ παιδία, tradit de desiderio Episcopatus, vel Politici muneris, quod vix absint à Φιλαρχίας vitio, & quæ contra Aristotolem μεγαλοψυχίαν annumerantem dispu- tat. Pauli certe verba εἴ τις Ἐπισκοπῆς ὀρέγεται καλᾶ ἔργα ἐπιθυμεῖ 1. Tim: III. 1. perperam ad ea restringuntur tempora, cum præfectura Ecclesiastica onus esset gravissimum mille periculis expositum, & frequentissimum habens exitum mortis violentæ. Nec de præfectura tantum Ecclesiastica loquitur Apostolus, sed Episcopi nomine generaliter pasto- res intelligit, ut Act. XX. 28. nec illa tantum tem- pora respicit, quæ & qualia tum erant, cum hæc scriberet. Sed communes regulas præscribit sine temporum distinctione, quemadmodum etiam communia Pastorum προσκείμενα, & munia illic designavit. Vers. 4. ὡς τὸ παιδίον τῦτο] ἑαυτὸν. Subauditur enim ταπεινόν ἐσι. In Psalmo CXXXI. quo manifestum est Chri- stum respicere, eadem est ἔμφασις LXX. sic habent : εἰ μὴ ἐ- ταπεινοφρόνεν ὡς τὸ ἀπογεγαλακτισμένον ἐπὶ τὴν μητέρα ἀυ- τῦ. Neque enim ταπεινοφρονεῖ τὸ βρέφος· sed ταπεινόν ἐσι. Quales igitur pueri natura sunt, ab ambitu scilicet alieni, tales nos esse jubemur τῇ προαιρέσει. Simile est quod Pau- lus, non vult τῇ κακίᾳ νηπιάζειν 1. Cor. XIV. 20. id est ἀκά- κως εἶναι quales sunt pueri. Clemens Alexandrin. Pæda- gogi l. cap. V. cujus hic est titulus ὅτι πάντες οἱ περὶ τὴν ἀλή- θειαν καταγινόμενοι παῖδες παρὰ τῷ θεῷ multa habet in hanc rem: istud inter cætera : παῖδες ἓν εἰκότως οἱ θεὸ μόνον ἐγνω- κότες πατέρα, ἀφελεῖς κὶ νήπιοι κὶ ἀκέραιοι. Notum illud Eu- ripidis: Νία γὰρ φροντὶς ἐκ ἀλγεῖν φιλεῖ. Et Menandri istud: Ἀγωνίαι, δόξαι, φιλοτιμίαι, νόμοι Ἅπαντα ταῦτ' ἐπίθετα τῇ φύσει κακά. Et Plato de juvenibus dixit ὐκ ἔχειν ἐν ἑαυτοῖς παραδείγματα ὁμοιοπαθῆ τοῖς πονηροῖς. Docebat Pythagoras, teste Jam blicho, τὸ τῶν ἐπιθυμιῶν τῶν ἰσχυρῶν, ὡσαύτως δὲ κὶ ἀυτὸ τὸ τῶν φιλοτιμιῶν γένος, ὁμοίως δὲ κὶ τὰς λοιπὰς ὁρμάς τε κὶ δια- θέσεις, ὅσαι τυγχάνωσιν ὖσαι τῇ χαλεπᾶ τε κὶ θορυβώδες γένες, ἐκ τῆς τῶ ἀνδρὸς ἡλικίας εἰς τὴν τῶν νεανίσκων ἀφικνεῖσθαι. Chalcidius ad Timæum: Avaritia, libido, crudelitas cæteræ- que hujusmodi pestes nihil in pueritia grande designant, sed sunt confirmata jam ætate noxia. Vers. 5. Δέξηται] δέχεσθαι quæ proprie hospitalitatem notat, hic pro omni beneficiorum genere accipitur, ut Act. XXI. 17. quod apparebit si Marci locum cap. IX. 41. cum isto conferas. Παιδίον τοιῦτο] Ex similitudine fit translatio, ut sæpe. Ergo παιδίον τοιῦτον est ὕτως ταπεινόφρονα : quivit sicut puer iste, ut vertit hic Syrus. Ostendit Christus quanti hanc virtutem faciat, cum non his tantum qui ea sunt præditi primas sedes pollicetur in regno cœlesti, sed & beneficia in ipsos collata imputari.

PARS II.

Monitio de scandalo.

## 18:6
Verse 6. whoever shall cause to stumble] It usually happens for the most part that those who conduct themselves humbly are despised by others. But that contempt cannot happen without often scaring away every best person from the pursuit of piety: Christ does not deny that this happens: but he threatens grave things to those who despise. Thus the word to cause to stumble, taken in this way, is at the same time opposed to the benefits about which it has been treated, and yet it has no meaning different from what follows. Of these little ones believing in me] That is, even of the little ones. Not only if he has despised some Prophet or another Christian of great progress, but if he has even spurned him who is in the least rank of those who truly believe. Thus the word little ones and least is accustomed to be taken. See what is above in chapter 5:19 and chapter 10:42 and below in chapter 25:40. Those who have reached the highest degree are also sometimes accustomed to be moved somewhat by the injuries of the wicked: which Origen does not seem to deny rightly here: but especially those who are in the apprenticeship of piety.

The discourse is not about little ones in progress, of whom there is no contention here with those who are more adult in progress, but about little ones in age, such as that little boy was who was set in the midst of the disciples, although we do not deny that twins are not excluded by the same simplicity of faith, humility, sincerity, readiness of imitation, and ease of seduction: nor does Christ deal with those not to be despised, but with those not to be affected by scandal: nor indeed could Grotius show where the word to cause to stumble is used regarding contempt, therefore this gloss is precarious: yet it is pleasing to the Anabaptists and Calvinists, who deny faith to infants, which Christ here expressly ascribes to the same: whence it is not to be conceded that his words should be so vexed, as has been done by Grotius, who also in verse 5 does not explain the words such a child, as they sound, about such a little child, but by thus humble: when, however, it is by no means right to depart from the propriety of words without necessity. It is only later, in verse 10, that the matter of not despising little ones is dealt with: see that you do not despise one of these little ones. The entire verse is a dissertation immediately following concerning scandals: and therefore the word to cause to stumble must also be taken properly here, so that the discourse may cohere. And the Interpreters commonly explain it thus with great consensus. Basil the Great, says in the Catena of Nicetas on Matthew: Let someone cause to stumble, by an iniquitous work or speech, another, as leading to transgression (as the serpent did Eve, and Eve Adam) or they prohibit them from fulfilling the will of God, as Peter did the Lord, saying, be it far from you Lord, this shall not be to you; or he who disposes the mind of the weak to something of those things which are forbidden, according to that which was said by the Apostle, 1 Corinthians 8:10. if therefore anyone sees you, who have knowledge, reclining in an idol's temple, will not his conscience, since it is weak, be built up to eat things sacrificed to idols? Nazianzen in the same place on this passage: It is good, he says, neither to be sinning, nor to be suspected, as much as possible, and reason dictates: not to place a scandal, or a stumbling block for many, since we know what an intolerable and heavy punishment is established by Him who does not lie, even for those who cause one of the little ones to stumble. What are scandals, says Chrysostom. Those things which prohibit the straight way, etc.

It is profitable for him] For it would be profitable for him. And the apodosis is missing, which from a comparison of those who relate the same things is to be supplied thus: Rather than he should commit such a thing.

Μύλος ὀνικὸς] Although the upper millstone is called ὄνος by the Greeks, not the lower part of the mill, as some please, but the upper, ὁ ἀλέτων according to Pollux: τὸ ἄνω τῆς μύλης according to Hesychius, and in Hebrew רכב, yet that it should be called μύλος ὀνικὸς itself is without precedent: nor does analogy allow it. It is therefore entirely true that the adjective ὀνικὸς is added to indicate a larger and heavier mill, such as that which is accustomed to be turned not by hand, but by the work of donkeys: just as both the Syriac and Latin interpreters understood. Thus Labeo, Cascellius, and Trebatius oppose animal-driven mills to hand-mills. By the name of μύλος, however, a millstone is understood here by synecdoche, in which sense John also said μύλον μέγαν in the Apocalypse, ch. XVIII. 21. Mark teaches this in this passage, who explains μύλον as λίθον μυλικόν, the lower one, that is, and the same one larger, which Paulus the Jurisconsult calls the meta, and the Greeks τράπεζαν: the teachers of the Hebrews, שכב. For they think רחים is a name common to both stones. I would hardly believe that this custom of drowning by hanging a stone to the neck was usual among the Jews, since no mention of it exists in the Law: indeed, it appears from all history and the consensus of interpreters that only four punishments were known among them: fire, stoning, the sword, and strangulation. Wherefore this manner of speaking was drawn from their Syrian neighbors. For we shall also find examples of drowning in Eusebius's history in Syria. The same custom existed in Greece. The Scholiast on Aristophanes's Knights: 'For when they drowned some, they hung a weight from their necks.'

Latin:

Vers. 6. ὃς δ' ἂν σκανδαλίσῃ] Evenire plerumque solet, ut qui demisse se gerunt contemnantur ab aliis. Is autem con- temtus fieri non potest, quin sæpe optimum quemque a stu- dio pietatis absterreat: Hoc Christus fieri non nugat: sed gravia minatur comtemtoribus. Ita sumta vox σκανδαλί- ζειν simul & beneficiis de quibus actum est opponitur, & sensum tamen a sequentibus diversum non habet. Τῶν μικρῶν τύτων πιστευόντων εἰς ἐμὲ] Id est, κᾂν τῶν μι- κρῶν. Non tantum si Prophetam aliquem aut alium magni profectus Christianum contemserit, sed si vel eum spre- verit qui in minimo est vere credentium censu. Ita vox μι- κρῶν & ἐλαχίστων accipi solet. Vide quæ supra cap. V. 19. & cap. X. 42. & infra cap. XXV. 40. Solent etiam qui ad summum gradum pervenerunt interdum commoveri non- nihil improborum injuriis: quod non recte hic negare vide- tur Origenes: sed illi maxime qui in tyrocinio sunt pietatis.
