Non de parvulis profectu, quorum hic nulla cum adultioribus profectu est contentio, sed de parvulis ætate sermo est, qualis erat puerulus ille, qui in medio fistebatur discipulorum, etsi non abnuamus, geminos iisdem fidei simplicitate, hu- militate, sinceritate, imitationis promtitudine, sedu- ctionis facilitate haud excludi: neque de non con- temnendis, sed scandalo non afficiendis aliis Chri- stus agit: nec vero ubi vox σκανδαλίζειν de con- temtu adhibeatur, ostendere potuit Grotius, pre- caria ergo est hæc glossa: grata tamen Anabaptistis & Calvinianis, fidem infantibus denegantibus, quam hic iisdem διαῤῥήδην adscribit Christus: un- de non concedendum, ut verba ejus ita vexentur, quemadmodum à Grotio factum, qui etiam v. 5. verba παιδίον τοιῦτον non, ut sonant, de parvulo ta- li explicat, sed per ὕτως ταπεινόφρονα: quum ta- men citra necessitatem fas minime sit à proprie- tate vocum discedere. De non contemnendis parvulis deinceps demum agitur v. 10. videte ne a contemnatis unum ex his pusillis. De scandalis v. to- ta est dissertatio immediate subsequens: ideoque hic etiam verbum illud σκανδαλίζειν proprie acci- piendum, ut cohæreat oratio. Et explicant id ita communiter magno consensu Interpp. Basilius M. Scandalizet, inquit in Catena Nicetæ in Matth. ali- quis iniquo opere, aut sermone alium, ut transgressio- nem adducens (ut serpens Evam, & Eva Adamum) aut prohibent Dei perficere voluntatem, ut Petrus Do- minum, dicens, propitius esto tibi Domine, non erit tibi hoc; aut qui disponit animum infirmi ad aliquid eorum, quæ vetita sunt, juxta id quod ab Apostolo di- ctum est, 1. Cor. VIII. 10. si quis igitur viderit te, qui habes scientiam in idoleo recumbentem, non- ne conscientia illius, cum sit infirma, ædificabi- tur ad manducandum idolothyta? Nazianzenus ibidem ad h. l. Bonum est, inquit, neque peccantem, neque suspectum esse, quantum fieri potest, & ratio fert: non ponere scandalum, aut offendiculum mul- tis, quandoquidem etiam unum de pusillis scandali- zantibus, sciamus quam intolerabilis gravisque ab eo, qui non mentitur, pœna sit statuta. Ecquid sunt scandala, ait Chrysostom. Ea quæ viam rectam prohibent, &c.

Συμφέρει ἀυτῷ] Pro συμφέρη ἂν ἀυτῷ. Et deest ἀνταπό- δοσις quæ ex collatione idem narrantium ita supplenda est: Potius quam tale quid committeret.

Μύλος ὀνικὸς] Quanquam catillus Græcis ὄνος dicitur, pars scilicet molæ non inferior, ut quibusdam placet, sed superior, ὁ ἀλέτων Polluci: τὸ ἄνω τῆς μύλης Hesychio, Hebrais רכב, tamen ut id ipsum dicatur μύλος ὀνικὸς sine exemplo est: neque id patitur ἀναλογία. Omnino ergo verum est adjectum ὀνικὸς ἐπίθετον ut molam indicet majo- rem ac graviorem, qualis est quæ non manu, sed asinorum opera versari solet: quomodo & Syrus & Latinus inter- pres intellexerunt. Ita jumentarias molas manuariis op- ponunt Labeo, Cascellius, Trebatius. μύλου autem nomine συνεκδοχικῶς hic intelligitur saxum molare, quo sensu & in Apocalypsi Johannes dixit μύλον μέγαν cap. XVIII. 21. Do- cet id Marcus hoc loco qui μύλον exponit λίθον μυλικόν, infe- riorem scilicet, eundemque majorem, quam metam vocat Paulus Jurisconsultus, τράπεζαν Græci: Hebræorum magi- stri שכב. Nam רחים putant nomen esse utrique sa- xo commune. Morem hunc καταποντισμοῦ saxo ad collum appenso usitatum Judæis fuisse vix crediderim, cum nulla ejus in lege exstet mentio: imo sola quatuor supplicia a- pud eos nota fuisse ex omni historia & interpretum consen- su appareat, ignem, lapidationem, gladium, strangulatio- nem. Quare a vicinis Syris tractum hoc loquendi genus. Nam & in Eusebii historia inveniemus exempla βυθισμοῦ in Syria. Mos idem in Græcia. Scholiastes ad Equites A- ristophanis: ὅται γὰρ κατεπόντουν τινας, βάρος ἀπὸ τῶν τρα- χήλων ἐκρέμων.

## 18:7
Vers. 7. ὀυαὶ τῷ κόσμῳ] By the name of the world, as often, the human race is understood here, in which are both those who cause offenses, and those who are offended, who, being offended by the wickedness of others, either fall away from piety, or otherwise sin gravely. Christ deals with these in verses 8 and 9, but with those in verse 10. Christ deplores the unhappiness of both kinds. For the Hebrew אוי, and the ὀυαὶ of the Hellenists taken from it, is for the most part a cry of one grieving: for which the LXX sometimes put ὄιμοι, as in Psalm CXX. 5.

Ἀνάγκη] Many think this saying is for indicating the necessity which they call of consequence, once that depravity is posited in which the world is situated, which John proclaims in 1 Epist. ch. V. 19. I, just as I do not deny that this is posited and laid down by Christ (in which sense the Emperor M. Antoninus said, 'it is possible for one not to be shameless in the world'), so I think the word ἀνάγκη is to be referred to something else, namely to the end for which God, in whose power are men and human actions, does not prevent stumbling blocks by greater force, but permits them. Aristotle, at the end of the second book of the Physics, and in the first chapter of the first book of the Parts of Animals, says that necessity is often spoken of not from matter, but from the end, when, namely, 'if that is to be for the sake of which, it is necessary that these things exist,' which necessity he says was passed over by the physicists who were before Democritus, although it is the most powerful. Thus he says a saw is made of iron so that it may have teeth, and has teeth so that it may be able to cut what is hard little by little. And in this way it is necessary for a saw to be of iron: which he applies with great judgment to the parts of living creatures. But this necessity flowing from the end is in physics a little more precise; but in morals and governments, according to the subject matter nature is to be taken more loosely, so that it may indicate a great utility of the thing, or its consistency with the proposed end. Wherefore, what Christ said here speaking generally about stumbling blocks, ἀνάγκη ἐστι, Paul, dealing with that species which excels most and consists in the propagation of false dogmas, expressed through δεῖ εἶναι that way the minds of men might be tested. Nor is it rare among Greek writers for ἀνάγκη or ἀναγκαῖον to signify that which must happen for some reason. Thus it appears that ἀνάγκην is used in Luke 14:18, Heb. 9:23, Jude 3, and ἀναγκαῖον in 2 Cor. 9:5, Phil. 2:25. Luke in this place said ἀνένδεκτόν ἐστι μὴ ἐλθεῖν τὰ σκάνδαλα: just as he said elsewhere ὐκ ἐνδέχεται προφήτην ἀπολέσθαι ἔξω Ἱερουσαλήμ, that is, it is not fitting. Thus also the Greeks often use ἀδύνατον. For what Plato had said in the Timaeus, ἀδύνατον ἓν Θεῶν παισὶν ἀπιστεῖν, Cicero translates, it is very difficult to do not to have faith in those born of the gods: and in the same book he interprets ἀδύνατον λέγειν as, it is a sin to reveal it to the common people. The sense therefore is: The greatest stumbling blocks will happen, and it should not seem strange that they are not inhibited by God, since it is just and right that they be permitted, so that the upright may be distinguished from the feigned, and the constant from the fickle.

This is commonly explained as the necessity which they call of consequence: that is, given that depravity in which John declares the world is situated, 1 Ep. 5:19. Grotius likes it to be singular. He wishes it to be taken from the necessity of the end, which, however, he understands more loosely, so that it may indicate a great utility of the thing or its consistency with the proposed end: since among the Greeks ἀνάγκη or ἀναγκαῖον sometimes signifies that which must happen for some reason, as for instance Luke 14:18, Heb. 9:23, Jude v. 3, and also 2 Cor. 9:5, Phil. 2:25. Even if we admit this, we do not think it should be granted that only the end for which God does not hinder but permits stumbling blocks is looked at here: because the matter concerns avoiding stumbling blocks and averting them as much as possible; which indeed happen necessarily, given the depravity of the world, so that one may not hope that the world will be free of stumbling blocks, or that stumbling blocks will ever cease: yet they must be avoided by us, so that we may not be the cause or authors of them, and that all the more carefully, the more easily they arise due to the wickedness of the world. There was no place here to speak of the end why God permits them to happen, nor is there mention in any word that they are permitted so that the upright may be distinguished from the feigned, and the constant from the fickle. The matter concerns the efficient cause, and woe is intimated to those through whom stumbling blocks come, not the final cause. It is certain, meanwhile, that a necessity is being discussed here that does not remove liberty; which Grotius rightly observes regarding this passage and ch. 26:24. (against the Stoic Calvinists) Grotius observes. When he said it is necessary (says Grotius) that stumbling blocks come, he does not remove the liberty of power, nor the power of free will, nor does he say these things by subjecting life to some necessity of things, but he predicts that it will absolutely happen. Therefore, the prediction of that does not induce the stumbling blocks, far from it, nor because he predicted it, for if they had not wished to act wickedly knowing them, they would certainly not have come, unless they were truly going to happen, he would not have predicted it at all, but since they were acting badly and suffering from an incurable disease, he came and predicted that it would happen.

πλὴν] This adversative shows that the guilt of the sinners is not lessened by the wise permission of God: whence it follows that a necessity is being discussed here that does not remove liberty. Thus also below ch. 26:24.

δι ὗ] Properly, therefore, stumbling blocks happen through men, not through God, although not without God. See what we said above at 10:29.

Latin:

Vers. 7. ὀυαὶ τῷ κόσμῳ] κόσμου nomine ut sæpe humanum genus hic intelligitur, in quo sunt & οἱ σκανδαλίζοντες, &c οἱ σκανδαλιζόμενοι, qui scilicet offensi aliorum improbitate aut a pietate deficiunt, aut alioqui graviter delinquunt. De his agit Christus commate 8. 9. de illis autem commate 10. Utriusque generis infelicitatem Christus deplorat. Nam אוי Hebræum & sumtum inde ὀυαὶ Hellenistarum, plerunque dolentis vox est: pro quo ὄιμοι interdum ponunt LXX. ut Psal. CXX. 5.

Ἀνάγκη] Multi hoc dictum putant ad indicandam ne- cessitatem quam vocant consequentiæ, posita scilicet illa pravitate in qua situm mundum Johannes prædicat Epist. I. cap. V. 19. Ego, sicut hanc a Christo poni atque sub- sterni non nego, (quo sensu M. Antoninus imperat dixit, δύναται ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ ἀναίσχυντος μὴ εἶναι) ita vocem ἀνάγκης alio referendum puto, ad finem nimirum ob quem Deus, in cu- jus potestate sunt homines humanæque actiones, offendi- cula non impedit vi majore, sed permittit. Aristoteles fine II. ἀκροαματικῶν, & capite primo libri primi de partibus ani- mantium, ait ἀνάγκην sæpe non ex materia, sed ex fine dici, quando scilicet εἰ ἐκεῖνο ἔσται τὸ ὗ ἕνεκα, ταῦτα ἀνάγκη ἐστιν ἔχειν, quam necessitatem ait præteritam a Physicis qui an- te Democritum, cum tamen sit potissima. Ita ser- ram ait ferream esse ut dentes habeat, dentes habere ut quod durum est paulatim secare possit. Et hoc modo necessarium esse serram esse ex ferro: quod magno cum judicio aptat ad partes animantium. Hæc autem necessitas ex fine manans in physicis paulo pressius; at in moribus gubernationibus pro rei subjectæ natura laxius sumenda est, ut magnam rei utilitatem, sive cum fine proposito convenientiam indicet. Quare quod hic Christus in genere de offendiculis loquens dixit ἀνάγκη ἐστι, idem Paulus agens de ea specie quæ maxime excellit, atque in falsorum dogmatum propagatione consistit, per δεῖ εἶναι extulit, ipsum etiam finem clare designans, nimirum ut eo modo explorentur hominum animi. Neque rarum est apud Græcos Scriptores ut ἀνάγκη aut ἀναγκαῖον id significet quod fieri aliqua de causa oportet. Ita ἀνάγκην sumi apparet Luc. XIV. 18. Hebr. IX. 23. Judæ 3. & ἀναγκαῖον 2. Cor. IX. 5. Philip. II. 25. Lucas hoc loco dixit ἀνένδεκτόν ἐστι μὴ ἐλθεῖν τὰ σκάνδαλα: quomodo alibi dixit ὐκ ἐνδέχεται προφήτην ἀπολέσθαι ἔξω Ἱερουσαλήμ, id est, non convenit. Sic & ἀδύνατον sæpe sumunt Græci. Nam quod Plato Timæo dixerat, ἀδύνατον ἓν Θεῶν παισὶν ἀπιστεῖν, Cicero vertit, difficillimum factu est à diis ortis fidem non habere: & in eodem libro ἀδύνατον λέγειν interpretatur, nefas in vulgus indicare. Sensus igitur est: Maxima offendicula evenient, neque mirum videri debet à Deo ea non inhiberi, cum æquum rectumque sit ea permitti, ut integri à fictis, constantes à levibus discernimentur.

Explicatur hoc communiter de necessitate, quam vocant, consequentiæ: posita sc. illa pravitate, in qua situm mundum Johannes prædicat 1. Ep. V. 19. Grotio placet singulari esse. De necessitate ex fine accipi vult, quam tamen laxius intelligit, uti sc. magnam rei utilitatem sive cum fine proposito convenientiam indicet: Siquidem apud Græcos ἀνάγκη aut ἀναγκαῖον quandoque id significet, quod fieri aliqua de causa oportet, utpote Luc. XIV. 18. Ebr. IX. 23. Jud. v. 3. nec non 2. Cor. IX. 5. Phil. II. 25. Quod etiamsi admittamus, hic tamen solum respici, ob quem finem Deus offendicula non impedit, sed permittit, haud concedendum existimamus: quia de scandalis cavendis, ac quantum fieri potest, avertendis agitur; quæ necessario quidem, posita mundi pravitate, fiant, ut sperare non liceat, mundum scandalorum expertem fore, aut unquam defitura scandala: cavenda tamen à nobis sint, ne nos eorum causa, aut autores existamus, idque tanto accuratius, quanto facilius illa ob improbitatem mundi oriuntur. De fine, cur Deus ea fieri permittat, hic non erat dicendi locus, nec ullo verbo mentio fit, quod ideo permittantur ut integri à fictis, constantes à levibus discernimentur. De causa efficiente agitur, & væ illis, per quos scandala veniunt, intimatur, non de causa finali. Certum interim, de tali hic agi necessitate, quæ libertatem non tollat; quod recte de hoc loco, & c. XXVI. 24. (contra Calvinianos Stoicos) observat Grotius. Cum necesse dixit (inquit Grotius) ut eveniant scandala, non potestatis libertatem tollit, nec liberi arbitrii potestatem, nec rerum cuidam necessitati vitam subdens hæc dicit, sed omnino futurum prædicit. Non igitur prædictio illius scandala inducit, absit, neque quia prædixit, ut nisi ea scientes maligne agere voluissent, utique non venissent, nisi vero eventura fuissent, neutiquam prædixisset, cum vero illi male agerent, & incurabili morbo laborarent, venit, futurumque prædicit.

πλὴν] Adversativa hæc ostendit sapiente Dei permisione culpam peccantium non levari: unde sequitur de tali hic agi necessitate quæ libertatem non tollat. Sic & infra cap. XXVI. 24.

δι ὗ] Proprie igitur σκάνδαλα eveniunt διὰ τῶν ἀνθρώπων, non διὰ τοῦ Θεοῦ, quanquam nec ἄνευ τοῦ Θεοῦ. Vide quæ supra X. 29.

## 18:8
Vers. 8. Σκανδαλίζει σε] See what we said in ch. 5:29. The argument is taken from the greater. Or, the dearest members of the body should be cut off so that eternal destruction might be avoided, since it is necessary that the same be done for the sake of avoiding death in this age. How much more should thoughts that are less right, which the wickedness of others suggests, be cast away by us?

This sense is not bad, yet we observe that the Ancients understand friends by members. He does not say this about members, says Chrysostom, far from it, but about friends, about relatives, whom we hold as necessary in the place of members. Nothing is so harmful to the flesh as the company of the depraved. For whatever necessity cannot do, friendship can very often do, both to detriment and to utility. And therefore with great vehemence he orders us to cut off those who are harmful, implying those who provide stumbling blocks. Photius explains it similarly in the Catena of the Greeks edited by Peter Possinus: However benevolently anyone may be disposed toward you: if he is the same worker and author of evils: cut yourself off from him, declining the destruction of the soul and guarding against the poison creeping forth from the contagion of that association. Add also Isidore from the Catena of Corderius. Theodorus Heracleota says a little differently that Christ is one body, the Church, that is, the congregation of the faithful: but the members are each one of these individually. But if any of these faithful and members of the Church has been the cause of a stumbling block to others, do not spare him, but cut him off and exterminate him from the Church. Which cutting off is not of individuals, whom Christ compels with these words, but must be done by the censure of the whole Church, Matt. 18:17. Our opinion is that all things, even if they are so useful, so dear to us, as eyes, hands, and feet, by whatever name they may come, are to be removed if they are a stumbling block to us: therefore, not only friends and necessary persons are understood: nor only thoughts, although these are also included, along with depraved desires and lusts of the flesh, as well as the nearest occasions of sin, from which sin is either clearly inseparable morally, or is separated with the greatest difficulty.

to enter into life halt or maimed] That is, you who have been lame or maimed. See what is below in chapter XXVI, verse 6.

Latin:

Vers. 8. Σκανδαλίζει σε] Vide quæ diximus cap. V. 29. Est à majori sumtum argumentum. Vel carissima corporis membra præcidenda essent, ut evitaretur æternum exitium, cum mortis in hoc seculo vitandæ causa id ipsum fieri oporteat. Quanto magis abjiciendæ sunt à nobis cogitationes minus rectæ, quas aliorum improbitas suggerit?

Non est malus hic sensus, observamus tamen, Veteres per membra amicos intelligere. Non de membris, inquit Chrysostomus, hæc dicit, ab- sit, sed de amicis, de affinibus, quos loco mem- brorum habemus necessarios. Nihil carni ita no- xium ut consortium pravorum. Quæcunque enim necessitas non potest, potest sæpenumero amicitia, cum ad detrimentum, tum ad utilitatem. Id- eoque magna cum vehementia nobis noxios abscin- dere jubet, illos insinuans, qui scandala præbent. Similiter explicat & Photius, in Catena Græco- rum à Petro Possino edita: Quamlibet benevole sit affectus erga te quispiam: sit autem idem opera- rius, & autor malorum: abscinde te ab illo, per- niciem animæ declinans & proserpens ex contagione consuetudinis istius venenum præcavens. Adde & Isidorum è Catena Corderii. Paulo aliter Theodorus Heracleota unum corpus dicit Christum Ecclesiam, hoc est, fidelium congregationem: membra vero sigillatim unumquemque istorum. Quod si quis ex fidelibus istis & membris Eccle- siæ causa fuerit aliis scandali, ne parcas ei, sed abscinde ipsum, & ex Ecclesia extermina. Quæ vero abscissio non est singulorum, quos his com- pellat Christus, sed totius Ecclesiæ censura fieri debet Matth. XIIX. vers. 17. Nostra sententia omnia, etiamsi tam utilia, tam cara nobis sint, ut oculi, manus, & pedes, quocunque veniant no- mine esse removenda, si scandalo nobis sint, indi- catur: non ergo solum amici ac necessarii intelli- guntur: nec cogitationes solum, etsi hæ etiam comprehendantur, juxta cum pravis desideriis, & cupiditatibus carnis, nec non proximis pec- candi occasionibus, à quibus peccatum vel pla- ne inseparabile est moraliter, vel perquam diffi- culter separatur.

εἰσελθεῖν εἰς τὴν ζωὴν χωλὸν ἢ κυλλὸν] Id est qui fueris claudus, aut mancus. Vide quæ infra cap. XXVI. vers. 6.

## 18:10
Ver. 10. their angels] Since Christ was accustomed to speak in the way he knew best would be understood by the Jews, and since the ancient and modern Jews believed that a guardian angel was assigned by God to at least every one of the pious, an opinion which flowed over even to the Christians, as appears from the passage in Acts XII. 15 and many ancient writers, it is highly probable that this view is here approved by Christ. It is certainly agreed that angels are ministers of divine providence: whence it is credible that the duties of angels are distinguished according to the degrees of providence. Besides universal providence, there is a certain common providence by which God preserves and directs the civil societies of men, which we call commonwealths. From Daniel, both Jews and ancient Christians gathered with great consensus that their own angels were attributed to these individual societies, and Clement of Alexandria places this as if beyond all controversy. But just as God generally ordains the affairs of kingdoms to the state of the universe, so he ordains the affairs of individuals to the state of kingdoms. But those who consecrate themselves to God by true faith, and are therefore considered his peculiar property, are exempted from this common lot. God, just as he cherishes these with a peculiar providence, so he seems to endow individuals with a guardian angel, who may, namely, assist their steps and endeavors, either perpetually, or at least until they have arrived at the fullest possession of the divine Spirit himself. For I see that the ancient Christians believed this. See Origen, Homily VIII on Genesis, and Tertullian on Baptism. Nor does Clement hesitate to assert that what is in Plato, that 'to each one is assigned a daemon as a guardian of his life and a fulfiller of what has been chosen,' proceeded from barbarian, that is, Hebrew wisdom. But whether an angel is given to every single human being, Clement leaves in ambiguity. Origen attempts to prove that both a good and an evil angel are attributed to each person from the books of the Shepherd and Barnabas: although the passage of Barnabas which he cites does not even say this: but that the angels of God preside over the light, and those of darkness over Satan. Gregory of Nyssa follows Origen's opinion in this matter, as in many others, in his Life of Moses. But we see many men lacking these distinguished men

Guardian angels: as to Jacob Gen. XXXII. verses 1, 2, to Elisha 2 Kings VI. 17. Moreover, that the administration of this world may at length turn out for the good of those who are to be partakers of future glory, all angels whatsoever are rightly said by the writer to the Hebrews to be sent or ordained for the sake of those who are to be heirs of salvation.

It is quite probable, in the judgment of Grotius, that Christ approved the opinion of the Jews—which he gathers from Acts XII. 15 to have passed over to the Christians—that an angel is added by God as a guardian to individuals, at least to the pious. And it is known that from the words of Christ that opinion is concluded by the Papists, whom our author here, as often elsewhere, wished to favor. One may look at Becanus the Jesuit on Angels, chapter VI, although many, such as Molina in prim. Thom. q. 113, Ignatius Derkennis in his Treatise on the One God, Disp. VI, on the Creator, chapter III, and others, admit that this opinion is not a matter of faith. Moreover, that was not the opinion of the ancient Jews, that individual angels were given to individual believers, but rather it has its origin from the Stoics, who said that a genius was given to each of us as a tutor: as Seneca testifies in Epistle CX. Nor was any such thing approved by Christ, who implies that believers only, and even little children, have angels, but not indeed that individual angels are assigned to individual believers: nor what

Acts XII. 15. do not teach this: since a common way of speaking contributes nothing to faith, and Peter's angel can be understood as that angel who was believed to have been seen in the form of Peter. Among the Fathers, not even Grotius himself could have anything certain here. He cites Origen, Homily VIII on Genesis, and Tertullian on Baptism, and Gregory of Nyssa on the Life of Moses: but they were occupied with the opinion of the poets, Platonists, and Stoics concerning geniuses: and Origen attributes to every human being both an evil and a good angel, as Grotius notes: which they prove from the books of the Shepherd and Barnabas. The former of which is apocryphal, and the latter is not held to be uncorrupted: nor does it have anything about that figment, but only says that the angels of God preside over the way of light, and those of Satan over the way of darkness, as Grotius himself observes. But he acknowledges that many guardian angels are given to eminent men from Gen. XXXII. 12, 2 Kings VI. 17. But Scripture testifies that not only concerning eminent men, such as Jacob and Elisha were, but concerning each one of the believers, angels are assigned to them for protection, Ps. XCI. 11, Heb. I. 13, just as also many angels are said to rejoice over the repentance of one sinner, Luke XV. 10. Compare what we have said about these in Tom. IV. System. Theol. cap. II. q. V. p. 77 seqq. Therefore, what Grotius defines, that a peculiar angel is given to each of the believers to assist his steps and endeavors, either perpetually or until they have arrived at the fullest possession of the divine Spirit itself, is rash: and if he posits that fullest possession here, he openly opposes the Holy Scriptures, which do not attribute perfection to this age, but declare it to be reserved for the future. If the Papists are to be heard, guardian angels must be assigned not only to believers but even to unbelievers, which Suarez on angels l. XVI. c. 77. n. 8. contends, as does also Henr. Lancellot in Anatom. Christian. deformat. page 329, who also tries to build this up from the words of Christ, since he is dealing with all infants, although Cajetan dissents, and the words of Christ concern believers, namely those little ones who believe in him, whence Felicianus Capito in his explanation of the places of the Old and New Testament Catholic on this passage admits that they do not apply. Concerning the guardian angels of provinces, because here also Grotius accedes to the opinion of the Papists, one may look at what we have disputed in the aforementioned place, question VI, page 80. Διὰ παντὸς βλέπουσι τὸ πρόσωπον τοῦ πατρός με τοῦ ἐν ὀυρανοῖς.] This pertains to the fact that not just any, but more distinguished angels are understood to be assigned to the custody of the pious. For the likeness is taken from the custom of kings, whom it is not permitted for just any of the ministers to see daily, but only the nobles of the kingdom 1. Kings X. verse 8. which the Hebrews think is signified by the word אחשׁדרפנים, whence the name of satraps flowed. Theopompus, in the passage which is in Photius, said Ἐξατράπην closer to the Persian idiom. It is the same thing to see the face of the king and to stand before the king. Thus 2 Kings XIV. 11, where that is in the Hebrew and Greek, the Latin has placed this. Such an angel is Gabriel ὁ παρεστηκὼς ἐνώπιον τοῦ Θεοῦ Luke I. 19, and in Isaiah מלאך פניו c. LXIII. 9, perhaps also שרפים עמדים in the same prophet c. VI. 2, but also Daniel says the dream of the four beasts was explained to him by one τῶν ἑστηκότων chapter VII. 16, when he had previously distinguished those standing by from other ministering ones. How can it be understood what the angel promises to Joshua in Zechariah, that if he walks in the ways of God he will one day be μετὰ τῶν ἑστηκότων בֵּין עֹמְדִים chapter III. 7? So also among kings and princes, those who are of intimate admission are called παρεστηκότες Deut. I. 16, 1 Sam. XXII. 6. and XXV. 27. Finally, many of their writings prove that this distinction of angels was famous among the Jews. Among these, seven were believed to excel as the primary angels, which I also believe proceeded from the Persian court, which lesser courts imitated. See Jer. LII. 25. There is mention of those seven in the Chaldean paraphrase of Gen. XI. 7, in Jachiades on Dan. X. 13, in the writer of Tobit, to whom Raphael is called one τῶν ἑπτὰ ἀγγέλων οἳ προσαναφέρουσι τὰς προσευχὰς τῶν ἁγίων κὴ ἐκπορεύονται ἐνώπιον τῆς δόξης τοῦ ἁγίου. I believe also in Revelation I. 5, with the added place c. IX. 2. To Daniel they are השרים הראשנים chapter X. 13. The Rabbis of the Hebrews call these the eyes of God, as can be seen in the book titled The Beginning of Wisdom, brief. Clement Strom. VI. ἑπτὰ τὰς τὴν μεγίστην δύναμιν ἔχοντας πρωτογόνους ἀγγέλους: mention of whom is also in the book which is called Θεολογύμενα τῆς ἀριθμητικῆς. Christ did not, however, wish to feed us with useless speculations, like those whom Paul says 'intrude into those things which they have not seen': but he showed most significantly how great a price pious men are at before God, when he said that the chief of the angels are given to them as guardians and messengers, who pass back and forth as it were between God and them, which the sacred scriptures call ascending and descending, Gen. XXIX. 12. from which it can be understood how great a crime it is to insult their innocence and simplicity. Grotius wishes this to pertain to the fact that not just any, but more distinguished angels are understood to be assigned to the guardianship of the pious: if indeed the comparison is taken from the custom of Kings, whom not just any of their ministers are permitted to see daily, but only the nobles of the Kingdom 1. Kings X. 8. But where is this handed down in the Holy scriptures, that only more distinguished angels are assigned to the guardianship of the pious? Two camps of angels accompanied Jacob, Genesis XXXII. Entire legions of heavenly horsemen and chariots surrounded and guarded Elisha: for there were more defending angels on his side than there were soldiers in the army of the Syrians, the persecutors of Elisha, 2. Kings VI. verses 16, 17. Were all in those camps and legions only more distinguished angels? But the support which Grotius seeks for that opinion in the phrase 'to see the face of GOD' is nothing: for all the elect in the other life see the face of GOD in the heavens: not only the more distinguished among them. And therefore there is no reason why we should derive that phrase from the custom of Kings, with Grotius, Calixtus in his dissertation on the mystery of the Trinity in the O.T., and those whom they follow, the Papists. For GOD does not act after the manner of worldly Kings, nor does he admit only more distinguished angels, or the chief of elect men, to the sight or vision of himself, but all angels see the face of GOD, and all the elect will see it, when they shall be ἰσάγγελοι, 1. Corinthians XIII. v. 12. 1. John III. verse 2. Many myriads of angels stand before the face of GOD, beholding him, and prompt at his nod, and executing his will, Daniel VII. verse 10. nor in the fact that they see the face of God, is there any diversity of angels. In vain, therefore, are those things which are brought forward concerning the sole nobles of kings enjoying daily sight, and that from thence the Hebrew אחשתרפנים, and the Latin name of Satraps is derived, which Theopompus in Photius says is closer to the Persian idiom ἐξατράπην. Although neither the sole nobles, nor those more than other ministers, enjoy the sight of Kings, which would be more truly said of ministers of a lower order, who are at the side and in the service of Kings: but as we have warned, that custom is ἀλλότριος to worldly Kings, which necessity imposes upon them, because they cannot admit all to their sight at once and continually, as God can and does deign to admit all to His sight, both angels and the elect. It is the same to see the face of the King, and to stand before the King, says Grotius: and therefore 2 Kings XIV. 11. where that is in the Hebrew and Greek, he wishes the Latin to have placed this. Now a thousand thousand are said to stand before God, and ten thousand times ten thousand of angels to serve God, Dan. VII. 10. that is, all the angels, of whom there are many myriads. For a certain number is put for an uncertain. Therefore all Angels see the face of God. What therefore is said of Gabriel, Luke I. 19. ὁ παρεστηκὼς ἐνώπιον τοῦ Θεοῦ, is not to be denied of others; not of the שרפים however much they are עמדים, of which the same Grotius speaks doubtfully, Is. VI. 2. not of the Angels, who are said to stand before God, Dan. VII. 10. (LXX. have the same word which Luke used.) Just as also in verse 16, one of those standing is commemorated: where Grotius rashly distinguishes with the Papists those STANDING BY from other MINISTERS: for it cannot be proven that those are set as distinct, to stand before God, and to serve God, Dan. VII. 10. since one can be explanatory of the other: and that hypothesis concerning some angels assisting and others ministering is rejected by the Pontificians themselves, namely Sanctius and Cornelius a Lapide on that passage of Daniel, as also Becanus de offic. angel. cap. 2. All ministering angels are called by the Apostle πνεύματα λειτυργικὰ Heb. I. 13. as Petavius admits, l. II. de Angel. c. V. as Didymus, Nyssenus, Cyrillus Alexandr. and others have observed from the Fathers: see T. IV. Syst. Theol. p. 83. But that at Zech. III. 7. more distinguished angels are understood by the name of those standing by, is rejected with the same ease with which it is asserted. To stand by, to appear, to be present, do not imply a communion of counsels, but a ministry. They assist for the sake of ministry as παραστάται, who are apparitors to the Latins, Job XVIII. 22. as Petavius acknowledges in the cited place. It is not attributed to the Angels that they are participants of counsel, but that they assist and perform a ministry, says Chrysost. hom. VIII. in Gen. Nor are they called παρεστηκότες in any other sense in 1 Sam. XXII. 6. and ch. XXV. 27., although those have nothing to do with Angels either. But that Angel of His face, Is. LXIII. 9. does not belong to this lot. For He is the uncreated Angel, the Son of God, the Redeemer of the people, who is the angel of the face in such a way that He is at the same time the brightness of the glory of God the Father, Heb. I. 3. and the image of the invisible God, Col. I. 15.

But that the distinction between ministering and assisting angels is famous among the Jews, as Grotius says, teaches nothing other than that the opinion of the Papists, who also not infrequently Judaize in other matters, has been derived from Rabbinical pits: To which also pertains the fiction concerning the seven leading angels, even if the writer of the Apocryphal book of Tobit also made it his own, counting Raphael among them, and designating their proper offices, but in a different way: who offer up the prayers of the saints, and go in before the glory

τῶν ἁγίων: with whom the seven Spirits of Apoc. I. 5 (as Grotius wrongly believed) or the seven angels sounding with trumpets, Apoc. VIII. 2, have no connection. For there the Holy Spirit is understood in His sevenfold office and in His manifold gifts diffusing Himself into the seven Asiatic Churches, as if there were as many Spirits; but here, indeed, created angels are meant, yet they are neither designated as the chief among the angels, nor are they taught to be the seven chief angels, but seven angels are introduced because there were seven trumpets to be sounded. As regards Dan. X. verse 13, we are taught nothing there other than that there are princes among the angels; which is here ἐξαγώνιον: where we do not raise a doubt concerning the orders among the angels, but we deny that the assisting angels are to be distinguished from the ministering ones. Finally, the opinion of the Rabbis, whom Grotius observes from the book titled: The Beginning of Wisdom, to call the seven leading angels the eyes of God, is nothing to us: even though some of the ancients also have some things concerning seven leading angels, but outside of scripture, drawn, as it seems, from the Platonists, from whom those things flowed also to the Jews: For those Ancients were learned in Platonic Philosophy. Such are those things of Clement, Strom. VI. seven who have the greatest power, the first-born angels: mention of whom Grotius says is also found in the book which is called the Theology of Arithmetic, which is Apocryphal, and perhaps fabulous, and similar things are observed in the Chaldean on Gen. XI. 7. and also in Jachiades on Dan. X. 13. Let us leave such things to the Jews, who feed on their own fictions and those of others. Grotius thinks that it proceeded from the Persian court, which other smaller courts imitated, Jerem. LII. 7. But shall we believe that the heavenly court also imitated the custom of the Persians, or shall we judge that the Persians were taught this from heaven and so ordered it? See concerning these things which we have said in the cited place, p. 85. I wish Grotius had thought of what he warns here at the end: Christ did not wish to feed us with USELESS speculations, (such as those Grotian ones, and many others among the Pontificians, especially from Pseudo-Dionysius) like those whom Paul says intrude into those things which they have not seen: but He shows most significantly how precious pious men are to God, when He said that the leading angels are given to them as guardians and messengers, who go back and forth as it were between God and them, which the sacred scriptures call ascending and descending, Gen. XXIX. 12. He would have spoken more correctly to say absolutely Angels, for all angels, the highest, the middle, and the lowest, or of whatever degree and order they may be, are ministering spirits, as are all angels, according to Dionysius. According to Petavius, in whatever order they are reckoned, they are sent by God and undertake the ministries assigned to them, on account of the passages of Scripture and the judgment and consensus of the ancients concerning this. Christ certainly testifies here indefinitely concerning the Angels, who serve the faithful, whom Paul teaches that all serve in Heb. I. 13, because they always behold the face of the Father in heaven; which is a description of the good angels, who, namely, are so confirmed in good that, because they never cease to see the face of God in heaven, they can never fall away either in holiness or in heavenly blessedness: since these things imply confirmation in good: see Psalm XVI. 11, John XIX. 27, Matt. V. 8, 1 Cor. XIII. 12, 1 John III. 2. Which confirmation is certainly not of the more distinguished angels only, but of all.

PART III. On the purpose of the coming of the Son of Man.

Latin:

Vers. 10. οἱ ἄγγελοι αὐτῶν] Cum Christus ita solitus sit loqui quomodo se loquentem à Judæis optime sciebat intelligi, Judæi autem veteres novique crediderint singu- lis saltem piorum additum à Deo custodem Angelum, quæ opinio ad Christianos etiam manavit, ut apparet ex loco Actor. XII. 15. & multis vetustis scriptoribus, pro- babile admodum est eam sententiam hîc à Christo appro- batam. Constat sane Angelos administros esse divinæ providentiæ: unde credibile est pro gradibus providentiæ munia Angelorum distingui. Præter universalem pro- videntiam est aliqua communis, qua Deus civiles homi- num societates, quas respublicas dicimus, conservat ac dirigit. His autem singulis suos attributos esse Angelos ex Daniele magno consensu & Judæi & Christiani vete- res colligebant, idque velut extra omnem controver- siam ponit Clemens Alexandrinus. Sicut autem res re- gnorum ad statum universi, ita res singulorum ad sta- tum regnorum plerunque Deus ordinat. Sed eximun- tur communi huic sorti hi, qui vera fide Deo se conse- crant, ac proinde ipsius peculium censentur. Hos Deus sicut peculiari providentia fovet, ita singulos donare videtur custode Angelo, qui scilicet ipsorum gressus conatusque adjuvet, aut perpetuo, aut certe donec ad plenissimam i- psius divini Spiritus possessionem devenerint. Ita enim ver- teres Christianos credidisse video. Vide Origenem homi- lia IIX. in Genesin, & Tertullianum de baptismo. Ne- que dubitat Clemens à barbara, hoc est Hebræa sapientia profectum asseverare, quod apud Platorem est, ἑκάστῳ ἐ- τιλετο δαίμονα τῆτοι φύλακα συμπέμπειν ᾧ βίῳ καὶ ἀπεπλη- ρωτὴ τῶν αἱρεθέντων. An autem unicuique hominum datus sit Angelus in ambiguo relinquit Clemens. Ori- genes unicuique & bonum & malum Angelum attribui probare conatur ex libris Pastoris & Barnabæ: quanquam Barnabæ quem citat locus ne hoc quidem dicit: sed vix lu- cis præesse Angelos Dei viz tenebrarum Satanæ. Origenis sententiam hac in re ut in multis aliis sequitur Greg. Nysse- nus de vita Mosis. At viris eximiis multos videmus carí

Angelos custodes: ut Jacobo Genes. XXXII. vers. 1. 2. Elisæo 2. Reg. VI. 17. Cæterum cœta hujus mundi ad- ministratio tandem bono cessura sit eorum qui futuræ gloriæ érunt participes, recte à Scriptore ad Hebræos o- mnes omnino Angeli dicuntur mitti sive ordinari in eo- rum gratiam, qui salutis hæredes sunt futuri.

Christum Judæorum sententiam, quod singu- lis, saltim piorum additus à DEO custos Angelus sit, quam ad Christianos manasse ex Actor. XII. 15. colligit, approbasse, admodum probabile est, Grotio judice. Et notum est, è verbis Christi illam à Pontificiis concludi, quibus hic noster, ut alias sæpe velificare voluit. Videri poterit è multis Becanus Jesuita de Angelis cap. VI. quamvis plerique, Molina in prim. Thom. q. 113. Ignatius Derkennis Tr. de Deo uno Disp. VI. de creatore cap. III. aliique fateantur, eam sententiam non esse de fide. Cæterum ne- que veterum ea Judæorum sententia fuit, quod singulis fidelibus singuli dati sint angeli, sed ori- ginem potius ea habet à Stoicis, qui unicuique nostrûm genium dari pædagogum dixere: teste Se- neca Epist. CX. nec à Christo tale quid appro- batum est: qui fideles solum, etiam parvulos habere angelos innuit, non vero singulis fide- lium singulos assignatos esse angelos: nec quæ

Actor. XII. 15. habentur, hoc docent: quum vulgaris loquendi ratio ad fidem nihil faciat, & angelus Petri de eo intelligi possit angelo, qui in forma Petri visus creditus sit. E Patribus nec ipse Grotius hic certi quid habere potuit. Origenem allegat homil. IIX. in Genes. & Ter- tullianum de Baptismo, ac Gregorium Nyssenum de vita Mosis: Sed illi Poetarum, Platonicorum & Stoicorum sententia de geniis occupati fuere: & tribuit Origenes unicuique hominum tum ma- lum, tum bonum angelum, notante Grotio: quod è libris Pastoris & Barnabæ probant. Quo- rum ille Apocryphus est, hic vero non habe- tur incorruptus: nec de eo & figmento quicquam habet, solum via lucis præesse Angelos Dei, ait, viæ tenebrarum Satanæ, ut observat ipse Grotius. Qui vero viris eximiis multos dari angelos custodes agnoscit è Genes. XXXII. 12. 2. Reg. VI. 17. At non tantum de viris eximiis, qualis Jacobus & Elisæus fuère, sed de unoquoque fidelium testa- tur Scriptura, angelos illis in custodiam assignatos esse Ps. XCI. 11. Ebr. I. 13. quemadmodum et- iam plures angeli de unius peccatoris resipi- scentia gaudere dicuntur Luc. XV. 10. Confer. quæ de his Tom. IV. System. Theol. cap. II. q. V. p. 77. seqq. diximus. Quod ergo Grotius definit, unicuique fidelium donari peculiarem An- gelum qui gressus ejusdem conatusque adjuvet, aut perpetuo, aut donec ad plenissimam ipsius Spiritus divini possessionem devenerint, temerarium est: atque si illam plenissimam possessionem hic statuit, aperte S. literis adversatur, quæ perfectionem non huic seculo tribuunt, sed futuro reservatam esse perhibent. Si Pontificii audiendi sint, non fi- delibus tantum sed infidelibus etiam angeli custo- des assignandi erunt, quod Suarez. de angel. l. XVI. c. 77. n. 8. contendit, nec non Henr. Lancel- lot. in Anatom. Christian. deformat. pag. 329. qui etiam è verbis Christi præsentibus, q. de omnibus infantibus agat, id astruere conatur, quamvis Ca- jetanus dissentiat, & verba Christi fideles concer- nant, parvulos scilicet illos, qui in ipsum cre- dunt, unde ea non stringere fatetur Felicianus Capito in explicat. locorum V. & N. T. Cathol. ad h. l. De provinciarum angelis tutelaribus, quia hic etiam Papistarum opinioni accedit Grotius, vi- vi- deri poterunt, quæ l. c. quæst. VI. p. 80. disputa- vimus. Διὰ παντὸς βλέπουσι τὸ πρόσωπον τοῦ πατρός με τοῦ ἐν ὀυρα- νοῖς.] Hoc eo pertinet ut non quivis sed insigniores Angeli intelligantur piorum custodiæ assignati. A regum enim more sumta est similitudo, quos aspicere quotidie non cui- vis ministrorum licet, sed solis regni proceribus 1. Reg. X. vers. 8. quod ipsum significari putant Hebræi voce אחשׁדרפנים unde fluxit nomen satraparum. Ἐξα- τράπην propius ad Persicum idioma dixit Theopompus lo- co qui est apud Photium. Idem est videre faciem regis & stare coram rege. Ita que 2. Reg. XIV. II. ubi illud in He- bræo est & Græco, hoc posuit Latinus. Talis Angelus est Gabriel ὁ παρεστηκὼς ἐνώπιον τοῦ Θεοῦ Luc. I. 19. & apud E- saiam מלאך פניו c. LXIII. 9. forte & שרפים עמדים apud eundem Prophetam c. VI. 2. sed & Daniel bestiarum quatuor somnium expositum sibi dicit ab uno τῶν ἑστηκότων cap. VII. 16. cum antea adstantes ab aliis ministrantibus discrevisset. Quomodo intelligi potest quod apud Za- chariam Angelus Josuæ pollicetur fore ut si vias Dei insti- stat degat aliquando μετὰ τῶν ἑστηκότων בֵּין עֹמְדִים cap. III. 7. Sic & apud Reges & Principes qui intimæ sunt ad- missionis, dicuntur παρεστηκότες Deut. I. 16. l. Sam. XXII. 6. & XXV. 27. Denique discrimen hoc Angelorum ce- lebre fuisse apud Judæos multa ipsorum scripta evincunt. In- ter hos primores Angelos septem eminere credebantur, quod ipsum quoque credo profectum ex aula Persica : quam imitatæ aulæ minores. Vide Jer. LII. 25. Est eorum septem mentio apud Chaldæum paraphrasten Genes. XI. 7. apud Jachiaden ad Dan. X. 13. apud Tobiæ scriptorem cui Raphael dicitur unus τῶν ἑπτὰ ἀγγέλων οἳ προσαναφέρουσι τὰς προσευχὰς τῶν ἁγίων κὴ ἐκπορεύονται ἐνώπιον τῆς δόξης τοῦ ἁγίου. Credo & in Apocalypsi I. 5. addito loco c. IX. 2. Danieli sunt השרים הראשנים cap. X. 13. Hebræo- rum Rabbini hos oculos Dei vocant, ut videre est in libro cui titulus Principium sapientiæ breve. Clemens Strom. VI. ἑπτὰ τὰς τὴν μεγίστην δύναμιν ἔχοντας πρωτογόνους ἀγγέ- λους: quorum mentio & in libro qui vocatur Θεολογύμενα τῆς ἀριθμητικῆς. Non voluit autem Christus nos pascere inutilibus speculationibus, ut illi quos Paulus dicit ἃ μὴ ἑωράκασιν ἐμβατεύειν : sed quanto pretio pii homines sint apud Deum significantissime ostendit, cum dixit Angelo- rum primores illis datos custodes & internuntios, qui vel- ut inter Deum atque ipsos commeent, quod ascendere & descendere vocant sacræ literæ Gen. XXIX. 12. unde in- telligi potest, quantum sit facinus eorum innocentiæ ac simplicitati insultare. Hoc eo pertinere vult Grotius, ut non quivis, sed insigniores Angeli intelligantur piorum custodiæ assignati: siquidem à Regum more desumta sit simi- litudo, quos aspicere quotidie non cuivis ministro- rum licet, sed solis Regni proceribus 1. Reg. X. 8. At ubi hoc in S. literis traditum, quod insigniores An- geli solum assignati sint custodiæ piorum? Jaco- bum comitabantur duo angelorum castra Genes. XXXII. Elisæum circumdabant, & custodiebant integræ legiones equitum & curruum cœlestium: erant enim plures ab ejus parte Angeli defenso- res, quam in Syrorum exercitu milites, Elisæi persequutores 2. Reg. VI. vers. 16. 17. Num omnes in illis castris & legionibus insigniores tantum fuêre angeli? Quod vero in phrasi videre faciem DEI pro ea opinione quærit Grotius præsi- dium, nullum est: nam omnes electi in altera vi- ta faciem DEI vident in cœlis: non tantum in- signiorès ex iisdem. Ideoque non est, quod il- lam phrasin à more Regum deducamus, cum Gro- tio, Calixto in dissertat. de mysterio Trinit. in V. T. & quos illi sequuntur, Pontificiis. DEUS enim non agit more Regum mundanorum, nec ad conspectum vel visionem sui admittit tantum angelos insigniores, aut electorum hominum præcipuos, sed universi angeli vident faciem DEI, & videbunt eam universi electi, cum erunt ἰσάγγελοι I. Corinth. XIII. v. 12. 1. Joh. III. vers. 2. Stant ante faciem DEI multæ ange- lorum myriades, ipsum intuentes, & ad nu- tum ejus promti, ac voluntatem ejus exequentes Daniel. VII. vers. 10. nec in eo, quod vide- ant faciem Dei, ulla angelorum est diversitas. Frustra ergo sunt illa, quae de solis proceribus re- gum quotidiano conspectu fruentibus adducuntur, & quod inde Ebraeum אחשתרפנים, ac Latinum Sa- traparum nomen deducatur, quod propius ad Per- sicum idioma Theopompus apud Photium ἐξατρά- πην dixerit. Quanquam nec soli proceres, nec magis illi, quam ministri alii conspectu Regum fruantur, quod de inferioris ordinis ministris, qui a latere & servitiis sunt Regibus, verius diceretur: sed uti monuimus consuetudo illa a mundanis Re- gibus ἀλλότριος est, quam necessitas ipsis impo- nit, quia simul & jugiter omnes ad conspectum suum admittere nequeunt, uti Deus omnes con- spectu suo dignari potest, & dignatur, cum angelos, tum electos. Idem est videre faciem Regis, & stare coram Rege, ait Grotius: atque ideo 2. Reg. XIV. 11. ubi illud in Hebraeo est & Graeco, hoc posuisse vult La- tinum. Jam millies millena stare coram Deo, & de- cies centies millena Angelorum servire Deo dicun- tur Dan. VII. 10. h. e. angeli omnes, quorum mul- tae myriades. Ponitur enim numerus certus pro incerto. Omnes ergo Angeli faciem Dei vident. Quod ergo de Gabriele dicitur Luc. I. 19. ὁ παρε- στηκὼς ἐνώπιον τοῦ Θεοῦ, de aliis non negandum; non de שרפים utut עמדים, de quibus dubitan- ter idem affirmat Grotius Es. VI. 2. non de Ange- lis, qui coram Deo stare dicuntur Dan. VII. 10. (LXX. habent idem verbum, quod Lucas adhi- buit.) Quemadmodum etiam versu 16. unus τῶν ἑστηκότων commemoratur: ubi temere Grotius cum Papistis ADSTANTES ab aliis MINI- STRANTIBUS distinguit: non enim probari potest, illa ut distincta poni, stare coram Deo, & servire Deo, Dan. VII. 10. quum unum alterius possit esse ἐξηγητικὸν: & hypothesin illam de an- gelis aliis adsistentibus, aliis ministrantibus e Pon- tificiis ipsis reprobant nonnulli, Sanctius nempe & Cornelius a Lapide ad locum illum Daniel, ut & Becanus de offic. angel. cap. 2.. Angeli omnes mi- nistrantes dicuntur Apostolo πνεύματα λειτυργι- κὰ Ebr. I. 13. fatente Petavio l. II. de Angel. c. V. uti e Patribus observarunt Didymus, Nyssenus, Cyrillus Alexandr. alii: vid. T. IV. Syst. Theol. p. 83. Quod autem Zach. III. 7. nomine astantium insi- gniores intelligantur angeli, parili facilitate rejici- tur, qua asseritur. Astare, apparere, praesto esse, non inferunt consiliorum communionem, sed mini- sterium. Assistunt ministerii causa ut παραστάται, qui apparitores Latinis Job. XIIX. 22. ut l. c. agno- scit Petavius. Non est Angelis tributum, ut sint con- silii participes, sed ut assistant, & ministerio fungantur, ait Chrysost. hom. IIX. in Gen. Nec alio sensu πα- ρεστηκότες 1. Sam. XXII. 6. cap. XXV. 27. dicuntur, quamvis nihil illa etiam ad Angelos. Ille vero מלאך פניו Es. LXIII. 9. ad hanc sortem non per- tinet. Est enim Angelus increatus, Filius Dei, Redemptor populi, qui sic angelus faciei est, ut si- mul ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης sit Dei Patris Ebr. I. 3. & imago Dei inconspicui, Col. I. 15.

Quod autem apud Judaeos discrimen inter an- gelos ministrantes & assistentes celebre esse, ait Grotius, nihil aliud docet, quam quod e lacunis Rabbinicis derivata sit Papistarum opinio, qui et- iam in aliis non raro Judaizant: Quo etiam pertinet commentum de septem primoribus ange- lis, etsi suum id quoque fecerit scriptor libri Tobiae Apocryphi, Raphaelem personatum illis accensens, & officia eorum propria, sed ἑτερο- γραφῶς designans: οἱ προσαναφέρουσι τὰς προσ- ευχὰς τῶν ἁγίων, καὶ ἐκπορεύονται ἐνώπιον τῆς δόξης

τῶν ἁγίων: cum quibus nihil commercii habent septem Spiritus Apoc. I. 5. (uti perperam credidit Grotius) aut septem angeli buccinis clangentes. Apoc. VIII. 2. Illic enim Spiritus Sanctus septi- formis munere: & donis suis multivariis in se- ptem Ecclesias Asiaticas ita se diffundens, ac si totidem essent Spiritus: hic vero angeli creati quidem intelliguntur, non autem vel primores ex angelis designantur, vel septem angeli pri- mores esse docentur, sed septem introducuntur angeli, quia septem buccinis clangendum erat. Dan. X. vers. 13. quod attinet, nihil aliud ibi do- cemur, quam quod inter angelos principes den- tur; quod hic ἐξαγώνιον: ubi non de ordinibus inter angelos dubium movemus, sed assistentes angelos à ministrantibus distingui negamus. De- nique Rabbinorum opinio, quos septem primores angelos oculos Dei dicere, è libro cui titulus: prin- cipium sapientiæ breve, observat Grotius, nihil ad nos: utut nonnulli veterum etiam de septem pri- moribus angelis aliqua habeant, sed extra scri- pturam, à Platonicis, ut videtur, hausta, à quibus ea ad Judæos etiam dimanârunt: Erant enim Veteres illi in Platonica Philosophia erudi- ti. Qualia sunt illa Clementis Strom. VI. ἑπτά τούς τήν μεγίςην δύναμιν ἔχοντας πρωτογόνες ἀγ- γέλες: quorum mentionem etiam in libro, qui vocatur θεολογήμλυα τῆς ἀριθμητικῆς Apocry- pho, forte & fabuloso, reperiri, ait Grotius, & apud Chaldæum ad Genes. XI. 7. nec non Ja- chiadem ad Dan. X. 13. similia haberi observat. Relinquamus Judæis talia, qui commentis pa- scuntur suis & aliorum. Ex aula Persica pro- fectum id putat Grotius, quam aliæ minores au- læ imitatæ, Jerem. LII. 7. Sed num aulam cœ- lestem etiam imitatam esse morem Persarum cre- demus, aut Persas id è cœlo edoctos ita ordi- nasse censebimus? Vid. de his, quæ diximus l. c. p. 85. Vellem id cogitasset Grotius, quod po- stremo hic monet: Non voluit Christus nos pa- scere INUTILIBUS speculationibus, (quales illæ Grotianæ, & aliæ plurimæ apud Pontificios, ma- xime è Pseudo Dionysio) ut illi, quos Paulus dicit ἃ μὴ ἑωράκασιν ἐμβατεύειν: sed quanto pretio pii homines sint apud Deum, significantissime ostendit, cum dixit, Angelorum primores datos illis custodes, & internuncios, qui velut inter Deum atque ipsos commeent, quod ascendere & descendere vocant sacræ literæ Gen. XXIX. 12. Rectius dixisset ab- solute Angelos, omnes enim angeli summi, me- dii & infimi, vel cujuscunque sint gradus atque ordinis, πνεύματα sunt λειτεργικά, uti angeli omnes, dicente Dionys. Petavio, quocunque cen- sentur ordine, à Deo mittuntur, & mandata sibi ministeria capessunt, ob Scripturæ loca & veterum de eo judicium ac consensum. Sane indefinite hic de Angelis Christus testatur, qui fidelibus inserviunt, quibus inservire omnes Paulus docet Ebr. I. 13. quod διὰ παντὸς βλέπεσι τὸ πρόσω- πον τῆς Πατρὸς ἐν ἐρανᾶις; quæ descriptio est bo- norum angelorum, qui scil. in bono ita confirma- ti sunt, ut quia nunquam non vident faciem Dei in cœlis, nunquam excidere vel sanctitate, vel cœlesti queant beatitudine: siquidem hæc con- firmationem in bono inferant: vid. Psalm. XVI. 11. Joh. XIX. 27. Matth. V. 8. 1. Cor. XIII. 12. 1. Joh. III. 2. Quæ confirmatio utique non est insigniorum tantum angelorum, sed omnium.

PARS III. De fine adventus filii hominis.

## 18:11
Verse 11. For the Son of Man came to save that which was lost] By comparing verse 16, it appears that the argument is drawn from the greater. God sent His Son so that He might draw to piety those who were still hostile to Him; how much more, then, does He not wish those already drawn to be turned away from the pursuit of piety by the injuries of others. See a similar argument of Paul at Rom. V. Add what is at Rom. XV. 15 and 1 Cor. VIII. 11. From this, however, the universality of Christ's redemption is deduced: for we were all lost; therefore He came for the sake of all. Cf. John III. 16, 1 John II. 2.

Latin:

Vers. 11. ἦλθε γὰρ ὁ ὑιὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου σῶσαι τὸ ἀπολωλὸς] Collato commate 16. apparet argumentum esse ductum a majori. Deus filium suum misit ut adversos adhuc a se homines ad pietatem pertraheret, quanto magis jam per- tractos non vult aliorum injuriis ab instituto pietatis averti. Vide similem Pauli argumentationem ad Rom. V. Adde quod est Rom. XV. 15. & 1. Cor. IIX. 11. Deducitur autem hinc universalitas redemtio- nis Christi: omnes enim perditi eramus; omnium ergo causa venit. Conf. Joh. III. 16. 1. Joh. II. 2.

## 18:12
Verse 12. If it happens to any man] Christ uses this comparison elsewhere as well, with a somewhat different purpose: which is also to be observed in other comparisons. The sense is that God greatly rejoices in the conversion of a sinful man. The rest are an accessory to the comparison, which it is not necessary to apply individually to the recompense. And one of them goes astray] Like those sheep in Jer. L. 6. Upon the mountains] I agree with the Syriac, which refers these to what precedes: for so also Luke: does he not leave the ninety-nine in the wilderness? Usually, mountainous places are more deserted than others. Hence Christ withdraws into the mountains, seeking solitude. And the mountainous regions, in which John was preaching, are called the wilderness.

Latin:

Vers. 12. ἐὰν γένηταί τινι ἀνθρώπῳ] Hanc comparatio- nem alibi quoque fine aliquantum diverso Christus usur- pat: quod & in aliis comparationibus observare est. Sen- sus est, magnopere gaudere Deum conversione hominis peccatoris. Cætera accessio sunt comparationis, quæ si- gillatim applicari ad ἀνταπόδοσιν nihil necesse est. καὶ πλανηθῇ ἓν ἐξ ἀυτῶν] Ut oves illæ Jer. L. 6. ἐπὶ τὰ ὄρη] Assentior Syro hæc retrahenti ad ea quæ præcedunt: nam ita & Lucas ἧ καταλείπει τὰ ἐννενήκοντα ἐν- νέα ἐν τῇ ἐρήμῳ; Plerumque montana loca sunt cæteris de- fertiora. Hinc Christus in montes secedit solitudinem ca- ptans. Et τὰ ὀρεινὰ, in quibus concionabatur Johannes, vocantur ἔρημος.

## 18:14
Verse 14. It is not the will before [the Lord] as in Exodus XXIII. 38, where the Septuagint translated it as acceptable before the Lord, just as Luke, following the same Septuagint, translated the acceptable year in chapter IV. 19. But elsewhere, from Psalm XL, the writer to the Hebrews translates will with the same Septuagint. But it is usually translated as good pleasure. It is, however, a litotes: It is not pleasing to God, instead of what would properly be said, it is most displeasing to God. Therefore, those who offend the pious act against the true and serious will of God. That one of these little ones should perish] To perish here is to be turned away from God, to which being saved is opposed, as appears from the passages to the Romans and Corinthians just cited.

PART IV. On fraternal correction.

Latin:

Vers. 14. ὀυκ ἔστι θέλημα ἔμπροσθεν [רצן לפנו יהוה ut Exodi XXIII. 38. ubi δεκτὸν ἔναντι κυρίῳ verterunt LXX. quomodo & שנת־רצן ἐνιαυτὸν δεκτὸν vertit eosdem LXX. secutus Lucas cap. IV. 19. At alibi ex Psalmo XL. רצון θέλημα vertit cum iisdem LXX. Scriptor ad Hebræos. Sed plerumque verti solet ἐυδοκία. Est autem λιτότης: Non est gratum Deo, pro eo quod proprie diceretur, Deo quam maxime displicet. Faciunt ergo qui pios offen- dunt contra veram ac seriam Dei voluntatem. ἵνα ἀπόληται ἓν τῶν μικρῶν τούτων] ἀπολέσθαι hic est a Deo averti, cui opponitur σώζεσθαι, ut apparet locis ad Roma- nos & Corinthios modo citatis.

PARS IV. De correptione fraterna.

## 18:15
Verse 15. But if your brother sins against you] Christ, as we have said elsewhere, just as He freely criticized whatever was in the Jewish traditions of the evil party, so He translated whatever made for piety and probity almost word for word into His own teachings, of which kind is that which follows, as is manifest from a comparison of the maxims received among the Hebrews, which others have cited. Christ had said above that he who is offended ought to strive strongly not to be moved from the state of his pious purpose: now He adds something more, to be translated as if something of that kind should happen, into an occasion for a benefit. Indeed, as the Mime said: If you bear a friend's faults, you make them your own. Cicero: Truth is troublesome, if indeed hatred is born from it: but compliance is much more troublesome, because, by indulging in sins, it allows a friend to be carried to his ruin. And what is in Plautus: To chastise a friend for a deserved fault is a thankless task, but in time it is useful and profitable. And we see that this kind of duty is explicitly commanded even in the law of Moses, Lev. XIX. 17: You shall not hate your neighbor in your heart; you shall surely rebuke him. But it must be carefully observed here that we do not seek our own advantages or victory by that chastisement rather than the salvation of our friend. For as Hierocles says, for maintaining and restoring friendships, our own long-suffering contributes most; and being not petty toward friends, nor inquisitive to the point of precision, but as much as possible indulgent. It is necessary, therefore, as he says, to consider all things outside the soul as small, and to forbid making a friend an enemy for the sake of these; but rather, by indifference regarding such things, to call back a friend who has fallen away. Many sin against this law, whom Justin graphically depicts to Zenas: those who profess to have zeal and practice frankness, because they wish to win, put on themselves a mask of every kind of freedom, being lovers of their own children, or having fallen from the ranks of the zealous. Furthermore, however, such effort must be devoted to correcting a friend that, at the same time, as much as possible, regard is had for his reputation and modesty, according to that saying of the Hebrews: It is better for a man to be cast into a furnace of fire than to publicly put his neighbor to shame: which, how it ought to be done, Christ explains here by certain steps. The scope, however, is that which Justin prescribes in the aforementioned book: one must admonish the sinner not in public, unless he should need it because of his arrogance. The word brother in this place signifies him who professes to follow the same norm of piety, the fellow-zealot as Philo speaks, which the following words declare. But it is properly about offenses which are wont to creep into human weakness from anger, envy, or the desire for possession, and which pertain to the injury of another. For this is what against you signifies. Hence the Syriac translates sins with the word that the Septuagint likewise often translates as to sin, sometimes more properly as to act foolishly, as in Genesis XXXI. 28. Luke makes this sense most clear to us, who, along with the chastisement, makes mention of forgiving in chapter XVII. 3, from which we learn that what Peter asks below in verse 21 pertains to this very type of act. But we are neither accustomed to nor able to forgive unless an injury has been done to us. So also in the Hebrew maxims: if your associate has afflicted you with an injury. And thus Ambrose, Jerome, Chrysostom, and Augustine correctly interpret this passage. But at the same time we ought to remember that it is the custom of divine law in a most noble type of act to indicate what should be followed in other matters, while maintaining the equity of proportion.

Rebuke] Thus the Septuagint translate the Hebrew in Leviticus, whom other Hellenists follow, as in Ecclesiastes XX. 15. This is what Plautus had called to chastise.

Between you and him alone] And that first with soft words: then, if there is need, with somewhat sharper ones, as the Hebrews rightly prescribe. Cicero: Regard and diligence must be had first that the admonition lacks bitterness, and then that the rebuke lacks insult.

ἐάν σου ἀκούσῃ] If he obeys the warnings, that is ἐὰν μετανοήσῃ as Luke explains.

ἐκέρδησας τὸν ἀδελφόν σου] Christ does not say, you have consulted your own interests, but your brother's: and this same thing ought to be the primary purpose proposed to us in these matters. For it is only our own affairs or temporary reputation that are at stake: his is eternal salvation. Κερδαίνειν is to recall to a good way of life and therefore to lead back into the path of salvation: thus this word is used in 1 Cor. 9.19, 20, 21, 22; 1 Pet. 3.1. James explains this: ὁ ἐπιστρέψας ἁμαρτωλὸν ἐκ πλάνης ὁδοῦ αὐτοῦ, σώσει ψυχὴν ἐκ θανάτου καὶ καλύψει πλῆθος ἁμαρτιῶν, ch. 5.20. A not dissimilar manner of speaking is in Gen. 12.5, ואת הנפש אשר עשו בחרן. The soul which they had made or acquired in Haran, that is, according to the Chaldean interpreter, the souls which they had subjected to the law.

Latin:

Vers. 15. ἐὰν δὲ ἁμαρτήσῃ εἰς σὲ ὁ ἀδελφός σου] Christus, ut alibi diximus, sicut quicquid erat in Judaicis traditioni- bus τοῦ πονηροῦ κόμματος libere reprehendit, ita quæcunque ad pietatem ac probitatem faciebant ad verbum prope in sua dogmata transtulit, cujus generis est id quod sequitur, ut ex collatione receptarum apud Hebræos sententiarum, quas alii citarunt, manifeste apparet. Dixerat supra Chri- stus eum qui offenditur fortiter obniti debere ne eo dimo- veatur de statu pii propositi: nunc addit aliquid amplius, vertendum si quid tale acciderit, in occasionem beneficii. Nimirum ut Mimus dixit: Amici vitia si feras facias tua. Cicero: Molesta veritas, siquidem ex ea nascitur odium: sed obsequium multo molestius, quod peccatis indulgens præcipi- tem amicum ferri sinit. Et quod apud Plautum est: Amicum castigare ob meritam noxiam Immune est facinus, verum in ætate utile Et conducibile. Videmusque hoc officii genus diserte præcipi etiam Mosis lege Levit. IX. 7. Ne odio habeas proximum tuum: arguen- do arguas eum. Sed observandum hic diligenter ne ea ca- stigatione nostra potius commoda aut victoriam sectemur quam amici salutem. Nam ut Hierocles inquit ad amici- tias tuendas restituendasque πλεῖστα συμβάλλεται τὸ ἡμέτε- ρον ἀνεξίκακον· κᾀ περὶ μηδενὸς πρὸς τοὺς φίλους μικρολογέμε- νον, μηδὲ ἐξεταστικὸν πρὸς ἀκρίβειαν ἀλλ' ὅσον οἷοντε ὑπομειη- τικόν. Oportet ergo ut idem ait τὰ ἔξω τῆς ψυχῆς πάντα μικρὰ λὶθειν, καὶ ἀπαγορεύειν μὴ φειδοῖ τούτων τὸν φίλον ἐχθρὸν ποιεῖν· ἀδιαφορίᾳ δὲ μᾶλλον τῇ περὶ τὰ τοιαῦτα κᾀ τὸ ἀποπέ- σοντα φίλον ἀνακαλεῖσθαι. In hanc legem peccant multi quos graphice depingit ad Zenam Justinus: οἱ ζῆλον ἔχειν ἐπαγ- γελλόμενοι κᾀ τὸ παῤῥησιαστικὸν ἐπιτηδεύοντες, διὰ τὸ βούλεσθαι νικᾶν πᾶν εἶδος ἐλευτερίας προσωπήτῳ περιτιθέασιν ἑαυτοῖς, οἱ Φιλότεκνοι, ἣ ζηλωτῶν καταπεπτωκότες. Præterea vero ita danda opera est amico corrigendo, ut simul quan- tum fieri potest famæ & pudoris ejus habeatur ratio, jux- ta illud dictum Hebræorum. Melius est homini ut conjicia- tur in caminum ignis, quam ut palam proximum suum ignominia afficiat: quod quomodo fieri debeat, Christus hic per gradus quosdam explicat. Scopus autem is est quem Justinus dicto libro præscribit: νουθετητέον δὲ ἁμαρτάνοντα μὴ κατὰ κοινὸν, ἐκτὸς εἰ μή χρήζοι διὰ τὸ ὑπεροπλι- κόν. Vox ἀδελφῷ hoc quidem loco significat eum qui eandem pietatis normam sequi se profiteatur, τὸν ὁμόζηλον ut loquitur Philo, quod sequentia declarant. Agitur au- tem proprie de delictis quæ imbecillitati humanæ ex ira, invidia, habendi cupidine solent obrepere, quæque ad al- terius injuriam pertinent. Hoc enim significat εἰς σέ. Hinc Syrus ἀμαρτήσῃ vertit אלכך eo verbo quod LXX. itidem ἀμαρτάνειν sæpe vertunt, interdum magis pro- prie ἀφρόνως πράττειν ut Genes. XXXI. 28. Hunc sensum Lucas nobis apertissimum facit, qui simul cum castigatione condonandi facit mentionem cap. XVII. 3. unde discimus quod infra Petrus interrogat commate 21. ad hanc ipsam facti speciem pertinere. Condonare autem neque sole- mus neque possumus nisi nobis sit injuria. Ita & in He- bræis sententiis: si te injuria socius tuus affecerit. Atque ita hunc locum recte interpretantur Ambrosius, Hiero- nymus, Chrysostomus, Augustinus. Sed simul me- minisse debemus morem esse divinæ legis in facti specie no- bilissima indicare quid in rebus aliis, servata tamen propor- tionis æquitate, sequendum sit.

ἔλεγξον] Ita Hebræum הוכח in Levitico transferunt LXX. quos sequuntur alii Hellenistæ, ut Eccles. XX. 15. Hoc est quod castigare dixerat Plautus.

μεταξύ σου κὶ ἀυτῦ μόνου] Idque primum verbis mollibus: deinde, si opus sit, paulo acrioribus, ut recte præcipiunt Hebræi. Cicero: Habenda ratio & diligentia est primum ut monitio acerbitate, deinde objurgatio contumelia careat.

ἐάν σου ἀκούσῃ] Si monitis pareat, hoc est ἐὰν μετανοή- σῃ ut Lucas explicat.

ἐκέρδησας τὸν ἀδελφόν σου] Non ait Christus, tibi bene con- suluisti, sed fratri: idemque præcipue propositum nobis is- tis esse debet. Nam nostra tantum aut res aut existimatio agitur temporaria: illius salus æterna. Κερδαίνειν est ad bo- nam frugem revocare ac proinde in salutis viam reducere: ita vox hæc sumitur I. Cor. IX. 19. 20. 21. 22. 1. Petr. III. 1. Explicat hoc Jacobus ὁ ἐπιστρέψας ἁμαρτωλὸν ἐκ πλάνης ὁδῦ ἀυτῦ, σώσει ψυχὴν ἐκ θανάτου κὶ καλύψει πλῆθος ἁμαρτιῶν, c. V. 20. Loquendi genus non dissimile Genes. XII. 5. ואת הנפש אשר עשו בחרן. Animam quam fece- rant sive acquisiverant in Charan, id est Chaldæo interprete, animas quas subjecerant legi.

## 18:16
Vers. 16. ἕνα ἢ δύο] So that in this way, if it is possible, shame may be pressed upon him, which the Hebrews add. Therefore such persons ought to be taken, whose authority may have some weight with him.

ἵνα ἐπὶ στόματος δύο μαρτύρων ἢ τριῶν σταθῇ πᾶν ῥῆμα] These are the very words of the law from Deut. 19.15. From the LXX version. עמד to stand here is to have force and effect: see ἀντίστησον in Ps. 33.9. The divine law wisely requires witnesses in every case, two or three, first rejecting singular testimonies, then showing that a man's reputation can be such that it is ἰσοτάλαντος (of equal weight) not just to one, but to two witnesses. Then, therefore, a third witness will not be required: for the weights of proofs cannot be circumscribed by narrow limits, but must be estimated according to the circumstances of persons and things by the judgment of a good man. Furthermore, this law of Moses, properly, as we have said, pertaining to controversies of fact, passed into a proverb, so that it was also used for other matters, as can be seen in John 8.17; 2 Cor. 13.1. The sense here is that he who has sinned, if he has not revered you alone, may at least revere those two or three who have been brought in, and moved by their consensus, may acknowledge the iniquity of his deed.

Latin:

Vers. 16. ἕνα ἢ δύο] Ut eo modo, si fieri potest, pudor il- li exprimatur quod addunt Hebræi. Ideo tales assumi de- bent, quorum aliquid apud ipsum auctoritas valeat.

ἵνα ἐπὶ στόματος δύο μαρτύρων ἢ τριῶν σταθῇ πᾶν ῥῆμα] Sunt ipsa verba legis ex Deut. XIX. 15. Ex versione LXX. עמד stare hic est vim atque effectum habere: vide ἀντί- στησον in Ps. XXXIII. 9. Sapienter lex divina exigit testes in quaque causa binos aut ternos, primum rejiciens singularia testimonia, deinde ostendens eam posse esse viri alicujus famam ut facile non uni tantum, sed & duobus testibus sit ἰσοτάλαντος. Tunc igitur tertius non exigetur testis: nam probationum pondera angustis finibus circumscribi non possunt, sed pro personarum rerumque circumstantia boni viri arbitrio æstimanda veniunt. Cæterum lex ista Mosis proprie ut diximus ad facti controversias pertinens, in proverbium transiit, ita ut & de rebus aliis usurparetur, quem- admodum videre est Joh. IIX. 17. 2. Cor. XIII. 1. Sensus hic est, ut is qui peccavit, si te unum non est reveritus, illos saltem duos aut tres adhibitos revereatur, & illorum con- sensu motus iniquitatem facti sui agnoscat.

## 18:17
Vers. 17. παρακούσῃ ἀυτῶν] That is, if he does not repent. A word frequent in Greek writers, but also used by the LXX interpreters.

By brother, Grotius understands one who professes to follow the same standard of piety, τὸν ὁμόζηλον, as Philo speaks: and by sin, the offenses which are accustomed to creep into human weakness from anger, envy, or the desire of possession, and which pertain to the injury of another, because of the words εἰς σὲ. While we concede the latter, and Ambrose, Jerome, Augustine, and Chrysostom explain the words of Christ in that way: even though it pleases some to refer the words εἰς σὲ to secret sins, as will be evident at v. 17 regarding Calvin: thus it is certain that sin is not to be forgiven only in a faith that is ὁμοψήφῳ (of one mind) against us. We readily grant, however, because the entire process is described as to be observed in the stages of admonitions, to such a ὁμόζηλον, and ὁμόψηφον in faith, who to

It pertains to the Church, to which the matter must finally be referred, to look primarily to these things. It was also rightly noted here by Grotius that it is the custom of divine law to indicate in a most noble instance of fact what must be followed in other matters, while preserving the equity of proportion. Bellarmine, lib. III. de Verb. Dei cap. 4, also acknowledges that Christ is speaking of private injuries, which one suffers from another: whence the Papists rashly drag these things to prove the infallible judgment of the Roman Pontiff in controversies of religion, which certainly are not private injuries. Although we do not deny that those things concerning injuries which are done to the whole Church and to God, such as heresy, are also to be understood from the greater, so that such things may be referred to the Church if private admonition finds no place, yet the Church to which Christ refers us—'Tell it to the Church,' likewise 'if he will not hear the Church, let him be to you as a Gentile and a tax collector'—is not either a prelate or a congregation of prelates, as the Papists wish. A single person certainly cannot be called the Church, since the Church is the people and kingdom of God, as Bellarmine admits, lib. III. de Eccles. cap. XVII. Nor does a congregation of prelates appear anywhere under the name of Church in the Scriptures. And it is manifest that this right pertains no less to other particular Churches than to the Roman one: to which, however, the Papists do not grant the privilege of infallibility. Therefore, it should not be granted to the Roman Church either. Finally, the Church, whatever it may be, is not to be heard in articles of faith or controversies, except insofar as it follows the voice of Scripture, which alone is ἀνυπεύθυνος and infallible. And concerning ecclesiastical discipline, the Canon Law also warned of this from Innocent III, C. à nobis extr. de sentent. excomm. in Decret. Gregorii I. V. tit. 39: The judgment of God always relies on truth, which neither deceives nor is deceived, but the judgment of the Church sometimes follows opinion, which it often happens is both deceived and deceives, because of which it sometimes happens that he who is bound before God is loosed before the Church, and he who is free before God is bound by an ecclesiastical sentence. Whence it is again clear that the absolute infallibility of the Church cannot be proven from this passage; in which it is not a matter of the Church's Magisterium in doctrine, but of the Church's ministry with respect to discipline and εὐταξία. Grotius acknowledged here at v. 17 that by the word τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ is understood not a congregation of prelates, but the Church or assembly of the faithful: concerning which he has this to say:

V. 17. τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ] Before many, says the book Musar, κατὰ κοινὸν says Justin. Namely, so that there may come to him ἐπιτιμία ὑπὸ πλειόνων, as Paul speaks in 2 Cor. II. 6, and ἔλεγξις ἐνώπιον πάντων, as the same says in 1 Tim. V. v. 20. It is indeed a matter of more serious sins in these places: but even those which are lighter in their beginning are made equal to serious ones by a stubborn contempt for admonitions. The book Musar adds the reason, so that hypocrites may be exposed. But this is secondary; the primary reason is so that he may be brought back to the way, if only by the movement of so many pious people disapproving of his deed by their consensus. We have already said that nothing new is commanded by Christ: but that a rightly introduced custom is approved. Therefore, it is not a new privilege given to the Pontiff or a congregation of prelates. The Jews, although they all came together into one temple and were associated with each other by the ceremonies of the temple, nevertheless had various bodies instituted for the sake of discipline. Thus the Pharisees were distinguished from the Sadducees, and both from the Essenes, by their own institutions and assemblies. Again, among those who followed the authority of the experts in the law, there were diverse schools. Philo calls them ὁμιλίας, κοινὰς, συλλόγους, κοινὰς συνόδους. The Pythagoreans called their assembly ὁμαῖον, which Hierocles interprets as ἱερὸν σύλλογον. In these assemblies, matters pertaining to the harmony and εὐταξία of each assembly were accustomed to be treated. Such an assembly, while the law still remained and no secession had been made by the Jews from the rest, Christ had already begun to gather: which he himself, in the manner of the Hebrews, called עדה, the disciples

Writing in Greek, they sometimes used ἐκκλησίαν and συναγωγήν, just as those words were once accustomed to be used indiscriminately. It is noted in the book פרקיאבות that ten men make an עדה, that is, an ἐκκλησίαν. The same is in the Gemara Melilah cap. III. They err who think that this is about public judges. For Christ does not teach here how we may most conveniently repair our loss, which he leaves to be estimated by everyone as a βιωτικὸν and by the rules of prudence and equity, but how we may bring back the erring one to the right way. But I think it is sufficiently apparent from what we have already brought forward that not only the πρεσβυτέριον τῆς συναγωγῆς is indicated. For it was the custom for the Hebrews to bring the matter in the last instance to the multitude of τῶν ὁμοζήλων, that is, of those who followed the same institutions, whose judgments, however, the elders moderated as presidents: which, like many other things, both other writers and Tertullian teach us was preserved by the Christians: We come together, he says, into an assembly and congregation [that is, ἐκκλησίαν] so that, as if by a force of numbers, we may pray to God with our petitions. Then: there also are exhortations, punishments, and divine censure. Soon after: the approved elders of every kind preside. We see similar things in Cyprian and others.

These are the words of Grotius, who afterwards became an advocate for the Roman Synagogue: whence we thought these things should be noted here.

ἔστω σοι ὥσπερ ὁ ἐθνικὸς καὶ ὁ τελώνης:] Let him be to you a vile associate, say the Hebrews: the sense is, then at last it will be right and lawful for you to dissolve the closer bond of friendship and to avoid his familiar company, so that hereafter you may live unmolested by him: you have already done enough for your duty. When he has despised all admonitions, being free from the care of him, hold him in the place where you hold a Gentile, that is, one who is clearly alien to religion, or indeed a Jew, but an ἁμαρτωλὸν, that is, such a one who is of a flagitious life; such as tax collectors and harlots were accustomed to be held. For we said at chapter V that the word ἁμαρτωλῶν is explained by these examples. But it was not thought that the common duties of humanity were owed to such people, as most of the Jews wrongly thought, but only those which pertain to closer friendship. Nor was there any reason why much effort should be spent in admonishing them, unless a new hope of repentance should show itself. Demosthenes: For it is a moderate justice from friends, if they seem to have done something terrible, no longer to share in the remaining friendship. Cicero: The salvation of him whose ears are closed to the truth, so that he cannot hear the truth from a friend, is to be despaired of. Aristotle: One must not break off with everyone, but with those who are incurable due to their wickedness. Chrysippus: It is fitting that some things be passed over entirely, some receive a little attention, some more, and some be deemed worthy of complete dissolution. I therefore feel that these words of Christ are those of one permitting, not commanding: nor is this a matter of excommunication, about whose antiquity and necessity there will be a place to speak elsewhere: although I would not deny that an argument can be drawn from this passage for it not absurdly. Otherwise, it is not the same thing to hold someone as a base companion and to make him an outcast from the synagogue.
