This belongs to the whole assembly: that belongs to individuals, especially indeed to him who has received the injury: in which sense, if I am not mistaken, most of the ancients have rightly understood this passage, which the following will also show.

It is not a question of the power to dissolve the bond of friendship and to avoid familiar association, which everyone has in his own hand, so that there is no need at last to ask the opinion of the Church: but it is a question of the right and power of ecclesiastical censure and excommunication, by which, with other preceding degrees of admonition, one is treated as one who, by the judgment of the Church, is to be held by all members of the Church as a Gentile and a tax collector. Therefore, the gloss of Grotius is not to be approved. By the common judgment of the Doctors, these words deal with excommunication: and the words themselves, which are very clear, draw us to that. For what else is it to hold someone as a Gentile and a tax collector by the judgment of the Church than that the same person is excommunicated? Nor is the power of binding committed to the Church for any other end than that it may use the same, when other means do not avail, by excommunicating such scandalous men who have been recalled to a better life in vain by milder methods and remedies. But Grotius goes in a completely different direction, and clearly perverts a very full text. He says, I feel that these words of Christ are those of one permitting, not commanding: nor is this a matter of excommunication. He admits, however, that an argument can be drawn from this passage for it not absurdly to be able: but otherwise, he says, it is not the same thing to hold someone as a vile associate and to make them an ἀποσυνάγωγον (excommunicated person). This belongs to the whole assembly: that to individuals, and especially to him who has received the injury, in which sense, if I am not mistaken, most of the ancients have rightly understood this passage, which the following will also show. But that is not merely a permission, but a command, both in these words, Tell the Church: and in the passage which Grotius brings forward as a parallel, 1 Tim. V. 20. ἐνώπιον πάντων ἔλεγχε (rebuke before all); and the application of the binding key is not placed in ἐν ἀδιαφορίᾳ (a matter of indifference), but is necessary, by the necessity of a divine command. And not only is an argument for excommunication drawn from here, but the same is ordained in this place; for the meaning of Christ is not to be learned from Demosthenes, Cicero, Aristotle, or Chrysippus, whom Grotius brings in here, inasmuch as Cicero says that the salvation of one whose ears are closed to the truth, so that he cannot hear the truth from a friend, is to be despaired of, and other such witticisms: but that is the true meaning of Christ's words which both the tenor and propriety of the words and the context of the discourse demand. Are those words of Christ not clear enough: If he will not hear it, let him be to you as a Gentile and a tax collector? For it is certain that the former are outside the Church, and the latter are unworthy of the communion of the Church. Those, therefore, who are ordered to be held as such are by that very fact ordered to be removed from the communion of the Church. And that gloss on the words of Christ, hold him as a vile associate, is not worth a hollow nut, which he derives from a certain witticism of the Hebrews, not from the precept of Christ. It is one thing to hold someone as a Gentile and a tax collector, another to hold him as a vile associate. But it does not appear at all from Christ's discourse that this is a matter for individuals, which is what is inculcated by Christ; for although individuals, by virtue of this precept, and even he who has received the injury, are ordered to hold such a person as a Gentile and a tax collector, yet no one ought to hold him so by his own judgment, but after the ecclesiastical censure, for the sake of which the words Tell the Church are placed first. For to what other end is it denounced to the Church, than that it may judge, and that by its judgment at last he may be held as a Gentile by us who have been affected by the injury, if he has rejected reconciliation and the sentence of the Church. From the consequences the matter becomes even clearer. For Christ affirms: Amen I say to you: whatsoever you shall bind on earth, shall be bound in heaven. Which cannot be understood of the renunciation of private friendship and familiar association: but they clearly set forth the power and effect of ecclesiastical excommunication and the binding key. Who will admit that to loose and to bind here is attributed to individual Christians? It is a far different thing when such things are attributed to both Christ and the pastors, to the former principally, to the latter ministerially, nor can one conclude from that, with Grotius, that the same is also to be extended to individuals. For pastors perform an embassy in the place of Christ, which cannot be said of individual Christians. And that Grotian explanation of binding and loosing is too diluted; he binds who convicts another of guilt, he looses who brings him back to repentance by right admonitions. That this duty pertains to the ministers of the Church, not to individual Christians, is evident from a comparison of Matt. XVI. 19. & John XX. 23. is evident: nor yet do they perform this duty in their own name, but in the name of the Church, to which the keys have been entrusted: just as is certain regarding excommunication: indeed, not by the authority and name of the Church, but of Christ, from whom the keys were delivered to the Church, 1 Cor. V. 3. Therefore Christ promises here that he will ratify what the Church prays for, and that he will be present to it, v. 19. 20. so that we may not doubt concerning the effect of those things which the Church and its ministers do in the name of Christ. The connection is in the open: if two agreeing in prayers obtain what they ask, much more will that be ratified in heaven which the

Church does. If Christ is present to those gathered in his name, what they do, Christ is considered to do through them. For he is so present to the Church, as directing all things in it and performing them through the ministers. But the subsequent Petrine question, how often we ought to forgive a brother sinning against us, dealing with private forgiveness, ought not to be mixed with this reformation of Christ concerning the degrees of admonition and ecclesiastical censure. The opinion of Augustine, hom. XV. on the words of the Lord: If you hold a brother as a Gentile and a tax collector, you have bound him on earth: if you have corrected a brother, you have loosed him on earth: is not an explanation, but an application of the words of the Lord. Theophylact, however, joins both: not only are those things loosed which the priests loose, but whatsoever we also, affected by injury, either bind or loose, they themselves will be bound or loosed. But that they do not stand in an equal relation or have the same value or effect, Theophylact teaches. For there it is the public censure of the whole Church, here only a private binding or loosing. And it is the common opinion of the ancients and moderns, otherwise, that this concerns ecclesiastical excommunication, from which Grotius rashly departs. Thus Chrysostom: He wished to deter us by that denounced supreme extermination from the Church, so that if we should happen to have fallen, we might never allow ourselves to be carried to that destruction, but might repent either at the first admonition, or at the second, or at least at the third. Similarly Hilary in his commentary on this passage. For the terror of the greatest fear, by which all might be restrained for the present, he set forth the immovable judgment of Apostolic severity, so that those whom they have bound on earth, that is, left entangled in the knots of their sins, and those whom they have loosed, namely, received into salvation by the confession of pardon: these, by the condition of the Apostolic sentence, may be either loosed or bound in heaven also. Jerome says that the power is attributed here to the Apostles, and also to their successors, so that they may know that those who are condemned by them have the sentence of men strengthened by the divine sentence. Euthymius and Anselm agree. Nor does Innocent III or the Canon Law differ, or those Papists who follow it, whose patron and advocate Grotius desires to be. Most of our own agree ὁμοθυμαδὸν (with one mind). B. Lyserus in Harm. Evangel. c. XCIII. It ought to be indicated to the Church, or as they say, denounced, not so that it may be defamed in the multitude, but so that it may be healed by the authority of the whole community. Thus Paul in 1 Cor. 5:1 judged and denounced the incestuous man to the Corinthians, and willed that they, being gathered together in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and with his Spirit, with the power of the Lord JESUS, should deliver such a one unto Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ. And this rebuke St. Paul calls in 2 Cor. 2:6 Ἐπιτιμίαν ὑπὸ τῶν πλειόνων, a rebuke inflicted by many. For thus Christ commands here: If he will not hear the Church, let him be unto thee as an Ethnic and a Publican, that is, let him be excommunicated, and held in the same place as Ethnics entirely segregated from the society of the Church, or men of most lost wickedness. For the explaining of Theophylact's opinion, the blessed Lyserus noted these things: The power of binding and loosing, as promised to Peter in Matt. 16:19, and delivered to all the Apostles in John 20:23: thus in this place it is delivered by Christ to the CHURCH, which can ordinarily delegate this power to persons legitimately called to it, but extraordinarily, and in a case of necessity, any one true member of the Church has the same right, and can use it for the glory of God and the salvation of his neighbor. The blessed Aegidius Hunnius has it thus: Christ teaches that this sentence of the Church denounced to an impenitent man will not be void before God, but most ratified and efficacious, and this he confirms with a grave and religious asseveration, adding, Amen I say to you, &c. To bind is to retain sins and to consign a man by the sentence of excommunication to the wrath of God, and to temporal, and unless repentance is made, to eternal punishments as well. To loose, furthermore, is to absolve from sins. The sense of Christ's asseveration is therefore: if the wrath of God and eternal damnation are denounced in the name of the Church to the impenitent, that will be ratified in heaven before God himself. Again, if Evangelical absolution from sins is announced to the repentant and believing, this too will be undoubtedly ratified, and joined with solid effect. Thus also Flacius in his gloss; Let him be to you as a Gentile: Here excommunication is now commanded. The sense is, let the ministers of the Church excommunicate him, and you as a private person avoid him, as one excommunicated, as a Gentile &c. In the same way Osiander explains it in his Paraphrase, and in the same way other interpreters of ours, L. L. C. C. writers, Casuists, Moralists, and others commonly. Nor do the Reformed disagree; Calvin thinks the particle IN YOU, if your brother sins against you, does not concern private injuries, and he holds this regarding them: It is asked whether this rule ought to be extended indiscriminately to any sins whatsoever? For there are very many who admit no public censures until the sinner has been admonished privately. But there is a manifest restriction in the words of Christ. For he does not command that whoever has sinned be simply and without exception admonished and argued with separately and without a witness: but he wishes this way to be tried by us where we have been privately offended: not indeed in our own business, but because it is fitting that we grieve for the wound, as often as GOD is offended. Nor does Christ here discourse about bearing injuries, but in general teaches that gentleness is to be cultivated among us, lest by treating the weak too harshly, we destroy those who were to be saved. Therefore the particle IN YOU does not designate an injury brought upon someone, but distinguishes between secret and manifest sins. For if anyone has sinned against the whole Church, Paul commands him to be argued with publicly &c. 1 Tim. V. 20. afterwards he adds these things: if anyone either stubbornly rejects previous admonitions, or by persisting in his vices shows that he despises them, when he has been admonished a second time with witnesses brought in, Christ commands him to be called to the judgment of the Church, which is the assembly of the elders, &c. Finally, Calvin warns that these things pertain to the discipline of excommunication, which is permitted to the Church. The rest of the Reformed follow Calvin regarding this interpretation of the discipline of excommunication; Bucer, Beza, and others. The Remonstrants alone are almost singular, acting in such a way as to render the Censorship and Ecclesiastical discipline doubtful, whence they contend that nothing is attributed here to the Church as such. Apolog. c. XXIV. f. 256. The Church is not commanded to consider a contumacious or impenitent sinner as a Gentile and a publican, but he with whom the matter was. We have warned those whom these things have wrongly held as opposites, and thus we have met their exception in the Consideration of Arminianism c. XXIV. q. VI. p. 527. which can be compared here. But that Lightfoot restricts the promise of Christ, whatever you shall have loosed shall be loosed, &c. to the Apostles alone, in that he is singular, and does not weigh the intention of Christ: because he gives such precepts about correction and forgiveness, which are to be observed perpetually in the Church.

Latin:

Vers. 17. παρακούσῃ ἀυτῶν] Id est ἐὰν ἦ μετανοήσῃ. Vox frequens Græcis Scriptoribus, sed & LXX. Interpretibus usitata.

Per fratrem intelligit Grotius qui eandem pie- tatis normam sequi se profiteatur, τὸν ὁμόζηλον, ut loquitur Philo: & per peccatum delicta quæ imbe- cillitati humanæ ex ira, invidia, habendi cupiditate solent obrepere, quæque ad alterius injuriam perti- nent, ob verba εἰς σὲ. Quod posterius uti conce- dimus, explicantque ea ratione Verba Christi Ambrosius, Hieronymus, Augustinus, Chrysostomus: etsi verba εἰς σὲ nonnullis placeat ad peccata oc- culta referre, quemadmodum ad v. 17. de Calvi- no id patebit: ita non tantum in fide ὁμοψήφῳ ad- versus nos peccatum condonandum esse, certum est. Facile tamen largimur, quia integer processus in gradibus admonitionum observandus describitur, ad ejusmodi ὁμόζηλον, & ὁμόψηφον in fide, qui ad

Ecclesiam pertinet, ad quam res deferenda deniq; est, hæc imprimis spectare. Recte etiam monitum hic à Grotio, morem esse divinæ legis, in facti specie nobilissima indicare, quid in rebus aliis, servata tamen proportionis æquitate, sequendum sit. De injuriis Christum loqui privatis, quas unus ab a- lio patitur, Bellarm. lib. III. de Verb. Dei cap. 4. quoque agnoscit: unde temere hæc ad proban- dum infallibile judicium Romani Pontificis in contro- versiis religionis trahunt Papistæ, quæ certe non sunt privatæ injuriæ. Quanquam vero haud dif- fiteamur, à majori etiam intelligenda illa de in- juriis esse, quæ fiunt in totam Ecclesiam, & in Deum, qualis est hærefis, ut nempe talia deferan- tur ad Ecclesiam, si privata admonitio locum non inveniat, non tamen Ecclesia, ad quam remit- tit nos Christus, Dic Ecclesiæ, item si Ecclesiam non audierit, sit tibi velut Ethnicus, & publicanus, est vel prælatus vel prælatorum congregatio, quod Pa- pistæ volunt. Una certe persona non potest dici Ecclesia, cum Ecclesia sit populus & regnum Dei, fatente Bellarmino lib. III. de Eccles. cap. XVII. Neque prælatorum congregatio uspiam Ecclesiæ no- mine venit in Scripturis. Et non minus ad alias particulares Ecclesias, quam ad Romanam hoc jus pertinere in propatulo est: quibus tamen Pa- pistæ privilegium infallibilitatis non concedunt. Nec ergo Romanæ concedendum id Ecclesiæ. Denique non aliter Ecclesia, quæcunq; illa sit, au- dienda est in fidei articulis, vel controversiis, nisi quatenus vocem Scripturæ, quæ sola ἀνυπεύθυνος est, & infallibilis, illa sequitur. Idque etiam de disciplina Ecclesiastica monuit ex Innocentio III. Jus Canonicum C. à nobis extr. de sentent. ex- comm. in Decret. Gregorii I. V. tit. 39. Judicium Dei veritati, quæ non fallit, nec fallitur, semper innititur, judicium autem Ecclesiæ nonnunquam opinionem sequitur, quam & fallere sæpe contingit, & falli, propter quod contingit interdum, ut qui li- gatus est apud Deum, apud Ecclesiam sit solutus, qui liber est apud Deum, apud Ecclesiam sit solutus, qui li- ber est apud Deum, Ecclesiastica sit sententia inno- datus. Unde iterum patet, ex hoc loco probari non posse absolutam Ecclesiæ infallibilitatem; in quo non de Ecclesiæ in doctrina agitur Magisterio, sed de Ecclesiæ, respectu disciplinæ, & εὐταξίας ministerio. Agnovit hic Grotius ad v. 17. voce τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ non prælatorum congregationem, sed Ecclesiam seu cœtum fidelium intelligi: de quo ita habet:

V. 17. τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ] Coram multis, inquit liber Musar. κατὰ κοινὸν Justinus. Nempe ut ei veniat ἐπιτιμία ὑπὸ πλειόνων, ut loquitur Paulus 2. Cor. II. 6. ἔλεγξις ἐνώπιον πάντων, ut idem ad 1. Tim. V. v. 20. Agitur quidem istis in locis de peccatis gravioribus: sed etiam quæ sui initio leviora sunt, pertinaci monitorum contemptu gravibus æquantur. Cau- sam addit liber Musar, ut detegantur hypocritæ. Sed hæc se- cundaria est, primaria autem est, ut vel sic ad viam reduca- tur, motus tot piorum factum suum improbantium consen- sione. Jam diximus, nihil à Christo novum præcipi: sed morem recte introductum probari. Non ergo novum est privilegium Pontifici aut prælatorum congregationi datum. Judæi, quamvis omnes in unum templum coirent, & templi ceremoniis inter se sociarentur, habebant tamen varia corpora disciplinæ causa instituta. Ita Pharisæi à Sadducæis, utrique ab Essenis, institutis & cœtibus pro- priis distinguebantur. Rursum inter eos, qui legisperi- torum auctoritatem sequebantur, Scholæ erant diversæ. Philo vocat ὁμιλίας, κοινὰς, συλλόγους, κοινὰς συνόδους. Py- thagoristæ ὁμαῖον vocabant cœtum suum, ἱερὸν σύλλογον interpretatur Hierocles. In his cœtibus tractari solebant, quæ ad concordiam atque εὐταξίαν cujusque cœtus per- tinebant. Talem cœtum, manente etiam lege, neque facta à Judæis cæteris secessione, Christus jam colligere cœperat: quem ipse more Hebræorum vocabat עדה, discipuli

Græce scribentes ἐκκλησίαν interdum & συναγωγήν, ut solebant olim eæ voces promisscue usurpari. Notatur in libro פרקיאבות decem homines facere עדה, id est ἐκκλησίαν. Idem est in Gemara Melilah cap. III. Er- rant, qui de judicibus publicis agi hic existimant. Non enim huc docet Christus, quomodo damnum nostrum commo- dissime sarciamus, quod ille, ut βιωτικὸν & prudentiæ & æquitatis regulis unicuique æstimandum relinquit, sed quomodo errantem reducamus in rectam viam. Sed ne- que πρεσβυτέριον τῆς συναγωγῆς solum indicari ex his, quæ jam adduximus, satis puto apparere. Mos enim fuit Hebræis rem ultimo loco ad multitudinem τῶν ὁμοζήλων, id est, eorum, qui eadem instituta sectarentur, perducere, cujus tamen multitudinis judicia, seniores tanquam præsides moderabantur: quod ut multa alia, servatum à Christianis tum alii scriptores, tum Tertullianus nos docet: Coimus, inquit, in cætum, & congregationem, [hoc est, ἐκκλησίαν] ut ad Deum quasi manu facta precationibus orantes. Deinde: ibidem etiam cohortationes, castigatio- nes & censura divina. Mox: præsident probati quique se- niores. Similia videmus apud Cyprianum atque alios.

Hæc Grotius qui postmodum causidicus Romà- næ Synagogæ factus est: unde ea hic observanda duximus.

ἔστω σοι ὥσπερ ὁ ἐθνικὸς καὶ ὁ τελώνης:] Esto tibi socius vilis inquiunt Hebræi: sensus est, tunc demum jus fasque tibi erit propius amicitiæ vinculum resolvere, & familiarem illius convictum defugere, ut posthac ab illo illacessitus vivas: satis fecisti jam officio. Quando o- mnia monita contemsit, libero de illius cura, habe eum quo loco habes ἐθνικὸν, hoc est, à religione plane alienum, aut Judæum quidem, sed ἁμαρτωλὸν, hoc est talem, qui vitæ sit flagitiosæ; quales haberi solebant τελῶναι καὶ πόρναι. Nam his exemplis declarari vocem ἁμαρτωλῶν diximus ad caput V. Talibus autem non delinebant deberi com- munia humanitatis officia, ut male sentiebant Judæorum plerique, sed ea tantum quæ ad propiorem amicitiam pertinent. Neque erat quod in illis monendis multum operæ poneretur, nisi nova spes pœnitentiæ se ostende- ret. Demosthenes: μετρία γὰρ δίκη παρὰ τῶν φίλων ἐστὶν ἄν τι δοκῶσι πεποιηκέναι δεινὸν μηκέτι τῆς λοιπῆς φιλίας κοινω- νεῖν. Cicero: Cujus aures veritati clausæ sunt, ut ab amico verum audire nequeat, hujus salus desperanda est. Aristo- teles: διαλυτέον ὀυ πᾶσιν, ἀλλὰ τοῖς ἀνιάτοις διὰ τὴν μο- χθηρίαν. Chrysippus: προσήκει τὰ μὲν ὅλως παραπέμπεσθαι, τὰ δὲ μικρᾶς ἐπιστροφῆς τυγχάνειν, τὰ δὲ ἐπὶ μεῖζον, τὰ δὲ ὅ- λως διαλύσεως ἀξιοῦσθαι. Permittenti igitur, non impe- rantis esse hæc Christi verba sentio: neque agi hic de ex- communicatione, de cujus antiquitate & necessitate alibi erit dicendi locus: quanquam ad eam ex hoc etiam loco non absurde argumentum duci posse non negaverim. A- lioqui non est idem, habere aliquem pro socio vili, & ἀποσυνάγωγον ποιεῖν. Hoc totius est cœtus: illud singulo- rum, maxime vero ejus qui injuriam accepit: quem in sensum hunc locum recte ni fallor acceperunt plerique veterum, quod & sequentia ostendent.

Non de potestate amicitiæ vinculum resolvendi, & familiarem convictum defugiendi, quam quis- que in manu sua habet, ut non demum Ecclesiæ opus sit rogare sententiam: sed de jure ac pote- state censuræ Ecclesiasticæ & excommunicationis, qua præviis aliis admonitionum gradibus, quis ab omnibus Ecclesiæ membris, ea ita censente, pro Ethnico & publicano habendus, agitur. Non probanda ergo Grotii glossa. Communi judicio Doctorum, hæc de excommunicatione agunt: atque eo verba ipsa nos trahunt, quæ luculenta ad modum sunt. Quid enim aliud est, habendum quemdam ceu Ethnicum & publicanum judicio Ecclesiæ quam eundem excommunicatum esse? Nec alio fine hic potestas ligandi committi- tur Ecclesiæ, quam ut eadem utatur, quum alia non proficiunt, excommunicando tales scan- dalosos homines, qui mitioribus modis & re- mediis frustra ad frugem revocati sunt. At Gro- tius in alia omnia it, & textum per quam difer- tum plane pervertit. Permittentis,inquit, non impe- rantis esse hæc Christi verba sentio: neque agi hic de excommunicatione. Fatetur tamen ad eam ex hoc etiam loco non absurde argumentum duci posse : sed alioquin, ait, non est idem, habere ali- quem pro socio vili, & ἀποσυνάγωγον ποιεῖν. Hoc totius est cœtus : illud singulorum, maxime vero ejus, qui injuriam accepit, quem in sensum hunc locum recte ni fallor, acceperunt plerique veterum, quod & sequentia ostendent. At non permissio tantum illa est, sed mandatum, tum in his verbis, Dic Ecclesiæ: tum in loco, quem pro parallelo confert Grotius 1. Tim. V. 20. ἐνώπιον πάντων ἔλεγχε; & clavis ligan- tis adhibitio non est ἐν ἀδιαφορίᾳ posita, sed neces- saria, necessitate mandati divini. Neque tantum argumentum hinc ducitur ad excommunicatio- nem, sed ordinatur eadem hoc loco; sensus enim Christi non ex Demosthene, Cicerone, Aristotele, aut Chrysippo addiscendus est, quos hic adducit Gro- tius, utpote quod Cicero dicat, cujus aures veritati clausæ sunt, ut ab amico verum audire nequeat, hu- jus salus desperanda est, & quæ hujusmodi alia sunt dictaeria: sed ea demum verborum Christi est sen- tentia, quam tum verborum tenor & proprietas, tum contextus orationis postulat. Annon vero satis clara sunt illa Christi verba: Si non audierit eam, sit tibi velut Ethnicus & publicanus? Illos e- nim extra Ecclesiam esse constat, & hos indignos Ecclesiæ communione. Qui ergo tales haberi ju- bentur, eo ipso ab Ecclesiæ communione juben- tur removeri. Neque cassa nuce digna est illa ver- borum Christi glossa, habeas eum pro vili socio, quam ex Ebræorum quodam dicterio, non è Christi præ- cepto habet. Aliud est habere aliquem pro Ethni- co & publicano, aliud habere pro vili socio. Id ve- ro è Christi oratione nullatenus apparet, quod singulorum hoc sit, quod à Christo inculcatur; nam etsi singuli, vi hujus præcepti, atque ille etiam, qui injuriam accepit, pro Ethnico & publicano ta- lem habere jubeantur, non tamen suopte judicio eum ita habere quisque debet, sed post censuram Ec- clesiasticam, cujus gratia præmittitur, dic Ecclesiæ. Nam quo alias fine denunciatur Ecclesiæ, quam ut hæc judicet, ejusque demum judicio à nobis, qui injuria affecti sumus, pro Ethnico habeatur, qui re- conciliationem ac sententiam Ecclesiæ reproba- rit. E consequentibus res adhuc clarior fit. Nam af- feverat Christus: Amen dico vobis: quæcunque liga- veritis in terra, ligata erunt in cælo. Quæ de renunciatione privatæ amicitiæ, & familiaris con- victus accipi nequeunt: excommunicationis autem Ecclesiasticæ, & clavis ligantis vim atque effectum luculenter sistunt. Ecquis admittet, solvere hic & ligare Christianis singulis tribui? longe aliud est, cum & Christo & pastoribus talia tribuuntur, illi principaliter; his ministerialiter, nec inde cum Grotio colligere licet, ad singulos eadem quoque extendenda. Nam Pastores funguntur legatione vice Christi, quod de Christianis singulis dici ne- quit. Et nimis diluta est illa ligationis & solutionis explicatio Grotiana; ligat qui alterum culpæ con- vincit, solvit, qui eum rectis monitis ad pænitentiam reducit. Ad Ministrorum Ecclesiæ, non singulorum Christianorum officium hoc pertinere, è collatio- ne Matth. XVI. 19. & Joh. XX. 23. evidens est: nec tamen suo, sed Ecclesiæ nomine, cui crediti claves sunt, funguntur illi hoc munere: quemadmodum de excommunicatione constat: imo non Eccle- siæ, sed Christi, à quo Ecclesiæ claves traditi sunt, autoritate ac nomine 1. Cor. V. 3. ideo Christus se rata habiturum, quæ precatur Ecclesia, eiq; præsto futurum hic pollicetur v. 19. 20. ut ne de effectu eorum, quæ Ecclesia, ejusque ministri nomine Chri- sti faciunt, ambigamus. Connexio in aprico est: si duo in precibus consentientes impetrant, quod petunt, multo magis ratum in cœlo erit, quod agit

Ecclesia. Si præsto est Christus congregatis in nomine suo, quod illi agunt, Christus per eosdem agere censetur. Sic enim adest Ecclesiæ, ut omnia in ea dirigens & per Ministros peragens. Quæ- stio autem subsequens Petrina, quoties fratri in nos peccanti remittere debeamus, de privata agens condonatione, cum hac de gradibus admonitionis & censura Ecclesiastica reformatione Christi com- misceri non debet. Augustini sententia hom. XV. de verbis Dom. Si fratrem habes pro Ethnico & pu- blicano, ligasti illum in terra: si correxeris fratrem, solvisti illum in terra: non explicatio est, sed appli- catio verborum Domini. Theophylactus vero u- trumque conjungit: non solum quæ solvunt Sa- cerdotes, sunt soluta, sed quæcunque & nos injuria affecti vel ligamus, vel solvimus, & ipsa erunt li- gata vel soluta. Sed non æquali ratione illa se ha- bent vel habere sese aut ejusdem prorsus esse va- loris vel effectus, docet Theophylactus. Ibi enim censura est publica totius Ecclesiæ, hic privata tan- tum ligatio vel solutio. Et communis cæteroquin doctorum veterum & recentiorum sententia est, agi hic de excommunicatione Ecclesiastica, à qua te- mere abit Grotius. Ita Chrysost. Voluit deterre- re nos denunciata suprema illa ex Ecclesia extermina- tione, ut si lapsi forte fuerimus, nunquam in eam us- que perniciem ferri nos sinamus, sed vel ad primam admonitionem, vel ad secundam, vel certe ad ter- tiam resipiscamus. Similiter Hilarius in comment. ad h. l. Ad terrorem metus maximi, quo in præsens omnes continerentur, immobile severitatis Apostolicæ judicium præmisit, ut quos in terris ligaverint, id est, peccatorum nodis innexos reliquerint, & quos solverint, confessione videlicet veniæ receperint in salu- tem: hi Apostolicæ conditione sententiæ in cælis quo- que aut soluti sint, aut ligati. Hieronymus pote- statem Apostolis, etiam eorum successoribus hic tribui ait, ut sciant, qui ab ipsis condemnentur, homi- num sententiam divina sententia roborari. Con- sentit Euthymius, & Anshelmus. Nec discrepat Innocentius III. aut jus Canonicum, quique id se- quuntur Pontificii, quorum Patronus & advoca- tus esse gestit Grotius. E nostris plerique annu- unt ὁμοθυμαδὸν. B. Lyserus in Harm. Evangel. c. XCIII. Ecclesiæ talis indicari, aut ut loquuntur, de- nunciari debet, non ut in multitudine diffametur, sed ut totius communitatis auctoritate sanetur. Sic Paulus 1. Cor. V. 1. incestuosum adjudicavit & denun- ciavit Corinthiis, & voluit, ut ipsis in nomine Jesu Christi congregatis & suo Spiritu, cum virtute Do- mine JESU talem tradant Satanæ in interitum car- nis, ut salvus sit spiritus in die Domini nostri Jesu Christi. Et hanc correptionem vocat D. Paulus 2. Cor. II. 6. Ἐπιτιμίαν ὑπὸ τῶν πλειόνων increpatio- nem à pluribus factam. Nam sic Christus hic præcipit: Si Ecclesiam non audierit, sit tibi velut Ethnicus & Publicanus, hoc est, excommunicetur, & eodem loco habeatur, quo Ethnici penitus ab Ecclesiæ sovieta- te segregati, aut perditissimæ improbitatis homines. Pro Theophylacti vero sententia explicanda hæc notavit B. Lyserus: Potestas ligandi & solvendi, ut Matth. XVI. 19. promissa est Petro, & Joh. XX. 23. tradita est omnibus Apostolis: sic hoc in loco traditur à Christo ECCLESIÆ, quæ hanc potestatem ordi- narie deferre potest personis legitime ad id vocatis, extraordinarie autem, & in casu necessitatis unum- quodlibet verum Ecclesiæ membrum idem jus habet, eoque ad gloriam Dei & proximi salutem uti potest. B. Ægid. Hunnius ita habet: Sententiam i- stam Ecclesiæ denunciatam homini impœnitenti do- cet Christus non fore coram Deo irritam, sed maxi- me ratam & efficacem, idque gravi & religiosa atte- statione confirmat subjiciens, Amen dico vobis, &c. Alligare est peccata retinere & excommunicationis sententia hominem irae Dei, ac temporalibus, & ni- si poenitentia fiat, aeternis quoque poenis addicere. Solvere porro est a peccatis absolvere. Est ergo sen- sus asseverationis Christi: si nomine Ecclesiae de- nuncietur impoenitenti ira Dei & aeterna damna- tio, fore id ratum in coelis coram ipso Deo. Rur- sum, si resipiscenti & credenti annuncietur Ev- angelica a peccatis absolutio, fore & hanc indu- bie ratam, & cum solido effectu conjunctam. Sic etiam Flacius in glossa; Sit tibi Ethnicus: Hic jam mandatur excommunicatio. Sensus est, ex- communicent eum ministri Ecclesiae, & tu privatus devita eum, ut excommunicatum, tanquam genti- lem &c. Eodem modo explicat Osiander in Pa- raphrasi, eodem modo alii Interpretes nostri, L. L. C. C. Scriptores, Casuistae, Moralistae, & alii communiter. Neque Reformati discrepant; Calvinus particulam IN TE, si peccaverit in te frater tuus, non concernere injurias privatas, pu- tat, atque ita de his habet: Quaeritur an promi- scue regula haec ad quaevis peccata extendi debeat? Sunt enim permulti, qui nullas admittunt publicas censuras, donec privatim admonitus fuerit pecca- tor. Atqui manifesta est in Christi verbis restri- ctio. Neque enim simpliciter & sine exceptione moneri, & argui seorsim & sine teste jubet, qui- cunque peccaverint: sed hanc viam a nobis tenta- ri vult ubi privatim offensi sumus: non quidem in proprio negotio, sed quia dolere nos vulneri conve- nit, quoties offenditur DEUS. Nec vero Christus hic de ferendis injuriis disserit, sed in genere man- suetudinem inter nos colendam docet, ne asperius tractando infirmos, perdamus qui servandi erant. Ergo particula IN TE non illatam alicui inju- riam designat, sed inter occulta & manifesta pecca- ta distinguit. Nam si quis in totam Ecclesiam pec- caverit, eum Paulus jubet publice argui &c. 1. Tim. V. 20. postea haec subjungit: si quis monitiones priores vel pervicaciter respuat, vel pergendo in suis vitiis, contemnere se ostendat, ubi secundo testi- bus adhibitis monitus fuerit, ad judicium Ecclesiae, quod est seniorum confessus, vocari Christus praeci- pit, &c. Denique monet Calvinus, hac ad di- sciplinam excommunicationis pertinere, quae Eccle- siae permissa est. Calvinus sequuntur, quoad hanc interpretationem de disciplina excommu- nicationis, caeteri Reformati; Bucerus, Beza, a- lii. Soli fere Remonstrantes singulares sunt, id agentes, ut dubia reddatur Censura & discipli- na Ecclesiastica, unde Ecclesiae, qua tali nihil hic tribui contendunt. Apolog. c. XXIV. f. 256. Non Ecclesia jubetur peccatorem contumacem, aut impoenitentem censere pro Ethnico & publicano, sed is, cui cum eo res fuit. Quos vero haec frustra pro oppositis habere monuimus, adeoque ex- ceptioni eorum occurrimus in Consideratione Arminianismi c. XXIV. q. VI. p. 527. quae hic conferri poterit. Quod vero Lightfootus pro- missionem Christi qua solveritis soluta erunt, &c. ad solos Apostolos restringat, in eo singularis est, nec intentionem Christi pensi habet: quia talia de correptione & condonatione dat prae- cepta, quae perpetuo in Ecclesia observanda sunt.

## 18:18
Vers. 18. ὅσα ἐὰν δήσητε ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς] Since the preceding discourse is directed to him who has received an injury, these things also, announced in a continuous discourse, pertain entirely to it: which is shown also by the interrogation of Peter that will follow shortly, how often injuries are to be forgiven. Rightly, therefore, Origen says these things seem to be said to all who have argued with sinners three times.

Augustine, on the Word of the Lord, homily XV. If he holds his brother as a Gentile and a Publican, you have bound him on earth: if you have corrected your brother, you have loosed him on earth. And Theophylact; If you, he says, being offended, hold him who has afflicted you with an injury as a publican and a gentile, he will be such also in heaven. But if you have loosed him, that is, forgiven him, it will be by force also in heaven forgiven. For not only those things which Priests loose are loosed, but whatever we also, having been afflicted with an injury, either bind or loose, they themselves will be bound or loosed. These are his words. Nor should it seem strange to us that this loosing and binding is attributed to individual Christians. For if these same things are attributed both to Christ and to pastors, with the ratio of proportion preserved, why could they not be extended to individuals with the same ratio preserved? For we see that σῴζειν, which is attributed now to Christ, now to pastors, is also attributed to individuals, in the same sense that is being treated here, James V. 20. He therefore binds who convinces another of guilt: he looses, who leads him to repentance by right admonitions, and also prays to God for him, as the following things declare.

ἐν τῷ ὐρανῷ] For ἐν τοῖς ὐρανοῖς. For we have said elsewhere that these are sometimes confused. See what is above XVI. vers. 19.

Latin:

Vers. 18. ὅσα ἐὰν δήσητε ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς] Cum qui praecessit sermo ad eum dirigatur qui injuriam accepit, omnino & haec continuo sermone enuntiata eo pertinent: quod o- stendit & ea quae mox sequetur Petri interrogatio, quo- ties condonandae sint injuriae. Recte igitur Origenes videri ait haec omnibus dicta qui peccantes ter arguerint.

Augustinus de Verbo Domini homilia XV. Si fratrem habet pro Ethnico & Publicano, ligasti illum in terra: si cor- rexeris fratrem, solvisti illum in terra. Et Theophylactus; Si tu, inquit, offensus, habes eum qui te injuria affecit, sicut publicanum & gentilem, erit ille & in cœlo talis. Si autem solveris eum, hoc est ignoveris, erit vi & in cœlo condonatum. Non enim solum quæ solvunt Sacerdotes sunt soluta, sed quæcunque & nos injuria affecti vel ligamus vel solvimus & ipsa erunt ligata vel soluta. Hæc ille. Ne- que mirum nobis videri debet solvere hoc & ligare Christianis singulis tribui. Nam si hæc eadem & Christo tribuuntur & pastoribus, servata proportionis ratione, quidni extendi possent ad singulos eadem ratione serva- ta? Nam & σῴζειν quod modo Christo, modo pastori- bus tribuitur, videmus & singulis tribui, eodem de- quo hic agitur sensu Jac. V. 20. Ligat igitur qui alterum culpæ convincit: solvit, qui eum rectis monitis ad pœni- tentiam perducit, atque etiam pro ipso Deum precatur, ut sequentia declarant.

ἐν τῷ ὐρανῷ] Pro ἐν τοῖς ὐρανοῖς. Interdum enim confundi hæc alibi diximus. Vide quæ supra XVI. vers. 19.

## 18:19
V. 19. ἐὰν δύο ὑμῶν] The connection with the preceding seems manifest to me. He said that what we shall have loosed here, will be loosed in heaven. He confirms that with a universal proposition: because God grants whatever two ask concordantly, just as in that species of which he treated; and he who has admonished his brother, and the brother admonished, or even others if any were brought in, pray to God that he may forgive the fault. This is what James says: Confess your sins to one another: pray for one another that you may be healed. For the effective prayer of a just man avails much, chap. V. 16. Often indeed God grants even to one praying what he asks, but to more who are in concord among themselves he bestows both more willingly, and more things, and more quickly. But if two, understand, if even two only, in the Hebrew manner.

Grotius explains this connection τῇ ὑποθέσει δουλεύων, because GOD grants whatever two agreeably ask, just as in that species of which he treated, both he who admonished the brother and the brother who was admonished, or even others if any were brought in, pray to GOD that He may forgive the fault. But since the discourse was about the Church, there is no reason why we should restrict this promise to those who have been reconciled. More correctly, the blessed Hunnius explains this reason for the συνεχείας, so that it may be manifest how much GOD values those things which the Church of the faithful undertakes according to His word, Christ attaches the sweetest promises, one concerning the hearing of prayers, the other concerning His perpetual presence among the faithful. The blessed Lyserus has twin points to these, clarifying the second reason thus: namely, that Christ is not far off from such an action (he indicates the excommunication of the Church) but is present at it, nay, presides over it, and therefore makes firm and ratified whatever is performed in His name. That ἐαν δύο ὑμῶν does not precisely look to those two reconciled among themselves, but to more, not even Grotius himself denies: If two however (these are the words of his Commentary) understand, if even only two or three have agreed in a certain matter to be asked for with a unanimous voice, that it will not be in vain: And however contracted the assembly may be, Christ will nonetheless be present to them, and will hold as ratified what they perform in His name. Grotius, however, seems to have followed the Arminians, or rather spoke from the mind of this sect, to which he himself perhaps was still addicted at that time: For these declared themselves thus concerning the promise of the presence of Christ made in Matthew 18, verse 20, in the Apology, chapter 25, page 282: What does this promise contribute to Synods, let alone to concluding their necessity? For if the scope of the Lord JESUS is attended to, this promise does not pertain to two or three gathered in the name of Jesus Christ, as such, but to two or three agreeing, or rather made concordant from being discordant, etc. But their opinion we discussed in the loc. cit. q. 18, p. 549 et seqq. Yet the Papists wrongly attribute infallibility to Synods gathered by the authority of the Pope from this promise. For where does this gloss have a foundation in Scripture, that to be gathered in the name of Christ is to be gathered by the authority of the Pope? And since this promise was made to all the faithful, are all the faithful infallible in faith, or any assembly of the faithful? Cons. Critic. Sacr. p. 884.

συμφωνήσωσιν] They shall have been in agreement. For the Greeks translate the Hebrew חברו thus.

περὶ παντὸς πράγματος] The universal term must be restricted by the nature of the matter, if good men ask for good things well for a good purpose. The first restriction is taught in John 9:31 and in the first epistle, chapter 3:21, 22. The second below in verse 11. The third in Luke 18:1, James 1:5, 6, 7. The fourth in James 4:3.

Latin:

V. 19. ἐὰν δύο ὑμῶν] Manifesta mihi videtur cum superio- ribus connexio. Dixit quod hic solverimus, in cœlo so- lutum fore. Id universali propositione confirmat: quia Deus præstat quicquid duo concorditer petunt, sicut in ea de qua egit specie; & is qui fratrem admonuit, & frater admonitus, aut etiam alii si qui fuerunt adhibiti, Deum precantur ut culpam condonet. Hoc est quod Ja- cobus dicit Fatemini peccata alter alteri: orate alter pro alte- ro ut sanemini. Multum enim valet efficax justi hominis de- precatio, cap. V. 16. Sæpe quidem Deus etiam uni precanti concedit quod rogat, sed pluribus inter se con- cordibus largitur & libentius, & plura, & citius. Si duo autem, intellige, si vel duo tantum, more He- bræo.

Connexionem hanc reddit Grotius τῇ ὑποθέσει δουλεύων, quia DEUS præstat, quicquid duo con- corditer petunt, sicut in ea, de qua egit specie, & is qui fratrem admonuit & frater admonitus, aut etiam alii si qui fuerint adhibiti, DEUM precan- tur, ut culpam condonet. Sed quum de Ecclesiæ sermo fuerit, non est quod hanc promissionem ad eos restringamus, qui reconciliati sunt. Re- ctius B. Hunnius hanc συνεχείας rationem reddit, ut palam fiat, quanti DEUS æstimet ea, quæ secundum verbum ejus suscipit Ecclesia fidelium in hoc mundo, dulcissimas promissiones subnectit Christus, alteram de exauditione precum, alte- ram de perpetua sua apud fideles præsentia. Qui- bus gemina habet B. Lyserus, alteram rationem ita dilucidans: quod nempe Christus non procul absit ab ejusmodi actione (excommunicationem indigat Ecclesiæ) sed illi intersit, imo præsit, & proinde firmum ac ratum efficiat, quicquid in no- mine suo peragitur. Illa ἐαν δύο ὑμῶν non præ- cise duos istos inter se reconciliatos, sed plures respicere, nec ipse Grotius inficiatur: Si duo autem (sunt verba Commentarii ejus) intellige, si vel duo duntaxat pli aut tres consenserint in rem certam unanimi voce petendam, non id fore irri- tum: Et utcunque contractus sit cœtus, non tamen minus illi præsto futurum Christum, & quæ per- agit in nomine suo, rata habiturum. Sequutus au- tem videtur Grotius Arminianos, vel ex men- te potius sectæ hujus, cui ipse tum forte adhuc addictus fuit, loquutus est: Hi enim de pro- missione præsentiæ Christi Matth. XIIX. vers. 20. facta sic Apol. cap. XXV. pag. 282. se decla- rarunt: Quid hec promissio ad Synodos, ne- dum ad earum necessitatem concludendam facit? Etenim si scopus Domini JESU attendatur, pro- missio hæc non pertinet ad duos vel tres in nomine Jesu Christi congregatos, qua tales, sed ad duos vel tres consentientes, sive potius ex discordibus concordes factos &c. Sed illorum sententiam dis- cussimus l. c. q. XIIX. pag. 549. seqq. Perpe- ram tamen ex hac promissione Pontificii Synodis 'autoritate Pontificis congregatis infallibilitatem tribuunt. Ubi enim hæc glossa in Script. fun- damentum habet, in nomine Christi congregari esse congregari autoritate Papæ? Et quum o- mnibus fidelibus hæc facta promissio sit, num o- mnes fideles infallibiles in fide sunt, aut quivis fidelium cœtus! Cons. Critic. Sacr. p. 884.

συμφωνήσωσιν] Concordes fuerint. Nam חברו He- bræum sic vertunt Græci.

περὶ παντὸς πράγματος] Universalis vox ex rei naturâ restringenda est, si boni petant bona bene ad bonum. Prima restrictio docetur Joh. IX. 31. & in epist. I. cap. III. 21. 22. Secunda infra commate 11. Tertia Luc. XIIX. 1. Jac. I. 5. 6. 7. Quarta Jac. IV. 3.

## 18:20
V. 20. Συνηγμένοι] Just as just now συμφωνεῖν was transferred from the mouth to the mind, so here συνάγεσθαι is by metaphor ὁμονοεῖν, just as we also say in Latin to convene. That the word συνάγεσθαι is taken in this way is manifest in Acts 4:27.

εἰς τὸ ἐμὸν ὄνομα] The Syriac בשמי, just as בשם is taken in Psalm 20:5 & 8 & 1 Sam. 17:45, to signify the confidence which we place in someone. Thus John 14:13, 14, ἐάν τι αἰτήσητε ἐν τῷ ὀνόματί με, by my confidence.

ἐκεῖ εἰμι ἐν μέσῳ ἀυτῶν] Again it is a metaphor, such as the one above for the word συνάγεσθαι. Thus in Latin, one is said to be present to someone who favors him and provides him aid. Moreover, this saying of Christ is very similar to a common sentiment among the Hebrews: 'Where two sit together and have words of the law between them, the Shechinah is between them.' Where two sit together having a conversation about the law, the Shechinah is among them.

It is not only about presence by reason of power and operation, as in Latin one is said to be present to someone who favors him and provides him aid—which meaning Grotius wishes it to be—but it is also a matter of the subject. Because this is a divine presence, which cannot exist without substantial presence. GOD does not act or operate anywhere while substantially absent, but wherever He acts or operates, He is present, and His power cannot be separated from His essence. Since therefore Christ acts not by any other than a divine presence, not like a Monarch through ministers, or like the sun and stars acting through virtual influx, even if they are not really present, but in a heavenly manner, as being true God, and thus is present there by reason of substance where He operates, and that not only with respect to the divine nature, but also with respect to the human, which is inseparable from the former and constitutes one ὑφισάμενον with it. Grotius himself notes that the saying of Christ is very similar to a common sentiment among the Hebrews: where two sit together having a conversation about the law, the Shechinah is among them. If Christ is present to us in that way, as GOD and man, as the Shechinah or divinity is present to the faithful, it is certain that He is present to us not only by reason of power, but also by reason of substance.

PART V. Concerning fraternal forgiveness.

Latin:

V. 20. Συνηγμένοι] Sicut modo συμφωνεῖν ab ore ad animum transferebatur, ita hic συνάγεσθαι per translationem est ὁμονοεῖν, quomodo Latine etiam dicimus convenire. Ita sumi vocem συνάγεσθαι manifestum est Actor. IV. 27.

εἰς τὸ ἐμὸν ὄνομα] Syrus בשמי quomodo בשם su- mitur Psalm. XX. 5. & 8. & 1. Sam. XVII. 45. ad signi- ficandam fiduciam quam in aliquo ponimus. Ita Johan. XIV. 13. 14. ἐάν τι αἰτήσητε ἐν τῷ ὀνόματί με, meâ fiducia.

ἐκεῖ εἰμι ἐν μέσῳ ἀυτῶν] Rursum translatio est qualis supra in voce συνάγεσθαι. Sic Latine adesse alicui dicitur qui ei favet auxiliumque præbet. Est autem hoc Christi dictum simillimum tritæ inter Hebræos sententiæ: שנים שיושבים ויש ביניהם דברי תורה שכינה שרויה ביניהם Ubi duo consident sermonem habentes de lege, Schechinah est inter ipsos.

Non tantum de præsentia ratione virtutis & operationis, ut Latine adesse alicui dicitur, qui ei favet, auxiliumque præbet, quem sensum esse vult Grotius, sed etiam ratione suppositi agitur. Quia divina hæc est præsentia, quæ non potest esse si- ne substantiali adessentia. DEUS non agit, aut operatur alicubi, substantialiter absens, sed u- bicunque agit vel operatur, præsens est, ejusque virtus ab essentia separari nequit. Quum ergo Christus non alia, quam divina præsentia, non instar Monarchæ per ministros, aut solis & stel- larum per virtualem influxum, utut realiter præsto non sint, operantium, sed cælesti modo, utpote verus Deus agit, adeoque substantiæ ratione ibi præsto est, ubi operatur, idque non tantum respectu divinæ naturæ, sed etiam respe- ctu humanæ, quæ ab illa inseparabilis est, & cum illa unum constituit ὑφισάμενον. Notat ipse Grotius dictum Christi simillimum esse tritæ inter Ebræos sententiæ: ubi duo consident sermonem habentes de lege, Schechina est inter ipsos. Si ea ratione nobis adest Christus, ut DEUS & ho- mo, ut Schechina vel divinitas adest fidelibus, non tantum ratione virtutis, sed etiam ratione substantiæ eum nobis adesse, certum est.

PARS V. De condonatione fraterna.

## 18:21
Vers. 21. ποσάκις ἁμαρτήσει εἰς ἐμὲ ὁ ἀδελφός με, κὶ ἀφήσω ἀυτῷ] A Hebraism, for which the Greeks would say, ποσάκις ἁμαρτήσαντι ἀφήσω: as above chapter 17:20, ἐρεῖτε τῷ μεταβήσεται, instead of κελευόντων ὑμῶν μεταβήσεται. But since forgiveness can be twofold—the one by which we neither demand vengeance and injury ourselves, nor ask for it from God or man; the other by which we retain someone or restore them to their former degree of friendship—we ought to use the former against everyone, the latter against those who truly repent, which Hierocles calls the recall from repentance. Peter seems to be dealing with the latter here. For Christ had said, as Luke testifies, 'if he turns to you saying, I repent, you shall forgive him.'

ἕως ἑπτάκις] From the tradition, as I believe, of the Jews: who did not extend the necessity of forgiving beyond this, even in lighter sins. For I do not think that Christ's words which are in Luke gave Peter the occasion for error, for there it is not simply ἑπτάκις, but ἑπτάκις τῆς ἡμέρας, which in the manner of the Hebrews signifies as often as possible, as in Prov. 24:16, Ps. 119:165.

Latin:

Vers. 21. ποσάκις ἁμαρτήσει εἰς ἐμὲ ὁ ἀδελφός με, κὶ ἀ- φήσω ἀυτῷ] Hebraismus, pro quo Græci dicerent, ποσάκις ἁμαρτήσαντι ἀφήσω: ut supra cap. XVII. 20. ἐρεῖτε τῷ μετα- βήσεται, pro κελευόντων ὑμῶν μεταβήσεται. Cum autem condonatio duplex esse possit, altera qua vindictam injuriamque neque exigimus per nos, neque à Deo homi- neve deposcimus, altera qua retinemus aliquem aut resti- tuimus in pristinum amicitiæ gradum, priore adversus o- mnes uti debemus, posteriore adversus vere resipiscentes quam ἐκ μεταμελείας ἀνάκλησιν vocat Hierocles. De po- steriore agere hic Petrus videtur. Dixerat enim Christus teste Luca, ἐὰν ἐπιστρέψῃ ἐπί σε λέγων, μετανοῶ, ἀφήσεις ἀυ- τῷ.

ἕως ἑπτάκις] Ex traditione ut credo Judæorum: qui non ultra extendebant condonandi necessitatem in peccatis etiam levioribus. Nam Christi quæ apud Lucam sunt ver- ba occasionem errandi Petro dedisse non arbitror, neque enim ibi est ἑπτάκις simpliciter, sed ἑπτάκις τῆς ἡμέρας, quod Hebræorum more significat quam sæpissime, ut Prov. XXIV. 16. Ps. CXIX, 165.

## 18:22
Vers. 22. ἕως ἑβδομηκοντάκις ἑπτά] This is not seventy times seven, but up to the number of seventy-seven. Nor did the Syrian mean anything else when he said: עַדְמָא לִשְׁבְעִין וְבַעְנִין שְׁבַע שְׁבַע that is, up to seventy-seven times: not as it seemed to others to interpret, fourteen times seventy. For שֶׁבַע שֶׁבַע does not signify fourteen, but seven each, as in Genesis VII. 2, just as Mark chapter VI. 7 said δύο δύο for two by two. Christ opposes this number as being much greater than the number seven, according to the custom of the Hebrews. For the same opposition is found in Gen. IV. 24, where what is שִׁבְעָתַיִם וְשִׁבְעִים must be interpreted as seventy times and that same seven times. Among the LXX, likewise as here ἑβδομηκοντάκις ἑπτά, although Josephus understood it otherwise. Furthermore, what is said here by Christ about forgiving offenses, I would not wish to be rashly extended to Ecclesiastical judgments concerning more serious offenses. For it is one thing to give of one's own, another to give of the public's; and it makes a great difference whether you privately receive a friend, or relax the rigor of common discipline, in which both the honor and health of the Church consist in large part. Wherefore the most ancient of Christians used to commend those who had fallen into idolatry, homicide, or adultery to the mercy of God, yet not so as to admit them to communion. Those defiled by such crimes they did not receive to communion merely upon a profession of repentance, but after the trials of a long time: those who had relapsed again or more often, they did not. Therefore, that saying of Chrysostom, χιλιάκις μετανοήσας εἴσελθε, spoken in the heat of the struggle against the Novatians, must be softened by a benign interpretation. Moreover, this passage of the Gospel in the Hebrew Codex, such as it was kept by the Nazarenes, held thus: If your brother sins in word, and makes amends to you, receive him seven times a day. Simon his disciple said to him: Seven times a day? The Lord answered and said to him: Even I say to you, up to seventy times seven. For indeed, in the Prophets also, after they were anointed with the Holy Spirit, a word of sin was found.

The occasion for error did not arise for Peter from Christ's words, because Christ did not say simply ἑπτάκις. But ἑπτάκις τῆς ἡμέρας, which in the manner of the Hebrews signifies as often as possible, as in Prov. XXIV. 16, Psal. CXIX. 165. But perhaps it was from the tradition of the Jews, who did not extend the necessity of forgiving beyond this, even in sins that were not lighter. Which Grotius observed not badly. Nor will it be inconvenient to say that mention was made of the number seven because this number is sacred and of perfection. Concerning it, there is also no doubt that ἕως ἑβδομηκοντάκις ἑπτά is not seventy times seven, but up to the number of seventy-seven: And Grotius rightly taught that the Syrian also indicates this here, however much it may have seemed otherwise to others: nor did he inconveniently warn that Christ opposes this number as being much greater than the number seven according to the custom of the Hebrews, just as the same opposition is found in Gen. IV. 24. According to the LXX Interpreters ἑβδομηκοντάκις ἑπτά. But whether the Hebrew text there should also be rendered in that way, could be a matter of doubt. Grotius certainly wishes שִׁבְעָתַיִם וְשִׁבְעִים to be explained as seventy times, and that same seven times. But he does not deny that Josephus understood it otherwise. Our B. Luther also rendered it there as sieben undsiebentzig mahl. The Vulgate also seems to be ambiguous. But this is beyond doubt, that a certain number is put for an uncertain one, and that it is indicated that one must forgive one's brother as often as he repents, just as God forgives us most often and infinitely when we truly repent of our sins. Nor does that saying of Chrysostom, χιλιάκις μετανοήσας εἴσελθε, imply anything else, which Grotius judges should be softened by a benign interpretation, as it was wrongly spoken as if in the heat of the struggle against the Novatians; namely, not about rashly receiving those who have relapsed a thousand times to the assembly of the Church; but concerning the most gracious mercy of GOD, not receiving a thousand times, provided only that we have done penance, Chrysostom especially wished this to be said: but he did not exclude such as have relapsed very often, whom the Ancient Church, but also defiled by crimes on repeated occasions, received not only to the profession of penance, but even to the communion: since the Church is an imitator of God, and ought not simply to exclude those whom Christ receives. Indeed, it is rightly cautioned that what is said here by Christ about forgiving offenses should not be rashly extended to Ecclesiastical judgments concerning more serious crimes; it is one thing to give of one's own, another to give of the public; and it matters much whether you privately receive a friend, or relax the rigor of common discipline, in which both the honor and health of the Church in great part consist. Nevertheless, because Christ proposes to us the example of God for imitation, who receives a sinner into grace as often as he himself, having relapsed, does penance, the Church ought also in that to imitate the example of divine grace; not so that all rigor of discipline perishes, but that, with discipline preserved, such a temperament may be applied, lest the sinner, having done penance, perish by despair. Justin certainly teaches concerning God that He, out of immense mercy, forgives us seventy times seven: Grace, he says, has established in the world the physician of sinners, penance itself: which obtains the power of healing even those who have fallen seventy-seven times, if only they induce their mind to use the counsel or prescription of penance. St. Athanasius, Questions to Antioch, XCIII. Vol. II. p. 307. Having perceived, he says, the mutability of human nature (the Greek text has τὸ ἔυτρεπτον τῇς ἀνθρωπίνης Φύσεως), even if a man has fallen a thousand times, and a thousand times has repented, he by no means casts him off. For He who announced to Peter that one must forgive a brother seventy times seven, He Himself will much more forgive a man who repents even seven thousand times. Origen also in this place: Christ, he says, understanding our innumerable falls in His service, commands that the number of our indulgences toward those who harm us also be defined as none. Chrysostom says that by this certain number the Lord shows an infinite force of perfect virtue and patience. See what we have disputed against the Novatians and Socinians in the Exegesis of the Augsburg Confession, article XII, chapter II, thesis I, and following. The addition which Grotius observes to be found in this place in the Hebrew Code of the Nazarenes is without doubt spurious. For to those words: Even I say to you up to seventy times seven, these things have been stitched on: For even in the Prophets, after they were anointed with the Holy Spirit, a word of sin was found.

Latin:

Vers. 22. ἕως ἑβδομηκοντάκις ἑπτά] Non est hoc septua- gies & septies, sed ad numerum usque septuagies se- ptenum. Neque aliud voluit Syrus cum dixit: עַדְמָא לִשְׁבְעִין וְבַעְנִין שְׁבַע שְׁבַע id est ad tempora usque septuagies septena: non ut aliis visum est interpretari, qua- tuordecim vicibus septuagies. Nam שֶׁבַע שֶׁבַע non significat quatuordecim, sed septena, ut Genes. VII. 2. quomodo δύο δύο pro binas dixit Marcus cap. VI. 7. Oppo- nit Christus hunc numerum ut multo majorem septenario ex more Hebræorum. Nam eadem oppositio invenitur Gen. IV. 24. ubi quod est שִׁבְעָתַיִם וְשִׁבְעִים inter- pretandum est septuagies & id ipsum septies. Apud LXX. itidem ut hic ἑβδομηκοντάκις ἑπτά, quanquam aliter acce- pit Josephus. Cæterum quod hic de donandis offensioni- bus a Christo dicitur, temere ad Ecclesiastica judicia de gra- vioribus delictis nolim extendi. Aliud enim est de suo largiri, aliud de publico: multumque interest privatim re- cipias amicum, an rigorem laxes communis disciplinæ, in qua & honos & sanitas Ecclesiæ magna ex parte consistit. Quare vetustissimi Christianorum in idololatriam, homi- cidium aut adulterium lapsos, Dei quidem misericordiæ commendabant, non tamen ut ad communionem admit- terent. Illis criminibus fœdatos non ad solam pœniten- tiæ professionem, sed post longi temporis experimenta ad communionem recipiebant: iterum aut sæpius relapsos non item. Chrysostomi igitur illud χιλιάκις μετανοήσας εἴσελθε dictum in calore certaminis adversus Novatianos benigna interpretatione molliendum est. Locus autem hic Evangelii in Hebræo Codice, qualis a Nazarenis servaba- tur, sic habebat: Si peccaverit frater tuus in verbo, & satis tibi fecerit, septies in die suscipe eum. Dixit ei Simon discipu- lus ejus: Septies in die? Respondit Dominus & dixit ei: Etiam ego dico tibi usque ad septuagies septies. Etenim in Prophetis quoque postquam uncti sunt Spiritu Sancto, inventus est sermo peccati.

Non è Christi verbis occasio errandi nata Pe- tro, quia non dixit simpliciter Christus ἑπτάκις. Sed ἑπτάκις τῆς ἡμέρας, quod Ebræorum more signifi- cat quam sæpissime, ut Prov. XXIV. 16. Psal. CXIX. 165. Sed fortassis ex Judæorum traditione, qui non ultra extendebant condonandi necessitatem in peccatis etiam non levioribus. Quod non male observavit Grotius. Neque inconveniens erit, dicere, mentionem factam septenarii, quia nu- merus hic sacer est, & perfectionis. De eo etiam dubium non est, ἕως ἑβδομηκοντάκις ἑπτά non esse septuagies & septies, sed ad numerum usque septua- gies septenum: Idemque etiam Syrum hic indicare, ut ut aliis aliter visum sit, recte docuit Grotius: nec incommode monuit, Christum hunc numerum ut multo majorem numero septenario ex more Ebræo- rum opponere, quemadmodum eadem oppositio inve- nitur Gen. IV. 24. Secundum LXX. Interpp. ἑβδο- μηκοντάκις ἑπτά. An autem ita etiam Ebræus textus ibi reddendus sit, dubium esse queat. Gro- tius sane vult שִׁבְעָתַיִם וְשִׁבְעִים exponi debere se- ptuagies, & id ipsum septies. At non diffitetur, a- liter accepisse Josephum. B. Lutherus etiam no- ster ibi reddidit sieben undsiebentzig mahl. Vul- gata etiam ambigua videtur esse. Id autem in- dubium, numerum certum poni pro incerto, at- que id indicari, sæpius, & toties, quoties fratrem pœnitet, condonandum ei esse, quemadmodum sæpissime, & infinities Deus nobis remittit, cum ve- re de peccatis nostris pœnitemus. Neque a- liud innuit Chrysostomi illud χιλιάκις μετανοή- σας εἴσελθε, quod perperam ceu in calore certaminis adversus Novarianos dictum benigna interpretatione molliendum esse, censet Grotius; nimirum non de temere recipiendis millies relapsis ad concionem Ecclesiæ; sed de gratiosissima DEI misericordia, millies non recipiente, dum modo pœnitentiam egerimus, imprimis hoc di- ctum voluit Chrysostomus: sed neque exclusit tales, qui sæpius relapsi, à communione Ec- clesiæ Vetus Ecclesia, sed iteratis etiam vici- bus criminibus fœdatos non ad solam pœniten- tiæ professionem, verum etiam ad communio- nem recepit: quum Ecclesia Dei imitatrix sit, nec eos, quos Christus recipit, ipsa excludere debeat simpliciter. Equidem probe monetur, quod hic de donandis offensionibus à Christo dici- tur, temere ad Ecclesiastica judicia de graviori- bus delictis extendendum non esse; aliud esse de suo largiri, aliud de publico: multumque in- teresse, privatim recipias amicum, an rigorem relaxes communis disciplinæ, in qua & honos & sanitas Ecclesiæ magna ex parte consistit. Verun- tamen quia Dei exemplum Christus ad imita- tionem nobis proponit, qui peccatorem in gra- tiam recipit, quoties ipse relapsus pœnitentiam agit, in eo etiam imitari exemplum gratiæ divi- næ Ecclesia debet; non ut rigor disciplinæ omnis pereat, sed ut servata disciplina tale adhibea- tur temperamentum, ne acta pœnitentia de- sperando pereat peccator. De Deo certe Ju- stinus docet, eum pro immensa misericordia ἑβδο- μηκοντάκις ἑπτὰ nobis condonare: Gratia, in- quit, in mundo medicum peccantium probatum constituit, pœnitentiam ipsam: quæ etiam septuage- sies septies lapsos sanandi potestatem obtinet, si modo in animum illi inducant pœnitentiæ uti consi- lio, vel præscripto. S. Athanasius quæst. ad An- tioch. XCIII. Tom. II. pag. 307. perspecta, in- quit, mutabilitate naturæ humanæ (τὸ ἔυτρεπτον τῇς ἀνθρωπίνης Φύσεως, habet Græcus textus) etsi millies homo lapsus sit, & millies resipuerit, ne- quaquam eum abjicit. Qui enim Petro annun- ciavit, septuagies septies fratri ignoscendum, multo amplius ipse, & vel septies millies homini ignoverit resipiscenti. Origenes etiam in h. l. Christus, inquit, intelligens innumerabiles nostros in ejus ob- sequio lapsus, nostris quoque erga eos, qui nos læ- dunt, indulgentiis numerum præcipit definiendum esse nullum. Chrysostomus hoc certo numero Do- minum infinitam vim perfectæ virtutis ac patientiæ ostendere, ait. Vid. quæ contra Novatianos & Socinistas Exeg. Aug. Confess. artic. XII. cap. II. th. I. seqq. disputavimus. Additamen- tum, quod in hoc loco in Nazarenorum Ebræo Codice reperiri Grotius observat, sine dubio no- thum est. Illis enim verbis: Etiam ego dico tibi usque ad septuagies septies hæc affuta sunt: Etenim in Prophetis quoque, postquam uncti sunt Spiritu Sancto, inventus est sermo peccati.

## 18:23
Verse 23. διὰ τῦτο] an ellipsis: for διὰ τῦτο λέγω ὑμῖν ὅτι ὡμοιώθη.

ἡ βασιλεία τῶν ὅρανῶν] A thing is compared to a thing: thus, he says, the matter will be in my kingdom, as if there were some King, and what follows. The heavenly kingdom is the time after the advent of the Messiah. A not dissimilar comparison is in Libanius concerning the Antiochene sedition: ὅσις ἐν ιοικίταις βύλεται θεοῖς, ἀφιεὶς τιμωρίας χαρίστω μᾶλλον ἢ λαμβάνων.

Ἀνθρώπῳ βασιλεῖ] That is, to a certain king, as below XX. 1, in the way that איש is accustomed to be taken by the Hebrews.

συνάραι λόγον] To settle accounts, as the Jurisconsults and Seneca speak.

μετὰ τῶν δύλων ἁυτῦ] Where it concerns kings, all subjects are called servants, but especially those who are in courtly service, as I Kings IX. 22, where the word עבד is found in the same clause with a double and indeed opposite meaning. But that I prefer ministers to be understood here is made clear by the whole series of the narrative, which you could not quite correctly apply to slaves, especially those things which are in verses 28 and 29.

Latin:

Vers. 23. διὰ τῦτο] ἑλλειψις: pro διὰ τῦτο λέγω ὑμῖν ὅτι ὡμοιώθη.

ἡ βασιλεία τῶν ὅρανῶν] Res rei comparatur: ita, inquit, se res habebit in regno meo, ut si Rex sit aliquis, & quæ se- quuntur. Regnum cœleste est tempus post adventum Messiæ. Comparatio non dissimilis apud Libanium de seditione Antiochena: ὅσις ἔν ιοικίταις βύλεται θεοῖς, ἀφιεὶς τιμωρίας χαρίστω μᾶλλον ἢ λαμβάνων.

Ἀνθρώπῳ βασιλεῖ] Id est βασιλεῖ τινι, ut infra XX. 1. quo- modo איש solet sumi Hebræis.

συνάραι λόγον] Rationes dispungere, ut Jurisconsulti & Seneca loquuntur.

μετὰ τῶν δύλων ἁυτῦ] Ubi de regibus agitur, servi di- cuntur omnes subditi, sed præcipue qui in aulico sunt ministerio, ut I. Reg. IX. 22. ubi vox עבד in eodem commate significatu duplici & quidem opposito inveni- tur. Ut autem ministros hic malim intelligi, facit tota narrationis series, quam mancipiis non satis recte aptave- ris, præsertim ea quæ sunt commate 28. & 29.

## 18:24
Verse 24. Μυρίων ταλάντων. The Greeks call a talent what the Hebrews call כִּכָּר: which if it be of silver, is 3000 shekels, that is, 1500 Joachimics: if of gold, it is 18000 Joachimics, as we taught in Vol. I of the Illustrated Bible, p. 184, seq. Wherefore 10,000 talents of silver are 150 tons of gold; as many talents of gold are 1800 tons of gold, as we call it in the ton of gold, counting one hundred thousand Joachimics.

Latin:

Vers. 24. Μυρίων ταλάντων. Τάλαντον Græci, quod Ebræi כִּכָּר vocant: quod si argenti sit 3000. Siclorum est, hoc est, 1500. Joachimicorum: si auri, est 18000. Joachi- micorum, ut Tom. I. Bibl. Illustr. p. 184. seq. do- cuimus. Quapropter 10000. talenta argenti sunt 150. tonnæ auri; totidem talenta auri sunt 1800. tonnæ auri, ut vocamus in auri tonnam computa- tis centum mille Joachimicis.

## 18:25
Verse 25. πραθῆναι] Free men with their wife and offspring, when they were not able to pay, became the slaves of their creditors, by Hebrew customs, which we are taught in IV Kings IV. 1. But also Josephus, most expert in the law of Moses according to the custom of his country, interprets the law concerning a thief: let him who has stolen a beast pay a fourfold penalty, except for an ox; but let him pay a fivefold penalty for that; and he who is unable to settle the penalty, let him be a slave to those who condemned him. The same notes in Antiquities XVI, c. 1, that Jews could not be sold except to Jews, nor indeed did that servitude last except for six years, arguing Herod of illegality, who had sold certain directarii for export. But slaves, not even excluding those whom parents had sold into servitude, could be sold by their masters, outside of that which is provided concerning a daughter sold in Exodus XXI. 8. The king therefore threatens sale by the right of a creditor.

καὶ τὴν γυναῖκα ἀυτοῦ καὶ τὰ τέκνα] For hands could be laid upon them too, as appears from the places already mentioned.

Latin:

Vers. 25. πραθῆναι] Liberi homines cum uxore & pro- le ubi solvendo non essent servi fiebant creditorum, mo- ribus Hebræis, quod docemur IV. Reg. IV. 1. Sed & Jo- sephus more patriæ peritissimus Mosis legem de fure inter- pretatur : βόσκημα δὲ ἐκλέψας τετραπλῆν τὴν ζημίαν ἀπο- τινύτω, πλὴν βοός· πενταπλῆ δὲ ὑπὲρ τότε καταβαλέτω· ὁ δὲ τὸ ἐπιτίμιον ἀπορῶν διαλύσασθαι, δῦλος ἔσω τοῖς καταδι- κασαμένοις. Idem Originum XVI. c. 1. notat vendi Judæos nisi Judæis non potuisse, neque vero durasse eam servitu- tem nisi in sexennium, Herodem παρανομίας arguens, qui directarios quosdam vendiderat ἐπ' ἐξαγωγῇ. At servi, ne iis quidem exceptis quos parentes in servitutem vendide- rant, vendi à dominis poterant, extra id quod de filia ven- dita cavetur Exod. XXI. 8. Minatur igitur rex venditio- nem jure creditoris.

καὶ τὴν γυναῖκα ἀυτοῦ καὶ τὰ τέκνα] Nam & istis manus in- jici poterat, ut ex dictis jam locis apparet.

## 18:26
Vers. 26. μακροθύμησον] The Hellenists call him μακρόθυμον whom the Hebrews call אֶרֶךְ אַפַּיִם, as can be seen in Ps. 86:14. In which sense both that noun and the verb μακροθυμεῖν are to be found several times in these books: and the Syriac follows this here. There is, however, a place where it signifies patient expectation without the meaning of anger, as in Heb. 6:15 and Jas. 5:7, which is how the Latin translates it here, more aptly to the sense, if I am not mistaken.

Latin:

Vers. 26. μακροθύμησον] μακρόθυμον vocant Helleni- stæ quem Hebræi אֶרֶךְ אַפַּיִם ut videre est Ps. LXXXVI. 14. Quo sensu & nomen istud & verbum μακροθυμεῖν ali- quoties in his libris invenire est: idque hic sequitur Syrus. Est tamen ubi fine iræ significatione patientem exspecta- tionem significat, ut Hebr. VI. 15. & Jac. V. 7. quomodo hic vertit Latinus, ad sensum, ni fallor, aptius.

## 18:27
Vers. 27. τὸ δάνειον] that is, ὀφειλὴν, as is said below. For just as a thing lent is properly mutuum to the Latins, from which it began to be transferred to other things, so is δάνειον to the Greeks. There is an old maxim: Τὰ δάνεια δούλες τὲς ἐλευθέρες ποιεῖ: which Publius translates thus: Alienum æs homini ingenuo acerba servitus (Debt is a bitter slavery to a free man).

Latin:

Vers. 27. τὸ δάνειον] id est ὀφειλὴν ut infra dicitur. Nam sicut res credita proprie Latinis est mutuum, inde ad alia transferri cœpit, ita δάνειον Græcis. Vetus est sen- tentia : Τὰ δάνεια δούλες τὲς ἐλευθέρες ποιεῖ: quamita vertit Publius: Alienum æs homini ingenuo acerba servitus.

## 18:28
Vers. 28. ὅ,τι ὀφείλεις] I would not dare to disturb this reading of the ancient codices. For εἰ is often accustomed to signify not a condition but a generality.

Latin:

Vers. 28. ὅ,τι ὀφείλεις] Non ausim movere hanc vete- rum codicum lectionem. Nam solet εἰ sæpe non condi- tionem sed generalitatem significare.

## 18:34
Vers. 34. τοῖς βασανισταῖς] Cάσανον in these books signifies not only an examination, but every kind of torture and distress whatsoever; as can be seen above in ch. 8:29, ch. 14:24, Mark 5:7, ch. 6:48, Luke 8:28, 2 Pet. 2:8, Rev. 18:7, and more often in the same book. Wherefore I think that by βασανιστὰς here are meant δεσμοφύλακας (jailers). Thus what follows will fit perfectly, ἕως ἀποδῷ πᾶν τὸ ὀφειλόμενον ἀυτῷ, so that the sense is the same as above in ch. 5:25, 26 and Luke 12:58, 59. For the prison itself is also called a torture of the body in the last book of the Code, title 'Qui bonis cedunt possunt'. The word שׁוֹטֵר, from which the name by which the Syriac translates τὲς βασανιστὰς is derived, means 'to draw' in Chaldean, as Joseph Kimchi notes. Moreover, that king here uses not only the right of a creditor, but also that of a judge.

Latin:

Vers. 34. τοῖς βασανισταῖς] Cάσανον in his libris non quæ- stionem solum, sed omnem omnino cruciatum atque molestiam significat; ut videre est supra c. IIX. 29. c. XIV. 24. Marc. V. 7. c. VI. 48. Luc. IIX. 28. 2. Petr. II. 8. Apoc. XIIX. 7. & eodem libro sæpius. Quare βασανιστὰς hic puto dici δεσμοφύλακας. Ita optime conveniet quod sequitur ἕως ἀποδῷ πᾶν τὸ ὀφειλόμενον ἀυτῷ, ut sensus sit idem qui su- pra c. V. 25. 26. & Luc. XII. 58. 59. Nam & ipse carcer vo- catur corporis cruciatus L. ult. c. qui bon. ced. poss. Ver- bum שׁוֹטֵר unde nomen quo transfert τὲς βασανιστὰς dedu- xit Syrus Chaldæis est trahere ut Joseph Kimchi notat. U- titur autem hic rex ille non solo creditoris jure, sed & judi- cis.

## 18:35
Vers. 35. ὕτως] This is a full comparison. For it has an ἀνταπόδοσιν (retribution), the sense of which is the same as in those words of James: ἡ κρίσις ἀνίλεως τῷ μὴ ποιήσαντι ἔλεος (judgment is without mercy to him who has not shown mercy): and above in chapter 6:15, except that here it is added that benefits already received will be of no profit to the unmerciful from divine indulgence. Whence it is often debated whether sins once forgiven are imputed again. The ancients clearly disagree among themselves. For some think there is nothing absurd in saying that the remission which is in this life has within itself the condition of new obedience, a great part of which is leniency toward other men: and that what was given under a condition vanishes if that is not fulfilled: or certainly, just as donations even purely bestowed are accustomed to be revoked on account of extraordinary injuries committed against the laws: so also this benefit of pardon is revoked: or rather taken away by way of punishment, just as goods, even those acquired by full right, are accustomed to be taken away from the condemned. Nor do they think it an obstacle that the gifts of God are said to be ἀμεταμέλητα (irrevocable): for that can rightly be said even of the liberality with which God gave the land of Canaan to the Hebrew people, because it did not stand by God that that people, persisting in the covenant, did not possess the promise, Neh. 9:32, 33. Others prefer the view that an obligation once extinguished does not revive, but that on account of subsequent crimes [as Prosper speaks] a man is affected with that death which was owed to him on account of those things which had been remitted. There are also those who reconcile both, by the temperament of a middle opinion. It pleases these that sins once remitted are not punished in themselves, but indirectly and by a certain consequence, insofar as their forgiveness increases the subsequent guilt by the crime of both pertinacity and ungrateful mind: which also the Jurisconsults establish against those who, having obtained pardon from a Prince, either fall back into the same crimes, or commit offenses against the Prince himself.

Grotius raises that dispute accustomed to be moved here, whether sins once remitted are again imputed? The ancients, he says, manifestly disagree among themselves: Some think that the remission which is in this life has the condition of new obedience; and that what was given under a condition vanishes if that is not fulfilled. But he does not teach who those are who think so. Nor does Scripture anywhere hand down that remission is made under that condition: even though it requires new obedience as the fruit of faith and justice from those who have obtained remission, as a proof of gratitude, and so that they do not fall from grace in turn by staining their conscience with sins. And the parable teaches that the debt was simply remitted to this servant. Therefore, sins are also simply forgiven us by God. Others therefore, as Grotius reports, although he does not report who they are, just as gifts, even those purely bestowed, are accustomed to be revoked on account of extraordinary injuries committed against the laws, so they say that this benefit of forgiveness is revoked, or rather taken away by way of punishment, just as the goods of the condemned, even those acquired by full right, are accustomed to be taken away. But neither that revocation is to be admitted, nor the punishment of those things which have once been forgiven by God. For the gifts of God are ἀμεταμέλητα. And we see in the example of this King, that God remits both the guilt and the punishment in full. That remission is indeed described in sacred writings in such a way that God wills to forget our sins, to remember them no more, to cast them behind his back, to throw them into the depth of the sea, and to blot them out. Whence neither is that to be approved, which he observes pleases others more, who acknowledge that an obligation once extinguished does not revive again, but on account of the latest crimes (as Prosper speaks) they think a man is affected by that death which was owed to him on account of those things which had been remitted. But what kind of forgiveness of guilt and punishment would this be, if the punishment which was owed for the remitted guilt must also be exacted, and is exacted, however new offenses may be added? Finally, he commemorates those who, as he thinks, reconcile the others by the temperament of a middle opinion: namely, that sins once remitted are not punished in themselves, but indirectly, and by a certain consequence, insofar as their forgiveness increases the subsequent guilt by the crime of both pertinacity and ungrateful mind: as the Jurisconsults establish against those who, having obtained pardon from a Prince, either fall back into the same crimes, or commit offenses against the Prince himself. Grotius defines nothing: but this latter opinion is altogether more probable. Thomas p. III. q. LXXXVIII. art. I. n. VII. makes these conclusions; The first holds thus: Since the work of GOD cannot be made void by the work of man, the stain and eternal punishment of guilt do not simply return, insofar as they proceeded from the acts of sins formerly dismissed, unless insofar as a man through a subsequent sin returns to the former state, in which he was deprived of grace and charity, and they are contained in the subsequent sin virtually. He explains this conclusion, however, thus: It happens, however, that the subsequent act of sin virtually contains the guilt of the prior sin, insofar as, namely, some man sinning a second time, from this very fact seems to sin more gravely than he had sinned before: according to that Rom. II. According to your hardness, and impenitent heart you treasure up for yourself wrath in the day of wrath, from this namely alone, that the goodness of God is despised, which waits for repentance. But the goodness of GOD is much more despised if, after the remission of a prior sin, the sin is repeated a second time: how much greater a benefit it is to remit a sin than to sustain a sinner. Thus therefore through a sin subsequent to repentance, the guilt of sins previously dismissed returns in a certain way, not insofar as it was caused by those sins previously dismissed, but insofar as it was caused by the last sin perpetrated, which is aggravated by the prior sins. And this is not for dismissed sins to return simply, but to return in a certain respect, insofar as namely they are virtually contained in the subsequent sin. The other conclusion of Thomas is this: Sins dismissed through repentance are said to return through a subsequent sin, insofar as by reason of ingratitude, their guilt is virtually contained in the subsequent guilt. Concerning which let the Interpreters of Thomas be consulted, and those who have published Disputations on him. One must take care, however, lest with the Papists, one establishes that after the remission of guilt, punishment still remains to be paid: because even from this parable we learn that God, after the manner of this King, mercifully remits and forgives to debtors not only the guilt, but also all the punishment. Great, says Chrysostom, is the power of repentance, but greater is that of divine clemency. The former frees the servant from guilt. The kindness of GOD remitted the entire debt to him. If the Papists object: But yet he demanded payment. It is answered that this pertains to legal exaction, but the Lord exhibited Evangelical grace in the subjoined forgiveness of punishment and guilt, and therefore Chrysostom answers thus.
