That the Lord ordered his sum to be made up for him by the price of the servant himself being sold, was not demanded of him absolutely or simply, or as if he really wished that to be fulfilled, but that he might terrify the servant with that threat, and lead him to implore grace from the Lord, ἵνα τὸν δοῦλον ἐκφοβήσῃ καὶ ἐς ρὸς παράκλησιν ἐπιστρέψῃ. Nor does the satisfaction in that prison, until he should pay the whole debt, imply: but eternal torture: It is manifest that he would never pay; who, ungrateful as he was, would always be going to be: It remains therefore that he be punished eternally, divine justice thus decreeing, as this Chrysostom says again. For he had nothing with which he might pay, although he promised that he would pay, because this is the custom of debtors, to promise that they will pay, so that they may be freed from present evils: as Nicetas says.

The objection of the Socinians, which they seek from this parable, namely that remission is made without any satisfaction, there is no reason for us to touch upon here. We have discussed it elsewhere. Let it only be observed that parabolic theology is not argumentative: nor should all the circumstances of a parable be heeded or pressed in its application, provided that account is taken only of the principal scope. (2.) Since satisfaction is demanded by the law by virtue of divine justice, which the King here also exacted from the servant, either that satisfaction has been performed by Christ the Mediator, or divine justice must be endangered. (3.) The cause of justification is not explained in this place; it is only taught that the pardon of sins is gratuitous, which with respect to us is truly gratuitous, because satisfaction can no more be performed by us than the ten thousand talents, that is, sixty tons of gold, could be paid by that servant; even if he had sold both himself and his own. (4). Sins are indeed called debts, but only figuratively, and therefore the nature of a pecuniary debt and of a fault or sin is not the same in all respects: because to remit the former is a matter of liberality, but the latter are pardoned not from liberality, but from grace and mercy: Those can be given by simple munificence and liberality without injury to justice and detriment to the public good; but that these should not be remitted by absolute grace, justice and the observance of the public good forbid. See Socinism. proflig. sect. VI. subsect. II. art. II. tit. III. quæst. I. But because Crellius, Contr. Grot. de satisf. Christ. p. 317, objects that even if some remission could concur with satisfaction, it will not, however, be a remission of the whole debt, nor will it be so called, which is nevertheless expressly said concerning the remission of our debt in Matt. 18:32. But if remission is to be reconciled with payment and compensation in this matter, it is necessary that it be said that neither the whole debt was remitted, nor the whole paid or compensated (through Christ). I reply: there is no such necessity. For, to say nothing of the fact that in law the remission of a penalty is spoken of even when full satisfaction is provided, which we noted in Disputat. de Satisfact. I. th. XIII. de Satisfact. I. th. XIII., Crellius confuses not only civil satisfaction with criminal, but also one's own with vicarious. For Christ provided payment in our stead. And therefore the payment, or compensation, of the whole debt and the remission of the whole debt can properly concur here; payment by reason of Christ, or the sponsor or mediator; remission by reason of us, or the debtors. Therefore, there is indeed no remission insofar as payment has been made: for the penalty was not remitted to Christ, but exacted from him: yet it is the same debt, and the whole of it, which is truly said to have been paid by Christ and remitted to us.

Verse 35. Τὰ παραπτώματα ἀυτῶν] The ancient codices, which have these words added, are supported by the Syriac interpreter along with Chrysostom and Theophylact. But offenses are often compared to monetary debts, not because there is not a great difference, but because just as a right of demanding arises from a debt, so from an offense a certain right seems to arise of dissolving a friendship, and he who does not use this right shows his kindness, being to that extent similar to him who frees a debtor by an acquittance. Therefore, the words χαρίζεσθαι and ἀφιέναι, and similar ones, are commonly used for both. See what is above on VI. 12.

The Vulgate version is deservedly noted for these omitted words, concerning which Beza says on this passage: The ancient interpreter does not read these, nor does Jerome: but, unless you add them, the verb ἀφιέναι will be placed absolutely, which you would hardly find elsewhere. Furthermore, I have found these written in all the Greek codices. Concerning the difference between debts and offenses, or sins, and the force of the verb χαρίζεσθαι against the Socinians, we have dealt with this in the disputations on the Nature of Satisfaction and Socinism Refuted, in the place cited.

Latin:

Vers. 35. ὕτως] Hæc plena est comparatio. Habet e- nim ἀνταπόδοσιν cujus sensus idem est qui in illis Jacobi verbis : ἡ κρίσις ἀνίλεως τῷ μὴ ποιήσαντι ἔλεος : & supra capit. VI. 15. nisi quod hic additur jam accepta benefi- cia divinæ indulgentiæ nihil profutura immisericordibus. Unde disputari solet an peccata semel remissa iterum imputentur. Veteres manifeste inter se dissen- tiunt. Alii enim existimant nihil in eo esse absurdi si di- camus remissionem quæ in hac vita sit, habere in se con- ditionem novæ obedientiæ, cujus magna pars est lenitas in homines alios: quod autem sub conditione datum est, ea non impleta evanescere: aut certe sicut donationes etiam pure collatæ revocari solent, ob eximias injurias legi- bus proditas: ita & beneficium hoc condonationis revo- cari: aut potius in modum pœnæ auferri, quomodo da- minatis bona etiam pleno jure quæsita auferri solent. Nec obstare arbitrantur quod dona Dei dicantur esse ἀμεταμέ- λητα : nam id recte dici posse etiam de liberalitate qua ter- ram Canaanis Deus donavit Hebræ populo, quia per Deum non stetit, quominus ille populus perstans in fœdere pro- missu potiretur, Neh. IX. 32. 33. Aliis magis placet extin- ctam semel obligationem non reviviscere, sed propter po- strema crimina [ut Prosper loquitur] affici hominem ea morte quæ ei propter ea quæ remissa erant debebatur. Sunt & qui utrosque concilient, mediæ sententiæ temperamen- to. His placet remissa semel peccata non per se puniri, sed indirecte & per consequentiam quandam, quatenus eorum condonatio auget culpam sequentem & pertinaciæ & in- grati animi crimine: quod & Jurisconsulti statuunt adver- sus eos qui veniam à Principe consecuti, aut in eadem cri- mina recidunt, aut in ipsum Principem delinquunt.

Disputationem illam hîc moveri solitam mo- vet Grotius, an peccata semel remissa iterum impu- tentur? Veteres, dicit, manifeste inter se dis- sentire: Nonnullos existimare, remissionem, quæ in hac vita sit, habere conditionem novæ obedientiæ; quod autem sub conditione datum, ea non impleta evanescere. Sed quinam ita censeant, non do- cet. Neque uspiam Scriptura remissionem sub conditione illa fieri tradit: etsi novam obedien- tiam ceu fructum fidei & justitiæ ab illis, qui re- missionem adepti sunt, in documentum gratitu- dinis, ac ne gratia vicissim excidant, per peccata fœdantes conscientiam, requirat. Et simplici- ter huic servo remissum fuisse debitum parabola docet. Itaque & simpliciter à Deo condonantur nobis peccata. Alii ergo, referente Grotio, quamvis nec illos referat, quinam sint, sicut do- nationes, etiam pure collatæ revocari solent, ob eximias injurias legibus proditas, ita & beneficium hoc condonationis revocari dicunt, aut potius in modum pœnæ auferri, quomodo damnatis bona, etiam pleno jure quæsita auferri solent. Sed nec illa revoca- tio admittenda, nec eorum, quæ semel à Deo con- donata sunt, punitio. Dona enim Dei ἀμετα- μέλητα sunt. Et videmus in exemplo Regis hu- jus, Deum in solidum & culpam & pœnam remit- tere. Illa vero remissio ita in sacris describitur, quod Deus peccatorum nostrorum oblivisci, non am- plius meminisse, post tergum ea rejicere, in profun- dum maris abjicere, ac delere velit. Unde nec illud probandum, quod aliis magis placere observat, qui agnoscunt, extinctam semel obligationem non amplius reviviscere, sed propter postrema crimina (ut Prosper loquitur) putant hominem ea affici mor- te, quæ ei propter ea, quæ remissa erant, debeba- tur. At qualis hæc foret culpæ & pœnæ condona- tio, si & pœna, quæ ob culpam remissam debe- batur, exigenda sit, & exigatur, utut novis acce- dentibus delictis? Denique eos commemorat, qui, ut putat, cæteros mediæ sententiæ temperamento, con- ciliant: nimirum remissa semel peccata non per se puniri, sed indirecte, & per consequentiam quan- dam, quatenus eorum condonatio auget culpam se- quentem & pertinaciæ, & ingrati animi crimine: ut JCti statuunt adversus eos, qui veniam à Princi- pe consecuti, aut in eadem crimina recidunt, aut in i- psum Principem delinquunt. Nihil definit Gro- tius: sed postrema hæc sententia omnino proba- bilior est. Thomas p. III. q. LXXXVIII. art. I. n. VII. has facit conclusiones; Prima ita habet: Cum opus DEI per opus hominis irritari non possit, macula & æterna pœna reatus simpliciter non rede- unt, quatenus ex actibus peccatorum olim dimisso- rum proveniebant, nisi quatenus homo per peccatum sequens redit ad priorem statum, in quo erat gratia & charitate privatus, & ipsa in peccato sequenti vir- tute continentur. Hanc conclusionem autem ita ex- plicat: Contingit autem, quod sequens actus pec- cati virtualiter continet reatum prioris pecca- ti, in quantum scil. aliquis homo secundo peccans, ex hoc ipso videtur gravius peccare, quam prius peccaverat: secundum illud Rom. II. Secundum duritiam tuam, & impœnitens cor thesaurizas tibi iram in die iræ, ex hoc scilicet solo, quod contemnitur Dei bonitas, quæ ad pœnitentiam expe- ctat. Multo autem magis contemnitur DEI bo- nitas, si post remissionem prioris peccati, secundo peccatum iteretur : quanto majus est beneficium peccatum remittere, quam peccatorem sustinere. Sic igitur per peccatum sequens pœnitentiam, redit quodammodo reatus peccatorum prius dimissorum, non in quantum causabatur ex illis peccatis prius di- missis, sed in quantum causabatur ex peccato ultimo perpetrato, quod aggravatur ex peccatis prioribus. Et hoc non est, peccata dimissa redire simpliciter, sed redire secundum quid, in quantum scilicet virtuali- ter in peccato sequenti continentur. Altera Thomæ conclusio hæc est: Peccata per pœnitentiam dimis- sa per sequens peccatum redire dicuntur, quatenus ingratitudinis ratione, eorum reatus in sequenti cul- pa virtualiter continetur. De quibus conferan- tur Interpretes Thomæ, & qui in eum Disputa- tiones edidêre. Cavendum tamen, ne cum Pon- tificiis, post remissionem culpæ pœnam adhuc luen- dam restare quis statuat: quia vel ex hac parabo- la discimus Deum adinstar hujus Regis debitori- bus non tantum culpam, sed & pœnam omnem misericorditer remittere, ac condonare. Ma- gna, inquit Chrysostomus, pœnitentiæ, major tamen clementiæ divinæ vis est. Prior servum culpa solvit. DEI benignitas universum ipsi remi- sit debitum. Si objiciant Pontificii: Atqui solu- tionem postulavit. Respondetur id ad legalem ex- actionem pertinet, Evangelicam autem gratiam in subjuncta condonatione pœnæ, & culpæ ex- hibuit Dominus, ideoque ita respondet Chryso- stomus. Quod pretio servi ipsius venditi confici sibi jusserit Dominus suam summam, non absolute vel simpliciter, vel q. reipsa id impleri vellet, ab ipso postulatum est, sed ut terreret ista comminatione servum, & ad implorandam à Domino gratiam per- duceret; ἵνα τὸν δοῦλον ἐκφοβήσῃ καὶ ἐς ρὸς παρα- κλησιν ἐπιστρέψῃ. Neque satisfactionem in carce- re illa, quoad usque redderet universum debitum, important: sed æternam torturam: Manifestum est, redditurum nunquam; qui ingratus ut erat, semper esset futurus: Superest igitur, ut æternum puniatur justitia divina sic decernente, ut iterum hic Chrysostomus. Nihil enim habuit, quod redderet, licet se redditurum promiserit, quia hic debitorum mos est, promittere, se reddituros, ut præsentibus ma- lis liberentur: dicente Niceta.

Socinianorum objectionem, quam ex hac para- bola petunt, quod nempe citra satisfactionem ul- lam fiat remissio, non est, quod hic tangamus. Dif- cussimus eam alibi. Observetur tantum, quod Theologia parabolica non sit argumentativa: nec omnes parabolæ circumstantiæ in applicatione at- tendi, vel urgeri debeant, dum solum principalis scopi ratio habeatur. (2.) Quum postuletur à lege satisfactio vi divinæ justitiæ, quam hic etiam Rex à ministro exegit, aut præstita illa est per Christum Mediatorem, aut justitiam divinam periclitari o- portet. (3.) Non explicatur hoc loco causa justi- ficationis, solum gratuitam esse peccatorum con- donationem docetur, quæ respectu nostri vere gratuita est, quia tam à nobis præstari nequit satisfactio, quam à servo illo solvi haud pote- rant decem talentorum millia, hoc est sexagin- ta tonnæ auri; etiamsi & se, & suos vendi- disset. (4). Peccata nominantur quidem debi- ta, sed figurate tantum, nec ergo per omnia de- biti pecuniarii & delicti vel peccati eadem est ra- tio: quia illa remittere liberalitatis est, hæc vero non è liberalitate, sed è gratia & miseri- cordia condonantur: Illa simplici munificentia, & liberalitate donari possunt citra læsionem justi- tiæ publicique boni detrimentum; hæc vero ne absoluta gratia remittantur, justitia, bonique publici observatio prohibent. Videat. Socinism. proflig. sect. VI. subsect. II. art. II. tit. III. quæst. I. Quia vero Crellius Contr. Grot. de satisf. Christ. p. 317. excipit, etiamsi remissio aliqua concurre- re queat cum satisfactione, non erit tamen ea totius debiti remissio, nec ita appellabitur, quod tamen de remissione nostri debiti expresse dicitur Matth. XIIX. 32. Si autem remissio cum solutione, ac compensatione in hoc negotio concilianda sit, neces- se est, ut dicatur, nec totum debitum remissum es- se, nec totum solutum, aut compensatum (per Christum) Resp. nulla hæc necessitas. Nam ut taceamus, in jure remissionem pœnæ dici etiam, ubi plena præstatur satisfactio, quod Disputat. de Satisfact. I. th. XIII. notavimus, confundi- tur à Crellio non tantum satisfactio civilis cum cri- minali: sed propria quoque cum vicaria. Quia Christus vice nostrûm præstitit solutionem. Id- eoque concurrere hic possunt probe totius debi- ti solutio, seu compensatio, & totius debiti re- missio; solutio ratione Christi, seu sponsoris, vel mediatoris: remissio ratione nostri, seu de- bitorum. Proinde nulla quidem est remissio, in quantum facta est solutio: Pœna enim Christo re- missa non fuit, sed exacta ab eodem: Idem ta- men est debitum, idque universum, quod à Chri- sto solutum, nobis remissum vere dicitur.

Vers. 35. Τὰ παραπτώματα ἀυτῶν] Vetustis codicibus, qui hæc verba habent adjecta, cum Chrysostomo & Theo- phylacto adstipulatur Syrus interpres. Sæpe autem of- fensæ debitis pecuniariis comparantur, non quod non multum intersit: sed quia sicut ex debito nascitur jus exi- gendi, ita ex offensa jus quoddam nasci videtur rescin- dendæ amicitiæ, quo jure qui non utitur, benignitatem suam ostendit, eatenus similis ei, qui debitorem per ac- ceptilationem liberat, Ideo & verbum χαρίζεσθαι & ἀφιέ- ναι, & similia communiter de utroque usurpantur. Vi- de quæ supra VI. 12.

Merito vulgata versio notatur ob verba hæc o- missa: de quibus ita Beza adh. l. Hæc non legit Vetus interpres, neque Hieronymus: sed, nisi ad- das, absolute ponetur verbum ἀφιέναι: quod vix alibi reperias. Præterea in omnibus Græcis codi- cibus hæc scripta inveni. De differentia inter de- bita & delicta, vel peccata, & vi verbi χαρίζε- σθαι contra Socinianos egimus in disputationibus de Natura Satisfactionis & Socinismo profligato, lo- co citato.

## 19:1 Argument
CHAPTER XIX. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

Jesus, coming into the borders of Judea beyond the Jordan, questions the Pharisees about divorce, recalls them to the primordial law of marriage, and teaches that a bill of divorce was permitted only because of the hardness of heart, and that divorce is not to be instituted outside the case of fornication, at the same time instructing them about those who are not fit for marriage. He wishes little children to be brought to him, and commands one asking what he must do to obtain eternal life to keep the commandments, and he rebukes his boasting, while he who is ordered to sell all and give to the poor, and thus follow Christ, departs sad: adding a warning of how difficult it is for a rich man to be saved. To Peter, testifying that they have followed Christ having left all things, he promises with the other Apostles that they will judge the twelve tribes of Israel, and promises a large retribution for the abandonment of all things, yet teaches that the first will be last, and the last first.

There are four parts. I. The resolution of the question about divorce, to verse 12. II. The warning about bringing little children, to verse 15. III. The testing of the rich young man and information about the rich, to verse 26. IV. The answer given to Peter concerning the retribution of the Apostles who, having followed Christ, left all things, to verse 30.

PART I. Resolution of the question about divorce.

Verse 1. ἐτέλεσεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς τοὺς λόγους τούτους] Christ first published the dogmas commanded to him by the Father in the borders of Galilee. All that follows pertains either to their explanation or to their sealing.

μετῆρεν] Thus is translated נסע Ps. 79:9.

πέραν τοῦ Ἰορδάνου] Namely at Aenon and Salim, John 10:40. See what is on Mark 10:1.

Beza does not like the passage through Peraea: The Vulgate, he says, and Erasmus [translate] word for word 'beyond the Jordan,' as if Christ, having crossed the Jordan or the Sea of Tiberias, came into Judea from Galilee through Peraea or Transjordania: which is not true, since the crowd is said to have followed him, and it is not said again that he crossed the river when he entered Judea. It is signified, therefore, that Christ did not go through Samaria, but kept his journey along the Jordan, leaving it to the right. But Ludovicus de Dieu rightly departed from Beza, concerning the parallel passage Mark 10, having it thus: Capernaum, into which he was said to have entered in chapter 9:33, and from which he is now said to have departed, lay very close to the further bank of the Jordan. So that from there they could have arrived at the further borders of Judea by a much shorter route along that bank than by the nearer shore. Add that in Matt. 11:1 Christ is said to have set out from Galilee and to have come into the border of Judea beyond the Jordan. For I prefer this with the Vulgate, rather than with Beza, on the other side of the Jordan. For if he set out from Capernaum into the borders of Judea along the nearer bank of the Jordan, with Samaria left to the right, it cannot be said that he departed from Galilee, because he would have had to cross the whole of lower Galilee, namely through the tribes of Zebulun and Issachar, in order to proceed through the tribes of Manasseh, Ephraim, and Benjamin to come into Judea. Nor does it follow from the version of the Vulgate that he came from Galilee into Judea by crossing the Jordan through Perea. Which I admit is not to be admitted, because a great crowd is said to have followed him. But the sense is that he made the journey on foot, διὰ τοῦ πέραν, as Mark speaks, along that bank which is beyond the Jordan, towards Judea. And there was no need to cross, because Capernaum lay very close to Perea. And as soon as he departed from Capernaum towards Perea, immediately μετῆρεν ἐκ τῆς Γαλιλαίας.

Latin:

CAPUT XIX. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Jesus in fines Judææ trans Iordanem veniens de divortio quæsit us Pharisæos ad legem conjugii primordialem revocat, nec nisi ob duritiem cordis permissum libellum re- pudii, & extra casum fornicationis non esse divortium instituendum docet, simul de illis, qui non idonei ad conjugium sint, instruens. Parvulos ad se adduci vult, & quærentem quid facere debeat, ut vitam æternam consequatur, jubet servare man- data, ejusque jactantiam retundit, dum omnia vendere, ac pauperibus dare, atque ita Christum sequi jussus tristis recedit: addens monitionem quam difficile sit divi- tem salvari. Petro autem testanti, quodo mnibus relictis Christum secuti sint, pollicetur cum aliis Apostolis, quod judicaturi sint XII. tribus Israëlus, & pro derelictione omnium largam retributionem promittit, primos tamen novissimos, & novissimos primos futuros docet.

Partes sunt IV. I. Resolutio quaestionis de divortio, ad v. 12. II. Monitio de adducendis parvulis, ad v. 15. III. Juvenis divitis probatio & de divitibus informatio, ad v. 26. IV. Petro de Apostolorum, qui Christum sequuti reliquère omnia; retributione data responsio, ad vers. 30.

PARS I. Resolutio quaestionis de divortio.

Vers. 1. ἐτέλεσεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς τοὺς λόγους τούτους] Dogmata sibi à Patre mandata Christus in Galilaeae finibus primum publicavit. Quae sequuntur omnia aut ad eorum explicationem aut ad obsignationem pertinent.

μετῆρεν] Sic vertitur נסע Ps. LXXIX. 9.

πέραν τοῦ Ἰορδάνου] Nimirum apud Aenon & Salim Johan. X. 40. Vide quae ad Marcum X. 1.

Bezae non placet transitus per Peraeam: Vulgata, inquit, & Erasmus ad verbum trans Jordanem, quasi per Peraeam sive trans Jordaninam Christus, trajecto Jordane vel lacu Tiberiadis, in Judaeam venerit ex Galilaea: quod verum non est, cum turba dicatur eum secuta, neque rursum dicatur fluvium trajecisse cum Judaeam ingrederetur. Significatur ergo Christus non per Samariam, sed ea ad dextram relicta iter tenuisse secundum Jordanem. Sed recte Ludovicus de Dieu discessit à Beza, ad locum parallelum Marc. X. ita habens: Capernaum quo c. IX. 33. ingressus dicebatur, & unde jam digressus dicitur, ulteriori Jordanis ripae proxime adjacebat. Ita ut inde per eam ripam compendiosiori longe itinere ad ulteriores Judae fines pervenire potuerint, quam per citeriorem oram. Adde quod Matth. XI. 1. dicatur Christus solvisse ex Galilaea, & venisse in finem Judaeae trans Jordanem. Sic enim malo cum Vulgato, quam cum Beza, secus Jordanem. Nam si Capernaum profectus est in fines Judaeae per citeriorem Jordanis ripam, Samaria ad dextram relicta, non potest dici solvisse ex Galilaea, quia universam Galilaeam inferiorem, per tribus nempe Zabulon & Isaschar, transire debuit, ut porro per tribus Manasse, Ephraim & Benjamin in Judaeam veniret. Neque sequitur ex versione Vulgati, eum per Peraeam trajecto Jordane ex Galilaea in Judaeam venisse. Quod fateor non admittendum, quia turba multa eum secuta dicitur. Sed sensus est, eum pedestri itinere, διὰ τοῦ πέραν, ut loquitur Marcus, per eam ripam quae est ultra Jordanem, iter fecisse Judaeam versus. Nec opus fuit trajicere, quia Capernaum Peraeae proxime adjacebat. Et simulac discessit Capernaumo Peraeam versus, statim μετῆρεν ἐκ τῆς Γαλιλαίας.

## 19:3
Vers. 3. πειράζοντες] That they might reconcile enmities to him from the definition of a disputed law, and find material for disparagement, both among the learned and among the common people of either sex, with which design they approached him more often, as below in chapter XXII. 16 and 36.

εἰ] That is, whether: in a locution not of the Greeks but of the Hebrews who thus use אם.

ἔξεστι] Is it lawful, as above in chapter XII. verse 2, 10, chapter XIV. verse 4. ἀνθρώπῳ, is τινὶ, as we just said.

κατὰ πᾶσαν αἰτίαν] As the School of Hillel affirmed, with a similar error, as if I should say, it is placed in the judgment of the judge either to condemn or to absolve; therefore, whichever he does, he will not sin. See what we said regarding the fifth chapter. Josephus said: for whatever reasons, treating this same argument.

Latin:

Vers. 3. πειράζοντες] Ut ex juris controversi definitione inimicitias ipsi conciliarent, & obtrectandi invenirent materiam, tum apud eruditos, tum apud plebem aut hujus aut illius sexus, quo consilio saepius eum adierunt, ut infra cap. XXII. 16. & 36.

εἰ] Id est an: locutione non Graecorum sed Hebraeorum qui sic usurpant אם.

ἔξεστι] Fasné est, ut supra cap. XII. vers. 2. 10. cap. XIV. vers. 4. ἀνθρώπῳ, est τινὶ, ut modo diximus.

κατὰ πᾶσαν αἰτίαν] Ut affirmabat Hillelis Schola, simili errore, ac si dicam, in judicis arbitrio est positum aut condemnare, aut absolvere; ergo utrumvis faciat, non peccabit. Vide quae ad caput quintum diximus. Josephus dixit: καϑ' ἅς δήποτετῶν αἰτίας, idem hoc argumentum tra- ctans.

## 19:4
Verse 4. Have you not read, that he who made them from the beginning] From the beginning בראשית as in Gen. I. or מראש as in Ecclesiastes III. 11. where in the Greek is what God made from the beginning. He does not press the little word ערות as Sameas did, because in truth Moses was not dealing with adultery, as that which was to be punished by death, and not even with a probable suspicion of that crime, because as we said above, that, if she is not pleasing in his eyes, extends more broadly. But he draws us back from the civil law, which is accustomed to adapt itself somewhat to the customs of the people, to the will of God which is primary, to that, namely, which first and of itself pleases God, and to which every dispute about duties must be referred. The whole force of the argument, however, is placed not in the words male and female, nor in the fact that it was said two, but in the word shall cleave, and in that which follows, into one flesh, which shows the following inference, so that they are no longer two, but one flesh. The rest, however, were added to weave the discourse together. Moreover, it is emphatic, what is said here from the beginning, that is, when God was adapting his institutions to the very nature of equity and goodness, not to the depraved characters of men, when that saying did not yet have a place: customs have brought laws under their own power.

Male and female he created them] Namely, first Adam, then from the very body of Adam, Eve: which Christ passes over in silence as it is sufficiently known. For to this points what follows for this cause.

Concerning the contention between those two schools of the Jews, Hillel and Sameas, Benedictus Arias Montanus has this to say on this passage: There were two most famous families of Scribes in Jerusalem, and in all Judea. The followers of the one were called the Samai, those of the other, however, the house of Hillel. These defended various opinions in various arguments and in explaining the reasons of doctrine: Among these, one question was about the causes of divorce. The house of Samai asserted that there was only one cause for which a divorce might be tolerated, and that this was the suspicion of adultery; they prove this from those words of Moses for some uncleanness. For the house of Samai said that only uncleanness could be the cause of repudiation, and they defined uncleanness only as unchastity. The house of Hillel, however, admitted every cause, or even the slightest offense, to the right of repudiation, using only those words, and she finds no favor in his eyes. There was a certain third opinion, which supported the house of Samai in the genus of the cause, but that genus, uncleanness, was extended into many species. Concerning this third opinion, Grotius on Matt. V. 3. Today the Jews follow neither Sameas nor Hillel: For they approve of divorce not for every cause as Hillel, but nevertheless for many causes besides adultery, which are enumerated in the Talmudic digests, and are now also anxiously weighed by the Masters.

That law of Moses, about which they were debating, is Deut. XXIV. 1. where ערות דבר, the LXX rendered as an unseemly thing, the Vulgate as some uncleanness, indicates that wives are not to be dismissed rashly, about which therefore the question is asked, whether they could be dismissed for any cause whatsoever, which Hillel, whom Josephus calls Pollio, wanted? Or whether that cause had to be judged first before a judge, or whether that right of dismissing caused it to be done rightly, or only that it might be done with impunity? Finally, what cause was indicated by Moses? As to the first, that divorce was not permitted for any cause whatsoever, those Mosaic words sufficiently teach, which were not added rashly. Grotius admits this in the cited place, that God intended by those words to warn the Hebrews not to dismiss their wives rashly. In which, however, Grotius does not seem to be consistent with himself, when he adds these words: It was therefore a right, that for ANY CAUSE a husband could expel his wife. He warns that this was not done rightly, because even the law of charity alone prohibits dismissing a wife for no cause or for a very slight one, yet he asserts that it was permitted by the force of this law: just as something is said to be permitted in common usage which is beyond punishment, and which can be hindered by no one from being done, even if one departs from the rule of equity and goodness, just as he said here, that it was placed in the discretion of the judge either to condemn or to absolve, yet that he is not immune from vice, whichever he does: and just as the Praetor is said to render justice, even when he decrees unjustly, as Paulus the Jurisconsult speaks, who also said elsewhere; not everything that is permitted is honorable. In which manner Grotius, by the force of the law established in Deuteronomy, seems to establish with the School of Hillel that it was PERMITTED to dismiss a wife for any cause, even the slightest, so that it might be done with impunity, from which, however, he testifies here that he departs in the opposite direction. On the contrary, whatever the law does not permit except under a certain cause, that was not permitted for any cause whatsoever.

As to the second, Grotius wants that cause to have been committed to the discretion of the husband, so that there was no need to refer the matter to a judge, concerning which he has this to say on Matt. V.: Moreover, so that graver evils might be avoided, (GOD) did not want the truth and gravity of the cause to be referred to the discretion of another: but permitted it to be estimated by the mind of the husband himself. That, however, is in no way likely: For thus any husband, when it did not please him to keep his wife, could have dismissed her with impunity, and by that reason a cause and occasion would have been provided for countless repudiations, and that by the divine law itself. Which God forbid that we should admit. Too rashly, therefore, does Grotius define that those err who think it was not permitted for the Jews to dismiss a wife unless the cause was proven before a judge. He brings forward two things for his opinion: First, the words of Christ in Matt. V. verse 31. For it is said, says Christ, whoever wishes to dismiss his wife, let him give a bill of divorce. But neither did Christ say that this was spoken by Moses, but simply, he says, regarding the traditions of the Jews, not the divine law: in which, just as the cause was expressly designated, so without doubt it, when a divorce was taking place before a judge, which was certainly necessary, had to be first recognized by the judge; by virtue of the divine law. Grotius admits that this act, no less than the cession of an inheritance and other more solemn acts, was accustomed to be performed before judges, and that the Talmudic digests teach this, but he says that this was a matter of voluntary, not contentious, jurisdiction, just as manumission was before the Praetor in Roman law: Therefore, the judge did not interpose his cognizance, unless a controversy had arisen concerning a dowry or a gift on account of marriage. He admits that the woman could have requested, if she trusted in her innocence, that it be testified in writing, either by the husband or the judges, that she was found guilty of no crime: but he says that as often as a divorce was made by mutual consent, there was no need for cognizance. But would not mere confusion have arisen from that, and indeed with the divine law permitting it, and an illusion of the primordial matrimonial law, and the highest contempt, if it had been permitted to a husband with impunity, at his own discretion, to dismiss his wife, with no cause for that matter rendered, nor the affair brought to the judges? Just as the Turks make divorces for many reasons, which it is easy for husbands to invent. For Grotius brings forward this formula for a bill of divorce: Of my own accord, by no one's compulsion, I have decided to dismiss, desert, and repudiate you, hitherto my wife, from me: and now therefore I dismiss, desert, and repudiate you, and cast you out from me, so that you may be of your own power, and at your own discretion and pleasure depart wherever you like, nor will anyone at that time prohibit it. And let it be dismissed in such a way that it is permitted for you to marry any man you wish. Then he brings forward a passage from Josephus, when, speaking of himself, he says thus: καθ᾽ ὅν δή καιρὸν κᾐ τὴν γυναῖκα μὴ ἀρεσκόμενον αὐτῆς τοῖς ἤθεσιν ἀποπεμψάμενον. But this does nothing for the sense of divine law, or the Mosaic constitution, and the custom of better times, about which the question is here for us. For it was possible to depart from that in later times, and without doubt it was departed from. Wherefore others teach that the cause ought to have been brought at the very least to the scribes, who were fortified with public authority, who ought to have first attempted reconciliation, and, having proposed the inconveniences, dissuaded the husband from the repudiation. Repudiations ought not to have been made by private rashness, but by the public authority of judges, advises B. Gerhard in Deut. XXIV. 1. p. 443. And S. Augustine observed this in book XVI. against Faustus, ch. 26. That the scribes drew up the bill of divorce by public authority.

As to the third point, Grotius maintains that that right established in Deuteronomy did not cause that which is being discussed to be done rightly; but only that it might be done with impunity: since Christ teaches that this permission was made because of the hardness of the Jews, namely, so that occasion might not be given for harsher treatment, or even for poisonings, for which end the mere concession of impunity is sufficient: and therefore he concludes that this permission, at least in some cases, freed them from punishment, not from vice. Regarding which he has us easily agreeing. For it is certain that divorces conflict with the original institution of marriage in Genesis II, and Christ demonstrates this here, which Moses neither wished nor was able to abrogate: and the Prophet sufficiently teaches that divorces were permitted not as a thing good in itself and pleasing to GOD, but only for the sake of avoiding a greater evil, Mal. II. 13. seqq. And from the very consideration of the law concerning the bill of divorce, it is clear that Moses by no means commands or approves of divorces because of foulness, but rather puts a curb on them, so that they would not hasten to them so easily. But especially the cause of the permission, which Christ taught to be the σκληροκαρδίαν of the Jews, that is, the hardness of husbands against their wives, is an argument that they were permitted only for the sake of avoiding a greater evil: concerning which Chrysostom in this place: Moses did not simply enact this law, but was compelled to adapt himself to the infirmity of those to whom he was giving the law. For since they were prone to slaughter, and were filling their houses with the blood of their kin, and spared neither their own nor others, lest they should kill their wives inside, who were ungrateful, he commanded them to be sent outside, so that a graver evil, namely the ease of homicides, might be removed. Theophylact in ch. V. of Matthew. Moses commanded, if anyone hated his wife, to dismiss her, ἵνα μὴ χεῖρόν τι γένηται, for perhaps those who were hated might even have been murdered. The ordinary gloss has the same: Moses wrote this commandment because of the hardness of your hearts, wishing, namely, to indulge the dissension rather than that a homicide should be committed. Lyranus in annotations to Deut. XXIV. 1. It must be said, he says, that such a repudiation (made outside the case of fornication) was never lawful; that it was conceded, or rather permitted, to avoid a greater evil, namely uxoricide, and this does not make it lawful. Thomas in the fourth book of the Sentences teaches that it is held MORE COMMONLY that [those who in the Mosaic law gave a bill of divorce were excused from the punishment to be inflicted according to the law, but not from the guilt, so that Moses permitted the bill of divorce to avoid a greater evil, namely uxoricide. And this is the opinion of Lombard, Bonaventure, Richard, Paludanus, Dominicus a Soto, Covarruvias part II.

on matrimony, ch. 7. Azorius, book V. of Moral Institutions, ch. XIII. q. 3. Franciscus Haraeus in annotations to ch. XXIV. of Deut., as well as Laurentius in Canon Law in the book Gaudemus concerning divorces. With whom others among the Papists deal, Scotus, Durandus, Burgensis in notes to Lyranus, Abulensis and Cajetan on this passage, Bellarmine on matrimony, ch. XVII. response to objection 14, and Bonfrerius on Deut. XXIV. 1. that, namely, repudiation was permitted to the Jews, not as a lesser evil, but as something in itself lawful before God, and that by the bill of divorce in the Old Testament the bond itself was dissolved, who for that reason argue thus, especially the Jesuits, so that they may maintain that Christ, as a new legislator, abrogated the divorce which had been conceded in the Old Testament, and by a new law made the bond of marriage indissoluble, and constituted marriage as a Sacrament. Confer our B. Gerhard's Commentary on Deut. XXIV. 1.

But as to the fourth point, regarding the cause, what did Moses indicate with the words ערות דבר? Not that these imply a suspicion of unchastity as the old Samaean interpretation held (to which the opinion of Tertullian is agreeable, that for the sake of the wife's fornication alone was repudiation lawful to the Jews, book IV. ch. 34 against Marcion, as well as Burgensis on this passage and Dionysius the Carthusian on Deuteronomy XXIV. v. 1.), Grotius proved this in his notes on Matthew V. For if Moses had granted divorce only in that species in which Christ grants it, Christ would not say that that concession was made because of the hardness of the Jews against the original institution to which he himself recalls us. Nor would Moses have rightly said then, if she does not find favor in his eyes. For what need is there to say that about an adulteress? In which most of the ancient and recent interpreters easily agree: Origen, Chrysostom, etc. namely, that these things are to be understood concerning other foulnesses of body and mind outside of manifest adultery, which was to be visited with capital punishment, Levit. XX. 10, Deuter. XXII. 22. That the suspicion of adultery was the cause, and of the repudiation, is evident from Drusius on the difficult passages of Deuteronomy and others. Concerning which Grotius on Matthew V. Truly, if a husband were asked to prove adultery to a judge, it would no longer be a matter of dissolving the marriage, but of punishing the adulteress. Therefore, that which is said to be a just cause for divorce, namely unchastity, must be referred either to mild husbands, who do not wish to demand the punishment of their wives, such as was Joseph, the husband of Mary, or to those who, because they believe it themselves, or perhaps have even certainly discovered it, yet despair of being able to prove it in court, to which that of Jerome pertains: wherever there is fornication and suspicion of fornication, the wife is freely dismissed. That filthiness, however, is not to be extended too broadly, judging from the mind of the legislator. I say, from the mind of the legislator. For in later times, with the manifold depravation of sacred laws and customs supervening, there is no doubt that it was sufficiently extended. See more on these matters in our Annotations to chapter V of Matthew.

But as for the force of Christ's argument, it is not placed entirely in the word προσκολληθήσεται, and in the following εἰς σάρκα μίαν, although these are entirely relevant here, but also in those words ἄρσεν καὶ θῆλυ, and also in the word δύο. For as the Lord created only one man, so also He created only one woman in the beginning, which beginning of the creation of men, and not that בראשית of Genesis I. 1, is regarded here, much less Ecclesiastes III. 11, which passage is clearly ἀπροσδιόνυσος. Concerning which Jerome says on this passage: Not male and females (He created), which was sought from the repudiation of the former, but male and female, so that they might be joined in the fellowship of one spouse. Can God be contrary to Himself, so that He commanded one thing before and may break his own opinion with a new authority. Chrysostom has this to say about divorce: If this had been the case, He would not have created one man and one woman, but having created one Adam, He would have made two women, if indeed He had wished for one to be cast out and another to be brought in. And in his Commentary on this passage: He who from the beginning created one man, not many, and likewise one woman, is to be thought to have prescribed this, that it is not proper for one to have many, or for one woman to have many men. Furthermore, force is also situated in the word δύο. For why did Christ expressly add this word, which is not expressed in the Mosaic words, even if it is gathered from them, unless to show the force of the inference, because God willed that two should be into one flesh; whence it is not permitted, without prejudice to God's ordinance, the spouse having been dismissed, to assume another: For thus they will not be two, but three: if indeed one has two spouses, or even more; namely, both the one dismissed and the one newly taken. Meanwhile, we do not deny that there is also significant force in the word προσκολληθήσεται, he shall be glued, in an individual partnership of life; because the metaphor is taken from those things which are joined together by glue in such a way that you would believe them to be one, and Christ teaches that a firm and indissoluble conjunction is thus insinuated, inferring from the same: What God has joined, let not man separate. Finally, those words εἰς σάρκα μίαν powerfully refute divorce. For those who have been glued into one flesh, or have grown into one flesh by divine conjunction, cannot be torn from each other by men or by human and personal will. But nothing, says Chrysostom, shows their indivisible and inseparable society as much as that which is added: and they were two into one flesh: for having already been fused into one flesh, they are no longer two; nor is it right or fair that those things which have been united by God should be disjoined by men. Whence it is also clear that the preposition εἰς is not redundant, which has seemed so to some, even to Grotius: because not only is the terminus indicated, that two are one flesh, which the Apostle expresses in 1 Cor. VI. 16, Eph. V. 28, and here Christ, ὥστε οὐκ ἔτι εἰσὶ δύο, ἀλλὰ σὰρξ μία. But also the medium or that act by which two become one flesh, which is the union, or that divine gluing, which is insinuated by the added particle εἰς; because they are not one flesh by themselves, but are IN ONE flesh, namely, glued and united. Before that conjunction they were two, but through the conjunction they are glued into one flesh, and thus they are no longer two, but one flesh, concerning which Grotius: Since בשר most often signifies man among the Hebrews, and the word σαρκὸς is used in the same sense by the Hellenists, as below XXIV. 22, Luke XII. 16, Acts II. 17, Rom. III. 21. and Cor. I. 29, that interpretation seems to me most simple, which Plato expressed, having received it, as is believed, from the Hebrews: ὥστε δύο ὄντας ἕνα γεγόνέναι. For there is no closer friendship than that of husband and wife, which requires a communion of affections, of body, of offspring, and finally of the whole of life. Although this sense can indeed be admitted here, the word of flesh is nevertheless used emphatically, nor did the Holy Spirit wish to say, ONE Man, but ONE FLESH, or rather they shall be INTO ONE FLESH; namely, He looked to the carnal copulation, without which there is no marriage: and thus He expressed that which is required for the nature of matrimony. For the defect of marriage is substantial, or of that which is necessary for the substance of matrimony, then two cannot be joined, or be into one flesh, on account of the defect and vice of the members which GOD ordained for that purpose; whence also afterwards in this very treatment He taught that Eunuchs are unfit for marriage. Chrysostom weighs the arguments of Christ thus: οὐδὲ εἰσελθεῖν πρὸς τὴν γυναῖκα ἁπλῶς ἐνομοθέτησεν, ἀλλὰ καὶ κολληθῆναι, τῷ τρόπῳ τῆς λέξεως τὸ ἀδιάσπαστον ἐμφαίνων. He did not simply command to approach the woman, but to be glued, signifying the indivisible society by the figure of the diction, and not even this sufficed, but He required an even greater conjunction. For they shall be, he says, two into one flesh, therefore they are no longer two, but one flesh: as therefore it is a sin to divide flesh, so also it is unjust to tear away a woman. Nor did He stop here, but He also brought in God, saying: what therefore God has joined, let not man separate; showing that this has been done both against nature and against the law; against nature indeed in that one flesh is dissected: against the law however in that, with God joining and commanding that they not be separated, they themselves presumed to do that.

Latin:

Verf. 4. Οὐκ ἀνέγνωτε, ὅτι ποιήσας ἀπ' ἀρχῆς] Ἀπ' ἀρ- χῆς בראשית ut Gen. I. aut מראש ut Ecclesiastæ III. 11. ubi in Græco ὃ ἐποίησεν ὁ Θεὸς ἐξ ἀρχῆς. Non urget vocu- lam ערות ut faciebat Sameas, quia revera Moses non agebat περὶ τῆς πορνείας, ut quæ morte erat punienda, ac ne de suspicione quidem probabili ejus criminis, quia ut supra diximus illud, si non gratiosa sit apud eum, latius patet. Sed à lege civili, quæ solet se nonnihil aptare po- puli moribus, nos retrahit πρὸς τὸ θέλημα Θεῦ τὸ προηγύμε- νον, ad id nimirum, quod primum ac per se Deo placet, & quo omnis de officiis disputatio referenda est. Vis autem argumenti tota posita est non in verbis ἄρσεν καὶ θῆλυ, neque in eo quod dictum est δύο, sed in voce προσκολληθήσεται, & in eo, quod sequitur, εἰς σάρκα μίαν, quod ostendit sequens illatum, ὥστε οὐκέτι εἰσὶ δύο, ἀλλὰ σὰρξ μία. Cætera vero addita sunt ad contexendam orationem. Est autem ἐμφατικὸν, quod hic dicitur ἀπ' ἀρχῆς, id est, cum Deus ad ipsam æqui bonique naturam, non ad depravata ho- minum ingenia instituta sua accommodaret, cum locum nondum haberet illud: mores leges perduxerunt in pote- statem suam.

Ἄρσεν καὶ θῆλυ ἐποίησεν ἀυτὸς] Nempe primo Adamum, deinde ex ipso Adami corpore Evam: quod ut satis notum reticet Christus. Huc enim spectat quod sequitur ἕνεκεν τούτου.

De contentione inter duas illas Scholas Judæo- rum Hillelis & Sameæ Benedictus Ariasmontanus ita habet in hunc locum: Duæ fuere celeberrimæ fa- miliæ Scribarum Hierosolymis, & in omni Judæa. Alterius sectatores dicebantur Samai, alterius vero domus Hillel. Hi variis in argumentis, atque do- ctrinæ rationibus explicandis varias sententias defen- debant: In his una quæstio erat de divortiorum causis. Domus Samai unam tantum causam esse asseverabat, quam ob rem divortium toleraretur, eam- que esse adulterii suspicionem, probant hoc ex verbis illis Mosis propter aliquam fœditatem. Domus enim Samai solam fœditatem ajebat esse posse causam repudii, & fœditatem tantum impudicitiam defi- niebant. Domus vero Hillel omnem causam vel mi- nimam quamque offensionem ad repudii jus admit- tebant, illis verbis tantum usurpatis, & non inve- nerit gratiam in oculis ejus. Erat tertia quædam opinio, quæ suffragabatur domui Samai causæ gene- re, sed in species multas genus illud fœditatem dilata- bat. De qua tertia opinione Grotius ad Matth. V. 3. Hodie Judæi neque Sameam sequuntur, ne- que Hillelem: Probant enim divortium non κατὰ πᾶσαν αἰτίαν ut Hillel, sed ob multas tamen cau- sas ἐκτὸς τῆς πορνείας, quæ enumerantur in dige- stis Thalmudicis, & nunc quoque à Magistris an- xie expenduntur.

Lex illa Mosis, de qua disceptabant, est Deut. XXIV. 1. ubi ערות דבר, LXX. ἄσχημον πρᾶγμα probrum, Vulgata fœditatem aliquam, reddidêre, indicat, non temere uxores dimittendas esse, de qua proinde quæritur, an ob quamcun- que causam, quod Hillel, quem Josephus Pollio- nem vocat, volebat, dimitti potuerint? an cau- sa illa apud Judicem prius fuerit dijudicanda, an jus illud dimittendi effecerit, ut recte id fieret, an duntaxat, ut fieret impune? Quæ denique causa à Mose indicata fuerit? Quod ad primum, non ob quamcunque causam licitum fuisse repudium, verba illa Mosaica satis docent, quæ non teme- re adjecta sunt. Fatetur id Grotius l. c. voluisse nempe Deum vocibus illis admonere Hebræos, ne temere uxores dimitterent. In quo tamen sibi non videtur constare Grotius, cum hæc addit: Jus ergo fuit, ut QUAVIS de CAUSA u- xorem maritus posset expellere. Quod quidem non recte factum monet, quia aut nulla aut le- ve vissima de causa uxorem dimittere vel sola chari- tatis lex prohibeat, licuisse tamen hujus legis vi, asserit: prout licere in communi usu aliquid dicitur, quod extra pœnam est, & quo minus fiat a nemine impediri potest, etiamsi ab æqui bonique regula dis- cedatur, uti hic dixit, in judicis arbitrio esse posi- tum aut condemnare aut absolvere, non tamen eum a vitio immunem esse, utrumvis faciat: & quem- admodum Prætor jus reddere dicitur, etiam cum in- juste decernit, ut Paulus Jurisconsultus loquitur, qui & alibi dixit; non omne quod licet honestum es- se. Quo pacto Grotius vi legis in Deuteronomio constitutæ LICUISSE, ob quamvis causam, et- iam levissimam, uxorem dimittere, ita ut id im- pune fieret cum Schola Hillelis statuere videtur, a qua tamen se hic in diversum abire testatur. Ex adverso, quicquid lex non nisi sub certa causa permittit, id licitum non erat quavis de cau- sa.

Quod ad alterum, arbitrio mariti causam il- lam commissam vult Grotius, ut opus non fue- rit rem deferre ad Judicem, quo de ad Matth. V. ita habet: Cæterum ut graviora mala evitaren- tur, & veritatem & gravitatem causæ noluit (DEUS) ad arbitrium alienum referri: sed ipsius mariti animo id æstimandum permisit. Id vero nullo modo est verisimile: Nam ita ma- ritus quilibet, quum non placuerit uxorem reti- nere, impune potuisset eandem dimittere, at- que ea ratione causa & occasio præbita fuisset in- numeris repudiis, idque ipsa lege divina. Quod absit, ut admittamus. Nimis ergo te- mere definit Grotius, errare eos, qui putant Ju- dæis non licuisse uxorem dimittere nisi causa apud judicem probata. Duo autem adfert pro sua opi- nione: Primum verba Christi Matth. V. vers. 31. Dictum, enim esse, ait Christus, qui uxorem dimissam vult, libellum det repudii. Sed nec Christus hoc a Mose dictum, sed simpliciter er- rede, inquit, traditiones respiciens Judæorum, non legem divinam: in qua uti causa expresse designata fuit, ita sine dubio ea, cum divortium fiebat coram Judice, quod necessarium utique erat, a judice primum dignoscenda erat; vi legis divinæ. Fatetur Grotius, hunc actum non minus quam hæreditatis cessionem atque alios solemniores solitos coram judicibus peragi, idque digesta Thalmudica docere, sed fuisse hoc ait, jurisdictionis voluntariæ, non contentiosæ, quo- modo manumissio fuerit apud Prætorem jure Ro- mano: Cognitionem igitur suam judicem non in- terposuisse, nisi de dote aut donatione propter nu- ptias incidisset controversia. Fatetur, postulare mulierem potuisse si innocentiæ suæ confideret, ut scripto testaretur, aut maritus aut judices, nul- lius se flagitii compertam: sed quoties bona gratia fiebat divortium, nulla opus fuisse cognitione, ait. Annon vero inde mera orta fuisset confu- sio, & quidem permittente lege divina, & primæ- væ legis matrimonialis illusio, summumque vi- lipendium, si impune licuisset marito, pro suo arbitrio, uxorem dimittere, nulla ejus rei cau- sa reddita, neque re ad judices delata? Uti Tur- cæ pluribus de causis, quas facile est maritis com- minisci, divortia faciunt. Hanc enim adfert Grotius libelli divortii formulam: Mea sponte, nullius coactu te uxorem hactenus meam dimittere a me, deserere, ac repudiare decrevi: jamque adeo te dimitto, desero ac repudio, atque a me ejicio, ut tuæ sis potestatis, tuo que arbitratu ac lubitu quo libet discedas, neque id quisquam illo tempore prohibebit. Atque ita dimissa esto, ut cui- vis viro nubere tibi liceat. Deinde locum è Jose- pho adducit, cum de se agens ita ait: καθ᾽ ὅν δή καιρὸν κᾐ τὴν γυναῖκα μὴ ἀρεσκόμενον αὐτῆς τοῖς ἤθεσιν ἀποπεμψάμενον. Sed is ad legis divinæ sensum, aut constitutionem Mosaicam, & con- suetudinem meliórum temporum nihil facit, de qua hic quæstio nobis est. Discedi enim sequio- ribus temporibus ab illa potuit, & sine dubio dis- cessum est. Quapropter alii ad minimum defe- rendam fuisse causam ad scribas autoritate publi- ca munitos docent, qui debuerint prius reconci- liationem tentare, ac propositis incommodis ma- ritum à repudio dehortari. Repudia non debebant fieri, privata temeritate, sed publica judicum au- toritate, monet B. Gerhard. in Deut. XXIV. 1. p. 443. Et observavit S. August. l. XVI. contra Faust. c. 26. Scribas publica autoritate libellum re- pudii confecisse.

Quantum ad Tertium, jus illud in Deuterdno- mio constitutum non effecisse ut recte id de quo agi- tur, fieret; sed duntaxat, ut fieret impune, Gro- tius statuit: siquidem ob duritiem Judæorum per- missionem hanc factam Christus doceat, nimirum ne duriori tractationi, aut etiam veneficiis dare- tur occasio, ad qualem finem sufficiat sola impu- nitatis concessio: ideoque concludit, permissio- nem hanc, saltem in nonnullis casibus à pœna, non à vitio liberasse. De quo facile nos consentien- tes habet. Nam & divortia cum prima conjugii institutione Genes. II. pugnare certum est, ac de- monstrat hic Christus, quam Moses abrogare nec voluit, nec potuit: & Propheta satis docet, divortia non ut rem per se bonam & DEO gra- tam, sed majoris mali vitandi causa tantum per- missa Mal. II. 13. seqq. & ex ipsa legis de repudii libello consideratione patet, Mosen nequaquam præcipere vel approbare divortia ob fœditatem, sed fræna potius injicere, ne tam facile ad ea properarent. Sed imprimis causa permissionis, quam Christus docuit σκληροκαρδίαν esse Judæo- rum, maritorum scil. adversus uxores duritiem, argumento est, majoris tantum mali vitandi causa permissa esse: quo de Chrysostom. in h. l. Moses non simpliciter hanc legem tulit, sed coactus fuit, sese attemperare eorum, quibus legem da- bat, infirmitati. Nam quoniam ad cædes promti erant, & domus cognato replebant sanguine, & neque suis, neque alienis parcebant, ne intus occide- rent uxores, quæ ingratæ erant, præcepit foras mit- tendas, quo gravius malum, nempe homicidio- rum facilitas tolleretur. Theophylact. in cap. V. Matth. Moses præcepit, si quis odio haberet uxorem dimittere eam, ἵνα μὴ χεῖρόν τι γένηται, μισό- μενα γὰρ ἴσως αῒ καὶ ἐφονεύθη. Similiter habet glossa ordinaria: ad duritiem cordis vestri scripsit Moses præceptum istud, malens scilicet indulgere dissidium, quam committi homicidium. Lyra- nus in annot. ad Deut. XXIV. 1. Dicendum, in- quit, quod nunquam tale repudium (extra casum fornicationis factum) fuerit licitum; quod fuit concessum, vel potius permissum, ad evitandum majus malum, scil. uxoricidium, & hoc non facit licitum. Thomas in IV. sententia docet, COM- MUNIUS teneri, quod [qui in lege Mosaica de- derunt libellum repudii, excusabantur à pœna se- cundum legem infligenda, non autem à culpa, ita quod Moses permisit libellum repudii ad vitandum majus malum scilicet uxoricidium. Atque hæc est sententia Lombardi, Bonaventuræ, Richardi, Paludani, Dominici à Soto, Covarruviæ part. II.

de matrim. cap. 7. Azorii l. V. Instit. moral. cap. XIII. q. 3. Francisc. Haræi in annot. ad cap. XXIV. Deut. nec non Laurentii in jure Canonico in l. Gaudemus de divortiis. Cum quibus transigant alii è Pontificiis, Scotus, Durandus, Burgenfis in not. ad Lyran. Abulensis & Cajet. ad h. l. Bellarm. de matrim. cap. XVII. resp. ad object. 14. & Bon- frerius ad Deut. XXIV. 1. quod nempe repudium permissum Judæis fuerit, non ut minus malum, sed ut aliquid per se coram Deo licitum, quodque per libellum repudii in V. Test. vinculum ipsum fue- rit solutum, qui ea de causa ita disputant, Jesuitæ imprimis, ut Christum ceu novum legislatorem, divortium, quod in V. Test. concessum fuerit, abrogasse, novaque lege matrimonii vinculum indissolubile fecisse, ac matrimonium Sacramen- tum constituisse, obtineant. Confer. B. Ger- hardi nostri Commentar. in Deut. XXIV. 1.

Quod autem quarto ad causam, quamnam in- dicarit Moses verbis ערות דבר? Non innuere ea suspicionem stupri ut habebat vetus Samæa interpre- tatio, (cui consentanea est Tertulliani sententia, ob solam uxoris fornicationem licitum fuisse Judæis repudium lib. IV. c. Marc. c. 34. nec non Burgen- sis ad. h. l. & Dionysii Carthus. ad Deuter. XXIV. v. 1.) Grotius hisce probavit ad Matth. V. Nam si Moses in ea duntaxat specie divortium concessisset, in qua eam concedit Christus, non diceret Christus, eam concessionem factam ob duritiem Judæorum contra originale institutum ad quod ipse nos revocat. Neque recte tum dixisset Moses, si non sit gratiosa apud eum. Quid enim id opus dicere de adultera? in quo Veteres ac recentiores Interpp. plerique facile consentiunt: Origenes, Chrysostomus, &c. intelligenda nempe hæc esse de aliis fœditatibus corporis & animi extra manifestum adulterium, quod pœna capitali afficiendum erat, Le- vit. XX. 10. Deuter. XXII. 22. Suspicionem vero adulterii causam fuisse, repudiique, è Dru- sio ad loca diffic. Deut. aliisque constat. Quo de Grotius ad Matth. V. Sane si maritus esset roga- tus probare adulterium judici, jam non de dirimen- do matrimonio, sed de punienda adultera ageretur. Quod ergo stuprum justa esse divortii causa dicitur, id referri debet aut ad maritos lenes, qui ad pœ- nam deposcere uxores nolunt, qualis erat Joseph Mariæ conjux, aut ad eos, qui quod ipsi credunt, aut forte etiam certo compererunt probare tamen se in judicio posse diffidunt, quo illud Hieronymi pertinet: ubicunque est fornicatio & fornicatio- nis suspicio, libere uxor dimittitur. Fœdita- tem tamen illam ex mente legislatoris non judica- ri nimis ample extendendam esse. Dico, ex men- te legislatoris. Nam sequioribus temporibus, ac- cedente multiplici depravatione legum & con- suetudinum sacrarum satis extensam fuisse, nul- lum est dubium. Plura de hisce Vid. in Annotat. nostris ad c. V. Matth.

Quod autem ad vim argumenti Christi, non posita ea est tota in voce προσκολληθήσεται, & in sequentibus εἰς σάρκα μίαν, etsi ea omnino huc faciant, sed etiam in illis verbis ἄρσεν καὶ θῆλυ, etiam in voce δύο. Nam ut unum tantum virum, ita etiam unam tantum fœminam creavit initio Do- minus, quod initium creationis hominum, non vero illud בראשית Genes. I. 1. hic spectatur, nedum Ecclesiast. III. 11. qui locus plane est ἀ- προσδιόνυσος. Quo de Hieronymus in h. l. Non masculum & fœminas (fecit) quod ex priorum re- pudio quærebatur, sed masculum & fœminam ut unius conjugis consortio necterentur. Nunquid potest Deus sibi esse contrarius, ut aliud ante jusserit & sententiam suam novo frangat imperio. Chryso- stomus ita habet de repudio: Si hoc fuisset, non unum virum & unam mulierem, sed uno Adamo condito duas fecisset mulieres, si quidem voluisset u- nam quidem ejici, alteram induci. Et in Com- mentario ad h. l. Qui ab initio unum creavit vi- rum, non multos, unam item mulierem, hoc præ- scripsisse putandus est, non oportere unum multas habere aut unam multos. Porro vis etiam sita est in voce δύο. Cur enim expresse hanc addidit vo- cem Christus, quæ in verbis Mosaicis expressa non est, etsi ex iisdem colligatur, nisi ut vim mon- straret illationis, quia Deus voluit, ut duo sint in carnem unam; unde non licet, salva Dei ordi- natione, conjuge dimissa, aliam assumere: Sic enim non duo erunt, sed tres: si nempe unus duas habet conjuges, vel plures etiam; nimirum tum dimissam, tum noviter ductam. Interim non diffitemur, insignem etiam vim esse in verbo προσκολληθήσεται agglutinabitur, individuo vitæ consortio; quia metaphora ab his, quæ sic glu- tine committuntur ut unum esse credas, desum- pta est, & firmam atque indissolubilem conjun- ctionem ita insinuatam esse, Christus docet, infe- rens ex eadem: Quod Deus conjunxit, homo ne separet. Denique verba illa εἰς σάρκα μίαν po- tenter refellunt divortium. Qui enim in unam sunt carnem conglutinati, vel in unam carnem coaluerunt divina conjunctione, illi non possunt ab hominibus vel humana, propriaque voluntate ab invicem divelli. Sed nihil æque, inquit Chry- sostomus, indivulsam atque inseparabilem eorum societatem ostendit, atque id, quod additur: & e- rant duo in carne una: in unam quippe jam con- flati carnem, duo amplius non sunt; nec fas, aut æ- quum est, ut quæ à Deo sunt unita, per homines dis- jungantur. Unde etiam patet præpositionem εἰς non πλεονάζειν, quod nonnullis, etiam Grotio, visum: quia non solum terminus indicatur, quod duo sint una caro, quem exprimit Apostolus 1. Cor. VI. 16. Ephes. V. 28. Et hic Christus, ὥστε οὐκ ἔτι εἰσὶ δύο, ἀλλὰ σὰρξ μία. Sed etiam medium vel a- ctus ille, quo duo fiunt una caro, quod est unio, vel conglutinatio illa divina, quæ insinuatur particu- la εἰς adjecta; quia non per se sunt una caro, sed sunt IN UNAM carnem, conglutinati scil. & uniti. Ante illam conjunctionem duo erant, sed per conjunctionem conglutinantur in unam car- nem, adeoque jam non duo amplius sunt, sed una caro, de quo Grotius: Cum בשר Hebræis sæpissi- me hominem significet, & vox σαρκὸς eodem sensu u- surpetur ab Hellenistis, ut infra XXIV. 22. Luc. XII. 16. Actor. II. 17. Rom. III. 21. & Cor. I. 29. videtur mihi simplicissima esse interpretatio illa, quam ab Hebræis, ut creditur, acceptam expressit Plato: ὥ- στε δύο ὄντας ἕνα γεγόνέναι. Nulla enim arctior a- micitia, quam mariti & uxoris, quæ communio- nem requirit affectuum, corporis, prolis, vitæ deni- que totius. Quanquam vero admitti hic sensus possit, emphatice tamen adhibita est vox carnis, nec dicere voluit Spiritus Sanctus, UNUS Ho- mo, sed UNA CARO, vel potius erunt IN UNAM CARNEM; Nimirum copulam carnalem respexit, sine qua conjugium nullum est: ad- eoque id quod ad naturam matrimonii requiri- tur, expressit. Defectus enim conjugii substan- tialis est, vel requisiti ad matrimonii substantiam necessarii, tum duo non possunt conjungi, vel esse in unam carnem, ob membrorum, quæ DEUS eam in rem ordinavit, defectum & vitium; unde etiam postmodum in hac ipsa tractatione Eunu- chos ineptos esse ad conjugium, docuit. Chryso- stomus ita argumenta Christi expendit: οὐδὲ εἰσελθεῖν πρὸς τὴν γυναῖκα ἁπλῶς ἐνομοθέτησεν, ἀλλὰ καὶ κολληθῆναι, τῷ τρόπῳ τῆς λέξεως τὸ ἀδιάσπαστον ἐμφαίνων. Non simpliciter ad mulierem accedere præ- cepit, sed agglutinari, figuræ dictionis indivulsam so- cietatem significans, ac ne hoc quidem suffecit, sed majorem etiam conjunctionem requisivit. Erunt e- nim, inquit, duo in carnem unam, itaque non amplius duo sunt, sed una caro: ut igitur carnem dividere nefas est: ita etiam mulierem divellere ini- quum. Neque hic substitit, verum etiam Deum indu- xit dicens: quod ergo Deus conjunxit, homo non separets ostendens tum contra naturam, tum con- tra legem hoc esse factum; contra naturam quidem eo quod una caro dissecetur: contra legem vero eo quod Deo conjungente, ac præcipiente non separari, ipsi illud facere præsumpserint.

## 19:5
Vers. 5. Καὶ εἶπεν] God Himself through His Prophet Moses: for these words are to be ascribed to him rather than to Adam. The interpreter of Matthew, however, translated this testimony from the LXX.

Προσκολληθήσεται] He shall be glued, namely, in an individual partnership of life, which the preceding words show: he shall leave his father and his mother. Great is the conjunction between parents and children, since children are as it were a part of the parents. Nevertheless, it is greater by divine institution between spouses, not without mystical signification, as Paul teaches us in Eph. V. 32. Thus it is said to the daughter of Pharaoh, Forget your people and your father's house, Ps. XLV. 11. Aristotle: for communion is by nature most of all in the female and the male. Menander: There is nothing so intimate, O Laches, if one considers it, as a husband and a wife. Hierocles in his book on marriage: the first and most elementary of communions is that which is according to marriage.

Καὶ ἔσονται οἱ δύο εἰς σάρκα μίαν] Since בשר among the Hebrews very often signifies a human being, and the word σαρκὸς is used in the same sense by the Hellenists, as below in chapter XXIV. 22, Luke III. 16, Acts II. 17, Romans III. 20, 1 Corinthians I. 29, it seems to me that the simplest interpretation is that which Plato expressed, having received it, as is believed, from the Hebrews: ὥςε δύο ὄντας ἕνα γεγονέναι [so that being two they have become one]: and an old proverb, which Aristotle says is about friends, calls them μία ψυχή [one soul]. For that εἰς, according to the Hebrew custom, is redundant here, as appears in 1 Corinthians VI. 16, Ephesians V. 28, 29, 30, 31. A similar manner of speaking is found in Deuteronomy XXIX. 13, 44, Psalm LXIX. 12, LXXII. 18, and XCIV. 22, 2 Samuel VII. 14, which passage is cited in Hebrews I. 5. There is, however, no closer friendship than that of husband and wife, which requires a communion of affections, of body, of offspring, and finally of the whole of life: which matter, that it is truly sacred—that is, discovered not by human but by divine means—the nations have believed with great consensus. The same expression is used by Paul when he treats of a harlot: but, of course, he who joins himself to a harlot uses it as for a wife. In the sense we have already mentioned, this very passage is explained in the constitutions which are called those of Clement, book VII, chapter 3: ἔσονται γάρ, φησὶν, οἱ δύο εἰς σάρκα μίαν· ἓν γάρ ἐστιν ἀνὴρ καὶ γυνὴ τῇ φύσει, τῇ συμπνοίᾳ, τῇ ἑνώσει, τῇ διαθέσει, τῷ βίῳ, τῷ τρόπῳ κεχωρισμένοι δὲ εἰσι τῷ σχήματι καὶ τῷ ἀριθμῷ [For they shall be, he says, the two into one flesh; for man and woman are one in nature, in agreement, in union, in disposition, in life, in manner, but they are separated in form and in number].

Latin:

Vers. 5. Καὶ εἶπεν] Deus ipse per Prophetam suum Mo- sem: ei enim potius adscribenda sunt hæc verba quam A- damo. Testimonium autem hoc transtulit Matthæi in- terpres ex LXX.

Προσκολληθήσεται] Agglutinabitur, individuo scilicet vi- tæ consortio, quod ostendunt præcedentia: καταλείψει τὸν πατέρα καὶ τὴν μητέρα. Magna est conjunctio inter parentes & liberos, cum liberi quasi pars sint parentum. Attamen major ex instituto divino inter conjuges, non sine mystica significatione, ut nos Paulus docet Ephes. V. 32. Ita Pha- raonis filiæ dicitur, Obliviscere populi tui & domus patris tui, Ps. XLV. 11. Aristoteles: κοινωνία γὰρ φύσει τῷ θήλει καὶ τῷ ἄῤῥενι μάλιστά ἐστιν. Menander: Οἰκεῖον οὕτως οὐδὲν ἐστιν, ὦ Λάχης, Ἐὰν σκοπῇ τις, ὡς ἀνήρ τε καὶ γυνή. Hierocles libro de nuptiis: πρώτην καὶ στοιχειωδεστάτην τῶν κοι- νωνιῶν ἦ κατὰ τὸν γάμον.

Καὶ ἔσονται οἱ δύο εἰς σάρκα μίαν] Cum בשר Hebræis sæpissime hominem significet, & vox σαρκὸς eodem sensu usurpetur ab Hellenistis ut infra cap. XXIV. 22. Luc. III. 16. Act. II. 17. Rom. III. 20. 1. Cor. I. 29. videtur mihi sim- plicissima esse ea interpretatio quam ab Hebræis, ut credi- tur, acceptam expressit Plato ὥςε δύο ὄντας ἕνα γεγονέναι: & vetus proverbium ait esse Aristoteles de amicis μία ψυχή. Nam illud εἰς more Hebræo hic πλεονάζει, ut apparet 1. Cor. VI. 16. Ephes. V. 28. 29. 30. 31. Simile loquendi genus Deut. XXIX. 13. 44. Ps. LXIX. 12. LXXII. 18. & XCIV. 22. 2. Sam. VII. 14. qui locus citatur Hebr. I. 5. Nulla au- tem arctior amicitia quam mariti & uxoris, quæ commu- nionem requirit affectuum, corporis, prolis, vitæ denique totius: quam rem esse vere sacram, id est non humanitus sed divinitus repertam magno consensu gentes crediderunt. Eadem locutio usurpatur à Paulo ubi de scorto agit: sed nimirum qui scorto se miscet ea utitur pro uxore. In eum quem jam diximus sensum explicatur hic ipse locus in con- stitutionibus quæ dicuntur Clementis lib. VII. cap. 3. ἔσον- ται γάρ, φησὶν, οἱ δύο εἰς σάρκα μίαν· ἓν γάρ ἐστιν ἀνὴρ καὶ γυνὴ τῇ φύσει, τῇ συμπνοίᾳ, τῇ ἑνώσει, τῇ διαθέσει, τῷ βίῳ, τῷ τρόπῳ κεχωρισμένοι δὲ εἰσι τῷ σχήματι καὶ τῷ ἀριθμῷ.

## 19:6
Vers. 6. ὥστε οὐκέτι εἰσὶ δύο, ἀλλὰ σὰρξ μία] We see here that two is not opposed to many, but to one: before the bond of matrimony they were two; afterwards they are reckoned as one by the interpretation of the law.

See what we have said about these things in the Commentary on Genesis II.

Ὁ ὖν ὁ Θεὸς συνέζευξε.] They are mistaken who refer this to the causes and occasions of contracting marriages. For it is not about those that the matter is concerned, but about the very nature of matrimony, in which God, as its author, willed that the closest bond of friendship should exist. If, therefore, without grave fault, κατὰ πᾶσαν αἰτίαν [for every cause], other friendships cannot be dissolved, how much less this one, which is held together by the bond of so many pledges, upon which depends the honorable propagation and education of the most noble living creature created in the divine image?

These are not opposites, but subordinate. God joins as the efficient cause, because marriages do not happen without divine providence, and therefore they are called fated. See Genesis XXIV. 7, 14, Judges XIV. 4, Proverbs II. 17, chapter XIX. 14, Tobit VI. 12. He also joins two into one, namely through the ordination and the matrimonial law, which concerns the very nature of matrimony, by which He willed it to be an indissoluble bond between two spouses.

Ἄνθρωπος μὴ χωριζέτω] Which he does who either an innocent wife casts out, or even refuses to tolerate those things which are tolerable. See 1 Pet. III.

Latin:

Vers. 6. ὥστε οὐκέτι εἰσὶ δύο, ἀλλὰ σὰρξ μία] Videmus hic duo non pluribus opponi, sed uni: ante fedus matrimo- nii duo erant: postea pro uno censentur legis inter- pretatione.

Vid. de his quæ ad Genes. II. diximus in Com- mentario.

Ὁ ὖν ὁ Θεὸς συνέζευξε.] Errant, qui hoc ad cau- sas & occasiones conjugiorum contrahendorum referunt. Non enim de istis agitur: sed de ipsa matrimonii natura, cui Deus auctor inesse voluit jus amicitiæ arctissimum. Si igitur sine gravi culpa κατὰ πᾶσαν αἰτίαν amicitiæ cæteræ dissui non possunt, quanto minus ista quæ tot pignorum vinculo continetur, unde pendet honesta tum propagatio tum educatio nobilissimi animantis creati ad divinam ima- ginem?

Non sunt hæc opposita, sed subordinata. Con- jungit Deus ceu causa efficiens, quia non sine di- vina providentia fiunt connubia, ideo dicuntur fatalia. Vid. Gen. XXIV. 7. 14. Judic. XIV. 4. Prov. II. 17. c. XIX. 14. Tob. VI. 12. conjungit etiam duos in unum, per ordinationem nempe, ac legem matri- monialem, ipsam matrimonii naturam concernen- tem, qua voluit esse vinculum indissolubile inter duos conjuges.

Ἄνθρωπος μὴ χωριζέτω] Quod facit qui aut innocentem uxorem extrudit, aut etiam tolerare recusat ea quæ sunt to- lerabilia. Vid. 1. Pet. III.

## 19:7
Vers. 7. Ἐνετείλατο] They do not wrongly infer a permission from the law prescribing a form for the business. He who commands the one repudiating his wife to give a bill of divorce, permits divorce to some extent. But not everything that is permitted, especially by civil laws, is right and pious, as Christ will show.

But it was not a mere permission that was being inferred here by the Pharisees, but, as the Vulgate rendered it, 'mandavit' [he commanded], a precept. Nor was a permission of law, if Grotius speaks of it, rightly inferred, because it is not pious to ascribe to God such a permission of law as is contrary to what is right and pious. Nor, finally, is there any reason why he should explain the word in this way, as he explained τὸ ἐπέτρεψεν in v. 8. Ἐπιτρέπεν is often among Greek writers to commit a matter to the discretion of someone: the Latin word for permitting is also used in this way: and this meaning is intermediate between a permission of law and a mere fact. For ἐνετείλατο imports something more, and properly signifies a mandate; just as ἐντολὴ is a precept. Whence others observe that Christ spoke differently about the constitution of Moses, and the Pharisees differently: the former [Christ] by the word ἐπέτρεψεν [permitted] only a mere permission, but the latter [the Pharisees] made a precept of it by the word ἐνετείλατο [commanded]. Nor is the argument firm, when such a permission is inferred from the law prescribing a form for the business: whence some explain the Mosaic text in such a way that divorce is not permitted, but it is only taught what is to be observed in the case of a divorce actually occurring, namely, that a husband should not marry again a wife once repudiated: See B. Gerhard on Deut. XXIV. 1, page 1451.

Ἀπολῦσαι] We have spoken of the meaning of this word in chapter V.

Latin:

Vers. 7. Ἐνετείλατο] Non male ex lege formam negotio præscribente permissionem inferunt. Qui repudianti uxo- rem præcipit, ut libellum det divortii, divortium aliquate- nus permittit. Sed non quicquid permittitur, legibus præ- sertim civilibus, fas, piumque est, ut Christus ostendet.

At non hic nuda permissio inferebatur à Phari- sæis, sed ut vulgata reddidit mandavit, præceptum. Neque permissio juris, si de ea loquatur Grotius, recte inferebatur quia Deo talem permissionem juris, quæ sit contra fas & pietatem, adscribere pium non est. Nec denique est, quod ita expli- cet vocem, ut v. 8. τὸ ἐπέτρεψεν exposuit. Ἐπιτρέ- πειν sæpe apud Græcos scriptores est rem arbitrio ali- cujus committere: Latine quoque permittendi vox ita usurpatur: estque hæc significatio inter permis- sionem juris, nudique facti, media. Nam ἐνετεί- λατο aliquid amplius importat, ac proprie man- datum significat; quemadmodum ἐντολὴ præceptum est. Unde alii observant, aliter loquutum esse de constitutione Mosis Christum, aliter Pharisæos: illum solum permissionem nudam voce ἐπέτρεψεν, hos vero præceptum inde fecisse voce ἐνετείλατο. Neque firmum est argumentum, cum ex lege for- mam negotio præscribente talis infertur permissio: unde nonnulli textum Mosaicum ita exponunt, ut divortium non permittatur, sed tantum doceatur, quid in casu facti divortii observandum, videlicet ne maritus uxorem semel repudiatam iterum du- cat: Vid. B. Gerhard. in Deuter. XXIV. 1. pag. 1451.

Ἀπολῦσαι] De hujus vocis significatu diximus ad ca- put V.

## 19:8
Vers. 8. Ὅτι Μωσῆς] With God as the author, as we said above: but he names Moses as the promulgator not of a common, primary, and perpetual law, but of a Jewish one given in accordance with the times.

Πρὸς τὴν σκληροκαρδίαν] That is, disobedience. Thus elsewhere 'unbelief and hardness of heart' are joined, Mark XVI. 14. Because they had hardened themselves against the equity prescribed by nature and God, therefore God wrote laws, not as for an ideal republic, but as for the dregs of Israel. Moreover, this is as it were a proper mark of that people, Ex. XXXIII. 3, XXXIV. 9, Deut. IX. 6, XXXI. 27, Is. XLVIII. 4, Ezek. II. 4, III. 7, Acts VII. 41. πρὸς here corresponds to the Hebrew על which means 'on account of'.

Disobedience and hardness of heart differ, even if they sometimes concur in the same subject. The hardness of husbands against their spouses is noted, which caused God to permit this, judging it better, as Isidore says, for wives to be sent away than to be killed inside. He permitted it, says Chrysostom, a thing not good, for fear of a greater evil. For if he did not permit those who had wives they loathed to marry others after casting them out, what else was to be expected from those inflamed by anger as well as lust, than that they would break a path to other marriages for themselves by the death of the loathed spouse; foreseeing which evil, Moses wrote that, declaring that he would not punish what he nevertheless did not at all approve. Furthermore, some observe that this was permitted by Moses, not as a Prophetic Teacher, but as a Political Legislator, who permitted divorces to a stubborn people to avert a greater evil, even though he was not ignorant that they were repugnant to the primary institution of marriage.

Ἐπέτρεψεν ὑμῖν] ἐπιτρέπειν is often among Greek writers to commit a matter to the discretion of someone: which is the true meaning of this passage: as has been shown elsewhere. The Latin word for permitting is also used in this way; and this meaning is intermediate between a permission of law and a mere fact.

ἐ γέγονεν ὕτως] I think it is rightly translated: it has not been done so, that the custom of a better age might approach the authority of the Lord's institution, for no one of the praised men is read to have dismissed his wife, not even then, when the causes for divorce seemed plausible: regarding which matter Malachi brings forward the example of Abraham.

This is a new version. Hitherto interpreters have by common consent both rendered and understood 'from the beginning', i.e., of the instituted marriage, 'it was not so', that is, by the force of the divine institution the matter had been otherwise, and there was no place for divorce at all. Chrysostom on this passage explained it thus: 'From the beginning it was not so': that is, by the very nature of things God commanded us the opposite from the beginning. For if this had been [the case] (as the same author says elsewhere), he would not have created one man and one woman, but having created one Adam, he would have created two women. That, therefore, is to him BY THE VERY NATURE OF THINGS.

Latin:

Vers. 8. Ὅτι Μωσῆς] Deo auctore ut supra diximus: sed Mosem nominat ut legis non communis primævæ atque perpetuæ, sed Judaicæ pro ratione temporum datæ pro- mulgatorem.

Πρὸς τὴν σκληροκαρδίαν] Id est ἀπείθειαν. Ita alibi jun- guntur ἀπιστία καὶ σκληροκαρδία Marc. XVI. 14. Quia ob- duruerant adversus æquitatem à natura Deoque præscri- ptam, ideo Deus jura scripsit, non tanquam optimæ rei- publicæ, sed tanquam fæci Israelis. Est autem hæc velut propria nota illius populi Ex. XXXIII. 3. XXXIV. 9. Deut. IX. 6. XXXI. 27. Es. XLVIII. 4. Ezech. II. 4. III. 7. Act. VII. 41. πρὸς hic respondet Hebræo על quod valet propter.

Differunt ἀπείθεια & σκληροκαρδία, etsi quandoque in eodem subjecto concurrant. Duri- ties notatur maritorum adversus conjuges, quæ fe- cit, ut hæc permitteret Deus, melius ducens, Isido- ro dicente, uxores extra dimitti, quam intus occidi. Permisit, inquit Chrysostomus, bene rem non bo- nam metu majoris mali. Tam si viris exosæ uxores habentibus non permittere ejectis iis alias ducere, quid erat expectandum aliud ab ira simul ac libidine inflammatis, quam ut nece conjugis exosæ ad alias sibi nuptias aditum rumperent; cui malo prævertens illa scripsit Moses, declarans, se non ulturum, quæ tamen minime probaret. Cæterum permissum hoc esse à Mose nonnulli observant, non ut Docto- re Prophetico, sed ut Legislatore Politico, qui con- tumaci populo divortia ad majus malum averten- dum permiserit, etsi ea primævæ conjugii institu- tioni repugnare non ignorârit.
