Ἐπέτρεψεν ὑμῖν] ἐπιτρέπειν sæpe apud Græcos scriptores est rem arbitrio alicujus committere: quæ vera est hujus loci sententia: ut alibi ostensum est. Latine quoque per- mittendi vox ita usurpatur; estque hæc significatio inter permissionem juris, nudique facti media.

ἐ γέγονεν ὕτως] Puto recte verti: non ita factitatum est, ut ad auctoritatem Dominicæ institutionis accedat ævi me- lioris consuetudo, nemo enim laudatorum virorum uxo- rem suam dimisisse legitur, ne tum quidem, cum proba- biles esse viderentur divortii causæ: quam in rem Abraha- mi exemplum affert Malachias.

Nova hæc est versio. Hactenus communi consensu interpretes & reddiderunt, & intellexe- runt ab initio, scil. instituti conjugii, non erat sic, quod nempe vi divinæ institutionis secus res ha- buerit, nec ullatenus divortii locus fuerit. Chry- sost. ad h. l. sic exposuit: Ab initio non erat sic: id est, rebus ipsis nobis Deus ab initio contraria præ- cepit. Si enim hoc fuisset (ut idem alibi) non unum virum & unam mulierem, sed uno Adam condito duas fecisset mulieres. Id ergo est eidem REBUS IPSIS.

## 19:9
Vers. 9. εἰμὴ ἐπὶ πορνείᾳ] Thus the old Complutensian edition. And thus the Syriac reads: that is, when she is not an adulteress. Which favors Origen, who says that the mention of fornication is not made by way of a strict exception, but for the sake of an example, namely so that graver vices may be distinguished from lighter ones. Seneca said that vices are to be pardoned, not monstrosities.

Καὶ γαμήσῃ ἄλλην μοιχᾶται.] That is, he makes that former one, dismissed by him, commit adultery. That these words ought to be explained thus is apparent from a comparison of the passage which is above, v. 32. He is rightly said to do a thing who provides the cause for the deed. It is an idiom of the Hellenists to express verbs of the Hiphil form through active ones, as in Rom. VIII. 26, Gal. IV. 6.

This is a notable depravation of Christ's words. Christ speaks openly about the adequate cause for dismissing a wife, outside of which her repudiation, as conflicting with the institution of marriage, cannot be done without prejudice to piety, which cause he makes adultery. Grotius, on the contrary, denies that adultery is the sole cause of a just repudiation, and maintains that it is brought in only for the sake of an example. Christ affirms that he who dismisses his wife outside the case of adultery, and marries another, commits adultery. Grotius, in order to serve his hypothesis, says he does not commit adultery, but causes her to commit adultery, namely the wife whom he dismissed. He opposes the Complutensian edition to the former, for the sake of which he himself boldly alters the text; and since the codices otherwise consistently have the exceptive εἰ μὴ, by omitting the particle εἰ he leaves a simple negative. To whom, however, not only the consensus of the remaining Codices can be opposed, but also the parallel passage in Matt. V. 32, which expressly employs the exceptive clause παρεκτὸς, that is, except for or the cause of fornication being excepted, as the Vulgate renders it, which also retains the exceptive clause in this place, nisi ob fornicationem. The latter corruption vainly pretends the custom of the Hellenists and the aforementioned parallel passage for the sense of Christ. For one must not rashly depart from the proper and more received meaning. It is certainly one thing for someone to commit adultery, and another to cause a wife to commit adultery, or to provide her with the occasion for committing adultery; both are asserted by Christ, the latter in Matt. V, the former in the present passage concerning him who puts away a wife for a reason other than fornication: which latter, however, only then has a place when that which Christ adds here occurs, he marries another wife, who has put away the former. Whence it is clear that the sense of these two statements, being so diverse, is not the same in every respect. For that sentence is one: He who dismisses a wife outside of fornication, causes her to commit adultery; but this one is another: He who dismisses a wife unless for fornication, and marries ANOTHER, commits adultery. Grotius perhaps wished to gratify the Papists, who deny that separation is made through adultery, not only as regards bed and board, but also as regards the bond of matrimony: and thus they deny that the innocent party, when a spouse is rejected on account of adultery, even if the separation is made by the sentence of a judge, can pass to other vows, since an anathema was vibrated in the Council of Trent, sess. XXIV, c. 7, against those who think so: so that, therefore, they may not seem contrary to Christ, they pretend that these words are to be taken not exceptively, but negatively, as if Christ only wishes to affirm that a wife who is not an adulteress, i.e., faithful and chaste, cannot be dismissed, but wishes to say nothing about the unfaithful and adulterous one, to avoid the odium of the Pharisees and the people, as if they thought impiously enough about Christ's truth.

Master Cornelius Lapideus holds here) although they cannot deny that the particle εἰ μὴ is exceptive in Matt. 11:27, 12:4, 39, 19:17, 21:19, 24:36, and elsewhere throughout, and that it is rendered thus by the Vulgate, which is authentic to them: nor does the comparison of Matt. 5:32 leave room for ambiguity, where the word παρεκτὸς cannot be taken otherwise than exceptively. And the ancient interpreters easily agree on this. Chrysostom teaches that the power of dissolving marriage is denied here, except to him who has caught his wife in fornication: Nazianzen, in the Greek Catena of Nicetas, says: The Law indeed in this place permits divorce for any cause, but Christ does not, but only to be separated from an adulteress. Isidore of Pelusium, Book III, Epistle 76: Christ himself ordered those who violate the law of marriage to be cast out. But unless this happens, he commanded that all other vices of wives be borne, nay, he pronounced it necessary. Nor is that indeed in vain and rashly. For other vices do not in the least concern each of those who are joined by the law of marriage; but adultery tends to the very pacts of marriage, and affects with insult the εὐγένειαν of children (which others render as nobility, Conr. Rittershusius prefers to explain as well-born character, but I would judge it more correctly rendered here as legitimate procreation), and tears apart kinships, and finally ruins and overturns all human life. Hence it was also defined in public Councils that the bond of marriage is dissolved by fornication: as Sixtus Senensis, Book VI, Biblioth. annot. 81, p. 582, grants us here the consensus not only of the ancient Fathers and some Pontificals, but also of Councils, such as Tertullian, Book IV against Marcion, and Ambrose on 1 Cor. 7, Pope Zachary I, and the Councils of Elvira, Mainz, and Tivoli, as well as Cardinal Thomas Cajetan on this passage. and Ambrose, Bishop of Conza, in Volume V of his Commentaries on 1 Corinthians; and he confesses furthermore that it is lawful to repudiate adulteresses by the force of Christ's words, and that these things are therefore to be understood exceptively, teaching with us Hilary, Canon IV on Matthew; the Author of the Opus Imperfectum on Matthew, Homily 32; Chrysostom, Homily 17 on Matthew and Homily on Divorce in 1 Cor. 7; Euthymius on Matthew 5; Theophylact on Luke 16; Chromatius, Bishop of Aquileia, on Matthew 5; as also Augustine in his book on Adulterous Marriages, as well as in his book on Faith and Works, chapter 19, although he contends regarding these latter that they only admit separation from bed and board, but not the dissolution of the marriage bond, which will hardly be proven from the same, if you except Augustine: nay, B. Gerhard demonstrates from the same in his Confessio Catholica, Book II, Part III. Art. 19, ch. 2, p. 257, that they speak of the dissolution of the marriage bond and grant access to another marriage. And that many Greek Fathers feel this way, and that the modern Greek Church in actual fact dissolves marriages and gives spouses the power to enter into other marriages in the case of adultery, is undoubtedly certain and notorious; see Bellarmine, Book on Matrimony, ch. 15, § 'sentiunt', Benedict Justinian in his Commentary on Romans, ch. 7, whence the formulators of the Canons in the Council of Trent had abstained from the word 'anathema', so as not to rashly condemn that opinion which was that of St. Ambrose and many Fathers of the Greek Church; and the Venetian ambassadors warned that, since their Republic has in its power the kingdoms of Cyprus, Crete, Corfu, Zante, and Cephalonia, inhabited by Greeks, among whom it has been the custom from the most ancient time to repudiate an adulterous wife and marry another—a rite most well-known to the whole Church, for which they were never condemned or reproved by any Council—it would be unjust to condemn those who are absent and not called to this Council. See Petr. Suavis, Book VIII, History of the Council of Trent, p. 869 and 879. Grotius praises on Matt. 5, p. 99, not only Canon 65 of the Council of Elvira: If any cleric's wife has committed adultery, and her husband knows that she is committing adultery, and does not immediately cast her out, he shall not receive communion at the end; lest from those who ought to be an example of good conduct, the masteries of crimes seem to proceed: but also the Constitutions of Clement: ὁ κατέχων τὴν παρεφθαρμένην, Φύσεως θέσμε παρανόμος : ἐπείπερ ὁ κατέχων μοιχαλίδα ἄφρων καὶ ἀσεβής; as also Canon 8 of the Synod of Neocaesarea: ἐὰν μετὰ τὴν χειροτονίαν μοιχευθῇ (γυνή τιν@) ὁ ὀφείλων ἀπολῦσαι αὐτήν. He also alleges Justin Martyr, who is closest to the Apostolic times, who in his oration to the Roman Senate praises a Christian woman who, using the benefit of Roman law, sent a bill of divorce to her husband who was lusting beyond what is lawful, and divorced him. Ὅπως μὴ κοινωνὸς τῶν ἀδικημάτων, καὶ ἀσεβημάτων γένηται, μένεσα ἐν τῇ συζυγίᾳ καὶ ὁ- μοδίαιτος & ὁμόκοιτος γινομένη. And although Grotius observes that in the case of even diminished modesty many Christians formerly abstained from a second marriage, he nevertheless rightly warned that Clement of Alexandria also approves of this very thing in such a way that he does not demand it as if it were necessary, and that this opinion arose more from a peculiar goodness than from a common and received law, and that this appears both from others and from Tertullian, who shows in more than one place that those who had dismissed a wife on account of adultery were accustomed in his time to be admitted to a second marriage: and Origen narrates that the same was permitted in his time by certain Bishops; but also that it was later decreed by the Councils of Elvira, Orléans, and the first Council of Arles that it is lawful; and that the Greeks observe this even now: He adds also that Lactantius said: he is an adulterer who marries one dismissed by her husband, and he who has dismissed his wife for a reason other than the crime of adultery, in order to marry another. And he bids one to see Chrysostom in his second oration concerning those who fasted with the Jews, near the end.

But that which Grotius writes to have been perpetually observed among Christians, that the wife of a man committing fornication could not for that reason depart from the marriage, will be difficult to prove. He praises the Greeks on Apostolic Canon XLVIII. But it has long since been demonstrated that those canons are spurious. He praises Basil in response IX. But we have been able to find nothing of the sort in either the longer or the shorter responses of Basil. He praises the Eliberine Canon IX, that the same was also observed in the West: A faithful woman who has left a faithful husband who is an adulterer and marries another, let her be prohibited from marrying. But that council was particular, and the sanctions of such councils were not general and perpetual, but for a time, and made for certain reasons; as Sixtus Senensis warned in the cited place; and Grotius admits that the right of the husband and the wife was equal under Roman laws, and that the Apostle Paul perhaps puts them on an equal footing in 1 Cor. VII. 25. To this also pertains the example praised by Justin and adduced by Grotius.

But Grotius says that it was not permitted for Jewish women to divorce their husbands of their own accord: Nor did Christ pronounce anything concerning them, not even in the case of adultery. Similarly Cajetan on this passage says: I understand from this law of the Lord Jesus Christ that it is permitted for a Christian to dismiss a wife on account of her carnal fornication, and to be able to take another wife. Nor should you understand from these things that a wife can also dismiss a fornicating husband, because JESUS, who is true GOD, did not grant this, nor is the reason equal, as is evident: nor even in the old law could a wife repudiate her husband. Concerning the Mosaic constitution of the state, it is certainly a matter of doubt: regarding which Josephus says, our law permits the right of divorce only to husbands, but it is not lawful for women, even when dismissed, to marry, unless with the permission of the former husband; but just as nothing is held in the divine law concerning the latter, so even if the former does not occur there αὐτολεξεὶ, nevertheless, because of the adultery of the husband, if that remained unpunished, wives could perform a divorce, as B. Gerhard rightly observes on Deut. XXIV. in his Commentary, page 1443. And the reason is not different in the case of adultery, as Cajetan thought: but entirely the same; because the Apostle compares the husband and the spouse on equal terms, as Grotius admits. The woman does not have power over her own body, but the husband SIMILARLY also the husband does not have power over his own body, but the woman, says the Apostle 1 Cor. VII. 4. For the unity of the flesh is no less broken by an adulterous husband than by a fornicating woman, and thus the bond of marriage is dissolved, and the substance of matrimony is abolished.

But why does Grotius argue whether what is said by Christ outside the cause of adultery should be taken so rigidly, that no other cause can render the mind tranquil? thinking that, because where the reason is the same, the law holds the same, the same equity has a place in other cases also: such as if a wife has plotted against the life of her husband with poison, if, as Origen posited, she has killed their common pledges; since marriage was instituted not for the sake of offspring alone, but also for mutual aid, nor can anything be more contrary to the contract of so close a Society than that which is committed against life. But here not only a certain example proposed by Christ, or some species of fact brought forward, but an exception, and that a unique and adequate one, besides which it is not for us to invent others, has been handed down: and therefore one must acquiesce in the explicit decision of Christ. Matth. V. 32. But I say to you, that everyone who dismisses his wife, except for the cause of fornication, makes her commit adultery and Matthew XIX. 9. But I say to you, that whoever dismisses his wife, unless for fornication, and marries another, commits adultery. And the reason is in the open, flowing from the very sanction of the matrimonial law: because through fornication the form of marriage is removed, and those two no longer remain one flesh: for an adulteress becomes one flesh with an adulterer 1 Cor. VI. 16. But through other causes, such as the killing of children or plots laid against life, the form of marriage is not removed, nor are the substantials of Matrimony abolished. For one must look not only to the end, which is outside the essence of the thing, but to the form, which gives being to the thing. Even if therefore the end of marriage does not find a place, or is not obtained, whether procreation or mutual aid, while the form of marriage remains safe, the marriage remains, nor can it be removed. Whence in more serious plots and dangers to life, separation is indeed granted as to bed and board, in order to avoid those things, until a reconciliation is made, and provision is made for the security of the spouse through sufficient caution, but the dissolution of marriage is not to be granted. When, however, someone is impotent for marriage due to a defect primarily of the members required for it, a divorce does not properly take place, when the male and female depart from each other and are separated by the authority of the Magistrate, because it was never a true marriage. Regarding which B. Benedict Carpzovius rightly defines in Jurisprud. Consistor. lib. II. Tit. XI. definit. Cc. n. 8. Spouses by the divine institution of marriage are one flesh, Genes. II. 24. Matth. XIX. 6. Therefore if that marriage cannot be obtained through impotence, it will be declared void. Nor, speaking properly, does a divorce then take place, but it is merely decreed that the marriage was null from the very beginning.

Latin:

Vers. 9. εἰμὴ ἐπὶ πορνείᾳ] Ita vetus editio Complutensis. Atque ita legit Syrus: id est, cum non sit adultera. Quod favet Origeni dicenti πορνείας mentionem non fieri in vim strictæ exceptionis, sed exempli gratia, nimirum ut gravio- res mores à levioribus discernantur. Seneca dixit, condo- nanda esse vitia, non portenta.

Καὶ γαμήσῃ ἄλλην μοιχᾶται.] Id est ποιεῖ μοιχᾶσθαι illam priorem à se dimissam. Ita hæc verba exponi debere ap- paret ex collatione loci qui supra est v. 32. Tacere recte dicitur qui facto causam præbet. Eysmos est Hellenistarum verba formæ Hiphil per activa exprimere, ut Rom. VIII. 26. Gal. IV. 6.

Insignis verborum Christi depravatio hæc est. Christus palam loquitur de adæquata causa dimit- tendæ uxoris, extra quam ejusdem repudium, ceu pugnans cum institutione conjugii, salva pietate fieri non possit, quam facit adulterium. Grotius contra adulterium unicam causam esse negat justi repudii, exempli solum gratia, adduci statuit. Christus eum, qui extra casum adulterii dimittit uxorem, & aliam ducit, mochari affirmat. Gro- tius ut hypothesi suæ serviat, non mochari eum, sed facere ut ipsa mœchetur, uxor nempe, quam di- misit. Priori obtendit editionem Complutensem, cu- jus gratia audacter ipse textum immutat; & quum cæteroquin Codices constanter habeant exceptivam εἰς μὴ, prætermissa particula εἰ sim- plicem negativam relinquit. Cui vero non tantum reliquorum Codicum consensus opponi potest, sed etiam locus parallelus Matth. V. 32. exceptivam diserte adhibens, παρεκτὸς præterquam vel ex- cepta fornicationis causa, ut vulgata reddit, quæ etiam hoc loco exceptivam retinet, nisi ob forni- cationem. Posteriori corruptelæ sensus Christi frustra morem Hellenistarum prætexit, locumque parallelum prædictum. Nam à proprio & rece- ptiori significatu temere recedendum non est. Aliud certe est mochari quempiam, aliud facere ut uxor mochetur, vel occasionem ei præbere mœchan- di; utrumque à Christo asseritur, hoc Matth. V. illud præsenti loco de eo qui extra fornicationem uxorem dimittit: quod posterius tamen tum de- mum locum habet, cum quod Christus hic addit, aliam ducit uxorem, qui priorem dimisit. Unde patet duarum istarum enunciationum utpote ad- eo diversarum non esse eundem per omnia sen- sum. Alia enim est sententia illa: Qui extra forni- cationem dimittit uxorem, facit eam mochari; Alia, vero hæc; Qui dimittit uxorem nisi ob fornicatio- nem, & ALIAM ducit, mochatur. Gratificari fortean voluit Grotius Papistis, qui negant per adulterium separationem fieri, non tantum quoad thorum & mensam, sed & quoad matrimonii vincu- lum: adeoque innocentem partem, cum ob ad- ulterium rejicitur conjux, etsi per sententiam Ju- dicis fiat separatio, ad alia vota transire posse, infi- ciantur, siquidem anathema vibratum est in Con- cilio Tridentino sess. XXIV. c. 7. adversus ita sen- tientes: ut ergo Christo ne contrarii videantur, fingunt, verba hæc accipienda esse non exceptive, sed negative, quasi Christus tantum velit affirma- re uxorem quæ non sit adultera, h. e. fidam & ca- stam non posse dimitti, de infida vero & adultera nil velit dicere, ad vitandam invidiam Pharisæo- rum & populi ut impie satis de Christo veritatis

Magistro Cornelius Lapideus hic habet) quum ta- men negare nequeant particulam εἰ μὴ excepti- vam esse Matth. XI. 27. c. XII. 4. 39. c. XIX. 17. c. XXI. 19. c. XXIV. 36. & alibi passim, atque ita reddita illa fit a vulgata ipsis authentica : nec locum ambigen- di relinquat collatio Matth. V. 32. ubi vox παρε- κτὸς aliter, quam exceptive accipi nequit. Et consentiunt facile in eo veteres Interpp. Chrysost. docet, negari hic facultatem conjugii solvendi, praeterquam ei, qui uxorem in fornicatione de- prehenderit: Nazianzenus in Caten. Graec. Nice- tae, Lex quidem, inquit, h. l. repudium propter quamcunque causam permittit, at Christus non item, sed a fornicaria solum separari. Isidorus Pelusio- ta lib. III. Epist. LXXVI. Christus ipse eas, qua ma- trimonii legem violant, ejicere jussit. Hoc autem nisi contingat, omnia alia uxorum vitia ferre praecepit, imo necessarium esse pronunciavit. Neque id quidem frustra & temere. Nam caetera quidem vitia unum- quemque eorum, qui matrimonii lege copulantur, minime intuentur; adulterium autem ad ipsa ma- trimonii pacta tendit, & filiorum εὐγένειαν (quod alii nobilitatem reddunt, Conr. Rittershusius bene natam indolem exponere mavult, at rectius hic censerem reddi legitimam procreationem) contu- melia afficit, & cognationes lacerat, ac denique hu- manam omnem vitam pessundat & evertit. Inde in Conciliis etiam publicis definitum fuit, per for- nicationem solvi vinculum matrimonii : quemad- modum non tantum Patrum veterum, Pontificio- rum nonnullorum, sed Conciliorum quoque con- sensum nobis hic largitur Sixtus Senensis libr. VI. Biblioth. annot. XXCI. p. 582. utpote Tertulliani, lib. IV. adv. Marc. & Ambrosii in 1. Cor. VII. Za- chariae I. Papae & Concilii Elibertini, Moguntini, & Tiburtini, nec non Thomae Cajetani Cardinal. in h. l. & Ambrosii Compsae Episcopi in volum. V. Commentar. in 1. ad Corinth. fateturque insuper adulter as repudiare licere, vi verborum Christi, adeoque haec exceptive esse intelligenda, nobiscum docere Hilarium Can. IV. in Matth. Autorem ope- ris imperfect. in Matth. homil. XXXII. Chrysosto- mum hom. XVII. in Matth. & homil. de repudio in 1. ad Cor. VII. Euthymium in Matth. V. Theo- phylactum in Luc. XVI. Chromatium Aquilejae E- piscopum in Matth. V. ut & Augustinum l. de ad- ulter. Conjug. ut & de fid. & oper. cap. XIX. etsi de his posterioribus contendat, eos tantum admitte- re separationem a thoro & mensa, non autem solu- tionem vinculi conjugii quod ex iisdem, si Augusti- num excipias, haud probabitur: imo demon- strat ex iisdem B. Gerhardus in Confess. Cathol: lib. II. part. III. Art. XIX. c. II. pag. 257. quod ipsi de dissolutione vinculi conjugii loquantur, & aditum ad aliud matrimonium concedant. Atque ita mul- tos Graecos Patres sentire, ac hodiernam Graecam Ec- clesiam re ipsa matrimonia dissolvere, & conjugi- bus alia matrimonia ineundi potestatem facere in causa adulterii, indubitato certum est, ac noto- rium; Vid. Bellarm. l. de Matrim. c. 15. §. sentiunt, Benedict. Justinian. in Comment. ad Rom. c. VII. unde in Concilio Tridentino ab anathematis voce Canonum formatores abstinuerant, ne opinio- nem illam, quae S. Ambrosii fuit, multorumque Pa- trum Graecae Ecclesiae, temere damnarent, Veneti- que Oratores monuerunt, quandoquidem Res- publica ipsorum habeat in potestate regna Cypri, Cretae, Corcyrae, Zacynthi, Cephaloniae a Graecis ha- bitata, quibus ab antiquissimo tempore in more positum uxorem adulteram repudiare, aliamque ducere, de quo ritu toti Ecclesiae notissimo nun- quam ab aliquo Concilio damnati aut reprehensi sunt, iniquum esse illos absentes, nec ad hoc Con- cilium vocatos, condemnare. Vid. Petr. Suavis l. VIII. Hist. Concil. Trident. p. 869. & 879. Grotius laudat ad Matth. V. pag. 99. non tantum Elibertini Concilii Canonem LXV. Si cujus Clerici uxor fuerit mœchata, & scierit eam maritus suus mœchari, & non statim eam projecerit, nec in fine accipiat com- munionem; ne ab his qui exemplum bonæ conversa- tionis esse debent, ab eis videantur scelerum Magi- steria procedere : sed etiam Clementis Constitutiones : ὁ κατέχων τὴν παρεφθαρμένην, Φύσεως θέσμε παρανόμος : ἐπείπερ ὁ κατέχων μοιχαλίδα ἄφρων καὶ ἀσεβής ; ut & Canonem VIII. Synodi Neo-Cæsa- riensis : ἐὰν μετὰ τὴν χειροτονίαν μοιχευθῇ (γυνή τιν@) ὁ ὀφείλων ἀπολῦσαι αὐτήν. Allegat etiam Justi- num Martyrem, qui Apostolicis temporibus pro- ximus in oratione ad Senatum Romanum laudat fœminam Christianam, quæ usa Romanæ legis bene- ficio marito ultra fas libidinanti repudium misit, & ab eo divortit. Ὅπως μὴ κοινωνὸς τῶν ἀδικημάτων, καὶ ἀσεβημάτων γένηται, μένεσα ἐν τῇ συζυγίᾳ καὶ ὁ- μοδίαιτος & ὁμόκοιτος γινομένη. Et quanquam observet Grotius; in casu etiam imminutæ pudici- tiæ multos Christianorum olim ab altero matrimonio abstinuisse, recte tamen monuit & Clementem Ale- xandrinum id ipsum ita probare, ut non exigat qua- si necessarium, & ortam eam sententiam esse magis ex bonitate peculiari, quam ex communi, receptaque le- ge, idque tum ex aliis, tum ex Tertulliano apparere, qui non uno loco ostendit solitos suo tempore ad matri- monium alterum admitti, qui ob adulterium uxorem dimississent: idemque suo tempore à quibusdam Epi- scopis permissum narrare Origenem; sed & serius con- ciliis Eliberino & Aurelianensi & Arelatensi primo decretum esse, id licere; atque id nunc quoque Græcos observare : Addit etiam Lactantium dixisse : adul- terum esse, qui à marito dimissam duxerit, & eum qui præter crimen adulterii uxorem dimiserit, ut al- teram ducat. Et videri jubet Chrysostomum ora- tione altera de his, qui cum Judæis jejunabant circa finem.

Quod autem Grotius perpetuo inter Christianos observatum fuisse scribit, viri scortantis uxorem eam ob causam discedere à matrimonio non potuisse, æ- gre docebitur. Laudat Græcos ad Canonem Apo- stolicum XLIIX. Sed Canones illos νοθευτὲς jam pridem demonstratum est. Laudat Basilium re- sponso IX. Sed nihil tale neque in responsis fu- fioribus neque in succinctioribus Basilii reperire potuimus. Laudat Eliberinum Canonem IX. quod idem in Occidente observatum quoque fuerit : Fœmina fidelis, quæ adulterum maritum reliquerit fidelem & alterum ducit, prohibeatur ne ducat. Sed concilium illud particulare fuit, & sanctiones ta- lium conciliorum non generales erant, & perpetuæ, sed ad tempus, idque certis rationibus factæ; ut Sixtus Senensis l. c. monuit; & fatetur Grotius, le- gibus Romanis par fuisse jus mariti, & fœminæ, ac pari forte eos componere Paulum Apostolum 1. Cor. VII. 25. Quo facit etiam exemplum à Justino laudatum, à Grotio adductum.

Sed ait Grotius, fœminis Judæis non licuisse sponte sua à marito divortere: Neque Christus quic- quam de illis pronunciavit, ne quidem in adulterii casu. Similiter Cajetanus in h. l. intelligo, inquit, ex hac lege Domini Jesu Christi, licitum esse Chri- stiano dimittere uxorem ob fornicationem carnalem ipsius uxoris, & posse ducere aliam uxorem. Nec ex his intelligas, uxorem quoque posse dimittere virum fornicantem, quia JESUS, qui est verus DE- US, hoc non concessit, nec est par ratio, ut pa- tet: nec etiam in veteri lege uxor poterat repudia- re virum. Reip. de constitutione Mosaica du- bium sane est: de qua Josephus, lex nostra, inquit, solis maritis jus repudii permittit, mulieribus au- tem, ne dimissis quidem, fas est nubere, nisi prio- ris viri permissu; sed uti de posteriori nihil in lege divina habetur, ita etsi prius αὐτολεξεὶ ibi non oc- currat, potuisse tamen, ob adulterium mariti, si impunitum id mansit, uxores divortium facere, recte observat B. Gerhard. ad Deut. XXIV. in Commentar. pag. 1443. Et ratio haud est dif- par, in casu adulterii, uti putavit Cajetanus: sed par omnino; quia pari sorte componit maritum & conjugem Apostolus, fatente Grotio. Mulier sui corporis potestatem non habet, sed Vir SIMILI- TER autem & Vir sui corporis potestatem non ha- bet, sed mulier, ait Apostolus 1. Cor. VII. 4. Non minus enim unitas carnis solvitur per maritum adulterum, quam per mulierem fornicatricem, ad- eaque vinculum conjugii dissolvitur, ac substan- tia matrimonii aboletur.

Cur vero disputat Grotius an quod dicitur à Christo extra adulterii causam tam rigide accipi- endum sit, ut nulla alia causa animum possit tran- quillum reddere? existimans, quia ubi eadem est ratio, jus idem valet, eandem æquitatem in aliis ca- sibus etiam locum habere: utpote si uxor veneno vitæ mariti insidiata fuerit, si, quod Origenes po- suit, communia pignora interfecerit; siquidem non prolis solius, sed & mutui auxilii causa conjugium institutum sit, nec quicquam possit contractui tam arctæ Societatis magis esse adversum, quam quod in vitam committitur. Sed hic non solum exem- plum quoddam à Christo propositum, aut spe- cies aliqua facti adducta, sed exceptio, eaque unica, & adæquata, præter quam alias fingere nostrum non est, tradita: ideoque disertæ Chri- sti decisioni acquiescendum. Matth. V. 32. E- go autem dico vobis, quia omnis, qui dimiserit uxo- rem suam, excepta fornicationis causa, facit eam mœchari & Matthæi XIX. 9. Dico autem vobis, quia quicunque dimiserit uxo- rem suam, nisi ob fornicationem, & aliam duxerit, mœchatur. Et ratio in aprico est ex ipsa legis matrimonialis sanctione fluens: quia per forni- cationem matrimonii forma tollitur, nec amplius duo illi manent una caro: nam adultera una fit caro cum adultero 1. Cor. VI. 16. At per alias causas, utpote interfectionem liberorum vel insi- dias vitæ structas non tollitur conjugii forma, nec substantialia Matrimonii abolentur. Non enim tantum ad finem, qui extra essentiam rei est, sed ad formam, quæ dat esse rei, respiciendum. Etsi ergo finis conjugii non inveniat locum, aut ob- tineatur, seu prolificatio, seu mutuum auxilium, dum salva manet conjugii forma, conjugium re- manet, nec tolli potest. Unde in gravioribus insidiis & vitæ periculis separatio quidem con- ceditur quoad thorum & mensam, ob ea decli- nanda, donec reconciliatio fiat, & per sufficien- tem cautionem de securitate prospiciatur conju- gi, non autem concedenda est matrimonii dis- solutio. Cum vero impotens quis ad matrimo- nium ob defectum imprimis membrorum ad id requisitorum est, divortium proprie non fit, cum discedunt ab invicem, & separantur autoritate Magistratus mas & fœmina, quia nunquam ve- rum fuit conjugium. Quo de recte B. Benedict. Carpzovius in Jurisprud. Consistor. lib. II. Tit. XI. definit. Cc. n. 8. Conjuges ex divina conju- gii institutione sunt una caro, Genes. II. 24. Matth. XIX. 6. Proinde si per impotentiam illud ob- tineri nequit conjugium declarabitur irritum. Nec proprie loquendo tum fit divortium, sed duntaxat de- cernitur, ab initio statim conjugium fuisse nullum.

## 19:10
Vers. 10. Αἰτία] Condition. דברה. For I clearly agree with the most learned man interpreting this word from Roman law. To Theophilus, the plaintiff is said to seek more τῇ αἰτίᾳ who πλῆ- θλονὰ μὲν ἐκοτᾶ, χείρονα δὲ τὴν αἵρεσιν ποιεῖ τῷ ἐναγομένῳ. It makes a great difference, says Pomponius, whether one was ignorant of the cause and fact of another, or was ignorant of his own right. Thus, the Jurisconsults say that not only the body, but also the cause of the thing must be restored l. præterea par. 1. de rei vind. L. Cum fundus si cert. pet. that is, its entire quality. Martial: Why do you ruin for me the cause of my Nomentan field, which was precious because of the neighbor.

It is evident from many indications that most ancient Christian writers, and among them the interpreter of Matthew, Mark and Luke, were not ignorant of legal expressions. If, say the Apostles, such is the condition of the husband, namely that it is not lawful for him to dismiss his wife at the whim of his own mind, it would be better to abstain from marriage than to clothe oneself in an inextricable evil. The inconvenient dispositions of women deter many from marriage. The wise Hebrew Eccles. XXV. 22. συνοικῆσαι λέοντι κᾴ δρά- κοντι ἐνδοκῶ ἢ συνοικῆσαι μετὰ γυναικὸς πονηρᾶς. Alexis: Ἐπὰν δὲ γήμῃς, ἐδὲ σαυτᾶ κύριον Ἔξεστιν εἶναι· πᾶς γὰρ εὐθύνας λόγον Ἐφημερινὰς τῷ βίῳ κεκτημένῳ. For this evil, the freedom of divorce seemed the best remedy: Ὡς τὴν κακὴν μὲν ἐξέβαλλε δωμάτων, Τὴν δ᾽ ἐσιὼν ἐσθλὴν ἠδίως ἐσώζετο, as Euripides says. And Antiphon meanwhile, among those to whom he dissuades marriage, brings forward also this, εἰ γὰρ τύχοι μὴ ἐπιτηδείᾳ γενο- μένῃ, χαλεπὸν ἐκπομπαὶ, χαλεπὸν δὲ κεκτῆσθαι κτῆμα τοιῦτον.

Grotius rightly explains the condition, conveying this sense: If, say the Apostles, such is the condition of the husband, namely that it is not lawful for him to dismiss his wife at the whim of his own mind, it would be better to abstain from marriage than to induce oneself into an inextricable evil. Similar is the interpretation of Chrysostom, as also of Peter of Laodicea, who has it thus in the Catena of Greek Fathers. For if, they said among themselves, a man and a woman are joined for this reason, that they may now be one, and never be torn from each other, however stiff-necked and stubborn the woman may be, it is not expedient to marry. For it is more prudent to abstain from marriage altogether, and to suppress the motions of an effervescent nature while celibate, than to be bound by the bond of such a relationship to a stubborn or ill-mannered woman. Indeed, they did not take the words of Christ otherwise than as they sound, that a marriage once entered into, outside the cause of fornication, whatever other causes there may be, cannot be dissolved.

Latin:

Vers. 10. Αἰτία] Conditio. דברה. Plane enim assen- tior viro doctissimo ex jure Romano hanc vocem interpre- tanti. Theophilo dicitur actor plus petere τῇ αἰτίᾳ qui πλῆ- θλονὰ μὲν ἐκοτᾶ, χείρονα δὲ τὴν αἵρεσιν ποιεῖ τῷ ἐναγομένῳ. Plu- rimum interest, inquit Pomponius, utrum quis de alterius causa ac facto nesciret, an de jure suo ignoraret. Sic non cor- pus tantum, sed & causam rei restituendam ajunt Juriscon- sulti l. præterea par. 1. de rei vind. L. Cum fundus si cert. pet. id est omnem ejus qualitatem. Martialis: Quid Nomentani causam mihi perdis agelli, Propter vicinum qui pretiosus erat.

Scriptores plerosque Christianos veteres atque inter eos Matthæi interpretem, Marcum & Lucam juris locutionum fuisse non ignaros plurimis indiciis patet. Si, inquiunt Apo- stoli, ea est mariti conditio, scilicet ut uxorem pro animi sui arbitrio dimittere ei fas non sit, satius esset abstinere a nu- ptiis, quam se induere in malum inextricabile. Incom- moda mulierum ingenia multos a matrimonio deterrent. Sapiens Hebræus Eccles. XXV. 22. συνοικῆσαι λέοντι κᾴ δρά- κοντι ἐνδοκῶ ἢ συνοικῆσαι μετὰ γυναικὸς πονηρᾶς. Alexis: Ἐπὰν δὲ γήμῃς, ἐδὲ σαυτᾶ κύριον Ἔξεστιν εἶναι· πᾶς γὰρ εὐθύνας λόγον Ἐφημερινὰς τῷ βίῳ κεκτημένῳ. Huic malo remedium optimum videbatur repudii libertas: Ὡς τὴν κακὴν μὲν ἐξέβαλλε δωμάτων, Τὴν δ᾽ ἐσιὼν ἐσθλὴν ἠδίως ἐσώζετο, ut Euripides inquit. Et Antiphon interea quibus matrimo- nium dissuadet, affert & hoc, εἰ γὰρ τύχοι μὴ ἐπιτηδείᾳ γενο- μένῃ, χαλεπὸν ἐκπομπαὶ, χαλεπὸν δὲ κεκτῆσθαι κτῆμα τοιῦτον.

Conditionem recte explicat Grotius, sensum hunc tradens: Si inquiunt Apostoli, ea est mariti conditio, scilicet ut uxorem pro animi sui arbitrio dimittere ei fas non sit, satius esset, abstinere a nu- ptiis, quam se inducere in malum inextricabile. Simi- lis est Chrysostomi interpretatio, ut & Petri Laodi- ceni, qui ita habet in Caten. Græc. Patr. Si enim, ajebant ipsi secum, propterea conjuncti sunt vir & mulier, ut unum jam sint, neque unquam ab invicem divellantur, quantumvis cervicosa & contumax mu- lier sit, non expedit nubere. Consultius enim est abstinere nuptiis omnino, & effervescentis naturæ motus utcunque opprimere cælibem, quam mulieri pervicaci aut male moratæ, vinculo tantæ necessitudi- nis adstringi. Nimirum verba Christi aliter non accipiebant, quam prout ipsa sonant, extra causam fornicationis matrimonium semel initum, quæ- cunque aliæ sint causæ, dissolvi non posse.

## 19:11
Vers. 11. ἑ πάντες χωρᾶσι τὸν λόγον τῦτον] Not all are sufficient for this matter, as the Syrian rightly interprets. Thus also Origen: ἀλλὰ κ᾿ ἄγεσθαι γυναῖκα ἐπέτρεψεν ἡμῖν ὁ θεὸς, ὡς ἐ πάν- των χωρέντων τὸ διαφέρον, τετέστι τὸ πάντῃ καθαρὸν. The poet, not inelegantly, whom people commonly but incorrectly call Phocylides, used χωρεῖν in this way: Οὐ χωρεῖ μεγάλην διδαχὴν ἀδίδακτον ἀκέειν· Οὐ γὰρ δὴ τοίοισ᾽ οἱ μηδίποτ᾽ ἐσθλὰ μαθόντες. And Plutarch in the life of Cato of Utica makes the Romans who were around him pray thus: εἰ Κάτωνες ἐκ εἰσὶν ἐδὲ τὸ Κά- τωνος φρόνημα χωρᾶσιν, οἰκτείρεσι τὴν ἀσθένειαν αὐτῶν. The sense is that many are too weak to be equal to a sublime purpose. Cyprian, concerning certain virgins, says: if they do not wish or are not able to persevere. Lactantius explains these words of Christ: If anyone, he says, is able to do this, he will have an excellent and incomparable reward. Because the kind of continence is, as it were, the pinnacle and consummation of all virtues.

Αλλ' οἷς δέδοται] Christ says this is given by God: yet not without the effort and struggle of men, as appears from what follows. Clement of Rome in his Epistle to the Corinthians: ὁ ἁγνὸς τῇ σαρκὶ μὴ ἀλαζονευέσθω γινώσκων ὅτι ἕτερός ἐστιν ὁ ἐ- πιχορηγῶν αὐτῷ τὴν ἐγκρατείαν. Tertullian seems to me to have transcribed this, as he did certain other things, in his book On the Veiling of Virgins: And if the virtue of continence is conferred by God, why do you boast, as if you had not received it? Clement of Alexandria: εὐτυχίαν μὲν κ' οἷς τῦτο δέδωκται ὑπὸ θεῶ μακαρίζομεν.

Grotius renders it thus: Not all are sufficient for this matter; and he notes that the Syrian interprets it thus: so that the sense is: that many are too weak to be equal to a sublime purpose. And thus also Chrysostom, saying that the Lord shows that this is not for everyone to grasp: he shows that this work stands in need of heavenly help, namely, the continence preserved throughout one's whole life. Many others explain it similarly. But by the power of receiving, this word does not designate a faculty of strength for performing this thing, that is, celibacy, but on the contrary, that the faculty of the intellect is denied, so that it might be able to reconcile eunuchism with the perpetual obligation of spouses, B. Hülfemann in Man. August. Confess. p. 143 teaches, and thus that Christ is not speaking of continence outside of marriage, or of the capacity of the will and appetite to desire celibacy, but of the capacity of the intellect, how a certain eunuchism can consist with the marital bond and the obligation of not dismissing a wife. In which manner the word to receive is taken in John 8:37, 1 Corinthians 2:14, namely, not to signify not having the faculty of performing something, but not understanding the sayings of someone, not approving. For it is evident from Mark 13 that the disciples did not understand. Therefore, what they themselves could not receive (according to this interpretation), Christ was explaining, namely, that eunuchism can entirely consist with the marital bond, not indeed that which is of the body; as it excludes from marriage by divine right, but the eunuchism of the mind, when one abstains with a consenting spouse for the sake of the kingdom of God, or for the sake of the Church, 1 Cor. 7:5, where, however, a vow of perpetual continence is not to be rashly taken: for that would be contrary to the Apostle 1 Cor. 7:5, 27. Compare what we have said in our Commentary on Genesis at chapter 2:18, p. 312 seqq. Thus Ignatius uses this saying regarding faith in Christ in his Epistle to the Smyrnaeans: let him who can receive it, receive it; let him who hears, hear.

Latin:

Vers. 11. ἑ πάντες χωρᾶσι τὸν λόγον τῦτον] Non omnes suf- ficiunt huic rei, ut recte interpretatur Syrus. Sic & Orige- nes: ἀλλὰ κ᾿ ἄγεσθαι γυναῖκα ἐπέτρεψεν ἡμῖν ὁ θεὸς, ὡς ἐ πάν- των χωρέντων τὸ διαφέρον, τετέστι τὸ πάντῃ καθαρὸν. Ita χωρεῖν usurpavit Poëta non inelegans quem vulgo Phocyliden non recte vocant: Οὐ χωρεῖ μεγάλην διδαχὴν ἀδίδακτον ἀκέειν· Οὐ γὰρ δὴ τοίοισ᾽ οἱ μηδίποτ᾽ ἐσθλὰ μαθόντες. Et Plutarchus vita Catonis Uticensis sic orantes facit Ro- manos qui circa ipsum erant: εἰ Κάτωνες ἐκ εἰσὶν ἐδὲ τὸ Κά- τωνος φρόνημα χωρᾶσιν, οἰκτείρεσι τὴν ἀσθένειαν αὐτῶν. Sensus est, multos esse imbecilliores, quam ut pares sint sublimi proposito. Cyprianus de virginibus quibusdam, si persevera- re, inquit, nolunt vel non possunt. Lactantius hæc Christi ver- baita explicat. Si quis hoc, inquit, facere potuerit, habebit e- ximiam incomparabilemque mercedem. Quod continentia ge- nus, quasi fastigium est omniumque consummatio virtutum.

Αλλ' οἷς δέδοται] Dari a Deo hoc dicit Christus: attamen non sine hominum nisu ac contentione, ut ex sequentibus apparet. Clemens Romanus in Epistola ad Corinthios: ὁ ἁγνὸς τῇ σαρκὶ μὴ ἀλαζονευέσθω γινώσκων ὅτι ἕτερός ἐστιν ὁ ἐ- πιχορηγῶν αὐτῷ τὴν ἐγκρατείαν. Quod ut alia quædam, Transscripsisse mihi videtur Tertullianus libro de virginibus velandis: Et si a Deo confertur continentiæ virtus, quid gloria- ris, quasi non acceperis? Clemens Alexandrinus: εὐτυχίαν μὲν κ' οἷς τῦτο δέδωκται ὑπὸ θεῶ μακαρίζομεν.

Reddit ita Grotius: Non omnes sufficiunt huic rei; & sic interpretari Syrum notat: ut sensus sit: multos imbecilliores, esse, quam ut pares sint subli- mi proposito. Atque ita etiam Chrysost. dicens Do- minus non omnium esse hoc capere: ostendit cœlesti auxilio indigere istud opus, continentiam videlicet tota vita servatam. Similiter plerique alii exponunt. At per potentiam capiendi verbum hoc non designa- tam facultatem virium ad praestandam rem hanc, id est, calibatum, sed contra, negatam esse facul- tatem intellectus, ut possit ἐυνεχίαν cum perpetua conjugum obligatione componere, B. Hülfemann. in Man. August. Confess. p. 143. docet, adeoque Christum non de continentia extra matrimonium, sive de capacitate voluntatis & appetitus ad expe- tendum calibatum loqui, sed de capacitate intelle- ctus, quomodo cum vinculo connubiali & obli- gatione non dimittendi uxorem ἐυνυχία quædam consistere possit. Quo pacto verbum capiendi accipitur Johan. VIII. 37. 1. Corinth. II. 14. ni- mirum non ut significet, non habere facultatem aliquid praestandi, sed non intelligere dicta alicujus, non approbare. Non enim discipulos intellexisse è Marci XIII. constat. Quod ergo ipsi capere non poterant (juxta hanc interpretationem) id explicabat Christus, nimirum consistere omni- no cum vinculo conjugali posse ἐυνεχίαν, non eam quidem, quæ corporis est; utpote quæ à Matrimonio divinitus excludit, sed ἐυνεχίαν ani- mi, cum consentiente conjuge ob regnum Dei, vel Ecclesiæ causa, quis abstinet 1. Cor. VII. 5. u- bi tamen votum continentiæ perpetuæ temere emit- tendum non est: id enim refragaretur Apostolo 1. Corinth. VII. 5. 27. Conf. quæ diximus in Com- ment. in Genes. ad cap. II. 18. p. 312. seqq. Sic usurpat dictum hoc Ignatius de fide in Christum in Epist. ad Smyrnens. ὁ χωρῶν χωρείτω, ὁ ἀκύων ἀκεέτω.

## 19:12
Verse 12. For there are eunuchs. These are added for the sake of completing the comparison. But just as the name of eunuchs is for the Greeks, so it is a general appellation for the Latins for castrated men, according to Ulpian, although there are also cases where castrated men are opposed to those who are eunuchs.

Those who were made eunuchs by men. Such a one is called אדם סריס in the Aruch: a eunuch by commission in the canons.

These things were added not only for the sake of completing the comparison; but either for the sake of explaining that difficulty, how eunuchism can have a place even while the bond of marriage is preserved: or so that, on the occasion of the saying about the gift of continence, one might be taught about eunuchs, that some are bound to abstain from marriage because of a defect of nature, who are eunuchs from their mother's womb, others because of the malice of men: who have been castrated by men either voluntarily or against their will: others finally because of a free and firm purpose of mind, who castrate themselves for the sake of the kingdom of heaven, or for the sake of the Church, so that they may serve the Gospel more expeditiously: whom Christ excludes entirely from marriage as being unfit for it, and teaches that they are not to be admitted in any way: but to these who voluntarily contain themselves, he casts no snare of conscience, but if they are endowed with the gift of continence, he implies that they can freely abstain from marriage. See the Commentary on Genesis, loc. cit., where we have taught at length that eunuchs, castrated men, and those who have been castrated are excluded from marriage, as being clearly unfit for wedlock because of a defect of the members destined for generation. Chrysostom warns that this is done out of necessity, because eunuchs, whose members have been cut out, abstain from marriage, according to the nature of things: for neither can a eunuch be joined to a woman. Namely, so that Christ might explain the matrimonial law more fully, since it pertains to the form of marriage, what he had said, that they should be two in one flesh, he openly restrains and excludes eunuchs who are such in body from marriage, but makes the use of marriage free for all others, and that voluntary continence can well consist with marriage, if indeed they abstain from the marital custom by mutual consent, with the bond of marriage preserved, 1 Cor. 7:5.

They made themselves eunuchs. By a determination of the mind, not seeking a wife, as Paul speaks in 1 Cor. 7:27. But to the purpose there must be added a solicitous guarding of oneself, prayers, fasts, and whatever else there is by which the body can be brought into subjection. For the achievement also requires our own diligence, as Chrysostom speaks when dealing with this matter at chapter 7 of the first Epistle to the Corinthians: which he executes more broadly in his work on Virginity, chapter 27. This comparison shows that only those things are crowned by God which are done freely.

For the sake of the kingdom of heaven. For the sake of love toward God, as Clement interprets in Stromata III, that is, so that they may better be able to care for the things of the Lord, that they may be holy both in body and in spirit, as Paul speaks in 1 Cor. 7:34. But to fulfill the precepts of Christianity more rightly, more freely, and more constantly: not that celibacy is in them, but that it is a great help toward them. Therefore, for the sake of the kingdom of God is the same as for the sake of the Gospel in Mark 10:29. Which Origen said in his first book against Celsus, for the sake of serving the divine more purely, not even touching the pleasures permitted by the law. For not only those who were set apart for the ministry of the word, but besides them many others of both sexes and every order of men have embraced this higher way of life from the beginning of Christianity. Justin Martyr. And many men and many women, sixty and seventy years old, who were discipled to Christ from childhood, remain incorrupt; and I pray to show such in every race of men. The same elsewhere: either we do not marry at the beginning unless for the rearing of children, or refusing to marry, we live in perfect continence. Tatian against the Greeks: you revile the virgins among us. Minutius Felix about the Christians: Most enjoy the virginity of an inviolate body rather than boast of it. Tertullian notes that in his age, the virgins of the churches were accustomed to be secluded in certain places, while in other places they were not secluded. The same on the resurrection of Christ: How many voluntary eunuchs, how many virgins married to Christ? See Cyprian, and others. But Christ deservedly added this cause of piety. For otherwise the αἱ σεμναὶ among the Indians, the Vestals of the Romans, and not a few athletes were doing the same, whom Clement names as those who practice self-control through bodily discipline and abstain from sexual pleasures. Eusebius adds that among Christians, virginity was observed by voluntary choice, not by necessity as among the Greeks. Chrysostom in VII to the Romans: For this reason, among the ancients, no one had yet appeared practicing virginity, and they were greatly astonished, but now the thing is spread everywhere in the inhabited world.

Grotius rightly understands this not as Origen did, concerning castration which is by hand—who castrated himself out of a misinterpretation of this sentence, as witnessed by Eusebius, Hist. Eccl. book VI, ch. VII—but as that which is by the determination of the mind. Concerning which Chrysostom, homily LXIII on Matthew: He does not speak of the cutting off of members, far from it: but he understands the cutting off of thoughts. For he who cuts off a member is subject to a curse: for he who attempts such a thing undertakes the work of a homicide, and provides an opportunity to those who criticize the workmanship of God. Whence in the Council of Nicaea, Canon I, such as castrated themselves were excluded from sacred offices. However, these things are not to be drawn precisely to perpetual celibacy, much less to a religious vow of the same. For one can also abstain for a time for the sake of the kingdom of heaven: which the Apostle taught in 1 Cor. VII. 1. Christ certainly does not understand here a vow of celibacy, but a firm purpose of mind, as Isidore of Pelusium, book III, Ep. 13, and others explain, of persisting in virginity, which Isidore refers to both sexes. Some, with B. Franzius in his book on Interpretation, p. 978, explain it as spiritual castration; but the comparison of the eunuchism of the body and of the mind implies something more, and spiritual castration is necessary even for the married; that, of which Matthew V. 28 speaks. Therefore, it must not be conceded to the Papists that these words refer to perpetual celibacy, just as Grotius seems to grant it to them, explaining these words 'they have made themselves eunuchs' thus: by the determination of the mind, 'not seeking a wife,' as Paul speaks in 1 Cor. VII. 27, whence he adds afterwards concerning celibacy: For not only those who were set apart for the ministry of the word, but many others besides them of both sexes and every rank, from the beginning of Christianity, have embraced this most sublime way of life. He says this was done to fulfill the precepts of Christianity more rightly, more freely, and more constantly, not because celibacy is in them, but because it is a great help toward them. Although indeed celibacy serves those who are endowed with the gift of continence, so that they may better be able to care for the things of the Lord, that they may be holy in body and in spirit, 1 Cor. 7:34, yet that gift is given to few, nor can those who contain themselves for a time promise or vow perpetual continence, on account of the fragility and weakness of the flesh, and the power and craftiness of Satan, and the scandals and malignity of the world: nor is marriage in itself an impediment to performing the precepts of Christianity, but on account of the calamity of the times, nay, according to the Apostle's warning, it serves to restrain the lusts of the flesh, since it is better to marry than to burn: and spouses who fear God may mutually excite one another to the duties of piety, by mutual instruction, exhortation, the governing of the family in the fear of the Lord, the holy education of children for the glory of God, and in cross and calamity may wholesomely edify one another by this domestic mutual consolation, and their houses, so that marriage, which is an image of our spiritual union with Christ, may be a signal help to the duties of Christianity, and in no way an impediment. Concerning which Claud. Espensæus on 1 Tim. 3: Marriages, although they may have much difficulty, can yet be assumed in such a way that they are not an impediment to a more perfect life: whence, although excessive estimators among the ancients have extolled the same with hyperbolic praises of celibacy, in which B. Rhenanus in the argument of Tertullian's book Exhortation to Chastity desires that they were too little fair to matrimony. Espensæus on Continence, book 1, ch. 9. It is wonderful, he says, how vehement they were for continence, not to mention Erasmus's censure of them: yet venerable antiquity was not lacking in celebrating the connubial state, but rather adorned the same with due praises: inasmuch as God Himself so proclaims it as a holy and honored state, that He protests that it is NOT GOOD for man to be alone, Gen. 1:28, see Ps. 128:2, Eph. 5:32, Heb. 13:1. Concerning which Amphilochius in his sermon on the meeting of the Lord: Honored matrimony surpasses every earthly gift, since it is a fruitful tree, since it is an elegant plant, since it is the root of virginity, since like a farmer it cultivates branches endowed with reason and life, since its blessing is the increase of the world, since it consoles the race, since it makes men, since it fashions the divine image like a painter, since it has the Lord, who blesses it, since it is able to bear the whole world. Let them compare the verses of Nazianzen concerning marriage, and what we have said concerning the end and dignity of marriage in our Commentary on Genesis, p. 320 seqq. For the rest, we acquiesce in the opinion of the Augsburg Apology: Yet we do not equate virginity with marriage. For just as one gift excels another, prophecy excels eloquence, the science of military affairs excels agriculture, eloquence excels architecture; so virginity is a more excellent gift than marriage. Yet it is as an orator is not more righteous before God on account of his eloquence, so a virgin does not merit justification more by virginity than a spouse by conjugal duties, but each one ought to serve faithfully in his own gift and believe that on account of Christ he obtains the remission of sins by faith, and is accounted righteous before God by faith. Which was also the opinion of our blessed Luther, that we may add this on account of the calumnies of the Papists, in 1 Cor. 7: Marriage and virginity are of equal value before GOD. For both are a gift and a creature of God, even though one excels the other, if one compares them between themselves. Nor could Bellarmine deny these things, book on matrimony, ch. 34, in response to 19. It can happen, he says, that virginity is joined in one man with less charity, humanity, and other virtues than marriage in another man; therefore we cannot prefer a virgin to a married person, unless it is certain that they are equal in other virtues.

The passage 1 Cor. 7:34, that the unmarried can better care for the things that are of the Lord, that they may be holy in body and spirit, is to be left in that incomparable sense, and not to be understood exclusively with the Papists: and besides, it treats of a certain time, on account of common necessity, and also of certain persons, namely regarding marriages with infidels, for times and cases can also occur in which spouses can better care for the things that are of the Lord, when both are believers; which Caslander warned in Consult. art. 23.

But the Papists wrongly snatch the words of Christ 'for the sake of the kingdom of heaven' to the merit of the kingdom of heaven: such as Albert Pighius in Controv. ch. 14, on vows: Monks castrate themselves for the sake of attaining the kingdom of God and meriting the grace of God. Petr. à Soto in the refutation of the Wurtemberg Confession: Celibacy is the greatest satisfaction for sins and a merit of the kingdom of heaven. There is nothing in these words of Christ about the attainment of the heavenly kingdom, and not even anything about the heavenly kingdom of the other life, but about the kingdom of grace, as we call it, in this age; much less about the merit of the heavenly kingdom. It is the same, as Grotius himself warns, 'for the sake of the kingdom of God', 'for the sake of the gospel', because celibacy is more ready for the duties of the Holy Ministry and other exercises of piety. Conf. B. Gerhard on Marriage, § 500.

ὁ δυνάμενος χωρεῖν, χωρείτω] That is, he who has so much spirit, let him be encouraged in that virtue, let him proceed with God's favor. Ignatius also uses this saying, but dealing with faith in Christ: ὁ χωρῶν χωρείτω· ὁ ἀκόων ἀκουέτω, in his Epistle to the Smyrnaeans.

PART II. Admonition concerning the bringing of little children.

Latin:

Vers. 12. ἔσι γὰρ ἐυνῦχοι] Hæc adduntur implendæ com- parationis gratia. Sicut autem Græcis nomen ἐυνύχων, i- ta Latinis Spadonum generalis appellatio est, teste Ulpia- no, quamquam est & ubi spadones castratis opponun- tur.

Οἵτινες ἐυνυχίσθησαν ὑπὸ τῶν ἀνθρώπων] Talis qui est אדם סריס dicitur in Aruch: ἐυνῦχος ἐξ ἐπιτροπῆς in ca- nonibus.

Non tantum comparationis implendæ causa hæc addita; sed sive explicandæ difficultatis istius gratia, quomodo etiam salvo matrimonii vinculo possit ἐυνυχία locum habere: seu ut occasione dicti de dono continentiæ, de Eunuchis doceatur, quod alii à conjugio abstinere teneantur ob naturæ vi- tium, qui Eunuchi sunt à matris utero, alii ob hominum maleficium: qui ab hominibus seu vo- luntario seu inviti castrati sunt: alii deniq; ob libe- rum & firmum animi propositum, qui se ipsos ca- strant ob regnum cœlorum, vel Ecclesiæ causa, ut Evangelio serviant expeditius: quorum illos & istos ceu ineptos ad conjugium ab eodem exclu- dit prorsus Christus, nec ullatenus admittendos docet: his autem voluntarie se continentibus la- queum conscientiæ minime injicit, sed si dono præ- diti continentiæ sint, à matrimónio libere eos abstinere posse innuit. Vid. Comment. in Ge- nes. l. c. ubi prolixe docuimus Eunuchos, Spado- nes & Castratos à matrimonio excludi, utpote pla- ne ineptos ad conjugium ob membrorum gene- rationi destinatorum defectum. Ex necessitate id fieri monet Chrysostom. quod Eunuchi, quibus membra exsecta sunt, à conjugio abstinent, κατὰ τὴν τῶν πραγμάτων φύσιν ex rei natura: ὔτε γὰρ ὁ ἐυνῦχος δύναται αὖ συγγενέσθαι γυναικί. neque enim Eunuchus conjungi potest mulieri. Nimi- rum ut plenius explicaret Christus legem matri- monialem, quum ad formam conjugii pertineat, quod dixerat, ut sint duo in carnem unam, arcet & excludit aperte Eunuchos corpore tales à conju- gio, cæteris autem omnibus liberum conjugii usum facit, ac probe consistere posse continen- tiam voluntariam cum conjugio, si nempe ex mu- tuo consensu connubiali abstineant consuetudine, salvo matrimonii vinculo, 1. Cor. VII. 5.

Εὐνούχισαν ἑαυτοὺς] Animi destinatione μὴ ζητοῦντες γυ- ναῖκα, ut Paulus loquitur 1. Cor. VII. 27. Sed ad proposi- tum accedere debet custodia sui sollicita, preces, jejunia, & quicquid præterea est quo potest τὸ σῶμα δουλαγωγεῖσθαι. Nam & ἡμετέρας σπουδῆς δεῖ τὸ κατόρθωμα, ut hac de re agens ad cap. VII. prioris ad Corinthios loquitur Chrysostomus: quod idem latius exequitur de Virginitate cap. XXVII. O- stendit hæc comparatio ea sola à Deo coronari quæ libere fiunt.

Διὰ τὴν βασιλείαν τῶν οὐρανῶν] Δι᾽ ἀγάπην πρὸς τὸν Θεὸν, ut Clemens interpretatur Strom. III. id est ut melius pos- sint μεριμνᾶν τὰ τοῦ κυρίου ἵνα ὦσιν ἅγιοι καὶ σώματι καὶ πνεύματι, ut Paulus loquitur 1. Cor. VII. 34. At implenda rectius, li- berius, atque constantius præcepta Christianismi: non quod in iis sit cælibatus, sed quod ad ea magno sit adju- mento. Idem ergo est διὰ τὴν βασιλείαν τοῦ Θεοῦ quod ἕνεκεν εὐαγγελίου Marci X. 29. Quod Origenes primo ad Celsum dixit, διὰ τὸ καθαρώτερον θεραπεύειν τὸ θεῖον, μηδὲ τῶν συγ- κεχωρημένων ὑπὸ τοῦ νόμου ἅπτεσθαι ἀφροδισίων. Neque enim ii tantum qui ad verbi ministerium erant segregati, sed præter eos alii complures utriusque sexus & omnis ordinis homi- nes ab initio Christianismi amplexi sunt ταύτην τὴν ὑψηλοτέ- ραν πολιτείαν. Justinus Martyr. κᾲ πολλοί τινες κᾲ πολλαὶ, ἑξη- κοντοῦται κᾲ ἑβδομηκοντοῦται, οἳ ἐκ παίδων ἐμαθητεύθησαν τῷ Χρι- στῷ, ἄφθοροι διαμένουσι· κᾲ εὔχομαι κατὰ πᾶν γένος ἀνθρώπων τοι- ούτους δεῖξαι. Idem alibi : ἢ τὴν ἀρχὴν οὐκ ἐγαμοῦμεν εἰ μὴ ἐπὶ παί- δων ἀνατροφῇ, ἢ παραιτούμενοι τὸ γήμασθαι τέλεον ἐγκρατευόμε- θα. Tatianus contra Græcos : τὰς παρ᾽ ἡμῖν παρθένους λοιδορεῖ- τε. Minutius Felix de Christianis: Plerique inviolati corpo- ris virginitate fruuntur potius quam gloriantur. Tertullianus notat sua ætate virgines Ecclesiarum in quibusdam locis recludi solitas, cum rursus aliis in locis non recluderentur. Idem de resurrectione Christi: Quot Spadones voluntarii quot virgines Christo maritata? Vide Cyprianum, atque alios Me- rito autem causam hanc pietatis adjecit Christus. Nam alioqui idem faciebant αἱ σεμναὶ apud Indos, Vestales Ro- manorum, & athletæ non pauci, quos Clemens nominat δι᾽ ἄσκησιν σωματικὴν ἐγκρατευομένους κᾲ ἀφροδισίων ἀπεχομένους. Eusebius addit apud Christianos observatum παρθενίαν καθ᾽ ἑκούσιον γνώμην, ἐ δι᾽ ἀνάγκην ὡς παρ᾽ ἕλλησι. Chrysostomus in VII. ad Romanos, διὰ τοῦτο ἐπὶ μὲν τῶν παλαιῶν, οὔπω τις ἐφάνη παρθενίαν ἀσκῶν, σφόδρα ἔκπληκτοι ἦν, νυνὶ δὲ πανταχοῦ τῆς οἰκουμένης τὸ πρᾶγμα ἔσπαρται.

Recte Grotius non cum Origene de castratione, quæ sit manu, qui se ex ψευδερμηνείᾳ hujus sen- tentiæ castravit, teste Eusebio lib. VI. Histor. Ec- cles. c. VII. Sed quæ animi destinatione sit, intelli- git. Quo de Chrysost. homil. LXIII. in Matth. Non de abscissione membrorum dicit, absit: sed cogitatio- nes intercisionem intelligit. Nam qui membrum in- cidit, maledictione subjectus est: Homicide enim opus, qui tale quid tentat, aggreditur, & Dei opifi- cium criminantibus occasionem præbet. Unde in Conc. Nicen. Can. I. tales ab officiis sacris exclusi sunt, qui seipsos castrarunt. Non autem præcise hæc ad cælibatum perpetuum, nedum ad religio- sum ejusdem votum trahenda. Nam & ad tempus quis continere potest διὰ τὴν βασιλείαν τῶν οὐρα- νῶν: quod Apostolus docuit 1. Cor. VII. 1. Chri- stus utique hic non votum cælibatus, sed firmum animi propositum intelligit, ut Isidor. Pelusiota l. III. Ep. 13. aliique explicant, in virginitate persi- stendi, quod ad utrumque sexum Isidorus refert. Nonnulli cum B. Franzio l. de Interpr. p. 978. de spirituali castratione explicant; sed collatio εὐνου- χίας corporis & animi aliquid amplius infert, & spiritualis castratio etiam conjugatis necessaria est; illa, de qua Matth. V. 28. Non ergo Pontifi- ciis concedendum, quod hæc cælibatum perpetuum respiciant, quemadmodum id iis largiri videtur Grotius, verba hæc εὐνούχισαν ἑαυτοὺς ita expli- cans, animi destinatione μὴ ζητοῦντες γυναῖκα, ut Paulus loquitur 1. Cor. VII. 27. unde de cælibatu sub- jicit postea: Neque enim ii tantum qui ad verbi mini- sterium erant segregati, sed præter eos alii complures utriusque sexus & omnis ordinis homines, ab initio Christianismi amplexi sunt ταύτην τὴν ὑψηλοτάτην πολιτείαν. Quod factum dicit, ad implenda rectius, liberius atque constantius præcepta Christianismi, non quod in iis sit cælibatus, sed quod ad ea magno sit ad- jumento. Quanquam vero illis, qui dono continen- tiæ præditi sunt, cælibatus inserviat, ut melius possint μεριμνᾶν τὰ τοῦ κυρίου ἵνα ὦσιν ἅγιοι κὴ σώ- ματι κὴ πνεύματι, 1. Cor. VII.34. donum tamen il- lud paucis datum est, nec qui ad tempus continet sefe, de perpetua continentia polliceri, aut vovere possint, propter carnis fragilitatem & imbecillita- tem, ac Satanæ vim & calliditatem, mundique scandala, & malignitatem: nec per sefe impedimen- to sit conjugium in præstandis Christianismi præ- ceptis, sed propter temporum calamitatem, imo ex Apostoli monito serviat ad coercendas carnis libi- dines quum melius sit nubere quam uri: conjuges- que Deum timentes mutuo se ad pietatis officia excitent, mutua informatione, cohortatione, fa- miliæ in timore Domini gubernatione, libero- rum sancta ad gloriam Dei educatione, in cruce ac calamitate huic statui domestica mutua conso- latione sese salutariter ædificent, ac domus suas, ut adeo conjugium, quod imago est spiritualis no- stræ cum Christo copulationis insigni sit ad officia Christianismi adjumento, nulli vero impedimen- to. Quo de Claud. Espensæus in 1. Tim. III. Nuptiæ licet plurimum difficultatis habeant, sic tamen assumi possunt, ut vitæ perfectiori impedimento non sint: unde quamvis nimii æstimatores è veteribus cæ- libatus laudibus hyperbolicis eundem deprædica- rint, in quibus B. Rhenanus in argumento libri Tertulliani Exhort. ad Castit. desiderat, quod ma- trimonio parum æqui fuerint. Espensæus de conti- nentia lib. 1. c. 9. Mirum, inquit, quam pro con- tinentia vehementes fuerint, ut Erasmi de illis tacea- mus censuram: non tamen veneranda antiquitas defuit celebrando statui connubiali, quin eundem debitis ornaret elogiis: utpote quem ceu sanctum & honoratum statum ita deprædicat DEUS ipse, ut protestetur BONUM non esse hominem esse solum Gen. I. 28. vid. Psal. CXXVIII. 2. Ephes. V. 32. Ebr. XIII. 1. De quo Amphiloch. in serm. de occurf. Do- min. Honorandum matrimonium superat omne do- num terrenum, quippe cum sit arbor fructuosa, cum sit elegans planta, cum sit radix virginitatis, cum more Agricolæ excolat ratione præditos ramos ani- matos, cum ejus benedictio mundi incrementum sit, cum genus consoletur, cum homines efficiat, cum di- vinam imaginem, quasi pictor effingat, cum Domi- num habeat: qui ei benedicat, cum totum mundum ferre valeat. Conferant Nazianzeni versus de conjugio, & quæ de fine ac dignitate conjugii dixi- mus Comment. in Genes. p. 320. seqq. De cætero acquiescimus sententiæ Apol. Augustanæ: Neque tamen æquamus conjugio virginitatem. Sicut enim donum dono præstat, prophetia præstat eloquentiæ, scientia rei militaris præstat agriculturæ, eloquentia præstat architectonicæ; ita virginitas donum est præ- stantius conjugio. Est tamen sicut Orator non est ma- gis justus coram Deo, propter eloquentiam, ita virgo non magis meretur justificationem virginitate, quam conjux conjugalibus officiis, sed unusquisque in suo dono fideliter servire debet ac sentire, quod propter Christum fide consequatur remissionem pecca- torum, & fide justus coram Deo reputetur. Quæ etiam B. Lutheri nostri sententia fuit, ut propter calumnias pontificiorum id addamus, in 1. Cor. VII. Idem coram DEO valet matrimonium & virginitas. Nam utrumque est donum & creatura Dei, tametsi alterum alteri antecellat, si quis inter se ct conferat. Neque abnuere his potuit Bellarm. l. de matrim. c. XXXIV. resp. ad 19. Potest fieri, in- quit, ut virginitas conjuncta sit in uno homine cum minore cacitate, humanitate, aliisque virtutibus, quam in altero homine conjugium; Idcirco non pos- sumus virginem anteponere conjugato, nisi constet in cæteris virtutibus illos esse pares.

Locus 1. Cor. VII. 34. quod cœlibes melius pos- sint curare ea, quæ Domini sunt, ut sancti sint cor- pore & spiritu incomparato illo sensu relinquendus est, non vero cum Pontificiis exclusive intelligen- dus: ac præterea de certo tempore, propter communem necessitatem, nec non de personis certis, quoad nempe conjugia cum infidelibus, imprimis agit, nam possunt etiam incidere tem- pora & casus, quibus melius queant conjuges cu- rare quæ sunt Domini, cum fideles utrique sunt; quod monuit Caslander in Consult. artic. XXIII.

Perperam vero verba Christi διὰ τὴν βασιλεί- av τῶν ὀυρανῶν abripiunt Papistæ ad meritum regni cælorum: utpote Albert Pighius in Controv. cap. XIV. de votis: Monachi castrant se propter regnum Dei assequendum & gratiam Dei promerendam. Petr. à Soto in ref. Wurtemberg. Conf. Cœlibatus est satisfactio peccatorum maxima & meritum regni cœ- lorum. Nihil in his Christi verbis de consecutione regni cœlestis, ac ne de regno quidem cœlesti alte- rius vitæ quicquam, sed de regno gratiæ, quod vo- camus, in hoc seculo; nedum de merito regni cœ- lestis. Idem est, monente ipso Grotio διὰ τὴν βασιλείαν Θεῦ, ἕνεκεν ἐυαγγελία, quod expeditior sit cœlibatus ad officia S. Ministerii & alia pietatis exercitia. Conf. B. Gerhard. de Conjug. §. 500.

ὁ δυνάμενος χωρεῖν, χωρείτω] Id est, cui tantum animi est, macte ista virtute esto, pergat Deo favente. Usur- pat hoc dictum & Ignatius, sed de fide in Christum agens: ὁ χωρῶν χωρείτω· ὁ ἀκόων ἀκουέτω, in Epistola ad Smyrnen- ses.

PARS II. Monitio de adducendis parvulis.

## 19:13
Verse 13.

παιδία] We have already said several times that this word is also accepted for a somewhat more advanced age. Nay, even the word βρέφος which Luke uses receives the same meaning, as is clear from 2 Tim. 3:15.

Τὰς χεῖρας ἐπιθῇ κὶ προσεύξηται] The laying on of hands among the Jews indicated an invocation of divine power: as we have said elsewhere. Whence it came about that public offices were also conferred by that rite, even civil ones, such as those of senators. But the same was also observed among the Archisynagogi and the elders of the Synagogue, whence the custom of τῆς χειροθεσίας passed to the Christians: concerning which there will be a place to treat elsewhere. That prayers were also accustomed to be conceived for children by that rite is manifest from Genesis 48:14, 15. From then on it was always observed by the Hebrews that they should bring children to those who were believed to excel others in holiness, to be commended to God by their prayers διὰ τῆς τῶν χειρῶν ἐπιθέσεως: which custom remains among them even today. Christ, however, by approving this custom, shows that the faith and prayers of others are of benefit even to that age.

Latin:

Vers. 13.

παιδία] Jam aliquoties diximus vocem hanc etiam de paulo provectiore ætate accipi. Imo & βρέφος vox quam Lucas usurpat eandem significationem recipit, ut liquet 2. Tim. III. 15.

Τὰς χεῖρας ἐπιθῇ κὶ προσεύξηται] Manuum impositio a- pud Judæos indicabat invocationem divinæ potentiæ: ut alibi diximus. Unde factum est ut & munia publica eo ritu conferrentur, etiam civilia, ut senatorum. Sed & in Archisynagogis & senioribus Synagogæ idem observatum, unde mos τῆς χειροθεσίας ad Christianos transiit: de quo alibi erit agendi locus. Pro pueris etiam eo ritu pre- ces concipi solitas manifestum est ex Genes. XLVIII. 14. 15. Exinde Hebræis semper observatum ut ad eos qui sancti- monia præstare cæteris crederentur pueros deferrent, ipsa- rum precibus Deo commendandos διὰ τῆς τῶν χειρῶν ἐπι- θέσεως: qui mos hodieque apud ipsos manet. Hunc au- tem morem Christus probans ostendit isti etiam ætati prod- esse aliorum fidem ac preces.

## 19:14
Vers. 14.

μὴ κωλύετε ἀυτὰ ἐλθεῖν πρός με] The Apostles thought it a matter less worthy of Christ to be occupied with touching children. But Christ does not reject even that age from his benefits. Nay, he shows that it is pleasing to him if children, as if designated for holiness and through this also for salvation, as Tertullian speaks, are from the very beginnings of life dedicated to Christian education. For certainly to be accustomed from tender years is a great thing, and 'The jar will long keep the scent with which it was once imbued when new.'

Irenæus de Christo: Ideo per omnem venit ætatem & infantibus infans factus sanctificans infantes, in parvulis parvulus sanctificans hanc ipsam habentes ætatem, simul & exemplum illis pietatis effectus & subjectionis. [Irenæus concerning Christ: Therefore he came through every age, and became an infant for infants, sanctifying infants, and in little children a little child, sanctifying those who have this very age, at the same time also becoming an example of piety and subjection to them.] On this saying of Christ, among other things, rests the custom of baptizing even infant children: that this was received through all the Churches in the times of Augustine is sufficiently evident from this very fact, that the Pelagians, when they were pressed by that argument by Augustine and others, never dared to deny that very thing. And to say nothing of Origen, to whom certain things that are ascribed are of uncertain authorship, and some interpolated, the epistle of Cyprian to Fidus, which both Augustine and Jerome use, makes it clear that it was not even doubted whether infants were rightly baptized, but whether some hesitated as to whether they could be baptized even before the eighth day: but the matter having been weighed in the Council, it seemed that baptism should not be denied even to those newly born if they were offered. In an ancient book entitled The Constitutions of Clement we read: 'And baptize your infants, and bring them up in the discipline and admonition of God.' Furthermore, it appears from the most ancient testimonies that the eucharist was offered to infants. Moreover, that opinion, that unbaptized infants are certainly consigned to eternal punishments, although lighter ones, so rigidly defended by Augustine, had not pleased even Augustine himself before he clashed with Pelagius. However, it seems to me that in ancient times the baptism of infants was much more frequent in Africa than in Asia or other parts of the world, and with a certain greater opinion of necessity. For in the councils you will not find mention of this custom older than the Council of Carthage. Tertullian, concerning the age at which those who were consecrated to Christian discipline by their parents should be baptized, shows that nothing had been defined in his own times by the very fact that he persuades the delay of baptism with so many reasons. Therefore, he says, according to the condition and disposition of each person's character, and also their age, the delay of baptism is more useful: especially, however, regarding little children. For what necessity is there (which is repeated here in some codices, if it is not so necessary, I do not see what convenient sense it receives) for sponsors also to be thrust into danger, who may themselves, through mortality, fail in their promises, or be deceived by the development of a bad character? The Lord indeed says, 'Do not forbid them to come to me.' Let them come therefore while they are growing up, let them come while they are learning, while they are being taught to where they are coming (I think it should be read 'while they are coming, let them be taught'). Let them become Christians when they have been able to know Christ: why does innocent age hasten to the remission of sins? The sense is: let them come to Christ so that they may be instructed, not so that they may be baptized, unless after they have understood the power of baptism. Nazianzen, dealing with those who depart without baptism, sets an example in those to whom baptism does not happen because of infancy. And this very Nazianzen, although he was the son of a bishop and educated for a very long time under the care of his father, was not baptized until he had emerged from his youth, as he himself teaches us in his life. John of Antioch, later called Chrysostom, born to Christian parents, as the truer opinion holds, instructed by Meletius the bishop, was baptized after his one and twentieth year. But especially worthy of note is the canon of the Synod of Neocaesarea held in the year 315, which is as follows: 'Concerning a pregnant woman, that she ought to be enlightened whenever she wishes; for in this the one giving birth does not share with the one being born, because each one's own choice is shown in the confession.' For however much interpreters may pull it in another direction, it appears that the question was raised concerning the baptism of pregnant women because it seemed that the offspring was being baptized at the same time as the mother, which, however, was not accustomed to be baptized except upon its own will and profession. And thus in the compendium of canons under title IV, Balsamon explains: 'As she can be enlightened because it has not yet come into the light, nor does it have the choice of the confession of divine baptism.' And Zonaras: 'The embryo needs baptism when it shall be able to choose.' The Synod defines that baptism proceeds rightly for this reason, because it pertained to the mother alone, who would issue a profession for herself, and not also to the womb. And most of the Greeks from every age to this day observe the custom of deferring the baptism of little children until they themselves can issue a confession of their faith. Walafrid Strabo on ecclesiastical matters, ch. 26: 'It should be noted then that in those first times the grace of baptism was accustomed to be given only to those who, in integrity of both body and mind, had already arrived at this point, that they could know and understand what benefit was to be obtained in baptism, what was to be confessed and believed, and finally what was to be observed by those reborn in Christ.' Moreover, just as those things indicate liberty, antiquity, and the custom of difference, so they bring forward nothing as to why the baptism of infants should be repudiated, whom parents or other sponsors offer to be consecrated to God through the prayers of the saints, with a vow of pious education: which, among other things, is not inconveniently signified by baptism. Nor should it be an obstacle that not all things which are accustomed to be signified by baptism in the same way, properly fit that age. For even repentance, which we know is designated by baptism, certainly had a greater place in those who, having led a long impure life, testified to a purpose of changing their whole life, than in others, but in Christ, whom John baptized, it had no place, who, as Tertullian speaks, was dipped as a debtor to no repentance. The writer of the questions and answers to the Orthodox, speaking concerning infants: 'They are deemed worthy of the goods through baptism by the faith of those who offer them to baptism.'

For of such [is the kingdom of heaven]. The less, says Christ, is that age to be despised as if it were profane, because even adults who give themselves to my discipline ought to become as it were children again, having stripped off the vices which a greater age has brought on. Above, Christ wanted his followers to become like children, in the emptiness of self-love. Here, however, the obedient docility of children seems to be more regarded. For thus Luke says, 'Whoever does not receive the kingdom of God as a child, shall not enter into it.' Childlike dispositions are accustomed to be compared to a blank slate, upon which you can easily write anything.

That by παιδία in this place are understood infants who are still carried in arms, the very circumstances of those who were brought here to Christ teach, Mark X. 16, whom Christ is said to have taken in his arms: and the comparison of Luke XVIII. 15 confirms this, who names them βρέφη: for this word denotes infants (βρέφος is said to be from τρέφω, because it is nourished by a nurse) and is understood of infants recently born, as also of those who are still enclosed in the maternal womb, Luke I. 41, 44, c. II. 12, 1 Peter II. 2, nor is this word used otherwise in 2 Tim. III. 15, for who would deny that the children of the faithful are informed in the word of God immediately from infancy? Nor is it to be presumed otherwise concerning Timothy, whose mother and grandmother are notably commended for piety, 2 Tim. I. 5. And παιδίον is said of an infant of eight days, Luke II. 21. Whence the present passage was accepted by the ancients concerning infants to be brought to Christ through prayers and baptism, and is rightly opposed by our theologians to the Anabaptists and Socinians who reject infant baptism, as also to the Calvinists who, together with them, derogate faith from infants, to whom nevertheless the kingdom of heaven is here said to belong, which no one enters without faith. Bernard, Epistle CXL to Count Hildoph, says: The way of Christ is blocked to the little ones of Christians while the grace of Baptism is denied, nor are they allowed to approach salvation, although the Savior piously cries out for them: Suffer the little children to come unto me. We add what Grotius has concerning this here at verse 14.
