On this saying of Christ, among other things, rests the custom of baptizing even infant children: that this was received through all the Churches in the times of Augustine is sufficiently established by this very fact, that the Pelagians, when they were pressed by that argument by Augustine and others, never dared to deny that very thing. And that I may say nothing of Origen, to whom certain things are ascribed which are of an uncertain author and certain things are interpolated, the letter of Cyprian to Fidus, which both Augustine and Jerome use, makes it clear that it was not even doubted whether infants were rightly baptized, but they hesitated whether they could be baptized even before the eighth day; but the matter having been weighed in a Council, it seemed that baptism should not be denied even to the recently born, if they were offered. In an ancient book titled The Constitutions of Clement we read: Baptize also your infants, and bring them up in the discipline and admonition of God. This is Grotius. If, therefore, the ancients are resting on this saying, baptizing infants, they either accepted it well concerning them, or badly. If well, why does Grotius not also offer his assent? If badly, how could they rest upon it, and why does he praise those who rest upon it? The testimony, however, from the Constitutions of Clement is not of great moment. For it is already sufficiently known that those Constitutions of the Apostles, which they say were compiled by Clement, are spurious, even though Franciscus Turrianus and Johan. Carolus Bovius, Bishop of Ostrina, fought fiercely for them, since they were already rejected by Athanasius himself in his Synopsis, and Bellarmine, in his book on Ecclesiastical Writers, p. 59, testifies that they have almost no standing in the Latin Church, and later Greeks in the Second Trullan Council condemned them as corrupted by heretics, and indeed the judgment concerning them is almost the same as that concerning the books of the Recognitions, which in book II on the Roman Pontiff, chapter 11, he holds as Apocryphal: but Bisciola in the Epitome of Baronius, p. 72, teaches: The Constitutions of Clement have been listed BY ALL among the Apocrypha. Indeed, those things which are in them concerning the ceremonies of Baptism

Books III and VII have been handed down, they do not savor of the age of the Apostles: nor does Cardinal Bellarmine doubt, in the place cited, that those things which are held in Book VI, chapter 15, concerning their re-baptism, who have been baptized by heretics, are erroneous. Petrus Halloixius teaches that the constitutions are held among the Apocrypha, in his notes to the life of Polycarp, chapter 6, and that they were written after the times of Ignatius, in his Notes on the life of Ignatius, chapter 7; and he judges that they were not compiled by one man, nor at one time, but by different men and at various times, in his Apology for the writings of Ignatius, chapter 3. Although Epiphanius does indeed praise the constitutions of Clement somewhere, Petavius nevertheless observed correctly, in his Scholia on the 70th heresy of the Audians, that those Constitutions which are circulated today seem different from those earlier ones, and nonetheless doubtful ones, which Epiphanius mentions. Alexius Aristenus in his Scholia on the 80th Apostolic Canon, still unpublished, Theodor Balsamon, and Johan. Zonaras reject the same by the authority of the Sixth Synod, on account of certain adulterated things inserted that are alien to piety, added in Jacob Ussher’s dissertation on the Epistle of Polycarp and Ignatius, p. 105. Photius, however, testifies that they were also once accused of Arianism in his Bibliotheca, no. 113. The most learned Lisserius, in the place cited, p. 63 et seqq., learnedly teaches that the corruptions of both the Ignatian Epistles and the Pseudo-Clementine Constitutions proceeded from the same workshop, and that they were finally interpolated in the fifth century after the departure of Clement, page 41; and he observes, chapter XVI, p. 118, that this masked Clement lived under Christian Emperors, and by his own indication, like a sewer, Book VI, chapter 24, betrayed himself. These things we have thought should be noted here, since Grotius not infrequently appeals to that Pseudo-Clement, or if not for the writing of that Roman Clement, he certainly hawks those constitutions as the writing of some ancient and Catholic Doctor.

But a more certain witness concerning the antiquity of infant baptism is St. Augustine: On Genesis to the letter, Book X, chapter 23: 'The custom of mother Church in baptizing infants is by no means to be scorned: nor in any way to be deemed superfluous: nor at all to be believed, unless it were an APOSTOLIC tradition' (certainly not unwritten, but founded in the Scriptures, as he teaches in Book IV on Baptism, chapter 24). And in Sermon X on the words of the Apostle, he warns concerning infant baptism: 'Let no one whisper alien doctrines to you. This the Church has always had, has always held: this it received from the faith of the Forefathers: this it preserves perseveringly until the end.' Concerning Cyprian also and the Council of 66 Bishops from the cited Epistle to Fidus, which is in Book III, number VIII, the matter is indubitable: whose words it is helpful to bring forward: 'This was our opinion IN THE COUNCIL, that from baptism, and from the grace of GOD, who is merciful and kind and pious to all, no one should be prohibited by us.' Which, as it must be observed and retained concerning all, so it must be observed more concerning INFANTS themselves, and the newly born: who by this very fact deserve more of our aid, and of divine mercy, because in the very first moment of their birth, weeping and crying, they do nothing else than pray. Which Epistle Augustine praised in Epistle XXVIII to Jerome, and Book IV against the two Epistles of the Pelagians, chapter VIII: as also did Jerome in Book III against the Pelagians near the end. St. Irenaeus was even older than Cyprian, who says in Book II, chapter XXXIX: '(The Lord) sanctifies EVERY age by that likeness which was toward it: He came to save ALL, I say, ALL through Himself: All, I say, who through Him are REBORN into GOD, INFANTS AND LITTLE ONES, and youths and elders.' Which rebirth of infants is not, except through Baptism.

Finally, it is certain concerning the Pelagians that they by no means denied, but they themselves confessed, that infants must be baptized, even though the Pontifical in the Life of Innocent III charges the contrary to them. Joseph Vice-Comes, in his Ecclesiastical Observations on the rites of Baptism, Book II, chapter 1, notes that Pelagius complained in an Epistle written to Innocent himself that this was attributed to him by calumny, and Augustine acknowledges that it was attributed to him undeservedly, in his book on Original Sin, chapters XIX and XXX, and Book I on the merit and remission of sins, chapter XXVI. 'They (the Pelagians),' he says, 'concede that infants must be baptized, who cannot, without doubt, go against the authority of the UNIVERSAL Church, handed down through the Lord and the Apostles.' Compare also Epistle LXXXIX to Hilary, and the book on the grace of Christ against the Pelagians and Caelestius, chapter XX.

But Grotius does not seem to be consistent with himself in this place, since he had already asserted that in the times of Augustine the custom of baptizing infants had been received THROUGH ALL Churches: but soon he adds: 'but it seems to me that in ancient times the baptism of infants was much more frequented in Africa than in Asia or other parts of the world, and with a certain greater opinion of necessity.' For you cannot find mention of it in the older Councils. The Council of Carthage. Councils do not make for this. For neither have the acts and decrees of all the Councils that were ever held been propagated to posterity, nor was business transacted in them concerning all things necessary to be believed and observed, but concerning those things which, according to the circumstances, were to be expedited, deliberated, and defined in the Church. But how could St. Augustine have urged the authority of the UNIVERSAL Church regarding the baptism of infants, and indeed from the tradition of Christ and the Apostles, if the baptism of infants had obtained only in certain particular Churches, not in the universal Church, nor had the baptism of infants been judged so necessary? What of the fact that St. Jerome in Book III against the Pelagians and in his Epistle to Laetus, and St. Augustine not only in the cited places Epistle XXVIII and on Original Sin, chapter XL, but also in Book II on Marriage and Concupiscence, chapter XX, Book III on the merit and remission of sins, chapter IX, and also Book IV against the Donatists on Baptism, chapter XXIV, Innocent in Epistle XXVI to the Council of Milevis, Paulinus in the life of Ambrose in Surius, Vol. II, p. 506, Theodoret in his Epitome of divine dogmas, chapter on Baptism, and Leo the Great in Epistle LXXXIV to the Bishops of Aquileia, testify that the baptism of infants had obtained in the Church in ancient centuries? Gennadius on Ecclesiastical Dogmas, chapter XXXI, some assert and testify. And therefore concerning Infant Baptism, this the Church said, Sermon X on the Words of the Apostle, says Augustine, this it has ALWAYS had, ALWAYS held: this it received from the FAITH OF THE ANCESTORS: and Caelestius himself in the booklet which he published at Rome, Augustine book II against Caelestius and Pelagius, confessed that infants are baptized for the remission of sins, according to the RULE OF THE UNIVERSAL Church, and according to the sentence of the Gospel. And the reason which the ancients allege for the necessity of Baptism concerns infants equally as adults, and makes for their baptism, so that it may not be deferred or denied to them: as is clear from Ambrose book II on the Patriarch Abraham, chapter XI. Neither the aged proselyte nor the infant born in the house is excepted: because every age is subject to sin, and therefore every age is fit for the Sacrament. For unless one has been born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God. Certainly he excepts no one, not an infant, not one prevented by some necessity. Grotius, however, appeals to Tertullian, whom he observes to teach that nothing was defined concerning the age at which those who were being consecrated to the Christian discipline were to be baptized, by the very fact that he urges the delay of baptism for so many reasons. He cites his passage thus: Therefore, he says, according to the condition and disposition, and even the age, of each person, the delay of baptism is more useful: especially, however, regarding little children. For what necessity is there (which is found here in some Codices, if not so necessary, I do not see what convenient sense it receives. But if Grotius did not see it, others have seen it: namely, the proposition is hypothetical, if baptism is not necessary, which Catholics do not concede to Tertullian, establishing the necessity of baptism entirely.) Sponsors are also brought into danger, who themselves can also fail in their promises through mortality, and be deceived by the emergence of a bad character. The Lord indeed says, Do not forbid them to come to me. Let them come therefore while they are growing up, let them come while they are learning, while they are being taught where to come (I think it should be read, and while they are coming let them be taught: which is an overly arbitrary correction, by no means necessary, nor approved by ancient Codices) Let them become Christians when they are able to know Christ, why does the innocent age hasten to the remission of sins? The meaning is (adds Grotius, namely primarily according to the correction which he had made at will) let them come to Christ, so that they may be instructed, not so that they may be baptized, unless after they have understood the power of baptism. The vexed passage of Tertullian is read in the book on Baptism, ch. XVIII. But what need was there for it to be defined by the Church, if this was handed down by Christ and the Apostles, if the necessity of baptism as a means ordained for salvation was evident from Scripture? Tertullian therefore erred in this, that he did not judge baptism to be necessary for salvation: he erred, that he deemed the infantile age to be INNOCENT, and not in need of the remission of sins, which opinion was later condemned in Pelagius. He erred, that he believed it was necessary for the efficacy of Baptism that the one being baptized be instructed beforehand about the power of baptism, by which hypothesis Infant Baptism is utterly overthrown, which the Church condemns today in the Anabaptists and Socinians. However, it is sufficiently evident from this passage of Tertullian that in his age infants were baptized in the Church. For what else would have been the need to refute this custom, concerning the baptism of infants, and concerning the sponsors accustomed to be employed in the same? What of the fact that that hypothetical, which Grotius wishes to be expunged, if not so necessary, seems to imply that Tertullian denies nothing other than the necessity of the baptism of infants outside the danger of death? To say nothing of the fact that some think Tertullian is dealing with the infants of unbelievers. Furthermore, it is clear from another book of Tertullian, namely on the soul, ch. XXXIX and XL. Otherwise (says the Apostle) they would be born unclean. Wishing, however, to be understood as if they were designated for holiness, and through this also for salvation, the children of the faithful: so that the pledges of this hope might patronize the marriage, which he had judged should be retained. Otherwise he remembered the Lord's definition: Unless one is born of water and the spirit, he will not enter into the kingdom of God, that is, he will not be holy. Thus every soul is reckoned in Adam until it is reckoned again in Christ: unclean for as long as it is reckoned again. These things are more consonant with the opinion of the orthodox Church.

Grotius also alleges Nazianzen, who, dealing with those who die without baptism, sets an example in those to whom Baptism does not happen because of

infancy, and he himself was not baptized until he had emerged from his youth, as he teaches in his life. But he did not deny the baptism of infants; indeed, if necessity and the case of death urge it, he commanded it, and thought it could be deferred outside that case until the fourth year of age, which, however, was only his private opinion. We shall transcribe the entire passage from Orat. XL, which is on Holy Baptism, so that the mind of the Theologian may be more correctly established: We must provide with all care and zeal, he says, lest we lack this common grace. Let these things be, someone might say, as far as they pertain to those who request baptism: but what will you say about those who are still of tender age, and feel neither loss nor grace? Shall we baptize them too? Yes, absolutely, if any danger urges it. For it is better to be sanctified without feeling than to depart without the seal and initiation. And the reason for this matter is circumcision, accustomed to be performed on the eighth day, which in a certain way bore the figure of baptism, and was offered to those who were still devoid of reason. In the same way also the anointing of the doorposts, which, applied to things lacking sense, brought salvation to the firstborn. Concerning the rest, I judge that, having waited for three years, or for a somewhat shorter or longer space of time (for then they can both hear something mystical and respond, and even if they do not understand clearly and exactly, they are nevertheless imbued and informed), only then should they sanctify both their minds and bodies through the Sacrament of the great Baptism. These things Nazianzen: who nevertheless adds: that because of unexpected and sudden onsets of dangers, and which cannot be repelled by any help and aid, it is altogether more beneficial to be fortified by the washing. For he was not diminishing the necessity of baptism, which is done by the Arminian Grotius, but he only desired some prior information in those being baptized, if danger is not present, which, however, he himself confessed that we have no remedy to avoid, and that we cannot by any reason know that it will be absent, because of unexpected cases, and therefore he judged it to be παντὶ λόγῳ λυσιτελέστερον [in every respect more beneficial] for infants to be fortified by the washing of baptism.

Nor does the Synod of Neocaesarea held in the year 315 hinder infant baptism in any way: for the canon cited by Grotius requires only the will and consent in adults, as in a pregnant woman: περὶ κυοφορούσης ὅτι δεῖ φωτίζεσθαι ὁπότε βούλεται. For the one giving birth shares nothing in this with the one being born, because each one's own choice is shown in the confession. The condition added, ὁπότε βούλεται, sufficiently teaches that the will of the pregnant mother is regarded, namely whether she herself, not yet baptized, wishes to be baptized: whatever may be the case regarding the explanation of Balsamon or Zonaras, whom Grotius alleges, as if the Synod had defined that baptism proceeds rightly because it pertains only to the mother, who would issue a profession concerning herself, and not also to the womb (the fetus), namely because the fetus could not issue a profession.

Finally, Grotius falsely asserts that most Greeks from every age to this day observe the custom of deferring the baptism of infants until they themselves can issue a confession of their faith. By the testimony of one Walafrid Strabo, who lived in the year 850, that cannot be established. It is to be noted, he says in his book on Ecclesiastical Matters, chapter 26, that in those first times the grace of baptism was accustomed to be given only to those who had already arrived at such integrity of body and mind that they could know and understand what benefit was to be obtained in baptism, what was to be confessed and believed, and finally what was to be observed by those reborn in Christ. That Walafrid was mistaken in this, trustworthy and far more certain testimonies have already shown, namely of Fathers three hundred years older than he, who testified that it was the custom and belief of the universal Church, which is ours even today, that baptism must not be denied to little children on account of its supreme necessity: to whom must be added from the Greeks Cyril of Jerusalem, Catech. Mystag. 1, Basil the Great, exhort. to Baptism, Chrysostom, homil. to the Neophytes. That the modern Greeks also observe the contrary of what Grotius asserted, to this very day, [namely] the custom of deferring the baptism of infants until they themselves can issue a confession of their faith, is evident from the first Response of the Patriarch of Constantinople, Jeremiah, rendered to the Württemberg Theologians in the year 1576, ch. II & IX. In the ninth (article) it is said that infants are to be baptized, and that a more adult age is not to be awaited. This is done among us also; so that nothing may happen, with the matter delayed. For unless someone is regenerated of water and the spirit, he does not enter the kingdom of heaven.

Latin:

Vers. 14.

μὴ κωλύετε ἀυτὰ ἐλθεῖν πρός με] Apostoli rem minus dignam Christo putabant, contingendis pueris occupari. At Christus istam quoque ætatem à suis beneficiis non rejicit. Imo ostendit gratum sibi esse si pueri, quasi desi- gnati sanctitatis ac per hoc etiam salutis, quomodo Tertulli- anus loquitur, à primis vitæ initiis addicantur Christianæ e- ducationi. Nam certè à teneris assuescere multum est, & Quo semel est imbuta recens servabit odorem Testa diu.

Irenæus de Christo: Ideo per omnem venit ætatem & infan- tibus infans factus sanctificans infantes, in parvulis parvulus sanctificans hanc ipsam habentes ætatem, simul & exemplum illis pietatis effectus & subjectionis. Huic Christi dicto inter cætera innititur mos pueros etiam infantes baptismo tin- gendi: quem Augustini temporibus per omnes Ecclesias fuisse receptum hoc ipso satis constat, quod Pelagiani, cum eo argumento ab Augustino atque aliis premerentur, negare id ipsum nunquam ausi fuerint. Et ut de Origene nihil dicam, cui quæ ascribuntur quædam sunt incerti au- ctoris, quædam interpolata, epistola Cypriani ad Fidum, qua & Augustinus & Hieronymus utuntur, apertum facit, an recte baptizarentur infantes ne dubitatum quidem, sed an possint baptizari etiam ante octavum diem quosdam hæsitasse: re autem in Concilio expensa visum ne recens quidem natis si offerrentur negandum baptismum. In libro antiquo cui titulus Constitutiones Clementis legimus: βαπτίζετε δὲ ὑμῶν καὶ τὰ νήπια, καὶ ἐκτρέφετε αὐτὰ ἐν παιδείᾳ καὶ νουθεσίᾳ θεοῦ. Quin etiam εὐχαριστίαν præbitam infantibus, antiquissimis testimoniis apparet. Cæterum illa senten- tia, infantes non baptizatos certo suppliciis æternis, quam- quam levioribus addici, tam rigide defensa ab Augustino, ne ipsi quidem Augustino placuerat, antequam cum Pela- gio collideretur. Videtur autem mihi antiquitus baptismus infantium, multo magis in Africa quam in Asia aliisve mun- di partibus fuisse frequentatus & cum majori quadam ne- cessitatis opinione. Nam in conciliis vetustioremejus mo- ris mentionem non invenias concilio Carthaginiensi. Ter- tullianus de ætate qua baptizandi essent qui Christianæ di- sciplinæ à parentibus consecrabantur, nihil definitum fuis- se suis temporibus hoc ipso docet quod dilationem bapti- smi tam multis rationibus suadet. Itaque, inquit, pro cujusque persona conditione ac dispositione, etiam ætate, cunctatio baptismi utilior est : præcipue tamen circa parvulos. Quid enim necesse est (quod hic in quibusdam codicibus repetitur, si non tam ne- cesse, non video quem commodum sensum accipiat) sponso- res etiam periculo ingeri, qui & ipsi per mortalitatem destituere promissiones suas possunt & proventu malæ indolis falli? Ait qui- dem Dominus, Nolite illos prohibere ad me venire. Veniant ergo dum adolescunt, veniant dum discunt, dum quo veniant docentur (legendum puto dum & veniunt doceantur :) Fiant Christiani quum Christum nosse potuerint: quid festinat innocens ætas ad remissionem peccatorum? Sensus est: veniant ad Christum ut instituantur, non ut baptizentur, nisi postquam vim ba- ptismi intellexerint. Nazianzenus agens de iis qui sine ba- ptismo decedunt, exemplum ponit in iis quibus baptismus non contingit διὰ νηπιότητα. Atque is ipse Nazianzenus episcopi cum esset filius patris sub cura diutissime educa- tus, baptizatus non fuit nisi cum ex ephebis exiisset, ut ipse in vita sua nos docet. Johannes Antiochenus, dictus po- stea Chrysostomus, parentibus natus Christianis, ut verior habet sententia, à Meletio episcopo institutus, baptizatus est post annum primum & vicesimum. Sed imprimis nota- tu dignus est canon Synodi Neocæsariensis habitæ anno CCCXV. qui sic habet : περὶ κυοφορούσης ὅτι δεῖ φωτίζεσθαι ὁ- πότε βούλεται· οὐδὲν γὰρ ἐν τούτῳ κοινωνεῖ ἡ τίκτουσα τῷ τικτομένῳ, διὰ τὸ ἑκάστου ἰδίαν τὴν προαίρεσιν τὴν ἐπὶ τῇ ὁμολογίᾳ δείκνυ- σθαι. Utcunque enim alioversum trahant interpretes, apparet, ideo de baptismo prægnantium motam quæstio- nem, quod videretur cum matre simul proles baptizari, quæ tamen baptizari non soleret nisi super propria volun- tate ac professione. Et sic in compendio canonum titulo IV. explicat Balsamo: ὡς δύναται φωτισθῆναι διὰ τὸ μηκέτι εἰς φῶς ἐλθεῖν, μηδὲ προαίρεσιν ἔχειν τῆς ὁμολογίας τοῦ θείου βαπτίσματος. & Zonaras: τὸ ἐμβρυον χρήζει βαπτίσμα- τος· ὅτε προαιρεῖσθαι δυνήσεται. Definit autem Synodus baptismum ideo recte procedere quia ad matrem solam, quæ de se professionem ederet, non etiam ad uterum per- tineret. Et Græcorum plerique ab omni ævo ad hunc diem morem servant differendi parvulorum baptismum, donec ipsi fidei suæ confessionem possint edere. Walafredus Stra- bo de rebus ecclesiasticis c. 26. Notandum deinde primis temporibus illis solummodo baptismi gratiam dari solitam, qui & corporis & mentis integritate jam ad hoc pervenerant, ut scire & intelligere possent, quid emolumenti in baptismo conse- quendum, quid confitendum atque credendum, quid postre- mo renatis in Christo esset servandum. Cæterum ista sicut li- bertatem, vetustatem, & consuetudinem differentiam in- dicant, ita nihil afferunt, cur repudiandus sit baptismus in- fantium, quos parentes aut sponsores alii Deo per sancto- rum preces consecrandos offerunt, cum voto piæ educa- tionis: quod præter cætera baptismo non incommode si- gnificatur. Neque obstare debet quod non omnia quæ iti- dem per baptismum significari solent, in istam ætatem pro- prie congruant. Nam & pœnitentia, quam scimus bapti- smo designari, majorem certe in iis qui cum vitam diu im- puram egissent, vitæ totius mutandæ propositum testaban- tur, quam in aliis locum habebat, in Christo vero quem Johannes baptizavit nullum, qui, ut Tertullianus loqui- tur, nullius pœnitentiæ debitor tinctus est. Scriptor quæ- stionum & responsionum ad Orthodoxos περὶ βρεφῶν lo- quens : ἀξιοῦνται δὲ τῶν διὰ τοῦ βαπτίσματος ἀγαθῶν τῇ πί- στει τῶν προσφερόντων αὐτὰ τῷ βαπτίσματι.

Τῶν γὰρ τοιούτων] Eo minus, inquit Christus, ætas ista quasi profana spernenda est, quia & adulti qui se in meam dedunt disciplinam debent quasi repuerascere, exutis scilicet vitiis quæ major ætas supervexit. Supra voluit Chri- stus sectatores suos pueris similes fieri, vacuitate τῆς φιλαυ- tias. Hic vero magis respici videtur obediens puerorum docilitas. Ita enim ait Lucas ὃς ἐὰν μὴ δέξηται τὴν βασιλεί- αν τοῦ Θεοῦ ὡς παιδίον, οὐ μὴ εἰσέλθῃ εἰς αὐτήν. Solent compa- rari puerilia ingenia tabulæ rasæ, cui facile quidvis inscri- bas.

Per παιδία hoc loco intelligi infantes qui in ulnis adhuc gestantur, ipsæ περιστάσεις docent eorum qui hic ad Christum adducti sunt Marc. X. 16. quos Christus dicitur ἐναγκαλισάμενος: & collatio Luc. XVIII. 5. confirmat, qui βρέ- φη nominat: hæc enim vox infantes notat (βρέ- φος ἀπὸ τρέφω dicitur, quod à nutrice alatur) ac de infantibus recens natis accipitur, ut & de iis qui adhuc utero materno concluduntur, Luc. I. 41. 44. c. II. 12. 1. Petri II. 2. nec aliter usurpatur hæc vox 2. Tim. III. 15. nam ab ipsa infantia sta- tim in verbo Dei informari liberos fidelium quis neget? neque de Timotheo aliter præsumendum, cujus mater & avia à pietate insigniter commen- dantur 2. Tim. I. 5. Et παιδίον de infante octo dierum dicitur, Luc. II. 21. Unde locus præsens à veteribus de infantibus ad Christum per preces & baptismum adducendis acceptus fuit, & à nostris Theologis merito Anabaptistis, Socinianis Pædo- baptismum reprobantibus, ut & Calvinianis jux- ta cum illis fidem infantibus, quorum tamen hic dicitur esse regnum cœlorum, quod nemo sine fide ingreditur, derogantibus opponitur. Bern- hardus Epistol. CXL. ad Hildoph. Comit: Par- vulis, inquit, Christianorum Christi intercluditur via dum Baptismi negatur gratia, nec saluti pro- pinquare sinuntur, Salvatore licet pie clamante pro eis: Sinite parvulos ad me venire. Addimus quæ de eo hic habet Grotius ad v. 14. Huic Christi di- cto inter cætera innititur mos pueros etiam infantes baptismo tingendi: quem Augustini temporibus per omnes Ecclesias fuisse receptum hoc ipso satis constat, quod Pelagiani, cum eo argumento ab Augustino, atque aliis premerentur, negare id ipsum nunquam ausi fuerint. Et ut de Origene nihil dicam, cui qua adscribuntur, quædam sunt incerti autoris, quæ- dam interpolata, epistola Cypriani ad Fidum, qua & Augustinus & Hieronymus utuntur, apertum facit, an recte baptizarentur infantes ne dubitatum quidem, sed an possint baptizari etiam ante octa- vum diem hesitasse; re autem in Concilio expensa visum ne recens quidem natis, si offerantur negan- dum baptismum. In libro antiquo cui titulus Con- stitutiones Clementis legimus: Βαπτίζετε δὲ ὑμῶν καὶ τὰ νήπια, καὶ ἐκτρέφετε αὐτὰ ἐν παιδείᾳ καὶ νουθε- σίᾳ Θεοῦ. Hæc Grotius. Si ergo huic dicto innixi veteres sunt, baptismo infantes tingentes, aut be- ne id de illis acceperunt, aut male. Si bene, cur non assensum etiam præbet Grotius? Si male, quomo- do inniti eidem potuêre, & cur innitentes illi lau- dat? Testimonium tamen è Clementis constitu- tionibus non magni est momenti. Notum enim jam satis, Constitutiones istas Apostolorum, quas à Clemente digestas dicunt νοθεύεσθαι, etsi pro iisdem acriter dimicarit Franciscus Turrianus, & Johan. Carolus Bovius Episcop. Ostrinensis siqui- dem jam ab ipso Athanasio in Synopsi reproba- tæ sint, & Bellarm. libr. de Script. Eccles. p. 59. testetur, in Ecclesia Latina nullum fere nomen eas- dem habere, Græcosque posteriores in Concilio Trul- lano II. easdem improbasse, ut ab hæreticis depra- vatas, imo idem fere judicium de illis esse, quod de recognitionum libris, quos l. II. de Rom. Pont. cap. 11. pro Apocryphis habet: Bisciola vero in Epitome Baron. p. 72. docet: AB OMNIBUS inter Apocrypha relatas esse Clementis Constitutio- nes. Sane quæ de Baptismi Ceremoniis in iisdem

Libr. III. & VII. tradita sunt, ætatem Apostolorum non sapiunt: neque erronea esse, quæ de ανα- βαπτισμῷ eorum, qui baptizati ab hæreticis sunt l. VI. c. 15. habentur, Bellarminus Cardinalis l. c. dubitat. Petrus Halloixius constitutiones in Apocryphis haberi, notis ad vitam Polycarp. cap. 6. & post Ignatii tempora conscriptas esse docet, Not. in vit. Ignat. c. 7. nec ab uno eas homine, nec uno tempore, sed à diversis hominibus & variis temporibus conflatas censet, in Apolog. pro script. Ignat. c. 3. Quanquam vero Epiphanius τὰς διαταγὰς Clementis alicubi laudet, observavit tamen Petavius probe, in Scholiis ad hæresin LXX. Audæanor. eas, quæ hodie circumfe- runtur Constitutiones à prioribus illis, ac nihilomi- nus dubiis, quarum meminit Epiphanius diversas videri. Alexius Aristenus in Scholiis ad Cano- nem Apostolicum LXXX. adhuc ἀνεκδότοις, Theodor. Balsamo, & Johan. Zonaras autoritate Sextæ Synodi rejiciunt easdem, ob adulterina quædam & à pietate aliena inserta, apud Jacob. Usserium in dissertatione ad Epist. Polycarpi & Ignat. addita p. 105. Photius vero Arianismi etiam eas olim insimulatas esse testatur in Bibliothec. n. 113. Doctissimus Lisserius l. c. p. 63. seqq. e- rudite docet, ex eadem officina & Ignatianarum Epistolarum, & Pseudo-Clementinarum Constitu- tionum corruptelas prodiisse, easque quinto post ex- cessum Clementis seculo demum interpolatas esse pag. 41. ac larvatum istum Clementem sub Chri- stianis Imperatoribus vixisse, suoque ipsius indi- cio, foricis instar. l. VI. c. 24. se prodidisse, obser- vat cap. XVI. p. 118. Quæ hic monenda duximus, quum non raro ad Pseudo-Clementem illum pro- vocet Grotius, aut si non pro Clementis illius Ro- mani, certe pro antiqui cujusdam & Catholici Do- ctoris scripto constitutiones illas venditet.

De antiquitate autem Pædobaptismi testis cer- tior S. Augustinus est: de Genesi ad liter. l. X. c. 23. Consuetudo matris Ecclesiæ in baptizandis parvulis nequaquam spernenda est: neque ullo modo super- flua deputanda: nec omnino credenda, nisi APO- STOLICA esset traditio: (non sane ἄγρα- φος, sed in Scripturis fundata, uti docet l. IV. de Bapt. cap. 24.) Et serm. X. de verb. Apo- stoli, de Pædobaptismo monet: Nemo vobis su- surret doctrinas alienas. Hoc Ecclesia semper ha- buit, semper tenuit: hoc à Majorum fide accepit: hoc usque in finem perseveranter custodit. De Cy- priano etiam & Concilio LXVI. Episcoporum è laudata ad Fidum Epistola, quæ libro III. nume- ro VIII. est, res indubitata est: cujus verba ad- ducere juvat: Hæc fuit IN CONCILIO nostra sententia, à baptismo, atque à gratia DEI, qui omnibus misericors & benignus & pius est, nemi- nem per nos debere prohiberi. Quod cum circa uni- versus observandum sit, atque retinendum: tum magis circa INFANTES ipsos, & recens natos, observandum: qui hoc ipso de ope nostra, ac de di- vina misericordia, plus merentur, quod in primo statim nativitatis suæ ortu plorantes ac flentes ni- hil aliud faciunt, quam deprecari. Quam Episto- lam Augustinus Epist. XXVIII. ad Hieronym. & lib. IV. contra duas Epist. Pelag. cap. VIII. lauda- vit: ut & Hieronymus lib. III. contra Pelagianos sub finem. Antiquior adhuc Cypriano fuit S. Ire- næus, qui lib. II. cap. XXXIX. OMNEM æta- tem, ait, sanctificat (Dominus) per illam, quæ ad ipsam erat, similitudinem: OMNES, in- quam, OMNES venit per semetipsum salvare: Omnes, inquam, qui per ipsum RENASCUN- TUR in DEUM, INFANTES ET PAR- VULOS, & juniores & seniores. Quæ infantum παλιγγενεσία non sit, nisi per Baptismum.

De Pelagianis denique certum est, quod neu- tiquam negarint, sed ipsimet confessi sint, in- fantes baptizandos esse, etsi contrarium iisdem impingat Pontificale in Vita Innocentii III. Jo- sephus Vice-Comes Observat. Eccles. de Bapti- smi ritib. lib. II. cap. 1. quod vero per calumniam sibi tribui questus est Epistola ad Innocentium i- psum exarata Pelagius, & immerito id ei tribu- tum esse, agnoscit Augustin. l. de peccat. Orig. cap. XIX. & XXX. & l. 1. de peccat. mer. & remiss. cap. XXVI. Parvulos, inquit, baptizandos esse (Pelagiani) concedunt, qui contra autoritatem U- NIVERSÆ Ecclesiæ, procul dubio, per Dominum & Apostolos traditam venire non possunt. Conf. et- iam Epist. LXXXIX. ad Hilar. & libr. de gratia Christi contra Pelag. & Cœlest. cap. XX.

Non satis autem sibi constare videtur Grotius hoc in loco, quum Augustini temporibus PER O- MNES Ecclesias fuisse receptum morem infantes baptizandi jam asseruerit: mox autem subjun- gat: videtur autem mihi antiquitus baptismus in- fantium multo magis in Africa, quam in Asia aliis- ve mundi partibus fuisse frequentatus, & cum ma- jori quadam necessitatis opinione. Nam in Conciliis vetustioremejus mentionem non invenias Concilio Carthaginensi. Concilia huc non faciunt. Nam nec omnium, quæ usquam habita sunt, ad po- steritatem propagata sunt Conciliorum acta & de- creta, neque de omnibus creditu & observatu necessariis in iisdem actum, sed de iis, quæ pro re nata in Ecclesia expediunda, deliberanda, & definienda erant. Quomodo autem UNI- VERSÆ Ecclesiæ autoritatem S. Augustinus quoad parvulorum baptismum, & quidem inde à Christi & Apostolorum traditione urgere po- tuisset, si in particularibus tantum Ecclesiis qui- busdam, non in universa Ecclesia obtinuisset par- vulorum baptismus, nec adeo necessarius judi- catus fuisset baptismus? Quid quod antiquis se- culis in Ecclesia parvulorum baptismum obtinuis- se S. Hieronymus l. III. contr. Pelagian. & Episto- la ad Lætum, S. Augustinus non locis citatis tan- tum Epist. XXVIII. & de pecc. Orig. c. XL. sed & l. II. de Nuptiis, & concup. c. XX. l. III. de peccat. mer. & remiss. cap. IX. nec non l. IV. contr. Donat. de Baptism. c. XXIV. Innocentius Epist. XXVI. ad Concil. Milevitan. Paulinus in vita Ambrosii apud Surium Tom. II. p. 506. Theodoretus Epitome divin. dogm. cap. de Ba- ptism. Leo M. Epist. LXXXIV. ad Episc. Aqui- lejens. Gennadius de Eccles. dogmat. cap. XXXI. alique perhibeant, ac testentur. Ideoque de Pædo-baptismo, Hoc Ecclesia dixit Serm. X. de V.A. inquit Augustin. hoc SEMPER habuit, SEMPER tenuit: hoc à MAJORUM FIDE accepit: & Cœlestius ipse in libello, quem Ro- mæ edidit, Augustino l. II. contra Cœlest. & Pelag. fassus est, infantes baptizari in remif- sionem peccatorum, secundum REGULAM U- NIVERSALIS Ecclesiæ, & secundum Evan- gelii sententiam. Et ratio, quam pro necessita- te Baptismi allegant veteres, infantes æque con- cernit, ac adultos, & pro ipsorum baptismo fa- cit, ne scilicet differatur, vel denegetur iisdem: uti ex Ambrosio liquet lib. II. de Patriarcha Abra- ham. c. XI. Nec senex proselytus, nec infans verna- culus excipitur: quia omnis ætas peccato obnoxia, & ideo omnis ætas Sacramento idonea. Nisi enim quis renatus fuerit ex aqua, & Spiritu Sancto non potest introire in regnum Dei. Utique nullum ex- cipit, non infantem, non aliqua præventum neces- sitate. Provocat autem Grotius ad Tertullianum, quem de ætate, qua baptizandi essent, qui Chri- stianæ disciplinæ consecrabantur, nihil definitum fuiffe, hoc ipso docere observat, quod dilationem baptismi tam multis rationibus suadet. Locum e- jus ita adducit: Itaque, inquit, pro cujuscunque personæ conditione ac dispositione, etiam ætate, cun- ctatio baptismi utilior est: præcipue tamen circa parvulos. Quid enim necesse est (quod hic in qui- busdam Codicibus reperitur, si non tam necesse, non video, quem commodum sensum accipiat. At si Grotius non vidit, viderunt alii: nimirum hypothetica est propositio, si non necessarius est baptismus, quam Catholici Tertulliano non con- cedunt, Baptismi necessitatem omnino statuen- tes.) Sponsores etiam periculo ingeri, qui & ipsi per mortalitatem destituere promissiones suas possunt, & proventu malæ indolis falli. Ait quidem Domi- nus, Nolite illos prohibere ad me venire. Veniant ergo dum adolescunt, veniant dum discunt, dum quo veniant docentur (legendum puto, dumque veniunt doceantur: quæ est arbitraria nimis corre- ctio, nullatenus necessaria, nec Codicibus anti- quis probata) Fiant Christiani cum Christum noffe potuerint, quid festinat innocens ætas ad re- missionem peccatorum? Sensus est (addit Grotius, scilicet imprimis juxta correctionem, quam pro lubitu fecerat) veniant ad Christum, ut instituan- tur, non ut baptizentur, nisi postquam vim ba- ptismi intellexerint. Locus Tertulliani vexatus legitur libro de Baptismo c. XVIII. At quid o- pus fuit ab Ecclesia definiri, si hoc traditum à Christo & Apostolis, si necessitas baptismi ceu medii ad salutem ordinati è Scriptura patuit? Erravit ergo in eo Tertullianus, quod necessa- rium esse baptismum ad salutem non judicavit: erravit, quod infantilem ætatem INNOCEN- TEM esse, nec remissione peccatorum indige- re censuit, quæ sententia postmodum in Pelagio damnata fuit. Erravit, quod opus esse credidit ad Baptismi efficaciam, ut de baptismi vi prius e- doceatur baptizandus, qua hypothesi penitus prosternitur Pædobaptismus, quod in Anaba- ptistis, & Socinianis hodie damnat Ecclesia. Constat autem id ex hoc Tertulliani loco satis, quod ejus ætate in Ecclesia baptizati fuerint par- vuli. Quid enim alias opus fuisset hanc consue- tudinem refutare, de baptismo infantum, & de sponsoribus in eodem adhibere solitis? quid quod hypothetica illa, quam expunctam cupit Grotius, si non tam necesse, videatur innuere, nihil aliud Tertullianum negare, nisi necessitatem baptismi infantum extra periculum mortis? ut taceamus, quod nonnulli Tertullianum de infantibus infide- lium agere existiment. De cætero aliud ex alio Tertulliani libro de anima nempe cap. XXXIX. & XL. liquet. Cæterum (inquit Apostolus) immundi nascerentur. Quasi designatos tamen sanctitatis, ac per hoc etiam salutis, intelligi volens fidelium fi- lios: ut hujus spei pignora matrimonii, quæ re- tinenda censuerat, patrocinarentur. Alioquin meminerat dominicæ definitionis: Nisi quis nasca- tur ex aqua, & spiritu, non introibit in regnum Dei, id est, non erit sanctus. Ita omnis anima eo usque in Adam censetur, donec in Christo re- censeatur: tamdiu immunda, quamdiu recenseatur. Hæc orthodoxæ Ecclesiæ sententiæ magis conso- na sunt.

Nazianzenum etiam allegat Grotius, qui de iis, qui sine baptismo decedunt agens, exemplum in iis ponit, quibus Baptismus non contingit dia

νηπιότητα, & baptizatus ipse non fuit, nisi cum ex ephebis exiisset, ut in vita sua docet. Sed is non ne- gavit baptismum parvulorum, imo si urgeat ne- cessitas & casus mortis, eundem præcepit, & exi- stimavit differri posse extra illum casum in quar- tum ætatis annum, quæ tamen privata ejus tantum sententia fuit. Locum adscribemus integrum ex Orat. XL. quæ est in S. Baptisma, ut de men- te Theologi rectius constet: Omni, inquit, cu- ra & studio nobis est providendum, ne communi hac gratia careamus. Sint sane hæc, dixerit aliquis quantum ad eos attinet, qui baptismum requirunt: quid autem de iis dices, quid adhuc tenera ætate sunt, nec aut damnum, aut gratiam sentiunt? An eos quoque baptizabimus? Ita prorsus, si quod pe- riculum urgeat. Præstat enim absque sensu san- ctificari, quam sine sigillo & initiatione abscedere. Atque hujus rei ratio nobis est circumcisio, die o- ctavo peragi solita, quæ baptismi figuram quodam- modo gerebat, atque iis, qui rationis adhuc exper- tes erant, offerebatur. Eodem quoque modo postium unctio, quæ rebus sensu carentibus adhibita, pri- mogenitis salutem afferebat. De reliquis ita cen- seo, ut triennio expectato, aut aliquanto breviori, vel longiori temporis spatio (nam tum & mystici quiddam audire, & respondere possunt, ac si minus plane & exacte intelligunt, imbuuntur tamen & in- formantur) ita demum per magni Baptismi Sacra- mentum & animos & corpora sanctificent. Hæc Nazianzenus: qui tamen addit: propter inopina- tos & repentinos periculorum impetus, quique nul- la ope atque auxilio propulsari queant, lavacro com- muniri omnino conducibilius esse. Non enim ne- cessitatem baptismi elevabat, quod à Grotio Ar- miniano fit, sed desiderabat solum præviam ali- qualem informationem in baptizandis, si non ad- sit periculum, cujus tamen declinandi nullum no- bis esse remedium, nosque id abfuturum ne sci- re quidem ulla ratione posse, propter casus ino- pinatos, fatebatur ipse, eoque παντὶ λόγῳ λυ- σιτελέστερον censebat, lavacro baptismi infantes communiri.

Nec Synodus Neo-Cæsariensis Anno CCCXV. habita Pædobaptismo quicquam officit: volunta- tem enim & consensum solum in adultis, utpote in muliere prægnanti requirit Canon à Grotio ad- ductus: περὶ κυοφορούσης ὅτι δεῖ φωτίζεσθαι ὁπό- τε βούλεται. οὐδὲν γὰρ ἐν τούτῳ κοινωνεῖ ἡ τίκτουσα τῷ τικτομένῳ, διὰ τὸ ἑκάστου ἰδίαν τὴν προαίρεσιν τὴν ἐπὶ τῇ ὁμολογίᾳ δείκνυσθαι. Matris enim gravidæ voluntatem, num scilicet ipsa, nondum baptizata baptizari velit, respici, conditio adjecta ὁπότε βού- λεται, satis docet: quicquid sit de explicatione Balsamonis, aut Zonaræ, quos allegat Grotius, ac si definierit Synodus baptismum ideo recte procede- re, quia ad matrem solam, quæ de se professionem ederet, non etiam ad uterum (fœtum) pertinet, sci- licet quia fœtus professionem edere non posset.

Falso denique affirmat Grotius Græcorum ple- rosque ab omni ævo ad hunc diem morem servare differendi parvulorum baptismum, donec ipsi fidei suæ confessionem possint edere. Testimonio unius Walafrædi Strabonis, qui anno DCCCL. vixit, id confici non potest. Notandum, inquit ille li- bro de rebus Ecclesiast. cap. XXVI. primis tempo- ribus illis solummodo baptismi gratiam dari solitam, qui & corporis & mentis integritate jam ad hoc per- venerant, ut scire, & intelligere possent, quid e- molumenti in baptismo consequendum, quid confi- tendum atque credendum, quid postremo renatis in Christo esset servandum. Falsum in eo fuisse Wa- lafredum, testimonia ἀξιόπιστα, longeque cer- tiora jam docuerunt, Patrum nempe trecentis annis eodem antiquiorum, qui universæ Ecclesiæ eam fuisse consuetudinem ac sententiam, quæ ho- dieque nostræ est, baptismum parvulis ob sum- mam ejus necessitatem, non esse denegandum: quibus addendi è Græcis sunt Cyrillus Hierosolymi- tanus Catech. Mystag. 1. Basilius M. exhort. ad Ba- ptism. Chrysost. homil. ad Neophist. De modernis etiam Græcis contrarium ejus, quod asseruit Gro- tius, ad hunc usque diem eos morem servare, differendi Baptismum parvulorum, donec ipsi confessionem fidei suæ edere possint, patet è Re- sponso primo Patriarchæ Constantinopolitani Jere- miæ Würtenbergens. Theologis reddito Anno 1576. cap. II. & IX. In nono (articulo) dicitur, ba- ptizandos esse infantes, nec adultiorem ætatem ex- spectandam esse. Hoc apud Nos quoque fit; ut ne quid accidat, re dilata. Nisi enim aliquis regene- retur ex aqua & spiritu, non ingreditur regnum cœ- lorum.

## 19:15
Ver. 15. laying his hands upon them] So that at the same time, according to the Hebrew custom, he might conceive prayers for them. For this is what ἐνλογεῖν means, Mark X. 16. Christ indeed had the power of conferring gifts even without prayers, but offering us an example, he for the most part interposed prayers.

PART III. The testing of the rich young worker.

Latin:

Vers. 15. ἐπιθεὶς ἀυτοῖς τὰς χεῖρας] Ita ut simul more Hæbræo preces pro iis conciperet. Hoc enim est ἐνλογεῖν Marc. X. 16. Habebat quidem Christus potestatem dona conferendi etiam sine precibus, sed exemplum nobis præ- bens plerumque preces interponebat.

PARS III. Iuvenis divitis operarii probatio.

## 19:16
Ver. 16. one approaching] Not that lawyer mentioned by Luke ch. X. 25, but a ruler, that is, one of the senators of his town, Luke XVIII. 18, otherwise a youth in age, below v. 20. I think John’s statement XII. 42, nevertheless even of the rulers many believed in him, is to be understood of this kind of rulers. But that he came not with the intention of slandering, like that lawyer, but desirous of learning, appears from Mark and Luke.

Eternal life] Which he heard being openly preached by Christ, though it was but thinly known to the Jews. See what will be said on Luke X. 25.

Latin:

Vers. 16. εἷς προσελθὼν] Non νομικὸς ille Lucæ memoratus cap. X. 25. sed ἄρχων id est unus oppidi sui senatorum Luc. XVIII. 18. cæterum ætate juvenis, infra v. 20. De hoc ἀρ- χόντων genere accipiendum puto Johannis illud XII. 42. ὅ- μως μὲν τοὶ κὶ τῶν ἀρχόντων πολλοὶ ἐπίστευσαν εἰς ἀυτὸν. Venisse autem hunc non calumniandi animo, ut νομικὸν illum, sed discendi cupidum, ex Marco & Luca apparet.

Ζωὴν αἰώνιον] Quam Judæis tenuiter cognitam aperte à Christo prædicari audiebat. Vide quæ ad Lucam X. 25. dicentur.

## 19:17
Ver. 17. Why do you ask me about the good; there is one who is good] Since both the older and more corrected copies prefer this reading, which not only the old Latin interpreter whom we now use followed, but also those codices which Augustine, Jerome, and others used, it is much more credible that the other reading was brought over here from Mark and Luke, which often happens, than that this one crept in from elsewhere. The antiquity of the diverse reading, however, appears even from the fact that in Origen (unless one wishes to suspect that something was added there too) there is mention of both: and the Syrian has it as in Mark and Luke. The sense comes to the same thing. That youth, although he recognized nothing in Jesus greater than a man, hoped nevertheless that by his showing he would arrive at the possession of that good by which eternal life is prepared, as if he needed only a shower for that matter, intending to accomplish the rest by himself. Just as the philosophers of whom Augustine treats in Epistle LII, who wished to fashion a blessed life for themselves, and thought it was rather to be achieved than obtained, when its giver is none but God. With this intention he also called Jesus a good teacher, that is, a shower of the good, and wished to be taught about the good by him. But Jesus, meeting this error, and at the same time offering us an example of modesty, says that there are not many sources of the good, but one only, namely God, by this very thing indicating that it is not enough for the good to be shown to us, unless God, illuminating the mind, suggests strength to us, to which pertains what follows below, but with God all things are possible. Some among the Gentiles also saw this, but those to whom, as I think, some spark of barbaric philosophy had reached. Plato in the Meno: but if now we have searched and spoken well of all things in this discourse, virtue would be neither by nature, nor teachable, but arriving by divine allotment. That these things are to be understood in such a way that the work of teachers is not excluded, nor the faculty of natural talent, but that God is believed to work virtue in us both through these and beyond these, Maximus Tyrius eloquently shows in his diatribe on whether one might become good by divine allotment, where he uses the testimony of Homer to the same opinion:

For I do not think that you were born and reared without the gods.

He uses this argument, however: for the Divine, being self-sufficient and perfect and powerful, would wish to accomplish good things, and according to its self-sufficiency it has [the will], and according to its power it is able to wish; but having good things and being able, why does it not give? For one who has and gives, also wishes; and one who wishes and does not have, also is able; but one who has and wishes, how is he not able? And he refers to this also the adversities and dangers which God casts before men, so that by exercising themselves in them they may turn out good. Hierocles in the Pythagorean school learned the same: for as regards the choice of good things, it is in our power, but also having that very thing which is in our power from God, we are in every way in need of the cooperation and perfection of those things chosen from Him; for it seems that what is striven for by us is like a hand extended for the taking of good things; but what is accomplished by God is the provision and source of the giving of good things. Shortly after: for when it is necessary only to be eager for good things as if they were in our power to accomplish, and we are in need of the help of God for the avoidance of evils and the acquisition of good things. Seneca: No mind is good without God. Porphyry also wrote that men cannot be perfected except through the paternal mind. Let Philo also teach us that the saner Jews felt the same: the soul must not attribute the labor for virtue to itself, but take it away from itself, and refer it to God, acknowledging that not its own strength nor its power procured the good, but He who bestowed the love for this. The same author elsewhere addresses God in the person of the Muses thus: therefore I pray and beseech that you accept the supplication of a man who is a suppliant and a lover of God and who deems it worthy to worship you alone. For as light, not being known by another, is a sign of itself to itself, so you alone could reveal yourself. And in the second book of Allegories: νᾶς γὰρ δίκαιον τῶν τῆς ψυχῆς κινημάτων ὅσα πρῶτα ἠ τάξει ἠ δυνάμει Θεῷ ὁμολογεῖν. For which reason I am the more surprised that there are those who everywhere traduce the Christian writers of that first and most holy antiquity, as if by them τὸ ἀυτεξύσιον were extolled to the injury of divine grace. Although it has been abundantly demonstrated of late by most learned men that those most holy men, by whose doctrine in part, and in part by whose blood, the Christian cause was established, were of a far different mind, I cannot but make it conspicuous to the readers here also by testimonies which, to me at least, seem most clear. Justin Martyr: ὀυδὲ ἂν ἡ- μᾶς ποτε ὦ ἄνδρες, νενοηκέναι δυνηθῆναι ἐν ταῖς γραφαῖς ταυ- τα, ἐιμὴ θελήματι τοῦ θελήσαντος ἀυτὰ ἐλάβομεν χάριν τῶ νοῆσαι; Clement of Alexandria, Strom. V.: & χάριθ- ἄνευ τῆς ἐξαιρέτου πτερῶταί τε κὶ ἀνίσταται κὶ ἄνω τῶν ὑπερκειμένων αἴρεται ἡ ψυχὴ, πᾶν τὸ βρῖθον ἀποτιθεμένη κὶ ἀποδιδοῦσα τῷ συγγενεῖ, where he also brings forward the passage from Plato which we have cited. Origen against Celsus, book VI.: Φησὶ δ' ὁ θεῖος λόγος ὐκ ἀυταρκὲς εἶναι τὸ λεγόμενον (κ' ἀυτὸ καθ' ἀυτὸ ἀληθὲς κὶ πισι- κώταῖον ἦ) πρὸς τὸ καθικέσθαι ἀνθρωπίνης ψυχῆς, ἐὰν μὴ καὶ δύ- ναμίς τις θεόθεν δοθῇτῷ λίγοιτι καὶ χάρις ἐπανθήσῃ τοῖς λεγομέ- τοις, κὶ ἄυτη ὐκ ἀθεεὶ ἐγγινομένη. Again elsewhere he requires πρὸς τὸ λογικὸν ἀγαθὸν τὴν συμπνέουσαν θείαν δύναμιν. Chrysostom, homil. XLIV. on John, makes Christ speak thus: τὸ τολυχὸν πρᾶγμα ἐστὶ τὸ πιστέυσαι εἰς ἐμὲ, ἀλλὰ τῆς ἄνωθεν ἀποκαλύψεως δεῖ, κὶ ψυχῆς ἐυγνωμόνως, δεχομέ- νης τὴν ἀποκάλυψιν. And Hom. XLV.: ὀυ γάρ τις ἰσχύσει πρὸς ἀυτὸν φοιτῆσ δεῖτες ἰλέως, ὃ δὲ ἀυτὸ κ' τὸ ἐφ' ἡμῖν ἀιαιρεῖ, ἀλ- λὰ μᾶλλον ἐμφαίνει ἡμᾶς βοηθείας δεομένες. When therefore Christ says here that there is only one good, namely God, he indicates by that that God is τὸ ἀυτοαγαθὸν, the fountain of true good, ἀφ' ὗ πᾶσα δόσις ἀγαθὴ, as James speaks: clearly so that the young man, not a stranger to the pursuit of virtue, but trusting more than was right in his own powers, might understand by that very thing that that good ought not only to be learned by questioning, but also to be sought by prayers. Moreover, ὃς ἐστὶν ὁ ἀγαθός, as the ancient Codices have it, the Syrian rightly interprets by adding the name of God. For as others have noted, one, even without any other addition, was accustomed to be called God by the Hebrews. Indeed, and by the Assyrians: Macrobius: For to the God whom they venerate as supreme and greatest, they gave the name Adad: the interpretation of which name signifies one. Philo of Byblos: Ἀδωδος βασιλεὺς θεῶν. Clearly the Assyrians said חד חד for which the Hebrews said אחד. Thus that passage in Job XIV. 4. לא אחד the Chaldean interprets as except God. Tertullian in the Testimony of the Soul recites as a common saying: God is good, but man is bad.

ἐισελεθεῖν εἰς τὴν ζωὴν] Clearly the eternal life about which the young man had asked: which is below ἐισελεθεῖν εἰς τὴν βασιλείαν τῦ Θεῦ. Moreover, just as we said above that ἔρχεσθαι is taken for πο- ρέυεσθαι, so also ἐισέρχεσθαι here signifies not the attainment of eternal life itself, but the journey directed toward it: just as also ἐισέρχεσθαι διὰ πύλης is said above in ch. VII. 13. And below the lawyers are said ὐ ἐισέρχεσθαι εἰς τὴν βασιλείαν τῶν ὀρανῶν, that is, not to enter upon the true way to the kingdom, nor to allow others to do so.

Τήρησον τὰς ἐντολάς] Prov. VII. 1. 2. He called them ἐντολὰς after the manner of the Hebrews, the precepts of Moses, that is to say, the law of works, not the law of the Spirit. See Luke I. 6. and in Paul several times. In these, however, Christ places not the whole way, but the beginning of the way. For this, as we have said elsewhere, was the righteousness of the lawyers and the Pharisees: Christ had taught that another, greater righteousness was required to attain the kingdom. But, as Paul says treating of the law of works, "the law has been our schoolmaster unto Christ," thus Christ begins from that which is less. Thus also the Baptist, the herald of repentance, had paved the way with a more perfect teaching.

Latin:

Vers. 17. Τί με ἐρωτᾷς περὶ τῦ ἀγαθῦ· εἷς ἐστιν ὁ ἀγαθὸς] Cum & vetustiora & emendatiora exemplaria hanc lectionem præ- ferant, quam secutus est non vetus tantum quo nunc uti- mur Latinus interpres, sed & illi codices quibus usi sunt Augustinus, Hieronymus, atque alii, multo est credibi- lius lectionem alteram ex Marco & Luca huc traductam, quod sæpe accidit, quam istam aliunde irrepsisse. Antiqui- tas tamen diversæ lectionis vel inde apparet, quod apud Origenem (nisi tamen & ibi aliquid afsutum suspicari libet) utriusque sit mentio: & Syrus ita habet, ut in Marco & Luca. Sensus eodem recidit. Juvenis iste, quamvis in Jesu majus homine nihil agnosceret, sperabat tamen eo mon- strante se perventurum ad possessionem ejus boni quo vita æterna paratur, quasi ad eam rem monstratore tantum ege- ret, cætera per se confecturus. Sicut Philosophi de quibus Epistola LII. agit Augustinus, qui beatam vitam ipsi sibi fa- bricare voluerunt, potiusque patrandam quam impetran- dam putaverunt, cum ejus dator non sit nisi Deus. Hoc animo & Jesum bonum magistrum vocabat, id est boni monstratorem, & de bono ab ipso volebat edoceri. At Je- sus occurrens huic errori, simulque modestiæ nobis præ- bens exemplum, ait non esse multos boni fontes, sed uni- cum, Deum scilicet, hoc ipso indicans, non satis esse bo- num nobis monstrari, nisi Deus mentem illustrans vires nobis suggerat, quo pertinet quod infra sequitur, παρὰ δὲ Θεῷ πάντα δυνατά ἐστι. Viderunt hoc etiam in Gentibus nonnulli, sed ad quos ut arbitror aliqua Barbaricæ philoso- phiæ scintilla pervaserat. Plato Menone: εἰ δὲ νῦν ἡμεῖς πάν- τα τῷ λόγῳ τούτῳ καλῶς ἐζητήσαμέν τε κὶ ἐλέγομεν, ἀρετὴ ἄν εἴη ὄυ- τε φύσει, ὄυτε διδακτὸν, ἀλλὰ θεία μοίρα παραγιγνομένη. Quæ ita esse intelligenda, ut non excludatur opera magistro- rum, neque naturalis ingenii facultas, sed ut Deus & per hæc & præter hæc operari in nobis credatur virtutem, fa- cunde ostendit Maximus Tyrius in diatriba εἰ γένοιτό τις θεία μοίρα ἀγαθὸς, ubi in eandem sententiam Homeri utitur te- stimonio:

ὦ γὰρ ὀΐω Οὐδέ σε Θεῶν ἀέκητι γενέσθαι τε τραφέμεντε.

Argumento autem hoc utitur: ἀυταρκὲς δὲ ὂν (τὸ Θεῖον) κὶ τέλειον καὶ ἰσχυρὸν, καλὰ μὲν ἂν τελεσδέργια [τὰ ἀγαθὰ] βούλοι- ται, κατὰ δὲ τὴν ἀυτάρκειαν ἔχον καλὰ δὲ τὴν ἰσχὺν δύναται βούλεσ- θαι· δὲ διὰ καλὰ ἔχων καὶ δυνάμενος κατὰ τί μὴ δῷ; ὃ μὲν γὰρ ἔχων κὶ διδὺς, κὶ βούλεται ὃ δὲ βουλόμενος ὐκ ἔχων, κὶ δύναται ὃ δὲ ἔχων καὶ βουλόμενος πῶς ὐ δύναται; Atque huc refert et- iam adversa ac pericula quæ Deus hominibus objiciat, ut in iis se exercendo boni evadant. Hierocles in Pythago- rica schola eadem didicit: ὡς γὰρ πρὸς τὸ ἐφ' ἡμῖν αἵρεσις τῶν κα- λῶν, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἀυτὸ τὸ ἐφ' ἡμῖν θεόθεν ἔχοντες, τῆς παρ' ἐκείνο συνεργείας, καὶ τελειώσεως τῶν αἱρεθέντων πάντως πὼ χρῄζομεν ἔοικε γὰρ τὸ μὲν παρ' ἡμῶν σπουδαζόμενον ἐκτεινομένῃ χειρὶ πρὸς λῆψιν τῶν καλῶν· τὸ δὲ παρὰ Θεῶ συντελούμενον χορηγία οὖσα καὶ πηγὴ τῆς δόσεως τῶν ἀγαθῶν. Mox: ὅτε γὰρ μόνον προθυ- μεῖσθαι δεῖ τὰ καλὰ ὡς ἐφ' ἑαυτοῖς ὄντα κατορθῶσαι καὶ χωρὶς τᾶ Θεῦ ἐπικουρίας χρῄζομεν πρὸς ἀποφυγὴν μὲν τῶν κακῶν, κτῆκτε- σιν δὲ τῶν ἀγαθῶν. Seneca: Nulla sine Deo mens bona est. Por- phyrius quoque scripsit non posse homines τελειῶσθαι nisi διὰ τοῦ νῦ πατρικοῦ. Judæos saniores idem sensisse vel Philo nos doceat: δεῖ τὸν ὑπὲρ ἀρετῆς πόνον μὴ ἑαυτῷ προσάγειν τὴν ψυχὴν, ἀλλ' ἀφελεῖν ἀφ' ἑαυτῆς, καὶ Θεῷ ἀνεῖγκεῖν, ὁμο λογᾶσαν ὅτι ἐχ ἡ ἰσχὺς αυτῆς ἐδὲ ἡ δύναμις περιεποίησε τὸ κα- λὸν, ἀλλὰ πρὸ τοῦτο ἔρωτα χαρισαμένου. Idem alibi Deum ex Musis persona ita alloquitur: διὸ δέομαι καὶ ποτνιῶμαι προσέσθαι τὴν ἱκεσίαν ἀνδρὸς ἱκέτε καὶ φιλοθέα καὶ μόνον θερα- πεύειν ἀξιῦντος. ὡς γὰρ τὸ φῶς ὑφ' ἑτέρου μὴ γνωριζόμενον ἀυ- τὸ ἑαυτῶ γνώρισμά ἐστιν, ὕτω καὶ σὺ σεαυτὸν μόνος ἂν φῆναι δύναιο. Et allegoriarum secundo: νᾶς γὰρ δίκαιον τῶν τῆς ψυχῆς κινημάτων ὅσα πρῶτα ἠ τάξει ἠ δυνάμει Θεῷ ὁμολογεῖν. Quo magis miror esse qui Scriptores Christianos primæ illius atque sanctissimæ vetustatis passim traducunt, qua- si ab illis τὸ ἀυτεξύσιον extollatur in divinæ gratiæ inju- riam. Longe aliter animatos fuisse viros sanctissimos, quorum partim doctrina, partim & sanguine stabilita est res Christiana, quanquam a viris doctissimis nuper abun- de demonstratum est, non possum non hic etiam apposi- tis testimoniis, ut mihi quidem videntur, aperrissimis, con- spicuum lectoribus facere. Justinus Martyr: ὀυδὲ ἂν ἡ- μᾶς ποτε ὦ ἄνδρες, νενοηκέναι δυνηθῆναι ἐν ταῖς γραφαῖς ταυ- τα, ἐιμὴ θελήματι τοῦ θελήσαντος ἀυτὰ ἐλάβομεν χάριν τῶ νοῆσαι; Clemens Alexandrinus Strom. V. & χάριθ- ἄνευ τῆς ἐξαιρέτου πτερῶταί τε κὶ ἀνίσταται κὶ ἄνω τῶν ὑπερκειμένων αἴρεται ἡ ψυχὴ, πᾶν τὸ βρῖθον ἀποτιθεμένη κὶ ἀποδιδοῦσα τῷ συγγενεῖ, ubi & locum ex Platone adducit quem citavimus. Orige- nes adversus Celsum libro VI. Φησὶ δ' ὁ θεῖος λόγος ὐκ ἀυταρκὲς εἶναι τὸ λεγόμενον (κ' ἀυτὸ καθ' ἀυτὸ ἀληθὲς κὶ πισι- κώταῖον ἦ) πρὸς τὸ καθικέσθαι ἀνθρωπίνης ψυχῆς, ἐὰν μὴ καὶ δύ- ναμίς τις θεόθεν δοθῇτῷ λίγοιτι καὶ χάρις ἐπανθήσῃ τοῖς λεγομέ- τοις, κὶ ἄυτη ὐκ ἀθεεὶ ἐγγινομένη. Rursum alibi requirit πρὸς τὸ λογικὸν ἀγαθὸν τὴν συμπνέουσαν θείαν δύναμιν. Chryso- stomus homil. XLIV. ad Johannem Christum sic loquen- tem facit; τὸ τολυχὸν πρᾶγμα ἐστὶ τὸ πιστέυσαι εἰς ἐμὲ, ἀλλὰ τῆς ἄνωθεν ἀποκαλύψεως δεῖ, κὶ ψυχῆς ἐυγνωμόνως, δεχομέ- νης τὴν ἀποκάλυψιν. Et Hom. XLV. ὀυ γάρ τις ἰσχύσει πρὸς ἀυτὸν φοιτῆσ δεῖτες ἰλέως, ὃ δὲ ἀυτὸ κ' τὸ ἐφ' ἡμῖν ἀιαιρεῖ, ἀλ- λὰ μᾶλλον ἐμφαίνει ἡμᾶς βοηθείας δεομένες. Cum ergo hic dicit Christus unum tantum esse bonum, nempe Deum, eo indicat Deum esse τὸ ἀυτοαγαθὸν, fontem veri boni, ἀφ' ὗ πᾶσα δόσις ἀγαθὴ, ut loquitur Jacobus: ni- mirum ut juvenis non alienus à virtutis studio, sed viri- bus suis plus æquo confidens eo ipso intelligeret bonum il- lud non interrogando tantum disci, sed & precibus posci debere. Cæterum ὃς ἐστὶν ὁ ἀγαθός, ut antiqui Codices ha- bent, recte Syrus interpretatur addito Dei nomine. Nam ut alii notarunt, unus, etiam sine alio adjectamento, Deus dici solebat Hebræis. Imo & Assyriis: Macrobius: Deo enim quem summum maximumque fenerantur Adad nomen dederunt: cujus nominis interpretatio significat unus. Philo Byblius: Ἀδωδος βασιλεὺς θεῶν. Nimirum Assyrii dicebant חד חד pro quo Hebræi אחד. Ita illud apud Jobum XIV. 4. לא אחד Chaldæus interpretatur nisi Deus. Tertullianus Testimonio Animæ recitat ut vulgi dictum: Deus bonus, sed bomo malus.

ἐισελεθεῖν εἰς τὴν ζωὴν] Nimirum τὴν αἰώνιον de qua juve- nis interrogaverat: quod infra est ἐισελεθεῖν εἰς τὴν βασιλείαν τῦ Θεῦ. Cæterum sicut supra diximus ἔρχεσθαι sumi pro πο- ρέυεσθαι, ita & ἐισέρχεσθαι hic non ipsam vitæ æternæ con- secutionem, sed iter eo directum significat: quomodo & ἐισέρχεσθαι διὰ πύλης supra dicitur c. VII. 13. Et infra dicun- tur legisperiti ὐ ἐισέρχεσθαι εἰς τὴν βασιλείαν τῶν ὀρανῶν, id est viam veram ad regnum non insistere, neque alios ut id faciant pati.

Τήρησον τὰς ἐντολάς] Prov. VII. 1. 2. ἐντολὰς vocavit more Hebræorum præcepta Mosis, legem factorum scili- cet, non legem Spiritus. Vide Luc. I. 6. & apud Paulum ali- quoties. In his aurem ponit Christus non viam totam sed initium viæ. Hæc enim ut alibi diximus, erat justitia legis- peritorum & Pharisæorum: aliam majorem exigi ad re- gnum adipiscendum Christus docuerat. Sed, ut Paulus dicit de lege factorum agens, ὁ νόμος παιδαγωγὸς ἡμῶν γέγονεν εἰς χριστὸν, ita Christus ab eo quod minus est incipit. Ita & Baptista pœnitentiæ præco perfectiori magisterio viam straverat.

## 19:18
Ver. 18. ποῖας] So among Plato sometimes ποῖα for τίνα. And no otherwise below ch. XXI. 23. ch. XXII. 36. ch. XXIV. 42. 43. John X. 32. Acts IV. 7. and elsewhere passim. Among the LXX also sometimes, as 1 Kings IX. 18. But the young man seems to ask this because, since there are very many commandments in the law of Moses, in any one of which it is easy to stumble, he seeks to know to which he ought especially to attend. Christ, however, answering the questioner, says that those are the most important commandments which consist in mutual duties, not those which consist in rites.

Latin:

Vers. 18. ποῖας] Ita apud Platonem aliquoties ποῖα pro τίνα. Nec aliter infra c. XXI. 23. c. XXII. 36. c. XXIV. 42. 43. Joh. X. 32. Act. IV. 7. & alibi passim. A- pud LXX. etiam aliquoties, ut 1. Reg. IX. 18. Videtur autem ideo hoc quærere juvenis, quia cum in lege Mofis plurima sint mandata, in quorum unum aliquod facile sit impingere, scire expetit ad quæ potissimum attendere de- beat. Christus autem ad interrogatum respondens ea po- tissima esse dicit mandata, quæ in officiis mutuis, non quæ in ritibus consisterent.

## 19:19
V. 19. "Thou shalt love thy neighbor as thyself." Since this commandment has a double sense, the one general, which shows that true and sincere love of men among themselves is most acceptable to God, in which respect this precept is called by Paul the fulfilling of the law, and by Christ the greatest commandment, from that which is about worshipping God: the other indeed more strict, insofar as that precept formed a part of the law of works, that is, as we have explained elsewhere, of the Hebrew civil law, the latter sense seems to agree more with this place, because the young man had asked about deeds: "what good shall I do?" Which Mark, if I am not mistaken, makes clear, who, omitting those words, puts "defraud not," by which word he embraces all other injustices which do not properly come under adultery, murder, theft, false witness. Thus Paul joined "to do wrong or to defraud" in 1 Cor. VI. 8. And among Aristophanes in the Plutus, after the question "have you stolen?" follows another, "but you have defrauded no one." But Mark well expressed in one word what is read in Leviticus XIX in many words: "Thou shalt not slander thy neighbor; thou shalt not wrong thy neighbor, and thou shalt not rob, nor shalt thou walk with deceit in thy nation." Thus the Romans used to include all those crimes which have no proper name under the name of stellionatus or evil deceit. The Hebrew עשק extends equally widely, which the Greeks translate as "to defraud" in Levit. VI. 2 and elsewhere, with David Kimchi in his book of roots explaining that generality of the Hebrew word very well at the place in Levit. XIX. 13. In the same sense יונה is placed in Levit. XXV. 14, 17, which the Greeks translate as "to oppress." Christ therefore looks in this place to this law insofar as it commands duty, not insofar as it shows the perfect achievement.

Grotius rightly notes that he was not that lawyer of Luke X. 25, because this history is different, mentioned in Luke XVIII. 42: where he is called a ruler: by which name he understands a senator of his town, and he perhaps not inappropriately takes the words of John XII. 42 concerning that kind of rulers. That he came eager to learn, not with the intention of slandering like that lawyer, is certain from Mark and Luke. But that Grotius says eternal life was thinly known to the Jews, which Christ openly preached, smacks of the Pelagian error of Socinianism: which we have already often refuted. For in the Old Testament not only bodily goods, but also promises of eternal life were given. Therefore this young man is also called back to the Old Testament, so that if anyone wishes to obtain eternal life through works, being informed from there of what Moses requires, he may recognize the inability to fulfill the law. Nor is the audacity to be tolerated that he boldly alters the text of v. 17, which is thus: "Why callest thou me good? There is none good but one, that is, God," into: "Why askest thou me about the good? One is good." For he has not proved that the older and more correct copies prefer this reading: only two are noted by Stephanus, three by Beza, which read thus. But all the rest consistently retain the vulgate and common reading. Although indeed the Latin vulgate, which Augustine followed, has it so, yet it is not permitted to correct the source from a translation; nor does it appear why we should suspect that our reading was brought here from Mark and Luke; rather, because Mark and Luke agree with our reading, one may instead conclude that this is to be judged the truer one, on account of the harmony of the Evangelists; for the Syrian also has it here as it is in Mark and Luke, and the Greek interpreters read it thus: therefore Nyssenus in the Catena on Matthew: Therefore he says; why callest thou me good?

By saying ME he indicates his human nature, and he refutes the Eunomians here, who, hearing the Lord say "there is none good but one, that is, God," say that goodness belongs only to the Father, but exclude the Son from this: which difficulty is also raised here by Basil in Matthew XIX, and by Nazianzen, as also by Chrysostom; whose reading as Greek Fathers is to be more attended to here, as they did not even doubt the truth of our reading. But that mention is made of both readings in Origen is suspicious even to Grotius himself, that something was added there. Nor would that connection or objection be appropriate, "why askest thou me about the good," because he could well ask Christ about the good, even if only one is good: but he could not call Christ good, whom he did not believe to be God, if only one God is good. Add that these have a relation to the address of the young man, by which he addressed Christ, "Good Master": but not to the object of the question; which also was not about the good, but about eternal life. Nor is that gloss of Grotius to be admitted, that this young man, although he recognized nothing in JESUS greater than a man, yet hoped that with him pointing the way he would arrive at the possession of that good by which eternal life is prepared, as if he only needed a guide for that matter, intending to accomplish the rest by himself. For he had not inquired concerning the attainment of that good by which eternal life is prepared, but concerning the method of attaining eternal life, as the very words of the inquirer teach: τί ἀγαθὸν ποιήσω, ἵνα ἔχω ζωὴν αἰώνιον; for he had been instructed in the Pharisaic schools, and thus believed that by his own ποιήσεΐ, or proper works, he could and ought to attain eternal life, nor did he wish to learn anything other than what that good was which, by doing, he himself might aspire to eternal life, not how he might arrive at the possession of that good by which life is prepared: then the answer of Christ also confirms this: If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments: which did not sound as if it concerned the attainment of the good necessary for eternal life, but the condition required by the law, and the mode of obtaining life according to the Law. For because that young man still savored nothing but the law, Christ refers him to the law: so that He might lead him to the acknowledgment of himself, since he himself or anyone else cannot fully keep the law, so that by that observance which the law requires, he might be able to enter into eternal life: so that he might consequently understand that there must be another method of salvation, or that the entrance to eternal life lies open to no man. Therefore, it must not be conceded to Grotius that εἰσέρχεσθαι here signifies not the attainment of eternal life itself, but the path directed toward it: and if indeed εἰσέρχεσθαι διὰ πύλης in Matt. VII. 13 is the same as εἰσελθεῖν εἰς τὴν ζωὴν, it is manifest that it distinguishes the path directed to life from the life itself, which we desire to enter, just as there the way, which must be insisted upon, is distinguished from the gate, into which one must enter. And who does not see how alien and false that interpretation of Christ's answer τήρησον τὰς ἐντολάς is: He called the precepts of Moses ἐντολάς after the manner of the Hebrews, namely the law of works, not the law of the spirit: See Luke I. 6 and several times in Paul. But in these Christ places not the whole way, but the beginning of the way! For since Grotius understands by the law of works, as he himself explains later, the HEBREW CIVIL law, that interpretation does not at all suit the usage of Scripture, especially of the New Testament: In Proverbs VII. 1, 2 (which passage he alleges), as also in Luke I. 6, it is sufficiently manifest that it is not a question of the civil or forensic law of the Hebrews, nor does the Apostle, when opposing the law of works to the law of the spirit, designate by it the law forensic, but rather the moral law in ἀντιθέσει to the Gospel, which it calls the law or doctrine of the spirit; then, even if the civil law were designated by τὰς ἐντολὰς elsewhere in the New Testament, here certainly that meaning has no place: because Christ explains immediately in v. 18, the precepts of the Decalogue regarding the second table understands: namely, not of the forensic law, nor of the ceremonial, but of the moral law. Add that the civil law was given to the Hebrews not for eternal life, but for civil life and the political state: and therefore its mention here would be ἀπροσδιόνυσος; which perhaps also occurred to no one besides Grotius in this place: whose own inventions these also are, that that commandment ἀγαπήσεις τὸν πλησίον σου ὡς σεαυτὸν has a double sense, the one general, which shows that true and sincere love of men among themselves is most acceptable to God, in which respect this precept is called by Paul the fullness of the law, and by Christ the greatest, distinct from that which is about worshipping God: the other indeed stricter, insofar as that precept, as he speaks, formed a part of the law of works, that is, of the Hebrew civil law; which latter sense seems to him to fit this place better, because (the young man) had asked about works. But where in the Scriptures is that double sense of this precept, where the stricter one, about which τὸ κρινόμενον is, that explanation founded? From the word ποιήσω which is general, and embraces works no less than the moral law, than what the forensic law requires, it is rashly carved out: but as for the collation of Mark, that sense certainly seems open to Grotius from the same, since by the word μὴ ἀποστερήσῃς he embraces all other ἀδικήματα which do not properly come under the name of adultery, murder, theft, false witness; But what, I ask, are such actual ἀδικήματα designated against the second table, which do not come under those names, nor are an ἀτιμία against parents (which Mark also peculiarly excludes), which might be indicated by τὸ ἀποστερεῖν? Grotius thinks that Mark expressed with this one word what is read in Leviticus ch. XIX with many words: οὐ συκοφαντήσεις ἕκαστοι τὸν πλησίον οὐκ ἀδικήσεις τὸν πλησίον, καὶ οὐχ᾽ ἁρπάσεις, οὐ πορεύσῃ δόλῳ ἐν τῷ ἔθνει σου. Just as the Romans embrace all offenses which do not have a proper name under the name of stellionatus or fraud: and he says the Hebrew עשק which the Greeks translate as ἀποστερεῖν in Lev. VI. 2 and elsewhere, extends just as widely; that ינה is placed in the same sense in Lev. XXV. 14, 17, which the Greeks translate as θλίβειν. These we do not examine but leave in their own place. The Vulgate rendered it in this place, do not commit fraud; but Beza notes that τὸ ἀποστερεῖν extends more broadly, and signifies to deprive someone of their property, whether you retain it, or take it away by fraud or force: and therefore he rendered it with a general word, do not inflict damage: and it seems to him that this commandment embraces all the former in a certain summary: and he observes that in one manuscript it is missing, and perhaps is redundant; which, however, because of the consensus of other codices and interpreters, is not to be said. Evang. cap. CXXXI. he advises that this clause is either an appendix to the seventh commandment, concerning theft; or placed in the stead of the ninth and tenth, concerning evil concupiscence, which is taught to be restrained by these words: And therefore it is not necessary that these words should be equivalent to those, you shall love your neighbor as yourself, much less does it follow, because Mark omitted these and set down those, that he understands the same law concerning the love of one's neighbor in a special sense, namely, insofar as the civil law requires it: or insofar as it commands τὸ καθῆκον, not insofar as it points out τὸ κατόρθωμα.

Furthermore, it is assumed only precariously that this was the righteousness of the Scribes and Pharisees: who wanted to obtain eternal life not through the observance of the civil law, but through the observance of the moral law: nor does the Apostle, when in Gal. III. 24 he calls the law a tutor to Christ, understand the civil law; and while Christ, as Grotius admits, answering the questioner, says that those are the most important commandments which consist in mutual duties, not in rites, he does not restrict mutual duties only to those which are necessary in civil life, but as his very words have it αὐτολεξεὶ, those which are required for that love of the neighbor, that we love him as ourselves: which in this imperfection, which the fall of our first parents brought about, it is certain is done by no one. Whence the Papists rashly use, or rather abuse these, when they argue from the present place even for the powers of free will in spiritual matters with Bellarmine l. V. de grat. & liber. arbitr. cap. XIX. because if it is not in our power to perform this condition, this would be a manifest mockery, if you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments, or also they conclude with the same l. IV. de Justific. cap. 2. that Evangelical promises are conditional, and further with Coster in Enchir. Controv. p. 84. that no one can be certain of his own salvation, for the reason that Evangelical promises also have a condition attached: because Christ does not wish here to teach the faculty of our powers, but rather our impotence from the law, seeing the presumption of this young man, and the Pharisaical pride, as if he had performed all these things perfectly; nor is it mockery when the law demands perfect obedience, because God had granted man the powers to perform it, which when man lost by his own fault, God is not bound to remit his right because of man's fault; nor does the law, which is a mirror of divine justice and a norm of our due obedience, remit anything, but rigorously demands all things, not to mock us, but to conclude us all under sin, that God may have mercy on us Rom. XI. 32. and in that way it is not a mockery of us, but a humiliation, that having been led to the acknowledgment of our ἀδυναμία it may be a tutor to Christ. This promise is therefore not Evangelical, but legal, distinguished from Evangelical promises in that the latter (Evangelical) requires only faith in Christ, in whom we have the remission of sins and righteousness, because he has been made righteousness for us by God; but the former (legal) involves the condition of obedience to the precepts of the Decalogue: therefore the Apostle teaches that it pertains to the certainty of grace and the promise of life, and is required, that such a condition not be involved in the Gospel, Rom. IV. 16. Grotius himself indeed acknowledges that the powers of free will are not asserted here, but rather that we are recalled to the fountain of grace, arguing against the Papists, whom he wonders that the writers of that first and most holy antiquity everywhere traduce, as if by them τὸ ἀυτεξύσιον were extolled to the injury of divine grace, (unless perhaps he is to be considered as wondering rather at the Calvinists here) such as Justin Martyr, Clement of Alexandria, V. strom. Origen against Celsus, book VI. Chrysostom, homily XLIV. and following on John, and taking the words of Christ present there: When he here calls Christ one only good, namely God, and indicates (these are the words of Grotius) that God is τὸ ἀυτὸ ἀγαθὸν: the fountain of true good, ἀφ' ὗ πᾶσα δόσις ἀγαθὴ, as James speaks; surely so that the young man, not a stranger to the pursuit of virtue, but trusting more than was right in his own powers, might understand by that very fact that that good ought not only to be learned by questioning, but also to be sought by prayers. With this sense prevailing, the Arians or Photinians can extract nothing from the words of Christ against the Deity of Christ; which words, moreover, are not directed toward excluding the Son of God from that most perfect and original goodness which is proper to the one God, since the Son and the Father are one (John 10:30), but toward excluding others who are outside the fellowship of the divine essence, as when he said 'good' to the youth, whom he believed to be a mere man, he was teaching that this title belongs to God alone, not to ψιλῷ ἀνθρώπῳ (a mere man), by which he denotes τὸ ἀυτοαγαθὸν (the self-good). Concerning which, see our Anti-Crellius in Theolog. natur. & revel. page 1120. Chrysostom has it thus concerning him in this place: 'This master of the Jews, because he believed Christ to be a pure man, and addressing him as such had called him a good master, deservedly heard from him: "No one is good in comparison with God"; wherefore he also adds, "except one God." Therefore, he says, if you call me good, considering me one of the common masters, you speak wrongly; for since perfect goodness implies a constant state of immutable virtue, there is no man who is not easily changeable: but if you acknowledge me as God, and address me as such, you speak most correctly. Similarly, Nazianzen says that 'no one is good' refers to the youth, as if he were ascribing goodness to Christ as a man: 'For the supreme goodness,' he says, 'is of God alone, even if men are also called so, to whom the influx of the first good arrives according to a second manner (of speaking).'
