Basil, however, notes that not only was the regard of the questioner taken into account here: 'Indeed, since the question was not directed to God the Word, it was fitting that the answer be given in the name of human nature to the petitioner: but it was also demonstrated in this way that the human race, established in malice through sin, is properly deprived of the title of good, ὄτι τὸ ἀνθρώπινον ἐν πονηρίᾳ διὰ τὴν ἁμαρτίαν γεννό- μενον ἀποκέκριται τῆς κυρίως τῷ ἀγαθῷ κλή- σεως (because the human [race], born in wickedness through sin, has been separated from the calling that is properly of the good).'

But the fact that Grotius thinks the name of GOD is foreign to the original text here, yet rightly added by the Syrian for the sake of interpretation, is refuted by a collation of other codices, and of many of them, as also by the Syriac version itself, in which that name is not added, but translated from the source. For the rest, we do not deny that 'one', even without another addition, was accustomed to be called GOD by the Hebrews: as also by the Assyrians; concerning which Macrobius says: 'For to the God whom they venerate as the highest and greatest, they gave the name Adad: the interpretation of which name signifies one.' And Philo Byblius: Ἀδωδὸς βασιλεὺς Θεῶν (Adad, king of the gods). Indeed, the Assyrians said חד, for which the Hebrews said אחד. Thus that passage in Job 14:14, לא אחד, the Chaldean interprets as 'except God.' Which things are not poorly observed here by Grotius.

Latin:

V. 19. ἀγαπήσεις τὸν πλησίον συ ὡς σεαυτὸν] Cum mandatum hoc duplicem habeat sensum, alterum generalem, qui monstrat acceptissimam esse Deo veram & sinceram homi- num inter se dilectionem, quo respectu præceptum hoc Paulo dicitur legis plenitudo, & Christo præceptum ma- ximum ab eo quod est de Deo colendo : alterum vero stri- ctiorem, quatenus præceptum illud partem efficiebat le- gis factorum, id est, ut alibi exposuimus, legis Hebrai- cæ civilis, posterior sensus huic loco magis convenire vide- tur, quia de factis interrogaverat juvenis : τί ἀγαθὸν ποιήσω; Quod apertum ni fallor, facit Marcus, qui istis verbis o- missis ponit μὴ ἀποστερήσῃς, quo verbo omnia alia ἀδικήμα- τα complectitur, quæ proprie non veniunt μοιχείας, φόνε, κλοπῆς, ψευδομαρτυρίας. Ita ἀδικεῖν ἤ ἀποστερεῖν junxit Pau- lus I. Cor. VI. 8. & apud Aristophanem Pluto post interro- gationem μῶν ἧ κέκλοφας; sequitur altera, ἀλλ’ ἐδὶ μέν γ’ ἀπεστέρηκας γ’ οὐδένα. Bene autem Marcus una voce ex- pressit quod in Levitico XIX. multis vocibus legitur ὀ συκο- φαντήσῃ ἕκαστος τὸν πλησίον· οὐκ ἀδικήσεις τὸν πλησίον, καὶ οὐχ ἁρπάσεις, ὧ πορεύσῃ δόλῳ ἐν τῷ ἔθνει σε. Ita Romani cœli- cta omnia quæ proprium non habent nomen, stellionatus aut doli mali nomine complectebantur. Æque late pa- tet Hebræum עשק quod Levit. VI. 2. & alibi per ἀποστερεῖν vertunt Græci, optime illam vocis Hebrææ generalitatem explicante Davide Kimchi libro radicum ad locum Levit. XIX. 13. Eodem sensu יונה ponitur Levit. XXV. 14. 17. quod ὄλιβειν vertunt Græci. Spectat igitur hoc loco Chri- stus hanc legem quatenus imperat τὸ καθῆκον, non quate- nus monstrat τὸ κατόρθωμα.

Recte notat Grotius non fuisse νομικὸν illum Lucæ X. 25. quia hæc historia diversa est, Lucæ XVIII. 42. memorata: ubi hic ἄρχων vocatur : quo nomine intelligit Senatorem oppidi sui, deque eo ἀρχόντων genere verba Johan. XII. 42. etiam ac- cipit forte non inconcinne. Discendi cupidum, non ut νομικὸν illum, calumniandi animo, venis- se certum est è Marco, & Luca: Quod autem ζωὴν αἰώνιον Judæis tenuiter cognitam, quam Chri- stus aperte prædicarit, Grotius dicit, Pelagianum Socinianismi errorem resipit: quam sæpius jam retudimus. In Veteri enim Testamento non tantum bona corporalia, sed vitæ etiam æternæ promissa. Ideo ad Vet. Testam. etiam juvenis iste revoca- tur, ut quod Moses requirat, si quis per opera æ- ternam vitam consequendi velit, inde informatus legis adimplendæ ἀδυναμίαν agnoscat. Nec feren- da est audacia quod textum v. 17. sic habentem : τί με λέγεις ἀγαθὸν; οὐδεὶς ἀγαθὸς, εἰ μὴ εἷς, ὁ Θεὸς audacter ita immutet, τί με ἐρωτᾶς περὶ τοῦ ἀ- γαθοῦ, εἷς ἐστιν ἀγαθός. Nam quod vetustiorem & e- mendatiora exemplaria hanc lectionem ait præferre, non probavit: duo tantum Stephano notata sunt, tria Bezæ, quæ sic legant. At reliqua omnia con- stanter vulgatam & communem lectionem reti- nent. Quamvis vero etiam Latinus vulgatus, quem Augustinus sequutus est, ita habeat, è ver- sione tamen emendare fontem non licet; neque apparet, cur suspicari debeamus, ex Marco & Luca lectionem nostram huc traductam esse, imo quia Marcus & Lucas nostræ consonant lectioni, hanc veriorem censendam esse, ob harmoniam Evan- gelistarum colligere potius licet; nam & Syrus ita hic habet, ut in Marco est, & Luca, & Græci In- terpretes sic legerunt: ideo Nyssenus in Catena in Matthæum: Propterea ait; quid me dicis bonum?

dicendo ME humanam naturam de se subindicat, qui & Eunomianos hic refellit, quod audientes Dominum dicere οὐδεὶς ἀγαθὸς εἰ μὴ εἷς ὁ Θεὸς, so- li Patri ajunt convenire bonitatem, at Filium ab hac excludunt: quæ difficultas etiam à Basilio hic in Matthæi XIX. movetur, & à Nazianzeno, ut &c. Chrysostomo; quorum ceu Græcorum Patrum le- ctio magis hic attendenda, utpote qui ne dubita- runt quidem de veritate nostræ lectionis. Quod vero apud Origenem utriusque lectionis mentio fit, ipsi etiam Grotio suspectum est, ibi aliquid affutum esse. Neque conveniens foret illa συνέ- χεια, vel objectio, cur me interrogas περὶ τοῦ ἀγα- θοῦ, quia Christum ἐπὶ τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ interrogare po- terat probe, etsi unus tantum sit bonus: at fore Christum bonum, quem non credebat Deum, si unus tantum Deus bonus est, non poterat. Adde quod relationem hæc habeant ad προσφώνησιν ju- venis, qua Christum compellavit, Magister bo- ne: non vero ad objectum quæstionis; quod etiam non περὶ τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ erat, sed περὶ τῆς ζωῆς αἰωνίου. Neque vero admittenda Glossa illa Grotii, quod Juvenis iste, quamvis in JESU majus homine nihil agnoverit, speravit tamen eo monstrante se perven- turum ad possessionem ejus boni, quo vita æterna paratur, quasi ad eam rem monstratore tantum e- guerit, cætera per se confecturus. Non enim de consecutione ejus boni, quo æterna paratur vi- ta, sed de ratione consequendi æternam vitam cum quæsivisse, cum verba ipsa docent quærentis τί ἀγαθὸν ποιήσω, ἵνα ἔχω ζωὴν αἰώνιον; informa- tus enim erat in Scholis Pharisæicis, adeoque cre- debat ποιήσεΐ sua, vel operibus propriis se consequi posse, ac debere vitam æternam, nec aliud discere volebat, quam quodnam illud bonum esset, quod faciendo ad vitam æternam aspirare ipse queat, non quomodo ad illius boni quo paratur vita, possessio- nem pervenire queat: tum responsum etiam Christi confirmat: Si vis ingredi vitam, serva mandata: quod non sonabat de consecutione boni ad vi- tam æternam necessarii, sed de conditione à lege requisita, & modo adipiscendi vitam secundum Legem. Quia enim non nisi legem sapiebat adhuc ille juvenis, Christus ad legem eum remittit: ut ad agnitionem sui perducat, quum non possit ipse vel quisquam alius legem plene servare, ut pen eam, quam lex requirit, observantiam, vitam æ- ternam ingredi queat: ut ita consequenter intel- ligat, aliam oportere esse salutis rationem, aut nul- li hominum ingressum patere ad vitam æternam. Non ergo concedendum Grotio, quod εἰσέρχε- σθαι hic non ipsam vitæ æternæ consequutionem, sed iter eo directum significet: & siquidem est εἰσέρχ χεσθαι διὰ πύλης Matth. VII. 13. quod εἰσελθεῖν εἰς τὴν ζωὴν, manifestum est, distinguit iter directum ad vitam ab ipsa vita, quam introire optamus, quemadmodum ibi via, Dei insistendum, à porta distinguitur, in quam ingrediendum. Et quis non videt, quam aliena, & falsa sit ista interpre- tatio responsi Christi τήρησον τὰς ἐντολάς: ἐντο- λὰς vocavit more Hebræorum præcepta Mosis, legem factorum scilicet non legem spiritus: Vid. Luc. I. 6. & apud Paulum aliquoties. In his autem ponit Christus non viam totam, sed initium viæ! Nam quum per legem factorum intelligat Grotius, uti postea ipse explicat, legem Hebraicam CIVI- LEM, interpretatio ea scripturæ, imprimis Nov. Testam. usui haud convenit: Proverbiorum certe VII. 1. 2. (quem locum allegat) ut & Luc. I. 6. sa- tis manifestum est, non agi de lege civili vel forensi Ebræorum, nec Apostolus legem factorum opponens legi spiritûs per illam designat legem forensem, sed potius legem moralem in ἀντιθέσει ad Evangelium, quod legem vel doctrinam spiritus vocat; tum si maxime alias per τὰς ἐντολὰς lex civilis in Nov. Testam. designetur, hic sane ea significatio locum non habet: quia explicat statim v. 18. Christus, præcepta Decalogi, quoad secundam tabulam, ejusdemque summam recensens, quænam præcepta intelligat: nimirum non legis forensis, neque ceremonialis, sed legis moralis. Adde quod lex civilis non ob vitam æternam, sed ob civilem vitam & statum Politicum Ebræis data fit: ideoque ejus commemoratio hic ἀπροσδιόνυσος sit: quæ etiam fortassis nemini præter Grotium hoc in loco in mentem venit: cujus propria quoque sunt hæc commenta, quod illud mandatum ἀγαπήσεις τὸν πλησίον σου ὡς σεαυτὸν duplicem habeat sensum, alterum generalem, qui monstrat acceptissimam esse Deo veram atque sinceram hominum inter se dilectionem, quo respectu præceptum hoc Paulo dicitur legis plenitudo, & Christo maximum, ab eo, quod est de Deo colendo: alterum vero strictiorem, quatenus præceptum illud, ut loquitur, partem efficiebat legis factorum, id est, legis Hebraicæ civilis; quem posteriorem sensum huic loco magis convenire ipsi videtur, quia de factis (juvenis) interrogaverat. At ubi in Sacris geminus ille hujus præcepti sensus, ubi strictior, de quo τὸ κρινόμενον est, explicatio illa fundatur? è verbo ποιήσω quod generale est, nec minus opera complectitur, quæ lex moralis, quam quæ lex forensis requirit, temere ea exsculpitur: quod vero ad collationem Marci, sane ex eadem sensus ille apertus videtur Grotio, quandoquidem verbo μὴ ἀποστερήσῃς omnia alia ἀδικήματα complectatur, quæ proprie non veniunt nomine μοιχείας, φόνου, κλοπῆς, ψευδομαρτυρίας; At quænam obsecro, sunt talia ἀδικήματα actualia adversus secundam tabulam designata, quæ illis nominibus non veniant, nec ἀτιμία sint adversus parentes (quam etiam peculiariter excludit Marcus,) quæ per τὸ ἀποστερεῖν indigitentur? Grotius hac una voce expressisse Marcum putat, quod in Levitico v. XIX. multis vocibus legitur: οὐ συκοφαντήσεις ἕκαστοι τὸν πλησίον οὐκ ἀδικήσεις τὸν πλησίον, καὶ οὐχ᾽ ἁρπάσεις, οὐ πορεύσῃ δόλῳ ἐν τῷ ἔθνει σου. Quemadmodum Romani omnia delicta, quæ proprium non habent nomen, stellionatus aut doli mali nomine complectuntur: & æque late patere, ait Hebræum עשק quod Lev. VI. 2. & alibi per ἀποστερεῖν vertunt Græci; eodem sensu ינה poni Lev. XXV. 14. 17. quod θλίβειν vertunt Græci. Quæ non excutimus sed suo relinquimus loco. Vulgatus reddidit hoc loco, ne fraudem feceris; Beza vero latius patere τὸ ἀποστερεῖν notat, & significare, quempiam re sua privare, sive eam retineas, sive fraude aut vi eripias: ideoque reddidit generali voce, ne damno afficito: videturque ipsi hoc mandatum compendio quodam omnia superiora complecti: & observat, in uno manuscripto id deesse, ac fortassis redundare; quod tamen ob aliorum Codicum & interpp. consensum dicendum non est B. Lyserus Harm. Evang. cap. CXXXI. hanc particulam monet vel appendicem esse septimi præcepti, de furto; vel appositam loco noni & decimi, de prava concupiscentia, quæ his verbis reprimenda doceatur: Ideoque necessum non est, ut verba hæc æquipolleant illis, diliges proximum tuum, sicut teipsum, nedum consequens est, quia his omissis illa posuit Marcus, eundem legem de dilectione proximi sensu speciali intelligere, quantum nempe lex civilis eam requirit: aut quatenus ea imperat τὸ καθῆκον, non quatenus monstrat τὸ κατόρθωμα.

Porro non nisi precario assumitur, hanc fuisse justitiam Legisperitorum & Pharisæorum: qui per non observantiam legis civilis vitam æternam con- sequi volebant, sed per observantiam legis moralis: neque Apostolus cum Galat. III. 24. le- gem pædagogum dicit ad Christum, legem civilem intelligit; & dum Christus, fatente Grotio, ad interrogatum respondens ea potissima esse dicit man- data, quæ in officiis mutuis, non quæ in ritibus con- sisterent, officia mutua non tantum ad ea restringit, quibus in vita civili opus est, sed quemadmodum ipsa ejus verba αὐτολεξεὶ habent, quæ requirun- tur ad eam proximi charitatem, ut ipsum diliga- mus, sicut nosmetipsos: quod in hac imperfectio- ne, quam lapsus conciliavit primorum paren- tum, à nemine fieri certum est. Unde temere his utuntur, vel abutuntur potius Papistæ, cum è præsenti loco vel pro viribus liberi arbitrii pu- gnant in spiritualibus cum Bellarmino l. V. de grat. & liber. arbitr. cap. XIX. quia si non sit in potestate nostra hanc conditionem præstare, manifesta hæc sit irrisio, si vis ad vitam ingredi, serva mandata, vel etiam colligunt cum Eodem l. IV. de Justific. cap. 2. promissiones Evangelicas esse conditionatas, & porro cum Costero in Enchir. Controv. p. 84. neminem de sua salute posse certum esse, eo quod pro- missiones quoque Evangelicæ adjectam habeant con- ditionem: quia non hic virium nostrarum facul- tatem, sed impotentiam potius è lege docere vult Christus, videns juvenis hujus præsumtionem, & fastum Pharisaicum, quasi hæc omnia ex asse præ- stiterit; neque irrisio est, cum lex postulat obe- dientiam perfectam, quia Deus vires homini ad eam præstandam concesserat, quas ubi culpa sua deperdidit homo, non tenetur Deus ob homi- nis culpam de jure suo remittere; neque lex, quæ speculum est justitiæ divinæ, & norma debi- tæ nostræ obedientiæ, aliquid remittit, sed o- mnia rigorose exigit, non ut illudat nobis, sed ut nos sub peccato concludat universos, ut Deus nostri misereatur Rom. XI. 32. eoque pacto est non irrisio nostri, sed humiliatio, ut ad agnitionem no- stræ ἀδυναμίας perductis pædagogus sit ad Chri- stum. Nec ergo Evangelica hæc est promissio, sed legalis, eo distincta ab Evangelicis promissio- nibus, quod hæc (Evangelica) fidem in Christum, in quo habemus remissionem peccatorum & ju- stitiam, quia factus à Deo nobis est justitia, tan- tum requirat; illa vero (legalis) conditionem obedientiæ præceptorum Decalogi involvat: ideo ad certitudinem gratiæ, & promissionis vitæ id pertinere, ac requiri docet Apostolus, ut non involvatur in Evangelio talis conditio Rom. IV. 16. Agnoscit sane Grotius ipse, hic non adstrui vi- res liberi arbitrii, sed ad fontem gratiæ potius nos revocari, adducens contra Pontificios, quos mi- ratur prima illius atque sanctissimæ vetustatis scri- ptores Christianos passim traducere, quasi ab illis τὸ ἀυτεξύσιον extollatur in divinæ gratiæ injuriam, (nisi forte Calvinianos potius hic mirari censendus sit) utpote Justinum Martyrem, Clementem Ale- xandr. V. strom. Origenem advers. Cels. l. VI. Chrysostomum hom. XLIV. & seqq. ad Johann. eoque verba Christi præsentia accipiens: Cum hic dicit Christum, unum tantum esse bonum nem- pe Deum, & indicat (verba Grotii sunt) Deum esse τὸ ἀυτὸ ἀγαθὸν: fontem veri boni, ἀφ' ὗ πᾶ- σα δόσις ἀγαθὴ, ut loquitur Jacobus; nimirum ut juvenis non alienus à virtutis studio, sed viribus suis plus æquo confidens eo ipso intelligeret bonum illud non interrogando tantum disci, sed & precibus po- sci debere. Quo sensu obtinente nihil Ariani aut Photinia- ni è verbis Christi adversus Deitatem Christi erue- re possunt: quæ etiam cæteroquin non ad exclu- dendum Filium Dei à Deitate, vel bonitate illa perfectissima, & originaria, quæ unius Dei propria est, directa sunt, quum Filius & Pater unum sint Johan. X. 30. sed ad excludendum alios, qui extra divinæ essentiæ consortium sunt, ut quum bonum diceret juvenis, quem hominem merum credebat, disceret, soli Deo hoc elogium conve- nire, non ψιλῷ ἀνθρώπῳ, qua τὸ ἀυτοαγαθὸν notat. Quo de videatur Anti-Crellius noster in Theolog. natur. & revel. pag. 1120. Chrysostomus ita habet de eo h. l. Magister hic Judæorum, quod purum hominem Christum crederet, & ipsum ut ta- lem alloquens Magistrum bonum ipsum appellasset, merito audivit ab eo: bonus nemo est in compara- tione Dei: quare & subdit, nisi unus Deus. Itaque sime, inquit, unum ex vulgaribus Magistris repu- tans bonum vocas, male loqueris; cum enim bonitas perfecta statum sonet constantem immutabilis virtu- tis, nullus non hominum facile mutabilis est: sin me autem ut Deum agnoscis, & ut talem sic alloqueris, rectissime dicis. Similiter Nazianzenus, illud nemo bonus refertur ad adolescentem, tanquam homini Christo bonitatem adscribentem: Summa enim bo- nitas, inquit, Solius Dei, etsi ita etiam homines vocentur ad quos influxus primi boni juxta secundam (dicendi) rationem pervenit. Basilius vero notat non tantum respectum hic habitum interrogan- tis: Sane cum non ad Deum Verbum interrogatio directa esset, par fuit humanæ naturæ nomine re- sponderi supplicanti: sed etiam ita demonstratum esse, humanum genus per peccatum in malitia con- stitutum proprie boni appellatione privari, ὄτι τὸ ἀνθρώπινον ἐν πονηρίᾳ διὰ τὴν ἁμαρτίαν γεννό- μενον ἀποκέκριται τῆς κυρίως τῷ ἀγαθῷ κλή- σεως.

Quod autem Grotius putat, nomen DEI hic alienum esse à textu originali, recte tamen à Sy- ro interpretationis gratia addi: è collatione alio- rum Codicum, eorumque plurium refellitur, ut & ex ipsa Syriaca versione, in qua non adjectum illud nomen est, sed è fonte translatum. De cætero non negamus, unum, etiam sine alio adjectamen- to, DEUM Ebræis dici consuevisse: ut & Assy- riis: de quo Macrobius: Deo enim, quem summum maximum venerantur, Adad nomen dederunt: cu- jus nominis interpretatio significat unus. Et Philo Byblius, Ἀδωδὸς βασιλεὺς Θεῶν. Nimirum Assy- rii dicebant חד pro quo Hebræi אחד. Ita illud apud Jobum XIV. 14. לא אחד Chaldæus interpre- tatur, nisi Deus. Quæ non male hic observata Grotio.

## 19:20
Verse 20. Πάντα ταῦτα ἐφυλαξάμην (All these things I have kept). That he did not say this falsely, as far as external and civil justice is concerned, we learn from Mark, in whose account Christ is narrated, after this profession, as having followed the youth with a certain peculiar favor, because it was true. Indeed, it is something to live socially. What follows, ἐκ νεότητός μυ (that is, from the time the use of reason began in me), is indeed read here and in the Syriac now; but the ancient Latin books did not have it: whence it is permissible to suspect it was added from Mark or Luke.

The youth boasted altogether falsely that he had observed the law: for neither was the discourse of Christ only about civil and external justice, nor does the law concerning the love of neighbor demand only that: and since he boasts that he had performed all these things from his youth, or from the time the use of reason began, he could not boast that from the truth even regarding civil and external justice: for shall we believe that he always showed the honor due to his parents, so that he never lacked even exterior reverence toward them? But Christ loved him because he desired to be further informed what still needed to be done, not as if he had performed those things which the law requires, just as he himself boasted. For Origen, Clement of Alexandria, Basil, Chrysostom, Theophylact, and among the Latins, Hilary, Jerome, Augustine, Ambrose, and Bede acknowledge that he lied. Nor is it right to amend the Greek text from Latin codices, even if they are ancient, since it is not likely that divine providence watched over the versions in the same way as over the original text, which it willed to be the perpetual Canon, not of this or that particular church, but of the whole Oecumenical Church: and why should we suspect that 'from his youth' was added from Mark and Luke, where there is no cause for suspicion in the Greek codices or even in the interpreters, and the Syriac version and others also agree with them? Moreover, Grotius also acknowledged that the Papists wrongly deduce their erroneous hypothesis from this passage, as if a man could fulfill the law, since he did not take these words as referring to the perfect fulfillment of the law, but only to civil and external justice; but neither did Christ approve this boast; rather, he taught by one example how much was still lacking to this youth regarding the perfect love of neighbor, as one who would rather have the poor and needy lack and perish than, at Christ's command, sell his own possessions for their sake, and expect treasures in heaven with the providence of divine sustenance, while Christ, who made him more certain of these things, was present. This certainly is not to love one's neighbor as ourselves: much less to love God above all things, from which love of God the true and sincere love of neighbor finally redounds. Whence Basil: 'The youth seemed to boast rashly by saying, "All these I have kept from my youth," for if he had loved his neighbor as himself, he would certainly not have had so many goods: for he who loves does not spare his money.' Who also rebukes this youth thus: 'You call him Master, and you do not do what belongs to a disciple: you confess him good, and you do not admit what is given. Certainly, if he is good, he is also altogether the giver of good things: and you ask indeed about eternal life, but you prove yourself bound by the enjoyment of the present life, and these things are by no means difficult, or heavy, or troublesome, as the word of the Master proposes.' These things are Basil's. Chrysostom, however, accuses him also of avarice, and not undeservedly: 'I, for my part, would not deny that he was avaricious and greedy for possession, since Christ also rebukes him as such.' And regarding those words, 'and you will have treasure in heaven,' he notes this: For since the discourse was about money, so that he might be stripped of all things, he exhorts him, showing that he is taking nothing away from his possessions, but adding to them, and that he will give more than he had ordered him to let go, and indeed not only greater things, but also things as much greater as heaven excels the earth, and besides that, more. Moreover, he called the treasure the excellence of the reward, τὸ δαψιλὲν τῆς ἀντιδόσεως, signifying stability and security, as far as he could insinuate it to the hearer in a human manner. Whence Thomas also in c. 2. q. 189. art. 1, with Jerome, and from the same: The young man lies; for if he had fulfilled in deed that which is set in the commandments, 'you shall love your neighbor as yourself,' how did he afterwards, hearing 'go, sell what you have,' go away sad. Maldonatus also acknowledges that the young man lied, praising not only Jerome, but also Hilary, the author of the imperfect work, Ambrose, Augustine, Bede, and the Greek interpreters for that opinion.

Τί ἔτι ὑστερῶ] What is lacking to me for persisting on the path of eternal life? For ὑστερῶ properly is nothing else to the Greeks than, 'this is lacking to me.' Therefore that young man believed that something more was required: but he was ignorant of what it was.

Latin:

Vers. 20. Πάντα ταῦτα ἐφυλαξάμην] Non falso hoc eum dixisse, quod ad exteriorem & civilem justitiam attinet, ex Marco discimus, apud quem Christus narratur post hanc professionem utpote veram, favore quodam peculia- ri juvenem prosecutus. Nimirum est aliquid vivere socia- liter. Quod sequitur ἐκ νεότητός μυ (id est, ex quo cœpit in me usus rationis) nunc quidem hic & apud Syrum legitur; sed antiqui libri Latini non habebant: unde suspicari li- cet ex Marco aut Luca adjectum.

Falso omnino se observasse legem jactavit juve- nis: nam nec de civili & exteriori tantum justitia sermo erat Christo, nec eam solam lex de dilectio- ne proximi postulat: & quum à juventute, vel ex quo rationis cœpit usus hæc omnia se præstitis- se glorietur, ne quidem quoad civilem, & exterio- rem justitiam id ex vero jactare poterat: num e- nim honorem semper parentibus debitum exhi- buisse credemus, ut nunquam etiam exteriori so- lum reverentia iis defuerit? Amavit autem Chri- stus eum, quod ulterius informari desiderârit, quid adhuc facto opus sit, non quasi ea præstite- rit, quæ lex requirit, quemadmodum ipse jacta- vit. Mentitum enim esse Origenes, Clem. Alex, Basil. Chrysost. Theophyl. & è Latinis Hilar. Hieron. Augustin. Ambros. & Beda agnoscunt. Neque fas est è Latinis Codicibus etsi antiquis Græcum textum emendare, quum ita vigilasse divinam providen- tiam pro versionibus, uti pro textu originario, quem Canonem perpetuum esse voluit, non hujus, aut illius particularis, sed totius Oecumenicæ Eccle- siæ, verisimile non sit: & cur suspicaremur ex Marco & Luca adjectum illud ἐκ νεότητος, ubi nulla in Græcis Codicibus, aut Interpp. etiam su- spicionis causa est, iisque Syriaca quoque versio & aliæ consonant? Cæterum perperam Pontificios ex hoc loco deducere hypothesin suam erroneam, quasi legem homo implere possit, etiam Grotius a- gnovit, cum non de perfecta legis impletione hæc accepit, sed de civili & exteriori tantum justitia; sed nec Christus approbavit hanc jactantiam, i- mo quantum ad perfectam proximi dilectionem huic juveni adhuc deesset, vel uno exemplo do- cuit, utpote, qui pauperes & egenos mallet de- ficere ac perire, quam Christi jussu sua ipsorum causa divendere, & thesauros in cælis, cum pro- videntia divinæ sustentationis, penes Christum, de iis certiorem ipsum reddentem, fiducialiter ex- spectare. Hoc certe non est diligere proximum sic- ut nos ipsos: nedum diligere Deum super omnia, è qua Dei dilectione demum verus & sincerus amor proximi redundat. Unde Basilius: Visus est juve- nis temere se jactare dicendo, omnia custodivi à ju- ventute mea, si enim dilexisset proximum suum sic- ut seipsum, utique non tot bona habuisset: qui enim amat, pecuniæ non parcit. Qui redarguit etiam ita hunc juvenem: Magistrum dicis, & quæ discipuli sunt, non facis: bonum confiteris, & quæ data non admittis. Certe si bonus est, bonorum omnino etiam largitor est: & interrogas quidem de vita æterna, fruitione autem vitæ præsentis te arguis astrictum, & hæc quidem nullo modo difficile quiddam, aut grave, aut molestum verbo Magistri proponente. Hæc Ba- silius. Chrysostomus vero avaritiæ eum etiam, nec immerito, accusat: Ego vero avarum & ha- bendi cupidum non negârim, cum Christus etiam talem arguat. Et ad verba illa, & habebis thesau- rum in cælis, hæc notat: Cum enim de pecuniis fo- ret sermo, ut omnibus denudetur, hortatur, osten- dens sese rebus illius nihil auferre, sed adjungere, ma- joramque quam dimittere jusserat, daturum, neque vero majora tantum, verum etiam tanto majora, quanto terram cælum antecellit, ac præterea plura. Thesaurum autem retributionis præstantiam τὸ δα- ψιλὲν τῆς ἀντιδόσεως appellavit, stabilitatem signi- ficans, & securitatem, prout humano more audienti poterat insinuare. Unde Thomas etiam c. 2. q. 189. artic. 1. cum Hieronymo, & ex eodem: Mentitur a- dolescens; si enim hoc quod positum est in mandatis, di- liges proximum tuum sicut teipsum, opere complevis- set, quomodo postea audiens, vade, vende quæ habes, tristis recessit. Mentitum etiam esse Adolescentem agnoscit Maldonatus, non Hieronymum tantum, sed Hilarium quoque autorem imperfecti operis, Ambrosium, Augustinum, Bedam & Græcos Inter- pretes in eam laudans sententiam.

Τί ἔτι ὑστερῶ] Quid mihi deest ad insistendum iter vi- tæ æternæ? Nam ὑστερῶ ἰδίως nihil aliud est Græcis quam, hoc mihi deest. Credidit igitur juvenis iste plus aliquid re- quiri: sed quid esset ignorabat.

## 19:21
Vers. 21. εἰ θέλεις τέλειος εἶναι] We showed above at the end of chapter V that any true Christian is called τέλειος. For indeed, this word, like many others, has different meanings according to the diversity of the comparison. Thus, whatever is in this life is rightly called ἀτελὲς if it is compared to that which we expect in the other life. And among Christians themselves, those who have progressed the most are called τέλειοι with respect to τῶν ἔλαττον προβεβηκότων. Aristotle in his Metaphysics says that every thing is τέλειον ὅταν κατὰ τὸ εἶδος τῆς οἰκείας ἀρετῆς μηδὲν ἐλλείπῃ. Thus we see this applies very well to what the young man had asked, what was lacking to him. In Mark, Christ answers, ἕν σοι ὑστερεῖ, that is: there is still something that you lack, and then he said what follows here. Luke: ἔτι ἕν σοι λείπει. From which it clearly appears that τέλειον is said here of him to whom nothing is lacking that is necessary for entering upon the path of eternal life: and the following discourse of Christ to the Apostles demonstrates this very thing.

Sell your possessions, and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me.] We have shown that this does not treat of the perfection by which Christians are compared among themselves. Nor does that perfection consist properly in the distribution of goods. Indeed, it can happen that someone distributes his goods and yet does not have the love which is necessary for a Christian, as Paul testifies in 1 Cor. 13:3, which Origen demonstrates here with the example of a certain Theban. But it is to be noted that it was Christ's custom, when those desiring to understand the way of salvation approached him, not to propose everything at once by way of aversion, but with the best counsel to demand of them that they follow him, that is, that they surrender themselves to his discipline, to progress little by little in the knowledge of piety. See above ch. 8:22, ch. 9:9. This, therefore, is what is also demanded of this young man by these words ἀκολύθει μοι, to which certain manuscripts of Mark add ἄρας τὸν σταυρὸν, so that the young man might understand that this following would not be without its inconveniences, which, however, were to be devoured with a brave spirit. That the word ἀκολυθεῖν is to be taken in this way is apparent from the words of Peter below, repeating that word in v. 27. All Christians ought to be prepared to lose their own things when God demands it, as in times of a troubled Church. Therefore, just as he tested others with things, so the Lord tests this one with words, whether he is prepared for this. He knew that the care of preserving and increasing his family estate would hinder this young man from surrendering himself in mind and body to the discipline of Christ: therefore he tests him to see if this impediment could be removed by him, by selling and distributing the things that were calling him away from the study of true wisdom: that is, either all that he possessed, or at least those things that were in excess of his own needs, in the way the word ὑπάρχοντα seems to be taken also below in Luke 12:33. It is told that Anacreon returned the five talents given to him by Polycrates, saying that they were not worth the worry they caused. Others are said to have thrown money into the sea, with the saying, 'Perish, lest you destroy me.' So important did it seem to them to remove the delays to right thinking. And for this purpose, it would have sufficed for him to unburden himself of his loads in any way. But Christ, so that what is good may be done as well as possible, urges that the goods be given to the poor at the same time: because by that method he would not only be preparing himself for discipline, but would be performing a work pleasing and acceptable to God, which we have seen called by the name of treasure at chapter 6. In the Gospel according to the Hebrews, as with certain other things, this passage also was interpolated in this manner: 'The other of the rich men said to him: Master, what good thing doing shall I live? He said to him: Man, do the law and the prophets. He answered him: I have done them. He said to him: Go, sell all that you possess and divide it among the poor, and come, follow me. But the rich man began to scratch his head, and it did not please him. And the Lord said to him: How do you say I have done the law and the prophets? Since it is written in the law, you shall love your neighbor as yourself: and behold, many of your brothers, sons of Abraham, are clothed in filth, dying of hunger, and your house is full of many goods, and nothing at all goes out of it to them.' And turning, he said to Simon his disciple sitting near him: Simon, son of Joanna, it is easier for a camel to enter through the eye of a needle than for a rich man into the kingdom of heaven. Doubtless, the Ebionite changed these things because he acknowledged Christ neither as the Son of God nor as a lawgiver, but as a mere interpreter of the law given through Moses. Just as, on the contrary, Marcion in Luke 10:25 deleted the word 'eternal,' lest he be forced to admit that the Jews had any knowledge of eternal life before the times of Christ: so,

While fools avoid vices, they run into the opposite ones.

How truth holds the middle ground between these things is to be seen at chapter 5. But if this young man had followed the counsel of Christ and surrendered himself to be formed by him, he would have learned from that master what the perfection of the law was; he would have learned at the same time not to depend on his own deeds, but on the mercy of God.

Latin:

Vers. 21. εἰ θέλεις τέλειος εἶναι] Ostendimus supra ad fi- nem cap. V. τέλειος dici quemvis vere Christianum. Nimi- tum vox ista ut aliæ multæ pro diversitate comparationis diversas habent fignificationes. Ita quicquid in hac vita est, recte dicitur ἀτελὲς si comparetur ad id quod in vita altera exspectamus. Et inter ipsos Christianos qui plurimum profecerunt τέλειοι dicuntur respectu τῶν ἔλαττον προβεβη- κότων. Aristoteles metaphysicis τέλειον esse dicit rem quam- que ὅταν κατὰ τὸ εἶδος τῆς οἰκείας ἀρετῆς μηδὲν ἐλλείπῃ. Ita vi- demus optime hoc consequi ad id quod juvenis interroga- verat quid sibi deesset. Apud Marcum Christus respon- det, ἕν σοι ὑστερεῖ, id est: est adhuc quod tibi desit, & dein- de id dixisse quod hic sequitur. Lucas: ἔτι ἕν σοι λείπει. Un- de liquido apparet τέλειον hic dici eum cui nihil desit quod ad insistendum vitæ æternæ iter sit necessarium: idque ipsum insequens Christi ad Apostolos sermo demonstrat.

Πώλησόν συ τὰ ὑπάρχοντα, κὶ δὸς πτωχοῖς. κὶ ἕξεις θη- σαυρὸν ἐν ὁρανῷ· κὶ δεῦρο, ἀκολύθει μοι.] De perfectione qua Christiani inter se comparantur, hic non agi ostendimus. Neque vero ea perfectio in bonorum dilargitione proprie consistit. Imo fieri potest ut quis bona sua dilargiatur & ta- men eam quæ Christiano necessaria est dilectionem non habeat, Paulo teste I. Cor. XIII. 3. quod hic Origenes The- bani cujusdam exemplo demonstrat. Sed notandum est, morem hunc Christo fuisse, ut viam salutis intelligere cu- pientibus, non omnia simul per aversionem proponeret, sed optimo consilio ab ipsis exigeret ut se sectarentur, id est ut se in disciplinam suam traderent, paulatim profecturi in cognitione pietatis. Vide supra c. VIII. 22. c. IX. 9. Hoc ergo est quod & ab isto juvene exigitur verbis istis ἀκολύθει μοι, quibus addunt Marci codices quidam ἄρας τὸν σταυρὸν, ut intelligeret juvenis istam sectationem non carituram suis incommodis quæ tamen forti animo essent devoranda. Sumendam hoc modo vocem ἀκολυθεῖν apparet ex verbis Petri infra eam vocem repetentis v. 27. Christiani omnes parati esse debent sua amittere, ubi Deus id exigit, ut in temporibus vexatæ Ecclesiæ. Ideo sicut alios rebus eratit, ita hunc verbis explorat Dominus, an in id paratus sit. Sciebat curam servandæ augendæque rei familiaris huic juveni obstituram, quominus animo ac corpore se in Christi disciplinam traderet: ideo eum tentat an hoc à se impedimentum removeri possit, divenditis elargitisque rebus quæ ipsum à veræ sapientiæ studio avocabant: id est, aut omnibus quæ possidebat, aut certe iis quæ usibus ipsius supererant, quomodo vox ὑπάρχοντα sumi videtur & infra Lucæ XII. 33. Narratur Anacreon talenta quinque à Polycrate sibi donata reddidisse εἰπὼν, ὧ τιμᾶσθαι ἀυτὰ τῆς ἐπ’ αὐτοῖς φροντίδος. Narrantur alii in mare pecuniam projecisse, cum dicto, pereas ne me perdas. Tanti illis videbatur amovere recte sapiendi moras. Et huic quidem sini suffecerit quovis modo se exonerare sarcinis. Sed Christus, ut quod bonum est quam optime fiat, suadet simul dari bona pauperibus: quia ea ratione non tantum se paraturus esset disciplinæ, sed opus editurus Deo gratum atque acceptum, quod θησαυρῦ nomine appellari vidimus ad caput VI. In Evangelio κατὰ ἑβραίυς, ut alia quædam ita hæc quoque περικοπὴ erat interpolata, hunc in modum, Dixit ad eum alter divitum: Magister quid bonum faciens viSam? Dixit ei: Homo, leges & Prophetas fac. Respondit ad eum, feci. Dixit ei: Vade vende omnia quæ possides & divide pauperibus, & veni sequere me. Cœpit autem dives scalpere caput suum, & non placuit ei. Et dixit ad eum Dominus: quomodo dicis legem feci & Prophetas? quum scriptum sit in lege, diliges proximum tuum sicut te ipsum: & ecce multi fratres tui filii Abrahæ amicti sunt stercore, morientes præ fame, & domus tua plena est bonis multis, & non egreditur omnino aliquid ex ea ad eos. Et conversus dixit Simoni discipulo suo sedenti apud se: Simon fili Ioanna, facilius est camelum intrare per foramen acus, quam divitem in regnum cœlorum. Nimirum hæc ideo mutavit Ebion, quia Christum nec Dei Filium nec νομοθέτην, sed nudum interpretem legis per Mosem datæ agnoscebat. Sicut contra Marcion apud Lucam X. 25. delevit vocem αἰώνιον, ne ullam Judæis vitæ æternæ cognitionem ante Christi tempora fuisse fateri cogeretur: ita,

Dum vitant stulti vitia in contraria currunt.

Quæ inter quomodo medium veritas teneat videre est ad caput V. Quod si juvenis iste Christi secutus consilium ipsi se formandum tradidisset, didicisset illo magistro quid esset τὸ τέλειον τῦ νόμε, didicisset simul non à factis suis sed à Dei misericordia pendere.

## 19:22
Verse 22. For he was having many possessions. Indeed. Care follows growing money.

It cannot be simply proven, as Grotius notes, that every true Christian is called perfect, as in ch. 5, last verse. For there it treats of the perfection of Christians, that is, those who have faith in Christ, working through love, to which they ought to strive; but here it treats of the perfection which the law demands if we wish to enter into life through the observance of its commandments. But that he thinks it appears clearly from the comparison of the words of Mark, 'one thing you lack,' and of Luke, 'still one thing you lack,' that 'perfect' is said here of him to whom nothing is lacking that is necessary for entering upon the path of eternal life, in that he is clearly mistaken. For the discourse is not about that perfection which is necessary for entering upon the path of eternal life, but which the law requires from those who wish to be justified by works for the sake of obtaining eternal life itself. For that rich young man still had first to be convinced by the law of the great imperfection of his love for his neighbor, so that, being convinced by those words, 'sell all that you have,' he might follow Christ all the more eagerly; for those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. Matt. IX. 12. Just as a physician, says our blessed Lyserus here, if he has a patient who does not recognize his illness due to phrensy, urges him to dance and run, so that, having recognized his infirmity, he may all the more easily accept the physician and the medicines; so Christ first proposes the law with its promises, so that, because the human mind flatters itself greatly regarding its own virtue out of a certain spiritual phrensy, it may experience in the very attempt that it cannot fulfill the law with perfect obedience, and thus learn that it has need of a Physician and of another righteousness for eternal life. Which very thing this young man experienced a little later. For as soon as Christ referred him, boasting of the external observation of the commandments, to the perfect love of a poor neighbor, he departed at once dismayed in his whole soul, he who was already thought to be about to ascend into heaven by ladders made of his own works. For the doctrine of the gratuitous righteousness of faith cannot have a place unless a man is first convinced that he cannot obtain salvation and eternal life by his own works from the law. And in this way the law is our schoolmaster unto Christ, Gal. III. 24, that He himself may be our righteousness. We add the confession of Johannes Ferus, a famous Papist, who likewise acknowledges that Christ is convincing this young man of not having observed the law, while he writes in this place: Just as a physician, if he perceives that he has applied the first medicine in vain, applies a stronger one: so Christ does here. The young man was sick, and indeed dangerously so: Christ had applied a medicine appropriate to his disease, namely, the remembrance of the commandments, which can easily remove presumption, but they were applied in vain in this young man; now therefore He applies a more effective one, who, though not in words, yet by his deed declared that he had not yet fulfilled the commandments. Whence it is clear that neither is perfect fulfillment of the law attributed to the young man, nor can it be proven from the present passage by the Papists, nor can these things be drawn, except very forcedly, to the counsels of Evangelical perfection; since Christ is convincing that young man of false boasting, and that he had lied, as we noted a little earlier with the Holy Fathers, Greek and Latin, Thomas, and Maldonatus, I add also Barradius, Stapleton, as also Guilb. Estius admit: to say nothing of the fact that a counsel of perfection, which the Papists invent, is, according to the interpretation of Bellarmine on Monks, ch. VII, a good work, not commanded by Christ, but demonstrated: not mandated, but commended: and that it is placed in the will of man, but does not bind by its own force: Which can be said neither of the selling and distribution of possessions, which Christ certainly commanded, even if this commandment was special here, to manifest the mind of the young man and to convince him of his imperfection: nor of the following of Christ, by which Bellarmine understands the imitation of Christ, which is certainly of commandment, not of counsel, and this obedience is necessarily due to God, of that which is treated here is owed, Bellarmine himself acknowledges, and thus he tries in vain to carve out counsels of perfection from this place, book on Monasticism, chapter IX. Chrysostom on this passage: It is not enough to despise money, but it is also necessary to feed the poor, and especially to follow Christ: that is, to do all things which have been commanded by him, and to be prepared for the same even unto death daily. Grotius explains this regarding the following of Christ thus: that he demanded that they should follow him, that is, that they should surrender themselves to his discipline; gradually to progress in the knowledge of piety, as in Matthew VIII. 22, chapter IX. 9, the words ἀκολύθοιμοι are accepted: since Peter, repeating those words, used the same in verse 27. Which sense also agrees more with the very words of the command, because he says, AND COME follow me, and not less in the following here, and in Mark chapter X. 22. But he, affected by trouble because of the saying, WENT AWAY sorrowing, he was not following Christ, ἀπῆλθε λυπέμενΘ. Grotius also rightly acknowledges against the Papists that the perfection by which Christians are compared among themselves is not treated here; nor does that perfection consist in the distribution of goods: indeed, it is possible that someone might distribute his goods and yet not have that love which is necessary for a Christian, as Paul testifies in 1 Corinthians XIII. 3. Furthermore, that by the name of treasure a work pleasing and acceptable to God is understood, which Grotius desires, is inappropriate, since it is not the work itself or its quality that is noted, but the reward of the work, which we have to expect in the heavens: as is clear from the response of Christ subsequently rendered to Peter.

Latin:

Vers. 22. ἦν γὰρ ἔχων κτήματα πολλά] Nimirum. Crescentem sequitur cura pecuniam.

Non simpliciter probari potest, quod annotat Grotius, τέλειον dici quemvis vere Christianum, ut c. V. v. ult. Nam illic de Christianorum, hoc est, qui fidem habent in Christum, δι ἀγάπης ἐνεργυμένην, perfectione, ad quam contendere debeant, agitur, hic vero de perfectione, quam lex postulat, si per observantiam mandatorum ejus vitam ingredi velimus. Quod autem è colla- tione verborum Marci ἓν σοὶ ὑςερεῖ, & Lucæ ἔτι ἓν σοὶ λείπει, apparere liquido, putat, τέλειον hic di- ci eum, cui nihil deest, quod ad insistendum vitæ æter- næ iter sit necessarium, in eo liquido fallitur. Non enim de ea perfectione sermo est, quæ ad insi- stendum iter vitæ æternæ necessaria sit, sed quam ad ipsam æternam vitam consequendam lex ab iis requirit, qui per opera justificari volunt. Nam pri- mum adhuc convincendus erat juvenis ille dives lege de magna amoris proximi imperfectione, ut convictus per illa, vende omnia quæ habes, Chri- stum eo avidius sequeretur; sani enim opus non habent Medico, sed ægroti. Matth. IX. 12. Quem- admodum Medicus, ait hic B. Lyserus noster, si ægrum habeat, qui ex phrenesi morbum suum non agnoscat, eum ad saltandum & currendum hortatur, ut agnita sua infirmitate Medicum & medicamenta tanto facilius admittat; ita Chri- stus legem cum suis promissionibus primum pro- ponit, ut quia humanus animus ex spirituali qua- dam phrenesi de sua virtute plurimum sibi blandi- tur, in ipso conatu experiatur, se legem perfe- cta obedientia implere non posse, & ita discat, o- pus sibi esse Medico, & alia justitia ad vitam æter- nam. Quod ipsum adolescens hic paulo post ex- pertus est. Quam primum enim Christus ipsum de externa observatione præceptorum glorian- tem ad perfectam proximi pauperis dilectionem remisit, mox toto animo consternatus discessit, qui jam scalis sua opera factis in cœlum conscen- surus putabatur. Neque enim potest doctrina de gratuita fidei justitia locum habere, nisi prius ho- mo sit convictus, quod operibus suis ex lege non possit salutem & vitam æternam consequi. Atq; hoc modo lex est pædagogus noster ad Christum Gal. III. 24. ut ipse sit nostra justitia. Addimus Johannis Fe- ri, celebris Papistæ, confessionem, qui agnoscit iti- dem, Christum hunc juvenem convincere de non observata lege, dum in h. l. ita scribit: Sicut Medicus si primam medicinam frustra se adhibuisse perspexe- rit, fortiorem apponit: sic Christus hic facit. Ægrota- bat adolescens, & quidem periculose: adhibuerat Chri- stus medicinam ei morbo congruentem, præceptorum scilicet memoriam, quæ facile præsumtionem tollere possunt, sed frustra in hoc juvene adhibita sunt; nunc igitur adhibet efficaciorem, qui convictus etsi non verbis, tamen opere declaravit se nec dum præcepta im- plesse. Unde liquet, nec perfectam legis impletio- nem juveni tribui, aut ex præsenti loco evinci à Pontificiis posse, nec hæc trahi, nisi perquam coa- cte, ad consilia perfectionis Evangelicæ; quum ju- venem illum Christus de falsa gloriatione convin- cat, eumque mentitum esse, cum S. Patribus, Græ- cis, & Latinis, quod paulo ante notavimus, Tho- mas, & Maldonatus, addo & Barradius, Stapleto- nus, ut & Guilb. Estius fateantur: ut taceamus, quod consilium perfectionis, quod comminiscuntur Pontificii, interprete Bellarmino de Monach. c. VII. opus bonum sit, à Christo non imperatum, sed de- monstratum: non mandatum, sed commendatum: quodque in hominis arbitrio positum sit, non autem vi sua obliget: Quod nec de venditione, ac distribu- tione facultatum, quam utiq; Christus præcepit, et- si hoc præceptum hic speciale fuerit, ad manifestan- dum animum adolescentis, eumque de imper- fectione sua convincendum: nec de sequela Chri- sti dici potest, per quam Bellarminus imitationem Christi intelligit, quæ utique præcepti est, non consilii, Deoque necessario hanc obedientiam, de qua hic agitur, deberi, agnoscit ipse Bellarminus, adesque nequicquam consilia perfectionis hinc exsculpere conatur l. de Monach. cap. IX. Chry- sost. in h. l. Non sufficit pecuniis despicere, verum etiam nutrire pauperes, & praesertim Christum se- qui oportet: id est, omnia, quae ab eo praecepta, fa- cere, ad eadem & mortem quotidie esse paratum. Grotius hoc de sequela Christi sic explicat, quod exegerit, ut se sectarentur, h. e. ut se in discipli- nam suam traderent; paulatim profecturi in cogni- tione pietatis, uti Matth. VIII. 22. c. IX. 9. verba ἀκολύθοιμοι accipiuntur: siquidem Petrus ita, verba illa repetens, eadem adhibuit v. 27. Qui sensus verbis etiam ipsis mandati magis con- gruit, quia ait, ET VENI sequere me, nec non sequentibus hic, & apud Marcum c. X. 22. At ille molestia affectibus propter sermonem DISCE- DEBAT moerens, non sequebatur Christum, ἀ- πῆλθε λυπέμενΘ. Recte etiam contra Pontifi- cios agnoscit Grotius, de perfectione, qua Christia- ni inter se comparantur, hic non agi; neque eam perfectionem in bonorum dilargitione consistere: imo fieri posse, ut quis bona sua dilargiatur, & ta- men eam, qua necessaria Christiano est, dilectio- nem non habeat, Paulo teste 1. Cor. XIII. 3. Cae- terum thesauri nomine opus Deo gratum atque acce- ptum intelligi, quod Grotius vult, inconveniens est, quum non opus ipsum, aut ejus qualitas, sed retributio operis notetur, quam in coelis expectare habemus: ut ex responso Christi deinceps Petro reddito liquet.

## 19:23
Verse 23. δυσκόλως] What he called difficult here is called impossible below in verse 26. These are indeed accustomed to be used interchangeably in matters of this kind. Thus also Plato: It is impossible for one to be exceptionally good and exceptionally rich. But Christ, repeating the same sentiment with different words from time to time, as appears here and even more so in Mark, wishes that which he says to be most certain to us, namely that riches are for the most part incitements to evil, or at least impediments to good. The reason is that for the most part those who are rich are accustomed to trust in their riches and as it were to place in them the highest good, as Mark indicates. Add Psalm XLIX. 7 and LII. 9. Therefore the wealthy are warned by Paul not to hope in the uncertainty of riches but in the living God, 1 Timothy VI. 17, that is, not to walk after gold, as the writer of Ecclesiasticus XXXI. 7 speaks. For that covetousness is with the best right called idolatry in Colossians III. 5, which ancient opinion of the Hebrews used by Paul was thus extolled by that same writer of Ecclesiasticus: Gold is a stumbling block to those who sacrifice to it, where stumbling block is an idol. A living image of this idolatry can be seen among the poets. Petronius: He possesses a locked-up Jupiter in a chest. Menander: Epicharmus says the gods are the sun, winds, earth, water, fire, stars. But I have assumed that only silver and gold are useful gods to us. For having set these up in the house, pray, whatever you wish will happen for you. See what we have said concerning the deceitfulness of riches at chapter XIII and what at chapters V and VI. And add that statement of Lactantius in book VII. Hence it happens that the poor and humble believe in God more easily, who are unencumbered, than the rich who are entangled by very many impediments: indeed, they are chained and fettered and serve at the whim of the mistress of greed, which ensnares them in inextricable bonds: nor can they look up to heaven, since their mind is prone to the ground and fixed to the earth. But the way of virtue does not admit those carrying heavy burdens. Rabbi Israel treats the same sentiment concerning the soul in chapter XXXIII.

Latin:

Vers. 23. δυσκόλως] Quod hic dixit δύσκολον infra voca- tur ἀδύνατον v. 26. Solent nimirum ista promiscue usur- pari in rebus istius generis. Sic & Plato: ἀγαθὸν ὄντα δια- φερόντως καὶ πλύσιον εἶναι διαφερόντως ἀδύνατον. Eandem autem sententiam diversis subinde verbis repetens Chri- stus, ut hic & magis etiam apud Marcum apparet, vult id quod dicit nobis esse certissimum, scilicet opus plerunque esse malorum irritamenta, aut certe bonorum impedi- menta. Causa est, quia plerunque hi qui divites sunt so- lent divitiis suis confidere & quasi in illis ponere summum boni, ut Marcus indicat. Adde Psal. XLIX. 7. & LII. 9. Ideo monentur opulenti à Paulo μὴ ἠλπικέναι ἐπὶ πλύτο ἀ- δηλότητι ἀλλ' ἐν τῷ Θεῷ τῷ ζῶντι, 1. Tim. VI. 17. id est, μὴ πορέυεσθαι ὀπίσω χρυσίε, ut loquitur Scriptor Ecclesiastici XXXI. 7. Nam ista πλεονεξία optimo jure εἰδωλολατρεία di- citur Col. III. 5. quam veterem Hebraeorum γνώμην à Pau- lo usurpatam ita extulit idem ille Ecclesiastici scriptor, Χρυ- σίον ξύλον προσκόμματός ἐσι τοῖς θυσιάζεσιν ἀυτῷ, ubi ξύλον προσκόμματος est εἴδωλον. Hujus εἰδωλολατρείας vivam effi- giem videre est apud Poëtas. Petronius, Clausum possidet arca Iovem. Menander: ῾Ο μὲν ΕπίχαρμΘ τὲς Θεὸς εἶναι λέγει Ηέλιον, ἀνέμες, γῆν, ὕδωρ, πῦρ, ἀσέρας. Εγὼ δ' ὑπέλαβον χρησίμες εἶναι Θεὸς Τ' ἀργύριον ἡμῖν καὶ τὸ χρυσίον μόνον. ἱδρυσάμενΘ τέτες γὰρ εἰς τὴν οἰκίαν, Εὖξαι, τι βύλῃ πάντα σοι γενήσεται. Vide quae diximus περὶ πλύτο ἀπάτης ad caput XIII. & quae ad caput V. & VI. Et adde Lactantii illud libro VII. Eo sit ut pauperes & humiles Deo credant facilius, qui sunt expediti, quam divites qui sunt impedimentis plurimis implicati: imo vero catenati & compediti serviunt ad nudum dominae cupidi- tatis, quae illos inextricabilibus vinculis irretibit: nec possunt in caelum aspicere, quoniam mens eorum in humum prona, ter- raeque defixa est. Virtutis autem via non capit magna onera portantes. Tractat eandem sententiam Rabbi Israel de a- nima cap. XXXIII.

## 19:24
Verse 24. It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle] Certain Greeks, as Theophylact also notes, have dragged these to a nautical cable, but wrongly, through ignorance of a proverb used among the Hebrews and Arabs, no less about an elephant than about a camel. Similar is that of the old Latin: Sooner shall a locust give birth to a Lucanian ox. In such proverbs, however, it is not necessary that an exact comparison be instituted between the parts compared, since they are accustomed to be adorned with hyperboles. Such is also that in Jeremiah XIII. 23. Indeed, this whole proverb, with the word camel changed to elephant, is in Rabbi Jacob in Caphthor.

Latin:

V. 24. εὐκοπώτερόν ἐσι κάμηλον διὰ τρυπήματΘ ῥαφίδος διελ- θεῖν] Graeci quidam, ut & Theophylactus notat, ad funem nauticum haec traxerunt, sed perperam, ignorantia adagii inter Hebraeos & Arabas usitati, non minus de elephante quam de camelo. Simile est illud Latini veteris: Citius locusta pepererit Lucam bovem. In talibus autem adagiis nihil necesse est exactam inter par- tes collatas comparationem institui, cum soleant ornari ὑπερβολαῖς. Tale est & illud Jer. XIII. 23. Imo totum hoc proverbium, mutata cameli voce in elephantem, est apud R. Jacobum in Caphthor.

## 19:25
Verse 25. Who then can be saved] It moved the Apostles because they saw that even those who were not rich were nevertheless touched by the desire for riches; perhaps also from a similarity of reasoning they believed there were other things, if not equal to riches, at least close to obstructing the way that would lead to heaven. Verse 26. With men this is impossible] It is not of human power to break such tenacious bonds. But with God all things are possible] A common sentiment among the Hebrews from the passage in Genesis XVIII. 14 and Jeremiah XXXII. 17 and Job XLII. 1. Luke expressed the words of the Septuagint Interpreters in Genesis: No word shall be impossible with God, chapter I. 37. Similar things can be found also among the Greeks: Linus: All things are easy for God to accomplish and nothing is impossible. Among Homer several times: And the gods can do all things. Epicharmus: Nothing escapes the divine; this you must know. He himself is our overseer; and nothing is impossible for God. Callimachus: If you know God, know that it is possible for a deity to do everything. Sophocles: Everything could happen if God is contriving it. The saying of Pythagoras is in Iamblichus: That there are not some things possible for God and others impossible, as those who play the sophist think, but all things are possible. Concerning the same Pythagoras, Chalcidius on the Timaeus: To assert that this is the virtue and power of God alone, that what nature cannot effect, God can easily do: as one who is more powerful and more excellent than all virtue, and from whom nature itself borrows its strengths. It is Ovid's: It is easy for God to do all things. But this maxim, just as elsewhere it is generally adapted to all those things which in any way can have existence, that is, either in themselves or in the nature of God do not have a contradiction, so here it is properly referred to those things which are either a part or aids of piety, just as Paul also said: I can do all things in Christ who strengthens me. Thus God, when humbly invoked, can by the inspiration of His grace render the rich immune from the contagion of riches, so that they may be as those having as though they had not, and using as though they were not using, 1 Cor. VII. 29, 30, 31. Which happens not only to those who once and for all distribute their goods to the needy, but also to those who do this bit by bit, content with their own frugal portion.

Grotius rightly notes from a comparison with verse 26 that τὸ δύσκολον (the difficult) is explained by ἀδύνατον (the impossible), because these are accustomed to be used interchangeably: but he less correctly wishes to imply only that riches are for the most part incitements to evils, or at least impediments to good things: because the matter is not simply about riches, or those who have riches, but about the trust that is placed in them: for which reason it is certainly not only difficult, but impossible for such a person to enter into heaven, unless he be converted by the omnipotent divine power. See Job XXXI. 24, Ps. XLIX. 7, LII. 9, LXII. 1, Sir. XXXI. 2, Col. III. 5, 1 Tim. VI. 17. Chrysostom says, He did not say this accusing money, but those held by it: for he calls him a rich man here not as one possessing, but as one desiring to have riches. And afterwards regarding verse 24: When he had said above that it was difficult, now he shows for the first time that it is impossible. For the words of Christ in verse 26 especially imply this: with men this is impossible, but not with God: that it can in no way be done by human power: but that it is not impossible for God, who through the grace of His Spirit changes hearts, regenerates, takes away hearts of stone, puts in hearts of flesh, creates new hearts, and so converts the hearts of the rich, that, being drawn away from the love and desire of temporal things, to which they were utterly devoted and attached, they desire only heavenly things, and despise all earthly things in comparison with them, and are prepared to leave them. Which change and spiritual transformation can be done by no human power, but requires the infinite creative and renewing power of God. Which is implied by this sentence, παρὰ δὲ τῷ πάντα δυνατά ἐστι; which is also found in Gen. XVIII. 14, Jer. XXXII. 17, Zech. VIII. 6, Job XLII. 1, Luke I. 37. Eph. III. 20 is found, and, as Grotius admits, is applied to all those things which in any way can have τὸ εἶναι (being), that is, either in themselves, or do not have τὸ ἀντιφατικὸν (the contradictory) in the nature of God. And therefore the explanation of Grotius does not exhaust the force of this, that God, when humbly invoked, can by the inspiration of His grace keep the rich immune from the contagion of riches, so that they may be ἔχοντες ὡς μὴ ἔχοντες [having as though they had not], καὶ χρώμενοι ὡς μὴ καταχρώμενοι [and using as though they used not], 1 Cor. VII. 29, 30, 31. For it is manifest that the subject is the conversion and change of the mind of the avaricious, and of those whose hearts are fixed on the riches of the world. εὐκοπώτερόν ἐςι κάμηλον διὰ τρυπήματος ῥαφί- δος διελθεῖν [It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle].

We agree with Grotius that by κάμηλον one should not, as some Greeks do, understand a ship's cable, as indeed Cyril of Alexandria and Theophylact have explained; but that the sentiment arose from an adage of the Hebrews and Arabs, because in R. Jacob in Caphtor that whole thing is read with the word camel changed to elephant, is not clear: since it is more likely, on the contrary, that this, like many other things from the New Testament and conversation with Christians and the reading of their writings, passed to others, than that it was taken from others. Nor do we admit that this was said ὑπερβολικῶς [hyperbolically]: for it is certainly a greater work of divine power to recall to spiritual life one who is dead in sins, for example in avarice and the desire of having, to change his heart thoroughly and convert it, and to create and implant in him a new heart, than to cause a camel, that very large animal, to enter through the eye of a needle, if indeed for conversion is required τὸ ὑπερβάλλον μέγεθος τῆς δυνά- μεως τοῦ Θεοῦ, κατὰ τὴν ἐνέργειαν τοῦ κράτους τῆς ἰσχύος αὐτοῦ, ἣν ἐνέργησεν ἐν τῷ χριστῷ ἐγείρας αὐτὸν ἐκ νεκρῶν [the exceeding greatness of the power of God, according to the working of the strength of his might, which he wrought in Christ when he raised him from the dead], as the Apostle testifies, Eph. I. 19, 20. There is therefore no reason for us to imagine, with some, that there was some very narrow gate in Jerusalem which went by the name of a needle, about which one reads nothing anywhere in

It is a history, which the camel could not enter. The common meaning must be retained, because κάμηλον signifies that animal destined for carrying burdens, as the Syrian, Arab, Ethiopian, and Persian have rendered it: concerning which the saying of Christ is also explained by Origen, Clement of Alexandria, book II of the Stromata, Ambrose on chapter XVIII of Luke, Hilary in Canon 19 on Matthew, the Author of the Imperfect Work on Matthew, homily 33, Jerome on chapter IX of Isaiah, Augustine in Questions on the Gospels, book II, question 47, Juvencus, Sedulius, etc., as also by our own writers quite commonly: for a ship's cable is called not κάμηλος, but κάμιλος. See Franz on the Interpretation of Sacred Scripture, chapter XXXVIII, Tarnovius in Exercitations, p. 122, and also Buxtorf, Lexicon Rabbinical, p. 1722, since it is not impossible for divine power to cause that large animal to pass through the eye of a needle: since that is tied to no quantity, nor does this involve a contradiction: for that local extension and commensuration is an accident: which can be absent without prejudice to the substance, just as is taught in philosophy against the Calvinists who restrict divine power here, who impiously argue that it cannot cause one body to be in several places, or that a body should not have an external local position of parts outside of parts, proportioned and commensurate to its place.

PART IV. The retribution promised to the Apostles. Verse 27.

Latin:

Vers. 25. Τίς ἄρα δύναται σωθῆναι] Movit Apostolos quod viderent etiam eos qui divites non essent, tangi tamen di- vitiarum cupiditate; forte & ex rationis similitudine cre- diderunt alia quoque esse, si non divitiis paria, saltem proxima ad obstruendam viam quæ in cœlum duceret. Vers. 26. παρὰ ἀνθρώποις τῦτο ἀδύνατόν ἐςι] Non est humanæ opis tam tenacia vincula abrumpere. παρὰ δὲ Θεῷ πάντα δυνατά ἐσι] Trita inter Hebræos sententia ex loco Gen. XVIII. 14. & Jer. XXXII. 17. & Jo- bi XLII. 1. Verba LXX. Interpretum in Genesi expressic Lucas : ἐκ ἀδυνατήσει παρὰ τῷ Θεῷ πᾶν ῥῆμα cap. I. 37. Simi- lia invenire est & apud Græcos : Linus : Ῥᾴδια πάντα Θεῷ τελέσαι κὶ ἀνήνυτον ἐδὲν. Apud Homerum aliquoties : Θεοὶ δὲ τε πάντα δύνανται. Epicharmus : Οὐδὲν ἐκφεύγει τὸ θεῖον· τῦτο γινώσκειν σε δεῖ. Αὐτός ἐσθ᾽ ἁμῶν ἐπόπτης· ἀδυνατεῖ δ᾽ ἐδὲν Θεῷ. Callimachus : εἰ θεὸν οἶσθα, Ἴσθ᾽ ὅτι κὴ ῥέξαι δαίμονι πᾶν δυνατὸν. Sophocles : Γένοιτο μὲν τ᾽ ἂν πᾶν Θεῦ τεχνωμένε. Pythagoræ dictum est apud Jamblichum : ἐκ εἶναι τὰ μὲν δυ- νατὰ τῷ Θεῷ, τὰ δὲ ἀδύνατα, ὥσπερ οἴεσθαι τὺς σοφιζομένως, ἀλλὰ πάντα δυνατά. De eodem Pythagora Chalcidius ad Timæum : Solius Dei hanc esse virtutem ac potentiam asserere, ut quod natura efficere nequeat, Deus facile possit : ut qui sit o- mni virtute potentior atque præstantior, & à quo natura ipsa vires mutuetur. Ovidii est · facile est omnia posse Deo. Hoc autem effatum sicut alibi generaliter aptatur ad omnia ea quæ ullo modo possunt habere τὸ εἶναι, hoc est, aut in se- metipsis aut in Dei natura non habent τὸ ἀντιφατικὸν, ita hic proprie ad ea refertur quæ aut pars sunt aut adminicula pietatis, quomodo & Paulus dixit : πάντα ἰσχύω ἐν τῷ ἐνδυ- ναμῶντι με χρισῷ. Ita potest Deus humiliter invocatus gra- tiæ suæ afflatu præstare divites immunes à divitiarum con- tagio, ut sint ἔχοντες ὡς μὴ ἔχοντες, κὴ χρώμενοι ὡς μὴ κατα- χρώμενοι, 1. Cor. VII. 29. 30. 31. Quod non tantum his con- tingit qui semel universim bona sua dilargiuntur egentibus, sed & his qui particulatim id faciunt, dimenso suo frugaliter contenti.

Per ἀδύνατον explicari τὸ δύσκολον recte notat Grotius è collatione v. 26. quod ista soleant pro- miscue usurpari : sed minus recte id tantum innui vult, quod opes plerumque irritamenta sint malo- rum, aut certe bonorum impedimenta : quia non simpliciter de opibus, aut opes habentibus, sed qua in iis fiducia collocatur, agitur: qua ratione certe non difficile tantum est, sed impossibile talem, nisi omnipotenti divina virtute convertatur, in cœlum ingredi. Vid. Job. XXXI. 24. Ps. XLIX. 7. LII. 9. LXII. 1. Syr. XXXI. 2. Col. III. 5. 1. Tim. VI. 17. Non dixit hoc, inquit Chrysostomus, pecunias accu- sans, sed ab iis detentos : divitem enim hic non pos- sidentem vocat, sed divitias habere cupientem. Et postea ad vers. 24. Cum dixisset superius difficile, nunc primum ostendit fieri non posse. Id enim verba Christi v. 26. imprimis inferunt : apud homines hoc impossibile est, sed non apud Deum : humana virtu- te id nullatenus fieri posse : sed Deo non esse impossi- bi-le, qui per Spiritus sui gratiam corda immutat, rege- nerat, lapidea corda eximit, carnea indit, nova cor- da creat, atque ita convertit corda divitum, ut à temporalium rerum amore, & cupiditate, quibus prorsus dedita & affixa erant, abstracta tantum cœlestia cupiant, & præ iis omnia terrena sper- nant, & relinquere parata sint. Quæ immutatio & spiritualis transformatio nulla virtute humana fie- ri potest, sed infinitam virtutem Dei creatricem, & innovatricem requirit. Quod innuitur hac senten- tia, παρὰ δὲ θ. ῷ πάντα δυνατά ἐσι; quæ etiam Gen. XVIII. 14. Jer. XXXII. 17. Zach. VIII. 6. Job. XLII. 1. Luc. I. 37. Eph. III. 20. reperitur, & fatente Grotio aptatur ad omnia ea, quæ ullo modo possunt habere τὸ εἶναι, hoc est, aut in semetipsis, aut in Dei natu- ra non habent τὸ ἀντιφατικὸν. Ideoque non ex- haurit his ejus vim explicatio Grotiana, quod pos- sit Deus humiliter invocatus, gratia suæ afflatu- praestare divites immunes à divitiarum contagio, ut sint ἔχοντες ὡς μὴ ἔχοντες, καὶ χρώμενοι ὡς μὴ καταχρώμενοι, 1. Cor. VII. 29. 30. 31. Nam de conversione, & mutatione animi avarorum, & di- vitiis mundi corde affixorum agi, manifestum est. εὐκοπώτερόν ἐςι κάμηλον διὰ τρυπήματος ῥαφί- δος διελθεῖν.

Per κάμηλον non esse cum Graecis quibusdam funem nauticum intelligendum, astipulamur Gro- tio, uti nempe Cyrillus Alex. & Theophylact. ex- posuere; quod autem ab adagio Ebraeorum & Ara- bum orta sit sententia, quia apud R. Jacobum in Caphtor illud totum legitur mutata cameli voce in Elephantem, non liquet: quum verisimilius con- tra sit, hoc, ut alia multa è N. Test. & conversa- tione cum Christianis, eorumque scriptorum le- ctione ad alios transiisse, quam ab aliis transsum- pta esse. Neque ὑπερβολικῶς hoc dictum esse, ad- mittimus: nam majus certe divinae potentiae opus est, eum qui in peccatis mortuus, v. g. in avaritia, & habendi cupiditate, in vitam spiritualem revoca- re, cor ejus immutare penitus, ac convertere, ei- que novum cor creare, atque indere, quam effi- cere, ut Camelus, animal illud praegrande per fo- ramen acus ingrediatur, siquidem ad conversio- nem requiritur τὸ ὑπερβάλλον μέγεθος τῆς δυνά- μεως τοῦ Θεοῦ, κατὰ τὴν ἐνέργειαν τοῦ κράτους τῆς ἰσχύος αὐτοῦ, ἣν ἐνέργησεν ἐν τῷ χριστῷ ἐγείρας αὐτὸν ἐκ νεκρῶν, teste Apostolo Eph. I. 19. 20. Non ergo est quod fingamus cum nonnullis, portam aliquam Hierosolymis perquam angustam fuisse, quae acûs nomine venerit, de qua nihil uspiam legere in

Historia est, quam ingredi nequiverit Camelus. Retinenda communis significatio, quia κάμηλον animal illud oneribus ferendis destinatum significat, ut reddidit Syrus, Arabs, Aethiops & Persa: de quo explicatur etiam dictum Christi, ab Origene, Clemente Alex. l. II. Stromat. Ambrosio in capite XVIII. Luc. Hilario Can. 19. in Matth. Auth. Oper. imperf. in Matth. hom. 33. Hieronymo in cap. IX. Es. Augustino qq. Evangel. l. II. q. 47. Ju- venco, Sedulio, &c. ut & à nostris fere communiter: funis vero nauticus non κάμηλος, sed κάμιλος dicitur. Vid. Franz. de Interpretat. Script. Sac. c. XXXVIII. Tarnovium in Exerc. p. 122. nec non Buxtorf. Lex. Rabb. p. 1722. siquidem divinae po- tentiae impossibile non sit efficere, ut animal illud grande per acus foramen transeat: quum illa ad nullam quantitatem alligata sit, nec contradictio- nem haec involvant: extensio enim illa localis, & commensuratio accidens est: quod abesse potest salva substantia, quemadmodum in Philosophia adversus Calvinianos divinam potentiam hic re- stringentes, docetur, quam efficere non posse, ut corpus unum in pluribus locis sit, aut ut corpus non habeat externam localem positionem par- tium extra partes, loco suo proportionatam & commensuratam, impie disputant.

PARS IV. Retributio Apostolis promissa. Vers. 27.

## 19:27
ἀφήκαμεν πάντα καὶ ἠκολουθήσαμέν σοι [We have left all and followed you]. Peter says that the two things which Christ had demanded of the young man had been performed by himself and his companions, truly, although, as some think, a little boastfully. He does not add the third, concerning goods sold and given to the poor, because Christ had neither demanded this of them, nor was it suitable to their poverty. For what would they sell? A hut? But that received wives, children, and perhaps parents and brothers. Whether the little boat in which they were accustomed to fish was their own or held in common with others is very uncertain. They did not have estates and the rest of the provision for life. Wherefore, since they had left both the care of their affairs and the trade by the fruit of which they were accustomed to sustain themselves and their family, in order to follow Christ, they had done no less than the young man was about to do if he had sold goods that were not necessary. With this confidence Peter asks what the reward will be. Christ could have rebuffed him by saying, what you have done, you have done for yourselves, not for me, so that you might receive from me the words of eternal life: there is no reason for you to impute it to me or to the Father. But out of his goodness he fosters their hope, and says that this tolerance of loss, whatever it may be, will not lack a special reward of honor.

Latin:

ἀφήκαμεν πάντα καὶ ἠκολουθήσαμέν σοι] Duo quae Chri- stus à juvene exegerat, Petrus à se sociisque suis ait praesti- ta, vere, quanquam, ut quidam putant, jactantius paulo. Tertium non addit, de bonis venditis donatisque paupe- ribus, quia neque hoc ab illis exegerat Christus, neque con- veniebat eorum tenuitati. Quid enim venderent? ca- samne? at ea uxores, liberos, forte & parentes ac fratres receptabat. Navicula qua piscari solebant, illorum pro- pria, an communis cum aliis fuerit perincertum est. Prae- dia & reliquum vitae χορήγημα non habebant, Quare cum & curam rerum suarum & artem, cujus fructu se ac fami- liam fuftentare folebant, reliquissent, ut Christum secla- rentur, fecerant non minus quam facturus erat juvenis si bona non necessaria vendidisset. Hac fiducia interrogat Pe- trus ecquid præmii sit futurum. Poterat eum Christus re- tundere dicendo, quod fecistis, vobis fecistis non mihi, ut verba a me acciperetis vitæ æternæ: non est quod mihi aut patri imputetis. Sed pro sua bonitate spem illorum fovet, aitque non carituram peculiari honoris præmio istam qua- liscunque jacturæ tolerantiam.

## 19:28
Verse 28.

ἐν τῇ παλιγγενεσίᾳ [in the regeneration]. These words are more correctly referred to the following clause. But I think that by παλιγγενεσία, that is, תחיה [resurrection] or of the new age, as the Syrian speaks with the word, is indicated here the very kingdom of the Messiah to be begun after the resurrection of Christ, concerning which Paul, dealing with it, says, ἰδὲ γέγονε καινὰ τὰ πάν- τα [behold, all things have become new], 2 Cor. V. 17. And elsewhere we have said that this time is also called by the Jews the age to come. For also what follows, ὅταν καθίσῃ ὁ ὑὸς τῶ ἀνθρώπε ἐπὶ θρόνε δόξης αὑτῶ [when the Son of man shall sit on the throne of his glory], is for the most part and properly referred to that, as is manifest from the compared passages. Moreover, Josephus teaches us that the appellation of regeneration was accepted in this sense among the Jews, who in the second book against Apion speaks thus: ὅτι τοῖς τὰς νόμως διαφυλά- ξασι κ᾿ ἂν εἰ δέοι θνήσκειν ὑπὲρ αὐτῶν, προθύμως ἀποθανῦσιν ἔδωκεν ὁ θεὸς γενέσθαι τε πάλιν καὶ βίον ἀμείνω λαβεῖν ἐκ περι- τροπῆς [that to those who have kept the laws, even if it were necessary to die for them, and who have willingly died, God has given to be born again and to receive a better life in the cycle]. Philo in this sense uses the very word itself in his book on Cain: πόθεν ἦλθεν ἡ ψυχὴ, πᾶ δὲ χωρήσει, πό- σον δὲ χρόνον ἡμῖν ἐμοδίωσε; ἔστι' τίς δὲ ὶει τὰν ὀσίαν ἔχομεν εἰ- πεῖν, πότε δὲ νὸν ἐκτησάμεθα ἀυτήν. πρὸ γενέσεως; ἀλλ᾿ ὐχ ὑπάρχομεν˙ μετὰ τὸν θάνατον; ἀλλ᾿ ἐκ ἰσόμεθα οἱ μετὰ σωμάτων σύγκριτοι˙ ἀλλ᾿ εἰς παλιγγενεσίαν ὁρμήσομεν, οἱ μὲν τὰ ἀσωμάτων ἀσύγκριτοι. For I think that passage, which is read corruptly, should be read thus. The Churches of Gaul, in their Epistle to the Asiatic Churches, when they had narrated that the ashes of the martyrs were cast into the Rhone, add: καὶ ταῦτ᾽ ἔπραττον ὡς δυνά- μενοι νικῆσαι τὸν Θεὸν κὴ ἀφελίσθαι ἀυτῶν τὴν παλιγγενεσίαν, ἵνα ὡς ἔλεγον ἐκεῖνοι μηδὲ ἐλπίδα χῶσιν ἀναστάσεως.

You also shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.] You shall occupy the honor next to me as King; κρίνειν here signifies as much as to preside, by metonymy, because those who preside are generally occupied with administering justice. Whence מדיני is called a prefecture by the Hebrews. The translation is taken from the ancient state of the Israelite kingdom, in which the heads of the tribes approached nearest to the royal majesty, and in public assemblies sat next to his throne in curule chairs. Christ uses the same translation elsewhere, Luke 22:29, where another thing is also added, that they themselves would sit at the royal table, which was the custom of the greatest nobles. And although because of the double portion of Joseph's children there were thirteen tribes, yet they are usually named as twelve, Acts 26:7. James 1:1, because the Levitical [tribe] had no seats apart, and therefore no proper ruler of a division; but what are called thrones here by the name of seats, as I said, are curule chairs placed next to the king's throne, the same is also to be found in the Apocalypse. Nor do I think it happened from any other source that the chief of the Angels were called thrones, Colossians 1:16.

Grotius understands by παλιγγενεσίαν the kingdom of the Messiah to be begun after the resurrection of Christ, but against the will of almost all interpreters, even the one he cites, the Syriac, rendering it by חדי a new age, and Ambrose by the generation to come; for the interpreters commonly understand the future age and the time of our resurrection to a blessed life thus far. Nor is the resurrection of Christ ever designated by the name of παλιγγενεσία; but that our resurrection is so called, the passages which Grotius adduced from Josephus, Book II against Apion, Philo's book on Cain, and the Epistle of the Churches of Gaul to the Asiatic Churches, testify. Nor is that which follows, 'when the Son of man shall sit on the throne of his glory,' referred so much to the resurrection of Christ as to his most recent coming in the resurrection of the blessed: nor can it be denied that the sitting of the Apostles upon twelve thrones must be referred to the final judgment, compare Luke 22:30. Furthermore, the gloss does not satisfy the promise of Christ, by which these things are drawn to the beginning of the kingdom of Christ after the resurrection, as if they then occupied the throne next to him as King, and judged the twelve tribes of Israel sitting in curule chairs, that is, presided over them. The Apostles were sent into the whole world, not as approaching nearest to the royal majesty of CHRIST, stretching itself forward and backward, and there is no looking toward a new kingdom begun after the time of Christ's resurrection. But these things are concerning Grotius's opinion.

There have not been wanting, however, those who have referred this word even to the present age and spiritual regeneration, such as the author of the Oper. imperf., Hilary, Macarius hom. VII., and Bede: for they seem to have recalled these words to the preceding clause: but Grotius concedes that they look to the following one, which is manifest no less from the text and a comparison of Mark X. 30 and Luke XVIII. 29 than from the common punctuation of the Codices, and they explain it concerning regeneration to the other life on the last day, as Augustine does in book III against the two Epistles of the Pelagians, ch. III, book IV, ch. XI, book II against Julian, and book XX of the City of God, ch. XXV. What he says, 'in the regeneration,' he undoubtedly intended the resurrection of the dead to be understood by the name of regeneration. For thus our flesh will be regenerated through incorruption, just as our soul has been regenerated through faith. Gregory the Great, book IV of the Morals, ch. XXIII. Bernard in his declamations; from the Greeks, Euthymius and Theophylactus. Some, however, refer that dignity of sitting to both ages, such as Maximus in Corderius's Catena of the Greek Fathers: 'This also,' he says, 'was done on earth; for He sent to the twelve (tribes) also a holy power, which coming, sat upon the seats of their minds (Acts II. 13) and Peter began to judge them, saying of Jesus: You crucified a man powerful in word and signs: many therefore were converted to repentance: Do you see how the principality of judgment appeared, and the power of sitting and judging was given to them in this world?' although it was to be that they would sit also and pass judgment at the appearing of the Lord in the resurrection of the dead.

But how then will they sit upon twelve thrones and be about to judge? All the saints are indeed said to judge the world (1 Cor. VI. 2) by assisting Christ in judgment, by approving His judgment, by testifying against the infidels, and by convincing them by the example of their own faith and repentance: but this is attributed to the Apostles in a peculiar way, because they were the first to announce the Gospel, and by the word which they preached, the infidels themselves will be judged.
