Special mention of the tribes of Israel is made, however, because they were sent to them first (Acts XIII. 46), to whom alone the Gospel had been preached up to that time, and by whom the Apostles were judged and condemned here, being about to judge them in turn later, and to condemn them on account of the word which they rejected through infidelity: just as Christ also promises to the Apostles not the glory of the heavenly kingdom in common, but a more eminent degree in that glory in particular above other elect: whence by judicial thrones their highest honor is rightly designated, because they are not only to go before the other citizens of the heavenly kingdom, but also are to judge the world together with Christ, the King of glory. Therefore some of our own also join both here, namely that by the preaching of the Gospel the Apostles were to call the Jews to repentance and faith, and to pronounce those not obeying guilty of eternal damnation, and later also to condemn them by Word, testimony, and example (John III. 18, ch. XII. 48), so that by the mention of the twelve tribes it is also hinted that, because they were sent primarily to them to gather the dispersed tribes of the people through the preaching of the Gospel, those not obeying the call were to be condemned here and hereafter. Compare B. Gerhard, Harm. Evang. ch. CLXXII. In which way Mark also promises retribution in this age and at the same time in the future (ch. X. 30), which Cyril explains concerning spiritual graces, which are much more excellent than these earthly ones, which are certain pledges of future goods, which those who have are in the greatest dignities, with all honors in a certain way running to the saints, so that through them they may enjoy divine grace. Therefore those things are not to be restricted to this age with Grotius: even if distinct mention is made afterward of eternal life; because these are not opposed, but joined. Therefore, what Origen, the writer of the responses to the Orthodox to question CX, and Theophylactus say in this place, that it is future, so that for Christians who have suffered the loss of such things, other Christians may be a necessity in place of them, and that they may receive from the estates of others as much as suffices for their own moderate desires, and draw much greater pleasure from this brotherly charity than pain from the offenses contracted or the loss of things endured, is not to be accepted in an exclusive sense, as if such things are not also to be expected a hundred times more excellent in the day of the restoration of all things: just as is evident from Theophylactus: 'For carnal relatives they will have familiarity and brotherhood with God, for fields Paradise, and for stone houses the heavenly Jerusalem.' For what is said about receiving back what we lose for the sake of the Gospel—parents, brothers, and possessions—and indeed with a hundredfold interest, is not to be understood of the same things in substance and number, but of similar things, and those to be held in the same place; because in place of corporal parents, brothers, children, and possessions, we receive spiritual ones a hundred times more excellent, here and in the future age; in place of spouses, Him to whom we have been betrothed through faith, a hundred times, nay, infinitely more excellent than a spouse in faith, love, and the communication of all His own, and in indissoluble union and society. Although, Cyril says again, other believers may not attain the same, they will nevertheless have, in place of carnal relatives, familiarity with God, and brotherhood with the holy city, the mother of the firstborn, to receive life without end, which is from everlasting fruition, and in delights, and with no deprivation of goods ever. They will not, therefore, receive many for one brother, or many for one mother, or many fields for a few, he says, but they will attain heavenly things that without controversy exceed all earthly things, so that those which remain will be far more excellent than those which are laid aside. Add that the 'hundredfold' can be rendered 'a hundred times as much,' because we receive things a hundred times more excellent.

Latin:

Vers. 28.

ἐν τῇ παλιγγενεσίᾳ] Rectius ad sequens comma refe- runtur hæ voces. παλιγγενεσία autem, id est תחיה sive novi fæculi, ut Syrus loquitur voce, indicari hic puto i- psum Messiæ regnum inchoandum post resurrectionem Christi, de quo agens Paulus, inquit, ἰδὲ γέγονε καινὰ τὰ πάν- τα, 2. Cor. V.17. Et alibi diximus Judæis quoque id tem- pus fæculum futurum appellari. Nam & quod sequitur, ὅταν καθίσῃ ὁ ὑὸς τῶ ἀνθρώπε ἐπὶ θρόνε δόξης αὑτῶ, plerumque & proprie eo refertur, ut collatis locis manifestum est. Ap- pellationem autem genituræ hoc sensu receptam fuisse a- pud Judæos etiam Josephus nos docet, qui secundo ad- versus Appionem ita loquitur: ὅτι τοῖς τὰς νόμως διαφυλά- ξασι κ᾿ ἂν εἰ δέοι θνήσκειν ὑπὲρ αὐτῶν, προθύμως ἀποθανῦσιν ἔδωκεν ὁ θεὸς γενέσθαι τε πάλιν καὶ βίον ἀμείνω λαβεῖν ἐκ περι- τροπῆς. Philo in hunc sensum ipsam etiam vocem usur- pat libro de Caino: πόθεν ἦλθεν ἡ ψυχὴ, πᾶ δὲ χωρήσει, πό- σον δὲ χρόνον ἡμῖν ἐμοδίωσε; ἔστι' τίς δὲ ὶει τὰν ὀσίαν ἔχομεν εἰ- πεῖν, πότε δὲ νὸν ἐκτησάμεθα ἀυτήν. πρὸ γενέσεως; ἀλλ᾿ ὐχ ὑπάρχομεν˙ μετὰ τὸν θάνατον; ἀλλ᾿ ἐκ ἰσόμεθα οἱ μετὰ σωμάτων σύγκριτοι˙ ἀλλ᾿ εἰς παλιγγενεσίαν ὁρμήσομεν, οἱ μὲν τὰ ἀσωμάτων ἀσύγκριτοι. Ita enim locum illum legendum censeo qui corrupte legitur. Ecclesiæ Galliæ in Epistola ad Asiaticas Ecclesias cum narrassent martyrum cineres in Rhodanum conjectas, addunt: καὶ ταῦτ᾽ ἔπραττον ὡς δυνά- μενοι νικῆσαι τὸν Θεὸν κὴ ἀφελίσθαι ἀυτῶν τὴν παλιγγενεσίαν, ἵνα ὡς ἔλεγον ἐκεῖνοι μηδὲ ἐλπίδα χῶσιν ἀναστάσεως.

Καθίσεσθε κὴ ὑμεῖς ἐπὶ δώδεκα θρόνες, κρίνοντες τὰς δώ- δεκα φυλὰς τῆ Ἰσραήλ.] Proximum mihi Regi honorem oc- cupabitis, κρίνειν hic tantum valet quantum præesse, μέτα- ληπτικῶς, quia plerumque præsides juri dicundo vacant. Unde מדיני Hebræis præfectura dicta est. Sumta est tralatio a veteri statu regni Israelitici in quo οἱ φυλάρχαι proxime ad regiam majestatem accedebant, & in publicis cœtibus juxta ejus solium sedebant in sellis curulibus. Ali- bi quoque Christus eadem tralatione utitur, Luc. XXII. 29. ubi & alterum additur, assessuros ipsos mensæ regiæ, quod esse solebat maximorum procerum. Quanquam autem ob duplam Josephi liberûm portionem factæ erant tribus tredecim, solent tamen plerumque nominari duo- decim, Act. XXVI. 7. Jac. I. I. quia Levitica nullas habe- bat sedes seorsim, ac proinde nec proprium μεριδάρχην; quod autem θρόνων nomine hic vocantur sellæ, ut dixi, curules juxta regis solium politæ, idem & in Apocalypsi invenire est. Neque aliunde factum arbitror, ut Ange- lorum primores θρόνοι vocarentur, Coloss. I, 16.

Per παλιγγενεσίαν Messiæ regnum post resurre- Etionem Christi inchoandum intelligit Grotius, sed invitis interpp. plerisque omnibus, ipso etiam quem allegat, Syro, reddente per חדי novum feculum, & Ambr, per generationem venturam; nam futurum seculum, & tempus resurrectionis nostræ ad beatam vitam hactenus intelligunt com- muniter Interpp. Nec vero uspiam Christi resur- rectio παλιγγενεσίας nomine indigitatur: resur- rectionem autem nostram ita vocari, loca etiam, quæ è Josephi l. II. contra Appion. Philon. libr. de Caino, Ecclesiæ Galliæ Epistola ad Asiaticas Eccle- fias adduxit Grotius testantur. Neque tam ad resurrectionem Christi, quam ad adventum ejus novissimum in resurrectione beatorum illud, quod sequitur, ὅταν καθίσῃ ὁ ὑὸς τῶ ἀνθρώπυ ἐπὶ θρόνε δόξης ἀυτῶ refertur: nec negari potest, quin ad judicium extremum referri debeat sessio Aposto- lorum super duodecim thronis, Conf. Luc. XXII. 30. Nec porro satisfacit promissioni Christi glossa, qua ad inchoationem regni Christi post re- surrectionem hæc trahuntur, quasi tum proxi- mum ipsi ceu Regi thronum occuparint, & duode- cim tribus Israel judicarint in sellis curulibus seden- tes, hoc est ipsis præfuerint. Emissi sunt Apo- stoli in totum terrarum orbem, non ceu acceden- tes proxime ad regiam majestatem CHRISTI, antrorsum & retrorsum se porrigentem, neque ad novum regnum post tempus resurrectionis Christi inchoatum respicitur. Sed hæc de Grotii sententia.

Non defuerunt tamen, qui vocem hanc etiam ad præsens sæculum, & spiritualem regenerationem retulerint, utpote autor. Oper. imperf. Hilarius, Macar. hom. VII. Beda: Videntur enim verba hæc ad præcedens comma revocasse: sed concedit Grotius ea ad sequens spectare, quod è textu, & collatione Marc. X. 30. Luc. XVIII. 29. non mi- nus, quam è Codicum communi interpunctione manifestum est, & de regeneratione ad alteram vitam in die novissima, exponunt Augustin. l. III. contr. duas Epist. Pelag. c. III. l. IV. cap. XI. l. II. contr. Julian. & l. XX. de Civit. DEI cap. XXV. Quod ait in regeneratione, procul dubio mortuorum resurrectionem nomine voluit regenerationis intelligi. Sic enim caro nostra regenerabitur per incorruptio- nem, quemadmodum est anima nostra regenerata per fidem. Gregor. M. l. IV. Moral. cap. XXIII. Bernhard. in declamat. è Græcis Euthymius, & Theophylactus. Illam tamen sessionis dignitatem ad utrumque sæculum nonnulli referunt, utpote Maximus in Caten. Græcor. Patr. Corderii: Hoc etiam, inquit, in terra factum est; misit enim ad duodecim (tribus) etiam sanctam potestatem, quæ veniens in sedibus animorum illorum sedit (Act. II. 13.) & cœpit eos Petrus judicare, de Jesu dicens: Virum potentem sermone, & signis vos crucifi- xistis: multi igitur ad pœnitentiam conversi sunt: Videsne quomodo apparuerit judicii principatus, da- taque illis sit in hoc mundo sedendi, & judicandi po- testas? licet futurum esset, ut sederent etiam; ac judicium ferrent in apparitione Domini in mortuorum resurrectione.

Quomodo vero tum super Duodecim thronis sedebunt, & judicaturi sunt? judicare sane mun- dum dicuntur omnes sancti 1. Cor. VI. 2. Christo ju- dici assistendo, judicium ejus approbando, de infide- libus testificando, eosque fidei & pœnitentiæ suæ exemplo convincendo: Sed peculiari ratione id tribuitur Apostolis, quia Evangelium primi annun- ciarunt, & verbo, quod prædicarunt, ipsi judica- buntur infideles. Tribuum autem Israëlis ideo fit specialis mentio, quia primo ad easdem missi fuêre Act. XIII. 46. quibus etiam solis eo usq; Evange- lium prædicatum fuit, & à quibus hic judicabantur Apostoli, & condemnabantur, olim vice versa eas- dem judicaturi, & ob verbum, quod per infidelita- tem reprobarunt, condemnaturi: quemadmodum etiam Apostolis Christus non communiter regni cælestis gloriam, sed peculiariter eminentiorem gra- dum in ea gloria præ aliis electis promittit: unde per thronos judiciarios recte honor summus eorum designatur, quod non solum cæteros regni cæle- stis cives præcessuri, sed etiam una cum Rege glo- riæ Christo mundum judicaturi sint. Ideo etiam è nostris utrumque nonnulli hic conjungunt, quod nempe per prædicationem Evangelii Apostoli ad pœnitentiam & fidem Judæos vocaturi essent, & non obedientes æternæ damnationis reos pro- nunciaturi, olim etiam Verbo, testimonio, & exem- plo eosdem damnaturi Job. III. 18. c. XII. 48. ut ita etiam duodecim tribuum mentione innuatur, quod ad easdem imprimis missi, ut dispersas po- puli tribus per Evangelii prædicationem collige- rent, vocationi non parentes hic & olim conde- mnaturi. Confer. B. Gerhard. Harm. Evang. cap. CLXXII. Quo pacto etiam retributionem Marcus in hoc sæculo promittit, simul & in futuro c. X. 30. quod Cyrillus de spiritualibus gratiis multum ter- renis his præcellentibus explicat, quæ sunt arrhæ quædam bonorum futurorum, quas qui habent, in maximis sunt dignitatibus, omnibus quodam- modo honoribus ad sanctos accurrentibus, ut per eos divina gratia fruantur. Non ergo tantum ad hoc seculum illa restringenda cum Gretio: etsi di- stincta deinde mentio fiat æternæ vitæ; quia hæc non opponuntur, sed conjunguntur. Quod itaque Origenes, scriptor responsionum ad Orthodoxos ad quæstionem CX. Theophylactus h. l. futurum di- cunt, ut Christianis talium jacturam passis alii Chri- stiani sint vice istarum necessitudinem, utque ex alio- rum prædiis tantum percipiant, quantum ipsorum mo- deratis desideriis sufficiat, multoque majorem vo- luptatem hauriant ex ista fraterna charitate, quam dolorem ex contractis offensis, aut tolerato rerum di- spendio, non accipiendum sensu exclusivo, ac si ta- lia in die ἀποκαταστάσεως πάντων etiam non sint expectanda centies præstantiora: quemadmodum è Theophylacto constat: Pro carnalibus cognatis fa- miliaritatem & fraternitatem cum Deo habebunt, pro agris Paradisum, ac pro lapideis ædibus cœlestem Hierosolymam. Nam quod de recipiendis, quæ propter Evangelium amittimus; Parentibus, fratribus, & fa- cultatibus dicitur, & quidem centuplici fœnore, non intelligi de iisdem qua substantiam, & numerum, sed de similibus, & eodem loco habendis; quia lo- co corporalium parentum, fratrum, filiorum, facultatum, spirituales centuplum præstantiores recipimus, hic & in futuro seculo; loco conju- gum eum, cui desponsati per fidem sumus, cen- ties, imo infinities conjuge præstantiorem fide, amore, omniumque suorum communicatione, & indissolubili unione ac societate. Licet non ea- dem, inquit iterum Cyrillus, alii fideles consequan- tur, habituri tamen sunt pro carnalibus quidem co- gnatis cum Deo familiaritatem, fraternitatemque sanctæ civitate primogenitorum matre, ad vitam sine fine accipiendam, quæ est ex fruitione sempiter- na, & in deliciis, ac nulla unquam bonorum priva- tione. Non multos igitur pro uno fratre, aut mul- tas pro una matre, aut agros pro paucis multos ac- cipient, inquit, sed terrestria omnia sine controversia excedentia cœlestia consequentur, ita ut iis, quæ im- ponuntur longe præstantiora, quæ restabunt. Adde quod τὸ ἑκατονταπλάσιον reddi possit, centies tanti, quod centies præstantiora recipiamus.

## 19:29
Vers. 29.

or wife] It is not a question of divorce here, but of putting a wife in the second place in the business of piety, no less than other affections, which is also called 'hating' in Luke XIV. 26.

So too Chrysostom: But when he says, everyone who puts away his wife, he does not mean this, that marriages should be simply dissolved, but what he said about the soul: he who loses his soul for my sake, shall find it; not that we should kill ourselves, nor that we should separate it from the body from now on, but that we should prefer piety to all other things, he says this also about a wife, and brothers. It seems to me, however, that he is also insinuating persecutions here. For when many fathers would drag their children and wives toward impiety; when they command these things, he says, let neither wives be held, nor fathers: which Paul also said (1 Cor. 7:15), If the unbeliever departs, let him depart. Grotius therefore acknowledged then that this passage was ineptly snatched by the Papists, such as Lorichius and others, for the celibacy of priests: just as Cornel. also confessed. Jansenius in Harm. cap. 100, that these things are not said so that Christ might dissolve marriages, but so that we might prefer both Him, and the Gospel, and the kingdom of God, even to the spouse himself: and Barradius, Vol. III, Conc. Evang. lib. III, cap. 17, that Christ does not wish parents and relatives to be pursued with hatred from the heart, but if they are contrary to our faith, or obedience owed to God, they are not to be heard. Therefore, Christ is dealing with a case of necessity in persecution, concerning a departure that is not voluntary but forced, and not out of positive hatred, but out of putting something else first, and that is not assigned to priests specifically, but to any Christians in general. Compare Matthew 16:25, chapter 10:37. Augustine, Epistle 89. There occurs sometimes an article of necessity, where either the wife must be dismissed, or Christ. And not without reason does Grotius here note that Irenaeus (whom Jerome criticizes without mentioning his name) is mistaken, when he also strives to prove by this testimony the earthly (thousand-year) happiness of the anticipated resurrection: which he thinks is clear from the words of Mark: For he says, ἐν τῷ καιρῷ τούτῳ: which signifies a continuous and uninterrupted course of this life.

ἑκατονταπλασίονα λήψεται] מֵאָה פְעָמִים as in 2 Samuel 24:3, 1 Chronicles 21:2. In this very age, as the opposition of the following member proves, and Mark clearly expresses. Salvianus: How much more are religious and holy men not to be thought miserable, who both take the delights of present faith and will obtain the rewards of future blessedness. Mark furthermore, by repeating the words for things, says it will come to pass that they receive houses, fields, parents, children, brothers, sisters, yet with tribulations. Which Origen, the author of the responses to the Orthodox, to question 110. Theophylact in this place, in my judgment, interprets correctly, saying that it will come to pass that for Christians who have suffered the loss of such things, other Christians will be in place of those relationships, and that from the estates of others they will receive as much as suffices for their moderate desires, and draw much greater pleasure from that brotherly love than pain from the offenses incurred or the loss of things tolerated. Of which matter we have a clear example in the Apostle Paul, whose ignominy was compensated by honor, contempt by nobility, pain by joy, poverty by an abundance of things in wonderful turns, as can be seen in 2 Corinthians 6:8, 9, 10. But that Irenaeus is mistaken [for he is the one whom Jerome criticizes without mentioning his name] when he strives to prove by this testimony also the earthly happiness of the anticipated resurrection, seems clear to me from the words of Mark. For he says, ἐν τῷ καιρῷ τούτῳ, which signifies a continuous and uninterrupted course of this life. But concerning the thousand years themselves, it will have to be spoken of elsewhere.

καὶ ζωὴν αἰώνιον κληρονομήσει] Which was once foreshadowed in the Levites, of whom Philo beautifully says: ὗτοι καταλελοίπασι τέκνα, γονεῖς, ἀδελφὸς, τὰ οἰκειότατα καὶ φίλτατα, ἵν' ἀντὶ θνητῶν ἀθάνατον κλῆρον εὕρωνται.

Latin:

Vers. 29.

ἢ γυναῖκα] Non de divortio hic agitur, sed de postha- benda in pietatis negotio uxore, non minus quam cæte- ris affectibus, quod & μισεῖν dicitur apud Luc. XIV, 26.

Ita & Chrysostomus: Cum vero dicit, omnis, qui dimiserit uxorem, non hoc ait, ut simpliciter dirimantur matrimonia, sed quod de anima dixit: qui perdiderit animam suam propter me, inveniet eam; non ut interficiamus nosmetipsos, neque ex nunc eam à corpore separemus, sed ut pietatem cæteris o- mnibus præferamus, hoc etiam de uxore ait, ac fra- tribus. Videtur autem mihi etiam hic persecutio- nes insinuare. Cum enim multi Patres ad impicta- tem pertraherent liberos, & uxores viri; cum hæc jubebunt, inquit, nec uxores habeantur, neque Patres: quod & Paulus dixit (1. Corinth. VII. 15.) Si vero infidelis discedit, discedat. Agnovit ergo tum Grotius, inepte hunc locum à Pontifi- ciis, utpote Lorichio, & aliis ad cælibatum Sacer- dotum abripi: quemadmodum etiam fassus est Cornel. Jansen. in Harm. cap. C. non hæc dici, ut nuptias dirimat Christus, sed ut ipsi quoque conjugi præponamus & ipsum, & Evangelium, & regnum Dei: & Barradius T. III. Conc. Evang. l. III. c. 17. non velle Christum, parentes & cognatos ex animo prosequendos esse odio, sed si fidei nostræ, vel Deo debita obedientia obsistant, non audiendos. Proinde agere Christum de causa necessitatis in per- secutione, de dimissione non voluntaria, sed coacta, nec de odio positivo, sed de posthabitatione, eaq; non Sacerdotibus in specie, sed Christianis quibusvis in genere demandari. Cons. Matth. XVI.25. c.X 37. August. Ep. XXCIX. Occurrit aliquando neces- sitatis articulus, ubi aut dimittatur uxor, aut Christus. Nec immerito notat hic Grotius Ire- næum, (quem nomine suppresso reprehendit Hie- ronymus) falli eum, tum hoc quoque testimonio pro- bare nititur terrenam (mille annorum) felicitatem anticipatæ resurrectionis: quod ex Marci verbis apertum esse censet: Is enim ait, ἐν τῷ καιρῷ τού- τῳ: quod continuum, neǵ; interruptum vitæ bujus cursum significat.

ἑκατονταπλασίονα λήψεται] מֵאָה פְעָמִים ut 2. Sam. XXIV. 3. 1. Par. XXI. 2. In hoc ipso sæculo, ut sequentis membri oppositio evincit, & clare exprimit Marcus. Sal- vianus: Quanto magis religiosi & sancti viri miseri non putandi sunt qui & præsentis fidei oblectamenta capiunt & beatitudinis futuræ præmia consequentur. Marcus insuper rerum vocabulis repetitis futurum ait, ut recipiant domos, agros, parentes, liberos, fratres, sorores, attamen cum ærumnis. Quod Origenes, Scriptor responsionum ad Orthodoxos ad quæstionem CX. Theophylactus hoc lo- co recte, me judice, interpretantur, dicentes futurum, ut Christianis talium jacturam passis alii Christiani sint vice istarum necessitudinum, utque ex aliorum prædiis tan- tum percipiant quantum ipsorum moderatis desideriis suf- ficiat, multoque majorem voluptatem hauriant ex ista fraterna caritate quam dolorem ex contractis offenfis, aut tolerato rerum dispendio. Cujus rei luculentum habe- mus exemplum in Paulo Apostolo, cujus ignominia ho- nore, comtemtus nobilitate, dolor gaudio, paupertas re- rum abundantia miris vicibus pensabantur, ut videre est 2. Cor. VI. 8. 9. 10. Falli autem Irenæum [is enim est quem nomine suppresso reprehendit Hieronymus] cum hoc quoque testimonio probare nititur terrenam felicita- tem anticipatæ resurrectionis, ex Marci verbis apertum mihi videtur. Is enim ait, ἐν τῷ καιρῷ τούτῳ, quod con- tinuum neque interruptum vitæ hujus cursum significat. De ipsis autem mille annis alibi dicendum erit.

καὶ ζωὴν αἰώνιον κληρονομήσει] Quod olim in Levitis erat adumbratum, de quibus pulchre Philo: ὗτοι καταλελοί- πασι τέκνα, γονεῖς, ἀδελφὸς, τὰ οἰκειότατα καὶ φίλτατα, ἵν' ἀντὶ θνητῶν ἀθάνατον κλῆρον εὕρωνται.

## 19:30
Verse 30. πρῶτοι ἔσχατοι καὶ ἔσχατοι πρῶτοι. This is a transition to the following treatment by which Christ indicates that it will come to pass that the Gentiles, while the Jews pride themselves on the antiquity of the covenant initiated with them, and among the Jews those who were most despised because of the sins of their former life, while others despised the remedy of repentance, are preferred by the most just judgment of God. But Christ is accustomed to indicate such things more obscurely, as we have noted elsewhere. Therefore, the fable that follows does not have a clear ἀνταπόδοσιν, but in its place a maxim common in general usage, which both begins and closes the narrative. The same maxim adapted to this sense of which I speak is found in Luke 13:28, 29, 30, with which place one should compare Matthew 8:11, 12, chapter 21:31, 32, and then indeed Luke 7:29, 30.

Cornelius Jansenius in his Concordance of the Gospels, chapter 101, explains the scope of this parable not dissimilarly. He says that it is signified by this parable that the Jews served God plainly as if they were mercenaries, but the Gentiles trusted more in His grace than the Jews, for which reason they are also signified to have been preferred to the Jews, not indeed by their own merit, but by the sole good pleasure of God, while the last are said by the Master of the house to be preferred to the first in such a way that they both received the reward before them, and a reward far exceeding the labor, when those only received what was agreed upon and owed: Jansenius further warns that the parable should not be extended beyond this scope: Although therefore in the parable the last and the first are said to have received the same reward, namely a denarius, it is not to be understood in the matter signified by the parable that the last and the first will receive the same reward from God:

but this only is to be understood as being signified, which has been said: that, however, which does not agree with the intended scope, is to be omitted, as only agreeing with the human example itself. And so it is not to be inquired what is mystically signified by the denarius. This is that Cornelius. Ludovicus Granatensis in his Epistle on the Concordance, page 124, observes that the whole parable looks primarily to this, to demonstrate the liberality and freedom of the Lord in the distribution of His gifts. Which things are in agreement with the opinion of our people, as from the Commentary of B. Hunnius. it is evident: who, although here he says generally that those words, many who are first are last, aim at this, that the sum of eternal salvation is demonstrated to be referred not to any labor or work of ours, but to the grace and beneficence of the most benign God alone, yet in the explanation of the parable in the following chapter he understands these things specifically concerning the Jews and Gentiles: namely, that it is indicated mystically that the Gentiles precede the Jews in the kingdom of God, and those who were last, and plainly cut off and alienated from the life of God, now become the first of all in the kingdom of Christ; furthermore, that those who had been first turn out to be last, and are plainly rejected, so that although they are in the number of the called, yet because of their trust in the labor and work performed, that is, because of an opinion of their own holiness and righteousness, and likewise because of their murmuring against God and envy toward their neighbor, they are not in the number of the elect, according to the saying of Christ, many are called, few are chosen. Whence it is clear that that parable, if you look at its proper scope, is so far from favoring the doctrine of the Papists concerning justification by works and the merits of works, that it rather plainly opposes it, even by the opinion of the Papists themselves, if indeed the whole parable tends to this, that trust in one's own labor and works may be confounded, and that in turn the goodness and clemency of the eternal Master of the house alone may reign and rule in the matter of salvation. The scope primarily intended by the Lord in the proposal of the parable, says Jansenius, seems to be this, that we may understand that on the last day, when the end of this day shall be in which it is permitted to work in the vineyard of the Lord, it will come to pass by the kindness of God that those who here have been reckoned the last shall then be preferred to those who here have been held as the first laborers in the vineyard of the Lord, and that, conversely, without any injustice and just complaint, those who here seemed to hold the first places shall then hold the last, that is, that the Apostles and abject men shall be preferred to the Scribes and Pharisees, and the Gentiles to the Jews, who were first called by the Lord and claimed for themselves the first parts in the vineyard of God and the kingdom of heaven. To which Vasquez the Jesuit does not dissent, T. I. in 1. Tim. Disp. XLVII. c. 4. Cornel. à Lapide in h. l.

Latin:

Vers. 30. πρῶτοι ἔσχατοι καὶ ἔσχατοι πρῶτοι.] Transgressio est ad sequentem tractationem qua Christus futurum indi- cat, ut Gentiles, Judæis fœderis secum initi antiquitate su- perbientibus, atque inter Judæos hi, qui ob prioris vitæ peccata erant comtemtissimi aliis pœnitentiæ remedium contemnentibus, æquissimo Dei judicio præferantur. So- let autem Christus tales obscurius indicare, ut alibi notavimus. Ideo quæ sequitur fabella non habet claram ἀνταπόδοσιν, sed ejus loco γνώμην tritam usu com- muni, quæ & inchoat & claudit narrationem. Eadem γνώμη huic quem dico sensui aptata invenitur Luc. XIII. 28. 29. 30. cum quo loco conferendum Matth. IIX. 11. 12. cap. XXI. 31. 32. tum vero Luc. VII. 29. 30.

Scopum etiam hujus parabolæ non absimili- ter explicat Cornelius Jansenius in Conc. Evang. cap. CI. Significari hac parabola, Judæos pla- ne velut mercenarios Deo serviisse, gentes vero magis illius confisos gratiæ, quam Judæos, propter quod etiam prælatæ Judæis non suo quidem me- rito, sed solo Dei beneplacito significantur, dum novissimi dicuntur à Patrefamilias sic prælati pri- mis, ut & reciperent ante illos mercedem, & mer- cedem longe excedentem laborem, cum illi tantum pactam & debitam reciperent: Monet adhæc Jansenius, extra hanc scopum non extendendam esse parabolam: Quanquam ergo in parabola no- vissimi, & primi eandem dicuntur accepisse mer- cedem, nempe denarium, non tamen in re per parabolam significata intelligendum, novissimos & primos eandem accepturos à Deo mercedem:

fed hoc tantum intelligendum est significari, quod dictum est: id vero, quod non convenit scopo in- tento, omittendum est, tanquam tantum conve- niens ipsi humano exemplo. Itaque nec inquiren- dum est, quid per denarium mystice significe- tur. Hæc Cornelius ille. Ludov. Granatensis in Epist. Conc. pag. 124. totam parabolam huc po- tissimum spectare observat, ut liberalitatem & libera- tatem Domini in donorum suorum distributione de- monstret. Quæ consonant nostrorum sententiæ, ut è B. Hunnii Comment. constat: qui etsi hic ge- neraliter illa, multi primi sunt novissimi, eo colli- mare dicat, ut æternæ salutis summam non ad ullum laborem, aut opus nostrum, sed ad solius Dei benignissimi gratiam & beneficentiam refer- ri demonstretur, in explicatione tamen parabo- læ cap. sequ. specialiter hæc intelligit de Judæis & Gentibus: id scilicet indicari mystice, gentiles prævenire in regno Dei Judæos, & qui ultimi e- rant, planeque abscissi, & abalienati à vita Dei, nunc in Christi regno fieri omnium primos; eos porro, qui primi fuerant, evadere ultimos, pla- neque reprobari, ut licet ex vocatorum sint nu- mero, tamen ob fiduciam præstiti laboris, atq; operis, hoc est, propter opinionem sanctitatis & justitiæ propriæ, similiter ob murmur in Deum, & invidentiam adversus proximum ex electorum numero non sint, juxta sententiam Christi, mul- ti vocati, pauci electi. Unde liquet, parabo- lam illam, si scopum proprium spectes, Ponti- ficiorum doctrinæ de justificatione per opera, & meritis operum adeo non favere, ut potius eidem plane repugnet, vel ipsorum Pontificiorum sen- tentia, siquidem huc tota Parabola tendit, ut confundatur fiducia proprii laboris, & operum, utque vicissim in ratione salutis regnet, ac domi- netur solius æterni Patrisfamilias bonitas, atque clementia. Scopus à Domino in parabolæ proposi- tione præcipue intentus, ait Jansenius, videtur is esse, ut intelligamus in novissimo die, cum finis e- rit hujus diei, in quo operari licet in vinea Domi- ni, ex Dei benignitate futurum, ut qui hic reputa- ti sunt novissimi, tunc præferantur his, qui hic ha- biti sunt primi in vinea Domini laboratores, utque contra fine omni injustitia, & justa querimonia, qui hic primas tenere visi sunt, tunc postremas teneant, hoc est, ut Apostoli & abjecti homines Scribis, & Pharisæis præferantur, & gentiles Judæis, qui pri- mo vocati fuerunt à Domino, & primas partes in vinea Dei & regno cælorum sibi vendicarunt. Quibus non abnuit Vasquez Jesuita T. I. in 1. Tim. Disp. XLVII. c. 4. Cornel. à Lapide in h. l.

## 20:1 Argument
CHAPTER XX.

ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

The parable of JESUS concerning the householder hiring laborers into his vineyard and freely distributing wages to each; and the taking of the disciples for the journey to Jerusalem, to whom he predicts his passion and resurrection on the way: he warns the sons of Zebedee, seeking to sit at his right hand and left, concerning the drinking of his cup and that sitting at his right and left is to be granted only to those for whom it is prepared by the Father, and also concerning dominion, which is not appropriate for them but for the princes of the world: and to the example of himself, who came to serve and to give his soul as a price of redemption he recalls, restoring sight to two blind men as he leaves Jericho. There are two parts: the former of which still pertains to the preceding matters, namely I. The parable of the laborers in the vineyard, up to v. 16, the occasion for which was given by the conversation of Christ with Peter at the end of chapter XX: The latter, however, looks to the journey to Jerusalem; concerning which three things are designated in this chapter: I. The prediction of the passion, death, and resurrection of CHRIST, up to verse 19. II. The petition of the sons of Zebedee, and the correction, up to v. 28. III. The healing of the two blind men near Jericho, up to v. 34.

PART I. OF THE CHAPTER. The parable of the laborers in the vineyard.

Vers. 1. The kingdom of heaven] That is, the equity of the divine dispensation concerning the heavenly kingdom behaves itself in the same way as if a Householder went out, and what follows.

The heavenly kingdom seems to be understood as the kingdom of the other life; but because the murmurers and the non-elect have no place in that; No one, says Chrysostom, contends by right, or accuses, concerning such in the kingdom of heaven. Far from it. For that region is devoid of envy and jealousy, it is more correctly understood as the kingdom of grace, or the Church in this age: which is also compared to a vineyard everywhere: Deut. XXXII. 32. Ps. LXXX. 9. Is. V. 1. Cant. II. 16. c. VI. 10. c. VII. 12. c. VIII. 11. Matt. XXI. 32.

Luke XX. 9. The laborers in the vineyard are both generally all the called, or all Christians, according to Origen hom. X. on Matthew, Nazianzen orat. XL. on Baptism, Chrysostom in this place, and Augustine Serm. LIX. on the Words of the Lord, and specifically the ministers of the Church, whom Irenaeus l. IV. c. LXX., Hilary Can. CXX. on Matthew, Jerome l. II. against Jovinian, the Author of the imperfect work hom. XXXIV., and Gregory the Great hom. XIX. on the Gospels understand.

into his vineyard] Eis for the Hebrew ל. The Syriac לכרמה that is, for the use of his vineyard.

Latin:

CAPUT XX.

ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Parabola IESV de Patrefamilias operarios in vineam conducente, & mercedem qui- busvis libere distribuente: & assumtio discipulorum ad iter Hierosolymitanum, quibus passionem suam, & resurrectio- nem in via prædicit: filios Zebedæi sessio- nem ad dextram, & sinistram expe- tentes de calicis sui bibitione, ac ses- sione ad dextram, & sinistram nonnisi quibus parata est à Patre concedenda, nec non de dominio non ipsis sed princi- pibus seculi competente, monet: & ad sui exemplum qui venit ut serviret, ani- mamque suam in pretium redemptionis poneret, revocat, sub egressum e Iericho duobus cæcis visum restituens. Partes sunt duæ: quarum prior pertinet adhuc ad antecedentia, utpote I. Parabola de operariis in vinea, ad v. 16. cui occasio data a colloquio Chri- sti cum Petro cap. XX. extremo relata : Posterior vero ad iter Hierosolymitanum spectat; circa quod in hoc capite tria designata sunt: I. Prædictio pas- sionis, mortis & resurrectionis CHRISTI, ad vers. 19. II. Filiorum Zebedæi petitio, & corre- ctio, ad v. 28. III. Duorum cæcorum circa Jericho sanatio, ad v. 34.

PARS I. CAPITIS. Parabola de operariis in vinea.

Vers. 1. Ἡ βασιλεία τ̃ οὐρανῶν ἀνθρώπῳ] Id est, similiter se habet æquitas divinæ dispensationis circa regnum cœle ste, ac si Paterfamilias exiret, & quæ sequuntur.

Regnum cœleste videtur de regno alterius seculi intelligere; sed quia murmurantes & non electi in illo locum non habent; Nemo, inquit Chrysost. de talibus jure contendit, aut accusat, in regno cœlo- rum. Absit. Livoris enim ac invidiæ expers est illa regio, rectius intelligitur regnum gratiæ, vel Ec- clesia in hoc seculo: quæ vineæ etiam comparatur passim: Deut. XXXII. 32. Ps. XXC. 9. Es. V. 1. Cant. II. 16. c. VI. 10. c. VII. 12. c. IIX. 11. Matth. XXI. 32.

Luc. XX. 9. Operarii in vinea sunt tum commu- niter omnes vocati, vel Christiani omnes, juxta Origenem hom. X. in Matth. Nazianz. orat. XL. de Bapt. Chrysost. h. l. & August. Serm. LIX. de Verb. Dom. tum speciatim ministri Ecclesiæ, de quibus Iren. l. IV. c. LXX. Hilarius Can. CXX. in Matth. Hieronymus l. II. contra Jov. Autor oper. imperf. hom. XXXIV. Gregor. M. hom. XIX. in Evang. intelligunt.

εἰς τ̃ ἀμπελῶνα ἀυτ̃] Eis pro ל Hebræo. Syrus לכרמה id est, in usum vineæ suæ.

## 20:2
Vers. 2. for a denarius a day.] A denarius is a daily stipend according to Tacitus.

For the sake of the ornamentation of the parable, the denarius seems to some to be mentioned. Therefore, Jac. de Voragine warned that we should not investigate what is mystically understood by the denarius. But whether it is called a denarius, or comes under any other name, some reward is nevertheless noted in the recompense. Some of the ancients understand eternal life, Augustine Serm. LIX. on the Words of the Lord, the Author of the book on the Calling of the Gentiles l. I. cap. V., which most Roman Catholics seize upon: but some who receive the denarius murmur and are envious: which can be said of no one attaining eternal life: as Gregory the Great rightly observed. Some of our own understand Christ by the denarius, B. Luther, B. Balduinus, B. Meisner: But Christ is not given to the laborers, or for works performed in the vineyard. Wherefore more conveniently S. Irenaeus [speaks] of the knowledge of Christ, which is given to the laborers in the vineyard: they all received one denarius having the image and inscription of the King, the knowledge of the Son of God, which is incorruptibility, (causally) and therefore he began to give the reward from the last, because in the last times the Lord manifested himself to all: or if you prefer, generally a retribution is insinuated, whether bodily or spiritual. But Grotius is less correct, To me, he says, nothing occurs more probable than to refer the likeness of the denarius to any recompense whatsoever for work done well or badly, carnally or spiritually. For also the writer to the Hebrews II. 2 [speaks] of the recompense of reward in a similar way. Add Rev. XXII. 12. For it is not about the punishments which await those working carnally, or sowing in the flesh Gal. VI.

Latin:

Vers. 2. ἐκ δηναρίε τὴν ἡμέραν.] Denarius diurnum stipen dium Tacito.

Ornatus parabolæ causa denarius commemo- rari nonnullis videtur. Ideo non esse, quod inda- gemus, quid per denarium mystice intelligatur, monuit Jac. de Voragine. Sed sive denarius dica- tur, seu alio quovis nomine veniat, merces tamen aliqua notatur in ἀνταποδόσεj. Veteres nonnulli vitam æternam intelligunt, August. Serm. LIX. de Verb. Dom. Autor libr. de Vocat. Gent. l. I. cap. V. quod arripiunt Pontificii plerique: sed denarium accipientes quidam murmurant, & invidi sunt: quod de nullo vitam æternam consequente dici potest: ut recte Greg. M. observavit. Nonnulli e Nostris Christum intelligunt per denarium, B. Lyterus, B. Balduinus. B. Meisnerus: Sed Chri- stus non datur operantibus, vel pro operibus in vi- nea præstitis. Quapropter convenientius S. Ire- næus de cognitione Christi, quæ operariis in vinea datur: omnes acceperunt unum denarium habentem imaginem & inscriptionem Regis, cognitionem Filii Dei, quæ est incorruptibilitas, (causaliter) ac pro- pterea a novissimis incepit dare mercedem, quia in novissimis temporibus manifestatus Dominus omni- bus se revelavit: aut si mavis, generaliter retributio insinuatur sive corporalis, sive spiritualis. Minus autem recte Grotius, Mihi, inquit, nihil occurrit pro- babilius, quam δηναρίε similitudinem referre ad qua- lemcunq́, ἀνταπόδοσιν bene aut male, Cαρκικῶς sive πνευματικῶς navatæ operæ. Nam & μισθαποδο- σίας simili modo ad Hebræos Scriptor. II. 2. Adde A- poc. XXII. 12. Non enim de pœnis, quæ manent Cαρκικῶς operantes, vel in carne seminantes Gal. VI.

## 20:3
Vers. 3. ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ] In the marketplace usually spent their time men given to leisure, whom Luke calls ἀγοραίους in Acts XVII. 5. Cicero often calls them forenses: Festus calls them Ordinarios: Plautus and others call them scoundrels; the Romans even call them subrostranos. Ammonius: Ἀγόραιοι δὲ ἰὼν προπαραξύνοντας, σημαίνει δὲ πονηρὸν, τὸν ἐν ἀγορᾷ τετραμμένον.

Latin:

Vers. 3. ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ] In foro plerumque versabantur ho- mines otio dediti, quos ἀγοραίους vocat Lucas Act. XVII. 5. forenses Cicero sæpe: Festus Ordinarios: Plautus atque a- lii scurras; Romani etiam subrostranos Ammonius: Ἀ- γόραιοι δὲ ἰὼν προπαραξύνοντας, σημαίνει δὲ πονηρὸν, τὸν ἐν ἀγορᾷ τετραμμένον.

## 20:4
Vers. 4. ὃ ἐὰν ᾖ δίκαιον] What will be equitable, as the Syrian rightly translates: which words are also repeated below in verse 7 by the Greek books now, which the Syrian follows: but formerly they were understood, as appears from the ancient Latin copies. Δίκαιον, as often שׁוֶּה, signifies equitable here, as also in Philipp. I. 7. Coloss. IV. 1. 2. Pet. I. 13. We are accustomed to hire the labor of some in two ways, either by a stipulated wage, or by an indefinite promise of that which was equitable, whence the jurists say that an action arises not from a contract of hiring, but from prescribed words. Although it is not at all necessary for the individual parts of the fable to be referred to the ἀνταπόδοσιν, yet it does not seem to be without purpose that mention is made of a double hiring: because under the dispensation of the Sinaitic covenant, the reward of obedience was proposed as certain, definite, and obvious to the senses, namely the blessed possession of the land of Canaan, long life, and whatever else the law proposes. But under the dispensation of the new Zionitic covenant, the hope of the obedient is placed not in conspicuous things, but in the divine goodness, from which we trust we shall obtain those things which neither eye has seen, nor ear has heard. These are also repeated in verse 7, but Grotius gathers from the Latin copies that they are redundant there: But rashly: for Latin texts are to be corrected from the Greek, not the other way around. And the Syriac, Arabic, and Ethiopic editions agree with the Greek; the Greek interpreters Chrysostom and Theophylact retain them. But Grotius rightly observes that δίκαιον here, as often שוה, signifies equitable, as also in Phil. I. 7. Coloss. IV. 1. 2. Petr. I. 13. just as it is also rendered by the Syrian, whence from this word the Papists cannot gather the merit of good works, to which a reward is owed out of justice. For the Master of the house here shows his equity and kindness rather toward those who relied on merits, in rendering the reward, as Granatensis and & Jansenius.

Latin:

Vers. 4. ὃ ἐὰν ᾖ δίκαιον] Quod æquum erit, ut recte trans- fert Syrus: quæ verba & infra commate 7. repetunt nunc li- bri Græci, quos Syrus sequitur: at olim subintellige bantur, ut ex priscis Latinis exemplaribus apparet. Δίκαιον, ut sæ- pe שׁוֶּה æquum hic significat, ut & Philipp. I. 7. Coloss. IV. 1 2. Pet. I. 13. Solemus duobus modis operâ aliquorum con- ducere, aut præstituta mercede, aut indefinita promissione ejus quod æquum erat, unde non locati & conducti, sed præ- scriptis verbis actionem nasci ajunt jurisconsulti. Quan- quam autem nihil necesse est singulas fabellæ partes referri ad ἀνταπόδοσιν, tamen non frustra videtur duplicis condu- ctionis fieri mentio: quia sub dispensatione fœderis Sinai- tici, obedientiæ merces proposita erat certa, definita ac sensibus obvia, beata scilicet terræ Cananææ possessio, vi- ta longæva & quæ alia lex proponit. At sub dispensa- tione novi fœderis Sionæi, spes obedientium posita est non in rebus conspicuis, sed in bonitate divina, à qua confidimus nos impetraturos ea quæ nec oculos vidit, nec auris audivit- Repetuuntur ea etiam vers. 7. sed ibi illa red- undare è Latinis exemplaribus colligit Grotius: Ast temere: Latina enim è Græcis emendanda sunt, non contra. Et consonant Græcis Syræ ac Arabicæ, & Æthiopicæ editiones: retinent ea Interpp. Græci Chrysost. Theophylact. Recte au- tem observat Grotius, δίκαιον hic ut sæpe שוה æquum significare, ut & Phil. I. 7. Coloss. IV. 1. 2. Petr. I. 13. quemadmodum à Syro etiam reddi- tur, unde ex hoc verbo colligere nequeunt Pa- picolæ meritum bonorum operum, cui ex ju- stitia debeatur merces. Nam æquitatem & be- nignitatem suam hic potius ostendit Paterfami- lias adversus eos, qui meritis nitebantur, in red- denda mercede, uti fatentur Granatens. & Jan- senius.

## 20:6
Verse 6. And about the eleventh hour] Very late. It was said to Dejotarus, who was founding a city in his old age: O King, you begin to build at the eleventh hour. Plutarch relates this in the Life of Crassus; and Appian in the Parthian History.

These things are also understood by Ambrose, Hilary, Jerome, Basil the Great, Chrysostom, Isidore of Pelusium, and Fulgentius as the eleventh hour of life, or the final age of man: others, however, with Irenaeus (Book IV, ch. 70), Origen (Homily 10 on Matthew), and Nazianzen (Oration 40 on Baptism), prefer to refer it to the evening of the world; the former divide the hours according to the microcosm, the latter according to the age of the macrocosm. But it is better to refer these to the ornaments of the parable, not to pry into them curiously. The vigilance of the Householder is noted, in that he went out frequently and hired laborers from time to time, and even now continues to hire, calling some sooner, some later. Therefore, he is twisting ropes from sand when he gathers that the evening was made from the distribution of the reward, as Becanus does in Treatise 1 on Beatitude, ch. 1, q. 12. The Fathers of the Old Testament were not admitted into the kingdom of heaven until after the death of Christ: What then is to be said of those who died some centuries after the death of Christ, or who die even today; is it because the reward has already been distributed after the death of Christ, that it is now no longer distributed to them? Since the hour of distribution, which Becanus assigns, has long since passed. Keeping the scope of the parable in mind, says Jansenius, whatever of those things which are placed in the parable contributes something to that which is intended by the parable, must be diligently noted: the rest, however, are to be passed over, as things which are placed there only for the sake of the convenient narration of the example from which the parable is taken. We do not, however, disapprove of the pious accommodations of the Ancients, if they are kept within the analogy of faith. Thus Chrysostom. He hires laborers, for whom this present life is the time prescribed for working. He says that the laborers were called at the third, and sixth, and ninth, and eleventh hour. Who then are these? Certainly those who have believed at different times and in different ages. Furthermore, some are called at the first hour, namely those from childhood. Others at the third, who are around the flower of adolescence. Others at the ninth, of an age that has turned, already verging into old age. Finally, others at the eleventh, namely those already advanced into deep old age. It is permitted to interpret these otherwise, so that the first hour designates the times of Enoch and Noah. The third, the age of Abraham. The sixth, the time when Moses flourished. The ninth, the times of the Prophets. Finally, the eleventh, our conversion, that is, of the Gentiles, which happened at the end of the ages. For we Gentiles were ceasing from every good work for the whole span of the world, because no one had hired us, that is, no Prophet had been sent to us.

Latin:

Vers. 6. περὶ δὲ τὴν ἑνδεκάτην ὥραν] Sero admodum. Dejotaro in multa senectute urbem condenti dictum est: ὦ βασιλεῦ ἕνδεκα τῆς ὥρας οἰκοδομῶν ἄρχῃ. Narrat Plutarchus Crassi vita : & Appianus Parthico.

De undecima vita hora, vel postrema hominis ætate ab Ambrosio, Hilario, Hieronymo, Basilio M. Chrysostomo, Isidoro Pelusiota, Fulgentio hæc etiam accipiuntur: alii tamen cum Irenæo l. IV. c. LXX. Origene hom. X. in Matth. Nazianzeno Orat. XL. de Bapt. referre malunt ad mundi vesperam; illi horas juxta μικροκόσμυς, hi juxta μακροκόσμος ætatem partiuntur. Sed præstat hæc ad ornamenta referre parabolæ, non curiose rimari. Notatur vigilantia Patrisfamilias, quod frequenter exierit, ac operarios subinde conduxerit, atque etiamnum conducat, alios citius, alios serius vocet. Ideo funiculos ex arena nectit, cum è mercedis distributione suo vesperam facta colligit Becanus tr. I. de Beat. c. I. q. XII. Patres V. T. non nisi post mortem Christi in regnum cælorum admissos: Quid ergo de illis, qui aliquot seculis post Christi mortem diem obiêre, aut hodienum obeunt, dicendum, an quia jam merces distributa est post Christi mortem, illis nunc non distribuitur amplius? Siquidem jam pridem hora distributionis, quam Becanus assignat, transiit. Scopum parabolæ animo retinentes, inquit Jansenius, quicquid eorum, quæ in parabola ponuntur, aliquid facit an id, quod per parabolam intenditur, diligenter est annotandum: reliqua vero prætereunda sunt, velut quæ tantum propter exempli, unde sumitur parabola, commodam narrationem sunt posita. Non improbamus tamen ac commodationes Veterum pias, si intra analogiam fidei sistatur. Ita Chrysostom. Conducit operarios, quibus operandi præscriptum est tempus vita hæc præsens. Jam operarios vocatos ait circa tertiam, & sextam, & nonam, & undecimam horam. Quinam ergo hi sunt? utique qui diversis temporibus & diversis ætatibus crediderunt. Alii porro vocantur circa horam primam, nimirum qui à pueritia. Alii circa tertiam, qui circiter adolescentiæ florem. Alii circa nonam ætatis flexæ, vergentes jam in senium. Alii deniq́; circa undecimam, nempe in profundam jam provecti senectutem. Licet & hæc aliter interpretari, ut prima hora Enochi & Noæ tempora designet. Tertia ætatem Abrahami. Sexta tempus, quo Moses floruit. Nona Prophetarum tempora. Undecima denique conversionem nostram, hoc est, gentium, quæ in seculorum fine contigit. Nos enim Gentiles ab omnium bono opere toto mundi spatio cessabamus, quoniam nemo nos conduxerat, hoc est, nullus Propheta ad nos missus erat.

## 20:8
v. 8. but about the rewards distributed here. Nor did Basil interpret this place as Grotius did. Perhaps, he says, not to be accused on account of the evil things which one has done is common to all the obedient: for to be crowned is proper to those who have lawfully fought the good fight. But (adds Basil) the covenanted reward can also be those hundredfold things which the Lord promised that those who for his commandment have left whatever it may be of present things would receive in this time. Which explanation is akin to ours. Nor can it be proven that Grotius restricts the reward promised in the O.T. to temporal goods: and under the N.T. he thinks only heavenly things are promised: which Jansenius also believed, that the Gentiles receive a reward far exceeding their labors, namely the happiness of eternal life, while the Jews only attain the temporal reward promised to them. Although it is not at all necessary, says Grotius, for the individual parts of the fable (parable) to be referred to the ἀνταπόδοσιν (correspondence), yet it does not seem to be without purpose that mention is made of a double hiring: because under the dispensation of the Sinaitic covenant, the reward of obedience was proposed as certain, definite, and obvious to the senses, namely the blessed possession of the land of Canaan, long life, and whatever else the law proposes. But under the dispensation of the new Zionitic covenant, the hope of the obedient is placed not in conspicuous things, but in the divine goodness, from which we trust we shall obtain those things which neither eye has seen, nor ear has heard. That error, that in the O.T. only temporal goods were promised, which Grotius holds in common with the Socinians, and indeed also with the Pelagians, we have already noted often. However, it is clear that Parabolic theology is not argumentative: especially where the application is instituted outside of Scripture, much less when it is against Scripture.

Latin:

v. 8. sed de premiis distributis hic agitur. Neq; ita hunc locum interpretatus est Basilius, ut Grotius. Forte, inquit, non accusari propter ea, quæ quis fe- cit mala, commune est omnium obedientium: nam coronari proprium est eorum, qui bonum certamen legitime decertaverunt. Potest autem (addit Basi- lius) pacta merces etiam esse centuplicia illa, quæ in hoc tempore recepturos esse promisit Dominus his, qui propter mandatum ipsius dimiserunt quodcunq; tandem ex rebus præsentibus. Quæ explicatio no- stræ affinis est. Neq; probari potest, quod Grotius in V. T. promissam mercedem restringat ad bona temporalia: & sub N. T. solum cælestia promissa censet: quod etiam Jansenius credidit gentes merce- dem accipere labores longe excedentem, felicitatem scilicet vitæ æternæ, cum Judæi tantum mercedem temporalem eis promissam consequantur. Quan- quam nihil necesse est, inquit Grotius, singulas fa- bellæ (parabolæ) partes referri ad ἀνταπόδοσιν, tamen non frustra videtur duplicis conductionis fieri mentio: quia sub dispensatione fœderis Sinaitici, obe- dientiæ merces proposita erat certa, definita, ac sensi- bus obvia, beata scilicet terræ Cananææ possessio, vita longæva, & quæ alia lex proponit. At sub dispensa- tione novi fœderis Sionæi, spes obedientium posita est non in rebus conspicuis, sed in bonitate divina, à qua confidimus nos impetraturos ea quæ nec oculus vidit, nec auris audivit. Errorem illum, quod in V. T. tantum temporalia promissa fuerint bona, quem cum Socinianis, imo & Pelagianis communem ha- bet Grotius, sæpius jam notavimus. Theologiam autem Parabolicam non esse argumentativam con- stat: imprimis ubi applicatio extra Scripturam instituitur, nedum cum contra Scripturam.

## 20:8
Verse 8. To his steward] This word, apotropus, had also reached the Hebrews. The same is oikonomos elsewhere, in Latin, dispensers.

From the last even unto the first] That is, with no regard for order among them, or in such a way that no one is passed over. Otherwise it should have been said, from the first even unto the last, as it is in John 8:9, from the eldest even unto the last. But when equality is denoted, the expression is accustomed to be inverted, as from the small even unto the great, Acts 8:10.

Latin:

Vers. 8. ἐπιτρόπῳ ἀυτῷ] Vox hæc אפוטרופוס etiam ad Hebræos pervenerat. Idem οἰκονόμῳ alibi, Latine dispensatos.

ἀπὸ τῶν ἐσχάτων ἕως τῶν πρώτων] Id est, nulla ordinis inter ipsos habita ratione, seu ita ut nemo prætermittatur. Alioqui dicendum fuerat, ἀπὸ τῶν πρώτων ἕως τῶν ἐσχάτων, quomodo apud Johannem est VIII. 9. ἀπὸ τῶν πρεσβυτέρων ἕως ἐσχάτων. Sed cum æqualitas denotatur, solet inverti locutio, ut ἀπὸ μικρῶ ἕως μεγάλυ Act. IIX 10.

## 20:9
Verse 9. They received each] Thus physicians use this word in a distributive sense; the Hebrews say she.

This way of speaking was added not only for the sake of equality, but because he wished to indicate that this order was observed, by which, starting from the last, to whom the denarius was paid, the first were left in suspense as to what they were to receive, v. 10. But the last are said to have received each, which word Grotius notes is taken here in the same distributive sense that physicians use, and that the Hebrews say she in the same sense. And he refers to equality likewise those things in v. 14, as also to you. He acknowledges, however, that these seem to cohere poorly with that which follows below in v. 16, and indeed with the connecting particle thus; since here equality seems to be designated: there, inequality: and so much the more, if we observe that same thing which is below, the agreement, is referred in Luke to the Jews excluded from the kingdom, but the foreigners admitted. He thinks that this knot, which is accustomed to be solved in many ways, can be untied in this way: if, namely, the likeness of the denarius is referred to any kind of recompense, whether good or bad, worked carnally or spiritually: but we have already said what might be desired in that solution. More correctly, therefore, by the name of the denarius is understood any gracious retribution, of gifts both corporal and spiritual, of which those working in the vineyard are not destitute, even if they do not work equally, or those called to the Church, which they also receive, who are said to receive a hundredfold because they leave their own things for the Lord's sake: to which can also be referred primarily the knowledge of the Son of God, which those called to the Church do not lack, which the Jews also had in the Old Testament, and thus benefits of every kind, by which each is gifted, without distinction, not indeed as to the identity of quality or quantity, but as to the truth of the divine promises, and with the liberty of divine distribution saved, so that nevertheless no one is passed over, no one has cause to complain of injustice. But because some complain, murmur, or speak against, and envy others, such as the Jews primarily were, Christ teaches that they themselves are finally to be rejected because of ingratitude toward God, confidence in their own merits, and envy against their neighbor: and although they were first in the calling, and received their reward here, yet in the end they will be the last, and will be excluded from the kingdom of heaven. To this contributes the explanation of Basil the Great, that those promised rewards are those hundredfold things which they receive in this time or age, leaving their own things for the Lord's sake, so that that 'take what is yours' is said concerning this reward in this present time; but when those who seemed to have been exhausted labored under the vice of envy against those who obtained an equal fruit, they are to be condemned in the future age because of envy, and will hear 'go'. For everyone, he says, is condemned in his own sin, murmuring in murmuring. Others indeed murmur for one reason, others for another: some indeed because those things which satisfy are lacking to them, as gluttons, making their belly their God; others, however, because equal things are given to them with the last, show themselves moved by envy at the partner in the reward; others, however, for some other reason. Similarly, Chrysostom explains the reward, not concerning eternal life, but concerning spiritual gifts in this life: Moreover, this reward is the grace of the Holy Spirit, which has recovered us, and restored us to our ancient dignity, and made us partakers of the divine nature. And Origen: although those also, who lived before the coming of Christ, were partakers of the Holy Spirit, etc. We have spoken before of the not dissimilar explanation of Irenaeus. Præfius follows Basil, B. Gerh. and B. D. Dietericus in the explanation of the Gospel for the Sunday. Seventh, understanding by the denarius the gratuitous gifts of God bestowed upon individuals in this mortality, whether they regard this life or the future one. So good, says this one, and liberal is the Lord, that He does not leave any good, of whatever kind it may be, unrewarded, Is. 40:10, Ps. 62:13, Wis. 3:15, and he teaches at length how even infidels obtain a reward for good deeds here and receive their denarius: how likewise He gives to the faithful their denarius, both corporal and spiritual of divine graces. To which denarius of the faithful, however, we do not refer the reward of eternal life in this parable, both because this denarius is given when hypocrites and infidels are still mixed with the faithful, and they receive, by the force of the parable, also murmuring about their denarius, which cannot be said of eternal life: For no one murmuring, according to Gregory the Great, homily on the Gospel, Vol. II, receives the kingdom of heaven: no one who receives it can murmur: both because the denarius is given to works by contract, whereas eternal life is not given to works, but is a mere gift of God, Rom. VI. last, Eph. II. 8, Tit. III. 5, and because it is inappropriate that those who labored the whole day should have demanded more than eternal life as a reward, for what more can be given? But it is even more absurd that eternal life should be given to those who are indeed called, but not chosen.

It is therefore now manifest that the Papists rashly abuse this parable when they gather from it that eternal life is rendered for the merits of works as a reward: because eternal life is understood neither by the name of denarius or reward, nor is the matter here about the method of obtaining eternal life, but about the gratuitous remuneration of goods, nor is the reward, which is said to be rendered to the workers, a reward of merit or of debt, but of grace: since this word is taken both strictly and properly for the debt of the merit of labors, or compensation for labor, according to an adequate proportion; and broadly and improperly for the gratuitous retribution of labor, made by virtue of a promise: in the former, reward and merit are related, and there is an adequacy of work and reward, in the latter not so: just as in Matt. VI. 1 it is called μισθὸς, which in Luke VI. 32 is called χάρις: and Ps. CXXVII. 3 the fruit of the womb is called a reward, which nevertheless is called an inheritance, or gift of GOD in the same place: and GOD, or the Son of GOD, calls Himself the reward of Abraham, Gen. XV. 1, which reward Abraham certainly could not merit, or obtain through merits. Eternal life certainly cannot be held as a reward of debt; because (1.) if you look at the principle, it is given out of mere grace, on account of the merit of Christ alone: Rom. VI. 23. It does not therefore redound from our merits, Rom. XI. 6. (2.) If you compare the condition of works and eternal life, those are also owed to God, therefore we can merit nothing there from God by them, Luke XVII. 10, and they are too imperfect, therefore they merit not salvation, but eternal death; nor are they ours, but God's, Is. XXVI. 12, 2 Cor. III. 5, and therefore they do not render God a debtor to us, but us to God, as Bernard, Sermon I on the Annunciation, concludes: nor do they bring any good or advantage to God, Job XXII. 2, how then could they merit anything from God? Finally, they have no proportion in order to eternal life, Rom. VIII. 18. But there must be a proportion between merit and reward. (3.) If you look at the end of our operation, eternal life itself is nowhere assigned in place of a reward, even though the rewards of this and the future life are promised to it, 1 Tim. IV. 8, and a reward in heaven, Matt. V. 12, but heaven itself is nowhere designated as a reward to the faithful: concerning which we have cited elsewhere the suffrages of the Walenburch brothers and other Papists, in the Exegesis, namely, of the Augsburg Confession, art. IV and XX. Those among the Fathers who wish eternal life to be designated here by reward, understand it not by reason of merit, but by reason of the promise, not of debt, but of grace: just as Hilary called it a reward of mercy in Ps. CXXIX, and Prosper, book I, on the calling of the Gentiles, ch. 17. Therefore, he says, in the parable concerning those who labor in the vineyard, the same prize and the same reward is given to all workers, whether they have labored much or little, so that those who have sweated with much labor, and received no more than the last, may understand that they have received a GIFT OF GRACE, not a REWARD OF WORKS. And Origen, book IV, on ch. IV to the Romans, says: I can scarcely persuade myself that there can be any work that demands remuneration from GOD as a DEBT, since we do even this very thing, that we can do, or think, or speak anything, by His gift and bounty. Concerning eternal life, Augustine himself decides thus in Epistle CV to Sixtus: Therefore, O man, if you are about to receive eternal life, it is indeed a stipend of justice, but to you it is grace, to whom justice itself is grace. For it would be rendered to you as if it were owed, if justice were from you, to whom it is owed. Faith believes nothing more wholesome than this, because the intellect finds nothing truer. And Gregory the Great, in the seven penitential Psalms: To that blessed life, in which one lives with God and from God, no labor can be equaled, no works compared, especially since the Apostle says, the sufferings of this time are not worthy of the future glory. So also Lyranus in ch. X of John: Celestial glory is not properly called a reward, but only broadly, in so much as everything that is rendered as a prize for labor is called a reward. The reason for this, however, is because an inheritance is distinguished from a reward properly so called, just as a son, to whom an inheritance is owed, is distinguished from a hired worker, to whom a reward is owed. But celestial glory is rendered to the faithful, like an inheritance to children, for which reason it does not have the nature of a reward. John Ferus in the Commentary published in the year 1559, on ch. XX of Matthew: This parable teaches that whatever is given to us by God is grace, not a debt. Also all our righteousnesses are as filthy rags, indeed not even the sufferings of this time are worthy of the future glory. But if we sometimes hear a reward promised, we ought to know that it is not owed for any other reason primarily than from the divine promise. He promised freely, and He renders it freely and out of justice (the truth of the promise). If therefore you desire to preserve the grace and favor of God, make no mention of merits. What of the fact that Bellarmine himself, book II on grace and free will, ch. 3, acknowledges that if God wished to give a greater reward to someone, He would not be a respecter of persons, even if He did not observe this with everyone, since this is not of JUSTICE, but of LIBERALITY, according to that, friend, I do you no wrong. And book I on justification, ch. XIX, he confesses that for works which are done out of grace, that which is rendered is not simply a reward, but also grace, indeed more grace than reward.

Latin:

Vers. 9. ἔλαβον ἀνά] Sic vocem hanc sensu distributivo usurpant medici, Hebræi שׁיא dicunt.

Non æqualitatis tantum gratia hæc addita est loquendi ratio, sed quia hunc ordinem observatum indicare voluit, quo initio facto à novissimis, quibus denarius solvebatur, in suspenso relinquerentur primi, quidnam accepturi sint, v. 10. Dicuntur autem novissimi accepisse ἀνά, quam vocem eodem sensu distributivo, quo ea utuntur Medici, hic accipi notat Grotius: Hebræosque eodem sensu שׁיא dicere. Et ad æqualitatem refert pariter illa v. 14. ὡς καὶ σοί. Agnofcit autem quod male hæc cohærere videantur cum eo quod sequitur infra v. 16. & quidem connectente particula ὕτως; siquidem hic æqualitas videtur designari: ibi inæqualitas: tanto- que magis, si observemus idem illud quod infra est συμφώνημα, apud Lucam referri ad Judæos exclusos à regno, alienigenas autem admissos. Quem nodum multis modis solvi solitum, ita se expedire posse pu- tat: si nempe denarii similitudo referatur ad qua- lemcunq́; ἀνταπόδοσιν, bene aut male, Cαρκικῶς sive πνευματικῶς navatæ operæ: sed quid in ea solutio- ne desiderari possit jam diximus. Rectius ergo denarii nomine intelligitur quæcunque gratiosa retributio, donorum tum corporalium, tum spiritua- lium, qua non destituuntur operantes in vinea, utut æque non operentur, vel vocati ad Ecclesiam, quam etiam recipiunt, qui quod sua relinquunt propter Dominum, centuplicia recipere dicuntur: ad quam imprimis etiam referri potest cognitio Fi- lii Dei, qua vocati ad Ecclesiam non carent, quam Judæi etiam habuerunt in V. Test. adeoq; omnis generis beneficia, quibq donatur ἀνὰ, citra discri- men, non quidem quoad qualitatis vel quantitatis identitatem, sed quoad promissionum divinarum veritatem, & salva distributionis divinæ libertate, ut tamen nullus prætereatur, nullus conqueri ha- beat de iniquitate. Quia vero nonnulli conque- runtur, murmurant, vel obloquuntur, & invident aliis, quales imprimis Judæi erant, docet Christus eosdem tandem ob ingratitudinem erga Deum, fiduciam in propria merita, invidiam adversus proximum, rejiciendos esse: ac quamvis primi fuerint in vocatione, mercedemque suam hic ac- ceperint, olim tamen novissimos fore, & exclu- sum iri à regno cœlorum. Quo facit explicatio Basilii M. quod merces illa pacta sint centuplicia illa, quæ in hoc tempore vel seculo recipiunt sua dimittentes propter Dominum, ita ut illud tolle quod tuum est, de hac mercede dictum sit ἐν τῷ νῦν καιρῷ; cum vero invidiæ vitio laborarint hi, qui defatigati esse videbantur, adversus eos, qui æqua- lem fructum consecuti sunt, in futuro seculo con- demnandos illos esse, propter invidiam, audituros- que ὕπαγε, Vade. Unusquisque enim, inquit, in suo peccato condemnatur, murmurantes in murmu- ratione. Alii vero ob aliud murmurant: alii si- quidem eo quod desint eis, quæ saturent, ut gulosi, Deumque facientes ventrem, alii vero, eo quod cum postremis eis æqualia dentur, invidia se motos ostendunt mercedis consorte; alii autem ob quid a- liud. Similiter mercedem explicat Chrysostomus, non de vita æterna, sed de donis spiritualibus in hac vita: Est porro hæc merces gratia Spiritus Sancti, quæ recuperavit nos, & restituit in antiquam digni- tatem, ac divina participes naturæ fecit. Et Origenes: tametsi & ii quoq;, qui ante adventum Christi vixerunt, Sancti Spiritus participes fue- rint &c. De Irenei non absimili explicatione antea diximus. Præfius Basilium sequitur B. Gerh. & B. D. Dietericus in explic. Evangel. Dom. Sept. dona Dei gratuita singulis in hac mortalitate col- lata, sive hanc, sive futuram vitam respiciant, per denarium intelligentes. Tam bonus, inquit hic, & liberalis Dominus est, ut bonum aliquod, quale qua- le sit, irremuneratum non relinquat Es. XL. 10. Ps. LXII. 13. Sap. III. 15. ac prolixe docet, quomodo et- iam infideles remunerationem bonorum hic conse- quantur & accipiant denarium suum: quomo- do item fidelibus suum donet denarium, tum corporalem, tum spiritualem divinarum gra- tiarum. Ad quem tamen fidelium denarium in hac parabola non referimus remuneratio- nem vitæ æternæ, tum quia hic denarius da- tur, cum adhuc fidelibus mixti sunt hypo- critæ & infideles, & accipiunt, vi parabolæ, etiam murmurantes suum denarium, quod non potest de vita æterna dici: Nullus enim murmu- rans, autore Gregorio M. homil. super Evan- gel. Tom. II. regnum cœlorum accipit: nullus qui accipit, murmurare potest: tum quia denarius da- tur operibus ex conducto, vita vero æterna non da- tur operibus, sed merum est Dei donum Rom. VI. ult. Eph. II. 8. Tit. III. 5. tum quia inconveniens est, eos, qui totam diem laborarunt, plus quam vi- tam æternam postulasse pro mercede, quid enim amplius dari potest? magis autem adhuc absur- dum illis, qui vocati quidem, non autem electi sunt, etiam æternam vitam dari.

Manifestum ergo jam est, temere hac parabola abuti Pontificios, quando vitam æternam reddi meritis operum pro mercede, ex eadem colli- gunt: quia nec denarii, vel mercedis nomine vita æterna intelligitur, neque de ratione æternam vitam consequendi hic agitur, sed de gratuita bonorum remuneratione, nec merces, quæ reddi dicitur operariis, est merces meriti, vel debiti, sed gratiæ: quum vox hæc & stricte accipiatur, ac proprie pro debito laborum merito, seu compen- satione laboris; secundum proportionem adæqua- tam: & late ac improprie, pro gratuita laboris re- tributione, vi promissionis facta: illic merces & meritum relata sunt, & adæquatio est operis & mercedis, hic non item: quomodo Matth. VI. 1. μισθὸς dicitur, quod Luc. VI. 32. χάρις vocatur: & Ps. CXXVII. 3. fructus ventris merces nuncu- patur, qui tamen hæreditas, seu donum DEI ibidem dicitur: & DEUS, vel Filius DEI se dicit mercedem Abrahæ Gen. XV. 1. quam certe mercedem mereri Abraham, vel per merita ob- tinere non potuit. Æterna utique vita non pot- est merces debiti haberi; quia (1.) si principium spectes, ex mera gratia donatur, ob meritum unius Christi: Rom. VI. 23. Non ergo ex nostris meritis redundat, Rom. XI. 6. (2.) Si conditionem operum & vitæ æternæ conferas, illa & debita sunt Deo, ideo iis mereri illic à Deo nihil possumus Luc. XVII. 10. & imperfecta nimis sunt, ideo non salu- tem, sed mortem æternam merentur; neque no- stra sunt, sed Dei, Es. XXVI. 12. 2. Cor. III. 5. ideo- que non Deum nobis debitorem reddunt, sed nos Deo, ut Bernhard. Serm. I. de annunc. concludit: neque Dei boni quid adferunt vel commodi, Job. XXII. 2. quomodo ergo à Deo quidquam mereri possent? Denique nullam ea proportionem habent in ordine ad vitam æternam, Rom. IIX. 18. At inter meritum & mercedem proportio sit, oportet. (3.) Si finem operationis nostræ respicias, nuspiam mercedis loco ipsa æterna vita assignata est, etsi præmia hujus & futuræ vitæ ei promissa 1. Tim. IV. 2.& merces in cælis Matth. V. 12. nuspiam vero i- psum cælum merces designatur fidelibus: quo de fratrum Walenburchiorum, & aliorum Pontificio- rum suffragia alias adduximus, in Exegem. nempe August. Confess. art. IV. & XX. Qui è Patribus hic vitam æternam per mercedem designari volunt, non ratione meriti, sed ratione promissi, non debiti, sed gratiæ mercedem intelligunt: uti Hilarius mer- cedem misericordiæ vocavit in Ps. CXXIX. & Pro- sper l. I. de vocat. gent. c. 17. Ideo, ait, in parabola de his, qui laborant in vinea, datur idem præmium, ea- demque merces omnibus operariis, sive multum sive parum laboraverint, ut ii, qui multo labore suda- runt, nec amplius quam novissimi acceperant, intel- ligant se DONUM GRATIAE, non OPERUM ac- cepisse MERCEDEM. Et Origenes lib. IV. in c. IV. ad Rom. vix mihi, inquit, suadeo, quod ullum possit esse opus, quod ex DEBITO DEI remunerationem deposcat, quum etiam hoc ipsum, quod agere aliquid possumus, vel cogitare, vel proloqui, ipsius dono, & largitione faciamus. De vita vero æterna ita decer- nit ipse Augustinus Epist. CV. ad Sixtum: Quapro- pter o homo, si accepturus es vitam æternam, justitiæ quidem stipendium est, sed tibi gratia est, cui gratia est ipsa justitia. Tibi enim tanquam debita redderc- tur, si ex te esset justitia, cui debetur. Hoc nihil salu- brius fides credit, quia nihil verius intellectus inve- nit. Et Gregorius M. in sept. Psalm. pœnit. Illi beatæ vitæ, in qua cum Deo, & de Deo vivitur, nullus pot- est æquari labor, nulla opera comparari, præsertim quum Apostolus dicat, non sunt condigna hujus tem- poris passiones ad futuram gloriam. Sic etiam Lyra- nus in c. X. Joh. Gloria cælestis non proprie dicitur merces, sed tantummodo large, in quantum omne, quod redditur in præmium laboris dicitur merces. Ratio autem hujus est, quia hæreditas distingui- tur à mercede proprie dicta, sicut filius, cui debe- tur hæreditas, distinguitur ab operario conducti- tio, cui debetur merces. Gloria autem cœlestis redditur fidelibus, sicut hæreditas liberis,propter quod non habet rationem mercedis. Joh. Ferus in Comment. editis Ann. 1559. in c. XX. Matth. Docet hæc parabola, gratiam esse, non debitum, quicquid à Deo nobis datur. Omnes etiam justitiæ nostræ tan- quam pannus menstruatæ, imo neque ipsæ quidem pas- siones hujus temporis sunt condignæ ad futuram glo- riam. Quod si aliquando mercedem audimus pollice- ri, scire debemus, non ob aliud potissimum esse debi- tam, quam ex promissione divina. Gratis promisit, gratis & ex justitia (promissionis veritate) reddit. Si igitur Dei gratiam & favorem conservare cupis, nullam meritorum fac mentionem. Quid quod Bel- larminus ipse l. II. de grat. & lib. arb. c. 3. agnoscat, Si Deus alicui majus præmium dare voluerit, non fore acceptorem personarum, etiamsi non cum omnibus id observet, quoniam hoc non est JUSTI- TIÆ, sed LIBERALITATIS, juxta illud, amice, Tibi non facio injuriam. Et l. I. de justif. c. XIX. fa- teatur, operibus, quæ fiunt ex gratia, id quod reddi- tur, non esse simpliciter mercedem, sed etiam gra- tiam, imo magis gratiam, quam mercedem.

## 20:11
Vers. 11. ἐγόγγυζον] The LXX translate the word לזן thus, as in Exod. XVII. 3, Num. XIV. 24, and elsewhere. You would not translate it badly into Latin as to murmur against.

Latin:

Vers. 11. ἐγόγγυζον] Ita vocem לזן vertunt LXX. ut E- xod. XVII. 3. Num. XIV. 24. & alibi. Latine obloqui non male verteris.

## 20:12
Vers. 12. ἐποίησαν] This passage is to be interpreted according to Hebraism, not Latinity. The Syriac עבדו, that is, they had done the work, is excellent, in the way Terence speaks. For the Hebrews use both עשה and פעל in this way. See Ex. V. 9, compared with the passage Lev. XXIII. 7. So also Ex. XX. 9, 10. Indeed, as has been noted before, a similar עשת exists among the Hebrews, and in it the same manner of speaking.

Latin:

Vers. 12. ἐποίησαν] Ex Hebraismo non ex Latinitate in- terpretandus locus. Optime Syrus עבדו id est, opus fece- rant, quomodo Terentius loquitur. Nam Hebræi ita & עשה & פעל usurpant. Vide Ex. V. 9. collato loco Lev. XXIII. 7. Sic & Ex. XX. 9. 10. Imo ut pridem notatum est, extat similis עשת apud Hebræos, & in eo idem loquendi genus.

## 20:13
Vers. 13. ἑταῖρε] This form of address, slightly adapted to the context, is found both in Hippocrates and others: the same is below in chapter XXII. 12. It is placed thus by the Hebrews as עמי. The Latins would say 'good man' or 'my fellow'.

Latin:

Vers. 13. ἑταῖρε] Est & apud Hippocratem & alios hæc compellatio leviter notis accommodata: eadem infra cap. XXII. 12. Hebræis עמי sic ponitur. Latini dicerent bone vir, aut, mi homo.

## 20:14
V. 14. θέλω δὲ] In this whole narrative, the vivid description (hypotyposis) is to be admired. For in this way we are accustomed to reject importunate respondents: thus I will; thus it seems to me. See also below v. 15.

ὡς καὶ σοὶ] This seems to cohere poorly with that which follows below in v. 16, and indeed with the connecting particle ὥστε. For here an equality seems to be designated; there, an inequality: and so much the more if we observe that the same epiphonema which is below in Luke refers to the Jews excluded from the kingdom, but the Gentiles admitted. I see this knot solved in many ways. Nothing occurs to me as more probable than that the analogy refers the similarity to any kind of recompense, whether good or bad, for work performed, whether carnally or spiritually. For the writer to the Hebrews also uses μισθαποδοσίαν in a similar way in chapter II. 2. Add Apoc. XXII. 12. And in this, indeed, divine equity appears; but in that, supreme goodness appears, in that God, winking at the times of ignorance, makes those taught long ago equal to those taught later. Nor has Basil interpreted this passage otherwise. See also what we said above on the word δίκαιον.

Latin:

V. 14. θέλω δὲ] In omni hac narratione admiranda est ὑ- ποτύπωσις. Nam hoc modo rejicere solemus importunos re- sponsatores: ita volo: ita mihi videtur. Vide & infra v. 15.

ὡς καὶ σοὶ] Male cohærere hoc videtur cum eo quod sequi- tur infra v. 16. & quidem connectente particula ὥστε. Hic enim æqualitas videtur designari: ibi inæqualitas: tan- toque magis si observemus idem illud quod infra est ἐπιφώ- νημα apud Lucam referre ad Judæos exclusos à regno, alie- nigenas autem admissos. Video multis modis hunc no- dum solvi. Mihi nihil occurrit probabilius, quam ἀναλογίᾳ similitudinem referri ad qualemcunque ἀνταπόδοσιν bene aut male, σαρκικῶς sive πνευματικῶς navatæ operæ. Nam & μισθαποδοσίαν simili modo usurpat ad Hebræos Scriptor cap. II. 2. Adde Apoc. XXII. 12. Et in hoc quidem æquitas divina: in eo autem summa & benignitas apparent, quod Deus ad ignorantiæ tempora connivens pridem edoctos se- rius edoctis adæquat. Neque aliter hunc locum interpreta- tus est Basilius. Vide & quæ diximus supra ad vocem δίκαιον.

## 20:15
Vers. 15. ἢ οὐκ ἔξεστί μοι ποιῆσαι ὃ θέλω ἐν τοῖς ἐμοῖς] I have already said that importunate people are accustomed to be rejected in this way. Nor should it be thought that nothing else can be said for the divine dispensation than that 'thus I will, thus I command,' since of this very dispensation the causes are more often rendered elsewhere, such as would most befit divine wisdom. But this is God's custom: He often renders the reasons for His counsels to those who humbly venerate Him, as in Genesis 13. To the contumacious, by right of authority, He imposes silence: as if a King were saying to thick-headed men asking about a most just law, 'Shall I render to you the reason for My counsels?'
