Grotius notes these things correctly, provided, however, that those things which we warned of before are observed. The Calvinists are therefore in vain when they strive to carve out their absolute decree from this: especially also, because this is not a matter of the causes of predestination, but of the mode of divine dispensation in the retribution of labors, and the equity of the divine dispensation is asserted alongside absolute power in such matters.

If your eye is evil] 'If' is not causal here but interrogative, as the Syrian and Latin have rendered it, as above in chapter 12, 10. An 'evil eye' among the Hebrews is properly the character of an envious person: just as the Greeks also say 'an envious eye' (βάσκανον ὀφθαλμὸν), whence the Latin 'fascinus' (bewitchment), the power of which was believed to be in the eyes. Hence it began to be transferred to the miser, as in Proverbs 23:6, because a miser envies the use of his property both to himself and to others. Therefore, the miser's eye is called not only 'evil' (πονηρὸς) but also 'envious' (φθονερὸς) in the same sense in Tobit 4:7 and 17: 'Let not your eye be envious in doing alms.' Ecclesiasticus 14:10: 'An evil eye is envious over bread.' One must also see what precedes in the same place. The Latins also, when they depict an envious person, say that his eyes ache from the advantages of others. In Libanius there is: 'Envy is a grievous eye' (φθόνος χαλεπὸς ὀφθαλμός).

Latin:

Vers. 15. ἢ οὐκ ἔξεστί μοι ποιῆσαι ὃ θέλω ἐν τοῖς ἐμοῖς] Jam dixi ita rejici solere importunos. Neque ideo cogitan- dum est nihil aliud dici posse pro divina dispensatio- ne quam illud sic volo, sic jubeo, cum hujus ipsius dispensationis causæ alibi sæpius reddantur, tales quæ di- vinam sapientiam maxime deceant. Sed is mos est Deo: humiliter se venerantibus exactas sæpe reddit confilio- rum suorum rationes, ut Genes. XIII. Contumacibus ju- re imperii silentium indicit: quasi Rex crassis hominibus de lege æquissima quærentibus diceret, vobisne ego con- filiorum meorum rationem reddam?

Recte hæc notat Grotius, observatis tamen iis, quæ antea monuimus. Frustra ergo sunt Calvi- niani, cum inde absolutum suum decretum exscul- pere satagunt: imprimis etiam, quia hic non de caufis prædestinationis, sed de modo dispensationis divinæ in retributione laborum agitur, & juxtà cum absoluta in talibus potestate æquitas divinæ dispensationis asseritur.

Εἰ ὁ ὀφθαλμός συ πονηρός ἐστι] εἰ non est hic causale sed percunctativum, quomodo Syrus & Latinus reddiderunt, ut supra cap. XII, 10. ὀφθαλμὸς πονηρὸς Hebræis proprie est χα- ρακτὴρ invidi: quomodo & βάσκανον ὀφθαλμὸν dicunt Græ- ci, unde Latinorum fascinus, cujus vis esse in oculis credi- ta. Hinc ad avarum traduci cœpit, ut Proverb. XXIII. 6. quia avarus & sibi & aliis rei suæ usum invidet. Itaque avari oculus, ut πονηρὸς ita & φθονερὸς dicitur sensu eodem Tobæ IV. 7. & 17. μὴ φθονησάτω συ ὁ ὀφθαλμός ἐν τῷ ποι- εῖν ἐλεημοσύνην. Ecclesiastici XIV. 10. ὀφθαλμὸς πονηρὸς φθονερὸς ἐπ’ ἄρτῳ. Videnda & quæ ibidem antecedunt. Latini quoque cum invidum depingunt, dolere ei oculos dicunt ex alienis commodis. Apud Libanium est: φθόνος χαλεπὸς ὀφθαλμός.

## 20:16
Verse 16. Thus] Since God will not look to the virtues of ancestors and external righteousness, in which the Jews are accustomed to trust, but to the obedience of faith, which is never fruitless, however late, if it is serious.

For many are called, but few are chosen] Just as the words 'to call' (καλεῖν) and 'to choose' (ἐκλέγειν) receive various meanings, so too do these verbal nouns, which approach most closely to the nature of passive participles, except that they denote a remaining quality rather than a transient act. Just as 'the anointed one' (ὁ κεχρισμένος) is he who has been anointed in any way; but 'Christ' (Χριστὸς) is he who retains a right from the anointing. But this distinction is not always observed. For below in chapter 22, the same people are called indiscriminately 'invited' (κεκλημένοι) and 'called' (κλητοὶ), who were, namely, invited to the wedding, both those who had come and those who had not come. But because the words themselves are also sometimes used in such a way that they include the intended effect in the action, therefore in many places 'called' (κλητὸς) is a name of honor, as in Romans 1:16, 1 Corinthians 1:1, 2, 24, Jude 1, just as also among the Hebrews 'those called to the assembly' (קראי מועד) are 'the called' (οἱ κλητοὶ) or, as the Septuagint translate, 'the called of the council' (οἱ συγκλητοὶ τῆς βυλῆς). And in this sense, when there is talk of Christians, they are sometimes used for the same thing, and are even joined exegetically as 'called and chosen' (κλητοὶ κὶ ἐκλεκτοὶ) in Revelation 17:14. Furthermore, it appears here that the word 'called' (κλητῶν) extends more widely than 'chosen' (ἐκλεκτῶν), as also below in chapter 22, where this opinion (γνώμη) is repeated in the same words. Greek writers also explain 'chosen' (ἐκλέκτον) as 'the selected' (τὸ ἐκκρίτον), 'the excellent' (τὸ ἐξαίρετον), which is distinguished in any matter, whether by its own quality or even by the estimation of others. The Hellenists, whom the writers of the New Testament follow throughout, are accustomed to interpret the Hebrew 'chosen' (בחור or בחיר) in this way: sometimes also other words, as behold Psalm 41:4, 'with their delights' (במנעמיהם), the Septuagint translate 'with their chosen ones' (μετὰ τῶν ἐκλεκτῶν αὐτῶν), and Isaiah 29:16, 'a tried stone' (אבן בחן), 'a precious chosen stone' (λίθον πολυτελῆ ἐκλεκτὸν), but Peter 'a chosen precious stone' (λίθον ἐκλεκτον ἔντιμον) in 1 Peter 2:4, 6. Again, the Septuagint, where it is in the Hebrew 'chosen' (בחור) concerning Saul in 1 Samuel 9:2, translated it 'of goodly stature' (ἐυμεγέθης). Thus also Salvianus said that testimonies of chosen and wise pagans were brought forward. And these indeed denote the most proper quality of the thing. That which is in Isaiah 42, where in the Hebrew 'my chosen' (בחירי) is 'my chosen' (ἐκλεκτός μυ) among the Septuagint, our writers, as we saw before, have placed 'beloved' (ἀγαπητός). Just as Justin also in his Epistle to Diognetus, refuting the Jews who think 'the circumcision of the flesh' (τὴν μείωσιν τῆς σαρκὸς) is 'a testimony of election' (μαρτύριον ἐκλογῆς), interprets that word as 'as if for this reason especially beloved' (ὡς διὰ τῦτο ἐξαιρέτως ἠγαπημένυς). But just as divine love has its degrees, so also the title of 'chosen' (ἐκλεκτῶν) is taken now more loosely, now more strictly. For now all Israelites are called 'chosen' (ἐκλεκτοὶ) universally, as the peculiar people of God, 'O sons of Jacob His chosen' (υἱοὶ Ἰα- κὼβ ἐκλεκτοὶ αὐτῶ) Psalm 105:6. Thus this word is taken in Psalm 106:5 and 83:13 and in the book of Ecclesiasticus 46:2. Elsewhere, not just anyone from the people is so called, but either those who excelled in strength, 2 Samuel 6:1, or in holiness or office, as Moses in Psalm 106:23, Saul, 2 Samuel 21:6, David, Psalm 89:3, Ecclesiasticus 47:25, Nehemiah in the same writer chapter 49:15. And the writer of the second book of Maccabees chapter 1:15, speaking of God, says, 'He who made the fathers chosen' (ὁ ποιήσας τὸν πατέρας ἐκλεκτὸς), which he explains

by 'having sanctified them' (ἁγιάσας αὐτούς). Often also truly pious men are called 'chosen' (ἐκλεκτοὶ), just as in Isaiah 65:9 and 22, GOD calls 'chosen' (ἐκλεκτούς) the same ones whom He also calls 'servants' (δούλους) and 'blessed seed' (σπέρμα εὐλογημένον), just as the writer of Ecclesiasticus seems to use that word in chapter 17, verse 7. For Sirachides also calls the same ones 'chosen' (ἐκλεκτούς) whom he calls 'holy' (ὁσίους) in chapter 3, verse 9. And this meaning is most accepted in the books of the New Testament, as in Romans 16:3, Colossians 3:12, where it is 'chosen of God, holy and beloved' (ἐκλεκτοὶ Θεῦ ἅγιοι κὴ ἠγαπημένοι): and 1 Peter 2:9 and often elsewhere, as we shall see in their places. Suidas from some ancient writer not badly: 'The flock which the Scripture has named chosen.' And that this word was customary among the ancient Christians in this sense appears also from Justin and Clement: which meaning also fits this passage. For as the comparison of the place which is below in chapter 22 shows, all those whom God deems worthy of the Evangelical calling are called 'called' (κλητοὶ): but 'chosen' (ἐκλεκτοὶ) are those who come when called and conduct themselves worthily of the calling, and whose obedience is therefore pleasing to God. See what we shall say about this word at Luke 23:35, and add to what has already been said. It appears, however, that this opinion (γνώμη) was also common in the speech of the Hebrews, which Theodoret explains in his book on practical virtue with this Greek adage: 'Many are the wand-bearers, but few are the Bacchants.'

Other Christians likewise cite in support of the same opinion that saying of Plato: ὦ Φημι δυνατὸν εἶναι κἀνθρώποις μακαρίοις τε κὴ ἐνδαίμοσι γενέσθαι πλὴν ὀλίγων. Sinai, a Hebrew teacher, as is read in the Talmudic writings, said: Only two out of six hundred thousand shall enter the land of Canaan. Thus the matter will stand in the times of the Messiah. In the Epistle of Barnabas, which both Clement and Origen use, we have these words: When you see such signs and wonders among the people of the Jews (and thus the Lord abandons them), let us take heed, therefore, lest by chance (as it is written) we be found many called, few chosen. This coheres, however, in this way, if I am not mistaken, with the preceding: There is nothing unjust in it, that many of the Jews who are very pleased with themselves are postponed to foreigners, or even to publicans and harlots. For those were no less than these seriously invited to repentance and faith, through which they would have been able to obtain equally with them the rewards proposed to all, if they had obeyed the one calling. Although I do not deny that it can be explained otherwise, as proverbial sayings are wont to be adapted in various ways. For the called can be understood as all those who will effectively receive the reward of their labor: but the chosen as those among them who, because of the guilt of their past life, had need of a certain singular mercy, such as were most of those converted from the Gentiles.

Although the name κλητῶν occurs in the same sense as the word ἐκλεκτῶν in Apoc. XVII. verse 14, here however it extends more broadly, which is evident from chapter XXII. 14, as Grotius rightly says, since all are called κλητοὶ whom God deems worthy of the Evangelical vocation: but ἔκλεκτοι are those who come when called, and conduct themselves worthily of the vocation, and whose obedience is therefore pleasing to God: according to the same interpreter. Which sense we admit in certain places, Rom. XVI. verse 13, Coloss. III. v. 12, 1 Petr. II. Ef. XXIIIX. But we desire here that meaning besides, by which Scripture uses the name of the elect even more strictly, namely of those who, finally persevering in the faith, are predestined to eternal life, which is proper to this passage and the parallel in Matth. XXII. verse 14, where the same maxim is repeated. Compare Ephes. I. verse 4. But when MANY are said to be called, either the solemn vocation is understood, which was made through the Ministry of the Prophets or other ministers of the word, in which sense it is certain that not all, yet many, have been called; Deuteron. XXIX. v. 29, Ps. CIII. v. 7, Ps. CXLVII. v. 10, Is. LII. verse 15, Acts XIV. v. 16, or vocation is spoken of generally, by which those called in any way are designated, and thus those many called are said comparatively to the few elect, as all men, because the multitude of men is great: nor, when many are said to be called, are only some implied, but the entire multitude of men: just as also in Roman. V. verse 19, many are said to have been made sinners through the disobedience of one, that is, all. The descendants of Adam, no one excepted, so that it is not right to conclude any particularity from the many. FEW, however, are the elect, certainly not because of some absolute decree of God, because many are called, with the same intention of salvation, as far as God is concerned, therefore not one of them is absolutely rejected by God: and the causes are disclosed here, why the Jews were rejected and made the last: because of murmuring against God, and trust in their own merits, while God's grace, along with Christ's merit and justice, was held in contempt: whence an absolute decree must be banished: But of these things elsewhere against the heretical Predestinarians, and their successors the Calvinists.

Yet one must not say with Huber that all men are elect in a participial sense, or ἐκλελεγμένοι, even if all men are seriously loved by God, and by the power of that love redeemed by Christ, and called by the Holy Spirit; since divine love, which is universal, is one thing, and election, which is particular, is another; whence few are called elect. Where the ἐκλεκτοὶ or elect taken nominally by Huber are rashly distinguished from the ἐκλελεγμένοι, the elect said in a participial sense: as if in this sense all were elect to eternal life by God, but in that sense, only a few are called elect, namely those who obey the divine election: because that distinction has no foundation in Scripture, and it is rightly observed by Grotius that κεκλημένους and κλητούς in Matthew 22 are used indiscriminately, namely those who were invited to the wedding, both those who had come and those who had not: and the elect are said to obey not the divine election, but the calling: for the election of a few is only because few obey the calling, and adhere to the calling God with true faith until the end. Therefore, Grotius not badly teaches the connection of this epiphonema with the preceding ones thus: There is nothing unjust in the fact that many of the Jews, who are very pleased with themselves, are postponed to foreigners, or even to tax collectors and harlots. For they no less than the others were seriously invited to repentance and faith, through which they would have equally obtained, alongside the others, the rewards proposed in common, if they had obeyed the one calling.

PART II. OF CHAPTER XX. Concerning those things which happened on the journey to Jerusalem. WHAT THEREFORE NOW FOLLOWS PERTAINS TO THE FOURTH PASSOVER OF CHRIST, INTO WHICH FALLS THE HISTORY OF THE PASSION, DEATH, AND RESURRECTION OF CHRIST. I. THE ANTECEDENTS OF THE PASSION OF CHRIST, WHICH OCCUR IN THIS CHAPTER. (I.) The prediction of the passion, death, and resurrection of Christ.

Latin:

Vers. 16. ὕτως] Quandoquidem non respiciet Deus ad majorum virtutes & exteriorem justitiam cui Judæi solent confidere, sed ad obedientiam fidei, quæ nunquam infru- ctuosa, quantumvis sera, si seria.

πολλοὶ γάρ εἰσι κλητοὶ, ὀλίγοι δὲ ἐκλεκτοὶ] Sicut verba κα- λεῖν & ἐκλέγειν varios accipiunt significatus, ita & nomina hæc verbalia ad participiorum passivorum naturam proxi- me accedentia, nisi quod manentem qualitatem potius quam actum transeuntem notant. Sicut ὁ κεχρισμένος est is qui quoquo modo unctus est;Χριστὸς autem, qui ex unctione jus retinet. Sed is discrimen non semper observatur. Nam infra cap. XXII. iidem dicuntur promiscue κεκλημένοι & κλη- τοὶ, qui scilicet ad nuptias erant invitati, tam qui venerant, quam qui non venerant. Quia vero verba quoque ipsa in- terdum ita usurpantur, ut actioni propositum effectum in- cludant, ideo multis in locis κλητὸς honoris est nomen, ut Rom. I. 16. I. Cor. I. 1. 2. 24. Judæ 1. sicut & Hebræis קראי מועד οἱ κλητοὶ aut ut LXX. vertunt οἱ συγκλητοὶ τῆς βυλῆς. Atque hoc sensu cum de Christianis sermo est, pro eodem interdum usurpantur, atque etiam ἐξηγητικῶς conjunguntur κλητοὶ κὶ ἐκλεκτοὶ Apoc. XVII. 14. Cæterum hic apparet κλητῶν quam ἐκλεκτῶν vocem latius patere, ut infra quoque cap. XXII. ubi hæc γνώμη totidem verbis re- petitur. Ἐκλέκτον etiam Græci Scriptores exponunt τὸ ἐκκρί- τον, τὸ ἐξαίρετον, quod in re quaque eximium est, sive pro- pria qualitate, sive etiam aliorum æstimatione. Hellenistæ, quos passim sequuntur Scriptores novi fœderis, ita solent in- terpretari Hebræum בחור sive בחיר: interdum & vo- ces alias, ut ecce Psal. XLI. 4. במנעמיהם, cum deliciis eo- rum, LXX. vertunt μετὰ τῶν ἐκλεκτῶν αὐτῶν, & Es. XXIX. 16. אבן בחן λίθον πολυτελῆ ἐκλεκτὸν, Petrus autem λίθον ἐκ- λεκτον ἔντιμον 1. Ep. II. 4. 6. Rursum LXX. ubi est in He- bræo בחור de Saule 1. Sam IX. 2. transtulerunt ἐυμεγέθης. Sic & Salvianus dixit afferri se testimonia paganorum ele- ctorum atque sapientum. Et hæc quidem propriam po- tissimum rei qualitatem notant. Ad æstimationem illud pertinet, quod Es. XLII. ubi in Hebræo בחירי apud LXX. ἐκλεκτός μυ, nostri Scriptores, ut ante vidimus, posuerunt ἀγαπητός. Quomodo & Justinus in Epistola ad Diogne- tum, refutans Judæos, qui putent τὴν μείωσιν τῆς σαρκὸς μαρτ τύριον ἐκλογῆς, vocem eam interpretatur ὡς διὰ τῦτο ἐξαι- ρέτως ἠγαπημένυς. Sicut autem divina dilectio suos ha- bet gradus, ita & ἐκλεκτῶν titulus modo laxius modo strictius sumitur. Nam modo ἐκλεκτοὶ vocantur univer- se omnes Israëlitæ, ut populus Dei peculiaris, υἱοὶ Ἰα- κὼβ ἐκλεκτοὶ αὐτῶ Psal. CV. 6. Ita vox hæc sumitur Ps. CVI. 5. & LXXXIII. 13. & libro Ecclesiastici XLVI. 2. Alibi ita vocantur non quivis de populo, sed aut qui ro- bore præstabant, 2. Sam. VI. 1. aut sanctitate aut mune- re, ut Moses Psal. CVI. 23. Saul, 2. Sam. XXI. 6. Da- vid, Psal. LXXXIX. 3. Ecclesiastici XLVII. 25. Nee- mias apud eundem Scriptorem cap. XLIX. 15. Et Scri- ptor Maccabaici secundi cap. I. 15. de Deo loquens, ὁ ποιήσας, inquit, τὸν πατέρας ἐκλεκτὸς, quòd explicat

ἁγιάσας αὐτούς. Sæpe etiam ἐκλεκτοὶ vocantur homines vere pii, sicut apud Esaiam LXV. 9. & 22. DEUS ἐκλεκτούς vocat eosdem quos & δούλους & σπέρμα εὐλογημένον, quomodo & Ecclesiastici Scriptor eam vocem usurpare videtur cap. XVII. v. 7. Nam & Sirachides ἐκλεκτούς eosdem vocat quos ὁσίους cap. III. v. 9. Et hæc significatio receptissima est in libris novi fœderis, ut Rom. XVI. v. 3. Coloss. III. v. 12. ubi est ἐκλεκτοὶ Θεῦ ἅγιοι κὴ ἠγαπημένοι: & 1. Pet. II. 9. & alibi sæpe, ut suis locis videbimus. Suidas ex veteri aliquo Scriptore non male: 𝒯 𝜑ωλῖων ἧς ἡ γραφὴ ἐκλεκτὺς ὠνόμασεν. Atque hoc sensu vocem hanc veteribus Christianis fuisse usitatam ex Justino etiam & Clemente apparet: quæ significatio huic etiam loco convenit. Nam ut ostendit collatio loci qui infra est cap. XXII. κλητοὶ vocantur omnes quos Deus dignatur Evangelica vocatione: ἐκλεκτοὶ autem qui vocari veniunt & vocatione condigne se gerunt, atque adeo quorum obedientia Deo grata est. Vide quæ de hac voce dicemus ad Luc. XXIII. 35. & jam dictis adde. Apparet autem & hanc γνώμην tritam fuisse Hebræorum sermonibus, quam Theodoretes libro περὶ πρακτικῆς ἀρετῆς explicat hoc Græcorum adagio: Πολλοὶ μὲν ναρθηκοφόροι, παῦροι δέ τε βάκχοι.

Alii Christiani itidem in eandem sententiam citant Platonis illud ὦ Φημι δυνατὸν εἶναι κἀνθρώποις μακαρίοις τε κὴ ἐνδαίμοσι γενέσθαι πλὴν ὀλίγων. Sinai magister Hebræus, ut in Talmudicis legitur, dixit: Introierint in terram Canaan duo tantum è sexcenties mille. Ita se res habebit temporibus Messiæ. In Epistola Barnabæ illa qua utitur & Clemens & Origenes habemus hæc: Cum videritis tanta signa & monstra in populo Iudæorum (& sic illos derelinquit Dominus) attendamus ergo, ne forte (sicut scriptum est. multi vocati, pauci electi inveniamur. Cohæret autem hoc modo, ni fallor, cum superioribus: Nihil in eo iniqui est, quod multi Judæorum qui sibi valde placent, postponentur alienigenis, aut etiam publicanis & meretricibus. Nam illi non minus quam isti serio ad pœnitentiam & fidem sunt invitati, per quam pariter juxta istos impetraturi fuerant præmia in commune proposita, si vocanti paruissent. Quanquam non nego, & aliter exponi posse, ut solent proverbiales sententiæ variis modis aptari. Possunt enim vocati intelligi cum effectu omnes qui laboris mercedem accipient: electi autem inter eos qui ob anteactæ vitæ culpam singulari quadam misericordia opus habuerunt, quales fuerunt plerique ex gentibus conversi.

Nomen κλητῶν etsi eodem sensu cum ἐκλεκτῶν voce occurrat Apoc. XVII. vers. 14. hic tamen latius patet, quod constat è cap. XXII. 14. ut recte Grotius, siquidem κλητοὶ vocentur omnes, quos DEUS dignatur Evangelica vocatione: ἔκλεκτοι autem qui vocati veniunt, & vocatione condigne se gerunt, atque adeo quorum obedientia Deo grata est: eodem interprete. Quem. sensum admittimus in quibusdam locis Roman. XVI. vers. 13. Coloss. III. v. 12. 1. Petr. II. Ef. XXIIIX. Illam autem præterea significationem hic desideramus, qua Scriptura adhuc frictius nomen electorum usurpat, de illis nempe, qui finaliter perseverantes in fide, ad vitam æternam prædestinati sunt, quæ huic loco, & parallelo Matth. XXII. vers. 14. ubi eadem gnome repetitur, propria est. Cons. Ephes. I. vers. 4. Cum vero MULTI vocati dicuntur, vocatio aut solemnis intelligitur, quæ per Ministerium facta Prophetarum, aut aliorum verbi ministrorum, quo sensu non omnes, multos tamen vocatos esse, certum est; Deuteron. XXIX. v. 29. Pf. CIII. v. 7. Pf. CXLVII. v. 10. Ef. LII. vers. 15. Actor. XIV. v. 16. vel vocatio generaliter dicta, qua quomodocunque vocati designantur atque ita multi illi vocati συγκριτικῶς paucorum electorum, dicti sunt omnes homines, quia hominum magna est multitudo: nec, dum multi vocati dicuntur, nonnulli tantum innuuntur, sed universa hominum multitudo: quemadmodum etiam Roman. V. vers. 19. multi per unius inobedientiam dicuntur facti peccatores, hoc est omnes Adamigenæ, excepto nemine,ut fas non sit ἐ πολ- λῶν nomine particularitatem aliquam concludere. PAUCI vero electi, non sane ob Dei absolutum quoddam decretum, quia multi vocati sunt, ea- dem, quantum ad Deum, salutis intentione, non ergo eorum quisquam absolute à Deo rejectus est: & recluduntur hîc causæ, cur Judæi rejecti, & novissimi facti sint: ob murmur adversus De- um, & fiduciam in propria merita, insuper habita Dei gratia, cum Christi merito & justitia: unde absolutum decretum exulare oportet: Sed de his alias contra Prædestinatianos hæreticos, eo- rumque posteros Calvinianos.

Nec tamen cum Hubero omnes homines electi dicendi participia- liter,seu ἐκλελεγμένοι, etsi omnes homines à Deo serio dilecti, & vi dilectionis illius à Christo re- dempti, à Spiritu S. vocati sint; siquidem aliud sit divina dilectio, quæ universalis, aliud electio, quæ particularis est; unde ὀλίγοι dicuntur ἐκλεκτοὶ. Ubi temere ἐκλεκτοὶ seu electi nominaliter accepti ab Hubero distinguuntur ab ἐκλελεγμένοις electis participialiter dictis: quasi hoc sensu omnes electi ad vitam æternam sint à Deo, illo autem, pauci tantum dicantur electi, qui scilicet obsequuntur divinæ electioni: quia distinctio illa in Script. nullum habet fundamentum, & promiscue dici κεκλημένυς, & κλητὺς Matth. XXII. qui scil. ad nu- ptias erant invitati, tam qui venerant, quam qui non venerant, recte observatum Grotio: neque obsequi electioni divinæ, sed obsequi vocationi di- cuntur electi: ideo enim electio paucorum tan- tum est, quia pauci vocationi obsequuntur, Deoq; vocanti vera fide adhærent usque ad finem. Id- circo non male Epiphonematis hujus συνέχειαν cum præcedentibus ita docet Grotius: Nihil in eo iniqui est, quod multi Judæorum, qui sibi valde placent, postponantur alienigenis, aut etiam publi- canis & meretricibus. Nam & illi non minus, quam isti serio ad pœnitentiam & fidem sunt invita- ti, per quam pariter juxta istos impetraturi fuerant præmia in commune proposita, si vocanti paruissent.

PARS II. CAPITIS XX. De iis quæ in itinere Hierosolymitano acciderunt. QUÆ ERGO JAM SEQUUNTUR, AD QUARTUM PASCHA CHRISTI PERTI- NENT IN QUOD INCIDIT HISTORIA PASSIONIS, MORTIS ET RESURRE- CTIONIS CHRISTI. I. ANTECEDENTIA PASSIONIS CHRISTI, QUÆ IN HOC CAPITE OCCURRUNT. (I.) Passionis, mortis, & resurrectionis Christi prædictio.

## 20:17
Verse 17. privately on the way] Apart from the rest of the crowd following: to whom he did not indicate these things, lest by predicting them he might seem to have stirred up the hatred of the Jews against himself. But he said the same things to the Apostles more often, and daily more expressly, so that they might be witnesses of his foreknowledge in the future. If he did not indicate these things to them to avoid the hatred of the Jews, why then did he later openly predict to the same ones in Mark 12:8 that the son of the Lord of the vineyard, the heir of the vineyard, they themselves were going to kill, and that that same stone was to be rejected by them as the cornerstone, which, although said in a parable, the Jews understood was said about him, as Mark 12:12 testifies. Therefore that is not the reason why these things were said to the Apostles privately, but because the Apostles were chosen as witnesses of the passion and resurrection, which he therefore wished to predict to them, so that, seeing the event with their own eyes, they might understand that nothing else had happened than what he had predicted, and not by chance, but by divine counsel, and freely, indeed by his own authority, he had laid down his life: which he also professed to the Jews themselves in John 10:18.

Latin:

Vers. 17. κατ' ἰδίαν ἐν τῇ ὁδῷ] Seorsim à cætera sequen- tium turba: cui hæc non indicavit,ne prædicendo irritasse in se Judæorum odia videretur. Apostolis autem sæpius eadem dixit, & indies expressius, ut in posterum testes essent præscientiæ ipsius. Si ad declinandum odium Judæorum illis hæc non indicavit, cur ergo iisdem postea Marc.XII.8. palam prædixit,quod filium Domini vineæ, hære- dem vineæ ipsi occisuri essent,quodq; idem ille la- pis ab ipsis rejiciendus futurus sit lapis angularis, quod etsi in parabola dictum, de se tamen intelli- gebant dictum esse Judæi,teste Marco v.12. Non er- go illa causa est, cur seorsim Apostolis hæc dicta, sed quia Apostoli electi erant testes passionis, & resur- rectionis, quam proinde prædicere voluit iisdem, ut eventum oculis usurpantes nihil aliud, quam quod prædixerit, evenisse, nec fortuito, sed divi- no consilio, & libere, imo αὐτεξυσίως se vitam posuisse, intelligerent: quod ipsis etiam Judæis professus est Joh. X. 18.

## 20:18
Verse 18. he will be delivered up] He does not yet say that this would happen to him by one of the Apostles, so as not to stir up quarrels among them.

To the chief priests and scribes.] He names these especially, although there were others in the Sanhedrin, because both the priests by their holiness and the experts in the law by their learning ought to have shone before others.

However, he did not remain silent about others: for he had already made mention of the elders at the same time in Matthew 16:21. Interpreters observe that Christ predicted his passion five times (1.) in the borders of Caesarea Philippi, Matthew 16, Mark 8, Luke 9. (2.) eight days later, when he was transfigured on the mountain and was being asked about Elijah, Matthew 17:12, Mark 9:12. (3.) after healing the lunatic in Galilee, Matthew 17:22-23, Mark 9:31, Luke 9:22. (4.) when he was setting out for Jerusalem, in this place: Matthew 20:18, Mark 10:32, Luke 18:31. (5.) two days before the passion, Matthew 26:2. These predictions were made to the Disciples: besides which, however, other less clear predictions of the passion occur, made not only to the disciples, such as the discourse concerning his departure to the Father, but also to the Jews, when he spoke more obscurely in John 2:21 about the destruction of the temple of his body, in Matthew 12:40 about the son of man being in the belly of the earth, like Jonah, for three days and three nights, and also in Matthew 21:39 about the killing of the son of the Lord of the vineyard; then more clearly about his life being given for the life of the world in John 6:51, and in John 10:15, 17, 18 about the laying down of his life for the sheep: not to mention what he said before Nicodemus about his exaltation figured in the bronze serpent in John 3:15, and also before the people about his departure to him who had sent him in John 7:33-34, about the exaltation of the son of man on the cross in John 12:32-34, and about the grain of wheat dying in the earth in verse 24. and at the hour of death v. 27. he foretold; and what he spoke in his transfiguration concerning the departure which was to be fulfilled at Jerusalem, Luke IX. v. 31.

κατακρινῶσιν ἀυτὸν θανάτῳ.] Not by pronouncing sentence with judicial power, but by the prejudice of their authority: Mark XIV. 64. concerning the Sanhedrin, 'and they all condemned him to be guilty of death.' And here the writer below XXVII. 3. 'Judas seeing that he was condemned.'

He hints at this meaning while he foretells that he must be delivered to the Gentiles, because a judicial sentence was to be pronounced by Pilate the Gentile, Matt. XXVII. 26. Mark XIV. 15. Luke XXIII. 25. For the Jews themselves professed that they could not kill anyone, or condemn them to death, John XVIII. 31.

Latin:

Vers. 18. παραδοθήσεται] Nondum dicit id sibi eventu- rum ab uno Apostolorum, ne rixas inter ipsos concitaret.

Τοῖς ἀρχιερεῦσι κὶ γραμματεῦσι.] Hos præcipue nominat, quanquam alii erant in Synedrio, quia & Sacerdotes sancti- monia, & legis periti eruditione aliis prælucere debuerant.

Non tacuit autem alios: nam & πρεσβυτέρων si- mul mentionem jam fecerat Matth. XVI. 21. Quin- quies autem observant Interpp. Christum prædi- xisse passionem suam (1.) in finibus Cæsareæ Phi- lippi Matth. XVI. Marc. IIX. Luc. IX. (2.) octiduo post, quum in monte clarificatus de Elia interro- garetur Matth. XVII. 12. Marc. IX. 12. (3.) post sa- natum Lunaticum in Galilæa Matth. XVII. 22. 23. Marc. IX. 31. Luc. IX. 22. (4.) cum Hierosolymam proficisceretur, hoc loco: Matth. XX. 18. Marc. X. 32. Luc. XIIX. 31. (5.) biduo ante passionem Matth. XXVI. 2. Quæ prædictiones Discipulis factæ sunt: præter quas tamen occurrunt & aliæ, etsi minus lu- culentæ passionis prædictiones, non modo ad disci- pulos, qualis est concio περαγονὴ de abitu ad Patrem, sed etiam ad Judæos factæ, cum obscurius Joh. II. 21. de templi corporis sui destructione Matth. XII. 40. de filio hominis in ventre terræ, instar Jonæ, per tres dies, & tres noctes hæsuro, nec non Matth. XXI. 39. de filii Domini vineæ in- terfectione; tum clarius de vita sua danda pro mun- di vita Joh. VI. 51. & Joh. X. 15. 17. 18. de vitæ suæ pro ovibus positione: ut taceam quod coram Nicode- mo, de sui exaltatione in serpente æneo figurata Joh. III. 15. nec non coram populo de abitu suo ad eum, qui miserat ipsum Joh. VII. 33. 34. de exaltatio- ne filii hominis in cruce, Joh. X. 32. 33. 34. deque semi- ne tritici in terra emoriente v. 24. & hora mortis v. 27. prædixit; & quæ in transfiguratione sua, de e- gressu, qui complendus erat Hierosolymis, loquu- tus est, Luc. IX. v. 31.

κατακρινῶσιν ἀυτὸν θανάτῳ.] Non sententiam judiciali potestate pronunciando, sed præjudicio auctoritatis suæ: Marcus XIV. 64. de Synedrio δι δὲ πάντες κατέκρινον ἀυτὸν εἶναι ἔνοχον θανάτῳ. Et hic scriptor infra XXVII. 3. ἰδὼν ὁ Ἰύ- δας ὅτι κατεκρίθη.

Innuit hunc sensum, dum Ethnicis se traden- dum prædicit, quia à Pilato Ethnico sententia Ju- dicialis pronuncianda erat Matth. XXVII. 26. Marc. XIV. 15. Luc. XXIII. 25. Nam professi ipsi Judæi sunt, se non posse quenquam interficere, vel ad mortem condemnare, Joh. XIIX. 31.

## 20:19
Vers. 19. Τοῖς ἔθνεσιν] That is, to the Gentiles, in the manner of the Hebrews, who call גוים not only entire nations, but also individual foreigners: in which way Paul also often uses it. It is also entirely clear that Pilate is understood with all his council and retinue, Acts IV. 10. Moreover, Christ shows the indignity of the crime, that the Jews would use the work of those to destroy him, whose very contact they avoided: 'You have killed him with the sword of the Ammonites,' 2 Sam. XII. 9.

εἰς τὸ] The Syrian well explains it as a consequence, in the way that εἰς τὸ, ἵνα, ὅπως are often taken. For although the punishment of the cross was by the destination of the Jews, yet the scourging came from the outside. But all the evils were deservedly imputed to them, who by their own wickedness provided the occasion for the evils.

(II.) The petition and correction of the sons of Zebedee.

Latin:

Vers. 19. Τοῖς ἔθνεσιν] Id est τοῖς ἐθνικοῖς more Hebræo- rum, qui גוים vocant non tantum nationes integras, sed & singulos ἀλλοφύλες: quomodo & Paulus sæpe usurpat. A- pertum etiam omnino est, Pilatum intelligi cum omni con- silio, ac satellitio suo, Act. IV. 10. Ostendit autem Christus indignitatem facinoris, quod Judæi ad se perdendum illo- rum usuri essent opera, quorum etiam contactum defugie- bant: Occidisti eum gladio Ammonitarum, 2. Sam. XII. 9.

εἰς τὸ] Bene exponit Syrus ἐκβατικῶς, quomodo sæpe εἰς τὸ, ἵνα, ὅπως sumuntur. Quanquam enim supplicium crucis erat ex destinatione Judæorum, at flagellatio extrin- secus advenit. Sed merito omnia mala illis imputabantur, qui suo scelere occasionem malis præbuerunt.

(II.) Filiorum Zebedæi petitio & correctio.

## 20:20
Vers. 20. ἀιτῶσά τι παρ' ἀυτὲ] Salome seems to have conceived this confidence from the fact that no other mother of the Apostles followed Christ so perpetually, and served him so diligently. She cherished the hope of maternal ambition, because she had understood that her sons were sometimes taken aside by Christ without the company of the other Apostles, so that Peter alone seemed to be able to contend with them. That 'something' (τι) indicates, if I am not mistaken, the preface to the petition; for those who are about to ask for something are accustomed to preface that they are not asking for many things, but for one thing, so that they do not appear shameless. See the history in 1 Kings II. verse 15. This is the Salome whose certain conversations with CHRIST were circulated among the Egyptians. Among other things, they narrated that it was said to her by CHRIST, 'I came to destroy the works of the female.' Then she asked, 'Until when will men die?' The Lord answered: 'Until women give birth.' Again, when she had inquired about other matters and, as it seems, had been rejected, the insistent ones asked πότε γνωσθήσεται τὰ περὶ ὧν ἤρετο, the answer from Christ was ὅταν τὸ τῆς αἰσχύνης ἔνδυμα πατήσητε, κἂν ὅτ᾽ ἂν γένηται τὰ δύο ἓν κἂν τὸ ἄῤῥεν μετὰ τῆς θηλείας ὔτε ἄῤῥεν ὔτε θῆλυ. All of which have a clear element of truth (about which the ancients also rightly doubted: for those things do not seem to savor of that simple majesty which everywhere shines forth in the words of Christ) and do not need the subtly devised wrappings of allegories, which the ancients employed in interpreting those things, since it seems clear to me that nothing else is signified in those words than what Christ says in Luke, ὅτι οἱ καταξιωθέντες τῆς ἀναστάσεως ὔτε γαμῦσιν ὔτε ἐκγαμίσκονται· ἰσάγγελοι γάρ εἰσι. But what is said, that death will remain until women are about to give birth, agrees with the interpretation of the Hebrew philosophers on the passage Prov. XXX.16. where the grave and the womb are said to be insatiable, which they explain as corruption and generation, which perpetually succeed one another in turn until the end of this age: just as Hippocrates joined light and the grave when he said: νομίζεται δὲ παρὰ τῶν ἀνθρώπων τὸ μὲν ἐξ ᾅδε εἰς φῶς αὐξηθὲν γενέσθαι, τὸ δὲ ἐκ τῶ φάε- ος εἰς ᾅδην μειωθὲν ἀπολέσθαι. In which passage Hippocrates makes fire and water the principles of living things, of which two Solomon also makes mention in the cited passage, so that this can appear to have been transferred into Greece from barbarian philosophy.

Latin:

Vers. 20. ἀιτῶσά τι παρ' ἀυτὲ] Videtur Salome hanc fi- duciam concepisse ex eo quod nulla aliorum Apostolorum mater Christum ita perpetuo sectaretur, eique tam sedulo inserviret. Fovit spem materni ambitus, quod filios aliquo- ties intellexisset seorsim à Christo abductos sine aliorum A- postolorum comitatu, ita ut Petrus solus contendere cum ipsis posse videretur. Illud τι ipsam ni fallor petitionis præfationem indicat; Solent enim qui aliquid sunt postu- laturi præfari, non multa à se, sed unam rem peti, ne invere- cundi videantur. Vide Historiam 1. Reg. II. vers. 15. Hæc est Salome cujus colloquia quædam cum CHRISTO apud Ægyptios ferebantur. Inter alia narrabant ei di- ctum à CHRISTO ἦλθον καταλῦσαι τὰ ἔργα τῆς θηλείας. Tum illam quæsiisse μέχρι τίνος οἱ ἄνθρωποι ἀποθανῶνται. Respondisse Dominum : μέχρις ἂν τίκτωσι αἱ γυναῖκες. Rursum cum illa de rebus aliis percunctata & ut videtur re- jecta, instans quæsiissent πότε γνωσθήσεται τὰ περὶ ὧν ἤρετο, re- sponsum à Christo ὅταν τὸ τῆς αἰσχύνης ἔνδυμα πατήσητε, κἂν ὅτ᾽ ἂν γένηται τὰ δύο ἓν κἂν τὸ ἄῤῥεν μετὰ τῆς θηλείας ὔτε ἄῤῥεν ὔτε θῆλυ. Quæ omnia liquid habent veri (de quo merito anti- qui etiam dubitarunt: neque enim videntur ista sapere sim- plicem illam majestatem quæ in verbis Christi ubique elu- cet) non opus habent subtiliter excogitatis ἀλληγοριῶν invo- lucris, quæ istis interpretandis veteres adhibuerunt, cum mihi apertum videatur nihil aliud in illis verbis significari, quam quod apud Lucam dicit Christus, ὅτι οἱ καταξιωθέντες τῆς ἀναστάσεως ὔτε γαμῦσιν ὔτε ἐκγαμίσκονται· ἰσάγγελοι γάρ εἰσι. Quod autem dicitur, mortem mansuram donec pari- turæ essent mulieres, convenit Hebræorum Philosopho- rum interpretationi ad locum Prov. XXX.16. ubi insatiabi- lia esse dicuntur ᾅδης & os uteri, quod illi exponunt φθορὰν καὶ γένεσιν, quæ perpetuo mutuis se vicibus excipiunt ad finem usque sæculi hujus: quomodo φῶς & ᾅδην con- junxit Hippocrates cum dixit: νομίζεται δὲ παρὰ τῶν ἀνθρώ- πων τὸ μὲν ἐξ ᾅδε εἰς φῶς αὐξηθὲν γενέσθαι, τὸ δὲ ἐκ τῶ φάε- ος εἰς ᾅδην μειωθὲν ἀπολέσθαι. quo loco Hippocrates principia animalium facit ignem & aquam, quorum duorum et- iam Salomo dicto loco meminit, ut videri hoc possit ex barbara Philosophia in Græciam tralatum.

## 20:21
Vers. 21. One at your right hand and one at your left in your kingdom. The mother had heard from the sons that a dignity, as it were a chieftaincy, had been promised to the Apostles in common, as we said above: but she also knew that among those who were of equal rank there was some order: just as in the ancient kingdom of Israel the two first places were those of the chieftains of the tribes of Judah and Joseph. These honors, therefore, she requests for her sons. To sit at the right hand of the king signifies the place of highest rank after the king. Thus Solomon, sitting on the royal throne, ordered his mother's seat to be placed next to him at his right side, 1 Kings II.19. Elsewhere the queen is said to sit at the right hand of the king, as in Psalm XLV.10. Nero, as is in Suetonius, placed Tiridates next to himself on his right side. Thus Christ himself, although a King in his own kingdom, when he is compared to God his Father, is said to sit at his right hand: or at the right of the throne, as the divine writer to the Hebrews speaks, chapter XII.3. To this also pertains that which we read in Daniel concerning polished thrones, two, namely, as Rabbi Akiba interprets, one for God the Father, the other for the Messiah. In exactly the same sense it was said of Minerva by Pindar: δεξιὰν κατὰ χεῖρα τῶ πατρὸς καθεζομένην, as cited by Aristides: which Horace expressed thus: Yet Pallas occupied the honors next to him.

The third place in the kingdom is consequently described by sitting at the left side of the king. For the greater anyone was in the kingdom, the closer he sat to the king in public assemblies.

To sit at the right hand of the King, according to Grotius, denotes the place of highest rank after the King, 1 Kings II.19, Psalm XLV.10. The third place in the kingdom is consequently described by sitting at the left side of the King. But that is wrongly applied to the sitting of Christ at the right hand of God; because this phrase is used of Christ in a far different sense, and is explained by the Holy Scriptures, namely by reigning, as is clear from a comparison of Psalm CX.1 and 1 Cor. XV.25. Therefore Christ does not hold the place next to the King, but is the King himself, and is distinguished by the same title as God the Father, King of Kings, Lord of Lords, 1 Tim. VI.16, Rev. XVII.14, ch. XIX.16, Lord of glory, 1 Cor. II.8, Lord of all, Acts II.36. And since there is but one Lord of Lords, Lord of glory, Lord of all, through whom are all things, 1 Cor. VIII.6, Eph. IV.5. Zech. XIV.9, Christ certainly does not occupy a different throne than the Father, nor is the dominion double, but the dominion of one Lord is only one, just as we are forbidden by the Christian religion to worship two Lords: there is one Lord, we profess in the Athanasian Creed, because just as we are compelled by Christian truth to confess each person individually as God and Lord; so we are forbidden by the Catholic religion to say there are three Gods or three Lords. But since the human nature of Christ must be believed to have been raised to the partnership of this one divine and supreme dominion and rule, so that our one Lord Jesus Christ may remain God and man, no other throne or inferior power can be assigned to Christ according to his human nature, who testifies that all that same power in heaven and on earth, which is God the Father's, has been given to him according to the flesh, Matt. XXVIII.18, and professes that he is placed not on another, but on the very throne of the Father, Rev. III.21. Therefore Grotius should not have lent his ears to the Jew rather than to Christ, who, following R. Akiba, asserts in Dan. VII.14 that one throne was placed for the Father, another for the Messiah: for those thrones are not said there to be placed for the Father and the Messiah, nor does the analogy of faith support that: See John V.22, 23. The phrase therefore indeed seems the same, when Christ is said to sit at the right hand of the Father and when the mother of Solomon had a seat at the right hand of the King, but the sense is far different: just as worldly honor is far different from divine: and the right hand of an earthly king is bodily, at which another is said to sit: but the right hand of God, at which Christ sits, is the infinite power of God metaphorically so named: to the communion of which power the human nature of Christ has been admitted, and by that name he is said to sit at the right hand of God, because, with divine power and authority communicated to him, he reigns and governs all things in heaven and on earth.

Latin:

Vers. 21. ἷς ἐκ δεξιῶν σε καὶ ἷς ἐξ εὐωνύμων ἐν τῇ βασιλείᾳ σε.] Audierat ex filiis mater, Apostolis communiter pro- missam dignitatem quasi φυλαρχίαν, ut supra diximus: sed sciebat etiam inter eos qui paris essent gradus aliquem esse ordinem: quemadmodum in veteri regno Israëlitico duo primi loci erant τῶν φυλαρχῶν tribuum Judæ & Josephi. Hos igitur honores filiis suis deposcit. Dextræ regis assi- dere significat locum à rege principem. Ita Salomo sedens in solio regio matris sedem collocari jussit proxime se ad dexterum latus 1.Reg.II.19. Alibi regina dicitur sedere ad dextram regis, ut Psal. XLV.10. Tiridatem, ut apud Sueto- nium est, Nero juxta se latere dextro collocavit. Ita Chri- stus ipse, quanquam in regno suo Rex, cum tamen Deo Pa- tri suo comparatur, dicitur sedere ad ipsius dextram: sive ad dextram solii, ut loquitur divinus ad Hebræos Scriptor cap. XII.3. Quo & illud pertinet quod apud Danielem legimus solia polita, duo scilicet ut interpretatur Rabbi Akiba, al- terum Deo Patri, alterum Messiæ. Eodem plane sensu de Minerva dictum est Pindaro: δεξιὰν κατὰ χεῖρα τῶ πατρὸς καθεζομένην citante Aristide: quod Horatius ita expressit: Proximos illi tamen occupavit Pallas bonores.

Tertius autem in regno locus consequenter describitur ses- sione ad sinistrum regis latus. Nam quoquisque in regno major, ita regi in publicis conventibus propior sedebat.

Dextræ Regis assidere, interprete Grotius, no- tat locum à Rege principem 1. Reg. II.19. Psal. XLV. 10. Tertio autem in regno locus consequenter describitur sessione ad sinistrum Regis latus. Sed id male trahitur ad sessionem Christi ad dextram Dei; quia longe alio sensu hæc phrasis de Chri- sto adhibetur, & à S.S. explicatur, nimirum per τὸ regnare, ut è collatione Psal. CX. 1. & 1.Cor. XV. 25. liquet. Non ergo proximum à Rege locum obtinet Christus, sed est ipse Rex, & eodem cum Deo Patre titulo Rex Regum, Dominus domi- nantium 1. Tim. VI.16 Apoc. XVII. 14. cap. XIX. 16. Dominus gloriæ 1. Cor. II. 8. Dominus omnium, Actor. II. 36. insignitur. Et quum non sit nisi unus Dominus dominantium, Dominus gloriæ, Do- minus omnium, per quem omnia, 1. Cor. VIII. 6. Eph. IV. 5. Zach. XIV. 9. non utique alium thro- num occupat Christus, quam Pater, nec geminum est Dominium, sed unum tantum unius Domini est dominium, quemadmodum duos Dominos venerari, religione Christiana prohibemur: unus est Dominus, profitemur in Symbolo Athanasia- no quia sicut singulatim unamquamque personam Deum ac Dominum confiteri, Christiana veritate compellimur; ita tres Deos aut tres Dominos dice- re, catholica religione prohibemur. At hujus au- tem unius divini & summi dominatus ac regiminis consortium evecta humana Christi natura quum credenda sit, ut unus maneat Dominus noster Je- sus Christus Deus & homo, non potest alius thro- nus, aut inferior potestas Christo secundum huma- nam naturam assignari, qui eandem illam omnem potestatem in cœlo & in terra, quæ Dei Patris est, tibi secundum carnem datam esse testatur, Matth. XXVIII. 18. seque non in alio, sed in ipso Patris throno collocatum esse profitetur Apoc. III. 21. Non ergo Judæo potius quam Christo hic aures præbere debuit Grotius, qui R. Akibam sequutus Dan. VII. 14. aliud solium Patris, aliud Messiæ po- situm asserit: nam illa solia non dicuntur ibi Patri & Messiæ posita, nec id fidei analogia fert: Vid. Joh. V. 22. 23. Phrasis ergo videtur quidem eadem, cum Christus ad dextram Patris sedere dicitur & cum mater Salomonis sedem habuit ad dextram Re- gis, sed sensus longe diversissimus est: quemadmo- dum longe alius est honor mundanus, alius divi- nus: ac dextra Regis mundani corporalis est, ad quam alius sedere dicitur: dextra autem Dei, ad quam Christus sedet, virtus Dei est infinita meta- phorice sic nuncupata: ad cujus virtutis commu- nionem admissa est humana Christi natura, eoque nomine ad dextram Dei sedere dicitur, quia com- municata divina virtute, ac potestate regnat; & gubernat omnia in cœlo, & in terra.

## 20:22
Ver. 22. You do not know what you are asking.] That is, when you demand the first places in my kingdom by interposing the person of your mother, you think you are asking for a thing full of many human advantages. But the matter is far otherwise. What Jerome said concerning the Episcopate can rightly be applied also to that preeminence desired among the Apostles: If anyone desires the Episcopate, he desires a good work: a work, not a dignity: labor, not delights: a work through which he may decrease in humility, not swell with pride in high station. Thus those who seemed to be pillars of the Church surpassed others in dangers and labors, not in external display of things and advantages, which are usually sought after. Join what will soon follow in verse 24 and the following.

Can you drink the cup] Can you, says Christ, perform that which pertains necessarily not only to that excellence among the prefects of my kingdom, but to that very prefecture itself, that you may endure with a brave spirit any adverse incidents, even death, if the matter should so require? It has been rightly noted by learned men that by the Hebrew כוֹס, to which the cup of the Hellenists corresponds, is signified a prosperous or unprosperous lot, which befalls each person with God watching and moderating. Whence we also read the word for 'part' sometimes joined to it, as in Psalm 11:6, 16:4. Hierocles, regarding that passage of the Golden Verses 'as you may have a lot,' says thus: 'For it is not as it happens that painful things are distributed to men, if indeed God and the boundaries of justice stand over us.' But even before Pythagoras, this tradition had migrated from barbarian wisdom into Greece, as can be seen in Homer in that passage: 'For two jars lie on the floor of Zeus:' where the same metaphor is used. But for an adverse lot, as in the Psalms, Isaiah, and Jeremiah several times, so in these books it is taken not only in this place, but also below in chapter 26:39, 42, Mark 14:30, Luke 22:42, John 18:11, and in the Apocalypse in several places.

About to drink] Because here in certain copies there follows 'and the baptism with which I am baptized to be baptized,' and in the following verse, 'the baptism with which I am baptized you shall be baptized,' since Hilary, Ambrose, and Jerome do not acknowledge these, they may appear to have been added from Mark for the sake of interpretation. And indeed the Greek Codices differ: yet it is apparent from the Syriac and Origen that this and other similar additions are ancient.

He says this to the sons, both because the prayers of the mother had descended from the will of the sons, as Jerome advises, and because the disciples themselves had also asked, Mark 10:35, even if they also employed their mother, because they believed her intercession would be of much value. Christ says they do not know what they are asking: not only because they were ignorant of what dangers those are exposed to who hold the first places in the kingdom of Christ, as Grotius opines, but primarily because they had anticipated in their minds an opinion about a worldly kingdom of Christ, in which they themselves desired the chief dignities, unaware that the kingdom of Christ is not of this world, John 18:36. Therefore he asks, 'What do you want?' not because he did not know, but to force them to an answer, and to lay open the ulcer, and thus apply a remedy. But Christ teaches that dignities in his kingdom are joined with afflictions, when he makes mention of the cup to be drunk, and the baptism of blood, or martyrdom, which they ought not to decline in the kingdom of Christ, especially those who hold the chief parts in it:

which words concerning Baptism, although they are not read here by the Latin interpreter, as also by Hilary and Ambrose, and are lacking in some Greek Codices, are not, however, to be said to have been added to this Mark with Grotius, but rather are to be judged as having been omitted through the carelessness of scribes in those few Codices, since they are found in most Greek Codices, and some things can be omitted more easily through the carelessness of scribes than added, and the Syrian interpreter, and Chrysostom, and Maximus, and others read and explain them. Do you see, says Chrysostom in this place, how he has led them away from this desire, dealing with them about the opposite things? For you indeed are dealing with me about honor and crowns, he says, but I am dealing with you about sweats and struggles. For this is not the time for rewards, nor is my glory shown as about to happen at some time, but these are the times of slaughter and wars and dangers. Observe, however, how he exhorts and entices by the very mode of questioning: for he did not say, can you be slaughtered, can you shed your blood: but how, can you drink the cup? Then, enticing them, he says, which I am about to drink, so that since they are participants in it, they may become more ready: and he calls them again to the baptism itself, showing that through those things which will have been done, there will be a great purification for the whole world. Maximus has it thus: Baptism is a type of voluntary labors, and of our own for the sake of virtue, by which, casting off the stains of conscience, we choose a voluntary death from a free purpose of mind: but the cup is a type of involuntary temptations, which come upon us against our will for the sake of the truth. But we leave this explanation of Maximus in its own place. For calamities are designated generally as a metaphor both of a bitter potion, and of the immersion of baptism or of waters, because the Cup is accustomed to be taken for the cross, Jer. 25, ch. 49. 12, Ezek. 23. 32. Ps. 116. 13. Cf. Ps. 110. 7. Matt. 26. 37. And by the likeness of deep waters, calamities are designated Ps. 19. 7, 32. 6, 42, 69, by which the faithful are submerged as if by whirlpools of water, as Beza explains this metaphor far more elegantly than the impure Piscator, saying it is derived from a shameful drenching, such as it is when someone is drenched with urine.

Latin:

Vers. 22. ὀυκ ὄιδατε, τί ἀιτεῖσθε.] Id est cum primas par- tes in regno meo interposita matris persona postulatis, exi- stimatis vos rem postulare multis humanis commodis ple- nam. At longe aliter se res habet. Quod Hieronymus dixit de Episcopatu, recte potest etiam ad istam concupi- tam inter Apostolos ὑπεροχὴν aptari: Si quis Episcopatum de- siderat, bonum opus desiderat: opus, non dignitatem: laborem, non delicias: opus per quod humilitate decrescat, non intumescat fastigio. Ita illi, qui columnæ videbantur esse Ecclesiæ, peri- culis ac laboribus, non externo rerum apparatu ac com- modis, quæ plerumque expeti solent, cæteros antecesse- runt. Conjunge quæ mox sequentur commate 24. & se- quentibus.

Δύνασθε πιειν τὸ ποτήριον] Potestisne, inquit Christus, id præstare, quod non modo ad excellentiam illam inter regni mei præfectos, verum ad ipsam illam præfecturam neces- sario pertinet, ut incidentia adversa quævis, etiam mortem, si ita res ferat, forti animo toleretis? Recte autem à viris doctis annotatum est per כוֹס Hebræum, cui respondet Hellenistarum ποτήριον, significari sortem prosperam aut improsperam, quæ Deo inspectante ac moderante cuique obtingit. Unde & vocem μέρους ei interdum adjunctam legi- mus, ut Psal. XI. 6. XVI. 4. Hierocles ad illud aurei car- minis ὡς ἄν μοῖραν ἔχῃς ita ait: ᾗ γὰρ ὡς ἔτυχε τὰ ἀλγεινὰ τοῖς ἀνθρώποις διανέμεται, ἔιπερ θεὸς, κὴ δίκης ὅροι προεστήκασιν ἡμῶν. Sed & ante Pythagoram hæc παράδοσις ex barbara sapien- tia in Græciam migraverat, ut apud Homerum videre est illo loco: Δοιοὶ γάρ τε πίθοι κατακέαται ἐν διὸς ὄυδει: ubi eadem est translatio. Pro adversa autem forte ut in Psal- mis, Esaia & Jeremia aliquoties, ita in his libris non hoc tantum loco, sed & infra c. XXVI. 39. 42. Marc. XIV. 30. Luc. XXII. 42. Joh. XVIII. 11. & in Apocalypsi locis ali- quot sumitur.

Μέλλον πίνειν] Quod hic in quibusdam exemplaribus se- quitur καὶ τὸ βάπτισμα ὃ ἐγὼ βαπτίζομαι βαπτισθῆναι, & commate sequenti, τὸ βάπτισμα ὃ ἐγὼ βαπτίζομαι βαπτι- σθήσεσθε, quando & Hilarius, Ambrosius & Hieronymus hæc non agnoscunt, videri possunt interpretamenti causa ex Marco adjecta. Et sane Codices Græci discrepant: Vete- rem tamen esse & hanc & huic similes alias adjectiones ap- paret ex Syro & Origene.

Filiis id dicit, tum quia preces matris ex filio- rum descenderant voluntate, ut Hieronymus monet, tum quia ipsi etiam discipuli petierant Marc. X. 35. et si matrem quoque adhibuerint, quod ejus interces- sionem multum valituram crederent. Nescire au- tem quid poscat, Christus dicit: non solum quia ignorabant, quibus periculis expositi sint, qui pri- mas partes in regno Christi tenent, ut Grotius o- pinatur, sed imprimis, quia animo præceperant opinionem de regno Christi mundano, in quo præ- cipuas desiderabant ipsi dignitates, nescii quod regnum Christi non sit de hoc mundo Johan. XVIII. 36. Ideo quærit, quid vultis? non quod nesciret, sed ut cogeret ad responsionem, ac ape- riret ulcus, atque ita remedium adhiberet. At Christus dignitates in regno suo cum afflictionibus conjunctas docet, cum poculi bibendi mentionem facit, & baptismi sanguinis, vel martyrii, quem detractare in regno Christi non debeant, imprimis, qui præcipuas in eo partes sustinent:

quæ verba de Baptismo etsi hic à Latino interprete, ut & ab Hilario, & Ambrosio non legantur, & in a- liquibus Græcis Codicibus deficiant, non tamen è Marco hoc adjecta cum Grotio dicenda, sed po- tius per incuriam librariorum in paucis illis Codicibus omissa censenda sunt, siquidem in plerisque Codicibus Græcis habeantur, & facilius omitti possint nonnulla, librariorum incuria, quam adjici, Syrusque interpres, ac Chrysostomus, & Maximus, aliique ea legant, & explicent. Videsne, inquit Chrysost. in h. l. quomodo ab hac cupiditate abduxerit, de contrariis cum iis agens? Vos siquidem de honore ac coronis agitis mecum, inquit, ego vero vobiscum de sudoribus, ac certaminibus. Neque enim hoc præmiorum tempus est, neque modo gloria mea olim futura monstratur, sed cædis ac bellorum periculorumque tempora hæc sunt. Cerne autem quomodo ipso interrogationis modo hortetur, & alliciat: neque enim dixit, potestis cædi, potestis sanguinem vestrum fundere: at quomodo, potestis bibere calicem? deinde alliciens ait, quem ego bibiturus sum, ut cum illius participes sint, fiant promptiores: & baptismum ad ipsum rursus vocat, ostendens magnam per ea, quæ facta fuerint, futuram toti orbi purgationem. Maximus ita habet: Baptismus typus est voluntariorum, ac nostrorum pro virtute laborum, quibus conscientiæ maculas abjicientes, voluntariam ex libero animi proposito eligimus mortem: calix autem typus est in voluntariarum tentationum, quæ præter voluntatem nobis pro veritate ingruunt. Quam vero Maximi explicationem suo relinquimus loco. Designantur enim generatim calamitates ut Metaphora & amaræ potionis, & immersionis baptismi vel aquarum, quia Calix pro cruce accipi solet Jer. XXV. c. XLIX. 12. Ezech. XXIII. 32. Psal. CXVI. 13. Conf. Pf. CX. 7. Matth. XXVI. 37. & aquarum profundarum similitudine calamitates designantur Pf. XIX. 7. XXXII. 6. XLII. LXIX. quibus veluti gurgitibus aquarum submerguntur fideles, ut Beza hanc metaphoram longe concinnius explicat, quam impurus Piscator, deductam eam dicens à contumeliosa perfusione, qualis est, cum quis lotio perfunditur.

## 20:23
Verse 23. 'You shall indeed drink my cup.' It seems to me more probable that by the word 'cup' death is not strictly denoted, but rather more loosely sufferings, especially the more severe ones, the more it corresponds to the outcome. For it is a certain fact that James was indeed struck by the sword. Chrysostom asserts more than once that the same happened to John his brother, with Theophylact following, as is his custom, but he is too late in age to be considered a suitable author for that matter, especially since there is nothing of the sort in Justin, Irenaeus, or Clement, and Origen, in this place, as also Tertullian, being so much closer, openly reject such an end for him. Nor does what Christ says, 'which I am about to drink,' stand in the way of this interpretation. For that can be quite correctly referred to the very kind of sufferings to be endured for the sake of the truth. Thus Rom. 8. 17, 'joint heirs with Christ, if so be that we suffer together.' 2 Cor. 1. 7, 'as you are partakers of the sufferings, so also of the consolation.'

Tertullian, however, reports concerning John in 'De praescriptione haereticorum' that he was cast into boiling oil, but preserved by divine aid; whence the will for martyrdom was not lacking, but the martyrdom for the will. Eusebius reports that he was driven into exile under Domitian, Hist. Eccles. book 4, ch. 16, where he endured grave calamities, Rev. 1. 9.

'It is not mine to give, but to those for whom it has been prepared by my Father.' There is no ellipsis here. They have hit the nail on the head who showed that 'but' here is 'except.' For what Matthew's interpreter said as 'not' above ch. 17. 8, Mark expressed by 'but' ch. 9. 8. Christ does not deny that he will distribute the offices of his kingdom. For what Paul attributes to God the Father in 1 Cor. 12. 28, he attributes the same to Christ in Eph. 4. 8, saying that from him, after he had ascended on high, some were appointed Apostles, some Prophets, some Evangelists, some Pastors and teachers. And therefore, even among the Apostles, to prefer these to those in the abundance of gifts and fruits was his own: but he says that this honor would not be given by him to others than those for whom it had been destined by the Father: referring, of course, the glory of the whole dispensation to the Father, as we have often observed. Compare what is in John ch. 17. 6; the word 'to prepare' signifies divine destination, as below 25. 34. 2 Cor. 2. 9. Heb. 11. 16. Nor did the ancient Hellenists use it otherwise. Tob. 6. 22, 'for this was prepared for you from eternity.' But mention of divine destination is introduced so that it might not be thought that this thing is obtainable by human ambition. For David also established the order among the priestly families, not by his own judgment, but by lot, as if by divine judgment, as Kimchi notes on 1 Chron. 24. But if anyone says that this sitting at the right and left was attributed to Peter and Paul by an inexplicable counsel of divine wisdom, in my judgment he will not stray from the truth.

Grotius says that he recognizes no ellipsis here, and that they hit the nail on the head who showed that 'but' here is 'except': because what is had above 17. 8 as 'except,' Mark expressed by 'but' 9. 8; nor does Christ deny that he will distribute the offices of his kingdom: because what Paul attributes to the Father in 1 Cor. 12. 28, he attributes the same to Christ, Eph. 4. 8, 11. But he says that this honor would not be given by him to others than those for whom it had been destined by the Father: referring, of course, the glory of the whole dispensation to the Father. Cf. John 17. 6. Which sense easily beats back the sophism of the Arians and Socinians, who elicit from this the inequality of the Son and the Father. And thus Grotius judges that the sitting at the right and left was attributed to Peter and Paul by an inexplicable counsel of divine wisdom, because they were preferred to others in the abundance of gifts and fruits. For the same reason, in an exceptive sense, Trostius also expressed the word 'except' in the Syriac here. And the sense returns to the same thing, assuming the ellipsis of the pronoun VOBIS, which the Vulgate adds for the sake of explanation, as does Ambrose, lib. V. de fid. c. 2. Others posit an ellipsis of the preceding verb, it is not mine to give, but (it will be given to those) for whom it is prepared: so that Christ only says that it is not his to give to those, whoever they may be, who ask for it, but that it will be given to those for whom it is destined, or that it does not pertain to him according to his human nature, and indeed in the state of humiliation, or by reason of his Mediatorial office, and thus he denies that it is his only in a qualified sense. Others, because the Disciples were anxious about a worldly kingdom, take Christ's words as entirely negative: It is not mine, insofar as I have been sent into this world, or as regards my mediatorial office, to give that one should sit at my right or left, namely in the way you ask: since Christ had not come to establish a worldly kingdom, much less to dispense worldly dignities at will. But how then will that antithesis, but for whom it is prepared, fit? Is the sitting at the right or left prepared by God for some in the worldly kingdom of Christ? Certainly, since Christ has no worldly kingdom, John XVIII, nor could any honor be prepared in a worldly kingdom of Christ. And would not the disciples have been confirmed in this way about a worldly kingdom of Christ, namely that in it the πρωτοκαθεδρίας would be distributed to those for whom they were prepared! For if you say that Christ was simply referring to the kingdoms of this world, that he was not sent to determine the πρωτοκλισίας in the kingdoms of the world, but that the same were otherwise (outside of this mission of his) destined and designated by the Father: that would have been nothing to the point: because they were not asking simply for a prerogative in some kingdom of the world, but in the kingdom of Christ, and the sitting at the right and the left of Christ. Such an answer concerning the kingdoms of the world might therefore seem more alien. They were seeking only this one thing, says Chrysostom, to obtain these prerogatives, and to be preferred before others, and that no one should be before them in the presence of Christ, and when they had heard of twelve seats, not knowing what it was that was being said, they were coveting the τὼ προεδρίαν preeminence. What he says, therefore, Chrysostom infers, is this: you will indeed die for my sake, and you will be killed for the sake of the preaching, and you will be partakers of my passion, yet this is not enough to bring it about that you should enjoy this prerogative, and obtain the first rank, &c. Therefore, without doubt, these things are more correctly understood either concerning the prerogative in the kingdom of grace, and the Church, or concerning the ἐξοχῇ in the kingdom of glory, regarding the more eminent degrees of glory in the heavens. But Christ is so far from derogating from himself the power to grant, or the power of granting, those prerogatives—to whom all power had been given in heaven and on earth—that by these words he rather claims the same for himself: for while he says: it is not mine to give, but to those for whom it is prepared, what else does he imply than that it is his to give to them, and that he has in his own power those for whom it is prepared? Just as he also testified in Luke 22:29 that he was appointing a kingdom for the Apostles, that they might sit upon thrones in his kingdom. Thus Cyril: it is not mine to give, not because he does not have the power of giving, but because rewards are given proportionally to those who contend: and Theophylact: It is not mine to give, regarding grace, crowns, but to those for whom it is prepared, that is, who have run and conquered. See in this place Epiphanius, heresy 69, and Chrysostom. And Jerome in this place. It is not mine to give to you, that is, to such proud ones as you are, but to the humble in heart, for whom it is prepared, says Rabanus: Others, it is not mine to give to those who merely and boldly ask for it, relying only on the external respect of kinship, but to those for whom it is prepared, i.e., who keep the faith. Compare John 5:22, Rev. 2 and 3, 2 Tim. 4:7. Thus Isidore in the Catena of Nicetas; It is not mine to give to those who simply ask, but to provide a reward to those who labor: it is not for a just Judge to neglect those who sweat, and to provide for the slothful: If therefore you love seats, do not decline the contests, for which the prize is prepared there for those who contend lawfully. We discussed the Crellian Φλυαρίας (trifles) concerning this passage in our Anti-Crellius §. 175 seqq. We add only the answer given to the Arian predecessors by St. Chrysostom: He did not say, it is not mine to give, but my Father's, lest anyone should think him weak or powerless for this very retribution. But how is it not mine, but theirs for whom it is prepared? So that what I say may be clearer, let us illustrate it with some likeness to him, and let us propose that there is some Agonothetes (judge of the games), and then that many and the best athletes descend into the contest, and that two who are most familiar to him approach the Agonothetes and say, bring it about that we may be crowned and proclaimed, relying on his benevolence and friendship: but that he should answer them: it is not mine to give, but to those for whom it is prepared by labors and sweats? Shall we therefore condemn him of weakness? By no means: but we shall admire his justice, and his disregard of persons. As therefore we do not consider him powerless to give the crown, but that he is unwilling to transgress the laws of the contests, nor to disturb the order of justice, so let us say that this must also be said of Christ; so drawing them on every side with the grace of God, that for the exhibition of their own right actions, they might have a conformable hope of salvation and of pleasing God: therefore he says: for whom it is prepared, for what does he say, if others seem to you better? What if they have done greater things? For not because you are my disciples will you therefore occupy the first places, unless you have been seen worthy. Which things were said concerning the more eminent degrees in the heavens, and the πρωτεῖα (first places), as Chrysostom had explained before: for if anyone should come by martyrdom, and another be adorned with all your virtues much greater, not because I now love you, and prefer you to others, will I therefore, having expelled him who shines with greater works, give to you the πρωτεῖα (first places). For rewards in the heavens, and degrees of glory, will be distributed according to works, even though glory itself is not conferred according to works, but out of mere grace.

Latin:

Vers. 23. Τὸ μὲν ποτήριόν μου πίεσθε] Ποτηρίου voce non strictè mortem, sed laxius paulo perpessiones, præsertim graviores, notari eo mihi videtur probabilius, quo magis eventui respondet. Nam Jacobum quidem gladio percussum res certa est. Johanni ejus fratri idem accidisse non semel asseverat Chrysostomus, sequente, ut solet, Theophylacto, sed ætate posterior, quam ut ejus rei idoneus autor haberi debeat, præsertim cum apud Justinum, Irenæum, Clementem nihil sit tale, & Origene, hoc loco, ut & Tertullianus, tanto propiores, talem illi exitum aperte abdicant. Neque obstat huic interpretationi quod dicit Christus ὃ ἐγὼ μέλλω πίνειν. Nam id satis recte ad genus ipsum perpessionum veri causa sustinendarum referri potest. Ita Rom. VIII. 17. συγκληρονόμοι δὲ χριστῦ εἴπερ συμπάσχομεν. 2. Cor. I. 7. ὥσπερ κοινωνοί ἐστε τῶν παθημάτων ὕτω καὶ τῆς παρα- κλήσεως.

Refert tamen de Johanne Tertull. de præscript. hæret. quod in fervens oleum injectus fuerit, sed divina ope servatus; unde non voluntas martyrio defuit, sed voluntati martyrium. In exilium pulsum sub Domitiano tradit Eusebius lib. IV. Hist. Eccles. cap. XVI. ubi graves calamitates sustinuit, Apoc. I. 9.

ὐκ ἐστὶν ἐμὸν δῦναι, ἀλλ᾽ οἷς ἡτοίμασται ὑπὸ τῦ πατρός με] Nulla hic est ἔλλειψις. Rem acu tetigerunt, qui ostenderunt ἀλλ' hic esse εἰ μὴ. Nam & quod οὐ μὴ dixit Matthæi in- terpres supra c. XVII. 8. Marcus per ἀλλὰ extulit cap. IX. 8. Non negat Christus se distributurum munia regni sui. Nam Paulus quod Deo Patri tribuit 1. Cor. XII. 28. Idem tribuit Christo Ephes. IV. 8. In dicens ab ipso, postquam in subli- me ascenderat, constitutos alios Apostolos, alios Prophe- tas, alios Evangelistas, alios Pastores atque doctores. Ac proinde etiam inter Apostolos hos illis præferre donorum & fructuum ubertate, ipsius fuit: sed hunc honorem ait à se non aliis datum iri, quam quibus à Patre is esset destinatus: gloriam scilicet totius dispensationis ad Patrem referens, ut sæpe observavimus. Confer quæ apud Johannem c. XVII. 6. vox ἑτοιμάζειν divinam destinationem significat, ut infra XXV. 34. 2. Cor. II. 9. Hebr. XI. 16. Neque aliter usurpa- runt veteres Hellenistæ. Tob. VI. 22. ὅτι σοι ἅυτη ἡτοι- μασμένη ἦν ἀπὸ τοῦ αἰῶνος. Ideo autem divinæ destinationis injicitur mentio ne putaretur hæc res esse humano ambitu impetrabilis. Nam & inter sacerdotales familias ordinem David, non suo arbitratu, sed sorte, velut divino judicio, constituit, ut notat Kimchi ad 1. Paral. XXIV. Quod si quis dixerit sessionem hanc ad dextram & sinistram, inexpli- cabili divinæ sapientiæ consilio, Petro & Paulo tributam, me judice à vero non aberrabit.

Nullam hic ἔλλειψιν agnoscit, & rem acu teti- gisse, ait Grotius, qui ostenderunt ἀλλ' hic esse εἰ μὴ: quia quod supra XVII. 8. habetur εἰ μὴ. Mar- cus per ἀλλὰ extulit IX. 8. nec negat Christus, se distributurum munia regni sui: quia quod Patri tribuit Paulus 1. Cor. XII. 28. idem tribuit Christo, Ephes. IV. 8. 11. Sed hunc honorem ait à se non aliis datum iri, quam quibus à Patre is esset desti- natus: gloriam scil. totius dispensationis ad Pa- trem referens. Conf. Johann. XVII. 6. Qui sen- sus facile retundit Arianorum & Socinianorum σόφισμα, hinc inæqualitatem Filii & Patris eli- cientium. Atque ita sessionem ad dextram, & si- nistram, inexplicabili divinæ sapientiæ consilio, Pe- tro, & Paulo tributam esse, judicat Grotius, quia illi donorum & fructuum ubertate aliis prælati fue- re. Eadem ratione, sensu exceptivo scil. vocem אלא in Syro hic expressit etiam Trostius. Et eo- dem redit sensus admissa ellipsi vel pronominis VOBIS, quod addit explicationis gratia vulga- tus, ut & Ambros. lib. V. de fid. c. 2. Alii ellipsin statuunt verbi præcedentis, non est meum dare, sed (dabitur illud iis) quibus paratum est: ut Christus solum dicat id suum non esse, dare illis, quicunq; id petierint, sed datum id iri, quibus destinatum est, vel quod sibi id non competat secundum hu- manam naturam, & quidem in statu exinanitio- nis, aut ratione muneris Mediatorii, adeoque solum secundum quid neget id suum esse. Alii quia de mundano regno solliciti erant Discipuli, prorsus negative accipiunt Christi verba: Non est meum, quatenus in hunc mundum missus sum, vel quod ad mediatorium officium, dare, ut ad dextram, aut sinistram quis sedeat, ita scil. ut vos petitis: siquidem Christus non venerat, ut regnum mundanum institueret, nedum ut dignitates mun- danas pro arbitrio dispensaret. Sed quomodo ita antithesis illa, sed quibus paratum est, congru- et? num paratum à Deo quibusdam in regno Christi mundano est τὸ sedere ad dextram vel ad sinistram? Certe quum Christus nullum habeat mundanum regnum Johan. XVIII. nec parari in mundano Christi regno ullus honor poterat. Et annon ita confirmati fuissent discipuli de regno Christi mundano in eo scil. πρωτοκαθεδρίας di- stributum iri illis, quibus eæ paratæ! Nam si dicas, respexisse Christum simpliciter regna hujus mun- di, se non esse missum, ut in regnis mundi πρωτο- κλισίας decerneret, sed eandem à Patre alioquin (extra hanc missionem suam) destinari, & desi- gnari: nihil id ad rem fecisset: quia non petebant simpliciter prærogativam in aliquo mundi re- gno, sed in regno Christi, & τὸ sedere ad dextram- & sinistram Christi. Alienior itaque videri posset talis de regnis mundi responsio. Id unum solum quærebant, inquit Chrysost. prærogativis hisce poti- ri, aliisque præpani, neminemque apud Christum ante eos esse, & quum duodecim sedes audivissent, ignorantes quid demum esset quod dicebatur, τὼ προεδρίαν præeminentiam affectabant. Quod igi- tur ait, infert Chrysostom. tale est: moriemini qui- dem propter me, & occidemini propter prædicatio- nem, & participes eritis meæ passionis, non tamen hoc sufficit ad efficiendum, ut hac prærogativa frua- mini, primumque ordinem obtineatis, &c. Ideo sine dubio rectius vel de prærogativa in regno gratiæ, & Ecclesiæ, vel de ἐξοχῇ in regno gloriæ, quoad gradus gloriæ eminentiores in cœlis hæc ac- cipiuntur. Quas vero prærogativas concedere, vel concedendi potestatem adeo non derogat sibi Christus, cui omnis data erat potestas in cœlo, & in terra, ut hisce verbis potius sibi vendicet ean- dem: nam dum ait: non est meum dare, sed quibus paratum est, quid innuit aliud, quam quod illis da- re suum sit, & in potestate sua habeat, quibus id paratum est? quemadmodum etiam Luc. XXII. 29. testatus est, sese disponere Apostolis regnum, ut se- deant, super thronis in regno suo. Ita Cyrillus: non est meum dare, non quia potestatem dandi non ha- beat, sed quia præmia proportionaliter certantibus dantur: & Theophylactus: Non est meum dare, ad gratiam, coronas, sed quibus præparatum est, hoc est, qui cucurrerint, & vicerint. Vid. h. l. Epiphan. hæres. LXIX. & Chrysostom. Et Hieronym. in h. l. Non est meum dare vobis, id est, superbis talibus, quales vos estis, sed humilibus corde, quibus para- tum est, ait Rabanus: Alii, non est meum dare illis, qui nude tantum & audacter illud petunt, freti so- lum externo cognationis respectu, sed quibus para- tum est, h. e. qui fidem conservant. Conf. Joh. V. 22. Apoc. II. & III. 2. Tim. IV. 7. Sic Isidorus in Caten. Nicetæ; Non est meum dare simpliciter pe- tentibus, sed mercedem præbere laborantibus: non est justi Judicis sudantes negligere, & præbere ignavis: Si igitur sedes amatis, non detrectate certamina, quorum ibi brabejum legitime certantibus præpa- ratum. Crellianas Φλυαρίας circa hunc locum in Anti-Crellio nostro discussimus §. 175. seqq. Ad- dimus solum responsum prædecessoribus Arianis datum à S. Chrysostomo: Non dixit, non est meum dare, sed Patris mei, ne quis infirmum, aut impotentem ad hanc ipsam retributionem esse opine- tur. At quomodo non est meum, sed illorum quibus paratum est? ut sit quod dico clarius, simi- litudine aliqua ad ipsum illustremus, ac Agonothe- tam aliquem esse proponamus, tum athletas plurimos optimosque in certamen descendere, ac duos quosdam illi maxime familiares accedentes ad Agonothetam, dicere, effice, ut nos coronemur, ac deprædicemur, fretos illius benevolentia, ac amicitia: illum vero istis respondere: non est meum dare, sed quibus la- boribus, ac sudoribus paratum est? Ergone illum infirmitatis condemnabimus? Minime: sed justi- tiam illius admirabimur, personarumq; neglectum. Ut igitur illum non impotentem ad dandam coro- nam existimamus: sed nolle certaminum transgredi leges, nec justitiæ ordinem turbare, ita utique dica mus hoc de Christo etiam esse dicendum; ita eos un- dique cum Dei gratia attrahente, ut ad suorum re- cte factorum exhibitionem, conformem spem salutis & beneplacendi Deo haberent: idcirco ait: quibus paratum est, ecquid enim ait, si vobis alii videantur meliores? quid autem si majora operati fuerint? Non enim quia discipuli mei estis idcirco primas oc- cupabitis, nisi digni visi fueritis. Quæ de gradibus in cœlis eminentioribus, & πρωτεῖα dicta sunt, uti antea exposuerat Chrysostomus: si quis enim ve- nerit martyrio, aliusque virtutibus omnibus vestris multo majoribus ornatus, non quia nunc vos amo, aliisque præpono, idcirco eo, qui majoribus nitet ope- ribus, expulso, Vobis τὰ πρωτεῖα PRIMAS dabo. Præmia enim in cœlis, & gradus gloriæ secundum opera distribuentur, etsi gloria ipsa non secundum opera, sed ex mera gratia conferatur.

## 20:25
Vers. 25. ὅτι οἱ ἄρχοντες τῶν ἐθνῶν κατακυριεύουσιν αὐτῶν.] Although I feel that what Synesius said is very true, that to join the kingdom to the priesthood is to weave together things that cannot be woven, yet I am compelled by many things not to think that this is the proper meaning of this place. For Christ recalls the Apostles to his own example, to which that does not apply, for he himself received all power in heaven and on earth, having been made king of kings and lord of lords. Furthermore, this seems to be his purpose, to appease the other disciples who were hostile to the sons of Zebedee: for which matter nothing could be brought forward more effectively than the explanation of that which he had just said, that they did not know what they were asking. This therefore seems to me to be what he is saying: do not be angry with them because they covet the πρωτεῖα (first places) in my kingdom: for they will bring with them neither external splendor, nor riches, nor pleasure, for the sake of which leadership is usually sought by men; but on the contrary, he who seeks the most sublime place in my kingdom, seeks dangers, inconveniences, and servitude. Wherefore if you weigh the matter by its own weights, you will see that what they are coveting is not at all to be envied. Thus in the Babylonian exile it was customarily said solemnly to the prince of the exiles: that he should not exalt himself: that an office was enjoined upon him, not power: and that from that day he must begin to serve everyone. That is noted in the Hebrew book which is named Tribes of Judah, which calls ἄρχοντας (rulers) those whom Luke calls βασιλεῖς (kings), not kings only but also governors to whom the disciples hoped they would be made equal: for we have seen above in chapter 10:18 that these also are called βασιλεῖς (kings) in a broader sense of the word.
