He seems to have said εἶπεν for the reason that the divine law prescribed something else to the Hebrew king, namely that he should not prepare for himself a great abundance of women, cavalry, and gold and silver, but should live with his fellow citizens under equal law. Although in truth there were few kings even among the people of God who lived up to that standard, if indeed there was even one. So true is what was said to him, that all good princes could most easily be inscribed on a single ring. Κυριεύειν or κατακυριεύειν δεσποτικῶς: מרד Gen. I. 28. Psal. CX. 3. Aristotle often says that δεσποτεύειν is for the advantage of the master. And although the law of nature itself teaches that the administration of the republic, as Cicero speaks, is like a guardianship, to be conducted for the utility of those who are entrusted to it, not of those to whom they are entrusted, and that famous saying of Antigonus is well known, that kingship is a splendid servitude, yet hardly anywhere is that adage truer: No one does not say these things are true, no one does not act to the contrary. To such an extent, not indeed in words, but in the very deeds from the times of Ninus, has the opinion been adopted which Thrasymachus defends in Plato: that justice is the advantage of the stronger; and as Varro said: He who can, presses harder: as the great fish often eats the small, as the hawk kills the birds. Petty kings and governors diligently imitate the examples of kings, seeking out from time to time new pretexts and various terms for plundering, as if sent for a golden harvest. Peter in 2 Epist. V. 2.3 well joins ἀναγκαστῶς and αἰσχροκερδῶς to shepherd with that word κατακυριεύειν. And Paul used κυριεύειν for that which is to act imperiously, 2 Cor. I. 24. And below we see this very thing expressed by the word διακονηθῆναι.

Grotius says that what Synesius said is most true. Which, however, he later, when he pleaded the cause of the Roman Antichrist, not obscurely retracted. Nor does he think here that this is the proper meaning of this passage, which, however, the ancients and more recent interpreters entirely believed. If you except the Papists, who sail for the Roman purple. For what reasons, indeed, is he driven to abandon the opinion of those men, expressed in the very words in this place? Certainly none. For as to his first point, that he says Christ recalls the Apostles to his own example, to whom would that not be appropriate, since he himself received all power in heaven and on earth, having been made King of kings and Lord of lords, it is easily dissolved. To his own example, regarding the zeal of humility and serving others, and the readiness to minister in the state of emptying himself and undergoing passion, he indeed recalls the Apostles, but what has this to do with the office of Christ, which he alone sustains in a twofold manner, priestly namely and Kingly, what to the state of exaltation, and the session of Christ at the right hand of God, and his power over all things in heaven, and on earth, in which he could not set himself as an example to others, Heb. 1:13. Furthermore, what Grotius says: that this seems to have been proposed to him, so that he might appease the other disciples who were hostile to the sons of Zebedee: for which matter he thinks nothing could have been brought forward more effectively than the explanation of that which he had just said, that they did not know what they were asking. This, therefore, he infers, seems to me to say: do not be angry with them because they covet the τὰ πρωτεῖα [first places] in my kingdom: for they will bring with them neither external splendor, nor riches, nor pleasure, for the sake of which leadership is usually sought by men: but on the contrary, whoever seeks the most sublime place in my kingdom, seeks dangers, inconveniences, and servitude. Wherefore, if you weigh the matter in its own scales, you will see that what they covet is by no means to be envied. Resp. He did not wish so much to appease the other disciples with these words, as to inform them all that his kingdom is far different from worldly kingdoms: and that it is not for ministers in his kingdom to lord it over others, but to serve. Whence it is spontaneously clear that dominion does not befit the ministers of the Word, such as Christ wished the Apostles to be: it befits kings over subject peoples, it does not befit the ministers of the Word over the clergy entrusted to them: just as Peter also warned, using the same word that Christ uses here: 1 Epist. 5:3, μηδ᾽ ὡς κατακυριεύοντες τῶν κλήρων [neither as being lords over God's heritage]. Therefore, Christ is not dealing with the accidents or concomitants of προεδρίας [presidency], but with an axiom proper to worldly kings, which does not befit the leaders of his kingdom. Nor does he, through ἄρχοντας [rulers], as Grotius wishes, understand presidents, to whom the disciples hoped to be made equal, but rather kings and princes, or lords, because Luke calls them βασιλεῖς [kings]: for no necessity compels us to take the word βασιλεῖς in a broader sense. And Grotius himself admits that Christ said ἐθνῶν [of the nations] for the reason that the divine law prescribed something else for the Hebrew King, namely, that he should not prepare for himself a great abundance of women, cavalry, and gold and silver, but should live with his citizens under equal law. Chrysostom wishes the mention of ἐθνῶν to have been made to confound the pride of the disciples: he shows by these words that it is a characteristic of the Gentiles to covet primacy, for this is a tyrannical affection, and sometimes it even disturbs great men, for which reason it also needs more vehement castigation. And therefore he pursues them even more sharply, repressing their swelling spirit by the comparison of the nations. But this name is general, denoting not only those who are Gentiles by religion, but φυτικῶς [by nature] peoples and nations: Matt. 24:7, Luke 7:5, John 11:48, Acts 2:5. Nor is only tyrannical dominion designated here, or forbidden to the Apostles as ministers of the Word, but all dominion: therefore Luke rendered the τὸ κατακυριεύειν & κατεξουσιάζειν [to lord it over and to exercise authority] of Matthew as κυριεύειν & ἐξουσιάζειν [to rule and to exercise authority] in ch. 22:25, and Mark as ἄρχειν [to rule]: nor does τὸ κατακυριεύειν imply tyrannical dominion, since the dominion committed to Adam was also expressed by this word in Gen. 1:28, who was constituted not a tyrant, but a lord and ruler of the earth. Add that Christ says those who are κατακυριεύοντας [lording it over] are called εὐεργέτας [benefactors]: which certainly does not befit tyrants. The Holy Scriptures do not disapprove of tyrannical dominion, such as that of some, though not all, Gentile Kings, in Christian Kings themselves. However, Christ grants that dominion which is treated here to Political Kings, and commands that it be alien to the Apostles. Add that he excludes such dominion as the Apostles sought. Whence the Papists, with Bellarmine leading the way in lib. 5 de Pont. c. 10, strive in vain to refute the force of our argument, derived from these words, concerning the forbidden dominion for Ecclesiastical persons: as if dominion were not simply prohibited to them, but only tyrannical dominion. Καὶ οἱ μεγάλοι κατεξουσιάζουσιν ἀυτῶν [And their great ones exercise authority over them]] you may not inconveniently refer ἀυτῶν [them] to ἄρχοντας [rulers], not to ἔθνη [nations], just as also what is in Mark, οἱ μεγάλοι ἀυτῶν [their great ones], namely, τῶν δοκούντων ἄρχειν [of those who are accounted to rule], so that the sense is: just as peoples are treated by Kings, so Kings themselves are treated by those who among them possess the most power, for example, the Roman Emperors who had instruments of servitude and kings. Indeed, as Papinius said: Everything is ruled by turns and they press in turn: all the earth is under its own kings: happy Rome presses the diadems of kings: it is given to her to curb them with leaders. King Agrippa in Philo: 'And who am I, of those who know that I have a master and lord.' ἐξουσιάζειν [to exercise authority] is the same as κυριεύειν [to rule], to command at will, not according to the custom of parents: just as ἐξουσιάζοντας [those exercising authority] is taken also in the Greek of Nehemiah 5:15. In Luke it is: οἱ ἐξουσιάζοντες ἀυτῶν (namely τῶν βασιλείων) ἐνεργέται καλῶνται [those who exercise authority over them (namely of the kingdoms) are called benefactors]: that is, those who command kings at their own pleasure are saluted as benefactors by the kings, by servile adulation, of course, just as Prusias professed himself a freedman of the Roman people. And there is no doubt that Herod called Caesar a benefactor. For both in Philo and Josephus, emperors are often called by that name. But especially relevant to this passage is what we read in Philo concerning Gaius Caligula: 'Immediately, therefore, not long after, having been thought to be a savior and benefactor, and that he would rain down some new fountains of good things upon Asia and Europe for indestructible happiness, both privately to each one and to all in common, he began this so-called [benefaction] from the hearth, having changed toward the untamable, or rather he overshadowed it with the savagery of the mask of hypocrisy which he displayed': and what follows. Moreover, if you refer ἀυτῶν [them] to ἔθνη [nations], the sense will be almost the same as in the previous member. Certainly, many of the successors of Alexander boasted of the name of benefactors: indeed, it appears that this name was also given to the Ethnarchs of the Jews. It is not surprising, therefore, that such empires are coveted, as they are wont to be turned to the utilities, pride, and pleasures of those who rule.

But this is a clear distortion. For it is not the authority of nobles over kings, but of kings over the people that is noted, who are called rulers, and those who are accounted to rule, and kings, and great ones: and it is also the mark of these to exercise lordship and to exercise authority, when this is composed by way of antithesis with whoever wishes to become great, or first. But those whom they rule are designated by the name of the nations. Furthermore, those who exercise authority in Luke ch. XXII. 25 are said to be called benefactors. But nobles are certainly not the benefactors of kings; if they are so called, Grotius acknowledges that it is said by servile adulation.

Latin:

Vers. 25. ὅτι οἱ ἄρχοντες τῶν ἐθνῶν κατακυριεύουσιν αὐτῶν.] Quanquam velissimum esse sentio quod dixit Synesius, τὸ συνάπτειν τὴν βασιλείαν τῇ ἱερωσύνῃ συγκλώθειν ἐστὶ τὰ ἀσύγ- κλωστα, tamen ut hanc non putem propriam esse hujus loci sententiam multis adigor. Nam Christus ad suum exem- plum Apostolos revocat, cui illud non convenit, ipse enim omnem accepit potestatē in cœlo & in terra, rex factus re- gum & dominus dominantium. Præterea hoc illi propo- situm videtur ut cæteros discipulos infensos Zebedæi filiis placet: ad quam rem nihil potuit afferri efficacius, quam explicatio ejus quod modo dixerat, nescire ipsos quod pete- rent. Hoc ergo mihi videtur dicere: nolite illis irasci quod τὰ πρωτεῖα in regno meo ambiunt: nam ea secum neque externum splendorem, neque divitias, neque voluptatem ferent, propter quæ ab hominibus principatus appeti solet; sed contra qui in regno meo locum appetit sublimissimum, pericula, incommoda, servitutem appetit. Quare si rem suis ponderib9 æstimetis, id quod ambiunt videbitis mini- me esse invidendum. Sic in Babylonico exsilio exsulum principi dici solenniter solebat: ne se efferret: officium ipsi, non potestatem injungi: & ab eo die incipiendum ipsi ser- vire omnibus. Notatum id in libro Hebræo cui nomen Tribus Juda ἄρχοντας vocat quos βασιλεῖς Lucas, non reges tantum sed & præsides quibus se æquandos sperabant disci- puli: nam & hos laxius sumta voce βασιλεῖς dici supra vidi- mus cap. X. 18. εἶπεν dixisse videtur ideo quod Hebræo regi aliud lex divina præscriberet, nimirum ne magnam sibi mu- lierum, equitii, aurique & argenti copiam pararet, sed æ- quabili jure cum civibus viveret. Quanquam profecto pauci etiam in populo Dei reges fuerunt ad eam normam, si tamen vel unus fuit. Adeo verum est quod illi dixit, o- mnes bonos principes uni annulo facillime inscribi posse. Κυριεύειν aut κατακυριεύειν δεσποτικῶς: מרד Gen. I. 28. Psal. CX. 3. Aristoteles sæpe dicit δεσποτεύειν esse πρὸς τὸ τῦ δε- σπότε συμφέρον. Quanquam vero lex ipsa naturæ docet procurationem reipublicæ, ut Cicero loquitur, velut tute- lam, ad utilitatem eorum qui commissi sunt, non eorum quibus commissi sunt esse gerendam, & celebre est illud Antigoni, regnum splendidam esse servitutem, tamen vix usquam verius est adagium illud: Nemo non hæc vera dicit, nemo non contra facit. Adeo non verbis quidem, sed rebus ipsis abusque Nini tem- poribus itum est in eam sententiam quam apud Platonem tuetur Thrasymachus: δίκαιον εἶναι τῷ κρείττονι συμφέρον; atque ut dixit Varro; Qui pote plus urget: pisces ut sæpe minutos Magnus comest, ut aves enecat accipiter. Regum exempla gnaviter imitantur reguli & præsides ex- quirentes subinde novos sinus & varia prædandi vocabula, quasi ad auream messem missi. Petrus 2. Epist V. 2.3. be- ne conjungit ἀναγκαστῶς & αἰσχροκερδῶς ποιμαίνειν cum ista voce κατακυριεύειν. Et Paulus dixit κυριεύειν pro eo quod est imperiose agere 2. Cor. I. 24. Et infra videmus hoc i- psum exprimi voce διακονηθῆναι.

Verissimum esse ait Grotius, quod dixit Synesius. Quod vero postea, ubi Anti Christi Romani cau- sam egit, non obscure revocavit. Neque hic pu- tat propriam esse hanc hujus loci sententiam, quod vero omnino crediderunt veteres & recentiores Interpp. Si Pontificios excipias, purpuræ Romanæ velificantes. Ob quas vero rationes adigitur, ut istorum sententiam verbis ipsis expressam deferat hoc loco? Nullas certe. Nam quod primum Chri- stum, ait, ad suum exemplum Apostolos revocare, cui illud non conveniat, siquidem ipse omnem acce- perit potestatem in cælo, & in terra, Rex factus re- gum, & Dominus dominantium, ἐυδιάλυτον. Ad suum exemplum, quoad studium humilitatis & in- serviendi aliis, ac ministrandi in statu exinanitio- nis, ac passionis subeundæ promptitudinem revo- cat sane Apostolos, sed quid hoc ad officium Christi, quod geminum ipse unus sustinet, sacer- dotale nempe ac Regium, quid ad statum exalta- tionis, & sessionem Christi ad dextram Dei, ac potestatem ejus super omnia in coelo, & in terra, in quibus aliis se in exemplum sistere non poterat Ebr. I. 13. Quod porro ait Grotius: hoc illi pro- positum videri, ut cæteros discipulos infensos Zebe- dæi filiis placet: ad quam rem nihil potuisse afferri efficacius censet, quam explicationem ejus, quod modo dixerat, nescire ipsos quod peterent. Hoc ergo, infert, mihi videtur dicere: nolite illis irasci quod τὰ πρωτεῖα in regno meo ambiunt: nam ea secum neque externum splendorem, neque divitias, neque voluptatem ferent, propter quæ ab hominibus prin- cipatus appeti solet: sed contra qui in regno meo lo- cum appetit sublimissimum, pericula, incommoda, servitutem appetit. Quare si rem suis ponderibus æstimetis, id quod ambiunt videbitis minime esse in- videndum. Resp. Non tam placare alios disci- pulos hisce, quam informare universos voluit, quod regnum suum longe diversum sit à munda- nis regnis: quodque ministrorum in regno suo non sit aliis dominari, sed inservire. Unde ultro patet, non convenire ministris verbi, quales Apo- stolos volebat esse Christus, dominium: regibus id convenire in populos subjectos, non convenire Verbi ministris in clerum sibi creditum: quemad- modum etiam Petrus monuit eodem, quo hic Christus, usus verbo: 1. Epist. V. 3. μηδ᾽ ὡς κατα- κυριεύοντες τῶν κλήρων. Non ergo de accidentibus, vel concomitantibus προεδρίας, sed de axiomate mundanis regibus proprio, regni sui primoribus haud competente, agit Christus. Neque per ἄρ- χοντας, quod Grotius vult, præsides intelligit, qui- bus se æquandos sperarint discipuli, sed reges po- tius, ac principes, vel dominos, quia βασιλεῖς vocat eosdem Lucas: ut enim laxius vocem βασιλεῖς ac- cipiamus nulla cogit necessitas. Et fatetur Gro- tius ipse, ἐθνῶν dixisse Christum ideo, quod Ebræo Re- gi aliud lex divina præscriberet, nimirum ne ma- gnam sibi mulierum, equitii, aurique & argenti co- piam pararet, sed æquabili jure cum civibus vive- ret. Chrysostomus ἐθνῶν mentionem factam vult ad confundendum tumorem discipulorum: osten- dit hisce gentilium esse primatum ambire, tyranni- cus enim hic affectus est, & nonnunquam etiam ma- gnos viros perturbat, quapropter etiam vehemen- tiori castigatione indiget. Ideoque acrius eos etiam insequitur, gentium comparatione tumentem eorum animum reprimens. Verum nomen hoc genera- le est, non tantum religione gentiles, sed φυτικῶς populos, ac gentes notans: Matth. XXIV. 7. Luc. VII. 5. Johan. XI. 48. Actor. II. 5. neque tyrannicus tantum dominatus hic designatus, aut Apostolis ut ministris verbi interdictus est, sed dominatus o- mnis: ideo τὸ κατακυριεύειν & κατεξουσιάζειν mat- thæi Lucas reddidit κυριεύειν & ἐξουσιάζειν c. XXII. 25. Marcus ἄρχειν: neq; τὸ κατακυριεύειν tyranni- cum infert dominatum, quum etiam Adamo com- missum dominium, hoc verbo expressum sit Gen. I. 28. qui non tyrannus, sed dominus, & rector terræ constitutus est. Adde quod Christus illos κατακυριεύοντας vocari εὐεργέτας dicat: quod Ty- rannis certe non convenit. Tyrannicum domina- tum, qualis quorundam est, non tamen omnium, gentilium Regum, improbat S. S. in ipsis Chri- stianis Regibus. Dominatum autem illum, de quo hic agitur, Politicis Regibus concedit Chri- stus, ab Apostolis alienum esse jubet. Adde, quod talem dominatum excludat, qualem Aposto- li expetierunt. Unde Pontificii, præeunte Bel- larmino lib. V. de Pont. c. 10. nequicquam elidere satagunt vim argumenti nostri, ex his verbis de- da ducti, de interdicto dominatu personis Ecclesia- sticis : quasi non simpliciter dominium ipsis pro- hibitum sit, sed tantum dominium tyrannicum. Καὶ οἱ μεγάλοι κατεξουσιάζουσιν ἀυτῶν] ἀυτῶν non incom- mode referas ad ἄρχοντας, non ad ἔθνη, ut & quod apud Mar- cum est οἱ μεγάλοι ἀυτῶν, nimirum τῶν δοκούντων ἄρχειν, ut sensus sit : quomodo populi tractantur à Regibus, ita Reges ipsi ab his, qui inter ipsos plurimum viribus pollent, exem- pli causa Romanorum Imperatores qui habebant instru- menta servitutis & reges. Nimirum ut Papinius dixit : Vice cuncta reguntur Alternisque premunt : propriis sub regibus omnis Terra : premit felix regum diademata Roma : Hanc ducibus frænare datum. Agrippa rex apud Philonem : κἀγὼ τίς εἰμι τῶν εἰδότων μὲν ὅτι δεσπότην ἔχω κὴ κύριον. ἐξουσιάζειν idem est quod κυ- ριεύειν, pro lubitu, non ex usu parentium imperare : quomo- do ἐξουσιάζοντας sumitur & in Græco Nehemiæ V. 15. Apud Lucam est : οἱ ἐξουσιάζοντες ἀυτῶν (nempe τῶν βασιλείων) ἐνερ- γέται καλῶνται : id est qui regibus pro arbitratu imperant à regibus ἐνεργέται salutantur, servili adulatione scilicet, quo- modo Prusias libertum se populi Romani profitebatur. Nec dubium est quin Herodes Cæsarem vocarit ἐνεργέτην. Nam & apud Philonem & Josephum imperatores sæpe eo nomine appellantur. Sed imprimis ad hunc locum facit quod legimus apud Philonem de Cajo Caligula : ἐνθὺς γοῦν ἐκ εἰς μακρὰν ὁ σωτὴρ κὴ ἐνεργέτης εἶναι νομισθείς, κὴ τινας ἀγα- θῶν πηγὰς νέας ἐπομβρήσειν Ἀσιάδι τε κὴ Εὐρώπη πρὸς ἐνδαιμο- νίαν ἀκαθαίρετον ἰδίᾳ τε ἑκάστῳ κὴ πᾶσι κοινῇ, τὸ λεγόμενον δὴ τοῦτο ἀφ᾽ ἑσίας ἤρξατο, μεταβαλὼν πρὸς τὸ ἀτίθασσον μᾶλλον δὲ ἢ συνεσκίασεν ἀγριότητι τῷ πλάσματι τῆς ὑποκρίσεως ἀναφά- νας : & quæ sequuntur. Cæterum si ἀυτῶν ad ἔθνη referas sensus erit ferme idem qui in membro superiore. Sane ex Alexandri successoribus multi ἐνεργετῶν nomine se jacta- bant : quin & Judæorum Ethnarchis id nomen datum appa- ret. Talia igitur imperia ambiri mirum non est, ut quæ ad imperantium utilitates, fastum ac voluptates converti so- leant.

Sed hæc luculenta est detorsio. Non enim Pro- cerum in Reges, sed Regum in populum imperium no- tatur, qui imperant, & ἄρχοντες, & οἱ δοκῦντες ἀρχᾶν, & βασιλεῖς, & μεγάλοι vocantur : & ho- rum etiam est τὸ κατακυριεύειν & τὸ κατεξουσιά- ζειν, cum hic κατ᾿ ἀντίθεσιν componitur ὅς ἐὰν θέ- λῃ γενέσθαι μέγας, ἢ πρῶτος. quibus vero illi imperant, τῶν ἐθνῶν nomine designantur. Acce- dit, quod οἱ ἐξουσιάζοντες apud Lucam c. XXII. 25. ἐυεργέται vocari dicantur. Proceres autem certę non sunt ἐνεργέται τῶν βασιλέων; si dicantur ita servili adulatione dici agnoscit Grotius.

## 20:26
Vers. 26. But it shall not be so among you] He teaches not only what their duty is: but he shows a lot contrary to the lot of kingdoms and earthly princes, which was most relevant to removing emulation. In the kingdom of Christ, those are to be considered to hold the primacy who have both received the greatest gifts, and by whose works very many are converted to the faith. But that was to happen only to those, by the disposition of Christ and the Father, who had surrendered themselves entirely with the most ardent zeal not to their own, but to the interests of others. Wherefore Christ says, whoever among you is held by a desire to excel in my kingdom, let him know that a greater burden of ministry and servitude is imposed upon him than upon the others. To be a minister and to be a servant is directly opposed to exercising lordship and exercising authority. This opposition shows why in the Prophets the empires of the world are depicted by the image of beasts, and the kingdom of Christ by the image of a man. Paul excellently in 1 Corinthians XII. 14, I seek not yours, but you. And I will most gladly spend and be spent for your souls. But just as here there is shall be, so also in the following words shall be is read more correctly than let me be, with many books supporting it.

Latin:

Vers. 26. ἐχ᾽ ὕτως δὲ ἔσαι ἐν ὑμῖν] Non tantum quid ipsorum sit officii docet : sed sortem ostendit contrariam regnum & principum terrenorum sorti, quod maxime ad tollendam æmulationem pertinebat. In regno Christi illi censendi sunt principatum obtinere, qui & maxima dona acceperunt, & quorum opera plurimi ad fidem convertun- tur. Id autem is duntaxat eventurum erat, Christi & pa- tris dispositione, qui se totos ardentissimo studio non suis sed alienis utilitatibus mancipassent. Quare Christus, qui vestrum, inquit, in regno meo excellendi desiderio tenetur, is sciat sibi majus quam cæteris onus ministerii ac servitutis imponi. Διάκονον εἶναι & δῦλον εἶναι directe opponitur τῷ κατακυριεύειν & κατεξουσιάζειν. Hæc oppositio ostendit cur apud Prophetas imperia mundi bestiarum, regnum Christi hominis imagine depingatur. Egregie Paulus 1. Corinth. XII. 14. ἐ ζητῶ τὰ ὑμῶν, ἀλλ᾽ ὑμᾶς. ἐγὼ δὲ ἥδισα δαπανήσω κὴ ἐκδαπανηθήσομαι ὑπὲρ τῶν ψυχῶν ὑμῶν. Sicut autem hic est ἔσαι, ita & in sequentibus verbis ἔσαι rectius legitur quam ἔσω, multis libris astipulantibus.

## 20:28
Vers. 28. Even as the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister.] Such as the king is, such ought the presidents of the kingdom to be. I have given you an example, says Christ: for I have done nothing for reasons of my own utility, nor have I acted the king with splendor or luxuries: but I have endured all inconveniences for the sake of my own, and furthermore I will endure greater ones, namely death itself, contrary to what is accustomed to happen in other kingdoms. For there the people die for the glory and greatness of kings.

And to give his life a ransom for many] Although many sometimes signifies all, I think nevertheless that here the word to give and the preposition for are to be understood with effect, and therefore that it concerns those who will believe in Christ, who are therefore called many in this place and in Daniel IX. 27, so that it may be understood that not only Jews but also foreigners belong to that number. For I think that the prophecy of Isaiah 53:10 is being looked to, where it is said that if Christ had given his life as אשם, which is rightly translated here as λύτρον (ransom), it would come to pass that by the knowledge of him he would justify many: and afterwards: he himself bore the sin of many. The same sense is found in John, when he says that it was necessary for Christ to die, not for the Jews only, but also that he might gather together in one the dispersed children of God, ch. 11:52, 53. And below it is said that the blood of Christ was to be poured out περὶ πολλῶν εἰς ἄφεσιν ἁμαρτιῶν (for many for the remission of sins): just as the writer to the Hebrews also says that Christ was offered εἰς τὸ πολ- λῶν ἀνενεγκεῖν ἁμαρτίας (to bear the sins of many), ch. 9:28. Moreover, a piacular sacrifice, which the Hebrews call אשם and the Hellenists call περὶ ἁμαρτίας (for sin) or ἱλασικόν (propitiatory), is rightly called λύτρον. For the word כפר, which signifies λύτρον, is also used in that sense, as in Lev. 10:17, whence it is also translated by the LXX as περικάθαρμα (expiation): and indeed the piacular victims of the Hebrews, by divine institution, paid the penalties for sins. In Latin also such victims were called lustral. For λύτρον is lustrum: just as Ennius, what is in Greek Ἕκτορος λύτρα (the ransoms of Hector), he inscribed in Latin as Hectoris lustra. And in these books we see placed everywhere, as mutually explanatory, καθαρισμόν (purification), ἱλασμόν (propitiation), λύτρον (ransom). The ancient Hebrews called the Messiah איש כפר, ἄνδρα λύτρου (a man of ransom). Daniel had said that the Messiah would come לכפר עון (to atone for iniquity), ch. 9:24. Joseph Albo admits in his disputation against the Christians that it was customary for the wise men among the Hebrews to bear in themselves the punishments due to the multitude of sinners: and thus Ezekiel was commanded to lie on his side and sustain punishment, by transferring to himself the iniquity of the house of Israel. And to Philo, ὁ σπεδαῖος τῷ φαύλῳ λύτρον (the virtuous man is a ransom for the wicked). Thus Joseph Jacchiades on Dan. 9:35 says that the teachers of the Israelites would suffer the hardest things, and that they would be an altar of expiation for the sins of the people. He says the same on the chapter of Isaiah 53:5. That other nations were expiated and God was appeased toward them through the punishments imposed on the Israelites. Abarbanel also says that Josiah bore the punishment of the sins of the people, not his own. Regarding Moses and Aaron, Moses Alschech says similar things, and regarding the righteous generally. The Chaldean says the same regarding Daniel, Cant. 7:8. And the Yalkut explains 'to take upon himself the sins,' which is in the cited place of chapter 53 of Isaiah, as 'to expiate.' And the Chaldean, concerning him of whom Isaiah treats, says that God will remit the guilt: that through him there will be remission of sins. Moses Alschech says on the same passage that the Messiah would endure punishments for Israel. The word λύτρον added here is therefore ἐξηγητικῶς (by way of explanation) so that the principal cause of the death of Christ might be explained in passing: but thus, what is proposed to be imitated is δῶναι τὴν ψυχὴν (to give the soul). The excellence, therefore, of those who hold offices in the kingdom of Christ is not to be estimated from smoky titles, not from the magnitude of revenues, but from spiritual gifts, from indefatigable diligence, from dangers, and finally from death itself. That first and more sincere age saw bishops striving competitively for this excellence: but gradually vices crept in, and they changed the care of the flock into the appearance of worldly empire: that this had already begun to happen in his own times, Origen complains in these words: And the divine word teaches us these things. But we, whether not understanding the divine will placed in the scriptures, or despising such a commendation of Christ, are such that we seem to exceed even the pride of the evil princes of the world: and we not only seek, like kings, to go before the battle lines, and show ourselves terrible and not easy of access, especially to the poor, and are such toward those who call upon us to entreat us for something, as not even tyrants are, and are more cruel to our subjects than worldly princes. And it is possible to see in certain churches, especially of the greatest cities, princes of the Christian people having no affability or allowing any to have it toward them. To illustrate this passage, those things which are in Ammianus Marcellinus, a man, as it seems, who was a pagan, serve wonderfully. For he, when he had narrated the bloody sedition that arose at Rome from the contest of Damasus and Ursicinus, adds this: Nor do I deny, considering the ostentation of urban affairs, that those desirous of this thing ought to quarrel with every exertion of their sides to obtain what they covet: since, having attained it, they will be so secure that they are enriched by the offerings of matrons, and proceed sitting in carriages, dressed circumspectly, providing profuse banquets, so that their feasts surpass royal tables. Who could be truly blessed if, having despised the magnitude of the city, which they oppose with vices, they lived in imitation of certain provincial prelates, whom the frugality of eating and drinking most sparingly, the plainness also of their garments, and their eyes looking to the ground, commend to the eternal Deity and his true worshippers as pure and modest. To these things agrees what Socrates says, that the Roman and Alexandrian Bishops had fallen into ἐπὶ δυναστείαν (a lust for power). And those things which are in Nazianzen in his oration after his return, where, when he had eloquently deplored the vices of his own time, he concludes the matter with a wish, saying, 'I wish there were μηδὲ προε- δρία, μηδέ τις τόπε πρόκρισεις, κὴ τυραννικὴ προνομία, ἵν᾽ ἐξ ἀρετῆς μόνης ἐγινωσκόμεθα' (neither presidency, nor any preference of place, and tyrannical privilege, so that we might be known by virtue alone). Grotius does not deny that πολλοὺς (many) sometimes signifies all: here, however, he thinks that the word δῦναι (to give), and the preposition ἀντὶ (for/instead of) are to be understood with effect, and therefore that it concerns those who are about to believe in Christ, who for that reason are called πολ- λοι (many) here, and are said to be so in Daniel 9:28, so that it may be understood that not only Jews, but also foreigners belong to that number. Is. 53:12, John 11:52, 53, Heb. 9:28. Although indeed this sense can be admitted here, while the universal redemption of the human race remains safe, yet the reason does not appear why here, just as in v. 16, all are not to be understood by 'many' equally; for the same little word ἀντὶ is used for all when he is said to have paid the λύτρον, 1 Tim. 2:6. who gave himself a ransom for all. Isa. LIII. 12. by many are understood not only the faithful, but all; for whose sins God cast upon him, their sins he bore. Regarding he cast the sins of all men upon him v. 6. But the passage of Daniel ch. IX. 27. is irrelevant, because there it is not a matter of redemption, but of the confirmation of the covenant: & v. 24. iniquities are said to be expiated generally, just as 1 John II. 2. a universal propitiation for the sins of the whole world is claimed for Christ. Whence, which is to be noted on account of the Calvinists, universal propositions are not to be explained from special ones, but special ones presuppose universal ones. For this reason, true confidence in believing can subsist, that Christ died for them, because he died for all 2 Cor. V. 14. 19. 1 Tim. I. 15. 16. Beautifully does Basil the Great speak of this passage. Every human soul was subject to the malignant yoke of the sin of the enemy of all, and was led captive, deprived of the liberty of God through sin: But every captive needs a ransom for his captivity: That which was found was such that it would suffice for redeeming all at once, which also IN FACT was given as the price of the redemption of our soul, the holy and precious blood of Christ, which was shed FOR ALL: Wherefore we have also been redeemed by this price. For man alone did not suffice for our redemption, because he himself was also liable to sin: therefore our Lord Jesus Christ, being man and God, delivered us, therefore he did not commit sin, nor was guile found in his mouth.

But the things which Grotius observed here for the emphasis of the word λύτρον are deservedly opposed both to Socinus and to Grotius himself, in the way he subsequently began to sail with the Socinians: inasmuch as λύτρον is said here, that he gave his soul, as in Isa. LIII. 10. and what further follows in Grotius. He adds, after some things brought forward from the Rabbis to the same effect, which are conformable to our faith. See more of this kind in our Socinianism Overthrown.

Things also seem worthy, which, for the sake of the Papists and of Grotius himself—who in his later age did not hesitate to pour cold water on the Papists and to offer flattery to the Pope—are here properly to be observed: which can not without merit be opposed to the Papizing Grotius.

(II.) THE HEALING OF TWO BLIND MEN NEAR JERICHO.

Latin:

Vers. 28. ὥσπερ ὁ ὑὸς τῶ ἀνθρώπῳ ἐκ ἦλθε διακονηθῆναι, ἀλλὰ διακονῆσαι.] Qualis rex tales esse debent regni præsi- des. Ego exemplum vobis dedi, inquit Christus : neque enim quicquam feci ex meæ utilitatis rationibus, neque splendote, aut deliciis egi regem: sed omnia incommoda sustinui meorum causa & porro majora sustinebo, ipsam mortem scilicet, contra quam in cæteris regnis fieri solet. Ibi enim populi moriuntur pro regum gloria ac magnitu- dine.

κὴ δῦναι τὴν ψυχὴν ἀυτᾶ λύτρον ἀντὶ πολλῶν] Quamquam πολλοὶ interdum omnes significat, puto tamen hic verbum δῦναι & præpositionem ἀντὶ cum effectu intelligendam, id- eoque agi de credituris in Christum, qui ideo vocentur πολ- λοὶ hoc loco & apud Danielem IX. 27. רבים, ut intelli- gantur ad eum numerum non Judæi tantum sed & alieni- genx pertinere. Puto enim respici vaticinium Esaiæ LIII. 10. ubi dicitur si Christus vitam suam dedisset אשם quod hic recte λύτρον vertitur, fore ut sui cognitione multos justifica- ret: & postea: ipse peccatum multorum tulit. Idem sensus est apud Johannem, cum dicit oportuisse Christum mori, non pro Judæis tantum, sed etiam ut dispersos Dei filios in unum congregaret, cap. XI. 52. 53. Et infra dicitur sanguis Christi fundendus περὶ πολλῶν εἰς ἄφεσιν ἁμαρτιῶν: quomo- do & ad Hebræos Scriptor oblatum ait Christum εἰς τὸ πολ- λῶν ἀνενεγκεῖν ἁμαρτίας, c. IX. 28. Sacrificium autem pia- culare, quod Hebræi vocant אשם Hellenistæ περὶ ἁμαρτί- ας, aut ἱλασικὸν, recte λύτρον dicitur. Nam & vox כפר quæ λύτρον significat, eo sensu usurpatur, ut Lev. X. 17. un- de & a LXX. vertitur περικάθαρμα: & sane victimæ piacu- lares Hebræorum ex divina institutione luebant pœnas pec- catorum. Latine quoque victimæ tales lustrales diceban- tur. Nam λύτρον est lustrum: quomodo & Ennius quod Græce est Ἕκτορος λύτρα Latine Hectoris lustra inscripsit. Et in his libris passim videmus se mutuo explicantia poni καθαρισμὸν, ἱλασμὸν, λύτρον. Hebræi veteres Messiam vo- cabant איש כפר ἄνδρα λύτρου. Daniel Messiam ventu- rum dixerat לכפר עון c. IX. 24. Fatetur Josephus Albo in disputatione adversus Christianos pro situm ab Hebræis so- ler sapientes in semetipsis tolerare supplicia multitudini peccatorum debita: atq; ita jussum Ezechielem recumbe- re in latus suum & sustinere supplicium, in se transferendo iniquitatem domus Israël. Et Philoni ὁ σπεδαῖος τῷ φαύλῳ λύτρον. Sic Joseph Jacchiades ad Dan. IX. 35. ait doctores Israëlitarum durissima quæque passuros, & fore eos altare expiationis pro peccatis populi. Idem dicit ad caput Esaiæ LIII. 5. Gentes alias expiatas Deumque eis placatum per pœnas Israëlitis impositas. Dicit & Abarbaniel Josiam pœnam tulisse peccatorum populi, non suorum. De Mose & Aarone Moses Alschech dicit similia, & de justis genera- tim. Idem de Daniele Chaldæus Cant. VII. 8. Et Jalcut suscipere in se peccata quod dicto loco LIII. cap. Esaiæ est, per expiare exponit. Et Chaldæus propter eum de quo Esaias agit, ait Deum reatum remissurum: propter ipsum so- re peccatorum remissionem. Messiam pœnas toleratu- rum pro Israele ad eundem locum ait Moses Alschech. Vox ergo λύτρω addita hic est ἐξηγητικῶς ut obiter explicaretur causa præcipua mortis Christi: ita autem quod imitandum proponitur est δῶναι τὴν ψυχὴν. Excellenria igitur eorum qui in Christi regno præfecturas obtinent, non ex fumofis ti- tulis, non ex obventionum magnitudine, se t ex donis spiri- tualibus, ex indefessa diligentia, ex periculis, ex morte ipsa denique æstimanda est. Ad hanc excellentiam certatim contendentes episcopos vidit prima illa ac sincerior ætas: sed paulatim irrepserunt vitia, & curam gregis in mundani imperii speciem mutarunt: quod jam suis temporibus cœ- pisse fieri, his verbis conqueritur Origenes: Et hæc docet nos sermo divinus. Nos autem sive non intelligentes voluntatem divinam positam in scripturis, sive contemnentes talem commen- dationem Christi, tales sumus, ut etiam malorum principum mundi excedere, superbiam videamur: & non solum quærimus sicut reges acies præcedentes, & terribiles non & accessu difficiles maxime pauperibus exhibemus, & tales sumus adversus eos qui nos interpellant ut propter aliquid deprecentur, sicut nec tyranni, & crudeliores principibus mundalibus ad subjectos. Et est vi- dere in quibusdam ecclesiis, præcipue civitatum maximarum, principes populi Christiani nullam affabilitatem habentes vel habere ad se permittentes. Cui loco illustrando mire inser- viunt ea quæ sunt apud Ammianum Marcellinum homi- nem, ut videtur, paganum. Is enim cum narraset cruen- tam seditionem ortam Romæ ex certamine Damasi & Ur- sicini, hæc subjicit: Neque ego abnuo, ostentationem rerum considerans urbanarum, hujus rei cupidos ad impetrandum quod appetunt omni contentione laterum jurgari debere: cum id adepti, futuri sint ita securi, ut ditentur oblationibus matro- narum, procedantq; vehiculis insidentes, circumspecte vestiti, e- pulas curantes profusas, adeo ut eorum convivia regales supe- rent mensas. Qui esse poterant beati revera, si magnitudine ur- bis despecta, quam vitiis opponunt, ad imitationem Antistitum quorundam provincialium viverent, quos tenuitas edendi po- tandique parcissime, vilitas etiam indumentorum & supercilia humum spectantia perpetuo numini verisque ejus cultoribus ut puros commendant & verecundos. His convenit quod dicit Socrates Romanum & Alexandrinum Episcopos prolapsos ἐπὶ δυναστείαν. Et quæ apud Nazianzenum sunt oratione post reditum, ubi cum sui temporis vitia facunde deploraf- set, voto rem concludit, utinam esset, inquiens, μηδὲ προε- δρία, μηδέ τις τόπε πρόκρισεις, κὴ τυραννικὴ προνομία, ἵν᾽ ἐξ ἀρετῆς μόνης ἐγινωσκόμεθα. Non negat Grotius πολλοὺς interdum omnes si- gnificare: hic tamen verbum δῦναι, & præpositio- nem ἀντὶ cum effectu intelligendum, ideoque de cre- dituris in Christum agi,existimat,qui ideo hic πολ- λοι vocentur, & apud Danielem IX. 28. dicantur, ut intelligantur ad eum numerum non tantum Judæi, sed & alienigenæ pertinere. Ef. LIII. 12. Joh. XI. 52. 53. Ebr. IX. 28. Quanquam vero admitti hic sensus possit, dum salva manet universalis generis humani redemptio, non apparet tamen ratio, cur hic non æque v. 28. uti v. 16. per multos omnes intelligendi sint; nam pro omnibus eadem vocula ἀντὶ adhibita λύτρον solvisse dicitur 1. Tim. II. 6. ὁ δὲς ἑαυτὸν ἀντίλυτρον ὑπὲρ πάντων. Neq; Ef. LIII. 12. per multos tantum fideles intelliguntur, sed omnes; quorum enim peccata in ipsum conjecit Deus, eorum peccata tulit. Ad conjecit omnium hominum peccata in ipsum v. 6. Locus vero Danielis cap. IX. 27. alienus est, quia ibi non de redemptione, sed de confirmatione fœderis agitur: & v. 24. generaliter iniquitates expiatæ dicuntur quemadmodum 1. Joh. II. 2. universalis propitiatio pro peccatis totius mundi Christo vendicatur. Unde quod propter Calvinianos notandum non universales propositiones è specialibus explicandæ, sed speciales præsupponunt universales. Ideo enim vera fiducia credendes subsistere possunt, Christum pro se mortuum esse, quia mortuus est pro omnibus 2. Cor. V. 14. 19. 1. Tim. I. 15. 16. Pulchre de hoc loco Bafilius M. Omnis humana anima subdita fuit maligno jugo peccati communis omnium hostis, ac Dei libertate privata captiva ducta est per peccatum: Omni autem captivo lytro opus est pro captivitate: Inventum id est tale quod redimendis simul omnibus sufficeret, quod & REIPSA datum est in pretium redemtionis animæ nostræ sanctus & pretiosus Christi sanguis, qui PRO OMNIBUS effusus est: Quapropter & hoc pretio redempti sumus. Solus enim homo ad redemtionem non sufficiebat nobis, quia & ipse peccato obnoxius erat: idcirco Dominus noster Jesus Christus homo & Deus existens liberavit nos, ideo peccatum non fecit, nec est inventus dolus in ore ejus.

Quæ vero hic pro emphasi vocis λύτρο observavit Grotius, merito & Socino & Grotio ipsi, qua postmodum Socinianis velificari cœpit, opponuntur: utpote quod λύτρον hic dicatur, animam suam dedisse, uti Ef. LIII. 10. & quæ porro apud Grotium sequuntur. Addit post aliqua è Rabbinis adducta in eandem sententiam, quæ fidei nostræ conformia sunt. Vid. plura ejusmodi in Socinismo nostro profligato.

Digna etiam videntur, quæ in gratiam Papistarum, & Grotii ipsius, qui posteriori ætate Papistis frigidam affundere, ac Pontifici palpum obtrudere non dubitavit, hic probe observentur: quæ Grotio Papizanti non præter meritum opponi possunt.

(II.) DUORUM CÆCORUM CIRCA JERICHO SANATIO.

## 20:30
Vers. 30. two blind men] But one was more notable than the other: therefore Mark and Luke mention one, to whom undoubtedly the principal circumstances of this narrative pertain, which Matthew sets forth collectively. Now this event happened as Jesus was going out of the town. Nor does it stand in the way that Luke says, as he was drawing near to Jericho. For drawing near does not always signify movement to a place, but often only distance. Wherefore the sense is, when he was not far from the town. Such also is that of Luke XIX. 20. as he drew near to Bethphage and Bethany. For he had already passed Bethany.

Grotius judges that there is one history, which Matthew relates here, and which Mark ch. X. 46. and Luke ch. XIIX. 35. relate, even though these mention only one blind man: which he says was done because one was more excellent than the other. Others, however, make two different histories, both because Matthew mentions two blind men healed, and because he reports that this happened as Jesus was going out of the town, so that that one reported by Luke was the third from those whom Matthew and Mark commemorate, but the first in the order of healing, who received his sight from him ἐν τῷ ἐγγίζειν αὐτὸν εἰς Ἰεριχὼ [while he was approaching Jericho]: Which is the opinion of S. Augustine, l. II. de consens. Evangel. c. LXV. and libr. Evangel. c. XLIIX. B. Lyserus, Hunnius, Winckelmann, B. Johan. Gerhard, Cornelius Jansen, and others. Grotius, to remove the difficulty, notes that ἐγγίζειν [to approach] does not always signify movement to a place, but often only distance: but the passage by which he attempts to prove this meaning is less evident, Luke XIX. 29. and that movement to a place is noted here is clear from chapter XIX. 1. καὶ εἰσελθὼν διήρχετο τὴν ἰεριχώ [and having entered, he was passing through Jericho]. Wherefore others with Chrysostom, Ambrose on chapter XVIII. of Luke, Theophylact, Dionysius the Carthusian, Franc. Lucas, Cornelius à Lapide, Maldonado, B. Walther, B. Glassius, Tossanus, establishing that it is one and the same history, either reconcile it thus, that the same blind man had previously asked to be enlightened by Christ at the entrance of the city, but since he was not heard by the crowd, he presented himself the next day at the gate of the city, and there again asked for sight from Christ as he was leaving, and obtained it; or that Matthew concisely embraced both blind men, and the one healed under the entrance of Luke, and this one of Mark, whom he calls Bartimaeus by name as being more famous, healed under the exit. But because Matthew explicitly says two were healed under the exit, not just one, the truth of the account being saved, it cannot be established otherwise than that in reality two were then healed, even if Mark, describing the same history, names only one, as being the more noble: whose designation cannot be considered an exclusion of the other healed at the same time. When this report had spread, that blind man who sat at the other gate of the city, having heard it, awaited the exit of the Lord, and likewise, as those two did, cried out to the Lord, and likewise obtained healing, as it is reported by Luke: who therefore describes another and different history, even if, for the reason already stated, it is very analogous regarding the circumstances of the petition and the obtained restoration of sight. Andr. Osiander in his Harmony distinguishes all those blind men; If, he says, we diligently observe the propriety of the words, we will discover that not only Luke, but also Matthew describes a history different from Mark's. For Bartimaeus was healed in the city of Jericho, or at least at the gate of the city: but those other two were cured sitting in the middle of the journey, between Jericho and Bethany. But that cannot be discovered from the words of Matthew and Mark: for they use the very same words: ἐκπορευεσθαι ἀπὸ ἱεριχὼ [to go out from Jericho], concerning Jesus, and concerning the blind men, that they sat παρὰ τὴν ὁδόν [by the way]; whence it is rather clear that the history of these two Evangelists is the same, not different: and that three blind men in total were healed here at the entrance and exit, and not four.

Latin:

Vers. 30. δύο τυφλοὶ] Sed alter altero nobilior: ideo unius meminerunt Marcus & Lucas, ad quem haud dubie præcipuæ circumstantiæ hujus narrationis pertinent, quam συνανάλως Matthæus enuntiat. Contigit autem res hæc Jesu exeunte ex oppido. Nec obstat quod Lucas dicit, τῷ ἐγγίζειν αὐτὸν εἰς ἰεριχὼ. Nam ἐγγίζειν non semper motum ad locum, sed sæpe distantiam tantum significat. Quare sensus est, cum non procul ab oppido esset. Tale est & illud Lucæ XIX. 20. ὡς ἤγγισεν εἰς βηθφαγῆ καὶ βηθανίαν. Nam Bethaniam jam transierat.

Unam esse historiam, quam hic Matthæus, quamque Marcus c. X. 46. & Lucas c. XIIX. 35. referunt, etsi unius tantum cæci hi mentionem faciant, censet Grotius: quod ideo factum dicit, quia alter altero excellentior fuit. Alii tamen duas diversas historias faciunt, tum, quia Matthæus duorum cæcorum sanatorum meminit, tum, quia hoc accidisse Jesu ex oppido exeunte perhi- bet; ut unus ille à Luca relatus tertius ab istis fue- rit, quos Matthæus & Marcus commemorant, sed ordine sanationis primus, qui ἐν τῷ ἐγγίζειν αὐτὸν εἰς Ἰεριχὼ visum ab eo receperit: Quæ est S. Augu- stinus sententia l. II. de consens. Evangel. c. LXV. & libr. Evangel. c. XLIIX. B. Lyseri, Hunnii, Win- ckelmanni, B. Johan. Gerhardi, Cornelii Janse- nii, & aliorum. Grotius, ut tollat difficultatem, notat, ἐγγίζειν non semper motum ad locum, sed sæpe distantiam tantum significare: sed locus, quo hanc significationem probare conatur, minus evi- dens est Luc. XIX. 29. & hic motum ad locum nota- ri, luculentum est è cap. XIX. 1. καὶ εἰσελθὼν διήρ- χετο τὴν ἰεριχώ. Quapropter alii cum Chrysost. Ambrosio in cap. XIIX. Luc. Theophylacto, Dionyf. Carthus. Franc. Luca, Cornelio à Lapide, Maldo- nato, B. Walthero, B. Glassio, Tossano, statuentes unam eandemque Historiam esse, vel ita conci- liant, quod idem cæcus prius in ingressu urbis pe- tierit à Christo illuminari, sed cum à turba non au- diretur, postridie se stiterit ad portam urbis, ibi- que à Christo egrediente rursus visum postularit, & impetrarit; vel quod Matthæus utrumque cæcum Cυντόμως complexus sit, & illum Lucæ sub ingres- sum sanatum,& hunc Marci, quem ceu celebrio- rem nomine suo Bartimæum vocat, sanatum sub egressu. Quia vero Matthæus diserte duos sub egressum sanatos dicit, non unum tantum, salva ve- ritate relationis aliter statui non potest, quam re- vera duos tum sanatos esse, etsi Marcus eandem historiam describens unum tantum, utpote no- biliorem nominet: cujus designatio non potest censeri alterius eodem tempore sanati exclusio. Quæ fama quum percrebruisset, cæcus ille, qui ad alteram urbis portam sedit, ea audita præstola- tus egressum Domini est, & pariter, ut duo illi Dominum ac clamavit, pariterq; sanationem im- petravit, uti à Luca id relatum est: qui proinde a- liam, ac diversam historiam describit, etsi ob cau- sam jam dictam, quoad circumstantias petitionis, & impetratæ restitutionis visus valde analogam. Andr. Osiander in Harmon. omnes illos cæcos distinguit; Si verborum, inquit, proprietatem dili- genter observaverimus, deprehendemus, non Lucam solum, sed etiam Matthæum diversam à Marco de- scribere Historiam. Nam Bartimæus in urbe Jeri- cho, aut certe ad portam urbis sanatus fuit: illi autem duo alii in medio itinere, inter Jericho & Bethaniam sidentes curati fuêre. Sed id deprehendi non potest è verbis Matthæi, & Marci: utuntur enim i- isdem plane verbis: ἐκπορευεσθαι ἀπὸ ἱεριχὼ, de Jesu, & de cæcis, quod sederint παρὰ τὴν ὁδόν; unde potius liquet, eandem duorum istorum Ev- angelistarum esse Historiam, non diversam: ac tres in universum cæcos in ingressu, & egressu hic sa- natos esse, non vero quatuor.

## 20:32
Vers. 32. Τὶ θέλετε ποιήσω ὑμῖν [What do you want me to do for you?] So that the faith of those asking might be made manifest, for otherwise they could have been believed to have asked only for alms, as those seem to have understood them who were ordering them to be silent as importunate.

Chrysostom has it thus concerning this: Why does he question them? Lest anyone think that he gave to those wishing for other things something else, for it is his custom everywhere to first make the virtue of those who are to be cured manifest and open to all, and only then to append the healing. First indeed to excite others also to imitation, but then to show that those who enjoy the gift are worthy. It was certainly in the interest that the miracles be more fully known, so that the glory of the Messiah might be more fully manifested, and what is the head of the matter, that Jesus might be recognized as the true Messiah, John II. 11. c. XX. 31.

Latin:

Vers. 32. Τὶ θέλετε ποιήσω ὑμῖν.] Ut fides poscentium manifesta fieret, poterant enim alioqui credi, stipem tantum rogasse, quomodo illos intellexisse videntur, qui ut impor- tunis silentium imperabant.

Chrysost. ita de eo habet: Cur eos interrogat? Ne quis existimet alia volentibus accipere alia eum dedisse, mos quippe illi ubique est, prius virtutem eo- rum, qui curandi sunt, manifestam facere omnibus- que aperire, ac tum demum subjungere sanationem. Primum quidem ut alios quoque ad imitationem ex- citet, deinde autem ut eos qui dono fruuntur, dignos esse ostendat. Intererat sane, miracula plenius innotescere, ut gloria Messiæ plenius manifesta- retur, & quod caput rei est, Jesus verus Messias agnosceretur, Joh. II. 11. c. XX. 31.

## 20:33
Vers. 33. Ἀνοιχθῶσιν [may be opened] as above chapter IX. 30. where mention is also made of touch. It is the work of God to open eyes, Genesis XXI. 19. 2 Kings VI. 17.

Latin:

Vers. 33. Ἀνοιχθῶσιν] ut supra cap. IX. 30. ubi & conta- ctus fit mentio. Dei est opus aperire oculos Genes. XXI. 19. 2. Reg. VI. 17.

## 20:34
Vers. 34. ἀνέβλεψαν [they received sight] as above chapter XI. 5. καὶ ἠκολούθησαν αὐτῷ [and they followed him] Because almost all the miracles had happened in the borders of Galilee, therefore Christ brought these two witnesses with him to Jerusalem.

Latin:

Vers. 34. ἀνέβλεψαν] ut supra cap. XI. 5. καὶ ἠκολούθησαν αὐτῷ] Quia in Galilææ finibus miracula ferme omnia contigerant, ideo hos duos secum testes Christus Hierosolyma adduxit.

## 21:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXI. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

JESUS approaching Jerusalem sent two disciples to bring an ass with a colt, so that what was said through the Prophet (Zech. IX. 9.) might be fulfilled, and he rides on them into the city, the people in the way crying out Hosanna, the whole city moved: he casts out those selling and buying from the temple, rebuking them severely (from Is. LVI. 7. Jer. VII. 11.) healing the blind and the lame, the Pharisees raging because of the miracles and the cry of the infants, whom he convicts (from Ps. VIII.): going out into Bethany, but returning in the morning into the city of Jerusalem he cursed a fig tree destitute of fruit, which the disciples marvel that it is withered, but are informed about the power of faith and prayers: The priests asking by what authority he teaches in the temple, he proposes another question about the baptism of John, whether it was from heaven, likewise parables about two sons, and about the vineyard let out by the Lord, whose servants were treated badly, the son as heir killed, and the authors of the slaughter likewise to be killed, and also the prophecy about the rejected cornerstone.

There are four parts: I. The solemn entry of Christ into the city of Jerusalem, and things done there in the temple, to v. 17. II. The curse of the fig tree and the power of faith, to v. 22. III. The conference about the authority of Jesus to teach, to v. 27. IV. The parables spoken against the Pharisees, and fortified by the oracle of David, to v. 46.

PART I. The solemn entry of JESUS into Jerusalem.

Vers. 1. Ἦλθον εἰς Βηθφαγῆ] That is, they were going, as we have said elsewhere. For they had not yet arrived, but were not far off, as Mark and Luke teach: and it is clearly likely that Βηθφαγῆ is the village to which the disciples are sent, so that Christ spoke these things in the valley, which had Bethany on one side, and Bethphage on the other. But the Syrian at Mark called Bethphage closer to the city: by the slope of Bethphage, and of Bethany. See the map of Judea edited by the Jews.

These things seem to be said not inappropriately. But because Mark and Luke have 'when they had approached Bethphage and Bethany,' and Christ had departed from Bethany, where John asserts a banquet was presented to Christ, and therefore a journey into Bethphage and Bethany cannot be understood, because he had approached Bethany, which was rather the terminus a quo of that journey: but it must be established that by Bethphage and Bethany, not the small villages so named, but that whole tract pertaining to those villages is designated, and therefore the customary sense of the word ἦλθον can be retained, so that they are said to have come from Bethany, not into the village of Bethphage, but into that tract which we have already mentioned. Bethany was distant from Jerusalem about fifteen stadia, John XI. 18, that is, nearly two thousand paces, or half a German mile; Bethphage was in the middle, distant about eight stadia. They came therefore from Bethany εἰς Βηθφαγῆ, not into the village of Bethphage, but into the tract named from it: and because Mark and Luke in the sequence of the history had not mentioned that Christ had come to Bethany on the preceding day, which from

We have in John, they wished to make mention of Bethany here, because indeed it was near Jerusalem, near Bethphage, and Bethany, in the tract belonging to those villages near Jerusalem, or as Grotius has it, in the valley which on one side had Bethany, on the other Bethphage. Moreover Bethphage, of which mention is not made elsewhere in the Biblical Codex, according to Jerome in Matthew, was a small village of the Priests situated on the Mount of Olives: whether because some Priests lived there, or because they withdrew there after the duty of their course was completed, as Remigius and Bede establish, because there was a precept in the law that no one should make a journey beyond a thousand paces on the Sabbath days. Jerome interprets the word in Epist. XXVII. to Eustoch. the village of the priestly jaws; Pagninus wishes it to be said from פוֹשׂ ôs, and גַּיְא valley, because it was the house of the mouth of the valley, because the village was situated at the foot of the mountain in the very orifice of the valley, where one would first enter into the valley: which does not agree with the description of Jerome: who places this village on the Mount of Olives itself: Tremellius calls it the house of the fountain: but the Talmudists indeed call a fountain by the Greek word פיגי pigi; but פגי pagi is said by neither the Hebrews nor the Talmudists. And therefore since פג to the Rabbis is fruit of every kind unripe, and פגים are the green figs, which the fig tree produces in place of flowers Cant. II. 13. and there was an abundance of figs there, where also Christ cursed the fig tree, Schindler in Lex. and B. Gerhard in Harm. judge that the village had its name from thence, because it is the house of green figs.

Latin:

CAPUT XXI. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

IESVS appropinquans Hierosolymæ binos discipulos allatum asinam cum pullo misit, ut impleretur dictum per Prophetam (Zach. IX. 9.) & iis equitat in urbem, populo in via Hosanna acclamante, civitate tota commota: è templo ejicit vendentes & ementes, corripiens eosdem graviter (ex Es. LVI. 7. Ier. VII. 11.) cæcos & claudos sanans, frementibus ob miracula & infantium clamorem Pharisæis, quos (è Ps. IIX.) convincit: egrediens in Bethaniam, mane autem regrediens in urbem Hierosolymam ficui fructu destituta maledixit, quam arefactum mirantur discipuli, sed informantur de vi fidei & precum: Sacerdotibus quærentibus qua potestate in templo doceat, aliam proponit quæstionem de baptismo Iohannis, an è cælo fuerit, item parabolas de duobus filiis, & de vinea à Domino elocata, cujus servi male tractati, filius ceu hæres interfectus, & autoribus cædis itidem interficiendis, nec non vaticinium de lapide angulari rejecto.

Partes sunt quatuor: I. Ingressus Christi solemnis in urbem Hierosolymam, ibique in templo gesta, ad v. 17. II. Maledictio fici & fidei vis, ad v. 22. III. Collatio de Jesu potestate docendi, ad v. 27. IV. Parabolæ in Pharisæos dictæ, & oraculo Davidis munitæ, ad v. 46.

PARS I. Solemnis IESV in Hierosolymam ingressus.

Vers. 1. Ἦλθον εἰς Βηθφαγῆ] Id est, ἐπορεύοντο, ut alibi diximus. Neque enim pervenerant, sed non longe aberant, ut docent Marcus & Lucas: planeque verisimile est Βηθφαγῆ esse κώμην quo mittuntur discipuli, ita ut Christus locutus hæc sit in valle, quæ ab uno latere habebat Bethaniam, ab altera Bethphagen. Sed Bethphagen urbi propiorem Syrus ad Marcum dixit: per declive Bethphage, & Bethaniæ. Vide tabulam Judææ à Judæis editam.

Non inconcinne hæc dici videntur. Sed quia Marcus, & Lucas habent cum appropinquassent ad Bethphage, & Bethaniam, & è Bethania, ubi convivium Christo exhibitum fuisse Johannes perhibet, egressus Christus fuerit, ideoq; profectus in Bethphage, & Bethaniam intelligi nequit, quod appropinquarit Bethaniæ, quæ terminus à quo potius fuit profectionis istius: sed statuendum, per Bethphagen, & Bethaniam non viculos ita dictos, sed totum illum tractum ad viculos illos pertinentem designatis, ideoq; verbi ἦλθον usitatus sensus retineri potest, ut venisse dicantur è Bethania, non in vicum Bethphage, sed in tractum illum, quem jam diximus. Bethania distabat Hierosolymis circiter quindecim stadiis Joh. XI. 18. h. e. duobus fere millibus passuum, seu dimidio milliari Germanico; media erat Bethphage, octo circiter stadiis distans. Venerunt ergo Bethania εἰς Βηθφαγῆ non in vicum Bethphage, sed in tractum inde denominatum: & quia Marcus & Lucas in serie historiæ Christum præcedenti die Bethaniam venisse non commemorarant, quod è

Johanne habemus, Bethaniæ hic mentionem fa- cere voluerunt, quod nempe prope fuerit Hiero- solymis, prope Bethphage, & Bethaniæ, in tractu ad vicos illos pertinentes prope Hierosolymam, vel ut Grotius habet, in valle, quæ ab uno latere ha- bebat Bethaniam, ab altero Bethphagen. Cæterum Bethphage, cujus alias in Codice Biblico mentio non fit, secundum Hieronymum in Matth. Sacer- dotum viculus erat situs in monte oliveti: seu quod Sacerdotes aliqui illic habitarint, seu quod eo per- acto officio vicis suæ diverterint, ut Remigius, & Beda statuunt, quia præceptum in lege fuit, ut nul- lus diebus Sabbatorum iter ultra mille passus face- ret. Vocem interpretantur Hieronymus Epist. XXVII. ad Eustoch. villam Sacerdotalium maxil- larum; Pagninus dictam vult à פּוֹשׂ ôs, & גַּיְא val- lis, quod fuerit domus oris vallis, quia ad pedem montis in ipso vallis orificio situs fuerit vicus, ubi primus in vallem ingressus esset: quod non con- gruit descriptioni Hieronymi: qui in ipso monte olivarum hunc vicum collocat: Tremellius do- mum fontis vocat: sed Talmudistæ fontem qui- dem Græca voce פיגי pigi vocant; פגי pagi au- tem nec Ebræis, nec Talmudistis dicitur. Ideoque cum פג Rabbinis fructus omnis generis immaturus sit, ac פגים grossi sint, quos loco florum ficus arbor producit Cant. II. 13. atque ibi copia ficuum fuerit, ubi etiam Christus ficui maledixit, inde nomen vi- cum habuisse, quod sit domus grossorum, Schindler. in Lex. & B. Gerhard in Harm. censent.

## 21:2
V. 2. ἀπέναντι.] In sight, as below XXVII. 24. Acts III. 16. It is the same as κατέναντι among Mark and Luke, which word Mark uses elsewhere in that sense XII. 41. XIII. 3. The LXX also use ἐναντίον in such a way, as Gen. XXXI. 32. 2 Sam. XII. 11. Thus also the Syrian explains it as before, over against: But Lyranus, Hugo, and Abulensis wrongly explained it as against you, concerning the morals of the Jerusalemites, the Apostles being adverse, out of ignorance of the Greek language, and understood the village as Jerusalem: whereas on the contrary by κώμην is designated not a city, but a village not surrounded by walls Matt. IX. 35. c. X. 11. By which village most here understand Bethphage, others a small village or farm, where someone lived, keeping donkeys for hire.

πὼ πῶλον μετ’ αὐτῆς] Upon which no one had yet sat, but yet of such size as to carry a rider comfortably. For they call young donkeys of that kind πώλους also the LXX Jud. X. 4. c. XII. 14.

Latin:

V. 2. ἀπέναντι.] In conspectu, ut infra XXVII. 24. Act. III. 16. Idem est κατέναντι apud Marcum & Lucam, quam vocem Marcus & alibi eo sensu usurpat XII. 41. XIII. 3. LXX. etiam ἐναντίον ita usurpant, ut Gen. XXXI. 32. 2. Sam. XII. 11. Sic etiam Syrus explicat coram, è regione: Male autem Lyranus, Hugo, & Abulensis contra vos, de moribus Hierosolymitanorum, Apostolis adversis, ex ignorantiâ Græcæ linguæ exposuère, & per vi- cum Hierosolymam intellexère: quum contra per κώμην non urbs, sed vicus mœnibus non cinctus designetur Matth. IX. 35. c. X. 11. Per quem vicum hic plerique Bethphagen, alii villulam vel præ- dium, ubi habitarit aliquis, asinas meritorias alens, intelligunt.

πὼ πῶλον μετ’ αὐτῆς] Cui nemo adhuc insederat, sed ejus tamen magnitudinis qui sessorem commode ferret. Nam id genus asellos juniores πώλους vocant etiam LXX. Jud. X. 4. c. XII. 14.

## 21:5
V. 5. πραῦς] Thus the LXX in this place, although from another version, as I think, πτωχὸς is added, עָנִי and עָנָו are used promiscuously by the Hebrews. For both עָנִי as has been said at chapter XI. often signifies a poor man, and עָנָו denotes a meek man, not only here but also in other places. But also Jonathan interprets this place of Zechariah in the same way, whom Kimchi also follows. To sit upon a donkey among the ancient Hebrews was not a sign of poverty, for nobles were carried on a donkey, as can be seen in the cited places of Judges (c. X. 4. XII. 14.) and elsewhere. But when in the times of Solomon the supply of horses among the Jews had increased through trade with Egypt, from that time donkeys became cheap. But also the very stature of the donkey and the company entering the city easily show that the kingdom which Jesus claimed for himself is very different from the kingdoms of the world. Moreover, the writer of Bereschith Rabba and Midras Koheleth acknowledge that this place of Zechariah pertains to the Messiah.

It is not badly observed that עָנִי and עָנָו are used promiscuously by the Hebrews: nor is there reason that we should conclude with Barth. Willius that the LXX Interpreters, when they render the word עָנִי as πραῦς, had read עָנָו: for also πραῦς among the Hellenists denotes an afflicted and humiliated person, just as עָנִי from עָנָה was oppressed; which we observed regarding the place in Zach. IX. Whence that the word πραΰς is accepted here for that reason, added for the sake of explanation, and was not translated from another version (for this is unusual, to compile different versions, the word πτωχὸς: to describe fully the state of emptying. But he was used for the donkey primarily, so that there might be some κεντήσιον of the Messiah, which we noted at the cited place. Because Grotius acknowledges here that he was designated by Zechariah, we wish it to be noted again, because he confesses in the place of Zechariah that even the Rabbis of the Jews themselves saw it, which he himself, fascinated by the inventions of other more recent Jews there, could not see when he was adorning the preface to the Prophet. Concerning which see our Annotations on Zechariah.

ὄνον] Since ὄνος in Greek is of common gender, just as the Hebrew חמור, as can be seen in 2 Sam. XX. 26. where also the LXX said ὄνον, the Latin interpreter rightly placed she-ass here. For the mother is best joined to the foal.

ὑποζυγίε] The Hebrew word is plural in sound, but singular in meaning because of the idiom. For אתונות you rightly translated as the son of one of the she-asses, thus also in the verse within 7. ἐπάνω αὐτῶν the Syrian rightly translated upon him, that is upon one of the beasts of burden, namely the foal, just as the Latin interpreter also accepted it. Similar are, he is buried in the cities of Gilead: he descended into the sides of the ship, and other things of that kind. In the codices of the LXX in the place of Zechariah there is πῶλον νέον, but it must be rewritten from Justin as πῶλον ὄνε.

Grotius rightly joined the foal and the she-ass, because the text is clear both in the Prophet and among the Evangelists: but he wrongly in the annotations on Zechariah understood the donkey alone or the foal born from donkeys, with the mother of the donkey excluded; for they are said to have brought the SHE-ASS and the FOAL, and to have placed their garments UPON THEM.

Latin:

V. 5. πραῦς] Ita LXX hoc loco, quanquà ex alia ut pu- to versione additur πτωχὸς, עָנִי & עָנָו Hebræis promi- scue usurpantur. Nam & עָנִי ut dictum est ad cap. XI. pau- perem sæpe significat, & עָנָו mansuetum notat, non hic ta- tum sed & aliis in locis. Sed & Jonathan eodem modo hunc Zachariæ locum interpretatur, quem & Kimchi sequitur. Asino insidere apud Hebræos veteres non erat paupertatis signum, nam proceres asino vectabantur, ut dictis Judicum locis (c. X. 4. XII. 14.) & alibi videre est. Sed cum Salomo- nis temporibus Ægypti commercio equorū copia apud Ju- dæos crevisset, ex eo eviluère asini. Sed & ipsa asini statura & comitatus urbem ineuntis facile ostendunt regnū quod sibi Jesus vindicabat diversissimum esse à regnis mundi. Locum autem hunc Zachariæ ad Messiam pertinere agno- scunt Scriptor Bereschith Rabba, & Midras Koheleth.

Non male observatur promiscue Ebræis עָנִי & עָנָו usurpari: nec est, quod cum Barth. Willio sta- tuamus LXX. Interpp. cum vocem עָנִי reddunt πραῦς legisse censeamus עָנָו: nam & πραῦς apud Hellenistas afflictum & humiliatum notat, uti עָנִי ab עָנָה oppressū fuit; quod ad locum Zach. IX. ob- servavimus. Unde ut ea ratione hic accipiatur vox πραΰς, addita ἐξηγήσεως gratia, non autem ex a- lia versione traducta fuit (hoc enim insolens est, diversas versiones compilare, vox πτωχὸς: ad ple- niῦ describendū exinanitionis statum. Asino autem adhibitus est imprimis, ut κεντήσιον aliquod habe- retur Messiæ, quod loco cit. notavimus. Quem quod Grotius hic agnoscat à Zacharia designatum esse, notari iterum cupimus, quia ipsos etiam Ju- dæorum Rabbinos id vidisse, fatetur in loco Za- chariæ, quod ipse fascinatus aliorum recentiorum Judæorum commentis ibi, cum anteposta ad Pro- phetam adornaret, videre non potuit. Quo de vid. Annot. nostra ad Zachar.

ὄνον] Cum ὄνος Græce sit ἐπίκοινον, quomodo Hæbræum חמור, ut videre est 2. Sam. XX. 26. ubi & LXX. ὄνον dixerunt, recte hic interpres Latinus asinam posuit. Nam pullo mater optime adjungitur.

ὑποζυγίε] Vox Hebræa pluralis est sono, significatu au- tem singularis propter ἰδίωμα. Nam אתונות recte ver- titis filium unius asinarum, Sic & commate intra 7. ἐπάνω αὐτῶν recte transtulit Syrus super eum, id est super al- terum ex jumentis, pullum videlicet, quomodo accepit & Latinus interpres. Similia sunt, sepultus est in urbibus Gala- ad: descendit in latera navis, & id genus alia. In codici- bus LXX. in Zachariæ loco est πῶλον νέον, sed rescribendum ex Justino πῶλον ὄνε.

Recte conjunxit pullum & asinam Grotius, quia textus & penes Prophetam & apud Evange- listas clarus est: at male in annot. ad Zachariam a- sinum solum vel pullum natum ex asinis, intelle- xit asinæ matre exclusa; adduxisse enim dicuntur ASINAM & PULLUM, & imposuisse SUPER EOS vestimenta sua.

## 21:8
V. 8. ὁ δὲ πλεῖστος ὄχλος] That saying of Horace agrees here: Sometimes the crowd sees rightly: as in David 1 Sam. XVIII. 6.

ἔστρωσαν ἑαυτῶν τὰ ἱμάτια] Concerning this custom see, besides those places which others have brought forward, the one which is in the Agamemnon of Aeschylus: "Handmaids, why do you delay, for whom the task has been commanded to strew the ground of the path with tapestries?" And many things which follow in the same place pertaining to the same thing. Plutarch in Cato the Younger: "He was escorted with tears and boundless embraces, with them placing their garments under his feet where he might walk," See 2 Kings IX. 13.

Verse of the same. And others cut branches and strewed them in the way. Not that they strewed garments and branches in the very path to be trampled under the feet of the donkey (this perhaps would have tripped up the rider), but they fashioned little tents and tabernacles out of garments and branches alongside the road, after the manner of the Feast of Tabernacles: as Lightfoot says here.

Latin:

V. 8. ὁ δὲ πλεῖστος ὄχλος] Convenit hic illud Horatii: In- terdum vulgus rectum videt: ut in Dvide 1. Sam. XIIX. 6.

ἔστρωσαν ἑαυτῶν τὰ ἱμάτια] De hoc more vide præ- ter eos locos quos alii adduxerunt eum qui est in Agamem- none Æschylis: Δμωαὶ τί μέλλεθ᾽ ὧν ἐπέσταλται τέλος Πέδον κελεύθῳ στρωννύναι πετάσμασιν; Et quæ ibidem sequuntur multa eodem pertinentia. Plutar- chus Catone Uticensi: προεπέμφθη δάκρυσι καὶ περιβολαῖς ἀ- πλήτοις ὑποτιθέντων τὰ ἱμάτια τοῖς ποσὶν ᾗ βαδίζοι, Vide. 2. Reg. IX. 13.

Vers. eod. ἄλλοι δὲ κλάδες ἔστρωννυν ἐν τῇ ὁδῷ. Non quod vestes & ramos in ipsa semita sub pedi- bus asini calcandos sternerent, (hoc forsan equitan- tem præsterneret) sed juxta viam tentoriola & ta- bernacula ex vestibus & ramis confinxerunt, ad mo- rem festi Scenopegiæ: ut hic Lightfootus.

## 21:9
Verse 9. Hosanna to the Son of David. The word Hosanna, consisting of a Hebrew verb and particle, is used for the hymn itself, as the paean is for the Greeks. For that interpretation is more suitable here and below in verse 15 than that it should signify palm branches. The sense is: we sing this auspicious hymn to King Messiah. It may be asked, since the rite of carrying palm branches or thyrsi made of palm and citron, as Josephus speaks, and of acclaiming Hosanna pertains to the Feast of Tabernacles (the same Josephus calls it the Feast of Wood-carrying), which fell in the month of September, as appears in Leviticus 23:39-40, how they were used now at a completely different time of year. It must be known, therefore, that it was constantly believed by the Jews that the feast days contained not only the memory of the Egyptian exodus, but also a presage of the times of the Messiah. And so, even today, the Jews in the Feast of Tabernacles say they wish that they might be able to spend joyful days in that manner when the Messiah reigns, and their enemies are defeated. That part of the people, therefore, which, moved by the miracles of Jesus, had firmly persuaded itself that this was the true Messiah, as if the presage were fulfilled, rightly uses the rites and words of the Feast of Tabernacles. Just as we read that the same signs of public joy were used in the new dedication of the temple under the Hasmoneans, 2 Maccabees 10:7 and 1 Maccabees 13:51 and Revelation 7:9. Moreover, it seems that the rite of carrying branches, like many others, passed from the Jews to the Greeks. For Clement notes from Orpheus that branches were accustomed to be given to those worshipping. And at Athens, among the feast days, there was the Feast of Tabernacles.

The word Hosanna, Hebrew הושע נא, is used in two ways: first, it is employed as a formula of acclamation from Psalm 118:25, Save, I beseech thee, or bring salvation, I pray: which the Jews were accustomed to use especially in the Feast of Tabernacles, carrying fronds and branches and singing Hosanna daily, with a very frequent repetition of the word to the names of GOD, For thy sake, GOD of gods, Hosanna, for thy sake, LORD of lords, Hosanna, etc., to the divine attributes: for thy truth, Hosanna, for thy Covenant, Hosanna. And furthermore they added to these things, by which they were congratulating the temple of the elect, Hosanna, the mount Moriah, Hosanna, etc., and then returning again to the names of God, they shouted: LORD Savior, Hosanna; Redeemer and Savior Hosanna, etc., and afterwards by antiphon, I beseech thee redeem the shoot of thy plantation, to which is sung in response, and Hosanna, etc. See Andr. Osiander, book III, Annotations on ch. xxxvi of the Harmony. Then that word is taken for the branches of trees themselves, which they carried in the public solemnity of the feast of tabernacles, according to the law of Lev. XXIII. 40, which are called by that word by the Jews, because they were accustomed to shout Hosanna so often when they carried them, as it is said in the Talmud to bind Hosannas: in which sense some, with Schindler, think it is taken here. But it is more correctly taken in this place for an acclamation repeated from the Jewish Litanies (for those songs were twin to our Litanies), or rather taken from Ps. CXVIII, which treats of the advent and passion of Christ, since, as Jerome teaches, the Jews for that reason accepted this Psalm concerning the advent of the Messiah. Since, therefore, they sang Hosanna no longer at the feast of tabernacles, but extraordinarily around the time of the Feast of the Passover in honor of Christ, there is no doubt that this was done by the special direction of God, so that Jesus of Nazareth, as the true Messiah, might be received with this acclamation: although Grotius's opinion does not displease, that the feast days of the Passover were believed by the Jews to contain not only the memory of the Egyptian exodus, but also a presage of the times of the Messiah. Therefore, as to the sense of the word, we do not much oppose the handed-down interpretation: we sing this well-omening hymn to King Messiah: as Theophyl. and Euthymius note that some understand by Hosanna a hymn or praise: to which Justin's interpretation in Q. 50 of the Questions and Answers to the Orthodox seems to return, that Hosanna is μεγαλωσύνη ὑπερκειμένη, excellent magnificence, and Clement of Alexandria, book 1, Paedagogus, ch. 5, that it signifies light, and glory, and praise. If, however, it is rendered word for word, the interpretation will be simpler, as being consonant with the Psalm from which that word is taken, in this way: Bring salvation, I beseech thee, or Save, I pray: to the Son of David, namely, we sing this in response, or we omen, or we pray. For as Casaubon rightly says in Exerc. p. 449 against Baronius, who objects that there would be no congruent sense if this Hosanna were taken in the sense in which he observes it in the Psalm, it is the custom in all languages that in such acclamations semi-complete sentences are uttered, and the words necessary to complete the sense are left to be supplied by the hearers: or if an abrupt or semi-complete speech does not please: it will be permitted to render the congratulatory song in this way: Hosanna, that is, bring salvation, I beseech thee, or grant prosperity to the Son of David: because the verb הוֹשִׁיעָה is also constructed with the third case, Jos. X. 6, Jud. VII. 2, 2 Sam. X. 11, Ps. XLIV. 4, Ps. LXXXVI. 16, Ps. XCVIII. 1, Ps. CXVI. 6, so that the acclamation is analogous to that, Long live the King, 1 Sam. X. 24, 1 Reg. I. 34. There are indeed not wanting those who would have the people pray for salvation for themselves from Christ by this Hosanna, which is the opinion of Jerome, Bede, Anselm, Thomas, Lyranus, and Abulensis: but it is better, by the force of the collation of the Psalm, to understand these as a congratulation made to the Messiah, by which they wish and pray for prosperity and happiness for him from God: to which sense those things which follow also favor.

Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord] From Ps. CXVIII. 26. May he be happy; or let it be, as the Latins used to shout. In the name of the Lord, by divine command and power.

Blessed, namely, let him be, may he be blessed by God, may he be heaped with every kind of blessing of the Lord, he who comes is the name of the Messiah, Matt. XI. 3, Luke VII. 19, John I. 15. Who was to come by the command and will of the Lord, and by the gracious economy of the divine: Rabbi Elias reports that the Jews formerly sang that formula, Blessed is he who comes, the King, in the name of the Lord, which is read here in Luke ch. XIX. 38, at the offering of sacrifices: which were a figure of Christ, who here presents himself as the lamb of God for the offering of his body.

Hosanna in the highest] In the Hebrew Gospel it was read ברמם as Jerome teaches us to Damasus. But I do not think this pertains to the designation of God, but that it is worth the same as 'highly': as if you were to say in Latin 'thrice and four times'. Thus the Hebrew במרומים and in Greek the words in the highest are found in the LXX interpreters, Ps. CXLVIII. 1, and elsewhere. And in the same sense במרום and in Greek in the highest in Psalm XCII. 4.

That sense of Grotius lacks examples. Those which are brought forward are equally doubtful. Nor does it appear why the words should not be taken properly as they sound: if, in the manner of Grotius, Hosanna is taken technically for a Hymn, will not the sense be plain, that we sing that Hymn in honor of God who dwells in the highest, or let Hosanna be heard in the highest. If it is taken for glory and praise, it will be consonant with that glory in the highest of Luke. But in our interpretation, saving the 'he who is in the highest'; who (art) God in the highest, so that there is an ellipsis of the article 'the', or the participle 'the one who is' is understood. Simply, save in the highest; because salvation is consummated in the heavens. Vossius makes a different acclamation, the former when Christ had ascended the foal of an ass; the latter after he arrived at the descent of the mount of Olives, book I, Harmony of the Gospels, ch. IV, § 7 & 9, but that cannot be gathered from the Evangelists. But it is akin to the truth, because the Evangelists report the acclamation in different ways, some from the crowd and the disciples as Matthew has it, others as the other Evangelists have it, having shouted with the same sense. In the temple, however, a new congratulation was made to Christ afterwards, with the boys shouting Hosanna to the Son of David, as Matthew testifies below v. 15.
