Τεθυμένα] Grammarians distinguish between θύειν & σφάττειν, so that σφάττειν may be for any reason, but θύειν is for the honor of God. But as with other words, so usage has extended this one beyond the nature of its origin. That is manifest in John X. 10. Thus also the Latin mactare, born in sacred rites, began to be extended to other things.

Latin:

Vers. 4. πάλιν ἀπέςειλεν ἄλλως] Invitatio apertior facta per Apostolos tum veteres, tum alios illis additos, eorumq; adjutores, postquam Christo resuscitato, in cælum evecto, & Spiritu desuper misso, nihil ultra divinæ liberalitatis non dicam requiri, sed nec optari poterat.

Τὰ σιτιςὰ] In quo genere erant vituli, μέχρι σιτεντοὶ non Athenzo tantum, sed & Lucæ XV. 23 & in Græco Jeremiæ XLVI. 21. & cortis aves. His altilium, illis saginatorum vox ex usu Latino rectius convenit.

Τεθυμένα] Θύειν & σφάττειν distinguunt Grammatici, ut (φάττειν sit quavis de causa, θύειν autem ἐπὶ τιμῇ Θεῦ. Sed ut alias voces ita & hanc usus extra originis suæ naturam produxit. Manifestum id est Joh. X. 10. Sic & Latinum mactare in sacris natum ad alia extendi cœpit.

## 22:5
Vers. 5. ἀπῆλθον, ὁ μὲν εἰς τ' ἴδιον ἀγρὸν] They put eternal benefits after the pursuit of perishable things.

Latin:

Vers. 5. ἀπῆλθον, ὁ μὲν εἰς τ' ἴδιον ἀγρὸν] Caducarum re- sum studio beneficia æterna posthabuerunt,

## 22:6
Vers. 6. ὕβρισαν] As Peter and John, and Paul also more than once.

ἀπέκτειναν] As Stephen and the two Jameses.

Latin:

Vers. 6. ὕβρισαν] Ut Petrum & Johannem, Paulum quoque non semel.

ἀπέκτειναν] Ut Stephanum & Jacobos duos.

## 22:7
Vers. 7. Τὰ ςρατεύματα ἀυτῦ] The angels, as in 1 Kings XXII. 19, 2 Chronicles XVIII. 18, Luke II. 13. Moreover, by the ministry of angels God governs both kingdoms and the lower nature: and consequently through them he sends wars, famine, and pestilence: all of which thundered down as if in one assault upon the city of Jerusalem.

They are not angels as in 1 Kings XXII. 19, 2 Chronicles XVIII. 18, Luke II. 13, as seemed to Grotius, nor does God always send wars, famine, and pestilence through angels. Others, with Theophylact, more correctly understand military armies, and B. Franzius and others think these were fulfilled in the Jews by the Roman Army.

Latin:

Vers. 7. Τὰ ςρατεύματα ἀυτῦ] Angelos, ut 1. Reg. XXII. 19. 2. Paral. XIIX. 18. Luc. II. 13. Angelorum autem mi- nisterio Deus & regna & naturam inferiorem gubernat: ac proinde per eos immittit bella, famem & pestilentiam: quæ omnia uno velut impetu in Hierosolymorum urbem detonuerunt.

Non sunt Angeli ut 1. Reg. XXII. 19. 2. Par. XIIX. 18. Luc. II. 13. quod Grotio visum, neque semper per angelos bella, famem & pestilentiam immittit Deus. Rectius alii exercitus militares cum Theo- phylacto intelligunt, & impleta hæc in Judæis per Exercitum Romanum B. Franzius aliique cen- sent.

## 22:8
Vers. 8. οὐκ ἦσαν ἄξιοι [they were not worthy]: a litotes, for what otherwise had to be said, μάλα ἦσαν ἀνάξιοι [they were very unworthy]. Thus Acts 13:46, where we have an example of this fulfilled prophecy, οὐκ ἀξίους κρίνετε ἑαυτοὺς τῆς αἰωνίας ζωῆς [you judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life]; that is, you show yourselves in reality unworthy of eternal life by contumaciously rejecting the life-giving word.

Latin:

Vers. 8. 8κ ἦσαν ἄξιοι] λιτότης, pro eo quod dicendum alioqui erat μάλα ἦσαν ἀνάξιοι. Sic Actor. XIII. 46. ubi consummati hujus vaticinii habemus exemplum, ἐκ ἄξιως κρίνετε ἑαυτὸς τῆς αἰωνία ζωῆς; id est, vosipsos vita æterna indignos reipsa ostenditis, sermonem vivificum contuma- citer repudiando.

## 22:9
Vers. 9. πορεύεσθε οὖν εἰς τὰς διεξόδους τῶν ὁδῶν [go therefore to the outlets of the ways]: The admirable wisdom of God seized the occasion to show His immense goodness from the malice of the Jews. Even if the Jews had done their duty, they still had no cause to complain of God if He had made the Gentiles also participants in His kindness, which the parable of the two sons, one thrifty and the other ἀσώτος [prodigal], teaches, and as could also be understood above from the comparison of the laborers. But so that God might remove every pretext for Jewish envy, He willed that they themselves be invited first, and not perfunctorily, but frequently, to the Evangelical dogma; but upon them refusing the benefit, that it be passed to the Gentiles, willing it to be both a most certain testimony of His goodness toward the whole human race and a punishment for Hebrew obstinacy. Thus Paul in the already mentioned place says, when it does not please you to hear, we turn to the Gentiles: who also in the Epistle to the Romans magnificently explains this divine counsel, saying that the crime of the Jews became the wealth of the world. Διιξοδοι [outlets] are תוצאות העיר [the exits of the city], viz., leading outside the city. For thus Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion translate that Hebrew word in Ezekiel 48:30. These διεξοδος [outlets] signify in this place the various opinions of philosophers and the diverse rites of superstitions into which the nations, having abandoned the ways handed down by Adam and Noah, had turned aside. For in the preceding centuries God permitted the nations to insist on whatever ways they pleased, Acts 14:16, not having sent prophets to them, as He was accustomed to do to the nation of the Jews, although otherwise He was daily meeting them with natural testimonies, nor was the approach to greater progress closed to them, especially since the time when the manifold diaspora of the Jews had filled the world, and the divine law was read in the Greek language.

ὅπως ἂν εὕρητε [that you may find]: God did not want anyone excluded from a general benefit by any prejudice.

Latin:

Vers. 9. πορεύεσθε ἕν εἰς τὰς διεξόδες ἢ ὁδῶν] Admirabi- lis Dei sapientia suæ ingentes profanas bonitatis ostenden- dæ occasionem arripuit ex Judæorum malitia, Etiamsi Ju- dæi fecissent officium, nullam tamen habebant causam de Deo querendi, si benignitates suæ etiam gentes fecisset par- ticipes, quod filiorum duorum alterius frugi, alterius ἀσώτυ fabella docet, & supra etiam ex vimtoruin comparatione intelligi potuit. Sed ut omnem πρόφασιν Judaicæ inviden- tiæ Deus adimeret, ipsos primum, nec perfunctorie, sed cre- bro invitari ad dogma Evangelicum voluit; ipsis autem be- neficium recusantibus, transiri ad gentes, idem esse volens & bonitatis suæ erga omne humanum genus certissimum te- stimonium, & pertinaciæ Hebraicæ pœnam. Ita Paulus jam dicto loco, quando vobis non libet inquit, audire, ad gentes vertimur: qui & in Epistola ad Romanos divinum hoc consilium magnifice explicat, dicens Judæorum crimē facti esse mundi opulentiam. Διιξοδοι sunt תוצאות העיר viz extra urbem ducentes. Nam ita Hebræum illud ver- tunt Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion Ezechielis XLIIX. 30. Hæ διεξοδος significant hoc loco varias Philosophorum opiniones, & diversos superstitionum ritus, in quos natio- nes, relictis viis ab Adamo & Noa traditis, deflexerant. Præ cedentibus enim sæculis permisie at Deus gentes fuis quan- que viis qua luberet insistere, Act. XIV. 16. non missis scili- cet ad eos Prophetis, ut ad gentem Judæorum facere sole- bat, cum alioqui naturalibus illos testimoniis quotidie con- veniret, nec clausus istis esset aditus majoris profectus, præ- sertim ex quo Judæorum multiplex διασπορὰ orbem im- pleverat, & divina lex Græco sermone legebatur.

ὅπως ἂν εὕρητε] A generali beneficio Deus neminem vo- luit ullo præjudicio exclusum.

## 22:10
V. 10. πονηρούς τε καὶ ἀγαθοὺς [both bad and good]: There was indeed some distinction among the Gentiles before the Evangelical invitation: for some wandered with loosened reins; others followed the guidance of reason a little more closely. But since all had turned aside to the worship of false gods, and add to that the pursuit of vain glory, God did not want account to be taken of that distinction: but He embraced all, as gravely guilty, in one formula of pardon: so that it might appear more that this gift is of purely gratuitous favor, οὐκ ἐξ ἔργων, ἀλλ' ἐκ τοῦ καλοῦντος [not of works, but of Him who calls]. Theophylact well notes that ἀγαθοὺς [good] is to be understood comparatively: for what is less evil is popularly accustomed to be called good.

ὁ Γάμος [the wedding]: So most codices: nor did Origen and Theophylact read otherwise: whence what others have, νυμφὼν [wedding hall], is to be believed to have come from an interpretation, which however the Syriac follows, whether because it reads it so, or because it wanted to render the sense more openly.

Latin:

V. 10. πονηρούς τε καὶ ἀγαθοὺς] Erat quidem inter gentiles ante invitationem Evangelica discrimen aliquod : nam alii laxa- tis habenis vagabantur: alii paulo propius sequebantur du- ctum rationis. Sed cum omnes ad falsorum Deorum cul- tus, adde & manis gloriæ studium deflexissent, noluit Deus ejus discriminis haberi rationem : sed omnes, ut graviter fontes, una veniæ formula complexus est: quo magis appa- reret mere gratuiti favoris esse hoc donum, ἐκ τῆς ἐγγύης, ἀλλ' ἐκ τοῦ καλέντος. Bene notat Theophylactus ἀγαθοὺς intel- ligendos comparate: nam quod minus malum est, bonum vocari solet populariter.

ὁ Γάμος] Ita plerique codices: nec aliter le- gerunt Origenes & Theophylactus : unde quod alii habent νυμφὼν, ex interpretamento credendum est venisse, quod tamen sequitur Syrus, sive quod ita legit, sive quod sensum reddere voluit apertiorem.

## 22:11
Vers. 11. ἔνδυμα γάμου [wedding garment]: Aristophanes in the Birds called it γαμικὴν χλανίδα [a wedding cloak]. This garment is a walk worthy of the vocation, Eph. 4:1, works which make the vocation sure, 2 Pet. 1:10. For also in the Apocalypse the white linen wedding garment is explained as τὰ δικαιώματα τῶν ἁγίων [the righteous acts of the saints], where δικαιώματα [righteous acts] are the very works testifying to our obedience, as Luke 1:6, Rom. 2:26. The same are called ἱμάτια λευκὰ [white garments] in the same Apocalypse 3:18. And so the ancients with great consensus on this place. By a similar metaphor we read the word to be clothed used of virtues in Col. 3:12 and elsewhere.

This is primarily the explanation of the Papists, who understand the wedding garment as works. How much indeed we are also commanded to put on virtues like garments, Col. 3:12. Yet that covering and ornament by which we stand before God, and are pleasing in His eyes, is the righteousness of Christ: a garment, I say, not of our own righteousness, which is imperfect and too unclean, and as a menstruous cloth, Isa. 64:6. But the righteousness of Christ, which is truly pure, and untouched, lacking all uncleanness, Isa. 61:10, Zech. 3:5, therefore we are said to put on Christ, Rom. 13:14, Gal. 3:27, and Christ Himself offers us white garments, Rev. 3:18, nor are τὰ δικαιώματα τῶν ἁγίων [the righteous acts of the saints], Rev. 19:8, other than that righteousness and obedience of Christ by which we are constituted righteous, Rom. 5:18, 19, which is appropriated to the saints through faith. And so the principal ones among the ancients in the Greek Church; Basil the Great in Isa. ch. 9. The garment of Christians, covering the shame of our sin, is faith, by which we believe in Christ. For whoever of you have been baptized into Christ, have put on Christ: Chrysostom, hom. 41, oper. imperf., the wedding garment is true faith. And in the Latin Church, Ambrose, book 4 de fid. c. 1, where he points out the wedding garment of faith: likewise Hilary on Matt. 24, Augustine, book 1 Qq. Evangel. q. 13, book 15 de Trinit. cap. 8, Gregory the Great, homily 38 in Evangel.

Latin:

Vers. 11. ἔνδυμα γάμου] γαμικὴν χλανίδα dixit Aristo- phanes Avibus. Vestis hæc est ambulatio digna vocatione Eph. IV. 1. opera quæ ratam efficiunt vocationem 2. Petr. I, 10. Nam & in Apocalypsi vestis byssina nuptialis, explica- tur τὰ δικαιώματα τ' ἁγίων, ubi δικαιώματα sunt ipsa opera obedientiam nostram testantia, ut Luc. 1. 6. Rom. II. 26, Eadem ἱμάτια λευκὰ dicuntur in eadem Apoc. III. 18. Atq; ita veteres magno consensu ad hunc locum. Simili trala- tione verbum indui de virtutibus usurpatum legimus Co- loss. III. 12. & alibi.

Est hæc imprimis Pontificiorum explicatio, qui de operibus vestem nuptialem intelligunt. Quan- tam vero etiam induere virtutes vestium instar jubeamur Col. III. 12. Tegumentum tamen & or- namentum illud, quo coram Deo consistimus, & in oculis ejus grati sumus, est justitia Christi: vestis inquam, non nostræ justitiæ, quæ imperfecta & immunda nimis, atque velut pannus menstruatæ Ef. LXIV. 6. Sed justitia Christi, quæ vere pura est, atque illibata omnis expers immunditiei, Ef. LXI. 10. Zach. III. 5. ideo Christum induere dici- mur Rom. XIII. 14. Gal. III. 27. & Christus ipse no- bis vestes offert candidas Apoc. III. 18. nec alia sunt τὰ δικαιώματα τ' ἁγίων Apoc. XIX. 8. quam il- la justitia & obedientia Christi qua justi nos con- stituimur, Rom. V. 18. 19. quæ per fidem sanctis ap- propriatur. Atque ita è Veteribus in Græca Ec- clesia præcipui; Basilius M. in Ef. IX. cap. Samis Christianorum vestimentum, obnubens peccati no- stri turpitudinem fides est, qua in Christum credi- mus. Quicunque enim in Christum baptizati estis, Christum induistis: Chrysost. hom. XLI. oper. im- perf. nuptiale vestimentum est fides vera. Et in La- tina Ecclesia Ambrosius l. IV. de fid. c. 1. ubi nuptia- le fidei vestimentum indigitat: nec non Hilarius in XXIV. Matth. August. l. I. Qq. Evangel. q. 13. 1. XV. de Trinit. cap. 8. Gregorius M. homil. XXXIIX. in Evangel.

## 22:12
Vers. 12. ἑταῖρε [friend]: We treated of this form of address above at ch. 20:13.

ἐφιμώθη] The inexcusability is shown: just as the binding of hands and feet soon denotes the irresistible and inescapable nature of the punishment divinely inflicted.

Latin:

Vers. 12. ἑταῖρε] De hac compellatione egimus supra ad c. XX. 13.

ἐφιμώθη] Ostenditur τὸ ἀναπολόγητον: sicut mox ligatio manuum & pedum notat τὸ ἄμαχον καὶ τὸ ἄφευκτον irroga- ti divinitus supplicii.

## 22:13
Vers. 13. into the outer darkness] Christ, by a certain summary, continues that which is the final stage of retribution with the comparison itself, because from there it is easy to understand how the rest is to be supplied. Regarding these darknesses, it was treated above at VIII. 12.

Latin:

Vers. 13. εἰς τὸ σκότος τὸ ἐξώτερον] Christus compendio quodam id quod est ultimum τῆς ἀνταποδόσεως cum ipsa comparatione continuat, quia inde facile est intellectu, quomodo supplenda sint cætera. De his tenebris actum supra IIX. 12.

## 22:14
Vers. 14. for many are called, but few are chosen] We had this maxim placed more obscurely above, which here has a most open sense: the Jews [for it is about them that it is treated] were all called, who are many in number: but some turned away from the fleeting word, and spurned the warnings: others, moreover, treated the monitors badly: some, having professed faith, did not show the sincerity and vigor of faith through pious works. Therefore, only a small remnant, approved by God through testimonies of docility, faith, and love, received the gifts of the Holy Spirit, but also in the future will receive the thing itself, of which the Spirit is the earnest.

PART II. On the case of Caesar's census.

Latin:

Vers. 14. πολλοὶ γάρ εἰσι κλητοὶ, ὀλίγοι δὲ ἐκλεκτοὶ] Ha- buimus hanc γνώμην supra obscurius positam, quæ hic aper- tissimum habet sensum: Judæi [de his enim agitur] vocati sunt omnes, qui sunt numero multi: sed alii ab caduca verfi, monita sprevere: alii insuper male tractarunt monitores : nonnulli fidem professi non ostenderunt piis operibus fi- dei sinceritatem & vigorem. Igitur parvum duntaxat κα- τάλευμμα Deo probatum per docilitatis, fidei & dilectionis testimonia, accepit dona Spiritus Sancti, sed & in posterum accipiet rem ipsam, cujus arra est spiritus.

PARS II. Casu de censu Cæsaris.

## 22:15
Verse 15. The Pharisees took counsel] Since public authority had accomplished nothing, the Pharisaic sect employs private machinations, as above in chapter XII. 14, where see what we have said.

that they might ensnare him in his speech] That is, that they might elicit something from him, by the pretext of which he could be accused of revolutionary activities before the Roman Governor. For otherwise there was no hope of putting him to death. It must be interpreted thus from Luke.

Latin:

Vers. 15. οἱ Φαρισαῖοι συμβούλιον ἔλαβον] Cum publica auctoritas nihil profecisset, secta Pharisaīca privatas molitio- nes adhibet, ut supra c. XII. 14. ubi quæ diximus vide.

ὅπως αὐτὸν παγιδεύσωσιν ἐν λόγῳ] Id est, ut aliquid ab ipso elicerent, cujus obtentu accusari posset rerum novata- rum apud Romanum Præsidem. Nam alioqui nulla spes erat illum interficiendi. Ita interpretandum ex Luca.

## 22:16
Verse 16. their disciples] Certain of the Pharisees, having followed Judas the Gaulonite, felt it was a sin to acknowledge a power foreign to the divine law. For I think that what Josephus says of them, 'they have supposed God alone to be leader and master,' must be interpreted in this way: namely, that they wished the command, 'you shall serve God alone,' to be understood not as if it conflicted with any supreme authority, such as that of Saul, David, or Solomon, but as if it opposed this very thing when profaned by the rule of foreign powers: just as it is written in Deuteronomy chapter XVII. 15, 'You shall not set over you a foreign man, but one who is of your brothers.' Nor was this opinion new, but, if I am not mistaken, it proceeded from the Hasideans of the Maccabean times: indeed, it is older. For those who so stubbornly refused surrender during the Chaldean siege, with whose obstinacy Jeremiah had to contend, seem to have thought the same. And just as in those times that opinion was the cause of great evils, as Jeremiah taught, so Josephus rightly notes of his own age that no evil can be imagined to which that dogma did not give rise. But it is one thing to invite an external yoke upon oneself voluntarily, and another to submit to servitude for the sake of preserving life, or to endure it once imposed, as Daniel and his companions did, which God would never have sent upon that people except as a punishment for grave sins. Some of the Greeks and Romans thought that servitude should be redeemed even by certain death. Truth itself teaches us otherwise through Jeremiah: for the delay of life, which gives space for repentance, ought to be held as the first among the goods of the body, and the foundation of other goods pertaining to the body. But that external servitude pertains to the body, not to the soul. It is Bion's: 'Good servants are free; but wicked men are free, yet slaves to their desires.' And that of Euripides: 'For the name will not corrupt a noble slave. And many are better than the free.' And this of the same: 'To many slaves the name is shameful; but the mind of those who are not slaves is freer.' But if even that domestic servitude does not hinder the virtue of the mind, how much less does that public one, which is often not even servitude. Seneca blames Brutus for thinking that liberty could not exist under the rule of one man. All of which could have had a place even if, with the republic standing, the Jews, placed in grave danger, had had to deliberate whether liberty or peace was preferable, and as Cicero poses this question, 'whether one must strive in every way for the dissolution of tyranny, even if the city is going to be endangered on account of this.' But truly, once the surrender was made, what consultation remained? For the promises we make when driven by the necessity of war bind our faith: for unless this were so, the whole sanctity of treaties would perish. Furthermore, there had been added the possession of a long time, which it is always unjust to wish to disturb in public affairs. Agrippa, arguing well against these zealots, speaks thus in Josephus: 'But indeed, to desire liberty now is untimely, when one ought to have struggled earlier so as not to lose it; for the experience of slavery is harsh, and the struggle not to begin it is just. But he who has once been conquered and then revolts is a headstrong slave, not a lover of liberty.' Following him, Josephus himself addressed the besieged Jerusalemites in this manner: 'For it is indeed noble to fight for liberty, but one ought to have done so first. But to have once submitted and yielded for long periods of time, and then to shake off the yoke, is the mark of those who are dying hard, not of those who love liberty.' Since there are diverse kinds of regimes, all liable to their own vices, although some more, some less, that man is both a good man and a good citizen, as Augustus used to say, who does not wish the present republic to be changed: who, to speak with Tacitus, desires good and legitimate rule by prayer, but tolerates whatever kind exists, just as one tolerates sterility or excessive rains and the evils of nature. The characters of those in power must be borne, and frequent changes are not useful. Sophocles: 'They are rulers; so one must yield; why not? For even terrible and most powerful things yield to honors.' And what follows. And we see that the ancient Christians prescribed this law for themselves, that they should render faith and obedience to whoever had obtained power, and not join any who were causing revolution under specious names. See Tertullian in his Apology.

rum, how the Gaulonite zealots were a part of the Pharisees, but distinguished by peculiar opinions from the rest of the flock of their name, has been evident from those things which were said at chapter XVI. 6: and the matter is clearer than that it should be doubted. It is more to be considered whether these also, like the Gaulonites, thought that Caesar's rule should be rejected, or the contrary. To me, they clearly seem to have been brought to Christ because they were most popular and most apt to elicit from Christ a response in favor of liberty. We have said that the dogma of the Herodians was born in the times of Herod the Great, who, although an Idumean by birth, yet since Idumea had become an accession to Judea, and he himself professed Judaism, could not be considered a foreigner. Therefore the Herodians willingly obeyed Herod, whom they also called the Messiah, as a Jew, and as the history of Josephus teaches, a great defender of the law, who even if he did anything for the sake of the Romans, solicitously excused himself to the Jews, 'as doing it not of his own accord but by the command and orders of others.' But with Jerusalem and the better part of Judea reduced to the form of a province, obeying not a circumcised king but powers foreign to the law did not sufficiently agree with the dogma of the Herodians. Moreover, the Sadducees, of whom the Herodians were a part, valued the liberty of the republic highly. For among other arguments, they tried to prove by this that there are no rewards after this life believed in by the ancestors, because otherwise they would never have taken up arms so often for the sake of liberty. Nor is it incredible that the children of Herod, although they openly flattered Caesar servilely, nevertheless through secret arts provided fuel for this dogma, not without hope that it would come to pass that they might one day be restored to the lost part of the kingdom by the zeal of the people.

Indeed, others also understand them as admirers or worshippers of Herod, who held him for the Messiah, Tertullian de praescript., Epiphanius haer. XX, Victor of Antioch on Mark XII, Damascenus de haeref., Theophylact in h. l., and Scaliger in Euseb., Casaubon Exerc. l. c. 5, Eman. Saa, B. Gerhard. But the interpretation of others seems simpler, who take them with the Syriac as Herod's ministers, or those who were of the house of Herod, which is also the opinion of the Persians and Ethiopians: approved by Origen, Eusebius Emissenus, Anselm, Dionysius the Carthusian, B. Luther, Chemnitius, Hunnius, Beza, Piscator, Gualtherus, Franc. Lucas, Salmeron, Barradius. For those [theories] about the Herodians worshipping their King as the Messiah, and constituting some part of the Sadducees, rest on no solid foundation. And the Herodians are clearly distinguished here by St. Matthew from the Sadducees. Cons. v. 16 and 23. Cons. and Sam. Petit l. II. Var. Lect. c. 1.

Ἀληθὴς εἶ] Ἀληθὴς here is frank, as in that of Terence: Compliance begets friends, truth begets hatred. Τὴν ὁδὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ] The divine law, the precepts of a life pleasing to God.

Οὐ μέλει σοι περὶ οὐδενός] Namely, that you do not hesitate to faithfully deliver those precepts.

Οὐ γὰρ βλέπεις εἰς πρόσωπον ἀνθρώπων] You do not court the favor of either Caesar or Pontius Pilate, nor do you fear their power. For the Hellenists, following the Hebrews, call πρόσωπον the quality of a man which is wont to stir up affections in others and thus lead them away from the respect of truth and justice. Hence προσωπολήπτης and προσωποληπτεῖν.

Latin:

Vers. 16. τοὺς μαθητὰς αὐτῶν] Pharisæorum quidam Ju- dam Gaulonitem secuti sentiebant nefas esse agnoscere potestatem à lege divina extraneam. Ita enim interpre- tandum puto quod de illis dicit Josephus μόνον ἡγεμόνα καὶ δεσπότην τὸν Θεὸν ὑπειλήφασι, nempe quod illud, uni Deo servies, ita intelligi voluerint, non quasi cum quovis imperio summo, puta Saulis, Davidis, Solomonis pugnaret, sed quasi adversaretur hoc ipsum imperiis profanatum potestatum: sicut in Deuteronomio c. XVII. 15. scriptum est, Non præficies tibi virum extraneum, sed qui de fratribus tuis sit. Neque nova erat hæc sententia, sed, ni fallor, ab Asidæis Macca- baicorum temporum profecta: imo antiquior. Nam idem sensisse videntur qui in Chaldaico obsidio deditionem tam præfracte recusabant, cum quorum pertinacia certandum habuit Jeremias. Et sicut illis temporibus illa opinio cau- sa fuit magnorum malorum, ut Jeremias docuit, ita recte de sua ætate Josephus notat, nullum posse malum excogitari cui istud dogma causam non dederit. Longe autem est a- liud, sponte in se externum jugum accersere, aliud vitæ ser- vandæ causa subire servitutem, aut jam impositam pati, ut Daniel fecit sociique ipsius, quam scilicet nunquam illi po- pulo Deus immissurus fuerat, nisi in pœnam gravium pec- catorum. Græcorum & Romanorum nonnulli existima- runt servitutem vel certa morte redimendam. Ad aliud per Jeremiam nos docet ipsa veritas: nam vitæ mora, quæ spatium dat pœnitentiæ, inter bona corporis primum ha- beri debet, & fundamentum aliorum bonorum ad corpus pertinentium. Servitus autem illa externa ad corpus non ad animum pertinet. Bionis est: οἱ ἀγαθοὶ οἰκέται, ἐλεύ- θεροι· οἱ δὲ πονηροὶ ἐλεύθεροι, δοῦλοι ἐπιθυμιῶν: Et Euripidis istud: Δοῦλον γὰρ ἐσθλὸν τοὔνομ᾽ οὐ διαφθερεῖ. Πολλοὶ δ᾽ ἀμείνους εἰσι τῶν ἐλευθέρων. Ejusdem & hoc: Πολλοῖσι δούλοις τ᾽ οὔνομ᾽ αἰσχρὸν· ἡ δὲ φρὴν Τῶν οὐχὶ δούλων ἐστ᾽ ἐλευθερωτέρα. Quod si illa etiam domestica servitus animi virtutem non impedīt, quanto minus publica illa quæ sæpe ne servitus quidem est. Seneca Brutum eo nomine culpat, quod existi- maverit sub unius imperio libertatem esse non posse. Quæ omnia locum habere poterant etiam si stante republica Ju- dæi in gravi periculo constituti consultandum habuissent libertas an pax placeret, & ut Cicero hanc quæstionem po- nit, εἰ παντὶ τρόπῳ τυραννίδος κατάλυσιν πραγματευτέον, κἂν μέλλῃ διὰ τοῦτο περὶ τῶν ὅλων ἡ πόλις κινδυνεύσειν. At vero semel facta deditione quæ supererat consultatio? Nam quæ belli necessitate adducti promittimus fidem obstrin- gunt: nisi enim id esset, periret tota fœderum sanctitas. Ac- cesserat deinde longi temporis possessio, quam movere velle semper iniquum est in publicis rebus. Bene adver- sus istos ζηλωτὰς disputans Agrippa apud Josephum ita lo- quitur: ἀλλὰ μὴν τόγε νῦν ἐλευθερίας ἐπιθυμεῖν ἄωρον, δέον ὑπὲρ τοῦ μηδὲ ἀποβαλεῖν αὐτὴν ἀγωνίζεσθαι πρότερον· ἡ γὰρ πεῖ- ρα τῆς δουλείας χαλεπὴ καὶ περὶ τοῦ μηδὲ ἄρξασθαι ταύτης ὁ ἀγὼν δίκαιος. ὁ δ᾽ ἅπαξ χειρωθεὶς, ἔπειτα ἀφιστάμενος αὐθάδης δοῦλός ἐστιν, οὐ φιλελεύθερος. Quem secutus Josephus ipse obsessos Hierosolymitas hunc in modum est affatus: εὖ γὰρ δὴ καὶ πολεμεῖν ὑπὲρ ἐλευθερίας καλὸν, χρῆναι δὲ πρῶτον. Τὸ δ᾽ ἅπαξ ὑποπεσόντας καὶ μακροῖς εἴξαντας χρόνοις ἔπειτα ἀπο- σείεσθαι τὸ ζυγὸν, δυσθανατούντων οὐ φιλελευθέρων εἶναι. Cum diversa sint regiminum genera, omnia vitiis suis, quanqum alia plus, alia minus, obnoxia, bonus ille & vir est & civis, ut Augustus dicebat, qui rempublicam præsentem mutari non vult: qui scilicet, ut cum Tacito loquar, bonum ac le- gitimum imperium voto expetit, qualecumque tolerat, quomodo sterilitatem aut nimios imbres & naturæ mala. Ferenda potentum ingenia, neque usui crebræ mutatio- nes. Sophocles: Ἄρχοντες εἰσιν· ὥσθ᾽ ὑπεικτέον· τί μή; Καὶ γὰρ τὰ δεινὰ, καὶ τὰ καρτερώτατα Τιμαῖς ὑπείκει· Et quæ sequuntur. Atque hanc legem videmus sibi præ- scripsisse Christianos veteres, ut cuivis imperium nacto fi- dem atque obedientiam præstarent, neque ulli sub specio- sis nominibus res novanti accederent. Vide Tertullianum Apologetico.

rum, quomodo Gaulonitici zelotæ pars erant Pharisæorum, sed peculiaribus opinionibus distinctos à cætero sui nomi- nis grege, ex iis quæ dicta sunt ad caput XVI. 6. patuit: & res est manifestior quam ut de ea ambigi debeat. Illud magis vivendum, an hi quoque, ut Gaulonitici, senserint recusanda Cæsaris imperia, an contra. Mihi plane videntur ad Chri- stum allegati qui maxime populares erant & aptissimi ad e- liciendum à Christo responsum pro libertate. Diximus He- rodianorum dogma natum temporibus Herodis magni, qui ortu quamvis Idumæus, tamen cum Idumæa facta esset Ju- dææ accessio, & ipse Judaismum profiteretur, extraneus haberi non poterat. Itaque Herodiani Herodi, quem & Messiam dicebant, libenter paruerunt ut Judæo, & quod Jo- sephi historia docet, magno legis vindici, qui etiam si quid faceret in Romanorum gratiam sollicite se Judæis excusa- bat, ὡς μὴ καθ' αὑτὸν ἀλλ' ἐξ ἐντολῆς καὶ προταγμάτων ποι- ῶν. At Hierosolymis & parte potiore Judææ in provinciæ formulam redacta, parere non jam circumciso regi sed alie- nis à lege potestatibus Herodianorum dogmati non satis consentiebat. Quin & Sadducæi, quorum pars erant He- rodiani, magni faciebant reipublicæ libertatem. Nam hoc inter cætera argumēto conabantur evincere nulla esse post hanc vitam præmia credita à majoribus, quia alioqui nun- quam pro libertate toties arma sumturi fuerant. Neque incredibile est Herodis liberos, quanquam palam Cæsari serviliter adulabantur, per occultas artes tamen fomenta subdidisse isti dogmati, non sine spe fore, ut aliquando po- puli studiis in amissam regni partem restituerentur.

Ita sane admiratores vel cultores Herodis, qui eum pro Messia habuerint, etiam alii intelligunt, Tertul. de præscript. Epiphan. hær. XX. Victor An- tiochenus in Marc. XII. Damasc. de hæref. Theo- phyl. in h. l. & Scaliger in Euseb. Casaubonus E- xerc. l. c. 5. Eman. Saa, B. Gerhard. Sed simplicior videtur aliorum interpretatio, qui de Herodia- nis ministris, vel iis qui è domo Herodis erant, cum Syro accipiunt, quæ etiam Persarum & Æthio- pum est sententia: Origeni, Eusebio Emisseno, Anshelmo, Dionys. Carthufiano, B. Luthero, Che- mnitio, Hunnio, Beza, Piscatori, Gualthero, Franc. Luca, Salmeroni, Barradio probata. Illa enim de Herodianis pro Messia Regem suum colentibus, & partem aliquam Sadducæorum constituenti- bus, nullo nituntur solido fundamento. Et di- stinguuntur Herodiani diserte à S. Matthæo hic à Sadducæis. Cons. v. 16. & 23. Cons. & Sam. Pe- titus l. II. Var. Lect. c. 1.

Ἀληθὴς εἶ] Ἀληθὴς hic est παῤῥησιαστικὸς, ut in illo Te- rentii: Obsequium amicos, veritas odium parit. Τὴν ὁδὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ] Legem divinam, præcepta vitæ Deo pla- centis.

Οὐ μέλει σοι περὶ οὐδενός] Nempe quominus ea præcepta fideliter tradas.

Οὐ γὰρ βλέπεις εἰς πρόσωπον ἀνθρώπων] Non captas gra- tiam aut Cæsaris aut Ponti Pilati, neque eorum poten- tiam formidas. Nam πρόσωπον Hellenistæ Hebræos secuti vocant qualitatem hominis quæ in aliis affectus ciere atque ita eos à veri justique respectu solet abducere. Hinc προ- σωπολήπτης & προσωποληπτεῖν.

## 22:17
Vers. 17. Ἔξεστι] It is lawful: as we have interpreted several times. For they are raising a question of divine, not human, law.

Κῆνσον] Φόρον, as Luke speaks. A metonymy. For tribute was paid from the census. The name of census, as we have said elsewhere, refers both to the burdens of estates and of heads, as can be seen in the Justinian Pandects, title de Censibus, where it is narrated that the poll tax was remitted by Vespasian for the Caesareans. For both censuses, an enrollment was necessary. Panegyric in praise of Constantine: You have remitted seven thousand heads, more than a fourth part of our censuses. Ammianus on Julian Caesar: Having entered those parts (of the Gauls), he found twenty-five gold pieces being demanded for each head in the name of tribute, but departing, only seven. Tertullian: Fields burdened with tribute are of less value: the heads of men assessed for payment are more ignoble. Whence we learn that the provinces of the Roman Empire paid tributes not only of fields, but also of human heads, outside of colonies, municipalities, and cities of Italian right. That Judea, from the time it was added to the provinces, was of a better right than the Gauls, is hardly credible. Wherefore, although κῆνσος or φόρος can also signify a burden on an estate, I do not see what stands in the way of our interpreting it here as a tribute on heads, not of fields but of men, with the Syriac interpreter, that which exists in Law III, Digest on Censuses, supports this interpretation of Ulpian: In the Syrian provinces, males from fourteen years of age and females from twelve up to the sixty-fifth year are obligated to the head tax. We showed above that the didrachmon is far different from this Roman tax.

Latin:

Vers. 17. Ἔξεστι] Fas est: ut aliquoties interpretati su- mus. Quæstionem enim divini non humani juris mo- vent.

Κῆνσον] Φόρον, ut Lucas loquitur. Μετωνυμία. Nam ex censu tributum pendebatur. Census nomen, ut alibi dixi- mus, & ad prædiorum & ad capitum onera refertur, ut videre est in Pandecte Justinianeo, titulo de Censibus, ubi Cæsariensibus narratur remissum à Vespasiano tributum capitis. Ad utrumque censum necessaria erat ἀπογραφή. Panegyricus in laudibus Constantini: Septem millia capi- tum remisisti, quartam amplius partem nostrorum censuum. Ammianus de Juliano Cæsare: Partes eas (Galliarum) in- gressus pro capitibus singulis tributi nomine vicenos quinos aureos reperit flagitari, discedens vero septenos tantum. Ter- tullianus: Agri tributo onusti viliores: hominum capita sti- pendio censa ignobiliora. Unde discimus provincias Ro- mani Imperii non agrorum tantum pependisse tributa, sed & humanorum capitum, extra colonias, municipia & civitates Italici juris. Judæam, ex quo provinciis ac- censa est, melioris fuisse juris quam Gallias, vix credibi- le est. Quare κῆνσος sive φόρος quanquam potest & præ- dii onus significare, quominus hic tributum in capita non agrorum sed hominum cum Syro interpretemur, quid obstet non video. Facit pro hac interpretatione Ul- piani illud quod exstat lege III. D. de censibus: In Syriis à quatuordecim annis masculi, à duodecim feminæ usq; ad sexage- simum quintum annum tributo capitis obligantur. Longe a- liud ab hoc Romano tributo esse τὸ δίδραχμον supra osten- dimus.

## 22:18
Verse 18. Why do you test me, you hypocrites? To test, as we warned before, is to contrive a calumny against someone. He calls them hypocrites, however, because they were concealing a cruel, no less than crafty, plan with words that professed piety. Cicero well says: Of all injustice, none is more capital than that of those who, when they most deceive, act in such a way that they appear to be good men.

Latin:

Vers. 18. τί με πειράζετε ὑποκριταὶ] πειράζειν, ut ante ad- monuimus, est calumniam alicui struere. Ὑποκριτὰς au- tem vocat quia consilium crudele non minus quam vafrum obregebant verbis pietatem præferentibus. Bene Cicero: Totius injustitiæ nulla capitalior est, quam eorum, qui tum cum maximè fallunt, id agunt, ut viri boni esse videantur.

## 22:19
Verse 19. The coin of the census. Give me some coin of that currency in which the tax is accustomed to be exacted. In that type of coin, however, the denarius was most common. And so, the error of those most learned men who thought the denarius was the measure of the tax has been deservedly criticized.

Latin:

Vers. 19. Τὸ νόμισμα τοῦ κήνσου] Date mihi nummum ali- quem ejus monetæ, in qua tributum exigi solet. In eo au- tem nummorum genere usitatissimus erat denarius. Itaque merito à viris doctissimis reprehensus est eorum error qui denarium tributi modum esse existimabant.

## 22:20
Verse 20. Whose is this image and inscription? Just as fixing a law is a sign of supreme power, so too is minting a coin: for a coin, as Aristotle teaches, has both its name and its very force from the law. Hence, debasing coins is reckoned among crimes of majesty. It is believed to be a Persian institution that coins are marked with the face and name of those who rule: whence the name of Darics. To this pertains that line:

Silver committed to titles and small faces.

And Philostratus in the life of Tyanaeus mentions a drachma that had become current for Tiberius. The coin itself, therefore, having value from the edict of Caesar, and bearing Caesar's name and face, testified that Caesar actually held supreme power over Judea, and that this was acknowledged by the Jews using that coin. It could be objected that, while in fact the Romans ruled the Jews and Caesar ruled the Romans, they did so by no right. But Christ shows that this is irrelevant to the proposed question. For since, as Tacitus says, neither the peace of nations can be had without arms, nor arms without pay, nor pay without taxes, it follows that taxes must be paid to him who rules, for as long as he rules, as the price of the common protection which whoever is the possessor of public power provides for us. Therefore, says Paul, you also pay taxes, and not only for fear of punishment, but for the sake of justice and equity, because by the protection of the authorities you are safe from violence and injury. It is certain, however, that this very thing is provided to some extent by all authorities—even if not with the equity and diligence that is fitting, and often even in such a way that they themselves do not abstain from violence and injury—so that it is much safer to live under them than without them: which is enough for taxes to be both able and required to be paid.

It is doubtful how the Pharisees could have been convinced by the image and inscription of the coin that they were under Caesar's jurisdiction. For we often use the coins of other princes to whom we are not subject. But it must be known that the Jewish people, while they were still their own masters, had their own currency which they used, not a foreign one. Furthermore, it is not about just any coin here, but the coin of the census, i.e., that type of currency by which the census was paid: which Jerome in this place observes was a denarius having the image of Caesar in the head tax. And the ancient Romans were accustomed, when nations were reduced into their empire, to impose such a tax as a sign of subjection and recognition of dominion, which could not be paid in any other kind of currency than Roman money marked with the names of the Consuls, as B. Gerhard notes in Harmony, chapter CLIV, page 1147. But just as in the time when the Consulship still lasted, the currency had the names of the Roman Consuls inscribed, so when the sum of affairs had devolved to the Emperors, they themselves wanted their head, crowned with the ornaments of the Emperor and the triumphal laurel, and the memory of the dignities they had held, to be publicly visible on the inscription: and they observed this most strictly in exacting the tax from the peoples subject to their power, so that they would accept from them only their own currency, that is, minted by their order and marked with their name. Regarding Nero (who was the third Emperor after Tiberius), Suetonius in chapter 44 mentions that he exacted taxes with such fastidiousness that he would accept his own coins only if they were rough, that is, still fresh from the workshop and as if hot from the anvil and glowing with a certain pleasing newness; that this was also done by Tiberius, who had already reigned for eighteen years, so that he would accept only his own minted currency, is likely inferred from this very passage. And not irrelevantly does Selden observe that it was customary to inscribe the regions and provinces captured on the reverse side of coins; now, indeed, if there was any inscription on the reverse (for it is clear that both the reverse and the obverse can be contained under the name of a simple inscription) containing something of that kind about Judea captured, subdued, or received, from which the Caesarean Empire and the Roman victories would necessarily have to be acknowledged, nothing would be more evident than that from the very coin which those questioning him were exhibiting and acknowledging, they were sufficiently affirming that they were conquered, captured, and subdued by the Roman, and therefore owed him the payments of obedience and subjection. For it is recognized everywhere that taxes are owed by the right of victory and the law of nations. What of the fact that even while the Tax, the Coin, the Census, and the Denarius are mentioned together in the way just described, it is clearly admitted that the custom of paying had already taken root, that is, that the surrender had preceded, and the payment was not only commanded by the victor's order, but also admitted by those paying as if by right. Finally, Christ knew by the power of his omniscience that the Pharisees had at hand such an inscription by which they could be convinced: who, however, were so blinded that they nevertheless exhibited to Christ the coin he was demanding, from which their subjection could be demonstrated in the very act.

Latin:

Vers. 20. Τίνος ἡ εἰκὼν αὕτη καὶ ἡ ἐπιγραφή] Sicut legem figere signum est summi imperii, ita & nummum cudere: nam νόμισμα, ut docet Aristoteles, & nomen suum & vim ipsam habet ἀπὸ τοῦ νόμου. Hinc majestatis crimini- bus accensetur nummos corrumpere. Nummos autem imperantium vultu ac nomine signari Persicum creditur esse institutum: unde Daricorum nomen. Huc illud per- tinet:

Comisum argentum in titulos, faciesq; minutas.

Et Philostratus in vita Tyanæi commemorat δραχμὴν ἀγο- ρὰν γενομισμένην εἰς Τιβέριον. Ipse igitur nummus, pre- tium habens ex edicto Cæsaris, Cæsarisque nomen & vul- tum præferens, testabatur Cæsarem summum in Judæam imperium reipsa obtinere, idque à Judæis nummo illo u- tentibus agnosci. Objici poterat, ipso quidem facto Ro- manos Judæis, & Cæsarem Romanis imperasse, at nullo jure. Sed Christus ostendit hoc ad propositam quæstio- nem nihil pertinere. Nam cum nec quies gentium sine armis, nec arma sine stipendiis, nec stipendia sine tributis haberi possint, ut loquitur Tacitus, sequitur ei qui imperat, tantisper dum imperat, pendenda tributa, ut pretium com- munis tutelæ quam præstat nobis quisquis est publici im- perii possessor. Propterea, inquit Paulus, etiam tributa pen- ditis, nec sola pœnæ formidine, sed juris & æqui respectu, quia potestatum præsidio tuti estis à vi atque injuria. Cer tum autem est ab omnibus potestatibus hoc ipsum, etsi non ea qua oportet æquitate ac diligentia, sæpe etiam ita, ut ipsæ à vi atque injuriis non abstineant, aliquatenus tamen præ- stari, ita ut sub illis, quam sine illis vivere multo sit tutius: quod satis est, ut tributa præstari & possint & debeant.

Dubium est, quomodo ex nummi effigie & in- scriptione convinci potuerint Pharisæi, quod sub Cæsaris essent jurisdictione? Nam sæpe num- mis utimur aliorum Principum, quibus subjecti non sumus. Sed sciendum, populum Judai- cum dum adhuc sui juris erat, propriam habuisse monetam qua usi sunt, non alienam: Adhæc non de quovis numismate hic agitur, sed numisma cen- sus, h. e. illud monetæ genus, quo census exolve- batur, requiritur: quod in censu capitationis dena- rium fuisse habentem imaginem Cæsaris, Hieron. in h. l. observat. Et solebant veteres Romani gen- tibus in imperium suum redactis, in signum subje- ctionis & recognitionem Dominii ejusmodi tri- butum imponere, quod non in alio quam Roma- næ monetæ genere Consulum nominibus insigni- tæ pendi poterat, notante B. Gerhardo Harm. cap. CLIV. pag. 1147. Ut autem tempore durantis ad- huc Consulatus moneta Consulum Romanorum no- mina habebat insculpta; ita cum rerum summa ad Imperatores esse devoluta, ipsi in moneta ca- put suum cum ornamentis Imperatoris & lauru triumphali redimitum ac dignitatum, quas ges- serant, memoriam in ἐπιγραφῇ publice conspici voluerunt: idque in tributo à subjectis suæ pote- stati populis exigendo strictissime observabant, ut non nisi suam, id est, jussu suo cusam & suo no- mine insignitam monetam ab eis acciperent. De Nerone (qui à Tiberio tertius fuit Imperator) Suetonius cap. 44. commemorat, quod eo fasti- dio tributa exegerit, ut nummos etiam suos nonnisi asperos, id est, ab officina adhuc re- centes ac veluti ab incude calentes & novitate quadam grata candentes acciperet, quod ipsam a Tiberio quoque qui jam octodecim annis regna- verat, factitatum fuisse, ut non nisi suam in- censum acciperet monetam, ex hoc ipso loco veri- similiter colligitur. Nec præter rem observat Seldenus aversæ parti nummorum inscribi con- suevisse regiones ac provincias captas; Jam ve- ro, si inscriptio aliqua inerat aversa (nam tam aversam quam obversam simplicis inscriptionis no- mine contineri posse palam est) ejusmodi quid de Ju- dæa capta, subacta, recepta continens, unde Im- perium Cæsarianum atque victoriæ Romanæ jus ne- cessario agnoscendum fuisset, nil apertius foret quam ex ipso quod interrogantes exhiberent agno- scerentque numismate, devictos, captos, subactos a Romano se satis affirmarent, adeoque ei obedi- entia & subjectionis præstationes debitas. Nam ex jure victoriæ & Gentium ejusdem usu tributa deberi passim agnitum est. Quid quod etiam dum Tri- butum, Numisma, Cenfus & Denarius modo jam dicto intellectus, ita simul memorantur, liquido admittitur inolevisse jam morem solvendi, id est, tum deditionem præcessisse, tum solutionem ex victo- ris jussu, non solum imperatam, sed & velut jure a solventibus admissam. Denique numinum census tale ἐπίγραφῆ qua convinci poterant, Pharisæos præsto habere Christus vi omniscien- tiæ suæ noverat: qui vero adeo excæcati fuêre, ut nihilo secius Christo nummum exigenti eun- dem exhibuerint, ex quo ἐπ' αυτοφόρῳ eorum subjectio demonstrari poterat.

## 22:21
Vers. 21. ἀπόδοτε] As a debt, as Paul explains: for when he had dealt with tributes, he adds: ἀπόδοτε πᾶσι τὰς ὀφειλάς.

and the things of God, to God] The payment of tribute has nothing in itself that is repugnant to divine law. Furthermore, if Caesar or any other power commands anything against divine law, one must obey God rather than men. Thus Christ, by a most wise answer, escaped the calumny of both stirred-up sedition and violated religion in a most insidious question: and at the same time he silently notes those who, under the guise of piety, were solicitous about matters pertaining to this age, while they despised and even violated the duties of true and solid piety. The sentiment of Polycarp is: Δεδιδάγμεθα ἀρχαῖς καὶ ἐξουσίαις ἀπὸ Θεοῦ τεταγμέναις τιμὴν κατὰ τὸ προσῆκον τὴν μὴ βλάπτουσαν ἡμᾶς ἀπονέμειν.

PART III. The case concerning the woman of seven husbands in the resurrection.

Latin:

Vers. 21. ἀπόδοτε] Tanquam debitum, ut Paulus expli- cat: nam cum de tributis egisset subjicit: ἀπόδοτε ὐυπᾶ- σιτὰς ὀφειλὰς.

καὶ τὰ τοῦ Θεοῦ, τῷ Θεῷ] Tributi pensitatio nihil in se habet quod divinæ legi repugnet. Cæterum si quid Cæsar aut alia potestas præcipiat adversum legi divinæ, Deo potius quam hominibus parendum est. Ita Christus sapientis- simo responso & seditionis motæ & violatæ religionis calumniam in quæstione insidiosissima effugit: ac simul tacite ipsos notat qui de rebus ad hoc sæculum pertinen- tibus pietatis specie solliciti: veræ solidæque pietatis officia contemnerent atque etiam violarent. Polycarpi est sen- tentia: Δεδιδάγμεθα ἀρχαῖς καὶ ἐξουσίαις ἀπὸ Θεῦ τετα- γμέναις τιμὴν κατὰ τὸ προσῆκον τὴν μὴ βλάπτουσαν ἡμᾶς ἀπο- νέμειν.

PARS III. Casus de muliere septem virorum in resurrectione.

## 22:23
Vers. 23. Σαδδουκαῖοι οἱ λέγοντες μὴ εἶναι ἀνάστασιν] The foundation of the Sadducaic opinion was that there is no substance outside of God besides sensible things. Luke teaches us this clearly in Acts XXIII. 8. Σαδδουκαῖοι μὲν γὰρ λέγουσι μὴ εἶναι ἀνάστασιν, μηδὲ ἄγγελον, μήτε πνεῦμα. Where by the word πνεῦμα must be understood that divine inspiration by which the Pharisees rightly believed the Prophets were impelled by God. The Sadducees, who did not receive the Prophetic Scriptures (unless perhaps as works of human wisdom), admitted, as it seems, no divine ἀποκάλυψιν; except by voice; in the way the law had been delivered: to which alone it appears the Sadducees rendered obedience, if I am not mistaken, both by other arguments and by the opposition of the Pharisees and Sadducees which is in Josephus XIII. Antiquities XVIII. where he says that many things are observed by the Pharisees; ἅπερ οὐκ ἀναγέγραπται ἐν τοῖς Μωϋσέως νόμοις. Wherefore also what follows concerning the Sadducees, ταῦτα δὲ ἀγνοεῖν νομίμα τὰ γεγραμμένα, is to be understood of those things which are written down in the law of Moses. It is more surprising how they denied that there were Angels, since they admitted the writings of Moses, in which there is mention of Angels so many times. It seems to me that one must answer that they thought what Justin affirms some Jews of his own age also thought, that Angels were ἀτμήτως καὶ ἀχωρίστως Θεοῦ δυνάμεις ἃς ὁ Θεὸς ὅταν βούληται προπηδᾷν ποιεῖ καὶ πάλιν ἀναστέλλει εἰς ἑαυτόν. To which opinion that same Martyr opposes this true one, that angels are always remaining and not being dissolved. It is no wonder that those who thought thus about angels thought similarly about the souls of men, namely that they were not such things as could subsist by themselves, but which would return to nothing, being deprived of bodies. "The Sadducees, however, the account says, cause the souls to perish along with the bodies," says Josephus. And elsewhere about the same: "They abolish the persistence of the soul, and the punishments and honors in Hades." Jerome about the same: "They thought the soul perished with the bodies": which was also noted by Abraham of Salamanca. From this it followed further that "there is no resurrection." For resurrection requires the persistence of souls. It is likewise a consequence that they had all their hope of piety stored up in the present life. For I am certain that those who, from the poorly understood words of Josephus, equate the Sadducees with the Epicureans, as if they denied that human affairs were a concern to God, are mistaken. For those who received the law of Moses, in which there is a famous passage concerning rewards and punishments, could not have been followers of that insane wisdom. And the ancient Hebrews, and among the moderns Josephus Albo, rightly note that the Sadducees acknowledged rewards for those keeping the law, but only of this life. Josephus himself, against Apion, pronounces concerning all the Jews: "as the account is in agreement concerning God, saying that He oversees all things." But this is what Josephus says, that the Sadducees established the choice of good and evil so much in the power of man, that they judged that no action of God intervened in that matter at all, much in the way Coelestius and Pelagius did among the Christians. But there is an error in Josephus: for it is read thus concerning the Sadducees: "The Sadducees, the second order, abolish fate entirely and place God outside of doing or overseeing any evil." No one could deny that God is the inspector of human crimes unless one wishes to argue that the flood, the Sodoms, Pharaoh, and the rest written by Moses are a lie. It must be read entirely as "outside of doing any evil or not doing": that is, they deny that God has any part in men either committing sins or abstaining from them: and this is the very thing he says is taken away by them, namely fate: for he calls providence fate, not concerning those things which we suffer, but concerning those things which we do. That what I say is true, the following things prove: "They say that for men the choice of good and evil is set before them, and that it is according to the will of each that one or the other comes to each person." What he had just said, "to do evil or not to do," he here called "good and evil," both of which the Sadducees placed equally in the mere power of man. The same is to be understood from the opposite opinion of the Pharisees, which the most diligent writer expresses thus: "they attribute all things to fate and to God." And that the doing of just things and not doing them lies for the most part with men. But that fate assists in each case. He says that according to the opinion of the Pharisees, not all things are simply done by fate, but are joined and bound to fate: which the Chaldaizing Jews express in Hebrew, כלא במסירא תליא. So that to act rightly or otherwise is indeed for the most part in the power of men, but that the power of providence concurs in both. Compare to these another passage of Josephus, Antiquities 13, where he explains the opinion of the Pharisees thus: "that some things, and not all, are the work of fate; but that some things exist in our own power, to happen or not to happen": the Sadducees, however, as he speaks in the same place, "abolish fate, deeming it to be nothing, nor that human affairs take their end according to it. But they place all things in our own power, as if we ourselves are the causes of good things, and receive the worse things through our own folly." In which manner it is said that Chrysippus also tempered the opinion of the Stoics, whose sect Josephus professes in his life to have been akin to the Pharisaic sect. Nor is that a wonder, since in Cyprus, from where Zeno had been, there were always many Jews. Josephus also ascribes the same mixture of free will in other places to the opinion of the Pharisees, so that it ought to be most certain that Epiphanius erred in the explanation of that opinion, which has been rightly noted heretofore by a man learned in every respect.

Grotius gathers not badly from Acts 23:8 that the foundation of the opinion of the Sadducees is that there is no substance outside of God except sensible things. But because they accepted the writings of Moses, in which mention of angels is often made, he judges that they thought that angels were indivisible and inseparable powers of God, which God, when He wishes, makes to spring forth and again draws back into Himself, just as Justin Martyr reported this opinion of certain Jews of his own age, to which he opposes this true one, that angels are always remaining and not being dissolved. And therefore he thinks the Sadducees thought similarly about the souls of men, namely that they were not such things as could subsist by themselves, but which would return to nothing, being deprived of bodies: from which it followed further that there is no resurrection. Since this requires the persistence of souls. Which things agree with those which the ancients, Josephus, Jerome, and others hand down concerning the Sadducees. But what he hands down concerning the Pharisees at verse 28, that they hoped for the resurrection more from tradition and conjecture than from certain arguments, cannot be admitted otherwise than that the blind guides could not see the arguments and testimonies of Scripture before their own traditions, to which they were fixed and clung. For that is not to be attributed to the obscurity of Scripture, which hands down sufficiently clear testimonies and documents, such as some have even been observed and produced by the Rabbis themselves, as witnessed by the book of R. Menasseh Ben Israel on the resurrection of the dead, but to the blindness of the Pharisees. Nor indeed were those things contained only under figures, or under words needing investigation, as Grotius wishes, who here indicates a hidden and more mystical sense, but although there is need for scrutiny of the scriptures, it is certain that this article concerning the resurrection, and other things to be believed, were proposed in the Old Testament in a literal sense. Testament: because certain arguments are sought from the literal sense alone; nor is there any faith which does not lean upon the word of God, from which Christ openly convinces those denying the resurrection from the Scriptures, having premised the cause of the error, ignorance of the scripture: "You err, not knowing the scriptures."

Latin:

Vers. 23. Σαδδουκαῖοι οἱ λέγοντες μὴ εἶναι ἀνάστασιν] Fundamentum opinionis Sadducaicæ fuit nullam sub- stantiam esse extra Deum præter res sensiles. Clare id nos docet Lucas Actor. XXIII. 8. Σαδδουκαῖοι μὲν γὰρ λέγουσι μὴ εἶναι ἀνάστασιν, μηδὲ ἄγγελον, μήτε πνεῦμα. Ubi voce πνεύ- ματος intelligendus divinus ille afflatus quo Prophetas a Deo impulsos recte credebant Pharisæi. Sadducæi qui Prophetica Scripta non recipiebant (nisi forte tanquam humanæ sapientiæ opera) nullam, ut videtur, admiserunt ἀποκάλυψιν divinam; nisi per vocem; quomodo lex erat tradita: cui soli obedientiam præstitisse Sudducæos appa- ret, ni fallor, tum aliis argumentis, tum ex oppositio- ne Pharisæorum & Sadducæorum quæ est apud Jose- phum XIII. Origin. XIIX. ubi ait a Pharisæis multa ob- servari; ἅπερ ἐκ ἀναγέγραπται ἐν τοῖς Μωϋσεως νόμοις. Quare & quod de Sadducæis sequitur, ταῦτα δὲν ἀγνοεῖν νόμιμα τὰ γεγραμμένα, intelligendum de iis quæ in Mo- sis lege sunt perscripta. Magis mirum quomodo Ange- los esse inficiati fuerint, cum Mosis scripta, in quibus toties Angelorum sit mentio, admitterent. Respon- dendum mihi videtur sensisse illos quod Judæorum non- nullos sua quoque ætate sensisse Justinus affirmat, An- gelos fuisse ἀτμήτως καὶ ἀχωρίστως Θεῦ δυνάμεις ἃς ὁ Θεὸς ὅταν βύληται προπηδᾷν ποιεῖ καὶ πάλιν ἀναστέλλει εἰς ἑαυτόν : cui sententiae idem ille Martyr hanc veram opponit, εἶναι ἀγγέλους ἀεὶ μένοντας καὶ μὴ ἀναλυομένους. Qui ita de Ange- lis sentiebant, eos non mirum est similiter sensisse de ani- mis hominum, non esse scilicet res tales, quae per se possent subsistere, sed quae in nihilum redirent, corporibus destitu- tae. Σαδδουκαῖοι δὲ τὰς ψυχὰς ὁ λόγος συναφανίζει τοῖς σώ- μασι, inquit Josephus. Et alibi de eisdem: ψυχῆς δὲ τὴν διαμονὴν, καὶ τὰς καθ᾽ ᾅδε τιμωρίας καὶ τιμὰς ἀναιρῦσι. Hie- ronymus de iisdem: Animam putabant interire cum cor- poribus: quod & Abrahamo Salmanticensi notatum. Hinc porro sequebatur ὐκ εἶναι ἀνάστασιν. Nam ἀνάστασις requi- rit permansionem animorum. Consequens item est, ut spem omnem pietatis repositam habuerint in vita praesen- te. Certum enim habeo errare eos qui ex Josephi ver- bis male intellectis Sadducaeos Epicureis aequant, quasi Deo res humanas curae esse negaverint. Nam qui legem Mosis recipiebant, in qua praeclarus est locus περὶ ἄθλων κὶ ἐ- πιτιμίων, istius insanientis sapientiae consulti esse non pot- erant. Et recte Hebraei veteres, & inter novos Josephus Albo, notant Sadducaeis agnita praemia legem servant- bus, sed hujus duntaxat vitae. Ipse Josephus adversus Appionem de Judaeis omnibus pronuntiat: ὡς δὲ λόγος ὁ- μᾶ σύμφωνος περὶ Θεῦ, πάντα λέγων ἐκεῖνον ἐφορᾷν. Sed hoc est quod dicit Josephus, Sadducaeos ita in hominis po- testate statuisse boni malique electionem, ut nullam ea qui- dem in re censerent intervenire Dei actionem, ferme quo- modo Coelestius & Pelagius inter Christianos. Sed men- dum est in Josepho: ita enim legitur de Sadducaeis: Σαδ- δουκαῖοι δὲ τὸ δεύτερον τάγμα τὴν μὲν εἱμαρμένην παντάπασιν ἀναιρῦσι καὶ τὸν Θεὸν ἔξω τῦ δρᾷν τι κακὸν ἢ ἐφορᾷν τίθενται. Deum negare inspectorem humanorum criminum nemo potuit nisi quisque de diluvio, de Sodomis, de Pharaone, caeteraque a Mose conscripta mendacii velit arguere. O- mnino legendum ἔξω τῦ δρᾷν τι κακὸν ἢ μὴ δρᾷν: hoc est, negant ullas in eo esse Dei partes ut homines peccata aut perpetrent, aut iisdem abstineant: & hoc ipsum est quod ait tolli ab ipsis fatum: fatum enim vocat providentiam non circa ea quae patimur, sed circa ea quae agimus. Verum esse quod dico, sequentia evincunt: Φασὶ δ᾽ ἐπ᾽ ἀν- θρώπων ἐκλογῇ τότε καλὸν κὶ τὸ κακὸν προκεῖσθαι, κὶ τὸ κατὰ γνώμην ἑκάστῳ τέτων ἑκατέρῳ προσίεναι. Quod modo di- xerat τὸ κακὸν δρᾷν ἢ μὴ δρᾷν, hic dixit καλὸν καὶ τὸ κακὸν, quorum utrumque Sadducaei aequaliter ponebant in me- ra hominis potestate. Idem intelligere est ex opposita Pharisaeorum sententia, quam ita exprimit Scriptor dili- gentissimus εἱμαρμένῃ τε καὶ Θεῷ προσάπτεσι πάντα. καὶ τὸ μὲν πράττειν τὰ δίκαια καὶ μὴ κατὰ τὸ πλεῖστον ἐπὶ τοῖς ἀνθρώ- ποις κεῖσθαι. βοηθεῖν δὲ εἰς ἕκαστον τὴν εἱμαρμένην. Ait ex Pha- risaeorum sententia non omnia simpliciter fieri ex fato, sed fato convexa esse & colligata: quod Chaldaizantes Hebraice exprimunt, כלא במסירא תליא. Ita ut recte aut secus agere sit quidem maxima ex parte penes homines, sed in utrumque tamen concurrat vis illa pro- videntiae. Compara his alterum Josephi locum XIII. Orig. ubi sententiam Pharisaeorum ita explicat: τινὰ κὶ ὐ πάντα τῆς εἱμαρμένης εἶναι ἔργον· Ἰινὰ δ᾽ ἐφ᾽ ἑαυτοῖς ὑπάρχειν, συμ- φαίνειν τε καὶ μὴ γίνεσθαι: Sadducaei autem, ut ibidem lo- quitur, τὴν εἱμαρμένην ἀναιρῦσιν ὐδὲν εἶναι ταύτην ἀξιῦντες, ὔτε κατ᾽ αὐτὴν τὰ ἀνθρώπινα τέλος λαμβάνειν. ἅπαντα δὲ ἐφ᾽ ἡμῖν αὐτοῖς τίθενται, ὡς καὶ τ' ἀγαθῶν αἰτίες ἡμᾶς αὐτὸς γι- νομένως, καὶ τὰ χείρω παρὰ ἡμετέραν ἀβελίαν λαμβάνοντας. Quem in modum dicitur etiam Chrysippus sententiam temperasse Stoicorum, quorum sectam Pharisaicae sectae affinem fuisse Josephus in vita sua profitetur. Neque id mirum, cum in Cypro unde fuerat Zeno, multi sem- per Judaei fuerint. Eandem mixturam fuit & liberae vo- luntatis aliis quoque in locis Josephus ascribit sententiae Pharisaeorum, ut certissimum esse debeat lapsum Epipha- nium in istius sententiae explicatione, quod recte antehac a viro undequaque doctissimo annotatum est.

Fundamentum opinionis Sadducæorum nullam Substantiam esse extra Deum præter res sensiles, ex Actorum XXIII. v. 8. colligit non male Grotius. Quia vero illi Mosis scripta suscepêre, in qui- bus sæpe Angelorum mentio fit, censet, sen- sisse eos, angelos esse ἀτμήτες καὶ ἀχωρίσες Θεῦ δυνάμεις, ἃς ὁ Θεὸς ὅταν βέλῃ προπηδᾶν ποιεῖ κὶ πάλιν ἀναστέλλ᾽ εἰς ἑαυτὸν, uti Judæorum quorundam suæ ætatis hanc sententiam retulit Justinus Martyr, cui hanc veram opponit εἶναι ἀγ- γέλλες ἀεὶ μένοντας, καὶ μὴ ἀναλυομένως. Ideoque similiter de animis hominum sensisse Sad- ducæos putat, non esse sc. res tales, quæ per se pos- sent subsistere, sed quæ in nihilum redirent corpo- ribus destitutæ: unde porro sequebatur, ἐκ εἶναι ἀνάςασιν. Siquidem hæc requirat permansionem animorum. Quæ cum illis, quæ veteres, Jose- phus, Hieronymus, alii de Sadducæis tradunt, con- gruunt. Quod autem de Pharisæis ad v. 28. tra- dit, eos resurrectionem magis ex traditione & con- jectura, quam certis argumentis sperasse, non aliter admitti potest, quam quod cæci ductores argu- menta ac testimonia Scripturæ præ traditionibus suis, quibus infixi hærebant, videre nequiverint. Non enim id Scripturæ obscuritati tribuendum, quæ satis diserta testimonia, & documenta tradit, qualia etiam nonnulla ab ipsis Rabbinis observa- ta & producta sunt, teste libro R. Menassis Ben Israel de resurrectione mortuorum, sed Pharisæo- rum cæcitati. Neque vero tantum sub figuris, aut sub verbis inquisitionis egentibus ea contineban- tur, uti Grotius vult, qui hic sensum reconditum & μυσικώτερον indicat, sed quamvis scrutinio opus sit ad scripturas, literali tamen sensu & hunc de re- surrectione articulum, & alia credenda in Vet. Test. proposita esse, certum est: quia è solo sensu literali argumenta certa petuntur; neque fides ul- la est, quæ non nititur verbo Dei, unde Christus palam e Scripturis convincit resurrectionem ne- gantes, præmissa erroris causa, ignorantia scri- pturæ: Erratis μὴ εἰδότες τὰς γραφάς.

## 22:24
Vers. 24. μὴ ἔχων τέκνα] Without children. Whose legal expert says: He is not without children who has even one son or one daughter. Since a daughter, in the absence of male children, was called to the inheritance by Hebrew law, it follows that the right of τῆς ἐπιγαμβρεύσεως (marriage by affinity) only then had a place if no offspring were left. Nor does it stand in the way that in Hebrew there is בן. For it is common to all languages that the masculine appellation includes the feminine sex. Therefore, the interpreter prudently placed here τέκνα, and immediately μὴ ἔχων σπέρμα, just as זרע is placed in Genesis 38:8, which pertains to both sexes. As also Luke: κᾀὐτὸς ἄτεκνος ἀποθάνῃ. Such a name, however, the languages of the East do not have. Therefore, the Syrian also placed here בניא. Nor does it stand in the way of this interpretation what is said in the law about the propagation of a name. For a grandson from a daughter could also be inserted into the grandfather's family. But certainly, I do not see how one who leaves a daughter can rightly be called ἄτεκνος (childless).

ἐπιγαμβρεύσει] This word signifies to become a relative by marriage, 1 Sam. 18:21, 22, and 1 Macc. 10:54, 56, where it is attributed both to the son-in-law and the father-in-law. But here it is used to express the force of the Hebrew word יבם, which signifies to marry someone by right of affinity: just as the LXX also use τὸ ἐπιγαμβρεύειν, not indeed in Deuteronomy, but in the history of Judah and Onan, Gen. 38:8. For this right is among those things which were first received by custom, and soon received the authority of divine law: that there are many such things in Moses, is not to be doubted.

ὁ ἀδελφὸς ἀυτῶ] Namely, one born of the same father, as the reason of the law demands, and as Abenesdra rightly interprets. Indeed, from the similarity of the reason, the necessity of marrying a childless widow began to be imposed even on more distant relatives, unless one wished to renounce the right of proximity to the goods of the deceased, by that rite of taking off the shoe which the law of Deuteronomy prescribes: But that this did not arise so much from the force of the law itself, as the Sadducees urge, as from the process of custom, Ruth 4:7 seems to indicate clearly enough, where that right is attributed to customs, not to the law. And the Hebrew legal experts note that this right is not designated by the verb יבם but by the verb גאל, which the LXX translate as ἀγχιτεύειν.

ἀναςήσει σπέρμα τῷ ἀδελφῷ ἀυτῶ] This is what is said in the history of Ruth: to raise up the name of the dead: because, of course, the law called that son born of the deceased the son of the deceased. Therefore, τῷ ἀδελφῷ is in memory and honor of the brother.

Latin:

Vers. 24. μὴ ἔχων τέκνα] Sine liberis. Cujus Jurisconsul- tus: Non est sine liberis cui vel unus filius, unave filia est. Cum filia deficientibus liberis maribus ad hæreditatem vo- caretur jure Hebræo, sequitur jus τῆς ἐπιγαμβρεύσεως tum demum locum habuisse si nulla proles esset relicta. Neque obstat quod in Hebræo est בן. Omnium enim linguarum commune est, ut masculina appellatione femininus sexus comprehendatur. Ideo prudenter interpres hic posuit τέκνα, & statim μὴ ἔχων σπέρμα, quomodo זרע ponitur Genes. XXXIIX 8. quod ad utrumque sexum pertinet. Ut & Lu- cas κᾀὐτὸς ἄτεκνος ἀποθάνῃ. Tale autem nomen linguæ Orientis non habent. Ideo & Syrus hic posuit בניא. Nec obstat huic interpretationi quod de nominis propagatione in lege dicitur. Nam poterat & ex filia nepos in avi fami- liam inseri. At certe qui filiam relinquit non video quo- modo ἄτεκνος recte dicatur.

ἐπιγαμβρεύσει] Vox hæc significat affinem fieri 1. Sam. XIIX. 21. 22. & 1. Maccab. X. 54. 56. ubi tum genero, tum socero tribuitur. Sed hic usurpata est ad exprimendam vim Hebrææ vocis יבם quæ significat jure affinitatis ali- quam ducere: quomodo & LXX. τὸ ἐπιγαμβρεύειν usur- pant, non quidem in Deuteronomio, sed in historia Judæ & Onani Gen. XXXIIX. 8. Est enim hoc jus inter ea quæ primum moribus recepta, mox legis divinæ auctoritatem acceperunt: qualia multa esse in Mose, non est dubitandũ.

ὁ ἀδελφὸς ἀυτῶ] Nempe ὁμοπάτριος, ut ratio legis po- stulat, & recte interpretatur Abenesdra. Cœpit quidem ex rationis similitudine etiam remotioribus affinibus imponi necessitas ducendi viduam illiberem, nisi jus proximitatis in bona defuncti à se abdicare vellet, eo ritu calcei exuen- di, quem lex Deuteronomii præscribit: Sed hoc natum non tam ex ipsa legis vi quam urgent Sadducæi, quam ex pro- cessu consuetudinis, aperte satis indicare videtur Ruth. IV. 7. ubi moribus, non legi jus istud acceptum fertur. Et notant Hebræi Jurisconsulti id jus non designari verbo יבם sed verbo גאל, quod ἀγχιτεύειν vertunt LXX.

ἀναςήσει σπέρμα τῷ ἀδελφῷ ἀυτῶ] Hoc est quod in Ru- thæ historia dicitur ἀναςῆσαι τὸ ὄνομα τῶ τεθνηκότος: quia nimirum lex illum postratum filium defuncti nuncupabat, Ergo τῷ ἀδελφῷ est inmemoriam atque honorem fratris.

## 22:25
Vers. 25. Ἀφῆκε] How an inheritance is said to be left. For among the Hebrews, inheritance and marriage are deferred by equal right, just as among the Romans, inheritance and guardianship. Hence, someone is said to κληρονομεῖν (inherit) who ἐπιδικάζεται it, that is, takes it by right of proximity, as we have said elsewhere.

Latin:

Vers. 25. Ἀφῆκε] Quomodo hæreditas relinqui dici- tur. Nam apud Hebræos pari jure deferuntur hæreditas & matrimonium, sicut apud Romanos hæreditas & tu- tela. Hinc κληρονομεῖν aliquam dicitur, qui eam ἐπιδι- κάζεται, hoc est proximitatis jure ducit, ut diximus ali- bi.

## 22:28
Vers. 28. Τίνος τῶν ἑπτὰ ἔσαι γυνή] The Pharisees hoped for the resurrection more from tradition and conjecture than from certain arguments. Hence such a diversity of opinions, about which we have dealt elsewhere. And just as now also the Talmudists imagine for themselves feasts in which they are to eat Behemoth and Leviathan, so then also a happy life; XXII, v. 29, 30. indeed, but similar to this one of ours, they had taught from the beginning: whence Josephus compares the Pharisaic opinion to those things which are celebrated among the Greeks regarding the fortunate.

For concerning these he said, he says in the 8th verse *, "for because they do not account for their own needs from themselves, their own presuppositions" nor to terminate; in words almost the same as those of Homer long ago: "but the other is good for us in abundance." In addition to these, there are also many among the holy Fathers: "To have is sweet, it is honorable in virtue; The rich, if they are not stripped, are turned about in the household." Which the following Horace said: "The eighth [hour] awaits us, scanning around: the city blessed, present deeds, books & treaties." And soon: "More, we shall admire the happy, so that neither the watery Eurus may scrape the fields with large rains, nor the women be burned by fictitious clods." And what follows. Wherefore it is not a wonder if the manuscripts, where they also persuaded themselves of the use of marriage, which Muhammad, like many other things, reported in the Alcoran taken from the tradition of the Jews.

The Sadducees, however, with whom there had been a struggle up to this point with the Pharisees, thought that the resurrection was taught by Christ, and [used] the same presuppositions which the Pharisees used, but hoping to strike a tooth against a fragile thing, they struck against a solid one.

Latin:

Vers. 28. Τίνος τῶν ἑπτὰ ἔσαι γυνή] Pharisæi resurrectio- nem ex traditione magis & conjectura, quam certis argu- mentis sperabant. Hinc tanta opinionum diversitas, de qua egimus alibi. Et quemadmodum nunc quoq; Thal- mudistæ epulas sibi fingunt in quibus Behemothum & Leviathanem sint esitaturi, ita tunc quoque vitam felicem; XXII, v. 29, 30. quidem, sed huic nostrae similem, a primo praeceperant: unde Josephus Pharisaicam sententiam comparat iis quae apud Graecos de fortunatis agilius celebrantur.

Nam de his dixerit ait viii. uers. *, ὅτι γὰρ μὴ ἀπὸ ἑαυτῶν τὰς ἐνδείας ἀπολογοῦνται τὰς ἑαυτῶν προϋποθεσεις neque terminare; verbi prope iisdem uerbis Ubius olim Homerus: “ ὁ δ' ἄλλος ἡμῖν ἀγαθὸς ἐν εὐχραδείᾳ” Adhaec quoque sunt apud sanctos Patres plerique: Τῷ ἔχει γλυκὺν ἔντιμον ἐστίν ἐπ᾽ ἀρετῇ· Οἱ πλούσιοι, ἂν μὴ ἀποδεδυκται, ἐν τῷ οἰκ. ἀναστρέφονται. Quae sequens Horatius dixit: “Nos manet Octavus circumscans: urbs beata Praesens acta, libellis & foedera.” Et mox: “Plurad, felices mirabimur, ut nec largis Aquosus Eurus arva radat imbribus, Pinguid nec fictis urantur femina glebis.” Et quae sequuntur. Quare mirum non est, si manusfrum, ubi quoque conjugii usum sibi persuaserint, quod Muhammedes, ut multa alia, in Alcorano sumtum ex Judaeorum traditione retulit.

Sadducaei autem, quibus cum Pharisæis hactenus certamen fuerat, à Christo putabant resurrectionem doceri, καὶ τὰς αὐτὰς ὑποθέσεις quibus utebantur Pharisaei, sed sperantes fragili dentem illidere, solido impegerunt.

## 22:29
Vers. 29. "not knowing the scriptures" Because, of course, they accepted nothing except what was written in the response of Matthew: yet the act itself is nothing, since it is a pattern of theirs by nature, so that under figures or certainly under words of inquiry, greater dogmas occur.

Which we have treated elsewhere concerning the matter. If anyone thus [argues] about God, not so much that he separates the parts of the body from God in the believer, as that they thought souls could not be sustained without a body: as appeared from the above. But since this contains no anticipation in itself, there was no just reason why it should be rejected as in every way, even with respect to God, impossible.

Physical reasons could be brought forward, taken from the operations of the mind, by which it would be proven in the very truth which the apostles [spoke] about the soul, as the Christian philosopher Athenagoras speaks: but because those arguments exceed the capacity of simpler men, who nevertheless are not to be excluded from the pursuit of piety, there is nothing safer than to rely on divine power. For if the resurrection is not impossible, certainly there is no reason why it should be said to be impossible for God. "For to conclude," as that same Athenagoras wisely says; "as it is unjust to Him because it is unjust, as it is unjust." But since neither can be said about the sustenance of souls outside the body, it follows that the matter is not incredible, indeed it is to be believed, when trustworthy authority is added.

What I said, that we are referred not to natural reasons, but to the power & will of God when it is a question of sustaining souls outside the body, that can be seen in Luke XXIII. 46.

Acts.

VII. 29.

Latin:

Vers. 29. μὴ εἰδότες τὰς γραφάς Quia nimirum nihil accipiebant nisi quod iis laus respondens Matthaei scriptum erat: actus tamen ipsius nihilum cum illorum ὑπόδειγμα est esse natura, ut sub figuris aut certe sub verbis inquisitionis generibus majora dogmata occurrent.

Quae de re egimus alibi. Si quis ita deum non tam quod credentem distolunat corporis partes a Deo non posse reconprobari, quam quod putarent non posse sustentari animas sine corpore: ut ex superioribus apparuit. Atqui cum hoc nullam in se continentia anticipationem, nulla erat justa ratio cur id tanquam omni modo, etiam ad Dei respectu, ἀδύνατον repudiaretur.

Poterant afferri rationes Physicae ex operationibus animi desumtae, quibus probaretur in ipsa ueritate quae ab apostolis de anima, ut loquitur Christianus Philosophus Athenagoras: sed quia ista argumenta rudiorum hominum, qui tamen a pietatis studio excendi non sunt, captiam excedunt, nihil est tutius quam divina potestate inniti. Nam si resurrectio non est ἀδύνατον, certe non est cur dicatur ἀδύνατον Deo. Το γὰρ συνεπαγω, ut idem ille Athenagoras sapienter dicit; ὡς ἄδικον αὐτῷ ἐστιν ὅτι ἄδικον ἐστιν ὡς ἄδικον. Cum vero neutrum de sustentatione animarum extra corpus dici possit, sequitur ut res sit non incredibilis, imo credenda, ubi auctoritas ἀξιόπιστος accedit.

Quod dixi non ad naturales rationes, sed ad Dei potentiam & voluntatem nos remitti cum de sustentandis extra corpus animis agitur, id videre est Luc. XXIII. 46.

Act.

VII. 29.

## 22:30
Vers. 30. "when they marry, when they are given in marriage" Christ, before he brings forward the proof of that dogma, which is truly the most solid foundation of piety, removes the false reverence upon which the objection of the Sadducees rested.

"To be given in marriage" is said here for what the Latins would call "to marry": as also below c. XXII. 30. & XXIV. 38. &c.

It is the prerogative of some daughters of families, as appears 1 Cor. VII. 38. That [saying] of Electra in Euripides is famous: "My father will have the care of my marriage, and he will not judge these things mine."

Ovid, or he who wrote the epistle of Hermione: "Tyndareus, a grave author in years, handed me over to you: he had the decision over the marriage." Here the question is usually treated concerning the right of parents in giving their children in marriage.

It is indeed most fair that honor & reverence be shown to parents: and in no matter more than that which looks to the propagation of the race, as has been rightly noted somewhere by Aristotle. But circumstances occur which offer exceptions. For what if parents, held by hatred, avarice, or other affections, cease to do their duty? Was it fair for natural liberty to be taken away from children? Certainly by Roman law, a daughter who, after her twenty-fifth year, has entered into marriage while her parents were negligent, is held innocent.

And we know how much the Apostle Paul abhors "greed," furthermore, that argument which many think is invincible, in my judgment does not proceed sufficiently: "that is not done rightly; therefore it is void." For how many things are there which are not done rightly, that is, not according to duty, and yet if they have been done, they are by no means held as not done. Certainly, if we remain within the natural limits of law, an act cannot be called void because it is vicious, unless there is added a power of defect or a base act, or a permanent one, which to say has a place here is indeed easy, but to demonstrate from the sense of the prince is difficult.

For by the law of nature, the authority of parents seems to be more of a duty than a power, that is, even as we see it instituted for the people and by customs. Thus the Roman fathers say that what they call power is proper to the citizens of the Romans, nor by that law is the father's consent required for marriages if the children are emancipated, although the laws of nature cannot dissolve the rights of emancipation: but if the mother's consent is lacking, marriages are never on that account held void by Roman law.

By Hebrew law it is most clear that the father had more [power] over them as if they were his own, Num. XXXIX. 54. but neither is it the same for all daughters now: therefore those who are under paternal power are distinguished from those who go out from his hand.

Nor do I see what can be brought forward to prevent what is established concerning vows and oaths from being extended to betrothals and marriages. Elsewhere the right of parents is not extended beyond a defined age for children: and even before that age, if the parents are too unjust, the magistrate, as the common parent of all, interposes his parts. To me, all these things seem to be moderated by fair laws, and what pleases this one or that one should not be thrust upon others as a divine rule of law.

To "And Jesus answered." Luke explains the sense: "the man said, having a brother."
