For they have in them the treatments which are carried out in the souls themselves, that is, an internal force, which would perpetually consist of the body for love of itself, whence such a body is no longer called "soulish," but "spiritual," 1 Cor. XV. Since, therefore, those bodies of the dead are no longer harmful, no more than the Angels, it follows that they do not need [such] dealings, by the help of which the universality is preserved by those arriving individually.

For those things which we said not long ago, "cohere with corruption." Nor do I see by what certain reasons it is that anyone would want the distinction of sexes to be manifest even in that age.

For it can seem that that distinction is to be removed, [as it is] a part of "weakness" which will then cease. Indeed, every species and figure seems to be veiled by "corruption," and this [is] a better sign. But "the corruptible" is an open indication of "the generative."

Not a few of the ancients indeed thought that there would not then be "male, or female," as Hilary. Theodoret also, following the authority of this place which is now at hand, demonstrates that there are no distinctions of sexes in the Angels: "For this is the division of those who are under death, [which] nature [has]. For since death enslaves it, for he who does not [exist] through procreation... the Creator devised the procreation of living things as a kind of repair of immortality. This nature, which was perfect, is necessary for mortals in need. But for the immortal, marriage is superfluous." Which things seem to be able to be adapted by the same reason to men who are "equal to angels."

But just as marriage differs from immortal life, so too do food & drink, since they were introduced to replenish particles perishing daily. Which it is a wonder the Jews do not see (I except a few, like Josephus Albo) when Homer saw: "for they eat food, and drink sparkling wine." In which place the old Plutarch proves, "not only the things [eaten] but also the food [is] a provision for dying." The same Plutarch elsewhere: "for divine things do not need to fight with the immortal, the generating no less than the generated. For change is [without] suffering."

Aristotle, Mechanics II. cap. IV. concerning the Gods of the Poets: "how could they be others [if they] needed food." This knowledge ought to excite us, so that in this fragile life also we might indulge as little as possible in bodily pleasures, "practicing for those [things]."

But there is here a "freedom" of the particle. "Angels in heaven," that is, "those in heaven" who lead the life of the heavenly ones in heaven, not the life of "ages." Thus below XXIV.

36. "the angels of the heavens": & Mark XIII. 32. "the angels who are in heaven."

Then the present is put for the future. Although the Sadducees indeed happily denied the Angels, as divine, Christ rightly makes a commemoration of this in this place: because he solves the argument, he does not argue.

Who answers, as he can, with suppositions denied by the adversary. It is erroneous that Grotius thinks here that the difference of sexes will be supported in the other life.

But indeed I see, he says, as much as there is in the reasons of natures, that nature indeed wanted the distinction of sexes to be manifest even in that age. For it can seem that that distinction is to be removed, [as it is] a part of "weakness" which will then cease.

Indeed, every species and figure seems to be veiled by "corruption."

and with the power of incorruptibility. And yet the corruptible is an open indication of the generative. That, however, is what must be denied. For the protoplasts were created in incorruptibility; in whom, nevertheless, there was a difference of sex; and generation would have taken place, without prejudice to their incorruptibility, if they had persisted in integrity. Nor because generation ends in the other world, will the distinction of sexes cease to be. Christ also does not deny that a woman will be a woman, but he denies that that relation of wife and husband, and the nature of nuptials or matrimony, will have a place there: And will Mary, the mother of Christ, cease to be a woman in the other world, and turn into a male? to say nothing of others: or will those members created by God, which the Holy Spirit wishes to be honored, 1 Cor. XIII. verses 23, 24, be utterly abolished? That not a few of the ancients, as he says, thought there would then be neither male nor female, had to be demonstrated. Hilary alone does not settle the matter. Theodoret, however, demonstrates only in the case of the angels that there is no distinction of sexes, which is beyond controversy. But he does not teach that we will be like the angels in that respect.

Latin:

Vers. 30. ὅτε γαμοῦσι, ὅτε ἐκγαμίζονται Christus antequam dogmatis istius, quod uere pietatis solidissimum fundamentum est, probationem afferat, tollit falsam reverentiam qua Sadducaeorum objectio nitebatur.

Exγαμίζεσθαι hic dicitur pro quod Latini dicerent nubere: ut & infra c. XXII. 30. & XXIV. 38. &c.

Aliquot proprium est filiarum familias, ut apparet 1 Cor. VII. 38. Celebre est illud Electi apud Euripidem: Νυμφευμάτων μὲν ἐμῶν πατὴρ ἐμός Μέριμναν ἕξει, κοὐκ ἐμὸν κρινεῖ τάδε.

Ovidius aut is qui scripsit Hermiones epistolam: Me tibi Tyndareus sita gravis auctor & annis Tradidit: arbitrium nuptiis habebat abus. Solet hic tractari quaestio de jure parentum in elocandis liberis.

Equissimum sane est honorem & reverentiam exhiberi parentibus: nullaque in re magis quam quae ad generis propagationem spectat, ut alicubi recte ab Aristotele notatum est. Sed incidunt circumstantiae quae exceptiones porrigant. Quid enim si parentes odio, avaritia, aliisve affectibus detenti cessent officium facere? aequumne erat libertatem naturalem liberis auferri? Certe jure Romano filia quae post annum vicessimum quintum cellantibus parentibus nuptias fecerit, innocens habetur.

Et scimus quantopere Paulus Apostolus abhorreat πλεονεξίαν, praeterea vero argumentum, illud quod multi invictum putant, meo judicio non satis procedit: istud non recte fit; ergo irritum est. Quam multa enim sunt quae non recte, id est non ex officio fiunt, & tamen si facta sint pro non factis nequaquam habentur. Certe si maneamus intra limites naturales juris, actus irritus dici non potest eo quod vitiosus est, nisi accedat potestas defectus aut actus turpis, do permanens, quae hic locum habere dicto quidem est facile, at ex sensu principis demonstrari difficilia.

Nam ex jure naturae auctoritas, magis parentum malci videtur, quam potestas, id est, etiam ut quam videmus pro populo institutis & moribus innumer. Ita Romani patres triant quam dicunt potestatem propriae esse dicunt civinth Romanorum neque eo jure ad nuptias, patris consensu requiritur si liberi sint emancipati, cum tamen emancipationis jura naturae nequeat dissolvere: matris autem consensu fit desit, nunquam ob id Romano jure irritae fiunt nuptiae.

Jure Hebraeo apertissimum est plus iis Parret habuisse in illas quasi in silos, Num. XXXIX. 54. sed nec in filias omnes jam idem est: distinguuntur ergo quae in sacris est paternis, ab ea quae de manu exit.

Nec video quid afferri possit, quominus quod de votis & juramentis sit statuitur, ad sponsalia ac nuptias produci debeat. Alibi jus parentum non ultra definitam aetatem liberum portigitur: & ante istam quoque aetatem, si iniquiores sint parentes, magistratus, ut conjuinant omnium parentes, partes suas interponunt. Mihi haec omnia moderanda videntur equis legibus, nec debere quod huic aut illi placet, aliis pro divinis juris regula obtrudi.

Ad ὁ δὲ ἀπεκρίθη ὁ Ἰησοῦς. Sensum explicat Lucas: ὁ μὲν ἄνθρωπος ἔφη ἀδελφὸς ἔχων.

Habent enim in iis tractatus quae in ipsis animabus geruntur, id est vim internam, quae perpetuo corpus consisteret ad dilectionem ipsi, unde corpus tale non jam ψυχικὸν, sed πνευματικὸν dicitur 1 Cor. XV. Cum igitur corpora ista mortuorum noxia amplius non sint, non magis Angeli, sequitur ut nec indigeant seuat commercia, cujus ope singulis perveniantis universitas conservatur.

Nam iisque non ita pridem diximus, τῇ φθορᾷ coherer. Neque ego video quam certis rationibus quod quicquam volunt etiam in illo saeculo manifestum fore discrimen sexuum.

Videri enim potest id discrimen tollenda, pars esse ἀσθενείας quae tunc erit cessatura. Imo species omnis ac figura et φθορᾷ obvelanda videtur & huic autem as melius signa. Atqui τὸ φθαρτὸν apertum indicium τὸ γεννητικόν.

Veterum sane non pauci arbitrati sunt, non futurum tum ἄρρεν, ὅτε θῆλυ, ut Hilarius. Theodoretus quoque hujus loci qui nunc est prae manibus auctoritatem sequens demonstrat in Angelis non esse sexuum discrimina: Ταύτης γὰρ δὴ τὰς διαίρεσις ὑμεῖς ὦ ὑπὸ τῷ θανάτῳ τελάντων ἡ φύσις. Ἐπειδὰ γὰρ ἐξανδραποδίζει αὐτὴν ὁ θάνατος, ὁ γὰρ μὴ διὰ τῆς παιδοποιίας αἰτισαι-ἡ τὸ διεπιστάμενον· οἷον γὰρ τινα ἐπισκευασὴν ἀθανασίαν ἐποιητὴς τὴν ὄντων ζωὴν τοῦ παιδοποιίαν ἐμηχανήσατο. Ταύτῃ τῇ ἀναγκαίᾳ τοῖς θνητοῖς ἰσχύει φύσις ἡ τέλειος ἦν χρεία. Τοῖς δὲ ἀθανάτοις γαμοῖς, ἰσχυμεῖς, τὸ θέλω γὰρ πάντπαυσι περιττόν: quae ad homines ἰσαγγέλους videntur eadem ratione posse aptari.

Si cut autem matrimonium ab immortali vita dissidet, ita cibus quoque & potus, quippe inducta ad supplendas particulas quotidie pereuntes. Quod mirum est non videre Judaeos (paucos excipio ut Josephus Albo) cum Homerus viderit: “ἡ γὰρ σῖτοι ἔδουσ᾽, ἐπίνουσ᾽ αἴθοπα οἶνον” Quo loco uetus Plutarchus probat, μὴ μόνον τὰ ἐπὶ ἀλλὰ κἀπὶ ἀποθέσκειν τὴν τροφὴν ἦτα ἐφόδιον. Idem Plutarchus alibi: τὰ γὰρ θεῖα θεῖα μὴ δέῃ τῇ ἀφθάρτῃ μάχεσθαι τὸ γεννᾶν ἐχ ἦτον ἢ τὸ γεννώμενον. Μεταβολὴ γάρ ἐστιν ἀνατὶ κἀπάθ.

Aristoteles Mechanicorum II. cap. IV. de Diis Poerarum: “πῶς ἂν εἶεν ἄλλοι δέοιντο τροφῆς.” Haec cognitio excitare nos debet, ut in hac etiam fragili vita quam minimum fieri potest indulgeremus corporeis voluptatibus, μελετῶντες τῆς ἐκείνων.

Est autem hic ἐλευθερία particuli. Ἄγγελοι τὸ Θεὸν ἐν οὐρανῷ, id est οἱ ἐν οὐρανῷ qui in caelo vitam caelitum degunt, non vitam αἰών-τέλη. Ita infra XXIV.

36. οἱ ἄγγελοι οὐρανῶν: & Marci XIII. 32. οἱ ἄγγελοι οἱ ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ.

Deinde praesens pro futuro positum est. Quanquam vero Angelos foeliciter negabant Sadducei, ut divinus, recte tamen hoc loco commemorationem Christi facit: quia solvit argumentum, non argumentatur.

Qui respondet, ut potest suppositionibus ab adversario negatis. Erroneum est, quod Grotius hic sexuum differentiam in altera vita fulciatum iri, putat.

At vero ego video, inquit, quantum est naturarum rationibus, quod natura in quidem voluit etiam in illo saeculo manifestum fore discrimen sexuum. Videri enim potest id discrimen tollenda, pars esse ἀσθενείας quae tunc erit cessatura.

Imo species omnis ac figura & φθορᾷ obvelanda videtur.

δύματι τ' ἀφθαρσίας. Atqui τὸ φθαρτὸ aper- tum indicium τὸ γεννητικὸν. Id vero est quod negandum. Nam ἐν ἀφθαρσίᾳ conditi erant pro- toplasti; in quibus tamen sexus erat differentia; & generatio locum habuisset, salva ἀφθαρσίᾳ eo- rum, si in integritate perstitissent. Nec quia definit generatio in altero seculo, sexuum dif- crimen esse desinet. Non negat etiam Chri- stus mulierem fore mulierem, sed negat rela- tionem illam uxoris & viri, ac nuptiarum, vel matrimonii rationem illic locum habituram: Et num Maria mater Christi in altero secu- lo desinet esse fœmina, ac mas evadet? ut de aliis taceamus: aut num membra illa a Deo condita, quæ Spiritus S. honorari vult, 1. Cor. XIII. vers. 23. 24. abolenda prorsus erunt? Quod veterum non paucos ait arbitratos esse non futurum tum ἄῤῥεν, ὔτε θῆλυ, ostendendum e- rat. Unus Hilarius rem non conficit. Theodo- retus vero solum in Angelis demonstrat non esse sexuum discrimen, quod est extra contro- versiam. Non autem docet, ea parte nos An- gelis similes fore.

## 22:31
But concerning the resurrection of the dead] That is, as far as the thing itself is concerned. For up to this point he has only been responding to an objection.

Latin:

περὶ δὲ τῆς ἀναστάσεως τῶν νεκρῶν] Id est, quod rem ipsam attinet. Nam hactenus objectioni tantum respondit.

## 22:32
Verse 32. God is not the God of the dead, but of the living] This argument, which has seemed obscure to many, will become clear if we employ the interpreter, the divinely inspired writer to the Hebrews 11:16. First, it must be posited that the word God, where it has a possessive case after it, signifies a most excellent and most powerful benefactor, which the Sadducees could not deny, since the formula of the covenant was thus: I will be your GOD, and you will be my people. Next, it must be added that when Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob are specifically named, it signifies that God is their God or benefactor in a peculiar and excellent way, namely, on account of their singular faith and obedience. Third, it is to be noted that in this life, some comforts indeed, but mixed with many hardships, befell Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. For they neither possessed any lands of their own, but wandered here and there with their family and flocks, not rarely even struggling with the injuries of men and fortune. Whence also Jacob called himself a stranger or sojourner, addressing Pharaoh, which that divine writer rightly urges. Hence it follows that they received nothing in this life from God that was exceptional above other men, for which God should be called their God so peculiarly. Indeed, many wicked or less upright men in Egypt, Canaan, and elsewhere, led a much happier life. It remains, therefore, that God was their God, not only when they lived on earth, but also when God spoke those things to Moses. For, as I said, in this age nothing had happened to them that would fulfill the magnificence of such a name. Furthermore, we do much more for him for whose sake we do good to others, if we are able. God does not lack the power, as Christ now shows in one word: and he says that he will do good to their posterity on account of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob: much more, therefore, will he do good to them themselves. But those who are dead are not capable of a benefit if they are to remain perpetually in a state of death. It follows, therefore, that they must be restored to life, so that God can be their God, that is, their benefactor, in a peculiar and excellent way, just as the Jew Abenesdra also explains those words, I will be your GOD. Philo also: The eternal God is equal to the one who bestows, not sometimes, but always and continuously. This is what the writer to the Hebrews indicates with those words: Therefore God is not ashamed to be called their God. For he has prepared a city for them, namely, to receive the promises, as appears from what precedes and follows. Luke explains that 'God is not the God of the dead but of the living' thus: for all live to him: that is, God both can and wills to restore them to life: and therefore, since God's promises have no less certainty than present things: they are to be considered as living even now: thus Athenagoras attributes a persistence to the lives of men, though interrupted by death, as if by sleep. Just as Christ had said of Jairus's daughter: she is not dead but sleeps: and of Lazarus, he sleeps: I go to wake him. Although, indeed, to remove the hypothesis of the Sadducees, it could have sufficed to prove the persistence of souls, yet it agrees more correctly with the words and purpose of Christ, which is to prove the resurrection, that Abraham should be taken not as a soul, which is only a part of Abraham, but as a person consisting of soul and body, to whom properly death and life are attributed. Among all the arguments that are accustomed to be used to prove the immortality of the soul, none seems to me more apt for moving the minds of men than that which Clement, Bishop of Rome, used to recite as having been received from Peter the Apostle: If GOD is just, the soul is immortal. A similar sentiment can be found in Paul, 1 Cor. 15:19. For certainly, if we posit no distinction between those who have done well and those who have done otherwise, if we acknowledge divine providence and justice, which not even the Sadducees dared to deny, and yet we see that it is worse for many good men here than for the bad, it follows that another judgment remains, and therefore also that which can receive reward or punishment: which argument Chrysostom explained more than once with a wonderful abundance of eloquence. But that light also shone upon some of the pagans. For Balaam, whether led by reason or stirred by the divine Spirit, exclaims in Moses: let my death be with the death of the righteous: by which words, as the teachers of the Hebrews rightly note, he shows that some rewards are laid up for pious Hebrews after this life. Indeed, even Plato, Cicero, and Plutarch fight with that weapon, and Hierocles, whose words are these: For if there were nothing of us remaining after death, and this having a nature to be adorned with truth and virtue, such as we say the rational soul is, there would be no pure desire for noble things in us. For the suspicion of corruption destroys the zeal for these things and leads to bodily enjoyments, whatever they may be and from wherever they might be procured. For how could it seem to be the part of sensible men, or those who are moderately composed, not to grant everything to the body, through which the subsistence of the soul is also preserved, being in itself equal, but coming to be in a certain way through the formation of the body? And how shall we abandon the body for the sake of virtue, being about to destroy the soul itself together with the body, so that the virtue for which we endured death would nowhere exist? Nor does this hold true only for the immortality of souls, but, as I began to say, for the restoration of bodies as well, whether you look at nature or at the equity of the matter. The natural love of the body, which we all perceive in the soul, shows that the human soul is an imperfect substance which, by perfecting the body, is itself perfected at the same time by the attainment of its end: which reasoning drove many philosophers to invent transmigrations. Equity does not allow that the body, which sustains many hardships under the command of the soul, should not also bear a part of the reward. Add that it is necessary for human nature, created by God, that some end be proposed, which cannot even be imagined as anything other than the blessed life of the whole man. For the end of one part is not the end of the whole: but God created the whole man. All these things, and others besides worthy of reading, can be found treated more fully in the one I just mentioned, Athenagoras: to whom, so that I may not be too long, I refer you: but if it is not convenient for anyone to return to him, let him at least read here this vigorous reasoning, which is most consistent with these words of Christ: 'But if just judgment is carried out upon the things done according to the composite being, and it is not right that the soul alone should receive the rewards of the things done with the body [for it is in itself unaffected by the transgressions that occur regarding bodily pleasures or nourishment and treatments], nor the body alone (for this is in itself without judgment by law and justice), but the human being composed of these receives the judgment for each of the things done by him. And this reasoning finds that it does not happen in the life here (for what is according to merit is not preserved in the present life. because many who practice all impiety and every lawlessness and wickedness continue until the end without experiencing evils, and on the contrary those who have demonstrated their life tested by every virtue live in pains, in insults, in slanders, in outrages and all kinds of sufferings) nor after death [for the composite being no longer exists, with the soul being separated from the body, and the body itself being scattered back into those things from which it was gathered, and retaining nothing of its former nature or form except the memory of things done], it is clear to everyone what remains, that it is necessary, according to the apostle, for this corruptible and scattered thing to put on incorruption, so that when the dead have been brought to life by resurrection and the separated parts have been reunited, or even those entirely dissolved, each may justly receive what he did through the body, whether good or evil. This is also worthy of note, which has been observed by the Hebrews, that God is not called in the Holy Scriptures the God of anyone while he still leads a mortal life.

We admit that the word 'God,' when it has a possessive case after it, signifies a most excellent and most powerful benefactor by the force of the covenant, I will be your God, and you shall be my people. But that benefit does not only look to bodily goods, but primarily to spiritual ones, from the nature and condition of that same covenant. We also concede that, because those Patriarchs received nothing in this life so exceptional above other men; indeed, many wicked or less upright men in Egypt, Canaan, and elsewhere led a terrestrial life not a little more happily; it remains, therefore, that God was the God of the Patriarchs, not only when they were living on earth, but also when God was speaking those things to Moses. But it does not appear that Christ uses that argumentation here. Who rather concludes the matter from the words of Moses: Those of whom He still professes Himself to be the God, they have not entirely ceased to be, they are not altogether dead, but it is necessary that they live; for of those who in no way live, and are altogether dead, and have ceased to be, God is not the benefactor, nor can He do good to them. But God at the time of Moses still professed Himself to be the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; therefore, they had not then entirely ceased to be. Hence, Grotius's conclusion is not correctly inferred: it follows, therefore, that they must be restored to life, so that God can be their God in a peculiar and exceptional way, that is, their benefactor; for that follows, by the force of Christ's inference, that they are still living, not altogether dead; and this is what Luke explicitly has: 'for all live to Him,' the sense of which is not what Grotius renders, that God can and wills to restore them to life, but that they actually already live to God, and enjoy heavenly life in God. Although Christ proves not only the permanence of souls, but also the resurrection, it is not necessary to understand here a person constant from soul and body by the voice of Abraham; for in that way, as regards soul and body, or the whole person, Abraham was not living then; but He teaches that Abraham and others, whose God is still God even after death, live as regards the soul, so that He nevertheless employs the names of the persons, and thus implies that, just as their souls could not have entirely perished, so neither would their body remain forever in death. Because otherwise He would not be the God of the whole Abraham, not of the whole Isaac or Jacob, who indeed had promised and testified that He would be their God even after death, not only of the soul of Abraham, Isaac, or Jacob, but of those persons who consisted of soul and body, concerning which argument of Christ we have spoken more fully in Socinianism Profligated. Therefore, Christopher Sandius did not grasp either the state of the question or the force of Christ's argument in his Paradoxical Interpretations of the Four Gospels, page 61, when he wishes to conclude for Christ: Therefore Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob live. And further: But their bodies do not live. Therefore the souls. Therefore the souls do not perish with the bodies. The state of the question was not about the life or immortality of souls, but about the resurrection of the dead, verse 31. To the confirmation of which Christ's argument entirely contributes. The author of the Paradoxes indeed replies that Christ here calls dead souls dead by the hypothesis of the Sadducees, and as the Apostle in 1 Corinthians 15:35 calls souls dead, allegorically or metaphorically, because they sleep as it were and rest from all works. But these things prove at least the lack of judgment of the man and the itch for perverting Scripture. If He called souls dead by the hypothesis of the Sadducees, in those words, 'Have you not read concerning the resurrection of the dead?' Christ said; but the Sadducees, which he himself wishes, denied the resurrection of both soul and body, and asserted that souls perish with the bodies; how can they be understood as metaphorically dead?

For those whom Sandius says are thus dead, he says they only sleep, to be awakened from that sleep, but not that they have entirely perished. These things are certainly inconsistent. Nor is the resurrection of the dead to be understood otherwise in the words of Christ than as Matthew, verse 23, understood the resurrection, of whom it is most manifest that he speaks not of an improper, but of a proper resurrection, not of the awakening of souls from sleep, but of the resuscitation of the dead; nor did Paul in 1 Corinthians 15:35 call souls dead; but he spoke openly of dead men being resuscitated, with explicit mention made of bodies. 'How are the dead raised? And with what body do they come?' But concerning the metaphorical death of souls, that is, sleep, he made no indication, not even by the smallest iota, in the whole chapter, which chapter Sandius himself acknowledges on page 62 to be most open for proving the resurrection of bodies. But it is characteristic of man to twist and slander the writings both of men inspired by God and of any others whatsoever; which was also done to me in this very place, when that Anti-Trinitarian did not fear to write through a horrible calumny: that Calovius in Anti-Crellius § 420 seems to confess that the Trinity approaches superstition and idolatry; from which specimen one may gather with what faith he compiled the testimonies of his own unbelief. But these things are by way of paraphrase. But what the generator of monsters will finally effect from the human soul, perhaps not even he, completely intoxicated by the poison of Pyrrhonism, would know. As an angel, he says on page 38, so also the soul is a name of office; the name of the nature of both is Spirit; which if it is sent to announce, it becomes an Angel; but if to inform a human body, it becomes and is called a human soul, and when united with flesh it is called a man. And although we are truly spiritual substances, yet usage has prevailed that a soul is not called a man nakedly, but with the body. He seems to posit a pre-existent soul as a person with the Platonists, and that it informs the body afterwards, since he wishes it to be sent for that reason, and to be united with flesh, and thus to be called a man, and nevertheless he implies that the body is only a garment of the man, and he seems to distinguish the soul from an Angel not so much by species as by office. Whether, however, he wishes to ascribe to an Angel, just as to the soul, sleep and metaphorical death, is not clear. But having dismissed those paradoxes, we must return to Grotius, who does not poorly urge here that which contributes to proving the immortality of the soul, which Clement of Rome reported as received from Peter the Apostle: If God is just, the soul is immortal, to which a similar sentiment is that of Paul in 1 Corinthians 15:19. Thus it may be permitted to conclude from this also regarding the restoration of bodies: whether you look at the nature of the thing, or the equity of the thing. The natural love of the body, he says, which we all perceive in the soul, shows that the human soul is ὐσίαν ἀτελῆ which, by perfecting the body, is itself perfected at the same time by the attainment of its end. Which reasoning drove many philosophers to invent μετενσωματώσεις. Equity does not allow that the body, which endures many troubles under the command of the soul, should not also bear a part of the reward. Add that it is necessary for human nature created by God that some end be proposed, which cannot even be imagined to be other than the blessed way of the whole man. For the end of one part is not the end of the whole: but God created the whole man. All of which Athenagoras has beautifully executed. Finally, Grotius notes that it has been observed by the Hebrews that God is not called in the Holy Scriptures the God of anyone while he still leads a mortal life, which however is not universally true: see Gen. XXVIII. 13. It is rather to be observed that not only regarding earthly goods, but especially regarding heavenly ones, not only in this age, but also in the other, God himself

That God will be of the faithful, he received by the force of the covenant, Gen. XXVII. Conf. Ap. XXI. 7. which is noted by both Philo and Aben-Ezra. Mr. D. Sebast. Schmied. in Coll. Bibl. post. p. 382, makes Christ argue thus: God is God to Himself of the living, and not to Himself of the dead, but of those sleeping, even if they are dead to men. But God is the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Therefore, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob are living to God, and not dead to God, but only sleeping, although they are dead to men. Furthermore: Whoever are indeed truly dead to men, yet are not dead to God, but living and only sleeping, they shall truly rise again some day from their sleep, &c. But we acquiesce in the explanation of Christ's argument previously handed down, as the simplest.

PART IV. Question concerning the greatest commandment.

Latin:

Vers. 32. ὀυκ ἐστι ὁ Θεὸς, Θεὸς νεκρῶν, ἀλλὰ ζώντων] Ar- gumentum hoc, quod multis obscurius visum est, perspi- cuum fiet si interpretem adhibeamus θεόπνευστον Scriptorem ad Hebræos XI. 16. Primo ponendum vocem Dei ubi pos- sessivum casum post se habet, significare ἐυεργέτην optimum atque potentissimum, quod negare Sadducæi non poterant, cum ita haberet formula fœderis: Ero DEVS vester, & vos eritis mihi populus. Deinde addendum est, cum Abraha- mus, Isaacus & Jacobus peculiariter nominantur, eo si- gnificari Deum peculiariter atque eximie esse ipsorum Deum sive ἐυεργέτην, ob singularem scilicet ipsorum fi- dem atque obedientiam. Tertio notandum in hac vita Abrahamo, Isaaco, Jacobo, commoda quidem aliqua, sed multis incommodis permixta accidisse. Nam neque terras ullas proprias habuerunt, sed cum familia ac gre- gibus huc illuc sunt vagati, non raro etiam conflictati cum hominum fortunæque injuriis. Unde & Jacobus ξένον sive παρεπίδημον se vocabat, Pharaonem alloquens, quod merito urget divinus ille Scriptor. Hinc sequitur, nihil illos in hac vita supra cæteros homines eximium a Deo recepisse, propter quod Deus tam peculiariter ipso- rum Deus dici debeat. Imo multi improbi aut minus probi in Ægypto, Cananæa atque alibi, vitam tersenam haud paulo felicius egere. Restat ergo ut Deus ipsorum Deus fuerit, non modo cum in terris agerent, sed etiam cum ad Mosem Deus ista loqueretur. Nam, ut dixi, in hoc ævo nihil illis contigerat quod tanti nominis magni- ficentiam impleret. Deinde vero propter quem benefa- cimus aliis, ei multo magis benefacimus si possumus. Deo potestas non deest, ut jam uno verbo ostendit Chri- stus: & dicit se benefacturum posteritati propter Abra- hamum, Isaacum, Jacobum: multo ergo magis ipsis be- nefaciet. Beneficii autem capaces non sunt qui mortui sunt, si perpetuo in mortis statu sunt mansuri. Sequitur ergo restituendos eos esse in vitam, ut peculiariter at- que eximie Deus ipsorum Deus, hoc est ἐυεργέτης esse possit, quomodo etiam Judæus Abenesdra explicat illa 'lesis, Ego ero DEVS vester. Philo etiam: Τὸ δὴ θεὸς ἀιώνιΘ ; ἶσον ἐστι τῷ ὁ χαριζόμενΘ ὀ ποτὲ μὲν, ποτὲ δὲ ὀυ, ἀεὶ δὲ κὴ συνεχῶς. Hoc est quod illis verbis indicat Scri- ptor ad Hebræos: διὸ ὀυκ ἐπαισχύνεται ἀυτὸς Θεὸς, Θεὸς ἐπικαλεῖσθαι ἀυτῶν. Ἡτοίμασε γὰρ ἀυτοῖς πόλιν, nimi- rum ad recipiendas τὰς ἐπαγγελίας, ut ex præcedentibus & sequentibus apparet. Lucas illud Θεὸς δὲ ὀυκ ἔστι νε- κρῶν ἀλλὰ ζώντων, ita explicat: πάντες γὰρ ἀυτῷ ζῶσιν: id est, & potest & vult eos Deus vitæ reddere: ac pro- inde cum Dei promissa non minorem certitudinem ha- beant quam res præsentes: jam nunc vivere censendi sunt: ita vitæ hominum διαμονὴν tribuit Athenagoras, morte tamen, velut somno, intercisam. Quomodo Christus de Jairifilia dixerat: ὀυκ ἀπέθανεν ἀλλὰ καθεύ- δει: & de Lazaro, dormit: vado ut excitem eum. Quan- quam vero ad tollendam hypothesin Sadducæorum suf- ficere poterat, probare permansionem animorum, tamen & verbis & proposito Christi, quod est probare τὴν ἀνά- sasi, rectius convenit, Abrahamum accipere non ani- mum, quæ pars tantum est Abrahami, sed personam constantem ex animo ac corpore, cui proprie mors & vita tribuitur. Inter omnia argumenta, quæ ad pro- bandam animi immortalitatem adhiberi solent, nullum mihi videtur aptius movendis hominum animis, quam illud quod à Petro Apostolo acceptum recitasse solebat Clemens Romæ Episcopus: Si DEVS est justus, animus est immortalis. Cui parem sententiam reperire est apud Paulum I. Cor. XV. 19. Nam certe, si nullum ponimus bene secusque factorum discrimen, si divinam providen- tiam & justitiam agnoscimus, quam nec Sadducæi negare audebant, videmus autem bonis multis pejus hic esse quam malis, sequitur aliud superesse judicium, ac pro- inde id etiam quod præmium pœnamve recipere possit: quod argumentum mira facundiæ ubertate non semel ex- plicavit Chrysostomus. Sed & paganorum quibusdan lux illa emicuit. Nam Balaamus sive ratione ductus, sive Spiritu divino agitatus, exclamat apud Mosem: sit mors mea cum morte justorum: quibus verbis, ut recte notant Hebræorum magistri, ostendit piis Hebræis præmia ali- qua post hanc vitam esse reposita. Quin & Plato, Ci- cero, Plutarchus isto telo pugnant, & Hierocles, cujus hæc sunt verba: Εἰ γὰρ μὴ ἔη τι ὑπομένον ἡμῶν μετὰ θάνα- τον, καὶ τῦτο φύσιν ἔχον ἀληθείᾳ καὶ ἀρετῇ κοσμεῖθαι, οἵον δὴ φαμὲν εἶναι τὴν λογικὴν ψυχὴν, ὠκ ἂν ἔφεσις ἡμῖν καθαρὰ γένοιτο τῶν καλῶν. Προαναιρεῖται γὰρ ἡ ὑποψία τῆς φθορᾶς τὴν περὶ ταῦτα σπυδὴν καὶ πρὸς ἀπολαύσεις ἄγει σωματικὰς, ὁ- ποῖαι ποτέ ἂν ὦσιν αὐταὶ καὶ πόθεν ἂν πορίζεσθαι δύναιντο Πῶς γὰρ ἂν δόξη ἔμφρονων εἶναι καθ' ἑυτὰς, ἢ μετρίως καθε- στηκότων, μὴ πάντα χαρίζεσθαι τῷ σώματι, δι ὃ καὶ ἡ τῆς ψυ- χῆς ὑπόστασις σώζεται, ἐκ ὔσης μὲν καθ᾽ ἑυτὴν, ἐπιγιγνο- μένης δὲ τῇ ποίᾳ διὰ πλάσει τῦ σώματος; πῶς δὲ προησόμεθα δι ἀρετὴν τὸ σῶμα, μέλλοντες καὶ τὴν ψυχὴν αὐτὴν ἅμα τῷ σώματι διαφθείρειν, ὥσε μηδαμῦ εἶναι τὴν ἀρετὴν ἧς ἐφιέμε τα θάνατον ὑπεμείναμεν. Neque vero ad immortalitatem animorum duntaxat id valet, sed, ut dicere cœpi, ad corporum quoque restitutionem, sive naturam spectes, sive rei æquitatem. Naturalis amor corporis, quem in animo omnes deprehendimus, ostendit animum huma- num esse ὐσίαν ἀτελῆ quæ corpus perficiendo simul ipsa perficiatur finis sui adeptione: quæ ratio multos Philoso- phos adegit ad comminiscendas μετενσωματώσεις. Æ- quitas non patitur ut corpus quod animi imperio multa molesta sustinet, non etiam partem ferat præmii. Adde quod humanæ naturæ à Deo conditæ necesse sit finem aliquem esse propositum, qui ne fingi quidem potest a- lius quam beata vita totius hominis. Nam finis partis alterius non est finis totius: at totum hominem Deus condidit. Quæ omnia, aliaque insuper lectu digna u- berius tractata invenire est apud eum quem modo dixi Athenagoram: ad quem te, ne longior sim, remitto: quod sicui eo recurrere non vacat, hanc saltem hic le- gat nervosam & his Christi verbis convenientissimam ratiocinationem: Εἰ δὲ κατὰ τὸ συναμφότερον φέρεται ἐπὶ τοῖς εἰργασμένοις δίκην ἡ δικαία κρίσις, καὶ μήτε τὴν ψυχὴν μόνην δεῖ κομίσασθαι τὰ ἐπίχειρα τῶν μετὰ τῦ σώματος ἐιρ- γασμένων [ἀπροσπαθὴς γὰρ ἄυτη καθ' ἑαυτὴν τῶν περὶ τὰς σω- ματικὰς ἡδονὰς ἢ τροφὰς καὶ θεραπείας γινομένων πλημμελη- μάτων] μήτε τὸ σῶμα μόνον (ἄκριτον γὰρ τῦτο καθ' ἑαυτὸ νόμῳ καὶ δίκης) ὁ δὲ ἐκ τέτων ἀνθρωπων τὴν ἐφ' ἑκάστῳ τῶν εἰρ- γασμένων ἀυτῷ δέχεται κρίσιν. Τοῦτο δὲ ὔτε κατὰ τὴν ἐν τῷ ζωὴν εὑρίσκοι συμβαῖνον ὁ λόγος (ὐ γὰρ σώζεται τὸ κατ᾿ ἀξίαν ἐν τῷ παρόντι βίῳ. διὰ δὲ τὸ πόλλες μὲν ἀθέες καὶ πᾶσαν ἀνομίαν καὶ κακίαν ἐπιτηδεύοντας μέχρι τελευτῆς διατελεῖν κακῶν ἀπειράτες καὶ τἀναντίον τὰς κατὰ πᾶσαν ἀρετὴν ἐξη- τασμένον τῶν ἑαυτῶν βίον ἐπιδειξαμένως, ἐν ὀδύναις ζῆν, ἐν ἐπη- ρείαις, ἐν συκοφαντίαις, ἀικίαις τε καὶ παντοίαις κακοπαθεί- αις) ὔτε δὲ μετὰ θάνατον [ὐδὲ γάρ ἐσιν ἔτι τὸ συναμφότε- ρον, χωριζομένης μὲν τῆς ψυχῆς ἀπὸ τῦ σώματος, σκεδαννυμέ- νε δὲ καὶ ἀυτῦ τῦ σώματος εἰς ἐκεῖνα πάλιν ἐξ ὧν συνεσφορήθη, καὶ μηδὲν ἔτι σώζοντος τῆς προτέρας φυῆς ἢ μορφῆς ἄπω γε τὴν μνήμην τῶν πεπραγμένων] ἔνδηλον παντὶ τὸ λειπόμενον, ὅτι δεῖ κατὰ τὸν ἀπόστολον τὸ φθαρτὸν τῦτο καὶ διασκεδασὸν ἐνδύσα- θαι ἀφθαρσίαν, ἵνα ζωοποιηθέντων ἐξ ἀναστάσεως τῶν νεκρωθέν- των καὶ πάλιν ἑνωθέντων τῶν κεχωρισμένων, ἢ καὶ πάντη διαλε- λυμένων, ἕκαστον κομίσηται δικαίως, ἃ διὰ τῦ σώματος ἔ- πραξεν, εἴτε ἀγαθὰ, εἴτε κακά. Dignum notatu & hoc, quod ab Hebræis est observatum, Deum non vocari in sa- cris literis Deum cujusquam dum is vitam adhuc morta- lem agit.

Admittimus vocem Dei ubi possessivum casum post se habet, significare εὐεργέτην optimum, atque potentissimum vi foederis, Ero Deus vester, & vos eritis mihi populus. Non autem tantum εὐεργε- σία illa corporalia spectat bona, sed imprimis spi- ritualia, ex ejusdem fœderis natura & conditio- ne. Concedimus etiam, quia nihil Patriarchae illi in hac vita supra cæteros homines eximium adeo re- cepêre, imo multi improbi, aut minus probi in Æ- gypto, Cananæa, atque alibi vitam terrenam haud paulo felicius egêre, restare igitur, ut Deus Patriar- charum Deus fuerit, non modo cum in terris age- rent, sed etiam cum ad Mosen Deus ista loquere- tur. Sed illa argumentatione Christum hic uti non apparet. Qui potius ex verbis Mosis rem conficit; Quorum Deus adhuc se profitetur Deum, illi non plane desierunt esse, non sunt prorsus mortui, sed vivant, necessum est: qui e- nim nullo modo vivunt, ac prorsus mortui sunt, & esse defierunt, illorum εὐεργέτης Deus non est, nec iis benefacere potest. At Deus tempore Mo- sis se adhuc Deum profitebatur Abrahæ, Isaaci, & Jacobi, E. illi tum non plane desierunt esse. Pro- inde non recte infertur conclusio Grotii: sequi- tur ergo, restituendos eos esse in vitam, ut peculia- riter atque eximie Deus ipsorum Deus hoc est εὐερ- γέτης esse possit: nam id sequitur, vi illationis Chri- sti, eos etiamnum vivere, non omnino mortuos es- se; atque hoc est quod Lucas diserte habet; πάν- τες γὰρ αὐτῷ ζῶσιν, quorum sensus non est, quem reddit Grotius, & potest & vult eos Deus vitæ reddere: sed quod actu illi jam vivant Deo, ac vita fruantur cœlesti in Deo. Quanquam vero Christus non tantum permansionem animorum, sed etiam τὴν ἀνάστασιν probet: non tamen Abra- hami voce personam constantem ex anima ac corpo- re hic intelligere necessum est; Ea enim ratione quoad animam ac corpus, vel integram personam non vivebat tum Abraham; Sed ita Abrahamum & alios, quorum Deus post mortem etiam Deus est, vivere docet, quoad animam, ut nomina tamen adhibeat personarum, adeoque innuat, quemadmodum animæ ipsorum non potuit plane interiisse, ita nec corpus eorum in morte perpe- tuo mansurum. Quia alias non totius Abraha- mi, non totius Isaaci, aut Jacobi Deus foret, qui vero Deum se fore non animæ solum Abrahæ, Isaaci, aut Jacobi, sed personarum istarum, quæ constabant anima & corpore, promiserat, ac te- status erat, etiam post mortem se ipsorum Deum esse, de quo argumento Christi fusius diximus in Socinisino profligato. Non ergo vel statum causæ, vel vim argumenti Christi assecutus est Christo- phorus Sandius in interpretationibus paradoxis IV. Evangel. pag. 61. cum Christum concludere vult: Ergo Abraham, Isaac, & Jacob vivunt. Et porro: Ast non vivunt eorum corpora. Ergo animæ. Ergo animæ non intereunt cum corporibus. Status erat non de vita, vel immortalitate anima- rum, sed de resurrectione mortuorum vers. 31. Ad quam confirmandam Christi argumentum omni- no facit. Reponit quidem autor Paradoxus, Christum hic animas mortuas vocare ex hypothesi Sadducæorum, & ut Apostolus 1. Corinth. XV. 35. animas mortuas vocat, Allegorice vel Metaphori- ce, quia dormiant quasi & quiescant ab omnibus o- peribus. Sed hæc ἀκρισίας hominis, & caco- ethes pervertendi scripturam saltim probant. Si ex hypothesi Sadducæorum animas mortuas, in il- lis, nonne legistis de mortuorum resurrectione? di- xit Christus; Sadducæi autem, quod ipse vult, ne- garunt & animæ, & corporis resurrectionem, & asseruerunt animas cum corporibus interire, quo- modo intelligi possunt metaphorice mortuæ?

Quas enim ita mortuas dicit Sandius, eas dormire tantum, e somno illo resuscitandas ait, non autem plane interiisse. Hæc certe ἀσύστατα sunt. Nec vel in verbis Christi resurrectio mortuorum aliter intelligenda, quam uti Matthæus vers. 23. resurre- ctionem intellexit, quem non de impropria, sed propria resurrectione, non de animarum excita- tione a somno, sed de resuscitatione mortuorum lo- qui, manifestissimum est; Nec Paulus 1. Cor. XV. 35. animas mortuas vocavit; sed de mortuis homini- bus resuscitandis aperte loquutus est, corporum diserta mentione facta. Πῶς ἐγείρονται νεκροὶ; ποίῳ δὲ σώματι ἔρχονται; De animarum vero meta- phorica morte, hoc est, dormitione, nullo vel mini- mo apice indicium in toto capite fecit, quod vero caput ad probandam resurrectionem corporum aper- tissimum esse, agnoscit Sandius p. 62. Sed proprium hominis est torquere, & calumniari scripta tum virorum θεοπνεύστων, tum aliorum quorumvis; Quod in hoc ipso loco mihi etiam factum, cum Anti-Trinitarius ille per horrendam διαβολὴν scribere haud veritus est: Calovium in Anti-Crel- lio §. 420. videri fateri, Trinitatem ad superstitionem & idololatriam accedere; ex quo specimine colli- gere liceat, qua fide compilarit ἀπιστίας suæ te- stimonia. Verum hæc παραφραστικῶς. Quid autem ex anima humana tandem effecturus sit monstro- rum genitor, forte nec ipse Pyrrhonismi veneno prorsus intoxicatus noverit. Sicut angelus, inquit pag. 38. ita & anima, officii nomen est, utriusque nomen naturæ Spiritus est; qui si mittitur ad an- nuntiandum, Angelus fit; sin ad informandum cor- pus humanum anima humana fit & dicitur, & uni- tus cum carne homo vocatur. Et licet vere substan- tiæ simus spirituales, tamen usus obtinuit, ut ani- ma non nuda; sed cum corpore homo diceretur. Ni- mirum animam personam præexistentem cum Pla- tonicis statuere videtur, eamque corpus postea in- formare, quum ideo mittatur, ac cum carne uni- ri, atque ita hominem vocari vult, & nihilominus corpus tantum esse vestimentum hominis innuit, animamque videtur non tam specie, quam officio, ab Angelo discernere. Num vero Angelo æque ut animæ dormitionem ac mortem allegoricam ad- scribere velit, non liquet. Missis autem paradoxis illis redeundum nobis ad Grotium, qui non male hic urget quod uti ad probandam animæ immorta- litatem facit illud, quod Clemens Romanus à Petro Apostolo acceptum retulit. Si Deus est justus, ani- mus est immortalis, cui similis sententia est Pauli 1. Corinth. XV. 19. Sic ad corporum quoque restitu- tionem inde concludere liceat: sive naturam rei spe- ctes, sive rei æquitatem. Naturalis, inquit, amor corporis, quem in animo omnes deprehendimus, o- stendit animum humanum esse ὐσίαν ἀτελῆ quæ corpus perficiendo simul ipsa perficiatur finis sui ade- ptione. Quæ ratio multos Philosophos adegit ad com- miniscendas μετενσωματώσεις. Æquitas non pati- tur ut corpus quod animi imperio multa molesta su- stinet non etiam partem ferat præmii. Adde quod hu- manæ naturæ à Deo conditæ necesse sit finem aliquem esse propositum, qui ne fingi quidem potest alius quam beata via totius hominis. Nam finis partis alterius non est finis totius: at totum hominem Deus condidit. Quæ omnia pulchre exequutus est Athenagoras. Notat denique Grotius, ab Ebræis observatum esse, quod Deus non vocetur in S. literis Deus cujusquam, dum is vitam adhuc mortalem agit, quod tamen u- niversaliter verum non est: vid. Gen. XXVIII. 13. Id potius observandum, quod non solum quoad bo- na terrena, sed imprimis quoad cælestia, non in hoc solum sæculo, sed etiam in altero Deus se

Deum fore fidelium receperit vi fœderis Genes. XXVII. Conf. Ap. XXI. 7. quod & Philoni & Aben- Ezræ notatum. Dn. D. Sebast. Schmied. in Coll. Bibl. post. p. 382. Christum ita argumentantem facit: Deus est Deus vivorum sibi, & non mor- tuorum sibi, sed dormientium, etsi hominibus mortui sint. Atqui Deus est Deus Abrahæ, Isaa- ci & Jacobi. E. Abraham, Isaac & Jacob sunt vi- vi Deo, & non mortui Deo, sed tantum dormien- tes, licet hominibus mortui sint. Porro: Qui- cunque hominibus quidem vere mortui, non ta- men Deo mortui sunt, sed vivi & tantum dormi- entes, illi revera aliquando è somno suo resur- gent, &c. Sed nos acquiescimus explicationi argu- menti Christi antea traditæ, ceu simplicissimæ.

PARS IV. Quæstio de præcepto maximo.

## 22:34
Ver. 34. Συνήχθησαν ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτὸ] It answers to the Hebrew יהקבצו יחדו which is in Joshua IX. 2. and elsewhere. Ver. 35. εἷς ἐξ αὐτῶν νομικὸς] Νομικὸς is the same as γραμματεύς: that is the name of the office: he was, however, a Pharisee by sect. πειράζων] This verb is not to be taken here in the sense of calumny: but in the way the Queen of Sheba is said to have come πειράσαι Solomon, 1 Kings X. 1. Ver. 36. μεγάλη] μεγίστη, that is, most worthy to be committed to memory, the first of the commandments: as below 38. and in Mark. There is no doubt that this question had been agitated: and some thought the chief commandments were those which concerned sacrifices, as seems to be gathered from the cited passage of Mark; others, as is credible, the law of circumcision, as Eleazar the Galilean was saying to Izates, as Josephus relates, or even of the Sabbath: whose errors the Prophets refute in many places. V. 37. ἐν ὅλῃ τῇ καρδίᾳ σε καὶ ἐν ὅλῃ τῇ ψυχῇ σε] A Hebraism. For what we say in Latin to do something with the whole heart, the Greeks, like the LXX in this place, ἐξ ὅλης τῆς καρδίας, the Hebrews say in the whole heart. καὶ ἐν ὅλῃ τῇ διανοίᾳ σε] ובכל מאדך which the LXX rendered quite properly, ἐξ ὅλης δυνάμεώς σε. Mark and Luke [add] ἐξ ὅλης τῆς ἰσχύος σε. Who, however, exegetically add also the word διάνοια: the sense of which here is that which is in Thucydides, διάνοιαν ἔχω πρὸς τὸ καλὸν τῆς πράξεως: that is, I am intent upon this. But it means the same thing whether you say with all one's strength, or with all zeal and contention. For that some Hebrew interpreters take מאד in this place for wealth, is foreign: just as is the superfluous diligence of those who distinguish καρδίαν, ψυχὴν, διάνοιαν too subtly here, when the accumulation of many words designates nothing but more intense zeal: just as the Latins also say with heart, mind, and strength, as has been noted by others. Therefore, in the same sense, you may find what we have here, sometimes in threes, sometimes singly, sometimes in pairs. Singly, as when in 1 Kings XIV. 8, God says of David: ἐπορεύθη ὀπίσω με ἐν πάσῃ τῇ καρδίᾳ αὐτῶ: and when Samuel addresses the people thus, 1 Sam. VII. 3, εἰ ἐν ὅλῃ καρδίᾳ ὑμῶν ὑμεῖς ἐπιστρέφετε πρὸς κύριον: and when it is told of Jehu, 2 Kings X. 31, οὐκ ἐφύλαξε πορεύεσθαι ἐν νόμῳ κυρίῳ Θεῶ Ἰσραὴλ ἐν ὅλῃ καρδίᾳ αὐτῶ. And in Psalm CXIX. 2, concerning the pious, ἐν ὅλῃ καρδίᾳ ἐκζητήσουσιν αὐτόν. To which can be added that saying in Ecclesiasticus concerning David, ch. XLVII. 10, ἐν πάσῃ καρδίᾳ αὐτῶ ὕμνησε κᾀ ἠγάπησε τὸν ποιήσαντα αὐτόν. In pairs, as Deut. IV. 29, to the people, ὅταν ζητήσετε αὐτὸν ἐξ ὅλης τῆς καρδίας σε καὶ ἐξ ὅλης τῆς ψυχῆς σε; 2 Chron. XV. 12, concerning the whole people. they went to seek the Lord God of their fathers with all their heart and with all their soul: and 2 Kings XXIII. 3, concerning Josiah: he agreed to walk after the Lord, and to keep his commandments, with all his heart and with all his soul. Nor is that of M. Antoninus in book XII unlike: ἐξ ὅλης τῆς ψυχῆς τὰ δίκαια ποιεῖν καὶ τ' ἀληθῆ λέγειν. But the Jews err gravely who think this commandment, as also that concerning not coveting, is sufficiently fulfilled if one does not depart from the law in external deeds. For it is too evident to be denied that by these words internal acts are also commanded, yet in conjunction with external ones: and it is to be noted that this clause exists not in the formula of the Sinaitic covenant, which is in Exodus, but ἐν ῇ ἐπινομίδι, as Philo, in the Platonic manner, calls that book which we commonly call Deuteronomy. In that book, however, there are very many things which call the people to the norm of the covenant, which has been fully revealed through Christ, and they contain certain rudiments of Evangelical piety. Again, Augustine and others who followed him think that by these words is signified that perfection which no one has had or could have in this life, as if it were prescribed not so much by what one should run, as to where one should run. Which opinion can have its use, so that men, warned of their infirmity, may be kept within the bounds of humility, and desire for the other life may be excited in them. But that this is not the proper interpretation of the words is clear by comparing the passages we have brought forward: for David, Josiah, and others are recorded to have done that which this law demands. For I judge it manifest that to seek and to love God in Hebraism mean the same thing. Thus also some are said to follow after God, which the Chaldean paraphrast explains as perfectly following the fear of God, as can be seen in Num. XIV. 24, XXXII. 12, Deut. I. 36. Furthermore, the law wills that this love be rendered according to one's strength, μετὰ δύναμιν, that is, as much as a man can. But that a man can [do] as much as he can, no sane person will deny. The middle and true opinion, therefore, is this: that it is required by God, not that we never think of or love anything besides Him, which the state of this life does not allow, but that we devote the chief zeal of our minds to God, doing this with all effort, so that we may carry out not some, but all of God's commandments. For that ἐξ ὅλης or πάσης καρδίας is the same as what is said elsewhere בלבב שלם, ἐκ καθαρᾶς καρδίας, as Paul translates in 1 Tim. I. 5, that is, with an integral and sincere heart, just as we also say in Latin, I am wholly in this. But man is to be understood as able, not only in what he can do by the powers of nature prostrated by the habit of sinning, but in what he can do aided by the divine Spirit, whom God even in those ancient times gave to certain few chosen ones, not by common law, but by peculiar grace, but in the new covenant liberally promises to all his covenanted ones, that is, to those who believe in his Son. Πάντα ἰσχύω, says Paul, ἐν τῷ ἐνδυναμῦντί με χριςῷ. But by how much greater an abundance of the Spirit is now given or offered, by so much more abundantly is this commandment also to be fulfilled.

The diligence of those who distinguish καρδίαν, ψυχὴν, διάνοιαν here is not to be considered superfluous with Grotius: For although it is certain that a more intense zeal is being designated, and sometimes three, sometimes one, sometimes two are used, yet the Holy Scriptures did not use all of them rashly, and those which do not occur somewhere else have a fuller sense from others: and they teach that the heart, soul, mind, and indeed all powers are required, as Mark and Luke [say], ἐξ ὅλης τῆς ἰσχύος. How shall we estimate as superfluous the diligence which weighs the force and emphasis of individual words used by the Holy Scriptures not without care: and does not God demand all the faculties of man, and whatever is in him, so that he may be carried wholly with all his powers, mind, will, and appetite into love for Him? Therefore not only Scholastic or more recent Theologians used that diligence; but also the Fathers, Origen, Ambrose, Nyssenus, Augustine, and others, indeed the Hebrews also, concerning whom see. B. Gerhard in Harm. Evang. CLVI, who is pleased to understand by the word καρδίας the rational appetite, or the will, as in Deut. IV. 29, Jos. XXII. 5, 1 Par. XII. 36, because it is of the heart to have ὁρμὴ & ὄρεξις: by ψυχὴν the sensitive life, and the senses or sensitive appetite, whose property is ἐπιθύμησις Gen. XXIII, c. XXXIV. 3, Deut. XII. 20: by διάνοιαν the intellect, τὸ ἡγεμονικὸν, because it is explained in Mark XII. 33 by σύνεσιν, etc. But in this Grotius hallucinates more gravely, indeed he approaches the Papistic and Socinian heresy, when he rejects the opinion of Augustine and other ancients, that by these words is signified that perfection which no one (after the fall) has had or could have had in this life, and, intending to sail for the Pelagians, he maintains that the law only wishes this love to be performed according to one's powers and as much as a man can: whereas that law demands a far most perfect love, absolute in all parts and in all respects; such as has been performed by no one, nor could be performed. For the examples which are brought forward to the contrary, of David 1 Kings xiv. 8, and of Josiah 2 Kings XXIII. 3, do not contain all those things which the law requires: of David it is said only that ἐν πάσῃ τῇ καρδίᾳ ἀυτᾶ ἐπορέυθη ὀπίσω θεᾶ: he walked after God with all his heart: of Josiah it is added; καὶ ἐν πάσῃ ψυχῇ: of no one is the third added at the same time, ἐν τῇ ὅλῃ τῇ διανοίᾳ ἀυτᾶ, with that guarantee ἐξ ὅλης δυνάμεως, or τῆς ἴσχυος ἀυτᾶ: nor is such a love of God [attributed] to anyone, but only an endeavor to follow God in that manner, namely with all the heart, and all the soul, that is, a sincere and unfeigned zeal for piety is attributed. Which God not only granted to a few select persons, or out of a peculiar grace alone in ancient times, as Grotius, following the aforementioned heretics, opines, but commonly bestows upon all the regenerate at all times; who serve God with grace from the Holy Spirit from a pure heart, for that from all or with all the heart, Grotius acknowledges to be the same as from a pure heart, 1 Tim. I. 5, that is, with an upright and sincere heart: by which reasoning, to serve God and to love God is fitting for all believers, whether they lived or live in the time of the Old or New Testament.

Latin:

Vers. 34. Συνήχθησαν ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτὸ] Respondet Hebræo יהקבצו יחדו quod est Josuæ IX. 2. & alibi. Vers. 35. εἷς ἐξ αὐτῶν νομικὸς] Νομικὸς idem est quod γραμματεύς: id nomen officii: erat autem Pharisæus τὴν αἵρεσιν. πειράζων] Non est hic sumendum verbum hoc in ca- lumniæ significationem: sed quomodo regina Sabæ dicitur venisse πειράσαι Salomonem 1. Reg. X. 1. Vers. 36. μεγάλη] μεγίστη, id est dignissima quæ me- moriæ commendetur, πρώτη τῶν ἐντολῶν: ut infra 38. & apud Marcum. Dubium non est quin agitata fuerit hæc quæstio: & alii præcipuas ἐντολὰς esse putaverint eas quæ de sacrificiis erant, ut colligi videtur dicto Marci loco; alii, ut credibile est, legem circumcifionis, ut ad Izaten dicebat E- leazar Gallæus narrante Josepho, aut etiam Sabbati: quo rum errores passim refellunt Prophetæ. V. 37. ἐν ὅλῃ τῇ καρδίᾳ σε καὶ ἐν ὅλῃ τῇ ψυχῇ σε] Hebraismus. Nam quod Latine dicimus facere aliquid toto corde, Græ- ci, ut LXX. hoc loco, ἐξ ὅλης τῆς καρδίας, Hebræi dicunt in toto corde. καὶ ἐν ὅλῃ τῇ διανοίᾳ σε] ובכל מאדך quod LXX. satis proprie reddiderunt, ἐξ ὅλης δυνάμεώς σε. Mar- cus & Lucas ἐξ ὅλης τῆς ἰσχύος σε. Qui tamen ἐξηγητικῶς ad- dunt etiam διανοίας vocabulum: cujus hic is est sensus qui apud Thucydidem, διάνοιαν ἔχω πρὸς τὸ καλὸν τῆς πράξεως: id est, in id intentus sum. Idem autem valet sive dicas pro viribus, sive omni studio atque contentione. Nam quod Hebræi quidam interpretes מאד hoc loco pro opibus acci- piunt, alienum est: sicut & illorum supervacua diligentia, qui καρδίαν, ψυχὴν, διάνοιαν nimium subtiliter hic distin- guunt, cum vocum multarum cumulatio nihil quam inten- sius studium designet: sicut & Latini dicunt corde, animo, atque viribus, ut ab aliis est annotatum. Itaque eodem sen- su quæ hic habemus, terna modo, modo singula, modo bina reperias Singula, ut cum 1 Reg. XIV. 8. Deus de Davi- de dicit: ἐπορεύθη ὀπίσω με ἐν πάσῃ τῇ καρδίᾳ αὐτῶ: & cum Samuel populum ita alloquitur 1, Sam. VII. 3. εἰ ἐν ὅλῃ καρ- δίᾳ ὑμῶν ὑμεῖς ἐπιστρέφετε πρὸς κύριον: & cum de Jehu nar- ratur 2. Reg. X. 31. οὐκ ἐφύλαξε πορεύεσθαι ἐν νόμῳ κυρίῳ Θεῶ Ἰσραὴλ ἐν ὅλῃ καρδίᾳ αὐτῶ. Et in Psalm. CXIX 2. de piis, ἐν ὅλῃ καρδίᾳ ἐκζητήσουσιν αὐτόν. Quibus addi potest illud in Ec- clesiasticis dictum de Davide c. XLVII. 10. ἐν πάσῃ καρδίᾳ αὐτῶ ὕμνησε κᾀ ἠγάπησε τὸν ποιήσαντα αὐτόν. Bina, ut Deut. IV. 29. ad populum, ὅταν ζητήσετε αὐτὸν ἐξ ὅλης τῆς καρδίας σε καὶ ἐξ ὅλης τῆς ψυχῆς σε 2. Paral. XV. 12. de populo toto. διῆλθον ζητῆσαι κύριον Θεὸν τῶν πατέρων αὐτῶν ἐξ ὅλης τῆς καρδίας καὶ ἐξ ὅλης τῆς ψυχῆς αὐτῶν: & 2 Reg. XXIII. 3. de Jo- sia: διέθετο πορεύεσθαι ὀπίσω κυρίε, καὶ φυλάσσειν τὰ δικαιώματα αὐτῶ, ἐν πάσῃ καρδίᾳ καὶ ἐν πάσῃ ψυχῇ. Nec dissimile illud M. Anto- ni ni lib. XII. ἐξ ὅλης τῆς ψυχῆς τὰ δίκαια ποιεῖν καὶ τ' ἀληθῆ λέγειν. Errant autem graviter Judæi qui præceptum hoc, ut & illud de non concupiscendo, satis impleri putant, si factis externis à lege non abeatur. Apertius enim est quam ut ne- gari possit istis verbis actus etiam internos præcipi, conjun- ctim tamen cum externis: notandumque est exstare parti- culam hanc non in formula Sinaitici fœderis, quod est in Exodo, sed ἐν τῇ ἐπινομίδι, quomodo Platonico more Philo eum librum vocat quem vulgo Deuteronomium appella- mus. In eo autem libro plurima sunt quæ ad normam fœde- ris, quod per Christum plene revelatum est, populum vo- cant, & rudimenta quædam continent Evangelicæ pietatis. Rursum Augustinus & eum secuti alii putant eam perfe- ctionem istis verbis significari, quam in hac vita nemo ha- buerit aut habere potuerit, quasi præscriberetur non tam qua currendum, quam quo currendum esset. Quæ sententia fuum habere potest usum, ut homines infirmitatis suæ ad- monitos intra humilitatis terminos contineat, & deside- rium in iis excitet vitæ alterius. Sed propriam non esse hanc verborum interpretationem, patet collatis quæ attulimus locis: nam David, Josias atque alii id quod lex ista postulat fecisse memorantur. Nam Deum ἐκζητεῖν & ἀγαπᾷν in He- braismo idem valere manifestum arbitror. Sic & implere post Deum quidam dicuntur, quod Chaldæus paraphrastes exponit, perfecte Dei timorem sequi, ut videre est Num. XIV. 24. XXXII. 12. Deut. I. 36. Præterea vult lex amorem istum præstari pro viribus, μετὰ δύναμιν id est, quantum ho- mo potest. Posse autem hominem quantum potest, nemo sanus negabit. Media igitur & vera sententia hæc est, exigi à Deo, non nequid unquam præter se cogitemus aut ame- mus, quod hujus vitæ status non patitur, sed ut potissimum animi nostri studium Deo impendamus, hoc omni conatu agentes, ut non aliqua sed omnia Dei mandata exsequamur. Nam illud ἐξ ὅλης vel πάσης καρδίας idem est quod alibi di- citur בלבב שלם ἐκ καθαρᾶς καρδίας, ut Paulus vertit 1. Tim. I. 5. id est corde integro atque sincero, sicut & Latinè dicimus, totus in hoc sum. Posse autem homo intelligendus est, non id duntaxat quod potest viribus naturæ peccandi consuetudine prostratis, sed quod potest adjutus divino spi- ritu, quem Deus etiam priscis illis temporibus paucis qui- busdam selectis, non ex communi lege, sed ex peculiari gra- tia dedit, in novo autem fœdere omnibus fœderatis suis, hoc est in filium suum crede. tibus, liberaliter admodum polli- cetur. Πάντα ἰσχύω, inquit Paulus ἐν τῷ ἐνδυναμῦντί με χριςῷ. Quo autem major nunc aut datur aut offertur Spiritus co- pia, eo præceptum quoque istud uberius præstandum est.

Non est supervacua cum Grotio censenda eorum diligentia, qui καρδίαν, ψυχὴν, διάνοιαν hic distin- guant: Etsi enim intensius studium designari cer- tum sit, ac modo terna, modo singula, modo bina ad- hibeantur, non temere tamen omnia illa adhibuit S. S. & quæ alicubi non occurrunt, ex aliis ple- niorem sensum habent: & cor, animam, men- tem, omnesq; adeo vires requiri docent, uti Mar- cus, & Lucas, ἐξ ὅλης τῆς ἰσχύος 58. Quomodo su- pervacuam diligentiam æstimabimus, quæ vocum singularum à S.S. non sine cura adhibitarum, vim & emphasin expendit: & annon omnes facultates hominis, & quicquid in ipso est, postulat Deus, ut totus cum omnibus viribus suis mente, voluntate & appetitu in amorem ejus feratur? Ideo adhibuê- re illam diligentiam non Schoiastici tantum aut re- centiores Theologi; Sed etiam Patres, Origenes, Am- brosius, Nyssenus, Augustinus alii, imo Ebræi quoq;, de quibus vid. B. Gerhard. in Harm. Evang. CLVI. cui placet per vocem καρδίας appetitum ra- tionalem, seu voluntatem intelligere, uti Deut. IV. 29. Jos. XXII. 5. 1.Par. XII. 36. quia cordis est ὁρμὴ & ὄρεξις: per ψυχὴν vitam sensitivam, ac sensus sive ap- petitum sensitivum, cujus est ἐπιθύμησις Gen. XXIII. c. XXXIV. 3. Deut. XII. 20. per διάνοιαν intellectum, τὸ ἡγεμονικὸν, quia explicatur Marc. XII. 33. per σύνεσιν, &c. In eo autem gravius hallucinatur, imo hæresi Papistica & Sociniana accedit Gortius, cum sententiam Augustini, & aliorum veterum, quod ea perfectio istis verbis significetur, quam in hac vita nemo (post lapsum) habuerit, aut habere potuerit, reprobat, & legem tantum amorem istum velle præ- stari pro viribus & quantum potest homo, Pelagia- nis velificaturus statuit: siquidem lex illa longe perfectissimum amorem postulet, omnibus parti- bus, omnibusq; numeris absolutum; qualis à nemi- ne præstitus est, nec præstari potuit. Exempla enim quæ in contrarium adferuntur, Davidis 1. Reg. xiv. 8. & Josiæ 2. Reg. XXIII. 3. non continent illa omnia, quæ lex requirit: de Davide dicitur tantum, quod ἐν πάσῃ τῇ καρδίᾳ ἀυτᾶ ἐπορέυθη ὀπίσω θεᾶ: ambulavit post Deum in omni corde suo: de Josia ad- ditur; καὶ ἐν πάσῃ ψυχῇ: de nemine tertium simul additum ἐν τῇ ὅλῃ τῇ διανοίᾳ ἀυτᾶ, cum illo au- ctoramento ἐξ ὅλης δυνάμεως, vel τῆς ἴσχυος ἀυτᾶ: neque cuiquam tantus Dei amor, sed conatus tan- tum sequendi ea ratione Deum, ex toto nempe- corde, & tota anima, hoc est, sincerum, & ἀνυπόκρι- τον pietatis studium tribuitur. Quod Deus non tan- tum paucis quibusdam selectis, aut ex peculiari so- lum gratia priscis temporibus concessit, ut Grotius prædictos hæreticos sequutus opinatur, sed com- muniter renatis omnibus omni tempore indul- get; qui S. S. gratia Deo ex puro corde serviunt, nam illud ex ὅλης vel πάσης καρδίας idem esse, quod ἐκ καθαρᾶς καρδίας 1. Tim. I. 5. id est corde integro, atque sincero, agnoscit Grotius: qua ratione Deo servire, Deumque amare, omnibus convenit fide- libus, seu Vet. seu Novi Test. tempore vixe- rint, aut vivant.

## 22:39
Vers. 39. Like unto it] Yet so that it yields in prior dignity, whence it is called second in Mark. It is called like, however, because it commands acts that are likewise not only external but also internal, and extends its force as widely as possible: add that it coheres with the former by a necessary connection, as John teaches in 1 Epistle IV. 20, whence what Christ is about to say concerning those two precepts is said by Paul concerning the latter, because of that coherence which I mentioned. For he who loves God obeys the precepts of God, among which is the love of another man: and he who loves another man as he ought, it follows that he loves him for the sake of God, and consequently loves God most of all. Indeed, as the Greek philosophers say, the virtues follow one another. Philo on Abraham: It is of the same nature to be pious and to be a lover of mankind, and to be both in the same person; holiness is considered toward God, but justice toward men. The same author on the Decalogue: It is impossible for the invisible to be worshipped by those who are impious toward those who are visible and near.

Thy neighbor] That is, by the primordial law of nature, to which Christ recalls us, any man whatsoever. Thus also Hierocles, following the precept of the Pythagoreans, advises to maintain friendship toward all men, yet with this tempering: with the distribution according to worth. That the law tends hither may appear even from this, that where it is forbidden to bear false witness against anyone, in the Hebrew it is in thy neighbor, where it is certain that no man is excepted: indeed the Hebrew and Chaldean word which the Chaldean Paraphrast uses, signifies a companion, but in such a way that by that kindly appellation he designates any man whatsoever: just as the Greeks also use the word the neighbor, which the LXX and our writers are accustomed to use, or even the fellow. Wherefore, what is here the neighbor, Paul also called the other, Rom. XIII. 8.

As thyself] As, as also the Hebrew kaph, often compares things: similar, but unequal, as John XVII. 21, Acts III. 22. It is therefore as thyself to love sincerely, in the way we are accustomed to love ourselves. Thus a friend is called another self. See what is above VII, 12. In this sincerity of friendship, however, it is included that we sometimes perform less for them than for ourselves, and sometimes even more. Hence also arises the communion of goods, tempered by the measure of our abundance and the need of others: for all things are common among friends.

Latin:

Vers. 39. ὁμοία ἀυτῇ] Ita tamen ut priori dignitate con- cedat, unde δευτέρα dicitur apud Marcum. Similis autem di- citur, quia actus itidem non externos tantum, sed & inter- nos præcipit, & vim suam quam latissime extendit: adde quod priori necessario nexu cohæret ut docet Johannes 1. E- pist. IV. 20. unde quod dicturus est Christus de duobus illis præceptis, à Paulo dicitur de posteriore, propter illam quam dixi cohærentiam. Nam qui Deum diligit, Dei præ- ceptis obsequitur, inter quæ est dilectio hominis alterius: & qui hominem alterum ita ut oportet diligit, sequitur ut eum propter Deum, ac proinde Deum maxime diligat, Nimirum ut dicunt Græci Philosophi ἀκολουθοῦσιν αἱ ἀρε- ταὶ. Philo de Abrahamo: Τῆς ἀυτῆς φύσεώς ἐστιν ἐυσεβῆ τε εἶναι καὶ φιλάνθρωπον, κἀμπερι τὸν ἀυτὸν ἑκάτερον, ὁσιότης μεν πρὸς Θεὸν, δικαιοσύνη δὲ πρὸς ἀνθρώπους θεωρεῖται. Idem ad Decalogum: ἀμήχανον ἐυσεβεῖσθαι τὸν ἀόρατον ὑπὸ τῶν ἐις τοὺς ἐμφανεῖς καὶ ἐγγὺς ἀσεβούντων.

Τὸν πλησίον σου] Id est, ex primæva naturæ lege, ad quam Christus nos revocat, hominem quemvis. Ita & Hie- rocles ex Pythagoricorū præcepto monet φιλίαν τηρεῖν πρὸς πάντας ἀνθρώπους, cum hoc tamen temperamento μετὰ τῆς πρὸς τὴν ἀξίαν ἀπονεμήσεως. Huc tendere legem vel ex eo appareat, quod ubi vetatur falsum testimonium perhiberi adversus quemquam, in Hebræo est ברעך, ubi certum est neminem hominem excipi: nempe רע Hebræum & Chal- dæum חבר quo Paraphrastes Chaldæus utitur, socium quidem significat, sed ita ut ea comi appellatione hominem quemvis designet: quomodo & Græci usurpant vocem τὸ πλησίον, qua uti solent LXX. & Scriptores nostri, aut etiam τὸ πέλας. Quare quod hic est τὸν πλησίον, Paulus dixit et- iam τὸν ἕτερον Rom. XIII. 8.

ὡς σεαυτὸν] ὡς ut & Hebræum כ sæpe comparat re: similes, sed inæquales, ut Johan XVII. 21. Act III. 22. Est ergo ὡς σεαυτὸν sincere diligere, quomodo nosmetipsos di- ligere solemus. Ita amicus dicitur alter ipse. Vide quæ su- pra VII, 12. In hac autem amicitiæ sinceritate comprehen- sum est, ut modo minus illis quam nobis ipsis, modo plus etiam præstemus. Hinc etiam nascitur bonorum commu- nio ex nostræ copiæ & aliorum inopiæ modo temperata: κοινὰ γὰρ φίλων πάντα.

## 22:40
Vers. 40. The law and the prophets hang] I agree with those who think it is a Latin idiom, such as are quite numerous in these books. For that the word to hang in Isaiah XXII, 23 signifies something similar, is from the continuation of the translation concerning a peg. The sense here is: In these two is situated the law and the admonitions of the Prophets: for it is of these that it is treated here: just as he had said above concerning the precept of loving one's neighbor: this is the law and the prophets: and Paul says that every commandment is summed up, that is, contained, in the same precept, as the Syriac translates. Rightly, for summation is for the writer of the book On the World, and not only for Aristotle, as has been noted heretofore by a most learned man, but also for Plato, to contract into a sum; the Hebrew teachers call this very precept of love the great rule of the law. But from universals flow particulars, in a twofold way, either by inference, in which way all natural and perpetual precepts emanate from those two by necessity of consequence, concerning which emanation Paul treats, or by the constitution of a species, in which way the precepts of rites and judgments, and if there are any others in the law of Moses of positive law, are born from the same two, with the act of the divine will intervening. And by these ways indeed, all other things are contained in these precepts taken generally and commonly, which is the true meaning of this passage. But if you take these precepts more strictly, insofar as they are distinguished from all other precepts, and command peculiar acts, especially internal ones, even so it will be possible to say that other precepts hang from these, and are contained in these, just as means to an end are contained in their end: which Paul explains 1 Tim. I. 5. It is not foreign to this passage that the teachers of the Hebrews report that the precepts of the law, which are six hundred and more, were reduced by holy men into a certain sum, as Psalm XV, Isaiah XXXIII. 15, more briefly by Micah 6. VI, 8, etc.: what has God required of thee, but that thou shouldst exercise justice and love kindness and walk modestly with thy God: and by Isaiah ch. LVI, 1: Observe justice, and exercise righteousness: but most briefly by Habakkuk ch. II. 4: The just shall live by his faith: where, since it is certain that faith working through love is to be understood, is it not said in reality the same thing as here by Christ? as one who requires love that is from faith. Therefore also in Mark this preface is placed before these two precepts: Hear O Israel: The Lord our God is one God.

Grotius's commentary is not bad here: indeed, he explains the matter elegantly. That, however, which is added concerning the stricter acceptance of these precepts concerning the love of God and neighbor does not sufficiently agree. That the sum of all precepts, not certain peculiar precepts, is contained there, is sufficiently clear both from the thing itself and indeed also from the words of Christ. But afterwards he subjoins things which cannot be proven, namely that in Habakkuk II. 4, by those words the just shall live by his faith, the same thing is said as here by Christ. For although Christ requires love that is from faith, yet in Habakkuk it is not a question of love from faith, but of faith, nor does the just man live by love that is from faith, but solely by faith, and through faith, as the Apostle demonstrates from Habakkuk in Rom. I, Gal. II, and Heb. X.

PART V. Counter-question concerning the Messiah, the son and Lord of David.

Latin:

Vers. 40. ὁ νόμος καὶ οἱ προφῆται κρέμανται] Assentio existimantibus Latinam esse locutionem, quales in his libris satis multæ sunt. Nam quod Esaiæ XXII, 23. vox pendere aliquid simile significat, est ex continuatione translationis de paxillo. Sensus hic est: In his duobus sita est lex & Pro- phetarum monita: de his enim hic agitur: quomodo & su- pra de præcepto diligendi proximi dixerat: ὗτός ἐστιν ὁ νόμος καὶ οἱ προφῆται: & Paulus in eodem præcepto omnem ἐντο- λὴν ἀνακεφαλαιοῦσθαι, id est, contineri, ut vertit Syrus Recte, nam ἀνακεφαλαίωσις scriptori libri de mundo, κεφαλαυὴ non Aristoteli tantum, ut antehac à viro doctissimo est annota- tum, sed & Platoni est in summū contrahere, Hebræi magi- stri istud ipsum dilectionis præceptum vocant כלל גדול le- gis. Ex universalibus autein fluunt particularia, duplici mo- do, aut per illationem, quomodo omnia præcepta naturalia atque perpetua ex illis duobus necessitate consequentiæ e- manant, de qua emanatione agit Paulus, aut per constitu- tionem speciei, quomodo præcepta rituum & judiciorum, & si qua sunt alia in lege Mosis juris θετικοῦ ex iisdem duo- bus nascuntur, intercedente actu divinæ voluntatis. Et his quidem modis præceptis istis generaliter atq; communiter sumtis alia omnia continentur, quæ vera est hujus loci sen- tentia. Quod si præcepta ista sumas strictius quatenus ab omnibus aliis præceptis distinguuntur, & peculiares actus, internos præcipue imperant, etiam sic dici poterunt præce- pta alia ab istis pendere, & in istis contineri, sicut media ad finem continentur in suo fine: quod explicat Paulus 1, Tim. I. 5. Non alienum est ab hoc loco quod tradunt Hebræo- rum doctores præcepta legis, quæ fexcenta sunt & ultra, à viris sanctis in summam quandam redacta, ut Psal. XV. Esaiæ XXXIII. 15. brevius à Micha 6. VI, 8. &c quid Deus requisivit abs te, nisi ut exerceas jus & ames benignitatem & modeste ambules cum Deo tuo: & ab Esaia c. LVI, 1. Obser- vate jus, & exercete justitiam: brevissime vero ab Abacu- co c. II. 4. Justus ex fide sua vivet: ubi cum intelligi certum sit fidem δι' ἀγάπης ἐνεργουμένην, reipsa idem dicitur quod hic à Christo? ut qui ἀγάπην requirat τὴν ἐκ πίστεως. Ideo & apud Marcum præmittitur duobus istis præceptis hoc an- teloquium: Audi Israel: Deus noster Deus unus est.

Non male hic habet Grotii commentarius: quin eleganter rem explicat. Id tamen quod de strictiori acceptione borum præceptorum de dilectio- ne Dei & proximi, additur, non satis convenit. Summam præceptorum omnium, non peculiaria quædam præcepta illic contineri tum è reipsa, tum vero etiam è verbis Christi satis liquet. Sed postea subjungit, quæ probari nequeunt, nempe quod Habacut II. 4. verbis illis justus ex fide sua vivet, idem dicatur quod hic à Christo. Etsi enim Christus ἀγάπην requirat τὴν ἐκ πίστεως, non tamen apud Habacucum de ἀγάπῃ ἐκ πίστεως agitur, sed de τῇ πίστει, nec per τὴν ἀγάπην τὴν ἐκ πίστεως, sed unice ἐκ πίστεως ex fide, & per fidem justus vivet, ut ex Habacuco demonstrat Apostolus Rom. I. Gal. II. & Ebr. X.

PARS V. Ἀντερώτησις de Messia filio & Domino Davidis.

## 22:42
Vers. 42.

[Concerning Christ] Christ did not wish to indicate openly those things which were to be revealed to all only after the resurrection. But in the meantime, he wished to instill this into the minds of men as a supreme oracle, that the kingdom of the Messiah would be of a more excellent kind than the Davidic, and therefore divine.

[To David] And by the prophecy of Isaiah 9:7, which Gabriel uses as most clear to Mary. And the matter is even now acknowledged among the Jews.

Latin:

Vers. 42.

Περὶ τοῦ χριστοῦ] Noluit Christus aperte indicare ea quæ post resurrectionem demum erant omnibus revelanda. Verum interim hoc velut supremo oraculo inferere homi- num mentibus voluit, Messiæ regnum generis excellen- tioris fore quam Davidicum, ac proinde divinum.

Τῷ Δαβίδ] Et vaticinio Es. IX. 7. quo tanquam apertif- simo utitur Gabriel ad Mariam. Et res est nunc quoque inter Judæos confessa.

## 22:43
[Verse 43. David] He names David as the writer of Psalm 110, which he would never have taken upon himself unless it had been beyond controversy at that time. And indeed the inscription in the Hebrew codices themselves is מזמור לדוד, which alone ought to suffice, lest Eliezer or someone from the times of Hezekiah be believed to be the writer of that hymn. For even if we grant that the titles were not added by the writers themselves, it is nevertheless certain that they are most ancient, the authority of which it is the mark of men insane with a desire for contention to tear down now, not by any arguments, but by the whim of their own minds. The Septuagint are accustomed to interpret that לדוד as τῷ Δαβίδ: but the other paraphrasts and the Hebrews themselves interpret it otherwise, who in the inscriptions of the Psalms, as well as in many other places, accept it in the meaning which we express by the genitive case. And indeed if we interpret it otherwise, there will be no Psalm that is David's, or at least that is known to be David's, even though they themselves also acknowledge that very many Psalms, and indeed those having the same inscription, were written by David.

Why then did Grotius show himself worse than the Jews in the explanation of that prophecy in his annotations on the cited passage of Isaiah, snatching it away to Hezekiah, if the prophecy concerning Christ is MOST CLEAR, and the matter is EVEN NOW acknowledged among the Jews?

[In the Spirit] For David was a prophet (Acts 2:30), and the Holy Spirit spoke through him (2 Samuel 23:2; Acts 1:16). Nor does it stand in the way that the Jews distinguish between prophecy and the Holy Spirit, so that the former is with a more vehement and expressive motion, while the latter moves more gently and leaves the man to himself. For it is not new for general terms to be restricted so that species may be distinguished. Otherwise, the Holy Spirit is attributed to the prophets everywhere, and those who were warned divinely even in a dream were called 'coarser' prophets, as can be seen in Maimonides' Guide for the Perplexed, book 2, chapter 45.

The distinction of the Jews deserves no approval. For Scripture frequently teaches that the prophets were agitated by the Holy Spirit, and it recognizes no such difference anywhere: for where is any trace of it in the Holy Scriptures? Therefore, it is deservedly rejected and disapproved of by Christian Rabbis. But concerning the passage of Psalm 110, let those things be seen which have been said at length in the Anti-Grotian annotations on the Psalms.

[He calls him Lord] The Hebrews are mistaken who think that this is read by us otherwise than they themselves read it, Adoni. Nor is an argument for the divinity of Christ sought directly from this: but it is proved by this that the Messiah is regarded and worshipped by David, so great a king, not only as greater than himself, but also as his own Lord. But how is the Messiah born of David the Lord of David, unless the Messiah himself was to have right and authority over David himself, and the benefits of the Messiah were to reach David? The ancient Hebrews acknowledged that this Psalm pertains to the Messiah: whom Isaac Benarama follows on Gen. XLVII. Those who were after the rise of Christianity began to deny that very thing out of mere hatred of Christianity: although David Kimchi himself and others with him, as also Trypho in Justin, interpret Psalm II concerning the Messiah, where the same thing is said about the Sceptre that is to go forth from Zion as in this Psalm. Nor indeed can what is said here about the Priesthood be fitted to any of the Hebrew kings. For while the law of Moses remained, the priesthood could not be transferred from the family of Aaron: whence it was proclaimed to King Uzziah, who is also called Azariah, it is not for you to offer incense but for the sons of Aaron, and a punishment was divinely inflicted upon him for not obeying. But the one objection that Kimchi raises, that no battles were fought by Jesus, is easily solved, since they themselves cannot deny that many things are said figuratively, especially in the Prophets. For, to say nothing of the members of God, those among them who are a little more discerning understand that the mountain of the Lord will be raised above other mountains, and that wild beasts will stable with cattle, otherwise than the words sound: just as Albo also interprets the feasts in the heavenly kingdom.

Latin:

Vers. 43. Δαβὶδ] Scriptorem Psalmi CX. Davidem no- minat, nunquam id sibi sumturus, nisi id tum fuisset extra controversiam. Et sane ἐπιγραφὴ ipsis Hebræorum codici- bus est מזמור לדוד, quod vel solum sufficere debeat, ne Eliezer aut aliquis Ezechiæ temporum, scriptor ejus hymni crederetur. Ut enim demus titulos ab ipsis Scripto- ribus non additos, tamen antiquissimos esse constat, quò- rum nunc fidem convellere non argumentis ullis, sed ani- mi lubidine, hominum est contentionis studio insanien- tium.
