Illud לדוד Septuaginta interpretari solent τῷ Δα- βίδ: sed aliter cæteri Paraphrastæ Hebræique ipsi qui tum in Psalmorum inscriptionibus, tum aliis multis in locis ea significatione accipiunt quam nos casu secun- po exprimimus. Et sane si aliter interpretemur, nullus erit Psalmus qui sit Davidis, aut certe quem Davidis esse constet, cum tamen Psalmos plurimos & quidem eandem habentes ἐπιγραφὴν à Davide scriptos ipsi quoque fateantur.

Quid ergo Judæis deteriorem se exhibuit Gro- tius in explicatione illius vaticinii in annot. ad lo- cum Esaiæ citatum, ad Ezechiam id abripiens, si vaticinium de Christo est APERTISSIMUM, & res inter Judæos NUNC quoque confessa est?

Ἐν πνεύματι] Erat enim David προφήτης Act. II. 30. & per ipsum loquebatur Spiritus S. 2. Sam. XXIII. 2. Act. I. 16. Nec obstat quod Judæi distinguunt inter προφητείαν ỳ ἅγιον πνεῦμα, ut illa sit cum motu vehementiore & expres- sius, hoc vero lenius movens & hominem sibi relinquens. Neque enim novum est vocabula generalia restringi ut spe- cies discernantur. Alioqui Prophetis passim tribuitur Spi- ritus S. & qui vel in somnio divinitus monebantur, pro- phetæ παχύτεροι vocabantur, ut videre est Maimonidæ Du- cis dubitantium lib. II. c. 45.

Distinctio Judæorum nullum meretur calcu- lum. Nam Scriptura Prophetas agitatos fuisse à Spiritu S. frequenter docet, nec discrimen illud uspiam agnoscit: ubi enim ullum ejus in S. literis vestigium: Ideo merito à Christianis Rabbinis id rejicitur, & improbatur. De loco autem Ps. CX. videantur, quæ in annotatis Anti-Grotianis ad Psalmos fuse dicta sunt.

Κύριον ἀυτὸν καλεῖ] Falluntur Hebræi qui aliter à no- bis hoc legi putant quam ipsi legunt Adoni. Neque hinc ἀμέσως argumentum petitur θεότητος Christi: sed hoc pro- batur, Messiam à Davide rege tanto, non modo tanquam majorem ipso, sed & ut ipsius Dominum suspici ac coli. At quomodo Messias e Davide natus Dominus Davidis, nisi ipse Messias jus atque imperium erat habiturus in ipsum Da- videm, & Messiae beneficia ad Davidem erant perventura? Ad Messiam pertinere hunc Psalmum agnoverunt Hebraei veteres: quos sequitur Isaac Benarama ad Gen. XLVII. Qui post ortum Christianismum fuerunt negare idipsum coepe- runt solo odio Christianismi: cum tamen ipse David Kim- chi & cum eo alii, ut & apud Justinum Tryphon Psalmum II. de Messia interpretentur, ubi de Sceptro ex Sione exituro idem dicitur quod hoc Psalmo. Neque vero potest ulli re- gum Hebraeorum aptari quod hic dicitur de Sacerdotio. Nam manente Mosis lege sacerdotium ab Aaronis familia transferri non poterat: unde regi Oziae, qui & Azarias no- minatur, edictum est, non tuum est adolere sed Aaronidarum, & poena divinitus inflicta est nec obedienti. Quod autem unum objicit Kimchi, nulla praelia ab Jesu pugnata, facile solvitur, cum ipsi negare non possint multa esse, in Prophe- tis praesertim, dicta figurate. Nam ut de membris Dei nihil dicam, montem Domini elevatum iri supra montes alios, & feras cum pecudibus stabulaturas aliter quam verba sonant intelligunt qui inter ipsos naris sunt paulo emunctioris: quomodo & convivia in regno coelesti interpretatur Albo.

## 22:44
Vers. 44. The Lord] Thus are not only the LXX but also other Hellenists, and among them our own writers, accustomed to speak where in the Hebrew there is the tetragrammaton. Nor does the Chaldean paraphrast speak otherwise. Other Greek interpreters used to place the Hebrew letters themselves יהוה, whence it was made by unskilled scribes into ΠΙΠΙ in Greek letters. Moreover, by this irrefutable argument it appears that that Hebrew name was accustomed to be read in Ptolemaic times as it is now read, Adonai. The opinion of a very learned man, that it is called unutterable because the Greek language would not tolerate the concurrence of so many vowels, does not please me. For the same thing happens in many other names, which nevertheless the LXX often express as they can, even with some letters omitted. Furthermore, what does that reasoning touch the Jews who use the Hebrew language? Wherefore there must have been another reason why the Jews ceased to pronounce that name. For formerly not only they themselves but also foreigners used to pronounce it, as often as they spoke of the God of the Hebrews, as King Hiram in 1 Kings V. 7. The most probable cause is that other names declared a certain general notion of God, or of a thing that was held for God: but that name was distinctive, by which the God of the Hebrews was distinguished from other gods: a name in which there is no participation between the creator and anything else, as Maimonides speaks. And so, first out of reverence for God, it began to be used rarely, and thus less and less, so that at length it ceased to be used except in the public blessing of the Priests, and in the sacred expiatory rite: which Philo teaches us, besides the Talmudists, when he says that it was lawful only to say and hear this name in holy places. Nor for any other reason does Josephus call this name the holy letters, these, he says, are the four vowels, where he treats of the Pontiff's crown. And elsewhere he says, an appellation, about which it is not lawful for me to speak. Eusebius calls this name unutterable to the many. Nevertheless, even in those times there were those who, out of impatience or insult, would pronounce that name. Josephus provides an example of the former in the fifth book of the Jewish War: The terrible, he says, name of God which is covered. Philo provides an example of the latter, narrating what had been said to him and the other legates by Gaius Caligula: You, he said, are the God-haters, who do not believe that I am God, who is already acknowledged by all others, but rather the one unnameable to you. And lifting his hands to heaven, he uttered an appellation which it is not lawful even to hear, let alone to interpret word for word. And in that sense Josephus not improbably interprets that which is in the history about the giant Goliath, 1 Sam. XVII. 43, and the Philistine cursed David by his gods, although it is commonly understood as in his gods. The words of Josephus are: he lays curses upon him from the appellation of God. For Josephus calls that name an appellation, as we have seen elsewhere. It is clearly the same thing that Josephus narrates about Goliath and Philo about Caligula. Therefore, it was not the difficulty of pronunciation, as some like to think, but religion that stood in the way of the pronunciation. With a similar religion, the Jews in the time of Josephus abstained from reciting the words of the decalogue. For thus he says: the words which Moses left behind written on the two tablets, which it is not lawful for us to speak openly word for word, we shall declare their powers. The Samaritans, however, wrote יחוח, which in Greek is Iabe, as Theodoret writes, and Epiphanius: nor is there a just cause for changing the reading. For that in proper names the vowels were not read in one way, but changed according to the variety of dialects, the Greek Codex alone and the New Testament compared with the Masoretic edition abundantly prove: to say nothing now of Darius, Cyrus, Nebuchadnezzar, which in Greek are Nabuchodonosor, Cyrus, Dareios. Wherefore it is indeed to be wondered at that the Tyrians read that name otherwise, namely יהוה, which Philo of Byblos wrote Ieuo: but others יהוה, as Orpheus, through whom that name flowed into Greece, and whose writing Diodorus Siculus follows, and the oracle of Apollo Clarius, and afterwards the Gnostics. Nor do I doubt that what is in Origen, Iao, named among the Hebrews, should be read as Iao or Ia, so that there are two names, יהוה and יה. Nor does Jerome think that this name should be read otherwise than IAO. Clement of Alexandria says Iaoou, unless there is a mistake in the Scripture. But the Tyrrhenians, who brought this name from Tyre into Italy along with other sacred rites, seem to have read it as it is now written when it has the points of Adonai, namely יְהוָה, or as it is when it has the points of Elohim יֱהֹוִה. For I do not doubt that the Latin Jovis is derived from there: but also the Africans, if I am not mistaken, received the same name with the same sound from the same Tyrians, the founders of Carthage. For among them too God was called I'óbas, which is written corruptly by the Latins as Juba, from which name the kings of the Africans were also called. But what is read in the Greek poem about the name of the seven vowels, I think is drawn to this name without cause. For the Greeks, following the example of the Egyptians as it seems, had inscribed individual sounds to the spheres of the seven stars: by the harmony of which they said God was celebrated. Just as this institution is, like many other things of the Gnostics, about which Irenaeus says: The first heaven utters the A, the one after it the E, the third the H, the fourth and middle of the seven utters the power of the I, the fifth the O, the sixth the U, and the seventh and fourth from the middle cries out the element Omega.

What is to be thought of this, whether the tetragrammaton name is read as Adonai, we have said at length in Natural and Revealed Theology. That argument from the LXX version is hardly a Topic, let alone irrefutable. For it could have happened for other reasons that the name יְהוָה was rendered by the word κυρίος: namely because they had no other name by which they could conveniently express it: and truly in all languages the tetragrammaton name is ἀνέκφραστον κὴ ἀνεκφώνητον, not because of the concurrence of vowels, but because of the dignity of its signification, which can be expressed in no language. But if it is asked whether the Jews pronounced that name or not? Grotius rightly acknowledges that not only they, but even foreigners once pronounced it, as often as they spoke of the God of the Hebrews, which he proves by the example of King Hiram. 1 Kings 5:7, provided it was a distinguishing name, by which the God of the Hebrews was distinguished from other gods. But that they subsequently abstained from this name for the sake of religion can be conceded for later times, but not for the times of the Prophets. Nor was this religion, but superstition contrary to the word of God: because God revealed himself by this name for the reason that he might be distinguished and worshipped by it. And the things which Grotius brings forward about the varied reading and writing of this name sufficiently testify that it was pronounced, and not read through Adonai, but according to its own proper letters. Those things contribute somewhat to illustrating what we said in the cited passage. But the things which Grotius has injected about the points and the name Adonai placed under the name יְהוָה, we have refuted in the Critico Sacro, where we sufficiently showed that the divine name has its own proper vowels, not foreign or vicarious ones.

Sit at my right hand] That is, be second to me, as we have explained elsewhere. They err who heap many things here to prove that the right side is less honored. For as we have said, the translation is taken from kings, to whom the nearest heir, or a prince associated with the king, sat on the right; he who followed next sat on the left. Thus also the name of heir is attributed to Christ: and Paul, for that which is to sit at the right hand, said to reign, 1 Cor. 15:25.

Elsewhere, in the annotations, namely to Ps. 110, he explained it thus: sit at my right hand, that is, be secure in the confidence of my help: which gloss, colder than ice, we refuted there in the Anti-Grotian Annotations. Nor is he constituted second to God by this phrase, but he is raised to the truly supreme dominion of God and over all things in heaven and on earth, because by the admission of Grotius this is explained by reigning, 1 Cor. 15:25. But there is no dominion over all things other than the divine, infinite, and supreme: (not two different subordinate empires, or two different Lords over all,) to the full communion of which Christ according to his human nature has been exalted by the session at the right hand of God.

ἕως ἂν θῶ] ἕως can also be taken in a general sense, if we understand sitting at the right hand as exercising that power which the Father gave to Him over the heavenly and earthly goods of the Church: the administration of which goodness is to cease after the resurrection, while the glory of the kingdom remains forever, as can be seen in Paul at the cited place.

Nimirum 1. Cor. XV. 25. But there, that mode of government is indeed said to be about to cease, and the economy of the administration, which serves the gathering of the Church in these lands, is to end, but not that the dominion of Christ will cease entirely. And if the word ἕως is taken in a general sense, will Christ not cease to sit at the right hand of God at the consummation of the age? But that is absurd. Therefore, the particle ἕως is explained by the interpreters in a sense not exclusive, but inclusive, not to bring about an end, but to designate the cause why He sits at the right hand of God, namely, that He may make His enemies and ours the footstool of His feet: or as some say, it is taken indeterminately, so that it is indicated that even at that time, when enemies rage the most, Christ will reign, and in such a way that He subjects His enemies to Himself: but it is not denied that He will rule when the enemies are subjected, because of His dominion and kingdom there will be no end, Luke I. 33.

Τοὺς ἐχθρούς σου] Every force opposed to the Church, and finally death itself.

ὑποπόδιον τῶν ποδῶν σου] Of servitude, and indeed of abject subjection, as we have said elsewhere.

Latin:

Vers. 44. Ὁ κύριος] Ita solent non LXX. tantum sed & Hellenistae caeteri, atque inter eos nostri Scriptores loqui ubi in Hebraeo est τὸ τετραγράμματον. Nec aliter Chaldaeus paraphrastes. Alii interpretes Graeci ipsas ponebant literas Hebraeas יהוה unde ab imperitis librariis factum est ΠΙΠΙ Graecis literis. Caeterum hoc argumento irrefragabili appa- ret id nomen Hebraeum temporibus Ptolemaicis lectitari solitum, ut nunc legitur Adonai. Quod viro pererudito pla- cet ideo dici ἀνεκφώνητον quod tot vocalium concursum ser- mo Graecus non pateretur, mihi non probatur. Idem enim usu venit in multis nominibus aliis, quae tamen, ut possunt, saepe etiam literis aliquot omissis exprimunt LXX. Deinde quid ea ratio tangit Judaeos Hebraeo utentes sermone? Qua- re aliam causam fuisse oportet cur Judaei nomen illud pro- nuntiare desierint. Nam olim pronuntiarunt non ipsi tan- tum sed & alienigenae, quoties de Hebraeorum Deo loque- bantur, ut Rex Hiromus I. Reg. V. 7. Causa maxime proba- bilis est, quod alia nomina generalem quandam Dei, aut rei quae pro Deo haberetur, notionem declararent: illud autem nomen esset διακριτικὸν quo Deus Hebraeorum a Diis caete- ris discernebatur: nomen in quo non est participatio inter creatorem & aliquid aliud, ut Maimonides loquitur. Itaque primum Dei reverentia coeptum est raro usurpari, atque ita minus minusque, ut tandem usurpari desierit nisi in publica Sacerdotum benedictione, & in sacro piaculari: quod praeter Thalmudistas Philo nos docet, cum hoc nomen tantum fas ait fuisse λέγειν κ' ἀκούειν ἐν ἁγίοις. Neque alia de causa Josepho hoc nomen vocat Τὰ ἱερὰ γράμματα, ταῦτα δὲ ἐστι, inquit, τὰ φωνήεντα τέσσαρα, ubi de Pontificis agit corona. Et alibi προσ- γορίαν, inquit, περὶ ἧς ὦ μοι θέμις εἰπεῖν. Eusebius hoc nomen vocat ἄλεκτον τοῖς πολλοῖς. Attamen illis quoque temporibus erant qui per impatientiam aut contumeliam id nomen pro- nuntiarent. Prioris exemplum exhibet libro Belli Judaici quinto Josephus: Τὸ φρικτὸν, inquit, ἐπικαλυμένον ὄνομα τῦ Θεῦ. Posterioris Philo, narrans quid sibi aliisque legatis di- ctum esset a Cajo Caligula: ὑμεῖς, εἶπεν, ἐστε οἱ θεομυσεῖς, οἱ θε- ὸν μὴ νομίζοντες εἶναί με τὸν ἤδη παρὰ πᾶσι τοῖς ἄλλοις ἀνωμολο- γημένον, ἀλλὰ τὸν ἀκατονόμαστον ὑμῖν. κᾀ ἀνατείνας τὰς χεῖρας εἰς τὸν ὐρανὸν ἐπεφήμισε πρόσρησιν ἣν ὐδὲ ἀκούειν θεμιτὸν, ὐχ ὅτι δι- ερμηνεύειν αὐτολεξει. Atque in eum sensum Josephus non im- probabiliter interpretatur id quod est in historia de gigante Goliatho ויקלל הפלשתי את דוד באלהיו I. Sam. XVII. 43. & maledixit Philistaeus Davidi in Deo ejus, cum vulgo intelligi soleat in Diis suis. Verba Josephi sunt: ἀρὰς αὐτῷ τίθεται ἐκ τῆς προσηγορίας τῦ Θεῦ. Nam nomen illud προσηγορίαν Jose- phus, ut vidimus etiam alibi, vocat. Plane idem est quod de Goliatho narrat Josephus & de Caligula Philo. Non ergo pronuntiandi difficultas, ut quibusdam placet, sed religio pronuntiationi obstitit. Simili religione Judaei Josephitem- pore a recitandis decalogi verbis abstinebant. Ita enim ille ait λόγων ὓς Μωυσῆς ἐν ταῖς δυσὶ πλάξιν γεγραμμένυς κατέλιπεν, ὓς ὐ θεμιτόν ἐστιν ἡμῖν λέγειν φανερῶς πρὸς λέξιν, τὰς δυνάμεις αὐτῶν δηλώσομεν. Scripserunt autem Samaritae יחוח quod Graece est Iαβὲ, quomodo Theodoretius scribit, & Epipha- nius: neque mutandae lectionis justa causa est. Nam in no- minibus propriis vocales non uno modo lectitatas, sed pro dialectorum varietate mutatas vel solus Codex Graecus & Novi Testamenti cum Masoritica editione collatus abun- de evincat: ut jam omittam דריוש כורש נבוכרנצר quae Graecis sunt. Ναβυχοδονόσορ, Κῦρος, Δάρεως. Quare re illud quidem mirandum Tyrios aliter legisse id nomen, nempe יהוה quod Philo Biblius scribebat ἰευώ: alios autem יהוה ut Orphea, per quem in Graeciam id nomen manavit, cujusque scripturam sequitur Diodorus Siculus, & oracu- lum Apollinis Clarii, ac postea Gnostici. Neq; dubito quin quod apudOrigenem est ἰὼ ἰαωὶα παρ' ἑβραίοις ὀνομαζόμενον, legendum sit ἰὰω ἢ ἰὰ ut duo sint nomina יהוה & יהּ. Neq; aliter quam IAO nomen hoc legendum Hieronymus arbi- tratur. Clemens Alexandrinus ἰαοὺ, nisi in Scriptura men- dum est. At Tyrrheni,qui e Tyro in Italiam cum cæteris sa- cris nomen hoc attulerunt ita legisse videntur ut nunc scri- bitur cum puncta habet Adonai nimirum יְהוָה, aut ut cũ puncta habet Elohim יֱהֹוִה. Nam inde Latinum Jovis esse non dubito:sed & Afri,ni fallor, ab iisdem Tyriis Cartha- ginis conditoribus nomẽ idem eodem sono accepere. Nam apud illos quoque Deus vocabatur I'óbas, quod Latinis cor- rupte Juba scribitur, à quo nomine & reges Afrorum sunt appellati. Quod autẽ in carmine Græco legitur de nomine septem vocalium, sine causa ad hoc nomen trahi existimo. Nam Græci, Ægyptiorum ut videtur exemplo, septem si- derum orbibus singulas voces inscripserant: quarum con- centu ajebant Deum celebrari. Sicuti sunt hoc institutũ,ut multa alia Gnostici,de quibus Irenæus:ὁ μὲν πρῶτος ὀυρανὸς φθέγγεται τὸ Α,ὁ δὲ μετ'αὐτὸν τὸ Ε, ὁ δὲ τρίτος τὸ Η, τέταρτος δὲ καὶ μέσος τῶν ἑπτὰ τὴν τοῦ Ι δύναμιν ἐκφωνεῖ, ὁ δὲ πέμπτος τὸ Ο, ἕκτος δὲ τὸ Υ, ἑβδομος δὲ καὶ τέταρτος ἀπὸ μέσου τὸ Ω στοιχεῖον ἐκβοᾷ.

Quid de hoc habendum, anne nomen tetra- grammaton Adonai lectum.sit, diximus prolixe in Theologia naturali & revelata. Argumentum illud à versione LXX. vix Topicum est, nedum irrefra- gabile. Nam ex aliis causis fieri potuit quod reddi- tum sit nomen יְהוָה per vocem κυρίος: quia scili- cet nomen aliud non habebant, quo idcommode exprimerent : & vere in omnibus linguis nomen tetragrammaton est ἀνέκφραστον κὴ ἀνεκφώνητον non ob vocaliũ concursum,sed ob significationis des- νότητα, quæ nulla lingua exprimi potest. Utrum autem Judæi pronunciarint nomen illud, nec ne ? si quæratur, recte agnoscit Grotius,non ipsos tantum, sed etiam alienigenas olim id pronunciasse, quoties de Deo Hebræorum loquuti sint, quod Regis Hirami exemplo probat. 1. Reg. V. 7. siquidem in nomen διακριτικὸν fuerit,quoDeus Ebræorum à Diis cæ- teris discernebatur. Quod vero religionis causa deinceps abstinuerint ab hoc nomine, de sequioribus temporibus concedi potest, non vero de tempori- bus Prophetarum. Neque religio hæc fuit,sed su- perstitio verbo Dei contraria: quia ideo revelavit Deus se hoc nomine, ut eodem insigniretur & co- leretur. Et quæ adducit Grotius de varia lectione, ac scriptione hujus nominis, satis testantur id pro- nunciatum fuisse, nec per Adonai lectitatum, sed juxta literas suas proprias. Faciunt illa nonnihil ad ea illustranda, quæ loco citato diximus. Quæ vero de punctis & Adonai nomini יְהוָה substratis ingessit Grotius, profligavimus in Critico sacro, ubi vocales proprias nomen divinum habere, non alienas,aut vicarias satis ostendimus.

κάθου ἐκ δεξιῶν μου] Id est, à me secundus esto, ut alibi ex- plicavimus. Errant qui multa huc congerunt, ut probent dextrum latus minus esse honoratum. Nam ut diximus, à regibus sumta est tralatio,quibus hæres proximus, aut asso- qui à rege princeps,dexter assidebat;is qui deinde sequeba- tur sinister. Sic & hæredis nomen Christo tribuitur:Et Pau- lus pro eo quod est sedere ad dextram dixit βασιλεύειν, 1. Cor. XV. 25.

Alibi, in annotatis sc. ad Ps. CX. ita exposuit: sede à Dextris meis, id est, securus esto fiducia auxilii mei:quam glossam glacie frigidiorem in Annota- tis Anti-Grotianis ibi confutavimus.Neque hic se- cundus à Deo constituitur ista phrasi, sed ad domi- nium Dei vere summum & super omnia in cælo & in terra evehitur, quia per βασιλεύειν fatente Gro- tio hoc explicatur 1.Cor.XV.25.Non est autem do- minium super omnia aliud,nisi divinum, infini- tum, & summum: (non duo diversa imperia sub- ordinata, aut duo diversi Domini super omnia,) ad cujus plenam communionem Christus secun- dum humanam naturam exaltatus est per sessio- nem ad dextram Dei.

ἕως ἂν θῶ] Potest ἕως etiam communiter accipi, si se- dere ad dexteram accipiamus pro eo quod exercere potesta- tem illam quam Pater ipsi super cœlestia ac terrestria bona Ecclesiæ dedit: cujus bonitatis administratio cessatura est post resurrectionem, gloria regni in æternum manente, ut apud Paulum videre est dicto loco.

Nimirum 1. Cor. XV. 25. At illic cessaturus qui- dem dicitur modus ille regiminis, & œconomia desi- tura administrationis, quæ inservit colligendæ in his terris Ecclesiæ, non autem plane cessaturum Christi dominium. Et si vocabulum ἕως communi- ter accipiatur, annon desinet Christus in consum- matione seculi sedere ad dextram Dei? Quod vero absurdum est. Ideo particula ἕως explicatur ab In- terpp. sensu non exclusivo, sed inclusivo, non ut fi- nem inferat, sed ut causam designet, cur sedeat ad dextram Dei, ut nempe ponat hostes suos & nostros scabellum pedum suorum: vel ut aliqui loquuntur, indeterminate accipitur, ut ita indicetur, etiam illo tempore, quo hostes maxime furiunt, regnaturum Christum, idq; ita ut hostes sibi subjiciat: non vero negetur subjectis hostibus ipsum dominaturum, quia dominii & regni ejus non erit finis, Luc. I 33.

Τοὺς ἐχθρούς σου] Omnem vim Ecclesiæ adversam, ac po- stremo mortem ipsam.

ὑποπόδιον τῶν ποδῶν σου] Servitutis & quidem abjectæ cir- cumscripto, ut alibi diximus.

For the direct expression would have been: εἰ ὑιὸς ἀυτῦ ἐςι, πῶς ἀυτὸν κύριον καλεῖ? But in whichever way you pronounce it, the force of the argument comes to the same thing. Thus also Mark said in chapter II. 23. ἤρξαντο ὁδὸν ποιεῖν τίλλοντες τὲς ςάχυας instead of ἤρξαντο ὁδὸν ποιοῦντες τὲς ςάχυας τίλλειν. ## 23:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXIII.

ARGUMENT AND DIVISION.

Concerning the hearing of the lawyers and Pharisees sitting in the seat of Moses, but not imitating their works: who, because of hypocrisy in widening their phylacteries, the pride from which they love the first places at table and to be called Rabbi, are rebuked, and are taught that there is one Father and one Master: woe is said to them, because they shut heaven to others, devour widows' houses under the pretext of long prayers, make proselytes for hell, teach vain things about swearing, leave behind those things which are greatest in the law, adorn themselves only outwardly with probity, are sons of the murderers of the prophets, fill up the measure of their fathers, by killing and persecuting those who are sent to them, and deriving upon themselves all the guilt of just blood. Jesus complains about Jerusalem, which kills the prophets and is unwilling to be gathered, and therefore is to be devastated.

There are two parts: I. The manifold hypocrisy of the Pharisees and lawyers, to v. 28. II. The slaughter of the prophets and other messengers of God, with the denunciation of the final total destruction, to v. 39.

PART I.

The manifold hypocrisy of the Pharisees and the experts in the law.

Latin:

CAPUT XXIII.

ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

De audiendis Legisperitis & Pharisæis in Ca- thedra Mosis sedentibus, non autem imitan- dis operibus eorum: qui ob hypocrisin in Phy- lacteriis dilatandis fastu ex quo primos ac- cubitus & Rabbi dici amant, reprehendun- tur, unumq́; esse Patrem & unũ Magistrum docentur: væ istis dicitur, quod alius cœlum claudant, viduarum domos prætextu longa- rum precum devorent, proselytos ad gehen- nam faciant, vana de jurandis tradant, ea quæ maxima in lege sunt relinquant, ex- trinsecus tantum se probitate ornent, Pro- pheticidarum filii, mensuram Patrum im- pleant, eos qui ad ipsos missi sunt, occidendo & persequendo, omnemq́; sanguinis justi re- atum in se derivando. Queritur Iesus de Hierosolyma Prophetas occidente, & con- gregari nolente, ideoq; devastanda.

Partes sunt duæ: I. Hypocrisis multivaria Pha- risæorum & legisperitorum, ad v. 28. II. Cædes Pro- phetarum, & aliorum legatorum Dei, cum denun- ciatione πανολεθρίας novissimæ, ad v. 39.

PARS I.

Hypocrisis Pharisæorũ & legisperitorum multivaria.

## 23:2
V. 2. 'The scribes and the Pharisees sit on Moses' seat'] It is manifest that this does not concern the High Priests and Priests. For these would be named first. But neither can it be understood of the whole Sanhedrin: for the Sadducees were in it no less than the Pharisees. It concerns, therefore, as appears from verse 8, those who were called Masters or teachers; who were almost all of the Pharisaic institution, and many also fulfilling the office of assessors: because it is their duty, as we have said above, to respond concerning the law and to be of counsel to the magistrates מושב פשו

The 'seat of Moses' is the chair in which the masters, sitting, interpreted the law either to the people publicly or to the disciples privately: in which way the word 'chair' is used by the Greeks and Latins also, whence Seneca spoke of 'chair-philosophers.' For they err, in my judgment, who assert for certain that the Jews interpreted the law standing. Certainly, if any power of speaking was given to one from the common people, these were accustomed to speak standing, so that they might be heard more correctly by the whole assembly: to which refers that which we have in Acts 13:16. But the rulers of the synagogue or others fulfilling the public office of teacher, no less than the Bishops of the Christians, interpreted the law sitting in a chair. In the Constitutions of Clement, Book II, ch. XI, it is said to the bishop: 'Sit in the church making a discourse.' Optatus of Milevis, book V: 'You have been chosen to teach the people while sitting.' But they read the very words of the law standing: then they spoke the rest sitting, which distinction, not correctly observed, has deceived some. Thus we read that Ezra stood in a high place, but while the book was open. For this is what פתחתו means, Neh. 8:5, 'when he opened the book,' according to the LXX. With which passage should be compared that which is in Luke 4:17 ff., where Christ is said to have been handed the book to 'unroll' it, that is, to 'open' it, as the LXX speak; he then read the passage: which having been read, 'having rolled up the book and given it back to the attendant, he sat down.' He stood, therefore, while the book was open: then, with the book closed, he spoke to the people while sitting. Josephus also says that the High Priest stood every seventh year on a 'high platform,' but undoubtedly to read the words of the law to the people beforehand, which he adds.

That the Priests or members of the Sanhedrin are not excluded, nor are the Teachers alone noted, but also those who fulfilled the office of rulers and judges, the various predicates of the text teach. Because it concerns those who had the power of commanding, v. 3; who imposed burdens on the shoulders of men by their precepts, v. 4; who claimed for themselves the first seats in the synagogues, v. 6; who wanted to be considered leaders of the people, v. 16 and 24; who had the right of judging concerning doctrine and of killing false prophets, v. 34. The 'seat of Moses,' therefore, is not a private one, to which Grotius also refers these things, but a public chair. Cf. 2 Kings 16:18, Acts 8:4, 22:3. Nor does it imply only the power of teaching, but also of judging and ruling the people, Ex. 18:13, Jud. 5:10, because they sat for the sake of both teaching and ruling in that chair which had its origin from Moses and was instituted in Num. 11:16. Lightfoot thinks this should be understood of a legislative rather than a merely doctrinal chair, and thus that Christ here asserts the authority of the Magistrate, that he must be obeyed in lawful things: and that the Scribes and Pharisees are not to be held as oracles, but as Magistrates.

Latin:

V. 2. ἐπὶ τῆς Μωσέως καθέδρας ἐκάθισαν οἱ γραμματεῖς κὶ οἱ Φαρισαῖοι] Non agi de Pontificibus & Sacerdotibus, manife- stum est. Nam hi imprimis nominarentur. Sed neq; de toto Synedrio intelligi potest: nam in eo Sadducæi erant non mi- nus quam Pharisæi. Agitur ergo, ut ex commate 8. apparet, de iis qui Magistri sive doctores vocabantur; qui ferme o- mnes erant Pharisæici instituti, & multi etiam adsessorũ fun- gentes munere: quia eorundem est, ut supra diximus, de ju- re respondere & magistratib9 esse à consilio מושב פשו

καθέδρα Μωσέως est cathedra in qua sedentes magistri legem aut populo publice, aut discipulis privatim interpretabantur: quomodo cathedræ vox Græcis quoq; & Latinis usurpatur, unde philosophos cathedrarios dixit Seneca. Errant enim, meo judicio, qui pro certo asseverant Iudæos stantes legem interpretatos. Certe si quis ex plebe potestas loquendi fie- bat, hi stantes proloqui solebant, ut rectius ab omni cœtu exaudirentur: quo spectat id quod habemus Act. XIII. 16. At archisynagogi aut alii publico magistri munere fungentes, non minus quam Episcopi Christianoru, in cathedra sedētes legem interpretabantur. In Constitutionibus Clementis L. L. II. c. XI. episcopo dicitur ἕτως ἐν ἐκκλησίᾳ καθίζῃ ἳ λόγον ποιέμενος. Optatus Milevitanus lib. V Electi estis qui sedentes populum doceatis. Stantes autem legebāt ipsa legis verba: de- inde cætera sedentes loquebantur, quod discrimen non re- cte animadversum quosdam fefellit. Ita stetisse Esdram legi- mus in loco excelso, sed dum apertus esset liber. Hoc enim vult פתחתו Neh. VIII. 5. ἥνικα ἤνοιξε τὸ βιβλίον juxta LXX. Cum quo loco conferendus is qui est Lucæ IV. 17 seqq. ubi Christus in Synagoga dicitur traditum sibi librum ἀναπτύ- ξαι, hoc est, ἀνοῖξαι ut loquuntur LXX. legit deinde περικοπὴν: qua lecta πτύξας τὸ βιβλίον ἀποδὺς τῷ ὑπηρέτῃ ἐκάθισε. Stetit ergo dum liber erat apertus: clauso deinde libro sedens ad populum verba fecit. Josephus quoq; stetisse ait pontificem Maximum septimo quoq; anno βήματὸς ὑψηλῶ, sed nimi- rum ad prælegenda populo legis verba, quod adjicit.

Non excludi Sacerdotes, aut membra Synedrii, neq; solos Doctores notari, sed eos etiam qui re- ctorum & judicum munere fungebantur, prædica- ta varia textus docent. Quia de illis agitur, qui po- testatem habebant jubendi, v. 3. qui onera præceptis suis in hominum humeros imponebant v. 4. qui pri- mas Cathedras in Synagogis sibi vendicabant v. 6. qui duces populi haberi volebant v. 16. & 24. qui jus de do- ctrina cognoscendi, & Pseudo-Prophetas occidendi ha- bebant v. 34. Καθέδρα Μωσέως ergo est non priva- ta, ad quam hæc etiam refert Grotius, sed publica Cathedra. Conf. 2. Reg. XVI. 18. Act. VIII. 4. XXII. 3. Neque potestatem solum docendi, sed etiam judi- candi & regendi populum infert Ex. XVIII. 13. Jud. V. 10. quia sedebant & docendi, & regendi causa in illa Cathedra, quæ à Mose originem habebat, & in- stituta erat Num. XI. 16. De legislativa potius quam mere doctrinali cathedra hoc accipiendum censet Lightfoot, adeoque asserere hic Christum auctoritatem Magistratus, quod ei in licitis paren- dum sit: quodque Scribæ ac Pharisæi non pro o- raculis habendi, sed pro Magistratibus.

## 23:3
V. 3. 'All therefore whatever they tell you to keep, keep and do'] We have often said that universal terms ought to be restricted by the nature of the subject matter and by the equity of the thing itself. In the law of Moses, just as there were many precepts, so in those precepts there were many things concerning the sense of which one could be in doubt. In explaining these, the 'experts in the law' devoted not bad effort, being learned in the language and ancient history, without the knowledge of which most things of the law could not be correctly understood. In these, therefore, Christ wants them to be heard by the people, and their interpretations, although perhaps inclining too much to the harsher side, to be received: which can also be extended to the more rigid determinations of things generally commanded in the law, which could not be settled without some determination. For in such things there had to be some certain law, which could not be obtained except by the authority of the interpreters. However, that does not pertain to this, that if they taught anything contrary to manifest precepts and to piety itself, such as the Corban being preferred to parents, they were to be followed as blind guides. But neither did Christ wish to bind anyone's conscience to those precepts which the 'experts in the law' invented plainly outside the office of interpreting and outside the law itself, especially if those precepts had been built upon a false and empty persuasion, such as was the precept about washing hands to the end that hands defiled by contact might not defile the soul: concerning which matter it was treated above. That 'whatever they tell you to keep,' therefore, is to be understood from the context of the preceding, whatever by right of the chair, or as interpreters of the law, they shall dictate to you must be done: which interpretation, if I am not mistaken, does not differ in reality from those things which Jerome, Hilary, and Theophylact treat on this passage.

For they say and do not.] To whom could be said that Euripidean line: 'I hate a sophist who...' and that of the old Latin: 'I hate a man of slothful deeds, but philosophical sentiment.' For they are like those physicians in Philemon: 'I know physicians who are not very [helpful] to the sick regarding self-control,' Πάντας λαλῆσαι, ἀλλ᾽ ἐπὰν πταίσωσί τι Αὐτὸς ποιῆσαι, παῖδ᾽ ὅς᾽ ἐκ ὤσει τότε. Grotius rightly advises that this must be understood from the context of what precedes: that which they shall have dictated to you by the right of the Chair, or as interpreters of the law, which interpretation he notes is consistent with the explanation of Jerome, Hilary, and Theophylact. Therefore, an absolute infallibility of the Priests is not designated, which is to be observed against the Papists. Augustine indeed, in De doctr. Christian. c. 27, says that Christ commands this because the Chair compelled them to hand down not false, but true doctrine: but this is to be understood of right, not of fact. For the rest, Barradius himself rightly says in this place: Just as a pulpit does not compel preachers to teach the truth, so the Chair did not compel the Scribes and Pharisees to teach the truth.

Latin:

V. 3. πάντα ὖν ὅσα ἂν ἔιπωσιν ὑμῖν τηρεῖν, τηρεῖτε καὶ ποιεῖτε] Sæpe jam diximus universales voces restringi debere ex na- tura subjectæ materiæ, & ex ipsa rei æquitate. In lege Mosis sicut multa erant præcepta, ita in illis præceptis multa erant, de quorum sensu ambigi poterat. In iis explicandis operam non malam navabant οἱ νομικοὶ, gnari linguæ & historiæ ve- teris, sine quarum cognitione legis pleraq; recte intelligi ne- quibant. In his ergo eos Christus vult audiri à plebe, & eo- rum interpretationes, quanquam forte in duriorem partem nimium inclinantes, recipi: quod extendi etiam potest ad rigidiores determinationes rerum in lege generaliter præce- ptarum, quæ sine determinatione aliqua expediri non pote- rant. Nam in his talibq debebat aliquid esse certi juris, quod obtineri non poterat nisi interpretum auctoritate. Cæterum id non eo pertinet, ut si quid docerent manifestis præceptis ipsiq; pietati contrarium, ut de Corbona parentibus præfe- renda, sequendi essent duces cæci. Sed neq; obligare cujus- quam conscientiam Christus voluit iis præceptis quæ plane extra interpretandi officium extraq; legem ipsam οἱ νομικοὶ comminiscebantur, præsertim si ea præcepta superstructa es- sent falsæ atq; inani persuasioni, quale erat præceptum de manibus abluendis eo fine ne manus contactu inquinatæ a- nimum inquinarent: qua de re actum est supra. Illud ergo ὅσα ἂν ἔιπωσιν ὑμῖν τηρεῖν, intelligendum ex connexu superio- rum, quicquid jure cathedræ, sive ut legis interpretes vobis faciendum dictaverint: quæ interpretatio, ni fallor, reipsa non discrepat ab iis quæ in hunc locum tractant Hierony- mus, Hilarius, & Theophylactus.

Λέγουσι γὰρ κὶ ἐ ποιοῦσι.] Quibus dici poterat illud Euripi- deum: Μισῶ σοφιστὴν ὅστις & Latini veteris: Odi hominem ignava opera, philosopha sententia. Similes enim sunt medicis illis apud Philemonem. Τοῖς ἰατροῖς οἶδ' ἐγὼ Ὑπὲρ ἐγκρατείας τοῖς νοσοῦσιν οὐ σφόδρα, Πάντας λαλῆσαι, ἀλλ᾽ ἐπὰν πταίσωσί τι Αὐτὸς ποιῆσαι, παῖδ᾽ ὅς᾽ ἐκ ὤσει τότε. Intelligendum hoc esse ex connexu superiorum re- cte monet Grotius: quod jure Cathedræ, sive ut le- gis interpretes vobis faciendum dictaverint, quam interpretationem Hieronymi, Hilarii & Theophy- lacti explicationi conformem esse notat. Non er- go absoluta infallibilitas Sacerdotum designatur, quod contra Papistas observandum. Augustinus sa- ne de doctr. Christian. c. 27. ait, ideo Christum hoc ju- bere, quia Cathedra eos coëgerit non falsam, sed ve- ram tradere doctrinam: sed hoc de jure, non de fa- cto intelligendum. De cætero recte Barradius ipse in h. l. Sicut suggestum concionatores non cogit vera docere, ita Cathedra non cöegit Scribas & Pharisæos vera docere.

## 23:4
V. 4. For they bind heavy burdens and grievous to be borne, and lay them on men's shoulders] Interpreters are said to burden men when they teach that this or that must be done. The teachers of the Hebrews call this שור, that is, to aggravate. Thus ἐπιθεῖναι ζυγὸν (to lay a yoke) is used in Acts XV. 10, and ἐπιτίθεσθαι βάρος (to lay a burden) in the same place, v. 28, as will be explained more fully when we come to that. Dionysius, Bishop of the Corinthians, writing under Aurelius Verus to the Bishop of the Cnossians, warned him not to lay a heavy burden of necessity upon the brethren concerning purity. The Law itself by itself was a burden sufficiently grievous to be borne, which, says Peter, neither we nor our fathers were able to bear, namely, because of the huge number of precepts and the weakness of human memory and attention. Since, however, it is the duty of a good jurist to relieve whatever is burdensome with a benign interpretation, the consultants of the Hebrews, on the contrary, urged the positive laws, which God had not commanded primarily, but for other reasons, rigidly, and extended them as widely as possible, nor did they admit probable exceptions. Let the example be of tithes, which Deut. XIV. 22 has thus: Thou shalt truly tithe all the increase of thy seed, that the field bringeth forth year by year, which the LXX translate: Thou shalt tithe all the produce of thy seed, the produce of thy field year by year. Here a more benign interpreter would first turn himself to the intent, and would say that this had been the will of the most good and great God, that the Levites should be sufficiently provided for regarding necessary things: but not that He should bind the minds of men with too anxious a religion: therefore, it did not seem credible to him that the trifles of herbs were included in that law, the tithes of which could not bring much profit to the Levites, and, if they were to be paid, would affect the Israelites with great inconvenience because of the uncertainty of the valuation, and because that matter touched the poor most of all. He would also bring an argument to strengthen his interpretation from Leviticus XXVII. 30, where the tithe is said to be given of the seed of the land, of the fruit of the tree, which the LXX translate: of the seed of the land, and of the fruit of the tree. And from that which follows in Deuteronomy, namely, that the tithe of corn, wine, and oil is to be given. For even if examples did not restrict the rule, they could still show about what kind of produce the author of the law had thought. To these he would add an argument from a like case: for even in the kind of animals, not all were to be tithed, but only those which were driven by the pastoral foot. But if an adversary were to urge the points of the words, such an interpreter would say that they did not oppose him. For herbs can hardly be called produce, just as Roman jurists handed down that herbs are more in use than in fruit: then, that a field is mostly a field, not a garden. But the lawyers and their followers, the Pharisees, stubbornly clung to the advantages of the Levites, as if the whole matter of piety consisted in them. They contended, therefore, that nothing should be excepted where the law openly excepted nothing: that the word for both produce and field could be taken more broadly and that the best reason was that which favored religion. Neither for the divine glory, nor for the dignity of the Levitical order, nor for true piety did it matter much which interpretation prevailed. Christ, with an admirable temperament in these and other questions of this kind, notes the rigor of the interpretation in such a way that, however, it is not for anyone to depart from received opinions where it is possible to consult for peace and order without serious loss. But that was least of all to be endured, that such great captious critics of words, as often as their own affairs were at stake, so easily forgave themselves, with the confidence of wit and erudition easily suggesting exceptions by which they might defend themselves against the letter.

Τῷ δακτύλῳ δὲ αὐτῶν ὀ θέλεσι κινῆσαι αὐτά] A proverbial expression, using which the Romans also say, to touch with the tip of the finger.

Latin:

V. 4. δεσμεύεσι γὰρ φορτία βαρέα καὶ δυσβάσακτα καὶ ἐπιτιθέα- σιν ἐπὶ τὲς ὤμες τῶν ἀνθρώπων] Interpretes dicuntur homines onerare, cum docent hoc aut illud faciendum. Hebræorum magistri id dicunt שור id est aggravare. Ita ἐπιθεῖναι ζυγὸν usurpatur Act. XV. 10. ἐπιτίθεσθαι βάρος ibidem v. 28. ut cum eo ventu erit fusius explicabitur. Dionysius Corinthiorum Episcopus sub Aurelio Vero ad Cnoffiorum scribens Epi- scopum, monebat eum, μὴ βαρὺ φορτίον ἐπάναγκες τὰ περὶ ἁ- γνείας τοῖς ἀδελφοῖς ἐπιτιθέναι. Lex ipsa per se erat onus satis δυσβάσακτον, quod nec nos, inquit Petrus, nec majores nostri perferre potuimus, nimirum ob ingentem numerum præce- ptorum & humanæ memoriæ atq; attentionis imbecillita- tem. Cum autem munus sit boni Jurisconsulti quicquid o- nerosum est sublevare benigna interpretatione, contra He- bræorum consulti τὰ θετικὰ, quæ Deus non imperaverat προη- γουμένως, sed ob res alias, urgebant rigide, & quam latissime extendebant, neq; admittebant probabiles exceptiones. Ex- emplo sit de decimis quæ Deut. XIV. 22. sic habet, עשר תעשר את כל־תבואת זרעך היצא השדה שנה שנה quæ vertunt LXX. δεκάτην ἀποδεκατώσεις παντὸς γεννή- ματος, τῶ σπέρματός σε, τὸ γέννημα τῶ ἀγρῶ σε ἐνιαυτὸν κατ᾽ ἐνιαυτὸν. Hic benignior interpres primu se verteret ad τὴν διάνοιαν, ac diceret, Dei optimi maximi hanc fuisse voluntatem, ut Levi- tis satis prospectum esset de rebus necessariis: non autem ut hominum animos anxia nimium religione obstringeret: proinde credibile sibi non videri olerum minutias ista lege comprehendi, quarum decimæ Levitis non multum adferre poterant emolumenti, &, si pendendæ essent, magno Israeli- tas afficerent incommodo ob æstimationis incertu, & quia pauperes maxime ea res tangebat. Adferret etiam firmandæ interpretationi suæ argumentum ex Levitico XXVII. 30. ubi decima dada dicitur מזרע הארץ מפרי העץ quod lxx. transferut, ἀπὸ τῶ σπέρματος τῆς γῆς, κὶ ἀπὸ τῶ καρπῶ τῶ ξυλίνε. & ex eo quod in Deuteronomio sequitur, dandam scilicet decimam frumenti, vini, olei. Nam ut maxime exempla re- gulam non restringerent, ostendi tamen per illa de quo pro- ventuum genere legis auctor sensisset. His adjungeret à pari argumentum: nam & in animalium genere non omnia ἀπο- δεκατῦσθαι sed ea demum quæ pastorali pede regerentur. Quod si verborum apices urgeret adversarius, etiam illos talis interpres dicere sibi non adversari. Nam olera vix dici posse תבואה quomodo Romani Jurisconsulti olera tradi- derunt in usu magis esse quam in fructu: deinde שדה ple- rumq; agrum esse non hortum. At νομικοὶ & eorum sectato- res Pharisæi Levitarum utilitatibus contumaciter aderant, quasi in illis tota res pietatis versaretur. Contendebant igi- tur nihil excipiendum, ubi lex nihil aperte exciperet: posse & proventuum & agri vocem latius accipi & optimam esse rationem quæ pro religione faceret. Neq; ad divinam glo- riam, neq; ad dignitatem Levitici ordinis, neq; ad veram pie- tatem multum referebat, utra interpretatio prævaleret, Christus admirabili temperamento in his atq; aliis hujusce- modi quæstionibus ita interpretatum rigorem notat, ut ta- men nemini sit auctor à receptis sententiis discedendi, ubi paci atq; ordini sit e gravi jactura consuli potest. Sed illud minime erat ferendum, tantos verborum aucupes, quoties ipforum res agebatur, tam facile sibimet ignoscere, fiducia ingenii atque eruditionis facile suggerentis exceptiones, quibus se contra τὸ ῥητὸν defenderent.

Τῷ δακτύλῳ δὲ αὐτῶν ὀ θέλεσι κινῆσαι αὐτά] Proverbialis locutio, qua utentes Romani etiam dicunt, extremo digito attingere.

## 23:5
V. 5. But all their works they do for to be seen of men] If they do anything according to the prescription of the law, they give it to popular favor: see what has been said at chapter VI.

πλατύνεσι δὲ τὰ φυλακτήρια ἑαυτῶν κὶ μεγαλύνεσι τὰ κράσπε- δα τ᾽ ἱματίων αὐτῶν] How they strive to prove their piety to the people is manifest from this, says Christ, that in observing rites which are not of great moment for piety, but are of value for external appearance, they claim something exceptional for themselves; which he proves by the example of two rites, of which one was received by custom, the other was instituted by law. For the fringes, that is, the borders, were indeed commanded by law, which Justin calls scarlet dyes, and about which we touched on something above, so that not only by a mark on the body, but also by a conspicuous habit, the Israelites might be distinguished from foreigners. But the phylacteries (which word the Syrian also puts here, which the Hellenists call phylacteries) had custom as their author. There are those who think they are commanded in Exodus XIII. 9 and 16, and Deut. VI. 8: nor is that a new opinion. For Josephus also thought so, and Justin in his Dialogue with Trypho. However, they do not yet persuade me of that: and I have Jerome agreeing with me. For in those places the Israelites are commanded nothing else than to fix in their minds the benefits of the liberation from Egypt and the precepts given divinely, no less than those things which we are accustomed to carry in our hands or place before our eyes for the sake of memory. For it is apparent that it is a proverbial kind of speaking from the place in Isaiah XLIX. 16, and what is called a memorial in the cited place of Deuteronomy is that which is called frontlets in Exodus. Compare also Cant. VII. 6, Prov. VI. 21, and III. 3. Nor did the LXX interpreters translate what is frontlet in Moses as phylacteries, but as immovable things: although I am not unaware that phylacteries are put there by the Chaldeans. The word φυλακτήριον began to be applied to those Jewish parchments for this reason, because they were similar to the περιάπτα which the Greeks, believing them to be effective against diseases, called φυλακτήρια from that fact: of which there is mention in Canon xxxvi of the Synod of Laodicea. Justin, in the cited passage, says that the Jewish φυλακτήριον consisted of characters written on very thin membranes: such as is now also in use among them. But those things which Christ speaks of here, both the κράσπεδα and the φυλακτήρια, they wore around themselves larger than the common ones. By κράσπεδα, which are ציצית κόκκινα βάμματα according to Justin, read precepts, so that Israelites might be distinguished from foreigners, Grotius understands: But he rightly denies that the φυλακτήρια, which are תפלין, are commanded in Ex. xiii. 9, 16; Deut. vi. 8: since there the Israelites are only commanded to fix in their minds the benefits of the deliverance from Egypt and the precepts given to all, no less than those things which we are accustomed to carry in our hands for the sake of memory, or to place before our eyes. Epiph. haeres. xv. and in Anacephal. by phylacteria he understands borders or bands, with which garments were edged: but we learn from Jerome on Matt. xxiii that plates or small membranes are rather meant, such as the Jews even today, enclosed in leather, bind partly to the forehead, partly to the left arm, with certain words from the law of Moses inscribed. The Pharisees wrote the ten words of the law on membranes, folding them and binding them on the forehead, and making them as it were a crown for the head, so that they might always be moved before their eyes, which the Indians, and Persians, and Babylonians do even to this day, and whoever has these is judged as if religious among the people. Cf. Paulus Fagius in the notes to the Chald. paraphr. Ex. xiii. We do not deny that the fringes were commanded by law. Num. xv. 38; Deut. xxii. 12, which Christ himself therefore wore, Luke viii. 44. But those which the Pharisees widened for ostentation. But they were not only ordained for the distinction of the people, but so that they might be taught by them that the conversation of the Israelites also ought to be distinguished from the conversation of the Gentiles, and conformed according to the divine law. Concerning the Phylacteries and Fringes of the Jews, see, if you please, the Syntagma of Antiquitatum Sacrarum by Lord Augustus Pfeiffer, p. 29 seqq. V. 6. Φιλέσι τε τὴν πρωτοκλισίαν] They desire the first places at table with prayers, as a huge good, and even when the occasion is given, they claim them for themselves as if by their own right, which Luke xiv. 7 called ἐκλέγεσθαι τὰς πρωτοκλισίας. Josephus called them πρωτοκλισίους with the same meaning, and concerning Herod who deceived Hyrcanus, he says he deceived him of the πρωτοκλισίων, to which the word in the same author, τὸ ὑποκατακλίνεσθαι, is opposed. and the first seats in the synagogues] By the most ancient custom of the Jews, those who performed no office in the synagogue sat distinguished by the order of their age: which the Essenes (a less corrupted portion of the Jews) observed, whose synagogues Philo describing, says, καθ᾽ ἡλικίας, ἐν τάξεσιν ὑπὸ πρεσβυτέροις νέοι καθέζονται μετὰ κόσμε τὸ προσῆκον ἔχοντες ἀκροατικῶς. That the same custom flourished not only in the synagogues of the Jews, but also in the first churches of the Christians, is noted by him whose commentaries on the Pauline Epistles are read under the name of Ambrose. But in many places a custom crept in, that those who had attained some fame of learning should sit more honorably, to which this passage pertains. And there exist in the books of the Hebrews decrees concerning this matter, in which place the lawyers, in which the Pharisees ought to sit. And from that was born the proverb, that the rude populace, whom they called the people of the earth, should be called the footstool of the Pharisees. Which very thing as it was to some extent tolerable (for Christ does not criticize the order of sitting but the ambition) so that thing is unworthy, that finally that honor began to be conferred not upon virtue nor upon learning, but upon riches, even in the Churches of Christians, which James criticizes with the severity that was fitting. What is called here πρωτοκαθεδρίας, Plutarch said for it ἕδρας τὰς πρώτας. Herod among Josephus deceived the πρωτοκλινίτων.

Latin:

V. 5. πάντα δὲ τὰ ἔργα αὐτῶν ποιῦσι πρὸς τὸ θεαθῆναι τοῖς ἀνθρώποις] Si quid ad legis præscriptum faciunt, id dant au- ræ populari: vide quæ dicta sunt ad caput VI.

πλατύνεσι δὲ τὰ φυλακτήρια ἑαυτῶν κὶ μεγαλύνεσι τὰ κράσπε- δα τ᾽ ἱματίων αὐτῶν] Quam studeant populo pietatem suam probare ex eo manifestum est, inquit Christus, quod in ob- servandis ritibus qui non magni sunt ad pietatem momenti, sed externa specie valent, eximium sibi aliquid vindicans; quod exemplo duorum rituum probat, quorum alter usu re- ceptus, alter lege erat institutus. Nam ציצית quidem, id est τὰ κράσπεδα, lege erant præcepta, quæ κόκκινα βάμματα vocat Justinus, & de quibus aliquid attigimus supra, ut non tan- tum corporis nota, sed & conspicuo habitu Israëlitæ ab alie- nigenis discernerentur. At תפלין (quam vocem & hic ponit Syrus (quæ φυλακτήρια vocant Hellenistæ, usum habebant auctorem. Sunt qui Exodi XIII. 9. & 16. Deut. VI. 8 ea putat imperari: neq; nova ea est opinio. Nam & Josephus ita sen- sit, & Justinus in Colloquio cum Tryphone. Mihi tamen id nondum persuadent: & consentientem habeo Hieronymu. Nam istis locis nihil aliud jubentur Israëlitæ, quam benefi- cia liberationis ex Ægypto & præcepta divinitus data animo infigere non minus, quam quæ memoriæ causa in manibus gerere aut ob oculos nobis ponere solemus. Nam παροιμιῶ- δες esse loquendi genus apparet ex loco Esaia XLIX. 16. & quod dicto Deuteronomii loco dicitur זכרון id quod in E- xudo טוטפות. Conf. & Cant. vII. 6. Prov. VI. 21. & III. 3. Nec quod in Mose est טוטפת LXX. interpp. verterunt φυλακτή- ρια sed ἀσάλευτα: quanquam non nescio תפלין ibi poni à Chaldæis. Vox autem φυλακτήριον ideo membranis istis Ju- daicis appari cœpit, quia similes erant τοῖς περιάπτοις quæ Græci adversus morbos valere credita inde φυλακτήρια nun- cupabat: quoru mentio in Canone xxxvI Synodi Laodicenæ Justinus dicto loco φυλακτήριον Judaicū ait fuisse ἐν ὑμέσι λεπ- τοτάτοις γεγραμμένων χαρακτήρων: quale nunc illis etiam in u- su est. Illi autem de quibus Christus hic loquitur & κράσπε- δα & φυλακτήρια sibi circumdabant majora vulgaribus. Per κράσπεδα ציצית κόκκινα βάμματα Justi- no, lege præcepta, ut discernerentur Israëlitæ ab alieni- genis, intelligit Grotius: At φυλακτήρια תפלין re- cte negat Ex. XIII 9. 16. Deut. VI. 8. imperari: quum ibi tantum jubeantur Israëlitæ beneficia liberatio- nis ex Ægypto, & præcepta omnibus data animo infigere, non minus quam quæ memoriæ causa in manibus gerere, aut ob oculos nobis ponere sole- mus. Epiph. hæres. XV. & in Anacephal. per phyla- cteria limbos sive fascias intelligit, quibus vestes præ- texebatur: sed laminas potius notari, seu membranu las, quales adhuc hodie Judæi corio inclusas, par- tim fronte, partim brachio sinistro alligant, inscri- ptis è Mosis lege verbis quibusdam ex Hieronymo discimus in c. XXIII. Matt. Pharisæi scribebant in membranis decem verba legis, complicantes ea, & li- gantes in fronte, & quasi coronam capiti facientes, ut semper ante oculos moverētur, quod usq; hodie Indi, & Persæ, & Babylonii faciunt, & qui hæc habuerit quasi religiosus in populis judicatur. Conf. Paulus Fagius in not. ad Chald. paraphr. Ex. XIII. Fimbrias autem lege præceptas non diffitemur. Num. XV. 38. Deut. XXII. 12. quas ideo Christus ipse gestabat Luc. VIII. 44. Quas vero Pharisæi ad ostentationem dilata- bant. Non autem tantum erant ordinatæ ad discre- tionem populi, sed ut docerentur iisdem, conver- sationem etiam Israëllitarum à conversione gentilium distingui debere, ac juxta legem divinam confor- mari. De Phylacteriis & Fimbriis Judæorum vide sis Antiquitatum Sacrarum Domini Augusti Pfeif- feri Syntagma p. 29. seqq. V. 6. Φιλέσι τε τὴν πρωτοκλισίαν] Votis expetunt primos accubitus, tanquam ingens bonu, atq; etiam data occasio- ne velut jure suo sibi vindicant, quod ἐκλέγεσθαι τὰς πρωτοκλι- σίας dixit Lucas XIV. 7. πρωτοκλισίους dixit Josephus eodē significatu, & de Herode qui Hircanu decepit, πρωτοκλισίων ait ἐξηπάτα, cui opposita vox apud eundē τὸ ὑποκατακλίνεσθαι. κὶ τὰς πρωτοκαθεδρίας ἐν ταῖς συναγωγαῖς] Vetustissimo Ju- dæorum more, qui nullo in Synagoga munere fungebantur, sedebant ætatis ordine distincti: quod servabant Esseni (mi- nus corrupta Judæorum portio) quorum Synagogas descri- bens Philo, καθ᾽ ἡλικίας inquit, ἐν τάξεσιν ὑπὸ πρεσβυτέροις νέοι καθέζονται μετὰ κόσμε τὸ προσῆκον ἔχοντες ἀκροατικῶς. Eundē morem non in Synagogis tantum Judæorum, sed & in pri- mis Christianorum Ecclesiis viguisse notatis cujus commen- tarii in Paulinas Epistolas sub Ambrosii nomine leguntur. Sed multis in locis irrepsit consuetudo, ut eruditionis famā aliquam consecuti honoratius sederent, quo pertinet hic lo- cus. Et extant in Hebræorum libris decreta de hac re, quo lo- co legisperiti, quo Pharisæi sedere debeant. Atq; inde natum proverbium, ut plebs rudis, quam populu terræ vocabant, diceretur scabellum pedum Pharisæorum. Quod ipsum ut erat aliquatenus tolerabile(neq; enim sedendi ordinem sed τὸ φιλότιμον reprehendit Christus) ita illud indignum,quod tandem non virtuti neq; eruditioni, sed divitiis is honos de- ferri cœpit, etiam in Christianorum Ecclesiis,quod Jacobus qua decebat severitate reprehendit. Quod hic dicitur πρωτο- καθεδρίας pro eo ἕδρας τὰς πρώτας dixit Plutarchus. Herodes apud Josephum Hyrcanum πρωτοκλινίτων ἐξηπάτα.

## 23:7
V. 7. And greetings in the marketplaces and to be called by men, Rabbi, Rabbi] They seek to be greeted by that name Rabbi: how, the greeter poet, Horace said. But Rabbi was more than Rab: nor were they in need of that title unless those who had received a testimony of learning from the Sanhedrin through the laying on of hands: which testimony was given in the dispersions by the prefects of the schools which they call ישיבות as now also the custom of Christians holds. But the word Rabbi was accustomed to be expressed twice in greetings, as appears in Mark XIV. 45.

Latin:

V. 7. κὶ τὰς ἀσπασμὸς ἐν ταῖς ἀγοραῖς κὶ καλεῖσθ ὑπὸ ꚍ ἀνθρώπων, ῥαββὶ ῥαββὶ] Expetunt salutari isto nomine Rabbi: quomodo, Poëta salutor, dixit Horatius. Plus autem erat Rabbi,quam Rab: neq; indigetabātur isto cognomento nisi qui à Synedrio per manuum impositionem testimonium e- ruditionis accepiffent: quod testimonium ἐν ταῖς διασποραῖς dabatur à præfectis scholarū quas vocant ישיבות ut nunc quoque mos habet Christianorum.Solebat autem in saluta- tionibus vox Rabbi bis exprimi,ut apparet Marci XIV. 45.

## 23:8
V. 8. But you must not be called Rabbi. For one is your teacher; the Christ] It must be read διδάσκαλος entirely, just as the Syrian also reads. For our writers everywhere render the word Rabbi and Rabboni as διδάσκαλος: nowhere as καθηγητά. Then Christ clearly distinguishes the title of καθηγητῶ from the title of Rabbi in verse 10. Besides the common reason of humility, Christ adds another peculiar one, why his followers ought not to seek those appellations, especially in that sense in which they were sought by the Jews. For those who were learned among the Jews, with the name of Doctor they also claimed for themselves authority over what seemed to be taught, and they wanted to be believed. But the followers of Christ ought not to teach the people those things as necessary to be observed, which seemed such to them, but only those things which Christ himself had pronounced necessary. Some of the Jews followed some masters and others followed others and depended upon their authority: but among Christians to be said in that way, I am of Cephas, I of Paul, I of Apollos is a sin. For they ought not to heap up teachers for themselves, as Paul speaks in 2 Tim. IV: 3: for all are inserted into one family through baptism, that is, the profession of Christianity. But that διδάσκαλος ὁ χριστὸς we said at chapter X is to be interpreted thus, an excellent doctor appointed by God: just as Christ is called ἱερεύς and Christ is called βασιλεύς. There are indeed also in the Christian Church those who are called διδάσκαλοι, both commonly, as Paul calls himself a teacher of the Gentiles in 1 Tim. II. 7, 1 Tim. I. 11, and peculiarly some distinguished from the Apostles, Prophets, and Pastors, Acts XIII. 1, 1 Cor. XII. 28, 29, Eph. IV. 1, but in another sense than those Jews, not as authors of dogmas, but as messengers of one common dogma. And James teaches us in chapter III. 1 how much of a danger this very office is, and how it is not only not to be sought after but not even to be undertaken unless one's strengths have been well explored.

Grotius wrongly changes the received reading. Almost all copies have the word καθηγητής. Beza notes only two Codices which read ὁ διδάσκαλος. Nor is it permitted to gather the contrary from the Syrian: for those Greek names are almost synonyms. And the Syrian retained only the Hebrew word. But that that sentence is repeated in verse 10 is not a tautology, but it was done both so that it might be shown that that vice of ambition has taken such deep roots in the minds of men that it can be pulled out with difficulty, and so that necessary doctrine might be the more inculcated. For that which is never sufficiently learned can never be sufficiently said.

ἀδελφοί ἐσε] Disciples of that one teacher, among yourselves fellow-students.

Latin:

V. 8. ὑμεῖς δὲ μὴ κληθῆτε ῥαββὶ. εἷς γάρ ἐστιν ὑμῶν ὁ διδάσκα- λος· ὁ χριστὸς] Omnino διδάσκαλος legendum, quomodo & Syrus legit.Nam vocem Rabbi & Rabboni scriptores no- stri ubiq; reddunt διδάσκαλος : nusquā καθηγητά. Deinde κα- θηγητῶ titulum à titulo Rabbi Christus manifeste distinguit commate 10. Præter communem rationem τῆς ταπεινοφρο- σύνης, aliam peculiarem addit Christus, cur sui sectatores i- stas appellationes expetere non deberent, eo præsertim sen- su, quo à Judæis expetebantur. Nam qui eruditi erant inter Judæos,cum nomine Doctoris etiam auctoritatem sibi ven- dicabant quod visum esset docendi,& credi sibi volebāt. At Christi sectatores non debebant populum ea docere tan- quam observatu necessaria, quæ ipsis talia videbantur, sed ea tantum quæ Christus ipse necessaria pronunciasset. Judæo- rum alii alios sectabantur magistros & ab eorum pendebant auctoritate: at inter Christianos eo modo dici, ego sum Ce- phæ, ego Pauli,ego Apollo nefas est. Neq; enim debent sibi ἐπισωρεύειν διδασκάλες, ut loquitur Paulus 2. Tim.IV: 3. o- mnes enim per baptismum, id est, professionem Christia- nismi uni familiæ inseruntur. Illud autem διδάσκαλος ὁ χρι- σὸς ad caput X. diximus ita esse interpretandum, doctor exi- mius à Deo constitutus: quomodo ἱερεύς ὁ χριςὸς, & βασι- λεὺς ὁ χριςὸς dicitur. Sunt sane & in Christiana Ecclesia qui dicuntur διδάσκαλοι, tum communiter, ut Paulus se διδάσκαλον ἐθνῶν vocat I.Tim. 11.7. 1. Tim. 1. 11. tum pecu- liariter quidam ab Apostolis, Prophetis, Pastoribusque di- stincti, Act. XIII.1. 1. Cor. XII. 28.29. Eph.IV.1. sed alio sensu quam illi Judæi, non ut dogmatum auctores, sed ut unius communis dogmatis nuntii. Atq; hoc ipsum munus quanti sit periculi, quamque non modo non ambiendum sed neque suscipiendum nisi bene exploratis viribus Jaco- bus nos docet cap III. 1.

Lectionem receptam perperam immutat Gro- tius. Pleraque omnia exemplaria habent vocem καθηγητής. Duos solum Codices notat Beza, qui legerint ὁ διδάσκαλος. Nec è Syro contrarium col- ligere licet: sunt enim illa nomina Græca fere Sy- nonyma. Et retinuit solum Syrus vocem Ebræam. Quod autē repetitur ea sententia v. 10. non ταυτο- λογία est, sed factū tum ut ostendatur quod vitium illud ambitionis tam altas radices egerit in animis hominum, ut difficulter evelli queat, tum ut do- ctrina necessaria eo magis inculcetur. Nunquam enim satis dicitur, quod nunquam satis discitur.

ἀδελφοί ἐσε] Unius illius doctoris discipuli, inter vos συμφοιτηταὶ.

## 23:9
V. 9. You must not call your father upon the earth] Those who followed some wise man as if he were the head of a school, and had sworn as it were into his name, were called sons of that wise man, they themselves called him אבי or as the Syrian also has here אבא. The interpretation is to be sought from the preceding. But because אבא was a greater title than רבי therefore Christ claims the latter for himself, and the former for the Father.

εἷς γάρ ἐστιν ὁ πατὴρ ὑμῶν, ὁ ἐν τοῖς ἐρανοῖς] One is the head of your Family and the author of dogmas, God, who through the Son himself revealed to you all things necessary to be known. You are taught by God, John VI. 45, God-taught, 1 Thess. IV. 9. Therefore in that sense in which the Jews called their wise men fathers, Christians ought to acknowledge no one as father. But in another sense they are rightly called fathers who have begotten us in Christ through the Gospel: 1 Cor. IV. 15.

Latin:

V. 9. πατέρα μὴ καλέσητε ὑμῶν ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς] Qui sapientem aliquem tanquam Scholæ principem sectabantur, & velut in nomen ejus juraverant, ejus Sapientis filii vocabantur, ipsi illum vocabant אבי vel ut hic habet etiam Syrus אבא. Interpretatio petenda ex superioribus. Sed quia אבא ma- jor erat titulus quam רבי ideo Christus hunc sibi, illum patri vindicat.

εἷς γάρ ἐστιν ὁ πατὴρ ὑμῶν, ὁ ἐν τοῖς ἐρανοῖς] Unus est vestræ Familiæ princeps ac dogmatum auctor Deus, qui per filium vobis ipse omnia scitu necessaria revelavit. Estis διδακτοὶ τῶ Θεῶ Joh. VI. 45. Θεοδίδακτοι 1. Thess. IV. 9. Itaque illo sensu quo Judæi sapientes patres suos vocabant, Christiani pa- trem neminem debent agnoscere. Sed alio sensu patres re- cte vocantur qui nos in Christo per Evangelium genuerunt: 1. Cor. IV. 15.

## 23:10
V. 10. καθηγηταὶ] That is guides, as Christ called the Pharisees above in chapter XV. 14 and below in verse 16. And thus the Syrian interprets in this place. So also Paul places these among the titles of the Hebrew wise men, a guide of the blind, a light in darkness, an instructor of the foolish, a teacher of infants, Rom. II. 19, 20.

Latin:

V. 10. καθηγηταὶ] Id est ὁδηγοὶ, quomodo supra Phari- sæos vocavit Christus c. XV.14. & infra v. 16. Atque ita hoc loco Syrus interpretatur, Sic & Paulus inter titulos sapien- tum Hebræorum ista ponit, ὁδηγὸν τυφλῶν, φῶς ἐν σκότει, παιδευτὴν ἀφρόνων, διδάσκαλον νηπίων Rom. II. 19. 20.

## 23:11
V. 11. But the greater of you shall be your servant] By how much anyone among you will obtain a greater dignity in the Church, by so much let him know that not more power has been granted to him, but more burden has been enjoined: whence it follows that there is no reason why titles, which are indicators of greater servitude, should delight you. See what is above at chapter XX. 26.

Latin:

V. 11. ὁ δὲ μείζων ὑμῶν, ἔσται ὑμῶν διάκονος] Quo quis in- ter vos majorem in Ecclesia dignitatem obtinebit, eo sciat sibi non plus imperii concessum, sed plus oneris injunctum: unde sequitur non esse cur vos delectent tituli majoris servitutis indices. Vide quæ supra ad caput XX. 26.

## 23:12
V. 12. But whoever will exalt himself will be humbled] A sentence frequently used by Christ, undoubtedly famous among the Hebrews: the Talmudists in this way: every man who has haughtiness of spirit in him will in the end be diminished. Solomon expressed it thus in Proverbs XVI. 18: Before contrition is pride, before ruin a high spirit; and chapter XXIX. 23: pride will depress a man. Among the Greeks there are many similar things, such as that which some attribute to Euripides, others to Menander: When you see someone raised to a height, and proudly boasting in wealth and birth, and having lifted an eyebrow greater than his fortune, expect swift retribution for him immediately; for he is raised higher so that he may fall greater.

And whoever shall humble himself shall be exalted] What Solomon said, before glory is humility, Prov. XV. 33. and he who is humble in spirit shall attain glory, ch. XXIX. 23. These sentences, however, applied to Christ, indeed have their own use also in human affairs: but the heavenly teacher looks primarily to that which is heavenly: Peter explains this in I Ep. V. 6. Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time. Aesop, being asked what God was doing, replied that he humbles the high things, and exalts the humble things.

Latin:

V. 12. ὅςις δὲ ὑψώσει ἑαυτὸν ταπεινωθήσεται] Sententia Christo sæpig usurpata, celebris haud dubie apud Hebræos: Thalmudistæ hoc modo כל אדם שיש וב גסות רוח לסוף מתמעט Salomon ita extulit Proverb. XVI. 18. Ante contritionem superbia, ante ruinam spiritus altus; & cap. XXIX. 23. superbia hominem deprimet. Apud Græcos multa sunt similia, ut illud quod alii Euripidi, alii Menandro tribuunt: Ὅταν δ᾽ ἴδῃς πρὸς ὕψος ἠρμένον τινα Λαμπρῶς τε πλούτῳ κᾀ γένει γαυρούμενον, Ὀφρύν τε μείζω τῆς τύχης ἐπηρκότα, Τούτῳ ταχεῖαν νέμεσιν εὐθὺς προσδόκα· Ἐπαίρεται γὰρ μεῖζον ἵνα μεῖζον πέσῃ.

καὶ ὅςις ταπεινώσει ἑαυτὸν ὑψωθήσεται] Quod Salomo dixit, ante gloriam humilitas, Prov. XV. 33. & humilis spiritu gloriam assequetur, c. XXIX. 23. Sententiæ autem istæ Christo usurpatæ, habent quidem suum quoque usum in rebus humanis: at cælestis doctor id quod cæleste est potissimum respicit: Explicat Petrus I Ep. V. 6. Ταπεινώθητε ὖν ὑπὸ τὴν κραταιὰν χεῖρα τῶ Θεῦ, ἵνα ὑμᾶς ὑψώσῃ ἐν καιρῷ. Æsopus interrogatus quid Deus faceret, re pondit eum τὰ μὲν ὑψηλὰ ταπεινοῦν, τὰ δὲ ταπεινὰ ὑψοῦν.

## 23:13
V. 13. you shut the kingdom of heaven] The keys being removed, as Luke speaks, that is, the true interpretation and daily inculcation of the passages in which the subject is the Messiah and his doctrine being suppressed, that is, of repentance, faith, and love unfeigned: these being omitted, you devote all your effort to urging and amplifying rituals.

to those who are entering] The present for the future: those who otherwise were about to enter if you had rightly opened the way. But now you not only do not open it, but you even obstruct it with the fences of rituals, by which minds occupied cannot penetrate to better things. Why this comma is read in many copies long since, and woe to you scribes and Pharisees hypocrites, because you devour the houses of widows and for a pretense praying long: therefore you shall receive greater judgment: I judge to be interpolated: of which thing a great indication to me is that those who have other codices place it before this sentence about the keys, others append it. For you may almost see that things which vary in position are added from elsewhere, as here from Mark and Luke, with words added and changed to complete the coherence. The Greek index of the Gospels, which they call the canon, to which Jerome is accustomed to appeal, and which was made from the best codices, does not have this comma in Matthew. Origen, such a diligent searcher of books, does not acknowledge it. The Syriac books indeed have it: but the most ancient Latin ones do not have it. Therefore this part seems the greater. Add that there was no cause for removing it: some cause for adding it. We shall interpret it according to Mark.

There is no cause why Grotius should argue this verse to be spurious, and conclude that it crept in here from Mark and Luke. For although the Syrian placed it before the immediately preceding comma, with certain more recent Greek codices, that is not an argument that it was not read at all in Matthew. And the Greek and Syriac codices of Matthew agree, as do Chrysostom, the author of the imperfect work, Theophylact, and Euthymius, on the authenticity of this comma, however much the Latin codices may vary, which cannot prejudice those. Nor is it likely, as our blessed Gerhard rightly says in his Harmony, that in this accurate and prolix discourse, in which Christ expressly taxes the vices of the Scribes and Pharisees, this very far most serious vice should have been omitted.

Latin:

V. 13. κλείετε τὴν βασιλείαν τῶν ὐρανῶν] Clavibus sublatis, ut Lucas loquitur, id est suppressa vera interpretatione & quotidiana inculcatione locorum in quibus agitur de Messia ejusque doctrina, id est, de pœnitentia, fide & dilectione non ficta: quibus omissis omnem operam impenditis ritibus urgendis & ampliandis.

ἐδὶ τὲς εἰσερχομένυς] Præsens pro futuro: eos qui alioqui intraturi erant si viam recte panderetis. At nunc non modo non panditis, sed obstruitis etiam rituum septis, quibus occupati animi ad meliora nequeunt penetrare. Quid hic in multis exemplaribus jam pridem legitur comma, καὶ δι ὑμῖν γραμματεῖς καὶ Φαρισαῖοι ὑποκριταὶ, ὅτι κατεσθίετε τὰς οἰκίας τῶν χηρῶν κᾀ προφάσει μακρὰ προσευχόμενοι· διὰ τοῦτο λήψεσθε περισσότερον κρῖμα: judico παρεμβεβλημένον: cujus rei mihi magnum indicium est quod qui habent codices alii præponunt isti sententiæ de clavibus, alii subtexunt. Ferme enim videas quæ situ variant, aliunde adjecta, ut hic ex Marco & Luca, additis mutatisque verbis ad implendam cohærentiam. Græcus Evangeliorum indiculus, quem canonem vocant, ad quem provocare solet Hieronymus, quique factus est ex optimis codicibus, in Matthæo hoc comma non habet. Origenes tam diligens librorum scrutator non agnoscit. Habent quidem libri Syriaci: at Latini antiquissimi non habent. Proinde hæc pars major videtur. Adde quod detrahendi nulla fuit causa: addendi aliqua. Interpretabimur ad Marcum.

Non est causa cur hunc versum νοθείας arguat, & è Marco, ac Luca huc irrepsisse statuat Grotius. Etsi enim Syrus proxime præcedenti commati eum præmiserit, cum quibusdam recentioribus Græcis Codicibus, id tamen argumento non est, eum apud Matthæum nullatenus lectum fuisse. Et consentiunt Græci, ac Syriaci Codices Matthæi, nec non Chrysostomus, Autor imperfecti operis, Theophylactus, & Euthymius in authentia hujus commatis, utut Latini Codices varient, qui istis præjudicare non possunt. Neque verisimile est, ut recte B. Gerhard. noster in Harmonia, in hac accurata & prolixa concione, in qua Christus ex professo Scribarum ac Pharisæorum vitia taxat, hoc ipsum longe gravissimum vitium fuisse prætermissum.

## 23:15
V. 15. you compass sea and land] A proverbial expression signifying the anxious labor of searching. Thus to wage war through the sea and through the land is in the Maccabean history I. ch. VIII. 32. But this is also a Hebrew expression, such as we have noted elsewhere. For the sense is: When you go about land and sea to make a proselyte, you soon deprave him.

proselyte] A proselyte here and in Acts is one who, being a Gentile by birth, bound himself to the law of Moses through circumcision, whom Philo also calls an immigrant, who in most matters has the rights of the natives. These are accustomed to be called gerim tzedek, guests of righteousness. Otherwise, ger to the Hebrews or georas to the Hellenists is also accustomed to be called one who, having abandoned the worship of idols, had devoted himself to the one God and the common laws of the human race: in which sense perhaps Justin distinctly placed georas and proselytes in his dialogue with Trypho: and Eusebius: proselytes and lesser georas.

Thus they are called גרים [proselytes] 1 Par. XXII. 2. The Rabbis call others גרי צדק proselytes of righteousness or of truth, who are also called proselytes of the covenant, who were bound to observe the Mosaic law: others גרי שער proselytes of the gate: who observed the seven precepts of the sons of Noah. But that distinction is perhaps more recent, and was by no means accepted in the times of Christ. Christ does not censure the zeal for Gentile conversion; but he notes the carnal affections of the Pharisees in their heart, such as ambition, avarice, and above all, that they did not convert them to the kingdom of the Messiah, but perverted them to heresy, and with such zeal made them sons of Gehenna.

υἱὸν γεέννης] A debtor to Gehenna, as בן מות 1 Sam. XX. 31. 2 Sam. XII. 5. In Greek υἱὸς θανάτου, a debtor to death. Deut. XV. 2. בן הכות, in Greek ἄξιος πληγῶν [worthy of stripes].

Διπλότερον ὑμῶν] Much more than you yourselves, because examples do not stop where they begin, but corrupt men with great interest, --- when they enter minds with great authors: especially if there is any vice that deceives with the appearance and shadow of virtue, when it is sad in habit, and severe in countenance and dress. Such is ambition and avarice clothed in the person of sanctity. We are all so docile to imitating base and wicked things. Whence also that saying: The age of our parents, worse than our grandparents, has brought us forth more wicked, soon to give birth to a more vicious progeny. The experience of subsequent times has confirmed this saying of Christ. Justin on the proselytes of the Jews in his own age: 'But the proselytes not only do not believe, but they blaspheme against his name' (he is addressing the Jews), 'twofold more than you,' namely, against Christ.

Latin:

V. 15. περιάγετε τὴν θάλασσαν κᾀ τὴν ξηρὰν] Proverbialis locutio sollicitum inquirendi laborem significans. Ita πολεμεῖν διὰ τῆς θαλάσσης καὶ διὰ τῆς ξηρᾶς est in Maccabaica historia I. cap. VIII. 32. Est autem & hic Hebraica locutio, qualem alibi notavimus. Sensus enim est: Cum terram & mare obeatis ut faciatis proselytum, mox eum depravatis.

προσήλυτον] προσήλυτος hic & in Actis est is qui ortu gentilis per circumcisionem se legi Mosis obstrinxit, quem Philo etiam ἐπηλύτην vocat, qui in plerisque rebus jura habeat τῶν ἀυτοχθόνων. Hi dici solent גרי צדק hospites justitiæ. Alioqui גר Hebræis γεώργας aut γηόρας Hellenistis etiam is dici solet, qui relicto idolorum cultu uni Deo & communibus humani generis legibus se addixerat: quo forte sensu γηόραν καὶ τὲς προσηλύτους distincte posuit Justinus colloquio cum Tryphone: & Eusebius: προσηλύτους τέτωτε καὶ μειους γηωρας.

Ita גרים dicta sunt 1. Par. XXII. 2. Rabbini alios dicunt גרי צדק proselytos justitiae sive veritatis, qui & proselyti foederis vocati, qui legem Mosaicam ob- servare tenebantur: alios גרי שער proselytos por- tae: qui septem praecepta filiorum Noae observabant. Sed ea distinctio forte recentior, temporibus Christi minime recepta fuit. Non taxat Christus studium conversionis gentilis; sed carnales affe- ctus Pharisaeorum in corde notat, utpote ambitio- nem, avaritiam, & imprimis, quod non ad regnum Messiae eos converterent, sed ad haeresin perverte- rent, filiosque gehennae tanto studio efficerent.

υἱὸν γεέννης] Gehennae debitum, ut בן מות 1. Sam. XX. 31. 2. Sam. XII. 5. Graece υἱὸς θανάτου morti debitus. Deut. XV. 2. בן הכות Graece ἄξιος πληγῶν.

Διπλότερον ὑμῶν] Multo magis quam vos ipsi, quia non consistunt exempla ubi incipiunt, sed magno cum foenore corrumpunt homines, --- magnis Cum subeunt animos auctoribus: praesertim si quod est vitium quod fallit specie virtutis & umbra Cum sit triste habitu, vultuque & veste severum. Qualis est ambitio & avaritia induta sanctimoniae perso- nam. Adeo dociles imitandis Turpibus ac pravis omnes sumus. Unde & illud: Aetas parentum pejor avis, tulit Nos nequiores, mox daturos Progeniem vitiosiorem. Dictum hoc Christi comprobavit sequentium temporum experientia. Justinus de Judaeorum proselytis sua aetate: οἱ δὲ προσήλυτοι ὐ μόνον ὐ πιστεύεσι, ἀλλὰ διπλότερον ὑμῶν (Ju- daos alloquiter) βλασφημοῦσιν εἰς τὸ ὄνομα αὐτῦ, Christi scilicet.

## 23:16
V. 16. ὃς ἂν ὀμόσῃ ἐν τῷ ναῷ, ὐδέν ἐστι] The teachers of the Hebrews considered some oaths great, others small. The great ones were by God himself, to which they equated the oath of κορβᾶν, which we saw translated above as δῶρον Θεῦ [gift of God], just as Josephus also translates it against Apion as δῶρον Θεῦ.
