That, however, was twofold, as we said at chapter V: either a gift that was placed upon the altar, of which there is frequent mention in Leviticus, where the LXX also translate it as δῶρον; or money sent into the treasury, which Matthew calls κορβανᾶ below. If anyone had sworn by either of these, he was considered to have sworn by God himself, because those gifts were proper to God. This was the pretext of the teachers: it pertained to gain that those gifts be held as most holy, even above the temple and the altar, as if God, forsooth, delighted in them especially. Oaths, however, by the temple and the altar were reckoned as lesser oaths, although even he who swears by them, swears (as we observed elsewhere that Ulpian speaks) with respect to the divine majesty. The Jewish teachers therefore easily granted a release from these oaths if anyone said that he had sworn in an unconsidered heat: but not so with the oath of κορβᾶν. It is not unlike what the Roman Emperors did: if anyone had perjured himself by their safety or genius, they subjected him to the most severe punishments; if anyone had perjured himself by God, they left the vengeance of that injury to God.

ὐδέν ἐστι] That is, he is not bound: as the opposite member ὀφείλει shows: חוב, which is nothing else here than 'he is bound,' 'he is obligated.' I judge that this concerns the fulfillment of a promise, not a penalty.

Latin:

V. 16. ὃς ἂν ὀμόσῃ ἐν τῷ ναῷ, ὐδέν ἐστι] Juramenta Hebraeo- rum Magistri alia magna, alia parva censebant. Magna per Deum ipsum, cui aequabant juramentum κορβᾶν quod δῶρον Θεῦ supra verti vidimus, sicut & Josephus contra Appionem vertit δῶρον Θεῦ. Id autem erat duplex, ut diximus ad cap. V. aut donu quod altari superponebatur cujus in Levitico saepe est mentio, ubi itide δῶρον vertunt LXX. aut pecunia missa in gazophylacium, quod κορβανᾶ infra vocat Matthaeus. Per u- trumvis horum si quis jurasset, per Deum ipsum jurasse cen- se batur, quia illa dona Dei erant propria. Haec at πρόσφασις magistrorum greve: a ad quaestum pertinebat dona illa habe- ri quam sanctissima, etiam supra templum & altare, quasi Deus scilicet illis praecipue gauderet. Iuramenta autem per templum & altare minoribus juramentis accensebantur, cum tamen etiam qui per ea jurat, juret(ut Ulpianum loqui alibi observavimus) respectu divini numinis. Istorum igitur Iuramentorum gratiam facile faciebant Judaei doctores si quis se inconsulto calore jurasse diceret: at juramenti κορβᾶν non item. Haud dissimile est quod Romani Imperatores, si quis per ipsorum salutem aut genium pejerasfet gravissimis cum poenis subjiciebant: si quis per Deum pejerasset, ejus injuriae ultionem Deo relinquebant.

ὐδέν ἐστι] Id est, non tenetur: ut ostendit oppositum mem- brum ὀφείλει: חוב quod nihil hic est aliud quam tenetur, obstrictus est. De implenda promissione, non de poena hic agi censeo.

## 23:17
V. 17. ὁ ναὸς ὁ ἁγιάζων τὸν χρυσὸν] For the money of the treasury served especially for the uses of the temple, and therefore it was of sacred right, just as the donaria were among the Romans, and the ἀναθήματα among the Greeks. The writer to the Hebrews says, 'The lesser is blessed by the greater,' c. VII. 7.

Latin:

V. 17. ὁ ναὸς ὁ ἁγιάζων τὸν χρυσὸν] Nam pecunia gazophy- lacii praecipue templi usibus serviebat, ideoq; sacri erat juris ut & apud Romanos donaria, apud Graecos ἀναθήματα. Scri- ptor ad Hebraeos τὸ ἔλαττον ὑπὸ τῦ κρείττονος εὐλογεῖται c. VII. 7.

## 23:19
V. 19. τὸ θυσιαστήριον τὸ ἁγιάζον τὸ δῶρον] According to the sense of the law, כל הנוגע במזבח יקדש, i.e., 'everything that touches the altar shall be sanctified,' or 'everyone who touches,' as it is now read in the LXX.

Latin:

V. 19. τὸ θυσιαστήριον τὸ ἁγιάζον τὸ δῶρον] Ex sententia legis כל הנוגע במזבח יקדש i. e. πᾶν τὸ ἁπτόμενον τῦ θυσια- στηρίκ ἁγιασθήσεται, πõ πᾶς ὁ ἁπτόμενος, ut nunc legitur apud LXX.

## 23:20
V. 20. ἐν αὐτῷ κ᾿ ἐν πᾶσι τοῖς ἐπάνω αὐτῦ] Because accessories follow the principal thing. Now these offerings were accessories of the altar: therefore, when the altar was named, they were to be considered named at the same time.

Latin:

V. 20. ἐν αὐτῷ κ᾿ ἐν πᾶσι τοῖς ἐπάνω αὐτῦ] Quia accessio- nes sequuntur rem principalem. Oblationes autem istae ac- cessiones erant altaris: itaque nominato altari simul nomi- nata censeri debebant.

## 23:21
V. 21. καὶ ἐν τῷ κατοικῦντι αὐτὸν] Here Christ shows that all those things which they called lesser oaths are to be equated with the greatest. For no one ought to be considered so foolish as to call an empty thing as a witness of his thought and an avenger of his perfidy. Wherefore, in those oaths, a metonymy ought to be considered to be present: and by the temple, one should understand Him whose the temple is.

Thus also the author of the imperfect work, homily XLIV: The Jews said that the gold in which they delighted, and the gifts by which they were fed, were holier than the temple and the altar itself, so that men might become more prompt to offer gifts than to pour out prayers in the temple and to do justice. Cf. also Jerome on this passage. V. 22. ἐν τῷ ὀυρανῷ] Christ illustrates what he had said with a similar example. For, he says, even those who swear by heaven are to be considered to invoke that witness whose throne is heaven, which we have said at chapter V how it is to be understood. Let one consult here the passage of the writer of the responses to the Greeks in the works of Justin: 'We call heaven the house and throne of God, not as if God needs this for a dwelling or for a seat, as if he were a merchant and entirely lacking nothing, but so that we, not looking toward the magnitude of his substance and the incorruptibility of his essence, might not suppose this to be God or equal in honor to God.' For this reason we call it the house and throne of God, by these names separating it from all communion with God according to essence and according to the appellations of essence. For just as the house and the throne are posterior to the one who made them, so also heaven is posterior to God, as the begotten is to the unbegotten. Furthermore, Christ reduces these formulas of swearing to the passage in Deut. VI. 13, X. 20, that one must swear in the name of God alone, and teaches that he who swears by a creature, reductively and indirectly swears by God himself: and especially he who swears by sacred things and things destined for divine worship is considered to swear by the God to whose worship those things are destined. An altar cannot be called to witness in itself, since it has nothing of divinity in it: but insofar as it serves for sacrifices, and that by the very ordinance of God, by which they are offered upon it in recognition of the divine majesty, to that extent the divine majesty shines forth in it: whence he who swears by the altar, swears by God himself, for whose worship the altar was consecrated by the performance of sacrifices. And although similar grave adjurations by creatures are found in the Scriptures, Gen. XLII. 15, Deut. IV. 26, 1 Sam. I. 26, XX. 3, yet oaths properly so called are only to be performed in the name of the Lord, and therefore the Pharisees sinned in two ways: both because they performed oaths by creatures, and because they judged that those same oaths, thus performed, which they themselves held as true oaths, were not to be kept, and thus they rashly committed perjury. For although those things which were done by creatures were not truly oaths, yet if you look at the mind of the one swearing, who held them to be oaths, by violating them perjury was altogether committed.

Latin:

V. 21. καὶ ἐν τῷ κατοικῦντι αὐτὸν] Hic ostendit Christus o- mnia ista quae illi vocabant minora juramenta maximis esse aequiparanda. Nemo enim tam stultus censeri debet, ut rem inanem testem advocet suae cogitationis & perfidiae vindi- cem. Quare in istis juramentis censeri debet inesse μετωνυ- μία: & per templum intelligi is cujus est templum:

Sic etiam autor operis imperfecti homil. XLIV. Judaei aurum quo ipsi delectabantur, & dona quibus ipsi pascebantur, sanctiora dicebant esse, quam ipsum templum & altare, ut homines promtiores fierent ad offerenda dona, quam ad preces fundendas in tem- plo, & justitias faciendas. Conf. & Hier. in h. l. V. 22. ἐν τῷ ὀυρανῷ] Illustrat Christus quod dixerat exem- plo simili. Nam, inquit, & qui per cœlum jurant, censendi sunt testem illum invocare cui cœlum pro solio est, quod quomodo sit intelligendum diximus ad caput V. Adeam hic locum Scriptoris responsionum ad Græcos in Justini operi- bus: οἶκον δὲ καὶ θρόνον λέγομεν τοῦ Θεοῦ τ' ὀυρανὸν, ὀυχ ὡς τοῦ Θεοῦ τούτου πρὸς οἴκησιν ἢ πρὸς καθέδραν χρήζοντος, ὥσπερ ἐγκάπηλιν κ' ἀνεν- δεῶς παντελῶς ὑπάρχοντος, ἀλλ' ἵνα μὴ πρὸς τὸ μέγεθος τῆς ἀυτοῦ ὑποστάσεως καὶ τὸ ἄφθαρτον τῆς ὀυσίας ἀυτοῦ ἀφορῶντες, Θεὸν τοῦτον ἢ ἰσότιμον Θεῷ ὑπολάβωμεν. διὰ τοῦτο ὀνομάζομεν ἀυτὸν οἶκον καὶ θρόνον τοῦ Θεοῦ ταύταις ταῖς ὀνομασίαις πάσας τῆς πρὸς τὸν Θεὸν κατ' ὀυσίαν καὶ κατὰ τὰς τῆς ὀυσίας προσηγορίας κοινωνίας ἀυτὸν χωρί- ζοντες. ὥσπερ γὰρ ὁ οἶκος καὶ ὁ θρόνος ὕστερός ἐστι τοῦ πεποιηκότος ἀυτὸν, ὕτως καὶ ὁ ὀυρανὸς ὕστερός ἐστι τοῦ Θεοῦ, ὡς γεννητὸς τοῦ ἀγεννήτου. Cæterum reducit Christus has formulas juran- di ad locum Deus. VI. 13. X. 20. quod in solius Dei nomine jurandum, ac docet, quod is qui per crea- turam jurat, reductive & indirecte per Deum ipsum juret: & maxime qui per res sacras & cultui divino destinatas jurat, per Deum ad cujus cultum illa destinata sunt jurare censeatur. Altare per se in testem vocari nequit, cum in se nihil divinitatis habeat: sed quatenus inservit sacrificiis, idque ex ipsius Dei ordinatione, qua in recognitionem di- vinæ majestatis super illo offeruntur, eatenus re- lucet in eo divina majestas: unde qui per altare ju- rat, per Deum ipsum jurat, cujus cultui per sacrifi- cia præstando altare est consecratum. Et quan- quam graves obtestationes similes per creaturas in Scripturis habeantur Gen. XLII. 15. Deuter. IV. 26. 1. Sam. I. 26. XX. 3. juramenta tamen proprie dicta non sunt nisi in nomine Domini præstanda, ideoq; duobus modis peccabant Pharisæi, & quod jura- menta per creaturas præstarent, & quod eadem sic præstita, quæ pro veris juramentis ipsi habebant, non servanda censebant, & ita temere perjuria co- mittebant. Licet enim illa vere juramenta non fue- rint, quæ per creaturas fiebant, tamen si animum jurantis spectes, qui ea pro juramentis habebat, o- mnino ea violando perjurium commissum fuit.

## 23:23
V. 23. ἀποδεκατοῦτε] Thus the LXX said δεκάτην ἀποδεκατοῦν for that which is to pay a tithe, Gen. XXVIII. 22, Deut. XIV. 21. And what comes closer to this phrase is ἀποδεκατῶσαι τὸ ἐπιδέκατον τῶν γεννημάτων τῆς γῆς, Deut. XXVI. 12. And thus the Hebrews use עִשֵּׂר in Pihel and הִעְשִׂיר in Hiphil. Tὸ ἡδύοσμον καὶ τὸ ἄνηθον καὶ τὸ κύμινον] Luke, omitting the dill and the cumin, gave the example of mint and rue, adding then the general name καὶ πᾶν λάχανον. And this moves me most of all, lest I think that that Talmudic question is being treated here about certain things to be tithed twice in seed and herb, when that question cannot pertain to all vegetables. The question, therefore, was about vegetables, whether they were included in the law of tithes: Christ, to show the τὸ ἀκριβὲς (exactness) of the Pharisees in matters of that kind, specifically named the smaller vegetables. In the Talmudic book on Tithes, it stands that hyssop and oregano and also vetch are to be tithed: and vetch indeed, because in time of famine it is used for food.

ἀφήκατε τὰ βαρύτερα τοῦ νόμου] You have long since cast aside the care of those precepts of the law which are of much greater weight. But, as we have said elsewhere, natural things outweigh established ones, and those for whose sake others exist outweigh the others.

Τὴν κρίσιν] They err who draw this only to the office of a judge. For the Hebrews used מִשְׁפָּט, and the Hellenists κρίσιν, more broadly. In the Maccabean history, 1 Macc. 8.32, where there is mention of the letter of the Roman Senate to Demetrius on behalf of the Jews: ἵν' ὦσιν ἔτι ἐντύχωσι κατὰ σοῦ ποιήσομεν ἀυτοῖς τὴν κρίσιν: that is, we will cause them to obtain their right. And a little before, ch. VII. 18, concerning Alcimus and those who were with him: ὀυκ ἔστιν ἐν ἀυτοῖς ἀλήθεια, καὶ κρίσις· παρέβησαν γὰρ τὴν στάσιν καὶ τὸν ὅρκον ὃν ὤμοσαν, where κρίσις is justice. In Ezekiel XX. 11, what is מִשְׁפָּטַי in Hebrew, the Greeks translate as δικαιώματα. But מִשְׁפָּט or κρίσις is taken like δικαιοσύνη by the Greeks, sometimes more broadly, so that it comprehends all the duties of men toward one another, in which way Maimonides says that by the word מִשְׁפָּט those precepts are signified which are not ritual; sometimes more strictly, so that it denotes those things which can be demanded by law, opposed to mercy or beneficence: in which way the same Maimonides elsewhere opposes מִשְׁפָּט and חֶסֶד. I believe these words of Christ are clearly taken from Micah ch. VI. 7, where when it had been said that sacrifices do not greatly please God and offerings, it is subjoined that these are the things which God, to be sure, as the weightier matters of the law, principally requires: to do justice, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with God. This third thing, which is the principal one, Luke, who under the name of judgment also includes mercy, called the love of God. Wherefore, so that the sense of Matthew may cohere more correctly both with the Prophet and with Luke, I judge that faith here is not that faith which is observed among men, but hope and confidence placed in divine mercy, which excites humble love and a zeal for obedience in us.

[These things you ought to have done] Christ does not define a controversy of law: but he says this, when it pleases you to interpret the law in such a way, that thing indeed ought to have been performed, but in such a way that the greater and more important things were not omitted.

Grotius rightly observes that judgment does not pertain solely to the office of a judge: since the Hellenists take the Hebrew mishpat, judgment, more broadly, 1 Macc. 8:32, ch. 7:18, Ezek. 22, so that it includes all the duties of men toward one another, or denotes only those things which can be demanded by law, opposed to mercy or beneficence: he thinks, however, that these words of Christ are taken from Micah 6:7, where, after it had been said that sacrifices and offerings do not greatly please God, it is subjoined that these are the things which God, to be sure, as the weightier matters of the law, principally requires: to do justice, to love, and to walk humbly with God. Which third and principal thing Luke, including mercy also under the name of judgment, called the love of God. Wherefore he thinks that faith here is not that which is observed among men, but confidence placed in divine mercy, which excites humble love and a zeal for obedience in us: It must be added, however, that by the word judgment here, the due administration of law and justice is also included: which was neglected by the Pharisees and scribes: since these performed the office of ruling and judging. Thus the Author of the Opus Imperfectum in Matthew, homily 44: In judgments they were unjust, toward their brothers without mercy, toward God always unbelieving. Nor is it sufficiently fitting to understand saving faith here: because Christ objects to the Pharisees those crimes which fell into the eyes of all: and he looks here to the weightier matters of the law: but that faith does not pertain to the law, but to the Gospel. And therefore some prefer to understand faith here not as faith toward men, but as fidelity in keeping pacts and promises, as Lev. 6:2. 2 Kings 12:15, just as also in Jer. 5:1 judgment and faith are joined in the same sense, and likewise 1 Sam. 26:15, 2 Sam. 15:20, Zech. 8:16, faith and mercy. Hilary, Canon 24 on Matthew: They had left behind mercy, and justice, and faith, and every affection of benevolence, which is the proper duty of charity: Luke said judgment and the charity of God: because the Pharisees pursued the judgment and charity of men, but neglected the judgment and charity of God: or he named the charity of God specifically: by which, to be sure, we love our neighbor for the sake of and according to God: for even the Gentiles and tax collectors love those by whom they are loved, Luke 6:32. But this is not yet the charity of God: for that is merely gratuitous, not mercenary, and extends itself even to enemies, and to those from whom no retribution can be hoped for.

Latin:

V. 23. ἀποδεκατοῦτε] Ita δεκάτην ἀποδεκατοῦν pro eo quod est decimam solvere dixerunt LXX. Gen. XXVIII. 22. Deut. XIV. 21. Et quod propius ad hanc phrasin accedit ἀποδεκα- τῶσαι τὸ ἐπιδέκατον τῶν γεννημάτων τῆς γῆς Deut. xxvi. 12. Atq; ita usurpant Hebræi עִשֵּׂר in Pihel & הִעְשִׂיר in Hiphil. Tὸ ἡδύοσμον καὶ τὸ ἄνηθον καὶ τὸ κύμινον] Lucas omisso aneto & cumino exemplum mentæ & rutæ posuit, adjiciens dein- de nomen generale καὶ πᾶν λάχανον. Atq; id vel maxime me movet, ne putem hic tractari quæstionem illam Thalmu- dicam de quibusdam rebus bis decemandis in semine & her- ba, quando ea quæstio ad omnia olera pertinere non potest. Quæstio ergo fuit de oleribus, an lege decimarum compre- henderentur: Christus ut τὸ ἀκριβὲς Pharisæorum in rebus istiusmodi ostenderet, minutiora olera speciatim nomina- vit. In Thalmudico libro de Decimis exstat & hyssopum & origanum & viciam quoque decemandam: & viciam qui- dem, quia famis tempore pro cibo usurpatur.

ἀφήκατε τὰ βαρύτερα τοῦ νόμου] Pridem absecistis curam eorum legis præceptorum quæ multo majoris sunt ponde- ris. Præponderant autem, ut alibi diximus, naturalia consti- tutis, & ea quorum causa cætera sunt cæteris.

Τὴν κρίσιν] Errant qui ad solum judicis officium hoc tra- hunt. Nam Hebræi מִשְׁפָּט, Hellenistæ κρίσιν sumebant la- tius. In Maccabaica historia l. I. 6. VIII. 32. ubi mentio est E- pistolæ Senatus Romani ad Demetrium pro Judæis: ἵν' ὦ- σιν ἔτι ἐντύχωσι κατὰ σοῦ ποιήσομεν ἀυτοῖς τὴν κρίσιν: id est, facie- mus ut jus suum obtineant. Et paulo ante c. VII. 18. de Alci- mo & qui cum eo erant: ὀυκ ἔστιν ἐν ἀυτοῖς ἀλήθεια, καὶ κρίσις· παρέβησαν γὰρ τὴν στάσιν καὶ τὸν ὅρκον ὃν ὤμοσαν, ubi κρίσις est justitia. Ezechielis XX. 11. quod in Hebræo est מִשְׁפָּטַי Græci vertunt δικαιώματα. Sumitur autem מִשְׁפָּט sive κρίσις ut δικαιοσύνη Græcis, modo latius, ut omnia homi- num inter se officia comprehendat, quomodo Maimoni- des voce מִשְׁפָּט ea præcepta ait significari quæ ritualia nõ sunt, modo strictius, ut ea denotet quæ jure exigi possunt, opposita misericordiæ sive beneficentiæ: quomodo & idem Maimonides alibi opponit מִשְׁפָּט & חֶסֶד. Ego hæc Chri- sti verba plane arbitror desumta ex Michea c. VI 7. ubi cum dictum esset Deo haud magnopere placere sacrificia & oblationes, subjungitur, hæc esse quæ Deus scilicet tanquam τὰ βαρύτερα τῦ νόμε præcipue requirat, ποιεῖν κρῖμα κὶ ἀγα- πᾷν ἔλεον, & humiliter cum Deo ambulare. Tertium hoc quod præcipuum est, Lucas, qui κρίσεως nomine etiam ἔλεον comprehendit, vocavit ἀγάπην τῦ Θεῦ. Quare ut Matthæi sensus & cum Propheta & cum Luca rectius cohæreat, ar- bitror πίσιν hic non esse eam quæ inter homines spectatur fidem, sed spem ac fiduciam collocatam in misericordia di- vina, quæ humilem dilectionem & studium obedientiæ in nobis excitat.

[Ταῦτα ἔδει ποιῆσαι] Non definit Christus juris con- troversiam: sed hoc dicit, quando ita vobis lubet legem in- terpretari, præstandum quidem illud fuerat, sed ita ut ma- jora ac potiora non omitterentur.

Recte observat Grotius κρίσιν non ad solum judicis officium pertinere: siquidem Ebræum משפט Hellenistæ κρίσιν latius sumant, 1. Macc. VIII. 32. c. VII. 18. Ezech. XXII. ut omnia hominum inter se officia comprehendat, vel ea tantum denotet, quæ jure exigi possunt misericordiæ, sive beneficentiæ op- posita: desumta autem putat hæc Christi verba ex Mich. VI. 7. ubi cum dictum esset, Deo haud magnopere placere sacrificia & oblationes, sub- jungitur, hæc esse, quæ Deus sc. tanquam τὰ βαρύ- τερα τῦ νόμε præcipue requirat, ποιεῖν κρῖμα ἄγά- πησιν, & humiliter cum Deo ambulare. Quod tertium ac præcipuum Lucas, nomine κρίσεως et- iam ἔλεον comprehendens, vocarit ἀγάπην ῦ Θεῦ. Quapropter πίσιν hic non eam, quæ inter homi- nes spectatur fidem esse existimat, sed fiduciam col- locatam in misericordia divina, quæ humilem dile- ctionem, & studium obedientiæ in nobis excitat: Addendum tamen, quod voce κρίσεως hic etiam comprehendatur administratio debita juris & ju- dicii: quæ neglecta fuit à Pharisæis & scribis: si- quidem hi officio regendi & judicandi functi sint. Sic Autor operis imperf. hom. XLIV. In judiciis erant injusti, in fratres sine misericordia, in Deum semper increduli. Neque satis convenit fidem sal- vificam hic intelligere: quia Christus ea objicit Pharisæis crimina, quæ in omnium oculos incur- rebant: & respicit hic τὰ βαρύτερα legis: fides autem illa non ad legem pertinet, sed ad Evange- lium. Ideoque de fide erga homines, sed fidelitate in servandis pactis & promissis alii πίσιν hic in- telligere malunt, ut Levit. VI. 2. 2. Reg. XII. 15. quemadmodum & Jerem. V. 1. eodem sensu con- jungitur judicium & fides, nec non 1. Sam. XXVI. 15. 2. Sam. XV. 20. Zach. VIII. 16. fides & miseri- cordia. Hilarius Can. XXIV. in Matth. Misericor- diam, & justitiam, & fidem, & omnem benevolen- tiæ affectum reliquerant, quod proprium est chari- tatis officium: Lucas judicium & charitatem Dei dixit: quia Pharisæi judicium & charitatem homi- num sectabantur, judicium & charitatem Dei ne- gligebant: vel charitatem Dei peculiariter nomi- navit: qua nempe propter & secundum Deum pro- ximus diligimus: nam & Ethnici ac publicani di- ligunt eos, à quibus diliguntur, Luc. VI. 32. Sed hæc nondum est charitas Dei: illa enim est mere gratuita, non mercenaria, & extendit se etiam ad inimicos, & ad eos, à quibus nulla retributio spe- rari potest.

## 23:24
Verse 24. Straining out the gnat. To strain out is zarak in Amos 6:6, just as to swallow is bala. A proverbial expression applying to those who wish to appear scrupulously just in minute matters, while they securely neglect the principal duties. And yet, as Philemon used to say, he is just: Not he who promises to take small things, But he who endures not taking great things, Being able to have and to hold them without loss.

Latin:

Vers. 24. διϋλίζοντες τὸν κώνωπα] διϋλίζειν est זרק A- mos VI. 6. sicut καταπίνειν est בלע. Proverbialis locutio in eos competens qui ἀκριβοδίκαιοι videri volunt in rebus mi- nutis, cum præcipua officiorum secure negligant, Atqui ut Philemon dicebat, justus est: Ὅυχ᾿ ὅς τὰ μικρὰ λαμβάνειν ὑπίσχετο, Ἀλλ᾽ ὅς τὰ μεγάλα καρτερεῖ μὴ λαμβάνων Ἔχειν δυνάμενος κό κρατεῖν ἀζημίως.

## 23:25
Verse 25. You cleanse the outside of the cup. The Pharisees indeed washed even cups, as Mark ch. 7:4 teaches us, and we touched upon above. But here the sense is entirely comparative: for Christ means this: when you wash the body, with the mind not cleansed, you do just as much as if you were diligently washing dishes and cups, while in the meantime the food and wine were full of impure filth. For just as this would not profit for health, so neither would that for salvation. It is frequent for Christ, or those describing the things of Christ, to mix in the apodosis of the thing compared for the sake of brevity. And so often one member is left without a corresponding part; the other is nothing but the apodosis: because, to be sure, the one can easily be understood from the other. See Paul, Rom. 9:38, Peter, 1 Ep. 2:6, the Epistle to the Hebrews 6:7, 8, ch. 11:6, ch. 12:25, and Daniel ch. 4:13. Such a thing occurs here too: for the full sentence would have been: but within they are full of cups and platters of evil, just as you indeed cleanse the outside; but within you are full of extortion and uncleanness. Luke similarly mixes the parts of the comparison: but he makes the apodosis more open, when he says: but the inside of you is full of extortion and wickedness. Thus Philo on the wicked woman: brightening the outside with purifications and washings, but being filthy on the inside. This reason moved the Latin interpreter to render for they are full, you are full. A not dissimilar mixture of the parts of comparison is found also among the Greeks, as in Sophocles' Iphigenia: Think of the man, like a polypus, To turn oneself to a genuine mind. For that genuine mind fits the man, not the polypus. Porphyry noted a similar custom in Homer: from the transposition, so that the apodosis may be anticipated by the likeness and the metaphor at the same time. Likewise: to often transpose the words placed appropriately for things into parables, and those from parables into things.

ἐξ ἁρπαγῆς] The ἐξ is pleonastic, just as the ב in the word תמלאמו in Exodus 15:9. It seems to refer to that which is in Ezekiel 28:16, מלו תוכך חמס, which some interpret as 'your midst is filled with iniquity,' which is the same as that in Luke, 'your inward part is full of extortion.' The LXX are accustomed to translate חמס as 'injustice,' 'lawlessness,' or 'transgression'; and that is undoubtedly the meaning. Moreover, the origin itself is ἁρπαγὴ: in the Targum, חטוף, which corresponds directly to the word ἁρπαγῆς, and it is also placed here by the Syrian. If anyone does not approve of the interpretation from us in another way, and says that the cups themselves are pure but full of extortion because they were wickedly acquired, he will be able to establish his interpretation with a not dissimilar passage from Xenophon, near the end of the Cyropaedia: 'He acquired a custom that if they have as much as possible, they are adorned in this way, but if it is clearly from injustice or contrived, they are not at all ashamed of this.'

Latin:

Vers. 25. καθαρίζετε τὸ ἔξωθεν τῦ ποτηρία] Lavabant qui- dem Pharisæi etiam pocula, ut docet nos Marcus c. VII. 4. & supra attigimus. Sed hic omnino sensus est comparativus: hoc enim vult Christus: cum corpus lavatis, animo non pur- gato, tantundem agitis ac si diligenter lavaretis patinas & pocula, cum interim cibus & vinum plena essent impura se- cis. Nam sicut hoc ad sanitatem non prodesset, ita nec illud ad salutem. Frequens est aut Christo aut res Christi descri- bentibus, ut breviloquentiæ causa ἀνταπόδοσιν rei compara- tæ permisceant. Itaque sæpe unum membrum est ἀνυπότακ- δοτον; alterum nihil nisi ἀνταπόδοσις: quia nimirum alterum ex altero facile potest intelligi. Vide Paulum Rom. IX. 38. Petrum 1. Ep. II. 6. Epistolam ad Hebr. VI. 7. 8. c. XI. 6. c. XII. 25. & Danielis c. IV. 13. Tale & hic occurrit: nam plena oratio fuerat ἔσωθεν δὲ γέμουσι τὰ ποτήρια κj οἱ πίνακες κακῶν διερσίας ὅπως κj ὑμεῖς τὸ μὲν ἔξωθεν καθαρίζετε· ἔσωθεν δὲ γέ- μετε ἐξ ἁρπαγῆς κj ἀκαθαρσίας. Lucas similiter partes com- parationis permiscet: sed apertiorem facit ἀνταπόδοσιν, cum dicit τὸ δὲ ἔσωθεν ὑμῶν γέμει ἁρπαγῆς κj πονηρίας. Ita Philo de improba muliere: καθαρσίοις κj λυτροῖς τὰ ἐκτὸς φαιδρυ- νομένη, τὰ δὲ ἐκτὸς ῥυπῶσα. Hæc causa Latinum interpretem movit, ut pro γέμουσι redderet pleni estis. Non dissimilis mix- tura partium comparationis & apud Græcos invenitur, ut Sophoclis Iphigenia: Νόει πρὸς ἀνδρὶ, σῶμα πολύπε ὁμᾶ, Πέτρα τραπέσθαι γνησίᾳ φρονήματι. Nam illud γνησίᾳ φρονήματι, viro convenit non polypo. Similem in Homero morem Porphyrius notavit: ἐκ μετα- πίδωσιν ὡς τῆς ὁμοιώσεως ἅμα καὶ μεταφορᾶς προέχηται τὴν ἀνταπόδοσιν. Item: τὰς οἰκείως τιθεμένας φωνὰς ἐπὶ τῶν πραγ- μάτων, πολλάκις εἰς τὰς παραβολὰς μετατιθέναι, καὶ τὰς ἀπὸ τῶν παραβολῶν εἰς τὰ πράγματα.

ἐξ ἁρπαγῆς] πλεονάζει τὸ ἐξ, quomodo & ב in voce תמלאמו Exodi XV. 9. Videtur respici id quod est Ezech. XXVIII. 16. מלו תוכך חמס, quod quidam exponunt, re- pletum est medium tuum iniquitate, quod idem est cum illo Lucæ, τὸ ἔσωθεν ὑμῶν γέμει ἁρπαγῆς. חמס LXX. solent ver- tere ἀδικίαν, ἀνομίαν, παρανομίαν; atq; ea est haud dubie signi- ficatio. Cæterū ipsa origine est ἁρπαγὴ: in Targum. חטוף, quod directe respondet voci ἁρπαγῆς, atque hic etiam posi- tum est a Syro. Si quis alla am modo a nobis interpretatio- nem non probat, & ipsa pocula pura dici plena raptinæ, quod improbe parta essent, is interpretationem suam stabi- lire poterit non dissimili Xenophontis loco, circa finem insti- tutionis Cyri: νόμιμον ἐκτησατο εἰ μὲν ὡς πλεῖστα ἔχοιεν, ὅὕτω καλλωπίζονται ἢ δ' ἐξ ἀδίκου φανερῶς ἦ μεμηχανημένα, οὐδὲν τοῦτο αἰσχύνονται.

## 23:26
Vers. 26. ἵνα γένηται κj τὸ ἐκτὸς αὐτῶν καθαρὸν] Similar is that saying of Epicharmus, 'If you have a pure mind, you are pure in your whole body.' Paul to Titus 1:15, 'To the pure all things are pure.' Christ says this, however, not because He was abolishing the law concerning legal uncleanness at this time, but because He wished to show that a mind well-conscious of itself is defiled by nothing, against the false persuasion of the Pharisees about which we treated above. Add the passage from Arrian's Epictetus 4.1: 'You would not find the uncleanness of the soul as you would that of the body, but what else would you find of the soul, other than that which renders it filthy in relation to its works?'

Grotius intends this saying, not because Christ wished the law concerning legal impurities to be abolished at this time, but because He showed that a mind well-conscious of itself is defiled by nothing. But Christ does not have regard to the laws concerning legal impurities; but only to the Pharisaic traditions, by which they urged various washings for divine worship, Marc. VII. 3. 4. Matth. XV. 11. 13. 20.

Latin:

Vers. 26. ἵνα γένηται κj τὸ ἐκτὸς αὐτῶν καθαρὸν] Simile est illud Epicharmi, καθαρὸν ἰὰν τὸν νοῦν ἔχῃς, ἅπαν τὸ σῶμα καθα- ρὸς εἶ. Paulus ad Titum I. 15. πάντα καθαρὰ τοῖς καθαροῖς. Hoc autem dicit Christus, non quod legem de immunditiis legalibus hoc tempore aboleret, sed quod ostensum vellet animum sibi bene conscium nulla re inquinari, adversus fal- sam Pharisæorum persuasionem de qua egimus supra. Adde locum Arriani Epicteti IV. 1. ψυχῆς ὡς σώματος ἀκαθαρσίαν οὐκ ἂν ἔυροις, ὡς ψυχῆς δὲ τί ἂν ἄλλο ἔυροις, ἢ τὸ παρίχον ἄυ- τὴν ῥυπαρὰν πρὸς τὸ ἔργα ἀυτῆς.

Dictum hoc vult Grotius, non quod legem de im- munditiis legalibus hoc tempore abolitam vellet Christus, sed quod ostenderit animum bene sibi con- scium nulla re inquinari. At nō respicit Christo leges de immunditiis legalibus; sed traditiones tantum Pharisæicas, quibus lotiones varias ad cultum divi- num urgebant, Marc. VII. 3. 4. Matth. XV. 11. 13. 20.

## 23:27
V. 27. κj πάσης ἀκαθαρσίας] This reading, which the Latin follows, I would prefer to the others if the authority of ancient codices supports it. From there, other readings also seem to arise from the proximity of the word: such as ἀκρασίας, which, although it seems to have been read by Origen, I reject, because the Pharisees, as far as I know, are nowhere accused of that vice: and ἀδικίας, from the interpretation which the Syrian follows; ἀκαθαρσία quite often embraces every kind of vice: nor does πορνεία, which Luke uses in its place, extend any less widely. It corresponds to the Hebrew טמאה.

Rashly, in place of ἀκρασίας, which word is read not only in Origen but is found in most Greek Codices, ἀκαθαρσία is substituted, and the Greek text is corrected from the Latin Vulgate without the authority of any ancient Codex. A few copies read ἀδικίας, because the insides are full of rapine and injustice of every kind: but ἀδικία is comprised under ἁρπαγῇ, and injustice of every kind under rapine as a species, and Christ reproves the Pharisees for both, both because they amassed wealth through rapine and injustice, and because they indulged their genius and pleasures through intemperance.

κεκονιασμένοις] That the comparison of whitewashed work was customary among the Jews to denote hypocritical characters, and whatever we are not openly, is apparent from the words of Paul in Acts 23:3. Conf. Psalm 5:9.

Latin:

V. 27. κj πάσης ἀκαθαρσίας] Hanc lectionem quam Latinus sequitur, si veterum codicum accedat auctoritas, cæteris præferam. Inde etiam naræ videntur lectiones aliæ propin- quitate vocis: ut ἀκρασίας quod quanquam Origeni lectum videtur repudio, quia nusquam Pharisæi, quod sciam ejus vitii arguuntur: & ἀδικίας, ex interpretamento quod Syrus sequitur; ἀκαθαρσία paulo sæpe omne genus vitiorum com- plectitur: nec minus late patet πορνεία quod hujus vice Lu- cas usurpat. Respondet Hebræo טמאה.

Temere loco ἀκρασίας, quæ vox non Origeni tantum lecta, sed in plerisque Codicibus Græcis reperitur, substituitur ἀκαθαρσία, & Græcus textus sine ullius Veteris Codicis auctoritate corrigitur è vulgata Latina. Pauca quædam exemplaria le- gunt ἀδικίας, quod interiora plena sint rapina, & omnis generis injustitia: sed ἀδικία sub ἁρπαγῇ, o- mnis generis injustitia sub rapina tanquam specie comprehenditur, & utriusque causa Christus Pha- risæos reprehendit, & quod per rapinam & inju- stitiam opes conflaverint, & quod genio ac volu- ptatibus per intemperantiam indulserint.

κεκονιασμένοις] Comparationem albarii operis fuisse u- sitatam Judæis ad notandos mores personatos, & quodcun- que palam non sumus, apparet ex Pauli verbis Actor. XXIII. 3. Conf. Psal. V. 9.

## 23:28
Vers. 28. You appear righteous to men, but within you are full of hypocrisy and lawlessness] Eltis. Base within, fair in a beautiful skin.

Latin:

Vers. 28. φαίνεσθε τοῖς ἀνθρώποις δίκαιοι, ἔσωθεν δὲ μεστοὶ ἐστε ὑποκρίσεως καὶ ἀνομίας] Eltis. Introrsum turpes, speciosi pelle decora.

## 23:29
Vers. 29. Because you build] This passage is to be read in one breath up to the end of verse 32. And verse 31 is nothing other than a parenthesis. In order that this passage may be more correctly understood, it must be known that God often interprets the works and sayings of men, not as they wish them to be taken, but in another sense far removed, which fits them most justly. Such is that which God complains of in Amos 5:26, that during the space of 40 years on the journey from Egypt toward Palestine, sacrifices were not made to Him, but to Moloch and other stars, because, forsooth, that people did not worship God with a sincere heart, but was silently inclining toward the worship of idols. Nor is that allusion of Christ to the Samaritan woman, who had said 'I have no husband' (John 4:17), unlike this. It is the same thing to observe in this place. For as to the fact that they confessed that the Prophets were killed by their fathers, Christ accepts this not in the sense they intended: for they called them their fathers by consideration of nature; but Christ [calls them so] also by similarity of character, which they had hitherto declared, and were about to declare more openly. Let this be the paraphrase: It will be ill for you, Pharisees and scribes. For you indeed wish to appear to hold in high regard the Prophets and other servants of God, whose monuments you restore not without ostentation, and you even profess in words that, if you had lived in those times, you would not have been participants in their cruelty (in which matter that is certainly true, more than you wish, that you are the offspring of the 'prophet-killers'), and meanwhile you are no better than they were. For you already carry in your mind what you are shortly about to produce in reality. You are meditating the same thing that they were doing. You honor the dead, because they cannot stand in your way. You pursue the living with hatred that is only satisfied by slaughter, teaching the same things as they did, and more perfectly. Indeed, if anything is lacking to their wickedness, you will fulfill it. In Luke, Christ turns against them not only the words by which they professed themselves the descendants of the 'prophet-killers,' but that very zeal for restoring monuments. For we willingly build the tombs of those whom we would not wish to be alive. Not unlike this is that passage of Demosthenes concerning the false testimony against Stephanus: 'And he did not perceive that the tomb which he was considering as a monument was such a building, but [a monument] of the injustice by which he wronged the man through this.' Nor does that remark of Dio concerning Caracalla go far from this: 'Being vexed at all good men, he pretended to honor some of them after they were dead.' Herod built a magnificent funeral for Aristobulus, whom he had killed. 'To build tombs' is said as in Virgil: 'They build a horse by the divine art of Pallas.' In Cicero: 'to build a fleet.'

Latin:

Vers. 29. ὅτι οἰκοδομεῖτε] Hæc περικοπὴ uno spiritu le- genda est usque ad finem commatis 32. Et comma 31. nihil est aliud quam παρένθεσις. Ut locus hic rectius intelligatur, sciendum est Deum sæpe hominum opera ac dicta interpre- tari, non quomodo illi ea accipi volunt, sed in aliam lon- ge sententiam quæ justissime in ipsos quadret. Tale est il- lud quod apud Amosum V. 26. conqueritur Deus, XL. an- norum spatio in itinere ex Ægypto Palæstinam versus non sibi sacra esse facta, sed Molocho aliisque sideribus, quia scilicet populus ille Deum sincero animo non colebat, sed tacitè vergebat ad cultum idolorum. Neque dissimilis est illa Christi allusio ad Samaritida quæ dixerat οὐκ ἔχω ἄνδρα Joh. IV. 17. Idem hoc loco est animadvertere. Nam quod illi farebantur à patribus suis occisos Prophetas, Christus accipit non in eum sensum quem ipsi volebant: nam ipsi eos patres suos vocabant naturæ intuitu: Christus autem etiam animorum similitudine, quam & declarassent hacte- nus, & apertius essent declaraturi. Paraphrasis hæc esto: Male vobis erit, Pharisæi & legisperiti. Nam vultis qui- dem videri magni facere Prophetas aliosque Dei servos, quorum monumenta non sine ostentatione reficitis, atque etiam verbis profitemini, si illis vixissetis temporibus, non futuros vos fuisse sævitiæ illorum participes (qua in re il- lud certe verum est plus quam vultis, vos esse prolem τῶν προφητοκτόνων) atque interim nihilo meliores estis quam illi erant. Jam enim animo geritis quod brevi prodituri estis reipsa. Idem meditamini quod illi faciebant. Mortuos honoratis, quia vobis obstare non possunt. Superstites eadem quæ illi, & perfectius, docentes odio non nisi per cædem satiando prosequimini. Imo si quid ad ipsorum im- probitatem deest, id vos explebitis. Apud Lucam non ver- ba tantum, quibus se τῶν προφητοκτόνων posteros profite- bantur, sed ipsum illud monumenta reficiendi studium Christus in ipsos torquet. Libenter enim eorum sepulchra extruimus quos nollemus superstites. Cui non dissimilis ille demosthenis locus de falso testimonio in Stephanum: καὶ οὐκ ἠσθάνετο ὅτι ᾧ τῷ τάφῳ μνημεῖον ἐσκεψᾶτο οἰκοδόμημα τοιοῦ- τον ὂν, ἀλλὰ τῆς ἀδικίας ᾗ τὸν ἄνδρα ἠδίκησεν ἐκείνη διὰ τοῦ- τον. Nec longe abit Dionis illud de Caracalla: πᾶσι τοῖς ἀ- γαθοῖς ἀνδράσιν ἀχθόμενος, τιμᾷν τινας αὐτῶν ἀποθανόντας ἐπλάττετο. Herodes Aristobulo quem interfecerat, fu- nus fecit magnificum. οἰκοδομεῖν τάφους dictum ut apud Virgilium: equum divina Palladis arte Ædificant. Apud Ciceronem: ædificare classem.

## 23:30
Vers. 30. In the blood] Just as the Greeks say 'slaughter' instead of 'blood,' so the Hellenists say 'blood' instead of 'slaughter.'

Latin:

Vers. 30. ἐν τῷ αἵματι] Sicut Græci φόνον dicunt ἀντὶ αἵματος, ita Hellenistæ αἷμα ἀντὶ φόνου.

## 23:32
Vers. 32. Fill up] Do this when you wish. Thus the Hebrews not rarely use the imperative mood, as do other nations. 1 Kings 22:22; John 13:27.

The measure] It is a Greek proverb: 'The mills of the gods grind late, but they grind fine.' Concerning this matter, there exists an excellent little book by Plutarch, 'On those who are punished by God slowly.' Thus, indeed, the matter stands: great is the patience of God; but when injured, it becomes fury, as the sacred writings speak in human terms, and He compensates for the slowness of the punishment with its severity: which, as it is sometimes to be seen in the affairs of individual men, so it appears most of all in the divine providence concerning whole peoples. For God punishes the sins of peoples, which have been overlooked, so severely when they have finally exceeded every measure of patience, that while He does no injustice to the men of that age, nor inflicts evils upon them beyond their own merit, yet that punishment appears so great that it seems able to suffice for the expiation of the crimes of all the preceding ages as well. This measure of sins expected by God is called the 'measure or completion of iniquity' (Gen. 15:16), to which there are those who think that which is in Eph. 27:8 and Job 20:22 pertains. Theodectes brings forward another cause for the divine slowness in punishing, which is not to be disapproved, in these verses: 'Whoever of mortals blames the divine, because it does not pursue the unjust immediately but in time, let him hear the reason. For if punishments were immediate, many would worship God for fear and not for a pious way; but now, since the punishment is far off, mortals use their nature, and when they are caught, having been seen to be evil, they pay penalties in later times.'

Latin:

Vers. 32. πληρώσατε] Quando vultis hoc agite. Ita mo- dum imperativum non raro usurpant Hebræi, ut & gentes aliæ 1. Reg. XXII. 22. Joh. XIII. 27.

Τὸ μέτρον] Græcum est adagium: Ὀψὲ θεῶν ἀλέουσι μύλοι, ἀλέουσι δὲ λεπτά. Qua de re egregius exstat Plutarchi libellus περὶ τῶν ὑπὸ τοῦ Θεοῦ βραδέως τιμωρουμένων. Ita nimirum se res habet: ma- gna est Dei patientia; sed læsa furor fit, ut sacræ literæ ἀν- θρωποπαθῶς loquuntur, & tarditatem supplicii gravitate compensat: quod ut in hominum singulorum rebus inter- dum conspicere est, ita maxime apparet in divina circa to- tos populos providentia. Nam populorum delicta diffi- mulata tandem ubi omnem patientiæ modum vicerunt, tam severe punit Deus, ut cum nullam ejus ætatis homini- bus faciat injuriam, neque iis supra proprium meritum ma- la infligat, ea tamen pœna tanta appareat, ut videatur suf- ficere posse omnium etiam antecedentium ætatum scele- ribus luendis. Hic delictorum modus à Deo exspectatus mensura aut complementum iniquitatis dicitur Gen. XV. 16. quo sunt qui pertinere putant quod est Ef. XXVII. 8. & Jobi XX. 22. Causam divinæ in puniendo tarditatis alteram quoque non improbandam affert Theodectes his versi- bus. Ὅστις δὲ θνητῶν μέμφεται τὰ θεῖ ὅτι Οὐκ εὐθὺς ἀλλὰ τῷ χρόνῳ μετέρχεται, Τῆς μὴ δικαίας, πρόφασιν ἐξακουσάτω. Εἰ γὰρ παραυτίκ᾽ ἦσαν αἱ τιμωρίαι, Πολλοὶ διὰ φόβον κᾀὐ δι᾽ εὐσεβῆ τρόπον Θεὸν σέβοιεν᾽ ἂν· νῦν δὲ τῆς τιμωρίας Ἄπωθεν οὔσης, τῇ φύσει χρῶνται βροτοὶ, Ὅταν δὲ φωραθῶσιν, ὀφθέντες κακοὶ, Τίνουσι ποινὰς ὑστέροισιν ἐν χρόνοις

## 23:33
Vers. 33. How shall you escape] Since you are such, how can it be that you avoid the most grievous punishment not only of this age but also of the other?

The judgment of Gehenna] 'The judgment of Gehenna' in the book Pirke Eleazar.

Latin:

Vers. 33. Πῶς φύγητε] Tales cum sitis, qui fieri potest ut gravissimum non hujus tantum sed & alterius sæculi supplicium evitetis.

Τῆς κρίσεως τῆς γεέννης] דינה של גיהנם in libro Pirke Eleazar.

## 23:34
Vers. 34. Therefore] Namely, so that the measure of divine patience may be most fully filled in you, even with me killed. Christ says here that He will send; in Luke He says that He said, that is, that He had determined that 'the wisdom of God' would send, so that, indeed, we might understand that in this embassy destined for the Jews, the divine wisdom appears magnificently. Although here also, at the word 'I send,' it can be understood as 'so that God [sends],' as sometimes among the Prophets.

Prophets, and wise men, and scribes] Luke [says] 'prophets and apostles': not using the word 'apostles' strictly, as some think, for the proper function of the new covenant, but in the way that the word 'shaliachim' was understood at that time, to signify any envoys whatsoever. For so also below in verse 37 and in the other place in Luke, 'prophets' and 'those sent' are joined. Christ says this: that the envoys who were to come to them would be in no way inferior to those whom they called Prophets, or those possessing human wisdom, whom they called 'scribes' (sopherim) and their leaders 'wise men' (chakamim). This, however, pertains to this: that if they do not hear them, they may be 'without excuse,' and by that judgment which they passed upon their own parents, 'self-condemned.' We said above in chapter 13:52 that duties and gifts, however new, are accustomed to be described by an old and more well-known name.

That which Christ says here that he will send, Luke attributes to τῇ σοφίᾳ τοῦ Θεοῦ: not as Grotius wishes, that divine wisdom appears magnificently in this embassy: for it is one thing to send WISDOM, another for wisdom to appear in the sending: but because Christ is the very hypostatic Wisdom of God, to whom that sending is attributed Prov. VIII. 23.

ἀποκτενεῖτε] As James the two and Stephen.

Σταυρώσετε] Christ also, as it seems, numbers himself among the envoys, just as the writer to the Hebrews calls him an apostle. Nor should it frighten us that ἀποκτενεῖτε preceded. For it is a figure which they call syllepsis, which joins many nouns to one verb; which, however, does not properly suit all the nouns. Grammarians note this regarding that line of Virgil: 'Inclusos utero Danaos & pinea furtim Laxat claustra Sinon.' And regarding that line of Lucretius: 'Quam sepire plagis saltum canibusq; ciere.' But also Simon, son of Cleopas, is reported to have been crucified by the work of the Jews.

Μαστιγώσετε ἐν ταῖς συναγωγαῖς ὑμῶν] As John and Peter. See what is above in ch. X. 17.

διώξετε] As Paul and Barnabas often. - There is no doubt that Simon, son of Cleopas, crucified by the work of the Jews, is noted. See Euseb. l. III. Hist. Eccl. c. 32. Hieron. in Catal. illustr. viror. But that Christ is looking to his own crucifixion, and numbering himself among the envoys, does not suit the text: because 'I send' precedes concerning Christ: who is the author and cause of the mission not only of some, but of all those who are said here to be sent; so that it cannot be excused by the figure which they call syllepsis; namely, that many nouns are joined to one verb, which however does not properly suit all the nouns. Because, as we have said, all these were properly sent, and the one sending them is Christ, the hypostatic Wisdom of God. And Christ had already spoken about himself; namely, that they would fill up the measure of their fathers' crimes by driving him to the cross: yet that he would send from heaven Prophets, those skilled in Scripture, and Wise men, whom they would kill and crucify.

Latin:

Vers. 34. διὰ τοῦτο] Scilicet ut mensura divinæ patien- tiæ plenissime in vobis impleatur, etiam me occiso. Chri- stus hic se missurum dicit: apud Lucam ait dixisse, id est constituisse τὴν σοφίαν τοῦ Θεοῦ se missuram, ut nimirum in- telligeremus in hac legatione ad Judæos destinata magni- fice apparere divinam sapientiam. Quanquam & hic ad verbum ἀποστέλλω, intelligi potest, ὥστε Θεὸς, ut interdum apud Prophetas.

Προφήτας, καὶ σοφοὺς, καὶ γραμματεῖς] Lucas προφήτας καὶ ἀποστόλους: vocem ἀποστόλων non stricte usurpans, ut quidam putant pro functione propria novi fœderis, sed quomodo tunc vox ista שליחים intelligebatur, ut legatos quos- vis significaret. Nam ita infra quoque v. 37. & apud Lu- cam altero loco junguntur προφῆται & ἀπεσταλμένοι. Hoc dicit Christus legatos qui ad ipsos venturi essent nihil omi- nores fore iis quos vocabant Prophetas, aut humana sa- pientia pollentes, quos appellabant γραμματεῖς סופרים & eorum principes σοφοὺς החכמים. Hoc autem eo pertinet, ut si eos non audiant sint ἀναπολόγητοι, & ex eo judicio quod ipsi in parentes suos ferebant αὐτοκατάκριτοι. Diximus supra c. XIII. 52. munia & dona quantumvis no- va solere describi veteri magisque noto nomine.

Quod Christus hic se missurum dicit, Lucas τῇ σοφίᾳ τοῦ Θεοῦ tribuit : non ut Grotius vult, quod magnifice divina sapientia in hac legatione appareat: aliud enim est SAPIENTIAM mitte- re, aliud in missione apparere sapientiam: sed quia Christus est ipsa Sapientia Dei hypostatica, cui missio illa tribuitur Prov. VIII. 23.

ἀποκτενεῖτε] Ut Jacobus duos & Stephanum.

Σταυρώσετε] Se quoque ut videtur Christus legatis an- numerat, quomodo cum ad Hebræos Scriptor ἀπόστολον vocat. Neque terrere nos debet quod præcessit ἀπο- κτενεῖτε. Est enim figura quam σύλληψιν vocant, quæ no- mina multra uni conjungit verbo; quod tamen nominibus omnibus proprie non convenit. Notant hoc Grammati- ci ad illud Virgilii: Inclusos utero Danaos & pinea furtim Laxat claustra Sinon. Et ad Lucretii illud: Quam sepire plagis saltum canibusq; ciere. Sed & Cleopæ filius Simon Judæorum opera crucifixus narratur.

Μαστιγώσετε ἐν ταῖς συναγωγαῖς ὑμῶν] Ut Johannem & Petrum. Vide quæ supra c. X. 17.

διώξετε] Ut Paulum & Barnabam sæpe. - Simonem Cleophæ filium Judæorum opera crucifixum notari dubium non est. Vid. Euseb. l. III. Hist. Eccl. c. 32. Hieron. in Catal. illustr. vi- ror. Sed Christum suam crucifixionem respicere, ac se legatis annumerare, non convenit textui: quia de Christo præcedit ἀποστέλλω ἐγώ: qui au- tor & causa est missionis non tantum nonnullo- rum, sed omnium eorum qui hic missi dicuntur; ut per figuram, quam σύλληψιν dicunt, id excusa- ri nequeat; quod sc. nomina multa uni conjunguntur verbo, quod tamen nominibus omnibus non pro- prie convenit. Quia ut diximus, omnes isti proprie missi sunt, & mittens eos est Christus, Sapientia Dei hypostatica. Et de se jam loquutus erat Chri- stus; nimirum mensuram paternorum scelerum eos in se impleturos, sese in crucem acto: missu- rum tamen se de cœlo Prophetas, Scripturæ peri- tos, & Sapientes, quos occisuri, & crucifixuri sint.

## 23:35
Vers. 35. ὅπως ἔλθῃ ἐφ' ὑμᾶς πᾶν αἷμα] αἷμα, which the Hebrews say in the plural דמים, just as it signifies slaughter, so it also signifies the very punishment of the slaughter, as Ps. IX. 12. 1 Kings II. 32. Whence it began to be transferred further to the punishment of other crimes as well, and even to the obligation of punishment, as can be seen in Lev. XX. 9. 13. Then also to the cause of any destruction whatsoever, as 2 Sam. I. 16. Ezek. III. 18.

ἐκχυνόμενον ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς] ἀπὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου, as Luke speaks. ἐκχυνόμενον here and in Luke is for the past, as elsewhere for the future below in ch. XXVI. v. 28. The sense is: the punishments of the Jews in the destruction of Jerusalem will be so horrible that they might seem able to suffice for the expiation of all the homicides that were anywhere perpetrated, when nevertheless they did not equal, let alone exceed, the merits of their punishment, especially those which were known to God more than to men. This consideration, if I am not mistaken, solves many knots of this kind. Compare the place in the Apocalypse, ch. XVIII. 24. It has not been poorly noted by others, however, that Abel and Zechariah of Abel that his blood cried out to God, Gen. IV. 10; but of Zechariah it is said by him as he was dying, May God see and judge, 2 Chron. XXIV. 22.

Zechariah son of Barachiah, whom you murdered between the temple and the altar] That the history touched upon here is the one handed down in the aforementioned place in Chronicles, besides the fact that the sacred scriptures mention no other murdered Zechariah, the very place of the slaughter might prove. For it happened in the open-air space which the Hebrews call חצר, the Greeks αὐλήν, and Josephus ὕπαιθρον, in which was the altar of burnt offerings, in such a way that some open-air part intervened between the altar and the temple building, which is strictly called here by the Hebrews היכל, and by the Greeks ναός: which place Josephus also names in the same way in his history of the war, book five, μέχρι τοῦ βωμοῦ καὶ τοῦ ναοῦ. The same author, in his description of the third enclosure, speaks thus: ὅπαιος ἐν τούτῳ καὶ πρὸ τούτου βωμὸς ἦν, ἐφ᾽ ᾧ τὰς θυσίας ὁλοκαυτῶμεν τῷ Θεῷ. And in the description of Solomon's temple: τό τε θυσιαστήριον τὸ χάλκεον ἵστησι πρὸ τοῦ ναοῦ ἀντικρὺς τῆς θύρας ὡς ἀνοιγεθείσης αὐτῆς καταπρόσωπον εἶναι καὶ βλέπεσθαι τὰς ἱερεργίας. Hecataeus of Abdera: ἐν ταῦθα δ᾽ ἐστὶ κατὰ μέσον μάλιστα τῆς πόλεως περίβολος λίθινος, μῆκος ὡς πεντάπλεθρος, εὖρος, πηχῶν ἑκατόν, ἔχων διπλᾶς πύλας· ἐν ᾧ βωμός ἐστι τετράγωνος. Philo on the Life of Moses: ὁ μὲν οὖν βωμὸς ἵδρυτο ἐν ὑπαίθρῳ τὴν εἴσοδον τῆς σκηνῆς ἀντικρύ, ἀφεστὼς τοσοῦτον ὅσον ἱκανὸν ἦν λειτουργοῖς εἶναι διάστημα πρὸς τὰς καθ᾽ ἑκάστην ἡμέραν ἐπιτελουμένας θυσίας. In the Babylonian Talmud, concerning the measures of the temple, ch. V, it is said that there was a space of 22 cubits between the porch and this altar. Jerome rightly refuted the fable about the father of John the Baptist, which is ownerless and for many reasons not at all likely. The father's name stands in the way: and the suspicion of an error is increased by the fact that, just as that Zechariah had Jehoiada as a father, so the Prophet had Barachiah as a father: so that the scribes might seem to have erred through reliance on memory, because they knew the father of the Prophet Zechariah, and it did not occur to them about the other Zechariah: to which is added that the Hebrew codex of the Nazarenes, which Jerome consulted not in vain so many times and also in this place, had these same things, but instead of the name of Barachiah, the name of Jehoiada: nor was there any reason why the trustworthiness of the Nazarenes or Ebionites should be questioned in this matter. Nevertheless, one thing can defend the antiquity of our reading, which the Greeks, Latins, and Syriac codices defend with great consensus: that among the Hebrews proper names were often changed into others of the same or similar meaning, just as King Solomon was called Jedidiah, but Uzziah was called Azariah. But this had begun to be used most of all in names in which some letters of the Tetragrammaton existed, such as the name יהוידע. Thus, instead of Judah, some preferred to say Thaddaeus, because the name of Judah begins with the letters of the Tetragrammaton. Thus King Jehoiakim was also called Eliakim, 2 Kings XXIII. 34, 2 Chron. XXXVI. 4, and in the history of Judith the same priest is Jehoiakim ch. XV. 10 and Eliakim ch. IV. 5, 10. But just as Thaddaeus means the same as Judas, and Eliakim the same as Jehoiakim, so the meaning is the same in the name of Jehoiada and in the name of Barachiah. For a similar reason, the Chaldean Paraphrast of Lamentations calls that Zechariah who was killed in the temple the son not of Jehoiada but of Iddo, which name was the grandfather of the prophet Zechariah. But the LXX also call this very Zechariah (unless there is a fault in the codex) Azariah. He says 'you murdered' because the people are the same through many centuries. A similar way of speaking is in Mark X. 3, John VI. 32, ch. VII. 19. & 22. Acts VII. 38, and among other writers. I will add this also, that Christ seems to be alluding here to the old history in such a way that there is simultaneously in his words a presage of the future. For the last of the good and distinguished men to be slaughtered by the Jerusalemites, and indeed in the temple itself, was also called Zechariah, and indeed the son of Baruch, which can be held to be the same as the name of Barachiah: whose slaughter was immediately followed by the siege, as can be seen in Josephus.

The explanation concerning the blood that comes upon the Jerusalemites is not inconvenient. We only add that of Augustine, book II, against the adversaries of the law, ch. 5: 'It is one kind, one lump, one mass of the impious succeeding one another by imitation,' just as Grotius also says later: He said 'you murdered' because the people are the same through all the centuries. A similar way of speaking is in Mark X. 3, John VI. 32, VII. 19 & 22, Acts VII. 38, and among other writers. But these things are to be understood concerning Zechariah, not the one who was killed shortly before the first destruction, but concerning that one who was killed around the second destruction. For as Grotius has it later, the last of the good and distinguished men to be slaughtered by the Jerusalemites, and indeed in the temple itself, was also called Zechariah, and indeed the son of Baruch, which can be held to be the same as the name of Barachiah: whose slaughter was immediately followed by the siege, as can be seen in Josephus. But what is to be held concerning the fact that Grotius thinks that the old history is indicated here, 2 Chron. XXIV. 22, and that a presage is simultaneously had of the future slaughter of Zechariah son of Baruch, already designated, we have said concerning that at Zechariah I. 1.

PART II. The slaughter of the Prophets and other messengers of God.

Latin:

Vers. 35. ὅπως ἔλθῃ ἐφ' ὑμᾶς πᾶν αἷμα] αἷμα quod He- bræi pluraliter dicunt דמים, sicut cædem, ita ipsam qunque cædis pœnam significat, ut Psal. IX. 12. 1. Reg. II. 32. Unde porro ad aliorum quoque criminum pœnam, atque adeo pœnæ obligationem cœpit transferri, ut vide- re est Levit. XX. 9. 13. Deinde etiam ad causam qualis- cunque exitii, ut 2. Sam. I. 16. Ezech. III. 18.

ἐκχυνόμενον ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς] ἀπὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου, ut loquitur Lucas. ἐκχυνόμενον hic & apud Lucam pro præterito, ut alibi pro futuro infra cap. XXVI. v. 28. Sensus est: tam horribiles fore Judæorum pœnas in excidio Hierosolymitano, ut sufficere posse videan- tur luendis homicidiis omnibus, quæ usquam erant perpetrata, cum tamen ex pœnæ illorum merita, præser- tim ea quæ Deo magis quam hominibus erant cognita, non æquarent, nedum excederent. Quæ consideratio, ni fallor, multos hujus generis nodos solvit. Confer Apo- calypseos locum cap. XVIII. 24. Non male autem ab aliis annotatum est Abelis & Zachariæ speciatim mentionem fieri, quod de Abele legamus, sanguinem ejus ad Deum clamasse, Gen. IV. 10. de Zacharia autem dictum ab eo moriente, Videat Deus & judicet, 2. Par. XXIV. 22.

Zachariæ υἱῦ Βαραχίου, ὃν ἐφονεύσατε μεταξὺ, τᾶ ναᾶ καὶ τᾶ θυσιαςηρίου] Historiam hic tangi eam quæ dicto Paralipo- menon loco traditur, præterquam quod nullius alterius Zachariæ occisi sacræ literæ meminerunt, vel ipse cædis locus evincat. Facta enim est in subdiali quod חצר vo- cant Hebræi, ἀυλὴν Græci, Josephus ὕπαιθρον, in quo erat altare holocaustorum, ita ut subdialis pars aliqua inter al- tare & ædem templi, quæ hic ναὸς stricte dicitur Hebræis היכל, intercederet: quem locum etiam in historia πε- ρὶ ἁλώσεως libro quinto Josephus eodem modo nominat μέ- χρι τᾶ βωμᾶ κὶ τᾶ ναᾶ. Idem in descriptione τρίτου περιβόλε ita loquitur: ὅπαιος ἐν τότῳ κὶ πρὸ τότε βωμὸς ἦν, ἐφ᾽ ᾧ τὰς θυσίας ὁλοκαυτῶμεν τῷ Θεῷ. Et in descriptione templi Sa- lomonici: τό τε θυσιαςήριον τὸ χάλκεον ἵσησι πρὸ τᾶ ναᾶ ἀντικρὺς τῆς θύρας ὡς ἀνοιγεθείσης ἀυτῆς καταπρόσωπον εἶναι κὶ βλέπεσθαι τὰς ἱερεργίας. Hecatæus Abderita: ἐν ταῦθα δ᾽ ἐςὶ κατὰ μέσον μάλισα τῆς πόλεως περίβολος λίθινος, μῆκος ὡς πεντάπλεθρος, εὖρος, πηχῶν ἑκατὸν, ἔχων διπλᾶς πύ- λας· ἐν ᾧ βωμός ἐςι τετράγωνος. Philo de vita Mosis: ὁ μὲν ὖν βωμὸς ἵδρυτο ἐν ὑπαίθρω τὴν εἴσοδον τῆς σκηνῆς ἀντικρὺ, ἀφεστὼς τοσῦτον ὅσον ἱκανὸν ἦν λειτεργοῖς εἶναι διάστημα πρὸς τὰς καθ᾽ ἑκάςην ἡμέραν ἐπιτελυμένας θυσίας. In Thalmu- de Babylonico de Mensuris templi cap. V. dicitur inter por- ticum & hoc altare spatium fuisse XXII. cubitorum. De Johannis Baptistæ patre ἀδέσποτον & multis de causis mi- nime verisimilem fabulam recte refutavit Hieronymus. Obstat patris nomen: & mendi suspicionem auget, quod ut iste Zacharias patrem Jojadam, ita Prophetæ patrem habuit Barachiam: ita ut videri possint exscriptores pec- casse memoriæ fiducia, quia Prophetæ Zachariæ patrem noverant, nec de altero Zacharia succurrebat: quibus ac- cedit quod codex Hebræus Nazaræorum, quem non fru- stra toties & hoc etiam loco consuluit Hieronymus, eadem hæc habebat, sed pro Barachiæ nomine nomen Jojadæ: nec quicquam erat causæ cur hac in re Nazaræorum, aut E- bionitarum fides argueretur. Vetustatem tamen lectio- nis nostræ, quam magno consensu tuentur Græci: La- tini, Syri codices, una res potest defendere, quod apud Hebræos propria nomina sæpe mutarentur in alia ejus- dem aut vicini significatus, quomodo rex Salomo dice- batur Jedidias, Ozias vero Azarias. Maxime autem id usurpari cœptum erat in nominibus in quibus aliquot literæ nominis τετραγράμματε exstarent, quale est no- men יהוידע. Sic pro Juda quidam malebant Thaddæum dicere, quia Judæ nomen à literis τᾶ τετραγράμματε incipit. Sic rex Jojakim idem dictus & Eliakim 2. Reg. XXXIII. 34. 2. Paralip. XXXVI. 4. & in Judithæ historia idem est Sacerdos Jojakim cap. XV. 10. & Eliakim c. IV. 5. 10. Sicut autem Thaddæus idem valet quod Judas, E- liakim idem quod Jojakim, ita eadem est significatio & in nomine Jojadæ, & in nomine Barachiæ. Simili de causa Chaldæus Paraphrastes Threnorum Zachariam eum qui in templo est occisus, vocat filium non Jojadæ sed עדו quod nomen fuit avo vatis Zachariæ. Sed & hunc ipsum Zachariam (nisi in codice vitium est) LXX. Aza- riam vocant. Ἐφονεύσατε autem dicit, quia populus idem est per multa secula. Simile loquendi genus Marci X. 3. Johan. VI. 32. cap. VII. 19. & 22. Act. VII. 38. & apud Scriptores alios. Addam hoc quoque, videri ita hic Chri- stum alludere ad veterem historiam, ut simul insit ejus ver- bis futuri præsagium. Nam virorum bonorum atque in- signium ultimus ab Hiecosolymitis trucidatus & quidem in ipso templo, dictus itidem est Zacharias, & quidem fi- lius Baruchi, quod cum Barachiæ nomine idem haberi potest: cujus cædem statim secuta est obsidio, ut apud Josephum videre est.

Explicatio de sanguine qui venit super Hie- rosolymitanos non incommoda est. Addimus tan- tum illud Augustini l. II. contr. advers. legis cap. 5. Unum genus, una conspersio, una massa est impio- rum imitatione sibi invicem succedentium, uti etiam postea Grotius: Ἐφονεύσατε autem dixit, quia po- pulus idem est per cuncta secula. Simile loquendi ge- nus Marc. X. 3. Joh. VI. 32. VII. 19. & 22. Actor. VII. 38. & apud Scriptores alios. De Zacharia autem hæc accipienda, non qui paulo ante primum ex- cidium occisus est, sed de illo, qui interfectus est circa excidium alterum. Nam ut postea habet Grotius, Virorum bonorum atque insignium ulti- mus ab Hierosolymitis trucidatus & quidem in ipso templo dictus itidem est Zacharias & quidem Filius Baruchi, quod cum Barachiæ nomine idem haberi potest: cujus cædem statim secuta est obsidio, ut apud Josephum videre est. Quid vero de eo habendum sit, quod Grotius putat & veterem historiam hic indicari, 2. Paral. XXIV. 22. & presagium simul ha- beri futuræ cædis Zachariæ filii Baruchi, jam desi- gnati, de eo diximus ad Zach. I. 1.

PARS II. Cædes Prophetarum & aliorum legatorum Dei.

## 23:37
Verse 37.

Ἱερουσαλὴμ] That is, the Jerusalemites: therefore he adds in the plural number, 'you would not': according to the construction which they call synthesis.

These things are rightly said. Christ addresses Jerusalem, or all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, by the name of Jerusalem, and not merely the leaders of the city, the Priests, Princes, and Doctors, as Gomarus, and following him Balduinus Walæus, perverts the text, lest this illustrious passage interfere with his Calvinist dogma. Thus also Maccovius, Colleg. de prædestin. Disp. IV. p. 13. Indeed, Jerusalem is one thing, and her children, who are expressly distinguished from the city itself, are another. By Jerusalem understand the Priests, Levites, Scribes, and finally the Princes of the people; all these are most opposed to Christ. By the children of Jerusalem understand the people. Christ says that He wished to gather these children, and there is no doubt that He gathered those whom He wished, although against the will of the leaders. Therefore, this passage does nothing for the antecedent will, which they claim here was not fulfilled, when in truth it was fulfilled when it seemed good to God. But this is a vain evasion: for God wished to gather those very people who did not wish to be gathered. For that is what the opposition between 'I would' and 'you would not' implies. To those who could have been gathered, and by the gracious intention of God ought to have been, but did not wish to be gathered, punishment is denounced: Behold, your house is left to you desolate. Which was brought upon not only the leaders of the city, but upon all the inhabitants of Jerusalem. Nor are only the leaders of the city, but the people themselves, and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, accused of having killed the Prophets and stoned those who were sent to them; of which crime not only the leaders were guilty. Finally, Christ did not wish to gather only the people or the rest, excluding the leaders, but the leaders themselves, the Priests, Doctors, Pharisees, and Scribes; for His sermons were directed to them, John V. 34: These things I say to you that you may be saved: which pertains to the antecedent will. Therefore He says Jerusalem, Jerusalem. The reduplication of the address is a demonstration of compassion according to Euthymius in this place. But the fact that most were rejected belongs to the consequent and judicial will, on account of their unbelief, concerning which there is an elegant paraphrase in the author of the Opus Imperfectum, Homily XLVI: You have struggled against my mercy with your sins, but now you have overcome it. For I wish to have mercy on you, but I do not have the strength to perform the mercy, nor can I bear you any longer. For by your incessant iniquities, my mercy, as if now exhausted, has failed in its purpose, etc. How will you be healed, you who allow no Physician to come to you? How shall I cure your infirmity, you who trample upon all medicine? I did not spare my saints, so that I might spare you, a sinner. I neglected their life, so that I might not see your death. All spiritual Physicians have failed in you, and you are not cured. incurable is your suffering, for it has overcome divine art. If I had rejoiced at your death, I would never have sent the Prophets to you. If I had wished to destroy you, I would never have come to you myself. What shall I do for you, if you yourself do not wish to live, etc.

Regarding the opposition of the sons, what Grotius handed down is more correct: namely, those things which will follow immediately.

Vers. 37. ἡ ἀποκτένουσα τοὺς προφήτας] As Isaiah. But also others whose names do not exist. See Nehem. IX. 26.

τοὺς ἀπεσταλμένους] Thus he calls those who were not ordinary Prophets, but were for a time endowed with the divine spirit, such as that Zechariah.

Not only are the times of the Old Testament regarded, or those sent immediately by God, but as the author of the Opus Imperfectum in Matthew, homily 46, rightly observed, also those who were sent in the time of the New Testament: who notes the emphasis in the present tense: He did not say, which you killed and stoned, but which you kill and stone, that is, which you have as a proper and, as it were, natural custom, that you kill and stone the holy ones. Whence Jerome in this place, in that which he says, how often I wished to gather your children, he testifies that all the Prophets sent from himself in the past [were sent].

πρὸς αὐτήν] A locution of the Oriental peoples who, after a relative pronoun or participle, append verbs or pronouns of the third person to the first and second person: which is to be observed in many places of the Hebrews, Syrians, and Arabs.

Such is that of the Syrian in Gal. IV. 21. Say to me you, who wish to be under the law: and in the Hebraism in Micah I. 2. hear all you peoples, Job XVII. 10. and indeed all you (instead of you) will return. Therefore he does not wish to agree with de Dieu against Beza, who said that αὐτὴν is the same as σεαυτὴν. It is, he says, a pure and unmixed Hebraism, which the Syrian and Arab, retaining, translated αὐτὴν by the third person, following the idiom of their languages. Nor is there reason for Camerarius to say that this is a harsh enallage of person. It is certainly not harsh in the Oriental languages: nor do the Ethiopians hesitate to translate: O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, which kills the Prophets and stones the Apostles, who were sent to her. These things are straightforward, and elegant in those languages, as Dievius says.

Ποσάκις ἠθέλησα συναγαγεῖν τὰ τέκνα σου] The children of Jerusalem are called all the Jews, whose metropolis was Jerusalem, to which they all gathered for the sake of sacred rites and judgments, and where they also had a refuge in time of war. Thus also Luke XIX. 24. Christ had already for a whole three years striven to lead these to true repentance and faith by many miracles, many exhortations, and threats, so that he might by this means deliver them from the imminent divine wrath. For this is to gather under the wings: which the LXX translate as ἐν σκέπῃ τῶν πτερύγων σκεπάζειν, Psalm XVII. 8. There is, however, a literal meaning in the word συνάγειν. For the brood, once collected, is covered by the mother's wings. Hence יכנף in Isaiah XXX. 20. The teachers of the Hebrews explain יאסף as συνάξεται, συναχθήσεται, and to them כנופיא is a collection of people, a gathering. By the same simile the Greeks depict singular care and protection: Megala Hercule furente: Οἳ δ᾽ ἡράκλειοι παῖδες ὣς ὑποπτέρους Σώζω, νεοσσὺς ὄρνις ὡς ὑφειμένη. Seneca follows: Qualis accipitris minas Fugit & sparsos metu Colligit faetus avis.

καὶ οὐκ ἠθελήσατε] The Son, the image of the Father, expresses a paternal manner of speaking: for thus God in Ezech. XXIV. 13. I have cleansed you, and you have not been cleansed. And Proverbs I. 24. I called and you refused. In Isaiah ch. LXV. 12. I called and you did not answer: I spoke and you did not hear. And similarly in Jer. ch. VII. 13. Compare also Deut. XXXII. 29, 30. But these whom Christ addresses not only rejected the counsel of God for themselves, as is said in Luke VII. 30, but also hindered other Jews entrusted to their faith from receiving the heavenly warnings, as was said above in verse 13, partly by the power of the Sanhedrin, partly by the authority of the doctors.

Not undeservedly are these compared as parallels. Indeed, Christ was addressing the Pharisees,

and the Scribes specifically: but afterwards, because the inhabitants of Jerusalem rendered themselves participants in similar crimes, the slaughter of the Prophets and others sent to them, he finally addressed the Jerusalemites in general, and threatened them with the punishment of destruction.

Latin:

Vers. 37.

Ἱερουσαλὴμ] Id est ἱεροσολυμῖται : ideo subdit plurali nu- mero, ὠκ ἠθελήσατε : κατὰ σύνθεσιν quam vocant.

Recte hæc dicuntur. Hierosolymam compellat Christus, seu Hierosolymitanos universos, nomine Hierosolymæ, non vero primores urbis tantum, Sacerdotes, Principes, Doctores, ut Gomarus, & ex eo Balduinus Walæus pervertit, ne Calviniano suo dogmati locus illustris officiat. Ita & Macco- vius Colleg. de prædestin. Disp. IV. p. 13. Nempe aliud sunt Hierosolyma, aliud ejus filii, qui diserte ab ipsa urbe distinguuntur. Per Jerosolymam in- tellige Sacerdotes, Levitas, Scribas, denique Princi- pes populi, hi omnes maxime Christo adversantur: Per filios Jerosolymorum intellige populum. Christus dicit voluisse hos filios colligere, nec dubium est, quin collegerit, quos voluit, quanquam invitis primori- bus. Nihil ergo facit hic locus ad voluntatem ante- cedentem, quam hic volunt non impletam, cum re- vera impleta sit, quando Deo visum est. Sed effu- gium vanum est: nam illos ipsos congregare Deus voluit, qui congregari noluerunt. Id enim infert oppositio ἠθέλησα, & ὠκ ἐθελήσατε. Illis qui con- gregari poterant, & ex gratiosa Dei intentione debebant, congregari autem noluerunt, pœna denunciatur: Ecce relinquitur vobis domus vestra deserta. Quæ non primoribus tantum urbis, sed omnibus Hierosolymitanis inducta fuit. Nec pri- mores tantum urbis, sed populus etiam ipse, ac Hierosolymitani universi arguuntur, quod occide- rint Prophetas, & lapidarint eos, qui ad ipsos missi erant; cujus criminis non soli primores rei erant. Denique non populum solum aut reliquos tan- tum Christus congregatos voluit, exceptis primo- ribus, sed ipsos etiam primores, Sacerdotes, Do- ctores, Pharisæos & Scribas, eo enim directæ erant ejus conciones Joh. V. 34. Hæc dico vobis ut salve- mini: quod ad voluntatem antecedentem pertinet. Ideo dicit Jerusalem, Jerusalem. Reduplicatio com- pellationis demonstratio est miserationis secundum Euthymium in h. l. Quod vero reprobati plerique fuerint, voluntatis est consequentis, & judiciariæ, ob incredulitatem nempe ipsorum, de quo elegans est paraphrasis apud autorem oper. imperf. hom. XLVI. Luctata es contra misericordiam meam tuis pecca- tis, nunc autem ipsam superasti. Volo enim in te mise- reri, sed vires misericordiæ faciendæ non habeo, nec possum te amplius jam sufferre. Incessabilibus enim iniquitatibus tuis misericordia mea quasi jam lassa- ta à proposito suo defecit, &c. Quomodo sanaberis, qua nullum ad te Medicum venire permittis? quo- modo curabo infirmitatem tuam, quæ omnem me- dicinam conculcas? Sanctis meis non peperci, ut tibi parcerem peccatrici. Illorum vitam negle- xi, ne tuam mortem viderem. Omnes Medici spirituales in te defecerunt, & tu curata non es. In- sanabilis est passio tua, vicit enim artem divinam. Si de morte tua gavisus fuissem, nunquam ad te mi- sissem Prophetas. Si te perdere voluissem, nunquam ad te ego ipse venissem. Ego tibi quid faciam, si tu ipsa vivere non vis, &c.

De oppositione filiorum rectius se habent, quae Grotius tradidit: quae nempe jamjam se- quentur.

Vers. 37. ἡ ἀποκτένουσα τοὺς προφήτας] Ut Esaiam. Sed & alios quorum non exstant nomina Vid. Nehem. IX. 26.

τοὺς ἀπεσταλμένους] Ita vocat eos qui Prophetae ordinarii non erant, sed ad tempus divino spiritu induebantur, qua- lis ille Zacharias.

Non tantum Vet. Testam. tempora respici- untur, aut immediate a Deo missi, sed ut recte au- ctor operis imperf. hom. XLVI. observavit, etiam illi, qui missi sunt Nov. Testam. tempore: qui no- tat emphasin in praesenti tempore: Non dixit, quae occidisti & lapidasti, sed quae occidis & lapidas, hoc est quae hoc proprium, & quasi naturalem consuetu- dinem habes, ut occidas & lapides sanctos. Unde Hieron. in h. l. in eo, quod dicit, quoties volui con- gregare filios tuos, omnes retro Prophetas a se mis- sos esse testatur.

πρὸς αὐτήν] Locutio Orientalium populorum qui pri- mae & secundae personae post pronomen relativum aut participium subjungunt verba aut pronomina personae ter- tiae: quod multis in locis Hebraeorum, Syrorum, Ara- bum observare est.

Tale est illud Syri Gal. IV. 21. Dicite mihi vos, qui volunt, ut sint sub lege: & in Ebraismo Mich. I. 2. audite populi omnes illi, Job. XVII. 10. & profe- cto omnes illi (pro vos) revertemini. Ideo non as- sentiri vult de Dieu Bezae, qui αὐτὴν dixit idem es- se, quod σεαυτὴν. Est enim, inquit, purus putus Ebraismus, quem Syrus & Arabs retinentes αὐτὴν verterunt per tertiam personam sequentes lingua- rum suarum idiotismum. Neque est quod Camera- rius dicat, duram hanc esse personae enallagen. Non est sane dura in linguis orientalibus: nec dubitant Aethiopes convertere: O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, quae occidit Prophetas & lapidat Apostolos, qui missi sunt ad eam. Expedita haec sunt, & elegantia in istis linguis dicente Dievio.

Ποσάκις ἠθέλησα συναγαγεῖν τὰ τέκνα σου] Filii Hierso- lymorump vocantur Judaei omnes, quorum μητρόπολις erat Hierosolyma, quo conveniebant omnes sacrorum, judiciorumque causa, quo & belli tempore receptum ha- bebant. Sic & Luc. XIX. 24. Hos Christus jam toto triennio multis miraculis, multis adhortationibus ac comminatio- nibus ad veram poenitentiam & fidem perducere studue- rat, ut eos hac ratione ab imminenti ira divina liberaret. Nam hoc est sub alas congregare: quod ἐν σκέπῃ τῶν πτε- ρύγων σκεπάζειν vertunt LXX. Psal. XVII. 8. Est autem κυ- ριολεξία in voce συνάγειν. Collecta enim pullities mater- nis aliis tegitur. Hinc יכנף Isaiae XXX. 20. Hebraeorum magistri exponunt יאסף συνάξεται, συναχθήσεται, & iis- dem כנופיא est populi collectio, σύναξις. Eadem si- militudine Graeci curam ac tutelam singularem depingunt: Megala Hercule furente: Οἳ δ᾽ ἡράκλειοι παῖδες ὣς ὑποπτέρους Σώζω, νεοσσὺς ὄρνις ὡς ὑφειμένη. Seneca sequitur: Qualis accipitris minas Fugit & sparsos metu Colligit faetus avis.

καὶ οὐκ ἠθελήσατε] Paternum loquendi genus filius, imago Patris, exprimit: ita enim Deus Ezech. XXIV. 13. Mundavi te, & te non mundasti. Et Proverb. I. 24. Voca- vi & renuistis. Apud Esaiam c. LXV. 12. Vocavi & non re- spondistis: locutus sum & non audistis. & similiter apud Jer. c. VII. 13. Confer & Deut. XXXII. 29. 30. Isti autem quos Christus alloquitur, non modo τὴν βουλὴν τοῦ Θεοῦ ἠθέτησαν εἰς ἑαυτούς, ut dicitur Luc. VII. 30. sed alios quoque Judaeos fidei suae creditos impediebant ne caelestia monita recipe- rent, ut supra dictum est commate 13. partim potestate Synedrii, partim doctorum auctoritate.

Non immerito haec ceu parallela conferun- tur. Nimirum compellabat Christus Pharisaeos,

& Scribas specialiter: sed postmodum quia cri- minum similium, cædis Prophetarum & aliorum ad ipsos missorum Hierosolymitani sese etiam participes reddiderunt, universim tandem Hie- rosolymitanos compellavit, iisque excidii pœnam comminatus est.

## 23:38
Vers. 38. ἀφίεται ὑμῖν ὁ οἶκος ὑμῶν ἔρημος] This place in which you, O Jerusalemites, dwell, shall be turned into a solitude. For I would prefer the city to be understood rather than the temple alone. For this is οἶκος, which in Hebrew is טירה Psalm LXIX. 26. for which the LXX translated ἔπαυλιν, whom Luke follows in the Acts: Jerome, a dwelling: unless one prefers that the words of Jeremiah be regarded, in whom God speaks thus c. XII. 7. עזבתי את־ביתי נטשתי את־נחלתי ἐγκαταλέλοιπα τὸν οἶκόν με’ ἀφῆκα τὴν κληρονομίαν με. or those of the same Prophet c. XXII. 5. כי לחרבה יהיה הבית הזה εἰς ἐρήμωσιν ἔσται ὁ οἶκος ὗτος. ὑμῖν here is clearly redundant, just as the ancient Latins used to say suum sibi. Thus in the Syrian in the following chapter, verse 43. דמטת לה & elsewhere often.

Latin:

Vers. 38. ἀφίεται ὑμῖν ὁ οἶκος ὑμῶν ἔρημος] Locus iste in quo vos o Hierosolymitæ habitatis, in solitudinem verte- tur. Urbem enim malim intelligi quam templum solum. Est enim hic οἶκος, quod in Hebræo טירה Psal. LXIX. 26. pro quo ἔπαυλιν verterunt LXX. quos in Actis sequitur Lucas: Hieronymus commorationem: nisi quis malit Jere- miæ verba respici, apud quem Deus ita loquitur c. XII. 7. עזבתי את־ביתי נטשתי את־נחלתי ἐγκαταλέλοι- πα τὸν οἶκόν με’ ἀφῆκα τὴν κληρονομίαν με. aut illa ejusdem Prophetæ c. XXII. 5. כי לחרבה יהיה הבית הזה εἰς ἔ- ρήμωσιν ἔσται ὁ οἶκος ὗτος. ὑμῖν hic manifeste παρέλκει, quo- modo Latini veteres suum sibi dicebant. Ita apud Syrum capite sequenti comminate 43. דמטת לה & alibi sæpe.

## 23:39
Vers. 39. ἕως ἂν εἴπητε] That is, until you shall be very willing to say. Recently they had suppressed the boys acclaiming auspicious things to Jesus. Jesus says that the time will come when they themselves will willingly use that acclamation, if by that means they could wheedle his favor, namely then, when they see him constituted by the Father as judge of the world. See Philipp. II. 10. which passage pertains to the same thing. For it seems harsh to me to draw this to the conversion of the Jews: since the whole discourse is comminatory, and pertains to the men of that age, which the word γενεᾶς indicates.

We do not disapprove of these: for the words of Christ are explained more conveniently in this way than if they were either drawn to conversion or understood negatively: that is, you will never see me, because you refuse to acknowledge me as the Messiah. The explanation of the blessed Gerhard in Harm. Evangel. c. CLVIII. p. 259 comes to almost the same thing. It is most simply taken as referring to the final coming of Christ for judgment, in which the unbelieving Jews, even against their will, are compelled to acknowledge that he himself is the true Messiah, to whom their ancestors deservedly shouted: Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.
