The sense therefore is: You shall not see me hereafter, that is, I shall withdraw from you my visible and gracious presence, you shall no longer enjoy the preaching of the Gospel and the benefits hitherto offered to you in it, until at length at my final return for judgment you shall say, that is, you shall experience in reality, and in your hearts you shall be compelled to acknowledge, being convinced, that I am the true Messiah: for by the words the thing itself is indicated according to a common Hebraism. Thus B. Gerhard, who observes concerning the little word ἀπ’ ἄρτι that it denotes a time not indeed already present, but immediately impending, as Chrysost. has it in Hom. LXXV. That à modo signifies not that hour, but the whole time up to the passion. Inconvenient is the explanation of Calixtus in Conc. Evang. You shall not see me by the light of intellect and faith, until you yield to the truth, and confess me blessed of the Lord, which is the same as if he said, you shall not acknowledge me as Christ, until you acknowledge me. The gloss in Cornelius à Lapide concerning the conversion of the Jews by Elijah towards the end of the world is unworthy of being cited.

Latin:

Vers. 39. ἕως ἂν εἴπητε] Id est donec libenter admodum dicturi sitis. Nuper pueros fausta Jesu acclamantes com- presserant. Ait Jesus venturum tempus cum libenter ipsi ea usuri sint acclamatione, si ea ratione ipsius gratiam pos- sent eblandiri, tum scilicet, cum ipsum videbunt à patre judicem mundi constitutum. Vide Philipp. II. 10. qui locus eodem pertinet. Nam ad conversionem Judæorum hæc trahere durum mihi videtur: cum tota oratio sit commi- natoria, & ad ejus ætatis homines pertineat, quod vox γενεᾶς indicat.

Non improbamus hæc: commodius enim ita explicantur verba Christi, quam si vel ad conver- sionem trahantur, vel negative intelligantur: id est, nunquam me videbitis, quia me Messiam a- gnoscere recusatis. Eodem fere redit B. Gerhardi explicatio in Harm. Evangel. c. CLVIII. p. 259. Simplicissime accipitur de ultimo Christi ad judi- cium adventu, in quo Judæi increduli etiam invi- ti agnoscere coguntur, ipsum esse verum Messiam, cui majores ipsorum merito acclamaverint: Be- nedictus, qui venit in nomine Domini. Sensus ergo est: Non videbitis me post hac, hoc est, subtraham vobis meam visibilem & gratiosam præsentiam, non fruemini amplius prædicatione Evangelii & be- neficiis in eo vobis hactenus oblatis, donec tandem in novissimo meo ad judicium reditu dicatis, hoc est, reipsa experiamini, & in cordibus vestris convicti agnoscere cogemini, me esse verum Messiam: per verba enim indicatur res ipsa juxta usitatum He- braismum. Hæc B. Gerhardus, qui de vocula ἀπ’ ἄρτι observat, quod denotet tempus non quidem jam præsens, sed statim instans, ut Chrysost. habet Hom. LXXV. Illud à modo non illam horam, sed u- niversum usque ad passionem tempus significat. In- conveniens est Calixti explicatio in Conc. Evang. Non videbitis me lumine intellectus & fidei, usque dum veritati manus detis, & me benedictum Domi- ni confiteamini, quod idem est ac si diceret, non agnoscetis me Christum, usque dum agnoscetis. Glossa apud Cornelium à Lap. de conversione Ju- dæorum per Eliam sub finem mundi, indigna est, quæ referatur.

## 24:1 Argument
CAPUT XXIV. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Monstrato à discipulis templi ædificio Jesus ejus devastationem prædicit, & in monte Oliveti quærentes signa excidii templi & mundi informat primum quidem πανωλεθρίαν templi antecessuros rumores belli, cum bellis variisque malis, persecutionibus Apostolorum, ortu falsorum Prophetarum, injustitia ac defectu charitatis: præconium etiam Evangelii prius futurum in toto orbe, world, but when the abomination of desolation is seen, that flight must be taken, and that a great calamity will be, but that the time will be shortened because of the danger of seduction by false Christs and Pseudo-Prophets. Then he proposes the signs that will precede the end of the world, and he treats of the coming of the Son of man in the clouds, and of the angels who will gather the elect, but that no one knows that day, and that the last times will be like the times of the flood, and so one must be vigilant, he teaches by the parable of the householder watching for a thief: and he praises the faithful servant, but threatens the unfaithful one with a reward with the hypocrites.

There are three parts: I. Concerning the destruction of the temple and the signs of the same, up to v. 28. II. Concerning the signs of the last coming of Christ, up to v. 35. III. An exhortation to perpetual vigilance because of the ignorance of the last day, up to v. 51.

PART I. Concerning the destruction of the temple, and the signs of the same.

Vers. 1. From the temple] Towards the mount of Olives, as Mark ascribes, from where there is an excellent view of the temple, because the part of the walls of the temple subject to that mountain was lower than the other parts. to show him the buildings of the temple] As those are accustomed to do who admire the magnitude and firmness of some work: The temple was of immense wealth, said Tacitus: and soon after: The temple in the manner of a fortress and its own wall by labor and work before others: the very porticoes which surrounded the temple, an excellent bulwark. Then: they built walls in peace, as if for war. Josephus calls it the most wonderful work of all that we have received by hearsay, both for its construction and size and for the luxury of each part. Add Philo on Monarchy II. and on the embassy to Gaius. Although, however, Herod the Great had renovated the temple from its foundations in order to enlarge it, yet since he also used the old material, and did not tear down the whole temple at once, but by parts as much as was to be renovated at each time, it is rightly said that this temple was the same as that which had been built by Zerubbabel. And thus Josephus says twice that the temple was destroyed, once by the Chaldeans, and a second time by Titus: and the teachers of the Jews call the destruction of Titus the destruction of the second temple, and the times which precede that destruction, the times of the second temple. While this temple stood, the Messiah was to be expected according to the prophecy not only of Daniel, but also of Haggai ch. II. 9. with the addition of what is in Malachi III. v. 1.

Latin:

CAPUT XXIV. ARGUMENTUM ET PAR- TITIO.

Monstrato à discipulis templi ædificio Jesus e- jus devastationem prædicit, & in monte O- liveti quærentes signa excidii templi & mundi informat primum quidem πανωλε- θρίαν templi antecessuros rumores belli, cum bellis variisque malis, persecutionibus Apostolorum, ortu falsorum Prophetarum, injustitia ac defectu charitatis: præconium etiam Evangelii prius futurum in toto orbe, orbe, visa autem abominatione desola- tionis fugam arripiendam esse, magnam- que calamitatem futuram, sed tempus ab- breviatum iri ob periculum seductionis à falfis Christis, & Pseudo-Prophetis. De- inde signa proponit finem mundi ante- gressura, & de adventu Filii hominis in nubibus, & angelis collecturis electos agit, diem autem illum neminem nosse, & tem- pora novissima similia fore temporibus di- luvii, adeoque vigilandum esse, parabola patrisfamilias ob furem vigilantis docet: ac servum fidelem laudat, infido vero mi- natur mercedem cum hypocritis.

Partes sunt tres: I. De excidio templi & si- gnis ejusdem, ad v. 28. II. De signis adventus Christi novissimi, ad v. 35. III. Adhortatio ad vi- gilantiam perpetuam ob ignorantiam diei novif- simæ, ad v. 51.

PARS I. De excidio templi, & signis ejusdem.

Vers. 1. Ἀπὸ τῦ ἱερῦ] Versus montem Oliveti, ut Mar- cus ascribit, unde optimus in templum despectus, quod subjecta ei monti pars murorum templi esset depressior partibus cæteris. ἐπιδεῖξαι αὐτῷ τὰς οἰκοδομὰς τῦ ἱερῦ] Ut solent qui operis alicujus magnitudinem ac firmitatem admirantur: Im- mensæ opulentiæ templum, dixit Tacitus: & mox: Tem- plum in modum arcis propriique muri labore & opere ante alios: ipsæ porticus quis templum ambiebant, egregium pro- pugnaculum. Deinde: struxére muros in pace, tanquam ad bellum. Josephus vocat ἔργον πάντων ὧν ὑφ᾽ ἡμῖν ἀκοῇ παρειλήφαμεν θαυμασιώτατον κατασκευῆς τε ἕνεκα καὶ μεγέ- θες ἔτι τῆς καθ᾽ ἕκαςον πολυτελείας. Adde Philonem de Mo- narchia II. & de legatione ad Cajum. Quanquam autem Herodes magnus templum ut augeret à fundamentis no- vaverat, tamen cum & materia usus sit veteri, & non totum simul templum diruerit, sed per partes quantum quoque tempore innovandum erat, recte templum hoc idem fuisse dicitur quod structum erat à Zorobabele. Atque ita Jose- phus bis dicit templum dirutum, semel à Chaldæis, iterum à Tito: & Judæorum magistri excidium Titi vocant exci- dium templi secundi, & tempora quæ id excidium ante- cedunt, tempora secundi templi. Hoc templo stante ex- spectandus erat Messias ex vaticinio non Danielis tan- tum, sed & Aggæi cap. II. 9. addito quod est apud Mala- chiam III. v. 1.

## 24:2
Vers. 2. that there shall not be left here one stone upon another, which shall not be thrown down] That was indeed true also of the city, which itself, as Josephus speaks, was uprooted from its foundations, and as the same says elsewhere, it was vanished, so leveled that it would never again provide a belief to those who approached that it had been inhabited, with a few towers excepted as a monument of victory, and a part of the wall which served in place of a rampart for the Roman soldier, but Christ speaks properly of the temple, whose magnificence and firmness, as we have said, the disciples were admiring. That, however, was clearly destroyed, with no part of it saved. Just as in the construction of the temple it is said that a stone is placed upon a stone, Haggai II. 16. so in the destruction it is said that a stone is not left upon a stone.

Latin:

Vers. 2. 8 μὴ ἀφεθῇ ὧδε λίθος ἐπὶ λίθον, ὃς ὐ μὴ κατα- λυθήσεται] Erat id quidem verum & de urbe, quæ & ipsa, ut Josephus loquitur, πόῤῥιζεν ἐκ βάθρων ἀνῄρηται, & ut alibi idem ait, ἠφάνισαι ὕτως ἐξομαλισθεῖσα ὡς μηδέποτ᾽ οἰ- κηθῆναι πίσιν ἂν ἔτι παρασχεῖν τοῖς προσελθῦσι, paucis turri- bus exceptis in monumentum victoriæ, & muri parte quæ valli vice esset Romano militi, sed proprie de templo agit Christus, cujus, ut diximus, & magnificentiam & fir- mitatem discipuli admirabantur. Id autem plane dirutum est, nulla ejus parte servata. Sicut in structione templi di- ctus est lapis poni super lapidem, Aggæi II. 16. ita in de- structione non relinqui lapis super lapidem.

## 24:3
Vers. 3. his disciples] The article here has the force of an indefinite pronoun. For the sense is, some of the disciples, whom Mark names as four. when shall these things be, and what is the sign of thy coming and of the end of the world?] On the occasion of what Christ had said about the destruction of the temple, the disciples, asking Christ about the time of that destruction, ask two things besides, which Matthew has set forth distinctly, not expressed in the same way by others: namely, what would be the epochs both of the coming of Christ and of the end of the ages; not that they thought these three questions fell into one and the same thing, but because they desired that the chief of the imminent events be predicted to them all at once. They thought they had already sufficiently imbibed the dogmas of Christ; now they desire to hear prophecies from him, relying on that promise by which Christ had said that he would reveal many secrets to them apart from the rest of the crowd. Many do not distinguish the coming of Christ from the consummation of the ages, deceived, if I am not mistaken, by the ambiguity of the word: for it is most certain that the word coming is used in a manifold meaning. But Matthew distinguishes this question no less from the third, than he does this and the third from the first: And Christ, if I see correctly, answers distinct questions distinctly, the first up to verse 23, the second from there to verse 30, the last in the following verses. Wherefore I interpret coming here, not as judgment, but as the kingdom of the Messiah, which the disciples thought would be illustrious with external splendor. The argument for my opinion is that those words, if they say he is here or there, do not go out, which Christ uses here to solve the question concerning the coming, as can be seen below in v. 23, 26, 27, are also found in Luke ch. XVII. 22, 23, where likewise the comparison of lightning appears. In the same place, however, Christ most clearly shows that he is dealing with his kingdom, which he calls the kingdom of God, according to the common Jewish manner of speaking, signifying that that very kingdom would come without observation. Let the diligent reader compare the passages: and he will see that it is almost always so, as I say. I confess indeed that by the word coming that advent of judgment is often signified: but that is not perpetual. For Peter, designating the efficacy of Christ by the word coming, joins power and coming 2. Ep. ch. 1. 16. And there are also other places in the Apostolic Scriptures which receive that interpretation. The ancient Christians also received that manner of speaking from the Apostles: as Justin, dealing with the growing number of Christians in their very punishments: for the more they are punished, the more others abound; these seem to be the works of men, these are of the power of God. These are the proofs of his coming. Chrysostom defines the gospel as the coming of the Lord Jesus Christ through the word.

Grotius notes that three things are asked: 1. concerning the destruction of the temple, 2. concerning the sign of the coming of Christ, 3. and the end of the ages. And so also Hilary, Canon XXV, and Jerome in this place. But they and most other ancients understand the second question concerning the second coming. Augustine, however, in Epistle 80 to Hesychius, seems to take it concerning the spiritual coming. To which the opinion of Grotius also tends: whose explanation does not seem to be disapproved. It is certainly better to have a distinct explanation of the signs and time of the Jewish destruction, the coming of the kingdom of Christ, and the final judgment, than if you were to say, as some do, that in Christ's response the questions concerning the destruction of the people and the consummation of the age are mixed together, and that the signs of the former are explained in such a way that the same signs are also established for the final coming of Christ: which confusion only produces various difficulties, and should not be rashly attributed to Christ, the heavenly Teacher and the best interpreter of divine things.

Latin:

Vers. 3. οἱ μαθηταὶ αὐτᾶ] Articulus hic vim habet pro- nominis indefiniti. Sensus enim est, τινὲς ἢ μαθητῶν, quos Marcus quatuor nominat. πότε ταῦτα ἔσαι, κὶ τί τὸ σημεῖον τῆς σῆς παρεσίας κὶ τῆς συν- τελείας τῷ αἰῶν;] Occasione ejus quod Christus de excidio templi dixerat, discipuli de ejus excidii tempore Christum interrogantes, duo præterea quærunt, quæ ab aliis non it- dem expressa Matthæus distincte posuit: nempe quæ futuræ essent ἐποχαὶ tum adventus Christi, tum finis sæculorum; non quod has tres quæstiones in unum idemque recidere existimarent, sed quod rerum imminentium præcipuas una opera sibi prædici cuperent. Dogmata Christi jam satis imbibisse se putabant; nunc vaticinia ab ipso audire de- siderant, freti ea pollicitatione qua Christus dixerat multa se arcana seorsim à plebe cætera ipsis revelaturum. Παρυ- σίαν Christi à consummatione sæculorum multi non distin- guunt, vocis ni fallor ambiguo decepti: nam multiplici si- gnificatu usurpari παρεσίαν certissimum est. At Matthæus distinguit hanc quæstionem non minus à tertia, quam hanc & tertiam à prima: Et Christus, si quid video, distinctis quæstionibus distincte respondet, primæ ad comma usque 23. secundæ inde ad comma 30. postremæ in sequen- tibus. Quare παρουσίαν hic interpretor, non judicium, sed regnum Messiæ, quod illustre fore splendore externo discipuli putabant. Argumentum sententiæ meæ est, quod verba illa, si dixerint hic aut illic est, ne exite, quæ hic Chri- stus usurpat ad solvendam quæstionem περὶ τῆς παρουσίας ut videre est infra v. 23. 26. 27. apud Lucam quoque inveniun- tur c. XVII. 22. 23. ubi itidem fulminis apparet compara- tio. Eodem autem loco clarissime ostendit Christus agere se de regno suo, quod regnum Dei, loquendi more Judaico usitato, appellat, id ipsum regnum venturum significans ὦ μέ- τα παρατηρήσεως. Conferat diligens lector loca: videbitque fere in habere, ut dico. Fateor quidem παρουσίας voce sæpe illum judicii adventum significari: sed id perpetuum non est. Nam Petrus παρουσίας voce efficaciam Christi designans conjungit δύναμιν καὶ παρουσίαν 2. Ep. cap. 1. 16. Et alia quoque sunt in Apostolicis Scriptis loca quæ eam recipiunt inter- pretationem. Veteres quoque Christiani ab Apostolis eum loquendi morem acceperunt: ut Justinus de crescente in ip- sis suppliciis Christianorum numero agens: ὅσῳ γὰρ πλείονες κολάζοντες, τοσούτῳ πλεονάζοντας ἄλλους; Ταῦτα ἀν- θρώπων δοκεῖ τὰ ἔργα, ταῦτα δυνάμεώς ἐστι τοῦ Θεοῦ. Ταῦτα τῆς παρουσίας αὐτοῦ δείγματα. Chrysostomus εὐαγγέλιον definit τὸ διὰ λόγου κυρίῳ Ἰησοῦ Χριστῷ παρουσίαν.

Tria quæri notat Grotius 1. de excidio templi, 2. de figno adventus Christi, 3. & finis seculorum. Atque ita etiam Hilarius Can. XXV. & Hieron. in h. l. Sed illi & plerique alii Veteres de adventu secundo quæ- stionem alteram intelligunt. Augustinus tamen Epist. XXC. ad Hesych. de spirituali adventu vi- detur accipere. Quo etiam sententia Grotii abit: Cujus explicatio non videtur improbanda. Præstat certe distincta de signis & tempore exci- dii Judaici, adventus regni Christi, & judicii no- vissimi explicatio, quam si cum nonnullis in re- sponsione Christi quæstiones de excidio populi, & consummatione seculi commisceri, & signa il- lius ita explicari dicas, ut eadem etiam signa con- stituantur adventus novissimi Christi: quæ confu- sio varias difficultates tantum parit, neque temere Christo cœlesti Doctori, & optimo rerum divi- narum interpreti tribuenda est.

## 24:4
Verse 4. βλέπετε μή τις ὑμᾶς πλανήσῃ [Take heed that no man deceive you]: Christ begins to explain those things which are to precede the destruction of the temple.

Latin:

Vers. 4. βλέπετε μή τις ὑμᾶς πλανήσῃ] Incipit Christus explicare ea quæ excidium templi sint antecessura.

## 24:5
Verse 5. ἐπὶ τῷ ὀνόματί μου [in my name]: The name, as we have said elsewhere, signifies many things: but often the office or dignity of someone. Therefore, it is said here that those will arise who would claim for themselves that dignity which is proper to Jesus: that is, as follows, who will say that they themselves are Christs. Otherwise, a Name is a mandate, in which sense those same people are said to come in their own name, John 5, verse 43, that is, instructed by no mandate, but by their own daring.

Ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ χριστός [I am the Christ]: Although ψευδόχριστοι [false Christs] are also ψευδοπροφῆται [false prophets] by a more general name, they are nevertheless usually distinguished, as can also be seen below in verse 24. By the name of Christ, the Jewish people understood a vindicator of liberty. For that 'but we trusted that it had been he which should have redeemed Israel' (Luke 24, verse 21) is a description of the name of Christ. Wherefore, whoever said they were divinely sent liberators of the Jewish people, by that very fact they professed themselves to be Christs, and were ψευδόχριστοι [false Christs]. Such was Theudas, not the one named by Gamaliel, but another impostor (γόης) of the same name, who, while Cuspius Fadus was governing Judea, called a great multitude of the common people to himself, promising that at the command of his word the waters of the Jordan would part, so that a way would be open for those crossing: but when he was captured with a great slaughter of his followers, he paid the penalty by being beheaded by Fadus. Such also were those πλάνοι, γόητες, καὶ ἀπατεῶνες [deceivers, impostors, and swindlers], as Josephus names them, who, while Felix was procurator, under the pretext of divine inspiration (προσχήματι θεασμοῦ), imposed upon men, persuading them to follow them into the wilderness, where they would see the greatest signs and miracles: which likewise was the destruction of many, and at the same times an impostor from Egypt, who is mentioned both in Josephus and in the Acts of the Apostles, who, having gathered thirty thousand to the Mount of Olives, had promised that the walls of Jerusalem would fall at his command: but being attacked by Felix, with his followers killed and captured, he took to flight. And again under Porcius Festus another impostor (γόης), announcing salvation and a cessation of evils, and with that hope led many into the wilderness, where he was crushed with his followers. To these can be added Simon Magus, who called himself the power (δύναμιν)

He preached [himself as] the power of God: and that Dositheus, who claimed for himself the title of Christ, concerning whom see Origen against Celsus book II and in Matthew tract 27. By Christ is understood not merely, as it seems to Grotius, a common vindicator of liberty, but one called specifically ὁ χριστὸς, namely the promised Messiah, even if falsely believed to be a vindicator of bodily liberty. Grotius notes that Theudas was such a one, and that impostor from Egypt in those same times, who is mentioned both in Josephus and in the Acts of the Apostles. See Josephus book XX of Antiquities, chapter 12; book II of the Jewish War, chapter 12. That this Egyptian was held by the Jews for the Messiah, Galatinus book IV of De arcanis catholicae veritatis, chapter 21, teaches from the Rabbis. Compare Acts 21:38. To these is deservedly added another sorcerer under Porcius Festus, book XX, chapter 7. To these can be added, in the judgment of Grotius, Simon Magus; who preached himself as the power of God; and that Dositheus, who claimed for himself the title of Christ, concerning whom see Origen against Celsus book II and in Matthew tract 27. Jerome in this place and Theophylact also list Simon Magus among the Pseudo-Christs, who, just as before Baptism he called himself the great power of God, Acts 8:9, so after Baptism, having rejected Christ, he sold himself as Christ. Compare Irenaeus book I against Heresies, chapter 20; Augustine on Heresies, chapter 1; Eusebius book II of Ecclesiastical History, chapter 13; whom Menander followed as a teacher, and he did not hesitate to sell himself also as the Savior, Irenaeus book I, chapter 21. Dositheus the Samaritan seems to be that impostor who is reported by Josephus in book XVIII, chapter 5, to have seduced many and lured them to Mount Gerizim, being crushed with his followers by Pilate, whom Theophylact notes in this place to have said that he was the Prophet predicted by Moses. Some also refer to this place other Pseudo-Christs after the destruction of Jerusalem; but because it is a matter of the signs of the destruction, they are irrelevant in this place.

καὶ πολλὺς πλανήσυσι] They will snatch away many, enticed by false hope, into destruction, as is apparent from the histories mentioned before.

Latin:

Vers. 5. ἐπὶ τῷ ὀνόματί μου] Nomen, ut alibi diximus, multa significat: sæpe autem officium aut dignitatem alicujus. Dicuntur ergo hic exstituri, qui sibi asseribant di- gnitatem eam quæ Jesu est propria: id est, ut sequitur, qui se dicturi sint Christos. Alias Nomen est mandatum, quo sensu iidem illi dicuntur venturi in suo nomine, Johan. V. vers. 43. hoc est, nullo instructi mandato, sed ausu proprio.

Ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ χριστός] Quanquam & ψευδόχριστοι sunt ψευ- δοπροφῆται generaliori nomine, distingui tamen solent, ut & infra videre est v. 24. Christi nomine populus Ju- daicus intelligebat vindicem libertatis. Nam illud ἡμεῖς δὲ ἠλπίζομεν ὅτι αὐτός ἐστιν ὁ μέλλων λυτροῦσθαι τὸν Ἰσραὴλ Luc. XXIV. v. 21 descriptio est nominis Christi. Quare quicunque se missos divinitus liberatores populi Judaici dicebant, eo ipso Christos se profitebantur, & erant ψευ- δόχριστοι. Talis fuit Theudas, non ille Gamalieli nomi- natus, sed alter ejusdem nominis γόης, qui Cuspio Fado Judæam regente magnam plebis multitudinem ad se voca- vit, pollicitus verbi sui imperio discessuras Jordanis aquas, ut via pateret transeuntibus: sed cum magna sectatorum strage captus à Fado capite pœnas luit. Tales & illi πλάνοι, γόητες, καὶ ἀπατεῶνες, ut eos nominat Josephus, qui Felice procuratore προσχήματι θεασμοῦ imponebant hominibus, persuadentes iis ut se in solitudinem sequeren- tur, maxima signa & miracula conspecturi: quod itidem multis exitio fuit, & iisdem temporibus ex Ægypto impo- stor, cujus & apud Josephum & in Actis Apostolicis est mentio, qui contracta manu triginta millium in montem Oliveti, casura jussu suo Hierosolymorum mœnia pro- miserat: sed à Felice oppugnatus, cæsis captisque sectato- ribus, in fugam se dedit. Iterumque sub Portio Festo γόης alius, σωτηρίαν ἀπαγγελλόμενος καὶ παῦλαν κακῶν, eaque spe multos in solitudinem pelli iens, ubi cum suis oppressus est. His addi possunt Simon Magus, qui se δύναμιν

Θεῦ predicabat: & Dositheus ille, qui sibi Christi titulum vindicabat, de quo vide Origenem adversus Celsum lib. II. & in Matthæum tract. 27. Per Christum non tantum communiter vin- dex libertatis, ut Grotio videtur, sed ὁ χριστὸς pe- culiariter dictus, promissus nempe Messias, etsi falfo creditus corporalis libertatis vindex, intel- ligitur. Tales fuisse notat Grotius Theudam, & illum iisdem temporibus ex Ægypto imposto- rem, cujus & apud Josephum & in Actis Aposto- licis est mentio. Vid. Joseph. lib. XX. antiq. cap. 12. l. II. de bello Jud. cap. 12. Quem Ægyptium à Ju- dæis pro Messia habitum fuisse Galat. lib. IV. de arc. Cath. ver. c. 21. è Rabbinis docet. Conf. Actor. XXI. 38. Quibus merito accensetur, sub Porcio Festo γόης alius, l. XX. c. 7. His addi possunt, judi- cio Grotii, Simon Magus; qui se δύναμιν θεῦ præ- dicabat; & Dositheus ille, qui sibi Christi titulum vindicabat, de quo vide Origenem adversus Celsum l. II. & in Matth. tract. 27. Simonem Magum recen- set etiam Hieronymus in h. l. & Theophyl. inter Pseudo-Christos, qui uti ante Baptismum se virtu- tem Dei magnam dixit, Actor. VIII. 9. ita post Ba- ptismum rejecto Christo seipsum pro Christo venditavit. Conf. Iren. lib. I. advers. Hæres. c. 20. August. de Hær. c. 1. Euseb. l. II. H. E. c. 13. quem se- cutus est ceu præceptorem Menander, seque et- iam pro Salvatore venditare non dubitavit, Iren. lib. I. cap. 21. Dositheus Samaritanus videtur esse impostor ille, qui à Josepho lib. XVIII. cap. 5. re- fertur multos seduxisse, & in montem Garizim pellexisse, oppressus cum suis à Pilato, quem Theophyl. notat in h. l. dixisse se Prophetam esse à Mose prædictum. Nonnulli etiam huc referunt Pseudo-Christos alios post excidium Hierosolymita- num; sed quia de signis agitur excidii, alieni illi hoc loco sunt.

καὶ πολλὺς πλανήσυσι] Multos spe falsa illectos in exi- tium abripient, ut ex ante dictis Historiis apparet.

## 24:6
Vers. 6. πολέμυς καὶ ἀκοὰς πολέμων] By wars here I understand the slaughters inflicted upon the Jews under the Emperor Gaius, both at Alexandria and around Babylon, of which Josephus makes mention in Antiquities XVIII. Philo accurately describes the Alexandrian [slaughter] in Against Flaccus. By rumors of wars, the fear of war from Gaius when he prepared to bring his image into the temple. Tacitus, Histories V: Ordered by Gaius Caesar to place his effigy in the temple, they took up arms instead: which movement the death of Caesar ended. And in Annals XII, dealing with the same time: The Jews had provided a show of movement when a sedition arose. How great the consternation of the Jews was then, both at Alexandria and in Judea, it is worth the effort to read in those Jewish writers whom I have mentioned.

Others more conveniently take these as an explanation: you are about to hear of wars, that is, rumors of wars: or you are about to hear of wars, i.e., those to come, and rumors of wars, which are being waged in other cities of Judea. For those things which are reported about wars in other parts of the world are irrelevant, as Chrysostom observes in Homily 76 on Matthew, because Christ is here predicting the signs of the destruction of Jerusalem.

ὁρᾶτε] μὴ θροεῖσθε] Consider these things diligently: but do not be so moved by them, as if they were the extreme of the evils that await the Jews, on account of so many exhortations to repentance being despised.

Δεῖ γὰρ πάντα] The Latin interpreter reads 'these things' instead of 'all things': but the Syriac [reads] 'all these things' together, which, since it is also supported by the authority of certain codices, I think is to be preferred. The sense is: more such things must happen before the end of the greater [events] is present. That 'must' [δεῖ], as we said at chapter 18 in a similar matter. It looks to the counsel of God, who wisely permits those evils toward which the Jews were moving of their own accord, so that His justice might be the more revealed.

οὔπω ἐστι τὸ τέλος] That is, the punishment of the Jews has not yet reached its height, as the comparison of verse 14 shows. Daniel said 'even to the time appointed' in chapter 11:35.

Latin:

Vers. 6. πολέμυς καὶ ἀκοὰς πολέμων] Πολέμυς hic intelli- go cædes in Judæos editas Cajo imperante, tum Alexandriæ tum circa Babylonem, quarum meminit Josephus ἀρχαιολο- γίας XVIII. Alexandrinam accurate describit Philo adver- sus Flaccum. Ἀκοὰς πολέμων, metum belli à Cajo cum ima- ginem suam templo inferre pararet. Tacitus Historiarum V. Iussi à Cajo Cæsare effigiem ejus in templo locare, arma potius sumpsere: quem motum Cæsaris mors diremit. Et Annalium XII. de eodem agens tempore: Præbuerant Judæi speciem motus orta seditione. Quanta tum fuerit Judæorum con- sternatio tum Alexandriæ, tum in Judæa, apud eos quos dixi scriptores Judæos legere est operæ pretium.

Alii commodius κατ’ ἐπεξήγησιν hæc accipiunt audituri estis bella, hoc est, rumores bellorum: vel au- dituri estis bella sc. ventura, & rumores bellorum, quæ in aliis Judææ civitatibus geruntur. Aliena enim sunt, quæ de bellis in aliis orbis partibus ad- feruntur, ut observat Chrysost. hom. LXXVI. in Matth. quia prædicit hic Christus signa excidii Hierosolymitani.

ὁρᾶτε] μὴ θροεῖσθε] Considerate ista diligenter: sed ne ita movemini istis, quasi extrema essent malorum quæ Iu- dæos manent, ob contemta tot ad pœnitentiam horta- menta.

Δεῖ γὰρ πάντα] Latinus interpres pro πάντα legit ταῦτα: Syrus autem conjunctim πάντα ταῦτα, quod cum & co- dicum quorundam fide muniatur, præferendum puto. Sensus est: plura talia accidere debent antequam majo- rum terminus adsit. Δεῖ istud, ut ad caput XIIX. in re simili diximus. Dei consilium spectat sapienter permittan- tis ea mala ad quæ Iudæi sua sponte ferebantur, quo ma- gis justitia ipsius patesceret.

οὔπω ἐστι τὸ τέλος] Id est, nondum ad summum perve- nit pœna Iudæorum, ut ostendit collatio commatis 14. Daniel dixit כרעוד למועד cap. XI. 35.

## 24:7
Vers. 7. ἐγερθήσεται γὰρ ἔθνος ἐπὶ ἔθνος κὰι βασιλεία ἐπὶ βασιλείαν] They are almost the very words of the Prophet Azariah to

King Asa, 2 Chronicles 15:6. Christ indicates that slaughters greater than those which had occurred under Gaius were impending in the final Claudian times and the principate of Nero. That 'nation shall rise against nation' signified that the Jews, and those who were of other nations dwelling in the same cities, were to be clashed against each other in mutual slaughters, which happened first at Caesarea, then at Scythopolis, Ptolemais, Tyre, Gadara, again at Alexandria, and then also at Damascus. But that 'kingdom against kingdom' signifies open wars between tetrarchs or provinces. For just as 'king' sometimes also signifies a prefect, according to the custom of the Hebrew language, as we have observed elsewhere, so also 'kingdom' [signifies] any prefecture: as the Nome of Egypt in Isaiah 19:2. To this must be referred the war of the Jews living in Perea against the Philadelphians on account of a boundary controversy, under the procurator Cuspius Fadus: the war of the Jews and Galileans against the Samaritans, under the procurator Cumanus: finally, the war undertaken first by those they called sicarii, then by the whole Jewish nation against the Romans and Agrippa and other allies of the Roman empire: which had its beginning under the procurator Gessius Florus. These same wars, if I am not mistaken, are noted in the Apocalypse by the 'fiery horse,' to whose rider it was given 'to take peace from the earth and that they should kill one another, and there was given unto him a great sword,' chapter 6, verse 4.

Jerome, as also Augustine Ep. XXI, refers these to the signs of the end of the age: but Hilary, Chrysostom, Theophylact, Euthymius, and Bede more correctly teach that the signs of the Jewish destruction are brought forward here, to which Grotius agrees. From Josephus, Hegesippus, and Eusebius it is clear how the Jews rose up against the Samaritans, Romans, and Syrians: how likewise the Caesareans rose up against the Jews living among them, who slaughtered 20,000 Jews, the Scythopolitans, who 13,000, the Ascalonites, who 2,500, the inhabitants of Ptolemais, who 2,000, the Alexandrians, who 50,000, the Damascenes, who 10,000, killed. From the same it is also evident concerning the perpetual seditions in Jerusalem, and in other parts of Judea, which arose in continuous succession not only under Cumanus and Florus, but also under the intermediate procurators Felix, Festus, and Albinus. Concerning the passage in the Apocalypse, in its own place, God willing.

κὶ ἔσονται λιμοὶ] Such as that great famine predicted by Agabus which fell upon Judea in the time of Claudius. Acts 11:28. For it is familiar to the Jews to call Palestine 'the inhabited world': whence that saying arose, that the city of Jerusalem is said to be situated in the middle of 'the inhabited world', which if you take it concerning the globe of the earth, is ridiculously fabulous: if concerning Judea, it is most true. For it is, as Josephus speaks, the navel of the land. Josephus speaks thus concerning this same famine, where it reached the procurator Tiberius Alexander: 'For upon these it happened that a great famine occurred throughout Judea': narrating also some relief brought to that scarcity by Izates, king of the Adiabenians, and his mother Helena. And I think this is the primary reason why Paul so solicitously commends the need of the brothers in Palestine to the churches of other nations. Nor do I think those err who refer to this what is in the Apocalypse, concerning him who sitting on a black horse held a balance in his hand, signifying the laws of grain.

κὶ λοιμοὶ] Famine and pestilence are often accustomed to be joined, as by the sound of the Greek words, so also linked together by a certain natural connection: as in Hesiod: 'Upon them from heaven the son of Cronus brought a great woe, famine together with pestilence; and the peoples perish.'

I refer this pestilence, however, to the times immediately following the famine already mentioned: according to the old saying 'after famine, pestilence': just as also in the Apocalypse after the black horse comes the pale one, upon which sits Death and his companion Hades: where what follows 'and authority was given to them to kill over the fourth part of the earth with sword and with famine and with death and by the wild beasts of the earth' ought to be referred to the riders of the second, third, and fourth horses, and by the word 'death' pestilence is to be understood from a Hebraism: for thus 'death' is taken in Jeremiah 15:2 and 18:21. Thus we read in Sirach chapter 39:30, 'famine and death', where likewise 'death' undoubtedly signifies pestilence. The Syrian also, both here and in Luke, translates 'pestilence' as 'death': and the Seventy translate the Hebrew 'pestilence', that is, plague, as 'death': as also the Chaldean and the Latin in Leviticus 26:25. By their example, Sulpicius Severus in the first book of his histories used 'death' for 'pestilence'.

See Josephus on these matters, Antiquities book XX, ch. 2. And Eusebius in the Chronicle, as well as Acts 11:29-30, Rom. 15:25, 1 Cor. 16:3, 2 Cor. 9:3. Josephus did not indeed note anything about the λοιμοῖς (pestilences), but there is no doubt that this plague also preceded the destruction of Jerusalem. According to the old saying: μετὰ λιμὸν λοιμός (after famine, pestilence), which are linked together as much by the sound of the Greek words as by a certain natural connection. It is not for us, with the author of the Opus Imperfectum in Matthaeum, homily 48, to understand either the spiritual famine of the word or the pestilences of various carnal vices, since one must not depart from the literal meaning of the words.

And there will be earthquakes in many places: as the Syrian rightly explained. Earthquakes, however, besides being signs of divine wrath—whether of the One who causes them or the One who chooses not to prevent them—often bring grave disasters to cities, as one may learn from what Tacitus reports in Annals II regarding the earthquake in Asia. Pliny: 'It is not a simple evil, nor is the danger only in the shaking itself, but it is an equal or greater omen.' The Roman city never trembled without it being a harbinger of some future event. These earthquakes predicted by Christ occurred partly in the times of Claudius and partly in the times of Nero. Philostratus mentions a grave earthquake that occurred in Crete during the reign of Claudius in his Life of Apollonius. Likewise, the earthquakes in Smyrna, Miletus, Chios, and Samos shortly before the time of the destruction of the city of Jerusalem. Tacitus mentions another in Asia when Nero and Cornelius Cossus were consuls. 'Laodicea,' he says, 'collapsed from an earthquake.' Eusebius adds Hierapolis and Colossae. Seneca mentions a later earthquake in the sixth book of his Natural Questions. This matter pertained to the Jews, because many Jews lived in the places already mentioned. In the Apocalypse, after the mention of the martyrs, there follows a σεισμὸς μέγας (great earthquake): which I believe points to the same thing.

Because these things contribute to explaining the prophecy through its fulfillment, they are not ill-suited. As for the Apocalyptic passages, they will be dealt with in their proper place, God willing. It seemed to the blessed Gerhard in his Harmony, ch. 160, p. 380, that the earthquake which occurred on the third day after this discourse, at the passion of Christ, could also be referred to here. Add, if you like, those things which Grotius observed on verse 9, as they contribute to illustrating the text. Regarding which, one may see Acts 4:3 ff., ch. 5:17 ff., ch. 6:12, ch. 7:58, ch. 8:1, ch. 9:2, ch. 12:2. And those things which are reported in Ecclesiastical History about Peter being affixed to a cross, Andrew likewise crucified in Achaia, Philip stoned to death, Bartholomew flayed, Matthew beheaded, Thomas pierced with spears, James the son of Alphaeus killed with a fuller's club, Jude of James killed in Persia by the assault of the high priests, Simon the Canaanite first beaten for many days and then crucified: all of which, however, did not precede the Jewish destruction, and therefore not all can be referred to the signs of the same that are commemorated here. What Grotius brought forward on verse 11 regarding the false prophets is not unworthy of being referred to here as well.

Latin:

Vers. 7. ἐγερθήσεται γὰρ ἔθνος ἐπὶ ἔθνος κὰι βασιλεία ἐπὶ βασιλείαν] Sunt prope ipsa verba Azariæ Prophetæ ad

Afam regem Paralip. II. XV. 6. Indicat Christus majores quam sub Cajo evenerant cædes imminere ultimis tem- poribus Claudianis, & Neronis principatu. Illud ἔθν ἐπὶ ἔθν ἐγερθήσεται, significavit Judæos, & qui aliarum erant gentium iisdem in civitatibus morantes muruis in- ter se cædibus collidendos, quod contigit Cæfareæ pri- mum, deinde Scythopoli, Ptolemaide, Tyri, Gadaris, rur- sum Alexandriæ, deinde & Damasci. Illud autem, βα- σιλεία ἐπὶ βασιλείαν significat tetrarcharum aut provincia- rum aperta inter se bella. Nam sicut βασιλεὺς interdum etiam præfectum significat, ex more Hebraici sermonis, ut alibi observavimus, ita & βασιλεία præfecturam quamvis: ut Nomos Ægypti Esaïæ XIX. 2. Huc referri debet Judæo- rum in Peræa habitantium bellum adversus Philadelphenos ob finium controversiam, Cufpio Fado procuratore: Judæo- rum & Galilæorum bellum adversus Samaritas, procurato- re Cumano: postremo bellum primum à sicariis quos voca- bant, deinde ab universa Judæorum gente sumtum adver- sus Romanos & Agrippam aliosque Romani imperii so- cios: quod initium habuit Gessio Floro procuratore. Hæc eadem bella, ni fallor, notat in Apocalypsi ἵππ πυῤῥὸς, cujus sessori datum est λαβεῖν εἰρήνην ἀπὸ τῆς γῆς καὶ ἵνα ἀλ- λήλους σφάξωσι, καὶ ἐδόθη αὐτῷ μάχαιρα μεγάλη cap. VI. v. 4.

Hieronymus, ut & August. Ep. XXI. refert hæc ad signa consummationis seculi: sed rectius Hila- rius, Chrysost. Theophyl. Euthym. & Beda signa excidii Judaici hic adferri docent, quibus acce- dit Grotius. Ex Josepho, Egesippo & Eusebio liquet, quomodo Judæi adversus Samaritanos, Romanos & Syros: quomodo item adversus Judæos inter se habitantes insurrexerint Cæsarienses, qui 20000. Judæorum trucidarunt, Scythopolitæ, qui 13000. Ascalonitæ, qui 2500. Ptolemaidis inco- læ, qui 2000. Alexandrini, qui 50000. Damasceni, qui 10000. interemerunt. Ex iisdem etiam con- stat, de perpetuis seditionibus Hierosolymis, & in aliis Judææ partibus, non sub Cumano tantum & Floro, sed & intermediis Præsidibus Felice, Festo, Albino continua succesfione exortis. De loco Apocalyps. suo loco, cum Deo.

κὶ ἔσονται λιμοὶ] Qualis ille λιμὸς μέγας ab Agabo prædi- ctus qui Claudio tempore Judææ incubuit. Actor. XI. 28. Nam Palæstinam vocare τὴν οἰκουμένην Judæis familiare est: unde illud natum, quod urbs Hierosolyma sita dicitur in meditullio τῆς οἰκουμένης, quod si de orbe terrarum accipias, ridicule est fabulosum: si de Judæa, verissimum. Est enim ut Josephus loquitur ὀμφαλὸς τῆς χώρας. Josephus de eadem hac fame ita loquitur, ubi ad Tiberium Alexandrinum pro- curatorem pervenit: ἐπὶ τέτοις γὰρ κὴ τ μέγαν λιμὸν κατὰ τὴν Ἰυδαίαν συνέβη γενέσθαι: narrans etiam subsidium ei penuriæ aliquod allatum ab Izate Adiabenorum rege & matre ejus Helena. Et hanc præcipuam esse causam arbitror ob quam fratrum in Palæstina necessitatem aliarum gentium Ecclesiis Paulus tam sollicite commendat. Neque errare puto, qui huc referunt quod in Apocalypsi est, de eo qui atro equo insidens libellam habebat in manu, leges anno- narias significantem.

κὶ λοιμοὶ] Conjungi sæpe solent λιμὸς & λοιμὸς, ut sono Græcarum vocum, ita & naturali quodam nexu inter se copulata: ut apud Hesiodum: Τοῖσιν δ᾽ ἐρανόθεν μέγ᾽ ἐπήγαγε πῆμα κρονίων Λιμὸν ὁμὲ καὶ λοιμόν· ἀποφθινύθουσι δὲ λαοί.

Hanc autem pestilentiam ad tempora famem jam di- ctam proxime sequentia refero: juxta vetus verbum μετὰ λιμὸν λοιμὸς: quomodo & in Apocalypsi post atrum e- quum χλωρὸς, cui insidet θάνατος & ei comes ᾅδης: ubi quod sequitur κὶ ἐδόθη αὐτοῖς ἐξουσία ἀποκτεῖναι ἐπὶ τὸ τέταρτον τῆς γῆς ἐν ῥομφαίᾳ καὶ λιμῷ καὶ ἐν θανάτῳ κὶ ὑπὸ τῶν θηρίων γῆς referri debet ad secundi, tertii & quarti equi insessores, & voce θανάτω intelligendus est λοιμὸς ex Hebraïsmo: Nam ita מות sumitur apud Ieremiam I. 20. & XIIX. 21. Sic apud Sirachidem legimus cap. XXXIX. 34. λιμὸς κὶ θάνα- τος, ubi itidem θανάτος haud dubie pestilentiam signi- ficat. Syrus quoque tum hic, tum apud Lucam λοιμὸς vertit מותנא id est θανάτος: & LXX. Hebræorum דבר id est, pestem, vertunt θάνατον: ut & Chaldæus & Latinus Levit. XXVI. 24. Horum exemplo Severus Sulpitius hi- storiarum primo mortem pro pestilentia posuit.

Vid. de his Josephus l. XX. Antiquit. c. 2. Et Eu- sebi in Chron. nec non Act. XI. 29. 30. Rom. XV. 25. 1. Cor. XVI. 3. 2. Cor. IX. 3. De λοιμοῖς pestilentiis non annotavit quidem quicquam Josephus, sed du- bium nullum est etiam hanc plagam Hierosolymi- tanum excidium antegressum fuisse. Juxta ve- tus verbum: μετὰ λιμὸν λοιμός, quæ ut sono Græcarum vocum, ita & naturali quodam nexu inter se copulatæ sunt. Non est, ut cum Autore ope- ris imperf. hom. XLIIX. vel famem spiritualem ver- bi, vel pestilentias diversorum carnalium vitiorum intelligamus, quum à proprietate verborum di- scedendum non sit.

καὶ σεισμοὶ κατὰ τόπους] Id est terræ motus erunt multis in lo- cis: ut recte exposuit Syrus. Terræ motus autem, præter- quam quod signa sunt iræ divinæ, eos aut procurantis, aut impedire nolentis, graves etiam clades sæpe urbibus adfe- runt, ut ex iis est cognoscere quæ de Asiæ terræ motu Annal. II. Tacitus refert. Plinius: Non simplex malum, aut in ipso motu tantum periculum est. sed par aut majus ostentum. Nunquam urbs Romana tremuit, ut non futuri eventus alicujus id præ- nuntium esset. Hi autem terræ motus à Christo prædicti partim in Claudii, partim in Neronis tempora inciderunt. Gravis terræ motus qui in Creta accidit Claudio imperante meminit Philostratus in vita Apollonii. Item terræ mo- tuum Smyrnæ, Mileti, Chii, Sami paulo ante tempora exci- sii urbis Hierosolymorum. Alterius in Asia Tacitus Ne- rone & Cornelio Cossa consulibus. Laodicea, inquit, tremo- re terræ prolapsa. Addit Eusebius Hierapolim & Colossas. Rursus posterioris cujusdam terræ motus Seneca meminit naturalium sexto. Pertinebat autem hæc res ad Judæos, quod dictis jam locis multi Judæi habitarent: In Apocaly- psi post mentionem martyrum sequitur σεισμὸς μέγας: quod eodem spectare arbitror.

Hæc quia ad vaticinium per complementum explicandum faciunt, non male se habent. De locis autem Apocalypticis suo loco cum Deo. Posse & huc referri terræ motum, qui tertio statim ab hac concione die in passione Christi conti- git, B. Gerhardo visum fuit in Harm. cap. CLX. pag. 380. Adde si lubet & ea quæ ad v. 9. observa- vit Grotius, utpote ad textum illustrandum faci- entia. De quibus videri possunt Act. IV. 3. seqq. c. V. 17. seqq. c. VI. 12. c. VII. 58. c. IIX. 1. c. IX. 2. c. XII. 2. & quæ in Historia Ecclesiastica perhibentur de Petro cruci affixo, Andreæ itidem in Achaia cruci- fixo, Philippo lapidibus obruto, Bartholomæo exco- riato, Matthæo decollato, Thoma lanceis diverbe- rato, Iacobo Alphæi instrumento fullonis occiso, Iuda Iacobi in Persia Pontificum impetu interemto, Si- mone Cananæo, multis diebus primum cæso, post cru- cifixo: quæ tamen omnia non antecesserunt exci- dium Judaicum, ideoque nec omnia ad signa ejus- dem antecedentia, quæ hic commemorantur, refer- ri possunt. Quæ de Pseudo-Prophetis Grotius ad v. 11. adduxit, non indigna sunt, quæ etiam huc re- ferantur.

## 24:8
Verse 8. The beginning of birth pains. Very often the writers of the Psalms and the Prophets compare the greatest sorrows to the pains of a woman in labor: where one may also find the word ὠδίνων (birth pains) throughout the Septuagint, as in Ps. 48:7, Isa. 13:8, 66:7 (where see the Chaldean), Jer. 30:6-7, and elsewhere. But Christ says more here: namely, that the evils he has already mentioned will not be so extreme that they should be compared only to the first pains of a woman about to give birth: after which a much heavier pain follows in the birth itself: as in the comedy:

The pains, my dear, are just beginning.

Latin:

Vers. 8. ἀρχὴ ὠδίνων] Sæpissime Psalmorum Scriptores & Prophetæ maximos dolores doloribus parturiginis compa- rant: ubi & vocem ὠδίνων apud LXX. passim reperire est, ut Ps. XLIIX. 7. Es. XIII. 8. LXVI. 7. ubi Chaldæum vide Ier. XXX. 6. 7. & alibi Sed plus hic dicit Christus: ea nempe, quæ jam memoravit mala adeo suprema non fore, ut pri- mis demum doloribus parituræ mulieris conferri debe- ant: post quos dolor multo gravior in partu ipso sequi- tur: ut in Comœdia:

Dolores, mea tu, occipiunt primulum.

## 24:9
Verse 9. Then. That is, around those times: for that is how 'then' is usually taken more loosely. For the things that follow occurred partly before the already narrated calamities of the Jews (which Luke clearly signifies in this place) and partly during them. For Christ, distinguishing the events themselves from the common evils of the Jews, makes a transition to the peculiar inconveniences of those who believe in him. But it is also to be noted that those very evils of which Christ has already spoken—earthquakes, famine, pestilence—were imputed to the Christians, as if those evils were happening to the human race because of their impiety: and that was seized upon as an occasion for cruelty: which the Apologetic books of the Christians teach us everywhere.

They will deliver you up to tribulation. The Jews, he says, will drag you Christians to councils and larger assemblies, as happened to Peter and John; partly also to kings, as James and Peter were dragged to Herod, and Paul to Nero; partly to governors, as the same Paul was to Gallio, Felix, and Festus. Tribulations are scourges, prison, and other vexations of that kind.

And they will kill you. They will cause some of you, 'of you,' as Luke says, to be killed, whether by popular tumult, as Stephen, or by the appearance of a trial, as the two Jameses—one struck by the sword by Herod, the other condemned by the council to be stoned.

By all nations. You will come into hatred not only of the Jews, but also of other nations throughout the world. This began especially under Nero, who, as Tacitus narrates, made the Christians the scapegoats for the rumor that he had set the city on fire, and subjected them to the most exquisite punishments. Tertullian in his Apology against the Gentiles: 'Consult your records: there you will find that Nero was the first to rage with the Caesarean sword against this sect, which was then especially rising at Rome: but we glory in such a dedicator of our condemnation. For he who knows him can understand that nothing but some great good was condemned by Nero.'

For my name's sake. On account of the mere profession of Christianity, 1 Pet. 4:16, which Tertullian proves well in the aforementioned Apology: 'They believe things about us that are not proven: and they do not want them to be investigated, lest they be proven not to be what they prefer to have believed, so that the name, hostile to that rivalry, may be condemned for presumed, unproven crimes based solely on its own confession. Therefore we are tortured when we confess, and punished when we persevere, and acquitted when we deny, because it is a battle over the name.' For that they were believed not to think rightly about the gods, Origen proves that this was not the true cause of the cruelty, from the fact that Epicureans and other philosophers who removed all divine providence entirely were spared. Whence it is manifest that this cruelty arose from the instigation of the evil spirits who were worshipped through idols. For they perceived that this was the one doctrine by which the entire force of errors would be most fully vanquished. Therefore, since the Jews attacked false gods no less than the Christians, the Jews bore this with impunity, while the Christians were dragged to punishments.

Latin:

Vers. 9. Τότε] Id est, circa ista tempora: ita enim solet Τότε laxius accipi. Nam quæ sequuntur partim ante jam narra- tas Judæorum calamitates (quod Lucas hoc loco aperte si- gnificat) partim inter eas acciderunt. Nam Christus res ipsas distinguens à communibus Judæorum malis, ad pe- culiaria in se credentium incommoda facit μετάβασιν. Sed & illud notandum, ei ipsa de quibus jam egit Christus ma- la, terræ motus, famem, pestilentiam, imputata Christianis, quasi ob ipsorum impietatem mala ista humano generi eve- nirent: idque raptum in sævitiæ occasionem: quod pas- sim nos docent Apologetici Christianorum libri.

παραδώσουσιν ὑμᾶς εἰς θλῖψιν] Judæi, inquit, vos Chri- ftianos rapient ad Synedria & conventus majores, ut Pe- tro & Iohanni accidit, partim etiam ad reges, ut ad Hero- dem pertracti sunt Iacobus & Petrus, ad Neronem Paulus, partim ad Præsides, ut idem Paulus ad Gallionem, Felicem, Festum. θλίψις sunt flagra, carcer, aliaque id genus vexa- tiones.

καὶ ἀποκτενοῦσιν ὑμᾶς] Efficient ut quidam vestrum, ἐξ ὑμῶν, ut Lucas inquit, etiam interficiantur, sive populari tu- multu, ut Stephanus, sive judicii specie, ut Iacobi duo, alter ab Herode gladio percussus, alter à Synedrio damnatus ut lapidaretur.

ὑπὸ πάντων ἐθνῶν] Non in Judæorum tantum venietis odium, sed & aliarum per orbem gentium. Quod cœpit maxime sub Nerone, qui incensæ à se urbis rumori Chri- stianos, ut Tacitus narrat, reos subdidit, & quæsitissimis pœ- nis affecit. Tertullianus Apologetico adversus Gentes: Consulite commentarios vestros: Illic reperietis primum Nero- nem in hanc sectam, tum maxime Romæ orientem, Cæsariano gladio ferocisse: sed tali dedicatore damnationis nostræ etiam gloriamur. Qui enim scit illum, intelligere potest non nisi gran- de aliquod bonum à Nerone damnatum.

διὰ τὸ ὄνομά συ] Ob nudam Christianismi professio- nem, 1. Petr. IV 16. quod bene Tertullianus probat dicto Apologetico: Credunt de nobis quæ non probantur: & nolunt inquiri ne probentur non esse, quæ malunt credidisse, ut nomen il- lius æmulationis inimicum præsumtis non probatis criminibus de sua sola confessione damnetur. Ideo torquemur confessi, & pu- nimur perseverantes, & absolvumur negantes, quia nominis præ- lium est. Nam quod de Diis non recte sentire crederen- tur, eam non fuisse veram sævitiæ causam, ex eo probat Ori- genes, quod Epicureis aliisque Philosophis omnem omni- no divinam providentiam tollentibus parcebatur. Unde manifestum est, ex malorum spirituum, qui per idola cole- bantur, instigatione ortam hanc crudelitatem. Sentiebant enim hanc unam doctrinam esse qua vis omnis errorum plenissime debellaretur. Ideo cum Judæi non minus quam Christiani falsos Deos oppugnarent, Judæi impune id fere- bant, Christiani rapiebantur ad pœnas.

## 24:10
Verse 10. σκανδαλισθήσονται πολλοὶ] Having observed that hatred of all nations against the Christians, many will fall away from the profession of Christianity. Thus, we showed above at chapter XIII that what Matthew calls σκανδαλίζεσθαι, Luke calls ἀφίστασθαι. That is, in Daniel ch. XI. 30, עזב ברית. This happened to Phygellus, Hermogenes, Demas, and undoubtedly to very many others whose names do not survive.

and they will betray one another, and will hate one another] The word ἀλλήλων generally signifies a certain mutual action passing to and fro. But here it is used a little more broadly for what we would say, one will hate and betray another, which the Syrian correctly expressed as חד לחד. Thus the same Greek word is used in Acts VII. 26. For the sense is that it will come to pass that Christians will betray one another, namely those who fall away from Christianity will betray those who persevere. Moreover, there are almost none more cruel toward the true religion than those who have sent a repudiation to the true religion, whether because God avenges the contempt of the light with the thickest darkness of mind, or because they themselves do anything whatever to free themselves from the suspicion of their former zeal.

Latin:

Vers. 10. σκανδαλισθήσονται πολλοὶ] Conspecto isto o- mnium gentium adversus Christianos odio, multi à Chri- stianismi proffeffione deficient. Ita supra ad caput XIII. ostendimus, quod Matthæus dicit σκανδαλίζεσθαι, Lucæ dici ἀφίστασθαι. Id est Danieli c. XI. 30. עזב ברית. Evenit hoc Phygello, Hermogeni, Demæ, & haud dubie plurimis aliis quorum nomina non exstant.

καὶ ἀλλήλους παραδώσουσι, κὴ μισήσουσιν ἀλλήλους] Vox ἀλ- λήλων, plerumque mutuam quandam & ultro citroque com- meantem actionem significat. At hic paulo latius poni- tur pro eo quod diceremus alter alterum odio habebit, ac tradet, quod recte expressit Syrus חד לחד. Sic eadem vox Græca sumitur Act. VII. 26. Sensus enim est, futurum ut Christianorum alii alios tradant, nimirum hi qui à Christia- nismo deficiunt, eos qui perseverant. Ferme autem nulli sunt in veram religionem crudeliores, quam qui veræ reli- gioni repudium miserunt, seu quia comtemtum lucis crassissi- ma mentis caligine Deus ulciscitur, seu quia & ipsi quidvis agunt, ut à suspicione prioris studii se liberent.

## 24:11
Verse 11. and many false prophets will arise and will deceive many] ἐγερθήσονται is יעמדו; just as prophets were called by the Hebrews not only those who predicted future events, but also those who interpreted the law, so Christ calls false teachers by the well-known term false prophets. There is no doubt that Satan, having stirred up the hatred of the world against the Christians, when he saw that the power of the truth was so great that many who desired to deny it could scarcely do so, with their minds resisting too much, added guile to force, inventing certain pretexts that would make defection easier. The constancy of the Christians could be shaken either by the removal of the use of all religion, or by the claim that any external worship is indifferent, or by sought-after reconciliations that would permit the Christian religion to be combined with some religion, either publicly approved, such as that of the Gentiles, or at least tolerated, such as that of the Jews. The use of religion was being removed by Hymenaeus and Philetus, who said that the resurrection had already taken place. For certainly, with the hope of another life removed, and with the experience of those times showing that it was not better, but worse, for the pious in this life than for the impious, nothing remained firm enough to keep the mind in religion. Some taught from the very beginning that all external worship is indifferent, from whom Elxaeus drew this. From this dogma it came about that some would recline in idol temples together with the others, 1 Corinthians VIII. 10, because, forsooth, an idol was nothing in reality, 1 Cor. VIII. 4, X. 19. Against them is that admonition of John, 'Little children, keep yourselves from idols,' 1 Epistle, chapter V, verse 21. Simon Magus was the first of all to attempt to mix the Christian religion with Paganism during the reign of Claudius. For he himself also, for He wished to be held as God. It is credible that the report of his counsel, which we read was given by Tiberius to the Roman senate, that Christ should be added to the number of the Gods, reached him: such a mixture of things clearly incompatible, Adrian, Severus, and Heliogabalus also later attempted to effect, but in vain. From this Carpocrates, who is believed to be the prince of the Gnostics, departed thus far, that because the name of Gods was more hateful to Christians, he substituted in their place angels or αἰῶνας, as he called them, having thus turned into Greek the word חיות which is in Ezekiel I. 5, transferring to them all the θεολογίαν of Orpheus, Hesiod, and Pythagoras. But he also numbered Christ among them. And this is, if I am not mistaken, that ψευδώνυμος γνῶσις which Paul mentions to Timothy. These are οἱ συλαγωγοῦντες διὰ τῆς φιλοσοφίας καὶ κενῆς ἀπάτης, as the same Apostle speaks to the Colossians. For because they were mixing pagan doctrine with Christian doctrine, they therefore sold themselves under the name of erudition, as can be seen in Irenaeus and Clement. Of these are the γενεαλογίαι, which are mentioned in 1 Tim. I. 4, Tit. III. 9. Of these is the ἀπόσπασμα, as Irenaeus speaks, the Nicolaitans. But we also read in Vopiscus that those in Egypt who worshipped Serapis wished to be called Christians: and that they had their own Patriarch. They mixed the Christian religion with Judaism, not by tolerating Jewish rites (which we know the Apostles did in those first times) but by acknowledging Judaism as the only way of salvation, which had been announced both by other Prophets and also by Christ; Cerinthus and Ebion, whose chief study it was to escape those evils which particularly pressed upon the Christians in that way, as Paul clearly teaches in Phil. III. 18 and Gal. VI. 12. Against the same there are many things extant in the first epistle of John: but also in the Apocalypse. These therefore all and those like them are whom Christ calls ψευδοπροφήτας, Paul ἄνδρας λαλοῦντας διεστραμμένα, Acts XX. 30, ψευδαποστόλους 2 Cor. XI. 13, μετασχηματιζομένους εἰς ἀποστόλους χριστοῦ, by whose dogmas the faith of many has been overturned, 2 Tim. II. 18.

Grotius [says] these things not inappropriately. But B. Gerhard rightly observes that Christ in the preceding [verses] was speaking chiefly of those who arose from the Jews, Acts XX. 30, Rom. XVI. 17. But that this part of the prophecy also, like the rest, is referred to the most recent times, can be granted κατ’ ἀναλογίαν and by way of accommodation, but not according to the proper and literal sense, according to which here it is still only a matter of the signs of the most recent destruction of Jerusalem: lest distinct questions be confused, or different senses be attributed to the same text.

Latin:

Vers. 11. καὶ πολλοὶ ψευδοπροφῆται ἐγερθήσονται κὴ πλα- νήσουσι πολλούς] ἐγερθήσονται est יעמדו sicut προφῆται dice- bantur Hebræis non hi tantum qui prædicebant futura, sed & qui legem interpretabantur, ita falsos magistros Christus noto vocabulo ψευδοπροφήτας appellat. Dubium non est, quin Satan excitato mundi odio adversus Christianos, cum videret tantam esse vim veritatis, ut eam abnegare multi qui cuperent vix possent, nimium reluctante animo, ad vim dolos adjunxerit, prætextus aliquos comminiscens qui de- fectionem redderent faciliorem. Poterat autem labefa- stari constantia Christianorum, aut religionis omnis sublato usu, aut posito quemvis cultum externum esse ἀδιάφορον, aut quæsitis conciliaturis quæ Christianæ religionem cum ali- qua religione, aut probata publice, qualis erat Ethnicorum, aut tolerata certe, qualis erat Judæorum, permisserent. Religionis usus tollebatur per Hymenæum & Philetum, qui dicebant resurrectionem jam esse factam. Nam certe sub- lata spe vitæ alterius, & ostendente experientia illorsi tem- porum, piis non melius, sed pejus in hac vita esse quam im- piis, nihil manebat satis firmum quod animum in religione retineret. Cultum omnē externum esse ἀδιάφορον jam inde ab initio aliqui docuerunt, à quibus id hausit Elxæus. Ex hoc dogmate factum, ut quidam ἐν εἰδωλείους una cum cæteris accumberent 1. Corinth. VIII. 10. quia scilicet εἴδωλον ré psa nihil esset, 1. Cor VIII. 14. X. 19. Adversùs quos est illa Johannis admonitio, Τεκνία φυλάξατε ἑαυτοὺς ἀπὸ ἱ εἰδώ- λων Epist I. capit. V. vers. 21. Cum Paganismo Christia- nam religionem miscere aggressus est omnium primus Simon magus Claudio imperante. Nam & ipse pro DEO haberi voluit. Credibile est pervenisse ad eum famam consilii ejus quod à Tiberio datum senatui Roma- no legimus, ut Christus adderetur Deorum numero: qualem rerum plane insociabilium mixturam postea quo- que Adrianus, Severus, Heliogabalus, sed frustra, efficere conati sunt. Ab hoc Carpocrates, qui Gnosticorum prin- ceps creditur, hactenus discessit, ut quia Deorum nomen Christianis erat odiosius, eorum vice angelos aut αἰῶνας quos vocabat, ita versa in Græcum voce חיות quæ est apud Ezechielem I. 5. substitueret, ad eos transferens o- mnem θεολογίαν Orphei, Hesiodi & Pythagoræ. Illis au- tem annumerabat etiam Christum. Et hæc est, ni fallor, illa ψευδώνυμος γνῶσις cujus ad Timotheum Paulus me- minit. Hi sunt οἱ συλαγωγοῦντες διὰ τῆς φιλοσοφίας καὶ κε- νῆς ἀπάτης ut ad Colossenses idem Apostolus loquitur. Quia enim doctrinam paganicam cum Christiana doctri- na permiscebant, ideo se venditabant eruditionis nomi- ne, ut apud Irenæum & Clementem videre est. Horum sunt γενεαλογίαι quarum mentio 1. Tim. I. 4. Tit. III. 9. Horum ἀπόσπασμα, ut loquitur Irenæus, Nicolaitæ. Sed & apud Vopiscum legimus in Ægypto qui Sarapidem adorarent Christianos dici voluisse: atque illis suum fuisse Patriarcham. Cum Judaismo Christianam religionem miscuerunt, non tolerando ritus Judaicos (quod Apo- stolos primis illis temporibus scimus fecisse) sed Judai- smum agnoscendo unicam salutis viam, quæ tum ab a- liis Prophetis, tum à Christo etiam esset annunciata, Cerinthus & Ebion, quorum id præcipuum erat stu- dium, ut mala illa, quæ Christianos peculiariter pre- mebant, ea ratione effugerent, ut clare docet Pau- lus Phil. III. 18. & Gal. VI. 12. Adversus eosdem multa extant in prima Johannis epistola: sed & in Apocalypsi. Hi igitur omnes horumque similes sunt quos Christus vocat ψευδοπροφήτας, Paulus ἄνδρας λαλῦντας διεστραμμένα, Actor XX 30. ψευδαποστόλες 2. Cor. XI. 13. μετασχηματιζο- μένως εἰς ἀποστόλες χριστῦ, quorum dogmatibus multorum fides eversa est, 2. Tim. II 18.

Hæc non incommode Grotius. Recte autem observat B. Gerhardus, Christum in præcedenti- bus de illis loquutum præcipue esse, qui è Judæis exsurrexerunt, Act. XX. 30. Rom. XVI. 17. Quod autem hanc etiam vaticinii partem, uti reliquas ad tempora quoque novissima refert, κατ’ ἀναλογίαν & quoad accommodationem concedi potest, non autem quoad sensum proprium, & literalem, juxta quem hic adhuc tantum de signis agitur no- vissimi excidii Hierosolymitani: ne distinctæ quæ- stiones confundantur, aut eidem textui diversi sensus tribuantur.

## 24:12
V. 12. Καὶ διὰ τὸ πληθυνθῆναι τὴν ἀνομίαν, ψυγήσεται ἡ ἀγάπη τῶν πολλῶν] After open deserters and after adulterators of the faith, Christ notes a third class of men, who desert the duties of charity διὰ τὸ πληθυνθῆναι τὴν ἀνομίαν, that is, on account of long-lasting and increasing cruelty. ἀγάπη is the love of God and of men whom piety joins. We have an illustrious example when Paul first pleaded his cause before Nero. No one, he says, stood by me, all deserted me, 2 Tim. IV. 16. For a similar reason many were deserting τὴν ἑαυτῶν ἐπισυναγωγὴν, whom the writer to the Hebrews notes in chapter X. 25.

Latin:

V. 12. Καὶ διὰ τὸ πληθυνθῆναι τὴν ἀνομίαν, ψυγήσεται ἡ ἀγάπη τῶν πολλῶν] Post apertos desertores & post adul- teratores fidei, tertium genus hominum Christus notat, qui charitatis officia deserunt διὰ τὸ πληθυνθῆναι τὴν ἀνο- μίαν, ;: est propter diu durantem & ingravescentem sæ- vitiam. ἀγάπη est dilectio Dei & hominum quos pietas conjungit. Exemplum habemus illustre cum primum Paulus causam dixit apud Neronem. Nemo, inquit, mihi affuit, omnes me derelinquerunt, 2. Tim. IV. 16. Simili de causa multi deserebant τὴν ἑαυτῶν ἐπισυναγωγὴν quos no- tat Scriptor ad Hebræos cap. X. 25.

## 24:13
Vers. 13. Ὁ δὲ ὑπομείνας εἰς τέλος, οὗτος σωθήσεται] ὁ ὑπομείνας, that is, he who shall have persevered, both in faith and in love, as the very opposition of the preceding [verses] shows: Whom neither distress, nor pressure, nor vexation, nor famine, nor nakedness, nor danger, nor sword shall have separated from that love which is borne toward God. What is σώζεσθαι here, is κτᾶσθαι τὰς ψυχὰς in Luke, and elsewhere εὑρίσκειν τὴν ψυχὴν, that is, to acquire blessed immortality. For it is promised not to those who begin, but to those who persevere. To which pertains that of Tertullian: No one is a Christian except he who has persevered to the end. And of Cyprian: And faith itself, like birth, does not vivify unless it is kept. And of Jerome: In Christians, beginnings are not sought, but the end.

Latin:

Vers. 13. Ὁ δὲ ὑπομείνας εἰς τέλος, ὗτος σωθήσεται] ὁ ὑπομείνας, id est is qui pertiterit, tum in fide, tum in dilectione, ut ipsa præcedentium oppositio ostendit: Quem neque angustia, neque pressura, neque vexatio, neque fa- mes, neque nuditas, neque periculum, neque gladius separaverit ab ea quæ in Deum fertur dilectione. Quod hic est σώζεσθαι, apud Lucam est κτᾶσθαι τὰς ψυχὰς, alibi ὑυρίσκειν τὴν ψυχὴν, id est, beatam immortalitatem ac- quirere. Ea enim non inchoantibus, sed perseverantibus promittitur Qu pertinet illud Tertulliani: Nemo Chri- stianus nisi qui ad finem usque perseveraverit. Et Cypriani: Et fides ipsa, ut nativitas, non accepta, sed custodita vivificat. Et Hieronymi: Non quæruntur in Christianis initia, sed fi- nis.

## 24:14
Vers. 14. Ἐν ὅλῃ τῇ οἰκουμένῃ] Mark said εἰς πάντα τὰ ἔθνη, as also follows here πᾶσι τοῖς ἔθνεσι. But this was fulfilled before the destruction of Jerusalem. Therefore Mark added πρῶτον. For what the Psalmist had said about the celestial spheres, Paul applies to the Gospel (which is accustomed to be signified by heaven), and indeed in such a way that he seems to me to clearly designate his own times, Rom. X. 18. For also writing to the Colossians he speaks no less γενικῶς, saying that the word of the Gospel παρῆναι ἐν παντὶ τῷ κόσμῳ and κηρυχθῆναι πάσῃ τῇ κτίσει τῇ ὑπὸ τὸν οὐρανόν. Nay, Paul even says that the faith of the Romans was preached ἐν ὅλῳ τῷ κόσμῳ, Rom. I. 8. But Chrysostom well concludes, if Paul alone carried the doctrine of Christ from Jerusalem even to Illyricum, and, as some think, even into Spain, what is to be thought of all the other Apostles and so many of their helpers. Certainly Clement of Rome also says that the Gospel had reached the lands across the Ocean. Doubtless, by the example of even barbarian nations, God wished to invite the Jews to the obedience of the Gospel, and to convince the disobedient of their stubborn incredulity among all peoples, before He poured out the treasures of His wrath upon them. This is εἰς τὴν ἐμβάλλουσαν τῶν κρίσιν. Mark teaches us this sentiment when he says, εἰς πάντα τὰ ἔθνη δεῖ πρῶτον κηρυχθῆναι τὸ εὐαγγέλιον. Add Ezech. III. 6, 7.

These things can be opposed to the Calvinists, whom even Chamier himself refutes in T. II. Panstr. LXVI. c. 3. §. 14, in that they deny that the whole world is denoted here. But that some infer from this passage that the Gospel must be preached again to all before the end of the world, even though most have maliciously rejected the grace of the preached Gospel, that neither agrees with the present text, in which there is no discussion of the signs of the most recent day, as we have already warned several times, nor can it be proved from elsewhere in the Holy Scriptures. Finally, the Papists are foolish when they conclude that the Anti-Christ has not yet come from the fact that the Gospel has not yet been preached through the whole world, for it is manifest from this prophecy of Christ and the testimony of the Apostle, Rom. X. 18, Col. I. 23, that it was already preached through the whole world in the time of the Apostles. Add to these the testimonies of History and Ecclesiastical antiquity, Justin in Dial. with Trypho. There is no people on earth to whom the name of Christ has not become known, Iren. b. I. ch. 2. The Church has been sown throughout the whole world, even to the ends of the earth, See also Tertul. against the Jews, ch. 7. Euseb. b. III. ch. 5. etc.

Εἰς μαρτύριον] It can take the sense which we discussed at chapter X. But it is more straightforward to say, as we have already begun to explain, that God as it were called all nations to witness, so that the stubbornness of the Jews might be known to them, before He exacted punishment.

Καὶ τότε ἥξει τὸ τέλος] Of the judgments of God against the Jewish nation, as we said above. קץ בא Ezech. VII. 2.

Latin:

Vers. 14. Ἐν ὅλῃ τῇ οἰκουμένῃ] Marcus dixit εἰς πάντα τὰ ἔθνη, ut & hic sequitur πᾶσι τοῖς ἔθνεσι. Hoc autem impletum est ante excidium Hierosolymorum. Ideo Mar- cus adje it πρῶτον. Nam quod de cœlestibus orbibus dixe- rat Psalmographus, ad Evangelium (quod per cœlum de- fig ari solet) aprat Paulus, & ita quidem ut mihi videatur apertè sua tempora designare Rom. X, 18. Nam & ad Co- lossenses scribens non minus γενικῶς loquitur, dicens ver- sui bum illud Evangelii παρῆναι ἐν παντὶ τῷ κόσμῳ & κηρυχθῆ- ναι πάσῃ τῇ κτίσει τῇ ὑπὸ τὸν ὀυρανὸν Quin & fidem Roma- norum Paulus ait prædicatam ἐν ὅλῳ τῷ κόσμῳ Rom. I. 8. Bene autem colligit Chrysostomus, si unus Paulus ab Hie- rosolymis ad Illyricum usque Christi doctrinam pertulit, &, ut quidam existimant etiam in Hispaniam, quid de omnibus aliis Apostolis & tot eorum adjutoribus sit existi- mandum. Certe Clemens Romanus etiam ad terras trans- Oceanum Evangelium ait pervenisse. Nimirum exemplo gentium etiam barbararum Deus Judæos invitare voluit ad obedientiam Evangelii, & non obedientes contumacis incredulitatis apud omnes populos convincere, antequam in eos iræ suæ thesauros effunderet. Hoc est εἰς τὴν ἐν- βάλεσαν τῶν κρίσιν. Hanc sententiam Marcus nos docet cum dicit, εἰς πάντα τὰ ἔθνη δεῖ πρῶτον κηρυχθῆναι τὸ ἐυαγγέλιον. Adde Ezech. III. 6. 7.

Opponi hæc possunt Calvinianis, quos refutat etiam ipse Chamier T. II. Panstr. LXVI. c. 3. §. 14. qua negant totum terrarum orbem hic denotari. Quod autem nonnulli ex h. l. colligunt, etiam ante finem mundi denuo omnibus Evangelium præ- dicandum esse, utut plerique gratiam Evangelii præ- dicati malitiose rejecerint, id neque textui præsen- ti convenit, in quo non agitur de signis diei novis- simi, ut aliquoties jam monuimus, neque aliunde e S. literis probari potest. Inepti denique sunt Papistæ, cum Anti-Christum nondum venisse inde concludunt, quod Evangelium nondum prædica- tum sit per totum orbem, id enim jam Apostolo- rum tempore per totum orbem prædicatum esse, ex hoc vaticinio Christi, & testimonio Apostoli, Rom. X. 18. Col. I. 23. manifestum est. Adde his testimonia Historiæ & antiquitatis Ecclesiasticæ Justin. in Dial. cum Tryph. Nullus in terra populus est, cui non innotuerit Christi nomen, Iren. l. I. cap. 2. Ecclesia per universum orbem imo ad fines terræ se- minata est, Vid. & Tertul. c. Jud. c. 7. Euseb. l. III. c. 5. &c.

Εἰς μαρτύριον] Potest eum sensum accipere de quo egi- mus ad caput X. Sed expeditius est, ut dicamus quemad- modum explicare jam cœpimus, Deum velut antestatum omnes gentes, ut nota illis esset Judæorum pertinacia, antequam pœnas exposceret.

Καὶ τότε ἥξει τὸ τέλος] Judiciorum Dei adversus gen- tem Judæorum, ut supra diximus. קץ בא Ezech. VII. 2.

## 24:15
Vers. 15. Ὅταν ὖν ἴδητε τὸ βδέλυγμα τῆς ἐρημώσεως] After the distant signs, Christ indicates the sign of the imminent destruction. In Luke it is: when you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies, then know that its desolation has drawn near. Elsewhere in Luke, Christ explains the same thing thus: your enemies will cast a bank about you and will surround you and hem you in on every side. This sign was both proper to the thing signified, and had certainty, not from natural consequence, but from divine decree. That it was proper appears from the fact that, from the time Christ said these things, it happened only once that the city of Jerusalem was surrounded by camps (for that is what χάραξ means). For Cestius Gallus attacked one part of the city from one side: but he did not surround the city with camps: add that he was not the leader of a regular army, which is indicated by the word ςρατοπέδων. Titus Vespasianus led a regular army to the city, he surrounded the city with camps, ςρατόπεδον περιέβαλεν, as Josephus speaks in the fifth book of the Wars, leading sixty thousand soldiers besides camp followers and servants. By this sight, Christ, commanding that certain destruction be expected, not only takes away from the Jews all hope of the city being liberated by divine power, as had happened once in the times of Ezekiel, but also the confidence they were about to conceive partly in the number of their own people, which can be gathered from the fact that Josephus says the siege consumed 110 myriads, partly in the ferocity of their spirits more than their boldness, partly in the weakness of the works, concerning which it is worth the effort to transcribe what the victor himself thought from Josephus: But Titus, having gone inside, marveled at the other fortifications of the city, and at the towers, which the tyrants left behind in their madness. For having seen then the height of their masonry, and the size of each stone. and the precision of the joining, and how great they were in breadth, and how tall they were in height; we have fought with God, he said, and it was God who cast down the Jews from these fortifications, since what can the hands of men or machines do against these towers? No other sign from Matthew and Mark, than from

That the words of Luke just cited indicate this, the identity of the preceding and following things clearly, if I am not mistaken, indicates. Add that Luke, using the word ἐρημώσεως, clearly looks to that same place in Daniel, whose words Christ uses here. Therefore, in order for us to understand what it is that Christ says, τὸ βδέλυγμα τῆς ἐρημώσεως, we must have recourse to Daniel. In him, chapter IX. 27, there is שקצים משמם, βδέλυγμα τοῦ ἐρημώσεων in the Greeks: in chapter XI. 31, השקוץ משמם, which the Greeks translate βδέλυγμα ἠφανισμένον: but in chapter XII. 11, there is שקוץ שמם, in the Greeks τὸ βδέλυγμα τοῖς ἐρημώσεως. I do not name the LXX interpreters here, because it is Theodotion's version in this part that we use, not the LXX, as Jerome teaches us regarding Daniel and as some words testify. But to return to the places in Daniel, we concede to the Jews that the latter two deal with Antiochus, and that therefore שקוץ there is εἴδωλον Διὸς ὀλυμπίου, which Antiochus had placed in the temple, and which the writer of the first book of Maccabees, looking back at the places of Daniel already mentioned, calls τὸ βδέλυγμα τῆς ἐρημώσεως. But the Hebrews draw the words of chapter IX to Antiochus in vain, since the weeks named there cannot be understood as days; for thus one would stop far short of the times of Antiochus: and the weeks of years run far beyond Antiochus, from whatever edict for the restoration of the city or temple you may have taken the beginning of the count. Moreover, Hebrew usage does not recognize other weeks. And indeed, the ancient Jews, along with us, referred this passage to Roman times. Daniel, says Josephus, καὶ περὶ ἧ ῥωμαίων ἡγεμονίας ἀνέγραψε καὶ ὅτι ὑπ’ αὐτῶν ἐρημωθήσεται, namely the temple, which had preceded: and since he often finds the fulfillment of the prophecies in the history of the destruction, he looks especially to this place: which was also observed by Chrysostom in his second book against the Jews. This being posited, let us see the words of the Prophet: ועל כנף שקוצים משמם עד-כלה ונחרצה תתך על־שומם. First, it is doubted what כנף is. The Greeks, who read that word not with the sound of the construct state, as we do with the Masoretes, but with the primitive sound, understood by the wing the Cherubim, and by the Cherubim, synecdochically, the temple itself: and so they translate ἐπὶ τὸ ἱερὸν, which can be understood either in the temple or against the temple. Those who read with the Masoretes, and therefore construct this word with the following nouns, others interpret as an army, or by example, if I am not mistaken, others as an expansion, just as in Malachi IV. 2, the expansion of light is called by the same name. Wherefore I think that is rather to be followed. Some Hebrews, and certain others who followed them, draw שמם to the meaning of being stunned. But others more correctly deny that there is a reason why one should depart here from the most proper and no less frequent notion of ἐρημώσεως. For שמם in Kal, as they call it, is ἐρημοῦσθαι, but in Pihel it is ἐρημοῦν, which can also be called ἀφανίζειν. Therefore, the Hebrew words can be rendered thus word for word: And upon the expansion of the abomination of desolation, and indeed until the consummation and destruction (supply: may it be present) shall pour itself out (either Christ, or that time remaining of the week: for it can be referred to either) upon him who is desolated. Now it is certain that the word שקוץ is for the most part taken for an idol, as can be seen in 1 Kings XI. 3 and 7, 2 Kings XXIII. 24, Ezekiel VII. 2, ch. VIII. 10, ch. XX. 7, Jeremiah XXXII. 34, and elsewhere: in which places the Greeks translate βδέλυγμα, which word exists in the same sense in Wisdom XIV. 11. Well does Chrysostom in his second book against the Jews say, ἅπαν εἴδωλον καὶ πᾶν τύπωμα ἀνθρώπου παρὰ τοῖς Ἰουδαίοις βδέλυγμα ἐκαλεῖτο.
