Nor is it otherwise taken where it deals with Antiochus, as is most evident from history itself. When the ancient Christians noticed this, they had not badly sought a similar meaning for τῷ βδελύγματος here too: but others refer it to the act of Pilate, which is certainly too far removed from the times of the destruction: indeed, it had already happened when Christ was speaking these things about what was to happen around the end of the city, as the very sequence of the words shows. Others have fled to the times of Hadrian: but even if we grant that a part of the city, that is, the towers which Titus had left remaining, and if anything had been built after the times of Titus, was destroyed when he had captured the city of Bither (which, because of the great consensus of writers, Appian, who lived in the age of Hadrian, then Eusebius and Jerome, I do not dare to deny), certainly he did not overturn the temple, which is the main subject here, but Titus, as the eyewitness Josephus teaches us. Wherefore others interpret βδέλυγμα as a statue of Titus placed in the temple, but that narrative has no author: add that it could not even have happened except after the victory of Titus. But here it deals with the signs preceding the victory. For which reason the cessation of the τῷ ἐνδελεχισμῦ cannot be understood as signified here either. For that preceded the destruction by a small moment, when no flight remained. I, having considered the matter, do not doubt that the Roman military standards are called βδέλυγμα, about which Tertullian says: The entire religion of the Romans is camp-based; it venerates the standards, swears by the standards, places the standards before all the gods, all those famous displays of images are the ornaments of the crosses. That the standards themselves had the figure of a cross has been abundantly demonstrated by many: but affixed to those standards were many shields, one above another, whence Tertullian said 'displays,' as Papinius said 'display of hair': in those shields were images, that is, busts, as Josephus speaks, of Caesar, namely of those who had been enrolled among the gods. Such standards with shields can be seen on coins. Tertullian has that from Justin, to whom he had said: ἧ παρ' ὑμῖν ἀποθνησκόντων ἀυτοκρατόρων ἐικόνας ἐπὶ τούτῳ τῷ σχήματι ἀνατίθετε. Arrian: Τὰ σημεῖα τῆς πολικῆς στρατιᾶς ἀετοὶ, ἐικόνες βασιλέων. In Tacitus, there is mention of those images on the standards throughout. Because of those images, the standards were adored, as we have already heard Tertullian saying. Suetonius: Artabanus, having crossed the Euphrates, adored the eagles and Roman standards and the images of the Caesars. For this reason, in Tacitus, the standards are called the divinities of the legions and the gods of wars. To him also belongs this: embracing the standards and the eagle, he protected himself with religion. Such standards Titus placed conspicuously in his camp, as if a temple contrary to the Jerusalem temple. For Tacitus also speaks elsewhere thus: with the eagles and standards and images of the gods shining, in the manner of a temple. And Josephus himself in The Jewish War, book III, chapter 8, what he had called standards, he soon calls the holy things. As also Herodian in book IV. To such standards placed around the city, Alexandra persuades the procurator of Herod, Josephus, to flee as to a temple, as the historian Josephus narrates in Antiquities, book XV. These very standards the victor soon brought into the ruins of the temple, where the soldiers even sacrificed to the standards, as Josephus himself speaks. Therefore, why they are called abominations of desolation or desolating, as the Hebrew idiom has it, is not obscure: because, namely, they threatened desolation (a word which Josephus uses very often in his history of the capture) not only to the Jewish cult (which that idol brought by Antiochus had also done) but also to the temple and the city: moreover, it is called an expansion of the abomination because the standards were accustomed to be set up in an open and most conspicuous place. Tacitus concerning Titus: Having placed the camp before the walls of Jerusalem, he displayed the drawn-up legions.

Daniel the prophet] By this name Josephus, the writer of the Annals, also often calls Daniel, nor does he hesitate to equate him with the greatest prophets: as also Josephus Iacchides, Daniel 1:17.

The discourse of Christ is about a proper and conspicuous sign of imminent destruction: and about the destruction which is going to bring an end to the city and to the entire state of Judea, whether political, civil, or ecclesiastical. Therefore, that sign cannot be understood as a statue or some image in the temple, as some interpret it concerning the statue of Olympian Jupiter, and the idols of Antiochus Epiphanes, and the profanation of the temple done by him (1 Maccabees 1; Josephus, Antiquities, book XII, chapter 7): some interpret it concerning the golden eagle of Herod placed over the greatest gate of the temple, in Josephus, The Jewish War, book I, chapter 21; others concerning the insignia and image of Tiberius Caesar brought by Pilate into the Sanctuary itself after the passion of Christ, from Josephus, Antiquities, book XIII, chapter 4 (who, however, says nothing about it being brought into the temple, let alone the sanctuary, but at least that it was brought into the city to the insult of the law, in the same place and in The Jewish War, book II, chapter 8, which Eusebius repeats in book II, History, chapter 6.) Others concerning the statue of Caligula, the successor of Tiberius, which, however, was prevented from being brought into the temple by the prudence and intercession of Petronius, the governor of Syria, and Aristobulus. Not all these things happened long before those times of which Christ speaks, and most even happened before this discourse of Christ, such as the deed of Antiochus, Herod, and Pilate. Even in the time of Caligula, such a hasty flight as Christ prescribes was not yet necessary. Add that by such things the temple may indeed have been profaned, but desolation was not brought about. Here, however, the discourse is about the desolating abomination. Nor is this sign to be explained as the sins of the priests, which were indeed truly abominations (Leviticus 18:26; Deuteronomy 7:25, chapter 18:9; Proverbs 11:1; Jeremiah 11:13) and the cause of desolation: but they were neither so manifest to all, being covered by hypocrisy, nor did they immediately and proximately precede the destruction, but they flourished in the city for a long time.

Nor is this to be understood concerning the profanation of the temple through sacrifices, which were abominations after the death of Christ, with Dionysius the Carthusian and the author of the Historia Scholastica in chapter X of Daniel, which could not have been a certain sign of the now imminent destruction, which finally happened 40 years after the death of Christ. Nor is this to be understood with Tostatus, Baronius, Hesselius, and Jansenius concerning the seditious Zealots in the city, of whom Josephus writes in book II of the Jewish War, chapter 22, book IV, chapter 3, and book V, chapter 2; for it was not they, but the Roman soldiers, who properly desolated the city: nor are their deeds and passing crimes conveniently explained by the abomination standing in the holy place, for which reason that explanation is refuted by Pererius himself. We have a most certain and highly infallible interpreter, St. Luke, chapter XXI, 20: When you shall see Jerusalem compassed about with an army, then know that the desolation thereof is at hand. This army, surrounding the city on every side, was the abomination of desolation and a most certain sign of destruction. Concerning which, therefore, these things are interpreted by Origen in tract XXIX on Matthew, Chrysostom in homily LXXVII on Matthew, and Augustine in Epistle LXXX to Hesychius. And truly the Roman army was the abomination of desolation, which consisted of Gentile idolaters, who were an abomination to the Jews (Acts 10:28), and they carried with them very many idols in statues and military standards, and brought extreme desolation upon the city and the temple.

Nor do the words of Daniel demand anything else, by which he did not indeed describe an army spread far and wide through the extension of wings, as some wish from Isaiah VIII:8, for here there is no mention of the extension of wings (concerning which see Graserus on chapter IX of Daniel, page 392), but the Roman army is expressed through the EXPANSION OF THE ABOMINATIONS THAT MAKE DESOLATE, through which, as the particle על is wont sometimes to denote an instrument and to be explained as BY, which Grotius in this place rightly rendered thus: it shall be poured out, Daniel saying, upon that which is desolated, namely the city, the temple, and the people, or Christ will pour it out, or it will drip: which is the immediate subject. The remainder of the last week does not pertain to this: because those weeks were to end long before the destruction of Jerusalem, namely in the fourth year from the passion of Christ according to the Prophetic oracle. Blessed Gerhard renders the preposition על as 'upon': and there shall be upon the extremity abominations of desolations, but because כנף is placed in the construct state, these ought to be rendered 'the extremity of abominations,' and thus there would be no sense: and there shall be upon the extremity of the abominations of desolations: for what would be said to be upon the extremity of the abominations? Graserus offers another interpretation: and upon the wing of detestable abominations a waster (shall rush), loc. cit. p. 391. But thus the object of the desolation is established as the wing of detestable abominations, by which Graserus understands the temple: whereas, however, the abomination of desolations, according to Christ's interpretation, is not the object but a sign of imminent destruction: nor does that name 'wing of abominations' suit the temple or the Sanctuary. The other words Graserus translates not badly on page 411. For even unto the final consummation, and the completion of the decree, it shall drip upon the desolated. Concerning the sense of which, this author may be compared.

Verse 15. ἑςὸς ἐν [τόπῳ ἁγίῳ] and says Mark: This is not in the temple itself, for that was not a sign of the coming slaughter, but the slaughter itself most present, but in the sight of the temple, on the ground around the city: which ground ought to have been sacred to God alone, not to the gods of the nations. Thus סביבות ירושלם is named as a place exceptionally holy even in Psalm LXXIX:3. And Alexander, son of Antiochus, wishes the immunity and sanctity of Jerusalem to extend ἕως τῇ ὅρων

of it, according to Josephus. Just as Demetrius in the indulgence which exists in the Maccabean history, book I, chapter X, 31: let Jerusalem be holy and free, and the borders thereof. Josephus says that the right of asylum in the temple was granted by Demetrius, and to the things pertaining to it. Similar is that in Tacitus, Annals III: They recalled the names of the Emperors who attributed the same sanctity not only to the temple (of Hierocaesarea) but to two miles around it. For this reason, when Vitellius was preparing to lead his forces against Aretas through Judea, the Jews, as Josephus says, παρητῶντο τὴν διὰ τῆς χώρας ὁδὸν : γὰρ ἀυτοῖς εἶναι πάτριον, περιορᾷν εἰκόνας εἰς ἀυτὴν φερομένας, πολλοὺς d' εἶναι σημαί αις ἐπικειμένας. Behold, they denied that it was lawful for standards to be seen on the soil of Judea, because in the standards there were many images. Vitellius obeyed this warning, which happened not long after Christ had said these things. But some time before He said these things, a sedition had arisen in Jerusalem, for the reason that Pilate had secretly brought standards into Jerusalem. Therefore, He wishes this to be taken as a presage of imminent destruction, when the Jews will be compelled not to hear of standards brought in secretly, but to see them placed openly in an illustrious place, and not in just any corner of Judea, but under the very walls of Jerusalem, a soil especially holy, and in which even the reverence of the temple would make it least fitting that this be done, nor indeed would it be done, unless God were abominating that temple and the entire worship of the Jewish nation, as having been in many ways imputed. Josephus often notes that God had turned away from the holy things. For it had been a holy house and one that was mocking.

These things, and what Grotius hands down concerning the βδελύγματι ἐρημώσεως, can be read more prolixly in the Harmonia Evangelica of Blessed Gerhard, whose work in these, and in most other things in this chapter especially, Grotius seems to have used, even though he concealed his name.

Let the reader understand] I agree with those who include these in a parenthesis. For the following parts cohere with the preceding ones, as is apparent also from Mark and Luke. Moreover, this is also from Daniel והבין ותשכל, where the Greeks have κὶ γνώσῃ κὶ συνήσεις, Chapter 9:25. It is to be noted that some prophecies are published more obscurely, others more clearly, by the certain counsel of God. For there are certain evils which God wishes to be avoided by the pious, such as those which are punishments for the greatest crimes. Among these evils was the destruction by Titus. Therefore, most open signs were added, by which the pious were also warned, as Epiphanius, Eusebius, and others note, and departed from Jerusalem in time. There are other evils which God wishes to serve for the testing of the constancy of men, such as the vexation of Antiochus. He indeed predicts these, so that when they happen it may appear that they were foreseen by God, but He does not provide signs by which, if observed, they might be avoided: because if that were done, the constancy of the pious would not be apparent. Therefore, He signified how long the evils under Antiochus would last, but He remained silent about when they would begin. See Jacchiades on Daniel 12:10. Therefore, concerning the prophecy of those evils, Daniel says שמעתי ולא אבין, that is, as the Greeks translate, κὶ ἐγὼ ἤκεσα κὶ ὁ συνῆκα: to whom God responds that those things ought to be closed and sealed until a certain time. But that which was predicted concerning the destruction by Titus also had a note of definite time in Daniel, and if anything could seem more obscure, it had been made manifest, with Christ saying that these things would come to pass when the profane army first approached the city with its standards.

which no one could make void by supplications, to destroy the people and cast them out of the land. And elsewhere God often denies that He will admit any deprecation. Such was the decree of God in the times of Titus, concerning the destruction of the temple and the city: which Josephus calls fate and necessity, noting often the blinded minds of the Jerusalemites, so that they stubbornly rejected all exhortations to peace, and after many examples of desperate audacity, they yielded to those final and most firm fortifications, and many other things which are worth the effort to read, God indeed, God, as he says, was turning these things in this way, having condemned the destruction of the city as polluted. And so it was blinded by necessity which was already present to the city and to them themselves. Titus himself, in Philostratus in the life of Apollonius, said after the victory that he had not done these things himself, but that God, having shown His wrath, had offered his own hands.

Latin:

Vers. 15. Ὅταν ὖν ἴδητε τὸ βδέλυγμα τῆς ἐρημώσεως] Post signa remota, Christus signum excidii proximum indicat. Apud Lucam est : ὅταν ἴδητε κυκλωμένην ὑπὸ ςρατοπέδων τὴν Ἱερυσαλὴμ τότε γνῶτε ὅτε ἤγγικεν ἡ ἐρήμωσις ἀυτῆς. Alibi apud Lucam Christus rem eandem ita exponit : περικαλῦσιν οἱ ἐχθροί σε χάρακα σοι καὶ περικυκλώσεσι καὶ συνέξεσι σε πάντοθεν. Signum hoc & proprium erat rei signatæ, & cer- titudinem habebat, non ex naturali consequentia, sed ex divino decreto. Proprium fuisse inde apparet, quod ex quo Christus hæc dixerat, semel duntaxat contigit urbem Hierosolyma castris (id enim est χάραξ) cingi. Nam Cestius Gallus ex urbis parte partem alteram oppugnavit: urbem autem castris non ambiit: adde quod nec erat du- ctor justi exercitus, qui indicatur voce ςρατοπέδων. Justum exercitum ad urbem duxit, castra urbi circumdedit Titus Vespasianus, ςρατόπεδον περιέβαλεν, ut ἁλώσεως quinto Jo- sephus loquitur, ducens sexaginta millia militum præter lixas & calones. Hoc conspectu Christus jubens certum excidium exspectari, non modo spem omnem Judæis eri- pit urbis divinitus liberandæ, ut quondam Ezechiel tem- poribus contigerat, sed & eam quam concepturi erant fi- duciam partim in suorum numero, qui colligi inde potest, quod obsidio absumtas dicit Josephus μυριάδας ἑκατὸν καὶ dέκα, partim in animorum feritate magis quam audacia, partim infirmitate operum, de qua quid ipse senserit vi- ctor operæ pretium est ex Josepho asscribere : παρελθὼν δὲ Τίτος εἴσω, τά τ’ ἄλλα τῆς ὀχυρότητος τὴν πόλιν, καὶ τῶν πύρ- γων ἀποθαύμασεν, ὓς οἱ τύραννοι κατὰ φρενοβλάβειαν ἀπέλι- πον. κατιδὼν γῦν τότε νασὸν ἀυτῶν ὕψος, καὶ τὸ μέγεθος ἑκάςης πέτρας. τήν τε ἀκρίβειαν τῆς ἁρμονίας, καὶ ὅσοι μὲν εὔρους, ἡλίκοι δὲ ἦσαν τὴν ἀνάτασιν· σὺν θεῷ γ’ ἐπολεμήσα- μεν, ἔφη, καὶ θεὸς ἦν ὁ τῶν δὲ τῶν ἐρυμάτων τὲς Ἰυδαίες καθε- λὼν, ἐπεὶ χεῖρες τε ἀνθρώπων ἢ μηχαναὶ, τί πρὸς τύτες πύργες δύνανται; Non aliud signum à Matthæo & Marco, quam à

Lucæ verbis modo citatis indicari, antecedentium & con- sequentium ταυτότης manifeste, ni fallor, indicat. Adde quod Lucas utens voce ἐρημώσεως manifeste eundem re- spicit Danielis locum, cujus verbis hîc utitur Christus. Ut ergo intelligamus quid sit quod Christus dicat τὸ βδέλυγμα τῆς ἐρημώσεως; recurrendum est nobis ad Danielem. Apud eum capite IX. 27. est, שקצים משמם βδέλυγμα τοῦ ἐρημώσεων Græcis: capite XI. 31. השקוץ משמם quod Græci transferunt βδέλυγμα ἠφανισμένον: capite autem XII. 11. est שקוץ שמם Græcis τὸ βδέλυγμα τοῖς ἐρημώ- σεως. LXX. Interpretes hîc non nomino, quia Theodo- tionis in hac parte est versio, qua utimur, non LXX. ut nos docet ad Danielem Hieronymus & voces nonnullæ testan- tur. Sed Danielis ad loca ut redeam, posterioribus duo- bus agi de Antiocho concedimus Judæis, atque adeo שקוץ ibi esse εἴδωλον Διὸς ὀλυμπίου, quod Antiochus in templo col- locaverat, quodque Maccabaici primi Scriptor, loca Danie- lis jam dicta respiciens, vocat τὸ βδέλυγμα τῆς ἐρημώσεως. At verba capitis IX. ad Antiochum frustra trahunt Hebræi, cum hebdomates ibi nominatæ dierum non possint intelligi; ita enim multum citra Antiochi tempora consisteretur: & an- norum septimanæ multum ultra Antiochum procurrunt, à quocunque tandem restaurandæ urbis aut templi edicto nu- merandi exordium sumseris. Alias autem hebdomadas Hebraicus usus non agnoscit. Et sane Judæi veteres ad Ro- mana tempora hunc locum nobiscum retulerunt. Δανιὴλ, inquit Josephus, καὶ περὶ ἧ ῥωμαίων ἡγεμονίας ἀνέγραψε καὶ ὅτι ὑπ’ αὐτῶν ἐρημωθήσεται, nimirum τὸ ἱερὸν, quod præcesse- rat: & cum in excidii historia sæpe reperit impletam vatici- niorum fidem, hunc præcipue locum respicit: quod & Chry- sostomo observatum altero adversus Judæos libro. Hoc posito verba Prophetæ videamus: ועל כנף שקוצים משמם עד-כלה ונחרצה תתך על־שומם. Primù כנף quid sit dubitatur. Græci, qui eam vocem legerunt non sono regiminis, ut nos cum Masoritis, sed sono primitivo, per alam intellexerunt Cherubim, per Cherubim autem συνεκδοχικῶς templum ipsum: itaque vertunt ἐπὶ τὸ ἱερὸν, quod intelligi potest vel in templum vel contra templum. Qui cum Masoritis legunt, ac proinde voce hanc cum no- minibus sequentibus construunt, alii interpretantur exerci- tum, sive exemplo, ni fallor, alii expansionem, sicut Mala- chiæ IV. 2. expansio lucis eodem nomine appellatur. Quare id potius sequendu puto. שמם Hebræi nonnulli, & qui- dam alii eos secuti ad obstupescendi significationem tra- hunt. Sed alii rectius causam esse negant cur à maxime propria nec minus frequenti notione ἐρημώσεως hîc disceda- tur. Nam שמם in Kal, ut vocant, est ἐρημοῦσθαι, in Pihel autem ἐρημοῦν, quod & ἀφανίζειν dici potest. Verba igitur Hebræa ita reddi possunt κατὰ πόδας: Et per expansionem abo- minationem desolantem, & quidem donec consummatio & exci- dium (supple adsit) effundet se (aut Christus, aut tempus illud septimanæ reliquum: nam utroque referri potest) super eum qui desolatur. Iam certum est vocem שקוץ plerumque pro idolo accipi, ut videre est 1. Reg. XI. 3. & 7. 2. Reg. XXIII. 24. Ezech. VII. 2. c. VIII 10. c. XX. 7. Ier. XXXII 34. & a- libi: quibus locis Græci vertunt βδέλυγμα, quæ vox sensu eodem exstat Sap. XIV. 11. Bene Chrysostomus II. adver- sus Judæos, ἅπαν εἴδωλον καὶ πᾶν τύπωμα ἀνθρώπου παρὰ τοῖς Ἰουδαίοις βδέλυγμα ἐκαλεῖτο. Nec aliter sumi ubi de Antiocho agitur ex ipsa historia apertissimum est. Quod cum animadverterent Christiani veteres, hic quoque simi- lem τῷ βδελύγματος significationem non male quæsive- rant: sed alii ad factum Pilati id referunt, quod sane ni- mium abest ab excidii temporibus: imo jam evenerat cum Christus hæc loqueretur de eo quod eventurum erat circa finem urbis, ut ipsa verborum series ostendit. Alii confu- gerunt ad Adriani tempora: sed ut demus Adriano partem urbis, id est turres quas Titus reliquas fecerat, & si quid post Titi tempora ædificatum erat, dirutum esse, cum urbem Bither expugnasset (quod propter magnam Scriptorum consensio nem, Appiani, qui vixit Adriani ævo, deinde Eusebii & Hieronymi, negare non audeo) certe tem- plum, de quo hîc vel præcipue agitur, non ille evertit, sed Ti- tus, quod nos docet oculatus testis Josephus. Quare alii βδέλυγμα interpretantur statuam Titi in templo colloca- tam, sed ea narratio nullum habet auctorem: adde quod ne potuit quidem id fieri nisi post Titi victoriam. At hic de notis victoriam præcedentibus agitur. Quam ob causam nec intermissio τῷ ἐνδελεχισμῦ hic intelligi potest signifi- cata. Nam ea parvo momento excidium antecessit, cum nulla superesset fuga. Ego re considerata non du- bito βδέλυγμα vocari signa Romanorum militaria, de quibus ita Tertullianus: Religio Romanorum tota castren- sis signa veneratur, signa jurat, signa omnibus Diis præpo- nit, omnes illi imaginum suggestus insignes monilia cru- cium sunt. Signa ipsa crucis habuisse figuram abunde à multis demonstratum est: affixi autem iis signis erant clupei multi alter super alterum, unde suggestus dixit Tertullianus, ut suggestum comæ Papinius: in iis culpeis erant imagines, id est προτομαὶ, ut Josephus loquitur, Cæsaris, eorum scilicet qui in divos erant relati. Ta- lia signa cum clupeis videre est in nummis. Habet au- tem illud Tertullianus ex Justino cui ita dixerat, ἧ παρ' ὑμῖν ἀποθνησκόντων ἀυτοκρατόρων ἐικόνας ἐπὶ τούτῳ τῷ σχή- ματι ἀνατίθετε. Arrianus: Τὰ σημεῖα τῆς πολικῆς στρατιᾶς ἀετοὶ, ἐικόνες βασιλέων. Apud Tacitum passim istarum in signis imaginum mentio. Propter eas imagines adorata signa, ut jam dicentem Tertullianum au- divimus. Suetonius: Artabanus transgressus Euphra- tem aquilas & signa Romana, Cæsarumque imagines adoravit. Ideo Tacito numina legionum & bel- lorum Dii vocantur. Ejusdem est illud: signa & aqui- lam amplexus religione sese tutabatur. Talia signa Titus conspicua in castris suis posuit, quasi templum templo Hierosolymitano contrarium. Nam & Tacitus alibi ita loquitur, fulgentibus aquilis signisque & simulacris Deum, in modum templi. Et ipse Josephus ἁλώσεως III. cap. 8. quas σημαίας dixerat, mox Τὰ ἱερὰ vocat. Ut & Herod a- nus libro IV. Ad talia signa περὶ τὴν πόλιν posita, ut ad templum confugere Iosepho Herodis procuratori suadet Alexandra, narrante historiæ scriptore Iosepho lib. XV. Antiquit. Hæc ipsa signa mox victor intulit templi rui- nis, ubi milites etiam ἔθυσαν ταῖς σημαίαις, ut ipse Iose- phus loquitur. Βδελύγματα igitur ἐρημώσεως aut ἐρημω- τικὰ, ut habet Hebræa locutio, cur vocentur, obscurum non est: quia scilicet ἐρημίαν (qua voce in τῆς ἁλώσεως hi- storia sæpissime Iosephus utitur) minabantur, non tantum cultui Iudaico quod fecerat & illud εἴδωλον ab Antiocho allatum) sed & templo urbique: expansio autem βδελύγ- ματος dicitur, quia in loco aperto maximeque conspi- cuo signa constitui solebant. Tacitus de Tito: Castris ante mœnia Hierosolymorum positis instructas legiones osten- tavit.

Δανιὴλ τῶ προφήτου] Hoc nomine Danielem sæpe etiam Iosephus Annalium scriptor nuncupat, neque eum du- bitat maximis Prophetis æquare: ut & Iosephus Iacchia- des Daniel. I. 17.

De signo proprio & conspicuo imminentis ex- cidii sermo est Christo: deque excidio quod fi- nem allaturum est urbi, & statui universo Judææ, sit politico tum civilis tum Ecclesiastico. Signum ergo illud non potest intelligi statua vel imago quædam in templo, uti de statua Jovis Olympii, & idolis Antiochi Epiphanis, ac prophanatione templi per ipsum facta 1. Macc. I. Joseph. l. XII. Antiquit. c. 7. nonnulli interpretantur: de Herodis aurea aquila super maximam portam templi posita, apud Jose- phum lib. I. Bell. Iud. c. 21. alii de Tiberii Cæsaris insignibus & imagine à Pilato post Christi passio- nem in ipsum Sacrarium illata, è Joseph. l. XIII. Antiquit. c. 4. (qui vero nihil de eo, quod in templum, nedum sacrarium illata sit, saltem ad le- gis contumeliam in urbem illatam dicit l. c. & l. II. de Bell. Iud. c. 8. quod repetit Eusebius l. II. Hist. c. 6.) Alii de statua Caligulæ successoris Tiberii, quæ tamen ne inferretur templo Petronii Præfidis Syriæ, & Aristobuli prudentia & intercessione de- clinatum fuit. Non hæc omnia longe ante illa tempora, de quibus Christus agit, pleraque etiam ante hunc sermonem Christi contigere, utpote factum Antiochi, Herodis, & Pilati. Caligulæ etiam tempore tam præceps fuga qualem Chri- stus præscribit, nondum necessaria fuit. Adde quod talibus prophanatum quidem templum fu- erit, non autem facta sit desolatio. Hic vero de abominatione desolante sermo est. Neque si- gnum hoc de peccatis Sacerdotum explicandum, quæ vere quidem abominationes erant, Lev. IIX. 26. Deuteronom. VII. vers. 25. cap. XIIX. vers. 9. Prov. XI. vers. 1. Ierem. XI. vers. 13. & causa deso- lationis: sed nec tam manifesta omnibus, utpote hypocrisi tecta, nec immediate & proxime an- tecedebant excidium, sed diu viguerunt in urbe.

Nec de prophanatione templi, per sacrificia, quæ post mortem Christi abominationes fuêre, hæc accipienda cum Dionys. Carthus. & autore Histor. Scholast. in cap. X. Danielis,quæ non potuit cer- tum fignum esse jamjam imminentis excidii, quod demum 40. annis post mortem Christi accidit. Neque cum Tostato, Baronio, Hesselio, Jansenio de seditiosis in urbe Zelotis hæc intelligenda, de qui- bus Joseph. l. II. de B. I. c. 22. l. IV. c. 3. l. V. c. 2. nam non illi, sed Romani milites proprie desolati funt urbem:neque facta ipsorum & scelera transe- untia de abominatione in loco sancto stante com- mode explicantur, unde ab ipso Pererio illa expli- catio refellitur. Habemus interpretem certissi- mum,maximeq; infallibilem S. Lucam c.XXI. 20. Quum videritis circumdari ab exercitu Hierusa- lem, tunc scitote,quia appropinquavit desolatio. Qui exercitus urbem undiquaque cingens abominatio desolatrix fuit, ac signum certissimum exitii. De quo proinde hæc interpretantur Origenes tr. XXIX. in Matth. Chrysostomus hom.LXXVII. in Matth. August. Ep. XXC. ad Hesych. Et vere erat Ro- manus exercitus abominatio desolationis, qui ex Ethnicis idololatris constabat, qui Judæis erant ab- ominatio, Actor. X. 28. & idola quam plurima se- cum habebant, in statuis,signisque militaribus, ur- bique & templo extremam desolationem attulit.

Nec aliud poscunt verba Danielis,quibus non qui- dem per extensionem alarum descripsit exerci- tum longe lateque dilatatum,ut nonnulli ex Es. IIX. 8. volunt, nam hic extensionis alarum non sit mentio: quo de vid. Graserus in cap. IX. Daniel. pag. 392. sed exercitus Romanus exprimitur per EXPANSIONEM ABOMINATIO- NUM DESOLANTEM, per quam, uti solet particula על quandoque instrumentum de- notare, & exponi PER, quam hoc in loco Gro- tius recte sic reddidit, effundetur dicente Daniele, super id quod desolatur,urbem nempe, templum & populum, vel effundet sese, aut stillabit Christus: quod subjectum proximum est. Reliquum Se- ptimanæ ultimæ huc non facit: quia Septimanæ illæ longe ante excidium Hierosolymæ exituræ erant, quarto nempe anno à passione Christi secun- dum oraculum Propheticum. B. Gerhardus red- dit præpositionem על super:& erunt super extremi- tatem abominationes desolationum, sed quia כנף in statu constructionis ponitur, reddi hæc deberent extremitatem abominationum, & ita sensus nullus esset: & erunt super extremitatem abominationum desolationum: quid enim fore super extremitatem abominationum dicetur? Graserus aliam profert interpretationem: & super alam abominationum detestandarum vastator (ingruet) loc. cit. p. 391. sed ita objectum vastationis constituitur ala abomi- nationum detestandarum, per quam templum in- telligit Graserus: quum tamen abominatio deso- lationum, juxta Christi interpretationem, non ob- jectum sed signum sit imminentis excidii: nec no- men illud ala abominationum conveniat templo vel Sacrario. Cætera verba non male vertit Grase- rus p. 411. Nam usque ad finalem consummationem, fat alisque decreti expletionem super desolatum stil- labit. De quorum sensu autor hic conferri po- terit.

Vers. 15. ἑςὸς ἐν [τόπῳ ἁγίῳ] ἔτυ & dii Marcus: Hoc est non in ipso templo, id enim nota venturæ cladis non erat, sed ipsa clades præsentissima,verum in templi conspectu,in solo circum urbem:quod solumDeo uni,non gentium Diis, sacrum esse oportebat. Ita סביבות ירושלם tan- quam locus eximie sacer etiam in Psalmo LXXIX. 3. no- minatur. Et Alexander Antiochi filius immunitatem & sanctimoniam Hierosolymorum extendi vult ἕως τῇ ὅρων

ἀυτῆς apud Josephum. Sicut Demetrius in indulto quod ex- stat Maccabaicæ historiæ lib. I. cap. X. 31. ἱεροσόλυμα ἤτω ἁ- γία κὶ ἀφημένη κὶ τὰ ὅρια ἀυτῆς. Josephus à Demetrio concessum ait jus confugii in templum xὶ εἰς τὰ ὑπ᾿ ἀυτῷ χρηματίζοντα. Simile illud apud Tacitum Annal.III. Me- morabantur Imperatorum nomina qui non modo templo (Hie- rocæsariensi) sed duobus millibus passuum eandem sanctitatem tribuerent: Hac de causa cum Vitellius copias adversus A- retam ducere per Judæam pararet, Judæi, ut Josephus ait, παρητῶντο τὴν διὰ τῆς χώρας ὁδὸν : γὰρ ἀυτοῖς εἶναι πάτριον, περιορᾷν εἰκόνας εἰς ἀυτὴν φερομένας, πολλοὺς δ' εἶναι σημαί αις ἐπικειμένας. Ecce negabant fas esse signa in solo Judææ conspici, quia in signis multæ essent imagines. Cui monito Vitellius paruit,quod non ita multo post evenit quatnChri- stus hæc dixerat. Aliquanto vero antequam hæc diceret, seditio Hierosolymis orta erat, ideo quod Pilatus clam signa Hierofolymis intulisset. Præsagium ergo imminentis ex- cidii hoc vult accipi, cum cogentur Judæi non audire signa clam illata, sed palam in loco illustri posita conspicere, nec in quovis Judææ angulo, sed sub ipsa Hierosolymorum mœnia, solo apprime sancto, & in quo vel templi reveren- tia minime id fieri deceret, neque vero fieret, nisi Deus tem- plum illud omnemque cultum Judaicæ gentis, ut multis modis imputatum, abominaretur. Sæpe annotat Jose- phus Θεὸν ἀπεςράφθαι τὰ ἅγια. Fuisse enim οἶκον ἅγιον και ταγέλοντα.

Hæc, & quæ de βδελύγματι ἐρημώσεως tradit Grotius prolixius legi possunt in Harm.Evangel. B. Gerhardi, cujus opera in his,& plerisq; aliis hoc imprimis capite usus videtur Grotius, etsi dissimu- lato ejusdem nomine.

ὁ ἀναγινώσκων, νοείτω] Assentior hæc parenthesi inclu- dentibus. Cohærent enim sequentia prioribus, ut ex Mar- co etiam & Lucæ apparet. Est autem hoc etiam à Daniele והבין ותשכל,ubi Græci κὶ γνώσῃ κὶ συνήσεις C.IX. 25.No- tandum est,vaticinia alia obscurius, alia clarius edita,certo Dei consilio. Sunt enim quædam mala quæ à piis vitari vult Deus, ut quæ scelerum maximorum supplicia sunt. In his malis erat excidium Titi. Ideo additæ sunt notæ apertisli- mæ,quibus etiam pii admoniti,utEpiphanius,Eusebius,atq; alii notant, in tempore Hierosolymis exierunt, Sunt mala alia,quæ Deus explorandæ hominum constantiæ vult infer- vire, qualis erat vexatio Antiochi. Ea prædicit quidem,ita ut cum eveniunt à Deo provisa appareat, sed non præmittit notas quibus animadversis caveri possint: quia id si fieret, non appareret piorum constantia. Itaque mala sub Antio- cho quamdiu duratura essent significavit, sed quando ince- ptura,subticuit. Vide Jacchiaden ad Dan.XII. 10. Ideo de illorum malorum vaticinio a tDaniel שמעתי ולא אבין, id est, ut vertunt Græci, κὶ ἐγὼ ἤκεσα κὶ ὁ συνῆκα : cui Deus respondet illas res occlusas & obsignatas esse debere ad tempus aliquod. At illa de excidio Titi prædicto & apud Danielem habebat definiti temporis notam,& si quid videri poterat obscurius, patefactum erat, Christo dicente hæc eventum cum exercitus primum profanus cum signis ad urbem adventaret.

ἣν ὀυχ ἱκεσίαις ἄν τις ἄκυρον ποιήσειεν, ἀπολέσαι τὸν λαὸν καὶ τῆς χώρας ἐκβαλεῖν. Et alibi sæpe Deus negat ullam se admit- tere deprecationem. Tale erat decretum Dei temporibus Titi, de perdendo templo & urbe: quod εἱμαρμένην & τὸ χρε- ὼν vocat Iosephus, notans sæpe occæcatas Hierosolymita- norum mentes, ut & omnia ad pacem hortamenta præfra- cte repudiarent, & post multa desperatæ audaciæ exempla postremis iisdemque firmissimis munimentis recordes ce- derent, multaque alia quæ legere est operæ pretium, Deus nimirum, Deus, ut ille ait, hæc ita versabat, κατακρίνας ὡς με- mιασμένης τῆς πόλεως ἀπώλειαν. Itaque πεπῆρωτο ὑπὸ τοῦ χρεὼν ὃ τῆτε πόλει κ᾿ αὐτοῖς ἤδη παρῆν. Titus ipse apud Philostratum in vita Apollonii ajebat post victoriam, μὴ ἀυ- τός ταῦτα εἰργάσθαι, θεῷ δὲ ὀργὴν φήναντι, ἐπιδεδωκέναι τὰς ἑαυτοῦ χεῖρας.

## 24:17
Vers. 17. He who is on the housetop, let him not come down to take anything out of his house] It seems that it was possible to descend from the roof other than through the house: namely, by stairs projected into the public way, such as Euripides describes in the Phoenissae. Thus also Aristotle in Oeconomica II says that there were, just as upper rooms, so also stairs projecting into the public roads. And in the Miles Gloriosus, when the servant had said that there was no passage from the house in which he lived into the neighboring ones, he gives the reason, that there was neither a roof nor a garden. These things, however, and those which follow, pertain to the depiction of a most swift flight. Thus it was said to Lot, Escape for your life, that is, with your life only, and do not look back.

Latin:

Vers. 17. ὁ ἐπὶ δώματος, μὴ καταβαινέτω ἆραι τι ἐκ τῆς οἰ- κίας ἀυτοῦ] Videtur de solario alia quam per domum de- scendi potuisse: per scalas nimirum in publicum projectas, quales describit in Phœnissis Euripides. Sic & Aristoteles Oeconomicon II. ait fuisse ut ὑπερῷα ita & ἀναβαθμοὺς ὑπε- ρέχοντας εἰς τὰς δημοσίας ὁδός. Et in Milite Glorioso servus cum dixisset nullum esse ex ædibg. quas habitabat in vicinas commeatum, causam reddit, quod nec solarium esset, nec hortus. Hæc autem, & quæ sequuntur, ad celerrimæ fugæ ὑποτύπωσιν pertinent. Ita Loto dictum est, Erue te על נפשך id est, cum vita tua tantum, & ne respice.

## 24:18
Vers. 18. The garments] The Syriac and Latin translate in the singular number. I do not doubt that the cloak is meant. Nor, however, would I change the Greek reading. For this word is among those in the number which have a singular meaning in a plural sound, as can be seen in John 13:4 and 19:23.

Latin:

Vers. 18. Τὰ ἱμάτια] Singulari numero vertunt Syrus & Latinus. Penulam intelligi non dubito. Neque tamen mutem Græcam lectionem. Est enim hæc yox earum in numero, quæ plurali sono fignificationem habent interdum singularem, ut videre est Ioh XIII. 4. & XIX. 23.

## 24:19
Vers. 19. But woe to those who are with child and to those who are nursing] The sense is the same as those words of Christ going to the cross: The days are coming in which it will be said: blessed are the barren, and the wombs that have not borne; and the breasts that have not nursed, Luke 23:29. Indeed, small children are great impediments to flight. We read of an infant found at Antioch, who was sucking the breasts of its dead mother. In the Gothic War through Italy, a goat nourished an infant abandoned by its mother through death or captivity. There is in Josephus, book 14, a miserable description of mothers fleeing with infants.

Latin:

Vers. 19. ὀυαὶ δὲ ταῖς ἐν γαστρὶ ἐχούσαις κ᾿ ταῖς θηλαζούσαις] Idem est sensus qui istorum verborum Christi euntis ad cru- cem: Venient dies in quibus dicetur: beatæ steriles, & uteri qui non pepererunt; & ubera quæ non lactarunt, Luc. XXIII. 29. Nimirum parvi liberi magna fugæ sunt impedimenta. Antiochiæ infantem repertum legimus, qui matris mortuæ sugeret ubera. Bello Gothico per Italiam matri morte aut captivitate desertum infantem capra aluit. Est apud Io- sephum libro XIV. miserabilis descriptio matrum cum in- fantibus fugientium.

## 24:20
Vers. 20. Nor on the Sabbath] Since travel was forbidden on the Sabbath, Exod. 16:29, which Josephus in book 13 of the Antiquities expresses thus: It is not permitted for us to travel on the Sabbaths or on the feast: and yet it was sufficiently established that not every walking was forbidden, for it was customary to go to the sanctuary on that day from the camps, Lev. 23:3, that matter had to be tempered entirely by a fair definition: in which kind of things there ought to be some authority of the wise. Now the wise Hebrews defined that space by two thousand cubits, which others measure by five, others by seven stadia. Christ therefore says it is to be prayed that the necessity of flight does not fall on a Sabbath, showing that one must flee far beyond two thousand cubits. Nor does it stand in the way that we read among the teachers of the Jews that the law of the Sabbath ceases in danger of life. For that exception was not approved by all. For first, Dositheus thought that one should not even move from one's place on the Sabbath: the Essenes, not even to relieve the bowels. And although in Maccabean times it had been decreed to defend life attacked by the enemy with arms even on the Sabbath, yet to many it was not sufficiently persuaded that this was lawful. Which occasion Ptolemy, first the son of Lagus, and then indeed Pompey and Sossius used to break into the city on the Sabbath. Agatharchides of Cnidus narrates this about Ptolemy, in words which Josephus produces in the first book against Apion: the rest Josephus himself. Then also those who stood by that decree still interpreted it most strictly, if indeed the enemy were attacking the walls. For Josephus shows in more than one place that he felt it was a sin to fight outside that necessity: and he says that this was the received opinion in his own times, so much so that they did not dare to disturb the works of the besiegers on the Sabbath: which the Rabbis have reported along with Josephus. Those who were of this opinion (and there were very many, among whom was that sailor mentioned by Synesius) were hindered by religion from forestalling imminent danger by flight: to which Christ looks: That strict obligation of the Sabbath was indeed going to cease before the destruction of Jerusalem: but in most Jews, even those who had embraced the Christian religion, the persuasion of the obligation as if remaining was not going to cease, as can be seen in Rom. 14:5. Indeed, we have shown elsewhere that the precepts of the law were observed by the Christians of Palestine (who were called Nazarenes) up to the times of Hadrian. Certainly, before the destruction of the temple, there were very few who understood their liberty. But as long as that persuasion remained, to do anything against it would have been a grave offense: as Paul teaches several times. But the things which are said here about flight pertain to the time of the beginning of the siege, not to the extremes of the slaughter, for then there was no place for flight.

of the world until now, and never shall be] These cohere with the preceding in this way: I have exhorted you to flight: and I have ordered you to pray that you may have it most expeditious. Do not believe that this is said by me in vain. For after the occasion of flight has passed, evils will threaten that are more grievous than all human evils, within, robberies, famine, pestilence, without, sword and flame. It has been most truly said by Josephus: that neither has any other city suffered such things, nor has any generation from the ages been more productive of wickedness.

This comparison of tribulations seems to some not to be about every tribulation or affliction that ever and anywhere existed in the human race: for without doubt the θλίψις (tribulation) at the time of the flood was more severe; but it is to be understood as that which ever was in Judea, or is to be in the future: for that is named expressly, and it is taught that one must flee from it v. 16. And thus Augustine explains it in Epist. 80. Chrysostom, however, takes it universally concerning all tribulations in Homily LXXVII on Matthew, to whom B. Gerhard agrees in Harm. c. CLX. p. m. 485, though restricting Christ's words to tribulations to be feared from enemies, since the flood was sent immediately by God, as was the conflagration of Sodom: but because Christ speaks simply of θλίψις, and does not determine it to a θλῖψις arising from the incursion of enemies, Christ's sentiment is to be accepted in such a way that in no province since the foundation of the world has such a θλίψις ever existed, or will exist: that which happened through the flood did not happen in any province or kingdom, but throughout the whole world: therefore it is called μεγάλη (great) not quantitatively or extensively, but qualitatively and intensively, on account of the gathering of most atrocious punishments, of most virulent plague, of most dire famine, of internal dissension, of most grave sedition and conflict, of external obsession, of most vehement assault and constriction, of most bitter affliction of consciences with horror, terror, and pain: Concerning which Josephus in b. VI and VII of the Jewish War, whom it is helpful to cite in part: When the temple was being burned, whatever happened to come into their hands was seized, and there was infinite slaughter of those caught. Nor was there any pity for age, or reverence for chastity: but both boys and old men, and sacred and profane were killed alike, and the calamity of war pursued every kind of man, and suppliants were killed together with those resisting: and the flame, advancing further, crackled with the groaning of those falling. And because of the height of the hill and the magnitude of the burning structure, one would believe the whole city was burning. But nothing greater or more horrible than that clamor can be imagined. For there was the roaring of the Roman legions, and the huge clamor of the seditious trapped by iron and fire, and the flight of the people caught above toward the enemies with stupor, and the lamentation of the calamity: and for those stationed on the hill, the multitude of the town also joined in the sound. Now indeed many, wasted by hunger to the point of death, their eyes almost dim, after they saw the fire of the temple, recovered their strength and clamor for lamentations in the meantime. Moreover, the region across the river resounded, and the surrounding mountains gave back a heavier sound: For one would think the hill on which the temple was, was being burned from the roots, so full of flame was it on all sides: and the blood seemed more abundant than the fire, and there were more killed than the killers: and the whole earth was covered with corpses, and the soldiers, walking over the bodies of the dead, followed the course of the fugitives. Josephus does not neglect to add at the end an incredible multitude of those succumbing. And of all the captives who were caught in the whole war, the number of ninety-seven thousand was reached, but of the dead throughout the whole time of the siege, eleven hundred thousand. Most of these were Gentiles, but not natives: for from all regions gathered for the feast day of unleavened bread, they were suddenly surrounded by war: where first indeed a pestilential plague was born to them from the narrowness of the place, then more quickly famine. That the city could hold such a multitude of men, however, was certain from those who had been enumerated under Cestius. Truly, to one perusing the histories of all times, it will be possible to find a calamity equal to this nowhere: as Walaeus says here.

Latin:

Vers. 20. μηδὲ ἐν σαββάτῳ] Cum Sabbato iter esset prohibitum, Exod. XVI. 29. quod Iosephus libro XIII. An- tiquitatum sic exprimit: ἐκ ἔστι δὲ ἡμῖν ἕτε ἐν τοῖς σάββασιν ἕτε ἐν τῇ ἑορτῇ ὁδεύειν: & tamen satis constaret non o- mnem ambulationem esse vetitam, nam ad sanctuarium eo die ex castris iri solebat, Levit. XXIII. 3. omnino temperanda ea res fuit æqua definitione: in quo rerum genere aliqua esse debet sapientum auctoritas. Sapientes autem Hebræi bis mille cubitis id spatium definierunt, quod alii quinque, alii septem stadiis metiuntur. Optandum igitur dicit Chri- stus, ne in Sabbatum incidat fugæ necessitas, ostendens longe ultra bis mille cubitos fugiendum. Nec obstat, quod apud Iudæorum magistros legimus, vitæ periculo cessare le- gem Sabbati. Ea enim exceptio non omnibus erat pro- bata. Nam primum Dositheus ne statu quidem dece- dendum Sabbato arbitrabatur: Esseni nec alvum le- vandam. Et quamquam Maccabaicis temporibus decre- tum erat, vitam ab hoste impetitam armis etiam Sabbato defendere, tamen multis id fas esse non satis erat persuasum. Qua occasione usi & Ptolemæus primum Lagi filius, deinde vero & Pompejus & Sossius urbem Sabbato irrupere. De Ptolemæo narrat id Agatharchides Cnidius, verbis quæ Iosephus producit primo contra Appionem: cætera Iose- phus ipse. Deinde etiam qui isti decreto stabant, tamen strictissime interpretabantur, si nempe hostis mœnia oppu- gnaret. Nam extra eam necessitatem pugnare nefas esse non uno loco sentire se ostendit Iosephus: eamque suis tem- poribus ait receptam fuisse sententiam, adeo quidem, ut nec obsidentium opera Sabbato turbare auderent: quod cum Iosepho & Rabbini prodiderunt. Hujus qui erant senten- tiæ (erant autem plurimi, quos inter nautæ ille Synesio me- moratus) religione impediebantur periculum imminens fuga antevertere: quo Christus respicit: Erat quidem ces- satura ante excidium Hierosolymitanum stricta illa obliga- tio Sabbati: at in plerisque Iudæis etiam Christianam reli- gionem amplexis non erat cessatura obligationis veluti ma- nentis persuasio, ut videre est Rom. XIV. 5. Quin ad tempo- ra usque Adriani Christianis Palæstinæ (qui Nazaræi voca- bantur) observata legis præcepta alibi ostendimus. Certe ante excidium templi paucissimi fuêre, qui libertatem suam intelligerent. Quamdiu autem ea manebat persuasio, con- tra quicquam facere grave fuisset delictum: ut aliquoties docet Paulus. Quæ vero de fuga hic dicuntur, ad tem- pus inchoati obsidii, non ad extrema cladis pertinent, tunc enim fugæ non erat locus.

τῆς κόσμε ἕως τῦ νῦν, ἐδ᾽ ὐ μὴ γένηται] Cohærent hæc cum superioribus hoc modo: Hortatus sum vos ad fugam: & optare vos jussi ut eam habere possitis expeditissimam. Ne credite frustra id à me dici. Nam post elapsam fugæ occasionem, mala imminebunt omnibus malis humanis graviora, intus latrocinia, fames, pestis, extra ferrum & flamma. Verissime à Josepho dictum est: μήτε πόλιν ἄλλην, τοιαῦτα πεπονθέναι, μήτε γενεὰν ἐξ αἰῶν© γεγοίναν κακίας γονιμωτέραν.

Comparatio hæc tribulationum quibusdam videtur non de omni tribulatione vel afflictione, quæ unquam & uspiam in humano genere fuit: sine dubio enim gravior fuit θλίψις tempore diluvii; sed quæ in Judæa unquam fuerit, aut deinceps futura sit, intelligenda: Ea enim nominatur diferte, & ex ea fugiendum esse docetur v. 16. Atq; ita explicat Augustinus Epist. 80. Chrysostomus tamen universaliter de omnibus tribulationibus accipit homil. LXXVII. in Matth. cui accedit B. Gerhardus Harm. c. CLX. p. m. 485. restringens tamen Christi verba ad tribulationes ad hostibus metuendas, quum diluvium immediate à Deo immissum fuerit, uti & conflagratio Sodomorum: sed quia simpliciter de θλίψε loquitur Christus, non vero determinat ad θλῖψιν ab hostium irruptione provenientem, ita accipienda Christi sententia, quod in nulla provincia inde ab orbe condito tanta θλίψις unquam extiterit, aut exitura sit: ea quæ per diluvium contigit, non in provincia vel regno aliquo, sed per totum orbem contigit: proinde μεγάλη dicitur non quantitative vel extensive, sed qualitative & intensive, ob pœnarum atrocissimarum συνάθροισμὸν, pestis virulentissimæ, famis dirissimæ, internæ dissensionis, seditionis & conflictationis gravissimæ, externæ obsessionis, oppugnationis & coangustationis vehementissimæ, afflictionis conscientiarum cum horrore, terrore, dolore, acerbissimæ: Quo de Josephus l. VI. & VII. de bello Judaico, quem ex parte adducere juvat: Cum templum incenderetur, etiam quicquid in manus forte venisset rapiebatur, & cædes erat infinita deprehensorum. Nec acta fuit ætatis miseratio, aut reverentia castitatis: sed & pueri & senes, & sacri & profani similiter interficiebantur, atque omne genus hominum belli calamitas persequebatur, unaque supplices cum repugnantibus necabantur: flammaque ulterius progrediens, cum gemitu occumbentium concrepabat. Et pro altitudine quidem collis, ardentisq́, operis magnitudine, totam quis ardere crederet civitatem. Illo autem clamore nihil majus aut horribilius excogitari potest. Nam & Romanarum legionum fremitus erat, & seditiosorum ferro ignique clausorum clamor ingens, & populi sursum deprehensi ad hostes fuga cum stupore, ac calamitatis conquestio: in colle autem constitutis, etiam multitudo oppidi consonabat. Jam vero multi fame martidi in mortem pene luminibus clarisis, postquam ignem templi videre, in questus interim vires clamoremque receperunt. Resonabat autem & transfluvium regio, & montes circumpositi graviorem sonitum reddebant: Nam collem quidem in quo templum erat, exuri radicitus quis putaret, ita undique flamma plenum: videbatur autem sanguis igne largior esse, pluresque interfectoribus interfecti: omnisqne terra cadaveribus tegebatur, & supra corpora mortuorum gradientes milites cursum fugientium sequebantur. Incredibilem multitudinem succumbentium non negligit Josephus sub finem adjicere. Et captivorum quidem omnium qui toto bello comprehensi sunt, nonaginta & septem millium comprehensus est numerus, mortuorum vero per omne tempus obsidionis undecies centum millia. Horum plerique gentiles fuêre, sed non indigenæ: ab omnibus enim regionibus ad azymorum diem festum congregati, bello subito circumfusi sunt: ubi primo quidem illis pestifera lues ex loci angustia nasceretur, deinde citius fames. Quod autem caperet tantam hominum multitudinem civitas, certum erat ex his qui sub Cestio fuerant enumerati. Profecto omnium temporum historias pervolventi, parem cladem nullibi reperire licebit: ut hic Walæus.

## 24:22
Vers. 22. And if those days had not been shortened, no flesh would have been saved] shortened here, which is cut short among the Greeks in Dan. IX. 24. Light for this passage from history. Before the city was besieged, first the assassins secretly slaughtered whom they pleased, then the Zealots, taking up war against the Romans, cut down all who were averse to the war, finally the leaders of the Zealots, contending among themselves with arms for the principate both in Galilee and in Judea, dragged the people into mutual factions and slaughters, all of which can be seen in Josephus: and so, if the siege of the city had not been accelerated, into which flowed not only from Judea, but also from Galilee and Idumea, whatever there was of the worst men, the victims and offscourings of the whole country as Josephus speaks, and if the whole war had been concluded within a six-month period, undoubtedly as many as were in Judea would have perished either by robbery or by mutual slaughters. What so great a thing, says the same Josephus, O most wretched city, have you suffered from the Romans, such as they entered upon you while purging the domestic pollutions. Similar is that which the teachers of the Hebrews do, the Babylonian exile of the Israelites compared to the year 450 from the law given: if it had come two years later, there would have been total destruction.

For the sake of the elect] That is, for the sake of the Christians, who, scattered through Judea and Galilee, would have been a peculiar possession in the rite of heaven by the assassins, zealots, and tyrants, as being averse to the counsels of war. For those most wicked men only confessed to murdering those worthy of salvation, as Josephus speaks. And before: the strife of those contending for war against those desiring peace is grievous; that the elect are called Christians as if by a proper name, as being the dearest pledges of God, we have noted above. Famous in the first times of the Christians was the saying of Matthias the Apostle: if the neighbor of an elect one sins, the elect one has sinned: by which is signified the duty of Christians in admonishing men joined by any relationship. Thus Clement of Alexandria: even if some hate an elect one (that is, a Christian) nonetheless their ignorance. Arrian also, in Epictetus, calls him who has been baptized chosen: and Caecilius Natalis in Minucius Felix calls Christians the elect. Mark said the elect whom he chose, i.e., the beloved whom he loved, with a richness of speech familiar to the Hebrews. Such is that: the honor of the honored one whom they honored below c. XXVII. 9. the tradition which you delivered Mark VII. 13. in the resurrection when they rise Mark XII. 23. the creation which God created Mark XIII. 10. But Euripides also said the will which he willed. These elect are those servants of God from the XII tribes whom the Angel is narrated to have sealed in the Apocalypse before that day of divine wrath arrived. For we are accustomed to seal those things which we wish to be rightly guarded.

those days will be shortened] By the counsel of God, to whom Mark expressly ascribes this: whose wise dispensation of counsel can be seen in history. Vespasian, slow with old age, and judging that it should be awaited while the Jews perished by mutual wounds, was warned by many to defend the city, and to save the remnants of the people. For because of their goodwill toward the Romans, many had been killed and those remaining were in danger. Impelled by these things, he prepares everything for a siege: soon he himself, turned to seizing and strengthening the empire, hands over the forces to Titus, whom it seemed useful to remain with the armies for all the new events and chances of the principate: as Tacitus writes. But to Titus, as a young man, Rome (as the same Tacitus notes) and wealth and pleasures were before his eyes, and if Jerusalem did not fall immediately, they seemed to be delaying. By these means the siege was precipitated, while meanwhile those who were in the city indulged in robberies, plunderings, and lusts, reproaching the Divine as being slow in the punishment upon them, as we read in Josephus. But the siege that had begun also had an end faster than all hope, while the besieged themselves accelerated famine by burning the grain, and abandoned the most fortified garrisons with fatal madness. Thus it happened that between the immolation of Christ, the true Passover, and the lost possession of the promised land, as many years intervened as had intervened between the Egyptian Passover and the attainment of the same land: and so for the forty days which were given to the Ninevites for repentance, as many years were granted to them, which had been mystically signified in Ezekiel c. IV. 6. to which can also be referred what we said elsewhere about the solemn time of fasts.

By the elect are understood not generally Christians, but the faithful predestined to eternal life. Because this is the stronger and accepted meaning in the sacred writings. Which the preceding things also demand, if those days had not been cut short, no flesh would be saved, that is, no flesh would be saved. See Gen. IV. 18. Deut. IIX. 19. Ps. CXLIII. 2. Dan. XI. 37. Rom. III. 20. Ephes. IV. 29. 1. Joh. III. 21. For the salvation is of the Elect. If those evils had continued longer, all would have perished either by famine, or by plague, or by the sword: and there would have been no nations left, from which a certain holy seed could have been saved, and the elect saved. Therefore, not only the faithful Christians, who had already actually believed, but also those from the Jews or proselytes who could still be led to the faith, and from whom the Lord had foreseen that a holy seed would be raised up, are understood. August. Ep. c. XXC. We ought not to doubt, when Jerusalem was overturned, that there were in that people the elect of God, who had believed from the circumcision, or who had been chosen to believe before the foundation of the world, for whose sake those days would be shortened. Conf. v. 24. & 31.

Latin:

Vers. 22. καὶ εἰ μὴ ἐκολοβώθησαν αἱ ἡμέραι ἐκεῖναι, οὐκ ἂν ἐσώθη πᾶσα σάρξ] ἐκολοβώθησαν hic quod συντμήθησαν apud Græcos Dan. IX. 24. Lux huic loco ab historia. Antequam urbs obsideretur, primum sicarii clam quos lubebat trucidabant, deinde Zelotæ bellum in Romanos sumentes omnes à bello aversos obtruncabant, postremo duces Zelotarum tam in Galilæa, quam in Judæa de principatu inter se armis certantes populum in partes mutuasque cædes rapiebant, quæ omnia apud Josephum videre est: itaque nisi accelerata esset obsidio urbis, in quam confluxit non ex Judæa tantum, sed & ex Galilæa & Idumæa quicquid erat pessimorum hominum, θύματα καὶ καθάρματα τῆς χώρας ὅλης ut Josephus loquitur, ac si bellum omne conclusum intra semestre tempus, haud dubie quotquot in Judæa erant concidissent aut latrocinio, aut mutuis cædibus. Τί τηλικοῦτον, inquit idem Josephus, ὦ τλημονεστάτη πόλις, πέπονθας ὑπὸ ῥωμαίων οἷον σὲ τὰ ἐμφύλια μύση περικαθαιροῦντες εἰσῆλθον. Simile est quod agunt Hebræorum magistri, exilium Israelitarum Babylonicum collatum in annum à lege latam CCCCL: si venisset biennio post, futuram fuisse πανωλετρίαν.

Διὰ δὲ τοὺς ἐκλεκτοὺς] Id est Christianorum causa, qui sparsi per Judæam & Galilæam peculium ritu cæli fuissent à sicariis, zelotis & tyrannis, utpote aversi à belli consiliis. Nam isti sceleratissimi homines μόνον ὠμολόγουν τὸ φονεύειν τοὺς σωτηρίας ἀξίους, ut Josephus loquitur. Et ante: ἡ δὲ ἐριζόντων τῷ πολέμῳ πρὸς τοὺς ἐπιθυμοῦντας εἰρήνης ἔρις χαλεπή· ἐκλεκτοὺς quasi proprio nomine dici Christianos, utpote charissima Dei pignora, annotavimus supra. Celebre erat primis Christianorum temporibus Matthiæ Apostoli dictum: ἐὰν ἐκλεκτοῦ γείτων ἁμαρτήσῃ, ἥμαρτεν ὁ ἐκλεκτός: quo significatur officium Christianorum in admonendis hominibus ulla necessitudine conjunctis. Sic Clemens Alexandrinus: κἂν μισῶσι τὲ ἐκλεκτόν τινες (id est Christianum) οὐδὲν ἧττον τὴν ἄγνοιαν αὐτῶν. Etiam Arrianus Epicteto eum qui baptizatus est, vocat ᾑρημένον: & Cæcilius Natalis apud Minutium Felicem Christianos vocat electos. Marcus dixit ἐκλεκτοὺς ὃς ἐξελέξατο, i. e. ἀγαπητοὺς ὃς ἠγάπησε, loquendi ubertate Hebræis familiari. Tale est illud: τιμὴν τοῦ τετιμημένου ὃν ἐτιμήσαντο infra c. XXVII. 9. παραδόσεως ἧς παρεδώκατε Marc. VII. 13. ἐν τῇ ἀναστάσει ὅταν ἀναστῶσι Marc. XII. 23. κτίσεως ἧς ἔκτισεν ὁ Θεὸς Marc. XIII. 10. Sed & Euripides dixit βούλησιν ἣν ἐβούλετο. Hi ἐκλεκτοὶ sunt servi illi Dei ex tribubus XII. quos in Apocalypsi Angelus narratur obsignasse antequam adventaret dies ille iræ divinæ. Nam obsignare solemus ea quæ recte custodita volumus.

κολοβωθήσονται αἱ ἡμέραι ἐκεῖναι] Consilio Dei, cui hoc diserte ascribit Marcus: cujus consilii sapientem dispensationem in historia conspicere est. Vespasianus senecta tardus, & oppetiendum censens dum mutuis vulneribus Judæi conciderent, à multis monebatur ἀμῦναί τῇ πόλει, καὶ τὰ τῶ δήμου περισῶσαι λείψανα. διὰ γὰρ τὴν πρὸς ῥωμαίους εὔνοιαν ἀνηρῆσθαί τε πολλοὺς καὶ κινδυνεύειν τοὺς περιόντας. His impulsus omnia ad obsidium parat: mox ipse versus ad capessendum firmandumque imperium Tito tradit copias, quem manere apud exercitus ad omnes principatus novi eventus casusque, utile videbatur: scribente Tacito. At Tito, utpote juveni, Roma, (ut idem Tacitus notat) & opes voluptatesque, ante oculos, ac ni statim Hierosolyma conciderent morari videbantur. His modis præcipitatum obsidium, cum interim qui in urbe erant latrociniis, rapinis, libidinibusque indulgerent, ὀνειδίζοντες τὸ Θεῖον ὡς βραδύτητα τῆς ἐπ᾿ αὐτοῖς κολάσεως, ut apud Josephum legimus. Sed & cæpta obsidio spe omni celerius finem habuit, dum ipsi obsessi ambustis frumentis famem accelerant, & munitissima præsidiorum fatali vecordia deserunt. Ita factum est, ut inter Christi, veri Paschatis, immolationem & amissam possessionem terræ promissæ, totidem anni intercederent, quot inter Ægyptiacum Pascha & ejusdem terræ adeptionem anni intercesserant: itaque pro diebus quadraginta, qui dati erant ad pœnitentiam Ninevitis, ipsis concessi sint anni totidem, quod mystice significatum erat apud Ezechielem c. IV. 6. quo & id referri potest quod de solenni jejuniorum tempore alibi diximus.

Per electos non generaliter Christiani, sed fideles ad æternam prædestinati vitam intelliguntur. Quia hæc potior & recepta in sacris est significatio. Quam etiam poscunt antecedentia, nisi decurtati fuissent dies illi, non fieret salva omnis caro, id est, nulla caro salvaretur. Vid. Gen. IV. 18. Deut. IIX. 19. Ps. CXLIII. 2. Dan. XI. 37. Rom. III. 20. Ephes. IV. 29. 1. Joh. III. 21. Salus enim Electorum est. Si diutius mala illa continuassent, omnes vel fame, vel peste, vel gladio periissent: nullæque fuissent gentes reliquæ, e quibus servari sanctum quoddam semen potuisset, & salvari electi. Non ergo tantum fideles Christiani, qui jam actu credi- dere, sed etiam illi e Judæis vel proselytis qui ad- huc ad fidem perduci poterant, & e quibus semen sanctum excitandum præviderat Dominus, intelli- guntur. August. Ep. c. XXC. Non debemus am- higere, quando eversa est Jerusalem fuisse in illo po- pulo electos Dei, qui ex circumcisione crediderant, sive fuerant credituri electi ante constitutionem mundi, propter quos breviarentur dies illi. Conf. v. 24. & 31.

## 24:23
Vers. 23. Then] Christ, proceeding to resolve the second question, makes a silent transition, connecting the latter things with the former. The question was concerning the kingdom of the Messiah: but because many false Christs were about to appear even after the destruction of Jerusalem (for he had already dealt with those who were about to precede the destruction), he therefore warns the Christians not to expect the kingdom with external display, with observation. If anyone therefore announces that Christ is present here or there in a visible manner, do not give credence.

Latin:

Vers. 23. Τότε] Christus ad quæstionem secundam sol- vendam progrediens, tacitam facit transitionem posteriora prioribus connectens. Quæstio erat de regno Messiæ: quia autem multi ψευδόχριςοι apparituri erant etiam post exci- dium Hierosolymorum (nam de his qui excidium præven- turi erant, jam egerat) ideo Christianos admonet, ne regnum exspectent cum externo apparatu, μετὰ παρατηρήσεως. Si quis igitur hic aut illic Christum adspectabili modo adesse nuntiet, nolite fidem adhibere.

## 24:24
Vers. 24. For there shall arise false Christs] Immediately after the destruction, Jonathan, a most wicked man, as Josephus speaks, led many into the Cyrenaic wilderness, promising to show signs and phantoms: which attempt Catullius, the governor of the province, dispersed with arms. In the times of Hadrian, Barchochebas, so called from Chochaba, a noble village of Galilee (which Epiphanius mentions), said openly to all, I am the Messiah. Hadrian besieged him in the city of Bether. He himself was slaughtered by a soldier when the city was taken: from which time he began to be called by the Jews not Bar Chochaba but Bar Chozaba, i.e., son of a lie. For those who think he was so called before are much mistaken. This is Barchochebas, the leader of the Jewish revolt, whom Justin mentions in his Apology. But because some think there were two Barchochebas or Barchozbas, they err, being deceived by the Jews, the worst teachers of history. For from the time they were expelled from their fatherland, all history among them has been defiled with gross errors and fables: to which, therefore, no credence should be given unless other witnesses come forward. And so one can see that they are also discordant among themselves. For some establish Akiba as a supporter of the former Barchochebas, others of the latter: and there are those who believe the former was besieged by Titus, the latter by Hadrian. But in truth, it is an error of a similar name: for he who was besieged by Titus was not Barchochebas, but Bargioras, as Josephus and Tacitus name him. But other Jews also confuse Barchochebas with the one I mentioned, Jonathan. For they say the war in Cyrene was stirred up by him. But all Jews call false Christs Barchochebas, just as the Greeks ascribe whatever has been done bravely anywhere to Hercules: afterwards in Egypt, Cyprus, Crete, and elsewhere, many other impostors existed, selling themselves as Christ. To whom can be added Menander the Samaritan.

and false prophets] By false prophets, from the connection of the discourse, I understand the assistants of the false Christs, who abused the testimonies of the Holy Scriptures to persuade the people that this or that impostor was the promised Messiah. Such was Akiba in the times of Hadrian, drawing Balaam's prophecy concerning the star (because the village, whence the name of Barchochebas comes, has the meaning of a star) and the prophecies of Haggai and other prophets to him. And not only Akiba, but if we believe the Jews themselves and Maimonides, who is the least trifling among the Jews, most of the wise men of his age. Nor is it to be doubted that other false Christs also had their false prophets in a similar way: just as that beast mentioned in the Apocalypse has its false prophet, ch. XVI. 13, ch. XIX. 20, ch. XX. 10.

and shall give great signs and wonders] Jerome narrates that Barchochebas was thought to vomit flames: similar to which is what the Apocalypse narrates concerning the second beast, ch. XIII. 13. When God had invited Pharaoh to obedience by the miracles performed through Moses, he providently permitted certain wonders to be performed also by the Egyptian magicians, yet so that the signs of Moses far excelled them in magnitude and multitude; by which act, the excuse of Pharaoh, who pretended to give credence to the miracles of the magicians and used that as a veil for his cruelty, was met. For no plausible reason could be brought forward why he should have given credence to the miracles of the magicians, if he was unwilling to give credence to the miracles of Moses. Moses foretold to the Israelites that it would come to pass that the ministers of false gods would attempt to lead them away from the worship of the true God, not without a display of signs: and that God would permit this, so that their faith in him might test, most justly indeed, after so many miracles performed by himself, which could be equaled by no other miracles, let alone surpassed, that if the Jews, led by such signs, should fall away to false gods, it would be a notable monument of their own levity and perfidy. In a similar way, God, after the authority of his Son had been proven by so many illustrious others who sold themselves as Christs should exhibit some signs: so that the Jews, if they followed them as if moved by signs, might be convinced by the very comparison of the works. By this reasoning, of course, it was established for the whole human race that nothing other than the holiness and purity of his doctrine itself stood in the way of the Jews obeying Christ. Therefore, upon such as did not receive τὴν ἀγάπην τῆς ἀληθείας, the ἡ ἐνέργεια τοῦ σατανᾶ is accustomed to have power ἐν πάσῃ δυνάμει καὶ σημείοις καὶ τέρασι ψεύδους καὶ ἐν πάσῃ ἀπάτῃ τῆς ἀδικίας 2. Thess. II. 9. 10. This is the ἐνέργεια πλάνης, so that all who have not believed the truth may be judged. Confer the said chapter of the Apocalypse.

These things are more correctly referred to those who arose after the destruction, than by others to those leaders of the three factions, Eleazar, Simon, and John, of whom Josephus, book VI of the Jewish War, ch. 1, reports that they existed at the time of the captivity and suborned many false prophets promising divine aid. For those did not sell themselves as Christ. And it seems that Christ here altogether passes to the second question concerning the time of his spiritual coming, as has been rightly observed by Grotius. That he is proceeding to the signs of the last day is indeed the opinion of Chrysostom, Hilary, Jerome, Theophylact, Euthymius, B. Hunnius, Barradius, and Maldonatus: but Abulensis dissents, and B. Gerhard proves that these do not pertain to the question concerning the signs of the last day. We do not, however, accept these with him regarding the time of the siege of Jerusalem: because at that time there existed neither such false Christs nor false prophets who deluded the people with false miracles. Regarding the false prophets after the destruction, Grotius rightly understands them from the context of the discourse to be the supporters of the false Christs, who abused the testimonies of the Holy Scriptures to persuade the people that this or that impostor was the promised Messiah, such as was Aquibas in the times of Hadrian, drawing to himself Balaam's prophecy about the star, and the prophecies of Haggai and other prophets. And not Aquibas only, but, as Maimonides testifies, most of the wise men of that age. Wherefore Jerome reports that Barchocheba was even claimed to vomit flames. Nor indeed are only those false Christs and false prophets who arose after Jerusalem and the Jewish polity were destroyed designated, but as many as have been stirred up by Satan in the centuries that followed them, and will be stirred up while the spiritual coming of Christ lasts, that is, until the end of the age. Such also were those whom St. Peter, St. Paul, St. John, and St. Jude noted in their time as false teachers, and who have been noted here and there in ecclesiastical history. Regarding Barchocheba, Dio the Historian reports that over five hundred thousand men perished by his sedition and seduction, and that 50 fortresses and strongholds, and 98 cities and villages inhabited by Jews, were destroyed.

ὥστε πλανῆσαι εἰ δυνατὸν κ̄ τοὺς ἐκλεκτούς.] What is said here by ὥστε, Mark explains thus: πρὸς τὸ ἀποπλανᾷν εἰ δυνατὸν καὶ τοὺς ἐκλεκτούς. There is a similar manner of speaking in a place in an old book, but outside the canon, which Clement of Alexandria cites: Τινὰ γὰρ ῥήματα ἀγαθὰ λαλεῖ: (namely the false prophet, of whom the discourse is, for the devil fills him with his own spirit, which he will be able to break even of the righteous). The sense is that those impostors would devote every effort to draw into their parties not only the unbelieving Jews, but also those who had seriously given their name to Christ (whom it is a most certain fact are called the elect here and there). That 'if possible' denotes the difficulty of the thing. For one can hardly be deceived; indeed, if we follow the propriety of words, even he who seems to be deceived is not deceived, but he deceives himself who, having been warned, does not take heed. Therefore Christ adds, 'Behold, I have told you beforehand,' to show that it is sufficiently provided for Christians so that they do not follow such impostors. For he who believes that Jesus is the true teacher Christ, knowing it was predicted by

Christ, that his kingdom would not come with observation, is sufficiently armed against that kind of trickery. See Origen here and Theophylact if you have time. In the Constitutions of Clement, book VI, ch. 18, this passage is explained in this manner: 'And false Christs and false prophets shall come, and shall give signs in heaven, so that if possible they may deceive even the elect; from whose deception may God deliver us through Jesus Christ our hope.' Nor do I wonder if in those times it could be reckoned as nearly impossible that those who had carefully imbibed the dogmas of Christ could be led away from them, since even among Galen it is proverbial, 'One would sooner re-teach those from Christ.' And Augustine reports the oracle of Apollo, who, to one asking how he could tear his wife away from Christianity, replied that it would be easier for him to write letters on a rapid river or to fly in the air. Moreover, although this would happen with difficulty, Tertullian rightly affirms against Marcion, book III, that it did happen sometimes. For since he declared that many would come, would perform signs, and would edit great mighty works, even the turning away of the elect, yet they were not to be admitted for that reason. Eusebius said, 'as if it were possible to scandalize even the elect.'

By the elect, Grotius again understands Christians in general: but because it is not among the impossibilities for Christians to be seduced, just as it is impossible for one elected from eternity to eternal life, not indeed to fall away entirely from grace, but to perish finally: because thus God's foreknowledge and predestination would fail, which is impossible: therefore Grotius employs a new twist, that in those times it could be considered nearly impossible that those who had carefully imbibed the dogmas of Christ could be led away from them. For Christ does not say nearly impossible: but indicates that the thing of which he speaks is altogether impossible. Conf. John X.38. Rom. XI. 7. concerning which August. tr. XLV. in John. If he is predestined, he erred for a time, he will not perish forever. Πλανῆσαι is taken here actively, so that the cause of the seduction of the Pseudo-Christ and the Pseudo-Prophet may be designated. Mark XIII. 22. it is πρὸς τὸ ἀποπλανᾷν for leading astray.

Latin:

Vers. 24. ἐγερθήσονται γὰρ ψευδόχριστοι] Statim post ex- cidium Jonatha πονηρότατος ἄνθρωπος, ut Josephus lo- quitur, multos in Cyrenaicam solitudinem perduxit, σημεῖα καὶ φάσματα δείξειν ὑπισχνόμενος: quem conatum Catullius provinciæ præses armis disjecit. Adriani temporibus Bar- chochebas ita dictus a Chochaba nobili Galilææ vico (cu- jus Epiphanius meminit palam omnibus dixit אנא משיחא ego sum Messias. Hunc Adrianus in urbe Bether obsedit. Ipse in potior urbe capta a milite trucidatus est: ex quo tem- pore a Judæis non בר כוכבא sed בר כוזבא, i. e. filius mendacii dici cœpit. Nam qui ante ita appellatum censent multum falluntur. Hic est Βαρχωχεβας ὁ τῆς Ἰουδαίων ἀπο- ςάσεως ἀρχηγίτης cujus in Apologetico Justinus meminit. Quod autem quidam putant duos fuisse Barchochebas aut Barchozbas, errant decepti a Judæis, pessimis historiæ magi- stris. Nam ex quo patria expulsi sunt, omnis apud illos hi- storia crassis erroribus & fabulis est inquinata: quibus pro- inde nihil credendum est, nisi alii testes accedant. Itaque videre est ipsos quoque inter se discordes, Nam alii Aqui- bam Barchochebæ prioris, alii posterioris fautorem statu- unt: & priorem a Tito, posteriorem ab Adriano obsessum sunt qui credant. Sed profecto error est vicini nominis: nam ille a Tito obsessus non Barchochebas fuit, sed Bargio- ras, quomodo eum Josephus & Tacitus nominant. Sed & alii Judæi Barchochebam cum eo quem dixi Jonatha con- fundunt. Ajunt enim ab ipso excitatum bellum in Cyrene. Sed Judæi omnes ψευδοχρίσους Barchochebas vocant, quo- modo Græci quicquid usquam fortiter gestum est adscribunt Herculi: postea in Ægypto, Cypro, Creta atque alibi mul- ti alii exstiterunt impostores pro Christo se venditantes. Quibus adjungi potest Menander Samaritanus.

καὶ ψευδοπροφῆται] Ψευδοπροφῆτας ex connexu orationis intelligo παραστάτας τῶν ψευδοχρίστων, qui sacrarum literarum testimoniis abutebantur, ut populo persuaderent hunc aut illum impostorem esse promissum Messiam. Qualis Adriani temporibus fuit Aquibas Balaami de stella vaticinium (quia vicus, unde Barchochebæ nomen, stellæ habet fignificatio- nem) Aggæique & aliorum Prophetarum vaticinia ad illum trahens. Nec Aquibas tantum, sed si ipsis Judæis & qui in- ter Judæos minime nugatur Maimonidæ credimus, plerique ejus ætatis sapientes. Nec dubitandum est, quin simili modo alii quoque ψευδόχριςοι suos habuerint ψευδοπροφήτας: sicut bestia illa in Apocalypsi memorata suum habet pseudopro- phetam, c. XVI. 13. c. XIX. 20. c. XX. 10.

καὶ δώσουσι σημεῖα μεγάλα καὶ τέρατα] Flammas evomere putatum Barchochebam narrat Hieronymus: cui simile est quod de bestia secunda narrat Apocalypsis c. XII. 13. Deus cum Pharaonem editis per Mosem miraculis ad æqui obe- dientiam invitasset, provide permisit & a magis Aegyptiis edi mira quæda, ita tamen ut Mosis signa magnitudine & mul- titudine longe illis antecellerent; quo facto Pharaoni simu- lanti magorum se miraculis fidem adhibere, & id velum obtendenti suæ sævitiæ occursum est. Nulla enim proba- bilis afferri poterat ratio, cur magorum miraculis habuisset fidem, qui Mosis miraculis fidem habere nollet. Israëlitis prædixit Moses futurum ut falsorum Deorum ministri ipsos a veri Dei cultu conarentur abducere non sine signorum pompa: idque permissurum Deum, ut ipsorum in se fidem exploraret, justissime nimirum, post tot à se edita miracula, quæ nullis aliis miraculis æquari, nedum superari, possent, ut si talibus signis adducti Judæi ad falsos Deos deficerent, id levitatis ipsorum & perfidiæ insigne esset monumentum. Simili modo Deus post Filii sui auctoritatem tot illustribus miraculis probatam permittere voluit, ut alii qui Christos sese venditarent, aliqua exhiberent signa: ut Judæi, si illos sequerentur velut signis permoti, ipsâ lignorum compara- tione convincerentur. Hæc scilicet ratione toti humano generi constitit, Judæis, quo minus Christo, parerent, nul- lam rem aliam, quam doctrinæ ipsius sanctimoniam & pu- ritatem obstitisse. In tales igitur qui τὴν ἀγάπην τῆς ἀληθείας οὐκ ἐδέξαντο vim habere solet ἡ ἐνέργεια τοῦ σατανᾶ ἐν πάσῃ δυνάμει καὶ σημείοις καὶ τέρασι ψεύδους καὶ ἐν πάσῃ ἀπάτῃ τῆς ἀ- δικίας 2. Thess. II. 9. 10. Hæc est ἐνέργεια πλάνης ἵνα κριθῶσι πάντες οἱ μὴ πιστεύσαντες τῇ ἀληθείᾳ. Confer dictum caput Apocalypseos.

Rectius hæc ad eos, qui surrexêre post exci- dium, referuntur: quam ab aliis ad Principes illos trium factionum, Eleazarum, Simonem, & Johan- nem, de quibus Joseph. l. VI. de bello Jud. c. 1. per- hibet, quod tempore captivitatis extiterint, mul- tosq; Pseudo-Prophetas auxilium divinum polli- centes subornarint. Illi enim se non vendita- runt pro Christo. Et videtur omnino hic Chri- stus ad secundum quæstionem de tempore adventus sui spiritualis transire, uti probe observatum à Grotio. Ad signa extremi diei eum progredi equidem Chrysostomus, Hilarius, Hieronymus, Theophyl. Euthymius, B. Hunnius, Barradius, Mal- donatus censet: sed dissentit Abulensis, probatque B. Gerhard. hæc non pertinere ad quæstionem de si- gnis extremi diei. Non tamen cum eodem de obsi- dionis Hierosolymitanæ tempore hæc accipimus: quia tum neque Pseudo-Christi tales extitêre, neque Pseudo-Prophetæ, qui falsis miraculis populum deluserint. De Pseudo-Prophetis vero post ex- cidium recte Grotius, intelligendos ex connexu ora- tionis esse παραστάτας τ̄ ψευδοχρίστων, qui sacra- rum literarum testimoniis abusi sunt, ut populo persua- derent hunc aut illum Impostorem esse Messiam pro- missum, qualis Adriani temporibus fuit Aquibas Balaami de stella vaticinium, Aggæi, & aliorum Prophetarum vaticinia ad ipsum trahens.
