Nec A- quibus tantum, sed Maimonide teste, plerique ejus ætatis sapientes. Quare Bochebam etiam flammas evomere jactatum refert Hieronymus. Nec vero illi solum tum Pseudo-Christi, tum Pseudo-Pro- phetæ, qui post destructam Hierosolymam, & Po- litiam Judaicam surrexêre, sed quotquot eorum sequutis etiam seculis excitati à Satana sunt, & ex- citabuntur dum adventus Christi spiritualis durat, h. e. usque ad consummationem seculi, designan- tur. Quales etiam erant quos suo tempore ceu falsos Doctores S. Petrus, quos S. Paulus, quos S. Johannes, quos S. Judas notarunt, & qui passim in historia Ecclesiastica notati sunt. De Barchocheba refert Dio Historicus, supra quingenta millia ho- minum ejus seditione & seductione interiisse, 50. arces & propugnacula, 98. civitates & vicos à Ju- dæis inhabitatos destructos esse.

ὥστε πλανῆσαι εἰ δυνατὸν κ̄ τοὺς ἐκλεκτούς.] Quod hic per ὥστε dicitur, Marcus ita explicat, πρὸς τὸ ἀποπλανᾷν εἰ δυνα- τὸν καὶ τοὺς ἐκλεκτούς. Simile loquendi genus est in loco li- bri veteris, sed extra canonem, quem citat Clemens Alexan- drinus: Τινὰ γὰρ ῥήματα ἀγαθὰ λαλεῖ: (nimirum ὁ ψευδοπρο- φήτης, de quo sermo est ὁ γὰρ διάβολος αὐτὸν πληροῖ τῷ ἑαυτοῦ πνεύματι, ἅτινα δυνήσεται ῥῆξαι κ̄ δικαίων. Sensus est, il- los γόητας omnem operam daturos, ut non tantum Judæos incædulos, sed & eos qui Christo nomen serio dederant (quos ἐκλεκτοὺς passim vocari res certissima est) in suas per- trahant partes. Illud εἰ δυνατὸν rei denotat difficultatem. Vix enim decipi potest, imo si verborum proprietatem se- quimur, et am cum decipi videtur non decipitur, sed ipse se decipit qui monitus non cavet. Ideo addit Christus, ἰδοὺ προείρηκα ὑμῖν, ut ostendat Christianis ne tales sequantur impostores satis esse prospectum. Nam qui Jesum esse Christum veracem doctorem credit, sciens prædictum a

Christo, regnum suum non venturum μετὰ παρατηρήσεως, armatus satis est adversus id genus præstigias. Vide si vacat Originem hic & Theophylactum. In Clementis constitu- tionibus lib VI. c. 18. hunc in modum explicatur hic locus: καὶ ἐλεύσονται ψευδόχριστοι καὶ ψευδοπροφῆται, καὶ δώσουσι ση- μεῖα ἐν ὀρανῷ, ὥστε εἰ δυνατὸν καὶ τὲς ἐκλεκτὲς ἀπατῆσαι· ὧν τῆς ἀπάτης ῥύσεται ἡμᾶς ὁ Θεὸς διὰ Ἰησοῦ Χριστῦ τῆς ἐλπίδος ἡμῶν. Neque miror si illis temporibus prope ἀδυνάτοις accenseri potuit, ut qui Christi dogmata cum cura imbibissent, ab iis abducerentur, cum etiam apud Galenum proverbiale sit, θᾶττον τις Τὺς ἀπὸ χριστῦ μεταδιδάξειε. Et Augustinus ora- culum Apollinis refert, qui sciscitanti quomodo uxorem à Christianismo posset avellere, respondit, facilius eum aut flumini rapido inscripturum literas, aut in aere volaturum. Cæterum, quanquam difficulter hoc fieret, factum tamen interdum recte affirmat Tertullianus adversus Marcionem III. Siquidem edicens multos venturos, signa facturos, & virtu- tes magnas edituros, aversionem etiam electorum, nec ideo tamen admittendos. Eusebius dixit ὡς εἰ δυνατὸν σκανδαλίσαι καὶ τὲς ἐκλεκτύς.

Per electos iterum Christianos Grotius intelli- git generatim: sed quia hoc non est ἐκ τῶ ἀδυνάτων Christianos seduci, uti ἀδύνατον est electum ab æ- terno ad vitam æternam, non quidem ὁλικῶς ex- cidere gratia, sed τελικῶς seu finaliter perire: quia sic falleret Dei præscientia, & prædestinatio, quod impossibile est: ideo novam στρεβλότητα adhibet Grotius, quod istis temporibus prope ἀδύνατον cen- seri potuerit, ut qui Christi dogmata cum cura îmbi- bissent, ab iis abducerentur. Christus enim non di- cit prope ἀδύνατον: sed indicat omnino ἀδύνα- τον id esse, de quo loquitur. Conf. Joh X.38. Rom. XI. 7. de quo August. tr. XLV. in Joh. Si prædesti- natus est, ad tempus erravit, in æternum non peribit. Πλανῆσαι hic active accipitur, ut causa seductio- nis Pseudo-Christi & Pseudo-Prophetæ designen- tur. Marc. XIII. 22. est πρὸς τὸ ἀποπλανᾷν ad le- ducendum.

## 24:26
Vers. 26. Behold in the desert he is] The Messiah, that is, which Mark adds. Such impostors were accustomed to lead men away into the wilderness, so that they might safely gather a band there, which can be seen everywhere in Josephus. Do not go out] Do not go so that you follow their lead. In the inner chambers] In the inner room of a house, as above c. VI. 6. For some, not trusting enough in their own strength, gathered followers secretly. The sense is the same as above, if anyone says behold here is Christ or there: which the opposition of the following clause shows.

Latin:

Vers. 26. ἰδὺ ἐν τῇ ἐρήμῳ ἐστὶ] Messias scilicet, quod Mar- cus addit. Solebant id genus impostores abducere homi- nes in solitudinem, ut tuto ibi manum colligerent, quod a- pud Josephum passim videre est. Μὴ ἐξέλθητε] Ne ite ut illorum ductum sequamini. ἐν τοῖς Ταμείοις] In conclavi domus, ut supra c. VI. 6. Nam quidam haud satis fidentes viribus clam colligebant secta- tores. Sensus idem est qui supra, ἐάν τις εἴπῃ ἰδὲ ὧδε Χρι- σὸς ἢ ὧδε: quod ostendit oppositio me brisequentis.

## 24:27
Vers. 27. For as the lightning comes forth] It is the property of lightning to pervade many places in a very short time. Hence Lucan on Alexander: And the lightning that would strike all peoples alike. And Plutarch on the same: One might liken it to lightning fire bursting forth. Elsewhere: as a star carried through the sky, from the east to the west. Christ says, therefore, that there is no reason why his kingdom should be sought particularly in this or that place, since it will pervade all the shores of the earth in one stroke, as it were, from one hinge of heaven to the other, according to those things which were predicted in the Psalms and Prophets concerning the kingdom of the Messiah, Joel says cap. II. כַּשַּׁחַר פָּרֹשׂ עַל־הֶהָרִים. as the dawn shall be spread upon the mountains. The coming] We have treated of this word above.

Latin:

Vers. 27. ὥσπερ γὰρ ἡ ἀστραπὴ ἐξέρχεται] Fulminis pro- prium est brevissimo tempore plurima loca pervadere. Hinc de Alexandro Lucanus: Fulmenq; quod omnes Percuteret pariter populos. Et de eodem Plutarchus: Ἦν ἄν τις εἰκάσειεν ἤ πυρὶ κεραυ- νίῳ ῥαγέντι; Alibi: ὥσπερ ἄστρω φερομένῳ δι’ διαπόντε, ἐπὶ δυσμὰς ἐξ ἀνατολῶν. Ait ergo Christus non esse cur hoc aut illo loco peculiariter quæratur regnum suum, cum uno vel- ut ictu pervasurum sit per omnes terrarum oras ab uno cœli cardine ad alterum, secundum ea quæ in Psalmis & Prophetis de Messiæ regno erant prodita, Joël dicit cap. II. כשחר פרש על־ההרים .2 ὡς ὄρθρος χυθήσεται ἐπὶ τὰ ὄρη. ἡ παρουσία] De hac voce egimus supra.

## 24:28
Vers. 28. For wherever the carcass is, there the eagles will be gathered] A Hebrew proverb taken from the nature of the eagle, which the book of Job celebrates. The nature of the vulture is the same, whence also the Latin adages: such as that, Whose vulture will this carcass be? Lucan on the sorceress Erichtho: And whatever carcass lies on the bare ground, she sits before the wild beasts and birds. But the Hebrew proverb pertains to those things which are not proper to one place, but behave in the same way everywhere: such as that of Philemon: All lions are brave; all hares, on the other hand, are cowardly. No longer a fox, which used to creep by nature, and another by habit; but if one were to gather thirty thousand foxes, he will see one nature in all of them, and one way. Such also is that proverb: a crest for all larks. And Hutnus Sandil among Procopius, having spoken of the nature of wolves and sheep, and these things on earth, I think they happen to all; for in the equality of all, no one, nor does the flock plot against the dogs nor does the wolf defend itself against them with blows. The sense, however, in this place is the same which Peter more openly declares in Acts 10:34: that God is no respecter of persons, but in every nation he that feareth him and worketh righteousness is accepted with him. If anyone should wish to allegorize the particles more subtly (although that is by no means necessary in proverbs), he could understand by the corpse the deeds of the body that are being put to death, and by the eagles the sublime gifts of the Holy Spirit, which are signs of the kingdom of the Messiah, just as those eagles so feared by the Jews were signs of the Roman empire. Why these things ought not to be drawn to the judicial advent, I have partly said before, and partly the very sequence of the discourse will show. For many things intervene before one comes to the description of the judgment. I marvel that it could have occurred to the ancients to call the venerable body of Christ, after it has been sent into the fullest possession of divine life, a corpse. But also in Luke this proverb is applied not to a universal judgment, but to that discernment of men which was to be made through the Gospel, as we shall see therein.

That these things pertain to the spiritual advent is manifest from Luke 17:24: The kingdom of God cometh not with observation, neither shall they say, Lo here, or lo there: for, behold, the kingdom of God is within us. For as the lightning that lighteneth out of the one part under heaven shineth unto the other part under heaven; so shall also the Son of man be in his day. Since these words sound without doubt concerning the sudden expansion of the kingdom of Christ through the whole world, it cannot be ambiguous that here, where the same things are held, even if spoken at a different time, the same advent is equally being treated, and that not secondarily, as pleased the blessed Gerhard, but directly and primarily; although it is not to be conceded that a double sense, one primary and another secondary, obtains here—namely, one concerning the bodily advent to judgment, and another concerning the spiritual advent through the Gospel: such a duality of sense Scripture nowhere admits. And the preceding things concerning the Pseudo-Christs and Pseudo-Prophets, saying 'Lo, here is Christ,' sufficiently teach that the discourse is about the spiritual advent: the sense of which the blessed Gerhard delivers in this way in Harmony of the Gospels, chapter 160, page 518: 'Beware of the conventicles of the Pseudo-Christs and Pseudo-Prophets, because the Church, which is my mystical body, will no longer be enclosed by the narrow limits of Judea, but will be propagated through the whole world through the preaching of the Gospel, and indeed immediately after the destruction of the city; just as lightning is not tied to any certain place, but illuminates the whole lower hemisphere: so the Church of the New Testament will not be restricted to a certain place, but wherever the Word and Sacraments will be in true use, in whatever place of the world, whether in the East or in the West, there will the Christians be gathered.' These are the words of the blessed Gerhard. who acknowledges also that this prophecy was fulfilled when, after Christ's ascension into heaven, the preaching of the Gospel was propagated by the Apostles among all nations, but especially when, after the destruction of Jerusalem, the whole world began to be called to the fellowship of the kingdom of Christ; and he provides an application of the simile that is suitable regarding the brightness, speed, and universality of the lightning. Jerome, in this place, says: 'Do not believe that the Son of man is in the desert of the Gentiles or in the inner chambers of heretics, but that his faith shines from the East even unto the West in the Catholic Churches.'

Nor is there any reason why it should be said that that proverbial sentence, 'Wheresoever the body is, thither will the eagles be gathered together,' refers to the final advent, Luke 17, last verse. For even there it is explained by some concerning the kingdom of Christ, of which we shall see in that place, God willing: nor is it inconvenient, because of analogy, for the same sentence to be referred to the spiritual and bodily advent in different places. And thus in this place is denoted the power and efficacy of the death of Christ: that it is so fragrant that it draws the elect to itself from the whole world, John 12:32, for whom the sweetest food is Christ crucified, not otherwise than that kind of eagle which they call the 'vulture,' which delights most intensely in corpses, to which it hastens with the swiftest flight, Job 9:26, Prov. 30:17, Hab. 1:8. Jerome, in this place. If irrational birds by natural sense, separated by such great spaces of lands and waves of the sea, perceive a small corpse, where it lies: how much more ought we, and the whole multitude of believers, to hasten to him whose lightning goes out from the East and extends even to the West! By the body, that is, the corpse, which is more significantly called 'cadaver' by the Latins, we can understand the passion of Christ, to which we are provoked, so that wherever it is read in Scripture, we are gathered, and through it we can come to the Word of God.

The Grotian explanation of the proverb, however, is inconvenient: who seems in reverse order to understand by the corpse the faithful who are putting to death the deeds of the body, and by the eagles the sublime gifts of the Holy Spirit, which are signs of the kingdom of the Messiah, just as those eagles so feared by the Jews were signs of the Roman empire. For shall we say that the gifts of the Holy Spirit fly and are gathered to the faithful, just as eagles fly and are gathered to corpses? And how shall we compare the gifts of the Holy Spirit to eagles, and how shall we compare the faithful to corpses? There are indeed not lacking those who compare the pious to corpses by reason of natural death and spiritual condition outside of Christ, as also of an abject status in this world: but who does not see that these things are foreign to this place. Others wish to compare Christ to the eagles from Deut. 32:10, both by reason of his divine and royal nature, and by reason of his fatherly care: but neither do those things sufficiently agree with this place. But as for one who compares spiritual gifts to an eagle, no one has been found. Nor indeed is this discourse about the dispersion and derivation of the sublime gifts of the Holy Spirit into the humble, but about the true and non-erroneous consecration of Christ, and his genuine communion, who by the most pure and most perfect fragrance of his benefits is to draw those who are not maliciously ferocious. See Zehner, Adag. Centur. I, p. 266. Grotius, however, is needlessly anxious lest anything should be detracted from the honor of Christ's body if it be called πτῶμα, inasmuch as it has been sent into the fullest possession of life: for Christ's body is not called a corpse because it is compared to a corpse in any respect, nor is the matter here so much about the body of Christ, the admission into the possession of life and glory, as it is about how it is offered to us in the Gospel as having been delivered up to death for us, and spreads abroad from itself the odor of a sweet fragrance and of salvation. It is the body, says Ambrose on chapter XVII. of Luke, concerning which it was said, My flesh is meat indeed: around this body are the true eagles, which fly around with spiritual wings. This is a singular interpretation of Lightfoot, whose entire opinion I am pleased to transcribe: I wonder, he says, that anyone can understand these words as referring to the pious fleeing to Christ, since the discussion here is about a far different matter: they are connected with the preceding as follows: Sudden vengeance will reveal Christ; for, when God shall have delivered the city and the nation, ripe for slaughter, like a corpse cast out, the Roman soldiers will fly thither immediately, like eagles, with their eagles, and will tear it to pieces and devour it. And the answer of Christ in Luke 18:42 also squares with this, when, after the same words which are said in this chapter, it was asked, Where, Lord? he answered, Wheresoever the body is, etc. tacitly hinting at this, that Jerusalem and the impious nation, which he had depicted throughout the whole chapter, would be that corpse to which the greedy and voracious eagles would fly, to devour it. Concerning the gathering to the Son of Man, not to the city of Jerusalem, interpreters commonly, no less the more recent than the ancient have explained it. I confess, however, that that explanation is not inappropriate, provided only that it agrees with the text: and B. Gerhard has already observed the same in Harm. Evangel. chap. CLX. p. m. 522, even though he follows the other one primarily because he thinks the discourse is about the most recent coming of Christ: Some, he says, maintain that, just as the former member speaks of the success and expansion of Christ's spiritual kingdom, so the excision and deletion not only of the temple but also of the hoped-for earthly kingdom is predicted to the Jews, so that the sense is: My spiritual advent through the preaching of the Gospel and my spiritual kingdom cannot be hindered, but what will become of the desperate kingdom of the Jews? The Romans, who are called eagles by right because of their standards marked with eagles, will reduce them to servitude, indeed they will be to them in the place of prey and a corpse. To this it could be applied, that just as the Jews before the first overthrow of the city are compared to the Chaldeans, the eagles, Habac. I. v. 8, so also in this place Christ seems to compare the Jews to a corpse, but the Romans to eagles. However, the continuity of the text stands in the way of that opinion: according to which he is now occupied not in describing the judgment against the Jews, but the spiritual advent of Christ, and the diffusion of the brightness of the Gospel through the whole world: and many things had already intervened concerning Pseudo-Christs and Pseudo-Prophets, which do not allow these things to be snatched away to those evils which the Roman army and its confluence to the city was about to bring. Nor does the sufficiently contorted interpretation of Arias Montanus, which Walaeus reports, deserve any approval: I think that by this expression the character of the Pseudo-prophets is rather noted, about whom in the preceding verses, who do not find material for nourishing ambition and avarice among the living members of Christ, but only among the dead: just as eagles, a rapacious genus of birds, do not live on bodies, but feed on corpses. Hence, therefore, we can know those Pseudo-prophets, because they will feign piety only for the sake of gain and ambition; and they fly thither where they see material suitable for their talents however far away, which will never be lacking among the followers of Christ, and therefore neither will the Pseudo-prophets flying thither.

PART II. Concerning the signs of the most recent advent of Christ.

Vers. 28. ὅπυ γὰρ ἐὰν ᾖ τὸ πτῶμα, ἐκεῖ συναχθήσονται οἱ ἀετοὶ] Proverbium Hebraicum defumtum ex aquilæ natura, quam Jobi liber celebrat. Idem est vulturis ingenium, unde & Latina adagia: quæ illud, Cujus vulturis hoc erit cadaver? De Erichtho venefica Lucanus: Et quæcunque jacet nuda tellure cadaver Ante feras volucresque sedet. Pertinet autem Hebraicum proverbium ad ea quæ non u- nius loci propria, sed ubivis locorum eodem modo se ha- bent: quale est illud Philemonis: Ἅπαντες οἱ λέοντές εἰσιν ἄλκιμοι· Δειλοὶ πάλιν δ’ εἶξ’ ἅπαντες οἱ λαγοὶ. Οὐκ ἔτ’ ἀλώπεξ, ἤ μὲν εἷρπεν τῇ φύσει, Ἡ δ’ ἀυθέκας®· ἀλλ’ ἐὰν Τρισμυρίας Ἀλώπεκάς τις συναγάγοι, μίαν φύσιν Ἁπαξάπασιν ὄψεται, Τρόπον θ’ ἵνα. Tale & illud proverbium: πᾶσι κορυδαλοῖς λόφος. Sensus autem hoc loco est idem quem apertius enuntiat Petrus Act. X. 34. o(/ti ou)k e)/sti proswpolh/pths o( Qeòs, a)ll' e)n pantì e)/qnei o( fo- bou/menos au)tòn kaì e)rgazo/menos dikaiosu/nhn, dektòs au)tw=| e)sti Si quis particulas subtilius velit a)llhgorei=n (quanquam id in proverbiis minime est necesse) poterit per cadaver intel- ligere tàs tàs pra/ceis tou= sw/matos qanatu=las, per aquilas sub- limia dona Spiritus S. quæ signa sunt regni Messiæ, ut aqui- læ illæ adeo Iudæis formidatæ signa erant Romani impe- rii. Cur hæc ad judicialem adventum trahi non oporteat, partim ante dixi, partim ipsa orationis series ostendet. Mul- ta enim intercèdent antequam ad judicii descriptionem veniatur. Venerandum Christi corpus, postquam missum est in plenissimam vitæ divinæ possessionem vocari ptw=ma miror veteribus venire in mentem potuisse. Sed & apud Lucam hoc proverbium non universali judicio, sed illi ho- minum discretioni quæ per Evangelium facienda erat, ap- plicatur, ut inibi videbimus.

Ad adventum spiritualem hæc pertinere è Luc. XVII. 24. manifestum est: non venit regnum Dei cum observatione, neque dicent, ecce hic, aut ecce illic: Ecce regnum Dei intra nos est. Nam sicut fulgur coruscans ex una regione cæli splendet in al- teram sub cælo regionem: ita quoque erit Filius ho- minis in die sua. Quæ cum de dilatatione subita re- gni Christi per totum orbem indubitato sonent, non potest ambiguum esse, hic, ubi eadem ha- bentur, etsi alio dicta tempore, de eodem adven- tu pariter agi, idque non secundario, quod pla- cuit B. Gerhardō, sed directè & primario; quan- quam nec id concedendum sit, geminum sensum, alium primarium, alium secundarium hic obtine- re, alium nempe de adventu corporali ad judicium, alium de adventu spirituali per Evangelium: qua- lem ditto/thta sensus Scriptura nuspiam admittit. Et satis docent antecedentia de Pseudo-Christis & Pseudo-Prophetis, dicentibus Ecce hic est Chri- stus, quod de spirituali adventu sermo sit: quo- rum sensum B. Gerhardus hunc tradit Harmon. Evang. cap. CLX. pag. 518. Cavete Pseudochristo- rum & Pseudoprophetarum conventicula, quia Ecclesia, quæ est corpus meum mysticum, non am- plius inclusa erit angustis Iudææ limitibus, sed in to- tum terrarum orbem per prædicationem Evangelii propagabitur, & quidem statim post urbis exci- dium; Sicut fulgur non alligatur certo alicui loco, sed totum inferius hemisphærium collustrat: Sic Ec- clesia N. T. non erit certo loco adstricta, sed ubicun- que erit verbum & Sacramenta in vero usu, quo- cunque loco orbis terrarum sive in Oriente, sive in Occidente, ibi congregabuntur Christiani. Hæc B. Gerhard. qui agnoscit etiam completum esse hoc vaticinium, quando post Christi in cælos ascensio- nem prædicatio Evangelii per Apostolos in omnes gentes fuit propagata, cumprimis vero cum post Hierosolymæ excidium ad consortium regni Christi universus terrarum orbis vocari cœpit; & applica- tionem similitudinis tradit convenientem qua fulguris claritatem, celeritatem, universalitatem. Hieron. in h. l. Nolite, inquit, credere quod Filius hominis sit in deserto gentium vel in penetralibus hæ- reticorum, sed quod ab Oriente usque in Occidentem fides ejus in Catholicis Ecclesiis fulgeat.

Neque est, quod dicatur illam proverbialem sententiam: ubi cadaver est, ibi congregantur a- quilæ, ad novissimum adventum referri, Luc. XVII. v. ult. Nam & illic de regno Christi explicatur à nonnullis, de quo istic loci videbimus, cum Deo: neque inconveniens est ob analogiam eandem sententiam ad adventum spiritualem & corpora- lem diversis locis referri. Et denotatur ita hoc loco virtus & efficacia mortis Christi: quod ea tam odorifera sit, ut electos ex toto terrarum orbe ad se alliciat Ioh. XII. 32. quorum suavissimus cibus est Christus crucifixus, non secus atque aquila- rum genus illud quod ὕπαετὸν vocant, cadaveri- bus impensissime delectatur, ad quæ celerrimo contendit volatu, Iob. IX. 26. Prov. XXX. 17. Hab. I. 8. Hieron. in h. l. Si irrationabiles volucres naturali sensu tantis terrarum spatiis & maris fluctibus se- paratæ parvum cadaver sentiunt, ubi jaceat: quanto magis nos, & omnis multitudo credentium debet festinare ad eum, cujus fulgur exit ab Orien- te, & patet usque ad Occidentem! Per corpus, id est, πτῶμα, quod significantius Latinis cadaver di- citur, possumus passionem Christi intelligere, ad quam provocamur, ut ubicunque in Scriptura legi- tur, congregamur, & per illam venire possumus ad verbum Dei.

Grotiana tamen proverbii explicatio inconve- niens est: qui videtur ordine inverso per cadaver intelligere fideles τὰς τὰς πράξεις τὣ σώματος θανατῶντας, per aquilas vero sublimia dona S. S. quæ signa sint regni Messiæ, ut aquila illa adeo Judæis formidata signa erant Romani imperii. Num enim dona Spiritus S. volare, ac congregari dicemus ad fideles, sicut aquilæ volant, ac congregantur ad cadavera? Et quomodo dona S. S. aquilis, quo- modo fideles cadaverib. comparabimus? Non de- sunt quidem, qui pios cadaverib9 componunt ra- tione mortis naturalis, & cõditionis spiritualis ex- tra Christum, ut & abjecti status in hoc mundo: sed quis non videt, hæc aliena esse hoc loco. Aquilæ vero comparari volunt Christum è Deut. XXXII. 10. tum ratione divinæ & regiæ naturæ, tum ra- tione paternæ curæ: sed nec illa satis huic loco congruunt. Qui vero dona spiritualia aquilæ comparet, nemo inventus est. Neque vero de donorum S. S. sublimium in humiles dispersione, & derivatione sermo hic est, sed de Christi vera, & non erronea consecratione, ejusque genuina com- munione, qui purissimo perfectissimoque benefi- ciorum suorum nidore tracturus sit non malitio- se feroces. Vid. Zehner. Adag. Centur. I. pag, 266. Nequicquam autem Grotius sollicitus est, ne corporis Christi honori decedat quid, si πτῶμα dicatur, utpote quod missum sit in plenissimam vi- tæ possessionem: nam non ideo cadaver dicitur Christi corpus, quod cum cadavere in aliquo id comparetur, nec tam de corpore agitur Christi, immissio in possessionem vitæ, & gloriæ, quam qua id in mortem pro nobis traditum in Evangelio no- bis offertur, ac odorem bonæ fragrantiæ & saluti- ferum de se spargit. Est corpus, inquit Ambro- sius in c. XVII. Lucæ, de quo dictum, Caro mea ve- re est cibus: circa hoc corpus veræ aquilæ sunt, quæ alis circumvolant spiritualibus. Singularis hic est Lightfooti interpretatio, cujus sententiam inte- gram adscribere placet: Miror, inquit, quemquam hæc verba de piis ad Christum confugientibus intel- ligere posse, cum de re longe alia sit hic dissertatum: cum præcedentibus sic connectuntur: Subitanea vin- dicta Christum revelabit; nam, cum urbem gen- temque internecioni maturam, cadaveris instar projecti, tradiderit Deus, advolabunt illico milites Romani, aquilarum instar, cum aquilis suis, at- que eam dilacerabunt, & exedent. Atque huc et- iam quadrat responsio Christi, Luc. XVIII. ult. cum post eadem dicta, quæ dicuntur in hoc capite, quæ- reretur, Ubinam hæc, Domine? respondit ille, Ubicunque est cadaver, &c. tacite hoc innuens, Hierosolymas, gentemque impiam, quam per totum caput depinxisset, cadaver illud futurum, quo con- volaturæ essent aquilæ avidæ & voraces, illud come- sturæ. De congregatione ad Filium hominis, non ad urbem Hierosolymam communiter Interpretes hactenus non minus recentiores, quam veteres exposuêre. Fateor tamen explicationem illam non inconcinnam esse modo textui congrueret: ac observavit jam eandem B. Gerhardus in Harm. Evangel. cap. CLX. p. m. 522. etsi alteram ideo im- primis sequatur, quod putet de novissimo Christi adventu sermonem esse: Quidam, inquit, sta- tuunt, ut prius membrum loquitur de regni Christi spiritualis successu ac dilatatione, ita prædici Ju- dæis excisionem & deletionem non solum templi, sed etiam sperati regni terreni, ut sit sensus: Meus adventus spiritualis per prædicationem Evangelii & regnum meum spirituale non poterit impediri, sed quid fiet de desperato Judæorum regno? Romani qui propter vexilla aquilis insignita aquilæ jure vo- cantur, in servitutem eos redigent, imo loco prædæ & cadaveris illis erunt. Huc applicari posset, quod ut Judæi ante primam urbis eversionem eicæ, Chal- dæi aquilis comparantur Habac. I. v. 8. ita quoque hoc loco Christus Judæos cadaveri, Romanos vero aquilis conferre videatur. Obstat vero illi sen- tentiæ συνέχεια textus: juxta quam nunc occupa- tur non in describendo judicio adversus Judæos, sed adventu Christi spirituali, & diffusione fulgoris Evangelici per totum orbem: & intervenerant jam multa de Pseudo-Christis, & Pseudo-Prophe- tis, quæ non patiuntur ad mala illa, quæ illaturus erat exercitus Romanus, ejusque confluxum ad urbem hæc abripi. Neque calculum ullum me- retur Ariæmontani interpretatio satis contorta, quam Walæus refert: Hac loquutione ingenium Pseudoprophetarum potius notari existimo, de qui- bus versibus antecedentibus, qui apud viva Christi membra materiam alendæ ambitioni & avaritiæ non reperiunt, sed apud mortua tantum: quemad- modum aquilæ, rapax avium genus, non vivunt corporibus, sed cadaveribus pascuntur. Hinc ergo posse nosci Pseudoprophetas illos, quod quæstus & am- bitionis tantum causa pietatem simulabunt; atque eo convolant ubi materiam suis ingeniis aptam quamlibet longe vident, quæ inter Christi sectatores nunquam deerit, ac proinde neque Pseudoprophetæ eo convolantes.

PARS II. De signis adventus Christi novissimi.

## 24:29
Vers. 29. But immediately after the tribulation of those days, the sun shall be darkened] Many things stand in my way against these being drawn to the judicial advent. First, that 'immediately' signifies a time not too far removed from the Jerusalem destruction and the frauds of impostors that followed, which Mark called 'in those days after that tribulation.' Then, the consummation of the age is described in other ways, namely by fire, as can be seen in Peter, 2nd epistle, chap. III. v. 12, but nowhere by the darkness of the Sun or Moon, or the falling of stars. Moreover, those expressions concerning the darkness of the Sun and Moon are found in many places, but nowhere in a physical sense, but in a figurative sense, as can be seen in Isa. XIII. 10, chap. XXIV. 23, chap. LX. 20, Ezech. XXXII. 7, Joel II. 10, 31, chap. III. 15, in which places both the Sun and Moon are named: then also Job XXX. 28, Jer. XV. 9. Amos VIII. 9, where there is mention of the Sun; in almost the same sense as Atticus writing to Cicero, in a calamitous time: The sun, he says, seems to me to have fallen from the world. Plato had said, 'For just as if someone were to take the light out of the established world, the whole remaining life would become difficult and grievous, so with these men removed, all the previous zeal of the Greeks has become darkness and great disrepute.' Eustathius on Homer's Odyssey T, 'And indeed, some did not understand the sun has perished from the sky as referring to an eclipse, but that the Sun had already failed the suitors as men about to die.' Chrysostom in the first oration on the overturned statues: 'The very circle of the solar rays seems to me now to contract and appear dimmer, not because the nature of the elements has changed, nor because the day is disappearing above, but because our eyes, being clouded by the cloud of despondency, are not able to receive the light from the rays clearly, nor with the same disposition.' To these is added that the falling of the stars in the Apocalypse is much earlier than the time of judgment. Furthermore, that what is said here will not be immediately joined with the day of judgment is apparent even from the fact that in Luke, Christ, when these things begin, commands us to stand erect awaiting our redemption. But there is no expectation of a present thing. By which arguments I am led to believe that it was Christ's purpose to signify to the disciples that, just as the Jerusalem destruction had its previous calamities, so the day of universal judgment would have them, of which the Jerusalem destruction was a figure and, as it were, a pledge. But these evils, for great reasons, were not clearly announced by him, but prophetically. This opinion is strengthened by the fact that the Apocalypse, which is written entirely in prophetic language, proposes these signs to us not only individually but also conjunctively. For after that earthquake of which we spoke above, these things follow in chap. VI. 12, 'The Sun became black as sackcloth of hair, and the moon became as blood. And the stars of heaven fell unto the earth, even as a fig tree casteth her untimely figs, when she is shaken of a mighty wind. And the heaven departed as a scroll when it is rolled together,' and what follows. I confess that in that place those evils are designated which were seen in Judea before the destruction of Jerusalem: for I am entirely persuaded that the matter there is about this thing: But as I said, Christ wants this, that similar things are about to happen in the Roman world to those which had happened in Judea, and therefore an equal end is to be expected. Nor are those things which had already happened mentioned in the Apocalypse for any other purpose than that the constancy of divine judgments might be evident from the comparison of the former and the latter. Although indeed it may seem that the darkness of the Sun and Moon in the Prophets signifies the taking away of glory and happiness, just as conversely the increased light of the Sun and Moon signifies an increase of glory, and in a similar way the shaking of the heavens indicates merely a huge change, just as Maimonides noted that it is said among the Arabs that the heaven falls upon the earth, just as a new heaven and a new earth signify a new state of things in Isa. LXV. 17, chap. LXVI. 22, Apoc. XXI. 1. To me, however, attending to the Apocalypse, it is more probable that the individual members have individual significations. For a woman is described by John (whom I posit without controversy to be the Church) who is clothed with the Sun, but treads the Moon under her feet, and has on her head a crown of twelve stars: from which passage it seems clear to me, which I remember has likewise been observed by others, that by the Sun is signified the knowledge of the divine law, by the Moon, the mutable star, the kingdoms of the world, whose power the patience of the Church overcomes, and by the stars, the teachers, of whom the twelve Apostles were the leaders. Therefore, that we may explain the oracle of Christ one by one, this is said first: that after the destruction of Jerusalem and the ruinous frauds of Barchocheba and those like him, it would come to pass that the knowledge of the divine law would gradually be obscured, namely, partly by false interpretations, partly by fictitious traditions, which, after the death of the Apostles and of the last of them, John, began to be scattered here and there, and as the centuries progressed, received greater and greater increase. To this pertains what he says in the Apocalypse of John, chapter VIII. 12, that the third part of the Sun was struck: then in chapter IX. 2, that the Sun was covered with darkness.

Καὶ σελήνη ὀυ δώσει τὸ φέγγος ἀυτῆς] Just as in Joel, Acts II. 20, and Apoc. VI. 12, the Jewish Republic, bloody with internal discords, is signified by the Moon, so here the Roman Empire is signified by the Moon, which, as if growing young again under Trajan (as Florus speaks), moved its muscles: under Hadrian it began to decrease: then indeed, partly by monsters having gained the empire, such as Commodus and Heliogabalus, and partly by many contending for the empire from all sides with price and arms, that old majesty of the Roman empire was much worn away, and at length it began to be prey to external nations, the Goths, Vandals, Franks, Picts, Lombards, Huns, and finally the Saracens and Turks. The beginning of this decay is noted in the Apocalypse when the third part of the Moon is said to be struck in chapter VIII. 12, but further ruin is indicated in the following.

Καὶ οἱ ἀστέρες πεσοῦνται ἀπὸ τοῦ ὀυρανοῦ] Οὐρανός is the Jerusalem above, Gal. IV. 26, the heavenly Jerusalem, Heb. XII. 22, that is, the Christian Church, which the Apocalypse also designates by the name of heaven in more than one place. The stars are all who perform the office of teachers: The seven stars, says Christ to John, are the angels of the seven churches. Falling stars are teachers failing from the truth, whom Jude calls wandering stars by another similitude. Augustine, explaining this passage in Epistle LXXX: Then the stars shall fall from heaven, and the powers of the heavens shall be shaken, because many who seemed to shine with grace will yield to persecutors and fall, and indeed the most steadfast believers will be tempted. Such a falling star was Marcion, denying that the Old Testament proceeded from the God and Father of Jesus Christ, and destroying the passion of Christ by positing an imaginary body. Such was Manes, positing two eternal principles and removing the pursuit of piety through a feigned predestination. Mixing their inventions with the errors of Ebion and others, Mahomet forged a new dogma, which is nothing other than a huge depravation of Christianity.

Such falling stars are often mentioned in the Apocalypse, repeated due to the diversity of times; as in ch. VIII. 10. 11. 12. ch. IX. 1. ch. XII. 4. just as also in ch. VI. 13. the multitude of false prophets, who had existed in Judea before the times of the destruction, had been denoted by the same image. But also long ago Daniel had described by this very mark the distinguished men among the people of God who were to fall away from the law in the times of Antiochus: where Jacchaides interprets the word for stars in the same way.

And the powers of the heavens shall be shaken] By this expression, as I have said, a great change of things is usually indicated, as in Is. XIII. 13. ch. 34. 4. Joel 3. 16. Heb. 12. 27. Here I think by all means that a very great change is indeed indicated, but for the worse, and that in the very Church which we have said is designated by the word heavens. It is true that powers here corresponds to the Hebrew צבא. For in Ps. 33. 6. the LXX have it thus: by the word of the Lord the heavens were established and by the spirit of his mouth all their power, where in the Hebrew it is כל־צבאם, just as also elsewhere in the Psalms כל־צבאיו is translated all their powers. And in Isaiah ch. 34. 4. All the powers of the heavens shall melt away, where in the Hebrew it is כל־צבא השמים: from which passage the words which we just now brought forward from Apocalypse 6. 12 are taken. There is also a place where צבא is translated by the LXX as host: elsewhere as world. That angels are usually signified by that word is taught to us by what is in 1 Kings 22. 19. But at Deut. 4. 19. the same Hebrew word denotes something visible in heaven distinct from the Sun, Moon, and Stars, where the name of stars seems to be referred to the planets. צבא to the lesser stars. And so it is taken here, but figuratively. For just as Daniel ch. 8. 10 calls the Jews צבא השמים the power of heaven, so here the powers of the heavens is the multitude of Christians, which after the times of the Apostles began to be wonderfully shaken by the tyranny of those who love to have the preeminence and who lord it over the clergy, by rash excommunications and the daily growth of schisms. Whoever wishes to see examples of tyranny and rash excommunication should read the Epistle of John the Presbyter concerning Diotrephes, and the pious admonitions of Irenaeus to Victor. We have examples of schisms in not a few others, to which Optatus of Milevis prudently ascribes three causes: anger, ambition, and avarice. Thus also that which is mentioned in Apoc. 6, the departing of the heaven, signifies the manifold sects of the Jews budding forth a little before the destruction: the Zealots, Essenes, Sebaeans, Dositheans, Gorthaeans.

The third question is resolved here concerning the signs of the final coming: to which this common opinion of the ancients and of recent interpreters pertains: except that the blessed Brentius in homily XLVII on Luke would have Christ still dealing with the calamities of the Jews, namely those who would live outside Jerusalem and Judea in other nations at that most calamitous time of destruction, which was fatal to all Jews. Grotius, however, understands these things as concerning the spiritual coming. But he denies by some reasons that they pertain to the judicial coming: but they are less valid: The first is from the word immediately, because he rashly assumes that it signifies a time not too far removed from the Jerusalem destruction and the frauds of impostors that followed, that the time of the Jerusalem destruction is being looked at, since in the preceding parts there had been talk of the spiritual coming of the Lord, with which the judicial coming is immediately connected: but Christ indicates that the frauds of impostors would be not only in those times nearest to the final destruction of the Jews, but that from then on such impostors would arise perpetually in all centuries until the final judgment, as he hints by the very immediate connection of his coming and its nearest signs. And that is also insinuated by Mark in ch. XIII. 24. in those days after that tribulation, in those days of impostors and after that spiritual calamity assigned immediately, which was to be so great that, if it were possible, even the elect would be seduced, the Sun and Moon shall lose their splendor, etc. Therefore there is no reason why these things should be referred to the bodily tribulation, which was to afflict Judea, about which there had been discussion concerning the first question, since they more conveniently look to the immediately preceding spiritual tribulation, which pertains to the second question. The second reason is that the consummation of the age is described in other ways, namely by fire, 2 Pet. II.

ch. III. 12. but nowhere by the darkness of the Sun and Moon, or the falling of stars. But these are not opposites: and that darkness and the falling of stars pertains to the preceding events, but the fire to the very consummation of the age. The third reason is that these expressions about the darkness of the Sun and Moon are never taken in a physical sense, but always in a figurative sense, Is. XIII. 10. XXIV. 23. LX. 20. Ezech. XXXII. 7. Joel II. 10. 31. III. 15. This partly proceeds from the undistributed to the distributed: for it does not follow that if that phrase is used improperly elsewhere, or if it is so used in the Old Testament, it is also taken improperly here, and that one must depart from the literal sense in this prediction of Christ: nor is it necessary to posit an improper expression in all those places, such as Is. XXIV. 23. ch. LX. 20. Cf. Apoc. XXI. 13. ch. XXII. 3. Some also understand the passage of Joel II. 32, as also III. 15, properly and concerning the final judgment.

Finally, Grotius urges that what is said here would not be immediately joined with the day of judgment, since in Luke, when these things begin, Christ commands us to stand erect and expect our redemption. But there is no expectation of a present thing. I reply: although most things do not immediately, yet these signs do proximately precede: because it is said that then the sign of the son of man would be seen, and the son of man himself would appear. And that is evident from the parable of the fig tree; because the leaves and buds of this tree announce that summer is near. Since, therefore, those arguments of Grotius are by no means solid, there is no reason why we should depart from the letter and the literal meaning of the words without necessity, which the words of Christ confirm, while He expressly predicts: THERE SHALL BE signs in the SUN and MOON: and He openly distinguishes these from the anguish of men, lest the Sun be thought to be obscured only in the opinion of men on account of the anxiety of the times: just as also the tribulation of the days is here clearly discriminated from the obscuration of the Sun: Immediately after the TRIBULATION of those days the Sun shall be obscured: or that we should rashly abandon the common explanation, in which interpreters easily agree. Add that in verse 30 the sign of the Son of man about to appear in heaven is subjoined to the other signs: And then shall appear the sign of the son of man in heaven: and that there, as also in Mark XIII. 26. Luke XXI. 27. it is expressly held concerning the appearance of Christ in the clouds: And then shall they see the son of man coming in a cloud: which advent, Grotius not denying, is judicial, and the final one Acts I. 11. 1 Thess. I. 17. Rev. I. 7. Nor do most interpreters take the similar description in Rev. VI. 12. ff., which Grotius here vainly drags to the destruction of Jerusalem, as anything other than the final day. Finally, it is undoubted that the things which are predicted concerning the Pseudo-Christs and false Prophets in verses 24, 25, 26, extend themselves even to the final times: as is clear from other places parallel to our prophecy 2 Thess. II. 4. 10. 11. 1 Tim. IV. 1. 2 Tim. IV. 3. 1 John II. 18. 2 Peter II. 1. 2. Rev. XIII. 8. 14. chap. XIV. 8. chap. XVI. 13. 15. Jerome on Matthew XXIV. Then, he says, according to some denotes the time of the devastation of Jerusalem; for there were no princes at the time of the Jewish captivity who said they were Christs: but it is better understood concerning the consummation of the age.

But here Grotius has devised new and hitherto unheard-of glosses for all these signs: by the Sun he understands the knowledge of the divine law: which was to be obscured partly by false interpretations, partly by fictitious traditions, which after the death of the Apostles and of the last of them, John, having begun to be scattered here and there, received greater and greater increase as the centuries progressed: by the Moon he wishes the Roman Empire to be signified, whose ancient majesty was much worn away partly by the political ministers of the Empire, such as Commodus and Heliogabalus, and partly by many contending for the empire from all sides with money and arms, and which finally began to be prey to foreign nations, the Vandals, Franks, Picts, Lombards, Huns, and finally the Saracens and Turks. Such a sense regarding the obscuration of the Sun and Moon never came into anyone's mind before Grotius, even in a dream. The falling stars are in this place the Teachers themselves who are failing from the truth, such as Marcion and Manes: the powers of the heavens shaken are the Christian populace, which after the times of the Apostles began to be shaken by the excessive tyranny of those presiding, who love to be first, and who lord it over the clergy, by rash excommunications, and by the daily crop of schisms. By the sign of the Son of man in heaven, Grotius understands the pure preaching of the Evangelical doctrine, which is to be restored with a certain wonderful efficacy through the ministry of those witnesses who are to come in the likeness of Moses and Elijah: so that just as the pure doctrine of the word sounded through all nations to the condemnation of the Jews, so it is to sound again, especially among the Jews, to the condemnation of many nations. Finally, Grotius explains the wailing of all the tribes of the earth as the mourning that will arise because of the most severe judgments, which are to be exercised by Christ at the same time as the truth shines forth. But since these glosses are supported by no arguments, we judge that they can be rejected with the same ease with which they are brought forward. They will not easily find credence with anyone. For they are destitute of all probability.

Indeed, some of the Fathers also explain these signs allegorically, Ambrose lib. X. in Luc. and Augustine Epist. XXI. to Hesychius; but in a far different manner, and not concerning that time which followed the departure of the Apostles, but concerning the last time: which, as Augustine holds, the Church, which is itself both Moon and Sun, because it is beautiful as the Moon, chosen as the Sun, will not appear, as the coming of the Lord Jesus approaches, then, he says, the stars will fall from heaven, and the powers of the heavens will be shaken, because many who seemed to shine with grace will yield to persecutors and fall, and some of the most firm believers will be troubled. Which allegorical explanation the blessed Gerhard does not simply repudiate, de extr. jud. §. 96. he professes; yet he maintains that the literal and proper explanation of these words should by no means be excluded by the same; but since that double interpretation cannot have a place at the same time, but there is only one genuine sense of the words of Christ, we rightly, having dismissed the allegorical explanation, adhere to the literal sense, from which, as the blessed Gerhard admits, one must not depart here without a compelling necessity. And indeed it appears from the words of Christ that Christ wished to indicate something singular, not seen before: but those apostasies, changes of empires, and troubles of the pious were sufficiently frequent at all times. And therefore they are not pointed out here. Compare what he has drawn to his own comments here from the Johannine Apocalypse in a clearly perverse manner, which we shall see in its proper place §.θ. Sandius raises a scruple in his paradoxes: Because astronomers demonstrate that the stars are many times larger than the earth, indeed according to the hypothesis of Hevelius even the smallest star of appearance exceeds the magnitude of the earth by many thousands of times, the words of Christ certainly cannot be understood in a literal sense. But neither are the stars said to fall to the earth, but simply πεσοῦνται ἀπὸ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ, and, if such a great magnitude of the smallest stars is admitted—which, however, that they are so large in the Milky Way is perhaps not yet proven—cannot, I ask, some parts of the stars fall to the earth, even if the whole stars do not fall, so that there is no need to understand through allegory the teachers falling from heaven, that is, from the true faith? Compare Luke XXI. 25.

Latin:

Vers. 29. Εὐθέως δὲ μετὰ τὴν θλίψιν τῶν ἡμερῶν ἐκείνων, ὁ ἥλιος σκοτισθήσεται] Quominus hæc ad judiciarium adven- tum trahantur, multa apud me obstant. Primum illud εὐθέως, tempus significat ab excidio Hierosolymitano & secutis im- postorum fraudibus non nimis longe remotum, quod Mar- cus dixit ἐν ἐκείναις ταῖς ἡμέραις μετὰ τὴν θλίψιν ἐκείνην. Deinde consummatio seculi aliis modis describitur, nimirum in- cendio, ut videre est apud Petrum epist. II. cap. III. v. 12. nusquam vero caligine Solis aut Lunæ, aut stellarum lapsu. Tum vero locutiones istæ de caligine Solis & Lu- næ multis in locis reperiuntur, nusquam autem sensu phy- sico, sed sensu figurato, ut videre est Esa. XIII. 10. c. XXIV. 23. cap. LX. 20. Ezech. XXXII. 7. Joel. II. 10. 31. cap. III. 15. quibus locis & Sol & Luna nominantur: deinde etiam Job. XXX. 28. Jer. XV. 9. Amos VIII. 9. ubi Solis est mentio; in eundem ferme sensum quo Atticus ad Cice- ronem scribens, calamitoso tempore: Sol, inquit, mihi e mundo excidisse videtur. Plato dixerat, ὥσπερ γὰρ εἴτις ἐκ τοῦ καθεστηκότος κόσμου τὸ φῶς ἐξέλοι, δυσχερὴς καὶ χαλεπὸς ἅπας ὁ λειπόμενος βίος γένοιτ’ ἄν, οὕτω τῶν δὲ τῶν ἀνδρῶν ἀναιρεθέντων ἐν σκότῳ καὶ πολλῇ δυσκλείᾳ πᾶς ὁ πρὸ τοῦ ζῆλος τῶν Ἑλλήνων γέ- γονε. Eustathius ad Homeri Odysseæ T. καὶ μὴν, τίνες, τὸ ἠέλιον ὀρανῶ ἐξαπόλωλεν, ὐκ ἐνόησαν ἐπὶ τῷ ἐκλιπεῖν, ἀλλ’ ὅτι τοῖς μνηστῆρσιν ὁ Ἡλιος ἤδη ἐπιλέλοιπεν ὡς τεθνηξομένοις. Chrysostomus prima oratione de statuis eversis: αὐτὸς τῶν ἡλιακῶν ἀκτίνων ὁ κύκλος συγτάζειν μοι δοκεῖ νῦν καὶ ἀμαυρότε- ρον φαίνεσθαι, ὐ τῶν στοιχείων τὴν φύσιν μεταβαλόντων, ὐδὲ ἄνω τῆς ἡμέρας ἀφανιζομένης, ἀλλὰ τῶν ἡμετέρων ὀφθαλμῶν τῷ τε- θολῶσθαι τῆς ἀθυμίας τῷ νέφει μὴ δυναμένων καθαρῶς, μηδὲ μετὰ τῆς αὐτῆς διαθέσεως τὸ παρὰ τῶν ἀκτίνων δέχεσθαι φῶς. His accedit, quod stellarum lapsus in Apocalypsi multo prius o- est judicii tempore. Præterea quæ hic dicuntur, non fore ἀμέσως conjuncta cum judicii die, vel inde apparet, quod apud Lucam Christus, cum ista incipient, jubet nos arrectos exspectare nostram ἀπολύτρωσιν. Rei autem præsentis nul- la est exspectatio. Quibus argumentis adducor, ut credam Christo propositum significare discipulis, sicut excidium Hierosolymitanum habuit suas prævias calamitates, ita ha- biturum & universalis judicii diem, cujus figura & quasi pignus fuit excidium Hierosolymitanum. Sed hæc mala, magnis de causis no plane ab eo enunciata, sed prophetice. Firmat hanc sententiam quod Apocalypsis, quæ tota scripta est sermone Prophetico, hæc signa non tantum singula, sed & conjuncta nobis proponit. Nam post terræ motum il- lum de quo diximus supra, hæc sequuntur cap. VI. 12. Ὁ Ἥλιος ἐγένετο μέλας, ὡς σάκκος τρίχινος, καὶ ἡ σελήνη ἐγένετο ὡς αἷμα. καὶ οἱ ἀστέρες τοῦ ὀυρανοῦ ἔπεσον εἰς τὴν γῆν, ὡς συκῆ βάλλει τοὺς ὀλύνθους ἀυτῆς ὑπὸ μεγάλου ἀνέμου σειομένη. Καὶ ὀυρανὸς ἀπεχωρίσθη ὡς βιβλίον ἑιλισσόμενον, & quæ sequuntur. Fa- teor eo loco designari ea mala quæ in Judæa conspecta sunt ante excidium Hierosolymorum: nam de hac re die ibi agi omnino mihi persuadeo: Sed ut dixi hoc vult Christus, si- milia eventura in orbe Romano iis quæ in Judæa evene- rant, ac proinde parem finem exspectandum. Neque in Apocalypsi ea quæ jam evenerant alio fine memorantur, quam ut constantia judiciorum divinorum ex priorum & posteriorum collatione evidenter apparet. Quanquam vero videri potest apud Prophetas Solis & Lunæ caligo signifi- care gloriæ & felicitatis ademptionem, sicut contra lux So- lis & Lunæ aucta gloriæ augmentum significat, ac simili modo cæli concussio mutationen duntaxat ingentem in- dicare, sicut Arabibus dici cælum cadere super terram ali- quam notavit Maimonides, quomodo cælum novum & terra nova novum rerum statum significant Esa. LXV. 17. c.LXVI. 22. Apoc. XXI.1. mihi tamen ad Apocalypsin at- tendenti probabilius est singula membra singulas habere si- gnificationes. Describitur enim à Johanne mulier(quam es- se ecclesiam extra controversiam pono)quæ amicta sit Sole, Lunam autem pedibus premat, & in capite fertum habeat stellarum duodecim: quo ex loco clarum mihi videtur, quod ab aliis itidem observatum memini, per Solem signifi- cari notitiam divinæ legis, per Lunam mutabile sidus mun- di regna, quorum vim superat Ecclesiæ patientia, per stellas autem doctores quorum principes fuerunt duodecim Apo- stoli. Ut ergo sigillatim Christi oraculum explicemus, primum hoc dicitur, post excidium Hierosolymorum & Barchochebæ eique similium exitiosas fraudes, futurum ut paulatim obscuretur divinæ legis cognitio, partim scilicet falsis interpretationibus, partim commentitiis traditioni- bus, quæ post mortem Apostolorum, eorumque ultimi Jo- hannis spargi hic illic cœpta, procedentibus sæculis majus majusque augmentum accepere. Huc pertinet quod in Apocalypsi Johannis primum capite VIII. 12. tertiam Solis partem percussam ait: deinde cap. IX. 2. caligine obductum Solem.

Καὶ σελήνη ὀυ δώσει τὸ φέγγος ἀυτῆς] Sicut apud Joëlem Act. II. 20. & Apoc. VI. 12. per Lunam significatur Judai- cæ Respublica intestinis discordiis cruenta, ita hic per Lu- nam significatur imperium Romanum, quod velut juve- nescens sub Trajano (ut Florus loquitur) movit lacertos: sub Adriano cœpit decrefcere: deinde vero partim mon- stris imperii potitis, quales erant Commodus & Heliogaba- lus, partim multis undique de imperio certantibus pretio & armis, vetus illa Romani imperii majestas multum detrita est, tandemque præda esse cœpit externis Gentibus, Got- this, Vandalis, Francis, Pictis, Longobardis, Hunnis, Sara- cenis denique & Turcis. Hujus labis initium in Apocalypsi notatur cum Lunæ pars tertia percussa dicitur cap. VIII. 12. ulterior autem ruina indicatur in sequentibus.

Καὶ οἱ ἀστέρες πεσοῦνται ἀπὸ τοῦ ὀυρανοῦ] Οὐρανός est ἡ ἄνω Ἱε- ρουσαλὴμ, Gal. IV. 26. Ἱερουσαλὴμ ἐπουράνιος Heb. XII. 22. id est, Ecclesia Christiana, quam etiam cæli nomine non uno loco designat Apocalypsis. Stellæ sunt omnes qui do- ctorum officio funguntur: Οἱ ἑπτὰ ἀστέρες, inquit Christus Johanni, ἄγγελοι τῶν ἑπτὰ ἐκκλησιῶν εἰσι. Stellæ cadentes sunt doctores à veritate deficientes, quos alia similitudine ἀστέρας πλανήτας vocat Judas. Augustinus hunc locum ex- plicans in Epistola LXXX. Tunc stellæ cadent de cælo, & vir- tutes cælorum commovebuntur, quoniam multi qui gratia ful- gere videbantur, persequentibus cedent, & cadent, & quidem fideles firmissimi tentabuntur. Talis cadens stella fuit Mar- cio, Vetus testamentum à Deo Patre Jesu Christi profe- ctum negans, & passionem Christi destruens supposito ima- ginario corpore. Talis Manes duo statuens æterna princi- pia, & tollens studium pietatis per fictam ἀποκλήρωσιν. Quorum commenta cum Ebionis aliorumque erroribus commiscens Mahumetes novum dogma procudit, quod nihil est aliud quam ingens depravatio Christianismi.

Talium stellarum cadentium sæpe in Apocalypsi est mentio pro temporum diversitate repetita; ut cap. VIII. 10. 11. 12. cap. IX. 1. cap. XII. 4. sicut & cap. VI. 13. eadem imagine de- notata fuerat multitudo ψευδοπροφητῶν, qui in Judæa ante excidii tempora exstiterant. Sed & olim Daniel hac ipsa no- ta descripserat eximios in populo Dei viros qui temporibus Antiochi à lege erant defecturi: ubi stellarum vocem eo- dem modo interpretatur Jacchaides.

Καὶ αἱ δυνάμεις τῶν ὀυρανῶν σαλευθήσονται] Solet hæc locu- tione indicari, ut dixi, magna rerum mutatio, ut Es. XIII. 13. c. 34. 4. Ioel 3 16. Heb. 12. 27. Hic omnino arbitror muta- tionem quidem indicari maximam, sed in pejus, idque in i- psa Ecclesia quam cœli voce designari diximus. Δυνάμεις hic respondere Hebræo צבא verum est. Nam in Ps. 33. 6. ita habent LXX. τῷ λόγῳ κυρίου οἱ ὀυρανοὶ ἐστερεώθησαν καὶ τῷ πνεύματι τοῦ στόματος ἀυτοῦ πᾶσα ἡ δύναμις ἀυτῶν, ubi in Hebræo est כל־צבאם, quomodo & alibi in Psalmis כל־צבאיו transfertur πᾶσαι αἱ δυνάμεις ἀυτό. Et in Esaiæ cap. 34. 4. Τακήσονται πᾶσαι αἱ δυνάμεις τῶν ὀυρανῶν, ubi in Hebræo est כל־צבא השמים: ex quo loco desumta sunt verba quæ modo adduximus ex Apocalypsi 6. 12. Est & ubi צבא à LXX. vertitur στρατία: alibi κόσμος. Angelos ea vo- ce significari solere docet nos, quod est 1. Reg. 22. 19. At Deut. 4. 19. eadem vox Hebræa notat aliquid in cœlo a- spectabile disjunctum à Sole, Luna & Stellis, ubi stellarum nomen ad planetas referri videtur. צבא alstellas minores. Atque ita hic sumitur, sed τροπικῶς. Nam sicut Daniel cap. 8 10. Judæos vocat צבה השמים δύναμιν τοῦ ὀυρανοῦ, ita hic δυνάμεις τῶν ὀυρανῶν est plebs Christianorum, quæ post Apostolorum tempora mire concuti cœpit, tyrannide τῶν προεστώτων φιλοπρωτευόντων καὶ κατακυριευόντων τὸν κλῆ- ρον, temerariis excommunicationibus & quotidiano σχισμάτων proventu. Tyrannidis & temerariæ excom- municationis exempla videre qui vult legat Iohannis Presbyteri Epistolam de Diotrephe, & pia monita Irenæi ad Victorem. Schismatum exempla habemus in aliis non paucis, quibus Optatus Milevitanus prudenter tres as- scribit caussas, iracundiam, ambitum, avaritiam. Sic & il- le qui Apoc. 6. memoratur cœli ἀποχωρισμὸς, multiplices Judæorum sectas paulo ante excidium pullulantes, Zelo- tas, Essenos, Sebæos, Dositheanos, Gorthæos signi- ficat.

Tertia hic quæstio expeditur de signis adventus novissimi: ad quem hæc communi veterum, & recentiorum Interpp. sententia pertinent: nisi quod B. Brentius hom. XLVII. in Luc. Christum adhuc de Judæorum calamitatibus agere velit, il- lorum scil. qui extra Hierosolymam & Judæam in aliis nationibus calamitosissimo illo ac omnibus Judæis fatali excidii tempore habitarent. Gro- tius verò intelligit hæc de adventu spirituali. Ad judiciarium autem adventum ea pertinere ratio- nibus nonnullis negat: sed quæ minus sunt vali- dæ: Prima è voce εὐθέως, quod ea tempus signifi- cet ab excidio Hierosolymitano, & secutis imposto- rum fraudibus non nimis longe remotum temere supponit, tempus respici excidii Hierosolymita- ni, siquidem in antegressis sermo fuerit de spiri- tuali Domini adventu, quo cum immediate co- hæret adventus judiciarius: Impostorum vero fraudes, non tantum proximis illis temporibus ab excidio novissimo Judæorum futuras indicat Christus, sed dehinc etiam perpetuo seculis o- mnibus usque ad novissimum judicium tales im- postores orituros ipsa immediata connexione ad- ventus sui & signorum ejus proximorum innuit. idque à Marco etiam insinuatur cap. XIII. 24. ἐν ἐκείναις ταῖς ἡμέραις μετὰ τὴν θλίψιν ἐκείνην, in diebus illis impostorum & post calamitatem istam spiritualem proxime assignatam, quæ tanta futura, ut si possibile esset, etiam electi seducerentur, Sol & Luna splendorem suum amittent &c. Non ergo est quod ad θλίψιν corporalem, Judæam afflictu- ram, de qua circa primam quæstionem actum erat, hæc referantur, quum immediate anteceden- tem spiritualem θλίψιν, quæ ad secundam quæ- stionem pertinet, convenientius respiciant. Altera ratio est, quod consummatio seculi aliis modis describatur, nimirum incendio 2. Petr. II.

cap. III. 12. nuspiam vero caligine Solis & Lunæ, aut stellarum lapsu. Sed hæc opposita non sunt: & caligo illa ac lapsus stellarum ad antecedentia per- tinet, incendium vero ad ipsam seculi consum- mationem. Tertia ratio, quod loquutiones istæ de caligine Solis & Lunæ nusquam sensu physico, semper sensu figurato accipiantur, Esa. XIII. 10. XXIV. 23. LX. 20. Ezech. XXXII. 7. Joel. II. 10. 31. III. 15. partim procedit à non distributo ad di- stributum: nec enim si alias ea phrasis adhibita est improprie, aut si in Vet. Test. ita adhibita, consequens est, etiam hic eam improprie accipi, & à sensu literali discedendum esse in hac Chri- sti prædictione: neque in omnibus illis locis ne- cessum est impropriam statuere loquutionem, ut- pote Esa. XXIV. 23. cap. LX. 20. Conf. Apoc. XXI. 13. cap. XXII. 3. Etiam locum Joel. II. 32. ut & III. 15. nonnulli proprie, & de extremo judicio in- telligunt.

Denique urget Grotius, quod quæ hic dicuntur non futura sint ἀμέσως conjuncta cum judicii die, si- quidem apud Lucam Christus, cum ista incipient, jubeat nos arrectos expectare nostram ἀπολύτρωσιν. Rei autem præsentis nulla est expectatio. Resp. licet pleraque non immediate, proxime tamen signa hæc antecedunt: quia dicitur tunc visum iri signum fi- lii hominis, & appariturum ipsum filium hominis. Idque ex similitudine ficus constat; quia folia & gemmæ hujus arboris æstatem prope adesse nun- ciant. Quum ergo argumenta illa Grotiana soli- da minime sint, non est cur vel à litera & proprie- tate vocum discedamus citra necessitatem, quam firmant verba Christi, dum expresse prædicit: ERUNT Signa in SOLE & LUNA: ea- demque ab angore hominum aperte distinguit, ne οἰομένως tantum Sol obscurandus hominibus ob anxietatem temporum censeatur: quemadmo- dum etiam tribulatio dierum à Solis obscuratione hic luculenter discriminatur: Statim post TRI- BULATIONEM dierum illorum Sol obscu- rabitur: vel temere communem explicationem, in qua facile consentiunt interpp. deseramus. Adde quod vers. 30. cæteris signis subjungatur signum Filii hominis in cælo apparituri: Et tunc apparebit signum filii hominis in cælo: quodque illic, ut & Marci XIII. 26. Luc. XXI. 27. diser- te habeatur de apparitione Christi in nubibus: Et tunc videbunt filium hominis venientem in nube: qui adventus non diffitente Grotio est judicia- rius, & novissimus Actor. I. 11. 1. Thess. I. 17. Apoc. I. 7. Nec aliter quam de novissimo die similem descriptionem Apoc. VI. 12. seqq. quam Grotius hic ad excidium Hierosolymorum nequicquam trahit: Interpp. plerique accipiunt. Denique indubium est, quæ de Pseudo-Christis, & falsis Prophetis prædicuntur vers. 24. 25. 26. sese ad tem- pora usque novissima extendere: ut ex aliis locis, parallelis nostro vaticinio, liquet 2. Thess. II. 4. 10. 11. 1. Tim. IV. 1. 2. Tim. IV. 3. 1. Joh. II. 18. 2. Petr. II. 1. 2. Apoc. XIII. 8. 14. cap. XIV. 8. cap. XVI. 13. 15. Hieronym. in Matth. XXIV. Tunc, inquit, se- cundum quosdam denotat tempus devastationis Hie- rosolymæ; nam nulli tempore captivitatis Judaicæ Principes extitere, qui Christos se esse dicerent: sed melius de consummatione seculi intelligitur.

Excogitavit autem hic Grotius novas & hacte- nus inauditas glossas horum signorum omnium: per Solem intelligit notitiam divinæ legis: quæ ob- scuranda fuerit partim falsis interpretationibus, partim commentitiis traditionibus, quæ post mor- tem Apostolorum eorumque ultimi Johannis spargi hic, illic coeptae, procedentibus seculis ma- jus majusque augmentum accepere: per Lunam significari vult imperium Romanum, cujus maje- stas antiqua partim ministris Imperii politicis, qua- les Commodus erat & Heliogabalus, partim multis undique de imperio certantibus pretio & armis mul- tum detrita est, quodque tandem praeda esse coepit externis gentibus, Vandalis, Francis, Pictis, Longo- bardis, Hunnis, Saracenis denique & Turcis. Qua- lis sensus in obscuratione Solis & Lunae nemini ante Grotium vel per somnium in mentem venit unquam. Stellae cadentes sunt ipsi hoc loco Do- ctores a veritate deficientes, utpote Marcion, & Manes: virtutes coelorum commotae plebs Christia- norum, quae post Apostolorum tempora nimia con- cuti coepit tyrannide τ̄ προεστώτων φιλοπρωτευόν- των, καὶ κατακυριευόντων τ̄ κλη̄ρον, temerariis ex- communicationibus, & quotidiano σχισμάτων pro- ventu. Per signum Filii hominis in coelo intelligit Grotius puram Evangelicae doctrinae praedicationem, quod per ministerium illorum testium, qui in specie Mosis & Eliae venturi sunt mira quadam efficacia restituenda sit: ut quemadmodum pura verbi do- ctrina per omnes gentes sonuit in condemnationem Judaeorum, ita sonitura iterum apud Judaeos praeser- tim sit, in gentium multarum condemnationem. Planctum denique omnium tribuum terrae de luctu extituro ob judicia severissima, quae simul ubi veri- tas emicuerit a Christo exercenda sint, explicat Grotius. Quas vero glossas quia nullis firmantur argumentis, eadem facilitate qua adferuntur, re- jici posse censemus. Non facile penes ullum fi- dem invenient. Omni quippe destitutae proba- bilitate.

Explicant quidem etiam Patrum nonnulli si- gna haec allegorice Ambros. lib. X. in Luc. & August. Epist. XXI. ad Hesychium; Sed longe alia ra- tione, neque de isto tempore, quod excessum Apostolorum sequutum est, sed de novissimo tem- pore: quod ut August. habet, Ecclesia, quae ipsa & Luna & Sol est, quia speciosa sicut Luna, electa est, sicut Sol, non apparitura sit, appropinquante ad- ventu Domini Jesu, tunc, inquit, Stellae cadent de coelo, & virtutes coelorum commovebuntur, quo- niam multi, qui gratia fulgere videbantur, perse- quentibus cedent & cadent, & quidam fideles fir- missimi turbabuntur. Quam allegoricam explica- tionem se non simpliciter repudiare B. Gerhar- dus de extr. jud. §. 96. profitetur; literalem ta- men & propriam horum verborum explicationem per eandem minime excludi debere statuit; Sed quum gemina illa interpretatio simul locum ha- bere nequeat, quin unicus tantum sit germanus verborum Christi sensus, merito, missa allegorica explicatione, literali sensui adhaerescimus, a quo fatente B. Gerhardo absque cogente necessitate hic discedendum non est. Et sane ex verbis Christi apparet, Christum aliquid singulare, antea non visum indicare voluisse: apostasiae autem illae, mutationes imperiorum, turbationes piorum o- mni tempore satis frequentes fuere. Ideoque illae hic indigitatae non sunt. Conf. quae ad Luc. cap. XXI. De locis quae ex Apocalypsi Johannea perversa plane ratione huc ad sua commenta per- traxit Grotius, ea propria sede ξ.θ. visuri sumus. Scrupulum movet Sandius in paradoxis: Quia Astronomici demonstrant stellas multoties terra ma- jores esse, imo juxta hypothesin Hevelii vel mini- ma apparentiae stella aliquoties mille vicibus superat magnitudinem terrae, utique verba Christi sensu literali intelligi non posse. Sed nec calurae di- di- cuntur stellæ in terram, sed simpliciter πεσοῦνται ἀπὸ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ, & annon admissa tanta minimarum stellarum magnitudine, quas tamen in via lactea tam grandes esse, fortassis nondum evictum, an- non, inquam, partes aliquæ stellarum in terram cadere possunt, etiamsi totæ stellæ non decidant ut opus non sit per allegoriam doctores cadentes de cælo, id est, de vera fide intelligere. Conf. Lucæ XXI. 25.

## 24:30
Vers. 30. And then shall appear the sign of the Son of man in heaven] Since after a few words inserted there follows the judicial coming, in those words and they shall see the Son of man coming on the clouds of heaven with power and great glory, that the sign which is treated here is that very glory, and thus that the same thing is said twice with certain words interposed, is something I can hardly believe. Wherefore I think that the Prophetic discourse is continued here, and all the more so because in Apocal. XII. 1, 3, and chapter XV, 1, mention is made of a sign in heaven. But I think that that sign, or the evident argument of the divine power of Christ, produced for the good of the Church (which is called heaven), is properly noted here, which is described in Apoc. XIX. 11, where John says that he saw heaven opened, and in it a white horse. But the white horse, as is gathered from a comparison of the history of Jewish affairs, which is in the same Apocalypse chapter VI, is the pure preaching of the Evangelical doctrine. This, therefore, Christ says is to be restored with a certain wonderful efficacy after so many corruptions of morals, doctrine, and government in not a few places: through the ministry (as it is right to believe) of those witnesses who are to come in the spirit of Moses and Elijah. For just as the pure doctrine of truth sounded through all nations to the condemnation of the Jews, so it is to sound again, especially among the Jews, to the condemnation of many nations. For, as I have said, the last things respond to the first.

And then shall all the tribes of the earth mourn] It could seem to be referable to the mourning on the day of judgment, which the Apocalypse chapter I. 7 uses the same words in that sense. But it is not new for the same words, especially those taken from the Prophets, to be adapted to different things. But these words are placed from Zechariah c. XII. 12, where it seems to be a matter of the repentance of the Jews whom the preaching of the Apostles converted. In this place, however, the order seems to require that these be referred to the mourning that will arise because of those most severe judgments, which will be exercised by Christ at the same time as the truth shines forth more clearly. That event will correspond to that part of Jewish history which immediately precedes the destruction of Jerusalem, just as this corresponds to the destruction of the world. And the kings of the earth, and the great men, and the rich, and the chief captains, and the mighty men, and every bondman, and every free man, hid themselves in the dens and in the rocks of the mountains: Which pertain to the greatest consternation of the Jews, with robberies spreading on every side. Therefore Christ will demand similar punishments, through all regions of the earth, from all those who, for the sake of their own honor or advantage, have corrupted or attacked with open force the sincere doctrine and its true use, through the illusions of sophisms and dogmas pleasing to sinners. And then follows the end: as the following things show. And thus far Christ has spoken obscurely and prophetically of those things which it was not necessary to know then, but which were to demonstrate the certainty of the prediction by the event itself; now he explains clearly that which it was of the greatest importance for all to know, namely the universal judgment, containing our redemption.

And they shall see the Son of man, coming on the clouds] What prevents me from agreeing with Augustine, who draws these things allegorically to the coming of Christ, either by the word or by the spirit, are both the things that follow, and especially that which we have in Acts 1:9, 11, where he is said to be about to return in a similar manner to how he had departed from the disciples, that is, by a visible cloud; with the addition of the passage which is 1 Thess. 4:17. Otherwise, even outside the time of judgment, the cloud is ascribed to Christ as a vehicle, as in Daniel chapter 7:13, and in the Apocalypse it is to be seen in many places, as a testimony, namely, of his own divine power, according to that which we read in Ps. 104:3.

That the clouds denote the Holy Spirit, Sandius very absurdly notes here in his paradoxes. For will the Son of man come upon the Holy Spirit, or are we to understand that the same Holy Spirit is said to have been assumed visibly, Acts 1:9?

With power and great glory] We can understand the host of angels as the powers here, as Paul explains in 1 Thess. 1:7. Add that which is below in chapter 25:31. But glory [means] the visible brightness, as that word is often taken.

Latin:

Vers. 30. Καὶ τότε φανήσεται τὸ σημεῖον τοῦ υἱοῦ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ] Cum post aliquot verba interjecta sequatur ju- dicialis adventus, in illis verbis καὶ ὄψονται τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ ἀνθρώ- που ἐρχόμενον ἐπὶ τῶν νεφελῶν τοῦ οὐρανοῦ μετὰ δυνάμεως καὶ δόξης πολλῆς, signum de quo hic agitur, esse illam ipsam δόξαν, at- que ita bis idem verbis quibusdam interpositis dici, vix est ut credam. Quare Propheticum sermonem continuari hic arbitror, eoque magis quod & in Apocal. XII. 1. 3. cap. XV, 1. mentio fit σημείου ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ. Proprie autem illud signum sive divinæ Christi potentiæ evidens argumentum, Ecclesiæ (quæ cælum dicitur) bono editum, notari hic ar- bitror, quod describitur Apoc. XIX. 11, ubi Johannes di- cit vidisse se cælum apertum, & in eo equum candidum. E- quus autem candidus, ut ex collatione historiæ rerum Judai- carum, quæ est in eadem Apocalypsi cap. VI, colligitur, est pura Evangelicæ doctrinæ prædicatio. Hanc igitur dicit Christus post tot non paucis in locis, morum, do- ctrinæ & regiminis corruptelas mira quadam efficacia resti- tuendam esse: per ministerium (ut par est credi) illorum testium qui venturi sunt in spiritu Mosis & Eliæ. Sicut enim pura veri doctrina per omnes gentes sonuit in condemna- tionem Judæorum, ita sonitura iterum est, apud Ju- dæos præsertim, in gentium multarum condemnatio- nem. Nam, ut dixi, respondent ultima primis.

Καὶ τότε κόψονται πᾶσαι αἱ φυλαὶ τῆς γῆς] Videri posset referendum ad planctum in die judicii, qui eadem verba eo sensu usurpat Apocalypsis cap. I. 7. Sed novum non est, eadem verba, præsertim ex Prophetis petita, diversis rebus aptari. Sunt autem hæc verba posita ex Zacharia c. XII. 12. ubi de pœnitentia Judæorum quos Apostolorum prædicatio convertit, agi videtur. Hoc vero loco videtur ordo exi- gere ut ad planctum hæc referantur, exstiturum ob judicia illa severissima, quæ simul ubi veritas clarius emicuerit, exercebuntur à Christo. Is eventus respondebit isti parti historiæ Judaicæ quæ excidium Hierosolymorum proxime præcedit, ut hæc orbis excidium. Καὶ οἱ βασιλεῖς τῆς γῆς, καὶ οἱ μεγιστᾶνες, καὶ οἱ πλούσιοι, καὶ οἱ χιλίαρχοι, καὶ οἱ δυνατοὶ, καὶ πᾶς δοῦλος, καὶ πᾶς ἐλεύθερος, ἔκρυψαν ἑαυτοὺς εἰς τὰ σπήλαια καὶ εἰς τὰς πέτρας τῶν ὀρέων: Quæ pertinent ad maximam Judæo- rum consternationem latrociniis undique grassantibus. Si- miles igitur pœnas Christus exposcet, per omnes terrarum regiones, ab iis omnibus qui honoris aut commodi sui cau- sa sinceram doctrinam & verum ejus usum, per sophisma- tum præstigias & grata peccantibus dogmata, corruperunt aut vi aperta oppugnarunt. Καὶ τότε ἑξῆς τὸ τέλος: ut se- quentia ostendunt. Et hactenus Christus obscure ac Pro- phetice ea elocutus, quæ tunc sciri nihil attinebat, sed even- tu ipso demonstratura erant prædictionis certitudinem, nunc illud quod omnes scire plurimum referebat, judicium scilicet universale, ἀπολύτρωσιν nostram continens, expla- nate disserit.

Καὶ ὄψονται τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου, ἐρχόμενον ἐπὶ τῶν νεφελῶν] Quominus assentiar Augustino hæc ἀλληγορικῶς trahenti ad Christi adventum, aut per verbum, aut per spiritum, tum quæ sequuntur me movent, tum præcipue id quod habe- mus Act. I. 9. 11. ubi simili modo rediturus dicitur quomo- do à discipulis recesserat, id est, per nubem aspectabilem; addito loco qui est 1. Thess. I. 17. Alioqui etiam extra ju- dicii tempus Christo nubes velut vehiculi loco adscribitur, ut apud Danielem cap. VII. 13. & in Apocalypsi multis locis videre est, in testimonium scilicet divinæ ipsius po- tentiæ, juxta id quod legimus Ps. CIV. 3.

Nubes Spiritum Sanctum denotare è Matth. XVII. 6. perabsurde hic in paradoxis annotat San- dius. Num enim super Spiritu Sancto venturus est Filius hominis, aut num Spiritum Sanctum eun- dem intelligemus dici assumpsisse visibiliter, Act. I. 9.

Μετὰ δυνάμεως καὶ δόξης πολλῆς] Δυνάμεις hic intelligere possumus Angelorum militiam, explicante Paulo 1. Thess. I. 7. Adde quod infra est cap. XXV. 31. Δόξαν autem ful- gorem aspectabilem, ut sæpe ea vox sumitur.

## 24:31
Verse 31. And he shall send his angels with a great sound of a trumpet] That is, with a sonorous trumpet, which Paul called with a voice and with a trumpet, surely one thing by two, just as here some copies have σάλπιγγΘ- and voice. This is another argument for the divine power of Christ, that trumpet which is attributed to God in Exodus XX. 18 and Psalm XLVII. 6. Moreover, the same trumpet, or the voice which is signified by the trumpet, is called Christ's, as in John XV. 25, namely as a king whose edicts are published by trumpet; at other times it is called the Angels', as here, as if they were the summoners or heralds of Christ. Some understand Christ himself by the voice of the archangel in Paul, 1 Thessalonians IV. 16; but the sequence of the discourse does not sufficiently allow for that: for it is said αὐτὸς ὁ κύ- ριΘ-, that is, the Lord who is to come, ἐν φωνῇ ἀρχαγγέλου. Wherefore it is more correct in Paul to understand by archangel, who is the great prince (שר הגדול) to Daniel, not Christ the king of the Angels himself, but a leader under the king of the angelic militia. For we almost always see that whenever God executes something through Angels, one of a more eminent position is given to the others as if he were a commander or taskmaster: as in Daniel IV. 13, 17. Zechariah II. 3. Revelation VII. 2. Moreover, this trumpet is called the last by Paul, because its own trumpet is also ascribed to the particular judgments of God, as can be seen in the Apocalypse. In summoning the people, not only the Hebrews, as noted above in chapter VI. 2, but also the Greeks and Romans used a trumpet.

Καὶ ἐπισυνάξουσι] An allusion to the custom of the Jews, among whom the gathering (ἡ ἐπισύναξις) was accustomed to take place at the sound of a trumpet, Numbers X. Compare Ezekiel XXXV. 21.

Τοὺς ἐκλεκτοὺς αὐτοῦ] That is, the Christians, namely the true and constant ones. See what is above.

Grotius again understands the true and constant Christians: but it is manifest that they are to be understood, as the word sounds, as the elect themselves, who, namely, have persevered in faith until the very end of life, and have been elected to eternal life according to the foreknowledge of faith. For those are signified whom the angels will gather at the end of the world and will separate from the reprobate. But those are not all Christians, but only the elect who have persevered in the faith. It is to be noted, however, that Grotius confesses that these things pertain to the final judgment: whence what is held in verse 30 in its entirety cannot be taken otherwise: and it is rashly torn apart, with one part of verse 30 being taken for the destruction of Jerusalem, and the other for the final advent of Christ, when they treat of one and the same advent. Therefore, the interpretation of Lightfoot at this place is foreign, as even Grotius himself confesses, regarding verse 31. When Jerusalem has been reduced to ashes, and that impious nation has been cut off and rejected, then the Son of man will send forth His ministers with the evangelical trumpet, and they will gather the elect among the Gentiles from the four corners of the heaven: so that God will not be without a Church, although that old people of His has been rejected and abdicated; but, with that Jewish one cut off, a new, Gentile one will be summoned.
