Ἐκ τῶν τεσσάρων ἀνέμων] An allusion to that which is in Isaiah c. XLIII. 5, 6. See also above c. IIX. 11. A similar manner of speaking is in Revelation VII and Zechariah II. 6. The opposite of this is in Jeremiah XLIX. 36.

Ἀπ' ἄκρων ὐρανῶν ἕως ἄκρων αὐτῶν] An explanation of that which had preceded. The LXX are accustomed to render מקצה. But it is the same thing whether you say from the end of the heaven to the end, as Psalm XIX. 7 and Deuteronomy IV. 32, or from the end of the earth to the end of it, as Deuteronomy XXIIX. 64. For by the ends of the heaven and the ends of the earth we understand the same thing. Therefore Mark was not afraid to mix both manners of speaking. For he said from the end of the earth to the end of the heaven. Similar to this is that in Philo in the book on Cain, from the ends of heaven to the ends of the earth.

Latin:

Vers. 31. Καὶ ἀποστελεῖ τοὺς ἀγγέλους αὑτοῦ μετὰ σάλπιγγος φωνῆς μεγάλης] Id est cum tuba canora, quod Paulus dixit ἐν φωνῇ καὶ ἐν σάλπιγγι, nimirum ἓν διὰ δυοῖν, sicut & hic quædam exemplaria habent σάλπιγγΘ- καὶ φωνῆς. Alterum hoc divinæ Christi potentiæ argumentum est tuba ista quæ Deo tribuitur Exodi XX. 18. & Ps. XLVII. 6. Dicitur autem eadem tuba aut vox quæ per tubam significatur, modo Chri- sti, ut Iohan. XV. 25. nempe ut regis cujus edicta per tubam publicantur; modo Angelorum ut hic, tanquam accen- sorum Christi aut præconum. Quidam ἀρχαγγέλου voce apud Paulum 1. Thess. IV. 16. Christum ipsum intelligunt; sed se- ries orationis id non satis patitur: dicitur enim αὐτὸς ὁ κύ- ριΘ-, id est Christus venturus ἐν φωνῇ ἀρχαγγέλου. Quare rectius est apud Paulum ἀρχαγγέλου, qui est שר הגדול Danieli, intelligere non ipsum regem Angelorum Chri- stum, sed sub rege militiæ Angelicæ ducem. Ferme enim videmus quoties Deus per Angelos aliquid exsequitur, u- num aliquem eminentioris loci velut imperatorem aut ἐρ- γοδιώκτην cæteris dari : ut Dan. IV. 13. 17. Zach. II. 3. Apoc. VII. 2. Hæc autem tuba Paulo ultima vocatur, quia etiam peculiaribus Dei judiciis sua asscribitur tuba, ut in Apoca- lypsi est videre. In convocando populo non Hebræi tan- tum, ut notatum supra cap. VI. 2. sed & Græci & Romani usi classico.

Καὶ ἐπισυνάξουσι] Allusio ad morem Iudæorum, apud quos ἡ ἐπισύναξις fieri solebat sono tubæ Num. X. Conf. E- zech. XXXV. 21.

Τοὺς ἐκλεκτοὺς αὐτοῦ] Id est Christianos, veros scilicet at- que constantes. Vide quæ supra.

Iterum Christianos veros & constantes intelligit Grotius: sed intelligendos esse, uti vox sonat, ipsos electos, qui scil. in fide ad finem usque vitæ perseverarint, & κατὰ πρόγνωσιν fidei ad vitam æter- nam electi sint, manifestum est. Isti enim signi- ficantur, quos in fine mundi colligent, & à re- probis segregabunt angeli. Illi autem non sunt Christiani omnes, sed soli electi qui in fide deci- serunt. Notandum autem quod fateatur Gro- tius hæc pertinere ad judicium novissimum: unde quæ vers. 30. integro habentur, aliter accipi ne- queunt: & temere pars altera vers. 30. ad excidium Hierosolymitanum, altera ad adventum Christi novissimum abripitur, quum de uno eodemque adventu agant. Aliena itaque hoc loco est Light- footi, ipso etiam Grotio fatente, interpretatio ad vers. 31. Cum in cineres redacta fuerit Hieroso- lyma, & gens ista impia excisa & rejecta, tunc e- mittet Filius hominis Ministros suos cum tuba Evan- gelica, & congregabunt illi electos inter Gentes, à quatuor cardinibus cœli: ita ut cariturus non sit Deus Ecclesia, quamvis rejectus & abdicatus sit vetus iste ejus populus; sed, excisa ista Judaica, convocabitur nova, Gentilitia.

Ἐκ τῶν τεσσάρων ἀνέμων] Allusio ad id quod est apud E- saiam c. XLIII. 5. 6. Vide & supra c. IIX. 11. Simile lo- quendi genus Apoc. VII. & Zach. II. 6. Contrarium hujus apud Ieremiam XLIX. 36.

Ἀπ' ἄκρων ὐρανῶν ἕως ἄκρων αὐτῶν] Explicatio ejus quod præcesserat. מקצה folent reddere LXX. Idem au- tem est sive dicas ἀπ' ἄκρου τοῦ ὐρανοῦ ἕως ἄκρου, ut Psal. XIX. 7. & Deut. IV. 32. sive ἀπ' ἄκρου τῆς γῆς ἕως ἄκρου αὐτῆς, ut Deut. XXIIX. 64. Nam per fines cœli, & fines terræ idem intel- ligimus. Ideo non veritus est Marcus utrumque loquen- di genus miscere. Dixit enim ἀπ' ἄκρου γῆς, ἕως ἄκρου ὐρανοῦ. Cui simile est apud Philonem istud libro de Caino, ἀπ' ἐ- ρανοῦ περάτων μέχρι γῆς ἐσχάτων.

## 24:32
Vers. 32. Καὶ τὰ φύλλα ἐκφύῃ] I think ἐκφύειν is the same as προϐάλλειν in Luke: and therefore I prefer to agree with those who interpret it actively, rather than with the Syrian who translates it with a passive meaning. Compare Song of Solomon II. 13. Τὰ φύλλα, that is, its leaves.

Latin:

Vers. 32. Καὶ τὰ φύλλα ἐκφύῃ] Ἐκφύειν idem esse puto quod apud Lucam προϐάλλειν: atque ideo active interpre- tantibus accedere malo, quam Syro vertenti significatu passivo. Conf. Cant. II. 13. Τὰ φύλλα, id est, folia sua.

## 24:33
V. 33. Πάντα ταῦτα] These words, and those placed in the next clause, not being correctly understood, have cast great darkness upon the interpreters. It is to be noted, therefore, that among the Greeks ταῦτα and ἐκεῖνα are accustomed to be opposed. Wherefore, since he soon names that hour (ἐκείνην τὴν ὥραν), this ταῦτα must be taken in opposition. We have already said that those things which were about to happen to the Jewish people had a figure and a pledge, as it were, of those things which awaited the whole world. Christ says, therefore, when you see these things which properly touch the Jews, believe also that the rest which I have said will follow.

Ὅτι ἐγγύς ἐστιν ἐπὶ θύραις] Namely, the Son of man; with the word repeated from verse 30, just as I believe the Syrian also understood it. But this is not to be taken as if the universal judgment were imminent immediately after the Jewish affairs. For both other things stand in the way, and that which follows below, 48, the Lord delays to come (χρονίζει ὁ κύριός μοι ἐλθεῖν). Therefore, the certainty of the event is indicated, not the proximity of time. Thus, sin lies at the door (לפתח חטאת רבץ) in Genesis IV. 7 signifies a certain punishment as a companion to guilt. Nor did James speak otherwise when he said the judge stands before the doors (c. V. 9). And in the same way ἐγγὺς is also accustomed to be used, as Philippians IV. 5, the Lord is near (ὁ κύριος ἐγγύς). Revelation I. 3, for the time is near (ὁ γὰρ καιρὸς ἐγγύς), concerning all those things which are contained in the book of the Apocalypse.

Grotius desires this sense: When you see these things, which properly touch the Jews, believe also that the rest which I have said will follow. But those things which he had just said did not properly touch the Jews. For they looked to the whole world and its imminent destruction. Therefore, in the apodosis of the buds and leaves, the things which Christ had predicted to the Jews are not signified by the likeness of the fig tree indicating summer by its buds and leaves: but the signs that will immediately precede the final day, just as by summer, he does not shadow forth the rest that will follow, but eternal life. Otherwise, the words immediately conjoined, that it is near at the doors (ὅτι ἐγγύς ἐστιν ἐπὶ θύραις), where Grotius, with the Syrian, understands the Son of man from verse 30, would imply a connection of the final advent of Christ with the Jewish destruction: but Grotius himself acknowledges that it is not indicated that the universal judgment is imminent immediately after the Jewish affairs.

Nor is there any reason for him to say that only the certainty of the event is noted, not the proximity of the time: for this exception is openly contrary to the words of Christ, who teaches by the similitude of the approaching summer, ὅτι ἐγγύς ἐστιν ἐπὶ θύραις, which properly means that the Son of man is at the doors, not merely that he is certainly to come. Nor do those passages teach otherwise, Gen. IV. 7. Jac. V. 9. Phil. IV. 5. Apoc. I. 3.

For sin is at the doors, which means not only that its punishment is certain, but that it immediately convinces us of it, and the guilt of the same awaits us at once: but Christ is said to be before the doors as Judge, because he is to be expected at all hours, at all moments, whether by the singular judgment of any man at his death, or by the universal one, on the day of general judgment.

The Lord is also near by his gracious coming to all who call upon him, Psalm CXLV. 18, if the Apostle is speaking of him in Phil. IV. 5. But the times of those things which are contained in the book of the Apocalypse are said to be near, Apoc. I. 3, because from that time their fulfillment was to begin, even if not all at once, since they are predicted to follow one another in their own order. Therefore, the beginning of them is indicated, which was altogether near.

Latin:

V. 33. Πάντα ταῦτα] Hæ voces & huic proximo commate positæ non satis recte intellectæ magnas tenebras interpre- tibus offuderunt. Notandum ergo, apud Græcos ταῦτα & ἐκεῖνα opponi solere. Quare cum mox nominet ἐκείνην τὴν ὥραν, hoc ταῦτα opposite accipiendum est. Diximus jam ea, quæ populo Iudaico erant eventura, figuram & pi- gnus quasi quoddam habere eorum quæ manebant orbem universum. Dicit ergo Christus, cum hæc videritis quæ Iudæos proprie tangunt, credite & cætera quæ dixi secu- tura.

Ὅτι ἐγγύς ἐστιν ἐπὶ θύραις] Nimirum ὁ ὐὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου: re- petita voce ex commate 30. quomodo & Syrum intellexis- se arbitror. Hoc vero non ita accipiendum est, quasi statim post res Iudaicas immineat judicium universale. Obstant enim tum alia, tum id quod infra sequitur 48. χρονίζει ὁ κύ- ριός μοι ἐλθεῖν. Certitudo ergo eventus, non propinquitas temporis indicatur. Sic לפתח חטאת רבץ præ foribus pec- catum est Gen. IV. 7. certam pœnam culpæ comitem signi- ficat. Neque aliter Iacobus dixit κριτὴς πρὸ τῶν θυρῶν ἕστηκεν c. V. 9. Atque eodem modo etiam ἐγγὺς sitmi solet, ut Phil. IV. 5. ὁ κύριος ἐγγύς. Apoc. I. 3. ὁ γὰρ καιρὸς ἐγγύς, de omnibus iis quæ Apocalypseos libro continentur.

Sensum hunc vult Grotius: Cum hæc videritis, quæ Judæos proprie tangunt, credite & cætera quæ dixi sequutura. Sed illa quæ proxime dixerat, non tangebant proprie Judæos. Spectabant enim ad universum orbem, ejusque imminentem interi- tum. Ideo simili à ficu per gemmas & folia æsta- tem indicante in ἀποδόσει gemmarum & foliorum non significantur ea quæ Judæis Christus prædixe- rat: sed signa proxime antecessura diem novissimum, uti per æstatem, non cætera sequutura, sed vitam æternam adumbrat. Alias omnino verba imme- diate subjuncta, ὅτι ἐγγύς ἐστιν ἐπὶ θύραις ubi sub- intelligit Grotius cum Syro Filium hominis è com- mate 30. inferent connexum adventus Christi novis- simi cum excidio Judaico: Atqui agnoscit Grotius ipse, id non indicari, quasi statim post res Judaicas immineat judicium universale.

Nec est, quod dicat, certitudinem solum notari eventus, non propinquitatem temporis: Hæc enim exceptio verbis Christi aperte contraria est, qui similitudine æstatis propinquæ docet, ὅτι ἐγγύς ἐστιν ἐπὶ θύραις, quod proprie sit, & præ foribus Filius ho- minis, non modo quod certo adventurus sit. Ne- que aliud loca illa docent Gen. IV. 7. Jac. V. 9. Phil. IV. 5. Apoc. I. 3.

Nam peccatum præ foribus est quod non modo certa ejus pœna sit, sed quod sta- tim nos de ea convincat, ejusdemque reatus illico nos maneat: Judex vero ante fores esse dicitur Christus, quia omnibus horis, omnibus momen- tis expectandus, seu qua judicium cujusvis hominis singulare in morte ejus, seu qua universale, in die pantocritico.

Dominus etiam prope est gratioso suo adventu omnibus, qui invocant eum Psalm. CXLV. 18. si de eo loquatur Apostolus Phil. IV. 5. Tempora vero illorum quæ Apocalypseos li- bro continentur prope esse dicuntur, Apoc. I. 3. quod ab isto tempore eorum incepturum sit comple- mentum, etsi non omnium simul, quum ordine suo se exceptura esse prædicantur. Initium ergo in- dicatur eorum, quod omnino prope erat.

## 24:34
Vers. 34. Ἡ γενεὰ αὕτη.] Those who understand by the word generation the whole of that time from Christ to the last day, enervate the force of the words. For Christ wishes it to be gathered from those things which are now about to be seen, to which the comparison of the fig tree pertains. Therefore, γενεὰ, corresponding to the Hebrew דור, signifies here, as above in chapter XXIII. 36, the men of that age. Similar is what he had said above, that some of those standing by would not die before the kingdom of the Messiah was begun, chapter XVI. 28. Certainly many of those who were then living, indeed who had already reached manhood, could have seen not only the destruction of Jerusalem, but also many things subsequent to that destruction, which is manifest even by the example of John alone.

πάντα ταῦτα] He said this, pointing to the Temple.

We admit that the whole of that time from Christ to the last day is not noted: yet it is not necessary that the men of that age be designated by the word generation, as Grotius does: because the discourse was previously about the final coming, which no one of that age reached by living. But it is signified in this sense by these words, that the Jewish nation, whose destruction Christ had predicted would be by far the most grievous, would nevertheless remain until the consummation of the age, and would not entirely cease: or by this word is noted generally the very generation of men: just as Jerome understands it generally of the generation of men: All those things which are predicted are to happen before the generation of men ceases, who nevertheless adds that it can also be accepted specifically concerning the generation of the Jews. The meaning of those who wish Christ to have spoken thus with the intention of using the universal particle πάντα, as if the day of his coming were near, so that it is always to be expected, does not seem to fit, because Christ explains the signs of his coming, when the deliverance is to be expected, as if it were about to happen soon: he could not, therefore, speak of it already as if he were to come before the passing of that generation, and within the age or span of human life; if he was not yet to come for several centuries. If, however, anyone should think that τὰ πάντα ταῦτα in this 34th verse should be understood of those things which Christ had said above would precede the destruction of Jerusalem (because it is one continuous discourse about that destruction and about the end of the world) and does not refer those things at the same time to the signs of the last day, γενεὰ αὕτη can be explained of the present generation and not inappropriately of the Jews of that time, without prejudice to the other things which are contained in the context; in which way Grotius, at Luke 21:32, explains πάντα as all those things which concern the Jews and the destruction of the city. But one must take care, however, that other things in the text are not perverted in the manner of Grotius, about which we have already warned.

Latin:

Vers. 34. Ἡ γενεὰ αὕτη.] Qui totum illud tempus à Christo ad ultimum diem γενεᾶς voce intelligunt, vim ver- borum enervant. Vult enim Christus ex iis quæ jamjam conspicienda sunt futura colligi, quo pertinet ficus compa- ratio. Significat ergo γενεὰ. Hebræo דור respondens, hic, ut supra cap. XXIII. 36. ejus ætatis homines. Simile est quod supra dixerat, quosdam adstantium non morituros antequam regnum Messiæ inchoaretur, cap. XVI. 28. Cer- te multi eorum quitum vivebant, imo qui ad virilem æta- tem jam pervenerant, potuerunt non excidium tantum Hie- rosolymorum, sed & multa eo excidio posteriora conspice- re, quod vel unius Iohannis exemplo manifestum est.

πάντα ταῦτα] Hoc dixit, Templum ostendens.

Non notari totum illud tempus à Christo ad ulti- mum diem, admittimus: neque tamen necesse est, ut cum Grotio ejus ætatis homines designentur voce γενεᾶς: quia sermo antea erat de novissimo adventu, quem nemo istius ætatis vivendo attigit. Significatur autem hoc sensu istis verbis, gentem Judaicam, cujus excidium prædixerat Christus longe gravissimum, remansuram tamen usque ad consummationem seculi, non plane desituram: aut notatur hac voce γενικῶς ipsa generatio homi- num: quemadmodum Hieronymus generaliter de generatione hominum intelligit: Illa omnia quæ prædicta sunt eventura esse antequam desinat homi- num generatio, qui tamen addit, specialiter etiam de Judæorum generatione accipi posse. Sententia illorum, qui Christum studio sic loquutum esse vo- lunt, adhibita vocula universali πάντα, ac si dies ad- ventus sui in propinquo sit, ut semper illa expectetur, non videtur congruere, quia Christus explicat si- gna adventus sui, quando expectanda sit liberatio, ceu in propinquo futuri: non ergo ita jam de eo loqui poterat, ac si ante transitum istius genera- tionis, & intra ætatem sive spatium vitæ humanæ adventurus sit; si aliquot adhuc seculis nondum e- rat adventurus. Si quis tamen τὰ πάντα ταῦτα hoc 34. commate intelligenda censeat, de iis, quæ su- pra antecessura excidium Hierosolymitanum dixerat Christus (quia una est continua Concio de illo ex- cidio, & de mundi consummatione) nec referat illa simul ad signa novissimi diei, γενεὰ αὕτη de præsente generatione & non incommode de Judæis istius temporis explicari poterit, salvis cæteris, quæ in contextu habentur; quo pacto Grotius ad Luc. XXI. 32. πάντα explicat, omnia illa, quæ Ju- dæos & excidium urbis spectant. Sed cavendum ta- men ita, ne alia in textu more Grotiano perver- tantur de quibus jam monuimus.

## 24:35
Verse 35. Παρελεύσονται] The Hebrews do not have a potential or hypothetical mood, therefore they use the future of the Indicative mood for it: which the Hellenists often follow. Therefore, this παρελεύσονται is placed here for παρέλθωσιν ἄν. For Christ uses a comparison of a thing which might seem most impossible, to show that it is much more impossible for his oracles not to be fulfilled. See what we said above in chapter 5:18. The author of this explanation, which Euthymius follows, is Luke for us, chapter 16:17.

Οἱ δὲ λόγοι με μὴ παρέλθωσι] That is, before my words pass away: as we explained in the place already cited. The same kind of speaking is clearly in Isaiah 54:9.

PART III. An exhortation to perpetual vigilance because of the ignorance of the last day.

Latin:

Vers. 35. Παρελεύσονται] Hebræi non habent modum δυνητικὸν sive ὑποθετικὸν, ideo pro eo usurpant futurum mo- di Indicativi: quod sæpe sequuntur Hellenistæ. Est ergo hic παρελεύσονται positum pro παρέλθωσιν ἄν. Compara- tione enim rei quæ videatur maxime ἀδύνατον utitur Chri- stus, ut ostendat multo esse ἀδυνατώτερον sua oracula non impleri. Vide quæ diximus supra cap. V. 18. Hujus expli- cationis, quam Euthymius sequitur, auctor nobis est Lucas cap. XVI. v. 17.

Οἱ δὲ λόγοι με μὴ παρέλθωσι] Id est πρὶν ἢ παρελθεῖν τοὺς ἐμοὺς λόγους: ut citato jam loco explicavimus. Idem plane loquendi genus Esa. LIV. 9.

PARS III. Adhortatio ad vigilantiam perpetuam ob i- gnorantiam diei novissimæ.

## 24:36
Verse 36. Περὶ δὲ τῆς ἡμέρας ἐκείνης] Namely, of the end of the age: about which day inquiry had been made in the third place, and about which Christ had already dealt in verses 30 and 31. This day is pre-eminently called the day of the Lord, 2 Peter 3:10.

Καὶ τῆς ὥρας] I do not understand ὥραν here as a particle of a day, but as a more broadly taken span of time, as in 1 John 2:18, Revelation 3:10, chapter 14:7, 15, and elsewhere passim. This is the very thing which Paul calls καιρὸν in 1 Thessalonians 5:1. Which meaning is frequent also in the Hebrew word עת, which the Syrian uses here.

Since Grotius had to admit in verses 30 and 31 that the subject is the last coming of Christ, it is manifest that the immediately coherent parts cannot be dragged to the destruction of Jerusalem. Nor does the particle ἐκείνης τῆς ἡμέρας allow πάντα ταῦτα to be snatched away to that destruction: but rather it clearly teaches that the same day of judgment, to be instituted not against the Jewish nation but concerning the whole world on the last day, is treated both here and in the immediately coherent parts. Add to these things what occurs in verse 37: which, as they are again most clear concerning the last coming, so they are explained by Grotius in a most perverse manner concerning the coming through the efficacy of the Word and Spirit: who therefore in this discourse of Christ imagines mere loose sweepings, and invents that Christ speaks now of the last day, now of the day of the destruction of Jerusalem, and that not without notable confusion.

οὐδὲ οἱ ἄγγελοι τῶν ὀυρανῶν] It does not matter much whether what some add, οὐδὲ ὁ υἱὸς, is read here or not: since no one deletes it in Mark. To me, however, it is more probable that it was added to some codices from Mark than deleted in Matthew. For there was no cause for deleting it, since it was left in Mark: but we often see things added from the collation of writers among themselves. Nor does it move me that Mark contracted Matthew's history: for he did not so bind himself to Matthew that he did not change words somewhere, or even add something, with Peter, as it is reasonable to believe, suggesting if he remembered anything above the others. Interpreters who make mention of the Son here looked to Mark: which appears from Origen, who deals with the Son here, although the copies published by Origen did not have those words in this place, as Jerome testifies. The Syrian and the Latin, and a much larger part of the codices, stand by this reading.

Grotius rightly observes that οὐδὲ ὁ υἱὸς was rashly added to some codices of Matthew from Mark. But what is said about the suggestion made to Mark by Peter lacks any foundation, nor does it agree with the divine inspiration of the Canonical writer, whom the Church by common consent has accepted to be Mark.

Εἰμὴ ὁ πατὴρ μόνος.] Εἰ μὴ can be taken properly here, and we may read those words οὐδὲ οἱ ἄγγελοι τῶν ὀυρανῶν as if included in a parenthesis: which I think should also be done in Mark. For οὐδὲις and εἰ μὴ cohere very well. As if you were to say: No one knows (I do not except the angels themselves) except the Father. It is, however, an old saying of the Hebrews that the time when the world will end has been revealed to no one. See Iachiades on Daniel 8:26.

Latin:

Vers. 36. Περὶ δὲ τῆς ἡμέρας ἐκείνης] Nimirum τῆς συν- τελείας τοῦ αἰῶνος: de qua die tertio loco erat quæsitum, & de qua jam egerat Christus commate 30. 31. Hæc dies eximie vocatur ἡ ἡμέρα κυρίου 2. Petr. III. 10.

Καὶ τῆς ὥρας] ὥραν hic non diei particulam sed latius sumti temporis ambitum intelligo, ut 1. Ioh. II. 18. Apoc. III. 10. cap. XIV. 7. 15. & alibi passim. Hoc ipsum est quod καιρὸν vocat Paulus 1. Thess. V. 1. Quæ significatio fre- quens est etiam in Hebræa voce עת quam hic Syrus u- surpat.

Quum fateri oportuerit Grotium v. 30. 31. de adventu Christi novissimo agi, manifestum est im- mediate cohærentia non posse trahi ad excidium Hierosolymitanum. Neque vero vocula ἐκείνης τῆς ἡμέρας permittit ut ad illud excidium πάντα ταῦτα abripiantur: quin potius eandem ipsam diem judicii non adversus gentem Judaicam, sed de toto mundo instituendi in die novissima, & hic, & immediate cohærentibus actum esse liquido docet. Adde autem his quæ v. 37. occurrunt: quæ uti luculentissima iterum sunt de adventu no- vissimo, ita non nisi perversissima ratione de ad- ventu per Verbi & Spiritus efficaciam à Gro- tio explicantur: qui proinde in hac concione Christi meras scopas dissolutas fingit, & modo de die novissimo, modo de die excidii Hieroso- lymitani Christum loqui, idque non sine insigni confusione comminiscitur.

οὐδὲ οἱ ἄγγελοι τῶν ὀυρανῶν] Non multum refert an hic lega- tur id quod addunt quidam οὐδὲ ὁ υἱὸς, nec ne: cum apud Marcum nemo deleat. Mihi vero probabilius est quibus- dam codicibus, additum ex Marco, quam deletum in Mat- thæo. Nulla enim delendi erat causa, cum in Marco relin- queretur: addita autem sæpe videmus aliqua ex scriptorum inter se collatione. Neque me movet, quod Marcus Mat- thæi historiam contraxit: non enim ita se Matthæo ad- strinxit, ut non alicubi mutaret verba, adderet etiam ali- quid, Petro, ut credi par est, si quid supra cæteros me- minerat, suggerente. Interpretes qui filii hic faciunt men- tionem, ad Marcum respexere: quod ex Origene appa- ret, qui de filio hic agit, cum tamen edita ab Origene ex- emplaria istas voces hoc loco non haberent, ut testatur Hieronymus. Ab hac lectione stant Syrus & Latinus, & codicum pars multo major.

Recte observat Grotius, temere additum qui- busdam Matthæi Codicibus è Marco ἰδὲ ὁ ὑὸς. Quod autem de Petri suggestione Marco facta dici- tur, omni fundamento caret, nec convenit τῇ θεοπνευσίᾳ Scriptoris Canonici, quem Mar- cum esse communi consensu recepit Ecclesia.

Εἰμὴ ὁ πατὴρ μόνος.] Potest εἰ μὴ hic proprie sumi, & illa ἰδὲ οἱ ἄγγελοι τῶν ὐρανῶν legamus velut parenthesi inclu- sa: quod & apud Marcum faciendum arbitror. Opti- me enim cohærent ὀὐδὲις & εἰ μὴ. Quasi dicas: Nemo novit (Angelos ipsos non excipio) præter Patrem. Est autem dictum vetus Hebræorum, tempus quo mundus finiet, nemini patefactum. Vide Iachiaden ad Daniel. VIII, 26.

## 24:37
Verse 37. ὧσπερ δὲ αἱ ἡμέραι τῦ Νῶε, ὕτως ἔσαι καὶ ἡ παρυσία τῦ υἱῦ τῦ ἀνθρώπυ] Since I have said above, and if I am not mistaken have shown, that this is the coming of Christ into the whole world through the efficacy of his word and spirit, which exerted itself especially in the first forty years, as we shall also say regarding Luke, I think that those things which follow are to be referred entirely to the affairs of that time. And if I am not mistaken, at a different time than when Christ said the former things, on an occasion given by the Pharisees as Luke narrates: but Matthew added it here because it pertained much to illustrating those things which had been said above concerning Jewish affairs and the progress of the Gospel. Just as Mark also inserted here another passage which is above in Matthew chapter 10:17, because of the coherence of the subject matter. Nor indeed does what follows concerning the thief prove that the universal judgment is being discussed here, since even particular judgments of God upon peoples or men (which nevertheless themselves contain a presage of the universal judgment) are accustomed to be compared to a nocturnal thief, as can be seen in Apoc. III. 3, chap. XVI. 15. This interpretation is strengthened by the fact that Peter compares Noah, saved in the flood, to Christians saved from common destruction through baptism.

These things are not to be taken with Grotius concerning the coming of Christ through the efficacy of the Word and Spirit, which exerted itself especially in the first 40 years, but concerning the final coming, which is compared with the final times of the ante-diluvian world. For the things that immediately preceded in verse 36 demand this: 'of that day no one knows except the Father,' as also that vigilance which it requires, since no one knows at what hour the Lord is to come, v. 42. Compare Luke XXI. 35, 36, and also the description of the manner of the coming, that he will come like a thief, 1 Thess. V. 4, and finally the final punishment, v. 51.

Latin:

Vers. 37. ὧσπερ δὲ αἱ ἡμέραι τῦ Νῶε, ὕτως ἔσαι καὶ ἡ πα- ρυσία τῦ υἱῦ τῦ ἀνθρώπυ] Cum παρυσίαν supra dixerim, & ni fallor ostenderim hic esse adventum Christi in orbem to- tum per verbi & spiritus sui efficaciam, quæ præcipue se exeruit annis primis quadraginta, ut ad Lucam quoque dicemus, omnino ea quæ sequuntur ad res ejus tem- poris referenda præcipue arbitror. Et ni fallor alio illa tempore, quam quo priora dixit Christus, occasione à Pharisæis data ut Lucas narrat: sed Matthæus ideo hic addidit, quia ad illustranda ea quæ de rebus Iudaicis & Evangelii profectu supra dicta erant, multum pertine- bant. Sicut & Marcus alium locum qui supra apud Mat- thæum est cap. X. 17. ob rerum cohærentiam hic infe- ruit. Neque vero quod de fure sequitur, evincit de u- niversali judicio hic agi, cum etiam peculiaria in popu- los aut homines judicia Dei (quæ tamen ipsa universalis judicii præsagium continent) furi nocturno comparari so- leant, ut videre est Apoc. III. 3. cap. XVI. 15. Firmat hanc interpretationem quod Noam servatum in diluvio Christianis per baptismum à communi pernitie servatis Pe- trus comparat.

Hæc non de adventu Christi per Verbi & Spiri- tûs efficaciam quæ se exeruit præcipue annis primis 40. cum Grotio accipienda: sed de adventu no- vissimo: qui cum novissimis temporibus mundi ante-diluviani confertur. Id enim immediate antegressa vers. 36. poscunt: de die illa nemo novit nisi Pater: ut & vigilantia illa quam postulat, siquidem nemo novit, qua hora Dominus venturus sit, v. 42. Conf. Luc. XXI. 35. 36. nec non descriptio modi adventus, quod instar furis ven- turus sit, 1. Thess. V. 4. & pœna denique novissima, v. 51.

## 24:38
Vers. 38. Τρώγοντες καὶ πίνοντες] Not only carefree, but placing all their effort in perishable things, and enslaved to their own pleasures, no less than he who inscribed on his tomb:

Τοσσ᾽ ἔχω ὅσσ᾽ ἔπιον καὶ ἐδήτυν. To this life is opposed that warning in Luke: προσέχετε ἑαυτοῖς μήποτε βαρυνθῶσιν ὑμῶν αἱ καρδίαι κραιπάλῃ καὶ μέθῃ καὶ μερίμναις βιωτικαῖς. Compare what is below in verse 49.

Γαμῦντες κὶ ἐκγαμίζοντες] Burning with the desire to propagate their name and race, as if the whole hope of immortality were situated in that. See Genesis IV. 7, 19. But even those who were born of pious parents were defiling themselves with the marriages of the impious out of a desire for power and glory, as can be seen in Genesis. Thus, everywhere, their souls were bent toward the earth: unmindful that they were created in the image of God, which the very posture of the body also testifies; for this reason God gave man a sublime face, and commanded him to look at the heavens, and to lift his eyes erect to the stars. Which ancient philosophers drew from the Theology of the Phoenicians, and from them the poets; the Phoenicians had drawn it from the Hebrews. To the memory of this condition of ours we are commanded ἀνακύψαι κὶ ἐπᾶραι τὰς κεφαλὰς ἡμῶν, as it is in Luke in this place. This ἀποκαραδοκία (as Paul calls it) is opposed to those μερίμναις βιωτικαῖς of the men of the ancient world; Emperor M. Antoninus in book IV, showing that men always do the same things, says thus: ἐπινόησον λόγυ χάριν τὺς ἐπὶ Οὐησπασιανῦ καιρὺς, ὄψῃ ταῦτα πάντα γαμῦντας, παιδοτροφῦν-

Εἰς τὴν κιβωτὸν] Thus the LXX translate the Hebrew תבה, which Peter also follows, and Philo as well. Josephus said λάρνακα, following that Nicolaus of Damascus celebrated for his friendship with Augustus: whose words were these: καί τινα ἐπὶ λάρνα- κος ὀχύμενον ἐπὶ τὴν ἀκρώρειαν ὀκεῖλαι. Apollodorus also in his Bibliotheca, when he mentions the flood, names λάρνακα, and Lucian in his De Dea Syria likewise in the history of the flood: and Alexander Polyhistor, whose words exist in Cyril. Abydenus in his Assyrian history called it πλοῖον. And in the aforementioned Damascenus, the place where it had settled is called Βᾶρις. Herodotus noted that a certain kind of ship is called thus by the Egyptians. I believe it was a crude mass made without any art. Ξύλινον ἔργον μέγιστον, says Philo. For among the arts discovered before the flood, shipbuilding is not mentioned: or at least they were not constructed such as are called תבות, just as the little basket in which Moses was exposed is also called [that]: just as the Greek poets also call that in which Perseus was exposed λάρνακα.

Latin:

Vers. 38. Τρώγοντες καὶ πίνοντες] Non securi tantum, sed omne studium ponentes in rebus caducis, & voluptatibus suis mancipati, non minus quam ille qui sepulchro inscri- psit:

Τοσσ᾽ ἔχω ὅσσ᾽ ἔπιον καὶ ἐδήτυν. Huic vitæ opponitur illa apud Lucam monitio: προσέχε- τε ἑαυτοῖς μήποτε βαρυνθῶσιν ὑμῶν αἱ καρδίαι κραιπάλῃ καὶ μέθῃ καὶ μερίμναις βιωτικαῖς. Confer quod infra est com- mate 49.

Γαμῦντες κὶ ἐκγαμίζοντες] Nominis generisque propa- gandi desiderio flagrantes, quasi in eo sita esset tota spes immortalitatis. Vide Genes. IV. 7. 19. Sed & qui piis editi erant parentibus, impiorum connubiis se inquinabant potentiæ & gloriæ studio, ut in Genesi videre est. Ita pas- sim omnibus curvæ erant in terras animæ: immemores conditas se ad Dei imaginem, quod ipsa etiam corporis positura testatur: ideo enim Deus Os homini sublime dedit, cælumque videre Iussit, & erectos ad sidera tollere vultus. Quod ex Phœnicum Theologia veteres Philosophi hause- runt, ex illis Poetæ: Phœnices ab Hebræis hauserant. Ad huius conditionis nostræ memoriam nos jubemur ἀνακύψαι κὶ ἐπᾶραι τὰς κεφαλὰς ἡμῶν, ut apud Lucam est hoc loco. Hæc ἀποκαραδοκία (ut eam Paulus appellat) opponitur illis μερίμναις βιωτικαῖς hominum τῦ ἀρχαία κόσμε, M. Anto- nius Imperator libro IV. ostendens homines semper ea- dem agitare, sic ait: ἐπινόησον λόγυ χάριν τὺς ἐπὶ Οὐησπα- σιανῦ καιρὺς, ὄψῃ ταῦτα πάντα γαμῦντας, παιδοτροφῦν-

Εἰς τὴν κιβωτὸν] Ita LXX. transferunt Hebræum תבה, quod & Petrus sequitur, sed & Philo. Josephus λάρνακα dixit secutus Nicolaum Damascenum illum Augusti amici- tia celebratum: cujus hæc erant verba: καί τινα ἐπὶ λάρνα- κος ὀχύμενον ἐπὶ τὴν ἀκρώρειαν ὀκεῖλαι. Etiam Apollodorus in Bibliotheca ubi diluvii meminit, nominat λάρνακα, & Lucianus de Dea Syria itidem in diluvii historia: & A- lexander Polyhistor, cujus verba apud Cyrillum exstant. Abydenus in historia Assyriaca πλοῖον vocavit. Et apud Damascenum, quem dixi, locus in quo consederat ca voca- tur Βᾶρις. Ita autem navis quoddam genus Ægyptiis dici notavit Herodotus. Credo molem fuisse rudem nullaque arte factam. Ξύλινον ἔργον μέγιστον inquit Philo. Nam in- ter artes ante diluvium repertas non memoratur ἡ ναυπη- γικὴ: aut certe non fuere constructæ, quales תבות vo- cantur, quomodo & cistella appellatur in qua expositus est Moses: sicut & Græci Poetæ id in quo expositus fuit Perseus λάρνακα vocant.

## 24:39
Vers. 39. ἐκ ἔγνωσαν] לא ידע for the Hebrews is often προσέχειν, as in Ecclesiastes 4:17, Isaiah 1:3; thus γινώσκειν is taken here and in many other places, as Luke 19:44, Hebrews 3:10. To which perhaps should also be referred that which is in Romans 7:7 and Acts 23:5. Opposed to this negligence is that which is in Luke, προσέχειν.

Καὶ ἦρεν ἅπαντας] ἦρεν is נשא in Genesis 7:23. ἅπαντας, the whole human race, the ancient world as Peter speaks, with only eight men excepted, among whom was Noah. For I cannot at all agree with those who restrict this generality to some portion of the human race. For we have a great argument that this flood reached the whole human race in the memory of all nations, which ends at that time. Varro, the most diligent investigator of all antiquity, divided all time into three periods: unknown, mythical, and historical, calling unknown whatever was before the great Cataclysm: fabulous, that which follows next: historical, from the destruction of Troy. Josephus cites Berosus, the writer of Chaldean affairs, Hieronymus of the Phoenician, Mnaseas also, and the aforementioned Damascenus, who all mention both the flood at that time and the ark. Abydenus calls Noah Sisithrus, and him who foretold the impending destruction to him, Cronus, doubtless because the Greeks were accustomed to translate the oriental word אלון in that way. For Philo of Byblos also says ὁ ἰλὸς. τῦτ᾽ ἐστιν ὁ κρόν@. For the Phoenicians, Assyrians, and Armenians in antiquity venerated that star most highly which the Greeks call Cronus, because it is carried in the highest orbit and with chief power, which Tacitus notes. That the same was worshipped by the Jews, many were persuaded by the rest of the day which the nations had dedicated to Cronus. The same Abydenus also mentions the sending out of birds, which narrative the Greeks transferred to their Deucalion, as we learn from Plutarch. But also in the writings of Empolemus and Artabanus there existed a memory of a universal flood. Nor is there any other place to refer what Pliny said about the city of Joppa, that it is older than the flood: which is also reported by Josephus. But also in the New World, as it is called, traces of this anciently handed-down report have been found. Nor is the argument for this matter to be despised which Tertullian brings forward: shells in mountains most remote from the sea. But as for what some ask, if the flood was universal, whence did peoples arrive in that new world and remote islands, it is vain. For they posit that that new world is not connected by any strait that is easily crossed with Scythia, nor with the known islands in the North: which I will not say is now uncertain, but it is also refuted by strong arguments. But what is more credible than that the peoples of the north, increased by excessive fertility, poured themselves further and further into empty lands? For both their customs and the appearance of their bodies and their language agree partly with the Scythians, partly with the Germans. Regarding the islands, the observation of experts is not to be despised, that there is almost no island so remote to which a view does not lie open from some shore, and that they have the language of the nearest lands. And these things have been said in passing. For to pursue them more fully would be foreign to my purpose.

Latin:

Vers. 39. ἐκ ἔγνωσαν] לא ידע Hebræis sæpe est προσέχειν ut Ecclesiastæ IV. 17. Es. I. 3. ita sumitur hic γινώσκειν aliisque multis in locis, ut Luc. XIX. 44. Hebr. III. 10. Quo re- ferendum forte & illud quod est Rom. VII. 7. & Act. XXIII. 5. Huic supinitati oppositum est illud apud Lucam προσέ- χειν.

Καὶ ἦρεν ἅπαντας] ἦρεν est נשא Gen. VII. 23. ἅπαντας, omne humanum genus, τὸν ἀρχαῖον κόσμον ut Petrus loqui- tur, octo duntaxat hominibus exceptis, in quibus erat Noe. Plane enim illis assentiri non possum, qui genera- litatem hanc ad aliquam humani generis portionem re- stringunt. Nam od omne humanum genus hoc diluvium pertigisse magnum argumentum habemus omnium gen- tium memoriam quæ in id tempus definit. Diligentissi- mus omnis antiquitatis indagator Varro omne ævum in tria tempora dividebat, ἄδηλον, μυθικὸν, καὶ ἱστορικόν, ἄδηλον vocans quicquid prius erat magno Cataclysmo: Fabulo- sum quod proxime sequitur: historicum à Trojæ excidio. Citat Josephus Berosum rerum Chaldaicarum Scriptorem, Hieronymum Phœniciarum, Mnaseam quoque, & quem dixi Damascenum, qui omnes meminerint καὶ τῶ κατακλυ- σμῶ τότε, καὶ τῆς λάρνακος. Abydenus Noam Σείσιθρον vo- cat, eum qui ei imminentem cladem prædixerit κρόνον, ni- mirum quia Græci ita transferre folebant vocem orienta- lem אלון. Nam & Philo Byblius ὁ ἰλὸς. τῦτ᾽ ἐστιν ὁ κρόν@. Phœnices enim, Assyrii Armenii antiquitus eam stellam, quam Græci κρόνον vocant, maxime sunt venerati, quod al- tissimo orbe & præcipua potentia feratur, quod notat Ta- citus. A Judæis eundem coli multis persuasit otium diei quem τῷ κρόνῳ gentes dicaverant. Idem Abydenus emissa- rum quoque avium meminit, quam narrationem Græci ad Deucalionem suum transtulerunt, ut ex Plutarcho discimus. Sed & in Empoleuni & Artabani scriptis exstabat memoria universalis diluvii. Nec alio referendum quod Plinius de Joppe urbe dixit, diluvio esse antiquiorem: quod & à Jose- pho proditum est. Sed & in Novo qui dicitur orbe reperta sunt hujus famæ παλαιπαραδότε vestigia. Nec spernendum ejus rei argumentum affert Tertullianus conchas in remo- tissimis a mari montibus. Quod autem quidam quærunt, si universale diluvium fuit, unde in novum illum orbem, & remotas insulas populi pervenerint, vanum est. Ponunt e- nim novum illum orbem nullo freto quod facile transeca- tur cum Scythia, neque cum notis in Septentrione insulis connecti: quod non jam dicam incertum est, sed & validis argumentis refellitur. Quid autem credibilius, quam au- ctos nimia fœcunditate septentrionis populos in vacua se longius ac longius effudisse? nam & mores habitusque cor- porum & sermo partim cum Scythis, partim Germanis con- gruunt. De insulis vero haud contemnenda peritorum ob- servatio, nullam ferme esse adeo remotam ad quam non ex aliquo littore prospectus pateat, & linguam ipsis quæ pro- ximis terrarum. Et hæc quidem obiter dicta sunt. Nam fusius prosequi ab instituto alienum sit.

## 24:40
Vers. 40. Εἶτα ἀγρῷ] In which men are unrefined, whom the experts of the law called the people of the land out of contempt, and of whom they said, 'This crowd that does not know the law are cursed.' But Christ shows that neither an unrefined nature nor a despised condition hinders anyone from having access to the glory of heaven.

Ὁ εἷς παραλαμβάνεται] That is, he will be led out of common danger as if by the hand. For it is an allusion to the history of Lot, which Matthew omitted for the sake of brevity, but Luke expressed. See Genesis 19:16. Add Luke 21:36. These things, however, pertain to that separation of men which was made through the preaching of the Gospel, especially in those first 40 years. A visible sign of which was also the preservation of the Christians from the evils of the siege of Jerusalem.

Grotius takes these things to refer to the separation which was made through the preaching of the Gospel, especially in those first 40 years, which speak openly in this place about the separation that will be on the last day, when Christ will take the elect (John 17:24, leaving the wicked behind), whom the angels gather from all corners of the world, v. 31, where eternal punishment is denounced to hypocrites and infidels, v. 51. Which Grotius also explains wrongly as διχοτομήσει αὐτὸν: A brief expression, he says, for that which would be said, 'by cutting the house he will separate it.' For it is a question of the cutting in two of the unfaithful servant, not of the cutting in two of the house, and by that is denoted the infernal punishment of the infidels, joined with weeping and gnashing of teeth. It can indeed be said that the cutting in two of the servant is done by 'separating,' but that separation is from the beatific vision of God, and from the company of the holy angels and the elect in heaven, which will happen in the other life, not in this age. Therefore, it is taught in the immediately following parable what kind of separation this will be: namely, that it will be similar to that by which the foolish virgins are separated and excluded from the joys of the wedding; and it is explained what kind of vigilance is needed, so that we may not be separated from the elect. Where it is also to be observed that four parables are employed, by a different path, as Chrysostom says in Homily LXXIX on Matthew, leading us to the same point: 1. from the householder watching against the breaking in of a thief. 2. from the servants commanded to watchfully await the return of the Lord. 3. from the ten virgins, who were supposed to observe the coming of the bridegroom. 4. from the servants entrusted with talents and bound to trade. All of which look toward the final coming of Christ the Lord; in which all interpreters agree. Only this Grotius is singular: but with the whole context resisting him. Who nevertheless acknowledges that that γρηγορεῖτε is explained by the parable of the ten virgins, who met the coming bridegroom. Which is manifest from the following chapter XXV, v. 13. Moreover, that the coming there is designated for the assumption of the elect to eternal glory is confirmed most openly not only by that parable of the virgins, but also by the following parable, a twin to our present one about the faithful servants, v. 14 seqq. 17, and the description of the coming and the judicial process; nor does Grotius deny this.

Latin:

Vers. 40. Εἶτα ἀγρῷ] In quo rudes sunt homines, quos per comtemtum populum terræ vocabant legisperiti, & de quo dicebant, ὁ ὄχλ@ οὗτος ὁ μὴ γινώσκων τὸν νόμον ἐπικαλά- ρατοί εἰσι. At Christus ostendit neque rude ingenium ne- que despectam conditionem cuiquam obstare quo minus ad cœli gloriam aditus ei pateat.

Ὁ εἷς παραλαμβάνεται] Id est, velut apprehensa manu e- ducetur è communi periculo. Allusio enim est ad Lothi historiam, quam brevitatis causa omisit Matthæus, Lucas autem expressit. Vide Gen. XIX. 16. Adde Luc. XXI. 36. Hæc autem pertinent ad discretionem illam hominum quæ facta est per Evangelii sermonem, præsertim primis illis an- nis 40. Cujus aspectabile etiam signum fuit conservatio Christianorum à malis obsidii Hierosolymorum.

Ad discretionem hæc rapit Grotius, quæ facta sit per Evangelii sermonem, præsertim primis illis annis XL. quæ palam loquuntur hoc in loco, de discretione in novissima die futura, cùm electos assumet Christus (Johan. XVII. 24. relictis impro- bis) quos colligunt angeli ex omnibus plagis mundi v. 31. ubi hypocritis & infidelibus pœna æterna denunciatur, v. 51. Quam perperam iti- dem explicat Grotius διχοτομήσει αὐτὸν: Brevis, inquit, loquutio, pro eo, quod diceretur διχοτό- μων τὴν οἰκίαν ἀφοριεῖ αὐτὴν. Nam de διχο- τομίᾳ servi infidelis, non de διχοτομίᾳ domus agitur, & per illam pœna infidelium denotatur infernalis, cumque fletu & stridore dentium con- juncta. Dici quidem potest quod fiat τὸ διχοτο- μεῖν servi per ἀφορίζειν, sed separatio illa sit, à beatifico Dei conspectu, & sanctorum Angelorum, & electorum in cælis consortio, quæ in altera vi- ta continget, non in hoc seculo. Ideo docetur parabola proxime sequente, qualis hæc futura se- paratio sit: quod nempe similis sit futura ei, quæ virgines fatuæ separantur, & excluduntur à gau- diis nuptiarum; & explicatur quali vigilantia o- pus sit, ne ab electis separemur. Ubi etiam ob- servandum, quod quatuor adhibeantur parabolæ, diverso itinere, ut Chrysost. hom. LXXIX. in Matth. loquitur, eodem nos deducentes 1. à Patre- familias adversus furis irruptionem vigilante. 2. à servis reditum Domini vigilanter expectare jussis. 3. à decem virginibus, quæ debebant observare ad- ventum sponsi. 4. à servis talentis concreditis nego- tiari obstrictis. Quæ omnes adventum novissi- mum Christi Domini respiciunt; in quo omnes consentiunt interpretes. Solus hic Grotius sin- gularis est: sed repugnante toto contextu. Qui tamen agnoscit illud γρηγορεῖτε ἐν explicari parabo- la decem virginum, quæ sponso adventanti occurre- runt. Quod è cap. XXV. sequenti v. 13. manife- stum est. Adventum autem illic ad assumtionem electorum ad æternam gloriam designari, non tantum illa parabola de virginibus, sed etiam parabola sequens, nostræ præsenti de servis fide- libus gemella v. 14. seqq. 17. & descriptio adven- tus & processus judicialis apertissime confirmant; nec id diffitetur Grotius.

## 24:41
Vers. 41. Two women grinding at the mill] This was the work of maidservants, as we are taught in Exod. XI. 5 and Isa. XLVII. 2. Here again, the distinction of Christ's kingdom from earthly kingdoms is shown. For in the kingdoms of the world, women are removed from all civil or public offices, and servants much more so, as those who are said not even to have a person. But Christ receives women, even servants. οὐκ ἔνι δοῦλος, οὐδὲ ἐλεύθερος, οὐκ ἔνι ἄρσεν καὶ θῆλυ, Gal. III, 28. All are exempted from common destruction, to whom that will apply: ὅτι σὲ εἶδον δίκαιον ἐναντίον μου ἐν τῇ γενεᾷ ταύτῃ, Gen. VII. 1. which Philo paraphrases excellently at the end of book II, περὶ βίου Μωσέως.

Latin:

Vers. 41. Δύο ἀλήθουσαι ἐν τῷ μύλωνι] Erat hoc ancillarum, ut docemur Exod. XI. 5. & Esa. XLVII. 2. Hic rursus à Christo discrimen ostenditur regni sui à regnis terrenis. Nam in regnis mundi feminæ ab omnibus officiis civilibus vel publicis remotæ sunt, Servi vero multo magis, ut qui ne personam quidem habere dicantur. At Christus mulie- res etiam servas recipit. οὐκ ἔνι δοῦλος, οὐδὲ ἐλεύθερος, οὐκ ἔνι ἄρσεν καὶ θῆλυ, Gal. III, 28. omnes communi exitio exi- mentur, in quos illud quadrabit: ὅτι σὲ εἶδον δίκαιον ἐναντίον μου ἐν τῇ γενεᾷ ταύτῃ, Gen. VII. 1. quod egregie παραφράζει Phi- lo fine lib. II. περὶ βίου Μωσέως.

## 24:42
Vers. 42. Watch therefore] These things are said to all Christians. But that which follows in verse 45 adapts the general admonition particularly to the Apostles and other Pastors of the Church, which Luke teaches us in chapter XII. 41.

Latin:

Vers. 42. Γρηγορεῖτε οὖν] Hæc omnibus Christianis di- cuntur. Illud autem quod sequitur commate 45. gene- ralem admonitionem peculiariter Apostolis aliisque Ec- clesiæ Pastoribus accommodat, quod nos docet Lucas cap. XII. 41.

## 24:43
Vers. 43. If he had watched] It is easy, says Christ, to guard against the danger of a single and predetermined time. But because many dangers have an uncertain time, therefore they must always be feared, and always guarded against, lest a huge loss be received διὰ τὸ ἀπροσδόκητον.

Διορυγῆναι] Breaking through is attributed to a thief, Exod. XXII and Jerem. II. 34.

Latin:

Vers. 43. Εἰ ἐγρηγόρησεν ἂν] Facile est, inquit Christus, præ- cavere periculum unius ac præfiniti temporis. Sed quia pericula multa tempus habent incertum, ideo semper me- tuenda, semperque cavenda sunt, ne ingens damnum ac- cipiatur διὰ τὸ ἀπροσδόκητον.

Διορυγῆναι] Perfossio tribuitur furi, Exod. XXII. & Jerem. II. 34.

## 24:44
Vers. 44. He comes] That is, he can come unexpected unless you are always expecting him. ἔρχεται for ἔρχοιτο ἂν.

Latin:

Vers. 44. Ἔρχεται] Id est venire potest inexspectatus ni- si eum semper exspectetis. ἔρχεται pro ἔρχοιτο ἂν.

## 24:45
Vers. 45. Who then is] This is not an interrogative 'who' here, but a hypothetical one, as we have said elsewhere.

Over his household] He describes the office of a steward, that is, a dispenser: to which the office of pastors in the Church corresponds. See I Cor. IV. 1.

Latin:

Vers. 45. Τίς ἄρα ἐστὶν] Non est hic τίς interrogativum, sed ὑποθετικὸν, ut diximus alibi.

Ἐπὶ τῆς θεραπείας αὑτοῦ] Describit munus οἰκονόμου, id est, dispensatoris: cui munus pastorum in Ecclesia respon- det. Vide I. Cor. IV. 1.

## 24:47
Vers. 47. He will set him over all his possessions] From a dispenser he makes him a procurator: which is a greater honor. This process can be seen in the history of Joseph, Gen. XXXIX. For the Lord first set him over his house,

αὐτᾶ, ver. 4. then he entrusted all that he had into the hands of Joseph, ver. 6. Moreover, by this similitude is signified the highest honor which will be held for him. Compare Apocal. II. 26.

Latin:

Vers. 47. Ἐπὶ πᾶσι τοῖς ὑπάρχουσιν αὑτοῦ καταστήσει αὐτὸν] Ex dispensatione procuratorem facit: qui major honos. Hunc processum videre est in Josephi historia Gen. XXXIX. Nam Dominus primum κατέστησεν αὐτὸν ἐπὶ τῷ οἴκῳ αὑτοῦ,

αὐτᾶ, vers. 4. deinde ἐπέτρεψε πάντα ὅσα ἦν αὐτῷ εἰς χεῖρας Ἰωσὴφ, vers. 6. Cæterum hac similitudine significatur honos summus qui illi habebitur. Compara Apocal. II. 26.

## 24:48
Ver. 48. But if that evil servant says in his heart] The Greek interpreter retained the Hebraism אמר בלבו as also the LXX, Ps. XIV, and elsewhere, since it signifies nothing other than to think.

Χρονίζει] יאחר Abac. II. 3.

Latin:

Vers. 48. Ἐὰν δὲ εἴπῃ ὁ κακὸς δοῦλος ἐκεῖνος ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ αὐτῶ] Retinuit Græcus interpres Hebraismum אמר בלבו ut & LXX, Ps. XIV, & alibi, cum id nihil aliud significet quam cogitare.

Χρονίζει] יאחר Abac. II. 3.

## 24:49
Ver. 49. To beat his fellow servants] Christ indicates that there will not be lacking in the Church pastors who, either having themselves received the right of the sword, or having obtained those to whom the sword belongs as their own dependents, cruelly harass other pastors or Christians from the laity on account of a free rebuke of vices and false dogmas, or on account of differing opinions regarding certain less necessary and less explored dogmas. And they will do this especially those who, while they wish to seem to do everything for the sake of Christ, in reality do not serve Christ, but their own belly, minding earthly things, Rom. XVI. 18. Phil. III. 19. And indeed it happens naturally that those who profess piety for the sake of their own advantages implacably hate and even in every way infest those whom they see opposing their advantages: as we also noted when we dealt with the tares. How greatly this manner of acting displeases Christ, and how it will not go unpunished, is shown by what follows in verse 51, a fuller explanation of which must be sought from the Apocalypse.

Ἐσθίῃ δὲ καὶ πίνῃ] So many codices: so the Syriac: so the Latin, and some Greek interpreters. Wherefore this part seems to be the major one.

Latin:

Vers. 49. Τύπτειν τὼς συνδέλες] Indicat Christus non defuturos in Ecclesia pastores, qui, aut ipsi accepto gladii jure, aut eos quorum est gladius sibi nacti obnoxios, alios pastores aut de plebe Christianos ob libertam vitiorum falsorumque dogmatum reprehensionem, aut ob diversas de dogmatibus quibusdam minus necessariis minusque exploratis sententias, crudeliter divexent. Id autem facturos eos præcipue, qui, cum videri velint omnia facere Christi causa, revera non Christo serviant, sed ventri suo, τὰ ἐπίγεια φρονῦντες, Rom. XVI. 18. Phil. III. 19. Et sane naturaliter evenit, ut qui pietatem commodorum suorum causa profitentur implacabiliter oderint atque adeo omnibus modis infestent eos quos commodis suis adversari vident: ut & cum de zizaniis actum est annotavimus. Hæc autem agendi ratio quantopere Christo displiceat, & quam non sit impune abitura, ostendunt quæ sequuntur commate 51. quorum fusior explicatio ex Apocalypsi petenda est.

Ἐσθίῃ δὲ καὶ πίνῃ] Ita multi codices: ita Syrus: ita Latinus, & Græci interpretes nonnulli. Quare pars hæc major videtur.

## 24:51
Ver 51. Διχοτομήσει αὐτὸν] A brief expression, for what might be said: cutting the house in two, he will separate him. For διχοτομεῖν properly corresponds to the Hebrew חצה which Aquila translates with the word ἡμίσευσε, similar to this one of ours, Gen. XXXIII. 1. Explanations are to be sought from those things which are below in chapter XXV. 30.

Τὸ μέρος αὐτῶ] Such is that: fire and brimstone and the spirit of a tempest is the portion of their cup. Psal. XI. 6. likewise; this is the portion of a wicked man from the Lord, Job. XX. 29. For everywhere among the Hebrews מנה and חלק signify retribution.

Μετὰ τῶν ὑποκριτῶν] with the unbelievers, says Luke. It is credible that Christ said both, so that he might signify that the same punishments await those who had despised the Gospel, and those who had professed the faith but denied it by their deeds. I prefer to interpret ἀπίστως as incredulous rather than unfaithful, because what follows, there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth, proves that there is a silent transition to retribution such as we also had above in c. XIII. 42. and c. XXII. 13. and will have below in c. XXV. 30. in all of which places the epiphonema is the same.

Latin:

Vers 51. Διχοτομήσει αὐτὸν] Brevis locutio, pro eo quod diceretur διχοτομῶν τὴν οἰκίαν ἀφοριεῖ αὐτὸν. Nam διχοτομεῖν proprie respondet Hebræo חצה quod ἡμίσευσε voce simili huic nostræ vertit Aquila Gen. XXXIII. 1. Explicant petenda ex iis quæ infra cap. XXV. 30.

Τὸ μέρος αὐτῶ] Tale est illud: πῦρ καὶ θεῖον καὶ πνεῦμα καταιγίδος ἡ μερὶς τῦ ποτηρία αὐτῶν. Psal. XI. 6. item; αὕτη ἡ μερὶς ἀνθρώπω ἀσεβᾶς παρὰ κυρία, Job. XX. 29. Passim enim Hebræis מנה & חלק ἀνταπόδοσιν significant.

Μετὰ τῶν ὑποκριτῶν] μετὰ τῶν ἀπίστων, inquit Lucas. Credibile est utrumque Christum dixisse, ut significaret eadem supplicia manere eos qui Evangelium contemsissent, & eos qui fidem professi factis eam abnegassent. ἀπίστως malo incredulos quam infidos interpretari, quia quod sequitur, ἐκεῖ ἔσται ὁ κλαυθμὸς καὶ ὁ βρυγμὸς τῶν ὀδόντων probat tacitam esse transitionem ad ἀνταπόδοσιν qualem & supra habuimus c. XIII. 42. & c. XXII. 13. & infra habebimus c. XXV. 30. quibus omnibus in locis idem est ἐπιφώνημα.

## 25:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXV.

ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

A parable about ten virgins going to meet the Bridegroom, five foolish ones carrying lamps without oil, five prudent ones carrying lamps filled with oil, these being awakened at midnight by the arrival of the Bridegroom and meeting him, while it was not permitted for the others to hasten to the meeting on account of the lack of oil, whence the former came to the wedding, the latter remained excluded with the door shut. By this parable Jesus excites everyone to vigilance: and another is added about different servants, to whom the Lord had entrusted his talents, of whom one had gained five other talents with five, another two other two, the third had buried in the ground the talent which he had received: whence the former were set over many things on account of their faithfulness: but the latter, on account of his sloth, was deprived of his talent and cast out as a useless servant into outer darkness. Finally, Christ described the process of the final judgment, when, about to come in his glory and to separate the sheep from the goats, he is to admit to the inheritance of the kingdom those who showed works of mercy to his brothers, but is to adjudge to eternal fire those who denied them.

There are three parts: I. The parable of the five wise and five foolish virgins, to v. 13. II. The parable of the different servants to whom talents were entrusted by the Lord, to v. 30. III. The process of the final judgment, to v. 46.

PART I. The parable of the ten virgins.

Vers. 1. Ten virgins] These are the בתולות רעות in Psalm 45:14. The companions in the epithalamium of Theocritus, the virgin companions in Pindar's third Pythian ode. They went out] A prolepsis: for when they went to meet him is said below in v. 6, 7, 11.

To meet the bridegroom] It is not for nothing that both the Latin and the Syriac add 'and the bride.' And one would believe that Origen read it so if one were to attend diligently to his reading. One may suspect it was omitted by those who did not see how virgins, that is, the faithful, could be said to meet the bride, since they themselves are the Church, that is, the bride: which has troubled most Latin interpreters. But that should have moved no one. For in these comparisons, individual parts are not to be pressed, but the scope of the comparison is to be looked at: the rest are to be held as having the role of accessories. The scope is what Christ himself indicates with the words 'but watch,' namely that we ought always to be solicitous about rightly ordering our life, and, as Luke speaks, 'to take heed to ourselves.' But in order that it may be known that that 'and the bride' does not conflict with the nature of the narrative, as some think, it is to be noted that among the praised customs which the Jews received from the Fathers, this also was one, that they celebrated marriage not privately, but in the assembly of the pious with a blessing, the formulas of which exist in their own rituals: which, like many other institutions of the Jews, the ancient Christians imitated, Ignatius to Polycarp: 'It is necessary for those who marry and those who are married to make the union with the consent of the bishop, so that the marriage may be according to the law and not according to desire.' Tertullian in the book on modesty: 'Therefore among us, secret unions also, that is, not first professed before the Church, are in danger of being judged as adultery and fornication.' The same elsewhere: 'Whence shall I suffice to narrate the happiness of that marriage which the Church conciliates and the oblation confirms.' Evaristus to the African Bishops: 'Marriage does not become legitimate otherwise, unless the wife is sought from those who seem to have authority over the woman herself, and by whom she is guarded, and is betrothed by parents and by closer relatives, and is endowed by laws, and in its own time is blessed by the Priest sacerdotally, as is the custom, with prayers and oblations.' Before this blessing, it was held as a sin by both Jews and Christians for a bridegroom to touch a bride by right of a spouse. To this blessing the bridegroom was led by elderly men, the bride by matrons. As they returned from the blessing, young men and maidens went to meet them, the sons and daughters of the bridechamber: of whom we spoke at the ninth chapter. Then the nuptial banquet was celebrated: This parable alludes to Psalm 45 and the Song of Songs.

Therefore, it is suspected that that 'to meet the bridegroom' was omitted: but the original Greek text is wrongly corrected from the Syriac and Latin text, whose codices consistently omit that mention of the bride; whose reading is also not found among the Greek Fathers, Basil in moral. cap. V, Chrysostom, Euthymius, Theophylact in this place. Add that afterwards it is not said: 'Behold the bridegroom and the bride are coming,' but, 'Behold the bridegroom comes,' and that, as Jansenius notes, according to the custom received by the Jews, they were not accustomed to have the bride meet the virgins together with the bridegroom, but the bride sat at home, awaiting the bridegroom, to whom the virgins went out to meet him.

Latin:

CAPUT XXV.

ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Parabola de decem virginibus Sponso obviam euntibus, quinque fatuis lampades sine oleo, quinque prudentibus lampades oleo repletas gestantibus, hisce media nocte adventu Sponsi excitatis eidem occurrentibus, quum illis ob olei defectum in occursum properare non liceret, unde illæ ad nuptias venere, hæ occlusa janua exclusæ mansere. Qua parabola omnes excitat Jesus ad vigilantiam: additaque alia de servis diversis, quibus talenta sua Dominus crediderat, quorum unus quinque talentis alia quinque, alter duobus alia duo lucratus erat, tertius talentum quod acceperat, in terram defoderat: unde illi ob fidem super multa constituti: hic vero ob desidiam talento suo privatus & ceu inutilis servus in exteriores tenebras projectus est. Postremo processum extremi judicii descripsit Christus, cum adventurus in gloria sua, ovesque ab hædis separaturus, illos ad hereditatem regni admissurus est, qui opera misericordiæ fratribus suis exhibuere, hos bcs autem qui ea denegarunt, æterno igni ad- judicaturus est.

Partes tres sunt: I. Parabola de quinque pru- dentibus & quinque fatuis virginibus, ad v. 13. II. Parabola de servis diversis quibus talenta à Domino concredita, ad v. 30. III. Processus ju- dicii novissimi, ad v. 46.

PARS I. Parabola de decem virginibus.

Vers. 1. Δέκα παρθένοις] Hæ sunt בתולות רעות in Psalmo XLV. 14. Συνανάγεραι in Epithalamio Theocriti, παρθένοι ἑταῖραι Pindaro tertia ode Pythiorum. Ἐξῆλθον] πρόληψις: nam quando in occursum iverint in- fra dicitur v. 6. 7. 11.

Εἰς ἀπάντησιν τῷ νυμφίῳ] Non de nihilo est quod & Lati- nus & Syrus addunt καὶ νυμφῆς. Atque ita legisse Origenem credet si quis ejus lectioni diligenter attenderit. Suspicari licet omissum ab his qui non videbant quomodo virgines, id est, fideles, dicerentur sponsæ occurrere, cum ipsi sint Ecclesia, id est sponsa: quod plerosque Latinos interpretes terfit. Sed id neminem movere debuit. Nam in his com- parationibus non sunt premendæ partes singulæ, sed intuen- dus scopus comparationis: cætera habenda accessionum vi- ce. Scopus est quem Christus ipse indicat verbis γρηγορεῖτε δὲ, debere nos scilicet semper sollicitos esse de vita recte in- stituenda, &, ut Lucas loquitur, προσέχειν ἑαυτοῖς. Ut au- tem sciatur illud κὶ νυμφῆς non pugnare cum natura narra- tionis, ut quidam existimant, notandum est inter laudatos mores quos à Patribus Judæi acceperunt, etiam hunc fuis- se, ut matrimonium non privatim, sed in piorum conventu celebrarent μετ' εὐλογίας, cujus formulæ exstant in ipso- rum ritualibus: quod, ut multa alia Judæorum instituta, imitati sunt Christiani veteres, Ignatius ad Polycarpum: πρέπει δὲ τοῖς γαμῦσι καὶ ταῖς γαμέσαις μετὰ γνώμης τῷ ἐπισκό- πε τὴν ἕνωσιν ποιεῖσθαι, ἵνα ὁ γάμος ᾖ κατὰ νόμον κὶ μὴ κατ' ἐπιθυμίαν. Tertullianus libro de pudicitia: Ideo apud nos occultæ quoque conjunctiones, id est non prius apud Ecclesiam professæ, juxta mœchiam & fornicationem judicari periclitan- tur. Idem alibi: Unde sufficiam ad enarrandam felicitatem ejus matrimonii quod Ecclesia conciliat & confirmat oblatio. Evaristus ad Africanos Episcopos: Aliter legitimum non fit conjugium, nisi ab his qui super ipsam fæminam dominatio- nem habere videntur, & à quibus custoditur, uxor petatur, & à parentibus & à propinquioribus sponsetur, & legibus dotetur, & suo tempore sacerdotaliter, ut mos est, cum precibus & obla- tionibus à Sacerdote benedicatur. Ante hanc εὐλογίαν spon- sam sponso conjugis jure attingere nefas & Judæis & Chri- stianis habitum. Ad hanc εὐλογίαν deducebatur sponsus à viris grandævis, sponsa à matronis. Redeuntibus ἀπὸ τῆς εὐλογίας obviam procedebant juvenes & puellæ, οἱ ὑοὶ κὶ αἱ θυγατέρες τῶ νυμφῶν: de quibus diximus ad caput nonum. Deinde celebrabantur convivium nuptiale: Alludit hæc parabola ad Ps. XLV. & Canticum Canticorum.

Suspicatur ergo illa εἰς ἀπάντησιν τῷ νυμφίῳ o- missa esse: sed è Syro & Latino textu perperam corrigitur textus Græcus originalis, cujus Codices consentienter omittunt illam sponsæ mentionem; cujus etiam lectio non reperitur apud Patres Græ- cos, Basilium in moral. cap. V. Chrysostomum, Eu- thymium, Theophylactum in h. l. Adde quod postea non dicatur: Ecce sponsus & sponsa veniunt: sed, Ecce Sponsus venit, quodque notante Janse- nio, more Judæis recepto, non consueverint sponsa simul cum sponso virginibus occurrere, sed sponsa domi sederit, sponsum operiens, cui in occursum virgines processerint.

## 25:3
Vers. 3. Lamps] These oil lamps seem to have served the same use in Judea that pine or thorn torches did in Rome.

Latin:

Vers. 3. Λαμπάδας] Lampades istæ oleariæ eundem u- sum in Judæa præstitisse videntur, quem Romæ pineæ aut spineæ faces.

## 25:4
Vers. 4. In the vessels] This word extends very widely, as does the other, 'skeuos,' by which the Hebrew 'keli' is rendered.

Latin:

Vers. 4. Ἐν τοῖς ἀγγείοις] Latissime patet hæc vox, ut & altera σκεῦος, per quam redditur Hebræum כלי.

## 25:5
Vers. 5. They all slumbered and slept] Even the wise ones: which is not added in vain: 'for in many things we all offend' James 3:2, especially in the beginnings of faith. Paul to the Romans 13:11, 'It is high time for us to awake out of sleep: for now is our salvation nearer than when we believed,' that is, than when we first began to believe and gave our name to Christ. Which passage explains this.

Latin:

Vers. 5. Ἐνύταξαν πᾶσαι κὶ ἐκάθευδον] Etiam αἱ φρόνιμοι: quod non frustra est additum: πολλὰ γὰρ πταίομεν ἅ- παντες Jac. III. 2. præsertim in fidei initiis. Paulus ad Rom. ΧΙΙΙ. 11. ὥρα ἡμᾶς ἤδη ἐξ ὕπνε ἐγερθῆναι· νῦν γὰρ ἐγγύτερον ἡμῶν ἡ σωτηρία ἢ ὅτε ἐπιστεύσαμεν, id est, quam cum primum cre- dere cœpimus & Christo nomen dedimus. Qui locus hunc explicat.

## 25:6
Ver. 6. At midnight] Later than usual: therefore 'while the bridegroom tarried' preceded it. Otherwise, that it was a most ancient custom for the bride to be led by the new husband at night, and that from this torches remained in weddings, is noted by Servius on Eclogues VIII.

A cry was made] A cry is heard more widely at night, as in Exod. XII. 30.

Latin:

Vers. 6. Μέσης δὲ νυκτὸς] Serius quam pro more: ideo præcessit χρονίζοντος δὲ τοῦ νυμφίου. Alioqui ut nocte du- ceretur sponsa à novo marito moris fuisse antiquissimi, at- que ex eo mansisse in nuptiis faces, notatum Servio ad Ecclef. VIII.

Κραυγὴ γέγονεν] Clamor nocte latius auditur, ut Exod. XII. 30.

## 25:7
Ver. 7. They trimmed] הטיב Exod. XXX. 8. where it treats of the lamps as it does here. The Greeks there translate it ἐπισκευάζειν: elsewhere κοσμεῖν, as in 2 Kings IX. 30.

Latin:

Vers. 7. Ἐκόσμησαν] הטיב Exod. XXX. 8. ubi de lych- nis ut hic agitur. Græci ibi ἐπισκευάζειν vertunt: alibi κοσ- μεῖν, ut 2. Reg. IX. 30.

## 25:8
Ver. 8. our lamps are going out] Which is a sacrilege in the lamps of the temple. Exod. XXVII. 20. The mystical sense is with Paul: 'quench not the Spirit' 1 Thess. V. 19. For the Spirit is oil, Heb. I. 9; 1 John II. 20, 27. See also Job XIX. 6, ch. XXI. 17.

Latin:

Vers. 8. αἱ λαμπάδες ἡμῶν σβέννυνται] Quod in lucernis templi nefas. Exod. XXVII. 20. Sensus mysticus apud Paulum: τὸ πνεῦμα μὴ σβέννυτε 1. Thess. V. 19. Spiritus enim oleum Hebr. I. 9. 1. Joh. II. 20. 27. Vide & Jo- bium XIX. 6. c. XXI. 17.

## 25:9
Ver. 9. Lest,] The correct and undoubted reading is an invocation of refusal, the reason for which is given. Such is that in Gen. XX. 11, 'for I said, lest there be no fear of God in this place.' For it is missing, 'I will conceal that Sarah is my wife.' Thus also it has been observed above that ὅτι is accustomed to be placed with the suppression of that for which the reason is given.

Latin:

Vers. 9. Μήποτε,] Recta lectio & haud dubia ἔκκλησις re- cusationis cujus ratio redditur. Tale est illud Gen. XX. 11. εἶπα γάρ, μήποτε ἐκ ἔστι θεοσέβεια ἐν τῷ τόπῳ τούτῳ. Deest enim, dissimulabo Saram esse uxorem meam. Sic & ὅτι po- ni solere cum subricentia ejus cujus ratio redditur, obser- vatum est supra.

## 25:12
Ver. 12. I know you not] See above ch. VII. 29.

Latin:

Vers. 12. ἐκ οἶδα ὑμᾶς] Vid. supra c. VII. 29.

## 25:13
Ver. 13. nor the hour] It is an interpretation which not all Greek codices add here, 'wherein the Son of man cometh,' unknown to the Syriac, Latin, and Arabic.

But that interpretation is altogether required for the integrity of the sense, and it is found in the better Greek codices, as we have observed in the S. Critic.

PART II. The parable concerning the different servants, to whom the Lord entrusted his talents.

Latin:

Vers. 13. ἐδὲ τὴν ὥραν] Interpretamentum est quod hic Græci codices non omnes adjiciunt ἐν ᾗ ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ἔρχεται, ignoratum Syro, Latino, Arabi.

Id vero interpretamentum omnino ad sensus integritatem requiritur, & in melioribus Codi- cibus Græcis repertum est, uti in Critico S. obser- vavimus.

PARS II. Parabola de diversis servis, quibus Domi- nus talenta sua concrededit.

## 25:14
Ver. 14. For as] An anantapodoton, such as grammarians observe in Homer in that passage: 'But if the great-hearted Achaeans shall give a prize.' Of which kind there are many in Paul, as Jerome noted. Very similar to this is that in Mark XIII. 34. Furthermore, both the time and occasion of the telling, and the circumstances of the narrative, persuade me that this is not the same history which is appended to the banquet of Zacchaeus in Luke. And what prevents Christ from having often illustrated very similar matters with comparisons that are similar rather than the same? Since, however, the gifts which we receive through Christ are some common, such as the doctrine of the Gospel and those things which follow it, but others are peculiar, such as the 'gifts of ministries or of workings,' which Christ distributed to whom he wished after his ascension into the heavenly palace, it seems to me that Christ, still pursuing his course, looked to the former, but being now closer to death, looked to the latter. Therefore in Luke they are entrusted as equal: here as unequal. See Paul Rom. XII. 6; 1 Cor. XII. 7, 11, 29; Ephes. IV. 11.

But why restrict these to peculiar gifts, or those to common gifts? Why to the ministering ones only, and not indeed to the sanctifying ones? Why to the Doctors of the word only, and not to other believers? All Christians are servants, says Theophilus of Antioch, lib. I. Allegor. For to all he gave some talent, i.e., grace, with which they might trade. We are all called by a holy calling, we all ought to be servants of GOD, Rom. VI. 12. He entrusted his gifts and talents to all as stewards of the ποικίλης χάριτος Θεοῦ 1. Petr. IV. 10. so that we might trade with them for the glory of God and the salvation of our neighbor. Conf. 2. Cor. VI. 1. Ebr. XII. 15. And therefore Basil in the Catena of Nicetas: I think that every gift of God is called a talent, so that everyone, whatever grace he has been proved to have from GOD, may multiply it, brought forth for the beneficence and utility of many: for there is no one who is not a participant in the kindness of God, but he who keeps whatever grace of God he has for his own enjoyment, and does not do good to others, is condemned as one hiding a talent: for it is necessary to communicate grace to him who has need. Auctor. Imperf. Oper. homil. LIII. Just as this bodily money, if it is in a purse, is always enclosed; but if it has been moved from hand to hand, it is multiplied by the very use, whence usury is called from use: so also the faith of Christ, if indeed it is held idle in the heart, not only remains what it was, but is even diminished in idleness, and becomes sluggish and slothful, and gradually, through carnal acts, is emptied and goes to nothing. But if it has been exercised by the Scriptures and stirred up by constant conversations, and quickened by good works (demonstrated alive, Jac. II. 18.), I say it will not only be multiplied, but will never cease to grow as long as a man lives. Cons. B. Gerhard. Harmon. Evang. P. II. pag. 871. Chrysostom homil. LXXIX. on Matthew: Let us help our neighbor with money, study, authority, and by whatever means we can, etc. Let no one say to himself, since I have one talent, I can accomplish nothing; you can surely be proved by one thing alone, etc. Nothing is more pleasing to God than that you should contribute your whole life to the common good. Therefore God has adorned us with reason and speech, has granted us mind and talent, has given us hands, feet, and the strength of the body, so that with all these we may protect both ourselves and our neighbors. Theophylactus in h. l. He who not only benefits himself, whether he has prudence, or riches, or power and authority among Kings, or any other art or faculty, but also wishes to benefit others, he doubles what has been given to him. And further: He who digs a talent into the earth is he who has care only for his own utility, and not that of others. If you see a man of good mind and studious, who abuses his talent for negotiations, deceits, and earthly works, of him you should say that he has buried his talent under the earth, that is, in earthly works. Cons. Eccl. XX. 32.

Τὰ ὑπάρχοντα αὐτω̃] הֹונוֹ is thus translated in Prov. VI. 31. chap. XI. 4.

Latin:

Vers. 14. ὥσπερ γὰρ] Ἀνανταπόδοτον quale in Homero observant Grammatici illo loco: Ἀλλ' εἰ μὲν δώσουσι γέρας μεγάθυμοι Ἀχαιοί· Cujus generis in Paulo sunt multa, ut notavit Hieronymus. Simillimum huic est apud Marcum XIII. 34. Cæterum & narrandi tempus atque occasio, & circumstantiæ narratio- nis multum differentes persuadent mihi hanc non esse ean- dem historiam quæ apud Lucam Zacchæi convivio subtexi- tur. Et quid vetat quominus Christus sæpe res multum similes comparationibus similibus magis quam iisdem il- lustraverit? cum vero dona quæ per Christum accipimus, alia sunt communia, ut doctrina Evangelii & quæ eam con- sequuntur, alia vero peculiaria qualia sunt τὰ χαρίσματα τῶν διακονιῶν ὴ τῶν ἐνεργημάτων, quæ post ascensum in cæ- lestem regiam Christus quibus voluit distribuit, videtur mi- hi Christus cursum adhuc suum peragens illa, morti vero jam propior hæc spectasse. Ideo apud Lucam credita sunt æqualia: hic inæqualia. Vide Paulum Rom. XII. 6. 1. Cor. XII. 7. 11. 29. Ephes. IV. 11.

Cur vero ad dona peculiaria hæc restringen- da, aut illa ad communia dona? Cur ad mini- strantia tantum, non vero ad sanctificantia? Cur ad Doctores tantum verbi, non ad alios fide- les? Servi sunt omnes Christiani, inquit Theo- philus Antiochenus lib. I. Allegor. Omnibus enim aliquod talentum dedit, h. e. gratiam, qua negotiarentur. Omnes sumus vocati sancta vo- catione, omnes servi DEI esse debemus, Rom. VI. 12. omnibus sua dona & ta- lenta credidit ceu dispensatoribus ποικίλης χάρι- τος Θεοῦ 1. Petr. IV. 10. ut iis ad Dei gloriam, & proximi salutem negotiemur. Conf. 2. Cor. VI. 1. Ebr. XII. 15. Ideoque Basilius in Catena Nicetæ: Talentum dici existimo, omne Dei donum, ut u- nusquisque quamcunque gratiam à DEO habere probatus fuerit, eam multiplicet ad beneficentiam ac utilitatem plurium prolatam: nemo enim est qui non sit particeps benignitatis Dei, qui vero qua- lemcunque tandem Dei gratiam apud seipsum in sui ipsius fruitionem detinet, & aliis non benefacit, velut occultans quis talentum condemnetur: ne- cessarium quippe est, communicare gratiam ei cui opus est. Auctor. Imperf. Oper. homil. LIII. Sicut pecunia hæc corporalis, si sit in sacculo, in- clusa ipsa est semper: si autem fuerit agitata de ma- nu in manum, usu ipso multiplicatur, unde usura dicitur ab usu: sic & fides Christi, si quidem otiosa teneatur in corde, non solum ipsa manet, qua fuit, sed adhuc minoratur in otio, & torpescit & segnis ef- ficitur, & paulatim per actus carnales exinanita ad nihilum vadit. Si autem exercitata fuerit Scriptu- ris & locutionibus assiduis suscitata, operibus bonis vivificata (viva demonstrata Jac. II. 18.) non solum dico multiplicabitur, sed nunquam desinet crescere, donec vivet homo. Cons. B. Gerhard. Harmon.Evang. P. II. pag. 871. Chrysostomus homil. LXXIX. in Matthæum: Pecunia, studio, autoritate & quibuscunque possumus modis, proxi- mum adjuvemus, &c. Nemo secum dicat, cum unum talentum habeam, nihil possum efficere; po- tes profecto ex una re sola comprobari &c. Nulla res Deo gratior, quam ut universam vitam ad com- mune commodum conferas. Idcirco ratione atque oratione nos Deus decoravit, mentem atque ingenium concessit, manus, pedes, vires corporis dedit, ut his omnibus & nos ipsos & proximos tutemur. Theophylactus in h. l. Qui non solum sibi prodest, sive prudentiam habeat, sive divitias, sive poten- tiam & autoritatem apud Reges, sive quamcunque aliam vel artem, vel facultatem, sed & aliis vult prodesse, is duplicat quod sibi datum est. Et por- ro: Qui talentum fodit in terram, is est, qui sua tantum utilitatis curam habet, & non aliorum. Si bonæ mentis & studiosum hominem videris, qui ingenio suo ad negotiationes, dolos & terrena o- pera abutitur, de illo dicas quod defoderit talentum suum sub terra, id est, in terrena opera. Cons. Eccl. XX. 32.

Τὰ ὑπάρχοντα αὐτω̃] הֹונוֹ sic vertitur Prov. VI. 31. cap. XI. 4.

## 25:15
Vers. 15. Κατὰ τὴν ἰδίαν δύναμιν] This pertains to the completion of the parable: nor does it require a specific application in the simile. For although I would not deny that in the calling to functions God sometimes looks at what is present in human talent before that calling, yet that this is not perpetual, even Jeremiah alone might prove.

Latin:

Vers. 15. Κατὰ τὴν ἰδίαν δύναμιν] Hoc ad apologi com- plementum pertinet: neque propriam in similitudi- ne applicationem desiderat. Quanquam enim negare nolim in vocatione ad functiones Deum interdum spe- ctare id quod ante eam vocationem inest humano inge- nio, id tamen non esse perpetuum, vel unus Jeremias evincat.

## 25:16
Vers. 16. Εἰργάσατο ἐν αὐτοι̃ς] The Greeks would say ἐργάζεσθαι αὐτοι̃ς or ἀπ᾽ αὐτω̃ν, as ἀφ᾽ ὕψας ἐργάζεσθαι to make gain by the body. ἐργάζεσθαι therefore is sufficiently Greek here. But that ἐν is Hellenistic, quite frequent in that signification which the Latins express by the sixth case.

Ἐποίησεν] It is a Latinism: for most say to make money: Sallust even says to do it. To do a thing is most customary. Among the ancient Greeks I do not know if that kind of speaking is to be found. Therefore by some the interpretation ἐκέρδησεν has been substituted.

Latin:

Vers. 16. Εἰργάσατο ἐν αὐτοι̃ς] Græci dicerent ἐργάζεσθαι αὐτοι̃ς aut ἀπ᾽ αὐτω̃ν, ut ἀφ᾽ ὕψας ἐργάζεσθαι quæstum corpore facere. ἐργάζεσθαι ergo hic satis Græcum est. Sed illud ἐν Hellenisticum, frequens admodum in ea significatione, quam Latini casu sexto exprimunt.

Ἐποίησεν] Latinismus est: nam pecuniam conficere plerique dicunt: Sallustius etiam facere. Rem facere usi- tatissimum est. Apud Græcos veteres nescio an id loquen- di genus sit reperire. Ideo à quibusdam substitutum est interpretamentum ἐκέρδησεν.

## 25:18
Vers. 18. ὤρυξεν ἐν τη̃ γη̃] Thus in Latin he is said to brood over buried gold who keeps useless money. And among the Hebrew wise man, hidden wisdom and an invisible treasure are compared, Eccl. XX. 31.

Latin:
