Vers. 18. ὤρυξεν ἐν τη̃ γη̃] Ita Latinis defosso auro incu- bare dicitur, qui inutilem pecuniam detinet. Et apud sa- pientem Hebræum comparantur σοφία κεκρυμμένη καὶ θησαυ- ρὸς ἀφανὴς, Eccl. XX. 31.

## 25:20
Vers. 20. Ἐκέρδησα ἐπ᾿ αὐτοι̃ς] Above the capital: wherefore the Latin translator very well used 'super lucratus sum' (gained over) here.

Latin:

Vers. 20. Ἐκέρδησα ἐπ᾿ αὐτοι̃ς] Supra sortem: quare La- tinus optime hic super lucratus sum.

## 25:21
Vers. 21. Εὖ], Of one praising, as also εὖγε, which because the Latins also use in the same sense, the Latin translator prudently placed here. Otherwise, he could have translated it 'Macte', or 'Bonum factum', or 'Bene habet'.

Ἐπ᾿ ὀλίγα η̃ς πιϲτὸς] For how small are the services even of the Apostles and martyrs, if they are compared with such a reward?

I will set you over many things] Concerning Cyrus the Younger, Xenophon narrates thus: 'And if he saw anyone being a capable manager according to justice, and both improving the land over which he ruled and making it productive, he would never take anything away from him, but would even add more to him.' The same in the Oeconomicus, concerning the King of the Persians: 'And whoever of the rulers he perceives providing for the land to be inhabited, and the earth to be active and full of the trees which each bears and of fruits, to these he adds other land.'

Into the joy of your lord] That is, be a partaker of your master's joy. A partaker of the consolation, 2 Corinthians 1:7. Reigning together, 2 Timothy 2:12. A tacit connection vividly with the parable, as also in the opposite part below verse 30, of the household, in

It is a Hebraism to use μετέχειν, as in εἰ εἰσελεύσονται εἰς τὴν κατάπαυσίν μου Ps. XCV. 11. Hebr. III. 11. χαρὰ שִׂמְחָה עוֹלָם eternal joy, Is. LXI. 7.

Latin:

Vers. 21. Εὖ], Laudantis, ut & εὖγε, quod quia Latini quoque eodem sensu usurpant, prudenter hic posuit Lati- nus Interpres. Alioqui Macte, aut Bonum factum, aut Be- ne habet, potuerat vertere.

Ἐπ᾿ ὀλίγα η̃ς πιϲτὸς] Quantilla enim sunt obsequia etiam Apostolorum & martyrum, si cum tanto præmio compa- rentur?

Ἐπὶ πολλω̃ν σε καταστήσω] De Cyro juniore sic narrat Xe- nophon: Εἰ δέ τινα ὁρῴη δεινὸν ὄντα οἰκόνομον ἐκ του̃ δικαίου, καὶ κατασκευάζοντά τε ἡ̃ς ἄρχοι χώρας καὶ προϲόδους ποιου̃ντα, οὐδένα ἂν πώποτε ἀφείλατο, ἀλλὰ καὶ πλείω προσεδίδου. Idem Oeco- nomico, de Rege Persarum, καὶ ὃς μὲν αἰϲθάνηται τω̃ν ἀρχόν- των συνοικουμένην τε τὴν χώραν παρεχομένους καὶ ἐνεργὸν οὐ̃σαν τὴν γη̃ν καὶ πλήρη δενδρων τε ὡ̃ν ἑκάση φέρει καὶ καρπω̃ν, τούτοις μὲν χώραν τὴν ἄλλην προϲτίθησι.

Εἰς τὴν χαρὰν του̃ κυρίου σου] Id est, particeps esto herilis gaudii. κοινωνὸς τη̃ς παρακλήσεως 2. Corinth. I. 7. συμ- βασιλεύων 2. Tim. II. 12. Tacita connexio ἐκτυπωδω̃ς cum apologo, ut & in opposita parte infra vers. 30. οἰκίσεως, in

Hebraïsmo est μετέχειν, ut εἰ εἰσελεύσονται εἰς τὴν κατάπαυσίν μου Ps. XCV. 11. Hebr. III. 11. χαρὰ שִׂמְחָה עוֹלָם εὐ- φροσύνη αἰώνιος, Ef. LXI. 7.

## 25:22
Vers. 22. He said to him] Christ does not weigh the works themselves, for the doing of which not everyone has small, not the same amount of time, not equal opportunity, but faithful zeal. And so often, In tenui labor, at tenuis non gloria (The labor is slight, but the glory is not slight). Justin in Apology II says that everyone will be required to give an account to God in proportion to the powers he has received.

Chrysostom explains this in Homily XLI on Genesis: why indeed the same praise falls to him who had gained five and to him who had gained two, because it was not the negligence of the one or the diligence of the other that caused the increase or decrease of gain, but the quantity of what was entrusted; for as far as diligence is concerned, both were equal, and therefore they obtained the same honor, and so the same sentence is passed for both, because in proportion to the gifts, the industry in trading and gaining was equal. Furthermore, Eucherius rightly says in his homily on the Nativity of a Confessor: Although all will be blessed, they will not all be equal; which is indeed signified by the fact that some are said to be set over ten, others over five cities.

Latin:

Vers. 22. ἔφη αὐτῷ] Non opera ipsa ponderat Christus ad quæ facienda non omnibus parvis, non temporis tan- tundem, non æqua occasio, sed fidele studium. Itaque sæ- pe, In tenui labor, at tenuis non gloria. Justinus Apologetico II. unumquemque ait πρὸς ἀναλογίαν ὧν ἔλαβε δυνάμεων παρὰ Θεοῦ λόγον αἰτηθήσεσθαι.

Explicat id Chrysostomus hom. XLI. in Ge- nes. cur nempe illi qui quinque lucratus erat, & il- li qui duo eadem laus obtingat, quia augmentatio- nem, vel imminutionem lucri non vel hujus ne- gligentia, vel illius diligentia fecit, sed concredi- torum quantitas; quod enim diligentiam attinet, ambo pares fuerunt, proinde & eundem honorem nacti sunt, adeoque eadem pro utroque fertur sen- tentia, quia pro ratione donorum in negotiando & lucrando par fuit industria. De cætero recte Eucherius homil. in Natal. un. Confess. Quamvis omnes beati erunt, non tamen omnes æquales e- runt; quod quidem in eo significatur, quod alii supra decem, alii supra quinque civitates consti- tuti dicuntur.

## 25:24
Vers. 24. He who had the one talent] In him to whom the least had been entrusted, Christ set an example of negligence, so that no one might hope to be excused from all labor because he had not received extraordinary gifts. For more will be required of him to whom more has been given, as Luke says. Therefore, he who received less does not owe nothing in fruits, but he owes less.

σκληρὸς] A hard and harsh man, like that one regarding the steward. Cicero called men harsh and unjust to everyone. And the following words show that he is indicated who is not only unhelpful, but also greedy.

Θερίζων ὅπου οὐκ ἔσπειρας (Reaping where you did not sow)] This is a proverb also among the Latins: as you sow, so shall you reap. Cic. de Oratore II. See also John IV. 37 and what is noted there.

Latin:

Vers. 24. ὁ τὸ ἕν τάλαντον] In eo cui minimum erat con- creditum negligentiæ exemplum posuit Christus, ne quis speraret excusatum se iri ab omni labore ideo quod non eximia dona accepisset. Plus videlicet exigetur ab eo cui plus datum est, ut ait Lucas. Non igitur nihil fructuum debet, qui minus accepit, sed minus debet.

σκληρὸς] Homo durus & asper, ut ille de procuratore. Asperos & omnibus iniquos dixit Cicero. Et sequentia ostendunt indicari eum qui non modo sit ἀνεπιβοήθητος, sed & πλεονέκτης.

Θερίζων ὅπου οὐκ ἔσπειρας] Proverbium est etiam apud Latinos: ut sementem facies, ita metes. Cic. de Oratore II. Vide & Joh. IV. 37. & quæ ibi notata.

## 25:25
Vers. 25. You have what is yours] Thus above, ἆρον τὸ σὸν (take what is yours), ch. XX. 14. A formula of one professing that he owes nothing more.

Latin:

Vers. 25. ἔχεις τὸ σόν] Ita supra ἆρον τὸ σὸν c. XX. 14. For- mula nihil ultra debere se profitentis.

## 25:26
Vers. 26. ὀκνηρὲ (slothful)] Thus the LXX are accustomed to translate the Hebrew עָצֵל, as in Proverbs several times. In Latin, one might translate it as 'idler': for that is what the Romans called slaves who did not perform their duty.

Jerome on this passage: He is called a wicked servant because he brings a calumny against his Master, and slothful because he did not want to double the talent, so that he is condemned in the one for pride, in the other for negligence. Bede on chapter XIX of Luke: He is called a worthless servant because he is slothful and sluggish in conducting business, and insolent and proud in accusing the judgment of the Master.

ᾔδεις (You knew)] A figure which they call concession. Be it as you say, you knew me to be harsh and demanding more than is fair: all the more reason you should have taken care not to defraud me of the fruit of my property.

Latin:

Vers. 26. ὀκνηρὲ] Ita solent transferre LXX. Hebræorum עָצֵל ut in Proverbiis aliquoties. Latine vertere liceat cessator: ita enim Romani vocabant servos officium non facientes,

Hieronymus in h. l. Servus malus appellatur, quia calumniam Domino facit, piger, quia noluit talentum duplicare, ut in altero superbiæ, in alte- ro negligentiæ condemnetur. Beda in cap. XIX. Lucæ: Servus nequam vocatur quia piger ac de- fes est ad exercendum negotium, & procax ac su- perbus ad accusandum Domini judicium.

ᾔδεις] Figura quam συγχώρησιν vocant. Esto ut dicis, noras me asperum & plus æquo petentem: tanto magis curandum tibi fuit ne me rei mei fructu fraudares.

## 25:27
Vers. 27. To the bankers] Do not say that you could not find those who had need of money. Bankers take money from everyone at interest: Plautus: I will calculate the little account, how much silver I might have with the banker.

ἐγὼ ἐκομισάμην ἂν τὸ ἐμὸν σὺν τόκῳ (I would have received my own with interest)] ἐκομισάμην here is ἦλθον κομιζόμενος, I would have gone to receive, that is, I would have exacted, as Luke says, ἔπραξα, and the Syriac in this place. The sense is: There is also no reason for you to plead danger in investing the money: it was mine; I would have exacted it not at your risk, but at my own. For those who administer the property of others are safe whenever they entrust it to those whose credit is publicly trusted. Thus also our Lord: 'He will not condemn a steward for himself, if he knows him, because he knows that the Lord is able, and having come, will demand his own from every banker who gives, but [he will condemn] him who for any reason whatsoever has hidden it.' These are the words of Justin to Trypho.

Latin:

Vers. 27. τοῖς τραπεζίταις] Ne dicas invenire te non po- tuisse quibus pecunia esset opus. Argentarii ab omni- bus pecunias sumunt fœnore: Plautus: Subducam ratiunculam, Quantillum argenti mihi apud trapezitam siet.

ἐγὼ ἐκομισάμην ἂν τὸ ἐμὸν σὺν τόκῳ] Ἐκομισάμην hic est ἦλ- θον κομιζόμενος, ivissem receptum, id est, exegissem, ut Lucas. ἔπραξα, & Syrus hoc loco. Sensus est. Non est etiam quod in collocanda pecunia periculum obtendas: mea erat: ego eam exegissem non tuo, sed meo periculo. Tuti enim sunt qui res alienas administrant quoties eis credunt quorum fidei publice creditur. Sic & Dominus noster ἓν οἰκονόμον ῤ ἑαυτῷ ὐ καταδικάσει, εἰ γνωρίζοι αὐτὸν, διὰ τὸ ἐπίσασθαι ὅτι δύνατός ἐστιν ὁ κύριος αὐτῦ καὶ ἐλθὼν ἀπαι- τήσεται τὰ ἴδια ἐπὶ πᾶσαν τράπεζαν διδόντα, ἀλλ̓ ὁ δι᾽ αὐτίαν οἱανδηποτοῦν κατακρύψαντα: Verba sunt Justini ad Trypho- nem.

## 25:28
Vers. 28. Give to him who has the ten talents] This is to be taken in the same way as that which is in the Apocalypse: hold fast what you have so that no one may take your crown: for comparisons of this kind are to be taken more broadly.

Latin:

Vers. 28. δότε τῷ ἔχοντι τὰ δέκα τάλαντα] Hoc ita su- mendum quomodo illud quod in Apocalypsi est: κράτει ὃ ἔχεις ἵνα μηδεὶς λάβῃ τὸν στέφανόν σου: similitudines enim ejusmodi accipiendæ sunt παχύτερον.

## 25:29
Vers. 29. For to him who has] See what we said above XIII. 12.

For the meaning is the same, although it does not deal with the same gifts there. To have here is to have rightly, that is, to use well: not to suffer the grace to be in vain, but to labor as Paul does 1 Cor. XV. 10. which he who does obtains more from divine liberality. It is to be noted, however, that in this parable the order which the signified matter has is not kept. For the increases of grace of which it is treated here are before that joy which was treated above in verse 23. But since Christ wished to say both, that to those who show themselves grateful both greater gifts are bestowed here and afterwards the greatest reward, it did not matter in what order these were placed in the comparison,

and what he has] what he has in fact, what he seems to have [as Luke speaks, which some codices also have here but from Luke if I am not mistaken] as far as the full right of ownership which he does not have. See what is above.

Chrysostom beautifully in homily XXXIX on Matthew. He who receives the grace of doctrine for the benefit of others, and does not use it, loses the grace itself entirely; but he who uses this studiously and diligently, will thus obtain greater grace, just as the other had lost even what he had received.

Latin:

Vers. 29. τῷ γὰρ ἔχοντι] Vide quæ diximus supra XIII. 12.

Eadem enim est sententia, quanquam non de iisdem donis ibi agitur. Exen hic est recte habere, id est bene uti: non pati χάριν κενὴν γενέσθαι, ἀλλὰ κοπιάζειν ut Paulus 1. Cor. XV. 10. quod qui facit à divina liberalitate plura im- petrat. Notandum autem non servari in hoc Apologo eum ordinem quem habet res significata. Nam augmenta gra- tiæ de quibus hic agitur sunt ante gaudium illud de quo a- ctum est supra commate 23. Sed cum utrumque dicere voluerit Christus, iis qui gratos se præbent & majora hic dona & postea maximum præmium tribui, nihil referebat quo ista ordine in comparatione ponerentur,

καὶ ὃ ἔχει] ὃ ἔχει facto, ὃ δοκεῖ ἔχειν [ut Lucas loquitur, quod & hic habent quidam codices sed ex Luca ni fallor] quoad jus plenum dominii quod non habet. Vide quæ supra.

Pulchre Chrysostomus homil. XXXIX. in Matth. Qui doctrinæ gratiam ad utilitatem alio- rum accipit, nec utitur ea, gratiam quoque i- psam omnino perdit; qui autem studiose ac sedu- lo utitur hac, majorem gratiam ita impetrabit, quemadmodum ille vel quod accepit, amiserat.

## 25:30
Vers. 30. Useless servant] The Syrian translates well בטילא. For it has the same value as slothful, that is, as we just said, a slacker. For thus the Hellenists used this word. Tob. IV. 14. For in uselessness there is diminution and great need. For in uselessness there is hunger. Nor do I interpret Luke XVII. 10 otherwise. Thus the Greeks translate נאלמו as they were made useless in Psalm XIV. 3. & LIII. 4.

To this effect is what Chrysostom has in sermon VI on the Priesthood. It did not profit that slothful servant that he did not diminish the talent, but this destroyed him, that he did not return it increased by some addition. Cf. Matt. VII. 17. 19. ch. III. 10. John XV. 2. Whence Augustine concludes in Ps. XXXVIII. The servant is punished not as a destroyer for wasting, but as lazy for not dispensing; what should those expect who have consumed with luxury, if those are condemned who have saved with laziness?

PART III. The process of the final judgment.

Latin:

Vers. 30. ἀχρεῖον δῦλον] Bene vertit Syrus בטילא Idem enim valet quod ὀκνηρὸς, id est, ut modo diximus, cessator. Ita enim hac voce utebantur Hellenistæ. Tob. IV. 14. ἦ γὰρ ἀχρειότητι ἐλάττωσις καὶ ἔνδεια μεγάλη. ἦ γὰρ ἀχρησότητα ἔστι, τὸ λιμῶ. Neque aliter interpretor Lut. XVII. 10. Sic נאלמו ἠχρειώθησαν vertunt Græci in Psalm. XIV. 3. & LIII. 4.

Quo facit, quod habet Chrysostomus serm. VI. de Sacerd. Non profuit servo illi ignavo quod non imminuit talentum, sed hoc eum perdidit, quod non reddidit accessione aliqua auctum. Conf. Matth. VII. 17. 19. cap. III. 10. Joh. XV. 2. Unde colligit Augustinus in Ps. XXXIIX. Punitur servus non eversor ad perdendum, sed piger ad erogandum; quid expectare debent qui cum lu- xuria consumserunt, si damnantur, qui cum pigri- tia servarunt?

PARS III. Processus extremi judicii.

## 25:31
Vers. 31. And all the holy angels with him] A description of divine power. For it alludes to the words of Zechariah ch. XIV. 5.

on the throne of his glory] A comparison taken from Kings, who, when they handle the greatest matters, sit upon a magnificent and sublime throne. See above XIX. 28. & Dan. V. 20. See also the Talmud under the title Ahoda Zara.

Latin:

Vers. 31. καὶ πάντες οἱ ἅγιοι ἄγγελοι μετ' ἀυτᾶ] Divinæ potentiæ descriptio. Alluditur enim ad Zachariæ verba c. XIV. 5.

ἐπὶ θρόνυ δόξης ἀυτᾶ] Similitudo à Regibus sumta, qui cum res maximas tractant, insident magnifico ac sublimi solio. Vide supra XIX. 28. & Dan. V. 20. Vide & Thal- mudem titulo Ahoda Zara.

## 25:32
Vers. 32. All the nations] It can be understood of all the living and dead of the whole inhabited world, as Acts X. 42. ch. XVII. 31. However, the opinion of those is probable who think that it is treated here properly of those who in all peoples will have professed the name of Christ: because they, mixed in this world with the good and the bad, will then finally be separated, as the comparison of the net and the field taught above. It is added that this exact inquiry of life seems to look peculiarly at those who are in the census of the Christian name, as can be seen above ch. VII. verse 2. For just as the laws say there are no parts for those who have confessed except to be condemned, so those who have despised the Gospel are already as if condemned by their own confession, he who does not believe is already judged, John ch. III. verse 18. Lactantius VII. institution ch. XX. Nor yet will all then be judged by God, but only those who have been engaged in the religion of God. For those who have not acknowledged GOD, since a sentence cannot be passed upon them for absolution, they are already judged and condemned; with the holy books testifying that the impious will not rise in judgment. Therefore those who have known God will be judged, and their deeds, that is, evil works compared with good ones, will be weighed. Jerome in dialogue I against Pelagius: The impious will not rise in judgment. For they are already prejudged to destruction. Theophylact hands down the same from the Greeks on the second chapter of John. Nor does Cyprian dissent in book III of testimonies, no. 31. The distinction of sheep and goats seems to look to the place of Ezekiel ch. XXXIV. 17.

Grotius acknowledged that it could be understood as referring to all the living and the dead of the whole οἰκουμένη, as in Acts X. 42.

Chapter XVII. 31. Not only do the words themselves πάντα τὰ ἔθνη (all the nations) introduce this meaning, but the description and execution of the judgment, which is not particular but universal, truly demand it. He mentions, however, the probable opinion of I know not whom, who think that it concerns those who will have professed the name of Christ among all peoples, because they, mixed with the good in this world, will only then be separated. Although this may be true, such a process will not be instituted with them alone, but with all who are to go, by a broad sentence, either into eternal life or into eternal fire; which latter will befall not only those infidels who have professed the name of Christ, but also those who have been strangers to the profession of the name of Christ, and who have despised the Gospel: for the fact that Grotius says these are already condemned by their own confession (by which those are also condemned) does not prevent them from being subjected to that solemn inquiry.

But it is entirely erroneous what he says, that the impious will not rise again for judgment. If this is the opinion of certain ancients, one will not easily find among them that distinction, that the impious who have been engaged in the religion of GOD are to be judged, but the rest, who have not acknowledged GOD, as if already judged and condemned, will not rise again for judgment. This is ἄγραφον (unwritten), nay, even ἀντίγραφον (contrary to scripture), since all must be presented before the tribunal of Christ, Rom. XIV. 10. 2 Cor. V. 10. Therefore, in the Apostolic Creed, we profess that Christ will come to judge the living and the dead. Polycarp the Martyr in his Epistle to the Philippians: We are before the sight of the eyes of the Lord, and we all must appear before the Tribunal of Christ, and each one give an account of himself. Although the incredulous are already judged by eternal reprobation, which must be said no less of those who are in the Church than of those who are outside, they will nevertheless be judged on the last pantocritic day, both by the solemn publication of the sentence and by the execution of the reprobation: which is the more common opinion of the Fathers, as is evident even from the Apostolic, Nicene, and Athanasian Creeds of the Church. Leo the Great, Sermon IV on Collections and Alms, ch. 13: The Lord, he says, will come in the glory of his majesty, as he himself foretold, and there will be present with him an innumerable multitude of angelic legions, radiating in their splendors. The peoples of all nations will be gathered before the throne of his power, and whatever of mankind has been born in all ages throughout the whole world will stand in the sight of the judge.

Latin:

Vers. 32. πάντα τὰ ἔθνη] Potest intelligi de omnibus vi- ventibus & mortuis totius οἰκουμένης, ut Actor. X. 42. cap. XVII. 31. Probabilis tamen est eorum sententia, qui pro- prie hic existimant agi de iis qui in omnibus populis Christi nomen erunt professi: quia illi, in hoc mundo permixti boni malis, tum demum segregabuntur, ut supra docuit retis & agri comparatio. Accedit quod ista exacta vitæ disquisitio videatur peculiariter spectare eos qui in censu sunt Christiani nominis, ut supra videre est cap. VII. vers. 2. Nam sicut jura dicunt in confessos nullas esse partes nisi condemnandi, ita qui Evangelium contemse- runt jam velut damnati sunt propria confessione, ὁ μὴ πι- στευων ἤδη κέκριται, Joh. cap. III. vers. 18. Lactantius VII. institutione cap. XX. Nec tamen universi tunc à Deo judicabuntur, sed ii tantum qui sunt in Dei religione versati. Nam qui DEUM non agnoverunt, quoniam sententia de his in absolutionem ferri non potest, jam judicati damnatique sunt; sanctis libris contestantibus non resurrecturos impios in judicium. Iudicabuntur ergo qui Deum scierunt, & faci- nota eorum, id est mala opera cum bonis collata ponderabun- tur. Hieronymus dialogo I. adversus Pelagium: Non resurgent impii in judicio. Iam enim in perditionem sunt præjudicati. Idem tradit ex Græcis Theophylactus ad II. caput Johannis. Nec dissentit Cyprianus testimo- niorum libro III. n. 31. discrimen ovium & hircorum re- spicere videtur Ezechielis locum c. XXXIV. 17.

Agnovit Grotius intelligi posse de omnibus vi- ventibus & mortuis totius οἰκουμένης, ut Act. X. 42.

cap. XVII. 31. quem sensum cum voces ipsæ πάντα τὰ ἔθνη inferunt, tum vero postulat descriptio, & exequutio judicii, quæ non particularis, sed univer- salis est. Probabilem tamen dicit sententiam ne- scio quorum, qui existimant agi de iis, qui in o- mnibus populis Christi nomen erunt professi, quia illi, in hoc mundo permixti boni malis, tum demum segregabuntur. Quod etsi verum sit, non tamen cum illis solis processus ejusmodi instituetur, sed cum omnibus, qui vel in vitam æternam, vel in æternum ignem, lata sententia, ituri sunt, quod posterius non illis tantum infidelibus obtinget, qui nomen Christi professi sunt, sed iis etiam, qui à professione nominis Christi alieni fuerunt, & qui Evangelium contemserunt: quod enim hos jam propria confessione damnatos dicit Grotius, (qua damnati etiam illi sunt) non impedit, quo minus solemni illi disquisitioni subjiciantur.

Id vero prorsus erroneum est, quod ait, impios non resurrecturos in judicium. Quæ si veterum quorumdam est sententia, non tamen inveniet fa- cile quis apud eos istud discrimen, quod impii qui in religione DEI versati sunt, judicandi sint, reli- qui autem, qui DEUM non agnoverunt, ceu jam judicati, damnatique in judicium resurrecturi non sint. Quod ἄγραφον est, imo & ἀντίγραφον, quum omnes oporteat sisti coram tribunali Christi, Rom. XIV. 10. 2. Cor. V. 10. Ideo in Symbolo A- postolico profitemur Christum venturum ad judican- dum vivos & mortuos. Polycarpus Martyr in Epi- stola ad Philippens. Ante conspectum oculorum Do- mini sumus, & omnes nos oportet apparere ante Tribunal Christi, & unumquemque de se rationem reddere. Quamvis vero increduli jam judicati sint æterna reprobatione, quod non minus de illis, qui in Ecclesia sunt, quam qui extra, dicendum, ju- dicabuntur tamen illi in novissimo pantocritico die tum solemni sententiæ publicatione, tum repro- bationis exequutione: quæ communior etiam Pa- trum est sententia, ut vel è Symbolo Ecclesiæ Aposto- lico, Niceno, & Athanasio constat. Leo M. serm. IV. de Collect. & Eleemos. c. 13. Veniet, inquit, in majestatis suæ gloria Dominus, sicut ipse prædixit, aderitque cum eo radians in splendoribus suis innume- rabilis angelocorum multitudo legionum. Congre- gabuntur ante thronum potentiæ ejus omnium gen- tium populi & quicquid hominum universis seculis to- to orbe progenitum est in conspectu judicantis adsta- bit.

## 25:33
Verse 33. ἐκ δεξιῶν (on the right hand)] The right hand denotes virtues, the left vices, Eccles. X. 2, Jon. IV. 11. Again, the right hand denotes τὴν εὐλογίαν (the blessing), the left τὴν ἄραν (the curse). Therefore, the blessings of the law were pronounced with the face turned toward Mount Gerizim, which, as the Hebrews teach, was situated to the south; and the Hebrews call the south ימין, that is, the right hand: but the curses were uttered with the mouth turned toward Mount Ebal, which was placed to the north, that is, to the left. Τὰ δ᾽ ἐρίφια ἐξ εὐωνύμων (but the goats on the left)] These are called the portion of Samael, that is, the devil, in Josephus Jacchai on Daniel VIII. Mention of the right and left in the judgment after this life is found also in Plato, where he treats of Er the Armenian. And just as the evil demons themselves are called שעירין, that is, goats, by the Hebrews, so their disciples are called kids. For that animal is both libidinous and foul-smelling.

Latin:

Vers. 33. ἐκ δεξιῶν] Dextra virtutes, sinistra vitia notat Eccles. X. 2. Jon. IV. 11. Rursum dextra τὴν εὐλογίαν, si- nistra τὴν ἄραν. Ideo εὐλογίᾳ legis pronuntiatæ sunt ob- verso vultu ad montem Garitim, qui ut Hebræi docent, si- tus erat ad meridiem, Meridiem autem ימין, id est dex- tram, Hebræi vocant: ἀραὶ vero prolatæ sunt ore obverso ad montem Hebal qui ad aquilonem, id est, ad sinistram e- rat positus. Τὰ δ᾽ ἐρίφια ἐξ εὐωνύμων] Hi dicuntur pars Samaëlis, id est diaboli, apud Josephum Jacchai ad IIX. Danielis. Dextræ & sinistræ in judicio post hanc vitam etiam apud Platonem mentio, ubi de Ere Armenio agit. Ac sicut ipsi mali dæ- mones שעירין, id est hirci. Hebræis dicuntur, sic eo- rum discipuli, hædi. Est enim id animal & libidinosum & olidun.

## 25:34
Verse 34. οἱ εὐλογημένοι (the blessed)] To whom, according to the covenant, that supreme happiness belongs, interrupted by no evils, which the blessings of the law shadowed forth under the guise of temporal things. Opposed to these below are the κατηραμένοι (cursed). See Deut. XXIX. κληρονομήσατε (inherit)] To possess by right of ownership, as we have interpreted the word κληρονομεῖν elsewhere. Peter 1, ch. III. 9: ἵνα τοῦτο ἐκλήθητε ἵνα τὴν εὐλογίαν κληρονομήσητε (that you were called to this, that you might inherit a blessing). τὴν ἡτοιμασμένην ὑμῖν (prepared for you)] That is, assigned to you divinely, as above XX. 23, 1 Cor. II. 9, Heb. XI. 16; for so the Hellenists were accustomed to use it: as Tob. VI. 22, concerning Sarah, the wife of Tobias: ὅτι σοι αὕτη ἡτοιμασμένη ἦν ἀπὸ τοῦ αἰῶνος (for this was prepared for you from eternity): which passage looks back to that of Genesis ch. XXIV. 44: αὕτη ἡ γυνὴ ἣν ἡτοίμασε κύριος τῷ ἑαυτοῦ θεράποντι Ἰσαάκ (this is the woman whom the Lord has prepared for his servant Isaac). אשר הכין. Thus Rabbi Israel mentions marriage designated from the foundation of the world in his exposition on Ps. LI.

ἀπὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου (from the foundation of the world)] See above XIII. 35, Luke XI. 50, Heb. IV. 3, ch. IX. 26, Rev. XIII. 8, ch. XVII. 8. But elsewhere ἀπὸ καταβολῆς designates the time after the world was founded: here, however, it is worth as much as πρὸ καταβολῆς (before the foundation), which is in Eph. I. 4 and 1 Pet. I. 20.

Latin:

Vers. 34. οἱ εὐλογημένοι] Ad quos ex federe spectat sum- ma illa & nullis malis interrupta felicitas, quam legis εὐ- λογίαι rerum temporalium specie adumbrabant. His op- ponuntur infra κατηραμένοι. Vid. Deut XXI IX. κληρονομήσατε] Mancupii jure possidere, ut vocem κλη- ρονομεῖν alibi sumus interpretati. Petrus 1. cap. III. 9. ἵνα τῶ- το ἐκλήθητε ἵνα τὴν εὐλογίαν κληρονομήσητε. τὴν ἡτοιμασμένην ὑμῖν] Id est assignatam vobis divini- tus, ut supra XX. 23. 1. Cor. II, 9. Hebr. XI. 16. ita enim solebant usurpare Hellenistae: ut Tob. VI. 22. de Sara To- biae conjuge: ὅτι σοι αὕτη ἡτοιμασμένη ἦν ἀπὸ τοῦ αἰῶνος: qui locus illum Geneseos respicit cap. XXIV. 44. αὕτη ἡ γυνὴ ἣν ἡτοίμασε κύριος τῷ ἑαυτοῦ θεράποντι Ἰσαάκ. אשר הכיח Sic matrimonium à conditu mundi designatum, memorat Rabbi Israel expositione ad Ps. LI.

ἀπὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου] Vide supra XIII. 35. Luc. XI. 50. Hebr. IV. 3. c. IX. 26. Apoc. XIII. 8. c. XVII. 8. Sed alibi ἀπὸ καταβολῆς tempus designat post orbem conditum: hic vero tantum valet quantum πρὸ καταβολῆς, quod est Eph. I. 4. & I. Petr. I. 20.

## 25:35
Verse 35. ἐπείνασα γὰρ (for I was hungry)] Among the true virtues, mercy stands out. Therefore, Christ, setting this forth for all, depicts it with examples that are most known and conspicuous: he names the works themselves rather than the affection of the mind, so that the figure of human judgment might be more expressed.

συνηγάγετέ με (you gathered me)] Athenaeus indeed says that for the Greeks συνάγειν is τὸ μετ' ἀλλήλων πίνειν (to drink together), citing Menander: but here it is undoubtedly a Hebraism. For among the Hellenists, συνάγεσθαι is said even of one who is received into hospitality, 2 Sam. XI. 27, concerning Bathsheba: καὶ συνήγαγεν αὐτὴν εἰς τὸν οἶκον αὐτοῦ (and he gathered her into his house) ויאספה.

Latin:

Vers. 35. ἐπείνασα γὰρ] Inter veras virtutes eminet mise- ricordia. Ideo hanc pro omnibus ponens Christus exem- plis depingit maxime notis atque conspicuis: opera autem ipsa potius nominat quam animi affectum, ut humani ju- dicii figura magis exprimeretur.

συνηγάγετέ με] Dicit quidem Athenaeus Graecis συνάγειν esse τὸ μετ' ἀλλήλων πίνειν, Menandrum citans: sed hic haud dubie Hebraismus est. Nam Hellenistis συνάγεσθαι dicitur etiam unus qui hospitio recipitur, 2. Sam. XI. 27. de Ber- sabea: καὶ συνήγαγεν αὐτὴν εἰς τὸν οἶκον αὐτοῦ ויאספה.

## 25:37
Verse 37. Λέγοντες κύριε (saying Lord)] Even from this it appears that many things are introduced into this description παραβολικά (parabolically). The meaning is that the pious will wonder at the goodness of Christ, who interprets their small deeds so kindly.

Latin:

Vers. 37. Λέγοντες κύριε] Vel hinc apparet multa huic descriptioni inferi παραβολικά. Sensus est, pios admira- turos bonitatem Christi ipsorum facta exigua tam benigne interpretantis.

## 25:40
Verse 40. ἐφ' ὅσον (inasmuch as)] In that: as Rom. XI. 8. In a similar sense καθ' ὅσον (inasmuch as) Heb. VII. 20.

τῶν ἐλαχίστων (of the least)] That is, even of the least, as we have already said several times. So great is the connection between Christ and Christians, and so close the relationship, that Christ constitutes himself the surety for benefits conferred upon them and the avenger of injuries inflicted upon them. See above ch. X. 42.

ἐμοὶ ἐποιήσατε (you did it to me)] That is, I consider it just as if you had done it to me, just as an injury done to a wife is considered done to the husband.

Latin:

Vers. 40. ἐφ' ὅσον] Eo quod: ut Rom. XI. 8. Pari sensu καθ' ὅσον Hebr. VII. 20.

τῶν ἐλαχίστων] Id est κ' ἂν ἐλαχίστων, ut jam diximus aliquo- ties. Tanta est connexio Christi & Christianorum, tam- que arcta necessitudo, ut Christus se pro beneficiis in illos collatis expromissorem & illatarum injuriarum vindicem constituat. Vide supra c. X. 42.

ἐμοὶ ἐποιήσατε] Id est perinde id habeo ac si mihi fecisse- tis, quomodo uxori facta injuria marito facta censetur.

## 25:41
Vers. 41. the eternal fire prepared for the devil] The prince of the evil Angels, who is preeminently called Satan and διάβολος, has been treated above. Moreover, the ancients note here that it is not said that that eternal punishment, which is designated here by the name of fire, was prepared or assigned from the foundation of the world, as was said concerning the kingdom, but neither is it said to have been prepared for men, but for the devil and his Angels: so that the supreme philanthropy of God may be understood, who prepared a heap of all good things for men not yet created and destined them by certain laws, moved by his own goodness. But he destined no torment primarily, but rather by the extortion of malice, first indeed of the rebellious Angels, then of those men who, imitating the guilt of another, and being invited moreover to repentance, which had not happened to the Angels, drew upon themselves the punishment of another: thus

It makes equal those whom it defiles: which the Roman Emperors, taken from Lucan, transferred into their laws. The older Latin vulgate interpretation was accustomed to have here, which the Father prepared for the devil: with a sense more expressed than the enumerated words.

There can be no doubt that eternal punishment was prepared for the Devil and his angels from the foundation of the world, just as the kingdom of God was prepared from eternity for the good angels and faithful men. For from eternity was foreseen both the apostasy of the Devil and his angels, and the final incredulity of men, who consequently, not indeed by an antecedent will, but by a consequent one, if you look at the moments in the sign of reason, as the Scholastics say, following one another in eternity, were already reprobated from eternity. Therefore in Isaiah 30:33, the infernal pit is said to have been prepared from yesterday. Compare concerning these things B. Gerhard's Harm. Evang. ch. CLXV. page 1020, 1023.

Latin:

Vers. 41. τὸ πῦρ τὸ αἰώνιον τὸ ἡτοιμασμένον τῷ διαβόλῳ] De principe malorum Angelorum qui Satan & διάβολος exi- mie dicitur, actum est supra. Caeterum notant hic vete- res non dici supplicium illud aeternum, quod hic ignis no- mine designatur, paratum aut assignatum esse ἀπὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου, ut de regno dictum fuit, sed nec dici, paratum fuisse hominibus, sed diabolo & Angelis ejus: ut intelligatur sum- ma Dei φιλανθρωπία, qui bonorum omnium cumulum ho- minibus nondum creatis paravit & certis legibus destinavit, motus sua bonitate. At cruciatum nullum destinavit προη- γουμένως, sed extorquente malitia, primum quidem Angelo- rum rebellium, deinde eorum hominum qui alienam cul- pam imitantes, ad poenitentiam insuper invitati, quod Ange- lis non contigerat, alienum supplicium in se traxerunt: ita

Facinus quos inquinat aequat: quod Imperatores Romani ex Lucano desumtum in leges suas transtulerunt. Latina vetustior vulgata interpretatio solebat hic habere, quem praeparavit Pater diabolo: sensu ma- gis expresso quam annumeratis verbis.

Non dubium esse potest aeque ἀπὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου paratum esse aeternum supplicium Diabo- lo & angelis ejus, nec non infidelibus, uti angelis bonis & fidelibus hominibus paratum ab aeterno est regnum Dei. Ab aeterno enim praevisa fuit tum apostasia Diaboli & angelorum ejus, tum homi- num finalis incredulitas, qui proinde non quidem voluntate antecedente, sed consequente, si mo- menta respicias in signo rationis, ut loquuntur Scholastici, in aeternitate sese consequentia ab ae- terno jam reprobati sunt. Ideo Es. XXX. 44. fo- vea infernalis parata dicitur ab heri. Conf. de his B. Gerhardi Harm. Evang. c. CLXV. pag. 1020. 1023.

## 25:46
Vers. 46. into eternal punishment] Reference is made to the passage of Daniel ch. XII. 2, where there is a similar repetition of the word eternal. These shall rise to eternal life, and these to reproach and to eternal shame. To which passage the paraphrast Jacchiades is to be seen, teaching things convenient to this place. These words of Christ are urged by the ancients against Origen, who had introduced into Christianity certain vicissitudes of rewards and punishments drawn from the Platonists. What Origen wrote is difficult to say from his own writings: so much have all things been interpolated by Rufinus. In this place indeed, whoever reads Origen will find nothing in his words that departs from the common opinion of Christians. Elsewhere he speaks obscurely, nor does he seem to be consistent with himself; Epiphanius, who is extensive in criticizing Origen, does not, however, properly touch upon this part, except that he says it is taught by him that souls pre-existing are sent into bodies for that reason. But Augustine describes Origen's error in this way: There are also other dogmas of this Origen which the Catholic Church has not received at all: in which it neither accuses him falsely, nor can he be excused by his defenders: especially concerning the purification and liberation and again after a long time the revolution to the same evils of the entire rational creation. For what Catholic Christian, whether learned or unlearned, would not vehemently shudder at that purification of evils which he speaks of? that is, even those who ended this life in the greatest possible disgraces and crimes and sacrileges and impieties, even the devil himself at last and his angels, although after the longest times they are purified and liberated and restored to the kingdom of GOD and to the light, and again after the longest times all who have been liberated fall back and return to these evils, and these alternating cycles of happiness and misery of the rational creature have always been and will always be? Which opinion, thus described, if it is Origen's, is undoubtedly peculiar to him among Christians, and drawn from the Platonists; which Augustine accurately refutes in his books on the City of God: otherwise, that the punishments of some, at least the sensible ones, would eventually cease, he seems not to have been the first to think. For Justin argues thus in his dialogue with Trypho: But I do not say that all souls die; for that would be a godsend indeed to the wicked; but what then? That the souls of the pious remain in a better place, while the unjust and wicked remain in a worse, awaiting the time of judgment then; thus those that are found worthy of God do not die anymore; but the others are punished as long as God wishes them to exist and to be punished. To which certain things leading one may read in Theophilus and in Tatian, and in Irenaeus book II. 64. whom Arnobius followed in the second book, saying that souls, as Christ taught, are of a middle quality, which can perish and be liberated from destruction: that destruction is true death, leaving nothing remaining: Souls, he adds, not knowing God are consumed by the fire-bearing torture of a very long time. But Tertullian: Indeed we who live under God, the overseer of all, and who foresee eternal punishment from him, we alone deserve to meet innocence, and because of the fullness of knowledge and the difficulty of the hidden things, and because of the magnitude of the torture, not temporary, but everlasting. And Lactantius: The same divine fire, with one and the same force and power, will both burn the impious and recreate them, and as much as it consumes from their bodies, so much will it replace, and will itself provide eternal food for itself: which the poets transferred to the vulture of Tityus. What he says about the poets will be best explained by those lines of Ovid in Ibis: Nor will a second death end the punishments of this one, and there will be no final hour for such great evils.

Among Minucius also you may read of eternal punishment and the greatest tortures. This opinion, especially concerning those who treat God, whom they know, with insult, is entirely favored by the Apocalypse ch. XIV. 11. ch. XX. 10. But if anyone wishes to know not the definitions but the doubts of the ancients on this matter, let him go to Jerome at the end of his Commentaries on Isaiah.

In Irenaeus nothing is found that renders his opinion on the eternity of infernal torments doubtful. He asserts the same in book IV. ch. 47. To whomever the Lord shall say, depart from me, you cursed, into everlasting fire, these will be always damned. Origen also in Ps. XXXVII. exhorts that a sinner should prepare himself in this age for the scourges, lest he be kept for eternal fires. And in homily XIV. on Leviticus, he teaches that eternal punishments must be weighed, and where the vengeance is not paid, he says, the sin remains to be exacted by those eternal fires.

Latin:

Vers. 46. εἰς κόλασιν αἰώνιον] Respicitur Danielis locus c. XII. 2. ubi similis est repetitio vocis αἰώνιον. ἐξεγερθήσονται ὗτοι εἰς ζωὴν αἰώνιον, καὶ ὗτοι εἰς ὀνειδισμὸν κὶ εἰς αἰσχύνην αἰώ- νιον. Ad quem locum videndus paraphrastes Jacchiades huic loco convenientia docens. Urgent haec Christi ver- ba veteres contra Origenem qui vicissitudines quasdam praemiorum & poenarum à Platonicis haustas in Christiani- smum invexerat. Quid Origenes scripserit, ex ipsius scriptis difficile est dictu: adeo omnia à Ruffino sunt interpolata. Hoc quidem loco qui Origenem leget, nihil in ejus verbis inveniet, quod à communi Christianorum sententia rece- dat. Alibi obscure loquitur, nec videtur sibi constare, Epi- phanius, qui multus est in reprehendendo Origene, hanc ta- men partem proprie non attingit, nisi quod dicit doceri ab eo animas προϋπαρχούσας causâ immitti corporibus. At Augustinus Origenis errorem hunc in modum describit: Sunt & alia hujus Origenis dogmata quæ Catholica Ecclesia o- mnino non recepit: in quibus nec ipsum falso arguit, nec potest ab ejus defensoribus excusari: maximè de purgatione & liberatione ac rursus post longum tempus ad eadem mala revolutione ratio- nalis universæ creaturæ. Quis enim Catholicus Christianus vel doctus vel indoctus non vehementer exhorreat, eam quam dicit purgationem malorum? id est etiam eos qui hanc vi- tam in flagitiis & facinoribus & sacrilegiis atque impietati- bus quamlibet maximis finierunt, ipsum etiam postremo dia- bolum atque angelos ejus, quamvis post longissima tempora purgatos atque liberatos regno DEI lucíque restitui, & rursus post longissima tempora omnes qui liberati sunt, ad hæc mala de- nuo relabi & reverti, & has vices alternantes beatitudinum & miseriarum rationalis creaturæ semper fuisse, semper fore? Quæ opinio ita descripta, si est Origenis, haud dubie inter Christianos propria est ipsius, & à Platonicis hausta; quam in libris de Civitate Dei accurate refutat Augustinus: cæte- rum aliquando desitura quorundam supplicia, saltem sen- sibilia, videtur non primus existimasse. Nam Justinus colloquio cum Tryphone ita disputat: ἀλλὰ μὴν οὐδὲ ἀπο- θνήσκειν φημὶ πάσας τὰς ψυχὰς ἐγώ· ἕρμαιον γὰρ ἦν ὡς ἀ- ληθῶς τοῖς κακοῖς· ἀλλὰ τί; τὰς μὲν τῶν εὐσεβῶν ἐν κρείττονί ποι χώρᾳ μένειν, τὰς δὲ ἀδίκους καὶ πονηρὰς ἐν χείρονι τὸν τῆς κρίσεως ἐκδεχομένας χρόνον τότε· οὕτως αἱ μὲν ἄξιαι τοῦ Θεοῦ φανεῖσαι, οὐκ ἀποθνήσκουσιν ἔτι· αἱ δὲ κολάζονται ἔστ' ἂν αὐτὰς καὶ εἶναι καὶ κολάζεσθαι ὁ Θεὸς θέλῃ. Quo ducentia quædam & apud Theophilum & apud Tatianum legere est, & apud Ire- næum libro II. 64. quos secutus Arnobius libro secundo animas ait Christo docente esse mediæ qualitatis, interire quæ possint & ab exitio liberari: interitum illum esse mor- tem veram nihil residuum facientem: Animæ, addit, ne- scientes Deum perlongissimi temporis cruciatu consumuntur ignifero. At Tertullianus: Enimvero nos qui sub Deo omnium speculatore disfungimur, quique æternam ab eo pœnam pro- videmus merito soli innocentiæ occurrimus, & pro scientiæ plenitudine & pro latebrarum difficultate, & pro magnitudi- ne cruciatus non diuturni, verum sempiterni. Et Lactan- tius: Idem divinus ignis, una eademque vi atque potentia & cremabit impios, & recreabit, & quantum è corporibus ab- sumet, tantum reponet, ac sibi ipse æternum pabulum submini- strabit: quod Poetæ in vulturem Titii transtulerunt. Quod de Poetis dicit, optime explicabitur istis Ovidii in Ibin: Nec mortu pœnas mors altera finiet hujus, Horaque erit tantis ultima nulla malis.

Apud Minutium quoque legas, pœnam sempiternam & cruciatus maximos. Huic sententiæ, præsertim circa eos qui Deum sibi notum contumelia afficiunt, omnino favet Apocalypsis c. XIV. 11. c. XX. 10. Quod si quis veterum hat de re non definitiones sed dubitationes velit noscere, adeat Hieronymum fine Commentariorum ad Esaiam.

Penes Irenæum nihil reperitur quod dubiam ejus reddat de æternitate cruciatuum infernalium sententiam. Asserit autem eandem lib. IV. c. 47. Quibuscunque dixerit Dominus, discedite à me maledicti in ignem perpetuum, isti erunt semper damnati. Origenes etiam in Ps. XXXVII. horta- tur, ut peccator in hoc seculo se præparet ad fla- gella, ne ignibus æternis asservetur. Et homil. XIV. in Levit. æterna supplicia expendenda esse docet, & ubi non est soluta, inquit, vindicta, pec- catum manet illis æternis ignibus exigendum.

## 26:1 Argument
HISTORY OF THE PASSION AND DEATH OF CHRIST. CHAPTER XXVI. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

JESUS, with the Passover imminent after two days, predicts to the disciples that the Son of man will be delivered up to be crucified, for which cause the Priests and lawyers gather a council at the house of Caiaphas. Concerning his anointing done in the house of Simon, for the sake of his burial. Judas offers himself for the betrayal, having agreed on the reward of 30 pieces of silver. The disciples are sent to prepare the Passover, during the eating of which Jesus predicts the betrayal, and designates the betrayer, and dissuades him with a grave warning. He celebrates the Holy Eucharist, and promises the disciples a drink in the kingdom of his Father. Towards the end, on the way to the Mount of Olives, he teaches about the scandalization of the disciples from the prophecy (Zachar. XIII. 7.), with the addition, however, of a promise about seeing them in Galilee after the resurrection. He predicts to Peter, who protests against it, a triple denial. In the garden of Gethsemane he is gravely saddened, and prays three times about the cup, but submits himself to the will of the Father, soon is betrayed by Judas with a kiss, and is apprehended by the cohort, he rebukes Peter who is cutting off the ear of the servant of the High Priest with a sword: the disciples flee, but Christ is led to Caiaphas and the council, with Peter following from afar: where false testimonies are sought in vain, and finally concerning the rebuilding of the temple within three days. But when the High Priest asks if he is Christ, Jesus not only professes it, but also predicts the coming of the Son of man in the clouds, which the High Priest considers blasphemy, and they all decree him guilty of death. Then Jesus is spat upon, beaten, and harassed: but Peter, terrified by a maidservant, denies him, and being recognized again by another, he swears with a denial: which he did again when he was accused by other disciples of Jesus: but having heard the cock crow, mindful of the words of Jesus, he went out and wept bitterly.

There are three parts: I. Acts before the departure to the passion, namely (1.) the prediction of the imminent betrayal, to v. 2. (2.) The council concerning the apprehending and killing of Jesus, to v. 5. (3.) The anointing of Jesus in Bethany, to v. 13. (4.) The pact of Judas concerning the betraying of Jesus, to v. 16. (5.) The eating of the Passover, with the prediction of the betrayal of Judas, to v. 25. (6.) The celebration of the Holy Eucharist, to v. 29. II. Acts during the departure to the Passion: (1.) The prediction of the scandalization of the disciples, to v. 32. (2.) as also of the triple denial of Peter, to v. 36. III. Acts of the passion: (I.) At the Mount of Olives, namely 1. the interior, and most grievous, passion of Christ, to v. 38. 2. The triple prayer against the cup of the passion, to v. 44. 3. The intimation of the imminent hour of his betrayal and the presence of the traitor, to v. 46. 4. The betrayal of Judas, to v. 49. 5. The apprehension of Jesus, with the striking of the servant by Peter, and the rebuke made by Christ to both Peter and the cohort, and the flight of the disciples, to v. 56. (II.) In the leading away to the Sanhedrin, and in the Sanhedrin: 1. The abduction of Jesus to Caiaphas, with Peter following, to v. 58. 2. The seeking of false testimonies, to v. 61. 3. The adjuration of the high priest as to whether he is the Christ, with the confession of Christ, to v. 64. 4. The proclamation of Jesus as guilty of death as a blasphemer, to v. 66. 5. The spitting upon, striking, and mocking of Jesus, to v. 68. 6. The triple denial of Peter, with his repentance, to v. 75.

PART I. Acts before the departure to the passion.

Vers. 1. πάνταs τῆς λόγος τέτυς] The office of teacher and prophet having been fulfilled, Christ undertakes the priestly office. Vers. 2. μετὰ δύο ἡμέρας τὸ Πάσχα γίνεται] The Passover is called here the very day ἐν ἧ ἐθυετό τὸ πάσχα, i.e., the fourteenth of Nisan; at the end of which that sacred rite was performed according to the law. Nor do I doubt that they err who interpret the words of the law as if it were commanded to be done at the end of the thirteenth day. For both reason and usage teach that the denomination is to be made from the prior and more important part. Wherefore, since it is commanded that the Passover be sacrificed on the fourteenth day between the two evenings, and the prior evening is that of the declining sun rather than the setting sun and has a much greater span, it follows that the law treats of the afternoon of the fourteenth day, and not concerning the beginning of its νυχθημέρῳ [day-night]: which is confirmed by the most ancient custom of the Jews, the best interpreter of the law. Added to this is that immediately after the Passover was sacrificed, the departure of the Hebrews from Egypt followed: but that fell on the 15th day, as Moses narrates. The same, if I am not mistaken, Josephus teaches us in Antiquities VI. 'A festival is at hand, called Passover, during which they sacrifice from the ninth hour until the eleventh.' A little before, he had called the same day the fourteenth day, just as Philo also does; 'around the fourteenth day, when the lunar cycle is about to become full, the Passover is celebrated, a festival visible to the people, what is called in Chaldean the Passover.' The Passover was therefore sacrificed from the ninth to the eleventh hour of the fourteenth day. For the former evening, that is, the part of the declining sun, is undoubtedly of the preceding day. Therefore, Augustus in an edict forbids the Jews to be summoned to court on days of preparation from the ninth hour. But the fourteenth day in that year was undoubtedly that which we call Friday. For that day, at the end of which the Jews were then about to eat the Passover, was the preparation, John 18:28, 19:14. But the preparation (ערב) is the day that precedes the day on which no work is done. The day on which no work is done following it was the great Sabbath, John 19:31, and therefore that preparation was the day before the Sabbath, Mark 15:42. But the day before the Sabbath is the day of Friday. It is difficult to assign the precise time when Christ said these things, because in that manner of speaking, 'after two days,' the limits are sometimes included, sometimes excluded. It is probable that these things were said at the end of Tuesday.

And the Son of man is delivered up to be crucified] That is, although this time is very short, yet in the meantime I shall be captured and condemned, so that I may be crucified on the very day of the Passover, so that in this part also the fulfillment of the law may be evident, John 19:36, 1 Cor. 5:7. For there was also a tradition among the Jews, which now also appears in the books of the Kabbalists: that on the same day the people were to be redeemed in the days of the Messiah as they had been redeemed of old, according to that saying: 'In the days of your exodus from Egypt I will show wonders.' But although the departure from Egypt fell on the 15th day, yet the people had prepared themselves for the journey on the 14th day, and so standing in readiness they ate the Passover. Hence it is that they attributed the liberty received to the 14th day: Josephus, 'the fourteenth day of the month Xanthicus, in which the Jews believe they were first delivered from the Egyptians.' Because of the speed of the action, the writer, using the present tense, said 'is delivered up': but I think this should be understood of the leaders of the Jews who are said to have delivered Christ to Pilate below in chapter 27:2, John 18:35.

These things are correct, with this exception, that the Jews ate the Passover on that legitimate day in this year of the crucifixion. For that they did not celebrate their Passover on the fourteenth day, which fell then on the fifth day of the week, or Thursday, but only on the following day, is taught by invincible arguments, along with Paul of Burgos, not only by most of our own, but even among the Reformed by Calvin, Piscator, Deodatus, Scaliger, Casaubon, the English Annotators, Bælius, and also among the Papists by Maldonatus, Jansenius, Petavius, namely that the Jews ate their Passover then at the end of the fifteenth day and the beginning of the sixteenth, as the sixth day was ending and the seventh beginning. For in John 18:28, when Christ had already been led by Caiaphas into the praetorium, the Jews did not want to enter, so that they would not be defiled, but that they might eat the Passover. Therefore, they had not yet eaten the Passover at that time. And what is clearer than that, in John 19:14, Christ is said to have been condemned on the Preparation of the Passover, and thus before the Passover of the Jews? Add that in John 19:31 the Sabbath that followed the death of Christ is said to be a great one: certainly for no other reason than that the first day of Unleavened Bread, according to the celebration of the Jews, fell upon it, whatever reason they themselves had for that observation, whether it seemed so to Petavius and Ludovicus de Dieu from an uncertain calculation of the new moons, or whether it resulted from the translation of the first day of Unleavened Bread to the Sabbath, so that two great solemnities would not follow one another immediately: which reason pleased most others. Nor indeed would the Jews, if they had celebrated the Passover on the fourteenth moon, have carried out capital trials on the following day, as the first day of Unleavened Bread, or have affixed Christ to the cross, they who so much wanted to appear observant of the ceremonial law that they were afraid to attempt such things on a feast day, lest by chance riots should arise, Matthew 26:5. What of the fact that on that day it was still the day before the Sabbath, as witnessed by Mark ch. 15:42 and the preparation of the Jews according to John ch. 19:31, 42? From which it is clearly evident that the Passover had not yet been celebrated by them at that time. However, it is not to be said that it was called the day before the Sabbath and the preparation by reason of the Sabbath; because it is so called by reason of the great Feast in John 19:31, and thus because of the concurrence of the Sabbath with the feast of the Passover among the Jews: and not only with respect to the common Sabbath. Finally, there is no reason for us to doubt that 'after two days' is to be understood precisely, which the Holy Scriptures define here (μετὰ δύο ἡμέρας τὸ πάσχα γίνεται), 'after two days the Passover will be': provided it is observed that the discourse is about the Passover that was to be in the future according to the law, not according to the tradition or observance of the Jews, when they sacrificed the Passover, Mark 14:12, that is, as Luke interprets, when they were obliged to sacrifice; when it was necessary (ἔδει) to sacrifice the Passover, by the tenor of the divine institution: and thus when those who were tenacious of the divine law were also sacrificing in act: which was also done by Christ and his disciples.

Regarding the explanation of the phrase 'between the two evenings' also, which Grotius takes from the Jews, one may compare B. Gerhard, Harmon. chap. CLXIX, p. 1165, who prefers the opinion of Scaliger, Cajetan, Masius, Schindler, and Casaubon, concerning the two evenings: the one named from the evening offering when the sun is already declining toward sunset, the other from the sunset itself; for the rest, they agree on the matter itself, namely that the time of the two evenings, or the interval between the two evenings, was the interval between the ninth and eleventh hour, that is, between our third and fifth hour in the afternoon. We observe here, however, from Bailius, book II of his Historical Work, p. 81, that the first day of Unleavened Bread was the fifteenth of the month; even though it is sometimes called the fourteenth day, as in Exodus 12:18, which must be cautiously observed for elucidating various passages of Scripture; for sometimes the day of the Passover and the first day of Unleavened Bread are joined as one and the same fourteenth day: sometimes they are separated as two distinct days; since the fourteenth is attributed to the Passover, and the fifteenth to the first day of Unleavened Bread, the reason for which is this: the days of the Hebrews began from the nights, and thus the fifteenth of Nisan began from the sunset of the fourteenth day; what was therefore done at the sunset of that fourteenth day is rightly referred either to the fourteenth or to the fifteenth: now, however, the Passover was commanded to be killed in the evening of the fourteenth day, which was not the beginning but the end of that day, for immediately after the lamb was eaten, in the early morning of the fifteenth day, the Israelite people were driven out of Egypt, Exodus 12:33. But when it is said in Leviticus 23:5 that the Passover was prepared 'between the two evenings,' beware of understanding it so loosely that it could have been prepared at any time between the first evening of that day, which began from the sunset of the thirteenth day, and the second, which ended at the sunset of the fourteenth day. For that בֵּין הָעַרְבַּיִם must be strictly understood as the second evening of the fourteenth day and the first of the fifteenth. For as Josephus, Philo, and Maimonides describe the Passover, the lamb was slaughtered, offered, and roasted at the ninth or third afternoon hour of the fourteenth day, three hours before sunset, so that, being thus prepared, it might be eaten at the twelfth hour at sunset, and the first hour of the fifteenth day after sunset. Thus it appears how the Passover, which was to be prepared at the end of the fourteenth day and eaten at the beginning of the fifteenth, is rightly 6. referred both to the fourteenth and to the fifteenth day. Certainly the celebrations of the Passover and of the first day of Unleavened Bread were neighboring and joined to one another, so that, although in the cited places they are distinguished by different days, yet men join several without distinction into one day, as is seen Luc. XXII. 7; Marc. XIV. 1; Matth. XXVI. 16. This is Basil.

Latin:

HISTORIA PASSIONIS ET MORTIS CHRISTI. CAPUT XXVI. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

IESUS imminente post biduum Paschate Fi- lium hominis traditum iri ut crucifigatur, discipulis prædicit, cujus causa concilium coëgere Sacerdotes & legisperiti penes Cai- pham. De unctione ejus in domo Simonis facta, sepulturæ ejus gratia. Iudas of- fert se ad proditionem mercedem pa- ctus 30. argenteorum. Emittuntur disci- puli ad Pascha adornandum, sub cujus manducatione Iesus proditionem prædicit, & proditorem designat, ac gravi commi- natione dehortatur. Sacram Euchari- stiam celebrat, & potionem in regno Pa- tris discipulis promittit. Sub exitum ad montem Oliveti de scandalizatione disci- pulorum è vaticinio (Zachar. XIII. 7.) do- cet, addita tamen promissione de ipsis post resurrectionem videndis in Galilea. Petro contra protestanti trinam abnega- tionem prædicit. In horto Gethsemane graviter contristatur, & ter deprecatur calicem, sed submittit sese voluntati Pa- tris, mox à Iuda osculo proditur, & à co- horte apprehenditur, Petrum servo Pon- tificis auriculam gladio amputantem cor- ripit: discipuli fugiunt, Christus vero ad Caipham & concilium deducitur, è longin- quo sequente Petro: ubi frustra falsa testi- monia conquiruntur, ac postremo de tem- plo intra triduum reedificando. Pontifi- ce vero quærente an sit Christus, id non tantum profitetur Iesus, sed etiam prædi- cit adventum Filii hominis in nubibus, quod pro blasphemia habet Pontifex, o- mnesque ipsum mortis reum decernunt. Inde conspuitur, verberatur & exagitatur Iesus: Petrus autem ab ancilla territus abnegat ipsum, & iterum ab alia agnitus cum abnegatione pejerat: quod denuo, quum ab aliis Iesu discipulis argueretur, ab ipso factum: audito autem gallicinio me- mor verborum Iesu exiit, amare flevit.

Partes sunt tres: I. Acta ante egressum ad pas- sionem, utpote (1.) prædictio imminentis tradi- tionis ad v. 2. (2.) Concilium de apprehendendo & occidendo Jesu, ad v. 5. (3.) Unctio Jesu in Be- thania, ad v. 13. (4.) Pactum Judæ de Jesu proden- do, ad v. 16. (5.) Paschatos manducatio, cum prædi- ctione proditionis Judæ, ad v. 25. (6.) Sacræ Eu- charistiæ celebratio, ad v. 29. II. Acta sub egressum ad Passionem: (1.) Scandalizationis discipulorum prædictio, ad v. 32. (2.) ut & abnegationis trinæ Pe- tri, ad v. 36. III. Acta passionis: (I.) Ad montem Oliveti, utpote 1. interior Christi, eademque gra- vissima passio, ad v. 38. 2. Trina calicis passionis deprecatio, ad v. 44. 3. Imminentis horæ traditio- nis suæ, & præsentiæ proditoris intimatio ad v. 46. 4. Judæ proditio, ad v. 49. 5. Jesu apprehensio, cum Petrina servi percussione, & à Christo facta tum Petri tum cohortis correptione, & discipulorum fuga, ad v. 56. (II.) In deductione ad Synedrium, & in Synedrio: 1. Abductio Jesu ad Caipham, sequen- te Petro, ad v. 58. 2. Falsorum testimoniorum con- quisitio, ad v. 61. 3. Pontificis obtestatio an Chri- stus sit, cum Christi confessione, ad v. 64. 4. Jesu ceu blasphemi mortis rei proclamatio, ad v. 66. 5. Jesu conspuitio, percussio, & illusio, ad v. 68. 6. Trina Petri abnegatio, cum ejusdem pœnitentia, ad v. 75.

PARS I. Acta ante egressum ad passionem.

Vers. 1. πάνταs τῆς λόγος τέτυς] Munere doctoris & va- tis impleto, Christus sacerdotale munus aggreditur. Vers. 2. μετὰ δύο ἡμέρας τὸ Πάσχα γίνεται] Pascha hic vocatur ipsa dies ἐν ἧ ἐθυετό τὸ πάσχα, i. e. decima quarta Nisan; cujus fine id sacrum ex lege peragebatur. Neque enim dubito quin er- rent, qui legis verba ita interpretantur, quasi fine diei deci- mæ tertiæ id fieri præciperetur. Nam & ratio & usus docet à priori ac potiori parte faciendam denominationem. Quare cum præcipiatur Pascha mactari die decimo quarto inter duas vesperas, prior autem sit vespera Solis declinantis quam occidentis multoque majorem tractum habeat, sequitur de tempore pomeridiano diei decimae quartae, non autem de e- jus νυχθημέρῳ initio in lege agi: quod confirmat mos Judæo- rum antiquissimus, optimus legis Interpres. Accedit quod statim post sacrificatum Pascha subsecuta est abitio Hebræo- rum ex Aegypto: ea autem incidit in diem XV, ut Moses nar- rat. Idem ni fallor nos docet Josephus Ἁλώσεως VI. Ἐνστάσης ἑορτῆς, πάσχα καλεῖται, καθ᾽ ἣν θύουσι μὲν ἀπὸ ἐνάτης ὥρας μέ- χρι ἑνδεκάτης. Eandem diem paulo ante vocarat ἡμέραν τεσσαρεσκαιδεκάτην, quomodo & Philo; περὶ τεσσαρεσκαιδε- κάτην ἡμέραν μέλλοντος τῶ σεληνιακῶ κύκλω γίνεσθ᾽ πλησιφαῦς ἄγεται τὰ διαβατήρια, δημοφανὴς ἑορτὴ, τὸ χαλδαϊστὶ λεγό- μενον πάσχα. Mactabatur ergo Pascha à nona ad undecimam diei decimæ quartæ. Nam prior vespera id est Solis decli- nantis pars est haud dubie diei antecedentis. Ideo Augustus in edicto vetat Judæos vadari diebus παρασκευῆς ἀπὸ τῆς ἐνά- της. Dies autem decima quarta isto anno haud dubie fuit ea, quam nos Veneris dicimus. Nam is dies, cujus fine Ju- dæi tunc manducaturi erant Pascha, erat παρασκευὴ Johan. XVIII.28. XIX. 14. παρασκευὴ autem ערב est dies qui diem ἄπρακτον antecedit. Dies ἄπρακτ@ eam sequens erat sabba- tum magnum, Johan. XIX. 31. ac proinde illa παρασκευὴ e- rat προσάββατον, Marc. XV. 42. Dies autem ante Sabbatum dies est Veneris. Præcisum tempus quando Christus hæc lo- cutus sit assignare difficile est, quia in illo loquendi genere, post biduum, termini modo includuntur, modo excludun- tur. Fine diei Martis hæc dicta probabile est.

καὶ ὁ ὑὸς τῶ ἀνθρώπω παραδίδοται εἰς τὸ σταυρωθῆναι] Id est, quanquam tempus hoc admodum breve est, tamen inter- ea capiar, & damnabor, ita ut crucifigar ipso die Paschatis, ut etiam hac in parte evidens sit τελείωσις τῶ νόμω, Joh. XIX. 36. 1. Cor. V. 7. Nam & παράδοσις erat apud Judæos, quæ nunc quoque in Cabalistarum libris apparet: eadem die redi- mendum populum in diebus Messiæ quo redemtus fuerat olim, juxta illud: In diebus exitus tui ex Aegypto ostendam mi- rabilia. Quanquam autem profectio ex Aegypto incidit in diem XV. tamen ad iter se accinxerat populus diei 14. ita- que in procinctu stantes Pascha ederant. Hinc est quod diei 14. libertatem acceptam ferebant: Josephus ἡμέρας τεσσα- ρεσκαιδεκάτης ξανθικῶ μηνὸς ἐν ᾗ δοκῦσιν οἱ Ἰυδαῖοι τ’ πρῶτον ἀπαλλαγῆναι καιρὸν αἰγυπτίων. Propter celeritatem actio- nis Scriptor præsens tempus usurpans dixit παραδίδοται: intelligendum autem hoc arbitror de primoribus Judæo- rum qui Christum dicuntur tradidisse Pilato infra c. XXVII. 2. Ioh. XIIX. 35.

Recte hæc se habent, hoc excepto, quod Judæi die illo legitimo comederint hoc Anno σταυρωσίμῳ Pa- scha. Nam illos non die decimo quarto, qui incidit tum in feriam quintam, seu diem Jovis, sed se- quenti demum Pascha suum celebrasse, argumen- tis invictis cum Paulo Burgensi docent non modo plerique è nostris, sed è Reformatis etiam Calvi- nus, Piscator, Deodatus, Scaliger, Casaubonus, An- notatores Anglicani, Bælius, nec non è Pontificiis Maldonatus, Jansenius, Petavius, quod nempe Judæi in fine die decimi quinti ac initio decimi sexti, feria sexta finiente, & septima incipiente Pascha suum tum comederint. Nam Joh. XIIX. 28. cum deductus jam est Christus à Caipha in prætorium intrare id noluere Judæi, ut non contaminarentur, sed ut manducarent Pascha. Nondum ergo tum Pascha ipsi manducarant. Et quid apertius eo, quod Joh. XIX. 14, condemnatus dicitur Christus in Parasceve Paschatos, adeoque ante Pascha Ju- dæorum: Adde quod Job. XIX. 31. Sabbatum mor- tem Christi insequutum dicatur magnum: non certe alia de causa, quam quod primus azymorum juxta celebrationem Judæorum in illud inciderit, quamcunque ejus observationis ipsi rationem ha- buerint, seu ex incerta Noviluniorum computatione, uti Petavio, & Ludovico de. Dieu, visum est, seu è translatione primi Azymorum in Sabbatum, ne duæ magnæ solemnitates se continuo seque- rentur, ea redundarit: quæ ratio plerisque aliis placuit. Neque vero Judæi, si decima quarta Luna Pascha celebrassent, sequenti die, ceu pri- ma Azymorum causas capitales peregissent, aut Christum cruci affixissent, qui adeo videri vole- bant observantes legis ceremonialis, ut talia die festo tentare veriti sint, ne forte tumultus orirentur Matth. XXVI. 5. Quid quod illo die adhuc fuerit προσάββατον, teste Marco c. XV. 42. & parasceve Judæorum secundum Jobannem cap. XIX. 31. 42. unde liquido constat, tum nondum Pascha ab ipsis celebratum fuisse. Non est au- tem, quod dicatur προσάββατον dictum fuisse, & παρασκευὴν ratione Sabbati; quia ratione magni Festi sic vocatur Job. XIX. 31. adeoque ob concur- sum Sabbati cum festo Paschatos penes Judæos: non vero solum respectu communis Sabbati. De- nique non est, quod ambigamus præcise biduum intelligendum esse, quod ita hic definit S. S. μετὰ δύο ἡμέρας τὸ πάσχα γίνεται), post biduum Pascha e- rit: modo observetur, quod de Paschate secundum legem futuro sermo sit, non secundum traditionem vel observantiam Judæorum, quando Pascha im- molabant Marc. XIV. 12. id est, interprete Luca, im- molare debebant; quando ἔδει necesse erat immolare Pascha, tenore institutionis divinæ: adeoque cum immolabant etiam actu, qui legis divinæ tenaces erant: quod à Christo, ejusque discipulis quoque factum est.

De explicatione quoque phraseos intra duas ve- speras, quam Grotius à Judæis habet, conferri poterit B. Gerhardus Harmon. cap. CLXIX. pag. 1165. qui sententiam Scaligeri, Cajetani, Masii, Schindleri, Casauboni præfert, de duabus vesperis altera ab oblatione vespertina cum jam Sol declinat ad occasum, altera à Solis occasu denominata: de cætero in reipsa conveniunt illi, quod nempe tempus duarum vesperarum, seu inter duas vesperas fuerit intervallum inter horam nonam & undeci- mam, hoc est, inter nostram tertiam & quintam pomeridianam. Observamus autem hic è Bailio lib. II. Operis Hist. pag. 81. diem primum Azy- morum fuisse mensis decimum quintum; etsi ali- quando vocatur dies decimus quartus, ut Exod. XII. 18. quod caute observandum est ad varios Scripturæ locos elucidandos; nam aliquando Pa- schatis dies & dies primus Azymorum conjun- guntur, ut unus & idem dies decimus quar- tus: aliquando disjunguntur, ut duo distincti; cum Paschati decimus quartus, & primo Azy- morum decimus quintus attribuuntur, quorum hæc ratio est: Hebræorum dies incipiebant à noctibus, itaque decimus quintus Nisan inci- piebat ab occasu solis diei decimi quarti, quod ergo gerebatur ad istius diei decimi quarti oc- casum, recte refertur vel ad decimum quar- tum vel ad decimum quintum: jam vero Pa- scha jussum est occidi in vespera decimi quarti diei, quæ fuit non principium sed finis istius diei, nam statim post comestum agnum primo mane diei decimi quinti extrusus est populus Is- raeliticus ex Ægypto, Exod. XII. 33. Cum autem dicitur Pascha Levit. XXIII. 5. paratum in- ter duas vesperas, cave intelligas tam laxe ut pa- rari potuerit quovis tempore inter primam vespe- ram istius diei, quæ incipiebat ab occasu solis diei decimi tertii & secundam, quæ definebat in occa- su solis diei decimi quarti. Illud enim בֵּין הָעַרְבַּיִם stricte intelligendum est de secunda vespera diei decimi quarti, & prima decimi quinti. Nam prout Josephus, Philo, ac Maimonides Pascha describunt hora nona seu tertia pomeridiana diei decimi quarti tribus horis ante solis occasum agnus mactabatur, offerebatur, & assabatur, ut ita paratus comederetur ad horam duodecimam in solis occasu, & hora prima diei decimi quinti post solis occasum. Sic apparet, quomodo Pascha, quod parandum erat in fine diei decimi quarti & comedendum initio decimi quinti, recte refe- 6. ratur tam ad diem decimum quartum quam ad decimum quintum. Certe celebrationes Paschatis & primi Azymorum tam erant sibi invicem vicinae ac junctae, ut, quamvis locis citatis diversis diebus distinguantur, tamen alias absque distinctione in unum diem conjungantur, ut videre est Luc. XXII. 7. Marc. XIV. 1. Matth. XXVI. 16. Haec Basilius.

## 26:3
Ver. 3. Τότε] About this time: for I think it is the same assembly which John describes, XI. 47. For often with Matthew one finds τότε; tumtum in a loose sense. οἱ ἀρχιερεῖς κὶ οἱ γραμματεῖς κὶ οἱ πρεσβύτεροι] A description of the Sanhedrists; by this name John calls that council, c. XI. 47. One of their functions was to inquire concerning false prophets. Latin does not read the word γραμματεῖς: but the Syriac and Arabic read it. εἰς τὴν αὐλὴν] Αὐλὴ properly means a subordinate court, as also elsewhere; but by synecdoche it may mean the palace; Athenaeus notes νῦν δὲ τὰ βασίλεια λέγεσθαι ἀνάκλας, which Eustathius also comments on in the Odyssey. Thus Marcus calls it the praetorium of Pilate. Such palaces were repeated at Jerusalem: as the house of the Asamoneans, mentioned by Josephus. τὸ ἀρχιερέως] Here κατ' ἐξοχήν νοεῖ τὸν ἀρχιερέα, it is taken pro eo qui dicebatur כהן גדול, with the previous clause generically removing Christ from the midst: this, however, occasioned grave reprehensions of Christ, and of the people's desire instituted a plan regarding the manner and time of taking him captive; for he must be seized by deceit, and not in a festival, lest uproar arise among the people; which counsel afterward they altered when opportunity was offered through the betrayal of the Jews. Both things Chrysostom observes in the cited place. Συμβουλεύσαντο] As signified before, Ps. II. 1, 2 and XLI. 8. Ver.

Latin:

Verf. 3. Τότε] Circa hoc tempus: puto enim eundem esse conventum quem Johannes describit XI. 47. Saepe enim apud Matthaeum invenire est τότε; tumtum laxo significatu. οἱ ἀρχιερεῖς κὶ οἱ γραμματεῖς κὶ οἱ πρεσβύτεροι] Synedrii descriptio, quo nomine hunc caetum appellat Johannes c. XI. 47. Ejus Synedrii munus erat de pseudoprophetis cognoscere. Vocem γραμματεῖς non legit Latinus: at Syrus & Arabs legerunt. εἰς τὴν αὐλὴν] Αὐλὴ proprie subdioele, ut & infra aliquoties; sed συνεκδοχικῶς palatium Athenaeus, νῦν δὲ τὰ βασίλεια λέγεσθαι ἀνάκλας: quod & Eustathio annotatum ad Odysseam. Ita Marcus aulam vocat Pilati praetorium. Talia autem palatia aliquoter antebantur Hierosolymis: ut domus Asamonoeorum, cujus meminit Josephus. τὸ ἀρχιερέος] Hic κατ' ἐξοχήν νοεῖ τὸ ἀρχιερέα, sumitur pro eo qui dicebatur כהן גדול, cum ante eodem commate generice de Christo è medio tollendo: haec vero occasione gravium reprehensionum Christi, & adhaesionis populi institutae est de modo & tempore eum captivandi, quod nempe dolo comprehendendus sit, idque non in festo, ne tumultus in populo oriatur, quod consilium postea occasione per Judaei proditionem oblata mutarunt. Utreque admodum Chrysostomus observat in h. l. Συμβουλεύσαντο] Ut praesignificatum Ps. II. 1. 2. & XLI. 8. Verf.

## 26:4
4. κὶ ἀποκτείνωσιν] Through the Roman governor. For that seemed safest to them under the circumstances. "To put to death" is said which furnishes the cause of death. See above XXI. 38. Peter to Judas: ἢ ἀρχηγὸν τῆς ζωῆς ἀπεκτείνατε. Ath. III. 15. Ver.

Latin:

4. κὶ ἀποκτείνωσιν] Per Romanum praefidem. Id enim tutissimum in ipsis videbatur. Necare autem dicitur qui caussam mortis praebet. Vid. supra XXI. 38. Petrus ad Judam: ἢ ἀρχηγὸν τῆς ζωῆς ἀπεκτείνατε. Ath. III. 15. Verf.

## 26:5
5. μὴ ἐν τῇ ἑορτῇ ἵνα μὴ θόρυβος γένηται ἐν τῷ λαῷ] This festival is called the whole time from the slaughtering of the lamb to the end of Unleavened Bread. Josephus, Antiquities II, ὅτε εἰς μνήμην τῆς τότε ἐνδείας ἑορτὴν ἄγομεν ἐφ' ἡμέρας ὀκτῶ. In Book II he treats the whole Paschal season: τὰ πάσχα... ἡ ἑορτὴ ἡ ἱ ἀζύμων — proper for disturbances when the multitude most assembles. The same Josephus in his book on the paschal observances: ἡ ἑορτὴ... καθ' ἣν... πολλὰ κὶ πανταχόθεν πλήθες συναχθέντες ἐπὶ τὴν ἑορτήν... Which also John c. VI. 14 records. Add what is said below c. XXVII. 15. I therefore wholly agree with those who suppose it seemed to the Sanhedrim, on account of the people's tumult, to deviate somewhat from the received custom. For they used, as the Talmudists note, to gather the more notable heads of families at these festivals, that example might reach further. Thus Herod intended to bring Peter forth to punishment immediately after the Passover, Acts XII. 4, that is, within those eight days. For besides the first and last day and the sabbath, if something intervened, the other days were nevertheless counted as festive. But to suppose that the punishment which they destined for Jesus was to be deferred beyond the usual time because of this season, I do not think likely; they feared Galileans rather more as being popular than the inhabitants of Jerusalem. Moreover this pertains to showing the singular providence of God in that fact, who, the opportunity being offered through Judas, caused that they should depart from that counsel, whereby it happened that many witnesses were present to the death of his Son, and that it fell into the very Passover time. Some think that the Sanhedrim formed a design to precipitate matters, lest the punishment should fall on the sabbath day and scandalize the people; for many reasons I do not approve: one of which is that it is not credible that Pilate would ever have pronounced sentence on the sabbath. For even when Jews acted outside Judea, an allowance had been granted by Augustus that they might not be compelled to travel on the sabbath (the same is attested in Josephus' edict), much more must it be supposed that the rulers of Judea were enjoined not to pass sentences on sabbaths. This was not changed under Tiberius, who first taught the perpetual observance of the customs instituted by Augustus as venerated oracles, and then Agrippa to Caius said: Τιβέριον ἀδὲν ἐθέλὰ τῶν ἡμετέρων καταλείπειν, apud Philo. Add that Titus in his address to the Roman emperors in general reports the Jews saying: τὸς πατρίοις νόμοις ἐτηρήσαμεν, κὶ ζῆν ἐμόνον καθ' ἑαυτές, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὰς ἄλλας ἐπετρέψαμεν ὡς ἐβλέπε. Therefore what some suppose, that in antiquity they did not travel on the sabbath, is not certain beyond doubt. Ver.

Latin:

5. μὴ ἐν τῇ ἑορτῇ ἵνα μὴ θόρυβος γένηται ἐν τῷ λαῷ] Haec vocatur tota illa festa a mactatione agni ad finem Azymorum. Josephus Antiquit. II, ὅτε εἰς μνήμην τῆς τότε ἐνδείας ἑορτὴν ἄγομεν ἐφ' ἡμέρας ὀκτῶ. Lib. II. Omne hoc tempus τὰ πάσχα ἡ ἑορτὴ ἡ ἱ ἀζύμων opportunum ad seditionibus ob maximum populi concursum. Idem Josephus libro XX de paschorum celebrandis: ἡ ἑορτὴ... καθ' ἣν ἔθῶν ἐστὶν ἡμῖν ἄζυμον... πολλὰ κὶ πανταχόθεν πλήθες συναχθέντες ἐπὶ τὴν ἑορτήν... Quod et Joannes c. VI. 14. Adde quae dicentur infra c. XXVII. 15. Omnino igitur iis accedo qui visum agunt Synedrio ob plebis murum nonnihil recedere à recepto more. Solebant enim, ut & Thalmudici notant, fontium insigniores plecti ἐν αὐταῖς ταῖς ἑορταῖς, quo ad plures exemplum pervenirent. Ita Herodes destinabat Petrum ad poenam producere statim post Pascha, Act. XII. 4. id est, intra illos octo dies. Nam praeter primum & ultimum diem & sabbatum, si quod interveniret, caeteri dies tamen festi nihilominus essent aestimati. Sed supplicium quod Jesum destinabant praeter morem differendum censent extra tempus; ut prius? Magis enim metuebant Galilaeos, tanquam ipsius se populares, quam Hierosolymitas. Pertinet autem hoc ad ostendendam singularem Dei in hoc facto providentiam, qui oblata per Judam occasione effecit, ut ab hoc consilio discederetur, quo factum ut & plures testes haberet mors filii sui, & in ipsum Paschale tempus incideret. Quod quidam existimant propositum Synedriorum praecipitare, ne supplicium incideret in Sabbati diem, idque populum offenderet, mihi multas ob causas non placet: quarum haec una est, quod credibile non est Pilatum unquam sabbatis jus dixisse. Nam cum Judaeis etiam extra Judaeam agentibus concessum ab Augusto fuerit sabbato hoc obtentu non vadari (idem in esto ἐγγύας ὁμολογῶν in edicto apud Josephum) multo magis censeri debet Judaeae praesidibus injunctum ne sabbatis jus dicerent. Hoc autem non mutatum à Tiberio, primum docet perpetuus ejus mos cuncta Augusti instituta tanquam oracula venerantis, deinde Agrippa ad Cajum verba: Τιβέριον ἀδὲν ἐθέλὰ τῶν ἡμετέρων καταλείπειν, apud Philonem. Adde his quod Titus de Imperatoribus Romanis in universum pronuntiat Judaeos alloquens: τὸς πατρίοις νόμοις ἐτηρήσαμεν, κὶ ζῆν ἐμόνον καθ' ἑαυτές, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὰς ἄλλας ἐπετρέψαμεν ὡς ἐβλέπε. Nam quod quidam putant etiam antiquitus Sabbatis exinde non vadari, non liquet esse satis certum. Verf.

## 26:6
6. ἐν Βηθανίᾳ ἐνοικία Σίμων] Nothing is more certain than that the writers of the Gospels refer many things not by the order of time but by the sequence of matters. Therefore some things are related earlier, some much later, some are reported retrospectively on account of wars and occasions; the causes for relating are not the same in all. Matthew and Mark seem to place this account here in order that they may note what drove Judas to the deed. For immediately follows what pertains to Judas. Luke likewise undertook to narrate this with certain speeches suitable to commendation of repentance. He wished likewise to confirm by that example how great a mercy Christ had shown to the woman, once much defiled by sins but drawn by penitence of soul.
