John, however, renders this history in his own time, both to confirm what he had said about Lazarus (for Lazarus was present at this banquet) and to connect the following matters: and that time was evening, the sabbath having just been completed, so that no religious prohibition hindered the anointing. Not only that it was the same woman, but also that the same deed occurred; I do not see that multiplicity of persons is to be rashly presumed. Matthew and Mark agree in all. Matthew, Mark and Luke agree that these acts took place at a supper in the house of Simon, that a woman approached bearing ἀλάβαστρον μύρου, with which she anointed Jesus. Matthew, Mark and John agree that this event was in Bethany at a supper, that the ointment brought by the woman was of very great price and that she was rebuked under that name by one of the disciples (the plural being used thus), John naming Judas; more properly that money would have been spent on the poor, which Christ defends the woman for, adopting a charitable interpretation that this honor pertained to her perfuming of him. These are the contingent arrangements which, at different times, fit together. Again Luke and John agree that the woman anointed Christ's feet and wiped them with her hair: which is expressed more plainly as to word and hair; and as John shows, he has explained it. Add that John describes Mary, the sister of Lazarus, as a peculiar mark, that she is the one who anointed and wiped Christ's feet. But one cannot certainly infer this solely from frequency of occurrence. And that John says it was by πρόληψις (in anticipation), is not more novel than that Judas, where there is the first mention of the Apostles, is distinguished by the surname of traitor. What is it, therefore, that compels us to invent different events? Is it because in Matthew and Mark there is mention of the head, and in Luke and John of the feet? But nothing prevents one from believing that the feet were anointed first, and then the head. in Luke there is a sinful woman, but the piety of Mary, the sister of Lazarus, is proclaimed? But the times must be distinguished. She had once lived more dissolutely: therefore she was called a sinner: soon she compensated for the faults of her former life with serious piety: wherefore it ought not to offend us that Jesus turned into her house, since it was already known to all that her life was amended. That this woman is the Magdalene, however, is not equally easy to prove. For the sister of Lazarus is never called by that name. And that opinion seems to have been born from the words of Christ concerning the preparation for burial: because the Magdalene went to prepare Christ for burial. But the words of Christ refer not to a future, but to a present duty, as the comparison of the Evangelists shows. Furthermore, the Magdalene seems to have been a Galilean, below XXVII. 56, Mark XV. 40. Lazarus, however, with his sisters, was a Judean from Bethany, John XI. 1. It is narrated of the Magdalene that she was delivered by Christ when she was possessed by seven demons: of the sister of Lazarus, nothing of the sort. And what is most to be noted, Luke, immediately after the narrative about the anointing woman, subjoins a mention of the women who were following Jesus, and among them the Magdalene, adding to her the note of having been freed from demons, and not from the act narrated a little before. In the constitutions also which are called Clement's, Mary Magdalene is distinguished from Mary the sister of Lazarus. The passage is book III, ch. 6. I would have some faith in those things which are narrated among the people of Marseille, if it were certain regarding the antiquity of her fame.

That this is the same history as that which is described by Mark ch. XIV. 3 and John ch. XII. 1 seqq., although Origen (tr. XXIV in Matt.), Chrysostom (hom. XXII in Matt. and hom. LX in John), as well as Euthymius in Matthew and Theophylact in Mark, and rashly Osiander in Annot. ad Harm. l. III. 5. 35 and Baronius (Tom. I. Annal. ad Ann. 32. num. 27) deny it, has been well observed by Grotius: concerning which Augustine (l. II. de conf. Evangel. c. LXXIX) says: There is no doubt that these three Evangelists are narrating the same event that took place in Bethany. Which is also the opinion of Dionysius the Carthusian, Faber Stapulensis, Jodocus Clichtoveus, Salmeron, Maldonatus, Jansenius, and Barradius; for all the circumstances agree, and convince that it is the same history. With Matthew and Mark, as Grotius rightly says, everything agrees. With Matthew, Mark, and John, [it agrees] that these things were done in Bethany, at a banquet, that the ointment brought by the woman was of the greatest value, that the woman was rebuked for this reason by one of the disciples (for the plural is usually taken in this way, but John names Judas) as a spendthrift, under the pretext that this expense would have been better made on the poor: that Christ defended the woman, with a benign, nay, most true interpretation, that this honor pertained to his preparation for burial. These circumstances are too precise to agree with different times. Nor does that note of two days before the Passover pertain to the present anointing: which Matthew and Mark mention here only by occasion: it was recounted in its own order and time by John, because it happened, namely, six days before the Passover. Nor does the house in which the banquet was celebrated create a diversity, if indeed it is not found in John that the banquet was prepared in the house of Lazarus, as Chrysostom and Theophylact wish; but it is said simply: and they made a supper for him there. Matthew and Mark, however, expressly specify the house of Simon. Furthermore, Grotius does not deserve assent in that he wishes the history of Luke also concerning the sinful woman (ch. VII) to be the same as this one of ours; even though Rupertus (comment. in John XII) was also of that opinion. For the time is repugnant: since that history of Luke concerning the action done by the sinful woman did not happen in the last year of the ministry, two days before the crucifixion-bound Passover, but in the second year, as sacred history teaches. The place is also repugnant: since that one happened in Galilee, this one in Judea in the village of Bethany: that one in the house of Simon the Pharisee, this one in the house of Simon the leper; which two persons, although Chrysostom homil. XXXI in Matthew, Ambrose l. VI in Luke c. VII, and the author of the sermon on the washing of the feet among the works of Cyprian, Gregory the Great, Cornelius Jansenius, Baronius T. I. Ann. 32, n. 17, as also the Jesuit Maldonatus in Matthew XXVI, following John Faber, Bishop of Rochester, in his book on the one Mary, and Natalis Beda, hold them to be one, yet Origen (tr. XXXV in Matthew), Basil of Seleucia (homil. de Lazar.), Jerome, Augustine (lib. II de consens. cap. 79), Beda in Luke VII, Theophylact, and Euthymius in this place distinguish them: because the Pharisee received Christ at a banquet with a hypocritical mind: but Simon the leper with an excellent and beneficent mind. Nor do other circumstances agree sufficiently: since the woman who is said to have anointed [him] in Luke was a notorious sinner: but this one is commended for her piety; that one both watered the feet of Christ with tears, and wiped them with her hair, and kissed them, which were signs of repentance: but this one is reported not to have shed tears for the sake of repentance, but only to have anointed the body of Christ as for burial: that one is said to have anointed the feet of Christ only with ointment: but this one, not only the feet (John XII. 3), but also the head (Matthew XXVI. 7, Mark XIV. 3). Concerning which Jerome says in this place: Let no one think that she who poured ointment on the head is the same as she who [poured it] on the feet. For that one washes with tears and wipes with her hair, and is manifestly called a harlot: but of this one, nothing of the sort is written. For a harlot could not immediately become worthy of the head of the Lord. Regarding her anointing, no one murmured because of the profusion of the ointment, but the Pharisee only thought within his own mind why Christ, if He is a Prophet, allows Himself to be touched by a sinner: here, however, Judas murmured because of the profusion of the ointment, which was sufficiently precious, and Christ defended that deed with an apology: there Christ informed Simon about true love, an undoubted sign and proof of justifying faith, and announced to the anointing woman the remission of sins through faith: something of which sort was not done in this place, but the avarice of Judas Iscariot was noted and the piety of the anointing woman was merely commended: Joh. XII. 6. 8. whence Irenaeus, lib. III. advers. haeres. c. XIV., when he enumerates those things which we know through Luke alone, reckons among them the conversion of the sinner and the parable about the two debtors spoken to Simon the Pharisee, because this history was described by Luke alone. But that the opinion has prevailed in the Roman Church that it was the same woman of whom Luke narrates, with her name passed over in silence, and who in John XI is called the sister of Lazarus: Lyranus notes that this came about because Gregory the Great was of this opinion, from whom it was brought into the ecclesiastical office, into which, indeed, who would doubt that many false, absurd, and ridiculous things have crept? See Casaub. Exercit. XIV. n. 17. p. 293.

But that neither woman is Magdalene is easily evident: For neither was the sister of Lazarus ever called by that name, and whereas he was of Bethany, it is implied that Magdalene was a Galilean, Matth. XXVII. 16, Marc. XV. 40, who is also said to have been delivered by Christ when she was possessed by seven demons, which is not established concerning the sister of Lazarus. Moreover, Grotius not badly infers from this that the anointing woman of Luke is different from Magdalene, because Luke, immediately after the narrative about the anointing woman, adds mention of the women who followed JESUS, and among them Magdalene, with the note added concerning the cast-out demons, and not concerning the act mentioned a little before. Therefore, the blessed Chemnitius, Harm. Evangel. c. LIIX., rightly observes that there were three different women: the sinner,

Luke 7:37. He says that Mary Magdalene, Luke 8:2, and Mary the sister of Martha, Luke 10:39, John 11:2, Matthew 26:6, are the same person, and that this is sufficiently manifest from the Evangelical History, and that this evidence cannot be denied by Cornelius Jansenius, even though he has nonetheless embraced the received opinion of one Mary, impiously preferring the sense of men to the testimony of the Gospel. Compare also B. Gerhard's Harmony, ch. 143, and Vossius's Evangelical Harmony, bk. 1, ch. 3, who, although he leans toward the opinion that there are not two women who anointed Christ according to Luke and the other Evangelists, nevertheless professes that he does not wish to strongly oppose the opinion that distinguishes them.

τῷ λεπρῷ] That is, to the one who was formerly a leper. For otherwise he would have been forbidden from the company of men. Such is that expression ἐκ τῆς ἰδίας ἀρετῆς. A similar manner of speaking is found above in chapter 11, verse 5, chapter 21:31, and often elsewhere. Now this man was indeed of the Pharisaic institution, but not abhorrent to the sermons of Christ: and a kinsman, as it seems, of Lazarus.

Latin:

6. ἐν Βηθανίᾳ ἐνοικία Σίμων] Nihil est certius quam à scriptoribus Evangeliorum multa referri non temporis ordine, sed ex rerum ductu. Itaque alia dicuntur praelix, alia multum retro gestae, alia in retro acta ob bella et occasiones: ipse occasiones narrandi non caedem omnibus. Hunc historiam videntur Matthaeus & Marcus hoc loco posuisse, ut notent quid Judam ad facinus impulisset. Nam ἀμέσως subsequitur id quod ad Judam pertinet. Lucas idem hoc narrare occupavit cum sermones quosdam recitasset ad poenitentiae commendationem pertinentes. Voluit enim simul illi exemplo confirmare quanta benignitate Christus profecisset mulierem multis olim peccatis inquinatam, sed ductam animi poenititudine. Johannes autem hanc historiam suo tempori reddidit, tum ad confirmandum quod de Lazaro dixerat (nam Lazarus huic convivio interfuit) tum ad connectendaque sequentia: id autem tempus fuit vespere, exacto jam Sabbati die, ita ut unctionem nullâ jam religio impedirent. Non tantum unam eandem fuisse mulierem, sed & factum idem, cur nequeo videre; neque enim temere multiplicanda sunt historia. Matthaeo & Marco omnia conveniunt. Matthaeo, Marco & Lucae convenit quod haec gesta in convivio, in domo Simonis, quod mulier adventat habens ἀλάβαστρον μύρου quo Jesum perfundit. Matthaeo, Marco & Johanni, quod haec gesta in Bethania, in convivio, quod unguentum a mulier allatum maximi erat pretii, quod reprehensa est hoc nomine mulier ab uno discipulorum (nam ita pluralis accisus) velut prodiga, Judam autem Ioannes nominant; rectius is sumptus factus esset in pauperes quod Christus mulierem defendit, interpretazione benigna ad pollincturam suam hunc honorem pertinere. Hae circumstantiae sunt taxis repent qui ad diversis temporibus congruunt. Rursus Luce cum Iohanne convenit, quod haec mulier pedes Christo perfudit & capillitio foveavit: quod idem aliter expressum fuit a verbo et capillo; utque a Iohanne constet, ipse enarravit. Adde quod Iohannes Mariam ...Lazari sororem haec velut peculiarì note describit, quod ea est quae Christi pedes perfudit & detersit. Non poterat autem certa fatis nota sumi ex eo quod saepius accideret. Quod autem per πρόληψιν id dicitur à Iohanne, non magis novum est, quam quod Judas, ubi prima Apostolo- rum sit mentio, proditoris cognomento insignitur. Quid igitur est quod nos cogat diversa facta fingere? An quod apud Matthæum & Marcum capitis, apud Lucam & Johan- nem pedum est mentio? Atqui nihil vetat credi prius pedes perfusos, deinde & caput. An quod apud Lucam est γυνὴ ἁ- μαρτωλὸς, Mariæ autem sororis Lazari pietas prædicatur? At distinguenda sunt tempora. Vixerat olim dissolutius: ideo ἁμαρτωλὸς dicta: mox delicta vitæ prioris seria pietate pensavit: quare nec offendere nos debet, quod in domum ejus Jesus diverterit, quippe cum jam de emendata vita omni- bus constaret. Hanc autem esse Magdalenam, non æque facile probatur. Nam soror Lazari nusquam eo nomine appellatur. Et nata ea opinio videtur ex verbis Christi de pollinctura: quia Magdalena Christum ivit pollinctum. At verba Christi non futurum, sed præsens officium respiciunt, ut collatio Evangelistarum ostendit. Deinde Magdalena videtur fuisse Galilæa infra XXVII. 56. Marci XV. 40. La- zarus autem cum sororibus Judæus Bethaniensis Joh. XI. 1. De Magdalena narratur liberatam à Christo cum obsessa es- set dæmoniis septem: de Lazari sorore nihil tale. Et quod maxime notandum, Lucas statim post narrationem de fœmi- na unctrice, subjicit mentionem mulierum quæ Jesum se- ctabantur, & inter eas Magdalenæ, addens ei notam ab eje- ctis dæmoniis, & non ab actu paulo ante narrato. In con- stitutionibus etiam quæ Clementis dicuntur, distinguitur Maria Magdalena à Maria sorore Lazari. Locus est lib. III. c. 6. His quæ apud Massilienses narrantur aliquid habe- rem fidei, si de ejus famæ antiquitate constaret.

Eandem hanc esse historiam cum ea, quæ à Marco c. XIV. 3. & Joh. c. XII. 1. seqq. descripta est, quod etsi præeunte Origene tr. XXIV. in Matth. Chrysoft. hom. XXII. in Matth. & hom. LX. in Joh. nec non Euthym. in Matth. Theophyl. in Marc. te- mere Osiander in Annot. ad Harm. l. III. 5. 35. & Baronius Tom. I. Annal. ad Ann. 32. num. 27. ne- gant, probe observatum est Grotio: de quo Au- gustinus l. II. de conf. Evangel. c. LXXIX. Non est dubium, quod hi tres Evangelistæ eandem rem narrent gestam in Bethania. Quæ etiam Dionys. Carthus. Fabri Stapulens. Jodoci Clichtovei, Salme- ronis, Maldonati, Jansenii & Barradii est senten- tia; Omnes enim circumstantiæ congruunt, ean- demque esse historiam convincunt. Matthæo & Marco, uti recte Grotius, omnia conveniunt. Matthæo, Marco & Johanni, quod hæc gesta in Bethania, in convivio, quod unguentum à mu- liere allatum maximi erat pretii, quod reprehen- sa est hoc nomine mulier ab uno discipulorum (nam ita pluralis accipi solet, Judam autem Jo- hannes nominat) velut prodiga, hoc obtentu quod rectius is sumtus factus esset in pauperes: quod Christus mulierem defendit, interpretatione be- nigna imo verissima, ad pollincturam suam hunc honorem pertinere. Hæ circumstantiæ sunt ἀκριβέστεραι, quam ut diversis temporibus congruant. Nec vero illa bidui ante Pascha no- tatio ad unctionem præsentem pertinet: quam ex occasione tantum hic referunt Matthæus & Mar- cus: recensitam suo ordine & tempore à Johanne, quod nempe sex diebus ante Pascha contigerit. Neque etiam domus in qua celebratum convi- vium, diversitatem parit, si quidem apud Johannem id non reperiatur, quod in domo Lazari paratum convivium sit, uti volunt Chrysostomus & Theo- phylactus; sed simpliciter dicatur: fecerunt autem ei cænam ibi. Matthæus autem & Marcus expri- munt domum Simonis diserte. Cæterum in eo assensum non meretur Grotius, quod Historiam etiam Lucæ de muliere peccatrice c. VII. eandem cum hac nostra esse vult; utut ejus etiam senten- tiæ Rupertus comment. in Joh. XII. fuerit. Nam repugnat tempus: quum illa Lucæ historia de a- ctione à peccatrice muliere facta non ultimo mini- sterii anno biduo ante Pascha σαυρώσιμον contige- rit, sed secundo anno, ut sacra historia docet. Re- pugnat etiam locus: siquidem illa in Galilæa, hæc in Judæa in castello Bethaniæ: illa in Simonis Pha- risæi, hæc in Simonis leprosi domo contigerit; quas duas personas etsi Chrysostom. homil. XXCl. in Matth. Ambrof. l. VI. in Luc. c. VII. & autor serm. de lotion. ped. apud Cyprianum, Gregor. M. Cor- nel. Jansenius, Baronius T. I. Ann. 32, n. 17. ut & Maldonatus Jesuita in Matth. XXVI. præeunte Jo- hanne Fabro Episcopo Roffensi in libro de una Maria, & Natali Beda, pro una habeant, rectius tamen Origenes tr. XXXV. in Matth. Basilius Se- leuciens. homil. de Lazar. Hieronymus, Augustinus lib. II. de consens. cap. 79. Beda in Luc. VII. Theo- phylactus & Euthymius in h. l. distinguunt: quia Pharisæus animo hypocritico Christum convivio excepit: Simon vero leprosus optimo & bene- fico animo. Neque congruunt satis aliæ circum- stantiæ: cum mulier quæ apud Lucam unxisse di- citur, peccatrix notoria fuerit: hæc autem à pietate commendetur, illa & lacrymis pedes rigarit Christi, & capillis terserit, atque osculata sit, quæ signa pœnitentiæ fuêre: hæc autem non pœnitentiæ causa fudisse lacrymas, sed tantum ὡς τὸ ἐνταφιάσαι unxisse corpus Christi perhibeatur: Illa pedes Christi tantum unguento dicitur unxis- se: hæc autem non pedes solum, Joh. XII. 3. sed & caput, Matth. XXVI. 7. Marc. XIV. 3. Quo de Hie- ronymus in h. l. Nemo putet eandem esse quæ super caput effudit unguentum, & quæ super pedes. Illa enim & lachrymis lavat & crine tergit, & manife- ste meretrix appellatur: de hac autem nihil tale scriptum est. Nec enim poterat statim capite Do- mini meretrix digna fieri. Circa illius unctionem non murmuravit quisquam ob profusionem un- guenti, sed Pharisæus solum penes animum suum cogitavit, cur Christus à peccatrice si Propheta sit, se attingi patiatur: hic autem murmuravit Ju- das ob profusionem unguenti satis pretiosi, & fa- ctum illud Christus apologia defendit: ibi Simo- nem Christus informavit de vera dilectione, fidei justificæ signo ac documento indubitato & unctri- ci remissionem peccatorum per fidem annuncia- vit: quale quid hoc loco non factum, sed Judæ I- schariotis avaritia notata mulieris unctricis pie- tas commendata solum est: Joh. XII. 6. 8. unde Ire- næus lib. III. advers. hæres. c. XIV. cum ea enume- rat, quæ per solum Lucam novimus illis accenset conversionem peccatricis, & parabolam de duo- bus debitoribus ad Simonem Pharisæum dictam, quod hæc historia à solo Luca descripta sit. Quod autem in Ecclesia Romana sententia illa obtinuerit, quod eadem mulier fuerit de qua Lucas narrat ta- cito ejus nomine, & quæ Joh. XI. dicitur soror La- zari: id inde factum notat Lyranus, quod Gregor. M. hujus opinionis fuerit, à quo ea in officium Ecclesiasticum relata est, in quod vero multa falsa, absurda, ridicula irrepsisse ecquis dubitet? Vide Casaub. Exercit. XIV. n. 17. p. 293.

Neutram autem mulierem Magdalenam esse, facile patet: Nam neque Lazari soror uspiam eo nuncupata est nomine, & quum ille Bethaniensis fuerit. Magdalena Galilæa fuisse innuitur Matth. XXVII. 16. Marc. XV. 40. quæ etiam liberata à Christo dicitur, quum obsessa esset septem dæmo- niis, quod de Lazari sorore non constat. Unctri- cem autem Lucæ à Magdalena diversam esse ex eo non male colligit Grotius, quod Lucas statim post narrationem de fæmina unctrice subjiciat mentio- nem mulierum quæ JESUM sectatæ sunt, & inter eas Magdalenæ, addita nota ab ejectis Dæmo- niis, & non ab actu paulo ante memorato. Ideo recte B. Chemnitius Harm. Evangel. c. LIIX. tres diversas fæminas fuisse observat: Peccatricem,

Luc. VII. 37. Mariam Magdalenam, Luc. IIX. 2. & Mariam sororem Marthæ Luc. X. 39. Joh. XI. 2. Matth. XXVI. 6. idque satis manifestum esse ex Historia Evangelica ait, nec à Cornelio Jansenio negari posse hanc evidentiam, etsi hic nihilomi- nus receptam opinionem de una Maria amplexus sit, impie hominum sensum præferens testimonio Evangelii. Conf. & B. Gerhardi Harm. cap. CXLIII. & Vossii Harm. Evangel. l. I. cap. III. qui etsi in eam propendeat sententiam, quod non duæ sint mulieres, quæ inunxerint Christum a- pud Lucam, & reliquos Evangelistas, profitetur tamen se nolle magnopere sententiæ, quæ illas distin- guit, adversari.

τῷ λεπρῷ] Id est, τῷ πρὶν λεπρῷ. Nam alioqui interdi- ctum ei fuisset hominum commercio. Tale est illud ἐκ τῆς ἰδίας ἀρετῆς. Simile loquendi genus supra cap. XI. vers. 5. cap. XXI. 31. & alibi sæpe. Fuit autem hic homo Phari- sæici quidem instituti, sed à Christi sermonibus non abhor- rens: & consanguineus ut videtur Lazari.

## 26:7
Verse 7. Ἀλάβαστρον μύρου] Since Mark narrates that this vessel was broken by the woman, no doubt so that the ointment might flow more freely, I entirely agree with Epiphanius, who explains it as βικίον ὑέλινον: and all the more so because the author of the Etymologicum also interprets ἀλάβαστρον as σκεῦός τι ἐξ ὑέλου, as has been observed by that man of highest erudition, Isaac Casaubon; who from this conjectures that what happened to this word is what happened to many others, that having been first used for a species, it gradually extended itself to the signification of a genus. But to me it seems much more probable that the word ἀλάβαστρον, or as others write it ἀλάβαστον, in its primitive notion signifies τὸ μυχηρὸν, as Pollux often interprets it, whence we also read of χρύσεα ἀλάβαστρα: and the LXX Interpreters in 2 Kings 21, what is in Hebrew צלחת, translate as ἀλάβαστρον, others as πυξίον: but because the onyx stone was usually used for this purpose, it began to be called not alabaster, but alabastrites. For Pliny and Dioscorides teach that it is the same as the Onyx. The Arabic interpreter has placed here قارورة, which greatly favors those who think it was a glass vessel. For by the same word among the Arabs a glass vessel is usually meant, in which the urine of the sick is kept for doctors to examine. An old Greek epigram: νάρδον ὑπὸ γλαυκῆς κλειομένην ὑέλου: in which place Salmasius, in his Plinian Exercises, a work of immense fruit, warned that by the word nard, nard ointment is understood. Now it is called an ἀλάβαστρον of ointment here, as in Horace, 'Nardi plenus onyx.' For here too, what Matthew and Luke call ointment in general, Mark and John teach was nard: whose scent is highly commended in Song of Solomon 1:11. An alabaster full of ointment is also mentioned by Cicero. In Aelian there is: ἔδωκε ἀλάβαστρον αὐτῷ κῇ εἶχεν αὐτῆ μύρον.

κατέχεεν ἐπὶ τὴν κεφαλὴν αὐτῷ] Thus Plato in Republic 3: μύρον κατὰ τῆς κεφαλῆς καταχεάντες. It appears, however, that this was done not for the sake of pleasure, but as a testimony of the highest honor. For in Plato it is preceded by: 'we would worship him as a sacred and wonderful being.' And Proclus on that passage: 'pouring ointment as is the custom for statues in the most holy temples.' See also Genesis 28:18. Nor did this woman have any other purpose, who also threw herself at his feet in the manner of a suppliant.

Latin:

Vers. 7. Ἀλάβαστρον μύρου] Cum vas hoc fractum à mulie- re narret Marcus, nimirum ut largius unguentum flueret, omnino Epiphanio assentior, exponenti βικίον ὑέλινον: eo- que magis quia & Etymologici auctor ἀλάβαστρον interpre- tatur σκεῦός τι ἐξ ὑέλου ut à summæ eruditionis viro Isaa- co Casaubono observatum est; qui hinc conjecturam fa- cit evenisse huic voci quod multis aliis, ut primum usur- pata de specie, paulatim ad generis significationem se porrigeret. At mihi multo probabilius videtur vocem ἀλάβαστρον, aut ut alii scribunt ἀλάβαστον, primitiva notio- ne significare τὸ μυχηρὸν ut sæpe Pollux interpretatur, un- de & χρύσεα ἀλάβαστρα legimus: & LXX. Interpretes 2. Reg. XXI. quod in Hebræo est צלחת vertunt ἀλάβα- στρον, alii πυξίον: at quia lapis onyx plerumque ei rei usur- pari soleret, inde cœptum dici eum lapidem non alaba- strum, sed alabastriten. Eundem enim esse cum Onyche docent Plinius & Dioscorides. Arabs interpres hoc loco posuit قارورة quod multum favet iis qui vitreum vas fuisse existimant. Nam eadem voce Arabibus dici so- let vitreum vasculum, in quo ægroti lotium à Medicis spectandum asservant. Vetus epigramma Græcum, νάρδον ὑπὸ γλαυκῆς κλειομένην ὑέλου: quo loco nardi voce nardi- num unguentum intelligi in Plinianis exercitationibus, immensæ frugis opere, monuit Salmasius. Ἀλάβαστρον autem μύρου hic dicitur, ut apud Horatium, Nardi ple- nus onyx. Nam & hic quod μύρον in genere vocant Mat- thæus & Lucas, Marcus & Johannes nardum docent fuis- se: cujus odor maxi ne commendatur Cant. I. 11. memo- ratur & Ciceroni alabaster plenus unguenti. Apud Ælia- num est: ἔδωκε ἀλάβαστρον αὐτῷ κῇ εἶχεν αὐτῆ μύρον.

κατέχεεν ἐπὶ τὴν κεφαλὴν αὐτῷ] Ita Plato de Republica III. μύρον κατὰ τῆς κεφαλῆς καταχεάντες. Apparet autem factum id non delectandi gratia, sed in honoris maximi testimonium. Nam præcedit apud Platonem προσκυνοῖ- μεν ἂν αὐτὸν ὡς ἱερὸν καὶ θαυμαστόν. Et Proclus ad eum lo- cum μύρον καταχέας ὡς ἂν ἐν τοῖς ἁγιωτάτοις ἱεροῖς ἀγαλμά- των θέμις. Vide & Gen. XXVIII. 18. Neque aliud huic mulieri propositum, quæ etiam pedibus advoluta est sup- plicum ritu.

## 26:8
Verse 8. οἱ μαθηταὶ] Either an enallage, as we have said, or because what one had begun wickedly, others were following imprudently.

εἰς τί ἡ ἀπώλεια αὕτη] That is, wastefulness: for thus, as has been noted by a most learned man, the Hebrews use תשחית. Such is that Latin saying: they know how to waste, they do not know how to give. It is well said by Epictetus that most things have two handles, as is the case here. Ointment of such value perishes uselessly: it is spent on a superfluous scent when the poor could have been fed: this is the left handle. But this is the right handle: The woman, weary of her former life, follows with every kind of honor him through whom she has been reformed: nor does she spare any expense or effort to make that testified to all. Praiseworthy is the repentance: praiseworthy is the humility of spirit: praiseworthy is the diligence. Love, grasping such handles, interprets everything that can be done in the more benign part, and loves not only virtues, but also the images of virtues: and if there is any fault in the manner of acting, it forgives the affection of the one acting.

Latin:

Vers. 8. οἱ μαθηταὶ] Aut enallage, ut diximus, aut quod unus improbe cœperat, alii imprudenter sequeban- tur.

εἰς τί ἡ ἀπώλεια αὕτη] Id est ἀσωτία: nam ita, ut nota- tum est a viro doctissimo תשחית usurpant Hebræi Ta- le est illud Latinum: perdere sciunt, donare nesciunt. Be- ne autem dictum ab Epicteto res plerasque binas habere ansas, ut hic. Tanti pretii unguentum inutiliter perit: odori supervacuo impenditur quo pasci pauperes poterant: sinistra hæc ansa est: Hæc vero dextra ansa: Mulier prio- ris vitæ pertæsa omni honoris genere eum prosequitur per quem emendata est: neque ulli sumtui aut operæ parcit, ut id omnibus testatum faciat. Laudanda pœnitentia: lau- danda animi demissio: laudanda sedulitas. Tales ansas arripiens dilectio, omnia qua fieri potest interpretatur in partem benigniorem, neque virtutes tantum amat, sed & simulachra virtutum: & si quid in modo agendi est vi- tii, condonat agentis affectui.

## 26:10
Verse 10. κόπους παρέχετε] The same manner of speaking is used not only here by Mark, but also elsewhere by Luke, ch. 11:7, ch. 18:5.

ἔργον γὰρ καλὸν εἰργάσατο εἰς ἐμὲ] The end especially distinguishes actions not clothed by law: now the end here is to affect Christ with honor.

Latin:

Vers. 10. κόπους παρέχετε] Idem loquendi genus non tantum hic Marcus, sed & alibi Lucas usurpat c. XI. 7. c. XIIX. 5.

ἔργον γὰρ καλὸν εἰργάσατο εἰς ἐμὲ] Actiones lege non ve- stitas finis præcipue discriminat: finis autem hic opumus Christum honore afficere.

## 26:11
Verse 11. πάντοτε γὰρ τὲς πτωχὺς ἔχετε μεθ' ἑαυτῶν] πτωχὸς in these books is not one who seeks a living by begging, as can be seen in many other places, especially 2 Corinthians 8:9: but one who barely has from his own wherewith to live; you would translate it more correctly as needy than as poor. For poverty is not having nothing, as Martial said. Therefore Servius teaches in the first book of the Aeneid that destitution is worse than poverty. Thus for the Hebrews אביון is more dejected than עני. However, what is said in Deuteronomy, to which Christ refers here, does not conflict: 'there shall not be among you one who is in need,' ch. 15:11, with what was said in the same chapter, verse 5: 'there shall be no one in you who is in need': for the latter is of one commanding, the former of one predicting. There will therefore be those who are in need, in such a great people, indeed: but the rest ought not to suffer them to remain in destitution: which sense the seventh verse indicates clearly enough. Tertullian saw this correctly in book 4 against Marcion: 'But let there not be,' he says, 'one in need among you,' that is, take care of your own accord that there is not: by which he the more prejudices that it must be given to the one asking in the following verses: 'if there shall be one in need from your brothers, you shall not turn away your heart nor close your hand from your needy brother.' And in this manner the Rabbi Solomon Benaderet reconciles those passages.

But me you do not always have] He signifies that his death is imminent: as often as there is doubt about which of several things ought to be done rather, the deeds themselves ought not to be estimated nakedly by themselves, but account must also be taken of the times and other circumstances. Thus, as often as laws are compared with one another, it must be seen, says Cicero in De Inventione II, whether it is necessary immediately: whether it admits of some delay and postponement: for that which must be done immediately ought to be completed first. Such was also the contention of deeds here. The needy could be helped at any time: for Christ who was present to be honored, there was need for haste. Mark expresses this sense most openly: 'For you always have the poor with you, and whenever you wish, you can do them good; but me you do not always have.'

Latin:

Vers. 11. πάντοτε γὰρ τὲς πτωχὺς ἔχετε μεθ' ἑαυτῶν] πτω- χὸς in his libris non est qui mendicando victum quærit, ut multis aliis in locis tum præcipue 2. Cor. IIX. 9. videre est: sed qui de suo vix habet unde vivat, egentem rectius quam pauperem verteris. Neque enim est paupertas nihil habe- re, ut Martialis dixit. Ideo pejorem esse egestatem pau- pertate, ad primum Æneidos docet Servius. Sic Hebræis אביון dejectus quam עני. Non pugnat autem quod in Deuteronomio dicitur quo hic respicit Christus: non deerit inter vos qui egeat, cap. XV. 11. cum eo quod eodem capite dictum erat commate 5. non erit in te qui egeat: nam hoc præcipientis est, illud prædicentis. Erunt igitur qui egeant, in tanto quippe populo: sed cæteri pati non de- bent, ut in egestate permaneant: quem sensum aperte satis indicat comma septimum. Vidit hoc recte Tertul- lianus IV. adversus Marcionem: Sed non sit, inquit, in- digens in te, id est cura ultro ne sit: quo magis petenti præ- judicat dandum etiam in sequentibus: si fuerit indigens ex fratribus tuis non avertes cor tuum nec constringes manum tuam à fratre indigente. Et hunc in modum illa loca con- ciliat Rabbinus Solomo Benaderet.

ἐμὲ δὲ ἐ πάντοτε ἔχετε] Mortem imminentem sibi signi- ficat: quoties quid de pluribus rebus potius faciendum sit ambigitur, non debent ipsa per se facta nude æstimari, sed temporum quoque & aliarum circumstantiarum habenda est ratio. Ita quoties leges inter se comparantur, viden- dum, ait Cicero de inventione II. utrum statim necesse sit: utrum habeat aliquam moram & sustentationem: nam id quod statim faciendum sit, perfici prius oportet. Ta- lis erat & hic factorum contentio. Egentibus quovis tempore succurri poterat: Christo præsenti ut honos habe- retur, properandum erat. Hunc sensum apertissime expri- mit Marcus πάντοτε γὰρ τὲς πτωχὲς ἔχετε μεθ' ἑαυτῶν, κὶ ὅ- τανθέλητε, δύνασθε αυτὲς ἐν ποιῆσαι· ἐμὲ ἐ πάντοτε ἔχει τε.

## 26:12
Vers. 12. 'For my burial she has done' Mark: 'She has anticipated anointing my body for burial.' John: 'She has kept it for the day of my burial.' The sense seems to me to be: You think it is extravagant spending that this woman has poured this precious ointment on me: and yet, if that expense had been spent on a dead body, no one would disapprove: for it is not only accepted by custom, but is also held to be praiseworthy: especially around kings, such as she believes me to be. Why is the honor that would be praiseworthy in a dead person invidious in a living one? Little remains for me until death: which I have often said to both you and others: and so this woman, when she understood that my death was imminent (for other women also had understood this, Luke 24:7), already holds me as if for dead, and has anticipated that solemn duty by only a short time. Mark signifies this sense most openly with the word 'anticipated'. Here 'to bury' is to be interpreted by the ellipsis of the little word 'as if': she did it as if to prepare me for burial. Which little word the Syriac interpreter prudently added here, as also in this history in Mark. And to John, 'the day of burial' is the day of the quasi-preparation for burial. Nor is it rare for the Hebrews that someone is said to do something to this or that end, which nevertheless is not intended by him, but the act follows from elsewhere, as Proverbs 28:36, chapter 17:19, 1 Kings 17:18, and often elsewhere. Thus also among Homer, interpreters note that 'as' is often understood as a comparative, as when the poet says 'like fire,' that is, as if fiery. The LXX had said 'to bury' for 'to prepare for burial' in the last chapter of Genesis: from which passage the antiquity of the custom is clear, which Ennius also mentions: 'A good woman washed and anointed the body of Tarquin.'

Doubtless the Tyrrhenians, offspring of the Tyrians, had introduced this rite among others into Italy. Moreover, this custom of anointing bodies, like most praiseworthy institutions of the Jews, was also observed by the ancient Christians as a testimony of the believed resurrection. Tertullian in his Apology: 'If the Arabians complain, let them know that the Sabaeans spend more and dearer merchandise on burying Christians than on fumigating the gods.' Pliny had said in book 12, chapter 18: 'heaped up in piles for the honor of corpses what is given to the gods in single grains.'

Latin:

Vers. 12. πρὸς τὸ ἐνταφιάσαι με ἐποίησεν] Marcus προ- έλαβε μυρίσαι με τὸ σῶμα εἰς ἐνταφιασμὸν. Johannes εἰς τὴν ἡμέραν τῶ ἐνταφιασμῶ μὲ τετήρηκεν ἀυτὸ. Sensus mihi esse videtur: Putatis sumtum esse nepotinum, quod hæc mulier me pretioso unguento perfudit: atqui, si is sumtus impensus esset in corpus mortuum nemo impro- baret: est enim id non tantum receptum moribus, sed & laudabile habetur: circa reges maxime qualem illa me credit. Qui honos in mortuo futurus erat laudabilis, cur in vivente est invidiosus? ad mortem parum mihi restat: quod & vobis & aliis sæpe dixi: ita que hæc mulier cum mor- tem meam instare intellexerit (nam & aliæ mulieres hoc intellexerant, Luc. XXIV. 7.) habet me jam quali pro mor- tuo, atque officium illud solenne modico tantum tempore antevertit. Hunc sensum apertissime significat Marcus vo- ce προέλαβε. Hic τὸ ἐνταφιάσαι interpretandum est per ἐλ- λειψιν voculæ ὡσεὶ: fecit quasi ad me pollinciendum. Quam voculam prudenter hic ut & in hac apud Marcum historia, addidit Syrus interpres. Et Johanni ἡμέρα ἐνταφιασμῶ est dies quasi pollincturæ. Nec rarum est Hebræis ut quis di- catur facere aliquid ad hunc aut illum finem, qui tamen ab ipso non intenditur, sed actum ejus aliunde consequitur, ut Proverb. IIX. 36. c. XVII. 19. I. Reg. XVII. 18. & ali- bi sæpe. Sic & apud Homerum ὡς comparativum sæpe subaudiri notant interpretes, ut cum dicit Poë a δέμας πυ- ρὸς, id est quasi igneum. ἐνταφιάζειν pro pollingire dixe- rant LXX. capite ultimo Geneseos: ex quo loco patet an- tiquitas moris, cujus & Ennius meminit: Tarquinii corpus bona femina lavit & unxit.

Nimirum Tyriorum proles Tyrrheni hunc inter cæteros ri- tum Italiæ intulerant. Morem autem hunc ungendorum corporum, ut pleraque instituta laudabilia Judæorum, ob- servarunt & Christiani veteres in testimonium creditæ re- surrectionis. Tertullianus Apologetico: Si Arabiæ que- runtur, sciant Sabæi pluris & carioris merces suas Christianis sepeliendis profligari quam diis fumigandu. Plinius dixerat libro XII. c. XIIX. acerbatim congesta honori cadaverum quæ diis per singulas micas dantur.

## 26:13
Vers. 13. 'Memorial'] Thus the LXX are accustomed to translate the Hebrew 'zikron,' which often signifies not so much a monument as a memory, as Exodus 17:14, 'write this as a memorial in a book,' and Numbers 5:18, 'a sacrifice of memorial.'

Latin:

Vers. 13. μνημόσυνον] Ita vertere solent LXX. Hebræum זכרון quod sæpe non tam monumentum, quam memo- riam significat, ut Exod. XVII. 14. κατάγραψον τῦτο εἰς μνημόσυνον ἐν βιβλίῳ, & Num. V. 18. θυσίαν τῶ μνημοσύνε.

## 26:14
Vers. 14. 'Then'] After the inserted narrative pertaining to connecting the matters, Matthew returns to the order of time. For this seems to have happened a little after the very consultation of the Sanhedrin which he had mentioned above. For this opportunity of Judas offering himself provided a reason for changing the plan.

Latin:

Vers. 14. τότε] Post interjectam narrationem ad res contexendas pertinentem, redit Matthæus ad temporis ordinem. Factum enim hoc videtur paulo post ipsam consultationem Synedrii cujus supra meminerat. Hæc- enim Judæ se offerentis occasio consilii mutandi causam præbuit.

## 26:15
Verse 15. ἔστησαν] They appointed, as the old Latin version translates very well here. For that is what it is to promise in law. It corresponds to the Hebrew וישקלו. Compare Mark chapter XIV. 11. Luke XXII. 5.

τριάκοντα ἀργύρια] Since Judas had left it to the discretion of the priests how much they valued Jesus, they valued him at the lowest amount any man could be valued. For τριάκοντα ἀργύρια, or silver shekels, are the same number of tetradrachms, which the LXX, because they use double drachmas, call didrachms. Thus in Exodus XXI. 32, the head of a slave is valued at thirty shekels, where in the Greek it is τριάκοντα δίδραχμα, and in Josephus the same number of tetradrachms. But in the prophecy of Zechariah, which will be examined below, the same LXX translate it as τριάκοντα ἀργύρους, where 'shekels' is to be understood: as here 'coins'. For to the Jews the shekel is the coin par excellence. The very passage of Zechariah itself shows that this sum has the meaning of a cheap price: and the Hebrews note that a male human was generally valued at fifty shekels, and a female slave at thirty. In the second book of Samuel also, chapter XXII. 11, כסף is translated in Greek as shekels of silver. Wherefore one should not think here of pounds or talents. This serves to note that Judas's mind was so enslaved to avarice that he could be driven to crime for any price whatsoever.

That passage of Zechariah has been treated at length in the Anti-Grotian annotations on Zechariah. Now thirty shekels make fifteen Vallenses. For a shekel was of the value of half a Joachimicus, or Vallensis, which we call Thalers. We have proven in our treatise on Coins that there is no distinction between the common and the sacred shekel. Compare Exod. XXI. 32, chap. XXX. 13, Lev. XXVII. 13, Num. III. 47, Ezech. XLV. 12. Grotius is correct, however: 'This serves to note that Judas's mind was so enslaved to avarice that he could be driven to crime for any price whatsoever.' For the fact that some of those people—Budé, for instance, Baronius, Spondanus, Torniellus—make those 30 pieces of silver into 30 silver pounds, or three hundred gold pieces, or even crowns, is vain and devoid of any foundation, nor does it seem consistent with the avarice of the High Priests. But the distinction between the masculine and feminine sex, which is brought forward from the Hebrews, is not recognized in the law, since male and female slaves are valued equally at the price of 30 shekels in Exod. XXI. 32.

Latin:

Vers. 15. ἔστησαν] Constituerunt, ut optime hic vertit vetus Latinus. Id enim in jure est promittere. Respon- det Hebræo וישקלו Confer Marci cap. XIV. 11. Luc. XXII. 5.

τριάκοντα ἀργύρια] Cum Judas Sacerdotum arbitrio permisisset quanti Jesum æstimarent, illi æstimarunt quanti minimi homo ullus æstimari poterat. Nam τριάκοντα ἀργύρια sive sicli argentei, sunt totidem τετράδραχμα, quæ LXX. quia duplaribus utuntur drachmis, δίδραχμα vo- cant. Itaque Exodi XXI. 32. caput servi æstimatur tri- ginta siclis, ubi in Græco est τριάκοντα δίδραχμα, apud Iosephum totidem τετράδραχμα. At in Zachariæ vatici- nio, quod infra examinabitur, iidem LXX. τριάκοντα ἀργύρους vertunt, ubi subintelligendum est σίκλους: ut hic νομίσματα. Nam Judæis σίκλος νόμισμα κατ' ἐξοχὴν. Qui ipse Zachariæ locus ostendit eam summam vilis pretii habere significationem: & notant Hebræi hominem ma- rem plerumque æstimatum quinquaginta siclis, ancillam triginta. Samuelis quoque secundo libro cap. XXII. 11. כסף Græce vertitur σίκλοι ἀργυρίου. Quare neque de libris neque de talentis hic cogitandum est. Facit hoc ad notandum Judæ animum ita avaritiæ mancipatum, ut quo- vis pretio impelli ad scelus potuerit.

De illo Zachariæ loco prolixe actum est in an- notatis Anti-Grotianis ad Zachariam. Triginta autem sicli efficiunt Vallenses quindecim. Siclus enim valoris fuit dimidii Joachimici, vel Vallen- sis, quos Taleros vocamus. Distinctionem au- tem inter vulgarem & sacrum siclum nullam esse, probavimus tract. de Nummis. Conf. Exod. XXI. 32. cap. XXX. 13. Lev. XXVII. 13. Num. III. 47. Ezech. XLV. 12. Recte autem Grotius; Facit hoc ad no- tandum Judæ animum ita avaritiæ mancipatum, ut quovis pretio impelli ad scelus potuerit. Nam quod XXX. libras argenteas, aut trecentos aureos, vel etiam coronatos nonnulli ex istis 30. argenteis fa- ciunt, Budæus puta, Baronius, Spondanus, Torni- ellus, vanum est, omnique fundamento destitui- tur, nec avaritiæ Pontificum consentaneum vide- tur. Discrimen vero inter masculinum & fœmini- num sexum, quod ex Ebræis adfertur, nullum in lege agnoscitur, siquidem ex æquo servi & ancillæ 30. siclorum pretio Exod. XXI. 32. æstimentur.

## 26:16
Verse 16. ἐυκαιρίαν] שׁעה.

Latin:

Vers. 16. ἐυκαιρίαν] שׁעה.

## 26:17
Verse 17. τῇ δὲ πρώτη τῶν ἀζύμων] Mark adds ὅτε τὸ πάσχα ἔθυον, the Jews, that is, which the Syriac expresses, that is, on the day on which it was the custom for the Passover to be sacrificed. Luke says ἐν ᾗ ἔδει θύεσθαι τὸ πάσχα: by comparing these passages with one another, I prove that the Passover was sacrificed by the Jews on that day on which it was necessary, if it is to be contended that 'de' must be taken for 'that which it behooves'. The days of Unleavened Bread are sometimes counted as seven, during which entire days it was forbidden to eat anything leavened, and sometimes eight, by counting the Paschal day, because the observance of Unleavened Bread began in its latter part. We just cited a passage from Josephus in which he attributes eight days to the Unleavened Bread, whereas elsewhere he assigns seven days to it. Thus the first of the Unleavened Bread is often called the first of the seven days during which nothing but unleavened bread was eaten. This is the first day on which they began to eat unleavened bread, that is, the Paschal day. For that is the peculiar character of the fourteenth of Nisan, as we said above. These writers, however, do not say that the hour of sacrifice had already arrived, but that the day itself had arrived. I do not understand this as if the sun had already set: for soon after follows ὀψίας δὲ γενομένης, but I think it describes the time when the sun was near setting: which Luke calls ἦλθε δὲ ἡ ἡμέρα, that is, the twenty-four hour period. For common speech also says that the day has come which is imminent. And Luke said elsewhere: γενομένης ἡμέρας, where Mark says πρωὶ ἔννυχον λίαν. Thus below in verse 71, ἐξελθόντα signifies one preparing to go out: for the following words show that Peter had not yet gone out at that time. These things were done, therefore, towards the sunset of the 13th day, at which time the fourteenth day began among the Jews. These things contribute much to the illustration of the controversy long debated in every direction among learned men, to which I hope to bring some light.

But that cannot be proven from a comparison of these passages. For the words of Mark, ὅτε τὸ πάσχα ἔθυον, refer to the law, namely that on that day the Passover ought to have been sacrificed by divine law, as the same are explained by Luke, and not that the Passover was sacrificed by the Jews at that time: nor is the word 'Jews' added:

and therefore it is better rendered indefinitely by the Syriac, 'on the day on which it was the custom for the Passover to be sacrificed.' But whether the Jews observed the custom on that same day in that year is not expressed.

Furthermore, Grotius indeed correctly observes that it is not said that the hour of sacrifice had already arrived, but that the day itself had arrived: but he does not correctly understand the day to have arrived as meaning that it had not yet arrived, but was imminent: so as to infer that these things were done towards the sunset of the 13th day, at which time the fourteenth day began among the Jews. But the Evangelists Matthew and Mark do not say πρὸ τῶν ἀζύμων, but τῇ πρώτῃ τῶν ἀζύμων: Luke, however, says explicitly: ἦλθε ἡ ἡμέρα τῶν ἀζύμων: whence Augustine, Ep. 86 to Casulanus, notes that although these things happened on the fifth day of the week, it is said to have happened on the first day of Unleavened Bread, because the day of the Passover, or the first of the Unleavened Bread, began around the evening of that day, so that these things happened in the morning of that day, as Theophylact thinks, in whose evening, according to the provision of the law, the first of the Unleavened Bread began, and not towards the sunset of the 13th day, as Grotius wishes.

Where do you want us to prepare for you to eat the Passover] Our Lord, most observant of the paternal law, was accustomed to eat the Passover according to the prescription at the time when all the Jews did, at the end of the fourteenth of Nisan. Now the Jews began to prepare the place in which they were to eat the Passover from that night which precedes the fourteenth day and is part of the νυχθημέρου of the fourteenth, which they still do now. A great part of that preparation is the anxious ἐκκάθαρσις τῆς ζύμης, to which Paul alludes in 1 Cor. 5:7. For anxiously on that night and in the following forenoon, they inquire whether any leaven remains anywhere, even gathering up crumbs. Then the couches are spread, the dining room is furnished, the foods are cooked. All these are works of that day, which is therefore called παρασκευὴ from the greater part, as the Passover is from the more worthy part. When therefore this night began, the disciples ask what place Christ wants prepared for himself for eating the Passover, thinking indeed that it was to be eaten according to custom at the end of that νυχθημέρου which had then begun. For I clearly cannot agree with those who think that in that year the Passover was celebrated by the Jews at a time other than it should have been. For even if some transfer of the feast day had fallen in that year, which is difficult to prove, and those who try to prove it differ greatly among themselves, that cause, for which the feast day was accustomed to be transferred by the Jews, seems to me so just that it should be considered an interpretation of the law rather than a change. For if the feast day of Unleavened Bread, which necessarily had to follow the Paschal sacrifice, were to be continued with the Sabbath, there would not indeed have followed the inconvenience that some think from the delayed cooking (for it was not permitted to cook on the Sabbath, but it was permitted on a feast day, Exod. 12:16), but after the manifold διασπορὰν of the Jews, many of whom lived in very hot places, there was a danger that the preserved carcasses would rot. Now indeed it was not credible that a ritual law, prescribed by God with such necessity that it would yield to no danger, to no inconveniences, when it has often been demonstrated elsewhere that in these laws especially τὸ ἐπιεικές ought to prevail. The transfer of the feast day to the day of the Sabbath was therefore equitable, and consequently to be observed: nor was that to be considered as conflicting with the law any more than the fact that in the time of Hezekiah the Passover was transferred from the 14th of Nisan to the fourteenth of the following month. For in these matters of rites the people safely followed the authority of the Sanhedrin, and were bound to follow it according to the law of Deuteronomy 17:8 and following. On which matter see what Maimonides prudently noted in the Guide for the Perplexed 3.41, and Moses of Coucy in the commanding precept 46. Add now that Christ, when he said: You know that within two days the Passover is at hand: he spoke of a known matter. And therefore he acknowledged no day of the Passover other than that which was publicly observed according to custom. To which must be added what we brought forward a little earlier from Mark and Luke on this matter.

Regarding the legitimate time of the Passover, Grotius easily agrees, as is evident from those things which he had noted against the second [passage]: but regarding the time of this Passover celebrated by the Jews, it can in no way be proven that he asserts they celebrated it according to the divine law: because they celebrated this Passover not on the 14th moon, but only on the following day, not on the fifth day of the week, but on the sixth: which we have confirmed above with undoubted documents. And Grotius himself saw that Christ did not celebrate the Passover with the Jews: If

ANNOTATIONS ON MATTHEW

Therefore, if the Jews observed the legitimate time, it is necessary that Christ, whom he acknowledges to have celebrated it at another time, ate the Passover at an illegitimate time: that is, he acted against the divine law, which is impious to say. Whence other authors, who affirm that the Jews celebrated this Passover on the ordinary day, namely the fourteenth moon, so that they might not have to assert that Christ acted against the law, say that he celebrated his own last Passover with the Jews: such as Alcuin, Thomas Aquinas, John Gerson, those four Cardinals Tostatus of Avila, Francisco de Toledo, Bellarmine, and Baronius, as also Cornelius a Lapide, Barradius, and Estius: and also from the Reformed, Broughton, the latest Anglican Annotators, and Cloppenburg: and finally from our own, Caspar Erasmus Brochmand, of pious memory. But why it should not be established that the Jews ate this Passover on the legitimate day, we have observed before.

Latin:

Vers. 17. τῇ δὲ πρώτη τῶν ἀζύμων] Addit Marcus ὅτε τὸ πά- σχα ἔθυον, Iudæi scilicet, quod exprimit Syrus, id est, quo die moris erat Pascha mactari. Lucas ἐν ᾗ ἔδει θύεσθαι τὸ πάσχα: quibus locis inter se collatis evinco eo die à Iudæis mactatum πάσχα, quo oportebat, si δὲ pro eo quod opor- te: sumi debere contenditur. Azymorum dies modo se- ptem numerantur, quibus integris nefas erat fermentato vesci, modo octo, annumerato die Paschali, quia parte ejus postrema incipiebat Azymorum observatio. Citavi- mus modo locum ex Iosepho in quo Azymis dies attribuit octo, cum alibi septem dies Azymis assignet. Ita prima Azymorum sæpe dicitur prima septem dierum quibus inte- gris non nisi Azyma edebantur. Hic dies prima qua edi incipiebant Azyma, id est dies Paschalis. Is enim peculia- ris est character decimæ quartæ Nisan, ut supra diximus. Non dicunt autem hi scriptores jam adventasse horam ma- ctationis, sed ipsum diem adventasse. Quod non ita intelli- go quasi jam occidisset Sol: mox enim sequitur ὀψίας δὲ γε- νομένης, sed puto describi tempus quo Sol erat prope occa- sum: quod Lucas dicit ἦλθε δὲ ἡ ἡμέρα, id est, τὸ νυχθήμε- ρον. Nam & popularis sermo venisse diem dicit qui de proximo imminet. Et Lucas alibi dixit: γενομένης ἡμέρας, ubi Marcus πρωὶ ἔννυχον λίαν. Sic infra commate 71. ἐξελ- θόντα significat exire parantem: nondum enim tum exiisse Petrum sequentia ostendunt. Facta ergo hæc sub occa- sum diei XIII. quo tempore incipiebat apud Iudæos dies decima quarta. Hæc multum faciunt ad illustrationem controversiæ inter viros eruditos in omnem partem diu versatæ, cui lucis ut spero nonnihil adferemus.

Id vero ex horum locorum collatione evinci nequit. Nam verba Marci, ὅτε τὸ πάσχα ἔθυον respi- ciunt jus, quod nempe eo die oportuerit Pascha ma- ctari jure divino, uti à Luca eadem explicantur, non vero quod tum temporis à Judæis Pascha ma- ctatum fuerit: nec de Judæis verbum additur:

ideoque indefinite à Syro melius redditur, quo die moris erat Pascha mactari. Num autem isto anno morem etiam eodem die observarint Judæi, non exprimicur.

Porro recte quidem observat Grotius, quod non dicatur jam adventasse horam mactationis, sed ipsum diem adventasse: verum non recte diem adventasse intelligit, quod nondum advenerit, sed de proximo imminuerit: ut hæc facta inferat sub occasum diei XIII. quo tempore incipiebat apud Judæos dies decima quarta. Ast Evangelistæ Mat- thæus, & Marcus non dicunt πρὸ τῶν ἀζύμων, sed τῇ πρώτῃ τῶν ἀζύμων: Lucas vero diferte: ἦλθε ἡ ἡμέρα τῶν ἀζύμων: unde Augustinus Ep. XXCVI. ad Casulan. advertit, etsi hæc contigerint feria quinta, primo tamen azymorum die contigisse dici, quia circa vesperam illius diei incipiebat Paschatos dies, vel primus azymorum, ut ita mane illius diei, ut Theophyl. censet, in cujus vespera juxta legis dispo- sitionem primus azymorum incipiebat, hæc contige- rint, non vero sub occasum diei XIII. ut vult Grotius.

Πῦ θέλεις ἑτοιμάσωμέν σοι φαγεῖν τὸ πάσχα] Dominus no- ster, observantissimus legis paternæ, solitus erat comedere Pascha ex præscripto quo tempore Judæi omnes, fine deci- mæ quartæ Nisan. Incipiebant autem Judæi locum in quo comesturi erant Pascha parare ab ea nocte quæ antecedit Solem decimum quartum & pars est τοῦ νυχθημέρου decimi quarti, quod nunc etiam faciunt. Ejus præparationis ma- gna est pars anxia ἐκκάθαρσις τῆς ζύμης, ad quam alludit Paulus 1. Cor. V. 7. Sollicite enim ea nocte & antemeridia- no tempore sequenti, inquirunt ecquid usquam fermenta- ti supersit, etiam micas colligentes. Deinde sternuntur le- cti, instruitur cœnaculum, coquuntur cibi. Hæc omnia sunt opera illius diei, qui propterea παρασκευὴ vocatur à parte majore, ut πάσχα à parte digniore. Cum ergo nox hæc inci- peret, interrogant discipuli quem locum Christus velit sibi parari edendo paschati, existimantes nempe edendum de more fine ejus νυχθημέρῳ quod tum cœperat. Plane enim assentiri illis nequeo qui putant eo anno à Iudæis Pascha ce- lebratum alio quam oportuit tempore. Nam etiamsi aliqua translatio diei festi in eum annum incidisset, quod probatu difficile est, & qui probare conantur valde inter se dissen- tiunt, ea tamen causa, propter quam à Iudæis dies festus transferri solebat, adeo mihi justa videtur, ut legis interpre- tatio potius quam mutatio sit censenda. Nam si continuare- tur dies festus Azymorum, qui Paschale sacrificium sequi necessario debebat cum Sabbato, non erat quidem secutu- rum id quod quidam putant incommodum ex dilatata co- ctione (nam coquere sabbato quidem non licebat, at lice- bat die festo Exod. XII, 16.) sed post multiplicem διασπορὰν Iudæorum quorum multi habitabant in locis callidissimis, periculum erat ne asservata cadavera putiscerent. Iam vero credibile non erat legem ritualem, à Deo præscriptam cum tali necessitate quæ nulli periculo, nullis incommodis ce- deret, cum alibi sæpe demonstratum sit in his potissimum legibus valere debere τὸ ἐπιεικές. Æqua igitur erat, ac proin- de observanda diei festi tralatio in diem Sabbati: neque id magis cum lege pugnare censendum erat, quam quod Eze- chiæ tempore Pascha tralatum est à XIV. Nisan in decimam quartam mensis sequentis. In his enim rituum rebus Syne- drii auctoritatem populus tuto sequebatur, & sequi debebat ex lege Deuteronomii XVII. 8. & deinceps. Qua de re vide quæ prudenter notavit Maimonides duce dubitantium III. 41. & Moses de Cotzi præcepto jubente XLVI. Adde jam quod Christus cum dixit: Scitis intra biduum Pascha instare: egit de re nota. Ac proinde diem Paschatis non alium a- gnovit quam eum qui publice de more observabatur. Qui- bus addenda quæ paulo ante ex Marco & Luca in hanc rem attulimus.

De tempore Paschatos legitimo facile consentit Grotius, quemadmodum ex iis, quæ adversum 2. annotarat, constat: at de tempore celebrati Judæis hujus Paschatis nullatenus probari potest, quod secundum legem divinam id celebrasse asserit: quia non XIV. Luna, sed sequenti demum die, non feria quinta, sed sexta hoc Pascha celebra- runt: Quod indubitatis documentis supra con- firmavimus. Et vidit Grotius ipse, quod Christus non cum Judæis Pascha celebrarrit: Si

ANNOT. AD MATT

ergo Judæi legitimum observarunt tempus, necef- sum est, ut Christus, quem alio tempore id cele- brasse agnoscit, tempore illegitimo Pascha comede- rit: hoc est, contra legem divinam egerit, quod dictu impium est. Unde alii auctores, qui Ju- dæos die ordinaria, Luna nempe decima quarta hoc Pascha celebrasse affirmant, ne Christum contra legem egisse asserere opus habeant, eun- dem Pascha suum ultimum cum Judæis celebrasse ajunt: ut puta Alcuinus, Thomas de Aquino, Job. Gerson, quattuor illi Cardinales Tostatus Abulen- sis, Franc. Toletus, Bellarminus, & Baronius, ut & Cornel. à Lapide, Barradius, & Estius: nec non è Reformatis Brugthonus, Annotatores Angli- cani ultimi, & Cloppenburgius: è nostris denique Casp. Erasmus Brochmand. p. m. Sed cur Judæos die legitimo hoc Pascha comedisse statui non de- beat, antea observavimus.

## 26:18
Verse 18. πρὸς τὸν δεῖνα] פלני, the Syrian. In Hebrew, אלמני or פלני אלני, as in Ruth 4:1, where certain Greeks translated it as 'secret one.' But the interpreter of Matthew in this place translates it into Greek quite appropriately as τὸν δεῖνα. For thus the Greeks speak when they do not mean any particular man, but some one designated person, whom it is not necessary to name. Christ, however, had not named this man, but had described him by certain signs, as can be seen in Mark. Matthew inserted that פלני into the words of Christ on his own account: a manner of narrating which can be found in 2 Samuel 15:2. The Arabs say the same word, فلان, whence it remained in Spanish as 'Fulano'.

ὁ καιρός μου ἐγγύς ἐστι, πρός σε ποιῶ τὸ πάσχα μετὰ τῶν μαθητῶν μου] We are bidden to learn from this, which many have failed to observe, that the Passover was anticipated by Christ, and the reason why he anticipated it. For that ποιῶ means 'I am doing it right now,' this very night, not in the afternoon, which was the legitimate time. The reason is not that the Jews had appointed the Passover to be slaughtered and eaten at a time other than they ought, but because the time of death was imminent for Christ, so that he would not survive until the legitimate time of the Passover. For in my judgment, that 'my time is near' cannot have another meaning. And in Luke, 'before I suffer.' It happened by divine providence that there was no need for delay. For the upper room was already prepared and everything was in readiness that was desired for eating the Passover; so that immediately after these words were spoken, Christ went into the house and reclined. Nor is that surprising in a city full of strangers for whom lodgings and suppers were being prepared everywhere. The Greeks object that if Christ anticipated the Passover, the law was violated by him. Others solve this knot in different ways: to me, the matter seems straightforward by applying a distinction regarding the Passover. For the Passover is a solemn, full θύσιμον (sacrificial offering); another, a commemorative θύσιμον (which Josephus calls 'Passover sacrifice'), could not be celebrated except in one place, where all the people would gather, which place from the times of David was Jerusalem. The law is in Deuteronomy 16:25. An example can be seen in 2 Chronicles 30 and 35, Luke 2:41, and in many places in Josephus. Trypho in his dialogue with Justin: 'We know that it is not possible for the lamb of the Passover to be sacrificed elsewhere.' This θύσιμον, however, because in it the lamb was slaughtered, not privately by the heads of families, as many think, but by the Priests, after the Priesthood was established—for before that, the heads of families were as it were Priests. I know it is said by Philo that 'each of the priests sacrifices on the day of the Passover, not waiting for the priesthood, the law having granted to the whole nation one day set apart for the performance of sacrifices.' But the Alexandrian himself is not a sufficiently certain authority on Hebrew customs. In the Books of Chronicles, where the history of Josiah is described, it is openly narrated that the Priests, with the Levites assisting, removed what had to be removed, and that in the temples, and then returned the Paschal animals to the families, where Josephus says: 'these things the priests explained to the crowds.' And hence it happened that the Priests, when Cestius asked what the number of Jews gathering in Jerusalem was, were able to say exactly how many lambs or kids had been sacrificed at the Passover. For they say that there were 256,500 victims: which indeed they could not have stated exactly unless they had intervened in the slaughtering. This θύσιμον Passover, just as it had a predefined place outside of which it could not be celebrated, so also it had a designated time: namely, between the two evenings of the fourteenth day ending and the fifteenth day beginning. Christ did not celebrate such a Passover this year. For it was not permitted to sacrifice outside the granted time: add that, as I said, the work of the Priests intervened, who would never have performed it except at the appointed time. But because in times of war the people could not gather, and much more so after the Babylonian exile, and other dispersions

with most of the Jews scattered further than they could come to Jerusalem, a commemorative Passover was substituted in place of the sacrificial Passover, more voluntary than commanded by law. For lest the memory of the Egyptian liberation should perish, the Jews instituted, even when they could not sacrifice the Passover (that they could do so outside the borders of Canaan, they themselves not unjustly deny), that they should nevertheless place a certain memory of the Passover before their eyes. Just as, therefore, in the Passover which we call θύσιμον, a ritual supper preceded the proper supper, by which they ate the lamb or kid with unleavened bread and bitter herbs according to the prescription of the law: I say for the sake of the ritual, not for satiety; for the lamb could not suffice for a proper supper for men never fewer than ten, often even twenty; for Josephus records that the 'brotherhoods' grew to that size: within which number we learn from Porphyry that the Phiditia of the Lacedaemonians also remained: then the proper supper followed. So also at the commemorative Passover, a certain meal ὄψλας χάριν was set before the meal, but without sacrifice. Therefore, in it, only something of the unleavened bread was eaten with bitter herbs. Of the other foods set out, nothing was tasted before the second meal, which was the ordinary one. Which the Jews observe even now. This commemorative Passover meal, however, although ἄθυτον as I said, is called πάσχα homonymously. For the song of that meal, which there is no doubt comes from Babylonian times, holds thus: כל דצריך ייתי ויפסח, that is, Let every needy person come and keep the Passover. And in this sense I accept what Chrysostom says, that even in his own time the Jews at Antioch kept the Passover: and what Procopius says in his Secret History, that they γίνεσθαι προβατείων κρεῶν. For it is not credible that they sacrificed. And therefore Tryphon, in the cited passage, does not say that it is forbidden to celebrate the Passover elsewhere, but τὸ πρόβατον τοῦ πάσχα θύειν. This memorial Passover, being undertaken by voluntary devotion, was not restricted to a place, nor to a time. Christ, therefore, since he could not use the sacrificial Passover, which was to be prevented by his death, nevertheless wished to celebrate the memory of the Passover with his disciples, as he was able: which he did in the same way as those who could not come to Jerusalem were accustomed to do, and at the nearest time he could, that is, eighteen hours or thereabouts before the very time of the sacrifice. Christ did not, therefore, sacrifice the Passover: nor indeed could he, being himself the true Passover to be sacrificed on the true day of the Passover: but he ate the Passover which I called memorial, which here is rightly called Passover in the Jewish manner: and so we nowhere read ἕθυσε πάσχα: indeed, that Christ did not sacrifice appears even from this, that as soon as he came into the house, he reclined. But ἔφαγε τὸ πάσχα. Nor is πάσχα ποιεῖν anything else here than the word עשה in the ritual song, as if you were to say παχατίζειν. From this it appears that nothing was done by Christ against the law: indeed, on the contrary, Christ was so observant of the law that, when he could not fulfill the sacrifice, he nevertheless celebrated the memory of the sacrifice by the received rite: What I said about the Passover is also to be seen on other feast days, the memory of which the Jews celebrated even outside Judea without sacrifices. Thus Philo, against Flaccus, narrates that the feast of tabernacles, τὴν ἐν σκηναῖς ἑορτὴν, was celebrated by the Jews living in Alexandria. But lest anyone suspect this new opinion of ours, let him know that it is very ancient: Photius mentions an anonymous writer against the Quartodecimans, who said that at the fifth hour our Lord Jesus Christ ate the Passover not having been sacrificed, for the time was not yet, but on the following day, and that he did not eat it legally. The same is said to have been defended by another very learned writer, who had published books on the Passover.

Grotius maintains that Christ anticipated the Passover and did not celebrate it at the legitimate time; yet he argues that the law was not violated by him, which he warns the Greeks to object to this opinion; understanding the older ones. For he does not have the more recent Greeks against him, since they likewise contend that Christ anticipated the legal term of the Passover, as can be seen in the Censura of the Augsburg Confession by Jeremiah, Patriarch of Constantinople, ch. XIII. Whose opinion, however, has been rejected by the Westerners. And deservedly so: because Christ celebrated his last Passover on the first day of unleavened bread, which was the fourteenth of the month of Nisan; and that he observed the law, as far as the time of the Passover is concerned, is explicitly indicated by Luke ch. XXII. 7, the day of unleavened bread came, ἐν ᾗ ἔδει θύεσθαι τὸ πάσχα, in which it was necessary (i.e., according to the law) for the Passover to be sacrificed. How then, when Christ himself introduces the law and implies that it must be observed by him, will he be said to have transgressed that very law, and to have anticipated the legitimate time of the Passover by eighteen hours or thereabouts?

That distinction of the Passover, which Grotius brings forward by way of excuse, that Christ did not indeed observe the θύσιμον (sacrificial) Passover, because it was restricted to a certain place and time, but that he did observe the μνημονευτικόν (memorial) one, because it was not so restricted, does not absolve Christ from the violation of the divine law, but rather convicts him of it more and more, because, forsooth, the Jewish superstition and that ἐθελοθρησκεία (will-worship) of the memorial Passover, nowhere sanctioned by God's law, were more important to him than the observation of the sacrificial Passover, which was sanctioned and circumscribed by God's law: and that Christ did not celebrate the true and proper Passover, but only a commemorative and ἄθυτον (non-sacrificial) Passover, which Grotius admits was called Passover ὁμωνύμως (equivocally). Would this not have been an open transgression of the divine law? Nor indeed was the preparation of the Paschal lamb restricted to the Priests, nor did it obtain the character of a sacrifice. For although the Paschal lambs were brought to the Priesthood, so that it might be inquired whether they were in proper condition, according to the qualities divinely required, yet it was not perpetual or necessary that the slaughtering be done by the Priests; as is abundantly evident from Philo, whose writings sufficiently show that, although he was an Alexandrian, the rites of the Hebrews were not unknown to him: who in book III of the Life of Moses, near the end, has this: 'On the fourteenth day of that month, about the very time when the moon is accustomed to fill its orb with light, the festival of the public migration is celebrated, which they call Passover in Chaldean, at which time, not as at other times do common people bring victims to the altar to be slaughtered by the Priests, but the whole nation sacrificed by the command of the law, while each one slaughters the victim with his own hands for himself, then with the whole people celebrating joyful feasts, each one acts as a Priest.' Similarly in the book on the Decalogue. The Passover is sacrificed by individuals in a popular manner, without waiting for the Priests, they themselves performing the Priesthood here by permission of the law. But that the Paschal lamb was not properly a sacrifice, but a Sacrament, may be gathered even from this, that in every sacrifice an offering was made to God: and that either the whole victim, or some part, was offered to God and consumed by sacred fire: but the Paschal lamb was not offered, nor consumed by fire, but roasted and eaten. Nevertheless, the sacrificial verb θύειν (to sacrifice) and θύεσθαι (to be sacrificed) is used even of the Passover which Christ celebrated (which Grotius wrongly denies here) Mark 14:12, Luke 22:7, even though Christ did not sacrifice in that Passover: because, forsooth, there is something analogous in the Paschal lamb to sacrifices, both in respect of the slaughtering and in respect of the signification and foreshadowing. Of the true sacrifice of the New Testament 1. Cor. 5:7. Add that sacrifices were also accustomed to be joined to the slaughtering and eating of the Paschal lamb, Num. 29:19, Lev. 23:8, Deut. 15:2, 2 Chron. 35:11.

But why could Christ not have observed the time prescribed in the law? For what Grotius says, that he was prevented by death, is nothing: since Christ had it in his power to lay down his life when he willed, John 10:18, 19, and it is false what Grotius assumes, that the time of the Passover according to the law fell on the sixth day, or Friday: which is rather gathered from the Evangelical Harmony to have fallen on the fifth day, or Thursday. For in John 13:1, before the feast day of the Passover, it is said that Christ celebrated the last supper, in which he ate the Paschal lamb, which cannot be taken otherwise than as our opinion holds, i.e., that he celebrated the last supper and in it the Passover before the day of the Jewish Passover feast, not on the very day of the Jewish Passover, just as also in John 19:14 he is said to have been condemned on the Preparation of the Jewish Passover, after he had already celebrated his Passover with his disciples the previous night. Wherefore it is certain that he celebrated his Passover on Thursday, the fifth day according to the law: but that it was celebrated by the Jews only on the following day: this Preparation was not for the true legal Passover, but for the traditional one of the Jews, which in that year was one day later than the legitimate one. Grotius followed Mark Antonio de Dominis in this discovery, book 5, On Festivals, ch. 6, §. 222, although he did not name him, so that he himself might be believed to be the author of this novelty as well. Nor indeed has it been proven by any example that the Jews ate such a memorial Passover in the Babylonian land: and whatever may be the case regarding it, that any Jew living in Jerusalem celebrated such a Passover of Unleavened Bread with bitter herbs without a Paschal lamb, and that Christ performed such a voluntary superstition, and ate a Passover without a Paschal lamb, is not free from blasphemy.

Nor is there any reason for anyone to say with Grotius: that it was fitting that Christ be slaughtered as the true lamb on the day and time that the typical lambs were slaughtered, and therefore he had need to anticipate the eating of the Passover, so that he might be offered at the true and legitimate time of the Paschal lamb: for it is not necessary that all things be found in the antitype, as regards all circumstances. Add that the true Paschal lamb was killed on the same day that the Passover was being celebrated: which had begun from the second evening of the fourteenth day, and continued to the end of the fifteenth day: nay, that he even hung on the cross during those hours when the lamb was accustomed to be offered for the evening sacrifice on the day of the legitimate Passover. Cf. Bælius, Historical and Chronological Work, book II, page 81.

μετὰ τῶν μαθητῶν με (with my disciples)] For this was a just phratria (brotherhood) between ten and twenty: similar to the Phiditia among the Lacedaemonians, which themselves consisted of fifteen or a few more or fewer guests: and the syssitia (common meals) of the Pythagoreans, which consisted of ten men: of the Nabataean Arabs, thirteen.

Latin:

Vers. 18. προς τ δεῖνα] פלני Syrus. Hebraice אלמני aut פלני אלני ut Ruth. IV. 1. ubi Græci quidam verte- runt κρύφιε. At Matthæi interpres hoc loco Græce ad- modum vertit τ δεῖνα. Ita enim Græci loquuntur cum non quemvis hominem, sed unum aliquem designatum vo- lunt, quem nominari nihil attinet. Hunc autem Chri- stus non nominarat, sed notis quibusdam descripserat, ut apud Marcum videre est. Interseruit autem verbis Chri- sti Matthæus illud פלני de suo: cujusmodi narrandi mo- dum invenire est 2. Sam. XV. v. 2. Arabes dicunt eadem voce فلان unde Hispanis mansit Fullano.

ὁ καιρός με ἐγγύς ἐσι, πρός σε ποιῶ τὸ πάχα μετὰ τ μα- θητῶν με] Discere hinc jubemur, quod non observatum multos fefellit, & anticipatum Pascha à Christo & causam cur anticipaverit. Nam illud ποιῶ est jamjam facio, hac ipsa nocte, non pomeridiano tempore quod erat legiti- mum. Causa est, non quod Judæi alio quam oportebat tem- pore constituissent Pascha mactare & edere, sed quia mor- tis tempus Christo imminebat, ita ut ad legitimum usque Paschatis tempus non esset provicturus. Nam alium sensum habere meo judicio non potest illud ὁ καιρός με ἐγγύς. Et apud Lucam πρὸ τᾶ με παθεῖν. Divina autem providentia factum est, ut nulla mora esset opus. Jam enim paratum erat cœnaculum & omnia in promptu quæ ad Pascha com- edendum desiderabant; ut ita statim post hæc dicta in do- mum iverit Christus, & discubuerit. Neque id mirum in urbe plena advenis quibus passim hospitia & cœna parabantur. Objiciunt Græci, si antevertit Christus Pascha, viola- tam ab eo legem. Quem nodum alii aliter solvunt: mihi res videtur expedita adhibita distinctione Paschatis. Pascha enim est θύσιμον solenne, plenum: aliud μνημονευτικον Θύσι- μον (quod πάσχα θυσίαν vocat Josephus) celebrari non pot- erat nisi uno in loco, quo populus omnis conveniret, qui lo- cus à Davidis temporibus fuit Hierosolyma. Lex est, Deut. XVI, 25. Exemplum videre est II. Par. XXX. & XXXV. Luc. II. 41. apud Josephum multis in locis. Tryphon in collo- quio cum Justino: Γνωρίζομεν ὅτι ἦν πρόβατον τᾶ πάσχα ἀλ- λαχε̃σε θύσει δυνατὸν. Hoc θύσιμον vero, quia in eo agnus mactabatur, non privatim à patribus familias, ut multi exi- stimant, sed à Sacerdotibus, post constitutum Sacerdotium, nam ante patres familiarum erant velut Sacerdotes. Scio Philoni dictum θύειν die Paschali ἑκαςον τες ἱερε̃ς ἐκ ἀναμέ- νοντας ἱερωσύνης τῷ νόμῳ χαρισαμένε τῷ ἔθνει παντὶ μίαν ἡμέραν ἐξαίρετον ἀνὰ πᾶν ἔτ@ εἰς αὐτεργίαν θυσιῶν. Sed in moribus Hebæis ipse Alexandrinus non satis certus est auctor. In Paralipomenis, ubi Josiæ describitur Historia, aperte narran- tur Sacerdotes, adjuvantibus Levitis, amovisse quæ amoven- da erant, idque in templis, & deinde pecudes Paschales red- didisse familiis, ubi Josephus: ταῦτα τ ἱερέων ἐξηγεμένων τοῖς ὄχλοις. Atque hinc factum, ut Sacerdotes, Cestio quærenti quis numerus esset Judæorum Hierosolyma convenientium, exacte dixerint quot fuissent in Paschate agni aut hædi sa- crificati. Ajunt enim fdisse θυμάτων εἴκοσι πέντε μυριάδας, πρὸς δὲ πεντακισχίλια ἑξακοσία: quod profecto exacte dicere non potuissent, nisi ipsi intervenissent mactationi. Hoc θύ- σιμον Pascha sicut locum habebat præfinitum extra quem celebrari non poterat, ita & tempus designatum: nempe inter duas ὀψίας decimæ quartæ diei exeuntis & inchoantis deci- mæ quintæ. Tale Pascha hoc anno non celebravit Chri- stus. Sacrificare enim extra tempus concessum non licuit: adde, quod & Sacerdotum, ut dixi, interveniebat opera, qui nunquam eam navassent nisi stato tempore. Sed quia bel- li temporibus convenire populus non poterat, multoque magis post Babylonicum exsilium, aliasque διασποράς

longius sparsis plerisque Judæorum quam ut possent venire Hierosolyma, in locum Paschatis θυσίμου surrogatum est Pa- scha μνημονευτικὸν, voluntarium magis quam lege præce- ptum. Nam ne excideret liberationis Ægyptiacæ memoria, instituerunt Judæi, etiam cum sacrificare Pascha non possent (posse autem extra Cananææ fines, non immerito ipsi ne- gant) memoriam tamen Paschatis quamdam ob oculos po- nere.
