Sicut ergo in Paschate quod θύσιμον vocamus ante cœnam justam antecedebat cœna ritualis, qua agnum aut hœdum cum azymis & herbis amaris ex legis præscripto comedebant: dicis inquam caussa, non ad saturitatem: ne- que enim agnus sufficere poterat ad cœnam justam homi- nibus nunquam paucioribus decem, sæpe etiam viginti; nam eo usque excrevisse τὰς Φρατρίας Josephus memorat: intra quem numerum stetisse & Lacedæmoniorum Phiditia ex Porphyrio discimus: sequebatur deinde cœna justa: ita & in Paschate commemorativo cœna quædam ὄψλας χάριν cœnæ præmittebatur, sed sine sacrificio. Itaque in eo edebatur tantum aliquid Azymorum cum herbis amaris. De cæteris cibis appositis nihil gustabatur ante cœnam se- cundam, quæ erat ordinaria. Quod nunc quoque Judæi observant. Hæc autem cœna commemorativa Paschatis, quanquam ἄθυτον ut dixi, vocatur πάσχα ὁμωνύμως. Nam ita habet carmen istius cœnæ, quod venire a Babylonicis temporibus non est dubium, כל דצריך ייתי ויפסח Id est, Omnis indigena Pascha faciat. Atque in hunc sen- sum accipio quod dicit Chrysostomus suo etiam tempore Judæos Antiochiæ Pascha fecisse: & quod Procopius in ar- cana Historia ait eos γίνεσθαι προβατείων κρεῶν. Nam sa- crificasse eos non est credibile. Atque ideo Tryphon di- cto loco non Pascha celebrare alibi ait vetitum, sed τὸ πρόβα- τον τοῦ πάσχα θύειν. Hoc Pascha μνημονευτικὸν, utpote volun- taria devotione susceptum, sicut loco non adstringebatur, i- ta nec tempore. Christus igitur cum πάσχα θύσιμον morte præveniendus usurpare non posset, voluit tamen cum disci- pulis suis memoriam Paschatis, qua poterat, celebrare: quod facit eodem modo quo solebant ii qui Hierosolyma venire non poterant, & quo proximo poterat tempore, id est, horis XIIX. aut circiter ante ipsum sacrificii tempus. Non sacrifica- vit igitur Pascha Christus: neque enim potuit, ipse verum Pa- scha vero Paschatis die sacrificandus: sed manducavit Pa- scha quod dixi μνημονευτικὸν, quod hic recte Judaico more Pascha appellatur: itaque ἕθυσε πάσχα nusquam legimus: imo non sacrificasse Christum vel hinc apparet, quod sta- tim ut in domum venit, discumbit. Sed ἔφαγε τὸ πάσχα. Nec aliud hic est πάσχα ποιεῖν quam עשה verbum in rituali carmine, quasi dicas παχατίζειν. Hinc apparet nihil à Christo factum contra legem: imo contra, adeo observan- tem legis Christum fuisse, ut cum sacrificium implere non posset, memoriam tamen sacrificii ritu recepto coluerit: Quod de Paschate dixi, idem videre est & in aliis diebus fe- stis, quorum memoriam etiam extra Judæam, Judæi sine sa- crificiis celebrabant. Ita Philo adversus Flaccum narrat alu- dæis Alexandriæ habitantibus celebratam τὴν ἐν σκηναῖς ἑορτὴν. Nequis vero novam hanc nostram sententiam su- spicetur, sciat esse antiquissimam: meminit Photius scripto- ris anonymi adversus Tessareskædecatitas, qui dixerit τῇ ὥ- ρᾳ τῇ πέμπτῃ μὴ τεθυμένον φαγεῖν πάσχα τ᾿ κύριον ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦν Χριστὸν, μηδὲ γὰρ εἶναι τότε τὸ καιρὸν, ἀλλὰ τῇ ἐπιούσῃ, καὶ ὅτι οὐδὲ νομικῶς τελῶν ἔφαγεν. Idem ait defensum ab alio scriptore valde erudito, qui de Paschate libros ediderat.

Christum anticipasse Pascha, nec id tempore le- gitimo celebrasse Grotius vult; nec tamen ab eo violatam esse legem, quod huic sententiæ objicere Græcos monet; Antiquiores intelligens. Nam re- centiores Græcos sibi adversos non habet, utpote qui pariter contendunt Christum legalem Pascha- tos terminum anticipasse, ut videre est in Jeremiæ Patriarchæ Constantinopolitani Censura Confessio- nis Augustanæ c. XIII. Quorum vero sententia ab occidentalibus reprobata est. Idque merito: quia Christus Pascha suum ultimum primo die azymo- rum celebravit, qui decimus quartus fuit mensis Nisan; & quod legem observârit, quantum ad tem- pus Paschatos, à Luca c. XXII. 7. diserte indicatur, venit dies azymorum, ἐν ᾗ ἔδει θύεσθαι τὸ πάσχα, in qua oportet (sc. secundum legem) mactari Pascha. Quomodo ergo Christus cum ipse legem introdu- cat, eamque sibi observandam esse innuat, illam ipsam legem transgressus dicetur, & horis XIIX. aut circiter anticipasse tempus legitimum Pascha- tos?

Distinctio illa Paschatos, quam excusationis gratia adfert Grotius, quod πάσχα θύσιμον quidem non observarit Christus, quod ad certum locum & tempus adstrictum fuerit, μνημονευτικὸν tamen quod ita adstrictum haud fuerit, observarit, Chri- stus non absolvit a legis divinæ violatione, sed de eadem magis magisque convincit, quod nempe potior ipsi fuerit superstitio Judaica, & ἐθελοθρη- σκεία illa Paschatos μνημονευτικοῦ, nuspiam a Deo lege sancita, quam observatio Paschatos θυσίμου quod a Deo lege sancitum, & circumscriptum e- rat: quodque Christus perum ac proprium Pascha non celebrariter: sed tantum Pascha commemorati- vum, & ἄθυτον, quod ὁμωνύμως Pascha voca- tum fatetur Grotius. Annon hæc aperta fuisset legis divinæ transgressio? Neque vero vel ad Sa- cerdotes adstricta fuit agni Paschalis præparatio, vel sacrificii rationem obtinuit. Etsi enim Sacer- dotio agni Paschales adducti, ut inquireretur an recte se haberent, juxta qualitates divinitus requi- sitas? non tamen perpetuum hoc aut necessarium fuisse, ut a Sacerdotibus fieret mactatio; e Philo- ne, cui etsi Alexandrino Ebræorum ritus non in- cognitos fuisse, scripta ipsius satis docent, ab- unde constat: qui libro III. de Vit. Mos. circa fi- nem ita habet: Ejus mensis die quarta decima sub ipsum tempus, quo Luna suum orbem solet implere lumine, celebratur migrationis publicæ festivitas, quam Chaldaice Pascha nominant, quo tempore, non ut alias plebeji homines victimas adducunt ad altare mactandas a Sacerdotibus, sed jubente lege tota gens sacrificabat, dum pro se quisque mactat hostiam suis manibus, tunc universo populo celebrante lætas epu- las, quisque se gerit pro Sacerdote. Similiter libr. de Decal. Pascha populariter singuli sacrificant, non expectatis Sacerdotibus, ipsi permissu legis hic fun- gentes Sacerdotio. Quod autem proprie sacrifi- cium non fuerit, sed Sacramentum agnus Paschalis vel hinc colligere est, quod in omni sacrificio Deo facta sit oblatio: quodque vel tota hostia, vel pars aliqua Deo oblata, & sacro igne absumta fuerit: agnus autem Paschalis non oblatus, vel igne con- sumtus sit, sed assatus & manducatus. Adhibetur tamen verbum sacrificiale θύειν, & θύεσθαι etiam de Paschate, quod Christus celebravit (quod per- peram Grotius hic negat) Marc. XIV. v. 12. Luc. XXII. 7. etsi Christus in illo Paschate non sacrifica- rit: quia nempe aliquid analogum est in agno Pa- schali sacrificiis, cum ratione mactationis, tum ra- tione significationis & adumbrationis. Veri sa- crificii Novi Test. 1. Cor. V. 7. adde quod & sacrifi- cia mactationi & manducationi agni Paschalis con- jungi consueverint Num. XXIX. v. 19. Lev. XXIII. 8. Deut. XV. 2. Par. XXXV. 11.

Cur autem non potuisset Christus tempus ob- servare in lege præscriptum? Nam quod morte præ- ventum fuisse Grotius dicit, nihil est: siquidem Christus in manu sua habuerit vitam tradere, quando voluit, Joh. X. 18. 19. & falsum sit, quod as- sumit Grotius, Paschatis tempus secundum legem sum incidisse in feriam sextam, vel diem Veneris: quod potius in quintam feriam, vel diem Jovis in- cidisse ex Harmonia Evangelica colligitur. Nam Johan. XIII. 1. ante diem festum Paschatos dicitur Christus celebrasse cœnam ultimam, in qua agnum Paschalem comedit, quod aliter accipi non potest, quam uti nostra habet sententia h. e. quod cœnam ultimam & in ea Pascha celebrariter ante diem festi Paschatos Judæorum, non in ipso Paschatos Judai- ci die, quemadmodum etiam Joh. XIX. 14. con- demnatus dicitur in Parasceve Paschatos Judaici, postquam jam præterita nocte Pascha suum cele- brasset cum discipulis suis. Quapropter certum est, ipsum die Jovis feria quinta secundum legem Pascha suum celebrasse: sequenti autem die de- mum à Judæis id celebratum esse: Parasceve hæc fuit non ad verum Pascha legale, sed ad traditionale Ju- dæorum, quod isto anno uno die serius fuit legiti- mo. Sequutus autem est in hoc εὑρήματι proprie Grotius Marc. Antonium de Dominis l. V. de Fest. c. VI. §. 222. etsi eum non nominarit, ut ipse hujus quoque novitatis auctor crederetur. Nec vero exemplo ullo comprobatum est, quod Judæi tale Pascha μνημονευτικὸν in terra Babylonica comede- rint: & quicquid de eo sit, Judæum tamen ullum Hierosolymis degentem ejusmodi Pascha Azy- morum cum herbis amaris sine agno Paschali ce- lebrasse, Christum vero ejusmodi voluntariam superstitionem exequutum esse, ac Pascha sine agno Paschali manducasse, non vacat blasphe- mia.

Nec est, quod dicat quis cum Grotio: quod convenerit, Christum eo die & tempore ceu verum agnum mactari, quo typice agni mactati sunt, ideoque comestionem Paschatos anticipare opus habuerit, ut vero & legitimo tempore Paschalis agni ipse offerre- tur: nam in antitypo omnia reperiri,quoad omnes περιστάσεις, necessum non est. Adde,quod eadem die occisus sit verus agnus Paschalis,qua Pascha ce- lebrabatur: quæ à vespera secunda diei decimæ quartæ inceperat, & ad finem diei decimi quinti perseverabat: imo quod illis etiam horis in cru- ce pependerit, cum agnus in sacrificium vesperti- num offerri solitum legitimi Paschatos die offer- retur. Conf. Bælii opus Histor. & Chronol. lib. II. pag. 81.

μετὰ τῶν μαθητῶν με] Erat enim hæc justa φρατρία inter decem & viginti: similis Phiditiis apud Lacedæmones quæ & ipsæ constabant quindecim aut paulo pluribus pauciori- busve convivis: Et Pythagoreorum συσσιτίοις quæ decem hominibus constabant: Arabum Nabatæorum tredecim.

## 26:19
Verse 19. ἡτοίμασαν τὸ πάσχα (they prepared the Passover)] The place was prepared, as we learn from Mark. It remained that those things which pertained to that memorial supper should be set out, unleavened bread and bitter herbs.

Grotius again introduces his fictitious Passover, a Passover without the Paschal lamb, which is a contradiction in terms, and he impiously attributes it to Christ the Savior, who came to fulfill the law, not to destroy it. But who will believe that Christ, with such great zeal, took care to prepare for himself ἄζυμα καὶ πικρίδας without the Paschal lamb, and a supper for the sake of the name, as Grotius speaks, and so called ὁμωνύμως, such as is laboriously described here in the preparation of the Passover.

Latin:

Vers. 19. ἡτοίμασαν τὸ πάσχα] Locus erat paratus ut ex Marco discimus. Restabat ut apponerentur quæ ad cœ- nam illam μνημονευτικὴν pertinebant, ἄζυμα καὶ πικρίδας.

Pascha suum commentitium, Pascha sine agno Paschali, quæ contradictio est in adjecto, ingerit iterum Grotius, idque impie Christo Servatori, qui venit ut legem impleret, non destrueret, tri- buit. Ecquis vero ἄζυμα καὶ πικρίδας sine agno Paschali, cænamque dicis gratia, uti loquitur Gro- tius, & ὁμωνύμως ita dictum Christum tanto stu- dio sibi præparari curasse, credet, quale hic in ap- paratu Paschatos operose describitur.

## 26:20
Vers. 20. ὀψίας δὲ γενομένης] When the sun had already set: which is not to be understood as in a moment. For whatever time there is after sunset is sometimes accustomed to be called by that name, as in Num. IX. 15, where כיום and בערב are opposed; Jer. V. v. 7, זאב ערבות, a nocturnal wolf, as Kimchi interprets from Psalm CIV. 20; I will omit other passages. That ὀψίας is taken in this way is manifest in John XX. 19 and Mark I. 32. Therefore, it is indicated that the supper was celebrated already at night, which was done deliberately by Christ, so that he might not seem to have exposed himself to danger. Nor was there anything new in that. For even now the Jews celebrate the πάσχα μνημονευτικὸν deep in the night. Indeed, even the πάσχα θύσιμον was indeed slaughtered between the two ὀψίας, but it was not accustomed to be eaten except at night. For thus custom had interpreted the law which exists in Exodus XII. 8, and all the Jews agree on that interpretation.

ἀνέκειτο] Many believe that the standing position in eating the lamb was not commanded for all time, but for that time of the exodus. Whether, however, reclining, a sign of secure liberty, as the Jews interpret, was used from the age of Joshua, can be doubted. For just as it is sufficiently certain that the first men took food while lying on the grass, to which that which is in Genesis chapter XVIII. 4, השענו, seems to pertain, so the same Genesis ch. XLIII, 33 teaches that the custom of sitting was either no less ancient, or next to the first custom. To which place may be added another, 1 Sam. XX, v. 25. Tacitus on the Germans: They take food with washing: separate seats for each: and a table for everyone. The same is reported by Strabo concerning the ancient Spaniards and Gauls. But what Philo says about that time, μὴ πὼ τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἐν ταῖς πομπικαῖς συνουσίαις κατακλισὶ χρωμένων, must be understood entirely of reclining on couches, which undoubtedly began later, as is credible, by the example of the Assyrians: the first mention of which custom among the Jews the most learned Casaubon observed in Amos ch. II. 8: unless there is an older mention of it in Cant. I. 11, where the Greeks translate מסב as reclining. There is no doubt that the custom of reclining increased by the example of the Greeks and finally the Romans. Today the Jews use a sitting posture at that commemorative supper; but one softer and more honorable than usual: and with a reclining of the body, which does not differ much from reclining.

Latin:

Vers.20. ὀψίας δὲ γενομένης] Cum jam Sol occidisset: quod non intelligendum ἐν συγμῇ. Nam quicquid est temporis post Solem occasum solet interdum eo nomine appellari, ut Num. IX. 15. ubi opposita sunt כיום & בערב Jer. V. v. 7. זאב ערבות lupus nocturnus, ut Kimchi interpre- tatur ex Psalmo CIV. 20. loca alia omittam, Ita sumi ὀψίας manifestum est Ioh. XX. 19. & Marc. II. 32. Indicatur ergo jam nocte celebrata cœna, quod consulto factum à Chri- sto, ne se periculo ingessisse videretur. Neque in eo quic- quam erat novi. Nam nunc quoque Iudæi πάσχα μνημο- νευτικὸν multa nocte celebrant. Imo & πάσχα θύσιμον mactari quidem inter duas ὀψίας, at edi non nisi noctu so- lebat. Ita enim usus interpretatus erat legem quæ exstat Exodi XII. 8. inque eam interpretationem Iudæi omnes consentiunt.

ἀνέκειτο] Stationem in agno edendo non in perpetuum præceptam, sed pro illo exitus tempore multi sentiunt. An tamen accubitus, signum securæ libertatis, ut Iudæi inter- pretantur, usurpatus sit ab ævo Iosuæ, dubitari potest. Nam sicut in herba jacentes cibum sumsisie primos hominum sa- tis constat, quo pertinere videtur id quod est in Genesicap. XIIX. 4. השענו, ita sedendi morem aut non minus anti- quum, aut primo mori proximum fuisse docet eadem Ge- nōfis cap. XLIII, 33. cui loco addi potest alter 1.Sam. XX. v. 25. Tacitus de Germanis: Lauti cibum capiunt: separatæ singulis sedes: & sua cuique mensa. Tantundem de Hispa- nis & Gallis veteribus traditum Straboni. Quod autem de eo tempore dicit Philo mήπω τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἐν ταῖς πομποτι- καῖς συνουσίαις κατακλισὶ χρωμένων, de accubitu in lectis ac- cipiendum omnino est, qui haud dubie serius cœpit, As- syriorum ut credibile est exemplo: cujus moris primam apud Judæos mentionem doctissimus Casaubonus apud Amosum c. II. 8. observavit: nisi vetustior ejus mentio Cant. I. 11. ubi מסב κατάκλισιν vertunt. Græci. Quin Græcorum ac postremo Romanorum exemplo mos ac- cumbendi increbuerit, non est dubitandum. Hodie Judæi sessionem in cœna illa commemorativa; sed solito mol- liorem atque honoratiorem, usurpant: & cum rectinatio- ne corporis, quæ ab accubitu non longe abscedit.

## 26:21
Vers. 21. καὶ ἐσθιόντων αὐτῶν] That is, when they were already eating supper late. For the former supper, as I said, was for form's sake: nor were any conversations held in it except for formulas. And that dish, concerning which it follows, contained broth: as the mention of the morsel in John shows. Wherefore I cannot approve the opinion of those who refer these things to bitter herbs dipped in vinegar, for which there was a place in the former supper.

Latin:

Vers. 21. καὶ ἐσθιόντων αὐτῶν] Id est, cum jam sero cœna- rent. Nam prior cœna, ut dixi, dicis causa erat: ne- que in ea habebantur ulli sermones præter formulas, Et τρύβλιον illud, pe quo sequitur, habebat in se jusculum: ut ostendit ψωμίε mentio apud Johannem. Quare probare non possumeorum sententiam qui hæc ad herbas amaras aceto tinctas referunt, quibus locus erat in cœna priore.

## 26:23
Vers. 23. ὁ ἐμβάψας μετ ἐμῶν ἐν τῷ τρυβλίῳ τὴν χεῖρα] It seems entirely that something more specific is indicated than what Christ had said above, one of you twelve. Wherefore I am persuaded that Judas reclined near Christ, in such a way that, since there were several bowls at the supper, he ate from the same bowl from which Christ was eating: for thus it could more easily happen that Christ, to him asking whether he was the one of whom He spoke, answered in a low voice and so that most did not hear, σὺ εἶπας, and that, this not being heard, John, warned by Peter, seeking who it was who would dare such a crime, received a certain sign from Christ, when he would give to this one, to whom Christ Himself was about to give a morsel dipped in the broth from the bowl. All of which things, if I am not mistaken, lead us to believe what I have said. And so here too it happens as in many other prophecies, that the words of David, Psalm XLI. 10, were fulfilled in Christ not only according to a proverbial mode of speaking, but also according to the most exact meaning of the words. Added to this is that Mark, when he had previously said ὁ ἐσθίων μετ᾽ ἐμῶν, afterwards added, ἗ις ἐκ τῶ δώδεκα ὁ ἐμβαπτόμενο μετ' ἐμῶ μῶ ἐνς τὸ τρυβλίον. Wherefore, since the same thing should not be considered to have been said twice, it follows that in the latter there is a more restrictive demonstration. And thus Christ brought forth the proofs of His foreknowledge by degrees, first including the future traitor in the number of twelve, then in the smaller number of those reclining nearest, and finally designating the man himself with certain marks.

Latin:

Vers. 23. ὁ ἐμβάψας μετ ἐμῶν ἐν τῷ τρυβλίῳ τὴν χεῖρα] O- mnino videtur propius quiddam indicari quam quod su- pra dixerat Christus, unus ex vobis duodecim. Quare per- suasum mihi est Judam prope Christum accubuisse, ita ut cum plures essent in cœna catini, ille ex eodem catino ede- ret ex quo edebat Christus: ita enim facilius fieri potuit ut Christus illi interroganti, an ipse esset de quo loqueretur, submisse & plerisque non audientibus responderet, σὺ εἶπας, utque eo non audito Johannes à Petro monitus, quærens quis ille esset qui tantum scelus esset ausurus, certum à Christo signum acciperet, cum hunc esse cui ipse Christus daturus esset de catino tinctam jure ossulam. Quæ omnia, ni fallor, indicia eo nos ducunt ut credamus quod dixi. At- que ita hic quoque accidit quod in multis aliis vaticiniis, ut verba Davidis Psal. XLI. 10. in Christo non tantum secun- dum proverbialem loquendi modum, sed etiam secundum exactissimam verborum significationem implerentur. Accedit huc, quod Marcus cum prius dixisset ὁ ἐσθίων μετ᾽ ἐμῶν, postea subjecit, ἗ις ἐκ τῶ δώδεκα ὁ ἐμβαπτόμενο μετ' ἐμῶ μῶ ἐνς τὸ τρυβλίον. Quare cum bis idem dictum censeri non debeat, sequitur in posteriori restrictiorem esse demonstra- tionem. Atque ita Christus præscientiæ suæ documenta per gradus edidit, primum duodenario numero includens futurum proditorem, deinde numero minore proxime accumbentium, postremo ipsum hominem notis certis de- signans.

## 26:24
Vers. 24. ὑπάγι καθὼς γέγραπται περὶ ἀυτῶ] Πορέυεται, says Luke: that is, he dies: for thus the Hebrews use הולך, as in Genesis XV. 2, where the LXX translate אנכי הולך as ἐγώ δὲ ἀπολύομαι. Thus also the Latins used to say that a dead person had departed. Elsewhere, ὑπάγειν used of Christ signifies His departure into heaven.

καὶ δὶ τῷ ἀνθρώπῳ ἐκείνῳ] The most wise decree of divine permission and the foreknowledge joined to it, since it imposes no necessity of crime, neither diminishes the guilt nor the merit of punishment.

Καλὸν ἦν ἀυτῷ, εἰ ὐκἐγεννήθη ὁ ἄνθρωπος ἐκεῖνος] Not that it can be well for him who does not exist, but that men can be so miserable that they rightly wish not to exist: which I am surprised is denied by some who philosophize too subtly, from whose unexpected opinion I appeal to common sense and this statement of Christ. For what impatience expressed for pious men, Job and Jeremiah, to say, that Christ here affirms truly and seriously concerning Judas: the wicked man, says Hierocles, wishes his soul to be immortal, so that he may not suffer while being punished. But to perish is the same as not to have been born: according to that of Seneca:

Do you ask in what place you lie after death? In the place where those not born lie.

Concerning the impious, therefore, it can truly be said what they say Silenus once said, and Theognis expressed in these words: Not to be born at all is best for those on earth, nor to see the rays of the swift sun.

Jerome: It is simply said that it is much better not to exist than to exist badly. Rabbi Israel says of the soul to him who in this world does not devote himself to divine contemplation, that it would be better never to have existed. The same in Zoaf concerning those ignorant of the law.

Latin:

Vers. 24. ὑπάγι καθὼς γέγραπται περὶ ἀυτῶ] Πορέυεται Lucas: id est moritur: ita enim Hebræi הולך usurpant, ut Genes. XV. 2. ubi LXX. אנכי הולך ver.untἐγώ δὲ ἀπο- λύομαι. Sic & Latini mortuum abiisse dicebant. Alibi ὑπά- γειν de Christo positum ἀνάλυψιν ejus in cœlum significat.

καὶ δὶ τῷ ἀνθρώπῳ ἐκείνῳ] Sapientissimum divinæ permis- sionis decretum eique juncta præscientia, cum nullam im- ponat sceleris necessitatem, neque culpam neque pœnæ meritum minuit.

Καλὸν ἦν ἀυτῷ, εἰ ὐκἐγεννήθη ὁ ἄνθρωπος ἐκεῖνος] Non quod esse bene ei possit qui non sit, sed quod homines ita possunt esse miseri, ut merito optent non esse: quod à qui- busdam nimium subtiliter philosophantibus negari miror,à quorum inopinata sententia ad sensum communem & hoc Christi effatum provoco. Nam quod viris piis, Jobo & Je- remiæ impatientia ut dicerent expressit, id hic vere ac serio de Juda Christus affirmat: ὑβλεται, inquit Hierocles, ὁ κακὸς ἀθάνατον εἶναι τὴν αὑτῶ ψυχὴν, ἵνα μὴ ὑπομένη τιμωρέμε- νος. Interire autem est perinde ac natum non esse: juxta illud Senecæ:

Quæris quo jaceas post obitum loco? Quo non nata jacent.

De impiis igitur vere dici potest, quod olim dixisse Sile- num ferunt, & Theognis istis verbis expressit: Ἀρχὴν μὲν μὴ φῦναι ἐπιχθονίοισιν ἄριστον Μηδ' ἐσιδεῖν αὐγὰς ὀξέος ἠελίου.

Hieronymus: Simpliciter dictum est, multo melius esse non sub- sistere quam male subsistere Rabbi Israel de anima ait ei qui in hoc mundo divinæ contemplationi non vacat, melius fu- turum esse nunquam extitisse. Idem in Zoaf de ignoran- tibus legem.

## 26:25
Vers. 25. Σὺ εἶπας] You have said it. For this speech is not of one leaving the matter in the middle, but of one conceding the question, as is clearly apparent by comparing places, below in this chapter v. 64 and Mark XIV. 62. Not unlike is that of Euripides, σὺ δὲ λέγεις τάδ᾽, τάδ'ἐγώ. But this was said to Judas in such a way that the others did not hear.

The mode of speaking, σὺ εἶπας, is rightly explained. Yet the observation of Lud. Capellus in Specileg. is not inelegant: that Christ, the knower of hearts, perceived that those by whom He was questioned were convinced inwardly of the truth of the matter, which they pretended by these questions not to know. But that this was said to Judas so that the others would not hear, although it may be conceded, yet it does not clearly appear from the text: nor was Judas reclining closer to Christ than the others. For the questioning of the disciple made by John, who was reclining on Christ's breast, by the nod of Peter, κύριε τίς ἐστιν, John XIII. 25, seems to have preceded this question of Judas himself; and the answer returned by Christ to him, otherwise than Vossius, book I, Harm. Evang. ch. XIV, § 16, 17, following Grotius, thinks.

Latin:

Vers. 25. Σὺ εἶπας] Rem dixisti. Est enim non in me- dio relinquentis, sed concedentis quæsitum ista oratio, ut collatis lolis, infra hoc cap. v. 64. & Marc. XIV. 62. liquido apparet. Non dissimile est illud Euripidis, σὺ δὲ λέγεις τάδ᾽, τάδ'ἐγώ. Sed hoc ita Judæ dictum est, ut cæteri non exaudirent,

Recte explicatur modus loquendi, σὺ εἶπας. Non inconcinna tamen est Lud. Capelli in Speci- leg. observatio : quod Christus καρδιογνώστης per- spexerit illos à quibus interrogabatur, convictos fuisse intus de veritate rei, quam hac interroga- tiones simulabant se nescire. Sed Judæ ira di- ctum hoc esse, ut non exaudirent cæteri, etsi con- cedi possit, haud luculenter tamen id è textu ap- paret : neque Judas propius Christo accumbebat, quam cæteri. Interrogatio enim nutu Petri à Jo- hanne ἐπιστηθίῳ Christo discipuli facta κύριε τίς ἐ- στιν Joh. XIII. 25. præcessisse videtur hanc ipsius Judæ quæstionem; ipsique à Christo redditam re- sponsionem, fecus atque Vossius l. I. Harm. Evang. c. XIV. §. 16. 17. sequutus Grotium putat.

## 26:26
Vers. 26. While they were eating] So also Mark: that is, while they were still dining. For wine indeed, according to the custom of the Jews, who even now observe this on the day of the Passover and on other feast days, was drunk both at dinner and after dinner with thanksgiving: and bread was broken and distributed while the dinner was still in progress, but nearly finished. Hence both Luke and Paul say specifically of the cup taken by Christ μετὰ τὸ δειπνῆσαι: which in the Latin Mass is explained as 'after they had supped': but Luke records that it was offered both at dinner and after dinner: but after dinner with the institution of the rite that was to remain. Even among the Greeks, the last cup, and that held as sacred, was drunk at the very time when the tables were being removed: Nicostratus, 'but let him who pours the wine bring me the table from my feet more quickly, by the good spirit.' Xenophon: 'and when the tables were removed and they had poured libations and sung the paean.' The Scholiast of Aristophanes on the Wasps: 'it was the custom whenever the table was about to be removed to drink to the good spirit.' Seneca in the Thyestes: 'let this, let this table be closed with a cup.' The Scholiasts on the third book of the Odyssey also mention this. The first Christians also celebrated this mystery while dining. 'Breaking bread from house to house, they partook of food in gladness and simplicity of heart,' says Luke in Acts II. 46. See and compare what is said in Acts XX. 7 and 11. This is what Pliny says, that Christians met to take food, but common and harmless: and this is the very thing which Paul calls the Lord's supper to the Corinthians: Ignatius in his Epistle to the Smyrnaeans calls it a feast, as does the very ancient writer of the constitutions which bear the name of Clement, who also interprets the feast as love. Tertullian thinks the name of Agape, which is in the epistle of Jude, came into this sense from the fact that the poor were helped by that refreshment. But it must be seen whether or not this name was given to the whole banquet synecdochically from the mystical cup, just as the Eucharist is called so from the very thing for which thanks were given. For that cup, being indeed the most certain testimony of the love with which Christ loved us, and which he proposed for us to imitate, was called love. Ignatius: 'I desire the drink, his blood, which is love, incorruptible, and everlasting life': whence his other passage to the Ephesians is to be understood: 'having been rekindled in the blood of Christ.' For he wishes to signify mutual love by participation. That custom in the banquet of celebrating this Sacrament in that first age had nothing of vice in most places. There was eaten, as Tertullian says, as much as the hungry took, there was drunk as much as was useful for the modest: which Josephus and Philo also state concerning the banquets of the Jews which are called common meals. But the irreverence of some caused it not to be retained for long. For Paul chastises the unequal feasts of the Corinthians, contrary to the nature of love, and the historian Socrates notes the intemperance of the Egyptians because, having filled themselves with all kinds of food, they participated in the mysteries. Hence it was decreed that the mysteries should not be taken except by those who were fasting, which Chrysostom rightly observes was not done so from the beginning. Justin describes for us the participation of the Eucharist outside the form of a banquet: and Clement stirs up a controversy about the name of love regarding those banquets which were celebrated in his time, namely when the mysteries had already been separated from those banquets. But Tertullian seems to indicate that in his time the mysteries were already celebrated mostly in pre-dawn assemblies: yet the testimony of the most ancient custom remained in the fact that it was done on the very day of the anniversary of the Lord's supper. The canon of the third Council of Carthage looks to this, that the sacraments of the altar should not be celebrated except by fasting people, except for one anniversary day on which the Lord's supper is celebrated: with which agrees the Epistle of Augustine to Januarius. But also, the banquets of the faithful having already been separated (as in Paul's time) were celebrated in the very buildings of the churches until the times of the Synod of Laodicea, and in Africa even later. Grotius notes that the Eucharist was instituted while they were still dining, comparing Mark: who, however, teaches nothing of the sort, only employing these same words. But since Luke and Paul teach that this was done μετὰ τὸ δεῖπνῆσαι, B. Gerhard rightly observes from book VI of Scaliger’s De emendatione temporum, p. 273, in Harm. Evang. cap. CLXXI, p. 1489, that ἐσθιόντων is most conveniently taken as placed in the second Aorist having the meaning of the past, comparing for this matter similar passages in Matt. XI. 17 [Luke VII. 33], Matt. XIV. 21, ch. XV. 38, Mark II. 6, and especially because in this very history of the most recent Supper, Jesus is said to have complained about his betrayer and revealed him to the Apostles ἐσθιόντων αὐτῶν, Matt. XXVI. 21, Mark XIV. 18, which happened not only after the Paschal and common supper, but also after the sacramental supper, in which Judas had still participated.

But that the first Christians celebrated this mystery while eating, Grotius tries in vain to prove from Acts II. 46; for it is neither certain that there is talk there of the Eucharist, nor if that be admitted, does it appear from that passage that it was celebrated while eating, even if the taking of food and the breaking of bread are joined in the account.

τὸ ἄρτον] Unleavened bread, contrary to what the Greeks think; for although the time was anticipated, Christ nevertheless kept everything that could indeed be kept while they were preparing.

ἐυλογήσας] It was always the custom for the Jews, as appears from the Talmudic writers and Philo, not to take any food or wine unless they had first offered praises and thanks to God as the creator and giver, with the addition of a prayer, which Josephus called γεραίρειν τὸν θεὸν ὡς χορηγὸν τῆς τροφῆς. They call the prayer itself קדוש, that is, sanctification, or ברכה, that is, blessing. Before this was done, the food was considered profane; after this was done, it was holy, that is, something that was lawful to eat; which custom Paul, approving as pious, says: Every creature of God is good, and nothing to be rejected if received with thanksgiving, for it is sanctified by the word of God and prayer. In which sense he also used ἁγιάζεσθαι, although in another matter, in I Cor. VII. 14. But Paul rightly explains thanksgiving in the cited passage with the word prayer; for those things were joined. Josephus: Since thanksgiving is just by nature and is made in return for things already done, and for the encouragement of things to come. Hence it is that everywhere in this matter, to bless and to give thanks are used for the same thing. What Matthew ch. XIV. 19, Mark ch. VI. 41, and Luke IX. 16 said in the history of the multiplied loaves, looking up to heaven he blessed, John said he gave thanks and gave, ch. VI. 11. Mark said he gave thanks and broke, ch. VIII. 6, just as our interpreter of Matthew does here in ch. XV. 16, in which passages of Mark and John the Syrian translates he gave thanks as וברך. But in this passage in Matthew, for he blessed he said ואודי וברך, that is, he gave thanks and blessed. Thus also Paul in 1 Cor. XIV. 16, 17 uses to pray, to bless, and to give thanks for the same thing; in the same passage the Latin interpreter translates thanksgiving as blessing. Thus where it is soon about the cup, having given thanks, Cyprian in his letter to Caecilius cites he blessed; and Paul hence calls the cup the cup of blessing. It is no wonder, therefore, if in reciting these words about the consecrated bread Luke and Paul said he gave thanks, which the interpreter of Matthew and Mark said he blessed; indeed, in this very passage some Greek codices had he gave thanks, and the ancients cite it thus, among others Basil in his moral rules, from the interpretation, of course. But the full and proper expression is to give thanks to God, which we find everywhere, and indeed in the mention of the breaking of bread in Acts XXVII. 35, to which to bless God is worth just as much, Luke I. 64, ch. II. 28, ch. XXIV. 53, James III. 9. But the Hebrews, and the Hellenists following them, love abbreviations of expressions; therefore they say to bless someone or something for to bless God on account of something; which way of speaking is to be found everywhere among the Septuagint and these authors of ours, as Mark X. 16, Luke II. 34, ch. IX. 16, ch. XXIV. 50, 51. Thus the writer to the Hebrews said to make atonement for sins, for to make atonement to God concerning sins. In the same way, to bless the sacrifice, 1 Sam. IX. 13, is to bless God for the sacrifice. Thus to bless the cup in this argument Paul said in 1 Cor. X. 16, and here he blessed is rightly construed with that which preceded, the bread; and in a similar way, what follows soon after, having given thanks, with that which preceded, the cup. For to give thanks for bread or a cup is said no less rightly than to bless; and Justin teaches us that the ancient Christians were accustomed to speak by the example of the Apostles, who said the bread and wine for which thanks have been given, then the food for which thanks have been given. The common formula of blessing or of thanksgiving among the Hebrews was this: Blessed are you, our God, King of the world, who brings forth bread from the earth; blessed be our God, the Lord of the world, who brought forth bread from the earth. Similarly, concerning wine they said: Blessed be our God, the world, creator of the fruit of the vine; blessed be our God, the Lord of the world, who created

the fruit of the vine. But on feast days there was added a mention of the benefit whose memory was then being celebrated; as at Passover, the liberation from Egypt. Thus also Christ, about to multiply the loaves, undoubtedly added to the common prayers those proper to the thing which was then being done. And in this passage, he poured out prayers not only for the old creation, but also for the new, for the sake of which he had come into this world, and gave thanks to God for the redemption of the human race as if already accomplished, as one for whose fulfillment not much time remained; which is the reason why the sacred writers use words of the present tense here: which is given, which is poured out. The ancient Christians followed Christ in this matter, joining in this thanksgiving old benefits with new ones. Justin is a witness: Jesus Christ our Lord commanded us to do this for the remembrance of the passion which he suffered for those whose souls are cleansed from all wickedness of men, so that we might at once give thanks to God for having created the world with all things in it for the sake of man, and for having freed us from the wickedness in which we were born, and for having destroyed the principalities and powers with a complete destruction through him who became capable of suffering according to his will. There also exists in the so-called constitutions of Clement, book VII, ch. XXVII, a thanksgiving, in which it is said that he prepared things for the use of men. Soon follows: who sent Jesus Christ upon the earth, and other things which pertain to that. Irenaeus, book V, ch. II. And since we are his members, and are nourished by the creature, and he himself provides the creature for us, making his sun rise and raining as he wills; when he confirmed the cup, which is a creature, as his blood which was poured out, from which he increases our blood, and that bread which is a creature, as his body, from which he increases our bodies. When therefore both the mixed cup and the broken bread receive the word of God, it becomes the Eucharist of the blood and body of Christ, from which the substance of our flesh is increased and consists. Origen, Book VIII against Celsus: αλλα το ευχαριστοι ειναι προς τ' Θεον περιισαμεθα, ου τ' ευεργεσιων πληρεις εσμεν, κ' δημιουργηματα οντες αυτου κ' προνοι- μενοι υπ' αυτου κριθεντες οπως ποτε ειναι κ' εξω του βιου τας παρ' αυτου ελπιδας εκδεχομενοι. εστι δε κ συμβολον ημιν της προς τ' Θεον ευχαριστιας αρτος ευχαριστια καλομενος. An ancient prayer appearing in the Latin Mass: O God, who wonderfully created the dignity of human substance and more wonderfully restored it. Ibidem: Through Christ our Lord, through whom you, O Lord, always create, sanctify, vivify, bless, and provide us with all these good things. Then: That which we have taken with our mouth, O Lord, may we receive with a pure mind, and may the temporal gift become for us an everlasting remedy.

Although the Sacred Writers interchange the terms ευλογιας and ευχαριστιας, and even include one under the other, yet ευχαριστια properly denotes thanksgiving directed to God the Father, whereas ευλογια refers to the external Symbols, bread and wine, which Christ consecrated into the communion of his body and blood: whence it cannot be proven that Grotius holds these to be the same. See what we said in Stereomat. against D. Bergium.

εκλασε] This breaking signifies both the sufferings of Christ, especially on the cross, whence Paul added concerning the body τουπερ υμων κλωμενον, and not a few Liturgies express this meaning, especially the Syriac, and at the same time also the liberality of Christ inviting us to the communion of all the goods which were to be produced through the cross. For because the loaves of the Hebrews were κλαστοι, it was therefore accepted among them to say 'to break bread' for 'to make others partakers of it,' as in Isaiah 58:7, Lamentations 4:4, Mark 8:19: 'when I broke the five loaves for the five thousand.' For the loaves of the Hebrews were so large that they sufficed for all the guests. Diogenes Laertius on Pythagoras: εκεινα αρτον οι παλαι τ' Φιλων ε- φοιτων καθαπερ κ' νυν οι βαρβαροι. Xenophon, Expedition, Book VII, concerning Seuthes, King of the Thracians: απολομεν@ τους παρα- κειμενες αυτω αρτους διεκλα κατα μικρον και διερριπτει οις αυτω εδοκει. Jamblichus, το αρχαιον βαρβαρικως παντες επι' ενα αρτον συνισαν οι φιλοι. Therefore, when the ancients treat of communion, they name parts, fragments, κλασματα. See Augustine, Sermon II on the words of the Apostle.

This breaking is rightly referred to the distribution of Christ from Isaiah 58:7, Lamentations 4:4, and therefore it should not be referred simultaneously to the sufferings of Christ on the cross: for the meaning of distribution cannot have a place in the same word as the meaning of breaking into pieces: which Christ neither suffered nor ought to have suffered.

Φαγετε] Among the various kinds of sacrifices, it was illustrious among the Hebrews that which they called שְׁלָמִים. Philo translates it σωτήριον: Josephus χαριςήριον, others εὐχαριςικὸν: but εὐχαριςικὸν is properly a species of תּוֹדָה of the σωτήρια. For σωτήρια sacrifices were performed not only for obtaining, but also for benefits already received. Now it is known to the Hebrews that שָׁלוֹם is said of every kind of good: but just as εὐχαριςεῖν was taken broadly by the Hellenists, so it is no wonder if they also spoke of εὐχαριςικῶν θυσιῶν in a broader sense. In these sacrifices, therefore, that was as it were peculiar, that a part of the victims fell to God and His priests, but a part to those offering: God wished this to be a testimony of His goodness toward them, as if, in the manner of friends, He were taking common meals with them: For those who eat the sacrifices, as Paul says, are partakers of the altar, 1. Cor. X. 18. and likewise among the Greeks and other nations it was practiced, that those who offered victims would feast upon their flesh, as can be seen everywhere among the poets: whether that took its origin from the example of the Hebrews, or, which is more probable, from the institutions of common parents. Thus also the Catilinarians, as Plutarch narrates, having sacrificed a man, tasted of the flesh. Christ, therefore, being about to perform a sacrifice, wishes to make those who believe in Him partakers of that sacrifice, just as if they themselves had offered this sacrifice, because it had been offered by Him who had taken upon Himself their nature; for He partook of flesh and blood, Heb. II, 14. This efficacy of His sacrifice, so that it could be clearly understood, He explained to them when He said to the Father, I sanctify Myself that they also may be sanctified in the truth Joh. XVII. 19. and soon after: I will that where I am, they also may be with Me, vers. 24. Both things, namely, both the knowledge and sealing of the truth, as the true food of souls, and the glorious joys which are expected after this life, the Jews also commonly knew were signified by the word eating. Of the former, Philo is a witness when he says thus in his book on Allegories: eating is a symbol of psychic nourishment, and the soul is nourished by the reception of good things and the performance of virtuous deeds: and in his book on the sacrifices of Abel and Cain: those who have already partaken and to whom nature might again be propitious know, being called to a participation in a feast, not one from which the pleasures of the belly, being filled, fatten the body, but from which the mind, being nourished and dancing with virtues, rejoices and is gladdened. Thus also Moses Maimonides in the opinions of the Hebrews says that to eat signifies to apprehend by the intellect: the place is in the Guide for the Perplexed, book I, chapter 29. which the places of the prophets also show to be true, Jerem. XV. 16. Ezech. III. 3. Prov. IX. 5. Apoc. X. 9. And Ecclesiasticus chapter XV. 3. c. XXIV. 29. The writer on the Lord's Supper, what food is to the flesh, this faith is to the soul. Servius on that in the III. Aeneid, He loosens the fillets: In the rationale of sacred rites, there is a cause for both the soul and the body. For often those things which cannot be done regarding the soul are done regarding the body. And elsewhere in book IV. In sacred rites, things which could not be exhibited were simulated and were taken for true. Tertullian on Baptism: That form which always precedes carnal things in the figure of spiritual ones. Evidence of the latter occurs often in the books of the Rabbis, where to eat and drink in the future world often appears. Therefore, following this received mode of speaking, the Pharisee said, Blessed is he who shall eat bread in the kingdom of God Luke XIV. 15. And Christ, whose speech was everywhere conspicuous and popular, shadowed forth future joys with the same image, not only among the Apostles as Luke XXII. 30. but also among the common people Matth. VIII. 11. But just as Christ in John had used the word ἁγιάζειν taken from sacrifices, so the writer to the Hebrews uses the same when he says: For both He who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are all from one. And Paul, just as he had said that those who eat the sacrifices are partakers of the altar, so he calls the bread the communion of the body. And the ancient Christians teach everywhere that this Sacrament was instituted so that we might share in the sufferings of Him who for our sake was made capable of suffering, bone of our bones, flesh of our flesh, and again in His glory, coalescing as it were into one flesh for the completion of that which had once been shadowed forth through the institution of marriage 1. Cor. VI. 17. it would be long to cite the places. The species of bread was well employed for the signification of the body, because it approaches most closely to its nature: all things are nourished by the same things from which they are, says Aristotle. And food is the matter of flesh according to Galen. And thus, not only to the Arabs does the word לַחַם, which is properly bread to the Hebrews, signify flesh, but the same word is found with that meaning among the Hebrews also, as in Zephaniah I. 17. Nor do some interpret that of Job VI. 7. otherwise, so that the sense may be: the languors of my flesh.

The Grotius comparison with the peace offering, because there a part fell to God and a part to those offering, is irrelevant here. For our sacrifice is celebrated here, and no part falls to God. The signification also of knowledge and sealing as the true food of souls or of heavenly joys does not apply here: because Christ wished this bread to be a medium not of signification, but of communication, and indeed of communion, not of our body, but of His body, which was delivered for us: then whatever is noted elsewhere by the word eating, here that word must be taken properly: for by the same word we are commanded to eat both the bread, which cannot be taken except by the mouth of the body, and the body of Christ. But that the species of bread was used for the signification of the body of Christ is a Calvinist gloss: for Christ does not say, the bread signifies My body, but this is My body.

Latin:

Vers. 26. ἐσθιόντων δὲ αὐτῶν] Ita & Marcus : id est, adhuc illis cœnantibus. Nam vinum quidem ex more Judæorum, qui nunc quoque in die Paschatis, aliisque diebus festis id observant, & in cœna & post cœnam cum gratiarum actio- ne bibebatur: ac panis frangebatur & distribuebatur cœna adhuc durante, sed ferme peracta. Hinc de poculo specia- tim dicunt & Lucas & Paulus sumtum à Christo μετὰ τὸ δειπ- νῆσαι: quod in Missa Latina exponitur postquam cœnatum est: Lucas autem & in cœna & post cœnam propinatum memo- rat : sed post cœnam cum mansuri ritus institutione. Etiam apud Græcos postremum poculum, idque pro sacro habi- tum, bibebatur eo ipso tempore quo tollebantur mensæ : Nicostratus, ἀλλ’ ἔγχεοντα θᾶττον ἀγαθῦ δαίμονθ’ ὐπενεγκά- τω μοι τὴν τράπεζαν ἐκ ποδῶν. Xenophon : ὡς δὲ ἀφηρέθησαν αἱ τράπεζαι κὴ ἐσπείσαντο κὴ ἐπαιάνισαν. Scholiastes Aristo- phanis ad Vespes : ἔθος ἦν ὁπότε μέλλοι ἡ τράπεζα αἴρεσθαι ἀγαθῦ δαίμονος ἐπιῤῥοφεῖν. Seneca Thyeste: hoc, hoc mensa claudatur scypho. Meminerunt & Scholiastæ ad tertium Odysseæ. Primi quoque Christiani inter cœnandum ce- lebrarunt hoc mysterium. Κλῶντες τε καθ’ οἶκον ἄρτον με- τελάμβανον τροφῆς ἐν ἀγαλλιάσει κὴ ἀφελότητι καρδίας, in- quit Lucas Act. II. 46. Vide & confer quod dicitur Act. XX. 7. & 11. Hoc est quod Plinius ait coïisse Christianos ad capiendum cibum sed promiscvum & innoxium: idque i- psum est quod δεῖπνον κυριακὸν Paulus ad Corinthios vocat:I- gnatius in Epistola ad Smyrnenses δοχὴν, ut & Scriptor vetu- stissimus constitutionum quæ Clementis nomen præferunt, qui & δοχὴν interpretatur ἀγάπην. Nomen Agapæ, quod in Judæ epistola est, in hoc sensu venisse putat Tertullianus inde quod inopes isto refrigerio juvarentur. Sed videndum an non συνεκδοχικῶς ex poculo mystico id datum sit nomen toti convivio, quomodo εὐχαριστία dicta est δι’ αὐτὸ τὸ εὐ- χαριστηθέντος. Nam poculum illud, certissimum quip- pe testimonium amoris quo nos Christus dilexit, quemque nobis imitandum proposuit, ἀγάπη dicebatur. Ignatius : πό- μα θέλω τὸ αἷμα ἀυτῦ ὅ ἐσιν ἀγάπη, ἄφθαρτος, κὴ ἀέναος ζωή : unde intelligendus alter ejusdem locus ad Ephesios : ἀναζωπυρήσαντες ἐν αἵματι χρισῦ. Vult enim μεταληπτικῶς significare dilectionem mutuam. Mos ille in convivio ce- lebrandi hoc Sacramentum prima illa ætate nihil habebat vitii plerisque in locis. Edebatur, ut ait Tertullianus, quan- tum esurientes capiebant, bibebatur quantum pudicis esset utile: quod & de Judæorum conviviis quæ σύνδειπνα vocantur, prædicant Josephus & Philo. Sed quorundam irreveren- tia effecit ne diu retineretur. Nam Corinthiorum inæquales epulas, contra naturam τῆς ἀγάπης, castigat Paulus, & So- crates historicus Ægyptiorum notat ἀκρασίαν quod παντοί- ων ἐδεσμάτων ἐμφορηθέντες participarent mysteria. Hinc constitutum ne mysteria sumerentur nisi à jejunis, quod ab initio ita non esse factitatum recte observat Chrysostomus. Justinus nobis τὴν τῆς ἐυχαριστίας μετοχὴν extra convivii for- mam describit : & Clemens istis quæ suo tempore celebra- bantur conviviis de nomine ἀγάπης controversiam movet, nimitum cum jam ab iis conviviis mysteria essent segregata. At Tertullianus indicare videtur jam suo tempore celebrata mysteria antelucanis maxime cœtibus: mansit tamen ant- quissimi moris testimonium in eo quod fiebat ipso die cœ- næ Dominicæ anniversario. Canon concilii Carthaginien- sis tertii huc spectat, ut sacramenta altaris non nisi à jejunis ho- minibus celebrentur, excepto uno die anniversario quo cæna Do- mini celebratur : quicum convenit Epistola Augustini ad Ja- nuarium. Sed & segregaris jam mysteriis fidelium convivia ut Pauli tempore) in ipsis Ecclesiarum ædibus celebraban- tur ad tempora Synodi Laodicenæ, in Africa etiam serius. Notat Grotius adhuc illis cænantibus institutam esse Eucharistiam, conferens Marcum: qui ve- ro nihil tale docet, eadem hæc verba solum ad- hibens. Sed quum Lucas & Paulus μετὰ τὸ δει- πνῆσαι hoc factum doceant, recte observat B. Ger- hard. è libro VI. Scaligeri de emendat. tempor. p. 273. in Harm. Evang. cap. CLXXI. p. 1489. quod ἐσθιόντων commodissime accipiatur positum in Ao- risto secundo præteriti significationem habente, con- ferens eam in rem similia loca Matth. XI. 17. [Luc. VII. 33.] Matth. XIV. 21. c. XV. 38. Marc. II. 6. & imprimis quod in hac ipsa novissime Cænæ Historia Jesus de proditore suo questus dicitur, eundemque manifestavit Apostolis ἐσθιόντων αὐτῶν, Matth. XXVI. 21. Marc. XIV. 18. quod factum est non solum post cœnam Paschalem & vulgarem, sed etiam post cœ- nam sacramentalem, cui Judas adhuc interfuerat.

Primos autem Christianos inter cœnandum cele- brasse hoc mysterium Grotius nequicquam probat ex Act. II. 46. nam neque constat, ibi de Euchari- stia sermonem esse: neque si id admittatur, ex eo loco apparet, quod inter cœnandum ea celebrata sit, utut conjungatur in relatione cibi sumtio; & ἀρτοκλασία.

τὸ ἄρτον] Azymum, contra quam sentiunt Græci: quan- quam enim anticipato tempore omnia tamen παρατιζόν- των servavit Christus quæ quidem servari poterant.

ἐυλογήσας] Moris semper Judæis fuit, ut ex Thalmudicis Scriptoribus & Philone apparet, cibum nullum aut vinum sumere nisi prius Deo tanquam conditori donatorique lau- des & grates egissent, addita precatione quod γεραίρειν τὸν θεὸν ὡς χορηγὸν τῆς τροφῆς dixit Josephus: Ipsam precatio- nem קדוש id est ἁγιασμὸν vocant: aut ברכה id est ἐυλο- γίαν. Antequam id fieret, cibus pro profano habebatur: hoc facto ἅγιον id est quo vesci fas esset: quem morem ut pium approbans Paulus πᾶν κτίσμα Θεῦ καλὸν, inquit, κὶ ἐδὲν ἀπό- βλητον μετὰ ἐυχαριστίας λαμβανόμενον, ἁγιάζεται γὰρ διὰ λόγω Θεῦ κὶ ἐντεύξεως. Quo sensu ἁγιάζεσθαι, quanquam in re alia, usurpavit & I. Cor. VII. 14. Bene autem Paulus dicto loco ἐυχαριστίαν explicat voce ἐντεύξεως: erant enim ista conjuncta. Josephus: δικαίας ὔσης φύσει τῆς ἐυχαριστίας κὶ γενομένης ἐπ᾿ ἀμοιβῇ μὲν ὧν ἤδη γεγονότων, ἐπὶ δὲ προτροπῇ τῶν ἐσομένων. Hinc est quod passim pro eodem ponuntur in hoc negotio ἐυλογεῖν καὶ ἐυχαριστῶν. Quod Matthæus cap. XIV. 19. Marcus c. VI. 41. Lucas IX. 16. dixere, in histo- ria panum multiplicatorum ἀναβλέψας εἰς ὸν ὀρανὸν ἐυλόγησε, Johannes ἐυχαριστήσας δέδωκε c. VI. 11. Marcus dixit ἐυχαρι- στήσας ἔκλασε c. VIII. 6. quomodo & hic noster Matthæi in- terpres c. XV. 16. in quibus locis Marci & Johani Syrus ἐυχαριστήσας vertit וברך Hoc autem loco apud Matthæum, pro ἐυλογήσας dixit ואודי וברך, id est, ἐυχαριστήσας καὶ ἐυλογήσας. Sic & Paulis 1. Cor. XV. 16. 17. pro eodem ponit προσεύχεσθαι, ἐυλογεῖν, ἐυχαριστῶν: eodem loco Latinus inter- pres ἐυχαριστίαν vertit benedictionem. Sic ubi mox est de poculo ἐυχαριστήσας, Cyprianus epistola ad Cæcilium ci- tat benedixit: & Paulus hinc calicem vocat ποτήριον ἐυλογίας. Non mirum igitur si in recitandis his verbis de sacrato pane Lucas & Paulus dixerunt ἐυχαριστήσας, quod Matthæi inter- pres & Marcus ἐυλογήσας: imo & hoc ipso loco quidam Græ- ci codices habuerunt ἐυχαριστήσας, atque ita citant veteres, inter alios Basilius regulis moralibus, ex interpretamento scilicet. Plena autem & propria locutio est ἐυχαριστεῖν τῷ Θεῷ, quod passim invenimus, & quidem in mentione fran- gendi panis Act. XXVII. 15. cui tantundem valet ἐυλογεῖν ὸν Θεὸν, Luc. I. 64. c. II. 28 c. XXIV. 53. Jac. III. 9. Sed Hebræi, & hos secuti Hellenistæ, amant dictionum compendia: ita- que ἐυλογεῖν τινα vel τι dicunt pro ἐυλογεῖν θεὸν ὑπὲρ τινθ: quod loquendi genus apud LXX. & hos nostros passim re- perire est, ut Marc. X. 16. Luc. II. 34. c. IX. 16. c. XXIV. 50. 51. Sic ἰλάσκεσθαι τὰς ἁμαρτίας dixit Scriptor ad Hebræos, pro i- λάσκεσθαι Θεὸν περὶ ῒ ἁμαρτιῶν. Pari modo ברך הזבח ἐυλο- γεῖν τὴν θυσίαν, 1. Sam. IX. 13. est ἐυλογεῖν ῒ θεὸν ὑπὲρ τῆς θυσίας. Sic ἐυλογεῖν τὸ ποτήριον in hoc argumento dixit Paulus 1. Cor. IX. 16. & hic ἐυλογήσας recte construitur cum eo quod præ- cessit τὸν ἄρτον: Similique modo quod mox sequitur, ἐυχαρι- στήσας cum eo quod præcessit τὸ ποτήριον. Nam & ἐυχαριστεῖν ἄρτον aut ποτήριον non minus recte dicitur quam ἐυλογεῖν: atque ita loqui solitos Apostolorum exemplo Christianos veteres Justinus nos docet, qui dixit ἰυχαριστηθέντα ἄρτον καὶ οἶνον, deinde ἐυχαριστηθεῖσαν τροφὴν. Formula communis τῆς ἐυλογίας sive τῆς ἐυχαριστίας apud Hebræos hæc erat: ברוך אתה אלהינו מלך העולם המוציא לחם מן הארץ: ἐυλογητὸς ὁ Θεὸς ἡμῶν ὁ κύριος τῶ κόσμω ὁ ἐυρήσας ῒ ἄρτον ἐκ τῆς γῆς. Similiter de vino dicebant ברוך אלהינו העולם בורא פרי הגפן ἐυλογητὸς ὁ Θεὸς ἡμῶν ὁ κύριος τῶ κόσμω ὁ κτίσας

το γεννημα της αμπελε. Sed diebus festis accedebat mentio be- neficii cujus tum memoria'celebrabatur; ut Paschate libe- rationis ex Ægypto. Sic & Christus panes multiplicaturus, haud dubie ad communes preces addidit proprias rei quæ tum agebatur. Et hoc loco, non pro veteri tantum crea- tione, sed & pro nova, cujus ergo in hunc orbem venerat, preces fudit gratiasq; Den egit pro redemtione humani ge- neris quasi jam peracta, utpote cui implendæ non multum temporis restaret: quæ causa est cur & præsentis temporis verba hic usurpent sacri Scriptores: το διδομενον, το εκχυνομενον. Secuti hac in re Christum sunt veteres Christiani, conjun- gentes in hac gratiarum actione beneficia vetera cum novis. Testis Justinus: η αρτου της ευχαριστιας εις αναμνησιν του παθους ου επαθεν υπερ τ καθαριζομενων τας ψυχας απο πασης πονηριας ανθρωπων, Ιησους χριστος ο κυριος ημων παρεδωκε ποιειν, ινα, αμα τε ευχαριστωμεν τω Θεω υπερ τε τ' κοσμον εκτικεναι συν πασι τοις εν αυτω δια τ ανθρωπον, κ υπερ του απο της κακιας εν η γεγοναμεν ηλευθερωκεναι ημας, κ τας αρχας κ τας εξουσιας καταλελυκεναι τελειαν καταλυσιν δια του παθητου γενομενου κατα την βουλην αυτου. Exstat & in Clementis quæ dicuntur consti- tutionibus libro VII. c. XXVII. gratiarum actio, in qua di- citur τα προς μεταληψιν προευτρεπισαι ανθρωποις. Sequitur mox: ο επισειλας επι γης Ιησουν τ' Χριστον, & alia quæ eo perti- nent. Irenæus lib. V. c. II. Et quoniam membra ejus sumus, & per creaturam nutrimur, creaturam autem ipse nobis præstat, solem suum oriri faciens & pluens quemadmodum vult; cum calicem, qui est creatura, suum sanguinem qui effusus est, ex quo auget nostrum sanguinem, & eum panem qui est creatura, suum corpus confirmavit, ex quo nostra auget corpora. Quando ergo & mixtus calix & fractus panis percipit verbum Dei, fit Eucharistia sanguinis & corporis Christi, ex quibus augetur & consistit carnis nostræ substantia. Origenes IIX. adversus Celsum: αλλα το ευχαριστοι ειναι προς τ' Θεον περιισαμεθα, ου τ' ευεργεσιων πληρεις εσμεν, κ' δημιουργηματα οντες αυτου κ' προνοι- μενοι υπ' αυτου κριθεντες οπως ποτε ειναι κ' εξω του βιου τας παρ' αυτου ελπιδας εκδεχομενοι. εστι δε κ συμβολον ημιν της προς τ' Θεον ευχαριστιας αρτος ευχαριστια καλομενος. Oratio ve- tus exitans in Missa Latina: Deus qui humanæ substantiæ di- gnitatem mirabiliter condidisti & mirabilius reformasti. Ibi- dem: Per Christum Dominum nostrum, per quem hæc omnia Domine semper bona creas, sanctificas, vivificas, benedicis & præstas nobis. Deinde: quod ore sumpsimus Domine, pia men- te capiamus, & de munere temporali fiat nobis remedium sem- piternum.

Quanquam ευλογιας & ευχαριστιας voces per- mutent S. Scriptores, & sub una alteram etiam comprehendant, ευχαριστια tamen proprie ad Deum Patrem directam gratiarum actionem infert, ευλογια vero respicit externa Symbola, panem & vinum, quæ in communicationem corporis & sanguinis sui consecravit Christus: unde probari nequit, quod Grotius hæc pro iisdem habeat. Vid. quæ in Stereomat. contr. D. Bergium dixi- mus.

εκλασε] Hæc fractio tum perpessiones Christi, in cruce præsertim, significat, unde Paulus adjecit de corpore τουπερ υμων κλωμενον, & Liturgiæ non paucæ hanc significationem exprimunt, præsertim Syriaca, tum simul etiam liberalita- tem Christi nos invitantis ad communionem omnium bo- norum quæ per crucem erant parienda. Nam quia panes Hebæorum erant κλαστοι, ideo receptum apud illos erat, ut frangere panem dicerent, pro ejus participes alios facere, ut Es. LIIX. 7. Thren. IV. 4. Marci IIX. 19. οτε τους πεντε αρ- τους εκλασα εις τους πεντακισχιλιους. Erant enim panes He- bræorum ita magni ut omnibus convivis sufficerent. Dio- genes Laërtius Pythagora: εκεινα αρτον οι παλαι τ' Φιλων ε- φοιτων καθαπερ κ' νυν οι βαρβαροι. Xenophon expeditionis VII. de Zeuthe rege Thracum: απολομεν@ τους παρα- κειμενες αυτω αρτους διεκλα κατα μικρον και διερριπτει οις αυτω εδοκει. Jamblichus, το αρχαιον βαρβαρικως παντες επι' ενα αρτον συνισαν οι φιλοι. Ideo cum de communione agunt veteres, nominant partes, fragmenta κλασματα. Vide Au- gustinum Serm. II. de verbis Apostoli.

Fractio hæc recte ad distributionem Christi refertur ex Es. LIIX. 7. Thren. IV. 4. ideoque non simul ad perpessiones Christi in cruce referri: non enim pariter distributionis significatio in eadem voce locum habere potest, & comminutionis in partes: quam etiam nullam passus est, aut pati de- buit Christus.

Φαγετε] Inter varia sacrificiorum genera illustre erat- apud Hebræos id quod vocabant שְׁלָמִים. Philo σωτήριον vertit: Josephus χαριςήριον, alii εὐχαριςικὸν: sed εὐχαριςικὸν proprie est תּוֹדָה species τῶν σωτηρίων. Nam σωτήρια sa- cra non tantum pro obtinendis, sed & pro obteptis benefi- ciis fiebant. Notum autem est Hebræis שָׁלוֹם dici o- mne bonorum genus: sed sicut εὐχαριςεῖν late sumtum est ab Hellenistis, ita non mirum si & εὐχαριςικῶν θυσιῶν largio- re significatu dixere. In his igitur sacris illud erat quasi peculiare quod victimæ pars Deo ejusque Sacerdotibus, pars vero offerentibus cedebat: id Deus bonitatis suæ erga ipsos testimonium esse volebat, quasi scilicet amicorum more communes cum ipsis epulas sumeret: Nam οἱ ἐσθί- οντες τὰς θυσίας: ut inquit Paulus, κοινωνοὶ τῦ θυσιαςηρίε εἰ- σι, 1. Cor. X. 18. atque itidem apud Græcos aliasque gen- tes usurpabatur, ut qui victimas offerrent, de earum carne epularentur, ut passim apud Poëtas videre est: sive id ab Hebræorum exemplo originem traxit, seu quod est pro- babilius, à communium parentum institutis. Itaque & Catilinarii narrante Plutarcho καταθύσαντες ἄνθρωπον ἐγεύ- σαντο τῶν σαρκῶν. Christus ergo sacrificium peracturus in se credentes vult participes facere ejus sacrificii, plane quasi ipsi hoc sacrificium obtulissent, quia oblatum erat ab eo qui ipsorum naturam susceperat; μετέσχε γὰρ σαρκὸς καὶ αἵματος, Hebr. II, 14. Hanc sacrificii sui efficaciam, ita ut clare posset intelligi, ipsis explicabat cum diceret ad Patrem, ἐγὼ ἁγιάζω ἐμαυτὸν ἵνα καὶ αὐτοὶ ὦσιν ἡγιασμένοι ἐν τῇ ἀληθείᾳ Joh. XVII. 19. & mox: θέλω ἵνα ὅπε εἰμὶ ἐγὼ κἀκεῖ- νοι ὦσι μετ' ἐμῦ, vers. 24. Utrumque scilicet, tum ve- ri cognitionem atque obsignationem, ut verum pastum animorum, tum gloriosa gaudia quæ post hanc vitam ex- pectantur, etiam vulgo sciebant Judæi manducandi ver- bo significari. Prioris testis est Philo cum ita ait libro de Allegoriis: τὸ φαγεῖν σύμβολον ἐςι τροφῆς ψυχικῆς, τρέφε- ται δὲ ἡ ψυχὴ, ἀναλήψει τῶν καλῶν, καὶ πράξει τῶν κατορθωμά- των: & libro de sacrificiis Abel & Cain: ἴσασιν οἱ κεκοινωνη- κότες ἤδη κὶ οἷς ἡ φύσις ἵλεως πάλιν γένοιτο αι, κληθέντες εἰς μετουσίαν θοίνης, ἐκ ἐξ ἧς, αἱ γαςρὸς ἡδοναὶ πιμπλαμένης τὸ σῶμα πιαίνεσι, ἀλλ' ἀφ' ἧς διάνοια ἐκτρεφομένη κὶ ἐγχορεύου- σα ἀρεταῖς γάνυται κὶ εὐφραίνεται. Sic & Moses Maimonides in Hebræorum ὑπονοίαις comedere dicit id valere quod in- tellectu apprehendere: locus est in ductore dubitantium lib. I. cap. 29. quod verum esse ostendunt & propheta- rum loca Jerem. XV. 16. Ezech. III. 3. Prov. IX. 5. Apoc. X. 9. Et Ecclesiasticus cap. XV. 3. c. XXIV. 29. Scriptor de cœna Domini, quod esca est carni, hoc anima fides. Ser- vius ad illud in III. Æneid. Vittasque resolvit: In ratione sa- crorum pars est & animæ & corporis causa. Nam plerumque quæ non possunt circa animam fieri, fiunt circa corpus. Etali- bi libro IV. In sacris quæ exhiberi non poterant, simulabantur & erant pro veris. Tertullianus de Baptismo: Ea forma quæ semper carnalia in figuram spiritualium antecedunt. Alterius indicia passim in libris Rabbinorum, ubi edere & bibere in mundo futuro sæpe occurrit. Itaque receptum hunc loquendi modum sequens Pharisæus di cebat, μακάρι- ος Φάγεται ἄρτον ἐν τῇ βασιλείᾳ τῦ θεῦ Luc. XIV. 15. Et Christus, cujus sermo ubique erat conspicuus ac popula- ris, futura gaudia eadem imagine adumbrabat, non tan- tum apud Apostolos ut Luc. XXII. 30. sed & apud ple- bem Matth. VIII. 11. Sicut autem Christus apud Johan- nem vocem ἁγιάζειν à sacrificiis desumtam usurpaverat, ita eadem utitur Scriptor ad Hebræos cum dicit: ὅτε γὰρ ἁ- γιάζων κὶ οἱ ἁγιαζόμενοι ἐξ ἑνὸς πάντες. Et Paulus sicut dixe- rat κοινωνὸς εἶναι θυσιαςηρίε τὲς ἐσθίοντας τὰς θυσίας, ita τὸν ἄρτον vocat κοινωνίαν τῦ σώματος. Ac passim docent Chri- stiani veteres institutum hoc Sacramentum ut perpessioni- bus ipsius qui propter nos factus est παθητὸς, os ex ossibus nostris, caro ex carne nostra, & rursum gloriæ communi- caremus, coalescentes velut εἰς σάρκα μίαν ad comple- mentum ejus quod olim per matrimonii institutionem fue- rat adumbratum 1. Cor. VI. 17. loca asserre longum esset. Bene autem panis species adhibita ad corporis significa- tionem, quia ad ejus naturam proxime accedit: ἅπαντα τρέφεται τοῖς αὐτοῖς ἐξ ὥσπερ ἐςιν inquit Aristoteles. Et σιτίον ὕλη σαρκὸς apud Galenum. Atque adeo non Ara- bibus tantum vox לַחַם, quæ panis proprie est Hebræis, carnem significat, sed & Hebræis vox eadem illo significa- tu reperitur, ut Sopkaniæ I. 17. Nec aliter nonnulli in- terpretantur illud Jobi VI. 7. ut sensus sit: languores carnis meæ.

Collatio Grotiana cum Sacrificio שׁלם, quod ibi pars Deo, pars offerentibus cederet, hic aliena est. Nostrum enim hic sacrificium cele- bratur, neque Deo aliqua pars cedit. Signi- ficatio etiain cognitionis & obsignationis ceu veri pastus animarum aut gaudiorum cælestium huc non facit: quia non fignificationis, sed commu- nicationis medium voluit esse Christus hunc pa- nem, & quidem τῆς κοινωνίας, non corporis no- stri, sed corporis sui, quod pro nobis traditum est: tum quicquid alibi manducationis voce no- tetur, hic proprie verbum illud accipiendum est: qui eadem voce & panem, qui non potest nisi ore corporis accipi, manducare jubemur, & corpus Christi. Speciem autem panis adhibi- tam esse ad fignificationem corporis Christi, glos- sa est Calviniana: non enim ait Christus, pa- nis significat corpus meum, sed hoc est corpus meum.

## 26:27
Vers. 27. τὸ ποτήριον] The cup was frequently passed around at the supper: but here it concerns the final draught, which was more solemn than the others even among the Gentiles: as we have already shown before. That there was wine tempered with water in that cup, the book Misnajoth concerning blessing VII teaches us. And the nature of that climate seems to have demanded this, so that wines, especially if taken a little more liberally than usual, would not be drunk unless tempered with water. See Prov. IX. 2, 5, Apoc. XVIII. 6, and the writer on Hebrew questions, who is read among the works of Jerome. This custom also passed to the ancient Christians. Justin [mentions] ποτήριον ὕδατος κὶ κράματος. Hence Irenæus called it the mixed cup. Clement: κέραται ὁ οἶνος τῷ ὕδατι. Cyprian calls it the Lord’s tradition, that the cup which is offered in commemoration of the Lord should be offered mixed with wine. Add Canon XL among the African [canons] and the ancient Syriac, Greek, Arabic, and Latin liturgies.

That the wine in the chalice was tempered with water, Grotius ineptly attempts to prove from the book of Misnajoth, Berakoth VII. What has that book to do with the most holy institution of Christ? And what is the relevance here of what the genius of his heaven seemed to demand? To everyone it is clear how much weight should be given to such quibbles. In divine matters, and especially in the institution of the Sacraments, one must rely upon the express word, not upon our own judgment, which here is either non-existent or fallacious. The testimonies of the rites of the Ancients, of Irenaeus, of Cyprian, and of Canon XL among the Africans, teach the ἀδιαφορίαν of that mixing, but they imply no necessity.

Εὐχαριστήσας] This has the same meaning as εὐλογήσας, as I said above. Paul expressed the very name of the cup that was received when he said ποτήριον εὐλογίας. For the Hebrews called it כּוֹס הַלּל. Moreover, בּרֵךְ and הלל are accustomed to be taken synonymously, as appears in Ps. X, 3, where one word explains the other. And in Isaiah LXIV, 11, הללו is translated by the LXX interpreters as ἐυλόγησαν.

πίετε ἐξ ἀυτῦ πάντες] In sacred rites (and consequently also in covenants which were concluded with a sacred rite interposed, Psalm 50:5), blood was indeed accustomed to be poured into bowls, as we read in the fourth book of Papinius Statius’s Thebaid and in other places: but because to drink blood was inhuman (although we read that this also was done in some covenants: for thus Plutarch in his Publicola says that young patricians, having sworn a covenant among themselves, drank the blood of a slaughtered man, and Tacitus in Annals XII called a covenant consecrated by gore; and Magellan found the same custom among the Americans; and Valerius Maximus, book IX, chapter 2, narrates that this was practiced by Tigranes in Armenia; by the Scythians, according to Solinus and Mela; by the Saracens, according to Nicetas Choniates; by the Danes, according to Saxo Grammaticus), it was established among more civilized peoples that wine should be drunk in place of blood, whence יין עבודה זרה is to the Hebrews the wine of profane sacrifices: to which Ezekiel alludes, chapter 39:19, 20. And wine is called the blood of the grape: and by its very color (for wines were almost always red, Ps. 75:9) it represented blood. Those who drank this wine were considered to be imbued with the very blood of the victim. Philo says, ἀπὸ τότε γέτοι φασὶ τὸ μεθύειν ὠνομάσθαι ὅτι μετὰ τὸ θύειν ἔθος ἦν τοῖς προτέροις οἰνοῦσθαι. Aristophanes in the Lysistrata shows that treaties also, as I have said, were accustomed to be confirmed by bringing forward a cup, and elsewhere, alluding to that custom, he said σπονδὰς ἐκπίομαι. And Diodorus Siculus says that the name σπονδαὶ was born from the libation of wine. Hence for Homer σπονδαὶ ἄκρητοι. Plutarch shows the origin, speaking of the Egyptians in his book On Isis: ἐκ ἔπινον οἶνον ἐδὲ ἐσπενδον ὡς φίλιον θεοῖς, ἀλλ᾽ ὡς αἷμα τῶν πολεμησάντων πότε τοῖς θεοῖς. Join to this what will follow shortly concerning the use of blood in a covenant. Certainly, not only in this, but also in the sacrament of baptism, Christ seems altogether to have accommodated Himself to the understanding not only of the Hebrews, but also of the Gentiles who were to be co-opted into the same covenant.

Grotius testifies to a profane mind, which gathers from profane sources that in sacred rites and also in treaties blood was accustomed to be poured into bowls, that in certain treaties they even drank blood, and that among more gentle peoples it was established that wine should be drunk in place of blood, and that those who drank this were considered to be imbued with the blood of the victim itself, and that Aristophanes testifies that treaties were accustomed to be confirmed by a cup being brought forward; finally, that not only in this, but also in the sacrament of Baptism, Christ seems to have accommodated himself not only to the Hebrews, but also to the Gentiles who were to be adopted into the same covenant. Away with profane rites, away with profane thoughts from this most divine Sacrament!

Latin:

Vers. 27. τὸ ποτήριον] Sæpius calix circumferebatur in cœna: sed hic de postrema poratione agitur, quæ cæte- ris solennior etiam apud gentes: ut jam ante ostendimus. Fuisse autem in eo calice vinum aqua temperatum docet nos liber Misnajoth de benedictione VII. Et videtur hoc postulasse cæli ejus ingenium, ut vina, præsertim pau- lo largius solito, nisi aqua temperata non biberentur. Vi- de Prov. IX. 2. 5. Apoc. XVIII. 6. & Scriptorem de quæ- stionibus Hebraicis, qui inter opera Hieronymi legitur. Hic quoque mos ad Christianos veteres transiit. Justinus ποτήριον ὕδατος κὶ κράματος. Hinc mixtum calicem dixit Irenæus. Clemens: κέραται ὁ οἶνος τῷ ὕδατι. Cyprianus dominicam traditionem vocat, ut calix qui in commemo- rationem Domini offertur mixtus vino offeratur. Adde Ca- nonem XL. inter Africanos & Liturgias veteres Syriacas, Græcas, Arabicas, Latinas.

Quod in calice fuerit vinum aqua tempera- tum, inepte probat Grotius e libro Misnajoth de benedictione VII. Quid liber ille ad sanctis- fimam Christi institutionem? & quid huc fa- cit, quod hoc videatur postulasse cæli ejus in- genium? qualibus argutiis quantum tribuendum sit, nemini non patet. Verbo expresso in re- bus divinis & maxime in Sacramentorum insti- tutione nitendum est, non judicio nostro, quod hic nullum est, aut fallax. Testimonia ritus Veterum Irenæi, Cypriani, & Canonis XL. in- ter Africanos ἀδιαφορίαν istius mistionis do- cent, necessitatem nullam important.

Εὐχαριστήσας] Idem valet quod εὐλογήσας ut supra dixi- mus. Ipsum nomen receptum poculi expressit Paulus cum dixit ποτήριον εὐλογίας. Nam Hebræi vocabant כּוֹס הַלּל. Solent autem בּרֵךְ & הלל sumi συνωνύμως, ut apparet Ps. X, 3. ubi altera vox alteram explicat. Et Esaiæ LXIV. 11. הללו ab interpretibus LXX. vertitur ἐυλόγησαν.

πίετε ἐξ ἀυτῦ πάντες] In sacris (ac proinde & in fœderi- bus quæ interposito sacro peragebantur Psal. L. 5.) sanguis quidem in pateras fundi solebat, ut quarto Thebaidos Pa- pinianæ & aliis in locis legimus: sed quia bibere sangui- nem inhumanum erat, (quanquam id quoque in fœderi- bus nonnullis factum legimus: sic enim Plutarchus Publi- cola juvenes patricios ait inter se fœderatos ἀνθρώπε σφα- γέντος ἐπισπείσαντες αἷμα, & fœdus cruore sacratum dixit Ta- citus Annalium XII. & morem eundem Magellan us apud Americanos reperit; & Tigrani in Armenia id factitatum narrat Valerius Maxim. lib. IX. cap. 2. Scythis Solinus & Mela; Saracenis Nicetas Choniates; Danis Saxo Sia- landicus) institutum est apud populos mansuetiores, ut vi- num sanguinis loco biberetur, unde יין עבודה זרה Hebræis est vinum profanorum sacrificiorum: quo alludit Ezechiel, cap. XXXIX. 19. 20. & vinum sanguis uvæ di- citur: & ipso colore (nam rubebant fere vina Psal. LXXV. 9.) sanguinem referebat. Hoc vinum qui potabant ipso vi- ctimæ sanguine imbuti censebantur. Philo ἀπὸ τότε γέτοι φασὶ τὸ μεθύειν ὠνομάσθαι ὅτι μετὰ τὸ θύειν ἔθος ἦν τοῖς προτέ- ροις οἰνοῦσθαι. Fœdera quoque ut dixi, admoto calice firmari so- lita ostendit Aristophanes Lysistrata, qui & alibi ad eum morem alludens σπονδὰς ἐκπίομαι dixit. Et Diodorus Sicu- lus à vini libatione natum dicit nomen σπονδῶν. Hinc Ho- mero σπονδαὶ ἄκρητοι. Originem ostendit Plutarchus libro de Iside de Ægyptiis loquens: ἐκ ἔπινον οἶνον ἐδὲ ἐσπενδον ὡς φίλιον θεοῖς, ἀλλ᾽ ὡς αἷμα τῶν πολεμησάντων πότε τοῖς θεοῖς. Conjunge quæ mox sequentur de sanguinis usu in fœde- re. Certe non in hoc tantum, sed & in baptismi sacra- mento videtur omnino Christus se non Hebræorum tan- tum, sed & gentium in idem fœdus cooptandarum captui accommodasse.

Profanum testantur mentem, quæ ex profanis congerit Grotius, quod in Sacris & fœderibus quoque sanguis in pateras fundi consueverit, quod in fœderibus etiam quibusdam sanguinem biberint, quodque apud mansuetiores populos sancitum sit, ut vinum loco sanguinis biberetur, & qui hoc potarent, censerentur ipso victimæ imbuti sanguine, & quod fœdera admoto calice firmari solita, Aristophanes te- stetur, denique quod non in hoc tantum, sed & in Baptismatis sacramento videatur Christus se non solum Ebræis, sed & gentium in idem fœdus cooptan- darum captuis accommodasse. Absint profani ri- tus, absint profanæ cogitationes ab hoc divinissi- mo Sacramento!

## 26:28
Vers. 28. My blood of the new covenant] In my judgment, the ancient grammarians are correct who say that the word sanction is derived from blood (sanguis). For in laws, that part which bound a man's life to the law was called a sanction: in treaties, it was the very shedding of the sacrificial blood, which contained a threat of similar destruction against him who did not stand by the treaty, Exodus 24:8. Thus, in Homer, in the treaties, this imprecation is read against those who did not stand by the pacts: 'May their brains flow upon the ground like this wine.' Eustathius on the third book of the Iliad: 'The king, cutting hair from the heads of the lambs that were to be placed upon the oaths, distributed it to the best of the Trojans and Achaeans through the heralds, so that all might seem to participate in the sacrifice. And this was a symbol that evils would turn upon the heads of those who perjured themselves.' That ancient formula refers to this: 'If he should be the first to depart, do you, Jupiter, strike him as I strike this pig today, and by so much the more as you are able and powerful.' Nor does that severe threat in the Epistle to the Hebrews look to anything else against 'him who has considered the blood of the covenant common,' in which place, as also here and in Exodus 24:8 and Zechariah 9:11, 'blood of the covenant' is the blood by which a covenant is solemnly sanctioned, which the divine writer of the said Epistle called 'to be renewed.' Tacitus in the Life of Agricola said that they sanctioned a conspiracy with sacrifices: and from there you may rightly supply what is in Luke and Paul, 'the new covenant in my blood' or 'in my own blood,' namely, 'having been renewed.' Moreover, the cup is called a covenant just as the bread is called a communion. The history in 1 Samuel 9 does not differ from this ancient nature of treaties, where beasts are cut asunder with a threat of punishment against deserters, but which is directed at their property, not at their persons. Zenobius: The Molossians, in their oaths, made their agreements by cutting up oxen into small pieces. In Apollodorus' Library we read about Peleus, who had cut up the wife of Acastus, and having divided the limbs, led the army through them. Thus also Abraham makes a covenant with God with divided beasts, Genesis 15:10, and Cyril, in his last book against Julian, reports that this was the custom of the Chaldeans for sanctioning faith. Livy, book 39: The middle of a slaughtered dog is cut, and the prior part is placed to the right with the entrails, the posterior to the left of the path: between this divided victim, the armed forces are led through. Plutarch in his Roman Questions: 'It is a public purification for the Boeotians to pass through the parts of a dog cut in two.' Add to the understanding of this place the passage in Luke 23:31.

Which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins] By 'many' here I understand those, both from the Jews and from the Gentiles, who embrace the conditions of the covenant. For I think the oracle of Daniel is being referred to, in which it is said of the Messiah, 'He shall confirm a covenant with many' (in Greek, 'he shall strengthen a covenant for many'). Since it had preceded, 'to atone for iniquity,' to expiate sins. Add what is in Romans 5:15. Thus also in the Epistle which is called Barnabas's: 'And he himself was about to offer the vessel of the spirit as a sacrifice for our sins.' At the same time, however, Christ passes from a comparison of covenants to a comparison of piacular sacrifices, in which the soul of the beast was offered as a substitute for the soul of the man who had deserved death: whence the victim was said in the law to bear sins. Hence, even the Greeks and Latins said that a victim dies for a man, and that a man is bought or redeemed by victims. Moreover, blood represented the soul, which is not visible, in a visible way: 'The soul of the flesh is in the blood,' says the law: 'but I have destined it for you on the altar to make expiation for your souls. For it is the blood that makes expiation for the soul.' Nor did the Gentiles signify anything else through blood in such sacrifices. Hence that line of Virgil, 'returns must be sought with blood, and atonement must be made with a soul.' And we read everywhere among the poets and others that peace is sought with blood, that the deity is appeased with blood, that blood is given for blood: looking to which custom, common to the Jews and other peoples, the writer to the Hebrews says: 'Without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness.' But just as by the name of the body the ancients understood the communication of the sufferings and glory of Christ, so by blood they understood the communication of his death and immortality, because blood, as we have said, signifies life. Hence Ignatius calls the blood of Christ 'incorruptible and everlasting life': Clement: 'This is to drink the blood of Jesus, to partake of the Lord's incorruptibility.' The oracle in the Latin Mass: 'May the blood of our Lord Jesus Christ guard my soul unto eternal life.' The author of the book on the Lord's Supper: 'Bread is food, blood is life': then: 'But we drink of the blood of Christ at his own command, partakers of eternal life with him and through him': which coheres very well with the remission of sins: because since death is from sin, then the fruit of the remission of sins will be perfectly perceived when death is abolished. 'Being poured out' signifies 'is about to be poured out': the present for the near future: so above in chapter 3:10, 'is cut down' is equivalent to 'is about to be cut down': and 'he who is coming after me,' who is about to follow me. And verse 23, 'if you are about to offer': chapter 6:6, 'when you are about to pray': and chapter 20:22, 'I am being baptized,' that is, I am about to be dipped. Mark IX. 31. παραδίδοται, that is, he shall be delivered: as appears in Matt. XV. II. 22. chap. XX. 22.
