Luke XVII. 12. εἰσερχομένῳ δὲ ἀυτῷ εἰς τινα κώμην, that is, when he was just about to enter: and chap. XXIII. 54. Σάββατον ἐπέφωσκε, that is, it was on the point of dawning shortly: chap. XXIV. 6. 48. ὑμεῖς δέ ἐσε μάρτυρες, that is, you shall be, as the same Luke himself interprets in Acts I. 8. chap. XXIV. 49. ἀποτέλλω, that is, I will send. ἔρχεται for ἐλεύσεται John IV. 21. Therefore the old Latin interpreter, and with him the so-called canon of the Mass, in this very place translates ἐκχυνόμενον as which shall be shed: and similarly in Mark XIV. 24. and what is said concerning the body of Christ in this same argument in I Cor. XI. 24. τὸ ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν κλώμενον, the same interpreter translates as which shall be delivered for you.

What the sanction made by blood with the threat of a similar destruction against him who had not stood by the covenant (Exod. XXIV. 8. 1 Sam. XI. Gen. XV. 10.) or the passage of Luke XXIII. 31. has to do with the understanding of this place, does not appear. For there is no threat here, but a sealing of grace: which, obtained through the shedding of the blood of Christ, is sealed to us through the cup of the New Testament. Grotius most wretchedly perverts the most sacred mysteries, who nevertheless was at last compelled to acknowledge that a comparison of expiatory sacrifices, in which the soul of the beast was offered as a substitute for the soul of the man who had deserved death, whence the victim was said in the law to bear sins, is hinted at here. But what he says, in those words of Heb. IX. ἄνευ αἱματεκχυσίας ὐ γίνεσθαι ἄφεσις, that he refers to the custom common to the Jews and other nations, by which they appeased the deity with blood, this is truly impious, since Christ is thus mixed with Belial, light with darkness, true religion with idolatrous superstition. Finally, we concede that the ancients understood by the body the communication of the suffering and glory of Christ, and by the blood the communication of death and immortality (which Grotius says), τελικῶς and as far as the end of the Sacrament is concerned, but not ὀσιωδῶς as regards its nature and form: because they acknowledged that the body and blood of Christ are exhibited here, so that we may be made partakers of the fruit which Christ acquired for us by his body and blood delivered and shed for us, and so also of the glory of immortality, as Grotius alleges this opinion from the author of the book on the Lord's Supper: We drink, however, of the blood of Christ, he himself commanding it, partakers of eternal life with him, and through him.

Latin:

Vers. 28. Τὸ αἷμά με τὸ τῆς καινῆς διαθήκης] Recte sentiunt me judice Grammatici veteres, qui sanctionem dictum ajunt à sanguine. Nam in legibus sanctio dicebatur ea pars quæ vitam hominis legi obligabat: in fœderibus ipsa effusio sanguinis victimalis, cui inerat comminatio simi- lis excidii adversus eum qui fœderi non stetisset, Exodi XXIV. 8. Sic apud Homerum ἐν ταῖς σπονδαῖς hæc le- gitur imprecatio in eos qui pactis non stetissent: Τῇδε σφ' ἐγκέφαλος χαμάδις ῥέοι ὡς ὅδε οἶνος. Eustathius ad III. Iliados: τῶν τιθησομένων ἐπὶ ὅρκοις ἀρνῶν τρίχας ἐκ κεφαλῆς τέμνων ὁ βασιλεὺς ἑνειμε τοῖς τῶν τρώων καὶ Ἀχαιῶν ἀρίστοις διὰ τῶν κηρύκων, ἵνα πάντες δοκῶσι συνεφά- πτεσθαι τῆς θυσίας. σύμβολον δὲ ἦν τῦτο τῦ εἰς κεφαλὴν τραπή- σεσθαι τὰ κακὰ τοῖς ἐπιορκήσασι. Hunc illa vetus formula: Si prior defexit, tu illum Jupiter sic ferito, ut ego hunc por- cum hodie feriam, tantoque magis quanto magis potes polles- que. Nec alio respicit severa illa comminatio in epistola ad Hebæros adversum τῆς κοινὸν ἡγησαμένως τὸ αἷμα τῆς διαθή- κης, quo in loco, ut & hic & Exodi XXIV. 8. & Zach. IX. 11. αἷμα τῆς διαθήκης est sanguis quo fœdus solenniter sanci- tur, quod ἐγκαινίζεσθαι dixit dictæ Epistolæ divinus Scriptor. Sacrificiis conspirationem sancire dixit Tacitus Agricolæ vita: atque inde recte suppleas quod apud Lucam & Paulum est ἡ καινὴ διαθήκη ἐν τῷ αἵματί με vel ἐν τῷ ἐμῷ αἵματι scilicet ἐγκαινισθεῖσα. Dicitur autem calix διαθήκη ut pa- nis κοινωνία. Ab hac antiqua fœderum natura non abludit Historia 1. Sam. IX. ubi pecudes discinduntur cum com- minatione pœnæ in desertores, sed quæ in res ipsorum, non in personas dirigitur. Zenobius: Οἱ μόλοττοι ἐν τοῖς ὁρκωμοσίοις εἰς μικρὰ τὰς βῦς τὰς συνθήκας ἐποιοῦντο. In Apol- lodori Bibliotheca legimus de Peleo, qui Acasti uxorem dissecuerat, κὶ διελὼν μέλη διήγαγε δι' αὐτῆς τὸν στρατὸν. Sic & Abrahamus cum Deo fœdus facit dissectis pecudibus, Genes. XV. 10. atque eum morem Chaldæis fuisse sancien- di fidem, tradit Cyrillus adversus Julianum ultimo. Livius lib. XXXIX. Caput mediæ canis præcisæ & prior pars ad dex- tram cum extis, posterior ad lævam viæ ponitur: inter hanc di- visam hostiam copia armatæ traducuntur. Plutarchus quæ- stionibus Romanis: Βοιωτοῖς δημοσίᾳ καθαρμός ἐστι, κυνὸς διχο- τομηθέντος τῶν μερῶν διεξελθεῖν. Adde ad loci hujus intel- lectum locum Luc. XXIII. 31.

Τὸ περὶ πολλῶν ἐκχυνόμενον εἰς ἄφεσιν ἁμαρτιῶν] πολλὲς hic intelligo eos tum ex Judæis tum ex Gentibus qui fœderis conditiones amplectuntur. Puto enim Danielis oraculum respici in quo de Messia dictum est גביר כרית לרבים Græce δυναμώσει διαθήκην πολλοῖς. Cum præcessisset לכפר העון ad expianda peccata. Adde quæ Rom. V. 15. Sic & in Barnabæ quæ dicitur Epistola κὶ ἀυτὸς ὑπὲρ τῶν ἡ- μετέρων ἁμαρτιῶν ἤμελλε σκεῦος τῷ πνέυματος προσφέρειν θυ- σίαν. Simul autem transit Christus à comparatione fœde- rum ad comparationem sacrificiorum piacularium, in qui- bus anima pecudis offerebatur velut succidanea animæ ho- minis qui mortem meruisset: unde victima ferre peccata dicebatur in lege. Hinc mori victimam pro homine, emi aut redimi hominem victimis, etiam Græci & Lati- ni dixere. Animam autem non visibilem visibiliter san- guis repræsentabat: Anima carnis in sanguine, inquit lex: ego vero destinavi eum vobis in altari ad expiationem facien- dam pro animis vestris. Nam sanguis est qui pro anima ex- piationem facit. Neque aliud gentes per sanguinem in sa- cris ejusmodi significabant. Hinc Virgilius illud, san- guine quærendi reditus exponit, animaque litandum. Et passim pacem sanguine exposci, numen sanguine pla- cari, sanguinem dari pro sanguine, apud Poëtas alios- que legimus: quem morem Judæis aliisque populis communem respiciens Scriptor ad Hebræos, ait: ἄνευ αἱματεκχυσίας κ' γίνεται ἄφεσις. Sicut autem per corpo- ris nomen veteres intellexerunt communicationem perspe- fionum & gloriæ Christi, ita per sanguinem, communi- cationem mortis & immortalitatis, quia sanguis ut di- ximus vitam significat. Hinc Ignatius αἷμα χριστῦ vocat ἄφθαρτον κὴ ἀέναον ζωήν : Clemens : τῦτ᾽ ἔστι πιεῖν τὸ αἷμα τῦ Ἰησῦ, τῆς κυριακῆς μεταλαβεῖν ἀφθαρσίας. Oraculum in Missa Latina: Sanguis Domini nostri Iesu Christi custodiat a- nimam meam in vitam æternam. Auctor libri de cœna Domini : panis est esca, sanguis vita: deinde : Bibimus autem de sanguine Christi ipso jubente, vitæ æternæ cum ipso & per ipsum participes: quod optime cohæret cum remis- sione peccatorum : quia cum mors sit ex peccato, tunc remissionis peccatorum fructus perfecte percipietur, cum mors abolebitur. ἐκχυνόμενον significat jam jam effundetur: præsens pro proxime futuro: ita supra capite III. 10. ἐκκόπτεται valet jam jam excidetur: & ὁ ὀπί- σω μᵾ ἐρχόμεν@, qui jam jam me est secuturus. Et vers. 23. ἐὰν ὖν προσφέρῃς si jam jamque sis oblaturus: cap. VI. 6. ὅταν προσεύχῃ jam jam oraturus: & cap. XX. 22. βα- πτίζομαι, id est tingar. Marc. IX. 31. παραδίδοται, id est tradetur: ut apparet Matth. XV. II. 22. cap. XX. 22. Luc. XVII. 12. εἰσερχομένῳ δὲ ἀυτῷ εἰς τινα κώμην, id est cum jam jam intraturus esset: & cap. XXIII. 54. Σάββατον ἐπέ- φωσκε, id est, in eo erat ut brevi illucesceret : c. XXIV. 6. 48. ὑμεῖς δέ ἐσε μάρτυρες, id est ἔσεσθε, ut idem ipse Lucas in- terpretatur Actor. I. 8. cap. XXIV. 49. ἀποτέλλω, id est ἀποστελῶ. ἔρχεται pro ἐλεύσεται Johan. IV. 21. Itaque vetus interpres Latinus, & cum eo canon Missæ qui dici- tur, hoc ipso loco ἐκχυνόμενον vertit qui effundetur: ac si- militer Marci XIV. 24. & quod de corpore Christi in hoc eodem argumento dicitur I. Cor. XI. 24. τὸ ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν κλώμενον, idem interpres vertit quod pro vobis tradetur.

Quid ad hujus loci intellectum, vel sanctio per sanguinem facta cum comminatione similis excidii adversus eum qui fœderi non stetisset Exod. XXIV. 8. 1. Sam. XI. Genes. XV. 10. vel locus Lucæ XXIII. 31. faciat, non apparet. Neque enim ulla hic comminatio, sed gratiæ obsignatio: quæ per ef- fusionem sanguinis Christi parta, per calicem Nov. Test. nobis obsignatur. Pessime pervertit sacratissima mysteria Grotius, qui tamen coactus tandem est agnoscere, comparationem sacrifi- ciorum piacularium, in quibus anima pecudis offe- rebatur velut succedanea animæ hominis, quæ mortem meruisset, unde victima ferre peccata in lege dicta, hic innui. Sed quod ait, verbis illis Ebr. IX. ἄνευ αἱματεκχυσίας ὐ γίνεσθαι ἄφεσις respici morem Judæis aliisque gentibus, qua nu- men sanguine placarunt, communem, hoc vero impium est, quum commisceatur ita Christus cum Beliale, lux cum tenebris, vera religio cum idololatrica superstitione. Denique veteres per corpus communicationem perpessionis & gloriæ Christi, per sanguinem communicationem mortis & immortalitatis intellexisse (quod Grotius ait,) τελικῶς & quantum ad finem Sacramenti atti- net, concedimus, non autem ὀσιωδῶς quod ad naturam & formam ejusdem: quia corpus ipsum & sanguinem Christi agnoverunt hic exhiberi, ut fructus participes reddamur, quem corpore & sanguine suo pro nobis tradito & effuso nobis acquisivit Christus, adeoque etiam gloriæ im- mortalitatis, uti ex autore libri de cœna Domini al- legat hanc sententiam Grotius: Bibimus autem de sanguine Christi ipso jubente, vitæ æternæ cum ipso, & per ipsum participes.

## 26:29
Vers. 29. λέγω δὲ ὑμῖν] It appears from Luke that these things were said at the supper itself, and therefore before the consecration of the bread and wine. But because the mention of wine had preceded here, it seemed good to Matthew to append that statement here. Luke also mentions the eating. Now it was customary among the Jews for the happiness of the other life to be described popularly through the words of eating and drinking: in which sense we also had ἀνακλίνεσθαι above in chap. VIII. 11.

Tῦ γεννήματ@ τῆς ἀμπέλε] Christ preferred to speak thus, rather than to call it nakedly wine, because in the Paschal supper and indeed in the very formula of the blessing (τῆς ἐνλογίας) it was not accustomed to be named otherwise than פרי הגפן. Philo also alluded to this in his book περὶ μέθης: τῦ γεννῶντ@ φυτῦ τὸν οἶνον ἀμπέλῳ.

Καινὸν] That is, this new thing, immortal joy, which was understood as shadowed forth by wine. For thus in the Oneirocriticon, Rabbi Hai signifies eternal life by the words of wine kept from the creation of the world, the mention of which wine is also found in Jonathan the paraphrast and others. See them at Ps. XXXV. 9. and at Cant. VIII. 2. and the book Berachot and the Zoar under the title Toldet. Similar is Ἱερουσαλὴμ καινὴ in the Apocalypse: for it is customary for things signified to be softened by some addition. Thus Paul said τὴν ἄνω Ἱερουσαλὴμ Gal. IV. 26. Such is ἐκ πνευματικῆς πέτρας 1 Cor. X. 4. οἶκος πνευματικὸς and ἀνενέγκαι πνευματικὰς θυσίας 1 Pet. II. 5. Thus also the Apocalypse says a certain city is called spiritually Sodom and Egypt. From a similar passage in Luke where the Paschal supper is treated, one may explain τὸν οἶνον τὸν πληρώμενον. For there are the intelligible fulfillments of the sensible things: concerning which matter more fully at Luke. Nor is it new that the same name, just as here the fruit of the vine, should serve in two senses. Thus water in John IV. 13, 14 is called both that which is common and another which is spiritual: thus in Mark X. 15 the kingdom of God signifies both heavenly doctrine and the glory of the other life: for he who receives the kingdom pertains to the former sense, he who does not enter into it to the second, as the collation of the passages which we cited above in chapter V. 20 teaches.

PART II. Acts during the departure to the Passion.

Latin:

Vers. 29. λέγω δὲ ὑμῖν] Ex Luca apparet dicta hæc in ipsa cœna, & proinde ante panis & vini consecrationem. Sed quia vini mentio hic præcesserat, ideo visum est Mat- thæo id dictum hic subtexere. Lucas etiam esus meminit. Solebat autem apud Judæos felicitas vitæ alterius per ver- ba edendi & bibendi populariter describi: quo sensu & ἀ- νακλίνεσθαι habuimus supra c. VIII. 11.

Tῦ γεννήματ@ τῆς ἀμπέλε] Ita loqui Christus maluit, quam nude vinum appellare, quia in cœna Paschali atque adeo in ipsa formula τῆς ἐνλογίας aliter nominari non sole- bat quam פרי הגפן Allusit & Philo περὶ μέθης libro : τῦ γεννῶντ@ φυτῦ τὸν οἶνον ἀμπέλῳ.

Καινὸν] Id est τὸ νέον τοῦτο, lætitiam immortalem, quæ per vinum adumbrata intelligebatur. Nam sic in Oniro- critico Rabbi Hai vita æterna significatur vocibus vini ser- vati à creatione mundi, cujus vini mentio etiam apud Jo- nathanem paraphrasten & alios. Vide eos ad Pf. XXXV. 9. & ad Cant. IIX. 2. & librum Berachot & Zoar titulo Toldet. Si- mile est Ἱερουσαλὴμ καινὴ in Apocalypsi : nam solent τὰ ἀναγ- γορόμενα aliquo additamento emolliri. Sic τὴν ἄνω Ἱερουσα- λὴμ dixit Paulus Gal. IV. 26. Tale est ἐκ πνευματικῆς πέτρας 1. Cor. X. 4. οἶκος πνευματικὸς & ἀνενέγκαι πνευματικὰς θυ- σίας 1. Pet. II. 5. Sic & Apocalypsis urbem quandam vocari ait πνευματικῶς Σόδομα κὴ Αἴγυπτον. Ex simili Lucæ loco ubi de Paschali cœna agitur exponere liceat τὸν οἶνον τὸν πληρώ- μενον. Sunt enim τὰ νοητὰ πληρώματα τῶν αἰσθητῶν : qua de re ad Lucam plenius. Neque novum est, ut idem nomen, quemadmodum hic γέννημα τῆς ἀμπέλου, duobus sensibus serviat. Ita aqua Joh. IV. 13. 14. dicitur & illa vulgaris & alia spiritualis: ita Marc. X. 15. βασιλεία τοῦ Θεοῦ & doctri- nam cœlestem significat, & gloriam vitæ alterius: nam δέξηται τὴν βασιλείαν ad priorem sensum pertinet, ὃ μὴ εἰ- σέλθῃ εἰς ἀυτὴν ad secundum, ut docet collatio locorum quos citavimus supra cap. V. 20.

PARS II. Acta sub egressum ad Passionem.

## 26:30
Vers. 30. ὑμνήσαντες] Learned men think that the hymns which were accustomed to be sung at the Passover were sung by Christ: such as Ps. CXIV and those following. But just as Christ added a new thanksgiving to the old, consistent with his own institution, so it is credible that he did the same concerning the hymn. And perhaps Christ said those very things in the manner of a hymn which we read in John chapter XVII. For the Hebrews were accustomed to pour forth hymns, which they call מזמורי, as the occasion arose, extemporaneously, bound by no meters, such as the songs of Deborah, Anna, Zacharias, the Jews in 2 Macc. X. 33, and that hymn of the Christians which exists in Acts IV. 24. Nor do I doubt that Paul also commends this kind of singing, or especially so, in Eph. V. 19, Col. III. 16. This custom remained for a long time in the ancient Church; Tertullian: After the washing of hands and the lights, each one is invited into the midst to sing to God from the Scriptures or from his own talent. Pliny also makes mention of the songs which were said to Christ: and the Council of Toledo IV, canon 12, and the writer against Artemon mentioned by Eusebius.

Εἰς τὸ ὄρος] That is, towards the mountain. For Gethsemane was between the torrent Cedron and the mountain itself.

Latin:

Vers. 30. ὑμνήσαντες] Censent viri eruditi cantatos à Christo hymnos qui Paschate cani solerent: quales sunt Pf. CXIV. & sequentes. Sed sicut ad veterem gratiarum a- ctionem Christus novam addidit, suo instituto congruen- tem, ita & de hymno fecisse credibile est. Ac forte ea ipsa hymni in modum dixit Christus quæ apud Iohannem cap. XVII. legimus. Nam solebant pro re nata, ex tempore hy- mnos, quos מזמורי vocant, effundere Hebræi, nullis nu- meris adstrictos, qualia sunt carmina Deboræ, Annæ, Za- chariæ, Judæorum 2. Macc. X. 33. & hymnus ille Christia- norum qui exstat Actor. IV. 24. Nec dubito quin & hoc ca- nendi genus vel præcipue commendet Paulus Ephes. V. 19. Col. III. 16. Mansit diu is mos in Ecclesia vetere Tertullia- nus: Post aquam manualem & lumina, ut quisque de Scri- pturis vel de proprio ingenio potest, provocatur in medium Deo canere. Meminit & Plinius carminum quæ Christo dice- bantur: & Synodus Toletan. IV. canone 12. & Scriptor contra Artemonem memoratus Eusebio.

Εἰς τὸ ὄρος] Id est versus montem. Nam Gethsemane erat inter torrentem Cedron & montem ipsum.

## 26:31
Vers. 31. Τότε] Around this time: for these things seem to be gathered from Luke and John to have been said before the departure from the house.

Σκανδαλισθήσεσθε ἐν ἐμοὶ] We had a similar way of speaking above in ch. XI. 16. There is, however, a widely extending meaning, but it must be restricted by the circumstances of the places. σκανδαλίζεσθαι here is to fail in the duty of a disciple and friend: and to think less worthily of the master. ἐν ἐμοὶ by the occasion of those things which will happen to me.

Γέγραπται γάρ. πατάξω τὸν ποιμένα κὴ διασκορπισθήσεται τὰ πρόβατα τῆς ποίμνης.] Christ seems to use this saying in the manner of a proverb: so that the sense is: That which is accustomed to be said, and which you remember is written somewhere, will come to pass: The shepherd having been struck, the sheep are scattered. And therefore Christ changed the imperative mood into the indicative, because it was more consistent with a proverbial expression. Nor does that πατάξω designate a certain person, but the first person is put for any one: nor is πατάξω τὸν ποιμένα anything other than πατάσσεται ὁ ποιμήν. But so far am I from thinking that Christ is directly referred to in the words of Zechariah, that I much rather believe that it treats there of some not good shepherd, and indeed, if I am not mistaken, of the same one about whom it had been treated at the end of chapter XI, where likewise he, whoever he is, is called my shepherd, and a sword is said to threaten him. Certainly those things which are thoughts placed in histories, when placed outside of histories become maxims, and then it is not looked at on what occasion they were originally said, but how widely the force of the maxim extends. Similar is that of Virgil concerning bees:

Rege incolumi, mens omnibus una, Amisso rupere fidem.

And of Livy: Just as the battle line is routed when the leader is killed, so they slipped away here and there. Homer had said concerning the death of Sarpedon:

— but he frightened all, since they saw the king with wounded heart lying in the gathering of the dead.

The corruption of this saying, to which he later gives credence from parallel passages, certainly excellent ones from Virgil, Livy, and Homer, has already been refuted at the passage of Zech. XIII. 7.

Latin:

Vers. 31. Τότε] Circa hoc tempus: nam hæc ante exi- tum è domo dicta ex Luca & Johanne videtur colligi.

Σκανδαλισθήσεσθε ἐν ἐμοὶ] Simile loquendi genus habui- mus supra c. XI. 16. Est autem late patens significatio, sed ex locorum circumstantiis restringenda. σκανδαλίζεσθαι hic est ab officio discipuli atque amici deficere: minusque di- gne de magistro sentire. ἐν ἐμοὶ occasione eorum quæ mihi evenient.

Γέγραπται γάρ. πατάξω τὸν ποιμένα κὴ διασκορ- πισθήσεται τὰ πρόβατα τῆς ποίμνης.] Videtur hoc dicto pro- verbiï in modum uti Christus: ut sensus sit: Fiet quod dici so- let, quodque alicubi scriptum meministis: Pastore percusso, oves disperguntur. Atque ideo Christus imperativum modum in Indicativum mutavit, quia proverbiali locutioni magis id congruebat. Neque illud πατάξω certam personam defi- gnat, sed prima persona pro quavis ponitur: nec aliud est πατάξω τὸν ποιμένα quam πατάσσεται ὁ ποιμήν. Tantum autem abest ut Zachariæ verbis directe Christum putem re- spici, ut multo magis credam agi inibi de aliquo non bo- no pastore, & quidem, ni fallor, de eodem de quo actum erat fine capitis XI. ubi itidem ille, quisquis est, vocatur pastor meus, & gladius illi imminere dicitur. Certe quæ in historiis posita νοήματα sunt, extra historias posita γνῶμαι fiunt, neque tum respicitur qua occasione sint primitus di- cta, sed quam late se vis γνώμης porrigat. Simile est illud Virgilii de apibus:

Rege incolumi, mens omnibus una, Amisso rupere fidem.

Et Livii: Sicut acies funditur duce occiso, ita dilapsi passim alii alio. Homerus circa Sarpedonis mortem dixerat:

———— ἀλλ’ ἐφόβηθεν Πάντας, ἐπεὶ βασιλῆα ἴδον βεβλαμμένον ἧτορ Κείμενον ἐν νεκύων ἀγύρῃ.

Depravatio hujus dicti, cui fidem postea con- ciliat è locis parallelis, præclaris certe Virgilii, Livii & Homeri, profligata jam est ad locum Zach. XIII. 7.

## 26:32
Vers. 32. I will go before you] Christ continues the metaphor: Again, in the manner of a shepherd, I will go before you into Galilee. John X. 4, concerning the shepherd: and when he puts forth his own sheep, he goes before them. The angel brings these very words of Christ back to the memory of the disciples below in chapter XXVIII, 7. he goes before you into Galilee.

Latin:

Vers. 32. Προάξω ὑμᾶς] Translationem Christus conti- nuat: Rursum pastoris more vos præibo in Galilæam. Joh. X. 4. de pastore: καὶ ὅταν τὰ ἴδια πρόβατα ἐκβάλῃ ἔμ- προσθεν αὐτῶν πορεύεται. Hæc ipsa Christi verba in memo- riam reducit discipulis Angelus infra cap. XXVIII, 7. δὲ προάγει ὑμᾶς εἰς τὴν γαλιλαίαν.

## 26:34
Vers. 34. Before the cock crows] Namely the early morning, as Aristophanes speaks, which Theocritus called the early-morning time. For otherwise, as has been rightly noted by Theophylact on Mark and others, the cock crows twice, first at midnight, then towards the approach of light: at the fourth watch, as Pliny says in book V of his Natural History, chapter XXII, and Solinus said that the sun is seen from the summit of Mount Casius at the fourth watch, and Ammianus speaks of the second cock-crowings: which term for second cock-crowings is also found in Mela. When the second cock crowed, in Aristophanes: the later crowing, as it is more noble and lively, is properly called the cock-crowing in Mark XIII. 35, the gallicinium in Gellius, Macrobius, Apuleius, and Censorinus. It seems that Mark expressed the very words of Christ received from Peter, 'before the cock crows twice,' that is, before the cock crows again, which Juvenal called the second cock-crowing: Synesius calls it the second song of the birds. But Matthew, Luke, and John were content to name the cock's crowing simply, knowing that where nothing is added, the morning one is understood.

You will deny me three times] These words of Christ are wonderfully emphatic: Peter had denied that he would depart from his duty. Christ shows that he would depart, not lightly, but gravely, that is, not only by flight, but by the abdication of his master: for that is what it means to deny, to deny that one knew who Jesus was, as Luke paraphrases it. Peter had said 'never': Christ teaches that he would do what he denied he would do that very night before the day arose, and would do it not once but three times: which was a sign not of some kind of passion, but of a lack of constancy. The cock praises God its maker: Peter denies his savior. After the cock's crowing, Christ begins his priestly office, as the high priest of the Hebrews was accustomed to do. That is written in Yoma.

Latin:

Vers. 34. Πρὶν ἀλέκτορα φωνῆσαι] Nimirum τὸ ὄρθριον ut Aristophanes loquitur quod ὀρθρινᾶς dixit Theocritus. Nam alioqui ut recte à Theophylacto ad Marcum atque alijs no- tatum est, bis canit gallus, primum medianoctio, deinde sub adventum lucis: quarta vigilia, ut ait Plinius lib. V. Hist. Nat. cap. XXII, & Casii montis è vertice conspici so- lem quarta vigilia Solinus dixit, secundis Gallicinijs Ammia- nus: quæ vox secundorum Galliciniorum etiam apud Me- lam est. ὅτε τὸ δεύτερον ἀλεκτρύων ἐφθέγξετο apud Aristopha- nem: posterior cantus ut nobilior atque alacrior proprie, vocatur ἀλεκτοροφωνία Marci XIII. 35. gallicinium, Gellio, Macrobio, Apulejo, Censorino. Videtur Marcus ipsam Christi verba expressisse à Petro accepta πρὶν ἢ δὶς ἀλέκτορα φωνῆσαι, id est, antequam gallus iterum canat, quod ad can- tum galli secundi dixit Juvenalis: Synefius δευτέρας ὀρνίθων ᾠδὰς vocat At Matthæus, Lucas, Johannes cantum gal- li simpliciter nominare contenti fuerunt, gnari ubi nihil ad- ditur matutinum intelligi.

Τρὶς ἀπαρνήσῃ με] Mire emphatica sunt hæc Christi ver- ba: negaverat Petrus se ab officio discessurum. Christus ostendit discessurum, non leviter, sed graviter, id est non so- lum fuga, sed magistri abdicatione: id enim est ἀπαρνεῖσθαι negare se Jesum qui esset nosse, ut Lucas παραφράζει. Di- xerat Petrus ὀδίποτε: Christus docet facturum eum quod facturum se negabat ea ipsa nocte antequam dies oriretur & facturum non semel sed ter: quod signum erat non qualiscunque πάθες sed expectoratæ constantiæ. Gallus Deum opificem suum laudat: Petrus servatorem negat. Post galli cantum Christus munus suum Sacerdotale au- spicatur, ut Pontifex maximus Hebræorum facere solebat. Scriptum id in Joma.

## 26:35
Vers. 35. even if it is necessary for me I will deny you] Peter says this in good faith, conscious of his purpose, but weighing neither the weakness of his own strength nor the magnitude of the impending danger: thus, indeed, it usually happens. A will imbued with some knowledge of the honorable is easily carried there, as long as there is nothing that moves the senses, and through the senses the irrational part of the soul. But when the things themselves begin to excite the passions, those beautifully thought-out ideas often fall away, because the mind, a judge corrupted by flatteries or fear, examines the truth poorly: Hence Philemon: 'It is one thing to suffer then, another to behold it perhaps.' Against this weakness, we must implore that spirit of fortitude which God did not give even to his own Apostles at the beginning of their discipline, so that, learning human infirmity by their own fall, they might the more sympathize with the infirmities of others, according to that saying:

Not ignorant of evil, I learn to succor the wretched.

It does not appear why one should depart from the customary meaning and common explanation concerning the double crowing of the cock: because Peter was more reminded by the double crowing than if only one morning cock-crowing had been heard. But since these things are everywhere obvious, and have been more fully deduced in the Harmony of the Gospels by the blessed Gerhard, it is not helpful to dwell on them; novelty has pleased Grotius everywhere. But what indeed could not be innovated, if it were not a matter of religion to innovate anything rashly in sacred things? Christ notably said, 'before the cock crows twice, you will deny me THREE times.' The cock will not even crow twice, and the denial will already have been made three times. We add, however, what Grotius has here: 'After the cock's crowing, Christ begins his priestly office, as the high priest of the Hebrews was accustomed to do. That is written in Yoma.' But Yoma is not Canonical Scripture. Nor is that tradition divine. We therefore leave it in its own place. What of the fact that from a comparison of the Evangelists it is evident that all three of Peter's denials were completed before midnight: and that the cock crows not only once, but twice before that time which is called the cock-crowing, in which it crows for the third time.

PART III. The acts of the Passion of Christ.

I. To the Mount of Olives.

Latin:

Vers. 35. κἂν δέῃ σε ἀπαρνήσομαι] Dicit hoc Petrus bona fide propositi sibi conscius, sed neque virium suarum im- becillitatem, neque periculi ingruentis magnitudinem sa- tis ponderans: ita nimirum fieri solet. Voluntas aliqua honesti cognitione imbuta facile eo fertur, quamdiu ni- hil est quod sensus, & per sensus τὸ τῆς ψυχῆς ἄλογον moveat. At ubi res ipsæ excitare cœperunt τὰ πάθη, sæpe illa pulchre cogitata excidunt, quia male verum examinat blanditiis aut metu corruptus judex animus: Hinc Philemon: Ἐτέραν τότ᾽ ἀλγεῖν ὡς θεωρεῖν ἔτ᾽ ἴσως. Adversus hanc imbecillitatem implorandus nobis est spiri- tus ille fortitudinis, quem ne Apostolis quidem suis initio disciplinæ dedit Deus, ut infirmitatem humanam lapsu suo discentes tanto magis aliorum infirmitatibus condolesce- rent, juxta illud:

Non ignara mali miseris succurrere disco.

Non apparet cur a consueta significatione ac communi explicatione de gemino cantu galli dis- cedendum sit: quia gemino cantu magis commo- nefactus est Petrus, quam si unus tantum matuti- nus galli cantus auditus sit. Sed quum hæc passim obvia, & in Harmon. Evang. B. Gerhardi plenius deducta sint, non juvat illis immorari, ubique no- vitas placuit Grotio. Ecquid vero non posses innovari, nisi religio in sacris foret temere quic- quam innovare? Notanter dixit Christus ante- quam bis gallus cantet, TER me abnegabis. Ne quidem binis vicibus cantabit gallus, & trina jam facta erit abnegatio. Addimus tamen quæ hic habet Grotius: Post galli cantum Christus munus suum Sacerdotale auspicatur, ut Pontifex maximus Hebræorum facere solebat. Scriptum id in Joma.. Sed Joma non est Scriptura Canonica. Neque traditio illa divina est. Suo ergo eam relinquimus loco. Quid quod è collatione Evangelistarum pateat, ante mediam noctem omnes tres abnega- tiones Petri peractas: quodque Gallus non semel tantum, sed bis canat ante illud tempus quod Gallicinium vocatur in quo ter- tium canit.

PARS III. Passionis Christi acta.

I. Ad montem Oliveti.

## 26:36
Ver. 36. Χωρίον] Thus the Greeks call a village outside the city, which later Latinity began to call a Villa, in which sense this word must be taken here by the Latin interpreter. The Arab translates it قرية, which is read interpreted in the Old Glossary as Villa, Vicus. In this village was that garden into which Christ went.

Γεθσημανῆ] גיא שמנים is called in Isa. XXVIII. 1. a part of the Israelite field, which is at the feet of the mountain of Lebanon. For a similar reason, or perhaps after that example, that village situated under the mount of olives had the same name. It is possible that this place was commonly called גיא את שמני, that is, the valley with oiliness. Aben Ezra notes that that young heifer, the mention of which is in Num. XIX., was accustomed to be burned on the mount of olives. It is credible that Christ looked to that when he withdrew to this place for the beginning of his suffering.

Lightfoot in his Hebrew and Talmudic hours on Matthew, p. 303, explains the place as the oil-press: thus also Capellus notes that גת שמני in Hebrew is an oil-press. That it was a place of oil-presses at the base of the olive grove was observed by both. Thus it seems that regard was had by Christ to the Prophetic prediction of Isa. LXIII. 3.

Καθίσατε ἀυτῦ] The words of Abraham when he went to offer his son, Gen. XXII. 5.

Latin:

Vers. 36. Χωρίον] Ita Graeci vocant vicum extra urbem, quem posterior Latinitas Villam coepit appellare, quo sensu hic sumenda ea vox apud Latinum interpretem. Arabs vertit قرية quod in Veteri Glossario interpretatum legitur Villa, Vicus. In hoc vico erat is hortus in quem ivit Christus.

Γεθσημανῆ] גיא שמנים vocatur Esa. XXVIII. 1. pars agri Israelitici, quae ad pedes est Libani montis. Similem ob causam, aut forte ad id exemplum, vicus iste sub montem olivarum situs idem nominis habuit. Fieri potest ut vulgo dictus sit hic locus גיא את שמני, id est vallis cum oleitate. Notat AbenEsdra junicem illam piaculam cujus mentio Num. XIX. in monte olivarum solitam comburi. Eo credibile est Christum respexisse cum huc locorum concessit inchoandae perpessioni.

Lightfootus in horis Ebr. & Talm. ad Matth. p. 303. exponit locum torcularium oleaciorum: sic & Capellus גת שמני Ebraice esse torcular olei notat. Fuisse locum torcularium oleaciorum ad basin oliveti utrique observatum. Ita videtur respectus habitus à Christo vaticinii Prophetici Esa. LXIII. 3.

Καθίσατε ἀυτῦ] Verba Abrahami cum filium iret oblatum Gen. XXII. 5.

## 26:37
Ver. 37. Πέτρον καὶ τὼς δύω ὑιὼς Ζεβεδαίς] As if 'more elect than the elect,' as Clement of Alexandria speaks elsewhere. Three witnesses, so that nothing can be excepted. See Deut. XVII. 6.

Latin:

Vers. 37. Πέτρον καὶ τὼς δύω ὑιὼς Ζεβεδαίς] Tanquam ἐκλεκτων ἐκλεκτοτέρες, ut alibi loquitur Clemens Alexandrinus. Testes tres, nequid excipi possit. Vid. Deut XVII. 6.

## 26:38
Ver. 38. Περίλυπός ἐσιν ἡ ψυχή με ἕως θανάτε] אפפוני חבלי מות. These are the words of David, generally bearing the type of Christ, Ps. CXVI. 3. In Greek, 'the pains of death compassed me about'; thus are called the greatest sorrows, and such as are wont to be around death, to which the very horror of death is not undeservedly compared, and indeed so bloody, so ignominious, hovering before the eyes: Ovid, 'And death has less of punishment than the delay of death.'

They err who take ἕως here as a limit of time. Compare also Ps. XLII. and XLIII.

You may see a similar meaning of the word ἕως, which is taken intensively, not extensively, in Isa. XXXVIII. 1, Jonah IV. 9. Beza derives that περίλυπος from the preposition περὶ, which he says increases the meaning in this way: to declare a soul besieged and surrounded by sorrow on every side, so that no exit lies open, just as the blessed Gerhard also explained. That does not please Erasmus Schmid: he prefers to derive it from the adverb περὶ, 'exceedingly,' 'greatly,' 'too much,' and to render it 'my soul is exceedingly sorrowful,' as in περιθέλω, 'I desire above measure,' about which he discourses at length. But it does not appear why the diffusion of sorrow should not have a place here; since by the intensive word ἕως being added, it is noted that sorrow besets my soul on every side and as if in a circuit even unto death, truly lethal, not only as much as temporal death brings, but as much as infernal death brings. For with this he wrestled here, nay, this Christ felt in this most grievous agony in our place, so that he even had need of angelic comfort. If one should say: if he already felt infernal sorrow when he began to 'be sorrowful and very heavy,' and thus complained of the sorrow of his soul, what then is it that he afterwards prays three times that the cup of wrath be taken away? I answer: that that sorrow was continued, or also that Christ understood that he would yet experience the same in a more intensive degree: just as it appears from the most sorrowful exclamation and complaint made on the cross concerning divine desertion that Christ again felt infernal sorrow, such as they feel who in hell are deserted by God.

Latin:

Vers. 38. Περίλυπός ἐσιν ἡ ψυχή με ἕως θανάτε] אפפוני חבלי מות. Verba sunt Davidis Christi plerumque typum gerentis Ps. CXVI. 3. Graece περίεχον με ὠδῖνες θανάτε, ita vocantur dolores maximi & quales circa mortem esse solent, quibus non immerito comparatur horror ipse mortis & quidem tam cruentae, tam ignominiosae ob oculos versantis: Ovidius Morsq; minus poenae quam mora mortis habet.

Errant qui ἕως hic pro temporis limite accipiunt. Confer & Ps. XLII. & XLIII.

Similem significationem vocis ἕως quae intensive, non extensive accipitur, videfis Es. XXXVIII. 1. Jon. IV. 9. Illud περίλυπος Beza ex praepositione περὶ deducit, quam augere significationem dicit hoc modo: ut animum declaret undiquaque maerore obsessum, & circumvallatum, ut nullus pateat exitus, quemadmodum etiam B. Gerhardus exposuit. Non placet id Erasmo Schmiedio: mavult ab adverbio περὶ, admodum, valde, nimis deducere, & reddere summe tristis est anima mea, ut in περιθέλω supra modum cupio, de quo fuse disserit. Sed non apparet, cur non diffusio doloris hic locum habeat; quum intensivo voce ἕως addita notetur? undiquaq; & veluti per circuitum tristitia animam meam obsidet usque ad mortem, vere lethalis, non modo quantam mors temporalis, sed quantam mors infernalis importat. Cum hac enim hic colluctatus est, imo hanc sensit in hoc agone gravissimo Christus nostri loco, ut etiam confortatione angelica opus habuerit. Si dicat quis: si jam tum infernalem dolorem sensit, cum cepit λυπεῖσθαι καὶ ἀδημονεῖν, & ita questus est de anima sua tristitia, quid ergo est, quod trina vice deinde adhuc deprecatur, ut calix irae auferatur? Resp. Continuatum illum dolorem fuisse, vel etiam intellexisse Christum gradu intensiori sese eundem experturum adhuc esse: quemadmodum è tristissima exclamatione ac querela in cruce facta de desertione divina apparet iterum sensisse Christum dolorem infernalem, qualem sentiunt, qui in inferno à Deo deserti sunt.

## 26:39
Ver. 39. ἔπεσεν ἐπὶ πρόσωπον ἀυτῦ] The custom of those praying with the utmost humility, Gen. XVII. 17, I Macc. ch. IV. 40, Eccl. L. 19.

Praying] with a strong cry and tears, as the Writer to the Hebrews says: which, although it can be referred to other prayers of Christ as well, yet pertains peculiarly to these. Father if it is possible, let this cup pass from me] What is here and in Luke is cup, is called both cup and hour in Mark. It could be doubted whether Christ was acting regarding imminent death, or regarding that man whom his mind was then sensing. But the very sense of horror conceived on account of death makes me believe that he spoke of this very thing, akin to that manner of speaking in Mark in the history of John, where Christ speaks thus: Now is my soul troubled; and what shall I say? Father, save me from this hour. But for this cause I came unto this hour. Where hour denotes the time of death entirely. But since these words of Christ and those which follow cohere in one connection, it is not to be thought that anything slipped out from him as if unpremeditated, and that what he had said earlier is truly and properly amended by that which is later: since it is said much more correctly that at one and the same time Christ wished to express both what he wanted, and what he wants: for it often happens that someone does something willingly with an unwilling mind. Indeed, in undergoing all troubles, such a mixed action, as Aristotle names it, is to be observed, an example of which he himself places in him who, while he would wish to have his goods safe, yet wishes to make a jettison for the sake of avoiding a greater evil: for no one would choose any of such things for their own sake. If therefore death alone joined with such ignominy and torture is looked upon, Christ would undoubtedly wish to decline it; since all nature and especially that of living creatures studies its own safety, and avoids things that will harm, but looking to the Father's will, he undergoes such death not unwillingly, and becomes obedient unto death, even the death of the cross Phil. II. 8. In this way he himself, although he was a son, learned obedience from the things which he suffered: by experiencing, namely, how arduous and difficult it is, especially at such a time, to fulfill all parts of obedience. But how does that condition if it is possible, which Mark also places with Matthew, cohere with that which follows in Mark, all things are possible to thee? Surely one must have recourse here to that trite distinction in the Schools of that which is impossible by itself, and that which is impossible with this or that posited. For by itself nothing is impossible to God, as we saw above in chapter XIX. 26, outside of those things which are in themselves inconsistent, or which are repugnant to the divine nature. But the sense is: if your decrees allow, that in another way your glory and the salvation of men might be equally provided for. Nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt] Namely let it be, which Luke adds. Here, in the manner of the Hebrews who have neither potential nor optative mood, I will is for I would, or as the Greeks speak, I was wanting. Thus Rom. IX. 3. I was wishing is I would. Thus below and he shall present is said for he would present, unless of course that definite decree stood in the way. Thus above c. XII. 34. how can you speak good things, being evil? i. e. how would you be able? & c. XIII. 6. it is profitable to him, that is, it would be better for him. It is advantageous in the same sense in Luke XVII. 2. & Luke XIII. 9. that they are just, as if they were just: & chapter XVI. 26. those wishing, if they wished anything. The sense therefore in this place is: I would indeed as much as possible decline this evil if you wished, Father: nevertheless let it be done not what I would otherwise wish but what you wish. That which Christ says he would otherwise naturally wish, is called will by Luke: namely according to things simply and with all the circumstances of the thing taken together, the same Christ wanted what the Father wanted: and this was the chief part of obedience, that he subjected his own will against natural desire to the Father's will. In a similar sense it is said to Peter in John XXI. 18. where when thou wilt: when yet that which is in Rev. XII. 11. they loved not their soul unto death, and what Paul says of himself in Acts XXI. 13. I am ready to die for the name of the Lord, is no less fitting to him than to other witnesses. Well therefore Origen in the seventh against Celsus: With piety toward God, prayer is also lifted up. standing over every circumstance, not thinking it primary to itself, but enduring that which is primary when it happens, when the time calls. But those things which were acceptable, and being virtuous in the things that happen, and meeting beforehand from providence the circumstances, the voice saying, nevertheless not what I will, but what thou. Verse 40. to Peter] To him especially, and through him to the others. For Peter also had led the others by promising too much about himself. Above in verse 35. so were you not able] I do not agree with those who punctuate so from the following words. For so, up to this point, is it so, is it thus, is accustomed to be connected with an interrogative, or rather an admiring, sentence. Thus in Mark I think it is best read: so how have you no faith. Verse 41. watch] With one word it signifies two things: for he does not only want this time to be for tempering sleep, but also for preparing oneself as much as possible for the battle with intent meditations. For to watch is to pay attention, as above in chapter XXIV. & XXV. several times: Acts XX. 31. 1 Cor. XVI. 13. Rev. III. 2. and elsewhere throughout.

Latin:

Vers. 39. ἔπεσεν ἐπὶ πρόσωπον ἀυτῦ] Mos cum summa demissione precantium, Gen. XVII, 17. I. Macc. c. IV. 40. Eccl. L, 19.

Προσευχόμενος] μετὰ κραυγῆς ἰσχυρᾶς καὶ δακρύων, ut ait Scriptor ad Hebræos: quod quanquam ad alias etiam Chri- sti preces referri potest, ad has tamen peculiariter pertinet. Πάτερ με εἰ δυνατόν ἐστι, παρελθέτω ἀπ' ἐμὲ τὸ ποτήριον τῦτο] Quod hic & apud Lucam est ποτήριον, Marco & ποτήριον & ὥρα dicitur. Dubitari poterat de imminenti morte ageret Christus, an de isto homine quem tum animus sentiebat. Sed præ horroris sensu ob mortem concepto hæc ipsa de- mor.e eum esse locutum ut credam facit affine isti quod a- pud Marcum loquendi genus in Johannis historia, ubi Chri- stus ita loquitur: νῦν ἡ ψυχή με τετάρακται· καὶ τί εἴπω πάτερ; σῶσον με ἐκ τῆς ὥρας ταύτης. ἀλλὰ διὰ τῦτο ἦλθον εἰς τὴν ὥραν ταύτην. ubi hora omnino mortis tempus denotat. Cum au- tem verba hæc Christi & quæ sequutur uno nexu cohæ- reant, non est putandum quicquam isti velut impræmedita- tum excidisse, & quod prius dixerat vere ac proprie per id quod posterius est emendari: cum multo rectius dicatur uno eodemque tempore Christum exprimere voluisse tum quid vellet, tum quid velit: sæpe enim accidit ut quis ali- quid faciat ἑκὼν ἀέκοντιγε θυμῷ. Imo in omnibus molestijs subeundis talem μικτὴν πρᾶξιν ut Aristoteles nominat, est animadvertere, cujus exemplum ipse ponit in eo qui cum vellet merces habere salvas, vult tamen majoris mali vitan- di causa jactum facere: ἑδεὶς γὰρ ἂν ἕλοιτο καθ' αὑτὸ τῶν τοιού- των ἐδέν. Si ergo mors sola conjuncta tanta cum ignomi- nia ac cruciatu spectetur, haud dubie vellet Christus eam declinare; quippe cum natura omnis præcipueque ani- mantium saluti suæ studeat, vitetque nocitura, at Patris vo- luntatem respiciens, mortem talem non invitus subit, καὶ γί- νεται ὑπήκοος μέχρι θανάτε, θανάτε δὲ σταυρῦ Phil. II. 8. Hoc modo ipse καίπερ ὗὸς ὢν ἔμαθεν ἀφ' ὧν ἔπαθε τὴν ὑπακοὴν: ex- periendo scilicet quam sit arduum ac difficile, tali præser- tim tempore, omnes obedientiæ partes explere. Quomo- do autem cohæret conditio illa εἰ δυνατόν ἐσι quam cum Mat- thæo etiam Marcus ponit, cum eo quod apud Marcum se- quitur πάντα δυνατά σοι; Nimirum recurrendum hic est ad illam tritam in Scholis distinctionem ejus quod ἀδύνατον sit per se, & ejus quod ἀδύνατον sit hoc vel illo posito. Nam per se nihil est Deo ἀδύνατον, ut vidimus supra cap. XIX. 26, extra ea quæ sunt in semetipsis ἀσύστατα, aut quæ divinæ na- turæ repugnant. At sensus est: si tua decreta ferunt, ut alio modo suæ gloriæ & hominum saluti æque consula- tur. Πλὴν ἐχ' ὡς ἐγὼ θέλω, ἀλλ' ὡς σύ] Scilicet γενέσθω, quod addit Lucas. Hic more Hebræorum qui neque potemia- lem neque optativum modum habent, θέλω est pro θέλοι- μι, vel ut Græci loquuntur ἤθελον. Sic Rom. IX. 3. ηὐχόμην est optarem. Sic infra καὶ παραστήσει est dictum pro παρα- στήσαι ἂν, nisi scilicet decretum illud definitum obstatet. Sic supra c. XII. 34. πῶς δύνασθε ἀγαθὰ λαλεῖν πονηροὶ ὄντες; i. e. quomodo possetis? & c. XIII. 6. συμφέρει αὐτῷ, id est, præsta- ret illi. λυσιτελεῖ sensu eodem Luc. XVII. 2. & Luc. XIII. 9. ὅτι εἰσὶ δίκαιοι, quasi essent justi: & cap. XVI. 26. οἱ θέλοντες, si quid vellent. Sensus ergo hoc loco est: Vellem quidem quam maxime declinare hoc malum si velles, pater: veruntamen solo fiat non quod alioqui ego vellem sed quod tu vis. Illud quod Christus alioqui se voliturum naturaliter dicit, Lucæ voca- tur θέλημα : nimirum κατὰ τὰ παραπλῶς & simul assumtis omnibus rei circumstantiis idem Christus volebat quod Pa- ter volebat: atque hæc præcipua pars erat obedientiæ, quod voluntatem suam contra naturale desiderium Patris volun- tati subjecit. Simili sensu Petro dicitur Joh. XXI. 18. ὅπῦ ὅταν θέλῃς: cum tamen ipsi non minus quam aliis Deitestibus conveniat illud Apoc. XII. 11. ἐκ ἠγάπησαν τὴν ψυχὴν αὐ- τῶν ἄχρι θανάτε, & quod Paulus de se dicit Actor. XXI. 13. ἑτοίμως ἔχω ἀποθανεῖν ὑπὲρ τῦ ὀνόματος τῦ κυρίῳ. Bene ergo Origenes septimo adversus Celsum: Μετὰ τῆς πρὸς τὸν θεὸν ἐυσεβείας κὶ ἡ ἐυχὴ ἄρηται. παντὸς ἐπιστῶσα τὸ περιστατικὸν 8 προηγύμενον αὑτῷ νομίζοντα, ἀλλ' ὑπομένοντα τὸ μὲν προη- γυμένως ὅταν συμβαίνοι, ὅταν καιρὸς καλῇ. ἀλλὰ τὰ μὲν ἀποδε- κτόν ἦν, ἐναρετημένη δὲ ταῖς συμβαίνεσι, καὶ προϋπαντῶτα ἀπὸ προνοίας περιστατικὰ, ἡ λέγεσα φωνὴ, πλὴν ἐ τί ἐγὼ θέλω, ἀλλὰ τί σύ. Vers. 40. τῷ Πέτρῳ] Ei præcipue, & per eum cæteris. Nam & nimium de se pollicendo Petrus aliis præiverat. Su- pra commate 35. ὕτως ἐκ ἰσχύσατε] Non assentior iis qui ὕτως à sequenti- bus interstingunt. Solet enim ὕτως, usque adeo, sicci- ne, adeone, connecti cum oratione interrogativa, aut ad- mirativa potius. Sic apud Marcum optime legi arbitror: ὕτω πῶς ἐκ ἔχετε πίσιν. Vers. 41. γρηγορεῖτε] Voce una duo significat: neque enim hoctantum vult tempus esse somno temperandi, sed & quam maxime se parandiad prælium intentis meditatio- nibus. Nam γρηγορεῖν est προσέχειν, ut supra cap. XXIV. & XXV. aliquoties: Act. XX. 31. 1. Cor. XVI. 13. Apoc. III. 2. & alibi passim.

## 26:41
Pray that you may not enter into temptation] I cannot subscribe to those who think the Apostles were commanded to pray to God that no temptation might come to them, which, given the decree concerning those things that were to happen to Christ, seems to be of the impossibilities. Therefore, it is more correct, as we also said above on chapter 6, that to enter here is what in 1 Timothy 6:9 is to fall into, namely to be immersed and to succumb. It is, however, a metonymy: for the effect is put for the cause. For Christ wishes the disciples to pray that a certain help greater than usual might be given to them, supported by which they might be able to achieve that they would not succumb when attacked. And hence it is clear that the help of even a more robust spirit was not so strictly withdrawn from them that it could not have been obtained by attention and prayers. But since this too had been neglected by them, they were permitted, some more, some less, to slip, so that they might the more, as we said above, learn to have compassion on the ignorant and those who are wandering: which was no small part of the duty entrusted to them.

The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak] The reason is given why help greater than usual must be implored, namely because they were still so constituted that the mind of the flesh did not sufficiently obey the reins of the mind. The Hebrews call the vital and sensitive faculty of the soul נפש, but that which uses reason, the ruling faculty, they call רוח. Thus Paul uses the word πνεῦμα in Romans 8:16, 1 Corinthians 2:11, chapter 6:20, and the writer to the Hebrews in chapter 4:12. The spirit of the mind is spoken of in Ephesians 4:23. It is called by Paul elsewhere both mind and the inner man, which are clearly used for the same thing in Romans 7:22-23 and Ephesians 3:16. Elsewhere, however, spirit signifies the whole soul, including even the affections, as we said above in chapter 5:4, thus in Acts 19:21. The mind, therefore, as being imbued with the doctrine of Christ, and add to this the participation in the mysteries, had in itself a willingness: but it had not yet progressed to the implanted power, namely that when danger was imminent it could easily subdue those affections which the soul, as the guardian of life and enemy of inconveniences, suggested: which is here and elsewhere called flesh, because it consults for the body. In this sense, those who lay the first rudiments of Christian piety, the infants in Christ, are also called carnal in 1 Corinthians 3:1, 3, because the mind of the flesh has not yet been sufficiently subdued by them. But it is to be noted that what was still rebelling against the mind in the Apostles at that time was not of that coarser dregs of affections concerning wealth and the pleasures of the senses and whatever things are similar, but the most natural desires, such as, for example, the care for life and the flight from pains. They were not, therefore, in the class of those whom Aristotle says are overcome by things that the many are stronger than, or are less affected by things that many both resist and are able to, but in the order of those whom he says are strong and surpass the rest in being overcome and resisting, which he says is most pardonable. Christ calls the flesh weak, not because it did not have strength, but because it did not have true health, as those who are insane from disease are wont to have. For the health of the soul is the command of the mind, to listen and to obey what it commands. Papinius says excellently: I hate the limbs, and this fragile use of the body, the deserter of the mind.

Latin:

Προσεύχεσθε ἵνα μὴ εἰσέλθητε εἰς πειρασμόν] Non possum iis subscribere qui præcipi putant Apostolis, ut orent Deum ne ullus ipsis πειρασμός adveniat, quod, posito decreto de iis quæ Christo erant eventura, videtur esse τῶν ἀδυνάτων. Itaque rectius est, ut & supra ad caput 6. diximus, εἰσέρχεσθαι hic esse quod 1. Timoth. VI. 9. ἐμπίπτειν, immergi scilicet & succumbere. Est autem μετωνυμία: nam effectus pro cau- sa ponitur. Vult enim Christus orare discipulos, ut detur ipsis auxilium quoddam majus solito, quo fulti possent id consequi ne oppugnati succumberent. Atque hinc liquet non ita destricte subtractum ipsis spiritus etiam robustioris auxilium, ut non potuerit attentione & precibus impetrari. Sed cum hoc quoque neglectum ab ipsis esset, permissi sunt alii plus, alii minus labi, quo magis, ut supra diximus, di- scerent, μετριοπαθεῖν τοῖς ἀγνοοῦσι καὶ πλανωμένοις: quæ non exigua pars erat muneris ipsis crediti.

Τὸ μὲν πνεῦμα πρόθυμον, ἡ δὲ σὰρξ ἀσθενής] Causa reddi- tur, cur implorandum sit solito majus auxilium, nimirum quod ita adhuc essent constituti, ut τὸ φρόνημα τῆς σαρκὸς non satis audiret habenas mentis. Hebræi animæ faculta- tem vitalem ac sensitivam vocant נפש, illam vero quæ ra- tione utitur, τὸ ἡγεμονικὸν, appellant רוח. Ita πνεῦμα τῷ νο- cem usurpat Paulus Rom. IIX. 16. 1. Cor. II. 11. cap. VI. 20. & Scriptor ad Hebræos c. IV. 12. πνεῦμα νοὸς dicitur Ephes. IV. 23. Dicitur Paulo alibi tum νοῦς tum ὁ ἔσω ἄνθρωπος, quæ pro eodem poni liquet Rom. VII. 22. 23. Eph. III. 16. Alibi vero πνεῦμα totum animum significat comprehensis etiam affectibus ut supra diximus c. V. 4. sic Act. XIX. 21. A- nimus igitur, utpote doctrina Christi, adde & mysteriorum participatione imbutus, habebat in se πρόθυμον: sed non- dum profecerat ad τὸ ἐμφυτευτικὸν, nempe ut instante pericu- lo facile posset edomare affectus illos quos anima vitæ tu- tatrix & incommodorum inimica suggerebat: quæ hic & alibi σὰρξ dicitur, quia corpori consulit. Hoc sensu hi qui pri- ma ponunt Christianæ pietatis rudimenta, οἱ νηπίοι ἐν χριστῷ etiam σαρκικοὶ vocantur 1. Cor. III. 1. 3. quia τὸ φρόνημα τῆς σαρκὸς nondum satis est ab ipsis edomitum. Sed notandum est id quod in Apostolis eo tempore adhuc menti rebella- bat, non fuisse de crassiore illa fæce affectuum circa opes & sensuum voluptates & siqua sunt similia, sed desideria maxi- me naturalia, ut puta vitæ curam, dolorum fugam. Non igi- tur erant in illorum genere quos Aristoteles ait ἡττᾶσθαι ὧν οἱ δὲ πολλοὶ κρείττους, aut ὀλιγώτους πρὸς ἃ πολλοὶ κ᾿ ἀντιστένουσι κ᾿ δύ- νανται, sed in eorum ordine quos ait ἰσχύειν καὶ ὑπερβάλλειν τῶν λοιπῶν ἡττᾶσθαι κ᾿ ἀντιστένοντας, quod maxime ait esse συγ- γνωμονικόν. Σάρκα autem ἀσθενῆ vocat Christus, non quod vires non haberet, sed quod non haberet veram sanitatem, ut solent qui morbo insaniunt. Nam sanitas ani- mæ est mentis imperium, ἀκούειν καὶ ὦ παραγγέλῃ. Egregie Papinius: Odi artus, fragilemque hunc corporis usum Desertorem animi.

## 26:42
Verse 42. If it is possible] If is put for since: for the decree of the Father was not unknown to Christ.

By flesh he understands the vital and sensitive faculty of the soul, which is called נפש by the Hebrews, which he wishes to be called flesh because it consults for the body and is rebellious to the mind, which Christ here calls weak, not because it does not have strength, but because it does not have true health, as those who are insane in mind are wont to have, because the health of the soul is the command of the mind: but by the word spirit he understands that faculty which uses reason, the ruling faculty, called רוח by the Hebrews: But where is this Hebrew acceptance founded in the sacred writings? No opposition or struggle of the vital and sensitive faculty with the rational, as the Socinians and Papists wish, is noted: because the whole man is by nature carnal, and is called flesh in John 3:5, and not merely some faculty of the soul: nor is the superior faculty of man free from carnal or sinful corruption: and therefore it is more correctly understood by others that by flesh is meant the animal man, and by spirit the spiritual man: Paul calls them the outer and inner man in Romans 7: by the former is designated the corruption adhering to us by nature after the fall, by which all faculties are affected: by the latter, however, that which is renewed in us by the Holy Spirit, concerning which [I have written] more fully in the Commonplaces.

This cup] See above chapter 20:22.

To pass from me so as not to drink] That is, since it has seemed so to you that you do not save me from death except through death. This is what the writer to the Hebrews says, that Christ cried out to him who was able to save him from death, namely by a speedy resurrection. To pass by here and in Mark 14:35 is to go away, just as העבר is to remove in 2 Kings 24:10, Zechariah 3:4, Psalm 119:39.

Your will be done] These are the words not merely of one bearing what cannot be avoided, but of one acquiescing with his whole soul, as in Acts 21:14.

Latin:

Vers. 42. Εἰ ὐ δύναται] Si positum pro quandoquidem: neque enim ignotum erat Christo decretum Patris.

Per σάρκα intelligit animæ facultatem vitalem, ac sensitivam, quæ Ebræis נפש dicatur, quam σάρ- κα vocari vult, quia corpori consulit, & menti re- bellas, quam hic ἀσθενῆ dicat Christus, non quod vi- res non habeat, sed quod non habeat veram sanita- tem, ut solent qui mente insaniunt, quia animæ sanitas est mentis imperium: per vocem πνεύμα- τος vero illam intelligit facultatem, quæ ratione utitur, τὸ ἡγεμονικὸν, Ebræis רוח dictum: Sed ubi hæc Ebræorum acceptio fundata in sacris? Non oppositio, aut lucta facultatis vitalis & sen- sitivæ cum rationali, ut Sociniani, & Papistæ vo- lunt, notatur: quia totus homo natura σαρκικὸς est, & σὰρξ dicitur Johan. III. 5. non vero solum facultas aliqua animæ: neque corruptionis car- nalis seu peccaminosæ expers est superior hominis facultas: ideoque rectius ab aliis per carnem in- telligitur homo animalis, per πνεῦμα spiritualis homo: Paulus vocat hominem exteriorem & inte- riorem Rom. VII. per illum corruptio designatur natura nobis adhærens post lapsum, qua omnes facultates: per hunc vero quod renovatum in no- bis est per Spiritum S. de quo in L.L. Communibus fusius.

Τοῦτο τὸ ποτήριον] Vide supra cap. XX. 22.

Παρελθεῖν ἀπ᾿ ἐμοῦ τοῦ μὴ πιεῖν] Id est, quando ita tibi visum est ut me non serves a morte nisi per mortem. Hoc est quod dicit Scriptor ad Hebræos clamasse Christum πρὸς τὸν δυνάμενον σώζειν αὐτὸν ἐκ θανάτου, nimirum festina resu- scitatione. παρελθεῖν hic & Marc. XIV. 35. est abire, quo- modo העבר est amovere 2. Reg. XXIV. 10. Zach. III, 4. Pf. CXIX. 39.

Γενηθήτω τὸ θέλημά σου] Voces sunt non ferentis tantum quod vitari nequeat, sed toto animo acquiescentis, ut Act. XXI. 14.

## 26:43
Vers. 43. The eyes heavy] Because of sorrow, and as Luke teaches, whence that sleepy torpor arises which the Greeks call καταφοράν.

Latin:

Vers. 43. Οἱ ὀφθαλμοὶ βεβαρημένοι] Præ mœstitia, ac Lucas docet, unde torpor ille somnolentus oritur quem καταφορὰν Græci vocant.

## 26:44
Vers. 44. For the third time] A solemn number for repeating prayers as often as something greater had occurred: Paul 2 Cor. XII. 8. I besought the Lord thrice.

Latin:

Vers. 44. Ἐκ τρίτου] Solennis numerus iterandarum pre- cum quoties quid majus inciderat: Paulus 2. Cor. XII. 8. τρὶς τὸν κύριον παρεκάλεσα.

## 26:45
Vers. 45. Sleep on now and take your rest] Above he had said, You could not watch one hour with me. Now he shows that their keeping watch can be of no further use to him: since he was already about to be torn away from them. The sense therefore is: As far as I am concerned, you may now sleep and rest as much as you like. And we are compelled to interpret it in no other way by what follows in Mark, ἀπέχει: for ἀπέχει in both Mark and Anacreon signifies the same thing that Virgil, Terence, and Seneca say in Latin, 'it is enough' [habet], to which word Seneca added 'it is finished' by way of interpretation. And so the Arabs and Syrians translate it in Mark, 'the end is present': by which it is given to be understood that the time had passed in which the Apostles could be a comfort to Christ.

The hour is at hand and the Son of man is betrayed] In the Hebrew manner, the copulative conjunction has the force of a relative: for the sense is: the time is near in which Christ is to be betrayed.

Sinners] Of the Roman soldiers. For the Jews properly called those living in a heathen manner ἁμαρτωλός, Gal. II. 15, that is, lawless, as in Acts II. 23, 1 Cor. IX. 21. Roman governors were accustomed on feast days, because then there was a great gathering of the people, to send a cohort to guard the temple, lest anything should be attempted there against the customs of the Jews, which John calls a band [σπεῖραν] in ch. XIII. 3, and Josephus a rank [τάξιν], whose words, already cited by us above, must be repeated here from the book of Antiquities VIII. c. 4. 'The feast called the Passover being at hand, at which it is our custom to offer unleavened bread, a great multitude having gathered from everywhere for the feast, the governor, fearing lest some innovation might arise from them, orders one rank of soldiers to take up their arms and stand upon the porticoes of the temple, suppressing the innovation if any should occur. And this also those who governed Judea before him were wont to do during the feasts.' Whence it is clear that this guard was transferred on feast days from the Antonia, which was in the power of the Romans, to the porticoes of the temple. The same Josephus, Wars V. cap. 15, dealing with the Antonia: 'But as was the custom for both of the holy feasts, it had descents, through which the guards (for a Roman cohort always sat upon it) descending and stationing themselves around the porticoes with their arms, kept watch over the people during the feasts, so that no innovation might be made. For the temple was a fortress overlooking the city, and the Antonia overlooking the temple. And at this place were the guards of the three.' Outside of feast days, the Priests guarded the Temple through their own Jewish watchmen, who are called ministers [ὑπηρέται], Acts V. 22, 26, Mark XIV. 65, John VI. 32, 45, ch. XVIII. 3, 12, 22, ch. XIX. 6. The Priests, however, entrusted the command to one of their own number, both over the daily watchmen and over the added soldiers: he was called the captain of the temple [στρατηγὸς τῦ ἱερῦ]: a magistracy not unlike that which the Romans called the prefect of the watch. Josephus shows that he was next in dignity to the High Priest, Antiquities VIII. 5. 'Those around Ananias the high priest and the captain Anatus': and cap. 8, 'they seize alive the scribe of the captain Eleazar; and this was the son of Ananias the high priest.' Mention of this magistrate is found in the same Josephus in several places, and in Luke Acts IV. 1, cap. V. 24, 26, whence we learn at the same time that it was committed to his office to apprehend those who transgressed the law, either in the Temple or even outside the Temple, by order of the Sanhedrin. For the Romans had permitted the Jews the right of apprehension and coercion short of death. But in this history Luke names in the plural number the captains [στρατηγούς] who had both taken part in the councils, ch. XII. 4, and through whom the apprehension was made, ch. XXII. 52, undoubtedly counting among the prefect of the watch the assistants added to his office, such as the one whom we saw called a scribe by Josephus: that is, שטר, which is a general name for all those who assist higher powers with counsel or effort. Thus also we learn from the same Josephus that the treasurer [γαζοφύλακι] had his own scribe. Those captains, therefore, fearing for themselves from Christ's followers, had taken to themselves the Roman cohort in addition to the daily Jewish watchmen of the Temple, in order to apprehend JESUS. These are they whom Christ here calls sinners, as being outlaws, whom no reverence for God restrained. That Latin cohort for guarding the Temple at that time The guard was called 'destinata', a term which our writer here uses. And that the command for that time had been entrusted to the priests for that guard, that saying of Pilate also teaches: 'You have a guard.' Concerning which more below when we have reached that point.

Latin:

Vers. 45. Καθεύδετε τὸ λοιπὸν καὶ ἀναπαύεσθε] Supra di- xerat οὐκ ἰσχύσατε μίαν ὥραν γρηγορῆσαι μετ' ἐμῦ. Iam o- stendit nulli amplius usui sibi esse posse ipsorum pervi- gilium: cum jamjam ab ipsis avellendus esset. Sensus er- go est: Per me jam vobis licet dormire & requiescere quantum lubet. Neque aliter ut interpreterur cogit nos quod apud Marcum sequitur ἀπέχει: omnino enim ἀπέχει & Marco & Anacreonti significat idem quod Latine Vir- gilius, Terentius, Seneca dicunt habet, cui voci interpre- tamenti loco Seneca addidit peractum est. Atque ita a- pud Marcum vertunt Arabs & Syrus, adest finis: quo da- tur intelligi præteriisse tempus quo Apostoli Christo pote- rant esse solatio.

Ἠγγικεν ἡ ὥρα καὶ ὁ ὑὸς τῦ ἀνθρώπυ παραδίδοται] Hebraico more conjunctio copulativa vim habet relativi: sensus e- nim est: prope esse tempus quo tradendus sit Christus.

Ἁμαρτωλῶν] Militum Romanorum. Nam ἀλλοφύλως gentiliter viventes Judæi proprie vocabant ἁμαρτωλὸς Gal. II. 15. id est ἀνόμως, ut Act. II. 23. 1. Cor. IX. 21. solebant Romani præsides diebus festis, quia tum magnus erat po- puli conventus, ad templi custodiam, nequid ibi contra mores Judæorum tentaretur, cohortem mittere quam σπείραν vocat Iohannes c. XIII. 3. τάξιν Iosephus, cujus ver- bi supra quoque allata a nobis hic repetenda sunt ex libro Ἀρχαιολογίας VIII. c. 4. Τῆς πάσχα προσαγορευομένης ἑορτῆς ἐνστάσης, καθ' ἣν ἔθος ἐστιν ἡμῖν ἄζυμα προσφέρεσθαι, πολλῆς κὶ παν- ταχόθεν πληθύος συνεληλυθυίας ἐπὶ τὴν ἑορτὴν, δείσας ὁ κύμων μὴ νεώτερον τι παρὰ τύτων προσπέση, κελεύει τῶν στρατιωτῶν μίαν τάξιν ἀναλαβῦσαν τὰ ὅπλα ἐπὶ τῶν τῦ ἱερῦ στοῶν ἑςάναι καταστε- λῦντας τὸν νεωτερισμὸν εἴ ἄρα τις γένοιτο. τῦτο δὲ κὶ οἱ πρὸ ἀυτῦ τῆς Ἰυδαίας ἐπιτροπεύσαντες ἐν ταῖς ἑορταῖς ἔπραττον. Unde apertum est hoc præsidium festis diebus translatum ex Antonia, quæ erat in potestate Romanorum, in por- ticus templi. Idem Josephus ἁλώσεως V. cap. 15. agens de Antonia: Καθὰ δὲ συνήθεια ταῖς τῶν ἱερῶν ἑοαῖς τίς ἀμφοτέραις εἶχε καταβάσεις, δι' ὧν κατιόντες οἱ φρυροὶ (καθῆστο γὰρ ἀεὶ ἐπ' ἀυτῆς τάγμα ῥωμαίων) καὶ διιστάμενοι περὶ τὰς σοὰς μετὰ τῶν ὅπλων, ἐν ταῖς ἑορταῖς τὸν δῆμον, ὡς μή τι νεωτερισθείη, παρεφύλαττον. Φρούριον γὰρ ἐπέκειτο τῇ πόλει μὲν τὸ ἱερὸν, τῷ ἱερῷ δὲ ἡ Ἀντωνία. κατὰ δὲ ταύτην οἱ τῶν τριῶν φύλακες ἦσαν. Extra festos dies Sa- cerdotes per suos vigiles Judæos Templum asservabant, qui ὑπηρέται vocantur, Act. V. 22. 26, Marc. XIV. 65. Job. VI. 32.45. c.XIIX. 3. 12. 22. c. XIX. 6. Sacerdotes autem uni ex suorum numero imperium tum in vigiles quotidianos, tum in additos milites mandabant: is στρατηγὸς τῦ ἱερῦ vocaba- tur: non dissimilis magistratus ei quem præfectum vigilum Romani vocabant. Josephus eum summo Pontifici di- gnitate proximum fuisse oftendit Ἀρχαιολογίας VIII. 5. Τὲς δὲ περὶ Ἀνανίαν τὸν ἀρχιερέα καὶ τὸν στρατηγὸν Ἄνατον: & cap. 8. συλλαμβάνεσι ζῶντα τὸν γραμματέα τῦ στρατηγῦντος Ἐ- λεαζάρυ' παῖς δὲ ἦν ὗτος Ἀνανίε τῦ ἀρχιερέως. Ejus ma- gistratus mentio est apud eundem Iosephum aliquot in lo- cis, & apud Lucam Act. IV. 1. cap. V. 24. 26. unde si- mul discimus ejusdem officio commissum fuisse ut ex Sy- nedrii jussu in legem delinquentes vel in Templo vel et- iam extra Templum prehenderet. Nam prehensionis jus & coercitionis citra mortem Judæis Romani permiserant. At in hac historia Lucas plurali numero στρατηγές nominat qui & consiliis interfuerant c. XII. 4. & per quos facta est prehensio c. XXII. 52. nimirum præfecto vigilum connu- merans adjutores ipsius officio additos qualis ille quem γραμματέα vocari a Iosepho vidimus: id est שטר quod ge- nerale nomen est omnium eorum qui majores potestates consilio aut opera juvant. Sic & γαζοφύλακι suum fuisse γραμματέα ex eodem Iosepho discimus. Isti ergo στρατηγοὶ metuentes sibi a Christo sectatoribus, præter quotidia- nos Templi vigiles Judæos, etiam Romanam co- hortem assumserant, ut IESUM prehenderent. Hi sunt quos hic Christus ἁμαρτωλὸς vocat, utpote ex- leges, quos nulla Dei reverentia tenebat. Latina cohors ista Templo custodiendo ad id tempus- destinata dicebatur custodia, quo nomine hic noster Scri- ptor utitur. Atque in eam custodiam imperium pro eo tempore permissum fuisse Sacerdotibus, illud quoque Pilati docet ἔχετε κωςωδίαν. De quo plura infra cum eo ventum erit.

## 26:47
Verse 47. 'From the chief priests and elders'—a periphrasis for the Sanhedrin, by whose decree the arrest was taking place.

'Elders of the people'—elsewhere we have said that the senators of the great Sanhedrin are so called, to distinguish them from the 'elders of the cities.' The same are called in Leviticus 4:15 'the elders of the congregation of the sons of Israel.'

Latin:

Vers. 47. Ἀπὸ τῶν ἀρχιερέων καὶ πρεσβυτέρων] περίφρασις Synedrii cujus decreto fiebat prehensio.

πρεσβυτέρων τῦ λαῦ] Alibi diximus ita dici magni Synedrii senatores ad discrimen τῶν πρεσβυτέρων τῶν πόλεων. Iidem in Levitico IV. 15. dicuntur οἱ πρεσβύτεροι τῆς συναγωγῆς τῶν ὑιῶν Ἰσραήλ.

## 26:48
Verse 48. 'To them'—namely, to the crowd of whom he had spoken: that is, especially to the Roman soldiers, who had not known Jesus. The chief priests seem to have preferred by a deliberate plan that Jesus be arrested by the hands of the Romans rather than by their own guards. See John 18:12.

Latin:

Vers. 48. Αὐτοῖς] Nempe τῷ ὄχλῳ de quo dixerat: id est præcipue militibus Romanis, qui Jesum non noverant. Videntur Pontifices certo consilio maluisse Jesum prehendi manibus Romanorum, quam suorum vigilium. Vide Joh. XIIX. 12.

## 26:49
Verse 49. 'He kissed him'—the Hebrews used a kiss as a sign of affection not only after a long absence or when saying goodbye, as some think, but also on other occasions, which we are taught especially in Luke 7:44. Christians received this custom from the Jews, as Tertullian teaches us both elsewhere and most clearly in his letter to his wife. This is the 'kiss of love' and the 'holy kiss,' of which there is such frequent mention in Paul. Justin in his Apology: 'We greet one another with a kiss when we have finished our prayers.' The same Tertullian in his book On Prayer calls it the 'kiss of peace,' which the Churches of the East use even now. To this pertains that which Athenagoras cites from ancient tradition: 'If anyone kisses a second time because it pleased him,' add 'woe to him': likewise, 'one must be so careful about the kiss, or rather the act of worship, that if it were slightly diverted in the mind, it would place us outside of eternal life.'

Latin:

V. 49. Κατεφίλησεν αὐτὸν] Hebræi non tantum post longam absentiam aut valedicentes, ut quidam existimant, sed alias etiam in signum dilectionis osculum adhibebant, quod præcipue docemur Luc. VII. 44. A Iudæis hunc morem ac- cepere Christiani, ut Tertullianus tum alibi, tum apertif- sime ad uxorem secundo nos docet. Hoc est φίλημα ἀγά- πης & φίλημα ἅγιον, cujus toties apud Paulum mentio. Iu- stinus Apologetico, ἀλλήλες φιλήματι ἀσπαζόμεθα παυσά μενοι τῶν ἐυχῶν. Osculum pacis vocat idem Tertullianus li- bro de Oratione: quod nunc etiam usurpant Orientis Ec- clesiæ. Huc pertinet illud quod ex veteri traditione citat Athenagoras, ἐάν τις διὰ τῦτο ἐκ δευτέρε καταφιλήσῃ ὅτι ἤρε- σεν αὐτῷ, supple væ illi: item, ὅτως ὖν ἀκριβώσασθαι τὸ φίλημα, μᾶλλον δὲ τὸ προσκύνημα δεῖ, ὡς εἴπε μικρὸν τῇ διανοίᾳ παρα- χαλαθείη ἔξω ἡμᾶς τῆς αἰωνίς τίθησιν ζωῆς.

## 26:50
Verse 50. 'For what purpose are you here?'—that is, with what intent do you come to kiss me? Was it not with the same intent as Joab once had toward Amasa? We interpret it thus from Luke. With a few words he both pricks the conscience of the treacherous man and shows himself to be a 'knower of hearts.' It has been rightly observed that 'ᾧ' is used here for 'τινι' (for what), which can be found elsewhere among the ancient Christians. For Justin, in his address to the Greeks, said 'δι᾿ ἣν αἰτίαν' (for which cause) in a question, instead of 'διὰ τινα αἰτίαν' (for what cause)?

Latin:

Vers. 50. Ἐφ᾿ ᾧ πάρει] Id est, quo animò me osculatum venis? Nonne eo quo olim Ioab Amasam? ita ex Luca interpretamur. Paucis verbis & conscientiam perfidi ho- minis verberat, & se καρδιογνώσην ostendit. Recte autem observatum est ᾧ hic pro τινι poni: quod & alibi apud Christianos veteres reperire est. Nam Iustinus ad Græcos dixit δι᾿ ἣν αἰτίαν interrogando, pro διὰ τινα αἰτίαν?

## 26:51
Verse 51. 'The ear'—'ὠτίον' to the Greeks, 'auricula' to the Latins, is the lowest part of the ear: hence the proverb, 'softer than an ear.' God so directed the blow aimed at the head that it resulted in the least possible damage: and Christ repaired that very damage by replacing the ear. For 'ἰᾶσθαι' (to heal) in this passage in Luke is used for 'ἀρτίζειν' (to make whole). Thus also above in chapter 15:31, the 'maimed' are said to be restored to 'sound' (ὑγιεῖς), that is, 'whole' (ἀρτίοι). I say this on account of certain people who, moved by that word, deny that the ear had been cut off.

Latin:

Vers. 51. Τὸ ὠτίον] ὠτίον Græcis auricula Latinis, est pars auris infima: unde adagium, auricula mollior. Ictum in caput destinatum Deus ita direxit, ut quam minimo damno abiret: idque ipsum damnum refarsit Christus re- posita auricula. Nam ἰᾶσθαι hoc loco apud Lucam est pro ἀρτίζειν. Ita & supra c. XV. 31. dicuntur οἱ κυλλοὶ redditi ὑγιεῖς id est ἀρτίοι. Quod propter quosdam dico qui eo verbo moti negant auriculam fuisse abscissam.

## 26:52
Verse 52. 'Into its place'—'אל־נדבהּ' (into its sheath), 2 Chronicles 21:27; 'into its sheath,' as John says here. The genus for the species.

'All who take the sword'—Christ brings forward the reason why he forbids Peter to use the sword: the decree of the Father, who wills that he suffer bonds and death and 'drink the cup' (John 18:11), ignorance of which decree, though declared more obscurely by the Prophets of old and now more clearly and frequently by Christ, could not excuse Peter. Nor does this admonition pertain only to Peter, but also to all Christians who are sought out by public authorities for punishment on account of their profession of piety. For God wills that, when such necessity threatens, our patience be testified to all and that we 'commit our souls to the Creator': for what is more equitable than that we should spend our life for the honor of Him from whom we received life? Peter, having been taught this by the voice of his Master, taught us the same in his first Epistle, chapter 4:16, 19. The right of natural defense is usually brought forward against this. But it makes a great difference whether that right is used against robbers and anything similar, against whom if anyone fights (although it is most certain that many pious men have not used even this right), he fights by the authority of the laws and of those to whom the care of the republic has been entrusted, as can be seen both elsewhere and especially in the title of the Code: 'When it is permitted to anyone to judge himself without a judge, or public devotion: or whether force may be prepared against the commands of supreme powers.' It is not said in vain that the Praetor renders justice even when he decrees iniquitously: for that is also called justice which, however unjust it may be, must nevertheless be borne, so that it ought not to be repelled by opposing force. Nor is this without reason. For 'ethics,' in which is also the method of administering the Republic, have their own rules, for the rectitude of which it is sufficient that they be useful 'for the most part': yet they do not lose their force if in some case that utility specifically fails. For that general utility of the example remains. But since no one fails to favor himself, if it were once admitted that private individuals injured by a magistrate could repel force with force, everything would be full of tumults: there would be no authority of laws, no authority of judgments: wherefore reason itself leads us to concede that there is some force that must be tolerated, lest place be given to unbridled license. Certainly, in the matter of religion, the examples of early Christianity teach us that such force as is brought to bear 'by the surpassing authority' must be patiently borne. For they err greatly who believe that Christians before the times of Constantine abstained from force out of an estimation of their own weakness. Let us hear even that of Tertullian: 'But far be it that a divine sect should be vindicated by human fire, or that it should grieve to suffer, in which it is proved. For if we wished to act not only as secret avengers but as open enemies, would we lack the strength of numbers and forces?' More, surely, are the Moors and Marcomanni, and the Parthians themselves, or whatever nations there are, even if they are of one place and their own borders, than those of the whole world? We are strangers, and we have filled all your places: cities, islands, castles, municipalities, meeting-places, the very camps, tribes, decuries, the palace, the senate, the forum. We leave you only the temples. For what war would we not have been fit, not ready, even if unequal in forces, who so willingly are slaughtered, if it were not that according to that discipline it is more lawful to be killed than to kill?' Cyprian to Demetrianus: 'Hence it is that none of us, when he is apprehended, struggles: nor does he avenge himself against your violent injustice, although our people is very great and numerous. The assurance of the coming vengeance makes us patient. The innocent yield to the guilty.'

For all who take the sword will perish by the sword] Let this be commonly explained as if this threat pertained to Peter. And yet that sentence does not strike those who defend the innocence of another from injury, even if by chance they exceed the measure in it, which Peter was doing here. For the fault of Peter was impatience, but not a lust for shedding blood, to which this statement properly looks. The sense therefore seems to me to be here: Do not, Peter, out of consideration for the injury brought upon me, be too stirred up to anticipate God in vengeance. For the wounds that can be suffered by you are light. For the sentence stands fixed, that those cruel and bloodthirsty men, even with you resting, will pay the most serious penalties to God with their own blood. Origen, Titus, Theophylact, and Euthymius seem to me to have thought the same. But this argument ought especially to commend patience to us, because we know that God will severely execute the injuries brought upon the pious. The divine Apocalypse strongly confirms this interpretation: If anyone kills with the sword, he must be killed with the sword; here is the patience and the faith of the saints. Paul Rom. XII 19. Do not avenge yourselves, beloved; but give place to wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, says the Lord. Tertullian: God is a sufficiently suitable trustee of patience. If you have deposited an injury with him, he is the avenger: if a loss, he is the restorer: if pain, he is the physician: if death, he is the resuscitator. How much is allowed to patience, that it should have God as its debtor? The saying of Christ was less obscure, because this sentence was worn by proverb among the Jews and was accustomed to be understood concerning divine judgment. Nor indeed was its truth ever more manifest than when the Roman sword exacted the penalties of Jewish cruelty.

This defense was not appropriate for Peter: who not only exceeded the measure through impatience, but also had no right of the sword, and thus was using it rashly: whence he is rebuked by Christ, and this threat strikes him. For although it is permitted to repel force with force against robbers, yet where the matter is conducted by the authority of the Magistrate, to whom the sword is girded, even if he abuses his power and the sword, which happened here, it is not permitted for private individuals to resist the Magistrate. God indeed exercises the penalty of retaliation against injustice, but that is ordinarily done also through the Magistrate, whence also the passage Apoc. XIII. 10. pertains to the vengeance of the Magistrate. Compare Rom. XIII. 4. Gen. IX. 6.

Latin:

Vers. 52. Εἰς τὸν τόπον ἀυτῆς] אל־נדבהּ εἰς τὸν κολεὸν ἀυ- τῆς 2. Par. XXI. 27. εἰς τὴν θήκην ἀυτῆς, ut hic Iohannes. Ge- nus pro specie.

Οἱ λαβόντες μάχαιραν] Causam cur gladio uti Petrum prohibeat Christus adfert decretum Patris qui velit se vin- cula & mortem pati κὶ πίνειν τὸ ποτήριον Ioh. XIIX. 11. cujus de- creti olim per Prophetas obscurius, jam vero per Christum sæpius clare enuntiati ignorantia Petrum excusare non po- terat. Neque vero ad Petrum tantum admonitio ista per- tinet, sed & ad Christianos omnes qui à publicis potestati- bus ad pœnam expetuntur ob pietatis professionem.
