Vult enim Deus, cum talis necessitas imminet, patientiam no- stram omnibus testatam esse & nos παρατιθεσθαι τὰς ψυχὰς τῷ κτίσῃ: quid enim æquius quam ut vitam impendamus ejus honori à quo vitam accepimus? Hoc nos Petrus Ma- gistri voce edoctus edocuit Epist. 1. cap. IV. 16. 19. So- let contra hoc adferri jus naturalis defensionis. Sed mul- tum interest id jus usurpetur adversus latrones & si quid est simile, contra quos si quis pugnat (quanquam pios multos etiam hoc jure non usos certissimum est) pugnat auctori- tate legum & eorum quibus reipublicæ cura mandata est, ut videre est tum alibi, tum imprimis titulo Codicis: Quando liceat unicuique sine judice se sindicare vel publicam devotionem: an vero contra summarum potestatum im- peria vis paretur. Non frustra dicitur Prætor jus redde- re etiam cum inique decernit: jus enim dicitur etiam id quod quamvis injustum est, ferendum tamen est, ita ut vi opposita depelli non debeat. Neque id ratione ca- ret. Nam τὰ ἠθικά, in quibus est & Reipublicæ admini- strandæ ratio, habent regulas suas, ad quorum rectitudi- nem satis est, ut ἐπὶ τὸ πολὺ sint utiles: neque tamen vim suam amittunt, si quo casu ea utilitas peculiariter de- ficiat. Manet enim utilitas illa generalis exempli. At- qui cum nemo sibi non faveat, si id semel admittatur posse privatos à magistratu injuria affectos vim vi repel- lere, omnia erunt tumultuum plena: nulla legum, nul- la judiciorum auctoritas: quare ipsa nos ratio eo ducit, ut concedamus aliquam esse vim quæ sit toleránda, ne effreni licentiæ detur locus. Certe in religionis negotio talem vim quæ infertur παρὰ τῆς ὑπερεχούσης ἐξουσίας patienter fe- rendam docent nos primæ Christianitatis exempla. Mul- tum enim errant qui ante Constantini tempora à vi absti- nuisse Christianos credant imbecillitatis suæ æstimatione. Audiamus vel illud Tertulliani: Sed absit ut aut igni humano vindicetur divina secta, aut doleat pati, in quo probatur Si enim & hostes exertos non tantum vindices occultos agere velle- mus, deesset nobis vis numerorum & copiarum? Plures ni- mirum Mauri & Marcomanni, ipsique Parthi, vel quan- tæcunque unius tamen loci & suorum finium gentes, quam totius orbis? Externi sumus & vestra omnia implevimus, urbes, insulas, castella, municipia, conciliabula, castra ipsa, tribus, decurias, palatium, senatum, forum. Sola vobis relinquimus templa. Cui bello non idonei, non promti fuissemus, etiam im- pares copiis, qui tam libenter trucidamur, si non apud istam disciplinam magis occidi liceret quam occidere? Cyprianus ad Demetrianum: Inde est quod nemo nostrum, quando appre- henditur, reluctatur: nec se adversus injustitiam violentam vestram, quamvis nimius & copiosus sit noster populus, ulci- scitur. Patientes facit de secutura ultione securitas. Innocen- tes nocentibus cedunt.

Πάντες γὰρ οἱ λαβόντες μάχαιραν ἐν μαχαίρᾳ ἀπολοῦνται] So- let hoc vulgo exponi quasi ad Petrum hæc comminatio per- tineat. Atqui sententia ista non ferit eos qui innocentiam alterius ab injuria defendunt, etsi forte in eo modum exce- dant, quod hic faciebat Petrus. Nam culpa Petri erat im- patientia, non autem libido effundendi sanguinis, quo pro- prie spectat istud enuntiatum. Sensus igitur mihi hic videtur esse: NoliPetre consideratione ejus quæ mihi infertur inju- riæ concitatior Deo præripere ultionem. Levia enim sunt vulnera, quæ à te pati possunt. Stat enim rata sententia, crudeles istos & sanguinarios, etiam te quiescente, gravissi- mas Deo daturos pœnas suo sanguine. Idem sensisse mihi videntur Origenes, Titus, Theophylactus, Euthymius. Hoc autem argumentum maxime patientiam nobis debet commendare, quod scimus Deum severe executurum illa- tas piis injurias. Hanc interpretationem valde confirmat divina Apocalypsis : Εἴ τις μαχαίρᾳ ἀποκτενεῖ, δεῖ αὐτὸν ἐν μα- χαίρᾳ ἀποκτανθῆναι˙ ὧδε ἐστιν ἡ ὑπομονὴ κῂ ἡ πίστις τῶν ἁγίων. Paulus Rom. XII 19. Μὴ ἑαυτοὺς ἐκδικοῦντες ἀγαπητοί˙ ἀλλὰ δότε τόπον τῇ ὀργῇ : γέγραπται γὰρ Ἐμοὶ ἐκδίκησις˙ ἐγὼ ἀντα- ποδώσω, λέγει κύριος. Tertullianus: Adeo satis idoneus pa- tientiæ sequester Deus. Si injuriam deposueris penes eum, ultor est: si damnum, restitutor est: si dolorem, medicus est: si mor- tem, resuscitator est. Quantum patientiæ licet, ut Deum ha- beat debitorem? Minus obscurum fuit Christi dictum, quia sententia hæc proverbio trita erat inter Judæos & de divino judicio solebat intelligi. Neque vero unquam manifestior ejus veritas fuit, quam cum Romanus ensis Judaicæ crude- litatis pœnas exegit.

Non conveniebat Petro hæc defensio: qui non tantum per impatientiam modum excedebat, sed nullum etiam jus habebat gladii, adeoque teme- rarie eundem adhibebat: unde à Christo repre- henditur, eumque ferit hæc comminatio. Quam- vis enim vim vi repellere liceat adversus latrones, tamen ubi autoritate Magistratus res geritur, cui gladius accinctus est, etiamsi potestate sua, & gla- dio abutatur, quod hic factum, non licitum pri- vatis est Magistratui resistere. Exercet quidem Deus adversus injustitiam talionis pœnam, sed id ordinarie etiam fit per Magistratum, unde & lo- cus Apoc. XIII. 10. ad Magistratus vindictam facit. Conf. Rom. XIII. 4. Gen. IX. 6.

## 26:53
Vers. 53. And he will present] That is, he would present, unless of course that decree stood in the way, which it is a sin for us to resist.

Twelve legions of angels] It would have been enough to compare twelve angels to twelve disciples: but Christ, that he might more openly show the power of the Father, named as many legions. See Dan. VII. 10. & 2. Kings VI. 17.

Latin:

Vers. 53. Καὶ παραστήσει] Id est παραστήσαι nisi scilicet de- cretum illud obstaret, cui nos reniti nefas est.

Δώδεκα λεγεῶνας ἀγγέλων] Satis fuerat duodecimAngelos duodecim discipulis comparare: sed Christus ut apertius Patris potentiam ostenderet, totidem legiones nomina- vit. Vide Dan. VII. 10. & 2. Reg. VI. 17.

## 26:54
Vers. 54. How then] If this arrest, and the things that are to follow it, were to be hindered in any way.

The scriptures that thus it must happen] Isaiah chap. LIII. 8. מעצר ומשפט לקח where מ as often, denotes the efficient cause, so that the sense may be, that Christ was taken from the living through captivity and judgment.

This explanation is to be observed against the distortion of the Prophetic passage to Jeremiah, concerning which we spoke at Is. LIII. 8.

Latin:

Vers. 54. Πῶς ὖν] Si prehensio hæc, & quæ eam secutura sunt, impediatur quocunque modo.

Αἱ γραφαὶ ὅτι ὕτω δεῖ γενέως] Esaias cap. LIII. 8. מעצר ומשפט לקח ubi מ ut sæpe, causam efficientem deno- tat, ut sensus sit, Christum è vivis ereptum per captivitatem & judicium.

Explicatio hæc observanda contra detorsio- nem loci Prophetici ad Jeremiam, de qua ad Es. LIII. 8. diximus.

## 26:55
Vers. 55. To the crowds] But especially to the leaders of the crowds, namely the commanders, to whom others were also present from the number of the chief Priests and Senators, so that the whole matter might be conducted with greater appearance. See Luke. That 'to you' pertains to the Jews.

Μετὰ ξύλων] ῥοπάλων which are מַקְלוֹת in Hebrew, as in Prov. XXV. 18.

Καὶ ἐκ ἐκρατήσατέ με] By divine providence, of course, when this seemed able to be done both easily and without noise, He restrained what now by the same most wise counsel He permits. Thus Luke.

Latin:

Vers. 55. Τοῖς ὄχλοις] Sed præcipue ducibus τῶν ὀχλῶν, nimirum στρατηγοῖς, quibus & alii aderant è Sacerdotum pri- mariorum & è Senatorum numero, quo res tota majori specie ageretur. Lucam vide. Ad Iudæos pertinet illud πρὸς ὑμᾶς.

Μετὰ ξύλων] ῥοπάλων quæ מַקְלוֹת Hebræis ut Prov. XXV. 18.

Καὶ ἐκ ἐκρατήσατέ με] Divina scilicet providentia, cum hoc & facile & sine strepitu fieri posse videretur, inhi- bente quod nunc eadem sapientissimo consilio permittit. Ita Lucas.

## 26:56
Vers. 56. ἵνα πληρωθῶσιν αἱ γραφαὶ τῶν προφητῶν] metonymy: the sense is: that the decree of the Father, previously announced through Isaiah, Daniel, and others, might have its outcome.

τότε οἱ μαθηταὶ πάντες ἀφέντες ἀυτὸν ἔφυγον] Some sooner, some a little later. For it seems that after Peter and Matthew, John remained for some time with a few others, and at that time occurred those things which he narrates particularly in ch. XVIII. 4 and following. For certainly the story of the wounding of Malchus is placed by John by way of retrocession.

If Grotius infers this from the fact that John reports that those who wished to apprehend Him were struck to the ground by the word of Christ, we rightly find the nerve of the consequence lacking. For those things were done before the flight of the disciples. Nor is it clear by any document that Matthew remained for some time: for the Evangelists declare that all fled immediately, except Peter and the disciple wrapped in a linen cloth. In the Johannine account also, the order has been duly observed.

II. Proceedings in the leading of Jesus to the Sanhedrin, and in the Sanhedrin.

Latin:

Vers. 56. ἵνα πληρωθῶσιν αἱ γραφαὶ τῶν προφητῶν] μετω- νυμία: sensus est: ut exitum habeat decretum Patris pri- dem enunciatum per Esaiam, Danielem, atque alios.

τότε οἱ μαθηταὶ πάντες ἀφέντες ἀυτὸν ἔφυγον] Alii citius: alii serius paulo. Videtur enim post Petrum & Matthæum aliquamdiu substitisse cum aliquot aliis Johannes, atque eo tempore accidisse ea quæ ille peculiariter narrat c. XIIX. 4. & deinceps. Nam certe vulnerati Malchi historia à Jo- hanne per retrocessum posita est.

Id si ex eo colligit Grotius, quod Johannes referat, in terram verbo Christi percussos esse, qui eum apprehendere volebant, nervum con- sequentiæ merito desideramus. Nam illa ante fugam discipulorum gesta sunt. Nec quod Mat- thæus aliquamdiu substiterit, ullo documento li- quet: omnes enim actutum aufugisse, præter Pe- trum & discipulum sindone amictum perhibent Evangelistæ. In Johannea etiam relatione ordo rite observatus est.

II. Acta in deductione Iesu ad Synedrium, & in Synedrio.

## 26:57
Vers. 57. πρὸς Καϊάφαν τὸν ἀρχιερέα] Who is therefore to be understood whenever the name of high priest is placed nakedly in John. For the others omit the leading of Christ to Annas, because nothing notable was done there: Christ seems only to have been detained there while the council was being gathered at Caiaphas'. But what John narrates in verse 24 is to be interpreted by way of retrocession, just like that other matter of which we have already spoken. But more fully on this matter at the place itself.

ὅπε οἱ γραμματεῖς καὶ οἱ πρεσβύτεροι] Because of their learning, the scribes are placed first, although otherwise the dignity of the elders was greater. And the order of the high priests is passed over in silence, because it was sufficiently understood from the person of Caiaphas. But soon he names them in verse 59 and expresses the proper name of the assembly, the Sanhedrin. In those times there was no נָשִׂיא other than the High Priest. Therefore, what had been said about the Nasi, Paul adapts to the High Priest in Acts XXIII. 5. For the Greeks translate נָשִׂיא as ruler: as can be seen in Levit. IV. 22, Exod. XXII. 28. Therefore the High Priest, like this Caiaphas, was accustomed to convene the Sanhedrin, which Josephus narrates concerning Ananus. Otherwise, if there had been another ruler besides the High Priest, as formerly, it would have been his place to convene the council. But we have dealt with this matter more fully elsewhere. The senators, however, sat in some portico, into which a view was given in the courtyard, that is, to those standing in the open air. In which respect Peter, who was in the open air, is said to have stood below, Mark XIV. 66.

Latin:

Vers. 57. πρὸς Καϊάφαν τὸν ἀρχιερέα] Qui proinde intel- ligendus quoties nomen ἀρχιερέως apud Johannem nude ponitur. Nam per ductionem Christi ad Annam omit- tunt cæteri, quia nihil ibi insigne gestum: tantum deten- tus ibi Christus videtur, dum apud Cajapham concilium co- gitur. Quod autem Johannes commate 24. narrat, per re- trocessum itidem, ut alterum illud de quo jam diximus, in- terpretandum est. Sed hac de re ad ipsum plenius.

ὅπε οἱ γραμματεῖς καὶ οἱ πρεσβύτεροι] Ob eruditionem præponuntur οἱ γραμματεῖς, cum alioqui πρεσβυτέρων ma- jor esset dignitas. Et reticetur ordo τῶν ἀρχιερέων, quia is ex Cajaphæ persona satis dabatur intelligi. At mox eos no- minat commate 59. & nomen confessus proprium exprimit συνέδριον. Illis temporibus nullus fuit נָשִׂיא alius à Ponti- fice Maximo. Itaque quod dictum erat περὶ τῶ Νασὶ, Pau- lus Pontifici Maximo aptat Actor. XXIII. 5. Nam נָשִׂיא Græci vertunt ἄρχοντα: ut videre est Levit. IV. 22. Exod. XXII. 28. Itaque Pontifex Maximus, ut hic Cajaphas, so- lebat καθίζειν συνέδριον, quod de Anano narrat Josephus. A- lioqui si alius fuisset Ἄρχων à Pontifice Maximo, ut olim, i- psius fuisset concilium cogere. Sed de hac re egimus alibi plenius. Consederunt autem Senatores in porticu aliqua, in quam prospectus dabatur ἐν τῇ ἀυλῇ, id est, sub dio con- sistentibus. Quo respectu Petrus, qui sub dio erat, dicitur constitisse κάτω Marc. XIV. 66.

## 26:59
Vers. 59. ἐζήτουν ψευδομαρτυρίαν] Not that they had leisure to seek out witnesses while sitting there, but that they instituted the inquiry, which the Greeks call an anakrisis, in such a way that they tried by all means to elicit something from the witnesses that would be valid for condemning Jesus. For that kind of inquiry, since it consists in the office and religion of a judge, provides a great opportunity for wicked men against the innocent. For witnesses, moved by authority and thanks, for the most part bend their words to where they see themselves being drawn by the inquisitor. And this they did, to whom the law had severely commanded the punishment of such a crime, Deut. XIX. 19. See Ps. XXVII. 11 and the whole of XXXV.

Latin:

Vers. 59. ἐζήτουν ψευδομαρτυρίαν] Non quod illis consi- dentibus conquirere testes vacaret, sed quod inquisitio- nem, quam ἀνάκρισιν Græci vocant, ita instituerent, ut omni- no à testibus conarentur aliquid elicere, quod ad damnan- dum Jesum valeret. Nam id genus inquisitiones, cum in officio ac religione judicis consistant, magnam præbent oc- casionem improbis hominibus adversum innocentes. Te- stes enim auctoritate & gratia permoti plerumque dicta sua eo flectunt, quo trahi se vident à quæsitore. Et hoc illi fecere, quibus lex talis criminis ultionem severe impera- verat, Deut. XIX. 19. Vide Ps. XXVII. 11. & XXXV. tot.

## 26:60
Vers. 60. ἐχ εὖρον] However eagerly they were set against Jesus, they nevertheless brought forward nothing of such a kind that could seem capital. For that phrase 'so that they might put him to death' must be repeated from the common sense, through the Roman governor, of course, for the persuading of whom this whole scene was constructed.

δύο] For the Hebrew law did not admit a single testimony in any case, Deut. XIX. 15.

False witnesses] They are deservedly so called because of the corrupted words of Christ. For Christ had not said 'I am able to destroy the temple' but 'Destroy this temple.' In which there is much difference. It was a matter of controversy among the Jews whether it was permitted to anyone to utter savage prophecies against the temple. For in Jeremiah the priests and prophets judged this to be a capital offense, while the nobles thought otherwise: and in the accusation of Stephen the first point is: 'He does not cease to speak blasphemous words against this holy place.'

Latin:

Vers. 60. ἐχ εὖρον] Utcunque cupide adversus Jesum restabantur, nihil tamen tale afferebant, quod capital posset videri. Repetendum enim ἀπὸ τῶ κοινῶ illud ὅπως ἀυτὸν θανατώσωσι, per præsidem Romanum scilicet, cui persua- dendo tota hæc scena struebatur.

δύο] Nam singulare testimonium nullo casu admittebat lex Hebræa Deut. XIX. 15.

Ψευδομάρτυρες] Merito ita appellantur ob depravata Christi verba. Neque enim dixerat Christus δύναμαι κατα- λῦσαι τὸν ναὸν sed λύσατε τὸν ναὸν τῦτον. In quo multum est discriminis. Controversum erat apud Judæos ac cuiquam liceret sæva vaticinia contra templum proferre. Nam in Je- remia id capital judicabant Sacerdotes & Prophetæ, contra censentibus proceribus: Et in Stephani accusatione primum est: ἐ παύεται ῥήματα βλάσφημα λαλῶν κατὰ τῶ τόπε ἁγίε.

## 26:61
Verse 61. 'In three days'] A brief locution of the Hellenists for 'three days having passed.' Thus 'after seven years' in Deut. 15:1. Luke, Acts 24:17, 'after more years.' See what is below in chapter 27:63.

We have treated of the sense and fulfillment of these words in the Biblical Chronicle, under the faith of the same.

Latin:

Vers. 61. διὰ τριῶν ἡμερῶν] Brevis locutio Hellenistarum pro διαγενομένων τριῶν ἡμερῶν. Ita δι ἑπτὰ ἐτῶν Deut. XV. 1. Luc. Actor. XXIV. 17. δι ἐτῶν δὲ πλειόνων. Vide quæ in- fra cap. XXVII. 63.

De sensu & complemento horum verborum in Chronico Biblico egimus, sub fidem ejus- dem.

## 26:62
Verse 62. 'Do you answer nothing?' Caiaphas saw that not even that act, which most pertained to the hatred of Christ, was sufficient for condemnation: which Mark said 'their testimony was not equal.' For he was prophesying no evil against the Temple, even if he says he will destroy it if he also adds that he will restore it: nor was a promise, however vain, to be punished by death. Therefore, distrusting the testimonies of others, he seeks to elicit from his own mouth something that might burden him. For he hoped that in a long defense something easily 'liable to accusation' would be found.

Latin:

Vers. 62. οὐδὲν ἀποκρίνῃ] Videbat Cajaphas ne illud qui- dem factum quod maxime ad invidiam Christi pertinebat sufficere ad damnationem: quod Marcus dixit ἴση αὐτῶν ἡ μαρ- τυρία οὐκ ἦσαν. Nihil enim mali Templo ominabatur, etiam qui demoliturum se dicit si & restituturum se addat: ne- que pollicitatio, utcunque vana, capite erat luenda. Ita- que testimoniis aliorum diffisus, quærit ex ipsius ore ali- quid elicere quod ipsum oneret. Sperabat enim in prolixa defensione facile aliquid repertum iri ἐνδιάβλητον.

## 26:63
Verse 63. 'He was silent'] Tacitus said somewhere: 'It did not matter to those killing him what he said.' And Christ knew that he was being provoked to a defense only so that a crime might be elicited from the defense: and that the things which had been objected by the witnesses were of such a kind that there was no need to refute them. Therefore Origen well says against Celsus: 'The silence of him (Jesus) under the scourges and many torments showed forth patience and endurance more than the speech of anyone who happens to be in such circumstances.' Maximus Tyrius in his dissertation: 'Whether Socrates did well by not defending himself,' has many things which you might more justly adapt to this our cause: 'For the sake of whom would he have defended himself? As before judges? But they were unjust. As before wise men? But they were wicked. As before kindly men? But they were angry. As before equals? But they were most unlike.' Item: 'For witnesses and faith and proof and evidence and tortures and other such things demonstrate other defenses, so that what is hidden may for a time be detected in court. But the proof of virtue and nobility is one: reverence for these things; if this is absent then, what need was there for speech? But also this: or who is the most shameful person standing in court, humble and begging and gathering the hope of living from others? For this was the form of the defense; which one ought to say, nothing humble or cringing or submissive, but something free and worthy of philosophy; you are not telling me a defense, but the tension and inflammation of anger.' To this also pertains that saying of Euripides: 'Silence is the answer for the wise.' Philo on the embassy: 'For it is possible in some way to defend oneself even through silence.' See Isaiah 53:7 and Acts 8:32.

I adjure you] 'To adjure' or 'to swear' in Hebrew 'hishbia' is sometimes to compel by an oath, as Gen. 24:3, ch. 50:6, 25, Exod. 13:19, Josh. 2:10, Ezra 10:5, in which history Josephus also uses this verb: but sometimes it is to instill religion into the mind of someone by a grave adjuration through the divine name, which the ancient Latins called 'to beseech': as Num. 5:19, Josh. 7:26, 1 Sam. 14:27, 28, 1 Kings 2:43, Cant. 5:9, which sense is proper to this place, as also in Mark ch. 5:7. Judges were accustomed to employ such an 'adjuration' so that they might extract testimony from witnesses or a confession from the accused. Concerning witnesses, the law exists in Lev. 5:1, where the witness is pronounced liable to guilt who keeps silent the truth after he has heard the 'voice of adjuration.' For that is the true meaning of that law, which has been wrongly understood by many. There were, however, certain solemn formulas of such 'adjurations' used in trials: 'I adjure you that you do not hide.' 1 Kings 22:16, 2 Chron. 18:15. In Greek 'I adjure you that you speak the truth to me in the name of the Lord.' Or thus: 'Give now glory to the Lord' Josh. 7:19, where in Greek it is 'Give glory to God,' which very formula exists in John ch. 9:24.

If you are the Christ, the Son of God] Above in ch. 14:33 we noted that even among the Jews that expected Messiah was accustomed to be called the Son of God from Psalm 2. Therefore also here in Luke, for the same thing, is placed first 'If you are the Christ,' then 'You are the Son of God.'

These are not synonyms, nor are they simply interchanged: which was shown against the Socinians in the Anti-Crellius. And so it is established from this only that the same one is the Son of God who is also the Christ: not that the same thing is denoted by both words.

Latin:

Vers. 63. ἐσιώπα] Dixit alicubi Tacitus: Non intererat occidentium quid diceret. Et Christus sciebat ad defensio- nem se prolici tantum, ut ex defensione crimen eliceretur: quæ vero à testibus objecta erant esse ejusmodi, ut refellere ea opus non esset. Bene ergo Origenes adversus Celsum: ἡ παρὰ ταῖς μάστιξι καὶ ταῖς πολλαῖς αἰκίαις ἀυτῶ (Ἰησῦ) σιωπὴ παντὸς τῦ εἰ ἵλασιν ἐι περιστάσεσι τυγχάνοντος φθεγξαμένε μᾶλλον ἐνέδειξε καρτερίαν καὶ ὑπομονήν. Maximus Tyrius in dissertatione: εἰ καλῶς ἐποίησε Σωκράτης μὴ ἀπολογησάμε- νος, multa habet quæ ad nostram hanc causam justius ac- commodes: Τίνων δ᾽ ἂν καὶ ἕνεκα ἀπελογήσατο ἐπ᾿ ἐκείνων ὡς ἐπὶ δικαστῶν; ἀλλὰ ἀδίκων· ὡς ἐπὶ φρονίμων; ἀλλὰ μοχθηρῶν· ὡς ἐπὶ ἐυμενῶν; ἀλλὰ οἱ ὀργίζοντο. ὡς ἐπὶ ἐμοίων; ἀλλὰ πτω- μοιότατοι. Item: Τὰς μὲν γὰρ ἄλλας ἀπολογίας μάρτυρες ἀ- ποφαίνεσι καὶ πίστις καὶ ἔλεγχος καὶ τεκμήρια καὶ βάσανοι καὶ ἄλλα τοιαῦτα ἵνα τὸ ἀφανὲς τίως ἐπὶ δικαστηρίῳ φωραθῇ. ἀρετῆς δὲ καὶ καλοκαγαθίας ὁ ἔλεγχος εἷς ἡ πρὸς ταῦτα αἰδώς· ἧς εἰ ἐξηλλα- μένης τότε, τί ἔδει λόγω. Sed & hoc: ἦ τίς αἰσχιστο ἐςᾶτα ἐν δικαστηρίῳ ταπεινὸν καὶ ἐπεηχότα καὶ τὴν ἐλπίδα τῶ ζῆν ἐρανιζό- μενον παρ᾽ ἄλλων; τῦτο γάρ πε τῆς ἀπολογίας τὸ σχῆμα ἦν· ὃ λέγειν ἐχρῆν ταπεινὸν μὲν ὐδὲν ὔτε ἐκτροὸς, ὔτε ὑφειμένον, ἀλλ᾽ ἐλευθερόν τι καὶ ἄξιον φιλοσοφίας; ἐκ ἀπολογίαν μοι λέ- γεις, ἀλλ᾽ ὀργῆς ξυντώσιν καὶ φλεγμονήν. Huc & Euripidis illud pertinet: Σιωπὴ τοῖς σοφοῖς ἀπόκρισις. Philo de lega- tione: ἔσι γάρ πως κὴ δι ἡσυχίας ἀπολογεῖσθ. Vide Esaiam LIII. 7. & Act. VIII. 32.

ἐξορκίζω σε] ἐξορκίζειν aut ὁρκίζειν Hebraice השביע mo- do est jurejurando adigere, ut Gen. XXIV. 3. cap. L. 6. 25. Exod. XIII. 19. Jos. II. 10. Esdr. X. 5. in qua historia & Jo- sephus hoc verbo utitur: interdum vero gravi obtestatione per nomen divinum religionem alicujus animo injicere, quod Latini veteres dicebant obsecrare: ut Num. V. 19. Jos. VII. 26. 1. Sam. XIV. 27. 28. 1. Reg. II. 43. Cant. V. 9. qui sensus huic loco est proprius, ut & apud Marcum c. V. 7. So- lebant Judices talem ὀρκισμὸν adhibere ut aut testibus testi- monium aut reis confessionem exprimerent. De testibus lex extat Lev. V. 1. ubi culpæ obnoxius pronuntiatur testis, qui verum subticet postquam audierit φωνὴν ὁρκισμῶ קול אלה. Ea enim vera est legis illius à multis perperam intellectæ sen- tentia. Erant autem formulæ quædam solennes talium ὀρ- κισμῶν in judiciis usitatæ: אני משבעך אשר לא תחבד 1. אוריך אמת בשם יהוה Reg. XXII. 16. 2. Par. XIIX. 15. Græce ἐγώ ὁρκίζω σε ὅπως λαλήσης πρὸς ἐμὲ ἀλήθειαν ἐν ὀ- νόματι κυρίω. Vel sic: שים נא כבוד ליהוה Jos. VII. 19. ubi Græce est δὸς δόξαν τῷ θεῷ, quæ ipsa formula extat apud Johannem cap. IX. 24.

εἰ σὺ εἶ, ὁ χριστὸς ὁ ὑὸς τῦ θεῦ] Supra cap. XIV. 33. notavi- mus etiam apud Judæos exspectatum illum Messiam vocari solitum Dei Filium ex Psalmo II. itaque & hic apud Lucam pro eodem ponitur primum εἰ σὺ εἶ ὁ χρισός: deinde σὺ εἶ ὁ ὁ ὑὸς τῦ θεῦ.

Non sunt hæc Synonyma, nec simpliciter inter se permutantur: quod contra Socinianos in Anti- Crellio ostensum. Adeoque id solum hinc con- stat, eundem esse Filium Dei, qui & Christus: non idem utraque voce notari.

## 26:64
Verse 64. 'You have said it'] Since he had previously said that they were not questioning rightly, who would neither believe him if he affirmed it, nor answer to the arguments he was about to bring: therefore it is 'I will ask' in Luke; with the Pontiff urging, at length he now gave his profession. For the many circumstances persuade me entirely that this is the same assembly of which it is treated here as that which Luke describes after the history concerning Peter is completed, because he preferred to weave that from beginning to end rather than to deliver it interrupted. But that 'when it was day' in Luke is when the day was approaching, and 'the eldership was gathered,' a Senate was being held: for the meeting was protracted until the day, with no adjournment made.

But others distinguish these meetings, and among our own, B. Gerhard in ch. 6 and 7 of the Harmony of the Passion, and not without reason: just as in the Harmony

of the Evangelists we show. For the one was made in the morning, which Matthew also reports in chapter XXVII. 1. as distinct. But here is held a continuation of the nocturnal acts. For what he had confessed by night, that they heard subsequently also in the morning council from Jesus: and thus at last, with the confession repeated, they sent him to Pilate, as one recognized anew as guilty of death. Nor indeed do those words ὡς ἐγένετο ἡμέρα : & συνήχθη τὸ πρεσβυτέριον grant place to the opinion of Grotius: therefore he had to twist them into this meaning, that the former does not signify what the words imply, when it was day, but when day was approaching: nor is the latter to be taken κτ' πόδα, the presbytery convened or was gathered, but a Senate was being held, that is, they were taking counsel, by which is not announced a new assembly instituted at the beginning of another day, but a new consultation in the nocturnal Sanhedrin. Which is truly not to interpret, but to pervert Scripture.

πλὴν λέγω] That is, although you do not believe me when I affirm that I am Christ.

καθήμενον ἐκ δεξιῶν τῆς δυνάμεως] Among the names of God the Hebrews recount הגבורה which is δύναμις: Luke here said δυνάμεως τοῦ θεοῦ. What is brought from Tobias I do not think pertains here. For the more received and better reading has τῇ βαάλ τῇ δαμάλει. Nor were the Hebrews accustomed to decorate the God of the true God with the titles of the gods of the nations. But what Christ says here, that the Jews will see themselves sitting at the right hand of God, I think should be referred to the day of the mission of the Holy Spirit, which was the most certain indication of the session at the right hand, as Peter teaches us in Acts II. 33, although if anyone adds the admirable progress of the Evangelical preaching, I will not gainsay it. That ἀπ' ἄρτι, which in Luke is ἀπὸ τοῦ νῦν, seems to favor the interpretation: which seem to note a thing now about to happen.

καὶ ἐρχόμενον ἐπὶ τῶν νεφελῶν τοῦ ὐρανοῦ] Above we said that this can also be understood of the power of Christ through the Gospel, according to that which is in Daniel and elsewhere: or also of the punishments which Christ caused to be inflicted upon the Jewish people, because a descent in a cloud is accustomed to signify wrath and vengeance, as Maimonides noted. Nevertheless, since Christ is also to descend in a visible manner in a cloud to judgment, just as he ascended in a cloud, nothing prevents referring these things to that advent: by which they will be compelled to acknowledge him who, from the sign of the sent Spirit, did not wish to acknowledge his majesty.

Latin:

Vers. 64. σὺ εἶπας] Cum prius dixisset non recte eos interrogare qui neque affirmanti sibi essent credituri, ne- que responsuri ad argumenta quæ esset allaturus: ide- nim est ἐρωτήσω apud Lucam: urgente Pontifice tandem jam edidit professionem. Omnino enim suadent mihi circumstantiæ plurimæ eundem esse conventum de quo hic agitur cum eo quem Lucas describit post historiam de Petro absolutam, quia eam ab initio ad finem pertexere quam interruptam tradere malebat. Illud autem ὡς ἐγέ- νετο ἡμέρα apud Lucam est tum dies adventaret, & συνήχθη τὸ πρεσβυτέριον Senatus habebatur: nam ad diem usque protractus est cœtus, nulla facta discessione.

At distinguunt alii hos conventus, & è nostris B. Gerhardus cap. VI. & VII. Harmon. de passione, nec id immerito: quemadmodum in Harmonia

Evangelistarum oftendimus. Alter enim mane factus est, quem refert quoque Matthæus cap. XXVII. 1. ceu distinctum. Hic vero continuatio actuum nocturnorum habetur. Nam quod con- fessus noctu erat, id deinceps etiam in matutino concilio ex Jesu audiebant: atque ita demum re- petita confessione ipsum ad Pilatum mittebant, ceu reum mortis denuo agnitum. Neque vero opinioni Grotii locum concedunt illa ὡς ἐγένετο ἡμέρα : & συνήχθη τὸ πρεσβυτέριον: ideo ea in hanc sententiam detorquere necessum habuit, ut prius non significet quod verba inferunt, cum dies esset, sed cum adventaret dies: nec posterius κτ' πόδα accipiendum sit, convenit vel congrega- tum est presbyterium, sed Senatus habebatur, id est consilium capiebant, quo non novus indice- tur conventus alterius diei initio institutus, sed nova in nocturno Synedrio consultatio. Quod vero non est interpretari, sed pervertere Scri- pturam.

πλὴν λέγω] Id est, quamquam mihi Christum me assir- manti non creditis.

καθήμενον ἐκ δεξιῶν τῆς δυνάμεως] Inter nomina Dei re- censent Hebræi הגבורה quod est δύναμις: Lucas hic dixit δυνάμεως τοῦ θεοῦ. Ex Tobia quod affertur huc perti- nere non arbitror. Nam receptior & melior lectio habet τῇ βαάλ τῇ δαμάλει. Neque solebant Hebræi gentium Deus Dei veri indigetamentis decorare. Quod autem hic Christus dicit fore ut Judæi se videant sedentem ad Dei dexteram, referendum arbitror ad diem missionis Spiritus S. quod certissimum erat indicium sessionis ad dexteram, ut nos docet Petrus Actor. II. 33. quanquam si quis adjun- gat admirabilem profectum Evangelicæ prædicationis, non refragabor. Favere interpretationi videtur illud ἀπ' ἄρτι, quod Lucæ est ἀπὸ τοῦ νῦν: quæ rem jamjam futuram videntur notare.

καὶ ἐρχόμενον ἐπὶ τῶν νεφελῶν τοῦ ὐρανοῦ] Supra diximus pos- se hoc etiam de virtute Christi per Evangelium intelligi, juxta id quod in Daniele est & alibi: aut etiam de pœnis quas Christus infligi curavit populo Judaico, quia descen- sus in nube iram ac vindictam solet significare, ut Mai- monides annotavit. Attamen cum visibili etiam modo in nube descensurus sit Christus ad judicium, sicut in nu- be ascendit, nihil prohibet ad eum adventum hæc refer- re: quo cogentur eum agnoscere qui ex signo missi Spi- ritus agnoscere ejus majestatem noluerunt.

## 26:65
Vers. 65. διέῤῥηξε τὰ ἱμάτια ἀυτοῦ] Which the Jews were accustomed to do, as often as they heard words contumelious against God, especially uttered by a Hebrew man: Whence the teachers of the Jews gather that Rabshakeh was a Jew, who had defected to ἀποφυλισμὸν, because upon hearing his words the Jerusalemites tore their garment, 2 Kings XIX. They err who think it was not permitted for the High Priest in any case to tear his garment. For the prohibition which exists twice in Leviticus pertains to a funeral cause, as the antecedents and consequents show. Otherwise, in public mourning, even the High Priest used to rend his garments. That is clear in 1 Maccabees XI. 71, where Jonathan the High Priest, after the slaughter received in Kadesh of Galilee, is narrated to have διαῤῥῆξαι τὰ ἱμάτια ἀυτοῦ. Josephus also in the War II, the powerful ones with the chief priests tore their garments. And afterwards: τοὺς δὲ ἀρχιερεῖς ἀυτοὺς ἦν ἰδεῖν καταμωμένους μὲν τῆς κεφαλῆς κόνιν, γυμνοὺς δὲ τὰ στέρνα τῶν ἐσθήτων περιεῤῥηγμένων. Even the King of the Persians in mourning tears his garment in Aeschylus' Persians, but the teachers of the Hebrews note that it was proper to the High Priest that he would tear the garment from the lower part, whereas others were accustomed to do so from the upper.

λέγων ὅτι ἐβλασφήμησε] He calls it blasphemy that Jesus professed himself to be Christ. And indeed it was, had Christ not been. For he who falsely arrogates that power to himself is contumelious against God. But this ought to have been inquired into: whether or not the prophecies agreed upon him: whether or not he had proved by most manifest miracles that he was he. These things they passed over and took it as manifest that Jesus could not be Christ, relying on futile arguments: such as that he was believed to be born at Nazareth, John I. 46, chapter VII. 52, because they thought his paternal and maternal origin was entirely known: chapter VII. 27. Especially, however, because he had exercised the carpenter's trade, and carried with him no external apparatus: above chapter XIII. 55, Mark VI. v. 3.

Latin:

Vers. 65. διέῤῥηξε τὰ ἱμάτια ἀυτοῦ] Quod facere judæi so- lebant, quoties verba audirent in Deum contumeliosa, præ- sertim prolata ab homine Hebræo: Unde Rabsacen fuis- se Judæum, qui ad ἀποφυλισμὸν defecerae, colligunt Ju- dæorum magistri, quia verbis ejus auditis Hierofolymitæ vestem lacerant, 2. Reg. XIX. Errant qui putant Ponti- fici Maximo non licuisse ullo casu vestem lacerare. Nam interdictum quod in Levitico bis exstat ad causam fune- brem pertinet, ut antecedentia & consequentia osten- dunt. Alioqui in luctu publico etiam Pontifex Maximus discindebat vestimenta. Clarum id 1. Mact. XI. 71. ubi Jonathan Pontifex Maximus post cladem acceptam in Ca- des Galilææ narratur διαῤῥῆξαι τὰ ἱμάτια ἀυτοῦ. Josephus quoque ἁλώσεως ΙΙ. οἱ δυνατοὶ σὺν τοῖς ἀρχιερεῦσι τὰς ἐσθῆ- τας περιεῤῥήξαντο. Et postea: τοὺς δὲ ἀρχιερεῖς ἀυτοὺς ἦν ἰδεῖν καταμωμένους μὲν τῆς κεφαλῆς κόνιν, γυμνοὺς δὲ τὰ στέρνα τῶν ἐσθήτων περιεῤῥηγμένων. Etiam Rex Persarum in luctu ve- stem scindit apud Æschylum Persis, sed notant Hebræo- rum magistri maximo Pontifici id fuisse proprium, quod vestem ab inferna parte laceraret, cum à superna alii sole- rent.

λέγων ὅτι ἐβλασφήμησε] Βλασφημίαν vocat quod Jesus se Christum profiterecur. Et sane erat, ni Christus fuis- set. Nam qui sibi eam potestatem falso arrogat, in Deuna est contumeliosus. At hoc quæsitum oportuit, an non in ipsum vaticinia congruerent: an non apercissimis mira- culis probasset se eum esse. His illi præteritis pro manife- sto sumunt Jesum, Christum esse non posse, futilibus nixi argumentis: ut quod Nazaretæ natus crederetur Joh. I. 46. cap. VII. 52. quod originem ejus paternam maternam- que notam omnino arbitrarentur: cap. VII. 27. Præci- pue vero quod fabrilem artem exercuisset, nihilque ex- terni apparatus secum ferret: supra cap. XIII. 55. Marc. VI. v. 3.

## 26:66
Vers. 66. Τί ὑμῖν δοκεῖ] As the prince of the Senate seeks opinions.

Οἱ δὲ ἀποκριθέντες εἶπον] The order is said to have done what the greater part did: nay, even all are said to have done it, as here in Mark. For that is used in senatorial decrees, just as in judgments. For there is no doubt that Nicodemus dissented: if indeed he was present: concerning Joseph of Arimathea we shall see elsewhere.

Ἔνοχος θανάτου ἐστί] בֶּן־מָוֶת as 2 Sam. XII. 5. Thus the Hebrew judges were accustomed to pronounce while capital judgments were in their power. With capital judgments removed, which happened after Judea was confiscated by Augustus (for previously, by the favor of Herod, some species of judgments had remained), although they could not carry out the sentence with effect, they nevertheless retained the old formula: the force of which was such that he concerning whom it was so pronounced was considered among all Jews worthy of death, that is, sacred and intestable, and finally, nothing was illicit against him. By which prejudice the people, incited, often sought punishments through force and tumult, although they were forbidden to do so by Roman laws. But this prejudice pertained to Jesus in such a way that the Jewish senators could, without prejudice to their religion, accuse Jesus before a profane judge and demand his execution, as one who no longer touched them by any bond, and had lost all the privileges of a Jewish man.

Latin:

Vers. 66. Τί ὑμῖν δοκεῖ] Ut princeps Senatus sententias exquirit.

Οἱ δὲ ἀποκριθέντες εἶπον] Ordo fecisse dicitur quod fecit pars major: imo & omnes id fecisse dicuntur, ut hic apud Marcum. Id enim ut in senatusconsultis, ita & in judiciis usurpatur. Nam Nicodemum dissensisse non dubium est: si tamen adfuit: De Josepho Arimatheensi alibi vi- debimus.

Ἔνοχος θανάτου ἐστί] בֶּן־מָוֶת ut 2. Sam. XII. 5. Ita pronunciare solebant judices Hebræi dum capitalia judicia penes ipsos erant. Ablatis capitalibus judiciis, quod post confiscatam ab Augusto Judæam factum est (nam antea Herodis beneficio manserat aliqua judiciorum species) quanquam cum effectu sententiam proferre non poterant, veterem tamen formulam retinebant: cujus ea vis erat, ut de quo ita pronuntiatum esset; is apud Judæos omnes morte dignus, id est sacer atque intestabilis haberetur, in eum denique nihil esset illicitum. Quo præjudicio po- pulus concitatus sæpe per vim ac tumultum pœnas expeti- vit, quanquam Romanis legibus id facere vetabatur. Perti- nebat autem hoc πρόκριμα in Jesum eo, ut scilicet senato- res Judæi possent salva religione Jesum accusare apud pro- fanum judicem ejusque supplicium flagitare, velut qui nul- la amplius necessitudine ipsos attingeret, & omnia homi- nis Judæi προνόμια amisisset.

## 26:67
Vers. 67. τότε] After that pronouncement, of course: upon hearing which, the Jewish officers began to vex Jesus as a man devoted to destruction, with every kind of mockery and contumely.

ἐνέπτυσαν εἰς τὸ πρόσωπον αὐτᾶ] A frequent sign of contempt among the Hebrews, Num. V. 16. What Isaiah says of himself, in a figuratively fashioned manner of speaking, ch. L. 5, that is fulfilled in Christ κατὰ τὴν τᾶ ῥητᾶ ἀκρίβειαν (according to the strictness of the word).

That this was predicted of Christ, not of Isaiah, Isa. L. 5, we have so asserted in the vindications of that passage that we have no need to add anything here. The completion, therefore, of that prediction is exhibited in this place.

Ἐκολάφισαν] κολαφίζειν, as the Greek scholiasts interpret it, is παίειν ἐπὶ κόῤῥης (to strike on the cheek), namely with a clenched fist: nor do Origen and Theophylact understand it otherwise here. Terence: 'Colaphis tuber est totum caput' (The whole head is a lump from blows). How insulting that kind of beating was considered can be understood from Demosthenes' oration against Midias, whose words the Roman jurists cite in the Digest, title 'De poenis'.

Ἐῤῥάπισαν] I do not think it should be doubted that by ῥαπίσματα (slaps) are meant blows with the palm. For so also the interpreter uses that word above, ch. V. 39. To which add what a most learned man has annotated for the understanding of this word from the Glossary, the jurists, the Greeks, and Sedulius. Add the Syriac of Mark XIV. 65. Nor is ῥαπίσμασι ἔβαλον in Mark anything else. For βάλλειν is to strike, to assail. Ignatius, referring to this history of Christ to the Trallians, says: ἐπὶ κόῤῥης ἐῤῥαπίσθη (he was slapped on the cheek): just as Nazianzenus also speaks, where κόῤῥη signifies the cheek, not the temples as it does elsewhere. Compare with the history of this passage and those things which Luke has, ch. XXII. 64, the prophecy of Isaiah, ch. L. 6, and ch. LIII. 3, 4, 5, 6, 7.

Latin:

Vers. 67. τότε] Post istam pronuntiationem scilicet: qua audita Judæi ὑπηρέται Jesum ut hominem devotum, omni ludibriorum atque contumeliarum genere vexare cœperunt.

ἐνέπτυσαν εἰς τὸ πρόσωπον αὐτᾶ] Contemtus signum fre- quens apud Hebræos Num. V. 16. Quod de se dicit Esaias, sorte figurato loquendi genere cap. L. 5. id in Christo im- pletum est κατὰ τὴν τᾶ ῥητᾶ ἀκρίβειαν.

De Christo, non de Esaia id prædictum esse, Esa. L. 5. in loci istius vindiciis ita asseruimus, ut nihil addere hic opus habeamus. Complemen- tum ergo istius prædictionis hoc loco exhibe- tur.

Ἐκολάφισαν] κολαφίζειν, ut Græci Scholiastæ interpretan- tur, est παίειν ἐπὶ κόῤῥης, contracto pugno scilicet: neque aliter hic Origenes & Theophylactus. Terentius, Colla- phis tuber est totum caput. Quam contumeliosum id ver- berandi genus habitum sit, ex Demosthenis adversus Mi- diam oratione intelligi datur, cujus verba citant Romani jurisconsulti in Pandecte titulo de pœnis.

Ἐῤῥάπισαν] Per ῥαπίσματα alapas intelligi dubitandum non puto. Nam ita & supra id verbum usurpat hic inter- pres cap. V. 39. Quibus adde quæ ex Glossario, Juris- consultis, Græcis & Sedulio vir eruditissimus ad hujus vocis intellectum annotavit. Adde Syrum Marci XIV. 65. Nec aliud est apud Marcum ῥαπίσμασι ἔβαλον. Nam βάλλειν est ferire, incessere. Ignatius ad Trallianos hanc de Christo historiam referens, ἐπὶ κόῤῥης ἐῤῥαπίσθη inquit: quomodo & Nazianzenus loquitur, ubi κόῤῥη genam significat, non ut alias tempora. Confer cum hujus loci historia & iis quæ Lucas habet c. XXII. 64. vaticinium Esaiæ c. L. 6. & c. LIII. 3.4.5.6.7.

## 26:68
Vers. 68. προφήτευσον] This is because they had blindfolded his eyes, as Mark adds. Now it was the role of prophets not only to predict future events (which the word properly indicates) but also other things which could not be known by natural cognition. Thus also the word μαντεύεσθαι is used by the Greeks. Aristotle, Rhetoric III. XVII, concerning Epimenides the Cretan: 'He did not prophesy about things that were to be, but about things that had happened, yet were unknown.'

Latin:

Vers. 68. προφήτευσον] Hoc ideo quia oculos obvelave- rant ut Marcus addit. Prophetarum autem erat non tan- tum futura prædicere (quod proprie vox indicat) sed & alia quæ naturali cognitione sciri nequibant. Sic & vox μαν- τεύεσθαι Græcis ponitur. Aristoteles III. Rhet. XVII. de Epi- menide Crete: περὶ τῶν ἐσομένων ἐκ ἐμαντεύετο, ἀλλὰ περὶ γεγονότων μὲν, ἀδήλων δέ.

## 26:69
Vers. 69. ἐκάθητο] Now sitting, now rising as is wont to happen: as the comparison teaches.

ἐν τῇ αὐλῇ] Which is the lower part of the house, the courtyard: whence Mark said κάτω (below). In the middle of it, coals were placed in a brazier, as is credible: as we learn from Luke and John.

μία παιδίσκη] A maidservant. Thus this word is taken both elsewhere and in Gal. IV. 22. Now this maidservant was ἡ θυρωρὸς (the doorkeeper), as is in John: see also Acts XII. 13.

Ἦσθα μετὰ] That is, you were of his party. A Hebraism, 2 Kings VI. 16, ch. IX. 32, Rom. VIII. 31. However, what is said affirmatively here does not conflict with what John expresses in the tone of a question. For among the Hebrews, a question with a negation affirms most vehemently.

τᾶ γαλιλαίυ] For the sake of distinction. For the name JESUS was among the most common at that time, as also appears from Josephus. In the same way below, 'Jesus the Nazarene.' Either the ignorance of history of the Jews is amazing, or before our Lord there was another Jesus likewise from Nazareth, whom the Talmudists make a contemporary of Hyrcanus, the son of Simon.

Latin:

Vers. 69. ἐκάθητο] Modo sedens, modo ut fieri solet assurgens: ut collatio docet.

ἐν τῇ αὐλῇ] Quæ pars domus inferior porticu: unde κάτω dixit Marcus. In ejus meditullio prunæ erant in ba- tillo, ut credibile est, positæ: ut ex Luca & Johanne di- scimus.

μία παιδίσκη] Ancilla. Ita vox hæc sumitur tum alibi, tum Gal. IV. 22. Erat autem hæc ancilla ἡ θυρωρὸς janitrix, ut est apud Johannem: vide & Act. XII. 13.

Ἦσθα μετὰ] Id est, fuisti partium ipsius. Hebraismus 2. Reg. VI. 16. c. IX. 32. Rom. VIII. 31. Non pugnat au- tem quod hic affirmate dicitur cum eo quod Johannes ex- primit interrogandi sono. Nam Hebræis interrogatio cum negatione vehementissime affirmat.

τᾶ γαλιλαίυ] Discriminis causa. IESU enim nomen eo tempore erat inter communissima, ut ex Josepho quo- que apparet. Eodem modo infra Ἰησᾶ τᾶ Ναζωραίυ. Aut mira est Judæorum ἀνιστορησία, aut ante Dominum nostrum alter fuit Jesus itidem à Nazaretha, quem Hyrcano Simo- nis filio coævum faciunt Talmuditæ.

## 26:70
Vers. 70. ἑκ οἶδα τί λέγεις] I neither know him, nor do I sufficiently understand what you want: for thus Mark connects this which is in Matthew with that which Luke and John have, undoubtedly at Peter's suggestion.

Latin:

Vers. 70. ἑκ οἶδα τί λέγεις] Neque ipsum novi, neque sa- tis intelligo quid velis: ita enim hoc quod apud Matthæum cum eo quod Lucas & Iohannes habent connectit Marcus, haud dubie Petro suggerente.

## 26:71
Vers. 71. ἐξελθόντα] Preparing to go out. For he did not go out, as the following [verses] show.

πυλῶνα] προαύλιον in Mark: A small open-air space outside the doors; the Syrian also understands it this way here.

ἄλλη] παιδίσκη in Mark, where the article designates not a certain, but an uncertain person, which also occurs often in these and other writers. In Luke it is ἕτερος. But it is common to all languages that the masculine is used ἀνεπικρίτως ἐπικοινῶς, when it does not matter much to know the sex. Therefore ἕτερος is some other person from the group of servants, whether male or female. Thus Plutarch said χαλεπαίνοντ' Ἀπόλλωνι when the discourse was about Thetis. Euripides in the Troades [uses] δύστηνος αἰχμάλωτος regarding Helen. Sopater in a declamation, speaking of a captive woman, [uses] τὸν μηδὲν ἀδικήσαντα: and Laërtius expresses an uncertain person in the masculine gender in the Life of Socrates, whom Plato in the Crito shows to have been a woman: and Cicero in [De] Divinatione I.

κᾀ λέγει αὐτοῖς] Thus the ancient codices and the Syrian: wherefore I think that τοῖς ἐκεῖ is an interpretation preferred by those who did not remember that αὐτοῖς is used by Hellenists in the Hebrew manner even when a noun has not preceded. See what [is said] above in ch. XI. 1.

Latin:

Vers. 71. ἐξελθόντα] Egredi parantem. Neque enim exiit ut sequentia ostendunt.

πυλῶνα] προαύλιον Marco: Subdiale minus extra fores; ita & Syrus hic accipit.

ἄλλη] παιδίσκη Marco, ubi articulus non certam, sed in- certam personam designat, quod & in his & in aliis Scri- ptoribus sæpe occurrit. Apud Lucam est ἕτερος. Sed com- mune est omnium linguarum, ut masculinum usurpetur ἀνεπικρίτως ἐπικοινῶς, quando sexum scire non multum refert. Itaque ἕτερος est alius quidam è servorum grege, seu mas seu femina. Sic Plutarchus dixit χαλεπαίνοντ' Ἀπόλλωνι cum de Thetide sermo esset. Euripides Troadibus δύστη- νος αἰχμάλωτος de Helena. Sopater in declamatione τὸν μηδὲν ἀδικήσαντα loquens de femina captiva: & Laërtius masculino genere exprimit personam incertam in vita So- cratis, quam mulierem fuisse ostendit Plato Critone: & Ci- cero de divinatione I.

κᾀ λέγει αὐτοῖς] Ita Codices antiqui & Syrus: quare illud τοῖς ἐκεῖ putem interpretamentum esse prælatum ab iis qui non meminerant αὐτοῖς Hellenistis more Hebræo dici et- iam ubi nomen non antecessit. Vide quæ supra c. XI. I.

## 26:73
Vers. 73. μετὰ μικρὸν δὲ] After an interval of an hour: or more (for Luke added ὡσεὶ) as much as intervenes between the first and second cock-crowing: for so Mark [says].

Οἱ ἑστῶτες] With Malchus's kinsman leading the way, and the others who were standing together by the fire agreeing: as Mark, Luke, and John teach us.

Ἀληθῶς] Certainly. Thus the Hebrew אָמֵן said elsewhere is accustomed to be translated.

Ἡ λαλία σου] Approaching closer to the Samaritan and Syriac idiom than the speech of the Jerusalemites: by which mark the Gileadites once distinguished the Ephraimites from their own countrymen, Judg. 12. The pronunciation betrayed Peter as a Galilean. Furthermore, Galileans were suspected as being disciples or supporters of Jesus. There was also another piece of evidence from him who thought he remembered having seen Peter in the garden.

Latin:

Vers. 73. μετὰ μικρὸν δὲ] Post horæ intervallum: aut eo amplius (nam ὡσεὶ addidit Lucas) quantum scilicet inter primum & secundum galli cantum intercedit: ita enim Marcus.

Οἱ ἑστῶτες] Malchi cognato præeunte, adstipulantibus cæteris qui una ad ignem astabant: ut docet nos Marcus, Lucas, Iohannes.

Ἀληθῶς] Certe. Ita verti solere Hebræum אָמֵן alibi di- ctum.

Ἡ λαλία σου] Ad Samaritanum & Syriacum idioma pro- pius accedens quam sermo Hierosolymitarum: quali no- ta olim Ephraimitas à suis popularibus dignoscebant Ga- laaditæ Iud. 12. Pronuntiatio Petrum Galilæum ducebat. Porro Galilæi suspecti tanquam Iesu discipuli aut fautores. Accedebat & aliud indicium ab eo qui Petrum à se in horto visum meminisse sibi videbatur.

## 26:74
Vers. 74. καταναθεματίζειν] I cannot agree with those who wish καταναθεματίζειν here to be the same as βλασφημεῖν in Acts XXVI and in Justin's Apology, or to curse Christ in Pliny. For just as the sin which Peter wept over with such great sorrow is not to be extenuated, so I do not see why we should seek out reasons to aggravate his fault: rather, καταναθεματίζειν here, like ἀναθεματίζειν in Acts XXIII. 14, is for the Hebrews החרים החרם, that is, to call down curses upon oneself. A formula which often occurs in the history of the Old Testament: "May God do this to me and add this if this is so." In that way then Peter bound himself with curses if he knew Christ, in addition to the oath which had also been added to the second denial: as we are accustomed to slip from bad to worse, unless timely repentance comes to our aid. In a very ancient manuscript which came from Greece to England, it is here καταθεματίζειν, just as also in Revelation XXII. 3. κατάθεμα, which word is in the same sense in Justin.

Οὐκ οἶδα τὸν ἄνθρωπον] It appears there was great consternation which drove Peter to such an incredible lie. For there was hardly any Jew who did not know Jesus by sight, famous for so many miracles. Nor could Peter bring forward any reason why he had come there, if he had not known him.

Latin:

Vers. 74. καταναθεματίζειν] Non possum iis assentiri qui καταναθεματίζειν hic idem esse volunt quod Actor. XXVI. & Iustino in Apologetico est βλασφημεῖν, apud Plinium maledicere Christo. Ut enim extenuandum non est deli- ctum quod Petrus tanto cum dolore deflevit, ita non vi- deo cur causas conquirere debeamus onerandæ ipsius cul- pæ: imo καταναθεματίζειν hic, ut ἀναθεματίζειν Actor. XXIII. 14. Hebræis החרים החרם est sibimet male precari Formula quæ sæpe in veteris fœderis historia occurrit τάδ' ἐπιθεματίσαι mihi Deus faciat & hæc addat si hoc ita se habet. Eo tum modo Petrus diris se obligavit si Christum nosset, super jusjurandum quod & secundæ ne- gationi accesserat: ut solemus ex malis in pejora prola- bi, nisi matura pœnitentia succurrat. In manuscripto vetu- stissimo qui ex Græcia in Angliam venit est hic καταθεμα- τίζειν, sicut & in Apocalypsi XXII. 3. κατάθεμα, quæ vox eodem sensu est apud Iustinum.

Οὐκ οἶδα τὸν ἄνθρωπον] Magnam apparet consternationem fuisse quæ Petrum adegit ad tam incredibile mendacium. Vix enim quisquam erat Iudæus qui Iesum de vultu non nosset, tot miraculis celebrem. Neque causam ad- ferre Petrus ullam poterat quorsum eo venisset, si eum non nôverat.

## 26:75
Vers. 75. And Peter remembered] He is awakened at once by the cock's crow, as those who are sleepy are wont to be, and by the sight of the Lord who was directing the gaze of his eyes upon him from a higher place, as it is in Luke. Thus in Isaiah 22:4, אמרד בבכי the Greeks translate 'I will weep bitterly'.

Latin:

Vers. 75. κᾀ ἐμνήσθη ὁ Πέτρος] Simul excitatur & galli cantu, ut somnolenti solent, & Domini adspectu qui de superiore loco aciem oculorum in ipsum dirigebat, ut a- pud Lucam est. Sic Esaiæ XXII. 4. אמרד בבכי Græci vertunt πικρῶς πλάνσομαι.

## 27:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXVII.

ARGUMENT AND DIVISION.

Early in the morning, a council having been held, they deliver the bound Jesus to Pilate, upon seeing whom Judas, repentant, returns the thirty pieces of silver, confesses his guilt, but in despair hangs himself: for these, however, the potter's field is bought for the burial of strangers, according to the prophecy of Jeremiah. When Pilate asks if he is the King of the Jews, Jesus answers in the affirmative, but to the accusations of the Priests and Elders he is silent, and when Pilate wished to release one of the prisoners according to the custom of the feast, and was warned by his wife not to have anything to do with Jesus, as he was a just man, and wished to release Jesus, the people asked for Barabbas to be released, but for Jesus to be crucified. Pilate, washing his hands, testified that he was innocent regarding the blood of this just man, but the people cried out, 'His blood come upon us and upon our children': and so, having released Barabbas, Pilate delivered Jesus, having been scourged, to be crucified: whom the soldiers mocked, having clothed him in purple, placed a crown of thorns upon his head, and put a reed in his hands, and furthermore led him out clothed in his own garments to crucify him, compelling Simon of Cyrene on the way to carry his cross: and having offered him vinegar mixed with gall at Golgotha, and having crucified him, they divided his garments according to the Prophet (Ps. 22:19) and kept watch over him, placed a title on the cross as the cause of his death, and crucified two thieves with him. Those passing by blasphemed Jesus, as did the Priests, and also the thieves: but darkness having arisen for three hours, Jesus cried out, 'Eli, Eli, Lama Sabachthani': and when vinegar was offered to him on a sponge, crying out again with a loud voice, he expired. Then indeed the veil of the Temple was torn, the earth shaken, the graves of the saints opened, who rose again, the Centurion converted, with some women standing by who had followed Jesus. Joseph of Arimathea, having obtained the body of Jesus, buried it in his own tomb, and rolled a great stone against it: but the Priests and Pharisees, with Pilate's consent, set guards and sealed the stone.

There are two parts: The former presents the Acts of the passion and death, up to verse 50, such as I. The delivery of Jesus led to Pilate, with the repentance of Judas, but joined with despair, up to verse 10. II. The Acts before Pilate, namely (1.) The examination of Jesus before Pilate, up to verse 14. (2.) Pilate's proposal to release Jesus rather than Barabbas, and the same repeated at the warning of his wife, up to verse 23. (3.) Pilate's testimony concerning the innocence of Jesus, and his delivery to crucifixion, up to verse 26. III. The Acts in the Praetorium by the cohort: the mockery of Jesus, up to v. 30. IV. The leading out of Jesus to the place of crucifixion, up to v. 34. V. The crucifixion of Jesus with related events, where also the division of garments, and the placing of the title, and the crucifixion of the thieves with Jesus, and the commemoration of various blasphemies and mockeries, up to v. 44, and also the cry concerning divine desertion, and the drink made of vinegar, up to v. 48. VI. The expiration of Jesus with a great cry, v. 50. The latter part concerns the things following the death of Christ, namely both the miracles which occurred, (1.) The tearing of the temple veil, verse 51. (2.) The shaking of the earth; (3.) The breaking of the rocks. (4.) The opening of the graves of the Saints, v. 52, and their effects, such as the conversion of the Centurion, v. 54, and the wonder of the pious women watching these things, v. 55, 56, and then the burial of Jesus; concerning which it is noted in advance the petition of Joseph of Arimathea, verses 57, 58, and of Pilate the Governor concession, verse 59. Then is described the wrapping of the body of Christ, verse 59, and his placement in the new monument of Joseph, and the rolling of a huge stone, verse 60, as well as the observation of Mary Magdalene, and the other Mary, v. 61. Finally is subjoined the obtaining of guards from Pilate at the insistence of the Priests, and the sealing of the stone, to v. 66.

PART ONE. The remaining acts of the passion of Christ.

Verse 1. συμβύλιον ἔλαβον] That so many senators should have departed in such a small space of time, and again have gathered from so many regions of the city, is neither credible, and it is invented without cause. The sense is, that after hearing Jesus, the senators deliberated separately among themselves what was to be done. Thus συμβύλιον ἔλαβον is taken elsewhere, to signify that a plan was formed. Above XII. 14. chap. XXII. 15. But more fully on this matter at Luke.

That agitation of the council in Matt. XII. 14. chap. XXII. 15. does not exclude, but includes, or presupposes a meeting of the council, as can be seen from Matt. XXVIII. 12: that it was a new meeting is taught by the circumstance of time, because that council was held in the morning, and to it gathered ἀρχιερεῖς μετὰ τῶν πρεσβυτέρων, καὶ γραμματέων, ἡ ὅλον τὸ συνέδριον, ἐυθέως ἐπὶ τὸ πρωὶ συμβόλιον πονήσαντες, as is had in Mark XV. 1. πρωίας γενομένης, as it is in this place: then indeed St. Luke indicates in chap. XXII. 66. expressly describing a new morning meeting: Ἐώς ἐγένετο ἡμέρα, συνήχθη τὸ πρεσβυτέριον τῶ λαῶ, ἀρχιερεῖς τε ἢ γραμματεῖς, έανήγαγον ἀυτὸν εἰς τὸ συνέδριον. Nor indeed did only a small space of night remain, because the Chief Priests and Pharisees departed before the second and third denial of Peter, and thus before the second cock-crowing, by which that cock-crowing is understood, not that which they are accustomed to give around dawn, but that which is heard around the middle of the night, as it is usually preceded by the first cock-crowing around the second watch of the night. Nor is it indeed likely that Peter would have wished to remain in the courtyard of the High Priest in such great danger of his life until dawn, and then it seems altogether probable that the Chief Priests, Pharisees, and Elders of the people devoted some hours after midnight to sleep, and for that reason withdrew, but on the condition that they would gather again in the morning: which is taught to have been done here. Calvin is therefore also mistaken, when he asserts that the Assessors of this Sanhedrin did not withdraw, nor cease for one moment in strenuously executing their crime, likewise openly contradicting St. Luke.

Verse same. ὥστε αὐτὸν θανατῶσαι] Not by treachery, which is infamous: nor by riot, which is dangerous: but by public judgment, which could not be done except through the Roman governor. Wherefore the whole deliberation turned on this, how that might be persuaded to the governor.

Latin:

CAPUT XXVII.

ARGUMENTUM ET PAR- TITIO.

Novo mane agitato concilio vinctum Iesum Pi- lato tradunt, quo viso Iudas pœnitens tri- ginta argenteos restituit, culpam fatetur, sed desperans seipsum suspendit: pro illis autem emitur ager figuli in peregrinorum sepulturam, secundum Ieremiæ vatici- nium. Pilato quærente an Iudæorum Rex sit, Iesus affirmative respondet, ad accusa- tiones vero Sacerdotum & Seniorum ta- cet, & quum ex festi consuetudine ali- quem captivorum dimittere vellet Pilatus, ac moneretur a conjuge ne cum Jesu, utpote justo, negotium haberet, Jesumque libe- rare vellet, Barabbam dimitti petebat po- pulus, Jesum vero crucifigi. Pilatus ma- nus lavans se innocentem esse quoad justi hujus sanguinem, testatus est, sed clama- vit populus, sanguis ejus veniat super nos & super liberos nostros: adeoque dimis- so Barraba Pilatus Jesum flagellatum tradidit, ut crucifigeretur: quem purpu- ra indutum, corona spinea capiti imposita & arundine in manus data exagitebant milites, ac porro propriis indutum vesti- bus eduxerunt ut crucifigerent ipsum, in via Simonem Cyreneum cogentes, ut cru- cem ejus portaret: & præbito ipsi in Gol- gatha aceto felle mixto, eoque crucifixo ve- stes ejus dividebant juxta Prophetam (Ps. XXII. 19.) ac custodiebant ipsum, cruci ti- tulum ceu causam mortis imponebant, & duos latrones cum ipso crucifigebant. Transeuntes Jesum blasphemabant, ut & Sacerdotes, nec non latrones: ortis autem tenebris per tres horas, exclamabat Jesus, Eli, Eli, Lama Sabachtani: & cum ipsi præberetur in spongia acetum, sonora voce iterum exclamans exspiravit. Tum vero scissum velum Templi, terra commota, se- pulcra sanctorum aperta, qui resurrexê- re, Centurio conversus, astantibus ali- quot mulieribus Jesum sequutis. Josephus Arimathensis impetrato corpore Jesu id in proprio monumento condidit, saxumque ingens ei advolvit: Sacerdotes autem & Pharisæi custodes Pilato annuente apposue- runt, saxumque obsignarunt.

Partes sunt duæ: Prior Acta passionis & mor- tis reliqua sistit, ad vers. 50. ceu sunt I. Jesu ad Pilatum traducti traditio, cum Judæ pœnitentia, sed cum desperatione conjuncta, ad vers. 10. II. Acta coram Pilato, utpote (1.) Jesu penes Pilatum examinatio, ad vers. 14. (2.) Pilati propositio de Jesu potius, quam Barraba dimittendo, ea- demque ad monitum uxoris iterata, ad vers. 23. (3.) Pilati testimonium de innocentia Jesu, ejus- demque ad crucifixionem traditio, ad vers. 26. III. Acta in Prætorio a cohorte: Jesu illusio, ad v. 30. IV. Eductio Jesu ad locum crucifixionis, ad v. 34. V. Crucifixio Jesu cum connexis, ubi & vestium divisio, & tituli impositio, & latronum cum Jesu crucifixio, & variarum blasphemiarum, & illusionum commemoratio, ad v. 44. nec noh exclamatio de divina desertione, & aceto facta potatio, ad v. 48. VI. Jesu cum clamore magno exspiratio, v. 50. Altera pars concernit τὰ ἑπό- μενα mortis Christi, utpote tum miracula quæ contigere, (1.) Veli templi scissionem, vers. 51. (2.) Terræ commotionem; (3.) Petrarum disru- ptionem. (4.) Sepulcrorum Sanctorum apertio- nem, v. 52. & eorum affecta ceu sunt Centurionis conversio, v. 54. & mulierum piarum ista spectan- tium admiratio v. 55. 56. tum sepulturam Jesu; circa quam in antecessum notatur Josephi Ari- mathensis petitio vers. 57. 58. ac Pilati Præsidis concessio vers. 59. dehinc describitur corporis Christi involutio vers. 59. ejusdemque in novo Josephi monumento repositio, ac lapidis ingen- tis obvolutio, vers. 60. nec non Mariæ Magda- lenæ, & Mariæ alterius observatio v. 61. De- nique subjungitur custodum ad instantiam Sacer- dotum à Pilato impetratio, & lapidis obsignatio, ad v. 66.

PARS PRIOR. Acta reliqua passionis Christi.

Vers. 1. συμβύλιον ἔλαβον] Tantillo temporis spatio dis- cessisse tot senatores, iterumque ex tot urbis regionibus convenisse, neque credibile est, & sine causa fingitur. Sen- sus est, post auditum Jesum seursim senatores inter se de- liberasse quid esset faciendum. Ita συμβύλιον ἔλαβον & ali- bi sumitur, ut captum consilium significet. Supra XII. 14. cap. XXII. 15. Sed de hac re ad Lucam plenius.

Illa consilii agitatio Matth. XII. 14. cap. XXII. 15. non excludit, sed includit, aut præsupponit concilii conventum, ut è Matth. XXVIII. 12. vi- dere est: novum vero conventum fuisse tum cir- cumstantia temporis docet, quod mane conci- lium illud celebratum fuerit, & ad illud con- voluerint ἀρχιερεῖς μετὰ τῶν πρεσβυτέρων, καὶ γραμματέων, ἡ ὅλον τὸ συνέδριον, ἐυθέως ἐπὶ τὸ πρωὶ συμβόλιον πονήσαντες, ut habetur Marc. XV. 1. πρωίας γενομένης, ut est hoc loco: tum vero S. Lucas indicat cap. XXII. 66. conventum novum matutinum diserte exprimens: Ἐώς ἐγένετο ἡμέ- ρα, συνήχθη τὸ πρεσβυτέριον τῶ λαῶ, ἀρχιερεῖς τε ἢ γραμματεῖς, έανήγαγον ἀυτὸν εἰς τὸ συνέ- δριον. Nec vero exiguum tantum supererat no- ctis spatium, quia discesserunt Pontifices & Pha- risæi ante secundam & tertiam abnegationem Pe- tri, adeoque ante secundum gallicinium, per quod ille galli cantus intelligitur, non quem circa auroram solent edere, sed qui circa medium noctis auditur, utpote quem præcedere solet primus galli cantus circa secundam noctis vigiliam. Neque enim vero simile est, Petrum usque ad auroram in atrio Pontificiis in tanto vitæ periculo manere voluisse, tum vero probabile omnino videtur, Pontifices, Pharisæos ac Seniores populi horas aliquot post mediam noctem somno tribuisse, ea- que de causa fecessisse, sed ea lege, ut mane iterum convenirent: quod hic factum esse doce- tur. Fallitur ergo etiam Calvinus, cum As- sessores hujus Synedrii non secessisse, nec unum momentum cessasse in scelere suo strenue exe- quendo, asserit, itidem palam S. Lucæ contra- dicens.

Vers. eod. ὥστε αὐτὸν θανατῶσαι] Non per insidias, quod infame: nec per tumultum quod periculosum: sed publico judicio, quod fieri non poterat nisi per Romanum præsidem. Quare tota deliberatio in eo vertebatur, quomo- do præsidi id persuaderetur.

## 27:2
Verse 2. δήσαντες] That is, δεδεμένον. Thus aorists are accustomed to signify even that which happened before. For Christ was bound immediately after his arrest, as we learn from John. See what [I wrote] at Mark XVI. 1.

The more common meaning can be retained. For it is likely that the Chief Priests had released Jesus from his bonds, so that his confession might seem freer, or even the soldiers, so that they might harass him all the more freely. It is better, therefore, to understand this as new bonds cast upon him again after the sentence of death was concluded. For it was the custom that whoever they had adjudged to death, they would present to the Governor bound and tied. Consult Harm. Pass. B. Gerhard. chap. 8.

παρέδωκαν] As was their custom if they had arrested someone as a capital criminal. Thus the Irenarchs were accustomed to interrogate those whom they had arrested in the Provinces, then to send them with the interrogations to the Governor. Law: Divine Hadrian in the Digests concerning the custody and exhibition of defendants. Jerome concerning the Jews: They had this custom, that whoever they had adjudged to death, they would hand over bound to the judge.

τῷ ἡγεμόνι] Thus also Josephus: Πιλάτῳ δὲ τῆς Ἰουδαίας ἡγεμών. The Latin translator rightly translates it as Governor, although it is sufficiently established that Pontius was procurator, even from Tacitus and Philo, who calls him ἐπίτροπον. For the name of governor, which the Greeks mostly translate as ἡγεμόνα, as Macer says, cited in the first law of the Pandects concerning the office of Governor, is general, by which all those ruling provinces are called. Although indeed the office of procurators was properly τὰ αὐτοκράτορος καὶ χρήματα διοικεῖν, as Dio speaks, it was nevertheless usurped in smaller Provinces, so that they might also administer justice outside of fiscal cases, and even punish with the sword. Such procurators are said to perform the duty of Governor in Law II. C. concerning punishments and Law IV. C. On the Fabian Law concerning kidnappers: and in Ulpian book IX. concerning the office of proconsul, as it is cited in the old collation of Mosaic laws with Roman ones. Therefore Josephus, dealing with such procurators, adds τῇ ἐπὶ πᾶσιν ἐξουσίᾳ, or having received authority up to the point of killing.

Therefore the passage of Tacitus book XV. of the Histories, 'The author of that name, Christ, who in the reign of Tiberius had been executed by the procurator Pontius Pilate,' does not stand against those who call Pilate Governor. Which some have rashly judged.

Latin:

Vers. 2. δήσαντες] Id est, δεδεμένον. Ita solent ἀόριστοι signi- ficare etiam id quod ante contigera. Nam vinctus erat Christus statim post prehensionem ut ex Iohanne discimus. Vide quæ ad Marc. XVI. I.

Retineri potest communior significatio. Nam vinculis Pontifices Jesum solvisse, ut libe- rior confessio videretur, aut etiam milites, ut tanto liberius exagitare ipsum possent, vero simile est. De novis ergo vinculis post con- clusam mortis sententiam denuo ei injectis præ- stat intelligere. Moris enim erat, ut quem n or- ti adjudicassent, eum vinctum ac ligatum Præ- sidi sisterent. Cons. Harm. Pass. B. Gerhard. cap. 8.

παρέδωκαν] Ut moris illis erat si quem prehendissent capitaliter noxirm. Ita solebant in Provinciis Irenarchæ- quos apprehenderant interrogare, deinde cum interroga- tionibus ad Præsidem mittere. L. Divus Hadrianus Digestis de custodia & exhibitione reorum. Hieronymus de Judæis: Habebant hunc morem, ut quem adjudicassent morti, ligatum judici traderent.

τῷ ἡγεμόνι] Sic & Josephus: Πιλάτῳ δὲ τῆς Ἰουδαίας ἡ- γεμών. Bene vertit Latinus interpres Præsidi, quanquam procuratorem fuisse Pontium satis constat vel ex Tacito & Philone, qui ἐπίτροπον vocat. Nam præsidis nomen, quod ἡγεμόνα plerunque Græci vertunt, ut ait Macer ci- tatus lege prima Pandecte de officio Præsidis, generale est, quo omnes provincias regentes appellantur. Quanquam vero procuratorum officium proprie erat τὰ αὐτοκράτορος καὶ χρήματα διοικεῖν, ut Dio loquitur, usurpatum tamen in minoribus Provinciis, ut etiam extra fisci causas jus dicerent, atque etiam gladio animadverterent. Tales procuratores dicuntur vice Præsidis fungi Lege II. C. de pœnis & L. IV. C. Ad Legem Fabiam de plagiariis: & apud Ulpianum lib. IX. de officio proconsulis, ut citatur in veteri collatione legum Mosaicarum cum Romanis. Ideo Josephus de talibus agens procuratoribus addit τῇ ἐπὶ πᾶσιν ἐξουσίᾳ, aut μέχρι τοῦ κτείνειν λαβὼν ἐξουσίαν.

Non ergo locus Taciti libr. XV. Histor. Au- tor nominis ejus Christus, qui Tiberio imperi- tante, per procuratorem Pontium Pilatum sup- plicio affectus erat, illis obstat, qui Pilatum Præsidem dicunt. Quod temere nonnulli cen- suêre.

## 27:3
Vers. 3. ὅτι κατεκρίθη] This must be referred entirely to the pre-condemnation of the Sanhedrin, concerning which see above c. XXVI. 66, which Judas accepted as a sign of the death that was to follow. For those branded by such a prejudice were rarely accustomed to escape.

μεταμεληθεὶς] I do not see that the distinction which is handed down by many between μεταμελείας and μετανοίας is observed. For both those outside and our own writers likewise interchange these, as see Heb. XII. 17, where μετάνοια is what they wish to be called μεταμέλεια, a repentance of a contract entered into, as the jurists also speak: on the contrary, μεταμεληθεὶς above c. XXI. 29 is said of one who has received a better mind. And Clement of Alexandria says there is a double τρόπον μετανοῦντος, the one more common, fear for what has been done, the other more specific, the shame of the soul toward itself from conscience. Nor, however, should the ambiguity of the word be thought to favor those who pronounce more mercifully than is right concerning Judas. For both Peter's speech in the Acts and the sharp words of Christ, calling him a son of perdition and adding that it would have been better for him if he had not been born at all, persuade otherwise. Therefore, from the circumstances of the history rather than from the mere property of the word, we ought to understand here that sorrow to which true amendment of life was not present, and that both by his own fault and by the judgment of God who hardens. Nor meanwhile do I disapprove of what Origen notes in the second book against Celsus, that there was such power in the documents of Christ that they struck even a man of desperate malice with some shame of sinning and with severe torment from sin.

Latin:

Vers. 3. ὅτι κατεκρίθη] Omnino referendum hoc ad Synedrii prædamnationem, de qua supra c. XXVI. 66. quam Judas accipiebat ut secuturæ mortis indicium. Raro enim elabi solebant tali præjudicio confossi.

μεταμεληθεὶς] Non video observari discrimen quod à multis traditur μεταμελείας & μετανοίας. Nam & οἱ ἔξω is- sta permutant, & nostri itidem Scriptores, ut ecce Hebr. XII. 17. μετάνοια elt id quod μεταμέλεια dici volunt, con- tractus initi pœnitentia, ut Jurisconsulti etiam loquuntur: contra μεταμεληθεὶς supra c. XXI. 29. is dicitur qui men- tem meliorem recepit. Et Clemens Alexandrinus du- plicem esse ait τρόπον μετανοῦντος, τὸν μὲν κοινότερον, φόβον ἐπὶ τοῖς πεπραγμένοις, τὸν δὲ ἰδιαίτερον τὴν δυσωπίαν τὴν πρὸς ἑαυτὴν τῆς ψυχῆς ἐκ συνειδήσεως. Neque tamen vocabuli ambiguitas iis favere censenda est, qui de Juda misericor- dius quam par est pronunciant. Aliud enim suadet & Pe- tri oratio in actis, & destricta Christi verba υἱὸν ἀπωλείας appellantus, addentisque melius ei futurum fuisse si natus omnino non esset. Ex circumstantiis igitur historiæ magis quam ex sola vocis proprietate eum mœrorem hic intelli- gere debemus, cui non adfuerit vera vitæ emendatio, id que tum ipsius culpa, tum Dei obdurantis judicio. Ne- que interim improbo quod adversus Celsum secundo no- tat Origenes, tantam vim fuisse documentorum Chri- sti, ut etiam deploratæ malitiæ homini pudorem quen- quam peccandi, & ex peccato cruciatum gravem incus- serint.

## 27:4
Vers. 4. αἷμα ἀθῶον] αἷμα to the Hellenists signifies any violent death whatsoever, as also below in verse 6. Here, metonymically, it signifies the very person who is destined for death.

σὺ ὄψει] Thus below in verse 24, ὑμεῖς ὄψεσθε. It is, however, a manner of speaking taken from the Latin language. For the Romans, when casting the care of some matter from themselves onto another, say, 'Tu videris' (See to it yourself): which the Greeks would say as σοὶ μελέτω. Wherefore it is not surprising that the force of this locution was not correctly grasped by the Syrian. They speak after the manner of Cain, the true offspring of Cain.

Latin:

Vers. 4. αἷμα ἀθῶον] αἷμα Hellenistis mortem quam- vis violentam significat, ut & infra commate 6. Hic μετωνυμικῶς ipsum eum qui morti destinatur.

σὺ ὄψει] Sic infra commate 24. ὑμεῖς ὄψεσθε. Est au- tem loquendi genus ex Latino sermone desumtum. Nam Romani curam rei alicujus à se in alium rejicientes ajunt, Tu videris: quod Græci dicerent σοὶ μελέτω. Quare mirum non est haud satis recte acceptam a Syro vim hujus locu- tionis. Ad modum Caini loquuntur vera progenies Caini.

## 27:5
Vers. 5. ἐν τῷ ναῷ] In that part of the Temple in which the Sanhedrin sat, which place was called לשכת הגזית.

Ἀπήγξατο] It is indeed for the Greeks ἀπάγξασθαι to take one's own life by hanging, as ἀπάγξασθαι με ποιήσεις in Theocritus. But that is reconciled with difficulty with Peter's narrative in Acts 1, where a different kind of death is attributed to Judas, namely, with his intestines poured out when he had fallen forward on his face. It is sufficiently well known what has been devised so that these might be reconciled with one another. Nor do those sufficiently extricate themselves who wish that Judas fell because the rope broke. For Peter seems to ascribe the cause of his destruction entirely to an unexpected fall, which divine providence directed, not to the act of Judas himself. Let us see, therefore, whether Matthew in this place is not dealing with the death of Judas, as something that happened later, and perhaps after the resurrection, as the conjecture of many holds: but rather with the most grievous torment of an ulcerated conscience. For that the compression of the spirit from extreme sorrow is indicated by this word, even the book of Tobit may teach us, where it is said of Sarah in chapter III. 12. ἐλυπήθη σφόδρα ὥστε ἀπάγξασθαι. And concerning Ahithophel, what was said by David, in Judas they agree perfectly, and concerning which we read similarly ἀπήγξατο, where in the Hebrew it is וַיֵּחָנַק, which word both the Syrian and the Arab use here; the not unlearned among the Hebrews feel that he perished not by a noose, but by sorrow. Ignatius may seem to ascribe the death of Judas by hanging in his Epistle to the Philippians where it is said of the Devil: μετάμελον ἐμβαλὼν τῷ προδότῃ ὃ βρόχον αὐτῷ δείκνυσι ἀγχόνην διδάσκει. But whoever reads that epistle with judgment will easily detect that the diction and χαρακτῆρα τοῦ λόγου are more flowery than those of Ignatius. For Ignatius had indeed written to the Philippians, as Polycarp remembers. But since that Epistle did not exist, another was substituted. Wherefore neither Theodoret nor Jerome nor Rufinus acknowledge this.

Grotius acknowledges that for the Greeks ἀπάγξασθαι means to take one's own life by hanging, as in ἀπάγξασθαι μὲ ποίησεις in Theocritus. Concerning which Salmasius also deserves to be heard: Matthew, he says, wrote that Judas hanged himself: For these words in Matthew admit of no other interpretation: καὶ ἀπελθὼν ἀπήγξατο. And rightly the Vulgate Interpreter, and going away he hanged himself with a noose. Greek writers use this word IN NO OTHER WAY. Nor can the words of Aelian be taken otherwise, Σωκράτης κωμῳδούμενος ἐγέλα πολίαγρός δὲ ἀπήγξατο. Socrates, being mocked on stage, laughed, but Poliagrus hanged himself. He did not die of anger, as they commonly accept. In the Greek Epigram Αἰσχυνθεὶς πετόσιρον ἀπήγξατο, that is, he hanged himself with a noose. In another Epigram ὃ γαμῶν ἀπήγξατο. This Greek word has never been accepted in any other sense. Which testimonies of most excellent Greek philologists are to be duly noted. For there is no reason why we should depart from the customary, and as Salmasius teaches, the uniquely accepted meaning among the Greeks. Thus also Thucydides used this word concerning strangulation, when someone chooses death for himself by a noose, καὶ ὅκ τῶν δένδρων τινὲς ἀ- πήγξαντο. Nor is the word חָנַק 2 Sam. XVII. 23 used otherwise, which the LXX interpreted at Nah. II. 12 as ἐπιπνίγειν: which the Syrian used here, because חנק נפשה strangled his soul, that is, Judas himself. Thus Heinsius himself observes that Chrysostom at Matt. XVIII explained ἄγειν τὸν δοῦλον as what the Evangelist called πνίγειν. And it is known that חנק is one of the four punishments of the Jews, namely strangulation, by which one striking father and mother, stealing someone from Israel, an old man contradicting the Consistory, a false prophet, and one prophesying in the name of an Idol, as well as one having relations with another's wife, and one seducing the daughter of a Priest, and lying with her, was affected.

But it is a new invention of Dan. Heinsius that Judas did not end his life by hanging, but died from sorrow of mind. Which Ludovicus de Dieu and this Grotius also embraced, even though he had to admit that that word means for the Greeks to take one's own life by hanging: to which opinion he also brought the Epistle of Ignatius to the Philippians, where it is said of the Devil μεταμέλον ἐμβάλλων τῷ προδότῃ ὃ βρόχον αὐτῷ δείκνυσι καὶ ἀγχόνην δι- δάσκει. He cast repentance into the traitor, and showed him a noose, and taught him the hanging by which he might be strangled. Which Epistle, even if it be supposititious, is perhaps not of such a recent author. But Grotius and Heinsius prove nothing from Tob. II. 12 regarding another meaning of this word, where it is said of Sarah, ἐλυπήθη σφόδρα ὥστε ἀπάγξασθαι. For the plain sense is that she was affected by great sorrow, as if she wished to exhale her soul with a choked throat, as the comparative particle ὥστε indicates, not that she wished to end her life by hanging, but that she was so affected by sorrow as if she were being strangled, and with an oppressed throat or constricted neck was about to exhale her soul: which comparative particle is not had here. Nor does the passage about Ahithophel 2 Sam. XVII. 23 teach the contrary: καὶ ἐνετείλατο τῷ οἴκῳ αὐτῶ, καὶ ἀ- πήγξατο, κ᾿ ἀπέθανε have the LXX Interpreters, where in the context itself is חנק. For the invention of certain Rabbis praised by Heinsius and Grotius, that the disease arose from great pain of mind and sorrow, by which he perished, does not agree with the words of the text: for immediately after he set his house in order ἀ- πήγξατο κ᾿ ἀπέθανε and he set his house in order because he wished to end his life by the Machanac: which do not agree with a perishing arising from sorrow and pain of mind.
