For he did not have it in his hand. And he could have been tormented for a long time by sorrow and pain of mind before he ended his life. But this is hinted to have been done immediately after he set his house in order, and in such a way that he inflicted death upon himself. Concerning which Josephus book VII, chapter 9, ταύτης θανάτω δικασὴν ἀυτὸν γνώμιμον, καθελόντες ἐκ τ᾿ ἀγχόνης ἐκήδευσαν οἱ προσήκοντες: his kinsmen, having taken him down from the noose, buried him, having been adjudged by his own judgment to such a death. Ἀγχόνη ὁ βρόχος, τὸ σχοινίον, A noose or rope, says Suidas. Nor does Lud. de Dieu at Matt. XXVII. 1 observe that חנק is that disease which the Greeks call ἀγχόνην, but that it is called אסכרה by the Hebrews: whence he ridiculously elicits an omen, that Judas was called אסכריותא by his parents, because as a boy he was seized by the disease אסכרה, and as an adult he perished by the same disease. Truly, for Critics, as for Poets, all things are permitted.

But as for the passage in Acts 1:18, no other kind of death of Judas is attributed there, as Grotius and Heinsius think, even if another circumstance which occurs in divine judgment concerning his death is expressed: Nor is it for us to think with Salmasius that the Evangelists neglected the minutiae of the circumstances, when they knew that the account of the truth stood firm for them concerning the principal history: because there was indeed a constant and true report that Judas brought death upon himself: but by what kind of death he perished, it was uncertain: that some handed down that he was extinguished by a precipice, others by hanging. For the Evangelists did not receive their histories from tradition or hearsay, but they wrote them down by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit. And there is no conflict here between Matthew and Luke, nor is there any need for us to take refuge with Oecumenius in the story derived from Papias, that Judas wished to end his life by hanging, but having fallen headlong to the ground he survived, his body so swollen that he could not walk, and that the road through which a wagon could be driven could not contain him, and finally when a wagon was passing by, he was crushed and bruised by it and poured out his bowels: or let us conclude with others that Judas, after the swelling of all his limbs, after pus and worms bursting forth from his whole body, and finally after many torments, died on his farm, etc. For could not Judas have hanged himself, as Matthew expressly states, and taken his own life with a noose, which the word used by him implies: and yet could that also have happened which Luke reports concerning him, καὶ πρηνὴς γενόμενος ἐλάκησε μέσος, καὶ ἐξεχύτη πάντα τα σπλάγχνα ἀυτῶ, and falling headlong he burst open in the middle, and all his bowels were poured out. What contradiction is there here, what opposition? For it is not even a wonder, much less impossible, that someone hanging himself from a height and strangling himself, should, upon the breaking of the noose, fall headlong, and being dashed against some rough rock or sharp wood, or even without such a dashing, burst in the middle and pour out his bowels, whether one concludes that the belly burst in the middle by the violence of the fall or by the singular judgment of a vengeful God. Although Epiphanius considers that he poured out his bowels first, and then died having used the ἀγχόνη, having employed hanging. But the former explanation accords better with the historical account.

Because, having thrown down the silver pieces in the temple, he departed and went away and hanged himself, and falling headlong he burst asunder in the midst, and all his bowels gushed out. Schmidius on Acts 1 has it thus: Without doubt, by these words a singular example of hanging is hinted at, that Judas, from a higher place, in which he had adapted a noose to his neck, fixed at a certain spot, afterwards in extreme desperation leaped headlong, so that in that sudden compression of the throat and the respiratory tract, because of the air included by breathing, not only the peritoneum, but also the skin of the abdomen was suddenly and with a crack ruptured, not without a sign of peculiar Divine vengeance. See Casaubon in Exerc. ad Baron. XVI. year 34. no. 69. But that either Pricaeus and Vossius assert that Judas threw himself headlong from on high out of desperation, or that some other person asserts he was snatched into the air by the Devil and cast down to the earth, is said without proof, nor does it agree with Matthew, who maintains that he took his own life by strangulation and hanging: in which agree Apollinarius of Hierapolis in Eusebius, Eccl. Hist. book V, ch. 14; Prudentius in Psychomachia; Chrysostom, Sermon III on Judas; Nazianzen on Christ Suffering; Augustine, book 50 of homilies, hom. 27; Leo II, sermon III on the passion; Juvencus, book IV of Gospel History; Arator, book X of History; Bede on ch. 1 of Acts; Oecumenius; Bernard; Rupert of Deutz; Drogo of Ostia; along with the Syriac and Arabic as well as the Ethiopic and Persian interpreters. Leo, sermon 3, says: You have been more wicked and more unhappy than all, Judas, whom not repentance recalled to the Lord, but desperation dragged to the noose. Of the ancients, those of the same opinion here are B. Luther, Osiander, Mr. Cramer, Arculanus, etc., and among the Reformed, Calvin, Gualther, Piscator, Junius, Casaubon, Salmasius; among the Papists, Salmero, Dionysius the Carthusian, à Rickes, Francis de Mendoza, Jansenius, Cornelius à Lapide, Tirinus, etc. Add to these what the blessed Mr. Dr. Danhawver has in his Program on the Theologian Thief of the blessed Dr. Dorscheus. Those who say Judas was snatched on high by the Devil and strangled, and cast headlong, so that being dashed to the ground he was broken in the midst—which, after John Lightfoot in his Hebrew Horae on Matthew, p. 307, also pleased Mr. Henry Möller of Rostock in his 'Jesus Suffering', p. 83—are destitute of all testimony and authority. For it does not follow that the Devil strangled him because he had already inhabited him for three days; the Devil was the moral cause of the strangulation, not the physical. Nor can it be proven, as Möller repeats at length from Lightfoot, that Judas Iscariot was so called only after his death, and that from אשכרא (strangulation); or if he was so named from strangulation, it follows that he was strangled by the Devil: for thus ropes are woven from sand, which is very common among critics. Vossius, Harm. Evang. book I, ch. 11, § 8, wishes Judas to be named from איש (man) and כריות (Carioth), which is a city of Judah, Josh. 15:25.

Latin:

Vers. 5. ἐν τῷ ναῷ] In ea parte Templi in qua considebat Synedrium, qui locus vocabatur לשכת הגזית.

Ἀπήγξατο] Est quidem Græcis ἀπάγξασθαι suspendio sibi vitam adimere, ut ἀπάγξασθαι με ποιήσεις apud Theo- critum. Sed difficulter id conciliatur cum Petri nar- ratione Actor. 1. ubi aliud mortis genus Judæ tribuitur, ef- fusis scilicet intestinis, cum pronus in faciem corruisset. Notum satis est quæ sint excogitata ut ista inter se concilia- rentur. Neque satis se expediunt qui laqueo fracto corruisse Judam volunt. Videtur enim Petrus omnino casui inopina- to, quem divina providentia direxerit, non Judæ ipsius fa- cto, exitii causam adscribere. Videamus igitur an hoc lo- co Matthæus non agat de morte Judæ, ut quæ serius con- tigerit, & forte post resurrectionem, ut multorum fert conjectura: sed de gravissimo exulceratæ conscientiæ tor- mento. Nam compressionem spiritus è mœrore summo hac voce indicari vel unus Tobiæ liber nos doceat, ubi de Sara dicitur cap. III. 12. ἐλυπήθη σφόδρα ὥστε ἀπάγξασθαι. Et de Achitophele in quem quæ dicta sunt à Davide, in Iudam apprime congruunt, & de quo similiter legimus ἀπήγξατο, ubi in Hebræo est וַיֵּחָנַק, quod verbum & Syrus, & Arabs hic usurpant, sentiunt Hebræorum non ineruditi non la- queo, sed mœstitia eum periisse. Videri potest suspendii mortem Judæ adscribere Ignatius in Epistola ad Philippen- ses ubi de Diabolo dicitur: μετάμελον ἐμβαλὼν τῷ προδότῃ ὃ βρόχον αὐτῷ δείκνυσι ἀγχόνην διδάσκει. Sed qui eam epi- stolam cum judicio leget, facile deprehendet dictionem & χαρακτῆρα τοῦ λόγου floridiorem quam est Ignatii. Nimi- rum scripserat ad Philippenses Ignatius, ut Polycarpus me- minit. Sed cum ea Epistola non exstaret alia supposita est. Quare nec Theodorecus nec Hieronymus nec Ruffinus hanc agnoscunt.

Agnoscit Grotius, quod Græcis ἀπάγξασθαι sit suspendio sibi vitam adimere, ut ἀπάγξασθαι μὲ ποίησεις apud Theocritum. De quo etiam audiri meretur Salmasius: Scripsit, inquit, Matthæus, Judam semetipsum suspendisse: Non enim aliam reci- piunt interpretationem hæc verba apud Matthæum: καὶ ἀπελθὼν ἀπήγξατο. Et recte vulgaris Inter- pres, & abiens laqueo se suspendit. Hoc verbo NON ALITER utuntur Græci Scriptores. Nec aliter verba Æliani capi possunt, Σωκράτης κωμῳδούμενος ἐγέλα πολίαγρός δὲ ἀπήγξατο. Socrates in sce- nam decisus ridebat, Poliagrus se suspendit. Non præ ira mortuus est, ut vulgo accipiunt. In Epigram- mate Græco Αἰσχυνθεὶς πετόσιρον ἀπήγξατο, id est, laqueo se suspendit. In alio Epigrammate ὃ γαμῶν ἀπήγξατο. Nunquam hoc verbum Græcum in alia notione acceptum est. Quæ testimonia Philo- logorum Græcorum excellentissimorum probe notanda. Non enim causa est, cur à consueta, & ut Salmasius docet, unice apud Græcos recepta significatione discedamus. Ita etiam Thucydides ad- hibuit hoc verbum de strangulatione, cum laqueo quis sibi mortem adsciscit καὶ ὅκ τῶν δένδρων τινὲς ἀ- πήγξαντο. Nec aliter vox חָנַק 2. Sam. XVII. 23. adhibetur, quam LXX. Nah. II. 12. pro ἐπιπνίγειν interpretati sunt: qua Syrus hic usus est, quod חנק נפשה strangulavit animam suam, hoc est, sei- psum Judas. Ita observat ipse Heinsius, quod Chrysostomus ad XVIII. Matth. ἄγειν τὸν δοῦλον ex- posuerit quod πνίγειν dixit Evangelista. Et notum est quod חנק unum sit è quatuor Judæorum sup- pliciis, strangulatio nempe, qua percutiens pa- trem & matrem, furans aliquem de Israel, senex contradicens Consistorio, Pseudopropheta, & prophetans in nomine Idoli, nec non rem habens cum uxore alterius, ac traducens filiam Sacerdo- tis, & subagitans eam, affectus est.

Novum autem commentum est Dan. Heinsii, quod Judas non suspendio vitam sibi finiverit, sed præ mœrore animi mortuus sit. Quod etiam am- plexus Ludovicus de Dieu, & hic Grotius est, etsi fateri necessum habuerit, verbum illud Græcis esse suspendio sibi vitam adimere: in quam senten- tiam adduxit quoque Ignatii Epistolam ad Philip- penses, ubi de Diabolo dicitur μεταμέλον ἐμβάλλων τῷ προδότῃ ὃ βρόχον αὐτῷ δείκνυσι καὶ ἀγχόνην δι- δάσκει. Pœnitentiam immisit proditori, & laqueum illi commonstravit, & suspendium, quo strangularetur, e- docuit. Quæ Epistola etsi supposititia sit, forte ta- men non adeo recentis autoris est. Nequicquam autem è Tob. II. 12. aliam vocis hujus significatio- nem Grotius cum Heinsio probant, ubi de Sara dicitur, ἐλυπήθη σφόδρα ὥστε ἀπάγξασθαι. Nam sensus planus est mœrore affectam valde, quasi obtu- rato gutture animam exhalare vellet, uti compara- tionem particula ὥστε indicat, non suspendio si- bi vitam voluisse finire, sed ita mœrore affectam fuisse, ac si strangularetur, & oppresso gutture, vel constricto collo animam esset exhalatura: qua- lis comparativa particula hic non habetur. Ne- que locus de Achitophele 2. Sam. XVII. 23. contra- rium docet: καὶ ἐνετείλατο τῷ οἴκῳ αὐτῶ, καὶ ἀ- πήγξατο, κ᾿ ἀπέθανε habent LXX. Interpp. ubi in contextu ipso חנק. Commentum enim Rab- binorum quorundam laudatuin Heinsio & Grotio, quod morbus ortus sit ex magno animi dolore, ac mœ- rore, quo interierit, non congruit verbis textus: nam statim postquam domum suam disposuit ἀ- πήγξατο κ᾿ ἀπέθανε & ideo domum disposuit, quia voluit τῷ Machanac vitam suam finire: quæ interi- tui è mœrore ac dolore animi oriundo non con- veniunt. Eum enim in manu sua non habuit. Et potuisset diu mœrore ac dolore animi angi, antequam vitam finiret. Hoc autem statim factum innuitur, postquam domum disposuit, & ita ut ipse sibi mortem afciverit. Quo de Josephus lib. VII. cap. 9. ταύτης θανάτω δικασὴν ἀυτὸν γνώμιμον, καθελόντες ἐκ τ᾿ ἀγχόνης ἐκήδευσαν οἱ προσήκοντες: suopte judicio tali morti addictum cognati ejus laqueo demtum funeraverunt. Ἀγχόνη ὁ βρόχος, τὸ σχοινίον, Laqueus vel funis ait Suidas. Neque חנק morbum illum, quem ἀγχόνην Græ- ci dicant, sed אסכרה Ebræis vocari Lud. de Dieu ad Matth. XXVII. 1. observat. unde ridicule omen elicit, quod Judas אסכריותא à parenti- bus dictus, quia puer morbo אסכרה correptus, a- dultus eodem morbo interierit. Nimirum Criticis, ut Poëtis, licent omnia.

Quod vero ad locum Actor. I. 18. non aliud ibi genus mortis Judæ tribuitur, ut Grotius atque Heinsius putant, etsi alia circumstantia, quæ ju- dicio divino circa mortem ejus occurrit, expri- matur: Neque est ut cum Salmasio censeamus, Evangelistas minutias τῶν περιστατικῶν neglexisse, cum de principali historia rationem veritatis sibi con- stare scirent: quia constans & vera fama quidem fuerit Judam sibi mortem conscivisse: quo vero gene- re mortis perierit, incertum fuerit: alios tradidisse præcipitio, alios suspendio ipsum extinctum fuisse. Non enim Evangelistæ historias suas è traditione aut fando accepere, se à Spiritus S. inspiratione easdem conscripsere. Et nulla hic pugna inter Matthæum, & Lucam, neque opus est, ut ad fabulam à Papia profectam cum Oecumenio nos re- cipiamus, quod Judas suspendio vitam sibi finire voluerit, sed præceps in terram prolapsus supervi- xerit in tantum corpore inflatus, ut progredi non posset, atque ut via, per quam agi plaustrum pot- erat, ipsum non caperet, ac tandem cum turrus transiret, eo compressus & obtritus viscera effude- rit: vel cum aliis statuamus, Judam post mem- brorum omnium inflationem, post saniem & vermes è toto corpore prorumpentes, post multa denique tormenta in pradio suo mortuum esse &c. Annon enim & suspendisse sese potuit Judas, ut διαῤῥή- δην habet Matthæus, atque vitam sibi ademisse la- queo, quod verbum ab eo usurpatum infert: & tamen id accidisse etiam, quod Lucas de ipso perhibet, καὶ πρηνὴς γενόμενος ἐλάκησε μέ- σος, καὶ ἐξεχύτη πάντα τα σπλάγχνα ἀυτῶ, & præcipitatus in terram crepuit medius, & effusa sunt omnia viscera ejus. Quæ hic est repugnantia, quæ oppositio? Nam ne mirum quidem, ne- dum ἀδύνατον quendam se ex alto suspendentem & strangulantem laqueo rupto præcipitem, sa- xo cuidam aspero, vel ligno acuto illisum, vel etiam absque tali illisione medium crepare, ac viscera effundere, sive violentia casus, sive sin- gulari vindicis Dei judicio, venter medius cre- puisse statuatur. Quanquam Epiphanius prius viscera effudisse, ac deinde ἀγχόνη χρησάμενον adhibito suspendio interiisse, æstimet. Sed prior explicatio relationi historicæ magis congruit.

Quia projectis argenteis in templo ἀνεχώρησε καὶ ἀπελθὼν ἀπήγξατο secessit, & profectus strangu- lavit sese, & præcipitatus crepuit medius, & effusa sunt omnia viscera ejus. Schmidius ad Act. I. ita habet: Haud dubie hisce singulare exemplum suspen- sionis innuitur, quod Judas ex altiore loco, in quo laqueum certo loco affixum, collo suo adaptavit, po- stea in extrema desperatione, præceps desilierit, ad- eo ut in subita illa compressione gutturis & viæ respi- rationis, propter aerem respirando haustum inclu- sum, non Peritonæum tantum, sed & cutis abdomi- nis, subito & cum crepitu disrupta fuerit, non si- ne indicio ultionis Divinæ peculiaris. Vide Casaub. in Exerc. ad Baron. XVI. anno 34. num 69. Quod vero vel Pricæus, & Vossius Judam se præcipitem ex alto dedisse è desperatione, vel alius quispiam ipsum à Diabolo in aerem raptum & in terram præ- cipitatum esse asserunt, ἄτεργράφως dicitur, nec cum Matthæo, qui strangulatione & suspendio eum vitam sibi ademisse perhibet, convenit: in quo consentiunt Apollinarius Hieropolitan. apud Euse- bium lib. V. Hist. Eccles. cap. 14. Prudentius in Psychopanaych. Chrysost. Serm. III. de Juda. Nazianz. de Christo patiente. Augustinus lib. L. homiliar. hom. 27. Leo II. serm. IIL de pass. Juvencus lib. IV. Evangel. Hist. Arator lib. X. Hist. Beda in c. 1. Actor. Oecum. Bernhardus, Ruper- tus Tuitiensis, Drogo Hostiensis, cum Syro & Arabe ut & Æthiope, ac Persa Interpp. Leo serm. 3. Sce- lestior, inquit, omnibus Juda & infelicior extitisti, quem non pænitentia revocavit ad Dominum, sed de- speratio traxit ad laqueum. Antiquis hic ὁμόψηφοι sunt B. Luther. Osiander, Dn. Cramerus, Arculanus &c. nec nor à Reformatis Calvinus, Gualterus, Pi- scator, Junius, Casaubonus, Salmasius: è Pontifi- ciis Salmero Dionys. Carthusianus à Rickes Franc. de Mendoza, Jansenius, Cornelius à Lapide, Tirinus &c. Adde his, quæ habet B. Dn. D. Danhawverus in Programm. ad Latronem Theologum B. D. Dor- schei. Qui dicunt Judam in sublime à Diabolo raptum & strangulatum, ac præcipitem datum, ita ut ad terram illisus medius rumperetur, quod post Joh. Lightfootum in Matth. Hor. Hebraic. p. 307. D. Henr. Möltero Rostochiensis etiam placuit in Jesu patiente p. 83. testimonio & autoritate o- mni destituuntur. Neque enim sequitur Diabo- lum eum strangulasse, quia eum jam per triduum inhabitarat; Causa moralis strangulationis Dia- bolus fuit, non physica. Neque post mortem de- mum Judam Ischariotham idque ab אשכרא strangulatio dictum, quod ex Lightfooto prolixe repetit Möllerus probari potest, aut si à strangula- tione ita nuncupatus fuerit, consequens est, eum à Diabolo strangulatum esse: nectuntur enim ita funiculi ex arena, quod Criticis oppido solemne est. Vossius Harm. Evangel. lib. I. c. 11. §. 8. Judam dici vult ab איש vir & כריות Carioth, quæ est urbs Judæ, Jos. XV. 25.

## 27:6
Verse 6. τὸν κορβανᾶν] Josephus, Wars II, calls it the sacred treasury; it is called κορβονᾶς. Elsewhere the same Josephus and Luke call it the treasury. Josephus also calls it money, and the treasury of God.

ἐπεὶ τιμὴ αἵματός ἐςι] An argument taken from the reason of the law. The law forbids the price of prostitution to be brought into sacred things. But among the Hebrews, the worship of idols, prostitution, and murder are considered as equals. Here the impure chief priests condemn themselves when they execrate in the seller the crime of which they themselves were the buyers. But certainly, he to whose advantage the crime is, has committed it.

Latin:

Vers. 6. τὸν κορβανᾶν] Josephus ἁλώσεως ΙΙ. τὸν ἱερὸν θη- σαυρὸν καλεῖται δὲ κορβονᾶς. Alibi γαζοφυλάκιον idem Jo- sephus & Lucas appellant. Josephus etiam χρήματα, & θεῦ θησαυρὸν.

ἐπεὶ τιμὴ αἵματός ἐςι] Argumentum à ratione legis de- sumtum. Vetat lex stupri pretium sacris inferri. At apud Hæbræos, cultus idolorum, stuprum, cædes velut paria cen- sentur. Damnant hic se impuri Pontifices cum in vendi- tore id facinus execrantur, cujus ipsi emtores erant. At certe cui prodest scelus is fecit.

## 27:7
Verse 7. τὸν ἀγρὸν τῶ κεράμεως] It must have been a place of little value, since it was not appraised at more than thirty silver shekels. Therefore, I understand here by the potter's field one whose entire richness had been exhausted for pottery works, so that no fruit could be hoped for from it.

from regions were arriving at Jerusalem for the sake of religion; and being overtaken by death, they had nowhere to be buried: the 'sojourners' in Acts 2:10. It is credible that there was a provision for their burial beforehand. But the huge multitude of those flowing in and dying one after another required more space.

Latin:

V. 7. τὸν ἀγρὸν τῶ κεράμεως] Exigui pretii locum fuisse o- portet qui triginta siclis argenteis non pluris licuerit. Quare ἀγρὸν κεράμεως hic intelligo eum cujus uber omne ad figlina opera exhaultum fuerit, ita ut nullus inde fructus sperari posset.

gionibus Hierosolyma adventabant religionis ergo; ac morte occupati non habebant ubi sepelirentur: οἱ ἐπιδημοῦν- τες Act. II. 10. Credibile est & ante prospectum fuisse eo- rum sepulturæ. Sed ingens confluentium & subinde mo- rientium multitudo plus loci desiderabat.

## 27:8
Verse 8. ἀγρὸς αἵματος.] In the Jerusalem dialect, חקל דמא, Acts 1:19. God willed that this name be given to this field so that the memory of the event might be more celebrated. In Peter's speech, Judas is said to have acquired this field, not as his own property, but as an eternal monument of infamy. For the people passing by would say, 'This is that field bought with the money by which Judas sold his master.'

Latin:

Vers. 8. ἀγρὸς αἵματος.] Dialecto Hierosolymitana חקל דמא Act. I. 19. id nomen huic agro datum Deus voluit quo celebrior esset rei memoria. In Petri oratione Judas hunc agrum acquisivisse dicitur, non tanquam rem suam, sed tanquam æternum infamiæ monumentum. Dicebat enim populus præteriens, hic est ager ille emtus ex pecu- nia qua Judas magistrum suum vendidit.

## 27:9
Verse 9. Διὰ Ἰερεμίου] It must be held for certain that many oracles of the ancient prophets were preserved among the Jews not in writing but by memory, although afterwards those who had received them from their parents annotated them privately, whence it happened that those oracles did not exist in the books compiled by Ezra. The expectation of a universal conflagration, celebrated even among the Greeks, could not but have originated from some prophecy, which prophecy Josephus does not fear to ascribe to Adam himself. Such also is that of Enoch: 'Behold, the Lord came with ten thousands of his holy ones,' and what follows in Jude 14, 15. Such is that: 'What eye has not seen, and ear has not heard, and has not entered into the heart of man, which God has prepared for those who love him,' which was celebrated in antiquity among the sayings of Elijah. Such also is that 'ancient saying of men' mentioned by Josephus: that the city would then be captured and the holy places burned by the law of war, if sedition should strike, and domestic hands should first defile the temple of God. And that oracle among the same: that the city and the temple would be captured when the sanctuary should become square. Now, indeed, it must also be known that later prophets were accustomed to use the words of the older prophets. Thus, Ezekiel has many things taken word for word from Jeremiah, as appears by comparing the passages Jer. 31:29, 30; Ezek. 18:1, 2, 3, 4, and elsewhere. So also in the Apocalypse of John, one can find many passages from Ezekiel and Daniel. And that which, from ancient tradition, of which Origen makes mention, and after him Jerome, as we cited of Elijah, Isaiah 64:3 borrowed from Elijah. Especially, however, Zechariah loves to imitate the expressions of Jeremiah. For who does not see that what is in him, ch. 1:4, is taken from Jer. 48:11? & XXXV. 15. which is with him I. 6. from Lam. Jer. II. 17. which is III. 8. from Jer. XXIII. 5. and other things of this kind: for which reason the Jews are also accustomed to say that the spirit of Jeremiah was in Zechariah, and indeed that Jeremiah and Zechariah are the same. Wherefore I do not see what prevents God from having willed that this saying also concerning the thirty shekels, originally used by Jeremiah and preserved in the memory of men, be repeated through Zechariah: which, however, is cited here by Christ in the name of the first author, although it does not exist in the books written by him. But Jerome says that a book was shown to him by a man of the Nazarene sect in which this existed under the name of Jeremiah, which book contained a private annotation of a tradition handed down from antiquity by the mouths of the Hebrews. Such annotations, however, because they were not made by public authority, are deservedly called ἀπόκρυφοι, yet that does not prevent many things both true and ancient from being contained in them. Thus the same Zechariah took that, The Lord rebuke thee O Satan! from an ancient tradition, which was afterwards written down in an apocryphal book whose title is the Assumption of Moses. Moreover, that passage among the Ephesians: ἔγειραι ὁ καθεύδων, καὶ ἀνάστα ἐκ τῶν νεκρῶν, καὶ ἐπιφαύσει σοι ὁ χριστὸς, the Greeks note was taken from the so-called apocrypha of Jeremiah. Just as that [saying] neither circumcision is anything nor uncircumcision, but a new creation: was celebrated in antiquity under the name of Moses. But that which some think, that the name of Jeremiah was added by a bold copyist when Matthew had named the Prophet, I cannot approve, because I see that from the times of Origen there was effort to resolve this knot: which labor would have been superfluous if any copies had lacked the name of Jeremiah. Nor indeed could the error of one transcriber have flowed into all copies. It is much more credible that the name was omitted by the Syrian, because it was known that this was not found in the writings of Jeremiah. But the Arab and the Latin and all the ancients acknowledge it. This saying of Jeremiah, repeated by Zechariah, is of the kind that would originally signify the affairs of their times, yet in such a way that they would also correspond even more to the times of Christ, which God made manifest by a singular direction of events. For with Zechariah this sense is primarily intended, such as it is credible to have been with Jeremiah: that God, in order to teach that his benefits bestowed upon the Hebrew people were received too ungratefully, says that the reward for the labor spent upon them was demanded by him. And a vile price was assigned to him by the people, at which the least of slaves are accustomed to be valued, thirty shekels. He, however, ordered that price to be thrown into some field into which fragments of pottery were accustomed to be thrown: by which act he wished to demonstrate that all the pomp of ceremonies, by which the Hebrews thought they were returning excellent thanks for divine benefits, when a pious mind was absent, was unworthy to be accepted by him. And this whole thing, just as it pertained to the times of Jeremiah and Zechariah, so was much more appropriate to the times of Christ. And therefore it happened by the governance of divine providence, that what was then said enigmatically, in the age of Christ, while the sense remained in analogy, was fulfilled even according to the literal meaning of the words: which kind of fulfillment of prophecies in this history of the death of Christ chief priests in Christ at thirty shekels, when the traitor was worth so much in Christ: and that money was truly cast into the potter's field not so much spent as contemptuously thrown, by the deed of the priests, but by divine counsel: whence what they did is rightly ascribed to God directing it.

κj ἔλαβον] ἔλαβον, and what follows ἔδωκαν are to be taken here indefinitely without any consideration of person or number. For the deed is noted, not who does it. Among Zechariah, it is commanded to Zechariah himself that he do it, and in that way render the ungrateful spirit of the people attested. Here, however, God took care that the very same thing be done through the priests: which the following clause shows: καθὼς συνέταξέ μοι κύριος. But by whomever it is done, the same meaning remains. Wherefore the Syrian, who used the first person verb here, did not sin at all: whom if we wish to follow, that ἔδωκαν will have to be changed into ἔδωκα.

τὰ τριάκοντα ἀργύρια] Supply νομίσματα as we said above. The LXX, Symmachus, Aquila, τριάκοντα ἀργυρὂς supply shekels. See what we said above.

τὴν τιμὴν τῶ τετιμημένα] אדר היקר in Zechariah. אדר is price, yet not as it signifies value, but as it signifies honor, but these are accustomed to be interchanged. But Matthew's interpreter seems to have read הַיְקָר. For יָקָר is an adjective; and it signifies both precious, or as it is brought out here, both valued, when יְקָר is a noun signifying glory or reverence. The LXX translate: Look if it is acceptable: clearly showing by that 'look' the irony of the saying. Aquila is sufficiently literal: the price is very great, an excellent price.

ὃν ἐτιμήσαντο ἀπὸ ὑιῶν Ἰσραὴλ] Matthew's interpreter referred what follows אֲשֶׁר to τετιμημένον, in the way we have already said it was taken by him from הַיָּקָר. Aquila to the price: therefore he translated which I was valued at by them. The LXX for how they translate: in what manner I was tested by them. For they put δοκιμάζειν entirely for τιμᾷν, as Plato does when he says to be tested by men. ἐτιμήσαντο is placed here for that which is in the Prophet ἐτιμήθην: rightly: because there God speaks: here the matter is narrated. ἀπὸ ὑιῶν is rightly explained as ἐξ ὑιῶν. For those prepositions are equivalent. Thus below in verse 21 it is said some of the two. But here is an ellipsis of the word some. A similar one is to be noted above XXIII. 34. Mark VI. 43. Luke XI. 44. ch. XXI. 16. Acts XXI. 16. Thus also Abydenus in the history of Sisithrus, by which name he calls Noah: some of the birds, that is, some of the birds. John ch. XVI. 17. εἶπον ὖν ἐκ ἦ μαθητῶν, that is, some of the disciples. Such also is that above, take from the garment, that is, something from the garment, ch. IX. 26.

Now the nearest Ucalegon burns:

That this field, which Zechariah mentions, was not far from the temple is indicated by that which is added בֵּית יְהוָה: whether this was also in Jeremiah's saying can be doubted. Perhaps from that field soil was accustomed to be taken for the pottery of the Temple: so that it is the same place as שַׁעַר הַחַרְסִית Jer. XIX. 2. with the ס clearly put for שׁ which is not without example. For what Kimchi interprets as treasurer, is without example: for wherever it is found, it signifies a potter, and therefore the LXX translate it potter. Isaiah XLI. 26. Lamentations IV. 2. Aquila in this place cast them to the potter. Among the LXX it seems to be called a smelting furnace abusively for that which should have been called a pottery: of which kind of abuses one can find examples among them everywhere.

Latin:

Vers. 9. Διὰ Ἰερεμίου] Pro certo haberi debet multa apud Judæos vatum veterum oracula conservata fuisse non scri- pto sed memoria, quanquam postea qui a Parentibus acce- perant ea privatim annotarunt, unde factum est ut ea oracu- la in libris ab Esdra digestis non exstarent. Ἐκπυρώσεως uni- versalis exspectatio, etiam Græcis celebrata, non potuit non ab aliquo vaticinio ortum habuisse, quod quidem vatici- nium ipsi Adamo adscribere non veretur Josephus. Tale est & Enochi illud: ἰδοὺ ἦλθε κύριος ἐν μυρίασιν ἁγίαις αὑτοῦ, & quæ sequuntur apud Judam 14. 15. Tale illud ὃ ὀφθαλμὸς οὐκ εἶδε, καὶ οὖς οὐκ ἤκουσεν, καὶ ἐπὶ καρδίαν ἀνθρώπων οὐκ ἀνέβη, ἃ ἡτοίμασεν ὁ θεὸς τοῖς ἀγαπῶσιν αὐτόν: quod inter Eliæ dicta antiquitus celebrabatur. Talis & ille παλαιὸς λόγος ἀνδρῶν Josepho memoratus: ὅτι τότε τὴν πόλιν ἁλώσεσθαι, καὶ καταφλεγήσεσθαι τὰ ἅγια νόμῳ πολέμου, στάσις ἐὰν κατασκήψῃ, καὶ χεῖρες οἰκεῖαι προ- μιάνωσι τὸ τοῦ θεοῦ τέμενος. Et illud λόγιον apud eundem: ἁλώσεσθαι τὴν πόλιν καὶ τὸν ναὸν ἐπειδὰν τὸ ἱερὸν γένηται τετράγω- νον. Jam vero & illud sciendum est, veterum Prophetarum verbis uti solitos Prophetas posteriores. Ita Ezechiel mul- ta habet verbotenus ex Jeremia desumta, ut apparet collatis locis Jer. XXXI. 29. 30. Ezech. XVIII. 1. 2. 3. 4. & alibi. Sic & in Apocalypsi Johannis multas περικοπὰς invenire est ex Ezechiele & Daniele. Et illud quod ex antiqua tradi- tione, cujus Origenes meminit, & post eum Hieronymus, ut Eliæ citavimus, ab Elia mutuatus est Esaias LXIV. 3. Impri- mis autem Zacharias amat imitari locutiones Jeremiæ. Quis enim non videt quod apud eum est c. I. 4. sumtum ex Jer. XIIX. 11. & XXXV. 15. quod est apud eum I. 6. ex Thren. Jer. II. 17. quod est III. 8. ex Jer. XXIII. 5. atque a- lia ejusmodi: quapropter dicere etiam solent Judæi, spiri- tum Jeremiæ fuisse in Zacharia, atque adeo Jeremiam eun- dem esse & Zachariam. Quare non video quid obstet, quo minus & dictum hoc de triginta siclis, ab Jeremia primitus usurpatum, hominumque memoria conservatum, per Za- chariam repeti Deus voluerit: quod tamen hic a Christo citetur primi auctoris nomine, quanquam in libris ab eo scriptis non exstat. At Hieronymus ostensum sibi ait a Na- zarenæ sectæ homine librum in quo id exstaret sub Jeremiæ nomine, qui liber privatam continuit annotationem famæ antiquitus traditæ per ora Hebræorum. Tales autem anno- tationes, quia publica autoritate factæ non sunt, merito vo- cantur ἀπόκρυφοι, neque tamen id obstat, quo minus in eis multa contineantur & vera & vetera. Sic idem Zacharias il- lud, Increpet te Deus ô Satan! sumsit ex antiqua traditione, quæ deinde perscripta est in libro ἀποκρύφῳ cui titulus ἀνά- ληψις Μωσέως. Quin & illud apud Ephesios: ἔγειραι ὁ κα- θεύδων, καὶ ἀνάστα ἐκ τῶν νεκρῶν, καὶ ἐπιφαύσει σοι ὁ χριστὸς, Græci notant desumtum ἐκ τοῦ Ἱερεμίου λεγομένων ἀποκρύφων. Sicut & illud ὄυτε περιτομή τί ἐστιν οὔτε ἀκροβυστία, ἀλλὰ καινὴ κτίσις: an- tiquitus sub Mosis nomine celebrabatur. Quod autem qui- dam existimant ab audace librario adjectum nomen Iere- miæ, cum Matthæus Prophetam nominasset, probare non possum, quia video jam ab Origenis temporibus laboratum, ut hic nodus solveretur: qui labor supervacuus fuerat si quæ exemplaria caruissent nomine Jeremiæ. Neque vero potuit unius exscriptoris error in omnia exemplaria manare. Mul- to credibilius est a Syro id nomen omissum, quia constabat in scriptis Jeremiæ istud non reperiri. At agnoscit Arabs & Latinus & quicquid est veterum. Dictum autem hoc Iere- miæ, repetitum a Zacharia, in eorum est genere, quæ primi- tus res illorum temporum significarent, ita tamen ut in Christi tempora etiam magis congruerent, quod Deus ma- nifestum fecit singulari eventuum directione. Nam apud Za- chariam sensus hic est primo intentus, qualem & apud Iere- miam fuisse credibile est: Deus ut sua beneficia in populum Hebræum collata ingrate nimis accepta doceat, ait operæ in illos impensæ mercedem a se postulatam. Assignatum autem sibi a populo vile pretium, quo minima æstimari so- lent mancipia, triginta siclos. Se vero illud pretium jussisse projici in agrum aliquem in quem fragmenta fictilium pro- jici solebant: quo facto demonstratum voluit omnem pompam cæremoniarum, qua impleta egregiam se benefi- ciis divinis gratiam referre Hebræi existimabant, cum abesset pius animus, indignam esse quæ a se acceptaretur. Hoc vero omne sicut ad Ieremiæ & Zachariæ tempora pertinebat, ita multo magis congruebat Christi temporibus. Atque ideo factum est divinæ providentiæ gubernatione, ut, quod aἰνιγ- ματικῶς tunc erat dictum, Christi ætate, manente sensu ino κατ' ἀναλογίαν, etiam secundum proprietatem verborum impleretur : quod genus impletionis vaticiniorum in hac mortis Christi historia sæpe occurret. Deus enim in Chri- sto æstimatus est à Pontificibus siclis triginta, cum tanti vmtus est in Christum proditor: atque ea pecunia vere in a- grum figlinum non tam impensa quam contemtim proje- cta est, facto quidem Pontificum, consilio autem divino: unde quodilli fecerunt, recte Deo dirigenti adscribitur.

κj ἔλαβον] ἔλαβον, & quod sequitur ἔδωκαν sumenda hic sunt indefinite sine ulla personæ aut numeri consideratio- ne. Factum enim notatur, non quis faciat. Apud Zacha- riam ipsi Zachariæ ut id faciat, atque eo modo ingratum populi animum testatum reddat, imperatur. Hic vero Deus curavit id ipsum per pontifices fieri: quod ostendit sequens clausula : καθὼς συνέταξέ μοι κύριος. Sed per quem- cunque fiat, eadem manet significatio. Quare nihil pec- cavit Syrus qui hic primæ personæ verbis usus est : quem si sequi volumus erit illud ἔδωκαν mutandum in ἔδωκα.

τὰ τριάκοντα ἀργύρια] Supple νομίσματα ut diximus supra. LXX. Symmachus, Aquila, τριάκοντα ἀργυρὂς sup- ple σίκλους. Vide quæ diximus supra.

τὴν τιμὴν τῶ τετιμημένα] אדר היקר apud Zachariam. אדר est τιμή, non tamen qua pretium, sed qua hono- rem significat, sed hæc solent inter se commutari. Legisse au- tem videtur Matthæi interpres הַיְקָר. Nam יָקָר est ad- jectivum; significatque & τιμήεντα, aut ut hic effertur & τετι- μημένον, cum יְקָר sit substantivum significans gloriam aut reverentiam. LXX. vertunt Σκέψαι εἰ δόκιμόν ἐστι : nimi- rum per illud σκέψαι ostendentes dicti εἰρωνικῶς. Aquila satis ad verbum: ὑπερμεγέθης ἡ τιμὴ, egregium hero pre- tium.

ὃν ἐτιμήσαντο ἀπὸ ὑιῶν Ἰσραὴλ] Matthæi interpres quod sequitur אֲשֶׁר retulit ad & τετιμημένον, quomodo acce- ptum ab eo הַיָּקָר jam diximus. Aquila ad τὴν τιμὴν : ideo ἣν ἐτιμήθην ὑπὲρ ἀυτῶν transtulit. LXX. pro quomo- do sui nunt: ὃν τρόπον ἐδοκιμάσθην ὑπὲρ ἀυτῶν. Nam δο- κιμάζειν omnino illi pro τιμᾷν ponetunt, ut Plato cum di- cit πρὸς ἀνθρώπων δοκιμάζεσθαι. ἐτιμήσαντο hic positum est pro eo quod apud Prophetam ἐτιμήθην : recte : quia ibi Deus loquitur: hic res narratur. ἀπὸ ὑιῶν recte exponitur ἐξ ὑιῶν. Nam istæ præpositiones sunt ἰσοδύναμοι. Ita in- fra commate 21. dicitur τινὰ ἀπὸ τῶν δύο. sed hic est ἔλλει- ψις vocis τινες. Similem notare est supra XXIII. 34. Mar- ci VI. 43. Luc. XI. 44. c. XXI.16. Act. XXI. 16. Sic & A- bydenus in historia de Sisithro, quo nomine Noam appellat: μετέαξ ἦ ὀρνίθων, id est τίνας ἦ ὀρνίθων. Iohannes c. XVI. 17. εἶπον ὖν ἐκ ἦ μαθητῶν, id est τίνες ἐκ ἦ μαθητῶν. Tale est & illud supra αἰρῇ ἀπὸ τῶ ἱματίε, id estτι ἀπὸ τῶ ἱματίε, cap. IX. 26.

Iam proximus ardet Ucalegon:

Neque longe à templo hunc agrum, cujus Zacharias me- minit, fuisse indicio est id quod additur בֵּית יְהוָה : quod an & in Ieremiæ dicto fuerit dubitari potest. Forte ex eo a- gro sumi solebat humus ad fictilia Templi: ut idem sit lo- cus qui שַׁעַר הַחַרְסִית Ierem. XIX. 2. ס nimirum posito pro שׁ quod non caret exemplo. Nam quod יוֹצֵר Kimchi interpretatur & γαζοφύλακα, sine exemplo est: u- bicunque enim reperitur, figulum significat, & proinde κερα- μέα vertunt LXX. Esaix XLI. 26. Thren. IV. 2. Aquila hoc loco ἔῤῥιψον ἀυτὰ πρὸς τ πλάστην. Apud LXX. videtur χω- νευτήριον dictum καταχρηστικῶς pro eo quod dicendum erat κεραμεῖον: cujusmodi abusiones passim apud eos reperire est.

## 27:10
καθὼς συνέταξέ μοι κύριος.] This is not added here in vain from the previous words of the Prophet, so that it may be understood that all these things happened by the dispensation of divine counsel. But when Matthew recites here this saying of Jeremiah repeated through Zechariah, he shows at the same time tacitly that those punishments were impending over the Jews which the same Prophet had once predicted to the men of his own time. For it would come to pass that that people, having been loathed by God and placed outside his protection, would be agitated by internal discords, and at one time would lose those three kinds of shepherds, the civil government as much as still remained, the Priesthood, and Prophecy.

The opinion of those who think the passage is corrupt and the name of Jeremiah was added by some scholar, or changed with the name of Zechariah in abbreviation, is rightly rejected, which Maldonado, Baronius, Jansen, Suarez, Beza, Piscator, Flacius, and Calixtus establish: but against the unanimous consent of the Greek Codices, as also of the Arabic, and the Vulgate Latin interpreter. Others say the book of Jeremiah is mutilated and corrupt: but since other things have been left in the Scripture of the O.T., why would this text have been erased by the Jews? The Socinians themselves attribute a mnemonic lapse to the Evangelist with Pigghe and Melchior Cano, Erasmus not denying it; but the Evangelist wrote carried by the Holy Spirit, and therefore could not slip: Augustine in book III de consensu [evangelistarum] says he put it so intentionally. Ev. ch. 7 wishes, to which the Glossa ordinaria and B. Gerhard agree: because both Jeremiah and Zechariah were moved by one spirit: but even if there is one principal author, his amanuenses should not have been confused: Some say Zechariah was binominal with Erasmus, Joh. Ferus, B. Hunnius, Balduinus, Tarnovius, Fr. Junius, and Francis Gomarus, but concerning the authority. It pleased some [to refer to] ch. XVIII of Jeremiah, where however nothing else occurs except the name of the potter. Others with B. Walther and Glassius recur to Jer. ch. XXXII, or with Sanctius wish the same to be joined with the Zechariah passage, as they are accustomed to be cited in the N.T. under one name, which are conflated from two writers of the O.T.: because at Jeremiah mention is made of the purchase of a field and a potter, and of strangers; but its price was seven and ten staters, or as many shekels, and Jeremiah bought that field for himself and his own. Heinsius wishes Jeremiah ch. XIX to be referred to, where there is mention of a field abominable because of slaughters; and he thinks that only a neat explanation of the Prophet's words is being made, not that a prophecy or a type is being held. But Rivetus himself, following Jerome, called this bending of Scripture, with the reason of sense and analogy neglected, a most vicious kind of speaking. From this, however, Mr. D. Christoph Schlegel took the occasion to establish that this prophecy must be sought not only in Zechariah, whose many words concerning the price are cited, but also in Jeremiah concerning the field, which was bought as to its location, name, and profanation in ch. XIX, which, however, he also wishes to be sought in Jer. ch. XXXI, v. 38, 39, 40, as to its subsequent sanctification in the times of the Messiah. Concerning which he treated at length in his חקל דמא or Field of Blood, published at Leipzig in the year 1665. But ch. XIX. 1. Jeremiah was only commanded to buy for himself a potter's jar (not a field), and to break it in the valley of Ben-Hinnom, because by that reason the city and the people ought to be broken; and to be buried in Topheth: because no other place will remain. But in ch. XXXI. 38 it is predicted that the valley of dead bodies with the whole field as far as the brook Kidron will be sanctified to God, all of which, into whatever forms they are turned, are entirely ἀλλότρια and foreign here, if I may say so with the author's permission, and contribute nothing to the present history, which even a mere inspection of the passages teaches. John Lightfoot in his Hebrew and Talmudic Exercitations on Matthew observed from the Bab. Bava Bathra a tradition of the Rabbis brought forward by David Kimchi in his preface to Jeremiah, that Jeremiah was accustomed to be placed in the first position in this order: Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Isaiah, and the twelve: hence therefore the name was given to the volume of the Prophets from the first in order, just as the volume of the Hagiographa in Luke XXIV. 44 received its naming from the Psalms, which occupy the first place in the same. But that that order of the Prophets prevailed in the time of Matthew, from where will it be taught? Nor are those things which are expressly alleged here read in any of the Prophets. Therefore, that observation of Lightfoot is not to be snatched at rashly, just as by D. Henr. Muller in

Jesu Patiente p. 69. factum, who furthermore touted it as his own, while concealing the name of the author, Lightfoot.

Since, therefore, this prophecy is found written in no text of Jeremiah, one must altogether admit that it was spoken by Jeremiah, whose testimony is here openly cited: nor is it permitted to doubt that it was correctly adduced in Matthew, just as it was once uttered by the Prophet: since his very words are recounted, even if they are not contained in the Prophecy of Jeremiah: not that it was erased, for the integrity of Scripture does not permit that, nor would divine providence have allowed it, but that it was handed down by word of mouth, and not at that time recorded in the Holy Scriptures, but now suggested by the Holy Spirit to St. Matthew, and by His inspiration reduced to the Canonical Scripture of the New Testament Code. The text teaches that the very words of St. Jeremiah are recited: Τότε ἐπληρώθη τὸ ῥηθὲν διὰ ἰερεμίου τοῦ Προφήτου λέγοντος, so that it might be fulfilled which was spoken by Jeremiah the Prophet SAYING. But what DOES Jeremiah the Prophet SAY? καὶ ἔλαβον τὰ τριά- κοντα ἀργύρια, τὴν τιμὴν τοῦ τετιμημένου, ὃν ἐτι- μήσαντο ἀπὸ υἱῶν Ἰσραὴλ, κὶ ἔδωκεν αὐτὰ εἰς έἀ- γρὸν τοῦ κεραμέως, καθ' συνέταξέ μοι Κύριος. Because he cites the words of the Prophet Jeremiah so extensively, and recites them αὐτολεξεὶ, though translated into Greek, who can doubt that they were uttered by the Prophet, whom the Evangelist thus makes DICENTEM, or asserts to have spoken? And Matthew notably says, not that it was written thus by the Prophet, but that it was spoken, τὸ ῥηθὲν: which, although it also occurs at times when Scripture is alleged, yet there is no doubt that it is strictly applied here, where such a prophecy is alleged which is nowhere read in the Old Testament; which is also detected in some other places, such as Matt. II. 23, Jude v. 14, 25. To this opinion of ours also B. D. Keslerus adds his support in his inaugural dissertation on the sayings of Scripture alleged in the New Testament, along with Origen and Jerome in this place. Tertul. l. IV. contr. Marc. c. XXXIX. Dionys. Carthus. Salmerone & others, as well as from the Reformed side Joh. Gerhard. Vossius Harm. Evang. de pass. & resurr. Christi page 210. and Fr. Gomarus T. I. Oper. p. 143. is not of a different mind, comparing the saying of Christ in Acts XX. 35. which is nowhere expressed by the Evangelists, and the appearance of Christ after the resurrection, both that which was made to more than 500 brethren, and that which was made to James, 1. Cor. XV. 6. which is nowhere described by the Evangelists.

Nor can the Papists seek anything from this for their ἀγράφοις traditions. For this testimony has divine authority, after the Canon of Scripture was completed, not as ἄγραφον, but because it was brought forward by the Holy Spirit Himself in the Canonical Scripture. Whence no patronage is provided here for ἀγράφοις traditions by any reasoning; because this tradition is not ἄγραφος, but is expressed and contained in the Canon of the N. T.

Furthermore, it cannot be approved in Grotius that he judges the Apostles to have drawn their material either from memory or from non-Canonical writings, whereas we know that they had everything they wrote from the inspiration of the Holy Scriptures: nor do those things which he relates from Josephus concerning the prophecy of Adam, and παλαιῷ λόγῳ ἀνδρῶν, and from others concerning the saying of Elijah, enjoy certainty, nor finally does that deserve approval which he says, that the more recent Prophets transcribed their material from the more ancient ones: although we do not deny that the same Spirit, the author of Scripture, sometimes inspired similar things in different Prophets, just as it pleased Him, in the way that this saying of Jeremiah was in part repeated by Zechariah. We also acknowledge no authority in what is brought forward from the Nazarene Sect: &

Whatever of this kind is brought forward here is ἀκανόνισον. But the things which Grotius subsequently added concerning the sense of tradition, or the genuine meaning of the words of Jeremiah or Zechariah, have already been examined at Chapter XI of Zechariah, so that there is no need to add anything to these.

Latin:

καθὼς συνέταξέ μοι κύριος.] Hoc ex superioribus Prophe- tæ verbis non frustra hic additum, ut intelligantur hæc o- mnia divini consilii dispensatione accidisse. Cum autem hoc dictum Ieremiæ per Zachariam repetitum hic recitat Matthæus, simul ostendit tacite eas pœnas imminere Iu- dæis quas eidem Prophetæ olim sui temporis hominibus prædixerant. Fore enim ut populus ille à Deo fastiditus, & extra ejus tutelam positus, intestinis discordiis agitaretur, atque uno tempore amitteret tria illa pastorum genera, im- perium civile quantum adhuc restabat, Sacerdotium & Pro- phetiam.

Recte reprobatur eorum sententia qui locum corruptum & nomen Jeremiæ à Sciolo quodam adjectum, vel cum Zachariæ nomine in abbrevia- tura commutatum putant, quod statuunt Maldo- natus, Baron. Jansen. Suarez, Beza, Piscator, Flacius & Calixtus: sed contra unanimem Codi- cum Græcorum, ut & Arabis, & Vulgati Latine interpretis consensum. Alii librum Ieremiæ mu- tilatum & corruptum esse dicunt: sed quum alia in Scriptura V. T. relicta sunt, qui hic textus era- sus esset à Judæis? Sociniani ipsimet Evangelistæ lapsum μνημονευτικὸν tribuunt cum Piggio, & Melch. Cano, non abnuente Erasmo; sed scripsit Evangelista ὑπὸ πνεύματος ἁγίε φερόμενος, ideoque labi non potuit: studiole ita posuisse eum Augustinus l. III. de consens. Ev. c. 7. vult, cui annuit Glossa ordinaria, & B. Gerhardus: quia uno & Ie- remias & Zacharias acti fuere spiritu: sed etiamsi unus autor sit principalis, confundi tamen ama- nuenses ejus non debuere: Nonnulli Zachariam fuille binominem ajunt cum Erasmo, Iob. Fero, B. Hunnio, Balduino, Tarnovio, Fr. Iunio, & Fran- cisco Gomaro, sed circa autoritatem. Quibusdam placuit c. XIIX. Ier. ubi vero nihil aliud præter no- men figuli occurrit. Alii cum B. Walthero & Glaslio recurrunt ad Ier. c. XXXII. vel cum San- ctio eundem cum loco Zachariano conjungi vo- lunt, uti solent in N. T. sub unius nomine allega- ri, quæ è duobus Scriptoribus V. T. conflata sunt: quia apud Ieremiam empti agri & figuli, & peregri- norum mentio facta; sed illius pretium septem & decem stateres, vel totidem sicli fuerunt, emitque eum agrum pro se & suis Ieremias. Heinsius respici vult Ierem. c. XIX. ubi agri ob cædes abominabilis mentio; & explicationem solum concinnam ver- borum Prophetæ fieri putat, non haberi vatici- nium, vel typum. Quam vero Scripturæ inflexio- nem, sensus & analogiæ ratione posthabita, vitiosif- simum dicendi genus Rivetus ipse nominavit ex Hieronymo. Inde tamen occasionem Dn. D. Chri- stophorus Schlegel. sumpsit statuendi, quod hæc Pro- phetia quærenda sit non modo apud Zachariam, cu- jus plura verba de pretio citata, sed etiam apud Ie- remiam de agro, qui emptus est quoad situm, no- men, & profanationem c. XIX. quam tamen etiam quæri vult Ier. c. XXXI. v. 38. 39. 40. quoad subse- quutam ejus sanctificationem temporibus Mes- siæ. De quo prolixe in חקל דמא vel agro san- guinis Lipsiæ Anno 1665. edito egit. Sed c. XIX. 1. Jeremias jussus tantum est sibi figulinam ollam (non agrum) emere, eamque in valle Ben Hinnon confringere, quod ea ratione civitas & populus confringi debeant; & in Topheth sepeliri: quia locus alius non supererit. At c. XXXI. 38. prædici- tur vallem funerum cum toto agro usque ad torren- tem Kidron Deo sanctificatum iri, quæ omnia, quas- cunque in formas vertantur, ἀλλότρια prorsus, & aliena hic sunt, ut pace Autoris id dicam, nec quic- quam ad præsentem historiam faciunt, quod vel sola inspectio locorum docet. Ioh. Lightfoot in horis Hebraicis & Talmudicis ad Matthæum observavit è Bab. Bava Bathra traditionem Rabbi- norum à Dav. Kimchio in præf. ad Jeremiam addu- ctam, quod Jeremias primo loco collocari con- sueverit hoc ordine, Ieremias, Ezechiel, Esaias, & duodecim: hinc ergo volumini Prophetarum à primo in ordine nomen datum, uti volumen Hagio- graphorum Luc. XXIV. 44. à Psalmis nuncupatio- nem accepit, primum locum in eodem obtinentibus. Sed tempore Matthæi obtinuisse illum Propheta- rum ordinem, unde docebitur? Neque illa quæ hic ῥητῶς allegantur, in ullo Prophetarum legur- tur. Ideo non temere arripienda illa Lightfooti ob- servatio, quemadmodum à D. Henr. Muliero in

Jesu Patiente p. 69. factum, qui eam insuper ceu propriam venditavit, dissimulato autoris Lightfoo- ti nomine.

Quum ergo in nullo textu Jeremiæ scriptum reperiatur hoc vaticinium, omnino fateri oportet id à Jeremia dictum esse, cujus hic aperte laudatur testimonium: neque dubitare licet, quin recte in Matthæo id adductum sit, quemadmodum à Pro- pheta id quondam prolatum fuit: quum ipsissima ejus verba recenseantur, etsi in Prophetia Jeremiæ non habeantur: non quod erasum sit, id enim in- tegritas Scripturæ non permittit, nec concessisset divina providentia, sed quod oretenus traditum, nec in S. Scripturas isto tempore relatum, jam vero à S. S. Matthæo suggestum, ejusque inspiratione in Codicis N. T. Scripturam Canonicam redactum sit. Verba ipsa S. Jeremiæ recitari textus docet: Τότε ἐπληρώθη τὸ ῥηθὲν διὰ ἰερεμίου τοῦ Προφήτου λέγοντος, ut impleretur quod dictum est per Jere- miam Prophetam DICENTEM. Quid vero DI- CIT Jeremias Propheta? καὶ ἔλαβον τὰ τριά- κοντα ἀργύρια, τὴν τιμὴν τοῦ τετιμημένου, ὃν ἐτι- μήσαντο ἀπὸ υἱῶν Ἰσραὴλ, κὶ ἔδωκεν αὐτὰ εἰς έἀ- γρὸν τοῦ κεραμέως, καθ' συνέταξέ μοι Κύριος. Quia tam prolixe verba Prophetæ Jeremiæ adducit, ea- demque αὐτολεξεὶ, translata tamen in Græcum, recitat, ecquis dubitare potest, eadem à Propheta, quem ita λέγοντα DICENTEM facit Evangelista, seu loquutum esse perhibet, prolata esse? Et no- tanter ait Matthæus, non scriptum sic esse à Pro- pheta, sed dictum, τὸ ῥηθὲν: quod quamvis et- iam interdum occurrat, cum Scriptura allegatur, tamen hic stricte adhibitum esse, dubitandum non est, ubi tale vaticinium allegatur, quod in Vet. Test. nuspiam legitur; quod etiam in aliis nonnul- lis locis deprehenditur, utpote Matth. II. 23. Jud. v. 14. 25. Accedit huic sententiæ nostræ etiam B. D. Keslerus disp. inaug. de dictis Scripturæ allega- tis in N. Test. cum Origen. Hieron. in h. l. Tertul. l. IV. contr. Marc. c. XXXIX. Dionys. Carthus. Sal- merone & aliis, nec non è Reformatis Joh. Gerhard. Vossius Harm. Evang. de pass. & resurr. Christi pag. 210. nec alienus est Fr. Gomarus T. I. Oper. p. 143. conferens dictum Christi Act. XX. 35. nullibi ab Evangelistis expressum, & apparitionem Christi post resurrectionem, tum quæ plusquam 500. fratribus, tum quæ Jacobo facta est, 1. Cor. XV. 6. ab Evan- gelistis nuspiam descriptam.

Ne vero quicquam inde pro traditionibus ἀ- γράφοις petere possunt Papistæ. Nam autorita- tem habet hoc testimonium divinam, post Cano- nem scripturæ absolutum, non ut ἄγραφον, sed quia in Scriptura Canonica ab ipso Spiritu Sancto adductum est. Unde hic traditionibus ἀγρά- φοις nulla ratione patrocinium præbetur; quia traditio hæc non ἄγραφος est, sed Canone N. T. expressa, & comprehensa.

Cæterum probari in Grotio non potest, quod vel è memoria, vel è Scriptis non-Canonicis sua de- promsisse Apostolos censet, quos novimus omnia è S. S. inspiratione habuisse, quæ scripsêre: neque certitudine gaudent, quæ è Josepho de Vaticinio Adami, & παλαιῷ λόγῳ ἀνδρῶν, ex aliis de dicto Eliæ, tradit, nec denique calculum meretur, quod ait, Prophetas recentiores ex antiquioribus sua ex- scripsisse: etsi non diffiteamur similia eundem Scripturæ autorem Spiritum quandoque diversis Prophetis inspirasse, prout nempe ipsi placuit, quomodo dictum hoc Jeremiæ ex parte à Zacha- ria repetitum. Nullius etiam autoritatis agno- scimus, quod è Secta Nazarena profertur: &

quicquid ejusmodi hic adducitur ἀκανόνισον. Quæ vero deinde subjunxit Grotius, de sensu traditionis, vel verborum Jeremiæ, aut Zachariæ genuino, excussa jam sunt ad Zach. XI. Caput, ut nihil his addere opus sit.

## 27:11
Vers. 11. σὺ εἶ ὁ βασιλεὺς τῶν Ἰουδαίων] For when the chief priests had delivered Jesus to Pilate with this title, because they thought that this charge of aspiring to a kingdom would be most effective for Pilate to sentence Jesus to death: they were meanwhile condemning themselves, as those who most eagerly expected a Messiah who would be a king of a visible kingdom and an overthrower of Roman rule.

σὺ λέγεις] This is that famous confession of which Paul makes mention in 1 Tim. VI. 13. But since Jesus here confesses himself to be a king, it seems to me impossible to deny that his kingdom was in some way begun when he began to teach the truth: for thus he himself interprets the kingdom in John. Nor is it an obstacle that the beginning of his kingdom is everywhere seen to be traced from his exaltation into heaven: for that can be understood of the full possession of the kingdom. And indeed it may seem that David also in this matter bore an image of Jesus. For he too was first anointed king, after that received some portion of the kingdom, and soon received the right of the kingdom in its entirety, 2 Sam. II. & V. Certainly the power of remitting sins, which Jesus exercised while leading a mortal life, pertained to the kingdom, as did also that most free power of dispensing miracles at will.

Latin:

Vers. 11. σὺ εἶ ὁ βασιλεὺς τῶν Ἰουδαίων] Nam cum hoc e- logio Pontifices Jesum Pilato tradiderant, quia hoc cri- men affectati regni maxime putabant valiturum ut Pilatus Jesum morti addiceret: semet interim capitis damnantes, ut qui Messiam Regem regni aspectabilis, & eversorem Romani dominationis, avidissime expectarent.

σὺ λέγεις] Hæc est præclara illa confessio, cujus memi- nit Paulus 1. Tim. VI. 13. Cum vero Jesus hic regem se fateatur, negari mihi videtur non posse regnum ejus ali- quomodo inchoatum esse cum veritatem cœpit docere: nam ita ipse apud Johannem regnum interpretatur. Ne- que obstat quod passim regni ejus initium duci videtur ab evectione in cœlum: id enim de plena regni possessione intelligendum potest. Et sane videri potest David etiam hac in re imaginem Jesu gessisse. Nam & is primum in re- gem unctus est, post id regni portione aliqua accepta, mox jusregni in solidum accepit, 2. Sam. II. & V. Certe potestas remittendi peccata, quam Jesus vitam mortalem agens ex- ercuit, ad regnum pertinebat, ut & liberrima illa miracu- lorum pro arbitrio dispensandorum potestas.

## 27:12
Vers. 12. καὶ ἐν τῷ κατηγορεῖσθαι αὐτὸν] This was the second and more intense accusation, when the chief priests had seen that Pilate was not much moved by the former charge, as we learn from Luke. This was done in the presence of the accused, according to Roman custom, Acts XXV. v. 16.

οὐδὲν ἀπεκρίνατο] The reason for his silence, besides a deliberate endurance of death, was this: that before a religious judge such an accusation would vanish of its own accord. For in cases of high treason, as Modestinus says, the person must be considered as to whether he could have committed it. But the very nature of the case sufficiently freed Jesus, a man of plebeian rank, having no forces of armed men and no garrisons, from this suspicion. But if Pilate, as was the case, wished to gratify his own religion to the Jews, all defense was superfluous. See what has been said above, chap. XXVI. 63. And compare that passage of Isaiah, ולא יפתח פיו, chap. LIII. 7.

Latin:

Vers. 12. καὶ ἐν τῷ κατηγορεῖσθαι αὐτὸν] Hæc erat secun- da & intentior accusatio, cum vidissent Pontifices Pilatum priori criminatione non multum moveri, ut ex Luca disci- mus. Hæc reo coram facta, more Romano, Act. XXV. v. 16.

οὐδὲν ἀπεκρίνατο] Causa silentii, præter deliberatam mor- tis patientiam, hæc erat, quod apud religiosum judicem accusatio ista sua sponte evanesceret. Nam in criminibus majestatis, ut Modestinus inquit, persona spectanda est an potuerit facere. Jesum autem, plebejæ sortis hominem, nullas habentem armatorum copias, præsidia nulla, res ipsa satis ab hac suspicione liberabat. Quod si Pilatus, ut fa- ctum est, vellet suam religionem Judæis gratificari, super- vacua erat omnis defensio. Vide quæ dicta sunt, supra cap. XXVI. 63. Et confer illud Esaiæ ולא יפתח פיו cap. LIII. 7.

## 27:13
Vers. 13. πόσα σου καταμαρτυροῦσι] They brought forward many things indeed, but partly those for which they could not provide assurance, as concerning the non-payment of tributes, and partly things not at all pertaining to His Majesty, as concerning the doctrine spread throughout all Judaea. Neither sort stood in need of refutation.

Ambrose says it beautifully; The Lord is accused, and he is silent, and he is rightly silent who does not need a defense. Let those who fear being defeated seek to be defended. Therefore, he does not confirm the accusation by being silent, but he shows contempt for it by not refuting it. And the Author of the imperfect work, homily 38: One can better overcome an evil man by being silent than by responding, because malice is not instructed by words, but excited. Therefore, the Lord strove to restrain by silence those whom he could not restrain by responding. Furthermore, whatever he had done and said had been done and said in the public light: therefore, they needed no excuse or declaration. And the things that were brought forward were openly false and notorious calumnies. Moreover, he knew that he would obtain nothing by a response. For since they could not endure with an even mind the calm silence and gentle patience of Christ, how would they hear his excuse with fair ears? Furthermore, he wished to testify by this silence that he was approaching death of his own accord and voluntarily. Those who die against their will are accustomed to bring forward various excuses. But Christ, standing before the governor, burdened with the sins of the whole world, is silent, so that he might show that he is willing to die on account of the sins laid upon him. Finally, he wished to go before us in this way by the example of patience: which is so great that Cyprian rightly marvels at it in his work On the Good of Patience. Among other admirable mighty works, by which he expressed the judgments of divine majesty, he also maintained fatherly patience through the tenor of his endurance.

Latin:

Vers. 13. πόσα σου καταμαρτυροῦσι] Multa quidem adfere- bant, sed partim ea quorum fidem implere non poterant, ut de non solvendis tributis, partim nihil pertinentia ad Maje- statem, ut de doctrina sparsa per omnem Judæam. Neutra refutationis egebant.

Pulcre Ambrosius; Accusatur Dominus, & ta- cet, & bene tacet qui defensione non indiget. Am- biant defendi qui timent vinci. Non ergo accusa- tionem tacendo confirmat, sed contemnit non refel- lendo. Et Autor oper. imperf. hom. 38. Ma- lum hominem melius tacendo aliquis potest vincere, quam respondendo, quia malitia non instruitur ser- monibus, sed excitatur. Ideo Dominus tacendo compescere studuit, quos respondendo compescere non potuit. Adhæc quæcunque egerat ac dixerat, in publica luce erant gesta & dicta: nulla igitur excusatione vel declaratione indigebant. Et quæ proferebantur, palam falsa erant, ac notoriæ ca- lumniæ. Tum vero noverat se nihil responso ob- tenturum. Quum enim non potuerint æquo a- nimo placidam taciturnitatem ac mansuetam pa- tientiam Christi sustinere, quomodo æquis auri- bus excusationem ipsius audirent? Porro testari hoc silentio voluit, se sponte ac voluntarie mor- tem adire. Qui inviti moriuntur, varias excu- sationes proferre solent. At Christus coram præ- fide stans totius mundi peccatis onustus tacet, ut propter peccata sibi imposita sese volentem mori ostendat. Denique præire ita nobis voluit ex- emplo patientiæ: quod tantum est ut merito mi- retur Cyprianus de bono patient. Inter cætera admirabilia virtutum, quibus judicia divinæ ma- jeftatis expressit, paternam quoque patientiam tolerantiæ tenore servavit.

## 27:14
Ver. 14. So that the governor marveled greatly] Compare Isaiah ch. XLIX. 7. Perhaps he was thinking of that Terentian line: Is there any judge who can know your just claims, when you yourself do not answer a word? But in truth, in criminal cases, not only can those who are silent not be condemned unless convicted by the most certain testimonies, but not even the confession of those wishing to perish is to be admitted.

Latin:

Vers. 14. ὥstε θαυμάζειν τὸν ἡγεμόνα λίαν] Confer Esaiam c. XLIX. 7. Cogitabat forte Terentianum illud: An quisquam judex est qui possit noscere Tua justa, ubi tute verbum non respondeas? At profecto in criminum causis non modo tacentes, nisi convicti certissimis testimoniis, damnari non possunt, sed neconfessio quidem perire volentium admittenda est.

## 27:15
Ver. 15. Now at the feast] The Passover, as John says. For it was preeminently called the feast, as above XXVI. 25. & John IV. 45, comparing the passage of the same book II. 13. Josephus: 'the feast called the Passover': elsewhere, 'the feast of unleavened bread, the Passover': again elsewhere 'the feast called the Passover': just as Luke also, 'at the Passover at the feast': in which places the Passover is called by synecdoche the whole time of the Unleavened Bread. I do not believe this was an ancient custom. For the law of Moses was 'without mercy,' as the writer to the Hebrews says ch. X. 28. 'In the law, it holds the inexcusable,' says the writer of the responses to the Orthodox. Nor was the power of pardoning given to any man: not to a King, not to the Sanhedrin, not to the whole people. For Jonathan, whose punishment the people were deprecating, was either being demanded for punishment by his Father contrary to justice, or certainly not by the law of Moses, but by a new royal edict: for he had sinned in nothing against the law. David did not dare to grant pardon to Absalom, until perhaps his purpose yielded to paternal affection, with Joab assisting. The punishment of Joab's homicide was also deferred, not forgiven. King Zedekiah also acknowledges that he could do nothing against the sentence of the Sanhedrin. And Sameas prophesied destruction to the Sanhedrin itself, because it had not condemned Herod when he was accused. Wherefore it is credible that this was from the Romans. For in Livy's history we find that on the days of the lectisternium, chains were removed from prisoners: it was then a matter of religion that those to whom the Gods had brought that aid should be bound. By this example I should think this favor was granted by Augustus to the Jewish people: and that it was included in the mandates of the procurators. For otherwise the Roman governors had no freedom of pardoning, as the laws teach us. Thus the Christian Emperors, Valentinian, Theodosius, and Arcadius, by a general law commanded the judges that on the first day of the Passover the chains of all those shut up in prison, unless for certain crimes which the law enumerates, should be dissolved.

That was a custom of the Jews rather than of the Romans, as is held in John XVIII. 39. 'It is a custom for you,' says Pilate. Which seems to have been confirmed by a decree of Caesar, as pertaining to public rites, or necessity seems to have gained force in the course of time among a people tenacious of traditions: because Luke XXIII. 17 says: 'And he had a necessity to release one to them at the feast.' And it drew its origin without doubt from the fact that the Jews recalled the memory of their liberation from Egyptian servitude at this feast, where they had been shut up as if in a house of prison: therefore they were also accustomed to release some captive, for the sake of recalling that benefit, in order to show mercy in the same way. But this custom was contrary to the word of God, Prov. XVII. 15, however much it may seem to have been introduced for the sake of counsel. Traditions and rites ought not to be estimated only from intention and end, but primarily from their internal form and goodness, and their agreement with divine law.

Latin:

Vers. 15. κατὰ δὲ ἑορτὴν] τὸ πάχα, ut ait Johannes. Nam eam eminenter ἑορτὴ dicebatur ut supra XXVI. 25. & Joh. IV. 45. collato loco ejusdem lib. II. 13. Josephus: τῆς πάχα προσαγορευομένης ἑορτῆς: alibi, ἀζύμων ἑορτὴ Φάσκα: rursum alibi ἑορτὴ καλευμένη Φάσκα: quomodo & Lucas, ἐν τῷ πάχα ἐν τῇ ἑορτῇ: quibus in locis Pascha συνεκδοχι- κῶς vocatur totum tempus Azymorum. Veterem hunc morem fuisse non credo. Nam lex Mosis erat χωρὶς οἰκτιρ- μῶν, ut ait Scriptor ad Hebræos c. X. 28. ἐ νόμῷ τὸ ἀσύγ- γνωστον ἴσχε, inquit Scriptor responsionum ad Orthodoxos. Nec cuiquam homini data ignoscendi potestas: non Re- gi, non Synedrio, non populo universo. Nam Jona- than, cujus pœnam populus deprecabatur, aut contra æ- quum ad pœnam poscebatur à Patre, aut certe non ex le- ge Mosis, sed ex novo edicto regio: nam in legem nihil peccaverat. David Absalomo veniam dare ausus non est, donec forte propositum paterno affectui, Ioabo annitente, succubuit. Ioabo quoque homicidii pœna dilata, non do- nata est. Rex etiam Sedecias agnoscit se contra Synedrii sententiam nihil posse. Ipsi autem Synedrio Sameas exi- tium vaticinatus est, quod Herodem accusatum non con- demnasset. Quare credibile est à Romanis hoc esse. Nam in Livii historia invenimus lectisternii indicti diebus vinctis demta vincula: religioni deinde fuisse quibus eam opem Dii tulissent vinciri. Ad hoc exemplum putem ab Augu- sto hanc gratiam concessam populo Iudaico: idque man- datis procuratorum fuisse comprehensum. Nam alioqui præsides Romani nullam habebant ignoscendi libertatem, ut leges nos docent. Sic Christiani Imperatores, Valenti- nianus, Theodosius, & Arcadius, generali lege judici- bus mandarunt, ut primo die Paschali omnium in carcere clausorum, nisi ob certa crimina quæ lex enumerat, vincu- la dissolverentur.

Judæorum potius quam Romanorum illa erat consuetudo, ut habetur Joh. XIIX. 39. Est con- suetudo vobis, inquit Pilatus. Quæ decreto Cæ- saris, ceu ad ritus publicos pertinens confirmata videtur, aut necessitas vim progressu temporis in populo traditionum pertinace obtinuisse: quia Luc. XXIII. 17. dicitur: Necesse autem habebat dimittere eis in festo unum. Et originem traxit sine dubio inde, quod memoriam liberationis suæ ex Ægyptiaca servitute recolerent hoc festo Judæi, ubi velut in domo carceris conclusi fuerant: ideo dimittere etiam consueverunt, recolendi ejus be- neficii gratia, aliquem captivum, ut exhiberent itidem misericordiam. Quæ vero consuetudo verbo Dei contraria erat Prov. XVII. 15. utcunque videatur pro consilio introducta. Traditiones & ritus non æstimari tantum ex intentione ac fine de- bent, sed imprimis ex interna forma ac bonitate, & cum lege divina consonantia.

## 27:16
Ver. 16. They had] Said impersonally, which kind of speaking we have already often noted: They had a certain prisoner, that is, a certain prisoner was held.

Notable] Infamous, as one who had been among the leaders of a sedition that had progressed even to slaughter. Wherefore 'robber' in John signifies 'murderer,' by which name Peter calls this Barabbas, Acts III. 14. But Josephus also calls the leaders of seditions 'robbers,' as also 'sicarii,' because they had weapons without public command: Marcianus says that he who was the author of a sedition is held by the Cornelian law concerning Sicarii, L. of the same, D. on the Cornelian law. Thus the word 'sicarii' is taken also in Acts XXI. 38.

Latin:

Vers. 16. ἖χον] Impersonaliter dictum, quod genus lo- quendi sæpe jam annotavimus: Habebant vinctum quen- dam, id est quidam vinctus habebatur.

ἐπίσημον] Famosum, ut qui inter capita fuisset seditio- nis ad cædem usque progressæ. Quare ληstὴς apud Iohan- nem significat φονέα, quo nomine hunc Barabbam Petrus appellat, Act. III. 14. Sed & Iosephus seditionum princi- pes ληsὰς appellat, ut & σικαρίυς, quia scilicet arma habe- bant publico injussu: lege Corneliana de Sicariis teneri eum qui auctor seditionis fuerit ait Marcianus L. ejusdem, D. ad legem Corneliam. Sic συκαρίων vox sumitur & Act. XXI. 38.

## 27:17
Ver. 17. When they were gathered together] The Sanhedrin, that is, having been gathered, with the people standing by. Thus we gather from Luke ch. XXIII. 13 and from that which follows below 20. That it was customary for this to be done appears from Josephus, among whom 'the chief priests and the powerful, and all the most notable of the city' approach the tribunal of Florus.

Called Christ] Christ is not placed here in place of a surname: for that word had not yet so increased that Jesus was called by it as if it were his own. But 'called Christ' signifies him because he was believed by many to be the promised Messiah. See John IX. 22. Mark here for the same said 'whom you call the King of the Jews.'

Latin:

Vers. 17. συνηγμένων ēν αὐτῶν] Synedrio scilicet coacto, adstante populo. Ita colligimus ex Luca c. XXIII. 13. & ex eo quod infra sequitur 20. Solitum id fieri ex Iosepho apparet, apud quem ad Flori tribunal accedunt οἵ τε ἀρ- χιερεῖς κὴ δυνατοὶ, τὸ, τε γνωριμώτατον τῆς πόλεως πᾶν.

λεγόμενον χρισὸν] χρισὸν hic non ponitur vice cognomi- nis: nondum enim ita increbuerat id vocabulum, ut Iesus eo velut proprio vocaretur. Sed λεγόμεν Χρισὸν significat eum quia à multis credebatur esse promissus Messias. Vide Ioh. IX. 22. Marcus hic pro eodem dixit ὅν λέγετε βασιλέα τῶν Ἰυδαίων.

## 27:18
Ver. 18. For now] Both from the preceding fame and from the modesty of Jesus himself, and because no crimes were brought against him. 'That for envy they had delivered him' (v. 18)] As once the brothers did Joseph.

Latin:

Vers. 18. ἤδη γὰρ] Tum ex antegressa fama tum ex ipsius Iesu modestia, & quod nulia in eum crimina adferrentur. ὅτι διὰ φθόνον παρέδωκαν ἀυτόν] Ut olim fratres Iose- phum.

## 27:19
Ver. 19. On the judgment seat] This act seems to me to have occurred not in the final hearing in which Christ was condemned to the cross, but in another earlier one. For Pilate proceeded to the tribunal several times from that place, that is, in which he held his council: for governors were accustomed to pronounce from the opinion of the council. That place was distinguished from the tribunal by a veil interposed, whence that 'with the veil lifted' in law, that is, with no consultation applied, to which is contrary 'with the veil interposed,' in the Constitutions which are called Clement's book II. cap. 52. Philostratus calls this place the 'secret tribunal' in the Life of Apollonius book IV. ch. XV., and the African Synod calls it the 'secrets of the tribunals.' 'Secretarium' is often in the martyrologies, as in Ado on the day before the Ides of August concerning Euplus: When he was outside the veil of the secretarium, he was brought in by the order of Calsisianus the consular into the auditorium. The same word exists in the Carthaginian collation, and L. 3. C. where the Senators: and L. in causis de accusat. and elsewhere. This former examination was followed by an interlocutory order concerning Christ being beaten with scourges, namely for the sake of an interrogation to be held upon him: which Luke Acts XXII. 24 called μάστιξιν ἀνετάζεσθαι. Tacitus concerning Heremius Gallus: With garment torn, body beaten, they order him to say at what price, with what accomplices he had betrayed the army. Cicero Verrina concerning Punishments: he says, the rod is more in torture than in punishment: Gordianus Emperor L. Nullam C. From which causes infamy is inflicted: Let not your uncle fear any infamy of reputation, subjected to blows of rods for a crime, an interrogation having been held. There is a vivid description of this custom in Chrysostom’s oration XIII. concerning the statues. Pilate indeed hoped for something else also from this scourging, namely the mercy of the people, but meanwhile it was necessary that some appearance of law be applied to the injury. That some wish Christ to have been beaten with scourges as part of the punishment, according to Roman custom, cannot stand. For John openly teaches that after Christ was beaten with scourges, some time intervened before Christ was sentenced to the cross. But in those who were beaten for the sake of punishment, there was one sentence, whose words were these by law: Move forward lictor, strip, beat, proceed by law, execute: wherefore what is below in verse 26, φραγελλώσας, is said by retrogression: that is, when he had already beaten him with scourges before, Josephus concerning certain Jews seized by Florus: ὃς μάστιξι προαικισάμενος, ἀνεσταύρωσεν. Thus there is no need to invent that Christ was beaten with scourges twice in so short a time, which some do without cause or probability.

But others wrongly judge that Jesus was scourged twice, once before the sentence of death was pronounced, so that the fury of the Jews might be calmed by this miserable spectacle, and then after the sentence of death was pronounced, so that he might be the forerunner of the crucifixion; which opinion D. Henr. Möllerus attributes to Calixtus and Drusius, B. Gerhard here agreeing with Grotio. For the Harmony of the Evangelists admits only one scourging, by which Pilate intended only that, the fury of the Jews being placated, he would have no need to adjudge him to death: so that they might greedily drink these mockeries, and not thirst further for the blood of Jesus, as Augustine has it in tract 116 on John. See Luke XXIII. 16, 22, and B. Gerhard rightly observes in Harm. Evangel. de Passion. c. XI. that those to be crucified were accustomed to be scourged on the way, or under the cross, but Christ was led away into the praetorium and there scourged by the soldiers.

ἡ γυνὴ ἀυτᾶ] It had become prevalent in the time of Tiberius, contrary to the old custom, that wives should accompany those sent into the provinces. Tacitus notes this in Annals III. He adds there that business was undertaken and transacted by them: that the departures of two were honored: that there were two praetoria. τῷ δικαίῳ] That is, the innocent one: as also below 24. For the innocence of Jesus was revealed to her by God through a dream, and perhaps also the evils which awaited Pilate from an unjust condemnation. And it could be that the woman was θεοσεβής, as it appears that the wives of other Roman governors sometimes were.

For a divine dream it is also held by Ambrose lib. X. in Luc. and Augustine in sermon CXXI. de Temp. Hieron. Chrysost. Theophyl. and Euthymius in this place. Whose opinion is more correct than those who ascribe this dream to the Devil, which B. attributes to Ignatius, Bede, Bernard, Rabanus, Lyranus, and Peter Damian. Gerhard, whose arguments among others against that opinion are in the cited place, p. 117. The priests and elders were burning so much at the instigation of the Devil to kill Christ, just as it is said of Judas that Satan sent into his heart that he should betray Jesus, John 13:2; with what appearance of truth, therefore, can it be said that at the same time a dream was sent by the Devil to this little woman to save Christ unharmed? If the Devil had wished to free Christ, he would rather have terrified the Jews, who were burning with greater hatred, than Pilate's wife with dreams. This dream attributes to Christ the praise of justice; therefore, it cannot be diabolical, but God sent it to the wife of Pilate so that her husband might be drawn back from his sin and not consent to the condemnation of an innocent man: the judge is terrified in his wife, and so that he might not offer consent to the crime of the Jews in the judgment, he endured judgment in the affliction of his wife: he who judges is himself judged, and is tormented before he torments. Furthermore, why this dream was sent to the wife rather than to Pilate himself, B. Gerhard has taught in the same place from Chrysostom, Homily 86 on Matthew, that it was done either because the woman was more worthy, or because if the Governor had said that he had seen this dream, it would not have been believed as much, or because he would not have proclaimed it but would have kept it to himself; therefore, by divine dispensation, the woman saw it so that it might become known to all. Examples teach that dreams were sometimes sent even to Gentiles, Gen. 20:3, ch. 41:1, Dan. 2:1.

Latin:

Vers. 19. ἐπὶ τῶ βήματὸς] Factum hoc mihi videtur non in ultima cognitione qua Christus cruci damnatus est, sed in alia priore. Nam aliquoties in tribunal processit Pilatus ex eo scilicet loco in quo habebat consilium suum: nam de consilii sententia præsides pronuntiare solebant. Is locus à tribunali velo interposito discernebatur, unde illud velo le- vato in jure, id est nulla adhibita consultatione, cui con- trarium est παραπετάσματος πίσιν, id est velo interposito, in Constitutionibus, quæ dicuntur Clementis lib. II. cap. 52. Hunc locum τὸ ἀπόῤῥητον δικαστήριον vocat Philostratus vita Apollonii lib. IV. c. XV. & ἀπόκρυφα τ δικαστηρίων, secre- ta judiciorum Synodus Africana. Secretarium sæpe est in martyrologiis, ut apud Adonem Pridie Eidus Augusti de Euplo: Cum esset extra velum secretarii, intromissus est jubente Calsisiano consulari in auditorium. Exstat eadem vox in col- latione Carthaginiensi, & L. 3. C. ubi Senatores: & L. in causis de accusat. & alibi.
