Priorem hanc cogni ionem se- cata est interlocutio de Christo flagris cædendo, nimirum quæstionis in eum habendæ ergo: quod μάστιξιν ἀνετάζεσθαι dixit Lucas Actor. XXII. 24. Tacitus de Heremio Gallo: Scissa veste, verberato corpore, quo pretio, quibus consciis prodi- disset exercitum dicere jubent. Cicero Verrina de Suppli- ciis: virgam, ait, magis in tormento esse quam in supplicio: Gordianus Imperator L. Nullam C. Ex quibus causis infa- mia irrogatur: Nullam existimationis infamiam avunculus tuus pertimescat ictibus fustium subjectus ob crimen quæstione habita. Est hujus moris viva descriptio in Chrysostomi o- ratione XIII. de statuis. Sperabat quidem Pilatus aliud quo- que ex hac flagellatione, populi scilicet misericordiam, ve- rum interim oportebat speciem aliquam juris adhiberi inju- riæ. Quod quidam volunt cæsum flagris Christum in partem pœnæ, ex more Romano, consistere non potest. Nam Johannes aperte docet post Christum flagris cæsum, aliquantum temporis intercessisse antequam cruci Christus addiceretur. At in his qui supplicii causa cædebantur, una erat sententia, cujus hæc erant verba legitima: Summove li- ctor, despolia, verbera, lege age, animadverte: quare quod infra est commate 26. φραγελλώσας, dictum est per retro- gressionem: id est, cum eum jam ante flagris cecidisset, Jo- sephus de Judæis quibusdam à Floro comprehensis: ὃς μά- στιξι προαικισάμενος, ἀνεσταύρωσεν. Ita nihil necesse est tan- tillo tempore bis flagris cæsum Christum comminisci, quod quidam sine causa ac probabilitate faciunt.

Perperam vero alii Jesum bis flagellatum cen- sent, semel ante prolatam mortis sententiam, ut furor Judæorum miserabili isthoc spectaculo se- daretur, & deinde post dictam mortis sententiam, ut esset crucifixionisantéambulo; quam opinio- nem D. Henr. Möllerus Calixto & Drusio tribuit, B. Gerhardohic & Grotio accedens. Harmonia enim Evangelistarum non nisi unam flagellatio- nem admittit, qua Pilatus id intenderit solum ut placato Judæorum furore opus non haberet ipsum morti adjudicare: ut hæc ludibria cupide bibe- rent, nec ulterius sanguinem Jesu sitirent, ut ha- bet August. tr. 116. in Johann. Vid. Luc. XXIII. 16. 22. & recte observat B. Gerhardus Harm. Evangel. de Passion. c. XI. quod crucifigendi consueverint in via, aut sub cruce flagellari, Christus vero in prætorium abductus ibi à militibus flagellatus fuerit.

ἡ γυνὴ ἀυτᾶ] Invaluerat Tiberii tempore contra morem veterem, ut in provincias missos uxores suæ comitarentur. Notat Tacitus Annalium III. Addit ibi Cæcina ab his nego. tia suscipi, transigi: duorum egressus coli: duo esse prætoria. τῷ δικαίῳ] Id est innocenti: ut & infra 24. A Deo enim patefacta ipsi per insomnium Jesu innocentia, forte & ma- la quæ Pilatum ex injusta damnatione manebant. Et fieri potuit, ut fuerit mulier θεοσεβής, quales interdum & aliorum præsidum Romanorum uxores fuisse apparet.

Pro divino somnio id etiam habetur ab Am- brosio lib. X. in Luc. & Augustino sermone CXXI. de Temp. Hieron. Chrysost. Theophyl. & Euthymio in h. 1. Quorum sententia rectius se habet, quam eorum, qui Diabolo hoc somnium adscri- bunt, quod Ignatio, Beda, Bernardo, Ra- bano, Lyrano, & Petro Damiano tribuit B. Gerhardus, cujus haec inter alia contra illam opi- nionem sunt argumenta l. c. p. 117. Sacerdotes & Seniores Diaboli impulsu tantopere ardebant ad Chri- stum interficiendum, sicut de Juda dicitur, quod Satanas miserit in cor ejus, ut Jesum traderet, Joh. XII. 2. qua igitur veritatis specie dici potest, eo- dem tempore a Diabolo fuisse huic mulierculae so- mnium immissum ad Christum incolumem servan- dum? Si Diabolus voluisset Christum liberare, Ju- daeos potius majoribus odiis flagrantes, quam Pila- ti conjugem insomniis terruisset. Tribuit hoc inso- mnium Christo laudem justitiae, proinde nequit esse Diabolicum, sed Deus immisit illud conjugi Pilati, ut maritus a peccato suo retraheretur, nec in conde- mnationem innocentis consentiret: Judex terretur in conjuge, & ut crimini Judaeorum non praebeat in ju- dicio consensum, pertulit in uxoris afflictione judi- cium: Judicatur ipse qui judicat, & torquetur, an- tequam torqueat. Caeterum cur conjugi potius quam Pilato ipsi immissum fuerit hoc somnium, e Chrysoft. homil. XXCVI. in Matth. ibidem B. Ger- hardus docuit, quod id factum sit vel quia mulier dignior erat, vel quia si Praeses hoc somnium se vidisse dixisset, non ita ipsi creditum fuisset, aut quia non edixisset, sed secum ipse tenuisset, ideo ex divina dis- pensatione mulier vidit, ut omnibus notum fieret. Ethnicis vero etiam immissa somnia quandoque fuisse exempla docent, Gen. XX. 3. c. XLI. 1. Dan. II. v. 1.

## 27:23
Verse 23. Why what evil has he done? A refusal of the demand is implied. I will not do it: for what evil has he committed? For our writers do not express the very words of Pilate, but the sense: and therefore, even when he is introduced speaking, it is to be observed as a Hebraism, as below in verse 24. Now it is the custom among the Hebrews to pass over in silence that for which a reason is given. Examples have been cited elsewhere.

They cried out the more, saying, Let him be crucified. Such are those shouts of the people in Tertullian: The Christians to the lion: the Christians to the beasts. In Lampridius: The informers to the lion. Thus in the Acts the Jews shout, Away with him, and away with him from the earth, ch. 21:36, ch. 22:22. Similar are Tiberius into the Tiber in Suetonius, Let Valens burn in Ammianus. Although Emperors have pronounced that such vain voices of the people are not to be heard, as in Law 1 of the Decurions, Code on Punishments, many magistrates were nevertheless moved by them more than was just. They desire the cross for Christ, because that was the most ignominious punishment. For the supreme punishment, that is, the cross, says Paul in his Sentences: Apuleius called it the extreme penalty. See also Cicero in the last Verrine.

Latin:

Vers. 23. Τί γὰρ κακὸν ἐποίησεν] Subintelligitur recusatio postulationis. Non faciam: quid enim mali patravit? Nam Scriptores nostri non ipsa verba Pilati exprimunt, sed sen- sum: atque ideo etiam cum ille loquens inducitur, observa- re est Hebraismus, ut infra 24. Hebraeis autem mos est reti- cere id cujus ratio redditur. Exempla alibi allata sunt.

περισσῶς ἔκραζον λέγοντες ςαυρωθήτω] Tales sunt illi cla- mores populi apud Tertullianum: Christianos ad leonem: Christianos ad bestias. Apud Lampridium: Delatores ad leo- nem. Sic in Actis clamant Judaei, αἶρε αὐτὸν, & αἶρε ἀπὸ τῆς γῆς c. XXI. 36 c. XXII. 22. Similia sunt Tiberium in Tiberim apud Suetonium, Ardeat Valens apud Ammianum. Tales vanas populi voces quanquam non audiendas esse Imperatores pronuntiarunt ut L.Decurionum C.de Poenis, multi tamen magistratus iis supra aequum movebantur. Crucem autem Christo optant, quia id ignominiosissimum erat supplicium. Summo supplicio, id est cruce, inquit Pau- lus in sententiis: Apulejus extremam poenam dixit. Vide & Ciceronem Verrina ultima.

## 27:24
Verse 24. A tumult is made. Since John narrates that it was said by the Jews, We have a law according to which he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God, and all the writers of this sacred history report that the matter was agitated with great clamors, it is likely that fear was injected into Pilate that the people might snatch Jesus to death through a tumult, and if he himself resisted, might plot a defection, as if the law of Moses were despised. For there had been others before who attempted to overwhelm Christ with stones: and afterwards the same happened in the case of Stephen. Which fear, as unworthy of a constant man, and not even to be excused by Roman, let alone divine laws, from the crime of condemned innocence, nevertheless much elevates his guilt in comparison with Jewish cruelty: which Christ seems to signify in John 19:11, and thus I interpret what is in Mark, wishing to satisfy the crowd, not that Pilate was courting popular favor (for he was by nature unbending and, with that stubbornness, implacable, as Philo writes of him, from whom what Josephus reports does not dissent), but because when he brought standards into Jerusalem, and when he wished to touch the treasury, he had experienced how easily that people could be driven to prepare for violence under the pretext of the law of the fatherland. He wished, therefore, to redeem this danger with the punishment of an innocent man: after the manner of those who violate law and equity for the sake of the republic, as they say, when meanwhile by that act they tear the republic up from its lowest foundations.

He washed his hands. I agree with those who think that the washing of hands to testify to innocence was not peculiar to the Jews, for which matter learned men have long since brought forward the passage in Deuteronomy 21:6, Psalm 26:6, and another from Aristeas (to which can be added the passage of Josephus, Antiquities 12, ch. 2), but was a mark known to other nations as well, because it is quite natural that purity should be signified by the element of water. Certainly, those who wished to sacrifice to the gods of the nations had to bring pure hands, and to testify to that very thing by the solemn washing of hands: whence those who were contaminated by some crime were accustomed, as Demosthenes speaks, to be excluded from the lustral waters. Sophocles: neither to make common with sacrifices nor to share in lustral waters. The Scholiast of Aristophanes mentions this custom in more than one place. See what we noted above on chapter 3. But it was also an ancient custom that judges, about to condemn someone according to the laws, would testify with hands raised to the sun that they were innocent of the blood of the man, as can be seen in a sufficiently ancient book, which is titled the Apostolic Constitutions of Clement, book 2, 52. To Philo, in the third book on the life of Moses, it is a symbol of a blameless life. The old custom still remains among the Jews of washing hands when coming from a funeral, by which they testify that they did not provide the cause for death, and that they provided all things necessary.

You see to it. See above 4.

Latin:

V. 24. Θόρυβος γίνεται] Cum narret Johannes dictum a Ju- daeis nos legem habemus secundum quam debet mori, quia filium Dei se fecit, & magnis clamoribus rem agitatam o- mnes Scriptores sacrae hujus historiae tradant, vero simile est metum injectum Pilato ne populus per tumultum Jesum ad mortem raperet, & si ipse obsisteret, defectionem molire- tur, tanquam Mosis lege contemta. Nam & ante fuerant qui Christum lapidibus obruere tentarent: & postea in Ste- phano idem accidit. Qui metus tanquam indignus viro constante, ac ne Romanis quidem, nedum divinis legibus Pilatum liberaturus a crimine condemnatae innocentiae, multum tamen culpam ejus in comparatione Judaicae sae- vitiae elevat: quod Christus significare videtur Joh. XIX. 11. atque ita interpretor quod apud Marcum est βουλόμενος τῷ ὄχλῳ ἱκανὸν ποιῆσαι, non quod popularem auram Pilatus captaret, ἦν γὰρ τὴν φύσιν ἀκαμπὴς κὴ μετὰ τῦ αὐθάδες ἀ- μείλικτος, ut de eo scribit Philo, a quo non dissident quae tradit Josephus) sed quod cum signa inferret Hierosolymis, & cum gazophylacium vellet attingere, expertus esset quam facile ad vim parandam impelli populus ille posset obtentu patriae legis. Hoc igitur periculum innocentis supplicio redemtum voluit: eorum more qui jus & aequum violant reipublicae, ut ajunt, causa, cum interim eo facto rempublicam ex imis sedibus convellant.

ἀπενίψατο τὰς χεῖρας] Iis assentio qui manuum lotio- nem ad testandam innocentiam putant non Judaeorum fuisse proprium, quam ad rem viri eruditi pridem locum Deuter. XXI. 6. Pf. XXVI. 6. & alium Aristeae attulerunt (quibus addi potest & Josephi locus originum XII. cap. II.) sed notam aliis quoque gentibus, quia puritatem aquae elemento defigi are admodum naturale est. Certe qui diis gentium sacrificare volebant, afferre debebant ὁσίας χεῖρας, idque ipsum testari solenni manuum lotione: unde qui scelere aliquo erant contaminati, solebant, ut Demosthe- nes loquitur, χερνίβων εἴργεσθαι. Sophocles: μήτε θύμασι κοι- νὸν ποιεῖσθαι μήτε χερνίβων νέμειν. Meminit ejus moris & Scholiastes Aristophanis plus uno loco. Vide quæ supra notavimus ad caput III. Sed & moris antiqui fuit, ut judi- ces ex legibus aliquem damnaturi manibus ad solem eleva- tis testarentur ἀθῶοι ὑπάρχειν τὲ αἵματος τῆ ἀνθρώπω, ut vi- dere est in libro satis antiquo, cui titulus est Constitutio- num Apostolicarum Clementis lib. II. 52. Philoni, tertio de vita Mosis, λυτῆρ σύμβολον ἀνυπαιτίς ζωῆς. Judæis mos vetus nunc etiam manet a funere venientibus manus la- vandi, quo testantur se causam morti non præbuisse, & o- mnia ministrasse necessaria.

ὑμεῖς ὄψεσθε] Vide supra 4.

## 27:25
Verse 25. His blood be upon us. That is, we shall be held responsible. Thus the LXX in Leviticus 20:9 and 11 well translate his blood is upon him and their blood is upon them as he is guilty and they are guilty. But in 1 Samuel 1:16, they preserved the Hebraism: Your blood be upon your head: just as the Romans also used to say, let it be upon your head. Witnesses were accustomed to say, Let the blood of that man be upon us. See the 105th of the commanding precepts.

and upon our children] An old custom not only of devoting oneself but also one's children: it is in the treaty of the Smyrneans with the Magnetes: 'may destruction come upon the perjurer, both upon himself and upon the race from him.' Seneca says that Rufus wished that what he had ill-omened might recoil upon himself and his children. Certainly, that posterity is also bound by great crimes was the opinion not only of the Hebrews but also of almost all nations. Histories teach this everywhere. Thucydides in book I, where he deals with the pollution of Cylon: 'and from this, those men and the race from them were called accursed and impious toward God.' Add what is narrated in 1 Sam. XXI and the passage from the Hebrew book of precepts brought forward by Johannes Drusius, a man who deserves very well of these letters. Plutarch has many things on this matter in his book on the slow punishment of the divine. Which will seem the less unjust to us if we add that posterity could be freed from the pollution of paternal crimes by a serious and solemn detestation. Certainly it is commanded to the Hebrews that they should humbly acknowledge not only their own individual sins but also those of their parents, which Daniel in chapter IX and Nehemiah in chapter IX also do in the name of the people.

Latin:

Vers. 25. τὸ αἷμα ἀυτῆ ἐφ᾽ ἡμᾶς] Id est nos tenebimur. Ita LXX. Levit. XX. 9. & 11. דמיו בו & דמיהם בם bene vertunt ἔνοχός ἐστιν & ἔνοχοί εἰσιν. At 1. Sam. I. 16. ser- varunt Hebraisinum: Τὸ αἷμά σε ἐπὶ τὴν κεφαλήν σε: quomo- do & Romani dicebant, sit capiti tuo. Testes solebant di- cere, Sit sanguis istius super nos. Vide præceptorum juben- tium CV.

καὶ ἐπὶ τὰ τέκνα ἡμῶν] Mos vetus non se modo sed & libe- ros devotandi: in fœdere Smyrnæorum cum Magnetibus est: ἐπιορκοῦντι μὲ ἐξώλεια, καὶ ἀυτῷ καὶ γένει τῷ ἐξ ἀυτῶ. Seneca Rufum ait optasse, ut quod male erat ominatus, id in se & fi- lios suos recideret. Certe magnis sceleribus etiam posterita- tem obstringi, non Hebræorum tantum, sed & omnium pr. pe gentium fuit opinio. Docent passim historiæ. Thu- cydides libro I. ubi de Cylonis piaculo agit: κὶ ἀπὸ τούτου ἐ- ναγεῖς καὶ ἀλειτήριοι τῷ Θεῷ ἐκεῖνοί τε ἐκαλοῦντο καὶ τὸ γένος τὸ ἀπ᾽ ἐκείνων. Adde quod narratur 1. Sam. XXI. & locum ex He- bræico libro præceptorum adductum a Johanne Drusio, viro optime de his literis merito. Multa hac de re habet Plutarchus libro περὶ τ̄ ὑπὸ τ̄ Θεῦ βραδέως τιμωρουμένων. Quæ eo minus iniqua nobis videbuntur, si addamus, potuisse posteros seria ac solenni detestatione paternorum scelerum piaculo solvi. Certe Hebræis præcipitur, ut non sua tan- tum singuli, sed & parentum delicta suppliciter agnoscant, quod & populi nomine facit Daniel cap. IX. & Nehemias c. IX.

## 27:26
Vers. 26. Φραγελλώσας] See what we said above at verse 19. Moreover, this word is transferred from Latin into the usage of the Greek language, like κωστωδία, and those which are read in Ignatius, δεσέρτωρ, δεπόσιτα, ἄκκεπτα, ἐξεμπλάριον.

Flagella Athenaeus in book IV and Apuleius in book VIII call thongs studded with knucklebones, chained with animal bones, and tessellated with many-jointed sheep-knuckles. Nazianzen in Oration 1 on Julian, Jerome in Epistle XXVII to Marcellus, Bede on the holy places, chapter 3, Paulinus in Epistle XXXIV, and others teach that Christ was tied to a column when he was to be scourged. Concerning the scourging, Jerome beautifully says: 'This was done so that, because it was written, "many are the scourges of the sinners," we might be freed from blows by his being scourged.' And Bernard: 'He was scourged for you, so that he might free you from the scourges of wrath. He was wounded for you, so that he might heal you.' Cf. Ps. XXXV. 18. Is. L. 6. chap. LIII. 4. Matt. XX. 9. Mark X. 34. Luke XVIII. 32.

παρέδωκεν ἵνα σταυρωθῇ] Some doubt whether Pilate merely permitted the Jews to have Christ, or whether he condemned him in the manner of a judge. Tertullian speaks ambiguously: 'But they were so exasperated at his teaching, by which the masters and leaders of the Jews were refuted, especially because a huge multitude was turning to him, that at last, when he was offered to Pontius Pilate, who was then governing Syria on the Roman side, they extorted from him by the violence of their votes that Jesus be delivered to them for the cross.' Lactantius, however, expressly denies that a sentence was pronounced by Pilate in book IV of the Institutions, chapter VIII, just as Chrysostom also thought in his second oration on Almsgiving. But many things prove the contrary: first, the place of the tribunal to which Pilate proceeded: then that the execution was carried out by Roman soldiers alone: the punishment itself, which is proper to Roman law (for the cross was unknown to Jewish laws): the title dictated by Pilate: the body requested from him, and other circumstances. Add to these that already before, when Pilate had said, 'Judge him according to your law,' the Jews had replied that the power of capital judgments had been taken away from them: wherefore also all the shouts that followed tended to nothing else than that Pilate should condemn Jesus with his own voice. And this is the point in which he lent compliance to a people raging against law and equity, and against the judgment of his own mind. But also the appeal of the Catholics and the Quartodecimans to the Acts of Pilate shows that the matter was conducted under the appearance of a trial. Add Tacitus: 'The author of his name, Christ, who' He had been put to death while Tiberius was reigning, through the procurator Pontius Pilate. Christ himself said of himself above in chapter 20, verse 19: 'they will deliver him to the Gentiles to be crucified.' Nor did the ancient Christians think otherwise. Ignatius on Christ: 'he received the sentence from Pilate.' Cyprian against Demetrianus: 'Their teachers and leaders, that is, those whom that doctrine and wisdom was refuting, inflamed with anger and provoked by indignation, had delivered him to Pontius Pilate, who at that time was governing Syria on behalf of the Romans, demanding his cross and death with violent and persistent votes.' That the cross was inflicted upon Christ as the author of sedition has been most truly noted by others. For Roman laws establish that punishment for that crime: as Paul notes in Sententiae, Book V, Title XXII, for which we now read 'fork' in the Pandects, since the use of the cross in executions was abolished by Constantine. You have examples of those crucified for the crime of sedition in Judea itself, both by Varus and by Florus, in Josephus.

Moreover, the cross of Christ puzzles philologists who are debating the shape of the cross. In which, however, Joseph Scaliger seemed to himself to have observed something peculiar beyond others in his Animadversiones on Eusebius, p. 110: 'What is chief in the history of the cross, and no one, as far as I have seen, has noted, is that in the middle of the upright beam there was a piece of wood driven in, upon which sat the one who was being fastened to the cross.' And again: 'And indeed there are two chief things in the history of the cross: the footrest and the projecting peg. For those about to be executed would ascend the cross with their foot placed on the footrest. Then, with their feet resting on the footrest, and riding the middle piece of wood—their feet were pierced with two nails into the footrest, and their hands likewise into the transverse beam.' But Claudius Salmasius removes the footrest, which Bartholomaeus Nihusius, following Jacob Gretser in Book I, On the Cross, chapter 29, and Nicolaus Fuller in Book IV, Miscellanea, chapter XII, had supposed. Salmasius, to whom Thomas Bartholinus yielded the palm in this matter in his Hypomnemata I on the Cross of Christ, p. 37: 'I have not brought myself to defend the footrest in this Apology, because the illustrious Salmasius recently satisfied me.' He refers to the letter of Salmasius written to him about the cross, which Bartholinus appended to his dissertation on the opened side of Christ. But Salmasius shows from antiquity the middle piece of wood of the cross, or peg, and the seat, which Fuller considers an imaginary invention, lest Scaliger pride himself on the same observation: having brought forward primarily Justin and Irenaeus, whom Fuller drags in vain in a different direction. 'The middle piece of wood of the cross,' says Salmasius on the cross in Bartholinus, p. 229, 'which projected from the front part, was the equivalent of a wooden horse which the crucified person straddled and rode. His body was therefore carried and supported by it.' Whence Justin also said in his Dialogue with Trypho that the crucified person 'rides' it: 'And that which is driven in the middle, like a horn, also projects, upon which those who are crucified ride.' That this cannot be understood as the footrest is more certain than certain. This piece of wood stood out from the middle of the cross's upright beam, fixed and driven into the beam itself. He says the crucified person was carried by it. Therefore he had this between his thighs, and as it were rode it, which is what 'to ride' means. For it is said of a horse that a rider sits upon, 'to become a rider' and 'to ride.' Eustathius in the passage cited above: 'to mount onto the horse and make one a rider.' They would sit as it were on that piece of wood, supported by their whole body, because they pressed it with their buttocks, with their legs hanging on either side. And further, p. 231: 'And Irenaeus clearly explains this in Book II against Heresies, chapter 46.' 'The very shape of the cross,' he says, 'has five ends and extremities, two in length, and two in breadth, and one in the middle where he rests who is fastened by nails.' That one end or extremity in the middle of the upright beam of the cross—it was 'the tip' in the Greek—Tertullian in Book II against the Nations calls the 'projection of the seat' with these words: 'A part of the cross, and indeed the greater part, is all the strength which is fixed in an upright position. But the whole cross is imputed to us, with its yardarm, of course, and with that projection of the seat.' The seat is that on which one sits, not that which is placed under the feet. It cannot therefore be understood as the footrest. He calls it the 'projection of the seat' because that piece of wood, projecting and standing out in the middle of the cross, served as a seat for supporting the crucified person sitting upon it. Justin calls it 'the projecting peg in the middle.' A 'peg' is everything that is composed of two pieces of wood. Therefore that piece of wood projecting from the middle of the upright beam of the cross, which would be fixed and driven into the beam itself, is called a 'peg.' And hence Salmasius discourses thus on the parts of the cross, page 235: 'The whole cross therefore consisted of three parts, and only three: the upright wood, or beam, or stake, which was fixed into the ground in an upright position.' The same Tertullian calls it the 'upright' and the 'support.' This is the chief part of the cross, or the greater part, as the same Tertullian affirmed in that place: 'A part of the cross, and indeed the greater part, is all the strength which is fixed in a direct position.' It is the greater part, however, because it is longer and thicker. The other part is the transverse one, which is therefore called the yardarm. For the upright part has the likeness of a mast, the transverse part that of a yardarm. This part was as it were clothed by the outstretched arms of the crucified person. The part which was fixed directly supported the whole body upright. The third was the seat, that is, the piece of wood which projected from the middle of the upright support or beam of the cross, upon which the crucified person sat. The whole cross consisted of these three parts integrating it. He also adds the figure of the Paschal Lamb from Justin, p. 244. Justin in another place in his Dialogue with Trypho says that the Paschal Lamb, which was roasted fixed on a spit, exhibited the figure of Jesus fastened to the cross: 'For the lamb being roasted is roasted shaped similarly to the shape of the cross. For one spit is pierced through from the lowest parts up to the head, and another again across the back, to which the hands are also attached.' The roasted lamb had the figure of the cross while it was being roasted. For one straight spit extended through, pierced from the lowest parts up to the head. The other again passed through the shoulders, to which the inner feet of the lamb were also fastened. There were therefore two spits in use among the Jews for roasting the paschal lamb, which intersected one another at right angles. One was longer, which he calls ὄρθιον ὀβελίσκον, an upright spit, which held the whole lamb transfixed from head to feet. The other pierced it transversely, at the part where the shoulders are; this figure, or this spit, represented the yardarm of a cross. But that longer one was the upright stake itself, τὸ ὄρθιον ξύλον. This was the form of the cross, that is, the highest part of the upright stake, protruding above the middle of the transverse wood. This is what Origen, and Jerome from Origen, handed down to be similar to the Samaritan Tau. But the Samaritan alphabet today presents nothing of the sort, in which the last letter Tau is exhibited expressed thus, N. But the last letter in the Egyptian alphabet is clearly a cross, and is called Dei or Di, and also Salebdi, that is, the form of the cross of Di. Origen therefore erred, and when he had read about the Egyptian, perhaps having lapsed in memory, he wrote that about the Samaritan; whom Jerome followed. There are therefore three parts of which an entire cross consists according to the description of the ancients: the upright wood on which the body hung fixed, the transverse wood to which the arms were extended and bound with the hands fixed on both sides by a nail, and the wood protruding from the middle on which the person being crucified sat. All these things Salmasius: who is very prolix in bringing forward this scaffold; and he provides two reasons for it: one, that the bodies might be able to last longer on the cross, sustained by this as it were seat and rack; the other so that the crucified might be more easily stretched out on the cross and fastened.

Latin:

Vers. 26. Φραγελλώσας] Vide quæ supra diximus ad com- ma 19. Est autem hæc vox e Latina translata in usum Græci sermonis, ut κωστωδία, & quæ apud Ignatium legun- tur, δεσέρτωρ, δεπόσιτα, ἄκκεπτα, ἐξεμπλάριον.

Flagella Athenæus l. IV. & Apulejus l. IIX. lora dicunt taxillata, pecuinis ossibus catenata, & multi- jugis ovium talis tessellata. Columnæ Christum alli- gatum fuisse, cum flagellandus esset, Nazianzenus Orat. 1. in Julian. Hieronymus Epist. XXVII. ad Marcell. Beda, de loc. sanct. c. 3. Paulinus E- pist. XXXIV. & alii docent. De flagellatione pulcre Hieronymus: Hoc factum est, ut quia scriptum erat, multa flagella peccatorum, nos il- lo flagellato à verberibus liberaremur. Et Bernhar- dus: Pro te flagellatus est, ut à flagellis ira te libera- ret. Pro te vulneratus est, ut te sanaret. Conf. Ps. XXXV. 18. Es. L. 6. cap. LIII. 4. Matth. XX. 9. Marc. X. 34. Luc. XIIX. 32.

παρέδωκεν ἵνα σταυρωθῇ] Dubitant quidam permiserit dum- taxat Judæis Christum Pilatus, an judicis more damnave- rit. Ambiguë loquitur Tertullianus: Ad doctrinam vero ejus, qua revincebantur magistri primoresque Judæorum, ita exa- sperabantur, maxime quod ad eum ingens multitudo deflecteret, ut postremo oblatum Pontio Pilato, Syriam tunc ex parte Ro- mana procuranti, violentia suffragiorum in crucem Jesum dedi sibi extorserint. Lactantius autem prolatam à Pilato sen- tentiam diserte negat lib. IV. Institutionum, cap. IIX. quo- modo & Chrysostomus sensit oratione secunda de Eleemo- syna. Sed contrarium multa evincunt: primum locus tri- bunalis in quem processit Pilatus: deinde quod per solos milites Romanos exactum supplicium: ipsa pœna propria Romani juris, (nam crux Judæis legibus ignota:) titulus à Pilato dictatus: corpus ab eo postulatum aliæque circum- stantiæ. His adde quod jam ante, cum Pilatus dixisset, vos de eo ex lege vestra judicate; Judæi responderant, sibi capi- talium judiciorum potestatem ablatam: quare & omnes in- secuti clamores non alio tendebant, quam ut Pilatus sua voce Jesum damnaret. Atque hoc est in quo populo fu- renti contra jus & æquum, & mentis suæ sententiam obse- quium commodavit. Sed & provocatio Catholicorum & τεσσαρεσκαιδεκατιτῶν ad Acta Pilati ostendit rem judicii spe- cie gestam. Adde Tacitum: Auctor nominis ejus Christus, qui- Tiberio imperitante per procuratorem Pontium Pilatum suppli- cio affectus erat. Ipse Christus supra c. XX. 19. dixit de se: πα- ραδώσουσιν αὐτὸν τοῖς ἔθνεσιν εἰς τὸ σταυρῶσαι. Nec aliter senserunt veteres Christiani. Ignatius de Christo, ἀπόφασιν ἰδίξατο πα- ρὰ τῦ Πιλάτυ. Cyprianus adversus Demetrianum: Hunc ma- gistri eorum atque primores, hoc est quos & doctrina ille & sa- pientia revincebat, accensi ira, & indignatione provocati, Pontio Pilato, qui tunc ex parte Romana Syriam procurabat, tradide- rant: crucem ejus & mortem suffragiis violentis ac pertinacibus flagitantes. Crucem autem irrogatam Christo, tanquam seditionis auctori, verissime ab aliis notatum est. Eam enim poenam ei crimini statuunt Romanae leges: ut notat Paulus V. Sent. Tit. XXII. pro qua nunc furcam in Pandectis legi- mus, quippe crucis usu in suppliciis per Constantinum sub- lato. Exempla crucifixorum seditionis crimine in ipsa Judaea & a Varo & a Floro habes apud Josephum.

Caeterum Christi crux Philologis crucem figit disceptantibus de figura crucis. In qua vero pe- culiare quid prae aliis sibi observasse visus Josephus Scaliger in animadvers. Euseb. p. 110. Quod in hi- storia de cruce praecipuum est, & nemo, quod viderim, annotavit, in medio stipitis erat lignum impactum, cui insidebat is qui cruci affigebatur. Atque iterum: Et sane duo praecipua in historia crucis sunt τὸ ὑ- ποπόδιον & τὸ ἐξέχον πῆγμα. - Nam supplicio affi- ciendi pede in suppedaneum posito crucem ascende- bant. - Deinde pedibus insistentibus suppedaneo, medio autem ligno inequitantes -- binis clavis pedes in sup- pedaneo, totidem ambas manus in transversario li- gno transfigebantur. Sed suppedaneum, quod cum Jacobo Gretsero l. 1. de Cruce c. 29. supposuit etiam Barth. Nihusius, & Nicol. Fullerus l. IV. Miscell. c. XII. submovet Claud. Salmasius, cui palmam in eo reliquit Thomas Bartholinus in hypomnem. I. de Cruce Christi p. 37. Non induxi in animum hypo- podion defendere hac Apologia, quia nuper mihi illu- stris Salmasius satisfecit. Respicit Epistolam Sal- masii, ad se de Cruce perscriptam: quam subjecit suae de latere Christi aperto dissertationi Bartholi- nus. Medium autem crucis lignum, vel pegma, & sedile, quod Fullerus pro invento imaginario ha- bet, ex antiquitate ostendit Salmasius, ne se ejusdem observatione efferat Scaliger: adducto imprimis Justino & Irenaeo, quos nequicquam Fullerus in di- versum abripit. Medium crucis lignum, ait Salma- sius de cruce apud Bartholinum, p. 229. quod emi- nebat ex anteriore parte, equi vicem fuit lignei quod incendebat & inequitabat cruciarius. Corpus itaque ejus illo portabatur, & sustentabatur. Unde & ἐπο- χεῖσθαι eo dixit crucifixum Justinus in Tryphonis dia- logo, καὶ τὸ ἐν τῷ μέσῳ πηγνύμενον ὡς κέρας κ̓ αὐ- τὸ ἐξέχον ἐστὶν ἐφ᾽ ᾧ ἐποχῦνται οἱ σταυρύμενοι: Et quod in medio impactum est, instar cornu & ipsum eminet, cui inequitant & quo vectantur qui cruci affiguntur. De suppedaneo hac accipi non posse cer- to certius est. E medio crucis stipite extabat hoc li- gnum, in ipso stipite infixum & impactum. Eo ve- ctatum dicit crucifixum. Ergo inter femina hoc ha- bebat, eique quasi inequitabat, quod est ἐποχεῖσθαι. Nam de equo dicitur cui eques insidet, ἔποχον γίνεσθαι, & ἐποχεῖσθαι. Eustathius in loco superius citato, εἰς τὸν ἵππον ἀνάγειν κ̓ ἔποχον ποιεῖν. In eo ligno veluti subsidebant toto corpore sustentati, quia illud na- tibus premebant, cruribus hinc inde pendulis. Et por- ro p. 231. Idque clare Irenaeus explicat lib. II. advers. Haereses cap. XLVI. Ipse habitus crucis, inquit, fines & summitates habet quinque, duos in lon- gitudine, & duos in latitudine, & unum in me- dio ubi requiescit qui clavis affigitur. Unum illum in medio stipitis crucis finem sive extremitatem, τὸ ἄκρον in Graeco fuit, Tertullianus in libro II. ad- versus Nationes sedilis excessum appellat his ver- bis: Pars crucis & quidem major, est omne ro- bur quod erecta statione defigitur. Sed nobis nobis tota crux imputatur, cum antemna scilicet sua, & cum illo sedilis excessu. Sedile est in quo sedetur, non quod pedibus subjicitur. Non potest ita- que accipi de suppedaneo. Excessum vocat sedi- lis, quia excedens illud & eminens in medio crucis li- gnum pro sedili fuit ad sustinendum cruciarium ei insi- dentem. Τὸ ἐξέχον ἐν μέσῳ πῆγμα appellat Justi- nus. Πῆγμα est id omne quod ex duobus lignis com- ponitur. Lignum igitur illud eminens è medio stipi- te crucis quod ipso stipiti infixum & impactum foret, πῆγμα appellatur. Atque hinc de partibus Cru- cis ita disserit Salmasius pag. 235. Tribus igitur par- tibus tota crux constabat, & solis, arrectario ligno, sive stipite, sive palo qui erecta statione in terram defigebatur. Staticulum & statumen appellat idem Tertullianus. Hæc præcipua pars crucis, sive ma- jor, ut idem Tertullianus eo loco affirmavit : Pars crucis, & quidem major, omne robur quod di- recta statione desigitur. Major autem est, quia longior & crassior. Altera pars transversaria est, quæ ideo antemna appellata. Nam arrectaria mali instar habet, transversaria antemnæ. Hæc pars dispersis brachiis cruciarii, & alligatis quasi vestita erat. Quæ directa defigebatur, totum corpus sustinebat rectum. Tertia fuit sedile, id est, lignum quod è medio staticulo sive stipite crucis erecto eminebat, cui insidebat cruciarius. His tribus partibus inte- grantibus tota crux constabat. Addit & figuram Agni Paschalis è Justino p. 244. Justinus alio loco in Tryphone Agnum Paschalem, qui veru infixus torrebatur, figuram Jesu cruci affixi exhibuisse dicit: Τό γὰρ ὀπτώμενον πρόβατον σχηματιζόμενον ὁ- μοίως τῷ σχήματι τῷ σταυρῦ ὀπτᾶται. Εἰς γὰρ ὄρ- θιῷ ὀβελίσκῷ διαπερονᾶται ἀπὸ τῶν κατωτά- τω μερῶν μέχρι τῆς κεφαλῆς, καὶ εἷς πάλιν κατὰ τὸ μετάφρενον, ᾧ προσαρτῶνται κὴ αἱ χεῖρες ἕπερ- βατος. Assatus agnus figuram habebat dum as- saretur crucis. Unum quippe directum veru ab infimis partibus usque ad caput transfixum perti- nebat. Alterum rursus transibat per armos cui & affixi erant pedes agni interiores. Bina igitur verua in assando agno paschali usui apud Judæos fuis- se, quæ se se invicem ad rectos angulos intersecarent. Longius unum, quem ὄρθιον ὀβελίσκον, rectum veru vocitat, quod à capite ad pedes totum agnum transfixum tenebat. Alterum è transverso ipsum transfigebat, qua parte armi sunt; Hæc figura, sive hoc veru antemnam crucis referebat. At illud longius ipsum erectum stipitem, τὸ ὄρθιον ξύλον. Hæc forma crucis fuit, hoc est, partem sum- mam recti stipitis, supra medium transversi ligni eminentem. Hæc est, quam Origenes, & ex Ori- gene Hieronymus, Tau Samaritano similem esse tra- diderunt. Sed Samaritanum Alphabetum nihil hodie præfert tale, in quo littera ultima Tau sic expressa exhibetur, N. At extrema littera in Ægyptiaco Alphabeto plane crux est, & Dei vel Di appellatur, atque etiam Salebdi, hoc est, Di crucis forma. -- Erraverit igitur Orige- nes, & cum de Ægyptiaco legisset, memoria fortassis lapsus, de Samaritano id scripsit; quem sequutus est Hieronymus. Tres igitur sunt par- tes quibus integra crux constat secundum veterum descriptionem, lignum rectum in quo corpus af- fixum pendebat, lignum transversum cui bra- chia extensa deligata erant manibus utrimque cla- vo fixis, lignum è medio imminens cui insidebat cru- ciarius. Hæc omnia Salmasius: qui proli- xus admodum est in hoc pegmate adferendo; ejusque duas causas tradit: unam ut diurnare in cruce longius possent corpora, hoc veluti- sedili & equuleo sustentata : alteram ut facilius in cruce extendi quirent & affigi cruciarii.

## 27:27
Verse 27. εἰς τὸ πραιτώριον] Pilate's tribunal was not inside the praetorium, but in the stadium which was not far from the praetorium. Josephus: ὁ Πιλάτος καθίζας ἐπὶ βήματος ἐν τῷ μεγάλῳ στα- δίῳ. Part of this area was paved with stones, as we learn from John: there was both the place of the consistory and the tribunal.

ὅλην τὴν σπεῖραν] another cohort than that which was assigned to the Temple and the Priests and which was called the guard: Σπεῖρα δὲ ἐστιν ὅ καλῦμεν νῦν νόμερον. Oecumenius.

Latin:

Vers. 27. εἰς τὸ πραιτώριον] Non erat tribunal Pilati in- tra prætorium, sed in stadio quod erat non longe à prætorio. Josephus: ὁ Πιλάτος καθίζας ἐπὶ βήματος ἐν τῷ μεγάλῳ στα- δίῳ. Pars hujus aræ lapidibus constrata, ut ex Johanne discimus : ibi erat & consistorii locus & tribunal.

ὅλην τὴν σπεῖραν] aliam cohortem ab ea quæ Templo & Sacerdotibus erat assignata & quæ custodia vocabatur : Σπεῖρα δὲ ἐστιν ὅ καλῦμεν νῦν νόμερον. Oecumenius.

## 27:28
Verse 28. περιέθηκαν αὐτῷ χλαμύδα κοκκίνην] Mark and John say purple, that is, of that color which would imitate purple. And in the same way here it is called a scarlet Chlamys, because it resembled a scarlet one: for its color and purple are neighboring colors. See L. si cui lana D. de legatis III. Par. verficoloribus, the Hebrews call תולע what we commonly call Crimson, which the Greek interpreters translate as κόκκιον. These things pertained to the mockery as if of a foolishly affected kingdom. Similar is the account where the Alexandrians, in order to mock Agrippa, who called himself king, as if he were unworthy of the majesty of that name, adorned a certain Carabas, a man of little sound mind, by way of mockery with certain insignia as if of a kingdom: which narrative in Philo's In Flaccum deserves to be compared with this. For what is here χλαμὺς κοκκίνη, there is χαμαιστρώτῳ δὲ τὸ ἄλλο σῶμα περιβαλόντες ἀντὶ χλαμύδος.

What Grotius said about the purple Chlamys, that is, of a color that would imitate purple, and scarlet, that is, referring to a scarlet one, is ridiculous to Salmasius, because of the diversity of each color: who prefers to think it was sufficient for the Evangelists for the credibility of the matter that we be taught that a garment of a bright color was cast upon Christ for the sake of mockery: that some called it scarlet, others purple: because those two colors were then excellent in garments. But this is too diluted: for the Evangelists do not indicate a bright color in general, such as snow-white and white also are, but one corresponding by the likeness of purple and scarlet: which Priceus also acknowledged because of the affinity and almost promiscuous use of these colors, although he thinks the Evangelists spoke more crudely and commonly. Granted that the color of scarlet is paler than that of purple, and that purple shines with the color of a blackening rose, which Pliny l. XXI. c. 8. l. IX. c. 36. says, and that a puniceus color, which shows the excellence and splendor of redness, is seen in purple, especially Tyrian, about which Salmasius notes to Solin. p. 1330: nor do we deny that the scarlet color is distinguished from the purple in Exod. XXV. v. 4. cap. XXVI. 1. c. XXVII. 16. 2. Par. II. 7. c. III. 14. Apoc. XIIX. 16. yet it is not unusual for the purple color in general to be taken for a pleasantly reddening one, just as Horace l. II. Satyr. 6. made the same garment dyed with scarlet and purple. Cassiodorus l. I. Var. Epist. 2. says of purple, that color, he says, blooming with excessive charm, a reddening obscurity, a bloody blackness distinguishes the ruler, while it makes him conspicuous, and provides for the human race so that there can be no mistake about the appearance of the Prince. Scarlet, says B. Gerhard, is the grain of a certain shrub staining garments with a red color, which comes very close to purple. Purple is a fish of the shellfish kind having in its throat a liquid of clotted blood and imbued with the color of a blackening rose. The soldiers therefore clothed Christ in a scarlet garment to mock him regarding the affected royal dignity, which he could not have attained; for just as that garment was not truly purple, but at least had a certain likeness to purple: so they wish to signify that Christ is not a true King, but had only affected royal honor without any success. It was not the soldiers' concern to clothe Christ in true purple, for that is very rare, and the garment of Emperors, Kings, and Princes, but they judge a scarlet chlamys thrown by some soldier into a corner of the praetorium to be sufficient for this game, so that they might use it in place of purple, and thus the feigned color might have a correspondence with the feigned King. These things are rightly stated by B. Gerhard in Harm. Pass. p. 124. Conf. Cant. VII. 5. Dan. V. 7. 1. Macc. X. 10. 62. 64. cap. XI. 58. c. XIV. 44. Luc. XVI. 19. And not only purple, but also scarlet chlamydes were used sometimes by Emperors and military commanders. An example is the Emperor Alexander, about whom Aelius Lampridius reports this. Pliny says that scarlet is dedicated to imperial military cloaks, book XXII. c. 2. The supreme Emperor is clothed in a military chlamys, because he had to fight against barbarian leaders. But the chlamys was purple, because he ought to shed blood.

Latin:

Vers. 28. περιέθηκαν αὐτῷ χλαμύδα κοκκίνην] Πορφύραν Marcus & Johannes, id est ejus coloris qui purpuram mentiretur. Atque eodem modo hic coccina dicitur Chla- mys, quod coccinam referret : nam ejus & purpuræ vicinus color. Vide L. si cui lana D. de legatis III. Par. verficolo- ribus, Hebræi תולע vocant id quod nos vulgo Cramosi- num, quod Græci interpretes vertunt κόκκινον. Pertinebant hæc ad exprobrationem velut stultæ affectati regni. Simi- le est quod Alexandrini, ut Agrippam, qui se regem di- ceret, tanquam ejus nominis majestate indignum, ir- riderent, Carbam quemdam, hominem mentis parum compotem, per ludibrium ornarunt quibusdam quasi re- gni insignibus : quæ narratio apud Philonem in Flaccum meretur cum hac comparari. Nam quod hic est χλαμὺς κοκκίνη, ibi est χαμαιστρώτῳ δὲ τὸ ἄλλο σῶμα περιβαλόντες ἀντὶ χλαμύδος.

Quod de Chlamyde purpurea, id est, ejus coloris qui purpuram mentiretur, & coccina, id est coc- cinam referente dixit Grotius, id Salmasio ridicu- lum est, ob diversitatem coloris utriusque : qui ma- vult satis visum fuisse Evangelistis ad rei fidem, nos doceri clari coloris vestem ludibrii causa Christo fuisse injectam: Hanc alios coccineam, alios pur- puream dixisse: quia duo isti colores in vestibus tunc eximii. Sed hoc nimis dilutum est : non enim in genere clarum colorem, qualis etiam niveus est, & albus, sed similitudine purpuræ & cocco respon- dentem indicant Evangelistæ : quod ob affinitatem & fere promescuum usum colorum istorum factum Priceus etiam agnovit, etsi crassius & commu- nius loquutos Evangelistas censeat. Esto color cocci, quam purpuræ, dilutior sit, & purpura ni- grantis rosæ colore subluceat, quod Plinius l. XXI. c. 8. l. IX. c. 36. ait, as puniceus color, qui exuperan- tiam & splendorem ruboris ostendit, in purpura cernatur, præsertim Tyria, quo de Salmasius ad So- lin. p. 1330. notat: neque negamus, colorem coc- cineum à purpureo distingui Exod. XXV. v. 4. cap. XXVI. 1. c. XXVII. 16. 2. Par. II. 7. c. III. 14. Apoc. XIIX. 16. non insolens tamen est purpureum colo- rem in genere pro suaviter rubente accipi, uti Ho- ratius l. II. Satyr. 6. eandem vestem tinctam cocco & purpuream fecit. Cassiodor. l. I. Var. Epist. 2. de purpura, color ille, inquit, nimio lepore ver- nans, obscuritas rubens, nigredo sanguinea regnan- tem discernit, dum conspicuum facit, & præstat hu- mano generi ne de aspectu Principis possit errari. Coc- cus, inquit B. Gerhardus, est granum cujusdam fruticis inficiens vestes colore rubro, qui proxime accedit ad purpureum. Purpura est piscis ex concharum genere in faucibus habens liquorem con- creti sanguinis & nigrantis rosæ colore imbutum. Milites ergo induerunt Christum veste coccinea ut illuderent illi de affectata dignitate regia, quam non potuerit assequi; ut enim illa vestis non erat vere purpurea, sed saltem similitudinem quandam cum purpura habebat: ita significare volunt Christum non esse verum Regem, sed affectasse solum honorem regium sine omni successu. Non fuit cura militibus ut veram purpuram Christo induerent, ea enim ad- modum rara est, & Imperatorum, Regum ac Prin- cipum vestimentum, sed judicant coccineam chla- mydem à quodam milite in angulum prætorii conje- Etam ad hunc lusum sufficere, ut loco purpuræ ea u- tantur, sicque color fictus cum ficto Rege convenien- tiam habeat. Hæc recte B. Gerhardus in Harm. Pass. p. 124. Conf. Cant. VII. 5. Dan. V. 7. 1. Macc. X. 10. 62. 64. cap. XI. 58. c. XIV. 44. Luc. XVI. 19. Nec purpurea tantum, sed etiam coccinea chla- myde usi fuêre quandoque Imperatores, & Belli duces. Exemplo est Alexander Imperator, de quo id refert Ælius Lampridius. Plinius coccum imperatoriis dicatum paludamentis dicit lib. XXII. c. 2. Chlamyde induitur summus Imperator mili- tari, quia adversus tartareos duces ei pugnandum erat. Chlamys autem erat purpurea, quia sangui- nem fundere debeat.

## 27:29
Verse 29. στέφανον ἐξ ἀκανθῶν] In the mentioned narrative of Philo: βύβλον μὲν εὐρύναντες ἀντὶ διαδήματος ἐπιτιθέασιν αὐτῷ τῇ κεφαλῇ. The curse began in thorns Gen. III. 18. it ends in thorns. A lily in the midst of thorns Cant. II. 2.

Concerning this crown Tertullian, book de coron. milit. Certainly, besides the figure of insult, there is readiness and shame and dishonor, and intertwined with these is cruelty, which then both defiled and lacerated the Lord's temples. Athanasius speaks beautifully about the use of the worn crown of thorns in his book on the Passion and Cross of the Lord: In another way (Christ) can be seen to wear the crown of thorns, namely to extirpate the anxieties of our life. For that wicked one cast, although unwillingly, our anxieties upon the Lord, not noticing that it would come to pass that by wearing them the Lord would bring all into security, by which he would also have the seed of the word purged of thorns. Cyril says that the crown of thorns shows that the curse has been removed, because on account of the curse thorns have sprung from the earth. For the type see Gen. XXII. 13. But it is a fabrication of certain Papists that they say Christ was crowned twice, first with a crown of thorns, then with a crown of briars: and that one is kept at Aachen, the other at Paris: it is said to have been ἐξ ἀκανθῶν, that is, from thorny shrubs.

καὶ κάλαμον ἐπὶ τὴν δεξιὰν αὐτοῦ] Philo: ἀντὶ δὲ σκήπτρου βραχύ τι παπύρου τμῆμα τῆς ἐγχωρίου καθ’ ὁδὸν ἐῤῥιμμένον ἰδών τις ἀναδίδωσιν. Then he adds what also fits this place: ἐπεὶ δὲ ὡς ἐν θεατρικοῖς μίμοις τὰ παράσημα τῆς βασιλείας ἀνει- λήφει, καὶ διεκικόσμητο εἰς βασιλέα.

saying: Hail, King] Philo: then others approached, some as if to greet: then from the crowd standing in a circle a strange shout rang out, calling him Marin; for they say that this is the word for Lord among the Syrians. Correct. For מרן is Syrian. Thus Livy relates that a man from Megalopolis was ordered by King Philip to be greeted as king in mockery. The custom of greeting even princes with the addition of 'ave' also existed: thus 'ave Caesar' in Martial's Apophoretis and Macrobius, Saturnalia II. 4.

Latin:

Vers. 29. στέφανον ἐξ ἀκανθῶν] In dicta Philonis narra- tione: βύβλον μὲν εὐρύναντες ἀντὶ διαδήματος ἐπιτιθέασιν αὐτῷ τῇ κεφαλῇ Maledictio in spinis cœpit Gen. III. 18. in spinis desit. Lilium in medio spinarum Cant. II. 2.

De hac corona Tertul. lib. de coron. milit. Cer- te præter figuram contumelia in promptu est & turpi- tudo & dedecoratio, & his implexa sævitia, quæ tunc Domini tempora & fœdaverunt, & lanciaverunt. Pulcre autem de usu gestæ coronæ spineæ Atha- nasius l. de Pass. & cruce Domini: Alia ratione spineam coronam gestare videri potest (Christus,) nimirum ut sollicitudines vitæ nostræ exstirpet. In- jecit enim scelestus ille, quanquam nolens, solici- tudines nostras super Dominum, non animadver- tens futurum esse, ut earum gestatione Dominus o- mnes in securitatem adsereret, quo & semen verbi de spinis depurgatum haberet. Cyrillus ait quod coro- na spinea ostendat sublatum esse maledictionem, quia propter maledictionem ex terra spinæ sunt ortæ. Ty- pus vid. Gen. XXII. 13. Commentum autem est Papistarum quorundam, quod Christum bis co- ronatum dicunt, prius corona spinea, deinde coro- na ex rubo: & alteram Aquisgrani, alteram Pari- siis asservari: ἐξ ἀκανθῶν fuisse dicitur, hoc est ex fruticibus spineis.

καὶ κάλαμον ἐπὶ τὴν δεξιὰν αὐτοῦ] Philo: ἀντὶ δὲ σκήπτρου βραχύ τι παπύρου τμῆμα τῆς ἐγχωρίου καθ’ ὁδὸν ἐῤῥιμμένον ἰδών τις ἀναδίδωσιν. Deinde addit quod & huic loco quadrat ἐπεὶ δὲ ὡς ἐν θεατρικοῖς μίμοις τὰ παράσημα τῆς βασιλείας ἀνει- λήφει, καὶ διεκικόσμητο εἰς βασιλέα.

λέγοντες· χαῖρε ὁ βασιλεὺς] Philo: εἶθ’ ἕτεροι προσήεσαν οἱ μὲν ὡς ἀσπασόμενοι: deinde εἶτ’ ἐκ περιεστῶτος ἐν κύκλῳ πλή- θους ἐξήχει βοή τις ἄτοπος Μάριν ἀποκαλούντων· οὕτως δέ φασιν τὸ κύριον ὀνομάζεσθαι παρὰ Σύροις. Recte. מרן enim Sy- rum est. Sic Livius narrat Megalopolitanum à Philippo re- ge ad ludibrium regem consalutari jussum. Mos autem sa- lutandi etiam principes addito ave: sic Cæsar ave, apud Martialem Apophioretis & Macrobium II. Saturn. 4.

## 27:31
Vers. 31. they led him away to crucify him] The execution of punishment by soldiers at the command of Roman magistrates, even outside the camp, has been noted by very learned men. Hence the tribune as the executor of death in Tacitus: in Suetonius, the soldier as the craftsman of beheading, who is the 'spiculator' to Marcus, to the Roman jurists, and to Julius Firmicus. Tertullian, where he dissuades a Christian from military service: 'And will he administer chains and the cross and punishments, and not be an avenger of his own injuries?'

Latin:

Vers. 31. ἀπήγαγον αὐτὸν εἰς τὸ σταυρῶσαι] Per milites sup- plicium exactum à Romanis magistratibus etiam extra ca- stra notatum est à viris doctissimis. Hinc tribunus exa- ctor mortis Tacito: Suetonio miles decollandi artifex, qui spiculator Marco, Jurisconsultis Romanis, Julio Firmico. Tertullianus ubi Christiano militiam dissuadet: Et vincula & crucem & supplicia administ rabit, nec suarum ultor injuria- rum?

## 27:32
Vers. 32. and as they were coming out] Outside the city, as John relates and the writer to the Hebrews observes in XIII. 12. This was consistent with Hebrew custom. For in the time of Moses, those who were guilty of capital crimes were put to death outside the camp, Num. XV. 35; once the republic was established, outside the cities, 1 Kings XXI. 13; but also with Roman custom: Seneca teaches concerning the camps: 'The condemned man had been led outside the rampart for punishment.' Vegetius: 'In former times they were led outside the rampart to be beheaded.' The author of Caesar's African War: 'Thus they were led outside the rampart and killed with torture.' Aggenus on cities: 'There are places in the suburbs designated for the punishments of criminals.' Cicero, Verrine V: 'When the Mamertines, according to their own custom and institution, had fixed the cross outside the city on the Pompeian Way.' Plautus: 'I believe that you will have to go immediately outside the city with your hands stretched out, when you have the cross-bar.' Testimonies to the same effect brought forward by others from Lampridius and Theodoret.

Cyrenian] Originating from the Cyrenaica in the Libyan Pentapolis, which was full of Jews, as Josephus most clearly teaches in his work on the Capture

VII. ch. XXXVIII. & Luke Acts II. 10. & VI. 9. Nor is there any doubt that those who take these things concerning another Cyrene are mistaken. Origen interprets correctly.

that he might take up his cross] Since Christ himself had already carried the gibbet through the city, as Plautus speaks, John XIX. 17, without doubt in the Roman manner, according to which he who is about to be crucified previously carried the cross: as is now known to all. But the soldiers seem to have seized this Simon to succeed to the burden for Christ at the instigation of the Jews, who knew that he favored Christ, which Mark confirms, naming also his sons, who were, of course, disciples of Christ. Thus it was expressed by a conspicuous sign, what Christ had commanded all his disciples, to follow him with the cross lifted onto their shoulders. For Luke also expresses this in this history: they laid the cross upon him to carry behind Jesus.

That Christ himself first carried the cross within the city, but that this Simon was substituted for him lest he perhaps fail under the burden, the ancients Origen, Jerome, Bede, Euthymius, Theophylact correctly observe in this place. Athanasius in the place cited. Augustine book III de Cons. Evang. ch. 10. Leo the Great Sermon XXVIII on the Passion. But Christ carries the cross, as Cyril says in book XII on John ch. 28, not for himself, but for us. He carries the cross owed to transgressors by the law, says Athanasius, so that he himself might display a trophy against the devil. But concerning the significance of the cross-bearing of Simon see Matthew XVI. 24, Luke XIV. 27.

Latin:

Vers. 32. ἐξερχόμενοι δὲ] Extra urbem, ut narrat Johan- nes, & observat Scriptor ad Hebræos XIII. 12. congruebat id Hebræo mori. Nam fontes Mosis tempore extra castra morte afficiebantur, Num. XV. 35. constituta republica ex- tra urbes, 1. Reg. XXI. 13. sed & Romano: De castris docet Seneca: Damnatus extra vallum ad supplicium deductus fu- erat. Vegetius: Decumana deducebantur olim extra val- lum ut capite plecterentur. Scriptor belli Africani Cæsaris: Sic extra vallum deducti sunt & cruciabiliter interfecti. De ur- bibus Aggenus: Sunt in suburbanis loca noxiorum pœnis desti- nata. Cicero Verrina V. Cum Mamertini more atque instituto suo crucem fixissent post urbem in via Pompeja. Plautus: Credo ego istuc extemplo tibi Esse eundum actutum extra urbem dispessis manibus, Patibulum cum habebis. Prolata in rem eandem ab aliis testimonia ex Lampidio & Theodoreto.

Κυρηναῖον] Ex Lybiæ Pentapoli Cyrenaica oriundum, quæ plena Judæis, ut apertissime docet Josephus ἁλώσεως

VII. cap. XXXIIX. & Lucas Act. II. 10. & VI. 9. Nec du- bium falli qui de alia Cyrene hæc accipiunt. Origenes re- cte interpretatur.

ἵνα ἄρῃ τὸν σταυρὸν αὐτοῦ] Cum jam ante Christus ipse pa- tibulum tulisset per urbem, ut Plautus loquitur, Ioh. XIX. 17. more haud dubie Romano, juxta quem ὁ μέλλων προση- λῦσθαι πρότερον σταυρὸν ἐβάσαζε: ut jam omnibus notum. Vi- dentur autem milites hunc Simonem arripuisse qui in onus Christo succederet Judæorum instigatu, qui eum sciebant Christo favere, quod Marcus confirmat, filios quoque ejus, Christi nimirum discipulos, nominans. Ita conspicuo signo expressum est, quod Christus omnibus discipulis suis præ- ceperat, sublata in humeros cruce ipsum sequi. Nam & hoc exprimit Lucas in hac historia: ἐπέθηκαν αὐτῷ τὸν σταυρὸν φέ- ρειν ὀπίσω τοῦ Ἰησοῦ.

Christum ipsum primum portasse crucem intra urbem, sed ne deficeret forte sub onere surroga- tum ei hunc Simonem esse, recte observant ve- teres Origenes, Hieronymus, Beda, Euthymius, Theophyl. in h. l. Athanasius l. c. August. l. III. de Cons. Evang. c. 10. Leo M. Serm. IIX. de Pass. Cru- cem autem portat Christus, dicente Cyrillo lib. XII. in Joh. cap. 28. non sibi, sed nobis. Debitam transgressoribus per legem crucem portat, ait A- thanasius, ut contra diabolum trophæum ipse o- stentet. De significatione autem σταυροφορίας Si- monis vid. Matth. XVI. 24. Luc. XIV. 27.

## 27:33
Verse 33. Golgotha] That the elision of the letter is not without example has been openly demonstrated by a most learned man. In the Zohar, as also here in the Syriac and Arabic, it is read fully. Wherefore it signifies nothing other than what is expressed in Greek by the interpreter of Matthew as the place of a skull. Nor do I think the cause of the name should be sought elsewhere than that men were accustomed to be beheaded there, such as were the places in Rome, the Sestertium and the Gemoniae. That bare skulls of heads remained in that place long after death I hardly believe: for that accords sufficiently with neither Jewish nor Roman custom, and the Hebrews call any head galgal, in imitation of which I think kranion was made by the interpreter: which, however, the Greeks themselves sometimes use for the head of the living, as the Latins use calva. But it seems to me that the expression of this name pertains not only to history, but also to the fulfillment of prophecy, namely that our reproach was rolled away from us there, just as the image of our Jesus was spoken of, who thence named a certain place galgal, which with the Syriac addition is ramatha, as from ramath galgalta it became ramatha. Josephus interprets that name galgal as anathema. Thus also the word Nazarene, signifying a fatherland, had a more abstruse meaning in another sense.

The place was rather called so from Calvary, because the mountain was similar to a human head, as Cyril of Jerusalem judges. But it is a fable that it received its name from the skull of the first man, which nevertheless pleased not a few of the Fathers. Who would believe that the Jews would have afflicted the place of the burial of the Protoplast with such ignominy, that criminals should be punished there, or that they would have wanted it defiled by their slaughters and burials?

Latin:

Vers. 33. γολγοθᾶ] Elisionem literæ non carere exem- plo aperte a viro doctissimo demonstratum est. In Zohar, ut & hic in Syriaco & Arabico plene legitur. Quare non aliud significat quam quod Græce exprimitur a Matthæi interpre- te κρανίου τόπον. Nec causam nominis aliunde quærendam arbitror quam quod ibi decollari homines solerent, qualia loca Romæ erant Sestertium & Gemoniæ. Mansisse eo lo- co diu post mortem nuda capitum ossa vix credo: nam ne- que Judaico, neque Romano mori id satis congruit, & Hæbræis גלגל quodvis caput appellant quorum imi- tatione κρανίον ab interprete factum puto: quod tamen i- psi quoque Græci interdum de viventium capite usurpant, ut calvam Latini. Videtur autem mihi expressio hujus no- minis non ad historiam tantum, sed & ad vaticinii imple- mentum pertinere, quod ibi scilicet avolutum a nobis sit opprobrium nostrum, quomodo loquebantur jejus nostri Je- su imago, qui exinde locum quemdam גלגל nomina- vit, quod cum additamento Syriaco est רמת ut ex רמת גלגלתא factum est רמתא. Id nomen גלגל Josephus ἀνα- θέριον interpretatur. Sic & Nazaræi vox patriam signifi- cans, alio sensu abstrusiorem habebat significationem.

Dictus potius ita locus est a Calvaria, quod mons humano capiti similis fuerit, censente Cyril- lo Hierosolymitano. Fabula autem est, quod no- men acceperit a primi hominis cranio, quæ tamen non paucis e Patribus placuit. Ecquis credat Ju- dæos locum sepulturæ Protoplasti insignem ea i- gnominia affecisse, ut illic facinorosi plecteren- tur, vel cædibus & sepulturis eorum inquinatum voluisse?

## 27:34
Verse 34. Vinegar mingled with gall] So most copies and the Syriac. Nor does Origen, a diligent seeker of copies, read it otherwise. Yet I do not blame the Latin interpreter who translated it as wine, nor those who added oinon to the Greek margin at the word oxos, for the sake of interpretation, which later crept into the context of certain books. For the Greeks call wine of a manufactured flavor oxos: such as the oxos of dates mentioned by Xenophon and others: but the same is also no less correctly called wine, just as Athenaeus calls barley beer oinos krithinos. Such was also this wine, seasoned either with frankincense, as the teachers of the Hebrews hand down, or with myrrh, as Mark says, which according to received custom was accustomed to be given to those going to execution. But also the Hebrew hamets which is in the Psalm signifies that which is fermented: as has been observed by a man of the highest diligence, with whom I also agree in this, that he takes cholen more loosely for all bitterness: since the Greek interpreters signify wormwood by that word in Proverbs V. 3, Lamentations III. 15. For the Hebrew rosh or rush also extends widely, and is translated by the word pikron in Jeremiah XXIII. 15, and thus it extends even to poisonous herbs of bitter taste: as is clear by comparing the passage Deuteronomy XXIX. 18 with Hebrews XII. 14. And thus the Syriac took the word choles here, translating it as merarta, which signifies bitterness, and therefore is no less suited to wormwood than to gall. Nor does Theophylact speak otherwise regarding Mark: and Augustine in book III on the consensus of the Evangelists: For he put gall for bitterness.

It moves me from this opinion that myrrhed wine was given to the guilty as if for a benefit. For this very thing abundantly notes the cruelty of the Jews, that they had taken care that Christ should be led to such evils, that a drink which would stupefy the mind should be offered to him as if for solace: by which act the words of David were fulfilled in Christ both literally and in meaning. We also read in the martyrology of the virgins Maxima and Donatilla in the persecution of Valerian, that they were given vinegar and gall to drink before their execution.

Tasting] When he had lightly tasted, only by fulfilling the prophecy: not so that he might drink, which is lambanein in Mark; just as lambanein to psomion is to devour bread dipped in broth. But Christ did not want to drink, because, as we have said, it was applied to stupefy the mind. But hanging on the cross afterwards, because he was thirsty, elabe to oxos that is he drank, John XIX. 30.

It is indeed read as oἶνον in Mark, yet oἶνον ought not here be read for ὄξος, as Beza and Corn. à Lap. indeed contend, and as we read in the Ethiopian, and also in one or two Greek Codices, just as the Latin version also has it, which Grotius rashly excuses: for it is not right for an Interpreter to substitute entirely different words, or to transmute vinegar into wine: since most all Greek Codices, Jerome, Hilary, and the Greek Interpreters commonly read ὄξος; Origen, Chrysost. Titus of Bostra, Euthym. Theophyl. the Syrian, likewise the Ambrose and Persian Interpreters. Erasmus, however, observes that the same drink was not given to Christ here as was given to him while hanging on the cross: which distinction we admit with respect to this v. 34 and the following v. 48: but here in v. 34 it seems one must side with those who think that myrrhed wine was indeed brought by the pious women according to the custom of the nation, Prov. XXXI. 6, Am. II. 8. 9. Zach. XII. 3. but that it had been mixed by the soldiers not only with gall and other bitter matter, such as wormwood, but also with vinegar, so that they might satisfy their own lust: whence Christ did not wish to drink it, as the Evangelist adds, and γευσάμενος οὐκ ἤθελε πιεῖν. Mark therefore calls it wine, but Matthew calls it vinegar: that vinegar was mixed with wine, but not that ὄξος denotes wine of a pleasant taste. And the opinion of Dievius here is correct, that nothing was done here according to the received custom of the Jews: who were accustomed to perform this office of humanity to those about to die, by offering them wine with a grain of frankincense. Here, on the contrary, instead of wine they offered vinegar, and instead of the frankincense of pleasant taste, they offered the bitterness of myrrh, so that nothing would be lacking to reveal their virulent spirit against the Savior. Bede and Strabo say that the wine was tempered with myrrh and gall together. But Calixtus is wrong, along with Baronius, Gretser, and Conzenius, to confuse the myrrh potion with the myrrhed one. For the latter is named from myrrh, in Greek σμύρνα, but the former from ointment, or μύρον. See Thom. Barthol. de cruce p. 125.

Latin:

Vers. 34. ὄξος μετὰ χολῆς μεμιγμένον] Ita pleraque exem- plaria & Syrus. Nec aliter legit Origenes diligens exem- plarium inquisitor. Neque tamen Latinum interpretem culpo qui vinum vertit, ut nec eos qui Græco margini ad vo- cem ὄξος adjecere οἶνον, interpretamenti gratia, quod postea in contextum quorundam librorum irrepsit. Nam ὄξος Græci vocant vinum factitii saporis: quale ὄξος αὐτῶν ex palmulis Xenophonti atque aliis memoratum: Idem au- tem & vinum non minus recte dicitur, sicut cerevisiam οἶνον κρίθινον appellat Athenæus. Tale erat & hoc vinum, sive thure, ut Hebræorum magistri tradunt, sive myrrha, ut Mar- cus ait, conditum, quod recepto more ad supplicium eunti- bus dari solebat. Sed & חמץ Hebræum quod in Psalmo est id quod infectum est significat: ut observatum est a sum- mæ diligentiæ viro, cui & in hoc accedo, quod χολὴν laxius sumit pro omni amaritie: quippe cum ea voce absinthium significent Græci Interpretes Prov. V. 3. Thr. III. 15. Nam & Hebræum ראש sive רוש late patet, & voce πικρὸν verti- tur Jer. XXIII. 15. atque adeo ad herbas etiam venenatas amari gustus porrigitur: ut liquet collato loco Deut. XXIX. 18. cum Hebr. XII. 14. Atque ita vocem χολῆς hic sumsis Syrus vertens מררתא quod amarorem significat, & pro- pterea absinthio non minus quam felli aptatur. Neque aliter ad Marcum Theophylactus: & Augustinus lib. III. de con- sensu Evangelistarum: Fel quippe pro amaritudine posuit.

dimovet me ab hac sententia quod myrrhatum vinum quasi pro beneficio sontibus dabatur. Nam hoc ipsum crudeli- tatem Judæorum abunde notat, quod Christum curassent eo malorum perduci, ut quasi pro solatio offerendus ei esset potus qui mentem extemaret: quo facto verba Da- vidis κατὰ λέξιν simul & κατὰ διάνοιαν in Christo impleta sunt. Etiam de virginibus Maxima & Donatilla in perse- cutione Valeriani ante supplicium aceto & felle potatis in martyrologio legimus.

γευσάμενος] Cum leviter degustasset, implendo tantum vaticinio: non ut imbiberet quod est λαμβάνειν Marco; sic- υτ λαμβάνειν τὸ ψωμίον est panem jusculo tinctum devorare. Noluit autem imbibere Christus, quia, ut diximus, menti extemnandæ adhibebatur. In cruce autem pendens postea, quia sitiebat, ἔλαβε τὸ ὄξος id est imbibit, Joh. XIX. 30.

Legitur sane oἶνον apud Marcum, non tamen hic ideo oἶνον pro ὄξος legi debet, ut quidem Be- za & Corn. à Lap. contendunt, & apud Æthiopem legimus, nec non in uno atque altero Græco Co- dice, prout etiam habet Latina versio, quam temere excusat Grotius: non enim integrum est Interpreti voces prorsus alias substituere, aut acetum in vi- num transmutare: siquidem Codd. Græci plerique omnes, Hieronymus, Hilarius & Interpretes Græci communiter ὄξος legunt; Origenes, Chrysost. Titus Bostrens. Euthym. Theophyl. Syrus, item Ambr. & Per- sicus Interpretes. Observat autem Erasmus, non eundem potum Christo hic datum, qui eidem da- tus in cruce pendenti: quam distinctionem respe- ctu hujus v. 34. & sequentis v. 48. admittimus: hic vero vers. 34. videtur iis accedendum qui putant vinum myrrhatum quidem adductum à piis mulier- culis more gentis Proverb. XXXI. 6. Am. II. 8. 9. Zach. XII. 3. sed à militibus non modo felle, aliaque materia amara, uti absinthio, sed etiam aceto com- mixtum fuisse, ut suam explerent libidinem: unde id bibere Christus noluerit, ut addit Evangelista, & γευσάμενος οὐκ ἤθελε πιεῖν. Vinum ergo Mar- cus quidem vocat, Matthæus autem acetum: quod vino acetum mixtum fuerit, non vero ὄξος vinum saporis tactitii denotetur. Et recte Dievii hic habet sententia, nihil ex recepto Judæorum more hic fa- ctum: qui hoc morituris humanitatis officium præstare solebant, ut vinum propinarent cum gra- no thuris. Hic contra pro vino acetum, pro beni- gni saporis thure amarorem myrrhæ propinarunt, nequid deesset, quo virulentum suum in Servato- rem animum proderent. Beda & Strabus vinum & myrrha & felle simul fuisse temperatum dicunt. Male autem Calixtus, cum Baronio, Gretsero, Conzenio myrrhinam potionem cum myrrhata confundit. Hæc enim à myrrha, Græce σμύρνα, illa vero ab unguento, seu μύρῳ dicta. Vide Thom. Barthol. de cruce p. 125.

## 27:35
Vers. 35. Διεμερίσαντο τὰ ἱμάτια αὐτοῦ, βάλλοντες κλῆρον] That is, they partly divided them, and partly assigned them by lot to the winner, as John teaches us: God, of course, directing the matter so that what David had said of himself figuratively might be fulfilled in Christ according to the most exact propriety. This, however, came from Roman custom. For the soldiers who were the executioners of the punishment claimed for themselves the spoils of the condemned, which the Emperor Hadrian forbade to be done except by the order of the governors: The pannicularia, he says, are those things which one taken into custody brought with him: the spoils with which one is clothed when he is led to punishment, as the very name shows. Let neither the guards claim these for themselves any longer; nor let the officers desire those things of which one is stripped at the moment he is punished. That which follows here in certain books, ἵνα πληρωθῇ, I do not doubt was added from John, because many of the best Greek copies, and even Latin ones, do not have it, nor does the Syrian or the Arabic, which is undoubtedly older, recognize it. Origen also does not read it.

How David predicted these things, we saw at Ps. XXII. Certainly not in such a way that he understood it figuratively of himself, as Grotius says: for we have refuted that in Calvin.

Latin:

Vers. 35. Διεμερίσαντο τὰ ἱμάτια αὐτοῦ, βάλλοντες κλῆρον] Id est partim diviserunt, partim alea addixerunt victori, ut nos docet Johannes: Deo scilicet rem ita dirigente, ut quod David de se dixerat figurate, in Christo secundum exactissi- mam proprietatem impleretur. Veniebat autem hoc ex more Romano. Milites enim supplicii exactores fontium spolia sibi vindicabant, quod Adrianus Imperator vetuit fieri nisi præsidum jussu: Pannicularia, inquit, sunt ea quæ in custodiam receptus secum attulit: spolia quibus indutus est, cum quis ad supplicium ducitur, ut & ipsa appellatio ostendit. Ista neque speculatores ultra sibi vindicent; neque optio- nes ea desiderent quibus spoliatur quo momento quis punitus est. Quod in quibusdam libris hic sequitur ἵνα πληρωθῇ ex Jo- hanne adjectum non dubito, quia Græca optima exempla- ria multa etiam Latina non habent, nec agnoscit Syrus Ara- be haud dubie antiquior. Etiam Origenes non legit.

Quomodo hæc David prædixerit, ad Ps. XXII. vidimus. Certe non ita, ut de se figurate id intelle- xerit, quod ait Grotius: id enim in Calvino profli- gavimus.

## 27:36
Vers. 36. καὶ καθήμενοι ἐτήρουν αὐτὸν ἐκεῖ] And this is from Roman custom. Petronius Arbiter in the Satyricon: the soldier who was guarding the crosses.

Latin:

Vers. 36. καὶ καθήμενοι ἐτήρουν αὐτὸν ἐκεῖ] Et hoc ex more Romano. Petronius Arbiter Satyrico: miles qui cruces asser- vabat.

## 27:37
Vers. 37. τὴν αἰτίαν] Did Dio Cassius say 'letters declaring the cause of the execution'? A title, as John does, Suetonius in two places, and Tertullian in his Apologeticus: πίνακι, Eusebius where he deals with Attalus. The cause of the punishment was usually indicated in brief words, either in writing or by the voice of a herald. In writing, as in Suetonius: 'IMPIE LOCUTUS PARMULARIOUS': in Eusebius in the said place: 'this is Attalus the Christian'. By the voice of a herald, which the jurisconsults call a superindictum, as 'do not swear rashly' L. si duo, D. de jurejurando: 'you have acted as a sycophant' L. fustibus ex quibus causis infamia: 'because he built the city, the war was ended' in Diodorus Siculus: 'DO NOT RASHLY EMBRACE THE LEGATE OF THE ROMAN PEOPLE, O PLEBEIAN MAN' in Spartianus: 'WHAT YOU DO NOT WISH FOR YOURSELF, DO NOT DO TO ANOTHER' in Lampridius: 'HE WHO SOLD SMOKE IS PUNISHED BY SMOKE' in the same: 'he confessed himself to be a Christian' in Eusebius: 'A SACRILEGIOUS VIRGIN BRINGING BLASPHEMY TO THE GODS, A PROSTITUTE GIVEN TO THE BROTHELS' in Ambrose: the αἰτία was written in the Latin language, because of the majesty of the empire: in Hebrew, because of the place in which the punishment was carried out: in Greek, because of the great crowd of Hellenists who had gathered for the Passover, although otherwise the Jews and neighboring peoples had been accustomed to the Greek language since the Macedonian times and in Palestine. Thus, in Josephus, C. Caesar the dictator commands the Sidonians, and M. Antony the Triumvir commands the Tyrians, that certain of their edicts be recorded on public tablets in both the Latin and also the Greek language. And the edict by which foreigners were forbidden to proceed within the τὸν δρύφακτον of the Temple was posted in both Greek and Latin letters. We also read that in the tomb of the Emperor Gordian there were letters of these three languages, and besides them, Persian and Egyptian as well. Not even this is unworthy of note, that by God's direction it was brought about that, in the manner of Emperors, the cross of Christ should carry the titles of nations not yet indeed subdued, but soon to be subdued. For He was the one to whom Jewish religion, Greek learning, and Latin strength had to yield. Nor is it new that Pilate, through mockery—but if I am not mistaken, wishing to mock the Jews more than Jesus—called Him King of the Jews in the title, since in Livy also a herald, by the order of Fulvius, is said to have proclaimed at the execution of Taurer Subellius: 'Lictor, add lashes to the brave man.' I believe the Latin inscription was JESUS NAZARENUS REX JUDAEORUM, as John places it. By Matthew and Luke, ὗτός ἐστι was added from the Hebrew, in which it would have been הוא ישוע.

Latin:

Vers. 37. τὴν αἰτίαν] γράμματα τὴν αἰτίαν τῆς θανατώ- σεως δηλῶτα dixit Dio Cassius? Titulum, ut Johannes, Sue- tonius duobus locis & Tertullianus Apologetico: πίνακι Eusebius ubi de Attalo agit. Brevibus verbis causa sup- plicii indicari solebat scripto, aut præconis voce. Scripto ut apud Suetonium: IMPIE LOCUTUS PARMULA- RIUS: apud Eusebium dicto loco: ὗτός ἐστιν Ἄτταλος ὁ Χριστιανὸς. Voce præconis quod superindictum Juriscon- sulti vocant, ut προπετῶς μὴ ὄμνυε L. si duo, D. de jurejuran- do: συκοφάντησας L. fustibus ex quibus causis infamia: ὅτι τὴν πόλιν ἕκτισεν ἐλύθη τε πόλεμος apud Diodorum Si- culum: LEGATUM POPULI ROMANI HOMO PLEBEJUS TEMERE AMPLECTI NOLI apud Spar- tianum: QUOD TIBI NON VIS, ALTERI NE FECERIS apud Lampridium: FUMO PUNITUR QUI VENDIDIT FUMUM apud eundem: πολυκᾴκηθ ὁ- μολόγησεν ἑαυτὸν Χριστιανὸν εἶναι apud Eusebium: AGNEM SACRILEGAM VIRGINEM DIIS BLASPHEMIAM INFERENTEM SCORTUM LUPANARIBUS DA- TAM apud Ambrosium: Latino sermone scripta αἰτία, ob majestatem imperii: Hebræo, ob locum in quo suppli- cium sumebatur: Græco, ob maximam turbam Helleni- starum quæ ad Pascha convenerat, quanquam alioqui Græ- co sermoni à Macedonicis temporibus & in Palæstina Ju- dæi vicinæque gentes assueverant. Itaque apud Josephum C. Cæsar dictator Sidoniis, atq; M. Antonius Triumvir Ty- riis imperant, ut edicta quædam sua in publicas tabulas refe- rantur tum Latino tum Græco etiam sermone. Et edictum quo vetabantur alisnegenæ procedere intra τὸν δρύφακτον Templi, proscriptum erat tam Græcis quam Latinis literis. In sepulchro etiam Gordiani Imperatoris legimus fuisse & harum trium linguarum literas, & Persicas præterea atque Ægyptiacas. Ne hoc quidem indignum notatu, Deo res di- rigente, factum ut more Imperatorum Christi crux præfer- ret titulos gentium nondum quidem subactarum sed brevi subigendarum. Ille enim erat cui cedere debebat religio Judaica, eruditio Græca, robur Latinum. Neque novum est quod Pilatus per ludibrium, sed ni fallor, Judæis magis quam Jesu illusum cupiens, eum in titulo vocavit Regem judæorum, cum apud Livium quoque præco jussu Fulvii in supplicio Taurer Subellii pronuntiasse dicitur: Lictor viro forti adde virgas. Inscriptionem Latinam fuisse arbitror JE- SUS NAZARENUS REX JUDÆORUM, quomodo eam ponit Johannes. A Matthæo & Luca additum ὗ- τός ἐστι ex Hebræo in quo fuerit הוא ישוע.

## 27:38
Vers. 38. σταυρῶνται σὺν ἀυτῷ δύο λῃσταὶ] For the cross is the punishment of robbers. Petronius: 'When meanwhile the governor of the province ordered the robbers to be fixed to crosses.' Seneca: 'Has someone committed robbery? What then has he deserved? That he be suspended.' Firmicus: 'He will make a murderer and a robber: caught in these crimes, he is cruelly raised up fixed to a cross.' They were called λῃσταὶ, and also by the name of sicarii, even those who had taken up arms without public order, as we just noted at verse 16. These two had been kept for the time of the approaching Unleavened Bread, so that they might be punished at the largest possible gathering of the people: for that was accepted in Judea, and deservedly retained by the Romans, since it did not differ from their institutions. For even at Rome, in the comitium, and later also at the sound of the trumpet, punishments were accustomed to be carried out. Quintilian also says that in executions it was taken care of that as many as possible could see and be moved by fear, with the cause added: For all punishment pertains not so much to the crime as to the example.

Latin:

Vers. 38. σταυρῶνται σὺν ἀυτῷ δύο λῃσταὶ] Nam crux pœna latronum. Petronius: Cum interim Imperator provinciæ la- trones jussit crucibus affigi. Seneca: Latrocinium fecit ali- quis? Quid ergo meruit? ut suspendatur. Firmicus: homici- dam & latronem efficiet: istis facinoribus comprehensus patibu- lo suffixus in crucem crudeliter erigitur: Vocabantur autem λῃ- σταὶ & sicariorum nomine etiam qui injussu publico ar- ma cepissent, ut modo ad comma 16. notavimus. Hiau- tem duo asservati erant ad tempus adventantium Azymo- rum, ut quam maximo populi conventu punirentur: id enim in Judæa receptum erat, meritoque à Romanis reten- tum, cum ab eorum institutis non dissideret. Nam & Ro- mæ olim in comitio, postea quoque ad classicum exigi pœ- næ solebant. Quintilianus quoque in suppliciis curatum ait, ut plurimi intueri, commoveri metu possint, causa addi- ta: Omnis enim pœna non tam ad delictum pertinet, quam ad exemplum.

## 27:39
Vers. 39. κινῶντες τὰς κεφαλὰς ἀυτῶν] A sign of insult: in which sense you will find κινεῖν κεφαλὴν in Psalm XXII. 8, 2 Kings XIX. 21, Isaiah XXXVII. 22, Lamentations II. 15; σαλέυειν κεφαλὴν in Psalm CX. 25. The writer of Ecclesiasticus XIII. 8 followed this Hebraism: τὴν κεφαλὴν ἀυτὲ κινήσει ἐπὶ σοὶ. It is to be noted here how easily the diverse fortune of Jesus shook all his benefits from the minds of the common people. Sophocles well says: 'Alas, alas, how quickly the favor of the dead flows away from mortals and is found to have slipped away.'

Latin:
