Vers. 39. κινῶντες τὰς κεφαλὰς ἀυτῶν] signum insultatio- nis: quo sensu κινεῖν κεφαλὴν reperies Psal. XXII. 8. 2. Reg. XIX. 21. Es. XXXVII. 22. Thren. II. 15. σαλέυειν κεφαλὴν Pf. CX. 25. Secutus est hunc Hebraismum Scriptor Eccle- siastici XIII. 8. τὴν κεφαλὴν ἀυτὲ κινήσει ἐπὶ σοὶ. Notandum hic quam facile diversa Jesu fortuna omnia ejus beneficia vulgi animis excusserit. Bene Sophocles: Φεῦ Φεῦ θανόντων ὡς ταχεῖα τοῖς βροτοῖς χάρις διαῤῥεῖ καὶ προδῦσ᾽ ἁλίσκεται.

## 27:40
Vers. 40. εἰ ὑιὸς τῇ Θεῖ] This does not pertain to birth, of which the common people had heard nothing, but to the special love of God, such as that with which fathers pursue their sons. Thus, what is below in v. 43 as Θεᾶ ὑιὸς, Luke called Θεᾶ ἐκλεκτός, that is, especially beloved by God. The writer of Wisdom introduces the impious thus disparaging the pious man: 'He boasts that he has knowledge of God, and calls himself a child of the Lord.' c. II. 15. And soon: 'He boasts that God is his father; let us see if his words are true, and let us test what will happen at his end. For if the righteous man is the Son of God, He will help him, and will deliver him from the hand of his adversaries.' However those who mocked Christ understood it, Christ certainly called Himself the proper and only-begotten Son of God, through birth from the substance of the Father, not through the special love of God: which is to be noted here because of the Grotian Gloss. For one should not depart to metaphorical and figurative meanings, abandoning the literal sense of things, unless necessity compels.

Latin:

Vers. 40. εἰ ὑιὸς τῇ Θεῖ] Non ad nativitatem hoc perti- net, de qua plebs nihil inaudiverat, sed ad specialem Dei a- morem, qualis est quo patres filios suos prosequuntur. Sic quod infra v. 43. est Θεᾶ ὑιὸς, Lucas dixit Θεᾶ ἐκλεκτός, id est, Deo eximie dilectus. Scriptor sapientiæ impios viro pio sic obtreclantes inducit: ἐπαγγέλλεται γνῶσιν ἔχειν Θεᾶ, καὶ παῖδα κυρία ἑαυτὸν ὀνομάζει. c. II. 15. & mox: ἀλαζονεύεται πατέρα θεόν· ἴδωμεν εἰ οἱ λόγοι ἀυτᾶ ἀληθεῖς, καὶ πειράσωμεν τὰ ἐν ἐκβάσει ἀυτᾶ. εἰ γάρ ἐστιν ὁ δίκαιος, ὑιὸς Θεᾶ ἀντιλή- ψεται ἀυτᾶ, καὶ ῥύσεται ἀυτὸν ἐκ χειρὸς ἀνθεστηκότων. Quomodocunque id intellexerint qui Christo illuserunt, Christus sane se proprium dixit & unigenitum Dei Filium, per nativitatem è sub- stantia Patris, non per specialem Dei amorem: quod ob Glossam Grotianam hic notandum. Non enim ad tralatitias & figurales significationes abeundum, relicta rerum proprietate, nisi cogat necessitas.

## 27:42
Vers. 42. εἰ βασιλεὺς Ἰσραήλ ἐστι] It appears from this that miracles were expected from the Messiah, which some of the Jews began to deny out of a spirit of contention, while others admitted them. καταβάτω νῦν ἀπὸ τοῦ σταυροῦ] The son of Satan speaks thus, as Satan did above in c. IV. 3. πιστεύσομεν αὐτῷ] I consider this reading to be more true. For they do not mean by this that they will place their trust in Him (which is usually said as πιστεύειν ἐπ᾽ αὐτόν, or ἐπ᾽ αὐτῷ), but that they will believe His assertion concerning the divine benevolence toward Himself: as we were just citing from the book of Wisdom: 'let us see if his words are true.' That sense of believing is usually expressed in these books by the dative.

Latin:

Vers. 42. εἰ βασιλεὺς Ἰσραήλ ἐστι] Apparet hinc à Messia exspectata miracula, quod quidam Judæorum contentionis studio negare cœperunt, aliisque fatentibus. καταβάτω νῦν ἀπὸ τοῦ σταυροῦ] Satanæ filius ita loquitur, ut Satanas supra c. IV. 3. πιστεύσομεν αὐτῷ] Hanc lectionem veriorem arbitror. Non enim hoc volunt ii id præstat fiduciam se in eo collocaturos (quod dici solet πιστεύειν ἐπ᾽ αὐτόν, vel ἐπ᾽ αὐτῷ) sed fidem habituros asseverationis ejus de divina in se benevolentia: ut modo citabamus ex libro Sapientiæ: ἴδωμεν εἰ οἱ λόγοι αὐτοῦ ἀληθεῖς. Is autem credendi sensus in his libris dativo exprimi solet.

## 27:43
Vers. 43. πέποιθεν ἐπὶ τὸν Θεὸν] It was brought about by divine dispensation that the wicked Senators and Chief Priests used the same words about Christ with which David, when he was miserably harassed, once complained in Psalm XXII, which very Psalm the writer of the Midrash Tehillim acknowledges to contain a prophecy about the Messiah. For there the words of the impious are expressed mimetically thus: גל אל־יהוה: where some think גל is an imperative, with the meaning of one insulting: but Kimchi and others think it is a participial noun: as if you were to say 'believing': supply 'is': which the LXX seem to have followed: ἤλπισεν ἐπὶ κύριον.

The whole Psalm cries out that David was not complaining about himself, but speaking from the person of the Messiah. Concerning which, it is treated at length in the Annotations of Anti-Grotius on the same.

Let him deliver him now if he wills him: This reading must in no way be questioned. For the Hellenists construct θέλειν with the accusative case in the sense of loving. For what follows in the Psalm וַיַלְטֵהוּ יַצִילֵהוּ כִי חָפַץ בּוֹ, the LXX translated thus: ῥυσάσθω αὐτὸν, σωσάτω αὐτὸν ὅτι θέλει αὐτὸν. Thus Psalm XIX. 20: ἠθέλησέ με. Ps. XLI. 12: τεθέληκάς με. But at 1 Sam. XVIII. 22, the same interpreters said θέλει ἐν σοὶ ὁ βασιλεὺς. There is also a place where they express this Hebrew manner of speaking by ἐγκεῖσθαι, as in Gen. XXXIV. 9, and by αἱρετίζειν in 1 Sam. XIX. 1, and by εὐδοκεῖν in Ps. CXLVII. 11. For he said that I am the Son of God: This also is from the Psalm we mentioned: but εἶπε γὰρ is a supplement of the Hebrew exposition. ὅτι Θεοῦ εἰμι υἱὸς is a simpler statement of that which is poetically said there: כִּי אַתָּה נֹחִי מִבָּטֶן, that is, σὺ εἶ ὁ ἐκσπάσας με ἐκ γαστρός.

Latin:

Vers. 43. πέποιθεν ἐπὶ τὸν Θεὸν] Divina dispensatione factum est, ut eadem verba Scelerati Senatores & Ponti- fices de Christo usurpavent quibus olim se incessi David miserabiliter querebatur Psal. XXII. quem ipsum Psalmum vaticinium de Messia continere agnoscit Scriptor Midras Thehillim. Ibi enim verba impiorum μιμητικῶς ita expri- muntur: גל אל־יהוה : ubi גל quidam putant esse imperativum, insultantis fignificatu: sed Kimchi atque a- lii nomen participiale: quasi dicas πίστων: supple est: quod secuti videntur LXX. ἤλπισεν ἐπὶ κύριον.

Non de se Davidem questum esse, sed loquu- tum ex persona Messiæ totus Psalmus clamat. Quo de in Annotat. Anti-Grot. ad eundem prolixe a- ctum.

ῥυσάσθω νῦν αὐτὸν εἰ θέλει αὐτὸν] Nulla modo sollici- tanda est hæc lectio. Nam Hellenistæ θέλειν cum quarto casu construunt in amandi notione. Nam quod in Psalmo sequitur וַיַלְטֵהוּ יַצִילֵהוּ כִי חָפַץ בּוֹ ita verterunt LXX. ῥυσάσθω αὐτὸν, σωσάτω αὐτὸν ὅτι θέλει αὐτὸν. Sic Psal XIX. 20. ἠθέλησέ με. Pf. XLI. 12. τεθέληκάς με. At 1. Sam. XIIX. 22. iidem Interpretes dixerunt θέλει ἐν σοὶ ὁ βασιλεὺς. Est & ubi Hebræum hoc loquendi genus exprimunt per ἐγκεῖσθαι ut Genes. XXXIV. 9. & per αἱρετίζειν 1. Sam. XIX. 1. & per εὐδοκεῖν Pf. CXLVII. 11. εἶπε γὰρ ὅτι Θεοῦ εἰμι υἱὸς] Hoc quoque ex eo quem dixi- mus Psalmo: sed εἶπε γὰρ est supplementum ἐκθέσεως He- braicæ. ὅτι Θεοῦ εἰμι υἱὸς simplicior enuntiatio ejus quod poetice ibi dicitur: כִּי אַתָּה נֹחִי מִבָּטֶן ὅτι σὺ εἶ ὁ ἐκσπά- σας με ἐκ γαστρός.

## 27:44
Vers. 44. λῃσταὶ: Ancient and modern interpreters have noted that the plural number is used when one out of many, but indefinitely, is indicated. Thus the writer to the Hebrews, speaking of the righteous of the Old Covenant, says they shut the mouths of lions and were sawn asunder: the former of which pertains to one Daniel, the latter to one Isaiah. But because it was of no importance to name them in that place, it was enough for the matter to be expressed in the plural. Thus in this very history Luke says: ἐπέπαισον δὲ αὐτῷ κ᾿ οἱ στρατιῶται προσερχόμενοι καὶ ὄξος προσφέροντες αὐτῷ. And John similarly: πλήσαντες σπόγγον ὄξους προσήνεγκαν. And yet Matthew will presently say clearly that this was done by one of the soldiers. I have gathered these things, pointed out by many, all the more willingly, lest anyone resort with some of the ancients to that interpretation which, with little probability, posits that the robber who believed in Christ was suddenly converted from reviling to that piety: with which fiction removed, there remains nonetheless a benefit to him, significant in many ways and not rashly to be drawn into consequences of example.

Montacutius not unaptly judges that this plural number does not properly indicate persons, but the quality of persons, as if it were said that Christ was mocked by any kind of men, even by robbers: but that this does not indicate whether one or more robbers mocked him.

Latin:

Vers. 44. λῃσταὶ] Pluralem numerum usurpari ubi unum è multis, sed indefinite, indicatur veteres novique interpre- tes monuerunt. Ita Scriptor ad Hebræos de justis loquens veteris fœderis, clauserunt inquit ora leonum & serra dissecti sunt: quorum illud ad unum Danielem, hoc ad unum E- saiam pertinet. Sed quia nominari eos eo loco nihil attine- bat, satis erat πληθυντικῶς rem efferri. Sic in hac ipsa histo- ria Lucas ἐπέπαισον δὲ αὐτῷ κ᾿ οἱ στρατιῶται προσερχόμενοι καὶ ὄξος προσφέροντες αὐτῷ. Et Johannes similiter πλήσαντες σπόγγον ὄξους προσήνεγκαν. Atqui ab uno militum id fa- ctum diferte mox dicet Matthæus. Hæc à multis indicata eo lubentius congesti, nequis cum antiquis aliquot ad eam interpretationem confugiat, quæ parum probabiliter statuit latronem qui in Christum credidit subito à convitiis ad eam pietatem conversum: quo commento sublato manet nihil- ominus beneficium in ipsum multis modis insigne & non temere trahendi in consequentias exempli.

Montacutius non inconcinne censet pluralem hunc numerum non proprie personas, sed qualita- tem personarum indicare, ac si diceretur, à quovis hominum genere Christum fuisse illusum, etiam à latronibus: non indicare autem hoc an unus an plures latrones ipsi illuserint.

## 27:45
Vers. 45. ἀπὸ δὲ ἕκτης ὥρας: At the third hour of the day, trials began to be conducted among the Romans.

The third hour occupies a few lawyers. The hearing of Pilate also falls into that time. Ignatius to the Trallians well says: τῇ ἓν παρασκευῇ τρίτῃ ὥρᾳ ἀπόφασιν ἐδέξατο παρὰ τοῦ Πιλάτου. So that Christ was crucified before the sixth hour: after the sixth hour the darkness began, but Christ died a little after the ninth. The same Ignatius says: ἕκτῃ ὥρᾳ ἐσταυρώθη, ἐννατῇ ἀπέπνευσε: which sense is also read in a sufficiently ancient book, which is named the Constitutions of Clement, book V. ch. 14 and VIII. ch. 24, which ought to move us not to change anything in the Scripture of Mark or John against the authority of the most ancient codices and translators. Nor indeed do they contradict one another: for the custom of speaking was born from the practice of the Temple, where sacrifices and prayers were accustomed to be made at the third, sixth, and ninth hour; as Jerome notes regarding Daniel VII, besides the Hebrews, which very times were signified on the most festive days by the sound of the trumpet: as we are taught in Num. X. 10. Whence it happened that these hours were commonly celebrated as being better known: nor will you find other names of hours where mention is made of fixed prayers. See Acts III. 1, X. 3, 9, and Tertullian on fasts, where he says these are the more notable hours in human affairs which distribute the day, which distinguish business, which resonate publicly. With which agree those things which Cyprian writes on the Lord's Prayer and Jerome both to Laeta and to Demetrias. And to this pertains that which is above XX. 3. 5, where between the third, sixth, and ninth no hour is named, since after the ninth mention is made of the eleventh. But it is said to have happened at the third or sixth hour, whatever had occurred between those fixed times of prayer, as things that are placed in the middle are accustomed to be referred now to this, now to that limit. For this is just as if it were said that something happened ἐν τῇ δευτέρᾳ τριώρᾳ, as the Genethliaci speak. Hesychius teaches us that parts of the day were signified by the sound of the trumpet even among certain Greeks, in which place he says that the hours without trumpets are called by Sophocles the dead of night.

These things are read in the Epistle of Ignatius, not to the Smyrnaeans, but to the Trallians. But the Grotian reconciliation is not to be approved. For thus the time of the crucifixion of Christ would be uncertain. For it is said to have happened at the third or sixth hour of the day, because it is doubtful at what hour, between those fixed times of prayer, it occurred. Others therefore establish a division of the day by three-hour periods or quadrants, so that in John the sixth hour is understood not of the second quadrant of the day named from the sixth hour, but of the hour itself, which is counted from the beginning of the day, although Mark perhaps designated the second quadrant of the day, to which he reconciles both the beginning and the naming of the third hour. But because this naming is also doubtful, it is better with Marcellus the Roman Monk, Daniel Heinsius, and Rob. Baillie, with Lud. de Dieu and Bald. not dissenting, Walaeus, to say that at the third hour, counting from the crucifixion, the division of the garments is indicated, Mark XV. 26, or that a certain third hour from the handing over to Pilate is understood, and thus the crucifixion happened at almost the sixth hour, or as Luke has it, about the sixth: just as we have shown more fully in the Biblical Chronicle.

σκότος ἐγένετο ἐπὶ πᾶσαν τὴν γῆν] The sun being obscured, of course, as Luke teaches us; not by the moon being interposed, as it was then full, nor by a cloud being drawn over, but in a manner unknown to men. ἐπὶ πᾶσαν τὴν γῆν here, which Mark called ἐφ᾽ ὅλην τὴν γῆν, just as it cannot be taken for the whole globe of the earth (for in many parts it was not day), so I would not have it taken for Judea alone, since ancient astrologers and chronographers have noted this darkness, with no name of a place added, from which it is given to be understood that it extended widely. Phlegon, 13th of the Olympiads. Τῷ Δ ἔτει τῆς ΣΒ ὀλυμπιάδος ἐγένετο ἔκλειψις ἡλίου μεγίστη τ᾽ ἐγνωρισμένων πρότερον, κὴ νὺξ ὥρα ς΄ τῆς ἡμέρας ἐγένετο ὥστε καὶ ἀστέρας ἐν ὐρανῷ φανῆναι. σεισμός τε μέγας κατὰ βιθύνιαν γενόμενος τὰ πολλὰ Νικαίας κατεστρέψατο. He names the place of the earthquake; he does not name the place of the darkness, and since he records it as having been seen before by elders, so that at high noon it was as if it were night, he sufficiently demonstrates that this spectacle was not peculiar to Judea. Eusebius cites another Greek whom he does not name, writing thus about this very matter: ὁ ἥλιος ἐξέλιπε. Βιθυνία ἐσείσθη. Νικαίας τὰ πολλὰ ἔπεσεν. That writer not named by Eusebius is undoubtedly Thallus, whom Africanus mentions thus: τοῦτο τὸ σκότος ἔκλειψιν ἡλίου Θάλλος ἀποκαλεῖ ἐν τρίτῃ τῶν ἱστοριῶν ὡς ἐμοὶ δοκεῖ ἀλόγως. Ἑβραῖοι γὰρ ἄγουσι τὸ πάσχα και τὰ σελήνης ΙΔ, πρὸ δὲ μιᾶς τοῦ πάσχα τὰ περὶ τὸν Σωτῆρα συμβαίνει, ἔκλειψις δὲ ἡλίου, σελήνης ὑπελθούσης τῷ ἡλίῳ γίνεται. ἀδύνατον δὲ ἐν ἄλλῳ χρόνῳ πλὴν ἐν τῷ μεταξὺ μιᾶς κὴ τῆς πρὸ αὐτῆς και τὰ τὴν σύνοδον αὐτῶν ἀποβῆναι. πῶς ὦν ἔκλειψις νομισθείη και τὰ διάμετρον σχεδὸν ὑπαρχούσης τῆς σελήνης ἡλίῳ; In which place Africanus interprets that statement of Thallus, ὁ ἥλιος ἐξέλιπε, strictly, as if Thallus had meant that it was a natural ἔκλειψις, whereas otherwise the sun can be said ἐκλείπειν when it fails in any way. Thus also in certain copies of Luke, Origen complains that it was written erroneously ἡλίου ἐκλείποντος, which he, likewise as Africanus, judges to pertain to the injury of the sense. Tertullian in the Apologeticus: Yet he showed the proper signs of that death even when fixed to the cross. For he dismissed his spirit with a word of his own accord, anticipating the office of the executioner. At that same moment, the day, with the sun marking the middle of the world, was withdrawn. They certainly thought it an eclipse, who did not know that this also had been predicted concerning Christ. And yet you have that disaster of the world recorded in your archives. Where I do not see why we should accept any archives other than the public Roman acts, to which, if I am not mistaken, Lucian the martyr also appeals in Eusebius. And when he calls it a disaster of the world, he sufficiently took care that it should not be believed to be peculiar to Judea. Wherefore I think πᾶσαν τὴν γῆν here should be taken as in Luke II. 1, πᾶσαν τὴν οἰκουμένην, for the Roman world, or at least for its most important part. Many dispute what God intended to be signified by these darknesses. I think entirely that this portent did not pertain only to the Jews, whose prophecies, when worn out, depict the saddest times with the darkness of the sun; but also to other nations. For this also was among those things by which the centurion was struck with amazement. Wherefore that signification is to be taken which can be understood as broadly as possible. Among all peoples, however, it was accepted that they should believe that by such portents some notable crime was indicated as having been committed. The Thyestean banquet is well known, where Seneca says: O we, created by a harsh fate, whether we wretched ones have lost the sun, or have driven it away. Concerning this matter, Euripides says thus in Iphigenia: ἀλλάξας Δ' ἐξέδρας᾽ ἱερὸν ὄμμ' αὐγᾶς ἅλιος. To the same point pertains that passage in Medea: Does the Sun, the sower of our race, behold these things and is he beheld, and sitting in his chariot does he run through the accustomed spaces of the pure sky? And in Phaedra: You, head of the stars, radiant Titan, do you behold the wickedness of your race? Virgil on the Sun: When he stained his shining head with dark rust, and the impious ages feared eternal night. Marcus Antonius the Triumvir in a letter to Hyrcanus the High Priest: διὸ κὶ τ' ἥλιον ἀπεστράφθαι δοκῦμεν ὃς καὶ αὐτὸς ἀηδῶς ἐπεῖδε ὼ ἐπὶ καίσαρα μῖσος. Lucan: Titan himself, when he was carrying his head in the middle of Olympus, hid his burning chariots in black darkness, and wrapped the world in shadows, and compelled the nations to despair of the day, such as the Thyestean Mycenae endured when the sun fled through the east. Moreover, this portent could specifically recall to the Jews the words of Amos, who had said that it would come to pass that the sun would set at noon, adding that there would be mourning as for an only-begotten son, ch. VIII. 9, 10. For those things which had once been fulfilled in a metaphorical sense were now being fulfilled also in a literal sense, as we have often said. Although, indeed, the darkness described here, as it was the greatest during the greatest wickedness of the Jews and Romans, I do not think it should be denied that at other times also, if not equal, at least similar signs of divine wrath against more serious sins have existed. Certainly, it was constantly believed by the ancient Christians. I will bring forward one passage from Tertullian: it is in his work to Scapula: All these are signs of the imminent wrath of God, which it is necessary that we, in whatever way we can, both announce and preach, and pray against, and that we understand it to be local. For those who interpret its examples otherwise will feel it universal and supreme in its own time. For that sun also in the Utican assembly, with its light almost extinguished, was such a portent that it could not have suffered this from an ordinary eclipse, being positioned in its exaltation and domicile: You have astrologers.

Whether the obscuration of the sun was caused by the interposition of the moon is not sufficiently clear. Nor, however, should it be denied that it was so caused because the moon was full at that time. For although in the natural way an eclipse of the sun does not occur at the time of the full moon, yet who would doubt that this obscuration, which was entirely supernatural, could have occurred even with a full moon, unless he wished to call into doubt the divine power, for whom it is so easy to draw back the moon, even if it were distant from the sun by half the part of the sky, even by a retrograde journey against its own and natural motion, which is from the West to the East, towards the sun at noon, so that it might place itself under the sun, just as in Isaiah XXXVIII. 8. at the prayers of Hezekiah the sun had gone back ten degrees: how easy it is to draw back the sun's rays, so that it does not cast them upon the earth, nor shine, or to wrap its light as if with a certain veil: in which manner, by the solar rays being drawn back, the moon would also necessarily have been obscured, and consequently have suffered a supernatural eclipse, which, however, the Evangelists did not record to have happened. Some indeed observe that on that same day of the crucifixion, at the fifth hour according to our clock at Jerusalem, an eclipse of the Moon occurred to seven digits, and thus beyond half of the Lunar body, which lasted until half-past seven in the evening: but that it was natural, and therefore not noted on account of the retraction of the Sun's rays, the holy amanuenses of God would have deservedly recorded the obscuration of both luminaries. It is therefore surprising that ὁ δεῖνα attempts to prove that the eclipse of the Sun, which not only Dionysius the Areopagite but also Phlegon and Thallus noted, was not a proper eclipse, but an obscuration made by the retraction of the Sun's rays, by an argument I believe not sufficiently consistent with infinite divine omnipotence: because, forsooth, it must be believed that the moon, which at full moon is opposite the Sun, being drawn from its place to the Sun so that it might stand between the Sun and the earth, is absurd and alien to divine power. For with God every word is not impossible (Luke 1:37). For those of the Fathers who say that the Sun was forced to retract its rays, not so that it would not look, do not describe the manner of the obscuration, but rhetorize about that obscuration according to their custom, which can be seen even from Cyprian, sermon on the good of patience, who says that the Sun retracted both its rays and its eyes. Chrysostom, sermon on the Passion. in the Catena, says, the creature could not bear the injury of the Creator, whence the Sun retracted its rays, so that it might not see the crimes of the impious. But although the whole globe of the earth may not be denoted by the whole earth, it is not to be explained only of the Roman world, but of the whole land which had the Sun above the horizon. For that meaning must be taken, Grotius admitting, which can be understood as broadly as possible. And because all the Evangelists ὁμοθυμαδὸν assert that those darknesses were spread over the whole earth, one must deservedly adhere to the propriety of the words. Which was also done by the Fathers Chrysostom and others. Add that from the testimony of the Gentiles that universal Eclipse is also established. Tertullian noted that the fall of the world was recorded in the archives of the Romans. Eusebius in the Chronicles, at the year of the Lord's passion, observes from the commentaries of the Gentiles the failure of the Sun and darkness over the whole earth, and brings forward Phlegon, who recorded a great and excellent failure of the Sun, among all that had happened before it, in the year 262 of the Olympiad, in Bithynia: saying, moreover, the day at the sixth hour was so turned into dark night that stars were seen in the sky, and an earthquake in Bithynia overturned many buildings of the city of Nicaea. Therefore Orosius, book VIII, ch. 3, says that the Sun was obscured in the whole world at the time of Christ's passion, not only, he says, does the faith of the holy Gospels attest this, but also some books of the Greeks.

ἕως ὥρας ἐννάτης] That is, until the time of the evening offering. For thus the Hebrews divided the day. See what is above on this chapter, v. 42.

Latin:

Vers. 45. ἀπὸ δὲ ἕκτης ὥρας] Tertia hora diei judicia apud Romanos exerceri incipiebant.

Exercet paucos tertia causidicos. In id tempus incidit & Pilati cognitio. Bene Igna- tius ad Trallianos: τῇ ἓν παρασκευῇ τρίτῃ ὥρᾳ ἀπόφα- σιν ἐδέξατο παρὰ τοῦ Πιλάτου) Ita ut ante sextam Christus sit crucifixus: post sextam cœperint tenebræ mortuus autem Christus paulo post nonam Idus Ignatius: ἔκ- τῃ ὥρᾳ ἐσταυρώθη, ἐννατῇ ἀπέπνευσε: qui sensus legitur & in libro satis antiquo, cui nomen est constitutiones Cle- mentis lib. V. cap. 14. & VIII. c. 24. quæ movere nos de- bent ne quid in Scriptura Marci aut Johannis immutemus contra vetustissimorum codicum & μεταφραστῶν auctorita- tem. Neque vero illi inter se pugnant: nam mos loquen- di natus ex Templi consuetudine, ubi sacrificia & preces fieri solebant hora tertia, sexta, nona; ut præter Hebræos Hieronymus notat ad Danielem VII. quæ ipsa tempora fe- stis maxime diebus tubæ sono significabantur: ut docemur Num. X. 10. quo factum ut hæ horæ tanquam notiores vul- go celebrarentur: neque alia nomina horarum reperies, u- bi statarum precationum fit mentio. Vide Act. III. 1. X. 3. 9. & Tertullianum de jejuniis, ubi has horas insigniores ait in rebus humanis quæ diem distribuunt, quæ negotia distinguunt, quæ publice resonant. Quicum congruunt, quæ scribunt Cyprianus de oratione Dominica & Hierony- mus tum ad Lætam, tum ad Demetriadem. Atque eo per- tinet quod est supra XX. 3. 5. ubi inter tertiam, sextam & nonam nulla hora nominatur, cum post nonam undecimæ fiat mentio. Factum autem tertia aut sexta hora dicitur, quicquid inter illa stata precandi tempora evenerat, ut so- lent quæ in medio sunt posita nunc ad hunc, nunc ad illum terminum referri. Perinde enim hoc est, ac si diceretur fa- ctum aliquid ἐν τῇ δευτέρᾳ τριώρᾳ, ut loquuntur Genethlia- ci. Tubæ sono partes diei etiam apud Græcos quosdam significatas docet nos Hesychius, quo loco ἀσάλπιγκτοι ὥ- ραι Sophocli vocari ait conticinium noctis.

In Epistola hæc leguntur Ignatii, non ad Smyr- nenses, sed ad Trallianos. Non autem probanda est user Grotiana conciliatio. Nam ita incertum foret tempus crucifixionionis Christi. Factum enim sic di- citur tertia aut sexta hora diei, quod, dubium, qua hora, inter illa stata precandi tempora contigerit. A- lii ergo distinctionem diei per trihoria vel qua- drantes statuunt, ita ut in Johanne sexta hora non de quadrante secundo diei à sexta hora denomi- nato, sed de hora ipsa, quæ à diei exordio numera- tur, sexta intelligatur, tametsi Marcus forte qua- drantem secundum diei designarit, cui tertia ho- ra & initium & denominationem conciliat. Verum quia & hæc denominatio dubia est, præstat cum Marcello Monacho Romano, Daniele Heinsio, & Rob. Bailio, non abnuente Lud. de Dieu, & Bald. Walao, dicere, quod hora tertia, inde à crucifixione numeratione facta divisio vestium facta indicetur Marc. XV. 26. vel certa hora tertia à traditione Pi- lato facta intelligatur, adeoque fere hora sexta, crucifixio facta sit, vel ut Lucas habet, quasi sexta: quemadmodum in Chronico Biblico fusius ostendi- mus.

σκότος ἐγένετο ἐπὶ πᾶσαν τὴν γῆν] Sole scilicet obscurato, ut Lucas nos docet; non interposita Luna, ut quæ tum plena esset, neque nube obducta, sed modo quodam hominibus ignoto. ἐπὶ πᾶσαν τὴν γῆν hic, quod Marcus di- xit ἐφ᾽ ὅλην τὴν γῆν, sicut pro toto telluris globo sumi non potest (multis enim in partibus dies non erat) ita de sola Judæa nolim accipi, cum veteres Astrologi & chronographi hanc caliginem annotaverint, nullo addito loci nomine, unde late eam patuisse datur intelligi. Phlegon. XIII. Olym- piadum. Τῷ Δ ἔτει τῆς ΣΒ ὀλυμπιάδος ἐγένετο ἔκλειψις ἡλίου με- γίστη τ᾽ ἐγνωρισμένων πρότερον, κὴ νὺξ ὥρα ς΄ τῆς ἡμέρας ἐγένετο ὥ- στε καὶ ἀστέρας ἐν ὐρανῷ φανῆναι. σεισμός τε μέγας κατὰ βιθύ- νιαν γενόμενος τὰ πολλὰ Νικαίας κατεστρέψατο. Terræ motus locum nominat; tenebrarum non nominat & cum majores ante visis memorat, ita ut mero meridie velut nox esset, satis demonstrat, non fuisse proprium Judææ hoc spectacu- lum. Eusebius Græcum alium citat quem non nominat, ita scribentem de hac ipsa re: ὁ ἥλιος ἐξέλιπεν. Βιθυνία ἐσείσθη. Νικαίας τὰ πολλὰ ἔπεσεν. Is scriptor Eusebio non nomina- tus haud dubie est Thallus, cujus ita meminit Africanus: τοῦτο τὸ σκότος ἔκλειψιν ἡλίου Θάλλος ἀποκαλεῖ ἐν τρίτῃ τῶν ἱστοριῶν ὡς ἐμοὶ δοκεῖ ἀλόγως. Ἑβραῖοι γὰρ ἄγουσι τὸ πάσχα και τὰ σελήνης ΙΔ, πρὸ δὲ μιᾶς τοῦ πάσχα τὰ περὶ τὸν Σωτῆρα συμβαί- νει, ἔκλειψις δὲ ἡλίου, σελήνης ὑπελθούσης τῷ ἡλίῳ γίνεται. ἀδύνα- τον δὲ ἐν ἄλλῳ χρόνῳ πλὴν ἐν τῷ μεταξὺ μιᾶς κὴ τῆς πρὸ αὐτῆς και τὰ τὴν σύνοδον αὐτῶν ἀποβῆναι. πῶς ὦν ἔκλειψις νομισθείη και τὰ διάμετρον σχεδὸν ὑπαρχούσης τῆς σελήνης ἡλίῳ; Quo loco Africanus Thalli illud ὁ ἥλιος ἐξέλιπε stricte interpretatur, quasi Thallus voluerit naturalem fuisse ἔκλειψιν, cum alio- qui ἐκλείπειν Sol dici possit cum quovis modo deficit. Sic & in Lucæ quibusdam exemplaribus Origenes conqueritur mendose scriptum fuisse ἡλίου ἐκλείποντος, quod ille itidem ut Africanus pertinere arbitratur ad sensus injuriam. Ter- tullianus in Apologetico: Tamen suffixus multo mortis illius propria ostendit insignia. Nam spiritum cum verbo sponte di- misit, prævento carnificis officio. Eodem momento dies, me- dium orbem signante Sole, subducta est. Deliquium utique pu- te taverunt, qui id quoque super Christo prædicatum non scierunt. Et tamen eum mundi casum relatum in archivis vestris habetis. Ubi non video cur archiva alia quam acta publica Roma- na, accipiamus, ad quæ, ni fallor, & Lucianus martyr provocat apud Eusebium. Et cum mundi casum vocat, sa- tis cavit ne Judææ peculiaris crederetur. Quare πᾶσαν τὴν γῆν hic ita sumendum arbitror ut apud Lucam II. 1. πᾶσαν τὴν οἰκουμένην de orbe Romano, aut certe de potissima ejus parte. Quid Deus his tenebris significatum voluerit mul- ti disputant. Ego omnino arbitror non ad Judæos tantum pertinuisse hoc ostentum, quorum Prophetiæ tritæ tristissi- ma tempora solis caligine depingunt; sed ad alias etiam gentes. Nam hoc quoque inter ea fuit quibus centurio in stuporem est datus. Quare ea significatio sumenda est quæ quam latissime possit intelligi. Apud omnes autem po- pulos receptum erat ut crederent talibus ostentis scelus ali- quod insigne patratum indicari. Nota est cœna Thyestea ubi Seneca: O nos dura Sorte creatos, seu perdidimus Solem miseri, sive expulimus. De qua re sic Euripides Iphigenia: ἀλλάξας Δ' ἐξέδρας᾽ ἱερὸν ὄμμ' αὐγᾶς ἅλιος. Eodem pertinet illud Medea: Spectat hæc nostri sator Sol generis & spectatur, & curru insidens Per solita puri spatia decurrit poli? Et Phædra: tuῦ siderum caput Radiate Titan, tu nefas stirpis tuæ Speculare? Virgilius de Sole: Cum caput obscura nitidum ferrugine tinxit, Impiaque æternam timuerunt sæcula noctem. Marcus Antonius Triumvir in Epistola ad Hyrcanum Pon- tificem Maximum: διὸ κὶ τ' ἥλιον ἀπεστράφθαι δοκῦμεν ὃς καὶ αὐτὸς ἀηδῶς ἐπεῖδε ὼ ἐπὶ καίσαρα μῖσος. Lucanus: Ipse caput medio Titan cum ferret Olympo Condidit ardentes atra caligine currus, Involvitq; orbem tenebris, gentesque coegit Desperare diem, qualem fugiente per ortus Sole, Thyesteæ noctem duxere Mycenæ. Cæterum Judæis peculiariter ostentum hoc in memoriam revocare potuit Amosi verba, qui dixerat futurum, ut Sol meridie occideret, addens luctum fore, velut super unige- nito, c. IIX. 9. 10. Nam & quæ olim impleta erant in sensu μεταφορικῶς, ea nunc implebantur etiam in sensu proprio, ut sæpe diximus. Quanquam vero quæ hic describitur ca- ligo, ut in summo Judæorum & Romanorum scelere summa fuit, non negandum tamen arbitror aliis quoq; temporibus, si non pares, at similes iræ divinæ adversus graviora peccata significationes exstitisse. Certe veteribus Christianis con- stanter id creditum. Unum adferam Tertulliani locum: is est apud Scapulam: Omnia hæc signa sunt imminentis iræ Dei, quam necesse est quoque modo possumus, ut & annuntiemus & prædicemus, & deprecemur, interan localem esse. Universa- lem enim & supremam suo tempore sentient, qui exempla ejus aliter interpretantur. Nam & Sol ille in conventu Uticensi ex- tinctopene lumine adeo portentum fuit, ut non potuerit ex or- dinario deliquio hoc pati, positus in suo hypsomate & do- micilio: Habetis Astrologos.

Obscuratio Solis anne facta sit Luna interposita non satis liquet. Nec tamen ita factam ideo ne- gandum, quod tum plena esset luna. Etsi enim naturali modo tempore plenilunii non fiat Solis eclipsis, hæc tamen obscuratio, quæ omnino super- naturalis fuit, quin Luna plena fieri potuerit, ec- quis ambigeret, nisi qui divinam potentiam in du- bium vocare vellet, cui tam facile est Lunam etsi dimidia cœli parte à Sole distantem, itinere etiam retrogrado contra proprium ac naturalem mo- tum, qui est ab Occidente in Orientem, retrahere ad Solem versus meridiem, ut Soli se supponat, quemadmodum Es. XXXIIX.8. ad preces Ezechiæ Sol decem gradibus retrocesserat: quam est facile retrahere Solis radios, ne in terram projiciat, neve luceat, aut lucem ejus velut peplo quodam obdu- cto involvere: quo pacto utique retractis Solari- bus radiis Lunam etiam oportuisset obscurari, ac proinde supernaturalem eclipsin pati, quod tamen factum esse non consignarunt Evangelistæ. Ob- servant quidem nonnulli, quod Luna eodem die σταυρωσίμῳ hora quinta secundum nostrum horo- logium Hierosolymis eclipsis Lunæ contigerit ad septem digitos, adeoq; ultra medietatem corporis Lunaris, quæ durarit usque ad dimidiam octavam vespertinam : Sed eam naturalem fuisse : ac proin- de non annotatam ab Evangelistis. Si autem non minus Lunæ quam Soli obscuratio supernatura- lis, ob retractionem radiorum Solis contigisset, utriusque luminaris obscurationem merito consi- gnassent sancti Dei amanuenses. Mirari itaque subit, quod ὁ δεῖνα eclipsin Solis, quam non Dionysius tantum Areopagita, sed etiam Phegon, atq; Thallus notarunt, non propriam eclipsin fuif- se, sed retractione radiorum Solis factam obscu- rationem, argumento haud satis credo infinitæ o- mnipotentiæ divinæ convenienti probet: quia sci- licet lunam, quæ in plenilunio ex adverso Solis est, è loco suo ad Solem detractam, ut inter Solem & terram consisteret, absonum, & à divina potentia alienum esse credendum sit. Apud Deum enim non est impossibile omne verbum Luc. I. 37. Qui è Patribus Solem ne adspicere faciuus cogeretur, radios suos retraxisse ajunt, non modum descri- bunt obscurationis, sed de obscuratione illa pro more suo rhetoricantur, quod vel è Cypriano serm. de bon. patient. videre est, qui & radios & o- culos suos retraxisse Solem dicit. Chrysostomus serm. de Passion. in Catena, non poterat, inquit, ferre creatura injuriam Creatoris, unde Sol retra- xit radios suos, ne videret impiorum facinora. Per universam terram vero etsi non totus telluris glo- bus denotetur, non tamen tantum de orbe Roma- no ea explicanda, sed de terra tota quæ Solem supra Horyzontem habuit. Ea enim, fatente Gro- tio, significatio sumenda est, quæ quam latissime possit intelligi. Et quia omnes Evangelistæ ὁμοθυ- μαδὸν asserunt, tenebras illas super universam ter- ram exporrectas, proprietati verborum merito in- hærendum. Quod etiam factum à Patribus Chry- sostomo, aliisque. Adde quod è testimonio gen- tilium universalis illa Eclipsis etiam constet. Mun- di casum in archiva Romanorum relatum Tertul- lianus notavit. Eusebius in Chronicis ad annum Do- minicæ passionis ex Ethnicorum commentariis observat Solis defectionem & tenebras super uni- versam terram, ac Phlegontem adducit, qui ma- gnam & excellentem inter omnes quæ ante eam acciderant, defectionem Solis anno 262. Olympia- dis consignavit, in Bithynia: Dies, inquiens por- ro, hora sexta ita in tenebrosam noctem versus, ut stellæ cœlo visæ sint, terræque motus in Bithynia Nicariæ urbis multas ædes subvertit. Ideo Oro- sius l. VIII. c. 3. Solem in toto orbe fuisse obscura- tum Christi passionis tempore, non solum, inquit, sancta Evangeliorum; fides, sed etiam aliquanti Græcorum libri attestantur.

ἕως ὥρας ἐννάτης] Id est, ad tempus usque oblationis ve- spertinæ. Nam sic Hebræi diem partiebantur. Vide quæ supra hoc capite v. 42.

## 27:46
Vers. 46. ἠλὶ ἠλὶ λαμὰ σαβαχθανὶ] And from this and elsewhere it is gathered that Christ used neither the old language of the Hebrews nor the Syriac: but a mixed dialect which then flourished in Judea. That language retained certain things of the ancestral pronunciation, such as ἠλὶ אלי for which the Syrians are accustomed to say אלהי: some things it had in common with the Syrians, such as שבק for עזב. The very sound, approaching most closely to Elias, proves that Eli was pronounced by Christ. Wherefore I persuade myself that in the Syriac version, both here and in Mark, the letters were transposed, and what had been written אלי was changed into איל, an error arising thence because אלי was unknown to the Syrians, but some of the Syrians called God איל. Philo Byblius wrote Ἶλος from Sanchuniathon. Thus in Ezekiel, who sometimes χαλδαΐζει, ch. XXXI. 11, where we now read איל, the Oriental books of the Jews had איל, and where there is now אלי in Ezekiel XXXII. 21, the same Codices had אלי. Indeed, as I said, it was not איל that was written by the Syrian, but either אלי or certainly אילי, as is indicated by his own interpretation which he adds in Mark, which is אלהי with the suffix of the first person. Why we should think that Mark also did not write ἐλωῒ, but ἠλεὶ, we shall say when we come to that point. But that some Latin copies had lamana azabtani in this place instead of lamma sabactani, if I judge correctly, is from the hand of Jerome, who thought that the very words of the Psalm should be placed here.

ἵνα τί] It is the voice of one praying. Thus Moses, Exod. XXXII. 11, ἵνα τί κύριε θυμοῖ ὀργῇ εἰς τὸν λαόν σε, Ps. X. 1 (in the Greek it is part of the ninth) ἵνα τί κύριε ἀφέστηκας μακρόθεν.

ἐγκατέλιπες] עזב ἐγκαταλείπειν means to forsake in help: as in Isaiah XLIX. 14 and elsewhere.

Latin:

Vers. 46. ἠλὶ ἠλὶ λαμὰ σαβαχθανὶ] Et hinc & aliunde colligitur Christum neque veteri usum Hebræorum sermo- ne, neque Syriaco: sed mixta dialecto quæ tum in Iudæa vigebat. Ea lingua quædam retinebat avitæ pronuntiatio- nis, ut ἠλὶ אלי pro quo Syri dicere solent אלהי: quædam cum Syris habebat communia, ut שבק pro עזב. Eli à Christo pronuntiatum ipse sonus ad Eliam proxime acce- dens evincit. Quare mihi persuadeo in Syriaca versione, tum hic, tum apud Marcum transpositas literas, & quod אלי scriptum fuerat mutatum in איל, inde nato errore quod אלי Syris esset incognitum, quidam autem Syrorum Deum איל appallarent. Ἶλος scribebat Philo Byblius ex San- chuniathone. Sic apud Ezechielem, qui interdum χαλδαΐ- ζει, c. XXXI. 11. ubi nunc איל legimus libri Orientales Iu- dæorum habebant איל & ubi nunc est אלי Ezechielis XXXII. 21. eidem Codices habebant אלי. Enimvero, ut di- xi, à Syro non איל scriptum, sed aut אלי aut certe אילי indicio est ipsius interpretatio quam subjungit apud Mar- cum, quæ est אלהי cum affixo primæ personæ. Marcum quoque non ἐλωῒ scripsisse, sed ἠλεὶ cur arbitremur, dice- mus ubi eo ventum erit. Quod autem Latina quædam ex- emplaria hoc loco pro lamma sabactani habuerunt lamana azabtani, si quid recte judico ab Hieronymi est manu, qui i- psa Psalmi verba hic ponenda existimavit.

ἵνα τί] Vox est deprecantis. Ita Moses Exod. XXXII. 11. ἵνα τί κύριε θυμοῖ ὀργῇ εἰς τὸν λαόν σε, Ps. X. 1. (in Græco est pars noni) ἵνα τί κύριε ἀφέστηκας μακρόθεν.

ἐγκατέλιπες] עזב ἐγκαταλείπειν est auxilio destituere: ut Esaiæ XLIX. 14. & alibi.

## 27:47
Vers. 47. τινὲς δὲ τ’ ἐκεῖ ἑστώτων] I think these were not Roman soldiers, to whom nothing was known about Elias, nor Palestinian Jews, but Hellenists who, since they did not understand the Hebrew words, thought they heard the name of Elias, which was known to them. But an old rumor about the returning Elias, drawn from misunderstood prophecies, had permeated not only the Palestinian Jews but also the Hellenists, as is most manifest from the book of Ecclesiasticus. His time was thought to be already at hand, Matt. XVII. 10.

Latin:

Vers. 47. τινὲς δὲ τ’ ἐκεῖ ἑστώτων] Hos puto fuisse non Ro- manos milites, quibus de Elia nihil erat cognitum, ne- que Judæos Palæstinos, sed Hellenistas qui cum Hebrea verba, non intelligerent Eliæ nomen sibi notum audire se existimabant. De redituro autem Elia vetus fa- ma ex vaticiniis male intellectis hausta, non Palæstinos tan- tum Judæos, sed & Hellenistas pervaserat, ut ex Ecclesia- stici libro manifestissimum est. Ejus tempus jam instare putabatur, Matth. XVII. 10.

## 27:48
Vers. 48. πλήσας τε ὄξες] Because Jesus had said that he was thirsty, as John teaches. But there stood by a vessel full of ὄξος (that is, of artificial wine, as we explained above), not to accelerate death, as some think, but against a fainting of the spirit. Hence someone gave Christ to drink, as if sustaining his life with help arriving from heaven.

Vossius also approved that end in Harm. Evangel. book II, ch. VIII, §. 23, by his own calculation: that, namely, this was given by those who wanted to see whether Elias would bring him help, and thus they wanted to refresh him, so that his life might be prolonged until Elias arrived. But Vossius understands vinegar, not artificial wine: since vinegar might refresh a soul fleeing in a faint even by its smell alone. But it is gathered from Luke ch. XXIII. 36 that this was done for the sake of insult rather than for refreshment.

περιθεὶς καλάμῳ] John says ὑσσώπῳ περιθέντες. The same word shows that κάλαμον was the same as ὕσσωπον: that is, a rod made of hyssop, which grew in Judea to a size suitable for a tree, no less than mustard; I see no sufficient reason why we should deny this. There is one argument brought against this from the history of Solomon, 1 Kings 4:33. But it is not dealing there with any hyssop, but with one of its smallest species which is called יצא בקיר, as if you would say in Latin 'wall-plant'. To this is opposed the cedar, not just any, but that of Lebanon, which is taller than the rest. And indeed אזוב for the Hebrews extends more broadly than ὕσσωπος for the Greeks: so much so that Kimchi says there are seven kinds of it, who also explains it as Origanum. Something similar is in Pliny concerning the mallow, book XIX. Authors report that in Arabia mallows grow into trees and provide the use of rods. See the same author on Origanum.

Salmasius sets forth at greater length this opinion, formerly approved by Origen, in Epist. 1 de Cruce: that ὕσσωπον was nothing other than κάλαμον, so that John used ὕσσωπον for a reed or a stalk of hyssop, and the other two said κάλαμον regarding the reed or stalk of hyssop. Dr. Henr. Müller follows him in Jesu patiente p. 181. But Salmasius sharply criticizes the opinion of Heinsius, who wishes ὕσσωπον to be taken for οἰσύπῳ, on page 292. The sacred Aristarchus, with the unhappiness and most miserable poverty of judgment that he has, omitting reeds and spears, because he is a lover of peace, had dreamed of a medical matter here, and had taught that ὕσσωπον should be taken for οἰσύπῳ. Which can be read there. Concerning that, however, the most famous man is ambiguous, whether it was an aromatic reed. For now he had embraced the opinion of Origen that 'κάλαμον' was said for a stalk or a thyrse; and thus for the hyssop shrub itself, where, however, he says not quite reverently that the Evangelists did not observe an exact manner of speaking, as unlearned in the Greek language, and neglected the minutiae of the circumstances, Ep. III. on the cross, pages 617, 618; now he asserts, not without reason, that a reed is put for hyssop, namely an aromatic one, whose odor could have accomplished the same thing as the fragrance of hyssop for refreshing the spirits. Yet he says that he does not approve of this opinion to the extent of presenting it as most certain, but that he showed it to have been devised by another (Ludov. de Dieu) to reconcile the Evangelists with one another. We readily agree with Grotius. Compare regarding these matters the Epistle added to the tract of Barthol. on the pierced side of Christ. The blessed Gerhard most excellently reviews the various opinions concerning this apparent contradiction in Harm. Passion. chap. XVII. page 198. It is most simply established that Matthew and Mark state the genus, namely that the sponge was tied to a reed or staff; but that John expresses the species, namely that that staff was prepared from hyssop. Nor is it absurdly established that John, who especially notes those things which contain some mystery, for that reason made mention of hyssop, which was used in the lustrations and sprinklings of the Old Testament, in order to admonish us of the fruit of the Lord's passion cleansing us from sins; to which the royal Prophet also looks in Psalm 51:9, 'You shall sprinkle me with hyssop and I shall be cleansed.'

Latin:

Vers. 48. πλήσας τε ὄξες] Quia sitire se dixerat Iesus, ut Iohannes docet. Adstabat autem vox ὄξος (id est vini fa- ctitii, ut supra exposuimus) plenum, non accelerandæ morti, ut quidam putant, sed adversus animi deliquium. Hinc Christo potandum aliquis dedit, quasi in sem adven- tantis cœlitus auxilii vitam ei sustentans,

Finem illum etiam Vossius Harm. Evangel. l. II. c. VIII. §. 23. calculo suo probavit: quod sc. datum hoc ab iis, qui videre volebant, utrum Elias illi es- set opem laturus, adeoque reficere eum voluêre, quo vita prorogaretur, donec Elias adventaret. Sed acetum Vossius intelligit, non vinum facti- tium: siquidem acetum vel solo odore in lipothy- mia fugientem animam refocillet. Verum con- tumeliæ potius causa, quam refocillationis ergo hoc factum è Luca colligitur c. XXIII. 36.

περιθεὶς καλάμῳ] ὑσσώπῳ περιθέντες inquit Iohannes. Verbum idem ostendit κάλαμον idem fuisse quod ὕσσωπον: id est bacillum ex hyssopo quam in aliquam magnitudinem arbori convenientem excrevisse in Iudæa, non minus quam Sinapi, cur negemus satis causæ non video. Unum est quod contra affertur argumentum ex historia Salomonis I. Reg. IV. 33. Atqui non ibi de quavis hyssopo agitur, sed de una ejus minima specie quæ vocatur יצא בקיר quasi Latine parietariam dicas. Huic opponitur cedrus, non quævis, sed Libani, quæ cæteris celsior. Et sane אזוב He- bræis latius patet quam ὕσσωπος Græcis: adeo ut septem ejus genera dicat esse Kimchi, qui & Origanum exponit. Simile quid apud Plinium de malva l. XIX. Tradunt autores in Arabia malvas arborescere, baculorumque usum præbere. Vi- de eundem de Origano.

Pluribus hanc sententiam Origeni olim proba- tam exequitur Salmasius Epist. 1. de Cruce: non aliud ὕσσωπον fuisse quam κάλαμον, ut ita ὕσσωπον pro calamo vel thyrso hyssopi posuerit Johannes, & alii duo κάλαμον dixerint de hyssopi calamo seu caule. Sequitur illum D. Henr. Müller. in Jesu patiente p. 181. Heinsii vero sententiam, qui ὕσσω- πον pro οἰσύπῳ accipi vult, acriter perstringit Salmasius pag. 292. Aristarchus sacer, qua infelici- tate est, & miserrima judicii paupertate, omissis calamis & hastis, quia pacis amator est, rem me- dicam hic somniaverat, & ὕσσωπον pro οἰσύπῳ esse accipiendum docuerat. Quæ illic legi pote- runt. De eo tamen vir clarissimus ambiguus est, anne calamus fuerit aromaticus. Nam mo- do Origenis amplexus fuit sententiam 'κάλαμον dictum pro scapo vel thyrso; adeoque ipso fruti- ce hyssopi, ubi tamen non satis reverenter Ev- angelistas ait non exactam loquendi rationem observasse, ut idiotas Græci sermonis, & minu- tias τῶν περιστατικῶν neglexisse, Ep. III. de cruce pag. 617. 618. modo non sine ratione calamum pro hyssopo poni asserit, nempe aromaticum, cu- jus odor idem efficere potuerit, quod Hyssopi fragrantia ad reficiendos spiritus. Quam vero sententiam vicissim non adeo se comprobare ait, ut pro certissima daret, sed ab alio (Ludov. de Dieu) excogitatam ostendisse ad conciliandos in- ter se Evangelistas facere. Nos facile annuimus Grotio. Conf. de his Epistola ad tract. Barthol. de latere Christi perfosso adjecta. Optime B. Gerhardus recensitis variis de hac ἐναντιοφανείᾳ sententiis Harm. Passion. cap. XVII. pag. 198. Sim- plicissime statuitur, Matthæum & Marcum ponere genus, quod scilicet spongia arundini sive baculo fue- rit alligata; Johannem vero exprimere speciem, quod baculus ille fuerit ex hyssopo paratus. Nec absurde statuitur, Iohannem, qui cumprimis notat ea, quæ mysterium aliquod continent, ideo fecisse mentionem hyssopi cujus erat usus in lustrationibus & aspersionibus Vet. Test. ut admoneat nos de fructu Dominicæ passionis à peccatis nos emundantis; quo respicit etiam Propheta regius Psal. LI. 9. Asperges me hyssopo & mundabor.

## 27:49
Verse 49. 'But the rest'—Together with him who was offering the vinegar, as we are taught from Mark. Therefore 'the rest' is not said in opposition, but so that it may be understood that more than one said this.

'Let be'—It is a redundant word, as 'let be' in Mark: not of one forbidding, but serving the following subjunctive: as if you were to say, 'come, let us see.' And thus even now some peoples speak. In the acts of the city of Constantinople, in which the sedition is described, which is named Nika, 'let us be punished' is nothing other than 'let us be punished.' The Greeks said 'one' for the same thing under Justin, as 'one come,' 'one fall' in the acclamations of the Synod under Mennas. Among the LXX in a similar sense, as Job 19:5.

Latin:

Vers. 49. οἱ δὲ λοιποὶ] Simul cum ipso qui ὄξος porri- gebat, ut ex Marco docemur. Itaque λοιποὶ non oppo- site dicitur, sed ut plures uno id dixisse intelligantur.

Ἄφες] Vox est πλεονάζουσα, ut ἄφετε apud Marcum: non prohibentis: sed subjunctivo sequenti inserviens: quasi dicas: age videamus. Et sic nunc etiam populi nonnulli loquuntur. In actis urbis Constantinopolitanæ, quibus describitur seditio, cui Νίκα nomen, ἄφες κολαζώ- μεθα nihil aliud est quam puniamur. Dixerunt pro eo- dem & εἷς Græci sub Justino, ut εἷς ἅτελθε, εἷς πέσον in acclamationibus Synodi sub Menna. Apud LXX. in si- mili sensu, ut Job. XIX. 5.

## 27:50
Verse 50. 'Crying with a loud voice, he yielded up the spirit'—Together with the cry itself, as we heard Tertullian saying: 'He dismissed his spirit with a word of his own accord.' That cry was 'it is finished' in John, and 'Father, into your hands I commend my spirit.' The Centurion accepted this very thing as a miracle, 'that crying out in such a way he breathed his last': for the thing itself, immediately responding to his words, showed that his soul was truly being received by GOD. For death was accelerated by divine counsel before his natural strength had failed. Otherwise, death could not yet have been expected, Mark 15:44, therefore the thieves were killed by the breaking of their legs. Origen seems to refer to this liberation from death accelerated by him that passage to the Hebrews ch. 5:7, 'Who in the days of his flesh, when he had offered up prayers and supplications with strong crying and tears unto him that was able to save him from death, and was heard in that he feared; though he were a Son, yet learned he obedience by the things which he suffered.' Cyprian against Demetrianus: 'Crucified, having anticipated the office of the executioner, he dismissed his spirit of his own accord.' But those words 'he yielded up the spirit' express one Hebrew word, 'azab, for which Mark and Luke have placed 'he breathed his last.' But the sense is in Isaiah 53:12.

PART II. The things following the death of Christ.

Latin:

Vers. 50. κράξας φωνῇ μεγάλῃ, ἀφῆκε τὸ πνεῦμα] Simul cum ipsâ clamore, ut Tertullianus dixentem audivimus: Spiritum cum verbo sponte dimisit. Clamor is fuit τετέλεσται apud Iohannem, & πάτερ εἰς χεῖρας σου παρατίθεμαι τὸ πνεῦ- μά μου. Hoc autem ipsum pro miraculo accepit Centurio ὅτι ὕτως κράξας ἐξέπνευσεν: nam verbis ejus res ipsa statim respondens ostendebat vere animam ejus à DEO suscipi. Accelerata quippe mors erat divino consilio antequam vi- res ejus naturales defecissent. Alioqui nondum mors ex- spectari poterat, Marc. XV. 44. ideo latrones crucifragio peremti. Videtur Origenes ad acceleratam hanc à morte liberationem referre illud ad Hebræos c. V. 7. Ὃς ἐν ταῖς ἡμέραις τῆς σαρκὸς ἀυτῦ δεήσεις τε καὶ ἱκετηρίας πρὸς ἳ δυνάμε- νον σώζειν ἀυτὸν ἐκ θανάτε μετὰ κραυγῆς ἰσχυρᾶς καὶ δακρύων προσενέγκας καὶ ἐισακουσθεὶς ἀπὸ τῆς ἐυλαβείας ἔμαθεν ἀφ' ὧν ἔ- παθε τὴν ὑπακοήν. Cyprianus adversus Demetrianum: Crucifixus, prævento carnificis officio, spiritum sponte dimisit. Il- la autem ἀφῆκε τὸ πνεῦμα exprimunt unam vocem Hebræam עזב, pro qua ἐξέπνευσε posuere Marcus & Lucas. Sensus autem apud Esaiam LIII. 12.

PARS II. Τὰ ἑπόμενα mortis Christi.

## 27:51
Verse 51. 'The veil of the temple was torn in two'—Both ancient and new Interpreters think it is not sufficiently agreed whether this concerns the inner veil, which was hung before the sanctuary, or the outer veil, which was hung before the doors of the priestly temple. In the times of Moses there were three curtains: the outermost of the court, Exodus 27:16; the middle of the temple, Ex. 26:36; the innermost of the holy of holies, Exodus 26:31, that is, of the adytum or sanctuary. In the temple of Solomon, and that which was substituted for it in place of the outermost curtain, there was a gate, as we learn from Josephus. Philo calls it the propylaeum. Therefore two curtains remained, which Josephus calls the inner veils in Antiquities 12.11. And hence the curtain hung before the adytum is called the second veil by the divine Writer to the Hebrews, ch. 9:3. Furthermore, where it is said 'the veil' without qualification, it must entirely be understood as that which was hung before the adytum: for that had properly and for the sake of a peculiar distinction occupied that name. Philo on the life of Moses: 'And from them [that is, from the hyacinth, scarlet, purple, and fine linen] both the veil and the so-called covering were constructed. The one inside, according to the four pillars, upon which the adytum was hung. The one outside, according to the five, so that no one from outside could gaze upon the holy things.' And after: 'And in the boundary of the four and five pillars, which is properly that which is kept by providence with two fabrics, the one which is inside is called the veil. The one outside is called the covering.' He distinctly calls the curtain hung before the adytum the veil, and the other hung before the priestly temple he calls the covering. For also to Moses that lower one is distinctly called paroketh in Exodus 26:33, and that outer one masakh. The LXX also translate the word paroketh as veil in Ex. 26:33, ch. 36:33. But the word masakh, which Philo translates as covering, they translate as epispastron in Exod. 26:36, ch. 36:33. Wherefore I do not doubt that 'the veil' ought to be understood as the curtain by which the sanctuary was defended. But neither is there more agreement among the ancients as to what the proper significance of this tearing was. But to me it does not even seem to be doubted that it was that which the Jews who were not stubborn could most easily conjecture from the thing itself. When the never-sufficiently-praised Writer to the Hebrews says that 'the holy places,' that is, 'the holy of holies' (for after the distinction placed at the beginning of the ninth chapter, always studying brevity, he calls the adytum 'the holy places') are 'the antitypes of the true ones,' namely of that highest heaven, he said nothing new, but assumed that which was confessed among all the Jews, which I shall show with clear testimonies. Josephus, Antiquities III, chap. 5: 'For the third part of it, that which is inside the four pillars, was inaccessible to the priests, as being the throne of God.' And chap. 8. The third part he assigned to God alone, because the heaven is inaccessible to men, Philo de vita Mosis, the inner sanctum of the tabernacle, which is symbolically intelligible. Wherefore concerning this principal part of the Temple it ought to be understood primarily, what is in the book of Wisdom, that the Temple was a copy of the holy tabernacle which God prepared from the beginning, namely that which is treated in Ps. XV, which is also hinted at in Ps. LXXIIX. 68. For those things which were outside the inner sanctum did not obscurely shadow forth this visible world. For in the curtain, scarlet signified fire, fine linen the earth, hyacinth the air, purple the sea: seven lamps denoted as many planets: twelve loaves denoted as many signs of the Zodiac and months: although some of these could have had another signification proper to the Israelites. It was not obscure, therefore, that the inner sanctum was a copy of the intelligible world, as Clement speaks in the fifth book of the Stromata: in which inner sanctum there had been of old the cherubim of glory overshadowing the mercy seat, the interpretation of which the writer to the Hebrews defers to another time. But Philo, without doubt, from ancient discipline says that the mercy seat was indeed a symbol of the propitious power of God: but through the cherubim he thinks are designated the powers of God, both the creative and the kingly. Josephus calls the cherubim the chariot of God: as if it were by transposition from the word רכב. Cf. Ps. XIIX. 11. and 2 Sam. XXII. 11. I think that these being understood, it is not obscure what the rending of the veil signifies. For it signifies the entrance opened through the death of Christ, first to Christ, then by his benefit to the holy and pious in the new covenant, to that invisible heaven which the sacred writers call the heaven of heavens, which is as it were the proper seat of the divine majesty. Paul Rom. III. 25. concerning Christ, whom God set forth as a propitiation through faith in his blood. The writer to the Hebrews IX. 8. the Holy Spirit indicating this, that the way into the holiest of all was not yet made manifest, soon 24. for Christ did not enter into holy places made with hands, which are copies of the true, but into heaven itself: certainly not in the blood of another, but through his own blood. For although he did not immediately obtain possession, but after forty and more days, yet the right was acquired for him and through him for others at that time, when he gave himself as a sacrifice for sin, as Isaiah had prophesied: the veil of sins being rent, which was interposed between this visible world and the propitious power of God, Is. LIX. 2. But that I understand sin by the veil is not at all repugnant to the writer to the Hebrews, who calls the very flesh of Christ, spread before his divinity, a veil. For that very flesh was not only in the likeness of sinful flesh, but partly, even among the Apostles, it bears the figure of sin itself, as appears from those places which treat of the crucifixion, death, and burial of sin. And thus some of the ancients explain that passage Rom. VI. 10. for in that he died, he died unto sin once for all, that is, in his mortal body. How perhaps could be understood also that passage to the Hebrews V. 3. because of this he ought, as for the people, so also for himself to offer for sins, insofar as that universal expression also includes Christ, where he calls that sin, which a little before he called infirmity: and more openly in the same Epistle ch. VII. v. 27. who does not have need daily, as the high priests before, to offer up sacrifices for his own sins, then for the people's: for this he did once for all, when he offered up himself: so that his own sins may be the inseparable qualities of a mortal body, which as in us are effects, and partly also causes of sin, so in Christ they were a figure of sin: just as the contact with a corpse, and other things which happen to those who are unaware or unwilling, were called sins in the Law: For Christ can also be said to have offered for those, insofar as by the paternal decree he could not be freed from them, except through death, as an example for us. Among the Romans, however, and men of other nations, this same miracle indicated not obscurely the atrocity of the crime committed against Christ. Philippides in his Comedy about Demetrius, speaking of the fact that he had allowed himself to be made equal to the gods, says thus: 'Because of whom, on account of impiety, the veil was torn in the middle.' Plutarch touches upon the same history: 'The divine power gave a sign to most people; for the veil, which they had decreed to weave together with the images of Zeus and Athena for Demetrius and Antigonus, was torn in the middle as it was being carried through the Ceramicus, a storm having fallen upon it.' But as for what the Talmudists narrate, that forty years before the destruction of the Temple the doors opened of their own accord, I greatly doubt whether it should be referred to this. For I fear that, as they are unreliable, they have confused those signs which occurred at the passion of Christ with those which immediately preceded the destruction, which also happened to others in the narration of the voice heard in the Temple, 'Let us depart from here.' Either I am very much mistaken, or what the Talmudists wish to say is the same as what Tacitus said briefly: 'The doors of the temple were suddenly opened'; but Josephus more broadly: so that it can in no way be understood of the veil of the sanctuary. I shall append the words: 'The eastern gate of the inner [perhaps it is better read as 'outer,' for the inner gates were gilded, the outer one of Corinthian bronze] being of bronze and very sturdy, and closed towards evening, with difficulty by twenty men, and supported by iron-bound bars, and having bolts sunk deep into the threshold which was one continuous stone, was seen at the sixth hour of the night to have opened of its own accord; the guards of the temple ran and reported it to the commander, and he, having gone up, was barely able to close it.'

But the way was not to be prepared for Christ through death, but for us: for he did not die for his own sake, but for us, and our sins. He himself was in the form of God (Phil. 2:6) and in the heavens, even when he was on earth (John 3:14), but he had to open heaven for us through his blood (Heb. 9:24), nor did he offer himself as a victim for himself, but for us (Eph. 5:2; 1 Pet. 2; Job 2; Isa. 53). However, by the veil, sin is wrongly understood: which is nowhere in Scripture so taken; and the veil is interpreted in the Holy Scriptures not of sin, but of the flesh of Christ (Heb. 10:30), which, even if on account of infirmities and the imputation of our sin, it is said to have been 'in the likeness of sinful flesh' (Rom. 8:3), in reality, however, it did not know sin (2 Cor. 5:21), but was most alien from sin (Heb. 7:26), nor is sin ever said to have been shadowed in it, even if, since it was crucified, dead, and buried on account of our sin, which was imputed to it by divine reckoning, our sin itself is considered to have been crucified, dead, and buried. That explanation of Rom. 6:10, by which a mortal body is understood through 'sin,' carries no weight: for 'he died to sin' because he died on account of our sin: not because he died with a mortal body. For what is this, to die with a mortal body? Especially when it concerns Christ, who did not die out of the necessity or condition of his body, but by his own authority, by free power (John 10:19). Nor indeed can that Apostolic description of the High Priest of the Old Testament (Heb. 5:3) be drawn to Christ, inasmuch as he was devoid of all personal sin: nor is it right to understand both sins and the infirmity devoid of sin by the word 'sins':

whence even that Socinian distortion of Heb. 7:27 to the personal sins of Christ is rightly rejected as blasphemous; for that 'personal sins' are inseparable qualities of a mortal body, which in us are effects, or even causes of sin, but in Christ were a figure of sin, is a mere distortion of the Apostle's words: for 'sins' denote sins, which had to be expiated by sacrifices, deserving the wrath of God and eternal punishment: nor can the same word have a double meaning in the same place. But the contact with a corpse and other similar things are called sins because they were prohibited by divine law, which cannot be said of inseparable qualities, which are themselves harmless and not at all absurd. It is also Socinian and heretical that Christ offered for his own sins, that is, infirmities, and could not be freed from them except through his sacrifice and death, and that as an example for us. Of which matters, elsewhere.

And the earth shook] In several places, not only in Judea. For God willed that the memory of this portent should remain. See what we have cited from Phlegon and Thallus. It is very true that among the prophets, an earthquake signifies elsewhere a change of affairs, elsewhere the majesty of God: but here that signification is clearer which could be understood equally by Jews and other nations, namely, of divine wrath on account of the crimes of men (Ps. 18:8; Joel 3:16). Thus Virgil added an earthquake to the darkness of the sun, and Lucan and Seneca did no differently. Indeed, the centurion and those who were with him interpreted the prodigy in that way. For from that they concluded that Jesus was unjustly condemned (Luke 23:45).

And the rocks were split] I think it is a consequence of the earthquake. For often when the earth moves, a multitude of stones comes to the surface, as Aristotle says in 2 Meteor. 8. Seneca in the Troades: 'When suddenly the earth, groaning with a blind rumbling, was shaken, it drew blind sounds from the deep: the forests moved their heads, and the high grove thundered with a vast crash, and the sacred wood: the rocks of Ida fell, their ridges broken.' But this also had a signification of divine wrath among the Hebrews (Nahum 1:6; 1 Kings 19:11). He joins the earthquake and the broken rocks also in Ps. 114:7-8.

Latin:

Vers. 51. τὸ καταπέτασμα τῦ ναῦ ἐσχίσθη εἰς δύο] Et vete- res & novi Interpretes parum constare arbitrantur, agatur ne hic de velo interiore, quod oppansum erat penetrali, an de velo exteriore, quod erat oppansum foribus templi sacerdo- talis. Mosis temporibus tria erant aulæa: extimum τῆς ἀυλῆς Exodi XXVII, 16. medium τοῦ ναοῦ Ex. XXVI. 36. intimum τοῦ ἁγίου τῶν ἁγίων Exodi XXVI. 31. id est, adyti sive penetralis. In templo Salomonis & quod ei surrogatum vice extimi au- læi fuit porta, ut ex Josepho discimus. Προπύλαιον vocat Philo. Manserant ergo duo aulæa, quæ τὰ ἐνδότερα κατα- πετάσματα vocat Josephus ἀρχαιολογίας ΙΙΧ. 11. Et hinc aulæum adyto oppansum δεύτερον καταπέτασμα vocat di- vinus ad Hebræos Scriptor c. IX. 3. Cæterum ubi unde dici- tur καταπέτασμα, omnino intelligendum est illud quod adyto erat oppansum: id enim proprie ac peculiaris dif- criminis causa id nomen occupaverat. Philo de vita Mo- sis: ἐκ δὲ τ' ἀυτῶν [id est ex hyacintho, coccino, purpura bysso] τό τε καταπέτασμα κᾴ τὸ λεγόμενον κάλυμμα κατε- σκευάζετο. Τὸ μὲν ἔσω κατὰ τὲς τέσσαρας κίονας, ἐφ' ἐπικρὖ πτετο τὸ ἄδυτον. Τὸδ' ἔξω κατὰ τὲς πέντε, ὡς μηδεὶς ἐξ ἀπόπλε δύναιτο ᾗ μὴ ἱερωμένοις καταθεάσασθαι τὰ ἅγια. Et post: ἐν δὲ τῇ μεθορίᾳ τῶν τεσσάρων κᾀπέντε κιόνων, ὅπερ ἐςὶ κυρίως ὑπὸ τῶν προνοιαν εἰργόμενον δυςὶν ὑφάσμασι, τὸ μὲν ἔνδον ὂν και λεῖται καταπέτασμα. Τὸ δ' ἐκτὸς προσαγορεύεται κάλυμμα. Distincte aulam adyto oppansum vocat καταπέτασμα, alterum oppansum templo Sacerdotali appellat κάλυμμα. Nam & Mosi distincte illud inferius vocatur פרכת Exodi XXVI. 33. istud exterius מסך. Vocem פרכת etiam LXX. vertunt καταπέτασμα Ex. XXVI. 33. c. XXXVI. 33. At vocem מסך, quam Philo transfert κάλυμμα, ἐπίσπαςρον Exod. XXVI. 36. c. XXXVI. 33. Quare non dubito quin καταπέτασμα intelligi debeat auleum quo penetrale de- fendebatur. Sed neque magis inter veteres convenit quæ propria fuerit significatio hujus scissuræ. Mihi vero ne dubitandum quidem videtur eam fuisse quam Judæi non pertinaces ex re ipsa facillime conjectare poterant. Cum dicit nunquam satis laudatus ad Hebræos Scriptor τὰ ἅγια, id est τὰ ἅγια τ' ἁγίων (nam post discrimen positum initio capitis noni semper brevitati studens adytum vocat ἅγια) esse ἀντίτυπα τ' ἀληθινῶν, summi illius cæli scilicet, nihil novi dixit, sed id sumpsit quod erat apud Judæos omnes confessum, quod perspicuis testimoniis ostendam. Josephus Α'ρχαιολογίας III. cap. 5. τὸ μὲν γὰρ τρίτον ἀυτῆς μέρος. τὸ ἐν- τος τ' τεσσάρων κιόνων; δι'τοῖς ἱερεῦσιν ἦν ἄβατον, ὡς κρατός ἂν εἴη τῷ Θεῷ. Et c. VIII. τὴν δὲ τρίτην μοῖραν μόνῳ περιέγραψε τῷ Θεῷ διὰ κᾀμὲ ἲ ὀυρανὸν ἀνεπίβατον εἶναι ἀνθρώποις Philo de vita Mosis, τὰ ἄδυτα τῆς σκηνῆς, ἅπερ ἐςὶ συμβολικῶς νοητό. Quare de hac parte præcipua Templi præcipue accipi de- bet, quod in libro est Sapientiæ, Templum fuisse μίμημα σκηνῆς ἁγίας ἣν ὁ Θεὸς προητοίμασεν ἀπ' ἀρχῆς, ejus scilicet de qua agitur Ps. XV. quod & Ps. LXXIIX. 68. innuitur. Quæ enim extra adytum erant, non obscure adumbrabant Mun- dum hunc aspectabilem. Nam in auleo coccinum ignem, byssus tellurem, hyacinthus aëra, purpura mare: septem Ly- chni totidem planetas: panes duodecim totidem Zodiaci signa & menses notabant: quanquam potuerunt horum quædam aliam Israëlitis propriam habere significationem. Obscurum igitur non erat, adytum κόσμυ τὲ νοητὲ ἐπιτύπωμα ὅντος, ut Clemens loquitur Stromateon quinto: in quo adyto antiquitus fuerant χερυβὶμ δόξης κατασκιάζοντα τὸ ἱ- λατήριον, quorum interpretationem in aliud tempus differt Scriptor ad Hebræos. At Philo haud dubie ex veteri disci- plina ἱλαςήριον quidem ait fuisse σύμβολον τῆς ἵλεω τῷ Θεῷ δυ- νάμεως : Per Cherubim vero arbitratur designari τὰς τῆς ὅτι τ Θε δυνάμεις τήντε ποιητικὴν κᾀμ βασιλικὴν. Josephus Che- rubim vocat τὸ ἅρμα τῷ Θεῦ: tanquam sit per μετάθεσιν ex verbo רכב. Conf. Ps. XIIX. 11. & 2. Sam. XXII. 11. Puto his intellectis non esse obscurum quid significet aulai scissura. Significat enim aditum per Christi mortem apertum Christo primum, deinde ejus beneficio sanctis piis in ovique fœde- ris ad cœlum illud inaspectabile quod ὀρανὸν τ' ὀρανῶν νο- cant sacri scriptores, quæ majestatis divinæ velut propria est sedes. Paulus Rom. III. 25. de Christo, ὃν προέθετο ὁ Θεὸς ἱλαςήριον διὰ τῆς πίσεως ἐν τῷ ἀυτὲ αἵματι. Scriptor ad He- bræos IX. 8. τῦτο δηλῶντα τῷ πνέυματα ἁγία μήπω πεφα- νερωθῆ τὴν ἳ ἁγίων ὁδὸν, mox 24. 8 γὰρ εἰς χειροποίητα ἅγια εἰσῆλθεν ὁ χρισὸς, ἀντίτυπα ἢ ἀληθινῶν, ἀλλ' εἰς ἀυτὸν τ' ὀρα- νὸν: utique ἐκ ἐν αἵματι ἀλλοτρίῳ sed per suum ipsius san- guinem. Quanquam enim possessionem non statim est adeptus, sed post quadraginta & quod excedit dies, jus tamen ipsi & per ipsum aliis quæsitum est eo tempore, quo se dedit θυσίαν περὶ ἁμαρτίας ut vaticinatus erat Esaias: scisso scilicet velo peccatorum quod inter hunc mundum aspectabilem & τὴν ἵλεων τῷ Θεῦ δύναμιν interjiciebatur, Es. LIX. 2. Quod autem per velum peccatum intelligam mini- me repugnat Scriptori ad Hebræos, qui ipsam Christi car- nem, divinitati ipsius oppansam, vocat καταπέτασμα. Nam ea ipsa caro non tantum erat ἐν ὁμοιώματι σαρκὸς ἁμαρτίας, sed parttim, etiam apud Apostolos, figuram getit peccati ipsius, ut apparet iis ex locis, quæ de peccati crucifixione, morte, sepultura agunt. Atque ita veterum nonnulli ex- plicant illud Rom. VI. 10. ὃ γὰρ ἀπέθανεν ἁμαρτίᾳ ἀπέθανεν ἐ- φάπαξ, id est, corpore mortali. Quomodo forte intelligi posset, & illud ad Hebræos V. 3. διὰ ταύτην ὀφείλῃ, καθὼς περὶ τῷ λαῦ, ὕτως κᾀμ περὶ ἑαυτῦ προσφέρειν ὑπὲρ ἁμαρτιῶν, quatenus scilicet universalis ista locutio etiam Christum complectitur, ubi ἁμαρτίαν vocat, quod paulo ante ἀσθέ- νειαν: & apertius eadem Epistola cap. VII. v. 27. ὅς ἐκ ἔχει καθ' ἡμέραν ἀνάγκην ὥσπερ οἱ ἀρχιερεῖς πρότερον ὑπὲρ τῶν ἰ- δίων ἁμαρτιῶν θυσίας ἀναφέρειν, ἔπειτα τῶν τοῦ Ἱῦτο γὰρ ποίησεν ἐφάπαξ ἑαυτὸν ἀνενέγκας : ut ἰδίοις ἁμαρτίαις sint qualitates inseparabiles mortalis corporis, quæ ut in nobis- sunt effecta, partim etiam causae peccati, ita in Christo erant figura peccati: quomodo contactus cadaveris, & alia quae inscijs aut invitis accidunt, in lege peccata dicebantur: Nam & pro illis obtulisse dici potest Christus quatenus ex decreto paterno liberari ab illis non potuit, nisi per mor- tem, nobis in exemplum. Apud Romanos autem & aliotum gentium homines idem hoc miraculum non ob- scure indicabat commissi in Christum facinoris atrocita- tem. Philippides in Comoedia de Demetrio, quod se Diis aequari passus esset, verba faciens, ita inquit: Δι ὃν δι᾿ ἀσέβειαν ὁ πέπλος ἐῥῥάγη μέσος. Plutarchus eandem historiam tangunt, ἐπεσήμαινε δὲ τοῖς πλείστοις τὸ θεῖον· ὁ μὲν γὰρ πέπλος ὧσπερ ἐψηφίσαντο μετὰ τῶν Διὸς καὶ τῆς Ἀθηνᾶς προσεπυφαίνειν Δημήτριον καὶ Ἀντίγονον, πεμπόμενος διὰ τοῦ κεραμεικοῦ μέσος ἐῥῥάγη θυέλλης ἐμπεσού- σης. Quod autem narrant Thalmudistae XL. ante exci- dium annis Templi fores sponte patuisse, valde dubito an huc referri debeat. Vereor enim ne, ut sunt ἀνυπό- στατοι, confuderint signa illa quae in Christi passionem inci- derunt cum illis quae excidium proxime antecesserunt, quod & aliis accidit in narratione vocis auditae in Templo μεταβαίνωμεν ἐντεῦθεν. Aut valde fallor aut id quod dicere volunt Thalmudistae idem est quod breviter dixit Tacitus, Expansae repente delubri fores: latius autem Josephus: ita ut de aulaeo adyti nullo modo possit intelligi. Verba appo- nam: ἡ δὲ ἀνατολικὴ πύλη τῆς ἐνδοτέρω (melius forte legitur τῆς ἐξωτέρω Nam portae interiores erant auratae, exterior ex aere Corinthio) χαλκῆ μὲν οὖσα καὶ στιβαρωτάτη, κλειομένη δὲ περὶ δείλην, μόλις ὑπ᾽ ἀνδρῶν εἴκοσι, καὶ μοχλοῖς μὲν ἐπερειδομένη σι- δηροδέτοις, καὶ καταπλῆγας δ᾽ ἔχουσα βαθυτάτυς, εἰς τὸ καδὸς ὄν- τα διηνεκῶς λίθον καθειμένους, ὤφθη κατὰ νυκτὸς ὥραν ἑκτην αὐ- τομάτως ἠνεωγμένη· δραμόντες δ᾽ οἱ τῦν ἱερῶν φύλακες ἤγγειλαν τῷ στρατηγῷ κἀκεῖνος ἀναβὰς, μόλις αὐτὴν ἴχυσεν κλεῖ- σαι.

At non Christo aditus parandus erat per mor- tem, sed nobis: neque enim sui causa mortuus est, sed propter nos, & peccata nostra. Ipse in forma Dei erat Phil. II. 6. & in caelis, etiam cum in terra esset Johan. III. 14. sed nobis aperire de- buit caelum per sanguinem suum. Ebr. IX. 24. nec pro se victimam obtulit sese, sed pro nobis, Ephes. V. 2. 1. Petr. II. 1. Job. II. Esa. LIII. Per velum autem perperam intelligitur peccatum: quod nus- piam in Scriptura ita accipitur; & interpretatur velum S. S. non de peccato, sed de carne Christi Ebr. X. 30. quae etsi propter infirmitates, & impu- tationem peccati nostri, ἐν ὁμιώματι σαρκὸς ἁμάρ- τίας fuisse dicatur, Rom. IIX. 3. revera tamen non noverat peccatum 2. Cor. V. 21. sed à peccato a- lienissima erat Ebr. VII. 26. nec in ipsa adumbra- tum peccatum uspiam dicitur, etsi cum ipsa crucifixa, mortua & sepulta propter peccatum no- strum, quod eidem imputatum fuit divino λο- γισμῷ, ipsum peccatum nostrum crucifixum, mortuum, sepultum censeatur. Illa vero expli- catio Rom. VI. 10. qua per ἁμαρτίαν mortale cor- pus intelligitur, nullum fert punctum: nam ἁ- μαρτίᾳ ἀπέθανεν quia propter peccatum nostrum mortuus est: non quia corpore mortali obiit. Quid enim hoc est mori mortali corpore? imprimis ubi de Christo agitur qui non ex necessitate aut con- ditione corporis sui mortuus est, sed αὐτεξυ- σίως, libera potestate Joh. X. 19. Nec vero A- postolica illa Pontificis Veteris Testamenti de- scriptio Ebr. V. 3. trahi ad Christum potest, ut- pote qui omnis peccati proprii expers fuit: neque simul voce ἁμαρτιῶν & peccata & peccati expertem ἀσθένειαν intelligere fas est:

unde Sociniana etiam illa detorsio Ebr. VII. 27. ad propria peccata Christi, ceu blasphema meri- to reprobatur; nam quod ἴδιοι ἁμαρτίαι qualita- tes inseparabiles sint mortalis corporis, qua in nobis effecta, aut etiam causa peccati sunt, in Christo vero figura fuerint peccati, mera est verborum Apo- stoli detorsio: ἁμαρτίαι enim peccata notant, quæ expianda sacrificiis fuerint, iram Dei me- rentia, & pœnam æternam: neque unius, ejus- demque vocis geminus esse potest in eodem lo- co sensus. Contactus vero cadaveris & alia si- milia, ideo peccata dicta, quia lege divina pro- hibita, quod de qualitatibus inseparabilibus, ipsis- que innoxiis, minimeque ἀτόμοις dici nequit. Socinianum etiam, atque hæreticum est, Christum obtulisse pro suis peccatis, id est, infirmitatibus, nec liberari ab iis potuisse, nisi per sacrificium & mor- tem suam, idque in nostrum exemplum. De qui- bus alias.

καὶ ἡ γῆ ἐσείσθη] Aliquot in locis, non in Judæa tan- tum. Voluit enim Deus ostenti hujus memoriam ex- stare. Vide quæ ex Phlegonte & Thallo citavimus. Ve- rissimum est apud Prophetas terræ motu alibi rerum mu- tationem, alibi Dei majestatem significari: sed hic aper- tior est ea significatio quæ pariter à Judæis & gentibus a- liis poterat intelligi, iræ scilicet divinæ ob hominum sce- lera Psal. XIIX. 8. Joël. III. 16. Ita Virgilius Solis cali- gni addidit terræ motum, nec aliter Lucanus & Seneca. Sane centurio & qui cum eo erant ita interpretati sunt prodigium. Inde enim colligebant Jesum inique damna- tum, Luc. XXIII. 45.

καὶ αἱ πέτραι ἐσχίσθησαν] Puto consequens esse terræ mo- tus. Sæpe enim cum terra movet ἐπιπολάζει πλῆθος ἁλ- θων ut ait Aristoteles 2. Meteor. IIX. Seneca Troadi- bus: Cum subito cæco terra mugitus fremens Concussa, cæcos traxit ex imo sonos: Movere silva capita, & excelsum nemus Fragore vasto tonuit, & lucus sacer: Idæa ruptis saxa ceciderunt jugis. Sed & hoc apud Hebræos iræ divinæ habebat significatio- nem Nahum I. 6. 1. Reg. XIX. 11. Terræ motum & saxa rupta conjungit & Psal. CXIV. 7. 8.

## 27:52
V. 52. And the tombs were opened] At the very moment of Christ's death the tombs were opened, so that it might appear more clearly that he 'through death destroyed him who had the power of death' (Heb. 2:14). Aristides in his description of the earthquake by which Rhodes was overturned: 'The tombs were broken open': And soon after: 'The tombs threw out those who were lying within.'

Vers. 52. καὶ πολλὰ σώματα ἳ κεκοιμημένων ἁγίων ἠγέρθη] Some immediately think that these dead rose when Christ died, which moved some to read in what follows not μετὰ τὴν ἔγερσιν αὐτῶ but αὐτῶν, among whom is the Arabic Interpreter and among the Greeks, Glycas. But it is truly more likely that the power of Christ's death was demonstrated by the opening of the tombs, yet that these dead did not come to life until after Christ had revived, so that it thus appears that He himself is the πρωτότοκον ἐκ ἳ νεκρῶν. For no one of the dead rose to immortal life, which it is reasonable to believe of these, in which opinion is the writer of the responses to the Orthodox to question LXXXV. Cf. Dan. XII. 2.

However, the critical judgment of Dan. Heinsius is to be disapproved, who newly punctuated the text thus: καὶ ἐξελθόντες ἐκ τῶν μνημείων, μετὰ τlὼ ἔγερσιν αὐτε εἰσήλθον εἰς τlὼ ἁγίαν πόλιν, as if they rose at the same moment when their tombs were opened, but did not appear in the holy city until after the resurrection of these Saints. St. Jerome is more correct: They did not rise before the Lord rose, so that He might be the firstborn of the resurrection from the dead.

Latin:

V. 52. καὶ τὰ μνημεῖα ἀνεῴχθησαν] In ipso mortis Christi ar- ticulo aperta sunt monumenta, quo clarius appareret ipsum διὰ τῦ θανάτε καταργῆσαι τὸν τὸ κράτος ἔχοντα θανάτε Hebr. II. 14. Aristides in descriptione terræ motus quo Rho- dus eversa est: μνήματα ἀνεῤῥήγνυτο: Et mox: ἴζω μὲν τὰ μνήματα ἀνέρῥιπτε τὲς κειμένως.

Vers. 52. καὶ πολλὰ σώματα ἳ κεκοιμημένων ἁγίων ἠγέρθη] Quidam statim putant mortuo Christo hos mortuos resur- rexisse quod aliquos movit ut in eo quod sequitur lege- rent non μετὰ τὴν ἔγερσιν αὐτῶ sed αὐτῶν, inter quos est Arabs Interpres & inter Græcos Glycas. Sed vero est si- milius in morte vim mortis Christi apertione monumento- rum demonstratam, neque tamen ad vitam pervenisse hos mortuos nisi postquam Christus revixerat, ut sic apparet ipsum esse πρωτότοκον ἐκ ἳ νεκρῶν. Nemo enim mortuorum autem ad vitam immortalem surrexit, quod de his credi par est, in qua sententia est scriptor responsionum ad Orthodo- xos ad quæstionem LXXXV. Cons. Dan. XII. 2.

Improbanda autem Crisis est Dan.
