Heinsii, qui textum noviter ita interpunxit: καὶ ἐξελθόντες ἐκ τῶν μνημείων, μετὰ τlὼ ἔγερσιν αὐτε εἰσήλθον εἰς τlὼ ἁγίαν πόλιν, ac si eodem momento, cum a- perirentur eorum monumenta, resurrexerint, sed non nisi post resurrectionem in urbe sancta appa- ruerint hi Sancti. Rectius S. Hieronymus: Non antea resurrexerunt quam Dominus resurgeret, ut esset primogenitus resurrectionis ex mortuis.

## 27:53
Vers. 53. εἰς τὴν ἁγίαν πόλιν] For they were buried in the suburban places: he called it the holy city according to the popular manner of speaking, as above IV. 5.

Ἐνεφανίσθησαν πολλοῖς] To those believing in Christ, as also Christ himself: not to all the people, as Peter speaks in Acts X. 41.

Some others deny that these saints rose to immortal life, and say that they died again, to whom Vossius has added himself in lib. III. Harm. Evang. c. 1. §. 10. To whom it seems otherwise, he says, they say if they had to die again, it would not be a benefit to them, but a torment. That, however, is nothing, because it was most delightful for these souls to behold Christ, and with him, without any pain, which it was easy for God to provide, carrying the body, to ascend into the place destined for blessed souls, where they would be eternally with Christ before the throne of GOD. But if they ascended into heaven with Christ, what need was there of death, or of the removal of the body, which it is clear was certainly not mortal? Since that ἐνεφανίσθησαν πολλοῖς refers to a free presentation with a disappearance, as in Acts X. 40 concerning Christ, and not a perpetual conversation. What, therefore, prevents them from having ascended into heaven with Christ in that spiritual body? Which Epiphanius, Haer. LXXV, Ambrose in the Psalms, and most recent theologians have seen.

Latin:

Vers. 53. εἰς τὴν ἁγίαν πόλιν] Sepulti enim in suburbanis locis fuerunt: ἁγίαν πόλιν dixit ex populari more loquen- di, ut supra IV. 5.

Ἐνεφανίσθησαν πολλοῖς] Credentibus in Christum, ut & Christus ipse: ὐ παντὶ τῷ λαῷ ut Petrus loquitur Act. X. 41.

Ad vitam immortalem hosce sanctos resurre- xisse alii nonnulli negant, eosque iterum mortuos ajunt, quibus accessit Vossius l. III. Harm. Evang. c. 1. §. 10. Quibus aliud videtur, inquit, ajunt si iterum fuisset moriendum, non beneficium iis fore, sed tor- mentum. Id vero nihil est, quia jucundissimum his ani- mis fuit Christum conspicere, & cum eo, sine dolore ullo, quod facile fuit Deo præstare, corpus deferentes adscendere in locum animis beatis destinatum, ubi æternum forent cum Christo ante DEI thronum. Sed si cum Christo ascenderunt in cœlum, quid opus morte, vel corporis delatione, quod utique non mortale fuisse patet. Siquidem illud ἐνεφα- νίσθησαν πολλοῖς liberam, ut de Christo Actor. X. 40. præsentationem cum disparitione sequu- ta, non vero perpetuam conversationem referat. In illo ergo spirituali corpore eos cum Christo in cœlum adscendisse, quid vetat? Quod vi- sum Epiphan. hæres. LXXV. Ambros. in Psal. & plerisque recentioribus Theologis.

## 27:54
Vers. 54. ἑκατόνταρχος] The centurion in charge of the execution, as Seneca speaks in book 1 de ira, chapter 12.

τηρῦντες] See what is above at verse 31. And note also that the soldiers remained after the death: lest anyone, as Petronius speaks, should drag the bodies away for burial: add, unless by public permission.

καὶ τὰ γενόμενα] The darkness of the Sun and, which Mark not in vain adds, the expiration immediately after the cry.

ἐφοβήθησαν σφόδρα] In themselves, as ministers of cruelty fearing the wrath of God.

Ἀληθῶς Θεῦ ὑὸς ἦν ὗτος] Since they were Romans who were saying this, I think they judged Jesus in the same way they judged Hercules, Bacchus, the Castors, Aesculapius, and Quirinus: And it is credible that they looked especially to the famous fable about Quirinus, around whose death both darkness and a crash were said to have occurred. Tertullian concerning Christ: He was received into heaven much more truly than the followers of Proculus are accustomed to assert concerning Romulus. Luke, as we have said, says that he himself said that Jesus was innocent. It is credible that this was said by them at the beginning: but with other portents being added to others, their admiration was increased, so that now they believed him to be not only an innocent man, but also greater than a man.

Things that are asserted from fables are foreign here. They teach that the conversion was truly περισσῶς (abundantly), with which those profane fables have no connection. Therefore, the centurion, with those who were present with him, acknowledged that Christ was truly the Son of GOD: namely, such as he had professed himself to be. But he had professed himself to be the true and proper Son of GOD, not so called in an adoptive or metaphorical sense.

Latin:

Vers. 54. ἑκατόνταρχος] Centurio supplicio præpositus, ut Seneca loquitur lib. 1. de ira cap. 12.

τηρῦντες] Vide quæ supra ad comma 31. Et nota etiam post mortem mansisse milites: nequis scilicet, ut Petronius loquitur, ad sepulturam corpora detraheret: adde, nisi pu- blico permissu.

καὶ τὰ γενόμενα] Caliginem Solis &, quod non frustra Marcus addit, exspirationem statim post clamorem.

ἐφοβήθησαν σφόδρα] In se, ut sævitiæ ministros iram Dei metuentes.

Ἀληθῶς Θεῦ ὑὸς ἦν ὗτος] Cum Romani fuerint qui hoc di- cebant, puto eos de Jesu ita existimasse quomodo de Hercu- le, Baccho, Castoribus, Æsculapio, Quirino existima- bant: Et maxime ad celebrem de Quirino fabulam respe- xisse eos credibile est, circa cujus mortem & tenebræ & fra- gor contigisse dicebantur. Tertullianus de Christo: In Cœlum est receptus multo verius quam apud vos asseverare de Romulo Proculi solent. Lucas, ut diximus, dictum ab ipsi sait Jesum esse innocentem. Credibile est id initio ab illis dictum: sed aliis ostentis ad alia accedentibus auctam admirationem, ita ut jam non hominem tantum innocen- tem, sed & homine majorem crederent.

Aliena hic sunt quæ è fabulis asseruntur. Ve- ram fuisse conversionem περισσῶς docent, cum qua fabulæ illæ profanæ nihil habent commercii. Agnovere ergo centurio cum iis, qui ipsi aderant, Christum vere esse Filium DEI: qualem nempe se professus erat. Professus autem erat se verum & proprium DEI Filium, non adoptivum, aut me- taphoricum ita dictum.

## 27:55
Vers. 55. ἀπὸ μακρόθεν] παρὰ τῷ σταυρῷ indeed, as John says, but not so as to touch the cross, which was surrounded by the crowd of soldiers.

διακονῦσαι αὐτῷ] Namely, ἀπὸ τῶν ὑπαρχόντων αὐταῖς, Luke VIII. 3.

Latin:

Vers. 55. ἀπὸ μακρόθεν] παρὰ τῷ σταυρῷ quidem, ut ait Johannes, sed non ut crucem attingerent quæ militum tur- ba cingebatur.

διακονῦσαι αὐτῷ] Nimirum ἀπὸ τῶν ὑπαρχόντων αὐταῖς, Luc. VIII. 3.

## 27:56
Vers. 56. Μαρία ἡ Μαγδαληνὴ] A Galilean woman, as we have learned from Luke.

Μαρία ἡ τῦ Ἰακώβυ καὶ Ἰωσῆ μήτηρ] The wife of Cleopas, according to John. For the fact that, besides the mother of the Lord, there were no more than two Marys who followed Jesus is an indication, XXVII. 61. Among many opinions, the simplest is that which establishes Cleopas as her father and Alphaeus as her husband. Some ancient codices, both Greek and Latin, had Joseph instead of Joses. But it is the same name, with a different pronunciation, concerning which matter elsewhere.

But in our judgment, others more correctly wish her to be called the wife of Alphaeus from her first husband, from whom James and Joses were born to her, and they make Cleopas, the brother of Joseph the husband of Mary the Mother of God, her other husband, and consider her to be the sister of the blessed Virgin Mary: She is called the Mary of Joses in Mark XV. 47 because she was his mother, as is said here, whom (along with James) she bore from Alphaeus, whence James is called the (son) of Alphaeus in Matt. X. 3. Upon his death, she married Cleopas, and from him she bore Simeon, the second Bishop of Jerusalem, as Eusebius has it in book III of his Ecclesiastical History, chapter 11, teaching from Hegesippus that Cleopas was the brother of Joseph. This Mary, however, John calls the sister of the mother of Christ, whence James, in the manner of the Hebrew language, which calls cousins brothers, is called the brother of the Lord in Gal. I. 9. Johann Gerhard is singular. Vossius's opinion, that Mary the mother of James and Joses is the very θεοτόκος [Mother of God], who was their stepmother, as being the children of Joseph betrothed to her, lib. III. Harmon. Evang. c. III. §. 2. Which rests on no solid evidence. For it is not likely that the mother of the Lord, along with the other women who had run to the sepulchre for the sake of anointing Christ, Mark XVI., doubted the resurrection of Christ, or did not believe it: of which ἀπιστία [unbelief] that intention of anointing was surely no obscure proof. But Sedulius indeed, lib. V. Carmin., maintains that the Blessed Mary was in the company of those women; but he does not say that she was Mary of Cleophas, which perhaps, apart from Nicephorus the fabulous writer, lib. I. Histor. c. 33, hardly anyone would say, nor is it to be presumed, because otherwise the Evangelists would have explicitly mentioned it, which was done by no one. The mother of the Lord certainly knew well that Christ did not need anointing, nor would his body see corruption, not to mention that anointing was not accustomed to be performed by close relatives or a mother, but by others.

ἡ μήτηρ τῶν ὑιῶν Ζεβεδαίου [The mother of the sons of Zebedee]: Salome, of whom above.

Latin:

Vers. 56. Μαρία ἡ Μαγδαληνὴ] Galilæa femina, ut ex Lu- ca didicimus.

Μαρία ἡ τῦ Ἰακώβυ καὶ Ἰωσῆ μήτηρ] Cleopæ Johanni. Nam eandem esse indicio est quod præter matrem Domini non fuerant plures duabus Mariæ nomine quæ Jesum se- ctarentur XXVII. 61. Inter multas sententias expeditis- sima est, quæ Cleopam ejus Patrem, Alphæum maritum statuit. Pro Jose veteres quidam codices & Græci & Lati- ni habebant Joseph. Sed idem est nomen, pronunciatio- ne diversa, qua de re alibi.

Nostro vero judicio rectius alii Alphæi dictam a primo marito volunt, ex quo nati sint ipsi Ja- cobus & Joses., & Cleopham Josephi sponsi Mariæ θεοτόκου fratrem alterum ejus maritum faciunt, eamque pro Mariæ virginis benedictæ sorore ha- bent: Vocatur Maria Joses Marc. XV. 47. quia ejus mater fuit, ut hic dicitur, quem (cum Jaco- bo) ex Alphæo suscepit, unde Iacobus Alphæi (fi- lius) dicitur Matth. X. 3. quo defuncto nupsit Cleophæ, & ex eo Simeonem secundum Hierosoly- morum Episcopum, suscepit, uti habet Euse- bius lib. III. Histor. Eccles. cap. 11. ex Egesippo do- cens, Cleopham fratrem fuisse Josephi. Hanc au- tem Mariam Johannes vocat sororem matris Christi, unde Jacobus more Ebrææ linguæ, quæ consobrinos vocat fratres, vocatur frater Domini Gal. I. 9. Singularis est Joh. Gerh. Vossii sententia, Mariam matrem Iacobi & Joses esse ipsam θεοτόκον quæ noverca istorum fuerit, utpote filiorum Jose- phi ipsi desponsati lib. III. Harmon. Evang. c. III. §. 2. Quæ nullo solido documento nituntur. Neque enim verosimile est, matrem Domini cum cæteris quæ ungendi Christi causa ad sepulchrum excur- rerant, Marc. XVI. mulieribus de resurrectione Christi dubitasse, aut eandem non credidisse: cu- jus ἀπιστίας non obscurum sane documentum erat illa unctionis destinatio. Sed dius quidem lib. V. Carmin. B. Mariam in comitatu istarum mulierum fuisse statuit; sed nec eam Mariam Cleophæ dicit, quod forte præter Nicephorum fabulosum scripto- rem lib. I. Histor. c. 33. haud facile quisquam di- xerit, nec præsumere licet, quia cæteroquin diser- te id Evangelistæ memorassent, quod à nemine fa- ctum. Noverat utique probe mater Domini Christum non indigere unctione, neque corpus ejus visurum corruptionem, ut taceam, quod un- ctio non à cognatis proximis aut matre, sed ab aliis præstari consueverit.

ἡ μήτηρ τῶν ὑιῶν Ζεβεδαίου] Salome, de qua supra.

## 27:57
Vers. 57. ὀψίας δὲ γενομένης [And when evening had come]: Immediately after the ninth hour; a hurried matter, so that Joseph could, according to custom, slaughter the Passover before the twelfth hour, once Christ was buried.

πλούσιος [Rich]: ἐυσχήμων [prominent/honorable], says Mark, that is, a man of honorable standing, since he was a βουλευτής [councillor], as he himself adds and Luke expresses. It is asked whether this Joseph was in the Great Sanhedrin. Many believe he was, because Luke says he did not consent to the counsel and deeds of the others, but that is not a sufficiently certain argument. For many disapprove of many things even who do not have the right of suffrage. Furthermore, there is no reason why those words should be taken precisely of that consultation of the last day, since it had been deliberated several times before about the matter of Jesus, as when it was decided that those who said Jesus was the Messiah should be held as ἀποσυνάγωγοι [excommunicated]. In which history John does not mention the Sanhedrin, but says, συνέθεντο οἱ Ἰουδαῖοι [the Jews agreed], so that it is credible that that matter was acted upon in a larger assembly, which we said was called συναγωγὴν μεγάλην [great synagogue], and into which, besides the judges of the Sanhedrin, others also holding magistracy were called, just as Gorionides also narrates that both the lesser and greater senate, that is, the urban and the common one of the people, met concerning more serious matters. Therefore, I believe this Joseph, who was indeed born at Arimathea, but who had his domicile and the seat of his fortunes at Jerusalem (to which the wealthier were accustomed to migrate), was a Senator of the senate of the city of Jerusalem. He is not called ἄρχων [ruler], which was the name of the members of the Sanhedrin, like Nicodemus in John III.1, but βουλευτής [councillor], which two terms Josephus also distinguishes in his history of the Jewish War, lib. II c. XXIX. βουλευτής is not badly translated by the Latin interpreter as decurio [decurion]. Thus also in more than one old Glossary: Decurio βουλευτής. Pomponius thinks that this word was first born in the Roman colonies, because in the beginning, when colonies were being led out, a tenth part of those who were being led out was accustomed to be enrolled for the sake of a public council. Afterwards, it certainly began to be transferred to other cities as well, as the laws teach us and the reciprocal letters of Pliny and Trajan, where the body of the Boule itself, and its participants in the cities of Bithynia, are called decurions. The Greek word itself, bulentæ, is read in the Latin language, just as by the Syrian interpreter of Mark, so also in the Pliny and Spartianus whom I mentioned. But as for what the learned man thinks, that this Joseph was from Pilate's council, that is clearly repugnant to Roman customs. For governors used the council of Roman citizens: indeed, even those who had obtained the right of Roman citizenship were forbidden to sit in that province from which they had originated. But the dignity of this man is described accurately, so that we may see that some beginnings of glory destined for Christ appeared immediately after his death. For honor is held for him dead, such as for Jacob, the prince of the nation, whose name Christ often bears in the Prophets. To him a disciple, who is likewise rightly called a son, to the other a son, both of Joseph, both placed in dignity, were the undertakers.

ἐμαθήτευσε τῷ Ἰησοῦ [He was a disciple of Jesus]: A man indeed of upright life, ἀγαθὸς κὴ δίκαιος [good and just], an imitator of Simeon and eagerly awaiting the divine kingdom promised through the Prophets, as Mark and Luke teach: and therefore recognizing the true doctrine of Christ, but, as John adds, not daring to profess it until then, with fear prohibiting him. Thus we see how the seeds of faith, oppressed for some time by human vices, sometimes suddenly erupt, God thus disposing the occasions.

ἀπὸ Ἀριμαθαίας [from Arimathea]: which is perhaps ארומה [Arumah] Jud. IX. 40. There are more words approaching this name, such as רמתים [Ramathaim] of the Ephraimites I. Reg. I. II. רמה [Ramah] which is also רמות [Ramoth] and ירמות [Jarmuth] in the part of Issachar Jos. XIX. 21. c. XXI. 27. another רמת [Ramath] called for the sake of distinction מצפה [Mizpah] within the borders of the Gadites Jos. XIII. 26. Again רמה [Ramah] in the portion of the Asherites Jos. XIX. 29. Nor should that seem strange, since the word itself signifies nothing other than a more elevated place, whence what in the Hebrew Deut. III. 28 is משכה [Mishkah], the Chaldean translates as רמתא [Ramatha], but since Luke explicitly calls this πόλιν Ἰουδαίων [a city of the Jews], where I do not doubt that those who lived around Jerusalem are strictly called Ἰουδαῖοι [Jews], I am led to believe that there is designated here the town of Benjamin, Ramah, mentioned in Josh. 18:25. It is thought to be the same as Ramoth in 2 Kings 23:36. Jerome and Eusebius report that in their times it was called Remtin; it is characteristic of the Syrians to say Armatha for Ramah: just as Josephus calls that Ephraimite seat of Samuel Armatha. Thus, Cana in Syriac is Qana: and for the Hebrew Qiryah, which signifies a city, the Syrians say Qarta, whence Tigranocerta and others are formed in that manner: Similar is Behemah among the Chaldeans for the Hebrew Beqer in Gen. 14:5, and for Hiddekel, which is the Hebrew name for the Tigris river, with the first guttural omitted, Diqlatha, Diglito in Pliny.

Latin:

Vers. 57. ὀψίας δὲ γενομένης] Statim post nonam; Festi- na res, ut posset Josephus Christo tumulato, ex more ante duodecimam Pascha mactare.

πλούσιος] ἐυσχήμων inquit Marcus, id est vir honesti loci, quippe βουλευτὴς ut ipse addit & Lucas exprimit. Quæritur an in Synedrio Magno Josephus hic fuerit. Fuisse multi cre- dunt, quia Lucas eum dicit non consensisse consilio & acti- bus aliorum, sed id non satis certum est argumentum. Im- probant enim multi multa etiam qui jus suffragii non ha- bent. Deinde non est quod verba illa præcise sumantur de illa consultatione postremæ diei, cum antea quoque delibe- ratum aliquoties de re Jesu fuerit ut cum constitutum est ut ἀποσυνάγωγοι haberentur qui Jesum esse Messiam dicerent. In qua historia Johannes non Synedrii meminit, sed dicit, συνέθεντο οἱ Ἰουδαῖοι, ut credibile sit eam rem actam in con- ventu majore, quam συναγωγὴν μεγάλην vocari diximus, & in quam præter Synedrii judices alii etiam magistratum ge- rentes vocabantur, sicut & Gorionides narrat convenisse su- per rebus gravioribus senatum & minorem & maiorem, id est urbanum & communem populi, Josephum igitur hunc oriundum quidem ab Arimathæa, cæterum domicilium & sedem fortunarum suarum habentem Hierosolymis (quo commigrare opulentiores solebant) credo fuisse Senatorem senatus urbis Hierosolymitanæ. Ii es non vocatur ἄρχων, quod nomen erat τῶν συνέδρων, ut Nicodemus Joh. III.1. sed βουλευτής, quæ duo etiam Josephus in belli Judaici historia distinguit lib. II c. XXIX. βουλευτὴς à Latino interprete non male vertitur decurio. Sic & in Glossario vetere non uno: Decurio βουλευτής. Putat Pomponius in coloniis Romanis primum natam eam vocem, quod initio, cum coloniæ de- ducerentur, decima pars eorum qui ducerentur, consilii pu- blici gratia conscribi solita esset. Postea certe ad alias quo- que urbes transferri cœpit, ut nos leges docent & ἀμοιβαῖαι literæ Plinii & Trajani, ubi corpus ipsum Bule, ejus partici- pes in Bithyniæ urbibus decuriones vocantur. Ipsa vox Græca bulentæ ut à Syro Marci Interprete, ita apud eum quem dixi Plinium & Spartianum in Latino sermone legi- tur. Quod vero putat vir doctus Josephum hunc ex Pilati consilio fuisse, id plane Romanis moribus repugnat. Nam Romanorum civium consilio præsides utebantur: imo et- iam qui jus nacti erant Romanæ civitatis, in ea provincia ex qua orti erant adsidere vetabantur. Accurate autem hu- jus viri dignitas describitur, ut videamus statim à morte quæ- dam gloriæ Christo destinatæ apparuisse initia. Honos e- nim ei mortuo habetur, qualis Jacobo gentis principi, cujus nomen in Prophetis sæpe fert Christus. Huic discipulus, qui item filius recte dicitur, illi filius, ambo Josephi, ambo in dignitate positi, pollinctores.

ἐμαθήτευσε τῷ Ἰησοῦ] Vir quippe probæ vitæ, ἀγαθὸς κὴ δίκαιος, Simeonis imitator & regnum divinum per Prophe- tas promissum avide exspectans, ut Marcus & Lucas do- cent: ac proinde veram agnoscens Christi doctrinam, sed, quod Johannes addit, profiteri eam non audens hactenus, metu prohibente. Ita videmus quomodo fidei semina, humanis vitiis oppressæ aliquamdiu, subito interdum e- rumpant Deo ita disponente occasiones.

ἀπὸ Ἀριμαθαίας] quæ forte ארומה Jud. IX. 40. Plu- res sunt voces ad hoc nomen accedentes, ut רמתים Ephraimitarum I. Reg. I. II. רמה quæ & רמות & ירמות in Ischaris parte Jos. XIX. 21. c. XXI. 27. alia רמת discriminis causa מצפה dicta intra Gaditarum ter- minos Jos. XIII. 26. Rursum רמה in portione Aseritarum Jos. XIX. 29. Neque mirum id videri debet, cum vox ipsa nihil aliud quam locum eminentiorem significet, un- de quod in Hebræo Deut. III. 28. & משכה Chaldæus ver- tit רמתא, sed cum Lucas diferte hanc vocet πόλιν Ἰουδαίων, ubi non dubito quin Ἰουδαῖοι stricte dicantur ii qui circa Hie- rosolyma habitabant, adducor ut credam designari hic oppi- dum Benjaminis רמה memoratum Jef. XIIX. 25. Eadem putatur esse רמות 2. Reg. XXIII. 36. Hanc suis tempo- ribus Remtin appellatam Hieronymus & Eusebius tradunt, Syrorum est pro רמה dicere ארמתא : quomodo Josephus illam Ephraimiticam Samuelis sedem vocat Ἀρμα- θᾶ. Sic Cana Syro est קנא: & pro Hebræo קריה quod urbem significat, Syri dicunt קרתא, unde Tigra- nocerta & alia ad eam formam: Simile est בהמה a- pud Chaldæum pro Hebræo בקר Gen. XIV. 5. & pro חדקל quod Hebræum nomen est Tigridi flumine omissa prima gutturali דקלתא Diglito apud Plinium.

## 27:58
ἠτήσατο τὸ σῶμα] Of those, says Ulpian, who are executed, the bodies are not buried otherwise than if it has been requested and permitted. Roman magistrates, however, are lenient in this matter. Ulpian in the cited passage: The bodies of those who are condemned to death must not be denied to their relatives. Diocletian and Maximian: We do not forbid the bodies of those guilty of crimes who have suffered the deserved punishment to be committed to burial. Verres, among other things, is accused by Cicero of having thrown the bodies of those struck by the axe to wild beasts, or of having sold the power of burial for a price. Ulpian in the cited passage excepts those condemned for high treason: whence it can be gathered that Pilate did not wish to have the crime of high treason (since it is by no means credible) ascribed to Christ so much as the crime of sedition. Although burial is sometimes granted even to those condemned for treason, as to those who had conspired with Catiline. For as Fabius well says, treating this argument about burying criminals in Declamation 6: even if there are laws that stand in the way, if nevertheless a narrow access is at least given, through which humanity can enter, true clemency is content with the opportunity. However, the bodies of the crucified, even of robbers, were accustomed to be kept on the cross for some time for display, as we learn from Petronius. But because it conflicted with the institutions of the Jews for the bodies of the executed to be displayed beyond evening, Deut. 21:23, it is credible that the Roman governors in that matter, as in many other things, followed the custom of the region. Josephus: The Jews are so careful about burials that they take down and bury even those who have been crucified after conviction before the sun sets. Wherefore this was not properly requested by the Jews in John 19:31, that the bodies should be removed before night, but that it should be done a little earlier, lest the beginning of the Sabbath should overtake the soldiers occupied in that work. For for the sake of greater caution, the Jews used to begin their rest about one hour before sunset: and at that time indeed more religiously, because the feast day that was impending would have been so even without the Sabbath.

Latin:

ἠτήσατο τὸ σῶμα] Eorum, inquit Ulpianus, in quos animadvertitur, corpora non aliter sepeliuntur quam si fuerit petitum & permissum. Faciles autem in hanc rem Romani magistratus. Ulpianus dicto loco: Corpora eorum qui ca- pitis damnantur cognatis eorum neganda non sunt. Diocletia- nus & Maximianus: Obnoxios criminum digno supplicio affe- ctos sepulturæ tradinon vetamus. Verri inter alia objicitur à Cicerone quod securi percussorum corpora feris objecif- set, aut pretio vendidisset sepeliendi potestatem. Excipit Ulpianus dicto loco majestatis damnatos: unde colligi potest Pilatum Christo non tam majestatis (quippe nequa- quam credibile) quam seditionis crimen asscriptum voluis- se. Quanquam & perduellionis damnatis indulta inter- dum sepultura, ut his qui cum Catilina conjuraverant. Nam ut bene Fabius declamatione VI. tractans hoc argu- mentum de sepeliendis facinorosis: etiam si qua sunt jura quæ obstent, si tamen angustus saltem detur accessus, per quem intrare humanitas possit, vera clementia occasione contenta est. Corpora tamen crucifixorum, etiam latronum, solebant aliquamdiu in cruce servari ostentui, ut ex Petronio disci- mus. Sed quia cum judæorum institutis pugnabat cor- pora peremtorum ultra vesperam ostentari, Deut. XXI. 23. credibile est præsides Romanos ea in re, ut in multis rebus aliis, secutos morem regionis. Josephus: Τοσαύτην Ἰυ- δαίων περὶ τὰς ταφὰς πρόνοιαν ποιουμένων ὥστε κᾀ τὺς ἐκ καταδί- κης ἀνασταυρωμένως πρὸ δύντος ἡλίε ἀνελῶν τε κᾀ θάπτειν. Qua- re non hoc proprie rogatum à Judæis Ioh. XIX. 31. ut ante noctem corpora demerentur, sed ut paulo maturius, ne milites in eo opere occupatos initium Sabbati deprehen de- ret. Nam majoris cautionis ergo hora ferme una ante so- lem occasum Judæi otium suum auspicabantur: ac tunc quidem eo religiosius, quia qui imminebat dies festus e- rat etiam absque sabbato fuisset.

## 27:59
Verse 59. Σινδόνι καθαρᾷ] The Hebrew word Sadin, by which is signified not silk, which we now call by a similar word (for even the Prince of the Senate could not often be clothed in silk), but a covering made of linen of no great price, as the Hebrews note it was instituted by Gamaliel the Elder: which can also be gathered from that history which exists in Mark 14:52. Herodotus, describing the embalming of the Egyptians: having washed the corpse, they wrap his whole body in a sindon. Although Matthew names only one, namely the principal one, with which the body was wrapped, it is certain that there were more, wherefore John rightly said linen cloths in chapter 19:40 and chapter 20:6, among which was also the sudarium for covering the head, which John distinguishes from the other coverings in chapter 20:7. The same is shown in the history of Lazarus, that besides the sudarium there were also grave-bands, of which we shall treat in their place, chapter 11:44. Interpreters explain ὀθόνας in Homer as linen fabrics. In the Glossary, ὀθόνη is a linen cloth: and elsewhere sindon is a linen tunic. Nonnus on Lazarus: And he was wrapped in a linen covering around his head. Mark also mentions the sindon in chapter 15:46, and Luke in chapter 23:53. John, however, in chapter 19:40, named linen cloths. Josephus seems to have wrapped the sindon around the naked body, but the linen cloths or bands or strips were added for that purpose; so that the sindon might be held fast by them, or so that the body might be wrapped further, which seems to have been enveloped not in one but in several linen cloths; indeed, that grave-bands were also used, B. Gerhard gathers from the history of Lazarus in John 11:44, so that, namely, the hands and feet might be bound with them. For in preparing the dead for burial, as Salmasius has it in De Cruce, page 381, they bound the hands, let down and joined at the sides, together with the body itself and to the body itself. Thus bound, the hands descended almost to the very knees. Thence also the legs and feet were accustomed to be bound with similar bands. If indeed for Hesychius ὀθόνη, sindon, girdle, and band are the same. But St. Athanasius in his Homily on Holy Friday distinguishes them: Let us see for a moment Joseph bringing gifts, and Nicodemus running together, wrapping the Lord of all in a sindon, a clean one, and linen cloths, and a sudarium. For the head was also covered with a sudarium, John 20:6. Although indeed linen cloths are mentioned only by John, and the sindon only by the other Evangelists, they are not therefore to be taken as the same. For what some of the Evangelists omit, one or another is accustomed to supply. To the sindon of the others, therefore, St. John added the bands, but he did not exchange these. There is no need, therefore, to say with Salmasius, l.c. page 383, that a large linen covering was bought by Joseph, which is the sindon, and that he himself tore it into many bands, with which he bound and wrapped the body of Christ. For Joseph is not said only to have bought the sindon, but to have wrapped the body of Christ in a clean sindon: and he wrapped it in a clean sindon. Salmasius acknowledges that Athanasius names those three, the sindon, and the linen cloths, and the sudarium, as if they were different: Behold, he says, with the words of the Holy Father already praised, he calls it a sindon, and linen cloths, and a sudarium, with all of which he was wrapped at the same time: namely, as he had said before, the body bound with bands, then also wrapped in a large sindon. This could seem to have been done in that way (Salmasius continues) if John did not contradict it, who named only the linen cloths, and makes no mention of the sindon. But Matthew, Mark, and Luke call it a sindon. We invert the argument: the linen cloths were named by John because the earlier Evangelists had already made mention of the sindon. Wherefore they were used together, but are not to be taken as the same, which in truth are different. No one of the Evangelists commemorates the sindon being torn into bands. But the greatest of critics seems at length doubtful: However it may be, he says, certainly the sudarium is far different from the sindon itself, in which the dead are now wrapped, or even from the very bonds (swaddling bands) with which formerly both Greeks and Jews as well as Latins used to bind the bodies of their deceased. Regarding what Matthew called σινδόνα καθαρὰν, Origen says beautifully: I think that that sindon received a better cleanliness from the time the body of Christ was wrapped in it than it had before.

Latin:

Vers. 59. Σινδόνι καθαρᾷ] Hebræa vox סדין quo signi- ficatur non sericum quod nos nunc simili voce appellamus (nam cum serico sepe iri ne quidem Senatus Princeps pot- erat) sed operimentum ex lino pretii haud magni, ut à Ga- maliele seniore institutum notant Hebræi: quod & ex ea historia colligere est quæ exstat apud Mar. um XIV. 52. He- rodotus Ægyptiorum polliancturam describens: λούσαντες τ νεκρὸν κατειλίσσουσι πᾶν ἀυτοῦ τὸ σῶμα σίνδονι. Σινδόνος Quan- quam autem unum nominat Matthæus, præcipuum vice- licet, quo corpus involvebatur, plura tamen fuisse certum est, quare ὀθόνια recte dixit Iohannes cap. XIX. 40. & cap. XX. 6. inter quæ erat & sudarium velando capiti,quod à re- liquis operimentis distinguit Iohannes cap. XX. 7. Idem in Lazari historia ostendit præter sudarium fuisse & κειρίας, de quibus suo loco agemus, cap. XI. 44. ὀθόνας apud Ho- merum interpretes exponunt ὑφάσματα λινᾶ. In Glossario est ὀθόνη linteamen: & alibi σινδὼν tunica lintea. Nonnus de Lazaro: Καὶ λινέῳ πεπύκαϲτο καλύμματι κυκλάδα κόρσην. Sidonis etiam meminit Marcus cap. XV. 46. & Lucas cap. XXIII. 53. Johannes vero cap. XIX. 40. nominavit ὀθόνια. Sindonem videtur Jose- phus nudo circumvolvisse corpori, ὀθόνια vero vel fascias, seu institæ ea fini accessisse; ut iis Sindon coërceretur, vel ut corpus etiam invol- veretur, quod non uno solum sed pluribus linteis videtur obvolutum, imo adhibitas etiam esse κειρίας, ex historia Lazari Johan. XI. 44. col- ligit B. Gerhardus, ut scil. iisdem manus, pe- desque colligarentur. Nam in mortuis pollin- gendis, ut habet Salmasius de cruce pag. 381. ma- nus demissas & ad latera junctas simul cum ipso corpore & ad corpus ipsum colligabant. Ita ligatæ manus pene ad genua ipsa descendebant. Inde & crura & pedes similibus fasciis ligari consueverunt. si Hesychio sane idem sunt ὀθόνη, σινδὼν, ζώνη, τε- λαμὼν. At S. Athanasius Homilia in S. Parasc. si distinguit illa: Ἴδωμεν τέως δωροφορῦντα τὸν Ἰω- σήφ, καὶ τὸν Νικόδημον συντρέχοντα, σίνδονι, tu- καθαρᾷ καὶ ὀθονίοις, καὶ σουδαρίῳ περιελίσσοντας τὸν τοῦ παντὸς κύριον. Nam & sudario caput vela- tum fuit, Johan. XX. 6. Quanquam vero ὀθόνια tantum à Johanne, σινδὼν verò à cæteris solum Evangelistis commemorentur, non tamen ea pro iisdem ideo habenda. Nam quod Evangelista- rum aliqui omittunt, unus vel alter supplere so- let. Sindoni ergo cæterorum S. Johannes insti- tas addidit, non vero hæc commutavit. Non ergo opus ut cum Salmasio l. c. pag. 383. dicamus emtum à Josepho grande linteum tegmen, quod est Sindon, eamque in multas ipsum scidisse fascias, quibus corpus Christi vinxit, & convolvit. Non enim emisse tantum Sindonem dicitur Josephus, sed corpus Christi sindone involvisse : & ἐνετύλιξεν αὐτὸ σινδόνι καθαρᾷ. Agnoscit Salmasius Atha- nasium tria illa, σινδόνα, & ὀθόνια, & σουδάριον qua- si diversa nominare : Ecce, inquit productis ver- bis S. Patris, jam laudatis, Sindonem vocat, & ὀθόνια, & sudarium, quibus omnibus simul cir- cumligatus : nimirum ut antea dixerat, corpus liga- tum fasciis, deinde & grandi sindone involutum. Hoc posset ita factum videri (pergit Salmasius) nisi Johannes repugnaret, qui sola ὀθόνια nominavit, nec σινδόνος meminit. At Matthæus, Marcus, & Lucas σινδόνα appellant. Invertimus nos argu- mentum: ideo ὀθόνια nominata à Johanne, quia priores Evangelistæ jam Sindonis mentio- nem fecerant. Quapropter eadem conjunctim adhibita esse, non vero pro iisdem habenda, quæ revera diversa sunt. In fascias scissam sindonem Evangelistarum nullus commemorat. Sed du- bius tandem videtur Criticorum maximus: Utut sit, inquit, sane sudarium longe aliud est ab ipsa Sindone, qua mortui nunc involvuntur, vel etiam ab ipsis vinculis, (fasciis) quibus olim tam Græci & Judæi quam Latini corpora suorum defunctorum circumligabant. Quod σινδόνα καθαρὰν dixit Matthæus, ad id Origenes pulchre : Puto Sin- donem illam meliorem accepisse munditiem, ex quo involutum ei fuit corpus Christi, quam habuerat prius.

## 27:60
Vers. 60. ὃ ἐλατόμησεν ἐν τῇ πέτρᾳ] For it was the custom of the Jews to excavate for themselves from a rock for the burying of bodies, as a man of the highest learning and diligence has observed. Luke calls it Λαξευτὸν μνῆμα: in Hebrew פָּסַל מָעוֹז. For λατομεῖν is to excavate according to the LXX interpreters in Deut. VI. 11, where it is about a cistern: and Isa. XXII. 16, where it is about a sepulcher. Moreover, all these things are so exactly noted by the writers of the Gospels, because they pertain greatly to establishing the faith concerning the death and resurrection of Christ: in which two heads the foundation of all Christianity is contained as it were. See Paul 1 Cor. XV. 3, 4, 5, and the speeches of the Apostles throughout the Acts.

Mark expressly testifies that that crypt where the body of the Lord was placed was cut out of a rock: καὶ κατέθηκεν αὐτὸν ἐν μνημείῳ ὃ ἦν λελατομημένον ἐκ πέτρας. Which it is not permitted to explain as having been a monument built of stone and vaulted, but cut out of a rock or cliff, as the Vulgate and Beza render it. But Luke, says Salmasius, removes every difficulty, who calls it μνῆμα λαξευτὸν: καὶ κατέθηκαν αὐτὸ ἐν μνήματι λαξευτῷ. I agree with all who know Greek here that they think nothing else is understood by the name μνήματος λαξευτοῦ than a monument built of polished and squared stone. But the Vulgate was one who knew Greek, who rendered it, in a monument cut out: Beza was also one, who interpreted it, in a monument which was cut into a rock. Erasmus Schmid was also one, explaining it as that which was cut into a rock. Casaubon was also one, who has it thus: Therefore μνημεῖον λαξευτὸν that is that place which is called in the writings of the Rabbis, qeber is a sepulcher, from the end, and me'arah is a cave or grotto from the form, since the place was hollowed out in a rock or stone: the reason for which must be sought from the fact that the whole ground around Jerusalem is rocky and hypopetron, as it is called by Strabo. Nor does Erasmus, most learned in Greek, think otherwise in his Annotations on Luke 24: 'In a monument hewn out': laxeyto: so that we may understand it was solid rock, not compact or built, but sculpted in its own native place. Nor does Matthew say 'which he hewed out of a rock' (ek petras), or 'in a rock' (petra), but 'in the rock' (en te petra). 'He should have said,' says Salmasius, 'lelatomemenon ek tes petras' (hewn out of the rock), if he had meant hewn out of the cliff that was there. Those skilled in Greek know what that 'ek petras' without the article is worth; it is indeed the same as if he had said 'ek lithou' (out of a stone). If this is the force of the article which Salmasius claims, it was not omitted by Matthew, even if it was not added by Mark. For thus Matthew has it: 'which he hewed in the rock.' And therefore nothing prevents the monument from being understood as hewn out of that cliff which was there. We add, however, what Salmasius rightly observes here: 'It is certain,' he says, 'that the Jews did not bury the bodies of the deceased in chests or beds or sarcophagi, but brought them into the monument covered and wrapped only in linen cloths torn into strips.' In the sides of the monument, as the Jewish masters relate, hollows were sculpted, suitable for receiving individual bodies, into which they were inserted just as they were veiled in strips or bandages. These hollows, excavated in the wall of the monument, into which the corpse was as it were delivered, served the purpose of the beds or chests in which bodies of the deceased were accustomed to be buried in Greece.

Rolling a great stone to the door of the monument] galal to the Talmudists, Polybius: 'but having brought him into what is called the Treasury, an underground chamber, so that it might take air, so that it might see light, so that it might have doors, but being closed up with a great stone rolled around, they deposited him there.'

Sopranes notes that the stone was rolled not to the entrance of the whole sepulcher, but at least to the inner one, with a straight and free entry to the vestibule, which some gather from Mark 16:6. Tradition according to Nicephorus, book 1, chapter 32, teaches that it was rolled to the highest lip of the monument: where the method of sealing the stone is also explained. Montacutius repeats that tradition, and from him Walaeus, p. 65, b. l.

Latin:

Vers. 60. ὃ ἐλατόμησεν ἐν τῇ πέτρᾳ] Is enim mos erat Ju- dæorum è rupe secum excavare condendis corporibus, ut observavit vir summæ eruditionis ac diligentiæ. Λαξευτὸν μνῆμα Lucas dicit : Hebræis פָּסַל מָעוֹז . Nam λατομεῖν excavare est LXX. interpretibus Deut. VI. 11, ubi de cister- na : & Esa. XXII. 16. ubi de sepulchro. Hæc autem omnia tam exacte notata sunt ab Evangeliorum Scriptori- bus, quia valde pertinent ad stabiliendam fidem de Chri- sti morte & resurrectione : in quibus duobus capitibus vel- ut fundamentum totius Christianismi continetur. Vide Paulum 1. Cor. XV. 3. 4. 5. & orationes Apostolorum pas- sim in Actis.

Ex rupe excisam cryptam illam, ubi corpus Domini repositum est, Marcus diserte testatur : καὶ κατέθηκεν αὐτὸν ἐν μνημείῳ ὃ ἦν λελατομημένον ἐκ πέτρας. Quæ exponere non licet, lapide structum & concameratum fuisse monumentum, sed ex petra vel rupe excisum, ut Vulgata & Beza reddunt. Sed Lucas, inquit Salmasius, omnem difficultatem amolitur, qui μνῆμα λαξευτὸν vo- cat : καὶ κατέθηκαν αὐτὸ ἐν μνήματι λαξευ- τῷ. Græce scientes omnes hic convenio quod a- liud putent μνήματος λαξευτοῦ appellatione intel- ligi, quam monumentum ex lapide politum at- que quadrato structum. At Græce sciens Vul- gatus fuit, qui reddidit, in monumento exciso: fuit & Beza, qui interpretatus est, in monu- mento quod erat in saxo incisum. Fuit & Era- smus Schmidius exponens, quod saxo incisum e- rat. Fuit & Casaubonus, qui ita habet Igi- tur μνημεῖον λαξευτὸν id est ille locus qui dicitur in Scriptis Rabbinorum קבר sepulchrum, à fine, & מערה spelunca sive antrum à forma, quoniam cavabatur locus in Petra sive saxo: cujus rei petenda ratio est ex eo, quod totum circa Jerusalem solum est saxosum & ὑπόπετρον, ut appellatur à Strabone. Nec aliter Erasmus Græce scientissimus Annot. ad Luc. XXIV. In monumento exciso: λαξευτῷ: ut intelligamus solidum fuisse saxum, non compa- ctile, aut structile, sed exsculptum suo loco nativo. Neque Matthæus dicit ὃ ἐλατόμησεν ἐκ πέτρας, vel πέτρᾳ, sed ἐν τῇ πέτρᾳ. Ad dicendum fuis- set, inquit Salmasius, λελατομημένον ἐκ τῆς πέ- τρας, si ex rupe excisum, quæ inibi erat, intellexis- set. Norunt Græce periti quid valeat illud abs- que articulo ἐκ πέτρας, idem quippe est ac si dixis- set ἐκ λίθου. Si articuli hæc vis est, quam Sal- masius dicit, non omissus ille à Matthæo est, et- si non additus à Marco sit. Ita enim Matthæus habet: ὃ ἐλατόμησεν ἐν τῇ πέτρᾳ. Ideoque ni- hil obstat quo minus ex rupe illa quæ inibi erat, excisum intelligatur monumentum. Addimus autem quæ hic recte observat Salmasius: Cer- tum, inquit, est, Judæos corpora defunctorum non condita in arcis aut lectulis sive sarcophagis, sed solis lineis taniatim scissis operta & amicta intulisse monumento. In monumenti lateribus, ut Judæi magistri tradunt, exculpti erant cavi singulis corpo- ribus recipiendis idonei, quibus ea immittebantur, sicut erant taniis vel fasciis velata. Hi cavi in pariete monumenti excavati, in quos veluti tradeba- tur cadaver, vicem lectorum vel arcularum præbe- bant, quibus in Græcia corpora defunctorum condi so- lebant.

προσκυλίσας λίθον μέγαν τῇ θύρᾳ τοῦ μνημείου] גלל Thalmudistis, Polybius: ἡμῖν ἀλλὰ κομίσαντες αὐτὸν εἰς ἳ καλούμενον Θησαυρὸν οἴκημα κατάγειον, ὥτε πνεῦμα λαμβάνειν ὥ- τε φῶς ἰξεῖδεν, ὥτε θύρας ἔχον, ἀλλὰ μεγάλῳ λίθῳ περιηγο- μένῳ κατακλειόμενον, ἐνταῦθα κατέθεντο.

Notat Sopranes advolutum esse lapidem non ad ostium totius sepulchri, sed interioris saltim, re- cto libero ingressu ad vestibulum, quod colli- gunt nonnulli è Marc. XVI. 6. Ad summum mo- menti labrum advolutum traditio apud Nicepho- rum lib. I. cap. 32. docet: ubi etiam modus ob- signationis lapidis explicatur. Repetit eam tra- ditionem Montacutius, & ex eo Walæus, p. 65. b. l.

## 27:62
Verse 62. After the preparation] He understands the first of the seven unleavened days, whose preparation was that day on which the lamb was eaten. For because the day of eating the lamb was most celebrated, therefore the following day not inappropriately received its name from it: as also Exodus 12:14, 15. Otherwise, the ordinary Sabbath was not fittingly noted from the pre-Sabbath.

The chief priests and the Pharisees] The Sanhedrin could not be held on that day: therefore neither elders nor scribes are mentioned here. But by private counsel, certain chief priests and some senators of the Pharisaic faction approached Pilate, as if to deal with a matter pertaining to the highest affairs of the state: nor did they have difficulty in obtaining from him a matter in which he thought nothing was at stake. We see, however, that the Jews believed then, as their most learned men believe now, that foreigners are not bound by the law of the Sabbath rest, since they themselves are the authors for the Romans to do those things which could not be expedited by the Jews without prejudice to the Sabbath religion.

Latin:

Vers. 62. μετὰ τὴν παρασκευὴν] Intelligit primam septem ἀζύμων, cujus παρασκευὴ erat is dies quo agnus edebatur. Quia enim dies edendi agni erat celeberrimus, ideo non male consequens dies, ab eo nomen accepit: ut & Exod. XII. 14. 15. Alioqui sabbatum ordinatium non convenie- bat notari ex prosabbato.

Οἱ ἀρχιερεῖς καὶ οἱ Φαρισαῖοι] Non potuit eo die syne- drium haberi: ideo nec πρεσβυτέρων nec γραμματέων hic fit mentio. Sed privato consilio Sacerdotum principes qui- dam & senatores aliqui Pharisæicæ factionis Pilatum con- venerunt, tanquam acturi de negotio ad summam rempu- blicam pertinente: nec difficulter ab eo impetrarunt rem in qua ille nihil situm existimabat. Videmus autem cre- didisse tunc Iudæos, quod & nunc credunt eorum doctis- simi, otii sabbatici lege alienigenas non teneri, cum ipsi auctores sint Romanis ut ea faciant quæ ab Iudæis salva sabbati religione expediri 'nequibant.

## 27:63
Verse 63. The deceiver] mat'eh. Masters of true and solid piety are accustomed to apply this nickname to men who shun the light. John says that certain Jews said this about Christ: 'He deceives the crowd,' ch. 7:12. Among Luke, the legates of the Sanhedrin accuse Jesus as 'perverting the nation,' ch. 23:2, that is, 'oker Yisrael' (troubler of Israel), as Ahab said about Elijah. For there too the LXX have 'the one who perverts Israel.' Justin, against Trypho, relates that legates were sent by the Palestinian Jews to the synagogues after the death of Jesus, 'proclaiming that a certain godless and lawless heresy has been raised by a certain Jesus, a Galilean deceiver.' Paul, 2 Corinthians 6:8, says that he and the other Apostles were held as 'deceivers'.

The same is called by the Philosophers a 'babbler,' a 'proclaimer of foreign gods,' Acts 17:18. Celsus called Christ and his Apostles by similar terms, as appears from Origen. Ulpian, who wrote several books on the punishments of Christians, when he says, 'if, to use the common word for impostors, he shall have exorcised,' undoubtedly notes the Christians: perhaps also the Jews.

He said while still living] Christ had never said that openly himself. But his mind, badly conscious of itself, interpreted what he had said more obscurely about the sign of Jonah and about the Temple in the direction it feared: unless perhaps Judas also betrayed something from familiar conversation.

After three days] That is, within three days: 'be'od sheloshet yamim' (in three days' time), Genesis 40:13, where the LXX have 'yet three days,' when nevertheless what is said there was fulfilled on the third day itself, as appears in the same place, verse 20. Thus Christ himself in Mark 8:31 says that it behooves him 'after three days to rise.' Thus 'miqets sheva-shanim' (at the end of seven years), Deuteronomy 15:1, the LXX translate 'after seven years' (in the way Josephus also speaks, and above 26:61 and Mark 14:58 it is written 'after three days'). To the same Hebrew words where the same matter is treated, Jeremiah 34:14, they are translated into Greek not so much word for word as according to the sense: 'when six years are completed,' as the most learned of the Rabbis, Abraham and Kimchi, also explain. But in Deuteronomy 31:10, retaining the Hebraism, they translated 'after seven years.' Similar is John 20:26, 'after eight days,' where the Syriac, as in this place, rendered that 'meta' word for word as 'katar,' while in Mark it explains it by 'l,' which corresponds to the word 'en'.

Latin:

Vers. 63. ὁ πλάνος] מתעה. Hoc cognomen re- ferre solent veræ ac solidæ pietatis magistri ab hominibus lucifugis. Ita Iudæos quosdam de Christo dixisse ait Iohan- nes: πλανᾷ ἳ ὄχλον c. VII. 12. Apud Lucam legati Synedrii accusant Iesum ut διαστρέφοντα τὸ ἔθνος c. XXIII. 2. id est עכר ישראל ut de Elia dicebat Achab. Nam & ibi LXX. habent ὁ διατρέφων τὸν Ἰσραὴλ. Iustinus adversus Trypho- nem narrat ab Iudæis Palæstinis missos legatos ad Synago- gas post Iesu mortem κηρύσσοντας ὅτι αἵρεσίς τις ἄθεος κὶ ἄ- νομος ἐγήγερται ἀπὸ Ἰησοῦ τινος γαλιλαίου πλάνου Paulus 2. Corinth. VI. 8. ait se aliosque Apostolos habitos ut πλάνους,

Idem à Philosophis vocatur σπερμολόγος, ξένων δαιμονίων καταγγελεὺς. Act. XVII. 18. Similibus vocabulis Christum ejusque Apostolos Celsus vocabat ut ex Origene apparet. Ulpianus, qui de pœnis Christianorum libros aliquot scri- ssit, cum dicit, si, ut vulgari verbo impostorum utar, exorci- zaberit, Christianos haud dubie notat: forte & Judæos.

Ἆπεν ἔτι ζῶν] Nunquam id Christus aperte ipse dixerat. Sed quæ de Jonæ signo & de Templo obscurius dixerat, a- nimus male sibi conscius in eam quam timebat partem in- terpretabatur: nisi forte etiam de familiari sermone Judas aliquid prodidit.

μετὰ τρεῖς ἡμέρας] Id est intra tres dies: בעוד שׁלשׁת ימים Gen. XL. 13. ubi LXX. ἔτι τρεῖς ἡμέρας, cum tamen quod ibi dicitur impletum sit ipso die tertio, ut apparet ibi- dem commate 20. Ita Christus ipse apud Marcum VIII. 31. dicit oportere se μετὰ τρεῖς ἡμέρας ἀναστῆναι. Ita מקץ שׁבע־שׁנים Deut. XV. 1. LXX. vertunt δι ἑπτὰ ἐτῶν (quomodo & Josephus loquitur, & supra XXVI. 61. & Marci XIV. 58. scriptum est διὰ τριῶν ἡμερῶν.) Ad eadem verba Hebræa ubi de eadem res agitur Jeremiæ XXXIV. 14. Græce non tam κατὰ λέξιν quam κατὰ διάνοιαν vertun- tur ὅταν πληρωθῇ ἓξ ἔτη, quomodo & Rabbinorum eruditis- simi exponunt Abraham & Kimchi. At Deut. XXXI. 10. Hebraïsmo retento verterunt μετὰ ἑπτὰ ἔτη. Simile est Joh. XX. 26. μετ' ἡμέρας ὀκτὼ, ubi Syrus ut & hoc loco il- lud μετὰ reddidit verbum verbo כתר cum apud Marcum explicet per ל, quod respondet voci ἐν.

## 27:64
Verse 64. And the last deception will be worse than the first] A proverbial expression as above 12:45, Luke 11:26, 2 Peter 2:20.

Latin:

Vers. 64. καὶ ἔσται ἡ ἐσχάτη πλάνη χείρων τῆς πρώτης] Lo- cutio proverbialis ut supra XII. 45. Luc. XI. 26. 2. Pet. II. 20.

## 27:65
Vers. 65. ἔχετε κωστωδίαν] You have. Thus rightly the Latin and the Syrian, not 'have' (imperative). The sense is entirely: You have a cohort which at this time has been committed to your command to ward off all tumults: use it at your discretion. For although that cohort properly served the Temple, yet that its use was also elsewhere, the very arrest of Christ teaches. They are called 'custodia' here who are 'φύλακες' in Josephus, as appears from the passage cited before. Thus Tibullus, 'Custodia visa est', that is, a guard. And Tertullian, acting on this very history: 'Custodia pavore disjecta'. And thus the Arab rightly understood it here; since otherwise 'custodia' in Latin signifies both the place and him who is guarded. This Greek word made from Latin is found among historians and lexicographers. It is true what a man of rare diligence and learning, Nicolaus Füllerus, recently observed, that when the Syrian here placed קסטורא for 'custodia', he did not intend the word 'custodia', but to express another of more recent Latinity. Namely 'quaestionarii', as in a later age those 'οἱ βασάνων ὑπηρέται' were called: in which sense that word exists both elsewhere and in the Scholiast of Juvenal, Sat. VI, from which it also appears that this interpreter is not as ancient as the Syrians believe: but he did not express the meaning sufficiently. For even those who had been present as the exactors of Christ's punishment were not peculiarly addicted to that ministry: but soldiers chosen for this under the command of a centurion. Theophylact says 'κωστωδία' are sixty soldiers, as a 'σπεῖρα' is two hundred. But Pilate is not dealing with these, who had already reported that that duty was completed: but with those who had been assigned to the Jewish leaders at that time against all 'νεωτερίζοντας'.

ὡς οἴδατε] As you know, you will judge how it ought to be done according to your diligence.

Latin:

Vers. 65. ἔχετε κωστωδίαν] Habetis. Ita recte Latinus & Syrus, non habete. Sensus omnino est: Habetis cohor- tem quæ hoc tempore ad omnes tumultus arcendos vestro imperio commissa est: ea utimini pro arbitrio. Nam quamquam proprie ea cohors Templo serviebat; tamen et- iam alibi ejus usum fuisse, docet ipsa prehensio Christi. Custodia vocantur hic qui Josepho φύλακες, ut ex loco an- te citato apparet. Ita Tibullus, Custodia vista est, id est, custos. Et Tertullianus de hac ipsa historia agens: Cu- stodia pavore disjecta. Atque ita recte hic accepit Arabs; cum alioqui custodia Latine & locum & eum qui custodi- tur significet. Vox hæc Græca facta ex Latina apud Histo- ricos & Lexicographos invenitur. Verum est quod vir ra- ræ diligentiæ & doctrinæ Nicolaus Füllerus nuper observa- vit cum Syrus hic pro custodia posuit קסטורא non vo- luisse eum vocem custodiæ, sed alteram recentioris Lati- nitatis exprimere. Quæstionarii scilicet, quomodo po- steriori ævo vocati sunt οἱ βασάνων ὑπηρέται: quo sensu ea vox tum alibi exstat, tum apud Juvenalis Scholiasten Sat. VI. unde etiam apparet non tam antiquum esse hunc in- terpretem quam Syri credunt: sed sententiam non satis ex- pressit. Nam & qui Christi supplicii exactores adfuerant, non erant peculiariter ei ministerio addicti: sed delecti ad hoc milites sub centurionis imperio. Theophylacto κωστωδία ἑξήκοντα εἰσι στρατιωτῶν, ut σπεῖρα διακοσίων. At vero de his non agit Pilatus qui jam expletum id officium renunciaverant: sed de illis qui Judæorum primoribus eo tempore attributi erant adversus omnes νεωτερίζοντας.

ὡς οἴδατε] Ut fieri oporteat pro solertia vestra judicabi- tis.

## 27:66
Vers. 66. σφραγίσαντες τὸν λίθον] Thus in the history of Daniel, ch. VI. 17, 'and they brought one stone, and placed it upon the mouth of the pit, and the king sealed it with his ring.' Josephus in the same history says that they 'sealed the stone lying upon the treasury instead of a door.' I am led by this passage of Daniel to believe that this stone was also sealed with Pilate's ring, God so acting that the things done before might shadow forth the things of Christ on every side. Just as it was established by the public faith of a seal that Daniel was delivered from danger by no human aid, so it was established by a similar faith that Christ's body was delivered from the sepulchre by no human hand. Add Rev. XX. 3.

μετὰ τῆς κωστωδίας] It is to be construed with the verb 'ἠσφαλίσαντο' in the sense which Tertullian expresses: 'They surrounded the sepulchre, where he was buried, with a great military force of guards.' Wherefore that 'σφραγίσαντες τὸν λίθον' is to be taken by way of 'παρεμβολῆς' or 'μεταξυλογίας'.

CHAPTER

Latin:

Vers. 66. σφραγίσαντες τὸν λίθον] Ita in Danielis histo- ria cap. VI. 17. καὶ ἤνεγκαν λίθον ἕνα, καὶ ἐπέθηκαν ἐπὶ τὸ στόμα τοῦ λακκῦ καὶ ἐσφραγίσατο ὁ βασιλεὺς ἐν τῷ δακτυλίῳ ἀυ- τοῦ. Josephus in eadem historia ait illos σφραγίση τὸν ἐπὶ τῷ ταμίῳ κείμενον ἀντὶ θύρας λίθον. Hoc autem Danielis loco adducor ut credam Pilati annulo & hunc lapidem si- gnatum, hoc Deo agente ut res anteactæ res Christi undi- que adumbrarent. Quemadmodum publica sigilli fide constitit Danielem nulla ope humana periculo exemtum, ita simili fide constitit Christi corpus nulla humana manu exemtum sepulchro. Adde Apoc. XX. 3.

μετὰ τῆς κωστωδίας] Construendum est cum verbo ἠσφα- λίσαντο eo sensu quem Tertullianus exprimit: Sepulchro con- ditum magna militari manu custodiædiligentia circumsede- runt. Quare istud σφραγίσαντες τὸν λίθον accipiendum est per modum παρεμβολῆς sive μεταξυλογίας.

CAPUT

## 28:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXVIII.

ARGUMENT AND DIVISION.

Mary Magdalene runs out with the other Mary to the sepulcher; an earthquake having occurred, an Angel descending from heaven rolls away the stone from the sepulcher, by which the guards were almost dead with terror. The Angel announces to the women the resurrection of Jesus, and commands it to be announced to the disciples, for which purpose they hasten to the disciples; but on the way Jesus meets them, and they touch his feet, and are sent to the disciples so that they may go into Galilee to see Jesus there. But as the guards report the event, the Elders, having taken counsel, bribe them to disseminate a lie about the body of Jesus being taken away: the Apostles indeed betake themselves into Galilee to a certain mountain: appearing to them, he testifies concerning all power in heaven and on earth given to him, and sends them to teach all nations, and to baptize in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, promising his perpetual presence until the consummation of the age.

There are three parts: I. The apparition made to the women having set out to the sepulcher, both of the Angel and of Jesus himself, to verse 10. II. The lie about the body of Jesus being taken away, disseminated by the Elders through the soldiers, to verse 15. III. The apparition of Jesus made to the Apostles with his sending them to teach and baptize all nations, to verse 20.

PART I.

The excursion of the women to the sepulcher, and the apparition made to them.

Verse 1. ὀψὲ δὲ σαββάτων] Since Mark so follows the footsteps of Matthew, that he often performs the role of interpreter for him, I do not doubt that the sense in these words is the same as it is in those words of Mark, διαγενομένου σαββάτου. Nor does it move me that in Mark it is ἠγόρασαν ἀρώματα, whence some have thought that this deals with an event immediately after the setting of the Sabbath sun. For since it is most clearly evident in Luke that the spices were prepared by these women not on the Sabbath, but on the day τῆς παρασκευῆς, that ἠγόρασαν in Mark must be interpreted as, they had bought spices. For when the women had gone out, it mattered much to say: that they had spices with them, because that indicates the cause of the going out: but when they had bought those spices, it mattered nothing to be known: wherefore that is expressed indefinitely. Thus Matt. XIV. 13. ἐδησεν αὐτὸν signifies not he binds, but he had bound. Add what is above in ch. XXVII. 2. Therefore no peculiar journey to the sepulcher is to be sought in Mark. But that in Matthew in this place it deals with some evening journey, during which nothing worthy of report happened, and that the morning one, to which all the following things pertain, is passed over in silence, has no probability. It could be said that ὀψίαν is sometimes called night by the Hellenists, as by the Hebrews ערב, which we noted above: and so that ὀψὲ here is at night, in which way the Syrian and Arab seem to have understood this passage: and some of the Greeks; to which also that can be adapted which the Hebrews call the whole night which is after the Sabbath מוצי שבת, the exit of the Sabbath: but two things stand in the way: first, that ὀψὲ with the genitive case is a purely Greek construction: then that as שבתות is to the Hebrews, so σάββατα is generally said by the Hellenists in the plural number, not the days themselves given to rest, but the whole week of days from the beginning of one Sabbath to the beginning of another: of which days the first is for that reason called μία σαββάτων (from a Hebraism which the LXX Interpreters also follow) both here and in Mark, John, Luke in the Gospel and in the Acts, and in Paul. But especially it could seem strange in this place that the same name-σαββάτων is used with only four little words interposed without any cause for a different meaning. Wherefore there is no simpler interpretation than that ὀψὲ σαββάτων here is, the week of days being finished. For ὀψὲ with the genitive case for the Greeks not only signifies that which happens late, (which, proved by many testimonies, does not properly pertain here) but whatever is later in the order of time. Philostratus concerning the Pythian games: τὴν Πυθῶ τοῖς εἰς αὐτὴν ἤκοιτας ἀὐλῷ τε πα- ραπέμπειν καὶ ᾠδαῖς καὶ ψάλσει, κωμῳδίας τε καὶ τραγῳδίας ἀξιοῦν· εἶτα τὴν ἀγωνίαν παρέχειν τὴν γυμνὴν ὀψὲ τούτων, that is, these all being performed. And elsewhere ὀψὲ τῶν τρωϊκῶν after the Trojan affairs. ὀψὲ τῶν βασιλείων χρόνων. Similarly Plutarch in the life of Numa.

τῇ ἐπιφωσκούσῃ εἰς μίαν σαββάτων] After an indication of a more broadly extending time, another more precise notation was required. Nor is there any doubt that in the designation of this time it was very fitting for the writers of these books. For what is it that ought to have been inquired into with greater diligence by them, or more faithfully handed down, than the certain time of that event in which the hinge of our faith turns? Wherefore both here and in many other places, if anything is obscure or contradictory, it proceeds not from the fault of the writers, but of the readers. Ἐπιφώσκειν or ἐπιφαίνειν (for these are of the same meaning) is said of any light, when it first begins to show itself: whether it be of the Sun, or of the stars. μήτε ἡλίου, μήτε ἄστρων ἐπιφαινόντων, says Luke in Acts XXVII. 20. In the same Luke in the Evangelical history ch. XXIII. 54. σάββατον ἐπέφωσκε is said by reason of either the Moon or the Stars. But it is said most properly of the light of the Sun, in the way it was said by Polybius τῆς ἡμέρας ἐπιφαινούσης, as is shown by him to whom not only Polybius but as much as there is of literature owes very much. Hence that translation in the song of Zacharias, Luke I. 78, 79, ἐπεσκέψατο ἡμᾶς ἀνατολὴ ἐξ ὕψους, ἐπιφᾶναι τοῖς ἐν σκότῃ. Thus also from Ignatius ἐπιφωσκούσης κυριακῆς, and from Epiphanius ἐπιφωσκούσῃ τῇ τετράδι, the same most learned man noted. But also in Herodotus it is said ἡμέρᾳ διαφωσκούσῃ. Nor is it to be taken otherwise here, τῇ ἐπιφωσκούσῃ. For ἡμέρᾳ is missing, as when the Greeks say, τῆς ἐπιούσης: our writer here above τὴν ἄυριον ch. VI. 34, as also Luke Acts IV. 3, 5, and James IV. 14. John indeed ch. I. 35, and ch. XII. 12. Luke Acts XX. 7, τῇ ἐπαύριον. But the Hebraism is to be noted in that which is said εἰς μίαν σαββάτων. For the sense is, when that day was dawning which was to be the first of the week. The dawn is therefore designated here: as also in Luke 24:22, γενόμεναι ὄρθριαι ἐπὶ τὸ μνημεῖον. John describes the first part of the dawn, saying: πρωῒ σκοτίας ἔτι ὔσης, chapter 20:1, when some of the night still remained, just as Mark also uses πρωῒ, adding ἐννυχον λίαν, chapter 1:35, and Luke for the same thing here says ὄρθρου βαθέος: the very end, which is early morning to the Latins, Mark notes here when he says λίαν πρωῒ, ἀνατείλαντος, or as other copies have it, ἀνατέλλοντος, or which comes to the same thing, ἔτι ἀνατείλαντος τοῦ ἡλίου. I do not see what such great difficulty there is in these narratives. Naturally, the women had risen at the first dawn: while one waited for another, while they prepared the spices, while they proceeded through the city and outside the city to the tomb, enough time easily passed so that when they arrived at the tomb, some of the sun was already appearing. However, individual circumstances have their own weight. The fact that the women rise at the first dawn shows that they feared that, with the Sabbath now passed, the body might be transferred elsewhere, as if it had been deposited there only for a time because of the impending Sabbath. That it had already dawned somewhat when they arrived at the tomb serves to ensure that what the women reported is established by the certain testimony of their eyes. On the same day of the seven that creation was begun, the same also for the new creation. There is μία in the Greek of Genesis 1:5, here is μία.

Μαρία Μαγδαληνὴ] Whom John names as the leader of the group: and I believe the expenses were mainly borne by her. She certainly seems to have been more noble than the others, because her name is usually placed before the others, above in chapter 27:56 and 61, in this place, and in Mark 15:40, chapter 16:1, Luke 8:2-3, chapter 24:10.

καὶ ἡ ἄλλη Μαρία] The daughter of Cleopas, the mother of Joses and James, as we said above. Matthew omits Salome, whom Mark names, and Joanna, namely the wife of Chuza who was Herod's steward, mentioned by Luke. There were therefore four named women, besides the ἀνωνύμους whom Luke indicates.

Θεωρῆσαι τὸν τάφον] ἵνα ἀλείψωσιν, Mark adds, which Luke also indicates not obscurely. They came, therefore, to see whether the tomb was accessible for the anointing. This is the ἐνταφιασμὸς of which we spoke above. That was accustomed to be done before bodies were committed to the tomb: but the haste of the burial had forestalled the duty.

Grotius explains the phrase of the Evangelist, which has caused difficulty for interpreters, in this way: ὀψὲ σαββάτων, that is, the week of days having been completed; so that ὀψὲ is not the same as 'late,' but denotes whatever is later in the order of time. τῇ ἐπιφωσκούσῃ, however, is spoken in the Hellenistic manner, since ἡμέρᾳ is missing, just as when the Greeks say τῆς ἐπιούσης, Matthew says τὴν αὔριον VI. 34, and Luke Acts XX. 7, τῇ ἐπαύριον, just as Ignatius has ἐπιφωσκούσης κυριακῆς, and Herodotus ἡμέρᾳ διαφωσκούσῃ, and Polybius τὴν ἡμέραν ἐπιφαινούσης. The sense, therefore, according to Grotius, is: The week of days having been completed, when that day was dawning which was to be the first of the week. For he notes a Hebraism in the fact that it is said εἰς μίαν σαββάτων: and therefore he reconciles the Evangelists in this way: that here the dawn is designated, as also in Luke ch. XXIV. 12. ὀψόμεναι ὄρθρου ἐπὶ τὸ μνημεῖον: and John describes the first part of the dawn as πρωῒ σκοτίας ἔτι οὔσης XX. 1, when some of the night still remained, and Luke for the same thing here says ὄρθρου βαθέος: Mark, however, notes the end of the dawn here, 'very early' being said first by the Latins, when he says, λίαν πρωῒ ἀνατείλαντος, or as other copies have it, ἀνατέλλοντος, or what amounts to the same thing, ἔτι ἀνατείλοντος τοῦ ἡλίου. With these things thus explained, Grotius adds: I do not see what difficulty there is in these narratives. Naturally, the women had risen at the first dawn: while some wait for others, while they prepare spices, while they proceed through the city and outside the city to the sepulcher, so much time easily passed that when they arrived at the sepulcher, some sun was already appearing, etc.

Regarding the first expression ὀψὲ δὲ σαββάτων, we easily agree, if that meaning of the word ὀψὲ is proven: because it is known that the days of the whole week are called Sabbaths by the Hebrews: and thus also Euthymius and some others have interpreted it, ὀψὲ σαββάτων, the week having ended. What Grotius has therefore handed down here does not do poorly in illustrating the expression of Matthew.

Nor does the more specific determination of time have any difficulty, when the day was dawning which was to be the first of the week, when compared with the other Evangelists. Mark has λίαν πρωῒ τῆς μιᾶς σαββάτων, 'very early' (which for Luke is ὄρθρου βαθέως, 'in the deep dawn,' as Erasmus renders it, 'very early,' as the Vulgate explained it; for John, πρωῒ σκοτίας ἔτι οὔσης, 'early when it was still dark') and Mark adds ἀνατείλοντος τοῦ ἡλίου: which word is of indefinite time, so that there is no need to interpret it as 'the sun having already risen,' but it can be understood as 'the sun about to rise': Gregory of Nyssa, in his sermon on the resurrection, is a witness that the more accurate copies have the word ἔτι added, which is also read in the Royal edition, so that it is noted that the sun had not yet fully risen, but was still in its rising.

Thus, therefore, the Grotian explanation is altogether more convenient (to which Vossius also added his support, explaining it as 'after the Sabbath or the week having already been completed, when the light of the first day of the Sabbaths first showed itself') than if it were said with others that there was a double excursion of Mary Magdalene and the other Mary to the sepulcher of Christ, designated here: so that they went to the sepulcher first in the evening after the Sabbath was completed, before night, because Matthew says ὀψὲ σαββάτων that they came: and that only to see the sepulcher, then went there again in the morning time, λίαν πρωῒ, and indeed, to anoint Christ: or, as is maintained with Ludovicus de Dieu, that they went out of the gates in the evening, stayed outside the gates the whole night, so that they might hasten to the sepulcher at the crack of dawn before the city gates were opened and they could be seen by anyone. We think, therefore, says Dievius, that the women, on the very evening of the Sabbath, when according to the custom of the Jews the first day of the week began, prepared themselves for the journey toward the sepulcher, bought spices on that journey, went out of the city, stayed the whole night in the suburb, from there Mary ran out while it was still dark, John XX. 1, and then the rest came to the sepulcher at the deep dawn, Luke XXIV. 1. Drusius brings forward another explanation: but that has already been refuted by Dievius. For there is no need to posit a double excursion, nor is it certain that the women went to the sepulcher for the sake of seeing it alone, but to see and anoint Jesus, which two things Mark joins: nor can they be separated, which Matthew adds in v. 2, about the earthquake and the angel who rolled away the stone: because they are connected by the particle καὶ ἰδὲ. And the women had already looked at the sepulcher before, when Christ was being buried, Mark XV. 42, and therefore they had no need of a special excursion for the sake of seeing the sepulcher, whence Grotius rightly says no special journey to the sepulcher is to be sought in Mark. But that in this place in Matthew there is talk of some evening journey, during which nothing worthy of report happened, and that the morning one, to which all the following things refer, is passed over in silence, has no probability. But the interpretation of Dievius has no place for this reason, because he joins ὀψὲ σαββάτων with τῇ ἐπιφωσκούσῃ (ἡμέρᾳ) and says that both Marys came then to see the sepulcher, but not that they prepared themselves then for the journey, did not buy spices on that journey (which also does not fit the history), did not go out of the city, and did not stay in the suburb.

In this, however, we cannot agree with Grotius. That he wishes the same thing to be indicated in the words of Mark, διαγενομένου σαββάτου, as in Matthew, when he says ὀψὲ δὲ σαββάτων: because Mark is dealing with the time of the buying of the spices; Matthew, however, with the time of the excursion to the sepulcher. Add that he openly distinguishes between the time of the buying and that excursion: for he says the buying was done διαγενομένου τοῦ Σαββάτου, when the Sabbath had passed: but the excursion λίαν πρωῒ, at the very dawn of the first day of the Sabbaths.

Grotius indeed objects that in Luke it is most clearly evident that the spices were procured by these women not on the Sabbath, but on the day τῆς παρασκευῆς, and therefore that that ἠγόρασαν in Mark must be interpreted as, they had the spices bought; but that what Grotius wants is most clearly evident in Luke, B. Bugenhagius certainly did not see: who says, Luke asserts indeterminately and without a notation of a certain time that the women, having returned from the sepulchre on the day of preparation, prepared spices and ointments: but lest it be thought that they prepared them that very evening, he explains himself, that they rested on the Sabbath according to the law, Luke 23:56. Which opinion, according to B. Gerhard, is confirmed by the short interval of time between the burial of Christ and the setting of the sun, with which, as Luke speaks, the Sabbath was dawning or beginning: since scarcely three hours had intervened: nor is it likely, in his judgment (although he does not here agree with Bugenhagius), that the women, stunned by the grief conceived from the death of Christ, would have immediately thought about anointing the body of Christ, especially because they had seen this duty performed for Christ by Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus. Nor indeed can it be proven that ἠγόρασαν is the same as they HAD bought spices, or were carrying them: as others explain: since that word imports the buying, not indeed the possession or the carrying; and the women are said to have carried the spices ὄρθρου βαθέος, Luke 24:1, which to Mark is λίαν πρωὶ, and is distinguished from the prior note of the past Sabbath time. It is necessary, therefore, that some interval be left, in which after the Sabbath had passed they bought and prepared the spices, which at the break of day of the first day of the Sabbath they took with them, running to the sepulcher of the Lord. Vossius, book II of the Harmony of the Gospels concerning the Passion of Christ, chapter XIV, judges that on the preparation day according to Luke, the women prepared spices, because there were several women, and the spices were bought by several, as if Mary Magdalene bought them immediately after the death of Christ before the setting of the sun, after which the Passover began: but Joanna, the wife of Chuza, did this after the Passover was finished, or in the evening which followed the Sabbath.

Latin:

CAPUT XXVIII.

ARGUMENTUM ET PAR- TITIO.

Excurrit Maria Magdalena cum altera Ma- ria ad sepulcrum, terra motu facto Ange- lus de cœlo descendens devolvit lapidem à sepulcro, unde custodes prae terrore prope- modum exanimati sunt. Annunciat An- gelus mulieribus resurrectionem Iesu, eam- que annunciari discipulis jubet, quo fine illæ ad discipulos properant, in via autem occurrit illis Iesus, tanguntque ejus pedes, & mittuntur ad discipulos ut illi in Gali- læam eant illic Iesum visuri. Custodibus vero rem gestam narrantibus Seniores consilio inito eosdem corrumpunt, ut men- dacium de ablato corpore Iesus dissemi- nent: Apostoli vero in Galilæam se confe- runt in montem quemdam: qui ipsis appa- rens de omni potestate in cœlo & in terra sibi data testatus emittit eos ad docendum omnes populos, & baptizandum in nomi- ne Patris & Filii & Spiritus Sancti pro- missa perpetua præsentia usque ad consum- mationem seculi.

Partes tres sunt: I. Mulieribus ad sepulcrum profectis facta apparitio cum Angeli tum ipsius Jesu, ad vers. 10. II. Mendacium de ablato corpore Je- su à Senioribus per milites disseminatum, ad vers. 15. III. Apparitio Jesu Apostolis facta cum emis- sione eorum ad docendum & baptizandum omnes po- pulos, ad vers. 20.

PARS I.

Mulierum excursus ad sepulcrum, & appa- ritio iisdem facta.

Vers. 1. ὀψὲ δὲ σαββάτων] Cum Marcus ita Matthæi le- gat vestigia, ut sæpe ei præstet interpretis vicem, sensum in his vocibus eundem esse non dubito qui est in illis Marci verbis διαγενομένου σαββάτυ. Neque me dimovet quod a- pud Marcum est ἠγόρασαν ἀρώματα, unde nonnulli puta- runt hic agi de re gesta statim post occasum Solis Sabbati. Nam cum apud Lucam apertissime liqueat, aromata ab his mulieribus non sabbato, sed die τῆς παρασκευῆς comparata, ἠγόρασαν illud apud Marcum interpretandum est, habebant emta aromata. Nam quando exiissent mulieres dici mul- tum attinebat: habuisse eas secum aromata itidem, quia id causam exitionis indicat: quando autem ea aromata comparassent, nihil referebat sciri: quare id ἀορίστως ex- pressum est. Sic Matt. XIV. 13. ἐδησεν αὐτὸν significat non vin- xit, sed vinxerat. Adde quæ supra c. XXVII. 2. Nulla igitur pe- culiaris itio ad sepulchrum apud Marcum quærenda est. A- pud Matthæum vero hoc loco agi de aliqua itione vesperti- na, qua nihil relatu dignum acciderit, matutinam ad quam sequentia omnia pertinent, silentio omitti, nihil habet pro- babilitatis. Poterat dici ὀψίαν Hellenistis dici interdum no- ctem, ut Hebræis ערב quod supra annotavimus: atq; ita ὀψὲ hic esse noctu, quomodo cepisse hunc locum videntur Sy- rus & Arabs: & Græcorum nonnulli; quo & illud aptari po- test quod totam noctem quæ est post Sabbatum Hebræi vo- cant מוצי שבת exitus Sabbati: sed duo obstant: primum quod ὀψὲ cum casu secundo plane Græca est constructio: deinde quod ut שבתות Hebræis, ita σάββατα Hellenistis multitudinis numero plerumque dicuntur non ipsi dies otio dati, sed tota dierum ἑβδομὰς ab unius Sabbati initio ad initium alterius: quarum dierum prima eam ob rem vo- catur μία σαββάτων (ex Hebraismo quem & LXX. Interpre- tes sequuntur) tum hic tum apud Marcum, Johannem, Lucam in Evangelio & in Actibus, & apud Paulum. Imprimis autem novum videri poterat hoc loco, quatuor duntaxat voculis interpositis idem nomen-σαββάτων fine ulla causa significatu diverso usurpari. Quare nulla est simplicior interpretatio, quam óψὲ σαββάτων hic esse, exa- cta dierum hebdomade. Nam óψὲ cum casu secundo Græcis non modo significat id quod sero fit, (quod mul- tis testimoniis probatum huc proprie non pertinet) sed quicquid temporis ordine est posterius. Philostratus de Pythiis ludis: τὴν Πυθῶ τοῖς εἰς αὐτὴν ἤκοιτας ἀὐλῷ τε πα- ραπέμπειν καὶ ᾠδαῖς καὶ ψάλσει, κωμῳδίας τε καὶ τραγῳδίας ἀξιοῦν· εἶτα τὴν ἀγωνίαν παρέχειν τὴν γυμνὴν ὀψὲ τούτων, id est, his omnibus peractis. Et alibi ὀψὲ τῶν τρωϊκῶν post res Tro- janas. ὀψὲ τῶν βασιλείων χρόνων. Similiter Plutarchus vi- ta Numæ.

τῇ ἐπιφωσκούσῃ εἰς μίαν σαββάτων] Post temporis latius patentis indicium altera pressior notatio requirebatur. Neque dubium est quin in hujus temporis designatione optime conveniebat horum librorum Scriptoribus. Nam quid est quod majore diligentia ab illis inquiri debuit, aut fidelius tradi, quam certum tempus ejus rei in qua fidei nostræ cardo vertitur? Quare & hoc & multis aliis in locis, si quid est obscurum aut ἐναντιοφανὲς, id profi- ciscitur non ex scribentium, sed ex legentium vitio. Ἐ- πιφώσκειν aut ἐπιφαίνειν (sunt enim hæc significatus ejus- dem) de quavis luce dicitur, cum primum se ostentare incipit: sive illa Solis sit, sive siderum. μήτε ἡλίου, μήτε ἄστρων ἐπιφαινόντων, inquit Lucas Act. XXVII. 20. Apud eundem Lucam in Evangelica historia cap. XXIII. 54. σάββατον ἐπέφωσκε dicitur aut Lunæ aut Siderum ratione. Maxime autem proprie de Solis luce dicitur, quomodo di- ctum à Polybio τῆς ἡμέρας ἐπιφαινούσης ostendit is cui non Polybias tantum sed & quantum est literarum plurimum debet. Hinc illa translatio in carmine Zachar. Luc. I. 78. 79. ἐπεσκέψατο ἡμᾶς ἀνατολὴ ἐξ ὕψους, ἐπιφᾶναι τοῖς ἐν σκότῃ. Sic & ex Ignatio ἐπιφωσκούσης κυριακῆς, & ex Epiphanio ἐπιφωσκούσῃ τῇ τετράδι idem vir doctissimus annotavit. Sed & Herodoto dictum ἡμέρᾳ διαφωσκούσῃ. Neque aliter hic sumendum, τῇ ἐπιφωσκούσῃ. Deest enim ἡμέρᾳ, ut cum Græci dicunt, τῆς ἐπιούσης: noster hic Scriptor supra τὴν ἄυριον cap. VI. 34. ut & Luc. Actor. IV. 3. 5. & Jac. IV. 14. Johannes vero cap. I. 35. & cap. XII. 12. Lucas Actor. XX. 7. τῇ ἐπαύριον. Est autem notandus Hebraismus in eo quod dicitur εἰς μίαν σαββάτων. Sensus enim est, cum ea dies illucesceret quæ erat futura prima hebdomadis. Designatur igitur hic diluculum: ut & apud Lucam XXIV. 22. γενόμεναι ὄρθριαι ἐπὶ τὸ μνημεῖον. Di- luculi primam partem Johannes describit, dicens: πρωῒ σκοτίας ἔτι ὔσης cap. XX. 1. cum adhuc noctis aliquid resta- ret, quomodo πρωῒ etiam Marcus usurpat, addens ἐννυ- χον λίαν cap. I. 35. & Lucas pro eodem hic dicit ὄρθρου βαθέος: finem ipsum, quod est mane primum Latinis, notat hic Marcus cum dicit λίαν πρωῒ, ἀνατείλαντος, aut ut alia exemplaria habent ἀνατέλλοντος, vel quod eodem recidit ἔτι ἀνατείλαντος τοῦ ἡλίου. Ego quid in his narra- tionibus tantum sit difficultatis non video. Nimirum primo diluculo surrexerant mulieres: dum alia aliam op- periuntur, dum parant aromata, dum progrediuntur per urbem & extra urbem ad sepulchrum, facile tantum temporis transiit, ut cum ad sepulchrum ventum esset a- liquid jam Solis appareret. Habent autem singulæ cir- cumstantiæ suum pondus. Quod primo diluculo surgunt mulieres ostendit metuisse eas ne sabbato jam transacto corpus alio transferretur, quasi illic duntaxat depositum pro tempore propter imminens sabbatum. Quod jam illuxerat nonnihil cum ad sepulchrum ventum est, eo facit ut certa oculorum fide comperta constet quæ mu- lieres renuntiarunt. Qua die de septem creatio inchoata est, eadem & nova creatio. Ibi μία in Græco Gen. I. 5. hic μία.
