Μαρία Μαγδαληνὴ] Quam ut ducem agminis Johannes nominat: & credo ab ea factos præcipue sumtus. Sa- ne cæteris nobilior fuisse videtur, quia nomen ejus aliis præponi solet supra cap. XXVII. 56. & 61. hoc loco & apud Marcum XV. 40. cap. XVI. 1. Luc. VIII. 2. 3. cap. XXIV. 10.

καὶ ἡ ἄλλη Μαρία] Cleopæ filia mater Jose & Jacobi, ut supra diximus. Omittit Matthæus Salomen quam Mar- cus nominat, & Johannam, uxorem scilicet Chuzzæ qui Herodis erat procurator, Lucæ memoratam. Fuerunt ergo mulieres quatuor nominatæ: præter ἀνωνύμους quas Lucas indicat.

Θεωρῆσαι τὸν τάφον] ἵνα ἀλείψωσιν addit Marcus, quod & Lucas non obscure indicat. Venerunt igitur, ut vide- rent an sepulchrum ad unctionem pateret. Hic est ἐντα- φιασμὸς de quo diximus supra. Solebat id fieri antequam corpora sepulchro mandarentur: sed sepeliendi festinatio d officium anteverterat.

Phrasin Evangelistæ, quæ difficultatem pepe- rit Interpretibus, ita explicat Grotius: ὀψὲ σαβ- βάτων, id est, exacta dierum hebdomade; ut ὀψὲ non sit idem, quod sero, sed notet, quicquid temporis ordine est posterius. τῇ ἐπιφωσκούσῃ vero sit ἐλ- ληνιστικῶς dictum, quum desit ἡμέρᾳ, ut cum Græci dicunt τῆς ἐπιούσης, Matthæus τὴν αὔριον VI. 34. & Lucas Act. XX. 7. τῇ ἐπαύριον, quemadmodum Ignatius habet ἐπιφωσκούσης κυριακῆς, & Herodo- tus ἡμέρᾳ διαφωσκούσῃ, ac Polybius τὴν ἡμέραν ἐ- πιφαινούσης. Sensus ergo est secundum Grotium: Exacta dierum hebdomade, cum illucesceret ea dies, quæ erat futura prima hebdomadis. Notat enim Ebrai- smum in eo quod dicitur εἰς μίαν σαββάτων: id- eoque ita conciliat Evangelistas: ut hic designetur diluculum, ut & apud Lucam cap. XXIV. 12. ὀψό- μεναι ὄρθρου ἐπὶ τὸ μνημεῖον: primamque diluculi partem describat Johannes πρωῒ σκοτίας ἔτι οὔσης XX. 1. cum adhuc noctis aliquid restaret, & Lucas pro eodem hic dicat ὄρθρου βαθέος: Marcus au- tem finem diluculi hic notet, mane primum Lati- nis dictum, cum ait, λίαν πρωῒ ἀνατείλαντος, aut ut alia exemplaria habent, ἀνατέλλοντος, vel quod eodem recidit ἔτι ἀνατείλοντος τοῦ ἡλίου. His ita explicatis addit Grotius: Ego quid in his narratio- nibus tantum sit difficultatis non video. Nimirum primo diluculo surrexerant mulieres: dum aliæ a- liam opperiuntur, dum parant aromata, dum pro- grediuntur per urbem & extra urbem ad sepul- chrum, facile tantum temporis transiit, ut cum ad sepulchrum ventum esset aliquid jam solis appa- ret, &c.

De prima loquutione ὀψὲ δὲ σαββάτων facile annuimus, si ea vocis ὀψὲ significatio probetur: quia notum est Ebrais dies totius septimanæ vocari Sabbata: atque ita etiam Euthymius, & alii nonnulli interpretati sunt, ὀψὲ σαββάτων finita septimana. Quæ ergo hic tradidit Grotius, ad illustrandam loquutionem Matthæi non male faciunt.

Neque difficultatem habet specialior determi- natio temporis, cum illucesceret dies, quæ futura deerat prima hebdomadis, collata cum reliquis Evan- gelistis. Marcus habet λίαν πρωῒ τῆς μιᾶς σαβ- βάτων, valde mane (quod Lucæ est ὄρθρου βαθέως profundo diluculo, ut reddit Erasmus, valde dilucu- lo, ut expoluit vulgatus: Johanni πρωῒ σκοτίας ἔτι οὔσης, mane cum adhuc tenebræ essent) additque Marcus ἀνατείλοντος τοῦ ἡλίου: quæ vox indefini- ti temporis est, ut non opus sit interpretari Sole jam orto, sed intelligi possit Sol jamjam oriturus: Gregorius Nyssenus serm. de resurr. testis est ἀκρι- βέστερα exemplaria vocem ἔτι additam habere, quæ etiam in opere Regio legitur, ut notetur, So- lem nondum plene ortum, sed adhuc in ortu fuisse.

Ita ergo commodior omnino est Grotiana ex- plicatio, (cui etiam calculum addidit Vossius, ex- ponens, post Sabbatum sive hebdomade jam exacta, cum primum se ostentaret lux primæ diei Sabbato- rum) quam si cum aliis dicatur geminum fuisse ex- cursum Mariæ Magdalenæ & alterius Mariæ ad Christi sepulchrum, hic designatum: ita ut pri- mum exacto Sabbato sub vesperam ante noctem ad sepulchrum abierint, quia Matthæus dicit ὀψὲ σαββάτων eas venisse: idque tantum ut viderent sepulchrum, deinde matutino tempore iterum eo abiisse, λίαν πρωῒ, & quidem, ut Christum unge- rent: vel cum Ludovico de Dieu statuatur, vespe- ri eas portis exivisse, totam noctem extra portas hæsisse, ut summo mane antequam portæ urbis aperirentur, & ab ullis conspici possent ad sepul- chrum contenderent. Existimamus itaque, in- quit Dievius, fæminas ipsa vespera Sabbati, quum ex more Judæorum primus dies septimanæ initium caperet, accinxisse se ad iter sepulchrum versus, in eo itinere emisse aromata, exiisse urbe, tota nocte hæ- sisse in suburbio, inde excurrisse Mariam σκοτίας ἔ- τι ὔσης Joh. XX. 1. reliquas deinde ad sepulchrum ve- nisse ὄρθρου βαθέως Luc. XXIV. 1. Drusius aliam adfert explicationem: sed ea à Dievio jam profli- gata est. Non enim opus est geminum excursum statuere, neque solius visionis gratia mulieres abiis- se ad sepulchrum, constat, sed ut viderent & unge- rent Jesum, quæ duo conjungit Marcus: nec sepa- rari possunt, quæ Matthæus addit v. 2. de terræ mo- tu, & angelo, qui lapidem devolvit: quia cohæ- rent particula καὶ ἰδὲ. Et sepulchrum antea jam intuitæ erant mulieres, tum sepeliretur Christus Marc. XV. 42. ideoque visendi sepulchri causa non opus habebant peculiari excursu, unde recte Gro- tius nulla peculiaris itio ad sepulchrum apud Mar- cum quærenda est. Apud Matthæum vero hoc loco agi de aliqua itione vespertina, qua nihil re- latu dignum acciderit, matutinam ad quam se- quentia omnia perærent silentio omitti, nihil ha- bet probabilitatis. Dievii vero interpretamentum id- eo locum nullum habet, quia ὀψὲ σαββάτων con- jungit cum τῇ ἐπιφωσκούσῃ (ἡμέρᾳ) & venisse tum dicitur Maria utraque ut viderent sepulchrum, non vero se accinxisse tum ad iter, non emisse in eo i- tinere aromata (quod Historiæ etiam non con- gruit) non exiisse urbe, & in suburbio hæsisse.

In eo tamen Grotio accedere non possumus. Quod in quod in verbis Marci διαγενομένου σαββάτου idem Grotii in- dici vult, quod apud Matthæum, cum ait ὀψὲ δὲ terpretatio- σαββάτων: quia Marcus agit de tempore emtionis ne desidera- tur ? aromatum; Matthæus autem de tempore excursus ad sepulchrum. Adde quod ille aperte distinguit inter tempus emtionis, & excursus istius: nam emtionem factam dicit διαγενομένου τοῦ Σαββά- του cum præteriisset Sabbatum: excursum autem λίαν πρωὶ summo diluculo diei primi Sabbatorum.

Obvertit quidem Grotius, apud Lucam apertis- sime liquere aromata ab his mulieribus non Sabbato, sed die τῆς παρασκευῆς comparata, ideoque illud ἠγόρασαν apud Marcum interpretandum esse, ha- bebant emta aromata; Sed id apertissime apud Lu- cam quod vult Grotius, liquere, B. Bugenhagius certe non vidit: qui, Lucas, inquit, indeterminate ac sine certæ notatione temporis asserit, mulierculas à sepulchro die parasceves reversas aromata & un- guenta parasse: ne vero existimetur, quod ipsa illa vespera ea paratint, ideo seipsum explicat, quod Sabbato quiēverint secundum legem, Lucæ XXIII. 26. Quam sententiam secundum B. Ger- hard. confirmat breve intervallum temporis inter sepulturam Christi & occasum solis, cum quo illuce- scebat, ut Lucas loquitur, sive incipiebat Sabbatum: siquidem vix tres horæ intercesserint: neque veri- simile est, eodem judice (etsi Bugenhagio hic non accedat) mulieres luctu ex morte Christi concepto attonitas statim de ungendo Christi corpore cogitasse, præsertim quia viderant hoc officii à Josepho Arima- thæo, & Nicodemo fuisse Christo exhibitum. Nec vero probari potest ἠγόρασαν esse idem, quod HABEBANT emta aromata, vel portabant ea: quemadmodum alii exponunt: quum em- tionem, non vero possessionem aut portationem id verbi importet; & portasse dicantur aromata mu- lieres ὄρθρου βαθέος, Luc. XXIV. 1. quod Marco est λίαν πρωὶ, & à priori nota temporis præteriti Sabbati distinguitur. Oportet ergo interval- lum aliquod relinqui, quo post Sabbatum præteri- tum emerint, & præpararint aromata, quæ summo diluculo diei primi Sabbati secum sumserint ex- currentes ad sepulcrum Domini. Vossius lib. II. Harmon. Evang. de Pass. Christi cap. XIV. censet, in parasceve juxta Lucam, mulieres parasse aro- mata, quia plures fuerint mulieres, & a pluribus empta aromata, ac si Maria Magdalena emerit mox a morte Christi ante occasum Solis, post quem incipiebat Pascha: Joanna autem Chusae id fecerit exacto Paschate sive vespera, quae excepit Sabbatum.

## 28:2
Verse 2. A great earthquake occurred. This motion was a sign of the vision that was to follow, well known to the Jewish people, Psalm 68:8, 9; 99:1; 114:17. This is shown by what follows, 'for an angel,' etc. Wherefore no other reason is to be sought. I would think, however, that this, as well as the rolling away of the stone, and even the flight of the guards, happened while the women were on their way: and that this was not known from the testimony of the women, but from the report of the other soldiers, who, having received money, did not maintain the silence they had bought: as is wont to happen. The proof is what Mark narrates concerning the women: 'and looking up they see that the stone has been rolled away.' Therefore they saw it rolled away when they least expected it: they did not see it being rolled away. Nor would they have dared to approach if they had seen the monument blocked by a military guard.

That earthquake, although it can be considered a sign of the future vision, yet that reason which the ancients gave should not be rashly denied, namely, that in that earthquake Christ descended into the underworld. Hilary, Canon XXXIII on Matthew; Chrysostom, sermon LXXIV; to whom are added our Blessed Luther and Blessed Gerhard, Harmony of the Resurrection, part 1.

He who descended from heaven. God has angels as ministers of daily providence. He also has them as it were as satraps, whose service He uses for matters of the greatest importance, as we have noted elsewhere. These are specifically said to descend from heaven, that is, as if sent from His side. Therefore, wherever there is mention of a descent from heaven, as in Revelation 10:1, chapter 18, chapter 20:1, you should understand that something great and excellent is being done.

He rolled away the stone from the door. Was it so that he might perform the office of a doorkeeper, not indeed necessarily, but honorably? Certainly, it cannot be denied that some of the ancients thought so, and they twist the words of those who deny it flatly. Others think differently: among whom is that whoever he is, the ancient writer (I am certain that there is not one author of that book, but a collection made from the writings of many of more than one age) in the responses to the Orthodox: 'For the removal of the stone from the tomb did not happen because of the resurrection, but so that the resurrection might be shown to those who see.' I do not see how the former opinion, even if it is not certain, can be refuted. This can be seen as prefigured in Jacob, Genesis 29:9. The words are the same.

This was done not so that the Angel might perform the office of a doorkeeper and open the sepulcher to Christ, which Grotius and Vossius, book III of the Harmony of the Gospels, chapter II, section 5, with most Calvinists maintain, but rather, as the ancient writer in the responses to the orthodox in the works of Justin teaches, so that the empty sepulcher might be shown to those desiring to see it: 'For the removal of the stone from the tomb did not happen because of his resurrection, but so that the resurrection might be shown to those who see.' For the ancients teach with great consensus that Christ rose while the sepulcher was still closed, along with that ancient writer in the cited question 117, Nazianzen in the Drama, Gregory of Nyssa on the resurrection, Ambrose, book X on chapter 24 of Luke, Chrysostom, homily 90 on Matthew and on chapter 20 of John, Jerome to Pammachius and in the Epitaph of Paula, Augustine passim, sermon 138 and 156 and 158 de tempore, etc., and others: and Calvin himself acknowledges this in the Harmony. of the Gospels. That Christ had risen before the sepulcher was opened by the Angel: add also Musculus on chapter 28 of Matthew, Marloratus in this place. Johann Casius, from the fact that Christ rose while the sepulcher was closed, proves the penetration of dimensions: which Goclenius also acknowledges as possible.

And he was sitting upon it. Matthew names one, as does Mark: Luke names two, as does John: For in John the same history is narrated as here, chapter 20:13. For I see nothing why we should think it is another, since so many circumstances agree. To John, Mary Magdalene sees this vision: to others, the same as the rest: for at the beginning John had named Magdalene as the one who remained: to which it is similar that to John two angels are named, to Luke two men, that is, angels in human form, to Matthew one angel, as also to Mark one young man: clearly because that one was both closer and spoke for the two: which the Hebrews note is customary from the passage in Genesis 18:1 and 3. Therefore, that which Luke reports the angels to have said, 'he is not here but has risen,' Matthew and Mark narrate that this was said by the angel. Thus, what is in Matthew 'do not be afraid,' in Mark 'do not be amazed,' in John 'why are you weeping?' John mentions white garments just as the other three do: he mentions the sitting just as Matthew and Mark do. There is absolutely no reason why the different narrations should be believed to be different, except that John narrates his own and Peter's going first, then those things which Magdalene had seen, whereas that there was a different order of time appears both from Luke's history in this place, and most openly from those things which Cleopas says on the journey toward Emmaus, Luke 24:22, 23, 24. But that does not move me, who know that, just like other founders of annals, these of ours do not always bind themselves to such straits that they narrate what happened first also first, since one can find many hystera protera, many prolepses, many returns everywhere. Nor was there a just cause lacking for John why he should invert the natural order here. He knew how weak the testimony of a woman would be among many, because of that weakness of judgment which is commonly attributed to that sex. For Celsus also, eluding that testimony against the Christians, called Magdalene a γυναῖκα πάροιστρον. Wherefore John, about to treat of a matter as most true as it was difficult to believe, placed his own and Peter's testimony before the narrative; Peter's, as one who had already sealed that very thing with his own death: his own, as one who, even when he was writing, was prepared to suffer all things for the truth of that testimony. This foundation being laid, which ought to have carried the greatest weight with fair judges, he then safely adds the testimony of the weaker sex. Nor, however, did he entirely discard the order of time. But when he had begun to speak of the going of Magdalene in chapter XX. 1, he then adds those things which he himself had discovered with Peter, soon returning to Magdalene, he wove together those things which had indeed been done earlier, but had been reported later, accurately and with their circumstances, by Magdalene to the Apostles. Wherefore that Μαρία δὲ εἱστήκει in chapter XX. 11 is to be understood as 'but Mary was standing,' and so on for the rest, with a return made to that which John had interrupted after the first comma. I have thought these things should be said in this place, so that, having proved that there is one and the same history among the four writers, those things which have been brought forth by others may serve for the interpretation of others. Let us see what difficulty remains. John says the Angels were sitting, along with Matthew and Mark; but Luke seems to say they were standing: but he only seems to: for ἐφιστάναι means to come upon: as when Hippocrates says: 'For just as the handmaidens and servants in the houses, making a noise and quarreling, when suddenly the mistress comes upon them, being frightened, they become quiet.' And Herodian: 'sooner than hope, he came upon the Britons.' And that word is used peculiarly by Luke for heavenly visions in his Gospel ch. II. 9, Acts XII. 7, and ch. XXIII. 11. Thus when Demosthenes had said in that which is on the crown, 'from the day that I came upon these things,' Ulpian notes: 'he speaks of the coming upon of some spirit of his own duty.' Concerning the place where the Angels sat, it is likewise doubted. For that the Angel whom Matthew mentions sat outside the cave is gathered from the fact that he is said to have sat upon the stone. But that stone, larger than the mouth of the cave, had undoubtedly been rolled away outward, not inward. But both Mark and John are thought to say the contrary, whence there are those who have said that the Angel sat not upon the stone rolled away from the mouth, but upon another stone which had been placed at the tomb of Christ. But what is it to contradict Matthew, if this is not? For he says most openly, 'he rolled away the stone from the door and sat upon it.' To me the matter seems settled if we interpret the words of Mark conveniently. He says, 'having entered into the monument they saw a young man.' But they had not yet entered into the cave: for afterwards the Angel says to them, 'come, see the place where he was lying.' Mark therefore calls the monument the part of the garden which was separated from the rest of the garden by some fence or enclosure. For the monuments, taken more broadly, had two parts: the courtyard, the open space, and the cave. In the oration of Demosthenes against Macartatus: 'the monument of the Beselidae, a large place enclosed as the ancients were accustomed to do'; and that open space was called a forum by Roman Pontifical law. Strabo, where he describes the monument of Augustus and his relatives: 'and in the middle of the plain is the enclosure of his funeral pyre (that is, the forum) having a circular iron fence placed around it.' Thus also among the Romans the monument was open for some many feet, as the inscriptions teach us. But I think those are entirely mistaken who think this garden served in place of an open space. For because it was a part of the monument, it was exempt from human uses. But that garden was cultivated and had its own gardener, John XX. 14; it was therefore a place outside the enclosure, pure land, such as that which the Romans called the protection of a monument, as in an old inscription: 'To this monument, in the name of protection, yield acres of pure fields' ten. And in Frontinus: For they have also Mausolea (for so it must be read) with the measures of their own gardens lying around them. That parapet which is called מעקה in Hebrew, Deut. XXII. 8, I judge to be rightly called γεῖσον in Greek. For Josephus teaches us sufficiently that not only projections are so called, in whom, in the description of the temple, the fence which kept the people from the priests, being a cubit in height, is called γείσιον. Just as he calls the other fence, by which foreigners were kept away, δρύφακτον λίθινον. The same author elsewhere, likewise describing the Temple, says that what the Greeks call θρίγκον is called γεῖσον in the local tongue, although that word is not Hebrew in origin, but, like many others, was translated from the Greek language into Hebrew. Again, elsewhere he calls it περίβολον, elsewhere ἑρκίον. Pausanias also uses the word θριγχοῦ concerning a monument: ἐνταῦθα ἐσι καὶ ὀφέλτε τάφος. Around it was a coping of stones, and within the enclosure an altar: where περίβολος is the חצר, which the Latins, as we have said, call a breastwork or also a fortification, as may be seen in L. Funeris, Dig. de Religiosis. Homer uses θεμείλια in that verse: Τορνώσαντο δὲ σῆμα θεμείλιά τε προβάλοντο. Such a δρύφακτον, θριγκόν, or γεῖσον—that is, a breastwork—Cyril undoubtedly calls a σκέπην, by which he says the monuments of the Jews were surrounded. But Augustine also, undoubtedly from ancient report, says that the women entered into the space enclosed by a wall. When, therefore, the women had come into this part of the garden within the breastwork, they beheld an Angel sitting upon a stone in that ὑπαίθρῳ, at the right side of the cave, toward which side I believe the head of the dead man to have been placed. For even in a dead body the head is the most important part, as Paulus the jurisconsult replies. Wherefore I think that John’s πρὸς τῇ κεφαλῇ and Mark’s ἐν τοῖς δεξιοῖς are the same thing. Therefore another Angel, passed over by Matthew and Mark, sat at the left side of the cave towards which the feet had been placed. If the description of Beda is true, the right side will have been towards the North, the left towards the South. The mouth of the cave itself will have looked towards the East.

Grotius maintains there is only one ἀγγελοψίαν, which not only Luke, together with Matthew and Mark, but also John in chapter XX. 13 describes, inasmuch as so many circumstances agree. Others elicit from this three or rather four different apparitions: the first, in which the angel was seen by the guards, whose appearance was terrible; the second, when two angels appeared to the women in the first, or rather, as they themselves assign, the second excursion (because they think the first was made solely for the sake of visiting the sepulchre), instituted for the sake of anointing, according to Luke; the third, when two angels were seen with Mary Magdalene, John XX. v. 11; the fourth, when the women returned again to the sepulchre, after they had perceived that Christ had appeared to Mary Magdalene, both for the certainty of the matter and so that they too might be blessed by the grace of the manifestation of Christ (which was their third excursion), in which manner the blessed Gerhard arranged his harmony, as did also the blessed Cluverus. But there is no need for that threefold excursion to the sepulchre, nor for four distinct appearances of angels: nay, according to some, not even for three; because that angel who, by Matthew’s testimony, rolled away the stone and sat upon it, delivered that address to the women which he himself immediately subjoins; provided that it is not implied that another came up, and the historical account is continued concerning the same angel in verse 5, ἀποκριθεὶς δὲ ὁ ἄγγελος εἶπε ταῖς γυναιξὶ, where the article is also not added idly, but points out the same angel whom Matthew had said rolled away the stone: for it would be inappropriate to introduce another here, since the Evangelist has made no mention of a second. Which opinion we have also approved heretofore. But now, upon more accurate consideration of the matter, we judge that the angel who is said to have rolled away the stone was different from both angels seen by the women at the monument, as is evident from our Evangelical Harmony: that the discourse described by Matthew, Mark, and Luke was indeed the same, and is to be harmoniously woven together from that triad of Evangelists; but that the angel who is recounted by Matthew as having rolled away the stone and sat upon it, by whom the guards were terrified, was not seen by the women, nor was he the same one who is said by Matthew to have addressed the women; or at any rate, that he did not deliver the discourse concerning the resurrection of Christ to the women from the stone, which they finally heard in the monument, which they entered after Mary Magdalene had departed. The Greek article in the word ὁ ἄγγελος certainly does not have such force that it demonstrates that same angel of whom mention was made before; since another angel, commemorated by other Evangelists, could have been designated; from whom the History, as is often the case, must be woven together.

That therefore the angel in Matthew, addressing the women, sat upon the stone, while Mark introduces the angel delivering the same address to the women καθήμενον ἐν τοῖς δεξιοῖς after the women had entered εἰς τὸ μνημεῖον, Grotius explains in vain by saying that Mark calls the μνημεῖον not a cave, because they had not yet entered it, but a part of the garden which had been separated from the rest of the garden (which was cultivated by the gardener, John XX. 14) by some fence or breastwork, being ὑπ’ αἴθρον and not a σπήλαιον: that, indeed, will be difficult to prove regarding this tomb (even if such a distinction may have had its place in other cases, which had their own enclosure, περίβολον, or coping, ϑριγκὸν); nor is it sufficient for proving it that Augustine says the women had entered into a space enclosed by a wall. Grotius, however, confidently, according to his custom, says that this arose without doubt from an old tradition, and adds: when the women had therefore come into this part of the garden within the enclosure, they saw an Angel sitting upon a stone in that ὑπαίθρῳ (open-air space), at the right side of the cave, towards which I believe the head of the dead man had been placed. For even in a dead man the head is the most important part, as Paulus the Jurisconsult replies. Wherefore I think that John’s πρὸς τῇ κεφαλῇ (at the head) and Mark’s ἐν τοῖς δεξιοῖς (on the right side) are the same, and thus the other Angel, passed over by Matthew and Mark, sat at the left side of the cave towards which the feet had been placed. But indeed those things are said without a solid foundation: and it will soon be clear that the history of John is different. However, that the women had not yet entered into the σπήλαιον (cave) or sepulcher cannot be gathered beyond doubt from the account of the Evangelists. For as to what Grotius urges later, that the Angel said to them, δεῦτε ἴδετε τὸν τόπον ὅπη ἔκειτο, come, see the place where he was laid, it is not clearly evident that this was done after the women had entered εἰς τὸ μνημεῖον (into the tomb): and Mark expressly says, εἰσελθῦσαι εἰς τὸ μνημεῖον εἶδον νεανίσκον (entering into the tomb they saw a young man). For the Angel, as if present in the cave, says demonstratively, ἴδε ὁ τόπος, ὅπη ἔθηκαν αὐτὸν, Behold the place where they laid him. Wherefore others say that the word εἰσελθῦσαι (entering) in Mark designates only an action begun, when they were beginning, or desiring, to enter the monument. To others it seems that the Angel first sat outside the sepulcher upon a stone, and was thus seen by the guards: afterwards the same one was seen in the sepulcher, and there seen by the women. Thus Victor of Antioch in chapter XVI. of Mark: It could have happened that they saw that very angel whom, according to Matthew, they had seen shining like lightning and gleaming with white clothing like snow, sitting upon the stone, after they had entered into the monument, as a guide of the way going before them, and also placing himself at the right side. It pleases others that the angels were different, one who is reported by Matthew to have sat upon the stone, another who was seen in the monument sitting at the right side, as Mark reports, even if the discourse of both was the same, so that they spoke and testified with one mouth? which I see was the opinion of St. Augustine in book III of the Harmony of the Evangelists, chapter 24. It can be questioned how according to Matthew an angel was sitting upon the stone rolled away from the monument, for Mark says that they, entering the monument, saw a young man sitting on the right, covered in a white robe, and were astonished: unless we understand either that Matthew was silent about that angel whom they saw entering, but Mark was silent about that one whom they saw outside sitting upon the stone, so that they saw two, and heard from the two separately what the angels said about Jesus; first from him whom they saw sitting outside upon the stone: then from him whom they saw entering into the monument, sitting on the right, by whose words they were exhorted to enter, he who sat outside saying, come and see the place where the Lord was laid! to which coming, as it is said, and entering, they saw him, about whom Matthew is silent, but Mark speaks, sitting on the right, from whom they similarly heard such things. Augustine now adds that explanation which was approved by Grotius: But that different meaning of τῶ μνημείω cannot be taught from the Holy Scriptures: and where it concerns the μνημείῳ of Christ, it is always understood as the cave into which his body was brought, or the sepulcher, Matt. XXVII. 60. ch. XXVIII. 8. Mark XV. 26. ch. XVI. 2. 3. 8. Luke XXIII. 55. ch. XXIV. 1. 2. 9. 12. 22. 24. John XIX. 41. 42. ch. XX. 1. 2. 3. 6. 8. 11. It is pleasing, however, to adduce also that declaration of Augustine, which holds thus: Or certainly we ought to accept that entering into the monument means into some enclosure of a wall, by which it is CREDIBLE that the place was then fortified in some space before the rock, by which, having been cut out, the place of burial had been made, so that they saw him in the same space sitting on the right, whom Matthew says was sitting upon the stone, which the earthquake had rolled away from the door of the monument, that is, from the place of the sepulcher, which had been dug out of the rock. Thus Augustine. Moreover, if it be urged that the angels were different, even though the address of both is almost the same, because the former angel invites the women to enter the monument: but the latter, once they have entered, points out with his finger, as it were, the place where he was laid, empty; the answer is at hand: that it is not an invitation to enter the monument, but to see the place of the monument (which they had already entered) which Mark points out δεικτικῶς: so that there is no need therefore to posit different angelic addresses here: because the Harmony holds up perfectly; Come, see the place where he was laid, ἰδὲ Behold, there is that place where they laid him.

Therefore, as far as the narrative of St. Luke pertains, ch. XXIV. 2, he seems to relate not a different history, but one entirely the same as Mark. For that there was a different excursion of the women, one instituted for the sake of anointing, the other for the sake of greater confirmation: and that the former was described by Luke, the outcome of which the women reported to the Apostles before they were ordered to announce the same to them; but the latter happened after the women understood that Christ had manifested himself to Mary Magdalene, is assumed without proof; nor can it be firmly proven from a comparison of the Evangelists. The circumstances are certainly the same in Luke as in Mark, except that Luke mentions two together to the same women, while they found the stone rolled away from the monument, about which they had been anxious on the way, having been seen: The sum of the address also held by those two angels expressed by Luke agrees: who nevertheless added some words of Christ, by which he had predicted these things, recalled to the memory of the women by the angels, so that the angelic address made to them might appear fuller. The form also, that they were seen in the appearance of men, in Mark and Luke, is the same: and therefore we do not deny here that Grotius asserts the same history is described by Luke: which is also the opinion of Dr. John Richardson, Bishop of Ardagh in the province of Armagh, praised by James Ussher, Archbishop of Armagh, in his Annals part II. p. 608, and also of John Gerhard Vossius in his Harmony of the Passion and Resurrection of Christ p. 369.

Three things, however, can be objected to this opinion: (1) that Luke reports that two men in flashing garments were seen by the women, when, having entered the sepulcher, they did not find the body of the Lord, and were mentally distraught περὶ τούτου about this. (2) that those two men are said to have stood beside the women: whereas the angel of Mark sat. (3) that in the history of Mark the women not only saw and heard the angel, but also on the return from the sepulcher Christ met them: which did not happen in the history of Luke, because they reported nothing about the appearance of Christ to the Apostles: from which they conclude that the excursion described by Luke happened earlier, with which the manifestation of Christ was not joined.

But these things cannot move us from that opinion: for as to (1) Luke reports in summary what is read more distinctly in Mark: introducing two angels, seen when the women had entered the sepulcher: and they were mentally distraught, partly because of the angelic sight, partly because of the empty sepulcher, even though the angel confirmed to them through the empty sepulcher the truth of the Lord's resurrection: to which they did not yet have faith, until the very words of Christ, which Luke recorded as a supplement to the history, were recalled to their memory by the angel; for Luke adds: καὶ ἐμνήσθησαν τῶν ῥημάτων αὐτοῦ, and they remembered his words.

As to (2) Grotius rightly observes, and after him Vossius and Walæus, that the words of Luke Δύο ἄνδρες ἐπέστησαν αὐταῖς, which the Vulgate and Erasmus rendered as "two men stood by them," should be explained as "they came upon them." Thus Grotius on these: "But Luke seems to say they stood: but it only seems so, for ἐφιστάναι means to come upon; as when Hippocrates says, 'for just as servants and handmaids in houses making a noise and quarreling, the mistress coming upon them suddenly makes them quiet.' And Herodian: 'sooner than expected he came upon the Britons.' And that word is used by Luke peculiarly concerning heavenly visions in his Gospel II, 9, Acts XII, 7, and XXIII, 11. Thus when Demosthenes in the speech on the crown had said, ἀφ' ἧς ἡμέρας ἐπὶ ταῦτα ἐπέστην ἐγὼ, Ulpian notes, ὥσπέρ τινὸς δαίμονος ἐπιστασίαν λέγει τῆς ἀυτοῦ κηδεμονίας τὴν παρουσίαν."

As to (3) the response: when Luke says that the women, having returned from the tomb, reported ταῦτα πάντα all these things to the eleven and to all the rest, and lists them as being Mary Magdalene, and Joanna, and Mary the mother of James, and the others who were with them, nothing prevents us from saying that they also reported to the Apostles the appearance of Christ which occurred on the return from the tomb, even though all those things seen were to them ὡσεὶ λῆρος: for the reason is added, κὶ ἠπίστουν ἀυταῖς, that they did not believe them. Because they believed nothing of what the women reported, it is no wonder that they also did not believe those things which they reported concerning the appearance of Christ. Indeed, they did not even give credence to Mary Magdalene when she reported the appearance of Christ, Mark XVI. 10, 11.

As for the fact that the disciples who set out for Emmaus present the summary of the report made by the women in Luke XXIV, verse 23, in such a way that they make mention only of the body of Christ not being found and of the angelic testimony, but not of the manifestation of Christ made to them, it cannot be concluded from this that the manifestation of Christ was either not yet made to the women when they brought these things to the Apostles, or that it was not reported to the Apostles. For could the disciples from Emmaus not have omitted this report, for the reason that it seemed too absurd to them, or whatever the cause of that omission may have been for us to leave room for the suspicion of Grotius, at verse 9. “that not even then did Mary Magdalene believe that the Lord had risen, after he had already appeared to her, but still suspected at that time that the body of Christ had been taken from the tomb, as if she had been addicted to the Pythagorean opinion of the Jews, that the soul also has a body which can be seen by the eyes, ὅτι δύναται ὀφθαλμοῖς αἰσθητοῖς φανῆναι ψυχῆς σῶμα ἀυγοειδὲς (which, however, whether it was the opinion of the ancient Hebrews, or whether, like many other things, it came to the later Hebrews from the Chaldeans and Greeks, he doubts) or, which seems more credible to Grotius, Magdalene thought that it was not the Lord, but an angel that had appeared to her, and this all the more, because it was not permitted to touch him, nor did he himself clearly declare that he was Jesus, whence Grotius thinks it happened that this epiphany also is comprehended under the name of the vision of angels in Luke 24:23. Indeed, it is better to confess ignorance as to why the two disciples from Emmaus did not mention the apparition of Christ made to the women, than with Grotius to attribute such monstrous opinions to the women and the disciples, and to pervert the most open texts. For what could be clearer than that Mary recognized Jesus when he had addressed her by her own name, calling him Rabboni (John 20:17), and that Jesus openly manifested himself to her when he said, 'Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father,' and gave her a command: 'Go to my brothers, and tell them: I am ascending to my Father and your Father, and my God and your God.' And how can there be doubt about the recognition of Christ, when the Evangelist adds, 'Mary Magdalene came announcing to the disciples, ὅτι ἑώρακε κύριον, that she had seen the Lord, and that he had said these things to her.' Can these things be understood as a vision of some angel? And how could Magdalene suspect an angel, not the Lord? Could any angel usurp these words: 'I have not yet ascended to my Father'? And 'Go to my brothers, and tell them, I am ascending to my Father,' etc. Who does not see how inept these things are? Then, indeed, is not that apparition also sufficiently manifest, which Matthew records as having been made to the women in chapter 28:9, where he reports not only that Jesus greeted them in the customary manner, but also testifies that he was touched and worshipped by them, and finally that he gave them a command to go to his brothers and announce that which they had seen, and that they themselves were also about to see the Lord in Galilee? These things are clearer than the sun, so that one must marvel that Grotius dared to obscure them with his inventions, or call them into doubt.

Therefore, as regards the apparition made to Mary Magdalene, described by Saint John, there is no doubt that it is different from that which is described by the other Evangelists. Grotius, and Vossius who has almost always followed him closely in these matters, certainly try to pass it off as that very same angelic apparition which is reported by the other Evangelists; but it is too manifest that those histories are different. For they differ (1) in time: the former happened before Peter and the other disciple ran to the tomb: the latter, however, is recorded to have happened after that run of Peter and the other disciple (to whom Magdalene, when she had seen the stone removed from the tomb and suspected that the Lord's body had been taken away, had announced it), John 20:2 ff. (2) In subjects. For those were made to the other women, Magdalene having departed: this one to Magdalene alone, John 20:11, 12. (3) In place. There the angels appeared in the tomb indeed, but sitting at the right: Here two angels were seen sitting in the tomb, where they had placed Jesus, one at the right, the other at the left. (4) In address. There all the women are addressed by the angelic speech, 'Do not be afraid.' Here, however, the angels address Mary alone thus: 'Woman, why are you weeping?' (5) In response: which was returned by no one from the women: here, however, the cause of the weeping is explained by Magdalene: 'They have taken away my Lord, and I do not know where they have laid him.' (6) In the consequent apparition of Christ. Which happened to no women at the tomb: here, however, Magdalene 'turned back' and saw Jesus standing. (7) In the consequent interrogation of Christ: 'Woman, why are you weeping? Whom are you seeking?' such as is found with none of the other Evangelists. (8) In the consequent suspicion of Mary: that she thought it was the gardener who was asking thus, about which the others are likewise silent. (9) In the consequent recognition of Christ: That by the customary address made by the name 'Mary,' she recognized the voice of Jesus, and called him 'Rabboni.' (10) In the inhibition of touching. For although Jesus is said to have manifested himself also to other women, Matt. 28:9 (which, however, was not done in the garden, but on the way), he nevertheless allowed himself to be touched by them: here, however, he did not want to be touched by Mary: 'Do not touch me,' and he gave the reason for it, 'I have not yet ascended to my Father.' (11) In a peculiar command: such as does not occur in the other Evangelists: that, namely, she ought to report these words of his to the brothers of Christ: 'I am ascending to my Father and your Father, and my God and your God.'

Although all these things are most manifest proofs that both a proper and peculiar ἀγγελοψίαν and χριστοφάνειαν are described by St. John, Grotius and Vossius nevertheless very badly confuse that Johannine history with the angelic apparition described by the other Evangelists, and the manifestation of Christ commemorated by St. Matthew: whence they had to labor at perverting almost all the circumstances: and the clear texts were often violently distorted. So that this may be a summary of words, we show it here immediately, lest we have need to repeat the same things again and again: For first, a πρωθύστερον is imagined without necessity in the Johannine narrative in chapter XX. 2, as if the apparition made to Magdalene, however later it is related, had preceded the excursion of Peter and John to the sepulcher: when nevertheless St. John relates them in such a way that it clearly appears they were done in the same order: and from a comparison of the Evangelists it is manifest that Magdalene, when she saw the stone removed from the sepulcher, the other women having been left at the sepulcher, had hastened to Peter and John, and had announced it to them, whence Peter and John, in order to explore the truth of the matter, immediately betook themselves to the sepulcher, as is held in John XX. 2-3 seqq., with whom Mary goes again to the sepulcher, or follows them from a distance, and they having departed, she still stands for some time at the sepulcher, looks into it with tears, and thus sees not only the angels, but Christ himself revived, v. 11 seqq. What is this ὑστερολογία here, or what is the cause for imagining it? Furthermore, in order to sustain it, Grotius invents that that Μαρία δὲ εἱστήκει in John XX. 11 must be rendered in the pluperfect: but Mary had stood, and not only that, but all the other things which follow must be understood in that way, which nevertheless cannot be understood in that way, unless we force the words.

Thirdly, he wishes that John named Magdalene before the others, although it is said in chapter XX. 2 that Magdalene alone ran from the sepulcher and came to Simon Peter and to that other disciple whom Jesus loved, even if she had come to the sepulcher first with other women: and afterwards, because she stood by the monument weeping v. 11, it is understood that she had returned to the sepulcher. But if she stood there from the first excursion to the sepulcher, how is it said that she ran and announced to Peter and John that Christ had been taken away: or if this happened after the apparition of the angels and the manifestation of Christ, as Grotius thinks, with what appearance of truth could she herself say that Christ, whom she had seen alive again and in whose name she ought to have announced that Christ was about to ascend to the Father, had been taken away by theft?

Fourthly, in order to maintain that the same vision of the angels is the one which John reports happened to Mary Magdalene, and which the other Evangelists say was seen by the other women, he says that the angelic address 'do not be afraid' is the same as 'woman, why are you weeping?' Which are, however, most different. For there, many are addressed; here, one. There, they are warned not to fear; here, however, it is asked of Mary what is the cause of her weeping.

Fifthly, to the same end he perverts the words of Luke 'having entered' so that he takes them not of several women, but of one Magdalene, and says by synecdoche that the plural is put for the singular at Matthew XXVIII. 5, although it is clear in Luke chapter XXIV. 3 that the discourse is about several women who, having entered the monument, did not find the body of the Lord, and being dismayed were raised up by the angels.

Similarly, sixthly, he twists the words of Matthew 'come, see the place where the Lord was laid' chapter XXVIII. 6 to Magdalene, and her alone, and after she herself had already 'looked into the monument' John XX. 11, as they say, by force: which were said to the women by the angel when Magdalene had first run to the sepulcher with them, but after Magdalene had already departed from them and hurried to Peter and John.

No less, seventhly, does he twist the words in John chapter XX. 14 'she turned back,' because Magdalene, I know not by what delay, returned from her journey to the monument: when the sense of them is plain, that having turned backwards she looked behind her, if indeed 'to turn' signifies to turn oneself and look back, Matthew XVI. 23, Luke VII. 9, 44, c. IX. 55; moreover, 'backwards' is added so that it may be implied that she turned herself backwards with her whole body, not with her face alone. And thus even Grotius himself rendered it at John XX. 14: she turned her eyes from the monument to the garden.

Eighthly, when Matthew says chapter XXVIII. 9 'he met them,' that the Lord met the women returning from the monument, so that they might announce to the disciples what they had seen and heard, he twists these to Magdalene, who had departed to Peter and John: and he contends that this is the same manifestation which is indicated in Mark XVI. 9 as having happened to Magdalene, and described in John XX. And therefore he invents here again a synecdoche, or an exchange of number, 'he met THEM' for 'HER,' or if that is not to be admitted, he thinks it credible that a handmaid of Magdalene was present. But force is thus brought upon the text in more than one way: For those women who had heard the angelic address, who having entered into the monument had seen the empty place, who had been ordered to go away and announce to the disciples of Christ that Christ is about to go before them into Galilee, who having departed from the monument with fear and great joy were running after those things seen and heard, so that they might announce them to the disciples. To them, I say, as they were thus going to announce to the disciples, as Matthew expressly repeats these things 'and as they were going to announce to the disciples,' Jesus met them and said 'Greetings.' And after they approached and held his feet and worshiped him, Jesus said to those very same ones: 'Do not fear, go, announce to my brothers that they may go into Galilee and there they will see me.' To drag all these things either to one Magdalene, or to her and her handmaid, what else is it than to twist the scripture most wickedly? Ninthly, when Matthew teaches that these women approaching Christ held his feet, 'and they approaching, held his feet,' Grotius, taking these things of Magdalene, whom Christ did not want to touch himself, and her handmaid, interprets them as if they indeed wanted to embrace the feet of Christ, but were ordered to abstain. But that word 'held' sounds not of an attempt only, but of an act. The cause, however, why Christ did not want to be touched by Mary, but suffered his feet to be grasped by other women, and even offered himself to be handled by the disciples, is this: that those women and the disciples doubted about the truth of the resurrection, to whom he wanted faith to be confirmed in this way; but Magdalene had already recognized Christ, but she still stuck in the common error about a worldly kingdom now being erected, as if he were now going to live familiarly with his own, whence Christ himself said to her: do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father, as if he were saying, there is no reason for you to stick in external embraces, and to expect from this a certain earthly conversation: for I must ascend into heaven: which ascension is not yet so near, because I must still manifest myself more to the disciples, and instruct them; it is now more necessary that you hasten to them, and refresh them with the joyful announcement of the resurrection, who are clearly dismayed by grief. Compare the writer of the Questions to the Orthodox among the works of Justin, q. XLIIX. 'Grotius rightly interpreted these things at John XX. 17, as if Jesus had said, you want to touch me, Mary, that is, you want to enjoy my friendship entirely: that is not allowed now, since I only show myself to be seen economically to strengthen your faith.' But when I shall have ascended to the Father, the time will come when you will be able to enjoy my friendship most perfectly, not by earthly contact, but by such as is suitable to that place, that is, heaven, a spiritual one. In the tenth place, Grotius acknowledges that the words καὶ προσεκύνησαν αὐτῷ were not said of the Magdalene alone: Let us understand, he says, that these women, although not yet sufficiently persuaded of the resurrection of the buried body, had nevertheless conceived in their minds something greater concerning Christ than ever before. But it is said of the same women that they grasped the feet of Christ, who worshipped Christ. Therefore, it is not to be understood of the Magdalene alone. Finally, in order to render the faith of Mary doubtful, which the words of John place beyond all doubt in ch. XX. 18, when she herself announced to the disciples ὅτι ἑώρακε τὸν κύριον, in his annotations on that place Grotius perverts them in such a way that she had seen someone whom she herself had believed to be the Lord. For, he says, she doubted again whether it had been an incorporeal vision. But how could she doubt, when she herself saw and recognized Christ alive again, and wished to touch him, and reported to the disciples, not someone whom she had taken for the Lord, but that she had seen τὸν κύριον, the Lord himself. But enough of these Grotian corruptions.

From what has been said, however, it is clear that there is a twofold ὀπτασία of the angels, which the Evangelists have described: the one of those who appeared to the other women after Mary had departed from them; the other of those who were seen by Mary after she had returned to the sepulchre with Peter and John, or at least had followed them: and that a twofold χριστοφάνεια has been expressed thus far: the former (which was the first of all the appearance after the resurrection (Mark XVI. 9.) made to Mary Magdalene; the other, which happened to the remaining women having departed from the tomb. Which was then followed by the appearance made to Simon Peter (Luke XXIV. 34.), just as this was followed by the manifestation which occurred to the disciples at Emmaus (Mark XVI. 12., Luke XXIV. 13.).

Latin:

Vers. 2. σεισμὸς ἐγένετο μέγας] Motus hic signum fuit se- cuturae ὀπτασίας satis notum Iudaico populo Psal. LXIIX. 8. 9. XCIX. 1. CXIV. 17. Ostendit hoc quod sequitur ἄγγελος γὰρ & caetera. Quare nulla alia quaerenda est ratio. Putem autem hoc, ut & lapidis devolutionem, sed & fugam custo- dum evenisse dum mulieres in itinere essent: neque id ex mulierum testimonio notum, sed ex aliorum militum rela- tu, qui accepta pecunia redemptum silentium non praestite- runt: ut fieri solet. Argumento est quod Marcus de mu- lieribus narrat: κ̓ ἀναβλέψασαι θεωρου̃σιν ό̨τι ἀποκεκύλισται ο̨ λίθος. Devolutum igitur viderunt cum id minime spera- rent: devolvi non viderunt. Neque ausae fuissent accede- re si monumentum obseptum vidissent militari custodia.

Motus ille terrae etsi haberi possit pro signo futurae ὀπτασίας, non neganda tamen temere illa ratio est, quam veteres dedere, quod nempe in illo terrae motu Christus ad inferos descenderit. Hilar. Canon. XXXIII. in Matth. Chrysost. serm. LXXIV. quibus accedit B. Lutherus noster, & B. Gerhard. Harm. Resurr. p. 1.

́ καταβὰς ἐξ οὐρανου̃] Habet Deus Angelos quotidianae pro- videntiae ministros. Habet & velut satrapas, quorum opera ad res maximi momenti utitur, ut alibi annotavimus. Hi peculiariter dicuntur ἐξ οὐρανου̃ καταβαίνειν, hoc est, tanquam a latere mitti. Itaque ubicunque κατάβασις ἐξ οὐρανου̃ est mentio, ut Apoc. X. 1. c. XIIX. c. XX. 1. magnum quiddam atque eximium agi intelligas.

ἀπεκύλισε τὸν λίθον ἀπὸ τη̃ς θύρας] An ut janitoris offi- cio, non necessario quidem, sed honorifico fungeretur? Certe veterum quosdam ita existimasse negari non potest, & torquent eorum verba qui id praefracte negant. Alii a- liter: quos inter ille quisquis est Scriptor antiquus (non u- num esse libri istius pro certo habeo, sed ex multorum non unius aevi scriptis factam collectionem) in responsionibus ad Orthodoxos: ἐ γὰρ διὰ τὴν ἀνάστασιν του̃ λίθου ἐκ του̃ μνήματος ἐγένετο η̨ ἀφαίρεσις, ἀλλὰ διὰ τὸ δηλωθη̃ναι τοι̃ς ο̨ρω̃- σι τὴν ἀνάστασιν. Prior sententia, ut certa non sit, qui refelli possit non video. Praefiguratum videri hoc potest in Iaco- bo Gen. XXIX. 9. Verba eadem.

Factum id non ut janitoris officio fungeretur Angelus, & Christo sepulcrum aperiret, quod vult Grotius, & Vossius lib. III. Harm. Evang. c. II. §. 5. cum plerisque Calvinianis, sed potius, ut scriptor antiquus in respons. ad orthodoxos in operibus Justi- ni docet, ut monstraretur vacuum sepulcrum vi- dere cupientibus: ἐ γὰρ διὰ τὴν ἀυτου̃ ἔγερσιν του̃ λίθου ἐκ του̃ μνήματος ἐγένετο η̨ ἀφαίρεσις, ἀλλὰ διὰ τὸ δηλωθη̃ναι τοι̃ς ο̨ρω̃σι τὴν ἀνάστασιν. Ma- gno enim consensu docent veteres Christum se- pulcro adhuc clauso resurrexisse, cum scriptore il- lo antiquo quaest. citata CXVII. Nazianz. in Dra- mate, Gregor. Nyssenus de resurrect. Ambrosius lib. X. in cap. XXIV. Lucae, Chrysost. hom. XC. in Matth. & in cap. XX. Joh. Hier. ad Pammach. & in Epitaph. Paul. August. passim serm. CXXXVIII. & CLVI. & CLVIII. de tempore &c. & alii: & a- gnoscit ipse Calvinus in Harmon. Evangel. Christus ante surrexisse, quam ab Angelo sepulchrum aperire- tur: adde & Muscul. in cap. XXVIII. Matth. Mar- lor. in h. l. Johan. Casius ex eo, quod Christus clauso sepulchro resurrexerit, probat dimensio- num penetrationem: quam etiam possibilem agno- scit Goclenius.

κ̓ ἐκάθητο ἐπάνω ἀυτου̃] Unum nominat Matthaeus, ut & Marcus: Lucas duos, ut & Iohannes: Nam apud Iohannem eadem quae hic historia narratur cap. XX. 13. Nihil enim vi- deo cur aliam putemus, cum tot circumstantiae congruant. Iohanni Maria Magdalena hanc ὀπτασίαν videt: aliis eadem cum cæteris: nam initio Johannes Magdalenam pro resta quis nominaverat: cui simile est quod Iohanni duo Angeli, Lucæ, duo ἄνδρες, id est Angeli virili specie, nominantur, Matthæo unus Angelus, ut & Marco unus νεανίσκος: ni- mirum quia unus ille & propior & pro duobus verba fecit: quod solenne notant Hebræi ex loco Gen. XIIX. 1. & 3. ita- que quod Lucas Angelos dixisse perhibet non est hic sed sur- rexit, id ab Angelo dictum narrant Matthæus & Marcus. Sic quod Matthæo est μὴ φοβεῖσθε, Marco, μὴ ἐκθαμβεῖσθε, Johan- ni, τί κλαίεις Vestes candidas Johannes memorat item ut tres alii: sessionis meminit ut Matthæus & Marcus. Cur diversæ narrationes credantur plane nihil est, nisi quod Jo- hannes suam & Petri itionem prius narrat, deinde ea quæ Magdalena viderat, cum alium fuisse temporis ordinem, tum ex Lucæ historia hoc loco appareat, tum apertessime ex iis quæ Cleopas dicit in itinere Emauntem versus, Lucæ XXIV. 22. 23. 24. At me id non movet, qui sciam, ut alios annalium conditores, ita & hosce nostros non semper se ad- stringere ad eas angustias, ut quod prius gestum est prius et- iam narrent, cum multa ubi que sit reperire προϋστερα, multas προλήψεις, multas ἐπανόδους. Neque Johanni cur na- turalem hic ordinem inverteret justa causa defuit. Sciebat quam imbecille futurum esset apud multos testimonium muliebte ob eam quæ sexui isto tribui vulgo solet judicii imbecillitatem. Nam & Celsus contra Christianos id te- stimonium eludens Magdalenam γυναῖκα πάροιστρον vocavit, Quare Johannes acturus de re ut verissima, ita creditu diffi- cili, suum & Petri testimonium narrationi præstruxit; Pe- tri, ut qui id ipsum morte sua jam obsignasset: Suum, ut qui tunc etiam cum scriberet paratus esset omnia perpeti pro- pter ejus testimonii veritatem. Hoc posito fundamento, quod apud æquos judices valere plurimum debebat, tuto deinde addit sexus sequioris testimonium. Neque tamen omnino abjecit temporis ordinem. Sed cum de itione Magdalenæ dicere cœpisset cap. XX. 1 adjicit deinde ea, quæ ipse cum Petro compererat, mox ad Magdalenam rediens ea pertexit quæ prius quidem gesta, sed posterius tamen ac- curate & cum suis circumstantiis per Magdalenam Aposto- lis erant renunciata. Quare illud Μαρία δὲ εἱστήκει cap. XX. 11. intelligendum est steteraat autem Maria, & ita deinceps cæte- ra, reditu facto ad id quod post commma primum Johannes intermiserat. Hæc ideo hoc loco dicenda sum arbitratus, ut probato unam esse eandemque historiam apud Scripto- res quatuor, ea quæ ab aliis sunt prodita, aliorum interpreta- tioni serviant. Videamus quid restet difficultatis. Sedere, ut dixi, Angelos dicit Iohannes, cum Matthæo & Marco; at Lucas eos sterisse videtur dicere: sed videtur tantum: nam ἐφιστάναι est supervenire: ut cum Hippocrates dicit: ὥσπερ γὰρ ὁμῶες κὴ δμωΐδες ἐν τοῖς οἴκοισι θορυβέοντες καὶ τασιά- ζοντες ὁκόταν ἐξαπιναίως ἡ δέσποινα ἐπιστᾶ πτοηθέντες ἐφησυχά- ζωσι. Et Herodianus: ἐλπίδα θᾶττον τοῖς βρετανοῖς ἐπίστη- Ac Lucæ peculiariter ea vox de cælestibus visis usurpatur Evangelio ejus cap. II. 9. Act. XII. 7. & c. XXIII. 11. Sic cum Demosthenes in ea quæ est de corona dixisset, ἀφ' ἧς ἡμέρας ἐπὶ ταῦτα ἐπέστην ἐγὼ, notat Ulpianus: ὥσπερ τινὸς δαίμονος ἐπιστασίαν λέγει τῆς ἀυτῦ καθηκονιῶ τῆς παρουσίας. De loco ubi sederint Angeli, itidem dubitatur. Nam extra specum sedisse Angelum illum cujus Matthæus meminit inde colli- gitur quod lapidi supersediffe dicitur. Is autem lapis major ore specus haud dubie extrorsum, non introrsum erat devo- lutus. At contrarium dicere purantur tum Marcus, tum Iohannes, unde sunt qui dixerunt Angelum sedisse non su- per lapidem ab ore devolutum, sed super lapidem alium qui Christi loculo impositus fuerit. At quid est Matthæo con- tradicere, si hoc non est? is enim apertiffime ait, ἀπεκύλισε τὸν λίθον ἀπὸ τῆς θύρας καὶ ἐκάθητο ἐπάνω ἀυτῦ. Mihi res vi- detur expedita, si Marci verba commode interpretemur. Is ait εἰσελθῦσαι εἰς τὸ μνημεῖον εἶδον νεανίσκον. Atqui in specum nondum intraverant: nam postea dicit eis Angelus δεῦτε ἴδετε τὸν τόπον ὅπε ἔκειτο. Vocat ergo Marcus μνημεῖον par- tem horti quæ ab horto reliquo, sepimento aliquo sive lori- ca, separabatur. Nam μνημεῖα laxius sumti partes erant duæ חצר τὸ ὕπαιθρον & מערה σπήλαιον. In oratione Demo- sthenis adversus Macartatum: τὸ μνῆμα Βεσελιδῶν πολὺς τό- πος περιβεβλημένῶ ὥσπερ οἱ ἀρχαῖοι ἐνόμιζον; & illud ὕπαιθρον jure Pontificio Romano forum vocabatur. Strabo ubi Au- gusti & cognatorum monimentum describit: ἐν μέσῳ δὲ τῷ πεδίῳ ὁ τῆς κάυστρας ἀυτῦ περίβολῶ (id est forum) κύκλῳ περικείμενον ἔχων σιδηρῦν περίφραγμα. Sic & apud Romanos in pedes aliquam multos monumentum patebat, ut nos do- cent inscriptiones. Omnino autem errare eos arbitror qui tutum hunc hortum putant fuisse vice ὑπαίθρου. Nam quod monumenti pars erat, exemtum erat humanis usibus. At hortus ille colebatur & suum habebat κηπυρὸν Ioh. XX. 14. erat ergo locus extra loricam terra pura, qualis illa quam Romani tutelam monumenti vocabant, ut in veteri inscri- ptione: Huic monumento tutela nomine cedunt agri puri jugera decem. Et apud Frontinum: Habent enim & Mausolea (ita enim legendum) juris sui hortorum modos circumjacentes. Loricam illam quæ Hebræis מעקה Deut. XXII. 8. recte Græce γεῖσον dici arbitror. Neque enim projecta tantum ita appellari fatis Josephus nos docet, apud quem in templi deseriptione γείσιον vocatur sepimentum ὅσον πηχυαῖον ὕψος quod populum à Sacerdotibus arcebat. Sicut alterum sepi- mentum quo ἀλλόφυλοι arcebantur vocat δρύφακτον λίθινον. Idem alibi itidem Templum describens, quod Græci vo- cant θρίγκον, id ait γεῖσον vocari κατὰ ἐπιχώριον γλῶτταν, cum tamen ea vox Hebræa non sit origine, sed ut multæ aliæ, ex Græco sermone in Hebræum traducta. Rursum alibi περίβολον, alibi ἑρκίον appellat. Vocem θριγχοῦ de mo- numento etiam Pausanias usurpat: ἐνταῦθα ἐσι καὶ ὀφέλτε τάφος. περὶ δὲ αὐτὸν θριγγὸς λίθων κὴ ἐντὸς τῦ περιβόλω βω- μός: ubi περίβολος est חצר Latini quam loricam diximus etiam munimentum vocant, ut videre est in L. Funeris Dig. de Religiosis. Homerus θεμείλια illo versu: Τορνώσαντο δὲ σῆμα θεμείλιά τε προβάλοντο. Tale δρύφακτον θριγκόν sive γεῖσον, id est loricam haud du- bie Cyrillus σκέπην vocat qua vallata ait fuisse Judæorum monumenta. Sed & Augustinus, ex vetere haud dubie fama, ingressas ait mulieres in spatium maceria communi- tum. In hanc ergo partem horti intra loricam cum venis- sent mulieres, in isto ὑπαίθρῳ super lapidem sedentem An- gelum conspexêre, ad dextram speluncæ partem quam versus caput mortui positum fuisse credo. Nam etiam in mortuo caput pars potissima est, ut Paulus jurisconsultus respondet. Quare idem esse puto Johanni πρὸς τῇ κεφαλῇ, & Marco ἐν τοῖς δεξιοῖς. Itaque alter Angelus, Matthæo & Marco dissimulatus, sedit ad sinistram speluncæ partem quam versus pedes positi fuerant. Si vera est Bedæ descri- ptio dextra pars versus Aquilonem fuerit, sinistra versus Austrum. Os ipsum specus orientem spectaverit.

Unicam vult ἀγγελοψίαν esse, Grotius, quam non Lucas tantum cum Matthæo & Marco, sed quam etiam Johannes cap. XX. 13. describit, iiqui- dem tot circumstantiæ congruant. Alii tres vel potius quatuor diversas apparitiones inde eruunt; primam qua conspectus est angelus custodibus, cu- jus aspectus fuit terribilis: alteram cum mulieribus in primo, vel potius, ut ipsi assignant secundo ex- cursu, (quia primum solum visendi sepulcri cau- sa factum putant) unctionis causa instituto apparue- re bini angeli apud Lucam: tertiam cum Maria Magdalene visi sunt duo angeli Johan. XX. v. 11. quartam cum mulieribus denuo ad sepulcrum, ubi Christum Mariæ Magdalenæ apparuisse per- cepissent, reversis, tum ob rei certitudinem, tum ut ipsæ quoque manifestationis Christi gra- tia bearentur (qui tertius fuerit earum excursus) quo pacto harmoniam suam digessit B. Gerhar- dus, ut & B. Cluverus. Sed neque trino illo ex- cursu ad sepulcrum opus est, neque quatuor di- versis apparitionibus angelorum: imo juxta quos- dam ne tribus quidem: quia angelus ille, qui Matthæo teste, saxum devolvit, eique insedit, concionem illam, quam ipse statim subjungit, habuit ad mulieres: siquidem alium supervenis- se non innuatur, & de eodem angelo continue- tur historica relatio vers. 5. ἀποκριθεὶς δὲ ὁ ἄγγε- λος εἶπε ταῖς γυναιξὶ, ubi etiam non otiose addi- tur articulus, sed eundem, quem lapidem de- volvisse dixerat Matthæus, demonstrat angelum: Alium enim hic ingerere inconveniens foret, cum alterius nullam mentionem fecerit Evange- lista. Quam sententiam etiam antehac probavi- mus. Sed nunc in re accuratius pensitata an- gelum illum qui lapidem dicitur devolvisse, diver- sum fuisse ab Angelo utroque in monumento viso mulieribus censemus, uti ex Harmonia nostra Evangelica patescit: eandem quidem fuisse con- cionem à Matthæo, Marco, & Luca descri- ptam, & ex triga illa Evangelistarum harmonice contexendam: sed Angelum illum qui à Matthæo recensetur devolvisse lapidem & super eum sedis- se, à quo terrefacti sunt custodes, visum non effe mulieribus, nec illum ipsum esse, qui mulieres allocutus à Matthæo dicitur: aut certe de saxo non habuisse concionem de resurrectione Christi ad mulieres, quam hæ denum in monumento, quód digressa Maria Magdalena ingressæ sunt, audie- runt. Articulus certe Græcus in voce ὁ ἄγγελος non habet tantam vim, ut eundem illum angelum demonstret, cujus antea facta mentio: quum alius potuerit designari angelus ab aliis Evangelistis commemoratus; è quibus contexenda, usalias sæpe est Historia.

Quod ergo angelus ille apud Matthæum allo- quens mulierculas, in lapide sedit, Marcus vero introducit angelum eandem concionem ad mu- lieres habentem καθήμενον ἐν τοῖς δεξιοῖς postquam ingressæ mulieres sunt εἰς τὸ μνημεῖον, frustra ita ex- pedit Grotius, quod Marcus μνημεῖον vocet non specum, quia eum nondum intraverint, sed par- tem horti, quæ ab horto reliquo (qui ab hortula- no colebatur Johan. XX. 14.) sepimento aliquo, sive lorica, separata fuerit ὑπ’ αἴθρον non σπή- λαιον: Illud sane de hoc monumento (etsi ea in a- liis sorte locum habuerit distinctio, quæ suam tu- telam περίβολον, vel ϑριγκὸν habuere) difficulter docebitur; nec ei probando sufficit, quod Augu- stinus ait mulieres in spatium maceria communitum ingressas. Confidenter tamen pro more suo Gro- tius, hoc ex veteri fama baud dubie ortum dicit, ad- ditque: in hanc ergo partem horti intra loricam cum venissent mulieres, in isto ὑπαίθρῳ super lapidem sedentem Angelum conspexere, ad dextram speluncæ partem quam versus caput mortui positum fuisse credo. Nam etiam in mortuo caput pars potissima est, ut Paulus Jurisconsultus respondet. Quare idem esse puto Johanni πρὸς τῇ κεφαλῇ, & Mar- co ἐν τοῖς δεξιοῖς, itaque alter Angelus, Matthæo & Marco dissimulatus, sedit ad sinistram spelun- cæ partem quam versus pedes positi fuerant. Verum etiam vero illa citra solidum fundamentum di- cuntur: & diversam esse historiam Johannis mox constabit. In σπήλαιον autem sive specum mulier- culas nondum ingressa esse, non potest indubita- to colligi ex relatione Evangelistarum. Nam quod urget Grotius postea demum, dixisse eis Ange- lum, δεῦτε ἴδετε τὸν τόπον ὅπη ἔκειτο, venite, vi- dete locum ubi positus erat, id indubitato non li- quet factum postquam εἰς τὸ μνημεῖον intravere mulieres: & diserte Marcus ait, εἰσελθῦσαι εἰς τὸ μνημεῖον εἶδον νεανίσκον. Angelus enim veluti præsens in specu δεικτικῶς, ἴδε ὁ τόπος, inquit, ὅπη ἔθηκαν αὐτὸν, Ecce Locus, ubi posuerunt eum. Quapropter alii dicunt,quod verbum εἰσελθῦσαι introeuntes apud Marcum actum solum inchoatum designet, cum inciperent, vel cuperent ingredi monu- mentum. Aliis videtur Angelum primum extra sepulchrum super saxum sedisse, atque ita custodi- bus conspectum fuisse: postmodum eundem in sepul- cro visum, ibique mulieribus conspectum. Ita Vi- ctor Antiochenus in cap. XVI. Marci: Contingere potuit, ut illum ipsum angelum quem secundum Mat- thæum fulguris more splendentem candidoque vestitu instar nivis micantem, lapidi insidentem viderant postquam in monumentum intraverant, quasi viæ ducem præeuntem, nec non à dextris se collocantem conspexerint. Aliis placet, angelos diversos fuis- se, alterum qui saxo supersedisse refertur à Mat- thæo, alterum qui in monumento visus est à dex- tris sedens, referente Marco, etsi eadem pe- neutriusque fuerit concio, ut uno loquerentur ac testarentur ore? quam S. Augustini video fuisse sententiam libr. III. de consens. Evangel. cap. 24. Potest moveri, quo modo secundum Mat- thæum Angelus super lapidem sedebat devolutum à monumento, Marcus enim intrantes eas monumen- tum dicit vidisse juvenem sedentem a dextris cooper- tum stola candida, & obstupuisse: nisi intelligamus aut Matthæum tacuisse de illo angelo quem intrantes viderunt, Marcum vero tacuisse de illo, quem foris viderunt sedentem super lapidem, ut duos viderint, & a duobus singulatim audierint, quæ dixerunt angeli de Jesu; prius ab illo quem foris viderunt se- dentem super lapide: deinde ab illo quem viderunt intrantes in monumentum, sedentem a dextris, quo ut intrarent illius qui foris sedebat verbis exhorta- tæ sunt, dicentis, venite & videte locum ubi posi- tus erat Dominus! quo venientes, ut dictum est, & intrantes, viderunt eum, de quo Matthæus tacet, Marcus autem loquitur, sedentem a dextris, a quo talia similiter audierunt. Addit jam Augusti- nus illam explicationem quæ Grotio probata: Sed illa τῶ μνημείω diversa significatio è S. literis do- ceri nequit: & ubi de μνημείῳ Christi agitur, sem- per spelunca in quam corpus ejus illatum est, vel sepulchrum intelligitur, Matth. XXVII. 60. cap. XXVIII. 8. Marc. XV. 26. c. XVI. 2. 3. 8. Luc. XXIII. 55. c. XXIV. 1. 2. 9. 12. 22. 24. Johan. XIX. 41. 42. c. XX. 1. 2. 3. 6. 8. 11. Adducere tamen placet eam quoque Augustini declarationem, quæ ita habet: Aut certe intrantes in monumentum in aliqua septa maceriæ debemus accipere, qua commu- nitum locum tunc fuisse CREDIBILE est in aliquo spatio ante petram, qua excisa locus factus fuerat sepulturæ, ut ipsum viderint in eodem spatio seden- tem a dextris, quem dicit Matthæus seden- tem super lapidem, quem terræ motus ab ostio mo- numenti revolverat, id est, a loco sepulcri, quod effossum erat è Petra. Hæc Augustinus. Cæterùm si id urgeatur, diversos fuisse Angelos, etsi pe- ne eadem utriusque concio sit, quod prior An- gelus invitet mulierculas ad ingressum in monu- mentum: posterior autem ingressis digito veluti locum, in quo positus erat, vacuum demonstret; responsio in promtu est: non esse illud invitatio- nem ad ingressum in monumentum, sed ad vi- dendum locum monumenti (quod ingressæ jam e- rant) quem δεικτικῶς monstrat Marcus: ut non opus ideo sit diversas conciones Angelicas hic sta- tuere: quia optime se habet Harmonia; Venite, videte locum, ubi positus erat, ἰδὲ Ecce, ibi locus ille est, ubi posuerunt eum.

Quod itaque ad S. Lucæ narrationem attinet, c. XXIV. 2. videtur ille non diversam, sed eandem omnino cum Marco historiam referre. Nam quod diversus muliercularum excursus fuerit, al- ter unctionis causa institutus, alter majoris confir- mationis gratia: quodque prior ille à Luca descri- ptus sit, cujus ἔκβασιν mulierculæ Apostolis retu- lerint, antequam jussæ sunt eandem annunciare iisdem; posterior autem acciderit, postquam Ma- riæ Magdalenæ Christum sese manifestasse intelle- xere mulierculæ, gratis assumitur; nec è collatio- ne Evangelistarum firmiter probari potest. Cir- cumstantiæ certe eædem sunt apud Lucam, quæ apud Marcum, nisi quod Lucas conjunctim duos commemorat iisdem mulierculis, dum repere- runt lapidem à monumento revolutum, de quo anxiæ fuerant in via, conspectos: Concionis et- iam ab Angelis illis duobus habitæ summa expres- sa a Luca congruit: qui tamen verba nonnulla Christi, quibus hæc prædixerat, ab angelis in memoriam mulierculis revocata, addidit, ut an- gelica concio ad easdem facta plenior exstaret. Forma quoque quod in virili visi sint specie, apud Marcum & Lucam, eadem est: ideoque hic non abnuimus Grotio eandem historiam à Luca descri- bi asserenti: quæ etiam sententia est D. Johannis Richardsoni Ardachadensis in provincia Armacha- na Episcopi, à Jacobo Usserio Armachano Archi- Episcopo laudata in Annalibus part. II. p. 608. nec non Johan. Gerhardi Vossii in Harmon. Evangel. Passion. & Resurr. Christi p. 369.

Tria autem objici possunt huic sententiæ: (1) quod Lucas refert, duos viros in vestibus fulguranti- bus visos mulieribus, cum ingressæ sepulcrum non in- venerunt corpus Domini, ac mente consternatæ περὶ τούτου super hoc essent. (2) quod stetisse duo illi viri juxta mulierculas dicantur: quum Angelus Mar- ci sederit. (3) quod in historia Marci mulieres non solum angelum viderint, & audierint, sed etiam in regressu à sepulchro Christus ipsis occurre- rit: quod in historia Lucæ factum non est, quia de apparitione Christi nihil retulerunt penes Apo- stolos: unde colligunt, excursum à Luca de- scriptum prius contigisse, cum quo conjuncta non fuerit manifestatio Christi.

Sed hæc dimovere nos non possunt ab illa sen- tentia: nam quod ad (1) Summatim refert Lucas, quæ distinctius penes Marcum leguntur: introdu- cens duos angelos, visos cum ingressæ muliercu- læ sepulchrum sunt: ac mente consternatæ essent, partim ob conspectum angelicum, partim ob se- pulchrum vacuum, utut Angelus per vacuum sepulcrum ipsis confirmaret veritatem resurre- ctionis dominicæ: quibus fidem nondum habe- bant, donec ab angelo in monumento ipsissima Christi verba, quæ Lucas in supplementum histo- riæ consignavit, iisdem in memoriam revocata essent; addit enim Lucas: καὶ ἐμνήσθησαν τῶν ῥημάτων αὐτοῦ, & recordatæ sunt verborum ejus.

Quod ad (2) Recte observat Grotius, & ex eo Vossius, ac Walæus. Verba Lucæ Δύο ἄνδρες ἐπέ- στησαν αὐταῖς quæ Vulgatus & Erasmus reddide- runt, duo viri adstiterunt iis, exponenda esse, super- venerunt iis. Ita de his Grotius: At Lucas eos ste- tisse videtur dicere: sed videtur tantum: nam ἐ- φιστάναι est supervenire: cum Hippocrates dicit," ὥσπερ γὰρ δμῶες κὶ δμωΐδες ἐν τοῖς ὄικοισι θορυ- βέοντες κὶ στασιάζοντες ὀικέταν ἐξαπιναίως ἡ δέσποι- να ἐπισταπτηθέντες ἐφησυχάζουσι. Et Herodianus: ἐλπίδα θᾶττον τοῖς βρετανοῖς ἐπέστη. Ac Lucæ" peculiariter ea vox de cœlestibus visis usurpa-" tur Evangelio ejus II, 9. Act. XII. 7. & XXIII. 11. Sic" cum Demosthenes in ea quæ est de corona dixis-" set, ἀφ' ἧς ἡμέρας ἐπὶ ταῦτα ἐπέστην ἐγὼ, notat Ul-" pianus, ὥσπέρ τινὸς δαίμονος ἐπιστασίαν λέγει τῆς ἀυτοῦ κηδεμονίας τὴν παρουσίαν."

Quod ad (3) Resp. cum Lucas ait, mulieres a monumento regressas nunciasse ταῦτα πάντα hæc o- mnia illis undecim, & cæteris omnibus, easque com- memorat, quod fuerint Maria Magdalena, & Jo- hanna, & Maria Jacobi, & cæteræ, quæ cum iis erant, nihil obstat quo minus dicatur, illas etiam apparitionem Christi quæ in regressu à monumen- to contigit, Apostolis retulisse, utut visa illa omnia ipsis sint ὡσεὶ λῆρος: additur enim causa, κὶ ἠπί- στουν ἀυταῖς, quod non crediderint illis. Quia nihil eorum, quæ retulere mulierculæ credidere, non mirum, etiam haud credidisse ea, quæ de appari- tione Christi retulêre. Siquidem nec Mariæ Magda- lenæ apparitionem Christi referenti fidem adhi- buerunt Marc. XVI. 10. 11.

Quod vero discipuli Emauntem profecti sum- mam relationis à mulieribus factæ ita proponunt Luc. XXIV. vers. 23. ut solum non inventi corporis Christi, & testimonii Angelici, non vero manife- stationis Christi ipsis factæ, mentionem faciant, ex eo concludi non potest, vel nondum factam mulierculis manifestationem Christi, cum hæc ad Apostolos deferrent, vel eam non commemora- tam Apostolis. Nam annon potuêre omittere di- scipuli Emauntici hanc relationem, eo quod nimis absurda illis videretur, aut quæcunque tandem il- lius omissionis causa fuerit? ubi tamen non est quod locum relinquamus suspicioni Grotii, ad v. 9. „quod ne tum quidem Maria Magdalena credi- „derit Dominum resurrexisse, postquam apparue- „rat jam eidem, sed adhuc suspicata tunc fuerit „corpus Christi sublatum ex monumento, quasi Judæorum opinioni addicta fuerit Pythagoricæ, quod anima etiam corpus habeat, quod oculis conspi- ci possit, ὅτι δύναται ὀφθαλμοῖς αἰσθητοῖς φανῆναι ψυχῆς σῶμα ἀυγοειδὲς (quæ tamen an Veterum E- bræorum fuerit sententia, num vero ut alia multa, à Chaldæis & Græcis ad posteriores Ebræos vene- „rit, dubitat) vel, quod credibilius Grotio vide- „tur, existimavit Magdalena, non Dominum, „sed angelum sibi apparuisse, idq; eo magis, quia „nec tangere eum licuerit, neque ipse Jesum se „esse liquido pronunciaverit, unde factum putat Grotius, ut hæc quoque ἐπιφάνεια comprehendatur sub nomine ὀπτασίας ἀγγέλων Luc. XXIV. 23. Ni- mirum præstat fateri ignorantiam, cur duo Disci- puli Emauntici non commemorarint mulierculis factam Christi apparitionem, quam cum Grotio talia opinionum portenta mulierculis, & discipu- lis tribuere, textusque apertissimos pervertere. Quid enim luculentius esse posset, quam quod Maria Jesum, cum compellasset eandem nomine proprio, agnoverit, eum Rabboni nuncupans Joh. XX. 17. quodque Jesus palam eidem sese manifesta- rit, cum ait, noli me tangere, nondum enim ascendi ad Patrem meum, & mandatum ei dedit: Vade ad fratres meos, & dic eis: Ascendo ad Patrem meum, & Patrem vestrum, & Deum meum, & Deum ve- strum. Et quomodo dubitari potest de agnitione Christi, quum subjicit Evangelista, venit Maria Magdalena annuncians discipulis, ὅτι ἑώρακε κύριον, quod vidisset Dominum, & ea dixisset sibi. Num hæc de ὀπτασίᾳ angeli alicujus intelligi possunt? Et quomodo suspicari poterat Magdalena Ange- lum, non Dominum esse: Num Angelus aliquis u- surpare hæc verba poterat? nondum ascendi ad Pa- trem meum: Et vade ad fratres meos, & dic eis, Ascendo ad Patrem meum &c. Quis non videt quam inepta hæc sint? Tum vero annon satis ma- nifesta etiam est illa apparitio, quam Matthæus mulieribus factam recenset cap. XXVIII. 9. ubi non tantum salutasse eas, consueto more, Jesum refert, sed contrectatum etiam ab iis, & adoratum testa- tur, ac denique mandatum iis dedisse, ut ad fratres suos eant, idque annuncient, quod viderant, & quod ipsi Dominum etiam visuri sint in Galilæa. Quæ Sole clariora sunt, ut mirari oporteat, Gro- tium eadem commentis suis ausum obfuscare, vel in dubium vocare.

Quod ergo tandem ad apparitionem Mariæ Mag- dalene factam, à Sancto Johanne descriptam, du- bitandum non est, eam diversam esse ab ea, quæ à cæteris Evangelistis descripta est. Conatur sane Grotius, & qui eum in hisce fere semper presse se- quutus est Vossius, eandem quoque venditare pro illa ipsa angelica apparitione, quæ à cæteris tradi- ta est Evangelistis; sed nimis manifestum est, diver- sas esse illas historias; Nam differunt (1) tempo- re: illa facta est antequam Petrus cum altero di- scipulo ad sepulchrum excurrerent: hæc vero post excursum illum Petri & alterius discipuli, (quibus Magdalena quum conspexisset, lapidem à sepul- cro remotum, & suspicata esset Dominicum cor- pus ablatum esse, id annunciarat) accidisse com- memoratur Joh. XX. 2. seqq. (2) Subjectis. Illæ enim facta mulierculis cæteris, digressa Magdale- na: hæc soli Magdalenæ Joh. XX. 11. 12. (3) Loco. Illic apparuêre angeli monumento quidem, sed ad dextram sedentes: Hic visi duo angeli in mo- numento sedentes, ubi Jesum posuerant, unus ad dextram, alter ad sinistram. (4) Alloquio. Ibi mu- lieres omnes compellantur oratione angelica, no- lite timere. Hic vero angeli Mariam solam ita com- pellant: Mulier quid ploras? (5) Responso: quod tibi nullum à mulieribus redditum: hic vero à Magdalena causa exposita ploratus: Tulerunt Do- minum meum, & nescio ubi posuerunt eum. (6) Consequente Christi apparitione. Quæ nulla ad mo- numentum mulieribus contigit: hic vero Magda- lena ἐστράφη εἰς τὰ ὀπίσω Conversa retrorsum Je- sum stantem vidit. (7) Consequente Christi interro- gatione: Mulier quid ploras? quem quæris? qua- lis nulla penes cæteros Evangelistas. (8) Conse- quente Mariæ suspicione: quod existimavit hortu- lanum esse qui sic quærebat, de qua itidem alii ta- cent. (9) Consequente Christi agnitione: Quod per consuetam appellationem nomine Maria factam, vocem Jesu cognoverit, eumque Rabboni vocarit. (10) Contrectationis inhibitione. Nam etsi Jesus etiam aliis mulieribus se manifestasse dicatur, Matt. XXVIII. 9. (quod vero non in horto factum, sed in via) ab illis tamen contrectari se passus est: hic vero contrectari à Maria noluit: Noli me tan- gere, & causam ejus reddidit, nondum ascendi ad Patrem meum. (11) peculiari præceptione: qualis apud alios Evangelistas non occurrit: quod nem- pe fratribus Christi hæc ejus verba referre debeat: ascendo ad Patrem meum & Patrem vestrum, & Deum meum & Deum vestrum.

Quæ omnia etsi manifestissima documenta sint, omnino propriam & peculiarem tum ἀγγελοψίαν tum χριστοφάνειαν describi à S. Johanne, Grotius ta- men & Vossius pessime confundunt illam Johan- neam Historiam cum angelica apparitione, à cæteris Evangelistis descripta, & Christi manifestatione à S. Matthæo commemorata: unde in omnibus pene circumstantiis pervertendis laborandum ipsis fuit: textusque luculenti sæpe violenter detorti sunt. Quod ut compendium verborum fiat, hic statim ostendimus, ne eadem subinde repetere opus habeamus: Nam primum fingitur citra necessita- tem πρωθύστερον in narratione Johannea cap. XX. 2. ac si apparitio Magdalenæ facta, utut posterius relata excursum Petri, & Johannis ad sepulcrum antecesserit: quum tamen S.
