Johannes ea ita re- ferat, ut eodem ordine gesta esse luculenter appa- reat: & è collatione Evangelistarum manifestum sit, Magdalenam cum lapidem à sepulcro remo- tum vidit relictis ad sepulcrum mulieribus cæteris, ad Petrum & Johannem properasse, eisque id annunciasse, unde Petrus & Johannes rei verita- tem exploraturi confestim ad sepulcrum sese contulerunt, ut habetur Joh. XX. 23. seqq. quibus- cum Maria iterum ad sepulcrum abit, vel cominus eos sequitur, iisque digressis aliquandiu adhuc se- pulcro adstat, cum lacrymis illud introspicit, atq; ita non solum angelos, sed Christum ipsum redivi- vum nonspicit v. 11. seqq. quæ hic ὑστερολογία, aut quæ causa eam fingendi? Porro ut eam sustineat, comminiscitur Grotius, illud Μαρία δὲ εἱστήκει Joh. XX. 11. in plusquamperfecto reddendum esse: stete- rat autem Maria, nec illud tantum, sed cætera omnia quæ sequuntur, ita intelligenda, quæ tamen ita intelligi nequeunt, nisi vim verbis inferamus.

Tertio Johannem vult Magdalenam præ reliquis no- minasse, quum tamen sola Magdalena cucurrisse à sepulcro, & ad Simonem Petrum, & ad alterum illum discipulum, quem amabat Jesus, venisse di- catur cap. XX. 2. etsi primo cum aliis mulieribus ad sepulcrum venerit: ac postmodum, quia ste- tit penes monumentum plorans v. 11. reversa ad sepulcrum fuisse intelligatur. Si autem à primo ad sepulcrum excursu ibi stetit, quomodo dicitur cucurrisse, & Petro, ac Johanni, Christum sublatum esse, nunciasse: aut si hoc accidit post apparitionem angelorum, & manifestationem Christi, quemad- modum putat Grotius, qua veritatis specie dice- re potuit ipsa, Christum furto sublatum, quem redivivum conspexerat, & cujus nomine annun- ciare debebat, Christum ad Patrem ascensu- rum?

Quarto ut eandem ὀπτασίαν angelorum esse sustineat Grotius, quam Johannes Mariæ Magdalenæ contigisse refert, & quam cæteri Ev- angelistæ dicunt mulierculis reliquis visam, in al- loquio angelico μὴ φοβεῖσθε ὑμεῖς idem esse ait, quod γυναι τί κλαίεις. Quæ vero maxime diver- sa sunt. Illic enim plures compellantur, hic una. Illic monentur ne metuant: hic vero quæritur ex Maria, quæ causa sit ploratus ejusdem.

Quinto eadem fini verba Lucæ εἰσελθοῦσαι ita pervertit, ut non de pluribus mulierculis, sed de una Magdale- na ea capiat, ac per Synecdochen plurale pro singu- lari positum dicat ad Matth. XXVIII. 5. tametsi luculentum sit apud Lucam de mulieribus pluri- bus, quæ ingressæ monumentum non invenere corpus Domini, & consternatæ ab angelis erectæ sunt, sermonem esse cap. XXIV. 3.

Similiter sexto verba Matthæi venite, videte locum ubi positus erat Dominus cap. XXVIII. 6. ad Magdalenam, eamq; solam, & postquam jam ipsa παρέκυψεν εἰς τὸ μνη- μεῖον Joh. XX. 11. detorto quòd ajunt, collo abripit: quæ ad mulieres ab angelo, cum primum Magda- lena cum iisdem ad sepulcrum excurrisset, dicta sunt, sed postquam digressa jam ab illis Magdalena ad Petrum & Johannem properasset.

Nec minus septimo verba apud Johannem cap. XX. 14. ἐστρά- φη εἰς τὰ ὀπίσω torquet, quod Magdalena, ne- scio quo mora ex itinere recurrerit ad monumen- tum: quum sensus eorum planus sit, quod conver- sa retrorsum in tergum respexerit, siquidem ςρά- φεσθαι significet sese convertere, & retrospicere, Matth. XVI. 23. Luc. VII. 9. 44. c. IX. 55. additur autem εἰς τὰ ὀπίσω, ut innuatur, quod toto corpo- re, non sola facie se retrorsum converterit. Atque ita etiam Grotius ipse ad Joh. XX. 14. reddidit: oculos à monumento ad hortum vertit.

Octavo cum Matthæus dicit cap. XXVIII. 9. ἀπήντησεν αὐτοῖς, quod occurrerit Dominus mulierculis à monumento regressis, ut scilicet discipulis, quod jussæ erant an- nunciarent quæ viderant, & audierant, detorquet hæc ad Magdalenam, quæ digressa ad Petrum, & Johannem erat: & contendit, eandem esse ἐπιφά- νειαν, quæ Magdalenæ contigit Marc. XVI. 9. in- dicatam, & Joh. XX. descriptam. Ideoque commi- niscitur hic iterum συνεκδοχὴν, sive numeri ἐναλ- λαγὴν, occurrit ILLIS, pro ILLI, aut si ea admit- tenda non sit, credibile esse putat Ancillam Magdale- næ adfuisse. At texui ita vis infertur non uno mo- do: Nam illis mulieribus, quæ concionem angeli- cam audierant, quæ in monumentum ingressæ locum vacuum viderant, quæ jussæ erant abire & discipulis Christi nunciare, quod Christus eos præcessurus sit in Galilæam, quæ digressæ à monu- mento cum timore & gaudio magno post illa visa & audita currebant, ut renunciarent ea discipulis. Illis, inquam, cum ita irent ad renunciandum di- scipulis, ut diserte Matthæus hæc repetit ὡς δὲ ἐπο- ρεύοντο ἀπαγγεῖλαι τοῖς μαθηταῖς occurrit Je- sus, & dixit Avete. Et postquam accesserunt, & tenue- runt pedes ejus & adoraverunt eum, dixit iisdem ipsis Jesus: Nolite timere, ite, renunciate fratribus meis, ut eant in Galilæam & ibi me videbunt. Quæ omnia vel ad unam Magdalenam, vel ad eam & ancillam ejusdem abripere, quid aliud est, quam pessime scripturam torquere? Nono cum Matthæus docet, mulieres hasce ad Christum accedentes pedes ejus te- nuisse, αἱ δὲ προσελθῦσαι, ἐκράτησαν ἀυτõ ἳὲς πό- δας, Grotius de Magdalena, quam noluit Christus se attingere & ancilla ejus hæc accipiens, ita ea inter- pretatur, ac si voluerint quidem pedes Christi ample- xari, sed jussæ sint abstinere. At verbum istud ἐκρά- τησαν non de conatu tantum sonat, sed de actu. Causa autem cur à Maria tangi noluerit Christus, ab aliis mulieribus passus sit pedes suos apprehen- di, discipulis etiam sese contrectandum præbuerit, hæc est, quod mulieres illæ, & discipuli dubita- rint de veritate resurrectionis, quibus fidem ita confirmari volebat; Magdalena autem agnoverat jam Christum, sed hærebat adhuc in vulgato er- rore de regno terreno jam erigendo, ac si cohabi- taturus nunc suis esset familiariter, unde ipsi Chri- stus dicebat: noli me tangere, nondum enim adscen- di ad Patrem meum, quasi dicat, non est quod in ex- ternis amplexibus hæreas, ac terrenam quandam conversationem deinsuper expectes: ascendendum enim mihi in cælum: quæ ascensio nondum ita in pro- pinquo est, quia adhuc magis me manifestare Discipu- lis debeo, eosque instruere; jam magis necessarium est, ut proinus ad eos properes, eosque læto resuscita- tionis nuncio recrees, luctu plane consternatos. Con- fer. Scriptor quæst. adOrthod. ap. Justinum q. XLIIX. „Recte vero Grotius ad Joh. XX. 17. hæc interpre- „tatus est, quasi dixerit Jesus, vis me tangere, „Maria, id est, vis omnino frui amicitia mea: id „nunc non licet, cum tantum οἰκονομικῶς ad fidem „vestram roborandam me do conspiciendum. „At ubi ad Patrem ascendero, veniet tempus cum „frui mea amicitia perfectissime poteris, non terre- „stri contactu, sed tali qui loco illi, id est cælo, con- „veniat, spirituali. Decimo agnoscit Grotius ver- „ba καὶ προσεκύνησαν ἀυτῷ non de sola Magdale- „na dicta esse: Intelligamus, inquit, has fœminas, „quaquam de resurrectione sepulti corporis non- „dum satis persuasas, majus tamen quoddam a- „nimo de Christo concepisse, quam unquam an- tea. At de iisdem dicitur, quod apprehenderint Christi pedes, quæ adorarunt Christum. Non er- go de sola Magdalena id intelligendum. Denique ut fidem Mariæ dubiam reddat, quam verba Jo- hannis extra omnem dubitationem ponunt c. XX. 18. quum ipsa nunciarit discipulis, ὅτι ἑώρακε ἳ κύ- ριον in annot. ad illum locum ea ita pervertit Gro- tius, quod aliquem vidisset, quem ipsa Dominum cre- diderat. Nam, inquit, dubitabat iterum annon fuisset visio incorporea. Quomodo vero dubitare pote- rat, quum Christum viderit, & agnoverit ipsa redi- vivum, eumque tangere voluerit, ac discipulis re- tulerit, non aliquem, quem pro Domino habuerit, sed τὸν κύριον Dominum ipsum se vidisse. Sed satis de corruptelis hisce Grotianis.

E dictis autem patet, geminam esse angelorum ὀπτασίαν : quam descripsere Evangelistæ: alteram eorum, qui apparuêre mulieribus cæteris postquam ab ipsis digressa esset Maria: alteram eorum, qui Mariæ visi sunt, postquam cum Petro & Johanne reversa esset ad sepulcrum, vel certe eosdem se- quuta: Geminam etiam hactenus χριςοφάνειαν ex- pressam esse: priorem (quæ omnium prima fuit apparitio post resurrectionem Marci XVI. 9.) Ma- ria Magdalena factam; alteram, quæ mulieribus reliquis digressis à monumento contigit. Quam excepit deinde apparitio Simoni Petro facta Luc. XXIV. 34. uti hanc sequuta est manifestatio, quæ Emauntinis discipulis evenit, Marc. XVI. 12. Luc. XXIV. 13.

## 28:3
Vers. 3. ἰδέα] I think it is nothing other than πρόσωπον. See above chapter XVII. 2. Although otherwise it extends more broadly, as when Plutarch says ἰδέαν τῷ σώματι & ἄμεμπτον. But here it is clearly distinguished from the clothed part of the body. Add that the passage of Daniel c. X. 6. is not obscurely referred to, ופניו כמראה ברק, where in Greek τὸ πρόσωπον αὐτᾶ ὡς ἡ ὅρασις ἀστραπῆς.

Τὸ ἔνδυμα] That garment reached to the ankles. For Mark calls it στολὴν: such as was the ποδήρης of the High Priest of the Jews: which στολὴ is often in Josephus. Thus Christ appears to John ἐνδεδυμέν& ποδήρη (Apoc. I. 13.). The angel is clothed in linen to Daniel (XII. 6.).

Λευκὸν ὡσεὶ χιὼν] See Acts I. 10. The highest whiteness is compared to snow, as among the Greeks and Latins, so also among the Hebrews (Num. XII. 10., Ps. L. 9., Lam. IV. 7.). Whiteness is undoubtedly a sign of purity and holiness (Dan. VII. 9., Apoc. III. 4. 5. 18., c. IV. 4., c. VI. 11., c. VII. 9. 13.). Therefore it was accepted among all nations to wear white when performing divine service, to which that of the Greek Comedy alludes: 'I justify myself to God thus throughout, not being bright in my robes as in my heart.' But to this whiteness in the garment of the angels, its own splendor was present, just as also to Christ in the transfiguration (above XVII. 2.). Therefore Luke: ἐν ἐσθήσεσιν ἀστραπτέσαις, which is a sign of heavenly honor. This is what Herod Agrippa wished to be admired, of whom Josephus says: 'where the silver, struck by the first rays of the sun, shone wonderfully, gleaming with something fearful and terrifying to those gazing upon him': at which sight the people called him superior to mortal nature. Luke (Acts XII. 22.) says it was acclaimed to him, 'the voice of a God and not of a man,' which amounts to the same thing. For God speaks through angels.

Latin:

Vers. 3. ἰδέα] Puto non aliud esse quam πρόσωπον. Vide supra cap. XVII. 2. Quanquam alioqui latius patet, ut cum Plutarchus dicit ἰδέαν τῷ σώματι & ἄμεμπτον. At hic manife- ste distinguitur à parte corporis vestita. Adde quod non ob- scure Danielis locus respicitur c. X. 6. ופניו כמראה ברק, ubi Græce τὸ πρόσωπον αὐτᾶ ὡς ἡ ὅρασις ἀστραπῆς.

Τὸ ἔνδυμα] Vestimentum id ad talos erat demissum. Στολὴν enim vocat Marcus: qualis erat ποδήρης Pontificis Maximi Judæorum: quæ στολὴ sæpe Josepho. Sic Christus Johanni apparet ἐνδεδυμέν& ποδήρη Apocal. I. 13. Angelus Danieli lineis indutus XII. 6.

Λευκὸν ὡσεὶ χιὼν] Vide Act. I. 10. summus candor nivi comparatur, ut apud Græcos & Latinos, ita & apud He- bræos Num. XII. 10. Psal L. 9. Thren. IV. 7. Candor haud dubie signum puritatis ac sanctimoniæ, Dan. VII. 9. Apoc. III. 4. 5 18. c. IV. 4. c. VI. 11. c. VII. 9. 13. Ideo apud omnes gentes receptum λευχημονεῖν cum rem divinam fa- cerent, quo illud alludit Comœdiæ Græcæ: Θεῶ δὲ ὧδε διὰ τέλες δικαιῶ ὢν, Μὴ λαμπρὸς ὢν ταῖς χλαμύσιν ὡς τῇ καρδίᾳ. Sed huic candori in veste Angelorum splendor suus aderat, quemadmodum & Christo ἐν τῇ μεταμορφήσει supra XVII. 2. Ideo Lucas: ἐν ἐσθήσεσιν ἀστραπτέσαις, quod signum honoris est cœlestis. Hoc est quod mirari voluit Herodes Agrippa, de quo Josephus: ἔνθα ταῖς πρώταις τῶν ἡλιακῶν ἀκτίνων ἐπιβολαῖς ὁ ἄργυρ& καταυγασθεὶς θαυμασίως ἀπέστιλβε, μαρ- μαίρων τι φοβερὸν καὶ τοῖς εἰς αὐτὸν ἀτενίζεσι φρικῶδες: quo conspectu populus eum vocavit κρείττονα τῆς θνητῆς φύσεως. Lucas Act. XII. 22. ait ei acclamatum φωνὴ Θεῦ καὶ ἐκ ἀν- θρώπυ, quod eodem redit. Nam per angelos Deus loquitur.

## 28:5
V. 5. Μὴ φοβεῖσθε] For fear had also pervaded them, not from an evil conscience like the soldiers, but from the weakness of human nature: just as we read that the pious were generally afraid in the Old and New Testaments whenever they saw visions: especially the more majestic ones, as Ezek. c. I. 28., Job V. 13. Luke adds that the faces of the women were cast down to the ground: which is likewise an indication of astonishment. See what is above XVII. 6. Magdalene, however, also wept, which happens to those who are mourning. Angels are accustomed to console the pious who are struck down in this manner (Judg. VI. 23., Luke I. 13. 30., Dan. X. 12.). Thus also Christ raises up John (Apoc. I. 17.).

Ζητεῖτε] Struck with awe, they were casting their eyes into the cave, seeing whether they might behold the body of Christ in that hollow of the cave, where they had seen it placed on the day of Preparation. For that hollow, as Bede testifies, was turned toward the mouth of the cave, so that some part of the body placed into the hollow (for that was the custom of the Hebrews) could be seen from the mouth of the cave. For on the day of Preparation, Magdalene and the other women had not entered into the cave, but were sitting opposite the tomb (above c. XXVII. 61.). That is, in the open air, at the mouth of the cave. From there they saw how and where the body was placed (Mark XV. 47., Luke XXIII. 55.). Thus also here Magdalene standing at the monument, that is, at the cave, which is strictly called a monument (John XX. 1.), and so as to be at the mouth of the cave (for which reason Luke said here, 'having entered,' using the plural for the singular by synecdoche), casts her eyes into the cave, but does not see the body. Luke, following the synecdoche, says 'they did not find the body of the Lord Jesus.' To these standing, the angel says that he sees that Jesus is being sought by them; Matthew here, Mark VI, Luke V, which she herself confesses, saying to the angel, 'They have taken away my Lord and I do not know where they have laid him' (John XX. 13.). Only afterwards is she warned by the angel to enter the cave and behold everything more closely (below 6, Mark XVI. 6.). Thus also John afterwards, not entering into the cave, but looking in with his head bent (which is παρακύπτον), sees the funeral wrappings (c. XX. 5.), namely, cast before the hollow itself, or in the hollow.

Latin:

V. 5. Μὴ φοβεῖσθε] Nam & illas timor pervaserat, non ex improba conscientia ut milites, sed ex naturæ humanæ im- becillitate: quomodo plerumque pios timuisse legimus in veteri novoque fœdere quoties viderunt ὀπτασίας: præsertim augustiores, ut Ezech. c. I. 28. Job. V. 13. Addit Lucas vul- tus mulierum in terram dejectos fuisse: quod itidem stupo- ris indicium est. Vide quæ supra XVII. 6. Magdalena vero etiam flevit, quod lugentibus accidit. Solent autem angeli pios perculsos hunc in modum consolari. Jud. VI. 23. Luc. 1. 13. 30. Dan. X. 12. Sic & Christus Johanne erigit, Ap. I. 17.

Ζητεῖτε] Perculsæ oculos imittebant intra specum, vi- derntes an Christi corpus in eo specus cavo conspicerent, ubi positum viderant ἐν τῇ παρασκευῇ. Nam cavum illud, te- stante Beda, qua patebat obversum erat ori specus, ita ut pars aliqua corporis in cavum immissi)is enim mos erat He- bræorum) ex ore specus conspici posset. Nam & die παρα- σκευῆς Magdalena aliæq; mulieres non intrarant in specum, sed erant καθήμεναι ἀπέναντι τῶ τάφε supra c. XXVII. 61. Id est ἐν τῷ ὑπαίθρῳ, ad os specus Inde videbant ὡς καὶ πᾶ ἐτέθη τὸ σῶμα. Marc. XV. 47. Luc. XXIII. 55. Sic & hic Magdale- na stans πρὸς τὸ μνημεῖον, id est, ad specum, qui stricte μνη- μεῖον dicitur Joh. XX. 1. atq; ita ut in ore esset specus (quam- obrem Lucas hic dixit, εἰσελθᾶσαι, κατὰ συνεκδοχὴν plurale pro singulari usurpans) oculos in specum injicit, sed corpus non videt. Lucas συνεκδοχὴν persequens ἐχ᾽ εὗρον inquit τῶ σῶμα τῶ κυρίε Ἰησῦ. Hi stanti dicit angelus videre se Je- sum ab iis quæri; Matth. hic, Marc. VI. Luc. V. quod ipsa faretur dicens angelo ἦραν τὸν κύριόν με καὶ ἐκ οἶδα πᾶ ἔθηκαν αὐτὸν, Joh. XX. 13. Postea demum ab angelo monetur ut intret specum, & propius omnia conspiceret, infra 6. Marci XVI. 6. Sic & Johannes postea non intrans in specum, sed capite inferto introspiciens (quod est παρακύπτον) videt fa- scias funerales c. XX. 5. nempe projectas ante ipsum cavum, aut in cavo.

## 28:6
V. 6. ὐκ ἔστιν ὧδε, ἠγέρθη] Luke adds what pertains to the same sentiment: 'Why do you seek the living among the dead?'

Ἴδετε] Believe with your eyes, which is the most certain way to the perception of truth. Mark XVI. 14., John I. Epist. I. 1.

Τὸν τόπον] That hollow in the cave. Bede calls it a 'loculus' (niche), Josephus sometimes calls it a 'θήκη' (receptacle). And from this we understand that it is not in vain what the describers of Palestine report about a double cave: for they call this hollow in the side of the cave, which is the proper place of the body, the inner cave.

Ὅπε ἔκειτο] Properly: where he was laid. Frequent in Greek epitaphs, ἐνθάδε κεῖται, as in Latin: Hic situs est (Here he is laid).

ὁ κύριος] Absolute: as if the angel were saying, not only your Lord, but ours as well. For by the resurrection that kingdom of Christ was being inaugurated, under which even the angels are.

Latin:

V. 6. ὐκ ἔστιν ὧδε, ἠγέρθη] Addit Lucas quod ad eandem sententiam pertinet: τι ζητεῖτε τὸν ζῶντα μετὰ τῶν νεκρῶν.

Ἴδετε] Oculis credite, quæ certissima ad veri perceptio- nem via. Marci XVI. 14. Joh. I. Epist. I. 1.

Τὸν τόπον] Cavum illud in specu. Loculum vocat Beda, θήκην Josephus aliquoties. Atque hinc inde intelligimus non vanum esse quod produnt descriptores Palæstinæ de spelunca duplici: nam cavum hoc in latere speluncæ, qui proprius corporis locus, vocant interiorem speluncam.

Ὅπε ἔκειτο] Proprie: ubi situs fuit. Frequens Græco- rum epitaphiis, ἐνθάδε κεῖται, ut in Latinis: Hic situs est.

ὁ κύριος] Absolute: quasi dicat angelus, non vester tan- tum, sed noster quoque Dominus. Nam resurrectione in- choabatur regnum illud Christi, sub quo sunt & angeli.

## 28:7
Vers. 7. ταχὺ] So that those who are wavering may be confirmed, and those weeping and mourning may enjoy consolation. See Mark here at verse 10. προάγει ὑμᾶς εἰς τὴν Γαλιλαίαν] Where Christ had more disciples to whom, as 'witnesses chosen beforehand,' as Peter speaks in Acts 10:41, he wished his resurrection to be testified: for there were five hundred to whom he gave himself to be seen, as we learn from Paul. Christ performed more than he promised. For he had promised that he would appear to them in Galilee: and while they were hesitating to go there, he appeared first in Jerusalem: then more often in Galilee. Concerning the word προάγειν see above XXVI. 32. and compare the words of Micah II. 13. Ἰδὲ εἶπον ὑμῖν] Both he foretold it, and I now proclaim it again. All these things pertained to shaking off the lethargy of 'little faith,' which was not shaken off even by this. Vers. 8. Μετὰ φόβε κὶ χαρᾶς μεγάλης] What the cause of the fear and also the amazement (for Mark puts 'trembling and astonishment') was, we have seen above at chapter V. They were rejoicing, however, not so much because they believed in Christ's resurrection (which they could not even comprehend in their minds) as because they had been deemed worthy of a heavenly vision. See Luke XXIV. 22. In a similar way, that fear through which salvation is effected, Philippians II. 12, is not separated from joy, 1 Peter I. 8, chapter IV. 13, 1 Thessalonians I. 6. ὡς δὲ ἐπορεύοντο ἀπαγγεῖλαι] They were indeed going to report what they had seen to the Apostles: but they dared not reveal the matter to anyone they met, for fear of the Jews. Thus we interpret that passage in Mark, 'they said nothing to anyone, for they were afraid.' However, since these words are in most Codices, and the Syrian and Greek interpreters acknowledge them, I would not dare to delete them. For the fact that καὶ παρελκὸ is a very well-known Hebraism, as above chapter IX. 10. Vers. 9. ἀπήντησεν αὐταῖς] A synecdoche or a change of number, unless we prefer to say, which is credible, that a handmaid was present with Magdalene. But Magdalene, moved by I know not what impulse, had returned from the journey to the monument. For thus I think that which John says, 'she turned back,' is rightly explained. It is the same appearance which Mark commemorates in chapter XVI. 9. For there is no reason why we should invent different ones, for 'having risen' in Mark is not 'as soon as Christ had risen,' but 'he himself who had risen.' For he wishes to indicate this, that the very body of Christ appeared to them, which could not have happened unless he had truly risen. 'Early on the first day of the week,' the same Mark added, to show that it was already clear morning when this happened. For the earlier events had happened 'very early' in the morning: this was 'early,' that is, in the clear morning. χαίρετε] Also addressing Mary by name, as those who greet are accustomed to do. Thus John. ἐκράτησαν ἀυτὲ τὲς πόδας] Christ ordered Mary, who was embracing his feet, to desist. For this was the reason why he said 'do not touch me' in John, that is, refrain from embracing me. Mary was hoping that she would now fully enjoy his presence, which a familiar embrace signified: but Christ teaches that those appearances were only 'economical' for the strengthening of faith: but that it would be granted to them to enjoy his presence only in the heavenly kingdom, to which he was going ahead to prepare a lodging for his own: to which when they themselves had one day arrived, then they would embrace Christ, in that manner, namely, in which Christ had declared he would eat and drink wine in the kingdom of the Father, leading them from sensible things to intelligible ones. It seems that Magdalene, because she was rejected from the embrace of Christ, concluded from this that what she had seen of Christ was not that body which had been buried in the sepulcher. Therefore, when she was reporting the whole matter to the Apostles, she did indeed tell of the 'vision' of angels, but said the body was not found, Luke XXIV. 22, suspecting even then that it had been taken away from the monument, John XX. 2. Certainly, in the minds of some of the Apostles, too, something of the sort had settled, which, so that Christ might uproot it, he says, 'a spirit does not have flesh and bones,' Luke XXIV. 39, and Thomas, not content with seeing, wished to explore the body with touch as well: moved by which arguments Origen, against Celsus II, thinks it was believed by the Jews that 'a luminous body of the soul can appear to sensible eyes,' following the Pythagoreans: and he refers to that passage of Homer: 'In all things resembling him in stature and beautiful eyes.' And the illustrious passage 'concerning the luminous body' (for he uses the same word) in Hierocles on that verse of the golden poem, 'Having set the charioteer, the best judgment, from above.' Where he, according to the opinion of the Pythagoreans, says that human souls, just like the stars, are 'neither body nor without a body,' but have a 'connatural immortal body': and that this is for Plato the 'winged pair' whose charioteer is the soul. He himself also calls it a 'psychical body,' which he opposes to the 'mortal body': and says the same is called in the oracles the 'subtle vehicle of the soul.' Porphyry: 'Blood is the pasture and food of the spirit. But the spirit is the soul itself or the vehicle of the soul.' The Chaldeans call this מַלְבּוּשׁ הַפְּנִימִי, and the Arab Meir Aldati explains it as a spirit intermediate between the soul and the body: the Greeks note that 'eidolon' is said in Homer: nor is it called otherwise in those poems which are ascribed to Zoroaster. But whether this opinion concerning the body of the soul, that it is such that it can be seen by human eyes, belonged to the ancient Hebrews, or whether, like many things, it was [derived] from the Chaldeans and Greeks to later [authors]

It may be doubted whether it came to the Hebrews. Josephus, describing the tenets of the Pharisees, says ψυχὰς μεταϐαίνειν εἰς ἕτερον σῶμα, which is far different. Wherefore it is more credible that Magdalene thought an Angel had appeared to her, and this all the more because she was neither permitted to touch him, nor did he himself clearly declare that he was Jesus: and from this I think it came about that this ἐπιφάνεια also is included under the name ὀπτασίας Ἀγγέλων, Luc. XXIV. 23.

Latin:

Vers. 7. ταχὺ] Ut nutantes confirmentur, flentes & lu- gentes fruantur solatio. Vide Marcum hic commate 10. προάγει ὑμᾶς εἰς τὴν Γαλιλαίαν] Ubi plures discipulos Chri- stus habebat quibus, tanquam μάρτυσι προκεχειροτονημένοις, ut loquitur Petrus Actor. X. 41. resurrectionem suam te- statan esse voluit: Nam quingenti fuerunt quibus vide- dum se dedit, ut ex Paulo discimus. Plus præstitit Christus quam promisit. Promiserat enim in Galilæa se ipsis appa- riturum: ac cunctantibus eo ire Hierosolymis primum ap- paruit: deinde in Galilæa sæpius. De voce προάγειν vide supra XXVI. 32. & confer verba Micheæ II. 13. Ἰδὲ εἶπον ὑμῖν] Et ille prædixit, & ego nunc iterum præ- dico. Hæc omnia pertinebant ad excutiendum τῆς ὀλιγο- πιστίας veternum, quod ne sic quidem excussum est. Vers. 8. Μετὰ φόβε κὶ χαρᾶς μεγάλης] Quæ timoris at- que etiam stuporis (nam τρόμον καὶ ἔκστασιν ponit Marcus) causa fuerit, vidimus supra ad caput V. Gavisæ autem erant non tam quod Christi resurrectionem crederent (quam ne animo quidem comprehendere satis poterant) quam quod dignatæ essent viso cœlesti. Vide Luc. XXIV. 22. Simili modo timor ille, per quem salus efficitur, Philipp. II. 12. non est abjunctus à gaudio, 1. Petr. I. 8. c. IV. 13. 1. Thess. I. 6. ὡς δὲ ἐπορεύοντο ἀπαγγεῖλαι] Ibant quidem ut Apostolis visa referrent: at nemini obvio rem aperire audebant, præ metu Judæorum. Ita interpretamur illud apud Marcum ἐδενὶ ἐδὲν εἶπον ἐφοβεῖντο γὰρ. Verba autem hæc cum sint in plerisque Codicibus, & Syrus Græcique interpretes agno- scant, delere non ausim. Nam quod καὶ παρελκὸ notissi- mus est Hebraismus, ut supra c. IX 10. Vers. 9. ἀπήντησεν αὐταῖς] συνεκδοχὴ sive numeri ἐναλλα- γὴ, nisi dicere malumus, quod credibile est, ancillam Mag- dalænæ adfuisse. Magdalenæ autem nescio quo mota ex iti- nere recurrerat ad monumentum. Ita enim recte exponi puto quod Johannes dicit ἐστράφη εἰς τὰ ὀπίσω. Eadem est ἐπιφάνεια, quam Marcus commemorat cap. XVI. 9. Nulla enim causa est, cur diversas comminiscamur, ἀναστὰς enim apud Marcum est, non simul ac resurrexerat Christus, sed i- pse qui resurrexerat. Hoc enim vult indicare, ipsum Chri- sti corpus ipsis apparuisse, quod fieri non poterat, nisi re- vera resurrexisset. πρωὶ πρώτῃ σαββάτων ideo addidit idem Marcus, ut ostenderet jam clarum mane fuisse cum id acci- dit. Nam priora acciderant λίαν πρωὶ primo mane: hoc πρωὶ id est, mane claro. χαίρετε] Etiam Mariam nomine compellans, ut salutan- tes solent. Ita Johannes. ἐκράτησαν ἀυτὲ τὲς πόδας] Mariam pedes suos ample- xantem abstinere Christus jussit. Hæc enim erat causa cur diceret μήπε ἅπτε apud Johannem, id est, parce me am- plexari. Futurum, ut illius præsentia jam plene frueretur, sperabat Maria, quod significabat familiaris amplexatio: at Christus docet istas ἐπιφανείας fuisse tantum οἰκονομικὰς fir- mandæ fidei: frui autem ipsius præsentia datum ipsis iri in regno demum cœlesti, quo præibat hospitium suis para- turus: quo cum ipsæ olim pervenissent tum amplexaturæ es- sent Christum, eo scilicet modo quo Christus se in regno Patris & Pascha esurum & vinum bibiturum pronuntiave- rat, ἀπὸ τῶν αἰσθητῶν εἰς τὰ νοητὰ ἀνάγων. Videtur Magdalē- na, quia ab amplexu Christi rejecta erat, hinc collegisse id quod Christi viderat non fuisse corpus illud quod sepul- chro conditum fuerat. Ideo cum rem omnem Apostolis renuntiaret, narravit quidem ὀπτασίαν angelorum, sed corpus dixit non repertum Luc. XXIV. 22. suspicata etiam tunc sublatum fuisse ex monumento Ioh. XX. 2. Certe A- postolorum quoq; nonnullis tale aliquid animo insederat, quod ut avellat Christus, ait, πνεῦμα σάρκα κὶ ὀσέα ἐκ ἔχει Luc. XXIV. 39. & Thomas conspicari non contentus tactu etiam explorare corpus voluit: Quibus argumentis permotus Origenes contra Celsum II. existimat creditum Judæis ὅτι δύναται ὀφθαλμοῖς αἰσθητοῖς φανῆναι ψυχῆς σῶμα ἀυγοειδὲς Pythagoreos secutus: atque eo refert Homeri illud: Πάντα δ' ἐοικώς μέγεθος τε καὶ ὄμματα καλὰ. Et illustris περὶ τὲ ἀυγοειδὲς σώματὸς (nam eadem voce uti- tur) locus apud Hieroclem ad illud aurei carminis, Ηνίοχον γνώμην σήσας καθύπερθεν ἀρίστην. Ubi ille ex Pythagoricorum sententia ait animos humanos Perinde ut astra μήτε σῶμα εἶναι μήτε ἄνευ σώματος, sed ha- bere συμφυες ἀθάνατον σῶμα: atque hoc esse Platoni ὑπόπτε- ρον ζεῦγος cujus auriga sit animus. Ipse etiam ψυχικὸν σῶ- μα vocat, quod τῷ θνητῷ σώματι opponit: idemque ait ἐν χρησμοῖς vocari ψυχῆς λεπτὸν ὄχημα. Porphyrius: τὸ αἷμα νομὴ κὶ τροφή ἐσι τᾶ πνεύματος. τὸ δὲ πνεῦμα ἐσιν ἀυτὴ ἡ ψυχὴ ἢ ὄχημα τῆς ψυχῆς. Chaldæi hoc vocant מַלְבּוּשׁ הַפְּנִימִי, & Arabs Meir Aldati exponit spiritum medium inter ani- mam & corpus: εἴδωλον apud Homerum dici notant Græci: nec aliter appellatur in iis carminibus, quæ ascribuntur Zoroastri. Cæterum an hæc opinio de corpore animi quod tale sit ut humanis oculis conspici possit veterum Hebræo- rum fuerit, an ut multa à Chaldæis & Græcis ad posteriores

Hebraeos venerit dubitari potest. Josephus Pharisaica scita deseribens ait ψυχὰς μεταϐαίνειν εἰς ἕτερον σῶμα, quod lon- ge est aliud. Quare credibilius est existimasse Magdale- nam Angelum sibi apparuisse, idque eo magis, quia nec tangere eum licuerit, neque ipse Jesum se esse liquido pro- nunciaverit: atque inde factum reor, ut haec quoque ἐπι- φάνεια comprehendatur sub nomine ὀπτασίας Ἀγγέλων, Luc. XXIV. 23.

## 28:9
καὶ προσεκύνησαν αὐτῷ] So also below in verse 17, concerning the disciples, προσεκύνησαν αὐτῷ. Christ was indeed accustomed, as were the Prophets of old, to be worshipped (προσκυνεῖσθαι) by those who approached to pray for something; but not in the same way by those who were more familiarly in his presence. Wherefore we understand from this that these women, although not yet sufficiently convinced of the resurrection of the buried body, had nevertheless conceived in their minds something greater concerning Christ than ever before.

Latin:

καὶ προσεκύνησαν αὐτῷ] Ita & infra commate 17. de disci- pulis προσεκύνησαν αὐτῷ. Solebat quidem Christus, ut & Prophetae olim, ab his qui aliquid oraturi accedebant προσ- κυνεῖσθαι: at non itidem ab iis qui familiarius ipsi aderant. Quare hinc intelligimus has feminas, quanquam de resur- rectione sepulti corporis nondum satis persuasas, majus ta- men quiddam animo concepisse de Christo, quam unquam antea.

## 28:10
Vers. 10. Τοῖς ἀδελφοῖς μᵾ] Not blood relatives, as some would have it, but disciples, whence also the alternative reading μαθηταῖς μᵾ from an ancient interpretation has penetrated into the text of certain codices. By this word Christ, alluding to the passage in Psalm XXII. 22, wished to signify what He had previously hinted at, above in chapter XII. 48, that through His death and resurrection He had been made the head of a certain new ἀδελφότητος, inasmuch as He had now been most openly declared the Son of God. John XX. 17, Πορεύου πρὸς τοὺς ἀδελφούς με, καὶ εἰπὲ αὐτοῖς, ἀναϐαίνω πρὸς τὸν πατέρα με, καὶ πατέρα ὑμῶν, Θεόν με, καὶ Θεὸν ὑμῶν. The writer to the Hebrews, chapter II. 11, ὅ τε γὰρ ἁγιάζων καὶ οἱ ἁγιαζόμενοι ἐξ ἑνὸς πάντες δι ἣν αἰτίαν ὀυκ ἐπαισχύνεται ἀδελφοὺς ἀυτὸς καλεῖν: where he also cites the aforementioned passage of the Psalm. Rom. VIII. 29, ὣς προέγνω καὶ προώρισε συμμόρφες τῆς εἰκόνος τᾶ ὑιᾶ ἀυτᾶ, εἰς τὸ εἶναι ἀυτὸν πρωτότοκον ἐν πολλοῖς ἀδελφοῖς.

PART II. The lie concerning the theft of the body of Jesus, spread by the Elders through the soldiers.

Latin:

Vers. 10. Τοῖς ἀδελφοῖς μᵾ] Non consanguineis, ut qui- dam volunt, sed discipulis, unde & lectio altera μαθηταῖς μᵾ ex veteri interpretamento in textum quorundam codi- cum penetravit. Hac voce Christus alludens ad locum Psal- mi XXII. 22. significare voluit, quod olim innuerat, supra cap. XII. 48. se per mortem & resurrectionem factum esse principem novae cujusdam ἀδελφότητος, quippe cum jam apertissime declaratus esset Dei filius. Johannes XX. 17. Πορεύου πρὸς τοὺς ἀδελφούς με, καὶ εἰπὲ αὐτοῖς, ἀναϐαίνω πρὸς τὸν πατέρα με, καὶ πατέρα ὑμῶν, Θεόν με, καὶ Θεὸν ὑμῶν. Scriptor ad Hebraeos cap. II. 11. ὅ τε γὰρ ἁγιάζων καὶ οἱ ἁγιαζόμενοι ἐξ ἑνὸς πάντες δι ἣν αἰτίαν ὀυκ ἐπαισχύνεται ἀδελφοὺς ἀυτὸς καλεῖν: ubi & dictum Psalmi locum citat. Rom. VIII. 29. ὣς προέ- γνω καὶ προώρισε συμμόρφες τῆς εἰκόνος τᾶ ὑιᾶ ἀυτᾶ, εἰς τὸ εἶναι ἀυτὸν πρωτότοκον ἐν πολλοῖς ἀδελφοῖς.

PARS II. Mendacium de furto ablato corpore Iesu, à Senioribus per milites divulga- tum.

## 28:11
Vers. 11. Πορευομένων δὲ ἀυτῶν] The present tense is used for the past: that is, when they had already gone away. For he does not mean that this happened while they were on the journey, but after they had departed from the sepulchre.

Ἰδού τινες τῆς κυστοδίας] The chief ones in the name of the rest.

τοῖς ἀρχιερεῦσιν] To whose commands they were so obedient, that nevertheless they owed the final account of their actions to the Governor, as we have said.

ἅπαντα τὰ γενόμενα] Earthquake, heavenly vision, rolled-away stone, body not found.

Latin:

Vers. 11. Πορευομένων δὲ ἀυτῶν] Praesens pro praeterito: id est cum jam abiissent. Neque enim vult hoc factum dum in itinere erant, sed postquam à sepulchro discesserant.

Ἰδού τινες τῆς κυστοδίας] Praecipui caeterorum nomine.

τοῖς ἀρχιερεῦσιν] Quorum imperiis ita parebant, ut ta- men ultimam actuum suorum rationem deberent Praesidi, ut diximus.

ἅπαντα τὰ γενόμενα] Terramotum, visum coeleste, devo- lutum lapidem, corpus non repertum.

## 28:12
Ver. 12. Μετὰ τῶν πρεσϐυτέρων] A description of the Sanhedrin: for now it could assemble, the Sabbath having passed. Here the prophecy of Hosea 12:1 is fulfilled.

Latin:

Vers. 12. Μετὰ τῶν πρεσϐυτέρων] Synedrii descriptio: jam enim convenire poterat Sabbato exacto. Impletur hic vaticinium Oseae XII. 1.

## 28:13
Vers. 13. Ἡμῶν κοιμωμένων] We see here τὸ ἀυτοκατάκριτον. Having heard the truth from witnesses who were not suspect, they redeem their lie with money. Truly, vices lead headlong. Ambition and envy attracted cruelty; that expelled what remained of conscience. The ancients well note here the blindness of depraved minds. For if anyone considers the matter with a calm mind, Σφόδρ᾽ ἐυάλωτον ἐσιν ἡ πονηρία. For how could the testimony be consistent regarding that which they said happened while they were sleeping? Furthermore, with what confidence would these men, both unarmed and fishermen, have dared this? If they themselves already felt within their minds that Christ was an impostor, why would they undergo danger for him? If they believed he was sent by God, what religion drove them to theft and lying? That a person should undergo death for an opinion he has conceived is possible, although even this is rare: but that anyone should do the same for the testimony of a matter which he knows to be false, and from which no good can be hoped for either by himself or by others, ought to seem incredible to all men of sound judgment.

Latin:

Vers. 13. Ἡμῶν κοιμωμένων] Videmus hic τὸ ἀυτοκατά- κριτον. Veritate audita ex non suspectis testibus, menda- cium pecunia redimunt. Nimirum vitia in praeceps ducunt. Ambitio & invidia crudelitatem attraxit, ea expulit quod superat conscientiae. Bene autem notant hic veteres im- probarum mentium caecitatem. Si quis enim placido a- nimo res consideret, Σφόδρ᾽ ἐυάλωτον ἐσιν ἡ πονηρία. Quomodo enim constare poterat fides testibus de eo quod se dormientibus dicerent evenisse: Deinde qua fiducia au- si hoc fuissent homines & inermes & piscatores? si imposto- rem Christum ipsi jam intra mentem animi sentiebant, cur pro ipso subirent periculum? si à Deo missum crederent, quae religio illos impellebat ad furtum & mendacium? ut pro concepta opinione mortem quis subeat, fieri potest, quanquam & hoc rarum est: at ut quis idem faciat pro te- stimonio rei quam falsam esse novit, & unde nihil aut ipsi aut aliis boni possit sperari, omnibus sani judicii homini- bus incredibile videri debet.

## 28:14
Vers. 14. Ἐπὶ τᾶ ἡγεμόνος] The Syrian well renders it קרם ההגמונר, for the Greeks speak in this way properly concerning the consistory of judges. Festus to Paul, Acts XXV. 9: θέλεις εἰς Ἱεροσόλυμα ἀναϐὰς ἐκεῖ περὶ τύτων κρίνεσθε ἐπ᾿ ἐμᾶ.

Ἐὰν ἀκυσθῇ τῦτο] Doubtless, poorly managed watches and a deserted post, which were severely punished among the Romans, the keen defenders of military discipline. See the title of the Digest concerning military affairs.

πείσομεν ἀυτὸν] That is, we will render him placid. John said in 1 Ep. III. 19, Πείσομεν τὰς καρδίας ἡμῶν. Nor do I think the origin of the Syriac word שיד, by which that same thing is signified, should be sought from elsewhere. For thus παῤῥησία also and other Greek words have received a certain peculiar meaning among the Syrians and Jews.

ἀμερίμνες ποιήσομεν] A legal term. For thus the Greeks say what the Latins call to hold harmless.

Latin:

Vers. 14. Ἐπὶ τᾶ ἡγεμόνος] Bene Syrus קרם ההגמונר Proprie enim de Judicum consistorio ita loquuntur Graeci. Festus ad Paulum Act. XXV. 9. θέλεις εἰς Ἱεροσόλυμα ἀναϐὰς ἐκεῖ περὶ τύτων κρίνεσθε ἐπ᾿ ἐμᾶ.

Ἐὰν ἀκυσθῇ τῦτο] Nimirum male curatas excubias & de- sertam stationem, quae graviter puniebantur apud Roma- nos acres militaris disciplinae vindices. Vide Digestorum titulum de re militari.

πείσομεν ἀυτὸν] Id est, placidum reddemus. Πείσομεν τὰς καρδίας ἡμῶν dixit Johannes I. ep. III. 19 Neque aliunde puto accersendam originem Syriaci verbi שיד quo idem illud significatur. Nam sic παῤῥησία quoque & aliae voces Graecae significatum quendam peculiarem apud Syros & Judaeos accepere.

ἀμερίμνες ποιήσομεν] Vox juris. Ita enim Graeci dicunt, quod Latini indemnem praestare.

## 28:15
Vers. 15. Καὶ διεφημίσθη ὁ λόγος ὗτος παρὰ Ἰυδαίοις μέχρι τῆς σήμερον] All the ancients with great consensus understand that lying rumor about the body of Christ being stolen by the disciples. If we accept this, we will not wrongly refer here to that embassy which Justin mentions in two places as having been sent by the Sanhedrin to the Jews of the whole world. For he teaches that the summary of that embassy was this: ὅτι αἵρεσίς τις ἄθεος καὶ ἄνομος ἐγήγερται ἀπὸ Ἰησοῦ τινος γαλιλαίου πλάνου ὃν σταυρωσάντων ἡμῶν οἱ μαθηταὶ αὐτοῦ κλέψαντες αὐτὸν ἀπὸ τοῦ μνήματος νυκτὸς ὁπόθεν κατετέθη ἀφηλωθεὶς ἀπὸ τοῦ σταυροῦ, πλανῶσι τοὺς ἀνθρώπους λέγοντες ἐγηγέρθαι αὐτὸν ἐκ νεκρῶν καὶ εἰς οὐρανὸν ἐληλυθέναι. Tertullian: Nevertheless, however, the leaders, whose interest it was both to divulge the crime and to recall the people who were warring and serving them from the faith, claimed that he was stolen by the disciples. And certainly it is more credible that this rumor was spread by them with all zeal, because without some such figment they were most openly convicted of the crime. For it could not happen that those who believed that God presides over human affairs, and at the same time that Jesus was brought back to life, could doubt his innocence. Wherefore, the Apostles rightly fix their stand here in all gatherings of disputes. Yet other diligent and learned interpreters of these writings prefer to take these words of Matthew as if it were said that this wicked trafficking of a lie between the Priests and the soldiers could not be so hidden that truth did not find some crack through which it might emanate into public view. Which I also believe to be most true, and that this was the beginning of the conversion of many to Christ. For the knowledge of this deceit seems to have reached Pilate also: since Tertullian adds these things to those which we cited from him: Pilate, already a Christian in his own conscience, reported all those things concerning Christ to Caesar, then Tiberius. These things having been weighed thus, just as I do not disapprove of either, so I prefer the former interpretation to the latter. Moreover, that expression μέχρι τῆς σήμερον, which often occurs in the writers of the Old Testament, and is also found above in this book c. XXVII. 8, provides an argument that Matthew wrote some time after these events had happened. When, however, he wrote, there is no reason for anyone to hope that he can obtain anything more certain than what has been handed down by ancient authors, among whom the most ancient, Irenaeus, speaks thus about this matter as if it were a known and confessed fact: ὁ μὲν δὴ Ματθαῖος ἐν τοῖς ἑβραίοις τῇ ἰδίᾳ διαλέκτῳ αὐτῶν καὶ γραφὴν ἐξήνεγκεν Εὐαγγελίου, τοῦ Πετροῦ καὶ τοῦ Παύλου ἐν Ῥώμῃ εὐαγγελιζομένων καὶ θεμελιούντων τὴν ἐκκλησίαν. Ancient tradition assigns the eighth year from the assumption of Christ to this book.

It is manifest that these things are to be understood in that sense, as all the ancients with great consensus understand, namely, concerning the lying rumor about the body of Christ being stolen by the disciples. Therefore, how that which Grotius observes—that certain learned interpreters take these words as if it were said that this wicked trafficking of a lie between the Priests and the soldiers could not be so hidden that truth did not find some crack through which it might emanate into public view—fits this passage, does not appear; so that one must wonder that Grotius does not disapprove of this explanation, even if he prefers the former. For the words of the Evangelist or the context do not bear that interpretation; since it is clear that the discourse is about a lying rumor spread by the Jews.

PARS III. The apparition of Jesus made to the Apostles in Galilee.

Latin:

Vers. 15. Καὶ διεφημίσθη ὁ λόγος ὗτος παρὰ Ἰυδαίοις μέχρι τῆς σήμερον] Veteres omnes magno consensu intelli- gunt famam illam mendacem de corpore Christi à discipu- lis subtracto. Quod si recipimus, non male huc referemus ad eam legationem quam à Synedrio ad totius orbis Ju- dæos missam Justinus duobus locis memorat. Ejus enim legationis hanc docet summam fuisse: ὅτι αἵρεσίς τις ἄθεος καὶ ἄνομος ἐγήγερται ἀπὸ Ἰησοῦ τινος γαλιλαίου πλάνου ὃν σταυ- ρωσάντων ἡμῶν οἱ μαθηταὶ αὐτοῦ κλέψαντες αὐτὸν ἀπὸ τοῦ μνή- ματος νυκτὸς ὁπόθεν κατετέθη ἀφηλωθεὶς ἀπὸ τοῦ σταυροῦ, πλα- νῶσι τοὺς ἀνθρώπους λέγοντες ἐγηγέρθαι αὐτὸν ἐκ νεκρῶν καὶ εἰς οὐρανὸν ἐληλυθέναι. Tertullianus: Nihilominus tamen primo- res quorum intererat & scelus divulgare & populum belligerantem & famularem sibi à fide revocare, surreptum à discipulis jacta- taverunt. Et certe sparsum ab eis omni studio hunc rumorem eo est credibilius, quia sine tali aliquo figmento apertissi- me sceleris convincebantur. Neque enim fieri poterat ut qui Deum rebus humanis præsidere, simulque Jesum ad vi- tam resuscitatum crederent de ejus innocentia dubitarent. Quare merito in omnibus disputationum congressibus hic gradum figunt Apostoli. Malunt tamen alii diligentes atque eruditi harum literarum interpretes, ita hæc Mat- thæi verba accipere, quasi dicatur non potuisse ita celari sce- leratam istam inter Sacerdotes & milites mendacii nundi- nationem ut non aliquam rimam inveniret veritas, per quam in publicum emanaret. Quod ipsum quoque ve- rissimum credo, & hoc initium fuisse multorum ad Chri- stum conversionis. Nam ad Pilatum quoque pervenisse videtur hujus doli notitia: quando Tertullianus his quæ ex illo citavimus ista subjicit: Ea omnia super Christo Pilatus, & ipse jam pro sua conscientia Christianus, Cæsari tum Tiberio nuntiavit. His ita expensis, ut neutram improbo, ita prio- rem interpretationem posteriori præfero. Locutio autem ista μέχρι τῆς σήμερον, quæ in Veteris Fœderis Scriptoribus sæpe occurrit, & in hoc libro supra quoque invenitur c. XXVII. 8. argumentum præbet, aliquanto post scripsisse Matthæum quam res istæ acciderant. Quando autem scri- pferit, non est quod quisquam speret se certius aliquid posse adipisci quam à priscis auctoribus proditum est, quos inter vetustissimus Irenæus ita hac de re tanquam nota confessaque loquitur: ὁ μὲν δὴ Ματθαῖος ἐν τοῖς ἑβραίοις τῇ ἰδίᾳ διαλέκτῳ αὐτῶν καὶ γραφὴν ἐξήνεγκεν Εὐαγγελίου, τοῦ Πε- τροῦ καὶ τοῦ Παύλου ἐν Ῥώμῃ εὐαγγελιζομένων καὶ θεμελιούντων τὴν ἐκκλησίαν. Vetus fama octavum ab assumtione Christi an- num huic libro assignat.

Manifestum est hæc eo intelligenda esse sensu, uti veteres omnes magno consensu intelligunt, de fama nempe mendace de corpore Christi à disci- pulis subtracto. Quod ergo observat Grotius ac- cipere eruditos quosdam Interpretes hæc verba ita, quasi dicatur, non potuisse ita celari sceleratam istam inter Sacerdotes & milites mendacii nundinationem, ut non aliquam rimam invenerit veritas, per quam in publicum emanaret, id quomodo huic loco con- veniat, non apparet; ut mirari oporteat, Grotium hanc explicationem non improbare, etsi priorem præferat. Non enim ferunt interpretationem il- lam verba Evangelistæ, aut contextus: quum lu- culentum sit de fama mendaci sermonem esse à Ju- dæis divulgata.

PARS III. Apparitio Jesu Apostolis in Galilæa facta.

## 28:16
Vers. 16. Ἕνδεκα] Judas abstaining himself from the sacred fellowship on account of the consciousness of his crime.

Nay, Judas having already been taken off to the majority. For Matthew had already taught in chapter XXVII. 6 that he ended his life for himself by hanging: which passage Grotius took in vain concerning grief of mind, as if it were said there, when it sounds of the hanging by which he was strangled. For Grotius himself acknowledged in the same place that ἀπάγξασθαι for the Greeks is to take one's life by hanging. Grotius observes that this is the conjecture of many, that the death of Judas happened after the resurrection: but he brings forward no authors, nor does he accede to that opinion except hesitantly. But the common opinion holds that immediately after the thirty pieces of silver were returned, Judas ended his life by hanging and breathed out his soul. The series of the Evangelist's narrative suggests this in such a way that no room for different conjecture remains.

to the mountain where [Jesus] had appointed for them. Matthew passes over many appearances of Christ made to Peter, to the Apostles without Thomas, and with Thomas: being content with one most illustrious one, which had many witnesses still alive when he was writing this. Yet he indicates these appearances incidentally and in passing, when he says that the mountain was named by Christ to them, to which they should gather, namely himself and those who were of the same institution. For since Christ had said nothing before about that mountain, it is understood that the commands were given by him to the Apostles while they were still staying in Jerusalem. That this mountain was Tabor, on which Christ had once given three disciples a taste of his majesty, is said probably and has the authority of ancient fame.

Latin:

Vers. 16. Ἕνδεκα] Juda se à sacro consortio abstinente ob sceleris conscientiam.

Imo Juda jam ad plures abrepto. Eundem e- nim suspendio sibi vitam finiisse, Matthæus jam cap. XXVII. 6. docuerat: quem locum nequic- quam de animi mœrore accepit Grotius, uti illic dictum, quum de suspendio, quo strangulatus est, sonet. ἀπάγξασθαι enim Græcis esse suspendio sibi vitam adimere, agnovit ibidem Grotius. Multo- rum quidem hanc esse conjecturam, mortem Ju- dæ post resurrectionem contigisse Grotius obser- vat: sed autores nullos adducit, nec nisi titubanter illi sententiæ accedit. Communis autem sententia- fert, statim post restitutos triginta argenteos Ju- dam sibi vitam suspendio finivisse, animamque exhalasse. Quam series narrationis Evangelistae ita suggerit, ut conjecturae diversae locus non su- perfit.

εἰς τὸ ὄρος οὗ ἐτάξατο αὐτοῖς [ἰησοῦς] Multas ἐπιφανείας Christi factas Petro, Apostolis sine Thoma, & cum Thoma praeterit Matthaeus: quippe una illustrissima, quae pluri- mos testes habebat, cum hoc scriberet superstites, contentus, Obiter tamen & in transcursu has ἐπιφανείας indicat, cum dicit à Christo nominatum ipsis montem in quem conve- nirent, ipsi scilicet & qui ejusdem erant instituti. Nam cum nihil ante de eo monte dixerit Christus, datur intelligi man- data ab ipso data Apostolis, cum adhuc Hierosolymis age- rent. Montem hunc fuisse Itabyrium in quo Christus olim tribus discipulis majestatis suae gustum dederat, probabili- ter dicitur & veteris famae habet auctoritatem.

## 28:17
Verse 17.

worshipping him] They, with the gathered company of believers, up to five hundred, as we learn from Paul. For I do not see why we should distinguish these appearances. And as I said, it is credible that the others are passed over by Matthew because this one was the most famous of all. If Ignatius wrote as Jerome wishes, and Sophronius following him, 'and after the resurrection they saw him in the flesh,' it would have to be believed that Ignatius was led to this mountain by his parents or those to whose care his tender age was entrusted: just as we are accustomed to bring boys to see new things, so that they may have something which, when they are old, they may tell others with eyewitness faith, not hearsay. But truly, if anyone inspects the passage of Ignatius with care, he will see that the correct reading is 'I know': and that it is not a matter of the sense of sight there, but of faith, which he confirms not by his own testimony, but by that of others. Add that Ignatius survived after John had been removed from human affairs. For he never mentions John, not even in the one which is to the Ephesians. But such was the longevity of John that it is hardly credible that anyone survived him who could remember having seen Jesus.

but some doubted] An indefinite time admits various meanings according to the circumstance of the place. Therefore I do not see why it is less permissible to translate here: 'but some had doubted,' namely before that time: which can seem to have been said especially on account of Thomas, who had persisted in doubting while the others were already believing. But this part of the history also has its own importance. For to those weighing the matter entirely, it removes all doubt about the truth of the fact, that certain faith was given even to those who had been so difficult to convince,

More correctly, without doubt, others refer these things to some of the five hundred brethren in 1 Cor. XV, outside the College of the Apostles, whom the Apostles had brought with them to the mountain, but who were still doubting about the resurrection, until by the accurate sight of Christ the doubt was put to flight.

Latin:

Vers. 17.

προσκυνήσαντες αὐτῷ] Ipsi cum collecta credentium manu ad quingentos, ut ex Paulo discimus. Nam cur has ἐπι- φανείας distinguamus non video. Et ut dixi credibile est ideo caeteras à Matthaeo dissimulari, quia haec erat omnium celeberrima. Si Ignatius ita scripsit, ut vult Hieronymus & secutus eum Sophronius καὶ μετὰ τὴν ἀνάστασιν ἐν σαρκὶ αὐτὸν εἶδον, credendum esset Ignatium à parentibus aut eis quo- rum curae tenera ipsius aetas erat mandata in hunc montem fuisse perductum: ut solemus ad res novas visendas pueros adducere, ut habeant quod olim senes aliis oculata non au- dita fide narrent. Sed profecto, si quis locum Ignatii cum cura inspiciat, videbit rectam esse lectionem οἶδα: neque de visus sensu ibi agi, sed de fide, quam non suo, sed aliorum testimonio confirmat. Adde quod Ignatius Johanne rebus humanis exemto superfuit. Nusquam enim Johannis me- minit, ne in ea quidem quae est ad Ephesios. At tanta fuit Johannis longaevitas, ut vix credibile sit quemquam ei su- pervixisse qui visum à se Jesum posset meminisse.

οἱ δὲ ἐδίστασαν] Indefinitum tempus pro circumstantia loci varias significationes admittit. Quare non video qui minus hic vertere liceat: quidam vero addubitaberant, nem- pe ante id tempus: quod maxime ob Thomam dictum vi- deri potest, qui caeteris jam credentibus dubitare persevera- verat. Habet autem & haec pars historiae suum momen- tum. Nam aeque rem aestimantibus omnem dubitationem de facti veritate adimit certa fides illis etiam facta qui ad credendum tam difficiles fuerant,

Rectius sine dubio alii haec referunt ad nonnul- los è quingentis fratribus 1. Cor. XV. extra Aposto- lorum Collegium quos Apostoli secum in montem adduxerant, sed dubitantes adhuc de resurrectio- ne, donec accurato Christi intuitu fugata est dubi- tatio.

## 28:18
Verse 18.

And Jesus coming up] In one summary Matthew embraces the chief heads of the discourses which Christ had with the Apostles not only on the mountain, but also at Jerusalem before and after, when he was about to ascend into heaven, at Bethany. See what is said on Luke at this place.

All authority has been given to me] Dan. VII. 14. He had also possessed authority while living a mortal life, as above c. VII. 29, c. IX. 6, Mark II. 27, which we noted above in the words of Christ to Pilate was also called a kingdom more loosely. But by death he acquired an infinite kingdom, 'all authority': as Paul says Phil. II. 8, 'He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even the death of the cross. Wherefore God also highly exalted him, and gave him a name which is above every name.' In this third dignity Matthew rightly ends the book, since, as we have noted, he had dealt first with his Prophetic office, then with his Priestly office.

in heaven] In this heavenly power is included the promise of the Spirit which Christ is said to have received from the Father, Acts II. 33. And dominion over the Angels, Phil. II. 10, Heb. I. 4, Eph. I. 10, Col. I. 16.

and on earth] The right of gathering a people from all the ends of the earth, as David, Isaiah, and Daniel had clearly predicted. In this right is included the remission of sins, Mark here XVI. 16, 'He who believes and is baptized shall be saved': which Joel had predicted: 'Whoever shall call upon the name of the Lord shall be saved.' Then, freedom from the law given through Moses, which Christ rightly hints at here. For that foreigners should be adopted into the people of God by undergoing the yoke of Moses was nothing new. But Christ shows that from those whom he desires to be adopted into his people, nothing else is required than the observation of those things which he himself commanded, c. XXVIII. 20. Whence he also sets the mark of profession, not circumcision, but baptism. But because the Apostles, accustomed to those rites, could less understand this, therefore what had been said here more obscurely was afterwards revealed most openly by the teaching of the Spirit.

By these words, Grotius wishes the right of gathering the people from all the ends of the earth, in which right the remission of sins is included, as well as freedom from the law given through Moses, to be contained: But that explanation is too restricted; since this power comprehends much more, nor is it to be determined only by those things which pertain to the Church: indeed πᾶσα ἐξουσία ἐν ὀυρανῷ & ἐπὶ γῆς designates divine, infinite, and immense power over all things that are in heaven and on earth, nor is the supreme and universal power of God himself described otherwise in the Holy Scriptures. Gen. XIV. 7. 1. Par. XXIX. 11. Ps. CIII. 19. Ps. CXXX. 6. Matth. XI. 24. Conf. Eph. I. 20. Ebr. II. 8. And Christ himself acknowledged that an infinite kingdom is designated in this place by the words πᾶσα ἐξουσία, comparing Phil. II. 8. We have argued against the Calvinists who dispute that all authority (ἐξουσία), not power (δύναμιν), belongs to Christ in heaven and on earth, and we have more fully defended this statement in the Examination of the doctrine concerning the person of Christ, p. 317 ff. & p. 493 ff.

Latin:

Vers. 18.

Καὶ προσελθὼν ὁ ἰησοῦς] Uno compendio Matthaeus complectitur praecipua capita sermonum quos Christus cum Apostolis non in monte tantum, sed & Hierosolymis antea & post, in coelum jamjam ascensurus, Bethaniae, habuit, Vide quae ad Lucam hoc loco.

Ἐδόθη μοι πᾶσα ἐξουσία] ישׂל Dan. VII. 14. Habue- rat & ante vitam mortalem agens ἐξουσίαν, ut supra c. VII. 29. c. IX. 6. Marc. II. 27. quam ipsam regnum etiam laxius appellari notavimus supra in verbis Christi ad Pilarum. At morte acquisivit regnum infinitum, πᾶσαν ἐξουσίαν: ut Paulus dicit Phil. II. 8. Ἐταπείνωσεν ἑαυτὸν γενόμενος ὑ- πήκοος μέχρι θανάτου, θανάτου δὲ σταυρῦ. διὸ καὶ ὁ Θεὸς αὐ- τὸν ὑπερύψωσε, καὶ ἐχαρίσατο αὐτῷ ὄνομα τὸ ὑπὲρ πᾶν ὄνομα. In hac tertia dignitate recte Matthaeus librum finit, cum, ut annotavimus, primum de Prophetico, deinde de Sacer- dotali ejus officio egisset.

ἐν ὀρανῷ] In hac coelesti potestate comprehensa est ἡ ἐ- παγγελία τῦ πνέυματος quam Christus à Patre accepisse di- citur Act. II. 33. Et imperium in Angelos Phil. II. 10. Hebr. I. 4. Eph. I. 10. Col. I. 16.

καὶ ἐπὶ γῆς] Jus congregandi populum ex omnibus terrae finibus, ut clare praedixerat David, Esaias, Daniel. In hoc jure comprehensa est remissio peccatorum, Marcus hic XVI. 16. ὁ πιστεύσας καὶ βαπτισθεὶς σωθήσεται: quod Joël praedixerat: Quisquis invocabit nomen Domini salvus erit. Deinde liber- tas à lege per Mosem data, quam Christus hic recte innuit. Nam ut alienigenae adsciscerentur in populum Dei subeun- do jugum Mosis nihil erat novi. At Christus ostendit ab his quos in populum suum adscisci cupit, nihil requiri aliud quam observationem eorum quae ipse praecepit c. XXVIII. 20. Unde & professionis notam ponit, non circumcisio- nem, sed baptismum. Sed quia hoc minus intelligere pot- erant Apostoli affueti istis ritibus, ideo quod hic dictum e- rat involutius, Spiritus magisterio postea apertissime reve- latum est.

Verbis hisce jus congregandi populum ex omni- bus terræ finibus, in quo jure comprehensa peccatorum remissio, ut & libertatem à lege per Mosen data con- tineri vult Grotius: Sed ea nimis restricta est ex- plicatio: quum multo plura comprehendat hæc potestas, nec ad ea determinanda tantum sit, quæ ad Ecclesiam spectant: imo πᾶσα ἐξουσία ἐν ὀυρα- νῷ & ἐπὶ γῆς divinam, infinitam, & immensam po- testatem super omnia, quæ in cælo & in terra sunt, de- signet, neque aliter ipsius Dei summa & universalis potestas in Sacris literis describatur. Gen. XIV. 7. 1. Par. XXIX. 11. Ps. CIII. 19. Ps. CXXX. 6. Matth. XI. 24. Conf. Eph. I. 20. Ebr. II. 8. Et agnovit Chri- stus ipse, ad verba πᾶσα ἐξουσία regnum infinitum designari hoc loco, conferens Phil. II. 8. Adversus Calvinianos ἐξουσίαν Christo, non δύναμιν omnem in cœlo & in terra convenire disputantes egimus dictumque hoc plenius vindicavimus Exam. do- ctrinæ de person. Christi p. 317. seqq. & p. 493. seq.

## 28:19
Vers. 19. πορευθέντες ὀν] It coheres very well with the preceding. When that right is given to me, be you the administrators and legates of that right.

Μαθητεύσατε] The word μαθητεύειν is formed after the manner of the Hebrew תלמד. Ignatius also uses this word in his Epistle to the Romans: ἃ μαθητεύοντες ἐντέλλεσθε. The writer of the Constitutions which are ascribed to Clement explains the sense: 'It is necessary for you first to remove all impiety, then to implant piety in them, and to deem them worthy of baptism.' This is the first faith of belief, canon XLII, of Elvira.

πάντα τὰ ἔθνη] Not as hitherto only the Jews, chap. X. vers. 5.

Βαπτίζοντες ἀυτὸς] For the people being gathered from all nations, a mark of profession was appropriate, which would have a clear meaning among all. We showed above that it was the custom among the Jews that those who were converting themselves from the worship of false gods to the worship of the one God should be baptized. But it was also used among the profane nations in ancient times, that those who wished to be initiated should first be washed over their whole body, undoubtedly testifying by that very act a purpose of innocence. For the mystagogues demanded a pledge of that purpose from them, as Libanius and Lampridius teach. Justin in his Apology: 'Finally, they also wash themselves before coming to the sacred places where they are established.' Clement, Strom. VI: 'Since they also deem it right to bring certain purifications to those about to be initiated before the delivery of the mysteries, as if they were laying aside the godless opinion to turn to the true tradition.' The same author elsewhere observes a certain image of baptism in Homer. Again elsewhere: 'In the mysteries among the Greeks, purifications come first, just as the bath does among the barbarians.' Tertullian on Baptism: 'But indeed, foreign nations, far from any understanding of spiritual powers, attribute the same efficacy to their idols, but they deceive themselves with empty waters. For they are also initiated into certain sacred rites by a washing; of some Isis or Mithras.' He adds shortly after: 'Certainly they are dipped at the Apollinarian and Pelusian games: and they presume that they are doing this for their regeneration and the impunity of their perjuries.' And in his Prescriptions: 'He (the devil) himself also dips some, certainly his own believers and faithful: he promises the expiation of sins from the washing.' Augustine on baptism against the Donatists: 'Men are said to be baptized in many sacrilegious rites of idols.' Nor is the name of the Baptae at Athens celebrated by Eupolis's comedy from any other source. The Scholiast on the first Epistle of Horace: 'Ter pure: as they dip three times who purify themselves.' The day of the purification of infants, which Festus mentions, seems to have had a similar meaning. Baptism indeed has many other meanings, which the Apostles teach us everywhere, but this one was most obvious, and even with no one teaching it, it forced itself upon the minds of all.

Neither the Jewish washings of those who were converting themselves from the worship of false gods to the worship of the one God (concerning which, however, there is nothing in the sacred writings, whence those as mere will-worships are by no means to be approved, much less worthy of imitation), nor those of the profane nations, which, if the Fathers perhaps compared them, was nevertheless done according to human fashion. But there is no doubt that Satan wished to emulate the sacred rites, or rather to mock them, through such ceremonies. Furthermore, this is to be rightly understood concerning the Baptism of water as Grotius teaches: Baptism indeed has other, more numerous meanings, which the Apostles teach us everywhere, but this one was most obvious, and even without a teacher, it forced itself upon the minds of all. Other proofs of this matter against Socinus and his followers, who think that the words of Christ are to be understood as referring to a baptism other than that of water, have been produced in Socinismus profligatus and the Exegesis of the Augsburg Confession. We have observed there that the followers of his heresy themselves do not approve of this Socinian opinion. We now add only a more recent testimony of Jeremias Felbinger, an Anti-Trinitarian, who in an unpublished letter to the Christians who rightly, as he says, acknowledge the one most high God the Father of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, written at Cruciburg on the 22nd of February 1666, in which the more serious errors of the Socinians (so his own inscription has it) are noted and succinctly refuted in their own words, teaches that the opinion of Socinus regarding baptism contradicts in every way, and detracts from, the divine ordinance made through Christ, and opposes the practice of the Apostles and the primitive Church after them; and from a comparison of John 3:5-6, that unless we are born anew through baptism of water and the Spirit, we are nothing but flesh, that is, carnal men, who have no communion with the spiritual Adam and his immortal life: and thus all ought to be baptized, with no one excepted, unless perhaps some unavoidable necessity prevents baptism.

εἰς τὸ ὄνομα] Since this expression has various meanings derived from Hebraism, I judge that one is to be preferred which is most proper to baptism. Now, to be baptized into someone, or into his name, is to pledge and devote oneself to him, and to wish to be called by his name. Paul, 1 Cor. 10:2, πάντες εἰς τὸν Μωσῆν ἐβαπτίσαντο, looking back to that in Exodus 14:31, They believed in God and Moses his servant, that is, they committed themselves with good confidence to be led by Moses as the minister of God. Thus Paul denies that anyone was baptized into his own name, 1 Cor. 1:13, 15, that is, enslaved to himself as the author of a new dogma. Maimonides on the war of the captured מטבילה בשם גירות, he baptizes her in the name of proselytes, that is, into that religion which the proselytes profess. Christians, therefore, were commanded to acknowledge three authors of their dogma, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and to admit nothing as necessary which had not proceeded from them, that is, which had not originated from the Father, been revealed by the Son, and been partly explained more openly and partly sealed by the Holy Spirit. For baptism was administered, as Hilary speaks, in the confession of the Author, the Only-begotten, and the Gift. In the 33rd Apostolic Canon we read: Δοξαζήσεται ὁ Θεὸς διὰ κυρίε ἐν ἁγίῳ πνεύματι, where what follows appears to have been wrongly added by a later hand. In the Constitutions of Clement, book 3, ch. 17, the memory of the Father as the cause and sender, of the Spirit as the co-receiver and witness. Book 6, ch. 16. Δηλῦμεν ὑμῖν Θεὸν παντοκράτορα ἕνα μόνον ὑπάρχειν παρ᾽ ὃν ἄλλος ἐκ ἔστι κἀι ἀυτὸν μόνον σέβειν κἀι προσκυνεῖν, διὰ Ἰησῦ Χριστῦ τῦ κυρίε ἡμῶν ἐν τῷ παναγίῳ πνεύματι, And in book 7, chapter 23, it is said that baptism is given in the name of τῦ ἀποσείλαντος πατρός, τῦ ἐλθόντος χριστῦ, τῦ μαρτυρήσαντος παρακλήτε. But what that doctrine was, they were briefly taught before baptism. This is the βαπτισμῶν διδαχή of Hebrews 6:2. what this instruction and κατήχησις was, we learn from Justin: ὅσοι ἂν πειθῶσι κἀι πισεύωσιν ἀληθῆ τᾶυta τὰ ὑφ᾽ ἡμῶν διδασκόμενα κἀι λεγόμενα εἶναι (Justin had dealt a little before with the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit and with the universal judgment) κἀι βιῶν ὕτως δύνασθαι ὑπισχνῶνται, εὔχεσθαί τε κἀι αἰτεῖν νησεύοντες παρὰ τῦ Θεῦ τῶν προημαρτημένων ἄφεσιν διδάσκονται, ἡμῶν συνευχομένων κἀι συννηστευόντων ἀυτοῖς· ἔπειτα ἄγονται ὑφ᾽ ἡμῶν ἔνθα ὕδωρ ἐστὶ κἀι τρόπον ἀναγεννήσεως, ὃν κἀι ἡμεῖς ἀυτοὶ ἀναγεννήθημεν, ἀναγεννῶνται. In the Martyrology of Ado on the 3rd of the Ides of May: Whom the blessed Callistus, having proclaimed a fast, catechized, and having brought water, baptized. Compare with these that saying of Tertullian: Those about to enter baptism ought to pray with frequent prayers, fasts, and genuflections and vigils, and with the confession of all past sins. And that of Theodotus: διὰ τῦτο νηστεῖαι, δεήσεις, ἐυχαὶ, χειρῶν γονυκλισίαι, ὅτι ψυχὴ ἐκ κόσμε κἀι ἐκ σόματος λεόντων ἀνασώζεται. It may be noted in passing that even pagan nations applied fasting to their washings. Eubulus: βαπτίζεται νῆστιν πόνηρον κέσγεως τρίβων βίον. Before baptism, as we see, two things were required of the candidates, faith and a purpose of a better life. Both were usually handled through questions and answers. Regarding faith in this way: Do you believe? I believe. εἰ πισένεις ἐξ ὅλης καρδίας ἔξεστι said Philip to the Ethiopian. He answered πιστεύειν τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ εἶναι τὸν Ἰησοῦν χριστόν. Nor indeed were the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit merely named in this interrogation of faith, but they were described by certain marks. The Father is described by Justin: ὁ πατὴρ τῶν ὅλων καὶ δεσπότης: in the Constitutions of Clement: ὁ ἐπὶ πάντων Θεός. In Irenaeus, who likewise explains τὸν κανόνα τῆς ἀληθείας ἀκλινῆ τὸν διὰ τοῦ βαπτίσματος εἰλημμένον, the Father is noted in this way: εἷς Θεὸς πατὴρ παντοκράτωρ ὁ πεποιηκὼς τὸν οὐρανὸν καὶ τὴν γῆν καὶ τὰς θαλάσσας καὶ πάντα τὰ ἐν αὐτοῖς. In Tertullian, where he similarly hands down that which he calls the rule of faith: One God and no other besides the creator of the world who produced all things from nothing through his Word sent forth first of all. Novatian likewise describing the rule of truth, that first of all we believe in God the Father and Lord Almighty, that is, the most perfect creator of all things. Justin briefly describes the Son: Ἰησοῦν χριστὸν τὸν σταυρωθέντα ἐπὶ Ποντίου Πιλάτου. In the said Constitutions of Clement: χριστὸς ὁ μονογενὴς Θεὸς ὁ ἀγαπητὸς υἱὸς, ὁ τῆς δόξης κύριος. A broader description is in Irenaeus, who says of him? the Son of God who was incarnate for our salvation, remembering at the same time his birth from a virgin, and the passion, and the rising from the dead, and the incarnate ascension into the heavens, and his coming from the heavens in the glory of the Father to sum up all things and to raise up all flesh of all humanity, so that to Christ Jesus our Lord and God and Savior and King, according to the good pleasure of the invisible Father, every knee should bow of things in heaven and things on earth and things under the earth, and every tongue should confess to him, and he should execute righteous judgment upon all, sending the spiritual forces of wickedness and the angels who have transgressed and fallen into apostasy and the impious and unjust and lawless and blasphemous of men into the eternal fire, but to the righteous and holy and those who have kept his commandments, and have remained in his love, some from the beginning, others from repentance, granting life, he may bestow incorruption and provide eternal glory. Tertullian speaks thus concerning the Son in the recitation of the said rule: That Word, called his Son, in the name of God, was seen in various ways by the Patriarchs, always heard in the Prophets, finally brought down by the Spirit and power of God the Father into the virgin Mary, made flesh in her womb, and born of her as a man, and is Jesus Christ: thenceforth he preached a new law and a new promise of the kingdom of heaven; he performed mighty works: he was fixed to the cross. On the third day he rose again: caught up into the heavens, he sits at the right hand of the Father: he sent the vicarious power of the Holy Spirit to act upon those who believe. He will come with glory to take up the saints into the fruit of eternal life and the heavenly promises, and to judge the profane with perpetual fire, after the resurrection of both parties has been accomplished with the resurrection of the flesh. With these passages is to be compared that of Ignatius to the Magnesians: who says that Christ was begotten before all ages by the Father, but begotten later from Mary the virgin without the intercourse of a man; and lived holily, and healed every disease and infirmity among the people, and performed signs and wonders for the benefit of men, and to those who had wandered into polytheism proclaimed the one and only true God, his own Father. And endured the passion and at the hands of the Christ-killing Jews under Pontius Pilate the governor and Herod the king, and endured the cross, and died, and rose again, and ascended into the heavens to him who sent him. And sat at his right hand and is coming at the consummation of the ages with the glory of the Father, to judge the living and the dead and to render to each according to his works. Justin notes the Holy Spirit: the Holy Spirit who through the prophets proclaimed all things concerning Jesus. Irenaeus indeed in this manner: the Holy Spirit who through the prophets proclaimed the dispensations and the advents and the birth from a virgin: and the rest which we have already noted. For he joins the mention of the Spirit to the affairs of the Son: just as Tertullian also does not mention him, except in the conception of the Son. There is a trace of that which Justin and Irenaeus recite concerning the Holy Spirit in the Rule in the Nicene formula: and in the Holy Spirit who spoke through the prophets. In the constitutions of Clement there is: the Holy Spirit, the Comforter, who is sent by Christ, and preaches him. The comparison of these passages can teach us that when the ancients say the rule of faith or of baptism is immutable, they do not look to a certain and everywhere received formula of words, but to the force and meaning of the interrogations: which briefly, as Luke is accustomed to do, he thus embraces in Acts 8:12: when they believed Philip preaching the things concerning the kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ, they were baptized. And indeed the most ancient teaching of baptism had seen that it stood within the limit which I have mentioned: which Tertullian recites in summary in his work On the Veiling of Virgins: The rule of faith is indeed altogether one; alone immovable and irreformable, namely, of believing in one God almighty, the creator of the world, and his Son Jesus Christ, born of the virgin Mary, crucified under Pontius Pilate, raised from the dead on the third day, received into the heavens, sitting now at the right hand of the Father, about to come to judge the living and the dead through the resurrection of the flesh also. This law of faith remaining, the rest of discipline and conduct admit the novelty of correction, with the grace of God, of course, working and progressing even to the end. Basil in

In his Disputation against Eunomius, he acknowledges this ancient formula: 'We believe in one God, the Father almighty, from whom are all things, and in one only-begotten Son of God, the Word of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, and in one Holy Spirit, the Comforter.' Hence the Nicene formula, with the insertion of certain words concerning the Son against Arius, ends in the name of the Holy Spirit. As the license for schisms grew, provision was made for unity by adding an interrogation concerning the Catholic Church. Tertullian, in his book on baptism, having said that the washing away of sins is sealed in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, whom he calls the witnesses of faith and the sponsors of salvation, says: 'The number of the divine names is sufficient for the assurance of our hope; but since both the attestation of faith and the promise of salvation are pledged under three, the mention of the Church is necessarily added, since where the three are, that is, the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, there is the Church, which is the body of the three.' At the same time, it seems that special interrogations were made concerning the remission of sins or baptism for the remission of sins, and likewise concerning the resurrection of the flesh and life everlasting, although otherwise those very things were contained clearly enough in the description of the Son. Tertullian, giving the reason why Christ himself did not baptize, says: 'Into whom was he to baptize? Into repentance? To what purpose then his forerunner? Into the remission of sins, which he gave by his word? Into himself, whom he was concealing by his humility?' 'Into the Holy Spirit, who had not yet descended from the Father? Into the Church, which the Apostles had not yet built?' Cyprian to the Numidian Bishops: 'But the very interrogation which is made in baptism is a witness of the truth. For when we say, "Dost thou believe in life everlasting and the remission of sins through the holy Church?" we understand that the remission of sins is given only in the Church.' These very words of Cyprian seem to me to show that the Symbol or rule of faith in his own age had not yet been restricted to those words in which it is found written later, although there is no doubt that the meaning of the rule was always the same. Indeed, even among later writers the order differs. For in Jerome and Rufinus it is, 'Dost thou believe the holy Church, dost thou believe the remission of sins?' But in Cyril: 'I believe in one baptism, for the remission of sins, and in one holy Catholic Church.' Nor is it unworthy of note that in many parts, against the Manichaeans, the mention of free will was added to the Symbol, which may be gathered from the beginning of Origen's *De Principiis*: and likewise from that Symbol which exists in the works of Jerome, which, although it was signed by Pelagius in order to prove his faith to the Roman Bishop, it does not therefore follow that this is more the work of Pelagius than that which we cited from Basil was the work of Eunomius, who used that ancient formula. Certainly, Charlemagne and the entire Synod of Frankfurt praise that very Symbol, which, as we have said, exists in the works of Jerome, under the name of Jerome, and approve it in every respect. And such indeed were the interrogations of faith either in the earliest times, or those next to the first, in respect of which baptism is called by Basil and others the *sphragis tes pisteos*: the sealing of faith by Tertullian in his book on repentance. The other kind of interrogation pertained to life: which in most places preceded the profession of faith itself. For those to be baptized had to promise that they would lead their lives according to the standard handed down by Christ, as we have heard from Justin: to which pertains entirely that which Peter calls baptism the 'answer of a good conscience.' Hence it was said to renounce the world: nor do I doubt that the use of those words was most ancient in this rite. Cyprian: 'We had renounced the world when we were baptized': looking back to which, perhaps, Paul warns the baptized 'not to be conformed to this world' (Rom. XII. 2). It was customary at the same time to renounce the devil and his worship, his pomp and his angels, or the devil, his pomps, spectacles, and works, which formula often occurs in Tertullian and others: but this seems to have been added properly on account of those who were giving their names to Christ from the worship of idols. Luke briefly embraces the response concerning both faith and the amendment of life in Acts II. 41: 'They then who gladly received the word' (for both were comprised in the discourse) 'were baptized.' The Greek formula was: 'I renounce thee, Satan, and I pledge myself to thee, Christ.' And more fully: 'I renounce Satan and all his works and all his pomps and all his worship.' After these stipulations and responses, therefore, which Tertullian calls the words of the Sacrament, alluding to the custom of military service, there followed baptism, to which were added prayers in which the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit were named. Justin seems to indicate that this prayer was directed properly to the Father: 'The name of the Father of all and Lord God is pronounced over him who chooses to be born again and has repented of his sins, they saying this alone over him.' Thence: 'And in the name of Jesus Christ and in the name of the Holy Spirit he who is enlightened is washed.' The solemn word of this invocation was 'Abba Father,' as Chrysostom notes (Hom. VIII on Rom. VIII. 15). If you add to these that which is reported in Acts XXII. 16 to have been said by Ananias to Paul, 'Be baptized, calling upon the name of the Lord,' you will see that both he who is baptized and those who were present at the baptism (for it was not performed in the whole assembly in the earliest times, which is shown by those words in Justin: 'They are led by us to where there is water': and what follows later: 'We, after having thus washed him who has been persuaded and has assented, lead him to those who are called brethren'). Indeed, even in the times of Constantine, fonts for the use of baptism existed, not in the buildings of the churches, but in the outskirts, and they were accustomed to pray to God the Father 'in the name of Christ,' just as he himself teaches us to pray in John XIV. 13, 14, that he might reward the faith of him who was being baptized and that free profession of Christianity with his Holy Spirit by certain degrees, the beginning of which was 'the illumination' (Cyprian): whence, the stain of the previous age having been wiped away by the help of the life-giving water, a light from above pours itself into the cleansed and pure breast; from which the baptism itself received that name *kata metalepsin*.
