Justin: 'And this washing is called illumination, as those who learn these things are enlightened in their understanding.' He may be seen to have had regard to the passage of Paul, Eph. II. 17, although there mention is made not of the beginning but of the increase of this gift in the baptized: ἵνα ὁ Θεὸς τᾶ κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ χριστᾶ ὁ πατὴρ τῆς δόξης δώῃ ὑμῖν πνεῦμα σοφίας κᾀ ἀποκαλύψεως ἐν ἐπιγνώσει αὐτᾶ, πεφωτισμένους τῆς ὀφθαλμὸς τῆς διανοίας ὑμῶν, εἰς τὸ εἰδέναι ὑμᾶς τίς ἐστιν ἡ ἐλπὶς τῆς κλήσεως αὐτᾶ & what follows. Hence the Syrian not badly interprets those who are baptized as Φωτισθέντες, which is in Hebrews VI. 4. & ch. X. 32. Mention of the Father, Son & Holy Spirit appears in the sense I have stated, just as in the passage of Paul, so also in Peter's address to the Jews, where the subject is properly baptism, Acts II. 38. Repent, and let each of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins, and you shall receive the gift of the Holy Spirit: for the promise is to you and to your children and to all who are afar off, as many as the Lord our God shall call. Paul also to Titus III. 5. joins the washing of regeneration and the renewing of the Holy Spirit. Tertullian on baptism: To our flesh emerging from the bath after old sins, the dove of the Holy Spirit flies, bringing the peace of God. It is indeed true that in those first times certain visible gifts of the Spirit also happened to the baptized, of which Mark also makes mention in this place: but they were nothing other than an accession and ornaments of that internal gift which pertains to all times, which the Prophets had especially looked forward to, that there would be those taught by God. We have, however, the more willingly placed this most ancient form of baptizing here with its testimonies, so that it may be clear how often, when mention is made of baptism in the Acts or elsewhere, if there is mention of Christ, but not likewise of the Father, or of Christ and the Spirit without the name of the Father, the whole matter is described in part, as it was sufficiently known to all. Irenaeus, b. III. c. 20, says excellently: In the name of Christ is understood he who anointed, and he himself who was anointed, and the anointing itself in which he was anointed. But what some object to weaken this precept of Christ, that the Apostles were not baptized with this baptism, lacks weight. For to them who had received the heavenly dogma from the mouth of Christ, Christ did not command to be baptized, but to baptize others, which they did. Tertullian in the book on Baptism: To them, the prerogative of the first choice and thenceforth of an inseparable familiarity could confer the compendium of baptism: but that they themselves were baptized not with this but with John's baptism, as is certain concerning some, so I do not see why it should be denied concerning the rest, especially since even publicans are read to have come to that bath.

We indeed readily admit that this expression, to be baptized into someone or into someone's name, is to devote oneself to him as author and to wish to be called by his name, but that meaning does not entirely exhaust its force: because it denotes not only the end, which is for worship, honor, and obedience, but also the efficient cause, origin, and authority, from which it has its force and efficacy, because by his authority and by the force of his institution and ordination the Baptism is administered and received, and has all its efficacy from him, whence the true Deity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit has been invincibly demonstrated by the Holy Fathers from this formula: because he, in whose name, by whose command and authority Baptism is administered and received as a medium and Sacrament of initiation and regeneration, to whose honor, worship, and obedience we are therefore obligated, is without doubt that one true God. Since therefore we are baptized in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, it follows infallibly that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are that one true God, concerning which argument it has been treated more fully in Vol. III of the System of Theology.

Even if, therefore, that 1 Cor. 10:2, 'all were baptized into Moses,' were to be explained here, because they committed themselves to the ministry of Moses, nevertheless that meaning is not here, where the discourse is primarily about the author of Baptism: by whose authority and power this Sacrament is performed.

Nor when Paul in 1 Cor. 1:13, 14 denies that anyone was baptized in his name, does he mean only that no one was enslaved to him as the author of a new dogma: but he rather implies that the authority of him in whose name we are baptized is divine; and therefore he considers it absurd to be baptized in the name of any mere man: just as it is equally absurd that a 'mere man' was crucified for us. Was Paul crucified for you? Were you baptized in the name of Paul? Nor does it fit the form of sound words, what Grotius says, that Christians are here ordered to acknowledge three authors of their dogma, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. For there is no one but one principal author of our dogmas, that one true God, and he is the same Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Because just as we are compelled by Christian truth to confess each person individually as God and Lord, so we are forbidden by the Catholic religion to say three Gods or three Lords, as the Athanasian Creed holds.

What Grotius observes concerning the doctrine delivered before baptism, or the 'catechesis,' and concerning the various Creeds, can be judged from those things which we have treated at length in the Calixtine Syncretism, in the first postulate concerning the Apostles' Creed. That 'doctrine of baptisms,' however, of which Heb. 6:2 speaks, does not apply here. For it does not designate the Catechesis itself, but a peculiar head of Catechesis distinct from 'repentance, and faith toward God,' and other heads of Apostolic Catechesis: concerning which see System of Theology, part II, near the beginning.

Latin:

Vers. 19. πορευθέντες ὀν] Optime cohæret cum superiori- bus. Quando id jus mihi datum est, vos estote ejus juris administri atque legati.

Μαθητεύσατε] Vox μαθητεύειν facta adinstar Hebraicæ תלמד. Utitur hac voce & Ignatius Epistola ad Romanos: ἃ μαθητεύοντες ἐντέλλεσθε. Sensum explicat Scriptor Consti- tutionum quæ Clementi adscribuntur. Δεῖ ὑμᾶς πρότερον πᾶσαν ἀσέβειαν ἐξελότας, τότε τὴν ἐυσέβειαν ἀυτοῖς ἐγκατα- βάλεσθαι, καὶ τῷ βαπτίσματι ἀξιῶσαι. Hæc est fides prima credulitatis, canone XLII, Eliberino.

πάντα τὰ ἔθνη] Non ut hactenus solos Judæos cap. X. vers. 5.

Βαπτίζοντες ἀυτὸς] Populo congregando ex omnibus gentibus competebat professionis nota, quæ perspicua a- pud omnes haberet significationem. Supra ostendimus a- pud Judæos moris fuisse, ut baptizarentur qui se à falsorum Deorum cultu ad cultum unius Dei convertebant. Sed a- pud gentes etiam profanas usurpatum antiquitus fuit, ut qui initiari vellent, prius toto corpore abluerentur, haud dubie eo ipso testantes propositum innocentiæ. Nam ejus propo- siti sponsionem ab iis mystagogi exigebant, ut Libanius docet & Lampridius. Justinus in Apologetico: Τέλος δὲ καὶ λουσθ᾽ ἀπιόντας πρὶν ἐλθεῖν ἐπὶ τὰ ἱερὰ ἔνθα ἵδρυνται ἐνεργοῦσι. Clemens Strom. VI. ἐπεὶ κὴ πρὸ τῆς ὦ μυτηρίων παραδόσεως και θαρμός τινας προσάγειν τοῖς μυεῖσθαι μέλλεσιν ἀξιοῦσιν ὡς διον τὴν ἄθεον ἀποθεμένους δόξαν ἐπὶ τὴν ἀληθῆ τρέπεσθαι παράδοσιν. Idem alibi imaginem quandam baptismi apud Homerum observat. Rursus alibi: ὦ μυστηρίων ὦ παρ' ἕλλησιν ἄρχει μὲν τὰ καθάρσια, καθάπερ καὶ τοῖς βαρβάροις τὸ λουτρόν. Tertul- lianus de Baptismo: Sed enim nationes extraneæ ab omni in- tellectu spiritualium potestatum eadem efficaciaidolis suis submi- nistrant, sed viduis aquis sibi mentiuntur. Nam & sacris quibus- dam per lavacrum initiantur; Isidis alicujus aut Mithræ Ad- jicit mox: Certe ludis Apollinaribus & Pelusiis tinguntur: id- que se in regenerationem & impunitatem perjuriorum suorum a- gere præsumunt. Et de præscriptionibus: Tingit & ipse (dia- bolus) quosdam, utique credentes & fideles suos: expositionem delictorum de lavacro repromittit. Augustinus de baptismo contra Donatistas: In multis idolorum sacrilegis sacris bapti- zari homines perhibentur. Nec aliunde Athenis Baptarum nomen Eupolidis Comœdia celebratum. Scholiastes ad primam Epistolam Horatii: Ter pure: ut ter mergunt qui se ex piant. Lustrici quoque infantium dies, quorum memi- nit Festus, similem habuisse videntur significationem. Ha- bet quidem baptismus alias plures significationes, quas passim Apostoli nos docent, sed hæc maxime erat obvia, & vel nullo docente omnium se animis ingerebat.

Nihil ad sacramentum Baptismi faciunt vel Ju- daicæ lotiones eorum, qui se à falsorum Deorum cul- tu ad cultum unius Dei convertebant, (de quibus vero nihil in sacris, unde illæ ceu meræ ἐθελοθρη- σκεῖαι minime probandæ, nedum imitatione dignæ) vel gentium profanarum, quas si forte contulere Pa- tres, κατ' ἄνθρωπον tamen id factum. Sacra autem æmulari, vel iisdem potius illudere Satanam vo- luisse per tales ceremonias, dubium nullum est. Cæterum recte de Baptismo aqua hæc accipienda effe docet Grotius: Habet quidem Baptismus alias plures significationes, quas passim Apostoli nos docent, sed hæc maxime erat obvia, & vel nullo docente o- mnium se animis ingerebat. Alia ejus rei documen- ta contra Socinum ejusque sectatores qui de alio quam aquæ Baptismo verba Christi accipienda ef- se putant, in Socinismo profligato, & Exegem. Aug. Confess. producta sunt. Quam Socinianam senten- tiam ipsis hæreseos ejus asseclis sese non probare, illic observavimus. Addimus nunc solum testimo- nium recentius Jeremiæ Felbingeri, Anti-Trinitarii, qui in Epistola ἀνεκδότῳ ad Christianos unum altissi- mum Deum Patrem Domini ac Salvatoris nostri Je- su Christi recte, ut ait, agnoscentes sub dato Crucibur- gi 22. Febr. 1666. exarata, in qua Socinianorum errores graviores (sic habet ejus inscriptio propria) suis i- psorum verbis notati succincte refutantur, docet, So- cini sententiam de Baptismo omnibus modis contradi- cere, & detrahere divinæ ordinationi per Christum factæ, & Apostolorum atque primitivæ post illos Ec- clesiæ exercitio adversari; & è collatione Joh. III. 5. 6. nos nisi ex aqua & Spiritu de novo generemur per baptismum nihil nisi carnem esse, h. e. carnales ho- mines, quibus nullum cum spirituali Adamo, & ejus immortali vita est commercium: adeoque omnes ba- ptizari debere, nemine recepto, nisi forte inevitabi- lis aliqua necessitas baptismum impediat.

εἰς τὸ ὄνομα] Cum locutio hæc varias habet ex He- braismo significationes, eam his præferendam arbitror, quæ baptismo maxime propria est. Est autem baptizari in aliquem, vel in ejus nomen, se ei auctorare atque devo- vere, & de ejus nomine appellari velle. Paulus 1. Cor. X. 2. πάντες εἰς τὸν Μωσῆν ἐβαπτίσαντο, respiciens illud Exo- di XIV. 31. Crediderunt in Deum & Mosem servum ejus, id est, Mosi tanquam Dei ministro cum bona fiducia regen- dos se commisêre, Sic Paulus negat quemquam baptiza- tum in suum nomen 1. Cor. I. 13.15. hoc est, sibi velut no- vi dogmatis auctori mancipatum. Maimonides de bello ca- ptæ מטבילה בשם גירות, baptizet eam in nomen pro- selytarum, id est in eam religiöuem quam profitentur profe- lytæ. Christiani igitur tres sui dogmatis auctores agnosce- re jubebantur, Patrem, Filium, & Spiritum Sanctum, nihilque, ut necessarium admittere, quod non ab iis esset profectum, id est, quod non à Patre ortum, à Filio prodi- tum, à Spiritu vero esset partim explicatum apertius, par- tim obsignatum, Administrabatur enim baptismus, ut lo- quitur Hilarius, in confessione & Auctoris & unigeniti & doni. In Canone Apostolico XXXIII. legimus: Δοξαζή- σεται ὁ Θεὸς διὰ κυρίε ἐν ἁγίῳ πνεύματι, ubi quæ sequuntur à manu posteriore perperam adjecta apparer. In Clementis constitutionibus lib. III. c. XVII. τὲ πάτρος ἡ μνήμη ὡς αἰτία κὶ ἀποστολέως, τὲ πνεύματος ὡς συμπαραλήψεως ὡς μάρτυρος Lib. VI. c. XVI. Δηλῦμεν ὑμῖν Θεὸν παντοκράτορα ἕνα μόνον ὑπάρχειν παρ᾽ ὃν ἄλλος ἐκ ἔστι κἀι ἀυτὸν μόνον σέβειν κἀι προσ- κυνεῖν, διὰ Ἰησῦ Χριστῦ τῦ κυρίε ἡμῶν ἐν τῷ παναγίῳ πνεύ- ματι, Et libro VII. cap. 23. dicitur baptismus dari in no- men τῦ ἀποσείλαντος πατρός, τῦ ἐλθόντος χριστῦ, τῦ μαρ- τυρήσαντος παρακλήτε. Quæ autem ea esset doctrina, bre- viter ante baptismum docebantur. Hæc est βαπτισμῶν δι- δαχή Hebræor. II.2. quæ institutio & κατήχησις qualis fuerit ex Justino discimus: ὅσοι ἂν πειθῶσι κἀι πισεύωσιν ἀληθῆ τᾶυτα τὰ ὑφ᾽ ἡμῶν διδασκόμενα κἀι λεγόμενα εἶναι (egerat autem paulo ante Justinus de Patre, Filio & Spiritu S. & de judicio universali κἀι βιῶν ὕτως δύνασθαι ὑπισχνῶνται, εὔχε- σθαί τε κἀι αἰτεῖν νησεύοντες παρὰ τῦ Θεῦ τῶν προημαρτημένων ἄφεσιν διδάσκονται, ἡμῶν συνευχομένων κἀι συννηστευόντων ἀυ- τοῖς· ἔπειτα ἄγονται ὑφ᾽ ἡμῶν ἔνθα ὕδωρ ἐστὶ κἀι τρόπον ἀνα- γεννήσεως, ὃν κἀι ἡμεῖς ἀυτοὶ ἀναγεννήθημεν, ἀναγεννῶνται. In martyrologio Adonis ad III. eid. Majas: Quem beatus Cal- listus indicto jejunio catechizavit, & allata aqua baptizavit. Quibus confer illud Tertulliani: Ingressuros baptismum, orationibus crebris, jejuniis & geniculationibus & pervigiliis orare oportet, & cum confessione omnium retro delictorum. Et illud Theodoti : διὰ τῦτο νηστεῖαι, δεήσεις, ἐυχαὶ, χειρῶν γο- νυκλισίαι, ὅτι ψυχὴ ἐκ κόσμε κἀι ἐκ σόματος λεόντων ἀνα- σώζεται. Obiter notari potest etiam profanas gentes suis lotionibus adhibuisse jejunium. Eubulus: βαπτίζεται νῆστιν πόνηρον κέσγεως τρίβων βίον. Ante baptismum ut videmus, duo exigebatur a candidatis, fides & propositum vitæ emenda- tioris. Utrumque per interrogationes & responsiones expe- diri solebat. De fide hoc modo: Credis? credo. εἰ πισένεις ἐξ ὅλης καρδίας ἔξεστι dicebat Philippus Æthiopi. Ille resp-on debat πιστεύειν τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ εἶναι τὸν Ἰησοῦν χριστόν. Neque ve- ro in hac fidei interrogatione Pater, Filius, Spiritus Sanctus nominabantur tantum, sed certis notis describebantur. Pa- ter apud Iustinum describitur: ὁ πατὴρ τῶν ὅλων καὶ δεσπό- της: in Constitutionibus Clementis: ὁ ἐπὶ πάντων Θεός. A- pud Irenæum qui itidem exponit τὸν κανόνα τῆς ἀληθείας ἀκλι- νῆ τὸν διὰ τοῦ βαπτίσματος εἰλημμένον, Pater hoc modo nota- tur: εἷς Θεὸς πατὴρ παντοκράτωρ ὁ πεποιηκὼς τὸν οὐρανὸν καὶ τὴν γῆν καὶ τὰς θαλάσσας καὶ πάντα τὰ ἐν αὐτοῖς. Apud Tertul- lianum ubi similiter tradit eam, quam vocat fidei regulam: Vnus Deus nec alius præter mundi conditorem qui universa de nihilo produxerit per Verbum suum primo omnium emissum. No vatianus itidem describens regulam veritatis, ut primo o- mnium credamus in Deum Patrem & Dominum omnipo- tentem, id est, rerum omnium perfectissimum conditorem Filium breviter Justinus describit: Ἰησοῦν χριστὸν τὸν σταυρωθέντα ἐπὶ Ποντίου Πιλάτου. In dictis Clementis Constitutionibus: χρι- στὸς ὁ μονογενὴς Θεὸς ὁ ἀγαπητὸς υἱὸς, ὁ τῆς δόξης κύριος. Latior descriptio est apud Irenæum, qui eum dicit? τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ τὸν σαρκωθέντα ὑπὲρ τῆς ἡμετέρας σωτηρίας, memorans simul τὴν ἐκ παρθένου γέννησιν, καὶ τὸ πάθος, καὶ τὴν ἔγερσιν ἐκ νεκρῶν, καὶ τὴν ἔνσαρκον εἰς τοὺς οὐρανοὺς ἀνάληψιν, καὶ τὴν ἐκ τῶν οὐρανῶν ἐν τῇ δόξῃ τοῦ πατρὸς παρουσίαν αὐτοῦ ἐπὶ τὸ ἀνακεφαλαιώσασθαι τὰ πάντα καὶ ἀναστῆσαι πᾶσαν σάρκα πάσης ἀνθρωπότητος, ἵνα χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ τῷ κυρίῳ ἡμῶν καὶ Θεῷ καὶ σωτῆρι καὶ βασιλεῖ κατὰ τὴν εὐδοκί- αν τοῦ πατρὸς τοῦ ἀοράτου πᾶν γόνυ κάμψῃ ἐπουρανίων καὶ ἐπιγείων καὶ καταχθονίων καὶ πᾶσα γλῶσσα ἐξομολογήσηται αὐτῷ καὶ κρί- σιν δικαίαν ἐν τοῖς πᾶσι ποιήσηται, τὰ μὲν πνευματικὰ τῆς πονηρίας καὶ ἀγγέλους τοὺς παραβεβηκότας καὶ ἐν ἀποστασίᾳ γεγονότας καὶ τοὺς ἀσεβεῖς καὶ ἀδίκους καὶ ἀνόμους καὶ βλασφήμους τῶν ἀνθρώπων εἰς τὸ αἰώνιον πῦρ πέμψῃ, τοῖς δὲ δικαίοις καὶ ὁσίοις καὶ τὰς ἐντολὰς αὐτοῦ τετηρηκόσι, καὶ ἐν τῇ ἀγάπῃ αὐτοῦ διαμεμενηκόσι, τοῖς μὲν ἀπʼ ἀρχῆς, τοῖς δὲ ἐκ μετανοίας, ζωὴν χαρισάμενος, ἀφθαρσίαν δω- ρήσηται καὶ δόξαν αἰώνιον περιποιήσῃ. Tertullianus de Filio in dictæ regulæ recitatione ita loquitur: Id verbum Filium ejus appellatum in nomine Dei varie visum Patriarchis, in Pro- phetis semper auditum, postremo delatum ex Spiritu Dei Patris & virtute in virginem Mariam, carnem factum in utero ejus, & ex ea natum hominem, & esse Iesum Christum: exinde præ- dicasse novam legem & novam promissionem regni cælorum; virtutes fecisse: fixum cruci. Tertia resurrexisse: in cælos ere- ptum sedere ad dexteram Patris: Misisse vicariam vim Spiritus Sancti qui credentes agat. Venturum cum claritate ad adsumen- dos sanctos in vitæ æternæ & promissorum cælestium fructum, ad profanos judicandos igni perpetuo, facta utriusque partis resuscitatione cum carnis resurrectione. Quibus locis comparan- dus est Ignatii ad Magnetios: qui Christum dicit πρὸ πάντων μὲν αἰώνων γεννηθέντα παρὰ τῷ πατρὸς, γεννώμενον δὲ ὕστερον ἐκ Μαρίας τῆς παρθένου δίχα ὁμιλίας ἀνδρὸς· καὶ πολιτευσάμενον ὁ- σίως, καὶ πᾶσαν νόσον καὶ μαλακίαν θεραπεύσαντα ἐν τῷ λαῷ, ση- μεῖα καὶ τέρατα ποιήσαντα ἐπʼ εὐεργεσίᾳ ἀνθρώπων, καὶ τοῖς ἐξο- κείλασιν εἰς πολυθεΐαν τὸν ἕνα καὶ μόνον ἀληθινὸν Θεὸν καταγγεί- λαντα τὸν ἑαυτοῦ πατέρα. καὶ τὸ πάθος ὑποστάντα καὶ πρὸς τῶν χριστοκτόνων Ἰουδαίων ἐπὶ Ποντίου Πιλάτου ἡγεμόνος καὶ Ἡρώδου βασιλέως καὶ σταυρὸν ὑπομείναντα, καὶ ἀποθανόντα, καὶ ἀναστάντα, καὶ ἀνελθόντα εἰς τοὺς οὐρανοὺς πρὸς τὸν ἀποστείλαντα. Καὶ καθίσαν- τα ἐν δεξιᾷ αὐτοῦ καὶ ἐρχόμενον ἐπὶ συντελείᾳ τῶν αἰώνων μετὰ δόξης πατρικῆς, κρῖναι ζῶντας, καὶ νεκροὺς καὶ ἀποδοῦναι ἑκάστῳ κατὰ τὰ ἔργα αὐτοῦ. Spiritum Sanctum notat Justinus: πνεῦμα ἅ- γιον ὃ διὰ τῶν προφητῶν προεκήρυξε τὰ κατὰ τὸν Ἰησοῦν πάντα. Irenæus vero hunc in modum: πνεῦμα ἅγιον τὸ διὰ τῶν προ- φητῶν κεκηρυχὸς τὰς οἰκονομίας καὶ τὰς ἐλεύσεις καὶ τὴν ἐκ παρθένου γέννησιν: & cætera quæ jam annotavimus. Nam Spiritus mentionem rebus Filii interjungit: quemadmodum & Ter- tullianus ejus non meminit, nisi in Filii conceptione. E- jus quod de Spiritu S.Iustinus & Irenæus in Regula recitant vestigium est in Nicena formula καὶ εἰς τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον τὸ λαλῆσαν διὰ τῶν προφητῶν. In Clementis constitutionibus est πνεῦμα ἅγιον, ὁ παράκλητος, τὸ ὑπὸ χριστοῦ πεμπόμενον, καὶ ἐ- κείνον κηρύττον. Horum locorum collatio docere nos potest, cum veteres regulam fidei aut baptismi immutabilem di- cunt, nos ad certam & receptam ubique verborum formu- lam eos respicere, sed ad vim atque sententiam interrogatio- num: quam breviter, ut solet Lucas, ita complectitur Actor. VIII. com. 12. ὅτε ἐπίστευσαν τῷ Φιλίππῳ εὐαγγελιζομένῳ τὰ περὶ τῆς βασιλείας τοῦ Θεοῦ καὶ τῷ ὀνόματι τοῦ Ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ, ἐβαπτί- ζοντο. Et antiquissima quidem τοῦ βαπτισμοῦ διδαχὴ intra cum quem dixi finem stetisse viderat: quam ita compendio reci- tat Tertullianus de Virginibus velandis: Regula quidem fidei una omnino est; sola immobilis & reformabilis, credendi sci- licet in unicum Deum omnipotentem mundi conditorem, & Filium ejus Iesum Christum, natum ex virgine Maria, cru- cifixum sub Pontio Pilato, tertia die resuscitatum à mortuis, receptum in cælis, sedentem nunc ad dexteram Patris, ventu- rum judicare vivos & mortuos per carnis etiam resurrectio- nem. Hac lege fidei manente cætera jam disciplina & con- versationis admittunt novitatem correctionis, operante sci- licet & proficiente usque in finem gratia Dei. Basilius in

Disputatione adversus Eunomium agnoscit hanc formulam veterem: Πιστεύομεν εἰς ἕνα Θεὸν, πατέρα παντοκράτορα, ἐξ ὗ τὰ πάντα, καὶ εἰς ἕνα μονογενῆ υἱὸν τῆ Θεῆ, Θεᾶ λόγον τὸν κύριον ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦν χριστὸν δι'ὗ τὰ πάντα, καὶ εἰς ἕν πνεῦ- μα ἅγιον τὸν παράκλητον. Hinc & Nicena formula, inser- tis quibusdam de filio verbis contra Arium, in nomine Spiritus Sancti desinit. Gliscente secessonum licentia u- nitati consultum est addita interrogatione de Ecclesia Catholica. Tertullianus libro de baptismo cum dixisset ab- lutionem delictorum obsignatam in Patre, Filio, & Spiri- tu sancto, quos arbitros fidei & spons res salutis vocat: Suf- ficit, inquit, ad fiduciam spei nostrae etiam numerus nominum divinorum quum autem sub tribus & testatio fidei & sponsio salutis pignerentur, necessario adjicitur Ecclesiae mentio, quo- niam ubi tres id est Pater & Filius & Spiritus sanctus, ibi Ecclesia quae trium corpus est Eodem tempore videntur de remissione peccatorum aut baptismate in remissionem, item de carnis resurrectione & vita aeterna speciales factae interrogationes, cum alioqui in descriptione Filii ea ipsa sa- tis aperte continerentur. Tertullianus rationem reddens cur Christus ipse non tinxerit: In quem, inquit, tingeret? in poenitentiam. Quo ergo illi praecursorem? In peccatorum remis- sionem, quam verbo dabat? In semetipsum, quem humilitate celabat? In Spiritum Sanctum qui nondum à Patre descen- derat? In Ecclesiam, quam nondum Apostoli struxerant? Cy- prianus ad Episcopos Numidas: Sed ipsa interrogatio quae fit in baptismo testis est veritatis. Nam cum dicimus credis in vi- tam aeternam & remissionem peccatorum per sanctam Eccle- siam, intelligimus remissionem peccatorum non nisi in Ecclesia dari. Quae ipsa Cypriani verba ostendere mihi videntur Symbolum sive regulam fidei ipsius aetate nondum ad- strictam fuisse illis verbis quibus postea scripta invenitur, cum tamen eandem semper fuisse regulae sententiam mi- nime sit dubitandum. Quin serius etiam apud Scriptores ordo discrepat. Nam apud Hieronymum & Rufinum est, Credis sanctam Ecclesiam, credas remissionem peccatorum? Apud Cyrillum vero: Credo in unum baptisma, in remis- sionem peccatorum & in unam sanctam Ecclesiam Catholicam. Nec indignum notatu multis in partibus adversus Mani- chaeos adjectam Symbolo & liberi arbitrii mentionem, quod ex Origenis Exordio περὶ ἀρχῶν datur colligere: itemq; ex eo Symbolo quod in Hieronymi exstat operibus, quod quanquam à Pelagio subsignatum est, ut fidem suam Ro- mano Episcopo probaret, non tamen sequitur magis hoc esse Pelagii quam illud quod ex Basilio citavimus Eunomii fuit opus, qui illa formula antiqua utebatur. Certe Carolus Magnus & tota Synodus Francofurtensis illud ipsum Sym- bolum, quod ut diximus in Hieronymi exstat operibus, lau- dat sub Hieronymi nomine, & omni ex parte approbat. Et tales quidem fuêre fidei interrogationes aut primis tempo- ribus, aut proxime prima, quarum respectu βάπτισμα Basi- lio & aliis dicitur σφραγὶς τῆς πίσεως: fidei obsignatio Ter- tulliano libro de poenitentia. Alterum interrogandi genus ad vitam pertinebat: quod plerisque in locis praecedebat ipsam fidei professionem. Promittere enim baptizandi debebant vitam se exacturos ad normam à Christo traditam ut ex Ju- stino audivimus: quo omnino illud pertinet quod Petrus baptisma vocat συνειδήσεως ἀγαθῆς ἐπερώτημα. Hinc dicebatur saeculo renuntiare: neque dubito quin earum vocum antiquis- simus fuerit usus in hoc ritu, Cyprianus: saeculo renuntiabera- mus cum baptizati sumus: quo forte respiciens Paulus monet baptizatos μὴ συσχηματίζεσθαι τῷ αἰῶνι τούτῳ Rom. XII. 2. So- lebat simul renuntiari diabolo & cultui, pompae & angelis e- jus, aut diabolo, pompis, spectaculis & operibus ejus, quae formula apud Tertullianum atque alios saepe occurrit: sed id proprie additum videtur propter eos qui ex Idolorum cultu Christo nomen dabant. Responsionem tum de fide tum de vita emendanda breviter complectitur Lucas Act. II. 41. οἱ μὲν ἓν ἀσμένως ἀποδεξάμενοι τὸν λόγον αὐτῷ (nam in oratione utrumque comprehendebatur) ἐβαπτίσθησαν. Graeca for- mula erat ἀποτάσσομαί σοι Σατανᾶ καὶ συντάσσομαί σοι χρι- στέ. Et plenior: ἀποτασσουμαι τῷ Σατανᾶ κὶ πᾶσι τοῖς ἔργοις αὐ- τῦ καὶ ταῖς πομπαῖς αὐτᾶ κὶ πασῃ τῇ λατρείᾳ αὐτᾶ. Post has er- go stipulationes atque responsiones, quas verba Sacramenti Tertullianus vocat ad militiae morem alludens, sequebatur baptismus, cui accedebant preces in quibus nominabantur Pater, Filius & Spiritus Sanctus. Orationem hanc proprie ad Patrem directam indicare vid. tur Justinus, ἐπονομάζεται τῷ ἑλομένῳ ἀναγεννηθῆναι καὶ μεῖανεήσαντι ἐπὶ ταῖς ἠμαρτημένοις τὸ τᾶ πατρὸς τῶν ὅλων κὶ δεσπότου Θεᾶ ὄνομα, αὐτὸ τᾶτο μόνον ἐπι- λέγοντες Deinde. κὶ ἐπὶ ὀνόματῷ δὲ ἰησῦ χρισᾶ καὶ ἐπ' ὀνόμα- τῷ πνεύματῷ ἁγίου ὁ φωτιζόμενῷ λούεται. Solenne ejus in- vocationis verbum erat Abba pater, ut notat Chrysosto- mus VIII. ad Rom. II. 15. His si addas id quod Act. XXII 16. refertur ab Anania dictum Paulo βάπτισαι ἐπικαλεσάμενῷ τὸ ὄνομα τᾶ κυρίου videbis tum eum qui baptizatur, tum eos qui baptismo aderant (neque enim in toto coetu exerceba- tur primis temporibus, quod oftendunt illa apud Justinum ἄγονται ὑφ' ἡμῶν ἔνθα ὕδωρ ἐστὶ : & quod postea sequitur ἡμεῖς δὲ μετὰ τὸ οὕτως λῦσαι τὸν πεπεισμένον καὶ συγκατατεθειμένον, ἐπὶ τὰς λεγομένους ἀδελφοὺς ἄγομεν. Quin & Constantinite mpo- ribus fontes in usum baptismi extant, non in Ecclesiarum ædibus, sed ἐν τοῖς περιοδοῖς) solitos orare Deum Patrem ἐν τῷ ὀνόματι χριστῦ, quomodo ipse orare nos docet Joh. XIV. 13, 14. ut fidem ejus, qui baptizabatur & liberam illam Chri- stianismi professionem muneraret Spiritu suo S. per gradus quosdam, quorum initium erat ὁ φωτισμὸς Cyprianus : unde genitalis auxilio superioris ævi labe detersa, in expiatum pectus ac purum desuper se lumen infundit, inde ipsum baptisma κατὰ μετάληψιν id nomen accepit. Justinus : καλεῖται δὲ τᾶτο λᾶτρὸν φωτισμὸς, ὡς φωτιζομένων τὴν διάνοιαν ἣν ταῦτα μανθανόντων. Respexisse videri potest locum Pauli Ephes. II. 17. quan- quam ibi non de initio sed de augmento hujus doni in baptizatis mentio est: ἵνα ὁ Θεὸς τᾶ κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ χρι- στᾶ ὁ πατὴρ τῆς δόξης δώῃ ὑμῖν πνεῦμα σοφίας κᾀ ἀποκαλύψεως ἐν ἐπιγνώσει αὐτᾶ, πεφωτισμένους τῆς ὀφθαλμὸς τῆς διανοίας ὑμῶν, εἰς τὸ εἰδέναι ὑμᾶς τίς ἐστιν ἡ ἐλπὶς τῆς κλήσεως αὐτᾶ & quæ sequuntur. Hinc Syrus non male quod est Hebræo- rum VI. 4. & cap. X. 32. Φωτισθέντες interpretatur baptiza- tos. Patris, Filii & Spiritus Sancti mentio in eam quam dixi sententiam ut dicto Pauli loco, ita & in Petri ad Judæos allocutione apparet, ubi proprie de baptismo agitur, Act. II. 38. Μετανοήσατε καὶ βαπτισθήτω ἕκαστος ὑμῶν ἐπὶ τῷ ὀνόματι Ἰησοῦ χριστᾶ εἰς ἄφεσιν ἁμαρτιῶν καὶ λήψεσθε τὴν δω- ρεὰν τᾶ ἁγίου πνεύματος: ὑμῖν γάρ ἐστιν ἡ ἐπαγγελία καὶ τοῖς τέκνοις ὑμῶν καὶ πᾶσι τοῖς εἰς μακρὰν, ὅσους ἂν προσκαλέση- ται κύριος ὁ Θεὸς ἡμῶν. Paulus quoque ad Titum III. 5. conjungit λυτρὸν παλιγγενεσίας κᾀ ἀνακαίνωσιν πνεύματος ἁ- γίου. Tertullianus de baptismo: Carni nostræ emergenti de lavacro post vetera delicta columba Sancti Spiritus advolat pa- cem Dei adferens. Verum quidem est primis illis tempo- ribus etiam aspectabilia quædam Spiritus dona baptizatis contigisse, quorum & Marcus hoc loco meminit : sed ea ni- hil aliud erant quam accessio & ornamenta doni illius inter- ni atq; ad omnia tempora pertinentis, quod præcipue Pro- phetæ spectaverant, vaticinationes fore θεοδιδάκτους. Hanc autem vetustissimam baptizandi formam eo liben- tius hic cum suis testimoniis posuimus, ut liqueat quoties in Actis aut alibi cum de baptismo agitur, Christi sit men- tio, non item Patris, aut Christi & Spiritus, sine Patris no- mine, ex parte rem totam, quippe satis omnibus notam, describi. Optime Irenæus l. III. c. 20. In Christi nomine sub- auditur qui unxit, & ipse qui unctus est, & ipsa unctio in qua unctus est. Quod autem nonnulli ad infirmandum hoc Christi præceptum objiciunt Apostolos non esse hoc ba- ptizato, baptismate, caret pondere. Nam ipsis qui ex Christi ore cœleste dogma acceperant, non præcepit Chri- stus baptizari, sed alios baptizare, quod fecerunt. Tertul- lianus libro de Baptismo: Illis vel prima adlectionis & exin- de individuæ familiaritatis prærogativa compendium baptismi conferre potuit: sed & ipsos baptizatos non isto sed Johan- nis baptismo, ut de quibusdam certum est, ita de cæteris cur negetur non video, præsertim cum etiam publicani ad id lavacrum venisse legantur.

Loquutionem hanc in aliquem, vel alicujus nomen baptizari esse ei se auctorem atque devovere, & de ejus nomine appellari velle, facile equidem admittimus, sed ea significatio non omnino ex- haurit vim ejusdem : quia non tantum finem de- notat, quod in cultum, honorem, & obsequium, sed etiam causam efficientem, originem & autori- tatem, à qua vim, & efficaciam suam habet, quod eo autore, & vi institutionis ac ordinationis e- jus Baptismus administretur, & suscipiatur, & ab eo omnem suam habeat efficaciam, unde vera Deitas Patris, Filii & Spiritus Sancti invicte à S. Patribus ex hac formula demonstrata : quia te- is, in cujus nomine, cujus mandato & auctori- tate Baptismus ceu medium & Sacramentum ini- tiationis & regenerationis administratur & susci- pitur, ad cujus proinde honorem, cultum & obsequium obligamur, sine dubio est unus ille verus Deus. Quum ergo in nomine Patris, Filii & Spiritus Sancti baptizemur, infallibiliter se- quitur Patrem, Filium & Spiritum Sanctum esse unum illum verum Deum, de quo argumento fusius Tom. III. Syst. Theol. actum.

Etiamsi ergo illud 1. Corinth. X. 2. πάντες εἰς τὸν Μωσῆν ἐβαπτίσαντο hic explicandum esset, quod ministerio Mosis sn commiserint, non tamen hic ea significatio est, ubi de autore Baptismi im- primis sermo est: cujus auctoritate & virtute hoc Sacramentum peragitur.

Neque cum 1. Cor. I. 13. 14. Paulus negat quenquam in suum nomen ba- ptizatum, id tantum vult, nullum sibi velut novi do- gmatis auctori mancipatum: Sed id potius innuit, divinam esse ejus, in cujus nomen baptizamur, au- ctoritatem; ideoque pro absurdo habet, in alicu- jus meri hominis nomine baptizari: æque uti absurdum ψιλὸν ἄνθρωπον pro nobis crucifixum esse. Num Paulus crucifixus pro nobis? num in nomi- ne Pauli baptizati estis? Neque formam sanorum verborum resipit, quod ait Grotius, Christianos tres sui dogmatis auctores agnoscere hic juberi, Pa- trem, Filium, & Spiritum Sanctum. Non enim est nisi unus auctor principalis dogmatum nostro- rum, unus ille verus Deus, idemque est Pater, Filius, & Spiritus Sanctus. Quia sicut singulatim unamquamque personam Deum ac Dominum confite- ri Christiana veritate compe limur, ita tres Deos aut tres Dominos dicere, Catholica religiones prohibe- mur, ut habet Symbolum Athanasianum.

Quæ de doctrina ante baptismum tradita, vel κατηχήσει Grotius observat, deque variis Symbo- lis, dijudicari possunt ex iis, quæ in Syncretismo Calixtino postulato primo de Symbolo Apostolico pro- lixe tradidimus. Illa tamen βαπτισμῶν διδαχὴ de qua Ebr. VI. 2. huc non facit. Non enim per il- lam ipsa Catechesis, sed peculiare Catecheseos ca- put distinctum à μετανοίᾳ, καὶ πίςει ἐπὶ θεὸν, aliis- que Catecheseos Apostolico capitibus designatur: de quibus Syst. Theol. part. II. sub initium.

## 28:20
Verse 20. 'teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you.' Christ does not order anything else to be taught than what he himself had commanded. Wherefore it ought to be certain that the whole substance of religion consists in those things: and nothing delivered by the Apostles necessary for salvation (for the reason for counsels and those things which are ordered for 'decency' according to the circumstances of places and times is different) is outside the precepts of Christ. Since there is a twofold method of teaching, one by way of 'introduction of the elementary,' the other by way of 'instruction,' the former seems to be indicated above by the word 'to make disciples': for that is as it were to initiate into discipline, and it is placed before baptism: the latter by the word 'to teach,' which is placed here after baptism. Thus Luke, writing to Theophilus about the life, death, and resurrection of Christ, says, 'that you might know the certainty of those words in which you have been instructed': where likewise 'instruction' is the first institution which is followed by 'knowledge of the certainty.' Thus Apollos is said to the same Luke in the Acts to have been 'instructed in the way of the Lord.' This distinction comes from the Hebrews, as do most things of ancient Christianity, among whom 'shema'ta' is the 'instruction' which was later followed by 'aggada'ta,' a fuller explanation, and 'moledet,' the 'delineation.' Clement of Alexandria, Stromata VI, says that 'knowledge' is the 'perfection of faith beyond instruction.' Elsewhere he makes a twofold 'kind of teaching,' one of 'pedagogy,' the other 'contemplative,' which he also calls 'trace' and 'spiritual.' The Pythagoreans, as the same Clement notes, called disciples of a common sort 'auditors,' but others who genuinely grasped philosophy they called 'mathematicians.' Now, as Malchus explains in the Life of Pythagoras, the 'mathematicians' are those who have learned the more thorough and precise discourse of science. The 'auditors' are those who have heard only the summary precepts of the writings, without a more precise explanation. Origen says it was common to all sects of wise men to have some 'exoteric' discourses, others 'esoteric.' See the beginning of ch. 6 to the Hebrews.

Because these things explain the different method of teaching not inconveniently, we do not disapprove of them. Yet they do not seem to have proceeded from the Hebrews, but rather to have passed from Christians to the Hebrews: because the Hebrews who can be brought forward are all more recent Christians; but concerning the more ancient ones, nothing certain is established.

And lo, I am with you. The ascension of Christ into heaven seems to have been so well known to all Christians in Palestine that there was no need for Matthew to speak of it. For when Christ appeared to those five hundred, he undoubtedly signified his future ascension to them. Yet it is indicated here in passing. For it is an 'anticipatory objection.' I am indeed about to go into heaven, and I will not be present with you in a visible manner: but I will be present by divine efficacy. For it is to be noted that 'to be with someone' is said peculiarly of God, Judg. 6:12, 13, Jer. 1:8, Acts 7:9. But Mark and Luke, since they were writing to those living outside Judea, rightly added the history of the ascension. John did not need to do that, as one who was writing 'omitted things,' leaving out what was said by others, unless the context of the history required something.

All the days, even to the end of the age. What the 'end of the age' is appears sufficiently above in ch. 13:39, 46, 49, ch. 24:3. After that time, when Christ is about to hand over the kingdom to the Father, he will be with us, but not in the way that is treated here, for the support of our weakness. Wherefore the 'until' can be taken properly here. From this, however, it appears most manifestly that Christ wanted the Apostles to commend that office of teaching to others, and they in turn to other 'faithful men who are able to teach others,' as can be seen in 2 Tim. 2:2. For since this promise extends itself to the consummation of the age, and the Apostles were not going to live that long, Christ must altogether be considered here to have addressed the successors of that office in the person of the Apostles.

The words of Christ are correctly explained regarding divine efficacy. But just as GOD is present with us by His power and efficacy, or His grace, not without His substantial presence, because the power of God cannot be separated from the divine essence, and the presence of grace presupposes, when there is talk of divine presence, the presence of the divine essence, which we showed against the Socinians in Vol. II. Syst. Theol. chap. VIII. q. 1. p. 391. we showed, so Christ the θεάνθρωπος, God and man, promises us His presence here, not by reason of power and grace only, but as regards the ἀδιαστασίαν of substance, not only by reason of the divine, but also by reason of the human nature: because the human nature cannot be separated by the διαστήματα of places from the divine, with which it is united most closely, by an indissoluble bond, and into whose hypostasis the same has been assumed, and that power, and grace, or divine efficacy, by which Christ assists us, is indeed proper to the divine nature, but communicated through the hypostatic union to the human nature itself: just as Christ testifies that all power has been given to Him in heaven and on earth. But concerning these things expressly in the Examination of the doctrine of the Reformed concerning the Person of Christ.

And with these we conclude our observations on Matthew: rendering devout thanks to Christ the Lord, and adoring Him, that He may deign to be with us, as He promised, in these proclaimed times of the end of the world, and that He may be willing to sanctify us even in these regions until the consummation of the age in the truth of His word. Amen, Lord Jesus, Amen!

II, 2. II. Syst. Theol. cap. VIII. q. 1. p. 391. ostendimus, ita Christus θεάνθρωπ©, Deus & homo suam no- bis præsentiam hic promittit, non ratione virtutis tantum atque gratiæ, sed quoad substantiæ ἀδια- στασίαν, non solum ratione divinæ, sed etiam ratione humanæ naturæ: quia nec separari per lo- corum διαστήματα potest humana natura a divi- na, cum qua unita est arctissime, vinculo indif- solubili, & in cujus hypostasin eadem assumta est, & potentia, atque gratia, vel efficacia illa divi- na, qua nobis assistit Christus, divinæ naturæ propria quidem est, communicata autem per u- nionem hypostaticam ipsi humanæ naturæ: quem- admodum testatur Christus sibi datam esse omnem potestatem in cœlo, & in terra. Sed de his ex pro- fesso in Examine doctrinæ Reformatorum de Perso- na Christi.

Atque his concludimus observationes no- stras ad Matthæum: Christo Domino gratias agen- tes devotas, eumque adorantes, ut, quod promi- sit, nobiscum esse dignetur, his conclamatis extre- mi mundi temporibus, nosque in his etiam oris ad consummationem usque seculi in veritate verbi sui sanctificare velit. Amen, Domine Jesu, Amen!

## 1:1 Introduction: Grotius' Preface
GROTIUS' PREFACE.

KATA' Μάρκον] That he was a Jew and more of a Hebrew-speaker than a Greek-speaker, although moderately skilled in both languages, his manner of speaking proves. Nor indeed could any Roman have been recognized by a common name shared by so many. But as often as Jews came into the inner parts of Asia or into Europe, they were accustomed to add to their Jewish name another, Greek or Roman, by which they might be known among men of a foreign nation. Thus Barsabas was called Justus; Simeon, Niger; and also that John, son of Mary, kinsman of Barnabas, with whom Paul had a slight disagreement, but one easily healed, as is wont to happen among good men, was called Mark, whom many think to be this writer of ours. I am moved not to agree with them by the authority of the ancients, who never call this writer John, but always Mark, and so add him as a companion and disciple to Peter, that they make no mention not only of Barnabas, but also of Paul, whom John Mark followed after that slight disagreement (Col. IV. 10; 2 Tim. IV. 11; Philem. v. 24). Add that John Mark was converted among the first Christians (1 Pet. V. 13). For the Apostles used to call such men their children in a special way (1 Cor. IV. 15; Gal. IV. 19; Philem. 10). It is possible that this writer had a Hebrew name not unlike that Latin one, just as Jesus, brother of Onias, wished to be called Jason, and Saul called himself Paul. For even today those who have the name Mordecai are called Mark. Clement in the sixth book of his Hypotyposes declared that this book was written by Mark while Peter was alive; with whom Irenaeus seems to conflict, who, after he had spoken of Peter and Paul, adds: 'But after their departure, Mark, the disciple and interpreter of Peter, also handed down to us in writing the things preached by Peter.' But 'departure' can be explained there not as the passing of the Apostles, which I admit is how that word is generally taken, but as their departure from the city of Rome. For the phrase 'of Peter and Paul preaching the Gospel in Rome' had preceded; so that Irenaeus notes the time of the writing, after Peter had returned from Rome to the parts of Babylon, and Paul had departed into Spain, from whence they returned to Rome after some years. But it will be more true to follow the ancient codex in which, instead of 'their departure,' there is 'the edition,' that is, after the edition of the Gospel written by Matthew. Tertullian teaches us that the Gospel of Mark was called by many the Gospel of Peter: 'Although,' he says, 'that which Mark published is affirmed to be Peter's, whose interpreter Mark was.' The same author elsewhere: 'We establish first that the Gospel instrument has the Apostles as authors, upon whom this duty of promulgating the Gospel was imposed by the Lord Himself; and apostolic men, not however alone, but with the Apostles and after the Apostles: since the preaching of the disciples could be rendered suspect of a desire for glory, if the authority of the masters does not stand by it.' Justin, however, in his book of Gospel history, calling them quite often 'memoirs of the apostles,' includes this book and that of Luke under that name. Perhaps someone might think this Gospel is called by the name of Peter by the same Justin when he says, 'And the saying that He renamed Peter one of the apostles, and that this also happened, is written in his memoirs.' But that ambiguous 'his' refers either to Peter or to Jesus, about whom those commentaries were written. In the first centuries other sayings of Peter were also circulated, which, being collected later, some had named the 'Preaching of Peter.' But Mark was content to write those things which pertained to the history of the life, death, and resurrection of Christ, omitting almost all dogmas, as things which, having been often inculcated by Peter, the Romans held well enough in their memory. See the words of Papias on this matter at the end of the third book of Eusebius. I would not deny that that John Mark was one of the seventy disciples of Christ. Regarding this Mark, I think enough has already been said as to why I believe that less. Nor indeed, if that had been believed in antiquity, would it have been passed over by Irenaeus, since the 'eyewitness' of the writer would have had the greatest momentum for defending the authority of the book against sectarians. But Papias also openly declared that the Lord was not heard by Mark, but that he wrote those things which, heard from Peter, his memory suggested. Mark wrote in Greek, although chiefly for the sake of the Romans, just as Paul also wrote his Epistle to the Romans in the Greek language, because the Jews who lived in Rome were for the most part ignorant of the Latin language, having learned the Greek language through their long habitation in Asia and Greece; and there was hardly anyone among the Romans who did not understand Greek. That the old Latin version of Mark is the same as that from which we have the other books of the Gospel, the similarity of the version itself makes probable; to which version it will appear in many places that certain Greek copies have been changed.

PRÆLOQVIVM GROTIANVM.

KATA' Μάρκον] Iudæum fuisse & ἑβραίζοντα magis quam ἑλληνίζοντα, quanquam sermonis utriusque mediocriter gnarum, locutio evincit. Neque vero Romanorum quisquam noscitari quisset ex communi tam multis prænomine. At Iudæi quoties in partes Asiæ interiores aut in Europam venirent, solebant sibi, ad Iudaicum nomen, alterum adsciscere Græcum aut Romanum, quo apud exteræ gentis homines noscerentur. Ita Barsabas, dictus Iustus: Simeon, Niger: Iohannes quoque ille Mariæ filius Barnabæ consanguineus, cui cum Paulo friusculum intercessit, sed facile sanatum, ut inter bonos fieri solet, Marcus vocabatur, quem multi hunc nostrum scriptorem putant. Quibus quo minus assentiar moveor veterum auctoritate, qui hunc Scriptorem Iohannem nunquam, Marcum semper vocant, & ita Petro addunt comitem ac discipulum, ut non tantum de Barnaba, sed & de Paulo, quem Iohannes Marcus post illud friusculum sectatus est Coloss. IV. 10. 2. Tim. IV. 11. Philem. v. 24. nihil meminerint. Adde quod Iohannes Marcus inter primos Christianos conversus 1. Pet. V. 13. Nam tales peculiariter filios suos Apostoli vocabant 1. Cor. IV. 15. Gal. IV. 19. Pilem. 10. Fieri potest ut hic Scriptor Hebræum nomen habuerit ab illo Latino non absudens, sicut Iesus Onia frater Iasonem se dici voluit, Saulus se Paulum vocavit. Nam & hodie quibus Mardochæo nomen est, Marci appellantur. Vivente Petro scriptum à Marco hunc librum Clemens ὑποτυπώσεων sexto prodidit: cum quo pugnare videtur Irenæus, qui cum de Petro & Paulo locutus esset, subjicit: μετὰ δὲ τὴν τούτων ἔξοδον Μάρκος ὁ μαθητὴς καὶ ἑρμηνευτὴς Πέτρου, καὶ αὐτὸς τὰ ὑπὸ Πέτρου κηρυσσόμενα ἐγγράφως ἡμῖν παραδέδωκε. Sed ἔξοδος potest ibi exponi non excessus Apostolorum, quomodo plerumque eam vocem sumi fateor, sed eorundem discessio ab urbe Roma. Præcesserat enim τὸ Πέτρου καὶ τοῦ Παύλου ἐν Ῥώμῃ εὐαγγελιζομένων: ut tempus scriptionis notet Irenæus, postquam Petrus à Roma in Babyloniæ partes reversus, Paulus autem in Hispaniam digressus sit, unde aliquot post annos Romam redierint. Sed verius erit veterem sequi codicem in quo pro τούτων ἔξοδον est τύτης ἔκδοσιν, id est, post editionem Evangelii à Matthæo conscripti. Docet nos Tertullianus à multis Marci Evangelium vocatum esse Petri: Licet & Marcus quod edidit, inquit, Petri affirmetur, cujus interpres Marcus. Idem alibi: Constituimus imprimis Evangelicum instrumentum Apostolos auctores habere, quibus boc munus Evangelii promulgandi ab ipso Domino sit impositum: & apostolicos, non tamen solos sed cum Apostolis & post Apostolos: quoniam prædicatio discipulorum suspecta fieri posset de gloriæ studio, si non adsistat illi auctoritas magistrorum. Iustinus autem Evangelicæ historiæ libro sæpiuscule appellans ἀπομνημονεύματα ἀποστόλων, hunc etiam & Lucæ librum eo nomine comprehendit. Putet forte aliquis hoc Evangelium vocari ex Petri nomine ab eodem Iustino cum dicit καὶ τὸ εἰπεῖν μετωνομακέναι αὐτὸν Πέτρον ἕνα τῶν ἀποστόλων, καὶ γεγράφθαι ἐν τοῖς ἀπομνημονεύμασιν αὐτοῦ γεγενημένον καὶ τοῦτο. Sed ambiguum illud αὐτοῦ ad Petrum, an ad Iesum, de quo scripti sunt illi commentarii, referatur. Circumferebantur primis seculis & alia Petri dicta, quibus postea collectis nomen quidam fecerant κήρυγμα Πέτρου. Sed Marcus ea scribere satis habuit quæ ad vitæ, mortis, & resurrectionis Christi historiam pertinebant, omissis ferme dogmatis, ut quæ à Petro sæpe inculcata satis Romani memoria tenebant. Vide sapiæ verba hac de re apud Eusebium fine libri III. Iohannem illum Marcum unum fuisse ex LXX. Christi discipulis negare nolim. De hoc Marco cur id minus credam, jam satis dictum arbitror. Neque vero si id creditum fuisset antiquitus, prætermissum esset ab Irenæo, cum ἡ αὐτοψία Scriptoris ad tuendam contra sectarios libri auctoritatem maximum habitura fuerit momentum. At Papias etiam aperte prodidit à Marco Dominum non auditum, sed scripta ab ipso quæ à Petro audita, memoria suggerebat. Græce autem scripsit Marcus, quanquam in gratiam præcipue Romanorum, sicut & Paulus ad Romanos Epistolam Græca scripsit lingua, quia Iudæi qui Romæ agebant plerique Latini sermonis ignari lon- per Asiam & Græciam habitatione Græcam linguam didi-çerant : & Romanorum vix quisquam erat non Græce intelligens. Latinam vero Marci versionem veterem esse, & ejusdem à quo versos habemus cæteros Evangelii libros si- psa versionis similitudo facit probabile : ad quam versio- nem quædam Græca exemplaria mutata esse multis locis apparebit.

## 1:1 Introduction: Notes on Grotius' Preface
NOTES ON GROTIUS' PREFACE.

Grotius makes Mark the Evangelist a Jew by birth, and distinguishes him from John Mark mentioned in the Acts and the Pauline Epistles: nor does he wish him to be one of the number of the LXX disciples; he attributes his Gospel, however, to Peter; and says it was recorded from his account. We can easily grant that he was a Jew: although the name Mark is not Hebrew: which he rashly suspects to have been at least the surname of the Evangelist, since it is always used as a proper name, unlike what is to be observed regarding the other Mark, who, called John by his proper name, was surnamed Mark. It is equally vain that he thinks Mark was called by the Hebrew name Mordecai. But as for his saying that the diction of Mark proves that he himself was a Jew and ἑβραΐζοντα [Hebraizing] more than ἑλληνίζοντα [Hellenizing], although moderately skilled in both languages, that does not stand on firm ground, because holy men, instructed from heaven by the gift of tongues, could use an idiom other than their native one, as it seemed good to the Holy Spirit, who gave them to speak as He willed, and what He willed, and therefore this judgment is not sufficiently pious, that the diction should prove the author to be only moderately skilled in both languages. For this contempt redounds upon the Holy Spirit Himself as the principal author, by whose inspiration the Evangelist wrote, 2 Pet. I. 21, 2 Tim. III. 16, whom there is no doubt dictated the words to him. But that the author of all languages should be only moderately skilled in this or that language cannot be said without prejudice to piety.

Opinions vary as to whether our Mark is the same as the one surnamed John Mark. For some think they are the same, such as Theophylact, Euthymius, Sixtus of Siena, whom the Magdeburg Centuriators, B. Winckelmann, and others support. It is more likely, however, that they are different: because he who is mentioned in Acts c. XII. 12 and by Paul in Col. IV. 10, 2 Tim. IV. 11, the cousin of Barnabas, adhered more to Paul and Barnabas than to Peter, to whom Eusebius, Hist. Eccl. b. II. c. 15, and Jerome in Catal. Script. Eccl. testify that the Evangelist adhered, by whom he is also called Son, 1 Pet. V. 13, which Jerome in Isa. LXV, Theodoret, and Oecumenius understand of the Evangelist. Add that that John was called Mark only by surname, whereas our own is never called by any other name than Mark.

The Papists prove with a less firm argument that the Evangelist was not one of the LXX disciples, because he is called the Son of Peter: from which they conclude that he was converted by Peter after the death of Christ: because he could be called the son of Peter, even if not converted by him, and could he not have been converted even before the passion?

of Christ by Peter? Luke IX. 1. What? That Grotius by that Mark, who is called the son of Peter 1 Pet. V. 13, understands not the Evangelist, but John Mark. Which is also the opinion of Nicephorus, Eccl. Hist. Book II, ch. 15. Whom, however, Grotius does not wish to deny was one of the 70 disciples of Christ. But what Irenaeus thinks—if the same had been believed of our Mark in ancient times, that he was one of the 70 disciples of Christ; that he would not have kept silent about it, since the ἡ ἀυτοψία (eyewitness account) of the writer would have had the greatest momentum for defending the authority of the book against sectarians—that has some appearance, yet it is not sufficiently firm. Because negative testimony proves nothing solidly. Origen certainly, Epiphanius in Heresies LI, and Dorotheus say that Mark was of the number of the 70 disciples of Christ. But the contrary testimony of Papias, namely that the Lord was not heard by Mark, but that those things were written by him which his memory suggested were heard from Peter, as being a man of by no means proven faith, is of no moment, nor does it much agree with the Canonical authority of this writing. For it is not what memory suggested from the relation of Peter, but what the Holy Spirit suggested, that Mark ought to have written, if he is to be held as a Canonical author, 2 Tim. III. 16, 2 Pet. I. 22. Therefore Grotius followed Papias rashly in this especially, and those things are not to be accepted except with a grain of salt, when some say that Mark had what he wrote from Peter, and when Tertullian says that Mark's Gospel was called Peter's, so that, namely, it might not be denied that it was written by Divine inspiration. Irenaeus indeed, Book III, ch. 1, seems to assert that after the ἔξοδον or departure of Peter and Paul, Mark wrote his Gospel: unless with Grotius you prefer to follow an old manuscript, in which for τάτων ἔξοδον is τέτω ἔκδοσιν, which is to say, he wrote after the Edition of the Gospel written by Matthew. Otherwise, from Book VI of Clement's Hypotyposes, Jerome proves in his Catalogue that this book was written by Mark while Peter was alive; and Eusebius reports in Book III, ch. 15, that Peter confirmed this Gospel by his authority to be read in the Churches. Concerning Mark and Luke, St. Augustine says thus in sermon 146: Mark and Luke were not the equals of the Apostles, but nearly their equals. Therefore the Holy Spirit already wished to choose two even from those who were not among the twelve to write the Gospel, lest it be thought that the grace of evangelizing had reached only as far as the Apostles, and that the fountain of grace had failed in them.

Finally, concerning the idiom in which the Gospel of Mark is written, Grotius rightly observes that Mark wrote in Greek. Although mainly for the sake of the Romans (which he has from Eusebius and Jerome), just as Paul also wrote to the Romans in the Greek language, because the Jews who lived in Rome, most of them being ignorant of the Latin language through long habitation in Asia and Greece, had learned the Greek language, and there was hardly anyone among the Romans who did not understand Greek. Which things are to be noted against Baronius in his Annals, Vol. 1, to the year 45, and Tirinus in his preface to Mark: as they are those who wish that Mark wrote in the Latin language, because Tirinus fabulates from some tradition or other that the Latin exemplar was afterwards translated by Peter himself into the Greek language at Aquileia: and he says that it is kept at Venice: which, however, Baronius peddles not as the Greek, but as the Latin original exemplar. But that the Greek text is the original, we show in Vol. I of our System. of Theology, nor is there any sacred book which was written by the Holy Spirit or his amanuensis, a Prophet and Apostle, in the same and original language, and transferred into another: finally, there is no book in the N.T. which was not written in the Greek language in the original.

Besides the general Biblical commentators, or those of the N.T. and the special interpreters of the Evangelists and the Gospel Harmonies, Franciscus Lambertus and B. Winkelmannus, who also explained Luke, as well as Lamb. Danæus and Franc. Junius, and also Cajetanus, have illustrated Mark with commentaries.

Furthermore, the Gospel of St. Mark can be distributed into the history of the life, and of the Passion and death, and the resurrection and ascension of the Lord following it. The history of the life of Christ is completed in thirteen chapters: the remaining three pertain to the Passion, death, and resurrection and ascension. Concerning the life of Christ, after a few things are premised in chapter 1 regarding the vocation, baptism, and preaching of St. John because of the baptism undertaken by him from John, the acts of the ministry of Christ are exhibited, which it pleases us to distribute according to distinct Passovers, for the sake of conformity with the other Evangelists: which the Baptism of Christ and his temptation in the desert precede.

As for what concerns those things which were done from the first Passover of Christ to the second, ch. I, the proclamation of Christ in Galilee, the calling of Simon, Andrew, then also of James and Zebedee, and after the sermon in Capernaum, the deliverance of one possessed: the healing of Peter's mother-in-law and of other sick persons is described: and how he preached in all Galilee, and restored a certain leper, is taught in the same chapter. Furthermore, in ch. II, he heals the paralytic in Capernaum, calls Levi from the tax office, and eats with publicans, and gives a reason concerning him, and why his disciples do not fast, up to v. 22.

From the second to the third Passover of Christ, these deeds are related by Mark in the remainder of ch. II: the defense of the disciples who had rubbed ears of grain on the Sabbath, in ch. III, the restoration of the withered hand, the withdrawal to the sea, the healing of many sick and possessed, the ordination of the Apostles, the refutation of the calumnies concerning Beelzebub, and the information concerning the sin against the Holy Spirit and concerning his true blood relatives, in ch. IV, parables are held concerning the seed, and concerning the light not to be hidden: and an admonition that to him who has it shall be given, illustrated by the similitude of the sprouting and growth of the mustard seed: and it treats of the storm of the sea being calmed. In the fifth chapter, in the land of the Gadarenes, one possessed is delivered, and the daughter of Jairus, with the woman with an issue of blood ἐν παρόδῳ healed, is raised from the dead. In the sixth chapter, Christ, despised at Nazareth, performs no miracles, sends out the twelve Apostles, and instructs them, whose fame penetrated to Herod, who had beheaded John: he feeds five thousand men in the desert, and walks on the sea.

From the third Passover to the fourth, these deeds are recounted by Mark in the remainder of chapter VI: the healing of very many sick persons in the land of Gennesaret. In the seventh chapter, the traditions of the Pharisees, because the disciples had not washed their hands, are reproved, the daughter of the Canaanite woman is healed, and a mute and deaf man is restored. In the eighth chapter, 4000 are fed: a blind man in Bethsaida is healed: Peter confessed Christ, and Christ predicted his passion, death, and resurrection, with Peter being rebuked for contradicting him, and he exhorted his own to the cross, and also to the confession of himself. In the ninth chapter, after the transfiguration of Christ, he answers the question concerning Elijah, and delivers a lunatic from an unclean spirit, which the disciples had not been able to do, and walking through Galilee he again predicts his passion, and in Capernaum sets a little child as an example of humility, and warns concerning not forbidding one casting out demons in his name, as well as concerning fleeing from scandal, and having salt. In the tenth chapter, he instructs concerning divorce, commands little children to come to him, tests the rich man boasting of the observance of the law, and warns concerning leaving all things for the sake of God.

To the history of the last Passover belongs the journey to Jerusalem, and in it the prediction of the passion, death, and resurrection, the instruction of those seeking to sit at his right and left, and the blind man near Jericho

healing, ch. 10. for the rest: and further ch. 11. the entry into Jerusalem made on an ass, the cursing of the fig tree, the cleansing of the temple, information concerning the efficacy of faith and being heard, and the answer given to the priests inquiring about the authority to teach. In the twelfth chapter is the parable of the vineyard, and the son of the Lord of the vineyard cast out, and the fulfilled prophecy concerning the rejected stone, as well as the answer concerning the tribute, concerning the resurrection of the dead, concerning the chief commandment, with the question concerning the son and Lord of David, and the warning to beware of the lawyers, and their pride and avarice: as also the observation of those who were casting a gift into the treasury, and among them the poor widow. In the thirteenth chapter the prophecy concerning the destruction of Jerusalem and concerning the most recent coming of the Son of God is proposed with an admonition to vigilance.

The history of the passion is exhibited in ch. 14 and ch. 15. In the former, the consultation of the priests and Pharisees, the anointing of Christ in Bethany; the pact with Judas; the Passover, and the prediction of the betrayal of Judas; the celebration of the Holy Eucharist; the prophecy concerning the scandal of the disciples, and the denial of Peter; as the antecedents of the Passion of Christ: the Passion in the garden; and the threefold prayer concerning the cup; the betrayal of Judas; the striking of the servant of the High Priest, the leading away of Jesus to the High Priest while the disciples were fleeing; the false testimonies; the confession of Jesus that he is Christ, the Son of God, about to sit at the right hand of God, and to come in the clouds; and the condemnation by the High Priest; and the mockery; and the threefold denial of Peter; and the weeping that followed. In this, the fifteenth chapter, a council having been held, Jesus is led away to Pilate and accused, who wishes the same to be released instead of Barabbas, but the people cry out that Jesus must be crucified, to satisfy whom Pilate delivered Jesus to be scourged and crucified. Whom, having been led into the praetorium, they clothe in purple, and having placed a crown of thorns upon him, they mock him, and further, having put his own clothes back on him, they lead him out to crucifixion, Simon the Cyrenian having been compelled to carry the cross, and at Golgotha, myrrh having been offered, they crucify him, they distribute his garments, they place a title upon the cross, at the same time crucifying two thieves with him, they mock him on the cross, who, darkness having been made for three hours, cries out Eli, Eli, lama asabthani: and crying out with a loud voice, he expires. The veil of the temple was then rent, the centurion was converted, the women watched from afar, Joseph of Arimathea, having obtained the body of Jesus from Pilate, wrapped in a linen cloth, laid it in a sepulchre.

In the last, which is the sixteenth chapter, the arrival of the women at the sepulchre, and the entry, and the sight of the Angel, announcing the resurrection, and commanding them to report to the disciples, by whom he is to be seen in Galilee, and the return from the sepulchre is set forth, with the appearances of Jesus made to Mary Magdalene, to two walking in the country, and to the eleven disciples: as well as the mission into the world to preach the Gospel, and the promise of signs. Finally, the ascension into heaven, and the sitting at the right hand of God, and while the Apostles were preaching everywhere, the cooperation of the Lord, and the confirmation of the word through signs.

Latin:

AD PRÆLOQVIUM GROTII ΥΠΩΜΝΗΜΑΤΑ.

Marcum Evangelistam natione Judæum facit Grotius, & distinguit eum à Johanne Marco in A- ctis, & Paulinis Epistolis commemorato : neque aliquem è numero LXX. discipulorum esse vult ; Evangelium vero ejus Petro tribuit ; & ex ejus re- latione consignatum dicit. Judæum fuisse facile largiri possumus : quamvis nomen Marci Ebræum non sit : quod cognomen saltem Evangelistæ fuisse, temere suspicatur, quum semper ut proprium no- men usurpetur, secus atque de altero Marco ob- servare est, qui Johannes nomine proprio dictus Marcus cognominatus est. Æque vanum est, quod putat Marcum Ebræo nomine Mardochæum vocatum esse. Quod autem locutionem Marci evincere dicit, ipsum Judæum fuisse & ἑβραΐζοντα magis quam ἑλληνίζοντα, quanquam sermonis utri- usque mediocriter gnarum, id nec firmo stat talo, quia sancti viri dono linguarum cœlitus instructi a- lio idiomate uti potuêre, quam nativo, prouti vi- sum Spiritui Sancto, qui ipsis dedit eloqui, ut vo- luit, & quæ voluit, adeoque nec satis pium hoc est judicium, quod locutio autorem arguat sermonis utriusque mediocriter gnarum. Hic enim contem- tus in ipsum Spiritum Sanctum ceu in principalem redundat autorem, cujus inspiratione scripsit Ev- angelista, 2. Petr. I. 21. 2. Tim. III. 16. quem ei ver- ba dictasse dubitandum non est. Illum autem linguarum omnium autorem hujus, vel illius lin- guæ mediocriter saltem gnarum esse, salva pieta- te dici nequit.

Utrum Marcus noster idem sit, qui Johannes Marcus cognominatus, variant sententiæ. Non- nulli enim eundem esse putant, ut Theophylactus, Euthymius, Sixtus Senensis, quibus Centuriatores Magdeburgenses, B. Winckelmannus, & alii as- surgunt. Vero tamen similius est, illos diver- sos esse : quia ille, qui in Actis c. XXII. 12. & à Pau- lo Col. IV. 10. 2. Tim. IV. 11. commemoratur Barna- bæ consobrinus, Paulo & Barnabæ magis adhæsit, quam Petro, cui adhæsisse Evangelistam Eusebius l. II. Hist. Eccl. c. 15. & Hieronymus in Catal. Script. Eccl. testantur, à quo etiam Filius vocatur 1. Petr. V. 13. quod de Evangelista Hieronymus in Esa. LXV. Theodoret. & Oecumen. intelligunt. Adde quod Johannes ille cognomento tantum Marcus dictus sit, noster autem nunquam alio quam Marci no- mine vocetur.

E LXX. tamen discipulis Evangelistam non fuisse, minus firmo argumento probant Pontificii, quod Petri dicatur Filius : unde conversum eun- dem à Petro post Christi mortem colligunt : quia fi- lius poterat dici Petri, etsi non conversus ab ipso, & annon converti potuit etiam ante passionem-

Christi à Petro? Luc. IX. l. Quid? quod Grotius per Marcum illum, qui filius Petri dicitur 1. Petr. V. 13. non Evangelistam, sed Johannem Marcum intelligat. Quæ etiam Nicephori l. II. Hist. Eccles. c. 15. est sententia. Quem tamen unum fuisse ex LXX. Christi discipulis negare non vult Grotius. Quod autem Irenæus putat, si de Marco nostro anti- quitus idem creditum fuisset, quod unus è LXX. Christi discipulis fuerit; illud non taciturum fuisse, siquidem ἡ ἀυτοψία Scriptoris ad tuendam contra sectarios libri auctoritatem maximum habitura fuerit momentum, id aliquam speciem habet, sa- tis tamen firmum non est. Quia testimonium ne- gativum nihil solide probat. Origenes certe, Epi- phanius Hæres. LI. Dorotheus Marcum è numero LXX. discipulorum Christi fuisse, dicunt. Papiæ autem contrarium testimonium, quod nempe à Marco Dominus auditus non sit, sed scripta ab ipso sint, quæ à Petro audita memoria suggerebat, ceu viri minime probatæ fidei, nullius est momenti, neque auctoritati Canonicæ hujus scripti admo- dum convenit. Nam non quæ memoria è Petri re- latione, sed quæ Spiritus Sanctus suggessit, Mar- cum scripsisse oportet, si autor sit habendus Ca- nonicus, 2. Tim. III. 16. 2. Petr. I. 22. Ideo temere in hoc imprimis sequutus est Papiam Grotius, nec nisi cum grano salis accipienda illa sunt, cum à Petro nonnulli habuisse Marcum quæ scripsit, ai- ferunt, & cum Tertullianus Marci Evangelium vocatum esse Petri dicit, ne sc. negetur Divina in- spiratione scriptum. Irenæus sane l. III. c. I. vide- tur asserere post Petri & Pauli ἔξοδον vel excessum Marcum Evangelium suum scripsisse: nisi cum Grotio malis veterem Codicem sequi, in quo pro τάτων ἔξοδον est · τέτω ἔκδοσιν quod sc. post Editio- nem Evangelii à Matthæo conscripti, scripserit. Cæ- teroquin è Clementis ὑποτυπώσεων l. VI. probat Hieronymus in Catal. quod liber hic vivente Petro à Marco scriptus sit; & perhibet Eusebius l. III. c. 15. Petrum Evangelium hoc Ecclesiis legendum sua auto- ritate confirmasse. De Marco & Luca ita S. Augusti- nus serm. 146. Marcus & Lucas Apostolorum non pares, sed suppares fuerunt. Ideo jam voluit Spiri- tus S. etiam ex his, qui inter duo decem non fuerunt, eligere ad Evangelium conscribendum duos, ne puta- retur gratia Evangelizandi usque ad Apostolos perve- nisse, & in illis fontem gratiæ defecisse.

Postremo de Idiomate, quo scriptum est Marci Evangelium, recte observat Grotius, Græce scri- psisse Marcum. Quanquam in gratiam præcipue Romanorum (quod ab Eusebio & Hieronymo habet) sicut & Paulus ad Romanos Græca scripsit lingua, quia Judæi, qui Romæ agebant, plerique Latini ser- monis ignari longa per Asiam & Græciam habitatio- ne, Græcam ling iam didicerant, & Romanorum vix quisquam erat, non Græce intelligens. Quæ con- tra Baronium in annal. T. 1. ad ann. 45. & Tirinum præf. ad Marcum notanda: utpote qui Marcum Latina Lingua scripsisse volunt, quod Latinum exemplar postmodum ab ipso Petro in Græcam lin- guam Aquilejæ transversum esse Tirinus è traditione, nescio qua, fabulatur: Idque Venetiis asservari, ait: quod tamen non de Græco, sed Latino primogeni- to exemplari venditat Baronius. Sed Græcum textum originalem esse, Tom. I. Syst. Theol. o- stendimus, neque ullus est liber sacer, qui à Spiritu Sancto vel amanuensi ejus, Propheta & Apostolo eodem & originali conscriptus lingua sit, & in a- liam transfusus: nullus denique in N. T. liber, qui non Græca lingua in originali scriptus.

Commentariis Marcum illustrarunt præter ge- nerales Biblicos, aut N. T. & speciales Evangeli- starum, & Harmoniæ Evangelicæ interpretes, Franciscus Lambertus, & B. Winkelmannus, qui & Lucam explicarunt, nec non Lamb. Danæus, & Franc. Junius, ut & Cajetanus.

Cæterum distribui potest Evangelium S. Marci in Historiam vitæ, & Passionis ac mortis, eamque consequentis resurrectionis, & ascensionis Domini- cæ. Historia vitæ Christi tredecim capp. absolvitur: tria reliqua ad Passionem, mortem ac resurrectionem & ascensionem spectant. Circa vitam Christi, præ- missis ob baptismum à Johanne susceptum cap. 1. paucis de vocatione, baptismo, ac concione S. Johan- nis, acta ministerii Christi exhibentur, quæ secun- dum distincta Paschata distribuere, conformitatis cum cæteris Evangelistis gratia, lubet: quæ Ba- ptisma Christi, & tentatio ejus in deserto antecedit.

Quod ergo ea quæ gesta sunt à primo Paschate Christi ad secundum attinet, c. I. præconium Christi in Galilæa, Simeonis, Andreæ, tum Jacobi quoque & Zebedæi vocatio, & post concionem in Caper- naum obsessi liberatio: socrus Petri, & aliorum æ- grotorum sanatio describitur: & quomodo in tota Galilæa prædicarit, ac leprosum quemdam resti- tuerit, eodem capite docetur. Porro II. cap. Paraly- ticum in Capernaum sanat, Levi è telonio vocat, & cum publicanis comedit, ac de eo, & cur disci- puli ipsius non jejunent, rationem reddit, ad v. 22.

A secundo ad tertium Pascha Christi hæc gesta referuntur à Marco cap. II. reliquo: defensio disci- pulorum qui spicas fricarant in Sabbato, c. III. ari- dæ manus restitutio, secessus ad mare, multorum ægrotorum & obsessorum sanatio, Apostolorum ordinatio, calumniæ de Beelzebub profligatio, & de peccato in Spiritum S. deque veris suis consan- guineis informatio, c. IV. Parabolæ habentur de semine, & de luce non occultanda: & commoni- tio quod habenti detur similitudine ortus & incre- menti seminis grani sinapis illustrata: & de maris tempestate sedata agitur. Quinto capite in terra Gadarenorum obsessus liberatur, & Jairı filia, hæ- morrhoosa ἐν παρόδῳ sanata, resuscitatur. Sexto ca- pite Christus Nazarethæ comtemtus nulla signa e- dit, duodecim Apostolos emittit, & instruit, cujus fama ad Herodem qui Johannem decollarat, pene- travit: in deserto quinque millia virorum cibat, & in mari ambulat.

A tertio Paschate ad quartum hæc gesta recensi- ta sunt à Marco capite VI. reliquo: plurimorum æ- grotorum in terra Genesareth sanatio. Septimo ca- pite Pharisæorum traditiones, quia non laverant manus discipuli, reprehensæ, Cananææ filia sanata, & mutus ac surdus restitutus est. Octavo capite 4000. cibati: cæcus in Bethsaida sanatus: Petrus Christum confessus est, & Christus passionem, mortem & resurrectionem suam, Petro contradi- cente reprehenso prædixit, & ad crucem suos hor- tatus est, nec non ad confessionem sui. Nono capite post transfigurationem Christi de Elia quæsitus re- spondet, & lunaticum, quod discipuli non po- tuerant, à spiritu immundo liberat, ac Galilæam perambulans iterum passionem prædicit, & Ca- pernaumi puerulum in exemplum humilitatis sistit, deque alieno in nomine suo dæmonia ejici- ente non prohibendo, ut de scandalo fugiendo, & sale habendo monet. Decimo capite de divortio informat, parvulos ad se venire jubet, divitem le- gis observantiam jactantem probat, & de relin- quendis propter Deum omnibus monet.

Ad historiam ultimi Paschatos pertinet iter Hie- rosolymitanum, & in eo passionis, mortis & resurre- ctionis prædictio, sessionem ad dextram & sinistram suam expetentium informatio, & cæci circa Jericho

sanatio, c. X. reliquo: & porro c. XI. ingressus Hie- rosolymae asina factus, fici maledictio, templi re- formatio, de fidei efficacia & exauditione infor- matio,, & Sacerdotibus de potestate docendi sci- scitantibus data responsio. Duodecimo capite para- bola de vinea, & filio Domini vineae ejecto, imple- toque vaticinio de lapide reprobato, nec non re- sponsum de censu, de resurrectione mortuorum, de praecipuo praecepto, cum quaestione de filio & Domino Davidis, ac monitio de cavendis legispe- ritis, eorumq; fastu & avaritia habetur: ut & ob- servatio eorum, qui gazophylacio munus injicie- bant, & inter eos pauperis viduae. Decimo & ter- tio capite vaticinium de Hierosolymae interitu & de adventu Filii Dei novissimo cum admonitione ad vigilantiam proponitur.

Historia passionis c. XIV. exhibetur & c. XV. Illo consultatio Sacerdotum & Pharisaeorum, unctio Christi in Bethania; pactum cum Juda; Pascha, & praedictio proditionis Judae; celebratio S. Eu- charistiae; vaticinium de scandalo discipulorum, & abnegatione Petri; ceu antecedentia Passionis Christi: Passio in horto; & trina calicis deprecatio; Judae proditio; servi Pontificis percussio, Jesu, discipulis fugientibus, ad Pontificem abductio; falsa testimonia; Jesu, quod Christus sit, Dei Fi- lius sessurus ad dextram Dei, & venturus in nubi- bus confessio; & à Pontifice condemnatio; atque illusio; & Petri trina abnegatio; & sequuta illa- chrymatio. Hoc, decimo & quinto, capite concilio habito ad Pilatum abducitur & accusatur Jesus, qui eundem dimissum prae Barraba cupit, sed populus clamat, Jesum crucifigendum esse, cui ut fatisface- ret Pilatus, Jesum ut flagellaretur, & crucifigere- tur, tradidit. Quem in praetorium deductum purpura induunt, & corona spinea imposita exa- gitant, ac porro indutis vestibus propriis ad cru- cifixionem educunt, Simone Cyrenaeo ad crucem portandam coacto, & in Golgatha, myrrha prae- bita, crucifigunt, vestes distribuunt, titulum cruci imponunt, simul crucifigentes cum eo duos latro- nes, in cruce exagitant, qui tenebris trium hora- rum factis exclamat Eli, Eli, lama asabthani: & so- nora voce clamans expirat. Templi velum tum scissum, centurio conversus est, mulieres de lon- ginquo spectarunt, Josephus Arimathensis corpus Jesu impetratum à Pilato linteo involutum in se- pulchrum condidit.

Ultimo, quod decimum & sextum est, capite adventus mulierum ad sepulchrum, & ingressus, ac conspectus Angeli, resurrectionem nuntiantis, & ut referant discipulis, à quibus videndus sit in Galilaea mandantis, reditusque à sepulchro exponitur, cum apparitionibus Jesu Mariae Mag- dalenae, duobus in campo ambulantibus, & unde- cim discipulis factis: nec non missio in orbem ad praedicandum Evangelium, & signorum promis- sio. Denique ascensio in coelum, ac sessio ad dextram Dei, & praedicantibus ubique Aposto- lis, Domini cooperatio, verbique per signa con- firmatio.

## 1:1 Argument
PART I. OF THE GOSPEL OF ST. MARK, exhibiting the Acts from the first Passover to the second, preceded by the inauguration of Christ through Baptism. CHAPTER I. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

Let the beginning be from the baptism and proclamation of John, predicted by Malachi (ch. 3. 5.) and Isaiah (ch. 40. 3.), to whom all Judea betook itself, who testified concerning the coming of one stronger and more worthy than himself, who was to baptize with the baptism of the Holy Spirit; by whom Jesus was baptized, the Holy Spirit descending from heaven upon him, and a heavenly voice proclaiming him the Son of God. Subjoined is the temptation of Jesus in the desert, and after John was delivered up, the preaching in Galilee, and the summary of it: who also called Simon and Andrew there, as well as James and John the brothers; and teaching in the synagogue at Capernaum with the admiration of all, he cast out an unclean spirit testifying about him; coming into the house of Simon, he freed his mother-in-law from a fever, and restored various sick and possessed people, going out in the morning into the desert for the sake of prayer, and preaching in all Galilee; he heals a leper, and sending him to the priests, which fame is spread abroad, whence he withdrew into desert places.

The parts are three: I. Introduction concerning John, and the baptism, and the temptation of Christ, to v. 13. II. The preaching of Jesus, and the calling of the disciples, and the deeds at Capernaum, to v. 34. III. The preaching in other synagogues of Galilee, and the healing of the leper, with the withdrawal of Christ, to v. 45.

PART I. The entry, concerning John the Baptist, and the baptism and temptation of Jesus in the desert.

Vers. 1. Ἀρχὴ τῦ ἐυαγγελίε Ἰησῦ χρισῦ] We have said in the commentary on Matthew that the ἐυαγγέλιον Ἰησῦ Χρισῦ is the very preaching pronounced by Christ. Mark says that the beginning of this is the preaching of John, as being prior to the preaching of Jesus. For the word ἀρχῆς is ambiguous, as Aristotle notes: of beginnings, some are inherent, others are external. Here ἀρχὴ is taken in the latter sense. For the baptism of John was a leading into the discipline of Christ.

τῦ υἱῦ θεῦ] In this very opening Mark prefaces this, intending to prove the truth of so great a surname by the magnitude of the things that follow. A comparison makes it clear that Mark used the Gospel of Matthew: which makes it seem the more wonderful that those things which pertain to the birth of Christ, although they had been handed down by Matthew, were passed over by Mark. It occurs to me that Mark had regard for both the people and the times. The Romans, certainly, at whose request he is believed to have written, being recent converts from paganism, were easily going to imagine something of such a kind as was narrated among themselves concerning Alcmene, Leda, Danae, and Ilia. For similar reasons, the Apostles, both in their speeches and in their Epistles, scarcely mentioned that matter. But if Peter judged that he should be silent about that matter, that one reason was sufficiently just for Mark not to touch upon this part of history, the necessity of preaching which everywhere began then most of all, when there arose those who would repeatedly call Christ a mere man.

Grotius rightly observes that Mark, in this very Exordium, intends to prove the truth of so great a surname by the magnitude of the things that follow. But that he made use of Matthew’s Gospel is asserted less correctly by him, as is evident from a comparison: for he neither had need to use it, nor is it likely that he did use it; since he ought not to have followed others, but to have written what the Holy Spirit suggested, and therefore what is said by Augustine, that he is an abbreviator of Matthew, must be understood with discernment: not that he had Matthew at hand, but that he relates more succinctly in some places what Matthew treats more fully: and Flacius observes in his preface to Mark, according to the opinion of other Doctors as well, which the reading itself confirms, that Mark neither follows the same order of events throughout as Matthew, nor does he narrate only those things which he himself does, but also certain things which are not found at all in Matthew, but certain things which are found in him he recites more copiously: because he also does not touch upon many histories of his, and those of the greatest importance. Whence Grotius had no need to wonder that he passed over those things which pertain to the birth of Christ, since they were handed down by Matthew. That reason, certainly, which Grotius gives is vain and profane: that the account of both men and times from paganism were easily going to imagine such a thing as was told among them about Alcmene, Leda, Danaë, and Ilia. And for similar reasons that the Apostles in their speeches, as well as in their Epistles, scarcely mentioned that matter, is equally futile and inept, nay, profane. For it is a matter of religion for us to believe that the Holy Writers wished to omit sacred things, however necessary to be believed, for the sake of profane fables.

Latin:

PARS I. EVANGELII S. MARCI PRÆMISSA CHRISTI INAUGU- ratione per Baptismum Acta à pri- mo Paschate ad secundum exhibens. CAPUT I. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.
