Principium sit à Iohannis prædicti à Malachia (cap. III. 5.) & Esaia (cap. XL. 3.) baptismo, & præconio, ad quem tota Iudæa se contu- lit, qui de adventu fortioris, & dignioris se, baptismo Spiritus S. baptizaturi, testa- tus; à quo baptizatus Iesus, Spiritu S. de cœlo descendente super ipsum, & voce cœle- sti eum Filium Dei proclamante. Subjungi- tur tentatio Iesu in deserto, & post tradi- tum Iohannem prædicatio in Galilæa, ejus- que summa: qui vocavit etiam ibi Simo- nem, & Andræam, nec non Iacobum, & Io- hannem fratres; & Capernaumi in Syna- goga cum admiratione omnium docens, im- pium Spiritum de ipso testantem ejecit; in domum Simonis veniens socrum ejus à fe- bri liberavit, & varios ægrotos & obsessos restituit, mane in desertum precum causa exiens, & prædicans in tota Galilæa; le- prosum sanat, & ad Sacerdotes remittens, quæ fama divulgatur, unde in deserta loca secessit.

Partes sunt tres: I. Ingressus de Johanne, & ba- ptismo, & tentatione Christi, ad v. 13. II. Præ- conium Jesu, & vocatio discipulorum, & gesta Capernaumi, ad vers. 34. III. Præconium in aliis Scholis Galilææ, & sanatio leprosi, cum secessu Christi, ad v. 45.

PARS I. Ingressus, de Iohanne Baptista, & baptismo ac tentatione Iesu in deserto.

Vers. 1. Ἀρχὴ τῦ ἐυαγγελίε Ἰησῦ χρισῦ] ἐυαγγέλιον Ἰησῦ Χρι- σῦ esse ipsum κήρυγμα à Christo pronunciatum diximus ad Matthæum. Hujus initium Marcus esse dicit τὸ κήρυγμα Johannis, quippe prævium τῷ Ἰησῦ κηρύγματι. Vox enim ἀρχῆς ambigua, ut notat Aristoteles: ἀρχῶν αἱ μὲν ἐνυπάρ- χυσαί εἰσιν, αἱ δὲ ἐκτός. Hic posteriore significatu ἀρχὴ su- mitur. Nam Iohannis baptisma manductio ad Christi di- sciplinam fuit.

τῦ υἱῦ θεῦ] Hoc in ipso exordio præfatur Marcus, tanti cognominis veritatem sequentium rerum magnitudine probaturus. Usum esse Marcum Matthæi Evangelio, a- pertum facit collatio: quo magis mirum videri potest, ea quæ ad nativitatem Christi pertinent, cum à Matthæo es- sent tradita, præterita esse a Marco. Mihi hoc succurrit, ha- bitam à Marco & hominum & temporum rationem. Ro- mani certe, quorum rogatu scripsisse creditur, recentes à paganismo, facile tale quid erant imaginaturi, quale apud ipsos de Alcmena, Leda, Danaë, Ilia narrabantur. Simi- libus de causis Apostoli tum in orationibus, tum in Epi- stolis vix ejus rei meminerunt. Quod si Petrus ea de re silendum sibi judicavit, ea vel una causa Marco satis justa fuit, non attingendi hanc historiæ partem, cujus passim prædicandæ necessitas tunc maxime cœpit, cum exstite- runt qui Christum ψιλὸν ἄνθρωπον dictitarent.

Præfari hoc Marcum in ipso Exordio, tanti cogno- minis veritatem sequentium rerum magnitudine pro- baturum, recte observat Grotius. At quod usus fuerit Marcus Matthæi Evangelio è collatione aper- tum esse minus recte asserit: nam nec opus habuit eodem uti, nec verisimile est, quod eodem u- sus sit; quum non sequi alios, sed quæ suggere- bat S. S. scribere debuerit, ideoque quod ab Au- gustino abbreviator Matthæi dicitur, dextre intel- ligendum: non quod præ manibus Matthæum ha- buerit, sed quod in nonnullis succinctius tradat, quæ Matthæus fusius exequitur: & observat Fla- cius præfat. in Marc. ex aliorum etiam Doctorum sententia, quam ipsa lectio confirmat, quod Mar- cus nec ordinem eundem per omnia sequatur rerum, quem Matthæus, nec solum illa narret, quæ ipse, sed etiam quædam quæ in Matthæo prorsus non habean- tur, quædam vero quæ in illo habentur copiosus reci- tet : quod etiam multas , easque , maximi momenti historias illius plane non attingat. Unde mirari opus non habuit Grotius, quod ea, quæ ad nativitatem Christi pertinent, cum à Matthæo tradita sint, præ- terierit. Illa certe causa, quam reddit Grotius, va- na & prophana est : quod & hominum & temporum ratio à paganismo facile tale quid imaginaturi erant, quale apud ipsos de Alcmena, Leda, Danaë, Ilia nar- rabatur. Et similibus de causis Apostolos tum in o- rationibus, tum in Epistolis vix ejus rei meminisse , æ- que futile atque ineptum, imo prophanum est. In gratiam enim profanorum commentorum res sacras omittere voluisse S. Scriptores, utut creditu necessarias, religio nobis est credere.

## 1:2
Verse 2. As it is written in Isaiah the prophet. I wonder that the truth of this Scripture is doubted, since, besides the authority of the codices and Irenæus citing it thus, the consensus of the ancient interpreters, the Syrian, the Latin, and the Arab, is manifest. Nor indeed would Porphyry have brought forward this passage against the Christians, unless that had been the constant reading of the codices: nor would the Christians have labored in solving Porphyry's objection. Add that the reason for changing this reading is apparent: there could be no reason for changing the other. Doubtless Matthew had cited Isaiah: whom Mark follows: but so that it might appear more certainly who that was of whom Isaiah treats, he adds to the greater prophet a lesser one, Malachi to Isaiah: whom he had to name besides, because the authority of Isaiah was more illustrious, and there was nothing in the words of Malachi whose sentiment did not also exist in Isaiah. But it seems to me that that 'as it is written' should be drawn to the preceding, so that Mark may say that the preaching of Christ had that preparation which the prophecies had predicted.

The bold alteration of the received Original text, which has 'in the prophets'. For as to what it appeals to the authority of the Greek Codices, those are very few, and scarcely three observed by Beza, with all the others retaining the received reading by great consensus: Nor is the citation of Irenæus, whose passage could have been corrupted just as easily, sufficient. But the Syrian, Latin, and Arab versions are more recent, and cannot prejudice the authentic text. But that Porphyry brought forward the passage in such a way, and that the received reading was not observed in the response to Porphyry's objection, proves only a particular reading. And the context entirely favors the received reading; in which not only the testimony of Isaiah, but also that of Malachi is brought forward: and what is especially to be observed, the passage of Malachi is placed first. Therefore that reading does not harmonize with the text: 'As it is written in the prophet Isaiah saying, Behold I send my angel': for that was nowhere said by the prophet Isaiah. But what Grotius says is vain, that Mark had Malachi besides, because the authority of Isaiah was more illustrious, and there was nothing in the words of Malachi whose sentiment did not also exist in Isaiah. For all the prophets, because they are equally inspired by God, are equally illustrious witnesses: nor is there anything in Isaiah about the mission of an angel: But about the voice of one crying in the desert.

Latin:

Vers. 2. ὡς γέγραπται ἐν Ἠσαΐᾳ τῷ προφήτῃ] De hujus Scripturæ veritate dubitari miror, cum, præter codicum au- ctoritatem & Irenæum ita citantem, manifesta sit vete- rum interpretum, Syri, Latini, Arabis, consensio. Neque vero Porphyrius adduxisset hunc locum contra Christianos, nisi ea constans fuisset codicum lectio : neque Christiani in solvenda Porphyrii objectione laborassent. Adde quod hujus lectionis mutandæ causa apparet : alterius mutandæ nulla esse potuit. Nimirum Esaiam citarat Matthæus: quem sequitur Marcus : sed ut certius appareret quis ille esset de quo agit Esaias, interpretem addit majori vati mi- norem, Esaiz Malachiam: quem nominare insuper ha- buit, quod Esaiæ autoritas esset illustrior, nec quicquam esset in verbis Malachiæ cujus non sententia & apud Esaiam extaret. Videtur autem mihi istud ὡς γέγραπται ad ante- cedentia trahendum, ut dicat Marcus Christi κήρυγμα eam habuisse προπαρασκευὴν quam vaticinia prædixerant.

Audax textus Originalis recepti, qui habet ἐν τοῖς προφήταις immutatio. Quod enim ad Codi- cum Græcorum auctoritatem provocat, pauci illi admodum sunt, & à Beza vix tres observati, cæ- teris omnibus magno consensu receptam lectio- nem retinentibus : Neque Irenæi citatio, cujus locus æque facile corrumpi potuit, sufficiens est. Syri autem, Latini, & Arabis versiones recentio- res sunt, nec textui authentico præjudicare pos- sunt. Quod vero Porphyrius ita adduxerit lo- cum, & quod in responsione ad objectionem Por- phyrii recepta lectio observata non sit, particula- rem solum lectionem probat. Et favet omnino receptæ lectioni contextus; in quo non Esaiæ tantum, sed etiam Malachiæ testimonium addu- citur: & quod præcipue observandum, Malachiæ locus præmittitur. Non consonat ergo textui le- ctio illa: Sicut scriptum est in Propheta Esaia dicen- te, Ecce ego mitto angelum meum: id enim nus- piam à Propheta Esaiâ dictum. Vanum vero est, quod ait Grotius, Marcum insuper habuisse Malachiam, quod Esaiæ auctoritas esset illustrior, nec quicquam esset in verbis Malachiæ, cujus non sen- tentia & apud Esaiam extaret. Nam Prophetæ o- mnes, quia æque θεόπνευστοι æque illustres sunt testes: neque apud Esaiam de angeli missione quic- quam: Sed de voce clamantis in deserto.

## 1:4
Verse 4. John was baptizing. This kind of speaking designates a continued act. Thus below v. 39 concerning Jesus, 'and he was preaching'. And concerning the disciples of John and the Pharisees, 'they were fasting' below c. II. 18.

Preaching a baptism of repentance for the remission of sins. Luke followed these words of Mark in c. III. concerning the interpretation of which, to omit the moderns, the ancients have handed down various things. Tertullian: He says, a baptism of repentance was acted out, as it were a candidate for the remission and sanctification that was to follow in Christ. For because he was preaching a baptism of repentance for the remission of sins, it was announced, he says, for a future remission. Since indeed repentance precedes, remission follows, and this is to prepare the way: but he who prepares does not himself perfect, but procures for another to be perfected. And elsewhere he shows that by the word repentance he does not understand the amendment of life, but certain external acts: which does not seem to agree entirely with the truth. I do not deny that the word 'repentance' is usually taken more strictly: but I am moved by many arguments why I do not think it should be taken so precisely here. First, Moses and the Prophets in many places command that the remission of sins be hoped for under the sole condition of repentance. But they usually add mention of the heart, so that they may teach that internal conversion is to be understood by them at the same time as the external, Deut. IV. 29. 1 Kings VIII. 47. 2 Chron. VII. 14. Neh. I. 28. Isa. I. 16, 17, 18. Jer. XVIII. 8. Ezek. XVIII. 11, c. XXXIII. 14. But it is not credible that John, being greater than the Prophets and bringing more light, demanded less repentance than the preceding Prophets had demanded. Then Christ proposed the sum of his doctrine with the same word, 'Repent' Matt. IV. 17. And Peter, the legate of Christ: 'Repent, and let each of you be baptized for the remission of sins' Acts II. 38. Wherefore it seems more true that John by the name of repentance understood all the parts of our duty and the true remission of sins, pre-signified in the Jubilee, in the mention of which the LXX interpreters use the word 'remission'. Neither, however, was fully and clearly explained by him. But repentance was delineated in its rudiments and as in a type, both by the flight from evil works and by a certain beginning of good ones, Luke III. 11, and the remission of sins was also described by immunity from divine wrath, Matt. III. 7. But that he wished for the consummated knowledge of both to be sought from Christ, to whose teaching he relegated his own, who were to receive by his benefit not only a doctrine most perfect in all its parts, but also the spirit of illumination, fortitude, and constancy.

The points which Grotius argues here concerning the interpretation of the word μετανοίας, whether they imply an internal conversion, and concerning ἀφέσει, whether they imply a true remission of sins, do not deserve to be retracted. He proceeds from a false hypothesis, as if conversion had not been so fully prescribed or the remission of sins delivered in former times: whence also it is claimed by him that neither was fully and clearly expounded by John himself, but that μετανοίαν was delineated in its rudiments καὶ ὡς ἐν τύπῳ, both by the flight from evil works and by a certain beginning of good ones, Luke 3:11, and that the remission of sins was also described as an immunity from divine wrath, Matthew 3:7. But how can it be doubted that the Prophets recalled to true conversion those who were entrusted to their faith, or that they announced the true remission of sins? This Pelagio-Socinian dogma has been refuted elsewhere. John, the herald of repentance, ought not only to have delivered the rudiments of μετανοίας, or to have delineated it ὡς ἐν τύπῳ, because he warned μετανοεῖτε, but he also ought to have delivered those things which pertain to μετανοίαν: which does not consist in the flight from evil works and the pursuit of good ones, but in contrition and faith in Christ, of which good works are the consequence, as fruits of repentance, Matthew 3:8. For fruits do not constitute the thing, but follow it. Now, John neither neglected those things which make for the acknowledgment of sins and true contrition, nor those which make for faith in Christ, nor ought he to have neglected them by the force of these Prophetic testimonies of Isaiah and Malachi. He also fully delivered the remission of sins, not merely an immunity from divine wrath, Luke 1:77, as is evident from his sermons in John 1 and 3. Nor, finally, is he called the precursor of Christ because he had to prepare the way for Him, because he had to teach that a consummate knowledge of repentance and of the remission of sins was to be sought from Christ, and to relegate his followers to His teaching, that they might receive by His benefit not only a doctrine most perfect in all its parts, but also the Spirit of illumination, fortitude, and constancy: as Grotius does in the manner of the Socinians; for Christ delivered no other doctrine than John, or even the Prophets in the Old Testament, which ought to have been perfect at all times, and was perfect, 2 Timothy 3:15, 16, 17; nor were the children and disciples of John or the Prophets destitute of the Spirit of illumination, or of fortitude and constancy: which the faithful have needed at all times, and have been divinely instructed. For that reason, indeed, the precursor The forerunner of the Lord preparing the way of the Lord is called the Baptist-herald, because he had to teach that Jesus of Nazareth, to whom he had to go before, was the Messiah promised to the world, and to point him out with his finger, and to testify so that faith might be had in him: just as John teaches in ch. 1. 7. which was also done diligently by him, so that, namely, there might be no doubt about the coming of the Messiah, or that another might be accepted for the Messiah, this one being rejected. Moreover, it is called the Baptism of repentance not only objectively, because it warned about repentance and looked toward the penitent, but also effectively, because it worked repentance for the remission of sins.

Latin:

Vers. 4. ἐγένετο Ἰωάννης βαπτίζων] Hoc loquendi genus actum continuatum designat. Ita infra v. 39. de Jesu, καὶ ἦν κηρύσσων. Et de discipulis Johannis & Pharisæorum, ἦ- σαν νηστεύοντες infra c. II. 18.

Κηρύσσων βάπτισμα μετανοίας εἰς ἄφεσιν ἁμαρτιῶν] Secu- tus hæc Marci verba est Lucas c. III. de quorum interpre- tatione, ut novos omittam, varia veteres tradidere. Ter- tullianus: Actum, ait, baptismum pœnitentiæ, quasi candi- datum remissionis & sanctificationis in Christo subsecuturæ. Nam quod prædicabat baptismum pœnitentiæ in remissionem delictorum, in futuram, inquit, remissionem enunciatum est Siquidem pœnitentia antecedit, remissio subsequitur, & hoc est viam præparare : qui autem præparat, non idem ipse perficit, sed alii perficiendum procurat. Et alibi ostendit pœ- nitentiæ se voce non vitæ emendationem, sed actus quos- dam externos intelligere: quod non videtur plane vero congruere. Non nego μετανοίας vocem strictius solere ac- cipi: sed cur hic ita præcise accipiendam non putem, mul- tis moveor argumentis. Primum Moses & Prophetæ mul- tis in locis remissionem peccatorum sperari jubent sub sola μετανοίας conditione. Plerumque autem addere solent cordis mentionem, ut internam conversionem simul cum externa a se intelligi doceant, Deut. IV. 29. 1. Reg. VIII. 47. 2. Par. VII. 14. Nehem. I. 28. Esa. I. 16. 17. 18. Jerem. XVIII. 8. Ezech. XVIII. 11. c. XXXIII. 14. Non est autem cre- dibile Johannem majorem Prophetis, & plus lucis affe- rentem minorem exegisse pœnitentiam, quam antegressi Prophetæ exegerant. Deinde Christus summam doctrinæ suæ eadem voce proposuit μετανοεῖτε Matth. IV. 17. Et Pe- trus Christi legatus : Μετανοήσατε, καὶ βαπτισθήτω ἕκαστος ὑ- μῶν εἰς ἄφεσιν ἁμαρτιῶν Act. II. 38. Quare verius videtur Johannem μετανοίας nomine intellexisse omnes officii no- stri partes & veram remissionem peccatorum, præsignifi- catam in Jubilæo, in cujus mentione LXX. interpretes vocem ἀφέσεως usurpant. Neutrum tamen ab ipso plene atque enucleate expositum. Sed τὴν μετανοίαν delineatam in suis rudimentis καὶ ὡς ἐν τύπῳ, tum malorum operum fuga, tum quadam bonorum inchoatione Luc. III. 11. remissio- ne quoque peccatorum descriptam immunitate ab ira divi- na, Matth. III. 7. Sed voluisse eum consummatam utrius- que cognitionem a Christo peti, ad cujus magisterium suos relegabat, accepturos ejus beneficio non tantum do- ctrinam omnibus suis partibus perfectissimam, sed & spiritum illuminationis, fortitudinis, atque constantiæ.

Quæ hic disputat Grotius de interpretatione vocis μετανοίας, utrum internam conversionem, & de ἀφέσει utrum veram remissionem peccatorum in- ferant? retractari non merentur. Procedit ex hypothesi falsa, quasi non ita plene olim vel conversio præscripta, vel remissio peccatorum tra- dita sit: unde etiam ab ipso Johanne neutrum plene atque enucleate expositum esse, sed τὴν μετανοίαν delineatam in suis rudimentis καὶ ὡς ἐν τύπῳ, tum malorum operum fuga, tum quadam bonorum inchoatione Luc. III. 11. remissionem quoque peccatorum descriptam immunitate ab ira divina Matth. III. 7. At quomodo dubitari potest, Prophetas ad veram conversionem revocasse eos, qui fidei ipsorum crediti, aut veram peccatorum remissionem annunciasse? Dogma hoc Pelagio- Socinianum alias profligatum est. Non solum rudimenta τῆς μετανοίας tradere, aut eam ὡς ἐν τύπῳ delineare debuit Johannes præco pœnitentiæ, quia monuit μετανοεῖτε, etiam quæ ad μετανοίαν pertinent, tradere debuit: quæ non consistit in malorum operum fuga, & bonorum studio, sed in contritione & fide in Christum, cujus conse- quentia sunt bona opera, ceu fructus pœnitentiæ Matth. III. 8. Fructus enim non constituunt rem, sed consequuntur eandem. Jam nec quæ ad peccatorum agnitionem, veramque contritio- nem faciunt, nec quæ ad fidem in Christum, ne- glexit Johannes, neque vi testimoniorum horum Propheticorum Esaiæ, & Malachiæ negligere de- buit. Remissionem etiam peccatorum plene tra- didit, non solum immunitatem ab ira divina Luc. I. 77. ut e concionibus ejus Johan. I. & III. constat. Nec denique ideo præcursor Christi dicitur, quod viam ipsi parare debuit, quod consummatam co- gnitionem pœnitentiæ, & remissionis peccatorum a Christo petendam esse, docere debuerit, & ad ejus Magisterium suos relegare, accepturos ejus beneficio non tantum doctrinam omnibus suis partibus perfe- ctissimam, sed & Spiritum illuminationis, fortitu- dinis atque constantiæ: uti Socinianorum more Grotius: nam nullam aliam doctrinam Christus tradidit, quam Johannes, vel etiam Prophetæ in V. T. quæ omnibus temporibus perfecta esse de- buit, ac perfecta fuit, 2. Timoth. III. 15. 16. 17. neque destituti fuêre vel Johannis vel Prophetarum filii & discipuli Spiritu illuminationis, aut fortitudinis ac constantiæ: quo omnibus temporibus eguêre fideles, & instructi sunt divinitus. Ideo vero præ- cursor Domini viam Domini præparans dicitur Præco-baptista, quia Jesum Nazarenum, cui præ- ire debuit, docere debebat esse Messiam, mundo promissum, eumque digito demonstrare, & ut fi- des ipsi haberetur, testari: quemadmodum Johan- nes docet c. 1. 7. quod etiam ab ipso sedulo factum, ne scil. vel de Messiæ adventu dubitaretur, vel alius pro Messia, hoc repudiato, susciperetur. Cæterum Baptisma pœnitentiæ dicitur non objective tan- tum, quod de pœnitentia moneret, & ad pœniten- tes spectaret, sed etiam effective, quod operaretur pœnitentiam in remissionem peccatorum.

## 1:7
Vers. 7. κύψας] Stooping. He expressed the gesture of a servant taking the shoe off his Lord.

Latin:

Vers. 7. κύψας] Cernuus. Gestum expressit famuli cal- ceum Domino exuentis.

## 1:10
Vers. 10. ἀναβαίνων ἀπὸ τẽ ὕδατος] It can be referred to John by hyperbaton. See what is said on Matthew. For both John and Christ had ascended from the water.

σχιζομένους] Matthew had said ἀνεῴχθησαν αὐτῷ οἱ ὀυρανοὶ, whence also this gloss ἠνεῳγμένως was born in this place. But Mark expressed the manner in which the heaven was seen to be opened, not gradually, but with one impetus, like those things which are torn. Which seems to have been a sign of the heavenly King suddenly breaking through obstacles.

Latin:

Vers. 10. ἀναβαίνων ἀπὸ τẽ ὕδατος] Potest per ὑπερβατὸν ad Johannem referri. Vide quæ ad Matthæum. Nam tam Johannes quam Christus ex aqua ascenderant.

σχιζομένους] ἀνεῴχθησαν αὐτῷ οἱ ὀυρανοὶ dixerat Matthæus, unde & glossema natum hoc loco ἠνεῳγμένως. Sed Marcus modum quo visum est aperiri cœlum expressit non sensim, sed uno impetu, ut ea quæ scinduntur. Quod fignum vi- detur fuisse perrupturi subito obstantia regi cœlestis.

## 1:11
Vers. 11. ἐν σοὶ ἠυδόκησα] So the Syriac and Latin and some Greek codices; what others have, ἐν ᾧ, is from Matthew.

But why is the received reading abandoned on account of one or another variant codex, and the translation of the Syriac and Latin interpreters preferred to the source itself? And whence is it certain that the little words ἐν ᾧ were transferred here from Matthew? We have a religious scruple against changing the text on account of such vain suspicions, when most copies agree. The change of person is frequent among the Hebrews.

Latin:

Vers. 11. ἐν σοὶ ἠυδόκησα] Ita Syrus & Latinus & codices Græci aliquot, quod alii habent ἐν ᾧ ex Matthæo est.

Cur vero recepta lectio ob unum atque alte- rum variantem Codicem deseritur, ac Syri & Lati- ni Interpp. translatio ipsi fonti præfertur? Et unde id constat, quod voculæ ἐν ᾧ è Matthæo huc traductæ sint? Ob vanas ejusmodi suspiciones tex- tum, consonantibus plerisque exemplaribus, im- mutare nobis religio est. Frequens est apud E- bræos personæ mutatio.

## 1:12
Vers. 12. ἐυθὺς] Not long after. For one or two days intervened, John I. 29. Nor is it unusual for ἐυθὺς to be used in this way, as in John XIII. 32. Why this time is so diligently noted, others bring forward different conjectures. It does not displease me what some have handed down, that perhaps in the person of Christ it is shown to us what threatens Christians after they have been baptized, that is, after they have renounced the world, namely, a new struggle against malignant spirits: concerning which matter we have said something on Matthew.

ἐκβάλλει] This word is put for ἄγειν in John X. 4, but a simpler exposition is 'he orders to depart,' in the way the same word is used in Matt. IX. 25 and below in this very chapter v. 43.

Latin:

Vers. 12. ἐυθὺς] Non multo post. Nam dies unus aut alter intercessit Ioh. I. 29. Neque inusitatum est, ut ἐυθὺς ita usurpetur, ut Ioh. XIII. 32. Cur tempus hoc tam diligenter notetur, alii alias adferunt conjecturas. Mihi non dis- plicet quod quidam tradiderunt, forte in Christi persona nobis ostendi quid Christianis postquam baptizati sunt, id est postquam sæculo renunciarunt, immineat, novum scili- cet certamen adversus malignos spiritus: qua de re ad Mat- thæum aliquid diximus.

ἐκβάλλει] Hæc vox pro ἄγειν ponitur Ioh. X. 4. sed sim- plicior expositio est jubet discedere quomodo eadem vox usurpatur Matth. IX. 25. & infra hoc ipso capite v. 43.

## 1:13
Vers. 13. μετὰ τῶν θηρίων] Not without cause did Mark add this, to signify that this was not just any wilderness, but a most desolate one. At the same time, it seems that an allusion can be made to the passage of Job V. 21.

Διηκόνουν αὐτῷ] After the temptation was finished, as Matthew teaches us, Mark delivers this history, like many others, in summary, hastening to greater things.

It is conveniently explained as 'not long after': since one or two days intervened, John I. 29, nor is it unusual for ἐυθὺς to be used in this way, as in John XIII. 32. But ἐκβάλλει is less correctly explained as 'he orders to depart.' For why should the proper meaning of the word not be retained, or explained by ἄγειν, as it is taken in John X. 4? For the Holy Spirit is no less to lead and guide than to order and impel. In Matthew it is rendered ἀνήχθη, c. IV. 1. But it is not a violent impulse, but only strong and powerful in the style of the Hellenists, since this word corresponds to the word שלח among the LXX, Exod. XII. 33, Ps. XLIII. 3. Cf. Matt. VII. 4, 5, c. IX. 25, 38, cap. XIII. 53, just as the word which the Syriac uses, אפק, signifies both to cast out and to send forth.

PART II.

The proclamation of Jesus, the calling of the disciples, and the city of Capernaum.

Latin:

Vers. 13. μετὰ τῶν θηρίων] Non sine causa hoc adjecit Marcus, ut significaret non quamvis sed desertissimam fuis- se hanc solitudinem. Simul allusum videri potest ad locum Iobi V. 21.

Διηκόνουν αὐτῷ] Post absolutum πειρασμὸν, ut Matthæus nos docet Marcus hanc historiam, ut multas alias, compen- dio tradit, ad majora properans.

Commode id exponitur, non multo post: siqui- dem dies unus aut alter intercesserit Joh. I. 29. ne- que inusitatum est, ut ἐυθὺς ita usurpetur, ut Joh. XIII. 32. ἐκβάλλει autem minus recte explicatur jubet discedere. Cur enim non retinenda propria verbi significatio, aut per ἄγειν explicandum, uti accipitur Joh. X. 4. Spiritus enim S. non minus est agere ac ducere, quam jubere, & impellere. Apud Matthæum redditur ἀνήχθης, c. IV. 1. Non autem est impulsus violentus, sed stylo Hellenistarum vali- dus tantum & potens, cum verbum hoc respondeat verbo שלח apud LXX. Exod. XII. 33. Psal. XLIII. 3. Conf. Matth. VII. 4. 5. c. IX. 25. 38. cap. XIII. 53. uti verbum, quod Syrus adhibet אפק & ejicere si- gnificat, & emittere.

PARS II.

Præconium Jesu, vocatio discipulorum, & ge- stain Capernaum.

## 1:15
Verse 15. πεπλήρωται ὁ καιρός] The time destined for the most abundant grace of God, predicted by the Prophets. τὸ πλήρωμα τῦ χρόνο Gal. IV. 3. τὸ πλήρωμα τῶν καιρῶν Eph. I. 23. צפירת היום Ezech. VII. 7.

πιστέυετε ἐν τῷ ἐυαγγελίῳ] It is true that the Hellenists use ἐν and εἰς after πιστέυειν in the same sense. But the fact that the Septuagint and the Apostles sometimes translate האמין with ב without a preposition by the Dative, as if it were הֶאֱמִין with ל, does not arise from the property of the words, but because the thing itself sometimes results in both expressions falling into the same meaning, especially where it concerns a promiser or a promise. Otherwise, as the Hebrews rightly note, הֶאֱמִין with ל is to have faith in a person or a statement; הֶאֱמִין with ב is to place trust in someone. Thus, πιστεύειν ἐν τῷ εὐαγγελίῳ would be to believe that the things being said were true, just as לֹא הֶאֱמַנְתִּי לִדְבָרִים is said in 1 Kings 10:7. But πιστεύειν εἰς τὸ εὐαγγέλιον or ἐν τῷ εὐαγγελίῳ is to place one's hope in that announcement, just as in Psalm 119:66 it is said בְמִצְוֹתֶיךָ הֶאֱמַנְתִּי, where, however, the LXX put ταῖς ἐντολαῖς σου ἐπίστευσα, surely because, as I said, the matter results in the same thing. Wherefore the old Latin interpreter also neglected this distinction in this place, which he observed elsewhere.

The Vulgate rendered it, believe the Gospel. Drusius wishes for believing God and in God to be the same thing: But although the use of those prepositions sometimes results in the same thing, nevertheless they are of different signification in themselves, since to believe someone is to have faith in him and expresses only assent: but to believe in someone is to place trust in him: which is not inconveniently observed here by Grotius.

Latin:

Vers. 15. πεπλήρωται ὁ καιρός] Tempus uberrimæ Dei gra- tiæ destinatum, prædictum à Prophetis. τὸ πλήρωμα τῦ χρόνο Gal. IV. 3. τὸ πλήρωμα τῶν καιρῶν Eph. I. 23. צפירת היום Ezech. VII. 7.

πιστέυετε ἐν τῷ ἐυαγγελίῳ] Verum est Hellenistas ἐν & εἰς post πιστέυειν eodem sensu usurpare. At quod האמין cum ב septuaginta & Apostoli sine præpositione per Dativum in- dum transferunt, quasi sit הֶאֱמִין cum ל, id non tamen ex vocum proprietate, quam quia interdum res ipsa efficit, ut in idem recidat utraque locutio, quippe ubi de promis- sore aut promissione agitur. Alioqui ut recte notant He- bræi הֶאֱמִין cum ל est fidem habere alicui personæ aut di- cto הֶאֱמִין cum ב est in aliquo fiduciam ponere. Ita πίς τεύειν ἐνευαγγελίῳ, esset credere dero esse quæ dicebantur, quomo- do לֹא הֶאֱמַנְתִּי לִדְבָרִים dicitur 1.Reg.X.7. At πιο τεύειν εἰς τὸ ἐνευαγγέλιον sive ἐν τῷ ἐνευαγγελίῳ est in ea annunciatio- ne spem suam locare quomodo Psal. CXIX. vers. 66. dicitur בְמִצְוֹתֶיךָ הֶאֱמַנְתִּי. ubi tamen LXX. ponunt ταῖς ἐντο λαῖς σου ἐπίστευσα, nimirum quia ut dixi res eodem recidit. Quare & vetus Latinus interpres hoc loco discrimen ne- glexit, alibi observatum.

Vulgatus reddidit, credite Evangelio. Drusius credere Deo, & in Deum idem esse vult: Sed quam- vis usus illarum præpositionum in idem quando- que recidat, tamen per se diversæ significationis sunt, cum credere alicui sit fidem ei habere & assen- sum tantum exprimat: credere autem in aliquem sit fiduciam in eum collocare: quod hic non incom- mode observatum à Grotio.

## 1:20
Verse 20. μετὰ τῶν μισθωτῶν] It has emphasis because they left their father, for whom their work was profitable: since he also used hired services.

Latin:

Vers. 20. μετὰ τῶν μισθωτῶν] Habet ἔμφασιν quod Patrem reliquerunt cui quæstuosa erat ipsorum opera: quando & conductis ministeriis utebatur.

## 1:21
Verse 21. τοῖς Cάββασι] That is, on the Sabbath, as the Syrian and Latin. See what is at Matt. 12:1. Mark also added this not without cause, so that he might ward off the calumny of the Sabbath being despised by Christ. This truly was to observe the Sabbath, to approach pious assemblies and to be occupied in meditating on the law. For thus the most ancient usage interpreted that which is in Lev. 23:3, as that passage of James in Acts 15:21 teaches us: "For Moses from ancient generations has in every city those who preach him, being read in the synagogues every Sabbath." And Paul says the voices of the prophets were accustomed to be read every Sabbath, Acts 13:27. Josephus testifies to the same against Apion: "He commanded that every week, leaving their works, they should gather for the hearing of the law, and learn it accurately, which indeed all lawgivers seem to have neglected." And Philo: "They perform this custom very well, using their ancestral laws as instructors, which it is impossible for a human soul to pour forth without divine inspiration; teaching these not only at other times, but especially on the sevenths in a different way. For the seventh is considered holy, on which, abstaining from other works, they arrive at holy places, which are called synagogues, where, according to age in ranks, the young sit under the elders, having themselves in an orderly and attentive manner; then one reads the books. For most things are philosophized among them through symbols in an ancient style. They are taught piety, holiness, justice, economy, citizenship, the knowledge of things truly good and evil and indifferent, the choices of what is necessary and the avoidances of the opposites; using these three ends and rules, the love of God, the love of virtue, and the love of man." Add Luke 4:16, 31; 13:10; Acts 13:14, 44; 17:2; 18:4.

And if the singular σάββα is not in use, and thus the plural has the meaning of the singular, which Grotius confirmed at Matt. 28:1, Acts 13:14, and at Matt. 12:1, yet here the plural number seems not without reason to have been used, since it could have been said τῷ σαββάτῳ from σάββατον, so that indeed the custom might be hinted at, how he was accustomed to teach on Sabbaths, since he did not teach only on that one Sabbath, and the Evangelist wards off the calumny of the Sabbath being despised by Christ. Because the Sabbath ought to be sanctified in that way. Compare Lev. 23:1; Luke 4:16, 31; ch. 13:10; Acts 13:7; ch. 15:21; ch. 17:2; ch. 18:4.

Latin:

Vers. 21. τοῖς Cάββασι] Id est, sabbato, ut Syrus & Lati- nus. Vide quæ ad Matt. XII.1. Adjecit & ad hoc Marcus non si- ne causa, ut contemti Sabbati calumniam à Christo arceret. Hoc vere eratSabbatum colere, adire pios cœtus & in medi- tanda lege occupari.Ita enim id quod est Lev.XXIII. 3. usus antiquissimus interpretabatur, ut nos docet illud lacœbi Act. XV. 21. Μῶσις γὰρ ἐκ γενεῶν ἀρχαίων κατὰ πόλιν τοὺς κηρύσσον- τας αὐτὸν ἔχει ἐν ταῖς συναγωγαῖς κατὰ πᾶν σάββατον ἀναγινωσκό- μενος. Et Paulus: τὰς φωνὰς τῶν προφητῶν ait solitas κατὰ πᾶν σάββατον ἀναγινώσκεσθαι Act. XIII. 27. Idem testatur Josephus contra Appionem: ἑκάστης ἑβδομάδος τῶν ἔργων ἀφεμένους ἐπὶ τὴν ἀκρόασιν τοῦ νόμου ἐκέλευσε συλλέγεσθαι, κ᾿ τῦτον ἀκριβῶς ἐκμαν- θάνειν, ὃ δὴ πάντας οἱ νομοθέται ἐοίκασι παραλιπεῖν. Et Phi- 1ο: Τὸ ἔθος τοῦ εὖ μάλα διαποιοῦσιν, ἀλείπταις χρώμενοι τοῖς πα- τρίοις νόμοις, ἃς ἀμάχανον ἀνθρωπίνῃ ἐκποῦσαι ψυχῇ ἄνευ κα- ταπληξῆς ἐνθέου· τότοις ἀναδιδάσκοντες μὲν κ᾿ παρὰ τὸν ἄλλον χρόνον, ἐν δὲ ταῖς ἑβδόμαις μάλιστα διαφορόντως. ἱερὰ γὰρ ἡ ἑβδόμη νενό- μισται, καθ᾽ ἣν τῶν ἄλλων ἀπέχοντες ἔργων εἰς ἱερὸς ἀφικνέονται τόπους, οἱ καλῦνται συναγωγαὶ, καθ᾽ ἡλικίας ἐν τάξεσιν ὑπὸ πρεσβυτέροις νέοι καθίζονται, μετὰ κόσμου τοῦ προσήκοντος ἔχοντες ἀκροατικῶς· εἶθ᾽ ὁ μὲν τὰς βίβλους ἀναγινώσκει. τὰ γὰρ πλεῖστα διὰ Cυμβόλων ἀρχαιοτρόπῳ ζηλώσῃ παρ᾿ αὐτοῖς φιλοσοφεῖται. παι- δεύονται δὲ εὐCέβειαν, ὁσιότητα, δικαιοσύνην, οἰκονομίαν, πολι- τείαν, ἐπιστήμην τῶν πρὸς ἀλήθειαν ἀγαθῶν κὴ κακῶν κὴ ἀδιαφό- ρων, αἱρέσεις ὧν χρὴ καὶ φυγὰς τῶν ἐναντίων; ὅροις κὴ κανόσι τρίτ- τοῖς χρώμενοι, τῷ τε φιλοθέῳ κὴ φιλαρέτῳ κὴ φιλανθρώπῳ. Adde Luc. IV. 16. 31. XIII. 10. Act. XIII. 14. 44. XVII. 2. XVIII. 4.

Et si singulare σάββα in usu non sit, adeoque plu- rale significationem singularis habeat, quod Grotius Matth. XXVIII. 1. Act. XIII. 14. ad Matth. XII. 1. confirmavit, hic tamen non immerito videtur pluralis numerus adhibitus, quum dici potuisset τῷ σαββάτῳ à σάββατον, ut nempe innueretur con- suetudo, quomodo in Sabbatis docere solitus fue- rit, quum neque in illo tantum Sabbato docuerit, & calumniam Sabbati contemti à Christo arceat Evangelista. Quia ita sanctificari debebat Sabba- tum. Conf. Lev. XXIII. 1. Luc. IV: 6. 31. c. XIII. 10. Act. XIII. 7. c. XV. 21. c. XVII. 2. c. XVIII. 4.

## 1:23
Verse 23. ἄνθρωπος ἐν πνέυματι ἀκαθάρτῳ] So also below in ch. 5:2, that is, with an unclean spirit. For the Hebrews used ב in that way, as in Exod. 15:19. Mark was the first to set down this history, which was either passed over by Matthew or included in general words, and after him Luke, having followed almost the very words of Mark; which he also does elsewhere.

Latin:

Vers. 23. ἄνθρωπος ἐν πνέυματι ἀκαθάρτῳ] Ita & infrà c. V. 2. id est, cum spiritu immundo. Nam ita ב usurparunt Hebræi, ut Exod. XV. 19. Historiam autem hanc Matthæo aut præteritam aut verbis generalibus comprehensam pri- mus posuit Marcus, & post eum Lucas, secutus prope ipsa Marci verba; quod & alibi facit.

## 1:24
Verse 24. ἔα] I do not agree with those who think it is either a verb or an interjection derived from a verb. For it is entirely the Hebrew הֵן and אָנָּא, from which the Greeks made ἔα. In the Prometheus of Aeschylus it is ἂ ἂ ἔα ἔα. The Latins are accustomed to say "ah" for the same.

τί ἡμῖν καὶ σοὶ] See Matt. 8:29.

From the Hebrew manner of speaking, Grotius explains this at Matt. VIII. 27, "why do you cause us trouble," from 2 Sam. X. 10, 2 Chron. XXXI. 21, and Joel III. 4. Yet that phrase is explained more fully by our blessed Chemnitz in Harmon. c. XXXVII: "What cause have you, or what right do you assume against us?"

Why do you invade us and disturb our kingdom? Attend to your own affairs, and leave us alone without trouble: You have your kingdom, leave ours to us: a doctrine added here that is very necessary today: Let this be observed diligently: that the devil is willing to tolerate the doctrine about the Holy One of God, and indeed to utter this very voice himself, if only he can keep his own in peace. I know, he says, and I myself confess, that you are the Holy One of God: only leave us alone in our kingdom. For by that commendation the demon wished to soothe Jesus, so that He might abstain from expelling him. This diabolical machination has many examples, especially in reconciliations of religions. Retain indeed, they say, and proclaim the pure doctrine, only leave the opposing party alone, what is that to us and you; attend to your own religion: do not agitate ours, etc.

Ἰησοῦ Ναζαρηνὲ) He calls him by a popular name. It is the same as Ναζωραῖος and Ναζαρηνός. For Stephanus rightly observed in his book on cities that those endings are used indiscriminately by the nations of the Orient. Thus ἐσσαῖος and ἐσσηνός.

ἦλθες ἀπολέσαι ἡμᾶς) I think it should be read as a question, as in Matthew: ἦλθες ὧδε πρὸ καιροῦ βασανίσαι ἡμᾶς; Nor indeed does ἀπολέσαι mean anything else here than βασανίζειν, as in the Comedies, 'May the gods destroy you' [Di te perduint]. It stands for the torment of an impure spirit whenever the power of doing evil is taken away from it. This is to send into the abyss, Luke VIII. 31. Conversely, when the reins are loosened for demons to vex men, it is said that the abyss is opened, as in the Apocalypse. To this character certain men accede, to whom that saying applies:

And if you had not done some harm, you would have died.

This interpretation also pleased Balduinus Walæus: but there is no reason why we should depart from the literal sense of the words. For it is known what ἀπολλύειν means, and what βασανίζειν means. Therefore, B. Chemnitius is more correct here: That perdition is to be understood (1.) of the destruction of the kingdom of the Devil, Luke XI. v. 22. and of the dissolution of his works. (2.) of the final damnation, when they will be sent into the abyss, Luke VIII. v. 31. Matthew XXV. v. 41. Chrysostom uses this simile; that the Devil is like a fugitive slave, who, after a long time, perhaps happening upon the sight of his master, can think of nothing else but lashes and torments.

οἶδά σε τίς εἶ. By many arguments already the evil spirits were beginning to gather that Jesus was that promised Messiah: as is evident in this chapter v. 34. and Luke IV. 41. But the evil demon wishes to soothe Jesus with flatteries, to whom he had experienced himself to be unequal in struggling.

ὁ ἅγιος τοῦ θεοῦ) The Messiah is called קדש קדשים by Daniel, according to the interpretation of Abenesdra as well. It is the same as υἱὸς θεοῦ in the exclamation of the other demon in Matthew VIII. 29. In Luke IV. 41. the demons exclaim ὅτι σὺ εἶ ὁ χριστὸς υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ.

ὁ ἅγιος τοῦ θεοῦ and υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ are not the same. For the latter is a name of person, the former of office: by the one, generation from the Father is indicated, by the other, sanctification and mission from the Father.

Latin:

Vers. 24. ἔα] Non assentior putantibus aut verbum esse aut interjectionem ex verbo. Est enim omnino Hebræum הֵן & אָנָּא unde Græci fecerunt ἔα. Apud Æschylum Promotheo est ἂ ἂ ἔα ἔα. Latini pro eodem ah solent di- cere.

τί ἡμῖν καὶ σοὶ] Vide Matth. VIII. 29.

Ex Ebræa loquendi consuetudine id explicat Grotius ad Matth. VIII. 27. cur nobis molestiam exhibes, è 2.Sam. X. 10. & 2. Paral. XXXI. 21. Joel. III. 4. Plenius tamen explicatur ea Phrasis à B. Chemnitio nostro in Harmon. c. XXXVII. Quid causæ habes, aut quid juris tibi sumis contra nos?

Quare nos invadis, & regnum nostrum perturbas? cures quæ tua sunt, & nos sine molestia missos facias: Habes tu tuum regnum, relinquas nobis nostrum: addita doctrina hodie perquam necessaria: Ob- servetur hoc diligenter: diabolum velle tolerare do- ctrinam de sancto Dei, & quidem ipsum hanc vo- cem sonare, si modo sua in pace retinere possit. No- vi, inquit, & ipse fateor, te esse sanctum Dei: tan- tum missos nos facias in nostro regno. Illa enim com- mendatione voluit dæmon Jesum delinire, ut ab expul- sione ejus abstineret. Hæc diabolica machinatio mul- ta habet exempla, præsertim in conciliationibus religio- num. Retineatis sane, inquiunt, & sonetis puram doctrinam, tantum adversariam partem missam fa- cite, quid nobis & vobis; curetis vestram religio- nem: non exagitetis nostram &c.

Ἰησοῦ Ναζαρηνὲ) Populari eum nomine appellat. Idem est Ναζωραῖος & Ναζαρηνός. Nam eas terminationes O- rientis nationibus promiscue usurpari recte observavit Ste- phanus libro de urbibus. Ita ἐσσαῖος & ἐσσηνός.

ἦλθες ἀπολέσαι ἡμᾶς) Percunctative legendum puto, ut apud Matthæum: ἦλθες ὧδε πρὸ καιροῦ βασανίσαι ἡμᾶς; Ne- que vero aliud hic ἀπολέσαι quam βασανίζειν, ut in Comœ- diis Di te perduint. Pro tormento est impuro spiritui quo- ties malefaciendi potestas ipsi adimitur. Hoc est mittere εἰς ἄβυσσον, Luc. VIII. 31. Contra cum Dæmonia l vexan- dos homines fræna laxantur, dicitur aperiri ἄβυσσος, ut in Apocalypsi. Ad hoc ingenium accedunt homines quidam, in quos illud quadrat:

Et si non aliqua nocuisses mortuus esses.

Placuit etiam Balduino Walæo hæc interpreta- tio: sed causa non est, cur à proprio vocum sen- su discedamus. Notum enim est, quid sit ἀπολλύ- ειν, quid βασανίζειν. Rectius ergo hic B. Chemni- tius: Perditio illa intelligenda est (1.) de destructione regni Diaboli, Luc. XI. v. 22. & de dissolutione operum ejus. (2.) de finali damnatione, quando in abyssum mittentur, Luc. VIII. v. 31. Matth. XXV. v. 41. Chry- sostomus utitur hac similitudine; quod Diabolus sit, sicut servus fugitivus, qui post multum temporis forte incidens in conspectum heri sui, nihil aliud, quam de verberibus & tormentis cogitare potest.

οἶδά σε τίς εἶ. Multis jam argumentis colligere incipie- bant mali Spiritus Jesum esse promissum illum Messiam: ut patet hoc capite v. 34. & Luc. IV. 41. Vult autem malus dæmon Jesum blanditiis demulcere, cui se certando impa- rem erat expertus.

ὁ ἅγιος τοῦ θεοῦ) Messias Danieli dictus קדש קדשים interprete etiam Abenesdra. Idem est quod υἱὸς θεοῦ in exclamatione alterius dæmonis Matth. VIII. 29. Apud Lucam IV. 41. dæmones exclamant ὅτι σὺ εἶ ὁ χριστὸς υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ.

Non sunt idem ὁ ἅγιος τοῦ θεοῦ, & υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ. Hoc enim nomen personæ, illud officii est: altero generatio à Patre, altero sanctificatio & missio à Pa- tre indigitatur.

## 1:25
Vers. 25. καὶ ἐπετίμησεν αὐτῷ Ἰησοῦς) See also Luke at the cited place. Tertullian gives the reason very well in Against Marcion IV. Jesus rebuked him: clearly, as one who was odious, and petulant in the very confession, and wickedly flattering. Shortly after: It was the duty of the unclean spirit to reject the proclamation of him to whom the holy ones abounded.

Φιμώθητι) Such is that below c. IV. 39. πεφίμωσο. Thus καταργήθητι below 41. διανοίχθητι chapter VII. 34. ἔγειραι Luke V. 24. Verbs of this kind have great force: for they do not demand a voluntary act, but show the effective power of the speaker, as much concerning natures using reason as concerning others: about which matter we have spoken elsewhere.

Latin:

Vers. 25. καὶ ἐπετίμησεν αὐτῷ Ἰησοῦς) Vide & Lucam dicto loco. Causam optime reddit Tertullianus contra Mar- cionem IV. Increpuit illum Jesus: plane, ut invidiosum, & in ipsa confessione petulantem, & male adulantem. Mox: Illius erat præconium immundi spiritus respuere cui sancti abunda- bant.

Φιμώθητι) Tale illud infra c. IV. 39. πεφίμωσο. Sic κατα- ργήθητι infra 41. διανοίχθητι cap. VII. 34. ἔγειραι Luc. V. 24. Vim magnam habent id genus verba: non enim actum voluntarium exigunt, sed ostendunt loquentis vim effecti- vam, tam circa naturas ratione utentes, quam circa alias: qua de re diximus & alibi.

## 1:26
Vers. 26. Σπαράξαν) Among other things, the Greeks use Σπαραγμὸν for a convulsion, which is otherwise more frequently called σπασμὸς: Nor do I think anything else is meant here. For those possessed by demons are accustomed to suffer convulsions of the nerves: which is followed by foaming at the mouth, Luke IX. 39. and here our own below 9. 20. where the word is the same. And this interpretation is to be admitted all the more in this place, because that vexation, just as it shows the anger of the demon, so it passed without harm to the body, as Luke teaches IV. 35.

There is a greater emphasis in this word, which our blessed Chemnitius unfolds properly: Mark, he says, uses a much more vehement word, σπαράττειν, which is also used for the convulsions of Satan in Mark IX. v. 26. and Luke IV. v. 47. It signifies, however, properly to tear with claws. And 2 Kings XXII. v. 8. the Greeks rendered the word רעש in this way, which signifies the convulsion of mountains and the collision of the waves of the sea. And thus in Luke IX. v. 39. the parent says: He convulses him with foam. The convulsion was therefore very atrocious. Luke adds that the demon threw the miserable possessed person, having been lifted up, into the middle of the Synagogue. The Evangelists therefore wished to describe the gestures of the Devil, when he was compelled against his will to depart by the violent authority of Christ. He shook the possessed person and, having lifted him up, dashed him to the ground, as if he wished to tear him apart: but he did him no harm, says Luke. This is not to be understood as if the limbs of the possessed felt no torture from that convulsion and tossing; but that no part of the body was harmed by any injury, mutilation, or mark, as would have necessarily happened in a natural way from such tossing. It also signifies that when the Devil departed, the man was immediately restored to wholeness without any injury and without remnants of weakness. Jerome, by this description of the tossing, thinks it is signified that the devil, when he is compelled to release a man from his dominion, then at last attacks him more hostilely, tosses him, and tears at him as if to rend him apart. For Pharaoh, when he is compelled to release the children of Israel, then pursues them hostilely: and the devil, being despised, rises up in scandals, as Jerome says. κράξας φωνῇ μεγάλῃ) with an inarticulate voice, which the impatience of pain expressed, when Christ had inhibited the articulate voice by his power.

Grotius explains the ἀνάρθρῳ φωνῇ not inappropriately, which the impatience of pain expressed, when Christ had inhibited the articulate voice by his power. For Christ had especially forbidden the devil to say more about himself and his doctrine, not only because he was flattering badly, as Tertullian has in book IV against Marcion, but also because he wanted to cast suspicion upon men by his confession, as if the doctrine and miracles of Christ had some commerce with him, as one who was offering mutual testimony to him.

Latin:

Vers. 26. Σπαράξαν) Σπαραγμὸν inter alia Græci usur- pant pro convulsione quæ σπασμὸς alioqui, frequentius di- citur: Neque aliud hic puto intelligi. Solent enim dæ- moniaci nervorum convulsiones perpeti: quas sequitur o- ris despumatio, Luc. IX. 39. & hic noster infra 9. 20. u- bi verbum idem est. Atque eo magis hoc loco hæc inter- pretatio admittenda est, quia vexatio ista, sicut iracun- diam dæmonis ostendit, ita transiit sine corporis noxa, ut Lucas docet IV. 35.

Major verbi hujus est ἔμφασις, quam evolvit probe B. Chemnitius noster: Marcus, inquit, utitur valde vehementiori verbo σπαράττειν, quod de convulsionibus Satanæ etiam usurpatur Marci IX. v. 26. & Luc. IV. v. 47. Significat autem proprie unguibus lacerare. Et 2. Reg. XXII. v. 8. Græci ita reddiderunt verbum רעש quod significat convulsio- nem montium, & collisionem fluctuum maris. Et ita Luc. IX. v. 39. parens dicit: Convellit ipsum cum spuma. Valde atrox itaque fuit convulsio. Lucas addit, quod dæmonium miserum obsessum elevatum projecerit usque in medium Synago- gæ. Gestus igitur Diaboli, cum violentia imperii Christi, contra voluntatem suam, exire compelle- retur, Evangelistæ describere voluerunt. Concus- sit obsessum & elevatum, ad terram allisit, quasi discerpere vellet: sed nihil illi nocuit, inquit Lucas. Quod non intelligendum est, quasi membra obsessi nullum cruciatum ex illa convul- sione & jactatione senserint: sed quod nulla pars corporis nocumento aliquo, mutilatione, aut nota aliqua læsa fuerit, sicut ex tali jactatione na- turali modo fieri necesse fuisset. Significat etiam, quod exeunte Diabolo, homo statim sine læsio- ne aliqua, & sine reliquiis debilitationis integræ restitutus fuerit. Hieronymus hac descriptione jactationis existimat hoc significari, quod diabo- lus, quando hominem ex suo imperio cogitur dimittere, tunc demum hostilius ipsum invadat, jactet, & quasi discerpturus convellat. Pharao enim, quando cogitur dimittere filios Israel, tunc hostiliter persequitur eos: & diabolus con- temptus consurgit in scandala, sicut inquit Hierony- mus. κράξας φωνῇ μεγάλῃ) ἀνάρθρῳ φωνῇ quam exprimebat doloris impatientia, cum ἔναρθρον Christus vi sua inhibuis- set.

De ἀνάρθρῳ φωνῇ non incommode explicat Grotius, quam exprimebat doloris impatientia, cum ἔναρθρον Christus vi sua inhibuisset. Prohi- buerat autem imprimis Christus, ne diabolus plu- ra de se & doctrina sua diceret, non solum quod male adularetur, ut Tertull. lib. IV. contra Marc. ha- bet, sed etiam quod sua confessione hominibus su- spicionem injicere vellet, quasi doctrina & mira- cula Christi aliquid commercii secum haberent, ut qui mutuum ipsi præbebat testimonium.

## 1:27
Vers. 27. κατ' ἐξουσίαν κὶ τοῖς πνεύμασι τοῖς ἀκαθάρτοις ἐπιτάσσει) The Jewish exorcists were indeed accustomed to put demons to flight by a certain invocation of the divine name. But no one before this time had done it by authority, as Christ. See below 9. 15. Rightly, therefore, they conclude that it must be a new and great dogma, which is armed with a new and hitherto unseen power.

Latin:

Vers. 27. κατ' ἐξουσίαν κὶ τοῖς πνεύμασι τοῖς ἀκαθάρτοις ἐπι- τάσσει) Solebant quidem Judæi exorcistæ invocatione qua- dam divini nominis fugare dæmones. Sed nemo ante hoc tempus id fecerat pro imperio, ut Christus. Vide infra 9. 15. Recte igitur colligunt oportere novum ma- gnumque dogma esse, quod nova neque visa hactenus po- testate armatur.

## 1:28
Vers. 28. εἰς ὅλην τὴν περίχωρον τῆς γαλιλαίας) It does not matter much whether this fame is believed to have been spread outside the borders of Galilee, or only outside Capernaum through Galilee. The Syriac and Latin versions embrace the latter sense here. And indeed ἡ περίχωρος is everywhere in these books the same as χώρα, as in Luke VIII. 37. And thus the Greeks translate פלך in Nehemiah III. 9 and the following. So below 6, 55 and 14, 35, it is called ἡ περίχωρος ἐκείνη without an addition: indeed, also in Luke in this very history 4, 37, as also among the Greek interpreters of Deuteronomy III, not once. Nevertheless, the other interpretation is favored by what is in Matthew around these times, καὶ ἀπῆλθεν ἡ ἀκοὴ ἀυτοῦ εἰς ὅλην τὴν Συρίαν.

But if Matthew explains it in the latter sense, then the phrase must certainly be taken in the same way: for without doubt Matthew's explanation is to be preferred to the interpretation of the Syriac and the Latin. Nor indeed is it of little interest whether this fame was spread outside the borders of Galilee through all of Syria, or fame spread only through Galilee: and if the former is true, as one must believe Matthew asserting, the latter must be false.

Latin:

Vers. 28. εἰς ὅλην τὴν περίχωρον τῆς γαλιλαίας) Non mul- tum refert fama hæc extra Galilææ fines, an duntaxat ex- tra Capernaumum per Galilæam sparsa credatur. Sensum posteriorem amplectuntur hic Syrus & Latinus. Et sane ἡ περίχωρος passim in his libris est idem quod χώρα, ut Luc. VIII. 37. Et sic פלך vertunt Græci Nehem. III. 9. & se- quentibus. Ita infra 6, 55. & 14, 35. dicitur ἡ περίχωρος ἐκείνη sine additamento: imo & apud Lucam in hac ipsa hi- storia 4, 37. ut & apud Græcos Interpp. Deut. III. non se- mel. Veruntamen alteri interpretationi favet quod apud Matthæum est circa hæc tempora, καὶ ἀπῆλθεν ἡ ἀκοὴ ἀυτοῦ εἰς ὅλην τὴν Συρίαν.

At si Matthæus explicat sensu posteriori, utique eodem etiam accipienda phrasis est: sine dubio e- nim Matthæi explicatio & Syri & Latini interpre- tationi præferenda. Neque sane parum hæc in- terest, famam sparsam extra Galilææ fines per totam Syriam, & famam sparsam tantum per Galilæam: ac si prius verum est, uti Matthæo asserenti creden- dum est, posterius falsum esse oportet.

## 1:30
Vers. 30. λέγουσιν ἀυτῷ περὶ ἀυτῆς) They were more anxious about this, because the fever was more dangerous in an elderly body. Μικρὰ γηραιὰ σώματ' ἐυτάξει ῥοπὴ.

Mark also learned and expressed the circumstances of this history more closely from Peter.

Latin:

Vers. 30. λέγουσιν ἀυτῷ περὶ ἀυτῆς) Hoc magis solliciti, quod periculosior esset febris in senili corpore. Μικρὰ γηραιὰ σώματ' ἐυτάξει ῥοπὴ.

Hujus quoque historicæ circumstantias ex Petro propius didicit expressitque Marcus.

## 1:32
Vers. 32. ὀψίας δὲ γενομένης, ὅτε ἔδυ ὁ ἥλιος] This is the second ὀψία as has been noted elsewhere at this word. But it is better that what is in Luke as δύνοντος be explained by the past tense, as the old Latin interpreter did there, than ἴδυ in this place by the present. For the Jews did not touch labors forbidden on the Sabbath before the sun had clearly set. Δύειν is rightly said by the Greeks of whatever withdraws itself from sight. The LXX in Joel II. 10: ἄστρα δύσουσι τὸ φέγγος αὐτῶν: where in the Hebrew it is אספו. It is found concerning the setting of the sun also in the Greek XIX. 14. Poets, even Aratus, said that stars sink when they withdraw themselves from our sight, because, as they were accustomed to express technical matters popularly, they called the horizons by the name of Ocean, as has been rightly observed by Strabo, Theon, and others.

Latin:

Vers. 32. ὀψίας δὲ γενομένης, ὅτε ἔδυ ὁ ἥλιος] Hæc est secun- da ὀψία ut alibi annotatum est ad hanc vocem. Potius au- tem quod apud Lucam est δύνοντος exponendum per præ- teritum, ut ibi fecit vetus Latinus interpres, quam ἴδυ hoc loco per præsens. Nam labores sabbato vetitos non attin- gebant Judæi ante Solem plane occasum. Δύειν Græcis recte dicitur quicquid visibus se subtrahit LXX. in Joele II. 10. ἄ- στρα δύσουσι τὸ φέγγος αὐτῶν: ubi in Hebræo est אספו. De Solis occasu reperitur & in Græco XIX. 14. Mergi autem sidera cum aspectui nostro se subtrahunt ideo dixerunt Poë- tæ, etiam Aratus, quia ut solebant τὰ τεχνικὰ eloqui popu- lariter, τοὺς ὁρίζοντας Oceani nomine appellabant, ut à Stra- bone, Theone, atque aliis recte observatum est.

## 1:34
Vers. 34. καὶ ἐθεράπευσε πολλοὺς] Not many of those who were being offered, but because those who were being offered were many.

ἐκ ἤφιε] A word truly unique: which no one has observed outside of Mark, who speaks thus again below. But neither will you easily find an analogous inflection: unless some learned in these matters think it is from ἀφίεω as ἤλιτε from ἀλιτέω. But this too is poetic. If any codices had ἤφιὲ there would be no doubt that that reading would also be preferred.

New readings are not to be invented, such as might be here or there: nor is cause to be given for suspicion of another reading as if it were better. Camerarius in his notes on this passage has it thus: ἐκ ἤφιε. He did not allow, or did not permit, that they should say what they themselves knew. The Iliad has: ἀλλὰ κακῶς ἀφίει: But both this and that ὡς ἑξημεῖς ἀφίεμεν are deduced from the form of the verb in μι, whereas that ἤφιε is from the less common ἀφίω.

ὅτι ἤδεισαν αὐτὸν] That they knew him, that is, his calling. For they truly know someone who knows his attributes. Because this seemed rather obscure, someone added from Luke for the sake of interpretation χριστὸν εἶναι: which ancient codices and ancient interpreters prove not to be genuine. See above what cause moved Christ. They err who think that ὅτι here is causal.

PART III. The proclamation of Jesus in other schools of Galilee, with the healing of the leper.

Latin:

Vers. 34. καὶ ἐθεράπευσε πολλοὺς] Non multos ex iis qui of- ferebantur, sed quia qui offerebantur multi erant.

ἐκ ἤφιε] Vox sane μονήρης: quam nemo observavit extra Marcum qui infra iterum sic loquitur. Sed neque ἀνά- λογον flexionem facile reperies: nisi quod quidam harum rerum eruditi putant esse ab ἀφίεω ut ἤλιτε ab ἀλιτέω.. Sed & hoc poëticum est. Si qui codices haberent ἤφιὲ dubi- tandum non esset, quin & ea lectio esset præferenda.

Non sunt fingendæ novæ lectiones, quales hic, aut illic esse possint: nec causa præbenda suspicio- ni alterius lectionis ceu meliori. Camerarius in notat. suis ad h. l. ita habet: ἐκ ἤφιε. Non sine- bat, vel non permittebat, ut dicerent, quod ipsum no- vissent. Iliados a est: ἀλλὰ κακῶς ἀφίει: Sed & hoc & illud ὡς ἑξημεῖς ἀφίεμεν à verbi forma in μι deducuntur, cum istud ἤφιε sit ab ἀφίω minus usitato.

ὅτι ἤδεισαν αὐτὸν] Quod ipsum nossent, id est ipsius κλῆ- σιν. Illi enim vere aliquem norunt, qui attributa ejus norunt. Quod cum videretur obscurius, adjecit aliquis ex Luca in- terpretamenti causa χριστὸν εἶναι: quod non esse genuinum vetusti codices & antiqui interpretes evincunt. Quæ causa Christum moverit, supra vide. Errant qui ὅτι hic putant esse αἰτιολογικὸν.

PARS III. Præconium Iesu in aliis Galilææ Scholis, cum leprosi sanatione.

## 1:35
Vers. 35. καὶ πρωῒ ἔννυχον λίαν] At night, but when the day was pressing on, which Luke calls γενομένης ἡμέρας. For that word γενομένης signifies at one time time already passed, at another present, at another imminent.

Latin:

Vers. 35. καὶ πρωῒ ἔννυχον λίαν] Noctu, sed cum dies insta- ret, quod Lucas dicit γενομένης ἡμέρας. Nam vox ista γενο- μένης modo jam exactum, modo præsens, modo imminens tempus significat.

## 1:37
Vers. 37. πάντες] The Capernaites.

Latin:

Vers. 37. πάντες] Capernauinitæ.

## 1:38
Vers. 38. Κωμοπόλεις] When Tacitus says in the fifth book of his Histories that works of peace were built not far from the camps in the manner of a municipality, he describes a κωμόπολις. Such a κωμόπολις had been Bethsaida, having recently acquired the appearance of a town. Luke called these πόλεις more loosely, as also in chapter V. 12. Some teachers of the Hebrews think that פרצות are κωμοπόλεις. There are those who disagree. Nor indeed do the LXX translate them so. It is evident from Josephus that there were in Judea κώμαι not lacking the size of a city. Hence our writers so often use πόλιν and κώμην interchangeably. Thus also among the Greek poets, places that are κῶμαι are called πόλιν, as Pollux and Harpocration note, and they bring forward an example in Euboea, of which Euripides said: Εὔβοὶ ἀθήναις ἐστί τις seilon πόλις.

εἰς τῦτο γὰρ ἐξελήλυθα] By the Father’s sending, as Luke explains. So also John XVI 28. He had received a mandate to promulgate His doctrine to all the Jews in Palestine, without any distinction of those inhabiting cities or fields.

Latin:

Vers. 38. Κωμοπόλεις] Tacitus cum dicit Historiarum V subsersa longe pacis opera haud procul castris in modum muni- cipii exstructa, κωμόπολιν describit. Talis κωμόπολις fuerat Bethsaida nuper oppidi speciem nacta. πόλεις his dix it Lu- cas καταχρηστικώτερον, ut & cap. V. 12. Hebræorum magistri quidam פרצות putant esse κωμοπόλεις. Sunt qui dissen- tiant. Neque vero ita vertunt LXX. Ex Josepho constat in Judæa fuisse κώμας πόλεως μέγεθος ἐκ ἀποδεούσας. Hinc toties Scriptores nostri πόλιν & κώμην promiscue usur- pant. Sic & Poëtis Græcis πόλιν dici quæ sunt κῶμαι, no- tant Pollux & Harpocratíon, & exemplum adferunt in Eu- bœa de qua dixerit Euripides: Εὔβοὶ ἀθήναις ἐστί τις seilon πόλις.

εἰς τῦτο γὰρ ἐξελήλυθα] Patris missu, ut Lucas explicat. Sic & Joh. XVI 28. Mandatum acceperat omnibus in Pa- læstina Judæis dogma suum promulgandi, nullo urbes aut agros habitantium discrimine.

## 1:39
Vers. 39. αὐτῶν] τῶν κωμοπόλεων. For there were synagogues also in the larger villages which approached the size of towns: as we have noted elsewhere.

Vers. 39. αὐτῶν] τῶν κωμοπόλεων. Nam & in majoribus vicis quæ ad oppidorum accedebant magnitudinem syna- gogæ erant: ut alibi annotavimus.

Ver. 40. γονυπετῶν] See Matthew ch. VIII. 2.

## 2:1 Argument
CHAPTER II. ARGUMENT AND DIVISION.

To Jesus again betaking himself to Capernaum, a paralytic is brought, let down through the roof, to whom he forgives sins, and that he may teach that this power belongs to him, he commands that he rise and walk, which was done immediately to the admiration of all: Then he calls Levi sitting at the tax office, and takes food in his house: and defends this against the Pharisees, that he came not for the righteous, but for sinners: and being asked why his disciples do not fast, as the disciples of John and the Pharisees, he answers; that guests do not fast while the bridegroom is present, nor is a new patch sewn onto an old garment, or new wine put into old wineskins. But he defends his disciples rubbing ears of corn on the Sabbath by the example of David, and teaches that the Son of man is Lord of the Sabbath.

There are two parts: The former pertains to the acts preceding the second Passover, concerning the healing of the paralytic, to v. 13, the calling of Levi, and the banquet at his house to verse 17, and concerning the resolution of the question about the disciples of Jesus not fasting, to verse 22. The latter to the acts from the second Passover of the ministry of Jesus, concerning the rubbing of the ears of corn, and his apology for it, to verse 28.

PART I. The remaining acts of Jesus up to the second Passover of his ministry.

Ver. 1. δι' ἡμερῶν] We have said what διὰ means here at Matt. XXVI. 61. But τίνων is missing here in the Hebrew manner, as in the LXX Gen. IV. 3. καὶ ἐγένετο μεθ' ἡμέρας.

Latin:

CAPUT II. ARGUMENTUM ET PAR- TITIO.

Iesu iterum Capernaum se conferenti adfer- tur paralyticus per tectum immissus, cui peccata remittit, & ut potestatem hanc si- bi convenire doceat, præcipit, ut surgat, & ambulet, quod cum omnium admiratione statim factum: Tum Levi in telonio seden- tem vocat, & in domo ejus cibum capit: id- que adversus Pharisæos defendit, quod non ob justos, sed peccatores venerit: ac quæsitus, cur discipuli ejus non jejunent, uti Johannis, & Pharisæorum discipuli, respondet; convivas sponso præsente non je- junare, nec veteri vesti novam laciniam assui, aut recens mustum in veteres utres mitti. Discipulos vero Sabbato spicas fri- cantes exemplo Davidis defendit, & Filium hominis Dominum sabbati esse docet.

Partes duæ sunt: Prior ad acta alterum Pascha antegredientia pertinet, de sanatione paralytici, ad v. 13. vocatione Levi, & convivio penes eum ad vers. 17. & de solutione quæstionis de non jejunan- tibus Jesu discipulis, ad vers. 22. Posterior ad acta à secundo Paschate Ministerii Jesu, de frica- tione spicarum, ejusque apologia, ad vers. 28.

PARS I. Acta reliqua Iesu usque ad alterum Pascha ministerii ejus.

Vers. 1. δι' ἡμερῶν] Quid διὰ hic valeat diximus ad Matth. XXVI. 61. Deest autem hic more Hebræo τίνων, ut apud LXX. Gen. IV. 3. κὶ ἐγένετο μεθ' ἡμέρας.

## 2:2
Ver. 2. μηδὲ τὰ πρὸς τὴν θύραν] That is, τὸ πρόθυρον. Vitruvius says that those things are called πρόθυρα in Greek which are the vestibules before the door.

τὸν λόγον] Thus in Matt. XIII. 20, below VIII. 32, ch. XVI. 20, Luke I. 2, and elsewhere throughout it is called, which is more fully called in Luke VIII. 11, 21, XI. 28, Acts XVIII. 11, and elsewhere ὁ λόγος τοῦ θεοῦ. You will also find it without the article λόγον in the same sense, as in Acts XVII. 11.

Latin:

Vers. 2. μηδὲ τὰ πρὸς τὴν θύραν] Id est τὸ πρόθυρον. πρό- θυρα Græce dicuntur, inquit Vitruvius, quæ sunt ante januam vestibula.

τὸν λόγον] Ita Matth. XIII. 20. infra VIII. 32. cap. XVI. 20. Luc. I. 2. & alibi passim vocatur, qui plenius Luc. VIII. 11. 21. XI. 28. Actor. XVIII. 11. & alibi ὁ λόγος τοῦ θεοῦ. In- venies & sine articulo λόγον eodem sensu, ut Act. XVII. 11.

Latin:

## 2:4
Vers. 4. χαλῶσι] Thus κατεχάλασαν is used in Josh. 2:15. Κράββατον] κλινίδιον in Luke. Nor did he interpret it badly as μιξοβάρβαρον. For as Phrynichus teaches, that was what the Attics called what is commonly κράββατον.

Latin:

Vers. 4. χαλῶσι] Sic κατεχάλασαν usurpatur Jos. II. 15. Κράββατον] κλινίδιον Lucas. Neque ille male μιξοβάρβα- ρον est interpretatus. Nam ut Phrynichus docet id Atticis erat quod communiter κράββατον.

## 2:7
Vers. 7. τίς δύναται ἀφιέναι ἁμαρτίας εἰ μὴ εἷς ὁ θεὸς] Mark explains more fully what Matthew had said was spoken by the lawyers, that he blasphemes. Did Christ not indeed say that he was forgiving the paralytic's sins? Yet they took it that way, naturally because it is the habit of hatred to drag everything toward that where there is room for calumny. That it is God who forgives sins is testified everywhere by the Psalms, the Prophets, and Moses himself. But it was nowhere read that this power was communicated to any man. A priest is indeed said to make atonement for a man in lesser offenses: but this making atonement is to prepare for forgiveness. For it follows, and it shall be forgiven him. But a priest is not said to forgive. Indeed, in Isaiah, God addresses the people most emphatically, ch. 43:25: I am he who blots out your iniquities, for my own sake. It is in Exod. 30:7; among the titles of God is placed נשא עון. But viewed properly, I think here is the passage of Job 14:4. For the Chaldean Paraphrast also explains it thus: Who can make him clean who is defiled by sins, except God who alone can forgive? Nathan announced to David that his crime was taken away: but the forgiveness itself is attributed to God alone: the Prophet coming into no part of it. Hence they concluded that this act was incommunicable. Christ, who had used those words which could also be taken otherwise, when he saw that the matter itself was being taken in that way, using the malice of his enemies, openly claimed for himself the right, as a man, from God the Father

conceded, performing a notable miracle directly in testimony of that right. Indeed, even before the miracle of healing, he performed another much more notable one, when he most openly showed that the innermost thoughts of those standing by were known to him, which the Holy Scriptures establish as no less proper to God than to forgive sins, as can be seen in 1 Sam. 16:7, 1 Chron. 29:9, 2 Chron. 6:36, Ps. 7:10, Jer. 17:10. Nor indeed was the argumentation of the lawyers valid: God never granted this right to anyone before; therefore, he cannot grant it. The prophets did not have it; therefore, the Messiah will not have it either.

Latin:

Vers. 7. τίς δύναται ἀφιέναι ἁμαρτίας εἰ μὴ εἷς ὁ θεὸς] Ube- rius explicat Marcus quos Matthæus dictum à legisperitis dixerat ὅτι βλασφημεῖ. Non dixerat quidem Christus se paralytico peccata remittere? at illi tamen id ita accipie- bant, nimirum quia is mos est odii omnia eo trahere qua pa- tet calumniæ locus. Deum esse qui condonet peccata passim testantur Psalmi, Prophetæ, ipse Moses. At potestatem hanc homini cuiquam communicatam nusquam legebatur. Di- citur quidem Sacerdos in minoribus delictis expiare homi- nem: sed hoc expiare est ad remissionem præparare. Sequi- tur enim & remittetur ei. Remittere autem Sacerdos non dicitur. Imo apud Esaiam Deus μάλισα ἐμφατικῶς populum sic alloquitur c. XLIII. 25. Ego is sum qui deleo iniquitates tuas, propter me. Est in Exod. XXX. V. 7. inter Dei indigetamenta ponitur נשא עון. Sed proprie spectatum hic puto Jobi lo- cum XIV. 4 Nam eum & Chaldæus Paraphrastes ita exponit: Quis potest mundum efficere eum qui inquinatus est peccatis, nisi Deus qui solus potest remittere? Annunciavit Nathan Da- vidi ablatum ab eo crimen: at ipsa condonatio Deo uni tri- buitur: in nullam ejus partem veniente Propheta. Hinc colligebant hunc actum esse ἀκοινώνητον. Christus qui ver- bis iis erat usus, quæ possent & aliter accipi, cum tamen ita udres ipsa erat accipi videret, usus inimicorum malitia, aparte sibi vindicavit jus sibi, ut homini, à Deo Patre con-

cessum, insigne edens miraculum directè in ejus juris testi- monium. Imo & ante miraculum sanationis, aliud edi- dit multo insignius, cum intimas astantium cogitationes apertissime sibi cognitas ostendit, quod sacræ literæ non minus proprium Dei statuunt quam peccata remittere ut videre est 1. Sam. XVI. 7. 1. Paral. XXIX. 9. 2. Paral. VI. 36. Pf. VII. 10. Jer. XVII. 10. Neque vero valebat legispe- ritorum argumentatio: Nunquam cuiquam id jus Deus concessit antehac: Ergo concedere non potest. Non ha- buerunt Prophetæ: Ergo nec habebit Messias.

## 2:8
Verse 8. τῷ πνεύματι ἀυτῦ] Not, as the prophets by inspiration, but by his own spirit, that is, τῇ ἀκρᾷ μετοχῇ τῦ ἀυτολόγε, as Origen speaks in Against Celsus. For what the ancient Christians, even Justin, call θείαν φύσιν, that which I mentioned Origen calls θείας φύσεως ἀπαύγασμα κὶ χαρακτῆρα, and the divine element in the man Jesus who was perceived, which was the only-begotten of God, is also accustomed to be called the Spirit, as in 1 Pet. 3:18. Tertullian in his Apology: And we also ascribe to the Word and Reason, and likewise to the Power, through which we have declared that God fashioned all things, a proper substance, the Spirit, in which there is both the Word for the one speaking, and Reason for the one disposing, and Power for the one performing. We have learned that this was brought forth from God, and generated by this bringing forth, and therefore called the Son of God and God from the unity of substance: for God is also Spirit. Even when a ray is extended from the Sun, a portion from the whole, but the sun will be in the ray, because it is the ray of the sun, nor is the substance separated, but extended. Thus, of spirit from spirit and of God from God, as light kindled from light: the matrix of the matter remains whole and unwearied, even if you borrow many offshoots of quality from it. Thus also, what has proceeded from God is God and the Son of God, and both are one. Thus, of spirit from spirit and of God from God, he made a second number by measure, not by state, and he did not depart from the matrix but went forth. The same concerning prayer: the Spirit of God, and the Word of God, and the Reason of God, the Word of Reason and the Reason of the Word, and the Spirit of both is Jesus Christ our Lord. Against Marcion I: Jesus deigned to flow from heaven as a saving spirit, and III: The Spirit is his person (of God the Creator), Christ the Lord. And shortly after: He (Christ) had then been in Moses who had heard such things, namely, the spirit of the Creator. Book V. In which Christ was to consist in the whole substance of the Spirit, not as if it were to come later to him who had always been the Spirit of God, even before the flesh. And against Praxeas: This Spirit of God will be the same as the Word: for just as, when John says the Word was made flesh, we also understand the Spirit in the mention of the Word, so here too we recognize the Word in the name of Spirit. Ibidem: Christ is the spirit of the Father's person. Book on the Flesh of Christ: The Word of God, and with the Word of God the Spirit, and in the Spirit of God the Power, and whatever is of God is Christ. Cyprian on the Vanity of Idols: The Holy Spirit is clothed in flesh. For so the manuscripts have it. Lactantius, Book IV of Wisdom, Chapter VI: He begat an incorruptible and irreproachable Spirit whom he named Son. And Chapter VIII: For in the first place we testify that he was born twice, first in spirit, afterwards in flesh. Then: For the Word is spirit brought forth with a voice signifying something. Shortly after: But he himself, while he is also Spirit, nevertheless proceeded from the mouth of God with voice and sound like a word. And Chapter XI: Descending therefore from heaven, that Holy Spirit chose the holy virgin, into whose womb he might insinuate himself. In the poem to Christ which is ascribed to Claudian: You, innocent Spirit. Prudentius on Christ:

who as spirit once, poured forth from the paternal mouth, was moving upon the waters not yet separated, nor enclosed by a fixed shore.

And what Moses had said, the Spirit brooding over the waters, the ancient writer translates as λόγον θεῦ; but the Christian of the Poimandres: therefore the divine and holy nature is called spirit, not only διὰ τὸ ἀσώματον, in the way that name befits the Father, but also because what is called generating for the sake of the distinction between the Word and the Holy Spirit, the Greeks sometimes also called ἀπαυγάζειν, they also called breathing by a looser term, indicating by that name any emanation whatsoever, or as Tertullian speaks, a projection. For Tertullian, in Against Praxeas, said that the Son proceeds no less than he is derived. How Lactantius and others can be defended, whom Jerome accuses along with Lactantius in this regard as being unskilled in the Scriptures. For certainly it cannot be doubted that Tertullian most openly acknowledged the Trinity. And because many think that this was peculiar to the Latins, I will show that the most ancient of the Christians who wrote in Greek spoke in the same manner. Hermas, of whatever authority, certainly of the first antiquity, as appears from Irenaeus and Clement using his words in the book of the Shepherd, as the division is now established, the third: That Holy Spirit which was infused first of all into the body in which God would dwell. Justin in the Second Apology: τὸ πνεῦμα ὆ν κὶ τὴν δύναμιν τὴν παρὰ τῦ θεῦ, Ὀδὲν ἄλλο νοῆσαι θέμις ἡ τὸν λόγον. Tatian: λόγον ὁ ἐποράν. τῷ πνεῦμα γεγονὸς ἀπὸ τῦ πατρός. Theophilus: ἔχω ἐν ὁ θεὸς τὸν ἑαυτῦ λόγον. And then: ἧτον ἐν ὧν πνεῦμα θεῦ ά περχὴ κὶ σοφία. Irenaeus V. 1: εἰ δὲ μὴ ὡς ἄνθρωπον ἐφαίνετο ἄνθρωπον ωτε ὅ ἦν ἐπ̓ ἀληθείας ἔμεινε

πνεῦμα θεῦ. Ibidem: The Word of the Father and the Spirit of God united to the ancient substance of the formation of Adam. But what is most to be noted, even after the controversy had arisen with the Arians and had been thrashed out in many Synods, those who wrote against the Arians spoke in such a way, as Phoebadius: Who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor? No one, certainly, but no one outside his own spirit: which Spirit the Prophet calls the wise architect and admirable counselor: and not undeservedly. For the same Spirit is the Word and Wisdom of God: from whose person Solomon says: When he was preparing the heavens, I was present with him. And afterwards: It appears therefore that one and the same was now in the name of Spirit, now in the word of Word, now in the appellation of Wisdom. Indeed, even after the struggle with Macedonius had arisen, this manner of speaking remained. The writer of the learned dialogue against the Apollinarist: χριστὸς πνεῦμα ζωοποιῶν ἐστὶ τῇ τῆς θεότητος λόγῳ. Epiphanius in the third book against heresies: ἐκὼν διὰ τῆς πρὸς Φιλιππησίους ἐπιστολῆς ἐδίδαξεν ἡμᾶς, πῶς ἡ ὑπόστασις τῷ υἱῷ ὁμοία ἐστιν τῇ ὑποστάσει τῷ πατρός. πνεῦ. α γὰρ ἐκ πατρός. The Chaldean paraphrast also, in what is in Job ch. IV. 9, 'by the breath of God,' translates it 'by the word of God.'

Grotius understands the divine nature of Christ, from 1 Pet. III. 18, which he wishes to be called so not only διὰ τὸ ἀσώματον, in the way that name befits the Father, but also because what is called 'to generate' in distinction to the Word and the Holy Spirit—and sometimes by the Greeks ἀπαυγάζειν—they also called 'to breathe' by a looser term, indicating by that name some sort of emanation, or as Tertullian speaks, a προβολή. Although he rightly shows this from the Fathers, it cannot, however, be taught from Scripture. Others understand by 'Spirit' here not the divine nature, but the soul of Christ: because according to his human nature he also tested hearts and kidneys, and recognized the thoughts of men; which, as a man, he is to bring into the light on the day of universal judgment, as judge of the whole world.

Latin:

Vers. 8. τῷ πνεύματι ἀυτῦ] Non, ut Prophetæ per affla- tum, sed suo spiritu id est τῇ ἀκρᾷ μετοχῇ τῦ ἀυτολόγε, ut O- rigenes adversus Celsum loquitur. Nam quod veteres Christiani, etiam Justinus, vocant θείαν φύσιν, is quem dixi Origenes θείας φύσεως ἀπαύγασμα κὶ χαρακτῆρα, & τὸ ἐν τῷ νουμένῳ ἀνθρώπῳ Ἰησῦ θεῖον ὅπερ ἧν ὁ μονογενὴς τῦ θεῦ, idem so- let & Spiritus dici, ut 1. Pet. III. 18. Tertullianus Apologeti- co: Et nos etiam sermoni atque rationi itemque virtuti, per quæ omnia molitum Deum ediximus, propriam substantiam spiri- tum inscribimus, cui & sermo insit pronuntianti, & ratio adsit disponenti, & virtus præsit perficienti. Hunc ex Deo prolatum didicimus, & prolatione generatum, idcirco filium Dei & Deum dictum ex unitate substantiæ: nam & Deus Spiritus. Etiam cum radius ex Sole porrigitur, portio ex summa sed sol erit in ra- dio, quia solis est radius, nec separatur substantia, sed extenditur. Ita de spiritu spiritus & de Deo Deus, ut lumen de lumine accen- sum: manet integra & indefessa materiæ matrix etsi plures inde traduces qualitatis mutuêris. Ita & quod de Deo profe- Etum est, Deus est & Dei Filius & unus ambo. Ita de spiritu spiritus & de Deo Deus modulo alternum numerum gradu non statu fecit, & à matrice non recessit sed excessit. Idem de ora- tione: Dei Spiritus, & Dei sermo & Dei ratio, sermo rationis & ratio sermonis, & Spiritus utrumque Jesus Christus Dominus noster. Adversus Marcionem I, Iesus de cælo manare dignatus est spiritus salutaris, & III, Spiritus persona ejus (Dei creatoris) Christus Dominus. Et mox: Ipse (Christus) tunc fuerat in Mose qui talia audierat, spiritus scilicet creatoris. Libro V. In quo Christus consistere haberet tota substantia Spiritus, non quasi postea obventura illi qui semper spiritus Dei fuerit, ante carnem quoque. Et adversus Praxean: Hic spiritus Dei idem erit sermo: sicut enim dicente Iohanne sermo caro factus est, spiritum quoque intelligimus in mentione sermonis, ita & hic sermonem quoque agnoscimus in nomine Spiritus. Ibidem: Christus paternæ personæ spiritus. Libro de carne Christi: Verbum Dei & cum Verbo Dei Spiritus & in Spiritu Dei vir- tus & quicquid Dei est Christus. Cyprianus de idolorum vanitate: Carnem Spiritus sanctus induitur. Ita enim ha- bent Manuscripti Lactantius lib. IV. de Sapientia cap. VI. Incorruptibilem & irreprehensibilem Spiritum genuit quem fi- lium nuncupavit. Et capite VIII. In primis enim testificamur illum bis esse natum, primum in spiritu, postea in carne. Dein- de: Nam sermo est spiritus cum voce aliquid significante prola- tus. Mox: Ipse vero cum sit & ipse Spiritus tamen cum voce ac sono ex Dei ore processit sicut verbum. Et capite XI. De- scendens itaque de cælo sanctus ille Spiritus sanctam virginem, cujus utero se insinuaret elegit. In carmine ad Christum quod Claudiano ascribitur: Tu Spiritus insons. Prudentius de Christo:

qui spiritus olim Ore superfusus patrio, solitabat in undis Nondum discretis, nec certo littore clausis.
