Et quod Moses dixerat, Spiritum aquis incubantem, id λό- γον θεῦ vertit Scriptor antiquus; sed Christianus Pemandri: vocatur ergo θεία κὶ χρισῇ φύσις spiritus, non tantum διὰ τὸ ἀσώματον, quomodo Patri id nomen convenit, sed etiam quia quod ad distinctionem verbi & Spiritus sancti vocatur generare, Græcis interdum & ἀπαυγάζειν, id laxiori voca- bulo etiam spirare appellabant, qualemcunque emanatio- nem, aut ut Tertullianus loquitur προβολὴν, eo nomine in- dicantes. Nam & procedere filium, non minus quam de- rivari, Tertullianus adversus Praxeam dixit. Quomodo de- fendi possunt & Lactantius & alii, quos cum Lactantio hac in parte ut Scripturarum imperitos accusat Hieronymus. Nam certe quin Trinitatem apertissime agnoverit Tertul- lianus dubitari non potest. Et quia plerique existimant Lati- norum fuisse hoc proprium, ostendam etiam antiquissimos Christianorum qui Græce scripserunt eundem ad modum locutos. Hermas, qualiscunque auctoritatis, certe vetusta- tis primæ, ut ex Irenæo & Clemente ejus verbis utentibus apparet Pastoris libro, ut nunc divisio instituta est, tertio: Illum spiritum sanctum qui infusus est omnium primus in cor- pore in quo habitaret Deus. Justinus Apologetico II. τὸ πνεῦ- μα ὆ν κὶ τὴν δύναμιν τὴν παρὰ τῦ θεῦ, Ὀδὲν ἄλλο νοῆσαι θέμις ἡ τὸν λόγον. Tatianus: λόγον ὁ ἐποράν. τῷ πνεῦμα γεγονὸς ἀπὸ τῦ πατρός. Theophilus: ἔχω ἐν ὁ θεὸς τὸν ἑαυτῦ λόγον.&dein- de: ἧτον ἔν ὧν πνεῦμα θεῦ ά περχὴ κὶ σοφία. Irenæus V. 1. εἰ δὲ μὴ ὡς ἄνθρωπον ἐφαίνετο ἄνθρωπον ωτε ὅ ἦν ἐπ̓ ἀληθείας ἔμεινε

πνεῦμα θεῦ. Ibidem: Verbum Patris & Spiritus Dei adunitus antiquæ substantiæ plasmationis Adæ. Sed quod maxime no- tandum, etiam post ortam cum Arianis controversiam & multis Synodis excussam ita locuti sunt hi qui adversus A- rianos scribebant, ut Phæbadius: Quis cognovit sensum Do- mini, aut quis consiliarius ejus fuit? Nemo utique, sed extra spiritum suum nemo: quem Spiritum Prophetæ sapientem archi- tectum, & admirabilem consiliarium dicit: nec immerito. Nam idem Spiritus sermo & sapientia Dei est: ex cujus persona Salo- mon: Quum pararet, inquit, cælos ego aderam illi. Et postea: Apparet ergo unum eundemque fuisse nunc in nomine Spiritus, nunc in vocabulo sermonis, nunc in appellatione sapientiæ. Quin etiam post natum cum Macedonio certamen mansit hoc loquendi genus. Scriptor dialogi eruditi adversus A- pollinaristam: χριστὸς πνεῦμα ζωοποιῶν ἐστὶ τῇ τῆς θεότητος λό- γῳ. Epiphanius tertio adversus hæreses: ἐκὼν διὰ τῆς πρὸς Φιλιππησίους ἐπιστολῆς ἐδίδαξεν ἡμᾶς, πῶς ἡ ὑπόστασις τῷ υἱῷ ὁμοία ἐστιν τῇ ὑποστάσει τῷ πατρός. πνεῦ. α γὰρ ἐκ πατρός. Chal- dæus quoque paraphrastes quod apud Jobum est cap. IV. 9. à flatu Dei, vertit, à sermone Dei.

Intelligit Grotius divinam Christi naturam, è 1. Petr. III. 18. quam ita vocari vult non tantum διὰ τὸ ἀσώματον, quomodo Patri id nomen convenit, sed etiam quia quod ad distinctionem Verbi & Spi- ritus S. vocatur generare, Græcis interdum & ἀπαυ- γάζειν, id laxiori vocabulo etiam spirare appella- bant, qualemcunque emanationem, aut ut Tertullia- nus loquitur, προβολὴν eo nomine indicantes. Quod uti recte è Patribus ostendit, è Scriptura ta- men doceri non potest. Alii per Spiritum intel- ligunt hic non divinam naturam, sed animam Chri- sti: quia secundum humanam naturam etiam cor- da & renes probabat, & cogitata hominum agno- scebat; quæ ut homo in die pantocritico in apri- cum producturus est, ceu judex universi orbis.

## 2:12
Verse 12. ὧστε ἐξίστασθαι πάντας] Matthew said 'they were amazed.' But Mark sought a more significant word by which great astonishment might be expressed. Luke also, following Mark, said ἔκστασιν: and not content with this, added καὶ ἐπλήσθησαν φόβου: just as we read ἐφοβήθησαν in the LXX, 1 Kings III. 28, and Acts II. 43, 'and fear came upon every soul.'

ὕτως] See Matt. IX. 33.

Latin:

Vers. 12. ὧστε ἐξίστασθαι πάντας] Ἐθαύμασαν dixit Matthæus. Sed Marcis significantius quæsivit vocabulum quo magnus stupor exprimeretur. Lucas quoque Marcum secutus ἔκ- στασιν dixit: neque hoc contentus adjecit καὶ ἐπλήσθησαν φόβου: quomodo ἐφοβήθησαν legimus apud LXX. 1. Reg. III. 28. & Act. II. 43. ἐγένετο δὲ πάσῃ ψυχῇ φόβος.

ὕτως] Vid. Matth. IX. 33.

## 2:14
Verse 14. καὶ παράγων] When he was going to the seaside, he had to go out through the maritime gate of Capernaum, near which there was undoubtedly a custom-house, since the publican's house was in the middle of the city. Concerning the name Levi, we have spoken in the notes on Matthew.

Latin:

Vers. 14. καὶ παράγων] Cum ad partes maritimas iret, ex- eundum illi fuit per portam Capharnaumi maritimam, apud quam haud dubie fuit vectigalarium, cum domus pu- blicani esset in media urbe. De Levi nomine ad Matthæum diximus.

## 2:15
Verse 15. ἦσαν γὰρ πολλοὶ καὶ ἠκολούθησαν αὐτῷ] The old Latin interpreter seems to me to have rendered the force of the Hebraism well: 'For there were many who followed him.' 'Him'—many here understand Christ. It seems to me rather that Levi himself is to be understood, whom Mark designated by this very name in this same verse, so that the sense is that at the time when he was called by Christ, many were present with him, such as lesser publicans and that sort of men whom the Jews called ἁμαρτωλούς. And that these, having followed Levi from death, also reclined at the table at the same time. And that Christ was not deterred.

It does not appear how this can be drawn to Levi, since the immediately preceding name is Ἰησοῦ, to which the pronoun is to be referred, and the text is clear: 'many publicans and sinners also reclined together with JESUS and his disciples: for there were many, and they had followed him;' whence most understand that they followed Christ, not Levi.

Latin:

Vers. 15. ἦσαν γὰρ πολλοὶ καὶ ἠκολούθησαν αὐτῷ] Bene He- braismi vim reddidisse mihi videtur Latinus interpres vetus: Erant enim multi qui sequebantur eum. Eum, multi hic Christum intelligunt. Mihi videtur potius ipse Levi intel- ligendus, quem αὐτῷ nomine hoc ipso commate designa- vit Marcus, ut sensus sit tunc cum à Christo vocaretur mul- tos adfuisse ipsi, ut ἀρχιτελώνῃ minores publicanos, & id ge- nus homines quos Judæi vocabant ἁμαρτωλούς. Eos autem Levin de morte sectatos simul etiam ad mensam accubuisse. Neque absterretum Christum.

Non apparet quomodo hoc ad Levin trahi possit, quum immediate antecedens nomen sit I' noῦ, ad quod referendum pronomen, & textus luculentus sit: multi etiam publicani & peccatores simul discubuerunt cum JESU, & discipulis ejus: e- rant enim multi, & sequuti fuerant eum; unde plerique Christum, non Levin sequutos intelli- gunt.

## 2:16
Verse 16. ἰδόντες αὐτὸν ἐσθίοντα] When they perceived that Jesus was taking food with the publicans, for they were not present.

τί] What is the meaning of this?

Latin:

Vers. 16. ἰδόντες αὐτὸν ἐσθίοντα] Cum intelligerent Jesum cum publicanis cibum sumere, neque enim aderant.

τί] Quid hoc rei est?

## 2:17
Verse 17. ὐκ ἦλθον καλέσαι δικαίους, ἀλλὰ ἁμαρτωλούς] 'To repentance' is understood: which is added in not all Greek codices, and in the Epistle of Barnabas, where the same sentiment is placed as is here; since the Syriac and Latin interpreters testify that it was absent of old, as does that most ancient manuscript which is in England. The sense, however, is undoubtedly rightly explained by that ancient addition. For the words that precede sufficiently show that ἁμαρτωλός is not used here in that common notion which embraces all men, but those who had hitherto lived an outlawed life. Wherefore also the δίκαιοι opposed to them are to be understood not as those in whom there is nothing of human infirmity, but such as that Nathanael, a true Israelite in whom there was no guile, or such as Zacharias and Elisabeth, living an unblamable life according to the divine precepts. These, by such a calling to a life

do not need the amendment of the whole, such as those former ones: in which sense a not inelegant writer of a prayer from the person of Manasseh says: You, he says, Lord God of the just, have not imposed repentance upon the just, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, those who had not sinned against you, but you have imposed repentance upon me who am a sinner. Christ does not deal here with the whole office imposed upon him, but with that part of the office which the Baptist had also performed and he himself was then most especially performing, κλήσεως εἰς μετάνοιαν [a calling to repentance]: which was a preparation for the heavenly kingdom. This, he says, I certainly cannot perform among men of amended life: there is need, therefore, that I should meet those who most need this remedy. Origen is not wrong against Celsus: ἐπέμφθη Θεὸς λόγος, καθὸ μὲν ἰατρὸς τοῖς ἁμαρτωλοῖς, καθὸ δὲ διδάσκα- λος τῶν μυστηρίων τοῖς ἤδη καθαροῖς [The Word of God was sent, as a physician to sinners, but as a teacher of mysteries to those already pure]. Christ neither concedes nor takes away from the Pharisees the holiness which they claimed for themselves in this particular place.

It is not understood, but added in most Greek Codices, if not in all, εἰς μετάνοιαν [to repentance], even in the Epistle of Barnabas, which the Syriac and Latin, and perhaps one English Greek Manuscript, cannot prejudice.

Latin:

Vers. 17. ὐκ ἦλθον καλέσαι δικαίυς, ἀλλὰ ἁμαρτωλοὺς] Sub- auditur εἰς μετάνοιαν: quod adjectum est in Codicibus Græcis non omnibus, & in Epistola Barnabæ, ubi eadem ponitur qua hic est sententia; cum olim abfuisse Syrus & Latinus interpretes testentur, & antiquissimus ille qui in Anglia est Manuscriptus. Sensus autem ea adjectione haud dubie antiqua recte explicatur. Nam quæ præcedunt verba satis ostendunt ἁμαρτωλὸς hic non dici communi illa notione quæ omnes homines complectitur, sed eos qui vitam vixe- rant hactenus exlegem. Quare & δίκαιοι his oppositi intelli- gendi sunt non in quibus nihil est humanæ infirmitatis, sed tales qualis ille Nathanael, verus Israelita in quo nihil erat doli, aut quales Zacharias & Elisabeth vitam viventes incul- patam secundum divina præcepta. Hi tali vocatione ad vitæ

totius emendationem, quales priores illi, non indigent: quo sensu Scriptor non inelegans precationis ex persona Manassis: Tu, inquit, Domine Deus justorum, non imposuisti poenitentiam justis Abrahamo, Isaaco & Iacobo, iis qui non pec- cave rant contra te, sed imposuisti poenitentiam mihi qui sum pec- cator. Non agit hic Christus de toto munere sibi imposi- to: sed de ea parte muneris qua & Baptista erat functus & ipse tunc maxime fungebatur κλήσεως εἰς μετάνοιαν: quae e- rat praeparatio ad regnum coeleste. Hanc, ait, ob- ire certe non possum circa homines emendatae vitae: opus igitur est eos conveniam qui maxime istius remedii indi- gent. Non male adversus Celsum Origenes: ἐπέμφθη Θεὸς λόγος, καθὸ μὲν ἰατρὸς τοῖς ἁμαρτωλοῖς, καθὸ δὲ διδάσκα- λος τῶν μυστηρίων τοῖς ἤδη καθαροῖς. Pharisaeis sanctimoniam quam sibi vindicabant hoc quidem loco nec concedit Chri- stus nec detrahit.

Non subauditur, sed additur in plerisque Co- dicibus Graecis, si non in omnibus, εἰς μετάνοιαν, etiam in Epistola Barnabae, quibus praejudicare Sy- rus & Latinus, & unus forte Graecus Anglicanus Manuscriptus non potest.

## 2:18
Verse 18. καὶ ἦσαν μαθηταὶ Ἰωάννου καὶ οἱ τῶν Φαρισαίων νηστεύοντες [And the disciples of John and those of the Pharisees were fasting]. Concerning this manner of speaking we have spoken at chapter I. I hold it certain that this does not deal with any defined time, but with that which happened more frequently. Among Matthew they themselves say of themselves νηστεύομεν πολλά [we fast much]. Among Luke οἱ μαθηταὶ Ἰωάννου νησ- τεύουσι πυκνά [the disciples of John fast often]. Which I would not point out if I did not see that there are those who interpret it otherwise.

καὶ ἔρχονται καὶ λέγουσιν αὐτῷ [And they come and say to him]. Both the disciples of John whom Matthew names, and the Pharisees whom Luke names: although it is not at all necessary that we say that this happened at one time.

Latin:

Vers. 18. καὶ ἦσαν μαθηταὶ Ἰωάννου καὶ οἱ τῶν Φαρισαίων νηστεύοντες] De hoc loquendi genere diximus ad caput I. Certum habeo non agi hic de aliquo definito tempore, sed de eo quod fiebat saepius. Apud Matthaeum ipsi de se di- cunt νηστεύομεν πολλά. Apud Lucam οἱ μαθηταὶ Ἰωάννου νησ- τεύουσι πυκνά. Quod non monerem nisi viderem esse qui ali- ter interpretarentur.

καὶ ἔρχονται καὶ λέγουσιν αὐτῷ] Tum Johannis discipuli quos Matthaeus nominat, tum Pharisaei quos Lucas: quam- quam nihil necesse est dicamus id uno tempore accidisse.

## 2:19
Verse 19. ὅσον χρόνον μεθ᾽ ἑαυτῶν ἔχουσι τòν νυμφίον, οὐ δύναν- ται νηστεύειν [As long as they have the bridegroom with them, they cannot fast]. Mark added this to signify that the interrogation has the force of a denial. Wherefore the Syriac here also placed nothing beyond a bare negation. Δύνανται [they can] here signifies not what can happen at all, but what is fitting: which also occurs elsewhere.

Latin:

Vers. 19. ὅσον χρόνον μεθ᾽ ἑαυτῶν ἔχουσι τòν νυμφίον, οὐ δύναν- ται νηστεύειν] Hoc addidit Marcus, ut significaret interro- gationem vim habere negandi. Quare & Syrus hic prae- ter nudam negationem nihil posuit. Δύνανται hic non quid fieri omnino possit, sed quid conveniat, significat: quod & alibi occurrit.

## 2:21
Verse 21. εἰ δὲ μή [But if not]. So also in Luke εἰ δὲ μήγε [but if not]. The verb is missing as in Apocal. II. 5. and elsewhere: which must be supplied from the sense. The sense here is: Unless he guards against that error.

PART II. OF CHAPTER II. In which also begins PART II. of the History of the life of JESUS by St. Mark; Pertaining to the Acts of the other part of the Ministry of JESUS at the Passover. Concerning the rubbing of the ears of corn on the Sabbath, and its Apology.

Latin:

Vers. 21. εἰ δὲ μή] Ita & apud Lucam εἰ δὲ μήγε. Deest verbum ut Apocal. II. 5. & alibi: quod ex sensu supplen- dum. Hic sensus est: Ni caveat eum errorem.

PARS II. CAPITIS II. Qua inchoatur etiam PARS II. Historiae vitae JESU S. Marci; Ad Acta ab altero Ministerii JESU Paschate pertinens. De fricatione spicarum in Sabbato, ejusque Apologia.

## 2:23
Verse 23. καὶ ἐγένετο παραπορεύεσθαι αὐτόν [And it came to pass that he was passing by]. The Syriac also follows this reading. Wherefore, that other less ancient codices have ἐγένετο πάλιν [it came to pass again], I think came from the Latin version in which 'iterum' [again] was placed μετατατικῶς [transpositively], if I am not mistaken. For that interpreter is accustomed sometimes to add something, as also below in verse 24.

Latin:

Vers. 23. καὶ ἐγένετο παραπορεύεσθαι αὐτόν] Hanc lectio- nem & Syrus sequitur. Quare quod alii minus vetusti co- dices habent ἐγένετο πάλιν, puto venisse ex Latina versione in qua iterum positum est μετατατικῶς, ni fallor. Solet enim iste interpres nonnunquam adjicere aliquid, ut infra quo- que commate 24.

## 2:25
Verse 25. ὅτε χρείαν ἔσχε [when he had need]. Mark added this deliberately, so that he might refer a special example to a general rule: which is this, that ritual laws lose their binding force where a sufficiently grave necessity urges, which is called χρεία [need] here: just as Greek writers are also accustomed to say ἐν χρείᾳ [in need]. Concerning the matter itself, we have dealt with it at Matthew.

Latin:

Vers. 25. ὅτε χρείαν ἔσχε] Addidit hoc consulto Marcus, ut speciale exemplum ad generalem referret regulam: quae haec est, Leges rituales vim obligandi amittere ubi satis gravis urget necessitas, quae χρεία hic dicitur: quomodo & Graeci Scriptores dicere solent ἐν χρείᾳ. De re ipsa ad Matthaeum egimus.

## 2:26
Verse 26. ἐπὶ Ἀβιάθαρ τοῦ ἀρχιερέως [in the time of Abiathar the high priest]. That Achimelech was named Abiathar and Abiathar his son was in turn named Achimelech, I do not yet see proven. For Achimelech who is named 2 Sam. VIII. 17 and 1 Par. XXIV. 3 is not called Pontifex Maximus [High Priest] but Priest, eminent indeed among others, as the son of the Pontifex, but nevertheless inferior to Sadoc, because Sadoc was, with Abiathar as Pontifex Maximus, the second Pontifex from the Maximus and the vicar of the Maximus, and סגן כהן הגדול [deputy high priest] or משנה כהן הגדול [second high priest]. The son of the Pontifex Maximus rightly follows him. But to name the Pontifex Maximus after his vicar would have been against reason and custom. Why therefore did Mark say that what was done under Achimelech the Pontifex Maximus happened under Abiathar the Pontifex? I find nothing more probable than that the name of Abiathar was better known, because of the Ephod brought to David 1 Sam. XXIII. 6 and because he held the Pontificatus Maximus for a long time under David. But he himself also, when this happened, was Pontifex, namely the vicar of his father, as one who succeeded him in the Pontificatus Maximus, as Vicars were accustomed to do: and he had been present at the event which is narrated here, and he himself approved the deed of both his father and David. For a similar reason Luke, in the designation of time, added Annas to Caiaphas the Pontifex Maximus, as a man of most celebrated fame.

These things are correct. Nor does the explanation of Luke disagree: that Abiathar was the son of Achimelech, who performed the paternal office under his father, and by the order of Saul was the companion of the Davidic flight when he was killed. Conf. Harm. B. Walsth. ad h. l. Addenda also the observation of B. Chemnitius Harm. c. XLVII. Lest anyone should say that God, by the slaughter of Achimelech, showed that that deed displeased Him, Christ names Abiathar, who did the same thing with his father, and yet was miraculously saved by God, and was exalted to the high priesthood and remained so for the whole time of the reign of David. God therefore shows, both by the reproof of the slaughter of Achimelech, Ps. LII, and by the preservation of Abiathar, that He does not disapprove of that deed.

καὶ ἔδωκε καὶ τοῖς σὺν αὐτῷ ὖσι] Mark added this prudently, although Matthew had also indicated it covertly when he said οὓς ἐκ ἐξὸν ἦν αὐτῷ φαγεῖν ὐδὲ τοῖς μετ' αὐτῶ. And the history in 1 Sam. XXI 4, 5 speaks that it is true. For with this added, the exception which could have been sought from David's dignity is excluded.

Latin:

Vers. 26. ἐπὶ Ἀβιάθαρ τοῦ ἀρχιερέως] Achimeleco no- men fuisse Abiathari & Abiathari ejus filio viciffim nomen Achimeleco, nondum video probatum. Nam Achimelec qui nominatur 2. Sam. VIII. 17. & 1. Par. XXIV. 3. non vo- catur Pontifex Maximus se I Sacerdos, eminens scilicet inter alios, ut Pontificis filius, sed Sadoco tamen minor, quia Sa- docus erat Abiathare Pontifice Maximo Pontifex à Maximo secundus & Maximi vicarius, & סגן כהן הגדול aut משנה כהן הגדול. Hunc recte sequitur filius Pon- tificis Maximi. At Pontificem Maximum post vicarium suum nominare contra rationem ac consuetudinem fuerat. Cur ergo Marcus dixit sub Abiathare Pontifice factum id quod factum est sub Achimeleco Pontifice Maximo? Nihil probabilius reperio, quam quod Abiatharis nomen erat no- tius. ob Ephod allatum ad Davidem 1. Sam. XXIII. 6. & ub diu gestum sub Davide Pontificatum Maximum. Sed & ipse cum hoc fieret erat Pontifex, Patris scilicet vicarius, ut cui in Pontificatum Maximum successit, ut solebant Vica- rii: & adfuerat rei quae hic narratur, atque ipse tum Patris, tum Davidis factum probaret. Simili de causa Lucas in designatione temporis, Cajaphae Pontifici Maximo Annam addidit, ut celeberrimae famae virum,

Recte se ista habent. Nec discrepat Lucæ ex- plicatio: Abiathar fuisse filium Achimelechi, qui sub patre functus sit officio paterno, eoque jus- su Saulis cæso comes fuerit fugæ Davidicæ, Conf. Harm. B. Walsth. ad h. l. Addenda autem B. Che- mnitii observatio Harm. c. XLVII. Ne quis diceret, Deum trucidatione Achimelech ostendisse factum il- lud sibi displicere, Christus nominat Abiathar, qui i- dem fecit cum patre, & tamen mirabiliter a Deo ser- vatus est, & ad summum Sacerdotium exaltatus to- to tempore regni Davidis mansit. Ostendit igitur Deus & reprehensione cædis Achimelech, Pf. LII. & conservatione Abiathar, se factum illud non impro- bare.

καὶ ἔδωκε καὶ τοῖς σὺν αὐτῷ ὖσι] Prudenter hoc addidit Marcus, quanquam tecte etiam Matthæos significarat, cum diceret οὓς ἐκ ἐξὸν ἦν αὐτῷ φαγεῖν ὐδὲ τοῖς μετ' αὐτῶ. Et verum esse loquitur historia 1. Sam, XXI 4. 5. Hoc enim addito, exceptio, quæ ex Davidis dignitate quæri pote- rat, excluditur.

## 2:27
Vers. 27. τὸ σάββατον διὰ τὸν ἄνθρωπον ἐγένετο] He calls the Sabbath here the law of rest on the seventh day. There are some things so honest in themselves that it is never possible to act against them without disgrace. There are others which come from established law, which does not flow from the fountains of honesty by a certain necessity, but is accustomed to be found for the sake of some utility. Thus that law of rest was found primarily for a double utility: first, so that under the pretext of any work, the assemblies instituted for the sake of piety might not be neglected, concerning which matter we treated above: then, so that there might be some breathing space from labors, which otherwise the harshness of masters would scarcely have granted to the family, Exod. XXIII, 12. To these, in place of an accession, the memory of Egyptian liberty and the signification of greater things was added. For we have proved elsewhere that the Sabbath was not instituted by God from the beginning with the necessity of resting. But things which are of this kind easily yield when an evident reason urges to the contrary. For equity itself dictates, which has also been produced in Roman law, that those things which have been found for the sake of utility ought not to be twisted into hatred by a harsher interpretation.

Grotius thinks that the law of the Sabbath rest is of established law, found primarily for a double utility: first, so that under the pretext of any work, the assemblies instituted for the sake of piety might not be neglected; then, so that there might be some breathing space from labors, which otherwise the harshness of masters would scarcely have granted to the family, Exod. XXIII. 12. To which, in place of an accession, the memory of Egyptian liberty and the signification of greater things was added: but that the Sabbath was not instituted by God from the beginning with the necessity of resting. But if the sanctification of the Sabbath was instituted from the beginning, for which rest from common labors is required, then the primordial necessity of this will also have to be established. But more on that elsewhere.

Latin:

Vers. 27. τὸ σάββατον διὰ τὸν ἄνθρωπον ἐγένετο] Sabbatum vocat hic legem otii die septimo. Sunt quædam ita per se honesta, ut nunquam sine flagitio contra ea fieri pos- sit. Sunt alia quæ ex jure constituto veniunt, quod non ex fontibus honesti necessitate quadam fluit, sed utilitatis alicujus causa reperiri solet. Ita lex illa otii ob duplicem ma- xime utilitatem reperta est: primum ne ullius operis ob- tentu negligerentur conventus pietatis causa instituti, qua de re egimus supra: deinde ut aliquod esset a laboribus spiramentum, quod alioqui dominorum durities familiæ vix erat concessura, Exod. XXIII, 12. His accessionis vice addita est Ægyptiacæ libertatis memoria & rerum majorum significatio. Nam ab initio non institutum fuisse a Deo sabbatum cum otiandi necessitate alibi probavimus. Quæ vero hujus sunt generis facile cedunt, ubi in contrarium ur- get evidens ratio. Nam æquitas ipsa dictat, quod & jure Romano proditum est, quæ utilitatis causa sunt reperta, ea non debere duriori interpretatione in odium retorqueri.

Putat Grotius legem otii Sabbati juris constituti esse, ob duplicem maxime utilitatem, repertam, pri- mum, ne ullius operis obtentu negligerentur conventus pietatis causa instituti, deinde ut aliquod esset a la- boribus spiramentum, quod alioqui dominorum durities familiæ vix erat concessura Exod. XXIII. 12. Quibus accessionis vice addita sit Ægyptiacæ libertatis memoria, & rerum majorum significatio: Ab ini- tio autem non institutum fuisse a Deo sabbatum cum otiandi necessitate. Sed si instituta ab initio Sabba- ti sanctificatio, ad quam requiritur otium a labori- bus communibus, etiam hujus necessitas primor- dialis statuenda erit. Sed de eo alias.

## 2:28
Vers. 28. κύριός ἐστιν ὁ ὑιὸς τῶ ἀνθρώπου καὶ τῶ σαββάτω] ὑιὸς τῶ ἀνθρώπων means any men whatsoever, as Mark also said below c. III. 28. Nor does this article stand in the way: for ὁ ὑιὸς τῶ ἀνθρώπω is correctly said when it concerns the universality of the human race. For often the article denotes τὸ καθόλκ. Ephraim of Antioch: δηλῶντες διὰ τῆς τοσαύτης προταγῆς τ' ἄρθρων ὅτι τινὰ ἄνθρωπον ποτ' ἄλλὰ τὸ ὁλικὸν. See what is said about these things in Matthew.

Latin:

Vers. 28. κύριός ἐστιν ὁ ὑιὸς τῶ ἀνθρώπου καὶ τῶ σαββάτω] ὑιὸς τῶ ἀνθρώπων homines quosvis Marcus etiam infra dixit c. III. 28. Neque obstat hic articulus: nam ὁ ὑιὸς τῶ ἀνθρώ- πω recte dicitur cum de generis humani universitate agitur. Sæpe enim articulus notat τὸ καθόλκ. Ephraim Antiochenus: δηλῶντες διὰ τῆς τοσαύτης προταγῆς τ' ἄρθρων ὅτι τινὰ ἄνθρωπον ποτ' ἄλλὰ τὸ ὁλικὸν. Vide quæ de his ad Matthæum.

## 3:1 Argument
CHAPTER III. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

JESUS in the Synagogue on the Sabbath heals a withered hand, asking first, whether it is lawful to do good on the Sabbath? The Pharisees consult with the Herodians about killing him. He withdraws to the sea, with many accompanying him from Galilee, Judea, Idumea, Tyre and Sidon, and he teaches from a boat, and heals many, and ascends a mountain, and ordains the Apostles, who are listed: many also gather in his house. But the lawyers coming from Jerusalem accuse him, because he has Beelzebub, He refutes them from the consistency of the Satanic Kingdom, and that he who binds Satan and snatches his prey from him must be stronger; and he warns them concerning the irremissibility of sin against the Holy Spirit: and he teaches that those who come to him, when his necessary ones arrive, are truly his kinsmen, who do the will of God.

Theophylact on Matt. 24. Although Origen said that the Dositheans were almost extinct in his time, Epiphanius nevertheless testifies that they still had some remnants in his own age. It seems more credible to me that they were different sects, but confused by the Talmudists because of a community of certain dogmas, and perhaps that one concerning the Sabbath. For the Herodians also agreed with the Sadducees in most things, as we have said elsewhere: and Tertullian records that Dositheus agreed with the Sadducees, although confused by the account of the times.

PART II. The information of the great crowd flowing to Jesus from the ship, sealed by miracles.

Latin:

CAPUT III. ARGUMENTUM ET PAR- TITIO.

IESUS in Synagoga in Sabbato manum ari- dam sanat, quærens primum, anne liceat in Sabbato benefacere? Consultant Pha- risæi cum Herodianis de ipso occidendo. Se- cedit ad mare, multis eum comitantibus e Galilæa, Judæa, Idumæa, Tyro ac Sido- ne, docetque e navi, ac sanat plurimos, & montem conscendit, ac Apostolos or- dinat, qui recensentur: congregan- tur etiam plurimi in domo ejus. Le- gisperiti autem Hierosolyma venientes criminantur, quod habeat Beelzebub, quos refellit à Regni Satanici consistentia, & quod fortiorem esse oporteat, qui Sa- tanam ligat, & prædam ei eripit; monet- que de peccati in Spir. S. irremiffibilitate: & advenientibus necessariis ejus, eos ve- re esse consanguineos suos, docet, qui vo- luntatem Dei faciunt.

Theophylactus ad Matth. XXIV. Dositheanos autem quamquam Origenes suo tempore extinctus serme dice- bat, Epiphanius tamen sua ætate aliquas habuisse reliquias testatur. Mihi credibilius videtur diversas fuisse sectas, sed confusas à Thalmudiftis ob quorundam dogmatum, ac forte istius de Sabbato communitatem. Nam & Herodia- ni in plerisque Sadducæis consentiebant, ut alibi diximus: & Dositheum Sadducæis consensisse tradit Tertullianus, quanquam temporum ratione confusa.

PARS. II. Magna turba ad Iesum confluentis è navi in- formatio, miraculis obsignata.

## 3:3
Vers. 3. ἔγειραι εἰς τὸ μέσον] So that the very sight of the man might soften hard hearts. The rest of this history has been explained at Matthew.

Latin:

Vers. 3. ἔγειραι εἰς τὸ μέσον] Ut vel ipse aspectus hominis dura corda emolliret. Cætera hujus historiæ ad Matthæum sunt explicata.

## 3:4
Vers. 4. ψυχὴν σῶσαι] Even, indeed, of a beast. For the word 'soul' is taken in this way in the Misnajoth, where questions of the Sabbath are treated. But if it is more fitting to save a beast from destruction on the Sabbath than to suffer it to perish, surely it is also more worthy on a joyful day to restore a man to health than to leave him in misery.

To explain the meaning of the N.T. from the Misnajoth is to illuminate darkness with light. The matter here was not about the soul of a beast, but about a man.

One or another codex of Beza, with the Latin version of Sym, and I add the Arabic, cannot excuse that audacity of Grotius, that having expunged the word ἀποκτεῖναι, which is read in all other copies, he substituted the word ἀπολέσαι. That has no inconvenience. For whether you understand 'man' by ψυχὴν synecdochically, the opposition of saving in life and slaughtering a man is clear, or if you take 'soul' for 'life', can life not be rightly said to be either saved or slaughtered? Indeed, what need is there to repeat the word ψυχῆς in the other member ἀπὸ κοινᾶ, when the antithesis holds itself correctly without repetition? For to slaughter and ψυχὴν ζῶσαι are opposites.

Latin:

Vers. 4. ψυχὴν σῶσαι] Quamvis, etiam pecudis. Nam ita vox animæ sumitur in Misnajoth, ubi sabbati quæstiones pertractantur. Quod si pecudem ab interitu servare con- venientius est sabbato quam pati ut pereat, sane & læto die dignius hominem sanitati reddere quam in miseria relin- quere.

E Misnajoth explicare N. T. sententiam est te- nebris lucem illustrare. Non de anima pecudis, sed de homine hic res erat.

Unus & alter codex Bezæ, cum versione Sym, Latina, addo & Arabica non potest excusare auda- ciam illam Grotianam, quod expuncta voce ἀπο- κτεῖναι, quæ in omnibus aliis exemplaribus legitur, substituit vocem ἀπολέσαι. Nil ista inconveni- entiæ habet. Nam sive per ψυχὴν Synechdochice hominem intelligas, oppositio salvandi in vita & trucidandi hominis luculenta est, seu animam pro vita accipias, annon vita vel servari, vel trucidari dici recte potest? Imo quid opus est ἀπὸ κοινᾶ in altero membro vocem ψυχῆς repetere, quum re- cte se habeat ἀντίθεσις, sine repetitione? trucidare enim & ψυχὴν ζῶσαι opposita sunt.

## 3:5
Vers. 5. μετ' ὀργῆς συνλυπέμεν] Christ teaches by his own example that one should be angry at sins in such a way that we simultaneously pity those who sin.

since that is not accustomed to happen except in words which receive Greek inflection: which that word does not receive, nor can it receive. But the Syrian also places this as a radical. But neither does רגש please me. For the noun רגש signifies nothing other than a gathering, which is far removed from the meaning of thunder. I do not doubt that it is the noun רעש. For it has been abundantly demonstrated that ע is transferred by r. Moreover, the noun רעש signifies a great commotion. The LXX translate it Σεισμὸν, Ezech. III. 14. Jer. X. 22. Job. XLI. 20. & XLVII. 3. Elsewhere Συσσεισμὸν, as 1. Reg. XIX. 12. Diodorus Siculus in book XIX says there was a certain prefecture in Media which was called ῥαγὰς: this name, however, was given to it because of the frequent earthquakes in that place. This, however, is not badly rendered by the word βροντῆς. For both thunder is a great Συσσεισμὸς, and every Συσσεισμὸς is accustomed to be called thunder by catachresis. The Arab correctly explains the word Boanerges as ابنا الرعد. Moreover, رعد is properly a tremor. It seems to me that Christ, in the imposition of this name, looked entirely to the prophecy of Haggai ch. II. 7, where that word appears from which this name is derived: עוד אחת מעט היא ואני מרעיש את השמים ואת ארץ ואת הים ואת החרבת Ἔτι ἅπαξ ἐγὼ σείσω τὸν οὐρανὸν καὶ τὴν γῆν καὶ τὴν θάλασσαν καὶ τὴν ξηράν. Which the writer to the Hebrews ch. XII. 26 explains concerning the preaching of the Gospel. To this great change of things, therefore, Christ signifies that the sons of Zebedee would be his eminent ministers. And certainly even this shows a certain excellence destined for them among the Apostles themselves, that they were taken as witnesses of many things apart from the others with Peter. Add now that James was the first of all the Apostles to seal the doctrine of Christ with his blood: and that John, surviving all the Apostles, bore witness to the truth for a very long time.

The derivation from רעם, which is Drusius's, or even Caninius's from רגש, does not please Grotius; he prefers to descend the word from רעש, which denotes a great commotion, and is translated by σεισμὸν by the LXX interpreters Ez. III. 14. Jerem. X. 22. But because it is explained by the word βροντῆς, Lud. de Dieu correctly warns that in Syriac it is said not as Caninius wants בְּנֵי רְגַשׁ but בְּנֵי רְגַשׁ which can be read βαναιργὲς, and from there, by a slight variation, easily arises βοανεργὲς.

Latin:

Vers. 5. μετ' ὀργῆς συνλυπέμεν] Docet exemplo suo Christus, ita irascendum peccatis, ut simul peccantium nos misereat.

cum id fieri non soleat nisi in vocibus quæ Græcam acci- piunt flexionem: quam vox illa non accipit, nec accipere potest. Sed & Syrus hic ponit ut radicale. Sed neque רגש mihi placet. Nam nomen רגש nihil aliud quam cœ- tum significat, quod à tonitrûs significatione longe abest. Non dubito quin sit nomen רעש. Nam ע per r trans- ferri abunde demonstratum est. Significat autem nomen רעש maximam commotionem. Σεισμὸν vertunt LXX, E- zech. III. 14. Jer. X. 22. Job. XLI. 20. & XLVII. 3. Alibi Συσσεισμὸν, ut 1. Reg. XIX. 12. Diodorus Siculus libro XIX. in Media præfecturam quandam ait fuisse quæ ῥαγὰς dice- retur: nomen autem hoc ei datum ex frequentibus eo loco terræ motibus. Hoc autem non male redditur voce βρον- τῆς. Nam & tonitru est maximus Συσσεισμὸς, & omnis συσ- σεισμὸς per κατάχρησιν tonitru dici solet. Arabs vocem Boa- nerges recte explicat ابنا الرعد. Est autem رعد pro- prie tremor. Omnino videtur mihi Christus in hujus no- minis impositione respexisse ad Aggæi vaticinium c. II. 7. ubi verbum illud comparet, unde nomen hoc derivatum est: עוד אחת מעט היא ואני מרעיש את השמים ואת ארץ ואת הים ואת החרבת Ἔτι ἅπαξ ἐγὼ σείσω τὸν οὐρανὸν καὶ τὴν γῆν καὶ τὴν θάλασσαν καὶ τὴν ξηράν. Quod de Evangelii prædicatione exponit Scri- ptor ad Hebræos c. XII. 26. Ad hanc ergo maximam re- rum mutationem significat Christus Zebedæi filios eximios sibi ministros fore. Et certe destinatam illis excellentiam quandam inter ipsos Apostolos vel hoc ostendit, quod cum Petro seorsim à cæteris multarum rerum testes sunt assum- ti. Adde jam quod Jacobus primus Apostolorum omni- um sanguine suo Christi doctrinam obsignavit: & quod Johannes omnibus Apostolis superstes diutissime testimo- nium perhibuit veritati.

Non placet Grotio derivatio à רעם quæ Drusii, vel etiam Caninii à רגש, mavult descendere vo- cem à רעש quod maximam commotionem notat, & per σεισμὸν vertitur à LXX. Interpretibus Ez. III. 14. Jerem. X. 22. Sed quia exponitur voce βροντῆς, recte Lud. de Dieu monet, Syriace dici non ut Caninius vult בְּנֵי רְגַשׁ sed בְּנֵי רְגַשׁ quod legi po- test βαναιργὲς, atque inde levi variatione facile oriri βοανεργὲς.

## 3:8
Verse 8. κὶ ἀπὸ τῆς ἰδουμαίας] Which in those times was joined with the Jews by a bond of religion, as appears from Josephus.

κὶ οἱ περὶ Τύρον κὶ Σιδῶνα] The Syriac and certain of the Greeks understand the Tyrians and Sidonians. To me, it seems rather that the Jews are indicated who were inhabiting the maritime coast in the borderland of Tyre and Sidon, which seems to be called παράλιθ Τύρου κὶ Σιδῶν& in Luke 6:17, μέρη Τύρου κὶ Σιδῶνθ in Matt. 15:21, and μεθόρια Τύρα κὶ Σιδῶν below in 7:24.

Latin:

Vers. 8. κὶ ἀπὸ τῆς ἰδουμαίας] Quæ iis temporibus cum Judæis religionis societate jungebatur, ut ex Josepho appa- ret.

κὶ οἱ περὶ Τύρον κὶ Σιδῶνα] Tyrios & Sidonios intelligit Syrus & Græcorum quidam. Mihi potius videntur indi- cari Judæi habitantes oram maritimam in confinio Tyri & Sidonis, quæ παράλιθ Τύρου κὶ Σιδῶν& dici videtur Luc. VI. 17. μέρη Τύρου κὶ Σιδῶνθ Matth. XV. 21. μεθόρια Τύρα κὶ Σιδῶν infra VII. 24.

## 3:9
Verse 9. προσκαρτερῇ ἀυτῷ] Mark uses this word quite properly, and in the same sense in which Luke said in Acts 8:13, ἦν προσκαρτερῶν Φιλίππῳ, he did not depart from Philip. It corresponds to the Hebrew שקד.

Latin:

Vers. 9. προσκαρτερῇ ἀυτῷ] Admodum proprie hac voce utitur Marcus, & eodem sensu quo Lucas dixit Actor. IIX. 13. ἦν προσκαρτερῶν Φιλίππῳ, à Philippo non discedebat. Respondet Hebræo שקד.

## 3:10
Verse 10. μάστιγας] Thus twice below Mark, and Luke chapter 7:21 distinguishes between νόσες κὶ μάστιγας, so that μάστιξ seems to be something more: just as also נגע for the Hebrews, which the LXX sometimes translate as μάστιγα, signifies more severe evils. And so it is accustomed to be said concerning leprosy, as μάστιξ below concerning the issue of blood. There is a similar meaning in the word שוט in Job 9:23, Prov. 26:3, Nahum 3:2.

Verse 11. προσέπιπτεν ἀυτῷ] The spirits are said here to have done that which those who were possessed did by their impulse, as appears below in chapter 7:25, which the Syriac here strove to avoid by ὑπ᾿ ἀυτῆν.

Nevertheless, the Spirits themselves are also said to bend their knees to Christ, Phil. 2:10, who are certainly included under the name of those under the earth (τῶν καταχθονίων).

PART III. The ordination of the Apostles.

Latin:

Vers. 10. μάστιγας] Sic bis infra Marcus, & Lucas cap. VII. 21. distinguit νόσες κὶ μάστιγας, ut μάστιξ plus aliquid esse videatur: quomodo & נגע Hebræis, quod LXX. inter- dum μάστιγα transferunt, mala graviora significat. Itaque περὶ τῆς λέπρας dici solet, ut μάστιξ infra de sanguinis fluxu. Par significatio in voce שוט Job. IX. 23. Prov. XXVI. 3. Nahum III. 2.

Ves. 11. προσέπιπτεν ἀυτῷ] Dicuntur hic fecisse spiritus id, quod eorum impulsu faciebant οἱ ἐνεργέμενοι, ut apparet infra cap. VII. 25. quam ὑπ᾿ ἀυτῆν hic vitare studuit Sy- rus.

Dicuntur tamen etiam Spiritus ipsi genua flecte- re Christo, Phil. II. 10. qui τῶν καταχθονίων no- mine utique comprehenduntur.

PARS III. Apostolorum ordinatio.

## 3:13
Verse 13. ἀναβαίνᾷ εἰς τὸ ὄρθ] As he was accustomed, whenever he had set out to pray to the Father more attentively. See in this place Luke 6:12. Thus he gave an example to his own, that they should always begin ordinations (χειροτονίαις) with prayers, which we see the Apostles following in Acts 1:24. But we also read in Acts 14:23 concerning Paul and Barnabas: χειροτονήσαντες δὲ ἀυτοῖς πρεσβυτέρες κατ᾿ ἐκκλησίαν προσευξάμενοι μετὰ νησειῶν.

προσκαλεῖται ὃς ἤθελεν ἀυτὸς] From the whole number of those following him, he takes to himself twelve perpetual companions, not those who wanted, but those whom he himself wanted. Thus Paul says in Eph. 1:1 that he is an Apostle διὰ θελήματῷ Θεῦ. And Christ himself says to them: You did not choose me, but I chose you, John 15:16. Not only ambition is excluded, but also every cause of election that could be investigated by human effort.

Latin:

Vers. 13. ἀναβαίνᾷ εἰς τὸ ὄρθ] Ut solebat, quoties pre- cari patrem attentius instituerat. Vide hoc loco Luc. VI. 12. Ita exemplum suis dedit, ut χειροτονίαις semper à preci- bus auspicarentur, quod videmus sequi Apostolos Actor. I. 24. Sed & Actor. XIV. 23. de Paulo & Barnaba legimus: χειροτονήσαντες δὲ ἀυτοῖς πρεσβυτέρες κατ᾿ ἐκκλησίαν προσευ- ξάμενοι μετὰ νησειῶν.

προσκαλεῖται ὃς ἤθελεν ἀυτὸς] Ex omni se sectantium nu- mero perpetuos sibi comites duodecim adsciscit, non qui volebant sed quos volebat ipse. Ita Paulus Eph. I. 1. dicit se Apostolum διὰ θελήματῷ Θεῦ. Et Christus ipse ad eos: Non vos me elegistis, sed ego vos elegi, Joh. XV. 16. Excluditur non tantum ambitus, sed omnis etiam causa electionis quæ humano studio posset indagari.

## 3:14
Vers. 14. κὶ ἐποίησε δώδεκα] The Syrian rightly translates it 'he chose'. The Greeks would say κατίση. And that עשה is taken in this way elsewhere, as well as in I Sam. XII. 6, has been rightly observed. But the LXX, even there: ὁ ποιήσας Μωσῆν κὶ ᾿Ααρὼν, that is, ὁ κατατήσας. You may also take δώδεκα not for the number but for the office, so that ἐποίησε δώδεκα is ἐποίησεν Αποστόλες, as we would say in Latin, he made twelve men. For the Apostles are called οἱ δώδεκα everywhere, even when they were eleven in number, as in 1 Cor. XV. 5. As for the fact that some codices add here ὡς κὶ ᾿Αποστόλες ὠνόμασεν, since the ancient interpreters do not recognize it, it was undoubtedly born from an interpretation.

The interpretation is to be preferred entirely to the Syriac. Concerning which Drusius, and from him Balduinus Walæus on this passage.

There are five parts: I. The healing of the withered hand, to v. 6. II. The information of the great crowd flowing to Jesus from the ship, confirmed by miracles, to v. 13. III. The ordination of the Apostles, to v. 20. IV. The defense of the miracles against the blasphemy of the lawyers, to v. 30. V. The admonition concerning his kinsmen, to v. 35.

PART I. The healing of the withered hand.

Latin:

Vers. 14. κὶ ἐποίησε δώδεκα] Bene vertit Syrus elegit. Græci dicerent κατίση. Atque ita עשה sumi rum alibi tum I. Sam. XII. 6. recte observatum est. At LXX, etiam ibi : ὁ ποι- ήσας Μωσῆν κὶ ᾿Ααρὼν, id est, ὁ κατατήσας. Potes etiam sume- re δώδεκα non pro numero sed pro officio, ut ἐποίησε δώδεκα sit ἐποίησεν Αποστόλες, quomodo Latine diceremus, fecit duodecim viros. Nam passim Apostoli vocantur οἱ δώ- δεκα, etiam cum numero essent undecim, ut 1. Cor. XV. 5. Quod enim nonnulli codices hic adjiciunt ὡς κὶ ᾿Αποστόλες ὠνόμασεν, cum prisci interpretes non agnoscant, haud dubi- to natum ex interpretamento.

Præferenda omnino Syriaco interpretatio. De qua Drusius, & ex eo Balduinus Walæus ad h. l.

Partes sunt quinque: I. Aridæ manus sanatio, ad v. 6. II. Magna turbæ ad Jesum confluentis è navi informatio miraculis confirmata, ad v. 13. III. Apo- stolorum ordinatio, ad v. 20. IV. Miraculorum ad- versus blasphemiam legisperitorum defensio, ad v. 30. V. De consanguineis commonefactio, ad v. 35.

PARS I. Aridæ manus sanatio.

## 3:18
Verse 18. Θαδδαῖον] Some copies have Λεββαῖον, for which I conjecture that others wrote λεὺιν from Origen. The place is in the first book against Celsus, which we cited on Matthew. It is credible that that reading pleased some, because James of Alphaeus had preceded, and this Levi, ὁ τελώνης, was also the son of Alphaeus. Certainly Theodoret also seems to have read it so. For he cites: Θαδδαῖον ὁ καὶ λεβὶ quest. 16 on Numbers.

Latin:

Vers. 18. Θαδδαῖον] Λεββαῖον habent quædam exempla- ria, pro quo alios scripsisse λεὺιν ex Origene conjicio. Locus est ad Celsum primo, quem citavimus ad Matthæum. Cre- dibile est eam lectionem nonnullis placuisse, ideo quod Jacobus Alphæi præcessisset, & iste etiam Levi, ὁ τελώνης, Alphæi fuerit filius. Certe & Theodoretes videtur ita legisse. Citat enim: Θαδδαῖον ὁ καὶ λεβὶ quæst. 16. ad Numeros.

## 3:20
Verse 20. καὶ ἔρχονται εἰς οἶκον) I see absolutely no reason why we should tear this away from those things which follow, with which it coheres in both construction and sense. For Mark wants to narrate that a great gathering took place when Christ had already entered the house to dine.

ὥστε μὴ δύνασθαι αὐτοὺς] So that Christ, and those who were with him, whether all the Apostles or some of them, could not take food, with the crowd obstructing on all sides.

Latin:

Vers. 20. καὶ ἔρχονται εἰς οἶκον) Plane nihil causæ video cur hoc avellamus ab iis quæ sequuntur, quibuscum & con- structione & sensu cohæret. Vult enim narrare Marcus, maximam concurfionem factam, cum Christus jam do- mum intrasset cœnaturus.

ὥστε μὴ δύνασθαι αὐτοὺς] Ita ut Christus, & qui cum eo e- rant, sive Apostoli omnes, sive illorum aliqui, non possent cibum capere, turba undique obstante.

## 3:21
Verse 21. οἱ παρ' αὐτοῦ] Kinsmen, as the Syrian interprets, or as the Latin, his own. Since, however, these things were done at Capharnaum, it seems that Christ also had relatives there. Indeed, it is credible that his mother, Joseph now being dead (for there is no mention of him anywhere after the beginning of Christ's κήρυγμα), had migrated there from Nazareth because of those things which are said below in verse thirty-two, and chapter six, verse 3.

ἐξῆλθον κρατῆσαι αὐτόν] To touch him. Namely, so that they might lead him away elsewhere from that house in which he was being pressed. For κρατεῖν is often ἅπτεσθαι with the accusative, as here and Matth. XXIX. 9. and below IX. 25. and Act. III. 11. or with the genitive, as above I. 31. and Matth. IX. 25, nor do the Syrian and Arab interpret it otherwise here.

ἔλεγον γὰρ] Impersonally in the Hebrew manner: that is, a rumor had gone out.

ὅτι ἐξέστη] We have said that we think so, not only the Arab, which a most learned man noted, but also the Syrian takes ἐξέστη in this place to signify either συγκοπὴν or λειποθυμίαν, both of which the Greeks call ἔκλυσιν. In which sense we read ἐκλύεσθαι, both in Matth. XV. 32. and below VIII. 3. It is the same for the Hebrews ויפג לבו Genes. XLVI. 26. Moreover, this is accustomed to follow then from fasting, as appears also in the stated places, and from the warmth of the surrounding air, which the excessive gathering of the crowd causes. Both causes then made this rumor credible even concerning Christ. In almost this sense Sophocles said καρδίας ἐξίσταμαι for my heart recoils. Cicero: What wonder if by the magnitude of fear, as usually happens, he departed from constancy and mind and from himself. Here he departed from himself is ἐξέστη, that is, he was not indeed driven into madness, but ἄπνοος ἐγένετο or ἰλιγγοψύχησε. And many peoples today express a fainting of the spirit with a similar locution. Moreover, all these things pertain to showing how famous the reputation of Jesus was. See Act. XXVI. 26.

To Heinsius, ἐξίσταθαι is to be alienated, which was proper to the Prophets while they were seized by the spirit, so that they were outside themselves and little in control. And under this name, and the pretext that the friends of the Lord might snatch him from the raging crowd, that most learned man, whom Grotius follows, who is Casaubon in Exerc. XVI. on the annotations of Baronius, page 247, wants to deny that he was in his own power. But Ludov. de Dieu refutes him just as he does Beza: This is indeed a pious sentiment, by which he attributes offices of charity to the kinsmen of Christ, whereas otherwise they would have acted impiously and iniquitously if, holding Christ for insane, they had sought to seize him. But I do not know whether we ought to be so fair to the kinsmen of Christ, who are said elsewhere not to have believed in him. The Arab certainly does not patronize them. The most learned man translates, because his heart was evil. He seems to have confused the roots, of which one signifies to be evil, the other Raphel translates to err. but properly it signifies to be carried away, not to consider what you are doing. Hence is ecstasis Acts II. 5. I saw a vision in a trance in ἐκστάσει. Thus in this place for ὅτι ἐξέστη, the Arab has that which would be carried away in mind, in an excess of mind. Rom. II. 8. πνεῦμα κατανύξεως, the Arab translates, a stupefied spirit, inept for considering things. Thus the same mind of the Arab, which is that of the Syrian, and which the Greek ἐξέστη carries before itself, namely that they had said that Christ had been made powerless of mind. Which coheres very well with the following verse, where the Scribes are said to have said, He has a demon. Namely, it agreed for the friends of Christ with the Scribes; those said he was powerless of mind, these said he was possessed: therefore worthy to be seized. These things Dievius. But since the mother of the Lord was among those relatives, as is to be gathered from verse 31, no such thing is to be presumed about the relatives: and therefore the explanation of Casaubon and Grotius seems to be preferred to the Dievian opinion, even if Beza and B. also agree with it. Winckelmann also agrees, the explanation of Casaubon and Grotius. Especially, however, the interpretation of our blessed Chemnitz pleases, Harmon. chap. LIX. that the relatives mean this, that he was so carried away as if out of himself by excessive zeal and fervor for propagating the kingdom of God, that he did not always consider the manner of acting, but was more often carried away by excessive vehemence, and that they were trying to appease the adversaries in this way: which Chemnitz opposes also to those who extol the holiness of Mary too much, comparing Ps. XXXI. 23. Ps. XLVIII. 6. Deut. XXIX. 28. and especially the passage 2 Cor. V. 13. εἴτε γὰρ ἐξέστημεν, Θεῷ εἴτε σωφρονοῦμεν, ὑμῖν, whether we were insane, for God: or whether we are sane, for you: by which the Apostle indicates that many things are done by the faithful ministers of Christ in the ministry with such zeal that the common people disapprove, and either interpret it as insanity, or at least complain of excessive excess, which things, however, both God and the outcome prove: Which Chemnitz also judges to have seemed to the relatives of Jesus concerning his ministry. Flacius in his gloss has it thus: They were thinking that such a great multitude, and so many occupations, were disturbing his head. Perhaps also in that great tumult, while one thing had to be answered to others, some of his words and gestures were taken sinisterly. Truly, to the world, those who serve God seriously always seem to be insane. Flacius brings forward another opinion there: and adds his own judgment about it: Molinæus, with the text agreeing, advises that it should rather be translated:

And when those who were with him had heard this, they went out to restrain him (that is, the crowd), saying that he was away, so that the sense is: the Apostles, seeing that they were too occupied, and also hindered by the crowd from taking necessary food, had gone out of the house to meet the gathering crowd, in order to restrain it from rushing into the house, pretending that the Lord was away: which sense is neither inconvenient nor alien to the words: but the following verse agrees more with the common opinion. See the union of Mol. part. 30. Others, whom Beza notes, refer not only the relative αὐτὸν to ὄχλον, but also those words, ὅτι ἐξέστη: and they take these things concerning those who were with him at home, that they went out to restrain the raging crowd. Which Beza disapproves, both because what is narrated at the end of the chapter seems to indicate that Christ's relatives were approaching, and that these things also should be understood concerning them: and because the word κρατῆσαι implies a certain force, by which they neither could nor would restrain the raging multitude, since such zeal was not in them at that time: having cited the passage of Cyprian, book 1, epistle 3. We see the Lord himself detained by his brothers, and betrayed by him whom he had chosen among the Apostles.

PART IV. Defense of the miracles against the blasphemy of the lawyers.

Latin:

Vers. 21. οἱ παρ' αὐτοῦ] Cognati ut Syrus interpretatur, aut ut Latinus sui. Cum autem hæc gesta sint Capharnaumi, videtur & ibi Christus propinquos habuisse. Imo credibile est matrem, Josepho jam mortuo (neque enim usquam il- lius post inchoatum Christi κήρυγμα fit mentio) Nazaretha eo migrasse ob ea quæ dicuntur infra com. trigesimo secun- do, & cap. sexto, com. 3.

ἐξῆλθον κρατῆσαι αὐτόν] Contingere eum. Nimirum ut eum ex ea domo, in qua premebatur, alio abducerent. Κρατεῖν enim sæpe est ἅπτεσθ cum accusativo, ut hic & Matth. XXIX. 9. & infra IX. 25. & Act. III. 11. aut cum Genitivo, ut supra I. 31. & Matth. IX. 25, neque aliter hic interpretantur Syrus & Arabs.

ἔλεγον γὰρ] Impersonaliter more Hebræo: id est, ru- mor exierat.

ὅτι ἐξέστη] Diximus ita nos arbitrari, non Arabem tan- tum, quod notavit vir eruditissimus, sed & Syrum ἐξέστη hoc loco accipere, ut significet aut συγκοπὴν aut λειποθυμίαν, quorum utrumque Græci ἔκλυσιν vocant. Quo sensu ἐκλύ- εσθαι legimus, & Matth. XV. 32. & infra VIII. 3. Idem est Hebræis ויפג לבו Genes. XLVI. 26. Solet autem id se- qui tum ex inedia, ut dictis etiam locis apparet, tum ex cir- cumstantis aëris tepore, quem facit nimius turbæ con- curfus. Vtraque autem caufa tunc & de Christo credibi- lem hunc rumorem faciebat. Hoc serme sensu καρδίας ἐξίσταμαι pro cor refugit dixit Sophocles. Cicero: Quid mirum si magnitudine timoris, ut plerumque fit, à constantia atque mente atque à se ipse decessit. Hic à se ipse discessit, est ἐξέστη, id est non quidem in furorem actus est, sed ἄπνοος θύμναν aut ἰλιγγοψύχησε. Et multi hodie populi simili locutione animi deliquium exprimunt. Pertinent autem hæc omnia ad ostendendum quam celebris Iesu fama fue- rit. Vide Act. XXVI. 26.

Heinsio ἐξίσταθαι est alienari, quod Propheta- rum fuit proprium, dum spiritu corriperentur, ex- tra se ac parum compotes ut essent. Atque hoc nomine, ac prætextu amicos Domini ut furenti turbæ eum eriperent, suæ eum potestatis esse, ne- gasse vult Vir ille eruditissimus, quem sequitur Grotius, qui Casaubonus est Exerc. XVI. ad an- not. Baron. pag. 247. Quem vero pariter, ut & Bezam Ludov. de Dieu ita refellit; Pia quidem hæc sententia est, qua cognatis Christi charitatis offi- cia tribuit, quum alioqui impiè & inique egissent, si Christum pro insano habentes capere stuaussent. Sed nescio, an tam æquos in Christi cognatos nos esse oporteat, qui alibi dicuntur in ipsum non credi- disse. Arabs certe ipsis non patrocinatur. Vir do- ctissimus vertit, quia malum esset ei cor. Videtur confudisse radices, quarum altera significat malum es- se, alteram Raphel. vertit errare; sed proprie significat abreptum esse, non considerare quid agas. Inde est ecstasis Actor. II. 5. vidi visionem in mentis excessu in ἐκστάσει. Ita hoc loco pro ὅτι ἐξέστη, Arabs habet, quod esset abreptus mente, in excessu mentis. Rom. II. 8. πνεῦμα κατανύξεως, Arabs vertit, spiritum stupentem, ad res considerandas ineptum. Ita ea- dem mens Arabis, quæ Syri, & quam Græcum ἐξέστη præ se fert, nempe dixisse eos, Christum mentis impotem factum esse. Quod optime co- hæret cum sequenti vers. ubi Scribæ dicuntur dixif- se, Dæmonium habet. Nempe conveniebat ami- cis Christi cum Scribis; illi mentis impotem, hi dæ- moniacum dicebant: dignum ergo qui comprehen- deretur. Hæc Dievius. Sed quum inter illos co- gnatos fuerit mater Domini, ut è vers. 31. collige- re est, non tale quid de cognatis præsumendum: ideoque præferenda videtur Dievianæ sententiæ, etsi ei Beza quoque ac B. Winckelmannus acce- dat, Casauboni, atque Grotii explicatio. Im- primis tamen placet B. Chemnitii nostri interpre- tatio Harmon. cap. LIX. quod id velint cognati, nimio studio ardere & zelo propagandi regni Dei ita quasi extra se raptum esse, ut non sem- per consideret modum agendi, sed sæpius abri- piatur nimia vehementia, quodque adversarios hoc modo placare conentur: quod opponit Che- mnitius etiam illis, qui Mariæ sanctitatem nimis extollunt, conferens Ps. XXXI. 23. Psal. XLIIX. 6. Deuter. XXIX. 28. & imprimis locum 2. Cor. V. 13. εἴτε γὰρ ἐξέστημεν, Θεῷ εἴτε σωφρονοῦμεν, ὑμῖν, sive insanivimus, Deo: sive sani sumus, vobis: quo in- dicat Apostolus à fidelibus Christi ministris multa in ministerio agi tali zelo, ut vulgus improbet, & vel insaniam interpretetur, vel saltim de nimio excessu conqueratur, quæ tamen ipsa & Deus & eventus probent: Quod etiam visum fuisse cognatis Jesu de ipsius ministerio censet Chemnitius. Flacius in glossa ita habet: Cogitabant illam tantam multitudinem, & tot occupationes perturbare caput. Forte etiam in illo tanto tumultu, dum aliud aliis respon- dendum fuit, aliqua ejus verba & gestus sinistre acci- piebant. Semper sane mundo insanire videntur, qui serio Deo serviunt. Adducit Flacius aliam ibi sen- tentiam: deque ea judicium suum addit: Molinæus consentiente textu monet, vertendum, potius esse:

Et cum id audissent, qui apud eum erant, exierunt, ut continerent eam (id est, turbam) dicentes eum abesse, ut sit sensus: Apostolos videntes se nimium occupari, & etiam in capiendo necessario cibo im- pediri a turba, egressos esse ex domo obviam tur- bæ confluenti, ut eam reprimerent, ne in domum irrueret, prætexentes Dominum abesse: qui sensus nec incommodus est, nec a verbis alienus: sed se- quens versus magis communi sententiæ astipulatur. Vide unionem Mol. part. 30. Alii quos notat Be- za, non relativum modo αὐτὸν ad ὄχλον referunt, sed & illa, ὅτι ἐξέστη: & hæc de iis accipiunt, qui apud ipsum domi fuerint, quod exierint, ut fu- rentem turbam compescerent. Quod improbat Beza, tum quia quæ extremo capite narrantur, de cognatis Christum accedentibus videantur indi- care, hæc quoque de iis accipienda esse: tum quod verbum κρατῆσαι, vim quandam inferat, qua fu- rentem multitudinem coërcere illi nec valuerint, nec voluerint, quum tantus iis eo tempore zelus non fuerit: adducto loco Cypriani l. I. epist. 3. Vi- demus ipsum Dominum a fratribus esse detentum, & ab eo, quem inter Apostolos delegerat, proditum.

PARS IV. Miraculorum adversus Legisperitorum blasphemiam defensio.

## 3:22
Verse 22. Βεελζεβοὺλ ἔχει) The Syrian well explains Beelzebub is in him, that is, he works through him. See Matt. IX. 34, ch. XII. 24, 27. Hence they also called Christ himself Beelzebub, Matt. X. 25, that is, the instrument and minister of Beelzebub. A similar expression is in Matt. XI. 18, δαιμόνιον ἔχει, that is, he uses it familiarly. The Platonists say Συγγίνεσθαι δαιμονίῳ, except that they interpret δαιμόνιον in a better sense. In another sense those men in John said he had a demon, wishing to signify that he was possessed.

Latin:

Vers. 22. Βεελζεβοὺλ ἔχει) Bene explicat Syrus Beelzebub in eo est, id est per eum operatur. Vide Matth. IX. 34. c. XII. 24. 27. Hinc & ipsum Christum Beelzebub vocabant, Matth. X. 25. id est Beelzebubi ὄργανον & ministrum. Si- milis locutio Matth. XI. 18. δαιμόνιον ἔχει, id est familiariter eo utitur. Συγγίνεσθαι δαιμονίῳ dicunt Platonici, nisi quod il- li δαιμόνιον in partem meliorem interpretantur. Alio sen- su illi apud Iohannem dicebant δαιμόνιον ἔχει, significare volentes eum esse ἐνεργούμενον.

## 3:26
V. 26. καὶ εἰ ὁ Σατανᾶς ἀνέστη ἐφ' ἑαυτὸν) It seems to me that Satan is said in this place, and in Luke XI. 18, to be the whole totality of evil spirits, just as man is used for the human race or human nature. For not only the Prince of spirits, but all impure spirits are reckoned by that name, as appears in this very place in verse 23, and Matt. XII. 26. Proclus on the second book of Plato's Republic: for the addition of the article either denotes only excellence, as when we say the poet said, assigning this as a prerogative to the greatest, or the whole multitude, as when we say, man is rational, attaching the article instead of the whole. Ἀνέστη with ἐπὶ is an expression of the Hellenists derived from Hebraism, by which a hostile attempt is indicated, קום על, as in Ps. III. 3, and elsewhere passim.

It does not appear how the whole totality can be understood: for will the whole totality rise up against itself? And v. 23, how can Satan cast out Satan; it is implied not that a totality casts out a totality, but that one Devil casts out another.

Latin:

V. 26. καὶ εἰ ὁ Σατανᾶς ἀνέστη ἐφ' ἑαυτὸν) Ὁ Σατανᾶς videtur mihi hoc loco dici, & Luc. XI. 18. tota universitas malo- rum spirituum, quomodo ἄνθρωπος pro genere humano aut natura humana. Non enim solus Princeps spirituum, sed omnes impuri spiritus eo nomine censentur, ut hoc ipso loco commate 23. & Matth. XII. 26. apparet. Proclus ad se- cundum Platonis de republica: ἡ γὰρ ἄρθρου πρόσθεσις, ἢ τὸ καθ' ὑπεροχὴν δηλοῖ μόνον, ὡς ὅταν λέγομεν ὁ ποιητὴς εἶπεν, τῷ ἀκρο- τάτῳ τοῦτο ἐξαίρετον ἀπονέμοντες, ἢ τὸ ὅλον πλῆθος, ὡς ὅταν λέγωμεν, ὁ ἄνθρωπός ἐστι λογικὸς, ἀντὶ τοῦ παντὸς τὸ ἄρθρον προσάπτοντες. Ἀνέστη cum ἐπὶ locutio est Hellenistarum ex Hebraismo, quo hostilis conatus indicatur קום על ut Ps. III. 3. & alibi passim.

Non apparet quomodo tota universitas intelli- gi possit: num enim tota universitas contra sei- psam insurget? Et v. 23. quomodo potest Satanas Sa- tanam ejicere; non universitas universitatem, sed unus Diabolus alterum rejicere innuitur.

## 3:27
Verse 27. τότε τὴν οἰκίαν αὐτοῦ διαρπάσῃ) Διαρπάσῃ is also in Matthew. Nor does the Syrian read otherwise. And it savors more of Hebraism. For the sense is: for then at last will he be able to plunder the house.

Latin:

Vers. 27. τότε τὴν οἰκίαν αὐτοῦ διαρπάσῃ) Διαρπάσῃ est & apud Matthæum. Nec aliter legit Syrus. Et magis He- braismum sapit. Sensus quippe est: tunc enim demum do- mum prædari poterit.

## 3:29
Verse 29. οὐκ ἔχει ἄφεσιν εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα) That is, never. For the Jews thought that certain crimes were ended by time.

ἀλλ' ἔνοχός ἐστιν αἰωνίου ἁμαρτίας) We find κρίσιν for condemnation or punishment everywhere in these books. But since ancient codices, besides the old Latin interpreter, have ἁμαρτίας, it is more probable that it was so written by Mark: and that κρίσιν was an interpretation of the Hebraism, by which sin is taken for the punishment of sin. The sense is: He is not only punished here by hardening, often also by visible punishments, which happened to the Jews, but also after this life by eternal punishments. He said more, he kept silent about what was less. Matthew had expressed both, to whom see what has been said.

Latin:

Vers. 29. οὐκ ἔχει ἄφεσιν εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα) Id est nunquam. Nam quædam crimina Judæi putabant tempore finiri.

ἀλλ' ἔνοχός ἐστιν αἰωνίου ἁμαρτίας) Κρίσιν pro condemna- tione aut supplicio passim in his libris reperimus. Sed cum præter veterem Latinum interpretem codices antiqui habe- ant ἁμαρτίας, probabilius est ita scriptum a Marco: Κρίσιν antem fuisse interpretamentum Hebraismi, quo peccatum sumitur pro pœna peccati. Sensus est: Non tantum hic punitur induratione, sæpe & pœnis aspectabilibus, quod Iudæis contigit, sed & post hanc vitam suppliciis æternis. Plus dixit, quod minus erat tacuit. Matthæus utrumque expresserat, ad quem quæ dicta sunt vide.

## 3:30
Verse 30. ὅτι ἔλεγον πνεῦμα ἀκάθαρτον ἔχει) Christ used this threat because he saw that they recognized within themselves a divine power, but out of envy and hatred were inventing calumnies to turn away the people: and thus to ascribe to the devil what was of God.

PART V. Admonition concerning relatives.

Latin:

Vers. 30. ὅτι ἔλεγον πνεῦμα ἀκάθαρτον ἔχει) Hæc commi- natione usus est Christus, quia videbat illos agnoscere in- tra se vim divinam, sed invidia & odio comminisci calu- mnias, ut plebem averterent: atque ita quod Dei erat, diabolo ascribere.

PARS V. De consanguineis commonefactio.

## 3:31
Verse 31. ἀδελφοὶ) Relatives, as in Gen. XIV. 14, ch. XXVII. 32, 2 Chron. XXXVI. 10.

Latin:

Vers. 31. ἀδελφοὶ) Cognati, ut Genes. XIV. 14. c. XXVII. 32. 2. Par. XXXVI. 10.

## 3:32
Vers. 32. ἔξω ζητῦσι σὲ) I agree with those who think the history begun in verse 2 is continued, but interrupted because of the conversations which Christ had at that time with those who had come from Jerusalem. For Luke says that when they had approached to enter the house, they could not because of the crowd standing in the way: which certainly coheres with those former things.

Latin:

Vers. 32. ἔξω ζητῦσι σὲ) Assentior putantibus continuari historiam cœptam commate 2. sed interruptam ob sermo- nes, quos sub id tempus Christus habuit cum iis qui Hiero- solymis venerant. Nam Lucas ait cum accessissent introire in domum, non potuisse ob urbam obstantem: quod cum illis prioribus certe cohæret.

## 3:34
Vers. 34. Τὺς περὶ ἀυτὸν καθημένυς) It is credible that some were sitting nearby: the rest were standing or sitting in the windows, as in Acts XX. 9.

Lud. de Dieu understands not those sitting around him, but those who were around him or with him, i.e., his relatives: which sense seems to be confirmed by a comparison of v. 21 and c. IV. 10, where the notes of Beza are to be compared. Concerning this very passage, Lud. de Dieu has this: There is no doubt that his disciples are understood, by a phrase most customary to the Greeks, among whom οἱ περὶ τινὰ are those who are addicted to someone and follow him. Whence I am also easily led not to construe τὺς περὶ ἀυτὸν in this passage with καθημένυς, but to take it absolutely for his disciples, in this sense: And when he had looked around at his disciples sitting in a circle. So he.

Latin:

Vers. 34. Τὺς περὶ ἀυτὸν καθημένυς) Credibile est proxi- mos aliquot sedisse: stetisse cæteros aut sedisse in fenestris, ut Act. XX. 9.

Lud. de Dieu non circa ipsum sedentes, sed eos, qui circa ipsum, vel cum eo fuere intelligit, h. e. cognatos ipsius: qui sensus confirmari videtur è collatione v. 21. & c. IV. 10. ubi conferendæ notæ Bezæ. De ipso loco Lud. de Dieu hic ita habet: Dubium non est, quin discipulis ejus intelligantur, phrasi Græcis usi- tatissima, apud quos οἱ περὶ τινὰ sunt qui alicui sunt addicti, eumque sectantur. Unde & facile adducor, ut hoc quoque loco τὺς περὶ ἀυτὸν non construam cum καθημένυς, sed absolute sumam pro discipulis e- jus, hoc sensu, Et quum circumspexisset in circui- tu suos discipulos sedentes. Hæc ille.

## 4:1 Argument
CHAPTER IV. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

Jesus teaches again from the boat, proposing and explaining parables about the seed and the fourfold field: and about the lit candle not to be hidden, and about retaliation in retribution: and he declares that to him who has it shall be given, with the parable of the earth germinating ἀυτομάτως, and the grain of mustard seed: and crossing the sea that evening, he calms the storm that had arisen, with the terror and admiration of all.

There are two parts: I. Christ's parabolic instruction from the boat, to v. 34. II. The miraculous calming of the storm of the sea, to v. 41.

PART I. Christ's parabolic instruction from the boat.

Latin:

CAPUT IV. ARGUMENTUM ET PAR- TITIO.

Iesus denuo è navi docet, parabolas de semine & agro quadruplici proponens, & expo- nens: & de candela accensa non occultan- da, ac de talione in retributione: & quod habenti dandum sit, declarat simili de ter- ra ἀυτομάτως germinante, & grano sina- pis: ac mare trajiciens illa vespera tempe- statem exortam compescit cum terrore & admiratione omnium.

Partes sunt duæ: I. Christi è navi parabolica in- formatio, ad v. 34. II. Tempestatis maris miracu- losa sedatio, ad v. 41.

PARS I. Christi è navi parabolica informatio.

## 4:2
Vers. 2. καὶ ἔλεγεν ἀυτοῖς ἐν τῇ διδαχῇ ἀυτῦ) The same kind of speaking is below XII. 38, nor does it occur outside of Mark. The sense seems to me to be that while he was discussing many other things, he also said this among the rest. The principal thing that Christ was teaching were the precepts themselves, which are also properly called by the name of διδαχῆς. He inculcated these to the people on every occasion: he then added for the sake of increase τὰ παραβολικῶς: and free rebukes.

Beza's interpretation is simpler. I accept διδαχὴν for the action of the verb διδάσκειν, so that it is the same as if Mark had said, ἐν τῷ διδάσκειν, while teaching. Nor can it be proven that Grotius says the precepts were the principal thing in the doctrine of Christ: for the better parts are owed to τῷ ἐυαγγελίῳ, for the sake of announcing which Christ had come, Mark I. 15.

Latin:

Vers. 2. καὶ ἔλεγεν ἀυτοῖς ἐν τῇ διδαχῇ ἀυτῦ) Idem genus loquendi est infra XII. 38. neque extra Marcum occurrit. Sensus mihi esse videtur cum alia multa differeret, tum hoc quoque dixit inter cætera. Præcipuum quod Christus do- cebat erant ipsa præcepta, quæ & proprie διδαχῆς nomine appellantur. Hæc omni occasione populo inculcabat: addebat deinde auctari causa τὰ παραβολικῶς: & liberas re- prehensiones.

Simplicior est Bezæ interpretatio. Accipio δι- δαχὴν pro actione verbi διδάσκειν, ut perinde sit, ac si dixisset Marcus, ἐν τῷ διδάσκειν inter docendum. Neque probari potest, quod præcepta Grotius præ- cipuum fuisse dicit in doctrina Christi: nam potio- res partes debentur τῷ ἐυαγγελίῳ, cujus annun- ciandi causa venerat Christus Marc. I. 15.

## 4:7
Vers. 7. καὶ συνέπνιξαν ἀυτὸ καὶ καρπὸν ἐκ ἔδωκε) It was not necessary for Καρπὸν ἐκ ἔδωκε to be said about the former seeds. For how could they yield fruit, either consumed by birds or dried up by the heat of the sun? But it is said about this seed not without cause: because the first growths gave hope of a good crop.

Latin:

Vers. 7. καὶ συνέπνιξαν ἀυτὸ καὶ καρπὸν ἐκ ἔδωκε) Καρπὸν ἐκ ἔδωκε de prioribus seminibus nihil necesse erat dici. Nam quomodo fructum ederent, aut ab avibus absumta, aut æstu Solis arefacta? sed de hoc semine non sine causa id dicitur: quia primi auctus spem faciebant bonæ fru- gis.

## 4:8
Vers. 8. ἐδίδυ καρπὸν ἀναβαίνοντα καὶ ἀυξάνοντα) Mark prudently separated the outcome of the fourth seed from the event of the three former ones. For the first did not rise, being consumed by birds: the second did rise, but did not grow, exhausted by the heat: the third both rose and grew, but did not yield fruit, oppressed by the crop of thorns that had grown up at the same time.

ἓν τριάκοντα, κᾲ ἓν ἑξήκοντα κᾲ ἓν ἑκατὸν) He placed ἓν as a distributive among the Hebrews, where the interpreter of Matthew uses the more Greek ὃ μὲν & ὃ δὲ. And thus it appears the ancient interpreters read it. Wherefore it should be read thus rather than ἓν. See what I have said below at verse 20.

Latin:

Vers. 8. ἐδίδυ καρπὸν ἀναβαίνοντα καὶ ἀυξάνοντα) Provi- de Marcus feminis quarti evenium à trium priorum eventu separavit. Nam primum ἐκ ἀνέβαινε ab avibus absumtum: alterum ἀνέβαινε μὲν, ἀλλ᾽ ἐκ ἠυξάνετο æstu exhaustum: ter- tium καὶ ἀνέβαινε καὶ ἠυξάνετο, καρπὸν δὲ ἐκ ἔδωκεν, oppres- sum ab ea quæ simul excreverat sentium segete.

ἓν τριάκοντα, κᾲ ἓν ἑξήκοντα κᾲ ἓν ἑκατὸν) ἓν distributivum apud Hebræos posuit, ubi Matthæi interpres magis Græce ὃ μὲν & ὃ δὲ. Atque ita apparet legisse veteres interpretes. Quare ita potius legendum quam ἓν. Vide quæ infra ad comma 20.

## 4:10
Vers. 10. καταμόνας) Apart from the crowd. Luke also uses it in chapter IX. 18, and Alexis in the comedy The Parasite.

οἱ περὶ αὐτὸν σὺν τοῖς δώδεκα) It could have seemed ambiguous, because Matthew had written that Christ explained these things to the disciples separately. For the disciples are sometimes called the twelve alone, sometimes also others, not indeed so familiarly, but yet following Christ quite assiduously, such as those seventy. Mark resolves the ambiguity when he says that Christ explained these things, not to the twelve alone, but also to others περὶ αὐτὸν. Now the ancients explained this περὶ αὐτὸν as μαθηταὶ αὐτῷ in a broader sense, which then penetrated into the text of certain codices. I judge that the little words σὺν τοῖς, which the Latin interpreter omitted, should be retained: for both the Greeks and the Syrian acknowledge them, as do the best codices.

Latin:

Vers. 10. καταμόνας) Seorsim a turba. Utitur & Lucas cap. IX. 18. & Alexis comœdia Parasito.

οἱ περὶ αὐτὸν σὺν τοῖς δώδεκα) Ambiguum videri poterat, quod Matthæus scripserat Christum seorsim discipulis hæc explicasse. Nam discipuli interdum dicuntur duodecim soli, interdum & alii, non ita quidem familiariter, sed satis assidue tamen Christum sectantes, quales illi septuaginta. Marcus ambiguitatem solvit, cum dicit hæc explicasse Christum, non solis duodecim, sed & aliis περὶ αὐτὸν. Hoc autem περὶ αὐτὸν veteres explicarunt μαθηταὶ αὐτῷ la- xiore notione, quod deinde in textum quorundam codi- cum penetravit. Voculas σὺν τοῖς quas omisit Latinus in- terpres retinendas censeo : nam & Græci agnoscunt & Sy- rus: & optimi codices.

## 4:11
Vers. 11. ἐκείνοις δὲ τοῖς ἔξω) What Matthew had said to them, Mark beautifully explains as τοῖς ἔξω. The ancient Christians called all those who were strangers to the discipline of Christ τοὺς ἔξω (1 Cor. V. 12, 13; Col. IV. 5; 1 Thess. IV. 12), and Clement and others do so throughout. Mark therefore well designated by that name those who indeed heard Christ, but not with the intention of learning piety: similar to those Athenians who οἱ οὐδὲν ἕτερον εὐκαίρουν ἢ λέγειν τὶ καὶ ἀκούειν καινότερον (Acts XVII. 21).

ἐν παραβολαῖς τὰ πάντα γίνεται) All things, that is to say, not those which pertain to repentance, but those which pertain either to the secrets of the divine dispensation or to the outcome of predictions. For mention of τῶν μυστηρίων preceded. And ἐν παραβολαῖς is to be understood as ἐν μόναις παραβολαῖς without their clearer explanation. Γίνεται, which is general, here by reason of the sense is worth the same as 'are proposed'.

Latin:

Vers. 11. ἐκείνοις δὲ τοῖς ἔξω) Quod Matthæus dixerat illis, pulchre explicat Marcus τοῖς ἔξω. Christiani veteres τοὺς ἔξω vocabant omnes, qui a Christi disciplina erant extra- nei 1. Cor. V. 12. 13. Col. IV. 5. 1. Thess. IV. 12. & passim Clemens atque alii. Bene ergo Marcus eo nomine desi- gnavit eos qui audiebant quidem Christum, sed non discen- dæ pietatis animo: similes Atheniensibus illis οἱ οὐδὲν ἕτερον εὐκαίρουν ἢ λέγειν τὶ καὶ ἀκούειν καινότερον Act. XVII. 21.

ἐν παραβολαῖς τὰ πάντα γίνεται) Omnia scilicet, non quæ ad pœnitentiam, sed quæ aut ad arcana divinæ dispen- sationis aut ad eventum prædictionum pertinent. Præ- cessit enim mentio τῶν μυστηρίων. Et ἐν παραβολαῖς intelli- gendum ἐν μόναις παραβολαῖς sine earum apertiori expli- catione. Γίνεται quod generale est, ex sensus ratione hic idem valet quod proponuntur.

## 4:12
V. 12. ἵνα βλέποντες βλέπωσι) Mark expressed not the very words of the Prophets, but the sense of the commination: namely, that it would come to pass that those who had not wanted to see while seeing, to hear while hearing, and to understand, would afterwards be able to read neither to see nor to hear those things which pertained to their own conversion. See what I have said regarding Matthew.

Latin:

V. 12. ἵνα βλέποντες βλέπωσι) Non verba ipsa Prophetarum, sed sensum comminationis expressit Marcus : futurum scil. ut qui videntes videre, audientes audire, & intelligere noluerant, postea nec videre nec audire legere possent ea, quæ ad ipsorum conversionem pertinebant. Vide quæ ad Matthæum diximus.

## 4:14
Vers. 14. ὁ σπείρων τὸν λόγον σπείρει) That sower of whom I had spoken in the little fable signifies the Teacher of the saving word.

Latin:

Vers. 14. ὁ σπείρων τὸν λόγον σπείρει) Is sator de quo dixe- ram in fabella, significat Doctorem salutaris verbi.

## 4:15
Vers. 15. ὅπου) Where, for 'in whom'. Thus the Latins often use unde for 'from whom', as Cicero: 'With him dead, there would be no one from whom I might learn'.

Latin:

Vers. 15. ὅπου) Ubi pro in quibus. Sic unde pro a quo La- tini sæpe usurpant, ut Cicero, Illo exstincto fore unde disce- rem neminem.

## 4:18
Vers. 18. ὗτοι εἰσιν οἱ τὸν λόγον ἀκούοντες) The repetition of the words ὗτοι εἰσι is not foreign to Hebraism: which gave cause for its unusual changes, and that in more than one way: which shows the truth of this reading.

Latin:

Vers. 18. ὗτοι εἰσιν οἱ τὸν λόγον ἀκούοντες) Repetitio vocum ὗτοι εἰσι non est aliena ab Hebraismo: quod ejus insolitis mutandi causam dedit, idque non uno modo: quod hu- jus lectionis veritatem ostendit.

## 4:19
Vers. 19, καὶ αἱ περὶ τὰ λοιπὰ ἐπιθυμίαι) That is, the pleasures of the body, which Matthew had not expressed because they are accustomed to accompany riches. However, τὰ λοιπὰ seems to be said euphemistically: as when we say things that cannot be named honestly.

εἰσπορευόμεναι) That is, overgrowing: Luke in turn said that they themselves were ὑπὸ μεριμνῶν καὶ πλούτου καὶ ἡδονῶν τοῦ βίου πορευομένους.

ἓν τριάκοντα, κᾲ ἓν ἑξήκοντα κᾲ ἓν ἑκατὸν) Here it appears that the Syrian read ἐν. Nor is there any doubt that many copyists preferred that, in order to avoid τὸ σολοικοφανές. It is more credible, however, that it was written thus as above in verse 8. For there is a similar repetition in Matthew. Nor does the transition into another gender move me. For in the explanation of these παραβολαῖς, one often returns in the apodosis through a figure to that which was placed in the comparison. But the discourse begun about the earth often ends in the seed: because, namely, in this kind of teaching, the whole matter is looked at, not individual particles.

Latin:

Vers. 19, καὶ αἱ περὶ τὰ λοιπὰ ἐπιθυμίαι) Id est volupta- tes corporis, quas Matthæus non expresserat, quia divitias comitari solent. Videtur autem σεμνῶς dictum τὰ λοιπὰ : ut cum dicimus, quæ honeste nominari nequeunt.

εἰσπορευόμεναι) Id est supercrescentes: Lucas vicissim ipsos dixit ὑπὸ μεριμνῶν καὶ πλούτου καὶ ἡδονῶν τοῦ βίου πορευομέ- νους.

ἓν τριάκοντα, κᾲ ἓν ἑξήκοντα κᾲ ἓν ἑκατὸν) Hic Syrum ἐν legis- se apparet. Neque dubium quin multi exscriptores id prætulerint, ut vitarent τὸ σολοικοφανές. Credibilius tamen est ita scriptum fuisse ut supra commate 8. Nam & in Mat- thæo est similis repetitio. Neque movet me transitio in a- liud genus. Nam in explanatione harum παραβολῶν sæ- pe ἐν ἀποδόσει reditur per figuram ad id quod in comparatio- ne erat positum. Sed & de terra cœptus sermo sæpe in se- men definit: quia scilicet in hoc docendi genere res tota inspicitur, non particulæ singulæ.

## 4:21
Vers. 21. And he said to them, 'Is the lamp...' The following statements might appear not so coherent with the preceding ones, nor even among themselves, as if gathered into one place by Mark, lest he interrupt the series of history too often with the recitation of such sayings. But since these are interspersed with two comparisons, which are also coherent in Matthew, and that final sentence, 'to him who has it will be given,' is also recited in Matthew around the narration of this time, I entirely believe that these things cohere with the preceding ones: nor does it stand in the way that the lamp and the measure are mentioned elsewhere in Matthew in a different sense. For those proverbs, worn by common usage, are accustomed to be adapted to different senses as the occasion arises, which nevertheless come under the same generality of the saying: which is often to be found both among the Greeks and Latins, and also in this history of ours. Indeed, Luke also placed this very saying about the lamp twice: and here he follows Mark, with a few things omitted.

ἔρχεται) I do not doubt that this is the true reading, even by the argument which I often use, that its diverse interpretations have crept into the text. For some codices have καίεται, others ἅπτεται: of which the latter is read by the Arab, يوقد. But the Syrian, being older than that, reads ἔρχεται, as does the Latin. Moreover, ἔρχεσθαι is to be brought into a room; which, since it seemed more obscure, provided an occasion for changing it.

ἢ ὑπὸ τὴν κλίνην) Luke also placed this in chapter VIII. 16. Popularity shines through everywhere in Christ's sayings. Because a bushel and a bed have a cavity under which a lamp could be hidden, he therefore named these.

ἀχ᾽ ἵνα ἐπὶ τὴν λυχνίαν ἐπιτεθῇ) This connection seems to me to be that the same thing is shown by another similitude as in the previous one, that saving doctrine is not given to us for this purpose, that it should lie torpid and sterile, but that it should shine in us through deeds consistent with piety. What was 'seed' above, here is 'lamp': what was 'to bear fruit' above, here is 'to be placed upon a lampstand.' See Matt. V. 16. 2 Pet. I. 12.
