The series of the sequence is more elegant in Chemnitz: that since the Word of God is so fruitful if it is rightly heard, both teachers and hearers are now warned that they should properly perform their duty, and treat and hear the Word of God as is fitting: the former indeed by not hiding the lamp of the Word under a bushel; the latter truly by devoutly hearing the Word: 'He who has ears to hear, let him hear.' See Harm. Evang. chap. LXI.

Latin:

Vers. 21. κᾲ ἔλεγεν αὐτοῖς, μήτι ὁ λύχνος) Possent videri quæ sequuntur ἀποφάσεις non tam cohærentes cum superiori- bus, atque etiam inter se, quam in unum locum a Marco congestæ, ne sæpius seriem historiæ ejusmodi dictorum re- citatione interrumperet. Sed cum hæc interferantur duabus comparationibus, quæ & apud Matthæum cohærent, & po- strema illa sententia, habenti dabitur, etiam apud Matthæum recitetur circa hujus temporis narrationem, omnino arbi- tror ista cum superioribus cohærere: neque obstat quod de lychno, & de remensione alibi apud Matthæum alio sensu sit mentio. Nam proverbia ista usu vulgi trita solent pro re nata sensibus diversis, qui tamen sub eandem dicti gene- ralitatem veniant, aptari: quod tum apud Græcos, Lati- nosque, tum & in hac nostra historia sæpe est reperire. Quin & Lucas hanc ipsam de Lychno sententiam bis posuit : Et hic Marcum sequitur, paucis omissis.

ἔρχεται) Non dubito quin vera hæc sit lectio vel eo argu- mento, quo sæpe utor, quod diversa ejus interpretamenta in textum irrepserunt. Alii enim Codices habent καίεται, alii ἅπτεται: quorum alterum legit Arabs يوقد. At Syrus eo antiquior legit ἔρχεται, ut & Latinus. Est autem ἔρχεσθαι inferri in conclave; quod cum obscurius videretur, mutandi occasionem præbuit.

ἢ ὑπὸ τὴν κλίνην) Hoc & Lucas posuit cap IIX. 16. Ma- gna ubique relucet in Christi dictis popularitas. Quia mo- dius & lectus cavitatem habent, sub qua condi lucerna pos- set, ideo ista nominavit.

ἀχ᾽ ἵνα ἐπὶ τὴν λυχνίαν ἐπιτεθῇ) Connexio hæc mihi esse videtur, quod alia similitudine idem quod superiore o- stenditur, non in hoc dari nobis salutarem doctrinam, ut sterilis torpeat, sed ut luceat in nobis per facta pietati con- sentanea. Quod supra semen, hic est lychnus: quod su- pra fructum ferre, hic super candelabrum ponere. Vide Matth. V. 16. 2. Petr. 11. 12.

Concinnior est τ᾿ ἀκολουθείας οἷρμος apud Che- mnitium: quod quam tam frugiferum sit Verbum Dei, si recte audiatur, moneantur nunc tum Docto- res, tum auditores, ut suo probe fungantur munere, ac Verbum Dei ut par est, tractent, atque audiant: illi quidem lucernam Verbi non sub modio occultando; hi vero Verbum devote audiendo: Qui aures habet ad audiendum audiat. Vid. Harm. Evang. cap. LXI.

## 4:22
Vers. 22. 'For there is nothing hidden, which shall not be manifested.' A universal expression is to be restricted from common sense to good and honest things. 'For everyone who does evil hates the light and does not come to the light, lest his works should be reproved. But he who does the truth comes to the light, that his works may be manifested,' John III. 20, 21. In this place, that sentence signifies that those things which are good are not taught even secretly or privately, except that they may bring forth the fruit of good works, and thus show themselves openly. Therefore, φανερωθῇ is placed for διὰ φανερωθῆναι, which is most evidently explained in the following member by ἵνα.

Grotius wishes this to be the meaning: that those things which are good are not taught even secretly or privately, except that they may bring forth the fruit of good works, and thus show themselves openly. But here reference is made rather to the manner of Christ's teaching: to which it could be objected that he himself delivered mysteries less clearly, when he warned that a lamp should not be hidden: so that by way of anticipation he might intimate that there is nothing hidden in his doctrine which is not to be manifested: since he himself also then explained to his disciples the things which were requested to be declared, and subsequently all things were to be delivered more explicitly once the Spirit of truth, the Teacher, had been sent.

ἐδὲ ἐγένετο ἀπόκρυφον) Supply τι from the previous member. And ἐγένετο here is what ἐστί is there. It is the custom of the Hebrews to repeat the same statement with changed words, which occurs very often in the Gnomology of Solomon. See a similar abundance of speech below in verse 30.

ἀλλ' ἵνα) Except that. Thus Matt. XX. 23 and below X. 40, 'it is not mine to give, but to those for whom it has been prepared'; Paul 2 Cor. II. 5, 'he has not grieved me, but in part.' Note here ch. IX. 8, 'they saw no one, but Jesus only.'

Latin:

Vers. 22. ὃ γάρ ἐστί τι κρυπτὸν, ὃ ἐὰν μὴ φανερωθῇ) Univer- salis locutio ex sensu communi restringenda est ad res pro- bas & honestas. Πᾶς γὰρ ὁ φαῦλα πράσσων μισεῖ τὸ φῶς καὶ ὐκ ἔρχεται πρὸς τὸ φῶς ἵνα μὴ ἐλεγχθῇ τὰ ἔργα αὐτοῦ. Ὁ δὲ ποιῶν τὴν ἀλήθειαν ἔρχεται πρὸς τὸ φῶς ἵνα φανερωθῇ αὐτοῦ τὰ ἔργα, Joh. III. 20. 21. Hoc loco ea sententia significat non doceri etiam clam aut privatim ea quæ bona sunt, nisi ut bonorum operum fructum proferant, atque ita se palam ostendant. Est ergo φανερωθῇ positum pro διη φανερωθῆ- ναι, quod in sequenti membro per ἵνα evidentissime expli- catur.

Grotius hanc vult esse sententiam: non doceri etiam clam aut privatim ea quæ bona sunt, nisi ut bonorum operum fructum proferant, atque ita se pa- lam ostendant. Sed respicitur hic potius ad modum docendi Christi: cui opponi poterat, quod minus perspicue ipse tradiderit mysteria, quum mone- ret lucernam abscondendam non esse: ut κατ' αἰ- θυποφορὰν innuat, nihil esse occultum in doctrina sua, quod non manifestandum sit: siquidem & tum ipse discipulis suis explicavit, quæ declarari pete- bant, & deinceps omnia explicatius misso spiritu veritatis Doctore tradenda erant.

ἐδὲ ἐγένετο ἀπόκρυφον) Supple τι ex membro superiore. Et ἐγένετο hic est quod ibi ἐστί. Mos Hebræorum est ean- dem ἀπόφασιν verbis mutatis repetere, quod in Gnomolo- gico Solomonis sæpissime occurrit. Vide similem dicendi copiam infra commate 30.

ἀλλ' ἵνα) Nisi ut. Ita Matth. XX. 23. & infra X. 40. ἐκ ἔστιν ἐμὸν δῦναι ἀλλ' οἷς ἡτοίμασται; Paulus 2. Corinth. II. 5. ὐκ ἐμὲ λελύπηκεν ἀλλ' ἀπὸ μέρες Nostet hic c. IX. 8. ἐδένα ἶ- δον ἀλλὰ τ' Ἰησοῦν μόνον.

## 4:23
Vers. 23. 'If anyone has ears to hear, let him hear.' See Matt. XI. 15. Understanding has been given to us by God especially so that we may apply it to teachings pertaining to piety.

Latin:

Vers. 23. εἴτις ἔχει ὦτα ἀκύειν ἀκυέτω) Vide Matth. XI. 15. Intellectus nobis a Deo potissimum datus est, ut eum in- tendamus documentis ad pietatem pertinentibus.

## 4:24
Vers. 24. 'And he said to them.' A new admonition, but one whose occasion flowed from the preceding. Christ had said that he did not open the mysteries of the kingdom to those who neglected the exhortations to repentance. He now reduces this act of his to a certain general rule. That sentence, 'to him who has it will be given,' in Matthew XIII. v. 12, shows this to be the meaning of what follows.

βλέπετε τί ἀκέετε) Consider again and again what and of what kind that is which you hear, so that you may apply your mind according to the magnitude of the matter. Luke said, 'How you hear.'

Latin:

Vers. 24. καὶ ἔλεγεν αὐτοῖς) Nova admonitio, sed cujus ex superioribus occasio manavit. Dixerat Christus se ar- cana regni non aperire his qui pœnitentiæ hortamenta ne- gligerent. Hoc factum suum nunc ad regulam quandam generalem revocat. Hunc esse sequentium sensum osten- dit sententia illa, habenti dabitur, apud Matthæum XIII. v. 12.

βλέπετε τί ἀκέετε) Etiam atque etiam considerate quid & quale sit quod auditis, ut pro rei magnitudine intendatis animum. Πῶς ἀκέετε dixit Lucas.

## 4:25
Ver. 25. ἐν ᾧ μέτρῳ μετρεῖτε μετρηθήσεται ὑμῖν, καὶ προς τεθήσεται ὑμῖν τοῖς ἀκέυσιν) The truth of this reading is defended by ancient codices and old Metaphrasts, from whose consensus, as I have often warned, one must not rashly depart. But what the use of this general proverb is here, those final words show, namely the same as that of the following sentence, to him who has it shall be given. Just as men receive the first and most necessary admonitions of piety with a grateful and faithful mind, so divine generosity pours forth more and more toward them. For to those hearing how one ought to hear, further benefits accrue, Cyprian in his letter to Donatus: 'For there is no measure or limit in the receiving of the heavenly gift, as is the custom with earthly benefits: the spirit flowing forth abundantly is pressed by no boundaries, nor is it restrained by confining walls within certain spaces of limits: it flows continuously, it overflows abundantly, if only our breast thirsts and lies open: as much as we bring of a capable faith to that place, so much of the cleansing grace do we draw.' For diverse reading see Beza. The blessed Chemnitz has excellently delivered the sense and coherence of the text in Harm. chap. LXI. col. 853. Attend diligently to what God in turn requires of you, lest you yourselves be wanting to your own salvation. Therefore, hearing the word, attend diligently, let nothing fly past your ears rashly: but receive each thing diligently, and having received it, ruminate with assiduous meditation, like clean animals, Lev. XI. 3, and direct it to this end, that they may bring forth worthy fruits in you. The parabolic reason is added: 'For with what measure you measure, it shall be measured to you again': that is, with whatever measure of talent, diligence, and industry you have used in receiving this divine benefit, with that same measure God will remeasure to you the fruits of hearing and the gifts of his Holy Spirit. Open therefore your mouths and your ears, and the Lord will fill them, Ps. LXXXI. verse 11. But if you bring minds dilated with the desire for heavenly goods, and faithfully guard those things which have been deposited with you through the hearing of the word, God will subsequently add more, which could aid your eternal salvation. For it shall be added to you who hear. For the heavenly Father is not so ungentle that he would not compensate his faithful work with great profit. For he is not so ungentle that he would not compensate his faithful work with great profit.

Latin:

Vers. 25. ἐν ᾧ μέτρῳ μετρεῖτε μετρηθήσεται ὑμῖν, καὶ προς τεθήσεται ὑμῖν τοῖς ἀκέυσιν) Lectionis hujus veritatem defendunt antiqui codices & veteres Metaphrastæ, à quo- rum consensu, ut sæpe monui, non est temere receden- dum. Generalis autem proverbii quis hic sit usus, verba illa postrema ostendunt, nimirum idem qui sequentis sententiæ, habenti dabitur. Prout homines prima & maxime neceffaria pietatis monita grato & fideli animo accipiunt, ita se in eos magis magisque effundit divina largitas. Audientibus e- nim quomodo audire oportet beneficia ulteriora contin- gunt, Cyprianus epistola ad Donatum: Non enim qui bene- ficiorum terrestrium mos in capessendo munere cælesti mensura ulla vel modus est: profluens largiter spiritus nullis finibus pre- mitur, nec coërcentibus claustris intra certa metarum spatia fre- natur: manat jugiter, exuberat affluenter, nostrum tantum sitiat pectus & pateat: quantum illuc fidei capacis afferimus, tantum gratiæ mundantis haurimus. De lectione diversa vid. Beza. Sensum & co- hærentiam textus eximie tradidit B. Chemnitius Harm. cap. LXI. col. 853. Diligenter attendite, quid Deus vicissim à vobis requirat, ne vestræ saluti ipsi defitis. Idcirco verbum audientes, diligenter atten- dite, nihil aures vestras temere prætervolet: sed singu- la diligenter excipite, excepta assidua meditatione, in- star mundorum animalium, Lev. XI. 3. ruminate, at- que eo dirigite, ut dignos in vobis fructus afferant. Ratio additur parabolica: Quæ enim mensura meti- mini, eadem fiet vobis admensio: id est, qua inge- nii, diligentiæ & industriæ mensura in recipiendo hoc divino beneficio usi fueritis, eadem mensura Deus vobis fructus auditus & dona sancti sui Spiri- tus remetietur. Aperite ergo ora & aures vestras, & Dominus implebit illa, Psal. LXXXI. vers. 11. Quod si animos cælestium bonorum desiderio dilata- tos attuleritis, & ea quæ per auditum verbi apud vos deposita fuerint, fideliter custodieritis, subinde Deus plura superaddet, quæ æternam vestram salu- tem juvare poterant. Nam adjicietur vobis, qui auditis. Non enim adeo immitis est cælestis Pater, quin magno cum lucro piis fidelem suam operam com- penset.

## 4:26
Vers. 26. ὡς ἐὰν ἄνθρωπος βάλῃ τ̃ σπόρον ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς] This παραβολὴ, omitted by others, since it does not have its explanation here, ought to be explained from a similar comparison which is in Matt. XIII. 14. Wherefore the sower here is not just any herald of the truth, but the first sower of it himself, Christ, Matt. XIII. 37. For he who is said to have sown is also said to be about to send reapers into the field below in v. 29. That person, however, is undoubtedly Christ, Matt. XIII. 39, 40, 41.

Latin:

Vers. 26. ὡς ἐὰν ἄνθρωπος βάλῃ τ̃ σπόρον ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς] Hæc παραβολὴ aliis omissa, cum suam hic explicationem non habeat, explicari debet ex simili comparatione quæ est a- pud Matth. XIII. 14. Quare sator non est hic quivis præco veritatis, sed ipse primus ejus sator Christus Matth. XIII. 37. Nam & hic qui sevit dicitur missurus in agrum messores in- fra v. 29. Is autem haud dubie est Christus Matth. XIII, 39. 40. 41.

## 4:27
Vers. 27. καὶ καθεύδῃ καὶ ἐγείρηται νύκτα καὶ ἡμέραν] A manner of speaking indicating the security of the farmer. However, the particles of the similitude are not to be pressed beyond that which is intended. The sense seems clear to me: that Christ, from the time the seed was sown until the time of harvest, would not be visibly present in the field.

Latin:

Vers. 27. καὶ καθεύδῃ καὶ ἐγείρηται νύκτα καὶ ἡμέραν] lo- quendi genus securitatem agricolæ indicans. Non sunt au- tem particulæ similitudinis præmendæ ultra id quod inten- ditur. Sensus mihi videtur perspicuus: Christum à facta se- mente ad messis tempus agro aspectabiliter non adfuturum

## 4:28
Vers. 28. ἀυτομάτη γὰρ ἡ γῆ] Of its own accord: for thus the Latins are also accustomed to speak about the earth. Theophylact thinks that τὸ ἐφ' ἡμῖν is indicated here in passing. Καρποφορεῖ πρῶτον χόρτον] A catachresis: for properly καρποφορεῖν is what he will say next, to bring forth fruit. That which first springs up the Latins also call grass, whence the proverb has arisen, 'To be in the grass,' and 'the harvest is in the grass.'

Latin:

Vers. 28. ἀυτομάτη γὰρ ἡ γῆ] Sponte sua: nam ita Latini etiam de terra solent loqui. Putat Theophylactus obiter hic indicari τὸ ἐφ' ἡμῖν. Καρποφορεῖ πρῶτον χόρτον] κατάχρησις: nam proprie καρ- ποφορεῖν est quod jam dicet, frugem proferre. Quod pri- mum enascitur herbam etiam vocant Latini, unde prover- bium natum est, In herbis esse, & messis in herba est.

## 4:29
Vers. 29. ἀποστέλλει τὸ δρέπανον] The Latins say 'to put in the sickle.'

Latin:

Vers. 29. ἀποστέλλει τὸ δρέπανον] Immittere falcem dicunt Latini.

## 4:30
Vers. 30. Τίνι ὁμοιώσωμεν τὴν βασιλείαν τῦ Θεῦ, ἢ ἐν τίνι παραβολῇ παραβάλωμεν ἀυτὴν] An imitation of the words of Isa. XL. 18.

Latin:

Vers. 30. Τίνι ὁμοιώσωμεν τὴν βασιλείαν τῦ Θεῦ, ἢ ἐν τίνι παραβολῇ παραβάλωμεν ἀυτὴν] Imitatio verborum Esa. XL. 18.

## 4:33
Vers. 33. καθὼς ἐδύναντο ἀκούειν] That is, as they were worthy to hear. See above at clause 11. Such is almost that of Demosthenes δυνάμεσθ' ἀντιλοιδορηθῆναι, that is, ἄξιόν ὄν. Thus also elsewhere τὸ πρέπον is explained by the verb δύνασθαι, as Matt. IX. 15, and here above chap. II. 9, μὴ δύνανται οἱ υἱοὶ τῦ νυμφῶν@ πενθεῖν. Concerning the sense, see what is in Matthew.

Latin:

Vers. 33. καθὼς ἐδύναντο ἀκούειν] Id est ut digni erant au- dire. Vide supra commate 11. Tale est ferme illud De- mosthenis δυνάμεσθ' ἀντιλοιδορηθῆναι, id est ἄξιόν ὄν. Sic & alibi τὸ πρέπον per verbum δύνασθαι explicatur, ut Matth. IX. 15. & hic supra cap. II. 9. μὴ δύνανται οἱ υἱοὶ τῦ νυμφῶν@ πενθεῖν. De sensu vide quæ apud Matthæum.

## 4:34
Vers. 34. ἐκ ἐλάλει ἀυτοῖς] Namely, the mysteries of the kingdom. For thus the breadth of the words must be restricted according to the meaning: as we have sometimes warned. ἐπίλυε] A similar manner of speaking to one who solves the enigmas of laws; in Chaldean משרא קטרין, λύων συνδεσμὸς, Dan. V. 12. 2 Pet. I. 29, ὅτι πᾶσα προφητεία γραφῆς ἰδίας ἐπιλύσεως ὐ γί- νεται: that is, ἰδίας ἑρμηνείας, as Paul calls that gift in 1 Cor. XIV. 29. For prophets also are accustomed to be αἰ- νιγματώδεις: and therefore for a certain interpretation the same Spirit is required who inspired the prophets.

PART II. The miraculous calming of the sea storm.

Latin:

Vers. 34. ἐκ ἐλάλει ἀυτοῖς] Nempe arcana regni. Ita enim ex sententia vocum latitudo restringenda est: ut ali- quoties monuimus. ἐπίλυε] Simile loquendi genus qui legum ænigmata solvit: Chaldaice משרא קטרין λύων συνδεσμὸς Dan. V. 12. 2. Pet. I. 29. ὅτι πᾶσα προφητεία γραφῆς ἰδίας ἐπιλύσεως ὐ γί- νεται: id est ἰδίας ἑρμηνείας, quomodo donum illud appel- lat Paulus 1. Cor. XIV. 29. Nam & Prophetiz solent esse αἰ- νιγματώδεις: ideoque ad certam interpretationem requiri- tur idem Spiritus qui afflavit Prophetas.

PARS II. Miraculosa tempestatis maris sedatio.

## 4:35
Vers. 35. ἐν ἐκείνῃ τῇ ἡμέρᾳ] This does not show that these things were done on the day on which Christ had taught the preceding things: but ἐκείνῃ ἡμέρᾳ is simply 'on a certain day,' as also Matt. XIII. 1, XXII. 23. Luke says for it ἐν μιᾷ τῶν ἡμερῶν V. 7, so the Hebrews בעת ההיא:

Latin:

Vers. 35. ἐν ἐκείνῃ τῇ ἡμέρᾳ] Non ostendit hæc eo die gesta quo præcedentia Christus docuerat: sed ἐκείνῃ ἡμέρᾳ simpliciter est quadam die, ut & Matth. XIII. 1. XXII. 23. Lucas pro eo dicit ἐν μιᾷ τῶν ἡμερῶν V. 7. ita Hebræi בעת ההיא:

## 4:36
Vers. 36. παραλαμβάνουσιν] That is, they take away, as above IV. 5. ὡς ἦν ἐν τῷ πλοίῳ] An elegant expression: thus the Latins, 'as she was, disheveled in her hair.' However, this manner of speaking signifies nothing other than the continuation of that which was before. Thus Christ was in the ship so that he might teach as if from a platform: he remained in the ship so that he might be carried out into the deep out of the sight of the crowd standing on the shore. The laying down of the body does not seem to be treated here. μετ᾽ αὐτοῦ] They followed him sailing nearby. For those who were in those ships said what is mentioned below in clause 41. That sense of the words ἐν ἐκείνῃ ἡμέρᾳ can hardly be proven solidly by parallel passages or from the usage of the language. Although if these things were done on the same day as the preceding, the order in Matthew would be greatly disturbed, according to the Chemnitian Harmony chap. LXIII. For thus one would have to go back from c. XIII to c. VIII, and a notable anticipation would have to be established in Matthew. Everything, however, is in good order, according to our Harmony. Nor is it fitting to invent new interpretations of words, and to snatch away to widely separated times those things which are said to have been done on the same day, in a historical commemoration where the circumstance of time is specifically designated. For such little words are clear indicators of the order of the event and of time. Nor in Matt. XIII. 1 and XXII. 23 are these words taken indefinitely, but definitely, as they properly sound, concerning the same day. But the reason for the phrase ἐν μιᾷ τῶν ἡμέρων and the Hebrew is different, by which not precisely the same day is denoted. Verse 37. λαῖλαψ ἀνέμου] Just as the City of Padua: the river of the Rhine. For λαῖλαψ is a 'whirlwind of wind with rain,' as Hesychius says, with the interpreters of Homer agreeing. γεμίζεσθαι] Thus the ancient interpreters, so that you may recognize that βυθίζεσθαι is an interpretation. Verse 38. ἐπὶ τῇ πρύμνῃ] The place of the helmsman in the stern. The traveler Jonah was sleeping on the rowing benches. Jon. I. 5. Jonah is awakened to pray, Christ to save. Verse 39. πεφίμωσο] The imperative of the present tense demands the utmost speed. καὶ ἐγένετο γαλήνη μεγάλη] suddenly, whereas otherwise the sea is usually agitated for a long time after the winds have ceased. Verse 40. τί δειλοί ἐστε ὕτω; πῶς οὐκ ἔχετε πίστιν;] I think this is the true reading: why are you timid? Are you so lacking in confidence? Such is 'so you were not able to watch one hour with me?' The little word πῶς, however, in such locutions signifies nothing by itself, but adds force to the speech. Christ expresses the cause of the fear as 'little faith.' Verse 41. ἐφοβήθησαν φόβον μέγαν καὶ ἔλεγον πρὸς ἀλλήλους] The verb is placed impersonally. It is understood not as the disciples, but the οἱ ἄνθρωποι, which Matthew expressed. It concerns those who were sailing nearby, and who were not equally accustomed to the miracles of Christ. Τίς ἄρα] Of one wondering: as Servius notes on that line of Virgil: 'What a crowd!'

Latin:

Vers. 36. παραλαμβάνουσιν] Id est, avehunt, ut supra IV. 5. ὡς ἦν ἐν τῷ πλοίῳ] Elegans locutio: ita Latini, ut erat dis- jecta capillos. Nihil autem aliud hoc genus loquendi signi- ficat, quam continuationem ejus quod prius erat. Ita Chri- stus erat in nave ut doceret velut e suggesto: mansit in navi ut in altum aveheretur extra conspectum turbae stantis in litore. Depositura corporis non videtur hic agi. μετ᾽ αὐτοῦ] Proxime navigantem sequebantur. Nam qui in istis navibus erant dixerunt quod infra memoratur com- mare 41. Sensus ille vocum ἐν ἐκείνῃ ἡμέρᾳ locis parallelis vel ex usu linguae probari solide vix poterit. Quanquam si eadem die haec gesta forent, qua prae- cedentia, valde turbetur ordo apud Matthaeum, juxta Harmoniam Chemnitianam cap. LXIII. Sic enim a c. XIII. regrediendum ad c. IIX. & antici- patio insignis penes Matthaeum statuenda erit. O- mnia tamen recte sese habent, juxta nostram Har- moniam. Neq; sane convenit novas vocum inter- pretationes fingere, & quae eadem die in histori- ca commemoratione, qua circumstantia temporis specifice designatur, facta dicuntur, ad tempora valde disjuncta abripere. Tales enim voculae or- dinis rei gestae, & temporis aperti sunt indices. Nec Matth. XIII. 1. c. XXII. 23. indefinite hae voces acci- piuntur, sed definite uti proprie sonant, de eadem die. Phraseos autem ἐν μιᾷ τῶν ἡμέρων & Ebraeae alia est ratio, qua non praecise eadem dies denotatur. Vers. 37. λαῖλαψ ἀνέμου] Sicut Urbs Patavii: flumen Rheni. Nam λαῖλαψ est ἀνέμου συστροφὴ μετὰ ὑετοῦ, ut ait Hesychius consentientibus Homeri interpretibus. γεμίζεσθαι] Ita interpretes veteres, ut agnoscas βυθίζε- σθαι esse interpretamentum. Vers. 38. ἐπὶ τῇ πρύμνῃ] Gubernatoris locus in puppi. Viator Jonas in transtris dormiebat. Jon. I. 5. Jonas exci- tatur ut oret, Christus ut sospitet. Vers. 39. πεφίμωσο] Praesenti temporis imperatio sum- mam exigit celeritatem. καὶ ἐγένετο γαλήνη μεγάλη] subito, cum alioqui diu soleat mare agitari postquam venti siluerunt. Vers. 40. τί δειλοί ἐστε ὕτω; πῶς οὐκ ἔχετε πίστιν;] Hanc ve- ram puto lectionem: quid timidi estis? Adeone caretis fi- ducia? Tale est ὕτως οὐκ ἰσχύσατε μίαν ὥραν γρηγορῆσαι μετ᾽ ἐμοῦ; Vocula autem πῶς in istiusmodi locutionibus nihil per se significat, sed vim addit orationi. Cansam timoris Christus exprimit ὀλιγοπιστίαν. Vers. 41. ἐφοβήθησαν φόβον μέγαν καὶ ἔλεγον πρὸς ἀλλήλους] Verbum impersonaliter positum. Subauditur non discipu- li, sed oi ἄνθρωποι, quod expressit Matthaeus. Agitur de il- lis qui in proximo navigabant, quique non aeque assueti e- rant Christi miraculis. Tίς ἄρα] Admirantis: ut notat Servius ad illud Virgilii: Quis globus!

## 5:1 Argument
CHAPTER V. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

Jesus, in the land of the Gadarenes, frees a possessed man who had met him, who lived in the tombs, when the demons begged him not to torment them, of whom there was an entire legion, and permits the demons to enter into the swine, a huge herd of which they cast into the sea; whence the Gadarenes ask that he depart from their borders; he, with the freed man proclaiming the benefit everywhere in the Decapolis, crossed back by ship, with a great crowd gathered to him. Jairus prays for his daughter who was in her death throes, to whose house while Jesus is going, he heals a woman with an issue of blood, who had spent all her substance in vain on physicians, by the touch of his garment, feeling that power had gone out from him, and he says she was restored through faith, and sends her away in peace; he encourages Jairus, to whom his household announces that his daughter has already died, not to fear, but only he trusts, and having taken the dead girl by the hand he commands her to arise, who immediately comes back to life, arises and walks, and he commands that food be given to her.

There are two parts: I. The deliverance of the possessed Gadarene to II: The restoration of the daughter of Jairus and the woman with the issue of blood, the latter healed, the former raised from the dead, to v. 43.

PART I. The deliverance of the possessed Gadarene.

Vers. 1. Γαδαρηνῶν] We learn from the maps of Judea which the Jews have published that גרגש & גדירון, that is, Girgasa and Gadara, are situated near the same part of the lake, so that the adjacent region could rightly be called Gadarene by Mark, no less than Gergesene by Matthew.

Thus Adrichomius teaches that those two cities, Girgasa and Gadara, are two hours distant from each other: whence it could have happened in the borders of either. Others, however, and among them B. Chemnitius, observing from Josephus, Jerome, and Ptolemy that the city of Gadara was distinguished and fortified, which was the primary city of the Gergesenes. There is certainly no need that, because of these different names, we should posit different histories described by Matthew c. VIII and Mark in this place. See the Harmony of Chemnitius c. LXII and LXV.

Latin:

CAPUT V. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Iesus in terra Gadarenorum obsessum obviam sibi factum, qui in sepulcris habitabat, cum daemones obtestarentur ne torqueret ipsos, quorum integra legio erat, liberat, daemoni- busque permittit, ut in porcos introirent, quorum gregem ingentem in mare praeci- pitant; unde Gadareni rogant, ut e fini- bus suis discedat; qui obsesso beneficium tantum passim in decapoli depradicante, vicissim navi trajecit, multa turba adi- psum congregata. Iairus orat pro filia in agone constituta, in cujus domum dum se confert Iesus, haemorrhoisam, quae o- mnem substantiam suam frustra in Medi- cos impenderat, contactu vestis suae sanat, virtutem de se exiisse sentiens, eamque per fidem restitutam dicit, & in pace dimittit; Iairum, cui domestici nunciant filiam jam obiisse, hortatur, ut ne metuat, sed tantum confidat, & apprehensa mortua jubet eam surgere, quæ confestim rediviva surgit & ambulat, eique cibum porrigi jubet.

Partes sunt duæ : I. Obsessi Gadareni liberatio ad II: Filiæ Jairi & hæmorrhousæ restitutio, hac sanata, illa à morte resuscitata, ad v. 43.

PARS I. Obsessi Gadareni liberatio.

Vers. 1. Γαδαρηνῶν] Discimus è tabulis Judææ quas Ju- dæi edidêre גרגש & גדירון, id est, Girgasa & Gadara ad eandem partem stagni vicino esse positu, ita ut adfita regio non minus Gadarenorum Marco, quam Matthæo Gergesenorum dici recte potuerit.

Sic Adrichomius duas illas urbes Girgasam & Gadaram docet ad duas horas ad invicem dissitas : unde in utriusque finibus id accidisse potuit. A- lii tamen, & inter hos B. Chemnitius, è Josepho, Hieronymo, Ptolomæo Gadaram urbem insignem & munitam observant, quæ fuerit primaria Ger- gesenorum. Non sane opus est ut propter hæc diversa nomina cum Andr. Osiandro diversas histo- rias statuamus à Matthæo c. IIX. & Marco hoc loco descriptas. Vid. Harmon. Chemnitii c. LXII. & LXV.

## 5:2
Vers. 2. ἄνθρωπος] He mentions the more notable of the two. ἐν πνεύματι ἀκαθάρτῳ] ἐν for cum. πνεῦμα ἀκάθαρτον from Zechariah XIII. 2.

Latin:

Vers. 2. ἄνθρωπος] De duobus insigniorem memorat. ἐν πνεύματι ἀκαθάρτῳ] ἐν pro cum. πνεῦμα ἀκάθαρτον ex Zacharia XIII. 2.

## 5:4
Vers. 4. διεσπᾶσθαι ὑπ’ αὐτῶν τὰς ἁλύσεις] Well does the author of the responses to the Orthodox say on this passage: ἡ θεία γραφὴ τῷ δαιμονιῶντι προσῆψε τῷ δαίμονος τὰ ἔργα. Thus, conversely, above III. 11, that which belonged to the possessed man is ascribed to the demon.

Latin:

Vers. 4. διεσπᾶσθαι ὑπ’ αὐτῶν τὰς ἁλύσεις] Bene ad hunc locum Scriptor responsionum ad Orthodoxos: ἡ θεία γρα- φὴ τῷ δαιμονιῶντι προσῆψε τῷ δαίμονος τὰ ἔργα. Ita con- tra supra III. II. dæmoni adscribitur id quod erat τῶ δαιμονι- ῶντος.

## 5:7
Vers. 7. τῦ ὑψίστε] עליון. Philo Byblius from Sanchuniathon in the history of the Phoenicians: Ἐλιῦν καλύμενος ὕψιστος: The Pœni, that is, the African Phoenicians, pronounced it Alon, as a very great man observed from Sisenna and Plautus's Pœnulus. Nor indeed is there any doubt that this name of God was most ancient among the old Canaanites, who were also Phoenicians. For Melchizedek, King of Salem, was also called Priest of לאל עליון, Gen. XIV. 18, ἱερεὺς τῦ Θεῦ ὑψίστε, Heb. VII. 1. Philo Judæus narrates in two places that Augustus Cæsar ordered sacrifices to be made for himself in Jerusalem to the Most High God. And in Josephus there exists an edict of Augustus for the Jews, where he wishes them to use their ancestral laws just as they were in the times of Hyrcanus, the High Priest of the Most High God.

ὁρκίζω σε τὸν Θεὸν] That is, νὴ τὸν Θεὸν: as ὁρκίζω τὸν κύριον I Thess. V. 27, ὁρκίζομεν ὴ᾿ Ἰησῦν Acts XIX. 13. They are mistaken, however, who think that an oath is being demanded here. There is indeed that meaning of the word ὁρκίζειν in some places. But in many other places, as we showed at Matt. XXVI, it signifies nothing other than to adjure, which in the old Roman language is to beseech. Luke said δέομαί συ, and an adjuration was accustomed to be joined to prayers: as Horace: I pray you by all the gods. Virgil: I pray you by your sacred things: to which similar examples can be found everywhere.

Latin:

Vers. 7. τῦ ὑψίστε] עליון. Philo Byblius ex Sanchn- niathone in historia Phœnicum Ἐλιῦν καλύμενος ὕψιστος: Pœni, id est Phœnices Africani, pronuntiabant Alon ut ex Sisenna & Plauti Pœnulo vir maximus observavit. Neque vero dubitandum, quin id nomen Dei apud Cananæos veteres, qui & Phœnices, antiquissimum fuerit., Nam & Melchisedec Rex Salem Sacerdos dicebatur לאל עליון, Gen. XIV. 18. ἱερεὺς τῦ Θεῦ ὑψίστε, Heb. VII. 1. Philo Judæus duobus locis narrat Augustum Cæsarem sacra pro se fieri jussisse Hierosolymis τῷ ὑψίστῳ Θεῷ. Et apud Josephum extat Augusti edictum pro Judæis, ubi eos vult uti patriis legibus ita ut ante temporibus Hyrcani ἀρχιερέως Θεῦ ὑ- ψίστε.

ὁρκίζω σε τὸν Θεὸν] Id est νὴ τὸν Θεὸν: ut ὁρκίζω τὸν κύριον I. Thess. V 27. ὁρκίζομεν ὴ᾿ Ἰησῦν Actor. XIX. 13. Errant au- tem qui hic jusjurandum exigi putant. Est quidem alicubi ea vocis ὁρκίζειν significatio. At multis aliis in locis, ut ostendimus ad Matth. XXVI. nihil aliud significat quam religionem injicere, quod est in lingua vetere Romana ob- secrare. Lucas dixit δέομαί συ, & solebat precibus adjun- gi obsecratio : ut Horatius : per omnes te deos oro. Virgi- lius: per te sacra precor: quibus similia passim reperire est.

## 5:10
Vers. 10. ἔξω τῆς χώρας] Why did the demons love to remain in that region? Undoubtedly because there were many Jews there who were מומרין, that is, apostates. For that tract was full of those who were Hellenizing, as we learn from Josephus. But over such Jews, as being outside the divine covenant, the devils, by divine concession, usurped dominion. Thus also the Hebrews hand down that a right was granted to a certain Angel over uncircumcised Jews at IV. Exodus, and Origenes from the Hebrews. Thus also Christians, failing from the rule of faith or life, became slaves of the devil 1 Cor. V. 5, 1 Tim. I. 20. And manifest signs of that divine judgment remained even after the age of the Apostles. Tertullian: An example happened of that woman who went to the theater, and returned from there with a demon. Therefore, in the Exorcism, when the unclean spirit was burdened because he had dared to attack a believer, he said constantly, and indeed most justly: I did it, for I found him in my own. Cyprian: How many daily, not doing penance nor confessing the consciousness of their own fault, are filled with unclean spirits? Naturally, as he had said elsewhere, with discipline receding, grace also receded.

Latin:

Vers. 10. ἔξω τῆς χώρας] Cur ea in regione manere ama- bant dæmones ? Haud dubie quia ibi multi erant Judæi מומרין id est ἀποστάται. Nam is tractus plenus erat ἐλλη- νιζόντων, ut ex Josepho discimus. In tales autem Judæos, ut- pote exsortes divini fœderis, diaboli divina concessione do- minium usurpabant. Sic & in Judæos incircumcisos Angelo cuidam jus fuisse concessum tradunt Hebræi ad IV. Exodi, ex Hebræis Origenes. Sic & Christiani, deficientes à regula fidei aut vitæ, mancipia diaboli fiebant 1. Cor. V. 5. I.Tim. I. 20. Atq; ejus judicii divini manifesta signa etiam post Apo- stolorum ætatem mansêre. Tertullianus : Exemplum acci- dit ejus mulieris quæ theatrum adiit, & inde cum dæmonio re- diit. Itaque in Exorcismo, cum oneraretur immundus spiritus, quod ausus esset fidelem aggredi, constanter, & justissime qui- dem, inquit, feci: in meo enim inveni. Cyprianus : Quam multi quotidie pœnitentiam non agentes nec delicti sui conscien- tiam confitentes, immundis spiritibus adimplentur? Nimirum ut idem alibi dixerat, recedente disciplina recessit & gratia.

## 5:11
Vers. 11. πρὸς τὰ ὄρη] Thus the Syriac reads. Luke: ἐν τῷ ὄρει. It can be understood that that herd was then in the lower part of the mountain.

Latin:

Vers. 11. πρὸς τὰ ὄρη] Ita Syrus legit. Lucas ἐν τῷ ὄρει. In- telligi potest grex ille tum fuisse in parte montis inferiore.

## 5:13
Vers. 13. ὡς δισχίλιοι. About two thousand. We speak thus when we do not wish to be bound exactly to a number.

Latin:

Vers. 13. ὡς δισχίλιοι. Bis mille admodum. Ita loquimur cum exacte ad numerum adstringi nolumus.

## 5:15
Vers. 15. σωφρονῦντα] שׂלון. This is added for this reason, because for the most part those who were possessed were seized by madness at the same time. John 10:20: He has a demon and is mad.

† ἐσχηκότα † λεγεῶνα] Since both the Syriac and the Arabic acknowledge it, I think it should be retained: and all the more so because it is more credible that it was deleted by those who thought it superfluous than added by others.

Grotius rightly defends here, although contrary to custom, the purity of the received Greek Codex, even if the Vulgate omits those things: which Beza notes he did not find in the old Greek Codex either, yet he acknowledges them as genuine, and confesses with Erasmus that they contribute much to the emphasis of the miracle.

Latin:

Vers. 15. σωφρονῦντα] שׂלון. Hoc ideo additum quia plerumque οἱ ἐνεργύμενοι simul furore corripiebantur. Joh. X. 20. δαιμόνιον ἔχει καὶ μαίνεται.

† ἐσχηκότα † λεγεῶνα] Cum & Syrus & Arabs agnoscant, retinendum censeo: eoque magis quia credibilius est de- letum ab iis qui supervacuum putabant, quam ab aliis ad- ditum.

Merito tuetur hic Grotius quanquam præter morem fere, Codicis Græci recepti puritatem, etsi vulgata illa omittat: quæ in veteri Codice Græco quoque se non reperiisse monet Beza, pro germanis tamen agnoscit, & multum ad Empha- sin miraculi facere, cum Erasmo fatetur.

## 5:18
Vers. 18. ἵνα ᾖ μετ' αὐτῦ] Fearing that if Jesus departed, he himself might fall back into the power of the demons. But Christ wished to show that even when absent, He is a protection to those who trust in Him, as Theophylact rightly observes.

Latin:

Vers. 18. ἵνα ᾖ μετ' αὐτῦ] Veritus ne digresso Jesu ipse in dæmonum potestatem recideret. At Christus ostendere voluit se etiam absentem præsidio esse eis qui sibi confide- rent, ut recte observat Theophylactus.

## 5:19
Vers. 19. Ἀνάγγειλον αὐτοῖς] Christ wished for some fame of Himself to spread even to the Gentiles; a presage of the calling that would follow.

καὶ ἐλέησέ σε] Thus the best codices, which the Latin follows. Nor do I see why it coheres badly. For why should it not be said in Greek ὅσα ἠλέησέ σε, since ἐλέησέ σε here is worth as much as ἐχαρίσατό σοι? It appears that those who added ὅτι were offended by the novelty of the construction. For the Syriac had its own reason for adding it, because that Greek manner of speaking would not be admitted in its own language. Christ uses here that modesty which removes envy from self-praise, as Plutarch wisely advises, when we rightly refer the things done by us to God as the author. You could also explain it as ὅσα σοὶ ὁ κύριος ἐποίησε ἐλεήσας σε, in the way we have often seen a copulative conjunction combined with a verb perform the function of a participle.

Grotius rightly deserted Beza here, even if he is otherwise not sufficiently fair to the Greek codices. Beza's boldness is deservedly to be reproved, because he amended the text on account of the reading of a single Codex, and inserted his own ὅτι. Whom the authority of the Syriac does not help. For it is accustomed sometimes to add something for the sake of the sense, which is not held in the original text.

PART II. The restoration of the daughter of Jairus and the woman with the issue of blood.

Latin:

Vers. 19. Ἀνάγγειλον αὐτοῖς] Voluit Christus etiam ad Gentes aliquam sui famam manare; vocationis secuturæ præsagium.

καὶ ἐλέησέ σε] Ita optimi codices, quos Latinus sequitur. Neque video cur male cohæreat. Nam Græce cur non dicatur ὅσαἠλέησέ σε cum ἐλέησέ σε hic tantum va- leat quantum ἐχαρίσατό σοι. Apparet offensos constru- ctionis novitate qui ὅτι addiderunt. Nam Syrus cur id adderet causam habuit suam, quod illud Græcum lo- quendi genus sua lingua non admitteret. Utitur hic Christus ea modestia quæ τῇ περιαυτολογίᾳ invidiam demit, ut sapienter Plutarchus monet, cum recte à nobis facta ad Deum referimus auctorem. Posses etiam exponere ὅσα σοὶ ὁ κύριος ἐποίησε ἐλεήσας σε, quomodo sæpe copulativam conjunctam cum verbo participii vicem explere vidi- mus.

Deseruit hic jure Bezam Grotius, etsi alias non satis æquus Græcis codicibus. Reprobanda me- rito Bezæ audacia, quod ob unius Codicis lectio- nem textum emendarit, & suum ὅτι ingesserit. Quem Syri autoritas non juvat. Solet enim is quandoque sensus causa aliquid addere, quod in textu originali non habetur.

PARS II. Filiæ Iairi, & hæmorrhousæ restitutio.

## 5:23
Vers. 23. ἐσχάτως ἔχει] In Hebrew לשאול הגיע Ps. 88:4.

ἵνα ἐλθὼν ἐπιθῇς] παρακαλῶ is understood from that which had preceded. This, however, is nothing other than a circumlocution of the precative mood. The interpreter of Matthew said ἐπίθες. Those who thought something was missing here added ἐλθέ: which the Syriac does not read, nor indeed does it repeat the verb of coming: but it correctly expressed the sense through the mood, as we have said, the precative. Similar is that of Aristophanes in the Clouds, ὅπως δὲ τῦτο μὴ διδάξῃς μηδένα, for here too παρακαλῶ or something similar is understood.

καὶ ζήσεται] It seems to me that he who annotated ζήσῃ was explaining a Hebraism. For to the Hebrews the future is in place of the subjunctive: and the Syriac and the Latin interpreter seem to me to have understood this passage in that way. Nor is it a tautology. For the sense is: that she may receive health, and thus escape imminent death.

Stephanus reports only one Codex which read ζήσῃ, as the Syriac also has, and the Latin. Grotius, however, implies that it was not a different reading, but only a marginal annotation. Which observation has its use even against Grotius himself, otherwise too prone to different readings. For if even then those are not to be established when Codices have it one way or another, because only a single reading is to be posited, and that which seems otherwise is to be held as a marginal note, how much less will it be permissible to invent another reading, where in no Greek Codex does a trace of it occur.

Latin:

Vers. 23. ἐσχάτως ἔχει] Hebraice לשאול הגיע Ps. LXXXVIII. 4.

ἵνα ἐλθὼν ἐπιθῇς] Subauditur παρακαλῶ σε ex eo quod præcesserat. Hoc autem nihil est aliud quam circumscri- ptio modi precativi. ἐπίθες dixit Matthæi interpres. Qui hic deesse aliquid putarunt, adjecerunt ἐλθέ: quod non legit Syrus, neque enim repetit veniendi verbum: sensum autem recte expressit per modum, ut diximus, precativum. Simile est illud Aristophanis Nubibus ὅπως δὲ τῦτο μὴ διδά- ξῃς μηδένα, nam & hic subauditur παρακαλῶ aut aliquid simile.

καὶ ζήσεται] Videtur mihi qui ζήσῃ annotavit explicassę Hebraismum. Nam Hebræis futurum est vici subjuncti- vi: atque ita intellexisse mihi hunc locum videntur Syrus, & Latinus interpres. Neque est ταυτολογία. Sensus e- nim est: ut sanitatem recipiat, atque ita mortem imminentem effugiat.

Stephanus non nisi unum refert Codicem, qui legerit ζήσῃ, uti Syrus etiam habet, ac Latinus. Non autem diversam fuisse lectionem, sed marginalem solum annotationem innuit Grotius. Quæ obser- vatio suum habet usum etiam adversus ipsummet Grotium, alias nimis proclivem in diversas lectio- nes. Si enim tum etiam eæ non sunt statuendæ, cum Codices aliter atque aliter habent, quia po- nenda unica tantum lectio, quæ vero videtur alte- ra habenda pro nota marginali, quanto minus id integrum erit fingere aliam lectionem, ubi in nul- lo Codice Græco ejus occurrit vestigium.

## 5:25
Vers. 25. ὖσα ἐν ῥύσει αἵματος] αἱμοῥῥοῦσα Matthew. I do not doubt that it is a Hebraism familiar to Mark, such as twice above, ἐν πνεύματι ἀκαθάρτῳ.

Latin:

Vers. 25. ὖσα ἐν ῥύσει αἵματος] αἱμοῥῥοῦσα Matthæus. Non dubito quin Hebraismus sit Marco familiaris qualis bis supra, ἐν πνεύματι ἀκαθάρτῳ.

## 5:26
Vers. 26. ἀπὸ πολλῶν ἰατρῶν] The old inscription: The crowd of physicians has ruined me.

κὶ μηδὲν ὠφεληθεῖσα] Naturally; It is not always that the patient is restored by the physician, sometimes the evil is stronger than the learned art: Which especially has a place in diseases that by their very age turn into nature.

εἰς τὸ χεῖρον ἐλθοῦσα] And no wonder: for it is hardly possible that medicines which do not help should not harm, especially in languid bodies, such as those must be whose blood is not turned into juice.

Latin:

Vers. 26. ἀπὸ πολλῶν ἰατρῶν] Vetus inscriptio: Turba medicorum me perdidit.

κὶ μηδὲν ὠφεληθεῖσα] Nimirum; Non est in medico semper reveletur ut æger, Interdum docta plus valet arte malum: Quod præcipue locum habet in morbis qui ipsa vetustate in naturam vertunt.

εἰς τὸ χεῖρον ἐλθοῦσα] Nec mirum: vix enim est ut non noceant medicamenta quæ non prosunt, præsertim in lan- guidis corporibus, qualia esse necesse est quorum sanguis in succum non vertitur.

## 5:29
Vers. 29. ἡ πηγὴ] ῥύσις in Luke. The Hebrews call every issue a fountain. Levit. XII. 7, concerning the natural flow of women: וטהרה ממקר דמיה. In the Greek, καὶ καθαριεῖ αὐτὴν ἀπὸ τῆς πηγῆς τοῦ αἵματος αὐτῆς.

ἔγνω τῷ σώματι] There is great emphasis in these words. For naturally no one recovers suddenly from an old disease, but long traces of the departing evil remain: that is signified in Luke in the words ἰάθη παραχρῆμα.

Latin:

Vers. 29. ἡ πηγὴ] ῥύσις Lucæ. Omnem scetebram Hebræi fontem appellant. Levit. XII. 7. de naturali mulierum pro- fluvio: וטהרה ממקר דמיה. Græcis καὶ καθαριεῖ αὐ- τὴν ἀπὸ τῆς πηγῆς τοῦ αἵματος αὐτῆς.

ἔγνω τῷ σώματι] Magna est ἔμφασις in his vocibus. Nam naturaliter nemo ex veteri morbo subito revalescit, sed longa manent cedentis mali vestigia: id apud Lucam signi- ficatur in verbis ἰάθη παραχρῆμα.

## 5:30
Vers. 30. δύναμιν ἐξελθοῦσαν] A popular way of speaking, but of great efficacy. For it signifies most clearly a certain power not adventitious, such as was wont to be exercised by God at the prayers of the Prophets, but which was subsisting in Him Himself, and from thence produced effects, which here is to go forth.

This observation of Grotius is to be noted against the Calvinists, who derogate the divine power from the flesh of Christ. Compare what is in the Examination of the Doctrine concerning the person of Christ, controversy VIII.

Latin:

Vers. 30. δύναμιν ἐξελθοῦσαν] Populare loquendi genus, sed magnæ efficaciæ. Significatur enim apertissime vis quædam non adventitia, qualis ad Prophetarum preces à Deo exerceri solebat, sed quæ esset in ipso ὑφισταμένη, atque inde effectus produceret, quod hic est ἐξέρχεσθαι

Hæc observatio Grotii contra Calvinianos no- tanda, vim divinam carni Christi derogantes. Conf. quæ in Exam. Doctr. de persona Christi controv. IIX.

## 5:33
Vers. 33. πᾶσαν τὴν ἀλήθειαν] So the ancient interpreters: nor do I doubt that what other codices have besides was added from the history of Luke.

Latin:

Vers. 33. πᾶσαν τὴν ἀλήθειαν] Ita veteres interpretes: nec dubito quin quod præterea Codices alii, adjectum sit ex Lucæ historia.

## 5:34
Vers. 34. ὕπαγε εἰς εἰρήνην] So also Luke. Some have wrongly changed it to ἐν εἰρήνῃ. For the sense is the same in both expressions: nor do the Hellenists rarely use εἰς for ἐν and ἐν for εἰς. But it also exists in the LXX, πορεύου εἰς εἰρήνην, 1 Sam. I. v. 17.

Latin:

Vers. 34. ὕπαγε εἰς εἰρήνην] Ita & Lucas. Male mutarunt quidam in ἐν εἰρήνῃ. Est enim in utraque locutione sensus idem: neque raro Hellenistæ εἰς pro ἐν & ἐν pro εἰς usur- pant. Sed & apud LXX. exstat πορεύου εἰς εἰρήνην, 1. Sam. I. v. 17.

## 5:35
Vers. 35. ἀπὸ τοῦ ἀρχισυναγώγου] The Syrian has well expressed the force of the expression, which is most common among the Latins. Thus in Virgil:

- - - - Ucalegon burns next.

σκύλλεις] תלאו Esa. VII. 13.

Latin:

Vers. 35. ἀπὸ τοῦ ἀρχισυναγώγου] Vim locutionis apud La- tinos usitatissimæ bene expressit Syrus. Sic apud Virgi- lium:

- - - - proximus ardet Ucalegon.

σκύλλεις] תלאו Esa. VII. 13.

## 5:36
Vers. 36. τὸν λόγον λαλύμενον] That which had been said: do not be troublesome to the master: which pertained to driving out all remnants of confidence from the mind of the archisynagogue, which Christ in his goodness forestalled.

μόνον πίστευε] To obtain visible benefits Christ requires nothing besides trust, to show that internal benefits also happen to those who trust in Him: concerning which matter it has been spoken elsewhere.

Latin:

Vers. 36. τὸν λόγον λαλύμενον] Illud quod dictum erat: noli magistro molestus esse: quod pertinebat ad omnes fidu- ciæ reliquias ex archisynagogi animo proturbandas, quod Christus pro sua bonitate antevertit.

μόνον πίστευε] Ad beneficia aspectabilia impetranda nihil præter fiduciam Christus exigit, ut ostendat etiam interna beneficia in se confidentibus contingere: qua de re alibi dictum.

## 5:38
Vers. 38. ἀλαλάζοντας] The Hellenists, who do not so much follow the precision of the Greek language as they take care to express the force of the Hebrew language as closely as possible, in order to render הילילו, which signifies to the Hebrews a clamor and especially a mournful one, have used Greek words similar in sound: there are two, ὀλολύζειν and ἀλαλάζειν, of which the Greeks used the former mostly in sacred rites, and the latter in war: in which sense I find ἀλαλαγμὸν even in Josephus. But the Hellenists, as I said, neglecting that propriety, indulged themselves in the liberty of catachresis. And ὀλολύζειν indeed occurs here and there in that sense, as in Is. 13:6, 15:2, 52:5, Jer. 48:20, 31, Zech. 11:2, Hos. 7:14, and Jas. 5:1; but ἀλαλάζειν in Jer. 25:34, הילילו הרעים ἀλαλάξατε ποιμένες, and 47:2, καὶ ἀλαλάξουσιν ἅπαντες οἱ κατοικοῦντες τὴν γῆν. But in another place of the same Prophet, which is 4:8, other Greek codices have ὀλολύξατε, others ἀλαλάξατε. The Syrian expressed the very word which is expressed by the Greek, מיילין. There is no reason to doubt the truth of this reading given such a consensus of codices.

These things were rightly said by Grotius: This word is one of joy among the Greeks. Whence some correct it and read ὀλολύζοντας: but Casaubon teaches that even that word does not fit; for it is properly said of the clamor which those who were present at the sacred rites raised when the victim was slaughtered: and that even the more eloquent Greeks did not use it otherwise than in a happy matter, so that it means to exclaim for joy. But Ludovicus de Dieu is right here: It is no wonder that ἀλαλάζειν is taken for to wail or to lament, even if there is no reference to flute-players, because ἀλαλαγμὸς is also ascribed to sheep whose pastures have been devastated, Jer. 25:36; nor is the usage of this word, as of others, to be sought from profane writers, but from the LXX interpreters, whose idiom the Sacred writers have followed throughout. By whom it is evident that this word is taken not only for to shout joyfully, but also for to lament sadly, from Jer. 25:34 and 48:3. And thus the author of the Glossary also explains ἀλαλάζειν as to wail. The same must be said of ὀλολύζειν, which, although those who spoke more elegantly in Greek used it only in a happy matter, as is learnedly proven by Casaubon, is nevertheless frequently used for to lament among the LXX and in the N.T. Which should not be turned into a fault for the Hellenists, since they learned from the Hebrews that הריע, which is properly used for joy, is not rarely used for sad shouting as well, as in Is. 15:4, Mic. 4:9, as Dievius holds here. Vers. 40. ἐκβαλὼν ἅπαντας] He took as many witnesses as were sufficient for proving the matter. To admit more could have had the appearance of ostentation. τοὺς μετ' αὐτοῦ] That is, the three disciples whom he had kept with him when entering the house. Therefore the Latin interpreter is excellent, who [translated it as] those who were with him, which is how it can be understood and what is in the Syrian and the Arab. ἀνακείμενον] On that very bed on which she had been sick. If the subtlety of the Greeks were to be followed, not even he who reclines at the table could be said to be ἀνακεῖσθαι; indeed, those who spoke that way were accustomed to be laughed at by the elegant, because those things which were upright, such as statues, were properly called ἀνακεῖσθαι. But the usage, the arbiter of words, does not allow itself to be bound by these straits. Vers. 41. αὐτῇ] Correct: and no reason to change it. For it is a construction according to the sense. Ταλιθὰ] This word exists in the Chaldean interpreter, Prov. 9. σοὶ λέγω] The force of the vocative is expressed by the added words, which we have observed the LXX also did in some places. Moreover, a direct command to a body devoid of reason signifies the divine power of the one commanding. Vers. 43. ἵνα μηδεὶς γνῷ τοῦτο] He did not want his power over death itself to be divulged at this time, as it was something that was to be published to the whole world only after his resurrection. Meanwhile, he wanted some signs of his power to be known to some, which would soon provide faith for the resurrection itself. εἶπε] that is, he commanded, יאמר, as also below in ch. 8:7. φαγεῖν] So that it might appear that she was not only alive but also properly healthy: for those who are gravely ill are hardly accustomed to take food.

Latin:

Vers. 38. ἀλαλάζοντας] Hellenistæ, qui non tam Græci sermonis ἀκριβολογίαν sequuntur, quam id curant ut quam proxime fieri potest exprimant vim linguæ Hebrææ, ut red- derent הילילו quod Hebræis clamorem præsertim vero lugubrem, significat, voces Græcas uæsfiverunt sono affines: sunt autem duæ ὀλολύζειν & ἀλαλάζειν, quarum illam in sa- cris, istam in bello maxime Græci usurpabant: quo sensu ἀλαλαγμὸν etiam apud Josephum reperio. Sed Helleni- stæ ut dixi ista proprietate neglecta abusionis libertatem sibi indulsêre. Et ὀλολύζειν quidem eo sensu passim occur- rit, ut Es. XIII. 6. XV. 2. LII. 5. Jer XLVIII. 20. 31. Zach. XI. 2. Os. VII. 14 & Jac. V. 1. ἀλαλάζειν vero Jerem. XXV. vers 34. הילילו הרעים ἀλαλάξατε ποιμένες XLVII. 2. καὶ ἀλα- λάξουσιν ἅπαντες οἱ κατοικοῦντες τὴν γῆν. Ejusdem vero Pro- phetæ loco altero qui est IV. 8. alii Codices Græci habent ὀλολύξατε, alii ἀλαλάξατε. Syrus ipsam vocem expressit quæ per Græcam exprimitur מיילין Quæ ede lectionis veritate in tanto codicum consensu non est dubitandum.

Recte ista à Grotio dicta: Vox hæc gaudii est a- pud Græcos. Unde nonnulli corrigunt, & legunt ὀλολύζοντας: sed nec eam vocem convenire Ca- saubonus docet: proprie enim dici de clamore, quem tollebant mactata victima, qui sacris intere- rant: Disertiores etiam Græcos non aliter usur- pare, nisi in re læta, ut sit præ gaudio exclamare. Sed recte hic Ludovicus de Dieu: Nihil mirum est ἀ- λαλάζειν pro ejulare aut lamentari accipi, etsi ad ἀυλητὰς non respiciatur, quia etiam ovibus vastata pascua lugentibus adscribitur ἀλαλαγμὸς Jer. XXV. v. 26. neque enim hujus vocis, ut & aliarum, usus ex prophanis scriptoribus, sed ex LXX. interpreti- bus est petendus, quorum idioma Sacri scriptores passim sunt secuti. Quibus hanc vocem accipi non solum pro læte vociferari, sed etiam pro triste lamentari è Jer. XXV. 44. & XLVIII. 3. constat. Atque ita Glossarii autor etiam ἀλαλάζειν expli- cat ejulare. Idem de ὀλολύζειν dicendum, quo quanquam qui elegantius Græce sunt locuti, non nisi in re læta sunt usi, ut docte à Casaubono probatur, apud LXX. tamen & in N. T. pro lamen- tari frequenter usurpatur. Quod Hellenistis vitio non verti debet, quippe qui ab Hebræis didicerunt, הריע quod in gaudio proprie ponitur, non raro de tristi etiam vociferatione usurpari, ut Esa. XV. 4. Mich. IV. 9. ut hic habet Dievius. Vers. 40. ἐκβαλὼν ἅπαντας] Tot testes assumebat quod rei probandæ sufficiebant. Plures admittere speciem ha- bere poterat ostentationis. τοὺς μετ' αὐτοῦ] Id est discipulos tres quos in domum in- trans secum retinuerat. Optime igitur Latinus interpres, qui secum erant, quomodo accipi potest & quod apud Syrum & Arabem est. ἀνακείμενον] In eo ipso lecto in quo ægrotaverat. Si Græ- corum subtilitas sequenda esset ne is quidem qui ad men- sam accumbit dici posset ἀνακεῖσθαι, imo rideri ab eleganti- bus solebant qui ita loquebantur, quia ἀνακεῖσθαι proprie di- cebantur ea quæ erecta erant, ut statuæ. Sed vocum arbites usus istis angustiis se adstringi non patitur. Vers. 41. αὐτῇ] Recte: neque mutandi causa. Est enim σύνταξις κατὰ τὸ σημαινόμενον. Ταλιθὰ] Exstat hæc vox in Chaldæo interprete Prov. IX. σοὶ λέγω] Vis vocativi additis vocibus exprimitur, quod & LXX. fecisse alicubi a nobis observatum est. Imperium autem directum in corpus rationis expers vim divinam im- perantis significat. Vers. 43. ἵνα μηδεὶς γνῷ τοῦτο] Imperium suum in mor- tem ipsam nolebat hoc tempore evulgari, ut quod post re- surrectionem demum ipsius omni mundo esset publican- dum. Interim aliqua ejus potentiæ signa nonnullis cogni- ta esse voluit, quæ mox ipsi etiam resurrectioni fidem ad- struerent. εἶπε] id est ἐκέλευσε יאמר ut & infra c. IIX. 7. φαγεῖν] Ut appareret non vivam tantum esse sed & recte valentem: nam graviter ægroti vix solent cibum sumere.

## 6:1 Argument
CHAPTER VI. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

Jesus heads to his own country, and teaches there, but because of contempt he performs no miracles there, and teaches in the towns: he sends out the Apostles with power over unclean Spirits, and with instruction, who preach here and there, and perform miracles. The fame of Jesus is reported to Herod, who thought he was John, whose head he had cut off: which history is related here, how he imprisoned John because of the rebuke concerning his brother's wife, and on the occasion of a birthday banquet, and the dancing of her daughter, he caused John's head to be cut off, and offered it to the daughter on a platter: as the Apostles of Jesus were telling what they had accomplished, and as he was withdrawing into the desert, many followed, and five thousand men were satisfied there with five loaves and two fishes, with twelve baskets of leftovers remaining: But as the disciples were heading by ship to Bethsaida, and were in danger on the sea, he himself, walking on the sea, comes to their aid, and when he was received into the ship, the tempest was calmed: As he comes into the land of Gennesaret, many sick are offered to him: wherever he stayed, he was begged that they might be permitted to touch even the hem of his garment, and those who touched were healed.

There are two parts: The former pursues the remaining things which were done up to the third Passover, such as I. The contempt of Jesus in his Country, to v. 6. II. The sending out of the Apostles to v. 13. III. The judgment of Herod concerning Christ, and the history of the beheading of John to v. 30. IV. The feeding of 5000 men in the desert, to v. 44. V. The walking of Christ on the sea, to v. 52. The latter begins to relate those things which were done from the third Passover of Christ's ministry to the fourth: to which belongs in this chapter the healing of many in the land of Gennesaret, and here and there in villages, towns, and hamlets, to v. 56.

PART I. The Contempt of Jesus in His Own Country.

Latin:

CAPUT VI. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Iesus in patriam suam tendit, ibiq́; docet, sed ob contemtum nulla illic edit miracula, do- cetq́; in oppidis: emittit Apostolos cum pote- state in immundos Spiritus, & instructione, qui passim prædicant, & miracula patrant. Fama de Iesu ad Herodem relata, qui censuit eum Iohannem esse, cui caput amputarat: quæ historia hic refertur, quomodo ob repre- hensionem ductæ uxoris fratris Iohannem captivarit, & occasione convivii genethlia- ci, & saltus ejus filiæ caput Iohanni ampu- tari curarit, & in patina id filiæ obtulerit: Apostolis Iesu narrantibus, quæ expedierant, eoque in desertum secedente, multi sequuti, & quinque millia virorum ibi quinque pa- nibus & duobus piscibus saturati, remanen- tibus duodecim reliquiarum cophinis: Disci- pulis autem nave Bethsaidam contendenti- bus, & in mari periclitantibus ipse in mari ambulans succurrit, quo navi recepto tem- pestas sedata: In terram Genesareth veni- enti offeruntur multi ægroti: ubicunque morabatur, rogabaturque ut vel oram vesti- menti tantum tangere permitterentur, tangentesque sanati sunt.

Partes sunt duæ: Prior reliqua quæ ad tertium usque Pascha gesta sunt persequitur, ceu sunt I. Contemtus Jesu in Patria, ad v. 6. II. Emissio A- postolorum ad v. 13. III. Judicium Herodis de Christo, & historia decollationis Johannis ad v. 30. IV. Cibatio 5000. virorum in deserto, ad v. 44. V. Ambulatio Christi in mari, ad v. 52. Posterior in- choat referre ea, quæ a tertio Paschate ministerii Christi ad quartum gesta sunt: quo facit hoc capite multorum in terra Genesareth, & passim in vicis, oppidis, & pagis sanatio ad v. 56.

PARS I. Contemtus Iesu in Patria.

## 6:2
Ver. 2. ἐξεπλήσσοντο] That which certain Codices have, ἐπὶ τῇ διδαχῇ αὐτῦ, I think was added from the Latin interpreter, who sometimes adds certain words to complete the sense. The cause of the admiration, as the comparison of Luke and John teaches us, was this: that Jesus, instructed by no human master, explained the words of the Prophets with the greatest clarity.

Grotius ought to have joined Matthew to Luke, not John. For John has nothing of these things, but Matthew ch. XIII. 54. In John, indeed, similar things are said to have been bandied about, but in the Capharnaite school, ch. IV. 42, not the Nazarene: nor on the occasion of a clear explanation of the Prophets, but because Christ said that he had come from heaven, which those hearers could not reconcile with his birth from Mary, believing him to be a mere man and the son of Joseph.

ἡ δοθεῖσα αὐτῷ, ὅτι καὶ δυνάμεις τοιαῦται διὰ τῶν χειρῶν αὐτῦ γίνονται] That his wisdom was given divinely, besides the fact that it was most well known that Jesus used no masters, they prove by a second argument from the miracles which he had performed at Capharnaum and elsewhere. Therefore ὅτι γίνονται is more correct than what they have, ἵνα γίνωνται.

Latin:

Vers. 2. ἐξεπλήσσοντο] Quod quidam Codices habent ἐπὶ τῇ διδαχῇ αὐτῦ puto additum ex Latino interprete, qui ad sensum explendum quædam interdum verba addit. Cau- sa admirationis ut collatio Lucæ & Johannis nos docet hæc erat: quod Jesus nullo humano magisterio institutus sum- ma cum perspicuitate Prophetarum verba explicaret.

Lucæ Matthæum conjungere debuisset Gro- tius, non Johannem. Nam Johannes de his nihil habet, sed Matthæus c. XIII. 54. Apud Johannem quidem similia jactata dicuntur, sed in Schola Ca- pernaitica c. IV. 42. non Nazarethana: nec occa- sione perspicuæ explicationis Prophetarum, sed quod diceret Christus se de cælo venisse, quod au- ditores isti non poterant conciliare cum ortu ejus è Maria, credentes ipsum esse merum hominem, & Josephi filium.

ἡ δοθεῖσα αὐτῷ, ὅτι καὶ δυνάμεις τοιαῦται διὰ τῶν χειρῶν αὐτῦ γίνονται] Sapientiam ipsius esse datam divinitus, præter- quam quod notissimum erat Jesum nullis usum magistris, altero argumento probant ex miraculis quæ Capharnaumi atque alibi ediderat. Ideo rectius est ὅτι γίνονται quàm quod illi habent ἵνα γίνωνται.

## 6:3
Ver. 3. ὁ τέκτων] See what is said on Matthew.

Ἰώσητος] This seems to me to be the true reading, the name having been brought to a Greek inflection. For also below, ch. XV. 40, the best Codices have it so, which those who did not understand replaced with an indeclinable word.

αἱ ἀδελφαὶ αὐτῦ ὧδε πρὸς ἡμᾶς] Since the Nazarenes here make special mention of the female relatives of JESUS living among them, I am led to believe what I also said above, that the mother of Jesus and some of his relatives lived at Capharnaum at this time.

Latin:

Vers. 3. ὁ τέκτων] Vide quæ ad Matthæum.

Ἰώσητος] Videtur mihi hæc vera esse lectio ad Græcam flexionem perducto nomine. Nam & infra c. XV. 40. ita habent optimi Codices, quod qui non intellexerunt re- posuerunt vocem ἄκλιτον.

αἱ ἀδελφαὶ αὐτῦ ὧδε πρὸς ἡμᾶς] Cum Nazarethan̄i hic specialiter meminerint cognatarum JESU apud se habitan- tium, adducor ut credam quod & supra dixi, matrem Je- su & cognatorum aliquos hoc tempore Capharnaumi ha- bitasse.

## 6:5
Ver. 5. οὐκ ἐδύνατο] We have already spoken above about the various meanings of the word δύνασθαι. Here I think is signified an affection in Christ which hindered him from doing many miracles at Nazareth. For so we also say in Latin, I cannot bring myself to do this. And that expression is wont to be used of evil as well as good affections. Thus in Gen. XXXVII, concerning the brothers of Joseph, it is said, ולא יכלו דברו לשלום and οὐκ ἠδύναντο λαλεῖν αὐτῷ οὐδὲν εἰρηνικὸν, hatred obviously standing in the way. John VII. 7, οὐ δύναται ὁ κόσμος μισεῖν ὑμᾶς, naturally because of the similarity of morals. Acts IV. 20, οὐ δυνάμεθα ἡμεῖς ἃ εἴδομεν καὶ ἠκούσαμεν μὴ λαλεῖν. Apoc. II. 2, οὐ δύνῃ βαστάσαι κακύς. So also 2 Cor. XIII. 8. Rightly Chrysostom: 'Thus he knows how to call the intention power in many places; and one might see this preserved also in common usage, as when someone says, I cannot love such a one, calling the vehemence of the will power.' Christ, having full power to perform miracles, was hindered from exercising it in this place by the hatred, not of men, but of most stubborn incredulity. For although they confessed that his doctrine and manner of teaching were excellent and divine, and were moved somewhat by the fame of the things done at Capharnaum, yet they were again called away by regard for his birth and upbringing, so that they could not think anything magnificent of him.

Latin:

Vers. 5. οὐκ ἐδύνατο] De variis significationibus vocis δύνασθαι jam diximus supra. Hic puto significari affectum in Christo qui obstiterit illi quominus miracula multa Na- zarethæ faceret. Nam ita & Latine dicimus, Impetrare hoc à me non possum. Soletque tam de malis quam de bonis af- fectibus ea locutio usurpari. Ita Genes. XXXVII. de fratri- bus Josephi dicitur ולא יכלו דברו לשלום καὶ οὐκ ἠδύ- ναντο λαλεῖν αὐτῷ οὐδὲν εἰρηνικὸν, obstante odio scilicet Joh. VII. 7. οὐ δύναται ὁ κόσμος μισεῖν ὑμᾶς, nimirum ob morum si- militudinem Act. IV. 20. οὐ δυνάμεθα ἡμεῖς ἃ εἴδομεν καὶ ἠκούσα- μεν μὴ λαλεῖν. Apoc. II. 2. οὐ δύνῃ βαστάσαι κακύς. Sic & 2. Cor. XIII. 8. Recte Chrysostomus: οὕτως οἶδε πολλαχῦ δύναμιν τὴν προαίρεσιν λέγειν˙ τῦτο δὲ κὰι ἐν τῇ κοινῇ συνηθείᾳ φυλαττό- μενον ἴδοι τις ἂν. ὡς ὅταν λέγῃ τις, ἐ δύναμαι αγαπῇν τὸν δεῖνα, τὸ σφοδρὸν τῆς βυλήσεως δύναμιν λέγων. Christus ple- nam habens miracula faciendi potestatem, quo minus eam hoc loco exerceret impediebatur odio non hominum sed pertinacissimæ incredulitatis. Nam cum illi doctrinam & do- cendi genus faterentur esse eximia ac divina, fama etiam rerum Capharnaumi gestarum commoverentur nonnihil, iterum tamen respectu natalium atque educationis avoca- bantur, quo minus magnificum aliquid de ipso sentirent.

## 6:6
Ver. 6. διὰ τὴν ἀπιστίαν αὐτῶν] So it seemed good to Mark to express what the Hebrews would say by ב־: just as our writers also sometimes speak, as Luke I. 21, 2 Thess. I. 10; elsewhere the same is wont to be expressed by ἐπὶ, as Luke IV. 22, ch. XX. 26, Acts III. 12.

περιῆγε τὰς κώμας κύκλῳ διδάσκων] Leaving his ungrateful country, he sought hearers whose minds were not equally occupied by depraved affections.

PART II. The Sending Forth of the Apostles.

Latin:

Vers. 6. διὰ τὴν ἀπιστίαν αὐτῶν] Ita visum est Marco ex- primere quod Hebræi dicerent per ב־: sicut & nostri Scri- ptores interdum loquuntur, ut Luc. I. 21. 2. Thess. I. 10. alias per ἐπὶ solet idem exprimi, ut Luc. IV. 22. cap. XX. 26. Actor. III. 12.

περιῆγε τὰς κώμας κύκλῳ διδάσκων] Patriam ingratam de- serens auditores quærebat quorum animi non æque essent pravis affectibus occupati.

PARS II. Emissio Apostolorum.

## 6:7
Vers. 7. the twelve] Mark is accustomed to speak thus: wherefore what others add, his disciples, has undoubtedly been added from Matthew.

two by two] For the full assurance of the testimony. Thus also John had sent the disciples of his own flock to Christ, Matt. XI. 2.

Latin:

Vers. 7. τὺς δώδεκα] Ita loqui solet Marcus: quare quod alii addunt μαθητὰς αὐτῦ haud dubie ex Matthæo adjectum est.

δύο δύο] Ad plenam testimonii fidem. Sic & Johannes sui gregis discipulos ad Christum legarat, Matth. XI. 2.

## 6:8
Vers. 8. that they should take nothing] That is, that they should carry nothing with them for the sake of the journey, beyond those things which were for daily use.

except a staff only] That staff with which they happened to be walking at that time, not another that would be for use among their baggage if by chance the former had failed. For the Lord wished in their first mission to give them a manifest proof of divine providence. The end of these precepts is perpetual: the precepts themselves are temporary: as we have noted regarding Matthew.

no wallet, no bread, no money in their belt] Namely, for the journey, that is, for the sake of the journey. For Christ did not want them, for the sake of the mission undertaken, to be even the slightest bit more anxious than they were before,

Latin:

Vers. 8. μηδὲν αἴρωσιν εἰς ὁδὸν] Id est ne quid viæ causa se- cum ferrent, extra ea quæ usus erant quotidiani.

εἰ μὴ ῥάβδον μόνον] Eam virgam cum qua tunc forte am- bulabant, non aliam inter sarcinas usui futuram si forte prior defecisset. Voluit enim Dominus in prima legatione ma- nifestum ipsis dare documentum divinæ providentiæ, Finis horum præceptorum perpetuus est: præcepta ipsa tempo- raria: ut ad Matthæum monuimus.

μὴ πήραν, μὴ ἄρτον, μὴ εἰς τὴν ζώνην χαλκόν] Nimirum εἰς ὁδὸν, id est viæ causa. Noluit enim Christus illos susce- ptæ legationis ergo vel tantillo sollicitiores esse quam ante erant,

## 6:9
Vers. 9. but to be shod with sandals] Go, he says. He speaks paradoxically. He commands them to go as they were, namely, wearing sandals. Although the ancient Christians walked much with bare feet (it is not very fitting for a man to be barefoot, says Tertullian: bare feet are more manly than those in shoes), they seem to me, however, to have done this more after the example of the Platonists, whose barefootedness is famous, so that, namely, they would not yield to the philosophers (whom they also imitated in that cloak) in any part of either frugality or fortitude, rather than from a primitive institution or example. For the history of Moses teaches us everywhere that the Jews generally had their own sandals, as Exod. III. 5, ch. XII. 11, Deut. XXV. 10, Ruth IV. 7, and Luke XV. 22. And that Christ did not depart from that custom is sufficiently manifest from the words of the Baptist in Matt. III. 11, and above in verse 7. That the Apostles were likewise shod, this passage proves, as does the other concerning Peter in Acts XII. 8. But the Jews used sandals greatly. Thus Isaiah is commanded to put off his sandals in the LXX version, ch. XX. 2, and Peter to put on sandals in the cited passage of Acts: and here the Apostles to take their way shod with sandals. Indeed, the Jerusalem Metaphrast everywhere put sandal for shoe. And therefore at a funeral they are commanded to lay aside their sandals by the old law which exists in the Talmudic writings: and Josephus, in his exposition of the law concerning a brother's widow, said sandals, which others called shoes. Although it appears from these same passages that the Jewish sandals were quite common shoes, it is nevertheless certain that the Jews also had other more exquisite shoes. Sandals seem to have corresponded properly to that kind of shoe which the Attics called konipodas. Suidas certainly explains konipoda as a kind of sandal, or because of the dust, the foot was covered in dust. To Pollux it is a thin shoe; Clement in the Pedagogue II, ch. XI. But if we are not strong, and we do not even bear being barefoot, we must use slippers or light shoes, and the Attics called them konipodas because they approach, it seems to me, the dust with the foot. The Jews relate that it was a custom for their ancestors to appear in the temple on feast days with sandals made of the skins of better animals. Christ therefore wishes his Apostles to set out on their journey, so to speak, wearing sandals, not shoes, intending to provide for them no less against the inconveniences of travel than against other difficulties. The Syrian calls sandals talaria, I believe because they were tied to the ankles. Thus also in Pedo's elegy, where there is 'sandalia', other books have 'talaria' from a glossarial exposition, if I am not mistaken. But concerning this passage I advise the reader to see what the man of incomparable learning, the illustrious Salmasius, noted on Tertullian's cloak.

and do not put on two tunics] That is, do not put on now this, now that tunic, as those who travel are accustomed to use some clothes on the journey and others when they have arrived in some city. See what is said on Matthew in this place. All these things, as I have said, pertain to this, that the Apostles may understand that they will have no need of greater preparation for their journey than if they were to remain at home,

Latin:

Vers. 9. ἀλλ' ὑποδεδεμένους σανδάλια] ἰθιγνῆται ὕπαγε. Dicit enim παραδόξως. Ire jubet ita ut erant, soleatos scilicet. Quanquam Christiani veteres multum incesserunt nudis pedibus (ἀνδρὶ οὐ μάλα ἁρμόδιον ἡ ἀνυποδησία, inquit Cle- Tertullianus: Pedes nudi viriles magis quam in cal- ceis) videntur tamen id mihi fecisse Platonicorum magis exemplo, quorum celebris est ἀνυποδησία, ne scil. Philoso- phis (quos & in illo pallio imitabantur) in ulla aut frugali- tatis aut fortitudinis parte cederent, quam ex primævo in- stituto aut exemplo. Nam Judæos plerumque sua habuisse ὑποδήματα passim nos docet Mosis historia, ut Exod. III. 5. c. XII. 11. Deuter. XXV. 10. Ruth. IV. 7. & Luc. XV. 22. Ne- que discessisse Christum ab eo more satis manifestum est ex verbis Baptistæ Matth. III. 11. & supra l. 7. Apostolos itidem fuisse ὑποδεδεμένους tum hic locus evincit, tum alter de Petro Act. XII. 8. Judæi vero scandaliis maxime usi. Ita que Esaias jubetur exuere τὰ σανδάλια in versione LXX. c. XX. 2. & Pe- trus induere σανδάλια dicto Actorum loco: & hic Apostoli viam capere ὑποδεδεμένοι σανδάλια. Quin & Metaphrastes Hierosolymitanus pro נעל ubiq; posuit סנדל. Et ideo in funere jubentur deponere sandalia lege veteri quæ in Thal- mudicis exstat:& Josephus in expositione legis de vidua fra- terna, σανδάλια dixit quæ alii ὑποδήματα. Quanquam au- tem iisdem ex locis appareat σανδάλια Judaica fuisse ὑπο- δήματα satis usitata, certum tamen est Judæis fuisse & alia ὑποδήματα exquisitiora. Σανδάλια proprie respondisse vi- dentur isti ὑποδημάτων generi quod κονίποδας vocabant At- tici. Suidas certe κονίποδα exponit γενὸς σανδαλίων ἢ διὰ τὴν κονιότητα ὁ πᾶς ἐκονιστᾶτο. Polluci est λεπτὸν ὑπόδημα; Clemens Pædagogo II. cap. XI. εἰ δὲ μὴ σθένοιμεν, ἀλλὰ μηδὲ φέροιμεν τὴν ἀνυποδησίαν, βλαύταις ἢ Φαικασίοις χρηστέον, καὶ κίποδας ἀυτὰ ἰκάλεν οἱ Ἀττικοὶ διὰ τὸ πελάζειν, μοι δοκεῖν, τῇ κόνει τῷ ποδί. Narrant Judæi morem fuisse majoribus suis, ut diebus festis in templo apparerent cum sandaliis e melium pellibus. Soleatos igitur, ut ita dicam, non calcea- tos vult Christus Apostolos suos iter arripere, non minus ad- versus itinerum incommoda, quam adversus difficultates a- lias illis consulturus. Syrus σανδάλια vocat talaria, credo quod ad talos allegarentur. Sic & in Pedonis elegia, ub bi est sandalia, alii libri habent talaria ex gloffematis expo- sitione, ni fallor. Sed de hoc loco moneo lectorem, videat quæ incomparabilis doctrinæ vir Cl. Salmasius ad Tertul- liani pallium notavit.

καὶ μὴ ἐνδύσασθε δύο χιτῶνας] Id est, ne modo hanc, modo illam tunicam induite, ut solent qui iter faciunt aliis in iti- nere vestibus uti, aliis ubi in urbem aliquam advenerunt. Vide quæ ad Matthæum hoc loco. Hæc omnia, ut dixi, eo pertinent, ut Apostoli intelligant nullo majore paratu sibi ad iter opus fore quam si domi essent mansuri,

## 6:10
Vers. 10. from there] from that city: as also in the following verse.

Latin:

Vers. 10. ἐκεῖθεν] ex ea urbe: ut & sequenti commate.

## 6:11
Vers. 11. for a testimony against them] As a testimony of the Gospel being despised by them: for in detestation of such contempt the dust was shaken off. See on Matthew.

Latin:

Vers. 11. εἰς μαρτύριον ἀυτοῖς] In testimonium contemti ab ipfis Evangelii: nam in ejus comtemtus detestationem pul- vis excutiebatur. Vide ad Matthæum.

## 6:12
Vers. 12. ἵνα μετανοήσωσι] The sum of the Apostolic embassy is the same as that of the Baptist's preaching, from which Christ also made his beginning. They admonished men that they should truly and seriously perform repentance, that is, that they should make their ways good from evil. The cause was added, because that long-expected time of the heavenly kingdom had now arrived. For in order that each one might receive within himself the benefits of this kingdom, the remission of sins and the Holy Spirit, minds had to be prepared through repentance. They said this briefly, so that those who were held by a zeal for repentance might come to hear all the precepts pertaining to it from Christ himself.

Latin:

Vers. 12. ἵνα μετανοήσωσι] Legationis Apostolicæ summa eadem quæ κηρύγματος Baptistæ, unde & Christus initium fecit. Admonebant homines, ut vere ac serio pœni- tentiam agerent, id est vias suas de malis bonas facerent Causa addebatur, quia jam adventasset tempus illud diu ex- spectatum regni cœlestis. Ut enim hujus regni beneficia, remissionem peccatorum & Spiritum sanctum, intra se quis- que reciperet, per pœnitentiam animi erant præparandi. Hoc illi dicebant breviter, ut qui studio pœnitentiæ tene- bantur omnia præcepta eo pertinentia ab ipso Christo au- ditum venirent.

## 6:13
Vers. 13. ἤλειφον ἐλαίῳ] According to the ancient custom of the Hebrews, who, just as they were accustomed to join the imposition of hands to prayers undertaken for someone, so also [they used] anointing with oil for the sick for whom they were undertaken, in the hope of obtaining from God the relief and joy which is signified by oil. Which custom the early Christian Church willingly adopted, yet not so that healings were never performed without oil. The passage of James concerning oil is known, and the histories of healings in the Acts [are known] without oil. We have said elsewhere that the ancient Christians expressed whatever was found said allegorically in the sacred scriptures with visible signs. Hence it happened that oil was applied to baptism and to the imposition of hands alongside baptism, and sometimes other anointings. Paul had said, 'God who establishes and anoints us' 2 Cor. I. 21, and John in his first Epistle, ch. II. 20, 27, 'You have the anointing.' Τὸ χρῖσμα ὃ ἐλάβετε ἀπ' ἀυτῦ διδάσκει ὑμᾶς περὶ πάντων: which passages most people understand concerning the Spirit; the ancients [understand them] concerning faith itself which is sealed by the Spirit, with little difference: as appears from Clement of Alexandria, who introduces Christ speaking to us thus: 'I will anoint you with the ointment of faith through which you cast off corruption, and I will show the form of righteousness naked, through which you ascend to God.' Cyprian calls this faith, which was designated by anointing, the grace of Christ.

Epistle to Januarius. Tertullian had said: 'Thus also in us the anointing runs carnally, but profits spiritually,' showing that the anointing is signified through which Christ constituted us Priests. The writer of the responses to the Orthodox teaches us that those who were converted from error and admitted to the Church without a new baptism were also accustomed to be anointed. 'The error,' he says, 'is corrected, of the false doctrine by the change of mind, and of the baptism by the anointing with the holy myrrh.' But also Philo, according to Moses, interpreted oil by ancient tradition, 'a leading, a most far-shining light to those who do not grasp it lightly, but strongly and firmly from an inseparable and continuous persistence of what they see.' The passage is in the book whose title is 'On the worse attacking the better.'

These things are to be observed on account of the Papists, who strive to carve out the Sacrament of extreme unction from this: to whom, in later times, Grotius did not hesitate to pour cold water. That this does not concern the Sacrament of extreme unction is acknowledged by Hugo Victorinus, Altisiodorensis, Lombard, Bonaventure, Alensis, also Bellarmine in 'On Extreme Unction,' chapter 2, Reihing in 'Enchiridion Catholicum' against D. Hoe, p. 564, Jansenius, Gregor. de Valentia, Tirinus, etc.

PART III. Herod's judgment concerning Christ, with the history of the beheading of John.

Latin:

Vers. 13. ἤλειφον ἐλαίῳ] Ex more antiquo Hebræorum, qui ut manuum impositionem precibus pro aliquo susceptis adjungere solebant, ita & unctionem per oleum circa ægro- tos pro quibus suscipiebantur, in spem impetrandi a Deo le- niminis & gaudii quod per oleum significatur. Quem mo- rem prima Christianorum Ecclesia libenter usurpavit, non ita tamen, ut nunquam ἰάματα sine oleo exerceretur. No- tus Jacobi locus de oleo: & historiæ sanationum in Actis sine oleo. Diximus alibi Christianos veteres, quicquid ἀλ- ληγορικῶς dictum in sacris literis reperiebatur id expressisse visibilibus signis. Hinc factum ut & baptismo, & manuum impositioni juxta baptismum oleum adhiberetur, interdum & aliæ unctiones. Dixerat Paulus ὁ βεβαιῶν κὶ χρίσας ἡμᾶς Θεός 2. Cor. I. 21. & Iohannes Epistola I. c. II. 20. 27. ὑμεῖς τὸ χρίσμα ἔχετε. Τὸ χρῖσμα ὃ ἐλάβετε ἀπ' ἀυτῦ διδάσκει ὑμᾶς περὶ πάντων: quæ loca de Spiritu plerique accipiunt: vete- res de ipsa fide quæ per spiritum obsignatur, modico discri- mine: ut apparet ex Clemente Alexandrino qui Christum ita loquentem nobis introducit: χρίσω ὑμᾶς τῷ πίστεως ἀλείμ- ματι δι' ὗ τὴν φθορὰν ἀποβάλλετε, καὶ γυμνὸν δικαιοσύνης ἐπιδείξω τὸ σχῆμα δι' ὗ πρὸς ἳ Θεὸν ἀναβαίνετε. Hanc fidem quæ per unctionem designabatur gratiam Christi vocat Cyprianus

epistola ad Januarium. Tertullianus dixerat: Sic & in no- bis carnaliter currit unctio, sed spiritualiter proficit, cam un- ctionem significari ostendens per quam Christus nos con- stituit Sacerdotes.
