Docet nos Scriptor responsionum ad Or- thodoxos inungi solitos etiam eos qui ab errore conversi sine novo baptismo ad Ecclesiam admittebantur. Tò σφάλμα, inquit, διορθῦται τῆς μὲν κακοδοξίας τῇ μεταθέσει τῦ φρονήματος, τᾶ δὲ βαπτίσματος τῇ ἐπιχρίσει τᾶ ἁγίς μύρα. Sed & Philo apud Mosem antiqua traditione oleum inter- pretabatur, ἀγωγὴν φῶς τηλαυγέσατον ἀπαστράπτεσαν τοῖς μὴ ἀψικόρως κραταιῶς δὲ καὶ παγίως ἐξ ἀδιαςάτε κὶ συνεχοῦς ἐ- πιμονῆς ἐκλαβομένης ὧν ὁρῶσιν. Locus est in libro cui titulus περὶ τῶ τὸ χεῖρον τῷ κρείττονι φιλεῖν ἐπιτίθεσθαι.

Observanda haec propter Pontificios, extremae unctionis Sacramentum hinc exsculpere nitentes: quibus, posterioribus temporibus, frigidam suf- fundere non dubitavit Grotius. Non agi hic de Sacramento extremae unctionis agnoscunt Hugo Victorinus, Altisiodor. Lombardus, Bonaventura, Alensis, etiam Bellarminus de extr. unct. cap. 2. Reihingius in Enchir. Cathol. contra D. Hoe p. 564. Jansenius, Gregor. de Valent. Tirinus &c.

PARS III. Iudicium Herodis de Christo, cum bistoria decollationis Iohannis.

## 6:14
Verse 14. 'And King Herod heard (for it became manifest) his name.' I think it should be read thus, so that 'name' is in the accusative case, for which some have substituted 'his hearing' in place of an interpretation. For since it is sufficiently established that ancient books lacked marks of punctuation, I think that free judgment in that matter should be permitted to everyone. The Syrian, because his language could hardly bear this construction, added two words: 'concerning JESUS.'

If it is permissible to establish parentheses at will, will it not be easy to pervert Scripture, just as the Socinians have taught by their example? In all the Codices, the parenthesis is finally closed after the words 'his name.' That ancient original books lacked all marks of punctuation is a precarious hypothesis, and one not free from danger.

And he said. Herod himself, just as Matthew also narrates: but with suspicion injected by others, as we learn from Luke. It must be seen whether any Codices have 'they said,' just as the Latins once read. For Luke follows Mark closely.

That suspicion concerning a faulty reading rests on no solid foundation. Why seek Codices that read otherwise, when everything is correct, and Matthew agrees with Mark, according to the received reading?

The baptizer. Both from this passage and from that which we had above, 'two by two,' and below, 'companies by companies,' and in many others, it appears to be true what we said, that Mark 'hebraizes' more than the others. For others say 'the Baptist,' as does Josephus.

Latin:

Vers. 14. κὶ ἤκυσεν ὁ βασιλεὺς Ἡρώδης (φανερὸν γὰρ ἐγένετο) τὸ ὄνομα ἀυτᾶ] Ita legendum censeo, ut ὄνομα sit quarti casus pro quo interpretamenti vice quidam substituerunt ἀκοὴν ἀυτᾶ. Cum enim satis constet veteres libros caruis- se distinctionum notis, liberum cuique ea in re judicium permittendum arbitror. Syrus, quia hanc constructionem sua lingua vix patiebatur, duas voces addidit, de IESU.

Si integrum id est, parentheses pro arbitrio constituere, annon facile erit Scripturam perver- tere, quemadmodum exemplo suo docuere Soci- niani. In Codicibus omnibus clauditur demum parenthesis post voces τὸ ὄνομα ἀυτᾶ. Veteres libros originarios omnibus distinctionum notis ca- ruisse, hypothesis precaria est, nec periculo va- cat.

κὶ ἔλεγεν] Ipse Herodes, ut & Matthæus narrat: cæterum injecta ab aliis suspicione, ut ex Luca discimus. Videndum num qui Codices habeant ἔλεγον, sicut olim Latini lege- bant. Nam Marcum ferme sequitur Lucas.

Illa suspicio de vitiosa lectione nullo solido ni- titur fundamento. Cur quaerendi Codices aliter legentes, quum omnia se recte habeant, & Mat- thæus consonet Marco, juxta receptam lectionem.

ὁ βαπτίζων] Et ex hoc loco & ex eo quod supra habui- mus δύο δύο & infra συμπόσια συμπόσια & multis aliis appa- ret verum esse quod diximus Marcum plus cæteris ἑβραίζειν. Nam alii dicunt ὁ βαπτιςὴς, ut & Josephus.

## 6:15
Verse 15. 'That he is Elias.' Matt. 16:14.

That he is a prophet, or as one of the prophets. I am surprised that there is doubt about this reading, which very many codices prefer, and besides them the Syrian, Arab, and Latin interpreters. Add that the inserted 'or' renders no convenient sense, since the meaning of this reading is clear. For this was the opinion of those men concerning Christ, that he was not the Messiah, not Elias, not John, but a Prophet raised up by God equal to the ancient Prophets. Those in Luke felt differently: 'that one of the ancients has risen.'

Not undeservedly does he here refute Beza, whom Heinsius also supported, because he did not hesitate to insert the particle 'or' into the text: 'that he is a prophet or as one of the prophets.' It is an unbearable audacity to change the received text, which has such consenting Codices, and no necessity for the change appears, since the sense is perfectly fine.

Latin:

Vers. 15. ὅτι Ἠλίας ἐςιν] Matth. XVI. 14.

Ὅτι προφήτης ἐςιν, ἢ ὡς εἷς τῶν προφητῶν] Miror dubitari de hac lectione quam codices plurimi præferunt & præterea Syrus, Arabs, & Latinus interpretes. Adde quod interpo- situm ἢ sensum nullum commodum reddit: cum hujus le- ctionis aperta sit sententia. Nam hæc istorum homi- num de Christo opinatio fuit, esse eum non Messiam, non Eliam, non Johannem, sed Prophetam à Deo suscitatum pa- rem veteribus Prophetis. Diversum sentiebant illi apud Lucam ὅτι εἷς τῶν ἀρχαίων ἀνέςη.

Non immerito hic refellit Bezam, cui astipula- tus etiam Heinsius, quod particulam ἢ inserere tex- tui non dubitavit, ὅτι προφήτης ἐξὶν ἢ ὡς εἷς τῶν προφητῶν. Audacia est non ferenda receptum textum immutare, qui tam consentientes habet Codices, neque ulla apparet mutationis necessi- tas: quum sensus optime se habeat.

## 6:17
Verse 17. Having sent. That is, through satellites sent by him. The same manner of speaking is in Matt. 2:16 and 14:10.

τὴν γυναῖκα τᾶ ἀδελφᾶ σε] That is, the former wife of your brother, as also in 1 Cor. 5:1. For it seems her husband was dead, as we have said regarding Matthew.

Latin:

Vers. 17. ἀποσείλας] Id est per missos à se satellites. Idem loquendi genus Matth. II. 16. & XIV. 10.

τὴν γυναῖκα τᾶ ἀδελφᾶ σε] Id est τὴν πρὶν γυναῖκα τᾶ ἀδελ- φᾶ σε, ut & 1. Cor. V. 1. Videtur enim maritus eum fuisse mortuus, ut ad Matthæum diximus.

## 6:19
Vers. 19. ἐνεῖχεν ἀυτῷ] He was intent upon his destruction: just as also in Luke ch. 11:53. In Hebrew שטמו, as in Gen. 49:23. It is one thing to have ἔχειν κατά τινος, for μομφὴν (blame) is understood.

Latin:

Vers. 19. ἐνεῖχεν ἀυτῷ] Exitio ejus imminebat: quomo- do & apud Lucam cap. XI. 53. Hebraice שטמו, ut Ge- nes. XLIX. 23. Aliud est ἔχειν κατά τιν®, Subauditur enim μομφὴν.

## 6:20
Vers. 20. ἐφοβεῖτο] 'Just as he was so persuasive to men,' as Josephus speaks concerning this matter. The authority of John among the people was formidable to Herod. Matthew signifies the same thing when he says he feared the crowd. Indeed, under such kings or petty rulers, there is greater danger from a great reputation than from a bad one, and because of virtues, certain destruction.

δίκαιον κὶ ἅγιον] Josephus called him a good man, and an advisor of justice and piety.

κὶ συνετήρει ἀυτὸν] These things seem to me to be explained by the pluperfect tense, as such things are wont to be confused in Hebraism and by the Hellenists. He had observed, he says, Herod himself had observed John for a long time, and had done many things by his counsel, and was accustomed to hear him gladly. For these things must be referred to the time that preceded the free rebuke: yet so that afterwards also the memory of those things, and from that a greater fear of infamy, often wandered through Herod's mind: even then when, as Matthew says, he desired to kill him, being subject to his wife. Thus his mind tossed between the small remnants of a good conscience and the considerations of the honest, the useful, and the pleasant, both public and domestic. So true it is that there is no peace for the wicked.

ἀκύσας ἀυτῶ πολλὰ ἐποίε] What Mark says here about Herod, Josephus declares about the Jews in general: 'for they seemed to have done everything by his counsel.' And Christ himself: 'they were willing to rejoice for a season in his light.' There is no doubt that a most holy man, not the least part of his country, gave worthy counsel even in matters concerning the public safety. 'Deep furrow through the mind reaping, from which noble counsels spring.'

Latin:

Vers. 20. ἐφοβεῖτο] ὥσπερ τὸ ἐπὶ τοσόυδε πιθανὸν ἀυτῶ τοῖς ἀνθρώποις, ut Josephus hac de re loquitur. Auctoritas Jo- hannis apud populum Herodi erat formidolosa. Idem si- gnificat Matthæus, cum dicit ἐφοβήθη ἲ ὄχλον. Nimirum sub ejusmodi regibus aut regulis majus periculum est ex magna fama quam ex mala, & ob virtutes certissimum exi- tium.

δίκαιον κὶ ἅγιον] ἀγαθὸν ἄνδρα dixit Josephus, & monito- rem δικαιοσύνης κὶ ἐυσεβείας.

κὶ συνετήρει ἀυτὸν] Hæc explicanda mihi videntur per tem- pus plusquamperfectum, ut solent ista in Hebraismo & ab Hellenistis confundi. Observaverat, inquit, ipse Herodes Johannem diu, multaque fecerat ejus consilio, & libentes eum audire erat solitus. Hæc enim referenda sunt ad tem- pus quod præcesserat liberam objurgationem: ita tamen, ut postea quoque earum rerum memoria & ex eo major in- famiæ metus sæpe animo Herodis oberraverit: etiam tum cum, ut Matthæus ait, interficere illum cuperet uxori obno- xius. Ita se volutabat animus inter exiguas reliquias bonæ mentis rationesque honesti, utilis ac jucundi, publicas ac domesticas. Adeo verum est pacem non esse impiis.

ἀκύσας ἀυτῶ πολλὰ ἐποίε] Quod de Herode hic dicit Marcus, idem de Judæis in universum Josephus prædicat: πάντα γὰρ ἐῴκεσαν τῇ συμβουλῇ ἀυτῶ πράξαντες. Et Christus ipse: ἠθέλησαν ἀγαλλιασθῆναι πρὸς ὥραν ἐν τῷ φωτὶ ἀυτῶ. Dubitandum non est, quin vir sanctissimus, pars patriæ suæ non minima, etiam in rebus publicam salutem spectanti- bus se digna consilia dederit. Βαθεῖαν ἄλοκα διὰ φρενὸς καρπέμενος Ἀφ' ἧς τὰ κεδνὰ βλάσανει βελέυματα.

## 6:21
Vers. 21. ἐυκαίρῳ] Opportuna (opportune) for the plotter, who, by wine, love, and the conspiracy of flatterers, easily hoped that the wavering mind of her husband could be impelled.

Μεγιςᾶσι] John also uses this word, famous in the East, in the divine Apocalypse ch. 6:15. Those who were called by the Chaldean word רברבנין, as in Dan. 5:33 and other places, were called by this Greek word, in Persian אחשדרפנים, that is, Satraps or rather ἄρχοντες σατραπῶν (rulers of satraps) as it is in the Greek version of Esther 9:3. The lesser courts imitated the words of the greater: 'The ox once broke his own, the great as the small.'

Χιλιάρχοις] For Herod had an army prepared at that time against Aretas, 'the force having been gathered,' says Josephus.

Τοῖς πρώτοις τῆς Γαλιλαίας] The magistrates of the towns. Τοῖς πρώτοις τῆς πόλεως in Novella 123. The old interpreter translated it 'the primates of the city.' They were called according to their number decemprimi, penteprimi, and in Latin quinqueprimi, decemprimi.

Latin:

Vers. 21. ἐυκαίρῳ] Opportuna insidiatrici, quæ vino, amo- re, & adulatorum conspiratione facile sperabat impelli pos- se nutantem mariti animum.

Μεγιςᾶσι] Usurpat hanc vocem, celebrem in oriente, etiam Johannes in divina Apocalypsi c. VI. 15. Vocabantur ita Græco vocabulo qui Chaldaico רברבנין ut Dan. V. 33. & aliis locis, Persice אחשדרפנים, id est Satra- pæ aut potius ἄρχοντες σατραπῶν ut est in Græca versione E- stheris IX. 3. Aulæ minores majorum vocabula imirabantur: Magnus ut exiguum bos suum ruperat olim.

Χιλιάρχοις] Nam exercitum sub id tempus paratum habe- bat Herodes adversus Aretam, Δυνάμεως συλλεγείσης inquit Josephus.

Τοῖς πρώτοις τῆς Γαλιλαίας] Magistratibus oppidorum. Τοῖς πρώτοις τῆς πόλεως in Novella 123. Vetus interpres transtulit primates civitatis. Vocabantur pro numero δε- καπρῶτοι, πεντεπρῶτοι, & Latine quinqueprimi, decemprimi.

## 6:23
Vers. 23. ἕως ἡμίσες τῆς βασιλείας με] See what I wrote on Matthew 14:7.

Latin:

Vers. 23. ἕως ἡμίσες τῆς βασιλείας με] Vide quæ ad Mat- thæum XIV. 7.

## 6:25
Vers. 25. Θέλω] I ask or I would like, as in Matt. 26:39. So it is several times in these books, among others John 6:21 and below 10:35. And in this sense you will often find the Hebrew word צפח.

ἐξ ἀυτῆς] Besides Paul, Luke uses this word several times in Acts 10:33, 11:11, 23:30. The Syrians are accustomed to sometimes suppress the word שעת in speech, which our writers imitate. But here and in other places, the Syrian has expressed what was lacking in the Greek language.

Latin:

Vers. 25. Θέλω] Peto aut vellem, ut Matth. XXVI. v. 39. Ita aliquoties in his libris, Inter alia Joh. VI. 21. & infra X. 35. Et hoc sensu sæpe reperies Hebræum צפח.

ἐξ ἀυτῆς] Præter Paulum Lucas hac voce utitur aliquoties Act. X. 33. c. XI. 11. c. XXIII. 30. Solent Syri in sermone supprimere interdum שעת quod imitantur nostri scripto- res. At hic atque aliis in locis Syrus quod Græco sermo- ni deerat expressit.

## 6:26
Vers. 26. ἀθετῆσαι] Greek grammarians also interpret ἀθετεῖν as ἀτιμάζειν, καταφρονεῖν. And it is used in this way also in Luke 7:30, 10:16, and John 12:48. It corresponds to the Hebrew פעם.

Latin:

Vers. 26. ἀθετῆσαι] ἀθετεῖν etiam Græcorum Gramma- tici interpretantur ἀτιμάζειν, καταφρονεῖν. Atque ita usur- patur etiam Luc. VII. 30. c. X. 16. & Joh. XII. 48. Respon- det Hebræo פעם.

## 6:27
Vers. 27. σπεκυλάτωρα] Emperor Hadrian in a letter to Aquilius Bradua: 'Let neither the speculators claim for themselves, nor the optiones desire, those things by which one is despoiled at the moment he is punished.' Valentinian, Theodosius, and Arcadius: 'The attendants of the ordinary judges who have attained the rank of either speculators or ordinarii.' Seneca: 'The centurion in charge of the execution orders the speculator to sheath his sword.' To which must be added the passages of Tacitus and Firmicus cited by others, who also proved this word, worn by the usage of the Hebrews, with clear testimonies.

Latin:

Vers. 27. σπεκυλάτωρα] Adrianus Imperator in epistola ad Aquilium Braduam: neque speculatores ultro sibi vindicent, neque optiones ea desiderent, quibus spoliatur quo momento quis punitus est. Valentinianus Theodosius & Arcadius: Ordi- nariorum judicum apparitores qui vel speculatorum vel ordina- riorum attigerint gradum. Seneca: Centurio supplicio præpo- situs condere gladium speculatorem jubet. Quibus addenda loca Taciti & Firmici citata ab aliis, qui & Hebræorum usu tritam hanc vocem manifestis testimoniis probarunt.

## 6:29
Vers. 29. τὸ πτῶμα] גויה.

PART IV. The miracle of the feeding of the 5000 men.

Latin:

Vers. 29. τὸ πτῶμα] גויה.

PARS IV. Miraculum cibationis 5000. virorum.

## 6:30
Vers. 30. πάντα κὶ ὅσα ἐποίησαν κὶ ὅσα ἐδίδαξαν] πάντα, that is, those diverse judgments of men concerning Christ about which he had treated above in verses 14-15. For while the Apostles were carrying out their mission, they had understood these things. Furthermore, they reported what they had taught, as well as what they had done: which pertains to the miracles. A similar expression is found in Luke, Acts 1: 'concerning all that Jesus began both to do and to teach.' It is the duty of ambassadors to report what has been done regarding each part of their mandate: Christ had commanded the Apostles to preach repentance, and to cast out demons and heal diseases in confirmation of their words.

Latin:

Vers. 30. πάντα κὶ ὅσα ἐποίησαν κὶ ὅσα ἐδίδαξαν] πάντα, id est, diversa illa hominum de Christo judicia de quibus a- gerat supra v. 14. 15. Nam dum legationem suam ob- eunt Apostoli ista intellexerant. Præterea vero renuntia- runt, tum quæ docuerant, tum quæ fecerant: quod ad miracula pertinet. Similis locutio apud Lucam Actor. I. περὶ πάντων ὧν ἤρξατο ὁ Ἰησῦς ποιεῖν τε κὶ διδάσκειν. Legato- rum est de singulis mandati partibus quid actum sit renun- tiare: Mandaverat autem Christus Apostolis κηρύσσειν με- τάνοιαν, & in fidem dictorum ejicere dæmonia & morbos sanare.

## 6:31
ANNOTATIONS ON MARK CH. VI. v. 31. 32. 33. 35.

Vers. 31. Δεῦτε ὑμεῖς, ὑπάγωμεν αὐτοὶ κατ' ἰδίαν] It seems to me that the Syrian read it in this manner, since in other codices ὑπάγωμεν is missing, and in others ὑμεῖς & αὐτοὶ. That reading does not displease me, provided that αὐτοὶ is placed for ἡμεῖς.

Grotius again corrects the text from mere suspicion. For he had no Codex that read it thus. Greek copies ordinarily and commonly have it thus: Δεῦτε ὑμεῖς αὐτοὶ κατ' ἰδίαν: and the sense is clear in itself: Come you yourselves apart. Erasmus interprets, you alone, i.e., with others dismissed: For it is placed, he says, αὐτοὶ for solis: there is no reason why this exposition should be judged by Beza as clearly violent: If, however, it pleases less, why should the Greek not be explained according to the letter and κατὰ πόδα, as they say? Beza reads δεῦτε ὑπάγωμεν in one ancient Codex. But why should that one Codex be preferred to the others?

Latin:

ANNOT. AD MARCI C. VI. v. 31. 32. 33. 35.

Vers. 31. Δεῦτε ὑμεῖς, ὑπάγωμεν αὐτοὶ κατ' ἰδίαν] Hunc in modum legisse mihi videtur Syrus, cum in aliis codicibus desit ὑπάγωμεν, in aliis ὑμεῖς & αὐτοὶ. Mihi ista lectio non displicet ut sit αὐτοὶ positum pro ἡμεῖς.

Iterum è sola suspicione textum corrigit Gro- tius. Nullum enim Codicem habuit, qui ita lege- rit. Ordinarie & communiter sic habent Græca exemplatia: Δεῦτε ὑμεῖς αὐτοὶ κατ' ἰδίαν: & sen- sus est per se luculentus: Venite vos ipsi seorsim. Erasmus interpretatur, vos soli, h. e. dimislis cæ- teris: Positum enim est, inquit, αὐτοὶ pro solis: quæ expositio cur violenta plane judicetur à Beza, cau- sa nulla est: Si tamen minus placeat, cur non se- cundum literam & κατὰ πόδα, ut ajunt, Græca ex- ponantur? Beza in uno vetusto Codice legit δεῦ- τε ὑπάγωμεν. Sed cur unus ille Codex cæteris præferretur?

## 6:32
Vers. 32. κῂ ἀπῆλθον εἰς ἔρημον τόπον] Even the reading ἀναβάντες εἰς τὸ πλοῖον, which has crept into certain Codices in this place, shows that the Greek text was interpolated by someone after the manner of the Latin version.

Latin:

Vers. 32. κῂ ἀπῆλθον εἰς ἔρημον τόπον] Etiam quæ hoc loco in Codices quosdam irrepsit lectio ἀναβάντες εἰς τὸ πλοῖον, ostendit ab aliquo interpolatum esse Græcum tex- tum ad modum Latinæ versionis.

## 6:33
Vers. 33. κῂ προῆλθον αὐτοὺς] That which our codices have here after those words, κῂ συνῆλθον πρὸς αὐτοὺς, is superfluous, and is recognized neither by the Syrian nor by the Latin. Wherefore, since other codices have ἦλθον & αὐτῷ, one might suspect that it was written at the beginning by scribes as κῂ ἦλθον πρὸ αὐτῦ, which was an interpretation of those words of Mark which we have placed. But afterwards, when it had crept into the text, it was changed so that the same thing would not be said twice.

Our Codices have not πρὸς αὐτοὺς, but πρὸς αὐτὸν. Why should that which makes sense be considered superfluous? Could they not have anticipated the Apostles into the desert, even if they did not come to Christ immediately? The suspicion about another reading, because it rests on no foundation, is vain.

Latin:

Vers. 33. κῂ προῆλθον αὐτοὺς] Quod hic nostri codices post illa verba habent, κῂ συνῆλθον πρὸς αὐτοὺς, supervacuum est, neque agnoscitur aut à Syro, aut à Latino. Quare cum alii codices habeant ἦλθον & αὐτῷ, suspicari liceat initio scriptum fuisse à librariis κῂ ἦλθον πρὸ αὐτῦ, quod inter- pretamentum erat eorum quæ posuimus Marci verborum. Sed postea cum in textum irrepsisset mutatum ne bis idem diceretur.

Non πρὸς αὐτοὺς, sed πρὸς αὐτὸν habent Codi- ces nostri. Cur supervacuum censeatur quod ad sen- sum facit? Annon prævenire Apostolos poterant in desertum, etsi ad Christum non venerint statim? Suspicio de alia scriptione, quia nullo nititur fun- damento, vana est.

## 6:35
Vers. 35. ὥρας πολλῆς γενομένης] He calls ὥραν not the whole day, but a part of the day, as below XI. 1. ὀψίας ἤδη ὄυσης τῆς ὥρας. Therefore he seems to call that part which is expressed by the name of a greater number, πολλὴν.

Latin:

Vers. 35. ὥρας πολλῆς γενομένης] ὥραν vocat non diem to- tum, sed partem diei, ut infra XI. 1. ὀψίας ἤδη ὄυσης τῆς ὥρας. Πολλὴν ergo dicere videtur eam partem quæ majoris numeri nomine exprimitur.

## 6:36
Vers. 36. κύκλῳ] See above this manner of speaking ch. III. 34. Thus κύκλῳ τῆς Ἱερουσαλὴμ LXX. Jer. XXXII. 44.

τί γὰρ φάγωσιν] for ὃ φάγωσιν. Thus in Matthew ch. XV. 32. ὀυκ ἔχουσι τί φάγωσι.

Latin:

Vers. 36. κύκλῳ] Vide supra hoc loquendi genus c. III. 34. Ita κύκλῳ τῆς Ἱερουσαλὴμ LXX. Jer. XXXII. 44.

τί γὰρ φάγωσιν] pro ὃ φάγωσιν. Ita apud Matthæum c. XV. 32. ὀυκ ἔχουσι τί φάγωσι.

## 6:37
Vers. 37. ἀπελθόντες ἀγοράσωμεν] Since it is established that Christ had a γλωσσόκομον, and in it some money from the collection of friends, both for the uses of his own and his twelve companions, and for the poor, I do not see why some should so abhor believing that he had two hundred denarii at this time when he had withdrawn from the towns into the fields as if to stay there for a while. For it is not for nothing that the Apostles name this sum of money; which, however, as we learn from John, in their own judgment could not suffice to satisfy such an immense multitude. The sense therefore seems to be what some have indicated: surely, so that nothing can be desired from us, we are prepared to spend as much money as we have with us on these men, not indeed to satisfy them, but to refresh them a little against hunger.

Latin:

Vers. 37. ἀπελθόντες ἀγοράσωμεν] Cum Christum con- stet γλωσσόκομον habuisse, & in eo ex amicorum collatione pecuniæ aliquid, tum in suos & duodecim comitum, tum in pauperum usus, non video cur aliqui adeo abhorreant cre- dere fuisse illi hoc tempore cum ab oppidis in agros velut i- bi mansurus aliquandin secessisset denarios ducentos. Ne- que enim de nihilo est quod hanc pecuniæ summam Apo- stoli nominant; quæ tamen, ut ex Johanne discimus, ipso- rum judicio sufficere non poterat tam immensæ multitudi- ni satiandæ. Sensus ergo esse videtur quem nonnulli indica- runt: sane ne quid à nobis desiderari possit parati sumus quantum apud nos est pecuniæ impendere his hominibus, non satiandis quidem, sed contra inediam parumper refo- vendis.

## 6:39
Vers. 39. ἀνακλῖναι πάντας] Thus ἀνακλῖναι αὐτὸν is in Lucian.

συμπόσια συμπόσια] By distinct groups of guests. The number of hundreds or even fifties is greater than that the name of a mess-group (contubernium) should sufficiently correspond to it, which name has its own use in the Paschal lamb which was eaten κατὰ φρατρίας by tens or twenties.

Latin:

Vers. 39. ἀνακλῖναι πάντας] Sic ἀνακλῖναι αὐτὸν est apud Lucianum.

συμπόσια συμπόσια] Per distinctos convivarum ordines. Numerus centenorum aut etiam quinquagenorum major est quam ut contubernii nomen ei satis respondeat, cui no- mini suus usus est in agno Paschali qui κατὰ φρατρίας de- num aut vicenum edebatur.

## 6:40
Verse 40. πρασιαὶ πρασιαὶ] A nominative in place of an indeclinable, as often among the Hebrews. See Ps. LXXIII. 28. Est, VI 7. The Syriac of Luke XX:II. 41. Such is John Ev. I. 14. πλήρης for πλήρους. Such is ἀπὸ τῦ ὁ ὢν Apoc. I. 4. & I. 5. ἀπὸ Ἰησῦ Χριςῦ ὁ μάρτυς ὁ πισός. Nor is the construction unlike that in Josephus: πάντων δι' ἀνθρώπων διημιέργημα ὄντων τῷ Θεῷ. Thus also in Euripides in the Phoenissae: Μολὼν δὲ πέμψον' μ' Ὀιδίπου κλεινὸς γόνος Ματρός τε κατὰ, λοξίω τ' ἐπ' ἐσχάρας Ἐντῷ δ' ἐπιστάτουσιν ἀργείοι πόλη. In which passage μόλων is openly placed for μόλοντος: as also in that of Herodotus: ἁλὸς γενομένη πᾶσα ἡ ὀθόνη, χεὶρ μεγάλη συνάγεται. Thus ἀσράπτων is placed for ἀστράπτοντα in the second book of the Iliad, as Eustathius noted: and πῖνον for πίνοντι in the first book of the Odyssey. Thus also in Proclus several times: καλὰ τῦτο, χαρίεν τῦτο.

ἀνὰ ἑκατὸν κῂ ἀνὰ πεντήκοντα] That is, neither more than a hundred, nor fewer than fifty. Therefore, sixty, seventy, or eighty could recline together.

Latin:

Vers. 40. πρασιαὶ πρασιαὶ] Nominativus vice ἀκλίτου, ut sæpe apud Hebræos. Vide Ps. LXXIII. 28. Est, VI 7. Syrum Luc. XX:II. 41. Tale est Joh. Ev. I. 14. πλήρης pro πλήρους. Tale ἀπὸ τῦ ὁ ὢν Apoc. I. 4. & I. 5. ἀπὸ Ἰησῦ Χριςῦ ὁ μάρτυς ὁ πισός. Nec absimilis apud Josephum constructio πάντων δι' ἀνθρώπων διημιέργημα ὄντων τῷ Θεῷ. Sic & apud Euripi- dem Phœnissis: Μολὼν δὲ πέμψον' μ' Ὀιδίπου κλεινὸς γόνος Ματρός τε κατὰ, λοξίω τ' ἐπ' ἐσχάρας Ἐντῷ δ' ἐπιστάτουσιν ἀργείοι πόλη. Quo in loco μόλων aperte positum est pro μόλοντος: ut & illo Herodoti ἁλὸς γενομένη πᾶσα ἡ ὀθόνη, χεὶρ μεγάλη συνάγε- ται. Sic ἀσράπτων pro ἀστράπτοντα positum in secundo I- liados notavit Eustathius: & πῖνον pro πίνοντι primo Odysseæ. Sic & apud Proclum aliquoties καλὰ τῦτο, χαρίεν τῦτο.

ἀνὰ ἑκατὸν κῂ ἀνὰ πεντήκοντα] Id est nec plures centenis, nec pauciores quinquagenis. Potuerunt igitur simul ac- cumbere sexageni, septuageni, octuageni.

## 6:43
Verse 43. καὶ ἀπὸ τῶν ἰχθύων] That is, some of the fish. Mark added this: yet he did not think it necessary to express how much it was. Thus Matt. XXVII, 9. ἀπὸ υἱῶν Ἰσραὴλ is placed for τινες τῶν υἱῶν Ἰσραὴλ.

PART V. The walking of Jesus on the sea.

Latin:

Vers. 43. καὶ ἀπὸ τῶν ἰχθύων] Id est τῇ τῶν ἰχθύων τι. Addi- dit hoc Marcus: neque tamen quantum fuerit putavit ex- primendum. Ita Matth. XXVII, 9. ἀπὸ υἱῶν Ἰσραὴλ posi- tum pro τινες τῶν υἱῶν Ἰσραὴλ.

PARS V. Ambulatio Jesu in mari.

## 6:46
Verse 46. καὶ ἀποταξάμενος αὐτοῖς] Namely, to the crowd. A construction according to the sense, as below VIII. 1. παμπόλλου ὄχλου ὄντος, καὶ μὴ ἐχόντων ἀπολύσας τοὺς ὄχλους is in Matthew. First Christ sent away the Apostles, then he bade farewell to the multitude: then he betook himself to the mountain to pray. This order is in Matthew: nor is there any doubt that Mark said the same thing in other words.

Latin:

Vers. 46. καὶ ἀποταξάμενος αὐτοῖς] Nimirum τῷ ὄχλῳ. Constructio πρὸς τὸ σημαινόμενον, ut infra IIX. 1. παμπόλλου ὄχλου ὄντος, καὶ μὴ ἐχόντων ἀπολύσας τοὺς ὄχλους est apud Mat- thæum. Prius Christus Apostolos ablegavit,tum valedixit multitudini: deinde in montem se oratum contulit. Hic ordo est apud Matthæum: nec dubium quin idem aliis ver- bis dixerit Marcus.

## 6:48
Verse 48. ἐν τῷ ἐλαύνειν] ἐλαύνειν concerning a ship is properly κωπηλατεῖν, to row. Xenophon: οἱ δὲ ἐλαύνειν διοι κατὰ μίσθον τὰς ναῦλας ἀνίσταυε. I see no reason why one should depart from this interpretation, which the Syriac and Latin follow. The difficulty of the navigation is described by the fact that it was necessary to struggle against the wind with oars.

ἤθελε παρελθεῖν αὐτοὺς] He did not intend to enter the ship, unless the Apostles had expressed this by prayers. This is what John says: ἤθελον οὖν λαβεῖν αὐτὸν εἰς τὸ πλοῖον, that is, they were praying, in the way we said above that τὸ θέλειν is taken.

Latin:

Vers. 48. ἐν τῷ ἐλαύνειν] ἐλαύνειν de navi proprie est κω- πηλατεῖν, remigare. Xenophon: οἱ δὲ ἐλαύνειν διοι κατὰ μίσθον τὰς ναῦλας ἀνίσταυε. Causæ nihil video cur ab hac in- terpretatione quam sequuntur Syrus & Latinus receden- dum sit. Molestia navigationis eo describitur quod con- tra ventum remis obniti necesse esset.

ἤθελε παρελθεῖν αὐτοὺς] Non intraturus navem, nisi Apo- stoli hoc precibus a vill expressissent. Hoc est quod Io- hannes dicit ἤθελον οὖν λαβεῖν αὐτὸν εἰς τὸ πλοῖον id est orabant, quomodo τὸ θέλειν sumi supra diximus.

## 6:51
Verse 51. ἐκστάσει] מִשְׁתָּאֶה as Gen. VIII, 6. Λίαν ἐκ περισσοῦ] This is what is said several times in Paul as περισσοτέρως: more than exceedingly. ἐξίσταντο καὶ ἐθαύμαζον] That is, they were amazed, wondering: as the Syriac also understood it.

Latin:

Vers. 51. ἐκστάσει] מִשְׁתָּאֶה ut Gen, VIII, 6. Λίαν ἐκ περισσοῦ] Hoc est quod apud Paulum aliquoties dicitur περισσοτέρως: plus quam vehementer. ἐξίσταντο καὶ ἐθαύμαζον] Id est θαυμάζοντες ἐξίσταντο: ut & Syrus accepit.

## 6:52
Verse 52. οὐ γὰρ συνῆκαν ἐπὶ τοῖς ἄρτοις] They had not attended sufficiently to the magnitude of the previous miracle: for if they had, there was no reason why this walking upon the sea and the calming of the storm should happen so contrary to their expectation. We have observed that συνιέναι is taken this way several times in Matthew. Nor did Luke use it otherwise in chapter II. 50.

πεπωρωμένη] Thus also below VIII. 17. οὔπω νοεῖτε οὐδὲ συνίετε; ἔτι πεπωρωμένην ἔχετε τὴν καρδίαν ὑμῶν; We have said that this word signifies any vice whatsoever that has become ingrained by age: such as was in the Apostles, a lack of attention, especially concerning those things which pertained to the divine power of Christ.

PART II. OF CHAPTER VI. Things which are begun to be done from the third Passover: and thus begins PART III. of the Gospel of St. Mark. The healing of many in the land of Gennesaret.

Latin:

Vers. 52. οὐ γὰρ συνῆκαν ἐπὶ τοῖς ἄρτοις] Non attenderant satis ad miraculi prioris magnitudinem: quod si se issent, non erat cur ista super mare ambulatio & sedatio tempesta- tis adeo illis præter opinionem eveniret. Ita συνιέναι sumi aliquoties apud Matthæum observavimus. Nec aliter usus est Lucas cap. II. 50.

πεπωρωμένη] Ita & infra IIX. 17. οὔπω νοεῖτε οὐδὲ συνίετε; ἔτι πεπωρωμένην ἔχετε τὴν καρδίαν ὑμῶν; Diximus hac voce signi- ficari qualecunque vitium vetustate inolitum: quale erat in Apostolis ἀπροσεξία, præsertim circa ea quæ ad divinam Christi potentiam pertinebant.

PARS II. CAPITIS VI. Quæ inchoantur a tertio Paschate gesta: & ita incipit PARS III. Evangelii S. Marci. Multorum in terra Genesareth sanatio.

## 6:54
Verse 54. ἐπιγνόντες αὐτὸν] ἄνδρες. It is understood which Matthew expressed: οἱ ἄνδρες τοῦ τόπου, which is also added here by the Syriac, and from an interpretation has insinuated itself into certain Greek codices, although the Latin does not recognize it.

Latin:

Vers. 54. ἐπιγνόντες αὐτὸν] ἄνδρες. Subintelligitur quod expressit Matthæus οἱ ἄνδρες τοῦ τόπου, quod & hic à Syro est additum, & ex interpretamento in quosdam Græcos codices se insinuavit, cum non agnoscat Latinus.

## 6:55
Vers. 55. ὅπου ἤκουον ὅτι ἐκεῖ ἐστι] Wherever they had understood him to be. ὅπου with ἐκεῖ is like אֲשֶׁר לְךָ. For thus the Syriac and Latin rightly understood it. So also ἧς θυγάτριον αὐτῆς below VII. 25.

Latin:

Vers. 55. ὅπου ἤκουον ὅτι ἐκεῖ ἐστι] Ubicunque esse cum in- tellexerant. ὅπου cum ἐκεῖ est ut אֲשֶׁר לְךָ. Ita enim re- cte acceperunt Syrus & Latinus. Sic & ἧς θυγάτριον αὐτῆς infra VII. 25.

## 6:56
Vers. 56. ἐν ἀγοραῖς] In more frequented places בַּחוּצוֹת. ἥπτοντο αὐτοῦ] of Jesus, not of the hem. In Matthew it is more simply ἥψαντο. It is credible, however, that by many not the hem was touched, but another part of the body or garment. In those, however, who were touching Christ are included also those who touched the hem.

Latin:

Vers. 56. ἐν ἀγοραῖς] In locis frequentioribus בַּחוּצוֹת. ἥπτοντο αὐτοῦ] τοῦ Ἰησοῦ nov τοῦ κρασπέδου. Apud Matthæum simplicius est ἥψαντο. Credibile autem est à multis non fimbriam tactam, sed aliam aut corporis aut vestis partem. In iis autem qui Christum tangebant comprehenduntur & hi qui tetigerunt fimbriam.

## 7:1 Argument
CHAPTER VII. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

The Pharisees and Jerusalem priests, seeing that the disciples of Jesus were taking food with unwashed hands, complain about the neglected traditions, but are convicted of hypocrisy from Isaiah (ch. XXIX. 13), because they taught the commandments of men, neglecting the precepts of God, such as that concerning the love of parents, to which they preferred Corban; and the people are instructed concerning those things which defile a man: In the borders of Tyre and Sidon, a Syrophoenician woman meets him, whose possessed daughter he delivered, after he had compared himself to the dogs to be satisfied with the crumbs of the children; and he healed a mute and deaf man, departing from those borders, by saying Ephphatha.

There are three parts: I. Information concerning the traditions of the Pharisees, to v. 23. II. The deliverance of the daughter of the Canaanite woman from a demon, to v. 30. III. The restoration of the mute and deaf, to v. 37.

PART I. Information concerning the traditions of the Pharisees.

Latin:

CAPUT VII. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Pharisæi, & Sacerdotes Hierosolymitani vi- dentes, quod illotis manibus cibum cape- rent discipuli Iesu, de neglectis traditioni- bus queruntur, sed hypocriseos ex Esaia (c. XXIX. 13.) arguuntur, quod docerent man- data hominum, Dei negligentes præcepta, utpote de parentum dilectione,cui præfere- bant Corban; & instituitur populus de iis, quæ hominem coinquinant: In finibus Tyri, & Sidonis occurrit ei Syrophœnissa, cujus obsessam filiam, postquam catellis de micis liberorum saturandis se compa- rarat, liberavit: mutumque ac surdum e- grediens è finibus illis, doce Hephetah sana- vit.

Partes sunt tres: I. De traditionibus Pharisaeorum informatio, ad v. 23. II. Filia Cananaeae à Daemone liberatio, ad v. 30. III. Muti & surdi restitutio, ad v. 37.

PARS I. De traditionibus Pharisaeorum informatio.

## 7:2
Vers. 2. ἐμέμψαντο) to them, that is, as in Heb. IIX. 18. First they were angry, then they also instituted an accusation, comm. 5.

Latin:

Vers. 2. ἐμέμψαντο) αὐτοῖς scilicet, ut Hebr. IIX. 18. Primum succensuerunt, deinde etiam accusationem instituêrunt comm. 5.

## 7:3
Vers. 3. καὶ πάντες οἱ ἰουδαῖοι) Mark shows that this was not a peculiar institution of Pharisaism: but a rite commonly observed, by those, namely, who followed the sentences received by all the masters: which was the greatest part of the Jews. For otherwise the Sadducees and certain others did not addict themselves to such institutions. The origin of the custom is from the contact of a corpse, with a translation made to foreigners as being no less impure than corpses.

πυγμῇ) Thus the LXX translate באגרף Exod. XXI. 18, with a clenched fist, as Cicero speaks. For they washed the hand composed into a fist with the other hand, as has been shown from Moses Gerundensis and others. The same Jacob Baalturim, a Hebrew master, hands down in the Path of Life. But what Theophylact says, ἄχρι τοῦ ἀγκῶνος (up to the elbow), he spoke the truth in that, but it is something that can hardly be adapted to the meaning of this word.

This explanation of Grotius is to be preferred to those which Scaliger, Camero, and Capellus brought forward in Balduinus Walaeus: which it is of no use to recount.

Νίψωνται) ירחצו of Leviticus XV. 11.

Latin:

Vers. 3. καὶ πάντες οἱ ἰουδαῖοι) Ostendit Marcus non fuisse hoc peculiare institutum Pharisaeîsmi: sed ritum communiter observatum, ab illis scilicet omnibus magistrorum receptas sententias sequebantur: quae Judaeorum pars maxima. Nam alioqui Sadducaei & alii quidam ejusmodi institutis se non addicebant. Origo moris à contactu cadaveris, translatione facta ad alienigenas ut non minus quam cadavera impuros.

πυγμῇ) Ita vertunt LXX. באגרף Exod. XXI. 18. facto pugno, ut Cicero loquitur. Nam manum in pugnum compositam manu altera lavabant, ut ex Mose Gerundensi atq; aliis ostensum est. Tradit idem Jacobus Baalturim magister Hebraeus in semita vitae. Quod autem Theophylactus dicit ἄχρι τοῦ ἀγκῶνος, in eo verum dixit, sed quod ad vocis hujus significationem aptari vix potest.

Praeferenda haec Grotii explicatio illis quas Scaliger, Camero, Capellus apud Balduinum Walaeum protulêre: quas recensere nihil attinet.

Νίψωνται) ירחצו Levitici XV. 11.

## 7:4
Vers. 4. ἀπὸ τῆς ἀγορᾶς) Supply γενόμενοι. Those who thought something was missing added ὅταν ἔλθωσι, which is not recognized by the Syriac, nor is it necessary. In the market and other public places there were many ἀλλόφυλοι (foreigners), by whom they feared they could be contaminated even unknowingly. For a similar reason, on the Preparation Day, they feared to enter the Praetorium, because it would be full of Roman men.

Βαπτίζωνται) They purged themselves with greater care from contact with the market, indeed not only by washing their hands, but also by immersing their body. But since this custom was received among almost all Jews due to the consenting authority of the masters, it is sufficiently understood from this that those who were called by the peculiar name of their sect ἡμεροβαπτισταὶ (daily-baptizers) did more than the others: namely, by using immersion even when they had not gone out of the house; or in the morning, as noted by Clement of Alexandria; or even more often, as that Batus in Josephus, ψυχρῷ ὕδατι τὴν ἡμέραν καὶ τὴν νύκτα πολλάκις λούμενος πρὸς ἁγνείαν (bathing in cold water day and night many times for the sake of purity). In the Constitutions of Clement, it is read concerning the same: καὶ ἡμεροβαπτισταὶ ἐὰν μὴ βαπτίσωνται οὐκ ἐσθίουσιν· ἀλλὰ καὶ τὰς κλίνας καὶ τοὺς πίνακας ἤτοι κρατῆρας καὶ ποτήρια καὶ καθίσματα ἐὰν μὴ καθάρωσιν ὕδατι οὐδενὶ χρῶνται (and the daily-baptizers, if they are not baptized, do not eat; but also they do not use beds, tables, or bowls, cups, and seats, unless they cleanse them with water). Wherefore in Justin, where the names of the Jewish sects are listed, I think it should be read, Φαρισαίων καὶ βαπτιστῶν, not βαριζαίων βαπτιστῶν.

ἐκ ἐσθίουσι) Lest a new pollution be added through food. They washed for the sake of religion before food and after food, as the Talmudic writings teach.

παρέλαβον) קבלו. παραλαμβάνειν and παραδιδόναι are related, as we noted regarding Matthew.

ξεστῶν) He understands sextarii. For Cicero also says a sextarius of water. But just as that word, derived from the Roman language through the whole world, underwent a transposition of letters among the Greeks, so also in the East. For the Arabs say قسط and the Syrians קסטא for כסטא. Josephus names ξέσας for a measure then most known to the Jews in his Life and in his books of Origins. Hadrian also said ξέστην to Epictetus.

καὶ χαλκίων) This is said cautiously; for bronze vessels were washed, earthenware ones were broken if they were believed to be defiled.

Latin:

Vers. 4. ἀπὸ τῆς ἀγορᾶς) Supple γενόμενοι. Qui deesse aliquid putârunt, addiderunt ὅταν ἔλθωσι, quod à Syro non agnoscitur, neque necessarium est. In foro aliisque locis publicis multi erant ἀλλόφυλοι, à quibus contaminari se etiam inscios posse verebantur. Simili de causa in parasceve metuebant Praetorium accedere, quod plenum esset hominibus Romanis.

Βαπτίζωνται) Majori cura se purgabant à fori contactu, quippe non manus tantum lavando, sed & corpus mersando. Cum vero hic mos apud omnes ferme Judaeos receptus fuerit ob consentientem magistrorum auctoritatem, satis hinc intelligitur eos, qui peculiari sectae suae nomine ἡμεροβαπτισταὶ vocabantur, plus fecisse quam caeteros: mersatione usos scilicet etiam cum domo non exiissent; aut mane, ut notatum Clementi Alexandrino; aut etiam saepius ut Batus ille apud Josephum ψυχρῷ ὕδατι τὴν ἡμέραν καὶ τὴν νύκτα πολλάκις λούμενος πρὸς ἁγνείαν. In Clementis constitutionibus de iisdem legitur: καὶ ἡμεροβαπτισταὶ ἐὰν μὴ βαπτίσωνται οὐκ ἐσθίουσιν· ἀλλὰ καὶ τὰς κλίνας καὶ τοὺς πίνακας ἤτοι κρατῆρας καὶ ποτήρια καὶ καθίσματα ἐὰν μὴ καθάρωσιν ὕδατι οὐδενὶ χρῶνται. Quare apud Justinum, ubi sectarum judaicarum nomina recensentur, legendum putem, Φαρισαίων καὶ βαπτιστῶν, non βαριζαίων βαπτιστῶν.

ἐκ ἐσθίουσι) Ne per cibum pollutum nova pollutio accedat. Lavabant religionis causa ante cibum & post cibum ut docent Scripta Thalmudica.

παρέλαβον) קבלו. Relata sunt παραλαμβάνειν & παραδιδόναι ut ad Matthaeum annotavimus.

ξεστῶν) Aquales intelligit. Nam & Cicero aquae sextarium dicit. Sicut autem vox ista ex Romano sermone per omnem orbem derivata apud Graecos passa est literarum μετάθεσιν, ita & in Oriente. Nam Arabes dicunt قسط Syri קסטא pro כסטא. Nominat ξέσας pro mensura tunc Judaeis notissima Josephus in vita sua & in Originum libris. ξέστην dixit & Adrianus Epicteto.

καὶ χαλκίων) Caute hoc dictum; aerea enim abluebantur, testacea frangebantur si polluta crederentur.

## 7:5
Vers. 5. ὦ περιπατοῦσι κατὰ τὴν παράδοσιν τῶν πρεσβυτέρων) Thus Acts XXI. 21. 'nor to walk according to the customs' הלך. The Hebrews call a certain manner of living and custom :הלוכה

κοιναῖς) ἀνίπτοις, which some Codices have as an interpretation and from verse 2 above. The Latin also reads κοιναῖς. Nor does the Syriac read otherwise: for it also interpreted above as κοιναῖς, that is, ἀνίπτοις, 'with unwashed hands'.

Latin:

Vers. 5. ὦ περιπατοῦσι κατὰ τὴν παράδοσιν τῶν πρεσβυτέρων) Ita Act. XXI. 21. μηδὲ τοῖς ἔθεσι περιπατεῖν הלך. Hebraei certam vivendi rationem ac consuetudinem vocant :הלוכה

κοιναῖς) ἀνίπτοις quod quidam habent Codices interpretamentum & ex commate 2. supra. Latinus quoque legit κοιναῖς. Nec aliter Syrus: nam & supra is pro κοιναῖς, τοῦτ᾽ ἔστιν ἀνίπτοις interpretatus est Illotis manibus.

## 7:8
Vers. 8. ἀφέντες) First, Christ says that the precepts of love are accustomed to be neglected, that is, less cared for, while men are entirely distracted by these laborious rituals, which itself is evil enough. But then, taking a step further, Christ demonstrates that there are certain παραδόσεις, which not only turn one away from the pursuit of internal piety, but even directly oppose the precepts handed down by God, as superstition is wont to proceed for the worse. ἀφιέναι is less than ἀθετεῖν and is properly the opposite of τῷ κρατεῖν.

καὶ ἄλλα παρόμοια τοιαῦτα) And other things of that kind similar to these, that is, ceremonies no less cold, of which the books of the Jews are full. The Greek codices and the Latin interpreter consistently support this reading: and the same expression occurs below.

Latin:

Vers. 8. ἀφέντες) Primum dicit Christus negligi, id est minus curari solere praecepta dilectionis, dum homines toti operosis istis ritibus distinentur, quod ipsum satis est mali. At deinde gradu factu, Christus insuper demonstrat esse quasdam παραδόσεις, quae non tantum avertant ab internae pietatis studio, verum etiam directe repugnent praeceptis à Deo traditis, ut solet superstitio in pejus procedere. Minus est ἀφιέναι quam ἀθετεῖν & proprie oppositum τῷ κρατεῖν.

καὶ ἄλλα παρόμοια τοιαῦτα) Et alia id genus istis similia, id est ceremonias non minus frigidas, quarum pleni sunt Ju- dæi dæorum libri. Lectionem hanc tuentur constanter codi- ces Græci & Latinus interpres : & infra locutio eadem oc- currit.

## 7:9
Vers. 9. καλῶς) Very Greek. The Scholiast on Aristophanes says that καλῶς is used for 'rejecting and refusing'.

Latin:

Vers. 9. καλῶς) Græce admodum. Scholiastes ad Aristo- phanem ἀποστρεφόμενοι καὶ παραιτούμενοι λέγᾶ τὸ καλῶς.

## 7:12
Vers. 12. κὴ ἐκ ἔτι ἀφίετε) There is a transition from direct to indirect speech. For the direct speech would have been: 'You say, if anyone says to father or mother, let that by which you could be helped by me be sacred to God, he has no need to perform any benefit for father or mother.' But because he who says this does not in fact permit, that is, he hinders the benefit, therefore, while the sense remains the same, the type of speech has been changed. Thus below XI, 32, when he had introduced the priests speaking ἐὰν' ὀὰν ἔιπωμεν ἐξ ἀνθρώπων, he immediately, without completing the sense, introduced indirect speech ἐφοβεῦντο τ` λαόν, which is very similar to this place. Conversely, the same Mark above c. VI 9, when he had said with indirect speech ὑποδεδεμένους, he immediately introduced direct speech κὴ μὴ ἐνδύσησθε δύο χιτῶνας. Such also is that of Clement of Rome in the book titled περίοδοι Πέτρε, where he says thus: κὴ ὀμόσας ἀπεκρίνατο μηδὲν τύτων ἀληθέστερον εἶναι ὧν ἔιπας. And Luke, when he had said with indirect speech, ὅτι ἄξιός ἐσιν ᾧ παρέξει τοῦτο, for whom Jesus should provide this [for it is unusual for these writers to be in the second person] he added with direct speech: ἀγαπᾷ γὰρ τὸ γένος ἡμῶν. Thus also Matthew, when he introduces Christ speaking, nevertheless inserts some things of his own c. IX, 6, c. XXVI, 18. But it is well said, 'you do not permit': because their dogmas called men away from such a duty. Regarding the matter itself, see what is in Matthew.

Latin:

Vers. 12. κὴ ἐκ ἔτι ἀφίετε) Est transitio ab oratione recta in obliquam. Nam recta oratio hæc fuerat : Dicitis, si quis di- xerit patri aut matri, Deo sacrum esto quo à me juvari posses, is non opus habet patri aut matri beneficium ullum præstare. Sed quia qui hoc dicit, reipsa non permittit, id est impedit bene- ficium, ideo, sensu eodem manente mutatum est sermonis genus. Sic infra XI, 32. cum Sacerdotes induxisset loquen- ces ἐὰν' ὀὰν ἔιπωμεν ἐξ ἀνθρώπων, statim sensu non impleto in- directa oratione intulit ἐφοβεῦντο τ` λαόν, quod huic loco si- millimum est. Contra idem Marcus supra c. VI 9. cum oratione indirecta dixisset ὑποδεδεμένους, statim directam ora- tionem intulit κὴ μὴ ἐνδύσησθε δύο χιτῶνας. Tale est & illud Clementis Romani in libro cui titulus περίοδοι Πέτρε, ubi sic ait : κὴ ὀμόσας ἀπεκρίνατο μηδὲν τύτων ἀληθέστερον εἶναι ὧν ἔιπας. Et Lucas cum obliqua oratione dixisset, ὅτι ἄξιός ἐσιν ᾧ παρέξει τοῦτο, cui hoc præstaret Iesus [nam ut secun- dæ sit personæ præter morem & horum Scriptorum] subje- cit oratione directa : ἀγαπᾷ γὰρ τὸ γένος ἡμῶν. Sic & Mat- thæus ubi Christum inducit loquentem quædam tamen de suo inte serit c. IX, 6. c. XXVI. 18. Bene autem dictum est, non sinitis : quia dogmata illorum à tali officio homines a- vocabant. De re ipsa vide quæ apud Matthæum.

## 7:15
Vers. 15. ἔξωθεν τῶ ἀνθρώπε) Outside the conscience of man. See below 19.

κοινῶσαι) To render profane, that is, invisible to God.

Latin:

Vers. 15. ἔξωθεν τῶ ἀνθρώπε) Citra hominis conscien- tiam. Vide infra 19.

κοινῶσαι) Profanum, id est Deo invisum, reddere.

## 7:19
Vers. 19. καρδίαν) The mind, from which alone sin is born.

καθαρίζον) If there is any natural impurity in food, it is purged by being ejected into the belly, leaving the food in the body.

Latin:

Vers. 19. καρδίαν) Animum ex quo solo delictum nasci- tur.

καθαρίζον) Si quid est in cibo naturalis immunditiæ, id alvo ejectum purgat relictum in corpore cibum.

## 7:22
Vers. 22. πλεονεξίαι) A desire for having, which itself, even if the methods of committing injustice are absent (which is rarely the case), is vicious in itself: indeed, as Paul says, a certain εἰδωλολατρεία. This word properly designates this, as the origin itself indicates, although usage has extended the meaning to the resulting things; Xenophon said ἢ τῷ πλεονεκτεῖν ἐραῖαι. And that it is used no differently by our writers is indicated by that passage of Luke: ὁρᾶτε κὴ φυλάσσετε ἀπὸ τῆς πλεονεξίας˙ ὅτι ἐκ ἐν τῷ περισσεύειν τινὶ ἡ ζωὴ αὐτῶ ἐσιν ἐκ τ ὑπαρχόντων ἀυτῶ. Moreover, Peter used the plural number πλεονεξίας in his second epistle, ch. II. 14.

Πονηρίαι] Πονηρία is where it is taken more broadly for all viciousness which the Greeks call κακίαν. But here it is only a certain species, if I am not mistaken, differing from the deceit that follows, as much as κακία exceeds πλεονεξία. The same is the use of this word in Rom. I. 29, where the old interpreter translates it as 'malice,' in my judgment, very well. Cicero, Tusculan Disputations IV: Malice is the name of a certain specific vice, viciousness of all. Akin to this is κακοήθεια.

Δόλος) Evil deceit: which Paul also places in the census of vices in the aforementioned passage to the Romans. Aquilius defined it: When one thing is feigned and another is done. Ulpian: A certain machination for the sake of deceiving another when one thing is feigned and another is done.

ἀσέλγεια) This word is found mostly joined with the word ἀκαθαρσίας in Paul, as in 2 Corinthians XII. 21, Galatians V. 19, Ephesians IV. 19. And here the Syrian translated it as 'stench,' from which it appears that obscenity in words and deeds is understood: so that a part of it is αἰσχρολογία, which Paul enumerates among the other vices in Colossians III. 8. Good codices, however, prefer the plural number: and the Latin reads it that way.

Why the plural number should be preferred, which was found in only three codices by Stephanus, there is no reason for the singular, which the other codices have: and therefore that change of the text made by Grotius is rash.

ὀφθαλμὸς πονηρὸς) Φθόνος in the aforementioned passage to the Romans. For in that sense the Hebrews mostly use רע עין, as in Deut. XV. 9.

Βλασφημία) This vice is also expressed, namely evil-speaking, in the aforementioned passage to the Colossians. And to the Romans two types of men suffering from that vice are noted, ψιθυριστὰς κὴ καταλάλους.

ὑπερηφανία) Paul also names ὑπερηφάνους in the aforementioned passage to the Romans. Moreover, ὑπερηφανία is, as Theophrastus defines it, καταφρόνησίς τις πλὴν ἀυτῶ τ' ἄλλων. Seneca: All pride comes from disdain.

ἀφροσύνη] I think ἀφροσύνην here is thoughtlessness and neglect of good things, which is the greatest source of sins. Thus Paul, Eph. V. 17: 'Therefore do not be foolish, but understand what the will of the Lord is.'

Latin:

Vers. 22. πλεονεξίαι) Studium habendi, quod ipsum, ut in- justære faciundæ rationes absint (quod fieri vix solet) per se vitiosum est : imo ut Paulus ait εἰδωλολατρεία quædam. Id proprie hæc vox designat, ut ipsa origo indicat, quanquam usus ad res consequentes significationem produxit, Xeno- phon dixit ἢ τῷ πλεονεκτεῖν ἐραῖαι. Nec aliter usurpari à nostris Scriptoribus indicio est Lucæ illud, ὁρᾶτε κὴ φυλάσσετε ἀπὸ τῆς πλεονεξίας˙ ὅτι ἐκ ἐν τῷ περισσεύειν τινὶ ἡ ζωὴ αὐτῶ ἐσιν ἐκ τ ὑπαρχόντων ἀυτῶ. Plurali autem numero πλεονεξίας dixit & Petrus epistola secunda c. II. 14.

Πονηρίαι] Πονηρία est ubi latius sumatur pro omni vitiosi- tate quam κακίαν Græci vocant. At hic certa est species tantum, ni fallor, à dolo qui sequitur distans, quantum κα- κὴ superat πλεονεξίαν. Idem hujus vocis usus est Rom. I. 29. ubi vetus interpres malitiam vertit meo judicio optime. Cicero Tusculanarum IV. Malitia certi cujusdam vitii nomen est, vitiositas omnium. Huic affinis est κακοήθεια.

Δόλος) Dolus malus : quem in censu vitiorum Paulus eta iam ponit dicto ad Romanos loco : Eum definiebat Aqui- lius : Cum aliud simulatum est aliud actum. Ulpianus : Machinationem quandam alterius decipiendi causa cum aliud simulatur & aliud agitur.

ἀσέλγεια) Reperitur hæc vox plerumque juncta cum voce ἀκαθαρσίας apud Paulum ut 2. Corinth. XII. 21. Gal. V. 19. Eph. IV. 19. Et hic Syrus fœtorem transtulit, unde apparet intelligi obscœnitatem in dictis factisque : ut pars ejus sit αἰσχρολογία, quam cæteris vitiis annumerat Paulus Coloss. III, 8. Pluralem autem numerum codices boni præferunt: atque ita legit Latinus.

Cur pluralis numerus præferri debeat, qui in tribus tantum codicibus repertus à Stephano, sin- gulari, quem cæteri Codices habent, causa nulla est : ideoque temeraria est illa mutatio textus à Crotio facta.

ὀφθαλμὸς πονηρὸς) Φθόνος dicto ad Romanos loco. Eo enim sensu plerumque Hebræi usurpant רע עין, ut Deut. XV. 9.

Βλασφημία) Exprimitur & hoc vitium, maledicentia scilicet, dicto ad Colossenses loco. Et ad Romanos duo genura notantur hominum eo vitio ægrotantium, ψιθυρι- στὰς κὴ καταλάλους.

ὑπερηφανία) ὑπερηφάνους nominat & Paulus dicto ad Ro- manos loco. Est autem ὑπερηφανία, Theophrasto defi- niente, καταφρόνησίς τις πλὴν ἀυτῶ τ' ἄλλων. Seneca : Ex fastidio venit omnis superbia.

ἀφροσύνη] Puto ἀφροσύνην hic esse incogitantiam at- que incuriam rerum bonarum quæ maxima delictorum sca- turigo est. Ita Paulus Eph. V. 17. διὰ τοῦτο μὴ γίνεσθε ἄ- φρονες, ἀλλὰ συνίεντες τί τὸ θέλημα τοῦ κυρίου.

## 7:23
Vers. 23. ἔσωθεν ἐκπορεύονται] They reveal themselves by their deeds. See what is said on Matthew.

PART II. The deliverance of the Canaanite woman's daughter from a demon.

Latin:

Vers. 23. ἔσωθεν ἐκπορεύονται] Factis se produnt. Vide quæ ad Matthæum.

PARS II. Filiæ Cananææ à Dæmone liberatio.

## 7:24
Vers. 24. ἠθέλησε γνῶναι] Lest he should seem to deliberately attract to himself men of profane nations, while neglecting the Jews.

Latin:

Vers. 24. ἠθέλησε γνῶναι] Ne de industria profanarum gentium homines ad se allicere videretur, posthabitis Iu- dæis.

## 7:27
Vers. 27. ἄφες πρῶτον χορτασθῆναι τὰ τέκνα] Let the Jews be filled with benefits first, so that they have nothing to complain about. Then the time will come to scatter heavenly benefits among other nations, when disdain for them has taken hold of the Jews.

Latin:

Vers. 27. ἄφες πρῶτον χορτασθῆναι τὰ τέκνα] Sine prius Iu- dæos impleri beneficiis, ut nihil habeant quod querantur. Tum tempus veniet spargendi cœlestia beneficia in gentes alias, cum Iudæos eorum fastidium ceperit.

## 7:29
Vers. 29. διὰ τοῦτον τὸν λόγον] A metonymy of the effect for the cause. For by 'word' is signified faith expressed in prayer, as can be seen in Matthew.

ὕπαγε] It must be taken as a parenthesis, so that the preceding words cohere with the following ones.

Latin:

Vers. 29. διὰ τοῦτον τὸν λόγον] μετωνυμία effecti pro causa. Per orationem enim significatur fides oratione expressa, ut apud Matthæum videre est.

ὕπαγε] Per παρένθεσιν accipiendum est, ut præcedentia sequentibus cohæreant.

## 7:30
Vers. 30. βεβλημένην ἐπὶ τῆς κλίνης] Lying softly on the bed without any tossing.

PART III. The restoration of the mute and deaf man.

Latin:

Vers. 30. βεβλημένην ἐπὶ τῆς κλίνης] In lecto molliter cu- bantem sine ulla jactatione.

PARS III. ​​Muti & surdi restitutio.

## 7:32
Vers. 32. μογιλάλον] I agree entirely with the Syrian, and with others who think this man was not mute but had an impeded tongue. For it follows 'he spoke plainly.' Nor does it stand in the way that it is said below 'he makes the mute speak.' For the particle α often signifies difficulty to the Greeks. But also the LXX translate the Hebrew אלם sometimes as μογιλάλον, as in Is. XXXV. 6, sometimes as ἄλαλον, as in Ps. XXVIII. 14. The Arab and Latin translators more correctly interpret it as 'mute,' as in Exod. IV. 11. אלם 'mute' is rendered as μογιλάλῳ by Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion, and in Is. XXXV. 6 by the LXX interpreters. Which also commends the miracle more. For if he only had an impeded tongue, the defect of deafness was accidental, not natural, or by κωφὸν not 'deaf,' but what Beza wants, 'hard of hearing' (δύσκωφος), will be understood in a similar way: and thus both defects were more curable. But if he was deaf at the same time, and clearly mute, it is understood that he was deaf by nature, for he is always mute, as Ludovicus de Dieu rightly says. Nor is that interpretation of the word ἀλάλους to be admitted, since it detracts not a little from the proper meaning, and from the glory of Christ's miracle, and also from the proclamation by which the greatness of Christ is celebrated.

ἵνα ἐπιθῇ αὐτῷ τὴν χεῖρα] See Matt. IX. 18 and above, chapter V. 23.

Latin:

Vers. 32. μογιλάλον] Omnino Syro assentior, atque aliis, qui hunc non mutum sed impeditæ linguæ fuisse arbitran- tur. Nam sequitur ἐλάλει ὀρθῶς. Neque obstat quod in- fra dicitur ἀλάλους λαλεῖν. Nam α particula Græcis sæpe difficultatem significat. Sed & LXX. Hebræum אלם modo vertunt μογιλάλον, ut Es. XXXV. 6. modo ἄλαλον, ut Psal. XXVIII 14. Rectius Arabs & Latinus mutum interpretantur, ut Exod. IV. 11. אלם mutus μογιλάλῳ reddi- tur ab Aquila, Symmacho, & Theodotione & Esa. XXXV. 6. à LXX. Interpp. Quod etiam miraculum magis commendat. Si enim impeditam solum- modo habuit linguam, surditatis vitium acciden- tale fuit, non naturale, aut per κωφὸν non surdus, sed quod vult Beza surdaster δύσκωφος, parili ra- tione intelligetur: adeoque utrumque vitium sa- nabile magis. Sed si surdus simul, & plane mutus fuit, intelligitur natura fuisse surdus, ille enim sem- per mutus, ut recte Ludovicus de Dieu. Neque ad- mittendum illud vocis ἀλάλους interpretamen- tum, quum id significationi propriæ, & miraculi Christi gloriæ, nec non præconii, quo Christus ce- lebratur magnitudini non parum deroget.

ἵνα ἐπιθῇ αὐτῷ τὴν χεῖρα] Vid. Matth. IX. 18. & supra cap. V. 23.

## 7:33
Vers. 33. [his fingers into his ears] Often Christ exhibited an observable efficacy as if to be looked upon by some external sign. Thus, by inserting his fingers into the ears and moistening the tongue, he made it testified that he was the one by whose power the closed passages were as if bored through, and the tongue adhering to the palate recovered its motion.

[and having spit] See below 8, 23. and John 9, 6. where the blind are similarly healed by saliva. And this seems to me to be referred to nothing else than what the former were, so that by this sign also it might be shown that this health-giving virtue proceeded from Jesus himself, since nothing had been applied to the affected body except those things which were proper to Jesus himself.

Latin:

Vers. 33. τοὺς δακτύλους αὑτοῦ εἰς τὰ ὦτα] Sæpe Christus ex- terno aliquo signo inspectabilem efficaciam velut spectan- dam exhibebat. Ita digitis in aures immissis irrigataque lingua testatum fecit se eum esse cujus vi clausi meatus qua- si perterebrarentur, & lingua palato adhærescens motum recuperaret.

καὶ πτύσας] Vide infra 8, 23. & Ioh. 9, 6. ubi cæci simi- liter per salivam sanantur. Nec alio hoc referendum mihi videtur quam quo superiora, ut hoc quoque indicio osten- deretur ab ipso Iesu prodiisse hanc salutiferam virtutem cum nihil admotum esset affecto corpori præter ea quæ i- psius Iesu erant propria.

## 7:34
Vers. 34. [having looked up to heaven] Matt. XIV. 19. above VI. 41. Luke IX. 16. By this sign he referred the glory of the work to the Father, John XI. 41. c. XVII. 4.

[he groaned] Pitying, as is credible, the labors of the human race.

[Ephphatha, which is, be opened] All impediments of the senses are as it were certain bonds: whence also he who uses his eyes rightly is called פקח and גלוי עינים, Exod. IV. 11. Num. XXIII. 4. and ἀνοιχθεὶς [opened] was said of eyes, Matt. IX. 30. c. XX. 33. and John IX. 14. 17. 21. 26. 30. 31. c. X. 21. 37. Wherefore also in this place it can be referred no less to the tongue than to the ears: although properly, as now follows, διανοίγεσθαι [to be opened] is suitable for ears, λύεσθαι [to be loosed] for the tongue. But those things are accustomed to be mixed by catachresis. Luke I. 64. concerning Zacharias, 'and his mouth was opened' [ἀνεῴχθη δὲ τὸ στόμα αὐτοῦ]. Concerning the mouth, indeed, you may often find that kind of speaking, Ps. XXXVIII. 14. 'as a mute not opening the mouth' [ὡσεὶ ἄλαλος οὐκ ἀνοίγων τὸ στόμα], XXXIX. 10. 'I was deaf and did not open the mouth' [ἐκωφώθην καὶ οὐκ ἤνοιξα τὸ στόμα]. Prov. XXXI. 8. 'open your mouth for the mute' [ἄνοιγε σὸν στόμα ἀλάλῳ] according to Aquila and

Symmachus. But this word Ephphatha, together with the saliva and the touching of the ears and tongue, were transferred from this act of Christ and the rite of baptism afterwards, so that it might be signified that the internal impediments of the mind are no less removed by the Spirit of Christ than the impediments of the senses had been removed in that man. For the heart also is said to be opened [διανοίγειν], Acts XVI. 14. Indeed, ears are also attributed to the heart, as we have seen elsewhere.

Latin:

Vers. 34. ἀναβλέψας εἰς τὸν οὐρανὸν] Matth. XIV. 19. supra VI. 41. Luc. IX. 16. Hoc signo referebat ad Patrem operis gloriam Ioh. XI. 41. c. XVII. 4.

ἐστέναξε] Miserans, ut credibile est humani generis la- bores.

ἐφφαθὰ ὅ ἐστι διανοίχθητι] Omnia sensuum impedimenta vel- ut vincula quædam sunt: unde etiam פקח & גלוי עינים dicitur qui oculis recte utitur Exod. IV. 11. Num. XXIII. 4. & ἀνοιχθεὶς de oculis dixit Matth. IX. 30. c. XX. 33. & Ioh. IX. 14. 17. 21. 26. 30. 31. c. X. 21. 37. Quare & hoc loco potest non minus ad linguam quam ad aures referri: quam- quam proprie, ut jam sequitur, διανοίγεσθαι auribus convenit, λύεσθαι linguæ. Sed solent ista per abusionem misceri. Luc. I. 64. de Zacharia ἀνεῴχθη δὲ τὸ στόμα αὐτοῦ. De ore quidem sæpe id loquendi genus reperias Ps. XXXVIII. 14. ὡσεὶ ἄλα- λος οὐκ ἀνοίγων τὸ στόμα XXXIX. 10. ἐκωφώθην καὶ οὐκ ἤνοιξα τὸ στό μα. Prov. XXXI. 8. ἄνοιγε σὸν στόμα ἀλάλῳ juxta Aquilam &

Symmachum. Hæc autem vox Ephhata simul cum saliva, & tactu aurium ac linguæ ex hoc Christi facto ac baptismi ri- tus postea translata sunt, ut significaretur, non minus inter- na mentis impedimenta tolli per Spiritum Christi quam in isto homine sublata fuerant sensuum impedimenta. Nam & cor dicitur διανοίγειν, Actor. XVI. 14. Imo & cordi aures tribuuntur, ut alibi vidimus.

## 7:35
Vers. 35. [Bond of the tongue] Thus also a disease is called a bond [δεσμὸς], Luke XIII. 16.

Latin:

Vers. 35. Δεσμὸς τῆς γλώσσης] Ita & morbus δεσμὸς dici- tur Luc. XIII. 16.

## 7:36
Vers. 36. [by how much] I see no reason why one should depart here from the interpretation of the Syrians and Latins. For it is very common for the apodosis in this kind of speaking to be omitted in silence, even among Latin authors, and it can be sufficiently understood from the following comparative: but ὅσον is said with the suppression of the little word, which is often accustomed to be suppressed, κατὰ. For the writer to the Hebrews uses it thus, III. 3. καθ' ὅσον πλείονα τιμὴν ἔχει, by how much more honor he has. This place shows the truth of the proverb: Glory follows the one fleeing it.

[More, exceedingly] Such is 'more you differ' [μᾶλλον διαφέρετε], Matt. VI. 26. 'more for the worse' [μᾶλλον εἰς τὸ χεῖρον], Mark VII. 26. 'more exceedingly' [περισσοτέρως μᾶλλον], 2 Cor. VII. 13.

[they proclaimed] Thus was fulfilled the prophecy of Isaiah XXXV. 6. תָרֹן לְשׁוֹן אִלֵּם, the tongue of the mute shall make a proclamation.

Latin:

Vers. 36. ὅσῳ] Cur à Syri & Latini interpretatione hic recedendum sit, causæ nihil video. Nam ἀπόδοσιν in hoc genere loquendi silentio omitti frequentissimum est, etiam apud Latinos auctores & potest ea satis intelligi ex sequen- te comparativo: ὅσον autem dicitur suppressa vocula, quæ sæpe supprimi solet κατὰ. Nam καθ' ὅσον ita usurpat Scri- ptor ad Hebræos III. 3. καθ' ὅσον πλείονα τιμὴν ἔχει, quanto majorem honorem habet. Ostendit hic locus veritatem proverbii: Gloria fugientem sequitur.

Μᾶλλον περισσότερον] Tale est μᾶλλον διαφέρετε Matth. VI. 26. μᾶλλον εἰς τὸ χεῖρον Marc. VII. 26. περισσοτέρως μᾶλλον 2. Cor. VII. 13.

ἐκήρυσσον] Sic impletum Esaiæ vaticinium XXXV. 6. תָרֹן לְשׁוֹן אִלֵּם præconium faciet linguamuti.

## 7:37
Vers. 37. [exceedingly] Thus Paul said ὑπερπερισσεύειν [to abound exceedingly].

[they were astonished] Again said impersonally. One must understand 'the people' [οἱ ἄνθρωποι], who were hearing those things. Thus also below 'they bring' [φέρουσι] in verse 22.

He has done all things well] The writer of Ecclesiasticus: the works of the Lord are all very good, XXXIX. 21.

Latin:

Vers. 37. ὑπερπερισσῶς] Ita ὑπερπερισσεύειν dixit Paulus.

ἐξεπλήσσοντο] Rursus dictum impersonaliter. Subin- telligendum oi ἄνθρωποι, qui ista audiebant. Ita & infra φέρουσι commate 22.

καλῶς πάντα πεποίηκε] Scriptor Ecclesiastici : τὰ ἔργα τοῦ κυρίου παντὰ καλὰ σφόδρα, XXXIX. 21.

## 8:1 Argument
CHAPTER VIII. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

A great crowd, which had adhered to Christ for three days in the desert, of four thousand men, fed with seven loaves, with seven baskets of fragments remaining. He crosses by ship into the borders of Dalmanutha: to the Pharisees asking for a sign from heaven, such a sign is denied: the disciples, warned about the Pharisaic and Herodian leaven and understanding it as a lack of bread, are rebuked, being reminded of the double miraculous feeding: a blind man in Bethsaida receives sight, first seeing men as trees. Setting out for Caesarea, Jesus asks what men think of him, and what the disciples think, and to Peter, who gives a confession, he predicts his passion, death, and resurrection, and gravely rebukes Peter for contradicting him: and he warns about taking up the cross and the confession of the Son of Man, and testifies that the coming of the kingdom of God is imminent.

There are five parts: I. The miraculous feeding of four thousand men, to v. 9. II. Concerning the Pharisees asking for a sign from heaven, and the warning to beware of their leaven, to v. 21. III. The healing of the blind man in Bethsaida, to v. 25. IV. The confession of Jesus, with the prediction of the passion and resurrection, to v. 33. V. Exhortation to the cross, and confession, with the prediction concerning the coming of the kingdom of God, to v. 39.

PART I. The miraculous feeding of four thousand men.

Latin:

CAPUT VIII. ARGUMENTUM ET PAR- TITIO.

Multa turba, quæ per triduum Christo adhæse- rat in deserto, quatuor millium virorum, se- ptem panibus cibata, remanentibus septem cophinis reliquiarum. Navi trajicit in fines Dalmanutha: Pharisæis signum postu- lantibus de cælo signum tale denegatur: discipuli de fermento Pharisæico & Hero- diano moniti de panis defectu id intelli- gentes commonefacti de gemina miraculo- sa cibatione redarguuntur: cæcus in Beth- saida visum recepit, primum homines ut arbores videns. Cæsaream proficiscens Ie- sus sciscitatur quid homines de se sentiant, quidve discipuli, & Petro confessionem e- denti prædicit passionem, mortem & resur- rectionem, ac Petrum contradicentem gra- viter increpat: deque tollenda cruce, & Filii hominis confessione monet, ac regni Dei adventum imminere testatur.

Partes sunt quinque: I. Quatuor millium viro- rum miraculosa cibatio, ad v. 9. II. De Pharisæis signum postulantibus de cælo, & fermento eorum ca- vendo monitio, ad v. 21. III. Cæci in Bethsaida sanatio, ad v. 25. IV. Confessio Jesu, cum prædi- ctione passionis & resurrectionis, ad v. 33. V. Ad- hortatio ad crucem, & confessionem, cum prædi- ctione de adventu regni Dei, ad v. 39.

PARS I. Miraculosa quatuor millium virorum cibatio.

## 8:10
Ver. 10. Δαλμανουθὰ) So the Syriac, the Arabic, the Latin, and the most excellent Codices, and the Greek writers on this passage: wherefore what other books formerly had, Μαγεδὰν or Μαδιγαδὰ, is an interpretation from Matthew. Christ came here through the lot of Reuben into the lot of Manasseh: thence through the lot of Gad into the lot of Dan, below 27, so that he might not omit any part of the land once divided among the descendants of Jacob. Ver. 11. Ἤρξαντο αὐτῷ) It was a very ancient custom of disputing by interrogations. Hence Aristotle places πλείω ἐρωτήματα in the number of sophisms. See also Luke II. 46. Hence it came about that συζητεῖν is said to mean to dispute. Ver. 12. ἀναστενάξας τῷ πνεύματι αὐτοῦ) He fetched sighs from the bottom of his chest: as the Latin poets say. For πνεῦμα in this place is the human spirit. See what [is said] on Matt. V. 3. εἰ δοθήσεται) As in Psalm CXXXI. 2, εἰ μὴ ἐταπεινοφρόνουν, CXXXII. 3, εἰ εἰσελεύσομαι: where the οὐ is now wrongly omitted in the Greek Codices, which is apparent from the following member κὶ εἰ ἀναβήσομαι. That which would make a full sentence, ἀρὰ, is suppressed, and that for the sake of a better omen. Which God also imitates ἀνθρωποπαθῶς in Ps. LXXXIX. 36 and Ps. XCV. 11. τῇ γενεᾷ ταύτῃ σημεῖον) One must repeat ἀπὸ τοῦ κοινοῦ what preceded, ἀπὸ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ. Ver. 15. βλέπετε) So also Paul said βλέπετε for to beware, Phil. III. 2, and our author here below 12, 38. Ἡρώδου) So the ancient interpreters. Wherefore what others have, Ἡρωδιανῶν, was born from an annotation. Moreover, the dogma of the Herodians is called Herod's, because they gave to Herod the honor which was due to the Messiah, whom we have said elsewhere were a part of the Sadducees. V. 17. πεπωρωμένην) See above 6, 52. Ver. 18. Ὀφθαλμοὺς ἔχοντες οὐ βλέπετε καὶ ὦτα ἔχοντες οὐκ ἀκούετε) Elsewhere perversity is noted as hindering teachableness. Here, however, it is inattention. Since my words sound in your ears, and miracles dazzle your eyes, you admit neither into your mind. Ver. 19. ἔκλασα) I distributed, from a well-known Hebraism.

PART III. The healing of the blind man in Bethsaida.

Latin:

Vers. 10. Δαλμανουθὰ) Ita Syrus, Arabs, Latinus & prae- stantissimi Codices, & Graeci scriptores ad hunc locum: quare quod alii libri pridem habuerunt Μαγεδὰν aut Μα- διγαδὰ interpretamentum est ex Matthaeo. Christus hic per sortem Rubenis venit in sortem Manassis: inde per sortem Gadis in sortem Danis, infra 27. ne quam partem terrae in- ter Jacobi posteros olim divisae omittat. Vers. 11. Ἤρξαντο αὐτῷ) Mos antiquissimus disputandi erat per interrogationes. Hinc πλείω ἐρωτήματα in Sophi- smatum numero ponit Aristoteles. Vide & Luc. II. 46. Hinc factum ut συζητεῖν dicatur disputare. Vers. 12. ἀναστενάξας τῷ πνεύματι αὐτοῦ) Suspiria duxit ab imo pectore: ut loquuntur Latini Poëtae. Nam πνεῦμα hoc loco est animus humanus. Vide quae ad Matth. V. 3. εἰ δοθήσεται) Ut Psalmo CXXXI. 2. εἰ μὴ ἐταπεινοφρόνουν CXXXII. 3. εἰ εἰσελεύσομαι: ubi male nunc in Graecis Co- dicibus οὐ omittitur, quod apparet ex membro sequenti κὶ εἰ ἀναβήσομαι. Subticetur, quae plenam orationem faceret ἀρὰ, idque melioris ominis causa. Quod & Deus ἀνθρω- ποπαθῶς imitatur Pf. LXXXIX. 36. & Psal. XCV. 11. τῇ γενεᾷ ταύτῃ σημεῖον) Repetendum ἀπὸ τῦ κοινῦ quod praecessit ἀπὸ τῦ ὐρανῦ. Vers. 15. βλέπετε) Ita & Paulus dixit βλέπετε pro cavere Phil. III. 2. & noster hic infra 12, 38. Ἡρώδου) Ita prisci interpretes. Quare quod alii habent Ἡρωδιανῶν, ex annotatione natum est. Vocatur autem He- rodianorum dogma Herodis, quia Herodi honorem dese- rebant, qui Messiae debebatur, quos partem fuisse Sadducaeo- rum alibi diximus. V. 17. πεπωρωμένην) Vide supra 6, 52. Vers. 18. Ὀφθαλμὺς ἔχοντες ὐ βλέπετε καὶ ὦτα ἔχοντες ὐκ ἀκύετε) Alibi perversitas notatur obstans docilitati. Hic ve- ro ἀπροσεξία. Cum verba mea vestris auribus insonent, mi- racula praestringant oculos, neutra in animum admittitis. Vers. 19. ἔκλασα) Distribui, ex Hebraïsmo satis noto.

PARS III. Caeci in Bethsaida sanatio.

## 8:23
Ver. 23. τῆς κώμης) He calls it so according to ancient custom, although it had recently received the status of a town, whence John calls it a town. Josephus concerning Philip: 'He bestowed the dignity of a city upon the village of Bethsaida, near the Lake of Gennesaret, by the multitude of its inhabitants and its other power, and named it Julia after the daughter of Caesar.' Christ judges the Bethsaidans unworthy to be witnesses of a miracle, and soon does not even permit the miracle to be told to them, because of that stubbornness of which he complains elsewhere. Ver. 24. ἀναβλέψας) I agree with the interpreter [who says] 'lifting up the eyes,' in which sense we have had ἀναβλέψας three times above. Ver. 25. κὲ ἐποίησεν αὐτὸν ἀναβλέψαι) Since the Syriac does not have this, and the Latin read it otherwise, whence the other reading κὲ ἤρξατο ἀναβλέψαι was born, it is possible that it was added by one who wished to express the force of the hands laid on a second time. From the Syriac and Latin, which did not always render the text word for word, as Grotius has more than once confessed, the original Greek text is not to be called into suspicion of corruption. Nor was that other reading found by Stephanus, except in one Codex only. — ἀποκατεστάθη) See above III. 5. ἐνέβλεψε) So Paul of himself in Acts XXII. 11, ὡς δὲ οὐκ ἐνέβλεπον. ἅπαντα) Since certain codices also have it so, and the Syriac and Latin read it so, this reading seems preferable. Stephanus did not find more Codices, but only one, as we have said, that reads ἅπαντα. Grotius therefore ought not to have changed the text here. Ver. 26. εἰς τὸν οἶκον αὐτοῦ) He seems to have lived in the country. τινὶ ἐν τῇ κώμῃ) He makes the place, which seemed obscure to many, clear by understanding the ellipsis. For the sense is: 'neither tell it to any of those in the village': namely, the inhabitants. He not only forbids him to go into the town, but also forbids him to tell the matter if any of the townspeople should meet him elsewhere. We have spoken about the omission of the article before prepositions on Matt. XXII. 30. Thus there is no need for those various readings which

Beza has collected, to trouble us. For the sense is plain in the received Codices according to this interpretation.

PART IV. The confession of Jesus and the prediction of his passion and resurrection.

Latin:

Vers. 23. τῆς κώμης) Ita vocat ex antiquo more, quam- quam nuper jus oppidi acceperat unde oppidum Johannes appellat. Josephus de Philippo: Κώμην δὲ Βηθσαῖδὰν πρὸς λίμνῃ δὲ τῇ Γεννησαρίτιδι πόλεως παρασχὼν ἀξίωμα πλήθει τε οἰκητόρων κὲ τῇ ἄλλῃ δυνάμει, Ἰουλία θυγατρὶ τῇ καίσαρος ὁμώνυ- μον ἐκάλεσε. Indignos Christus Bethsaïdenses judicat, qui testes essent miraculi, & mox ne narrati quidem ipsis mira- culum permittit, ob eam scilicet contumaciam, de qua alibi conqueritur. Vers. 24. ἀναβλέψας) Assentio interpretanti Oculos tol- lens, quo sensu ἀναβλέψας habuimus ter supra. Vers. 25. κὲ ἐποίησεν αὐτὸν ἀναβλέψαι) Cum hoc non ha- beat Syrus, & aliter legerit Latinus, undenata est altera le- ctio κὲ ἤρξατο ἀναβλέψαι, fieri potest ut adjectum sit ab eo qui vim impositarum secundo manuum voluit exprimere. E Syro & Latino, qui non semper κτὰ πόδα tex- tum reddidere, ut non semel fassus est Grotius, non est in suspicionem corruptionis vocandus textus Graecus originalis. Neque lectio illa alte- ra reperta est a Stephano, nisi in uno tantum Co- dice. — ἀποκατεστάθη) Vide supra III. 5. ἐνέβλεψε) Ita de se Paulus Actor, XXII. 11. ὡς δὲ ὐκ ἐνέ- βλεπον. ἅπαντα) Cum & codices quidam ita habeant, atque ita legerint Syrus & Latinus, praeferenda haec lectio videtur. Non plures Codices, sed unum tantum, ut diximus, invenit Codicem Stephanus, qui legit ἅπαντα. Non debuerat ergo hic textum immu- tare Grotius. Vers. 26. εἰς τὸν ὆κον αὐτῦ) Videtur in agro habitasse. τινὶ ἐν τῇ κώμῃ) Locum qui multis obscurus est visus perspicuum facit intellecta ἔκστρεψις. Sensus enim est μηδὲ εἴπῃς τινὶ τῶν ἐν τῇ κώμῃ: scilicet οἰκύντων. Non modo vetat eum ire in oppidum, sed & si quis oppidanorum alibi ei fiat obvius rem narrare prohibet. De articuli reticentia ante praepositiones diximus ad Matth. XXII. 30. Ita non opus est diversis illis lectionibus, quas

Beza congessit. nos angi. Planus enim sensus in receptis Codicibus juxta hanc interpretationem.

PARS IV. Confessio Jesu & prædictio passionis & re- surrectionis ejus.

## 8:30
Ver. 30. περὶ αὐτοῦ) That, that he was the Christ. For he wanted to be called a teacher of truth and a Prophet by the Apostles: but he said to few that he was the Messiah: not wishing that very thing to be spread publicly before his death was triumphed over. Moreover, Peter seems to have passed over in modest silence that magnificent promise made to him by Christ in the recitation of this history: since he narrated most openly whatever there was in which he himself could be blamed, which form of narrating Mark followed in good faith.

Grotius assumes without proof that Mark wrote what he wrote from Peter's account: whereas he himself wrote everything through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, just as the other God-inspired men did. But Beza rightly notes here that it is not credible that either Peter himself or Mark would have passed over that, 'Thou art Peter,' if they had thought that the foundation of the Christian Church was situated in these words.

Latin:

Vers. 30. περι αυτου) Illud, Christum se esse. Nam veri doctorem & Prophetam, se dici ab Apostolis volebat: Mes- siam vero se esse paucis dixit: nolens id ipsum publice vul- gari ante triumphatam mortem. Videtur autem Petrus in hujus historiæ recitatione magnificam illam promissionem à Christo sibi factam modesto silentio præteriisse: cum quicquid erat in quo culpari ipse posset apertissime narra- verit, quam formam narrandi bona fide secutus est Marcus.

Assumit Grotius precario, quod ex Petrina re- latione Marcus scripsit, quæ scripsit: quum potius per Spiritus S. inspirationem ipse omnia, uti cæ- teri viri θεοπνευστοι, scripserit. Recte au- tem hic Beza notat, credibile non esse vel ipsum Petrum, vel Marcum præteriturum fuisse illud, Tu es Petrus, si Ecclesiæ Christianæ fundamentum in his verbis situm esse, existimassent.

## 8:31
Vers. 31. αποδοκιμασθηναι) An allusion to the passage in Ps. CXVIII. 22, which Christ and his Apostles often mentioned. There, in the Hebrew, it is מאס, which the Hellenists translate sometimes as αποδοκιμαζειν, sometimes as εξουθενειν. Rejection had its degrees, but it reached its peak at that time when Christ was handed over by the Sanhedrin to the Roman power as unworthy of the name of Jew.

That Psalm CXVIII. 22 treats of Christ is undoubted: and Grotius acknowledged this here. Why, therefore, did he call it into doubt elsewhere in his annotations on the book of Psalms? Whoever wishes to see him corrected there, will see it in our Anti-Grotian Annotations.

μετα τρεις ημερας) See what [is said] at Matt. XXVII. 63. I will add this: it is not wrongly said by the Hebrews that God is accustomed to fulfill His benefits more abundantly than His words were. To perform within three days what you promised to do after three days have passed is a goodness to be praised, not a vanity to be accused. For in promises, time is added so that they may not be done too late, not so that they may not be done sooner than said. And thus the Jews say that the liberation from Egyptian servitude was promised after four hundred years, [but] was performed after two hundred and some odd years.

At Matt. XXVII. 63 he had correctly explained: μετα τρεις ημερας, that is, within three days, בעוד שלשת ימים Gen. XL. 13, where the LXX [have] ετι τρεις ημεραι, although what is said there was fulfilled on the third day itself, as appears in the same place, verse 20. Thus Christ himself in Mark VIII. 31 says that it is necessary for him μετα τρεις ημερας αναστηναι. Thus מקץ שבע שנים Deut. XV. 1, the LXX translate δι επτα ετων (just as Josephus also speaks, and above XXVI. 61, and Mark XIV. 58, it is written δια τριων ημερων). But the same Hebrew words, when the same matter is treated in Jer. XXXIV. 14, are translated into Greek not so much κατ' λεξιν (word for word) as κατ' διανοιαν (according to the sense) as οταν πληρωθη εξ ετη, just as the most learned of the Rabbis, Abraham and Kimchi, also explain. But in Deuteronomy XXXI. 10, with the Hebraism retained, they translated μετα επτα ετη. Similar is John XX. 26, μεθ' ημερας οκτω, where the Syrian, as also in this place, rendered that μετα word for word as בתר, whereas in Mark he explains it by ל, which corresponds to the word εν. These things [are] in the same place. Which are confirmed by those things which Beza and Ludov. de Dieu have here, which can also be read in Balduinus Wæleus on this passage, and are far sounder than this Grotian observation. For the goodness of GOD is to be preached in such a way that the divine truth is not detracted from. How that calculation of the 400 years of servitude stands, we have explained elsewhere.

Latin:

Vers. 31. αποδοκιμασθηναι) Allusio ad locum Ps. CXVIII. 22. cujus sæpe meminerunt Christus ejusque Apostoli. Ibi in Hebræo est מאס quod Hellenistæ modo vertunt αποδοκιμαζειν, modo εξουθενειν. Habuit εξουθενησις suos gra- dus ad summam autem pervenit eo tempore cum Christus à Synedrio, tanquam indignus Judæi nomine, traditus est Romanæ potestati.

Psalmūm ergo CXVIII. 22. de Christo agere indubium est: idque hic agnovit Grotius. Cur ita- que alias id in dubium vocavit in annotatis ad li- brum Psalmorum? Quem proinde ibi castigatum qui volet, in Annotatis nostris Anti-Grotianis vide- bit.

μετα τρεις ημερας) Vide quæ ad Matth. XXVII. 63. Hoc addam, non male ab Hebræis dici solere Deum beneficia sua cumulatius implere quam verba fuerunt. Intra triduum præstare, quod exacto triduo facturum te promiseris, boni- tatis est laudandæ, non accusandæ vanitatis. Nam in pro- missis tempus adjicitur, ne serius fiant, non ne citius dicto. Atque ita ajunt Judæi liberationem ex Ægyptiaca servitute promissam post annos quadringentos, præstitam post du- centos & quod excurrit.

Ad Matth. XXVII. 63. recte exposuerat: μετα τρεις ημερας id est, intra tres dies בעוד שלשת ימים Gen.
