ἐδίδασκεν αὐτοὺς] Locum Johannis baptismo nobilem & doctrina & miraculis faciebat nobiliorem, ipsa rerum comparatione homines ad sui admirationem excitans. Vide dima loca Matthæi & Johannis.

## 10:2
Vers. 2. ἀπολῦσαι] Namely for any cause whatsoever, which Matthew expressed. For they did not doubt that they could [do so] for some cause.

Latin:

Vers. 2. ἀπολῦσαι] Scilicet quavis de causa, quod Matthæus expreffit. Nam aliqua de causa posse non duqitabant.

## 10:3
Vers. 3. ὃ δὲ ἀποκριθεὶς] When they brought forward the authority of Moses for the promiscuous right of divorce, Christ urges them to recite the very words of Moses.

Latin:

Vers. 3. ὃ δὲ ἀποκριθεὶς] Cum Mofis auctoritatem adferrent pro divortiorum promiscuo jure, Christus urget ut ipsa Mofis verba recitent.

## 10:4
Vers. 4. ἐπέτρεψε] He permitted [them] to repudiate by giving a bill of divorce: or, which amounts to the same thing and is in Matthew, he commanded you to give a bill of divorce if you were to repudiate.

Latin:

Vers. 4. ἐπέτρεψε] Permisit repudiare dato libello: aut quod eodem recidit & apud Matthæum est, repudiare vos lenti præcepit libellum dare.

## 10:5
Vers. 5. τὴν ἐντολὴν ταύτην] ἐντολὴ signifies in a general sense any laws whatsoever, even those that permit. For a permission also obligates: first, all others not to hinder such a thing, and then, if a form is added to the permitted act, it obligates him who is about to act not to act otherwise.

Beza distinguishes more correctly here: teaching that by ἐντολὴν is understood the commandment about writing a bill of divorce, if anyone for his hardness could not bear his wife. For Moses did not give a commandment about repudiating wives, but rather provided for wives against the inflexible hardness of husbands. Mal. II. 15. See, however, what we have said regarding these matters in Matthew, where this subject is so elucidated that what Grotius has perhaps handed down here still in a peculiar way regarding Mark can be judged from there without difficulty. Therefore, there is no need to dwell on them. Selden, and Walæus following him, notes that in the Old Covenant, for seven hundred years or thereabouts after the law was given, the mention of divorce occurs nowhere: indeed, traces of it are rare somewhere afterwards; an example while the Hebrew Republic stood is either non-existent or very rarely mentioned. From this information of Christ, however, it appears that the use of divorces, even of wives dismissing husbands, had increased by then.

Latin:

Vers. 5. τὴν ἐντολὴν ταύτην] ἐντολὴ generali significatione leges quascunque, etiam permittentes significat. Nam & permissio obligat, primum alios omnes ne tale quid impediant, deinde si forma actui permissio addatur obligat eum qui acturus est ne aliter agat.

Rectius hic distinguit Beza: per ἐντολὴν docens intelligi mandatum de scribendo divortii libello, si quis pro sua duritia non posset uxorem ferre. Nec enim Moses præceptum dedit de repudiandis uxoribus, sed uxoribus potius contra inflexibilem maritorum duritiem prospexit. Mal. II. 15. Vide tamen quæ ad Matthæum de his diximus, ubi hæc materia ita enucleata, ut quæ hic forte adhuc peculiariter tradidit ad Marcum Grotius, inde dijudicari citra difficultatem possint. Ideo illis immorari opus non est. Seldenus, & ex eo Walæus notat in fœdere veteri per septingentos a lege lata, aut circiter annos, divortii mentionem nullibi occurrere: Rara quidem alicubi post, ejusdem vestigia, Exemplum stante Rep. Ebraica aut nullum, aut rarissime memoratum. Ex hac tamen Christi informatione apparet usum divortiorum, etiam uxorum dimittentium maritos tum increvisse.

## 10:6
Vers. 6. ἀπὸ δὲ ἀρχῆς κτίσεως] κτίσις signifies not the act of creating but the things created, in the way the Latin [translator] understood it. Thus also below XIII. 19 and XVI. 15 and 2 Peter III. 4. And thus the whole six days are the ἀρχὴ κτίσεως, that is, of the creatures, whereas the first day is properly the ἀρχὴ τῆς κοσμοποιΐας.

Latin:

Vers. 6. ἀπὸ δὲ ἀρχῆς κτίσεως] κτίσις non actum condendi sed res conditas significat, quomodo accepit Latinus. Sic & infra XIII. 19. & XVI. 15. & 2. Petri III. 4. Atque ita toti sex dies sunt ἀρχὴ κτίσεως, id est τοῦ κτισμάτων, cum primus dies proprie sit ἀρχὴ τῆς κοσμοποιΐας:

## 10:7
Vers. 7. ἕνεκεν τούτου] Understand λέγων.

Latin:

Vers. 7. ἕνεκεν τούτου] Sub intellige λέγων.

## 10:8
Vers. 8. εἰς σάρκα μίαν] Thus the LXX, which signifies nothing other than what is in Matthew and follows here, σὰρξ μία. For among the Hebrews, a substantive noun loves such a construction.

ὥστε οὐκέτι εἰσὶ δύο, ἀλλὰ μία σάρξ] That is, from that act and words of God it appears to be just and most pleasing to God that the union of spouses should be indivisible, as if they had coalesced into one man. See what [we said] regarding Matthew.

Latin:

Vers. 8. εἰς σάρκα μίαν] Ita LXX. quod non aliud significat quam quod apud Matthæum est & hic sequitur σὰρξ μία. Nam apud Hebræos vox substantiva amat talem constitutionem.

ὥστε οὐκέτι εἰσὶ δύο, ἀλλὰ μία σάρξ] Id est, ex isto Dei facto & verbis apparet æquum esse & Deo gratissimum, ut conjugum individua sit copula, quasi in unum hominem coaluissent. Vide quæ ad Matthæum.

## 10:11
Vers. 11. καὶ γαμήσῃ ἄλλην] by which act he shows himself to be averse to reconciliation. μοιχᾶται ἐπ᾿ αὐτὴν] Matthew [says] "makes her commit adultery." He is said to commit a crime who gives cause for sinning through his own fault, for in that case the crime is deservedly imputed.

This is held before God as adultery, because he who has cast her out provides the occasion for unchastity; as we have explained elsewhere. ἐπ᾿ αὐτήν, that is, by that very act which he commits against her. Vers.

Latin:

Vers. 11. καὶ γαμήσῃ ἄλλην] quo facto ostendit alienum se à reconciliatione, μοιχᾶται ἐπ᾿ αὐτὴν] Matthaeus ποιεῖ αὐτὴν μοιχᾶσθαι. facere delictum dicitur qui causam dat delinquendi sua culpa, illic enim delictum merito imputatur.

Haec apud Deum adulterii tenetur qui expulsa praebet impudicitiae occasionem; ut alibi explicavimus. ἐπ᾿ αὐτήν, id est isto facto quod in ipsum committit. Vers.

## 10:12
12. κἂν ἐὰν γυνὴ ἀπολύσῃ τὸν ἄνδρα αὐτῆς κὶ γαμήσῃ ἄλλῳ, μοιχᾶται] Other writers pass over this, because it was less doubted.

There were, however, those who dared this against the law of Moses. Thus Michal once deserted David by her father's authority, 1 Sam. XXV. 44. There was also one who sent a bill of divorce to her husband. Josephus: "When time had passed, since it happened that Salome quarreled with Costobarus, she sent immediately a bill of divorce, dissolving the marriage, according to the Jewish laws; for it is permitted among us for men to do so; but for a woman, if she is separated, to marry on her own, not if she is released by her husband." Herodias had followed the example of Salome. A woman, therefore, since she is not the mistress of herself, if she leaves her husband and betakes herself to another marriage, commits adultery entirely, not by some interpretation or by consequence, but directly. Therefore, it should not have been added here, ἐπ᾿ αὐτόν. II.

Admonition concerning the receiving of infants to himself.

Vers.

Latin:

12. κἂν ἐὰν γυνὴ ἀπολύσῃ τὸν ἄνδρα αὐτῆς κὶ γαμήσῃ ἄλλῳ, μοιχᾶται] Id praetereunt alii scriptores, quia de eo minus dubitabatur.

Erant tamen quae hoc auderent contra Mosis legem. Sic Michol olim Davidem deseruit patre auctore, 1 Sam. XXV. 44. Fuit & quae libellum divortii marito mitteret. Josephus: χρόνῳ δὲ διελθόντος, ἐπεὶ συνέβη τὴν Σαλώμην σασιάσαι πρὸς Κόστοβαρον, πέμπει μὲν εὐθὺς ἀντὶ τῷ γραμματείῳ ἀπολυομένη τὸν γάμον, ἐκατὰ τοὺς Ἰουδαίους νόμους· ἀνδρὶ μὲν γὰρ ἔξεστι παρ᾿ ἡμῖν τῶν ὁποίων· γυναικὶ δὲ ἐὰν διαχωρισθείσῃ καθ᾿ αὐτὴν γαμηθῆναι, μὴ τὸ κότερον ἀνδρὸς ἀφίεντο. Salomes exemplum secuta erat Herodias. Mulier ergo, cum domina sui non sit, si marito relicto ad aliud matrimonium se conferat omnino adulterium committit, non interpretatione aliqua aut per consequentiam, sed directe. Ideo non debuit hic addi, ἐπ᾿ αὐτόν. II.

Admonitio de infantibus ad se admittendis.

Vers.

## 10:15
15. ὃς ἐὰν μὴ δέξηται] Children are compared to blank slates; such must those be who are to judge the truth of dogmas.

Christ properly said δέξεται, because the Hebrews were said to receive the heavenly kingdom into themselves when they subjected themselves to the Law: whence also some ancient Latins read "Word of God" in this place, interpreting "Kingdom of God." We have said something about this passage of Mark at Matt. XXVI. 29. Vers.

Latin:

15. ὃς ἐὰν μὴ δέξηται] Pueri tabulae rasae conferuntur; tales esse oportet qui de dogmatis veritate sunt judicaturi.

Proprie autem dixit Christus δέξεται, quia suscipere in se regnum coeleste dicebantur Hebraei qui legi se subjiciebant: unde & Latini quidam veteres pro regnum Dei hoc loco legebant interpretantes Verbum Dei. Diximus aliquid de hoc Marci loco ad Matth. XXVI. 29. Vers.

## 10:29
29. ἢ γυναῖκα] The Syriac and the codices acknowledge it: nor do I see a reason to introduce it. For the fact that the mention of wives is not repeated in the frequent clause is not so surprising, since from the others that are mentioned, this also can be understood κατ᾿ ἀναλογίαν (by analogy). Perhaps Mark omitted it because the restoration of wives could admit a more calumnious interpretation than the others. For Julian mocked this: as Theophylact notes. Therefore, when the other affections are mentioned, the wife is not mentioned; from this we learn that the loss of a wife will be fulfilled by the restoration of all the duties which are provided by a wife, except for that which cannot be provided except by a wife.

Vers.

Latin:

29. ἢ γυναῖκα] Agnoscit Syrus & codices: neque inducendi causam video. Nam quod in frequenti commate uxorum mentio non repetitur haud adeo mirum est, cum ex caeteris quae memorantur κατ᾿ ἀναλογίαν hoc quoque possit intelligi. Forte & ideo omisit Marcus quod restitutis uxorum posset calumniosam interpretationem admittere magis quam caetera. Nam & Julianus hoc irrisit: ut monet Theophylactus. Ergo cum caeteri affectus memorantur, uxor non memoratur; hinc discimus uxoris jacturam expletum iri restitutione omnium officiorum quae ab uxore praestantur, excepto eo quod nisi ab uxore praestari non potest.

Vers.

42. οἱ δοκοῦντες ἄρχειν] Δοκοῦντες here means to be in honor, as in Gal. II. 2 and 6, and that [phrase] in Euripides' Hecuba is opposed to those who are "the apparent ones." The construction, however, is similar to that in the history of Susanna: clause 5, "from the elder judges who seemed to govern the people": from the elder judges to whom it had come to govern the people. οἱ μεγάλοι αὐτῶν] That is, those who are eminent among the princes themselves, as we said regarding Matthew.

Constructio autem similis illum in Susannae historia: commate 5. ἐκ πρεσβυτέρων κριτῶν οἱ ἐδόκουν κυβερνῶν τὸν λαόν: ex senioribus judicibus quibus venerat populum gubernandi. οἱ μεγάλοι αὐτῶν] Id est qui inter ipsos Principes eminens, ut ad Matth. diximus.

## 11:1 Argument
CHAPTER XI. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

Jesus, having sent his disciples from Bethphage, causes the foal of an ass to be brought, and upon it, while those who go before and follow cry out Hosanna, he proceeds to Jerusalem, enters the temple, and in the evening returns to Bethany. The following day, having left Bethany, he curses the fig tree, casts out the sellers and buyers from the temple, because the Temple is a house of prayer, with the Pharisees attempting to kill him. The next morning, on the occasion of seeing the withered fig tree, [he speaks] of the efficacy of faith for moving mountains, and of obtaining by prayers what we ask: having entered the temple, he is asked by what authority he teaches, but by asking in turn about the Baptism of John, and receiving no answer, he also refuses to answer concerning his own authority.

There are five parts: I. Jesus' entry into Jerusalem, to v. 11. II. The cursing of the fig tree, to v. 14. III. The casting out of the sellers and buyers from the temple, to v. 19. IV. Information concerning the efficacy of faith, to v. 26. V. The question concerning the authority of teaching, with the αὐτερωτήσει of Christ, to v. 33.

PART I. Jesus' entry into Jerusalem.

Vers. 1. εἰς Βηθφαγῆ καὶ Βηθανίαν) The Syriac mentions both places: as do the Talmudic [writings]; what some books have as Βηθσφαγὴ I think is from a corrupt pronunciation. For the Hebrew ת declines to the sound of σ.

The Vulgate commemorates only Bethany. Which Beza also notes in the Syriac, but as a ἁμάρτημα μνημονικὸν, since both the Syriac and the Arab have both places.

Latin:

CAPUT XI. ARGUMENTUM ET PAR- TITIO.

Iesus è Bethphage missis discipulis adduci cu- rat asinae pullum, eoque, acclamantibus qui praecedunt & sequuntur Hosianna, tendit Hierosolymam, templumque ingreditur, & vesperi Bethaniam regreditur. Sequenti die Bethania egressus ficui maledicit, è templo venditores & emtores ejicit, quod Templum domus precationis sit, Pharisaeis tentantibus ipsum interficere. Altero mane occasione visae arefactae ficus de efficacia fidei ad montes transferendos, & precibus impe- trandis, quae petimus: in templum ingres- sus rogatur, qua potestate doceat, sed iterum quaerens de Baptismo Iohannis, nullumque responsum accipiens etiam renuit de sua po- testate respondere.

Partes sunt quinque: I. Ingressus Jesu Hieroso- lymitanus, ad v. 11. II. Ficus maledictio, ad v. 14. III. Venditorum & emtorum è templo ejectio, ad v. 19. IV. De fidei efficacia informatio, ad v. 26. V. De potestate docendi quaestio, cum αὐτερωτήσει Christi, ad v. 33.

PARS I. Ingressus Iesu Hierosolymitanus.

Vers. 1. εἰς Βηθφαγῆ καὶ Βηθανίαν) Utriusque loci memi- nit Syrus: ut & Talmudici quod aliqui libri habent Βηθσφαγὴ puto esse ex corrupta pronunciatione. Nam ת Hebraeum declinat ad solum τοῦ σ.

Vulgatus solam Bethaniam commemorat. Quod etiam in Syro notat Beza, sed per ἁμάρ- τημα μνημονικὸν, siquidem & Syrus, & Arabs u- trumque locum habeant.

## 11:2
Vers. 2. ἐφ' ὃν οὐδεὶς ἀνθρώπων κεκάθικε) A most learned man rightly advises that animals not yet subjected to human uses were accustomed to be used for sacred purposes. The Latins called them 'injuges' (unyoked): as is in Festus and Macrobius. See the history in 1 Sam. VI. 7. Ovid: 'A heifer, Phoebus says, will meet you in the lonely fields, that has borne no yoke, and is immune to the curved plow.' Seneca: 'Ordered to go as a companion to the wandering cow: which neither the plowshare nor the curved yokes of a dragging cart had bent.' Μόσχοι ἀδάματοι πόσημα is in the Phoenissae of Euripides.

Nor did the Lord wish this to be done rashly, adds Beza, as if this foal had been destined for this very use, Christ thus testifying to his royal majesty by this pomp, though in appearance cheap, to the blind Jews. Which especially also ought to have been a character and κειμήλιον of the Messiah: from which he could be recognized.

Latin:

Vers. 2. ἐφ' ὃν οὐδεὶς ἀνθρώπων κεκάθικε) Bene monet vir doctissimus ad sacros usus solitas adhiberi animantes non- dum humanis usibus mancipatas. Injuges Latini vocabant: ut apud Festum & Macrobium est. Vide historiam I. Sam. VI. 7. Ovidius: Bos tibi, Phoebus ait, solis occurret in arvis Nullum passa jugum, curvique immunis aratri, Seneca: - - - Iussus erranti Comes ire vacca: quam non flexerat Vomer aut trudi juga curva plaustri. Μόσχοι ἀδάματοι πόσημα est in Phoenissis Euripidis.

Neque temere, addit Beza, hoc ita factum voluit Dominus, quasi ad hunc ipsum usum destinatus hic pullus fuerit, sic regiam suam majestatem hac licet in speciem vili pompa Christi caecis Judaeis testificante. Quae imprimis etiam character & κειμήλιον esse debebat Messiae: unde is dignosci poterat.

## 11:5
Vers. 5. Τί ποιεῖτε λύοντες τὸν πῶλον) That is, why are you untying him? The same manner of speaking is in Acts XXI. 13.

Latin:

Vers. 5. Τί ποιεῖτε λύοντες τὸν πῶλον) Id est, quorsum eum solvitis? Idem loquendi genus Actorum XXI. 13.

## 11:8
Vers. 8. στοιβάδας) It signifies a heap among the Hellenists. Hence στοιβάσειν ξύλα ἐπὶ τὸ πῦρ, καὶ στοιβάσουσι οἱ ἱοὶ Ἀαρὼν οἱ ἱερεῖς τὰ διχοτομήματα & what follows. Levit. I. v. 7. 8

Latin:

Vers. 8. στοιβάδας) Struem significat apud Hellenistas. Hinc στοιβάσειν ξύλα ἐπὶ τὸ πῦρ, καὶ στοιβάσουσι οἱ ἱοὶ Ἀαρὼν οἱ ἱερεῖς τὰ διχοτομήματα & quae sequuntur. Levit. I. v. 7. 8

## 11:10
Vers. 10. Βασιλεία τοῦ πατρὸς ἡμῶν Δαβὶδ) That some codices repeat here from the previous clause ἐν ὀνόματι κυρίου is not ancient, as the Latin teaches besides the Syriac. But the Arab has it, whose version appears by many signs to be more recent.

Latin:

Vers. 10. Βασιλεία τοῦ πατρὸς ἡμῶν Δαβὶδ) Quod hic ex superiore cominate quidam codices repetunt ἐν ὀνόματι κυ- ρίου vetus non est, ut praeter Syrum Latinus docet. Sed ha- bet Arabs, cujus seriorem esse versionem multis indiciis apparet.

## 11:11
Vers. 11. ὀψίας ἤδη οὔσης τῆς ὥρας) Phrynichus is the authority that ὄψιος is said as an adjective: and so I would take it here. Thus above, ὥρας πολλῆς γενομένης.

PART II. The cursing of the fig tree.

Latin:

Vers. 11. ὀψίας ἤδη οὔσης τῆς ὥρας) ὄψιος adjective dici au- ctor est Phrynichus: atque ita hic acceperim. Sic supra ὥρας πολλῆς γενομένης.

PARS II. Ficus maledictio.

## 11:12
Vers. 12. τῇ ἐπαύριον) Polybius speaks in this way also. ἐπείνασε) The salvation of the Jewish people figured in the fig tree. For it was not the time of year when the fig tree would bear fruit. He did not, therefore, look at the tree in this act; which, if it is unfruitful, is no less free from blame in the spring or summer than in the winter time.

Yet Christ was truly hungry, and properly so. This ought not, therefore, to be explained improperly and figuratively concerning the hunger for the salvation of the people, even if that is shadowed forth here. The typical signification presupposes the truth of the history: the spiritual hunger for the fruits of the Jews [corresponds to] the bodily hunger for the fruits of the fig tree. Furthermore, it is not for us to await the coming of Elijah to understand this passage, or with Heinsius to amend the passage against the constant consensus of all Codices, and thus read in a sense plainly contrary ἦ γὰρ ἦν, καιρὸς σύκων, for where it was, it was the time of figs: since in the East in the month of Nisan, or March, figs are born, as Pliny testifies. There is no need, I say, for this bold alteration of the text: for even if it was not yet the time of figs, in which, namely, they would mature universally and in abundance, whence most fig trees had nothing but leaves, yet this fig tree, peculiarly cultivated and enjoying convenience above others for bearing fruit, both could and ought to have had at least some figs, therefore Christ approached it, to see if he might find something of figs εἴ ἄρα εὑρήσει τι ἐν αὐτῇ, but he found nothing in it except mere leaves only, and not any fruits at all, which explanation does not entirely argue ignorance, since God himself is said to have descended to explore the life and actions of the Sodomites ἀνθρωποπαθῶς, and that approach and exploration was done not for the sake of Christ, but of others, so that the sterility of the tree might be made manifest. universally and in abundance, whence most fig trees had nothing but leaves, yet this fig tree, peculiarly cultivated and enjoying convenience above others for bearing fruit, both could and ought to have had at least some figs, therefore Christ approached it, to see if he might find something of figs εἴ ἄρα εὑρήσει τι ἐν αὐτῇ, but he found nothing in it except mere leaves only, and not any fruits at all, which explanation does not entirely argue ignorance, since God himself is said to have descended to explore the life and actions of the Sodomites ἀνθρωποπαθῶς, and that approach and exploration was done not for the sake of Christ, but of others, so that the sterility of the tree might be made manifest. For however it may be that it was not yet the καιρὸς of dried figs, or mature and timely figs, or that figs might break forth universally, which time was in the antitype when the Apostles were sent out into the whole world, yet grossi, that is, immature and untimely figs, which are noted in Hos. IX. 10 and Nah. III. 12 by the name of first-fruits on the fig tree, could then be had, especially in Judea; as it is said in Cant. II, the fig tree brought forth its grossos, for the winter has passed: from which early fruits Bethphage, to which the Lord was then near, seems to have its name: because to the Hebrews פגי are grossi, which not only means that more figs were there, but that they were mature and early, or came forth sooner than elsewhere in the East: where nothing is more pleasing than σύκα πρόδρομα (as Heinsius observes from Is. XXVIII. 4 and Hesychius that the Hellenists call that which is early and mature before the usual time,) and Hesychius, Heinsius observes,) if indeed such figs are placed among summer fruits, or those which immediately precede summer, Matt. XXIV. 12, Mark XIII. 28, and are for that very reason in delights and are pleasing, as things which rarity alone is accustomed to commend. Add that Pliny, book XV of Natural History, ch. 18, mentions from Cato that grossi are found in fig trees in winter if they are covered with manure after autumn; which, when dug up in milder weather with the tree and brought back into the light, receive new suns and others than those in which they lived, greedily as if born again, and mature with the flower of those coming in, early in a strange year even in the coldest tract; which we also observe in these regions if fig trees are brought into warmer cellars, and fruitful trees, which sometimes even through the winter preserve certain remnants of their fertility. What wonder, then, if in Palestine, a very warm region, figs were desired at that time? That reason, therefore, 'it was not the time of figs,' was not added for the sake of excusing the sterility, but rather so that the cause of Christ's approach and investigation might be rendered, because when it was not yet the time of mature figs or dried figs, or even of the universal bursting forth of figs, he wished to seek in this tree, situated in a more fertile and convenient place, luxuriating in leaves, whether at least something might be found in it, whether concerning the remnants of fertility, or concerning the gross, and early, or early-ripening figs, προδρόμοις σύκοις. Add that by those words, that the tree had nothing but leaves, it is implied that this tree was not only then, but also in previous years, always such—namely, abundant in leaves, but empty of fruit mystical meaning, and easily resolve the difficulties which Interpreters here vainly invent and fix.

Latin:

Vers. 12. τῇ ἐπαύριον) Ita & Polybius loquitur. ἐπείνασε) Salutem populi Judaici in ficu figurati. Tem- pus enim non erat anni quo ficus fructum ferret. Non ergo arborem spectavit in hoc facto; quae si infrugifera est, non minus culpa caret verno aut æstivo, quam hyberno tempore.

Vere tamen esurivit Christus, ac proprie. Non ergo improprie & figurate de esurie salutis populi explicari hoc debet, etsi ea hic adumbra- ta sit. Significatio typica præsupponit historiæ ve- ritatem: esuries spiritualis fructuum Judæorum e- suriem corporalem fructuum ficus. Cæterum non est, ut ad hunc locum intelligendum Eliæ ad- ventum expectemus, vel cum Heinsio locum contra omnium Codicum constantem consensum emen- demus, atque ita legamus sensu plane contrario ἦ γὰρ ἦν, καιρὸς σύκων, ubi enim erat, tempus erat fi- cuum: quum in oriente mense Nisan, vel Martio fi- ci, Plinio teste, nascantur. Hac, inquam, audaci tex- tus immutatione opus non est: nam etiamsi tempus nondum erat ficuum, quo scil. universaliter & in copia maturescerent, unde nil nisi folia ficus ple- ræque habebant, hæc tamen ficus peculiariter culta, & præ aliis commoditate gavisa ad feren- dos fructus opportuna, & poterat & debebat ha- bere minimum quasdam ficus, ideo ad eam ac- cessit Christus, num inveniret aliquid ficuum εἴ ἄρα εὑρήσει τι ἐν αὐτῇ, sed nihil in ea, nisi mera tantum folia, ac nec quicquam fructuum invenit, quæ explicatio non omnino arguit ignorantiam, quum & Deus ipse descendisse exploraturus So- domitarum vitam & actiones ἀνθρωποπαθῶς di- catur, & accessio & exploratio illa non Christi, sed aliorum, ut palam fieret sterilitas arboris, gratia facta. Nam utut caricarum, seu maturarum & tempestivarum ficuum nondum καιρὸς fuerit, aut ut ficus universaliter prorumperent, quod tem- pus in antitypo fuit, cum emitterentur Apostoli in totum orbem, grossi tamen, hoc est, immaturæ & in- tempestivæ ficus, quæ Hos. IX. 10. Nah. III. 12. pri- mitivorum in ficu nomine notantur, tum haberi poterant, imprimis in Judæa; uti Cant. II. dici- tur, ficus protulit grossos suos, hyems enim transiit: à quibus fructibus præcocibus Bethphage, ad quam versabatur tum Dominus, nomen habere videtur: quia Ebræis פגי grossi, quod non mo- do plures ibi, sed maturi & præcoces aut citius, quam alibi in oriente, provenirent ficus: ubi ni- hil gratius quam σύκα πρόδρομα (uti præcocem & ante tempus solitum maturam Hellenistas dice- re, ex Es. XXVIII. 4. & Hesychio observat Hein- sius,) siquidem ficus ejusmodi æstivos inter fru- ctus, aut qui proxime æstatem præcedunt, po- nantur Matth. XXIV. 12. Marc. XIII. 28. ac vel id- eo in delitiis & gratæ sint, ut quas commendare so- la raritas soleat. Adde quod Plinius l. XV. Hist. natur. c. 18. ex Catone memoret, deprehensas in fi- cubus hyeme grossos, si post autumnum fimo contegan- tur; quæ mitiore cœlo refossæ cum arbore, atque in lucem remissæ novos soles aliosque, quam quibus vi- xere avide tanquam iterum natæ accipiunt, & cum venientium flore maturescunt alieno præcoces anno in tractu vel gelidissimo; quod & in hisce oris, si cali- dioribus cellis inferantur ficus, deprehendimus, arboresque fœcundæ, quæ etiam per hyemem interdum fertilitatis suæ reliquias quasdam con- servent. Quid ergo mirum, si in Palæstina, re- gione calidissima isto tempore ficus desideratæ fuerint? Illa ergo ratio, non erat tempus ficuum, non excusandæ sterilitatis gratia addita est, sed po- tius, ut accessus & indagationis Christi causa redderetur, quod quum nondum tempus matura- rum ficuum vel caricarum esset, aut etiam univer- salis prostrusionis ficuum, in hac arbore, fertilio- ri & commodiori loco sita, foliis luxuriante, quære- re voluerit, anne saltim aliquid in ea reperiretur, seu de reliquiis fertilitatis, seu de grossis, & præco- quis, aut præcocibus ficubus προδρόμοις σύκοις. Ad- de quod verbis illis, quod arbor non habuerit nisi fo- lia, innuatur, quod arbor ista non tunc tantum, sed etiam superioribus annis talis fuerit semper foliis nempe abundans, fructibus autem vacua, propter- ea maledictione digna. Quæ omnia mystica signifi- cationi apprime conveniunt, & difficultates, quas hic frustra fingunt, & figunt Interpretes, facile ex- pediunt.

## 11:15
Vers. 15. ἤξατο ἐκβάλλειν] That is, ἐξέβαλε, just as we noted that the word πλεονάζειν is used above in ch. X. 32. For learned men seem to correctly conclude that a similar act was performed by Christ previously, which is narrated by John, but omitted by others because of the similarity of the deed.

PART III. The ejection of those selling and buying from the temple.

Latin:

Vers. 15. ἤξατο ἐκβάλλειν] Id est ἐξέβαλε, quomodo ver- bum illud πλεονάζειν supra annotavimus c. X. 32. Viden- tur enim viri eruditi recte colligere, antea quoque rem si- milem à Christo factam, quæ à Johanne narretur, præterita ab aliis ob facti similitudinem.

PARS III. Venditorum & emtorum è templo ejectio.

## 11:16
Vers. 16. διενέγκη σκεῦος] According to the subject matter, it ought to be understood as a vessel pertaining to making profit.

Therefore, those things which Walaeus brings forward here from Cunaeus out of Talmudic trifles are irrelevant; let no one come onto the mount of the temple with a staff, or shoes on their feet, or with a satchel, or money wrapped in linen. What do these things have to do with the present passage, or the trifles of the Rabbis with the reformation of Christ?

Latin:

Vers. 16. διενέγκη σκεῦος] κατὰ τὸ ὑποκείμενον intelligi de- bet σκεῦος ad quæstum faciendum pertinens.

Aliena ergo sunt, quæ è Cunæo hic Walæus ad- fert è nugis Talmudicis; nemo in montem templi ve- niat cum baculo, aut calceamentis pedum, neque cum mantica, aut pecuniis linteo involutis. Quid ista ad præsentem locum, aut næniæ Rabbinorum ad re- formationem Christi?

## 11:18
Vers. 18. ἐφοβοῦντο γὰρ αὐτὸν] I refer this to the word ἐζήτουν, which signifies solicitude. He says, therefore, that they were solicitous because they feared him, that is, the multitude of those who esteemed him highly. Ἐφοβήθησαν τὺς ὄχλυς, says Matthew, ἐπειδὴ ὡς προφήτην αὐτὸν εἶχον. Luke says exactly the same in ch. XIX. 47, 48, who, describing the helplessness of their plans more accurately, adds: ὐκ ἑυρισκον τὸ τι ποιήσωσι.

Latin:

Vers. 18. ἐφοβοῦντο γὰρ αὐτὸν] Refero ad verbum ἐζήτουν quod sollicitudinem significat. Sollicitos igitur dicit fuisse quia ipsum metuebant, id est multitudinem eorum qui ipsum magni faciebant. Ἐφοβήθησαν τὺς ὄχλυς, inquit Mat- thæus, ἐπειδὴ ὡς προφήτην αὐτὸν εἶχον. Idem plane dicit Lu- cas c. XIX. 47. 48. qui consiliorum ἀπορίαν accuratius de- scribens addit: ὐκ ἑυρισκον τὸ τι ποιήσωσι.

## 11:19
Vers. 19. ἐξεπορεύετο ἔξω τῆς πόλεως] Lest he should give, or seem to give, any occasion for new disturbances in the restless city by his presence at night.

PART IV. Instruction concerning the efficacy of faith.

Latin:

Vers. 19. ἐξεπορεύετο ἔξω τῆς πόλεως] Ne quam noctu in urbe inquieta rerum novarum occasionem præsentia sua daret, aut dare videretur.

PARS IV. De fidei efficacia informatio.

## 11:20
Vers. 20. Παραπορευόμενοι] When they were passing by the fig tree: as also in Matt. XXVII. 39, οἱ δὲ παραπορευόμενοι. The word 'to walk along' does not seem to me to be correctly used where it is not a matter of a river or a similar extended thing, but of a tree.

Latin:

Vers. 20. Παραπορευόμενοι] Cum ficum præterirent: ut & Matth. XXVII. 39. οἱ δὲ παραπορευόμενοι. Adambulandi vox non videtur mihi recte usurpari ubi non de amne aut simili re extensa, sed de arbore agitur.

## 11:22
Vers. 22. Πίστιν Θεῦ] That is, εἰς τὸν Θεὸν: it is similar to the type of 'trust of you' and 'trust of our art' in Tullius. Thus Acts III. 16, ἐπὶ πίστει τῦ ὀνόματος αὐτῦ, and Gal. II. 20, ἐν πίσῃ τῇ τῦ υῦ τῦ Θεῦ.

Latin:

Vers. 22. Πίστιν Θεῦ] Id est εἰς τὸν Θεὸν: simile est generis fiducia vestri & fiducia artis nostræ apud Tullium. Sic Act. III. 16. ἐπὶ πίστει τῦ ὀνόματος αὐτῦ. & Gal. II. 20. ἐν πίσῃ τῇ τῦ ὑῦ τῦ Θεῦ.

## 11:23
Vers. 23. ὃς ἂν εἴπῃ τῷ ὄρει τύτῳ] Mountains in the Prophets are often, as also in Rev. VIII. 8, great empires. The meaning in this place is: If the Jewish people had faith in God, the Roman yoke would be taken away from it.

This does not refer to the removal of the Roman yoke, nor is the discourse about the Jewish people, but about the disciples: and the efficacy of faith is commended, because not only the withering of the fig tree, but also the moving of a mountain into the sea—that is, whatever is impossible by nature (the species being changed, so that a judgment may be made from it about the genus)—can be done through faith: because divine power is expressed through the moving of a mountain in Job IX. 5. Therefore, the moving of mountains is to be understood literally. Cf. 1 Cor. XIII. 2.

Latin:

Vers. 23. ὃς ἂν εἴπῃ τῷ ὄρει τύτῳ] Montes in Prophetis sæ- pe, ut & Apocal. VIII. 8. sunt magna imperia. Sensus hoc loco est: Si fidem Deo haberet populus Judaicus, Roma- num jugum ab eo auferretur.

Non hic respicitur Romani jugi amolitio, nec de populo Judaico sermo est, sed de discipulis: & fi- dei commendatur efficacia, quod non solum ficus arefactio, sed etiam montis in mare translatio, hoc est, quicquid per naturam impossibile est (mutata specie, ut ex ea de genere judicium fiat) per fidem fieri possit: quia divina potentia per montis trans- lationem exprimitur Iob. IX. 5. Proprie ergo mon- tium translatio intelligenda. Conf. 1. Cor. XIII. 2.

## 11:25
Vers. 25. τάκητε προσευχόμενοι] See Matt. VI. 6. εἴ τι ἔχετε κατά τινος] The right of complaining about someone. See what [is said] regarding Matt. V. 23.

Latin:

Vers. 25. τάκητε προσευχόμενοι] Vide Matth. VI. 6. εἴ τι ἔχετε κατά τινος] Jus conquerendi de aliquo. Vi- de quæ ad Matth. V. 23.

## 11:26
Vers. 26. εἰ δὲ] Why in this place 'εἰ' should be taken more causally than oppositely, I truly do not see. Therefore, it seems to me that the Syrian and the Latin [versions] have translated it correctly.

PART V. The question concerning the authority of teaching, and the αἰτέρωσις [questioning] of Christ.

Latin:

Vers. 26. εἰ δὲ] Cur hoc quidem loco εἰ magis causaliter quam opposite accipi debeat sane non video. Itaque recte vertisse mihi videntur Syrus & Latinus.

PARS V. De potestate docendi quæstio, & Christi αἰτέρωσις.

## 11:27
Vers. 27. κὼ πρεσβύτεροι] What is added in certain books, λαῦ, is from an old interpretation: for neither the Syrian nor the Latin recognize it. Furthermore, who the πρεσβύτεροι τῦ λαῦ are, we have said elsewhere.

Latin:

Vers. 27. κὼ πρεσβύτεροι] Quod additur in libris quibus- dam λαῦ ex veteri interpretamento est: nam nec Syrus nec Latinus agnoscunt. Cæterum qui sint πρεσβύτεροι τῦ λαῦ alibi diximus.

## 11:32
Vers. 32. ἐφοβῦντο τὸν λαὸν] See above ch. VII. 12. ἖ιχον Ἰωάννην ὅτι ὄντως προφήτης ἦν] The customary construction would have been, as in Matthew, ἔχυσι τὸν Ἰωάννην ὡς προφήτην, or ἐδόκει περὶ Ἰωάννε ὅτι ὄντως προφήτης ἦν. Now he has mixed two types of speaking, and thus made the construction κατὰ τὸ σημαινόμενον [according to the meaning].

The parable of the vineyard, and of the servants of the Lord of the vineyard punished and killed, and the only son slain, and the punishment of the killers illustrated from the prophecy concerning the rejected cornerstone; and the plots of the Pharisees; who, with the Herodians, send out certain men to catch Jesus in his words, asking about the tribute to be paid to Caesar, but [they are] dismissed by that answer, which they admired. The Sadducees propose a doubt about the wife of seven brothers, but, being informed about the resurrection of the dead, they are dismissed. A lawyer asks about the greatest commandment, and he receives not only that one about loving God, but also the one next to it about the love of neighbor, and he approves that answer. Jesus asks about Christ being the son of David, why David calls him his Lord, and warns about the pride and avarice of the Scribes. He observes those putting coins into the treasury of Jesus, and among them he praises especially the poor widow.

There are seven parts: I. The parable of the vineyard, and its illustration, to v. 12. II. The temptation concerning giving tribute to Caesar, to v. 17. III. The question of the Sadducees concerning the resurrection, to v. 27. IV. The information of the lawyer concerning the greatest commandment of the law, to v. 34. V. The questioning concerning Christ being the son and Lord of David, to v. 37. VI. The warning concerning the pride and avarice of the lawyers, to v. 41. VII. The commendation of the alms of the poor widow, to v. 44.

PART I. The parable of the vineyard, and its illustration.

Latin:

Vers. 32. ἐφοβῦντο τὸν λαὸν] Vide supra c. VII. 12. ἖ιχον Ἰωάννην ὅτι ὄντως προφήτης ἦν] Confueta constructio fuerat, ut apud Matthæum, ἔχυσι τὸν Ἰωάννην ὡς προφήτην, aut ἐδόκει περὶ Ἰωάννε ὅτι ὄντως προφήτης ἦν. Nunc duo lo- quendi genera miscuit, atque ita constructionem fecit κα- τὰ τὸ σημαινόμενον.

Parabola de vinea, & servis Domini vineæ castigatis & occisis, filioque unico interfe- cto, & pœna interfectorum illustrata è va- ticinio de lapide angulari reprobato; ac insidiis Pharisæorum; qui cum Herodianis emittunt quosdam, qui verba Iesu captent, quærentes de censu Cæsari reddendo, sed responso eo, quod admirabantur, dimissos. Sadducæi dubium proponunt de uxore se- ptem fratrum, sed informati de resurre- ctione mortuorum dimittuntur. Legisperi- tus quærit de præcipuo præcepto, non illud tantum de diligendo Deo, sed etiam ei pro- ximum de dilectione proximi percipit, eamque responsionem approbat. Iesus in- terrogat de Christo Davidis filio, cur Do- minum suum ipsum vocet David, & monet de Scribarum fastu & avaritia. Iesu Gazo- phylazio nummos imponentes observant, & inter eos imprimis viduam pauperem lau- dat.

Partes sunt septem: I. Parabola de vinea, ejus- que illustratio, ad v. 12. II. Tentatio de censu Cæsa- ri dando, ad v. 17. III. Sadducæorum quæstio de re- surrectione, ad v. 27. IV. Legisperiti de præcipuo le- gis mandato informatio, ad v. 34. V. De Christo Davidis filio, & Domino interrogatio, ad v. 37. VI. De legisperitorum fastu, & avaritia commonitio, ad v. 41. VII. Eleemosynæ viduæ pauperis com- mendatio, ad v. 44.

PARS I. Parabola de vinea, ejusque illustratio.

## 12:1 Argument
Vers. 1. ἐν παραβολαῖς] משלים is among those things which often have a singular meaning with a plural sound, as Ez. XIV. 8.

Latin:

Vers. 1. ἐν παραβολαῖς] משלים inter ea est quæ plu- rali sono singularem sæpe habent significationem, ut Ez, XIV. 8.

## 12:2
Vers. 2. τῷ καιρῷ] τῶν καρπῶν as Matthew adds.

Latin:

Vers. 2. τῷ καιρῷ] τῶν καρπῶν ut addit Matthæus.

## 12:4
Vers. 4. ἐκεφαλαίωσαν] In Aristophanes, γαστρίζειν is formed in a similar way: about which matter a most learned man has well advised. The Scholiasts explain it as ἐν γαστρὶ τύπτειν [to strike in the belly].

ἠτιμωμένον] What the Greeks call ἀτιμάζειν, ἀτιμοῦν, and ἀτιμεῖν, later Latins called inhonorare and exhonorare. Both words are in Salvianus, a writer who is by no means base.

Latin:

Vers. 4. ἐκεφαλαίωσαν] Apud Aristophanem γαστρίζειν si- mili modo formatum est: qua de re bene monuit vir do- ctissimus. Scholiastæ exponunt ἐν γαστρὶ τύπτειν.

ἠτιμωμένον] Quod Græci dicunt ἀτιμάζειν, ἀτιμοῦν & ἀ- τιμεῖν, Latini posteriores dixerunt inhonorare & exhonora- re. Utraque vox apud Salvianum est minime sordidum Scriptorem.

## 12:6
Vers. 6. ἀγαπητὸν ἀυτᾶ] The Greeks note that by Hesiod and others ἀγαπητὸν is used to mean τὸν μονογενῆ (the only-begotten), thus יחיד which is μονογενὴς the LXX translate as ἀγαπητὸν, Jer. VI. 26, Gen. XXII. 2, where Aquila placed μονογενῆ. In the Canticle of Isaiah V. concerning the vineyard, דוד is translated as ἠγαπημένῳ & ἀγαπητός.

Latin:

Vers. 6. ἀγαπητὸν ἀυτᾶ] Notant Græci ab Hesiodo aliis- que ἀγαπητὸν dici τὸν μονογενῆ, sic יחיד quod est μονογενὴς LXX. vertunt ἀγαπητὸν, Jer. VI. 26. Gen. XXII. 2. ubi A- quila posuit μονογενῆ. In Cantico Esaïæ V. de vinea דוד ver- titur ἠγαπημένῳ & ἀγαπητός.

## 12:8
Vers. 8. κὶ ἐξέβαλον ἔξω τᾶ ἀμπελῶνος] This could be understood concerning the dead body in the fable, and in the meaning of the fable concerning the insults with which the Jews affected the name of Christ after his death: but since in Matthew there is a different order, it is better that we interpret κὶ ἐξέβαλον in the Hebrew manner as ἐκβληθέντα.

PART II. The temptation of the Pharisees and Sadducees concerning the tribute to Caesar.

Latin:

Vers. 8. κὶ ἐξέβαλον ἔξω τᾶ ἀμπελῶνος] Posset hoc intelligi de corpore mortuo in fabula, & in significatione fabulæ de contumeliis quibus Judæi nomen Christi post mortem affecerunt: sed cum apud Matthæum alius sit ordo, satius est more Hebræo κὶ ἐξέβαλον interpretemur ἐκβληθέντα.

PARS II. Pharisæorum & Sadducæorum de censu Cæsa- reò tentatio.

## 12:14
Vers. 14. δῶμεν ἢ μὴ δῶμεν] ἐθελοπτικῶς. Are you the author for us to give or not? Nor is this entirely the same as the previous question: but if Jesus had said it was lawful, another question remained, whether it was expedient.

Latin:

Vers. 14. δῶμεν ἢ μὴ δῶμεν] ἐθελοπτικῶς. Auctor es nobis de- mus an non? neque hoc idem omnino est cum superiore quæstione: sed si Jesus licere dixisset, supererat altera quæ- stio, an expediret.

## 12:15
Vers. 15. ὑπόκρισιν] For he perceived that they spoke with a feigned mind. He preferred the appearance of those desiring to learn, when their mind was plotting calumny.

PART III. The question of the Sadducees concerning the resurrection.

Latin:

Vers. 15. ὑπόκρισιν] Sensit enim simulata mente locu- tos. Discere cupientium præferebat speciem, cum animus calumniam strueret.

PARS III. Sadducæorum de resurrectione quæstio.

## 12:19
V. 19. τέκνα] I think it is well translated as children. See at Matthew.

Latin:

V. 19. τέκνα] Bene verti puto liberos. Vide ad Matthæum.

## 12:20
Vers. 20. ἑπτὰ ἀδελφοὶ ἦσαν] So most Codices and the Syriac, wherefore ἐν seems to have been added from the Latin: nor is it necessary. For the appearance of the fact begins a new sentence.

Erasmus also omitted the particle ἦν: nor did Beza find it except in one Codex. Therefore, the act of his audacity deserves no excuse, because he may not have feared to add this particle to the text. But it is very characteristic of this man, not vainly corrected by Grotius, though in other places he is no less rash.

Latin:

Vers. 20. ἑπτὰ ἀδελφοὶ ἦσαν] Ita plurimi Codices & Sy- rus, quare ἐν ex Latino videtur adjectum: neque necessa- rium est. Species enim facti novam sententiam inchoat.

Omisit etiam particulam ἦν Erasmus: nec inve- nit eam Beza nisi in uno Codice. Nullam ergo ex- cusationem meretur factum audacia ejus, quod adjicere veritus non sit textui hanc particulam. Sed perquam solennis illa est huic viro, non vane casti- gata a Grotio, in aliis tamen locis non minus teme- rario.

## 12:23
Vers. 23. ἐν τῇ οὖν ἀναστάσει ὅταν ἀναστῶσι] Mark delights in this kind of repetition of paronyms, as we have shown by several examples at Matt. XXIV. 22.

See Mark VII. 13. ch. XIII. 19. & 20. That repetition is rashly omitted by the Syriac, and in two of Beza's Codices. For the Arabic and the Vulgate Latin have it.

Latin:

Vers. 23. ἐν τῇ οὖν ἀναστάσει ὅταν ἀναστῶσι] Gaudet hujus- modi παρωνύμων iteratione Marcus ut exemplis aliquot o- stendimus ad Matth. XXIV. 22.

Vid. Marc. VII. 13. c. XIII. 19. & 20. Temere omit- titur illa repetitio a Syro, & in duobus Bezae Codi- cibus. Habent enim Arabs, & vulgatus Latinus.

## 12:24
Vers. 24. ὀυ διὰ τοῦτο πλανᾶσθε μὴ εἰδότες] It is clear from Matthew, or at least his interpreter, that an interrogation is placed here after the manner of the Hebrews for a vehement affirmation: who has πλανᾶσθε. Moreover, there is here again a σύνταξις κατὰ τὸ σημαινόμενον: for he said διὰ τοῦτο as if he were about to introduce ὅτι μὴ οἴδατε, whereas he has now said μὴ εἰδότες.

PART IV. Information of the lawyer concerning the chief commandment.

Latin:

Vers. 24. ὀυ διὰ τοῦτο πλανᾶσθε μὴ εἰδότες] Interrogatio- nem ex more Hebraeorum pro vehementi affirmatione po- sitam ex Matthaeo aut certe ejus interprete liquet: qui ha- bet πλανᾶσθε. Est autem hic rursus σύνταξις κατὰ τὸ σημαινό- μενον: nam διὰ τοῦτο dixit quasi illaturus esset ὅτι μὴ οἴδατε cum nunc dixerit μὴ εἰδότες.

PARS IV. Legisperiti de praecipuo mandato informatio.

## 12:29
Vers. 29. ἄκουε ἰσραὴλ κύριος ὁ Θεὸς ἡμῶν κύριος εἷς ἐστι] The very words of the LXX Interpreters, Deut. VI. 4. Mark added this well, because it pertains to the illustration of the following precept. For to the substance of religion it is not enough to worship any deity whatsoever, but a certain deity must be set before the mind, whose mark is unity, by which he is distinguished from the gods of the nations who were believed to be many, and likewise from the Angels.

Latin:

Vers. 29. ἄκουε ἰσραὴλ κύριος ὁ Θεὸς ἡμῶν κύριος εἷς ἐστι] Ipsa verba LXX. Interpretum Deut. VI. 4. Bene hoc addidit Marcus, quia ad sequentis praecepti illustrationem pertinet. Ad religionis enim substantiam non satis est quodvis nu- men colere, sed certum numen animo proponendum est, cujus nota est unitas, qua distinguitur a Deis gentium qui multi esse credebantur, item ab Angelis.

## 12:30
Vers. 30. ἐξ ὅλης τῆς διανοίας σου] Mark added this for the interpretation of that which preceded, τῆς ψυχῆς: just as below ἐξ ὅλης τῆς συνέσεως is added with a similar sense.

Latin:

Vers. 30. ἐξ ὅλης τῆς διανοίας σου] Addidit hoc Marcus ad interpretationem ejus quod praecessit τῆς ψυχῆς: uti & in- fra additum est ἐξ ὅλης τῆς συνέσεως simili sensu.

## 12:31
Vers. 31. ὁμοία ἀυτῇ] The Syriac and Latin read thus in agreement with Matthew, from whom I do not see why one should depart.

Latin:

Vers. 31. ὁμοία ἀυτῇ] Ita congruenter Matthaeo legerunt Syrus & Latinus a quibus cur discedendum sit non video.

## 12:32
Vers. 32. εἶπεν ἀυτῷ ὁ γραμματεὺς] He had come to test the wisdom of Christ; he bears witness to what he has heard.

Latin:

Vers. 32. εἶπεν ἀυτῷ ὁ γραμματεὺς] Exploraturus sapien- tiam Christi venerat, auditae testimonium praebet.

## 12:33
Vers. 33. πλεῖον] More and better and more pleasing to God. See what we have said concerning the order of the commandments at Matt. VII. 13.

τῶν ὁλοκαυτωμάτων καὶ θυσιῶν] עלה וזבח as in 2 Kings 5:17, 2 Chronicles 7:1. For the Septuagint sometimes use θυσίαν for מנחה, as we said above, and sometimes for זבח. But זבח is also used sometimes more broadly to signify all sacrifices except ὁλοκαυτώματα, and sometimes more strictly for those which are called χαριστήρια, as in Psalm 40:7, which the writer to the Hebrews cites in 10:5.

Latin:

Vers. 33. πλεῖον] Prius ac potius Deoque gratius. Vide quae de ordine praeceptorum diximus Matth. VII. 13.

τῶν ὁλοκαυτωμάτων καὶ θυσιῶν] עלה וזבח ut 2. Reg. V. 17. 2. Par. VII. 1. Nam LXX. modo pro מנחה ut supra diximus, modo pro זבח ponunt θυσίαν. Sed & זבח modo laxius ponitur ut omnia sacrificia significet praeter ὁλοκαυ- τώματα, modo strictius pro iis quae χαριστήρια dicuntur, ut Ps. XL. 7. quem citat scriptor ad Hebraeos X. 5.

## 12:34
V. 34. ὀυ μακρὰν εἶ ἀπὸ τῆς βασιλείας τοῦ Θεοῦ] There are many degrees of those who have not yet received the spirit of the kingdom, among whom he is not far removed from the kingdom in whom are men who understand the sum of piety and approve of it. Hence, by assiduous prayers, a passage to the kingdom is given. See Rom. VII.

For it is not enough to know and approve. If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them, John 13:17. Nor indeed is it enough only to understand the law, but it is required above all that Christ be rightly acknowledged from the Gospel and received by true faith, John 1:12, Rom. 9:4. This scribe did not yet acknowledge Him. Therefore Chrysostom says: He did not honor Him, he says, with perfect praise (Christ), but showed that something was lacking in Him. For although he is not far off, he is nevertheless away, wherefore that defect had to be supplied. Silently, therefore, He invited him to faith and stirred him up, so that he might strive toward further things and studiously inquire into what was still lacking to him. The reasoning of that one in Rom. 14 is different: for this one, already established in the kingdom of God, complains at least of the lust of the flesh against the spirit. Cf. Gal. 5:17.

PART V. Questioning concerning Christ the son and Lord of David.

Latin:

V. 34. ὀυ μακρὰν εἶ ἀπὸ τῆς βασιλείας τοῦ Θεοῦ] Eorum qui spiritum regni nondum acceperunt multi sunt gradus, quos inter non longe a regno remotus est ille in quo sunt homi- nes qui intelligunt summam pietatis & eam approbant. Hinc assiduis precibus ad regnum transitus datur. Vid. Rom. VII.

Non enim sufficit nosse & approbare. Haec si sciveritis, beati si feceritis Joh. XIII. 17. Nec vero tantum legem intelligere sufficit, sed imprimis re- quiritur, ut Christus ex Evangelio recte agnoscatur, & vera fide suscipiatur, Joh. I. 12. Rom. IX. 4. Quem nondum agnoscebat Scriba iste. Ideo Chry- sostomus: Non honoravit eum, inquit, consummata laude (Christus) sed nonnihil deesse ei ostendit. Nam etsi non procul abest, abest tamen, quare defe- ctus ille supplendus erat. Tacite igitur ad fidem eum invitavit, atque excitavit, ut ad ulteriora niteretur, & quae ipsi adhuc deerant, studiose inquireret. Alia est illius Rom. XIV. ratio: Hic enim in regno Dei jam constitutus, queritur saltim de carnis adversus spi- ritum concupiscentia. Conf. Gal. V. 17.

PARS V. De Christo Davidis filio & Domino interrogatio.

## 12:35
Verse 35. πῶς λέγουσιν οἱ γραμματεῖς] That is, how can what the experts in the law say stand? This question was proposed to the Pharisees, who in the explanation of the Prophets trusted much in the experts in the law. Therefore, Christ addresses them as those whom He knew would not depart from the authority of the experts in the law.

Latin:

Vers. 35. πῶς λέγουσιν οἱ γραμματεῖς] Id est, quomodo consistere potest quod dicunt legisperiti? Proponebatur haec quaestio Pharisaeis qui in explicatione Prophetarum multum credebant legisperitis. Itaq; Christus eos sic alloquitur quasi quos sciret ab auctoritate legisperitorum non discessuros.

## 12:37
Verse 37. πόθεν] πῶς in Matthew. Thus also for the Hebrews אֵין is how, as in Jer. 5:17; thus πόθεν μοι τοῦτο in Luke 1:43. The sense is, how can it come to pass that the same one is Lord and son? See what is said regarding Matthew.

PART VI. Admonition concerning the pride and avarice of the experts in the law.

Latin:

Vers. 37. πόθεν] πῶς Matthaeus. Sic & Hebraeis אֵין est quo- modo & Jer. V. 17. sic πόθεν μοι τοῦτο Luc. I. 43. Sensus est qui fieri potest, ut idem sit Dominus & filius? Vide quae ad Matthaeum.

PARS VI. De legisperitorum fastu & avaritia commonitio.

## 12:38
Verse 38. ὁ πολὺς ὄχλος] A great part of the common people.

and not about all the experts in the law but about certain exceedingly wicked ones is this being treated, so that ὗτοι is added for the sake of clarity. For Luke, who follows Mark in these things that are peculiar to Mark in such a way that he often takes the place of an interpreter, expresses this sentiment in this manner: οἱ κατεσθίουσι τὰς οἰκίας τῶν χηρῶν καὶ προφάσει μακρὰ προσεύχονται· ὗτοι λήψονται περισσότερον κρίμα, that is, Who indeed of the experts in the law devour the substance of widows under the pretext of prayer, upon them a proper and heavier punishment than upon others hangs.

Latin:

Vers. 38. ὁ πολὺς ὄχλος] Plebis pars magna.

dus, neque de omnibus legisperitis sed de quibusdam exi- mie improbis hic agi, ut ὗτοι additum sit perspicuitatis cau- sa. Nam Lucas quiMarcum in his quæ Marco sunt peculiaria ita sequitur ut sæpe interpretis sit loco, hanc sententiam in hunc exprimit modum: οἱ κατεσθίουσι τὰς οἰκίας τῶν χηρῶν καὶ προφάσει μακρὰ προσεύχονται· ὗτοι λήψονται περισσότερον κρί- μα, id est, Qui vero legisperitorum insuper viduarum sub- stantiam devorant orationis obtentu, his propria & gravior quam cæteris imminet pœna.

## 12:40
τὰς οἰκίας τῶν χηρῶν] Such as those whom Paul describes to Timothy, entering into houses and taking captive silly women laden with sins. The female sex, as it is more prone to superstition, is so much the more exposed to these frauds. But Christ said widows, because this burdens their guilt, that they were plundering those whom the divine law especially commends to them to be protected.

προφάσει μακρὰ προσευχόμενοι] Thus Paul said he was not engaged ἐν προφάσει πλεονεξίας, 1 Thess. 2:5. For these men are accustomed to pretend certain honest causes under which they may make gain: such as that they insist on tireless prayers before God for others: for which work they are not unjustly gifted with presents: when meanwhile they do not teach those for whom they say they are praying the true way of piety: and they do not allow gifts to be given to them, but they actively seek them: often even greater than the means of the giver. Therefore, here προφάσει is said for εἰς πρόφασιν πλεονεξίας. The comparison with Luke shows this.

PART VII. Commendation of the alms of the poor widow.

Latin:

τὰς οἰκίας τῶν χηρῶν] Quales & illi quos ad Timotheum Paulus describit, εἰς δύνοντες εἰς τὰς οἰκίας καὶ αἰχμαλωτεύοντες τὰ γυναικάρια σεσωρευμένα ἁμαρτίαις. Sexus muliebris ut ad superstitionem pronior, ita magis patet ad eas fraudes. Viduas autem dixit Christus, quia culpam ipsorum hoc o- nerat, quod eas expilabant quas tutandas lex divina præ- cipue illis commendat.

προφάσει μακρὰ προσευχόμενοι] Sic Paulus dixit se non ver- satum ἐν προφάσει πλεονεξίας 1. Thess. II. 5. Solent enim isti homines honestas quasdam causas prætendere sub quibus quæstum faciant: ut quod pro aliis apud Deum indefessis precibus instent: pro qua opera non injuria muneribus donentur: cum interim eos pro quibus precari se dicunt non doceant veram pietatis viam: & munera non dari sibi pariantur sed captent ultro: sæpe & majora quam pro facul- tatibus donantis. Est ergo hic προφάσει dictum pro εἰς πρό- φασιν πλεονεξίας. Ostendit hoc Lucæ collatio.

PARS VII. Eleemosynæ viduæ pauperis commendatio.

## 12:41
Verse 41. κατέναντι] That is, in the sight of the chest. Thus κατέναντι is taken above in ch. 11:2 and below in 13:3.

γαζοφυλακίῳ] γαζοφυλάκιον here, as also Luke calls the chest into which gifts were put: κιβωτὸν in the LXX, 2 Kings 12:10, 11; 2 Chron. 24. Others call it γλωσσόκομον, 2 Chron. 24:8; Josephus calls it ξυλινὸν θησαυρὸν. Otherwise, γαζοφυλάκιον was accustomed to be called that part of the Temple which was extended behind the holy house on either side toward the west, in which that chest was, and other treasures of the Temple, and then indeed purple, scarlet, spices, and whatever else was kept for the uses of the Temple. Concerning which Josephus, Wars 6:41; likewise wine, oil, grain, and the remaining food of the Priests, as can be seen in Neh. 10:37, where what is in the Hebrew as לשכה is translated γαζοφυλάκιον, as also in Neh. 13:5, for which in 1 Chron. 28:12 we read παστοφόρια, as also in Jer. 35:4, when in the same chapter of Jeremiah, verse 2, the same word לשכות is rendered by the word ἀυλὰς. Thus also in Ez. 40:17, the LXX translate the same word לשכות as παστοφόρια, Aquila as γαζοφυλάκια, Symmachus as ἐξέδρας. In this way John uses γαζοφυλάκιον in chapter VIII. 20. One of the order of the priests, who was called γαζοφύλαξ, was set over this γαζοφυλάκιον. Josephus mentions it several times, who also says that a golden chain, hung by Agrippa in memory of his chains, was within the Temple ὑπὲρ τὸ γαζοφυλάκιον: and elsewhere he says that there were two thousand talents ἐν τῷ γαζοφυλακίῳ.

χαλκὸν] For the reason that follows, I think χαλκὸν is taken here for any money, even gold and silver, just as aes is for the Latins. Nor is it otherwise in Matt. X. 9.

Latin:

Vers. 41. κατέναντι] Id est, in conspectu arcæ. Ita κα- τέναντι sumitur supra c. XI. 2. & infra XIII. 3.

γαζοφυλακίῳ] γαζοφυλάκιον hic ut & Lucas vocat arcam in quam dona mittebantur: κιβωτὸν LXX. 2. Reg. XII. v. 10. 11. 2. Par. XXIV. Alii γλωσσόκομον 2. Par. XXIV. 8 Jo- sephus ξυλινὸν θησαυρὸν. Alioqui solebat γαζοφυλάκιον dici pars illa Templi quæ pone ædem sacram in latus utrumque versus occasum porrigebatur, in qua & arca illa erat, & alia Templi κειμήλια, tum vero purpura, coccus, aromata & quicquid præterea in usus Templi asservabatur. De quibus Josephus Ἁλώσεως VI. 41. item vinum, oleum, fru- mentum & reliqua Sacerdotum alimenta, ut videre est Neh. X. 37. ubi quod in Hebræo est לשכה vertitur γαζοφυλά- κιον, ut & Neh. XIII. 5. pro quo 1. Par. XXVIII. 12. legimus παστοφόρια, ut & Jer. XXXV. 4. cum eodem Jeremiæ capite commate 2. vox eadem לשכות reddita sit voce ἀυλὰς. Sic & Ez. XL. 17. eandem vocem לשכות LXX. vertunt πα- στοφόρια, Aquila γαζοφυλάκια, Symmachus ἐξέδρας. Hoc mo- do γαζοφυλάκιον usurpat Johannes c. VIII. 20. Huic γαζο- φυλακίῳ præpositus erat unus ex Sacerdotum ordine, qui vocabatur γαζοφύλαξ. Meminit Josephus ali quoties, qui & catenam auream ab Agrippa in memoriam vinculorum suo- rum suspensam ait intra Templum ὑπὲρ τὸ γαζοφυλάκιον: & alibi ἐν τῷ γαζοφυλακίῳ fuisse ait duo millia talentorum.

χαλκὸν] Ob id quod sequitur arbitror χαλκὸν hic pro qua- vis etiam aurea & argentea pecunia sumi, ut æs Latinis. Nec aliter Matth. X. 9.

## 12:43
Vers. 43. προσκαλεσάμενος τὲς μαθητὰς] He said this to them privately, because it was not appropriate for either the widow or the others to hear this. But he wished to teach the disciples what the true estimation of liberality is before God and those who imitate God.

In which nothing is to be valued except the love of the giver. πλεῖον] Because ἀπὸ ἐλαττόνων, as Aristotle speaks. In all things the mind is especially to be regarded, not merely external deeds. Moreover, it is a more liberal affection to give a little from a very small amount than much from a large heap. Xenophon, Anabasis VII: 'For it is not the number that defines the much and the little, but the power of the one giving and the one receiving.' Andronicus Rhodius: 'For liberality is not judged according to the size or the quantity of the things given, but according to the proportion which the things given have to the substance of the giver.' Salvianus well says: 'It is not the mind of the giver that is commended by the gifts, but the gifts by the mind, nor does money insinuate faith, but faith insinuates money.' Chrysostom, Homily XIX on John. μόνον σὺ μὴ κατοκνήσῃς· κ' ἂν ὀβόλες δύο καταβάληῃς, ἐκ ἀποστραφήσεται, ἀλλ' ὡς πολὺν δέχεται πλῦτον· ἐπειδὴ γὰρ αἰτεῖται, ὡς εἰς χρείαν ἕνεκεν ταῦτα λαμβάνει εἰκότως ἂν ἐν τῷ μέτρῳ τῷ διδομένῳ, ἀπ' ἐν τῇ προαιρέσει τῶ παρέχοντος τὸ πᾶν ὁρίζεται. The same in the ninth chapter of II Corinthians v. 7: 'For the much and the little is not defined by the measure of the things given, but by the power of the substance of the giver.'

Latin:

Vers. 43. προσκαλεσάμενος τὲς μαθητὰς] Seorsim hoc il- lis dixit, quia nihil attinebat aut viduam hoc audire aut cæ- teros. Sed discipulos docere voluit quæ vera esset liberali- tatis æstimatio apud Deum & Dei imitatores.

In qua censendum nil nisi dantis amor. πλεῖον] Quia ἀπὸ ἐλαττόνων, ut Aristoteles loquitur In re- bus omnibus præcipue spectandus animus, non nude facta externa. Est autem affectus liberalioris de minimo paulum dare, quam multum de magno acervo. Xenophon. exped. VII. ὀ γὰρ ὁ ἀριθμὸς ὁρίζει ἴσι τὸ πολὺ κὶ ὀλίγον, ἀλλ' ἡ δύναμις τῆ τε ἀποδιδόντος κὶ τῆ λαμβάνοντος, Andronicus Rhodius, γὰρ πρὸς τὸ μέγεθος ἤ τὸ πλῆθος τῶν διδομένων ἡ ἐλευθεριότης κρί- νεται, ἀλλὰ κατὰ τὴν ἀναλογίαν ἧς ἔχουσι τὰ διδόμενα πρὸς τὴν ὀ- σίαν τῶ διδόντος. Bene Salvianus: Non animus dantis datis, sed animo commendantur data, nec pecunia fidem insinuat, sed pe- cuniam fides. Chrysostomus homil. XIX. in Joh. μόνον σὺ μὴ κατοκνήσῃς· κ' ἂν ὀβόλες δύο καταβάληῃς, ἐκ ἀποστραφήσεται, ἀλλ' ὡς πολὺν δέχεται πλῦτον· ἐπειδὴ γὰρ αἰτεῖται, ὡς εἰς χρείαν ἕνεκεν ταῦτα λαμβάνει εἰκότως ἂν ἐν τῷ μέτρῳ τῷ διδομένῳ, ἀπ' ἐν τῇ προαιρέσει τῶ παρέχοντος τὸ πᾶν ὁρίζεται. Idem in nonum cap. II ad Corinthios v. 7. τὸ γὰρ πολὺ κὶ τὸ ὀλίγον ἐ τῷ μέ- τρῳ τῶν διδομένων θέσεός ὁρίζει, ἀλλὰ τῇ δυνάμει τῆς ὀσίας τῶ διδόντος.

## 12:44
Vers. 44. ἐκ τῶ περισσεύοντος] Not πᾶν τὸ περισσεῦον, which nevertheless would have been less than what the poor widow was giving, but some amount from a great abundance. Thus Luke called that which remains over our needs τὸ περισσεῦον in XII. 15.

ἐκ τῆς ὑστερήσεως] Thus περίσσευμα and ὑστέρημα are found opposed to each other in Paul, 2 Cor. VIII. 14, who also elsewhere uses the word ὑστέρημα in the meaning of ἔνδεια, חסר. In the Greek version of the Old Covenant, ἔνδεια and ὑστέρημα are used indiscriminately.

Τὸν βίον] βίος is that by which life is sustained: Hence Βιόθεν βίου δεόμενοι ὧν ἔσιν βίος.

More loosely, all things that we possess for our uses are also called βίον, as in Luke 8:43, 15:2, 30. Thus also the Hebrews use חַיִּים. However, I think that in this passage βίον is taken by a man of rare erudition, Arias Montanus, as only so much as suffices for the daily nourishment of a man; for the daily sustenance of the very poorest men was provided for a mere farthing.

Latin:

Vers. 44. ἐκ τῶ περισσεύοντος] Non πᾶν τὸ περισσεῦον, quod tamen minus futurum fuerat quam quod dabat pau- percula, sed de magna copia aliquantum. Ita τὸ περισσεῦον Lucas dixit id quod necessitatibus nostris superest XII. 15.

ἐκ τῆς ὑστερήσεως] Sic περίσσευμα & ὑστέρημα inter se oppo- sita inveniuntur apud Paulum 2. Cor. VIII. 14. qui & alibi vocem ὑστέρηματος usurpat in significatione ἐνδείας, חסר In Græca veteris fœderis versione promiscue ponuntur ἔνδεια & ὑστέρημα.

Τὸν βίον] βίος est id quo vita sustentatur: Hinc Βιόθεν βίου δεόμενοι ὧν ἔσιν βίος.

Laxius etiam βίον vocantur omnia quæ in usus nostros pos- sidemus, ut Luc. VIII. 43. c. XV. 2. 30. Sic & Hebræi usur- pant חַיִּים. Bene autem hoc loco arbitror à viro raræ erudi- tionis Aria Montano βίον accipi tantum, quantum quoque die homini alendo sufficit; nam pauperrimorum hominum diurnus victus quadrante admodum parabatur.

## 13:1 Argument
CHAPTER XIII. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

As the disciples admire the building of the temple, He predicts its destruction, and on the Mount of Olives He prophesies concerning its signs, concerning false Christs, wars and earthquakes, the delivering of the disciples to the council and synagogues, and the preaching of the Gospel through all nations: the assistance of the Holy Spirit is promised to the Apostles, and a warning is added concerning flight when the abomination of desolation shall be seen, and concerning guarding against false Christs and false prophets: and with the signs of the final coming of the Son of Man subjoined, whose day the Father alone knows; by a parable about a householder going on a journey, they are stirred to vigilance.

There are two parts: I. The prediction of the destruction of the temple and the signs of the same, with necessary admonition, to verse 22. II. The prediction of the signs of the final coming of the Son of Man, with an exhortation to vigilance, to verse 37.

PART I. The prediction of the destruction of the temple and the signs of the same with necessary admonition.

Verse 1. ποταποὶ λίθοι] A voice of one admiring, as in Matthew 8:27. Concerning these stones, Josephus says thus: The temple was built of white and strong stones of such size; each about 6 in length, and in height, and in breadth about 12.

Latin:

CAPUT XIII. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Admirantibus discipulis ædificium templi de- structionem ejus prædicit, & in monte Oli- veti de signis ejus vaticinatur, de Pseudo- Christis, bellis & terræmotibus, tradendis curiæ & Synagogis discipulis, Evangelio prædicando per omnes populos: promissa Apostolis Spiritus Sancti assistentia, addi- taque monitione de fuga, cum videbitur a- bominatio desolationis, & de cavendis fal- sis Christis, falsisque Prophetis: Subjun- ctisque signis novissimi adventus filii ho- minis, cujus diem solus Pater novit; para- bola de patrefamilias peregre proficiscente, ad vigilantiam excitantur.

Partes sunt duæ: I. Prædictio destructionis tem- pli, & signorum ejusdem, cum admonitione necessaria ad v. 22. II. Prædictio signorum adventus Filii hominis novissimi, cum parænesi ad vigilantiam, ad v. 37.

PARS I. Prædictio destructionis templi & signorum e- jusdem cum admonitione necessaria.

Vers. 1. ποταποὶ λίθοι] Admirantis vox ut Matth. VIII. 27. De his lapidibus ita Josephus : ᾠκοδομήθη δὲ ὁ ναὸς, ἐκλι- θῶν μὲν λευκῶν τε κὶ κρατερῶν τὸ μέγεθος· ἑκάστου περὶ ἓξ κὶ ἕ- χων ἐπὶ μῆκος, ἡ δὲ ὕψος, εὖρος δὲ περὶ ιβ.

## 13:4
Verse 4. πάντα ταῦτα συντελεῖσθαι] That is, τότο τὸ πᾶν, this whole universe. See John 1:3. For Matthew shows that there is another question, distinct from the destruction of Jerusalem, where the same sense is expressed here by the words: what is the sign of the end of the age.

Latin:

Vers. 4. πάντα ταῦτα συντελεῖσθαι] Id est, τότο τὸ πᾶν hoc universum. Vid. Joh. I. 3. Nam alteram esse quæstionem diversam ab excidio Hierosolymorum ostendit Matthæus ubi hic idem sensus istis exprimitur verbi τί τὸ σημεῖον τῆς συντελείας τῶ αἰῶνος.

## 13:6
V. 6. ἐγώ εἰμι, אֲנִי הוּא I am he whom you expect.

Latin:

V. 6. ἐγώ εἰμι, אֲנִי הוּא Ego sum ille quem exspectatis.

## 13:8
V. 8. ταραχαὶ] A metonymy. For it indicates the prodigies which Luke calls Φοβητρὰ. See what will be said there.

Latin:

V. 8. ταραχαὶ] Μετωνυμία. Indicat enim prodigia quæ Φο- βητρὰ Lu. as vocat. Vide quæ inibi dicentur.

## 13:9
Vers. 9. βλέπετε δὲ ὑμεῖς ἑαυτοὺς] The use of the verb βλέπειν is different from that which we noted above. Thus 2 John 8, βλέπετε ἑαυτοὺς, that is, προσέχετε ἑαυτοῖς, attend to yourselves. In Matthew it is προσέχετε ἀπὸ τῶν ἀνθρώπων, chapter 10:17. For from there, because of the coherence of the matters, that part was transferred here, as will be apparent to one comparing them.

and you will be beaten in the synagogues] I do not doubt that this is the true reading which the ancient codices prefer, having been variously interpolated by those ignorant of that manner of speaking. For some added καὶ after the word συναγωγὰς, others replaced εἰς τὰς συναγωγὰς with ἐν ταῖς συναγωγαῖς. He was baptized into the Jordan and is into the house, and below, he who is into the field: the Latins also say to be into the power and similar things.

Beza notes this. But because most copies use a punctuation mark after συναγωγὰς, I see no reason why they could not rightly be preferred to the fewer? It must not be concealed, however, that the edition of Stephanus in the year 1550 has it as Grotius does.

Latin:

Vers. 9. βλέπετε δὲ ὑμεῖς ἑαυτοὺς] Alius est usus verbi βλέ- πειν ab eo quem supra annotavimus. Sic II. Joh. 8. βλέ- πετε ἑαυτοὺς, id est, προσέχετε ἑαυτοῖς, vobis attendite. In Matthæo est προσέχετε ἀπὸ τῶν ἀνθρώπων c. X. 17. Nam in- de ob cohærentiam rerum pars ista huc transsumta est, ut conferenti apparebit.

κὶ εἰς τὰς συναγωγὰς δαρήσεσθε] Veram hanc esse lectio- nem quam præferunt antiqui codices non dubito ab ignaris ejus dicendi generis varie interpolatam. Num alii καὶ post vo- cem συναγωγὰς addiderunt, alii pro εἰς τὰς συναγωγὰς re- posuerunt ἐν ταῖς συναγωγαῖς.ἐβαπτίσθη εἰς Ἰορδάνην & εἰς οἶκον ἐστι, & infra ὁ εἰς τὸν ἀγρὸν ὢν: Latini quoque dicunt esse in potestatem & similia.

Notat Bezam. Sed quia pleraque exemplaria post συναγωγὰς distinctionem adhibent,cur non ea paucioribus præferri potuerint jure, nullam video causam? Non dissimulandum tamen, quod ita ut Grotius, Stephani editio Anno ʆƆ ʆL. ha- beat.

## 13:11
Verse 11. ἀνάγωσιν] A literal expression. For he who drags another into court is properly said to be ἄγειν: whence Agere and Actio for the Latins.

μηδὲ μελετᾶτε] Luke 12:11.

Latin:

Vers. 11. ἀνάγωσιν] κυριολογία. Nam ἄγειν proprie dicitur is qui alium in jus rapit: unde Agere & Actio Latinis.

μηδὲ μελετᾶτε] Luc. XII. 11.

## 13:14
Verse 14. τῆς ἐρημώσεως] I think that which is added here in certain codices, 'that which was spoken by Daniel the prophet,' was added from Matthew. For the Latins do not acknowledge it.

The argument from the Latin codices is not sufficiently solid. In the received Greek texts, and even in those praised by Robert Stephanus, these things are not omitted.

ὅπυ ᾀ δεῖ] ᾀ δεῖ is לֹא כֵן, just as we said regarding Matthew that διδάσκοντες ἃ μὴ δεῖ, Tit. 1:11, signifies τὰ κύκλῳ Ἱεροσάλυμ.

Latin:

Vers. 14. τῆς ἐρημώσεως] Quod hic in quibusdam codici- bus additur τὸ ῥηθὲν ὑπὸ Δανιὴλ τῦ προφήτυ puto ex Matthæo adjectum. Nam Latini non agnoscunt.

Non satis solidum est argumentum à Latinis co- dicibus. In Græcis receptis,etiam in Rob. Ste- phani laudata hæc non omittuntur.

ὅπυ ᾀ δεῖ] ᾀ δεῖ est לֹא כֵן ut διδάσκοντες ἃ μὴ δεῖ, Tit. I. 11. significari τὰ κύκλῳ Ἱεροσάλυμ diximus ad Matthæum.

## 13:19
Verse 19. κτίσεως] That is, κόσμου, as Matthew has it. We said this above in chapter 10:6.

PART II. The prediction of the signs of the coming of the Son of Man, with an exhortation to vigilance.

Latin:

Vers. 19. κτίσεως] Id est κόσμου ut habet Matthæus. Di- ximus supra c. X. 6.

PARS II. Signorum adventus filii hominis novissimi prædictio cum parænesi ad vigilantiam.

## 13:27
Verse 27. ἐπισυνάξει] He is said to do himself what he commands the angels to do: for so Matthew says.

Latin:

Vers. 27. ἐπισυνάξει] Ipse facere dicitur quod angelos fa- cere jubet: ita enim Matthæus.

## 13:32
Verse 32. ὀὐδὲ ὁ υἱὸς] It seems to me, unless I am taught better, that this passage can be explained without impiety in this manner, that we say the divine wisdom impressed its effects upon the human mind of Christ according to the requirements of the times. For what else is it, if we do not twist the words, that he προέκοπτε σοφίᾳ, Luke 2:52? Just as, therefore, after the resurrection he received all power, so also he received all knowledge. And lest anyone think this opinion was condemned by antiquity, that statement of Ambrose can sufficiently admonish us: 'According to the flesh, indeed, the wisdom of God was being filled, and grace.' But for the time of his ἀποστολῆς, there was no need for Jesus to know the day of the universal judgment, which God the Father wished to remain hidden. And that Irenaeus did not think otherwise is indicated by the fact that he says, in book 2, chapters 48 and 49: 'The Son did not blush to refer the knowledge of that day to the Father, and he said what is true.' Item: 'And thus, according to knowledge, the Father is announced as being superior by the Lord.' Leontius on the Sects: 'It should be known that many of the fathers, and indeed almost all, appear to say that he was ignorant. For if he is said to be consubstantial with us in all things, and we are ignorant, it is clear that he also was ignorant, and the Scripture also says concerning him that he increased in stature and wisdom.'

Those words in Luke 2:52 concern habitual or experimental knowledge. Furthermore, Christ as man had all power even in the state of humiliation κτ᾽ τὴν κτῆσιν, John 3:34, Colossians 2:9, which he received after the resurrection κτ᾽ τὴν χρῆσιν, so that he might exercise it fully in heaven and on earth. This must also be held regarding the knowledge communicated through the hypostatic union. For all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge were hidden in him, Colossians 2:3, even if, by reason of use, the knowledge of all things was not in readiness, which he had communicated by reason of possession: because he was dwelling in the state of humiliation. After the resurrection he did not answer in that way: 'Of that day and hour no one knows, neither the Son,' but 'It is not for you to know the times,' Acts 1:7. Therefore, one must, with Cyril, book 9 of the Thesaurus, chapter 4, admire the mercy of God the Word, because he did not refuse for our sake to descend to such great humility that he took upon himself all our things, and even human ignorance itself. Therefore, the Papists are wrong to assert that Christ knew the day of judgment by the very act according to his human nature, but pretended that he did not know: from whom Jacobus Faber Stapulensis dissents, acknowledging the truth: 'Christ in these words looks to the infirmity of the nature assumed, before it shone in its glory of immortality.' We have dealt with this passage at greater length in the Anti-Crellius, where we also stopped the mouths of the Socinians, who abuse the same passage for the denial of the divine nature of Christ.

Latin:

Vers. 32. ὀὐδὲ ὁ υἱὸς] Videtur mihi, ni meliora docear, hic locus non impie posse exponi hunc in modum, ut dicamus divinam sapientiam menti humanæ Christi effectus suos im- pressisse pro temporum ratione. Nam quid aliud est, si ver- ba non torquemus, προέκοπτε σοφίᾳ, Luc. II. 52. Sicut igi- tur post resurrectionem accepit omnem potestatem, ita & omnem scientiam. Ac ne quis hanc sententiam ab antiqui- tate damnatam putet, satis admonere nos potest illud Am- brosii: secundum carnem utique sapientia Dei implebatur & gratia. Pro tempore autem ἀποστολῆς suæ Jesu opus non erat scire diem universalis judicii, quem Deus Pater latere vo- luit. Nec aliter sensisse Christianorum vetustissimos indicio est Irenæus, qui lib. II. cap. XLVIII. & XLIX. Scientiam, in- quit, diei illius filius non erubuit referre ad Patrem, & dixit quod verum est. Item: & secundum agnitionem itaque præ- positus esse pater annuntiatus est à Domino. Leontius de Se- ctis: ἰσέον ὅτι οἱ πολλοὶ τῶν πατέρων, σχεδὸν δὲ πάντες, φαί- νονται λέγοντες αὐτὸν ἀγνοεῖν. εἰ γὰρ κατὰ πάντα λέγεται ἡμῖν ὁ- μούσιος, ἀγνοοῦμεν δὲ κὰμεῖς, δηλονότι κὰὐτὸς ἠγνόει, κὰὶ ἡ γρα- φὴ δὲ λέγει περὶ αὐτῦ, ὅτι προέκοπτεν ἡλικίᾳ ό σοφίᾳ.

Illa Luc. II. 52. concernunt scientiam habitualem vel experimentalem. Cæterum habuit omnem po- testatem Christus ut homo etiam in statu exinani- tionis κτ᾽ τὴν κτῆσιν, Johan. III. 34. Coloss. II. 9. quam κτ᾽ τὴν χρῆσιν, ut plenarie in cœlo, & in ter- ra exerceret, accepit post resurrectionem. Quod etiam de scientia per unionem hypostaticam com- municata habendum. Omnes enim thesauri sapientiæ & agnitionis in ipso reconditi fuére Col. II. 3. etsi ra- tione χρήσεως non in promtu fuerit omnium re- rum notitia, quam ratione κτήσεως communica- tam habebat: quia in statu exinanitionis versaba- tur. Post resurrectionem non ita respondit: de die illa & hora nemo novit, neque Filius, sed non est vestrum nosse tempora Act. I. 7. Oportet ergo cum Cyrillo l. IX. Thesaur. c. 4. misericordiam Dei Ver- bi admirari, quod non recusaverit propter nos ad tantam humilitatem descendere, ut omnia nostra & i- psam etiam ignorantiam humanam susciperet. Per- peram igitur Pontificii Christum actu ipso scivisse diem judicii secundum humanam naturam, sed se scire dissimulasse asserunt: à quibus dissentit Jac. Faber Stapul. veritatem agnoscens: Christus his verbis naturæ assumtæ infirmitatem respicit, ante- quam in sua immortalitatis fulgeret gloria. Pluribus de hoc loco egimus in Anti-Crellio, ubi Socinianis quoque eodem ad inficiationem divinæ Christi naturæ abutentibus os oppilavimus.

## 13:34
Vers. 34. ἐξουσίαν] Thus the Syriac. It is clear that the management of domestic affairs is to be understood.

τὸ ἔργον αὐτῦ] Ministry. This word is taken in this way in John 4:34, 6:29, 1 Cor. 16:10.

κὰι τῷ θυρωρῷ] The κὰὶ here is redundant in the Hebrew manner, which has been observed elsewhere as well.

Beza thought it should be clearly expunged: But such audacity is not to be tolerated. Nor does any necessity appear for us to believe that it is even redundant, since the sense holds correctly while it remains intact. However, that was not poorly observed by Beza: that this type of expression is taken from the custom of the ancients, who were accustomed to have household slaves and a doorkeeper in particular, given the abundance of servants.

Latin:

Vers. 34. ἐξουσίαν] Ita Syrus. Procurationem rerum do- mesticarum patet intelligi.

τὸ ἔργον αὐτῦ] Ministerium. Ita vox hæc sumitur Johan- nis IV. 34. VI. 29. 1. Cor. XVI. 10.

κὰι τῷ θυρωρῷ] κὰὶ hic παρέλκει more Hebraico, quod alibi quoque observatum.

Beza plane expungendum duxit: Sed audacia non ferenda. Neque ulla necessitas apparet, ut vel παρέλκειν credamus: quum sensus ea integra manente recte habeat. Id autem non male Beza observatum: genus hoc dicendi ex veterum consuetu- dine petitum esse, qui atrienses servos & janitorem in primis habere consueverunt, abundante servorum multitudine.

## 14:1 Argument
THE HISTORY OF THE LORD'S PASSION, CHAP. XIV. & XV. described by St. Mark.

CHAPTER XIV. ARGUMENT AND DIVISION.

With the Passover imminent, when the priests were seeking how they might kill Jesus, yet not at the feast, because some had taken it indignantly that Jesus had been anointed in Bethany, and that the nard had not rather been sold, Judas betook himself to the priests to betray him for mon- as they were promising: Jesus, however, having sent two disciples, took care to have the Passover prepared for himself, and eating with the disciples, he foretold the betrayal, denouncing woe to the betrayer, and distributing his body with the blessed bread and his blood with the blessed chalice, he celebrated the holy Eucharist, and having sung a hymn, going out to the Mount of Olives, he said that all would be scandalized this night, and that the shepherd being struck, the flock would be scattered; but that he himself would go before them into Galilee after the resurrection; and when Peter protested to the contrary, he prophesied that he would deny him three times: and in the estate of Gethsemane he began to tremble, to be terrified, and to be sad, and falling to the ground three times he prayed that, if it were possible, this chalice might pass: he exhorted the sleeping disciples to watch: for the hour was at hand for him to be betrayed. Soon Judas is present with an armed cohort, and by a sign, a kiss given to him, and by the word Rabbi addressed, he himself was apprehended: the disciples fleeing, but Jesus being led to the Priests, with Peter following from afar. But the Priests, and the whole Sanhedrin seeking testimonies against Jesus, when none were found, some testified, but with discordant testimony, that he had said he would destroy the temple, and in three days rebuild it; but the High Priest asking whether he is the Christ, Jesus affirmed it, and foretold that the son of man would sit at the right hand of power, which the High Priest proclaimed to be blasphemous, and thus they condemned him with a unanimous sentence, as guilty of death: some mocked him, and spat in his face, and the servants struck him, while Peter, when he was accused that he had been with Jesus, denied Jesus three times, and wept at the second crowing of the cock.

There are two parts: (I.) The antecedents of the passion; namely 1. on the part of the Priests the plan, who were seeking a way to kill him; and of Judas, who had taken it ill that the nard was not sold, and having been promised money, receives the betrayal, to verse 11. 2. On the part of Jesus the celebration of the Passover and the Holy Eucharist, to verse 26. 3. On the part of the disciples to whom he foretold the scandalization of all, and the triple denial of Peter, to verse 31. (II.) Things done in the passion itself: 1. The passion of Jesus in the estate of Gethsemane, to verse 42. 2. The apprehension of Jesus, Judas betraying him, to verse 52. 3. The abduction of Jesus to the High Priest and the council of the Priests, with Peter following him, to verse 54. 4. The deposition of false witnesses, to verse 61. 5. The question of the High Priest whether he is the Christ the Son of God, and upon the answer of Jesus, his condemnation, mockery, and striking, to verse 65. 6. The triple denial of Peter, with his tears, to verse 72.

PART I. The antecedents of the Passion of Christ.

I. The plan of the Priests, and the pact of Judas, offended by the anointing of Jesus, concerning the betrayal.

Vers. 1. ἦν δὲ τὸ πάσχα καὶ ἄζυμα] That is, the Passover, which day is the beginning of the Unleavened Bread. For our writers count eight days of Unleavened Bread, the first of which is the one at the end of which the lamb was sacrificed. See what is at Matt. XXVI. 17.

Latin:

HISTORIA PASSIONIS DOMINICÆ, CAP. XIV. & XV. à S. MARCO descripta.

CAPUT XIV. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.
