Paschate imminente, cum quærerent Sacer- dotes, quomodo Jesum interficerent, non tamen in festo, quia Jesu in Bethania uncto aliqui indigne id tulerant, quod nardus non potius vendita esset, Judas ad Sacer- dotes se contulit, ut eum proderet pecu- niam promittentibus : Iesus vero, missis duobus discipulis, sibi Pascha præparari curavit, & manducans cum discipulis, proditionem prædixit, vœ proditori denun- cians, sacram Eucharistiam, distribuens cum pane benedicto corpus suum, cum ca- lice benedicto sanguinem suum, celebravit, & hymno decantato in montem Oliveti ex- iens, omnes se ista nocte scandalizaturos, ac percusso pastore dissipatum iri; Se au- tem post resurrectionem ipsos præcessuros in Galilæam; Petro vero contra protestan- te, ter ipsum se abnegaturum esse vaticina- tus est : atque in prædio Gethsemane cœpit tremere, pavere, ac tristari, & trinis vi- cibus in terram procidens oravit, ut si pos- sibile sit calix iste transeat: discipulos dormientes, ut vigilarent hortatus : ho- ram enim adesse ut tradatur. Mox Iudas cum cohorte armata adest, signo que, osculo ipsi dato, & voce Rabbi compellato, ipse apprehensus est : aufugientibus discipu- lis, Iesu autem ad Sacerdotes ducto, de lon- ginquo sequente Petro. Sacerdotibus vero, & toto Synedrio testimonia adversus Iesum conquirentibus, quum nulla invenirentur, testati nonnulli sunt, sed dissonotestimonio, quod dixerit se templum destructurum, & trib9 diebus reædificaturum; Pontifice vero quærente, num Christus sit, affirmavit id Ie- sus, & prædixit, filium hominis ad dextram virtutis sessurum, quod blasphemum esse Pontifex proclamavit, atq; ita condemna- runt ipsum unanimi sententia, ceu mortis reum: nonnulli illuserunt ei, & expuerunt in faciem, ac servi percusserunt eum, Petro, cum argueretur, quod cum Iesu fuerit, Ie- sum ternis vicibus abnegante, & ad galli i- teratum cantum illachrymante.

Partes sunt duæ: (I.) Antecedentia passionis; utpote 1. ex parte Pontificum propositum, qui modum quærebant ipsum interficiendi; & Judæ, qui indigne tulerat nardum non esse venditam, ac pecunia promissa recipit proditionem, ad vers. 11. 2. Ex parte Jesu Paschatos & S. Eucharistiæ cele- bratio, ad v. 26. 3. Ex parte discipulorum quibus scandalizationem omnium, trinamque abnegatio- nem Petri prædixit, ad v. 31. (II.) In passione ipsa ge- sta : 1. Passio Jesu in prædio Gethsemane, ad v. 42. 2. Jesu Juda ipsum prodente apprehensio, ad v. 52. 3. Jesu ad Pontificem & Sacerdotum concilium, Petro ipsum sequente, abductio, ad v. 54. 4. Fal- sorum testium depositio, ad v. 61. 5. Pontificis an sit Christus Dei filius, quæstio, & ad responsio- nem Jesu, ejus condemnatio, illusio, & percussio, ad v. 65. 6. Trina Petri abnegatio, cum lacrymis ejusdem, ad v. 72.

PARS I. Passionis Christi antecedentia.

I. Pontificum propositum, & Judæ per unctio- nem Jesu offensi, de proditione pactum.

Vers. 1. ἦν δὲ τὸ πάσχα καὶ ἄζυμα] Id est, Pascha, qui dies initium est Azymorum. Nam octo Azymorum dies nume- rant nostri scriptores, quorum primus est cujus fine agnus mactabatur. Vide quæ ad Matth. XXVI. 17.

## 14:3
Vers. 3. Νάρδου πιστικῆς] So also John. That πιστικὴ is derived here from πίνειν cannot be proven to me: because since this is not about drink, I do not see why Nard is called drinkable here. That it is called πιστικῆς because it is of proven faith is true, but only among writers some centuries later. Wherefore, since Mark and John use this word, who follow the Hebrew language more than the others, I am altogether led to believe that the Latin word spicata, which the Greeks also call σπικάτην and σπεκάτην, was pronounced more corruptly among the Jews, namely פיסטקא for פשיטא with a clearly similar transposition, such as we observed above in the word sextus or sextarius. Similar is the word Σαξίφραγον, which the Greeks put for saxifraga, and in the Arabic word زرنبيح how they call Arsenicum: in the Jewish language אספני for ἀσφάλτια and many things of that kind. The Syrian has Gogoltha for Golgatha. But what is in the Syrian ܫܝܪܬܝܐ does not signify headed, if I am not mistaken, but excellent, such as it is established that spicata was. Nonnus also seems to have understood the word πιστικῆς in this way, because he also produces the middle syllable against the nature of the Greek word, and what he adds φωτιζομένης properly suits spicated Nard. For I think there is not even any doubt that the Latin interpreter understood it so. The Arab in John put حالص, that is, pure, which is an epithet of nard also among Latin Poets. Pliny said sincere for the same, to which is opposed Pseudonardum, of which the same Pliny makes many species.

Grotius does not approve, and rightly, that πιστικὶν is derived from πίνειν: which was the opinion of Beza and Casaubon: for it is not a question of drink here, nor is πιστικὸν found anywhere with that meaning, as Vossius notes. But he wants the Latin word spicata, which the Greeks also call σπικάτην and σπεκάτην, to have been pronounced more corruptly among the Jews, namely פיסטקא; which opinion Vossius also approves, praising Grotius here, but to Capellus it deservedly seems quite harsh, and that transposition of letters clearly intolerable: nor could Grotius teach that this word was so pronounced among the Hebrews: who nevertheless acknowledged here that πιστικὸν is said because it is of proven faith, even if he says that it only occurs among writers some centuries later. To whom let Vossius reply in lib. 1. Harm. Evang. cap. III. §. 13. Since it is admitted that later writers speak thus, who can guarantee to us that they had not already begun to speak thus long before? Capellus praises Artemidorus, to whom πιστικὴ γυνὴ is a faithful wife: so that πιστικὴ νάρδος is pure and sincere nard, and not at all adulterated. To which also the Syriac version ܫܝܪܬܝܐ tends, which should be explained not as headed, but as excellent: of the most excellent nard. The Arab here clearly omitted πιστικῆς. But Josephus has similarly, of good nard: so also the Ethiopian has it: and thus also Theophylact rendered it by ἄδηλον, genuine, not adulterated. Which is also approved by Lud. de Dieu. Pliny said sincere, to which is opposed Pseudonardum, of which he himself makes many species. Casaubon notes that nard ointment was of great value then, because in those times Laodicea was the only city that would prepare ointment of this kind with praise. It is a wonder that he did not judge the passage corrupt, and that instead of πιστικῆς one should rewrite ὀπιστικῆς, (which pleased some, especially Job. Hartungus from the Persian city of Opis,) for Grotius is otherwise too prone to admitting corruptions of the sacred text. But Vossius refutes Hartungus's invention in book I of Harm. Evang. ch. III, § 9, where he also [refutes] Scaliger's opinion that πιστικὴ is put for something expressed from elsewhere into the liquid, from πίσσω.

συντρίψασα] Not breaking into small pieces, but causing it to gape wide: in the way that συντετριμμένον λάκκον [is used in] Jer. 2:13. Thus also elsewhere συντρίβειν is to wound, Ezek. 34:4, 1 Kings 20:27. 'Aperuit' [opened] is used here by the Syrian.

Less suitable is Erasmus's version 'comminuto alabastro' [with the alabaster broken into small pieces], and Beza's 'confracto' [broken]. The Vulgate's is more suitable: 'fracto' [broken], for the situation did not allow for the vessel to be broken into minute parts: because either the ointment would have fallen to the ground, or the fragments of the vessel would have fallen onto Christ's head along with the ointment. Nor does it stand in the way that συντρίβειν properly means to grind down. For it is used more broadly among the LXX for שבר, as Dievius [notes] here: who He also observes that the life had restored the Syrian and the Ethiopian: and he opened that alabaster jar, having made a hole in it.

(II.) The celebration of the Passover and the Holy Eucharist.

Latin:

Vers. 3. Νάρδου πιστικῆς] Ita & Johannes. πιστικὴ hic de- rivare παρὰ τὸ πιεῖν probari mihi non potest : quia cum de potu học non agatur, non video cur Nardus hìc potulenta dicatur. πιστικῆς dici, quod fidei est exploratæ, verum est, sed non nisi apud Scriptores aliquot seculis seriores. Quare cum Marcus & Johannes usurpent hanc vocem, qui plus cæteris sequuntur Hebræum sermonem, omnino eo ducor ut credam vocem Latinam spicatæ, quam & Græci dicunt σπικάτην & σπεκάτην, corruptius apud Judæos pronuntia- tam, nimirum פיסטקא pro פשיטא plane simili trans- positione, qualem supra in voce sexti aut sextarii observavi- mus. Similis est in voce Σαξίφραγον, quod Græci posuêre pro saxifraga, & in Arabica voce زرنبيح quomodo Ar- senicum vocant: in Judaica lingua אספני pro ἀσφάλτια multaque id genus. Syrus pro Golgatha habet Gogoltha. Quod autem apud Syrum est ܫܝܪܬܝܐ non capitatum ni fallor, sed eximium significat, quale fuisse spicatum con- stat. Videtur & Nonnus ita accepisse vocem πιστικῆς, quia & producit mediam contra naturam Græcæ vocis, & quod addit φωτιζομένης proprie convenit Nardo spicatæ. Nam Latinus interpres quin ita acceperit ne dubitandum quidem arbitror. Arabs apud Johannem posuit حالص, id est, pu- rum, quod nardi epitheton est & apud Latinos Poetas. Plinius sincerum dixit pro eodem, cui opponitur Pseudo- nardum, cujus multas species facit idem Plinius.

Non probat Grotius, & recte, πιστικὶν παρὰ τὸ πίνειν derivari: quæ Bezæ & Casauboni fuit sen- tentia: non enim hìc de potu agitur, nec uspiam πιστικὸν ea significatione reperitur, notante Vossio. Vult autem vocem Latinam spicatæ, quam & Græ- ci dicunt σπικάτην & σπεκάτην corruptius apud Judæos pronunciatam, nimirum פיסטקא; quam sententiam approbat etiam Vossius Grotium hic laudans, sed merito Capello dura admodum vide- tur, & plane intoleranda illa literarum μετάθεσις: neque ita apud Ebræos pronunciatam hanc vocem esse docere potuit Grotius: qui tamen πιστικὸν di- ci, quod fidei est exploratæ hic agnovit, etsi id tan- tum apud scriptores aliquot seculis seriores occurrere dicat. Cui respondeat Vossius lib. 1. Harm. Evang. cap. III. §. 13. Cum in confesso sit, sic loqui posteriores, quis spondeat nobis, non jam cæpisse multo ante sic loqui? Artemidorum laudat Capellus, cui πιστικὴ γυνὴ est fida uxor: ita ut πιστικὴ νάρδος sit nardus pura & sincera, minimeque adulterata. Quo etiam abit Syriaca versio ܫܝܪܬܝܐ quod non capitatum exponi debet, sed eximium: nardini præstantissimi. Arabs πιστικῆς hic plane omisit. At Josephus ha- bet similiter, nardini boni: sic habet quoque Æ- thiops: atque ita etiam Theophyl. reddidit per ἄ- δηλον germanum non adulteratum. Quod proba- tur etiam Lud. de Dieu. Plinius sincerum dixit, cui opponitur Pseudonardum, cujus multas ipse facit species. Nardinum unguentum magni tum fuisse pretii notat Casaubonus, quia illis temporibus uni- ca fuit urbs Laodicea, quæ unguentum hujusmodi cum laude conficeret. Mirum quod non corruptum censuerit locum, & pro πιστικῆς rescribendum ὀπι- στικῆς, (quod nonnullis placuit, imprimis Job. Har- tungo à civitate Persiæ Opis,) nimis enim pronus a- lias est Grotius in admittendis textus sacri corru- ptelis. Sed Hartungi commentum refellit Vossius l. I. Harm. Evang. c. III. §. 9. ubi etiam Scaligeri sen- tentiam πιστικὴ poni pro expresso aliunde in li- quorem, à πίσσω.

συντρίψασα] Non comminuens, sed efficiens, ut late hiaret: quomodo συντετριμμένον λάκκον Jer. II. 13. Sic & alibi συντρίβειν est vulnerare, Ezech. XXXIV. 4. I. Reg. XX. 27. Aperuit positum hic à Syro.

Minus commoda est Erasmi versio comminuto alabastro, & Bezæ confracto. Commodior vulga- tæ: fracto, ut enim in minutas partes confringe- retur vasculum, res non ferebat: quia aut unguen- tum in terram, aut una cum unguento fragmenta vasculi in caput Christi cecidissent. Nec obstat quod συντρίβειν proprie sit conterere. Latius enim usurpatur apud LXX. pro שבר, ut hic Dievius: qui observat etiam vita reddidisse Syrum & Æthiopem: & aperuit illud alabastrum, facto in eo foramine.

(II.) Paschatos & S. Eucharistiæ celebratio.

## 14:13
Verse 13. κεράμιον ὕδατος βαστάζων) With this mark Christ described him without expressing his name: whence Matthew said 'a certain one'. There is no doubt that many Jerusalemites rented out furnished dining rooms to those arriving at that time: and he seems to have been of that sort, as one who was carrying a water jar to the prepared dining room. And if I am not mistaken, the word κατάλυμα indicates this very thing.

Latin:

Vers. 13. κεράμιον ὕδατος βαστάζων) Hac nota illum Chri- stus descripsit nomine non expresso: unde τὸν δεῖνα dixit Matthæus. Dubitandum non est quin multi Hierofoly- mitæ cœnacula instructa sub id tempus advenis elocave- rint: cujus sortis & hic fuisse videtur, ut qui hydriam fer- ret ad paratum cœnaculi. Et ni fallor id ipsum indicat vox κατάλυμα.

## 14:15
Verse 15. ἐστρωμένον) In some books ἕτοιμον is added from Matthew, for the Latin does not recognize it: although the Syrian has it: as also some other things which were added from Matthew.

Robert Stephanus also retained that ἕτοιμον: nor does it appear why anything added here should be judged to be from Matthew. Grotius is too ready in his suspicion of the corruption of the text.

Latin:

Vers. 15. ἐστρωμένον) In quibus dam libris ἕτοιμον ex Mat- thæo additum, neque enim agnoscit Latinus: quanquam ha- bet Syrus: ut & alia nonnulla quæ ex Matthæo sunt addita.

Retinuit & Rob. Stephani illud ἕτοιμον: neque apparet, cur ex Matthæo additum hic quicquam censeri debeat. Nimis facilis est Grotius in suspi- cione corruptionis textus.

## 14:18
Verse 18. ὁ ἐσθίων μετ' ἐμῦ) Mark added this, having received it from Peter. It signifies a participant of the same table, which the ancients considered a great bond of friendship. 'A table and salt are true symbols of friendship for men,' says Philo. But what follows, ὁ ἐμβαπτόμενος, is a closer designation, as we said regarding Matthew.

Latin:

Vers. 18. ὁ ἐσθίων μετ' ἐμῦ) Hoc addidit Marcus à Petro acceptum. Id significat mensæ ejusdem participem, quod magnum amicitiæ vinculum veteres existinabant. Τράπε- ζα κὴ ἅλες σύμβολα γνησία φιλίας ἀνθρώποις inquit Philo. Quod vero sequitur ὁ ἐμβαπτόμενος, propior est designatio, ut ad Matthæum diximus.

## 14:19
Verse 19. εἷς καθ' εἷς) So also John VIII. 9. It is not Κάθεις for καὶ εἶτα εἷς, but καθ' εἷς, as clearly appears in Romans XII. 5. ὁ δὲ καθ' εἷς ἀλλήλων μέλη. Doubtless, as we said above VI. 40. Those accustomed to the Hebrew language not rarely take the nominative indeclinably. And so καθ' εἷς here has the same value as καθ' ἕνα in I Corinthians XIV. 31. In the same way καθ' εἷς is found in Lucian's 'Solecist' and some Christian writers.

Μήτι ἐγώ) The most diligent man rightly warns that in some codices the addition of καὶ ἄλλος μήτι ἐγὼ seems to have been born from an interpretation. For neither the Syrian nor the Latin nor the Arab recognize it. Nor does it cohere with that καθ' εἷς.

He now approves Beza's opinion that those words are redundant. But they were not found in only two codices. Nor should they seem foreign: indeed, one might suspect, as B. Gerhard rightly does here in his Harmony, that by that ἄλλον, Judas is specifically denoted, of whom Matthew specifically records that he said to Christ, 'Am I the Rabbi?' which specific question of betrayal Mark omitted.

Latin:

Vers. 19. εἷς καθ' εἷς) Ita & Ioh. VIII. 9. Non est Κάθεις pro κὴ εἶτα εἷς, sed καθ' εἷς, ut clare apparet Rom. XII. 5. ὁ δὲ καθ' εἷς ἀλλήλων μέλη. Nimirum ut supra diximus VI. 40. Sueri Hebraïco sermoni non raro nominativum sumunt ἀκλίτως. Itaque καθ' εἷς hic idem valet quod καθ' ἕνα I. Cor. XIV. 31. Eodem modo καθ' εἷς reperitur apud Lucianum Solœcista, & Christianos scriptores aliquot.

Μήτι ἐγώ) Recte monet vir diligentissimus, quod in qui- busdam codicibus adjicitur καὶ ἄλλος μήτι ἐγὼ ex interpre- tamento natum videri. Nam nec Syrus nec Latinus nec Arabs agnoscunt. Neque cohæret cum illa καθ' εἷς.

Approbat jam Bezæ sententiam, quod illa ver- ba redundent. At in duobus tantum codicibus non inventæ sunt. Nec aliena videri debent: imo su- spicari quis possit, ut hic recte B. Gerhardus in Harm. per illum ἄλλον in specie denotari Judam, de quo Matthæus speciatim memorat, quod Chri- sto dixerit, Nunquid ego sum Rabbi? quam specia- lem proditionis quæstionem Marcus prætermisit.

## 14:22
Verse 22. λάβετε) φάγετε, which some codices have added here, comes from Matthew. For the ancient translators do not recognize it: and it is missing in certain codices. Thus also below in verse 34, some books have added μετ' ἐμῦ.

Although this word is missing in one or another codex, the rest nevertheless all have it. We should not so easily imagine additions: since it is not likely that anyone would have presumed to enrich the text with additions taken from elsewhere. For the sacred codices were held as holy.

(III.) The prediction of the scandal and the Petrine denial.

Verse 31. ἐκ περισσᾶ μᾶλλον) Thus above ch. VII. 37. μᾶλλον περισσότερον ἐκύρισσον. Wherefore no other construction is to be sought.

PART II. Concerning the events in the Passion itself, such as (I.) The Passion on the estate of Gethsemane.

Latin:

Vers. 22. λάβετε) φάγετε quod hic aliqui codices additum habent, ex Matthæo venit. Nam veteres Metaphrastæ non agnoscunt: & deest in codicibus quibusdam. Sic & infra commate 34. quidam libri additum habent μετ' ἐμῦ.

Licet in uno & altero codice desit hoc verbum, cæteri tamen id omnes habent. Non tam facile additamenta fingere debemus: quum non verisi- mile sit præsumsisse quempiam textum addita- mentis aliunde ascitis locupletare. Sanctius enim habebantur codices sacri.

(III.) Scandali & abnegationis Petrinæ prædictio.

Vers: 31. ἐκ περισσᾶ μᾶλλον) Ita supra c. VII. 37. μᾶλλον περισσότερον ἐκύρισσον. Quare non est quærenda alia con- structio.

PARS II. Gestain ipsa Passione concernens, uti sunt (I.) Passio in prædio Gethsemane.

## 14:35
Verse 35. ἡ ὥρα) See what [is said] on Matthew at this place.

Latin:

Vers. 35. ἡ ὥρα) Vide quæ ad Matthæum hoc loco.

## 14:36
Verse 36. ἀββᾶ ὁ πατήρ) So also Paul Rom. VIII. 15. & Gal. IV. 6. The Hebrews using the Greek language seem to have retained this word, because children naturally greet their fathers with that sound. The Greeks say παπία παπίδιον: nor is πάππος from elsewhere. Thus what is אבא to the Hebrews is μάμμη to the Greeks. But the Latins also from that sound said pappare and mammas. Moreover, the double word is placed for the sake of testifying affection. Similar is that ναὶ ἀμὴν Apoc. I. 6.

Capellus is singular here beyond reason: although he is not certain of his own opinion: namely, it does not please him that a Syriac word was used by Christ in that invocation of his Father, although he notes that ALL, as far as he knows, interpreters state this: but he is mistaken in this, that he affirms that all judge the Greek word to have been added by the Evangelist as an exegetical [explanation] of it, since not for the sake of explanation do all say it was added either by Christ or by the Evangelist, but so that by the repetition of the same word, albeit in a different idiom, he might move the bowels of paternal affection: how the force, grace, and charm of such a gentle and familiar address is lost and diluted by this, does not appear. More correctly PERHAPS, says Capellus, IT MIGHT SEEM, if we say it is a formula most well-known to the Greeks, by which children gently and familiarly addressed their parents: But the things which lead him to this conjecture do not deserve to be brought forward. Why could the Greek not equally be joined to the Syriac word: just as the Hebrew was joined to the Greek in Apoc. I. 6. καὶ ἀμήν.

Οὐ τὶ ἐγὼ θέλω, ἀλλὰ τί (ὺ) Supply 'let it be done'. The Hebrews writing in Greek use the particles τὶ & ὅ indiscriminately.

Latin:

Vers. 36. ἀββᾶ ὁ πατήρ) Ita & Paulus Rom. VIII. 15. & Gal. IV. 6. Videntur Hebræi Græco utentes sermone reti- nuisse hanc vocem, quia naturaliter pueri eo sono patres sa- lutant. Græci dicunt παπία παπίδιον: nec aliunde πάπ- πος. Sic quod אבא Hebræis Græcis est μάμμη. Sed & Latini ab eo sono dixerunt pappare & mammas. Duplex autem vox posita est affectus testandi causa. Simile illud ναὶ ἀμὴν Apoc. I. 6.

Singularis hic est præter causam Capellus: quam- vis haud certus de sua sententia: nimirum non placet ipsi adhibitam à Christo vocem Syriacam fuisse in illa Patris sui invocatione, licet ita O- MNES, quantum sciat, interpretes statuere notet: qui vero in eo fallitur, quod omnes ab Evangelista subjectam esse vocem Græcam tanquam exegeti- cam illius censere affirmet, quandoquidem non ἐξηγήσεως causa sive à Christo sive ab Evangeli. sta subjici eam dicant omnes, sed ut repetitione vocis ejusdem, diverso licet idiomate, viscera affe- ctus paterni moveret: quo quomodo amittatur at- que diluatur vis, gratia & venustas tam blandæ & familiaris compellationis, non apparet. Rectius FORTE, inquit Capellus, VIDERI POSSET, si dicamus eam esse Græcis notissimam formulam, qua filii parentes blande & familiariter compellabant: Sed quæ eam in conjecturam adducit, adduci non merentur. Cur non æque conjungi Syriacæ voci Græca potuit: uti Ebræa Græcæ adjuncta A- poc. I. 6. καὶ ἀμήν.

Οὐ τὶ ἐγὼ θέλω, ἀλλὰ τί (ὺ) Supple fiat. Hebræi Græce scribentes particulas τὶ & ὅ promiscue usurpant.

## 14:44
Verse 44. Cύ([sημον) This word and the word Cημεῖον among the Greek interpreters of the sacred scriptures mean exactly the same thing Isa. V. 26. ch. XLIX. 22. ch. LXII. 10. Judg. XX. 40.

κρατήsατε ἀυτὸν κὴ ἀπαγάγετε ἀ([φαλῶς) Hold him and lead him away with care. Thus ἀ([φαλῶς τηρεῖν is to guard exactly, which you would less correctly translate into Latin by the word 'tuto' (safely). The Syrian well refers ἀ([φαλῶς as much to κρατήsατε as to ἀπάγετε.

Latin:

Vers. 44. Cύ([sημον) Vox hæc & vox Cημεῖον apud Græ- cos sacrarum literarum interpretes plane idem valent Esa. V. 26. c. XLIX. 22. c. LXII. 10. Judic. XX. 40.

κρατήsατε ἀυτὸν κὴ ἀπαγάγετε ἀ([φαλῶς) Tenete & duci- te cum cura. Ita ἀ([φαλῶς τηρεῖν est exacte custodire, quod Latine per vocem tuto minus recte verteris. Bene autem Syrus ἀ([φαλῶς refert tam ad κρατήsατε quam ad ἀπάγε- τε.

## 14:45
Verse 45. Ῥαββὶ ῥαββί) Thus the best Codices and the Syrian, wherefore the other reading flowed from Matthew.

And yet no other reading has been found, except that the Latin adds 'ave': whose version, however, cannot be sold as another manuscript, since he did not always render word for word.

Latin:

Vers 45. Ῥαββὶ ῥαββί) Ita optimi Codices & Syrus, qua- re lectio altera ex Matthæo profluxit.

Atqui nulla alia lectio reperta est, nisi quod La- tinus ave addit: cujus vero versio pro alio codice venditari non potest: quum non semper verbum verbo reddiderit.

## 14:49
Verse 49. ἀλλ᾽ ἵνα) Supply τῦτον ὅλον γέγονε from Matthew.

Latin:

Vers. 49. ἀλλ᾽ ἵνα) Supple τῦτον ὅλον γέγονε ex Matthæo.

## 14:51
Verse 51. κὴ εἷς τις νεανίσκος) Not from the flock of the Apostles, which I am surprised could have come into the minds of the ancients, nor from the house in which Christ had stayed in the city, but from some villa near the garden, awakened by the noise of the soldiers, and suddenly running up to see what was being done.

Σινδόνα) For they were accustomed to sleep ἐν λινῷ ἱδηώματι, as Isaac Casaubon, a man of the highest learning, showed from the epistle of Dionysius of Alexandria. And thus this youth had leapt from his bed.

οἱ νεανίσκοι) That is, the Roman soldiers, whom both the Greeks call νεανίσκους and the Latins often call the youth. These men, however, apprehended that youth, thinking him to be one of the disciples of Jesus: which Mark added for this reason, to signify that it had been determined not only to seize Jesus, but also his disciples.

The opinion of those is not to be approved who think he was one of the disciples of Christ, or even John himself: who would believe that he stood naked among his friends during all that time? We add what Casaubon has about him: Indeed, he says, who this youth was is a curious and vain inquiry; since the object of the search cannot be found. Theophylact, who reports several opinions on that question, puts this one first of all: ὅτι ὁ νεανίσκος εἰκὸς ὅτι ἐκ τῆς οἰκίας ἐκείνης ἦν, ἐν ᾗ ἔφαγον τὸ πάσχα. It is likely that this youth was from that house where they ate the Passover. And the same words are also found in Euthymius. This conjecture seems to me the most probable of all: for as for what the greatest men think, that the youth burst forth from his bed at the tumult which the cohort of Judas stirred up, and ran up from elsewhere in the neighborhood: that I approve less. For the Evangelist says ἠκολύθει ἀυτῷ, therefore he was following Christ, even before the traitor came with the soldiers. It is possible that this youth, after he had retired to bed, had heard something about the danger of Christ whom he venerated; and immediately rushed from his bed, clothed only in a linen cloth, and began to follow Christ. That he rose from his bed, his nakedness proves, for which no other probable cause can be devised: nor is this alien to the circumstance of the time. For as we learn from Theophylact, the night was advanced, and the second watch had already passed. Thus Casaubon: not with Grotius from some villa near the garden, but summoning that youth from the house into which Christ had turned aside in the city.

Latin:

Vers. 51. κὴ εἷς τις νεανί([κος) Non de Apostolorum gre- ge, quod miror veteribus in mentem venire potuisse nec è domo in quaen Christus in urbe diverterat, sed ex villa ali- qua horto proxima, strepitu militum excitatus, & subito accurrens ut conspiceret quid ageretur.

Σινδόνα) Solebant enim cubare ἐν λινῷ ἱδηώματι ut ex Dionysii Alexandrini epistola vir summæ eruditionis Isaac. Casaubon.monstravit. Atque ita hic juvenis lecto exsilierat.

οἱ νεανί([κοι) Id est, milites Romani, quos & Græci νεανί- ([κους & Latini sæpe juventutem vocant. Hi autem adole- scentem istum apprehenderunt unum discipulorum Jesu esse existimantes: quod ideo addidit Marcus, ut signifi- cares constitutum fuisse non Jesum tantum prehendere, sed & discipulos ejus.

Non probanda illorum sententia, qui aliquem è discipulis Christi putant, aut etiam ipsum Johan- nem: quem toto illo- tempore inter amictos nu- dum stetisse, ecquis credet? Addimus quæ habet de eo Casaubonus: Enimvero, inquit, quis fuerit hic juvenis, quærere curiosum est & vanum; quando inveniri τὸ ζητέμλυον non potest. Theophylactus, qui plures super ea quæstione refert sententias, pri- mam omnium ponit hanc: ὅτι [ῷ ὁ νεανίσκος εἰκὸς ὅτι ἐκ τ͂ οἰκίας ἐκείνης ἦν, ἐν ᾗ ἔφαγον τ᾿ πάχα. Verisimile est hunc juvenem ex illa domo fuisse, ubi Pa- scha comederunt. Et sunt eadem verba etiam apud Euthymium. Hæc conjectura mihi videtur omnium maxime probabilis: nam quod summi viri arbitran- tur, ad tumultum quem cohors Judæ excitavit, pro- rupisse juvenem è lecto, & aliunde è vicinia accurrisse: id ego minus probo. Ait enim Evangelista ἠκολύθει ἀυτῷ, sequebatur igitur Christum, etiam prius quam proditor cum militibus veniret. Fieri potest, ut hic juvenis, postquam cubitum se recepisset, de periculo Christi quem venerabatur, aliquid inaudie- rit; ac statim lecto se proripuerit, sindone tantum amictus, & Christum sequi cœperit. Quod è le- cto surrexerit, nuditas arguit, cujus causa proba- bilis alia excogitari vix potest: neque hoc à temporis circumstantia est alienum. Nam ut è Theophylacto discimus, nox fuit provecta, & altera jam præterie- rat vigilia. Hæc Casaubonus: non cum Grotio è villa aliqua horto proximia, sed è domo in quam Christus in urbe diverterat, juvenem illum arcessens.

## 14:54
Verse 54.

πρὸς τὸ φῶς] At the shining fire, which is אור for the Hebrews. And Mark owed this also, as Heinsius notes, to his Hellenists, as he did other things. He can be compared, and Walæus from him.

Latin:

Vers. 54.

πρὸς τὸ φῶς] Ad focum lucentem, qui אור Hebræis. Et hoc etiam, notante Heinsio, Hellenistis suis debuit Marcus, ut cætera. Conferri is poterit, & ex eo Walæus.

(IV.) Falsorum testium depositio.

## 14:56
Verse 56.

Ἴσαι] The meaning is not that the testimonies disagreed among themselves (for I do not see how that can be said of the following testimony, in which, once recited, the same thing is repeated), but that they were not weighty enough to equal the voices of the High Priests, who were seeking not just any testimony, but one that would be valid for death, εἰς τὸ θανατῶσαι, as he said before. Therefore, ἴση here is what the Hebrews say about testimonies, כשר, sufficient for the proof of that which is sought. For the fact that a very learned man places the disagreement of the witnesses in the fact that one testified to the statement δυνάμαι καταλῦσαι, and the other καταλύσω, is not proven to me. For I think these signify the same thing, or at least that one is included in the other. For Mark, who received these things from the mouth of Peter, recites the testimony of both using the word καταλύσω.

Beza retorted to Erasmus, who translated it in the same sense, 'sufficiently suitable,' that he had never read ἴσον used in this meaning. But nothing prevents this word from being explained in this way. It is clear that Beza tried in vain to prove a discrepancy from Matthew and Mark, which Grotius notes in these.

Latin:

Vers. 56.

Ἴσαι] Sensus non est testimonia inter se discrepasse (ne- que enim video, quomodo id dici possit de testimonio se- quente, quo recitato idem repetitur) sed non tam gravia fuisse, ut æquarent vocum Pontificum, quærentium μαρ- τυρίαν non quamvis sed quæ ad mortem valeret, εἰς τὸ θα- νατῶσαι ut ante dixit. Est ergo ἴση heic quod Hebræi de testi- moniis dicunt כשר ad probationem ejus quod quæritur sufficiens. Nam quod vir apprime doctus dissidium te- stium in eo collocat, quod alter testatus sit dictum δυνά- μαι καταλῦσαι, alter καταλύσω, mihi non probatur. Idem enim hæc significare arbitror, aut certe alterum altero in- cludi. Nam Marcus qui hæc ex Petri ore accepit, utrius- que testimonium recitat per verbum καταλύσω.

Beza Erasmo, qui in eandem sententiam reddi- dit, satis idonea, regessit, nusquam τὸ ἴσον se le- gisse hac significatione usurpatum. Sed nihil obstat, quo minus ita explicetur hæc vox. Discrepantiam certe è Matthæo & Marco nequicquam probasse Bezam, quam his notat Grotius, in aprico est.

## 14:69
Verse 69.

ἡ παιδίσκη] that is, a certain maidservant, as it is certain that the article is sometimes taken. For Matthew teaches that it was another than the former.

πάλιν ἤρξατο] I entirely agree with those who connect πάλιν with ἤρξατο, so that it is signified that the same thing was said to Peter again, as the Latin interpreter also seems to have understood it. Nor should the authority of the codices frighten anyone in this part: for since it is sufficiently established that ancient books were accustomed to be written without punctuation, it follows that it was added later by the judgment of the scribes: wherefore the judgment concerning them ought to be free even now.

That it was another, there is no room to doubt, because Matthew asserts it. But since that former doorkeeper also; at this second time, addressed Peter; because Mark bears witness to this. But it is not right to change anything in the text. Indeed, all the codices agree: whose authority is not to be disregarded. And if it were free for anyone to punctuate the sacred scriptures according to their pleasure, who could prevent errors from being introduced, or divine testimonies from being corrupted? Luke adds, and another seeing him (Peter) said. Must a corruption be feigned here too, because he said another instead of another woman? Since John testifies that several said such things to him, is it not better to say that Peter was addressed by several, and among those persons both the other one of Matthew, and that very doorkeeper who is in Mark, who, confirming the assertion of her fellow servant, adds, And this man was with Jesus the Nazarene, and also the other one of Luke, who took up the words of the maidservant and thus convicted Peter, And you are of them, which was also confirmed by others? It is likely, says Lyranus, that many gathered around Peter at those words of the maidservant, and uttered similar words to accuse him, whence it happened that one Evangelist notes one person, another another, that is, one or several.

ἐξ αὐτῶν εἶσι] He is of that sect.

Latin:

Vers. 69.

ἡ παιδίσκη] id est παιδίσκη τις, quomodo articulum in- terdum sumi certum est. Nam aliam fuisse à priore Mat- thæus docet.

πάλιν ἤρξατο] Omnino assentior iis qui πάλιν cum ἤρξατο conjungunt, ut significetur iterum idem dictum Petro, quomodo & Latinus interpres videtur accepisse. Neque terrere quemquam debet hac in parte codicum auctoritas: nam cum veteres libros sine distinctionibus scribi solitos satis constet, sequitur postea ex describentium judicio addi- tas: quare & nunc de illis judicium liberum esse debet.

Aliam fuisse dubitandum non est, quia Mat- thæus asserit. Sed cum illa etiam prior ostiaria; hac secunda vice, Petrum compellavit; quia Marcus de hac testimonium perhibet. Non vero in textu fas est quicquam immutare. Consentiunt sane Codices omnes: quorum auctoritas posthabenda non est. Et si cuilibet liberum sit pro placito di- stinguere sacra scripta, qui non errores ingeri, quæ non testimonia divina corrumpi possent? Lu- cas addit, & alius videns eum (Petrum) dixit. Num & hic corruptela fingenda, quod alium pro alia dixerit? Annon quum Johannes testetur plures ei talia dixisse, præstat dicere Petrum plures com- pellasse, & inter illas personas tum aliam Mat- thæi, tum ipsam etiam ostiariam, quæ apud Mar- cum est, quæ conservæ assertionem confirmans subjicit, Et hic cum Jesu Nazareno erat, tum a- lium quoque Lucæ, qui verba ancillæ excepit & Petrum ita convicit, Et tu ex illis es, quod ab a- liis etiam confirmatum fuit. Verisimile est, in- quit Lyranus, quod multi ad illa verba ancillæ con- currerint circa Petrum, & consimilia verba protule- rint ad accusandum, unde factum, ut unus Evan- gelista unam personam notet, alius aliam, unam sc. vel plures.

ἐξ αὐτῶν εἶσι] Est illius sectæ.

## 14:72
Verse 72.

κᾀ ἐπιβαλὼν ἔκλαιε] He not only remembered in his soul those things which Christ had said, but furthermore also testified to his grief with weeping. Thus the Hebrews say נפל with the addition of a verb. Luke in the same way says προσθεὶς εἶπε παραβολὴν c. XIX. 11, that is, he furthermore told a parable, and in another construction προσέθετο πέμψαι, Luke XX. 11. Among other meanings, however, ἐπιβάλλειν is also προστιθέναι. Thus Basil in his book on baptism, depicting the Christian life, places these two words with the same meaning: ἁγιάζονόμενος προστίθ. τυπτόμενος ἐπιβάλλ.

Dievius, with the meaning of the word ἐπιβάλλειν retained in the sense of adding or increasing, asks whether it could be translated as 'increasing,' that is, he wept abundantly. Yet he does not dare to affirm it. For no similar example of that meaning can be brought forward. In Beza's judgment, it could be explained as ἐπιβαλὼν meaning 'when he had noticed': that is, the matter having been noticed. In which way Casaubon took it for νοήσας or κατανοήσας: to which interpretation John Bois gives the palm over others. But Mark had already designated the noticing or reflection with the word ἀναμνησθεὶς. And Beza himself rendered it otherwise, namely, that it is the same as Matt. XXVI. 75, ἐξελθὼν, And when he had rushed out. Which also pleased our Erasmus Schmid. And thus the Arab translated: and he turned himself (departed) weeping. Examples from the LXX Interpreters Dievius brings forward similar ones, so also Stephanus: when he had thrown himself outside. Nor is that explanation of Casaubon alien, by which he rendered it as ἐγκαλυψάμενος, that he hid himself, and thus suddenly rushed out. The Vulgate, Erasmus, and B. Luther rendered it: And he began to weep; which explanation is also observed by Theophylact, ἐπιβαλὼν instead of ἀρξάμενος, and not disapproved by Erasmus Schmid, and is especially defended by Dan. Heinsius. And these two latter ones are, in our judgment, superior to the others, of which I would prefer the former, if a comparison of them were to be made. Another is also noted by Theophylact: Ἐπιβαλὼν, that is, ἐπικαλυψάμενος τὴν κεφαλὴν, he wept with his head covered. Which Salmasius approves with his own vote, comparing the rite of the Jews in Jer. XIV. 3 and other nations, and that of Socrates in the Trapeziticus, ἐγκαλυψάμενος ἔκλαιε. But although ἐπιβάλλειν occurs regarding the casting of garments in Lev. XIX. 9, Num. IV. 14, Mark XI. 7, it is nowhere placed nakedly, but it obtains that meaning with the addition of garments.

Latin:

Vers. 72.

κᾀ ἐπιβαλὼν ἔκλαιε] Non tantum recordatus est in anima eorum quæ Christus dixerat, sed præterea etiam fletu testatus est mœrorem. Sic Hebræi dicunt נפל addito ver- bo. Lucas eodem modo προσθεὶς εἶπε παραβολὴν c. XIX. 11 id est, praeterea dixit comparationem, & alia constructione προσέθετο πέμψαι, Luc. XX. 11. Inter alias autem significa- tiones ἐπιβάλλειν est etiam προστιθέναι. Sic Basilius in libro de baptismo vitam Christianam depingens duo haec verba ponit significatu eodem : ἁγιάζονόμενος προστίθ. τυπτόμε- νος ἐπιβάλλ.

Dievius vocis ἐπιβάλλειν significatione sensu ad- jiciendi, augendi retenta, quaerit annon possit verti augens, id est abunde flevit. Nec id tamen audet affir- mare. Nam exemplum simile istius significationis adferri nequit. Bezae judicio explicari posset ἐπι- βαλὼν tum animadvertisset : id est, re animadversa. Quo pacto Casaubonus pro νοήσας seu κατανοήσας accepit:cui interpretationi prae aliis palmam tribuit Johannes Boisius. Sed animadversionem, vel recogi- tationem jam designarat Marcus verbo ἀναμνη- σθεὶς. Et Beza ipse aliter reddidit,nimirum ut sit i- dem quod Matth.XXVI.75. ἐξελθὼν, Et quum se proripuisset. Quod etiam placuit Erasmo Schmidio nostro. Atque ita vertit Arabs : & vertit se, (dis- cessit) flens.Exempla e LXX.Interpp. similia addu- cit Dievius, Sic & Stephanus : quum se projecisset foras.Nec aliena est illa Casauboni explicatio, qua per ἐγκαλυψάμενος reddidit, quod se occulta- rit, adeoque se subito proripuerit. Vulgatus,Era- smus, & B. Lutherus reddidere : Et coepit flere ; quae explicatio etiam Theophylacto observata ἐπιβα- λὼν ἀντὶ τοῦ ἀρξάμενος, nec improbata Erasmo Schmidio, imprimis defenditur a Dan. Heinsio. Atque hae duae posteriores caeteris, nostro judicio praestant, e quibus priorem, si earum instituatur comparatio,praetulerim. Annotata est & alia a Theophylacto : Ἐπιβαλὼν,τουτέστιν, ἐπικαλυψά- μενος τὴν κεφαλὴν capite operto flebat. Quam cal- culo suo comprobatSalmasius,conferens ritum Ju- daerum Jer. XIV. 3. aliarumque gentium, & illud Socratis in Trapezitico ἐγκαλυψάμενος ἔκλαιε. Sed quamvis ἐπιβάλλειν de injectione vestimen- torum occurrat Levit. XIX. 9. Num. IV. 14. Marc. XI. 7. nuspiam tamen ea nude posita, sed cum adjectione vestimentorum eum sensum obtinet.

## 15:1 Argument
CHAPTER XV. ARGUMENT AND DIVISION.

In the morning, a council having been held, Jesus, bound, was led to Pilate, by whom, being asked whether he was the King of the Jews, he affirmed it; but to the most serious accusations of the priests he answered nothing: and when Pilate wished to release him according to the custom of the feast, at the instigation of the priests the people sought the release of Barabbas, but the crucifixion of Jesus: to satisfy whom, Pilate handed over Jesus to be crucified: The soldiers, however, having led him into the praetorium, clothed him in purple, and having crowned him with a crown of thorns, mocked him first, then put his own clothes on him again, and led him out to be crucified, Simon of Cyrene having been compelled to carry the cross. In the place Golgotha they offered him wine mixed with myrrh, which he refused, and they crucified him, and distributed his garments, and placed a title on the cross, with two thieves, one at his right, the other at his left, crucified at the same time, that the Scripture might be fulfilled, that he was reckoned among the transgressors. On the cross he was mocked by those passing by, as also by the priests, and darkness having arisen for three hours, he cried out, Eli Eli lama asabthani, some thinking that he was calling for Elias, a certain even while he was offering him vinegar. Jesus, however, expired with a loud cry. Soon the veil of the temple was torn, the Centurion professing him to be the Son of God: and Mary Magdalene and other women watched everything: in the evening, because it was the Preparation, Joseph of Arimathea begged the body of Christ from Pilate, and he buried it, and rolled a stone to the sepulcher, with Mary Magdalene and Mary of Joses watching where he had been laid.

There are five parts: I. Proceedings before Pilate, where (1) The abduction to Pilate v. 1. (2) Pilate's question whether he is the King of the Jews? v. 2. (3) The accusation of the Priests, to v. 5. (4) The solicitation that Jesus be crucified after Barabbas was released, to v. 14. (5) The handing over of Jesus by Pilate for crucifixion, v. 15. II. Deeds by the soldiers in the praetorium: the mockery and striking of Jesus, to v. 20. III. The crucifixion of Jesus: where (1) His leading out with Simon carrying the cross, to v. 22. (2) The crucifixion of Jesus after being offered myrrhed wine, v. 23. 24. (3) The distribution of garments, v. 24. (4) The designation of the hour of crucifixion, v. 25. (5) The inscription of the cross, v. 26. (6) The placement among thieves, vers. 27. v. 28. (7) The mockery of the crucified one, to v. 32. (8) Jesus' exclamation on the cross, v. 34. 35. 36. (9) Jesus' death with a loud cry, v. 37. IV. The consequences of the death: such as the tearing of the temple veil, vers. 38. and the Centurion's confession, with a list of the women spectators, to v. 41. V. The burial of Jesus, to v. 47.

PART I. Proceedings before Pilate.

Ver. 1.

Συμβούλιον ποιήσαντες) That is, λαβόντες, as the interpreter of Matthew speaks. For Mark also spoke thus above at III. 6, Συμβούλιον ἐποίουν, that is, they took counsel, not, as some interpret, they convened the senate.

Most people here, and at Matt. XXVII. 1, think that another meeting was instituted early in the morning: so that what had been done in the previous night, in a more restricted meeting of the Priests and Elders, might be repeated publicly in the morning in a formal meeting of all the assessors, and the sentence of death against Christ might be confirmed by the votes of the whole Sanhedrin. To Grotius, however, it does not seem that a new meeting was instituted. Regarding which at Matt. XXVII. 1, Συμβούλιον ἔλαβον. That so many senators departed in such a short space of time, and gathered again from so many parts of the city, is neither credible, and is imagined without cause. The sense is, after Jesus was heard, the senators deliberated among themselves separately as to what should be done. Thus συμβούλιον ἔλαβον is taken elsewhere to signify that counsel was taken. Above XII. 14, XXII. 15. This is Grotius. But in Luke a new meeting is expressly said to have been held, c. XXII. 66, to which certainly credit must be given. And as it dawned συνήχθη τὸ πρεσβυτέριον the elders of the people gathered, and the chief Priests, and the Scribes, and they led him back into their council.

καὶ ὅλον τὸ Συνέδριον) The full Senate, whose parts he has already named,

Latin:

CAPUT XV. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Mane concilio habito Jesus ligatus ad Pilatum ductus, a quo rogatus, an sit Judaeorum Rex, affirmavit, ad Sacerdotum autem accusa- tiones gravissimas nihil respondit: & quum eum pro more Festi dimittere vellet Pila- tus, Sacerdotum instinctu populus Barra- ba dimissionem expetiit, Jesu vero crucifi- xionem: cui ut satisfaceret, Jesum crucifigen- dum tradidit Pilatus: Milites autem in praetorium ductum,purpura indutum,& co- rona spinea coronatum exagitarunt pri- mum, tum vestes proprias ipsi iterum in- duerunt, eumque crucifigendum eduxe- runt, Simone Cyreneo, ut crucem portaret, coacto.In loco Golgatha myrrhatum vinum praebuere ipsi,quod renuit, & crucifixerunt eum,ac vestes distribuerunt, titulumque cruci imposuerunt, duobus latronibus, uno ad dextram, altero ad sinistram ejus simul crucifixis, ut impleretur Scriptura, quod inter praevaricatores computatus sit. In cru- ce illusus a praetereuntibus, ut & a Sacer- dotibus,exortisque tenebris trium horarum exclamavit, Eli Eli lama asabthani,censeni tibus nonnullis,quodEliam vocarit,quodam etiam ei acetum porrigente. Iesus vero cum clamore sonoro expiravit. Mox velum tem- pli scissum est, Centurio professus ipsum Fi- lium Dei esse: spectaruntque omnia Maria Magdalena, & aliæ mulieres: vesperi, quia parasceve erat, Iosephus Arimathensis a Pilato exoravit corpus Christi, idque con- didit, & lapidem ad sepulchrum volvit, Maria Magdalena, & Maria Ioses spectan- tibus, ubi repositus esset.

Partes sunt quinque: I. Acta coram Pilato, ubi (1) Abductio ad Pilatum v. 1. (2) Quæstio Pilati an Rex Judæorum sit? v. 2. (3) Accusatio Sacer- dotum, ad v. 5. (4) Solicitatio, ut Barraba di- misso Jesus crucifigeretur, ad v. 14. (5) Traditio Jesu a Pilato facta ad crucifixionem, v. 15. II. Ge- sta a militibus in prætorio: illusio & percussio Jesu, ad v. 20. III. Crucifixio Jesu: ubi (1) Ejus eductio Simone crucem portante, ad v. 22. (2) Jesu myr- rhato vino præbito crucifixio, v. 23. 24. (3) Ve- stium distributio, v. 24. (4) Horæ crucifixionis designatio, v. 25. (5) Crucis inscriptio, v. 26. (6) Inter latrones collocatio, vers. 27. v. 28. (7) Cru- cifixi illusio, ad v. 32. (8) Jesu in cruce exclama- tio, v. 34. 35. 36. (9) Jesu cum valido clamore o- bitus, v. 37. IV. Consequentia mortis: utpote ve- li templi scissio, vers. 38. & Centurionis confessio, cum mulierum spectatricum recensione, ad v. 41. V. Sepultura Jesu, ad v. 47.

PARS I. Acta coram Pilato.

Vers. 1.

Συμβούλιον ποιήσαντες) Id est, λαβόντες, ut Matthæi in- terpres loquitur. Nam sic & Marcus supra III. 6. locutus est, Συμβούλιον ἐποίουν, id est, consilium ceperunt, non ut qui- dam interpretantur, senatum convocarunt.

Plerique hic, & Matth. XXVII. 1. alium conven- tum summo mane institutum esse censent: ut quæ nocte antegressa, in conventu Sacerdotum ac Se- niorum contractiori, gesta erant, ea mane in so- lenni omnium assessorum conventu publice re- peterentur, ac sententia mortis contra Christum lata totius Synedrii suffragiis comprobaretur. Grotio autem non videtur novus conventus insti- tutus. Quo de ad Matth. XXVII. 1. Συμβούλιον ἔλα- βον. Tantillo temporis spatio discessisse tot senatores, iterumque ex tot urbis regionibus convenisse, neque cre- dibile est, sine causa fingitur. Sensus est, post audi- tum Jesum seorsim senatores inter se deliberasse quid esset faciendum. Ita συμβούλιον ἔλαβον & alibi sumitur ut captum consilium significet. Supra XII. 14. XXII. 15. Hæc Grotius. Sed apud Lucam di- serte novus conventus celebratus dicitur, c. XXII. 66. cui utique fides habenda. Atque ut illuxit συνήχθη τὸ πρεσβυτέριον convenerunt seniores ple- bis, & principes Sacerdotum, & Scribæ, & reduxe- runt illum in concilium suum.

καὶ ὅλον τὸ Συνέδριον) Pleno Senatu, cujus partes jam no- minavit,

## 15:3
Ver. 3. πολλὰ) What some Codices add here ἀυτὸς δὲ ὀυδὲν ἀπεκρίνατο has been added from Matthew. For neither the Latin nor the Syrian nor the Arab recognize it.

Latin:

Vers. 3. πολλὰ) Quod hic addunt Codices quidam ἀυτὸς δὲ ὀυδὲν ἀπεκρίνατο ex Matthæo adjectum est. Nam nec La- tinus nec Syrus nec Arabs agnoscunt.

## 15:7
Ver. 7. ἐπεποιήκεισαν) I judge this reading to be preferred, which both the Syrian and the Latin have followed.

Latin:

Vers. 7. ἐπεποιήκεισαν) Hanc lectionem præferendam censeo, quam secuti sunt & Syrus & Latinus.

## 15:8
Ver. 8. καὶ ἀναβοήσας) It appears that the Syrian and the Greeks read it thus: wherefore what the Vatican codex has, ἀναβὰς, adds to those arguments by which I am moved to believe that certain Greek copies of Mark were changed to the Latin version.

Latin:

Vers. 8. καὶ ἀναβοήσας) Apparet ita legisse Syrum & Græ- cos: quare quod Vaticanus codex habet ἀναβὰς, accedit ad ea argumenta, quibus moveor ut credam quædam Mar- ci exemplaria Græca ad Latinam versionem mutata.

## 15:11
Ver. 11. ἀνέσεισαν τὸν ὄχλον) I do not think the Syrian read it otherwise: nor the Arab, who often follows the Syrian, in whom is حرك they stirred up.

Latin:

Vers. 11. ἀνέσεισαν τὸν ὄχλον) Non puto aliter legisse Sy- rum: nec eum qui Syrum sæpe sequitur Arabem, apud quem est حرك commoverunt.

## 15:15
Ver. 15. Τὸ ἱκανὸν ποιῆσαι) This kind of speaking was transferred from the Roman language into Greek, as were many other things after Greece and the East had become subject to Roman law. Thus in the Acts, Luke said λαμβάνειν ἱκανὸν, which in Roman law is to receive satisfaction. Theophilus in the Institutes, under the title 'On the division of things': εἰ δὲ πωλήσας τραδιτίνζῃ οὐχ' ἑτέρως ἐπὶ τὸν ἀγοραστὴν ἡ δεσπότεια μέτεισιν ἐὰν μὴ ὁ ἀγοραστὴς τῷ πρά- τῃ τὸ τίμημα καταβάλῃ τοῦ πράματος ἢ τὸ ἱκανὸν αὐτῷ ποιή- σῃ ἐπὶ τιμήματι: where Tribonian wrote: 'Venditæ vero res & traditæ non aliter emptori acquiruntur, quam si is ven- ditori pretium solverit, vel alio modo ei satisfecerit.' But to satisfy here in Mark, as often in Latin writers, is to ensure that the other party has nothing to complain about. Φραγελλώσας) Since he had already beaten him with scourges before: as we explained in the commentary on Matthew.

PART II. Deeds done by the soldiers in the praetorium.

Latin:

Vers. 15. Τὸ ἱκανὸν ποιῆσαι) Ex Romano sermone genus hoc loquendi in Græciam traductum, ut multa alia post- quam Græcia & Oriens facta erant Romani juris. Sic in Actis Lucas dixit λαμβάνειν ἱκανὸν quod in jure Romano est satis accipere. Theophilus in institutionibus titulo de Rerum divisione : εἰ δὲ πωλήσας τραδιτίνζῃ οὐχ' ἑτέρως ἐπὶ τὸν ἀγοραστὴν ἡ δεσπότεια μέτεισιν ἐὰν μὴ ὁ ἀγοραστὴς τῷ πρά- τῃ τὸ τίμημα καταβάλῃ τοῦ πράματος ἢ τὸ ἱκανὸν αὐτῷ ποιή- σῃ ἐπὶ τιμήματι : ubi Tribonianus fcribebat: Venditæ vero res & traditæ non aliter emptori acquiruntur, quam si is ven- ditori pretium solverit, vel alio modo ei satisfecerit. Est au- tem satisfacere hic apud Marcum, ut apud Latinos Scripto- res sæpes, efficere ne alter habeat quod queratur. Φραγελλώσας) Cum jam ante eum flagris cecidisset: ut ad Matthæum exposuimus.

PARS II. Gesta à militibus in prætorio.

## 15:16
Ver. 16. ἔσω τῆς αὐλῆς) I take αὐλὴν here, not for an open courtyard, as is often the case elsewhere, but for the praetorium itself, as Mark explains. Thus also Matthew calls the house of the High Priest αὐλὴν, XXVI. 3. But Latin historians also are accustomed to translate praetorium as αὐλὴν. Therefore, from the tribunal which was in the stadium, as we said in the commentary on Matthew, Jesus was led into the inner part of the house.

But they seem to have led him into the middle of the courtyard or praetorium, where scourging was not otherwise performed, so that with the crowds removed, they could mock him more freely and satisfy their own lust.

PART III. The crucifixion of Jesus.

Latin:

Vers. 16. ἔσω τῆς αὐλῆς) αὐλὴν hic sumo, non pro subdia- li, ut alias sæpe, sed pro ipso prætorio, ut exponit Marcus. Sic & Matthæus Pontificis domum αὐλὴν vocat XXVI. 3. Sed & Latinæ historiæ scriptores prætorium solent vertere αὐλὴν. A tribunali ergo quod erat in stadio, ut ad Mat- thæum diximus, in partem domus interiorem abductus est Jesus.

Ideo vero in medium aulæ vel prætorium, in quo alias flagellatio non fiebat, abduxisse eum vi- dentur, ut remotis turbis liberius ipsi illudere, ac libidini suæ satisfacere possent.

PARS III. Crucifixio Iesu.

## 15:21
Ver. 21. Ἀλεξάνδρου καὶ Ῥούφου) Who were living when Mark wrote this, and if I am not mistaken, at Rome, where he was writing these things, so that he rightly appeals to their testimony, who could narrate to others the matter received from their father. For among those who professed Christ at Rome, Paul greets Rufus. It is said that this Alexander and Rufus had a third brother, named Lucius, who sowed the seed of the Word in Germany. To a Hebrew father, sons with Greek and Latin names—the beginnings of the calling of the Gentiles.

Latin:

Vers. 21. Ἀλεξάνδρου καὶ Ῥούφου) Quæ vivebant cum hæc scriberet Marcus, & ni fallor, Romæ, ubi ista scribebat, ita ut merito provocet ad eorum testimonium, qui rem a patre acceptam narrare aliis poterant. Nam inter eos qui Romæ Christum profitebantur, Rufum salutat Paulus. Di- citur huic Alexandro & Rufo frater tertius fuisse, Lucius nomine, qui in Germania Verbi semen sparserit. Patri Hebræo filii Græci Latinique nominis, initia vocationis gentium.

## 15:23
Ver. 23. ἐσμυρνισμένον) See what is said on Matthew. οὐκ ἔλαβε) He did not drink, as we said on Matthew.

Latin:

Vers. 23. ἐσμυρνισμένον) Vide quæ ad Matthæum. οὐκ ἔλαβε) Non imbibit, ut ad Matthæum diximus.

## 15:25
Ver. 25. ἦν δὲ ὥρα τρίτη) That is, the trumpet of the third hour had already been heard, which was accustomed to be said until the trumpet of the sixth hour sounded. See what is said on Matthew. For I see no reason for the reading to be changed, given the consensus of the Syrian, the Arab, and the Latin. Nor is there any argument to prove that numbers were written by signs in the original codices.

It is to be approved here in Grotius that he does not prove the corruption of the text, which others, especially the Papists, such as Thomas Aquinas, Cajetan on this passage, Sixtus Senensis in Book VI of the Bibliotheca Sancta, annotation 131, Melchior Canus, and Dionysius Petavius, assert. For where the Sacred Codices and also the ancient interpreters agree entirely, no suspicion of corruption is to be admitted. Whence there is no room for the opinion of Wilhelm Lang, who suspects that here a Γ crept in for an E by the removal of two lower lines, even though something similar is read in the commentary on the Psalms ascribed to Jerome: since it cannot be proven that numbers were written with such signs in the original text, as Grotius rightly says here. Whose explanation, however, about the trumpet of the third hour having already been heard, lacks a foundation and leaves the time defined in too loose a manner. For if that interval is designated from the third hour until the sixth, at what hour, then, was Christ properly crucified? And when afterwards it is said that darkness occurred at the sixth hour, v. 33, and at v. 34 that Christ cried out at the ninth hour, Eloi, Eloi, will an indefinite time, or one designated in such a breadth, be established there as well? Heinsius rendered these words thus: ἦν δὲ ὥρα τρίτη καὶ ἐσταύρωσαν αὐτὸν, 'It was indeed the third hour from when he began to be crucified,' or, 'The third hour was already passing from when he had been driven onto the cross.' Namely, when the garments were divided: the mention of which act precedes in v. 24, ὅτε καὶ σταυρώσαντες αὐτὸν διεμέρισαν τὰ ἱμάτια αὐτοῦ: Which explanation Heinsius proves at length: namely, that the hour

Let the third division of Christ's garments from the crucifixion be said to have been made. Which was also the ἔκθεσις of the most learned Roman monk Marcellus, as R. Bailius observed. That sense is clearer if ἐςαύρωσαν is taken in the pluperfect in this way: 'And it was the third hour, after they had crucified him.' How the Arab also explained the mind of St. Mark: joining that about the third hour, when he had been crucified, with the preceding verse, where it is about the division of Christ's garments, done in this way: 'That was done at the third hour from the crucifixion.' To which the Persian interpretation also seems to go: 'from when they had hung him on the cross'; and likewise the Syriac: 'when they had crucified him'; concerning which see Lud. de Dieu. Perhaps it would also not be inconvenient if it were said that the third hour from the tradition made to Pilate is designated here: which interpretation we have left for the learned to weigh in our Biblical Chronicle.

Latin:

Vers. 25. ἦν δὲ ὥρα τρίτη) Id est jam audita erat tuba ho- ræ tertiæ, quod dici solebat donec caneret tuba horæ sextæ. Vide quæ ad Matthæum. Lectionis enim mutandæ cau- sam non video, tanto Syri, Arabis, Latini consensu. Neque vero per notas scriptos fuisse numeros in primigenis Codi- cibus ullo argumento constat.

Probandum hic in Grotio, quod textus cor- ruptionem, quam alii imprimis Pontificii, utpote Thomas Aquinas, Cajetanus in h. l. Sixtus Senensis lib. VI. Bibl. annot. 131. Melchior Canus, Diony- sius Petavius statuunt, non probat. Nam ubi con- sentiunt ex asse Codices Sacri, nec non Interpre- tes antiqui, nulla corruptelæ suspicio admittenda. unde nec Wilhelmi Langii opinioni locus, qui hic pro E extritis binis inferioribus lineis Γ irrepsisse suspicatur, etsi simile quid legatur in comment. in Psalm. Hieronymo adscripto : quum probari ne- queat, talibus notis scriptos fuisse numeros in tex- tu originali, ut recte hic Grotius. Cujus tamen ex- plicatio, de jam audita tuba horæ tertiæ, funda- mento caret, nimisque laxa ratione tempus defini- tum relinquit. Nam si intervallum illud ab hora tertia usque ad sextam designatum, quanam ergo proprie hora crucifixus Christus ? Et cum postea hora sexta tenebræ factæ dicuntur, v. 33. ac v. 34. ho- ra vero nona Christus clamarit, Eloi, Eloi, num etiam illic indefinitum, aut in tanta πλάτει desi- gnatum tempus statuetur ? Heinsius ita reddidit hæc verba: ἦν δὲ ὥρα τρίτη καὶ ἐσταύρωσαν αὐτὸν, E- rat vero hora tertia, ex quo crucifigi cœpit, vel, Ter- tia vero jam agebatur hora ex quo actus fuerat in cru- cem. Nimirum quando divisa vestes sunt: cujus actus mentio præcedit v. 24. ȣ καὶ σταυρώσαντες αὐ- τὸν διεμέρισον τὰ ἱμάτια αὐτοῦ : Quam explicatio- nem pluribus probat Heinsius: quod nempe hora-

tertia inde a crucifixione divisio vestium Christi facta dicatur. Quæ etiam fuit Marcelli Monachi Romani doctissimi ἔκθεσις, ut observavit R. Bailius. Planior est sensus ille, si ἐςαύρωσαν in plusquamperfecto accipiatur hoc modo: Erat autem hora tertia, postquam crucifixerant eum. Quomodo etiam exposuit Arabs mentem S. Marci: illud de tertia hora, cum crucifixus esset, conjungens cum versu præcedenti, ubi de divisione vestium Christi, actum hoc modo: Id factum tertia hora a crucifixione. Quo abire quoque videtur interpretatio Persica: ex quo eum in cruce suspenderant; nec non Syriaca: quum crucifixissent eum; de quibus vid. Lud. de Dieu. Forte etiam non incommodum fuerit, si dicatur hora tertia inde a traditione Pilato facta hic designata: quam interpretationem eruditis expendendam reliquimus in Chronico nostro Biblico.

## 15:28
Verse 28.

καὶ μετὰ ἀνόμων ἐλογίσθη] The LXX in Isaiah have Ἐν τοῖς ἀνόμοις ἐλογίσθη. Christ had predicted in Luke 22:37 that this prophecy was to be fulfilled in himself; it may be translated: 'he was numbered with the wicked.' The Hebrew grammarians wish פשעים to be called those who sin both deliberately and with a certain notable perfidy; ἄνομοι are called oi ἀλλόφυλοι elsewhere: but here those who are held by no reverence for law or divine or human laws, having justice in their hands. Moreover, the whole of that prophecy of Isaiah, just as Philip did in the Acts, so also the old Chaldean Paraphrast explains concerning the Messiah.

Grotius acknowledges that these things were taken from Isaiah chapter 53:12, where the LXX have ἐν τοῖς ἀνόμοις ἐλογίσθη. He acknowledges that Christ predicted in Luke 22:37 that this prophecy was to be fulfilled in himself: He acknowledges that the whole of that prophecy of Isaiah 53 is to be accepted concerning the Messiah, and that Philip in Acts chapter 8 and the old Chaldean Paraphrast explained it concerning the Messiah. It is therefore mere trickery of his own, contrary to the interpretation of Christ himself, St. Mark, St. Philip, and the Chaldean text, that he twisted that whole prophecy to the Prophet Jeremiah, whose arrogance regarding Isaiah 53 we have corrected, as was fitting.

Latin:

Vers. 28.

καὶ μετὰ ἀνόμων ἐλογίσθη] Ἐν τοῖς ἀνόμοις ἐλογίσθη habent LXX. apud Esaiam. Implendum autem hoc vaticinium in se Christus prædixerat Luc. XXII. 37. vertere liceat: facinorosis annumeratus est. פשעים Hebræi Grammatici eos dici volunt, qui & deliberato & cum insigni quadam perfidia delinquunt, ἄνομοι alibi dicuntur oi ἀλλόφυλοι: hic vero ii qui nulla juris aut legum divinarum humanarumve reverentia tenentur, δίκην ἐν χερσὶν ἔχοντες. Totum autem illud Esaiæ vaticinium, sicut in Actis Philippus, ita & vetus Chaldæus Paraphrastes de Messia exponit.

Agnoscit Grotius hæc ex Esaia cap. LIII. 12. ubi LXX. habent ἐν τοῖς ἀνόμοις ἐλογίσθη desumta. Agnoscit Christum prædixisse Luc. XXII. 37. hoc vaticinium in se implendum: Agnoscit totum illud vaticinium Esa. LIII. de Messia accipiendum esse, idque in Actis Philippum cap. VIII. & veterem Chaldæum Paraphrastem de Messia exposuisse. Mera ergo κυβεία ipsius Christi, S. Marci, S. Philippi, & Chaldaici textus interpretationi contraria est, quod detorserit totum illud vaticinium ad Jeremiam Prophetam, quam πρεβλότητα ejus ad Es. LIII. prout par erat, castigavimus.

## 15:29
Verse 29.

Οὐὰ] The Latin interjection 'vah' is used by Mark in this place. It has the meaning of detesting rather than, as Jerome judged, insulting. Plautus: 'Vah, what worse thing can be remembered of that woman,' and 'Vah, shameless man.' It corresponds to the Hebrew אָח, but which is mostly of one admitting, ὀὰ in Aeschylus in the Persians, whence 'ovare'.

Latin:

Vers. 29.

Οὐὰ] Latina interjectio vah a Marco hoc loco usurpata est. Habet autem detestandi potius quam quod Hieronymus censuit, insultandi significationem. Plautus: Vah quid illi potest pejus quicquam muliere memorarier: & Vah homo impudens. Respondet Hebræum אָח, sed quod plerumque est admittantis, ὀὰ Æschylo in Persis, unde ovare.

## 15:32
Verse 32.

ἵνα πιστεύσωμεν] That we may have faith in him affirming himself to be the Messiah.

Latin:

Vers. 32.

ἵνα πιστεύσωμεν] Ut fidem habeamus ipsi se Messiam affirmanti.

## 15:34
Verse 34.

ἐλωὶ] Not all old copies had it so. For Eusebius cites ἠλεὶ (which is the same as that which is in Matthew, ἠλὶ). And in the Syriac in this place it is איל איל, but undoubtedly with the letters transposed by a scribe when it should have been written אלי אלי, as we noted at Matthew. But that in so many copies that ἐλωὶ has penetrated into this place, I think it happened because, just as Luke's Gospel was most celebrated in the beginning through the churches founded by Paul, so Mark's through the whole Babylonian dispersion, over which Peter had presided: and therefore it was copied by men skilled in the Syriac language, to whom אלהי was better known than אלי.

It cannot be proven by any codex that it was read otherwise than ἐλωὶ in Mark. If Eusebius's citation was made from Mark, not Matthew, it should be considered a mistake of memory or of the scribes, rather than calling the text of Scripture into suspicion of corruption. But that Syriac איל is not an argument that Mark did not write ἐλωὶ. Perhaps the Syrian used that word so that he might explain it by אלהי. Nor is there need for us to establish that אלי should be read in the Syriac. For איל is also accepted by the Syrian, as is evident from Psalm 22:20. Moreover, Ludov. de Dieu thinks the affixed pronoun is omitted because that affix, even when written, is not accustomed to be pronounced by the Syrians: furthermore, because it is also not accustomed to be written everywhere. But what Grotius suspects from that, that the name ἐλωὶ penetrated into all those copies that exist, is vain: for thus a universal corruption of all codices would have to be established. Christ spoke in Syriac, which language was familiar to him, and not unknown in Jerusalem. Moreover, in the Syriac text of Psalm 22:1, there is אלהי אלהי, not indeed אלי or איל. Therefore Mark expressed the name in the language familiar to Christ, which Matthew brought forward as it is in the Hebrew text; by which, as far as this word is concerned, Christ seems to have used it, so that he would not entirely pass over the Hebrew text as authentic, whence also the slander arose about calling Elias, because in the Hebrew it is Eli, Eli. But because it pleased Christ also to use the customary dialect in this exclamation, and therefore he used the Chaldeo-Syriac word שבקתני, therefore Mark seems also to have used the Syriac name אלהי in the commemoration of this saying. For that the Syrians also have their אלהי Elohi, Mart. Petr. Cheitomæus rightly notes against Lud. de Dieu in Græco-Barbaris no. 6, p. 65.

Latin:

Vers. 34.

ἐλωὶ] Vetera exemplaria non omnia ita habuere. Nam ἠλεὶ (quod idem est cum eo quod apud Matthæum ἠλὶ) citat Eusebius. Et apud Syrum hoc loco est איל איל, sed haud dubie transpositis a librario literis cum scribendum fuerit אלי אלי, ut ad Matthæum monuimus. Quod autem in tam multa exemplaria illud ἐλωὶ hoc loco penetraverit, factum inde arbitror, quod sicut Lucæ Evangelium initio maxime celebratum est per Ecclesias a Paulo fundatas, ita Marci per omnem Babylonicam διασπορὰν, cui Petrus præfuerat: ac proinde descriptum ab hominibus Syrium sermonem callentibus, quibus notius erat אלהי quam אלי.

Nullo codice probari potest aliter quam ἐλωὶ lectum esse in Marco. Eusebii citatio si e Marco facta, non Matthæo, vel memoriæ, vel librariorum ἁμάρτημα potius habenda, quam in suspicionem corruptelæ textus Scripturæ vocandus. Illud vero Syri איל argumento non est, quod Marcus non scripserit ἐλωὶ. Forte Syrus eam adhibuit vocem, ut eam exponeret per אלהי. Neq; opus est, ut statuamus apud Syrum אלי legendum esse. Nam etiam איל Syro receptum est, ut e Psal. XXII. 20. constat. Pronomen autem affixum omitti censet Ludov. de Dieu, quia id affixum etiam scriptum non solet pronunciari a Syris : deinde quia etiam non ubique adscribi solet. Quod vero inde suspicatur Grotius, nomen ἐλωὶ penetrasse in omnia illa, quæ habentur Exemplaria, vanum est: Ita enim universalis statuenda foret omnium codicum cor- ruptio. Syriace loquutus Christus fuit, quæ lin- gua ipsi familiaris erat, nec ignota Hierosolymis. In Syriaco autem textu Psalmi XXII. 1. habetur אלהי אלהי non vero אלי aut איל. Expressit ergo Marcus nomen lingua Christi familiari, quod Matthæus, ut in Ebræo habetur textu, ad- duxit; quo, quantum ad hanc vocem, Christus videtur usus, ut textum Ebræum ceu authenticum non plane præteriret, unde etiam nata est calu- mnia de vocato Elia, quia in Ebræo est Eli, Eli. Quia vero placuit Christo etiam uti dialecto con- sueta in hac exclamatione, atque ideo adhibuit vocem Chaldeo-Syram שבקתני, ideo Marcus vi- detur etiam nomen Syrum אלהי in commemora- tione hujus dicti adhibuisse. Nam אלהי Elohi suum etiam Syros habere, recte contra Lud. de Dieu notat Mart. Petr. Cheitomæus in Græco-Bar- baris n. 6. p. 65.

For as to what some think, that he was so called to distinguish him from his uncle, I do not see what certainty that has. For when Judas is called the son of James in Luke 6:16, the word 'brother' is to be understood rather than 'son,' for Judas of James himself calls himself a brother. And as for the fact that they wish that James the greater to have been the father not only of Judas but also of Joses, they are undoubtedly mistaken in that, especially since they establish this James as the son of Alphaeus. For this James had the same mother as Joses, as appears in this passage.

THE HISTORY OF THE LORD'S RESURRECTION.

Idem enim esse hoc nomen cum Josephi nomine inter veteres Origenes recte censuit.

HISTORIA RESUR- RECTIONIS DOMINI.

## 16:1 Argument
CHAPTER XVI.

That the history of the resurrection, which is the most important part of the Gospel, was omitted by Mark, is incredible to believe. That it was written by him, but lost, and this part supplied by another, seems to me equally incredible. For whence could such a corruption have come to a book which, as soon as it was published, was undoubtedly copied into very many examples and distributed far and wide? Moreover, if someone supplied it, why would they not have followed the very words of Matthew? Add now that the Latin, Syriac, and Arabic [versions] acknowledge it, and Irenæus, whose authority in this matter ought to be great. Wherefore, that in certain Greek copies this part was omitted, either in whole or from the words ἀναστὰς (for Gregory of Nyssa teaches that some books ended at the words ἐφοβοῦντο γὰρ, and certain manuscripts show this), is to be attributed to the copyists, who thought there was an irreconcilable conflict in this part with the words of Matthew, which cause for omission Jerome also gives: whereas the matter stands far otherwise, as has been demonstrated by others, and we have briefly touched upon at Matthew.

ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

The women, who had bought spices, coming early to the sepulcher, anxious about the stone, see it rolled away from the door of the sepulcher; to them, having entered, an angel in a long white garment appeared, who testified that Jesus had risen, the empty sepulcher being shown: and he ordered them to announce this to the disciples, and that Jesus would go before them into Galilee. They, however, fled from the sepulcher with terror. Jesus appeared first to Mary Magdalene, who, announcing this, did not find belief; then to two going into the country, to whom, when they announced it, belief was likewise not given: finally to the eleven Apostles, whom he rebuked for their unbelief. The Apostles were sent into all the world to preach the Gospel, and the signs that would follow were recounted. Finally, the Lord, taken up into heaven, sits at the right hand of God: the Apostles, however, going forth, preached everywhere, the Lord working with them.

There are two parts: I. The history of the manifestations of Christ after the resurrection: (1) Through the testimony of the Angel made to the women, to v. 8. (2) Through the various appearances of Jesus with the sending of the Apostles into the world, to v. 18. II. The ascension of Christ into heaven, with his sitting at the right hand of God, and the cooperation that took place everywhere, where the Apostles preached, to v. 21.

PART I. The history of the manifestations of Christ.

Ver. 1.

διαγενομένου τοῦ σαββάτου] When the Sabbath had passed: Thus Plato, διακοσίων ἐτῶν διαγεγονότων. Luke Acts 25:13, ἡμερῶν δὲ διαγενομένων τινων: and ch. 27:9, ἱκανοῦ δὲ χρόνου διαγενομένου.

ἠγόρασαν] They already had them bought, as we said at Matthew.

Latin:

CAPUT XVI.

Omissam a Marco resurrectionis historiam, quæ Evan- gelii vel potissima pars est, indignum sit creditu. Scri- ptam ab ipso, sed perditam, & ab alio partem hanc sup- pletam, æque mihi videtur incredibile. Unde enim ista labes advenire potuit libro, qui, statim ut est editus, haud dubie plurimis exemplis descriptus, & longe lateque distra- ctus est? Tum vero qui supplevit, cur non ipsa secutus esset Matthæi verba? Adde jam quod Latinus, Syrus, Arabs agnoscunt, &, cujus magna in hac re debet esse auctoritas, Irenæus. Quare quod in quibusdam Græcis exemplari- bus hæc pars aut tota, aut ab illis verbis ἀναστὰς (nam in verbis ἐφοβοῦντο γὰρ desiisse quosdam libros & Gregorius Nyssenus docet, & manuscripti quidam ostendunt) omissa fuit, exscriptoribus tribuendum est, qui in hac parte esse pu- taverunt cum Matthæi verbis ἄσπονδον πόλεμον, quam omis- sionis causam & Hieronymus reddit: cum res longe aliter se habeat, ut ab aliis demonstratum est, & nos ad Matthæum breviter attigimus.

ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Mulieres, quæ aromata emerant, mane ad se- pulchrum venientes, solicitæ de saxo vident id devolutum a sepulcri janua, quibus in- gressis angelus veste longa candida visus, testatus est surrexisse Jesum, monstrato se- pulcro vacuo: jussitque eas, id discipulis nuntiare, & quod præcessurus ipsos Jesus sit in Galilæam. Illæ vero cum terrore fu- gerunt a sepulcro. Apparuit autem Jesus primum Mariæ Magdalenæ, quæ id nun- cians fidem non invenit; tum duobus rus euntibus, quibus illud nuntiantibus itidem habita non est fides: denique undecim Apo- stolis, quos ob incredulitatem redarguit. Apostoli missi in omnem orbem ad prædi- candum Evangelium, & signa sequutura recensita. Tandem sublatus Dominus in cælum sedet ad Dextram Dei: Apostoli vero exeuntes ubique prædicarunt, coope- rante Domino.

Partes sunt duæ: I. Historiæ manifestationum Christi post resurrectionem: (1) Per Angeli testi- ficationem mulieribus factam, ad v. 8. (2) Per ap- paritiones Jesu diversas cum emissione Apostolo- rum in orbem ad v. 18. II. Ascensio Christi in cæ- lum, cum sessione ad dextram Dei, & coope- ratione ubique locorum facta, ubi Apostoli præ- dicaverunt, ad v. 21.

PARS I. Historia manifestationum Christi.

## 16:7
Vers. 7.

and to Peter] Strabo in book VIII says that it is a not infrequent figure of speech to include the part with the whole, citing both other things and that line of Alcman: 'Leaving lovely Cyprus and sea-girt Paphos': and of Aeschylus: 'Having come from Cyprus and Paphos, all the inheritance.' Thus in Homer: 'Phoenicia and the Sidonians, the Trojans and Hector, I saw also Gargaron, and Phalae and Eretria': which are noted by Eustathius on Odyssey A. Donatus on the Prologue to the Andria: because it is of the highest authority, he called Ennius the last. Servius on Aeneid I. 'Of the Danaans and of cruel Achilles': he rightly separated the leader from the people according to Homer. The same he observes in that passage of Aeneid III.

The chosen ones of the people to the nobles and the father himself.

And on X. After the general statement he introduced the specific. But almost whenever the species is subjoined to the genus (I use 'species' here in the manner of the jurists), there is something exceptional in the species, as Ps. 18:1, 1 Kings 11:1, 2 Sam. 2:30, Acts 1:14. But Peter is named here specifically as the leader of the Apostolic group, and therefore as a notable example proposed to all of human infirmity, of the festival of repentance, and of restored faith. There appears here that which Christ spoke of regarding the joy of the angels over a repentant sinner.

As has been rightly observed by Grotius from Strabo book VIII that it is a not infrequent figure of speech to include the part with the whole, and that this almost always occurs when there is something exceptional in the species, as Ps. 18:1, 1 Kings 11:1, 2 Sam. 2:30, Acts 1:14: so Peter is not named here specifically because he was the leader of the Apostolic group, as not only Grotius but also Cardinal Baronius opines; of which axiom regarding Peter, Scripture knows nothing, but because he, having fallen more notably than the other Apostles, had the greatest need to be specifically raised up. That excellence is to be sought in the transgression and in the contrition over it, and not in the primacy of Peter: which has nothing to do with the matter. More correctly, therefore, Victor of Antioch on this passage. By the fact that he wishes the indication of this matter to be made to Peter, he admonishes them that he who could have seemed rejected on account of his denial is now, through and because of his repentance, taken up again and numbered once more among the other Apostles just as before. Similarly, the Roman Bishop Gregory the Great, homily 21 on Mark: 'If the Angel did not name him specifically, he who had denied his Master would not have dared to come among the disciples.' He is called, therefore, by name, so that he might not despair because of his denial.

Vers. 7.

καὶ τῷ Πέτρῳ] Strabo libro VIII. σχῆμα esse ait non in- frequens συγκαταλέγειν τὸ μέρος τῷ ὅλῳ, adducens tum alia, tum illud Alcmanis: Κύπρον ἱμερτὰν λιπῦσα καὶ Πάφον περιῤῥύταν : & Æschyli: Κύπρου Πάφου θ' ἵκουσα πάντα κλῆρον. Sic apud Homerum: Φοινίκην καὶ Σιδονίους, Τρῶας καὶ Ἕκτο- ρα, ἴδον καὶ γάργαρον, Φαλαῖδά τ' Εἰρετρίην τε: quæ notata Eustathio ad Odysseæ A. Donatus ad Prologum Andriæ: quod est summæ auctoritatis Ennium ultimum dixit. Servius ad I. Æneid. Danaum atque immitis Achilli: bene secundum Homerum segregavit ducem à populo. Idem observat in il- lo III. Æneid.

Delectos populi ad proceres ipsumque parentem.

Et ad X. Post generalitatem intulit speciem. Ferme autem u- bi generi species subjungitur) speciem hic jurisconsulto- rum more usurpo) in specie aliquid est eximii, ut Psalm. XVIII. 1. I. Reg. XI. 1. 2. Sam. II. 30. Act. I. 14. Petrus au- tem peculiariter hic nominatur, ut dux Apostolici cœtus, ac proinde exemplum insigne propositum omnibus infirmita- tis humanæ, feriæ pœnitentiæ & instauratæ fidei. Appa- ret hic, illud de quo Christus dixit angelorum gaudium super converso peccatore.

Ut recte observatum Grotio è Strabone lib. VIII. σχῆμα non infrequens esse συγκαταλέγειν τὸ μέ- ρος τῷ ὅλῳ, idque ferme occurrere, cum in specie aliquid est eximii, ut Ps. XVIII. 1. 1. Reg. XI. 1. 2. Sam. II. 30. Act. I. 14: ita non ideo hic peculiariter no- minatur Petrus, quod dux Apostolici cœtus fuerit, quemadmodum non modo Grotius, sed etiam Baronius Cardinalis opinatur; de quo vero axio- mate Petri Scriptura nihil novit, sed quod ipse præ aliis Apostolis insigniter lapsus peculiariter erigi maxime opus habuerit. Ἐξοχὴ illa in præ- varicatione, & super ea contritione quærenda est, non vero in primatu Petri: qui nihil ad rem facit. Re- ctius itaque Victor Antiochenus in h. l. Per hoc quod rei hujus indicium Petro vult fieri, admonet illos, eum qui propter negationem rejectus videri poterat, nunc per & propter pœnitentiam denuo assumtum, & in- ter cæteros Apostolos æque atque ante rursus nume- ratum. Similiter Episcopus Romanus Gregorius Magnus hom. XXI. in Marc. Si hunc Angelus nomi- natim non exprimeret, qui Magistrum negaverat, venire inter discipulos non auderet. Vocatur ergo ex nomine, ne desperaret ex negatione.

Therefore, 'having risen' is he himself who had risen: but not as soon as he had risen. Thus below, 'him having been raised' denotes the person, not the time. Those who did not understand this expunged this clause, with the same rashness with which we said this whole reading was omitted by some.

Hoc qui non intellexerunt, expunxerunt hoc comma, simili teme- ritate, qua totam hanc lectionem à quibusdam omissam di- ximus.

κὶ ἐθεάθη ἀπ' αὐτῆς] A Magdalena: Johannes: ἔρχεται Μαρία ἡ Μαγδαληνὴ ἀπαγγέλλουσα τοῖς μαθηταῖς ὅτι ἑώρακε τὸν κύριον.
