## 16:12
Vers. 12.

Verse 12. To two of them] Those who were there with him, as he said above. For by this name others also outside the Twelve are reckoned, especially those who were of the number of the Seventy. Wherefore Euthymius wrongly thinks that a different history is indicated here than that which is described at length by Luke.

in another form] In a different habit than that which he was accustomed to use. Therefore they thought he was a stranger. Their eyes were divinely hindered from recognizing him himself because of his countenance. Thus I think Mark is best reconciled with Luke, and a similar thing happened concerning the Magdalene. For she had the habit of a gardener, her own face, but one that would not be recognized immediately. Thus also above, 'he was transfigured' is referred to his habit, 9. 2. 3.

Going into the country] Into the village which was outside the city, namely Emmaus. For it is customary for the Hebrews to contrast עִיר and שָׂדֶה, and for the Hellenists to contrast city and country, as in Deut. 28. 3.

Andreas Osiander therefore approached this rashly, as we noted at Luke 24. 30. Vossius, Harm. Evang. Book III, ch. 4, § 3, asks: whence Jesus had clothes, and thinks he either created them himself or took them from elsewhere, with the author of the responses (attributed to Justin) to the orthodox questions, ch. 16, and that it was a rustic garment, such as those of inhabitants in the Jerusalem countryside, or of travelers. But because the Lord did not wish to be recognized immediately even from his face, their eyes were restrained, as Luke has it: that the features of his face were changed, which seemed to be the case to Theophylact and certain others even in the time of Augustine (see Epist. 70 to Paulinus), does not agree so well with the words of Luke: as Augustine observed in his work On the Consensus of the Evangelists, Book III, ch. 25. Doubtless the Lord wished to be unknown at the beginning, so that he might draw out the inner thoughts of these disciples, and convince them all the more of their unbelief, and once convinced, convert them to faith.

Latin:

Vers. 12.

Verf. 12. Δυσὶν ἐξ ἀυτῶν] ῟ῌ μετὰ ἐκεῖ γενομένων, ut su- pra dixit. Nam hoc nomine etiam alii extra XII. censentur, præcipue qui de numero erant illorum LXX. Quare imme- rito Euthymius hic aliam putat historiam indicari quam eam quæ à Luca copiofe describitur.

ἐν ἑτέρᾳ μορφῇ] Habitu alio quam quo uti solebat. Ideo πάροικοι putabant. Ex vultu quominus ipsum agnosce- rent oculi divinitus impediebantur. Ita optime puto con- ciliari Marcum cum Luca, & simile contigit circa Magdale- nam. Nam habitum habebat olitoris, vultum suum, sed qui non repente agnosceretur. Sic & supra μετεμορφώθη ad habitum refertur IX. 2. 3.

Πορευομένοις εἰς ἀγρὸν] In pagum qui erat extra urbem, Emmauntem scilicet. Solent enim Hebræis opponi עִיר & שָׂדֶה, Hellenistis πόλις & ἀγρὸς ut Deut. XXVIII. 3.

Temere ergo hic accessit Euthymio Andr. Osi- ander, quod ad Luc. XXIV. 30. notavimus. Vossius l. III. Harm. Evang. c. IV. §. 3. quærit: unde vestes habuerit Jesus, & putat eas vel creasse ipsum, vel ali- unde sumsisse, cum autore responsionum (Justino tri- butarum) ad orthod. q. c. XVI. ac rusticam fuisse vestem, qualis habitantium in agro Hierosolymi- tano, vel peregrinantium. Quia vero nec è vultu statim agnosci voluit Dominus, oculi illorum de- tenti sunt, ut Lucas habet: vultus lineamenta im- mutata fuisse, quod Theophylacto & aliis quibus- dam etiam tempore Augustini (vid. Epist. LXX. ad Paulin.) visum fuit, verbis Lucæ non adeo con- gruit: ut l. III. de consens. Evang. c. 25. observavit Augustinus. Nimirum ignotus initio voluit esse Dominus, ut discipulorum horum interiora elice- ret, eosque eo magis de ἀπιστίᾳ convinceret, & convictos ad fidem converteret.

## 16:13
Verse 13. And they did not believe them] Most of them, that is. Nor does it stand in the way that Luke says that before those two arrived, Jesus had appeared to Simon, and that this very thing was announced to the assembly. For they did not sufficiently admit even this into their minds. Indeed, even when Jesus had already arrived, Luke adds 'while they still did not believe.' All these things pertain to this, that we might believe more firmly those who themselves believed so slowly.

When they saw these things, because the Apostles did not yet believe the disciples to whom Christ had appeared in a different form, Euthymius and Andreas Osiander in his Harmony judged that the account of Mark concerning the two disciples going to the country, and that which is commemorated by Luke concerning the two who were traveling to Emmaus, were a double appearance; but the circumstances show that it is the same appearance, and that the middle of the journey is expressed by Mark and the destination by Luke; which Augustine also teaches in his work On the Consensus of the Evangelists, Book III, ch. 25. Although indeed some said the Lord was truly raised, others nevertheless did not yet believe it: nor perhaps did those others assert it without the wavering of doubt: for in the same Luke, even when Christ had later stood among them and shown his hands and feet, v. 41, that 'while they still did not believe' is read; therefore in Mark 16, v. 14, the unbelief and hardness of heart of those eleven (or rather ten) was rebuked, if not of all, at least of some of them; where without doubt Peter is excepted, for the Lord had already appeared to him. Compare the Harmony of the Resurrection by B. Gerhard, ch. 7, p. 278.

Latin:

Verf. 13. κἀκεῖνοις ἐπίστευσαν] Plerique eorum scili- cet. Nec obstat, quod Lucas ait, antequam illi duo adven- tarent, Simoni visum fuisse Jesum, idque ipsum cœtui re- nunciatum. Nam & hoc in animum non satis admittebant. Imo & cum Jesus jam supervenisset, adjicit Lucas ἔτι ἀ- πιστούντων ἀυτῶν. Hæc omnia eo pertinent, ut nos firmius credamus, his qui ipsi tam tarde crediderunt.

Quum viderent hæc, quod nondum discipulis, quibus in aliena forma apparuerat Christus, Apo- stoli crediderint, Lucæ relationi quod Apostoli dixerint c. XXIV. 34. ὅτι ἠγέρθη ὁ κύριος ὄντως, non convenire, geminam apparitionem esse cen- suerunt Euthymius, & Andr. Osiander in Harm. il- lam Marci de duobus discipulis rus euntibus, & eam, quæ à Luca de duobus qui in Emaus contende- bant, commemorata est; sed circumstantiæ do- cent, eandem esse apparitionem, & à Marco viæ medium à Luca terminum expressum esse; quod etiam docet Augustin. l. III. de consens. Evangel. c. 25. Etsi vero nonnulli dixerint Dominum ὄντως resuscitatum, alii tamen id nondum credidere: ne- que isti fortasse citra dubitationem fluctus id asse- ruêre: nam apud eundem Lucam etiam tum, ubi se postea Christus ipse stitisset, & manus pedesque monstrasset, v. 41. illud ἔτι δὲ ἀπιστούντων αὐτῶν le- gitur, ideo Marc. XVI. v. 14. increpata fuit, si non omnium, quorundam saltem ex illis undecim (vel decem potius) ἀπιστία, καὶ σκληροκαρδία; ubi si- ne dubio Petrus exemtus est, illi enim Dominus jam apparuerat, Conf. Harm. Resurr. B. Gerhardi c. VII. p. 278.

## 16:14
Verse 14. Afterward] 'Afterward' is not 'lastly,' but 'then.' Thucydides says 'a little afterward,' Plutarch 'a little afterward,' when they wish to signify something done a little later. I entirely agree with those who refer these words of Mark to the same history which is in Luke 24. 36. Wherefore 'afterward' here signifies an interval of a short time, as in Matt. 4. 2, or it is the same as 'again,' as it is sometimes accustomed to be taken.

Lud. de Dieu also has it thus: Syriac, 'at length,' 'lastly.' It is certain, however, from the remaining Evangelists, which the illustrious Beza also acknowledges in his most learned commentary on this passage, that this was not the last appearance of Christ. Erasmus therefore preferred to translate it 'afterward.' As also the Arab, 'after that.' Excellent. For 'afterward' does not always signify 'lastly,' but also often 'then,' 'afterward,' as

Matt. 21. 32, 'and you did not repent afterward,' not 'you were not converted then,' after, namely, you saw the publicans and harlots believe John the Baptist. Thus John 13. 36, 'and afterward you will follow me,' 'hereafter you will follow me.' See also Heb. 12. 11, Matt. 4. 2, and elsewhere. Furthermore, if that meaning of the word 'afterward' as 'lastly' is retained, it will not denote the newest appearance of Christ, which happened on the day of the ascension, but the last of those which occurred on the day of the resurrection, because Mark wished to exhibit them synoptically; hence he teaches how 'first' on that day he appeared to Mary Magdalene, v. 9, how likewise 'after these things' he was seen by the two disciples, v. 12, and how finally 'afterward,' on the same day, he stood before the eleven disciples, v. 14.

reclining at table] At the end of the supper. For the reason of the interval and time does not conflict, as will be evident at Luke. But the Apostles seem to have used for their meals that same upper room which Christ had last used.

The Greek word is more correctly translated 'sitting together': Luke has 'gathered together': John 'assembled': for Beza rightly shows that 'ana' is placed for 'syn.' And this word is used in this way in Mark 5. 40. For this appearance happened around late at night, at which time a supper would not have been appropriate.

σκληροκαρδίαν] σκληροκαρδία is used here, just as above in ch. VI. 52. 'for their heart was hardened.' Elsewhere both this and that word signify a more serious evil: as we noted at the cited passage.

Latin:

Verf. 14. ὕστερον] ὕστερον non est postremo, sed deinde. Thucydides μικρὸν ὕστερον dicit, Plutarchus ὀλίγον ὕστερον, cum quid volunt paulo post factum significare. Ego totus assen- tior referentibus hæc Marci verba ad eandem historiam, quæ est apud Lucam XXIV. 36. Quare ὕστερον hic parvi temporis intervallum significat, ut Matth. IV. 2. aut idem est quod ἄν- θις, ut interdum sumi solet.

Sic etiam habet Lud. de Dieu: Syrus, tandem, ul- timo. Certum tamen est ex reliquis Evangelistis, quod & in doctissimo ad hunc locum commentario Cl. Beza agnoscit, non fuisse hanc ultimam Christi appari- tionem. Maluit ergo Erasmus vertere postea. Ut & Arabs, post illud. Optime. ὕστερον enim non semper postremo, sed & sæpe deinde, postea, significat, ut

Matt. XXI. 32. & μετεμελήθητε ὕσερον, non conver- fi estis deinde, postquam nempe vidistis publicanos & meretrices Johanni Baptistæ credere. Sic Joh. XIII. 36. ὕσερον δὲ ἀκολυθήσεις μοὶ, posthac me sequeris. Vide & Hebr. XII. 11. Matt. IV. 2. & alibi. Cæterum si retineatur illa vocis ὕσερον significatio postremo, non novissima Christi apparitio, die sc. affumtionis facta, sed ultima earum, quæ die resurrectionis con- tigerunt, notabitur, quia illas Synoptice exhibere voluit Marcus, hinc docet quomodo πρῶτον pri- mum illa die Mariæ Magdalenæ apparuit v. 9. quo- modo item μετὰ ταῦτα post hæc duobus discipulis visus sit v. 12. quomodo deniq; ὕσερον postremo, ea- dem die, se stiterit undecim discipulis v. 14.

ἀνακειμένοις αὐτοῖς] In fine cœnæ. Neque enim repugnat intervalli & temporis ratio, ut ad Lucam patefcet. Videntur autem Apostoli ad convivia sua usi eodem illo cœnaculo, quo Christus postremo usus fuerat.

Rectius vertitur Græca vox una sedentibus: Lu- cas habet συνηθροισμένοις: Johannes συνηγμένοις: poni enim ἀνὰ pro σὺν recte ostendit Beza. Et ita adhibetur hoc verbum Marc. V. 40. Contigit enim hæc apparitio circa multam noctem, quo tempore non opportuna fuisset cœnatio.

σκληροκαρδίαν] σκληροκαρδία hic dicitur, quomodo supra c. VI. 52. ἦν γὰρ καρδία αὐτῶν πεπωρωμένη. Alibi & hæc & illa vox gravius malum significat: ut ad dictum locum annota- vimus.

## 16:15
Vers. 15. κέ εἶπεν αὐτοῖς] That is, during the whole time of the XL days, both in Judea and in Galilee, he spoke to them about these matters. Therefore, soon after, in verse 19, he adds 'after he had spoken to them'.

Mark does not teach that he spoke with them during that whole time of XL days, but he now reports what he commanded them in his final appearance, as is evident from a comparison with Matt. XXIX. And it is added here, what he said to them? Namely, that he ordered them to go into all the world to preach the Gospel and to baptize, which he certainly did not speak to them about during that whole time of XL days. The things which he spoke to them on the last day of the resurrection are not reported here; but Mark now passes over, having left aside the other appearances, those made to Thomas and at the Sea of Tiberias, which are described by other Evangelists, to that manifestation which occurred before the disciples on a certain mountain in Galilee.

εἰς ᾄ κόσμον ἅπαντα] This is to be understood kindly, so that no nation is excluded, and the Apostles may be stirred up to scatter the seed of the Gospel as widely as they could. Thus it is also said below, 'everywhere'.

πάση τῇ κτίσει] The Hebrews call man by way of eminence בּריּתא, as the most excellent work of God.

But why should that which is stated universally be understood so restrictively? And why should he not have willed the Gospel to be preached throughout the whole world? One must certainly not depart from the letter without cause. Nor is the mention of EVERY creature added without reason: just as the Apostle also testifies concerning the fulfillment, that the Gospel was preached to every creature which is under heaven, Col. I. 16. Furthermore, some understand the word 'Gospel' more broadly as the whole doctrine which was preached by the Apostles: others properly and strictly as the Gospel, as it is the proclamation of grace and the remission of sins in Christ, and in him now exhibited. This explanation is favored not only by the propriety of the letter, but also by the mention of faith: which is the correlate of the Gospel, as they call it. But the Gospel is not to be understood in that way exclusively, but specifically, because while the Apostles must teach all nations, as in Matt. XXIX, they must also specifically inform them about this joyful message, as is added here in Mark. Although, therefore, the law itself is not included in the word 'Gospel', it is certain that the Gospel cannot be preached according to the command of God unless the law is preached, so that through this proclamation hearts may be crushed and, through contrition, prepared for the doctrine of the Gospel.

Latin:

Vers. 15. κέ εἶπεν αὐτοῖς] Toto sc. XL. dierum tempore tum in Judæa tum in Galilæa his de rebus illos est allocu- tus. Ideo mox commate 19. subjicit μετὰ τὸ λαλῆσαι αὐτοῖς.

Non quod toto illo tempore XL. dierum cum illis loquuto fit, docet Marcus, sed tradit nunc quid in postrema apparitione ipsis præceperit, ut è col- latione Matth. XXIX constat. Et additur hic, quid ipsis dixerit? Quod nempe jusserit eos ire in omnem terrarum orbem prædicare Evangelium & baptizare, quod utique non toto illo XL. dierum tempore ipsis loquutus est. Non hic ea quæ in no- vissima diei resurrectionis apparitione ipsis lo- quutus est, referuntur; sed transit jam Marcus reli- ctis cæteris apparitionibus, Thomæ, & ad mare Tiberiadis factis, quæ ab aliis Evangelistis deseri- buntur, ad eam Φανερωσιν, quæ coram discipulis in monte quodam Galilææ contigit.

εἰς ᾄ κόσμον ἅπαντα] Benigne hoc intelligendum, ut gens nulla excludatur, & excitentur Apostoli ad spargen- dum quam latissime possent Evangelii semen. Sic & infra dicitur πανταχῦ.

πάση τῇ κτίσει] Hebræi hominem κατ’ ἐξοχὴν vocant בּריּתא, ut excellentissimum Dei opus.

Cur vero ita restricte intelligendum, quod uni- versaliter dictum est? & quidni voluerit per totum mundum prædicari Evangelium? Non difceden- dum utiq; à litera citra causam. Nec præter rem ad- ditur OMNIS creaturæ mentio: quemadmodum etiam Apostolus de complemento testatur, prædi- catum esse Evangelium omni creaturæ quæ sub cœlo est Col. I. 16. Cæterum vocem Evangelii nonnulli latius de tota doctrina intelligunt, quæ prædicata ab Apostolis: alii κυρίως proprie & stricte de Evan- gelio, ut est concio gratiæ & remissionis peccatorum in Christo, eodemque jam exhibito. Cui explica- tioni favet non tantum literæ proprietas, sed etiam fidei mentio: quæ Evangelii correlarum est, ut vocant. Sed ita Evangelium non exclu- sive intelligendum, verum εἰδικῶς, quod cum docere debeant Apostoli omnes gentes, ut est Matth. XXIX. tum speciatim informare de hoc læto nuncio, ut additur hic apud Marcum. Quan- quam ergo in voce Evangelii non includatur ipsa lex, prædicari tamen non posse Evangelium ex præscripto Dei certum est, nisi prædicetur lex, ut per hoc præconium animi conterantur & per con- tritionem ad Evangelii doctrinam præparentur.

## 16:16
Verse 16. He who has believed and has been baptized) That is, he who has not believed merely contemplatively, but has also in act professed that faith. For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation, Rom. X. 10. Moreover, this profession is wont to be called baptism from its solemn beginning.

Baptism was solemnly instituted in this discourse of Christ, as is evident from a comparison of Matt. XXIX with this passage, as a sacrament and means of salvation: not indeed merely as a profession of faith: for Christ had already professed before, John III. 5, 6, that whoever had been baptized could not be regenerated; but these things are in the proper places and in the Disputations against the Socinians and Calvinists.

shall be saved) He shall receive the remission of sins, the Holy Spirit, and eternal life. For this word is wont to embrace all these things.

but he who has not believed) He who has not believed the Gospel, in such a way as is fitting, that is, with a profession of a holy life. Thus he who has not believed is opposed both to the believer and to the baptized,

Mention of baptism is not repeated here, not because this word is opposed both to the believer and to the baptized, but because there is not the same reason of necessity regarding faith and baptism. Because without faith it is impossible to please God, Heb. XI. 6. And so faith is simply necessary for all who are to be saved: baptism is not likewise. For although this is an ordinary means of salvation, to which God binds all, just as the Israelites were once bound to circumcision, yet God has not bound the hands of His grace so that He cannot confer grace and salvation upon us without baptism.

shall be condemned) By the retention of sins, by obduration, and by eternal punishments greater than those which await those to whom this message has not been announced.

Latin:

Vers. 16. ὁ πιστεύσας κὴ βαπτισθεὶς) Id est, qui non credide- rit tantum contemplative, sed actu quoque fidem istam pro- fessus fuerit. Nam corde creditur ad justitiam, ore fit pro- fessio ad salutem, Rom. X. 10. Haec autem professio à so- lenni ejus exordio baptismus vocari solet.

Institutus est in hac oratione Christi solenniter Baptismus, ut è collatione Matth. XXIX. cum hoc loco patet, ceu sacramentum & medium salutis: non vero tantum ut professio fidei: nam ipsi quis baptizatus fuerit, eum regenerari non posse, jam ante professus erat Christus Joh. III. 5. 6. sed haec in LL. CC. & Disputationibus adversus Socinia- nos & Calvinianos.

σωθήσεται) Accipiet remissionem peccatorum, Spiritum Sanctum, & vitam æternam. Hæc enim omnia vox ista complecti solet.

ὁ δὲ ἀπισήσας) Qui non crediderit Evangelio, ita ut opor- tet scilicet, id est, cum sanctæ vitæ professione. Ita ὁ ἀπισή- σας opponitur & credenti & baptizato,

Non repetitur hic mentio baptismi, non quod vox hæc opponatur & credenti & baptizato, sed quia non eadem necessitatis est ratio, quantum ad fidem & baptismum. Quia sine fide impossibile est Deo placere Ebr. XI. 6. Adeoque fides simpliciter necessaria est omnibus salvandis: non item Bapti- smus. Etsi enim hic medium sit ordinarium salutis, ad quod omnes adstringit Deus, uti olim ad cir- cumcisionem adstricti erant Israëlitæ, tamen sibi non ligavit Deus manus gratiæ, quo minus sine baptismo nobis gratiam & salutem conferre pos- sit.

κατακριθήσεται) Retentione peccatorum, obduratione, & suppliciis æternis majoribus quam quæ eos manet, qui- bus hic sermo non est annuntiatus.

## 16:17
Verse 17. To those who have believed) not all things to all. For there are diversities of gifts, 1 Cor. XII, 4. Yet in such a way that to each one who believes as is fitting, some admirable faculty was then given, which would manifest itself not always indeed, but when the occasion was given. For this is what the prophecy of Joel signifies when it says: upon all flesh, namely, that which is serving God. Chrysostom on Romans VIII: God gave different gifts to all those who were then baptized, which were indeed called spirits,

They shall cast out demons) Mark places this gift in the first place, because it was commonly given to all believers: which the history of subsequent times also proves to be true. Justin Martyr in his dialogue with Trypho: And now we who believe in Jesus, our Lord, who was crucified under Pontius Pilate, have all demons and evil spirits exorcised and made subject to us. And elsewhere: Which also trembles at the name of Jesus, and even today, being exorcised according to the name of Jesus Christ, who was crucified under Pontius Pilate, who became procurator of Judea, it is made subject. From which places it is also possible to learn the formula used in exorcisms in ancient times. Irenaeus, book 2. For some cast out demons surely and truly, so that often those very ones who have been cleansed from evil spirits even believe and are in the church. Origen says to Celsus: The name of Jesus, when named against demons, is most effective when those who speak it do so from a healthy and genuinely believing disposition. Tertullian in his Apology: Let someone be brought forth under your tribunals who is known to be possessed by a demon. Commanded by any CHRISTIAN to speak, that spirit will confess himself to be a demon as truly as he elsewhere confesses God to be false. Again, Yet all this our domination and power over those demons is valid through the naming of Christ, and through the commemoration of those things which they expect to be imminent upon them from God through Christ as arbiter. Fearing Christ in God, and God in Christ, they are made subject to the servants of God and of Christ. Thus, from our contact and from our breathing upon them, through the contemplation and representation of that fire, they even depart from bodies at our command, unwilling and grieving, and blushing in your presence. And soon: But who would snatch you from those hidden enemies that are everywhere ravaging your minds and your health? I mean from the incursions of demons, which we drive away from you without reward, without payment. Minucius Felix: Most of you know that the demons themselves confess this about themselves, as often as they are driven from bodies by us and by the torments of our words and the fires of our prayer. Soon: They leap out immediately or vanish gradually, just as the faith of the sufferer assists, or the grace of the healer inspires. Origen against Celsus, book seven: The race of demons is driven out by not a few of the Christians from those who are suffering, with no curious and

magical or pharmaceutical practice, but by prayer alone and simpler adjurations, and whatever a simpler man might be able to bring forward: for as a rule, unlearned people do such things, the grace of Christ in the word making the worthlessness and weakness of the demons—and their need in every way to be defeated and to depart from the soul and body of a man—evident through certain wise and powerful proofs in the arguments concerning the faith. Lactantius: But they (the demons) fear the righteous, that is, the worshippers of GOD, by whose name they are adjured and depart from bodies: being beaten by their words as if by scourges, they not only confess that they are demons, but even give their names, those which are worshipped in temples, and which they often do in the presence of their worshippers, not indeed to the disgrace of religion, but to their own honor: because they cannot lie either to God, by whom they are adjured, or to the righteous, by whose voice they are tormented. But since even much later centuries are full of testimonies of this matter, I do not know by what reason some are moved to restrict that gift only to the first times: to whom, while I readily concede that there was a more abundant supply of miracles for laying the foundations of so great an edifice against the force of the world, I do not see why we should believe that this promise of Christ expired with them. Wherefore, if anyone even now, to Gentiles ignorant of Christ (for to them miracles properly serve, 1 Corinthians XII, verse 22), should announce Christ, just as He Himself wished to be announced, I do not doubt that the power of the promise will endure. For the gifts of God are without repentance. But we, the fault of which matter lies in our own sloth or lack of faith, are accustomed to cast it back upon God.

γλώσσαις λαλήσουσι καιναῖς) This gift also extended very widely: for it was granted not only to the Apostles and Evangelists, but also to many other believers, as can be seen in Acts 11:46, chapter 19:6, and from the Epistle to the Corinthians. He called them καινας γλώσσας, which one was not accustomed to speak.

Latin:

Vers. 17. Τοῖς πιστεύσασι) non omnibus omnia. Sunt enim διαιρέσεις χαρισμάτων 1 Cor. XII, 4. Ita tamen, ut cuilibet ut oportet credenti aliqua tunc data sit admirabilis facultas, quæ se non semper quidem, sed data occasione explicaret. Hoc enim significat Joëlis vaticinium cum ait: ἐπὶ πᾶσαν σάρκα, nempe ἣν δόλων τῶ Θεῶ. Chrysost. in IIX ad Roman. διάφορα πᾶσι τοῖς τότε βαπτιζομένοις ἐδίδε χαρίσματα ὁ Θεὸς, ἃ δὴ κὴ πνεύματα ἐκαλεῖτο,

Δαιμόνια ἐκβαλῶσι) Primo loco hoc donum ponit Mar- cus, quia communiter dabatur omnibus credentibus: quod verum esse etiam secutorum temporum historia evincit. Ju- stinus Martyr colloquio cum Tryphone: κὴ νῦν ἡμεῖς οἱ πι- σεύοντες ἐπὶ τὸν σαυρωθέντα ἐπὶ Ποντίε Πιλάτε ἰησῶν κύριον ἡ- μῶν, τὰ δαιμόνια πάντα κὴ πνεύματα πονηρὰ ἐξορκίζοντες ὑπο- τασσόμενα ἡμῖν ἔχομεν Et alibi: ὅ κὴ ἐπὶ τῶ ὀνόματῶ ἰησῦ ἡ τὰ δαιμόνια τρεμᾷ κὴ σήμερον ἐξορκιζόμενα κατὰ τῶ ὀνόματῶ ἰησῶ Χρισῶ τῶ σαυρωθέντῶ ἐπι Ποντίε Πιλάτε τῶ γενομένε ἐπιτρόπε τῆς ἰεδαίας ὑποτάσσεται. Ex quibus locis etiam formulam in exorcismis antiquitus usurpatam est discere. Irenæus lib. 2. οἱ μὲν γὰρ δαίμονας ἐλαύνεσι βεβαίως κὴ ἀληθῶς, ὥσε πολλάκις κὴ πιστεύειν αὐτὸς ἐκείνες καθαρισθέντας ἀπὸ τῶν πονηρῶν πνευμάτων κὴ εἶναι ἐν τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ, Origenes ad Celsum ait: Τὸ ὄνομα τῶ ἰησῦ κατὰ τῶν δαιμόνων ὀνομαζόμενον ἀνύειν μάλισα ὅταν οἱ λέγον- τες ἀπὸ διαθέσεως ὑγιῶς κὴ πεπιστευκυίας γνησίως αὐτὸ λέγωσι. Jussus à quolibet CHRI- STIANO loqui spiritus ille tam se dæmonem confitebitur de vero, quam alibi Deum de falso, Rursum, Atquin omnis hæc nostra in illos dæmonibus) dominatio & potestas de nomi- natione Christi valet, & de commemoratione eorum, quæ sibi à Deo per arbitrum Christum imminentia expectant. Christum timentes in Deo, & Deum in Christo, subjiciun- tur servis Dei & Christi. ## 16:18
Vers. 18. ὄφεις ἀρῢσι) Doubtless καὶ εἰ μὴ ἀυτὸς βλάψουσι, which from the following must also be referred here. ἀίρῢσι means they shall lift up with their hands. Thus that viper hung harmless from Paul's hand. It is to be noted, however, that all these σημεῖα are not only benefits in themselves, but also contain within themselves expressed images of those benefits which come to souls through the Gospel.

κἂν θανάσιμόν τι πίωσιν) Which some report concerning John the Apostle: Eusebius from Papias concerning Barsabas: the martyrology of Ado on the day before the Ides of May concerning Victor the Cilician soldier: Gregory of Tours concerning Sabinus, bishop of Canusium: and others concerning others. But the Talmudists also narrate that a certain kinsman of Joshua son of Levi, when he had drunk poison, recovered upon the name of Jesus being pronounced.

ἐπὶ ἀῤῥώστως χεῖρας ἐπιθήσουσι) The δῶρον ἰαμάτων seems to have been granted almost generally to all who had received the governance of the Church, James 5:14. For the laying on of hands is a visible sign of the prayer which James mentions. Luke joined the sign to the thing signified: προσευξάμενος ἐπιθεὶς τὰς χεῖρας ἀυτῷ ἰάσατο ἀυτὸν. Acts 28:8.

PARS II. Ascension into heaven.

Vers. 18. ὄφεις ἀρῢσι) Nimirum καὶ εἰ μὴ ἀυτὸς βλάψουσι quod ex sequentibus huc quoque referendum est. ἀίρῢσι est manibus tollent. Ita vipera illa innoxia pendebat à Pauli manu. Notandum autem est omnia hæc σημεῖα non per se tantum esse beneficia, sed & expressas in se conti- nere imagines eorum beneficiorum quæ animis per Evan- gelium contingunt.

κἂν θανάσιμόν τι πίωσιν) Quod quidam de Johanne Apo- stolo referunt: de Barsaba Eusebius ex Papia: De Victo- re milite Cilice martyrologium Adonis ad Pridie Eidus Maji: de Sabino Canusino episcopo Gregorius Turonen- sis: de aliis alii. Sed & Thalmudistæ cognatum quendam Josuæ filii Levi cum venenum bibisset pronuntiato Jesu nomine convaluisse narrant.

ἐπὶ ἀῤῥώστως χεῖρας ἐπιθήσουσι) δῶρον ἰαμάτων videtur communiter ferme concessum omnibus qui regimen Ec- clesiæ acceperant, Jac. V. 14. Nam manuum impositio vi- sibile signum est precationis cujus Jacobus meminit. Con- junxit signum rei signatæ Lucas: προσευξάμενος ἐπιθεὶς τὰς χεῖρας ἀυτῷ ἰάσατο ἀυτὸν. Act. XXIX. 8.

## 16:19
Vers. 19. μετὰ τὸ λαλῆσαι) When he had given all these precepts and promises to them, and nothing now remained except that the same should be sealed by the Holy Spirit.

ἀνελήφθη) The Apostles gladly use this word concerning Christ's ascension into heaven, Luke 9:51, Acts 1:2, 2:22, Paul 1 Tim. 3:16. Among the LXX, Elijah says to Elisha, 2 Kings 2:10, ἐὰν ἴδῃς με ἀναλαμβανόμενον ἀπὸ σῢ. And for that reason the same interpreters a little later translate יעל (he went up) as ἀνελήφθη, looking more to the sense than to the word, and there was an ancient book among the Jews containing narratives about the body of Moses, which had the name ἀνάληψις Μωσέως. Nor should it be omitted that it is said of Elijah ἀνελήφθη ἕως εἰς τ᾿ ὐρανὸν, 1 Maccabees 2:58; but of Christ not only εἰς ὐρανὸν, as in this place and elsewhere, but εἰς ὐρανὲς, Acts 2:34, Eph. 6:9, Col. 2:1, 1 Thess. 1:10, Heb. 8:1, concerning which distinction we have treated at Matthew 3.

Discrimen illic assignavit Grotius: that by the singular number ὐρανῢ the Greeks denote the aerial or starry region, but by the plural the highest and invisible heaven is designated: whether this difference is perpetual, I do not inquire. But what does that have to do with the matter here? Was Elijah only received into the aerial or starry heaven? Did he not come from the highest, invisible heaven when he was seen with Christ on the mountain, Matthew 17? Do not the Elect all taken up into the highest heaven, or as Paul calls it, the third? Scripture certainly teaches this everywhere. Therefore they are with Christ 1 Thess. IV. 17. and before the throne of God, Rev. VII. And this is what Paul desires: I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ Phil. I. 23.

ἐκάθισεν ἐν δεξιᾷ) What this expression signifies, we have said elsewhere. Moreover, ἐκάθισεν means he sat down.

Latin:

Vers. 19. μετὰ τὸ λαλῆσαι) Cum omnia hæc præcepta & promissa illis dedisset, nec quicquam jam restaret nisi ut eadem per Spiritum Sanctum obsignarentur.

ἀνελήφθη) Vocem hanc de Christi in cœlum ascensione libenter Apostoli usurpant Luc. IX. 51. Actor. I. 2. c. II. 22. Paul. I. Tim. III. 6. Apud LXX. Elias dicit Elisæo 2. Reg. II. 10. ἐὰν ἴδῃς με ἀναλαμβανόμενον ἀπὸ σῢ רקה. Propter- eaque iidem interpretes paulo post יעל ascendit vertunt ἀνελήφθη ad sensum magis quam ad vocem respicientes, & erat inter Judæos liber veteres narrationes de Mosis cor- pore continens cui nomen ἀνάληψις Μωσέως. Nec omit- tendum de Elia dici ἀνελήφθη ἕως εἰς τ᾿ ὐρανὸν, I. Maccab. II. 59. de Christo vero non tantum εἰς ὐρανὸν, ut hoc loco & alibi, sed εἰς ὐρανὲς Actorum II. v. 34. Eph. VI. v. 9. Coloss. II. 1. 1. Thess. I. 10. Hebr. VIII. 1. de quo discrimine egimus ad Matth. III.

Discrimen illic assignavit Grotius: quod nume- ro singulari ὐρανῢ aëream, aut sideream regionem Græci notent, plurali vero cælum supremum atque inspectabile designetur: quæ differentia an perpetua sit, non disquiro. Quid vero ea hic ad rem facit? num Elias solum receptus in cœ- lum aëreum, aut sidereum? annon de cœlo su- premo inaspectabili venit, quando cum Christo in monte visus est, Matth. XVII. Annon Electi omnes in cœlum supremum, vel ut Paulus vocat tertium, suscipiuntur? Id utique passim Scriptura docet. Ideo cum Christo sunt 1. Thess. IV. 17. & coram throno Dei, Apoc. VII. Atque hoc est quod optat Paulus: Cupio dissolvi & esse cum Christo Phil. I. 23.

ἐκάθισεν ἐν δεξιᾷ) Quid hæc locutio significet, alibi di- ximus. Est autem ἐκάθισεν ibit sessum.

κηρύξαν) The teachings of Christ, his life, death, resurrection, and ascension into heaven.

## 1:1 Introduction: Preface of Grotius
PREFACE OF GROTIUS.

KATὰ Λυκᾶν) Origen teaches us in his Annotations on the Epistle to the Romans that there were those who believed that Lucius, who is named in the same Epistle ch. XVI. v. 21, is this very Luke: and that Lucius is said in the Roman inflection, Lucan in the Greek. I think that Lucius, whom Paul mentions there, is none other than the Cyrenian whom our author names here, Acts XIII. 1. But I judge that his name was indeed Roman, but somewhat longer. For names that end in ᾶς are accustomed to cut off the last part of the name. Thus Δηυᾶς is Δημήτρειος, Μνᾶς is μηνόδωρος, Ἀπελλᾶς is Ἀπελλόδωρος, Θευδᾶς is Θεόδωρος, ἐπαφρᾶς is ἐπαφρόδιτος, ἀρποκρᾶς is ἀρποκράτης, ἀλεξᾶς is ἀλέξανδρος, κλεοπᾶς is κλεόπατρος. From Artemidorus comes Artemas, as in Varro in book VII. de lingua Latina. Herod the Father in his lesser fortune was Antipas, in his greater Antipater, according to Josephus. Thus Posides was made from Posidonius, Harpocras from Harpocration by diminution. And to come to Latin names, ῥυφᾶς is Rufinus. Wherefore also Lucas, if I see correctly, is contracted from a Roman name, which I suspect was Lucillius. For that family was flourishing at Rome at that time, from which also was he to whom Seneca's letters are extant. This man of ours was a Syrian, as the ancients agree: and he practiced medicine. For why should we think he is someone other than the one about whom Paul writes to the Colossians, Λυκᾶς ὁ ἰατρὸς, I see no reason: the antiquity of the fame supports it. Syria, however, provided many slaves to the Romans: and medicine, as we learn from Pliny and others, was a servile task. Freedmen, however, took the name of their patron, as the writer of comedies, though he was an African, was called Terentius from his patron Terentius: Alexander Polyhistor from his patron Cornelius Lentulus was called Cornelius, according to Suidas. Thus this man from Lucillius was called Lucillius, and contractedly Λυκᾶς. It is credible that, when he had practiced medicine at Rome for some time, having received his freedom, he returned to his homeland. Whether he imbibed the Jewish religion at home or at Rome is uncertain. At Rome, indeed, many of the freedman condition were daily passing over to Judaism, such as that Caecilius with whom Cicero contended in accusing Verres. See Plutarch in his Cicero. Philo in his book on the embassy to Gaius [writes] how he would have received the great section of Rome across the Tiber river, which he did not ignore was held and inhabited by Jews, and the majority were Romans who had been manumitted. But also at Antioch there was a great community of Jews and a huge number of proselytes: which both Josephus teaches us and the Roman laws. He drank in the language of the Hellenists along with their religion: and Greek literature while he was studying medicine. Traces of both are manifest in his writings. But also his diction, often inclining toward the Syriac idiom, betrays his homeland: and you may recognize that he lived at Rome from certain Roman expressions. I think he embraced the Christian dogma at Antioch, after he had returned there from Rome, with Paul teaching, to whom he clung as a companion from that time, as appears from the book of Acts, unless perhaps when he was sent by Paul to the Churches, to foster the seed which Paul had sown, which I think happened quite often. Nor does it displease me, what most of the ancients think, that that of Paul in 1 Corinthians 8:18, 'The brother whose praise is in the gospel through all'

working together) For we are God's fellow workers, says Paul in 1 Corinthians 3. Likewise: 'I labored more abundantly than them all, yet not I, but the grace of God which is with me.' The same man elsewhere attributes to the messengers of the word the planting and watering, but to God the giving of the increase. Indeed, the faithful heralds of the Gospel, as some of the ancients not badly said, are both ministers of God by effect, and partners by voluntary consent.

through those who followed) Just as he had just said 'these signs shall follow'.

And these things regarding the Gospel of Mark. Grant, good JESUS, that with the four living creatures in the midst of the throne we may eternally sing 'Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Almighty, who was and is and is to come.' Amen.

PRÆFATIO GROTII.

KATὰ Λυκᾶν) Docet nos Origenes in Annotationibus epistolæ ad Romanos, fuisse qui crederent Lucium eum qui in eadem Epistola nominatur c. XVI. v. 21. esse hunc ipsum Lucam: & Lucium dici flexione Roma- na, Lucan Græca. Ego Lucium illum cujus ibi memi- nit Paulus, puto non alium esse à Cyrenensi quem noster hic nominat, Actor. XIII. 1. Nostro autem nomen quidem Romanum fuisse arbitror, sed aliquanto longius. Nam quæ in ᾶς terminantur nomina solent partem nominis postre- mam ἀποκόπτειν. Ita Δηυᾶς est Δημήτρειος, Μνᾶς est μηνόδωρος, Ἀπελλᾶς est Ἀπελλόδωρος, Θευδᾶς est Θεόδωρος, ἐπαφρᾶς est ἐπαφρόδιτος, ἀρποκρᾶς est ἀρποκράτης, ἀλεξᾶς est ἀλέξανδρος, κλεοπᾶς est κλεόπατρος. Ex Artemidoro fit Artemas, ut apud Varronem est libro VII. de lingua La- tina. Herodes Pater in minore fortuna Antipas in majore Antipater Josepho. Sic Posides ex Posidonio, Harpocras ex Harpocrate diminuendo factus. Et ut ad Latina veniam ῥυφᾶς Rufinus. Quare & Lucas, si quid video, contractum est ex Romano nomine, quod suspicor fuisse Lucillium. Nam ea gens tum Romæ florebat, ex qua erat & ille ad quem exstant Senecæ epistolæ. Erat noster hic Syrus, ut veteres consentiunt: & medicinam fecit. Cur enim alium esse putemus de quo Paulus scribit Colossensibus, Λυκᾶς ὁ ἰατρὸς, causæ nihil video: accedit famæ vetustas. Syria au- tem multos Romanis servos exhibebat: & medicina, ut ex Plinio atque aliis discimus, munus erat servile. Manumissi autem nomen patroni induebant, ut Comœdiarum Scri- ptor, Afer cum esset, dictus est à patrono Terentio Teren- tius: Alexander Polyhistor à patrono Cornelio Lentulo Cornelius, Suida referente. Ita hic à Lucillio Lucillius, & contracte Λυκᾶς. Credibile est, cum Romæ medicinam fa- ctitasset aliquamdiu, accepta libertate rediisse in patriam. Judaicam Religionem domi an Romæ imbiberit incertum. Romæ sane multi libertinæ conditionis quotidie ad Judai- smum transibant qualis Cæcilius ille quicum Cicero de Ver- re accusando certavit. Vide Plutarchum Cicerone. Philo li- bro de legatione ad Cajum πῶς ἂν ἀπεδέχετο τὴν πέραν τᾶ Τι- βέρεως ποταμᾶ μεγάλην τῆς ῥώμης ἀποτομὴν, ἣν ἐκ ἠγνόει κατε- χομένην καὶ οἰκουμένην πρὸς Ἰεδαίων, ῥωμαῖοι δὲ ἦσαν οἱ πλείους ἀπελευθερωθέντες. Sed & Antiochiæ magna erat Judæorum universitas & ingens προσηλύτων numerus: quod & Jose- phus nos docet & leges Romanæ. Hellenistarum sermonem cum religione hausit: Græcanicam literaturam dum medi- cinæ studet. Utriusque manifesta sunt in Scriptis ejus ve- stigia. Sed & ad Syriacum ἰδίωμα sæpe inclinans ejus di- ctio patriam prodit: & Romæ versatum ex Romanis qui- busdam locutionibus agnoscas. Christianum dogma puto ab ipso susceptum Antiochiæ, postquam eo Roma rediis- set, Paulo docente, cui ab eo tempore comes hæsit, ut ex Actuum libro apparet, nisi si quando à Paulo ad Ecclesias legabatur, fovendæ sementi quam fecerat Paulus, quod sæpiuscule factum arbitror. Neque mihi displicet, quod plerique veterum sentiunt, Pauli illud 1. Corinth. IIX. 18. Τὸν ἀδελφὸν ὗ ὁ ἔπαινος ἐν τῷ ἐυαγγελίῳ διὰ πασῶν 7

## 1:1 Introduction: Annotations on the Gospel According to Luke
ANNOTATIONS ON THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO LUKE.

of the churches is to be understood of Luke, especially since Ignatius in his epistle to the Ephesians (which I do not doubt to be genuine) draws those very words to Luke: 'As,' he says, 'Luke testifies, whose praise is in the gospel through all the churches.' Nor do I think, however, that this book is indicated by the word gospel, but the office of evangelist. But I think that both this book and the one which is about the Acts of the Apostles were written not long after Paul left Rome for Spain. For the book of Acts ends at that time, which if it had been written later, would have extended the narrative into even further times. I think, however, that Luke went from Rome into Achaia, and that the books we have were written by him there, which Jerome also reported. There are those who narrate that this was done in the fifteenth year after Christ's ascension, there are those who say the twenty-second.

Neque ta- men εὐαγγελίου voce librum hunc indicari sentio, sed munus εὐαγγελιστῦ. ## 1:1 Introduction: On the Preface of Grotius
ON THE PREFACE OF GROTIUS.

Grotius gives a new name for the Evangelist, hitherto unheard of in the Church, Lucillius. Because that clan flourished at Rome at that time. And since Luke was an Antiochene, as Eusebius testifies in book III of Ecclesiastical History, chapter 4, Jerome on Ecclesiastical Writers, and Dorotheus in his Synopsis, Grotius is led by another suspicion, namely that medicine, which Luke is believed to have practiced, was a servile office. Syria, however, gave many slaves to the Romans; who, having been manumitted, took the name of their patron, whence from Lucillius he was called Lucillius, and by contraction Luke. But in this way the original name of the Evangelist will be unknown: and whence will he provide assurance, if anyone does not wish to embrace these things, that he practiced medicine at Rome, that he served under Lucillius, and that he took his name after being manumitted by him?

More certain are the things he reports about the skill of the Hellenistic and Greek language, although that conjecture is likewise uncertain, that he as a proselyte absorbed the language of the Hellenists with his religion, and Greek literature while he devoted effort to medicine. Certainly he is commended by Jerome in chapter 6 of Isaiah because he was most skilled in the Greek language, who says that the Greek speech which Luke used is more polished, into which Hebraisms are sometimes interspersed. Casaubon, however, in Exercitations II, chapter 1, says it is known to the learned that he observed pure Hellenism more diligently than the other Evangelists. Anyone will detect that by reading, says our blessed Gerhard in Exegesis on Holy Scripture, chapter 253, that Luke used an idiom not unlike that which is used in the Greek version of the Old Testament, which it is gathered from that fact that he studied diligently.

Of the profession however of Luke the physician, not only is the tradition of the ancients constant, but the Apostle also testifies in Col. IV. 14, in which place, as well as 2 Tim. ch. IV. 11 and Phil. v. 24, it seems not obscure that our Luke is being dealt with, and most interpreters agree, Theodoret, Ambrose, Oecumenius, and others. Whom the Apostle also celebrates, whose inseparable companion and fellow-worker he was, according to Irenaeus LIII. c. 14, and whose follower he was, according to Tertullian in IV. c. Marci, 2 Cor. IIX. 18: We have sent with him the brother whose praise is in the Gospel throughout all the churches. That he was not of the 70 disciples, which Origen, Epiphanius, Dorotheus, and Gregory the Great judge, but an Apostle's disciple and an Apostolic man, not only Irenaeus and Tertullian, but also Eusebius, Jerome, and Bede maintain.

From which place some gather that the Gospel of Luke was already known and approved throughout the churches at that time, when indeed the Apostle was heading from Macedonia to Jerusalem under Claudius. Baronius thinks the Gospel was written in the 26th year from the death of Christ, the third of Nero: But Cornelius à Lapide teaches that it was written earlier: nor are there wanting those who assign it to the fifteenth year after Christ's ascension, which was the fifth of Claudius, the eleventh of the Apostle's conversion. But because nothing certain is established about it, we rightly leave this in doubt.

Beza and Gomarus gather that it was not written before the Gospel of Matthew and Mark, because those who undertook to compose the evangelical history before Luke did not compose it correctly, according to Luke ch. I. 1, and because the work would not otherwise have been needed for recognizing the truth or certainty by Luke's writing, as it could have been had from Matthew and Mark.

But it is not necessary that we judge the canonical writers Matthew and Mark to be included under the name of 'many' in Luke I. 1, or that, having admitted that, we interpret the word 'undertook' as an unfortunate attempt, as Grotius himself admits: and although certainty could be had from Matthew and Mark, Luke nevertheless wished to procure it particularly for Theophilus (and no less for others), having diligently repeated everything from the beginning from above, and having recorded everything one by one in order, some of which had been omitted by Matthew and Mark, which nevertheless contributed to judging the narratives of others and knowing the truth of things. And since the ancients with great consensus report that Luke wrote after Matthew and Mark, there is no reason why we should depart from them. We have here Grotius agreeing. The words follow a little later at ch. I. 1.

Furthermore, the Gospel of Luke can be divided into

The prologue, ch. I. 1 to 4, and the History, which exhibits both the life of Christ, and his passion and death, and his resurrection, with the consequent ascension into heaven. The life of Christ before the beginning of his office: and regarding the course of his office. There is handed down his conception, and birth, and circumcision, with the manifestation by which his infantile age: then his growth, and manifestation in his youthful age made in the Jerusalem temple: then his baptism, and inauguration to his office, when he was 30 years old, with his genealogy. Concerning the conception of Jesus, there is reported first the conception of the forerunner announced by the angel, and the annunciation of the conception of Jesus made by the same angel, with the consequences, the visitation of Elizabeth, and the birth and circumcision of John in the rest of chapter I. Concerning the birth of Jesus, its description, and the consequences, the angel's annunciation, with the angelic hymn, the shepherds' investigation, and Jesus' circumcision, as well as his presentation in the temple, with those things which were done then. Then his growth in age and manifestation in his twelfth year, with further progress are commemorated. And all those things are in chapter II. Of the baptism of Christ, and his inauguration to his office, through theophany, the mission of John to baptize is commemorated by way of thanks, and his execution of it, and at the designated age of Jesus, his genealogy is woven: Which are contained in chapter III.

Regarding the course of the ministry of Jesus, first the preparation through temptations in the desert, at the beginning of chapter four: then the proclamation of Christ is described in Nazareth, and Capernaum, with the miraculous liberation of one possessed, and the healing of Peter's mother-in-law, and others c. IV. and the confirmation of Peter and his companions in their office after the miraculous catch of fish, also the restoration of a certain leper, and of a paralytic, and the calling of Levi the tax collector, and the instruction of the disciples of John concerning fasting, c. V. Which things were done before the second Passover of Christ and the second-first Sabbath.

From the second Passover of Christ to the third, these things are described by St. Luke: the defense of the disciples plucking ears of grain, the withered hand, and the healing of many sick people, the election of the Apostles, and the sermon on blessedness, and other things in chapter VI. The restoration of the centurion's servant, the raising of the widow's son in Nain, the absolution of the sinful woman in chapter VII. with the proposal of parables, the miracle of the calmed storm, the liberation of the Gadarene possessed man, the raising of Jairus's daughter, the healing of the woman with the issue of blood c. IIX. And these things before the sending out of the Apostles. There follows c. IX. the sending out of the Apostles, and the feeding of the five thousand: which were done before the third Passover of Christ.

From the third to the fourth St. Luke describes these things: Peter's confession concerning Christ, warnings about following Christ, his transfiguration, the healing of the lunatic, the sermon concerning the passion and resurrection, the contention of the disciples concerning primacy, the hospitality denied to Christ in Samaria, and concerning the three who wished to accompany Christ, in the same ninth chapter. And further c. X. the sending out of the LXX disciples and their return, the blessedness preached by Christ, and the confession of the expert in the law concerning his neighbor: and also the conversation with Martha. Then c. XI. the form of prayer, the parable concerning prayer, the casting out of a mute demon, the rebuke of the Pharisees for hypocrisy is exhibited: and c. XII. various instructions concerning the leaven of the Pharisees, and other things, concerning blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, concerning avarice, concerning the signs of storms, concerning reconciliation. And c. XIII. an exhortation to repentance from the example of the Galileans, and from the parable of the unfruitful fig tree. The history concerning the sick woman healed, and a similar one concerning the man with dropsy, and the great banquet: concerning the one about to build a tower, and such a foolish person. C. XV. concerning the lost sheep and drachma, and the prodigal son. Chapter XVI. concerning the unjust steward, and the rich glutton. Chapter XVII. concerning scandal, and fraternal forgiveness: concerning the ten lepers, the coming of the kingdom of God, and the last times. Chapter XIIX. concerning always praying, concerning the Pharisee and the Publican, concerning the little children brought to Jesus: concerning a certain rich prince, and the inheritance of the disciples who left all things.

To the fourth and crucifying Passover of Christ these things pertain antecedently according to Luke: the journey to Jerusalem, and the prediction of the passion, the healing of two blind men, the conversion of Zacchaeus, and the parable of the talents, and the entry into Jerusalem, the lamentation over Jerusalem and the reformation of the temple, Chapter XIX. concerning the question of Christ's authority, the parable of the vineyard let out: the temptation concerning the census of the Sadducees, concerning the resurrection of the experts in the law, concerning the greatest commandment, concerning Christ as the son and Lord of David, concerning the ambition of the Pharisees. chapter XX. concerning the alms of the poor widow, concerning the destruction of the temple, and the signs of the ruin of the city and the world, c. XXI.

Thence St. Luke proceeds to describe the very History of the Passion of Christ: the council concerning Christ, the pact with Judas, the Passover, the institution of the Holy Supper, the repeated prediction of the betrayal of Judas, the contention of the disciples, the passion on the Mount of Olives, the capture of Christ, and the examination in the Sanhedrin with the denial of Peter, chapter XXII exhibiting: and chapter XXIII the leading away to Pilate and Herod, the condemnation of Pilate and the crucifixion, the death and burial of Christ.

Concerning Christ alive again, the testimony of the angels to the women, the appearance made to the disciples in Emmaus and Jerusalem: the promise of the Holy Spirit and the ascension into heaven is proposed in c. XXIV. And these things are concerning the Economy of the Gospel of St. Luke.

Commentators on St. Luke, besides the general ones who wrote on Holy Scripture or the New Testament, and the special ones who expounded the Evangelical quartet, are those who are contained in the Catena edited by Balthasar Corderius, 65 Greek Fathers; likewise Ambrose, Augustine, Bonaventure, Dominicus Leonus, Hubertus Leonardus, Michael Angrianus, Barthol. Bononiensis, and Bartholomæus Pareus, most of whom published Postils on Luke. John Beverclavius wrote Commentaries (Ann. 721), Didacus Stella moral commentaries: Christianus Druthmarus, Franc. Lambertus, and B. D. Joh. Winckelmannus also wrote on Luke, as did the Jesuit Franc. Toletus.

PART I. OF THE GOSPEL OF LUKE, Concerning those things which precede the ministry of Christ.

Latin:

AD PRÆFATIONEM GROTII.

NOmen Evangelistæ novum hactenus in Ec- clesia inauditum dat Grotius Lucillii. Quod ea gens tum Romæ floruerit. Ac quum Antiochenus fuerit Lucas, teste Eusebio l. III. Hist. Eccles. cap. 4. Hieronymo de Scriptor. Ecclesiast. & Dorotheo in Synopsi, alia suspicione ducitur Grotius, quod nempe Medicina, quam fecisse creditur Lucas, munus servile fuerit. Syria autem multos Romanis servos dederit; qui manumissi nomen Patroni in- duerint, unde à Lucillio Lucillius, & contracte Λου- κᾶς dictus. Sed ita primævum Evangelistæ no- men ignorabitur: & unde illis, quod Romæ me- dicinam fecerit, quod apud Lucillium servierit, & ab eo manumissus nomen ejus induerit, fidem facturus est, si quis hæc amplecti nolit?

Certiora sunt, quæ de peritia linguæ Helleni- sicæ, & Græcanicæ tradit, licet conjectura illa incerta itidem sit, quod Hellenistarum sermonem proselytus cum religione hauserit, Græcanicam li- teraturam dum medicinæ operam dedit. Sane commendatur ab Hieronymo in cap. Es. VI. quod Græca lingua fuerit peritissimus, qui sermonem Græcum, quo usus est Lucas, dicit comtiorem esse, cui Hebraismi quandoque sint inspersi. Casau- bonus vero Exercit. II. cap. 1. purum Hellenismum eum diligentius, quam cæteros Evangelistas obser- vasse, notum esse eruditis, ait. Illud legendo qui- libet deprehendet, inquit, B. Gerhardus noster in Exeg. de Script. S. cap. 253, Lucam idiomate esse usum non absimili illi, quod in versione Græca V. T. usurpatur, quam studiose ipsum evolvisse, ex eo col- ligitur.

De Professione tamen Lucæ Medicanon solum constans est veterum traditio, sed testatur etiam Apostolus Col. IV. 14. quo loco, nec non 2. Timoth. cap. IV. 11. Phil. v. 24. de Luca nostro agi haud obscurum videtur, & consentiunt plerique Interpretes, Theodoret. Ambrof. Oecumenius, aliiq;. Quem celebrat quoque Apostolus, cujus, teste Irene LIII. c. 14. inseparabilis comes & cooperarius, ac Tertulliano in IV. c. Marci teste, sectator fuit, 2. Cor. IIX. 18. Misimus cum illo fratrem cujus laus est in Evangelio per omnes Ecclesias. Non ex LXX. discipulis, quod Origenes, Epiphanius, Dorotheus, Gregorius M. censent, sed Apostolorum discipulum & Virum Apostolicum fuisse, non Ireneus & Tertullianus tantum, sed etiam Eusebius, Hieronymus & Beda statuunt.

E quo loco colligunt nonnulli, Evangelium Luca isto tempore jam per Ecclesias notum fuisse ac probatum, cum nempe Apostolus sub Claudio ex Macedonia tenderet Hierosolymam. Baronius 26. à morte Christi anno, Neronis tertio, conscriptum Evangelium putat: Sed Cornelius à Lapide id citius esse conscriptum docet: nec desunt, qui decimo quinto post Christi ascensum anno id assignent, qui quintus Claudii fuit, undecimus conversionis Apostoli. Sed quia nihil certi de eo constat, merito in dubio hoc relinquimus.

Beza & Gomarus id ante Matthæi & Marci Evangelium conscriptum non esse inde colligunt, quod ante Lucam, qui Evangelicam historiam componere aggressi sunt, eam non recte composuere, teste Luca c. I. 1. quodq; opus alias non fuisset ad veritatem seu certitudinem agnoscendam scriptione Lucæ, utpote quæ haberi potuisset è Matthæo & Marco.

Sed non necessum est, ut τῶν πολλῶν nomine Luc. I. 1. Canonicos Scriptores Matthæum & Marcum comprehensos censeamus, aut admisso eo vocem ἐπεχείρησαν de infelici susceptione interpretemur, fatente ipsomet Grotio: & quamvis è Matthæo & Marco haberi poterat certitudo, Theophilo tamen peculiariter eam conciliare Lucas volebat, (nec minus aliis) ἄνωθεν inde à principio diligenter repetitis, & καθεξῆς sigillatim consignatis omnibus, quorum nonnulla à Matthæo & Marco prætermissa fuerant, quæ tamen ad aliorum narrationes dijudicandas, & veritatem rerum cognoscendam faciebant. Et quum magno consensu veteres Lucam scripsisse post Matthæum & Marcum perhibeant, non est, cur ab iis discedamus. Habemus hic Grotium consentientem. Verba paulo post ad cap. I. 1. sequuntur.

Cæterum dispesci potest Evangelium Lucæ in

Proæmium, c. I. 1. ad 4. & Historiam, quæ tum Christi vitam, tum passionem & mortem, tum resurrectionem exhibet, cum consequenti ascensione in cælum. Vitam Christi ante muneris auspicium: & quoad muneris cursum. Illic traditur ejusdem conceptio, & nativitas, ac circumcisio, cum manifestatione, qua infantilem ætatem: dehinc incrementum, & manifestatio juvenili ætate in templo Hierosolymitano facta: tum baptismus, & inauguratio ad officium, cum 30 annorum esset, cum genealogia ejusdem. Circa conceptionem Jesu refertur primum conceptio prodromi ab angelo annunciata, & annunciatio conceptionis Jesu per eundem angelum facta, cum consequentibus, visitatione Elisabethæ, & nativitate ac circumcisione Iohannis cap. I. reliquo. Circa nativitatem Jesu, ejusdem descriptio, & consequentia, Angeli annunciatio, cum hymno angelico, pastorum exploratio, & Jesu circumcisio, nec non in templo præsentatio, cum iis quæ tum gesta. Dehinc ætatis incrementum & manifestatio anno duodecimo, cum ulteriori profectu comme- morantur. Atque ea omnia cap. II. Baptismi Christi, & inaugurationis ad officium, per θεοφα- νείας, gratia commemoratur missio Johannis ad ba- ptizandum, ejusdemque exequutio, & designata ætate Jesu, ejus genealogia texitur: Quæ capite III. sunt contenta.

Quod ad cursum muneris Jesu, primum præpa- ratio per tentationes in deserto, initio cap. quarti: dehinc præconium Christi describitur in Naza- reth, & Capernaum, cum miraculosa obsessi libera- tione, & socrus Petri, aliorumque sanatione c. IV. ac Petri & sociorum post miraculosam piscaturam in officio confirmatione, leprosi etiam cujusdam, & pa- ralytici restitutione, & Levi publicani vocatione, ac discipulorum Johannis de jejunio informatione, c. V. Quæ ante Pascha secundum Christi & Sabba- tum δευτερόπρωτον gesta sunt.

A secundo autem Paschate Christi ad tertium hæc à S. Luca describuntur: Discipulorum spicas fricantium defensio, arida manus, & ægrotorum mul- torum sanatio, Apostolorum electio, & concio de bea- titudine, alijsque cap. VI. Servi centurionis restitu- tio, filii viduæ in Nain resuscitatio, mulieris pecca- tricis absolutio cap. VII. cum parabolarum propo- sitione, miraculo tempestatis sedatæ, obsessi Gadarens liberati, filiæ Jairi excitatæ, hæmorrhousæ sanatæ c. IIX. Atq; hæc ante Apostolorum ablegationem. Suc- cedit c. IX. Apostolorum ablegatio, & quinq; mil- lium cibatio: quæ ante Pascha tertium Christi gesta.

A tertio ad quartum S. Lucas hæc describit: con- fessionem Petrinam de Christo, monitiones de se- quela Christi, transfigurationem ejus, lunaticicura- tionem, concionem de passione & resurrectione, discipulorum de primatu contentionem, hospi- tium Christo in Samaria denegatum, & de tribus Christum comitari cupientibus, cap. eodem nono. Et porro c. X. emissionem LXX. discipulorum & re- ditum, beatitudinem à Christo prædicatam, & legis- periti de proximo confessionem: nec non collo- quium cum Martha. Tum c. XI. orationis formu- la, parabola de oratione, dæmonis muti ejectio, Pha- risæorum ob hypocrisin increpatio exhibetur: & c. XII. variæ informationes de fermento Pharisae- rum, aliisque, de blasphemia in Spiritum S. de ava- ritia, de prognosticis tempestatum, de reconcilia- tione. Et c. XIII. ab exemplo Galilæorum exhor- tatio ad pœnitentiam, & à parabola de ficu infru- gifera. Historia de muliere ægrota sanata, & similis de hydropico, & magno convivio: de turrim extru- cturo, & tale fatuo. C. XV. de ove & drachma per- ditis, & filio prodigo. Cap. XVI. de injusto œconomo, & divite Epulone. Cap. XVII. de scandalo, & condo- natione fraterna: decem leprosis, adventu regni Dei, & temporibus novissimis. Cap. XIIX. de semper orando, de Pharisæo, & Publicano, de parvulis ad Ie- sum adductis: principe quodam divite, & discipu- lorum, qui omnia reliquerunt, hæreditate.

Ad Pascha Christi quartum & σαυρώσιμον hæc antecedenter faciunt penes Lucam: profectio Hie- rosolymitana, & prædictio passionis, duorum cæco- rum sanatio, Zachæi conversio, & parabola de ta- lentis, & ingressus Hierosolymitanus, deploratio Hie- rosolymæ & reformatio templi, Cap. XIX. de po- testate Christi erotema, de vinea elocata parabola: de censu Sadducæorum tentatio, de resurrectione le- gisperitorum, de maximo præcepto, de Christo Da- vidis filio & Domino, de Pharisæorum ambitione. cap. XX. de eleemosyna viduæ pauperculæ, de templi destructione, & signis interitus urbis, & orbis, c. XXI.

Dehinc progreditur S. Lucas ad ipsum Pas- sionis Christi Historiam describendam: concilium de Christo, pactum cum Iuda, Pascha, institu- tionem S. Cænæ, iteratam proditionis Judæ præ- dictionem, contentionem discipulorum, passionem in monte oliveti, capturam Christi, & examen in Synedrio cum abnegatione Petri cap. XXII. ex- hibens: & cap. XXIII. adductionem ad Pilatum, & Herodem, condemnationem Pilati & crucifixio- nem, mortem ac sepulturam Christi.

De Christo redivivo angelorum testimonium ad mulieres, apparitio discipulis in Emaus, & Hierosolymis facta: promissio Spiritus S. & ascen- sio in cælum c. XXIV. proponitur. Atque hæc de Oeconomia Evangelii S. Lucæ.

Commentatores in S. Lucam præter generales qui in Scripturam S. vel Novum T. scripsêre, & speciales qui quadrigam Evangelicam exposuêre, sunt qui in Catenâ à Balthas. Corderio edita con- tinentur LXV. Græci Patres; Ambrosius item, Au- gustinus, Bonaventura, Dominicus Leonus, Hu- bertus Leonardus, Michael Angrianus, Barthol. Bononiensis, & Bartholomæus Pareus, qui plerique Postillas in Lucam edidêre. Joh. Beverclavius Commentationes scripsit (Ann. 721.) Didacus Stella commentaria moralia: Scripsere etiam in Lucam Christianus Druthmarus, Franc. Lamber- tus & B. D. Joh. Winckelmannus, ut & Franc. To- letus Jesuita.

PARS I. EVANGELII LUCAE, De iis quæ ministerium Christi antecedunt.

## 1:1 Argument
CHAPTER I.

ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

After the preface, the parents of John are recounted, the prediction of his birth, as also that of Christ, the visitation of Mary with her hymn, and the birth and circumcision of John, with the hymn of Zechariah, and a summary of the life of John up to his public ministry. There are five parts: I. The preface of Luke, to v. 5. II. The prediction of the birth of John, and his conception, to v. 25. III. The prediction of the birth of Jesus, to v. 38. IV. The visitation of Mary, with her canticle, to v. 56. V. The birth and circumcision of John, with the canticle and prophecy of Zechariah, to v. 80, with a short narrative added of the growth of John.

PART I. The preface of St. Luke.

' Verse 1. Πολλoὶ.] It appears that when Luke was writing, many books had existed concerning the things of Christ: naturally, the very magnitude of the events had drawn many into that concern. But while others collected rumors, it is no wonder if they mixed true things with false: among whom I count the most ancient writer of the Egyptian Gospel. For the other Gospels that are circulated are most putrid figments of a much later age. But others, namely Matthew and Mark, who had written down what they had either seen or heard from certain authors, just as they were beyond all blame of negligence, so they had not closed the way to one desiring to add something to their labor in such a rich subject. Add that it is credible that at that time the book of Matthew had existed only in the Hebrew language: but Mark had written in Greek more a summary of history than a history. But as for what some think, that Luke was prior to Matthew and Mark in writing, I simply cannot be induced to believe that. The most ancient order of books among all nations contradicts it: ancient tradition, supported by the witnesses Irenæus and Tertullian, contradicts it: Luke himself contradicts it, who so augmented the history of Matthew and Mark with added narratives that he narrates the same things there and not rarely uses the same words.

ἐπεχείρησαν] A most learned man has well noted that the word is middle: and that it cannot be gathered from it that what those writers had undertaken was not accomplished. For Plato, Isocrates, and others also often use ἐπεχείρησαν even regarding successful study.

Regarding what must be observed against Gomarus, that a vain attempt is designated, which he tries to prove from the usage of the word in Acts 9:29 and 19:13: the most learned Casaubon explains τὸ ἐπιχειρεῖν not as 'to undertake' but as 'to do': that Luke says he was impelled by the example of others, not because he held their faith in suspicion, but so that he might trace the whole matter a little further back, and at the same time ensure that the credibility of this most holy history might be supported by more witnesses. If Luke had spoken of Pseudo-Apostles, says Casaubon, I do not know if he would have touched upon them so lightly. B. Chemnitius also observes the emphasis of the verb ἀναγράψασθαι and the copulative particle: These words, he says, can indeed also be understood of the Evangelical books of Matthew and Mark, published before Luke's writing. For Ἐπιχειρεῖν does not signify a vain attempt: but literally it signifies: to set one's hand to a work or to undertake something. And just as ἀναγράφεσθαι is used regarding public and authentic writing: as when laws are described on tablets, or when something is referred to public records. So Luke, by the verb ἀνατάξασθαι, seems to approve the Evangelical narrative composed by his predecessors. The conjunction (AND) also seems to insinuate the same thing, (it seemed good to me also, κἀμοὶ). For if he understood the Pseudo-Evangelists, he would simply say: Since many have written unfaithfully, it seemed good to me. But now he says, (it seemed good to me also:) numbering himself among those who previously treated this subject: And if the words are accepted in this sense, then in this preface of Luke the writings of the former Evangelists are approved, and as we commonly say, canonized, and indeed by a very illustrious testimony: namely, that they wrote those things which in the first Apostolic Church were of most certain faith: and that they wrote them just as the remaining Apostles were then handing them down by living voice in the Church. Ambrose, however, weighs those words, 'since many have undertaken,' in this way: they have undertaken, who could not fulfill; he who has undertaken, has undertaken to order by his own labor, and has not fulfilled. For gifts and the grace of God are without undertaking, which, where it has infused itself, is accustomed to irrigate, so that the writer's talent does not lack, but overflows. Matthew did not undertake, Mark did not undertake, John did not undertake, Luke did not undertake, but with the divine spirit providing the abundance of all things said, they completed what was begun without any effort. Titus of Bostra has similar things: Matthew attempted, οὐκ ἐπεχείρησεν, but wrote being affected by the heavenly spirit. You may conclude the same about Mark and John; similarly also about Luke. Nor does Theophylact think otherwise, who observes of all the Evangelists that they did not merely attempt, but accomplished: τὸ γὰρ τελέσποιον πνεῦμα εἶχον, because they had the spirit that works perfectly. To which we subscribe without hesitation: because this preface is general from the intention of the Spirit of the author of all the Evangelists, even though he willed the same to be prefixed specifically to the Gospel of St. Luke.

πεπληροφορημένων ἐν ἡμῖν πραγμάτων] Concerning things which are sufficiently and abundantly proven to us. The proof of facts consists mostly in witnesses, in whom it is observed whether they wish to tell the truth, and whether they know the truth. Those are to be judged as wishing to tell the truth who are of integrity of life, and have no advantage to hope for from their testimony. Such, however, were the witnesses chosen beforehand (οἱ προκεχειροτονημένοι μάρτυρες) of the things done by Christ: men of most holy life, and who were so far from hoping for advantages that, on the contrary, for the sake of that testimony they endured every kind of disadvantage.

Latin:

CAPUT I.

ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Post præloquium referuntur parentes Johan- nis, prædictio nativitatis ejusdem, ut & Christi, visitatio Mariæ, cum hymno ejus- dem, & nativitas, ac circumcisio Jo- hannis, cum hymno Zachariæ, & com- pendio vitæ Iohannis usque ad publicum ministerium. Partes sunt quinque I. Præfatio Lucæ, ad v. 5. II. Prædictio nativitatis Johannis, ejusdemque conceptio, ad v. 25. III. Prædictio nativitatis Jesu, ad v. 38. IV. Visitatio Mariæ, cum ejusdem can- tico, ad v. 56. V. Nativitas, & circumcisio Johan- nis, cum cantico, & vaticinio Zachariæ, ad v. 80. addita narratiuncula incrementi Johannis.

PARS I. Præfatio S. Lucæ.

' Vers. 1. Πολλoὶ.] Apparet cum Lucas scribere aliquam multos extitisse libros de rebus Christi: nimirum ipsa rerum magnitudo multos in eam curam pertraxerat. Sed alii dum rumores colligunt non mirum est si vera falsis mi- scuerint: quos inter numero Evangelii Ægyptiaci vetustis- simum scriptorem. Nam quæ alia circumferuntur Evan- gelia putidissima sunt figmenta ævi multo posterioris. Alii vero, Matthæus & Marcus scilicet, qui aut visa aut ex certis autoribus audita perscripserant, sicut extra omnem erant negligentiæ culpam, ita addere aliquid ad ipsorum laborem cupienti in materia tam ubere viam non præcluserant. Ad- de quod credibile est ad id tempus Matthæi librum non nisi Hebræo sermone exstitisse: Marcus autem Græce com- pendium magis historiæ quam historiam scripserat. Quod vero quidam existimant Matthæo & Marco priorem in scribendo Lucam fuisse, plane ut credam induci non possum. Refragatur vetustissimus librorum ordo apud omnes nationes: refragatur traditio vetus, Irenæo & Tertulliano testibus suffulta: refragatur ipse Lucas qui ita Matthæi & Marci historiam auxit additis narrationibus, ut ibi res easdem narrat eadem quoque verba non raro usurpet.

ἐπεχείρησαν] Bene notavit vir eruditissimus vocem esse mediam: neque ex ea colligi posse non præstitum ab il- lis scriptoribus, quod aggressi erant. Nam & Plato, Iso- crates, aliique ἐπεχείρησαν sæpe de studio etiam felice usur- pant.

Quod contra Gomarum observandum, irri- tum conatum designari, ex usu vocis Actor. IX. 29. & XIX. 13. probare conantis: eruditissimus Ca- saubonus explicat τὸ ἐπιχειρεῖν non per aggredi, sed per facere: quod exemplo aliorum se impul- sum dicat Lucas, non quod eorum fidem suspi- ctam haberet, sed ut rem totam paulo altius re- peteret, & simul efficeret, ut pluribus testibus hu- jus sanctissimæ historiæ fides fulciretur. Sunt, inquit Casaubonus, de Pseudo-Apostolis si locutus fuisset Lucas, nescio, an tam leviter eos perstrin- xisset. B. Chemnitius observat etiam ἔμφασιν verbi ἀναγράψασθαι & particulæ copulativæ: Possunt vero, inquit, etiam hæc verba intelligi de Matthei & Marci libris Evangelicis, ante Lucæ scriptionem edi- tis. Ἐπιχειρεῖν enim non significat vanum cona- tum: Sed ad verbum significat: manum operi ad- movere vel aliquid aggredi. Et sicut ἀναγράφεσθαι de publica & authentica scriptum usurpatur: ut cum leges in tabulis describuntur, vel cum aliquid in acta publica refertur. Ita Lucas verbo ἀνατάξασθαι, contextam à prioribus Evangelicam narrationem videtur approbare. Idem etiam conjunctio (ET) videtur insinuare, (visum est κἀμοὶ & mihi.) Si enim Pseudo- Evangelistas intelligeret, simpliciter diceret: Quoniam multi infideliter scripserunt, vi- sum est mihi. Jam vero dicit, (visum est & mihi :) annumerans se illis, qui prius hoc argumentum tra- ctarunt: Atque si hoc sensu verba accipiantur, tunc in hoc proæmio Lucæ approbantur, & ut vulgo lo- quimur, canonisantur priorum Evangelistarum scripta, & quidem testimonio valde illustri: quod scilicet scripserint ea, quæ in prima Apostolica Eccle- sia certissimæ fidei fuerint: quodq; ea ita scripserint, sicut reliqui Apostoli viva tunc voce in Ecclesia tra- debant. Ambrosius tamen illa verba, quoniam multi conati sunt, ita ponderat, conati sunt, qui im- plere nequiverunt qui conatus est, ordinare suo la- bore conatus est, nec implevit. Sine conatu sunt enim donationes & gratia Dei, quæ ubi se infuderit rigare consuevit, ut non egeat, sed redundet scriptoris inge- nium. Non conatus est Mattheus, non conatus est Marcus, non conatus est Johannes, non conatus est Lucas, sed divino spiritu ubertates dictorum rerum omnium ministrante, sine ullo molimine cœpta com- pleverunt. Similia habet Titus Bostrensis Mattheus intentavit οὐκ ἐπεχείρησεν, sed spiritu affectus cœlesti conscripsit. Idem statuas de Marco & Johanne; similiter & de Luca. Nec aliter Theophylact. qui de omnibus Evangelistis observat, quod non atten- tarint duntaxat, sed perfecerint: τὸ γὰρ τελέσποιον πνεῦμα εἶχον, quia spiritum habuerunt qui perfecte operatur. Quibus non cunctanter subscribimus: quia præfatio hæc ex intentione Spiritus autoris omnium Evangelistarum generalis est, etsi ean- dem in specie Evangelio S. Lucæ præmissam vo- luerit.

πεπληροφορημένων ἐν ἡμῖν πραγμάτων] De rebus quæ sa- tis atque abunde nobis probatæ sunt. Probatio factorum in testibus maxime consistit, in quibus spectatur an verum di- cere velint, & an verum norint. Velle censendi sunt qui sunt vitæ integræ, & ex testimonio nihil sperandi habent com- modi. Tales autem erant οἱ προκεχειροτονημένοι μάρτυρες re- rum à Christo gestarum: vitæ sanctissimæ homines & quid spe commodorum tam longe aberant, ut contra ejus testi- monii causa omne incommodorum genus tolerarent.

## 1:2
Verf. 2. καθὼς παρέδοσαν ἡμῖν] either by voice like the others, or also by writing, like Matthew. For the word 'tradition' (παραδόσεως) pertains to both.

Therefore these things cannot be snatched away with the Papists to prove unwritten traditions.

follows, because he mentions witnesses, whose credibility he has followed. For unless the Spirit had breathed upon him, he could have erred in the selection of witnesses and in the reporting of their testimonies. But that he wrote everything truly and conveniently is owed to divine inspiration; nor will Grotius find any ecclesiastical author who thought otherwise, as Rivetus has it in his Apologeticus p. 224. Epiphanius certainly, Haer. LI, Alogor., says that the Holy Spirit stirred up St. Luke with certain hidden impulses and compelled him to write: Ambrose compares him to the Prophets who prophesied infused with the divine Spirit. The same is the opinion of Titus, Bishop of Bostra, as well as of Theophylact. The Jesuit Toletus himself, on the words, it seemed good, says that the Holy Spirit induced Luke to write by His own instinct: And a little later: because indeed the Holy Spirit, while inspiring, requires the counsel of man, it is said in Acts XV, it seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us. Therefore, even in writing those things which Luke saw Paul doing, there was need for the breath of the Holy Spirit dictating.

Latin:

Verf. 2. καθὼς παρέδοσαν ἡμῖν] aut voce ut cæteri, aut etiam scripto, ut Matthæus. Nam vox παραδόσεως ad u- trumque pertinet.

Non ergo hæc abripi possunt cum Pontificiis ad probandas traditiones non-scriptas.

quitur, quod testium meminit, quorum fidem est se- quutus. Nisi enim afflavisset eum spiritus, potuisset in testium delectu, & in eorum testimoniis refe- rendis errare. Quod autem omnia vere & conve- nienter scripserit, id debetur inspirationi divinæ; nec ullum autorem Ecclesiasticum reperiet Gro- tius, qui aliter senserit, ut habet in Apologetico Ri- vetus p. 224. Epiphanius certe hær. LI. Alogor. ait S. Lucam occultis quibusdam stimulis excitasse, & coegis- se adscribendum: Ambrosius comparat eum Pro- phetis qui divino infusi spiritu prophetaverunt. Ea- dem Titi Bostrorum Episcopi, ut & Theophylacti est sententia. Jesuita ipse Toletus ad verba, visum est, Sp. S. ad scribendum suo instinctu Lucam induxis- se ait: Et paulo post: quia vero Sp. S. inspirans consilium hominis requirit, dicitur Act. XV. visum est Spiritui S. & nobis. Ergo etiam in iis, quæ Lu- cas Paulum agentem vidit, scribendis, afflatu S. S. dictante opus fuit.

## 1:3
παρηκολουθηκότι ἄνωθεν πᾶσιν ἀκριβῶς] παρακολουθεῖν means to attain knowledge. Galen said παρακολουθεῖν βιβλίοις παλαιοῖσιν; Josephus, μετὰ πάσης ἀκριβείας παρακολουθεῖν τοῖς ἡμετέροις γράμμασι. Paul, 1 Tim. IV. 6, τῆς καλῆς διδασκαλίας ἧ͂ παρηκολούθηκας, and 2 Tim. III. 10, σὺ δὲ παρηκολούθηκάς με τῇ διδασκαλίᾳ. But what Luke says here, ἄνωθεν πᾶσιν ἀκριβῶς παρακολουθεῖν, is worth as much as that which is in Plautus in the Trinummus,

If one should inquire even from the root, the authority. Thus Thucydides wrote history, as he himself professes, παρὰ τῶν ἄλλων ὅσον δυνατὸν ἀκριβείᾳ περὶ ἑκάστου ἐπεξελθών. Luke signifies that he did not write before he had inquired from the root into the testimonies of the things which various writers had produced, so that by distinguishing the explored from the uncertain, he might not consign to writing anything that he had not well ascertained, for which thing Paul's journeys into Judea offered him a fine opportunity. But I also believe that Luke was sent into Judea several times with the money of the churches by Paul. Being there, therefore, he could learn everything from the primary authors. This, however, undoubtedly pertains to those things which were written not by Matthew nor by any other, but by others.

Grotius wishes to indicate by this word that Luke inquired into testimonies from the very root, so that by distinguishing the explored from the uncertain, he might not consign to writing anything that he had not well ascertained, for which thing he thinks Paul's journeys into Judea offered a fine opportunity, and when he was sent into Judea by Paul with the money of the churches. But he had no need of that exploration in Judea, who received from the Holy Spirit what he should write and consign. He says indeed that he attained everything thoroughly, and that through the tradition of those who were eyewitnesses and ministers of the Word, so that from that he might also gain some credibility for himself, but when he wrote those things which he had attained, he did not draw them from the reasoning or memory of others, but from the divine inspiration of the Holy Spirit, who directed his mind and pen, and suggested to him both the things to be written and the words in which they were to be written. In this way also Franciscus Gomarus explains that ἄνωθεν, from above, that is, from heaven and divinely, with the grace of God inspiring and directing: from a comparison of John III. 31, ch.
