XIX. 11, James III. 15. But the word it seemed good to me, which is placed before, and the things which follow, παρηκολουθηκότι ἄνωθεν πᾶσιν ἀκριβῶς, indicate that it is more correctly rendered ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς, from the beginning or from an earlier time, as it is used in Acts XXVI. 5, so that it may be referred to knowledge in this way: after I had thoroughly attained all things from the beginning. The Syrian and the Arab omit that word: and the former refers τὸ πᾶσιν to persons, in this way: since I have carefully devoted effort to be present with all those who were eyewitnesses of our Lord, and have followed them as an inseparable companion, and was always near to them, it seemed good to me to write everything down in order. Here, however, the Arab referred τὸ πᾶσιν to the matter, translating it thus: it seemed good to me also, since I had attained every matter in certainty. For Luke undertook to begin everything from higher up, namely from the conception, birth, circumcision, and upbringing, both of the Baptist and of Christ, which had been omitted by others.

καθεξῆς] Those are mistaken who infer from this that Luke’s purpose is to follow the order of times more strictly than others had done before him. For on the contrary, it appears that he has more than once connected things because of their coherence, which were separated in time, a fact that will be made clear in its proper place. But Luke’s καθεξῆς is nothing other than 'in detail,' as can be seen in Acts 11:4 and 18:23. Such a narrative is opposed to the universal, which generally and in a summary fashion, and as the philosophers say, 'in outline,' reported that Jesus had come, had performed many miracles, was condemned by Pontius Pilate, died, and was resurrected, as is apparent from those things which we said regarding baptism in Matthew.

B. Chemnitius also notes that neither is the order precisely regarded, nor is the narration done in detail, but rather the coherence of things: καθεξῆς, that is, in a certain order and context of consequence or coherence. For although St. Luke does not everywhere strictly preserve the order of events, he nevertheless has his own certain method of weaving histories, which the Syrian also indicates here. And not only that; but the Evangelical Harmony teaches that, compared to the other Evangelists, the order of events is observed accurately by St. Luke: whence it is clear that not those who infer from this word that such was Luke’s purpose are mistaken, but Grotius, who thinks that they are mistaken for that reason. Let those things which were said about it in his preface be compared.

Κράτιστε θεόφιλε] Learned men do not wrongly infer from this form of address that this Theophilus was of some rank. I believe he held some magistracy in the cities of Achaia and was baptized by Luke. Thus Festus, thus Felix are addressed by this term in the Acts. Plutarch calls Fundanius 'most excellent' (κράτιστον). Josephus similarly, dedicating his book on his own life to Epaphroditus, a freedman and procurator of Trajan if I am not mistaken, says: 'most excellent of men, Epaphroditus.' And Justin, writing out a brief instruction of Christianity to Diognetus, prefaces it thus: 'Since I see, most excellent Diognetus, that you have been exceedingly eager to learn the piety of the Christians.' The Latin translator does not translate badly here as 'most excellent.' Thus Octavius is 'most excellent' to Horace.

Latin:

παρηκολουθηκότι ἄνωθεν πᾶσιν ἀκριβῶς] παρακολουθεῖν est notitiam consequi. Galenus παρακολουθεῖν βιβλίοις παλαιοῖσιν Josephus, μετὰ πάσης ἀκριβείας παρακολουθεῖν τοῖς ἡμετέροις γράμμασι dixit. Paulus 1. ad Tim. IV 6. τῆς καλῆς διδασκα- λίας ἧ͂ παρηκολούθηκας, & 2. Tim. III. 10. σὺ δὲ παρηκολούθηκάς με τῇ διδασκαλίᾳ. Quod autem hic dicit Lucas ἄνωθεν πᾶσιν ἀκριβῶς παρακολουθεῖν, tantundem valet quantum id quod apud Plautum est Trinummo,

Quod si exquiratur usq; ab stirpe auctoritas. Sic Thucydides historiam scripsit, ut ipse profitetur, παρὰ τῶν ἄλλων ὅσον δυνατὸν ἀκριβείᾳ περὶ ἑκάστου ἐπεξελθών. Significat Lucas se non ante qui esse quam rerum quas diversi Scripto- res prodiderant testimonia radicitus inquisivisset, ut ita ex- plorata ab incertis discernens nihil ipse non bene comper- tum literis consignaret, cui rei bellam occasionem ei præ- buerunt Pauli itinera in Judæam. Sed & cum Ecclesiarum pecuniis a Paulo in Iudæam missum Lucam aliquoties cre- do. Ibi ergo cum esset, potuit omnia ex primis auctoribus discere., Hoc autem non dubie ad ea pertinet quæ scripta erant non à Matthæo neq; ab astosia aliquo, sed ab aliis.

Radicitus sese & ab ipsa stirpe inquisivisse testimo- nia Lucam hac voce indicare vult Grotius, ut ita ex- plorata ab incertis discernens nihil ipse non bene com- pertum literis consignaret, cui rei bellam occasionem præbuisse Pauli itinera in Judæam putat, & quando cum Ecclesiarum pecuniis à Paulo in Judæam missus est. Sed ea exploratione in Judæa opus non habuit, qui à Spiritu S. quæ scribere & consignaret, acce- pit. Omnia sane se penitus assequutum ait, idque per traditionem eorum, qui spectatores & Ministri Verbi fuerunt, ut inde etiam aliquam sibi fidem concilia- ret, sed cum illa scriberet, quæ assequutus erat, non ex aliorum ratione aut memoria sua ea depromsit, sed è divina Spiritus S. inspiratione, qui mentem & calamum direxit, ipsiq; & res scribendas, & verba, quibus eædem scriberentur, suggessit. Quo pacto etiam Franciscus Gomarus illud ἄνωθεν explicat, su- perne, id est, cælitus ac divinitus Dei gratia inspiran- te ac dirigente: è collatione Iob. III. 31. c. XIX. 11. Iac. III. 15. Sed verbum visum est & mihi, quod præ- mittitur, ac quæ sequuntur παρηκολουθηκότι ἄνω- θεν πᾶσιν ἀκριβῶς indicant, rectius id reddi ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς, a principio vel superiori tempore, ut Act. XXVI. 5. adhibetur, ut ad cognitionem referatur hoc modo; post quam omnia inde ab initio gesta peni- tus assequutus sum. Syrus & Arabs omittunt eam vocem: & ille τὸ πᾶσιν ad personas refert h. m. quandoquidem curiose operam dedi, ut omnibq illis, qui spectatores Domini nostri fuerunt, adessem, eosq; asse- ctatus sum individuus comes, & illis semper propin- quus, visum mihi fuit, ordine omnia perscribere. Hic vero, Arabs, τὸ πᾶσιν ad rem retulit ita vertens: visum fuit mihi etiam quam fuerim assequutq omnem rem in certitudine. Aggressus enim Lucas altius est omnia exordiri à conceptione scil. nativitate, cir- cumcisione, & educatione, tum Baptistæ, tum Christi, quæ ab aliis prætermilsa erant.

καθεξῆς] Falluntur qui hinc colligunt propositum Lucæ temporum ordinem pressius sequi, quam alii ante ipsum fecissent, Nam contra apparet istum non semel ob rerum cohærentiam connexuisse, quæ temporibus erant discre- ta, quod suis locis patefiet. Sed καθεξῆς Lucæ nihil aliud est quam sigillatim, ut videre est Actor. 11, 4. c. 18, 23. Ta- lis narratio opponitur τῇ καθολικῇ, quæ generaliter κ' πα- χυμερῶς, & ut philosophi loquuntur ὡς ἐν τύπῳ tradebat Iesum venisse, fecisse miracula multa, damnatum à Pon- tio Pilato, mortuum, resuscitatum, ut ex iis apparet, quæ de baptismo ad Matthæum diximus.

Notat & B. Chemnitius, nec ordinem præcise respici neque enarrationem sigillatim factam, sed rerum cohærentiam : καθεξῆς h. e. certo quodam consequentiæ vel cohærentiæ ordine & contextu. Licet enim ordinem præcise rerum gestarum S. Lucas ubique non servet, habet tamen suam quandam rationem contexendi historias, quam etiam Syrus hic indicat. Nec id tantum; sed præ reliquis Evangelistis ἀκριβῶς ordinem re- rum gestarum observari à S. Luca, Harmonia Evangelica docet : unde non illos, qui ex hac voce colligunt id Lucæ propositum fuisse, sed Grotium, qui eos ideo falli putat, falli luculen- tum est. Conferantur quæ in procœmio ejusdem de eo dicta.

Κράτιστε θεόφιλε] Theophylum hunc alicujus fuisse di- gnitatis non male viri docti ex hac compellatione colligūt. Ego in aliqua Achajæ urbium magistratu functum arbitror, & à Luca baptizatum. Ita Festus, ita Felix in Actibus hoc vocabulo appellantur. Plutarchus Fundanium vocat κρά- τιστον. Iosephus similiter librum de vita sua Epaphrodito, Trajani ni fallor liberto ac procuratori, dedicans, κράτιστε ἀνδρῶν Ἐπαφρόδιτε, inquit: & Iustinus brevem Christianismi institutionem perscribens ad Diognetum ita præfatur: ἐπειδὴ ὁρῶ κράτιστε Διόγνητε ὑπερεσπουδακότα σε τὴν θεοσεβείαν τῶν χριστιανῶν μαθεῖν. Latinus interpres non male hic ver- tit, optime. Ita Octavius optimus Horatio.

## 1:4
Verse 4. ἵνα ἐπιγνῶς περὶ ὧν κατηχήθης λόγων τὴν ἀσφά- λειαν.] So that those things which you had received before baptism by a certain general instruction, you may now know in detail and consequently more certainly. For as the Philosopher rightly says, 'It is a good thing that what I learn, I should know in one way, and in another way be ignorant of it; for it is not strange if he knows how he learns, but if he knows in order that he may learn and how.'

PART II.

The prediction of the birth of John.

Latin:

Vers. 4. ἵνα ἐπιγνῶς περὶ ὧν κατηχήθης λόγων τὴν ἀσφά- λειαν.] Ut quæ ante baptismum generali quadam institu- tione acceperas, nunc sigillatim ac proinde certius cogno- scas. Nam ut recte Philosophus, ὠδὶν καλὸν ὁ μανθάνω ἵνε ἔστιν ὡς ἐπίστασθαι, εσι δ' ὡς ἀγνοεῖν· ὠκ ἄτοπον γὰρ, εἰ οἶδε πως ὁ μανθάνη, ἀλλ' εἰ ὠδὶ, ἵνα ἦ μανθάνη κὶ ὡς. Vide quæ ad Mat- thæum capite ultimo.

PARS II.

Prædictio nativitatis Iohannis.

## 1:5
Verse 5. ἐγένετο ἐν ταῖς ἡμέραις Ἡρώδε τῦ βασιλέως] A Hebrew custom of beginning, as in the book of Ruth: 'And it came to pass in the days when the judges judged.' I cannot approve of what some think was looked to here by Luke, namely the prophecy of Jacob. For, to pass over what has been accurately argued by very learned men on this matter, the simplest sense of that oracle is that the Messiah would be before the desolation of the Jewish polity: which concerns Herod. Furthermore, those who had fashioned him as the restorer of the Prophets had arisen from the time of their manifestation, as we see done regarding Elijah, Elisha, and others. Thus also Mark had made the beginning of the history of Christ his own and his precursor’s manifestation. But Luke, since he saw that a curious reader would desire to know what the births of both this one and that one had been, and at the same time foresaw that in the progress of time many fabulous things could be handed down, thought that he should begin from there.

Grotius speaks not as of one divinely inspired, but as of a common writer. But it should have been considered that these things were written by the inspiration of the divine Spirit, not by human choice.

ἱερεύς τις] Luke took sufficient care by adding 'a certain' (τις), so that it would not be understood that Zacharias was the high priest, which many of the ancients falsely believed, or which the 'course' (ἐφημερία) sufficiently refutes. But it is not credible that he was the head of a family either: regarding which matter we spoke at Matthew 14:2. This narrative, however, pertains to indicating the nobility of John. Josephus: 'Just as among each people there is some other basis for nobility, so among us the participation in the priesthood is a proof of the brilliance of one’s lineage.' Indeed, Philo dared to say: 'By as much as God differs from men in excellence, by so much does the high priesthood differ from kingship. For the one is the service of God, the other the care of men.' Which, as it was said rather boldly, must be mitigated by a kind interpretation. We know otherwise that kings were greeted as lords even by the high priests, and that it pleased God that the forerunner of the Messiah should be born from

a priestly [lineage], but the Messiah himself should be born from a royal lineage.

ἐξ ἐφημερίας Ἀβία] There is a metonymy here also. For by 'course' (ἐφημερία) is understood the 'family' (πατριὰ), which fulfilled its ministry (λειτουργίαν) in a certain space of days (namely weekly, as Theophylact, a diligent investigator of Jewish matters, rightly notes) according to the institution of David and the ancient Prophets, after the race of the Aaronids had grown to such a number that it could not be occupied with the business of the Temple at the same time. Properly, however, the Hellenistic word 'courses' (ἐφημερίαις), or, as Josephus speaks, 'courses' (ἐφημερίσι), corresponds to the Hebrew word 'watches' (משמרות). The interpreters of Nehemiah (whom I suspect on many grounds to be later than the Seventy), Nehemiah 13:30, 'I appointed courses': where in the Hebrew it is 'and I appointed watches,' and 2 Chronicles 31:16 (of which books the interpreter seems to be Theodotion) 'for the ministry of the course of their arrangement,' and in the following verse again 'for their ministry in their courses.' The LXX interpreters, however, are accustomed to translate the word 'watch' (משמרת), which signifies 'ministry' (λειτουργίαν), but not yet distributed into cycles of time, as 'guard' (φυλακὴν), as can be seen in Numbers 3:7, 25, 28, 31, and elsewhere. 'Division' (מחלקת) is the arrangement or distribution itself: although sometimes because of the affinity of meaning it is translated as 'course' (ἐφημερία). 'Visitation' (פקדה), however, is the oversight or inspection, that is, the care of those who were in charge of the others, as we are clearly taught in 1 Chronicles 23:24. The Hebrews seem to have been led by this example to attribute the families of the other tribes to the priestly families, to which those who belonged were free, not indeed from the ministry of the temple, but from prayers and fasting at the time appointed for them. The memory of that matter exists here and there in the book of Musar and others. But that I may believe it to be an ancient institution, the notable passage 2 Chronicles 23:6 makes me do so: 'Let all the people keep the watches of the Lord.' After this was accepted, they called that common λειτουργία of all the tribes משמרת, a guard, but that one proper to the Priests, for the sake of distinction, a station מעמד. That some think this succession of perpetual ministry was disturbed, and how much they are mistaken in that, since it has been demonstrated heretofore by Joseph Scaliger, a man of admirable both learning and diligence, to wish to show the same further would be to do what is already done. A few names, forsooth, of the times of Zerubbabel which have a fortuitous συνέμπτωσιν with the Davidic ones, while so many more differ, have brought forth this hallucination. But Joseph, both a priest and a most diligent investigator of his country's history, could certainly not be mistaken in these matters, who, narrating the history of David, says expressly, διέμεινεν ἕως ὀ μερισμὸς ἄχρι τῆς σήμερον ἡμέρας. There had indeed intervened the times of the impious kings, then of the Babylonian exile, and finally the three years of Antiochus. But even in those times the pious priests performed what they could not do in the temple, where they could, and as they could, not indeed by the slaughter of cattle, which was forbidden outside the temple, but by the solemn recitation of those prayers which were accustomed to accompany the sacrifices. Of which both Philo and Josephus make mention in several places. To nothing else pertains what God praises in Ezekiel regarding the priests οἵτινες ἐφυλάξαντο τὰς φυλακὰς τῶν ἁγίων: as far as they could, of course: which itself sufficed for retaining the memory of the τῶν ἐφημεριῶν which Hezekiah, Josiah, and finally Judas Maccabaeus brought back into the temple as if continued from the first institution.

Concerning the ancient institution of the Ephemeriae, one may read 2 Chron. XXIII. 6. But that the succession of the perpetual ministry was never disturbed, not even in the times of the Babylonian exile and the persecution of Antiochus, and that Grotius thinks it was so demonstrated by Scaliger that to wish to show the same further would be to do what is already done, in this how much he himself is mistaken, Dionysius Petavius, to whom Grotius attributes much, and Fried. Spanheim have endeavored to show. To whom, although Robert Baillie attempts to respond in lib. II. of his Historical and Chronological works, p. 45, he nevertheless confesses that the subtle demonstration of Scaliger rests upon so many hypotheses, that if one should slip, the whole edifice would collapse, so that to him indeed it seems sufficiently doubtful. Nor do the most excellent Chronologists concede what Scaliger wishes to construct from the Ephemeriae of the Priests, that John was conceived at the end of July or the beginning of August, and Christ indeed six months later, at the beginning of January, and thus that Christ was born at the beginning of October: Wilhelm Lang certainly, in lib. II. de annis Christi, page 359, thinks that he has removed the foundation of Scaliger, namely that the Ephemeria of Joiarib served at the Dedication of Maccabaeus, and other beginnings

It is believed to be certain and demonstrated by the calculation of the calendars that the true birthday of Christ falls on December 25th. On which matter, more elsewhere.

And his wife was of the daughters of Aaron] The law exists in Lev. 21.14, where the high priest is commanded to take a wife from his people, מעמיו, from his people, as the LXX translate it; others, from his kin, which gave occasion for a double interpretation. Philo thinks marriages outside the Aaronic kin were forbidden to the high priest. I shall append his words from the work On the Laws in the Special Categories. 'In addition to this, he also strictly regulated the lineage of those who were to be married, commanding the high priest not only to take a virgin wife, but also a priestess from priests, so that the bridegroom and bride might be from one house and in a certain way of the same blood, showing forth a most stable harmony of character throughout their whole life; but it was permitted to the others not to marry a priestess daughter, partly because their purifications are small, and partly because the nation did not wish to be deprived of the Israelite lineage in its entirety or to be severed from its instruction.' for which reason he did not forbid the other priests from making marriages with those from the nation. He clearly feels that this law pertains so peculiarly to the high priest that it does not include the other priests. But Josephus, being much more experienced in Jewish customs, interprets עמ not as tribe, but, which is a more frequent meaning, as nation, and with other Hebrews connects those things which are said in Levit. 21.13 and following, with the beginning of the same chapter, which had been said about the high priest in verses 10 and 11, enclosing them as if in a parenthesis: from which it followed that it was not permitted for any priest to marry anyone except one born of Hebrew parents, while men of the common people were not forbidden to marry a foreign woman who was Judaizing, with the exception of certain nations with whom there was no right of intermarriage. Josephus brings forward the cause of the law as the concern for unmixed blood in the priests. The passage is remarkable, Against Apion I: 'For they not only from the beginning appointed the best men and those attending to the worship of God for these offices, but they also took care that the lineage of the priests should remain unmixed and pure. For it is necessary that he who partakes of the priesthood should beget children from a woman of the same nation, and not look toward money or other honors, but examine the lineage, taking the succession from the ancients, and providing many witnesses; and we do these things not only in Judea itself, but wherever there is a system of our race, even there the accuracy is preserved for the priests regarding marriages.' I mean those in Egypt and in Babylon and wherever else in the inhabited world there are some of the race of the priests scattered; for they send to Jerusalem, having written down the name of the parents and of the ancestors above, and who the witnesses are; but if war should break out, as has already happened many times, with Antiochus the Illustrious invading the country, and Pompey the Great, and Quintilius Varus, and especially in your own times, those of the priests who remain again establish and test the remaining wives from the ancient records; for they no longer accept those who have been taken captive, suspecting that a communion with a foreigner has occurred; and the greatest proof of this accuracy is this: for the high priests among us have been named in the records from father to son for two thousand years; but for those of the aforementioned who might fall into transgression, it is forbidden either to stand by the altars or to partake of the other sacred rites.' I have transcribed this passage the more willingly because it appears from it that the things which Luke produced concerning John's paternal and maternal lineage could have had their assurance sought from public records. Moreover, I do not doubt that Josephus's explanation is truer than Philo's. For not only did Barzillai, a priest of the lesser families, take a wife from the lineage of Gilead, Ezra 2.61, but also Jehoiada had as a spouse the daughter of King Joram, the sister of Ahaziah, from the posterity of Judah, 2 Kings 11.2, both of which are narrated without any sign of reproach. Therefore, that Zechariah took an Aaronic woman does not signify an obedience rendered to the law, as some wish, but commends the nobility of John from both bloodlines. Moreover, no law stood in the way of Mary, who was from the stock of Judah, being related by blood to Elizabeth, an Aaronite. For the law which commands virgins to marry within the tribe pertains only to heiresses, as has been said elsewhere, and that because of the rights of estates which did not belong to the Levites. Therefore, one of Mary's ancestors could have taken as a wife one born of the same parents as Elizabeth, a descendant of David taking a granddaughter of Aaron. For as for Theophylact tracing this kinship from the times of Aaron, it is sought too far.

and her name Elizabeth] It is the Hebrew name אלישבע, Exod. 6.23. But the Arabs and Syrians often change the y at the end in this way, and the LXX followed that.

Latin:

Vers. 5. ἐγένετο ἐν ταῖς ἡμέραις Ἡρώδε τῦ βασιλέως] Mos Hebræus ordiendi, ut in libro Ruth : ויהי בימי שפט השפטים. Quod quidam spectatum hic à Luca putant Ia- cobi vaticinium, probare non possum. Nam ut præteream quæ à viris doctissimis accurate super hac re sunt disputata, simplicissimus oraculi illius sensus est, acfore Messiam ante τῆς Ἰουδαϊκῆς πολιτείας ἐρήμωσιν : quod molla. Herodem pertinet. Cæterum qui eum res Prophetarum finpserant, exorti erant à tempore ἀναδείξεως ἀυτῶν, ut de Elia, Elisæo atque aliis factum videmus. Ita & Marcus initium histo- riæ Christi fecerat ipsius & præcursoris Φανέρωσιν. At Lu- cas, cum videret curiosum lectorem scire desideraturum, qui & hujus & illius natales fuissent, simulque prospiceret progressu temporum multa posse tradi fabulosa, inde auspi- candum sibi existimavit.

Loquitur Grotius non ut de θεοπνεύστῳ, sed ut de vulgari Scriptore. At cogitandum erat, hæc inspiratione divini Spiritus scripta esse, non hu- mano arbitrio.

ἱερεύς τις] Satis cavit Lucas addito τις, ne Pontifex maxi- mus fuisse Zacharias intelligeretur, quod à veterum multis falso creditum vel ἐφημερία satis evincit. Sed nec princi- pem familiæ fuisse credibile est: qua de re ad Matthæum diximus XIV. 2. Pertinet autem hæc narratio ad indican- dam Iohannis nobilitatem. Iosephus: ὥσπερ δὲ παρ' ἑκά- στοις ἄλλη τίς ἐστιν εὐγενείας ὑπόθεσις, ὕτως παρ' ὑμῖν ἡ τῆς ἱερω- σύνης μετουσία τεκμήριόν ἐστι γένες λαμπρότητος. Imo Philo ausus est dicere ὅσῳ θεὸς ἀνθρώπων διαφερή κατὰ τὸ κρεῖττον, το- σούτῳ καὶ βασιλείας ἀρχιερωσύνη. τὴν μὲν γὰρ εἶναι θεῦ θερά- πειαν, τὴν δὲ ἐπιμέλειαν ἀνθρώπων. Quod ut calidius di- ctum benigna interpretatione mitigandum est. Scimus alioqui reges à Pontificibus etiam maximis dominos salutatos, & Deo placuisse ut Messiæ anteambulo ex

Sacerdotali, ipse autem Messias ex regio genere nascere- tur.

ἐξ ἐφημερίας Ἀβία] Est & hic μετωνυμία. Nam per ἐφη- μερίαν intelligitur ἡ πατριὰ, quæ certo dierum spatio (ἑβδομαίῳ scilicet, ut recte notat Theophylactus, dili- gens rerum Judaicarum inquisitor) λειτουργίαν suam imple- bat ex Davidis & veterum Prophetarum instituto, post- quam gens Aaronidarum in eum numerum excreverat, ut eodem tempore occupari Templi negotiis non posset. Pro- prie autem respondet vox Hellenistica ἐφημερίαις, aut, ut Jo- sephus loquitur, ἐφημερίσι, voci Hebrææ, משמרות. In- terpretes Nehemiæ (quos multis argumentis suspicor po- steriores esse τῶν ὀ) Nehem. 13, 30. ἔστησα ἐφημερίας: ubi in Hebræo est ואעמידה משמרות, & 2. Par. 31, 16. (quo- rum librorum interpres videtur esse Theodotion) εἰς λειτουρ- γίαν ἐφημερίας διατάξεως αὐτῶν, לעבודתם במשמרותם במשמרותיהם, & sequenti versu iterū לעבודתם ἐν ταῖς ἐφημερίαις αὐτῶν. LXX. autem Interpretes vocem משמרת, quæ λειτουργίαν significat; sed nondum in orbes temporum distributam, φυλακὴν solent vertere, ut Num. III. 7. 25. 28. 31. atque alibi videre. מחלקת est ipsa διάταξις aut μερισμός: quanquam interdum ob affinitatem significationis vertitur ἐφημερία. פקדה autem est ἡ ἐπισκο- πὴ aut ἐπίσκεψις, id est eorum cura qui cæteris præerant, ut clare docemur I. Par. XXIII. 24. Videntur autem Hebræi exemplo hoc inducti ut cæterarum tribuum familias attri- buerent sacerdotalibus familiis, ad quas qui pertinebant, non quidem templi ministerio, sed orationibus & jejunio indicto sibi tempore vacabant. Ejus rei memoria passim extat in libro Musar atque aliis. Ut autem vetus institu- tum credam facit locus insignis 2. Par. 23. 6. πᾶς ὁ λαὸς φυ- λασσέτω φυλακὰς κυρίου. Quod postquam receptum est, communem illam omnium tribuum λειτουργίαν dixerunt משמרת φυλακὴν, illam autem Sacerdotum propriam discriminis causa stationem מעמד. Quod quidam pu- tant successionem hanc perpetui ministerii turbatam, in eo quam fallantur cum a viro & doctrinæ & diligentiæ admi- rabilis Josepho Scaligero demonstratum sit antehac, idem ostendere amplius velle sit actum agere. Pauca scilicet no- mina Zorobabelis temporum quæ cum Davidicis habent fortuitam συνέμπτωσιν, cum tanto plura discrepent, hanc hallucinationem pepererunt. At falli certe in istis rebus Josephus, & sacerdos, & diligentissimus patriæ historiæ inquisitor non potuit, qui Davidi historiam enarrans di- serte ait, διέμεινεν ἕως ὀ μερισμὸς ἄχρι τῆς σήμερον ἡμέρας. Intervenerant quidem tempora regum impiorum, dein- de exilii Babylonici, postremo triennium Antiochi. Sed illis quoque temporibus pii sacerdotes, quod in templo non poterant, ubi poterant, & qua poterant, præstabant, non quidem pecorum mactatione, quod extra templum nefas erat, sed solenni recitatione earum precum quæ sa- crificiis accedere solebant. Quarum & Philo & Josephus aliquot locis meminerunt. Non alio pertinet quod apud Ezechielem laudat Deus sacerdotes οἵτινες ἐφυλάξαντο τὰς φυλακὰς τῶν ἁγίων: quatenus poterant scilicet: quod ipsum sufficiebat ad retinendam memoriam τῶν ἐφημεριῶν quas tanquam ex prima institutione continuatas in tem- plum reduxerunt Ezechias, Josias & postremo Judas Mac- cabæus.

De veteri Ephemeriarum instituto legere est 2. Paral. XXIII. 6. Quod autem successionem perpetui ministerii non perturbatam unquam, ne temporibus quidem exilii Babylonici, & perse- quutionis Antiochi fuisse, a Scaligero ita demon- stratum esse arbitratur Grotius, ut idem ostendere amplius velle, sit actum agere, in eo quam fal- latur ipse, Dionysius Petavius, cui multum tri- buit Grotius, & Fried. Spanhemius ostendere sa- tegerunt. Quibus etsi Robertus Bælius respon- dere conetur lib. II. oper. Histor. & Chron. p. 45. fatetur tamen demonstrationem subtilem Scaligeri tot niti hypothesibus, quarum una labente totum ruat ædificium, ut sibi quidem satis dubia videatur. Ne- que concedunt Chronologi præstantissimi, quod e Sacerdotum Ephemeriis conficere vult Scaliger Iohannem Iulii fine, vel Augusti initio, Christum vero sexto post mense, ineunte Ianuario conceptum, adeoque Christum Octobris initio natum esse: Wil- helmus certe Langius lib. II. de annis Christi pag. 359. fundamentum Scaligeri, quod nempe Encæniis Maccabæi Ephemeria Jojaribi mini- strarit, se submovisse putat, aliaque inita

Ephemeriarum ratione certum esse, ac demon- stratum credit, verum Christi natalem incidere in 25. Decembris. Qua de re alias.

Καὶ ἡ γυνὴ ἀυτῦ ἐκ τῶν θυγατέρων Ἀαρὼν] Lex exstat Lev. 21.14. ubi Pontifex maximus jubetur uxore ducere מעמיו ἐκ τῦ λαῦ ἀυτῦ, ut vertunt LXX. alii ἐκ τῦ γένυς ἀυτῦ, quod duplici occasionem præbuit interpretationi. Philo vetita putat summo Pontifici matrimonia extra genus Aa- ronicum. Verba ejus apponam ἐκ τῦ περὶ τῶν ἐν ἔδει νό- μων. Πρὸς δὲ τύτῳ κὶ τὸ γένν͵ ἠκρίβωσε τῶν μελλεσῶν γαμεῖ- σθαι, προστάξας τῷ μὲν ἀρχιερεῖ, μηδὲ μὴ μόνον γυναῖκα παρ- θένον ἀλλὰ καὶ ἱερεῖαν ἐξ ἱερέων, ἵνα ἐκ μιᾶς οἰκίας κὶ τρόπον τινὰ τῦ ἀυτῦ αἵματν͵ ὦσιν νυμφίος τε κὶ νύμφη, πρὸς ἁρμονίαν ἐπι- δειξόμενοι παρ᾽ ὅλον τὸν βίον κρᾶσιν ἠθῶν βεβαιοτάτην· ἐπεῖρά- πη δὲ τοῖς ἄλλοις καὶ μὴ ἱερείαν γαμεῖν θυγατέρν͵, τῇ μὲν ὅτι μικρὰ τύτων καθάρσια, τῇ δ᾽ ὅτι τὸ ἔθνος ἐκ ἠβυλήθη γενεᾶς εἰς ἅπαν ἰσραϊτικῆς ἀμοιρῆσαι καὶ παιδείας ἀποξεῦξαι. δι ἣν αἰτίαν ἐκ ἐκώλυσε τὲς ἄλλες ἱερέας ἐπιγαμίας ποιεῖσθαι πρὸς τὲς ἀπὸ τῦ ἔθνες. Aperte sentit legem hanc ita peculiariter ad pontifi- cem maximum pertinere, ut Sacerdotes cæteros non com- plectatur. At Josephus in moribus Judaicis multo exerci- tatior עמ interpretatur non φυλὴν, sed, quæ frequentior est significatio, ἔθνος, & cum Hebræis aliis ea quæ dicuntur Levit. 21.31. & sequentibus, connectit cum ejusdem capitis initio, quæ de Pontifice maximo dicta erant commatibus 10.& 11. velut parenthesi includens: unde sequebatur, ut sa- cerdotum cuivis ducere non liceret nisi Hebræis parentibus natam, cum de plebe homines peregrinam ἰυδαϊζεσαν duce- re non vetarentur, exceptis quibusdam nationum cum quibus jus connubii non erat. Causam legis adfert Josephus curam impermixti sanguinis in Sacerdotibus. Locus est in- signis contra Appionem I. οὐ γὰρ μόνον ἐξ ἀρχῆς ἐπὶ τύτων τὲς ἀρίστας κὶ τῇ θεραπείᾳ τῦ θεῦ προσεδρεύοντας κατέστησαν, ἀλλ᾽ ὅ- πως τὸ γένν͵ τῶν ἱερέων ἄμικτον καὶ καθαρὸν διαμένῃ προυόη- σαν. δεῖ γὰρ τὸν μετεχοντα τῆς ἱερωσύνης ἐξ ὁμοεθνῦς γυναικὸς παι- δοποιεῖσθ', καὶ μὴ πρὸς χρήματα μηδὲ τὰς ἄλλας ἀποβλέπειν τι- μὰς, ἀλλὰ τὸ γένν͵ ἐξετάζειν ἐκ τῶν ἀρχαίων λαμβάνοντα τὴν διαδοχὴν, καὶ πολὺς παρασχόμενον μάρτυρας· κὶ ταῦτα πράττο- μεν, ᾃ μόνον ἐπ᾿ ἀυτῆς Ἰυδαίας, ἀλλ᾽ ὅπυ πότε σύστημα τῦ γένυς ἐστὶν ἡμῶν, κἀκεῖ τὸ ἀκριβὲς ἀποσώζεται τοῖς ἱερεῦσι περὶ τὲς γάμες. λέγω δε τὲς ἐν Αἰγύπτῳ κὶ ἐν Βαβυλῶνι κὶ εἴπε τῆς ἄλλης οἰκουμένης τῷ γένες τῶν ἱερέων εἰσὶ τινες διεσπαρμένοι· πέμπεσι γὰρ εἰς Ἱεροσόλυμα συγγράψαντες πατρόθεν τὔνομα τῶν γεινα- μένων κὶ τῶν ἐπάνω προγόνων, κὶ τίνες οἱ μαξτυρῆντες· πόλεμν͵ δ᾽ εἰ καλάβοι, καθάπερ ἤδη γέγονεν πολλάκις, Ἀντιόχε τε τῦ ἐπιφανῦς εἰς τὴν χώραν ἐμβαλόντν͵, καὶ Πομπηΐς μάγνε, καὶ Κυιντιλις υ᾿άρυ, μάλιστα δὲ καὶ ἐν τοῖς καθ᾽ ὑμᾶς χρόνοις, οἱ περι- λειπόμενοι τῶν ἱερέων καινὰ πάλιν ἐκ τῶν ἀρχαίων γραμμάτων συνιστᾶσι καὶ δοκιμάζυσι τὰς ὑπολειφθείσας γυναῖκας· ἐ γὰρ ἔτι τὰς αἰχμαλώτες γενομένας προσίενται πολλάκις γενομένην τὴν πρὸς ἀλλόφυλον κοινωνίαν ὑφορώμενοι· τεκμήριον δὲ μέγι- σον τῆς ἀκριβείας· οἱ γὰρ ἀρχιερεῖς οἱ παρ᾽ ἡμῖν ἀπὸ δισχιλίων ἐτῶν ὀνομαστὶ παῖδες ἐκ πατρὸς εἰσιν ἐν ταῖς ἀναγραφαῖς· τοῖς δὲ τῶν εἰρημένων ὅτι ᾔν γένοιτο εἰς παράβασιν ἀπηγόρευται μή- τε βωμοῖς παρίστασθ', μήτε μετέχειν τῆς ἄλλης ἁγιστείας. Quem locum transcripsi libentius, quod inde appareat quæ de Jo- hannis paterno maternoque genere Lucas prodidit, eorum fidem ex Actis publicis peti potuisse. Josephi autem expli- catio quin verior sit quam Philonis non dubito. Neque enim Barzillajus tantum, minorum gentium sacerdos, ex Galaadis prosapia uxorem duxit, Esdr. II. 61. sed & Jojada conjugem habuit regis Jorami filiam, Achaziæ sororem, ex posteritate Judæ, 2.Reg.XI.2. quorum utrumque sine ulla reprehensionis significatione narratur. Quare quod Za- charias Aaronida mulierem duxit, non obsequium legi præ- stitum significat, ut quidam volunt, sed nobilitatem Johan- nis ex utroque sanguine commendat. Quominus autem Maria ex stirpe Judæ profata Elisabetham Aaronida sangui- ne contingeret lex nulla obstitabat. Nam lex quæ intra tri- buin virgines nubere jubet, ad solas ἐπικλήρες pertinet, ut dictum est alibi, idque ob prædiorum jura quæ ad Levitidas non pertinebant. Potuit igitur aliquis majorum Mariæ uxorem ducere iisdem cum Elisabetha parentibus prosa- tam, Davidis nepos Aaronis neptem. Nam quod Theo- phylactus hanc cognationem ab Aaronis temporibus repe- tit, nimis longe petitum est.

καὶ τὸ ὄνομα ἀυτῆς Ἐλισάβεθ] Hebræorum nomen est אלישבע Exod. VI.22. Sed Arabes & Syri sæpe y in fine fic mutant, & id secuti LXX.

## 1:6
Verse 6. And they were both righteous before God] That is, they strove for piety with a sincere heart. For because God is the knower of hearts, therefore those who think small things, their heart is said not to be right before God, as in Acts 8.21. Conversely, those who do not feign piety, but are devoted to it from the soul, are said to serve God in righteousness before him, as below 1.75. Nor should it be thought that those of whom this is said were exempt from the common weakness of human nature or even of those times. For David also is said to have done what was right in the sight of God, and never to have departed from his precepts, except for that which he committed against Uriah, although besides that atrocious crime there are many of his transgressions to be observed in sacred history, but by which that pursuit of piety which God especially regards was not interrupted, and while it remained, he overlooks those lesser things. Which the law itself also signified not obscurely, as the writer of the Responses to the Orthodox wisely notes on this passage to question 141. 'For he who sins,' he says, 'against the law, having received forgiveness for the sin by the offering of sacrifices and by the confession of the fault, becomes clean and blameless according to the righteousness of the law.'

walking in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord blameless] Many of the ancients refer this also to the estimation of God. To me it seems that this rather indicates that they had not only a pure conscience, but also an unblemished reputation, which contributed not a little to the commending of John. Providing for honest things not only in the sight of the Lord but also in the sight of men, says Paul, 2 Cor. 8:21. Wherefore, since Luke has already dealt with the former part, I think these pertain to the latter, especially since Paul also refers the word blameless to the estimation of men, when he says that he lived blameless according to the righteousness which is in the law, which righteousness is here distributed into commandments and ordinances. Deuteronomy 4:40, where in the Hebrew it is 'and you shall keep his statutes and his commandments', the LXX have 'and you shall keep his commandments and his ordinances'. I agree, however, with the Hebrews who think that by the word 'commandments', which the Hellenists translate as ordinances, are indicated those things which the law prescribes generally, such as those which contain natural equity in themselves. For so also Paul speaks: 'if then the uncircumcision keeps the ordinances of the law' Rom. 2:26, and John in the Apocalypse calls the works of Christians ordinances. Josephus also calls those things which are honest by nature the ordinances of nature. Therefore, 'statutes', that is, commandments, or as the LXX translate elsewhere, 'legal requirements', we shall rightly interpret with the same Hebrews as those special determinations which are wont to be called positive law; especially since Paul also calls the same law the law of commandments, Eph. 2:15. I know that this distinction is not observed perpetually: for commandments are also called precepts of morals, and ordinances certain things which pertain to rites. But that which I have stated is the most proper and accepted meaning of the words: sometimes also 'statutes', that is, the commandments, are distinguished into that part which, contained under the name of the genus, signifies ritual law, and 'judgments', which word then properly denotes that civil law by which the mutual society of citizens is maintained: which part of the law, since it pertains not only to judges but to all citizens altogether, ought here to be considered as included in the broader meaning of the commandments.

They are said to have been righteous before God by imputed righteousness, which is of faith, Rom. 4:5, 6, ch. 5:18, 19. For faith causes that sins are not imputed, which God does not indeed overlook, but forgives to those who believe: by faith also the obedience of Christ performed for us is apprehended, so that by the same we are constituted righteous before God, Rom. 5:19, 2 Cor. 5, Phil. 3:9. The righteousness begun is dealt with in the following words: walking in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord blameless. Although Grotius confesses that many of the ancients refer this to the testimony of God, he himself prefers to refer it to an unblemished reputation: thinking that by commandments positive law is designated, and by ordinances laws which contain natural equity in themselves: whereas this Scripture rather inverts these, and by 'statutes, commandments, and judgments' understands moral, Levitical or ceremonial, and judicial precepts: the last of which are omitted in this place, because judgments were for the most part then in the hands of the Romans: but mention is made of ordinances, because Zacharias was one of the priests. They are called blameless, however, not because they were without any sin, as the Pelagians wished, but because they were not guilty on account of public fault, as the Syrian rendered it: for blameless is he who does not deserve to be reproved by public and just judgment: just as one is called irreproachable in 1 Tim. 3:2. Whence Augustine replies to the Pelagians in Epistle 95.

That it is not just any sin of human temptation, but a grave crime that is to be understood, which comes into complaint, when they are said to have lived without complaint.

Latin:

Vers. 6. ἦσαν δὲ δίκαιοι ἀμφότεροι ἐνώπιον τῦ Θεῦ] Id est, sincero corde studebant pietati. Nam quia καρδιογνώστης est Deus, ideo qui parva cogitant, eorum cor dicitur non esse rectum ἐνώπιον θεῦ, ut Actor VIII.20. Contra qui non fingunt pietatem, sed ex animo ei sunt dediti, dicuntur Deo servire ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ ἐνώπιον ἀυτῦ, ut infra 75. Neque ideo putandum est, de quibus id dicitur, eos communi na- turæ humanæ, aut etiam temporum illorum imbecillita- te fuisse exemptos. Nam & David dicitur fecisse quod re- ctum erat in conspectu Dei, neque à præceptis ejus re- cessisse unquam, extra id quod commisit adversus Uriam, cum tamen præter illud atrox facinus multa ejus πλημ- μελήματα sit animadvertere in sacra historia, sed quibus non interrumpebatur studium illud pietatis quod Deus præcipue respicit, & quo manente minora illa dissimu- lat. Quod lex etiam ipsa non obscure significabat, ut ad hunc locum sapienter notat Scriptor responsionum ad orthodoxos ad quæstionem CXLI. ὁ γὰρ ἀμαρτάνων, in- quit, παρὰ τὸν νόμον συγγνώμη ἁμαρτίαν τῆ προσαγωγῆ τῶν θυσινῶν καὶ τῆ ἐξαγορεύσει τῶ πταίσματος λαβὼν τὴν ἄφεσιν γίνεται καθαρὸς καὶ ἄμεμπτος κατὰ τὴν ἐκ νόμο δικαιοσύ- νην.

πορευόμενοι ἐν πάσαις ταῖς ἐντολαῖς καὶ δικαιώμασι τῶ κυ- ρίο ἄμεμπτοι] Veterum multi hoc quoque ad Dei æsti- mationem referunt. Mihi videtur hic illud potius indicari, non conscientiam tantum puram illis fuisse, sed & famam integram, quod ad Johannem cominendandum non pa- rum pertinebat. Προνοούμενοι καλὰ ἐ μόνον ἐνώπιον κυρία ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐνώπιον ἀνθρώπων, inquit Paulus 2. Cor. VIII. 21. Qua- re cum de priori parte jam egerit Lucas, puto hæc ad poste- riorem pertinere, præsertim cum & Paulus vocem ἀμέμπτος ad hominum existimationem referat, cum se vixisse ait ἄμεμπτον κατὰ δικαιοσύνην τὴν ἐν νόμῳ, quæ quidem δικαιοσύνη hic in ἐντολὰς & δικαιώματα distribuitur. Deuteronomii IV. 40. ubi in Hebræo est ושמרת את חקיו ואת מצותיו LXX. habent κὴ φυλάξη τὰς ἐντολὰς ἀυτᾶ κὴ τὰ δικαιώματα ἀυ- τᾶ. Assentior autem Hebræis existimantibus voce מצות. quam δικαιώματα vertunt Hellenistæ, indicari ea quæ gene- raliter lex præscribit, qualia sunt quæ æquitatem in se natu- ralem continent. Nam ita & Paulus loquitur ἐὰν ὖν ἡ ἀκρο- βυςία τὰ δικαιώματα τῶ νόμο φυλάσση Rom. II. 26. & Johan- nes in Apocalypsi Christianorum opera vocat δικαιώματα. Josephus quoque ea quæ natura honesta sunt vocat τῆς φύ- σεως δικαιώματα. Proinde חקים id est ἐντολὰς, aut ut alibi vertunt LXX. νόμιμα cum eisdem Hebræis recte interpre- tabimur speciales illas determinationes, quæ jus positivum vocari solent; quippe cum & Paulus idem jus vocet νόμον ἐντολῶν Ephes. II. 15. Scio non observari perpetuo hoc di- scrimen: nam & ἐντολὰς vocati præcepta morum & δικαιώ- ματα quædam quæ ad ritus pertinent. Sed ea quam dixi maxime propria & recepta est vocum significatio: inter- dum & חוקים id est αἱ ἐντολαὶ distinguuntur in eam par- tem quæ generis nomine contenta jus rituale significat,& משפטים quæ vox tum proprie notat jus illud civile, quo mutua civium societas continetur: quæ pars juris cum non ad judices tantum, sed ad cives omnino omnes perti- neat, hic ampliori significatu τῶν ἐντολῶν comprehensa cen- seri debet.

Justi dicuntur coram Deo fuisse qua justitiam imputatam, quæ fidei est, Rom. IV. 5. 6. cap. V. 18. 19. Fides enim facit, ut non imputen- tur peccata, quæ Deus non dissimulat quidem, sed condonat credentibus: Fide etiam appre- henditur obedientia Christi pro nobis præstita, ut eadem justi coram Deo constituamur Rom. V. 19. 2. Corinth. V. Phil. III. 9. De justitia incho- ata agitur verbis sequentibus πορευόμενοι ἐν πά- σαις ταῖς ἐντολαῖς καὶ δικαιώμασι τᾶ κυρία ἄ- μεμπτοι. Quæ cum ad Dei testimonium multos Ve- terum referre fateatur Grotius, ipse tamen ad famam integram referre mavult: ut per ἐντολὰς jus positivum, per δικαιώματα vero leges, quæ naturalem in se æquitatem continent designari pu- tat: quum invertat potius hæc Scriptura, & per מצות תחוקים ושפטים ἐντολὰς, δικαιώμα- τα, κρίματα præcepta moralia, levitica vel cæremo- nialia, & judicialia intelligat: quorum postre- ma hoc loco omittuntur, quia judicia maximam partem tum penes Romanos erant: τῶν δικαιωμά- των vero mentio facta, quia Zacharias unus ex Sa- cerdotibus erat. Ἄμεμπτοι autem dicuntur non quod sine omni peccato fuerint, ut Pelagiani vo- lebant, sed quod non rei propter publicam cul- pam, ut Syrus reddidit: ἄμεμπτος enim est, qui publico & justo judicio reprehendi non me- retur: sicut ἀνεπίληπτος dicitur 1. Tim. III. 2. Un- de Augustinus Pelagianis respondet Epist. XCV.

Non qualecunque peccatum tentationis humanae, sed grave crimen intelligendum esse, quod in que- relam veniat, quando dicuntur sine querela vixis- se.

## 1:7
Vers. 7. οὐκ ἦν ἦν αὐτοῖς τέκνον] Meanwhile, among the things that are usually sought in this life, there is also offspring: for through it, as the Philosopher says, ἡ φύσις ἀναπληροῖ τὸ ἀεὶ εἶναι, ἐπεὶ κατ᾽ ἀριθμὸν ὀ δύναται, ἀλλάγε κατὰ τὸ εἶδος. But they are especially held by the desire for it who have ample means to sustain themselves. For, as Menander says, Ὀδυνηρόν ἐστιν εὐτυχοῦντα τῷ βίῳ Ἔχειν ἔρημον διαδόχων τὴν οἰκίαν. Wherefore the divine law promulgated through Moses, just as it promises the happiness of other things, so it also promises offspring to its worshippers, Exodus 23:26, Leviticus 26:9, Deuteronomy 7:14, ch. 28:11. Yet that did not prevent God, the dispenser and arbiter of His law, from sometimes testing the patience of the pious with this, as with other adversities, while meanwhile providing them with greater goods within the soul than the external ones that were denied. For it is no wonder if those who had received a greater spirit from God than the capacity of the times allowed were treated less indulgently in perishable matters, divine providence even then demonstrating in a few what was to be, as it were, common to the pious under the new and more august covenant. Thus Moses, pious and meek beyond every example, touched hardly any part of the goods promised by him, vexed by the continuous seditions of an ungrateful people. Thus, to pass over the examples of barren women before the law, the wife of Manoah and Anna the wife of Elkanah, though they were pious, were tested by long infertility of the womb. Which happened all the more grievously to them of old, and to Zechariah and Elizabeth, because the people, judging everything by external things, while they had nothing in their lives to criticize, nevertheless suspected that some guilt clung to them because of the denied offspring. Hence sterility is usually called a reproach.

προβεβηκότες ἐν ταῖς ἡμέραις] He doubled the miracle by adding the impediment of age to the old defect. The Greeks, however, translate the Hebrew בא בימים in this way, Gen. XVIII, 1, ch. XXIV, 1, Jos. XIII, 1, I Reg. I, 1.

Latin:

Vers. 7. οὐκ ἦν ἦν αὐτοῖς τέκνον] Interea quae in hac vita expeti solent, est etiam proles: nam per eam, ut ait Philo- sophus, ἡ φύσις ἀναπληροῖ τὸ ἀεὶ εἶναι, ἐπεὶ κατ᾽ ἀριθμὸν ὀ δύ- ναται, ἀλλάγε κατὰ τὸ εἶδος. Praecipue autem ejus deside- rio tenentur quibus ample est unde se sustentent. Nam, ut Menander ait, Ὀδυνηρόν ἐστιν εὐτυχοῦντα τῷ βίῳ Ἔχειν ἔρημον διαδόχων τὴν οἰκίαν. Quare lex divina per Mosem promulgata, sicut aliarum re- rum felicitatem, ita progeniem quoque cultoribus suis pol- licetur Exodi 23, 26. Levit. 26, 9. Deut. 7, 14. c. 28 11. Ne- que id tamen impedijt, quominus Deus legis suae dispensa- tor & arbiter interdum piorum patientiam, ut aliis adversi- tatibus, ita & in foecunditate experiretur, majora interim il- lis bona praestans intra animum, quam externa erant quae negabantur. Nam qui majorem a Deo spiritum, quam ca- ptus temporum ferebat, acceperant, non mirum est si in re- bus caducis minus indulgenter habebantur, jam tum divina providentia in paucis id praemonstrante, quod quasi com- mune piis futurum erat sub novo atque augustiori foedere. Sic Moses supra omne exemplum pius ac mitis bonorum a se promissorum partem vix ullam attigit, continuis ingrati populi seditionibus vexatus. Ita, ut sterilium feminarum ante legem exempla praeteream, Manoae uxor & Anna uxor Elcanae, piae cum essent, tentatae sunt longa uteri infoecun- ditate. Quod eo gravius & illis olim, & Zachariae atque Elisabethae accidit, quod populus ex rebus externis cuncta dijudicans, cum in vita ipsorum nihil haberet quod repre- henderet, tamen culpam aliquam in illis haerere ex nega- ta sobole suspicabatur. Hinc sterilitas opprobrium dici so- let.

προβεβηκότες ἐν ταῖς ἡμέραις] Duplicavit miraculum ad vetus vitium accedens impedimentum aetatis. Vertunt au- tem hoc modo Graeci Hebraeum בא בימים Gen. XVIII, 1. cap. XXIV. 1. Jos. XIII. 1. I. Reg. I. 1.

## 1:8
Vers. 8. ἱερατεύειν] This is what the Hebrew canons call עבד to perform sacred duties, λειτουργεῖν.

ἐν τῇ τάξει τῆς ἐφημερίας αὐτοῦ] That is, when the order had returned to the family of Abijah, which happened after an interval of 168 days, as a very great man has noted. τάξις is what the Hebrews call סדר. Porphyry also ascribes τάξεις to the Egyptian priests.

ἔναντι τοῦ θεοῦ] That is, לפני יהוה as Moses speaks in Exodus 27:21 and ch. 30:8, where the LXX have ἔναντι κυρίου. This kind of speaking is usually used of that whole priestly ministry, both that which was performed in the temple and that which was performed in the open air. Concerning the rites of the temple, it is apparent from the said passages. Concerning the altar of burnt offerings, the same kind of speaking is used several times in Leviticus.

Latin:

Vers. 8. ἱερατεύειν] Hoc est quod Hebraei canones dicunt עבד operari sacris, λειτουργεῖν.

ἐν τῇ τάξει τῆς ἐφημερίας αὐτοῦ] Id est, cum ad familiam Abiae ordo rediisset, quod fiebat post intervallum CLXVIII. dierum, ut vir maximus annotavit. τάξις est quod Hebraeis סדר. Etiam Aegyptiis Sacerdotibus τάξεις adscribit Porphy- rius.

ἔναντι τοῦ θεοῦ] Id est לפני יהוה ut loquitur Moses E- xodi 27, 21. & cap. 30, 8. ubi LXX. habent ἔναντι κυρίου. So- let id genus loquendi usurpari de toto illo ministerio Sa- cerdotali tam quod in templo, quam quod subdio perage- batur. De templi ritibus apparet dictis locis. De altari τῶν ὁλοκαυτωμάτων idem loquendi genus usurpatur in Levitico aliquoties.

## 1:9
V. 9. κατὰ τὸ ἔθος τῆς ἱερατείας ἔλαχε τοῦ θυμιᾶσαι] I think these are rightly joined in that manner. For ἱερατεία is ἡ ἱερατικὴ λειτουργία: which, since it had many parts, as can be seen in I Par. 23:27 and following, it was introduced not by law, but by custom, that those who were of the same family and ἐφημερία would cast lots among themselves as to which part of the ministry fell to each. And so by lot it fell to Zechariah הקטרת τὸ θυμιᾶσαι.

εἰσελθὼν εἰς τὸν ναὸν τοῦ κυρίου] It should not be doubted that by the word ναός here is understood the priestly sanctuary in which was the altar of incense. The Hebrews properly call that sanctuary היכל: Philo also calls it the adytum, which word, however, seems to fit the holy of holies, which the Hebrews call הדביר, more, but the added mention of the priests and the first veil removed the ambiguity, thus dealing with that altar: ὁ δὲ χρυσοῦ μὲν κατεσκεύασται, ἵδρυται δ᾽ ἐν ἀδύτῳ ἔσω τοῦ προτέρου καταπετάσματος, ὃς οὐδενὶ τῶν ἄλλων ἐστιν ὁρατὸς ὅτι μὴ τοῖς ἁγνεύουσι τῶν ἱερέων πρὸς γίγονε πρὸς χρείαν τῶν θυμιαμάτων. The priests call those ἁγνεύοντας whose turn of duty it was: for they were in a state of purity at that time.

Latin:

V. 9. κατὰ τὸ ἔθος τῆς ἱερατείας ἔλαχε τοῦ θυμιᾶσαι] Puto haec recte eum in modum conjungi. Nam ἱερατεία est ἡ ἱερα- τικὴ λειτουργία: quae cum partes haberet plures, ut videre est I. Par. 23, 27. & deinceps, non lege, sed consuetudine intro- ductum erat, ut qui ejusdem familiae & ἐφημερίας essent, inter se sortirentur quae pars ministerii cuique obtingeret. Itaque forte obtigit Zachariae הקטרת τὸ θυμιᾶσαι.

εἰσελθὼν εἰς τὸν ναὸν τοῦ κυρίου] Dubitati non debet ναῦ voce hic intelligi aedem Sacerdotalem in qua erat altare τῶν θυμιαμάτων. Hebraei eam aedem proprie היכל vocant: Philo etiam adytum, quae tamen vox τῷ ἁγίῳ τῶν ἁγίων, Hebraeis הדביר, magis videtur convenire, sed addita Sa- cerdotum & veli prioris mentione ambiguitatem sustulit, ita agens de altari illo: ὁ δὲ χρυσοῦ μὲν κατεσκεύασται, ἵδρυται δ᾽ ἐν ἀδύτῳ ἔσω τοῦ προτέρου καταπετάσματος, ὃς οὐδενὶ τῶν ἄλλων ἐστιν ὁρατὸς ὅτι μὴ τοῖς ἁγνεύουσι τῶν ἱερέων πρὸς γίγονε πρὸς χρείαν τῶν θυμιαμάτων. Sacerdotes ἁγνεύοντας vocant eos quorum erat ἐφημερία: nam illi eo tempore in casto erant.

## 1:10
Vers. 10. πᾶν τὸ πλῆθος] Those of the Israelites who were in Jerusalem belonging to that watch, and if any had come of their own accord to assist the priest's prayers with their own prayers, as was the custom.

Because mention is made of the whole multitude, B. Chemnitius concludes that it was not simply the time of incense, such as was placed daily morning and evening, but that it was one of the more solemn feasts, to which the whole multitude flocked from all sides from all of Judea: if indeed God wished there to be many and various witnesses of this history, so that on that occasion it might be spread more widely, and the minds of all might be excited to the expectation of the impending visitation and redemption: and that the opinion of the ancients is not to be disapproved, that these things happened in the seventh month, into which the feast of trumpets, of atonement, and of tabernacles falls. Ambrose refers it to the feast of atonement, Chrysostom to the tabernacles.

ἔξω] In that part which was called of the Israelites. τῇ ὥρᾳ τοῦ θυμιάματος] Morning. Exod. XXX. 7.

Latin:

Vers. 10. πᾶν τὸ πλῆθος] Qui Israelitarum Hierosoly- mis erant ad eam φυλακὴν pertinentes, & si qui sponte ac- cesserant suis precibus preces Sacerdotes adjuturi, ut mos habebat.

Quia multitudinis universae mentio fit, B. Chemnitius colligit, non simpliciter fuisse tempus incensi, quale quotidie mane & vesperi ponebatur, sed fuisse unum ex festis solemniori- bus, ad quae tota multitudo undique ex tota Ju- daee confluebat: siquidem voluerit Deus mul- tos & varios hujus historiae testes esse, ut ea oc- casione latius spargeretur, & omnium animi ad expectationem instantis visitationis & redem- ptionis excitarentur: nec improbandam esse veterum sententiam, quod hæc septimo mense, in quem festum tubarum, propitiationis, & tabernaculorum incidit, facta sint. Ad festum propitiationis refert Ambrosius, ad tabernaculorum Chrysostomus.

ἔξω] In ea parte quæ Israelitarum dicebatur. τῇ ὥρᾳ τοῦ θυμιάματος] Mane. Exod. XXX. 7.

## 1:11
Vers. 11. ἐκ δεξιῶν] Which is a sign of good omen: hence among the Poets: Be present on the right, and assist on the right with a favorable foot for the sacred rites.

Latin:

Vers. 11. ἐκ δεξιῶν] Quod boni ominis signum: hinc apud Poëtas: Dexter ades, & dexter adi pede sacra secundo.

## 1:12
Vers. 12. φόβος ἐπέπεσεν ἐπ᾿ αὐτόν] See Jud. XIII. 21. Dan. X. 8.

Latin:

Vers. 12. φόβος ἐπέπεσεν ἐπ᾿ αὐτόν] Vide Jud. XIII. 21. Dan. X. 8.

## 1:13
Vers. 13. Μὴ φοβοῦ] See what I wrote on Matthew XXIX. verse 10.

εἰσηκούσθη ἡ δέησίς σου] The opinion of those who think that this concerns prayers for obtaining offspring cannot approve itself to me. For how is it credible that Zechariah at that age hoped for what he so hardly believed when the Angel promised it, when Abraham himself, the father of believers, could not conceive such a thing in his mind, as can be seen in Gen. 17. 18. The circumstances of the place also do not allow these to be referred to prayers for a time already passed. For the Priest was accustomed to offer prayers at the same time with incense: δίκαιον γάρ, as Hierocles says, τῶν συμβολικῶν τεθεσθαι καὶ τὸ προφερόμενον φυλάττειν καὶ τὸ ἐπωτοούμενον. There is a similar sentiment in Philo περὶ ἀποικίας. Now τὸ θυμίαμα signifies, as Philo in the book περὶ θυόντων not badly said, τὸ πνεῦμα λογικόν, or as the divine Apocalypse speaks more expressly V. 8. τὰς προσευχὰς τῶν ἁγίων. Simul ego cum suffitu, as I said, the Priest offered prayers to God: and not the Priest only, but also the Israelites standing outside, as we have already heard. Those prayers were conceived for the people of God, nay, if we believe Josephus and Philo, for the salvation of the whole world. The Angel says these prayers were heard: for the coming of the Messiah was now at the door, for whom he who was to be born as a son to Zechariah was destined as a forerunner. If anyone weighs the following things correctly, he will see that no other meaning should be sought. Add that it appears from the writings of the Hebrews that appearances were accustomed to happen to the Priests especially at the time when they were burning incense. The excellent Drusius taught this from the writings of the Rabbis. But a passage of Josephus must be added, Antiquities XIII. 18, where God gives an oracle to Hyrcanus while he was burning incense.

Non agi hic de precibus ob impetrandam prolem, we easily admit: since it is not credible that Zechariah, who could not apply faith even to the angel promising the same, expected offspring at that age: and therefore with the blessed Chemnitz we judge that both the Priest and the people poured out prayers that God might at last visit the people and make redemption by sending the Messiah: which the words of Gabriel and the song of Zechariah show; to which those things which Grotius brings forward from Josephus and Philo are not dissonant: that indeed prayers were accustomed to be made for the people of God, nay, and for the salvation of the whole world: which the Angel therefore said were heard, for the coming of the Messiah was now at the door, for whom he who was to be born as a son to Zechariah was destined as a forerunner.

Τὸ ὄνομα αὐτοῦ Ἰωάννην] יוחנן properly is God has had mercy or has shown favor. Now both this word among the Hellenists, as also that Hebrew one, is accustomed often to signify the exhibition of notable joy: wherefore I do not doubt that in the following words καὶ ἔσται χαρά σοι καὶ ἀγαλλίασις καὶ πολλοὶ ἐπὶ τῇ γεννήσει αὐτοῦ χαρήσονται there is an explanation of this name. For the Hellenists say χάριν instead of χαρᾶς, and the reason for a name divinely bestowed is accustomed to be indicated sometimes by the preceding, sometimes also by the following words, as appears in Matt. I. 21. and chapter XVI. 18. in which place καὶ is similarly as here explanatory.

Latin:

Vers. 13. Μὴ φοβοῦ] Vide quæ ad Matthæum XXIX. vers. 10.

εἰσηκούσθη ἡ δέησίς σου] Probare se mihi eorum opinio non potest qui de precibus ob impetrandam prolem agi hic putant. Nam qui credibile sit ea senectute sperasse Zachariam, quod promittenti Angelo tam ægre credidit, cum Pater ipse credentium Abrahamus rem tantam non potuerit animo concipere, ut videre est Gen. 17. 18. Ad temporis etiam exacti preces hec referre circumstantiæ loci non patiuntur. Solebat enim Sacerdos simul suffitu preces offerre: δίκαιον γάρ, ut Hierocles ait, τῶν συμβολικῶν τεθεσθαι καὶ τὸ προφερόμενον φυλάττειν καὶ τὸ ἐπωτοούμενον. Cui par sententia est apud Philonem περὶ ἀποικίας. Significat autem τὸ θυμίαμα, ut Philo libro περὶ θυόντων non male dixit, τὸ πνεῦμα λογικόν, aut ut expressius loquitur divina Apocalypsis V. 8. τὰς προσευχὰς τῶν ἁγίων. Simul ego cum suffitu, ut dixi, preces Deo offerebat Sacerdos: nec Sacerdos tantum, sed & Israelitæ foris stantes, ut jam audivimus. Eæ preces concipiebantur pro Dei populo, imo, si Josepho & Philo credidimus, pro mundi totius salute. Has preces Angelus dicit exauditas: jam enim præ foribus esse adventum Messiæ, cujus anteambulo destinatus sit is qui Zachariæ nasciturus erat filius. Sequentia si quis recte expendat videbit non alium sensum quæri debere. Adde quod ex Hebræorum scriptis apparet solitas Sacerdotibus ἐπιφανείας contingere eo maxime tempore cum adolebant. Docuit hoc ex Rabbinorum scriptis optimus Drusius. Sed addendus est Josephi locus XIII. Originum 18. ubi Hyrcano θυμιῶντι Deus oraculum reddit.

Non agi hic de precibus ob impetrandam prolem, facile admittimus: quum credibile non sit, ea senectute prolem exspectasse Zachariam, qui ne angelo quidem eandem promittenti fidem adhibere poterat: ideoque cum B. Chemnitio & Sacerdotem & populum preces fudisse censemus, ut Deus visitaret tandem populum, & redemptionem faceret Messiam mittendo: quod Gabrielis verba, & canticum Zachariæ ostendunt; quibus non dissonant, quæ è Josepho & Philone adfert Grotius: quod nempe preces fieri consueverint pro Dei populo, imo & pro totius mundi salute: quas proinde exauditas dixit Angelus, jam enim præ foribus esse adventum Messiæ, cujus anteambulo destinatus sit is, qui Zachariæ nasciturus erat filius.

Τὸ ὄνομα αὐτοῦ Ἰωάννην] יוחנן proprie est θεὸς ἠλέησεν aut ἐχαρίσατο. Solet autem utrumque verbum hoc apud Hellenistas, ut & Hebræum illud, sæpe significare insignis gaudii exhibitionem: quare non dubito quin in verbis sequentibus καὶ ἔσται χαρά σοι καὶ ἀγαλλίασις καὶ πολλοὶ ἐπὶ τῇ γεννήσει αὐτοῦ χαρήσονται nominis hujus sit explicatio. Nam χάριν Hellenistæ dicunt ἀντὶ χαρᾶς, & nominis divinitus inditi ratio modo antecedentibus, modo etiam subsequentibus verbis solet indicari, ut apparet Matth. I. 21. & cap. XVI. 18. quo loco καὶ similiter ut hic est αἰτιολογικόν.

## 1:14
Vers. 14. ἔσται χαρά σοι καὶ ἀγαλλίασις, [יהן Zach. IV. 7. Deservedly: for: If anything ever happens to one desiring and wishing for it, while not hoping, this is properly pleasing to the mind. Wherefore what could be sweeter to Zechariah than to obtain offspring long desired, but now despaired of? I cannot but add the most sweet verses of Euripides: Woman, this light of the sun is dear, and it is beautiful to see the flow of the sea with fair winds, and the earth blooming in spring, and rich water. And it is in my power to speak the praise of many beautiful things: But nothing is so bright, nor beautiful to behold, as for those who are childless and bitten by the desire of children, to see the light of newborn ones in their homes.

Beyond these common reasons for rejoicing, another was added: the exceptional dignity of the son, which the Angel predicts. 'Many will rejoice at his birth' (rejoicing in his light, John 5:35). Verse 15. 'For he will be great before the Lord'—'before the Lord' here is 'before God,' as of Moses in Acts 7:46: 'he found grace before God.' Opposed to this is being 'an abomination before God' below in chapter 16:15. 'Strong drink'—concerning him who had vowed the Nazirite vow, it was written in the law: 'he shall abstain from wine and strong drink' (Num 6:3). For thus the word שכר is expressed there by the LXX. But the same was also commanded to the Priests at the time of their service (Lev 10:9), where the same word 'strong drink' is in the Greek. I entirely agree with those teachers of the Hebrews who think that 'strong drink' is called whatever intoxicates, whether it is wine or something else, such as the Zythum of the Egyptians, the 'drink from barley' in Aeschylus's Suppliants, and the drink of the Babylonians made from the palm. Philo understood the law of the Nazirite in this way, describing it thus: 'neither to drink anything made from grapes, nor any other intoxicating drink.' Thus also in 1 Sam 1:15, שכר is translated as 'intoxicating drink.' The original word, from which the name also comes, the Arabs also retain. For with them too, سكر means 'to be intoxicated.' Just as, therefore, those who were consecrated to God for a time were required to abstain for a time from wine and strong drink, which were signs of all things by which reason is disturbed, as has been rightly noted by Philo: so Samson, formerly granted to his parents not without a miracle and the announcement of an Angel, and now the Baptist, given to Zechariah in a similar way, as being set apart for God forever, and born for this purpose, are also commanded to live an abstemious life forever. See Jud 13:14, where the LXX likewise have 'let him not drink wine and strong drink.' Concerning Samuel, likewise obtained through a miracle, his mother had vowed a similar vow (1 Sam 1:11). Josephus in the history of Samson: 'it was clear that he would be a prophet from the temperance regarding his diet.' He has similar things about Samuel. Plutarch in his Roman Questions: 'Is it lawful for a priest to be intoxicated? For wine is above the heads of those who are intoxicated, and it presses them down and humbles them, whereas they ought to be superior and to master this pleasure, not be mastered by it.' The same author concerning the Egyptians: 'Those who serve the god in Heliopolis do not bring wine into the temple at all'; then, 'they have many wine-free purifications.' 'He will be filled with the Holy Spirit'—the Holy Spirit loves dry hearts. Nor is the Holy Spirit opposed to wine here only, but also in Acts 2:15, 17 and Eph 5:18. 'Even from his mother's womb'—'even' is either redundant, as often in Greek writers, or it has the same value as the Latin word which seems to be derived from the Greek as well. For Luke also uses this word below in chapter 14:26, and the writer to the Hebrews in 11:36. However, 'from the womb' is used for 'out of the womb,' that is, from the time when he will be in the womb: as the ancient Syriac and Arabic versions have it here. Thus Paul in Gal 1:15: 'who set me apart from my mother's womb,' looking back to that which had been said to Jeremiah by God in chapter 1:6: 'before you came out of the womb I consecrated you.' In the same sense, Acts 3:2: 'lame from his mother's womb.' Thus 'from the belly' (Ps 22:10), 'from the womb' (Ps 51:3). But as to the fact that the Angel says here that John will be filled with the Holy Spirit from the very time he was in the womb, I would not dare, with Augustine, to refer it to divine destination alone, for the words demand something more. But it should be noted that a fetus which is in the womb is not held to be an existing human, but is considered as a part of the mother. Thus to the Stoics: 'just as fruit is a part of the plants, so is the embryo.' And to Empedocles: 'the embryos in the mother's womb are parts.' 'Offspring before they are brought forth are a portion of the woman or of her viscera,' says Ulpian, book 1, section. 1. Concerning inspecting the belly. The Greeks say 'that which is being carried is a part of the pregnant woman.' Philo, in the second book of Special Laws: 'And yet, things still in the womb are said to be parts of the mothers who carry them, both by natural philosophers, to whom the theoretical life is devoted, and by the most approved physicians.' This saying of the Angel was therefore fulfilled when Elizabeth, in whose womb John was hidden, 'was filled with the Holy Spirit,' as Luke speaks below, repeating the very words of the Angel (verse 41). It has been well observed by a most learned man that those are accustomed to be called 'full of the Holy Spirit' not in whom the Holy Spirit is, but in whose words and deeds his efficacy abounds: which also happened to Elizabeth, who, moved by the Holy Spirit, began to prophesy; and through her, in a certain way, John, whom God wished to be commended by this miracle. However, this inspiration of the mother was an indication of that destination of which Augustine treats, and a presage of a Spirit more than Prophetic, which God was about to bestow upon the Baptist 'on the day of his manifestation to Israel.' Thus also 'from the womb' or 'out of the womb,' that is, from the time he will be in the womb, as the Syriac and Arabic have translated, and from the comparison of Acts 3:2. Galatians 1:5, it is clear, Grotius rightly acknowledges; but that, just as it cannot be referred to divine destination alone with Augustine, because the words demand something more, so he rashly snatches it away to Elizabeth on the pretext that a fetus which is in the womb is not held to be an existing human, but is considered as a part of the mother: for the Angel is not speaking here of the mother but of her fetus: and all the predicates pertain to John himself: nor is there any doubt that it was fulfilled in John, when 'he leaped for joy in his mother's womb' at the presence of the Messiah. For that spiritual joy is proof that he was filled with the Holy Spirit.

Latin:

Vers. 14. ἔσται χαρά σοι καὶ ἀγαλλίασις, [יהן Zach. IV. 7. Merito: nam: Si quicquam cupidoq; optantiq; obtigit unquam Insperanti, hoc est gratum animo proprie. Quare quid Zachariæ dulcius esse poterat quam prolem adipisci diu optatam, jam vero desperatam? Non possum non adjicere suavissimos Euripidis versus: Γύναι· φίλον μὲν φέγγος ἡλίου τόδε, Καλὸν δὲ πόντου χεῦμ᾿ ἰδεῖν εὐήνεμον, Γῆ τ᾽ ἠρινὸν θάλλουσα, πλούσιόν θ᾽ ὕδωρ. Πολλῶν τ᾽ ἔπαινον ἐστί μοι λέξαι καλῶν: Ἀλλ᾽ οὐδὲν οὕτω λαμπρὸν, οὐδ᾽ ἰδεῖν καλὸν, Ὡς τοῖς ἄπαισι καὶ πόθῳ δεδηγμένοις Παίδων, νεογνῶν ἐν δόμοις ἰδεῖν φάος.

Super has communes gaudendi causa accedebat alia, exi- mia filii dignitas, quam prædicit Angelus. Πολλοὶ ἐπὶ τῇ γεννήσει αὐτ̄ χαρήσονται) ἀγαλλιώμενοι ἐν τῷ φωτὶ αὐτ̄ Joh. V. 35. Vers. 15. ἔσαι γὰρ μέγας ἐνώπιον τ̄ θε̄) ἐνώπιον ̄τ θε̄ hic est apud Deum, ut de Mose Act. 7, 46. εὗρε χάριν ἐνώπιον τ̄ θε̄. Huic opponitur esse βδέλυγμα ἐνώπιον τ̄ θε̄ infra cap. XVI. 15. Σίκερα) Qui Naziræatum voverat, de eo scriptum erat in lege ἀπὸ οἴνου καὶ σίκερα ἁγνισθήσεται Num 6, 3. Ita enim & ibi vox שכר exprimitur à LXX. Sed & Sacerdotibus idem imperabatur tempore λειτουργίας Lev. 10, 9. ubi eadem vox σίκερα in Græca. Omnin illis Hebræorum magistris assentio, qui siceram dici putant quicquid inebriat, sive il- lud vinum est, sive aliud, ut Zythum Ægyptiorum ἐκ κρι- θῶν μέθυ Æschylo Supplicibus, & Babyloniorum potus è palma. Philo ita accepit legem Naziræatus, hoc modo describens: μηδ' ὅσα ἐκ σαφυλῆς κατεργάζεται, μηδ' ἄλλό τι μέθυσμα πίνειν. Sic & 1. Sam. 1. 15. שכר vertitur μέθυσμα. Verbum originale, unde & nomen venit, etiam Arabes re- tinent. Nam & illis سكر est μέθυειν. Sicut ergo hi qui ad tempus Deo consecrabantur, abstinere ad tempus debebant vino & sicera, quæ signa erant rerum omnium, quibus ratio perturbatur, ut recte à Philone annotatum est: ita Samson olim parentibus non sine miraculo & An- geli annuntiatione concessus, & nunc Baptista simili mo- do datus Zachariæ, ut in perpetuum Deo sepositi, & in hoc nati, perpetuo etiam jubentur abstemiam vitam vive- re. Vide Jud. 13, 14. ubi itidem LXX. habent οἶνον καὶ σί- κερα μὴ πιέτω. De Samuele itidem per miraculum ob- tento simile votum mater voverat 1. Sam. I. 11. Josephus in Samsonis historia: δῆλον ἦν προφητεύσων ὑπὸ τῆς περὶ τὴν διαίταν σωφροσύνης. Similia habet de Samuele. Plu- tarchus quæstionibus Romanis: ἦ θεμιτὸν τῷ ἱερεῖ μεθύσκε- σθαι' τῶν γὰρ μεθυσκομένων ὑπερκεφαλῆς ὁ οἰνός ἐσι καὶ πιεζόν- των, καὶ ταπεινῶν, δέον ὑπερτέρες εἶναι, κ̄ κρατεῖν ἀνὶ τῆς ἡδονῆς ταύτης, ἀλλὰ μὴ κρατεῖσθαι. Idem de Ægyptiis: οἶνον δὲ οἱ μεν ἐν Ἡλίου πόλει θεραπεύοντες τὸν θεὸν, ἐκ εἰσφέρουσι τοπαράπαν εἰς τὸ ἱερὸν: deinde, πολλὰς δὲ ἄοινος ἁγνείας ἔχουσιν. πνεύματ̄ ἁγίς πλησθήσεται) Amat Spiritus sanctus sic- ca corda. Neque hic tantum vino Spiritus sanctus op- ponitur, sed & Actorum II. vers. 15. 17. & Ephes. V. v. 18. ἔτι ἐκ κοιλίας μητρὸς αὐτ̄) ἔτι aut παρέλκ̄, ut sæpe apud Græcos Scriptores, aut idem valet quod Latina vox quæ ex Græca derivari videtur etiam. Nam & sic hanc vocem Lucas infra usurpat cap. 14, 26. & Scriptor ad Hebræos 11, 36. ἐκ κοιλίας autem positum est pro ἀπὸ κοιλίας, id est ab eo tempore quo erit in utero: quomodo hic veteres Syrus & Arabs. Ita Paulus Gal. I, 15. ὁ ἀφορίσας με ἐκ κοιλίας μητρός μυ: respiciens illud quod ad Jeremiam di- ctum erat a Deo cap. 1, 6. πρὸ τ̄ σε ἐξελθεῖν ἐκ μήτρας ἡγία- κά σε. Eodem sensu Actor. III. 2. χωλὸς ἐκ κοιλίας μητρὸς. Sic ἀπὸ γαστρὸς Psal. 22, 10. ἀπὸ μήτρας Psal. 51, 3. Quod au- tem hic dicit Angelus Johannem impletum iri Spiritu san- cto jam ab eo tempore quo erat in utero, non ausim cum Augustino ad solam destinationem divinam referre plus enim aliquid verba exigunt. Sed notandum est fœtum qui in utero est non haberi pro homine exsitente, sed ut par- tem matris censeri. Ita Stoicis ὥσπερ τῆς καρπὸς μέρη τῶν φυτῶν ὕτω κ̄ τὸ ἔμβρυον. Et Empedocli, τὰ ἔμβρυα τὰ ἐν τῇ γαςρὶ τῆς μήτρας μέρη. Partus antequam edatur mulieris portio est vel viscerum ait Ulpianus lib. I. §. I. de ventre inspic. Græci dicunt τὸ κυοφορέμενον μέρος τῆς ἐγκύε. Philo secundo de legibus specialibus: καί τοι τὰ μὲν ἔτι κ̄ τὴ γαςρὸς παρεχόμενα τῇ μήτρα τῶν κυεσῶν εἶναι μέρη λέγεται παρά τε φυσικοῖς ἀνδράσιν οἷς ὁ θεωρητικὸς διαπονεῖται βί̄ κ̄ παρ' ἰατρῶν τοῖς δοκιμωτάτοις. Impletum est ergo hoc Angeli dictum tunc cum Elisabeth, in cujus visceribus Jo- hannes latebat, ἐπλήσθη πνεύματ̄ ἁγίε, ut infra ipsa Angeli verba repentens Lucas loquitur 41. Bene autem à viro doctissimo observatum est, plenos Spiritus sancti eos dici solere, non in quibus sit Spiritus sanctus, sed in quorum sermonibus factisque ejus efficacia exundet: quod & Elisabethæ contigit quæ Spiritu sancto mota vati- cinari cœpit: & per ipsam quodammodo Johannes, quem Deus hoc miraculo commendatum volebat. Hic autem afflatus matris indicium fuit ejus destinationis de qua agit Augustinus, & præsagium Spiritus plus quam Pro- phetici, quem Deus baptistæ collocaturus erat τῇ ἡμέρᾳ ἀ- ναδείξεως αὐτ̄ πρὸς τὸν Ἰσραήλ. Ita etiam ἐκ κοιλίας vel ἀπὸ κοιλίας, id est, ab eo futurum tempore, quo in utero erit, ut Sy- rus, & Arabs verterunt, & è collatione Actor. III. 2. Galat. I. 5. patet, recte agnoscit Grotius; id vero, uti non ad solam destinationem divi- nam cum Augustino referri posse, fatetur, quia plus aliquid verba exigunt, ita ad Elisabetham temere abripit hoc prætextu, quod fœtus, qui in utero est, non habeatur pro homine existen- te, sed ut pars matris censeatur : nam non de matre hic loquitur Angelus sed de fœtu ejusdem: & prædicata omnia ad ipsum Johannem perti- nent: neque dubium est, impletum id in Jo- hanne esse, cum ἐσκίρτησεν ἐν ἀγαλλιάσει ἐν τῇ κοιλίᾳ μητρὸς præ gaudio exultavit in utero matris suæ ad præsentiam Messiæ. Illud enim spirituale gaudium documentum est, quod Spiritu S. re- pletus fuerit.

## 1:17
Verse 17. 'Before him'—see what is said on Matt 3:3.

And with power—as often as 'power' is named when the Spirit is named, a certain force of the Spirit greater than usual is indicated, as below in verse 35, Acts 10:38, 1 Cor 2:4, 1 Thess 1:5.

Elijah—see Matt 11:14 and 17:12.

ἐπιστρέψαι καρδίας πατέρων ἐπὶ τέκνα) In the times of the Baptist, the Jews were divided into three principal sects and several smaller ones, differing in both rites and opinions. The Sadducees and Pharisees, moreover, were agitated by sharp hatreds among themselves. Added to this were the diverse schools of the lawyers, and new conflicts arising from them. Hence Christ called them scattered sheep. It usually happens, however, that such dissensions penetrate even into families themselves. The Angel therefore says that the Baptist will be sent for this purpose, that he may draw men from so many masters to one master, namely Christ, and thus reconcile those who are at variance. In the Talmudic tractate concerning the King, this passage is explained thus: I will send you Elijah, he will make peace in the world. The LXX in Malachi (as they are accustomed to paraphrase more obscure passages) made this sense clear by adding a few words. For they translate it thus: ὃς ἀποκαταστήσει καρδίαν πατρὸς πρὸς υἱὸν, καὶ καρδίαν ἀνθρώπυ πρὸς τὸν πλησίον ἀυτῶ. For by that addition they sufficiently signify that the name of fathers and sons is placed for the sake of a more illustrious example: but that the sense is that the embassy would look to this, that the Jews might agree in the same form of doctrine, and be καρδία καὶ ψυχὴ μία: which counsel of God, however, was not to be fulfilled in all the Jews, as the Angel himself signified when he said πολὺς τῶν ὑιῶν Ἰσραὴλ. For others rejected that counsel of God.

Καὶ ἀπειθεῖς ἐν φρονήσει δικαίων) Ἀπειθεῖς are those who are not obedient to God, the מָרִים of the Hebrews: for the Greeks render this word as ἀπειθεῖς: such as those whom John called γεννήματα ἐχιδνῶν. But ἐν is placed here for εἰς, which not one person notes, and which was observed long ago not only by the Latin interpreter, but also by the Syrian. For he translates it לִידַעְתָא. Φρόνησις δικαίων is that wisdom which leads men to true justice.

Λαὸν κατεσκευασμένον) That is, a people who may be prepared for receiving the kingdom of heaven. And so the past tense word here should be taken indefinitely in the Hebrew manner, as also below in verse 19, παρεστηκώς. Nor should it offend us that the same thing seems to be said twice, because ἑτοιμάζειν and κατασκευάζειν hardly differ in sense, since Hebrew and Hellenistic speech abounds in such pleonasms.

Not only are the dissensions looked at, which among the Jews, from diverse sects, had penetrated into the families themselves, so that the Baptist might bind them from so many Masters to the one Master, namely Christ, and thus reconcile those who are at variance, so that the Jews might agree in the same form of doctrine, and be καρδία καὶ ψυχὴ μία: But that formula of speaking also looks to the reintegration to the communion of the Holy Fathers, or as the added explanation has it, to the φρόνησιν δικαίων, by whose name the Patriarchs are noted, from whom the Jews had fallen away in both doctrine and morals: whence John was sent, that he might recall those later ἀπειθεῖς to a true conjunction with their Fathers, as B. Chemnitius and Beza explain. Compare what we have said on Malachi ch. IV.

Latin:

Vers. 17. ἐνώπιον ἀυτῶ) Vide quæ ad Matth. III, 3.

Καὶ δυνάμει) Quoties δύναμις nominatur Spiritus nomi- nato, vis quædam Spiritus solita major indicatur, ut infra 35. Actor. X. 38. 1. Cor. II. 4. 1. Thess. I, 5.

Ηλίυ) Vide Matth. XI. 14. & XVII. 12.

ἐπιστρέψαι καρδίας πατέρων ἐπὶ τέκνα) Baptistæ tempori- bus Judæi in tres præcipuas pluresque minores sectas & ri- tibus & opinionibus discrepantes erant divisi. Sadducæi autem & Pharisæi etiam acribus odiis inter se agitaban- tur. Accedebant diversæ legisperitorum Scholæ, & no- va inde certamina. Hinc disjectas oves Christus eos vo- cavit. Solet autem accidere ut ejusmodi dissidia in ipsas etiam familias penetrent. Dicit ergo Angelus in hoc mis- sum iri Baptistam, ut à tot magistris homines ad unum magistrum, Christum scilicet, alleget, atque ita dissiden- tes secomponat. In Thalmudico titulo de Rege locus hic sic exponitur, mitto vobis Eliam, is pacem faciet in mundo. Hunc sensum in Malachia LXX. (ut solent locos obscuriores παραφράζειν) additis vocibus aliquor perspicuum fecerunt. Ita enim vertunt ὃς ἀποκαταστήσει καρδίαν πατρὸς πρὸς υἱὸν, καὶ καρδίαν ἀνθρώπυ πρὸς τὸν πλησίον ἀυτῶ. Satis enim ea ad- jectione significant patruum & filiorum nomen exempli il- lustrioris causa positum: sensum autem esse, huc specta- turam legationem, ut Judæi in eandem doctrinæ formam conveniant, & sint καρδία καὶ ψυχὴ μία: quod tamen con- silium Dei non in omnibus Judæis impletum iri pse Ange- lus significavit cum dixit πολὺς τῶν ὑιῶν Ἰσραὴλ. Nam alii illud Dei consilium ἠθέτησαν.

Καὶ ἀπειθεῖς ἐν φρονήσει δικαίων) Ἀπειθεῖς sunt Deo nec au- dientes מָרִים Hebræis: nam hanc vocem per ἀπειθεῖς reddunt Græci: quales erant quos γεννήματα ἐχιδνῶν Jo- hannes vocabat. Ἐν autem hic pro εἰς positum, quod non unus monet, pridem etiam non à Lantino tantum interpre- te, sed & à Syro observarum est. Vertit enim לִידַעְתָא. Φρόνησις δικαίων est ea sapientia, quæ homines ad veram ju- stitiam adducit.

Λαὸν κατεσκευασμένον) Id est populum qui paratus sit ad accipiendum regnum cælorum. Itaque præterita vox sumenda hic ἀορίστως more Hebræo, ut & infra v. 19. παρε- στηκώς. Neque offendere nos debet quod bis idem dici vi- detur, quia ἑτοιμάζειν & κατασκευάζειν sensu vix differunt, cum ejusmodi πλεονασμοῖς abundet sermo Hebræus & Hel- lenisticus.

Non tantum respiciuntur dissidia, quæ inter Judæos, è sectis diversis in familias ipsas penetra- rant, ut à tot Magistris ad unicum Magistrum, Christum scilicet alliget, atque ita dissidentes re- componat Baptista, ut Judæi in eandem doctrinæ formam conveniant, & sint καρδία καὶ ψυχὴ μία : Sed loquendi illa formula etiam spectat redinte- grationem ad S. Patrum communionem, vel ut ex- plicatio addita habet ad φρόνησιν δικαίων, quo- rum nomine Patriarchæ notantur, à quibus & doctrina & moribus desciverant Judæi: unde mis- sus Johannes, ut posteros illos ἀπειθεῖς ad veram cum suis Patribus conjunctionem revocaret, ut B. Chemnitius, & Beza explicant. Conf. quæ ad Malach. c. IV. diximus.

## 1:18
Vers. 18. Κατὰ τί γνώσομαι) The words themselves are those which the LXX use in the history of Abraham speaking similarly, Gen. XV. 7. If the bare words are looked at, they do not seem to deserve the punishment which God immediately inflicts. But God looked at the heart itself, in which diffidence was discerned: which the following words also indicate to some extent, where he opposes his own and his wife's advanced age to the divine promise through the Angel, when he ought to have turned his mind from natural causes to the power of the first cause, as Abraham ὃς

He considered his own body now dead, and the deadness of Sarah's womb Rom. IV. 18. Abraham indeed seems to have hesitated somewhat at the beginning, when he said, Shall a child be born to me a hundred years old, and shall Sarah, who is ninety years old, bear?
