But this sudden thought was overcome by faith, and was more excusable in him, because he had no examples of a similar thing before him, than in Zechariah, who could not have been ignorant of the history of both Abraham and Manoah, but, struck by the magnitude of the matter, remembered it little, which is a habit of the human mind, whereby it happens that we are wiser in the affairs of others than in our own. That some think the only cause of Zechariah's doubting was that he did not know whether the Angel who appeared to him was a good Angel, I cannot approve. For in such a doubt, what fault there is, especially one to be punished in such a way, I do not see. Nor, however, do I deny that in what happened to Zechariah there was an image of the Jewish people, who, when they had ceased to speak through the gift of Prophecy, and were shadowing forth future things only by the signs of ceremonies, brought forth Christ in their exhausted age: but that signification does not take away the merit of the punishment in Zechariah, which the Angel clearly expresses when he says, because you did not believe. And thus this passage, among others, can teach us that not as soon as God remits His anger to a man are all those things also removed which have the nature of a temporal punishment or rather of a medicine: which kind of punishment philosophers call admonition, not retribution.

Latin:

Vers. 18. Κατὰ τί γνώσομαι) Verba ipsa sunt quæ LXX. in Abrahami similiter loquentis historia usurpant Gen. XV. 7. Nuda verba si spectentur, non videntur eam me- reri pœnam quam Deus mox infligit. Sed Deus cor ipsum spectavit, in quo diffidentia cernebatur: quam & sequen- tia verba aliquatenus indicant, ubi ætatem provectam & suam & uxoris, divinæ per Angelum pollicitationi op- ponit, cum animum à naturalibus causis ad primæ causæ potentiam debuisset advertere, ut Abrahamus ὃς

κατενόησε τὸ ἑαυτῦ σῶμα ἤδη νενεκρωμένον κὶ τὴν νέκρωσιν τῆς μήτρας Σάῤῥας Rom. IV. 18. Videtur quidem & Abraha- mus initio aliquid hæsitasse, cum diceret, Itane mihi cen- tenario nascetur proles & Sara nonagenaria pariet? Sed hæc repentina cogitatio per fiduciam superata, ignoscibilior in eo erat, quia nullâ ante se habebat rei similis exem- pla, quam in Zacharia, qui & Abrahami & Manoæ histo- riam non poterat ignorare, sed magnitudine rei perculsus parum meminerat, qui mos est humani ingenii, quo fit ut in alienis negotiis quam in nostris sapiamus magis. Quod quidam putant unicam dubitandi causam Zacha- riæ fuisse, quod nesciret an is qui sibi apparebat Angelus bonus esset, probare non possum. Nam in tali dubi- tatione quid culpæ sit, præsertim ita castigandæ, non video. Neque tamen nego in eo quod Zachariæ accidit imaginem fuisse Judaici populi, qui cum per donum Pro- phetiæ loqui desiissent, & solis cæremoniarum nutibus fu- tura adumbraret, effœta ætate protulit Christum: sed ea significatio non tollit meritum pœnæ in Zacharia, quod Angelus diserte exprimit, cum dicit ἀνθ' ὧν ἐκ ἐπίστευσας. Atque adeo hic inter cæteros locus docere nos potest, non simulatque Deus iram suam homini remittit, ea etiam tol- li omnia quæ pœnæ temporalis aut medicinæ potius ha- bent rationem: quod pœnæ genus νουθεσίαν non τιμωρίαν Philosophi vocant.

## 1:19
Vers. 19. Gabriel) Angels, since they do not need names among themselves, receive names by which their ministries are indicated. Gabriel is the power of God. Thus, therefore, this Angel is so called, because God uses him as a minister to explain His supreme power. Now the supreme power of God is the Gospel of Christ Rom. I. 16. I. Cor. I. 24. Therefore, this same Gabriel was commanded to announce not just any things, but those which pertained either directly or antecedently to Christ, to Daniel of old, now to Zechariah, and soon to Mary. By the recitation of this name, therefore, Zechariah is recalled to the book of Daniel, as if the Angel were saying: do not wonder if God now brings about something extraordinary and surpassing the order of nature. For those times indicated to Daniel are at hand, in which God is about to exert His power most amply. The teachers of the Hebrews say that Michael is the minister of severity, Gabriel of mercy: therefore the former flies with one wing, the latter with two. And for a similar reason they call Michael fire, but Gabriel water.

He who stands before God) An expression taken from Oriental courts: for it is as much as to say, not that he is just any minister, but a satrap of the heavenly kingdom. See what was said on Matt. XVIII. 10.

Latin:

Vers. 19. Γαβριὴλ) Angeli, cum inter se nominibus non indigeant, nomina accipiunt quibus ministeria ipso- rum indicentur. גבריאל est δύναμις θεῦ. Ita ergo hic An- gelus dicitur, quia eo ministro Deus utitur ad summam po- tentiam suam explicandam. Summa autem δύναμις θεῦ est Evangelium Christi Rom. I. 16. I. Cor. I. 24. Ideo idem hic Gabriel res non quasvis, sed quæ ad Christum aut dire- cte aut antecedenter pertinerent, jussus est nuntiare, Danie- li olim, jam Zachariæ, mox & Mariæ. Hujus igitur nominis recitatione Zacharias ad Danielis librum revocatur, quasi dicat Angelus: mirari noli, si quid nunc eximium & na- turæ ordinem superans Deus efficit. Instant enim illa tem- pora Danieli indicata, quibus potentiam suam Deus am- plissime est exerturus. Hebræorum magistri ajunt severi- tatis ministrum esse Michaelem, Gabrielem misericordiæ: ideo illum una ala volare, hunc duabus. Similique de causa Michaelem vocant ignem, Gabrielem vero aquam.

Ὁ παρεστηκὼς ἐνώπιον τῦ θεῦ) Locutio ex aulis Orientali- bus sumta: tantundem enim est quasi dicat, non quemvis ministrum sed satrapam se esse regni cælestis. Vide quæ dicta ad Matth. XVIII. 10.

## 1:20
Vers. 20. You shall be silent and not able to speak) There is such grace between the mouth and the ears, that it is no wonder if words suitable to the one are transferred to the other. Wherefore the opinion of Theophylact, Titus, and Euthymius is not improbable, who, lest the same or almost the same thing be said twice here, think that to be silent here means to become deaf, especially since the Hebrew word charash signifies both to be silent and to be deaf, which the LXX also translate by to be silent in those places where the meaning of being deaf seems to be proper: whence also the adjective charash, deaf, Levit. XIX. 14. and elsewhere. Certainly, that the faculty of hearing was also taken away from Zechariah appears sufficiently from the fact that below his friends are said to have addressed him by signs: which, however, will be passed over in the Angel's words, unless we admit that catachresis of the word to be silent of which I speak. This interpretation is favored by the fact that a little later, as if concerning a matter already once indicated, it is said and he remained deaf: for although that word is ambiguous in Greek, yet even among the LXX it signifies deaf more often than dumb in these books.

With Theophylact, Titus, and Euthymius, Grotius thinks that to be silent here means to become deaf. But that argument, namely, that the same or almost the same thing should not be said twice here, is not firm; for first he is said to be silent, or you shall be silent, or dumb: but that this may not be extended forever, it is added, and you shall not be able to speak, until the day in which these things shall happen. Nor does the word deaf here denote deaf, but rather by the force of the context it denotes dumb: nor is the faculty of hearing taken away firmly inferred from the fact that below his friends are said to have addressed him by signs: which also happens not rarely when the person we are addressing is not at all deaf. There is nothing, therefore, in the text that favors this opinion. Nor does that reason contribute anything here, that naturally the dumb are also deaf: for Zechariah was made dumb not by a natural defect, but by a miracle. And it is a greater miracle that Zechariah, retaining the faculty of hearing, with the organs of forming the voice also intact and uninjured, could not speak: nor is it improbable, in the judgment

of the blessed Chemnitius, that Zechariah was a hearer of the conversation of Mary and Elizabeth, and from that knew that the Messiah was already conceived, just as she indicates in her canticle.

These things shall happen) Up to the imposition of the name of which he had treated above v. 13.

Because of which) Hellenists are accustomed to say this for what the Hebrews say ya'an, as Levit. XXVI. 43. because they despised my judgments. Ezech. V. 11. because you have defiled my holy things. In the same sense of merit Luke uses this word below chapter IX. 44. and Acts XII. 23. But also Paul 2. Thess. II. 10. You may find that because of which in exactly the same sense in Sophocles: there is also where it is placed illatively, as below chapter XII. 3.

εἰς τὸν καιρὸν ἀυτῶν) Thus also Gen. XVIII. 10. καιρὸς is called the just time of delivery.

Latin:

Vers. 20. ἔσῃ σιωπῶν κὶ μὴ δυνάμενος λαλῆσαι) Tanta est inter se χάρις oris & aurium, ut non mirum sit verba horum alteri convenientia ad alterum transferri. Quare non im- probabilis est sententia Theophylacti, Titi, Euthymii, qui, ne bis hic idem aut pæne idem dicatur, existin ant σιωπᾷν hic esse surdum fieri, præsertim cum חרש & ההרש He- bræis & silere & obsurdescere significet, quod per παρασιω- πᾷν vertunt LXX etiam quibus locis propria esse videtur obsurdescendi significatio: unde & adjectivum חרש sur- dus Levit. XIX. 14. & alibi. Certe Zachariæ etiam audiendi facultatem esse ademtam satis ex eo apparet quod infra a- mici dicuntur ipsum nutibus allocuti: quod tamen in An- geli verbis subticebitur, nisi vocis σιωπᾷν eam quam dico admittamus κατάχρησιν. Favet huic interpretationi quod paulo post tanquam de re jam semel indicata dicitur κὶ διέ- μεινε κωφὸς: quanquam enim ea vox Græce ambigua est, tamen & apud LXX. ab his libris sæpius surdum quam mu- tum significat.

Cum Theophylacto, Tito, & Euthymio putat Grotius σιωπῶν hic esse surdum fieri. Sed argu- mentum illud, ne scil. bis hic idem aut pene idem di- catur, firmum non est, primum enim silens dicitur, vel tacens eris, aut mutus: id vero ne in perpetuum extendatur, subjicitur, & non poteris loqui, usque in diem, quo hæc fiant. Neque vox κωφὸς hic sur- dum, sed potius vi contextus mutum notat: nec ademta facultas audiendi firmiter inde colligitur, quod infra ipsum nutibus dicuntur alloquuti ami- ci: quod etiam fit non raro, cum surdus minime est, quem alloquimur. Nihil ergo est in textu quod faveat huic opinioni. Nec ratio illa quic- quam huc facit, quod naturaliter muti etiam surdi sint: Non enim vitio naturali, sed miraculo factus mutus est Zacharias. Et majus est miraculum, quod Zacharias retinens facultatem audiendi, or- ganis etiam formandæ vocis integris & illæsis, lo- qui non potuit: nec improbabile est, judicio

B. Chemnitii, Zachariam auditorem fuisse collo- quii Mariæ & Elisabethæ, atque inde cognovisse Messiam jam conceptum esse, sicut ea cantico suo indicat.

Γενήσεται ταῦτα) Ad impositionem usque nominis de qua egerat supra v. 13.

Ἀνθ' ὧν) Ita solent Hellenistæ dicere quod Hebræi יַעַן ut Levit. XXVI. 43. ἀνθ' ὧν τὰ κρίματά με ὑπερεῖδον. Ezech. V. 11. ἀνθ' ὧν τὰ ἁγιά με ἐμίανας. Eodem meriti sensu hanc vocem usurpat Lucas infra cap. IX. 44. & Actor. XII. 23. Sed & Paulus 2. Thess. II. 10. Invenias eodem plane sensu illud ἀνθ' ὧν apud Sophoclem: est & ubi illative po- nitur, ut infra cap. XII. 3.

εἰς τὸν καιρὸν ἀυτῶν) Sic & Gen. XVIII. 10. καιρὸς voca- tur justum partitudinis tempus.

## 1:21
Vers. 21. ἐν τῷ χρονίζειν ἀυτὸν ἐν τῷ ναῷ) Beyond the hour of the incense, which being finished, the priests were accustomed to go forth to the people. Wherefore either the Angel prolonged the discourse, the sum of which is related here, or astonishment detained Zacharias.

Latin:

Vers. 21. ἐν τῷ χρονίζειν ἀυτὸν ἐν τῷ ναῷ) Ultra horam τῆς θυμιάσεως, qua peracta solebant Sacerdotes ad populum progredi. Quare aut diutiustraxit Angelus sermonem cu- jus hic summa refertur, aut stupor Zachariam detinuit.

## 1:22
Vers. 22. ἐπέγνωσαν ὅτι ὀπτασίαν ἑώρακεν) Not by conjecture, which could hardly happen, but from the signification of his gestures. Therefore I judge that the καὶ which follows here, as often elsewhere, is put for γὰρ. And ὀπτασία is ἐπιφάνεια, as below chapter XXIV. 23. Acts XXVI. 19. 1 Cor. XII. 1.

Latin:

Vers. 22. ἐπέγνωσαν ὅτι ὀπτασίαν ἑώρακεν) Non ex con- jectura, quòd fieri vix poterat, sed ex nutuum significatio- ne. Itaque καὶ quod sequitur hic, ut alibi sæpe, pro γὰρ po- situm arbitror. Et ὀπτασία est ἐπιφάνεια, ut infra cap. XXIV. 23. Actor. XXVI. 19. 1. Cor. XII. 1.

## 1:23
Vers. 23. ὡς ἐπλήσθησαν αἱ ἡμέραι τῆς λειτουργίας ἀυτῦ) He persevered therefore in the priesthood for the legitimate time, even until the morning incense of the following Sabbath.

Latin:

Vers. 23. ὡς ἐπλήσθησαν αἱ ἡμέραι τῆς λειτουργίας ἀυτῦ) Perseveravit ergo ἐν τῇ ἱερατείᾳ per tempus legitimum, ad matutinum usque suffitum sabbati sequentis.

## 1:24
Vers. 24. περιέκρυβεν) Declining rumors, but with God so disposing it, that nothing might be disclosed concerning John before it was established by certain testimonies concerning his conception, for whose sake John was being born.

λέγουσα) Rejoicing to herself, with only her husband aware.

Latin:

Vers. 24. περιέκρυβεν) Rumores declinans, cæterum Deo ita disponente, ne quid de Johanne dispalesceret an- tequam certis testimoniis constaret de ejus conceptione, propter quem Johannes nascebatur.

λέγουσα) Sibi gaudens, solo marito conscio.

## 1:25
Vers. 25. ἐπεῖδεν ἀφελεῖν) There is no ἕλκυσις. But ἐπεῖδεν ἀφελεῖν must be translated 'he took care to take away' from the Hebrew idiom.

Τὸ ὀνειδος) ἀφεῖλεν θεὸς μὲ τὸ ὀνειδος is found among the LXX in the words of Rachel, Gen. XXX. 23. See what we have said above concerning barrenness.

PART III. The prediction of the birth of Jesus.

Latin:

Vers. 25. ἐπεῖδεν ἀφελεῖν) Nulla est ἕλκυσις. Sed ἐπεῖ- δεν ἀφελεῖν vertendum est curavit auferre ex locutione He- braica.

Τὸ ὀνειδος) ἀφεῖλεν θεὸς μὲ τὸ ὀνειδος est apud LXX. in verbis Rachelis Gen. XXX. 23. Vide quæ diximus supra de sterilitate.

PARS III. Prædictio nativitatis Jesu.

## 1:27
Vers. 27. Παρθένον) Mary bears the image of the Church, which is a chaste virgin (2 Cor. XI.), which also brings forth Christ (Apoc. XII. 5.), not of the will of man but of God (John I. 13.). That saying of Philo pertains here: 'For the union of men for the begetting of children makes virgins into women; but when God begins to commune with a soul, He first makes it a woman, and then shows it to be a virgin again.'

Ἐξ οἴκυ Δαβὶδ) This is said directly of Joseph, as appears below in chapter II. 4. By consequence it pertains to Mary also. But why should we not refer it directly to Mary, as was done by Chrysostom, who says that 'ἐξ οἴκε Δαβὶδ must be understood concerning the virgin,' and thus he does not refer this to the husband or man of Mary, seeing that it was already established from Matthew chapter I. 20. that he was a Son of David. From a comparison with Luke II. 4. it does not appear that it is said here of Joseph that he was of the house of David. The contrary is rather gathered from it: for what purpose would it serve for the same thing to be said twice by Luke. It is more convenient rather that, since there the matter concerns the origin of Joseph from the family of David, here the matter concerns the origin of Mary from the house of David, and that the same thing is not repeated in vain.

Latin:

Vers. 27. Παρθένον) Maria Ecclesiæ fert imaginem, quæ παρθένος ἁγνὴ 2. Cor. XI. quæ & Christum parit, Apoc. XII. 5. ἐκ ἐκ θελήματῶν ἀνδρὸς ἀλλ' ἐκ θεᾶ Joh. I. 13. Pertinet huc illud Philonis: ἀνθρώπων μεν γὰρ (male in editis libris ἀνθρώ- πῳ) ἡ ἐπὶ γενέσει τεκνων σύνοδος τὰς παρθένες γυναῖκας ἀπο- φαίνῃ· ὅταν δε ὁμιλεῖν ἄρξηται ψυχῇ θεὸς πρότερον ὖσαι γυναῖ- κα, παρθένον αὖθις ἀποδείκνυσιν.

Ἐξ οἴκυ Δαβὶδ) Directe hoc de Josepho dicitur, ut ap- paret infra cap. II. 4. Per consequentiam ad Mariam quo- que pertinet. Quidni vero directe ad Mariam referamus, uti à Chrysostomo factum, qui illud ἐξ οἴκε Δαβὶδ περὶ τῆς παρθένε ὑποληπτέον dicit, adeoque hoc non refert ad ἄνδρα seu virum Mariæ, utpote de quo jam è Matthæo cap. I. 20. constabat, quod Filius Davidis fuerit. E collatione Lucæ II. 4. non apparet, hic de Josepho dici, quod de domo Da- vit fuerit. Contrarium potius inde colligitur: quid enim attinebat bis idem à Luca dici. Con- venientius potius est, quum illic de Josephi origi- ne è familia Davidis agatur, hic de origine Ma- riæ è Davidis domo agi, non vero frustra idem repeti.

## 1:28
Vers. 28. εἰσελθὼν) Into that house in which she was being kept under the care of her nearest kin, not yet having been brought into the house of Joseph, as we said regarding Matthew.

Kecharitomene) מְחֻנָּן. For the Hebrew חָנַן is properly charizein: as in Ephesians 1:6, whence in Hophal חֻנַּן charitosetai, for which the LXX translated eleethesētai in Proverbs 21:10. Thus also eleethe Aquila and Theodotion in Isaiah 26:10. For among the Hellenists, eleein is said of any benefit or of beneficence itself. Without doubt it is the same as what is said below, heures charin para tō theō (you have found grace with God).

Ho kyrios meta sou) It can be an exegesis of what he said, kecharitomene, so that a verb of the indicative mood is understood, or of what he said, chaire, so that it is of the precative mood, which I rather believe, because it was a Hebrew custom of greeting, Ruth 2:4, even formerly used by angels, as in Judges 6:12, kyrios meta sou dynatos tē ischy.

eulogemene sy en gynaixin) I take this also not in an indicative, but rather in a precative sense. For it is taken from

In the book of Judges, ch. V. 24, where we read תברך מנשים יעל in Greek εὐλογηθείη ἐκ γυναικῶν Ἰαήλ. So also Ruth III. 10. εὐλογημένη σὺ τῷ κυρίῳ θεῷ. And I Sam. XXV. 33. εὐλογημένη σὺ is of one praying well. So below εὐλογημένη σὺ ἐν γυναιξὶν and εὐλογημένος ὁ καρπὸς τῆς κοιλίας σου. And Matt. XXI. 9. and below XIII. 35. and John XII. 13. εὐλογημένος ὁ ἐρχόμενος ἐν ὀνόματι κυρίου. Similar is the form of speech εὐλογητὸς ὁ θεὸς below 68, 2 Cor. I. 3, Eph. I. 3, 1 Pet. I. 3. However, I interpret both what preceded, κεχαριτωμένη, and this, εὐλογημένη σὺ ἐν γυναιξὶν, the more willingly in this way, because this whole speech is only of one greeting, but not yet of one explaining a mission. Therefore it is called ἀσπασμὸς. It is to be noted also that this σὺ here is nothing other than a mark of the vocative, as Acts IV. 24. So Gen. XLIX. 8, in the Hebrew יהודה אתה O Judah.

Latin:

Vers. 28. εἰσελθὼν) In eam domum in qua sub proxi- morum cura custodiebatur, nondum traducta in domum Josephi, ut ad Matthæum diximus.

Κεχαριτωμένη) מְחֻנָּן. Nam חָנַן Hebræum proprie est χαρίζειν: ut Ephes. I. 6. unde in Hophal חֻנַּן χαριτώσεται, pro quo ἐλεηθήσεται verterunt LXX. Prov. XXI. 10. Sic & ἠλεήθη Aquila & Theodotio Esa. XXVI. 10. Nam Helleni- stis ἐλεεῖν dicitur quodvis beneficium aut ipsa beneficentia. Haud dubie idem est quod infra dicitur ἑυρες χάριν παρὰ τῷ θεῷ.

Ὁ κύριος μεθὰ σε) Potest ἐξήγησις esse ejus quod dixic κεχαριτωμένη, ut subaudiatur verbum modi indicativi, aut ejus quod dixit χαῖρε ut sit modi precativi, quod magis cre- do, quia mos erat Hebræus salutandi, Ruth. II. 4. etiam olim Angelis usurpatus, ut Jud. VI. 12. κύριος μετὰ σε δυνατὸς τῇ ἰσχύι.

ἐυλογημένη σὺ ἐν γυναιξὶν) Hoc quoq; sumo non indicativa, sed potius upprecativa significatione. Sumtum enim est ex

Judicum libro c. V. 24. ubi legimus תברך מנשים יעל Græce εὐλογηθείη ἐκ γυναικῶν Ἰαήλ. Sic & Ruth. III. 10. εὐλογημένη σὺ τῷ κυρίῳ θεῷ. Et I. Sam. XXV. 33. εὐλογημέ- νη σὺ est bene precantis. Sic infra εὐλογημένη σὺ ἐν γυναιξὶν κ̀ εὐλογημέν@ ὁ καρπὸς τῆς κοιλίας σῶ. Et Matth. XXI. 9. & infra XIII. 35. & Joh. XII. 13. εὐλογημέν@ ὁ ἐρχόμε- ν@ ἐν ὀνόματι κυρίε. Simile est loquendi genus εὐλογητὸς ὁ θεὸς infra 68. 2. Cor. I. 3. Eph. I. 3. 1. Pet. I. 3. Tam au- tem quod præcessit κεχαριτωμένη, quam istud εὐλογημένη σὺ ἐν γυναιξὶν eo libentius ita interpretor, quod tota hæc oratio salutantis tantum sit, nondum autem exponentis legatio- nem. Ideo ἀσπασμὸς dicitur. Notandum & hoc σὺ hic nihil esse aliud quam notam vocativi, ut Actor. IV. 24. Sic Gen. XLIX. 8. in Hebræo יהודה אתה O Juda.

## 1:29
Vers. 29. ἡ δὲ ἰδοῦσα] So the Syriac also reads. Nor were some rightly moved to change it because there follows διεταράχθη ἐπὶ τῷ λόγῳ. For nothing prevents her from having been astonished both by the sight and the hearing.

Ποταπὸς] Of one wondering. Matt. VIII. 27, Mark XIII. 1. She was especially stunned, not understanding what that celebrity above all the female kind was, which the Angel was predicting to her.

Latin:

Vers. 29. ἡ δὲ ἰδῦσα] Ita legit & Syrus. Neque recte ad mutandum quosdam movit quod sequitur διεταράχθη ἐπὶ τῷ λόγῳ. Nihil enim vetat attonitam fuisse & aspectu & auditu.

Ποταπὸς] Admirantis. Matth. VIII. 27. Marci XIII, 1. Præ- cipue obstupuit non intelligens quæ illa esset supra omne genus muliebre celebritas quam ipsi Angelus ominabatur.

## 1:30
Vers. 30. εὗρες γὰρ χάριν παρὰ θεῷ] One must not quibble about the propriety of the Greek word εὑρίσκειν. For it is a known Hebrew idiom מצא חן which the LXX translate word for word εὗρε χάριν, as Gen. VI. 8, ch. XVIII. 3, ch. XXXIX. 4, Esth. II. 16, and elsewhere. Stephen speaks thus also in Acts VII. 46, and the writer to the Hebrews IV. 16. Moreover, מצא in these and other places is simply to obtain, whether by effort or without effort.

Latin:

Vers. 30. εὗρες γὰρ χάριν παρὰ θεῷ] Non est argutandum in proprietate Græcæ vocis εὑρίσκειν. Est enim nota locu- tio Hebraica מצא חן quod LXX. vertunt ad verbum εὗρε χάριν, ut Gen. VI 8. cap. XVIII. 3. c. XXXIX. 4. Esth. II. 16. atq; alibi. Loquitur sic & Stephanus Act. VII. 46. & Scriptor ad Hebræos IV. 16. Est autem מצא tum istis tum aliis in lo- cis simpliciter consequi, sive studio, sive citra studium.

## 1:31
Vers. 31. ἰδὲ συλλήψῃ ἐν γαστρὶ καὶ τέξῃ ὑὸν καὶ καλέσεις τὸ ὄνομα ἀυτοῦ] The Angel quite openly points his finger to those words of Isaiah cited by Matthew I. 23, which among the LXX stand thus: ἰδὲ παρθένος ἐν γαστρὶ λήψεται καὶ τέξεται ὑὸν καὶ καλέσεις τὸ ὄνομα ἀυτοῦ Εμμανυηλ.

Ἰησῦν] For that which Isaiah had said Emmanuel, the Angel said Jesus, performing the role of an interpreter, whence it appears that the same meaning is in both: For whether you say this is he through whom God is propitious to us (which the word Emmanuel signifies) or this is our savior, the sense is the same. Wherefore Matthew also says that that prophecy was fulfilled by the imposition of the name Jesus. See what is to Matthew.

Grotius thus acknowledges that the prophecy in Isa. VII. 14 is held not concerning Hezekiah, but concerning Christ: because there a prediction was made concerning a virgin birth according to the angel's explanation, and concerning Jesus, who was designated by the name Immanuel. But how poorly the same man corrupted that remarkable prophecy in his annotations on the Old Testament, which we have vindicated there. Furthermore, the word עמנואל is not fully enough explained thus, through whom God is propitious to us: For אֵל joined with נָוֹ is God with us, as the angel also interpreted in Matt. I. But God is with us, both with the assumption of our flesh, or communion of our nature, by which the Word, who is God, was made flesh, and with the propitiation of our race, by which he was made our Mediator, in order to reconcile God to us.

Latin:

Vers. 31. ἰδὲ συλλήψῃ ἐν γαστρὶ κ̀ τέξῃ ὑὸν κ̀ καλέσεις τὸ ὄνο- μα ἀυτῶ] Aperte satis Angelus digitum intendit ad illa E- saiæ citata à Matthæo I. 23. quæ apud LXX. ita se habent: ἰδὲ παρθέν@ ἐν γαστρὶ λήψεται κ̀ τέξεται ὑὸν κ̀ καλέσεις τὸ ὄνο- μα ἀυτῶ Εμμανυηλ.

Ἰησῦν] Pro eo quod Esaias dixerat Emmanuel, Ange- lus Jesum dixit interpretis fungens vice, unde apparet ean- dem in utroque esse significationem: Sive enim dicas hic est per quem Deus nobis est propitius (quod significat vox Emmanuel) sive hic est sospitator noster, idem est sensus. Quare & Matthæus impositione nominis Jesu vaticinium illud ait impletum. Vide quæ ad Matthæum.

Agnoscit ita Grotius Esa. VII. 14. non de His- kia, sed de Christo vaticinium haberi: quia ibi de partu virgineo juxta angeli explicationem prædi- ctio facta, & de Jesu, qui nomine Immanuel de- signatus. Quam vero insignem Prophetiam pessi- me idem depravavit in annot. ad Vetus Test. ibi à nobis vindicatam. Cæterum vox עמנואל non plene satis ita explicatur, per quem nobis Deus est propitius: Nam אֵל con|iunctum cum נָוֹ est Deus nobiscum, ut in- terpretatus etiam est angelus Matth. I. Deus au- tem nobiscum est, cum carnis nostræ assumtione, seu naturæ nostræ communione, qua Verbum, quod Deus est, caro factum est, tum generis no- stri propitiatione, qua noster Mediator factus est, ut Deum nobis reconciliaret.

## 1:32
Vers. 32. ὗτος ἔσται μέγας] The Angel looks to the words of the same Isaiah IX. 6, where he is called μεγάλης βουλῆς ἄγγελος and θαυματός.

κ̀ ὑὸς ὑψίστου] He thus interprets what Isaiah had said he would be called אל גבור, the mighty God. Add what is to Mark V. 7.

Δώσει ἀυτῷ κύριος ὁ Θεὸς τὸν θρόνον Δαβὶδ τοῦ πατρὸς ἀυτοῦ] Isaiah names the throne of David in the same place. But that the Messiah would be the grandson of David, and that this throne would be given to him by God, he signified typically in Ps. CXXXII. 11. Add Isaiah IX. 6, Amos IX. 11. Moreover, the empire of the Messiah is called the throne of David, because it is shadowed forth by the throne of David. And Isaac Ben Arama explains the place 2 Sam. VII. 3 here.

Latin:

Vers. 32. ὗτ@ ἔσαι μέγας] Spectat Angelus ejusdem Esaiæ verba IX, 6. ubi μεγάλης βυλῆς ἄγγελ@ & θαυματὸς dicitur.

κ̀ ὑὸς ὑψίσυ] Ita interpretatur quod Esaias dixerat voca- tum eum iri אל גבור θεὸν ἰσχυρόν. Adde quæ ad Marc. V. 7.

Δώσει ἀυτῷ κύρι@ ὁ Θεὸς τὸν θρόνον Δαβὶδ τῦ πατρὸς ἀυτῶ] Δρόνον Δαβὶδ eodem loco Esaias nominat. Davidis autem nepotem fore Messiam, & dandum ei à Deo hoc solium tu- πικῶς significabat Psal. CXXXII. 11. Adde Esaiam IX. 6. A- mos IX. 11. Dicitur autem Messiæ imperium Davidis soli- um, quod Davidis solio adumbratur. Et hic locum 2. Sam. VII. 3. explicat Isaac Ben Arama.

## 1:33
Vers. 33. βασιλεύσει ἐπὶ τὸν οἶκον Ἰακὼβ] For first he was destined to seek the sheep of the Israelite people, from which people he enrolled into his kingdom whosoever wished to receive him. But also those converted from the nations come by right under the same name as if by adoption. For just as David, when he ruled even over the Idumeans and other peoples, was nevertheless called King of Israel only, because they were, as it were, incorporated into the people of Israel through the victories of David; so also whosoever were brought to it through the arms of the Messiah, that is, the word of the Gospel, so that they might worship the God of Israel, were made Israelites. Isaiah XIV. 1. The stranger shall join himself to them and shall cleave to the house of Jacob, ch. XLIV. 5, likewise concerning the stranger: He shall be surnamed by the name of Israel. And the name of Jacob is deservedly used for this matter. For it is, as Philo notes, Jacob the supplanter, that is, he who acquires virtue without sweat.

εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας] עדי־עד as said in Ps. 132. 12, עד־עולם, as Micah IV. 7 speaks. And Isaiah I. 7. And this kingdom

שלטן עלם in Daniel 7:14. But because the Sadducees wished לעולם to be understood everywhere as a long time, not an infinite one, it was therefore established by the wise that, for the sake of distinction, an infinite duration should be expressed in the plural לעולמים, which locution and interpretation this Angel confirms. καὶ τῆς βασιλείας ἀυτοῦ οὐκ ἔσται τέλος] Isaiah: μεγάλη ἡ ἀρχὴ ἀυτοῦ καὶ τῆς εἰρήνης οὐκ ἔστι τέλος, 9:7. Daniel, ἡ βασιλεία ἀυτοῦ οὐ διαφθαρήσεται 7:14. This is not added in vain, for it explains what εἰς τοὺς ἀιῶνας means, not for a long time, but without end. And thus this empire is distinguished from human empires, which history teaches are all perishable and temporary, and which was shown to Daniel by the examples of the most noble kingdoms. When Plato had described the republic which he could conceive in his mind as the best, he adds: ὅδ' ἡ τοιαύτη ξύστασις τὸν ἅπαντα μενεῖ χρόνον, ἀλλὰ λυθήσεται.

We accept Grotius's admission that, according to the Angel's explanation, Isaiah ch. 9 v. 6 dealt with Christ. Why then did Grotius dare, against a heavenly and indubitable interpretation, to twist that prophetic prediction likewise toward King Hezekiah? We accept that he acknowledges 2 Sam. 7:14 as being about the Messiah, and approves of Isaac ben Arama's explanation concerning the scion of the Messiah. And therefore the Grotian interpretation, by which he took that passage to be about Solomon, is to be rejected. We accept that Grotius explains the passage in Dan. 7:14 as being about Christ: whom, however, he himself perverts most badly in his annotations on Daniel. See what we have written in our annotations on Isa. 9:6, 2 Sam. 7:14, and Dan. 7.

Latin:

Vers. 33. βασιλεύσει ἐπὶ τὸν οἶκον Ἰακὼβ] Primo enim de- stinatus erat ad quærendas oves populi Israelitici, ex quo populo quicunque eum recipere voluerunt eos in regnum suum adscripsit. Sed & è gentibus conversi merito eodem veniunt nomine quasi per acceptionem. Sicut enim David, cum etiam Idumæis atque aliis populis imperaret, Rex ta- men Israelis duntaxat dicebatur, quia illi per victorias Da- vidis in populum Israelis erant velut incorporati; ita & qui- cunque per Messiæ arma id est verbum Evangelii, eo addu- cti sunt ut Deum Israelis colerent, facti sunt Israelitæ. Esaias XIV. 1. Adjunget se eis extraneus & adhærebit domo Iacob, c. XLIV. 5. itidem de extraneo: In nomine Israel cognominabi- tur. Et merito nomen Jacobi in hanc rem usurpatur. Est enim ut Philo annotat Jacob ὁ πτερνισὴς, id est, ὁ τὴν ἀρε- τὴν ἐκ ἀκονιτὶ κτώμεν@.

εἰς τὲς ἀιῶνας] עדי־עד dicto Psal. 132. 12. עד־עולם, ut loquitur Micheas IV. 7. Et Esaias I. 7. Et regnum hoc

שלטן עלם Danieli VII. 14. Sed quia Sadducæi לעולם ubique volebant accipi pro longo non pro infinito tempore, ideo à sapientibus erat institutum, ut discriminis causa infinita duratio pluraliter enunciaretur לעולמים, quam locutionem & interpretationem Angelus hic comprobat. καὶ τῆς βασιλείας ἀυτοῦ οὐκ ἔσται τέλος] Esaias: μεγάλη ἡ ἀρχὴ ἀυτοῦ καὶ τῆς εἰρήνης οὐκ ἔστι τέλος, 9, 7. Daniel, ἡ βασιλεία ἀυτοῦ οὐ διαφθαρήσεται 7, 14. Non frustra autem hoc adjicitur, explicat enim quid sit εἰς τοὺς ἀιῶνας, non in longum tempus, sed sine fine. Atque ita imperium hoc ab humanis imperiis distinguitur, quæ omnia caduca esse & temporaria, tum historiæ docent, tum nobilissimorum regnorum exemplis Danieli ostensum est. Plato cùm eam quam optimam mente complecti poterat descripsisset rempublicam, addit: ὅδ' ἡ τοιαύτη ξύστασις τὸν ἅπαντα μενεῖ χρόνον, ἀλλὰ λυθήσεται.

Acceptamus confessionem Grotii, quod juxta Angeli explicationem Esaias c. IX. v. 6. de Christo egerit. Cur ergo ausus est Grotius contra cœlestem & indubitatam interpretationem vaticinium illud Propheticum itidem ad Hiskiam Regem detorquere? Acceptamus, quod 2. Sam. VII. 14. de Messia agnoscat, & Isaaci Ben Arama explicationem de folio Messiæ approbet. Ideoque reprobanda Grotiana interpretatio, qua locum illum de Salomone accepit. Acceptamus, quod locum Dan. VII. 14. de Christo explicet Grotius: Quem vero pervertit ipse pessime in annotat. ad Danielem. Vid. quæ in annot. nostris ad Esa. IX. 6. 2. Sam. VII. 14. & Dan. VII.

## 1:34
Verse 34. πῶς ἔσται τοῦτο; ἐπεὶ ἄνδρα οὐ γινώσκω] I judge this to be the words not of one doubting, but of one wondering. The Angel's words seem to have been received by the virgin as if a thing were being indicated that was about to happen immediately. And οὐ γινώσκω means, "up to this point I am untouched by a man." Rightly, therefore, she wonders how she is to conceive without the work of a man, since there existed no example of that thing. "To know a man" is found even in Ovid. If it is true what Epiphanius narrates from ancient hearsay, that Joseph was quite old when Mary was betrothed to him, it will be all the more probable, as most of the ancients think, that by these words a certain purpose of perpetual virginity is also indicated by Mary, as one who was going to be married to an elderly kinsman, not with the hope of offspring, but so that she might have someone under whose protection she might hide, being exposed to the injuries of the sex. However, the purpose of virginity was not as unknown to the Jews as some think: because I see this has been less solidly proven by others, I will adduce a notable passage from Philo: συνεστιῶνται δὲ καὶ γυναῖκες, ὧν πλεῖσται γηραιαὶ παρθένοι τὴν ἁγνείαν, οὐκ ἀνάγκῃ, καθάπερ ἔνιαι τῶν παῤ ἕλλησιν ἱερειῶν, διαφυλάξασαι μᾶλλον ἢ καθ' ἑκούσιον γνώμην, διὰ δὲ ζῆλον καὶ πόθον σοφίας ᾗ συμβιοῦν σπουδάσασαι τῶν περὶ σῶμα ἡδονῶν ἠλόγησαν, οὐ θνητῶν ἐκγόνων, ἀλλ' ἀθανάτων ὀρεχθεῖσαι, ἃ μόνη τίκτειν ἀφ' ἑαυτῆς οἵα τε ἐστιν ἡ θεοφιλὴς ψυχὴ, σπείραντος εἰς ἀυτὴν ἀκτῖνας νοητὰς πατρὸς οἷς δυνήσεται θεωρεῖν τὰ σοφίας δόγματα. The Hebrews called such votaries of virginity פרושות, such as was also the daughter of Jephthah.

Thus far Grotius is correct. But we have handed down the origin of the Pharisees in our Commentary on Gen. 4:1. Furthermore, if this sense is genuine (as Grotius does not doubt), οὐ γινώσκω means "up to this point I am untouched by a man": how will a purpose of perpetual virginity be indicated by these words; even if it were true what Epiphanius narrates, that Joseph was quite old when Mary was betrothed to him? For since those words sound as if in the present, and imply that she is up to this point untouched by a man, how can the same words sound simultaneously of a virginity to be kept perpetually in the future? Nor does betrothal agree with a vow of virginity, 1 Cor. 7:4-5.

Latin:

Vers. 34. πῶς ἔσται τοῦτο; ἐπεὶ ἄνδρα οὐ γινώσκω] Non dubitantis esse arbitror, sed admirantis. Videntur ita Angeli verba à virgine accepta, quasi res jamjam futura indicaretur. Et οὐ γινώσκω est, hactenus viro sum intacta. Merito igitur admiratur, quomodo conceptura sit sine virili opera, cùm ejus rei nullum extaret exemplum. Virum cognovit etiam apud Ovidium est. Si verum est quod Epiphanius ex veteri auditione narrat, senem admodum fuisse Josephum cùm Maria ipsi desponderetur, tanto erit probabilius, quod veteres plerique existimant, his verbis et jam propositum quoddam perpetuæ virginitatis indicari à Maria, ut quæ agnato seni nuptum iret, non prolis spe, sed ut haberet cujus sub tutela delitesceret sexus injuriis obnoxius. Propositum autem virginitatis non tam incognitum Judæis fuit, quam quidam existimant: quod quia ab aliis minus solide probatum video, adducam insignem Philonis locum: συνεστιῶνται δὲ καὶ γυναῖκες, ὧν πλεῖσται γηραιαὶ παρθένοι τὴν ἁγνείαν, οὐκ ἀνάγκῃ, καθάπερ ἔνιαι τῶν παῤ ἕλλησιν ἱερειῶν, διαφυλάξασαι μᾶλλον ἢ καθ' ἑκούσιον γνώμην, διὰ δὲ ζῆλον καὶ πόθον σοφίας ᾗ συμβιοῦν σπουδάσασαι τῶν περὶ σῶμα ἡδονῶν ἠλόγησαν, οὐ θνητῶν ἐκγόνων, ἀλλ' ἀθανάτων ὀρεχθεῖσαι, ἃ μόνη τίκτειν ἀφ' ἑαυτῆς οἵα τε ἐστιν ἡ θεοφιλὴς ψυχὴ, σπείραντος εἰς ἀυτὴν ἀκτῖνας νοητὰς πατρὸς οἷς δυνήσεται θεωρεῖν τὰ σοφίας δόγματα. Hebræi tales votrices virginitatis vocabant פרושות, qualis fuit & Jephthæ filia.

Hæc ita recte Grotius. Pharisæos autem hujus originem in Commentar. ad Gen. IV. 1. tradidimus. Cæterum si sensus hic genuinus est, (uti non dubitat Grotius) οὐ γινώσκω hactenus viro sum intacta: quomodo his verbis propositum perpetuæ virginitatis indicabitur; etiamsi verum esset, quod Epiphanius narrat senem admodum fuisse Josephum, cùm Maria ipsi desponderetur. Nam quum verba illa sonent de præsenti, & id inferant, quod hactenus viro intacta sit, quomodo eadem de virginitate imposterum perpetuo servanda simul sonare possunt? Nec convenit voto virginitatis desponsatio, 1. Cor. VII. 4. 5.

## 1:35
Verse 35. πνεῦμα ἅγιον ἐπελεύσεται ἐπὶ σε] Thus Acts 1:8, Λήψεσθε δύναμιν ἐπελθόντος τοῦ ἁγίου πνεύματος: which our Evangelist had said elsewhere in ch. 24:49, ἕως ἂν ἐνδύσησθε δύναμιν ἐξ ὕψους.

καὶ δύναμις ὑψίστου] See what we said above on clause 17.

ἐπισκιάσει σοι] The LXX are indeed accustomed to translate סכך as ἐπισκιάζειν, as in Ps. 91:4, 140:8, and elsewhere. However, the opinion of those who think the translation is taken from birds hatching their young pleases me more, from which Theophylact does not depart far: so that the Angel thus shows that this fetus will arise by that power by which the world itself took its beginning. For in the history of Moses there is ורוח אלהים מרחפת על־פני המים, which word מרחפת the most learned Hebrews explain as such a brooding. And the use of the same word is evident in Deut. XXXII. 11, where the LXX use σκεπάσας with a similar meaning.

To verse 17 he had handed down this rule: Whenever δύναμις is named, with the Spirit named, a certain power greater than the usual power of the Spirit is indicated, Acts X. 38, 1 Cor. II. 4, 1 Thess. I. 1. But that is particular, and does not fit here: where the discourse is not about a power of the Holy Spirit greater than the usual, but about the power of GOD the Father, who is designated by the name of the Most High, and the power is indicated not as non-subsistent (ἀνυπόστατος), but as self-subsistent (αὐθυπόστατος): to which a personal action is attributed: just as in Gen. I. 2 one must understand the Spirit as self-subsistent, the very person of the Holy Spirit, because of the action attributed to him. For actions belong to supposita and persons. But since in this place Gabriel speaks distinctly of the coming upon (ἐπελεύσει) of the Holy Spirit and of the overshadowing (ἐπισκιασμῷ) of the power of the Most High, he expressed the action of the Holy Spirit without doubt by the former word: because that coming upon (ἐπίλευσις) is not idle, but operative, and by the force of the underlying matter brings about that operation in the womb of the virgin Mary, by which she could conceive without male agency: Namely, the Spirit comes upon her, not indeed spermatically, but creatively, the blood droplets of Mary, from which the flesh of the Lord was to be conceived by sanctifying, by rendering them fruitful, and by forming from them a human body, which coming upon (ἐπίλευσις) is analogous to the word מרחפת. Therefore, the latter word, overshadowing (ἐπισκιάσει σοι ἡ δύναμις), does not designate the action of the Holy Spirit himself, but of the power of the Most High, which he distinguishes from the Holy Spirit, and implies that it is likewise distinct from that. For in such a vigorous explanation of this mystery, the angel is not to be considered to say the same thing or almost the same thing twice. And therefore by the power of the Most High we more correctly understand the Son of GOD, who comes by this name in 1 Cor. I. 24, just as a son is otherwise also called the power of his Father, Gen. XLIX. 3, Deut. XXI. 7. Who by his overshadowing (ἐπισκιάσων) filled the body formed by the Holy Spirit with his majesty, through hypostatic union and communication, inasmuch as it was brought about that the fullness of divine majesty filled the flesh of Christ, and dwells in it bodily (σωματικῶς) Col. II. 9, of which there was once some figure in the tabernacle of the covenant, as also in the temple of Solomon, which, when both were built, the divine majesty filled through an overshadowing (ἐπισκιασμὸν) and a certain clouding over, Ex. XL. 35, 1 Kings VIII. 10, where the word ἐπισκιασμὸν is likewise used by the LXX interpreters in Exodus concerning the typical cloud, through which the glory of the Lord filled the tabernacle, cf. Heb. I. 3. Thus the Holy Fathers in the Latin and Greek Church explained the words of the Angel. From these we first present Gregory of Nyssa in his oration on the day of the Nativity of Christ: But the power of the Most High will overshadow thee. What does this mysterious discourse signify? Christ is the power and wisdom of God, as the Apostle says. Therefore the power of the Most High, which is Christ, is formed in the Virgin through the coming of the Holy Spirit. For just as a shadow is fashioned according to the figure of the preceding bodies, so the form and indication of the divinity of God will be shown in the power of him who is born, and the image, and the sign, and the adumbration, and the splendor of the exemplar will be demonstrated through the admirable effectuation of things. Next we also produce Damascene, book III of the Orthodox Faith, ch. 2: The substantial wisdom and power of God the Most High, the Son of God, consubstantial with the Father, overshadowed her; he overshadowed her. From those Latin Fathers, Gregory the Great, book XXX, ch. 3, has it thus. Because a shadow is not expressed otherwise than through light and a body, the power of the Most High overshadowed the virgin, because in her womb incorporeal light assumed a body. And book XVIII of the Morals, ch. 12: A shadow, however, is formed by light and a body: but the Lord is light through his divinity, who deigned to be made in the womb of the virgin through the soul by means of a body of humanity. Because, therefore, incorporeal light was to be embodied in the womb of the virgin, it is said to her who conceived the incorporeal one for the body, the power of the Most High will overshadow thee, that is, the incorporeal light of divinity will receive in thee a body of humanity. We also add Bede in his homily on the Annunciation. who says, The Sun, that is, the divinity of Christ, covered itself with the covering of human nature as if with a certain shade, by means of which the womb of the virgin would suffice to bear him, and thus the power of the Most High overshadowed her, while the divine power of Christ both filled her presently, and so that it could be grasped by her, it clouded itself with the substance of our mortality. Franc. Gomarus brings forward a new explanation, that the power of the Most High was going to protect and defend Mary: which he thinks was done when Joseph was thinking of deserting her. But that was not the question here; where Mary was rather inquiring how this could happen, that she might both conceive while preserving her virginity, and bear the Son of the Most High? The former of which the Angel taught would happen through the coming upon (ἐπέλευσιν) of the Holy Spirit, the latter through the overshadowing (ἐπισκιασμὸν) of the Power of the Most High.

Therefore also that which is born of thee shall be called holy, the Son of God] I judge that that 'of thee' (ἐκ σοῦ) must be entirely retained. For besides the Syrian, the Arab also acknowledges it, and ancient writers, Irenaeus book III. 26, Tertullian against Praxeas, Novatian on the Trinity: and after these Epiphanius against the Ebionites. It is credible that it was introduced by the Eutychians, a sect afterwards long dominant, whose opinion this passage strongly opposed. I think, however, that the present is used for the future, 'that which is born', that is, 'that which shall be born', as in Matthew II. 4. For if it were a matter of conception, it would rather have been said 'in thee' (ἐν σοὶ), as in Matt. I. 20, 'that which is born in her'. And Luke used 'to be born' (γεννᾷν) concerning birth also above in verse 13, and below in XXIII. 39, and Acts VII. 20. But also Paul, Gal. IV. 4, says Christ was 'born of a woman' (γενόμενον ἐκ γυναικὸς), where 'to become' (γίνεσθαι) is the same as 'to be born' (γεννᾶσθαι), as in Plato when he says 'each of us was not born for himself alone' (οὐχ αὑτῷ μόνον γέγονε), not 'has become' for himself alone, as Cicero translates. Moreover, that which was to be born of Mary is called holy, because it was exempt from the common law of human origin. The same, says the Angel, shall be called the Son of God; naturally as the second Adam. For the first Adam is also called the son of God, Luke 3:38, because God performed in him what fathers perform in others. Justin in his dialogue with Trypho: 'that from above and through a human womb God was about to beget him according to the will of the Father of all.' Moreover, that 'and' is a connection of lower things with higher ones. For what Novatian brings to this passage is more subtle than is consistent with the simplicity of the words. Nor are there lacking better arguments by which that very thing which he intends may be proved.

That ἐκ σοῦ is deservedly asserted, which is entirely genuine, which besides the cited authors, Cyprian also, book II of Testimonies against the Jews, Jerome on this passage, Athanasius, Vol. I, Epistle to Epictetus, likewise against heresies, pp. 580, 882, adduce. Whence not only the ancient Eutychian heretics, but also the modern Weigelians and Anabaptists, who dream that the flesh of Christ did not originate from the substance of the Virgin Mary, but was I know not what heavenly thing, are solidly refuted by this little word. Nor is there any reason why we should doubt that the conception is being discussed here, even if the preposition ἐκ is used. For the conception took place not only in the womb of Mary, but also from Mary: because the flesh of Christ was formed from the bloody drops of Mary, and not indeed brought down from heaven. So that there is no need to take the present for the future. But as for the comparison with Luke 3:38, Christ is called the Son of God in one way, Adam in another: the latter by creation; the former not by conception from the Holy Spirit, as the Socinians and Arminians wish, but by eternal generation from the Father: Psalm 2:7.

Nor is it deduced here from that conception which took place through the Holy Spirit that that holy thing is to be the Son of God, but just as that holy thing began to be holy through the conception, when indeed it was conceived in Mary, so that that holy thing conceived in and from Mary should be the Son of God, the overshadowing of the power of the Most High brought it about. For when the Son of God, the hypostatic power of God the Father, assumed that body, conceived by the power of the Holy Spirit, into the unity of his person, Therefore that holy thing was truly the Son of GOD by, and because of the hypostatic union of the divine and human nature. And thus the inference (διὸ καὶ) holds correctly. Compare what we have said against the Socinians in our Anti-Crellius regarding this passage. That GOD provided in the generation of Christ what the Fathers provide in others, we have refuted in the Socinians in our Socinismus profligatus. He was conceived, says Justin Martyr in Apolog. c. II. for the Christians, 8 διὰ συνουσίας ἀλλὰ διὰ δυνάμεως, not by intercourse, but by the power of the Holy Spirit, through which Mary was made pregnant. He was conceived, says Augustine, serm. VI. de tempore, not from the substance of the Holy Spirit, but from the power, and not by generation, but by command and blessing. Vers. 36. καὶ ἰδὲ] As if he were to say, do not doubt that God uses new methods of acting for this great renewal of things, behold a domestic example for you. But by how much less of a miracle it is in the birth of a sterile old woman than in the birth of a virgin, by so much will your birth be greater than that one. ἕκτος ἐστὶν] At which time the certain signs of a pregnant womb are accustomed to show themselves: thus a visible sign is given for the strengthening of the virgin's confidence, as was done for Hezekiah of old. Τῇ καλουμένῃ στείρᾳ] Καλεῖσθαι in Hebrew idiom signifies the fame of a thing with the thing itself. See what we wrote on Matt. c. I. Vers. 37. ὅτι] An explanatory particle for things passed over in silence, which we have also observed elsewhere. For the things that precede look toward Mary believing more firmly: the reason why this should happen is rendered here. οὐκ ἀδυνατήσει παρὰ τῷ Θεῷ πᾶν ῥῆμα] I think this sentiment does not pertain only to promises, but that the infinite omnipotence of God is indicated, just as the Syrian also understood it. For it is a proverb worn by the usage of the Hebrews, לא יפלא ממך כל דבר, which the LXX translate as οὐ μὴ ἀποκρυφῇ ἀπό σου οὐδὲ Jerem. XXXII. 27. The interpreter of Matthew expressed the same thing thus: παρὰ δὲ Θεῷ δυνατά ἐστι c. XIX. 16. whom Mark follows X. 27. & XIV. 36. We have cited elsewhere the verses of Linus, Epicharmus, and Callimachus to the same sentiment. Nor should it deter us from this interpretation that GOD is said to be unable to violate a given faith, and similar things. For the thing itself teaches that universal expressions ought not to be extended to those things which, with the name of God understood, ought to be understood as excluded. Origen well says against: Δύναται καθ' ἡμᾶς πάντα ὁ Θεὸς ἅπερ δυνάμενος τῷ Θεὸς εἶναι καὶ τῷ ἀγαθὸς εἶναι καὶ σοφὸς εἶναι οὐκ ἐξίσταται· ὁ δὲ κελσος φησιν (ὡς μὴ νοήσας πῶς λέγεται ὁ Θεὸς πάντα δύνασθαι, ὅτι οὐκ ἠθελήσει κἂν ἄδικον διδὰς) ὅτι δύναται μὲν καὶ τὸ ἄδικον, οὐ θέλει δὲ· ἡμεῖς, δὲ φαμὲν ὅτι ὥσπερ οὐ δύναται τὸ πεφυκὸς γλυκαίνειν τῷ γλυκὺ τυγχάνειν πικράζειν παρὰ τὴν αὐτῷ μόνην αἰτίαν, οὐδὲ τὸ πεφυκὸς φωτίζειν τῷ εἶναι φῶς σκοτίζειν, οὕτως οὐδὲ ὁ Θεὸς δύναται ἀδικεῖν· ἐναντίον γάρ ἐστιν αὐτῷ τῇ θεότητι καὶ τῇ κατ' αὐτὴν πάσῃ δυνάμει ἡ τοῦ ἀδικεῖν δύναμις. The same author in the same disputation in book IV says that that πᾶν δυνατὸν τῷ Θεῷ must be understood not concerning non-existent things nor concerning inconceivable things; but we say, he adds, even that God cannot do shameful things, since God would be able not to be God, alluding to the well-known verse of Euripides: εἰ θεοί τι δρῶσιν αἰσχρὸν οὐκ εἰσιν θεοὶ. Isidorus Pelusiota, to the question εἰ Θεῷ πάντα δυνατὰ, briefly answered: all things that are fitting for Him. Vers. 38. ἰδοὺ ἡ δούλη κυρίου] A Hebrew expression denoting a purpose of obedience. Thus Samuel to Eli 1 Sam. III. 6. & 8. ἰδοὺ ἐγώ. And soon to God: λάλει κύριε, ὅτι ἀκούει ὁ δοῦλός σου. γένοιτό μοι] The virgin does not only consent, but also desires, by an excellent example of confidence. Nor is there doubt that the promise began to be fulfilled simultaneously with the consent and desire, so that in this part also Mary might bear the person of the Christians. Wherefore also after this statement the Angel departs, as if having completed his mission, as has been not poorly noted by the ancients.

PART IV.

The Visitation of Elizabeth, and the Hymn of Mary.

Latin:

Vers. 35. πνεῦμα ἅγιον ἐπελεύσεται ἐπὶ σε] Sic Actor. I. 8. Λήψεσθε δύναμιν ἐπελθόντος τοῦ ἁγίου πνεύματος: quod alibi dixerat hic noster Evang. c. XXIV. 49. ἕως ἂν ἐνδύσησθε δύναμιν ἐξ ὕψους.

καὶ δύναμις ὑψίστου] Vide quæ supra diximus ad Comma 17.

ἐπισκιάσει σοι] Solent quidem LXX. סכך vertere ἐπισκιάζειν ut Ps. XCI. 4. CXL. 8. & alibi. Magis tamen mihi placet sententia putantium tralationem sumtam ab avibus pullos excludentibus, à qua non longe abit Theophylactus: ut ita ostendat Angelus ea virtute oriturum hunc fœtum, qua mundus ipse exordium sumsit. Nam in Mosis historia est ורוח אלהים מרחפת על־פני המים quod verbum מרחפת de tali incubitu exponunt Hebræorum doctissimi. Et aperte est is ejusdem verbi usus Deut. XXXII. 11. ubi LXX. σκεπάσας pari significatu.

Ad comma 17. hanc regulam tradiderat: Quo- ties δύναμις nominatur Spiritu nominato vis quæ- dam Spiritus solita major indicatur Actor. X. 38. 1. Cor. II. 4. 1. Thess. I. 1. Sed ea particularis est, & huc non quadrat: ubi non de virtute Spiritus S. solita majori, sed de virtute DEI Patris, qui nomine altissimi designatur, sermo est, ac virtus non ἀνυ- πόσατος, sed αὐθυπόσατος indicatur: cui actio personalis tribuitur: æque uti Gen. I. 2. Spiritum intelligere αὐθυπόσατον, ipsammet Spiritus Sancti personam oportet propter actionem ei tributam. Actiones enim suppositorum, & personarum sunt. Quum vero hoc loco distincte Gabriel agat de ἐπελεύσει τῶ πνεύματος ἁγίε & de ἐπισκια- σμῶ τῶ δυνάμεως ὑψίσε, actionem Spiritus Sancti sine dubio priori voce expressit: quia ἐπίλευσις il- la non est otiosa, sed operosa, & vi materiæ substra- tæ infert operationem illam in utero Mariæ virgi- nis, qua ipsa concipere sine virili opera poterat: Nimirum supervenit Spiritus non quidem σπερ- ματικῶς, sed δημιεργικῶς guttulas sanguineas Ma- riæ, è quibus concipienda caro Domini sanctifican- do, easdem fæcundas reddendo, & ex iisdem corpus hu- manum efformando, quæ ἐπίλευσις verbo מרחפת analoga est. Posterior itaq; verbo ἐπισκιάσει σοι ἡ δύ- ipsius Spiritus Sancti actionem, sed virtutis altissi- mi, quam à Spiritu Sancto distinguit, designat, eam- que ab illa distinctam itidem esse innuit. Non e- nim in tam nervosa mysterii hujus explicatione angelus idem aut pene idem bis dicere censendus est. Ideoque per virtutem altissimi Filium DEI re- ctius intelligimus, qui hoc nomine venit 1. Cor. I. 24. quemadmodum filius alias etiam virtus Patris sui dicitur Gen. XLIX. 3. Deut. XXI. 7. Qui ἐπισκιά- σων suo corpus à S. S. efformatum majestate sua implevit, per unionem & communicationem hy- postaticam, utpote qua factum est, ut plenitudo majestatis divinæ impleevit carnem Christi, & in ea habitet σωματικῶς Col. II. 9. cujus aliqua figura olim fuit in tabernaculo fœderis, ut & in templo Salomonico, quod utrumque cum exstructum es- set, majestas divina per ἐπισκιασμὸν & obumbra- tionem aliquam adimplverit Ex. X. 35. 1. Reg. VIII. 10. ubi pariter verbum ἐπισκιασμὸν adhibetur à LXX. Interpp. in Exod. de nube typica, per quam δόξα κυρίε ἐνεπλήσθη ἡ σκηνὴ, Conf. Ebr. I. 3. Ita ex- plicarunt verba Angeli S. Patres in Latina & Græca Ecclesia. Ex his primum Gregorium Nyssenum ora- tione in diem Natal. Christi sistimus: Sed & virtus altissimi obumbrabit tibi. Quid significat arcanus hic sermo? Christus DEI virtus est & sapientia, ut ait Apostolus. Virtus igitur Altissimi, quæ Christus est, per adventum Spirit. S. formatur in Virgine. Quem- admodum enim umbra ad præcedentium corporum figuram effingitur, sic forma & indicium divinitatis DEI in virtute ipsius, qui paritur, ostendetur, & i- mago, & signum, & adumbratio, & splendor exem- plaris per admirabilem rerum effectionem demon- strabitur. Deinde etiam Damascenum producimus l. III. de Orthodox. fid. c. 2. ἐπισκίασεν ἐπὶ αὐτὼ ἡ τῶ θεῶ ὑψίσε ἀυθυπόσατος σοφία κὶ δύναμις ὁ ὑὸς τῶ θεῶ, ὁ τῶ πατρὶ ὁμούσιος; obumbravit eum Dei altissimi substantialis sapientia & potentia, Filius Dei Patri coëffentialis. Ex illis Latinis Patribus Grego- rius M. l. XXX. c. 3. ita habet. Quia umbra non aliter exprimitur, nisi per lumen & corpus, virtus altissimi virgini obumbravit, quia in ejus utero lux incorpo- rea corpus assumsit. Et l. XVIII. Moral. c. 12. Umbra autem lumine formatur, & corpore: Dominus au- tem per divinitatem lumen est, qui mediante anima à in utero virginis fieri dignatus est per humanitatis corpus. Quia ergo lumen incorporeum in virginis utero erat corporandum, ei quæ incorporeum concepit ad corpus, dicitur, virtus Altissimi obumbrabit tibi, id est, corpus in te humanitatis accipiet incorporeum lumen divinitatis. Addimus & Bedam in homil. de annunc. qui, Sol, inquit, id est, divinitas Christi te- gmine se humanæ naturæ quasi umbraculo quodam obtexit, quo mediante virginis eum viscera ferre suf- ficerent, sicque virtus Altissimi obumbravit ei, dum divina Christi potentia & eam præsentialiter imple- vit, & ut capi posset ab ea, substantia se nostræ morta- litatis obnubilavit. Franc. Gomarus novam adfert explicationem, quod potentia Altissimi Mariam protectura sit, & defensura: quod factum putat cum Josephus eam deserere cogitaret. Sed de eo non erat hic quæstio; ubi Maria potius sciscitabatur, quo- modo hoc fieri possit, ut ipsa & salva virginitate concipiat, & Filium Altissimi pariat? quorum prius Angelus futurum docuit per Spiritus S. ἐπέ- λευσιν, posterius per Virtutis Altissimi ἐπισκιασμὸν.

διὸ καὶ τὸ γεννώμενον ἐκ σοῦ ἅγιον κληθήσεται υἱὸς Θεοῦ] Illud ἐκ σοῦ omnino retinendum censeo. Nam præter Syrum Arabs quoque agnoscit, & veteres scriptores, Irenæus l. III. 26. Tertullianus adversus Praxeam, Novatianus de Trinitate: & post hos Epiphanius contra Ebionæos. Credibile est in- ductum ab Eutychæis secta postea diu præpotente, cujus sententiæ valide hic locus adversabatur. Puto autem præ- sens pro futuro positum, quod nascitur, id est, quod nasce- tur, ut Matthæi II. 4. Nam si de conceptione ageretur, po- tius dictum esset ἐν σοὶ, ut apud Matth. I 20. τὸ ἐν αὐτῇ γεν- νηθέν. Et γεννᾷν de partu etiam supra commate 13. usurpa- vit Lucas, & infra XXIII. 39. & Act. VII. 20. Sed & Pau- lus Gal. IV. 4. Christum dicit γενόμενον ἐκ γυναικὸς, ubi γίνεσθαι idem est, quod γεννᾶσθαι, ut Platoni cum dicit ἕκαστος ἡμῶν οὐχ αὑτῷ μόνον γέγονε, non sibi soli natus est, ut vertit Cicero. ἅγιον autem dicitur id, quod ex Maria erat nasciturum, quia exemtum communi legi humanæ originis. Id ipsum, inquit Angelus, filius DEI vocabitur; nimirum ut secun- dus Adam. Nam & primus Adam DEI filius dicitur Luc. III. 38. quia DEUS in illo præstitit quod in aliis præstant pa- tres. Justinus colloquio cum Tryphone: ὅτι ἄνωθεν καὶ διὰ γαστρὸς ἀνθρωπείας ὁ Θεὸς κατὰ πατρὸς τῶν ὅλων γεννᾷν αὐτὸν ἔμελλε. Illud autem καὶ connexio est inferiorum cum superio- ribus. Nam quod in hunc locum Novatianus adfert, ar- gutius est, quam ut verborum simplicitati conveniat. Ne- que desunt meliora argumenta, quibus id ipsum probetur quod ille intendit.

Merito adseritur illud ἐκ σοῦ, quod omninoyνή- σιον est, quod præter citatos Autores etiam Cypria- nus l. II. testim. contr. Judæos. Hieronymus in h. l. Athanaf. Tom. I. Epist.ad Epictet.item contr. hæ- ref. p. 580. 882. adducunt. Unde non veteres hære- tici Eutychiani tantum, sed & hodierni Weigelia- ni, ac Anabaptistæ, qui carnem Christi non è Ma- riæ virginis substantia oriundam, sed cælestem, nescio quam, somniant, solide hac vocula refellun- tur. Non est autem causa, cur hic de conceptione agi dubitemus, etiamsi præpositio ἐκ adhibeatur. Nam non tantum in Mariæ utero, sed etiam ex Maria conceptio facta est: quia caro Christi è Ma- riæ sanguineis guttis efformata, non vero cælo deducta. Ut ita non opus sit præsens accipere pro futuro. Quod vero ad collationem Luc. III. 38. longe aliter Christus Filius DEI dicitur, aliter A- dam: hic per creationem: ille non per conceptio- nem è S. S. uti Sociniani & Arminiani volunt, sed per æternam à Patre generationem: Pf. II. 7.

Neque hic è conceptione illa per S.S. facta de- ducitur, quod sanctum illud Filius DEI futurus sit, sed uti τὸ ἅγιον sanctum illud esse cœpit per conceptionem, cum nempe conceptum in Ma- ria est, ita ut sanctum illud in & è Maria conce- ptum Filius DEI esset, effecit ἐπισκιασμὸς virtu- tis Altissimi. Quum enim Filius DEI, virtus hy- postatica DEI Patris, corpus illud, virtute S. S. conceptum, assumserit in unitatem personæ suæ, ideo sanctum illud vere fuit Filius DEI per, & pro- pter divine & humane naturæ unionem hypostati- cam. Atque ita recte se habet illatio διὸ καὶ). Conf. quæ adversus Socinianos in Anti-Crellio nostro de hoc loco diximus. DEUM in Christi generatio- ne præstitisse, quod in aliis præstant Patres in Soci- nianis refutavimus in Socinismo profligato. Conce- ptus est, inquit, Justinus Martyr. in Apolog. c. II. pro Christian. 8 διὰ συνουσίας ἀλλὰ διὰ δυνάμε- ως, non per concubitum, sed per virtutem S. S. per quam Maria prægnans reddita est. Conceptus est, ait Augustin. serm. VI. de tempore, non de substan- tia S. S. sed de potentia, nec generatione, sed jussione & benedictione. Vers. 36. καὶ ἰδὲ] Quasi dicat, ne dubites ad magnam hanc rerum renovationem uti Deum novis agendi rationi- bus, en domesticum tibi exemplum, Quanto autem minus est miraculum in partu anus sterilis, quam in partu virgi- nis, tanto tuus partus illo erit major. ἕκτος ἐστὶν] Quo tempore certa solent se prodere indicia prægnantis uteri: ita confirmandæ virginis fiduciæ signum datur aspectabile, ut Ezechias olim. Τῇ καλουμένῃ στείρᾳ] Καλεῖσθαι in Hebræa locutione cum re significat fama n rei. Vide quæ ad Matth. c. I. Vers. 37. ὅτι] Αἰτιολογικὸν τῶν σιωπωμένων quod & alibi observavimus. Nam quæ præcedunt, eo spectant ut fir- mius credat Maria: quod cur fieri debeat causa hic reddi- tur. οὐκ ἀδυνατήσει παρὰ τῷ Θεῷ πᾶν ῥῆμα] Puto non ad pro- missa tantum pertinere hanc sententiam, sed infinitam Dei omnipotentiam indicari, quomodo & Syrus accepit. Est e- nim proverbium tritum usu Hebræorum, לא יפלא ממך כל דבר, quod LXX. vertunt οὐ μὴ ἀποκρυφῇ ἀπό σου οὐδὲ Jerem. XXXII. 27. Idem ita extulit Matthæi interpres παρὰ δὲ Θεῷ δυνατά ἐστι c. XIX. 16. quem sequitur Marcus X. 27. & XIV. 36. Citavimus alibi Lini, Epicharmi & Callimachi versus in eandem sententiam. Neque abster- rere nos ab hac interpretatione debet, quod DEUS di- citur fidem datam violare non posse, & similia. Nam res ipsa docet universales locutiones extendi non debere ad ea quæ nomine Dei intellecto exclusa intelligi debent. Bene Origenes adversum : Δύναται καθ' ἡμᾶς πάντα ὁ Θεὸς ἅπερ δυνάμενος τῷ Θεὸς εἶναι καὶ τῷ ἀγαθὸς εἶναι καὶ σο- φὸς εἶναι οὐκ ἐξίσταται· ὁ δὲ κελσος φησιν (ὡς μὴ νοήσας πῶς λέγεται ὁ Θεὸς πάντα δύνασθαι, ὅτι οὐκ ἠθελήσει κἂν ἄδικον διδὰς) ὅτι δύναται μὲν καὶ τὸ ἄδικον, οὐ θέλει δὲ· ἡμεῖς, δὲ φα- μὲν ὅτι ὥσπερ οὐ δύναται τὸ πεφυκὸς γλυκαίνειν τῷ γλυκὺ τυγχάνειν πικράζειν παρὰ τὴν αὐτῷ μόνην αἰτίαν, οὐδὲ τὸ πε- φυκὸς φωτίζειν τῷ εἶναι φῶς σκοτίζειν, οὕτως οὐδὲ ὁ Θεὸς δύ- ναται ἀδικεῖν· ἐναντίον γάρ ἐστιν αὐτῷ τῇ θεότητι καὶ τῇ κατ' αὐτὴν πάσῃ δυνάμει ἡ τοῦ ἀδικεῖν δύναμις. Idem & Scriptor in eadem disputatione libro IV. ait illud πᾶν δυνατὸν τῷ Θεῷ intelligendum esse ἐκ ἐπὶ τῶν ἀνυπάρκτων ἠδ' ἐπὶ τῶν ἀ- διανοήτων φαμὲν δὲ, adjicit, κᾀν ὅτι οὐ δύναται αἰσχρὰ ὁ Θεὸς, ἐπεὶ ἔσται ὁ Θεὸς δυνάμενος μὴ εἶναι Θεὸς, alludens ad no- tum Euripidis versum: εἰ θεοί τι δρῶσιν αἰσχρὸν οὐκ εἰσιν θεοὶ. Isidorus Pelusiota ad quæstionem εἰ Θεῷ πάντα δυνατὰ, breviter respondit πάντα τὰ πρέποντα αὐτῷ. Vers. 38. ἰδοὺ ἡ δούλη κυρίου] Locutio Hebræa obedien- tiæ propositum notans. Ita Samuel ad Heli 1. Sam. III. 6. & 8. ἰδοὺ ἐγώ. Et mox ad Deum: λάλει κύριε, ὅτι ἀκούει ὁ δοῦ- λός σου γένοιτό μοι] Non consentit tantum virgo, sed & deside- rat, eximio fiduciæ exemplo. Nec dubium quin simul cum consensu & desiderio impleri promissio cœperit, ut hac quoque in parte personam Christianorum Maria gere- ret. Quare & post hoc dictum discedit Angelus, ut peracta legatione, quemadmodum à veteribus non male nota- tum est.

PARS IV.

Visitatio Elisabethæ, & Hymnus Mariæ.

## 1:39
Vers. 39. ἀναστᾶσα] A redundant word, as also below IV. 28. And not otherwise 1 Macc. XII. 40. c. XIII. 24. μετὰ σπουδῆς] Lest she should neglect the sign which God had assigned for the increasing of her own confidence. εἰς πόλιν ἰούδα] I accede to the opinion of those who judge that Hebron is signified. For πόλις, like the Hebrew קִירְיָה, is accustomed to be placed so as to signify a metropolis. And indeed Jerusalem was the head of the kingdom, but Hebron was the principal city of the portion of Judah, as is gathered from 2 Sam. II.

Latin:

Vers. 39. ἀναστᾶσα] Vox παρέλκουσα, ut & infra IV. 28. Nec aliter 1. Macc. XII. 40. c. XIII. 24. μετὰ σπουδῆς] Ne negligeret signum quod augendæ ipsius fiduciæ Deus assignaverat. εἰς πόλιν ἰούδα] Accedo eorum sententiæ qui Hebronem significari judicant. Nam πόλις, ut Hebræum קִירְיָה ita so- let poni, ut significet μητρόπολιν. Et erat quidem Hieroso- lyma caput regi, At peculiariter portionis Judæ urbs præcipua Hebron, ut colligitur 2. Sam. II.

## 1:41
Vers. 41. ἐσκίρτησε] Physicians are indeed accustomed to denote by this word the natural movement of an infant in the womb, which for others is ἀσκιαρίζειν. But to me it seems certain that this movement was not natural but divinely procured: just like that collision of the infants in the womb of Rebecca. For both this and that had a mystical meaning.

There is no need for conjectures or arguments where the Holy Spirit Himself explains what that leap was: which indeed was done in v. 44. For it is clearly taught that the infant leaped at the presence of the Messiah, not by natural movement, but by ἀγαλλιάσει, spiritual exultation, when the salutation of Mary was heard by Elizabeth. Nor could Grotius deny this: This, he says, Elizabeth seems to indicate, that just as infants in the womb naturally leap when delighted by warmth, so, without a natural cause and in a non-natural way, her infant leaped. But that Grotius understands only gesticulation by the word ἀγαλλιάσει, such as is accustomed to be in those who are rejoicing, and not true joy, that does not agree with the propriety of the word, from which it is by no means right to depart. For that word imports joy of the mind: nor is the verb ἀγαλλιάομαι understood otherwise than as joy of the mind a little later in v. 47, or anywhere in the New Testament. See Matt. V. 12. Luke X. 21. John V. 35. c. VIII. 56. Acts II. 26. c. XVI. 34. 1 Pet. I. 8. c. IV. 13. Rev. XIX. 7. or even the noun ἀγαλλίασις. See Luke I. 14. Acts II. 46. Heb. I. 9. Jude v. 24. in all of which places there is no doubt that it is taken for joy of the soul, and almost for spiritual gladness. Why, therefore, must a new meaning of Scripture be invented here, one clearly unusual? The leaping of the body had already been expressed by the word ἐσκίρτησε: here, however, the affection and joy of the soul is expressed. Whence Grotius wrongly denies the use of reason to our little John: who, even if it does not naturally befit infants enclosed in the womb, yet in a supernatural way, as he acknowledges this leaping took place, who would doubt that joy of the soul could also be excited? Therefore, against the Calvinists, Socinians, and Anabaptists who deny faith to infants, we prove from this example that GOD can entirely excite faith in their tender souls: which indeed He actually excited in John while still enclosed in the womb. For joy and spiritual exultation is an effect of faith. But although we are ignorant of the τὸ πῶς, that is, how infants believe, yet because of our ignorance of the mode of the thing, the thing itself is by no means to be denied: since GOD can do ὑπὲρ ἐκ περισσῦ [exceedingly] beyond all that we ask or think, Eph. III. 20, and with Him nothing is impossible, Luke I. 37.

Latin:

Vers. 41. ἐσκίρτησε] Solent quidem medici hoc verbo notare motum naturalem infantis in utero, quod ἀσκιαρίζειν est aliis. Mihi autem certum videtur motum hunc non naturalem sed divinitus fuisse procuratum: perinde ut collisionem illam infantium in Rebeccæ utero. Nam & hoc & illud μυστικὴν habuit ὑπόνοιαν.

Non conjecturis, aut rationibus opus, ubi Spiritus S. ipse explicat, quasi saltus ille fuerit: quod vero v. 44. factum. Non enim naturali motu, sed ἀγαλλιάσει exultatione Spirituali subsiliisse infantem ad præsentiam Messiæ, audita ab Elisabetha salutatione Mariæ, diserte docetur. Nec id diffiteri potuit Grotius: Hoc, inquit, videtur indicare Elisabet, sicut infantes in utero calore delectati naturaliter subsultant, ita citra causam naturalem, & modo non naturali infantem suum subsultasse. Quod autem Grotius tantum gesticulationem per vocem ἀγαλλιάσει intelligit, qualis scil. esse solet lætantium, non vero lætitiam, id proprietati vocis non convenit, à qua fas minime est discedere. Illa enim lætitiam animi importat: nec aliter verbum ἀγαλλιάομαι quam de lætitia animi accipitur paulo post v. 47. aut uspiam in N. Testam. Vid. Matth. V. 12. Luc. X. 21. Joh. V. 35. c. VIII. 56. Act. II. 26. c. XVI. 34. 1. Petr. I. 8. c. IV. 13. Ap. XIX. 7. aut etiam nomen ἀγαλλίασις. Vid. Luc. I. 14. Act. II. 46. Ebr. I. 9. Jud. v. 24. in quibus locis omnibus de gaudio animi, & fere de lætitia spirituali accipi nullum est dubium. Cui ergo nova hic fingenda significatio Scripturæ, plane inusitata? Subsultatio corporis jam per verbum ἐσκίρτησε expressa erat: hic vero affectus & gaudium animi exprimitur. Unde perperam denegat Grotius usum rationis Johannulo nostro: qui etsi infantibus utero conclusis non conveniat naturaliter, supernaturali tamen modo, ut hanc subsultationem factam agnoscit, etiam lætitiam animi excitari potuisse, quis dubitaret? Ideo contra Calvinianos, Socinianos, & Anabaptistas infantibus fidem derogantes, ab hoc Exemplo probamus, posse omnino DEUM in tenellulis eorum animis fidem excitare: quam utique in Johanne utero adhuc concluso reipsa excitavit. Nam lætitia, & exultatio spiritualis effectus est fidei. Etsi autem τὸ πῶς ignoremus, quomodo scilicet infantes credant, ob ignorantiam tamen nostram modi rei res ipsa neganda minime est: quum DEUS ὑπὲρ ἐκ περισσῦ facere possit ὑπὲρ πάντα ὧν αἰτῶμεθα ἢ νοῦμεν Ephes. III. 20. & apud eum nihil sit impossibile Luc. I. 37.

## 1:42
Vers. 42. Blessed art thou among women] She uses the very words of the Angel, so that it may appear she was moved by the same God. And blessed is the fruit of thy womb] These are the words of Deuteronomy ברוך פרי בטנך c. XXVIII. 4. Elizabeth therefore shows that the promises of the law are now being fulfilled excellently and above the common sense.

Latin:

Vers. 42. ἐυλογημένη σὺ ἐν γυναιξὶ] Ipsa verba Angeli usurpat, ut ab eodem Deo motam appareat. καὶ ἐυλογημένΘ ὁ καρπὸς τῆς κοιλίας σε] Sunt verba Deuteronomi ברוך פרי בטנך c. XXIV. 8. Ostendit ergo Elisabet legis promissiones nunc excellenter & supra communem sensum impleri.

## 1:43
Vers. 43. Whence is this to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me] Preluding the modesty of the son who would one day say to Christ, 'comest thou to me?' Matt. III. 14. She calls the Messiah Lord by the example of David, Ps. CX.

Latin:

Vers. 43. πόθεν μοι τῦτο, ἵνα ἔλθῃ ἡ μήτηρ τῦ κυρίυ πρός με] Modestiæ filii præludens qui olim Christo erat dicturus σὺ ἔρχῃ πρός με; Matth. III. 14. Κύριον vocat Messiam exemplo Davidis Ps CX.

## 1:44
Vers. 44. As the voice of thy salutation came into my ears] It is permitted to translate it simply, as it reached the ears. For our writers and other authors often use γενέσθαι for 'to come.' The Syrian uses נפל, 'it fell' to the ears. In exultation] It is accustomed to be transferred to the soul: properly, however, it signifies a gesticulation, such as is wont to be of those rejoicing. And this Elizabeth seems to indicate, that just as infants in the womb, delighted by warmth, naturally leap, so, apart from a natural cause and in a non-natural way, her infant had leaped. But that some infer from this that the use of reason was anticipated in John, seems to me, and indeed to Augustine, not sufficiently correct.

Latin:

Vers. 44. ὡς ἐγένετο ἡ φωνὴ τῶ ἀσπασμῦ σε ἐις τὰ ὦτά μꙋ] Vertere simpliciter licet, ut pervenit ad aures. Nam γενέσθαι pro venire sæpe usurpant nostri & alii Scriptores. Syrus נפל accidit auribus. ἐν ἀγαλλιάσει] Solet ad animum transferri: proprie tamen gesticulationem significat, qualis esse lætantium solet. Atque hoc videtur indicare Elisabet, sicut infantes in utero calore delectati naturaliter subsultant, ita citra causam naturalem & modo non naturali infantem suum subsultasse. Quod autem quidam hinc colligunt rationis usum in Johanne anticipatum, nec Augustino, neque vero mihi satis rectum videtur.

## 1:45
Vers. 45. Blessed is she that believed, for there shall be a performance of those things which were told her from the Lord] I think it is a general statement, but raised from woman to woman in the feminine gender. Blessed is she who believes that those things which were announced to her divinely will have an outcome: as the Syrian takes it. Just as Christ said: 'Blessed are they that hear the word of God and keep it,' see below XI. 28. and 'blessed are those who have not seen and have believed' John XX. 29. A thing believed is usually expressed by ὅτι, as in Matt. IX. 28. Mark XI. 24. But very similar to the phrasing of this passage is that in Mark XI. 23. 'believe that what he says comes to pass.' That παρὰ κυρίε is well interpreted by the Syrian as מן לות מריא.

Latin:

Vers. 45. μακαρία ἡ πιστεύσασα, ὅτι ἔσαι τελείωσις τοῖς λελαλημένοις ἀυτῇ παρὰ κυρίε) Puto generalem esse sententiam, sed à muliere ad mulierem elatam feminino genere. Beata quæ credit exitum habitura ea quæ divinitus ipsi sunt nuntiata: quomodo accipit Syrus. Sicut Christus dixit: μακάριοι οἱ ἀκούοντες τὸν λόγον τῶ Θεῦ καὶ φυλάσσοντες ἀυτὸν infra XI. 28. & μακάριοι οἱ μὴ ἰδόντες κὶ πιστεύσαντες Johan. XX. 29. Solet autem res credita per ὅτι exprimi, ut Matth. IX. 28. Marc XI. 24. Simillima autem hujus loci locutioni est illa apud Marcum XI. 23. πιστεύσῃ ὅτι ἃ λέγει γίνεται. Illud παρὰ κυρίε bene interpretatur Syrus מן לות מריא.

## 1:46
Verse 46. and Mary said] If I understand Origen correctly, he said that in some codices the name of Mary was omitted here, and consequently it was believed by some that this song belonged to Elizabeth: the authority of books, interpreters, and the ancients who use words taken from here refutes them. Hebrews, like other nations, were accustomed to use songs to stir up either joyful or mournful emotions, as can be seen throughout the history of the Old Testament. The writer of the responses to the Orthodox well says: according to the narratives contained in the odes, the rhythms of the melodies were appropriately made, leading souls to the disposition suited to what was being sung. Moreover, the ῥυθμοὶ or rhythms of the Hebrews were not metrical but free from law: of which kind their dances also were, and still are today. This song refers not obscurely to the times of the exodus from Egypt: to which the times of the Messiah were prefigured, with circumstances concurring not without the admirable arrangement of God. There is Mary the prophetess, leader of the female host: and here is Mary overshadowed by the Holy Spirit, to be celebrated above all women. Elizabeth, wife of Aaron, holds the second place there: here is another Elizabeth married to a priest from the lineage of Aaron.

The song of Hannah in 1 Sam. II is especially to be considered; a comparison of both teaches that, while Mary similarly to Hannah exults in her Savior, celebrates the name of the Lord, that is, his power, holiness or justice, and his mercy, and proclaims the rule of God and in it the works of divine power, justice, and grace, she nevertheless refers all these things most especially to the present matter, and to those things which had been announced to her by the Angel and confirmed by Elizabeth. Compare what Grotius annotates here on verses 47 and 48.

my soul magnifies the Lord] Thus in Psalm XXXIV. 4. magnify the Lord with me, in Greek magnify the Lord with me. In songs, the same things are usually expressed by many names, and here she first said soul, then Spirit. Yet the observation of Origen, who referred magnifying to the intellect and exulting to the subsequent emotion, does not seem to be despised.

Latin:

Vers. 46. κὶ εἶπε Μαριὰμ] Si recte Origenem intelligo, hic dixit in quibusdam codicibus omissum Mariæ nomen, ac proinde à quibusdam creditum hoc carmen esse Elisabethæ: quos refellit & librorum & interpretum & veterum qui verbis hinc depromtis utuntur auctoritas. Solebant Hebræi, ut & gentes aliæ, ad movendos affectus aut lætos aut lugubres uti carminibus, ut passim in veteris fœderis historia videre est. Bene scriptor responsionum ad Orthodoxos: κατὰ τὰ ἐν ταῖς ὠδαῖς ἐμφερόμενα διηγήματα ἁρμοδίως οἱ ῥυθμοὶ τῶν μελῶν ἐγίνοντο, ἄγοντες τὰς ψυχὰς εἰς τὴν ποίησαν τοῖς ἀδομένοις αἵρεσιν. Erant autem ῥυθμοὶ sive numeri Hebræorum non ἔμμετροι sed lege soluti: cujusmodi etiam erant, & nunc quoque sunt ipsorum saltationes. Respicit hoc carmen non obscure ad tempora exitus ex Ægypto: quibus tempora Messiæ figurabantur non sine admirabili Dei dispositu congruentibus circumstantiis. Est ibi Maria προφᾶτις dux feminei agminis: & hic Maria obumbrata sancto Spiritu, supra omnes feminas celebranda. Secundas ibi tenet Elisabet Aaronis uxor: hic alia Elisabet nupta Sacerdoti ex Aaronis genere.

Respici imprimis carmen Hannæ 1. Sam. II. collatio utriusque docet, quum Maria similiter ut Hanna in Salutari suo exultet, nomen Domini, hoc est potentiam, sanctitatem vel justitiam, ac misericordiam ejus celebret, & regimen Dei, atque in eo opera divinæ potentiæ, justitiæ & gratiæ deprædicet, hæc tamen omnia maxime referens ad rem præsentem, & ea quæ sibi ab Angelo annunciata, ab Elisabetha confirmata erant. Conf. quæ Grotius hic ad vers. 47. & 48. annotat.

μεγαλύνει ἡ ψυχή με τὸν κύριον] Ita Psalmo XXXIV. 4. גדלו ליהוה אתי Græce μεγαλύνετε τὸν κύριον σὺν ἐμοί. Solent in carminibus res eædem πολυωνύμως exprimi, atque hic prius animam dixit, deinde Spiritum. Neque tamen contemnenda videtur Origenis observatio, qui μεγαλύνειν ad intellectum, ἀγαλλιᾷσθαι ad affectum subsequentem retulit.

## 1:47
Verse 47. my spirit has exulted in God my Savior] Contracted from Psalm XXXIV. 9. where the LXX say, and my soul shall exult in the Lord, it shall rejoice in his salvation. But also in the Song of Hannah: she rejoiced in his salvation. It is the custom of the Hebrews to put the past or future for the present.

Latin:

Vers. 47. ἠγαλλίασε τὸ πνεῦμά με ἐπὶ τῷ Θεῷ τῷ σωτῆρί με] Contractum ex Psalm. XXXIV. 9. ubi LXX. ἡ δὲ ψυχή με ἀγαλλιάσεται ἐπὶ τῷ κυρίῳ, τερφθήσεται ἐπὶ τῷ σωτηρίω αὐτῦ. Sed & in Annæ Cantico: εὐφράνθη ἐν σωτηρίω σε. Præteritum aut futurum pro præsenti ponere mos est Hebræorum.

## 1:48
Verse 48. he has looked upon the lowliness of his handmaid] A most learned man has well noted that lowliness is עני, that is, misery, or at any rate an abject condition, as can be seen in Phil. III. 21. In the Old Testament, besides the passage in Gen. XXIX. 32, there are other illustrious ones where the LXX translate it thus, and indeed where mention is likewise made of looking upon, as 2 Kings XIV. 26. The Lord saw the lowliness of Israel. Psalm XXIV. 18. look upon my lowliness. But the words of Hannah, which I do not doubt are referred to by Mary since she imitates her words in other places as well, are most relevant here. They are thus in Greek: if looking you will look upon the lowliness of your handmaid, 1 Sam. I. 11. whence it is to be understood that what follows there also ought to be referred mystically to Christ. I will give him before you as a gift until the day of his death. Not much differently Valerius Maximus, speaking of himself to Tiberius Caesar, says, my smallness.

all generations will call me blessed] She alludes, but with an addition, to that which Leah had said: women will call me blessed, Gen. XXX. 12.

Latin:

Vers. 48. ἐπέβλεψεν ἐπὶ τὴν ταπέίνωσιν τῆς δέλης αὐτῦ] Bene notavit vir doctissimus ταπέινωσιν esse עני id est, miseriam, aut certe conditionem abjectam, ut Phil. III. 21. videre est. In veteri instrumento præter locum Gen. XXIX. 32. sunt illustres alii, ubi LXX. ita vertunt, & quidem ubi itidem respiciendi fit mentio, ut 2. Reg. XIV. 26. ἗δε κύριος τὴν ταπείνωσιν Ἰσραήλ. Psalmo XXIV. 18. ἴδε τὴν ταπείνωσίν με. Sed maxime huc faciunt Annæ verba quæ non dubito respici a Maria cum & in cæteris ejus verba imitetur. Ea sic habent Græce: ἐὰν ἐπιβλέπων ἐπιβλέψῃς ἐπὶ τὴν ταπέίνωσιν τῆς δύλης σε, I. Sam. I. 11. unde intelligendum, & quæ ibidem sequuntur, ad Christum mystice referri debere. δώσω σεδιὰυτὸν ἐνώπιόν σε δοτὸν ἕως ἡμέρας θανάτε αὐτῦ. Non multo aliter Valerius Maximus de se loquens ad Tiberium Cæsarem, mea, inquit, parvitas.

μακαριῦσι με πᾶσαι αἱ γενεαὶ] Alludit, sed cum augmento, ad id quod Lea dixerat: μακαρίσι με αἱ γυναῖκες Genes. XXX. 12.

## 1:49
V. 49. he has done great things for me] The LXX translate the Hebrew גדלות word for word as great things, as can be seen in Deut. XI. 2. Psalm LXXI. 19. you have done great things for me, where for me is added by the LXX, which passage I think is referred to here. A similar phrasing is in Deuteronomy X. 21. he has done for you the great things, where the LXX say, he has done for you the great things. Luke uses the word great things again in Acts II. 11. The sense is: he has performed great and wonderful things for me. Compare also Psalm CXXVI. 2.
