the Mighty One] That is גבור. For that is an attribute of God, which the LXX translate thus in Psalm XXIV. 8.

as in Ephes. III. 21. Coloss. I. 26. The sense is: that God perpetually and without end does good to those who serve him religiously.

But observe that Mary here uses not a legal phrase, such as is in Exod. 20:6, that He shows grace to those who love Him and keep His commandments: but an Evangelical one, that He shows mercy to those who fear Him: that is, those who humble themselves with true contrition of heart, and fear the wrath of God because of their sins: concerning which contrite and humbled heart see Ps. 51:19, Isa. 57:15, Matt. 5:3, 4, 5, ch. 11:28. And concerning those who thus fear the Lord, Ps. 103:11. Let the Evangelical proclamation of the Son of God be compared, Exod. 34:6, 7.

Latin:

V. 49. ἐποίησέ μοι μεγαλεῖα] LXX. Hebræum גדלות ad verbum transferunt μεγαλεῖα, ut videre est Deut. XI, 2. Psalmo LXXI. 19. עשית גדלות ἐποίησάς μοι μεγαλεῖαν, ubi μοι additum à LXX. quem locum hic respici puto. Similis locutio Deuteron. X. 21. עשה אתך את־הגדלת, ubi LXX. ἐποίησέ σοι τὰ μεγάλα. Utitur voce μεγαλείων Lucas iterum. Act. II 11. Sensus est res magnas & miras mihi præstitit. Confer & Psal. CXXVI. 2.

ὁ δυνατός] Id est גבור. Id enim Dei attributum, ita vertunt LXX. Psal. XXIV. 8.

ut Ephes. III. 21. Coloss. I. 26. Sensus est: Deum perpetuo ac sine fine benefacere iis qui religiose severentur.

Observare vero Mariam hic uti phrasi non legali, qualis est Exod. XX. 6. quod gratiam illis faciat, qui diligunt se, & custodiunt præcepta sua: sed Evangelica, quod misericordiam exhibeat his, qui timent ipsum: hoc est qui vera cordis contritione sese humiliant, iramque Dei ob peccata metuunt: de quo contrito corde & humiliato Psal. LI. 19. Es. LVII. 15. Matth. V. 3. 4. 5. c. XI. 28. Deque timentibus ita Dominum Psal. CIII 11 Con- feratur Evangelica Filii Dei concio, Exod. XXXIV. 6. 7.

## 1:51
Ver. 51. ἐποίησε κράτος ἐν βραχίονι ἀυτῶ] Again, with an augmentation, she has exalted what is in the Psalm, δεξιὰ κυρίε ἐποίησε δύναμιν Ps. 118:15 & 16. The great efficacy of God is indicated by the finger, greater by the hand, greatest by the arm. Compare the passage Exod. 15:16. See Ps. 76:16, 89:14, 97:1, Isa. 40:10, 62:8, Job 40:4. κράτος or δύναμις is called a most powerful work, such as was the virginal conception.

Why we believe she has exalted with an augmentation what is held in Ps. 118:15 & 16, when it is sung there of the victory of infinite virtue obtained in the passion and resurrection of Christ, as we have said regarding that passage. Nor do those degrees have a place in GOD and divine virtue, because His virtue is infinite and ἀμέριστος: and by the finger of GOD, as well as by His right hand, the equally infinite virtue of GOD is designated, as by the arm of GOD. Comp. Luke 11:20. But concerning the meaning of this verse, see the blessed Chemnitius p. 49. What follows, concerning the arm of the Lord, can indeed be understood in general of the power of GOD toward the proud: but it is much more illustrious if it is referred to the places of the Prophets from whence it is taken, where the struggle of the Messiah against the Devil, sin, and death, and His victory, is described. Therefore the Syrian rendered it, He wrought victory, as Isa. 59:16: God saw that there was no man, nor any to interpose: and His own arm brought salvation to Him, and 63:3. I have trodden the winepress alone: I looked around and there was no helper, I sought and there was none to assist, and my arm brought salvation. Moreover, the Messiah is called the arm of the Lord, Isa. 53:1, 52:10. The Lord has prepared His holy arm in the eyes of all the nations: and all the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of our God. So that the sense is: that the Messiah, in crushing our spiritual enemies and delivering us from their hand, would perform with His arm κράτος, which signifies either strength and power, or perhaps a famous, notable deed. Christ is not only called the arm of GOD with respect to the Father, but the divine arm is also attributed to Him, because He is ὁμοούσιος to the Father: and when the Θεοτόκος here celebrates GOD her Savior, whom Elizabeth had professed to be her Lord, she describes His own proper works, and attributes divine virtue to Him by the mention of the arm: because He wrought power by His own virtue.

Διεσκόρπισεν ὑπερηφάνες διανοίᾳ καρδίας ἀυτῶν] It is a part from Ps. 89:11, אתה דכאת כחלל רהב בזרוע עזך פזרת אויביך where they commonly explain רהב as Egypt, since the LXX took it for an adjective, thus they translate it σὺ ἐταπείνωσας ὡς τραυματίαν ὑπερήφανον, ἐν τῷ βραχίονι τῆς δυνάμεώς σε διεσκόρπισας τες ἐχθρές σε. Moreover, there is in the verb διασκορπίζειν almost the same force as in the verb διασκεδάζειν, as appears below ch. 15:13, ch. 16:1, Acts 5:37. Add Matt. 15:24, 26, ch. 26:31, Mark 14:27, John 11:52. But the LXX are accustomed to use διασκεδάζειν where it is a matter of dissipating counsels, which Luke here called διανοίας. 2 Sam. 15:34, διασκεδάσεις μοι τὴν βουλὴν Ἀχιτοφέλ. And Ps. 33:9, which passage seems to be looked back upon here together with the preceding one: διασκεδάζει βουλὰς ἐθνῶν. The sense therefore here is, He has dissipated the proud as far as the counsels of their hearts are concerned. There is an old proverb of the Hebrews which, like many others of that kind, has been preserved for us in the Eclogues of Jesus the son of Sirach, which book we call Ecclesiasticus. The passage is thus in ch. 10:15, ὅτι ἀρχὴ ἁμαρτίας ὑπερηφανία καὶ ὁ κρατῶν ἀυτῆς ἐξυβρίσει βδέλυγμα

and it shall be destroyed unto the end. For this reason the Lord accepted the afflictions and destroyed them unto the end. This very sentiment is what Moses pursues at length in the Epinicion. It was fulfilled, however, when GOD willed the Messiah to be born, not from those who were proud either of the scepter or of the knowledge of the law, but from a virgin of despised lot. And the same is fulfilled daily in the calling of Christians, of which this conception was an image. See Rom. X. 3. Matt. XXIII. 12. To the same point pertains that maxim likewise worn by use, as appears from the writings of two Apostles: GOD opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble. James IV. 6. 1 Pet. V. 5. But Seneca also said: God, the avenger, follows the proud from behind.

Latin:

Vers. 51. ἐποίησε κράτος ἐν βραχίονι ἀυτῶ] Rursum cum augmento extulit quod est in Psalmo δεξιὰ κυρίε ἐποίησε δύναμιν Psal. CXVIII. 15. & 16. Efficacia Dei magna per digitum indicatur, per manum major, per brachium maxima. Confer locum Exod XV. 16. Vide Psal. LXXVI. 16. LXXXIX. 14. XCVII. 1. Es. XL. 10. LXII. 8. Job. XL. 4. κράτος aut δύναμις dicitur opus potentissimum, qualis erat virginalis conceptio.

Cur credamus cum augmento extulisse, quod in Psalmo CXVIII. 15. & 16. habetur, quum ibi de victoria infinitæ virtutis in passione & resurrectio- ne Christi obtenta canatur, ut ad locum illum diximus. Neque in DEO & virtute divina illi gradus locum habent, quia virtus ejus infinita est, & ἀμέριστος: & per digitum DEI, nec non per dextram ejus æque infinita DEI virtus designatur, ac per brachium DEI Conf. Luc. XI. 20. De sententia vero hujus commatis optime B. Chemnitius p. 49. Quod sequitur, de brachio Domini, potest quidem in genere intelligi de potentia DEI erga superbos: sed multo illustrius est, si referatur ad loca Prophetarum unde sumtum est, ubi certamen Messiæ contra Diabolum, peccatum, & mortem, & victoria ejus describitur. Ideo Syrus reddidit, fecit victoriam, ut Es. LIX. v. 16. Vidit DEUS quia non est vir, nec qui se interponat: & salvavit sibi brachium suum, & LXIII. v. 3. Torcular calcavi solus: circumspexi & non erat auxiliator, quæsivi & non fuit qui adjuvaret, & præstitit salutem brachium meum. Vocatur autem Messias brachium Domini, Es. LIII. v. 1. LII. v. 10. Paravit Dominus brachium sanctum suum in oculis omnium gentium: & videbunt omnes fines terræ salutare DEI nostri. Ut sensus sit: Messiam in conterendis hostibus nostris spiritualibus, & liberandis nobis de manu ipsorum, præstiturum brachio suo κράτος, quod vel robur, & potentiam, vel forte, præclarum, insigne facinus significat. Christus non tantum dicitur brachium DEI respectu Patris, sed tribuitur ei etiam brachium divinum, quia est ὁμοούσιος Patri: & quum celebret hic Θεοτόκος DEUM Servatorem suum, quem Dominum suum Elisabetha professa erat, opera ejus propria describit, eique mentione brachii virtutem divinam tribuit: quia propria virtute fecit potentiam.

Διεσκόρπισεν ὑπερηφάνες διανοίᾳ καρδίας ἀυτῶν] Pars est ex Psalmo LXXXIX. 11. אתה דכאת כחלל רהב בזרוע עזך פזרת אויביך ubi רהב vulgo Ægyptum exponunt, cum LXX. sumserint pro adjectivo, ita er im vertunt σὺ ἐταπείνωσας ὡς τραυματίαν ὑπερήφανον, ἐν τῷ βραχίονι τῆς δυνάμεώς σε διεσκόρπισας τες ἐχθρές σε. Est autem in verbo διασκορπίζειν eadem ferme vis quæ in verbo διασκεδάζειν, ut apparet infra c. XV. 13. c. XVI. 1. Act. V. 37. Adde Matth. XV. 24. 26. c. XXVI. 31. Marc. XIV. 27. Johan. XI. 52. διασκεδάζειν autem ponere solent LXX. ubi de dissipandis consiliis, quas hic Lucas διανοίας dixit, agitur. 2. Sam. XV. 34 διασκεδάσεις μοι τὴν βουλὴν Ἀχιτοφέλ. Et Psalm. XXXIII. 9. qui locus hic simul cum illo præcedente videtur respici: διασκεδάζει βουλὰς ἐθνῶν. Sensus ergo hic est, dissipavit superbos quod consilia cordis ipsorum attinet. Vetus est proverbium Hebræorum quod, ut multa alia ejus generis, servatum est nobis in Eclogis Jesu Sirachidæ, quem librum Ecclesiasticum vocamus. Locus ita habet c. X 15. ὅτι ἀρχὴ ἁμαρτίας ὑπερηφανία καὶ ὁ κρατῶν ἀυτῆς ἐξυβρίσει βδέλυγμα

καὶ καταστραφήσεται εἰς τέλος. διὰ τοῦτο παρεδέξατο κύριος τὰς ἐπαγωγὰς καὶ κατέστρεψεν εἰς τέλος αὐτούς. Hæc ipsa sen- tentia est quam in Epinicio late prosequitur Moses. Imple- ta autem est cum DEUS Messiam nasci voluit, non ex iis qui aut sceptro aut legis scientia superbiebant, sed ex virgi- ne contemtæ sortis. Atque idem quotidie impletur in vo- catione Christianorum, cujus imago fuit hæc conceptio. Vide Rom. X. 3. Matth. XXIII. 12. Eodem pertinet illa γνώ- μη itidem usu trita, ut ex duorum Apostolorum Scriptis ap- paret: ὁ Θεὸς ὑπερηφάνοις ἀντιτάσσεται, ταπεινοῖς δὲ δίδωσι χάριν. Jacob. IV. 6. 1. Petr. V. 5. Sed & Seneca dixit: Sequitur superbos ultor à tergo Deus.

## 1:52
Verse 52. He has put down the mighty from their thrones and has exalted the humble] The sentiment is the same as in Ps. CXIII. 6 and 1 Sam. II. 8, where the LXX translate נדיבים as mighty ones. But the words approach more closely to another Hebrew proverb which the son of Sirach exhibits to us in the rubric already mentioned: The Lord has put down the thrones of rulers and has seated the meek in their place from within: whence we also learn what is meant here by 'has exalted,' namely, 'onto the thrones.' For we have noted elsewhere that 'humble' and 'meek' are accustomed to be used indiscriminately by the Hellenists. And this very thing ought to warn us that by 'humble' in this place we are to understand those who are not only humble in fortune, but also humble-minded in spirit, in the way that word is used in Matt. XI. 25 and in the cited passages of James and Peter, but also elsewhere throughout. Conversely, by 'mighty' are to be understood the proud, such as those powerful ones or rulers usually are. There is a noble example of this sentiment in Saul and David. To which pertains that which is written in 2. Sam. VI. 22, which passage illustrates this. See if you like also Josephus, Jacchiades on Dan. II. 20 and ch. IV. 14.

Latin:

Vers. 52. καθεῖλε δυνάστας ἀπὸ θρόνων καὶ ὕψωσε ταπεινούς] Sententia eadem est quæ Psal. CXIII. 6. & 1. Reg. II. 8. ubi נדיבים LXX. vertunt δυνάστας. At verba propius accedunt ad alterum proverbium Hebraicum quod dicta jam rubrica nobis exhibet Sirachides: θρόνους ἀρχόντων καθεῖλεν ὁ κύριος καὶ ἐκάθισε πραεῖς ἀντ᾽ αὐτῶν ἔνδοθεν: unde etiam discimus quid hic sit ὕψωσε, nempe ἐπὶ τοὺς θρόνους. Nam ταπεινὸς & πραῢς ab Hellenistis promiscue dici solere alibi annotavimus. Idq; ipsum monere nos debet ταπεινὸς hoc quidem loco intel- ligendos eos qui non fortis tantum sint humilis, sed animo quoque ταπεινόφρονες, quomodo ea vox usurpatur Matth. XI. 25. & dictis Jacobi & Petri locis, sed & alibi passim. Contra δυνάσας intelligendi sunt oi ὑπερήφανοι, quales ple- rumque sunt ei δυναταὶ live ἄρχοντες. Est hujus sententiæ no- bile exemplum in Saule & Davide. Quo pertinet id quod scriptum est 2. Sam. VI. 22. qui locus hunc illustrat. Vide si libet & Josephum Jacchaiad Dan II. 20. & c. IV. 14.

## 1:53
Verse 53. He has filled the hungry with good things and has sent away the rich empty] A maxim similar to the preceding ones. The sense is the same as in the song of Hannah, 1 Sam. II. 5, where likewise a general statement pertains to the benefit of childbirth. Those are said to be 'sent away empty' whoever compel someone for the sake of obtaining something and do not obtain it, as can be seen below in ch. XX. 10 and 11. The LXX in Job XXII. 9: 'and you have sent away widows empty.' So also in Judith X. 11: 'they sent back his messengers empty.'

Grotius refers these things to the fact that the Messiah willed to be born not from those who were proud either of the scepter or of the knowledge of the law, but from a virgin of despised lot: just as also v. 53, 'He has filled the hungry with good things,' according to the same interpreter, pertains to the benefit of childbirth. To which he wrongly drags the passage 1 Sam. II. 5: for the benefit of childbirth is celebrated there in other words, namely, that the barren woman brought forth seven children, that is, very many: just as also the remaining sentiments have nothing in common with the benefit of childbirth: as they are about the weak girded with strength, about the poor enriched, about the humble exalted from the dust, about the dead made alive, about those brought down to the underworld and brought back from it, except that they all exhibit proofs of divine omnipotence and of the most free government of the Sovereign. And therefore the blessed Chemnitius more correctly taught that that dispersion of the proud pertains either to the work of redemption, by which He Himself dissipated the proud army of spiritual enemies, or to the government of the kingdom of the Messiah: and similarly that Mary adapts the general sentiments concerning the humble, the hungry, and the rich to her own purpose in this way: Kings, when they distribute spoils after a victory, are accustomed to confer the richer portions upon the powerful, the noble, and the wealthy. But the Messiah distributes the spoils of His victory in His kingdom, not to the powerful and the wealthy, who are swollen with the persuasion of their own righteousness, but to those who humble themselves in true repentance and hunger for righteousness. Thus He cast off the Jews and called the Gentiles. Likewise: because GOD did not choose many wise, powerful, and noble men, but the foolish and weak things of the world, 1 Cor. I. 26. And to this point makes what Grotius himself in v. 54 explains 'He has helped Israel' thus: Just as once GOD led the people of Israel as if by His own hand out of Egypt, so now again He has led them out of the darkness of ignorance and the slavery of sin: and what he notes regarding verse 55, that then especially GOD showed Himself mindful of His mercy, as He spoke to Abraham, when He willed the Messiah to be born from the Israelites, and to dwell among them, and for the word of salvation to be announced to them before other nations with great testimonies of miracles: and especially what he observed regarding verse 71, that 'salvation from our enemies, and from the hand of all who hate us' is liberation from the body of sin, from the world, from death, and from the devil: just as Grotius also acknowledged in v. 69 that by the 'horn of salvation' raised up, the saving kingdom about to arise from the house of David was signified. But the dispersion of the proud seems to pertain especially to the confusion of diabolical pride, by which, not content to exalt itself against God, when it wished to raise its throne above the throne of God, seducing men to pride so that they too might desire to be like God, it strove to withdraw them from God and subject them to itself, but through the Messiah the human race was snatched away and the proud Spirits were dispersed with their prince in the counsels of their heart, and confounded in the thought of their heart, 1 John III. 8; they themselves were crushed under our feet, Gen. III. 15, Rom. XVI. 20, after the Lord made or exerted His strength in His arm, and Christ our Savior put down those powerful ones from their throne: concerning which the Apostle says in Col. II. 15: 'Having disarmed principalities and powers, He made a show of them openly, triumphing over them in it.' And thus the same God the Savior 'has exalted the humble' v. 47, 52, us who were wretched and humbled even to the underworld by diabolical seduction, crushing his head, He exalted, having raised our nature into the divine hypostasis, and to the right hand of the majesty of God, and having translated us through it into the heavenly places, Heb. I. 3, 10, Eph. II. 6.

Latin:

Vers. 53. πεινῶντας ἐνέπλησεν ἀγαθῶν καὶ πλουτοῦντας ἐξαπέ- στειλε κενούς] Γνώμη similis superioribus. Sensus idem qui in Annæ carmine 1. Sam II. 5. ubi itidem dictum generale per- tinet ad partus beneficium. Ἀποστέλλεσθαι κενοὶ dicuntur qui- cunque rei alicujus obtinendæ causa aliquem compellant neque eam obtinent, ut videre est infra c. XX. 10. & 11. LXX. in Jobo XXII. 9. χήρας δὲ ἐξαπέστειλας κενὰς. Sic & Ju- dithæ X. 11. ἀπέστρεψαν τοὺς ἀγγέλους αὐτῶ κενούς.

Refert hæc eo Grotius, quod Messias nasci vo- luit non ex iis qui aut sceptro, aut legis scientia super- biebant, sed ex virgine contemtæ sortis: quemadmo- dum & v. 53. πεινῶντας ἐνέπλησεν ἀγαθῶν, eodem interprete, ad partus beneficium pertinet. Quo perperam locum 1. Sam. II. 5. trahit: nam partus beneficium ibi aliis verbis celebratum est, quod nempe sterilis septem liberos, id est plurimos, pro- crearit: quemadmodum & reliquæ sententiæ cum partus beneficio nihil commune habent: utpote de infirmis, fortitudine cinctis, de pauperibus dita- tis, de humilibus è pulvere exaltatis, de mortuis vi- vificatis, de deductis in infernum reductis ex eo- dem, nisi quod omnes divinæ omnipotentiæ, & li- berrimæ τοῦ αὐτοκράτορος gubernationis docu- menta exhibeant. Ideoque rectius B. Chemnitius docuit illam dispersionem superborum vel ad redem- tionis opus pertinere, qua dissipavit ipse superbum exercitum spiritualium hostium, vel ad guberna- tionem regni Messiæ: ac similiter quod ad reliqua de humilibus, esurientibus, divitibus generales sen- tentias Mariam instituto suo accommodare hoc modo: Reges, quando post victoriam spolia distri- buunt, solent opimiora conferre potentibus, nobilibus & opulentis. Messias vero spolia victoriæ suæ in regno suo, non potentibus & divitibus, qui persuasione pro- priæ justitiæ tument, sed iis qui se in vera pœnitentia humiliant, & esuriunt justitiā distribuit. Ita Judæos abjecit, & gentes vocavit. Item: quia non multos sapientes, potentes & nobiles DEUS elegit, sed stul- ta & infirma mundi, 1. Cor. I. 26. & huc facit, quod Grotius ipse v. 54. ἀντελάβετο Ἰσραὴλ ita expli- cat: Sicut olim DEUS populum Israël quasi manu sua ex Ægypto, ita nunc rursus eum e- duxet ex ignorantiæ tenebris & peccati servitute: quodque ad vers. 55. notat, tunc præcipue ostendis- se DEUM memorem se esse misericordiæ suæ, sicut loquutus est Abrahamo, cum Messiam ex Israeli- tis nasci, atque inter ipsos versari voluit, & illis an- te cæteras nationes verbum salutare cum magnis miraculorum testimoniis annunciari: & imprimis quod ad versum 71. observavit, σωτηρίαν ἐξ ἐχ- θρῶν ἡμῶν, καὶ ἐκ χειρὸς πάντων τῶν μισούντων ἡ- μᾶς esse liberationem à corpore peccati, à mundo, à morte, & diabolo: quemadmodum etiam agno- vit Grotius v. 69. per erectum cornu salutis nota- tum esse regnum salutiferum ex domo Davidis sur- recturum. Videtur autem dispersio superborum ma- xime ad diabolicæ superbiæ confusionem pertinere, qua non contentus se efferre adversus Deum, cum thronum suum supra thronum Dei evehere vel- let, homines ad superbiam seducens, ut & ipsi si- milis Deo esse cuperent, eosdem Deo subduce- re, & sibi subjicere sategit, sed per Messiam erepto humano genere dispersi sunt superbi Spiritus cum principe suo in consiliis cordis sui, atque confusi διανοίᾳ καρδίας αὐτῶν 1. Joh. III. 8. ipsi sub pedes nostros contriti sunt, Genes. III. 15. Rom. XVI. 20. postquam fortitudinem suam fecit vel exeruit Do- minus in brachio suo, & potentes illos deposuit de throno suo Christus Servator noster: quo de Apo- stolus Col. II. 15. ἀπεκδυσάμενος τὰς ἀρχὰς καὶ τὰς ἐξουσίας ἐδειγμάτισεν ἐν παῤῥησίᾳ, θριαμβεύσας αὐτοὺς ἐν αὐτῷ. Atque ita idem Deus Servator ὕψωσε ταπεινοὺς v. 47. 52. miseros nos, & ad infer- num usque humiliatos seductione diabolica, caput ejus conterens, exaltavit, evecta natura nostra in hypostasin divinam, & ad dextram majestatis Dei, nobisque per ipsam in cœlestia translocatis Ebr. I. 3. 10. Eph. II. 6.

## 1:54
Vers. 54. ἀντελάβετο Ἰσραὴλ παιδὸς αὐτοῦ] There is indeed a place where ἀντιλαμβάνεσθαι corresponds to the Hebrew תמך, which we have noted is also translated as αἱρετίζειν, and sometimes by other words. But here, if I am not mistaken, it corresponds to the verb החזיק, which is to sustain, and sometimes also to lead by the hand. For in the passage of Isaiah XLI. verse 9, from which this is taken, when God had said ישראל עבדי Ἰσραὴλ παῖς μου, there follows אשר החזקתך, which the LXX translate as ὃν ἀντελαβόμην. Moreover, ἀπ’ ἄκρων τῆς γῆς is added. The same interpreters often translate the same verb as κρατεῖν τῆς χειρὸς, and sometimes also ἐπιλαβέσθαι τῆς χειρὸς, as in Jer. XXXI. 32, from which translation the writer to the Hebrews VIII. 9 does not depart; in which places there follows ἐξαγαγεῖν αὐτοὺς ἐκ γῆς Αἰγύπτου; our Actor also said ἐπιλαβέσθαι χειρὸς in XXIII. 19. The sense of the Holy Spirit in this place is: Just as God once led the people of Israel out of Egypt as if by His own hand, so now He will again lead them out of the darkness of ignorance and the slavery of sin. In the song of Moses there is ὡδήγησας τῇ δικαιοσύνῃ σου τὸν λαόν σου ὃν ἐλυτρώσω Exod. XV. 13, where δικαιοσύνη signifies mercy, for in the Hebrew it is בחסדך.

μνησθῆναι ἐλέους] So that He might show Himself mindful of His mercy. The finger is pointed to Psalm XCVIII. 3, where in the Hebrew it is זכר חסרו ואמונתו לבית ישראל, and in the Greek ἐμνήσθη τοῦ ἐλέους αὑτοῦ τῷ Ἰακὼβ καὶ τῆς ἀληθείας αὑτοῦ τῷ Ἰσραήλ. Compare also the last words of Micah, where there is a similar mention of the mercy of both Jacob and Abraham. Moreover, God is said to remember His people as often as He relieves them, when oppressed by long-standing evils, with a notable benefit. See 2 Chron. VI. 42, and here below 72.

Latin:

Vers. 54. ἀντελάβετο Ἰσραὴλ παιδὸς αὐτοῦ] Est quidem ubi ἀντιλαμβάνεσθαι respondet Hebræo תמך quod & αἱρετί- ζειν transferri notavimus, nonnunquam & aliis vocibus. Sed hic ni fallor respondet verbo החזיק quod est sustenta- re, atque interdum etiam manu ducere. Nam in loco Esaïæ XLI. vers. 9. unde hoc desumtum est, cum dixisset Deus ישראל עבדי Ἰσραὴλ παῖς μου, sequitur אשר החזקתך quod vertunt LXX. ὃν ἀντελαβόμην. Additur autem ἀπ’ ἄκρων τῆς γῆς. Idem verbum sæpe iidem interpretes vertunt κρατεῖν τῆς χειρὸς, interdum & ἐπιλαβέσθαι τῆς χειρὸς, ut Jer. XXXI. 32. à qua versione non discedit Scriptor adHebræos VIII. 9. quibus locis sequitur ἐξαγαγεῖν αὐτοὺς ἐκ γῆς Αἰ- γύπτου˙ ἐπιλαβέσθαι χειρὸς dixit & hic noster Actor. XXIII. 19. Sensus Spiritus Sancti hoc in loco est: Sicut olim Deus populum Israël ticum eduxit quasi manu sua ex Ægypto, ita nunc rursus eum educet ex ignorantiæ tenebris & pec- cati servitute. In carmine Mosis est ὡδήγησας τῇ δικαιοσύνῃ σου τὸν λαόν σου ὃν ἐλυτρώσω Exod. XV. 13. ubi δικαιοσύνη mi- sericordiam significat, nam in Hebræo est בחסדך.

μνησθῆναι ἐλέους] Ut memorem se misericordiæ suæ osten- deret. Intenditur digitus ad Psalmum XCVIII. 3. ubi in Hebræo est זכר חסרו ואמונתו לבית ישראל in Græco ἐμνήσθη τοῦ ἐλέους αὑτοῦ τῷ Ἰακὼβ καὶ τῆς ἀληθείας αὑτοῦ τῷ Ἰσραήλ. Confer & ultima Michææ verba, ubi similiter misericordiæ mentio & Jacobi & Abrahami. Dicitur autem Deus populi sui meminisse, quoties eum longis malis op- pressum insigni beneficio sublevat, Vide 2. Paral. VI. 42. & hic infra 72.

## 1:55
Vers. 55. εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα] There are those who think it is placed for the Hebrew סלה, which Aquila and Jerome interpret in this sense. But that meaning does not seem to fit in all places; and many Hebrews, as well as the LXX interpreters, explain it otherwise. To me, after others, this εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα seems to be referred to ἐλάλησε, so that the sense is: just as He promised to Abraham and Isaac forever. That is entirely regarded which the covenant entered into with Isaac is called ברית עולם לזרעו אחריו Gen. XVII. 19, which the LXX explain thus: διαθήκην αἰώνιον εἶναι αὐτῷ Θεὸς καὶ τῷ σπέρματι αὐτοῦ μετ’ αὐτόν. But just as the LXX rightly supply there εἶναι αὐτῷ Θεὸς from the preceding words of the same chapter, verse 7, where the covenant is struck with Abraham himself, so here too the same must be understood: for this is that which God ἐλάλησε τῷ Ἀβραὰμ καὶ τῷ σπέρματι αὐτοῦ. And the same clause of perpetuity, just as it ought to be considered to be present in the renewal of the covenant made with Jacob from the nature of the original pact, so it is openly repeated to David, as can be seen in Psalm CXXXII. 14, where the LXX have εἰς αἰῶνα αἰῶνος. And looking to this nature of the covenant, Paul says, ἀμεταμέλητα εἶναι τὰ Θεοῦ χαρίσματα καὶ κλῆσιν. Roman. XI. 29, undoubtedly by which it is fixed and ratified with God to always pursue the Israelites with a certain extraordinary mercy: which He showed then especially, when He caused the Messiah to be born from them and to dwell among them he willed, and that the saving word be announced to them before other nations with great testimonies of miracles.

Latin:

Vers. 55. εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα] Sunt qui positum putant pro He- bræo סלה quod in hunc sensum interpretatur Aquila & Hieronymus. Sed videtur ea significatio non omnibus lo- cis congruere: multique Hebræi, ut & LXX. interpretes aliter id exponunt. Mihi post alios hoc εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα referen- dum videtur ad ἐλάλησε, ut sensus sit: quemadmodum A- brahamo & Isaaco in perpetuum promisit. Omnino id re- spicitur, quod fœdus cum Isaaco initum dicitur ברית עולם לזרעו אחריו Gen. XVII. 19. quod ita explicant LXX. διαθήκην αἰώνιον εἶναι αὐτῷ Θεὸς καὶ τῷ σπέρματι αὐτοῦ μετ’ αὐτόν. Sicut autem ibi recte supplent LXX. εἶναι αὐ- τῷ Θεὸς ex superioribus verbis ejusdem capitis commate 7. ubi cum ipso Abrahamo fœdus feritur, ita & hic idem subintelligendum est: hoc enim est illud quod Deus ἐλά- λησε τῷ Ἀβραὰμ καὶ τῷ σπέρματι αὐτοῦ. Atque eadem per- petuitatis clausula sicut in fœderis renovatione cum Jaco- bo facta ex pacti originalis natura inesse censeri debet, ita Davidi aperte repetita est, ut videre est Psal. CXXXII. 14. ubi LXX. habent εἰς αἰῶνα αἰῶνος. Et ad hanc fœde- ris naturam respiciens Paulus ait, ἀμεταμέλητα εἶναι τὰ Θεοῦ χαρίσματα καὶ κλῆσιν. Roman. XI. 29. nimirum qua fixum ratumque sit apud Deum Israëlitas semper eximia quadam misericordia prosequi: quod tunc præcipue o- stendit, cum Messiam ex ipsis nasci atque inter ipsos versari voluit, & illis ante cæteras nationes verbum salutare cum magnis miraculorum testimoniis annuntiari.

## 1:56
Vers. 56. About three months] Avoiding the crowd, as it seems, she departed near the time of childbirth. For if she had been present at the birth, as some wish, she would have remained also through the times of the lochia to care for the woman in labor: which would have extended beyond the third month.

PART V. The nativity and circumcision of John, with the hymn and prophecy of Zechariah.

Latin:

Vers. 56. ὡσεὶ μῆνας τρεῖς] Turbam ut videtur vitans discessit sub tempus partitudinis. Nam si partui intersuisset, quod volunt quidam, mansisset etiam per tempora λοχείας curatura puerperam: quod excurrisset extra mensem tertium.

PARS V. Nativitas & circumcisio Iohannis, cum hymno & vaticinio Zachariæ.

## 1:58
Vers. 58. The Lord magnified his mercy] In the same sense the LXX translate μεγαλύνειν δικαιοσύνην for showing great benefits, Gen. XIX. 19.

Latin:

Vers. 58. ἐμεγάλυνε κύριος τὸ ἔλεος αὐτᾶ] Eodem sensu μεγαλύνειν δικαιοσύνην vertunt LXX. pro magnis beneficiis afficere גדל חסדו Gen. XIX. 19.

## 1:59
Vers. 59. On the eighth day] To which God had willed that circumcision be deferred, lest the very recent birth might not be sufficient for bearing the pain. Moreover, the circumcision of infants showed that the covenant was familial.

they came to circumcise] Friends invited for that matter came into the house of Zechariah. For no certain place is prescribed for circumcision by the law, just as there is no certain circumciser, but he who is most practiced in that art is accustomed to be employed for that matter. See I Macc. I. 63. The presence of the woman in labor shows that this circumcision was celebrated at home. Nor do the Jews today circumcise boys in the Synagogue as if that were necessary, but so that the matter may be established by more witnesses.

The ordinary minister of circumcision was a minister of the word, or an ecclesiastical person, which Mr. Dr. Sebastian Schmied teaches in his treatise on circumcision, page 350, by the example of Abraham, and from a comparison with Lev. XII. 3. Extraordinarily, in a case of necessity, circumcision was administered by others, even by women, which the passage from the Maccabees testifies.

they called him by the name of his father] Immediately after the circumcision was performed, a name was imposed upon the infant, Gen. XXI. 3, 4. Thus also among the Romans the day of infants was called the lustric and nominal day from the same custom, and among the Athenians sacred rites were performed on the tenth day, and a name was imposed upon the infant, as the Birds of Aristophanes and the Scholiast on it teach us: and Suidas under the word Amphidromia. Nor do I think anything else was looked to in that matter than that, since many were invited to the circumcision or lustration, the same ones could remember the imposed name if any controversy should arise later. Moreover, the names of parents or grandfathers were imposed upon descendants, so that by the very recollection of the name they might be kindled to imitate their virtues. Thus also among the Greeks, many Pyrrhi from Pyrrhus, Philippi from Philip, Ptolemies from Ptolemy. And among the Carthaginians, Hannibal bore the name of his grandfather. Aristophanes in the Birds: Callias begets Hipponicus, and Hipponicus begets Callias. Ulpian on the Oration of Demosthenes concerning the Maliciously Conducted Embassy: For it was likely that Proxenos used the name of Harmodius on purpose. For that Proxenos traced his lineage from Harmodius. Demosthenes against Boeotus: He himself, as being older, is worthy to have the name of his paternal grandfather. See also Plutarch in the Life of Cimon, where he says that Thucydides was the son of Olorus, tracing the homonymy to his ancestor.

Latin:

Vers. 59. ἐν τῇ ὀγδόῃ ἡμέρᾳ] In quem Deus circumcisionem differri voluerat, ne recens nimium partus non sufficeret ferendo dolori. Infantium autem circumcisio ostendebat fœdus esse gentilitium.

ἦλθον περιτεμεῖν] Amici ad eam rem advocati in domum Zachariæ venerunt. Nullus enim locus certus circumcisioni ex lege præscribitur, ut nec certus circumcisor, sed solet ad eam rem adhiberi qui maxime est in ea arte exercitus. Vide I. Macc. I. 63. Domi autem celebratam hanc circumcisionem ostendit puerperæ præsentia. Neque hodie Judæi in Synagoga pueros circumcidunt tanquam id necessarium esset, sed quo pluribus testibus res constet.

Ordinarius minister circumcisionis fuit verbi minister, vel persona Ecclesiastica, quod docet Dn. D. Sebastianus Schmied tract. de circumcis. pag. 350. exemplo Abrahami, & è collatione Lev. XII. 3. Extra ordinem in casu necessitatis ab aliis administrata fuit circumcisio, etiam à mulieribus, quod locus è Maccabaicis testatur.

ἐκάλεν αὐτὸ ἐπὶ τῷ ὀνόματι τῦ πατρὸς αὐτᾶ] Statim post circumcisionem peractam nomen infanti imponebatur Genes. XXI. 3. 4. Sic & apud Romanos dies infantium lustricus dicebatur & nominalis ab eodem more, & apud Athenienses decimo die sacra fiebant, & imponebatur nomen infanti, ut nos docent aves Aristophanis & ad eum Scholiastes: & in voce Ἀμφιδρόμια Suidas. Nec aliud ea in re spectatum arbitror, quam quod cum multi ad circumcisionem aut lustrationem advocarentur, iidem meminisse possent impositi nominis, si qua olim controversia oriretur. Parentum autem aut avorum nomina posteris imponebantur, ut ipsa nominis recordatione ad imitandas eorum virtutes accenderentur. Sic & apud Græcos à Pyrrho plures Pyrrhi, à Philippo Philippi, à Ptolemæo Ptolemæi. Et apud Pœnos Annibal avi nomen ferebat. Aristophanes avibus: ἱππόνικος καλίε, κᾀξ ἱππονίκε καλίας. Ulpianus ad Orationem Demosthenis de male obita legatione: εἰκὸς γὰρ ἦν τὸν Πρόξενον τῦ Ἁρμοδίε ὀνόματι κεχρῆσθαι ἐπίτηδες ὑέ. Is enim Proxenos ab Harmodio genus ducebat. Demosthenes in Bœotum: ἄξιος δὲ αὐτὸς ὡς δὴ πρεσβύτερος ὢν, τόνεμ᾽ ἔχειν τὸ τῦ πρὸς πατρὸς πάππε. Vide & Plutarchum Cimone, ubi Thucydidem ait fuisse πατρὸς Ὀλόρε εἰς τὸν πρόγονον ἀναφέροντα τὴν ὁμωνυμίαν.

## 1:60
Vers. 60. The mother] Full, clearly, of the Holy Spirit on account of her son, as was said above, by which Spirit she knew that which Zechariah had learned from the angel.

Latin:

Vers. 60. ἡ μήτηρ] Plena scilicet Spiritu Sancto ob filium, ut supra dictum est, quo Spiritu id cognovit quod ab angelo didicerat Zacharias.

## 1:63
Vers. 63. John is his name] As if he were to say that no consultation remained in a matter which God had already defined. Therefore he says is, not shall be. We spoke of the name of John above.

Latin:

Vers. 63. Ἰωάννης ἐστὶ τὸ ὄνομα αὐτᾶ] Quasi dicat nullam superesse consultationem in re quam Deus jam definisset. Itaque ἐστὶ inquit non ἔσται. De nomine Iohannis diximus supra.

## 1:64
Vers. 64. And his tongue] How the opening is referred to the tongue we said in the notes on Mark c. VII. 34, which those who did not understand thought should be added, was articulated. But the ancient Paraphrasts do not acknowledge that.

Latin:

Vers. 64. καὶ ἡ γλῶσσα αὐτᾶ] Quomodo τὸ ἀνοίγεσθαι ad linguam referatur diximus ad Marcum c. VII. 34. quod qui non intellexerunt addendum putarunt διηρθρώθη. Sed veteres Paraphrastæ id non agnoscunt.

## 1:65
V. 65. φόβος] That is, reverence for God, as in Acts 2:43.

Latin:

V. 65. φόβος] Id est reverentia Dei, ut Act. II. 43.

## 1:66
Vers. 66. ἔθεντο πάντες οἱ ἀκύσαντες ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ αὐτῶν] Luke speaks in the same way below in chapter 9:44. Elsewhere he said διατηρεῖν ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ in chapter 2:51. The LXX are accustomed to say τάττειν ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ as in Ezekiel 40:4. In Haggai 2:19, Aeschylus in Prometheus said θυμῷ βάλλειν.

Τί ἄρα τὸ παιδίον τῦτο ἔσται] What will this child become? For it is the same kind of expression as in Acts 12:18.

καὶ χεὶρ κυρίε ἦν μετ' αὐτᾶ] As often as the inspiration of prophecy is described, it is usually said χεὶρ κυρίε ἦν ἐπ' αὐτὸν, not μετ' αὐτᾶ, as in Ezekiel 1:3, chapter 3:22, chapter 37:1, chapter 40:1. Wherefore, by this mode of speaking which we have here, it is not prophecy, but the singular help of God that is indicated. Thus 2 Samuel 14:19, μὴ ἡ χεὶρ Ἰωὰβ ἐν παντὶ τύτῳ μετὰ σῦ; הֲיַד not עליך, that is, was he not your helper?

Latin:

Vers. 66. ἔθεντο πάντες οἱ ἀκύσαντες ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ αὐτῶν] Sic & infra loquitur Lucas cap. IX. 44. Alibi dixit διατηρεῖν ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ c. II. 51. LXX. solent dicere τάττειν ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ ut Ezech. XL. 4. Aggæi II. 19. θυμῷ βάλλειν dixit Æschylus Prometheo.

Τί ἄρα τὸ παιδίον τῦτο ἔσται] Quo evadet puer iste? Est enim genus idem loquendi quod Act. XII. 18.

καὶ χεὶρ κυρίε ἦν μετ' αὐτᾶ] Quoties afflatus Prophetiæ describitur, dici solet χεὶρ κυρίε ἦν ἐπ' αὐτὸν non μετ' αὐτᾶ, ut Ezech. I. 3. cap. III. 22. cap. XXXVII. 1. cap. XL. 1. Quare hoc quod hic habemus loquendi genere non προφητεία, sed singulare Dei auxilium indicatur. Sic 2. Sam. XIV. 19. μὴ ἡ χεὶρ Ἰωὰβ ἐν παντὶ τύτῳ μετὰ σῦ; הֲיַד non עליך id est an tibi adjutor fuit?

## 1:68
Vers. 68. ἐυλογητὸς κύριος ὁ Θεὸς τῶ ἰσραήλ] That is, ἐυλογηθείη, as we said above. Noah had spoken of Shem in Genesis 9:26, ברוך יהוה אלהי שם, ἐυλογητὸς κύριος ὁ Θεὸς τῶ Σήμ. For so the LXX. For He who is the Lord of all is called in a peculiar way the God of the pious. Philo says, περὶ τὸ ὄν, the first and greatest powers are, the one that is beneficent, God, since according to this He established and ordered the whole; the other, Lord, according to which the power over all things is attached: which he also repeats often elsewhere. But after most nations had lapsed into the worship of false gods, that name began to be restricted to the one people of Israel. Psalm 41:14, ἐυλογητὸς κύριος ὁ Θεὸς Ἰσραὴλ. So also Psalm 72:18 and 106:48.

ὅτι ἐπεσκέψατο] Namely, τὸν λαὸν, which is to be repeated here from the following member, to which you may find similar modes of speaking in Proverbs 31:30, Genesis 3:29, and elsewhere. The sense is: He has turned His attention to the people. The Chaldean, when פקד is taken in a good sense, translates it as זכר. I agree with those who think the passages in Exodus are being referred to, chapter 3:16 and 4:31, where in the Greek the word is the same.

καὶ ἐποίησε λύτρωσιν τῷ λαῷ ἀυτῶ] It is from the same Psalm from which Mary recited a part, namely 111: where concerning the benefit of the exodus from Egypt (which is an image, as we have said, of the times of the Messiah), פדות שלח לעמו, which the LXX translate λύτρωσιν ἀπέστειλε τῷ λαῷ ἀυτῶ. Whence it appears that liberation is rightly translated here, and that it is not so much a matter of Christ's sacrifice alone as of the whole counsel of God in liberating the Israelites, which at that time began to be put into effect. The LXX, as often as the matter requires mention of a price, say ἀπολύτρωσιν rather than λύτρωσιν.

Grotius thinks that it is not so much a matter of Christ's sacrifice alone as of the whole counsel of God in liberating the Israelites, which at that time began to be put into effect. But although redemption, as it is applied or ought to be applied primarily to the people of Israel, which happens through faith, is being looked at, yet the redemption itself, accomplished by the price of Christ's blood, and the acquisition of salvation are properly expressed by this word. Beza rightly observes that, since there are many kinds of liberation, that one is signified by the name of λυτρώσεως which is obtained neither by force (as happened of old, when the Lord snatched the people from Pharaoh) nor with the good will of the enemies (as when the people returned from Babylon), but by a just price paid, not to Satan himself, by whom they were held captive, but to GOD the Father himself, who had delivered us by His just judgment to Satan, to sin, and to death. Therefore the Apostle so often repeats that we are redeemed by the blood of Christ, namely by that huge price which was once foreshadowed by the gore of victims, so that it is a sin to doubt our redemption.

Latin:

Vers. 68. ἐυλογητὸς κύριος ὁ Θεὸς τῶ ἰσραήλ] Id est ἐυ- λογηθείη ut supra diximus. Dixerat de Semo Noachus Ge- nes. IX. 26. ברוך יהוה אלהי שם, ἐυλογητὸς κύριος ὁ Θεὸς τῶ Σήμ. Ita enim LXX. Nam qui omnium est Dominus peculiariter Deus piorum dicitur. περὶ τὸ ὄν inquit Philo αἱ πρῶται καὶ μέγισται δυνάμεις εἰσιν, ἥτε ἐυεργέτις, Θεὸς, ἐπει- δαὶ κατὰ ταύτην ἔθηκε καὶ διεκόσμησε τὸ πᾶν; δ' ἑτέρα, κύ- ριος, καθ' ἣν ἀνῆπται τῶν ὅλων τὸ κράτος: quod & alibi sæpe repetit. Postquam vero gentes pleræque ad falso- rum Deorum cultus erant dilapsæ, cœpit nomen illud ad unum Israëlis populuin restringi. Pfal XLI. 14. ἐυλογητὸς κύριος ὁ Θεὸς Ἰσραὴλ. Sic & Pf. LXXII. 18. & CVI. 48.

ὅτι ἐπεσκέψατο] Nimirum τὸν λαὸν, quod hic repeten- dum ex membro sequente, cui similia loquendi genera reperias Proverb. XXXI. 30. Genes. III. 29. & alibi. Sensus est: animadvertit ad populum. Chaldæus פקד cum in bo- nam partem sumitur, vertit זכר. Accedo putantibus Exo- di loca respici cap. III. 16. & IV. 31. ubi in Græco vox est eadem.

καὶ ἐποίησε λύτρωσιν τῷ λαῷ ἀυτῶ] Ex eodem Psalmo est ex quo partem Maria recitavit, CXI. scilicet: ubi de bene- ficio exitus ex Ægypto, (quæ imago, ut diximus Messiæ temporum) פדות שלח לעמו quod vertunt LXX. λύ- τρωσιν ἀπέστειλε τῷ λαῷ ἀυτῶ Unde apparet recte liberationem hic verti, neque tam de solo Christi sacrificio hic agi, quam de toto Dei consilio in liberandis Israëlitis, quod eo tem- pore cœptum est in rem conferri LXX. quoties pretii men- tionem res exigit ἀπολύτρωσιν potius quam λύτρωσιν di- cunt.

Non tam de solo sacrificio Christi hic agi, quam de toto Dei consilio in liberandis Israëlitis, quod eo tempore cœptum est in rem conferri, putat Grotius. Sed quanquam redemtio ut applicatur, vel appli- cari debebat imprimis populo Israëlis, quod per fidem fit, respiciatur, ipsa tamen pretio sanguinis Christi facta redemtio & salutis acquisitio proprie hac voce exprimitur. Recte observat Beza, cum multæ sint liberationis species, eam demum signi- ficari λυτρώσεως nomine, quæ nec vi (ut olim conti- git, cum Dominus populum eriperet Pharaoni) nec cum bona hostium gratia (ut cum populus Babylone reverteretur) sed justo persoluto pretio, non ipsi Sa- tanæ a quo captivi tenebantur, sed ipsi DEO Patri persoluto, qui nos justo suo judicio Satanæ, peccato, morti manciparat, impetratur. Ideo toties repetit Apostolus non sanguine Christi redemtos, ingenti videlicet illo pretio, quod olim adumbratum vi- ctimarum cruore, ut de redemtione nostra dubi- tare sit nefas.

## 1:69
Vers. 69. καὶ ἤγειρε κέρας σωτηρίας ἡμῖν ἐν τῷ οἴκῳ Δαβὶδ τῶ παιδὸς ἀυτῶ] Because the strength of a beast does not consist in its horns alone, therefore all power is called a horn by the Hebrews, as can be gathered from the passage in Deuteronomy 33:17, but especially royal power, as can be seen in Zechariah 1:18 and Daniel 7:24 and 8:21. And for that reason the ancient paraphrasts translate the word קרן in 1 Samuel 1:10, Jeremiah 48:25, and elsewhere as מלכות or מלכו. However, I do not think the word ἠγείρεν corresponds so much to the Hebrew הרים as to the word הצמיח. For two passages are being looked at together, the one in Psalm 132:17, שם אצמיח קרן לדוד where the LXX have ἐξανατελῶ κέρας τῷ Δαβὶδ: the other in Ezekiel 29:21, ביום ההוא אצמיח קרן לבית ישראל where they have, ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ ἐκείνῃ ἀνατελεῖ (perhaps ἀνατελῶ as in the previous passage) κέρας παντὶ τῷ οἴκῳ Ἰσραὴλ. Moreover, God is called in Psalm 18:3, קרן ישעי, κέρας σωτηρίας μυ. Zechariah prophesies that a saving kingdom will arise from the house of David.

Although it may be understood not inappropriately as a saving kingdom, I would prefer that Christ himself be understood here by κέρας σωτηρίας, who is called the horn of salvation in Psalm 18:3 and Psalm 132:17, which latter passage Zechariah is looking at here, implying that what was predicted there has now been fulfilled. Nor do I have any doubt about the prophecy of Psalm 89:18, And by your grace you will exalt our horn, where the discourse is about the Messiah, just as in the same Psalm later in verse 25, the kingdom of the Messiah, of which he speaks there, is designated by the same word: And his horn will be exalted in my name. The LXX in the former passage have, ἐν τῇ ἐυδοκίᾳ σὲ ὑψωθήσεται τὸ κέρας ἡμων: but in the latter, καὶ ἐν τῷ ὀνόματί μὲ ὑψωθήσεται τὸ

a horn for him. The author of the Psalm, Ethan, is joined in office with Heman, 1 Chronicles 16:9, of whom it is said in 1 Chronicles 26:5 that he was the King's Seer (Prophet) in the words of God, to exalt a horn, which it will be permissible to understand in the same way regarding this horn of David, as being that in the exalting of which all the prophets were occupied, Acts 10:43. Compare also Psalm 148:14. Hannah also sang of the same horn in her canticle, when her son Samuel had been divinely gifted to her: recalling to herself in true faith the Messiah promised to the people of the Lord, 1 Samuel 2:1. My heart has exulted, and my horn has been exalted in my God: my mouth has been widened over my enemies: because I have rejoiced in your Salvation. Those things which are brought forward in both passages in the place of a reason explain each other: because my horn has been exalted in God: and, because I have rejoiced in your Salvation. The horn of Hannah, in which she trusted, is the Messiah, whom she calls the salvation of the Lord. Regarding whom, and his kingdom, Hannah also prophesied toward the end of her song: verse 11. The Lord will judge the ends of the earth, and will give power to his king, (who is that if not Christ, to whom all judgment has been given, John 5:22) and will exalt the horn of his Christ, which latter things are explanatory of the former. For the horn of Christ the Lord is the kingdom of the Messiah, whom the holy men of God did not easily omit in their prophetic hymns. Thus by the word horn, when the discourse is about the Messiah, sometimes the Messiah himself is designated, so called because of his strength, whose name is El Gibbor, Isaiah 9:6, and sometimes the kingdom of the Messiah. But here Zechariah had especially in mind through the Holy Spirit the Psalm of degrees 132:17, 'There I will make a horn to sprout for David.' Let those things which we have annotated on that Psalm be compared.

Latin:

Vers. 69. καὶ ἤγειρε κέρας σωτηρίας ἡμῖν ἐν τῷ οἴκῳ Δαβὶδ τῶ παιδὸς ἀυτῶ] Quia non unius bestiæ vis in cornibus con- sistit, ideo potentia omnis cornu Hebræis dicitur, ut colli- gere est ex loco Deut. XXXIII. 17. præcipue vero potentia regalis, ut videre est Zach. I. 18. & Daniel. VII. 24. & VIII. 21. Atque ideo vocem קרן I. Samuel. I. 10. Jerem. XLVIII. 25. & alibi veteres Paraphrastæ vertunt מלכו מלכות aut. Vocem autem ἠγείρεν non tam respondere arbitror Hebrææ הרים quam voci הצמיח. Duo enim loci conjunctim respiciuntur, alter Psal. CXXXII. 17: שם אצמיח קרן לדוד ubi LXX. ἐξανατελῶ κέρας τῷ Δαβὶδ: alter vero Ez. XXIX. 21. ביום ההוא אצמיח קרן לבית ישראל ubi illi, ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ ἐκείνῃ ἀνατελεῖ forte ἀνατελῶ ut loco superiori) κέρας παντὶ τῷ οἴκῳ Ἰσραὴλ. Dicitur autem Deus Pfal. XVIII. 3. קרן ישעי κέρας· σωτηρίας μυ. Regnum salutiferum ex domo Davidis surrecturum Za- charias vaticinatur.

Quanquam de regno salutifero non incom- mode accipiatur, malim tamen hic intelligi per κέρας σωτηρίας ipsummet Christum, qui cornu sa- lutis vocatur Pfal. XVIII. 3. Pfal. CXXXII. 17. quem locum posteriorem hic respicit Zacharias, imple- tum jam innuens, quod ibi prædictum erat. Ne- que dubium mihi de eo est vaticinium Pf. XXCIX. 18. Et per gratiam tuam cornu nostrum exaltabis, ubi de Messia sermo est, quemadmodum eodem Psalmo postea v. 25. voce eadem regnum Messiæ, quo de illic loquitur, designatur: Et cornu ejus in nomi- ne meo exaltabitur. LXX. priori loco habent κ, ἐν τῇ ἐυδοκίᾳ σὲ ὑψωθήσεται τὸ κέρας ἡμων: poste- riori vero καὶ ἐν τῷ ὀνόματί μὲ ὑψωθήσεται τὸ

κέρας αὐτῷ. Autor Psalmi Ethan conjungitur in officio Hemani 1. Paral. XVI. 9. de quo 1. Paral. XXVI. 5. dicitur, quod fuerit Videns (Propheta) Regis in Verbis Dei, ad exaltandum cornu, quod itidem de hoc Davidis cornu intelligere licebit, utpote in quo exaltando omnes Prophetæ occu- pati fuêre, Actor. X. 43. Conf. & Psal. CXLVIII. 14. De eodem cornu cecinit quoque Hanna in Cantico suo, cum ei filius Samuel divinitus dona- tus esset: in memoriam sibi vera fide revocans Messiam populo Domini promissum 1. Sam. II. 1. Exultavit cor meum, & exaltatum est cornu meum in Deo meo: dilatatum est os meum super inimicos meos: quia lætata sum in Salutari tuo. Ex- plicant se mutuo illa, quæ in utroque commate rationis loco adducta sunt: quia exaltatum est cornu meum in Deo: &, quia lætata sum in Saluta- ri tuo. Cornu Hannæ, in quo confidebat, est Messias, quem vocat σωτηρίαν τοῦ κυρίου. De quo, & regno ejus, sub finem carminis itidem vatici- nata est Hanna: vers. 11. Dominus judicabit fines terræ, & dabit imperium regi suo, (quisnam ille nisi Christus, cui datum est omne Judicium, Jo- hann. V. 22.) & sublimabit cornu Christi sui, quæ posteriora exegetica priorum sunt. Cornu e- nim Christi Domini est regnum Messiæ, quem non facile in hymnis Propheticis Sancti Dei homines prætermiserunt. Ita per cornu, cum de Messia sermo est, modo Messias ipse, sic dictus ob for- titudinem, cujus nomen est אל גבור Es. IX. 6. mo- do regnum Messiæ designatur. Sed hic imprimis in mente habuit per Spiritum Sanctum Zacharias Psalmi graduum CXXXII. v. 17. ἐκεῖ ἐξανατελῶ κέρας τῷ Δαβίδ. Conferantur quæ ad Psalmum il- lum annotavimus.

## 1:70
Verse 70. 'As he spoke by the mouth of his holy prophets from of old'—Peter uses the same words in Acts 3:21: 'As God spoke by the mouth of his holy prophets from of old': where it is manifest that Moses and the prophets who followed him are understood. Thus also here 'from of old' is not from the foundation of the world, but from ancient times, which is sufficient to show the singular dispensation of God. Learned men have rightly noted that a similar way of speaking exists in Genesis 6:4, where in Greek it is 'the giants who were from of old'; that is, the ancients, and Psalm 25:6. But also elsewhere. Nor do I doubt that in this place Zechariah signifies those prophets from whose prophecies the following things are taken. For I agree with those who refer that 'he spoke' to the following things: so that it is 'he spoke salvation,' and 'he spoke to perform mercy,' and 'he spoke an oath.'

This is rashly restricted to Moses and the prophets who followed him: since it sounds openly of the prophets from the foundation of the world: for that 'from of old,' if it be taken properly, is not only from ancient times but from the foundation of the world. And GOD certainly spoke also through the mouth of the holy Patriarchs before and after the flood, who were also prophets, indeed through the mouth of Adam, and thence from the foundation of the world, after the Proto-Evangelium was promulgated in Genesis 3:15, of which the holy Patriarchs had to be the interpreters, no less than Moses and the prophets who followed him.

Latin:

Vers. 70. καθὼς ἐλάλησε διὰ στόματος τῶν ἁγίων τῶν ἀπ' αἰῶ- νος προφητῶν αὐτῷ] Eadem verba Petrus usurpat Actor. III. 21. ὡς ἐλάλησεν ὁ Θεὸς διὰ στόματος ἁγίων αὐτῶ προφη- τῶν ἀπ' αἰῶνος: ubi manifestum Mosen & eum secutos Prophetas intelligi. Ita & hic ἀπ' αἰῶνος non est ab orbe condito, sed ab antiquis temporibus, quod satis est ad ostendendam singularem Dei dispensationem. Re- cte notarunt viri eruditi simile loquendi genus exstare Ge- nes. VI. 4. ubi Græce est οἱ γίγαντες οἱ ἀπ' αἰῶνος; id est, οἱ ἀρχαῖοι, & Psal. XXV: 6. Sed & alibi. Neque dubito quin hoc quidem loco Zacharias eos Prophetas significet ex quorum vaticiniis desumta sunt quæ sequuntur. Nam ἐλάλησε illud ad sequentia referentibus assentio: ut sit ἐλάλησε σωτηρίαν, & ἐλάλησε ποιῆσαι ἔλεος & ἐλάλησε ὅρκον.

Temere hoc restringitur ad Mosen, & eum sequutos Prophetas: quum sonet aperte de Prophe- tis ab orbe condito: non enim illud ἀπ' αἰώνων si proprie accipiatur, est non tantum ab antiquis temporibus sed ab orbe condito. Et loquutus est sa- ne DEUS etiam per os sanctorum Patriarcharum ante, & post diluvium, qui etiam Prophetæ fuê- re, imo per os Adami, & inde ab orbe condito, postquam Gen. III. 15. Prot-Evangelium promul- gatum fuit, cujus interpretes esse debuêre S. Pa- triarchæ, non minus, quam Moses, & eum sequu- ti Prophetæ.

## 1:71
Verse 71. 'Salvation from our enemies and from the hand of all who hate us'—namely, liberation from the body of sin, from the world, from death, and from the devil: which liberation was first figured in the liberation from Egypt: of which the Psalmist sings thus in 106:10, 'He saved them from the hand of those who hated them and redeemed them from the hand of the enemies.' Then in the liberation of David from the power of Saul, of which David says in Psalm 18:17, 'He will deliver me from my strong enemies and from those who hate me.' Add the passage in Hosea 13:14 and his interpreter Paul in 1 Corinthians 15:55. Moreover, among the Hebrews, 'enemies' and 'those who hate' are often joined exegetically, as in Psalm 18:17 and 41.

Latin:

Vers. 71. σωτηρίαν ἐξ ἐχθρῶν ἡμῶν καὶ ἐκ χειρὸς πάντων τῶν μισούντων ἡμᾶς] Liberationem scilicet à corpore peccati, à mundo, à morte, & diabolo: quæ liberatio figurata est primum in liberatione ex Ægypto: de qua ita canit Psal- tes CVI. 10. ἔσωσεν αὐτὸς ἐκ χειρὸς μισούντων καὶ ἐλυτρώσατο αὐτὸς ἐκ χειρὸς ἐχθρῶν. Deinde in liberatione Davidis à vi Saulis, de qua David Psalm. XVIII. 18. ῥύσεται με ἐξ ἐχ- θρῶν μᾶ δυνατῶν καὶ ἐκ τῶν μισούντων με. Adde locum Oseæ XIII. 13. & ejus interpretem Paulum I. Cor. XV. 55. Solent autem apud Hebræos sæpe ἐξηγητικῶς conjungi οἱ ἐχθροὶ & οἱ μισοῦντες, ut Psal. XVIII. 18. & 41.

## 1:72
Verse 72. 'To perform mercy with our fathers'—these are the very words of the Decalogue explained more mystically, existing in Exodus 20:6 and Deuteronomy 5:10, where God says that He is 'performing mercy' unto many generations to those who love Him, such as were the first sowers of the Hebrew race. Although it is true, as Origen and others warn here, that the fruit of Christ's benefits flowed to those very progenitors, if one attends to the words of the law, he will find the sense to be that those benefits which happen to posterity on account of them are conferred upon the parents themselves: which Theophylact also noted on this passage. Aristotle in his book on Ethics, Book 1, Chapter 11: 'That the fortunes of descendants and of all friends contribute nothing at all seems very unfriendly and contrary to opinions': then, 'The successes of friends do therefore seem to contribute something to those who have passed away.' Thus Christ shows it is right for her to be relieved by him who is a daughter of Abraham, chapter 13:16. And elsewhere he says he was sent especially to save the sheep of the house of Israel, Matthew 10:6. So also Peter in Acts 3:25: 'You are the sons of the prophets': where it follows that here too there is a mention of the covenant; Paul in Romans 11:28: 'Beloved for the sake of the fathers.'

Although that phrase 'performing mercy' in Exodus 20:6 is held among the Septuagint, yet here it is not the legal promise to pious progenitors about grace being shown to posterity that is regarded, but the Evangelical promise made to the Patriarchs concerning the Messiah, just as the following things concerning the covenant and the divine oath confirm.

And to remember his holy covenant—taken from Leviticus 26:42, where, after God had dealt with repentance, he adds, 'And I will remember the covenant of Jacob and the covenant of Isaac and the covenant of Abraham I will remember.' See what we said above regarding those 'to remember mercy' in the song of Mary.

Latin:

Vers. 72. ποιῆσαι ἔλεος μετὰ τῶν πατέρων ἡμῶν] Verba sunt ipsa Decalogi explicata μυστικώτερον, Exstant Exodi XX. 6. & Deut. V. 10. ubi Deus dicit se esse עשה חסד ποιῆσαι ἔλεος in multam progeniem iis qui se diligant, quales fuerant He- brææ gentis primi Satores. Quanquam autem verum est quod Origenes atque alii hic monent, ad illos ipsos proge- nitores fructum beneficiorum Christi manasse, si quis tamen ad verba legis attendat, reperiet sensum esse, ipsis genitori- bus conferri ea beneficia quæ propter ipsos contingunt po- steris: quod & Theophylactus notavit ad hunc locum. A- ristoteles libro de Moribus I. cap. XI. τὰς δὲ τῶν ἀπογόνων τύ- χας καὶ τῶν φίλων ἁπάντων τὸ μὲν μηδοτιοῦν συμβάλλεσθαι, λίαν ἄφι- λον φαίνεται κὰι ταῖς δόξαις ἐναντίον : deinde, Συμβάλλεσθαί μὲν ἔν τε φαίνονται τοῖς κεκμηκόσιν αἱ εὐπραξίαι τῶν φίλων. Ita Christus ostendit æquum esse à se eam sublevari quæ sit filia Abra- hami c. XIII. 16. Et alibi missum se præcipue ait ad servan- das oves domus Israëlis Matth. X. 6. Sic & Petrus Act. III. 25. ὑμεῖς ἐστε υἱοὶ τῶν προφητῶν : ubi sequitur ut & hic mentio τῆς διαθήκης Paulus Rom. XI. 28. ἀγαπητοὶ διὰ τοὺς πατέρας.

Licet phrasis illa ποιῶν ἔλεος Exod. XX. 6. ha- beatur apud LXX. non tamen hic promissio legalis piis progenitoribus de gratia posteris exhibenda, sed promissio Evangelica Patriarchis de Messia fa- cta respicitur, quemadmodum sequentia de fœde- re & juramento divino confirmant.

κὰι μνησθῆναι διαθήκης ἁγίας αὑτοῦ] Sumtum ex Levitico XXVI. 42. ubi cum de pœnitentia Deus egisset, subjicit, κὰι μνησθήσομαι τῆς διαθήκης Ἰακὼβ κὰι τῆς διαθήκης Ἰσαὰκ κὰι τῆς διαθήκης Ἀβραὰμ μνησθήσομαι. Vide quæ supra diximus ad illa μνησθῆναι ἐλέους in carmine Mariæ.

## 1:73
Vers. 73. The oath which he swore to Abraham our father] I think this also, no less than the preceding infinitives, is best referred to that which preceded, 'as he spoke.' For the discourse ascends by degrees from the covenant to the oath, just as God first makes a covenant with Abraham, Gen. XVII. 7, and then also swore, ch. XXII. 16, 17, rewarding the confidence shown by Abraham in the offering of his son with a new confirmation of confidence, as Philo not badly observes. I would cite words worthy of being read: 'God, admiring the faith shown toward him, gives back to him as a prize the confirmation by oath of the gifts which he promised, and not only as God to a man, but also as a friend conversing with a friend.' The same writer elsewhere says that God's oath is 'a help for our weakness,' adding an excellent reason: 'for we are not able to store up in our own soul the worthy sum of the causes continuously, this is why God [speaks] in a human-like way, so that we may rise above all things that are spoken of in human terms.' Nor indeed is God accustomed to add an oath to any promises whatsoever, but only to those which extend into all time: by which is noted 'the immutability of his counsel,' says the writer to the Hebrews VI. 17. Now, that such is the promise concerning the singular favor of God toward the Israelites above the other nations, Paul shows in the Epistle to the Romans, which nevertheless did not prevent some who were notably stubborn from falling away from the fruit of that favor, as we are taught in the same place. It is worthy of note, however, that in these few words the force of the names which had fallen to both the son and the parents, not without divine arrangement, is indicated. For 'to perform mercy' explains the name of John: 'to remember' the name of Zacharias: 'oath' the name of Elizabeth.

Latin:

Vers. 73. ὅρκον ὃν ὤμοσε πρὸς Ἀβραὰμ τὸν πατέρα ἡμῶν] Puto & hoc non minus quam infinitivos præcedentes opti- me referri ad id quod præcessit καθὼς ἐλάλησε. Nam grada- tim ascendit oratio à fœdere ad jusjurandum, sicut Deus primo fœdus facit cum Abrahamo, Gen. XVII. 7. deinde & juravit c. XXII. 16. 17. fiduciam nimirum Abraham in obla- tione filii ostensam nova fiduciæ confirmatione remune- rans, ut non male observat Philo. Verba legi digna affcri- bam: Θεὸς τῆς πρὸς αὐτὸν πίστεως ἀγάμενος τὸν ἄθλα πίστιν ἀν- τιδίδωσιν αὐτῷ τὴν δι’ ὅρκυ βεβαίωσιν ὧν ὑπέσχετο δωρεῶν, καὶ ἔτι μόνον ὡς ἀνθρώπῳ Θεὸς, ἀλλὰ κὰι ὡς Φίλω γνώριμος διαλε- γόμενος. Idem Scriptor alibi Dei jusjurandum ait esse τῆς ἡμετέρας ἀσθενείας ἐπικουρίαν, rationem egregiam addens, ὧ γὰρ δυνάμεθα διηνεκῶς τὸ ἄξιον τῶν αἰτίων κεφάλαιον ἐν ψυχῇ τα- μιεύσασθαι τῇ ἑαυτῶν, τόδ̓ χ̓ ὡς ἀνθρωποειδῆ ὁ Θεὸς ἵνα ἅπαντα τὰ ἀνθρωπολογούμενα ὑπερκύψωμεν. Neque vero quibus vis promissionibus, sed eis duntaxat quæ se in omne tempus extendunt, jusjurandum Deus adjicere solet: quo no- tari τὸ ἀμετάθετον τῆς βυλῆς ait Scriptor ad Hebræos VI. 17. Talem autem esse pollicitationem de singulari favore Dei erga Israëlitas supra gentes cæteras ostendit Paulus in Epi- stola ad Romanos, quæ tamen non impedivit quo minus quidam insigniter contumaces ejus favoris fructu excide- rent, ut ibidem docemur. Dignum autem notatu est paucis hisce verbis vim nominum quæ & filio & parentibus non si- ne divina disposite one contigerant indicari. Nam ποιῆσαι ἔλεος explicat Johannis nomen: μνησθῆναι nomen Zacha- riæ: ὅρκος nomen Elisabeth.

## 1:74
Vers. 74. That he would grant unto us that we being delivered out of the hand of our enemies might serve him without fear] The Holy Spirit paraphrases the words of the oath: 'Thy seed shall possess by hereditary right the gate of his enemies.' He rightly called 'the oath that he would grant' the oath by which God promises that he will give something. But the Holy Spirit teaches us here through Zacharias, as he often does through the Apostles, that 'fleshly things' had in themselves a shadow 'of spiritual things.' This explanation, however, indicates not obscurely the excellence of the new and now to be promulgated covenant over the old.

ἀφόβως] To be joined with λατρεύειν. Of the old covenant there was a spirit of bondage unto fear, Rom. VIII. 15. For there were those who belonged to that covenant, subject to bondage, through fear of death, Hebr. II, 15. But to the new people is everywhere attributed the Spirit of liberty and confidence. It is well noted, however, that ἀφόβως here is equivalent to לבטח. See Leviticus XXV. 18 and Jeremiah XXIII. v. 6. The LXX in both places translate it πεποιθότες. But properly it seems here to look back to the passage in Deuteronomy where, just as that לבטח leans upon the mention of liberation from enemies, so here the LXX there have: and he shall cause you to rest from all your enemies round about, and you shall dwell in safety.

That distinction of time before Christ and after Christ was exhibited, which the Socinianizing Grotius refers to here, has no foundation: for although by the power of the legal pact we are under fear, that is nevertheless just as much the case now, after Christ was exhibited, as it was of old: because the law only works wrath, Rom. IV. 11, and brings condemnation, 2 Cor. III. 9. By the power of the new Evangelical covenant, however, the ancients were just as much as we were liberated from the fear of death, and rejoiced in the spirit of confidence and liberty, Act. XV. 10, 11.

ἐκ χειρὸς τῶν ἐχθρῶν ἡμῶν ῥυσθέντας λατρεύειν αὐτῷ] A manifest allusion to the words of God in Exodus III. 12. Who the enemies are to be understood as being has been said above. We are liberated from them for this reason, that we may serve God, Rom. VI. 18, 22.

Latin:

Vers. 74. τῦ δῦναι ἡμῖν ἀφόβως ἐκ χειρὸς τῶν ἐχθρῶν ἡμῶν ῥυ- σθέντας λατρεύειν αὐτῷ] Παραφράζει Spiritus Sanctus verba jurisjurandi: Semen tuum hæreditario jure possidebit portam hostium suorum. ὅρκον τῦ δῦναι recte dixit jusjurandum quo Deus aliquid se daturum promittit. Docet autem nos hic per Zachariam Spiritus Sanctus quod sæpe per Apostolos, τὰ σαρκικὰ habuisse in se umbram τῶν πνευματικῶν. Explica- tio autem hæc non obscure indicat excellentiam novi & jam promulgandi fœderis supra antiquum.

ἀφόβως] Conjungendum cum λατρεύειν. Veteris fœderis erat πνεῦμα δυλείας εἰς φόβον Rom. VIII. 15. Erant enim qui ad illud fœdus pertinebant ἔνοχοι, δυλείας, φόβῳ θανάτυ, Hebr. II, 15. At novo populo passim tribuitur Spiritus libertatis & fiduciæ. Bene autem notatum est ἀφόβως hic valere quod לבטח. Vide Levitici XXV. 18. & Jer. XXIII. v. 6. LXX. utroque loco vertunt πεποιθότες. Sed proprie videtur hic respici Deuteronomii locus ubi ut itidem istud לבטח adnitur mentioni liberationis ab hostibus, ut hic LXX. ibi habent καὶ καταπαύσῃ ὑμᾶς ἀπὸ πάντων τῶν ἐχθρῶν ὑμῶν τῷ κύκλῳ καὶ κατοικήσετε μετ᾽ ἀσφαλείας.

Illa temporis ante Christum, & post exhibitum Christum distinctio, quam respicit hic Socinizans Grotius, nullum habet fundamentum: Nam licet vi legalis pacti nos sub metu simus, id tamen perinde nunc, post exhibitum Christum, ita est, ut olim: quia lex tantum iram operatur, Rom. IV. 11. & condemnationem affert 2. Cor. III. 9. Vi autem Novi fœderis Evangelici æque veteres, ac nos, liberati à metu mortis spiritu fiduciæ, & libertatis gaudebant, Act. XV. 10. 111.

ἐκ χειρὸς τῶν ἐχθρῶν ἡμῶν ῥυσθέντας λατρεύειν αὐτῷ] Manifesta allusio ad verba Dei Exodi III. 12. Qui hostes sint intelligendi supra dictum est Ab his ideo liberamur ut Deo serviamus, Rom. VI. 18. 22.

## 1:75
Vers. 75. ἐν ὁσιότητι κὰι δικαιοσύνῃ ἐνώπιον ἀυτῦ] That is, in that justice and holiness which does not consist in laborious rites, but in the sincerity of the heart, of which God is the inspector. This is what Paul says, in righteousness and holiness of truth, Eph. IV. 24. Christ, in spirit and truth, John IV. 23.

πάσας τὰς ἡμέρας τῆς ζωῆς ἡμῶν] Without an interrupted course of obedience, which that Spirit promised in the new covenant provides. See Jer. XXXII. 39, 40.

Latin:

Vers. 75. ἐν ὁσιότητι κὰι δικαιοσύνῃ ἐνώπιον ἀυτῦ] Id est, in ea justitia & sanctitate quæ non in operosis ritibus consistit, sed in sinceritate cordis cujus inspector est Deus. Hoc est quod Paulus dicit ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ κὰι ὁσιότητι τῆς ἀληθείας Eph. IV. 24. Christus, ἐν πνεύματι καὶ ἀληθείᾳ Joh. IV. 23.

πάσας τὰς ἡμέρας τῆς ζωῆς ἡμῶν] Non interrupto obedientiæ cursu quod præstat Spiritus ille in novo fœdere promissus. Vide Jer. XXXII. 39. 40.

## 1:76
Vers. 76. προφήτης ὑψίστε κληθήσῃ] προφήτης, from the origin of the word, is one who predicts future things: but it is so called more broadly, to use the words of Philo, as an interpreter of things to be said, prompted from within by God.

προπορέυσῃ γὰρ πρὸ προσώπε κυρίε] The words of the Angel above v. 17. The office of a forerunner is described.

ἑτοιμάσαι ὁδὺς αὐτῦ] From Isaiah XL. 3.

John was not only a Prophet in such a way that interpreters of the word are accustomed to be called by this name, but also in the stricter meaning of the word; because he was predicting future things entirely, concerning the Messiah and the final Judgment, Matthew III, John I and III.

Latin:

Vers. 76. προφήτης ὑψίστε κληθήσῃ] προφήτης ex vocis origine qui futura prædicit: sed latius ita vocatur, ut Philonis utar verbis, ἑρμηνεὺς ἔνδοθεν ὑπηχῶντος τὰ λεκτέα τῶ Θεῷ.

προπορέυσῃ γὰρ πρὸ προσώπε κυρίε] Verba Angeli supra v. 17. Munitoris officium describitur.

ἑτοιμάσαι ὁδὺς αὐτῦ] Ex Esa. XL. 3.

Non tantum ita Propheta fuit Johannes, ut appellari hoc nomine Interpretes verbi solent, sed strictiori etiam vocis significatione; quia prædicebat omnino futura, de Messia & de extremo Judicio, Matth. III. Joh. I. & III.

## 1:77
Vers. 77. Τῦ δῦναι γνῶσιν σωτηρίας] That is, διὰ τῦ δῦναι: for he now explains in what that preparation consists: namely, in the provision of saving doctrine concerning repentance, to be commended in summary by John, but in such a way that a fuller knowledge was to be sought from Christ, John himself indicating this very thing.

It does not appear that the preparation is explained here: rather, each is distinctly attributed to John, both that he was to prepare the way for the Messiah, and that he himself was also to give the knowledge of salvation. The former looks to the legal, the latter to the Evangelical sermons of John. Therefore there is no need for an ellipsis. Nor should the different heads of doctrine be confused, concerning repentance and concerning salvation, the former of which, as we have said, pertains to the law: the latter to the Gospel: because we have salvation only in Christ.

ἐν ἀφέσει ἁμαρτιῶν αὐτῶν] Here, as in many other places, ἐν is put for εἰς. For that knowledge of salvation is the very baptism of repentance for the remission of sins, Mark I. 4, Luke below III. 3.

Latin:

Vers. 77. Τῦ δῦναι γνῶσιν σωτηρίας] Id est, διὰ τῦ δῦναι: jam enim explicat qua in re illa præparatio consistat: nimirum in subministratione doctrinæ salutaris de resipiscentia, summatim commendanda per Johannem, sed ita ut plenior cognitio à Christo esset petenda, Johanne hoc ipsum indicante.

Explicari hic preparationem non apparet: imo distincte utrumque tribuitur Johanni, & quod viam preparaturus sit Messiæ, ut quod daturus sit etiam ipse cognitionem salutis. Illud ad legales, hoc ad Evangelicas Johannis conciones spectat. Ideo opus non est Ellipsi. Neq; confundi debent diversa doctrinæ capita, de resipiscentia, & de salute, quorum prius ut diximus, ad legem pertinet: posterius ad Evangelium: quia non nisi in Christo salutem habemus.

ἐν ἀφέσει ἁμαρτιῶν αὐτῶν] Omnino hic, ut aliis multis in locis, ἐν est pro εἰς positum. Nam γνῶσις illa σωτηρίας est ipsum βάπτισμα μετανοίας εἰς ἄφεσιν ἁμαρτιῶν, Marcus I. 4. Lucas infra III. 3.

## 1:78
Vers. 78. Through the bowels of the mercy of our God] In Hebrew books you will find these placed separately, as in Isa. LXIII. 15. מעיך ורחמיך. Likewise: Jer. XVI. 5. את החסד ואת הרחמים: So also Paul, Phil. II. 1, σπλάγχνα κὰι οἰκτιρμοὶ. But a very similar manner of speaking is found here in the same Paul, Col. III. 12. σπλάγχνα οἰκτιρμῶν, by which undoubtedly inward compassion is signified. See what is said on Matt. IX. 36. Many think this 'through the bowels of the mercy of our God' should be referred to the 'remission' which was mentioned before, so that it is said that this forgiveness proceeds from the mercy of God, which is most certain. But to me, these words seem to be referred to the whole of what preceded, namely, to the very mission of John and the Messiah and the call to repentance commanded to them both from the most merciful counsel of God, which the following words also seem entirely to require. But the Apostles often refer this extraordinary calling to the supreme mercy of God, and they contrast that mercy with human works.

Baptism and the knowledge of salvation are entirely different things; they are rashly confused: nor is there any need for 'ἐν' to be taken as 'εἰς' here, since the knowledge of salvation is in that remission of sins which comes to us through the bowels of the mercy of our God, in which the dayspring from on high has visited us. For those 'bowels' do not pertain to the mission of John and the Messiah, and the call to repentance, as Grotius wishes, but to the immediately preceding 'remission', namely of sins: since these cohere like a chain and the causes of justification are rendered, both the ministerial, which is John and similar ministers of the word, and the instrumental, of the knowledge of salvation, that is, of faith, and the formal, in which Salvation consists, by the mention of the remission of sins, and the principal, which is the mercy of God, and the meritorious, which is comprehended by the visitation of the dayspring from on high, and finally the final, so that those illuminated by divine light may direct their feet into the way of peace.

Through which mercy, he says, that heavenly light shone upon us. 'ἀνατολὴ' is indeed used by the LXX in several places for 'צֶמַח', which others translate as 'βλάσημα' (sprout), for in Greek also 'φυτὰ' (plants) are said to 'ἀνατέλλειν' (sprout up). But truly, the following words show that it is not to be taken in this way here: but that 'ἀνατολὴ' is the very thing which Isaiah called 'אוֹר' (light) in chapter IX. 2, which passage is clearly looked back upon here, and is referred to Christ and his doctrine even by Matthew. Moreover, the word 'אוֹר', although it is accustomed to be taken for all light, yet properly and peculiarly signifies morning light, or the rising sun; thus Nehem. VIII. 3, 'מִן אוֹר' the LXX translate as 'from the hour of the brightening of the sun'. And the verb 'פָּנָה שֶׁמֶשׁ' is taken for 'ἀνατέλλειν' (to rise), as Gen. XLIV. 3, 'הַבֹּקֶר אוֹר' (the morning was light) 'τὸ πρωὶ ἔφαυσε' (the morning shone). Philo defines the 'ἀνατολὴν ψυχῆς' (rising of the soul) as when the brightness of virtues rises like the rays of the sun.

Scultetus prefers to interpret the word 'ἀνατολὴ' as 'germine' (sprout/branch), supposing that Zechariah looked with both eyes to the Prophets Zech. III. 8 and Jer. XXXIII. 5, which, however, is not placed beyond the hazard of doubt, since he does not say simply 'ἀνατολὼ' (branch), as the LXX have there, but 'ἀνατολὼ ἐξ ὕψυς' (dayspring from on high) for Christ: for that Zechariah adds this of his own, to indicate that this sprout differs from other plants which sprout from the earth, since this sprout is from heaven, is more subtle than solid: and Heinsius rightly warns of this. Those who wish 'ἀνατολὴ' in this place to be a sprout, let them see what they will answer to the Evangelist, when he adds 'to shine upon those in darkness' etc., by which words he alluded to the most well-known passage of Isaiah chapter IX. Cf. also Scaliger in Elench. Trihæref. The Syrian uses a word which signifies to come forth from the east, and the rising of the Sun.

Latin:

Vers. 78. διὰ σπλάγχνα ἐλέυς Θεῦ ἡμῶν] In Hebræis libris invenies hæc disjuncte posita ut Es. LXIII. 15. מעיך ורחמיך. It: Jer. XVI. 5. את החסד ואת הרחמים: Sic & Paulo Philipp. II. 1, σπλάγχνα κὰι οἰκτιρμοὶ. At simillimum hic loquendi genus est apud eundem Paulum Coloss. III. 12. σπλάγχνα οἰκτιρμῶν, quo haud dubie intima miseratio significatur. Vide quæ ad Matth. IX. 36. Putant multi hoc διὰ σπλάγχνα ἐλέυς Θεῦ ἡμῶν referendum ad ἄφεσιν cujus mentio præcessit, uti dicetur ea venia ex Dei misericordia proficisci, quod certissimum est. At mihi hæc verba ad totum id quod præcessit referenda videntur, nimirum ad ipsam missionem Johannis atque Messiæ & vocationem ad pœnitentiam illorum utrique mandatam ex misericordissimo Dei consilio, quod & sequentia omnino videntur exigere. Sæpe autem Apostoli hanc extraordinariam vocationem referunt ad summam Dei misericordiam, eamque misericordiam humanis operibus opponunt.

Diversa omnino sunt Baptismus & cognitio sa- lutis; quæ temere confunduntur: neque opus est ἐν pro εἰς hic accipi, quum cognitio salutis sit in remissione illa peccatorum quæ dia σπλάγχνα ἐλέ- υς Θεῶ ἡμῶν nobis obtingit, in quibus visitavit nos oriens ex alto. Illa enim διὰ σπλάγχνα non ad missionem Johannis ac Messiæ, & vocationem ad pœnitentiam, quod vult Grotius, sed ad immedia- te præcedentia ad ἄφεσιν, nempe ἁμαρτιῶν per- tinent: quum hæc instar catenæ coæreant & causæ reddantur justificationis, tum ministerialis quæ est Johannes, eique similes verbi ministri, tum instru- mentalis, cognitionis salutis, hoc est, fidei, tum for- malis, in quo consistat Salus, remissionis peccato- rum mentione, tum principalis, quæ est misericor- dia Dei, tum meritoria, quæ visitatione orientis ex alto comprehenditur, tum denique finalis, ut illu- minati divina luce pedes suos dirigant in viam pacis.

ἐν οἷς ἐπεσκέψατο ἡμᾶς ἀνατολὴ ἐξ ὕψυς] Per quam mise- ricordiam, inquit, affulsit nobis illa lux cœlestis. ἀνατολὴ quidem à LXX. aliquot locis ponitur pro צֶמַח quod alii vertunt βλάσημα, nam & Græcis φυτὰ dicuntur ἀνατέλλειν. Sed profecto quæ sequuntur ostendunt hic non ita accipi- endum: sed ἀνατολὴ esse id ipsum quod אוֹר dixit Esaias cap. IX. 2. qui locus hic aperte respicitur, & ad Christum ejusque doctrinam refertur etiam à Matthæo. Vox autem אוֹר quanquam pro omni luce accipi solet, proprie tamen & peculiariter lucem matutinam, sive orientem significat; ita Nehem. VIII. 3. מִן אוֹר LXX. vertunt ἀπὸ ὥρας τῶ δια- φωτίσαι τὸν ἥλιον. Et verbum פָּנָה שֶׁמֶשׁ sumitur pro ἀνα-τέλλειν, ut Gen. XLIV. 3. הַבֹּקֶר אוֹר τὸ πρωὶ ἔφαυσε. Phi- lo ἀνατολὴν ψυχῆς definit ὅταν ἡλιακῶν ἀκτίνων τρόπον ἀνάσχῃ τὸ ἀρετῶν φέγγος.

Scultetus mavult vocem ἀνατολὴ de germine in- terpretari, supponens Zachariam utroque oculo re- spexisse ad Prophetas Zach. III. 8. & Jerem. XXXIII. 5. quod vero extra dubitationis aleam constitutum non est, quum non simpliciter ἀνατολώ, ut ibi LXX. habent, sed ἀνατολὼ ἐξ ὕψυς Christum di- cat: nam quod hoc de suo addat Zacharias, ut indi- cet germen hoc à reliquis plantis differre, quæ è terra germinent, quum hoc germen à cælo sit, subtilius est, quam solidius: & recte monet Heinsius. Qui ἀνατολὴ hoc loco germen esse volunt, videant quid Evangelistæ responsuri sint, cum addit ἐπιφᾶναι τοῖς ἐν σκότῳ &c. quibus verbis notissimum Esaiæ allu- sit locum cap. IX. Conf. & Scaliger in Elench. Tri- hæref. Syrus ea voce utitur, quæ prodire ex oriente, & ortum Solis significat.

## 1:79
Vers. 79. To shine upon those sitting in darkness and the shadow of death] See Matt. IV. 16. The sense is that this light shone upon the Hebrew people at the time when they were living in the deepest darkness of ignorance.

To direct our feet into the way of peace] The metaphor is continued. For light directs us so that we may walk securely, John XII. 35, Eph. V. 8, 1 John II. 7, Rev. XXI. So also Ps. CXIX. 105. The word of God is called a light to the path. We interpret 'peace' here as security, just as Josephus explains 'Soluma' as 'security'.

The light shone not only upon the Hebrew people in the darkness of ignorance, but also upon the Gentiles established in the darkness and shadow of death, of sin no less than of ignorance, of whom Isa. IX. 2 treats particularly. Cf. Isa. LX. 1, 2. The horrible gloom is noted, which strikes the evil of death, and is deadly and brings death, as the blessed Chemnitius observes. By peace, however, he understands both the peace of conscience toward God in this life, Rom. V. 1, and the tranquility secure from all evils in the other: which is the end of this illumination of light. Nor does that light only show the way, but it directs our feet into that way, which leads from these miseries of the world to eternal peace and blessedness. For to direct is to rule, or to lead, so that the feet may not wander, but may rightly hold the way which leads to peace.

Latin:

Vers. 79. ἐπιφάναι τοῖς ἐν σκότῳ καὶ σκιᾷ θανάτυ καθη- μένοις] Vid. Matth. IV. 16. Sensus est populo Hebræo afful- sisse hanc lucem tunc cum in summis ignorantiæ tene- bris versaretur.

τῶ κατευθῦναι τὺς πόδας ἡμῶν εἰς ὁδὸν εἰρήνης] Continua- tur translatio. Nam lux dirigit nos ut secure ambulemus Joh. XII. 35. Eph. V. 8. 1. Joh. II. 7. Apoc. XXI. Sic & Psal. CXIX. 105. Verbum Dei lumen semitæ dicitur. εἰρήνην hic securitatem interpretamur, sicut Josephus σόλυμα exponit ἀσφάλειαν.

Non populo tantum Ebræo affulsit lux in te- nebris ignorantiæ, sed etiam gentibus in tenebris & umbra mortis constitutis, non minus peccati quam ignorantiæ, de quibus Esa. IX. 2. peculiariter agi- tur. Conf. Es. LX. 1. 2. Notatur horribilis caligo, quæ malum mortis incutiat, & mortifera sit & mortem inferat, observante B. Chemnitio. Per pacem au- tem tum pacem conscientiæ erga Deum in hac vita Rom. V. 1. tum tranquillitatem ab omnibus malis se- curam in altera intelligit: quæ finis est illuminatio- nis hujus lucis. Nec vero tantum ostendit lux illa viam, sed dirigit pedes nostros in illam viam, quæ ex his mundi miseriis ad æternam pacem, & beati- tudinem perducit. Dirigere enim est regere, seu ducere, ne pedes aberrent, sed viam, quæ ad pa- cem ducit, recte teneant.

## 1:80
Vers. 80.

He grew strong in spirit] That is, in wisdom: as below concerning the Lord himself, chapter II. 52, 'he increased in wisdom'.

ἐν ταῖς ἐρήμοις] They are mistaken who think that the paternal home of John is understood here. For that was in the city, as we have already seen. Therefore, just as the herald of repentance composed himself for a more severe way of life, so he chose a place suitable for that severity, thus also expressing Elijah. That what I say is true will appear to one who does not read the very words of Christ inattentively, Matt. XI. v. 7.

ἀναδείξεως ἀυτῦ πρὸς τὸν Ἰσραὴλ] When God wished to make his calling known. Thus concerning Jesus, John I. 31, "that he might be made manifest to Israel."

Latin:

Vers. 80.

Ἐκραταιῦτο πνεύματι] Id est, sapientia: ut infra de ipso Domino cap. II. 52. προέκοπτε σοφίᾳ.

ἐν ταῖς ἐρήμοις] Errant qui hic paternam Iohannis do- mum intelligi putant. Ea enim erat in urbe ut jam vidi- mus.
