Sicut ergo ad victum severiorem se composuit pœni- tentiæ præco, ita & locum ei severitati convenientem ele- git, Eliam sic quoque exprimens. Quod dico verum esse apparebit non supine legenti ipsa Christi verba Matth. XI. v. 7.

ἀναδείξεως ἀυτῦ πρὸς τὸν Ἰσραὴλ] Cum Deus vocatio- nem ipsius innotescere voluit. Sic de Iesu Ioh. I. 31. ἵνα φανερωθῇ τῷ Ἰσραὴλ.

## 2:1 Argument
CHAPTER II. ARGUMENT AND DIVISION.

The birth of Christ is described according to time, place, family, and manner, which the angel announces to the shepherds, the angelic host celebrates, and the shepherds find the child born in Bethlehem and make it known: who, circumcised on the eighth day, was called Jesus, and when the days of purification were completed, was presented in the temple, received in the arms by Simeon, who sought his dismissal because he had seen the Savior, and prophesied about him to Mary: the prophetess Anna also celebrating the Lord and testifying about him. Jesus grows, and the ten-year-old boy disputes with the Doctors in Jerusalem, then returning to Nazareth, subject to his parents, he advances in wisdom, age, and grace.

There are four parts: I. The birth of Christ, and its announcement, and its publication by the shepherds, to v. 20. II. The circumcision, v. 21. III. The presentation in the Temple, and what happened there, to v. 39. IV. His childhood, and the disputation in the Temple, to v. 52.

PART I. Description of the birth of Christ.

Verse 1.

Ἐξῆλθε δόγμα παρὰ καίσαρος Αὐγύστ8] I do not understand this as if a census were made throughout the whole world where there was a Roman at one and the same time: but since Augustus wished to know the full strength of the Roman empire, he ordered a census to be taken through all kingdoms and provinces, now here, now there, as was convenient. This is what Dio says, "he sent others to different places to register the property of individuals and of cities." Claudius, in the oration which is preserved at Ancyra, the abbreviator of Livy, and Dio mention the census taken through Gaul by the order of Augustus. The word ἐξῆλθε signifies a publication, Dan. II. 12, c. IX. 25, Esther I. 19.

ἀπογράφεσθαι πᾶσαν τὴν οἰκεμένην] That is, as I have already said, a census taken throughout the Roman world: just as the Syriac here correctly interprets it. For what is in the abbreviator of Livy as "a census was taken," Dio called "he made registrations." However, they are mistaken who think that by this census a poll tax was imposed on the Jews by the Romans. For that was not done before the confiscation of the property of Archelaus. Before that, the Jewish people paid tribute to Herod: but Herod gave to the Roman Empire, as other allied kings did, as Appian says, "fixed tributes." Therefore, this census pertained to this, that it might be known what each kingdom and province was worth in terms of the abundance of men and money. For the purpose of a census, as Florus teaches, is that all distinctions of property, dignity, age, arts, and duties be recorded in tables. Cicero, in the third book of Laws: "Let the censors register the ages, offspring, families, and property of the people." And Claudius in the said oration says that nothing further was sought by the census taken by him than that their resources should be publicly known.

Latin:

CAPUT II. ARGUMENTUM ET PAR- TITIO.

Nativitas Christi secundum tempus, locum, familiam, & modum describitur, quam pa- storibus annuntiat, angelus, celebrat exer- citus angelicus, puerumq́; natum in Bethle- hem inveniunt & divulgant pastores: qui octavo die circumcisus Iesus vocatus, & ex- actis dieb9 purificationis in templo præsen- tatus, à Simeone brachiis exceptus, dimissio- nem ob visum Salvatorem expetente, & de ipso ad Mariam vaticinante: celebrante et- iam Hanna Prophetissa Dominum, & de i- pso testificante. Crescit Iesus, & puer de- cennalis cum Doctoribus disputat Hieroso- lymis, inde Nazarethā reversus parentib9 subditus proficit sapientia, ætate & gratia.

Partes sunt quatuor: I. Nativitas Christi, ejus- que annunciatio, & per pastores divulgatio, ad v. 20. II. Circumcisio, v. 21. III. Præsenta- tio in Templo, & quæ ibi contigere, ad vers. 39. IV. Ætas puerilis, & disputatio in Templo, ad v. 52.

PARS I. Nativitatis Christi descriptio.

Vers. 1.

Ἐξῆλθε δόγμα παρὰ καίσαρος Αὐγύστ8] Non ita intel- ligo quasi uno eodemque tempore factus esset census per totum orbem qua Romanus erat: sed cum Augustus o- mnem vim imperii Romani pernôsse vellet, per omnia re- gna & provincias constituit censum agi, modo hic scilicet, modo illic, ut commodum erat. Hoc est quod Dion in- quit, ἔπεμψεν ἄλλες ἄλλῃ τάτε τῶν ἰδιωτῶν καὶ τὰ τῶν πόλεων ἀπογραψομένως. De censu per Galliam actu Augusti jussu meminerunt Claudius in oratione quæ Ancyræ servatur, breviator Livii & Dio. Vox ἐξῆλθε publicationem signifi- cat Dan. II. 12. c. IX. 25. Esther. I. 19.

ἀπογράφεσθαι πᾶσαν τὴν οἰκεμένην] Id est, ut jam dixi, censum agi per orbem Romanum: quomodo Syrus hic recte interpretatur. Nam quod apud Livii abbreviatorem est census actus, Dio dixit ἀπογραφὰς ἐποιήσατο. Errant autem qui putant hoc censu à Romanis capitationem Judæis in- dictam. Id enim factum non est ante confiscationem rerum Archelai. Antea populus Iudæus Herodi tributa pendebat: Herodes autem Imperio Romano, ut alii Reges socii, da- bat, ut Appianus loquitur, φόρες τεταγμένως. Quare census hic eo pertinebat, ut notum esset quid regna quæque & provinciæ hominum copia, quid pecuniis valerent. Nam ea vis census Floro docente, ut omnis patrimonii, dignita- tis, ætatis, artium officiorumq́; discrimina in tabulas referantur. Cicero de legibus tertio: Censores populi ævitates, suboles, familias, pecuniasq́; censento. Et Claudius in dicta oratione censu à se acto nihil ultra exquisitum ait quam ut publice notæ essent facultates.

## 2:2
Vers. 2. πρώτη ἐγένετο] That is, this was the first census taken by the Romans in Judea. Justin to Trypho: "When a registration was being made in Judea then for the first time under Quirinius, he had gone up from Nazareth, where he lived, to Bethlehem, from whence he was, to be registered." For we do not find any taken before. But this census reminded the Jews of the fulfilled prophecy concerning the destruction of the kingdoms of Syria and Egypt, after the overthrow of which the Messiah was to be expected.

quibus Quirinus legitur. Κυρηνίον, that name is written by Luke, by Josephus, and by Justin Martyr. But the prefect of this census business was Sentius Saturninus, who was governor of Syria, who was undoubtedly joined to Quirinius. And just as Luke calls Quirinius "governor of Syria," so Justin says that it happened in Judea as "procurator." Indeed, the word for both "governorship" and "procuratorship," as has been correctly demonstrated by learned men, signifies any commands, even those mandated out of the ordinary. For we cannot translate ἐπίτροπον as procurator of Judea, since no Roman procurator was in Judea, or could have been, while Herod was reigning: and besides, procurators were chosen from the equestrian order: Quirinius, although he was not a Patrician, had earned the consulship by his good conduct of affairs in Cilicia, as Tacitus teaches, and thus had reached the Senate: Josephus: Κυρήνιος εἰς τὴν βουλὴν συναγομένων ἀνὴρ τά τε ἄλλας ἀρχὰς ἐπιτετελεκὼς καὶ διὰ πασῶν ὁδεύσας ὑπατος γενέσθαι. And elsewhere about the same man: ἀνὴρ ὑπατικός. Thus also Eusebius had said, κυρήνιος ἀπὸ συγκλήτου βουλῆς ἐπέμφθη, that is, Quirinius was sent as one of the Senators, not by the counsel of the Senate, as Jerome translates. But men of that order were accustomed to be placed in charge of the census. Thus we read that censuses were conducted by Drusus and Germanicus, but also by other senators. Tacitus book XIV. Censuses were conducted throughout Gaul by Qu. Volusius and Sex. Africanus, and Trebellius Maximus, with Volusius and Africanus being rivals among themselves on account of their nobility. It is certain from Tertullian that Sentius Saturninus was Governor of Syria at this time: whose words are: but it is also established that censuses were conducted under Augustus now in Judea through Sentius Saturninus. However, Tertullian could not have been mistaken in that matter, since censuses were accustomed to be recorded in registers, and those registers were first publicly displayed, then kept in Archives where there was an opportunity for inspection. Therefore Justin appeals to the registers themselves, 'You can learn,' he says, 'from the registrations made under Quirinius.' where he calls the census registers ἀπογραφὰς, as they are called in the code. Thus also Dio about Caligula: 'he asked for the registrations of the Gauls.' Tertullian himself often mentions the registers of this census. For in the stated passage he adds: 'among whom they could have inquired about his lineage.' Elsewhere: 'Finally, concerning the census of Augustus, which the Roman archives, the most faithful witness of the Lord's birth, keep.' Again elsewhere: 'So that no one could easily have been ignorant about his lineage, or about the recent Augustan censuses then perhaps still pending.' Where that 'pending' refers to the Roman custom of publicly displaying Acts, just as Plautus said laws hang fixed with iron nails. In another place again: 'Just as Mary, from whom Christ is born, is described in the census among the Romans.' Nor is it a wonder that these registers existed in the age of Tertullian, since Chrysostom testifies that they existed even in his own time: His words are: 'Whence it is clear that he was born during the first registration; and it is possible for anyone who wishes, by encountering the ancient codes lying publicly in Rome and having learned the time of the writing, to know it accurately.' However, it seems that Augustus had placed Quirinius in charge of conducting this census throughout Syria, because he had learned the affairs of the East exactly when he was waging war in Cilicia, which is near Syria. And for the same reason, this very Quirinius was given as a guide to Gaius Caesar, who was sent to the affairs of the East: and some years later, when Judea had already been reduced to the form of a province, he was sent to both govern Syria and at the same time impose Roman tributes on the Jews, which had not been done before that time. Josephus, regarding this census which Luke touches upon here, had nothing further to record, because since the imposition of tributes did not follow, nothing memorable had happened in it: but he rightly mentions the imposition of tributes by Quirinius, because then for the first time arose, under the leadership of Judas the Gaulonite, the sedition of those who denied that tribute could be paid to 'aliens,' such as the Romans were, without prejudice to religion. Those who think that Josephus, such a diligent investigator of Jewish affairs and to whom the Roman archives were also open, was deceived in a matter so obvious, I do not doubt that they themselves are greatly deceived.

The census was not made at one and the same time throughout the whole world where it was Roman, according to Grotius, but now here, now there, nor was a head-tax imposed on the Jews by the Romans by this census, but it pertained to this, that it might be known what each kingdom and province was worth in abundance of men and in money. And therefore πρώτη ἐγένετο, this was the first census conducted by the Romans in Judea. Which reminded the Jews that the prophecy about the destroying of the kingdoms of Syria and Egypt was fulfilled, after the overthrow of which the Messiah was to be expected. But since the Jews had already been made tributary under Pompey the Great, and seventy talents had been exacted from them by Gabinius, it seems rather to be called 'first' in a relative sense, because it was indeed the first in the prefecture of Quirinius, as the Syriac rendered it; or PRIOR, with respect to a later one, about which in Acts V and in Josephus book XVIII, near the beginning, or because as such, i.e., with the completion of the records it was the first: because such a description had never before been made in Judea. And although Sentius Saturninus was then President of Syria, as Tertullian testifies in book IV against Marcion, Quirinus is nevertheless not undeservedly called ἡγεμονῆσαι έ Συρίας for this reason, because he was appointed there out of the ordinary to this business of the census, so that in this way there is no discrepancy between Luke and Tertullian. Compare here what we have said in the Chronicle.

Latin:

Vers. 2. πρώτη ἐγένετο] Id est, hic in Iudæa primus à Ro- manis census actus est. Iustinus ad Tryphonem: ἀπογρα- φῆς ὔσης ἐν Ἰεδαιᾳ τότε πρώτης ἐπὶ κυρηνίε ἀνεληλύθει ἀπὸ Ναζαρὲτ ἔνθα ὤκει εἰς Βηθλεὲμ ὅθεν ἦν ἀπογράψασθαι. Nam ante ullum actum non invenimus. Hic autem census com- monebat Iudæos impleti vaticinii de destruendis regnis Syriæ & Ægypti, post quorum eversionem expectandus erat Messias.

quibus Quirinus legitur. Κυρηνίον id nomen cum Luca scri- bunt tum Josephus tum Justinus Martyr. Præfectus autem fuit huic negotio census, cum præses Syriæ esset Sentius Sa- turninus qui adjunctus haud dubie Quirinio. Sicut autem Lucas Quirinium dicit, ἡγεμονεύοντος τῆς Συρίας ita eam ἐν Ἰου- δαίᾳ γενέσθαι ἐπίτροπον dicit Justinus. Nimirum vox & ἡγε- μονίας & ἐπιτροπῆς, ut recte ab eruditis viris demonstratum est, imperia quævis etiam extra ordinem mandata significat. Nam ἐπίτροπον procuratorem Judææ interpretari non pos- sumus, cum nullus procurator Romanus in Judæa fuerit, aut esse potuerit regnante Herode: ac præterea procurato- res ex equestri ordine legebantur: Quirinius, quanquam Patricius non erat, rebus in Cilicia bene gestis consulatum meruerat, ut Tacitus docet atque ita in Senatum pervene- rat: Josephus: Κυρήνιος εἰς τὴν βουλὴν συναγομένων ἀνὴρ τά τε ἄλλας ἀρχὰς ἐπιτετελεκὼς καὶ διὰ πασῶν ὁδεύσας ὑπατος γενέσθαι. Et alibi de eodem: ἀνὴρ ὑπατικός. Sic & Eusebius dixerat, κυρήνιος ἀπὸ συγκλήτου βουλῆς ἐπέμφθη, id est Qui- rinius Senatorum unus missus est, non ex consilio Senatus, ut vertit Hieronymus. Ejus autem ordinis homines censui præfici solebant. Ita a Druso & Germanico actos census legimus, sed & ab aliis senatoribus. Tacitus lib. XIV. Cen- sus per Gallias a Qu. Volusio & Sex. Africano, Trebellioque Maximo acti sunt, æmulis inter se per nobilitatem Volusio atq; Africano. Sentium Saturninum hoc tempore Syriæ fuisse Præsidem ex Tertulliano certum est: cujus verba sunt: sed & census constat actos sub Augusto nunc in Iudæam per Sen- tium Saturninum. Non potuit autem falli ea in re Tertul- lianus, cum solerent census in tabulas referri, eæque tabulæ primum publice proponi, deinde servari in Archivis ubi in- spectandi erat copia. Itaque Justinus ad ipsas tabulas provo- cat, Μαθεῖν δύνασθε, inquit, ἐκ τῶν ἀπογραφῶν τῶν γενομένων ἐπὶ κυρηνίου. ubi ἀπογραφὰς vocat tabulas censuales quomo- do in codice appellantur. Sic & Dio de Caligula: ἤτησε τὰς τῶν γαλατῶν ἀπογραφὰς. Ipse Tertullianus tabularum hu- jus census sæpe meminit. Nam dicto loco adjicit: apud quos genus ejus inquirere potuissent. Alibi: De censu deniq; Augusti, quem testem fidelissimum Dominicæ nativitatis Ro- manæ archivæ custodiunt. Rursum alibi: Ut nemo facile igno- rare de genere potuisset, vel de recentibus Augustianis censibus tunc adhuc forte pendentibus. Ubi illud pendentibus ad mo- rem Romanum refert Acta publice proponendi, quomodo leges pendere fixas clavis ferreis dixit Plautus. Alio iterum loco: Sicut apud Romanos in censu descripta est Maria ex qua nascitur Christus. Nec mirum exstitisse has tabulas Tertul- liani ævo, cum suo etiam exstitisse testetur Chrysostomus: Verba ejus sunt: ὅθεν δῆλον, ὅτι κατὰ τὴν πρώτην ἀπογραφὴν ἐτέχθη· κᾀ τοῖς ἀρχαίοις τοῖς δημοσία κειμένοις κώδιξιν ἐπὶ τῆς ῥώμης ἔξεστιν ἐντυχόντα κᾀ τὸν καιρὸν τῆς γραφῆς μαθόντα ἀκριβῶς εἰδέναι τὸν βουλόμενον. Videtur autem Quirinium Augustus huic censu per Syriam agendo præfecisse, quod cum bel- lum in Cilicia Syriæ vicina gereret exacte didicisset res Ori- entis. Eademque de causa C. Cæsari misso ad res Orientis hic ipse Quirinius rector est datus: & aliquot post annis Ju- dæa jam in provinciæ formulam redacta missus, qui & Sy- riæ præesset, & simul Judæis Romana tributa indiceret, quod ante id tempus factum non erat. Josephus de censu hoc quem Lucas hic attingit memorare insuper habuit, quia cum tributorum indictio non accederet, nihil in eo evenerat memorabile: at indictionis tributorum per Qui- rinium merito meminit, quia tum primum orta est duce Juda Gaulonita seditio eorum qui negabant ἀλλοφύλοις, quales erant Romani, tributum posse salva religione per- solvi. Qui Josephum tam diligentem rerum Judaicarum inquisitorem & cui Romana quoque archiva patuerunt, deceptum putant in re tam obvia, eos ipsos valde decipi non dubito.

Non uno eodemq; tempore factus census est, per totum orbem qua Romanus erat, interprete Gro- tio, sed modo hic, modo illic, nec hoc censu Judæis capitatio a Romanis indicta, sed eo is pertinuit, ut notum esset, quid regna quæq; & provinciæ hominum copia, quid pecuniis valerent. Ideoq; πρώτη ἐγένετο, primus hic census a Romanis in Judæa actus. Qui commonebat Judæos impleti vaticinii de de- struendis regnis Syriæ & Ægypti, post quorum eversionem expectandus erat Messias. Quum ve- ro sub Pompejo Magno Judæi jam vectigales red- diti, & a Gabinio ipsis septuaginta talenta expres- sa sint, πρώτη potius videtur secundum quid dici, quod nempe prima in præfectura Quirinii fuerit, ut Syrus reddidit; vel PRIOR, respectu posterio- ris, de qua Act. V. & apud Josephum lib. XVIII. sub initium, vel quod ut talis, h. e. cum confectione tabularum prima fuerit : quia ejusmodi descriptio in Judæa nunquam antea facta. Etsi autem Præses tum Syriæ Sentius Saturninus fuerit, Tertulliano teste lib. IV. c. Marc. Quirinus tamen ἡγεμονῆσαι έ Συρίας non immerito ea de causa dicitur, quod extra ordinem huic census negotio ibi præfectus fuerit, ut ita nulla sit Lucæ & Tertulliani discrepantia. Conf. hîc quæ in Chronico diximus.

## 2:3
Verse 3.

Ἀπογράφεσθαι] The Latin interpreter translates this very well as 'to register'. For it is a census term: as has been shown by others.

ἕκαστὸν εἰς τὴν ἰδίαν πόλιν] The Romans retained in individual provinces and kingdoms the custom of taking a census that had been used there from ancient times. Now, this was the custom of the Jews, that the census should be made by tribes, clans, and families, as the inquiry made by Joshua teaches us, the casting of lots by which King Saul was created, and finally the census instituted by David. But this could not be done after the many dispersions of the Jews, unless individuals betook themselves to those places which had formerly fallen to their clan and family.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

Ἀπογράφεσθαι] Optime vertit Latinus interpres profiteri. Est enim ea vox censualis : ut ab aliis ostensum est.

ἕκαστὸν εἰς τὴν ἰδίαν πόλιν] Romani in singulis provinciis ac regnis morem censendi antiquitus ibi usurpatum retinebant. Judæorum autem mos hic erat, ut census fieret per tribus, gentes & familias, ut docet nos inquisitio per Josuam facta, sortitio qua Saul rex creatus est, & postremo census à Davide institutus. Hoc autem post multas Judæorum disjectiones fieri non poterat, nisi singuli se ad ea loca conferrent, quæ olim genti ac familiæ suæ obvenerant.

## 2:4
Verse 4.

Ἐξ οἶκε κὶ πατριᾶς] It seems here that πατριὰ is a part of οἶκος, as in the tribe of Judah οἶκος is of the descendants of Ram, and πατριὰ of those who are from David: as at Rome the Cornelia gens, the family of the Scipios. Thus in the history of Joshua, שבט, that is, tribe, is distinguished into משפחות which the LXX call δήμους. משפחה again into בתים. Now the Bethlehemite region was not David's own, but that of his clan from which David was, as the history of Ruth teaches us. But Joseph was not only from that clan, but also from the very family of David.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

Ἐξ οἶκε κὶ πατριᾶς] Videtur hîc πατριὰ pars esse οἴκυ, ut in tribu Judæ οἶκος sit posterorum Ram, πατριὰ eorum qui ex Davide : ut Romæ gens Cornelia, familia Scipionum. Sic in Josuæ historia שבט, id est tribus, distinguitur in משפחות quas δήμυς vocant LXX. משפחה rursum in בתים. Bethlehemitica autem regio non Davidis erat propria, sed gentis ejus ex qua erat David, ut Ruinæ historia nos docet. At Josephus non tantum ex gente illa erat, sed ex ipsa etiam Davidis familia.

## 2:5
Verse 5.

συν Μαριὰμ] Luke shows clearly enough that Mary also was of the lineage of David. For otherwise she would have had to register in the city of her own family: nor did Joseph take her there while pregnant without cause. But the providence of God in this matter is to be admired, who willed that both the birthplace and the lineage of His Son, predicted by many prophecies, should be attested by public records. For the heads of infants were also registered: and Justin, Tertullian, and Chrysostom affirm that the name of Jesus was inscribed in the records. Ulpian, cited in the Digests, Book III, on censuses: 'It is necessary to indicate age in the census: because age grants to some that they be burdened with tribute: for instance, in Syria, males from fourteen years, females from twelve, up to the sixty-fifth year are obligated to the poll tax.' Now age is considered at the time of the census.

τῇ μεμησευμένῃ αὐτῷ γυναικὶ] She was not only a betrothed, but also a wife. But Luke preferred to say 'betrothed', because Joseph had Mary as a betrothed. For those betrothed who are forbidden to men (the Hebrews say) are just like those in their menstrual period. That word 'wife' offends some, which the Latin and ancient copies acknowledge.

Grotius acknowledges here that it is taught clearly enough that Mary was descended from the lineage of David: therefore this is not to be learned only from the genealogy of Joseph, to whom Mary was betrothed. Regarding which, see on Luke III. We do not, however, reject the argument by which, through consequence, Mary's family is gathered from the family of Joseph, by virtue of the law of Num. XXXVI. v. 8. 9. Inasmuch as the same is to be understood concerning an heiress, not only one who is such at present, but one who could become or turn out to be such, as we said on that passage. For if individuals were bound to betake themselves to those places which had formerly belonged to their clan and family, it was necessary for Mary to be a Bethlehemite, who had to register in Bethlehem. Since this city pertained to the family of David, to which Joseph therefore also betook himself because he was 'of the house and family of David', it is confirmed from this more abundantly that Mary also, having registered in the same city, was of the Davidic clan.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

συν Μαριὰμ] Aperte satis ostendit Lucas etiam Mariam ex genere Davidis fuisse. Nam alioqui ipsa in familiæ suæ urbe profiteri debuerat : neque sine causa prægnantem eo duxit Josephus. Admiranda autem in hoc negotio est Dei providentia qui & natalem locum & genus Filii sui multis vaticiniis prædictum voluit testatum esse publicis tabulis. Nam & infantum capita censebantur : & Jesu nomen ascriptum tabulis affirmant Justinus, Tertullianus, Chrysostomus. Ulpianus in digestis relatus L. III. de censibus : Ætatem in censendo significare necesse est : quia quibusdam ætas tribuit, ut tributo onerentur : veluti in Syriis à quatuordecim annis masculi, à duodecim feminæ usque ad sexagesimum quintum annum tributo capitis obligantur. Ætas autem spectatur censendi tempore.

τῇ μεμησευμένῃ αὐτῷ γυναικὶ] Non sponsa tantum erat, sed & nupta. At sponsam maluit Lucas di ere, quia Josephus Mariam habebat ut sponsam. Nam sponsæ interdictæ viris (inquiunt Hebræi) perinde ut αἱ ἐν ἐμμηνίοις. Offendit quosdam male illud γυναικὶ quod agnoscit Latinus & vetera exemplaria.

Agnoscit hic Grotius Mariam aperte satis doceri ex genere Davidis oriundam fuisse : non ergo id demum è Josephi genealogia discendum, cui Maria desponsata fuit. Quo de ad Luc. III. Non tamen respuimus argumentum, quo per consequensiam è familia Josephi colligitur Mariæ familia, vi legis Num. XXXVI. v. 8. 9. Siquidem eadem de ἐπικλήρῳ intelligenda, non tantum quæ in præsenti talis, sed quæ talis fieri aut evadere poterat, ut ad locum illum diximus. Nam si ad ea loca se conferre tenebantur singuli, quæ olim gentis & familiæ suæ fuerant, Mariam oportuit esse Bethlehemiticam, quæ in Bethlehem debuit ἀπογράφεσθαι. Quæ urbs cum ad Davidis familiam pertinuerit, ad quam ideo etiam se contulit Josephus, quod ἐξ οἴκυ καὶ πατριᾶς Δαβὶδ fuerit, confirmatur inde uberius, Mariam quoque in eadem urbe professam ex gente fuisse Davidica.

## 2:6
Verse 6.

ἐν τῷ εἶναι αὐτὺς ἐκεῖ] Doubtless the profession of the time required something because of the multitude of people.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

ἐν τῷ εἶναι αὐτὺς ἐκεῖ] Nimirum professio temporis aliquid desiderabat ob hominum multitudinem.

## 2:7
Vers. 7.

πρωτότοκον] See at Matt. I. 25.

ἐν τῇ φάτνῃ] That this manger or stable was in a cave, the ancients Justin, Origen, Eusebius, Athanasius, Gregory Nyssen, Jerome, Epiphanius, Theodoret, and others who followed them, report with great consensus. Nor is it a wonder, since that whole field was rocky, as a learned man observes from Strabo. Moreover, the custom of placing mangers in caves existed even among the Greeks. Euripides in the Bacchae: 'He shut him up near the horse-mangers, that he might see the dark gloom.'

Διότι ὐκ ἦν ἀυτοῖς τόπος ἐν τῷ καταλύματι] The καταλυμα calls that house into which they had come for the sake of seeking lodging. In this house there was no empty space because of the crowd of guests: therefore they were forced to hide themselves in a cave because the birth required solitude. The ancient author Justin reported that this house was not in the city itself, but very near the city, to whom this is more to be believed, because he was born and raised not far from Judea, being a Samaritan: and in his time the memory of the matter was fresh enough. 'He lodged,' he says, 'in a cave near the village.' For he calls Bethlehem a village, as being a small town, as also John VII. 42. Following which report, the old writer of the homily which used to be edited among the works of Chrysostom says: 'A new thing, they enter into an inn: they do not enter into the city.' The describers of Palestine who say that this cave was near the walls of Bethlehem may seem to have thought the same. And indeed in many regions there are inns outside the gates which receive those arriving at any time. And although it cannot be denied that in times of peace there was open access to the cities of Judea, since Christ often went out from Jerusalem late at night, it was nevertheless easier, and they were less observed, for the shepherds to come to an inn established outside the city walls than to penetrate into the city. I see nothing at all that stands in the way, except that he is said to have been born below ἐν πόλει Δαβὶδ, and that the temple built in honor of his cave is said to be in Bethlehem. But it is customary among all peoples that adjacent buildings, such as those we often see attached even to small towns, come under the name of the towns, by the right of accession, of course. Thus Christ is said to be about to die in Jerusalem, Luke IX. 31 and ch. XIII. 33, though it is certain he was crucified outside the walls. Thus Joshua is said to have been in Jericho, ch. V. 13. & Gabaone, c. X. 10. when he was besieging those cities. And in Luke V. 12, Jesus is said to have met a leper in one of the cities, when it is certain that lepers remained outside the walls. And Herod himself showed by his action that he had understood the prophecy of Micah in this way.

That great consensus is indeed boasted of by others as well, especially by Baronius. But it is only boasted of. Justin alone, in Dial. cum Tryph., designated a cave near the fortress, p. m. 237. But as it appears, this is through a false interpretation of the words of Isaiah ch. XXXIII, v. 16, whether ὗτος οἰκήσει ἐν ὑψηλῷ σπηλαίῳ πέτρας ἰχυρᾶς be rendered here as "he shall dwell in a cave of a strong rock": which also sound otherwise in Hebrew (which text Montacutius, in his Originibus p. 27, rashly asserts was falsified by the Rabbis in order to support Justin), and they speak not of Christ, but of the faithful. Origen, in book 1 against Celsus, has it thus: δείκνυται τὸ ἐν Βηθλεὲμ σπήλαιον ἔνθα ἐγεννήθη: "The cave IN (not OUTSIDE) BETHLEHEM, where he was born, is shown." Eusebius, book VII, demonstr. Evangel. Those who are accustomed to travel to Bethlehem for the sake of visiting the place, he says, bring their own testimony, giving assurance to the truth and pointing out the field where the virgin, having given birth, laid the infant: where it is manifest that for ἀγρὲ one should read τὲ ἄντρου; since the infant was not laid in a field: and thus the δόξις ἄντρου of that Origen will correspond to his δείκνυται σπήλαιον. Gregory of Nyssa, in his oration on the day of Christ’s Nativity, makes mention of a CAVE, but IN BETHLEHEM, in the city of our God, not outside the city; and he says that Christ the King was adored by the Magi in a cave, which is also asserted by Justin: but the Magi did not find Christ in a grotto outside Bethlehem, but in a house, as Matthew chapter II testifies. Athanasius, in his account of the census of the Blessed Mary and Joseph, at least names τὸν οἰκισκον ἔνθα ἡ παρθέν ἀπεκύησιν, the little house where the virgin gave birth, prefiguring the Church, whose altar is the manger. Jerome in his epistle. XVIII. To Marcellus, he mentioned only the Savior’s cave. But in Epist. XXVII, he does not place it outside Bethlehem, but in Bethlehem. On the right side of the road, he says, she stood at the tomb of Rachel, and thence HAVING ENTERED Bethlehem, and going into the Savior’s grotto, after she saw the holy lodging of the virgin, and the stable, etc., and therefore Jerome acknowledged both the cave and the grotto, who it is certain lived for a long time in Bethlehem, not outside the city, but in the city, in which the virgin mother, as he says, brought forth the Lord infant. Nor does Epiphanius have it otherwise in book I, Title I, near the end. And he was born IN Bethlehem, circumcised in a cave: nor can the contrary be taught either from Theodoret or others, so that Casaubon rightly wrote in Exerc. II to Baron. ann. n. 1, All to a man agree, except Justin, that the virgin gave birth in Bethlehem in the city or village of Bethlehem, and the same ones show not obscurely that the cave itself, of which they make mention so often, was in the city itself. But how they call the stable in which Christ was born a cave, the most learned Casaubon explains thus: The stable, he says, in which the Lord was born, Greek and Latin Fathers everywhere call σπήλαιον, a cave: nor is it a wonder; for since Bethlehem was situated on a rocky hill, most houses seem to have been hewn into the rocks. Strabo observes that the whole region around Jerusalem, up to the sixtieth milestone, is πετρέπετρον, stony. But Bethlehem is only four miles from the city, as James of Vitry says: or six, as the Arab Geographer. Which learned writer observes that there are in that tract many houses cut into the rocks, or rather, cells, in which, he says, men shut themselves up for the sake of religion. The same man, mentioning the place where the Messiah was born, calls it a cave, as the Greeks and Latins generally do. Properly indeed it was not a cavern, that is, naturally born, such as are celebrated by Poets and Geographers as the Trophonian, Corycian, Themisonian and the like; but a place prepared for the use of a stable, as the manger placed there demonstrates: because, however, that stable had been excavated within the rocks, it prevailed, partly because of the nature of the place, partly to declare its utility, that it should be called a cave everywhere. For thus it is the custom to speak, of the hovel of the poor: nor is that saying in Theocritus much otherwise, ἰλεὸν ἐν οἴκησω, that is, the lair of a serpent, not a house: for properly ἰλεὸς is θηρὶς φωλεός, a hole where a serpent lies hidden, or the den of some wild beast. Jerome calls this hole, or cave, a hole, to Marcella: Behold in this small hole of the earth the creator of the heavens was born: unless you prefer to interpret these words concerning the little town of Bethlehem itself. This is Casaubon. Furthermore, the same man confirms that Christ was not born outside the city, both from the temple of Helena, and also from the fact that it is not likely that that small village had suburbs. It is known, from history, that Helena built a magnificent temple in that very place where Christ had been born. If it were true, what Justin writes, that it was not in the city, but at the city of Bethlehem, that temple would have been built. Who of the ancients said this? who of them does not speak of that temple as if it were situated in the city itself? Sozomen, book 11, concerning Helena, ὠκοδόμησε ναὸν ἐν Βηθλεὲμ, ἀμφὶ τὸ τ̄ γυνήσεως χρισοῡ σπέ- λαιον, he built a temple in Bethlehem, at that cave in which Christ was born. Those who place the cave or stable, where Christ was born, in the suburbs, ought to teach us that Bethlehem had suburbs, Luke II. 4. Bethlehem is named a city, πόλις Δαβὶδ: but John VII. 42 it is called κώμη a village. And Jerome sometimes calls it a villa, as in the Epistle to Marcella, sometimes also a little villa, as in another to the same, sometimes even a small village, as at chapter V of Micah. Theodoret, Sermon V, Curat. χορίον ἄδοξον ἰς σμικρὸν, an ignoble and small place. That such a little town, or village, had suburbs, to whom will it seem likely? This again is Casaubon.

Nor does that opinion, which is held in the same place by Rob. Montagu, concerning the birth of Christ outside the city, or in the field, or in the Bethlehemitic territory, sufficiently agree with the description of the Evangelist. Because Joseph is said to have gone up with Mary εἰς πόλιν INTO the City of David, Luke II. 4, and when they were ἐκεῖ THERE, she brought forth Jesus, v. 6. And the angel testifies v. 11 that Christ was born ἐν πόλι IN the City of David, when he sends the shepherds there. But he would have said without doubt that he was born outside the city, or near, or by the city, if the birth had not happened in the city itself. Also those words v. 7, he laid him, ἐν τῇ Φάτνῃ, in the manger, because there was no place for them ἐν τῷ καταλύματι, the emphasis of which Casaubon weighs well, imply that they had no place in the inn in Bethlehem, except in the stable, in which it was necessary for them to place the newborn infant in the manger. Salmasius wants it to be read ἐν Φάτνῃ without the article; and by that word he understands a stable: but as St. Luke said ἐν τῷ καταλύματι not without emphasis, namely that they had approached some Bethlehemitic inn, and having been received into it, had not found an empty place which might be granted to them for sleeping: whence they were forced to withdraw into a stable. Thus he notably said ἐν τῇ Φάτνῃ: for he restricts the general appellation of a manger peculiarly to that manger which was in the stable belonging to the inn, of which mention is made here. Finally, it is evident from Matt. II. v. 12 that Christ was adored by the Magi in a house in Bethlehem: which without doubt was that κατάλυμα or inn, of which Luke makes mention here. For the census having been completed, and the lodging, which was occupied, having been made empty by the departure, it is very probable that Joseph and Mary, having left the stable, transferred themselves and the infant into the inn itself, which was near or joined to it.

To the doubt, which Baronius and Montagu especially urge, how the shepherds could have entered the city at night, if Christ was born within the walls, Casaubon answers, If Bethlehem was a κώμη village, it is likely that it was ἀτείχιστον and had no walls: If it was a town surrounded by walls, it is likely that in such deep peace the gates were for the most part left open, or certainly it happened by divine providence that night that the gates were open.

Our countrymen generally agree that there was an inn in the city itself; B. Franzius, in his De interpret. script. orac. CXVI, does not indeed entirely reject that opinion, that Christ was born in the suburb of Bethlehem, yet he does not hold it as certain, but conjectures that the whole place was perhaps called THE MANGER. B. Chemnitius, however, observes that the tradition comes from an Apocryphal source, the Proto-Evangelium of James the brother of the Lord, in which it is narrated that Mary, overtaken by labor in the middle of the journey, entered a certain cave in a deserted place and gave birth: and that the Legends thus hold that a certain excavated rock not far from the gate of Bethlehem is where Christ was born; and the blessed man adds: we owe these things to traditions, because, led away from the Word of God, we have almost lost the thing itself. For if Christ was not born in the city of Bethlehem, he cannot be the true Messiah, according to the prophecies of the Prophets, Matt. II. 5. But enough of these.

Latin:

Vers. 7.

πρωτότοκον] Vide apud Matth. I. 25.

ἐν τῇ φάτνῃ] Fuisse hoc præsepe sive stabulum ἐν σπηλαίῳ, magno consensu produnt veteres Justinus, Origenes, Eusebius, Athanasius, Gregorius, Nyssenus, Hieronymus, Epiphanius, Theodorethus & eos secuti alii. Nec mirum cum ager ille omnis ὑπόπετρος fuerit, ut ex Strabone vir doctus observat. Mos autem præsepia ponendi in speluncis etiam apud Græcos fuit. Euripides Bacchis : Καθείρξατ’ αὐτὸν ἱππικαῖς πέλας Φάτναισιν ὡς ᾔ σκότιον εἰσορᾷ κνέφας.

Διότι ὐκ ἦν ἀυτοῖς τόπος ἐν τῷ καταλύματι] τὸ κατα- λυμα dicit eam domum, in quam venerant hospitii quæ- rendi causa. In hac domo nullus erat locus vacuus ob tur- bam hospitum: itaque in specum coacti sunt se abdere ideo quod partus solitudinem desideraret. Domum hanc non in ipsa urbe, sed proxime urbem fuisse vetus auctor Justi- nus prodidit, cui hoc magis credendum est, quod non pro- cul Judæa natus & educatus fuit, quippe Samarites: & ejus temporibus satis recens erat rei memoria. ὑποπανδάνω, inquit, τοῦ συνεγγὺς τῆς κώμης κατέλυσε. Nam Bethlehemum κώμην vocat, utpote exiguum oppidum, ut & Joh. VII. 42. Quam famam secutus Scriptor vetus homiliæ quæ inter Chrysostomi opera edi solebat: Rem novam, inquit, ingrediuntnr in diversorium: non ingrediuntur in civitatem. Pos- sunt videri idem sensisse descriptores Palæstinæ qui specum istam fuisse ajunt juxta muros Bethlehemi. Et sane multis in regionibus diversoria sunt extra portas quæ quovis tem- pore adventantes recipiant. Et quanquam pacis tempori- bus exitum atque aditum patuisse in urbes Judææ non est negandum, cum Christas sæpe nocte multa exierit Hiero- solymis, facilius tamen, & minus observati potuerunt pa- stores in diversorium extra urbis mœnia constitutum veni- re, quam in urbem penetrare. Nihil sane video quod ob- stet, nisi quod infra natus dicitur ἐν πόλει Δαβὶδ, & quod templum in ejus specus honorem ab Helena structum dicitur in Bethlehem. Sed apud omnes populos usitatum est, ut continentia ædificia, qualia adhærere etiam parvis op- pidis sæpe videmus, oppidorum veniant nomine, jure sci- licet accessionis. Sic Christus dicitur moriturus in Jerusa- lem Luc. IX 31. & c. XIII. 33. quem constat extra mœnia crucifixum. Sic Josue dicitur fuisse Hierichunte c. V. 13. & Gabaone, c. X. 10. cum eas urbes obsideret. Et Lucæ V. 12. Jesus dicitur in una urbium obviam factus leproso, cum constet leprosos extra mœnia mansisse. Et ipse He- rodes ostendit facto, se Micheæ vaticinium in hunc modum intellexisse.

Magnus ille consensus jactatur quidem etiam ab aliis, imprimis Baronio. Sed jactatur. Solus Justinus Dial. cum Tryph. Speluncam castello pro- pinquam designavit. p. m. 237. Sed ut apparet falsa interpretatione verborum Esaiæ c. XXXIII. v. 16. sive ὗτος οἰκήσει ἐν ὑψηλῷ σπηλαίῳ πέτρας ἰχυρᾶς sit hic habitat in spelunca rupis validæ inductus: quæ & aliter in Ebræo sonant (quem textum Montacu- tius inde Originib. p. 27. temere à Rabbinis fal- satum, ut Justino patrocinetur, asserit,) nec de Christo, sed de fidelibus loquuntur. Origenes l. 1. contr. Celsum ita habet: δείκνυται τὸ ἐν Βηθλεὲμ σπήλαιον ἔνθα ἐγεννήθη: Ostenditur IN (non EX- TRA) BETHLEHEM spelunca, ubi natus est. Eu- sebius lib. VII. demonstr. Evangel. Qui visendi loci gratia, inquit, Bethlehem petere consueverunt, testimonium suum adferunt, veritati fidem fatientes, agrumq; demonstrantes, ubi virgo enixa infantem deposuit: ubi manifestū est pro d' ἀγρὲ legen- dum esse τὲ ἄντρου; quum in agro depositus infans non sit: atq; ita δόξις ἄντρου illi Origenis δείκνυται σπήλαιον respondebit. Greg. Nyssenus orat. in diem Natal. Christi ANTRI mentionem facit, sed IN BETHLEHEM, in civitate Dei nostri, non extra civitatem; Et in antro esse à Magis Christum Regem adoratum dicit, quod à Justino quoque asseritur: at Magi non in specu extra Bethlehem invenerunt Christum, sed in domo, teste Matthæo cap. II. Athanasius in census Descript. B. Mariæ & Josephi saltim nominat τὸν οἰκισκον ἔνθα ἡ παρθέν ἀπε- xύησιν ædiculam, ubi virgo peperit, Ecclesiam præ- figurantem, cujus altare est præsepe. Hieronymus in epist. XVIII. ad Marcel. speluncam tantum Salvatoris nominavit. Epist. vero XXVII. eam non ponit extra Bethlehem, sed in Bethlehem. In dextra, inquit, parte itineris stetit ad sepulcrum Rachel, atq; inde Bethlehem INGRESSA, & in specum Salvatoris introiens, postquam vidit sacrum virginis diversorium, & stabulum &c. ideoque & speluncam, & specum agnovit Hieronymus, quem constat diu Bethlehem habitasse non extra civita- tem, sed in civitate, in qua virgo puerpera, ut ait, Dominum fudit infantem. Nec aliter habet Epi- phanius in lib.I. Tit. I. sub fin. Natusq; est IN Beth- lehem, circumcisus in spelunca: neq; vel è Theodo- reto vel aliis contrarium doceri poterit, ut adeo ex vero Casaubon. Exerc. II. ad Baron. ann. n. 1. scri- pserit, Omnes ad unum consentiunt, præter Justinu, peperisse virginem ἐν Βηθλεὲμ in urbe aut vico Bethle- hem, & ipsam speluncam, cujus toties mentionem fa- ciunt, in ipsa urbe fuisse non obscure iidem ostendunt. Quomodo autem speluncam vocent stabulum, in quo natus est Christus, ita explicat eruditissimus Casaubonus: Stabulum, inquit, in quo natus est Dominus, passim Græci Latinique Patres appellant σπήλαιον, speluncam: nec mirum; nam cum esset Bethlehem in saxoso colle sita, videntur pleræq; do- mus in saxis fuisse excisæ. Strabo observat totam regionem circa Ierosolyma, ad sexagesimum usq; la- pidem, esse πετρέπετρον, petrosam. Bethlehem autem quatuor millia passuum duntaxat ab urbe, ut ait Ja- cobus de Vitriaco: vel sex, ut Arabs Geographus. Qui eruditus scriptor observat, esse in illo tractu multas domus saxis incisas, vel potius, cellas, in qui- bus, ait ille, homines sese incluserunt religionis causa. Idem locum ubi natus est Messias commemorans, speluncam vocat, ut fere Græci & Latini. Proprie quidem antrum id non erat, ἀυτοφυὲς hoc est, spon- te natum, qualia celebrantur à Poetis & Geogra- phis Trephonium, Gorycium, Themisonium & similia; sed locus concinnatus in usum stabuli, ut præsepe ibi po- situm demonstrat: quia tamen intra saxa illud sta- bulum fuerat excavatum, obtinuit, partim pro- pter loci naturam, partim ad declarandam ejus utilitatem, ut spelunca passim appellaretur. Sic enim loqui moris est, de angusti gurgustio lis: nec multo aliter dictum illud apud Theocritum, ἰλεὸν ἐν οἴκησω, hoc est, serpentis Catibulum, non do- mum: nam proprie ἰλεὸς est θηρὶς φωλεός, fora- men ubi latet serpens, vel alicujus feræ cubile. Hieronymus hoc foramen, sive speluncam, appellat foramen, ad Marcellam: Ecce in hoc parvo terræ foramine cœlorum conditor natus est: nisi malis de ipso oppidulo Bethlehem hæc verba interpretari. Hæc Casaubonus. Confirmat porro idem non extra urbem natum esse Christum, tum ex Helenæ templo, tum inde etiam, quod non verisimile sit suburbia habuisse parvum illum viculum. Notum est, ex historia, Helenam eo ipso in loco ubi na- tus fuerat Christus, templum extruxisse magnifi- cum. Si verum esset, quod Justinus scribit, non in urbe, sed ad urbem Bethlehem, templum illud fuisset structum. Quis veterum hoc dixit? quis illorum de eo templo non sic loquitur, tanquam in ipsa urbe sito? Sozomenus lib. 11. de Helena, ὠκοδόμησε ναὸν ἐν Βηθλεὲμ, ἀμφὶ τὸ τ̄ γυνήσεως χρισοῡ σπέ- λαιον, ædificavit templum in Bethlehem, ad spelun- cam illam, in qua Christus natus est. Qui antrum si- ve stabulum, ubi natus Christus, ponunt in subur- biis, docere nos deberent, habuisse Bethlehem suburbia, Luc. II. 4. Nominatur Bethlehem urbs, πόλις Δαβὶδ: sed Joh. VII. 42. dicitur κώμη vicus. Et Hieronymus modo appellat villam, ut in Epist. ad Marcell. modo etiam villulam, ut in altera ad eandem, aliquando vix parvum viculum, ut ad ca- put V. Micheæ Theodorets Serm. V. Curat. χορίον ἄδοξον ἰς σμικρὸν, locum ignobilem & par- vum. Tantulum igitur sive oppidulum, sive vi- cum, suburbia habuisse, cui fiet verisimile? Hæc iterum Casaubonus.

Neque Evangelistæ descriptioni satis congruit ista de nativitate Christi extra civitatem, vel in a- gro, vel in territorio Bethlehemitico, uti Rob. Mon- tacutio hæc eodem habentur loco, facta, opinio. Quia εἰς πόλιν IN Urbem Davidis ascendisse Jose- phus cum Maria dicitur Luc. II. 4. & cum essent ἐ- κεῖ ILLIC, peperisse Jesum, v. 6. Et angelus testatur v. 11. natum esse Christum ἐν πόλι IN Urbe David, cum pastores eo remittit. Dixisset autem sine du- bio extra urbem natum, vel prope, aut juxta ur- bem, si non in ipsa urbe nativitas contigisset. Ver- ba etiam illa v. 7. reclinavit eum, ἐν τῇ Φάτνῃ, in præsepi, quod non erat eis locus ἐν τῷ καταλύματι, quorum emphasin probe expendit Casaubonus, id inferunt, quod in diversorio in Bethlehem locum non habuerint, nisi in stabulo, in quo in præsepe oportuit eos infantem recens natum reponere. Salmasius vult legendum esse ἐν Φάτνῃ sine articu- lo; & per vocem illam stabulum intelligit: sed uti ἐν τῷ καταλύματι dixit S. Lucas non sine ἐμφά- σει, quod nempe aliquod diversorium Bethlehe- miticum ipsi adierint, atque in eo cætera excepti locum vacuum non invenerint, qui ipsis ad cuban- dum concederetur: unde coacti sunt in stabulum concedere. Ita notanter dixit ἐν τῇ Φάτνῃ: gene- ralem enim appellationem præsepis restringit pe- culiariter ad illud præsepe, quod erat in stabulo per- tinente ad diversorium, cujus hic habetur mentio. Denique è Matth. II. v. 12. constat, Christum in domo à Magis adoratum in Bethlehem: quæ sine dubio illud κατάλυμα vel diversorium fuit, cujus meminit hic Lucas. Nam confecta descriptione, & hospitio, quod occupatum erat discessione va- cuefacto, probabile admodum est, Josephum & Mariam relicto stabulo in ipsum diversorium, quod ei propinquum vel conjunctum erat, se atq; infantem transtulisse.

Ad dubium, quod imprimis urget Baronius, & Montacutius, quomodo potuerint pastores noctu ur- bem ingredi, si intra muros natus Christus, respon- det Casaubonus, Si Bethlehem erat κώμη vicus, verisimile fuisse ἀτείχιστον nec muros habuisse: Si oppidum fuit muris cinctum, verisimile est in tam alta pace portas ut plurimum relictas fuisse apertas, aut certe divina providentia evenisse illa nocte, ut paterent portæ.

Consentiunt communiter nostrates, diverso- rium in ipsa urbe fuisse, B. Franzius de interpret. script. orac. CXVI. non quidem prorfus rejicit illam sententiam, quod in suburbio Bethlehemi Christus natus sit, non tamen eam pro certa ha- bet, sed totum locum fortasse vocatum PRÆSE- PE conjectat. B. Chemnitius vero observat tra- ditionem ex Apocrypho, Prot-Evangelio Jacobi fratris Domini, in quo narratur, Mariam in medio itinere partu præoccupatam in loco deserto in spe- luncam quandam ingressam, enixam esse: atque ita Legendas habere, quod rupes quædam excavata non procul à porta Bethlehem, ubi natus sit Chri- stus; & addit ὁ μακαρίτης: hæc debemus traditioni- bus, quod à Verbo Dei abducti rem ipsam ferme amisimus. Si enim Christus non est in civitate Bethlehem natus, non potest esse verus Messias, juxta vaticinia Prophetarum Matth. II. 5. Atqui hæc de istis.

## 2:8
Vers. 8.

κὶ ποιμένες] For the field around Bethlehem is very suitable for pasture, 1 Sam. XVII. 13.

ἀγραυλῶντες] living in the open air: for in this word there is no indication of night, which the following words express. But since shepherds are hardly ever accustomed to live in the field in winter, especially at night, it may seem strange that the birthday of the Lord was placed by the Roman Church, for which it was easy to inspect the census records, on the 25th of December, which custom the Antiochene Church (for the oration that testifies to this was delivered in that city) began to follow only in the times of Chrysostom: but the whole East not before the times of the Emperor Justin: as observed by Nicephorus. That most diligent investigator of times thinks this opinion arose from another false one concerning the high priesthood of Zacharias: for from the day of atonements, on which the high priest was accustomed to enter the inner sanctuary, the times of Elizabeth's conception were reckoned, and six months later those of Mary: although he himself, having begun the calculation from the course of Abijah, thinks the Lord's birthday corresponds to September, at which time shepherds spend their time in the open air. Certainly it is agreed that the tradition varied in antiquity. For he who, approaching most closely to the age of Christ, makes mention of this matter is Clement of Alexandria, whose words are these: 'There are some who are more curious about the birth of our Savior, not only adding the year, but also the day, which they say was the 25th of Pachon in the 25th year of Augustus. And the followers of Basilides celebrate the day of his baptism, spending the night before in readings; and they say it is the 15th year of Tiberius Caesar, the 15th day of the month of Tybi.' The former of these opinions placed the Lord's birthday almost in May: at which time there is no doubt that shepherds in Judea were accustomed to live in the fields. For Pachon is the seventh of the Egyptian months, the first of which, Toth, almost coincides with the month of September. But the other opinion of the followers of Basilides referred this day to the fifth month of the Egyptians, which almost agrees with the Roman tradition. The same opinion held that the day on which Christ was born and the day on which he was baptized were one and the same, which many of the ancients believed because of what is read below in canon III. 23. And we also learn from Cassian, Conference X, chapter 2, that the Egyptian churches followed this. Epiphanius departs from this opinion, yet in such a way that he does not dissent much regarding the birthday. For he maintains that Christ was born on the eighth of the Ides of January, which would be the eleventh of the Egyptian month Tybi, but was baptized on the sixth of the Ides of November, which would be the twelfth of the Egyptian month Atyr. And the churches of Asia and Egypt once celebrated this day of January as the birthday of Christ, and the Armenians long after. Nyssen and Ambrose in their respective places testify only to this, that the Lord's birthday was celebrated when the days begin to lengthen. I shall finish with Jerome's sermon on the birth of Christ: Whether Christ was born today or baptized, a different opinion is indeed held in the world, and according to the variety of traditions, the opinion is different.

Φυλάσσοντες φυλακὰς τῆς νυκτὸς] That is, succeeding one another in the care of the flock through divided intervals of time.

From this expression 'living in the open air,' and the mention of night added, Grotius renders the Lord's birthday on December 25th in doubt, since shepherds are hardly accustomed to live in the field in winter, especially at night: which argument of Scaliger, Casaubon and Vossius held for nothing, who testify that they saw flocks of sheep grazing in the fields in England around the time of Christ's birth, as did also Wilh. Langius, who reports that in Denmark sheep live in the fields throughout the winter, unless the ground is so completely covered with snow that they can have no fodder outside the farmsteads. But what has Judea to do with Denmark, subject to the frozen north?

But as for the opinions brought forward by Grotius from Clement of Alexandria, of which the former placed the Lord's birthday almost in May, and the latter that of the followers of Basilides in the fifth month of the Egyptians, the former certainly, which was the singular opinion of some, does not deserve consideration. For Chrysostom is a witness in his Sermon on the Nativity that that opinion concerning the Lord's birthday on December 25th was brought to Constantinople from Rome ten years earlier, handed down by those who relate these things exactly, παρὰ τῶν ἀκριβῶς ταῦτα εἰδότων, which was indeed new at Constantinople, but to the Romans it was ancient, παλαιὰ ἐξ ἀρχαία. Doubtless, as Langius holds, the ancient Roman Senators, to whom it was permitted to inspect the Censorian records, after they had received Christianity, revealed the true birthday to others. And so that day was celebrated at Rome, knowledge of which they finally transmitted to Constantinople in the times of Chrysostom, and taught others also to observe the day which they themselves celebrated from ancient and infallible tradition. Since, therefore, the opinion of the Romans is supported by such and so certain arguments, it should not be called merely probable, but clearly true. For it was taken from the ancient Censorian records, which Chrysostom is a witness were at Rome even in his own times; namely, Quirinus, who had received a mandate from

Augustus, who wished to compile a summary of the empire, to register all the males, and to write down the age of those who were below puberty, so that he might have knowledge of the time when they could be useful to the empire if they lived, also recorded the name of Jesus and his age in the register, when, the census having been taken, he was not a full year old, but at least some days old. This is Langius. He also adds that Clement of Rome, Can. VIII. J. V., handed it down thus: 'Let the birthday be celebrated by you on the twenty-fifth of the ninth month.' Which ninth month is December according to the calculation of the Passover, by which April is the first. Suslyga the Pole also alleges the tradition of Evodius, successor of Peter in the Alexandrian See, in support of that same opinion, as well as the Acts of the Martyrs. Furthermore, Grotius acknowledges that the other opinion of Clement of Alexandria does not depart from the Roman tradition, and Epiphanius confesses that he does not dissent much regarding the birthday: Nor indeed do Nyssen and Ambrose testify in any other sense that the Lord's birthday was celebrated when the days begin to lengthen. And although many made the Lord's birthday on January 6th, most nevertheless agreed on December 25th, whence Spanheim, although he defines nothing here, but according to his custom in chronological matters, renders everything doubtful, so as to fill up, for instance, the Evangelical doubts, acknowledges that this is the opinion of the Ancient Church, or at least of the majority in the Ancient Church, which even today obtains in the practice of the Christian Church, handed down by Chrysostom, Augustine, Orosius, Sulpicius Severus, Cassiodorus, and INNUMERABLE others, and by the Christian Church for MANY centuries.

That the Asian and Syrian [churches], as Epiphanius testifies in book II against heretics, and the Egyptian [churches], as Cassiodorus reports in collation X, chapter 11, and not even the churches of the Armenians, as Grotius admits, transferred the birthday of the Lord to the 6th of January, Spanheim judges that John Kepler does not suspect without reason that this difference arose from a certain slip of the scribes, who for the 8th of the Kalends of January, that is, the 25th of December, substituted the 8th of the Ides of January, and he assumes that for this reason the ancients observed twelve nights as if they were sacred, which were interposed between the 25th of December and the 6th of January, because they were in doubt as to which opinion should be preferred. We leave this conjecture in the middle; from wherever the difference arose, the greater and more important part of the Church celebrated the birthday of the Lord on the 25th of December, which the whole Church observes to this day.

Latin:

Vers. 8.

κὶ ποιμένες] Est enim valde pascuus circa Bethlehemum ager 1. Sam. XVII. 13.

ἀγραυλῶντες] agentes sub dio: nam in hac voce nulla est noctis significatio quam sequentia exprimunt. Cum autem vix usquam hyeme soleant in agro agere pastores, nocti- bus præsertim, mirum videri potest natalem Domini ab Ec- clesia Romana, cui censuum tabulas inspicere promptum fuit, collocatum in diem xxv. Decembris, quod institutum Antiochena Ecclesia (in ea enim urbe habita est oratio, quæ id testatur) sequi cœpit temporibus demum Chrysostomi: totus autem Oriens non ante Justini Imperatoris tempora: ut Nicephoro observatum. Diligentissimus temporum in- dagator putat natam hanc opinionem ex altera falsa de pontificatu maximo Zachariæ: nam à die expiationum, quo Pontifex maximus ingredi penetrale solebat, putata conceptus Elisabetæ tempora, ac sex mensibus posterius Mariæ: cum ipse inita numeratione ἀπὸ τῆς ἐφημερίας Abia natalem Domini in Septembrem putet congruere, quo tempore sub dio agunt pastores. Antiquitūs certe variasse traditionem constat. Nam qui proxime ad ætatein Christi accedens ejus rei meminit est Clemens Alexandrinus, cu- jus hæc sunt verba: εἰσὶ δέ οἱ περιεργότεροι τῇ γενέσει τῦ σωτῆ- ρος ἡμῶν ἐ μόνον τὸ ἔτος, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὴν ἡμέραν προστιθέντες ἣν φασιν ἔτυς κη Αὐγύστυ ἐν πέμπῃ παχὼν καὶ εἰκάδι· οἱ δὲ ἀπὸ βασιλείδε καὶ τῆ παπίσματος αὐτῦ τὴν ἡμέραν ἑορτάζυσι, προδιανυκτερεύοντες ἀναγνώσεσι· φασὶ δὲ εἶναι τὸ πεντεκαιδέκατον ἔτος Τιβερίυ Καίσαρος, τὴν πεντεκαιδεκάτην τῦ Τυβὶ μηνὸς. Prior harum sententiarum in Majum ferme Domini natalē conferebat: quo tempore non dubium est pastores in Iudæa solitos ἀγραυλεῖν. Est enim παχὼν septimus mensium Ægy- ptiorum, quorum primusToth cum mense Septemb. ferme συμπίπτει. At altera sententia Basilidis sectatorū referebat hunc diem in mensem Ægyptiorum quintum, quod ferme cum traditione Romana congruit. Eadem sententia unum esse diē statuebat quo natus est Christus & quo baptizatus, quod veterū multi crediderunt ob id quod infra legitur can. III. 23. Atq; id secutas Ægypti Ecclesias etiam ex Cassiano discimus, collatione X, cap. 2. Ab hac sententia diversus abit Epiphanius, ita tamen, ut de die natali non multum dissentiat. Natum enim Christum vult octavo Eidus Ja- nuarias, quæ esset undecima Ægyptii mensis Tubi, bapti- zatum autem sexto Eidus Noveœnbris, quæ esset duodeci- ma Ægyptii mensis Atyr. Atque hunc diem Januarii ut natalem Christi olim celebrabant Asiæ & Ægypti Ecclesiæ, & multo post Armenii. Nyssenus & Ambrosius suis locis testantur hoc tantum, celebratum Domini natalem cum crescere dies incipiunt. Finiam cum Hieronymo sermone de Christi nativitate: Sive hodie Christus natus est, sive ba- ptizatus est, diversa quidem fertur opinio in mundo, & pro traditionum varietate sententia est diversa.

Φυλάσσοντες φυλακὰς τῆς νυκτὸς] Id est, per dispartita tem- porum intervalla alii aliis succedentes in curam gregis.

Ex hac voce agentes sub dio, additaque noctis mentione nequicquam dubium reddit Grotius natalem Domini 25. Decembris, cum vix usquam hyeme soleant in agro agere pastores, noctibus præser- tim: quod argumentum Scaligeri pro nullo habuit Casaubonus, Vossius, quæ circa natalem Christi gre- ges ovium in agris pascentes in Anglia se vidisse testantur, ut & Wilh. Langius, qui perhibet in Dania oves tota hyeme in agris degere, nisi terra ita nive penitus tecta sit, ut nihil pabuli extra villas habere possint. Quid autem Judæa ad Daniam ge- lidis trionibus subjectam?

Quod vero ad sententias è Clemente Alex. à Grotio adductas, quarum prior in Majum ferme Domini natalem contulerit, altera Basilidis secta- torum in mensem Ægyptiorum quintum, prior cer- te, quæ singularis quorundam fuit opinio, calcu- lum non meretur. Nam Chrysostomus testis est Sermone de Natali sententiam illam de 25. De- cembris Domini natali ante decennium Roma Con- stantinopolin allatam, ab illis traditam, qui exacte hæc narrant, παρὰ τῶν ἀκριβῶς ταῦτα εἰδότων, quæ Constantinopoli quidem nova fuerit, Roma- nis vero antiqua παλαιὰ ἐξ ἀρχαία. Nimirum, ut Langius habet, antiqui Senatores Romani, quibus Censorias tabulas inspicere permissum erat, post- quam Christianismum receperant, verum nata- lem aliis prodiderunt. Atque ita dies ille Romæ celebratus fuit, cujus rei notitiam demum tem- poribus Chrysostomi Constantinopolin trans- miferunt, diemque, quem ipsi ex antiqua & infal- libili traditione celebrabant, etiam alios observa- re docuerunt. Cum ergo Romanorum opinio ta- libus, ac tam certis argumentis subnitatur, non ultra verisimilis dicenda erit, sed plane vera. Ex antiquis enim tabulis Censoriis deprompta est, quas Romæ suis quoque temporibus fuisse Chry- sostomus testis est; Nimirum Quirinus, qui ab

Augusto breviarium imperii consicere volente, mandatum acceperat, omnes mares notare, eo- rumque qui infra pubertatem erant, ætatem ad- scribere, ut cognitum haberet, quo illi tempore imperio utiles esse possent, si viverent, nomen et- iam Jesu, & ætatem ipsius in tabula consignavit, cum censu acto non annum integrum, sed aliquot saltim dies natus esset. Hæc Langius. Addit etiam, quod Clemens Roman. Can. VIII. J. V. ita tradiderit τὴν γενέθλιον ἥτις ὑμῖν ἐπιτελείσθω εἰκάδι πέμπτῃ τοῦ ἐννάτου μηνός. Qui nonus mensis December est juxta rationem Paschatis, qua Aprilis primus est. Suslyga Polonus traditionem Evodii, Petri in Ca- thedra Alexandrina successoris, in eam etiam al- legat sententiam, nec non Acta Martyrum. Por- ro à Romana traditione haud abire alteram Cle- mentis Alex. sententiam agnoscit Grotius, neque multum dissentire de die natali Epiphanius fate- tur: Nec sane alio sensu Nyssenus & Ambrosius testantur natalem Domini celebratum, cum cre- scere dies incipiunt. Etsi autem multi VI. Januarii natalem Domini fecère, plerique tamen consen- sêre in XXV. Decembris, unde Spanhemius, etsi hic nihil definiat, sed pro more sibi in Chronolo- gicis solemni, omnia dubia reddat, ut scil. dubia Evangelica impleat, agnoscit hanc esse sententiam Veteris Ecclesiæ, vel plerorumque saltem in Veteri Ec- clesia, quæ hodieque obtinet in praxi Ecclesiæ Chri- stianæ à Chrysostomo, Augustino, Orosio, Sulpitio Se- vero, Cassiodoro, & INNUMERIS aliis, & Ec- clesia Christiana per COMPLURA secula tradi- tam.

Quod vero Asiatica & Syra, teste Epiph. lib. II. contra hæret. & Ægyptiaca, referente Cassiodoro collat. X. c. 11. nec Arminianorum Ecclesiæ, fatente Grotio, in diem VI. Januarii natalem Domini transtulerunt, Joh. Keplerum non præter rationem suspicari, censet Spanhemius, discrimen illud ex lapsu quodam librariorum ortum, qui pro VIII. Kal. Januarii, hoc est, XXV. Decemb. substitue- rint VIII. Id. Januarii, atque ideo Veteres duode- cim noctes quasi sacras observasse autumat, quæ inter XXV. Decembr. & VI. Jan. interjectæ, quod dubii fuerint, utra sententia præferenda sit. Quam conjecturam in medio relinquimus, undecunque ortum discrimen sit, major & potior Ecclesiæ pars XXV. Decemb. natalem Domini celebravit, quem hodieque tota observat Ecclesia.

## 2:11
Verse 11.

Ἐτέχθη ὑμῖν] For you Jews, but for the public good of the world. Zechariah calls the angels the superior family of God, and men the inferior. The superior family rejoices in the good of the inferior.

σωτήρ] Whom Zechariah in chapter IX, 9 called נושע, where the LXX said σώζοντα.

χριστὸς κύριος] Not just any anointed one, but that anointed one above all, the Lord of all, named by that title by David.

ἐν πόλει Δαυίδ] As Micah predicted: and so that it may appear by public testimony that this one is from the blood of David.

The Grotian depravation is therefore to be rejected, regarding Micah 5:2, by which he twisted the prophecy of Micah to Zerubbabel: concerning which it has been spoken there.

Vers. 11.

σωτήρ] Quem Zacharias c. IX. 9. נושע vocavit, ubi LXX. σώζοντα dixerunt.

χριστὸς κύριος] Non quilibet unctus sed ille unctus su- pra omnes, omnium Dominus, à Davidi eo nomine nun- cupatus.

ἐν πόλει Δαυίδ] Ut prædixit Micheas: & ut publico te- stimonio appareat hunc esse ex Davidis sanguine.

Reprobanda ergo depravatio Grotiana, ad Mich. V. 2. qua ad Zorobabelem Micheæ vatici- nium detorsit: de qua illic dictum.

## 2:12
Verse 12.

Verse 12.

τὸ. σημεῖον] A mark by which you may distinguish this infant from others. Thus also rhetoricians use this word. ἐν τῇ φάτνῃ] The angel described both the house and the cave. But Luke, since he had mentioned the place before, was content to say with the article τῇ φάτνῃ, signifying that manger of which he had treated before. Thus writers often intermingle their own words with the direct speech of others, as we have observed elsewhere. Most similar is that in Matt. 26:18. Such is also that in Virgil: "And never sufficiently allowed to be moved / Camarina appears from afar." For the poet's words are inserted into the words of Aeneas.

Sed Lucas, cum loci ante meminiffet, satis habuit cum ar- ticulo dicere τῇ φάτνῃ, id præsepe significans de quo ege- rat ante. Ita sæpe Scriptores sua verba aliorum directis ora- tionibus permiscent, ut alibi quoque observavimus. Si- millimum est illud apud Matth. XXVI. 18. Tale est & a- pud Virgilium : Et nunquam satis concessa moveri Apparet Camarina procul. Poetæ enim verba Æneæ verbis inseruntur.

## 2:14
Verse 14. δόξα ἐν ὑψίστοις Θεῷ καὶ ἐπὶ γῆς εἰρήνη, ἀνθρώποις εὐδοκία] I think it is more correct to understand ἔστω than ἐστὶ, but in such a way that a joyful approval of that which was is signified, not a desire for that which was absent.

let a joyful approval of that which was be signified, not a longing for that which was absent. Such is that of Virgil: "Run, spindles, run, the Fates have said, by destiny's unchanging thread." That ἐν ὑψίστοις, as we have said elsewhere, is sometimes the same as "most excellently." But here, since a place also seems to be expressed by the mode, it is as if ἐν ὑψίστοις and ἐπὶ γῆς were opposites, just as in the Lord's Prayer ἐν Ὀρανῷ κὶ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς. Here that of Isaiah XLIV. 23 and XLIX. 13 is fulfilled: "Shout for joy, O heavens"; by εἰρήνην here I understand, in the Hebrew manner, שׁלום, that is, happiness. εὐδοκία, not εὐδοκίας or εὐδοκίᾳ, has the consensus of the Greek codices: and it appears that Chrysostom and other Greek writers consistently read it in that way. For what is brought forward from Origen’s homily on this passage is of no weight, since we do not possess the Greek of Origen, and it is no wonder if the Latin interpreter of Origen followed the Latin version of Luke: the Latin interpreter of Luke, I think, was offended by the unusual apposition εἰρήνη εὐδοκία, whence he rendered the latter member by a genitive, which can have the same sense as the Greek. But the Syrian and the Arab, having retained the nominative, inserted a copula, as if the speech would otherwise be disjointed. But what offended them ought not to offend us, since both sacred and profane codices abound with constructions of this kind. Thus below, σωτήριον is called φῶς, v. 30, 32; I interpret it thus: let happiness come upon the earth, not earthly, however, but heavenly, namely the favor of God toward the human race, which He abundantly testifies by the mission of His Son and is going to testify more and more through the same Son. For εὐδοκία sometimes signifies the decree and counsel of God, and sometimes His benevolent affection, which in a sense like this is accustomed to be construed with ἐν, as in ἐν ᾧ εὐδόκησα, Matt. ch. III. 17, and ch. XVII. 5, ἐν σοὶ εὐδόκησα, and below ch. III. 22. Thus εὐδοκεῖ κύριος ἐν τῷ λαῷ αὐτοῦ, Psalm CXLIX. 4. Similarly, Paul says that his εὐδοκία is ὑπὲρ τοῦ Ἰσραήλ, that is, that he wishes them well from the bottom of his heart. Therefore, Chrysostom does not interpret εὐδοκίαν in this passage badly as καταλλαγήν, nor Theophylact as ἐπανάπαυσιν. Thus in Psalm V. at the end, ὅπλῳ εὐδοκίας ἐστεφάνωσας ἡμᾶς, where in the Hebrew it is רָצון. Grotius wishes ἔστω to be understood rather than ἐστὶ, but in such a way that it signifies His joyful approval of that which was, not a desire for that which was absent. Gomarus, on the contrary, urges that these things were uttered not in the sense of wishing, but of praising: because the angels are said to have sung a hymn. But because the hymn is not only eucharistic, but also votive, and we praise God even when we pray for something in His praise, nothing seems to stand in the way of these being understood in the mode of wishing and praying, just as Grotius explained: in which we also praise those things, that he acknowledges the passages of Isa. XLIV. 23 and XLIX. 13 to pertain to this: which elsewhere, for instance in his annotations on the Old Testament, he referred to the Babylonian captivity. This is fulfilled, he says, that of Isa. XLIV. 23 and XLIX. 13, shout for joy, O heavens. By εἰρήνην he understands, after the manner of the Hebrews, happiness: concerning the reading of the word εὐδοκία he has this: εὐδοκία, not εὐδοκίας or εὐδοκίᾳ, has the consensus of the Greek codices: and it appears that Chrysostom and other Greek writers consistently read it in that manner. For what is brought forward from Origen’s homily on this passage is of no weight, since we do not possess the Greek of Origen, and it is no wonder if the Latin translator of Origen followed the Latin version of Luke: the unusual apposition εἰρήνη εὐδοκία offends the Latin translator of Luke, I think; whence he rendered the latter member by the genitive, which can have the same sense as the Greek. But the Syrian and the Arab, having retained the nominative, inserted a copula, as if the speech would otherwise falter. But what offends them ought not to offend us, since both sacred and profane codices abound with constructions of this kind. Thus below, σωτήριον is called φῶς 30. 32; I interpret it thus: let happiness come upon the earth, not earthly, however, but heavenly, namely the favor of God toward the human race, which He abundantly testifies by the mission of His Son, and is going to testify more and more through the same Son. For εὐδοκία sometimes signifies the decree and counsel of God, sometimes His benevolent affection, in which sense, as here, it is accustomed to be construed with ἐν, as ἐν ᾧ εὐδόκησα Matth. III. 17. and XVII. 5. ἐν σοὶ εὐδόκησα, c. III. 22. Thus εὐδοκεῖ κύριος ἐν τῷ λαῷ αὐτοῦ Psal. CXLIX. 4. Similarly Paul says his εὐδοκία is ὑπὲρ τοῦ Ἰσραὴλ, that is, that he from his inmost soul wishes them well. Therefore, Chrysostom does not interpret εὐδοκίαν in this place badly as καταλλαγὴν, nor Theophylact as ἐπανάπαυσιν. Thus in Psalm V. at the end ὅπλῳ εὐδοκίας ἐστεφάνωσας ἡμᾶς, where in the Hebrew is רָצוֹן. These are the words of Grotius. In which opinion the blessed Chemnitius went before him, having noted the Hebraism by which nouns retain and imitate the construction of their verbs: because the verb εὐδοκέω is accustomed to be construed with the dative by means of the preposition ἐν, 2. Reg. XXII. 20. Psal. XLIV. 4. Matth. III. 17. 1. Cor. X. 5. and having observed the figure of the golden plate, which the High Priest wore on his forehead, upon which was engraved: holy to the Lord ὑπὲρ εὐδοκίας αὐτῶν. Before the Lord Exod. XXVIII. 38. but because in the first member they now desire and pray that the Lord be glorified, in the highest, in the second they vow and give thanks for peace, which properly signifies the pacification and reconciliation with God, made by Christ on earth: in the third εὐδοκίαν ἐν ἀνθρώποις, good pleasure in men, by which they acquiesce in that pacification made in Christ, it is not to be doubted is designated. For thus in all the members the force and emphasis of the same preposition ἐν is retained, and those members remain distinct, and furthermore there is a descent from the heavens to the earth, and on earth peculiarly to men, whose proper good this is: from the glory of God shining forth in turn, and peace being reborn, to the εὐδοκία in men rising again. In the highest glory to God, on earth peace to all, in men peculiarly εὐδοκία is restored, and is desired to be restored, on account of the glory of God again exerting itself, the glory especially of grace and mercy, and also of divine power and wisdom, which appears in the work of redemption, and the reconciliation, and pacification of all things in heaven and on earth; which sense the blessed Chemnitius does not reject, but confirms: because the word εὐδοκίας is sometimes also used in such a way that it is a certain εὐδοκία actively, (if I may so say) in men towards God Phil. I. 17. 2. Thess. I. 11. 2. Cor. V. 8. & XII. 10. Some in this passage interpret εὐδοκίας concerning the apprehension and application of peace, which is offered in the born Savior. And true faith can be most beautifully described from this sentiment: that it is εὐδοκία in men.

Latin:

Vers. 14. δόξα ἐν ὑψίστοις Θεῷ καὶ ἐπὶ γῆς εἰρήνη, ἀνθρώ- ποις εὐδοκία] Puto ἔστω rectius quam ἐστὶ subaudire, sed ita ut

significetur læta approbatio ejus quod erat, non desiderium ejus quod aberat. Quale est illud Virgilii : Talia sæcla suis dixerunt currite fusis Concordes stabili fatorum numine Parcæ. Illud ἐν ὑψίστοις ut alibi diximus interdum idem est quod excellentissime. Sed hic cum modo locus quoque exprimi videtur, ut opposita sint ἐν ὑψίστοις & ἐπὶ γῆς quemadmo- dum in oratione dominica ἐν Ὀρανῷ κὶ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς. Impletur hic illud Esaiæ XLIV. 23. & XLIX. 23. ovate cæli, εἰρήνην hic intelligo, more Hebræo, שׁלום, id est felicitatem. εὐ- δοκία non εὐδοκίας aut εὐδοκίᾳ habet consensus Græcorum codicum: & apparet Chrysostomum atque alios Græcos Scriptores constanter eum in modum legisse. Nam quod ex Origenis homilia in hunc locum affertur, nullius est pon- deris, cum Græca Origenis non habeamus, & mirum non sit si Latinam Lucæ versionem secutus sit Latinus Origenes interpres: offendit ut puto Latinum Lucæ interpretem in- solens appositio εἰρήνη εὐδοκία: unde posterius membrum per genitivum extulit, quod sensum habere cum Græco eundem potest. At Syrus & Arabs retento nominativo copulam interjecerunt, quasi aliter hiaret oratio. Sed quod illos offendit, offendere nos non debet, cum ejusmodi constructionibus abundent & sacri & profani codices. Sic infra σωτήριον, dicitur φῶς v. 30. 32. ita autem interpretor: super terram felicitas veniat, non terrena tamen, sed cœle- stis, Dei scilicet favor erga genus humanum, quem abunde testatur missione filii & per eundem filium magis magisq; testaturus est. Nam εὐδοκία interdum decretum & consi- lium Dei, interdum affectum ejus benevolum significat, quod sensu ut hic, cum ἐν constrtui solet, ut ἐν ὧ εὐδόκησα Matth. c. III. 17. & c. XVII 5 ἐν σοι εὐδόκησα, infra c. III. 22. Sic εὐδοκεῖ κύριος Θ ἐν τῷ λαῷ αὐτῦ Psalm. CXLIX. 4. Simi- liter Paulus ait εὐδοκίαν suam esse ὑπὲρ τῦ Ἰσραὴλ, id est, se ex intimo animo bene illis velle. Itaque non male εὐδο- κίαν hoc loco Chrysostomus καταλλαγὴν, Theophylactus ἐπανάπαυσιν interpretantur. Sic Psalmo V. in fine ὅπλῳ εὐ- δοκίας ἐστεφάνωσας ἡμᾶς, ubi in Hebræo רָצון. Subintelligi vult Grotius ἔστω potius, quam ἐστὶ, sed ita ut significetur læta approbatio ejus, quod erat, non desiderium ejus quod aberat. Gomarus contra non sensu optandi, sed laudandi ea prolata esse, urget: quia hymnum cecinisse angeli dicuntur. At quia hymnus non tantum evcharisticus, sed etiam votivus est, & Deum laudamus etiam cum in laudem ejus aliquid precamur, nihil obstare vi- detur, quo minus hæc optandi, & precandi mo- do, ita ut exposuit Grotius, intelligantur: in quo laudamus etiam illa, quod loca Esa. XLIV. 23. & XLIX. 13. huc pertinere agnoscat: quæ alias, in annotatis puta ad Vetus Testamentum ad captivita- tem Babylonicam retulit. Impletur hic, inquit, illud Esa. XLIV. 23. & XLIX. 13. ovate cæli. Per εἰρήνην intelligit, more Ebræorum felicitatem: de lectione vocis εὐδοκία hæc habet: εὐδοκία non εὐδοκίας aut εὐδοκίᾳ habet consensus Græcorum co- dicum: & apparet, Chrysostomum atque alios Græ- cos scriptores constanter eum in modum legisse. Nam quod ex Origenis homilia in hunc locum af- fertur, nullius est ponderis, cum Græca Origenis non habeamus, & mirum non sit, si Latinam Lucæ ver- sionem secutus sit Latinus Origenis interpres: Offen- dit ut puto Latinum Lucæ interpretum insolens appositio εἰρήνη εὐδοκία: unde posterius membrum per genitivum extulit, quod sensum habere cum Græco eundem potest. At Syrus & Arabs retento nominativo copulam interjecerunt; quasi aliter hia- ret oratio. Sed quod illos offendit offendere nos non debet, cum ejusmodi constructionibus abundent & sacri & profani codices. Sic infra σωτήριον dicitur φῶς 30. 32. ita autem interpretor: super terram fe- licitas veniat non terrena tamen, sed cœlestis, Dei scilicet favor erga genus humanum, quem abunde testatur missione Filii, & per eundem Fi- lium magis magisq́; testaturus est. Nam εὐδοκία in- terdum decretum & consilium Dei, interdum affe- ctum ejus benevolum significat, quo sensu, ut hic, cum ἐν construi solet, ut ἐν ᾧ εὐδόκησα Matth. III. 17. & XVII. 5. ἐν σοὶ εὐδόκησα, c. III. 22. Sic εὐδοκεῖ κύριος ἐν τῷ λαῷ αὐτοῦ Psal. CXLIX. 4. Similiter Paulus ait εὐδοκίαν suam esse ὑπὲρ τοῦ Ἰσραὴλ, id est, se ex intimo animo bene illis velle. Itaq́; non ma- le εὐδοκίαν hoc loco Chrysostomus καταλλαγὴν, Theophylactus ἐπανάπαυσιν interpretantur. Sic Psalmo V. in fine ὅπλῳ εὐδοκίας ἐστεφάνωσας ἡμᾶς, ubi in Hebræo רָצוֹן. Hæc Grotius. In qua sententia præivit B. Chemnitius notato Ebraismo, quo nomina constructionem suorum verborum retinent, & imi- tantur: quia verbum εὐδοκέω cum dativo mediante præpositione ἐν construi solet 2. Reg. XXII. 20. Psal. XLIV. 4. Matth. III. 17. 1. Cor. X. 5. & observata figura Lamine aureæ, quam Pontifex in fronte ge- rebat, cui insculptum erat: sanctum Domini ὑπὲρ εὐδοκίας αὐτῶν. Coram Domino Exod. XXVIII. 38. sed quia primo membro glorificari nunc Do- minum optant & ominantur, in excelsis, altero pa- cem, quæ proprie pacificationem & reconciliatio- nem cum Deo, à Christo factam in terris, vovent, ac gratulantur: tertio εὐδοκίαν ἐν ἀνθρώποις, com- placentiam in hominibus, qua in illa pacificatione in Christo facta acquiescunt, designari dubitan- dum non est. Sic enim in omnibus membris re- tinetur vis & emphasiseadem præpositionis ἐν, & distincta manent illa membra, ac porro à cælis ad terram descensus sit, & in terra peculiariter ad ho- mines, quorum proprium hoc est bonum: à glo- ria Dei vicissim effulgente, ac pace renascente ad εὐδοκίαν in hominibus resurgentem. In excelsis glo- ria Deo, in terra pax universis, in hominibus pe- culiariter εὐδοκία restituitur, & restitui optatur, ob Dei gloriam iterum sese exerentem, gloriam imprimis gratiæ & misericordiæ, nec non potentiæ & sapientiæ divinæ, quæ apparet in opere redem- ptionis, & reconciliationem, ac pacificationem omnium in cælo & in terra; quem sensum non re- probat, sed confirmat B. Chemnitius: quia voca- bulum εὐδοκίας aliquando etiam ita usurpatur, ut sit quædam εὐδοκία activè, (ut sic dicam) in homi- nibus erga Deum Phil. I. 17. 2. Thess. I. 11. 2. Cor. V. 8. & XII. 10. Quidam hoc loco εὐδοκίας interpre- tantur, de apprehensione & applicatione pacis, quæ in nato Salvatore offertur. Et vera fides pulcher- rime ex hac sententia describi potest: quod sit in hominibus εὐδοκία.

## 2:15
Ver. 15.
