That was called צבא, a word derived from military affairs, which the LXX translate as λειτουργεῖν in some places. Elsewhere they do not so much express the word as the custom denoted by the word. For they call the women λειτουργούσας, the הצב אות, 'those who stood by the doors of the tabernacle of the testimony,' 1 Sam. 2, 24. But in Exodus 38, 8, 'those who fasted, who fasted by the doors of the tabernacle of the testimony,' in which place there is neither a fault of the Greek codex, which a most diligent man suspects, nor did the LXX read otherwise in the Hebrew, but as they are accustomed, they used a freer interpretation explaining the thing itself. For that service, or its most important part, consisted in fastings and prayers. But both in Exodus and in Samuel, as Jonathan and Abenesdra think, it is not about matrons who, as we said, did not celebrate the temple perpetually, which the nature of domestic affairs did not allow, but at certain times. Indeed, as Paul said, 'the married woman' that she may devote herself to piety as much as possible, yet at the same time 'is anxious about the things of the world, how she may please her husband.' But widows, freed from that care, could continue that service and thus not depart from the temple, that is, hardly ever be elsewhere, being free for prayers and fastings day and night. The Christian Church, just as it retained whatever was praiseworthy among the Jews, so it retained this too. For Paul, dealing with the widow, uses almost the same words that Luke uses here about Anna, 'she continues in supplications and prayers night and day.' From this order of widows were accustomed to be chosen not only the deaconesses, who cared for poor women, but also the elder women who were also called presiding ones, the instructors of other women and teachers of morals. Paul mentions these in Titus 2, 3. Tertullian teaches us that these were accustomed to be solemnly ordained in the book I mentioned earlier, which is inscribed 'Exhortation to Chastity': and Balsamon and Zonaras acknowledge this. The Synod of Laodicea abolished that ordination: just as the Synod of Nicaea abolished the laying on of hands for deaconesses.

serving night and day) Supply 'God'. A similar idiom in Acts 26, 7.

Latin:

Vers. 37. Νηστείαις καὶ δεήσεσι) Conjungi hæc solere dixi- mus ad Matthæum 17, 21. supra retulisse nos meminimus, partem Israelitarum solitam convenire ad templum, distri- butis in id temporibus, ut precibus vacarent. Id dicebatur צבא à re militari deducto vocabulo, quod λειτουργεῖν ali- cubi vertunt LXX. Alibi non tam vocem exprimunt quam morem voce denotatum. Nam feminas λειτουργύσας הצב אות vocant τὰς παρεσηκυίας παρὰ τὰς θύρας τῆς σκηνῆς τῦ μαρτυρίε, 1. Sam. 2, 24. At Exodi 38, 8. τὰς νησευσάσας, αἱ ἐνήσευσαν παρὰ τὰς θύρας τῆς σκηνῆς τῦ μαρτυρίε, quo in lo- co neque Græci codicis vitium est, quod suspicatur vir dili- gentissimus, neque in Hebræo aliter legerunt LXX. sed ut solent, usi sunt liberiore interpretatione rem ipsam expli- cantes. In jejuniis enim & precibus consistebat ista λειτουργία aut ejus pars potissima. Sed tum in Exodo, tum in Samuele, ut Jonathan & Abenesdra existimant, ne matronis agitur, quæ ut diximus non perpetuo, quod non ferebat rei dome- sticæ ratio, sed certis temporibus templum celebrabant. Nimirum ut Paulus dixit ἡ γαμήσασα ut maxime pietati se dedat simul tamen μεριμνᾷ τὰ τοῦ κόσμου πῶς ἀρέσῃ τῷ ἀνδρὶ. At viduæ ea cura liberatæ continuare poterant eam λειτυρ- γίαν atque adeo non abscedere à templo, id est, vix unquam alibi esse, vacantes precibus & jejunis diu noctuque, Chri- stiana Ecclesia, ut quicquid apud Judæos erat laudabile, ita hoc quoque retinuit. Nam Paulus de vidua agens eadem prope verba usurpat, quæ hic de Anna Lucas, προσμένῃ ταῖς δεήσεσι κᾀ ταῖς προσευχαῖς νυκτὸς καὶ ἡμέρας. Ex hoc viduarum ordine legi solebant non tantum αἱ διάκονοι, quæ feminas pauperes curabant, sed & πρεσβύτιδες quæ & προκαθήμεναι dicebantur, aliarum mulierum σωφρονίστριαι & morum ma- gistræ. Harum meminit Paulus Tit. 2, 3. Has solenniter or- dinari solitas docet nos Tertullianus libro quem dixi priore qui exhortatio ad castitatem inscribitur: & agnoscuntBalsa- mo & Zonaras. Antiquavit eam ordinationem Laodicena Synodus : ficut διακονισσῶν χειροθεσίαν Synodus Nicena.

λατρεύουσα νύκτα κὶ ἡμέραν) Supple θεῷ. Similis ἰδιωτισμός Actor. 26, 7.

## 2:38
Ver. 38. ἀνθωμολογεῖτο τῷ κυρίῳ) That is, she gave praise and thanks to God. Nor is there any force of the preposition ἀντὶ here. For the LXX use ἀνθομολογεῖσθαι for ἐξομολογεῖσθαι, as in Psalm 79 near the end: ἀνθομολογησόμεθα σοὶ ὁ θεὸς εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα. And no otherwise in Ezra 3:11, Sirach 17:21 & 22, ch. 20:2.

Grotius neglects the particle ἀντὶ in this word, but Scultetus teaches that it should not be neglected, as it indicates that Anna sang in response to Simeon, ἀντισυμφωνολογῆσαί, such as is described in Ezra 3:11: κὶ ἀπεκρίθησαν ἐν αἴνῳ κὶ ἀνθομολογήσῃ τῷ κυρίῳ, they responded in praise and thanksgiving to the Lord; thus the version of the LXX elders. Jerome from the Hebrew: & concinebant in hymnis & confessione Domino. Word for word: and they sang together in praising and confessing to the Lord. Much better is Luther: und sungen umbeinander mit loben und dancken dem HErrn. Thus, in this passage of Luke, the same Luther has expressed the meaning most excellently: Dieselbige trat auch hinzu zu derselbigen Stunde / und preisete Gott. In Latin I would say: She therefore, coming up at that very hour, was herself also celebrating the Lord.

τοῖς προσδεχομένοις ἀπολύτρωσιν ἐν Ἱερουσαλὴμ) I think the construction is τοῖς ἐν Ἱερουσαλὴμ προσδεχομένοις τὴν ἀπολύτρωσιν. For Luke is frequent in transpositions. Moreover, that this reading is true, besides the consensus of the Greek Codices, the Syriac teaches, and Irenaeus, who reads it thus.

PART IV.

The childhood of Jesus, and the disputation in the Temple.

Latin:

Verf. 38. ἀνθωμολογεῖτο τῷ κυρίῳ) Id est Deo laudes gra- tesque agebat. Neque ulla hic vis est præpositionis ἀντὶ. Nam ἀνθομολογεῖσθαι pro ἐξομολογεῖσθαι usurpant LXX. ut Psalmo 79. circa finem : ἀνθομολογησόμεθα σοὶ ὁ θεὸς εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα. Nec aliter Efdr.3. 11. Sirachides 17,21. & 22.c.20,2.

Negligit Grotius particulam ἀντὶ in hac voce: sed Sculterus non negligendam esse docet: quæ in- dicet, Annam Simeoni succinuisse ἀντισυμφω ó- μολογῆσαί , qualis describitur Esdræ III.2. κὶ ἀπε- κρίθησαν ἐν αἴνῳ κὶ ἀνθομολογήσῃ τῷ κυρίῳ, respon- derunt in laude & florilegio & Domino: sic versio LXX. seniorum. Hieronymus ex Ebræo : & concine- bant in hymnis & confessione Domino. Ad verbum : & concinebant in laudando & confitendo Domino: Melius multo Lutherus, und fungen umbeinan- der mit loben und dancken dem HErrn. Sic hoc loco Lucæ mentem optime expressit idem Luthe- rus: Dieselbige trat auch hinzu zu derselbigen Stunde / und preisete Gott. Latine dixerim : Hæc igitur ea ipsa hora superveniens celebrabat & ipsa Dominum.

τοῖς προσδεχομένοις ἀπολύτρωσιν ἐν Ἱερουσαλὴμ) Puto con- structionem esse τοῖς ἐν Ἱερουσαλὴμ προσδεχομένοις τὴν ἀπο- λύτρωσιν. Nam creber est in trajectionibus Lucas, Lectio- nem autem hanc esse veram, præter Græcorum Codicum consensum, Syrus docet, & Irenæus, qui ita legit.

PARS IV.

Ætas puerilis Iesu, & disputatio in Templo.

## 2:40
Ver. 40. τὸ δὲ παιδίον ηὔξανε κὶ ἐκραταιοῦτο πνεύματι) These are the same words that he had used above concerning John: yet they must be interpreted differently κατ' ἀναλογίαν, and those who have not observed this have dared to delete the word πνεύματι here.

πληρούμενον σοφίας) And this signifies an act, unusual indeed, but yet successive, as they say. Such also is below, προέκοπτε σοφίᾳ. See what was said at Mark 13:32.

κὶ χάρις θεῦ ἦν ἐπ' ἀυτὸ) As concerning John, κὶ χεὶρ κυρίκ ἦν μετ' ἀυτῦ. Therefore χάρις here is the singular protection of God and the bestowing of gifts.

Latin:

Vers. 40. τὸ δὲ παιδίον ηὔξανε κὶ ἐκραταιοῦτο πνεύματι) Eadem sunt verba quæ de Johanne supra usurpaverat: di- verse tamen κατ' ἀναλογίαν interpretanda, quod qui non observarunt, ausi hic sunt delere vocem πνεύματι.

πληρούμενον σοφίας) Et hoc actum, insolitum quidem, sed tamen successivum ut loquuntur significat. Tale est & infra προέκοπτε σοφίᾳ. Vide quæ dicta ad Marci XIII, v. 32.

κὶ χάρις θεῦ ἦν ἐπ' ἀυτὸ) Ut de Johanne κὶ χεὶρ κυρίκ ἦν μετ' ἀυτῦ. Est ergo χάρις hic singularis Dei protectio & donorum collatio.

## 2:41
Ver. 41. κατ' ἔτος εἰς ἱερουσαλὴμ τῇ ἑορτῇ τοῦ πάσχα) Not that Joseph did not also go to Jerusalem at the time of Pentecost and the Feast of Tabernacles, since it was commanded to all men inhabiting Judea to go three times a year to the place of sacred assemblies, but that he did not go with his wife. For women, since no law existed concerning them, visited the sacred assemblies once a year by their own religious practice. Thus we read of Anna and Peninnah, the wives of Elkanah, that they went yearly to the house of the Lord, 1 Sam. 1:7. Which is altogether credible to have been done at the time of the unleavened bread, which is here called Passover συνεκδοχικῶς, as also sometimes in Josephus.

Latin:

Vers. 41. κατ' ἔτος εἰς ἱερουσαλὴμ τῇ ἑορτῇ τοῦ πάσχα) Non quod non & tempore πεντηκοστῆς & σκηνοπηγιῶν Jose- phus Jerosolyma iret, cum præceptum esset omnibus viris Judæam habitantibus ter anno adire locum sacrorum con- ventuum, sed quod non cum uxore. Nam feminæ, cum de iis lex non exstaret, propria religione semel anno sacros cœtus invisebant. Sic de Anna & Phenana Elcanæ uxoribus legimus quotannis eas ivisse ad ædem dominicam I. Sam. I.7. Quod omnino credibile est factum tempore azymo- rum, quod συνεκδοχικῶς hic vocatur πάσχα, ut & apud Jose- phum aliquoties.

## 2:42
Ver. 42. κὶ ὅτε ἐγένετο ἐτῶν δώδεκα) The law which exists in Exodus and Deuteronomy is conceived for all males. But since reason and equity themselves taught that this did not pertain to a very tender age, there was room for an equitable interpretation. For it mattered nothing to bring to feast days those who had no understanding of these things. Another law exists in Exodus 12:27, by which parents are commanded to explain to their children the history of the things done in Egypt, as soon as they began to inquire into the causes of that ceremony, that is, as soon as they had arrived at some use of reason: which time, since it was not defined by law, seems to have been left to the discretion of the wise, and defined by them at the age of twelve years, at which the Romans also judge women to be capable of marriage, and boys to be near to being troubled. The Hebrew words also indicate this difference of age, for within the twelfth year they were called קטנים, and upon its completion נערים. But when it is a question of inflicting punishments, he who had completed his thirteenth year was held by the laws, and was called בר מצוה, a son of the commandment. See Aben Ezra on Gen. 17:14. But the pious did not wait until then, according to the received opinion. זריזין מקדימים למצות, the diligent anticipate the commandment.

Latin:

Vers. 42. κὶ ὅτε ἐγένετο ἐτῶν δώδεκα) Lex quæ in Exodo & Deuteronomio exstat in mares omnes concepta est. Sed cum ipsa ratio & æquitas doceret id ad teneram admodum ætatem non pertinere, locus fuit æquæ interpretationi. Ni- hil enim referebat ad festos dies deduci eos, qui rerum istarum nullum habebant intellectum. Extat lex altera Exo- di 12,27. qua jubentur parentes liberis suis exponere histo- riam rerum in Ægypto gestarum, simul atque ceremoniæ istius causas inciperent inquirere, id est simul atq; ad ratio- nis usum aliquem pervenissent:quod tempus cum lege defi- nitum non esset, videtur relictum arbitrio sapientum, atque ab iis definitum ætate annorum duodecim, qua & feminas Romani viri potentes judicant, & pueros perturbari proxi- mos. Discrimen hoc ætatis indicant & voces Hebrææ, nam intra annum duodecimum dicebantur קטנים, eo impleto נערים. At ubi de pœnis irrogandis agitur, is qui annum implevit XIII. legibus tenebatur, & vocabatur בר מצוה filius præcepti. Vide Aben Esdram Gen. 17, 14. At pii non eousq; exspectabant juxta receptam sententiam. שורי זין מקדימים למצות expediti antevertunt præceptum.

## 2:43
Ver. 43. τελειωσάντων τὰς ἡμέρας) The legitimate days of the unleavened bread.

Because we have here a certain prelude to the office of Christ, it is helpful to note a few things about it. I. Regarding the time. Why did Christ institute the conversation at the boyish age of scarcely twelve years? Why at the feast of the Passover?

This was done on account of the type of Samson, Jud. 13:15, and of Samuel, 1 Sam. 2:18, as also of Josiah, 2 Chron. 34:1; both on account of the revelation of divine Wisdom, which he had not drawn from elsewhere, being instructed in no public school, and which far exceeded his age; and on account of the sanctification of his childhood. See Irenaeus, book 2, chapter 32. Moreover, he wished to institute the colloquy on the Feast of the Passover not only so that the specimen of Wisdom might be more illustrious, and his fame might spread more widely, but so that at that feast the first specimen of his office might be produced, by which it was destined to be concluded in these lands, and so that the primary feast of the Jews might be honored and rendered more solemn. II. Regarding the place. It is said that he sat ἐν τῷ ἱερῷ (in the temple). Where it is understood not as the temple itself, but the treasury adjacent to the temple, which, joined with the name of the temple, comes to be understood as the place in which, as in a school, the Doctors were accustomed to meet with their disciples. See Jer. 39:20; 2 Kings 16:18. Job 8:20, ch. 18:20. But he did not sit at their feet merely in the manner of disciples, as Burgensis and H. Grotius wish, but ἐν τῷ μέσῳ τῶν διδασκάλων (in the midst of the teachers) as the Doctor of Doctors, since one must not depart from the literal meaning, which is further confirmed by the examination instituted by Christ through questions and inquiries, as well as by the admiration of the Doctors themselves. III. Regarding the subject matter of the colloquy. It is not indeed expressed, but there is no doubt that he spoke about matters accommodated to the time of his advent, Rom. 12:11. Titus of Bostra and Euthymius think that it was about the rites of the law. Blessed Chemnitius thinks it was a specimen produced of the doctrine which he was about to deliver concerning the person and office of the Messiah, concerning the distinction between the law and the Gospel, concerning the true worship of God in the New Testament, concerning the abrogation of Levitical things, and concerning the traditions of the Pharisees. It can also be said that, on the occasion of the Feast of the Passover, he held a colloquy about those things which specifically befitted this Feast, just as he was accustomed to accommodate his discourses to festive times. IV. Regarding the form. He instituted this colloquy in an orderly and distinct manner, with modest listening, profound questioning, and vigorous answering, and with such boldness of speech and gravity that divine wisdom shone forth from it, on account of which all who heard, even the Doctors themselves, were astonished, i.e., they did not merely admire the boy, but were utterly stunned, as if rapt out of themselves, as in Gen. 42:18. That Hebraism: 'My heart has gone forth,' is rendered by this word; then his parents were struck, ἐξεπλάγησαν (they were astonished), v. 48, not only on account of the unexpected discovery, but primarily on account of the most profound instruction, just as others marveled ἐπὶ τῇ συνέσει, κὶ ταῖς ἀποκρίσεσιν αὐτῤ (at his understanding and his answers), not as Grotius too dryly [suggests], as if the boy were being questioned in turn by the Masters for the sake of testing his progress. For thus there would have been no cause for admiration, let alone stupor; not on account of his answers, but because the Doctors, hearing most wise questions about greater mysteries, questioned him in turn, for the sake of instruction. V. Regarding the end. Why did Christ wish to make this, as it were, a prelude to his office in the temple? It seems to have been done (1) for the illustration of the glory of the latter temple, Hag. 2:10. (2) For the manifestation of his advent, by which they might understand that that great Prophet had been raised up, Deut. 18:18. (3) For the demonstration of divine Wisdom, which, although it had been veiled otherwise, in the state of κένωσις (emptying), here scattered most illustrious rays, so that even in that childhood age it might not be entirely hidden, John 1:14, Col. 2:3. (4) For the instruction of the Doctors, so that they might be taught about the most grave matters, and might be led to the recognition of the truth by this miracle also of the boy's divine Wisdom, who, never having used public instruction, was superior to any public Doctors. Compare Mark 6:6, John 7:15. VI. As to the recording of this colloquy, it can be asked: Why is this single colloquy, above other discourses or sayings held by Christ, the only one commemorated? This was done not because he could not produce documents of singular wisdom before he was instructed in heaven, as the Socinians dream, which even this specimen of his childhood age refutes; nor is there any doubt that the rays of divine Wisdom subsequently exercised themselves more and more, Luke 2:52, but because (1) the Holy Spirit did not wish to present to us the sayings of Christ, except those which were uttered in his public office and in an admirable specimen of it. (2) Because authority had to be reconciled to Christ first by the solemn proclamation of the heavenly voice, Matt. 3:17. (3) Because the Evangelists had to report those things especially which they or other ministers of the word had drawn from the mouth of Christ, Luke 1:2, 1 John 1:1, so that at that age there was no lack of eyewitnesses. (4) Add that this was the chief among all the colloquies and sayings of Christ before the initiation of his office. (5) Since the Evangelists constantly keep this law of writing, as Blessed Chemnitius warns, that they diligently describe those things which happened to Christ in an extraordinary way, but those things in which he wished to differ in nothing from other men, they either pass over in silence or note in a few words taken from the common custom of men, it could be gathered from this that nothing extraordinary, which it would concern us to know, intervened before the public initiation of his office, except this colloquy.

Latin:

Vers. 43. τελειωσάντων τὰς ἡμέρας) Legitimos Azymo- rum dies.

Quia hic præludium quoddam habemus officii Christi, juvat paucula de illo annotare. I. Qua tempus. Cur ætate puerili vix duodecennalis col- loquium instituerit Christus? Cur festo Paschatos?

Illud factum est ob typum Simsonis Jud. XIII. 15. & Samúelis 1. Sam. II. 18. ut & Josiæ 2. Par. 34, 1. tum ob Sapientiæ divinæ patefactionem, quam aliunde non hauserat, in nulla quadam publica Schola in- formatus, quæque longe ætatem ejus superabat; tum ob puerilis ætatis sanctificationem. Vid. Iren. lib. II. cap. 32. In Festo autem Paschatos collo- quium instituere voluit non modo, ut eo illustrius esset specimen Sapientiæ, eoque amplius fama e- jus sese diffunderet, sed ut illo festo primum spe- cimen muneris ederetur, quo id in his terris con- cludi debebat, utq; primarium Judæorum festum honoraretur, ac solemnius redderetur. II. Qua lo- cum. Ἐν τῷ ἱερῷ dicitur sedisse. Ubi non ipsum templum, sed vicinum templo gazophylacium cum templi nomine conjuncta loco veniant, intel- ligitur, in quo ceu Schola solebant Doctores con- venire cum discipulis. Vid. Jer. 39, 20. 2. Reg. 16. 18. Job. 8, 20. c. 18, 20. Non autem sedit ad pedes tantum more Discipulorum, prout Burgensis & H. Grot. volunt, sed ἐν τῷ μέσῳ τῶν διδασκάλων ceu Doctor Doctorum, cum a literæ proprietate discedendum non sit, quod insuper confirmat exa- men per interrogata & quæstiones institutum à Christo, ut & admiratio ipsorummet Doctorum. III. Qua materiam Colloquii. Non exprimitur quidem ea, sed dubium non est de materiis tem- pori adventus sui accommodatis Rom. 12, 11. col- locutum esse. Titus Bostrensis & Euthymius de ri- tibus legis actum fuisse arbitrantur. B. Chemnitius specimen editum existimat doctrinæ, quam tra- diturus erat de persona & officio Messiæ, de discri- mine legis & Evangelii, de vero cultu Dei in N. T. de abrogatione Leviticorum, & de traditionibus Pha- risæorum. Dici etiam potest, quod occasione Festi Paschatos de iis quæ speciatim huic Festo con- gruebant, colloquium habuerit, prout consuevit sermones suos ad tempora festiva accommodare. IV. Qua formam. Instituit hoc colloquium ordi- nate ac distincte, modesta auscultatione, profun- da interrogatione, nervosa responsione, idque ea dicendi παῤῥησίᾳ ac gravitate, ut divina inde elu- cesceret sapientia, ob quam omnes audientes, et- iam ipsimet Doctores ἐξίσταντο h. e. non admira- bantur tantum puerum, sed obstupescebant penitus qs. extra se rapti ut Genes. 42, 18. Ebraïsmus ille: Egressum est cor meum hoc verbo redditur, tum Parentes ejus perculsi ἐξεπλάγησαν v. 48. non so- lum ob insperatam inventionem, sed imprimis ob profundissimam informationem, prout alii mira- ti sunt ἐπὶ τῇ συνέσει, κὶ ταῖς ἀποκρίσεσιν αὐτῤ, nõ ut jejune nimis Grotius, quemadmodum pueri explo- randi profectus causa vicissim à Magistris interro- gari solebant. Sic enim nulla fuisset admirationis, nedum stuporis causa; non ob responsa ejus, sed quod Doctores audientes sapientissimas interro- gationes de majoribus mysteriis vicissim eum in- terrogarint, informationis gratia. V. Qua finem. Cur Christus hoc qs. præludium muneris sui face- re voluerit in templo? Factum id videtur (1.) ob gloriæ templi posterioris illustrationem Hagg. 2, 10. (2.) Ob adventus sui manifestationem, quo ma- gnum illum Prophetam suscitatum esse intellige- rent Deut. 18, 18. (3.) Ob Sapientiæ divinæ demon- strationem, quæ cum velata alias fuerit, in statu 𝔠- τενώσεως, hic radios sparsit illustrissimos, ut in il- la etiam puerili ætate non penitus lateret Johan. 1, 14. Col. 2, 3. (4.) Ob Doctorum informationem, quo de materiis gravissimis erudirentur, & ad agnitio- nem veritatis hoc quoque miraculo divinæ pueri Sapientiæ perducerentur, qui nunquam publica usus institutione quibusvis Doctoribus publicis superior erat. Conf. Marc. VI. 6 Johan. VII. 15. VI. Quod ad consignationem hujus colloquii, quæri potest, Cur unicum hoc colloquium præ aliis à Christo habitis sermonibus vel dictis solum commemoratum sit? Factum id non quod nulla singularis sapientiæ documenta edere potuerit priusquam in cœlis informaretur, uti somniant Sociniani, quos vel hoc puerilis ætatis specimen refellit: neque dubium est, radios divinæ Sapien- tiæ deinceps se magis magisque exercuisse Luc. 2, 52. sed quod (1.) Spiritus S. dicta Christi nobis si- stere non voluerit, nisi quæ in munere publico, ejusque admirando specimine prolata. (2.) Quod autoritas Christo solemni proclamatione vocis cœlestis Matth. 3, 17. prius concilianda fuerit. (3.) Quod Evangelistæ illa potissimum referre de- buerint, quæ ipsi vel alii ὑπηρέται τῶν λόγων è Chri- sti ore hauserant Luc. I, 2. 1. Joh. I, 1. ita ut ista æta- te testes ἀυτόπται non defuerint. (4.) Adde quod hoc præcipuum fuerit inter omnia colloquia ac dicta Christi ante muneris ejus initiationem. (5.) Cum Evangelistæ hanc quasi legem scribendi perpetuo servent, monente B. Chemnitio, ut ea quæ extraordinario modo Christo acciderunt, diligenter describant, ea vero in quibus nihil vo- luit à cæteris hominibus differre, vel silentio præ- tereant, vel paucis, & è media hominum consue- tudine petitis verbis annotent, Colligi hinc pos- set, nihil extraordinarii, quod scire nostra refer- ret, præter hoc colloquium ante publicam mune- ris initiationem intervenisse.

## 2:44
Verse 44. ἐν τῇ συνοδίᾳ εἶναι (to be in the company). Great was the crowd of those traveling together from Galilee to Judea, and back. By day, as occasion offered, they gathered together for the sake of conversation; in the evening they returned to their own, for the sake of taking rest. And so it is not a wonder that the boy was first missed in the evening. Συνοδία is that which the Persians call a caravan, the Hebrews ארחה, the Arabs قافلة, Gen. 37:25, the Ethiopians ነግደ. Thus, those who had undertaken a journey with Nehemiah are called a συνοδία in Nehemiah 7:64.

ἐν τοῖς συγγενέσι καὶ τοῖς γνωστοῖς (among relatives and acquaintances). Among kinsmen and friends, who were ἐν τῇ συνοδίᾳ (in the company), among whom they suspected he had remained.

Heinsius does not want the word to be taken as referring to the company, but to the relatives who had set out together, because they believed the Lord was still staying and lingering among the relatives and friends who had betaken themselves together to the feast; but [they think] they would have sought him here in Jerusalem in that way. Why then are they said to have come to Jerusalem only afterwards, and to have sought him there? Therefore, Grotius's explanation is to be preferred.

Latin:

Vers. 44. ἐν τῇ συνοδίᾳ εἶναι] Magna erat turba simul iter facientium è Galilæa in Judæam, & contra. De die his atq; illis, prout ferebat occasio, se aggregabant colloquii causâ: vesperi ad suos se referebant, capiendæ quietis causâ. Itaque mirum non est vesperi primum desideratum esse puerum. Συνοδία id est quod Persæ Caravanam vocant, Hebræi ארחה, Arabes قافلة Gen. 37, 25. Æthio- pes ነግደ Sic qui cum Nehemia iter susceperant, συνοδία dicuntur Nehemiæ VII. 64.

ἐν τοῖς συγγενέσι καὶ τοῖς γνωστοῖς] Inter cognatos & ami- cos, qui erant ἐν τῇ συνοδίᾳ apud quos eum hæsisse suspi- cabantur.

Non vult Heinsius vocem de comitatu accipi: sed de propinquis qui una profecti, quod credi- derint Dominum apud propinquos & amicos, qui una ad festum se contulerant, adhuc versari ac hæ- rere: sed ita quæsiissent hic ipsum Hierosolymis. Cur ergo postea demum dicuntur venisse Hierso- lymam, ibique eum quæsiisse? Præferenda igitur Grotii explicatio.

## 2:46
Vers. 46. μεθ’ ἡμέρας τρεῖς] That is, on the third day, as in Matt. 27:63, Mark 8:31. They had traveled for one day, on the second they had retraced the same journey, and finally on the third they find the one they were seeking.

ἐν τῷ ἱερῷ] In the open-air portico of the Israelites, as can be gathered from Baruch and the Talmudic writings.

ἐν μέσῳ τῶν διδασκάλων] That is, in the crowd of the Masters. Otherwise, they did not sit mixed together, but the elders were separated from the younger ones. Thus Paul says he was instructed at the feet of Gamaliel, Acts 22:3. Philo on the Essenes says: 'they sit in order according to age'; and elsewhere: 'according to their ages in ranks, the young sit under the elders.' The author whose expositions on the epistles of Paul are read under the title of Ambrose at 1 Corinthians 14:31 notes this custom.

κὶι ἐπερωτῶντα αὐτὺς] Proposing questions from the Law and the Prophets.

Latin:

Vers. 46. μεθ’ ἡμέρας τρεῖς] Id est die tertio ut Matth. 27, 63. Marc. 8, 31. Diem unum iter fecerant, altero re- mensi erant idem iter, tertio demum quæsitum inve- niunt.

ἐν τῷ ἱερῷ] In porticu subdialis Israelitarum, ut ex Ba- rucho & Thalmudicis datur colligi.

ἐν μέσῳ τῶν διδασκάλων] Id est in turba Magistrorum. Alioqui non permixti sedebant, sed distincti senes à junio- ribus. Ita Paulus institutum se dicit ad pedes Gamalielis Actor. 22, 3. Philo de Essenis, καθ’ ἡλικίαν ἑξῆς καθίζονται: & alibi: καθ’ ἡλικίας ἐν τάξεσιν ὑπὸ πρεσβυτέροις νέοι καθίζον- ται. Annotat hunc morem is cujus in Pauli epistolas expositiones sub Ambrosii titulo leguntur ad Corinth. 14. v. 31.

κὶι ἐπερωτῶντα αὐτὺς] Proponentem quæstiones ex lege & Prophetis.

## 2:47
Vers. 47. Καὶ ταῖς ἀποκρίσεσιν ἀυτῦ] For the sake of testing progress, boys were questioned in turn by the masters, as appears from the book Musar. See Josephus in his Life.

Latin:

Vers. 47. Καὶ ταῖς ἀποκρίσεσιν ἀυτῦ] Nam explorandi profectus causa à magistris pueri vicissim interrogaban- tur, ut ex libro Musar apparet. Vide Josephum vita sua.

## 2:48
Vers. 48. Ὀδυνώμενοι] Because of the tenderness of their affection, not paying enough attention to those things which, otherwise, they could not have been ignorant of regarding this boy. For the things which Origen brings forward here have little probability.

Latin:

Vers. 48. Ὀδυνώμενοι] Præ affectus teneritudine non sa- tis attendentes ad ea quæ de hoc puero alioqui ignorare non poterant. Nam quæ Origenes hic adfert parum habent probabilitatis.

## 2:49
Vers. 49. Τὶ ὅτι ἐζητεῖτέ με, ὀυκ ᾔδειτε. Which words are not indeed those of one recriminating, as the impious Piscator is in this place against the clear letter of Scripture, 1 Pet. 2:23, and yet, not as Costerus wishes, excusing Mary from negligence, but 1. justly rebuking, as the anonymous Greek in the Catena has it, and arguing, as Ambrose explains, both because of that sorrowful and anxious inquiry, joined with a certain diffidence which word implies vehement pain, such as that of women in labor: the Syriac renders it Bethurah athebar; when someone beats his breast and laments over something, then because of that public expostulation, which Stapleton by no means excuses, and which Maldonatus, Burgensis, Salmero, and Jansenius change into a private one, made only after the assembly was dissolved, although Scripture immediately subjoins it, as if it were done in the temple. Salmero himself acknowledges here that the words are somewhat harsh and sub-acrid and a small rebuke of Christ, Stapleton. an unusual freedom of speech. Jansenius says Christ's words sound somewhat harsh; Maldonatus confesses that Christ had assumed the habit of one rebuking. 2. Gravely correcting. For he desired in them, not only a more ordered love, but also a fuller knowledge of the heavenly Father and of his own office, οὐκ ᾔδειτε, did you not know: which phrase B. Chemnitius observes, and Burgensis agrees, is used concerning matters about which there had been discussion among some before, so that it could and should have been known about them, Rom. 6:3, 1 Cor. 3:16, ch. 6:19. 3. More rightly informing, ὅτι ἐν τοῖς τοῦ πατρός μου δεῖ εἶναί με, by which he partly recalls them to the true and proper Father, correcting the Mother's statement, by which Joseph had been named Father, and partly embraces the sum of his office, which 1. he proposes not as arbitrary but as necessary from the hypothesis of the divine decree of the prediction of Scripture and the salvation of men. Δεῖ, it is necessary. Cf. John 9:4. Therefore Maldonatus does not sufficiently explain this by 'it behooves.' 2. He teaches that he consists in those things which are his Father's, which were not so much those things which were at home, as those which were being performed in the temple. 3. He does not recall them to his own office, those things which are the Father's by reason of general conservation and sustenance, but by reason of the gathering and government of the Church, for he was found occupied in these things then. Cf. regarding the phrase εἶναι ἐν τοῖς, the passage 1 Tim. 4:15.

That I must be in my Father's [things/places]. The Syriac [has] in the house of my Father, that is, in the temple, just as the man of exquisite diligence, Nicol. Fullerus, recently noted that Chrysostom also speaks, ἐν τοῖς τοῦ δεσπότου, in the master's places: also bringing forward that of John 19:27, ἔλαβεν εἰς τὰ ἴδια, he received into his own home. To which can be added that the word בַּיִת, which signifies house, is translated τὰ ἴδια, Esth. 5:10, 6:12. Nor indeed is this interpretation new. For Origen, most learned in Greek, accepted it no otherwise, and Euthymius, an interpreter of great judgment: the number of these is joined by Theophylact. But it coheres best with the preceding. For he was not to be sought elsewhere rather than where it most behooved him to be; and that was in the paternal house. There exists a diatribe of the excellent Musonius, in which he teaches that there are certain things excepted from the commands of parents. For a son who is a physician will not treat the sick as the father wishes, but according to the precept of the art. In the same place this sentiment exists: 'Your father will forbid you to philosophize; but the common Zeus of men and gods commands and urges you.' Hierocles: 'He who is not overcome by the succession from them (the parents), this one is released free from the dominion of them, by the law, and is exhorted to seek the truly Father (that is, God) and to hold to him and to take the greatest care of the likeness to him.' Thus also elsewhere the Lord denies that the Mother has authority over the miracles to be performed by him.

Epiphanius could also have been added to them, Heresy 30, Augustine in a sermon on the parents of Christ, as also Hugo. Furthermore, I do not disapprove of that explanation. Piscator, following Castalio, expounded it, 'in the business of my Father': which Fullerus disapproves: For we see, he says, that it is rightly said εἶναι ἐν τοῖς πράγμασι, to attend to or administer business; who, I pray, would grant that εἶναι ἐν τοῖς means the same thing, or that it was ever customary for those speaking Greek; and would he not rather consider it unheard of, unusual, and discordant? Moreover, there is no doubt that the Lord answered the mother's words accurately. But she speaks not of any business, but of a place. Behold (she says) your Father and I were seeking you in sorrow. For those things are sought which are, or are thought to be, outside their place. Thus also the Syriac, 'in the house of my Father': Therefore, Fullerus wishes that the word ἐν τοῖς τοῦ πατρός μου denotes 'in the places of my Father,' i.e., in the house or home. Cf. also Capellus on this place.

Latin:

Vers. 49. Τὶ ὅτι ἐζητεῖτέ με, ὀυκ ᾔδειτε. Quæ verba sunt non quidem recriminantis, ut impie Piscator in h. l. contra apertam Scripturæ literam, 1. Petr. II. 23. nec tamen, ut Costerus vult, Mariam à negligentia excusantis, sed 1. juste in- crepantis, ut habet Græcus anonymus in Catena, & arguentis, ut exponit Ambrosius, tum ob illam dolorosam & anxiam inquisitionem, cum diffiden- tia quadam conjunctam. Quid est, quod me quære- batis, ὀδυνώμενοι sc. (dolentes) quæ vox dolorem vehementem, qualis est parturientium, infert: Syrus reddit Bethurah athebar; cum quis pectus tundit & plangit super aliqua re, tum ob publicam illam expostulationem, quam nequaquam excu- sat Stapletonus, & Maldonatus aut in privatam, soluto conventu demum factam, commutant Burgensis, Salmero & Jansenius cum Scriptura eandem imme- diate subjungat, ceu in templo factam. Agnoscit ipse Salmero hic, verba aliquantisper aspera & sub- acerba & objurgatiunculam Christi, Stapleton. in- solitam dicendi libertatem. Jansenius duriusculum quid Christi verba sonare ait, Maldonatus Chri- stum reprehendentis habitum induisse facetur. 2. Graviter emendantis. Desiderabat quippe in iisdem, non modo magis ordinatam dilectionem, sed & ampliorem cognitionem Patris cælestis & offi- cii sui, ὐκ ᾔδειτε annon sciebatis : quam phrasin ob- servat B. Chemnitius, annuitque Burgensis adhiberi de rebus, de quibus antea inter aliquos actum fuerit, ut de illis constare potuerit ac debuerit Rom. VI. 3. 1. Cor. III. 16. c. VI. 19. 3. Rectius infor- mantis, ὅτι ἐν τοῖς Ῡ πατρός με δεῖ εἶναί με, quibus partim ad Patrem verum propriumque revocat, corrigens dictum Matris, quo Josephus Pater no- minatus erat, partim officii summam complectitur, quod 1. proponit non ut arbitrarium sed ex hypo- thesi divini decreti prædictionis Scripturæ & salu- tis hominum necessarium. Δεῖ oportet. Conf. Joh. IX. 4. Non ergo satis id explicat Maldonatus per decet. 2. Consistere docet in his, quæ Patris sua sunt, qualia non tam erant ea, quæ domi, quam quæ in templo peragebantur. 3. Non revocat ad pro- prium suum officium, ea, quæ Patris sunt ratione conservationis & sustentationis generalis, sed ratione collectionis & gubernationis Ecclesiæ, in his enim occupatus tum inveniebatur. Conf. quoad phrasin εἶναι ἐν τοῖς locus 1. Tim. IV. 15.

Ὅτι ἐν τοῖς τῶ πατρός με δεῖ με εἶναι] Syrus in domo Patris mei, id est, in templo, quomodo & Chrysostomum loqui, ἐν τοῖς τῶ δεσπότε in locis herilibus, annotavit nuper vir exquisitæ di- ligentiæ Nicol. Fullerus: etiam illud Johannis adferens XIX. 27. ἔλαβεν εἰς τὰ ἴδια, in domum suam recepit. Cui addi potest quod vox בַּיִת, quæ domum significat, τὰ ἴδια vertitur Esth. V. 10. VI. 12. Neque vero nova est hæc interpretatio. Nam Origenes non aliter accepit, Græce eruditissimus, at necku- thymius magni judicii interpres: accedit horum numero Theophylactus. Optime autem cohæret cum superioribus. Neq; enim alibi quærendus erat potius quam ubi esse eum maxime decebat; id autem erat in æde paterna. Exstat egre- gii Musonii diatriba, qua docet esse quædam parentum im- periis excepta. Neque enim filium medicum curaturum æ- grotos, ut Pater volet, sed ex artis præcepto. Ibidem hæc ex- stat sententia: ὁ πατὴρ ὁ σὸς κωλύσε σε φιλοσοφεῖν· ὁ δὲ γε κοινὸς ἀνθρώπων τε κὶ θεῶν Ζεὺς κελεύει σε κὶ προτρέπει. Hierocles : ὁ δὲ τῆς ἀπ’ ἐκείνων (τ γονέων) διαδοχῆς ὐκ ἥττηται, τῦτο ἐλεύθερον τῆς ἀπ’ ἐκείνων δεσποτείας ἀφίεται, ὁ νόμῷ, κὶ τ᾿ ὄντως πατέρα (id est Deum) ζητεῖν παρακελεύεται κάκείνω ἔχεσθαι κὶ τῆς πρὸς ἐκεῖνον ὁμοιώσεως πλείστην ἐπιμέλειαν ποιεῖσθαι. Sic & alibi Do- minus in miracula à se edenda jus esse Matri negat.

Addi illis poterat & Epiphanius hæresi XXX. Augustinus serm. de Christi parentibus, ut & Hugo. Cæterum non improbo istam explicationem. Pi- scator Castalionem sequutus expoluit, in negotiis Pa- tris mei: quod improbat Fullerus: Nam videmus, inquit, recte dici εἶναι ἐν τοῖς πράγμασι, negotia obi- re vel administrare, quis obsecro dederit; εἶναι ἐν τοῖς, idem valere, aut unquam Græce loquentibus usita- tum fuisse; ac non potius inauditum, insolens, absonum existimet? insuper dubium non est, quin ad verba matris accurate responderit Dominus. Illa autem non de negotio aliquo, sed de loco verba facit. Ecce (in- quit) Pater tuus & ego dolentes quærebamus te. Quæruntur enim, quæ extra locum suum aut sunt, aut esse putantur. Ita & Syrus, in domo Patris mei: Ad verbum ergo ἐν τοῖς τ͂ πατρός μȣ denotare in locis Patris mei, h. e. in æde, sive in domo vult Fülle- rus. Conf. & Capellus in h. l.

## 2:50
Verse 50. They did not understand. I think συνιέναι here and elsewhere is not so much to understand, as to consider with sufficient attention, as we have warned in another place. Christ had pointed his finger to the prophecy of Malachi: 'The Lord whom you desire will come into his temple, that messenger of the covenant whom you desire.' These things were finally understood fully only afterwards when the same Jesus taught publicly in the Temple, and purged the temple of the filth of the merchants: by which deeds the boy was even then preluding.

Latin:

Vers. 50. ȣ συνῆκαν] συνιέναι & hic & alibi puto non tam esse intelligere, quam attente satis considerare, ut alio loco monuimus. Intenderat Christus digitum ad Malachiæ vati- cinium: veniet in templum suum Dominus quem vos optatis, nuntius ille fœderis quem desideratis. Hæc plene postea de- mum intellecta sunt cum idem Jesus in Templo publice docuit, & templum à nundinantium sordibus repurgavit: quibus factis jam tum puer præludebat.

## 2:51
Verse 51. And he was subject to them. Luke rightly added this to show that Jesus had so occupied himself with divine things that he did not meanwhile withdraw the due duties from his parents. Thus, says Hierocles, 'it is possible for both to happen, so that we may keep divine goods and also in human ones, and yet we shall not neglect to serve the parents through the virtue of the house.'

She kept all the words. Thus above [verse] 19. Which seems to have been expressed by Luke because he had the very author of these narratives.

Latin:

Vers. 51. κὴ ἦν ὑποτασσόμεν@ αὐτοῖς] Recte hoc adjecit Lucas ut ostenderet ita divinis rebus vacasse Jesum, ut pa- rentibus interim debita officia non subtraheret. Οὕτως, in- quit Hierocles, ἀμφότερα δυναιὸν συμβαίνειν, ὥστε θεῖα ἀγαθὰ τηρεῖν κἀν ἀνθρωπίναις, κὴ ἔτι δι᾽ οἴκου ἀρετῆς γονέων θεραπέυειν ὀ- λιγωρήσομεν.

Διετήρει πάντα τὰ ῥήματα] Ita supra 19. Quod ideo vide- tur à Luca expressum, quia ipsam habebat harum narra- tionum auctorem.

## 2:52
Verse 52. Stature, as Matt. 6:27, below 19:2. And in favor with God and men. Grace is taken here a little differently than above in verse 40. For it signifies that Jesus was pleasing in the highest degree both to God and to men. Thus it is said of the boy Samuel [whom we have observed to have borne the image of Christ]; וטוב גם עם־יהוה וגם עם־אנשים : that is, He was gracious before God and men; from which passage these words seem to have been taken. Josephus said almost the same things about Moses.

Latin:

Vers. 52. ἡλικίᾳ] Statura, ut Matth. VI. 27. infra XIX. 2. καὶ χάριτι παρὰ Θεῷ κὴ ἀνθρώποις] χάρις hic paulo aliter su- mitur quam supra com. 40. Significat enim summopere placuisse Jesum & Deo & hominibus. Ita de Samuele puero [quem Christi gestisse imaginem observavimus] dictum est; וטוב גם עם־יהוה וגם עם־אנשים : id est, Gratio- sus erat apud Deum & homines; ex quo loco desumpta viden- tur hæc verba. Eadem serme de Mose dixit Josephus.

## 3:1 Argument
CHAPTER III. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

The time of the calling of John is designated, by which the year of the Emperor, and of the Governor, in Judea and other provinces, as well as the High Priests, and the command of God and the office of John according to the prophecy of Isaiah, (c. XL. 3.) the rebuke of the brood of vipers, and the exhortation to bring forth fruits of repentance, to beneficence; and of the Publicans to avoid iniquity: and of the soldiers, that they inflict violence or injury upon no one, and that they be content with their wages. John protests that he is not the Christ, whom he predicts will baptize with the Spirit, and will purge his threshing floor: concerning whom also Luke, on the occasion of these corrective sermons, reports proleptically how he was cast into prison because of his rebuke of Herod. There follows the manifestation of God in the baptism of Christ: and his age and genealogy ascending even to Adam created by God.

The parts are V. I. The preaching of John the Baptist, to v. 14. II. His prediction concerning Christ, to v. 18. III. The imprisonment of John, to v. 20. IV. The revelation of the Holy Trinity in the baptism of Christ, to v. 22. V. The commemoration of the age and ancestors of Christ, to the final v. 38.

PART I. The preaching of John the Baptist.

V. 1. ἐν ἔτει δὲ πεντεκαιδεκάτῳ] just as the Prophets, after the division of the Israelite kingdom had been made, were accustomed to note the times both of the Kings of Judah and of the kings of Samaria, who then divided the promised land among themselves, so also Luke, about to narrate the public appearance to Israel of two Prophets, John and the Messiah himself, employs an accurate description of the time, having named all who then held any part of the promised land in their own name or in another's.

τῆς ἡγεμονίας] He expressed the Roman term for empire, by which then, in order to avoid envy, a truly royal power was concealed. See Appian.

Regarding these matters, let those things be compared which have been said in the sacred Chronicle. Ἡγεμονεύοντος) That is, ἐπιτροπεύοντος, which interpretation has occupied the text in certain Codices. This ἡγεμονεύων is taken not from Roman, but from common usage: just as Peter calls all τοὺς διὰ βασιλέως πεμπομένους ἡγέμονας. We have said that in this meaning it corresponds to the word praeses, which is general, and also includes those procurators who had received the power of the sword. Τῆς Ἰτουραίας καὶ Τραχωνίτιδος χώρας) Trachonitis is also accustomed to be called by the name of Ituraea. But here Ituraea seems to be called specifically Batanaea and Auranitis. For Philip was in charge of those parts together with Trachonitis. κᾀ Λυσανίου τῆς Ἀβιληνῆς Τετραρχοῦντος) You will not find this Lysanias, as a dynast of a small portion, expressly mentioned in the history of Josephus. But since the same author says that a certain part of the house of Zenodorus, that is, of Abilene, which he therefore also calls the Tetrarchy of Zenodorus from its possessor, was attributed to Philip, by that very fact he indicates that the better part of it was in the hands of another: and that person was Lysanias, whom Luke mentions here, being of the posterity, no doubt, of that Lysanias who obtained the same region—called Abilene from the city of Abila, or Chalcidene by others from the city of Chalcis, the same region—while Antony was ruling over the East, after Ptolemy the son of Mennaeus: from whom that region of Lysanias had begun to be called everywhere the house of Lysanias, or Tetrarchy, or even the kingdom, or Abila of Lysanias. But just as after the death of this former Lysanias this region was called the tetrarchy of Zenodorus, so after the death of Zenodorus, or when his lease was finished (for he had obtained it as a leased property), when this other Lysanias, of the same name as the former, and who I do not doubt was descended from him (for the Romans were accustomed to honor the memory of ancestors in their descendants), held the same region, it began to be called again the tetrarchy of Lysanias. Vers. 2. ἐπὶ ἀρχιερέων Ἄννα κᾀ Καϊάφα) It appears from Josephus that Caiaphas was then holding the high priesthood. But Annas or Ananus, who was the second priest after him, that is, סגן, is named first, because he was the father-in-law of Caiaphas, and therefore of the highest authority at that time, being the father of the High Priest, and having held the high priesthood before Caiaphas: indeed, as is credible, the son-in-law had obtained this honor by the favor of his father-in-law. But Josephus also is accustomed to call those who have once held the priesthood high priests. Moreover, the name Annas which is placed here is the same as that which is pronounced Hanno by the Phoenicians. For it is the way of the Syrians to pronounce a long A as O. This is the opinion of Scaliger, Casaubon, and Constantine L'Empereur: which Selden, however, calls into doubt, proposing another conjecture about these matters. Walaeus repeats the Seldenian view at length. And that might seem plausible enough, provided it could be taught that the name of high priests denotes a prefecture or civil dignity, by which the Pontiffs stood out above the rest. Which I do not see proven. B. Chemnitius thinks that the two Pontiffs are joined because they administered the Pontificate by turns, which some think happened even in the same year, which opinion Selden observes is ancient, and that manifest traces of it are held in Augustine, Tract. XLIX on John; for which I see no solid reason why we should reject it. ἐγένετο ῥῆμα Θεῦ ἐπὶ Ἰωάννην) Above we said that it is customary to say of prophetic inspiration ἐγένετο χεὶρ κυρίυ ἐπὶ τὸν δεῖνα. But of a command it is customary to say ἐγένετο λόγος κυρίε πρὸς τὸν δεῖνα, as can be seen in more than one place from the books of Isaiah and Jeremiah. Luke, because both phrases denote the same thing, mixed the types of speaking, and said ῥῆμα, where others said λόγον, as also Paul does sometimes, and the writer to the Hebrews. The same type of speaking, which appears here, is in the Greek at the beginning of Jeremiah. ἐν τῇ ἐρήμῳ) In which he was staying, preparing himself for his duty. He imitated that Batus in Josephus who was living in the wilderness. Vers. 3. εἰς πᾶσαν τὴν περίχωρον τῶ Ἰαρδάνε) He was exercising baptism in various places situated at the Jordan, as now in Bethabara, John ch. I, vers. 28, now in Aenon near Salim, John ch. III, vers. 22, but wherever he was, the region about the Jordan flocked to him, as Matthew teaches us. Vers. 5. πᾶσα φάραγξ πληρωθήσεται, καὶ πᾶν ὄρος καὶ βω- νὸς ταπεινωθήσεται καὶ ἔσαι τὰ (κολιὰ εἰς εὐθεῖαν καὶ αἱ τρα- χεῖαι εἰς ὁδὲς λείας) Luke pursues the words of Isaiah a little further than the others, because for them it had been enough to indicate the place, but here he preferred to append all the words that were relevant to the matter. Moreover, Luke follows the LXX Interpreters word for word, as he often does. Their curiosity is too anxious, who in allegorized sayings examine individual parts minutely, and ask what corresponds to what, when it is enough that the comparison be understood in the whole matter. Thus here Origen and others argue much, in order to explain who the mountains are, who the valleys: when that should suffice, which I said elsewhere, that the duty of a road-builder is described: in type indeed in Isaiah, so that it may be signified that all things are now prepared for the people to be led back from Babylon into Judea by a return; but through the type, to announce the liberation from the slavery of sin and death, which were prefigured by that return. It is known, however, how often great Kings, especially with an army, make a journey, those are sent ahead who solidify the gaping places, level the protruding ones, and make a shortcut through the pathless areas, so that nothing may obstruct the journey or cause delay. Histories are full of this. When Josephus describes the arrival of Titus at Jerusalem: He says, the hollows and the trench-like places of the site were filled in; and working the rocky projections with iron, they made the whole area level. Plutarch in the Gracchi: when the hollows were being filled and bridged over wherever torrents or ravines cut through, and the height on either side was taken to be equal and parallel, it had a smooth and beautiful appearance because of the work. Xenophon calls those chosen for this service road-makers. I think, however, that those things which are announced in the Prophet and Luke for the future time are rightly explained by the Imperative, yet analogically: so that, namely, that command received concerning the return from Babylon signifies the power of GOD; but in the ministry of the Baptist it simultaneously demands human obedience. For it is not new for something to have a figure unlike that which is signified by the figure. Thus also the conversion of man is compared now to creation, now to resuscitation from death: since in conversion the voluntary aspect of the human will has its parts, in those actions it has none.

Latin:

CAPUT III. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Designatur tempus vocationis Johannis, qua annum Imperatoris, & Præsidis, in Judæa & aliis provinciis, nec non Pontifices, & mandatum Dei atque officium Johannis juxta vaticinium Esaiæ, (c. XL. 3.) corre- ptio geniminum viperarum, & adhorta- tio ad edendos fructus pœnitentiæ, ad be- neficentiam; & Publicanorum ad vitan- dam iniquitatem: ac militum, ne alicui vim, aut injuriam inferant, & ut stipen- diis contenti sint. Protestatur Iohannes quod non sit Christus, quem baptizaturum Spiritu, & aream suam purgaturum præ- dicit: de quo etiam ista concionum epanor- thoticarum occasione Lucas proleptice re- fert, quomodo ob correptionem Herodis in carcere conjectus sit. Sequitur manife- statio Dei in baptismo Christi: hujusque ætas & genealogia adscendendo usque ad Adamum à Deo conditum.

Partes sunt V. I. Johannis Baptistæ prædica- tio, ad v. 14. II. Ejusdem de Christo prædictio, ad v. 18. III. Johannis captivatio, ad v. 20. IV. S. Trinitatis in Baptismo Christi patefactio ad v. 22. V. Ætatis & majorum Christi commemora- tio, ad v. 38. finalem.

PARS I. Iohannis Baptistæ prædicatio.

V. 1. ἐν ἔτει δὲ πεντεκαιδεκάτῳ] sicut Prophetæ post regni Is- sraelitici factam divisionem tempora solent notare tum Re- gum Judæ, tum regum Samariæ, qui tum terram promissam inter se partiebantur, ita & Lucas, narraturus τὴν ἀνάδειξιν πρὸς τ͂ Ἰσραὴλ duorum Prophetarum, Johannis & Messiæ ipsius, temporis accuratam descriptionem adhibet, nomi- natis omnibus qui tum ullam terræ promissæ partem suo aut alieno nomine obtinebant.

τῆς ἡγεμονίας] Romanam imperii vocem expressit, quæ tum nomine, ad declinandam invidiam, potestas vere re- gia occultabatur. Vide Appianum.

De his conferantur quæ dicta sunt in Chro- nico sacro. Ἡγεμονεύοντος) Id est, ἐπιτροπεύοντος, quod interpreta- mentum in Codicibus quibusdam contextum occupavit. Hic ἡγεμονεύων non ex Romano, sed ex communi usu sumi- tur: quomodo Petrus ἡγέμονας vocat omnes τοὺς διὰ βασι- λέως πεμπομένους. Diximus respondere in hoc significatu vo- cabulo præsidis, quod generale est, & eos etiam compre- hendit procuratores, qui gladii acceperant potestatem. Τῆς Ἰτουραίας καὶ Τραχωνίτιδος χώρας) Solet & Tracho- nitis Iturææ nomine appellari. Sed hic Ituræa peculiariter dici videtur Batanæa & Auranitis. Nam illis partibus una cum Trachonitide Philippus præfuit. κᾀ Λυσανίου τῆς Ἀβιληνῆς Τετραρχοῦντος) Lysaniam hunc, ut exiguæ portionis Dynastam, in Josephi historia diserte me- moratum non invenias. Sed cum idem dicat partem aliquã οἴκου Ζηνοδώρου, id est, Abilenæ, quam & ideo à possessore vo- cat Ζηνοδώρου Τετραρχίαν Philippo attributam, eo ipso indicat partem ejus potiorem penes alium fuisse: is autem fuit Ly- sanias, cujus hic Lucas meminit, ex posteritate nimirum Ly- saniæ illius qui eandem regionem, Abilenam dictam ab ur- be Abila Chalcidenem aliis ab urbe Chalcide tractg ejusdẽ, Antonio per Orientem imperante, obtinuit, post partem Ptolemæum Mennæi filium: à quo Lysaniæ regio ista pas- sim Λυσανία οἶκος, aut Τετραρχία, aut etiam βασιλεία, aut Ἄβιλα Λυσανία dici cœperat. At sicut post hujus prioris Ly- saniæ mortem regio hæc dicta est Zenodori tetrarchia, ita post Zenodori mortem, aut conductione ejus finita (nam locatam obtinuerat) cum alter hic Lysanias, priori cogno- minis, & quod non dubito ab eo ortus [solebant enim Ro- mani majorum memoriam in posteris honorare, eandem re- gionem tenuit, dici iterum cœpit detrarchia Lysaniæ. Vers. 2. ἐπὶ ἀρχιερέων Ἄννα κᾀ Καϊάφα) Caiaphan tunc functum pontificatu maximo ex Josepho apparet. Sed Annas sive Ananus, qui secundus ab illo pontifex erat, id est, סגן, prior nominatur, quod Caiphæ esset Socer, ac pro- inde summæ eo tempore auctoritatis patre genitus Ponti- fice maximo, & ante Caiaphan functus maximo pontifica- tu: imo ut credibile est Soceri gratia huuc honorem gener impetraverat. Sed & Josephus semel functos pontificatu solet ἀρχιερέας appellare. Quod autem hic nomen ponitur Annas, idem est quod Pœnis effertur Hanno. Nam Sy- rorum est A longum ut O efferre. Scaligeri hæc, Casauboni, & Constantini Lemper. est sententia: Quam vero in dubium vocat Selde- nus aliam proponens de his conjecturam. Sel- deniana repetit prolixe Walæus. Et plausibilis satis illa videri queat, modo doceri possit, nomen ἀρχιερέων præfecturam seu dignitatem civilem, qua Pontifices præ cæteris emicuêre, notare. Quod probatum non video. B. Chemnitius censet con- jungi duos Pontifices, quod illi per vices Pontifi- catum administrarint, quod etiam in eodem anno factum esse nonnulli putant, quam sententiam ve- tustam esse, ejusq, vestigia manifesta haberi apud Augustin. in Joh. Tract. XLIX. observat Seldenus; quam cur reprobemus, nullam solidam rationem video. ἐγένετο ῥῆμα Θεῦ ἐπὶ Ἰωάννην) Supra diximus de afflatu Prophetico dici solere ἐγένετο χεὶρ κυρίυ ἐπὶ τὸν δεῖνα. At de mandato dici solet ἐγένετο λόγος κυρίε πρὸς τὸν δεῖνα ut ex Esaïæ & Jeremiæ libris non uno loco videre est. Lu- cas, quia utraque locutio rem eandem notat, loquendi ge- nera permiscuit, & ῥῆμα dixit, ubi alii λόγον, ut & Paulus ali- quoties, & Scriptor ad Hebræos. Idem, quod hic apparet, loquendi genus est in Græco initio Jeremiæ. ἐν τῇ ἐρήμῳ) In qua versabatur, muneri se præparans. Imitatus est Batus ille apud Josephum κατὰ τὴν ἐρημίαν δια- τρίβων. Vers. 3. εἰς πᾶσαν τὴν περίχωρον τῶ Ἰαρδάνε) Diversis in locis ad Jordanem sitis baptismum exercebat, ut modo in Bethabara Johann. cap. I. vers. 28. modo in Ænon apud Salim Johann. cap. III. vers. 22. ubi autem ille erat, eo confluebant ἡ περίχωρος τῶ Ἰορδάνε, ut Matthæus nos do- cet. Vers. 5. πᾶσα φάραγξ πληρωθήσεται, καὶ πᾶν ὄρος καὶ βω- νὸς ταπεινωθήσεται καὶ ἔσαι τὰ (κολιὰ εἰς εὐθεῖαν καὶ αἱ τρα- χεῖαι εἰς ὁδὲς λείας) Paulo ulterius quam cæteri verba Esaïæ prosequitur Lucas, quia illis satis fuerat locum indicare, hic omnia quæ ad rem faciebant verba, appo- nere maluit. Sequitur autem Lucas verbotenus LXX. Interpretes, ut sæpe. Nimium est anxia eorum περιερ- γία, qui in dictis ἀλληγορουμένοις singulas partes minuta- tim excutiunt, & quærunt quid cui respondeat, cum sa- tis sit in re tota comparationem intelligi. Ita hic multa Origenes atque alii argutantur, ut explicent qui sint montes, qui valles: cum illud sufficere debeat, quod alibi dixi, munitoris officium describi: ἐν τύπῳ quidem apud Esaiam, ut significetur omnia jam parata esse ad populum è Babylonia in Judæam postliminio reducen- dum: διὰ τύπυ vero, ad annunciandam liberationem à servitute peccati & mortis, quæ reditu illo figura- bantur. Notum autem est, quoties magni Reges, cum exercitu præsertim, iter faciunt, præmitti qui hiantia so- lident, exstantia complanent, per devia compendium faciant, nequid itineri obstet, aut morem faciat. Plenæ sunt historiæ. Josephus cum Titi adventum ad Hiero- solyma describit. Ἀνεπλάσθη, inquit, τὰ κοῖλα καὶ χαρακώ- δη τῶ τόπω· τάς δὲ πετρώδεις ἐξοχὰς σιδήρῳ κατεργαζόμενοι ὁμαλισμὸν ἐποίυν πάντα τὸν χῶρον. Plutarchus Gracchis: πιμπλαμένων δὲ τῶν κοίλων καὶ ζευγνυμένων γεφύραις ὅσα χεί- μαῥῥοι διέκοπτον ἢ φαράγγες, ὕψος δὲ τῆς ἑκατέρωθεν ἴσον καὶ παράλληλον λαμβανόντων ὁμαλὴν καὶ καλὴν ὄψιν εἶχε διὰλε τὸ ἔργον. Xenophon ad hoc ministerium dilectos ὁδοποιὺς vocat. Recte autem arbitror quæ apud Prophetam & Lucam futuro tempore enunciantur, per Imperati- vum exponi: ἀναλογικῶς tamen: ut nempe imperium illud de reditu ex Babylonia acceptum DEI potentiam significet: in Baptistæ autem ministerio simul exigat humanum obsequium. Neque enim novum est habere aliquid dissimile figuram, & id quod per figuram in- nuitur. Sic & conversio hominis modo creationi, mo- do resuscitationi ex morte comparatur: cum in conver- sione suas habeat partes humanæ voluntatis τὸ ἑκούσιον, in illis actionibus nullas.

## 3:6
Verse 6. And all flesh shall see the salvation of God) Luke continues the words of the Prophet with a few words omitted. But in the Prophet it is: And all flesh shall see together that which has been pronounced by the mouth of the Lord. The LXX, however, explain the pronoun by adding the noun quite conveniently: and all flesh shall see the salvation of God, because the Lord has spoken: from where Luke took this. We have said that σωτήριον and σωτηρίαν are used interchangeably among the LXX. The sense is: that this saving benefit would be conspicuous to all men, as had been the liberation from the Babylonian captivity. For the grace of God that brings salvation has appeared to all men, Tit. ch. II. verse 11. Thus Simeon: the salvation which you have prepared before the face of all peoples.

We have defended this whole prophecy against the depravations of Grotius here, and those occurring at Is. XL., in our defenses of Isaiah, so that there is no need to add anything in this place, lest we seem to be doing what has already been done.

Latin:

Vers. 6. καὶ ὄψεται πᾶσα σὰρξ τὸ σωτήριον τῦ Θεῦ) Pau- cis verbis omissis prosequitur Lucas Prophetæ verba. Sed apud Prophetam est: Et videbit caro omnis pariter id quod ore Domini est pronunciatum. LXX. autem prono- men addito nomine explicant satis commode: καὶ ὄψεται πᾶσα σὰρξ τὸ σωτήριον τῦ Θεῦ, ὅτι κύριος ἐλάλησε: unde hoc desumsit Lucas. Diximus σωτήριον & σωτηρίαν pro- miscue poni apud LXX. Sensus est: beneficium hoc sa- lutare omnibus hominibus conspicuum fore, ut fuerat liberatio ex Babylonica captivitate. Ἐπεφάνη γὰρ ἡ χάρις τῦ Θεῦ ἡ σωτήριος πᾶσιν ἀνθρώποις Tit. cap. II. vers. 11. Sic Simeon: σωτήριον ὃ ἡτοίμασας κατὰ πρόσωπον πάντων λαῶν.

Totum hoc vaticinium vindicavimus adver- sus Grotianas depravationes hic, & ad Es. XL. occurrentes, in vindiciis Esaiæ, ut opus non sit hoc loco quicquam addere, ne videamur actum agere.

## 3:8
Verse 8. And do not begin to say within yourselves) That is, do not say. A similar pleonasm is in Matt. XI. 7, 20, ch. XI. 1, ch. XVI. v. 22, ch. XXIV. 29, Mark I. 45, ch. VI. 7, ch. X. 28, ch. XIII. 5, and quite often in this author of ours, as ch. IV. 21, ch. V. v. 21, ch. VII. 24, 38, ch. XII. 45, ch. XIV. 18, 19, 30, ch. XIX. 45, Acts I. 1.

Latin:

Vers. 8. καὶ μὴ ἄρξησθε λέγειν ἐν ἑαυτοῖς) Id est, μὴ λέγε- τε. Similis πλεονασμὸς Matth. XI. 7. 20. c. XI. 1. c. XVI. v. 22. c. XXIV. 29. Marc. I. 45. c. VI. 7. c. X. 28. c. XIII. 5. & apud hunc nostrum sæpiuscule, ut c. IV. 21. c. V. v. 21. cap. VII. 24. 38. c. XII. 45. c. XIV. 18. 19. 30. c. XIX. 45. Act. I. 1.

## 3:10
Verse 10. What then shall we do) The first movement toward repentance reveals itself in seeking counsel for amending one's life. Thus in Acts ch. II. 37, the Jews, after they were pricked in their heart, ask of the Apostles, What shall we do, men and brethren? And the jailer, suddenly struck with fear, addresses Paul and Silas similarly, What must I do to be saved? For men corrupted by a long habit of sinning, it is not enough to be commanded generally to bring forth fruits worthy of repentance: but one must come to certain particular precepts. others live in miserable poverty. John expresses this very thing by the example of both clothing and food, because human usage desires these things most of all, and it is in heaping them up beyond measure and squandering them through luxury that the greatest sin is committed. See what is below in chapter XVI. 1, where a rich man is described in splendid clothing and fare, while meanwhile the poor man of the people was being consumed by extreme hunger. Not far removed from this is that saying of Martial: From such great wealth you give nothing to an old and faithful companion, and you say, Candidus, κοινὰ φίλων.

Wherefore what is said here, δύο χιτῶνας, it clearly appears is not to be taken as if we are forbidden to have more than one garment (for neither Peter nor Paul interpreted these things so superstitiously, as appears from their own example, Acts XII. 8, 2 Timothy IV. v. 13), but that it is meant to signify that an abundance of those things is condemned, by the lack of which we see others heavily oppressed. Thus also βρώματα are to be understood as τὰ περισσεύοντα. Moreover, Luke well uses the word μεταδιδόναι here, which Aristotle also employs in a similar sense. Thus also with Paul, ὁ μεταδιδοὺς is he who exercises beneficence toward others, Rom. XII. 8.

Latin:

Vers. 10. Τί ὖν ποιήσομεν) Primus ad pœnitentiam mo- tus se prodit in petendo emendandæ vitæ consilio. Ita Act. c. II. 37. Judæi postquam κατενύγησαν τῇ καρδίᾳ, quærunt ex Apostolis, Τί ποιήσομεν ἄνδρες ἀδελφοί; Et Commentari- ensis timore subito perculsus Paulum & Silam similiter af- fatur Τί με δεῖ ποιεῖν ἵνα σωθῶ; Hominibus longa peccandi consuetudine corruptis, non satis est generaliter præcipi, ut dignos pœnitentia fructus faciant: sed veniendum est ad præcepta quædam particularia. penuria alii miserabiles vivant. Exprimit autem hoc ipsum Johannes exemplo tum vestium tum ciborum, quia ea maxime usus humanus desiderat, & in iis supra modum congerendis, & per luxum prodigendis maxime peccatur. Vide quod infra est cap. XVI. 1. ubi homo dives describi- tur splendido vestitu victuque, cum pauper interim po- pularis extrema fama consumeretur. Non longe hic abit Martialis illud: Ex opibus tantis veteri fidoque sodali Das nihil & dicis, Candide κοινὰ φίλων.

Quare quod hic dicitur δύο χιτῶνας, satis apparet non ita ac- cipiendum quasi plus una veste habere vetemur (nam neq; Petrus neque Paulus ita superstitiose hæc sunt interpretati, ut ex ipsorum exemplo apparet Actor. XII. 8. 2. Timoth. IV. v. 13.) sed ut significetur damnari earum rerum affluentiam quarum inopia alios graviter premi videamus. Sic & βρώ- ματα intelligenda sunt τὰ περισσεύοντα. Bene autem voce μεταδιδόναι hic utitur Lucas, quam & Aristoteles usurpat simili sensu. Sic & apud Paulum ὁ μεταδιδοὺς est is qui be- neficentiam in alios exercet Rom. XII. 8.

## 3:12
Vers. 12. Τελῶναι) Namely, Jews who were associates or tax-farmers of the Romans.

Latin:

Vers. 12. Τελῶναι) Judæi scilicet Romanorum socii aut redemtores.

## 3:13
Vers. 13. μηδὲν πλέον παρὰ τὸ διατεταγμένον ὑμῖν πράσσετε. Beyond those precepts of living which pertain commonly to all, classes of men and individual men must be diligently taught to recognize those vices with which they struggle more than others. Now, tax collectors were accustomed to demand from merchants or travelers, and from those for whom it was inconvenient to seek judgment against them, much more than had been publicly established. There is a verse of the comic poet Xenon: Πάντες τελῶναι πάντες εἰσιν ἅρπαγες. Concerning the greed of the publicans, see Strabo. Add Philo, On the Special Laws, at the end. In Suidas, the life of publicans is described by an ancient writer thus: πεπαῤῥησιασμένη βία, ἀνεπίτιμητ̃ ἁρπαγὴ, ἀναίσχυντ̃ πλεονεξία, πραγματεία λόγον μὴ ἔχουσα, ἀναιδὴς ἐμπορία. See Tacitus, Annals XIII, and what other names the publicans had invented for illicit exactions. The Scholiast on the Knights of Aristophanes: Διεβέβλητο γὰ τὸ τελώνε ὄνομα, ὡς κᾳὐτ̃ κλέω- ν̃ ὄντ̃ τελώνε κᾳὐπὲρ τὸ τέλ̃ τελωνῦντ̃. What great audacity, what great temerity, says Ulpian, the factions of the Publicans possess, there is no one who does not know. For this reason, the Praetor, to restrain their audacity, proposed this edict. Paulus the Jurisconsult: That which is illicitly exacted publicly and privately is paid back to those who have suffered the injury with an additional equal amount; but that which is extorted by force is restored with a triple penalty; furthermore, they are punished extra ordinem: for the one the utility of private individuals demands, the other the vigor of public discipline. The Publicans were, of course, waiting to see whether John would forbid them from the farming of public revenues: since many of the Jews considered it a sin for tribute to be paid to a foreign people, and for that reason alone detested the publicans as accursed and intestabiles. But the best forerunner of Christ in this respect also distinguished the charges against his way of life from the very manner of his living, demonstrating that his teachings do not stand in the way of public tranquility, which in such great malice of men cannot be defended without tributes and taxes: nor indeed does it pertain to piety under whose rule one lives. But what John said here to the publicans, there is no doubt that he would have said the same to Herod, and would have said it to other kings if there had been an opportunity to address them: for what the civil law also forbids publicans to do, reason and the very law of nature dictate is wicked for kings to do. Just as public power, so also tributes are established not for the use of this person or that, but for the common good. Wherefore it is their duty to balance public burdens with public necessities: in such a way, indeed, that it may be permitted to those who preside over the republic to sustain themselves from public revenues in accordance with the requirements of their dignity, but not likewise to seek the measure of their exactions from the luxury and lust of themselves and their courtly minions, which have no measure. Those who do this truly πράσσουσι παρὰ τὸ διατεταγμένον, exacting, that is to say, more than the law permits of Him whose supreme authority is over all kings.

Latin:

Vers. 13. μηδὲν πλέον παρὰ τὸ διατεταγμένον ὑμῖν πράσ- σετε. Præter illa vivendi præcepta quæ communiter ad omnes pertinent, hominum ordines hominesque singuli diligenter docendi sunt agnoscere ea flagitia quibus præter cæteros laborant. Solebant autem publicani ab homini- bus mercatoribus aut iter facientibus & quibus incommo- dum erat adversus ipsos judicium exposcere, multo plus exigere quam publicitus erat constitutum. Xenonis comici versus est: Πάντες τελῶναι πάντες εἰσιν ἅρπαγες. Διὰ τὴν πλεονεξίαν τ̃ δημοσιωνῶν apud Strabonem. Adde Philonem de specialibus legibus ultimo. Apud Suidam veteri Scriptori publicanorum vita sic describitur: πεπαῤῥη- σιασμένη βία, ἀνεπίτιμητ̃ ἁρπαγὴ, ἀναίσχυντ̃ πλεονε- ξία, πραγματεία λόγον μὴ ἔχουσα, ἀναιδὴς ἐμπορία, Apud Tacitum XIII. Annal. Et quæ alia exactionibus illi- citis nomina Publicani invenerant. Scholiastes ad Equites Aristophanis: Διεβέβλητο γὰ τὸ τελώνε ὄνομα, ὡς κᾳὐτ̃ κλέω- ν̃ ὄντ̃ τελώνε κᾳὐπὲρ τὸ τέλ̃ τελωνῦντ̃. Quantæ audaciæ, quantæ temeritatis, inquit Ulpianus, sint Publi- canorum factiones nemo est qui nesciat. Iccirco Prætor ad com- pescendam eorum audaciam hoc edictum proposuit. Paulus Ju- risconsultus: Quod illicite publice privatimque exactum est cum altero tanto passis injuriam exfolvitur: per vim vero ex- tortum pœna triplici restituitur: amplius extra ordinem ple- ctuntur: alterum enim utilitas privatorum, alterum vigor publicæ disciplinæ postulat. Exspectabant nimirum Publi- cani an Johannes ipsis interdicturus esset, publicorum re- demtione:quippe cum multi Judæorum nefas ducerent ve- ctigal pendi populo extraneo, & vel ob id solum publi- canos ut sacros atq; intestabiles, abominarentur. Sed opti- mus hac quoque in parte Christi anteambulo vitæ cri- mina ab ipso vivendi genere discrevit, demonstrans sua mo- nita non obstare tranquillitati publicæ, quæ in tanta ho- minum malitia sine tributis & vectigalibus defendi non potest: neque vero ad pietatem referre quorum sub im- perio vivatur. Quod vero hic Johannis publicanis dixit, dubium non est quin idem Herodi dixerit, dicturus & aliis regibus si eos compellandi fuisset occasio: nam quod pu- blicanos facere vetat lex etiam civilis,idem regibus esse ne- fas dictat, ratio & lex ipsa naturæ. Ut publica potestas, ita & tributa,non in usum hujus aut illius,sed ad bonum com- mune sunt constituta. Quare illorum est muneris publica onera cum publicis necessitatibus æquare: ita quidem ut liceat his qui reipublicæ præsident ex publicis obventionibq semet pro dignitatis ratione sustentaret, non item modum exigendi petere à suo & aulicorum mancipiorum luxu,ac libidine quæ modum non habent. Hoc qui faciunt vere πράσσουσι παρὰ τὸ διατεταγμένον, plus scilicet exigentes quam lex ejus permittit cujus in reges omnes summum est imperium.

## 3:14
Vers. 14. στρατευόμενοι) The Jews serving as soldiers either for Herod or Philip, or even for the Romans. For the Romans guarded Judea partly with their own soldiers, partly with those of Sebaste, and partly with those of Caesarea, as Josephus teaches us at the end of the 19th book of the Antiquities. Now the Caesareans were Jews. But just as the Jews did not avoid military service in garrisons, so they could hardly follow expeditions without prejudice to their religion: because by the law they were forbidden to carry arms and make long journeys on the Sabbath; add to this that, being mixed with foreigners, they could hardly observe the prescribed manner of diet, which two causes were accustomed to be pleaded by the Jews to obtain exemption from military service (ἀστρατίαν), as is clear from the letters of Dolabella to the Ephesians, which exist in Josephus: who also relates that the Jews obtained a discharge from L. Lentulus for the sake of religion. Another cause which sometimes kept the Jews from military service was this, if they were to fight against their own countrymen. For to take up arms against those of the same race is unlawful, says the same Josephus. When the Jews had been ordered to depart from the city of Rome at this very time, Josephus relates that four thousand of them were enrolled in the military and sent to Sardinia: others were punished for being μὴ θέλοντας στρατεύεσθαι διὰ φυλακὴν τῶν πατρίων νόμων. But the same Josephus relates that many Jews served in the army under Alexander the Macedonian, but only after having first stipulated that they should not be compelled to do anything contrary to their religion. For this is what he says, ἐμμένοντας τοῖς πατρίοις ἔθεσι καὶ κατὰ ταῦτα ζῶντας. And in his discourse against Apion, he cites Hecataeus as a witness to this fact, whose words are these: συνηκολούθησέ τις μετὰ τῶν ἄλλων τῶν παραπεμπόντων ἡμῖν ἱππέων Ἰυδαίων ὄνομα Μοσόλλαμος: That is, משלם, which name appears in I Chronicles III, v. 19. But also, in order to prove that the Jews served in the army of Xerxes, Josephus brings forward these verses of Choerilus concerning the expedition of Xerxes: [Greek text]. By which words Josephus proves that the Jews are described as horsemen under the name of the Solymi, and by the mention of the lake which he says is the Asphaltite. But against this interpretation of Josephus, a man of great judgment objects two things. The first is that by the Solymi mountains the ancient Lycians are understood. But that does not move me: since the Romans undoubtedly received it from the Greeks, that they should call the Jews, whose capital is Jerusalem, by the truncated name of Solymi: from which manner of speaking the opinion mentioned by Tacitus of those who thought the Jews originated from the Lycians is known. And indeed, who would believe that the Lycians used the Phoenician language, that is, the Syrian or one approaching it? The other point is valid, that those horsemen are called [Greek text], whereas the law of Moses, Leviticus XIX. 27, forbids the Jews to be shorn in a circle. Since this cannot be denied, nor is it credible that the Jews had so commonly departed from the precept of the law, it is probable that by Choerilus certain Arabs, neighbors of the Jews, are described, but with the boundaries of the peoples confused, just as the poets also use Idumea for Judea: for the ancient scholia on the said passage of Leviticus relate that the Saracens were accustomed to be shorn in a circle. But concerning the Jews who served in the army of Alexander, the other passage of Hecataeus which I mentioned is illustrious, in which he narrates [Greek text]. For those words entirely: [Greek text] seem to demand that these things be understood concerning the Jews serving under Alexander, not concerning those who lived in Babylon from the time of Nebuchadnezzar. Appian in the second book of the Civil Wars is a witness that there were Jews even in the camp of Pompey. Strabo relates that there were five hundred Jews in the army of Aelius Gallus in book XVI. Josephus, the writers of the Maccabees, and Eusebius teach that they served both Antiochus and Demetrius and the Ptolemies: Appian that there were Hebrews in the army of Pompey: Plutarch that they were sent by Herod to serve Antony against Caesar. As to why the fact that a learned man thinks that the cohort which was accustomed to be granted to the high priests by Pontius Pilate was from the Jews cannot be proven to us, the reader will find in the history of the Lord's passion in Matthew. We have shown elsewhere that Christians abstained from military service partly by counsel rather than by precept: unless at some time military service was joined with the necessity of impious worship, or with the vexation of the pious, at which times they deemed it entirely wicked to serve. Certainly, not all Christians in those first times abstained from military service, besides that which is narrated concerning the Emperor Marcus and the Theban legion, the testimonies of the ancients exist. Clement of Alexandria, where he prescribes the habit suitable for a Christian, wishes women indeed to be shod, but men not so, unless in military service: [Greek text], he says, [Greek text]. Tertullian in the Apology: We sail with you, we serve in the army, and we farm, and we trade: soon in the same book he says the camps were filled by Christians: and in the book on the Crown he narrates that by one of many Christian soldiers a crown was not placed upon his head, whom praising he says, O soldier glorious in God! Likewise: He alone, forsooth, is brave among so many brother-soldiers, he alone is a Christian. But in the book on Idolatry he debates whether a believer can be converted to military service, and whether military service can be admitted to the faith, even the booted or any inferior kind, for which there is no necessity of sacrifices or capital judgments: and to these words of John and the praised faith of the centurion, he responds that every soldier afterwards was disarmed in Peter. You treat the same question somewhat more hesitantly in the said book on the Crown, thinking it must be asked whether it is entirely for Christians military service is appropriate. But those things which he brings forward so that it might not seem permitted, as also those things which we were bringing forward above concerning the Jews, were proper to those times, such as that they were often compelled to stand guard for temples and to dine in the temple, and that the bodies of the dead were cremated, not buried. And finally he distinguishes, so that the condition of those whom the later faith finds already caught up in military service is different, such as those whom John was admitting to the washing, provided that once the faith was accepted, either military service was to be resigned, or in every way it must be guarded against that nothing be committed against God: where he also adds this: In this one, Christ, a faithful soldier is just as much a soldier as an unfaithful pagan is a soldier; the state of faith does not admit the plea of necessity. Eusebius relates that in the times of Diocletian, Christian soldiers ceased to serve ἵνα μὴ ἐξερσι γένωνται. But Lactantius, who lived already under a Christian Emperor, at which time the dangers of military service, if not all, yet most, were ceasing, when he denies that it is possible for one who is truly just to wage war, seems to understand by 'truly just' not just anyone, but a Christian of great progress. For he also denies that he should go on a voyage. Origen has the same sense in that statement: ὐκ ἔτι γὰρ λαμβάνομεν ἐπ’ ἔθνος μάχαι- ραν, ὐδὲ μανθάνομεν ἔτι πολεμεῖν γενόμενοι διὰ τὸν Ἰησῦν υἱοὶ τῆς εἰρήνης ὅς ἐσιν ἡμῶν ἀρχηγός. Likewise Origen, to Celsus who was objecting to the refusal of military service by Christians, responds in this manner: εἶτα δὲ κὰι ταῦτ’ εἴποιμεν ἂν πρὸς τὸς ἀλλοτρίυς τῆς πί- σεως κὰι ἀξιῦντας ἡμᾶς σρατεύεσθαι ὑπὲρ τῶ κοινῶ κὰι ἀνθρώπως ἀναι- ρεῖν, ὅτι κὰι οἱ καθ’ ὑμᾶς ἱερεῖς ἀγαλμάτων Ἰνιῶν κὰι νεωκόροι ὧν νο- μίζετε Θεῶν, τηρῦσιν ἑαυτῶν ἀμίαντων τὴν δεξίαν διὰ τὰς θυ- σίας, ἵν’ ἀναιμάκτοις χερσὶ κὰι καθαραῖς ἀπὸ φόνων προσάγωσι τὰς νενομισμένας θυσίας οἷς φατὲ Θεοῖς. κὰι ὀ δήπε πολέμυ καταλα- βόντος κἃκῖνυς ἱερεῖς σρατεύετε. Εἰ ἐν’ ἐκ἖ν’ εὐλόγως γίνεται, πόσῳ μᾶλλον ἄλλων σρατευομένων κὰι ὗτοι σρατευονται, ὡς ἱερεῖς τῦ Θεῦ κὰι θεραπευταὶ, καθαρὰς τηρῦντες τὰς δεξιὰς, αγωνιζόμενοι δὲ διὰ ᾿τ πρὸς Θεὸν εὐχῶν ὑπὲρ τῦ δικαίως σρατευομένων κὰι ὑπὲρ τῦ δικαίως βασιλεύοντος. Concerning the Nicene Canon, and other things pertaining to this matter, we have treated them at the head of Matthew V.

Μηδένα διασείσητε) The Greek scholiasts indeed use this word, but after Greece had been made subject to Roman law. I entirely believe it is expressed from the Latin word 'concutere', whence in the Pandects there is the title 'de Concussione', in the Basilics περὶ διασεισμῶν. Now 'concutere' is to extort money or something similar from someone by injecting terror: which is all too familiar to soldiers. Everything, says Tacitus, they burn, devastate, and plunder as if they were cities of enemies: whom Curtius well calls the ravagers of the land which they ought to have protected from ravages. Juvenal, or whoever is the writer of the Satire on the advantages of military service:
