Let us treat of the advantages, first the common ones, of which not the least will be this, that a civilian may not dare to strike you: nay, even if he is struck, he should dissemble, nor dare to show his knocked-out teeth to the Praetor, and the black lump on his face with swollen bruises, and an eye left with the doctor promising nothing.

And soon after: It will be worthy, therefore, of the mule-like heart of the declaimer Vagellius, when you have two legs, to offend so many soldiers' boots.

Against this insolence of soldiers, there exists that edict in Cassiodorus: Let them live with the provincials by civil law, nor let the spirit grow insolent which feels itself armed, because that shield of yours ought to provide quiet for the civilians. The Hellenists, for what Luke said here διασείειν, are accustomed to express it with the verb ἀπο- βιάζειν, as the LXX in Prov. XXII. 22. Aquila and Theodotion in Prov. XXIIX. 24. It is the same as ἐκπιέζειν in I Sam. XII. 3 & 4.

μηδὲ συκοφαντήσητε) The Hebrew word עשׁק, which the LXX often express by συκοφαντεῖν, is sometimes general, and extends as widely as ἀδικεῖν, as in Jer. ch. XXII. v. 3, where the LXX translate it as διαρπάζειν, and in this writer below ch. XIX. v. 8; sometimes it is special, or signifies more closely to the usage of Greece, to steal something by deceit or at least secretly, not openly by force, which Rabbi Solomon judges to be the proper meaning of the word עשׁק. Now soldiers are accustomed sometimes (for it is not always desired) to use as a pretext for injuries some causes, however false and absurd. Which custom Aesop described not unaptly under the fable of the wolf, whose sentiment Phaedrus expresses thus in Latin verses:

To the same stream a wolf and a lamb had come, driven by thirst: the wolf stood higher up, and the lamb far below: then the robber, incited by his wicked nature, brought up a cause for a quarrel: Why, he said, have you made the water muddy for me drinking? The wool-bearer, fearing, replied: How, I pray, can I do what you complain of, wolf? The liquid flows down from you to my draughts. He, repulsed by the forces of truth;

Six months ago, he says, you spoke ill of me. The lamb replied: I was not even born. But by Hercules, your father, he said, spoke ill of me. And thus, having seized him, he tears him apart with an unjust death. This fable is written for those men who oppress the innocent with feigned causes. The writer of the Satire I mentioned: you could sooner produce a false witness against a civilian than one speaking the truth against the fortune of an armed man, and against his sense of shame. But what is said here διασείειν and συκοφαντεῖν refers to the passage in I Samuel ch. XII. verse 3. לא עש קתנו ולא רצוחנו.

καὶ ἀρκεῖσθε τοῖς ὀψωνίοις ὑμῶν) The Greeks call ὀψώνια not only stipends, but all the earnings of military service, as Marcianus speaks, among which is also the provision of rations and other advantages which, under the Roman empire, were not to be envied, if a just account of military labors is taken: just as the Jews use the word אספניא derived from that Greek word. Therefore, just as John had prescribed to the tax collectors that they should not exact more than the law of the public revenue allowed, so here he commands the soldiers to be content with the rewards established by the public. For they are accustomed to find a thousand words for plundering: and indeed it is a trite proverb in the mouths of many, that it is better to live off another's than to have nothing from which to live. But to live for them is not to satisfy the desires of nature, but to indulge in taverns and brothels. Josephus seems to have had this precept of the Baptist in mind when he instructed the soldiers entrusted to his care: μὴ ἁρπαγῇ λαμβάνειν τὰς χώρας, ἀλλὰ σκηνοῦν κατὰ τὸ πεδίον, ἀρκουμένους τοῖς ἑαυτῶν ἐφοδίοις. For we have noted elsewhere that Josephus followed the tenets of John to some extent. Similar is that statement of Aurelian in Vopiscus concerning the soldier: Let him be content with his own ration: let him live off the spoils of the enemy, not the tears of the provincials. And that of Valentinian and Valens: In the name of the Cænatici, let the soldiers and those stationed above them dare to accept nothing at all from the provincials. For let the soldiers know that it is fitting that they, receiving their own benefits which they obtain in the receipt of rations, should not inflict losses upon the provincials from outside. I am wonderfully pleased by what a man most learned in Greek, and of rare piety, noted on this passage, saying that the Baptist said these things to legitimate soldiers, who spent the greatest part of their life in garrisons, and were not led against the enemy except for great causes (such was the gravity of the Romans). But if such men had come to him as most soldiers are now, not addicted to one empire, but hunting for wars throughout the whole world, and 'venal hands, where there is the most pay, there is right,' who for greater pay from the other side strip away justice and right, and do not see why, but for how much, they either slaughter others or are slaughtered themselves, truly the Baptist would have said nothing else to them than that if they wished to be saved, they must abandon a way of life that is, I will not now say abhorrent to all piety, but abhorrent to all humanity and truly beastly.

PART II. The prophecy and prediction of John the Baptist concerning Christ.

Latin:

Vers. 14. στρατευόμενοι) Aut Herodi aut Philippo,aut etiam Romanis militantes Judæi. Nam Romani Ju- dæam partim suo, partim Sebasteno, partim Cæsarensi milite custodiebant, ut nos docet Josephus fine XIX. Ori- ginum. Cæsarienses autem Judæi erant. Sicut autem militiam in præsidiis non defugiebant Judæi, ita expedi- tiones sequi salva religione vix poterant: quia sabbato ferre arma & magna itinera facere per legem vetabantur: adde quod permixti externis vix poterant observare tradi- tam victus rationem, quas duas causas à judæis obtendi so- litas ad impetrandum ἀστρατίαν liquet ex Dolabellæ literis ad Ephesios, quæ apud Josephum exstant: qui & à L. Len- tulo Iudæos religionis causa missionem impetrasse nar- rat. Alia causa quæ interdum Judæos à militia arcebat hæc erat, si adversus populares essent pugnaturi. Nam κατὰ δὲ ὁμοφύλων ὅπλα λαβεῖν ἀθεμιτὸν, inquit idem Jose- phus. Cum Judæi urbe Roma sub hæc ipsa tempora jussi essent excedere, narrat Josephus quatuor millia eo- rum militiæ ascripta & missa in Sardiniam: punitos alios μὴ θέλοντας στρατεύεσθαι διὰ φυλακὴν τῶν πατρίων νόμων. At Alexandro Macedoni multos Judæorum militasse narrat idem Josephus, sed prius pactos nequid adversum religioni suæ facere cogerentur. Hoc enim est quod ait ἐμμένοντας τοῖς πατρίοις ἔθεσι καὶ κατὰ ταῦτα ζῶντας. Et in disputatione adversus Appionem testem ejus rei laudat Hecatæum cujus hæc sunt verba: συνηκολούθησέ τις μετὰ τῶν ἄλ- λων τῶν παραπεμπόντων ἡμῖν ἱππέων Ἰυδαίων ὄνομα Μοσόλ- λαμος: Id est, משלם, quod nomen exstat I. Paral. III. v. 19. Sed & ut Xerxi militasse Judæos probet, adfert Jo- sephus hos Chœrili versus de expeditione Xerxis: Τῷ δ᾽ ὄπιθεν διέβαινε γένος θαυμαστὸν ἰδέσθαι Γλῶσσαν μὲν φοίνισσαν ἀπὸ στομάτων ἀφιέντες, Ὠικεῦν δ᾽ ἐν Σολύμοις ὄρεσι πλατέῃ ἐνὶ λίμνῃ Αὐχμαλέοι κορυφὰς, τροχοκέφαδες, αὐτὰρ ὕπερθεν Ἵππων δαρτὰ πρόσωπ᾽ ἐφόρουν ἐσκληκότα καπνῷ. Quibus verbis Judæos equites describi Josephus probat nomine Solymorum, & mentione lacus quem ait esse Asphaltiten. At contra hanc Josephi interpretationem duo objicit magni judicii vir. Prius est Solymos mon- tes antiquis Lycios intelligi. Sed id me non movet: cum haud dubie Romani à Græcis acceperint, ut Judæos, quorum caput est Hierosolyma, truncato nomine So- lymos appellarent: ex quo loquendi more nota est opi- nio Tacito memorata eorum qui Judæos ex Lyciis ortos putarent. Et sane Lycios lingua usos Phœnissa, id est Syriaca aut ad eam accedente quis credat? Alterum validiq est, quod equites isti vocantur τροχοκέφαδες cum Judæis in orbem tonderi interdicat lex Mosis Levit. XIX. 27. Hoc cum negari non possit, neque vero credibile sit Judæos ita comuniter à legis præcepto recessisse, probabile est à Chœrilo Arabas quosdam Judæorum vicinos describi, sed confusis populorum finibus, quemadmodum & Idu- men pro Judæa ponunt Poëtæ: Nam Saracenos in orbem tonderi solitos narrant vetera scholia ad dictum Levitici locum. Sed de Judæi qui Alexandro militaverunt illu- stris est ejus quem dixi Hecatæi locus alter, quo narrat ᾿Αλεξάνδρου ποτὲ ἐν Βαβυλῶνι γενομένου καὶ προελομένου τὸ τοῦ Βήλου πεπτωκὸς ἱερὸν ἀνακαθᾶραι καὶ πᾶσιν αὐτοῖς τοῖς στρατιώ- ταις ὁμοίως φέρειν τὸν χοῦν προστάξαντος, μόνους τοὺς ἰυδαίους ἐ προσεῖν, ἀλλὰ καὶ πολλὰς ὑπομεῖναι πληγὰς καὶ ζημίας ἀποτί- ζειν μεγάλας, ἕως αὐτοῖς ξυγγνόντα τὸν βασιλέα δῦναι τὴν ἄ- δειαν. Omnino enim verba illa: τοῖς στρατιώταις exigere videntur, ut hæc de Judæis Alexandro militantibus, non de his qui à Nabuchodonosori tempore Babylone habi- tabant, intelligantur. Etiam in Pompeji castris fuisse Judæos testis est Appianus Civilium bellorum libro se- cundo. Lib. XVI. in Ælii Galli exercitu quingentos fuisse Judæos Strabo narrat. Militasse eos & Antiocho & Demetrio & Ptolemæis docens Josephus, Maccabæi- corum Scriptores & Eusebius: In Pompeji exercitu He- bræos fuisse Appianus: missos ab Herode qui Antonio contra Cæsarem militarent, Plutarchus. Quod vir eru- ditus putat eam cohortem, quæ à Pontio Pilato pontifici- bus concedi solebat, è Judæis ftisse, cur probari nobis non possit, ad historiam Dominicæ passionis in Matthæo lector inveniet. Christianos partim consilio magis quam præce- pto abstinuisse à militia alibi ostendimus: nisi siquando mi- litia conjuncta erat cum necessitate impii cultus, aut cum piorum vexatione, quibus temporibus omnino militare ne- fas ducebant. Non omnes sane Christianos primis illis temporibus abstinuisse à militia, præter id, quod de Marco Imperatore & de Thebæa legione narratur, exstant veterum testimonia. Clemens Alexandrinus, ubi convenientem Christiano habitum præscribit, feminas quidem vult esse calceatas, at viros non item, nisi in militia: εἰ δὲ μὴ μάλων ἁρμόδιον, inquit, ἀνυποδησία, πλὴν εἰ μὴ στρατεύοιτο. Ter- tullianus Apologetico: Navigamus & nos vobiscum, mili- tamus & rusticamur & mercamur: mox eodem libro castra dicit impleta à Christianis: & libro de Corona narrat ab uno multorum Christianorum militum coronam capiti non im- positam, quem laudans ait, O militem in Deo gloriosum! Item: Solus scilicet fortis tot fratres commilitones, solus Christianus. At libro de Idololatria disputant an fidelis ad militiam converti possit, & an militia ad fidem admitti, etiam caligata vel inferior quæque, cui non sit necessitas immolationum, vel capitalium Judiciorum: & ad hæc Jo- hannis verba & centurionis laudatam fidem, respondet, omnem postea militem in Petro exarmando discinctum. Paulo suspensius tractas quæstionem eandem dicto de Corona libro, quærendum putans, an in totum Christianis militia conveniat. Sed quae adfert ne licere videatur pleraque, ut & illa quae de Judaeis supra afferebamus, il- lorum temporum erant propria, ut quod pro templis ex- cubare saepe, & coenare in templo cogerentur, quod cor- pora mortuorum cremarentur, non sepelirentur. Ac tan- dem distinguit, ut alia sit eorum conditio quos militia prae- ventos fides posterior invenit, quales erant quos Johannes ad lavacrum admittebat, suscepta certe fide aut deferen- dam militiam, aut omni modo cavendum nequid adversus Deum committatur: ubi & hoc adjicit: Apud hunc, Chri- stium, tam miles est paganus fidelis, quam paganus est miles in- fidelis, non admittit status fidei allegationem necessitatis. Narrat Eusebius Diocletiani temporibus Christianos milites mili- tasse desiisse ἵνα μὴ ἐξερσι γένωνται. At Lactantius, qui jam sub Christiano vixit Imperatore, quo tempore militiae peri- cula, si non omnia, pleraque tamen cessabant, cum negat fieri posse, ut qui vere justus sit belligeret, vere justum non quemvis sed magni profectus Christianum videtur intelli- gere. Nam & navigaturum eum negat. Eundem sensum ha- bet Origenis illud: ὐκ ἔτι γὰρ λαμβάνομεν ἐπ’ ἔθνος μάχαι- ραν, ὐδὲ μανθάνομεν ἔτι πολεμεῖν γενόμενοι διὰ τὸν Ἰησῦν υἱοὶ τῆς εἰρήνης ὅς ἐσιν ἡμῶν ἀρχηγός. Item Origenes Celso detrecta- tionem militiae Christianis objicienti, hunc in modum re- spondet: εἶτα δὲ κὰι ταῦτ’ εἴποιμεν ἂν πρὸς τὸς ἀλλοτρίυς τῆς πί- σεως κὰι ἀξιῦντας ἡμᾶς σρατεύεσθαι ὑπὲρ τῶ κοινῶ κὰι ἀνθρώπως ἀναι- ρεῖν, ὅτι κὰι οἱ καθ’ ὑμᾶς ἱερεῖς ἀγαλμάτων Ἰνιῶν κὰι νεωκόροι ὧν νο- μίζετε Θεῶν, τηρῦσιν ἑαυτῶν ἀμίαντων τὴν δεξίαν διὰ τὰς θυ- σίας, ἵν’ ἀναιμάκτοις χερσὶ κὰι καθαραῖς ἀπὸ φόνων προσάγωσι τὰς νενομισμένας θυσίας οἷς φατὲ Θεοῖς. κὰι ὀ δήπε πολέμυ καταλα- βόντος κἃκῖνυς ἱερεῖς σρατεύετε. Εἰ ἐν’ ἐκ἖ν’ εὐλόγως γίνεται, πόσῳ μᾶλλον ἄλλων σρατευομένων κὰι ὗτοι σρατεύονται, ὡς ἱερεῖς τῦ Θεῦ κὰι θεραπευταὶ, καθαρὰς τηρῦντες τὰς δεξιὰς, αγωνιζόμενοι δὲ διὰ ᾿τ πρὸς Θεὸν εὐχῶν ὑπὲρ τῦ δικαίως σρατευομένων κὰι ὑπὲρ τῦ δικαίως βασιλεύοντος. De Canone Niceno, aliaque ad hanc rem pertinentia ad caput Matthaei V. tractavimus.

Μηδένα διασείσητε) Usurpant quidem hanc vocem Grae- corum Scholiastae, sed postquam Graecia facta erat Romani juris. Omnino arbitror expressam ex Latina voce concu- tere, unde in Pandectis titulus de Concussione, in Basilicis περὶ διασεισμῶν. Est autem concutere terrore injecto pe- cuniam aut simile quid alicui exprimere:quod militibus ni- mium quam familiare. Omnia, inquit Tacitus, tanquam urbes hostium urere, vastare,rapere: quos bene Curtius vocat populatores terrae quam à populationibus vindicare debebant. Juvenalis aut quisquis est Scriptor Satyrae de commodis militiae:

Commoda tractemus, primum communia,quorum Non minimum illud erit, ne te pulsare togatus Audeat: imo & si pulsetur dissimulet, nec Audeat excussos Praetori ostendere dentes, Et nigram in facie tumidis livoribus offam, Atque oculum medico nil promittente relictum.

Et Mox: Dignum erit ergo Declamatoris mulino corde Vagelli Cum duo crura habeas offendere tot caligatos.

Adversus hanc militum insolentiam extat edictum illud apud Cassiodorum: Vivant cum provincialibus jure civili, nec insolescat animus, qui se sentit armatum, quia clypeus ille exercitus tui quietem debet praestare paganis. Hellenistae, quod hic Lucas dixit διασείειν, solent exprimere verbo ἀπο- βιάζειν, ut LXX. Prov.XXII.22. Aquila & Theodotio Prov. XXIIX. 24. Idem est ἐκπιέζειν I. Sam. XII. 3. & 4.

μηδὲ συκοφαντήσητε) Vox Hebraea עשׁק quam per συκοφαντεῖν saepe exprimunt LXX. modo generalis est, & tam late patet quam ἀδικεῖν, ut Jer. cap. XXII. v. 3. ubi LXX. vertunt διαρπάζειν, & apud hunc Scriptorem infra c. XIX. v. 8. modo specialis, aut significet propius ad usum Graeciae, dolo aut certe occulte,non vi aperte aliquid sur- ripere, quam propriam vocis עשׁק esse significationem judicat Rabbinus Salomo. Solent autem milites inter- dum (neque enim semper id lubet) injuriis causas aliquas, quantumvis falsas atque absurdas, praetexere. Quem morem sub lupi fabula Aesopus non illepide descripsit, cujus sententiam Latinis versibus ita exprimit Phae- drus :

Ad rivum eundem lupus & agnus venerant Siti compulsi: superior stabat lupus, Longeǫ, inferior agnus: tunc facie improba Latro incitatus jurgii causam intulit: Cur, inquit, turbulentam mihi fecisti aquam Istam bibenti? laniger contra timens: Qui possum, quaeso, facere, quod quereris lupe? A te decurrit ad meos haustus liquor. Repulsus ille veritatis viribus;

Ante hos sex menses male, ait, dixisti mihi. Respondit agnus: equidem natus non eram. At pater hercle tuus, inquit, maledixit mihi. Atque ita correptum lacerat injusta nece. Hæc propter illos scripta est homines fabula, Qui fictis causis innocentes opprimunt. Scriptor ejus quam dixi Satyræ: citius falsum producere testem Contra paganum possis quam vera loquentem Contra fortunam armati, contraq; pudorem. Quod autem hic dicitur διασείειν & συκοφαντεῖν respicit lo- cum I. Samuel. cap. XII. verf. 3. לא עש קתנו ולא רצוחנו.

καὶ ἀρκεῖσθε τοῖς ὀψωνίοις ὑμῶν) ὀψώνια Græci vocant non sola stipendia, sed omnia, ut Marcianus loquitur, militiæ merita, in quibus est & annonæ præbitio & alia commoda quæ sub imperio Romano erant non invidenda, si laborum militarium justa habeatur ratio: ut sic Judæi usurpant vocem אספניא ex Græca illa deductam. Sicut ergo publicanis præscripserat Johannes ne plus exigerent quam ferret lex publici, ita hic jubet milites publicitus constitutis præmiis contentos esse. Solent enim invenire mille prædandi vocabula: atque adeo tritum est in mul- torum ore proverbium, satius esse de alieno vivere, quam unde vivas non habere. Vivere autem est illis non na- turæ desideriis satisfacere, sed popinis & lupanaribus in- dulgere. Videtur hoc Baptistæ præceptum in animo ha- buisse Josephus cum militibus suæ curæ traditis præcepit, μὴ ἁρπαγῇ λαμβάνειν τὰς χώρας, ἀλλὰ σκηνοῦν κατὰ τὸ πεδίον, ἀρκουμένους τοῖς ἑαυτῶν ἐφοδίοις. Nam Josephum Johannis placita sectatum aliquatenus fuisse alibi monuimus. Si- mile illud Aureliani apud Vopiscum de milite: Annona sua contentus sit: de præda hostis, non de lacrymis provin- cialium vivat. Et Valentiniani ac Valentis: Cænatico- rum nomine milites & super his stantes nihil penitus à pro- vincialibus accipere audeant. Sciant enim milites quod oportet eos commoda sua, quæ in annonarum perceptione adi- piscuntur, accipientes extrinsecus detrimentis provinciales non afficere. Mirum in modum mihi placet quod hunc in lo- cum annotat vir Græce doctissimus, & raræ pietatis, dixisse, hæc Baptistam legitimis militibus, qui in præsidiis agebant maximam vitæ partem, nec nisi magnis de causis (quæ erat Romanorum gravitas) in hostem ducebantur. Quod si ad eum venissent quales nunc plerique sunt militum, non uni imperio addicti, sed per omnem orbem terrarum bella aucupantes, Venalesq; manus, ibi fas, ubi plurima merces, qui majore ex diverso mercede jus fasque exuunt, neq; vi- dent cur, sed quanti aut alios jugulent, aut ipsi jugulen- tur, profecto non aliud illis dixisset Baptista, quam si salvi esse vellent, relinquendum vitæ genus, non jam dicam ab omni pietate, sed ab omni humanitate abhorrens & vere belluinum.

PARS II. Iohannis Baptistæ de Christo vaticinium, & prædictio.

## 3:15
Verse 15. προσδοκῶντος δὲ τοῦ λαοῦ) An ἐκπεπτική (expectant) discourse. The meaning is, while the people were waiting to see how John would turn out, what God was going to determine concerning him.

Latin:

Vers. 15. προσδοκῶντος δὲ τοῦ λαοῦ) Oratio ἐκπεπτική. Sen- sus est, exspectante populo quo evasurus esset Johannes, quid de illo constituturus esset Deus.

## 3:16
Verse 16. ἀπεκρίνατο Ἰωάννης ἅπασι λέγων) Namely, after the Senators of the Jews, moved by the various reports of the people, had sent envoys to him, as the Apostle John narrates. This indeed happened after Christ was baptized: but it is opportunely connected by Luke to the narration of the rumors that were being spread about John: so that it might be known no less whom he professed himself to be than who he was considered to be by others. Certainly Luke also disregarded the order of time below, when he mentions John being thrown into chains before Christ being baptized. But he wished to run through the history of John first, so that he might then weave together the affairs of Christ in a continuous series: which even the best compilers of Annals are accustomed to do, as we have said elsewhere. It does not stand against this interpretation that John says, μέσος δὲ ὑμῶν ἕστηκεν, while the other three say, ἔρχεται, or ἐρχόμενος. For the sense is that he, who was about to drench his disciples with a most abundant spirit, was even then living among the Jews, but that the time was approaching when he would become more and more known to all.

Latin:

Vers. 16. ἀπεκρίνατο Ἰωάννης ἅπασι λέγων) Postquam scilicet diversis populi sermonibus permoti Senatores Ju- dæorum legatos ad ipsum miserant, ut Apostolus Johannes narrat. Contigit quidem hoc post Christum baptizatum:sed opportune à Luca connectitur narrationi rumorum qui de Johanne spargebantur: ut non minus sciretur quem ipse se professus esset quam quis esset ab aliis habitus. Certe & in- fra Lucas temporum ordinem posthabuit, cum de Johanne in vincula conjecto quam de Christo baptizato prius me- minit. Sed voluit primum Johannis historiam percurre- re, ut deinde res Christi continua serie pertexeret: quod fa- cere solent etiam optimi Annalium conditores, ut alibi di- ximus. Non obstat huic interpretationi, quod Johannes di- cit, μέσος δὲ ὑμῶν ἕστηκεν, tres autem alii, ἔρχεται, aut ἐρχόμενος. Sensus enim est eum, qui spiritu copiosissimo discipulos su- os esset perfusurus, jam tum quidem vivere inter Judæos, sed tempus instare quo magis magisque omnibus innote- sceret.

## 3:17
Verse 17. εἰς τὴν ἀποθήκην ἀυτοῦ) This ἀυτοῦ ought to be referred to Christ no less than the preceding ἅλωνα ἀυτοῦ. Nor did the ancient Interpreters take it otherwise.

Latin:

Vers. 17. εἰς τὴν ἀποθήκην ἀυτοῦ) Non minus hoc ἀυτοῦ ad Christum referri debet quam quod præcessit ἅλωνα ἀυτοῦ. Neque aliter acceperunt veteres Interpretes.

## 3:18
Verse 18. ἐυηγγελίζετο τὸν λαὸν) That is, he was imbuing the people with good doctrine. A Hellenistic construction: such as that in Acts 8:25, πολλάς τε κώμας τῶν Σαμαρειτῶν ἐυηγγελίσαντο. And ch. 8:40, ἐυηγγελίζετο τὰς πόλεις πάσας. Etc. 14:21.

and preaching the gospel to that city.

PART III. The imprisonment of John.

Latin:

Vers. 18. ἐυηγγελίζετο τὸν λαὸν) Id est, bono dogmate po- pulum imbuebat. Constructio Hellenistica: qualis & illa in Actis IIX. 25. πολλάς τε κώμας τῶν Σαμαρειτῶν ἐυηγγελίσαντο. Et. c.IIX. 40. ἐυηγγελίζετο τὰς πόλεις πάσας. Etc. XIV.21.

εὐαγγελίζομενοί τε τὴν πόλιν ἐκείνην. Hinc & passive dicitur πτωχοὶ εὐαγγελίζονται.

PARS III. Iohannis captivatio.

## 3:19
Ver. 19. of the evil things which Herod did] The noun is repeated in place of a pronoun, in the Hebrew manner: Thus 1 Cor. I. 8. 1 Thess. c. III. 12. 2 Thess. III. 7. 8. Add if you please Gen. XIX. 24. Num. X. 29. Ps. LXXXII. 1.

Latin:

Vers. 19. ὧν ἐποίησε πονηρῶν ὁ Ἡρώδης] Repetitum no- men vice pronominis, more Hebræo: Sic. 1. Cor. I. 8. 1. Thess. c. III. 12. 2. Thess. III. 7. 8. Adde si placet Genes. XIX. 24. Num. X. 29. Ps. LXXXII. 1.

## 3:20
Ver. 20. he added this also above all] As crimes are wont to lead to crimes: see what we have said regarding Matthew.

PART IV. The manifestation of the Most Holy Trinity at the baptism of Christ.

Latin:

Vers. 20. προσέθηκε καὶ τοῦτο ἐπὶ πᾶσι] Ut solent scelera in scelera ducere: vide quæ ad Matthæum diximus.

PARS IV. S. S. Trinitatis in baptismo Christi patefactio.

## 3:21
Ver. 21. and praying] Christ shows by his own example that prayers are to be joined with baptism, which we have noted from Justin was observed by those who were baptized according to the discipline of Christ,

PART V. The commemoration of the age and ancestors of Christ.

Latin:

Vers. 21. καὶ προσευχομένου] Ostendit Christus suo exem- plo cum baptismo jungendas preces, quod observatum ab his, qui ex Christi disciplina baptizabantur ex Justino an- notavimus,

PARS V. Aetatis & majorum Christi commemoratio.

## 3:23
Ver. 23. and Jesus himself was about thirty years of age being] The construction seems altogether more correct if we join ὢν to the preceding words. For it is not correctly said ἄρχομαι ἤ τριάκοντα, but rather ἄρχομαι ἔτος τριακοστὸν, which is I am in my thirtieth year. But ἄρχομαι ὢν ἐτῶν τριάκοντα is I am beginning now to be a thirty-year-old, which is not said unless after the thirtieth year is completed: just as someone is called a one-year-old by the authors of Roman Law not immediately when he is born, but on the three hundred and sixty-fifth day. Which, as a man supreme in every kind of literature rightly observed, so I cannot agree with him when he thinks that ὡσεὶ in this passage of Luke is placed in place of the Caph of truth as the Hebrews call it. For the Greeks express that Caph by ὡς, as when it is said glory as of the only begotten: which place itself does not hold unless when one thing is a sign of another, as that majesty taught that Jesus was the only son of God. But here it is not ὡς but ὡσεὶ, which added to a number or measure signifies that which we call about or approximately, as Matt. XIV. 21. Mark VI. v. 44. Below IX. 14. XXII. 41, XXIII. 44. John IV. 6. VI. 10. XIX 14. Nor does that notation of one thing by another have a place here. Many of the ancients, when they perceived this clearly enough, thought that by ὡσεὶ it was signified that something was lacking to Christ for the thirtieth year; among whom are Irenaeus and Epiphanius, who wishes Christ to have been baptized in November, when his birthday was approaching in January. But if Luke had wished this, what need would there have been to add that ἀρχόμενος? Furthermore, this very accurate description altogether looks to some legitimate time. The law which exists in Num. IV. 3. and 47. with the history added in 1. Chron. XXIII. 2. expressly teaches that the Levites finally undertook their proper function when they were בְּנֵי שְׁלֹשִׁים שָׁנָה, that is, thirty years old, although as another law teaches Num. VIII. 24. after the twenty-fifth year was completed they laid the foundations of their ministry, just as also among the Achaeans and other nations the thirtieth year was the legitimate one for holding magistracies. To this example God wished both the Baptist (who being six months older than Christ by birth, also began his office that much earlier) and Christ himself, only after the thirtieth year was completed, to begin the function commanded to them. Nor yet is there no force in the particle ὡσεὶ. For it is customary for something to be said to have been done about a certain time, no less where something has exceeded, than where it is lacking to the precise notation, as can be seen also below XXII. 59. and most clearly XXIII. 44. when compared with the passage of Mark XV. 33. Luke therefore signifies that Christ did not come to baptism on his very birthday, but some days after, which was the beginning of his undertaking the office. And lest this interpretation be believed to be destitute of all authority of the ancients, it should be known that Chrysostom thought so, who says that Christ came to baptism after thirty years. Add what Moses notes concerning Joseph the son of Jacob, who bore no doubtful image of Christ, at the time when he is set over Egypt, that he was בֶּן שְׁלֹשִׁים שָׁנָה, that is, as the LXX translate, thirty years old. Following the example of the Hebrew law, and of the Lord himself, Justinian ordained that he who was to be chosen Bishop must exceed the thirtieth year of his age, Novella CXXXVII. formerly not even a presbyter was ordained before that age, as can be seen in the eleventh canon of the Synod of Neocaesarea.

There is no need that we join the participle ὢν to the preceding words: which coheres more correctly with the following, being as was supposed the son of Joseph of Heli. Nor is it necessary that that thirty years of age with

ἀρχόμενος should be construed: since it can be referred to the verb ἦν: He was thirty years of age. But the verb ἀρχόμενος seems to be referable to the ministry of Christ, so that the sense is not that Christ began to be, or was thirty years of age, but that being born about 30 years, he began to teach, and to enter upon the course of his ministry. B. Chemnitius in Prolegomena to the Harmony, chapter III, says that this explanation is not inconsistent, and agrees very well with grammar, and Spanheim proves it in part II, Dubia Evangelica, doubt XI, page 204, both from the underlying subject matter, because he truly began to manifest himself after he had been inaugurated by a heavenly voice in baptism as if by a solemn vocation: and from parallel passages, where Luke uses the same phrase in a similar sense, c. XXIII. 5, Acts I. 22, chapter X. 27. And thus Origen, Bede, Jansenius, and others refer this word to the ministry of Christ: to which opinion Wilh. also brings Justin and Euthymius. Langius, book II, on the years of Christ, chapter III, page 364, if he explains this passage of ours from similar passages, Acts I. 22, chapter XV. v. 32, with the elliptical phrase completed: καὶ αὐτὸς ἦν ὁ Ἰησῦς ὡς ἐτῶν τριάκοντα ἀρχόμενος (τὴν διακονίαν) ὢν ὡς ἐνομίζετο. Which is a tautology rather than a true explanation. And Spanheim rightly says, l. c. page 200, It will indeed be well said ἦν ἀρχόμενος for ἤρχετο, but ἦν ἀρχόμενος ὢν for ἤρχετο εἶναι is very harsh. What need was there for this circumlocution of words? The sense of Luke's words is certainly much more fluid with separate participles than with combined ones. Otherwise, one or the other would seem to be redundant, either ὡσεὶ or ἀρχόμενος. Furthermore, Grotius rightly proves against that great man that ὡσεὶ is not placed in place of the Caph of truth: nor is there any doubt from the perpetual use of this little word that it signifies about or approximately, so that either an excess or a defect is noted, and indeed a defect was seen to be noted by Irenaeus and Epiphanius for this reason, because Christ was born in the 42nd year of Augustus, and baptized in the 15th of Tiberius, but the reign of Augustus is extended to only 56 years, whence, adding the remaining 14 years of the reign of Augustus to the 15th of Tiberius, 29 years emerge, and not 30. But to these Spanheim replies that not 56 but 57 years are attributed to Augustus by many, and that the chronology which binds the birth of Christ to the 42nd year of Augustus is not sufficiently certain. Nor is that opinion of Irenaeus approved by Grotius: who from the phrase of Luke gathers rather that some excess is designated, so that he did not come to baptism precisely 30 years old, or on his very birthday, but some days after: for which opinion, that Christ was baptized after his 30th year, he cites Chrysostom: others also allege Ignatius, Jerome, Augustine, Eusebius, Euthymius, Theophylact, Cedrenus, Bede, Bernard, the ancient Roman ritual: to whom are added Salmero, Baronius, Scaliger, Gordanus, Torniellus, Barradius, Franciscus Lucas, Wilhelm Langius, etc. Nor, however, is the opinion of Deckers and Suslyga to be approved, that Christ was baptized only in the 32nd year of his age, much less that of Kepler concerning the 33rd year, to which Spanheim rashly rises in those paradoxical opinions, that Luke in such an accurate notation of time spoke not mathematically but popularly, and that these things do not conflict with each other, to be about thirty years of age, and to have precisely 32 or 33 years, at least so that he may favor his Pyrrhonism, that we have nothing certain about the baptismal year of Christ. Which skepticism of this man one must altogether marvel at: since, as Mr. Langius rightly says, Luke had described this epoch with such diligence that a greater one could be expected from no historian or can be demanded. Thus indeed Langius, l.c. p. 365, concerning the time of Christ’s baptism: The Savior was born in the year of the Julian period 4713, at the end of December 25; but was baptized in the year 4744, at the beginning of January 6. And at that time he was exactly 30 years and 13 days old. This is clearly ἦν ὡσεὶ ἐτῶν τριάκοντα. But if he is said to have been brought into the light at the beginning of the year 4713 (which Lansbergius maintains), he would have been 31 years old exactly, or if the baptism is moved back to November, 30 years and 10 months exactly. But this is not ὡσεὶ ἐτῶν τριάκοντα, but ὡσεὶ ἐτῶν τριάκοντα ἑνός. For the number approaches closer to thirty-one than to thirty. On the other hand, if we follow the calculation of Petavius, Christ, when he was baptized, would have been 32 years old exactly, but according to Kepler 33, which is clearly contrary to the Scriptures. So far Mr. Langius, who in the preceding chapter had treated at greater length of the day of Christ’s Baptism, and the same on the 6th. January 6 by the consensus of antiquity, if indeed that was the ancient and consenting opinion of the Fathers, as well Greeks as Latins, and to this expression, that Christ was ὡς ἐτῶν τριάκοντα, it best agrees: since he was thus 30 years and 13 days old when he was baptized, not precisely 30 years of age. And let these things concerning the time of the baptism of Christ suffice for the present. See more in our Biblical Chronicle.

Verse 23. υἱὸς Ἰωσὴφ τοῦ Ἡλὶ] In reconciling the genealogy which is in Matthew, and that which Luke has placed, the wits of ancient and recent writers have labored greatly: nor is that a wonder, since such a great disagreement at the very threshold was wont to be objected to these books daily by the enemies of Christianity. But those who are acquainted with the customs of the Jewish people know that there can be many genealogies which seem to conflict, yet do not conflict: and that this is wont to happen in more than one way, as it is easy to prove from those books which the Jews acknowledge with us. But since there are many methods of reconciliation, which is the best after so many centuries, with the records and all memory long since lost, is difficult to say: and truly here that old saying has a place, I will deem him the best prophet who has guessed well. They extricate themselves most easily from this, who, where υἱὸς Ἡλὶ is said, interpret son as son-in-law, or even do not refer it to Joseph but to Jesus, so that he himself is υἱὸς Ἡλὶ, that is to say, grandson: but as it is not to be denied that sons-in-law can be called sons, so in a list of a lineage, with no sign of distinction added, which would have been most easy, that a thing so different should be indicated by a common word, is hardly credible, nor does that perpetual order allow that τοῦ Ἡλὶ be referred to that which was more remote, especially since if that were the case, the word ἐνομίζετο would demand another opposite word, for instance ἦν δὲ or the like. Those who say that the Hebrews were multinominal, say what is true, and it can be proved by many places of the ancient scripture. But that between David and Salathiel no name should agree, nor likewise between Zorobabel and the end of the genealogy, especially since from Abraham to David all the names agree, he who is sound in judgment will not easily concede that this happened for the sole reason of τῆς πολυωνυμίας.

Wherefore they are to be thought to have judged much more correctly who bring forward this as the cause of the diversity, that the succession of blood and of law sometimes agrees, and sometimes disagrees. Nature is the arbiter of the former: civil law of the latter. And children are indeed also heirs: but not also those who are heirs, children: since often agnates from a sufficiently remote degree are called to inherit the estate, as often as a closer degree is lacking. But those who saw this correctly, most thought that there was not even room for doubt that Matthew follows the order of nature, Luke that of law: for they say the words are open, in Matthew indeed ἐγέννησε, but in Luke ἐνομίζετο, of which the former is natural, the latter legal. This has the appearance of truth and is supported by the authority of the ancient African writer. But it is easy to prove that that writer also in many matters is lacking not so much in diligence as in judgment and knowledge of languages, and falls into error: and as far as the force of the words is concerned, that first word ἐνομίζετο does not pertain to the whole context of the genealogy, but to Jesus alone who was not the son of Joseph, but was commonly thought to be: but in the rest, ἐνομίζετο has no place, unless one chooses to say that David also was νομισθῆναι the son of Jesse and Jesse the son of Obed and so on in order to Adam.

I, however, not led by conjectures, but by clear reasons, if I am not mistaken, judge it most certain that the succession of law is regarded by Matthew. For he lists those who obtained the kingdom, which was the right of the firstborn, with no private person admitted. Then, he says, Jechonias ἐγέννησε τὸν Σαλαθιὴλ. And yet Jeremiah 22:30 had not obscurely predicted by the command of God that the same Jechonias would depart this life without children because of his merits. Wherefore, since Luke ascribes Neri as the parent to the same Salathiel (for I do not see why we should think them different), and Matthew ascribes Jechonias, it is most clear that the right of blood is regarded by Luke, and the right of succession, and especially the right to royal dignity, by Matthew: which right, Jechonias having died without children, and if there were any others among the descendants of Solomon, devolved in legitimate order to Salathiel, the head of the family of Nathan. For among the sons of David, Nathan followed Solomon: for the fact that some think the posterity of Solomon failed in Achazias, does not conflict with any place of sacred history. But that error is to be pardoned not so much in men, as in an age miserably deceived by the Annian Pseudo-Philos.

That what we have said is true, the writer of Chronicles shows, who, since he could not be ignorant of the very well-known fact about Jeconiah dying without children, makes Assir the son of Jeconiah, or Shealtiel the son of Assir or of Jeconiah himself (for the construction is ambiguous) 1 Chron. 3:16. For I prefer with the Hebrews and the LXX to take אסר as a proper name rather than as an appellative, since the construction itself, if I am not mistaken, demands this more. He calls him son, therefore, as a successor in law, for in that manner he is accustomed to genealogize. Nor does he allow us to be ignorant of this himself. For a little before in the same place he had made Zedekiah the son of Jeconiah: whom it cannot be denied was the uncle of the same Jeconiah, since we have a manifest testimony in 2 Kings 24:19, in which place, although the Hebrew reading has no ambiguity, certain Greek codices correctly have patradelphon, just as Josephus does in this history, while others from the passage in Chronicles have uion. Just as, therefore, he is called the son of the writer of Chronicles who is the successor in law, even an uncle, so he is said by Matthew to beget who leaves behind some heir: by a fiction of law, that is. Just as the Latins also call adoptive parents progenitors through a similar catachresis. And the Hebrews, which is more, call the offspring of the brother of a dead man the seed of the dead man himself. In a similar way, he is said by Xenophon in the Laconian Republic to beget children who admits another man to his wife, so that he himself, according to Laconian institutions, may be called the father of the offspring. Similarly, Ovid calls Augustus the son of Caesar at the beginning of the Metamorphoses. Germanicus, moreover, calls Augustus his progenitor in the Aratean poem. To these is added, moreover, that the Hebrew word yaled, which is expressed by begetting, extends its use widely beyond the bounds of origin, so that the deeds of someone are called by the Hellenists, who love to follow Hebraisms, generations, as in Gen. 6:9, Num. 3:1, and elsewhere.

Since, therefore, it is most evident in the person of Shealtiel that the right of succession is regarded by Matthew, but the right of blood by Luke, if any say elsewhere that Matthew shifts to the right of blood and Luke to the right of succession in a desultory manner, I do not see what probable causes they can bring forward for such inconstancy. Africanus, as I have said, more diligent than of sound judgment in all things, while he relies more than is right upon those words 'he begat' and 'was supposed,' was both deceived himself and drew many of those who followed into the assent of his error. For the writer of the responses to the orthodox, Eusebius, Nazianzen, and others, as if in a formed line, follow him, and wish Eli, named by Luke, to be the father of Joseph by legal right, but Jacob, named by Matthew, to be the father of the same by natural right: although the reasons brought forward by us above persuade rather the contrary.

Add to these that Luke traces the lineage to Adam, the natural sower of all: but Matthew begins from Abraham, from whom the promises begin, from which the right especially arises. To these is added also that the number of Luke is much fuller than that of Matthew. For Luke counts nineteen persons between Shealtiel and Joseph, as the Vulgate editions have, or seventeen as we judge, while Matthew recites only ten, which is a manifest indication that some persons were omitted by Matthew. For who would believe that out of two families from the same time to the same time, one had only half as many generations as the other? This is altogether incredible. But Matthew himself quite openly professes that persons are not being counted by him, but that the sum of the lineage is briefly indicated, digested into three sets of fourteen for the sake of memory. For he also passes over in silence between King Joram and Uzziah, who are Ahaziah, Joash, and Amaziah: namely, to consult the order instituted for the ease of memory: which matters little in demonstrating a right of succession. For, as it is accustomed to be said, the heir of my heir is my heir. But he who wishes to follow the natural series, which Luke does (for that is the reason he mentions men of private fortune from David to Shealtiel, so as not to depart from that order), it becomes him to proceed from degree to degree, where the blood leads, which we do not doubt he has done. And if anyone correctly reckons the times from Zerubbabel to Christ, he will see, according to what for the most part happens, that the whole of that time is correctly filled by the persons recited by him: not so by Matthew. Wherefore we learn from this also that the legal is regarded by Matthew, and the natural by Luke.

But just as I am compelled to depart from Africanus thus far, so I think that what has been handed down by him, and than which we have nothing more ancient, should not be entirely despised. He used to praise the kinsmen of our Lord as the authors of that narrative, whom for that reason they called Δεσποσύνες. But the interval of time which intervenes between Christ and Africanus easily allows for some adulteration of the report. I believe, however, that what he had correctly received was corrupted by the interpretation of Africanus himself, while he strives to serve the ὑπόθεσις which he had set before himself, the order of nature observed by Matthew, that of the law by Luke. I do not wish for credit to be given to this conjecture of mine, unless he himself destroys his own credibility by his own words. Mathan, he says, tracing his lineage from Solomon, had taken Estha as his wife, and from her had begotten a son, Jacob. The same Estha, after Mathan was dead, married another man, Melchi, from the posterity of Nathan, and from him begat Eli. Eli having died without children, Jacob his brother, not indeed by blood, but uterine, that is, ὁμομήτριος, took the widow according to the law, from whom Joseph was born, who would be the son of Jacob by nature, but by the law the son of Eli. Who does not see that many errors are made here? For the law of τῆς ἐπιγαμβρεύσεως pertained to preserving the rights of families. Families are reckoned by agnation: wherefore, Eli having died without children, it was not the uterine brother, who was not an agnate, who ought to have begotten offspring for him, but the nearest of the same family and name. Nor if the uterine brother had voluntarily performed that duty, could the son for that reason have been reckoned by any right under the name of the deceased and been entered into the genealogy. Wherefore, even if it be true that Melchi and Mathan used the same wife, that cannot avail for reconciling these genealogies.

There is also another ancient tradition, mentioned by Epiphanius: that this Joseph of ours was the son of Jacob, called by the surname Panther: which I do not think should be spurned at all: for Joseph himself is also called by the same cognomen. Indeed, Celsus also says that Mary conceived from a certain Panther, a carpenter, which he had undoubtedly received from the Jews: for the same people call Jesus our Lord the son of Panther, as in the book מדרש קהלת and in the book עבודה זרה: another report mentioned by Greek writers has also flowed down to posterity, that Mary's father was called Jehojakim, his father Panther, Panther's father Barpanther, and Barpanther's father Levi, the son of Melchi, which is not to be rashly condemned. For since the matter itself speaks, as we have shown elsewhere, that Mary was an ἐπίκληρον, and therefore, as Epiphanius rightly speaks, κλήρων εἰς τοῦτο ἀναγκασάντων, she married the nearest agnate, it follows that Joseph and Mary were joined to each other in a close degree: wherefore the lineage of Mary is proposed to us to be learned from the genealogy of Joseph. That, however, will appear most true: if we say, as that narrative signifies, that the same Levi was uncle to Joseph, but great-great-grandfather to Mary. But that Panther and Barpanther are called the grandfather and great-grandfather of Mary, I believe it happened because the gentile cognomen was placed in this way in place of the name through forgetfulness, as is wont to happen. For Panther seems to have been a common name for those who had descended from Melchi, perhaps also traced back through a longer series of parents from the Maccabean times from the event of some memorable thing. For in those times certain gentile cognomens had begun to be used, either from the name of a progenitor, as the cognomen of the Hasmoneans, or from some chance event. Now, because, with the traditions collected into one, and accepted in such a way that they dissent neither with Matthew nor with Luke, it seems most likely to me, I shall submit it to the judgment of the readers, having testified what I have already said, that these things are arbitrary, not proven.

But I think that what the οἱ δεσπόσυνοι said to Africanus, that Estha was first the wife of Mathan, then of Melchi, and that therefore they were ὁμοχρόνους. And that in Mathan the natural line of Abiud was extinguished, which was the first of the lines descended from Zorobabel. Wherefore, by the law of the widow, marriage to raise up offspring in the name of the dead was owed to him who was the head of the second family coming through Resa from the same Zorobabel. And that he was Melchi, who begat Jacob, commonly called Panther by the cognomen of his natural father, but by the estimation of the law the son of the deceased Mathan and the successor of all his right. The right of this Jacob, who died without children, devolved to Joseph: and thus Joseph is called the son of Jacob, not by the law of τῆς ἐπιγαμβρεύσεως, but because his inheritance had come to him, just as Zedekiah is the son, as we have said, of Jeconiah. Joseph, however, if I rightly reckon the account, was the son of Jacob's brother, and therefore Jacob was Joseph's uncle. But Mary, since she came from the other son of Melchi, and was an ἐπίκληρος, was married to Joseph, because no one existed who was closer to whose guardianship she might flee.

These knots having been untied, one difficulty seems to remain, how both Matthew and Luke say Zorobabel is the son of Salathiel, when the writer of Chronicles says he is the son of Pedaiah, who seems to have been the brother of Salathiel. To me it seems plain that it is not a question there of the Ethnarch Zorobabel, whom it was most well known to all to be the firstborn of Salathiel, but of another of the same family, who is named among the others of the royal line. For the children of that Zorobabel also have other names than those which exist in Matthew or Luke: so that it is not permitted here to flee to a solution of natural and legitimate succession. And in Ezra, Nehemiah, and Haggai, the Ethnarch Zorobabel is nowhere called the son of Pedaiah, but always, as here in both Matthew and Luke, the son of Salathiel. And thus Joseph, a diligent investigator of these matters, often calls him. To this Zorobabel, however, most ample promises had been made by God concerning the establishing of the kingdom in his posterity, whence Matthew and Luke converge upon his person no less than upon those of David and Abraham. In these things which we have said before, we have set forth the matter as if those two names Matthat and Levi did not exist between Eli and Melchi in the context of Luke: the causes of which estimation of ours, as also of the omitted Cainan, will soon be rendered in their own place.

But since truth is fixed in the minds of men more by ocular proof than through the ears (as the Jurisconsults speak, when they treat of the degrees of kinship), I will exhibit both the line of Matthew and that of Luke to be viewed, with the line of Matthew on the right, that of Luke on the left, with the names which both mention cast into the middle space. And those persons whom Matthew omitted, in order to round out his τεσσαρεσκαιδεκάδας, I will submit in a different style of letters: and I will subjoin to the same the Genealogy of Mary:

ADAM. SETH. ENOS. CAINAN. MALELEEL. JARED. ENOCH. MATHUSALA. LAMECH. NOE. SEM. ARPHAXAD. SALA: HEBER. PHALEC. RAGU. SARUCH. NACHOR. THARE.

ABRAHAM. ISAAC. JACOB. JUDA. PHARES. ESROM. ARAM or RAM. AMINADAB. NAASSON. SALMON. BOOZ. OBED. JESSE. DAVID.

SALOMO. ROBOAM. ABIA. ASA. IOSAPHAT. IORAM. Achazia. Ioas. Amasia. OZIAS, who is also AZARIAS. IOATHAM. ACHAZ. EZECHIA. MANASSE. AMON. IOSIAS. IECHONIAS, that is, Iehojakim. IECHONIAS the second: died without children. SEDECIAS, uncle and heir of the latter Iechonias. ASSIR, heir of Iechonias after Sedecias. NATHAN. MATTATHA. MAINAN. MELEA. ELIAKIM. IONAN. IOSEPH. IUDA. SIMEON. LEVI. MATTHAT. IORIM. ELIEZER. IOSE. ER. ELMODAN. COSAM. ADDI. MELCHI. NERI.

SALATHIEL son of Neri, heir of Assir and Iechonias. ZOROBABEL son and heir of Salathiel.

ABIUD. ELIAKIM. AZOR. RESA. IOHANNA. IUDA. SADOC.

SADOC. ACHIM. ELIUD. ELEAZAR. Anonymous. Anonymous. Anonymous. Anonymous. Anonymous. Anonymous. Anonymous. MATHAN, the first husband of Estha, died without children. JACOB, who is also Panther, the legal son of Matthan by Estha: brother of Eli and Levi by nature. JOSEPH. SEMEI. MATTATHIAS. MAATH. NAGGA. ESLI. NAUM. AMOS. MATTATHIAS. JOSEPH. JANNA. MELCHI, the second husband of Estha, the natural father of Jacob. ELI-LEVI.

JOSEPH, son of Eli by nature, heir of Jacob: the nearest kinsman of Mary. I. BARPANTHER. I. PANTHER. I. JEHOJAKIM, who is also Eliakim. I. MARY married to Joseph.

I have interposed some persons, whose names do not exist, between the times of Zerubbabel and Christ, because without them the times cannot be filled out sufficiently conveniently. Nor is that new in Matthew, since, as I said, he omits three consecutive Kings. How many were omitted here is difficult to say, since families compared among themselves often have one or another more or fewer generations in the same space of time, which can be seen in all genealogies.

But because Mary's great-great-grandfather was called Levi, from there arose the error of the ancients who thought that the right of the Levitical priesthood was acquired for Christ also by birth: in which there is much to be criticized. For as far as names are concerned, they were common to all tribes, so that both a Levite could be called Judah and one born from Judah could be called Levi, which no one moderately versed in these letters is ignorant of. But then, the right of the Levitical priesthood could not be transferred except through males from males, as the Romans say. How much better it would have been to believe the divine writer to the Hebrews, who expressly denies that the tribe of Judah, from which Jesus arose, has any right of succeeding to the priesthood: and therefore that Christ's pontificate is not Levitical, but an unchangeable royal one, such as Melchizedek's had been. I will add that I entirely believe that Luke's genealogy was taken from such public records: for Josephus testifies that in them lineages were accustomed to be described and kept quite accurately even until the destruction.

TO THE ANIMADVERSIONS. Entrance.

The opinion of the Calvinist Doctor Abraham Scultetus, which he vomited forth in his Evangelical Exercises, book 1, chapter XLI, is not pious enough, to say nothing more serious: The Economic rule, he says, is: Buy not what is needed, but what is necessary. The Theological rule is: Learn necessary things, dismiss unnecessary things. This has a place especially in the Genealogy of Christ, where these and those doubts occur to the reader, about which one should not anxiously dispute. For what is it to piety? Nor did the Evangelists themselves follow accuracy. He thought that the doubts which occur in the Genealogy of Christ were unnecessary, to be dismissed, or to be neglected: without which, however, the truth of the scriptures cannot stand in all respects. How will the effort spent on the reading, collation, reconciliation, and interpretation of the sacred letters not be necessary? How is it to be neglected or dismissed? Without a doubt, all things contribute to piety which the Holy Spirit Himself, the Best Teacher of Piety, wished to be inserted into the Scripture that instructs us in piety, to whose judgment one must piously acquiesce. The Rabbis, although blind guides in the Scriptures, certainly felt much more religiously about Scripture: that there is no apex in the sacred letters from which great mountains of doctrines do not hang. And why would that scrutiny not contribute to piety, without which it cannot stand

the reason for the mysteries of piety concerning Christ: for which it is absolutely necessary that, if it is to be established concerning the promised Messiah, in whom one must believe, if the fundamental article of faith, that Jesus of Nazareth is the promised Messiah, is to be placed beyond doubt and in safety, so that we do not doubt that he, because according to the flesh he is without a father, draws his origin with respect to his mother from the stock of Judah and the family of David. How will it be possible to satisfy the Jews who stubbornly deny this origin and pit Matthew against Luke, so as to render the Christian faith doubtful (not to mention others who are anxious about the origin of Christ's mother from the stock of Judah), with this dispute omitted! Such a category or rather calumny of R. Joseph Albo the Spaniard in his book Ikkarim, Sermon III, chapter 25, p. 93, is known. How much less can a Jew bring himself to believe those things which are held in the law of Jesus, where he laughs at that which they have placed as the foundation of their faith, namely that Jesus is the Messiah, the son of David! Not yet, indeed, says that Rabbi, is it established among them whether he is the son of David or not. But in the first chapter of his Gospel, Matthew deduces the lineage of Joseph, the husband of Mary, or as they wish, her betrothed, according to their opinion, from Solomon, and says that he is from the Royal seed; but in the third chapter of his Gospel, Luke denies that he is from the Royal seed, and refers his lineage to Nathan, the son of David, which two genealogies concern only Joseph. But this genealogy of Joseph has nothing at all to do with Jesus. From where, then, is Mary's lineage established? So says that Jew. But is the faith of the Scripture of the New Testament not to be asserted? Is the foundation of the Christian religion not to be defended against the circumcised? Is the reconciliation of the Evangelists not to be shown? Who, being imprudent, will judge that effort unnecessary or superfluous? But in what way can it be excused that Scultetus was not afraid to accuse the Evangelists of not having followed accuracy? For this accusation redounds upon the Holy Spirit Himself, whose amanuenses they were. Nor indeed do those who, as is fitting, scrutinize the Genealogy of Christ lose their oil and effort, because a certain Sylvester Stejerus, a Leovalla Silesian, lost his, whom Scultetus says was an old Theologian who had worn out his whole life in elucidating the genealogy of Christ, and finally published his work at Prague in 1644, but that it did not quench the thirst of many, but rather increased it. Did Franciscus Gomarus also lose his, did Fridericus Spanhemius, and all others who among the Reformed have been diligent in that study? Nor indeed is the entire work of the Theologians, both ancient and modern, who have labored in reconciling Matthew and Luke, to be considered in vain, because Theodore Beza found in a certain codex this Genealogy, just as in Matthew descending, so in Luke ascending, with only those added whom Matthew had passed over in establishing the groups of fourteen, deduced to Solomon, not to Nathan, with the others unchanged upwards as far as Adam, namely in this series, υἱὸς Ἰωσὴφ, τῦ Ἰακὼβ, τῦ Ματθὰν, τῦ Ἐλεαζὰρ, Ἴᾶ Ἐλλιὲδ, Ἴᾶ Ἰαχεὶμ, τῦ Σαδὼκ, τῦ Ἐλιακεικὰ, τῦ Ἀβιὲδ, τῦ Ζόροβαβὲλ, τῦ Ἰωσία, τῦ Ἀμὼς, τῦ Μανακᾶ, τῦ Ἐζεκία, τῦ Ἄχας, τῦ Ἰωαθὰμ, τῦ Ὀζία, τῦ Ἀμασίκ, τῦ Ἰνὰς, τῦ Ὀχοζίε, τῦ Ἰωρὰμ, τῦ Ἰωσαφὰτ, τῦ Ἀσὼ, τῦ Ἀβιὰ, Ἰᾶ Ῥοβοὰμ, τῦ Σολομῶν. One ought rather to marvel that both Beza and Scultetus indulge in that conjecture, that the Genealogy of Christ was corrupted by the Jews, in the very times of the Evangelists, and that this fraud easily prevailed, not having been noticed by most: which is contrary to the constant consensus of the remaining Codices, of the ancient translations likewise consenting, and of the Fathers treating this Genealogy, strengthened by the agreement of those, nor does it in any way accord with divine providence: and therefore it was deservedly rejected by Spanheim in Dub. XXII. near the end. But having dismissed Scultetus, we turn ourselves to Grotius, intending to examine briefly his divinations in this cause, as well as those things which he peddles as resting upon certain and clear reasons.

ANIMADVERSIONS ON THE GENEALOGY OF CHRIST.

§. I. Grotius rightly observes at the beginning that there are many genealogies which seem to conflict, yet do not conflict, as the books of the Jews themselves testify, and that it is difficult, after so many centuries, with the records long since lost and all memory gone, to find the true reconciliation. But one should not for that reason despair of reconciliation, nor indulge in conjectures or one's own inventions, much less should the words of Scripture be twisted or vexed for their sake, and least of all should trifles, uncertainties, and copies be peddled as clear, certain, and consistent with the Scriptures.

§. II. Now since Grotius brings forward diverse methods of reconciliation, he certainly did not choose the best or the easiest. He acknowledges that those who understand 'son-in-law' where Joseph is called τοῦ Ἡλὶ (of Eli) extricate themselves most easily, in this manner: ὁ Ἰησοῦς ἦν ὡς ἐνομίζετο υἱὸς Ἰωσὴφ (υἱἳ) τοῦ Ἡλὶ, Jesus was, as was supposed, the son of Joseph (son) of Eli: or they even refer this not to Joseph, but to Jesus, so that he himself is τοῦ Ἡλὶ, that is to say, grandson: in this manner: ὁ Ἰησοῦς ἦν ὡς ἐνομίζετο, υἱὸς Ἰωσὴφ, (υἱὸς) τοῦ Ἡλὶ: Jesus was, as was supposed, the son of Joseph, (son) of Eli, that is, grandson. Yet he does not cast his vote for that opinion, which he confesses is most convenient for resolving many knots, even though it has been approved by the authority of great men.

§. III. But as for what seems hardly credible to Grotius, that in a list of lineage, with no added sign of distinction, sons are sometimes called sons-in-law through the genitive τοῦ, it is surely more convenient and much more likely that that bare pronoun ᾖ, which is common and general, is taken in different ways, than that the word ἐγέννησε (begat), which is special in Matthew in the list of the Genealogy, should be understood in such a disparate sense that in most cases it obtains the notion of generation, but in some denotes only succession, which is never expressed by that word, nor can it be. I pass over the fact that under the name of daughters in Gen. XXXVII, daughters-in-law are also included: where it is held in Rabboth thus: No one is prohibited from calling his son-in-law a son, and his daughter-in-law his daughter. That pronoun τοῦ, when referred to the origin of Adam, is certainly taken in another sense, who was of God not by generation, but by creation; but it demands another sense in other relations, when Seth is called τοῦ Ἀδὰμ (of Adam), which is understood entirely of generation.

§. IV. Nor is it inconvenient for that τοῦ Ἡλὶ to be referred to a more remote name, namely Jesus, provided the words ὡς ἐνομίζετο υἱὸς Ἰωσὴφ are read as a parenthesis, which reading is favored by the fact that those words cohere, and are not separated by a comma inserted at the word ἐνομίζετο, and thus they are also read by the Syrian, which interpretation, after Augustine, is approved by Theodatus in the Italian version of the Bible, Franciscus Junius, Immanuel Tremellius in the annotations to Luke III, and Fridericus Spanhemius in part I, Dub. Evangel. XX, page 24, and also B. Hülsemann in Gen. X, v. 22. Which interpretation Joh. Gerb. Vossius prefers for the reason that it is more in accordance with the custom of Scripture that someone should be called the son of his grandfather by nature rather than by the law of the levirate, especially since in the very Genealogy constructed by Matthew, examples are at hand where someone is said to have begotten him who is his grandson or great-grandson, as even Grotius acknowledges. Pricæus, however, thinks that he has found a more ready method of resolving the whole matter, if, with the mark of parenthesis removed, ὃς is read instead of ὡς, induced by two passages, Acts VII. 20 and Luke II. 36, where the relative is placed after ἦν. But all the codices read ὡς, the pronoun ὃς is found in none, and the most ancient versions agree. And Pricæus is thus forced to place a comma after the word ὤν, and to connect it with the preceding, not the following words, in this manner: Ἕαυτὸς ἦν ὁ Ἰησοῦς ὡσεὶ ἐτῶν τριάκοντα ἀρχόμενος ὢν, ὃς ἐνομίζετο υἱὸς Ἰωσὴφ, and he wishes the particle ὃς to be rendered in a copulative sense, i.e., and Jesus himself was about thirty years old beginning to be, and was supposed to be the son of Joseph. Which new reading and interpretation still leaves a scruple, how the following words & Ἠλὶ are to be taken, whether they are to be referred to Jesus, the grandson of Eli, or indeed to Joseph, the son-in-law of Eli?

§. V. Grotius not undeservedly rejects another method of reconciliation, that all the names inserted between David and Salathiel, and likewise between Zerubbabel and the end of the lineage, were multi-named, since on the contrary, from Abraham to David, all the names agree. Concerning which see Augustine, lib. II, Quæst. Evangel. c. V.

§. VI. Nor do we deny that the opinion of those, which is brought forward in the third place by Grotius, who seek the cause of the diversity in the diversity of the succession of blood and law, is to be preferred to it, although we do not judge that one must acquiesce in it. For in our judgment, that reconciliation of the Evangelists is truer, that the genealogy of Mary is woven here, than that the lineage of Joseph was recounted by both Evangelists, Matthew and Luke, under this distinction, that the one followed the order of nature, the other of law, which Grotius embraced along with Joh. Clichtoveus in Damascenus, Salmeron, Maldonado, and Calixtus, and which among the ancients, with Julius Africanus leading the way, Ambrose in Luke III, Anselm in Matthew, Epeberius in questions on the New Testament, and Damascenus entered upon. book on the Orthodox Faith, chapter 15. In explaining which, since the authors do not agree, some attributing the order of nature to Matthew, and the order of law to Luke with Damascenus and Nicetas in the catena; others inverting this with Ambrose. Grotius thinks that they were led into the former opinion by the authority of Africanus, but he himself prefers the latter. But as to what he opposes to the opinion of Africanus, that Luke refers the τὸ ἐνομίζετο not to the whole context of the pedigree, but to Jesus alone, who was not the son of Joseph but was commonly thought to be, the followers of Africanus will perhaps say that they by no means intend that all the ancestors of Christ in Luke are legal, but that only one is, namely Joseph, and that it suffices for the reconciliation that some were ancestors of Heli, whom Luke mentions, and others of Jacob, whom Matthew commemorates. Which is the response of Maldonado in Matthew I, col. 28.

§. VII. Furthermore, as to the Grotian opinion, for which it is most certain that the succession of law is looked to by Matthew, it does not rest on clear reasons, as he boasts, but on mere conjectures. So that one must wonder that Mr. Dr. Georg König was so prone to go over to it in his Sacred Vindications, disp. XXXIII, §. 6. et seqq. among our own, and among the Jesuits Petrus Possinus in his Diallacticon Theogenealogicon, p. 541, who however followed Corderius rather than Grotius; whom Grotius himself had as a predecessor. For Grotius is to Possinus a man of almost Academic liberty, of a sect ἀντεξυσίᾳ, κ᾿ ἀνυπευθύνῳ, page 558. For as to what Grotius urges first: that Matthew, with no private person mixed in, lists only those who obtained the kingdom, which was that of the firstborn, that this was done not on account of a succession of right, but of blood, and because both successions concur in that line of Solomon. An evident argument for this matter is that where only succession, and not generation, whether immediate or mediate, has a place, the succeeding persons have not been listed; as the example of Zedekiah proves, who was substituted not in the place of Jehoiakim his parent, but of his uncle Jeconiah, and therefore was passed over by Matthew; which the example of Assir would also teach, if that were a person's name, as Grotius wishes: placing Assir after Zedekiah, as the heir of Jeconiah by succession of right, not of blood. But the name אסיר, as R. Mordecai Nathan rightly observes, is an appellative, not a proper name, and he notes that it is the same as אסור, that is, bound and fettered. Cf. Gen. XXXIX. 20. 22. For the text holds thus: And the sons of Jeconiah, Assir, the bound, Shealtiel his son, with which Matthew agrees, and Jeconiah begat after the captivity Shealtiel. And thus B. Luther, Piscator, the Genevans, the Italian version, the Latin of Junius and Tremellius, etc., render the passage of Chronicles. Furthermore, is that claim of Grotius not openly false, that all those listed by Matthew obtained the kingdom? Did Abiud, Eliakim, Azor, Mathan, and Jacob, who are reported in the genealogy of Matthew, also possess the empire? Had not the Prophet Ezekiel already predicted that not only the crown, but also the turban would be taken away, chap. XXI. 32.

§. VIII. As to what Grotius urges secondly: that Jeconiah died without children on account of his merits, Jer. XXII. v. 30. And therefore that that statement of Matthew, 'Jeconiah begat Shealtiel,' cannot be understood of generation, but indicates succession in the right of royal dignity, its entire force lies in an alien sense of the words of Jeremiah. For the word ערירי does not only denote childless, but destroyed, or unhappy and miserable, which the second edition of Aquila explains by ἀνάυξητον, 'not growing,' and the LXX and Theodotion by ἐκκήρυκτον, which is the same as 'cast out by the voice of a herald': Jerome rendered it 'abdicated' and 'abominable.' The Arabic rendered it 'a despised man.' Rabbi Solomon on Gen. XV. notes that this word has the sense of destruction, whence, according to the circumstance of the text, it signifies an exile, a vacuum, and an abdicated person, rather than sterile or childless. Sixtus Senensis, lib. VIII. Bibl. says that Jeremiah is speaking, not of the loss of offspring, but of the loss of the kingdom. Which sense the following words, which are added by way of explanation, confirm. 'No man of his seed shall prosper.' For יצלח means 'he shall prosper.' Because the descendants of Jeconiah fell from the royal height, and were reduced to an inferior state, and that for the most part a mournful one, and exposed to various calamities. Jerome also leans toward this, whose words cited on the passage of Jeremiah are these: 'From Jehoiakim was born Jeconiah, from Jeconiah Shealtiel, from Shealtiel Zerubbabel, and by order one comes to Christ. But in the days of Jehoiakim, a king his son did not succeed him, as he himself had succeeded his father, but he was in captivity, and Shealtiel, and Zerubbabel, and up to Christ no one obtained royal power.' Francis Gomarus brings forward yet another solution concerning the Genealogy of Christ by distinguishing, namely, the time spent before the captivity from the time of the captivity, that Jeconiah was childless before the captivity, not after. But the threats of Jeremiah XXII were not absolute, but with the tacit condition of stubbornness understood, upon the ceasing of which Jeconiah was both exempted from prison and gifted with offspring: to say nothing of the fact that some, who say that all power was abrogated to the descendants of Jeconiah by virtue of this curse, judge the Shealtiels and Zerubbabels of Matthew and Luke to be so different that those who were born from Jeconiah lived as private citizens, with the Ducal power transferred to the Shealtiel and Zerubbabel who were born from the line of Nathan. A comparison of the passage of Matthew with the book of Chronicles certainly teaches clearly that a certain Shealtiel was begotten by Jeconiah, whether or not he succeeded him in the government. For both the author of the book of Chronicles says that Shealtiel was the son of Jeconiah, and the Evangelist Matthew says that Jeconiah begat Shealtiel. Since these things are clear and manifest, they can in no way be elided as if he were called begotten by Jeconiah and the son of Jeconiah only by catachresis, because he succeeded him in the government. For Grotius cannot prove with suitable examples that the writer of Chronicles genealogizes in that manner: much less does that have a place in the listing of the Pedigree of Christ by St. Matthew, for whom it is in no way likely that he used the word 'begat' so improperly that it denotes only succession in government, when he is exhibiting the lineage and ancestry of Christ.

§. IX. But as to what he thinks, 1 Chron. III, that Zedekiah is called the son of Jeconiah; who was his uncle or paternal uncle, as witnessed by the later book of Kings, chap. XXIV. 19, he is deceived by an alien interpretation of the passage of Chronicles, whose words hold thus, v. 16: 'And the sons of Jehoiakim, Jeconiah his son, Zedekiah his son.' Zedekiah is not called the son of Jeconiah there, but the brother, and both Jeconiah and Zedekiah are established as sons of Jehoiakim: furthermore, besides Zedekiah the brother of Jeconiah, another Zedekiah is still commemorated in verse 15; the uncle of Jeconiah, the son of Josiah, called Mattaniah in 2 Kings XXIV. v. 17, both of whom of the same name Grotius confuses. Matthew commemorated neither, because neither belonged to the genealogy of Christ, neither the brother nor the uncle of Jeconiah, whence it is manifest that Matthew did not look to a succession of right in royal or agnatic dignity, but a succession of blood, as we warned before.

§. X. From which it can now easily be explained what Mr. Dr. Georg König brought forward for Grotius, against other theologians of ours, in the cited book: Namely, he wished to prove that the word gennan, which Matthew used, does not always presuppose a natural father, but sometimes admits an adoptive one as well; and he thinks that this becomes sufficiently clear from the example of Jeconiah: concerning whom it is read in Matthew 1:12 that he begat (egennese) Salathiel: but Salathiel in Luke 3:27 was the true son of Neri, merely the heir of Jeconiah, since indeed concerning the sons of Jeconiah properly so called it is expressly stated that no one of his seed shall sit upon the throne of David, or rule anymore in Judah. Jer. 22:30. whereas the contrary is read concerning Salathiel, that he was a leader of the Jewish people, Ezra 5:16. Because, however, with the posterity of Solomon failing in Jeconiah, the principal dignity devolved in legitimate order to Salathiel, the son of Neri from the family of Nathan, who was still surviving, Jeconiah is said to have begotten him, that is, to have left him as his heir, and to have transmitted the right of succession, and especially the right of leadership, to him. These are König's words: which, however, deserve no approval. For 1. the verb gennao properly denotes generation: from which propriety of the word one must not depart without a most serious reason. 2. In other generations it is accepted properly by Matthew in this genealogy: Why therefore would Matthew have used it here alone in such an improper signification concerning adoption, or succession, or the transmission of the right of succession in the case of Salathiel alone? 3. No example of this metaphorical signification of that word can be brought forward either from Matthew or from other sacred writers. However, it is not permitted to introduce meanings unusual to the Holy Spirit, much less to insert genealogical lines. 4. There will be no certainty about the generations, once that homonymy of the word is admitted, and many doubts will subsequently be raised, whether this or that son is natural or truly legal, even if the progenitor from whom he was begotten is expressly designated. 5. That Salathiel, the natural son of Neri, is the same as he who is said by Matthew to have been begotten by Jechonias, is vain-glorious: nor can it be proved by any solid reason. Jechonias certainly had a son, called Sealthiel, 1 Chron. III. v. 17. But he was not as the son of Neri; for how could the same person have had two natural fathers? so it does not appear why, in the case of St. Matthew when he says that Jechonias begat Salathiel, leaving aside his son, properly begotten by him, another Sealthiel must be understood, who indeed was the son of Neri, (since Jechonias himself begat a son of that name from himself) and that the Sealthiel of Luke, according to the mind of König, was merely the heir of Jechonias. 6. That Salathiel, the parent of Zorobabel, was a leader of the people is not solidly proved from the fourth book of Ezra, which book is apocryphal and fabulous. 7. That the posterity of Solomon failed in Jechonias is contradicted by the Canon of Scripture, 1 Chron. III. 17 seqq., where the descendants of Jechonias, sons and grandsons, etc., are enumerated: and among his sons, Sealthiel is commemorated in the first place: whom, although Jechonias did not have as heir and successor to the scepter, because of the edict of the Lord, Jer. XXII. v. 30, he nevertheless truly begat from himself. 8. Therefore, that Sealthiel, the son of Neri in Luke, is different from the Sealthiel whom Matthew commemorated. In this opinion, that the Sealthiel and Zorobabel of Matthew are different from the Sealthiel and Zorobabel of Luke, and that all the ancients were of this view, Cornel. Jansen, comment. in Concord. Evangel. c. XIV. p. 104, observes, and he thinks this is evident from the fact, with the agreement, or rather the leadership, of our blessed Chemnitz, that Africanus, Damascenus, Ambrose, and the rest, who labored much in solving that scruple of how Joseph was born both from Jacob and was the son of Eli, did not mention this scruple, of how Salathiel and Zorobabel are referred both to the Solomonic line and among the descendants of Nathan, but all constantly affirmed that Jacob descended from Solomon, but Heli from Nathan. 9. Add that Jechonias could not even be said to have transmitted the right of succession or the right of leadership to Sealthiel, the son of Neri, much less to have begotten him. Not the right of succession, because he had sons who would succeed to the paternal goods. Nor the right of leadership, because if Salathiel was raised to leadership, he obtained it not by any right of succession, but by a free divine transfer: since God, as a punishment for Jechonias, excluded his family from this dignity and transferred it to the line of Nathan and the family of Neri. 10. Finally, neither is any adoption proved here; and even if it had a place, it would contribute nothing to the genealogy of Matthew. Whence it was most correctly said by our blessed Wilhelm Lyser, disp. de genealogia Christi q. XV. & H., that adoption can indeed grant an inheritance, but does not bring about a genealogical relationship.

§. XI. Where Mr. Dr. König objects in vain against the blessed Lyser that there is a contrary example in Scripture itself. For Zedekiah, the uncle of Jechonias, 2 Kings XXIV. v. 17, is mixed into the genealogy of Jechonias and is called his son, 2 Chron. III. v. 16. For a response has already been given to this example by Grotius, that it is not Jechonias's son who is said to be there, but Jehoiakim's, from whom, however, the uncle, also called Zedekiah, is different, who was the son of Josiah and was made King, previously called Mattaniah, 2 Kings XXIV. v. 17. Which is clear from 1 Chron. III. 15 compared with v. 16: not to mention that R. Abarbenel denies that the word דודו in 2 Kings XXIV. v. 17 should be translated as his uncle. He calls him, he says, דודו not because he was the brother of Jehoiachin, but because he was in the affections of the King of Babylon. For it is from that meaning by which it is said (Cant. II. v. 16) my beloved is mine, and I am his! But that genealogies do not always describe generations in a continuous series, but also successions of families, whether such successions of the flesh, or obtained by the benefit of adoption or another right, should not have been asserted nakedly against the blessed Lyser, but demonstrated by suitable examples from the Scriptures, which, if they were given at all, still one should not conclude from these to the genealogy woven by Matthew with the word BEGAT, unless certain documents are at hand. And where those improper generations lead, the Jesuit Posfinus taught, and he even went so far as to call into doubt the generation of Ahaz, whether Hezekiah was begotten by him, and suspected that Ahaz was only the legal father of Hezekiah, in Diallact. p. 551, as did the Jesuit Torniellus, who made Nathan, the son of David, legal only or by adoption, and not by nature or by generation, whom he says was begotten by Uriah, annalib. ad Ann. M. 3987. n. 5. & ad Ann. M. 4037. num. 3, who nevertheless confesses that St. Matthew enumerates only natural generations, and that the word Begat, repeated through each one, clearly indicates this, ad ann. 4017. n. 15. Which fabrication about Nathan was already refuted in Lyranus by the blessed Luther in the book Schemphamorasch, Tom. VIII. Jen. Germ. t. 127, who likewise touted Nathan as the adopted son of David and the same as the Prophet: by which pact Christ would turn out to be the son of Uriah the Hittite, a Gentile man: which is most absurd. We pass over other inconveniences of a similar stamp with a dry foot.

§. XII.
