But what Grotius gathers from foreign writers, what adoptive parents are to the Latins, what τεκνοποιήσεσθαι is to Xenophon, what born and progenitors are to the poets, what is called תולדות by the Hebrews, γόνος by the Hellenists, and what are called deeds, how likewise the offspring born from the brother of a dead man is called the seed of the dead man himself, proves nothing, and is irrelevant and ἀπροσδιόνυσα here, where the matter concerns the phraseology of Holy Scripture, and the word ὀξυνεᾶν is being discussed, and the review of the genealogy, where the same method is applied regarding all in the descending line, so that it denotes generation, either immediate or mediate. There is no reason, therefore, for Grotius to criticize Africanus in this, as being more diligent than of accurate judgment in all things, because he relies on those words ἐκλόγως and εἰνομίζετο. Nor is it to be rashly believed that the greatest men followed Africanus in this without accurate investigation, with blind impulse, as the writer of the responses to the orthodox, Eusebius, Nazianzen, and others, in a dense column, namely that Jacob, called by Matthew the father of the same, was his father by natural right, but was called Joseph or Eli by St. Luke for another reason.

§. XIII. Furthermore, what Grotius observes thirdly, that Luke traces the lineage to Adam, the natural sower of all, but Matthew begins from Abraham, from whom the αἱ ἐπαγγελίαι: whence the right especially arises, begin, that can in no way help Grotius's cause. For Matthew did not begin from Abraham because he only wished to weave together the series of those who had some succession of right, without regard for blood, but because, with the genealogy deduced from the lineage of Abraham, the origin of the rest of Christ's ancestors could not be hidden, who were most known to all from Moses. Although in the meantime we do not deny that the descendants of Abraham and David were primarily recorded for that reason, because such notable promises had been made to them concerning the Messiah who was to come from their own seed. And the observation of the blessed Luther on Matthew 1 is beautiful. Just as Matthew wishes to prove that Christ came to the Jews according to the promise made to Abraham and David, so Luke wishes to show that the same Christ does not himself and his seed, that is, to all the nations of the whole world.

§. XIV. For lest we should doubt that the genealogy was woven from the stock of Abraham and David, the Evangelist himself took care, while he prefixed to this catalogue the title Βίβλον γενήσεως, while he testified that he was weaving the pedigree of Christ the son of David, the son of Abraham (for it is confessed by all that the name of son is not taken there in a legal sense, but of a natural son), while he always used the word ἐγέννησε, and it could be proven that it was not used improperly here in any generation, while he sometimes commemorated mothers and brothers, lest it be ambiguous that the pedigree of blood and family was being woven, while he concluded the whole genealogy with the generation of Christ from Mary v. 16, so that it might be clear that he had dealt not with the succession of right, but with the generation and lineage of Joseph, the husband of Mary, from whom Jesus was born. Finally, while he counted the generations and distributed them into groups of fourteen, and thus signified that they all held the same status, that is, that they were properly designated as generations, such criteria for genealogies and natural series Luke did not produce. For although he commemorates Adam as the natural father of all, yet he did not stop there, but ascended to God, and says that Adam was of God, from whom he himself was certainly not naturally procreated, and at the very beginning of the pedigree he prefixed the word ἐνομίζετο not without cause.

§. XV. It is still more trivial what Grotius asks fourthly regarding the number, namely that Luke counts seventeen persons between Salathiel and Joseph (for he strikes out two, namely Mathat and Levi, placed between Eli and Melchi, which audacity of his the consensus of the editions and versions of the sacred Code refutes), whereas Matthew recounts only ten. For by what artifice he is to conclude from that that the succession of blood was looked at by Luke, but not likewise by Matthew, we indeed cannot attain by conjecture, even if it be posited that Salathiel is one, and likewise Zorobabel is one in both Evangelists, in whom the two lines of Nathan and Solomon converged, whom, however, not a few affirm to be different. For it is not a wonder that in one line more intermediate persons are found than in the other. That it happens very easily that some family counts ten generations in that space of time in which another scarcely counts five, according to whether fathers began to be made at an older age than others, Possinus acknowledges in his Diallactic c. XLVIII, nor does Grotius deny it: often in the same space of time families compared among themselves have one or two more or fewer generations; so that we do not have the necessity to take refuge in the idea that the succession of blood was looked at by one Evangelist, and the succession of right by the other. And whence will it be proven that the succession of blood was looked at by Luke rather than by Matthew, against so many illustrious documents already brought forward for Matthew?

§. XVI. Nor is it of any moment that fifthly Matthew himself quite openly professes that persons are not counted by him, but the sum of the lineage is briefly indicated, digested into three groups of fourteen for the sake of memory. For whatever the cause of this digestion may have been (which Possinus in his Diallactic c. XXIX strives to prove was not done for the sake of memory alone, but because the names omitted were absent from the genealogical tables accustomed to be kept in the temple, as Josephus testifies in his book 1 against Apion, having been erased by priestly judgment, that is), it cannot at any rate be concluded from that that Matthew did not recount the lineage and pedigree of Christ according to natural succession: for it is not necessary that he who weaves a genealogy (which Matthew testifies he is doing here) should proceed from degree to degree, where the blood leads, without omitting any order; rather, led by his own plan, even if perhaps it is not sufficiently clear to us, he can freely omit some persons; in which matter it is by no means our place to prescribe a norm to the Holy Spirit, by whom Matthew was moved. The reason for this method, however, is not unlike the truth, which the blessed Chemnitius cites from Jerome, that Matthew distributed the genealogy into three groups of fourteen not so much to consult the reader's memory as to show that that line of Christ was designated by certain circumstances or signs in the principal changes of the status of this people, and that three times especially, in Abraham, in David, and in Salathiel or Zorobabel, that is, in the Patriarchs, in the Kings, and in the Leaders.

§. XVII. Finally, as regards the sixth point, the computation of times from Christ up to Zorobabel, it does not appear why that whole time cannot be filled by the persons recounted by Matthew, even if he followed the natural order, nor does anything prevent one from asserting that here too one or two persons were omitted by Matthew: just as Grotius himself in his Diatyposis brings forward seven persons anonymously, as if omitted by Matthew. In which part he indulges his own genius, as he does elsewhere, and assumes for himself a dictatorship over the sacred code, according to his own whim, which perhaps even more modest philologists would not grant him in profane authors.

§. XVIII. Furthermore, the things he argues against Africanus, the things he assumes from Africanus at his own pleasure, the things he asserts about others, whether from tradition or from his own genius, are not of such importance that we should dwell on discussing them. He himself professes that they are arbitrary and not examined, and indeed they are too arbitrary.

§. XIX. Of greater importance is the difficulty which he examines in the last place, how Zorobabel is called the son of Salathiel by both Matthew and Luke, when the writer of Chronicles calls him the son of Pedaiah. Where Pareus indeed thinks that Zorobabel was the natural son of Pedaiah and the legal son of Salathiel, having been raised up for him after his death by his brother from the wife left behind, according to the right of Levirate in Deut. XXV. 5. But for that reason, Salathiel, inasmuch as he died without children, could not be reckoned among the ancestors of Christ, but Pedaiah should have been reckoned by the Evangelist. Whence others think thus concerning Zorobabel, that he is called both the son of Pedaiah, because he was his parent, and the son of Salathiel, because he was not begotten immediately by him, but through Pedaiah. But this opinion is opposed, first, by the fact that Malchiram, Pedaiah, Shenazzar, Jekamiah, Hoshama, and Nedabiah seem to be brought forward as brothers of Salathiel in 1 Chron. III. 18. Now to insert here that בני 'sons', so that they may be referred to Shealtiel as the parent, which is done in the Dutch version, is to add something to Scripture. Secondly, that the sons and descendants of the Zorobabel mentioned by the writer of Chronicles are far different from those who are recounted by Luke or by Matthew, nor is any one named by the Evangelists found in that genealogy of the sons of Pedaiah of Zorobabel in the book of Chronicles. Thirdly, that the Ethnarch Zorobabel is perpetually called the son of Shealtiel, and nowhere, not even once, is he called the son of Pedaiah.

§. XX. For these reasons, therefore, we cannot cast our vote for those who derive this Ethnarch Zorobabel from that passage in Chronicles. Wherefore he was undoubtedly different from the Ethnarch: which opinion I see is also approved by

Grotius. But it is not yet concluded from that, unless other documents are brought forward and called in as support, that that one Zorobabel the Ethnarch is understood by both Evangelists, whom Matthew makes the father of Abiud, and whom Luke makes the father of Rhesa. Whom others wish to be different persons of the same name. Because Matthew's Zorobabel was born after the Babylonian captivity: but Luke's either before him, or in the first years of the same: inasmuch as the people returned from captivity under his auspices when he was already of mature years: from whom also seventeen generations occur to Mary, when between the Zorobabel of Matthew and Joseph there intervene only nine generations. And since it was predicted in Jer. XXII. 30, that no leaders of Judah would sit upon the throne of David from the seed of Jechoniah, B. Chemnitius in Harm. on Matt. I. c. III. gathers from that prophecy of Jeremiah that Salathiel and Zorobabel, who were leaders of Judah after the captivity, are different in Luke than those who are derived from Jechoniah in Matthew, and that the descendants of the latter lived deprived of public authority. Which also pleased others. And although it is admitted that Zorobabel the Ethnarch, the son of Salathiel the son of Neri, and both Abiud and Rhesa were begotten by that Zorobabel, it is not, however, to be conceded in any way that the Salathiel the son of Neri, shining with princely dignity, is the Salathiel of Matthew, nor is it true that Jechoniah died without children, for seven children of his are listed in 1. Par. III. 17. 18. and it is rashly introduced by Grotius into the genealogical line of Matthew, Assir, with Sedecias, of whom there is no trace in Matthew: nor is any genealogical relationship of Sedecias detected in this line. But Assir is a merely fictitious person. Whence it is clear that the Grotian scheme is as uncertain and rash as he was prompt in assuming or devising some hypotheses for weaving together the pedigree of Joseph and Mary, convenient to his own opinion.

§. XXI. Yet a doubt seems still to remain, when we establish that in 1 Par. III. 18. it is not Zorobabel the Prince who is listed, but some private individual, which resulted in the pedigree and mention of the distinguished Prince being neglected, with the private person's lineage being recorded? And since without doubt Zerubabel the Prince arose from the royal lineage, and thus his parent Salathiel must be derived from the same origin, whence it is not to be doubted that he was that Salathiel his parent, whom the author of the Chronicles and Matthew say begat King Jechoniah, why was he passed over, who was more worthy of being commemorated than others, while his father and grandfather and their descendants were mentioned in the genealogy? We think there is no other cause for this matter than that it was notorious that Zorobabel was the son of Salathiel, and that the Holy Spirit indicated the same thing elsewhere more often, namely in the books of Ezra, Nehemiah, Haggai, and Malachi, even if He did not make mention of this matter here.

§. XXII. Thus, therefore, we now exhibit the genealogy of Christ more correctly from both Evangelists in the subjoined scheme, having supplied only three kings in Matthew, omitted either for the sake of rounding off the sets of fourteen, or for any other cause whatsoever (whom we insert in smaller type), and having omitted Cainan, whom the Vulgate codices of Luke report, but which we have argued at length in the Sacred Critic to be an interpolation, and Grotius does not deny it. Which schematism will teach that the genealogy of Christ in the Evangelists is not in itself as perplexed as the various opinions of authors have rendered it, without serious causes.

§. XXIII. The difficulties introduced by others, the unfortunate error of Grotius did not so much diminish as increase. Which he seems to have received from Johannes Cordesius de Cordes, a priest and canon of Louvain, in his animadversions on Luke III., and which Petrus Possinus, a Jesuit of Toulouse, embraced, striving to prove in his Theogenealogical Dialectic that Luke held the natural lot everywhere, but Matthew, where that failed, followed the right of succession. But this Jesuit departed from Grotius in several points, and enriched his opinion with new discoveries, as is wont to happen. For not to mention that Possinus, page 517, says that the stock of the Salomonids failed completely in Jechoniah, which he proves by an excellent testimony worthy of a Jesuit, namely from the Revelations of Bridget c. XIX., and he omits Sedecias in the line of Solomon (whom Grotius introduced), and because, having left out Jechoniah, he very absurdly inserts MARY the Mother of God as the other of the third set of fourteen on page 511, he has invented that Joseph, whom he makes the natural son of Heli with Grotius, is called the son of Jacob only by this reason of adoption, because when he was born from the stock of Zara (the Jesuit perhaps meant to say Rhesa), the son of the other Zorobabel, he succeeded to the inheritance of the blessings upon the death of Jacob without children (which Jacob was the last of the line of Abiud, the firstborn of Zorobabel), and afterwards died before the adult age of Christ without leaving any offspring, and thus had Christ Himself as the legitimate successor of the inheritance of the blessings: drawing the right to these successions from HIMSELF, however, not deriving it from others. To have commemorated which discovery is to have solidly refuted it: whose author, the Jesuit, Possinus praises as another Johannes Bessonus, who in his lucubrations on the Song of Songs was the first to affirm that Joseph was the paternal uncle of Mary, which one thing he professes is worth a thousand to him.

§. XXIII. But Grotius explains his error to us thus on page 654. Truly I think that what the Desposyni said to Africanus, that Estha was first the wife of Mathan, then of Melchi, and thus they are of the same blood. But in Mathan the natural stock of Abiud was extinguished, which was the first of the stocks sprung from Zorobabel. Wherefore by the law of the widow, marriage was owed to the offspring to raise up a name for the dead, to him who was the prince of the second family coming from the same Zorobabel through Rhesa. And that he was Melchi, who begat Jacob, commonly called Panther by the surname of his natural father, but by the estimation of the law the son of the dead Mathan, and the successor of all his right. The right of this Jacob, who died without children, devolved to Joseph: and thus Joseph is called the son of Jacob, not by the law of the levirate, but because his inheritance had come to him, just as Sedecias is the son, as we have said, of Jechoniah. Joseph, however, if I calculate the reasoning correctly, was the son of Jacob's brother, and consequently Jacob was Joseph's paternal uncle. Mary, moreover, since she came from the other son of Melchi and was an ἐπίκληρος, was married to Joseph because no one closer existed to whose guardianship she might flee. These things Grotius, accepting from the opinion of Africanus what he saw to be subservient to his own ὑπόθεσις, while rejecting the rest at his own discretion.

§. XXIV. But why should we establish that the natural line of Abiud was extinguished in Mathan, and not extend it further with Matthew to Jacob and Joseph, when Matthew in the same tenor of words, verse 15, says: 'Matthan begat Jacob, and Jacob begat Joseph!' Why should we have recourse to the law of ἐπιγαμβρεύσεως, when the Evangelist persists in the natural series of generations! Furthermore, whence is it evident to Grotius that Jacob died without children, that he affirms this so boldly, and therefore abandons the explicit letter of Matthew, by which Joseph is called his son? Whence will it be taught that from the right of Jacob devolved to Joseph, this Joseph is called Jacob's son, and to have been begotten by him, even apart from the law of the Levirate, or, as Grotius speaks, not from the law of ἐπιγαμβρεύσεως [marriage by affinity], but because his inheritance had come to him! Certainly no suitable example from the Scriptures could be shown for such a thing. For concerning Zedekiah, an answer has already been given. Not to mention that Grotius assumes as certain that Mary was an ἐπίκληρον [heiress], to whom immovable goods had fallen by hereditary right. Which does not sufficiently agree with her poverty insinuated in Luke 2:7, 24: whom Theodoret, in his sermon to the Greeks VIII, called παρθένον χερνῆτιν, a virgin seeking her living with her own hands. By what right can she be called an ἐπίκληρον who could not transmit even a footstep to a son? He himself testifies that he had no little hut, nest, or cave where he might lay his head, says Jac. Cappel in his vindication for Casaubon, page 59. Casaubon, whom he ought to have vindicated against Andr. Eudaemon-Joannes in that, that he asserted Mary was an ἐπίκληρον, Exerc. 1. §. XIII.

§. XXV. It must also be carefully noted here that the old tradition, which Grotius reports from Epiphanius, agrees with Matthew in testifying that Jacob was begotten by Matthan, and Joseph by Jacob. Namely, that this Joseph of ours was the son of Jacob, called by the surname Panther, which Grotius does not think should be entirely rejected: since Joseph himself is also called by the same surname of his father. For Celsus also says that Mary conceived from a certain Panther, which he thinks he received from the Jews, who also call Jesus our Lord Panther in the book Midrash Kohelet and in the book Avodah Zarah. Thus, therefore, even by this tradition of both Jews and Christians, it is confirmed that Joseph was begotten by Jacob.

§. XXVI. And thus far the opinion of Africanus holds correctly, that Joseph was by nature the son of Jacob. However, he errs from the truth in that he makes the father of Eli to be Melchi, who begat him from Estha: since according to Luke, Matthat is the father, but Melchi is the great-grandfather of the same. Nor is that tradition of Africanus consistent with itself, in that it claims that Melchi married Estha, the widow of Matthan, and from her begat Eli, and that Eli having died without children, Jacob, his brother by the same mother (whom Estha had borne to Matthan), begat Joseph from his widow, who therefore was the natural son of Jacob, but the legal son of Eli. For as was rightly observed by Grotius, the law of ἐπιγαμβρεύσεως [marriage by affinity] pertained to preserving the rights of families. But families are reckoned by agnation; wherefore, when Eli died without children, it was not a uterine brother, who was not an agnate, who ought to have raised up offspring for him, but the nearest of the same family and name. Add that Melchi had no need to marry the widow of Matthan in order to raise up seed for a brother or a fellow-tribesman, since he was not so near to him, being sprung from the stock of Nathan, nor did Matthan die childless, but left a son, Jacob, according to Africanus. Therefore, that tradition, which Africanus in Eusebius, Hist. Eccl. book I, chap. VIII, seems to refer to the Desposyni, the kinsmen of the Lord, does not deserve belief, to which Africanus himself attributes little, concluding the same reasoning thus: Whether, therefore, this matter stands in this way or otherwise, in my judgment no one will be able to find an exposition clearer than these. But whoever is endowed with a fair mind will take care of the same thing as we do. Even if CERTAIN TESTIMONY IS LACKING, for the reason, clearly, that he could not bring forward a better and sharper exposition. Which things teach that that tradition was not held to be sufficiently certain by Africanus himself. Nor is the suspicion of B. Chemnitius perhaps vain, that those things were then spread by the Jews as if they had been handed down by the kinsmen of Christ, so that they might have a more plausible occasion and pretext for mocking our faith.

§. XXVII. It is certainly absurd that two Evangelists should have wished to weave the genealogy of one Joseph, and indeed under different names, whence there is material for the weak to fall and for the malicious to cavil, when yet Christ was not born from Joseph, nor ought to have been born, nor could have been. It is absurd that both Evangelists should have kept silent about the lineage of Mary, from whom, however, Christ was born: that neither should have demonstrated what had to be demonstrated: that Christ was born from the seed of David. For although it may be said with probability that Joseph, a pious man, married a wife from the same tribe and from the same family of the tribe, yet other contrary examples occur: and it will be easy for the enemies of the Gospel to object that in Mary, as a poor woman, the law was not in danger, and that many from the tribe of Judah itself also took foreign wives, and could have taken them, just as that was sometimes done in other tribes: and that nothing stood in the way of Joseph, however much he was sprung from Judah, taking a wife from the tribe of Levi. But how would it have been so evident at that age that our Lord has sprung from Judah, Heb. 7:14? Who would also believe that either Evangelist would so anxiously report the legal father of Joseph and his genealogy, while passing over that which was of the chief moment, who were the ancestors of Mary, the Virgin Mother of God? Concerning which see Andr. Osiander, annotations to book 1 of the Harmony, chap. XVI. It is not enough that Mary was inserted into the family of David through marriage; since she gave birth as a virgin, it is necessary that she herself also be the seed of David, if we are to believe that her son Christ was promised in the Law and the Prophets. And further: What is more alien to the providence of God than that the genealogy of Joseph should be proposed twice, and that in such a way that no one can explain its reason: but that the genealogy of the virgin should be entirely neglected, upon which, however, the highest certainty of the matter depends.

§. XXVIII. Some also urge this against Africanus, who says that Melchi, although he was sprung from another line, namely that of Nathan, married Estha, the widow of Matthan, who was sprung from the line of Solomon? Would not this marriage have been repugnant to the law, since Melchi was indeed a fellow-tribesman of Estha, but not a kinsman and near relative, let alone the nearest, being sprung from another line! But they assume that kinship was required by the law for the marriage of widows even in common cases outside the instance of ἐπιγαμβρεύσεως and the Levirate, when seed had to be raised up with a brother who died childless, which claim, how it can be proved or reconciled with other examples, does not appear. That, however, is by far the most false thing, which some followers of Africanus suppose, that it is sufficient that Christ was the LEGITIMATE successor of David, even if he were not his natural son, since he had to come forth from the loins of David according to the flesh, and thus by reason of his mother: since with respect to his temporal birth he was ἀπάτωρ.

§. XXIX. Wherefore it is altogether better, for the sake of reconciling the Evangelists, to establish that one of them weaves the genealogy of Mary, and the other explains the pedigree of Joseph; which latter, since it is too clear that it is done by Matthew, is most rightly assigned to Luke as the genealogy of Mary the Mother of God. Which opinion, as far as concerns the pedigree of Matthew, that a natural genealogy, or way of generation, was observed by him, has patrons, besides Julius Africanus himself in his Epistle to Aristides (in Eusebius, book 1, ch. 7), the writer of the Responses to the Orthodox, Eusebius, Gregory Nazianzen, Damascenus, and very many others, whom Grotius confesses follow Africanus in a body, and also St. Augustine, book II, On the Harmony of the Evangelists, chap. III. The reason for this is entirely ἀδιάλυτος [indissoluble]: Matthew, saying, Abraham begat Isaac, and thus persisting in this verb, which is begat, until he said at the end, and Jacob begat, sufficiently expressed that he had led the origin of the begetters back to that Father from whom Joseph was not adopted, but begotten. B. Luther. Vol. VIII. Jena. Germ. page 126. Schemhamphor. destroys the legal succession in Matthew by the fact that he omits three generations, saying: Joram begat Uzziah, who was distant from Joram by about a hundred years, and thus could not be his legal son: whence, having dismissed the distinction between legal and natural Father, he thus reconciles the different Fathers assigned to Joseph by Matthew and Luke: That Jerome writes, Jacob was Joseph's natural father according to St. Matthew's thread, but Eli, whom he also calls Eliakim and Joakim, (for all three are supposed to be one name, as with us Nicolaus, Nickel, Claus) was his father, according to Luke's thread, that is, his father-in-law, or father in the manner where a son-in-law is also called a son, and a son's wife is also called a daughter, and according to the law where a brother must let himself be called the father of his deceased brother's children, and be so, that pleases me so well, and better than Eusebius and Lyra, who thinks Jacob took his brother Eli's widow, and begat Joseph with her, then Mary (Joakim, or Eli's daughter) and Joseph would be children of the same mother, and natural siblings, that Moses does not suffer Lev. 18. But as far as St. Luke's genealogy is concerned, that the pedigree of Mary is woven by him, this opinion was defended besides the ancients, whose tradition Osiander praises, that Joseph was the natural son of Jacob, but the son-in-law of Eli himself, that is, that Eli who was truly called by the name Jehoiakim, was the Father of the virgin Mary, and the grandfather of Jesus Christ according to the flesh: Petrus Galatinus L. VII. de arcan. Cathol. Verit. c. XII. Dominicus a Soto in IV. sent. Dist. XXX. q. 2. art. 1. Genebrardus, Didacus Stella, Jansenius, Barradius, Vincentius Regius, and others among the Papists: and neither Bibliander, Aretius, Lavaterus, Deodatus, Franc. Junius, Pareus, Gomarus, Spanhemius among the Reformed: and after the great Luther, B. Chemnitius, Andr. Osiander, Hunnius, Gerhardus, Hülsemannus, Brochmandus, Winstrupius, Helvicus, Dn. D. Müllerus in Judaism. and most others of our side. B. Gerhardus Annotat. in Matth. p. 56. praises Osiander, who opposes two things to that distinction between natural and legal Father: 1. That it is unheard of among the Jews that the dead man is said to be the father of this firstborn and the son himself his, when it is not read in the Hebrew, and he shall raise up seed to his brother, but ויבמה and he shall levirate her, that is, he shall have her by the right of a levir. 2. That no one can beget such a successor, or legal son, from the wife of the deceased, unless he is the full brother of the deceased. But now Jacob and Eli were not full brothers: because Matthew traces the genealogy of Christ from David through Solomon, but Luke through Nathan, neither of whom died without children. It pleases me to bring here the whole discourse of Osiander, whose book is in few hands, since it is worthy of being heard, from Annot. ad Harm. Evang. l. I. c. XVI. Among all the Jews it is unheard of, and entirely like a monster, that they imagine that the dead man is called the father of such a firstborn, and the son himself his, of which they will certainly be able to elicit no testimony or example, neither from the sacred nor from the profane writings of the Hebrews, even if they had labored by investigating throughout their whole age. But it is entirely incredible, and indeed even impossible, that this custom of the Jews, by which such a firstborn is imagined to be called the son of that dead brother, if the law had established it, and the practice had once prevailed, could have been so obliterated, and torn from the memory of all the Jews, that no trace of it existed in any kind of literature. The cause of this error is that the Latin edition has, his brother shall take her, and shall raise up seed to his brother, to which that in the Gospel seems to assent, he shall raise up seed to his brother. Likewise that in Gen. thirty-eighth: Onan knowing that the sons would not be born to him. For from these words they gathered that the son of the dead man is also rightly called, if the survivor raised up seed not his own, but of the deceased brother, and knew that the sons were not born to him, but to the deceased brother. But as I said they are mistaken, for these words, he shall raise up seed to his brother, are not in the Hebrew, but in their place is read ויבמה which we have rendered paraphrastically, he shall have her by the right of a levir, since it sounds, he shall levirate her, if it were permitted to say so, and not even in the Greek edition do we read anything about the raising up of fraternal seed, but only καὶ συνοικήσει αὐτῇ, that is, and he shall cohabit with her. Furthermore, what is read in the Gospel, he shall raise up seed to his brother, is not to be understood of the seed of the deceased, but of the seed of the survivor: for those words of Christ say exactly the same thing as these words of the law, namely that the firstborn shall stand in the place of the dead: for if he ought to stand, he ought certainly to be erected, or raised up, by his Father: and if in the place of the dead, he is certainly raised up for the dead. Thus also it ought to be understood, what Judah speaks to Onan, Go in to your brother's wife, that you may raise up seed to your brother: for he does not say, that you may raise up his seed. For what is read in the vulgate translation about the same thing, Knowing that children would not be born to him, it is not so in the Hebrew, but it is read in this way: and Onan knew that that seed would not be his: by all of which words, and indeed by the law itself, nothing else is effected than that if a brother, who having taken a wife, could have already provided a citizen for the fatherland, and if it were necessary, a soldier, and could have increased the family with a new house, died without children, so that such a great ruin brought about by the death of one man might not go unrepaired, the brother is commanded to marry the wife of the deceased brother, and to substitute the firstborn from her in his place, having handed over to the same the inheritance of the deceased, which he had received together with his wife: which while he does, he is compelled to lose a son, not so that he ceases to be the son of the survivor, and begins to be the son of the deceased, but so that he who otherwise would have been a son under authority and perpetually under paternal power, as long as the father lived, he, now freed from paternal power, and entirely emancipated, may be placed as the head of a household in the house and inheritance of the deceased. And in this sense all the Jews, as well the ancient as the more recent, accept these words, wherever they may be met with יקום על שם אחיו that is, and he shall be raised up, or shall stand, upon the name, or in the place, of this or that man. But how difficult it was at that time to lose a son in this way, and to constitute him a head of a household in another's house, when many daughters gathered riches, and a large offspring was like a kingdom, can easily be estimated. Whence it is no wonder if the impious Onan was burdened to do this, since he thought that his seed, if it had grown up, would not remain in his own power. But that such a successor should have been reputed the son of him in whose place he succeeded is completely unheard of among all the Jews, and is nothing else than a monstrous figment of those men to whom it is evident that neither the sacred scriptures nor the civil law of the Jews were sufficiently known. But let us grant, however unfair the condition, that such a firstborn had obtained two fathers, and could be considered the son of either, yet it will still do nothing to remove the present difficulties. For no one can beget such a successor, or legal son, as they call him, from the wife of the deceased, except the brother, the own brother of the deceased: this is beyond controversy among the Jews, and is most evidently proved from the words of Moses. For he says: When brothers dwell together: which indeed does not happen unless they are from the same father: for those who have different fathers also receive different inheritances, in which, when they dwell, they do not dwell together. Then it follows: the wife of the deceased shall not be given to an outsider: but she is given to an outsider, whoever she is given to a husband who is not from the house of her former father-in-law. Finally, he commands that the Levir, that is, her יבם, should take her. But יבם signifies nothing else in the whole Scripture than the own brother of the husband. But since it is certain that Matthew traces the Genealogy of Christ from David through Solomon, and Luke through Nathan, his own brother, neither of whom died without children, it is clear and clearer than the sun that the posterity of neither could, according to this law, raise up a successor of this kind, or legal son, to the posterity of the other. How great, therefore, O immortal God, is the insanity that some imagine, that Jacob was the natural father of Joseph, and Eli the legal father of the same, or vice versa (for it makes no difference), when the natural and legal father of the same son must be own brothers? But Eli and Jacob are separated by so many degrees that they can now hardly be called kinsmen. For Jacob, descending from David through Solomon, drew his origin, and is, if I am not mistaken, the twenty-fifth from him. But Eli is descended from David indeed, but through Nathan, so that he is the fortieth from him. Let us go now, and hold as distinguished theologians those who dream up such monstrosities and foist them upon the world as oracles, I speak of those who first brought these figments to light: for to others, who were seduced by their authority, pardon is due. But those who have reviewed them as uncertain, to be discussed and judged, even deserve praise. All these things are Osiander's. Blessed Gerhard cites also the opinion of Augustine, lib. II. de Consens. Evangel. cap. 3. and lib. III. contra Faust. cap. 3., that Joseph had two fathers: one by whom he was born, the other by whom he was adopted. The former is described by Matthew, the latter by Luke. But the blessed one adds: The answer is very simple, that Heli, or Joachim, was the natural parent of Mary, but that he is called the father of Joseph in Luke by the custom used among the Hebrews, because Joseph, the son of the natural Jacob, was the son-in-law of Heli. Where indeed Osiander has also not irrelevantly noted that Luke does not call Joseph the son of Eli, but simply placed after his name, who was of Eli, so that it would be free for us to understand son-in-law, and not son. He adds: And lest it should trouble anyone that in other names son must necessarily be understood, he takes pains to carry the genealogy up to Adam, to whom, although he adds, who was of God, yet no one is so foolish as to accept that he is the son of God, but a creature. Thus the beginning and the end agree beautifully: For just as Adam is said to be of God, when he is not his son, but a creature: so Joseph is said to be of Eli himself, when he is not his son, but his son-in-law. Wherefore the interpreters seem to me to have committed no light offense (may it be permitted to say so with their respect and kind pardon) because they added son, since that is nowhere found in the Greek source. Although even if it were expressed, nevertheless this opinion of ours, or rather of the ancients, could still stand: for nothing would prevent it from being referred to Jesus and not to Joseph, so that the meaning would be: And he himself was Jesus, beginning to be about thirty years old, as was supposed, the son of Joseph, who however was the son, or grandson, of Eli. For since he was born alone from a virgin mother without male agency, he had no one on earth whose son he could truly be called, except Eli, his maternal grandfather. And lest anyone should wonder that the Evangelist, in weaving the genealogy, immediately leaped from the grandson to the grandfather, he interposed the reason: because Joseph, whom he ought to have called his father, was not truly his father, but only his putative one. But let us hear first of all Blessed Chemnitz, a diligent and accurate writer on the reconciliation of the Evangelists, who here carries off the palm from many in explaining the genealogy of Christ. The simplest, says Blessed Chemnitz, and most certain is that method which leaves and establishes the descriptions of the Evangelists as simply distinct and diverse without any change, or confusion, or addition: that Matthew weaves the royal line from David through Solomon, which held the scepter, down to Jeconiah, whose posterity, having been deposed from the throne of David (Jer. XXII. 30) and living a private life, produced Joseph, the spouse of Mary, from Jacob. But Luke weaves the line of David through Nathan: which lived privately until Salathiel, to whose posterity the succession to the throne of David, with the line of Solomon removed, devolved under the title of Dukes or Princes, down to Joanna. And because it is certain that after that Joanna, no one sat upon the throne of David, or that there was no Duke afterwards from the house of David; therefore from that Joanna the line of Christ must descend. From his posterity, therefore, the Virgin Mary arose, from whom, since by birth she was of the ducal stock of David, and by betrothal had passed into the family of Joseph, which was royal, Jesus Christ was born, King and Duke, or Prince promised by GOD through the Prophets. Thus there is no need to attribute two fathers to Joseph, but Jacob alone, who according to Matthew begat Joseph, was his true and natural father. But Luke does not say that Heli begat Joseph, but names Joseph of Heli; which phrase does not necessarily convince that he was the natural son of Heli. For Adam also is called there of God, when he was his creature. And Acts I. 13, Judas is called of James, i.e., brother, and Mark XVI. 1, Mary is called of James, i.e., mother. The Syrian paraphrast indeed adds to each בר son: but one is called the son of another not only by natural generation, but also in other ways: as the Apostle John is called the son of Mary, John 19:26. Just as therefore Naomi calls her daughters-in-law daughters, Ruth 1:13, so Joseph, the spouse of Mary, is called the son of Heli or Joachim, the father of Mary.

§. XXX. These things the blessed Chemnitius [says], whose learned reconciliation most others embrace with both hands, as being solid and immovable. In this way they make Joseph the son of Jacob by reason of consanguinity, as being the one by whom he was begotten, and [the son of] Heli by reason of affinity, as being the one whose daughter he took in marriage. And in this sense, Mr. Dr. Winstrupius affirms in Pandect. Sacr. on Matthew, page 59, that Heli was designated by Luke as the legal father of Joseph, whose natural father according to Matthew was Jacob. Who also, disputing against Calixtus, provides the reason, following the lead of the blessed Chemnitius with the blessed Brochmann and others, why it was necessary for the genealogy of Mary to be described by Luke, namely because once the tribe and family of the husband are known, the tribe and family of the wife are not immediately known, since it was permitted to enter into marriage outside the tribe, if there were no danger. the transfer of possessions through marriage, can be proven by the examples of Aaron, who married the sister of Nahshon from the tribe of Judah, Exod. VI. 25; of David, who married the daughter of Saul from the tribe of Benjamin, 1 Sam. XVIII. 17; of Jehoiada the priest, who joined to himself in marriage Jehosheba from the royal tribe, 2 Kings XI. 2; and in this very genealogy, little women occur—Canaanites, Moabites, Hittites—whose husbands were of the tribe of Judah; and even if it were most strongly established that Christ was from the tribe of Judah because his mother's betrothed and husband, Joseph, was descended from that tribe, it would not therefore be established that he himself was from the family of David; who, he says, is so blind that he does not see that it was absolutely necessary that, besides the genealogy of Joseph, the genealogy of Mary also be described by one of the Evangelists?

§. XXXI. To these, although Fried. Spanheim, Dub. XIV. p. 68, strives to respond, as does D. König, l. c. §. 12, that Israelite girls who were ἐπίκληροι and without consanguineous brothers could not, by the law of Num. XXXVI. 8, marry outside the tribe and not even outside the family: yet this response is as uncertain as it is uncertain that Mary was an ἐπίκληρος: and was it not permitted for Joseph to take a wife from the tribe of Levi? How then can it be certainly inferred that Mary is from the tribe of Judah, from the fact that she married Joseph, who was descended from that tribe? Where Spanheim indeed responds that it was permitted for Joseph, but that it was not done by him, as is evident from the genealogy of Mary, which is traced from the tribe of Judah by Luke. But D. König cannot use this response, because he denies that Luke describes the lineage of Mary. Wherefore he could not solidly respond to R. Lipmann and other Jews in this doubt, which they urge, as from R. Isaac Ben. Abraham it can be seen that Mary was from the tribe of Levi, which is also the hypothesis of Socinus. For from the marriage entered into with Joseph alone, it cannot be clearly established that she was from the house of David, if she herself is ἀγενεαλόγητος in the sacred writings. Concerning which the blessed Aegidius Hunnius has dealt more fully in his commentary on Matthew V. 1.

§. XXXI. Nor indeed is the opinion of Episcopius to be admitted in any way, that the genealogy of Mary is entirely superfluous, and that whether she originated from the tribe of Judah, or from the tribe of Levi, or from another by natural generation, it matters nothing, because she ought not to be reckoned from that, but from the tribe into which she had passed through betrothal, T. II. opert. resp. ad quæst. Theolog. LXIV. p. 1. q. 2. For since the Son of God assumed human nature only from the Virgin Mary, how could he be from the tribe of David with respect to that nature? If Mary, from whom alone he was born according to the flesh, is from the tribe of Levi or any other! It is a twin invention of Marcus Antonius de Dominis that Christ, through his legal father (Joseph) alone, civilly obtained the tribe of Judah and the lineage of David, by which the origin of Christ from the fathers according to the flesh is entirely undermined. Concerning which see Tertullian, lib. de carne Christi c. XXII. If from the loins of David, how much more from the loins of Mary FOR WHICH (not for whose betrothed) in the loins of David. And chapter XXII: From the seed of David is the flesh of Christ, but according to the flesh of Mary from the seed of David, not according to a legal respect and because of a legal Father who is from David. Conf. Fried. Spanheim, Dub. Evangel. p. 1. p. 129; Joh. Cloppenburg, Gangr. Anabapt. disp. IX.

§. XXXII. But if anyone says: thus the genealogy of Joseph would be superfluous, since the origin of Christ is sufficiently established from the genealogy of Mary, and Joseph was only the father of care, not indeed the begetter of Christ, unless this hypothesis is admitted, that from the genealogy of Joseph it can be solidly deduced that Mary was of the tribe of Judah, because Joseph, her betrothed, was of that tribe? Resp. It was known at that time that Joseph and Mary were of the same tribe, indeed of the same family, and since the History declares St. James to be of the house of David, Luke II. 4, into whose family Mary had passed through betrothal, so that the origin from the tribe of Judah and the family of David might be established on all sides, it seemed good to the Holy Spirit to deduce not only the lineage of Mary, but also that of Joseph himself, from the Patriarchs and from the Davidic stock. For since both lineages of Solomon and Nathan were reduced to a small number, with the near female relatives failing, from the line of Solomon, Joseph seems to have joined to himself in marriage Mary, who was descended from Nathan. Whence the Evangelists deduced both lineages, how Mary drew her origin from Nathan and Joseph from Solomon, and thus they were of the same tribe and family, and the common stock of both was King David. This doubt has now been clearly resolved by the theologian of exquisite judgment, the blessed Chemnitz: But that the Evangelists judged it not sufficient to have traced the genealogy of Mary, but also described the kinship of Joseph the betrothed, they did nothing alien to their office: because that very thing serves the confirmation of faith. For a wife, because she is made one flesh with her husband, passes by law into the family of the husband, whence she is also reckoned after betrothal and marriage: as the examples of the little women in the very Genealogy of Christ show. For that is done not only through what is called carnal copulation: but Moses also names and judges the betrothed themselves to be wives, Deut. XXII. 23. Luke therefore shows that Mary is by birth or origin from the seed of David, but Matthew adds that she did not pass into another house or family through betrothal, being betrothed to Joseph, who himself was also of the house and family of David: so that thus it is most firmly proven on all sides that our Christ is from the house and family of David, whether he be reckoned from the family of David, or be reckoned from the family of his mother, from whom he was born a virgin, or be reckoned from that family into which Mary passed through betrothal. These are the words of the blessed Chemnitz: Whom the blessed Winckelmann follows entirely in his commentary on Luke III, and Andreas Osiander agrees in his Annotations on the Harmony of the Gospels in chapter V. who observed that Matthew proposed the genealogy of Joseph especially for the sake of those who, although they did not deny that Mary was sprung from the house of David and that Jesus was born of her without male agency, nevertheless, if Joseph had drawn his origin from another tribe than that of Judah, were going to assert: that Mary with her son ought to be referred not to the tribe from which she was born, but to that into which she had been placed by marriage, for the reason that spouses, even if still virgins, are nevertheless one flesh. Therefore, that the Evangelist wished to either assist their error or heal their infirmity, etc. & chap. XVI. It was brought about by divine providence that Luke wrote the genealogy of the virgin, just as Matthew wrote the genealogy of Joseph her spouse, so that wherever you turn, whether you consider Mary from her parents or from her husband, you always find her with her son in the house and family of David. Blessed Gerhard followed this also in his annotations on Matthew, page 67. Matthew wished to describe the lineage of Joseph, Luke that of Mary, so that both persons, Joseph the putative parent of Christ and Mary his wife, might be shown to have descended from David, so that it might be manifested from both genealogies that Christ is the son of David, both by nature and by the right of marriages. Nor does he disapprove, p. 68, of the opinion of St. Augustine, book II de consens. Evangel. chap. 1. That it suffices that Joseph was held to be the father of Christ, nay, that he was indeed the father of Christ, because he was the husband of Mary the mother of Christ, not indeed by the commingled bond of the body, but by the guarded affection of the mind, not by the conjunction of bodies, but by what is dearer, the conjunction of souls. For he adds: Since by legitimate marriage Joseph was joined to the virgin Mary, and Mary was therefore a body, his body, and indeed he himself was one flesh with her, by right, even if not in fact (for spouses are one flesh by right before they come together, but in fact afterwards), the offspring born from Mary's flesh is deservedly considered to be born from his flesh. This is from the blessed Gerhard. Add to these things which the blessed Chemnitz has near the beginning and in chapter III of his Harmony: Because it might seem strange that the Nazarene virgin, betrothed to the Nazarene carpenter Joseph, should become the Mother of the Messiah, that former point must therefore not only be asserted, but demonstrated by a certain and firm reason, which Luke briefly states, that Joseph, to whom Mary had been betrothed, was of the house of David: and what Gabriel says in his embassy, the Lord God will give to him the throne of David his father. And because the Jews pretended that they were rejecting this Jesus for the reason that he was not from the seed of David, but originated from Galilee, John VII. 41. Matthew therefore shows that Joseph and Mary, although poverty had driven them into Galilee, were nevertheless certainly and truly from the seed of David, according to the promise. This again is from the blessed Chemnitz.

§. XXXIII. These things are certainly more solid than if we were to say with others, either that Matthew weaves the genealogy of Joseph only for the sake of a common, albeit false, opinion that Christ was believed to be the son of Joseph, and thereby teaches that, even if he were descended from Joseph, he would nonetheless be the son of David: or that it was done because it was most well-known to the men of that age, especially in Galilee, that Mary and Joseph were of the same tribe, and indeed descended from the same paternal grandfather, namely Matthan, whose sons were Jacob, the father of Joseph, and Heli, the father of Mary, from which it is easy to conclude infallibly that if Joseph descends from the royal family of David, Mary must necessarily also have sprung from that lineage: or that Matthew, writing to the Hebrews, had regard for the rule and law of the Hebrews concerning heiresses (ἐπικλήροις), who could not be married except by those who were of the same tribe and family, since once the tribe and family of Joseph were known, it was immediately permissible to determine the tribe and family of Mary. For the former reason is utterly absurd, that the Holy Scriptures would weave an entire genealogy for the sake of a false opinion, which it would have done not to destroy, but rather to confirm the same.

§. XXXIV. The other [argument] runs to this, that it was very well known at the time when the Evangelists were writing that Joseph and Mary were from the same family and house, which, even if it is easily conceded, yet the lineage and family of Mary would not be proven from the genealogy of Joseph, but from elsewhere, namely from the knowledge of the men of that age, as the blessed Chemnitz rightly warns, and so, with respect to them, there would have been no need for that proof of a notorious matter through the exhibition of Joseph's genealogy; but for subsequent centuries, to whom that kinship is not known, the origin of Mary from the Davidic stock could not be demonstrated from the bare genealogy of Joseph. But the point assumed in the same opinion, that Mary and Joseph had one and the same paternal grandfather, is built upon a foundation that is too slippery, uncertain, and indeed false, regarding a matter of such importance as the birth of the Messiah from the Davidic tribe. For from where will that hypothesis about one grandfather be proven solidly and firmly? And that the Matthan of Matthew is the Matthat of Luke is not only doubtful, but openly false: for Matthan was the son of Eleazar, the grandson of Eliud; but Matthat was the son of Levi, the grandson of Melchi: The former descends from Solomon, the latter from Nathan: and both ancestors are most distinct.

§. XXXV. The third likewise relies partly on a slippery hypothesis, namely, that Mary was the sole heiress of her paternal estates: for this is both uncertain and does not sufficiently agree with the description of Mary's poverty, nor does it appear how one could thus counter the Jews, Celsus, Porphyry, Julian, Faustus the Manichaean, the Socinians, and others, who contend that Christ, by reason of his mother, did not descend from the tribe of Judah, but from the tribe of Levi, since Joseph, even if he originated from the tribe of Judah, was prohibited by no law from taking a wife from the tribe of Levi, and in Leviticus XXII. 12 it is indeed holy that a priest's daughter marrying outside the tribe of Levi must abstain from eating the sanctified things, but it was by no means forbidden that she should marry outside that tribe.

§. XXXVI. Furthermore, a not insignificant difficulty seems still to remain: how Mary descended from the house of David, if her lineage is not to be derived from the royal stock through Solomon, but from the family of Nathan: since that royal house propagated through Solomon obtained the name of Davidic properly or principally. This was so certain to Calvin that he did not hesitate to assert that whoever strikes Solomon out of the genealogy of Christ, at the same time obliterates and deletes the promises in which he must be acknowledged as the son of David. But since the lineage of Christ is nowhere restricted to the line of Solomon, nor were those promises made to Solomon which were made to David concerning the Messiah who would come from his loins (2 Sam. VII. 14, Ps. CXXXII. 17), there is no necessity to restrict the origin of the Messiah to the Solomonic line. For the promises that were made to David remain safe, even if the birth of the Messiah is traced from Nathan, since Nathan was no less a son of David than Solomon. Whence the Reformed Doctors themselves here desert and refute their patriarch Calvin, especially Franc. Gomarus and Frid. Spanheim, the latter of whom is mistaken in that he still refers that promise of 2 Sam. VII. 14 to Solomon, albeit under the aspect of a type. For this is to be understood solely of Christ.

§. XXXVII. Add that it seems probable to some that the line of Nathan, from which Mary came, was joined with the Solomonic line through marriages, and that they converge, so that the paternal line of Mary the χρισοτόκꙋ descends indeed from Nathan, but the maternal from Solomon: Thus if Eli, the father of Mary, married the daughter of Matthan, the sister of Jacob, the natural father of Joseph, and from her begat Mary, the maternal grandfather of Mary will be Matthan from the Solomonic line, who was the paternal grandfather of Joseph, which will be more correct than if it is said that Neri, originating from Nathan, married the daughter of Jeconiah, who was born from Solomon, and from her begat Shealtiel, so that Zerubbabel the Ethnarch derived his origin by reason of his mother from Solomon, and by reason of his father from Nathan; from which Zerubbabel Joseph was begotten by Jacob through Abiud, but the mother of the Messiah arose through Rhesa, the other son of Joachim. However that convergence of the lines may be: let it suffice that Nathan was just as much a son of David by Bathsheba as was Solomon, 1 Chron. III. 5, and that God transferred the lineage of the Messiah from Solomon to Nathan regarding the mother's paternal family, whose descendants were Ethnarchs and leaders of the people.

§. XXXIX. Pareus indeed, in his Commentary on Matthew I, as also Maldonatus, Col. 28, maintains that Jeconiah married the daughter of Neri, from whom he begat Shealtiel, so that Neri was the maternal grandfather of Shealtiel, but Jeconiah was his natural father: and thus both the line of Solomon and the line of Nathan were common to Joseph and Mary, and furthermore that a specific line, as Pareus explains, ought to be established for Joseph from Abiud, the son of Zerubbabel, but for Mary from Rhesa, the other son of Zerubbabel. But Many things stand in the way of this genealogy, primarily that it was predicted in Jer. XXII. 30 that no one of the sons of Jechoniah would occupy the throne of David; how then are Sealthiel and Zorobabel established on that throne, as son and grandson of the same? Add that Mary, according to the paternal line, draws her origin from Nathan, as Luke demonstrates; and Neri is established as the father of Sealthiel, not the maternal grandfather in Luke's genealogy: Finally, it is assumed in this way that that Sealthiel, who is introduced in 1 Par. III. 17 as the firstborn of Jechoniah, was the father of Zorobabel the Ethnarch, when yet Sealthiel is left childless there, or rather no sons of his are enumerated, and only the sons of his brother Phadaja are commemorated, and among these someone called by the name of Zorobabel.

§. XL. Pareus indeed meets this doubt with this reasoning, that Zorobabel the Ethnarch was the grandson of Sealthiel through his brother Pedajah, and is called his son only by legal right, because he succeeded to his goods by adoption, or by another legal reason. But this reconciliation cannot be admitted. For first, the Evangelist Matthew observes a series of generation, not of legal succession, and says that Sealthiel begat Zorobabel, not indeed that he adopted him, or had him as heir and successor by some other reason: he thus passes over Pedajah entirely in this genealogical line. Furthermore, secondly, Zorobabel the Ethnarch is nowhere called the son of Pedajah; whenever that leader of the people is designated, he is named the son of Sealthiel. But how would the Holy Spirit describe him only by his legal father, while neglecting his natural one? Thirdly, that Zorobabel, who was by natural generation the son of the son of King Jechoniah, and had Jechoniah as grandfather, but Pedajah as the natural father of Jechoniah, could not be the heir of the Davidic throne or the leader of the people by the power of the prophecy and the edict of the Lord in Jerem. XXII. 30: for thus the divine sentence held: Write this man childless, for no man of his seed shall prosper, sitting upon the throne of David, and ruling anymore in Judah: whence neither Sealthiel the son of Jechoniah in 1 Par. III. 17, nor anyone else from his sons, or the sons of his sons, can be admitted to dominion in Judah, without prejudice to the truth of the divine edict.

§. XLI. Our Chemnitius, therefore, of blessed memory, with the guidance of Andr. Osiander, rightly establishes different Salathiels and Zorobabels, namely some in the line of Solomon according to Matthew, others in the line of Nathan according to Luke: he asks, however, in the former book of Chronicles, chapter III. 19 seqq., whether any names are found in the lineage of Zorobabel that correspond to Luke's enumeration? And these names seem to him to correspond. The grandson, he says, of Zorobabel, who is called Joanna in Luke III. 27, is called Hananiah in 1 Par. III. 19, and his great-grandson Semei in Luke III. 26 seems to correspond to Semeja in 1 Par. III. v. 22, just as Joanna, who is almost the last in 1 Par. c. III. 24, seems to correspond with Janna, who is the fifth from Heli in Luke III. 24. But since it is manifest in the aforementioned place of the Chronicles that Zorobabel is referred to from the line of Solomon, and his grandson Hananiah, and his great-grandson Semaja, and from the sons of Elionai, Joanna, it does not therefore appear how they can be referred to the descendants of the Zorobabel who descends from Nathan. Osiander thus brings out two Zorobabels: 1 Par. III. From Phadaja were born Zorobabel and Semei. Zorobabel begat Mosollamus. -- I ask you, reader, to remember that Zorobabel the father of Mosollamus is the son of Phadaja. Likewise, in Haggai I, it is written thus, that the word of the Lord came by the hand of Haggai to Zorobabel the son of Sealthiel, the leader of Judah. -- Behold for you, reader, now another Zorobabel. Where further, after some many things, Osiander has it thus: But rather it seems worthy of the greatest admiration that there have been those who thought that Sealthiel and Zerobabel in Luke are the same as those in Matthew. As if it were not most customary for the same names to be given to many, especially, however, to distinguished, illustrious, and praised men. From how few periods did I enumerate above three Mosollamuses, and those contemporaries? And do we wonder that there were several Zorobabels and several Sealthiels? Who hereafter, reader, will be able to convince you that two men who are of the same name are in reality two, and not one, if when you have heard the parent of each, different from the other, you do not acquiesce, but imagine besides that those two fathers, even called by different names, were one and the same man? But what can be said more manifest to prove two Sealthiels than that Sealthiel, in Luke, is the son of Neri, and not of Jechoniah, especially when the same Neri is said to have had Melchi as father, and not Joachim the father of Jechoniah? But if nothing else, certainly the meaning of the name will convince us that there were many Zorobabels at that time, if we note that it signifies 'deserter of Babylon.' For what father, provided he was pious, did not have in his prayers that all his sons be Zorobabels, who, when the time of captivity was completed, might happily abandon Babylon and return to the land of Israel? This is Osiander.

§. XLII. We add, however, a conjecture of the highest theologian (the blessed Chemnitius) from Josephus, book XII, ch. IV and V, perhaps not an unsuccessful one. He writes, he says, that in the time of Ptolemy Euergetes and Eupator, Joseph (whose name is clearly placed in Luke in this way) was an illustrious leader of Judah, and his son Hyrcanus, to whom the name of John was given, was his successor in the leadership, who, having laid hands on himself for fear of Antiochus Epiphanes, ended the principate of his family, and was the last leader from the tribe of Judah and the house of David. For the Maccabees afterwards drew the dominion to themselves. That John was commonly called Jannaeus then is indicated by Alexander called Jannaeus. Jannaeus, therefore, in Luke III. 24 is that John Hyrcanus in Josephus. And in 2 Mach. III. 11, the treasures deposited in the Jerusalem temple are written to be in the care of Hyrcanus, a man in a position of great authority, which seems to be a description of a leader or prince. This observation of our blessed Chemnitius does not seem to lack probability.

§. XLIII. But first of all, the change in the Jewish Republic is to be noted, which he deduces from Ezek. 21:26: namely, that after the return from Babylon, it was to be administered not by scepter and crown, that is, royal power, but by the miter, that is, the title of Leader or Prince, from the house of David. For Zedekiah also is called there not king, but leader, or Prince. And in those words, where the prophet says: cast down the high, exalt the low: he predicts the transfer of the government from the stock of Solomon, which had hitherto been high with scepter and crown, so that hereafter it would not even be distinguished by the miter, that is, by ducal dignity, and that the government was to be transferred to the stock of Nathan, which had hitherto been low and private. Therefore, with the scepter and crown removed from the royal line of Solomon, nevertheless, from the fruit of the womb of David, although from another line, the stock of Nathan sits in the miter upon the throne of David. The Prophet further adds that it will come to pass that after the crown or royal dignity has been removed from the posterity of Solomon, the miter or ducal power or dignity shall also be taken away from the other stock of Nathan, and shall be handed over, along with the miter and his crown, to him whose the judgment is, that is, to whom, according to the promise made to the seed of David, it is owed. He prophesies, therefore, that the miter and the crown, toward the end would yield for a time to others, who are not of the house and family of David. And he repeats three times, I will overturn, overturn, overturn the miter and the crown. For after the last leader Iannas, who was of the house of David, FIRST the Maccabees, who were of the house of Aaron of the first course 1 Chron. VI. 50. and 1 Macc. ch. II. v. 54. transferred to themselves the miter, that is, the power of the leaders. SECONDLY, the priests succeeding them, not content with the title and dignity of leaders out of private ambition, having put on the crown, claimed royal power for themselves. THIRDLY, to the family of Herod the Idumeans was transferred first the miter, under the name of guardianship to Antipater: then the crown, with the royal title, to Herod. These three changes the Prophet insinuated by that triple repetition, I will overturn, overturn, overturn, namely the miter and the crown. But the Prophet always adds; This, not this, because against the promise made to the house of David, they invaded the empire for themselves and administered it tyrannically. And the Prophet indicates that those changes were to be about that time when the promised Messiah was to come, when he says, until he comes to whom it is rightfully owed, the miter, namely, and the crown; and I will deliver it to him. These things agree most beautifully with the histories, and with that which Gabriel says of Christ; The LORD GOD will give him the throne of his father David, and he will reign over the house of Jacob etc. It was not therefore by chance or against the prophecies of the Prophets that it happened that some years before the birth of Christ, both the kingdom and the leadership ceased in the house of David, indeed in the very line of the Messiah. For in Amos IX. 11., cited by James in Acts XV. 15., it is written: The tabernacle of David at the time of the coming of the Messiah would not only be interrupted, but would have collapsed. And that stock of David, when the blessed shoot was about to come forth from it, had to stand, not as if it were flourishing in the dignity and power of David like a tall cedar, Ezek. XVII. 12. but as the stock of Jesse Is. XI. 1. obscure, ignoble, and private, from which it would not be judged that the scepters of rulers could be fashioned Ezek. XIX. 13. and from that it happened that the posterity of Iannas, being private, was thrust into Galilee. For Hyrcanus also ordered his son Alexander Iannaeus, to whom he wanted the kingdom to descend, to be raised as a private citizen in Galilee. All these things [are from] the blessed Chemnitius, which it pleased me to repeat in his own words, although they are a little prolix, because they contribute entirely to the illustration of both genealogies.

§. XLIV. But we must return to Grotius: Who now brings in some things from Greece, but without naming the place or the author: and relies here on a rumor alone, the author of which is uncertain. And another, he says, is a rumor mentioned by Greek writers, that Mary's father was called Iehojakim, his father Panther, Panther's father Barpanther, Barpanther's father Levi the son of Melchi, which is not to be rashly disapproved. It is not for us to divine where he has these inventions. He praised Damascenus afterwards: but those things do not agree with the account of Damascenus, even if this also is fabulous, and not easily accepted by anyone. For here he derives from Levi the son of Melchi in the series of Nathan, and Panther as brothers. Panther, he says further, begat Barpanther, so named from him. This Barpanther begat Iojakim, but Iojakim begat the holy Mother of God. Which Nicetas repeats in the chain of Greek Fathers on Matthew. But if you listen to Grotius, Melchi descended from Ianna, and from Melchi [came] Panther, or Jacob, as also Eli and Levi. From Levi, however, [he derives] Barpanther, not indeed from Jacob or Panther; from Barpanther he derives another Panther: and from this one Iojakim. Whence therefore Grotius has these dreams, which in no way agree with the inventions of Damascenus, let those see who rashly agree with him.

§. XLV. Who furthermore will convince, as is proper, that Mary's father was Jojakim, distinct from Eli? Which, even if it is asserted by some, has no foundation in the Holy Scriptures. And should it not rather be established that that Jojakim, who is also called Eliakim according to Grotius, is the very same as Eli, which the blessed Chemnitius makes a name contracted from that one? In which way also Galatinus, book VII of the secrets of the Catholic truth, ch. XII, judges that Eli was the very same as Jehojakim and teaches from Philo that those names Jehojakim, Eli, and Eliakim were the same. Indeed, he also proves by the authority of the Rabbis, especially R. Hakkadosch: that Mary's father was called both Eli and Jehojakim. To which opinion Iac. Capellus alleges this in the cited book from Gale Razeja; Heli is the same as Ioakimus. And from 2 Kings XXIII. 34. and 2 Chron. XXXVI. 4. it is clear that the names Iehojakim and Eliakim are the same: from which the latter, the name Eli could easily arise, the common people pronouncing that same thing more briefly. Osiander in Paraph. and the blessed Gerhard in his annotations on Matthew p. 57. observe that the names Eli and Iehojakim agree. Inasmuch as Iehojakim signifies To be raised up, Eli [signifies] the sublime: in which they have as a predecessor Andrew Osiander the Elder, who in his annotations on book I of the Harmony of the Gospels, ch. XVI, has it thus: For the name Iehojakim is of such a kind that, because of the first three letters which it has in common with the name of God יהוה, it was not permitted to profane it in daily use, whence no one will doubt that another was substituted in its place, which would be familiarly called Iehojakimus, who has diligently and exactly weighed those things which we wrote above in ch. 6. But that Eli succeeded into the place of the name Iehojakim is most credible, both because of the testimonies of the ancient Hebrews and Christians, and also because of the signification of both names; for יהוֹיָקִים signifies, to be raised up, to be exalted and to be made sublime, but עֵלִי (for far be it that we should believe it was called אֱלִי according to Annius) signifies, high or sublime. Similarly, for the same names, the blessed Luther has these: Iojakim, Eliakim, and Eli, in his tract on the Schem Hamph., the passage of which we cited above. And in this most people agree, that Eli and Ioachim are the same person, the father of Mary: just as most people [agree] concerning the mother of the virgin Mother of God with Epiphanius, Heresy LXXIX against the Collyridians, and Damascenus, book IV of the Orthodox Faith, chapter 15, and also Nicephorus, book II of Ecclesiastical History, ch. 3. and whom he cites, Hippolytus the Martyr, they determine to have been Anna, the wife of Joachim: although some derive her from the tribe of Levi, even B. Luther in the cited place, but only conjecturally, because, as Christ had to be both King and priest, the paternal family of Mary was Royal, the maternal was Priestly: which indeed seems rather to be derived from the Royal Davidic tribe in respect to both maternal and paternal family, since Christ was designated High Priest not according to the Levitical order, but according to the order of Melchizedek, and it is manifest that the Lord sprang out of Judah, Heb. VII. 14. just as Damascenus in his second oration on the Nativity of Mary said to St. Anna, how blessed is the house of David, from which you have come forth! concerning which compare what we said in question XXXVII. Iob. Maldonatus agrees in his commentary on Matthew, ch. I, col. 26. It is not established that Christ had any priestly lineage from the tribe of Levi; indeed, some remarkably learned men, and Catholics, have precisely denied this in our time, which St. Paul also seems to deny in the entire seventh chapter of the Epistle to the Hebrews. Where Maldonatus also responds to the objection concerning the kinship of the Blessed Virgin with Elizabeth, who was of the lineage of Aaron, Luke ch. I, v. 36, that it is easily resolved if the father or some grandfather of Elizabeth from the tribe of Levi had at some time taken a wife from the tribe of Judah and the family of David, whence that kinship arose. Which is also the answer of many others, and satisfies the doubt. For in order for that kinship to be consistent, there is no need for Mary to descend from the tribe of Levi; it suffices if some one of Elizabeth's progenitors had taken a wife from the family of David. Thus our blessed Gerhard answers in Annot. ad Matth. p. 20. That a certain Levite, to whom it was permitted by law to marry into any tribe (because they were not counted among the twelve tribes and had no proper lot of land, and therefore would introduce no confusion of possessions by marrying), had taken a certain woman from the ancestors of Elizabeth, who was descended from the tribe of Judah, in such a way that Elizabeth could be both a kinswoman of Mary and a daughter of Aaron. Similarly Cloppenburg in Gangr. Anabapt. disp. IX. th. 15. Spanhem. in dub. Evangel. part. 1. p. 71.

Luke's genealogy, if it be said that Eli or Jojakim, the natural father of Mary, who was descended from the line of Nathan, which Luke traces without interruption, had taken a wife from the Solomonic line, exhibited by Matthew, Anna, the daughter of Matthan—which name is commonly attributed to the mother of the θεοτόκy—the sister of Jacob, the father of Joseph: for by this reasoning the maternal grandfather of the Mother of God will be Matthan, and the same will be the paternal grandfather of Joseph, according to nature, nor will there be any need for a confusion of natural and legal generation, which introduces mere confusion and inexplicable complications, and MARY will descend, by reason of her paternal family, from Nathan, but by reason of her maternal family, from Solomon, nor will anyone in the line of either Matthew or Luke have been mentioned in vain, or hold any merely legal respect; and that assertion of the blessed Luther will remain, Tom. IIX. Jen. Germ. f. 26. That both Evangelists introduce only children of David, and both remain in the house of David, counting no children of the cot, or of strange blood. But finally there must be exhibited

§. XLVI. Therefore, having dismissed uncertain, apocryphal, and false traditions, it seems more agreeable to the certain, Canonical, and in no way doubtful Matthew, and SCHEMATISM OF THE GENEALOGY OF CHRIST, ACCORDING TO BOTH EVANGELISTS.

Latin:

Vers. 23. κὶ αὐτὸς ἦν ὁ Ἰησοῦς ὡσεὶ ἐτῶν τριάκοντα ἀρχόμενος ὢν] Omnino rectior videtur constructio si ὢν superioribus jungamus. Neque enim recte dicitur ἄρχομαι ἤ τριάκοντα, sed potius ἄρχομαι ἔτος τριακοστ͂, quod est annum ago tri- cesimum. At ἄρχομαι ὢν ἐτῶν τριάκοντα est incipio jam esse tricenarius, quod non dicitur nisi post impletum annū tri- cesimum: sicut anniculus quis dicitur Juris Romani aucto- ribus non statim ut natus est, sed trecentesimo sexagesimo quinto die. Quod ut recte observavit vir in omni litera- rum genere summg, ita eidé assentiri non possum cum ὡσεὶ hoc Lucæ loco putat esse positum vice Caph veritatis ut He- bræi vocant. Nam id Caph Græci per ὡς exprimunt, ut cum dicitur δόξαν ὡς μονογενοῦς: quod ipsum locum non ha- bet nisi cum res altera alterius nota est, ut majestas illa do- cebat Jesum esse Dei filium unicum. At hic non est ὡς sed ὡσεὶ, quod numero aut mensuræ additum significat id quod dicimus circiter aut admodum, ut Matth. XIV. 21. Marc, VI. v. 44. Infra IX. 14. XXII. 41, XXIII. 44. Joh. IV. 6. VI. 10. XIX 14. Neque illa rei alterius per alteram notatio hic lo- cum habet. Veterum multi, cum hoc satis perspicerent, putarunt per ὡσεὶ significari aliquid ad annum tricesimum Christo defuisse; quorum sunt Irenæus & Epiphanius qui Novembri Christum vult baptizatum, cum natalis ejus Ja- nuario immineret. At hoc si Lucas voluisset quid opus fu- erit addere illud ἀρχόμενος; Deinde omnino hæc tam accu- rata descriptio tempus aliquod legitimum respicit. Lex quæ extat Num. IV. 3. & 47. addita historia 1. Paral. XXIII. 2. di- serte docet Levitas justam functionem demum aggressos cum essent בְּנֵי שְׁלֹשִׁים שָׁנָה, id est, tricenarii, quan- quam ut alia lex docet Num. IIX. 24. anno vicesimo quinto exacto jaciebant ministerii sui rudimenta, quomodo & apud Achæos aliasque gentes tricesimus annus legitimus ad gerendos Magistratus. Ad hoc exemplum voluit Deus & Baptistam (qui sex mensibus natu major Christo, tanto etiam ante munus suum est auspicatus) & ipsum Christum anno demum tricesimo peracto, exordiri functionem ipsis mandatam. Neque tamen nulla vis est particulæ ὡσεὶ. So- let enim circiter tempus aliquod factum aliquid dici, non minus ubi aliquid excessit, quam ubi deeft ad præcisam no- tationē, ut videre est & infra XXII. 59. & apertissime XXIII. 44. collato Marci loco XV. 33. Significat ergo Lucas Chri- stum non ipso natali die, sed aliquot post diebus venisse ad baptismum, quod ipsi auspicandi muneris initium fuit. Ac ne hæc interpretatio omni veterum auctoritate destituta credatur, sciendum est, ita sensisse Chrysostomum, qui Christum ait venisse ad baptismum post annos triginta.
