XXII. 30. privatam vitam agens, ex Iacobo produxit Josephum sponsum Ma- riæ. Lucam vero contexere lineam Davidis per Na- thanem: quæ privata vixit usque ad Salathielem, ad cujus posteritatem successio in solium Davidis, re- mota Salomonis stirpe, titulo Ducum sive Princi- pum, devoluta fuit usque ad Iohannam. Et quia certum est post Iohannam illum, nullum sedisse super solium Davidis, seu nullum postea fuisse Ducem ex domo Davidis; ideo ex illo Iohanna oportet lineam Christi descendere. Ex hujus igitur posteritate Ma- ria virgo orta est, ex qua cum nativitate esset ex stirpe Davidis ducali, & per desponsationem in Jose- phi familiam, quæ regia erat, transiisset, natus est Iesus Christus, Rex & Dux, vel Princeps a DEO per Prophetas promissus. Ita non opus est Josepho duos attribuere patres, sed solus Iacobus, qui se- cundum Matthæum Josephum genuit, verus & natu- ralis ipsius pater fuit. Lucas vero non dicit Heli genuisse Josephum, sed Josephum nominat τοῦ Ἡλὶ; quæ Phrasis non necessario convincit, quod filius na- turalis fuerit Heli. Nam & Adam ibi dicitur τοῦ Θεoῦ, cum ejus esset creatura. Et Act. I. 13. vocatur Judas Ἰακώβου scil. frater & Marc. XVI. 1. vocatur Maria Jacobi, scil. mater. Syrus quidem Pa- raphrastes singulis addit בר filius: sed non tantum naturali generatione, verum etiam aliis modis vo- catur quis filius alterius: ut Johannes Apostolus vocatur filius Mariæ, Iohan. XVI, 26. sicut igitur Noë- mi nurus suas vocat filias Ruth. I. 13 ita Joseph Sponsus Mariæ vocatur τοῦ Ἡλὶ seu Ioachim Patris Mariæ gener.

§. XXX. Hæc B. Chemnitius, cujus eruditam conciliationem plerique alii ambabus amplectun- tur manibus, utpote solidam, atque immotam. Quo pacto Josephum Jacobi filium faciunt ratio- ne consanguinitatis, utpote à quo generatus sit, Heli ratione affinitatis, utpote cujus filiam in matrimonium duxerit. Atque hoc sensu He- li à Luca Josephi Patrem legalem designatum es- se, cujus Pater secundum Matthæum naturalis Jacobus fuerit, affirmat Dn. D. Winstrupius in Pandect. Sacr. ad Matth. pag. 59. Qui et- iam adversus Calixtum disputans, causam, præeunte B. Chemnitio cum B. Brochmanno, & aliis, reddit, cur opus fuerit genealogiam Ma- riæ a Luca describi, quod nempe cognita tribu, ac familia mariti, non statim cognoscatur tri- bus, & familia uxoris, siquidem licuisse con- jugium extra tribum inire, si periculum nullum esset translationis possessionum per nuptias, exemplis probari possit Aaronis, qui sororem Nahassonis de tribu Juda duxit Exod. VI. 25. Davidis, qui filiam Saulus de tribu Benjamin, 1. Sam. XVIII. 17. Jojadæ sacerdotis, qui Jesebam è tribu Regia sibi matri- monio junxit 2. Reg. XI. 2. & in hac ipsa genealogia mulierculæ occurrant Chananææ, Maobitides, He- thææ, quarum mariti de tribu Juda erant; ac si ma- xime Christum è tribu Juda esse exinde constaret, quod matris ejus sponsus, & maritus, Josephus ex illa tribu oriundus esset, haud tamen ideo i- psum è familia Davidis esse, constiturum; quis non cæcus, inquit, non videt omnino necesse fuisse, ut præter Josephi genealogiam etiam genealogia Mariæ ab aliquo Evangelistarum describeretur?

§. XXXI. Ad quæ etsi Fried. Spanhem. Dub. XIV. p. 68. respondere satagat, ut & D. Köning. l. c. §. 12. puellas Israeliticas quæ ἐπίκληροι & sine fratri- bus consanguineis fuere vi legis Num. XXXVI. 8. non potuisse extra tribum ac ne quidem extra familiam nu- bere: tam incerta tamen hæc responsio est, quam incertum, Mariam ἐπίκληρον fuisse: & annon Jo- sepho integrum erat, conjugem ex tribu Levi ducere? Qui ergo certo inferri potest, Mariam è tribu Juda esse, eo quod Josepho ex illa tribu oriun- do nupserit? Ubi respondet quidem Spanhem. integrum id Josepho fuisse, sed id ab eo non factum esse è genealogia Mariæ, quæ è tribu Juda texitur à Luca, constare. Verum hac responsione uti non potest D. König, quia negat Lucam stemma Mariæ delcribere. Quapropter R. Lipmanno aliisque Ju- dæis solide respondere non potuit, in hoc dubio, qua illi urgent, ut è R. Isaac. Ben. Abraham videre est, Mariam e tribu Levi fuisse, quæ etiam Socin. est hypothesis. Ex solo enim matrimonio cum Jo- sepho inito constare liquido non potest, eam fuisse ex domo Davidis, si ipsa in sacris sit ἀγενεαλό- γητ⃝. De quo fusius egit B. Æg. Hunnius in comment. in Matth. V. 1.

§. XXXI. Nec vero ullatenus admittenda Epi- scopii opinio, supervacaneam prorsus esse Mariæ ge- nealogiam, ac sive ex tribu Juda, sive ex tribu Levi, sive ex alia orta illa sit per naturæ generatio- nem, nihil referre, quia censeri illa non debuerit ex ea, sed ex illa tribu, in quam per desponsatio- nem transierat, T. II. opert. resp. ad quæst. Theolog. LXIV. p. 1. q. 2. Nam quum nonnisi à Maria Vir- gine humanam naturam affumserit Filius DEI, quomodo naturæ istius respectu è tribu David es- se potuit? Si Maria, è qua sola ortus est secun- dum carnem è tribu Levi aut alia quacunque sit! Gemellum est commentum M. Antonii de Domi- nis Christum per solum patrem legalem (Josephum) civiliter & tribum Judæ sortitum esse, & stirpem David, quo labefactatur prorsus Origo Christi è patribus secundum carnem. Quo de Tertul. l. de carn. Christi c. XXII. Si ex lumbis David, quan- to magis ex lumbis Mariæ OB QUAM (non ob cu- jus sponsum) in lumbis David Et cap. XXII. Ex semine David caro Christi, sed secundum Mariæ carnem ex semine David, non secundum legalem respectum & ob Patrem legalem, qui è Davide sit. Conf. Fried. Spanhem. Dub. Evangel. p. 1. p. 129. Joh. Cloppenb. Gangr. Anabapt. disp. IX.

§. XXXII. Si quis vero dicat; ita supervaca- neam fore genealogiam Josephi, quum è Mariæ ge- nealogia origo Christi satis constet, ac Josephus Pater curæ tantum fuerit, non vero genitor Chri- sti, nisi admittatur hæc hypothesis, quod ex Josephi genealogia solide deduci possit, Mariam de tribu Juda fuisse, eo quod Josephus sponsus ipsius ex ea tribu fuerit? Resp. Notum erat tum temporis Jose- sephum & Mariam esse contribules, imo ejusdem esse familiæ, & quum Historia S. Jacobum de domo Davidis esse perhibeat, Luc. II. 4. in cujus familiam per desponsationem transierat Maria, ut undiqua- que stabiliretur origo è tribu Juda, & familia Da- vidis, visum fuit S.S. deducere non tantum stemma Mariæ, sed ipsius quoque Josephi, inde à Patriar- chis, & ex stirpe Davidica. Prosapia enim utraque Salomonis & Nathanis ad exiguum redacta nume- rum, deficientibus propinquis fœminis, è Salo- monis linea, Josephus Mariam à Nathane oriun- dam matrimonio sibi junxisse videtur. Unde u- trumque stemma deduxêre Evangelistæ, quomo- do & è Nathane ortum traxerit Maria, & è Salomo- ne Josephus, adeoque ejusdem & tribus & familiæ fuerint, & utriusque stirps communis Rex David extiterit. Expedivit jam dubium hocce luculenter exquisiti judicii Theologus B. Chemnitius; Quod vero Evangelistæ judicarunt, non sufficere Mariæ ge- nealogiam texuisse, sed & Josephi sponsi cognationem descripserunt, nihil ab officio suo alienum fecerunt: quia illud ipsum servit confirmationi fidei. Uxor e- nim, quia cum marito una caro efficitur, lege trans- it in familiam mariti, unde etiam post desponsatio- nem & nuptias censetur: sicut exempla muliercula- rum in ipsa Genealogia Christi ostendunt. Illud enim non tantum per carnalem, quod dicitur, co- pulam fit: sed & ipsas sponsas Moses nominat & ju- dicat uxores, Deut. XXII. 23. Lucas igitur ostendit, Mariam nativitate seu origine esse ex semine Davidis, Matthæus vero addit, ipsam per desponsationem non transiisse in aliam domum vel familiam, despon- satam Josepho, qui & ipse fuit de domo & familia Davidis: ut ita undique firmissime probetur, Chri- stum nostrum esse ex domo & familia Davidis, sive censeatur ex familia Davidis, sive censeatur ex fa- milia matris, ex qua virgine natus est, sive ex illa familia, in quam Maria per desponsationem transiit, censeatur. Hæc B. Chemnitius: Quem ex asse se- quitur B. Winckelm. commentar. in Luc. III. con- sonatque Andr. Osiander Annot. in Harm. Evang. in c. V. qui observavit, propter eos præcipue Ge- nealogiam Josephi proposuisse Matthæum, qui li- cet Mariam de domo Davidis ortam, Jesumque ex ea sine opera virili natum esse non abnuerent, tamen si Josephus ex alia, quam tribu Juda originem duxisset, asserturi erant: Mariam cum filio suo, non in eam tribum, ex qua nata, sed in quam fuisset matrimo- nio collocata, referri debere, propterea quod con- juges, quamvis adhuc virgines, una tamen caro sint. Eorum igitur vel errori fuccurrere, vel infirmi- tati mederi voluisse Evangelistam, &c. & cap. XVI. Divina providentia factum est, quod Lucas scripserit genealogiam virginis, sicut Matthæus scripsit genealogiam Josephi sponsi ejus, ut quo te vertas, sive Mariam ex parentibus æstimes, sive ex marito, semper tamen eam cum filio suo in domo & familia Davidis invenias. Sequutus hoc etiam B. Gerhard. ann. in Matth. pag. 67. Matthæus Jo- sephi, Lucas Mariæ genus describere voluit, ut sit utraque persona Joseph putativus Christi parens & Maria ipsius uxor ostenderetur à Davide descendisse, ut ex utraque genealogia manifestaretur, Christum esse Davidis filium, tum naturæ, tum connubiorum jure. Nec improbat p. 68. S. Augustini senten- tiam l. II. de consens. Evangel. cap. 1. Suffice- re, quod Josephus habitus fuerit Christi pater, quin & fuisse ipsum Christi patrem, quia fuerit Mariæ matris Christi conjux, non quidem permixto corpo- ris nexu, sed custodito mentis affectu, non conjun- ctione corporum, sed quod carius est conjunctio- ne animorum. Addit enim. Cum legitimo ma- trimonio conjunctus esset Josephus virgini Mariæ, es- setque proinde Maria corpus, corpus illius, quin & ipse cum ea esset una caro, jure, etsi, non re (sunt e- nim conjuges una caro jure, priusquam convenirent, re autem post) proles ex Maria carne genita ex ejus carne genita merito censetur. Hæc B. Gerhardus. Adde his, quæ B. Chemnitius sub initium ac cap. III. Harmoniæ suæ habet: Quia mirum videri pos- set, Nazarethanam virginem Josepho fabro Naza- rethano desponsatam, Matrem Messiæ fieri, illud i- gitur prius non tantum asseverandum, sed certa ac firma ratione demonstrandum est, quod Lucas bre- viter dicit, Josephum, cui Maria desponsata fue- rat, de domo Davidis fuisse: & quod Gabriel in sua legatione inquit, dabit ei Dominus Deus thronum Davidis Patris ipsius. Et quia Judæi prætendebant, se ideo Jesum hunc repudiare, quod non ex semine Davidis, sed ex Galilæa esset oriundus Joh. VII. 41. Matthæus igitur ostendit, Josephum & Mariam, li- cet paupertas ipsos in Galilæam expulisset, fuisse ta- men certo ac vere ex semine Davidis, juxta promis- sionem. Hæc iterum B. Chemnitius.

§. XXXIII. Quæ sane solidiora sunt, quam si cum aliis dicamus, vel quod solum communis, etsi falsæ opinionis gratia, quod Christus Josephi fi- lius creditus fuerit, Matthæus Josephi genealo- giam pertexat, eoque doceat, etiamsi maxime è Josepho oriundus esset, fore ipsum nihilomi- nus Davidis filium: vel quod ideo id factum, quia tum illius seculi hominibus maxime in Ga- lilæa notissimum fuerit, Mariam & Josephum contribules esse, imo ab eodem avo paterno, nem- pe Matthan descendere, cujus filii fuerint Jacobus, Josephi, & Heli Mariæ Pater, unde infallibiliter colligere promptum sit, si Joseph è regia Davidis familia descendat, necessario etiam Mariam ex ea prosapia ortam esse: vel quod Matthæus, Ebræis scribens, Ebræorum regulam & legem respexerit de virginibus ἐπικλήροις, quæ duci non potuerint, nisi ab iis, qui ejusdem tribus & familiæ essent, quum ita cognita Josephi tribu & familia proti- nus statuere licuerit de Maria & tribu, & familia. Prior enim ratio perquam absurda est, quod S. S. in gratiam falsæ opinionis integram genealogiam pertexat, quod non ad profligandam, sed confir- mandam eandem potius fecisset.

§. XXXIV. Altera eo decurritur, notissimum tunc, cum Evangelistæ scriberent, fuisse, Jose- phum & Mariam ex eadem familia & domo fuis- se, quod etsi facile concedatur, ita tamen non ex genealogia Josephi, sed aliunde genus & familia Mariæ probaretur, nempe ex notitia hominum, istius seculi, ut recte monet B. Chemnitius, adeo- que istorum quidem respectu ea probatione rei no- toriæ opus non fuisset, per exhibitionem nempe genealogiæ Josephi, subsequentibus vero secu- lis, quibus ea συγγένεια nota non est, ex nuda genealogia Josephi Mariæ origo è stirpe Davidica demonstrari non posset. Qua vero in eadem sententia assumitur, unum eundemque Mariæ & Josephi avum fuisse paternum, res tanti momenti, de ortu Messiæ è tribu Davidica, fundamento ni- mis lubrico, incerto, imo falso superstruitur. Un- de enim illa hypothesis de uno avo probabitur so- lide, ac firmiter? Et Matthanem Matthæi esse Mat- thatum Lucæ non dubium modo, sed aperte fal- sum est: nam Matthan filius Eleazari, nepos E- liudi fuit: Matthat vero fuit filius Levi, nepos Melchi: Ille à Salomone, hic à Nathane descendit: & utrique majores sunt distinctissimi.

§. XXXV. Tertia itidem partim lubricæ inni- titur hypothesi, nempe, quod Maria unica fuerit paternorum prædiorum hæres: hoc enim & incer- tum est, & cum descriptione paupertatis Mariæ non satis convenit, nec apparet, quomodo Ju- dæis, Celfo Porphyrio, Juliano, Fausto Mani- chæo, Socinianis, aliis, Christum ratione matris non e tribu Juda, sed e tribu Levi descendere conten- dentibus ita obviam iri possit, siquidem Josephus etsi e tribu Juda oriundus, e tribu Levi uxorem du- cere nulla lege prohibitus fuerit, & Levit. XXII. 12. sanctum quidem sit, quod filia Sacerdotis extra tribum Levi nubens a sanctificatorum esu abstinere debeat, ni autem extra tribum illum nuberet, neu- tiquam interdictum fuerit.

§. XXXVI. Cæterum difficultas non levis ad- huc superesse videtur: quo pacto Maria e domo Davidis descenderit, si non e stirpe Regia per Salo- monem prosapia ejus derivanda, sed e Nathanis familia: siquidem Regia illa domus per Salomo- nem propagata nomen Davidicæ proprie, aut præ- cipue obtinuerit. Quod Calvino adeo certum fuit, ut asserere non dubitarit, quisquis Salomonem ex- pungit e Christi genealogia, illum simul promissiones, in quibus agnosci debeat filius Davidis, obliterare ac delere. Sed quum nuspiam ad Salomonis lineam adstringatur Christi prosapia, nec factæ Salomoni eæ promissiones sint, quæ Davidis, de Messia e lum- bis ejus prodituro 2. Sam. VII. 14. Ps. CXXXII. 17. nulla est necessitas originem Messiæ ad Salomo- neam lineam restringendi. Quæ enim Davidi fa- ctæ sunt promissiones, salvæ manent, etiamsi ortus Messiæ a Nathane deducatur, siquidem Nathan non minus, quam Salomo Davidis filius fuerit. Unde Patriarcham suum Calvinum hic deserunt, & refellunt ipsimet Doctores Reformati, Franc. Gomarus imprimis, & Frid. Spanhemius, qui po- sterior in eo fallitur, quod adhuc ad Salomonem, quanquam sub ratione typi promissionem illam 2. Sam. VII. 14. referat. Hæc enim unice de Chri- sto intelligenda.

§. XXXVII. Adde, quod probabile quibusdam videatur, lineam Nathanis, e qua Maria prodiit, cum Salomonica per matrimonia copulatam fuisse, ac concurrere, ita ut Mariæ χρισοτόκꙋ pater- na linea descendat quidem a Nathane, materna vero a Salomone: Ita si Eli Mariæ pater duxit fi- liam Matthanis Jacobi Patris Josephi naturalis so- rorem, & ex ea procreavit Mariam, avus mater- nus Mariæ erit Matthan e linea Salomonica, qui paternus Josephi avus fuit, quod rectius se habe- bit, quam si dicatur, Neri a Nathane oriundum du- xisse Jechoniæ, qui e Salomone ortus est, filiam, & ex eadem Salathielem suscepisse, ut ita Zorobabel Ethnarcha ratione matris e Salomone, ratione Patris e Nathane ortum traxerit; e quo Zoroba- bele per Abiud Josephus a Jacobo, procreatus sit, per Rhesam vero alterum filium a Joachimo mater Messiæ exorta. Quomodocunque vero ille con- cursus linearum sese habeat: sufficiat, quod Na- than æque filius Davidis e Bathseba fuerit, ac Salomo 1. Par. III. 5. quodq; Deus a Salomone ad Nathanem Messiæ prosapiam qua matris paternam familiam, transtulerit, cujus posteri Ethnarchæ, & duces po- puli fuere.

§. XXXIX. Pareus equidem, Comment. in Matth. I. ut & Maldonat. Col. 28. Jechoniam vult duxisse filiam Neri, ex qua procrearit Sealthie- lem, ut sic Neri Sealthielis avus maternus, Jechonia vero Pater naturalis fuerit: adeoque & linea Salo- monis, & Nathanis linea communis Josepho & Mariæ extiterit, ac porro linea propria, ut Pareus explicat Josepho ex Abiud filio Zorobabelis, Mariæ vero ex Rhefa altero Zorobabelis filio statui debeat. Sed- huic genealogiæ obstant plurima, imprimis quod Jer. XXII. 30. prædictum neminem de filiis Jecho- niæ thronum Davidis occupaturum; quomodo ergo Sealthiel & Zorobabel in throno illo consti- tuuntur, ceu filius & nepos ejusdem? Adde, quod Maria secundum lineam paternam è Nathane or- tum trahat, Luca demonstrante; ac Neri Sealthie- lis pater constituatur, non avus maternus in Lucæ genealogia: Denique ita assumitur Sealthielem il- lum, qui 1. Par. III. 17. ceu primogenitus Jecho- niæ introducitur, Zorobabelis Ethnarchæ patrem fuissse, quum tamen illic Sealthiel ἄτεκνος relin- quatur, vel potius filii ejus nulli recenseantur, & fratris ejus Phadaja filio solum commemorentur, atque inter hos aliquis Zorobabelis nomine voca- tus.

§. XL. Cui dubio succurrit quidem Pareus hac ratione, quod Zorobabel Ethnarcha nepos fuerit Sealthielis ex fratre Pedajah, ac filius ejus dicatur tantum legali jure, quia bonis ejus adoptione, vel a- lia legali ratione successit. Sed hæc conciliatio admitti nequit. Nam primo Matthæus Evange- lista observat seriem generationis, non successionis legalis, ac generasse dicit Sealthielem Zorobabelem, non vero adoptasse, aut alia quadam ratione hære- dem ac successorem habuisse: Pedajam adeò pla- ne præterit in hac linea genealogica. Adhæc se- cundo nuspiam Zorobabel Ethnarcha filius Pedajah dicitur, semper ubi Dux ille populi designatur, filius Sealthielis nuncupatur. Quomodo vero Spiritus Sanctus ipsum describeret solum à Patre legali, neglecto ejusdem naturali? Tertio Zoro- babel ille, qui fuit naturali generatione Regis Je- choniæ filii filius, ac avum Jechoniam, Patrem vero Jechoniæ naturalem filium Pedaja habuit, vi Prophetiæ & edicti Domini Jerem. XXII. 30. non potuit hæres esse throni Davidici, aut Dux po- puli: sic enim habebat sententia divina: Scribi- te virum istum orbum, non enim prospere aget de semi- ne ejus Vir sedens super solium Davidis, & qui do- minetur, ultra in Juda: unde nec Sealthiel Je- choniæ filius 1. Par. III. 17. nec quisquam alius ex filiis, aut filiorum filiis ad dominium in Juda ad- mitti potest, salva veritate edicti divini.

§. XLI. Chemnitius ergo noster ὁ μακαρίτης præ- eunte Andr. Osiandro merito statuit diversos Sala- thieles & Zorobabeles, alios nempe in linea Salomo- nis apud Matthæum, alios in linea Nathanis apud Lucam: quærit vero in lib. Chron. priori cap. III. 19. seqq. anne aliqua nomina in stirpe Zorobabelis in- veniantur recensioni Lucæ convenientia? Et vi- dentur ei convenire hæc nomina. Nepos, inquit Zo- robabelis, qui vocatur Johanna Luc. III. 27. is appel- latur Hananias 1. Par. III. 19. & hujus pronepos Se- mei Luc. III. 26. convenire videtur Semeja 1. Par. III. v. 22. sicut & Johannam qui ultimus ferme est, 1. Par. c. III. 24. convenire videtur cum Janna, qui Luc. III. 24. quintus est ab Heli. Sed quum manifestum sit in prædicto Chronicorum loco Zorobabelem è linea Salomonis referri, ejusque nepotem Hananiam, ac hujus pronepotem Semaja, & è filiis Elionai Jo- hannam, non ergo apparet, quomodo illi ad Zoro- babelis à Nathane descendentis posteros referri queant. Duos Zorobabeles ita Osiander eruit: 1. Par. III. De Phadaja orti sunt Zorobabel & -Se- mei. Zorobabel genuit Mosollamum. -- Quæso te lector, ut memineris Zorobabelem patrem Mo- sollami esse filium Phadaja. Item Haggæi I. sic scri- ptum est, factum esse verbum Domini in manu Hag- gæi ad Zorobabelem filium Sealthielis ducem Juda. -- En tibi lector jam alterum Zorobabelem. Ubi porro post aliquam multa ita habet Osiander: Quin potius summa admiratione dignum videtur, quod fuerint, qui putarint Sealthielem & Zeroba- belem apud Lucam esse eosdem, qui sunt apud Mat- thæum. Quasi vero non sit usitatissimum, eadem nomina pluribus imponi, imprimis autem insignium, illustrium & laudatorum virorum. Ex quam pau- cis periodis ego supra enumeravi tres Mosollamos, e- osque contemporaneos? & miramur fuisse plures Zorobabeles, pluresque Sealthieles? Quis posthac tibi lector persuadere poterit, duos homines, qui eo- dem nomine sunt, esse revera duos, & non unicum, si cum utriusque parentem, ab alterius diversum, audieris, non acquiescis, sed fingis insuper, duos illos patres, etiam diversis nominibus appellatos, fuisse unum eundemque hominem? Quid autem ad proban- dum duos Sealthieles manifestius dici potest, quam Sealthielem, apud Lucam, esse filium Neri, & non Jechoniæ, præsertim cum idem Neri patrem ha- buisse dicatur Melchi, & non Joachimum patrem Je- choniæ? Multos autem eo tempore fuisse Zorobabeles si nihil aliud, certe, vel significatio nominis persuade- bit, si animadverterimus, significare desertorem Ba- bylonis. Quis enim pater, modo pius fuerit, non in votis habuit, filios suos omnes Zorobabeles, qui tem- pore captivitatis expleto, feliciter derelinquant Ba- bylonem, & redeant in terram Israëlis? Hæc O- siander.

§. XLII. Addimus tamen conjecturam Theolo- gi summi (B. Chemnitii) è Josepho l. XII. c. IV. & V. forte non infelicem. Scribit ille, inquit, tempore Pto- lomæi Evergetis & Eupatoris, Josephum (cujus no- men plane ita in Luca ponitur) fuisse illustrem Du- cem Juda, & ejus filium Hircanum, cui Johannis no- men impositum fuit, in Ducatu successorem fuisse, qui cum metu Antiochi Epiphanis manum sibi intulisset, principatum familiæ suæ finivit, & ultimus Dux ex tribu Juda & domo Davidis fuit. Machabæi enim postea dominationem ad se traxerunt. Johannem vulgo tunc Jannæm dictum indicio est Alexander di- ctus Jannæus. Jannæ igitur Luc. III. 24. est Johannes ille Hyrcanus apud Josephum. Et 2. Mach. III. 11. thesauri in templo Hierosolymitano depositi scribun- tur, Hyrcano ἀνδρὶ σφόδρα ἐν ὑπεροχῇ κειμένῳ, quæ Ducis seu Principis descriptio esse videtur. Hæc B. Chemnitii nostri observatio probabilitate non videtur carere.

§. XLIII. Sed imprimis notanda mutatio Reip. Judaicæ, quam ex Ezech. XXI. 26. deducit: quod illa scil. post reditum ex Babylone, non sceptro & corona, id est, regia potestate, sed cidari, hoc est, Du- cis seu Principis titulo, à domo Davidis, admi- nistranda esset. Nam & Sedechias ibi non rex, sed dux, seu Princeps appellatur. Et in illis verbis, ubi propheta dicit: sublimem dejice, humilem ex- alta: prædicit translationem gubernationis à stirpe Salomonis, quæ sceptro & corona hactenus sublimis fuerat, ut posthac ne cidari quidem, hoc est, ducali dignitate insignis futura sit, & ad Na- thanis stirpem, quæ hactenus humilis & privata fuerat, gubernationem transferendam. Sublato igitur sceptro & corona à regia Salomonis linea, nihilominus tamen de fructu ventris Davidis, li- cet ex alia linea, in cidari sedet stirps Nathanis su- per solium Davidis. Addit autem Propheta fore, ut post coronam seu regiam dignitatem, à Salomo- nis posteritate sublatam, etiam cidaris seu du- calis potestas seu dignitas, à stirpe altera Natha- nis auferatur, & tradatur, cum cidaris, tum corona ejus ei, cujus est judicium, hoc est, cui, juxta pro- missionem semini Davidis factam debetur. Va- ticinatur ergo cidarim & coronam sub finem cessuram ad tempus aliis, qui non sint de domo & familia Davidis. Et ter repetit, obliquam, obli- quam, obliquam ponam cidarim & coronam. Nam post ultimum ducem Iannam, qui de domo Da- vidis fuit, PRIMUM Machabæi, qui fuerunt de domo Aaronis primæ sortis 1. Par. VI. 50. & 1. Macc. c. II. v. 54. cidarim, hoc est, potestatem Ducum ad se transtulerunt. SECUNDO Sacerdotes illis suc- cedentes non contenti Ducum titulo & dignitate ex privata ambitione, imposita corona, regiam sibi potestatem vendicarunt. TERTIO ad Hero- dum familiam Idumæorum translata fuit primo ci- daris, tutorio nomine ad Antipatrum: deinde co- rona, regio titulo, ad Herodem. Hasce tres mu- tationes Propheta insinuavit, trina illa repetitio- ne obliquam, obliquam, obliquam ponam, cidarim scilicet & coronam. Semper autem addit Pro- pheta; Hæc, non hæc, quia contra promissionem, domui Davidis factam, imperium illi invaserunt, & tyrannice administrarunt. Ac futuras illas mu- tationes circa id tempus, quando adventurus erat promissus Messias, Propheta indicat, cum inquit, donec is veniat, cui jure debetur, cidaris, scil. & co- rona; & huic tradam eam. Hæc pulcerrime con- veniunt ad historias, & ad illud, quod Gabriel di- cit de Christo; Dabit ei DOMINUS DEUS se- dem patris sui Davidis, & regnabit super domum Iacob &c. Non igitur vel casu vel contra Prophe- tarum vaticinia factum fuit, quod aliquot annis ante nativitatem Christi, & regnum & Ducatus in domo Davidis, imo in ipsa Messiæ linea cessavit. Nam Amos IX. 11. citante Jacobo Act. XV. 15. scri- ptum est: Tabernaculum Davidis tempore venien- tis Messiæ non tantum interruptum, sed collapsum fore. Et stirps illa Davidis, quando surculus be- nedictus inde proditurus erat, debebat stare, non quasi Davidis esset dignitate & potentia florens tanquam cedrus excelsa, Ezech. XVII. 12. sed ut stirps Iesse Es. XI. 1. obscura, ignobilis, & privata, unde non judicarentur fabricari posse sceptra domi- nantium Ez. XIX. 13. atque inde factum fuit, quod Iannæ posteritas privata, in Galilæam detrusa fuit. Nam & Hyrcanus Alexandrum Iannæum filium su- um, ad quem volebat regnum devenire, jussit privatum in Galilæa educari. Hæc omnia B. Che- mnitius, quæ propriis ejus verbis etsi paulo proli- xioribus repetere placuit, quod ad illustrationem genealogiæ utriusque omnino faciant.

§. XLIV. Redeundum autem nobis ad Gro- tium: Qui jam nonnulla è Græcia, sed non nomi- nato loco, vel autore advehit: soliq; famæ incerto autore sparsæ hic innititur. Et alia, inquit, fama Græcis scriptoribus memorata, Mariæ Patrem di- ctum Iehojakimum, ei Patrem Pantherem, Pantheri Patrem Barpantherem, Barpantheri Levim Melchi filium, quod non est temere improbandum. Nostrum non est divinare, unde hæc commenta habeat. Damascenum postea laudavit: sed non consonant ista Damasceni relationi, etsi hæc etiam fabulosa sit, & à nemine facile recepta. Hic enim in serie Nathanis è Levi Melchi deducit, & Panthera ceu fratres. Panther, inquit porro, genuit Barpanthe- ra, sic ab eo denominatum. Hic Barpanther genuit Io- jakim, Iojakim vero genuit sanctam Deiparam. Quæ repetit Niceta in catena Græcor. Patrum in Matth. At Grotium si audias Melchi è Janna de- scendit, & è Melchi Panther, vel Iacobus, ut & Eli ac Levi. E Levi vero Barpanthera non vero è Jacobo, vel Panthere; E Barpanthere alium Pan- thera deducit: & ab hoc Iojakimum. Unde ergo hæc somnia, quæ cum commentis Da- masceni nullatenus consonant, habeat Grotius, viderint qui ei temere annuunt.

§. XLV. Quis porro fidem faciet, prout par est, Mariæ Patrem fuisse Jojakim, diversum ab Eli? Quod etsi à nonnullis asseratur, in S. literis fundamentum nullum habet. Et annon potius statuendum, Jojakim illum, qui Eliakim etiam dicitur secundum Grotium, esse ipsummet Eli, quod contractum ex illo nomen facit B. Chemnitius? Quo pacto etiam Galatinus l. VII. de arcan. Cathol. verit. c. XII. Eli censet fuisse ipsum Jehojakim eaque nomina Jehojakim, Eli & Eliakim eadem fuisse è Philone docet. Imo etiam autoritate Rabbinorum, maxime R. Hakkadosch probat: Mariæ Patrem & Eli & Jehojakim dictum esse. In quam sententiam hoc allegat Iac. Capellus l. c. è Gale Razeja; Heli idem est, quod Ioakimus. Et è 2. Reg. XXIII. 34. 2. Par. XXXVI. 4. liquet, eadem esse nomina Iehojakim & Eliakim : è quo posteriori facile oriri potuit nomen Eli, vulgo brevius id ipsum ita pronunciante. Osiander in Paraph. & B. Gerhard. annot. in Matth. p. 57. observant, quod nomina Eli & Iehojakim conveniant. Siquidem Iehojakim significet Erigendum, Eli sublimem: in quo prævium habent Andream Osiandrum Seniorem, qui annotat. in lib. I. Harmon. Evangel. c. XVI. ita habet: Est enim nomen Iehojakim ejusmodi, quod propter tres primas literas, quas habet cum nomine Dei יהוה communes, non licebat usu quotidiano profanare, unde aliud in locum ejus substitutum fuisse, quod Iehojakimus familiariter appellaretur, nemo dubitabit, qui ea, quæ supra c. 6. scripsimus, diligenter & exacte perpenderit. Eli autem in locum nominis Iehojakimi successisse, cum propter veterum Hebræorum, atque Christianorum testimonia, tum etiam propter utriusque nominis significationem, maxime credibile est; יהוֹיָקִים enim significat, erigendum, exaltandum & sublimandum, עֵלִי vero (absit enim ut juxta Annium אֱלִי appellatum fuisse credamus) significat, altum seu sublimem. Similiter pro iisdem nominibus hæc Iojakim, Eliakim, & Eli habet B. Luth. tract. de Schem Hamph. cujus locum supra adduximus. Atque in eo plurimi consentiunt, eundem esse Eli & Ioachim Mariæ Patrem : quemadmodum de matre Deiparæ virginis plerique cum Epiph. Hæres. LXXIX. contra Colyridian. & Damascen. l. IV. de Orth. fid. cap. 15. nec non Nicephoro l. II. Hist. Eccl. c. 3. & quem is allegat, Hippolyto Martyre, Annam fuisse statuunt, Joachimi conjugem: etsi nonnulli eam è tribu Levi deducant, etiam B. Luther l. c. sed σοχασικῶς solum, quia, ut Christus & Rex & sacerdos esse debuit, Paterna Mariæ Regia, materna Sacerdotalis fuerit familia : quæ vero potius & materna, & paterna familiæ respectu deducenda videtur è tribu Regia Davidica, quum Christus non secundum ordinem Leviticum, sed secundum ordinem Melchisedech sit Pontifex designatus, & πρόδηλον, sit quod ex Iuda ortus sit Dominus Ebr. VII. 14. quemadmodum Damascen. orat. II. de Nativ. Mar. ad S. Annam dixit, quam beata domus David, de qua prodiisti! de quo conf. quæth. XXXVII. diximus. Adstipulatur Iob. Maldonatus comment. in Matth. c. I. Col. 26. Non constat Christum ex tribu Levi Sacerdotalis aliquid generis habuisse; quin viri nonnulli insigniter docti, atque Catholici id nostro tempore præcise negarunt, quod D. etiam Paulus toto septimo capite Epistolæ ad Ebræos negare videtur. Ubi respondet etiam Maldonatus ad objectionem de συγγενείᾳ B. virginis cum Elisabetha, quæ ex genere Aaron erat Luc. c. I. s. 36. quod ea facile salvetur, si Pater, aut avus aliquis Elisabetha ex tribu Levi aliquando uxorem duxit è tribu Juda & familia Davidis, unde orta illa cognatio. Quæ etiam responsio multorum aliorum est, dubioque satisfacit. Nam ut cognatio illa constet, non opus est, Mariam è tribu Levi de- scendere, sufficit, si Elisabethæ progenitorum aliquis è Davidis familia uxorem habuerit. Ita B. Gerhard noster respondet Annot. ad Matth. p. 20. Levitam quendam cui per legem in quamvis tribum adnubere licebat (eo quod inter duodecim tri- bus non numerarentur ac sortem terræ propriam nul- lam haberent, ideoque nullam confusionem possessio- num adnubendo inducerent) duxisse quandam ex ma- joribus Elisabethæ è tribu Judæ oriundam, quomodo Elisabetha & cognata Mariæ & filia Aaronis esse potuerit. Similiter Cloppenburg. in Gangr. Ana- bapt. disp. IX. th. 15. Spanhem. in dub. Evangel. part. 1. p. 71.

Lucæ genealogia, si dicatur, Eli vel Jojakim Patrem Mariæ naturalem è linea Nathanis oriundum, quam sine interruptione pertexit Lucas, duxisse conjugem è linea Salomonea, à Matthæo exhibita, Matthanis filium Annam, quod nomen matri θεοτό- κy communiter tribuitur sororem Iacobi, Patris Jo- sephi: Hac enim ratione maternus Deiparæ avus e- rit Matthan, idemq; avus paternus erit Josephi, secun- dum naturam, nec opus erit confusione naturalis generationis, & legalis, quæ meram confusionem tricasque inexplicabiles insert, & descendet MA- RIA, ratione paternæ familiæ è Nathane, ratione vero familiæ maternæ è Salomone, nec quisquam in linea seu Matthæi, seu Lucæ frustra commemoratus erit, aut respectum aliquem mere legalem obtine- bit; manebitq; illud B. Lutheri assertum Tom. IIX. Jen. Germ. f. 26. Daß beyde Evangelisten eitel Davids-Kinder einführen, und bleiben beyde im Hause David, zehlen keine Kōt-Kinder, oder frembd Geblüts. ## 3:24
Verse 24. τοῦ ἠλὶ, τοῦ μελχὶ [of Eli, of Melchi] That it was so in ancient copies, I am persuaded by arguments which have been brought forward in two dissertations by a man who is a lover of truth, and who is also most dear to me by this and other names, Johannes Cordesius. For Irenæus explicitly teaches that in his time there existed only LXXII generations in Luke, and he expresses that number with such signs that there can be no doubt about the truth of the reading. But the matter cannot be reduced to that number unless both Matthat and Levi are omitted in this place, and Cainan below. Africanus, however, no less openly cites the words of Luke with these two names omitted in this place, and clearly signifies that for him the father of Eli was Melchi, without an intermediary, whom Eusebius also follows: and Nazianzen in a hexameter poem about the Genealogy: and Jerome regarding Matthew, and Augustine elsewhere. I might think the reason for the added name Matthat was that it was another name for Melchi: for that has been handed down by Damascenus and certain others from hearsay, or from lost books. But I might think the name of Levi was likewise wrongly inserted by those who had heard that Melchi himself had a son named Levi, which name they perhaps thought should be substituted for Eli, although that Levi did not pertain to Joseph, whose lineage is handed down here, but to Mary, to whom the lineage is not traced. Nor is it unworthy of note that almost all the names of the descendants of Nathan carry in themselves the hope of the kingdom which had been promised to the posterity of David.

§. I. Grotius, having omitted those τοῦ Ματθὰτ, τοῦ Λευὶ [of Matthat, of Levi], judges that one should read τοῦ Ἠλὶ, τοῦ Μελχί [of Eli, of Melchi], nor does he doubt that it existed thus in ancient copies, but he could produce no Codex that would give credence to this reading of his. And therefore his suspicion is deservedly held to be vain and rash. He appeals to the two Dissertations of Johannes Cordesius, by which the arguments for this opinion were brought forward. Whom, a priest and Canon of Limoges, he celebrated among the more moderate ones honored in a peculiar Epigram on religion, because it was done by his care that the truthful writings of Cassander are worn out, and therefore without doubt he honored him here with this eulogy, because the man

MAATH. 63. NAGGA. 64. ESLI. 65. NAUM. 66. AMOS. 67. MATHATHIAS. 68. JOSEPH. 69. JANNA. 70. MELCHI. 71. LEVI. 72. MATTHAT. 73. ELI. 74. MARIA.

Matthan maternal grandfather of Mary. Jacob paternal grandfather of Joseph. Joseph's natural father. JOSEPH.

has been a lover of truth, and by that name most friendly to himself. But how much truth Cassander's writings contain, or rather how much harm his syncretistic counsels have brought to the Christian world, the Church has hitherto experienced as a great evil, which Grotius, as he was able, attempted to promote, and Calixtus, who is nearly his equal, likewise.

§. II. What truly compelling arguments could be brought forward against the constant consensus of the Greek and other codices? First, he cites Irenaeus, because he expressly teaches that in his time there existed only 72 γενεὰς in Luke, and since he expresses the number with those signs; so that there can be no doubt about the truth of the reading, and the matter cannot be reduced to that number unless both Matthat and Levi are omitted in this place, and Cainan below.

Concerning Cainan there is no doubt for us, but why Matthat and Levi should be omitted, there is no cause, for thus the number of 72 generations would be deficient, which, as can be seen from the appended diagram, is most correctly consistent with itself. For he did not count the extremes, the first and the last, Adam and Christ. Because Seth was brought forth in the first generation, Eli was begotten by Matthat in the seventy-second generation. But natural generations proceed only up to Eli in Luke, whose son Joseph was not, except in that sense in which sons-in-law are called sons. Whence the authority of Irenaeus is directly opposed to Grotius, but it entirely supports the truth of the received reading, especially because Irenaeus assigns the 72 not indeed as persons, but as generations, in such a way that it is openly evident that he admitted neither more nor fewer. According to the number of languages, which were believed to be LXXII throughout the world, he also calculated LXXII generations. The passage is book III, chapter XXXIII. On account of this, Luke shows that the genealogy which is from the generation of our Lord up to Adam has LXXII generations, joining the end to the beginning, and signifying that He Himself, who recapitulated in Himself all the nations dispersed from Adam, and all the languages, and the generation of men with Adam himself.

§. III. Then he praises Africanus and Eusebius because they cite the words of Luke with these two names omitted, which Nazianzen in his poem, Jerome on Matthew, and Augustine elsewhere have followed. But how much Grotius attributed to Africanus, the passages recently adduced can teach. And why should the error be established in the Fathers rather than in the Holy Codices, and those authentic ones, when to admit a universal corruption is contrary to Divine Providence? Could it not have happened that Africanus used a mutilated or defective codex of the Gospel, in which two names were missing, or that, having neglected an inspection, he placed faith in some tradition of the Evangelist? Which often happened to the ancients. Certainly, if Africanus deserves faith in that account to Aristides, which Eusebius brought forward in book I of the Ecclesiastical History, chapter VII, the natural father of Jacob would have been Matthan, whom Grotius, however, affirms to have died without children: and furthermore, the natural father of Joseph would have been Jacob, whom Grotius, however, contends was the natural son of Eli; finally, Grotius makes Jacob the brother of Eli by nature, from the same father and the same mother: whom, however, Africanus derives from a different lineage, as far as the fathers are concerned, and establishes them only as ὁμοπατρίως (having the same father).

§. IV. Eusebius, however, does not approve the opinion of Africanus with a full vote, but recounts it only historically: Eusebius certainly did not approve by any little word that omission of the two generations, namely of Matthat and Levi.

§. V. Augustine, however, although he praises Africanus in book XI of the Retractations, chapter III, did not diminish the number of generations in Luke, but rather increased it, because he counted LXXVII generations in Sermon XV on the Words of the Lord according to Matthew, and in book II of Questions on the Gospels, chapter V, he teaches that forty-three generations are recounted by Luke from Christ to David, by which number it is clear that Matthat and Levi are included.

§. VI. Nor can anything be extracted from Jerome for the omission of those two generations, who only notes that Africanus, the writer of chronicles, and Eusebius of Caesarea had disputed more fully about it in their books on the disagreement of the Gospels, how Matthew called Joseph the son of Jacob, and Luke the son of Eli.

§. VII. Finally, Nazianzen, although in his poem on the genealogy of Christ he reconciled Matthew with Luke in the same manner as he had received from Africanus, he did not, however, in the review of the genealogies of Christ according to Luke subjoined in the same place, omit those two generations which Grotius thinks should be omitted, but retained them: for he has it thus: Μελχὶ, κ’ Λευὶ, c' Ματθὰν, Ἠλεὶ, ἰωσήφ. How, therefore, could Grotius have relied on the authority of Nazianzen?

§. VIII. These, therefore, were all the testimonies which Grotius sought to borrow from his Cordesius, produced against the constant fidelity of the Holy Codices, by which, however, not even Possinus, the Jesuit, could be moved by Cordesius, but that he professed to the contrary in Diallact. p. 533, that it is an example of rashness to lay critical hands upon the Holy Scriptures, and to condemn as faulty and mark with an obelus words or sentences received in that vulgate reading. The rest which Grotius adds are mere divinations. I might think, he says, that the reason for the added name Matthat was that it was the other name of Melchi: for that has been handed down by Damascenus and certain others from hearsay or lost books. In Damascenus it is said that a certain Melchi was the son of Levi, the brother of Panther, and that he married the wife of Matthan, who was of the line of Solomon, the mother of Jacob, and from her begat Heli, so that Jacob and Heli were uterine brothers, Jacob from the tribe of Solomon, but Heli from the tribe of Nathan. But those things differ no less from the Grotian opinion than from the Genealogy of Luke. For according to Grotius, Matthan died without children; but according to Damascenus, Matthan begat Jacob; according to Grotius, Melchi was the natural father of Jacob, the legal son of Matthan; but according to Damascenus, he was the natural father not of Jacob, but of Heli. According to Grotius, Jacob, and Eli, and Levi were brothers by nature, sons of Melchi by Estha; but according to Damascenus, Melchi was not the father of Levi, but his son; and Jacob and Eli were only uterine brothers. Therefore, Grotius cannot appeal to Damascenus here.

§. IX. Furthermore, is the hypothesis that Eli is the brother of Levi not vain and merely precarious? Concerning which, indeed, he could produce no testimony or evidence from antiquity; and not even from Africanus. And how can Barpanther be derived from Levi, when not Levi, but his brother, whom Grotius assigns, is said by him to be Jacob Panther? But let Barpanther be the son of Panther? Moreover, by what solid document will it be demonstrated that another Panther was begotten by Barpanther, and that from this second Panther, Jehoiakim, the father of Mary, drew his origin, so that he dared to insert these two so confidently into the generation of Mary? But we have already discussed these trifles before.

§. X. But for that reason we readily accept what Grotius confesses, that Levi pertains not to Joseph, but to Mary. Since, therefore, Levi is commemorated by Luke in the genealogy, and that by the consensus of all codices, what is more certain than that it is not the genealogy of Joseph, but of Mary, that is woven by Luke.

§. XI. Finally, if the Grotian opinion prevails, that both Joseph and Mary descend from Melchi by a natural series of generation, and that the natural son of Melchi was both the father of Joseph, whom he makes Eli, and the great-grandfather of Levi, as he thinks, of Mary, what need would there have been for the genealogy handed down by Matthew, and deduced through the line of Solomon? Since that Melchi, from whom Joseph as well as Mary descends, drew his origin not from the family of Solomon, but of Nathan, could not Matthew, describing the origin of Christ, have more rightly superseded that distinct review of the Solomonic stem? Since it is evident that it provided the cause for so many and such great difficulties.

§. XII. And these things concerning the Genealogy of CHRIST according to Luke, which, just as Grotius acknowledges it to have consisted of public records in his time, so it must not be denied that it was consigned by divine inspiration by Luke, the amanuensis of the Holy Spirit, since all things in Scripture are θεόπνευστα, 2 Tim. III. 16. That matter was indeed so certain in the age of Christ's conversation on earth and of the writing of the Gospel, that it was never called into doubt by anyone, not even by the most bitter enemies of Christ and the Apostles, the chief priests, scribes, or Pharisees; Christ was celebrated by all as the son of David, the blind, and the lame, and all the beggars, and the whole people had him as such and preached him, Matt. IX. 28, c. XII. 23, 48, c. XV. 22; he was proclaimed as such by public voice in his solemn entry into the city, Matt. XXI. 9. nor did his accusers raise a question about his family to him, either before the governor or before the people, which they certainly would not have omitted, if it had not been clearly established that Christ was of the lineage of David; whence it was evident, clear, and manifest among the Hebrews, the Apostle testified in Heb. VII. 14. that our Lord has sprung from Judah, and it was a matter of glorious importance that Christ should be according to the promise and likewise according to the gospel from the seed of David according to the flesh, Rom. I. 3, 2 Tim. II. 8, which is certainly to be understood of his mother, since according to the flesh he is without a father. Those who deny that the mother of Christ sprang from the family of David utterly overturn this axiom of faith; but they easily render the matter doubtful who, content only with a legal respect, eliminate the genealogy of his mother of God from the Gospel, and make her, along with the fruit of her womb—on account of whom the Spirit especially loves to genealogize in the Holy Scriptures—without a genealogy.

Latin:

Vers. 24. τοῦ ἠλὶ, τοῦ μελχὶ] Sic in antiquis exemplaribus fuisse, persuadeor argumentis, quæ à viro veri amante, eoq; & aliis nominibus mihi amicissimo Johanne Cordesio dua- bus dissertationibus allata sunt. Nam Irenæus diserte do- cet suo tempore tantum LXXII. extitisse γενεὰς in Luca, e- umq; numerum eis signis exprimit, ut de lectionis veritate dubitari non possit. Ad eum vero numerum res reduci non potest, nisi & Matthat, & Levi hoc loco omittantur, & infra Cainan. Africanus vero non minus aperte citat Lucæ verba his duobus nominibus hoc loco omissis, & clare significat ipsi Eli patrem ἄμεσον fuisse Melchim, quem & Eusebius se- quitur: & in hexametro carmine de Genealogia Nazian- zenus: & ad Matthæum Hieronymus, & alicubi Augusti- nus. Putem causam additi nominis Matthat fuisse quod id alterum esset nomen Melchis: nam id à Damasceno aliisq; quibusdam ex fama, aut libris amissis proditum est. Levis autem nomen itidem perperam insertum putem ab iis qui audissent ipsi Melchi filium fuisse Levin, quod nomen forte pro Eli substituendum putarunt, cum tamen is Levi non ad Josephum, cujus hic genus traditur, sed ad Mariam pertihe- ret, ad quam stemma non perducitur. Nec indignum nota- tu, nomina fere omnia Nathanis posterum spem in se ferre regni quod Davidis posteritati promissum fuerat.

§. I. Grotius prætermissis illis τοῦ Ματθὰτ, τοῦ Λευὶ, legendum censet, τοῦ Ἠλὶ, τοῦ Μελχί, neque dubitat in antiquis exemplaribus ita extitisse, sed nullum Codicem, qui huic suæ lectioni fidem fa- ciat, producere potuit. Ideoque vana merito ac temeraria habetur ejus suspicio. Ad Johannis Cordesii duas Dissertationes, quibus argumenta hujus sententiæ adducta, provocat. Quem Lemovicensem presbyterum & Canonicum inter moderatiores in religionis Epigrammate peculiari honoratos celebravit, quod ejus cura factum, quod Cassandri veracia scripta terantur, atque ideo sine dubio hic eo ornavit elogio, quod vir

46. ELIEZER. 47. JOSE. 48. ER. 49. ELMODAM. 50. KOSAM. 51. ADDI. 52. MELCHI. 53. NERI. 54. SALATHIEL. 55. ZOROBABEL. 56. RESA. 57. JOANNA. 58. JUDA. 59. JOSEPH. 60. SEMEI. 61. MATHATHIAS. 62. MAATH. 63. NAGGA. 64. ESLI. 65. NAUM. 66. AMOS. 67. MATHATHIAS. 68. JOSEPH. 69. JANNA. 70. MELCHI. 71. LEVI. 72. MATTHAT. 73. ELI. 74. MARIA.

TUS JESUS. αλογίας proximæ s exhibitum.

Matthan avus Mariæ maternus. Josephi paternus Jacob. Josephi Pater naturalis. JOSEPH.

fuerit veri amans, eoque nomine sibi amicissimus. Sed quantum veritatis Cassandri scripta conti- neant, imo quantum damni syncretistica ejus Consilia orbi Christiano attulerint, magno malo Ecclesia experta est hactenus, quæ, ut potuit, provehere conatus est Grotius, & eidem suppar Calixtus.

§. II. Quænam vero argumenta tam strin- gentia adferri potuerunt adversus constantem co- dicum Græcorum & aliorum consensum? Primum Irenæum adducit, quod is diserte doceat, suo tempore tantum LXXII. extitisse γενεὰς in Luca, cumque numerum eis signis exprimat; ut de lectio- nis veritate dubitari non possit, ad eum vero numerum res reduci nequeat, nisi & Matthat & Levi hoc loco omittantur, & infra Cainan.

De Cainan nobis dubium nullum est, sed cur omitti debeat Matthat & Levi, causa non est, nam ita deficeret numerus LXXII. generationum, qui, uti è Schematismo ap- posito videre est, sibi quam rectissime constat. Extremos enim primum & ultimum, Adamum & Christum non computavit. Quia Seth prima generatione editus, Eli à Matthat septuagesima secunda generatione procreatus fuit. Ad Eli antem tantum generationes naturales procedunt a- pud Lucam, cujus filius non fuit Josephus nisi ea ratione, uti generi filii dicuntur. Unde Irenæi autoritas Grotio directe adversatur, veritati au- tem lectionis receptæ omnino patrocinatur, im- primis, quia LXXII. non quidem personas, sed ge- nerationes Irenæus ita assignat, ut nec plures nec pauciores ipsum admisisse, palam constet. pro numero linguarum, quas LXXII. esse, per or- bem credebatur, generationes etiam LXXII. computavit. Locus est l. III. c. XXXIII. Propter hoc Lucas genealogiam, quæ est a generatione Domi- ni nostri usque ad Adam LXXII. generationes habe- re ostendit, finem conjungens initio, & significans, quoniam ipse, qui omnes gentes exinde ab Adam dispersas, & universas linguas, & generationem ho- minum cum ipso Adam in semetipso recapitulatus est.

§. III. Deinde Africanum, & Eusebium laudat, quod Lucæ verba citent, hisce duobus nominibus omissis, quos Nazianzenus in carmine, Hieronymus ad Matthæum, & Augustinus alicubi secuti sint. Sed quantum Africano tribuerit Grotius, proxi- me adducta docere possunt. Et cur non potius in Patribus, quam in S. Codd. iisque authenticis error statuendus, quum corruptionem universa- lem admittere divinæ Providentiæ adversum sit? Annon contingere potuit, ut Africanus mutilo vel manco Evangelii codice uteretur, in quo duo defuerint nomina, aut ut neglecta inspectio- ne Evangelistæ traditioni alicui fidem haberet? Quod sæpe antiquis accidit. Africanus certe si fidem mereatur in illa ad Aristidem relatione, quam Eusebius l. I. Histor. Eccles. c. IIX. adduxit, Jacobi Pater naturalis fuerit Matthan, quem ve- ro Grotius sine liberis mortuum esse affirmat: ac porro Josephi pater natura fuerit Jacobus, quem vero Grotius Eli filium naturalem fuisse contendit, denique Jacobum fratrem Eli natura facit, ex eo- dem Patre eademque matre, Grotius: quos tamen Africanus ex diverso genere, quantum ad Patres, deducit, & solum ὁμοπατρίως constituit.

§. IV. Eusebius vero Africani sententiam non probat pleno suffragio, sed historice solum recen- set: Illam profecto duarum generationum, nimi- rum Matthai & Levi omissionem nullo verbulo approbavit Eusebius.

§. V. Augustinus vero quamvis Africanum l. XI. Retract. c. III. laudet, generationum nume- rum in Luca non imminuit, sed auxit potius, quia LXXVII. generationes numeravit Serm. XV. de Verb. Dom. secundum Matth. & l. II. Quæst. Ev ang. c. V. à Christo ad David quadraginta tres ge- nerationes apud Lucam recenseri docet, quo nu- mero comprehendi Mathat & Levi, palam est.

§. VI. Neque ex Hieronymo quicquam pro o- mittendis illis duabus generationibus exsculpi potest, qui solum notat, Africanum temporum scriptorem & Eusebium Cæsariensem libris διαφω- νίας Εὐαγγελίων plenius de eo disputasse, quomodo Matthæus Josephum filium dixerit Jacobi, & Lucas filium Eli.

§. VII. Denique Nazianzenus etsi in carmine de genealogia Christi Matthæum cum Luca ad eundem modum conciliarit, ut ab Africano acce- perat, non tamen in recensione Genealogias Chri- sti secundum Lucam ibidem subjuncta prætermisit duas illas generationes, quas omittendas censet Grotius, sed easdem retinuit: sic enim habet: Μελ- χὶ, κ’ Λευὶ, c' Ματθὰν, Ἠλεὶ, ἰωσήφ. Quomodo er- go Nazianzeni autoritati inniti potuit Grotius.

§. IIX. Hæc ergo fuêre testimonia omnia, quæ à Cordesio suo mutuo petiit Grotius adversus con- stantem S. Codicum fidem producta, quibus vero à Cordesio ne Possinus quidem, Jesuita permoveri potuit, quin in Diallact. p. 533. contra profiteretur, præcipitis exempli esse Criticas manus inferre S. lite- ris, mendique damnare atque obelo figere receptas in illa vulgata lectione voces aut sententias. Cætera quæ attexit Grotius, meræ divinationes sunt. Putem, inquit, causam additi nominis Matthat fuisse, quod id alterum esset nomen Melchis: nam id a Damasce- no, aliisque quibusdam ex fama aut libris amissis pro- ditum est. In Damasceno dicitur quidam Melchi fuisse filius Levi frater Pantheris, & nupsisse uxori Matthan, qui erat ex serie Salomonis, matri Jacob & ex ea Heli genuisse, ut fratres uterini fuerint Jacob & Heli, Jacob ex tribu Salomonis, Heli vero ex tribu Nathan. Sed illa non minus a Grotiana sen- tentia, quam a Genealogia Lucae discrepant. Nam juxta Grotium Matthan sine liberis mortuus est: juxta Damascenum vero Matthan genuit Jacobum; juxta Grotium Melchi pater naturalis Jacobi fuit, Matthanis filius legalis: juxta Damascenum vero non Jacobi, sed Heli pater naturalis fuit. Juxta Grotium Jacob, & Eli, & Levi fratres natura fue- re, filii Melchi ex Estha: juxta Damascenum vero Melchi non fuit Levi Pater, sed filius: Jacob vero & Eli fratres solum uterini fuere. Non ergo ad Da- mascenum hic provocare potest Grotius.

§. IX. Porro quod Eli frater Levi sit, annon va- na & mere precaria est hypothesis? De qua pro- fecto nullum ex antiquitate testimonium aut in- dicium proferre potuit; ac ne ex Africano qui- dem. Et quomodo ex Levi Barpanther deduci potest, quum non Levi, sed frater ejus, quem assignat Grotius, Jacob Panther secundum ipsum dictus sit? Barpanther autem sit filius Pantheris? In- super quo documento solido demonstrabitur Pantherem alium a Barpanthere procreatum, & ab hoc Panthere secundo Jehojakimum, Mariae Pa- trem, ortum trahere, ut duos hosce tam confi- denter inferere Mariae generationi ausus fuerit? Sed hasce naenias antea jam discussimus.

§. X. Ideo vero prompti acceptamus, quod fatetur Grotius, Levin non ad Josephum, sed ad Mariam pertinere. Quum ergo a Luca Levi commemoratus in genealogia sit, idque omnium codicum consensu, quid certius, quam quod a Luca non Josephi, sed Mariae genealogia pertexatur.

§. XI. Denique si Grotiana obtineat sententia, a Melchi & Josephum & Mariam naturali serie ge- nerationis descendere, filiumque Melchi natura- lem, tum Patrem Josephi, quem Eli facit, fuisse, tum Levi abavum, uti putat, Mariae, ecquid opus fuisset genealogia a Matthaeo tradita, & per lineam Salomonis deducta? Quum Melchi ille, a quo de- scendit Josephus pariter ac Maria, non e Salomo- nis, sed Nathanis familia ortum traxerit, annon ista distincta stemmatis Salomonei recensione Mat- thaeus originem Christi describens, rectius super- sedere potuisset? Quam tot, ac tantis difficultati- bus causam praebuisse, constat.

§. XII. Atque haec de Genealogia CHRISTI secundum Lucam, quam uti e tabulis publicis ejus tempore constitisse, agnoscit Grotius, ita inspira- tione divina a Luca S. S. amanuensi, consignatam esse negandum non est, quum omnia in Scriptura sint θεόπνευστα, 2. Tim. III. 16. Fuit sane ista conver- sationis Christi in terris, & ευαγγελιογραφίας aetate res adeo certa, ut a nemine, nec infensissimis Chri- sti & Apostolorum hostibus, Pontificibus, Scribis aut Pharisaeis, unquam in dubium vocata sit; Chri- stus ab omnibus celebrabatur filius David, talem habebant & praedicabant ipsum caeci, & claudi, ac mendici omnes, & universus populus Matth. IX. 28. c. XII. 23. 48. c. XV. 22. talis proclamabatur voce publica in solemni in urbem ingressu Matth. XXI. 9. nec accusatores ejus vel apud praesidem vel apud populum quaestionem de familia ei moverunt, quod profecto non intermisissent, nisi liquido constitasset, Christum e genere Davidis esse; unde id πρόδηλον liquidum & manifestum apud Ebræos fuisse, testatus est Apostolus Ebr. VII. 14. ὅτι ἐξ Ἰούδα ἀνατέταλκεν ὁ κύριος ἡμῶν & κυρίᾳ δόξα erat secundum ἐπαγγελίαν pariter & secundum εὐαγγέλιον Christum esse ἐκ σπέρματος Δαβὶδ κατὰ Σάρκα Rom. I. 3. 2. Tim. II. 8. quod utique de matre ipsius intelligendum, quum secundum carnem ἀπάτωρ sit. Quod fidei axioma penitus evertunt, qui matrem Christi è Davidis familia ortum esse pernegant: facile autem dubium reddunt, qui legali solum respectu contenti genealogiam ipsius θεοτόκε ex Evangelio eliminant, eamque cum fructu ventris ejus, ob quem præcipue spiritus γενεαλογεῖν amat in sacris literis ἀγενεαλόγητον faciunt.

## 3:33
Vers. 33. of Aram] Thus the LXX at the end of the book of Ruth, and 1 Chron. ch. II. 19, where the Hebrews have Ram, but the Syrian here Aram. It is therefore from the Syriac that the Aleph was added to the front of the word. For the Syrians themselves were called Ramim by the Hebrews and Arabs, as in Job ch. XXXII. 2 and 2 Chron. XXII. 6, when they called themselves Aram, which name also prevailed in use among other nations: whence the Arimi of the ancient Greeks. Similar is the fact that the city called Ramatha was called Aramatha, Arimathea, as we said above.

Latin:

Vers. 33. τῦ Ἀράμ] Ita LXX. fine libri Ruth, & I. Par. c. II. 19. ubi Hebræi habent רם at Syrus hîc ארם. Est igitur ex Syriamo additum Aleph fronti dictionis. Nam & Syri ipsis Hebræis & Arabibus רמים vocabantur, ut Jobi c. XXXII. 2. & 2. Par. XXII. 6. cum ipsi se vocarent ארם quod nomen apud alias quoque gentes usu invaluit: unde Ἄριμοι Græcis veteribus. Simile est quod רמתא urbs dicta est ארמתא Ἀριμαθαία ut supra diximus.

## 3:36
Vers. 36. of Sala, of Arphaxad] So have some Greek manuscripts, which Beza mentions, and what is most important, one written in the most ancient lettering which was of the Church of Lyons, later brought to Cambridge: and another recently sent to England from Greece. The number of Irenaeus also shows that the name of Cainan was not read at that time: nor indeed would you find indications of the reading which now appears before the fourth century. I entirely agree with Cordesius, who thinks that the name of Cainan did not exist in this place in the primitive books of Luke, nor in the LXX interpreters. Concerning Luke, besides those things which we have said, Africanus makes the matter credible, who does not acknowledge that name: concerning the LXX interpreters, what Procopius of Gaza notes, that the passage which is in Genesis about Cainan was marked with an obelus as supposititious: that Theophilus of Antioch, in the calculation of times following those seventy in the review of names, omitting Cainan, makes Arphaxad the father of Sala: and likewise Eusebius, as he is edited in Greek by Scaliger, and that in that genealogy which he himself says is according to the seventy; and that others, professing that the times are calculated by them according to the same interpreters, so calculate them that the account cannot be consistent unless this Cainan is omitted: among whom are Epiphanius in heresy LV and Orosius. Add to these that the Septuagint cannot be said to have drawn this name from any tradition, since the Samaritan writing and the Chaldean version, and others which followed it outside the Greek, agree with the Hebrew codex, nor has any of the Hebrew masters handed down such a thing. Add that Abraham is the tenth from the flood, who with Cainan inserted would be the eleventh, which not only the Hebrews, among whom is Josephus, affirm, but also Berosus among the Chaldeans, brought forth by Josephus himself, and Eupolemus among the Greeks, whose passage Eusebius preserved. Which conjectures induce me to believe that by some writer of the book, from which many copies flowed, the name of Cainan was replaced in this place by some error from the penultimate chapter of this section, such as vicious repetitions which occur in many books from wrongly inspected archetypes or the hallucination of a dictator. Then, when that reading had begun to be spread widely through the copies of Luke, the Greek Christians also in the version of Genesis according to the LXX interposed the name of Cainan between Arphaxad and Sala, with years also added, so that the authority of Luke, whom they thought had written thus, might be more established. But the rashness of these is refuted both by other things which we have said, and by the fact that the Greek book of Chronicles, whoever its interpreter may be, makes no mention of this new Cainan in the older books.

This only still remains in the Genealogy of CHRIST, that we should look at the Greek copies concerning the Cainan whom they insert here. For thus they have: of Sala, of Cainan, of Arphaxad. Grotius eliminates Cainan. That he is entirely spurious, and not genuine, we taught at length in the Critici Sacri, page 57 and following. And therefore he is deservedly omitted by Grotius, who here appeals to some codices. Thus, he says, have some Greek manuscripts, which Beza mentions, and what is most important, one written in the most ancient lettering which was of the Church of Lyons, later brought to Cambridge: and another recently sent to England from Greece. But James Ussher, Archbishop of Armagh, renders that report about the codices in England doubtful in Chronol. Sacr. page 102, alleging, however, another codex which omits Canaan. It is helpful to hear him himself: But we ourselves saw the book of the blessed Luke written in Greek on the most ancient parchments, in capital letters, without breathings and accents: where in the Greek, of Phalec, of Eber, of Sala, of Arphaxad, of Sem, in the Latin which was Phalec, who was Eber, who was Arphaxad, who was Sem, it was clearly read; with the mention of this Cainan entirely passed over. That codex, comprising the histories of the four Gospels and the Acts of the Apostles, formerly brought from Greece into Gaul, was deposited in the monastery of St. Irenaeus in the suburb of Lyons, and there, upon the outbreak of the civil war in the year 1581, was donated to the public library of the Cambridge Academy. Nor is there any other Greek MS of this kind, either commemorated by Beza or recently sent to England from Greece: whatever Hugo Grotius may say in his annotations to this place of Luke. These are Ussher's words. Moreover, the illustrious Scaliger observed in the prolegomena to the Chronicle. Eusebius in the most ancient copies of the Gospel according to Luke that Cainan does not exist. Other arguments also have been brought forward to this matter by Grotius, which we do not reject: primarily from the authority of Irenaeus and Africanus. The number of Irenaeus also, he says, shows that the name of Cainan was not read at that time, nor indeed will you find indications of the reading which now appears before the fourth century. I entirely agree with Corderius, who thinks that the name of Cainan did not exist in this place in the primitive books of Luke, nor in the seventy interpreters. Concerning Luke, besides those things which we have said, Africanus makes the matter credible, who does not acknowledge that name. Nor did he bring forward evidence only concerning the present passage, but also concerning Genesis, into which Cainan has crept: he warns concerning the LXX interpreters, that Procopius of Gaza notes that the passage in Genesis concerning Cainan has been marked with an obelus as supposititious: that Theophilus of Antioch, in his calculation of times, following those seventy, in his review of names omits Cainan and makes Arphaxad the father of Sala, and likewise Eusebius as he is edited in Greek by Scaliger, and that in that genealogy which he himself says is according to the seventy: and that others, professing that times are calculated by them according to the same interpreters, calculate in such a way that the account cannot be consistent unless this Cainan is omitted: among whom are Epiphanius in heresy 55 and Orosius. Add to these that the seventy cannot be said to have drawn this name from any tradition, since the Samaritan writing and the Chaldean version and others which followed it outside of the Greek, agree with the Hebrew codex, nor has any of the Hebrew masters handed down such a thing. Add that Abraham is the tenth from the flood, who would be the eleventh if Cainan were inserted, which not only the Hebrews, among whom is Josephus, affirm, but also Berosus from the Chaldeans, produced by Josephus himself, and Eupolemus from the Greeks, whose passage Eusebius preserved. Finally, Grotius adds a conjecture as to the reason why Kainan crept both into this passage of ours and into Genesis: Which conjecture leads me to believe that by some writer of the book, from which many copies flowed, the name of Cainan was replaced in this place by some error from the penultimate chapter of this verse, such as vicious repetitions which have occurred in many books from wrongly inspected archetypes or the hallucination of a dictator. Then, when that reading had begun to be spread widely through the copies of Luke, Greek Christians also, in the version of Genesis according to the seventy, inserted the name of Cainan between Arphaxad and Sala, with years also added, by which they might the more [support] Luke, whom they thought had written thus, so that his authority might remain firm. But other things which we have said refute the rashness of these people, as does the fact that the Greek book of Paralipomenon, whoever its translator may finally be, makes no mention of this new Cainan in the older books. By a not dissimilar line of reasoning, the Criticus Sacer will teach that Oedipus was once here I saw Grotius: from which it is pleasing to repeat these things. To us, I say, p. 760, it truly seems more likely that the genuine Kainan, son of Enos, from verse 37, simultaneously introduced the interpolated Kainan into the immediately preceding verse 36, or that a marginal note, a memorandum, was inscribed in some codex at this place, designating the true Kainan, which another person thought was a new generation perhaps omitted in the description of the genealogy, and introduced it into the text, so that in this way another, supposititious Kainan was born from it: or that the true Kainan had been omitted entirely in some exemplar, and was noted in the margin either by the scribe himself or by a corrector reading through the text, and from there was later brought by someone else, not in its proper place, from the margin into the context; and because Kainan, the son of Enos, is found both in the context of Moses and in the version of the LXX, it could easily have happened that the same name was inserted by others into the following verse as well, without noticing the error of the former, so that in place of one omitted Kainan, a double Kainan was substituted. But there is no doubt that once one codex was corrupted, the error could have spread into countless others; whence it further followed that from the corrupted copies of the Greek text, corrupted translations—Syriac, Arabic, Latin—had to emerge, since the error had already prevailed in the authentic text before them. These things concerning the interpolated or creeping-in Kainan of the present text.

Concerning the passage of Genesis in the Greek Bibles, our conjecture at the cited place held as follows. For as to the corruption of the version of the LXX Interpreters, it seems to have arisen from this: that perhaps someone, ignorant of that error and taking the supposititious Kainan for the genuine one, decided to amend the edition of the LXX Interpreters according to the authority of Luke in that place from which this part of the genealogy was taken: not noticing that the same was repeated in the Chronicles, and therefore instituting no amendment there. But when Kainan was likewise annotated in the margin at the passage of Gen. X, by one person he was indeed ascribed to Arphaxad in the text, but by another he was referred to among the sons of Shem (who succeed each other closely in Luke; the interpolated Kainan could be taken by someone for the son of Shem with the same ease with which he was taken by another for the son of Arphaxad), whence there arose in the edition of the LXX a double supposititious Kainan in Gen. X, one the son of Shem, the other the son of Arphaxad. Finally, when in the 11th chapter of Genesis the interpolated Kainan required certain years, years were likewise ascribed to him, which, borrowed from Salah, completed this new generation. Thus far the conjecture approved by us. We have added the divination of others, however, not having entirely rejected it. Others, however, think that the name of Kainan first crept into the Greek codices of the LXX Interpreters and from there was deduced into the exemplars of the Gospel of Luke by those who, when they read it in the Greek text of the O.T., thought it should not be omitted in the text of the N.T. where the same genealogy was repeated. In such matters as these, everyone's conjecture must be granted, since no one can have indubitable certainty. The rest, and what especially teach that Kainan is an intruder, we do not repeat, having added them more laboriously there.

Latin:

Vers. 36. τῦ Σαλὰ, τῦἈρφαξὰδ] Sic habent Manuscripti Græci aliquot, quorum meminit Beza, & quod potissimum est, antiquissima litera scriptus unus qui Lugdunensis Ecclesiæ fuit, Cantabrigiam postea delatus: & alter in Angliam è Græcia nuper missus. Irenæi quoque numerus ostendit Cainani nomen non lectum eo tempore: nec certe ejus quæ nunc apparet lectionis indicia reperias ante quartum seculum. Omnino Cordefio assentior existimanti Cainani nomen hoc loco nec in primitivis Lucæ, nec in LXX. Interpp. libris exstitisse. De Luca, præter ea quæ diximus, rem credibilem facit Africanus, qui id nomen non agnoscit: de interpretibus LXX. quod Procopius Gazæus notat eum qui est in Genesi de Cainano locum ὠβελίσθαι tanquam supposititium: quod Theophilus Antiochenus in temporum supputatione septuaginta illos sequens in nominum recensione omisso Cainane Arphaxadum Salæ patrem faciat: itemque Eusebius, ut Græce à Scaligero est editus, idque in ea genealogia quam ipse ait esse secundum septuaginta; quodque alii secundum eosdem interpretes tempora à se putari profitentes, ita putent, ut constare ratio non possit, nisi omittatur hic Cainan: quos inter sunt Epiphanius hæresi LV. & Orosius. His adde quod Septuaginta nomen hoc ex traditione aliqua hausisse dici non possint, cum Samaritana scriptio & Chaldæa versio, & quæ eam secutæ sunt aliæ extra Græcum, codici Hebræo consentiant, nec quisquam Hebræorum magistrorum tale quid tradiderit. Adde quod Abrahamum à diluvio esse decimum, qui Cainano interjecto esset undecimus, non Hebræi tantum, quos inter Josephus, affirmant, sed & ex Chaldæis Berosus ab ipso Josepho proditus, & ex Græcis Eupolemus, cujus locum servavit Eusebius. Quæ conjecturæ me inducunt, ut credam à Scriptore aliquo libri, unde multa exemplaria fluxerunt, ex penultimo hujus commatis capite, nomen Cainanis hoc loco errore quodam repositum, quales repetitiones vitiosas ex perperam inspectis archetypis, aut dictantis hallucinatione, multis in libris occurrunt. Deinde cum late spargi ea lectio per Lucæ exemplaria cœpisset, Græcos Christianos etiam in versione Geneseos secundum LXX. inter Arphaxadum & Salam interposuisse nomen Cainanis, annis etiam additis, quo magis Lucæ, quem sic scripsisse arbitrabantur, sua auctoritas constaret. Sed horum temeritatem tum alia quæ diximus refellunt, tum quod Paralipomenon liber Græcus, cujuscunque tandem is sit interpretis, in antiquioribus libris Cainanis hujus novi nullam faciat mentionem.

Id tantum in Genealogia CHRISTI adhuc restat, ut de Caináne quem hic ingerunt, Græca exemplaria dispiciamus. Ita enim habent Σαλὰ τῦ Καϊνὰν τῦ Ἀρφαξὰδ. Grotius eliminat Cainanum. Quem omnino νοθεύεσθαι, nec genuinum esse in Critico Sacro prolixe docuimus pag. 57. & seqq. Ideoque merito omittitur à Grotio, qui hîc ad codices nonnullos provocat. Sic, inquit, habent manuscripti Græci aliquot, quorum meminit Beza, & quod potissimum est antiquissima litera scriptus unus qui Lugdunensis Ecclesiæ fuit, Cantabrigiam postea delatus: & alter in Angliam è Græcia nuper missus. Ast relationem illam de Codicibus in Anglia du- biam reddit Jac. Userius Armachanus Archiepisco- pus in Chronol. Sacr. pag. 102. alium tamen co- dicem, qui Canaanem omittit, allegans. Juvat ipsum audire: Atqui librum, inquit, B. Lucæ Græ- co in antiquissimis membranis, litteris majusculis, si- ne spiritibus & accentibus, descriptum ipsi vidimus: ubi in Græco, τῶ Φαλὲκ, τῶ Εβὲρ, τῶ Σαλὰ, τῶ Ἀρφαξὰδ, τῶ Σὴμ, in Latino qui fuit Phalec, qui fuit Eber, qui fuit Arphaxad, qui fuit Sem, exerte legebatur; Cainanis hujus mentione prorsus prætermissa. Codex ille, quatuor Evangeliorum & Actorum Apostolicorum historias complectens, ex Græcia olim in Galliam perductus, in monasterio S. Irenæi in suburbio Lugdunensi est repositus, ibique o- riente bello civili Anno 1581. publica Cantabrigiensis Academiæ Bibliothecæ est donatus. Neque hujus generis Græcus ullus MS. est alius, vel à Beza commemoratus, vel in Angliam è Græcia nuper missus: quicquid in notationibus suis ad hunc Lu- cæ locum dicat Hugo Grotius. Hæc Usserius. Cæterum observavit Illustris Scaliger in prolegom. in Chron. Euseb. in vetustissimis exemplaribus Evangelii secundum Lucam Kainanen illum non extare. Alia etiam in hanc rem argumenta ad- ducta à Grotio sunt, quæ non reprobamus: Ab Irenæi imprimis & Africani autoritate. I- renæi quoque numerus, inquit, ostendit Cainani nomen non lectum eo tempore, nec certe ejus, quæ nunc apparet lectionis indicia reperies ante quar- tum seculum. Omnino Corderio assentior existiman- ti Cainani nomen hoc loco nec in primitivis Lucæ, nec in septuaginta interpretum libris extitisse. De Lucæ, præter ea quæ diximus, rem credibilem fa- cit Africanus, qui id nomen non agnoscit. Ne- que de loco tantum præsenti, sed etiam de Ge- nesi, in quam irrepsit Cainan documenta addu- xit: De interpretibus LXX. monet, quod Pro- copius Gazæus notet eum, qui est in Genesi de Cai- nano locum ὠβελίσθαι tanquam supposititium: quod Theophilus Antiochenus in temporum supputa- tione septuaginta illos sequens in nominum recensione omisso Cainane Arphaxadum Sale Patrem faciat, i- temque Eusebius ut Græce à Scaligero est editus, idque in ea genealogia, quam ipse ait esse secun- dum septuaginta: quodque alii secundum eosdem interpretes tempora à se putari profitentes, ita pu- tent, ut constare ratio non possit, nisi omittatur hic Cainan: quos inter sunt Epiphanius hæresi LV. & Orosius. His adde quod septuaginta nomen hoc ex traditione aliqua hausisse dici non possint, cum Samaritana scriptio & Chaldæa versio & quæ eam secuta sunt alia extra Græcum, codici Hebraico consentiant, nec quisquam Hebræorum magistrorum tale quid tradiderit. Adde quod Abrahamum a diluvio esse decimum, qui Cainano, interjecto esset undecimus, non Hebræi tantum, quos inter Josephus, affirmant, sed & ex Chaldæis Berosus ab ipso Josepho productus & ex Græcis Eupolemus, cujus locum servavit Eusebius. Addit denique Grotius conjecturam, qua ratione irrepserit Kainan tum in hunc nostrum locum, tum in Genesin: Quæ conjectura me inducunt, ut credam a Scriptore aliquo libri, unde multa exemplaria fluxerunt ex penultimo hujus commatis capite, no- men Cainanis hoc loco errore quodam repositum, qua- les repetitiones vitiosas ex perperam inspectis arche- typis, aut dictantis hallucinatione, multis in libris oc- currerunt. Deinde cum late spargi ea lectio per Lu- cæ exemplaria cæpisset, Græcos Christianos etiam in versione Geneseos secundum septuaginta, inter Ar- phaxadum & Salam interposuisse nomen Cainania annis etiam additis, quo magis Lucæ, quem sic scripsisse arbitrabantur, sua auctoritas constaret. Sed horum temeritatem tum alia quæ diximus, refel- lunt, tum quod Paralipomenon liber Græcus; cujus- cunque tandem is sit interpretis, in antiquioribus libris Cainanis hujus novi nullam faciat mentionem. Non absimili ratione Oedipum me quondam hic fuisse antequam Grotium viderim, Criticus Sacer docebit: è quo hæc repetere placet. Nobis, in- quam, p. 760. id vero magis simile videtur, quod γνήσιος Kainan, filius Enos è versu 37. simul inve- xerit ἐμβολιμαῖον Kainanem in versum immedia- te præcedentem 36. sive quod nota marginalis μνημό- συνον in Codice quopiam ad hunc locum adscripta fuerit, designans verum Kainanem, quam alius existi- marit novam generationem in descriptione genealo- giæ forte prætermissam, eamque in textum invexe- rit, ut ita enatus hinc sit alter Kainan supposititius: sive quod omnino in exemplari aliquo verus Kainan prætermissus fuerit, & vel a descriptore ipso, vel a Correctore textum relegente in margine notatus, in- deque post ab alio, non suo loco, è margine in contex- tum illatus; & quia Kainan Filius Enos & in contex- tu Mosis & in versione LXX. repertus, facile fieri po- tuit, ut ab aliis idem nomen, non animadverso priorum errore versui sequenti quoque infereretur, ut ita pro uno Kainane omisso geminus Kainan substitueretur. Uno autem corrupto Codice, errorem in alios innu- meros diffundi potuisse, nullum dubium est; unde porro quoque corruptis apographis textus Græci, o- portuit prodire corruptas translationes Syriacam Arab. Latinam, quum ante easdem jam error in textu authentico invaluerit. Hæc de textus præ- sentis Embolimeo vel irreptitio Kainane.

De loco vero Geneseos in Græcis Bibliis ita no- stra conjectura habuit cit. loco. Quod enim ad versionis LXX. Interpretum corruptionem, ea vide- tur hinc enata, quod forte aliquis erroris istius nescius, Kainanque supposititium pro genuino habens emenda- re statuerit LXX. Interpp. editionem ad fidem Lucæ in eo loco, unde desumta est hæc genealogiæ pars: non animadvertens, eandem repetitam in Chronicis, ad- eoque nullam ibi emendationem instituens. Quum au- tem ad locum Gen. X. pariter annotatus esset Kainan in margine, ab alio quidem Arphachfado adscriptus fuit in textu, ab alio vero relatus inter filios Semi (qui sibi proxime succedunt apud Lucam, potuit ea facili- tate Kainan adscriptitius à quopiam haberi pro Semi filio, qua habitus est ab alio pro Arphachsadi filio) unde enatus est in editione LXX. geminus Kainan Supposititius Gen. X. alter filius Semi, alter filius Ar- phachsadi. Tandem quum Gen. XI. cap. Kainan ἐμ- βολιμαĩῶ annos certos desideraret, adscripti pari- ter eidem anni, qui à Sale mutuo accepti, compleverunt novam istam generationem. Hactenus conjectura nobis probata. Aliorum tamen divinationem adjecimus, non omnino reprobavimus. Alii ta- men censent nomen Kainanis primum irrepsisse in Co- dices Græcos LXX. Interpp. indeque deductum fuis- se in Exemplaria Evangelii Lucæ ab iis, qui cum illud legerent in Textu Græco V. T. existimarunt non o- mittendum esse in textu N. ubi eadem repeteretur ge- nealogia. Concedenda est in hisce talibus cuique sua conjectura, quum certitudinem indubiam habere possit nemo. Cætera & quæ imprimis irreptitium Kainanem esse docent, Illic operiosius addita non repetimus.

## 3:38
Vers. 38. Of Adam, of God. The Syriac and Arabic, although they expressed the name of son everywhere, here changed the manner of speaking: nor did they say Adam who is the Son of God, but who is from God: lest he be believed to be begotten from the divine substance. I rather agree with those who think Adam is called the son of God by right of creation: and that by that degree minds are raised to believe in the generation of Christ. For He who could produce the first man from the earth without a father, the same could bring it about that Christ was born from a virgin without a father, not only to cleanse that divine image to which Adam was created from the stains of sin, but also to reform it into a much better lot. Certainly Paul also praises that Aratean saying: For we are also his offspring: And God himself in this sense calls himself a father, Deut. xxxii. 6.
