I will add a passage of Philo where he both names God the father of Adam and eloquently explains the causes of the name: speaking in this manner concerning the first and earth-born man: who, on account of his nobility, is comparable to no mortal, having been fashioned in his bodily form by divine hands into a statue with the perfection of plastic art; and having been deemed worthy of a soul from none of those things that have come into generation, God having breathed in as much of the divine power as a mortal nature could receive; he was, therefore, not an excess of nobility, with none of the others being able to come into comparison even by self-learning; for the glory of the others is from the nobility of ancestors; but the ancestors were men, perishable and corruptible animals, and their successes are uncertain and ephemeral and many; but for him, no mortal was a father, nor was he himself; but God, to whom having become in a certain way an image according to the ruling mind in the soul, it was necessary to keep the image unblemished as far as it was possible: having followed the virtues of the one who begat him, being set before choices and flights of opposites, of good and evil, and of the beautiful and the base, and of the true and the false, he eagerly chose the false and the base and the evil, and neglected the good and the beautiful and the true. Josephus also, dealing with the first men, says he was made by God himself. Nor does the observation of the ancients displease me, who wish that Matthew, writing to the Jews, carried the matter to the point of showing that Jesus is the heir of Abraham and David, and consequently their Messiah: but Luke, as one who was writing to the Greeks, wove the pedigree to the very origin of the human race, to signify that this is he who, born for the common good of the human race, was about to confer upon those believing in him the right of the sons of God, which Adam and the men who followed him had lost: and indeed by so much the more excellently, by how much he himself was begotten in a more excellent manner.

Latin:

Vers. 38. τῦ Ἀδὰμ τῦ θεῦ] Syrus & Arabs, cum ubique filii nomen expresserint, hic mutarunt loquendi genus: neque dixerunt Adam qui Filius Dei, sed qui ex Deo est: ne scilicet ex substantia divina genitus crederetur. Ego illis potius as- sentio, qui filium Dei dici putant Adamum creationis jure: atq; eo gradu attolli animos ad credendam Christi genitu- ram, Nam qui ex terra sine patre hominem primum potuit producere, idem efficere potuit ut Christus ex virgine sine patre nasceretur, imaginem illam divinam ad quam Adamus erat conditus, non purgaturus tantum a peccati maculis, sed & in multo meliorem sortem reformaturus. Certe & Paulus illud Arateum laudat: τοῦ γὰρ καὶ γένος ἐσμέν: Et Deus ipse hoc sensu patrem se vocat Deut. xxxii. 6. Addam Philonis locum ubi & Deum patrem Adami nominat & causas nominis fa- cunde explicat: περὶ τοῦ πρώτου καὶ γηγενοῦς hunc in modum lo- quens: ὃς ἕνεκα ἐυγενείας οὐδενι θνητῷ σύγκριτος, χερσὶ μὲν θείαις εἰς ἀνδριάντα τὸ σωματοειδὲς τυπωθεὶς ἀκρότητι τέχνης πλα- στικῆς· ψυχῆς δὲ ἀξιωθεὶς ἀπ᾿ οὐδενὸς ἔτι τῶν εἰς γένεσιν ἡκόντων, ἐμπνεύσαντος θεοῦ τῆς θείας δυνάμεως ὅσον ἠδύνατο δέξασθαι θνητὴ φύσις· ἦν ἄρ, οὐχ᾽ ὑπερβολὴ τῆς ἐυγενείας, μηδεμίας τῶν ἄλλων οὐ δὲ ἀυτομάθουσαι εἰς σύγκρισιν ἐλθεῖν δυναμένης· τῶν μὲν γὰρ τὸ κλέος ἐκ προγόνων ἐυγενείας· ἄνθρωποι δὲ οἱ πρόγονοι, ζῶα ἐπί- κηρα καὶ φθαρτὰ, καὶ αἱ τούτων ἀβέβαιοι καὶ ἐφήμεροι ?αὶ πολλοὶ ἔυπρα- γίαι· τῷ δὲ πατὴρ μὲν θνητὸς οὐδεὶς, οὐδὲ αὔτος· ἀλλ᾽ ὁ θεὸς ᾧ τρόπον τινὰ γενόμενος εἰκὼν κατὰ τὸν ἡγεμόνα νοῦν ἐν ψυχῇ, δέον ἀκηλίδωτον τὴν εἰκόνα φυλάξαι καθ᾽ ὅσον οἷον τε ἦν: ἐπακολουθήσαντα ταῖς τοῦ γεννήσαντος ἀρεταῖς, προτεθένται εἰς αἱρέσεις καὶ φυγὰς τῶν ἐναν- τίων ἀγαθοῦ καὶ κακοῦ καὶ καλοῦ καὶ αἰσχροῦ καὶ ἀληθοῦς καὶ ψευδοῦς, τὰ μὲν ψευδῆ καὶ αἰσχρὰ καὶ κακὰ προθύμως ἑλέσθαι, τῶν δὲ ἀγαθῶν καὶ κα- λῶν καὶ ἀληθῶν ἠλόγησεν. Josephus quoque de primis homi- nibus agens ὑπ᾽ ἀυτοῦ τοῦ θεοῦ γενομένου. Neque vero displicet mihi veterum observatio, qui Matthæum Judæis scribentem eo rem perduxisse volunt, ut ostenderet Jesum esse hæredem Abrahami & Davidis, ac proinde ipsorum Messiam: Lucam autem, ut qui Græcis scriberet, ad ipsam generis humani originem stemma pertexuisse, ut significaret hunc illum es- se qui communi bono generis humani natus in se credenti- bus collaturus esset jus filiorum Dei, quod Adamus & eum secuti homines amiserant: & quidem tanto excellentius, quanto ipse genitus erat modo excellentiore.

## 4:1 Argument
PART II. OF THE GOSPEL OF ST. LUKE, Concerning the Acts of the Ministry of Christ up to the Passion of Christ. SECTION I. OF THE ACTS OF THE MINISTRY OF CHRIST. Acts from the first Passover to the second. CHAPTER IV. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

Under the auspices of the office of Christ, he had to fight with the Devil, by whom he was variously tempted in the desert. Then he preached in the Synagogue of his native Nazareth, teaching that that prophecy from Isaiah (c. LXI. 1.) was fulfilled, to the admiration of the hearers, although some demanded miracles: to whom he replies that a Prophet is not accepted in his own country, by the example of Elijah helping the woman of Zarephath, and Elisha helping Naaman, who were not fellow-countrymen: whence, when the Nazarenes wished to cast him down from the hill, he passed through the midst of them. Thenceforth he taught in Capernaum, and freed one possessed, the fame of him spreading into the surrounding lands. Afterwards he healed Peter's mother-in-law, and restored many other sick and possessed persons: and departing thence, testifying that he must also preach the Gospel to other cities, he preached in the synagogues of Galilee.

There are three parts: I. The temptations of Christ in the desert, to v. 13. II. Christ's Nazarene sermon with the consequences, to v. 29. III. The Capernaum deeds, to v. 44.

PART I. The temptations of Christ in the desert.

Vers. 1. ἐν τῷ πνεύματι] Below v. 13. ἐν τῇ δυνάμει τοῦ πνεύματος. See above c. II. 27. and what pertains to Matthew in this place. Vers. 2. ἡμέρας] He understands civil days, that is, periods of twenty-four hours, which others in the Hebrew manner have called ἡμέρας τεσσαράκοντα καὶ νύκτας τεσσαράκοντα. Nor does that prevent Christ from having truly been within the bounds of that time in Jerusalem

on the pinnacle. For since he was immediately carried back into the wilderness with the greatest speed, a short time is reckoned as nothing.

Latin:

PARS II. EVANGELII S. LUCÆ, De Actis Ministerii Christi usque ad Passionem Christi. SECTIO I. ACTORUM MINISTERII CHRISTI. A Paschate primo ad secundum acta. CAPUT IV. ARGUMENTUM ET PAR- TITIO.

Sub auspicium officii Christi pugnandum ei fuit cum Diabolo, à quo varie tentatus est in de- serto. Tum prædicavit in Synagoga patriæ Nazareth, ex Esaia (c. LXI. 1.) vaticinium il- lud impletum docens, cum auditorum admi- ratione, etsi nonnulli miracula postularent: quibus respondet, Prophetam non esse acce- ptum in Patria, exemplo Eliæ, Sareptanam, & Elisæ, Naamanum juvantis, qui non erant Sympatriota: unde cum ipsum præcipitare de colle vellent Nazarekani, per medium eorum transivit. Dehinc docuit in Caper- naum, & obsessum liberavit, fama dima- nante de eo in circumjacentes terras. Post- modum Petri socrum sanavit, & multos a- lios ægrotos & obsessos restituit: & digre- diens inde testatus se etiam aliis civitatibus oportere prædicare Evangelium, in Scholis Galilææ prædicavit.

Partes tres sunt: I. Tentationes Christi in deserto, ad v. 13. II. Concio Christi Nazaretha- na cum consequentibus, ad v. 29. III. Gesta Ca- pernaitica, ad v. 44.

PARS I. Teutationes Christi in deserto.

Vers. 1. ἐν τῷ πνεύματι] Infra v. 13. ἐν τῇ δυνάμει τοῦ πνεύ- ματος. Vide supra c. II. 27. & quæ ad Matthæum hoc loco. Vers. 2. ἡμέρας] Dies civiles, id est νυχθήμερα intelligit, quod alii Hebraico more dixerunt ἡμέρας τεσσαράκοντα καὶ νύκτας τεσσαράκοντα. Neque id impedit, quo minus reve- ra Christus intra ejus temporis terminos Hierosolymis

ἐν τῷ πτερυγίῳ fuerit. Nam cum statim relatus fuerit in so- litudinem summa celeritate, exiguum tempus pro nullo re- putatur.

## 4:2
being tempted] In many ways: of which the principal ones are reported here.

Latin:

πειραζόμενος] Multis modis: quorum præcipui hic refe- runtur.

## 4:3
Verse 3. to this stone] To any one of these stones: which Matthew expresses in the plural, as he often does elsewhere.

Latin:

Vers. 3. τῷ λίθῳ τούτῳ] Cuivis horum lapidum: quod pluraliter exprimit Matthæus, ut alibi sæpe.

## 4:5
Verse 5. Having led up] הֶעֶלָה.

in a moment of time] in an atom, as some of the Greeks speak. It has been well translated recently as in a point of time, in which way Cicero and Caesar speak. For the meaning of a moment extends further. It is Hebrew כְרֶגַע Isa. XXIX. 5.

Latin:

Vers. 5. Ἀναγαγὼν] הֶעֶלָה.

ἐν στιγμῇ χρόνου] ἐν ἀτόμῳ ut Græcorum quidam loquun- tur. Bene nuper versum in puncto temporis quo modo lo- quuntur Cicero & Cæsar. Nam momenti significatio lon- gius porrigitur. Hebræum est כְרֶגַע Esa. XXIX. 5.

## 4:6
Verse 6. this authority] That is, all this dominion, the Syrian rightly שׁוּלְטָנָא. For the LXX also translate שׁלט as to exercise authority. Hence one may see everywhere that rule and authority are joined, and that it is transferred from an abstract sense to what they call a concrete one.

and their glory] The Latin also reads it thus. But the Syrian reads it as 'its' so that it may refer to authority. But I think 'their' is correct so that it may refer to the things themselves that were demonstrated: just as shortly after 'all these things'.

it] the glory, just as the Syrian also reads. The Devil in this place and elsewhere, as Sophists are wont to do, mixes truth with falsehood. For he was not so impudent as to deny God's right over empires: therefore he says 'it has been delivered'. But he boasts of his own power in conducting and managing human affairs, on account of which he is called the ruler of the world even to Christ himself. It is especially false in that 'to whom I will'. For that signifies a freedom not subject to another's will, which is attributed to God in those very words as his own in Daniel IV. 22. The Devil therefore says just as much, as if he were saying that God had turned his care away from the regard of human affairs, which opinion is the source of atheism.

Latin:

Vers. 6. τὴν ἐξουσίαν ταύτην] Id est omne hoc imperium, Syrus recte שׁוּלְטָנָא. Nam & LXX, שׁלט vertunt ἐξουσιά- ζειν. Hinc passim videre est conjungi ἀρχὴν & ἐξουσίαν, & à sensu abstracto ad concretum quem vocant transferri.

καὶ τὴν δόξαν αὐτῶν] Ita & Latinus legit. At Syrus αὐτῆς ut referatur ad ἐξουσίαν. Sed rectum puto αὐτῶν ut ad res ipsas demonstratas referatur: quomodo mox ἅπαντα ταῦτα.

αὐτὴν] τὴν δόξαν quomodo & Syrus legit. Diabolus hoc loco & alibi, ut Sophistæ solent verum falso permiscet. Neque enim tam impudens erat ut Deo jus in imperia ab- negaret: ideo dicit παραδέδοται. Sed jactat vim suam in rebus humanis agendis ferendisque, ob quam ἄρχων τοῦ κόσμου ipsi quoque Christo dicitur. Falsum præcipue est in illo ᾧ ἐὰν θέλω. Id enim libertatem significat alieno arbi- trio non subjectam, quæ Deo illis ipsis verbis ut propria tribuitur Daniel IV. 22. Tantundem ergo dicit Diabolus, quasi diceret Deum ab humanarum rerum respectu cu- ram suam avertisse, quæ opinio fons est ἀθεότητος.

## 4:7
V. 7. before me] In my honor: which Matthew's interpreter called 'to me'. For what is often said by the Dative is expressed elsewhere by לִפְנֵי or עַל־פְּנֵי, in Greek 'in the presence of' or 'before someone'. The Dative is Hebrew and Greek in 3 Kings XIX. 18 and Greek in Rom. XI. 4, where it is 'before' in Latin; what is in the Dative in Jerem. XXIX, that is in 2 Par. XXV. 14 by לִפְנֵי, in Greek 'in their presence'.

Latin:

V. 7. ἐνώπιόν μου] In mei honorem: quod μοι dixit Matthæi interpres. Nam quod sæpe per Dativum dicitur id alibi ex- primitur per לִפְנֵי aut עַל־פְּנֵי, Græce ἐναντίον aut ἐνώπιόν τινος. Dativus est Hebraice & Græce 3. Reg. XIX. 18. & Græce Rom. XI. 4. ubi Latine coram; quod Jerem. XXIX. in Da- tivo, id 2. Par XXV. 14. est per לִפְנֵי Græce ἐναντίον αὐτῶν.

## 4:8
Verse 8. Jesus said it is written, you shall worship] This is undoubtedly an older reading which both the Latin and the Syrian acknowledge: and Origen and Ambrose. After all these, it is added in Greek codices and even Arabic ones: 'get behind me', or even 'get behind me Satan': and after 'it is written' 'for' is added, no doubt from a collation of other passages: Nor is there anyone among the Greeks older than Theophylact who acknowledges those words in this place, and so other scribes have transposed certain clauses in this history, so that they might restore the order of the temptations to that which is in Matthew. But there was no reason why Luke should follow the order so anxiously in matters of this kind.

From the Latin and Syrian version, it is a matter of conscience for us to correct the Greek codices, which constantly retain those words 'get behind me' with the Arabic. Nor can it be proven from Origen or Ambrose that that is an older reading: since Ambrose may have followed the Latin text, and neither Origen nor other commentators, when they perhaps omit this or that which is held in the codices of the original text, prove that it was also omitted in that codex which they had before their eyes: since they have often deliberately quoted the words of the text concisely. Yet those things which are sometimes inserted into the text by more recent scribes from the commentaries of the ancients provide a certain argument as to how the ancient interpreters read. Therefore, there is one reason for the omission of some words, which sometimes happens for the sake of brevity, and another for the express insertion of words, as if pertaining to the sacred text; which we readily admit should not be called into doubt so rashly.

Latin:

Vers. 8. εἶπεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς γέγραπται, προσκυνήσεις] Hæc haud dubie vetustior est lectio quam & Latinus & Syrus agnoscit: & Origenes & Ambrosius. Post quos omnes addit in Græ- cis codicibus atque etiam Arabicis cœpit: ὕπαγε ὀπίσω μου, aut etiam ὕπαγε ὀπίσω μοῦ Cατανᾶ: & post γέγραπται addi- tum γάρ, nimirum ex aliorum locorum collatione: Nec quisquam est Græcorum Theophylacto antiquior, qui ista verba hoc loco agnoscat, sic & alii exscriptores commata quædam in hac historia transposuerunt, ut ordinem τῶν πει- ρασμῶν eum restituerent qui est apud Matthæum. Sed nulla fuit causa cur Lucas in rebus ejusmodi ordinem tam anxie sequeretur.

E versione Latina, & Syra corrigere Græcos codices, qui constanter illa ὕπαγε ὀπίσω μου cum Arabe retinent, religio nobis est. Nec vetustio- rem illam lectionem esse ex Origene, vel Ambrosio probari potest: Siquidem Latinum secutus tex- tum sit Ambrosius, neque seu Origenes, seu alii commentatores, cum omittunt forte hoc vel illud, quod in codicibus textus originalis habetur, evin- cant, id omissum etiam in illo codice fuisse, quem præ oculis habuere: cum sæpe de industria ver- ba textus concise allegarint. Ea tamen quæ è textu nonnunquam à recentioribus exscriptori- bus inserta commentationibus veterum sunt, ar- gumentum quoddam præbent, quomodo lege- rint antiqui interpretes. Alia itaque ratio est o- missionis verborum nonnullorum, quæ compen- dii causa quandoque fit, alia expressæ verborum insertionis, ceu pertinentium ad textum sacrum; quæ non ita temere in dubium vocari debere, fa- ciles admittimus.

## 4:9
Vers. 9. εἰ ὁ υἱὸς εἶ τοῦ θεοῦ] Above he said εἰ υἱὸς εἶ τοῦ θεοῦ. How this also is to be read, the learned interpreter advises, not with empty conjectures. Nor do I disagree, if the authority of some codices is added. For not even the Arab added the article.

Therefore, the authority of the codices being deficient, the conjecture of Beza is vain, even though the Arab did not add the article. If it is permitted to indulge in suspicions concerning the reading of the sacred text or to amend it from versions, what certainty of the authentic text will finally remain?

Latin:

Vers. 9. εἰ ὁ υἱὸς εἶ τοῦ θεοῦ] Supra dixit εἰ υἱὸς εἶ τοῦ θεοῦ. Quomodo & hic legendum non vanis conjecturis monet eruditus interpres. Nec refrager, si codicum aliquot au- toritas accedat. Nam ne Arabs quidem articulum addi- dit.

Deficiente ergo codicum autoritate conjectu- ra Bezæ vana est, utut Arabs non addiderit arti- culum. Si suspicionibus indulgere liceat circa textus sacri lectionem aut è versionibus eandem emendare, quæ tandem supererit textus authenti- ci certitudo?

## 4:10
Vers. 10. τὸ διαφυλάξαι σε] Which is in the Psalm לִשְׁמָרְךָ, the LXX translated it thus. Thus also elsewhere in these Scriptures you will find τὸ placed for the Hebrew לְ.

Latin:

Vers. 10. τὸ διαφυλάξαι σε] Quod est in Psalmo לִשְׁמָרְךָ ita verterunt LXX. Sic & alibi in his Scriptis reperies τὸ positum pro Hebræo לְ.

## 4:13
Vers. 13. ἄχρι καιρῦ.] About to attack with force later, whom he had not been able to corrupt with allurements Joh. XIV. 30. so that there would be nothing of evils, in overcoming which our leader had not gone before us πεπειρασμένον κατὰ πάντα καθ᾽ ὑμοιότητα Hebr. IV. 15.

PART II. The Nazarene Sermon of Christ.

Latin:

Vers. 13. ἄχρι καιρῦ.] Vi aggressurus postea quem illece- bris corrumpere non potuerat Joh. XIV. 30. ut nihil esset malorum, in quo vincendo dux noster nobis non præivis- set πεπειρασμένον κατὰ πάντα καθ᾽ ὑμοιότητα Hebr. IV. 15.

PARS II. Concio Christi Nazarethana.

## 4:14
Vers. 14. κὰ ὑπέσρεψεν ὁ Ἰησῦς ἐν τῇ δυνάμει τῦ πνεύματος, εἰς τὴν γαλιλαίαν] That is, the Spirit leading him, he betook himself there. For this interpretation pleases above others because of that which we had above in verse 1. Δύναμις πνεύματος is τὸ πνεῦμα Act. I. v. 8.

Latin:

Vers. 14. κὰ ὑπέσρεψεν ὁ Ἰησῦς ἐν τῇ δυνάμει τῦ πνεύματος, εἰς τὴν γαλιλαίαν] Id est Spiritu ducente eo se contulit. Hæc enim interpretatio præ cæteris arridet ob id quod supra ha- buimus commate 1. Δύναμις πνεύματος est τὸ πνεῦμα Αετ. I. v. 8.

## 4:16
Vers. 16. κατὰ τὸ εἰωθὸς αὐτῷ] כמשפטו just as he was accustomed to do at Capharnaum.

άνέση αναγνῶσαι] There was accustomed to be an ἀναγνώσης in the Synagogues: as we shall say below at the word ὑπηρέτης: After he had read the passage assigned to the day, the opportunity for discussing was made: Act. XIII. 15. Philo: ὁ μὲν τὰς βίβλους ἀναγινώσκει λόγων· ἕτερος δὲ τῶν ἐμπειροτάτων, ὅσα μὴ γνώριμα παρελθὼν, ἀναδιδάσκει (so it must be read from Eusebius, where the codices of Philo wrongly repeat the word ἀναγινώσκει) τὰ γὰρ πλῖσα διὰ συμβόλων ἀρχαιοτρόπῳ ζηλώσει παρ᾽ αὐτοῖς φιλοσοφεῖται. But for the sake of honor, if any grave man had arrived, the book was given to him with the power of reading, and if he judged himself equal, also of explaining.

Latin:

Vers. 16. κατὰ τὸ εἰωθὸς αὐτῷ] כמשפטו ita ut Caphar- naumi facere solebat.

άνέση αναγνῶσαι] Solebat in Synagogis esse ἀναγνώσης: ut dicemus infra ad vocem ὑπηρέτης: Postquam is legerat at- tributam diei περιοχὴν fiebat differendi copia: Act. XIII. 15. Philo: ὁ μὲν τὰς βίβλους ἀναγινώσκει λόγων· ἕτερος δὲ τῶν ἐμπει- ροτάτων, ὅσα μὴ γνώριμα παρελθὼν, ἀναδιδάσκει (ita legen- dum ex Eusebio, ubi Philonis codices male repetunt vocem ἀναγινώσκει) τὰ γὰρ πλῖσα διὰ συμβόλων ἀρχαιοτρόπῳ ζηλώσει παρ᾽ αὐτοῖς φιλοσοφεῖται. Sed honoris causa, si quis vir gra- vis advenisset, dabatur ei liber cum potestate legendi, & si parem se judicaret etiam explicandi.

## 4:17
Vers. 17. ἐπεδόθη αὐτῷ βιβλίον] Since on the Sabbath passages were read both from the Law and also from the Prophets, the book which was thought more difficult to explain was given to him, and that by the order of the archisynagogue through him who is called below ὑπηρέτης.

ἀναπτύξας] Ἀναπτύσσειν βιβλίον is to unroll: πτύσσειν to roll up. For the books of the Hebrews, as also of the Latins, were volumes: hence to unroll a book among Cicero and others. It is the same as to unroll in Livy and Martial, which word the Latin interpreter also used correctly here. Books of this kind can be seen even now in the Synagogues.

τὸν τόπον] Thus Plutarch and others are accustomed to speak: others even say χωρίον. Cicero called a place of a book several times: and Terence: Cum Plautinus locum reliquit integrum. Our author here Act. VIII. 32. said περιοχὴν: Justin Martyr and Jerome said Περικοπὴν following the example of the Greeks: and they are mistaken who explain that word otherwise in Philoponus and Basil.

Latin:

Vers. 17. ἐπεδόθη αὐτῷ βιβλίον] Cum & ex lege & ex Pro- phetis quoque sabbato περιοχαὶ legerentur, datus est ei li- ber qui expositu difficilior credebatur, idque jussu archisy- nagogi per eum qui infra vocatur ὑπηρέτης.

ἀναπτύξας] Ἀναπτύσσειν βιβλίον est evolvere: πτύσσειν convolvere. Nam Hebræorum, ut & Latinorum, libri e- rant volumina: hinc evolvere librum apud Ciceronem at- que alios. Idem est revolvere Livio & Martiali, qua voce & hic usus est recte Latinus interpres. Ejusmodi libros etiam nunc in Synagogis videre est.

τὸν τόπον] Sic Plutarchus atque alii loqui solent: alii etiam χωρίον dicunt. Cicero locum libri aliquoties dixit: & Terentius: Cum Plautinus locum reliquit integrum. No- ster hic Act. VIII. 32. περιοχὴν dixit: Περικοπὴν dixerunt Græcorum exemplo Justinus Martyr & Hieronymus: & falluntur qui apud Philoponum & Basilium eam vocem aliter exponunt.

## 4:18
Vers. 18. πνεῦμα κυρίο ἐπ᾽ ἐμέ] Just as the liberation from the Babylonian captivity was both an image and a pledge of the liberation of souls which the Messiah was about to effect, so also those things which Isaiah had said about himself were so directed by God that they applied more excellently to the Lord Jesus. Kimchi also adapts these to the Messiah.

἗ ἕνεκεν ἔχρισέ με] ἗ ἕνεκεν seems to designate a consequence: whereas, contrary to the usage of the Hellenists, it signifies an antecedent; for it corresponds to the Hebrew יען, which word signifies not 'therefore,' but 'because'; as in Gen. XXII. 16, ἗ ἕνεκεν ἐποίησας τὸ ῥῆμα τῦτο κὰι ἐκ ἐφείσω τῦ υἱῦ συλῦ ἀγαπητῦ, ἦ μὴν ἐνλογῶν ἐυλογήσω σε. Where likewise, as here, in the Hebrew there is יען, which word the LXX elsewhere translate by διά ὁ, as we said above in chapter I. 20. ἔχρισε here does not signify the gift of the Spirit (for the same would be rendered as the cause of itself) but an enjoined office, as also what follows, ἀπέσαλκε. The manner of speaking is taken from the fact that both Kings and Priests were accustomed to be inaugurated by anointing. Because that office of annunciation was formerly Isaiah's, but now more augustly imposed upon Christ, therefore both were equipped with gifts suitable to the office.

πτωχοῖς] Among the diversities of readings that occur in Hebrew codices, none is more frequent than that which has arisen from the interchange of the letters ו and י. Wherefore this very word which exists here in the Prophet is written by some as עניום and by others as ענוים in Ps. XXXIV. 3, Ps. IX. 13 & 19, and Prov. XVI. 19, with the Masoretes, whose authority the Jews follow, acknowledging it. But also elsewhere, where only ענוים is read, as we have it written in this passage of the Prophet, the LXX translate it as πένητες: as in the passage of the Psalm in the Hebrew X. 17 and XXII. 27. Certainly the origin of the word shows that misery is properly signified by this word: but afterwards it was transferred to the denotation of modesty and a submissive mind, which we also said concerning the word ταπεινῶν. And in this passage, that signification of a miserable state is much more apt than that of a modest mind.

Latin:

Vers. 18. πνεῦμα κυρίο ἐπ᾽ ἐμέ] Sicut liberatio ex capti- vitate Babylonica & imago & pignus fuit liberationis ani- morum quam facturus esset Messias, ita & quæ Esaias de se dixerat ita directa sunt à Deo, ut Domino Jesu excel- lentius convenirent, Etiam Kimchi ad Messiam hæc ap- ptat.

἗ ἕνεκεν ἔχρισέ με] Videtur ἗ ἕνεκεν aliquid consequens designare: cum contra ex usu Hellenistarum antecedens si- gnificet: respondet enim Hebræo יען quæ vox significat non propterea, sed eo quod; ut Gen. XXII. 16. ἗ ἕνεκεν ἐποί- ησας τὸ ῥῆμα τῦτο κὰι ἐκ ἐφείσω τῦ υἱῦ συλῦ ἀγαπητῦ, ἦ μὴν ἐν- λογῶν ἐυλογήσω σε. Ubi itidem ut hic in Hebræo est יען quam vocem alibi LXX. vertunt per διά ὁ, ut diximus su- pra cap. I. 20. ἔχρισε hic non donationem Spiritus significat (idem enim sui ipsius causa redderetur) sed injunctum mu- nus, ut & quod sequitur ἀπέσαλκε. Genus loquendi inde sumtum quod & Reges & Sacerdotes unćtione inaugurari solebant. Quia minus illud annuntiationis Esaiæ olim, jam vero augustius Christo erat impositum, ideoque uter- que instructus est donis muneri convenientibus.

πτωχοῖς] Inter diversitates lectionum quæ in Hebræis codicibus occurrunt, nulla est frequentior ea, quæ nata est ex literarum ו & י inter se commutatione. Quare hæc ipsa vox quæ hic apud Prophetam exstat in Psal. XXXIV. 3. Ps. IX. 13. & 19. & Prov. XVI. 19. ab aliis עניום ab aliis ענוים scribitur, agnoscentibus Masoritis quorum au- ctoritatem Judæi sequuntur. Sed & alibi, ubi non nisi ענוים legitur, quomodo hoc Prophetæ loco scriptum habemus, LXX. vertunt πένητες: ut in loco Psalmi apud Hebræos X. 17. & XXII. 27. sane origo vocis ostendit pro- prie miseriam hac voce significari: postea vero translatam ad modestiæ & submissi animi denotationem, quod & de voce ταπεινῶν diximus. Ethuic loco multo aptior est illa miseri status, quam animi modesti significatio.

## 4:19
κηρύξαι] That some codices have before this word ἰάσασθαι τὺς συντετριμμένυς τὴν καρδίαν, it appears from Origen that it was not in the old Greek books. But that it did not appear in the most ancient Latin codices is also easy to gather from the explanation of Ambrose on this passage. Wherefore, since there still survive ancient codices which do not have this particle, it is much more probable that it was added from Isaiah and the LXX interpreters than omitted by other scribes. For in the same way the Latin edition has added from Isaiah the com- the following morning, and the day of retribution, which exists neither in the Greek nor in the Syriac. Our writers, however, often use such liberty with the passages of the Prophets that they omit certain words in the middle, which could be done here with the less damage to the sense, because the Prophet often expresses the same thing with a varied manner of speaking.

and recovery of sight to the blind] In reality, it is clear that the same thing is said as in the preceding. The propriety of the words is in dispute: it seems to me that the LXX, whom Luke follows, interpreted the Hebrew quite considerately. If anyone wishes to weigh the places in which the word פקח appears, it does not signify any opening like פתח, but only that which pertains to the eyes, except that it is also transferred to the ears, just as פצה is proper to the mouth. Now, as for what follows, that קור is a prison, as many wish, is proved by no testimony. Wherefore I do not see why we should disapprove of what the most learned of the Hebrews feel, that there is one word פקחקוח but in which the later letters are repeated αὐξητικῶς. Of this kind are אדמרם and ירקרק and סחרחר and הפכפך. The Hebrew grammarians dispute whether such a repetition of letters is ὑποκοριστικὴ or αὐξητικὴ. But even if the matter is doubtful regarding אדמרם and ירקרק, the two remaining words I mentioned absolutely demand an intensive meaning, as can be seen in Ps. XXXVIII. 11 and Prov. XXI. 8. They seem, therefore, to think very well who, in this passage of the Prophet, refer פקחקוח to the fullest freedom of turning the eyes hither and thither wherever one pleases. The interpreters of the LXX, however, in order to continue the translation, translated what precedes אסורים as blind, undoubtedly because, as we have said, פקח pertains to the eyes and does not pertain to a prison. And for that reason, it is usually said of the blind, as in Ps. CXLVI. 8 and Is. XLII. 7. But the Hebrews love to connect both proper and figurative meanings and other figures to others. Those who live in darkness are accustomed to be called blind, which especially suits those whom a prison encloses. And so, in the same Isaiah XLIX. 9, those in bonds and those in darkness are placed with the same meaning, and in chapter XLVII. 7, the blind and the bound. Therefore, blind captives, as the Latins say, those captured in their eyes. Each simile signifies the highest misery, such as was that of the Jews in the Babylonian exile, and much more that of all men in that state of gross ignorance before the times of the Messiah. Compare the same Isaiah chapter XLIII. 8, where the Jews in that exile are likewise called blind, however much they may have eyes: because, clearly, the highest misery had taken away from their eyes the freedom of seeing.

to send away the broken in liberty] This is nothing other than a popular explanation of that which might have seemed to be said more obscurely by the words immediately preceding. For it appears that this expression was commonly used from the other passage of Isaiah LVIII. 6, where the LXX have the same words that Luke placed here. And for that reason, I believe that because Luke was about to add this for the sake of explanation, he omitted above that equivalent, to heal the broken in heart. For how little do the broken and the crushed differ? But those to be understood in this place are the broken in spirit, not those who are touched by the repentance of sins, but those dwelling in the highest straits of affairs: as also in Ps. CXLVII. 3. For it is about that first calling, if I am not mistaken, which catches most men thinking of nothing good. For the discourse is not about the benefit of liberation itself, but about the announcement of that liberation already prepared: which the following also show.

Verse 19. to preach] לקרא to call. A simile taken from the year of Jubilee, which was accustomed to be announced by a herald with the sound of a trumpet.

Concerning this whole prophetic passage and the present Grotian explanation, as well as that which he handed down on Is. LXI, we have seen in the Anti-Grotian Annotations on Isaiah. It is helpful, however, to add what we have otherwise publicly proposed here concerning the same. The first public sermon held at Nazareth is described here, concerning which we note (1.) The text of the sermon. It is pleasant to observe that in the first sermon, which, as Origen and Theophylact note, he deigned to have in his own country, while explaining the book of the Prophet Isaiah, he immediately found the classic passage concerning his prophetic office: The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, etc. Is. LXI. 1. For in this most sweet text, not only is the doctoral office of the Messiah proposed, and his anointing to the office, and his divine mission, which he was then beginning to exercise publicly, so that he might thus demonstrate to all first the foundation of his whole ministry, his calling and his mission; but also it is so described that it can scarcely be read expressed in sweeter words anywhere in the whole code. Namely, that he was sent, not to sharpen the law but to evangelize, not to some few with selection, or according to some absolute election of God, but to any poor people whatsoever: That is, to all the afflicted, and indeed to the whole human race, constituted in a state of sin and misery, that he was sent to announce the glad tidings to afflicted mortals, so that, namely, the broken in heart might be healed, that release might be preached to the captives, sight to the blind, and sending away in liberty to the broken, so that the acceptable year of the Lord might truly be a Jubilee to all the afflicted, but the day of retribution might be denounced to spiritual enemies. Some think the words to send away the broken in liberty were taken from Isaiah LVIII. 6, as if Christ had joined two passages. But it is better to say that those were inserted by CHRIST for the sake of explanation, not indeed so that they might declare the immediately preceding, sight to the blind, which Maldonatus wishes, but so that the whole sentiment of the Prophet might be illustrated, and the sum of the preceding might be comprehended by those words. For if you wish to say in one word those afflicted in heart, the broken, the captives, and finally the blind, you would say the broken, who are clearly broken by misery and affliction, by the curse of the law, by the contrition of sin, and by the yoke and captivity of Satan, and also by spiritual blindness; if you wish to express the sum of preaching the Gospel and thus also to embrace it in a few words, the healing of the broken, the release of the captives, the restoration of the blind, you would say that the broken are sent away in liberty or true freedom. The preceding words καὶ τυφλοῖς ἀνάβλεψιν, which Christ did not weave in from his own [authority], as Rabbi Isaac Ben-Abraham accuses, but repeated from the Septuagint version and a collation of the Isaianic text, chapter XLII, are not difficult to reconcile with the Hebrews. The Hebrews, along with the Chaldean and Sanctius, render it thus: 'and to the shut, the opening of the prison'; they can be explained in such a way that those who are shut up in a dark prison live in darkness like the blind: But the words פקח קוח are more correctly explained as an opening, such as that of the eyes: סנורים concerning the shut, or captured eyes; since the Hebrews are accustomed to understand the blind by these. Compare Ps. CXLVI. 8, Isa. XLII. 7, as פקוחים [means] opened, seeing, or possessing sight, which word signifies not just any opening, but only that which pertains to the eyes. פקח קוח contracted into one word, as Grotius observes in this place, carries an intensive meaning toward the fullest freedom of turning the eyes hither and thither, wherever one pleases.

II. The sum and argument of the explanation.

Christ, having closed the book, sat down, claiming for himself the office of Teacher by right (whereas others of the common people were accustomed to do so while standing when discoursing on the Sacred Scriptures), where the eyes of all were turned upon him: He said, because today this Scripture is fulfilled in your ears. This is the sum of Christ's sermon, which he undoubtedly explained at greater length. Because Luke reports that all bore witness to him, and were amazed at the grace of the words which proceeded from his mouth. But Luke did not express what the sermon itself was; yet it is rightly gathered from the emphasis of the words of Isaiah, a comparison having been instituted with the recitation of the same by the Evangelist, how sweetly Christ instructed his fellow citizens in his first sermon, partly concerning the diverse state of men, then concerning the state of destitution, in which, outside of Christ, we are truly miserable and afflicted in heart, servants and captives in will, blind in the eyes of the mind, and thus destitute of all spiritual powers and utterly broken; then of restoration, to be procured through the Messiah, who brings and procures for the afflicted joy, for the contrite health, for the captives liberation, for the blind sight, for the broken liberty, situated in the remission of sins: partly concerning the Doctrine of the Messiah, by which he had to inculcate both the law and the Gospel; because through the law there is recognition of misery and contrition, as well as brokenness. But the Gospel is the joyful message concerning healing and restoration and the free remission of sins; that is as it were preliminary and is rather presupposed by Christ, inasmuch as Moses inculcated it most: but this is proper to Christ, John 1:18.

III. The object of the Prophetic prophecy. With a sonorous voice Christ teaches, and Luke repeats from his mouth that which is the chief point here in the Isaianic prophecy, concerning whom it speaks, while he says, today this Scripture is fulfilled; whence it is manifest that Isaiah predicted these things concerning Christ, for the Prophet undoubtedly prophesied concerning him in whom Christ taught in the explanation of this prophecy that it was fulfilled: But he testified that it was fulfilled in no one else but himself. Therefore, the Chaldean and the Rabbis are in vain here, as well as the Judaizing Papists, whom Lyranus notes, and especially Thomas and those who follow him, that Isaiah speaks here of himself, that he was sent to the Jews to announce to them liberation from the Babylonian captivity. To whom also Calvin and Wolfg. Musculus in their Commentaries on this place accede. The former not obscurely hints that the Jews rightly see that those things are inconsiderately drawn to Christ alone which were said of other Prophets also: the latter, however, says that the present passage of Isaiah is so constituted that it cannot without shame be referred to Christ alone, others being excluded. Similarly, Hugo Grotius in his annotations on this place thinks that Isaiah speaks of himself, but that the image of Christ is seen not obscurely in him. He refutes them (1.) The anointing, ἐξοχικὴ, from which he has the name above others, Dan. 11:2, 2 Sam. 23:1, done immediately by the Lord, bringing in the fullness of the Holy Spirit, who therefore is said simply and in the most eminent manner to be upon him, for the reason that he is anointed with the same not by measure and above his fellows, Ps. 45:7. (2.) A peculiar mission made to evangelize, to any blind, to any bound; which befits none of the Prophets, all were sent to some, the one Messiah to all, and for the sake of all. (3.) Preaching joined with the highest efficacy; for since others preach the Gospel, this anointed one of the Lord alone also grants efficacy to the proclamation, and in very deed provides liberation to the captives, opening to the closed, he himself binds the broken in heart, gives a crown for ashes, the oil of joy, the mantle of praise for the spirit of heaviness, which certainly no Prophet can perform except him. (4.) The calling of the Gentiles, of which v. 5. Another shall stand and feed your flocks; he predicts Pastors, Husbandmen, Vinedressers of the Church, foreigners or Gentiles, which also Christ is read to have predicted to the Jews, Matt. 21:41. Therefore, it is concerning that anointed one of the Lord that it is treated here, through whom the universal calling of the Gentiles was to be. Concerning the mission of him who was to be the universal Evangelist. Which certainly can be said neither of Isaiah, nor of any other Prophet, but uniquely of Christ. (5.) The designation of the divine nature of the Messiah. He who speaks in v. 1: The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, he testifies in v. 8, I am Jehovah loving justice and hating robbery for a burnt offering. But who else of the anointed of the Lord can profess this of himself than the Messiah, that he loves justice and simply hates robbery, and that he is Jehovah? Whence that anointed one, because he loves justice and hates robbery, is introduced as the universal judge of good and evil, who also promises a blessing to all nations, which befit none but the Messiah. (6.) A comparison of the preceding things. As in the preceding chapter 60:1 it is treated of Christ the great light, of the author of the calling of the Gentiles, as well as of the joy of eternal life, so here Christ himself is introduced to announce the Gospel concerning eternal salvation to the Jews and the Gentiles; therefore it is concerning that great Evangelist, and not concerning a messenger of the Babylonian captivity released or to be released; concerning Christ, I say, who is also the Redeemer, ch. 59:20. and is the light of Israel and of the Gentiles, and that Lord who will be the eternal light to the Elect, ch. 60:19, and not concerning Isaiah or any minister. (7.) The cohesion of the following things. For the sake of which thing in this very chapter 61:10 a Eucharistic song is sung, that must undoubtedly be attributed to this Evangelist, his proclamation having been received. But that song does not sound of the Babylonian captivity released, but of the salvation and everlasting Justice which is obtained in the Messiah. (8.) The application of Christ himself, who after the Spirit of the Lord descended upon him in Baptism, now prepares himself to undertake the Prophetic office, says that this scripture is fulfilled in himself: Today this Scripture is fulfilled. But he adds in your ears, not because it is fulfilled in others in the Prophets, but in the Nazarenes in Christ as Musculus wishes: but since he treats of Christ's proclamation in general, it is said that the same was also fulfilled among his fellow citizens hearing him. (9.) The interpretation of the more important Doctors. With unanimous vote, all our countrymen, Oecolampadius, likewise Piscator, Junius, Tremellius, the authors of the Belgian Version, and most Papists, along with the Greek and Latin Fathers, explain it of Christ alone according to the letter: nor does any reason move one to depart from them; nay, the text is too clear for anyone to be able to oppose this interpretation, which is approved by Christ and the Church.

IV. Christ's judgment concerning the complaint of certain hearers. He anticipated their thoughts. You will surely say this proverb to me: Physician, heal yourself. By this proverb, common among the Hebrews, they looked both to Christ himself, who, being himself miserable and afflicted, announced joy to the afflicted and an acceptable year to the miserable; and also to Christ's native country, as the words subjoined teach: What things we have heard done in Capernaum, do also here in your native country; namely, they understood the healing predicted by Isaiah concerning bodily care; therefore, they demanded that the same miracles of healing, which he had performed elsewhere, be done in his native country, partly out of ambition, partly out of incredulity; which, however, the Lord refused to do on account of their very incredulity, Matt. XIII. 58. Therefore, Christ here refutes that provocation, and that in two ways:

(1) by another proverb confirmed by his own assertion, Amen I say to you, that no Prophet is accepted the first of which is in the Fatherland, of which elsewhere. (2.) By examples of the free divine economy, of two distinguished Prophets who shone forth beyond other miracles; Elijah, who in the time of famine was sent to no widow in Israel, although there were many widows there, but only to the Sareptan woman in Sidonia outside his own Fatherland 1 Kings XVII. 9. Likewise Elisha, who was sent to no leper among the Israelite people, but only to Naaman the Syrian 2 Kings V. 8. Therefore the particle εἰ μὴ is exclusive, not exceptive as in Gal. II. 16. Because the Sidonian widow and Naaman the Syrian are not contained under the Jewish widows and lepers. But by these examples not only was the most free dispensation, the extraordinary divine calling through miracles to the true faith, set forth, which detracts nothing from the universal grace of the calling, just as the Israelites were by no means destitute of it in the time of Elijah and Elisha, and the Nazarenes in the time of Christ: but the citizens of Christ were also rebuked as being equally ungrateful toward Christ, as once the Israelites were toward Elijah and Elisha; indeed, the transfer of grace from the Jews to the Gentiles was also signified. Whence the Nazarenes, gnashing with anger, wished to cast Christ down from the mountain, but he himself passed through the midst of them, not by a divine hand restraining their force or changing their will, or holding their eyes, but by withdrawing his visible presence. Conf. Luke XXIV. 21. John VII. 59.

Let the following documents be observed here: I. The proper office of Christ is not to establish new laws, but to announce the Gospel to the contrite, John I. 18, 17. II. Christ is the chief and supreme Evangelist, and the sole cause and author of every evangelical proclamation: he is a Catholic Evangelist, announcing saving grace to all the afflicted, to all the contrite, to all the bound, excluding no one, Matt. XI. III. The extraordinary particular grace of God is not to be opposed to the universal grace of God. But if God shows extraordinary singular grace to these over others, that is to be attributed to the most free dispensation, but not for that reason is his equal, catholic, saving benevolence to be denied. For one must distinguish between the saving grace of God, by which he embraces all equally, and the mode of the dispensation of this grace, which is most free, tempered by divine justice and wisdom. IV. It is generally so arranged that those who help others cannot help themselves, just as physicians cure others, but generally do not know how to cure themselves. But he tastes ill who is wise for others but not for himself. V. The proverb; Physician, heal thyself, can also be applied to those who teach others but do not teach themselves, Romans II. 21, Luke VI. 40, etc.

Latin:

κηρύξαι] Quod ante hanc vocem habent codices qui- dam, ἰάσασθαι τὺς συντετριμμένυς τὴν καρδίαν non fuisse in libris Græcis veteribus ex Origene apparet. Sed nec in an- tiquissimis Latinorum codicibus apparuisse ex Ambrosii ad hunc locum explicatione facile est collectu. Quare cum & nunc antiqui Codices supersint qui hanc particulam non habeant, probabilius multo est additam ex Esaia & inter- pretibus LXX. quam ab aliis exscriptoribus omissam. Nam eodem modo Latina editio ex Esaia additum habet com- mate sequenti, & diem retributionis, quod neque in Græcis neque in Syriacis exstat. Sæpe autem nostri Scriptores Prophetarum locis utuntur ea libertate, ut verba quædam in medio omittant, quod hic eo minore sensus damno fie- ri potuit, quia Propheta variato sæpe loquendi genere rem eandem exprimit.

καὶ τυφλοῖς ἀνάβλεψιν] Reipsa constat idem dici quod su- perioribus. Verborum proprietas in controversia est: mihi videntur LXX. quos sequitur Lucas, Hebræa satis con- siderate interpretati. פקח si quis expendere velit loca in quibus ea vox apparet, non significat quamvis aperturam ut פתח, sed eam duntaxat quæ ad oculos pertinet, nisi quod & ad aures transfertur, quomodo & פצה oris est proprium. Jam vero quod sequitur קור esse carcerem, ut multi volunt, nullo testimonio probatur. Quare non vi- deo cur improbemus, quod doctissimi Hebræorum sen- tiunt unam esse vocem פקחקוח sed in qua literæ dinal posteriores αὐξητικῶς repetantur. Cujusmodi sunt אדמרם & ירקרק & סחרחר & הפכפך. Disputant Hebræorum Grammatici, talis literarum repetitio sitne ὑποκοριστικὴ an αὐξητικὴ. Sed ut de אדמרם & ירקרק res sit dubia, duæ reliquæ quas dixi voces omnino auctivam significationem postulant, ut videre est Ps. XXXVIII. 11. & Prov. XXI. 8. O- ptime ergo videntur sentire, qui hoc Prophetæ loco פקחקוח referunt ad plenissimam libertatem oculos huc atque illuc qua lubet circumferendi. Interpretes autem LXX. ut continuarent tralationem, quod præcedit אסורים verterunt τυφλοὶ, nimirum quia ut diximus פקח ad oculos pertinet, ad carcerem non pertinet. Atque ideo plerun- que de cæcis dicitur, ut Ps. CXLVI. 8 Es. XLII. 7. At Hebræi amant & propria figuratis & alias figuras aliis connectere. Cæci autem dici solent qui in tenebris vivunt, quod præ- cipue convenit his quos carcer claudit. Itaque apud eundem Esaiam XLIX. 9. eodem significatu ponuntur οἱ ἐν δεσμοῖς & οἱ ἐν σκότῳ & cap. XLVII. 7. οἱ τυφλοὶ & οἱ δεδεσμένοι. Ca- ptivi igitur cæci, ut Latinis cæci oculis capti. Utraque simili- tudo summam miseriam significat, qualis erat Judæorum in exsilio Babylonico, multoque magis hominum omnium in illo crassæ ignorantiæ statu ante tempora Messiæ. Confer eundem Esaiam cap. XLIII. 8. ubi itidem Judæi in exsilio illo cæci dicuntur, quantumvis oculos habeant: quia scilicet summa miseria oculis videndi libertatem ademerat.

ἀποστεῖλαι τεθραυσμένους ἐν ἀφέσει] Nihil aliud est quam popularis explicatio ejus, quod obscurius verbis ἀμέσως antecedentibus dictum videri poterat. Nam locutionem hanc fuisse vulgo usitatam apparet ex altero Esaiæ loco LVIII. 6. ubi LXX. eadem habent verba quæ hic Lucas po- suit. Atque ideo credo, quia hoc explicandi causa adje- cturus erat Lucas, omisit supra ἰσοδύναμον illud, ἰάσασθαι τοὺς συντετριμμένους τὴν καρδίαν. Quantillum enim differunt συντετριμμένοι & τεθραυσμένοι? Intelligendi autem hoc loco fracti animo, non qui pœnitudine peccatorum tanguntur, sed versantes in summis rerum angustiis: ut & Ps. CXLVII. 3. Nam de prima illa vocatione, ni fallor, agitur, quæ ho- mines plerosque nihil boni cogitantes deprehendit. Non enim de ipso liberationis beneficio sermo est, sed de annun- tiatione ejus liberationis jam paratæ: quod & sequentia ostendunt.

Vers. 19. κηρύξαι] לקרא καλέσαι. Similitudo sumta ab anno Jubilæo, qui per præconem buccinæ sono indici solebat.

De toto hoc loco Prophetico, & explicatio- ne præsenti Grotiana, nec non ea quam tradidit ad Esa. LXI. vidimus in Annotatis Anti-Grotianis ad Esaiam. Addere tamen juvat, quæ alias de eodem publice hic proposuimus. Publica pri- ma Concio Nazareth habita hic describitur, cir- ca quam notamus (1.) Concionis textum. Jacun- dum est observatu, quod in prima Concione, quam uti Origen. & Theophyl. annotant, habere dignatus est in Patria, librum explicans Esaiæ Prophetæ statim invenerit locum Classicum de munere suo Prophetico: Spir. Domini super me &c. Esa. LXI. 1. Siquidem suavissimo hoc textu, non tantum officium Doctorale Messiæ, ejusdem- que ad officium unctio, & missio divina propo- natur, quod tum publice exercere incipiebat, ut ita omnibus primo fundamentum totius Mi- nisterii vocationem & missionem suam demon- stret; Sed & ita illud descriptum habeatur, ut vix uspiam in toto codice suavioribus verbis ex- pressum legatur. Quod nempe missus sit, non ad legem acuendam sed ad evangelizandum, non paucis quibusdam cum delectu, aut juxta electio- nem quandam Dei absolutam, sed quibusvis pau- peribus: Hoc est, omnibus afflictis, totique ad- eo humano generi, in statu peccati & miseriæ constituto, quod missus sit ad lætum annuncian- dum nuncium afflictis mortalibus, ut nempe con- triti corde sanentur, captivis dimissio, cæcis visus, confractis emissio in remissionem prædicetur, ut annus Domini acceptus vere Jubilæus omnibus af- flictis, dies autem retributionis hostibus spiritua- libus denuncietur. Verba emittere confractos in remissionem, nonnulli ex Esaiæ LVIII. 6. de- prompta censent, quasi duo loca conjunxerit Christus. Sed præstat dicere, illa à CHRISTO explicationis gratia inserta esse, non quidem ut immediate præcedentia, cæcis visum, quod Maldonatus vult, declarentur, sed ut tota sen- tentia Prophetæ illustretur, ac summa superio- rum verbis istis comprehendatur. Si enim af- flictos corde, contritos, captivos, ac deni- que cæcos uno verbo dicere velis, τεθραυσμένους dicas, qui miseria & afflictione, legis maledictio- ne, contritione peccati, & Satanæ jugo ac captivi- tate, nec non spirituali cæcitate confracti plane sint; si velis exprimere, Evangelii prædicandi sum- mam atque adeo etiam paucis complecti, contri- torum sanationem, captivorum dimissionem, cæ- corum restitutionem, dimitti dicas confractos in remissionem vel veram libertatem. Verba præce- dentia καὶ τυφλοῖς ἀνάβλεψιν, quæ Christus non de suo, uti Rabbi Isaac Ben-Abraham criminatur, intexuit, sed è LXX-virali versione & textus Esaia- ni c. XLII. collatione repetiit, cum Ebræis haud æ- gre conciliantur. Ebræi reddunt ita cum Chaldæo & Sanctio & clausis apertionem carceris; eà ita expli- cari possunt, quod qui carceri tenebricoso inclu- duntur, in tenebris instar cæcorum degant: Sed rectius exponuntur verba פקח קוח per apertio- nem, qualis oculorum est: סנורים de clausis, vel captis oculis; Siquidem Hebræi per hos cæcos in- telligere solent. Conf. Ps. CXLVI. 8. Esa. XLII. 7. uti פקוחים apertos videntes seu visu pollentes, quæ vox non aperturam quamlibet, sed eam tan- tum, quæ ad oculos pertinet, significat. פקח קוח in unam vocem contracta uti Grotius in h: l. observat, auctivam significationem important ad plenissimam libertatem oculos huc atque illuc, qua lubet circumferendi.

II. Explicationis summam atque argumentum.

Christus libro complicato, ἐκάθισε sedit munus Doctoris jure sibi vindicans, (cum alii de plebe dissertantes de Sacris stantes id facere consueverint) ubi omnium oculi in ipsum converterentur: Dixit, quia hodie impleta est hæc Scriptura in auribus vestris. Summa hæc est Concionis Christi, quam proculdubio prolixius explicavit. Quia perhibet Lucas, quod omnes testimonium ipsi tulerint, & super gratia sermonum, qui procedebant ex ore ipsius, admirati fuerint. Quæ autem fuerit ipsa Concio non expressit Lucas, recte tamen ex Emphasi verborum Esaiæ, collatione instituta, cum recitatione eorundem penes Evangelistam colligitur, quam suaviter Christus in prima Concione cives suos informarit, partim de statu hominum diverso, tum de statu destitutionis, quo extra Christum vere sumus miseri & afflicti corde, voluntate servi & captivi, oculis mentis cæci, adeoq; omnibus spiritualibus viribus destituti ac prorsus confracti; tum restitutionis, per Messiam conciliandæ, qui afflictis lætitiam, contritis sanitatem, captivis liberationem, cæcis visum, confractis libertatem, in remissione peccatorum sitam affert & conciliat: partim de Doctrina Messiæ, qua legem atque Evangelium, quam utramque inculcare Christus debuit; quia per legem agnitio est miseriæ & contritio, nec non confractio. Evangelium vero lætum est nuncium de sanatione ac restitutione gratuitaque remissione peccatorum, illa est veluti præcedanea ac præsupponitur magis à Christo, utpote quam Moses inculcavit maxime: Hæc vero Christo est propria Ioh. I. 18.

III. Vaticinii Prophetici objectum. Sonora voce docet Christus, & ex ore ejus repetit Lucas, id quod hic præcipuum est, in vaticinio Esaiano, de quonam id loquatur, dum hodie, inquit, impleta est hæc Scriptura; unde manifestum est, de Christo hæc prædixisse Esaiam, de eo enim sine dubio vaticinatus est Propheta, in quo id impletum esse Christus in vaticinii hujus explicatione docuit: At in nullo alio quam in se hoc impletum esse testatus est. E. frustra hic sunt Chaldæus & Rabbini, nec non & judaizantes Papistæ, quos notat Lyranus, imprimis vero Thomas & qui eum sequuntur, Esaiam hic de se ipso loqui, quod missus sit ad Judæos, ut eis annunciaret liberationem è captivitate Babylonica. Quibus etiam Calvinus & Wolfg. Musculus in Comment. super h. l. accedunt. Ille haud obscure innuit, merito hoc videre Judæos, quod inconsiderate ista trahantur ad solum Christum, quæ de aliis etiam Prophetis dicta: hic vero præsentem locum Esaiæ sic comparatum dicit, ut sine pudore nequeat ad solum Christum aliis exclusis referri. Similiter Hugo Grotius in annot. ad h. l. Esaiam de se loqui, sed in eo non obscuram conspici Christi imaginem, existimat. Refellit illos (1.) Unctio, ἐξοχικὴ, à qua præ aliis nomen habet Dan. XI. 2. Sam. XXIII. 1. immediate à Domino facta Spiritus sancti plenitudinem inferens, qui proinde simpliciter & eminentiffima ratione dicitur super ipsum esse, ideo quia unctus est eodem non ad mensuram & supra consortes, Ps. XLV. 7. (2.) Peculiaris missio facta ad evangelizandum, quibusvis cæcis, quibusvis vinctis; Quæ nulli Prophetarum convenit, omnes ad quosdam missi sunt, unus Messias ad omnes, & propter omnes. (3.) Prædicatio cum summa efficacia conjuncta; cum enim alii Evangelium prædicent, solus hic unctus Domini largitur etiam præconio efficaciam, ac re ipsa præstat captivis liberationem, clausis apertionem, ligat ipse contritos corde, dat coronam pro cinere, oleum gaudii, pallium laudis pro spiritu mœroris, quod certe nemo Pro- phetarum pheta præstare potest præter ipsum. (4.) Gentium vocatio, de qua v. 5. Stabit alius & pascet pecora ve- stra; Pastores, Agricolas, Vinitores Ecclesiæ peregri- nos seu Gentiles prædicit, quod etiam Matth. XXI. 41. Christus Judæis prædixisse legitur. De illo ergo uncto Domini hic agitur, per quem vocatio gen- tium universalis futura erat. De illius missione qui universalis Evangelista futurus. Quod utique nec de Esaia, nec de ullo alio Propheta, sed unice de Christo dici potest. (5.) Divinæ naturæ Messiæ desi- gnatio. Qui v. 1. loquitur: Spiritus Domini super me, ille v. 8. testatur, Ego Jehova diligens justitiam & odio habens rapinam pro holocausto. At quis alius ex unctis Domini hoc de se profiteri potest, quam Messias, quod diligat justitiam & odio simpliciter habeat rapinam, quodq; Jehova sit? Unde unctus ille, quia diligit justitiam & odio habet rapinam introducitur ceu judex universalis bonorum & malorum, qui benedictionem quoque pollicetur omnibus gentibus, quæ non nisi Messiæ conve- niunt. (6.) Antecedentium collatio. Ut præcedente cap. LX. 1. de Christo luce magna, de autore vocatio- nis Gentium, nec non gaudii vitæ æternæ agitur, ita hic Christus ipse ad Evangelium de salute æterna annunciandum Judæis atque gentibus introduci- tur; de illo ergo Evangelista magno, non vero de nuncio solutæ vel solvendæ captivitatis Babylon. de Christo, inquam, qui & Redemptor c. LIX. 20. & lux Israelis ac Gentium est, & Dominus ille qui æterna lux Electis erit c. LX. 19. non vero de Esaia aut mi- nistro aliquo agitur. (7.) Consequentium cohæsio. Cujus rei gratia hoc ipso capite LXI. 10. canticum Eucharisticum canitur, illa fine dubio huic Evan- gelistæ, ejus præconio accepto ferri debet. At non de Babyl. captivitate soluta, sed de salute & Justitia sempiterna quæ in Messia obtinetur, sonat illud Canticum. (8.) Christi ipsius applicatio, qui post- quam in Baptismo Spir. Domini super ipsum de- scendit, nunc Propheticum munus aggredi ipse parat, hanc scripturam in se completam esse dicit: Hodie impleta est Scriptura hæc. Addit autem in au- ribus vestris, non quod impleta sit penes alios in Prophetis, penes Nazarethanos vero in Christo uti Musculus vult: sed cum de Christi præconio in genere agat, de eodem apud concives suos con- cionante eadem quoque impleta fuisse dicitur. (9.) Potiorum DD. interpretatio. De Christo solo unanimi suffragio cum PP. Græcis & Latinis no- strates omnes, Oecolampadius, item, Piscator, Junius, Tremellius, Autores Versionis Belgicæ, & plerique Pontif. exponunt secundum literam: nec ulla ratio movet, ab illis discedere, imo luculentior est tex- tus, quam ut huic interpretationi quis refragari possit, à Christo & Ecclesia approbatæ.

IV. De auditorum quorundam ἐγκλήματι Chri- sti judicium. Præoccupabat eorum cogitata. Uti- que dicetis mihi hanc parabolam: Medice cura te- ipsum: Quo proverbio apud Ebræos vulgari, tum Christum ipsum respexerunt, qui miser & affli- ctus ipse afflictis lætitiam & miseris annum acce- ptum annunciabat: tum etiam Patriam Christi, ut verba subjuncta docent: Quanta audivimus facta in Capernaum fac & hic in Patria tua; nempe sana- tionem ab Esaia prædictam de corporali cura intel- ligebant, eadem ergo sanationum miracula, quæ alibi patrarat, partim ex ambitione, partim ex incredulitate in patria fieri poscebant; quæ vero ob ipsam incredulitatem eorum Dominus facere renuebat Matth. XIII. 58. Ideo provocatio- nem illam diluit hic Christus, idque bifariam

(1) proverbio alio abs se asseveratione confirma- to, Amen dico vobis, quia nemo Propheta acceptus est in Patria, de quo alias. (2.) Exemplis liberæ œ- conomias divinæ, insignium duorum Propheta- rum qui præ cæteris miraculis claruerunt; Eliæ qui tempore famis ad nullam viduam in Israel missus est, utut plures ibi essent viduæ, sed solum ad Sare- ptanam in Sidonia extra Patriam suam 1. Reg. XVII. 9. Nec non Elisæi, qui ad nullum leprosum in Israe- litico populo, sed ad solum Naamannum Syrum missus 2. Reg. V. 8. Particula itaque εἰ μὴ est Exclusi- va, non exceptiva uti Gal. II. 16. Quia Sydonia vi- dua & Naaman Syrus non continentur sub Judaicis viduis ac leprosis. Quibus vero exemplis non tantum liberrima dispensatio, divina vocatio ex- traordinaria per miracula ad veram fidem expo- nebatur, quæ nihil derogat universali Gratiæ vo- cationis, uti tum nequaquam ea destituti fuere Israelitæ tempore Eliæ & Elisæi, & Nazaretani tempore Christi: sed reprehensi etiam sunt Cives Christi ceu æque ingrati adversus Christum, ut o- lim Israelitæ adversus Eliam & Elisæum, imo signi- ficata quoque fuit translatio Gratiæ à Judæis ad Gentes. Unde ira frendentes Nazaræi Christum præcipitare volebant de monte, sed ipse per me- dium ipsorum transibat non divina manu vim eo- rum cohibens aut voluntatem immutans, aut ocu- los eorum detinens, sed præsentiam suam visibilem subtrahens. Conf. Luc. XXIV. 21. Joh. VII. 59.

Observentur hic sequentia Documenta: I. Christi officium proprium non est novas leges con- dere, sed Evangelium contritis annunciare, Joh. I. 18. 17. II. Christus Evangelista princeps & sum- mus est, omnisque Evangelici præconii causa & auctor unicus: Evangelista est Catholicus, omnibus afflictis, omnibus contritis, omnibus vinctis, Gra- tiam salutiferam annuncians, neminem exclu- dens Matth. XI. III. Gratia Dei extraordinaria particularis non est opponenda Gratiæ Dei univer- sali. Quod si Deus his præ aliis extraordinarie singularem gratiam exhibeat, id liberrimo dispen- sationi tribuendum, non vero ideo benevolentia ejus æqualis catholica, salutifera neganda. Di- stinguendum enim inter gratiam Dei salutiferam, quo omnes ex æquo complectitur, & modum dispen- sationis hujus Gratiæ, qui liberrimus est, à justitia ac sapientia divina temperatus. IV. Plerun- que ita comparatum est, ut qui aliis opitulantur, sibi ipsis opitulari nequeant, uti Medici alios cu- rant, seipsos vero plerunque curare nesciunt. Ma- le autem sapit, qui aliis non sibi sapit. V. Pro- verbium; Medice cura teipsum etiam adhiberi po- test de iis, qui alios docent, seipsos non docent Roman. II. 21. Luc. VI. 40. &c.

## 4:20
Verse 20. τῷ ὑπηρέτῃ] After the ruler of the synagogue and the elders there were in the synagogue ὑπηρέται, who performed lesser duties by their decree: just as John Mark is said to have been a ὑπηρέτης of Paul and Barnabas, Acts XIII. 5. To the Hebrews they are called חזנים, as can be seen both elsewhere and in the Talmudic title concerning the Sabbath, chapter I. Their duty among others was to guard the book of the law, and also, if there were need, to read from it, which in the Christian Church the ἀναγνῶσται did: which was a species of deacons. For formerly, when the multitude was small, the same deacons performed all those things which the presbyters did not have time to perform: afterwards the labors were distributed and some became deacons, others archdeacons, others subdeacons, others doorkeepers, others acolytes of the bishops, others readers, others singers. Jerome also says that reading in the Church belongs to the deacons. In Massechah Succa we read וחזן הכנסת עומד לקרות בתורה, that is, And the minister or ὑπηρέτης stands to recite from the law. See what we said above on the word ἀναγνῶναι. Epiphanius, in the title concerning the Ebionites, dealing with Joseph the Apostle of the Jews, which was the dignity next after the first of the patriarch, says that many in the synagogues were moved from their place by him, where he enumerates the synagogue offices thus: Πολλὲς τῶν κακῶν καταταθέντων ἀρχισυναγώγων καὶ ἱερέων καὶ πρεσβυτέρων κὶ ἀζανιτῶν ϛ παρ' αὐτοῖς, διακόνων ἑρμηνευομένων ἢ ὑπηρετῶν καθαρῶς τε κὶ μετακινῆι τε ἀξιώματος, ὑπὸ πολλῶν ἐπεκοτᾶτο. He openly says that those who were called חזנים by the Hebrews were called in Greek either deacons or ὑπηρέται. For these words mean the same thing. In the Constitutions of Clement, book II, chapter XXVIII, διὰ τῶν ὑπηρετῶν ἁ' βούλονται σημαινέτωσαν, that is, through the deacons. Ignatius in the Epistle to the Trallians: δεῖ δὲ τοὺς διακόνους ὄντας μυστηρίων Χριστοῦ Ἰησοῦ κατὰ πάντα τρόπον ἀρέσκειν· οὐ γὰρ βρωτῶν κὴ ποτῶν εἰσὶ διάκονοι ἀλλ' ἐκκλησίας Θεοῦ ὑπηρέται. Wherefore Pliny also calls the deacons of the church of the Christians ministers. Cyprian: The Apostles appointed deacons for themselves after the ascension of the Lord as ministers of their episcopate and of the Church. And Optatus of Milevis in more than one place places ministers between the laity and the deacons, understanding those who were called subdeacons. Canon XVIII of the Synod of Nicaea: Ἐμμενέτωσαν οἱ διάκονοι τοῖς ἰδίοις μέτροις εἰδότες ὅτι τῷ μὲν ἐπισκόπῳ ὑπηρέται εἰσί. But just as hardly anyone was accustomed to be chosen for the presbyterate unless they were already advanced in both age and wisdom, so the ὑπηρεσία or diaconate was generally entrusted to young men. Philo: ὑπηρετοῦσι τοῖς διακονικὰς χρείας οἱ νέοι τῶν ἐν τῷ συστήματι μετὰ πάσης ἐπιμελείας ἀρισίνδην ἐπικριθέντες.

Ἐκάθισε] Claiming for himself the office of teacher by his own right. For others of the common people, even if they discussed something about sacred matters, did so standing. It is evident from Acts XIII. 16, 1 Cor. XIV. 30. See what we noted on Matt. XXIII. 2, where we also noted that the teachers themselves stood while the words of the law were read either by them or by others.

Οἱ ὀφθαλμοὶ ἦσαν ἀτενίζοντες αὐτῷ] This is what Virgil says: And they held their faces intent.

Latin:

Vers. 20. τῷ ὑπηρέτῃ] Post archisynagogum & Presby- teros erant in Synagoga ὑπηρέται, qui minora munia ex il- lorum decreto obibant: quomodo Johannes Marcus dicitur ὑπηρέτης fuisse Pauli & Barnabæ Actor. XIII. 5. Hebræis ὑπη- ρέται vocantur חזנים, ut videre est tum alibi tum Thal- mudico titulo de Sabbato cap. I. horum munus inter cætera erat legis librum custodire, atque etiam, si opus esset, ex eo legere, quod in Ecclesia Christiana faciebant ἀναγνῶσται: quæ erat species διακόνων. Nam olim cum exigua esset multitudo, iidem διάκονοι omnia ea obibant quæ presbyte- ris obire non vacabat: postea distributi sunt labores & fa- cti sunt alii διάκονοι, alii ἀρχιδιάκονοι, alii ὑποδιάκονοι, alii jani- tores, alii ἀκόλουθοι Episcoporum, alii ἀναγνῶσται, alii ψαλ- κωδοί. Etiam Hieronymus lectitare in Ecclesia dicit esse diaconorum. In Massechah Succa legimus וחזן הכנסת עומד לקרות בתורה, id est, Et minister sive ὑπηρέτης stat ut recitet de lege. Vide quæ diximus supra ad verbum ἀνα- γνῶναι. Epiphanius titulo de Ebionæis, de Josepho Judæo- rum Apostolo agens, quæ erat dignitas proxima à prima τοῦ πατριαρχοῦ, ait ab eo multos in Synagogis loco suo motos, ubi Synagogæ munera ita enumerat: Πολλὲς τῶν κακῶν κατα- ταθέντων ἀρχισυναγώγων καὶ ἱερέων καὶ πρεσβυτέρων κὶ ἀζανιτῶν ϛ παρ' αὐτοῖς, διακόνων ἑρμηνευομένων ἢ ὑπηρετῶν καθαρῶς τε κὶ μετακινῆι τε ἀξιώματος, ὑπὸ πολλῶν ἐπεκοτᾶτο. Aperte ait eos qui Hebræis dicebantur חזנים Græce dictos aut διακόνους aut ὑπηρέτας. Nam hæ voces idem valent. In Clementis Constitutionibus lib. II. cap. XXVIII. διὰ τῶν ὑπηρετῶν ἁ' βούλονται σημαινέτωσαν, τουτέστι διὰ τῶν διακόνων. Ignatius in Epistola ad Trallianos: δεῖ δὲ τοὺς διακόνους ὄντας μυστηρίων Χριστοῦ Ἰησοῦ κατὰ πάντα τρόπον ἀρέσκειν· οὐ γὰρ βρωτῶν κὴ ποτῶν εἰσὶ διάκονοι ἀλλ' ἐκκλησίας Θεοῦ ὑπηρέται. Quare & Plinius τοὺς διακόνους τῆς τῶν χριστιανῶν ἐκκλησίας vocat ministras. Cy- prianus: Diaconos autem post ascensum Domini Apostoli sibi constituerunt Episcopatui suo & Ecclesiæ ministros. Et Opta- tus Milevitanus non uno loco ministros ponit inter laicos & diaconos, eos intelligens qui ὑποδιάκονοι vocabantur. Ca- non Synodi Nicænsis XVIII. Ἐμμενέτωσαν οἱ διάκονοι τοῖς ἰδίοις μέτροις εἰδότες ὅτι τῷ μὲν ἐπισκόπῳ ὑπηρέται εἰσί. Sicut autem ad presbyterium vix legi solebant nisi qui jam pro- vectæ essent & ætatis & sapientiæ, ita ὑπηρεσία sive διακονία ferme juvenibus mandabatur. Philo : ὑπηρετοῦσι τοῖς διακο- νικὰς χρείας οἱ νέοι τῶν ἐν τῷ συστήματι μετὰ πάσης ἐπιμελείας ἀρισίνδην ἐπικριθέντες.

Ἐκάθισε] Munus doctoris suo sibi jure vindicans. Nam alii de plebe, etiamsi quid de sacris dissertabant, id facie- bant stantes. Patet Act. XIII. 16. 1. Cor. XIV. 30. Vide quæ notavimus ad Matth. XXIII. 2. ubi & illud annotavi- mus ipsos quoque doctores stetisse, dum verba legis aut ab ipsis aut ab aliis legebantur.

Οἱ ὀφθαλμοὶ ἦσαν ἀτενίζοντες αὐτῷ] Hoc est quod Virgi- lius ait: Intenti que ora tenebant.

## 4:21
Vers. 21. Today this scripture is fulfilled in your ears] With this opening Jesus explained the passage of the Prophet, and by explaining it he fulfilled it, announcing, that is, that liberation which was at the door. For he did not hitherto profess himself to be the Messiah and deliverer, which he did later: but he acted as an evangelist and messenger of the prepared liberation, that is, he set before them that which had been done in figure through Isaiah, not that which was done through Cyrus. Moreover, Luke seems, having omitted many things which others record, to have begun the acts of the Lord Jesus from this Nazareth discourse: because he thought the office of the same should be placed before the acts, which he could not express better than in the words of the Prophet and of Jesus himself. It is entirely true, contrary to what others feel, that in this whole history Luke attends more to the order of things than of times.

Latin:

Vers. 21. σήμερον πεπλήρωται ἡ γραφὴ αὕτη ἐν τοῖς ὠσὶν ὑ- μῶν] Hoc exordio usus Jesus explicavit Prophetæ locum, & explicando implevit, annuntians scilicet liberationem illam quæ præ foribus erat, Nam Messiam & liberatorem se- se hactenus non profitebatur, quod fecit postea: sed agebat εὐαγγελιστὴν & nuntium paratæ liberationis, hoc est, hoc præ se ferebat quod per Esaiam erat gestum in figura, non quod per Cyrum. Videtur autem Lucas omissis rebus multis, quas alii memorant, ab hac dissertatione Nazarethana ex- orsus acta Domini Jesu: quia actis præmittendum putavit officium ipsius, quod melius exprimere non potuit quam Prophetæ ipsiusque Jesu verbis. Omnino verum est, contra quam alii sentiunt, in omni hac historia Lucam ad rerum magis quam ad temporum ordinem attendere.

## 4:22
Vers. 22. They bore witness to him] That is, they were compelled to confess concerning him, as that word is taken in Matt. XXIII. 31 and Rom. X. 2. But what were they confessing? Namely, that very thing which follows, that they were astonished because of that singular manner of teaching.

Words of grace] Doubtless it could truly be said of him: Persuasion sat upon his lips. Thus he charmed; and he alone of the orators left a sting in his hearers. Not that persuasion of human wisdom, but of divine efficacy, as Paul says 1 Cor. II. 7. Reference is made to that of Psalm XLV. 3. הוצק חן בשפתותיך.

And they said, Is not this the son of Joseph] Wondering they said this: but struck by the force of the truth rather than by a sincere zeal for piety. Therefore, fluctuating between the authority of the doctrine and the vile and ignoble state of Jesus, they easily cast their minds headlong into the worse part, the word of hearing did not profit them, not being mixed with faith in those who heard, Heb. III. v. 2.

Latin:

Vers. 22. ἐμαρτύρουν αὐτῷ] Id est fateri cogebantur de eo, ut ea vox accipitur Matth. XXIII. 31. & Rom. X. 2. Quid autem fatebantur? Nempe id ipsum quod sequitur, attoni- tos se ob singularem illam docendi rationem.

Λόγοις τῆς χάριτος] Nimirum vere de illo dici poterat: Πειθώ τις ἐπεκάθιζεν ἐπὶ τοῖς χείλεσιν. Οὕτως ἐκήλει· κὴ μόνος τῶν ῥητόρων Τὸ κέντρον ἐγκατέλιπε τοῖς ἀκροωμένοις. Non illa humanæ sapientiæ πειθὼ, sed efficaciæ divinæ, ut Paulus ait 1. Corinth. II. 7. Respicitur illud Psalmi XLV. 3. .הוצק חן בשפתותיך

κὴ ἔλεγον οὐχ οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ ὑἱὸς Ἰωσήφ] Admirantes hoc dice- bant: sed vi veritatis perculsi magis quam sincero pietatis studio. Ideo inter doctrinæ auctoritatem & vilem atque ignobilem Jesu statum fluctuantes, animos facile in pejo- rem partem præcipites dedere, οὐκ ὠφέλησεν ὁ λόγος τῆς ἀκοῆς ἐκείνοις μὴ συγκεκραμένους τῇ πίστει τοῖς ἀκούσασιν, Hebr. III. v. 2.

## 4:23
Vers. 23. This parable] That is, proverb: as in turn John calls that a proverb which is properly a parable, which is a communication of names born from the Hebrew mashal, by which both this and that is accustomed to be comprehended. Moreover, this is a proverb, Physician, heal thyself, most common by the usage of the Hebrews, Syrians, and Arabs; and it first pertained to those who, while they do not know the path for themselves, show the way to another. Just as the Greeks also say: A physician of others, himself teeming with sores: and Aeschylus: A bad physician is he who, having fallen into sickness himself, is disheartened and cannot find with what medicines he is curable. Later it began to be extended even further to those who are more beneficent to strangers than to their own kin. Such is that of Virgil, Protect this house first. And thus it is used here.

Country] See Matt. XIII. 57.

Latin:

Vers. 23. τὴν παραβολὴν ταύτην] Id est παροιμίαν : ut vi- cissim Johannes παροιμίας vocat quod proprie παραβολὴ est, quæ nominum communicatio nata ex Hebræo משל quo & hoc & illud comprehendi solet. Est autem hoc pro- verbium, medice cura te ipsum, usu Hebræorum, Syrorum & Arabum triussimum; & primum quidem ad eos perti- nuit, Qui cum sibi semitam non sapiunt, alteri monstrant viam. Quomodo & Græci dicunt : ἄλλων ἰατρὸς αὐτὸς ἕλκεσι βρύων: & Æschylus: Κακὸς δ' ἰατρὸς ὅστις αὐτὸς εἰς νόσον Πεσὼν ἀθυμεῖς κὴ σεαυτὸν οὐκ ἔχεις Εὑρεῖν ὁποίοις φαρμάκοις ἰάσιμος. Postea etiam longius produci cœpit ad eos qui in alienos magis quam in conjunctos sunt benefici. Tale est illud Virgilii, Hanc primum tutare domum. Atque ita hic usurpatur.

πατρίδι] Vide Matth. XIII. 57.

## 4:24
Vers. 24. Is accepted] He has honor, John IV. 44. According to that saying, Ungrateful country: concerning the cause of which matter we have dealt at Matthew.

Latin:

Vers. 24. δεκτός ἐστι] τιμὴν ἔχει, Joh. IV. 44. Juxta il- lud dictum Ingrata patria: cujus de rei causa ad Matthæum egimus.

## 4:25
Vers. 25. The heaven was shut] Thus also Moses, Gen. VII. 2, says the windows of heaven were shut when it ceased to rain.

For three years and six months] From the tradition which James also follows V. 17, wherefore that which is 1 Kings XVIII. 1, if I am not mistaken, one may thus interpret: rather many days (that is, six months) had passed since God had spoken to Elijah in the third year, that is, at the end of the third year after it had ceased to rain: so that Elijah received the command at the end of the third year, but it was something to be carried out after a six-month period. It seems, however, that God deliberately defined this calamity by three years and a six-month period. For the desolation (ἐρήμωσις) which occurred through Antiochus was defined by an equal span of time; and while Christ was active on earth, the heaven was opened for an equal span of time.

Although it might have been possible to know from that tradition, yet Christ, in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden (Col. 2:3), and James, being carried along by the Holy Spirit (ὑπὸ πνεύματος ἁγίου φερόμενος), did not need tradition. And from where, pray, is it clear to Grotius that this was the tradition, or that James followed not his own Master Christ, about whose Nazareth sermon he was undoubtedly informed, but a common tradition?

ὡς ἐγένετο] At which time there was a great famine. Thus I see that expression ὡς ἐγένετο is generally taken in these books, and never, as far as I know, in an intensive sense (ἐπιτατικῶς).

Latin:

Vers. 25. ἐκλείσθη ὁ οὐρανός] Sic & Moses Gen. VII. 2. clau- sos dicit cœli cataractas cùm pluere desiit.

ἐπὶ ἔτη τρία κὴ μῆνας ἕξ] Ex traditione quam & Jacobus se- quitur V. 17. quare quod est 1. Reg. XVIII. 1. ni fallor, ita inter- pretari licet, Dies aliquam multi (id est sex menses) præterie- rant ex quo Deus allocutus erat Eliam anno tertio, id est fine anni tertii postquam pluere desierat: ut mandatum accepe- rit Elias fine tertii anni, sed quod exsequendum fuit post semestre tempus. Videtur autem consulto Deus hanc ca- lamitatem definiisse annis tribus & semestri tempore. Nam & ἐρήμωσις quæ per Antiochum contigit pari tempo- ris spatio definita est; At Christo in terris agente apertum fuit cœlum, pari temporis spatio.

Quanquam ex traditione ista constare potue- rit, Christus tamen, in quo reconditi omnes Sapien- tiæ & cognitionis thesauri Col. II. 3. ac Jacobus ὑπὸ πνεύματος ἁγίου φερόμενος traditione non ege- bant. Et unde nam Grotio liquet hanc fuisse πα- ράδοσιν, aut Jacobum sequutum esse non Magi- strum suum Christum de cujus concione Nazare- tana, sine dubio, informatus fuit, sed vulgarem traditionem?

ὡς ἐγένετο] Quo tempore fuit fames maxima. Ita plerun- que in his libris sumi video illud ὡς ἐγένετο, nec unquam quod sciam ἐπιτατικῶς.

## 4:26
Vers. 26. Σάρεπτα τῆς Σιδῶνος] Pliny mentions it. In Hebrew it is צָרְפַת. Furthermore, I thought I should not leave unmentioned that a very ancient manuscript here has Σιδωνίας instead of Σιδῶνος, so that the word for the region might be clearer, although I know that names of cities and regions are often interchanged. The stupidity of the Hebrews is admirable, who in Obadiah interpret צרפת as the kingdom of the Franks: and on the confidence of that interpretation, supported by no reason, they promise themselves great things. But it happens to them as to others, that what one has said, all believe, and no one judges.

πρὸς γυναῖκα χήραν] By this example and the following one, Christ shows that miracles are not dispensed according to private affections, but by the most free and most wise judgment of God, who knows where they, once published, will produce the best fruit. For by what reasoning the Nazarenes thought it fair that they should be preferred by Christ to others in that kind of benefit, if it had any validity, it ought also to have been valid in Elijah's time, so that he would have preferred Israelite women to the Sareptan woman: which he did not do.

Latin:

Vers. 26. Σάρεπτα τῆς Σιδῶνος] Meminit Plinius. He- bræis est צָרְפַת. Cæterum non tacendum duxi ve- tustissimum Codicem hic pro Σιδῶνος habere Σιδωνίας, ut a- pertius regionis sit vocabulum, quanquam scio urbis & re- gionis nomina sæpe permiscere. Admirabilis est Hebræo- rum stupor, qui apud Obadiam צרפת interpretantur regnum Francorum: atque ejus interpretationis nulla ra- tione suffultæ fiducia res magnas sibi pollicentur. Sed accidit illis quod & aliis, ut quod unus dixerit credant o- mnes, dijudicet nemo.

πρὸς γυναῖκα χήραν] Ostendit hoc exemplo & sequente Christus miracula non dispensari pro privatis affectibus, sed & liberrimo & sapientissimo Dei arbitratu, qui norit ubi edita optimam frugem sint paritura. Nam qua ratione Na- zarethani æquum putabant se à Christo præferri cæteris in isto beneficiorum genere, ea si quid valeret, valere etiam debuisset Eliæ tempore, ut nempe mulieres Israelitidas Sa- reptanæ anteponeret: quod non fecit.

## 4:27
Vers. 27. ἐκαθαρίσθη] A word proper to leprosy. In the history of Naaman, עֹהַר, the LXX [use] καὶ ἐκαθαρίσθη: and often in Leviticus.

εἰ μὴ Νεεμὰν ὁ Σύρος] The LXX are accustomed to often translate ע with ε. Thus from עֶמֹרָה was made Νεεμὰν. Nor is there any doubt that in those times it was accustomed to be read that way. Regarding this Syrian, who also here seems to be commended silently for a certain integrity of mind, which God mercifully regarded, it is usually discussed by the learned what it is that he asks to be forgiven for when departing from the Prophet. As for those who think that pardon is being asked by him for an act of idolatry (εἰδωλολατρικοῦ), I do not see how they can prove it. Add that this seems to conflict directly with the preceding words, in which he had professed that he would not sacrifice henceforth to any God except that God whom Elisha worshipped, where by sacrifice, as the noblest species, the whole genus of external worship seems to be included. Furthermore, if his mind had been so perverse, who thinks that Elisha would have let it pass without any rebuke?
