For as for what some say, that the Syrian erred openly even in another matter, when he carries Israelite soil with him upon which to sacrifice, because it was not permitted to sacrifice outside Jerusalem, they wrongly assume for themselves that it was not permitted to perform sacred rites outside Jerusalem, when the law given to the Hebrew people alone did not bind foreigners. Moreover, the earth that he carried with him was not superstitious: but by that sign he wanted to testify that he worshipped that very God who was worshipped in the land of Israel. Wherefore, what he says about the bowing down of the body in the Temple of Rimmon, it seems to me it must be understood in such a way that it is not a plea for a sin not yet committed (which no wise man would admit) but rather an interpretation of an ambiguous act. For since that prostration of the body among the Syrians was as much a sign of religion as of that veneration which was shown to kings, Naaman wanted to testify that he, as often as he accompanied the king into the temple, would bow down there, would do so in honor not of Rimmon but of the royal majesty, being prepared, of course, to profess this openly before the king and others. Wherefore he was praying not so much that God would forgive this, but that He would interpret it favorably. For סָלַח, which the LXX translate as ἱλάσκεσθαι, does not reject this sense, as can be seen in Num. 30:6, and יִסְלַח in Greek is καθαριεῖ, it means he will hold him innocent. Indeed, deeds and words of doubtful meaning are accustomed to be purged by such a declaration. Thus we learn from Eusebius that a certain Christian, when he had adored the King in the manner of the Persians, refrained from adoration after he was provoked to deny Christ: and from Tertullian that the ancient Christians attributed the title of Lord to the Emperors, when they were not compelled to say Lord in place of God (that is, as if he were God).

Grotius discusses this Syrian, what it is that he asks to be forgiven for when departing from the Prophet? For he rightly denies that pardon is being asked by him for an act of idolatry (εἰδωλολατρικοῦ), since that would conflict directly with the preceding words, in which he had professed that he would not sacrifice henceforth to any God except that God whom Elisha worshipped, nor should it be thought that Elisha would have let it pass without any rebuke if his mind had been so perverse. Yet what the Syrian said about the bowing down of the body in the temple of Rimmon is not to be understood with Grotius, although that interpretation has pleased many, as if it were an interpretation of an ambiguous act, by which Naaman testified that he, as often as he accompanied the king into the temple, would bow down there, would do so in honor not of Rimmon, but of the royal majesty. For if this had been his intention, he would not have had need to plead for it, and to ask that God might deign to be propitious to him in it: which was done by him, 2. 2 Kings 5:18. For the exception which Grotius makes, that God was prayed to not so much to pardon this as to take it in good part, does not at all agree with the text; since סלח, which the LXX interpreters render as ἰλάσκεσθαι, implies pardon, nor is the contrary proven from Num. 30:6. Grotius used another exception in his annotations to 2 Kings 5:18, namely that that law concerning not worshipping idols was not prescribed to foreigners: but he dismisses it here. More correctly, therefore, the words of Naaman are taken in the past tense, namely that he asked to be pardoned for the fact that he had previously bowed himself in the house of Rimmon. Nor is it to be approved that Grotius judges the transfer of Israelite soil into Syria, done for the sake of sacrifice, to be free from superstition, excusing it in such a way that by that sign he wished to testify that he himself worshipped that very God who was worshipped in the land of Israel: but could he not have testified to that in another way, so that he had no need to transfer the soil? and he would have testified to it very obscurely by standing on Israelite earth and sacrificing upon it: which in any case could not have been acquitted of will-worship. Let those things which we have said against Grotius regarding these matters and the sense of the words of 2 Kings 5 be seen at that passage.

Latin:

Vers. 27. ἐκαθαρίσθη] Vox propria vitiligini. In Hi- storia Neemanis עֹהַר LXX. καὶ ἐκαθαρίσθη: & in Levitico sæpe.

εἰ μὴ Νεεμὰν ὁ Σύρος] Solent LXX. ע sæpe per ε transfer- re. Ita ex עֶמֹרָה factum est Νεεμὰν. Neque dubium quin illis temporibus ita legi solitum sit. De hoc Syro, qui & hic tacite videtur ob quandam animi probitatem, quam Deus misericorditer respexerit, commendari, disquiri ab eruditis solet, quid sit quod à Propheta discedens con- donari sibi postulat. Qui putant veniam ab eo posci a- ctus εἰδωλολατρικοῦ, non video quomodo id probent. Adde quod directe hoc pugnare videtur cum verbis antecedenti- bus, quibus professus erat non sacrificaturum se posthac ulli Deo præterquam Deo illi quem colebat Elisæus, ubi sacri- ficio, tanquam nobilissima specie, genus omne cultus ex- terni comprehendi videtur. Deinde si tam læva illi mens fuiffet, quis putat Elisæum sine ulla castigatione id trans- missurum fuisse? Nam quod ajunt nonnulli aperte errasse Syrum etiam in re alia, cum humum Israeliticum secum defert, super qua sacrificet, quippe quia extra Hierosoly- ma sacrificare non liceret, male sibi sumunt etiam ἀνακόλουθος licitum non fuisse sacra facere extra Hierosolyma, cum ea de re lex Hebræo tantum populo data exteros non con- stringeret. Terram autem quod secum deferebat non erat superstitiosum: sed eo signo volebat testatum illum ipsum à se Deum coli qui in terra Israelitica coleretur. Quare quod de corporis procubitu in Templo Remmanis dicit, intelligendum ita mihi videtur, ut sit non peccati necdum perpetrati deprecatio (quam nemo sapiens admiserit) sed potius interpretatio facti ambigui. Nam cum corporis ista dejectio apud Syros tam θρησκείας esset signum quam ejus venerationis quæ regibus exhibebatur, testatum vo- lebat Neeman se, quoties regem in templum comitatus, ibi- dem esset procubiturus, facturum id in honorem non Rem- manis sed regiæ majestatis, paratus scilicet id ipsum coram rege atque aliis palam profiteri. Quare non tam ut hoc condonaret quam ut æqui consuleret DEUS precabatur. Nam סָלַח quod ἱλάσκεσθ vertunt LXX. hunc sensum non respuit, ut videre est Num. XXX. 6. & יִסְלַח Græce καθα- ριεῖ valet innocentem habebit. Scilicet facta & dicta du- biæ significationis tali testatione purgari solent. Ita ex Eu- sebio discimus Christianum quendam, cum more Persarum Regem adorasset abstinuisse ab adoratione postquam ad Christum abnegandum erat provocatus: & ex Tertulliano Christianos veteres Imperatoribus tribuisse Domini appel- lationem, quando non cogebantur ut Dominum Dei vice (id est quasi Deum) dicerent.

Disquirit Grotius de hoc Syro, quid sit, quod à Propheta discedens condonari sibi postulat? Recte enim negat, posci ab eo veniam actus εἰδωλολατρικοῦ, siquidem id directe pugnet cum verbis antecedentibus, quibus professus erat non sacrificaturum se posthac ulli Deo, præterquam Deo illi, quem colebat Elisæus, nec si tam læva illi mens fuisset, sine ulla castigatione id transmissurum fuisse Elisæum putandum sit. Non tamen quod de corporis procubitu in templo Remmanis dixit Syrus, ita intelligendum cum Grotio, quamvis multis ea placuerit interpretatio, ut interpretatio credatur facti ambigui, qua testatus Naaman sit, se quoties regem in templum comitatus, ibidem esset procubiturus, facturum id in honorem non Remmanis, sed regiæ majestatis. Nam si hæc mens ejus fuisset, non opus habuisset id deprecari, & ut Deus sibi propitius esse in eo dignetur, rogare: quod ab ipso factum est, 2. Reg. V. 18. Quod enim excipit Grotius, non tam ut hoc condonaret, quam ut æqui consuleret Deus, ipsum precatum esse, textui haud consonat; cum סלח, ἰλάσκεσθαι LXX. Interpp. condonationem inferat, nec contrarium è Num. XXX. 6. probetur. Alia usus exceptione Grotius annot. ad 2. Reg. V. 18. nempe quod alienigenis lex illa de simulacris non colendis haud præscripta fuerit: sed eam hic dimittit. Rectius proinde verba Naamanis in præterito accipiuntur, quod nempe condonari sibi petierit, quod antea in æde Remmanis se incurvaverit. Neque probandum, quod terræ Israeliticæ translationem in Syriam, sacrificii causa factam superstitione vacare censet Grotius, ita eam excusans, quod eo signo testatum voluerit illum ipsum à se Deum coli, qui in terra Israelitica coleretur: at annon alia ratione id testari poterat, ut opus non habuerit terram transferre? & valde obscure id testatus fuisset humo Israeliticæ insistendo, & super eam sacrificando: quod utique ab ἐθελοθρησκείᾳ absolvi non potuisset. Videantur autem de his & de sensu verborum 2. Reg. V. quæ ad locum illum contra Grotium diximus.

## 4:28
Verse 28. hearing these things] Because they were being argued against as unworthy of miracles by a silent comparison.

Latin:

Vers. 28. ἀκούοντες ταῦτα] Quia indigni miraculis tacita comparatione arguebantur.

## 4:29
Verse 29. of the brow] It is well known that the Latins call not only the prominences above the eyes eyebrows, but the Greeks do as well: Homer: 'on the brows of the beautiful hill'; Apollonius: 'on the brows of the shore.' Plutarch, Numa: 'an earthy brow extending far.' Herodotus, 'of those dwelling on the brow.'

to cast him down headlong] Not in the manner of a trial, but by the movement of an excited mob: just as at another time the Jews wished to stone him.

Latin:

Vers. 29. τῆς ὀφρύος] Non Latini tantum eminentias vocant supercilia, ut notum est, sed & Græci Homerus: ἐπ' ὀφρύσι καλλικολώνης Apollonius: ἐπ' ὀφρύσιν αἰγιαλοῖο. Plutarchus Numa: ὀφρῦς γεώδης παρατείνουσα πόῤῥω. Herodotus, τῶν ἐν τῇ ὀφρύϊ κατωκημένων.

εἰς τὸ κατακρημνίσαι αὐτὸν] Non judicii more, sed motu concitatæ plebis: sicut & alio tempore Judæi eum lapidare voluerunt.

## 4:30
Verse 30. through the midst of them] Unharmed by the crowd obstructing him on all sides. The same manner of speaking is found in John 8:59, where it is clearly signified that Christ was made invisible to his enemies by divine power: wherefore it is credible that he escaped in this way here as well.

PART III. Capernaum Deeds.

Latin:

Vers. 30. διὰ μέσου αὐτῶν] Nihil læsus a turba undique obstante. Idem loquendi genus reperitur Joh. VIII. 59. ubi clare significatur Christum divina virtute factum inimicis inconspicuum: quare eodem modo hic quoque elapsum credibile est.

PARS III. Gesta Capernaitica.

## 4:31
Verse 31. and he went down to Capernaum, a city of Galilee] Wonderful was the audacity of Marcion, who, having omitted all those things which we read in Luke up to this point, began his book from here, with such words as Tertullian teaches: 'In the fifteenth year of the principate of Tiberius, God descended into the Galilean city of Capernaum': subsequently appending that which we had above concerning what was done at Nazareth, having introduced the rest which had preceded. Epiphanius indicates the same. Whoever wishes to see in how many places Marcion or those who preceded him interpolated the books of both Luke and Paul, let them consult both the writers whom I have mentioned. To refute such forgeries, Tertullian rightly appeals to those churches which Paul, with Luke also as his helper, had founded, which all with the greatest consensus followed the edition which we have.

Latin:

Vers. 31. καὶ κατῆλθεν εἰς Καπερναοὺμ πόλιν τῆς Γαλιλαίας] Mira fuit Marcionis audacia, qui omissis omnibus iis quæ apud Lucam ad hunc usque locum legimus, hinc librum auspicabatur, talibus verbis ut Tertullianus docet: Anno quintodecimo principatus Tiberiani Deus descendit in civitatem Galilææ Capharnaum: subtexens deinde illud quod Nazarethæ factum supra habuimus, cæteris quæ præcesserant, inductis. Idem indicat Epiphanius. Qui videre volet quot locis Marcio aut qui ei præiverant tum Lucæ tum Pauli libros interpolaverint, consulant utrumque Scriptorem quem dixi. Ad revincenda id genus παραχαράγματα merito Tertullianus provocat ad eas Ecclesias quas Paulus, Luca etiam adjutore, fundaverat, quæ omnes maximo consensu eam quam nos habemus ἔκδοσιν sequebantur.

## 4:32
Verse 32. his word was with authority] He openly carried himself as a teacher sent from God, and confirmed that with admirable deeds. See regarding this meaning of authority what we said at Matt. 7:29.

Latin:

Vers. 32. ἐν ἐξουσίᾳ ἦν λόγος αὐτῦ] Palam se ferebat doctorem divinitus missum, atque id factis admirandis confirmabat. Vide de hoc significatu ἐξουσίας quæ ad Matth. VII. 29.

## 4:34
Vers. 34. ἔα] See the note on Mark 1:24. For Luke described these things entirely from Mark, with a few words changed.

Latin:

Vers. 34. ἔα] Vide ad Marcum I. 24. Nam hæc omnino ex Marco Lucas descripsit paucis vocibus mutatis.

## 4:36
Vers. 36. τίς ὁ λόγος ὗτος;] Luke placed this in place of what Mark had said, τί ἐστι τοῦτο: wherefore that interpretation, 'what is this thing?', is more true. For the LXX also, when they signify the word דבר, often translate it as λόγον or ῥῆμα: and above we have seen λόγος and ῥῆμα used by Luke in that sense. The Jerusalem Paraphrast is accustomed to translate it פתגם.

Ἐξουσίᾳ καὶ δυνάμει] I would prefer to translate δύναμιν as 'potentia' (power). For 'potestas' (authority), when one must speak accurately and distinctly, corresponds more to the word ἐξουσία and is usually translated that way by jurists. Ἐξουσία is a right or moral faculty: Δύναμις is active force, or a natural faculty, or one similar to natural.

Latin:

Vers. 36. τίς ὁ λόγος ὗτος;] Posuit hoc Lucas pro eo quod Marcus dixerat τί ἐστι τοῦτο: quare verior est interpretatio illa quid hoc est rei? Nam & LXX. cum דבר rem significat λόγον aut ῥῆμα sæpe vertunt: & supra λόγος & ῥῆμα eo sensu à Luca usurpatum vidimus. Hierosolymitanus Paraphrastes solet vertere פתגם.

Ἐξουσίᾳ καὶ δυνάμει] Δύναμιν malim potentiam vertere. Nam potestas, cum accurate & distincte loquendum est, magis respondet voci ἐξουσία atque ita verri solet à Jurisconsultis. Ἐξουσία est jus sive facultas moralis: Δύναμις vis activa, sive facultas naturalis, aut naturali similis.

## 4:38
Vers. 38. Συνεχομένη] The interpreter of Matthew uses this word in this way in chapter 4:24.

Ἠρώτησαν] It seems to be a Latinism: because the Latins say 'rogare' (to ask) for 'orare' (to pray). The interpreter of Matthew speaks in a similar way in chapter 5:23, John in chapter 4:16, our author here below in 7:3 and Acts 23:20, and Paul in 2 Thessalonians 2:1. But the Hellenists also use the word ἐρωτᾷν in the sense of a request or prayer, as can be seen in Psalm 122:6.

Latin:

Vers. 38. Συνεχομένη] Ita hanc vocem usurpat & Matthæi interpres c. IV. 24.

Ἠρώτησαν] Videtur esse Latinismus: quia Latini rogare dicunt pro orare. Simili modo loquitur Matthæi interpres c. V. 23. Johannes c. IV.16. Noster hic infra VII. 3. & Act. XXIII. 20. Paulus 2. Thess. II. 1. Sed & Hellenistæ vocem ἐρωτᾷν in sensu postulationis aut precationis usurpant, ut videre est Psal. CXXII. 6.

## 4:39
Vers 39. ἐπιστὰς ἐπάνω αὐτῆς] We have spoken about the word ἐπιστῆναι in the notes on Matthew 28. However, with ἐπάνω added, it seems to signify nothing other than an approach from nearby. Thus, in 2 Samuel 1:9, the LXX translate עמד נא עלי as ἐπίστηθι ἐπάνω μου, that is, 'approach closer to me'.

Latin:

Vers 39. ἐπιστὰς ἐπάνω αὐτῆς] De voce ἐπιστῆναι diximus ad Matth. XXVIII. Videtur autem addito ἐπάνω nihil aliud quam accessus de proximo significari. Ita 2. Samuel. I.9. עמד נא עלי vertunt LXX. ἐπίστηθι ἐπάνω μου, id est propius ad me accede.

## 4:40
Vers. 40. δύνοντος δὲ ἡλίου] When the sun had set. For the present participle is used here for the past. See Mark. The ancient interpreter is correct: 'when the sun had set'.

Latin:

Vers. 40. δύνοντος δὲ ἡλίου] Sole occaso. Nam præsens usurpatur hic pro præterito. Vide Marcum. Vetus interpres recte: cum sol occidisset.

## 4:42
Vers. 42. Γενομένης δὲ ἡμέρας] When the day was dawning. For ἐγένετο is sometimes accustomed to be used in such a way that it signifies 'that which is in coming-to-be' more than 'that which is in being'. See what I wrote on Mark.

κατεῖχον αὐτόν] Namely, for the sake of those benefits which they were receiving from the miracles. For they were looking primarily to that: but Christ teaches in the following words that the primary thing is the preaching of the kingdom, of which miracles are the seal.

Latin:

Vers. 42. Γενομένης δὲ ἡμέρας] Cum dies immineret. Ita enim ἐγένετο usurpari interdum solet, ut magis significet τὸ ἐν γενέσει quam τὸ ἐν εἶναι. Vide quæ ad Marcum.

κατεῖχον αὐτόν] Nempe eorum commodorum causa quæ ex miraculis percipiebant. Id enim præcipue spectabant: at Christus verbis sequentibus docet præcipuum esse τὸν εὐαγγελισμὸν τῆς βασιλείας, cujus sigillum sint miracula.

## 4:43
Vers. 43. πόλεσιν] Luke calls villages that are like towns πόλεις, which Mark calls κωμοπόλεις. Thus also below in chapter 5:12, 'in one of the cities', that is, 'town-villages'.

Latin:

Vers. 43. πόλεσιν] Vicos oppidorum instar πόλεις vocat Lucas, quas Marcus κωμοπόλεις. Sic & infra c. V. 12. ἐν μιᾷ τῶν πόλεων, id est κωμοπόλεων.

## 5:1 Argument
CHAPTER V. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

Christ preaches at the Sea of Gennesaret, and after a miraculous catch of fish, confirms Peter with his companions for the fishing of men: in a certain city he heals a leper, and many others, especially a paralytic let down through the roof, whose sins he also forgives, and defends this: he calls Levi from the tax office, who prepared a great banquet; and he gives the reason why he associates with publicans and sinners, and why the disciples of John and the Pharisees fast, but Christ's do not. There are three parts: I. The miraculous fishing of Peter and his calling, up to verse 11. II. The miraculous healings, of the leper, of others, and of the paralytic, up to verse 26. III. The calling of Levi the publican, and his banquet with related matters, up to verse 39.

PART I. The miraculous catch of Peter, and his calling to the catching of men.

Ver. 1. ἐπικεῖσθαι αὐτῷ] When they crowded upon him: The Syriac, indeed, and Matthew and Mark in a similar event use the word συνάγεσθαι (Matt. XIII. 2; Mark IV. 1). But this word seems to signify not just any gathering, but one with pressure: whence the Latin interpreter not badly translates it as 'to rush upon' (irruere). See Acts XXVII. 20, and the Greek of Job XIX. 3, ch. XXI. 23.

Latin:

CAPUT V. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Christus concionatur admareGenezareth, & post miraculosam piscaturam Petrum cum sociis confirmat ad piscaturam hominum: in civitate quadam leprosum sanat, mul- tosque alios, imprimis paralyticum per te- ctum immissum, cui etiam peccata remit- tit, idque defendit: Levi è telonio vocat, qui magnum convivium paravit; & cau- sam reddit, cur cum publicanis & peccato- ribus conversetur, & cur Johannis & Pharisæorum discipuli jejunent, non item Christi. Partes tres sunt: Miraculosa Petri piscatura & vocatio, ad v. 11. II. Miraculosæ sanationes, le- prosi, aliorum, paralytici, ad v. 26. III. Levi pu- blicani vocatio, ejusque convivium cum conne- xis, ad v. 39.

PARS I. Miraculosa Petri piscatura, ejusque ad pisca- turam hominum vocatio.

Vers. 1. ἐπικεῖσθαι αὐτῷ] Cum ad eum coiret: Syrus sane & Matthæus & Marcus in facto simili usurpant vocem συνάγεσθαι Matth. XIII. 2. Marc. IV. 1. Sed videtur hæc vox non quemvis concursum, sed cum pressura significare: unde irruere non male vertit Latinus interpres. Vide Actor. XXVII. 20. & Græca Job. XIX. 3. c. XXI. 23.

## 5:2
Ver. 2. οἱ δὲ ἁλιεῖς ἀποβάντες ἀπ' αὐτῶν ἀπέπλυναν τὰ δίκτυα] Since what follows below in verse 19 seems to show that the same event is being treated here as that which Matthew and Mark also narrate, it should be understood that with the ships drawn up, the fishermen were occupied with different tasks, as is wont to happen: there were those who were cleaning the nets, there were those who were mending them: and some were also testing from the shore whether they could catch anything. And so, a part of them were in the ships, and a part on the shore.

Latin:

Vers. 2. οἱ δὲ ἁλιεῖς ἀποβάντες ἀπ' αὐτῶν ἀπέπλυναν τὰ δίκτυα] Cum quod infra sequitur com. 19. ostendere videa- tur de eadem re hic agi, quam Matthæus quoque & Mar- cus narrant, intelligendum videtur navibus subductis pi- scatores alios aliis ministeriis fuisse distentos, ut fieri solet: fuisse qui purgarent retia, fuisse qui refarcirent: quosdam & ex littore expertos nunquid capere possent. Itaque partem eorum in navibus fuisse, partem in littore.

## 5:3
Ver. 3. ἐμβὰς δὲ εἰς ἓν τῶν πλοίων] Matthew and Mark had omitted the history of this miracle, perhaps because, however much it was certain to them that nothing was done here except by the singular disposition of God, it might nevertheless seem to others that this matter could be attributed to chance: and therefore there was no reason why, in such a great multitude of miracles, they should dwell on this matter. Luke restored this narrative, passed over by them, to its proper place, that is, between the fishermen found at the shore and that calling by which, having heard it, Peter, Andrew, John, and James left their affairs and followed Christ familiarly.

ἐπαναγαγεῖν] A nautical term: it signifies to be carried out into the deep, 2 Maccab. XII. 4, ἐπαναχθέντας αὐτὸς ἐβύθισαν. 'To lead back' (reducere), which the Latin interpreter uses here, is not so much to be despised. For to lead back from the shore is to move away, just as Virtue is the mean between vices, led back from both sides.

Latin:

Vers. 3. ἐμβὰς δὲ εἰς ἓν τῶν πλοίων] Omiserant huius mira- culi historiam Matthæus & Marcus, forte quia quantum vis ipsis constaret nihil hic gestum nisi singulari Dei dispo- sitione, tamen videretur ab aliis res ista ad casum posse re- ferri: ac proinde non esse cur in tanta miraculorum multi- tudine huic rei immorarentur. Lucas hanc narrationem ab illis præteritam suo loco reddidit, id est inter repertos ad littus piscatores, & inter illam vocationem, qua audita Petrus, Andreas, Johannes, Jacobus rebus relictis Chri- stum familiariter sunt secuti.

ἐπαναγαγεῖν] Vox nautica: significat in altum provehi, 2. Maccab. XII. 4. ἐπαναχθέντας αὐτὸς ἐβύθισαν. Redu- cere quod hic Latinus interpres usurpat, non adeo sper- nendum est. Nam à littore reducere est amovere, ut Virtus est medium vitiorum utrinque reductum.

## 5:4
Ver. 4. χαλάσατε] That χαλᾷν among other things means to let down is most evident even from one passage in Acts, ch. IX. 25. The Latins translate τὸ χαλᾷν as 'to loosen' (laxare) when it concerns a sail: which the old interpreter follows here by catachresis.

Latin:

Vers. 4. χαλάσατε] χαλᾷν inter cætera esse demittere, apertissimum est vel ex uno Actuum loco c. IX. 25. Latini τὸ χαλᾷν per laxare vertunt, cum de velo agitur: quod hic per abusionem sequitur vetus interpres.

## 5:5
Ver. 5. ἐπιστάτα] No one of these writers except Luke uses this word. It appears that it seemed to him that this Greek word best corresponds to the Hebrew רב. For a comparison of what is in Mark IX. 5 and below in this author IX. 33 makes this manifest. Matthew's interpreter is accustomed to put κύριε for the same word, Mark also διδάσκαλε: as can be seen by comparing the passages Matt. VIII. 25, Mark IV. 38, and Luke VIII. 24; likewise Matt. XVII. 4, the said passage Mark IX. 5, and Luke IX. 33; likewise Mark IX. 38 and Luke IX. 49. Doubtless Luke thought that in the word רבי there was something less than in the word κύριε, that is אדוני, but more than in the word διδασκάλῳ. Just as Ammonius says that διδάσκαλος is of words, but ἐπιστάτης of deeds. And so he sought a middle Greek word, to which the Latin 'master' (magister) responds quite properly, which is wont to be referred to every eminent dignity, whence the name 'master of the horse' (magister equitum) and the word 'magistrate' (magistratus). The LXX in Isaiah ch. XIX. 20 translate it κεῖνον, in the history of Esther I. 8, οἰκονόμους. The same people translate the Hebrew words מנצח, נגש, נגיד, שר, ררה and similar ones with the word ἐπιστάτης, as others have noted before. But what the word ἐπιστάτης properly designates, Callicratides the Pythagorean teaches us best, whose words are these: 'Among the practical and rational authorities, some are despotic, others are epistatic; and those are despotic which rule for the benefit of the ruler, and not of the ruled. For in this way the master rules the slaves, and the tyrant the subjects; but epistatic authorities are for the sake of the ruled, and not for themselves; and in this way those authorities rule: the trainers of athletes, and the physicians of the sick, and the teachers of the students; for they do not provide the benefit for themselves, but for the ruled: the physicians for the sick, the trainers for the athletes, and the knowledgeable for the ignorant.'

It does not mean only this, 'at your command,' but 'relying solely on your authority,' when all other things are contrary to our hope. And so ἐπὶ is properly taken here: but it is an ellipsis of the word πεποιθὼς; the word loves such a construction, as can be seen in Mark X. 24, below XVIII. 9, 2 Cor. I. 9, Heb. II. 13.

They called them to themselves with a sign, because they were wandering too far for a voice to reach them. For what Theophylact says, that they could not speak because of astonishment, is not likely, nor do the following things support it.

For fishermen of several ships are accustomed to form a partnership among themselves.

The same expression is found in Plutarch and Phil. IV. 3.

That which is added here, παρά τι, seems to me to have been added by those who thought this manner of speaking should be softened, whom the Syriac also followed for the sake of avoiding ambiguity. The most ancient of the Latin codices seem not to have had this. Indeed, ὥσε sometimes signifies to the Greeks not what is, but what is near. It is also possible for βυθίζεσθαι to be understood not as to be submerged, but to sink deeper on account of the burden. For even in Mark chapter IV. 37, βυθίζεσθαι had been placed by ancient expositors in place of γεμίζεσθαι.

Just as pious men feared to see angels, from a consciousness of common weakness, so also they feared the presence of those whom they recognized as sent singularly by GOD, as the Sareptan woman feared that the hospitality of Elijah might have harmed her. Wherefore it is less to be wondered at that Peter feared for himself from the sight of him to whom he saw the whole nature of things yielding: the dominion being restored to him which Adam had in great part lost. See Psalm VIII. 9, where fish are also named. The word ἁμαρτωλὸς is usually employed for the most part concerning those who, having cast off the fear of the divine majesty, live according to the lust of their mind: such as Peter never was, whose ἐυλάβειαν even this one history sufficiently testifies. For it is the greatest indication of an upright mind to exercise the most severe censure upon oneself. Thus Paul calls himself the first of sinners, by which he does also what we remember citing from Barnabas. That Adam had such dominion over the sea and the fish will not be taught, nor is Psalm VIII about Adam, but about Christ: nor was it restored to Christ, but through Christ to us, what we lost in Adam. Moreover, all of nature yielded to Christ as Lord, who has power over all things, in and of himself, as true GOD, and by another, and through the grace of the hypostatic union, as man, or according to his human nature.

Latin:

Vers. 5. ἐπιστάτα] Vocem hanc nemo horum Scripto- rum præter Lucam usurpat. Apparet ei visum hanc vocem Græcam optime respondere, Hebraicæ רב. Nam id ma- nifestum facit collatio ejus quod est apud Marcum IX. 5. & infra apud hunc IX. 33. Matthæi interpres pro eadem voce ponere solet κύριε, Marcus etiam διδάσκαλε: ut videre est collatis locis Matth. VIII. 25. Marc. IV. 38. & Luc. VIII. 24. item Matth. XVII. 4. dicto loco Marc. IX. 5. & Lucæ IX. 33. item Marci IX. 38. & Luc. IX. 49. Nimirum existima- vit Lucas in voce רבי minus aliquid esse quam in voce κυρίε id est אדוני, plus autem quam in voce διδασκάλῳ. Sicut Am- monius διδάσκαλον ait esse λόγων, at ἐπιστάτην ἔργων. Itaque mediam vocem Græcam quæsivit, cui satis proprie respon- det Latina, magister, quæ ad omnem eminentem digni- tatem referri solet, unde magistri equitum nomen, & vox magistratus. LXX. in Esaia cap. XIX. 20. vertunt κεῖ- νον, in Estheris historia I. 8. οἰκονόμῳς. Iidem Hebræas vo- ces מנצח נגש נגיד שר ררה & similes vertunt voce ἐπιστάτης ut alii notare anteverterunt. Quid autem proprie vox ἐπιστάτης designet, optime nos docet Callicratides Py- thagoreus, cujus hæc sunt verba: ἐπὶ τὰς πρακτικὰς καὶ κατὰ λογισμὸν ἀρχὰς, ἁ μέν ἐσι δεσποτικὰ, ἁ δὲ ἐπιστατικὰ, καὶ δεσποτικὰ μὲν ἐντὶ ἁ τῶ ἰδίω συμφέροντῶ ἄρχοντῶ, ἀλλ᾿ ὀὐ τῶ ἀρχομένω. ταύται γὰρ ἄρχοι τὰν κεχὰν ὁ μὲν δεσπότας τῶ δόλων, ὁ δὲ τύραννῶ τῶ ὑποτεταγμένων· ἐπιστατικὰ δὲ ἕνεκα τῶ ἀρχομέ- νω, ἀλλ᾿ ὀὐχ᾽ ἁυτᾶς· ταύται δ᾽ ἄρχονταὶ αἱ ἀρχαὶ τοὶ μὲν ἀλείπται τῶ ἀθλητᾶν, καὶ τοὶ ἰατροὶ τῶ νοσεόντων, κὶ τοὶ διδάσκοιτες τῶ διδασκομένων· ὀὐ γὰρ ἀυτοῖς τὸ συμφέρον, ἀλλὰ τοῖς ἀρχομένοις ποτικοιῦντι· τοῖς μὲν καμνόντεσσι τὸ ἰατροὶ, τοῖς δὲ ζωμασκεῦ- σι τοὶ ἀλεῖπται, τοῖς δ᾽ ἀνεπισάμοισιν οἱ ἐπισάμονες.

Non hoc tantum vult, te jubente, sed, fretus solo imperio tuo, cum res cæteræ omnes spei nostræ adversentur. Itaque ἐπὶ proprie hic sumitur: sed est ἕλλειψις vocis πεποιθὼς vox talem constructionem amat, ut videre est Marci X. 24. infra XVIII. 9. 2. Corinth. I. 9. Hebr. II. 13.

Signo eos ad se vocarunt, quia longius aberrant, quam ut vox eo pervenire posset. Nam quod Theophylactus ait, præ stupore loqui nequisse, verisi- mile non est, neque id ferunt quæ sequuntur.

Solent enim plurium navium piscatores societatem inter se coire.

Eadem locutio est apud Plutarchum & Philip. IV. 3.

Quod hic additur παρά τι videtur mi- hi adjectum ab his qui genus hoc loquendi emolliendum putabant, quos & Syrus ambiguitatis evitandæ causa est secutus. Latinorum codicum vetustissimi videntur hoc non habuisse. Sane ὥσε Græcis interdum non quod est, sed quod prope est significat. Potest & βυθίζεσθαι intelligi non submergi, sed præ onere profundius sidere. Nam & in Marco cap. IV. 37. pro γεμίζεσθαι ab antiquis explicatoribus positum erat βυθίζεσθαι.

Sicut Angelos videre metuebant pii homines, communis imbe- cillitatis conscientia, ita etiam verebantur eorum præsen- tiam quos à DEO singulariter missos agnoscebant, ut Sa- reptana mulier metuit, ne Eliæ hospitium sibi nocuisset. Quo minus mirandum est Petrum sibi metuisse ab ejus conspectu cui omnem rerum naturam cedere videbat: re- stituto ei dominio quod Adam magna ex parte amiserat. Vid. Psalm. VIII. 9. ubi & pisces nominantur. Solet vox ἁμαρτωλὸς plerumque usurpari de iis qui projecto metu di- vini numinis ex animi lubidine vivunt: qualis nunquam fuit Petrus, cujus ἐυλάβειαν vel hæc una historia satis te- statur. Nam probi animi vel maximum est indicium, seve- rissimam in se censuram exercere. Ita Paulus se primum vocat τῶν ἁμαρτωλῶν, quo facit & quod ex Barnaba citasse meminimus. Dominium tale maris & piscium habuisse Adamum non docebitur, nec de Adamo Psal. VIII. agitur, sed de Christo: neque restitutum Christo est, sed per Christum nobis, quod in Adamo amisimus. Cedebat autem omnis rerum natura Christo ceu Domino, qui potestatem in omnia habeat, καθ' αὑτὸ per se, ut verus DEUS, κατ' ἄλλο, & per unionis hypostaticae gratiam, ut homo, vel secundum humanam naturam.

There is a similar expression among the Latins: horror stood around. A not dissimilar meaning is in the Hebrew word אפף. In the catch of the fish which they took] There is a similar expression: a great herd of swine feeding, Mark V. 11, where Luke has feeding. For ἄγρα, like the Latin captura, does not always signify the act, but often the totality of things caught at once.

Simile est apud Latinos circumstitit horror: Non dissimilis significatio in voce Hebraea אפף. τῇ ἄγρᾳ τῶν ἰχθύων ᾗ συνέλαβον] Simile est ἀγέλη χοίρων μεγάλη βοσκομένη, Marc. V. 11. ubi Lucas habet βοσκομένων. Nam & ἄγρα ut Latine captura, non actum semper, sed saepe universitatem rerum simul captarum significat.

## 5:10
Verse 10. Do not fear] The more he was displeased with himself, the more he pleases the Lord. From now on you will be catching men] Luke seems to have said this on purpose, not ἀγρεύων, but ζωγρῶν. For this word is accustomed to be used in a better sense, and to signify such a capture by which the danger of death is redeemed, just as the Latins said that slaves (servos) were named from saving (servando). Thus he prays in Homer: Save me, son of Atreus, that is, the scholiasts say, keep me alive. A similar literal usage is to be observed in Paul, 2 Timothy II. 26: having been captured by him for his will. God thus captures us, who are his enemies, and enslaves us to himself, so that he keeps us safe from death. These words of Christ, however, teach us that in the aforementioned miracle there was not only a benefit, but also a deeper meaning: and just as this kind of interpretation is not to be laboriously pursued where no occasion presents itself, so it is not to be despised where the Spirit of God himself provides some indication of it. I therefore gladly follow the ancients here, who think this is the allegorical meaning of the preceding history: that the Apostles, not by their own industry, but by the command and power of Christ, having spread the nets of the Gospel, would make such a catch that they would need the subsidiary work of many evangelists: and thus not one ship would be filled, namely that of the Jews, and another of the Gentiles, but that there would be a close and inseparable partnership of these ships.

Latin:

Vers. 10. μὴ φοβοῦ] Quo magis sibi displicebat hoc magis Domino placet. ἀπὸ τοῦ νῦν ἀνθρώπους ἔσῃ ζωγρῶν] De industria videtur Lucas dixisse, non ἀγρεύων, sed ζωγρῶν, Solet enim haec vox in partem meliorem usurpari, & talem capturam significare, qua redimatur mortis periculum, sicut & Latini servos à servando dixêre. Ita ille apud Homerum precatur Ζώγρει ἀτρέος ὗε, id est, inquiunt Scholiastae, ζῶντά με φύλαττε. Similem κυριολογίαν observare est apud Paulum 2. Timoth. II. 26. ἐζωγρημένοι ὑπ' ἀυτῦ εἰς τὸ ἐκείνε θέλημα. Deus nos sibi inimicos ita capit, & sibi mancipiat, ut à morte incolumes servet. Haec autem Christi verba nos docent, in supra memorato miraculo non beneficium tantum fuisse, sed & ὑπόνοιαν: quod genus interpretandi sicut non est operose sectandum ubi nulla se praebet occasio, ita contemnendum non est, ubi ipse Dei Spiritus aliquod ejus indicium praebet. Libenter igitur hic veteres sequor, qui praecedentis historiae hoc putant esse τὸ ἀλληγορέμενον: Apostolos non suapte industria, sed Christi imperio ac virtute expansis Evangelii retibus tantam facturos capturam, ut opus habituri sint subsidiaria multorum ἐυαγγελιστῶν opera: atque ita impletum iri non unam navem, Judaeorum scilicet, & alteram gentium, sed quarum navium futura sit arcta atque indivulsa societas.

## 5:17
Verse 17. To heal them] I understand 'them' here as the men of that place: for it cannot conveniently be referred to the lawyers or Pharisees, whom we do not read were healed: nor is this about a power that did not have an effect. A similar way of speaking, where the word 'them' ought to be referred not to those most recently named, but to those who are understood rather than named, appears in Matthew XI. 1: And it came to pass when Jesus had finished instructing his twelve disciples, he departed from there to teach and preach in their cities, to which passage we have brought other similar examples. For the fact that mention is made here of the lawyers and Pharisees pertains to showing that they were both spectators and slanderers of this deed. See Mark.

Simile loquendi genus, ubi vox ἀυτῶν non ad proxime nominatos, sed ad eos qui intelliguntur magis quam nominantur, referri debet, apparet Matth. XI. 1. καὶ ἐγένετο ὅτε ἐτέλεσεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς διατάσσων τοῖς δώδεκα μαθηταῖς ἀυτῦ, μετέβη ἐκεῖθεν τοῦ διδάσκειν καὶ κηρύσσειν ἐν ταῖς πόλεσιν ἀυτῶν, ad quem locum similia alia attulimus. ## 5:26
Verse 26. Amazement seized everyone] That is, they marveled, as the interpreter of Matthew said. It is therefore not the same as what follows, they were filled with fear, that is, they were filled with reverence for the divine majesty, as we have shown the word 'fear' is accustomed to be taken. I say these things so that no one might approach thinking that something here should be deleted. Paradoxical things] נפלאות. Cicero translates παράδοξα as 'admirable things': and hence Olympic victors and other winners of contests were called 'paradoxical'. The people judged the matter to be admirable with the best right, not so much because health had been restored to the sick man (which had already happened quite often) as because by that miracle Jesus had proven that the right to forgive sins had been given to him while living among men. For he had healed the man in confirmation of that fact. See Matthew in this history.

Haec ideo dico ne quis accedat aliquid hic delendum suspicantibus. παράδοξα] נפלאות. Παράδοξα admirabilia vertit Cicero: atque hinc Olympionicae & alii certaminum victores dicti παράδοξοι. Rem autem admirandam optimo jure populus judicabat, non tam quod aegroto sanitas esset reddita (quod jam contigerat saepius) quam quod eo miraculo Jesus probasset sibi inter homines viventi datum jus condonandi peccata. Nam in ejus rei fidem hominem sanaverat. Vide Matthaeum in hac historia.

## 5:30
Vers. 30. And the scribes of them murmured] Learned men torture themselves here in vain: and those who translate it 'murmured at them' prove by no example that γογγύζειν ἀυτῶν is said. It should have been said γογγύζειν κατὰ ἀυτῶν: although not even that has a place here: since all this murmuring was not directed at the publicans, whom they hardly placed in the number of men, but at the disciples of Christ who are clearly named a little later. Therefore, 'the scribes of them' are the lawyers of that place, and consequently the teachers of the Capharnaites in general. For we have demonstrated above that the word ἀυτῶν is accepted in this way without a preceding noun.

Latin:

Vers. 30. καὶ ἐγόγγυζον οἱ γραμματεῖς ἀυτῶν] Frustra hic se torquent viri eruditi: & qui vertunt obmurmurabant illis, nullo exemplo probant γογγύζειν ἀυτῶν dici. Dicendum erat γογγύζειν κατὰ ἀυτῶν: quanquam ne id quidem hic locum habet: cum omnis hic γογγυσμὸς non in publicanos directus fuerit, quos illi vix hominum in numero ponebant, sed in Christi discipulos qui paulo post diferte nominantur. Sunt ergo οἱ γραμματεῖς ἀυτῶν legisperiti ejus loci, ac proinde magistri Capharnaum tarum communiter. Nam ita vocem ἀυτῶν accipi fine præcedente nomine, supra demonstravimus.

## 5:39
Vers. 39. And no one having drunk old wine immediately desires new. For he says the old is better] The Syriac translates this χρηστότερος very well: it is sweeter. For that word properly has the meaning of mildness, as in Matt. 11:30, below 6:35, Rom. 2:4, Eph. 4:32. Old wines are accustomed to be of a milder flavor: new ones, on the contrary, are more austere. The writer of Ecclesiasticus 9:13 says: 'New wine is a friend; if it becomes old with joy, you shall drink it,' where you must beware of reading πίεσαι with a learned man and translating it 'comprehend.' For it is not from πιέζειν: but is the future from πίνω, the same form as φάγεσαι. Alexis says of wine when it has settled and attained age: 'And when it has settled again, it is sweet and continues to be so thereafter.' Because, therefore, old wine is milder, those who are accustomed to it cannot be suddenly brought to love the new. By this proverb Christ signified that men are not to be suddenly drawn to a more austere life, but are to be accustomed to it by certain degrees, which was most appropriate to the matter that was being dealt with: just as what is usually asserted here by many concerning the distinction between the Law and the Gospel is foreign to the subject.

This, concerning which one may read in Jansenius, Concord. chap. 33, is rightly reproved: yet the sense of the proverb is not well expressed by Grotius. The application of our own theologians is far more correct; from whom it is a pleasure to hear the blessed Polycarp Lyser, my father-in-law's predecessor, in Harm. Evang. c. 66, p. 953. He wishes to say: The same thing happens to you, regarding my doctrine, as to those who have been accustomed to old and milder wine. For just as they bear new wine less well, even though it is more generous, because it has a certain sourness and penetrates the taste more sharply: so you, who have been accustomed to the traditions of the fathers and to superstitions which are composed for pomp and display before men, cannot admit my doctrine, which is indeed humble and simple, yet penetrates into the minds of men in such a way that it requires the innovation of the whole man, because those old things are far more pleasing to you. Therefore that old mind must be put off and inveterate custom renounced, if you wish to progress in true piety.

SECTION II. OF THE ACTS OF THE MINISTRY OF CHRIST. Acts from the second Passover to the third.

Latin:

Vers. 39. καὶ ἐδεὶς πιὼν παλαιὸν ἐυθέως θέλει νέον. λέγει γὰρ ὁ παλαιὸς χρηστότερός ἐσιν] Hoc χρηστότερος optime vertit Syrus, suabius est. Proprie enim habet ea vox lenitatis significationem, ut Matth. XI. 30. infra VI. 35. Rom. II. 4. Eph. IV. 32. vetera vina solent esse saporis lenioris: nova contra austeriora Scriptor Ecclesiastici IX. 13. οἶνος νέος φίλος, νέος ἐὰν παλαιωθῇ μετ᾽ ἐυφροσύνης, πίεσαι ἀυτὸν, ubi cave cum viro erudito πίεσαι legas & vertas comprehende. Non est enim à πιέζειν: sed futurum à πίνω, eadem forma quæ φάγεσαι. Alexis de vino ubi despumavit, & ætatem nactus est, ait: κἂμ καταστῆαι πάλιν Ἡδύς᾽ ἀπαλειφτ᾽ ἐπιλοιπὸν διατελεῖ. Quia ergo lenius est vinum vetus, ideo qui ei sunt assueti, non possunt subito adduci, ut ament novum. Significavit hoc proverbio Christus homines non subito ad austeriorem vitam pertrahendos, sed per gradus quosdam assuefaciendos esse, quod accommodatissimum erat ei rei, de qua agebatur: sicut quod hic asserri à multis solet de discrimine legis & Evangelii, ab instituto alienum est.

Recte hoc de quo Jansenius in Concord. cap. XXXIII. legi potest, reprobatur: non tamen sensus proverbii à Grotio probe exprimitur. Longe rectius se habet nostratium Theologorum applicatio; è quibus audire juvat B. Pro-Socerum Polycarp. Lyserum in Harm. Evang. c. LXVI. p. 953. Vult dicere, Idem vobis, quoad meam doctrinam, accidit quod iis qui vino veteri & leniori assueverunt. Uti enim illi vinum novum, etsi est generosius, minus ferunt, eo quod acorem quendam habeat, & gustum acutius penetret: Ita vos qui assuevistis Patrum traditionibus, & superstitionibus, quæ ad pompam & ostentationem coram hominibus sunt compositæ, meam doctrinam, quæ humilis quidem est & simplex, in hominum tamen animos ita penetrat, ut totius hominis innovationem requirat, admittere non potestis, quia vetera illa vobis longe magis allubescunt. Idcirco exuendus est ille vetus animus & inveteratæ consuetudini renunciandum, si in veræ pietate proficere velitis.

SECTIO II. ACTORUM MINISTERII CHRISTI. Acta à Paschate secundo ad tertium.

## 6:1 Argument
CHAPTER VI. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

The disciples of Christ rubbing ears of corn on the Sabbath are excused, and the healing of the withered hand on the Sabbath is defended. The twelve Apostles are chosen, and a lengthy sermon is delivered concerning blessedness, the love of one's neighbor, and mercy, concluding with an exhortation regarding good fruits and the hearing of the word of God.

There are IV parts: I. The defense of the disciples of Christ rubbing ears of corn on the Sabbath, to verse 5. II. The healing of the withered hand on the Sabbath, and its defense, at v. 12. III. The election and enumeration of the XII Apostles, at v. 17. IV. The sermon delivered by Christ to the disciples, at v. 49.

PART I. The defense of the disciples on account of the rubbed ears of grain.

Ἐν σαββάτῳ δευτεροπρώτῳ] Gregory of Nazianzus wittily eluded Jerome, who was consulting him about this passage, by promising that he would speak about it, but in the Church, where Jerome, with the whole populace applauding, would be forced to know what he did not know, or if he alone remained silent, it would happen that he would be condemned by all for stupidity: recounting which matter, Jerome adds this epiphonema: Nothing is so easy as to deceive a base and unlearned audience with the volubility of one's tongue, which admires all the more whatever it does not understand. How many are there today for whom bold assertion passes for erudition, especially as often as they speak from a higher place, where they have no one to contradict them? As for the rest, concerning the interpretation of the word δευτεροπρώτου, it can almost be said: as many heads, so many opinions: the Syrian and the Arab, being so much closer to that time and place than we are, show clearly enough that they did not know what this word meant: wherefore it is more equitable that others be forgiven to whom nothing is left but conjectures, which it is easier to refute than to bring forward anything certain. That they are mistaken who wish for a certain feast day to be understood here, and not the day which we call Saturn's day, is evident from the fact that the whole dispute which arose from this does not pertain to feast days, on which rest was not observed so rigidly, but to that day which is properly and peculiarly called the Sabbath, which those on the outside call Saturn's day. But neither can the opinion of those be accepted who explain δευτερόπρωτον in such a way that it is a name suitable for many days: since Luke used this name so that a certain day of the year might be understood: these things having been rightly observed, most of the divinations of the ancients fall away, as has been prudently noted by certain recent authors. The authority of a great man has drawn many into agreement: who explains δευτερόπρωτον as πρῶτον ἀπὸ τῆς δευτέρας τοῦ πάσχα. But these things stand in my way against subscribing to him: First, because I have seen no example of such a formation, as would be the case if δευτερόπρωτον were derived from the word δευτέρας and the word πρώτου. Then, because the Law which exists in Leviticus does not say that Sabbaths are named from the day after the Passover, so that this Sabbath is called the first, that the second, and so on, but that those fifty days ימים תמימת τὰς ἡμέρας τῆς πεντηκοστῆς are counted and on that same day, so that the day after the Passover is the first of those fifty, the one that follows it the second, and so on up to the fiftieth, which method of counting the Jews even now anxiously observe: yet they do not repeat that name δευτέρας in naming the days. But as each night arrives, they are accustomed to say, this is the first day of the Omer: this is the second day, and so on. Therefore, that opinion, which has been defended with great arguments by its author, since it does not approve itself to me, for the reasons I have stated, I will indulge myself also, after so many others, in the liberty of judging: the Jews today still call the Sabbath day which immediately precedes the Passover שבת הגדול. But even if the day of the Passover fell on the Sabbath itself, that day was called by the same name, as appears in John XIX. 31. ἦν γὰρ μεγάλη ἡ ἡμέρα ἐκείνη τοῦ σαββάτου. There is also mention of a σαββάτου μεγάλου in the history of the martyrdom of Polycarp in Eusebius. Others instead of הגדול said הראשון, that is, τὸ πρῶτον σάββατον. For in the preaching of Peter it was: σάββατον ἐκ ἄγουσι τὸ λεγόμενον πρῶτον. But since besides the Passover there are two other most celebrated feasts of the Jews, namely τὸ πλήρωμα τῆς πεντηκοστῆς and the feast of tabernacles, the Sabbaths which touched those feasts most closely were also called μέγαλα ἢ καὶ πρῶτα for a similar reason. For Josephus also calls the Sabbath which fell εἰς τὴν σκηνοπηγίαν the μάλισα θρησκευόμενον σάββατον, in the Jewish War, book II, ch. XXXVII. And thus, since there were three Sabbaths πρῶτα, that is, greatest, it was discovered for the sake of distinction that the Paschal Sabbath, which precedes in order, should be called πρωτόπρωτον, the first of the first, the Sabbath of Pentecost δευτερόπρωτον, the second of the first, the Sabbath of the feast of tabernacles, τριτόπρωτον, the third of the first. Thus in municipalities where there were δεκαπρῶτοι, the first of the order could be called πρωτόπρωτος, the second δευτερόπρωτος, and so on. It should be noted, however, that the harvest, as the Hebrews teach, fell almost in the month of Elul, which corresponds partly to June, partly to July: therefore, in Exodus XXIII. 16, the feast of Pentecost is called the feast of the harvest, but the feast of tabernacles, which fell at the end of August or the beginning of September, is the feast of the gathering of fruits into the barns. For because on the day after the Passover, the δράγμα ταχύων was brought to the altar, it was done for the sake of the sign from the green ears of grain which were roasted by fire, as Josephus teaches us from the passage in Lev. II. 14, whence also the month of Nisan has another name, אביב, which signifies a green ear: and these very first fruits were smoked from barley, the grain that reveals itself earlier. See Josephus. And this formation of δευτεροπρώτου does not exceed the rule of analogy. Add that among

the Hellenists, whose speech Luke is undoubtedly expressing here, there existed a word of similar form. For those tithes which the Levites paid to the priests, they called δευτεροδεκάτας, that is, second tithes, as Jerome notes in chapter XL of Ezekiel. The same are called δευτέρας δεκάτας in Tobit I. 6. Therefore, the same are δευτέρα δεκάτη and δευτεροδεκάτη: likewise the Sabbath δεύτερον πρῶτον or δευτερόπρωτον.

ψώχοντες] Rubbing.

Concerning the interpretation of this word, there are not indeed as many opinions as there are heads, yet there is a great discrepancy. Robert Baillie, in his Historical and Chronological Works, book II, ch. XII, p. 74 ff., after our B. Chemnitz in his Harmony of the Gospels, ch. XLV, distributes the principal opinions of authors into certain classes and carefully weighs them, and has enumerated nine or ten opinions: as many as are also enumerated by others, by Dr. Sebastian Schmieden and Dr. Henr. Müller, in their Disputation on the Deuteroproto Sabbath. Moreover, not only the Syrian and Arab, but also the Persian and Ethiopic interpreters pass over this word; nor does anything that Erasmus and Maldonado have read about this word, whether among the ancients or the moderns, please them. We readily agree, however, that no day other than the Sabbath is meant, not so much because rest on other feast days is not observed as rigidly by the force of divine law as on the weekly feast, or the Sabbath day, but because it is expressly called the Sabbath by Luke, which word is to be taken in its more familiar meaning, and that one is not to be rashly set aside, especially because in v. 6 mention is also made of the weekly Sabbath in these words, ἐγένετο δὲ κὴ ἐν ἑτέρῳ (αββάτῳ: nor do we rashly approve the opinion of those who explain δευτερόπρωτον in such a way that it is a name applicable to many days, since Luke used this name so that a specific day might be understood. B. Chemnitius proceeds thus: such a second-first Sabbath was altogether one in which, according to the law, it was permitted to do no work. But there are three kinds of it: namely, the ordinary Sabbath of every seventh day; then the first and last day in great feasts. But the word δευτερόπρωτον indicates that the first day of a feast is not to be understood, nor the Sabbath, which, outside of great feasts, was always celebrated on the seventh day. It will therefore be either the last day of a feast, or an ordinary Sabbath when it fell on the intermediate days of some great feast: or when the first or last day of a feast fell on the Sabbath itself. This, therefore, is certain to him, that the second-first Sabbath pertains to one of the great and more solemn feasts. And therefore he inquires, which feast that might be? He teaches that it is not the feast of Trumpets and Atonement, because these feasts consisted of only one day: but Mark named Sabbaths in this history, and the word δευτερόπρωτον indicates a relation to several days. That it cannot be understood of the Feast of Tabernacles either, because the disciples pluck and rub the ears of grain, which in the month of September, especially in Palestine, is in no way fitting: there remain, therefore, still two feasts: the Passover and Pentecost. And some indeed try to interpret this history concerning Pentecost, because in Lev. XXIII. 16, Pentecost is called the solemnity of the harvest of firstfruits, as also in Num. XXVIII. 26. But the matter is plain, says B. Chemnitius, if the descriptions of the feasts are diligently considered. For in Lev. XXIII. 15, on the second day of the feast of the Passover, the firstfruits of the ears of grain were offered: and then in Deut. XVI. 9, the sickle was put to the crops. The text also in Lev. XXIII. 10 says: When you have harvested the crop, you shall offer a sheaf of ears of grain: and he adds v. 14: You shall not eat parched or cooked grain from the crop before the offering of the ears of grain has been made on the second day of the Passover. These descriptions point as if with an outstretched finger that the feast of the Passover is to be understood in the history of Luke. For after the offering of the ears of grain, it was permitted to rub them and thus eat the grains. Thus the blessed mnitius; who furthermore wishes the last day of Passover to be called deuteroproton, because it was just as holy and celebrated as the first: Which is also the opinion of Brentius, Osiander, and Flacius, as well as Aretius and Antonius Waleus; to which, however, two things are opposed in particular (1) that on the last day of Passover or unleavened bread it was also permitted to prepare food, and to pluck ears of grain: and that (2) the feast of Scenopegia also had two feast days, whence it is left uncertain which feast is indicated here, or which one is that deuteroproton sabbaton. But the former can be met if it is said that it was not only the last day of Passover, but also an ordinary or weekly Sabbath: but the latter has already been satisfied by the blessed Chemnitius, because the plucking and rubbing of ears of grain does not befit the feast of tabernacles, inasmuch as it falls in the month of September.

Epiphanius explains it a little differently in heresy XXX. Ebion. n. 32. After the day of unleavened bread was made, the day of the Sabbath defined, on the Sabbath by nature, which was counted into the Sabbath after the day of unleavened bread, they were found passing through the sown fields. Casaubon, Petavius, and Bailius take these words of Epiphanius in such a way that he understood the natural Sabbath after the first day of unleavened bread: whence Bailius observes that according to Epiphanius the second-first Sabbath was the first ordinary or weekly Sabbath after the solemnity of Passover, which is called deutero because it is second in time and later than the feast of Passover, but proton because it is prior in dignity to Passover and to every other extraordinary feast. Scaliger, having embraced the same opinion, derives the word from there: because from the Passover, that is, from the 16th day of the month Nisan, on which the offering of the fruits was made, the law commands to count seven weeks Lev. XXIII. 15. Deut. XVI. 9. and thus seven Sabbaths until the feast of Pentecost, whence the first Sabbath from the second of the Passover was called deuteroproton; the second deutero-deuteron, the third deutero-triton, and so on: which explanation others have subsequently embraced, even our blessed Gerhard in Harm. C. CLXVI. p. 1074, and Bailius defends it against Petavius and others in the place cited.

However, the opinion of Scaliger does not please Grotius for two reasons; to which Bailius responds with some things: To the former, that there is no example of such a composition, he replied: Besides the many examples which Scaliger has in Canonib. Isagog., what need is there of any example where the matter is manifest? Grotius does not deny that the masculine deuteros and the neuter deuteron are correctly compounded with protos, what then prevents the feminine deutera from founding a composition with the same? especially since the express command of God to count from the second provides the best foundation for this composition. But from the command of GOD, even if the counting had been instituted from the Passover, it can by no means be deduced that deuteroproton can be compounded from it: not to mention that the noun deuteras is not found in Lev. XXIII. 15. The latter argument of Grotius is that God did not command to count the Sabbaths from the second day of unleavened bread, but only the days, from which Pentecost has its name. Bailius responds that God commands not only the days, but expressly the Sabbaths and weeks to be counted from the second day of unleavened bread in Levit. XXIII. 15. Where, however, it can be countered: it is one thing to count the weeks or the cycle of seven days, which GOD commanded, and another to count the Sabbaths; it is necessary that those (weeks) intervene entirely seven from the feast of Passover to Pentecost, but not likewise seven Sabbaths. For if Passover falls on the sixth day of the week, only six, not seven, Sabbaths will intervene from the second day of Passover to Pentecost. For the seventh Sabbath would coincide with the very day of Pentecost. Nor did Scaliger prove that the Sabbaths intermediate between Passover and Pentecost were so called, second-first, second-third, etc., since he could bring forward no foundation from scripture nor from the writings of the Hebrews.

But perhaps it is not a wonder that Scaliger had many followers, Piscator, Casaubon, Junius, Drusius, Cocceius, Bailius, Calixtus, Frieschmutius, Hackspanius, Erasmus Schmied, Wilh. Lang, Quislorpius, as well as Didac. Stella, Vasquez, Barradius, Petavius, Cœlestinus de monte Mariano, Joseph de Voisin, and Lightfoot, because in other much more serious errors, on account of the authority which he possessed in chronological matters, he had not a few followers, nor those of the lowest rank. Although indeed that Scaligerian etymology of the deuteroproton, and the numbering of the seven Sabbaths exhibited in his list, does not rest on a solid foundation, yet the opinion of Epiphanius, that the Sabbath nearest to the feast of unleavened bread is understood, is not to be immediately rejected. Since another reason for the denomination can be given: namely that the Sabbath is called deuteroproton because it is second in time, inasmuch as it is later than the Sabbath or feast of Passover: but first both in dignity and also in a certain respect of time, namely with respect to the day of the offering of the firstfruits: because the natural Sabbath nearest to that is designated by that word.

The other explanation of Epiphanius does not depart much, indeed it seems to agree with the former, which is held in heresy LI, which is of the alogoi: Where he calls the natural Sabbath the first Sabbath, but the legal one the second, and it can be judged that he called the natural or weekly Sabbath nearest to the legal Sabbath of Passover by the compound word deuteroproton. Nor is the interpretation of the word (we speak of the word, not of the thing signified) unlike this, concerning the weekly Sabbath which immediately preceded a festive Sabbath, inasmuch as when a feast day falls on the preparation of the weekly Sabbath or on Friday, so that the weekly Sabbath follows immediately, and the day of Saturn or the Sabbath is then called the deuteroproton Sabbath, i.e., the second Sabbath with respect to the preceding feast as the prior one, and the first, because this Sabbath is the most principal of the Sabbaths: In which way Theophylact's interpretation holds: The Jews, he says, called every feast a Sabbath. For the Sabbath is rest. Therefore, the feast occurred more often on the Preparation day. And they called the Preparation day the Sabbath on account of the Feast, but they called the principal Sabbath the second-first; because it was second, with another feast and Sabbath preceding it: but first, because as a weekly and ordinary one it surpassed in dignity any extraordinary one. To this is akin the explanation of Chrysostom: What is second-first? When there was a double cessation, both of the principal Sabbath and of the following feast. For he does not place the double cessation on one day: because he makes one that of the τοῦ Σαββάτου τοῦ κυρίου, the principal Sabbath, the other that of ἑτέρας ἑορτῆς διαδεχομένης, of another following feast. Theophylact differs only from Chrysostom: in that the former says the feast is not following, but preceding: and that τὸ δευτερόπρωτον fell upon the natural or weekly Sabbath, but the latter upon the legal Sabbath, or a festive one following the natural Sabbath.

But Cornelius Jansenius, Augustine, Torniellus, Thomas Cartwright with Marianus Victorius, and Lucas Brugensis depart from both, saying that the second-first Sabbath is when a feast day, or Sab- Sabbath, and the weekly Sabbath fall on the same day. But those opinions are primarily opposed by the fact that they render uncertain the day which the Evangelist nevertheless intended to designate with certainty by this term, as the same authors admit: since it could be noted as σάββατον δευτερόπρωτον not only when the feast of Passover coincides with the Sabbath, but also in other cases for that reason. But Luke does not say that this happened on a certain Sabbath δευτερόπρωτῳ, but simply that it happened on the second-first Sabbath. If, however, it is excepted, or proposed, that the Passover feast is understood from the designation of the ears of grain, and thus even if the feast is not precisely expressed by the term δευτερόπρωτυ, yet it is evident from the subject matter, one will not easily render the praise of probability ambiguous for those opinions.

This was the opinion of Isidore of Pelusium, that by the second-first Sabbath one should understand the first day of unleavened bread. He says, Δευτερόπρωτον is called that which was the second of Passover, but the first of unleavened bread. For those sacrificing the Passover in the evening would gather the feast of unleavened bread following, which they also called δευτερόπρωτον, because it was the second of Passover, but the first of unleavened bread. They call this day a Sabbath; because the whole week of Passover was festive, and thus consisted of seven Sabbaths: the first because it was the first of unleavened bread: the second, because it was the second of Passover. Which is also the explanation of Euthymius, and Suidas. Moreover, Bailius notes the oversight (παρόραμα) of Baronius in introducing the opinion of Isidore, l. c. But Isidore does not deserve to be counted. For the first of unleavened bread was not such a feast in which it was not permitted to prepare what pertained to food; for that was permitted on all days of Passover and unleavened bread. Mr. D. Sebast. Schmidius thinks the opinion of Isidore is sufficiently refuted by the fact that he made the first feast day of Passover and the first of unleavened bread different. Since although the Passover was sacrificed on the fourteenth day of the month Nisan, yet this was not the feast day in itself, nor the first of Passover: because the Passover was eaten after sunset, after the night of the fifteenth day began, and the same night was also that of the first feast day of Passover and unleavened bread. But when it is said in Num. XXXIII. 3, from the morrow of the Passover, he says the meaning is that which followed the eating of the Passover, or which followed the Paschal night.

Many overturn the opinion of the blessed Luther, who seems to have followed Stapulensis, even if it is not understood of any feast day, but of the day following the first feast day of Passover, for the same reason: that that day, which followed the first, which was most holy, was not equally holy and celebrated, as they wish it to be called not πρωτόπρωτον, but δευτερόπρωτον, for which reason it was permitted to work on it: whereas on the contrary Luke testifies that that Sabbath, which he designates by this term, was held so holy that the plucking and rubbing of certain ears of grain was considered a great violation of the Sabbath. Yet there is not lacking what can be replied in favor of that explanation of the opinion of the blessed Luther: For if that day following the Paschal Sabbath is said to be the weekly Sabbath, that objection will be null.

Other opinions also occur but newly devised, one of Cloppenburg, another of Capellus, a third of Constant. l'Empereur, the first two of which Bald. Walaus brought forward: but we do not value them so highly that they should be recounted here, much less that we should dwell on refuting them: And our Mr. D. Sebastian Schmidius has sufficiently demolished them, as well as Robert Bailius, whom anyone may consult. We must return to

Who also wishes to indulge himself after so many others in the freedom of judging, as if he had devised something new: but his opinion, that the Sabbath δευτερόπρωτον should be understood of Pentecost, which is the second solemnity after Passover, is not new: For it has already been held by many, as well from the Papists as from the Protestants, which Maldonatus, Cornelius a Lapide, Mercator, Piscator and others have embraced, and it has already been refuted by many: which also S. Chemnitius l. c. demolished, as did Petavius in his animadversions on Epiphanius, heresy XXX. and LI.

Nor indeed is it proven that those three feasts of Passover, Pentecost, and Tabernacles were called πρῶτα, because they were the greatest, much less that the feast of Pentecost was named δευτερόπρωτον, or the feast of Tabernacles τριτοπρωτον. We concede that it is said of the feast of Passover that it is הראשון, which Grotius wishes to prove was also once called πρῶτον by the Greeks from I know not what Πάτρα κηρύγματι: But concerning the other feasts, that they had the name δευτεροπρώτα or τριτοπρώτα, he had nothing to bring forward. Nor can the present history be referred to the feast of Pentecost: both because mention is made here of Sabbaths, when in the feast of Pentecost there was only one Sabbath, and because on the Sabbath δευτερόπρωτῳ it was not permitted to prepare what pertained to food, which was entirely permitted on the feast of Pentecost: whereas it was also permitted on the Passover itself, Ex. XII. 16. and because the context of the history proves that it did not happen around the feast of Pentecost, but of Passover, as B. Chemnitius, Jansenius, and Barradius show, and because in Judea the barley harvest was celebrated around the feast of Passover, after the offering of the fruits or the sheaf of ears was made on the second day of Passover, just as the loaves of the firstfruits of wheat were to be offered on the feast of Pentecost and that was followed by the wheat harvest, which double distinct harvest in Judea is observed by B. Chemnitius from Ruth II. 23, Jer. XXIII. 11, 15, Exod. IX. 31, chap. XXXIV. 22. But that Grotius says that the green ears were offered on the second day of unleavened bread only for the sake of saying so, seems not without reason to Bailius to be said very rashly and profanely: because the offering of the sheaf was very strictly and solemnly enjoined by God, and before it every eating of new fruits was expressly prohibited: but by the testimony of Maimonides, in Ainsworth on Lev. XXIII. 1, those ears were not green, but ripe, from which, when threshed, a gomer of flour had to be offered to GOD on the second day of unleavened bread.

Having thus weighed the various opinions concerning the second-first Sabbath, it appears that most of the others brought forward are not devoid of their probability, but that the Grotian one, above the others hitherto brought forward by us, is to be rejected; for it is entirely evident from history that the Sabbath δευτερόπρωτον fell not around the feast of Pentecost, but of Passover. Whether the Mosaic Sabbath coincides with the natural Sabbath on the same day, or whether the Sabbath immediately or mediately following, or even the final feast day of the Passover is intended, we judge that it does not matter much in Chronology or History: nor is there need that that stricter observance, which the οἱ ἐξ ἐναντίας urged against the disciples of Christ according to the interdict of the law which they themselves pretended, be referred to, since they adhered to that interdict of the law according to their own δευτερώσεις, or Cabala, which they boasted was received from Moses; which is here neither approved nor disapproved by Christ directly, nor is it taught, except at most by examples alone, that the Apostles had not contravened the interdict of the law (understood according to the mind of the legislator). But as for what seems to some, that the accusatory words of the Pharisees are to be taken in such a way that the disciples are doing ὃ ὐκ ἔξεστι, and that moreover ἐν

they do not fear to do on the Sabbaths: but that they wish the ὅ ὐκ ἔξεςι [which is not lawful] concerning the eating of the ears of corn before the offering, which ought to have been done at the feast of the Passover, to be understood, does not stand on a sufficiently firm footing. Indeed, Mr. D. Schmied thinks that nothing prevents the words of the Pharisees from being taken thus: Behold, thy disciples do what it is not yet lawful to do at this time, and indeed, which aggravates the matter, on the Sabbath, and that Christ's defense is sufficiently suited to this accusation, since in it the Lord does not only excuse the violation of the Sabbath by the example of the Priests, but also the eating of a forbidden thing by the example of David Matth. XII. 45. Yet he himself admits in Levit. XXIII. 14. that the discourse is only about the ordinary use of ears of corn in food, when the crops are used to make bread, or to cook porridge, or to prepare roasted grain, which, as he proves from the Chaldean, R. Solomon, and R. Meir, the plucking of ears of corn and rubbing them for eating did not pertain to that culinary use.

Moreover, Mr. D. Schmidius, in the cited dissertation on the δευτεροπρώτῳ [second-first] Sabbath, brings forward a not inappropriate explanation, that by that is understood the second Sabbath in the Ecclesiastical year, which began from the Month of Nisan, so that the first weekly Sabbath was called πρωτόπρωτον [first-first], and the second δευτερόπρωτον [second-first]: because those two Sabbaths, or the two weeks before the Passover, had this peculiarity, that they were called פרס הפסח [half of the Passover], and the second Sabbath of the year could be called by the name of the first, because it was called by the Jews the great Sabbath, and it is so called even in the Calendars of the Jews. Which explanation, as it is much more convenient than the Scaligerian one, learnedly refuted by Mr. D. Schmidius, so we would receive it with a grateful mind, if these things did not stand in the way in our judgment: (1) that it cannot be taught from antiquity that the earlier Sabbaths of the Ecclesiastical year were so called πρωτόπρωτον and δευτερόπρωτον. (2) that that denomination of the great Sabbath is more recent and more obscure than that Luke should have had regard for it. (3) Nor does a reason appear why the second Sabbath in the Ecclesiastical year is called the great Sabbath: whatever may be the case regarding the Rabbinic appellation. (4) If the second Sabbath of the year were being noted, it should have been called δευτεροσάββατον [second-sabbath] rather than δευτερόπρωτον [second-first]. (5) Most interpreters establish that this Sabbath followed, and did not precede, the Passover, from whose almost common opinion it does not seem that one should rashly depart. (6) Nor does it appear why the opinion of Epiphanius should be abandoned, as it is explained before concerning the weekly Sabbath, which followed the Feast of the Passover: with which the opinion of the Blessed Luther is easily reconciled, if it be assumed that the day of the Passover was the weekly Sabbath immediately following the festive Sabbath, because Luke calls it the Sabbath; with which also the explanation of Theophylact agrees, and the interpretation of Ludovicus de Dieu is not much different: And that very thing, he says, I think is called δευτερόπρωτον, because lying between two other Sabbaths, namely the first of the Unleavened Bread and the seventh, it was nearest to the first, and immediately followed it. I say this: the first of the Passover was the πρῶτον Σάββατον [first Sabbath], which then followed the weekly Sabbath, was the δευτερόπρωτον [second-first]. He does indeed add that the seventh day of the feast was then the τρίτον [third] Sabbath. But that is less likely.

That doubt which is raised, that it is too harsh a composition for δευτερόπρωτον to be called second and first; second by reason of order, first by reason of dignity, can also be raised against the opinion concerning the second Passover of the Ecclesiastical year, by which indeed it is called second by reason of time, but is believed to be designated by the name of first by reason of dignity, because it was called the great Sabbath. But these things have been said concerning the δευτεροπρώτῳ [second-first] Sabbath.

Latin:

CAPUT VI. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Discipuli Christi spicas fricantes in Sabbato excusantur, & sanatio manus aridæ in Sabbato defenditur. Duodecim Apostoli eliguntur, & prolixa de beatitudine, ac amore proximi, & misericordia concio habetur, finita parænesi de fructibus bonis, & audiendo Dei verbo.

Partes IV. sunt: I. Discipulorum Christi in Sabbato spicas fricantium defensio, ad vers. 5. II. Manus aridæ in Sabbato sanatio, ejusque apo- logia, ad v. 12. III. Apostolorum XII. electio, & recensio, ad v. 17. IV. Concio Christi ad discipulos habita, ad v. 49.

PARS I. Discipulorum ob spicas fricatas defensio.

Ἐν σαββάτῳ δευτεροπρώτῳ] Facete de hoc loco consulentem se Hieronymum elusit Gregorius Nazianzenus, promittens dictum se ea de re, sed in Ecclesia, ubi Hieronymus, toto populo acclamante, cogeretur scire quod nesciret, aut si solus tacuisset, futurum ut ab omnibus stultitiae condemnaretur: quam rem narrans Hieronymus, hoc ἐπιφώνημα subjicit: Nihil tam facile, quam vilem plebeculam & indoctam concionem linguae volubilitate decipere, quae quicquid non intelligit plus miratur. Quam multi sunt hodie quibus pro eruditione est audax asseveratio, praesertim quoties de loco superiore loquuntur, ubi contradictorem non habent? Caeterum de vocis δευτεροπρώτου interpretatione dici ferine potest, quot capita tot sententiae: Syrus & Arabs, tanto quam nos sumus illi & saeculo & loco propiores, satis manifeste ostendunt se quid haec vox velit ignorasse: quo aequius est aliis ignosci quibus praeter conjecturas nihil est relictum, quas refellere est promtius, quam certi aliquid adferre. Falli eos qui non diem, quem Saturni dicimus, sed festum aliquem diem hic volunt intelligi, ex eo apertum est, quod tota quae hinc orta est disputatio non ad festos dies pertinet, quibus non tam rigide otium servabatur, sed ad diem illum qui proprie ac peculiariter Sabbatum appellatur, quem οἱ ἔξω Saturni vocant. Sed neque eorum sententia recipi potest, qui δευτερόπρωτον ita exponunt, ut nomen sit multis diebus conveniens: cum Lucas hoc nomine usus sit, ut certus anni dies intelligeretur: quibus recte animadversis pleraeque veterum ariolationes concidunt, ut a recentioribus quibusdam prudenter notatum est. Traxit multos in assensum viri magni auctoritas: qui δευτερόπρωτον exponit πρῶτον ἀπὸ τῆς δευτέρας τοῦ πάσχα. Sed ei quominus subscribam apud me haec obstant: Primum quod nullum viderim talis formationis exemplum, quales esset si δευτερόπρωτον deduceretur a voce δευτέρας & voce πρώτου. Deinde quod Lex quae exstat in Levitico, non hoc dicit, sabbata denominari a postridie Paschatis, ut hoc sabbatum dicatur primum, illud secundum, atque ita deinceps, sed dies illos quinquaginta ימים תמימת τὰς ἡμέρας τῆς πεντηκοστῆς numerari ac eodem illo die, ita ut postridie Paschatis, sit dies illorum quinquaginta primus, qui hunc sequitur secundus, atque ita usque ad quinquagesimum, quem numerandi modum Judaei nunc quoque anxie observant: neque tamen in nominandis diebus repetunt nomen illud δευτέρας. Sed quaeque nox ut advenit, solent dicere, hic est dies primus Omer: hic est dies secundus, atque ita porro. Sententia igitur ista, quae magnis argumentis a suo auctore defensa est cum mihi se non probet, ob eas quas dixi causas, indulgebo mihi quoque post tot alios censendi libertatem: Judaei diem Sabbati, qui Pascha proxime antecedit, hodieque vocant שבת הגדול. Sed & si Paschatis dies in ipsum Sabbatum inciderit, appellabatur is dies eodem nomine, ut apparet Joh. XIX. 31. ἦν γὰρ μεγάλη ἡ ἡμέρα ἐκείνη τοῦ σαββάτου. Est & σαββάτου μεγάλου mentio in historia de martyrio Polycarpi apud Eusebium. Alii pro הגדול dixerunt הראשון, id est, τὸ πρῶτον σάββατον. Nam ὠ τῷ Πέτρου κηρύγματι erat: σάββατον ἐκ ἄγουσι τὸ λεγόμενον πρῶτον. Cum vero praeter Pascha duae sint praeterea celerrimae Judaeorum ἑορταὶ, nempe τὸ πλήρωμα τῆς πεντηκοστῆς & σκηνοπηγία, etiam quae eas ἑορτὰς proxime contingebant sabbata, μέγαλα ἢ καὶ πρῶτα vocata simili ratione. Nam & Sabbatum quod incidebat εἰς τὴν σκηνοπηγίαν, Josephus vocat μάλισα θρησκευόμενον σάββατον, Belli Judaici lib. II. c. XXXVII. Atque ita cum tria essent Sabbata πρῶτα, id est maxima, distinctionis causa repertum, ut sabbatum Paschale, quod ordine antegreditur, diceretur πρωτόπρωτον primorum primum, Sabbatum Pentecostes δευτερόπρωτον, primorum secundum, sabbatum σκηνοπηγίας, τριτόπρωτον primorum tertium. Sic in municipiis ubi erant δεκαπρῶτοι primus ordinis dici poterat πρωτόπρωτος, alter δευτερόπρωτος, atque ita deinceps. Notandum autem est messem, ut Hebraei docent, incidisse ferme in mensem Elul, qui partim Junio, partim Julio respondet: itaq; Exodi XXIII. 16. Pentecostes solenne vocatur solenne messis, tabernaculorum autem solenne, quod in finem Augusti, aut initium Septembris incidebat, festum collectarum in horrea frugum. Nam quod postridie Paschatis, δράγμα ταχύων ad altare adferebatur, fiebat id dicis causa ex spicis virentibus quae igne torrebantur, ut Josephus nos docet ex loco Lev. II. 14. unde & mensi Nisan nomen alterum אביב quod spicam virentem significat: & hae ipsae ἀπαρχαὶ fumebantur ex hordeo, fruge temporius se prodente. Vide Josephum. Et haec δευτεροπρώτου formatio ab ἀναλογίας regula non excedit. Adde quod apud

Hellenistas, quorum haud dubie sermonem hic Lucas ex- primit,exstabat vox similis formæ. Nam decimas illas quas Levitæ pendebant sacerdotibus, vocabant δευτεροδεκάτας, id est secundas decimas,ut notat Hieronymus in caput XL. Ezechielis Eædem vocantur δευτέρας δεκάτας Tobiæ I. 6. Sunt ergo idem δευτέρα δεκάτη & δευτεροδεκάτη : item Sab- batum δεύτερον πρῶτον aut δευτερόπρωτον.

ψώχοντες] Fricantes.
