Παρ' ὧν ἐλπίζετε ἀπολαβεῖν] This pertains entirely to that kind of benefit which the Greeks call ἐρανισμὸν, concerning which the most learned Casaubon has noted excellent things in his commentary on Theophrastus. If anyone had lost much property through shipwreck, fire, or some other sad event, friends were accustomed to contribute money to him, not to be paid back on a certain day, but when it was convenient. They were hardly accustomed to provide this, however, except to those who had the hope of emerging from adverse fortune into better: so that at some time they might be able to repay not only the money, but also the turn of the benefit, which was called ἀντερανίζειν. Luke calls ἐρανίζειν by the more common word δανίζειν: and ἀπολαμβάνειν to receive a benefit: as shortly after ἀπολαμβάνειν τὰ ἴσα: just as the Latins say to make things equal, to return like for like.

Latin:

Vers. 34.

Παρ' ὧν ἐλπίζετε ἀπολαβεῖν] Omnino hoc pertinet ad illud beneficii genus quod ἐρανισμὸν Græci vocant, de quo præclara annotavit doctissimus Casaubonus ad Theo- phrastum. Si quis naufragio, incendio, aut alio casu tri- stiore multum rei amisisset, solebant amici pecunias ei contribuere, non ad certum diem solvendas, sed ubi com- modum esset. Id vero præstare vix solebant nisi his quos spes esset ex adversa fortuna in meliorem emersuros: ita ut aliquando possent non pecuniam tantum, sed & bene- ficii vicem rependere, quod vocabatur ἀντερανίζειν. Lu- cas ἐρανίζειν communiore vocabulo δανίζειν vocat: & ἀ- πολαμβάνειν recipere beneficium: ut mox ἀπολαμβάνειν τὰ ἴσα: sicut Latini dicunt paria facere, par pari referre.

## 6:35
Vers. 35.

Μηδὲν ἀπελπίζοντες] The Syriac version reads entirely μηδὲν ἀπολπίζοντες and takes ἀπελπίζειν actively, as it does ἀποτοπατίζειν and other words which the Hellenists form according to the pattern of the Hiphil: but the Greeks also sometimes use ἀπελπίζειν in this way. He therefore thought the sense to be: give a loan to all who ask: [do not] to anyone frustrate the hope which he conceived from your generosity. But the Greek writers and the old Latin interpreter read μηδὲν and interpret ἀπελπίζειν as hoping for something from things, which sense fits this passage very well. For he wishes the opposite to be done of what he had said above. Non-Christian men are accustomed to lend hoping to receive back: Christ commands his own to lend hoping for nothing, that is, hoping for nothing back, expecting no return of the favor. Not far from this is that saying of Plutarch: To lend to the needy, not seeking to acquire some relief for one's own poverty, but giving both a witness and a worthy guarantor, that he has something to be trusted with, he might lend not to be lent to. But indeed, as Lactantius says, that is just, that is pious, that is humane which you have done without hope of receiving. I do not think the question of usury properly belongs here, which nevertheless is accustomed to be treated in this place by most of the ancients: for which reason, and because by consequence the forbidden avarice of usurers ought to be judged here, it will not be irrelevant to discuss a few things on that matter. Moreover, there can be a fourfold question: concerning natural law, concerning the law of Moses, concerning the law of Christ, and concerning the customs of the ancient Christians, which is accustomed to be called Canon law. But about to treat this matter, I will first preface this: that I approve the piety of those who would wish this whole kind of profit-making to be removed from human affairs, since it is most manifest that many evils are born from it, which Plutarch eloquently narrates in a book on this subject: but again I see it happening for the most part that excessive rigor gives occasion for unbridled license. For when men see that what is stretched too far is not proven by sufficiently firm reasons, having lapsed into the opposite, they indulge themselves without end or measure. Wherefore there is nothing safer than to bind precepts to the limits of either right reason or divine oracles: thus it will happen that neither are forbidden things condoned, and those things which are not forbidden are, if need be, dissuaded rather than forbidden. To begin from the law of nature: many, to prove that every gain from the use of money or a similar thing granted to another is illicit, say that money by its nature is sterile: but in this argument there is a manifest fallacy. For money is said to be sterile by nature, not because the law of nature commands it, but because human industry, not nature itself, gave origin to such fruit: just as a house is sterile by nature, whose rent, however, no one would say is unjustly received by the landlord. Others urge that point, that ownership is transferred in a loan: but the fruit of the thing ought to remain with the owner. But in this way also, the subtlety of words does nothing for natural equity. For in things which receive function by their kind, such as money, grain, wine, that right to receive the same in kind is in place of ownership. But all admit that he receives more who receives something immediately than he who receives it after a long time, on account of those utilities which natural possession brings with it, which proceeds no less in a loan than in a thing lent for use, if we look at the moments of the thing and not the niceties of words. This very thing, however, which is situated in the delay of time, can undoubtedly be valued and therefore also be brought into a stipulation. For if I lend a hundred to someone, and I agree that he should give me back a hundred at another time, which is a true exchange, how will this agreement be proven to be more unjust than if I had lent an ox to a neighbor for farm work, on the condition that he provide me the same amount sometime later? Now indeed, that obligation of giving a loan in return, like all things, can be valued by a common measure, that is, money. Nature dictates that no one is bound to benefit another to his own detriment. But he who lacks money for a time for the sake of another could have spent it on fields or houses and received the fruits of the intervening time, which if anyone says are uncertain, that very uncertainty, like every gamble, has its own price, so that it is also accustomed to be sold. Again, if he is considered wealthier to whom the usufruct of money is bequeathed without ownership, it is apparent that this use itself is something that receives a valuation: and the same therefore must be said about annual use. I see that most of those who condemn stipulations of usury do not disapprove of usury from delay: and therefore it is conceded that, if the loan is not returned on the appointed day, I may stipulate for usury. But what is this other than to fix laws with words, not with business? For it will be permitted, if that opinion is accepted, to agree thus: if you do not return it within three days, you will pay so much for the delay; but if mention of that three days is omitted, the agreement will be illicit. This subtlety in the Schools has evasions of words by which it protects itself; when it is applied to business, only then does its emptiness appear. Wherefore it must be held that, with nature not opposing, he who lacks the use of money for the sake of another can, in turn, agree to something on that account. But so that it may be known how much equity itself permits, one must not look, as some think, at how much profit he makes who took the money, but how much is absent from him who counted out the money to the other: just as in buying and in other contracts, the valuation must never be made from that which is the interest of the receiver, but from that which is absent from the giver. But there is absent as much as each person can and is accustomed to save from money according to his way of life: for example, from fields, from houses, from trade, having subtracted the valuation of the risk, which in other things is greater, in others less, just as is accustomed to be done among merchants in a contract of averted risk, which they call insurance. I come to that law which God gave to the Hebrew people. The law of Deuteronomy is conceived thus in chapter XXIII, v. 19: You shall not lend at interest to your brother, interest of money, interest of food, interest of any thing that is lent at interest. You shall lend at interest to a foreigner: but to your brother you shall not lend at interest. Here, those who think all usury is contrary to natural law want what is said about lending to a stranger to be a permission of fact, not of law: which neither the words admit, nor has it ever been understood in that way by that people to whom the law was given. I will bring as witnesses Josephus and Philo, with whom all the Rabbis agree. These are the words of Josephus from Antiquities IV: 'Let it be permitted to no one of the Hebrews to lend at interest, neither food nor drink, for it is not right to profit from the misfortunes of those of the same race, but rather, having helped their needs, to consider as profit both their thanks and the reward that will come from God for kindness.' Philo, in his book On Philanthropy, explains this law thus: 'He forbids, therefore, lending to a brother, calling a brother not only him who is born of the same parents, but also whoever is a fellow citizen or of the same race.' And shortly after: 'But if one is not able to give, let him at least lend most readily and most eagerly, intending to receive back nothing beyond the principal. For thus neither would the poor be likely to become most destitute, being forced to pay back more than they received, nor would those who contributed be likely to be wronged, [but rather they would gain] kindness, magnanimity, good reputation, and glory, the possession of which is worth striving for.' Clement of Alexandria, in his Stromata, translated this passage of Philo for his own uses in such a way that he interprets it at the same time. II. Where he speaks thus: 'The law forbids lending to a brother, calling a brother not only him who is born of the same parents, but also whoever is of the same race and of the same mind and shares in the same reason. It is not right to exact interest on money, but rather to give to those in need with open hands and minds. For God the Creator is the author of such thanks. And the generous man receives a notable interest, the most precious things among men: gentleness, kindness, magnanimity, good reputation, and glory.' From this it appears, if I am not mistaken, that that law of Deuteronomy is understood regarding the duty of citizens toward citizens: which the words of Leviticus also indicate; for there too usury is forbidden with this added reason, that your brother may live with you, chapter XXV. 36. Wherefore, also, when in the Psalms and in the writings of Ezekiel he who has abstained from practicing usury is praised, that is to be understood according to the prescription of the law. Ambrose and certain others who followed him think that the foreigners are to be understood as those seven nations against whom the Hebrews had a just war; nor does he think it a wonder if it was permitted to practice usury against those whom it was permitted to kill. But not even this interpretation agrees with the words of the law; for since foreigners are opposed to brothers, that is, to citizens, it is certain that not these or those, but all are meant. Add that it was by no means consistent with the gravity of the law to permit usury against those whom it was necessary to destroy completely. The reason for the distinction, therefore, was that God did not want for the Hebrews among themselves only those precepts which are common to all men among themselves, and which are owed by a strict interpretation of the law, but also many duties of a certain closer necessity and charity, as can be seen in the law concerning servants, pledges, gleaning, and many other things. It is added that the most important livelihood of the Hebrew people lay in agriculture and livestock. Josephus, in the first book Against Apion: 'We, therefore, neither inhabit a maritime region nor do we delight in commerce, nor in the associations with others through these things; but our cities are situated far from the sea, and, occupying good land, we cultivate it.' Wherefore, since most of the neighbors of the Jews made great profit from trade, such as the Sidonians, Tyrians, the dwellers by the Red Sea, and the Egyptians, the permission of usury against them, and the non-permission against Hebrew farmers and shepherds, had the highest reason. For in the laws of other peoples, too, usury which is practiced against farmers is most hateful. But that law of Moses, since it looks specifically at the state of that people and was given to one people, does not bind others, except insofar as it offers some indication of natural equity. What Christ wants us to do, since a specific precept about this matter does not exist, must be drawn from general precepts. When every covetousness is forbidden, there is no doubt that equality in transactions is required of us. Wherefore, just as by this law it is not permitted even to sell one's own thing except at a fair price, so neither is it permitted to bargain for more for the use of money than what is needed to compensate for our loss. But the rule of charity requires more; for if money is to be given as a loan to the needy, with no hope of compensation, it must certainly be given without usury, since otherwise it would not be a benefit, but a bane. rather. For the ancients did not wrongly call interest the poison of one's patrimony. Lactantius, Book IV, expresses this sense thus: If he has lent money, let him not accept interest: so that the benefit may be intact which provides for necessity, and he may abstain entirely from what is another's. For in this kind of duty he ought to be content with his own, he who ought not even to spare his own property to do good: but to receive more than he gave is unjust. Thus also Tertullian shows that the Hebrew law was a certain rudiment for those things which are to be performed by Christians. Book IV against Marcion: It was therefore first necessary to eradicate the fruit of interest, so as to accustom man more easily to the interest itself, if by chance, by losing it, he had learned to lose the fruit. For this was the divine work of the law preparing for the Gospel. It was then gradually informing the faith of some, still stammering at every first precept, to the perfect brightness of Christian discipline and kindness. But this caution does not pertain to those who use another's money for the sake of making greater profit. In the ancient Canons I find no one who indiscriminately removes all who practice usury from communion, which was done in later centuries. Only to those who were conspicuous in the Church by some office, whom they call τοὺς ἐν κανόνι, is that profit forbidden by the Apostolic canon, as they call it, XLIV, Laodicean IV, Nicene XVII, African V and XVI. The reason seems to have been that those who were in the sacred order ought to be free not only from every crime, but also from the suspicion of avarice. For thus the African fathers speak in the said Canon: τὸ ἐν λαϊκοῖς ἐπιλήψιμον, πολλῷ μᾶλλον ἐν κληρικοῖς ὀφείλει καταδικάζεσθαι, where ἐπιλήψιμον is that which is wont to be reprehended, τὸ ἐπίμεμπτον. Moreover, in the said canon XVI, it is forbidden at the same time as usury for bishops, presbyters, and deacons to undertake the management of others' affairs, or to provide patronage for the causes of others, with the added reason that it does not befit those who have given their name to the sacred warfare to be entangled in worldly affairs. Nor indeed does Hermenopulus bring forward any other cause. For when he had said τὸν ἱερωμένον τόκους ἢ συγχωρητῶς λαμβάνειν, and had cited the said canons, he adds: πῶς γὰρ ὃς ὧδε πράγματα ἔχειν συγχωρεῖται ἢ βιωτικοῖς κἀ ἐκ ἐκκλησιαστικοῖς (this negation is wrongly omitted in the Vulgate codices) ἐνσχολείσθαι. Leo, the first of the Emperors, as the same Hermenopulus notes, thinking all usury forbidden to a Christian, sanctioned the same by a common law: whereas before, the churches themselves were accustomed to take money at three percent interest. If anyone thinks those ancient Canons should be restored, I will not object. For it is right that those from whom others seek an example of living should live according to a more exact standard. As for the others, first they ought to take care not to exact more than is fair in the name of interest, which, because it is not placed ἐν στιγμῇ, but has some πλάτος according to the diversity of regions and peoples, must be defined by civil laws: yet in such a way that the pious remember that one must often stop short of what the laws permit. For laws connive at many things because corrupt morals do not bear a remedy: Then also, within this measure of equality, usury is not to be practiced against the needy, or those who it is credible have fallen into poverty through usury. For to such, money must either be denied if they have no need of it, or given if we are able, but certainly one must take care not to abuse the misery or imprudence of others for profit.

Dievius observes that the phrase μηδὲν ἀπελπίζοντες can be similarly explained, as the Syriac version has it, hoping for nothing from anyone, τῷ πλησίῳ neighbor, ἐπὶ τὸν πλησίον: since ἀπελπίζειν is sometimes to cause to despair, to take away hope from someone: yet Salmasius's interpretation is to be preferred, which is confirmed by the ἀντίθεσις of those who give nothing as a loan except with the hope that they will receive τὰ ἴσα: so that μηδὲν ἀπελπίζοντες is μηδὲν ἐλπίζοντες ἀπ' αὐτῶν: and hoping for nothing from him to whom you have given a loan. Which is also Casaubon's explanation. Therefore, the law does not deal with an official loan, in which τὰ ἴσα are returned at a set time; but with a loan, so to speak, of alms, in which something is given to the poor so that nothing at all returns to him who spends the money. For to them, by the law of charity, alms are owed, and therefore it is to be given to them in such a way that nothing at all is hoped for from it. See B. Gerhard on the Magistrate, n. 251. The question of usury therefore does not properly pertain here: about which Grotius discourses learnedly in this place from natural law, the law of Moses, the law of Christ, and the customs of the ancient Christians or Canon law, because the avarice of usurers is forbidden here by consequence. Yet some things occur about which one must be warned. Concerning the law of nature, it is rightly taught that not every profit from the use of money or a similar thing granted to another is illicit: But as regards the law of Moses, Deut. XXIII, v. 19: You shall not lend at interest to your brother, interest of money, interest of food, interest of anything that is lent, to a foreigner you may lend: but to your brother you shall not lend, the hand rightly explains it, as if any stranger were indicated by the same, if indeed only usury from the Canaanites conquered for destruction was permitted, as Ambrose rightly says in his book On Tobias, ch. XV, where there is the right of war, there also is the right of usury: On which see B. Aegidius Hunnius on 2 Corinthians VIII. That God granted this to the Israelites, so that they might transfer to themselves those possessions which had otherwise been decreed to them, by this intervening means from the Canaanites as unjust enemies and possessors, which matter today can neither be drawn into an example, nor ought to be, because of the reason of diversity. Nor is that to be approved, which explains that law as concerning any profit and gain, so much so that it judges even annual monetary censuses approved by civil laws to be contrary to this law: since the Mosaic law deals only with usury properly so called, which fights against the law of charity, with biting and gnawing usury, as the Hebrew word נשך, from which the serpent has its name, implies. And therefore it deals indeed with a true loan, which by its nature is gratuitous, but it is owed to the needy: who are bitten, gnawed, and consumed by usury, Micah III, v. 2. And therefore Lev. XXV, v. 35 is held: if your brother has been weakened: Cf. Exod. XXII, verse 25. Since, however, Grotius acknowledges that it does not conflict with the law of nature if a moderate interest is taken for the use of money from those who can profit by it, how can that be considered simply forbidden by divine law among the Jewish people, which is not illicit by the law of nature?

Furthermore, it must by no means be conceded that the Mosaic prohibition of usury pertained only to forensic laws: because its observance pertains to all, Ps. 15:5, Ezek. 18:8, and usury conflicts with the very law of charity: and therefore, just as the opinion of Socinus is deservedly rejected by our people, who in Epist. 4 to Morf. in Vol. Epistol. p. 503, maintains that usury is prohibited in the New Testament; so neither should it be conceded to Grotius that it is not clear what Christ wishes us to do, but that it must be drawn from general precepts. For Christ did not bring a new law, but recalled us to the Mosaic law and purged it of corruptions. Nor does the rule of charity require more in the New Testament, as Grotius thinks. For the same rule of charity flourished in the Old Testament also: that money must be given as a loan to the needy with no hope of compensation, and therefore also without usury, Lev. 25:35. In vain, therefore, does he say with Tertullian that the law of the Hebrews was a certain rudiment for those things which are to be performed by Christians, from book 4 against Marcion: because Christ came not for the sake of perfecting the law, but of fulfilling it in our place, nor is any perfection of the Mosaic constitutions detected in this law in the New Testament.

Finally, as regards Canon law: Grotius acknowledges that in the ancient Canons no one is found who indiscriminately removes all who practice usury from communion, which was done in later centuries, but that this gain is forbidden to those who were conspicuous in some office in the Church by the Apostolic Canon, as they call it, 44, Laodicean 4, Nicene 17, African 5 and 16, which seems to be understood only in a certain respect, namely, if it was done not for the sake of necessary sustenance, but out of avarice. As for the rest, regarding the constitution of Emperor Leo, whom he says was the first to sanction it by common law, as Hermenopulus notes, because he thought all usury was forbidden to Christians, when previously the churches themselves were accustomed to take money at one-third interest, the opinion of Grotius is not to be disapproved, that not all interest is prohibited, or ought to be prohibited: care must be taken, however, that under the name of interest more than is fair is not exacted, nor should a loan be practiced upon the needy, or those whom it is credible have fallen into poverty through a loan. καὶ ἔσαι ὁ μισθὸς ὑμῶν πολὺς.] Confer the things we have cited from Josephus & Philo. Abraham, when he had liberally testified to his beneficence toward the King & citizens of Sodom, heard from God, I am thy exceeding great reward, Gen. XVI. 1. Vers. 36. καθὼς κὶ ὁ πατὴρ ὑμῶν οἰκτίρμων ἐσί.] The Talmudists, Chaldeans & Arabs call God by a name as if it were his own רחמן, that is, οἰκτίρμονα. And that this very sentiment was worn by the usage of the people (as many others which Christ uses as indubitable) is apparent from the Talmudic Pandect. It must be known, however, that words signifying mercy among the Hebrews & Hellenists are extended to every kind of beneficence: as Gen. XX. 13. & elsewhere. See the things [written] on Matthew. Vers. 37. κὶ ἀπολύετε κὶ ἀπολυθήσεσθε] Just as καταδικάζειν is to take the doubtful deeds of others in the worse part, so I think ἀπολύειν here is to consider and interpret all things as favorably and kindly as possible: which the Latins, even when it concerns private matters, call to absolve. Thus Josephus said ἀπολύειν τὰς διαβολὰς to wash away calumnies, XVI. of the Origins, c. XII. Vers. 38. (ςεσαλευμένον] Ἀγγεῖα σαττόμενα in Aristotle Probl. Sect. XXI. Δώσουσιν] To be interpreted impersonally, that is, a just measure, pressed down, shaken together, running over shall be given to you. τῷ γὰρ αὐτῷ μέτρῳ ὧ μετρεῖτε ἀντιμετρηθήσεται ὑμῖν] That is, as Hesiod speaks, αὐτῷ τῷ μέτρῳ κί λώϊον: so that the measure is the same in kind, but exuberant. The sense is, that God will treat those who are kind & merciful, kindly & mercifully. Vers. 39. εἶπε δὲ παραβολὴν αὐτοῖς] I think it is labor in vain to seek a connection of this passage with the prior or subsequent ones. For Luke, when he had recited many of Christ's sayings, thought these also, although perhaps pronounced at another time & occasion, should be referred here. This εἶπε δὲ παραβολὴν αὐτοῖς is therefore such as that κὶ τόδε Φωκυλίδεω. Moreover, εἶπε is to be answered by the Hebrew אמר, which the Hebrews use of noble teachers when they wish to signify that some sentiment either flowed from that author, or at least was frequent in his mouth. It is not to be thought with Grotius that these do not cohere with the preceding, but that diverse sentiments said at another time & occasion are patched together. For since it is confessed that the same mountain sermon is described by Luke which was proposed by Matthew, & it is evident from Matt. VII. that Christ exhorted [his hearers] to beware of False Prophets, such as the Pharisees were especially at that time: this proverb, squaring generally with all hypocrites, especially those who judge others but do not examine themselves, nevertheless specifically looks to the Pharisees; as they were such hypocrites, and by their rash judgments were seducing others: whom he also called blind guides elsewhere by a similar reason & proverb, Matt. XV. 14. just as in this place from v. 49 compared with Matt. VII. 14. seqq. it is clear that that general rule about the bad tree was handed down for the sake of the Pharisees and similar False Prophets: which a similar passage, Matt. XII. 33., also confirms. Nor is the connection of these sentiments obscure: because such rash hypocritical judges judge and correct others, while they themselves are blind, nor do they recognize their own vices or the beam in their own eyes: they want others to be perfect, whom they instruct, and they dare to reform, when they themselves are not perfect, not thinking that a disciple is not above his Master, nor is that required, but it suffices if the disciple makes things equal to the master: by which the Pharisees & Scribes are wittily noted, who boasted themselves to be guides of the ignorant, and claimed for themselves the key of scripture, and superciliously despised others before them, when they themselves were blinder than a mole in divine matters: by whom the simpler folk were most wickedly seduced. For although this sentiment, a disciple is not above his Master, is taken elsewhere to mean that followers are perhaps in no better condition than he whom they follow, here, however, it is not the lot that is looked to, as Grotius wants, but erudition or perfection, as the word κατηρτισμένος teaches, and the connection of the context convinces.

Latin:

Vers. 35.

Μηδὲν ἀπελπίζοντες] Legit omnino Syrus μηδὲν ἀπολπίζοντες & ἀπελπίζειν sumit active ut ἀποτοπατίζειν atque alia quæ ad formam Hiphil fingunt Hellenistæ: Sed & Græci interdum ἀπελπίζειν ita usurpant. Sensum igitur esse exi- stimavit: omnibus petentibus date mutuum: neminem frustrantes spe ea, quam de vestra beneficentia concepit. At Græci scriptores & Latinus interpres vetus legunt μη- δὲν & ἀπελπίζειν interpretantur ἀπὸ τῶν πράγματων τι ἐλ- πίζειν, qui sensus optime huic loco congruit. Vult enim contrarium fieri ejus quod supra dixerat. Homines non Christiani solent δανείζειν ἐλπίζοντες ἀπολαβεῖν: Suis præci- pit Christus δανείζειν μηδὲν ἀπελπίζοντας, id est, μηδὲν ἐλ- πίζοντας ἀπολαβεῖν, nullam exspectantes vicem beneficii. Non longe hinc abit Plutarchi illud: Τοῖς ἀπόροις ὢ δανεί- ζειν ζητῶν, ἀλλὰ ἐκλυόμενοις ἀπορίαν τινα ἑαυτοῖς κτᾶσθαι καὶ μάρ- τυρα δίδωσι καὶ βεβαιωτὴν ἄξιον, ὅτι ἐχεὶ πιστεύεσθαι, δανείζοιτο μὴ δανείζεσθαι. At vero, ut ait Lactantius, id juste, id pie, id humane sit quod sine speresipiendi feceris. Non arbitror proprie huc pertinere quæstionem fœnebrem quæ ta- men in hunc locum à plerisque veterum tractari solet: qua de causa, & quia per consequentiam censeri hic debet vetita avaritia fœneratorum, non alienum erit pauca ea de re differere. Potest autem quadruplex esse quæstio, de jure naturali, de lege Mosis, de lege Christi, de mori- bus veterum Christianorun quod jus Canonicum dici solet. Sed hac de re acturus illud primum præfabor, probare me eorum pietatem qui totum hoc lucrandi ge- nus sublatum vellent è rebus humanis, quando multa inde mala nasci manifestissimum est, quæ facunde enar- rat in istius argumenti libro Plutarchus: sed rursum vi- deo fieri plerumque ut nimius rigor occasionem det ef- fræni licentiæ. Nam cum vident homines non satis fir- mis rationibus probari id quod nimium tenditur, in con- trarium lapsi sine fine modoque sibi indulgent. Quare nihil est tutius quam præcepta adstringere aut rectæ ra- tionis aut divinorum oraculorum finibus: ita fiet ut nec vetita condonentur, & quæ vetita non sunt, si opus est, dissuadeantur potius quam vetentur. Ut à jure naturæ incipiam: multi ut probent illicitum esse omnem quæ- stum ex usu pecuniæ aut rei similis alteri concesso, di- cunt pecuniam natura sua esse sterilem: sed in hoc argu- mento manifestus est παραλογισμός. Dicitur enim pecu- nia sterilis natura, non quod jus naturæ id præcipiat, sed quod hominum industria non ipsa natura tali fructui o- riginem dederit: quomodo & domus natura est steri- lis, cujus tamen pensiones inique à Domino percipi nemo dixerit. Alii illud urgent, mutuo transferri do- minium: fructum autem rei penes Dominum esse debe- re. Sed ita quoque subtilitas vocum ad æquitatem na- turalem nihil facit. Nam in rebus quæ genere recipiunt functionem, ut pecunia, frumentum, vinum, jus illud ad recipiendum idem genere est vice dominii. Faten- tur autem omnes plus eum recipere qui statim aliquid re- cipit quam qui multo post tempore, ob utilitates eas quam secum fert ἡ φυσικὴ κατοχὴ, quod non minus in mutuo quam in re commodata procedit, si rei momenta non verborum apices spectamus. Hœc ipsum autem, quod in temporis mora situm est, haud dubie æstimari ac pro- inde & in stipulationem deduci potest. Nam si cui dem mutua centum, & paciscar ut alio tempore mihi det itidem centum mutua, quæ est vera ἀνταλλαγὴ, quo- modo iniqua probabitur magis esse hæc pactio quam si bovem vicino ad opus ruris commosem, ea lege ut idem aliquando post mihi tantundem præstet? Jam ve- ro illa iterum mutuum dandi obligatio, ut res omnes, communi mensura, id est, pecunia æstimari potest. Dictat natura non teneri quenquam prodesse alteri cum detrimento suo. At is qui pecunia ad tempus caret in gratiam alterius, poterat eam in agros aut domos im- pendere ac medii temporis percipere fructus, quos si quis dicat incertos, illud ipsum tamen incertum, ut omnis alea, suum habet pretium, ita ut vendi quoque soleat. Rursum si locupletior censetur, cui sine proprie- tate legatus est pecuniæ ususfructus, apparet hunc ipsum usum aliquid esse quod æstimationem recipiat: atque idem proinde de annuo usu dicendum est. Video à plerisque eorum qui usurarum stipulationes damnant, usuras ex mora non improbare: ac proinde concedi, ut, ni præfinito die mutuum reddatur, usuram stipu- ler. Hoc autem quid est aliud quam verbis non nego- tiis leges figere? Licebit enim, si ea sententia recipitur, ita pacisci, ni intra triduum reddas solves tantum pro mora; quod si tridui illius omissa sit mentio pactio erit illicita. Hæc subtilitas in Scholis habet verborum effu- gia quibus se tueatur, negotiis cum aptatur tum de- mum ejus inanitas apparet. Quare ita habendum est, posse non repugnante natura eum qui pecuniæ usu in gratiam alterius careat, vicissim aliquid eo nomine pacisci. Ut autem sciatur quantum reipsi æquitas permittat, non est spectandum, ut quidam censent, quantum lucri fa- ciat qui pecuniam sumsit, sed quantum ei absit alteri pecuniam numeravit: sicut in emptione quoque & in aliis contractibus nunquam æstimatio facienda est ex eo quod intersit accipientis, sed ex eo quod absit danti. Ab- est autem tantum, quantum quisque pro vitæ suæ gene- re ex pecunia compendifacere potest ac solet: puta ex agris, ex domibus, ex mercatura, detracta æstimatione periculi, quod in aliis rebus majus, in aliis minus est, ita ut fieri inter mercatores solet in contractu aversi periculi, quem assecurationis vocant. Venio ad jus illud quod Deus Hebræo populo dedit. Lex Deuter. ita concepta est cap. XXIII. v. 19. Non fænerabis fratri tuo in usuram pecuniæ, in usuram cibi, in usuram rei ullius fænerabilis. Alienigenæ fænerabis: fratri autem tuo non fænerabis. Hic qui omnem usuram juri naturali contrariam putant, quod de extraneo fænerando dicitur, permissionen esse vo- lunt facti, non juris: quod neque verba admittunt, ne- que unquam ita intellectum est ab eo populo cui lex fe- rebatur. Testes adducam Josephum & Philonem, qui- bus consentiunt Rabbini omnes. Josephi hæc sunt verba Originum IV. Δανείζειν δὲ Ἑβραίων ἐπὶ τόκοις ἐξέστω μηδενὶ, μηδὲ βρωτὸν, μήτε ποτὸν, ἐ γὰρ δίκαιον προσοδεύεσθαι τὰς ὁμοφύλως τὰς τύχας, ἀλλὰ βοηθήσαντα ταῖς χρείαις αὐτῶν, κέρδος εἶναι νομίζειν τὴν τ᾽ ἐκείνων εὐχαριστίαν καὶ τὴν ἀμοιβὴν τὴν παρὰ τῦ Θεῦ γενησομένην ἐπὶ χρηστότητι. Philo libro περὶ φιλανθρωπίας ita hanc legem explicat: ἀπαγο- ρεύει τοίνυν ἀδελφῷ δανείζειν, ἀδελφὸν ὀνομάζων, ἐ μόνον τὸν ἐκ τῶν αὐτῶν φύντα γονέων, ἀλλὰ κᾂ ὃς ἂν ἀςὸς ᾖ ὁμόφυλος ᾖ. Et mox: εἰ δὲ κῂ μὴ εὔκολο δωρεῖσθαι, κιχράτω γῶν ἑτοι- μότατα καὶ προθυμότατα, μηδὲν ἔξω τῶν ἀρχαίων ἀποληψομέ- νος. ὅτω γὰρ ὕθ᾽ ἁ πένητες ἔμελλον ἀπορώτατοι γίνεσθ, πλείονα ὧν ἔλαβον, εἰσφέρειν ἀναγκαζόμενοι, ὕθ᾽ οἱ συμβαλόντες ἀδι- κεῖσθαι, χρηστότητα, μεγαλόνοιαν, εὐφημία, ἔυκλειαν, ὧν κτῆσις ἐφάμιλλος. Quem Philonis locum ita in suos usus transtulit, ut simul interpretetur Clemens Alexandrinus strom. II. ubi ita loquitur: ὁ νόμος ἀπαγορεύει ἀδελφῷ δα- νείζειν. ἀδελφὸν ὀνομάζων, ἐ μόνον τὸν ἐκ τῶν αὐτῶν φύντα γο- νέων, ἀλλὰ καὶ ὃς ἂν ὁμόφυλος ᾖ ὁμογνώμων τε κᾂ τῷ αὐτῷ λό- γῳ κεκοινωνικώς· ἐ δίκαιον, ἐκλέγειν τόκους ἐπὶ χρήμασιν ἀλλ᾿ ἀνειμέναις χερσὶ καὶ γνώμαις χαρίζεσθαι τοῖς δεομένοις. Θεὸς γὰρ ὁ κτίστης τοιάσδε χάριτος. ἤδη δὲ ὁ μεταδοτικὸς καὶ τόκος ἀξιολόγες ἀπολαμβάνῃ, τὰ τιμιώτατα τῶν ἐν ἀνθρώ- ποις ἡμερότητα, χρηστότητα, μεγαλονοίαν, ἐυφημίαν, ἔυ- κλειαν. Satis hinc, ni fallor, apparet legem illam Deute- ronomii intellectam de officio civium erga cives: quod & Levitici verba indicant: nam & ibi fœnus vetatur hac addita ratione, ut tecum vivat frater tuus, cap. XXV. 36. Quare & cum in Psalmis & apud Ezechielem laudatur qui ab exercendo fœnore abstinuit, id intelligendum est ex legis præscripto. Ambrosius & quidam eum secuti, alie- nigenas intelligendos putant septem illos populos, in quos Hebræis justum bellum erat: nec mirum putat, si fœnerari eis licuerit, quos licuerit occidere. Sed ne hæc quidem interpretatio verbis legis congruit: nam cum fra- tribus, id est civibus, opponuntur extranei, certum est non hos aut illos, sed omnes intelligi. Adde quod legis gravitati neutiquam conveniebat permittere in eos fœnus quos plane interfici oportebat. Causa igitur discrimi- nis hæc fuit, quod Deus Hebræis inter se non ea tan- tum præcepta vellet, quæ sunt hominibus omnibus inter se communia, & quæ stricta juris ratione debentur, sed multa etiam propioris cujusdam necessitudinis ac carita- tis officia, ut in lege de servis, pignoribus, de spicilegio, a- liisque multis videre est. Accedit quod potissimus He- bræi populi quæstus in agricultura & re pecuaria situs erat. Josephus primo contra Appionem: ἡμεῖς τοίνυν ὕτε χώ- ραν οἰκῶμεν παράλιον ὕτ᾿ ἐμπορίαις χαίρομεν, ὐδὲ ταῖς πρὸς ἄλλως διὰ τύτων ἐπιμιξίαις· ἀλλ᾿ εἰσὶν μεν ἡμῶν αἱ πόλεις μακρὰν ἀπὸ θαλάσσης ἀπῳκισμέναι, χώρῃ δὲ ἀγαθῆ νε- μόμενοι ταύτην ἐκπονῦμεν. Quare cum finitimi plerique Judæorum ex mercatura magnum quæstum facerent, ut Sydonii, Tyrii, accolæ maris rubri, & Ægyptii, fœ- nus in illos permitti, in Hebræos agricolas & pastores non permitti summam habebat rationem. Nam & alio- rum populorum legibus odiosissimum est fœnus quod in agricolas exercetur. Sed lex ista Mosis, cum illius popu- li statum peculiariter spectet, unique populo sit data, cæ- teros non obstringit, nisi quatenus indicium aliquod præbet naturali æquitati. Quid nos Christus facere ve- lit, cum peculiare de hac re præceptum non exstet, ex præceptis generalibus hauriendum est. Cum vetatur o- mne πλεονέκτημα, dubium non est, quin exigatur à no- bis ἡ ἐν τοῖς συναλλάγμασιν ἰσότης. Quare sicut ex hac le- ge ne vendere quidem rem suam licet, nisi æquo pre- tio, ita nec pro pecuniæ usu plus pacisci, quam quo de- trimentum nostrum sarciatur. At caritatis regula plus ex- igit: nam si egenti danda est pecunia mutua, nulla spe compensationis, sane danda etiam est sine usura cum alioqui non beneficium sit futurum, sed veneficium potius. Non male enim veteres fœnus venenum patrimo- nii vocabant. Hunc sensum Lactantius lib. IV. sic expri- mit: Pecunia, si quam crediderit, non accipiat usuram: ut & beneficium sit incolume quod succurrat necessitati, & abstineat se prorsus alieno. In hoc enim officii genere debet sua esse conten- tus, quem oporteat alias ne proprie quidem parcere ut bonum faciat: plus autem accipere quam dederit injustum est. Sic & Tertullianus legem Hebræam ostendit fuisse rudimentum quoddam ad ea quæ à Christianis præstanda sunt. Libro IV. adversus Marcionem: Prius ergo fuit ut fructum fœno- ris eradicaret, quo facilius assuefaceret hominem ipsi quoque fœnori, si forte, perdendo, cujus fructum didicisset amittere. Hanc etenim divinus operam legis fuisse procurantis Evangelio. Quorundam tunc fidem paulatim ad perfectum disciplinæ Christianæ nitorem, primis quibusque præceptis balbutientis ad- huc benignitatis informabat. Sed hæc cautio ad eos qui quæ- stus majoris faciendi causa pecunia aliena utuntur non per- tinet. In antiquis Canonibus nullum invenio qui fœnus exercenres omnes promiscue à communione submoveat, quod factum est posterioribus sæculis. Solis his, qui in Ec- clesia munere aliquo conspicui erant, quos dicunt τοὺς ἐν κανόνι, is quæstus interdicitur canone Apostolico, ut vo- cant, XLIV. Laodiceno IV. Niceno XVII. Africano V. & XVI. Causa fuisse videtur, quod hi qui in sacro erant ordine, non tantum crimine omni, sed & suspicione avaritiæ vaca- re deberent. Ita enim loquuntur Afri patres dicto Canone: τὸ ἐν λαϊκοῖς ἐπιλήψιμον, πολλῷ μᾶλλον ἐν κληρικοῖς ὀφείλει καταδικάζεσθαι, ubi ἐπιλήψιμον est id, quod reprehendi solet, τὸ ἐπίμεμπτον. Quin dicto canone XVI. simul cum fœnore prohibetur episcopis, presbyteris, diaconis, procurationem rerum alienarum suscipere, aut aliorum causis patrocinium præstare, addita ratione quod non deceat eos qui sacræ mi- litiæ nomen dederint sæculi rebus implicari. Neque sane aliam causam affert Hermenopulus. Nam cum dixisset τὸν ἱερωμένον τόκους ἢ συγχωρητῶς λαμβάνειν, & dictos canones ci- tasset, addit: πῶς γὰρ ὃς ὧδε πράγματα ἔχειν συγχωρεῖται ἢ βιωτικοῖς κἀ ἐκ ἐκκλησιαστικοῖς (male in Vulgatis codicibus negatio hæc omittitur) ἐνσχολείσθαι. Primus Imperatorum Leo, ut idem Hermenopulus notat, existimans omne fœnus Christiano interdictum, lege id ipsum communi sanxit: cum ante ipsæ Ecclesiæ solerent pecunias sumere sub trien- talibus usuris. Priscos illos Canones si quis instaurandos putet non refragabor. Par enim est ad exactiorem nor- mam eos vivere, à quibus cæteri vivendi exemplum pe- tunt. Cæteros quod attinet, primum cavere debent ne usurarum nomine plus æquo exigant, quod quia non posi- tum est ἐν στιγμῇ, sed πλάτος aliquod habet pro regionum ac populorum diversitate, legibus civilibus definiendum est: ita tamen ut pii meminerint, sæpe citra id quod leges permittunt consistendum. Ad multa enim leges connivent, quia corrupti mores remedium non ferunt: Deinde etiam intra hanc æqualitatis mensuram non exercendum fœnus in egentes, aut eos quos credibile sit fœnore in egestatem prolapsos. Nam talibus aut pecunia neganda est, si ea o- pus non habent, aut donanda si id possumus, certe id ca- vendum ne aliorum aut miseria aut imprudentia in quæ- sturn abutamur.

Illud μηδὲν ἀπελπίζοντες similiter exponi pos- se, ut Syriaca habet versio, nullius rei spem aufe- rentes τῷ πλησίῳ proximo, ἐπὶ τὸν πλησίον obser- vat Dievius: cum ἀπελπίζειν quandoque sit de- sperare facere, spem alicui auferre: Salmasii tamen præferenda interpretatio, quam firmat ἀντίθεσις eorum, qui nihil mutuum dant nisi ea spe, ut τὰ ἴσα re- cipiant: ut μηδὲν ἀπελπίζοντες sit μηδὲν ἐλπίζον- τες ἀπ' αὐτῶν: & nihil ab eo, cui mutuum dederitis, sperantes. Quæ & Casauboni est explicatio. Agitur ergo in lege non de mutuo officioso, in quo τὰ ἴσα redduntur constituto tempore; sed de mutuo, ut ita dicam, eleemosynario, in quo pauperibus aliquid donatur, ut nihil plane redeat ad eum, qui pecuniam erogat. Illis enim de lege charitatis debetur elee- mosyna, ideoque ita iis dandum ut nihil quicquam inde speretur. Vide B. Gerhardum de Magistratu n. 251. Quæstio itaque fœnoris huc proprie non pertinet: de qua ex jure naturali, lege Mosis, lege Christi, & moribus veterum Christianorum vel jure Canonico erudite disserit hoc loco Grotius, quia per consequentiam hic vetita avaritia fœneratorum. Oc- currunt tamen nonnulla, de quibus monendum. De jure naturæ recte docetur, illicitum non esse omnem quæstum ex usu pecuniæ aut rei similis alteri concesso: At quod ad legem Mosis attinet Deuter. XXIII. v. 19. non fœnerabis fratri tuo in usuram pe- cuniæ, in usuram cibi, in usuram rei fœnerabilis, alienigenæ fœnerabis: fratri autem tuo non fœnera- bis, eam manus recte explicat, quasi quivis ex- traneus eadem indigitetur, siquidem solum fœ- nus a Cananæis exitio devictis permissum fuerit, ut recte Ambrosius lib. de Tobia cap. XV. ubi jus belli, ibi etiam jus usuræ: Quo de B. Ægidius Hun- nius in 2. Corinth. VIII. Concessisse hoc Deum Is- raelitis, ut possessiones eas, quæ alioquin ipfis decretæ fuerant, hoc interveniente medio a Cananæis tan- quam hostibus injustis possessoribus ad se traducerent, quæ res hodie in exemplum trahi nec possit, nec pro- pter diversitatis rationem debeat. Neque id pro- bandum est, quod legem illam de quovis quæstu & quæstu explicet, adeo ut Census etiam annuos pecuniarios legibus civilibus comprobatos huic legi adversari censeat: quum lex Mosaica solum de usura proprie dicta, quæ cum lege charitatis pugnat, agat, de usura mordace, & corrodente, uti vox Ebræa נשך, a qua serpens nomen habet, infert. Ideoque agitur quidem de vero mutuo, quod sua natura est gratui- tum, sed id egentibus debetur: qui per usuram mor- dentur, corroduntur, ac consumuntur, Mich. III. v. 2. Ideoque Lev. XXV. v. 35. habetur: si attenua- tus fuerit frater tuus: Conf. Exod. XXII. vers. 25. Quum vero agnoscat Grotius, non pugnare cum lege naturæ si ab illis, qui pecunia lucrari possunt, pro ejus usu census moderatus accipiatur, quomodo id simpliciter lege divina interdictum censeri potest in populo Judaico, quod lege naturæ illicitum non est?

Porro interdictum usuræ Mosaicum ad leges tantum forenses spectasse, minime concedendum est: quod ad omnes pertineat ejus observatio, Ps. XV. v. 5. Ezech. XXX. v. 4. & usuræ pugnent, cum ipsa charitatis lege: Ideoque uti merito im- probata a nostris est Socini sententia, qui Epist. IV. ad Morf. in Vol. Epistol. pag. 503. in Novo Te- stamento prohibitam usuram statuit? ita nec Grotio concedendum, non constare, quid Christus nos facere velit, sed ex præceptis generalibus haurien- dum id esse. Christus enim non novam legem tu- lit: sed ad legem Mosaicam nos revocavit, eamq; a corruptelis repurgavit. Neque charitatis regula plus exigit in Novo Testamento, quemadmodum censet Grotius. Nam eadem charitatis regula in Veteri Testamento quoque viguit: egenti dandam esse pecuniam mutuam nulla spe compensationis, ad- eog, etiam sine usura, Lev. XXV. 35. Frustra ergo cum Tertulliano legem Ebræorum dicit rudimentum quoddam fuisse ad ea, quæ a Christianis præstanda sunt, e lib. IV. advers. Marcion: quia neque Christus legis perficiendæ, sed nostri loco im- plendæ causa venit, nec in hac lege ulla in Novo Testamento deprehenditur perfectio Mosaicarum constitutionum.

Denique quod ad jus Canonicum attinet: agno- scit Grotius, in antiquis Canonibus nullum inveniri, qui fœnus exercentes omnes promiscue a communio- ne submoveat, quod posterioribus seculis factum, sed quod his, qui in Ecclesia munere aliquo conspi- cui erant, is quæstus interdicatur Canone Apostoli- co, ut vocant XLIV. Laodiceno IV. Niceno XVII. Africano V. & XVI. secundum quid tantum acci- piendum videtur, si nempe non neceffariæ susten- tationis causa, sed ex avaritia id factum fuerit. De cætero quod ad Leonis Imperatoris constitutio- nem, quem quod existimavit omne fœnus Christia- nis interdictum, Hermenopulo notante, primum lege communi id sanxisse, ait, eum ante ipse Eccle- siæ solerent pecunias sumere sub trientalibus usuris, non improbanda sententia Grotii, non omnem usuram prohibitam, aut prohibendam esse: caven- dum autem ne usurarum nomine plus æquo exiga- tur, nec exercendum fœnus in egentes, aut eos quos credibile sit fœnore in egestatem prolapsos. καὶ ἔσαι ὁ μισθὸς ὑμῶν πολὺς.] Confer Josephi & Philonis quæ citavimus. Abrahamus cum beneficentiam suam in Regem & cives Sodomorum liberaliter esset testatus à Deo audivit, Ego sum merces tua magna valde, Gen. XVI. 1. Vers. 36. καθὼς κὶ ὁ πατὴρ ὑμῶν οἰκτίρμων ἐσί.] Thalmu- distæ, Chaldæi & Arabes Deum quasi proprio nomine vo- cant רחמן, id est, οἰκτίρμονα. Et hanc ipsam sententiam usu populi tritam fuisse (ut multas alias quibus utitur Chri- stus tanquam indubitatis) apparet ex Pandecte Thalmudico. Sciendum autem est voces misericordiam significantes apud Hebræos & Hellenistas ad omne beneficentiæ genus extendi: ut Gen. XX. 13. & alibi. Vide quæ ad Matthæum. Vers. 37. κὶ ἀπολύετε κὶ ἀπολυθήσεσθε] Sicut καταδικάζειν est dubia aliorum facta in partem pejorem rapere, ita ἀπο- λύειν hic esse arbitror omnia quatenus fieri potest æqui bo- nique consulere, & interpretari benignius: quod Latini, etiam cum de privatis agitur, dicunt absolvere. Sic Jose- phus dixit ἀπολύειν τὰς διαβολὰς diluere calumnias, XVI. Originum, c. XII. Vers. 38. (ςεσαλευμένον] Ἀγγεῖα σαττόμενα Aristoteli Probl. Sect. XXI. Δώσουσιν] Impersonaliter interpretandum, id est, mensu- ra justa, coacta, succussata, superfluens vobis dabitur. τῷ γὰρ αὐτῷ μέτρῳ ὧ μετρεῖτε ἀντιμετρηθήσεται ὑμῖν] Id est, ut Hesiodus loquitur, αὐτῷ τῷ μέτρῳ κί λώϊον: ut eadem sit mensura in genere, sed exuberans. Sensus est, Deum eos qui sunt benigni & clementes, benigne & clementer habiturum. Vers. 39. εἶπε δὲ παραβολὴν αὐτοῖς] Frustra laborari puto in quærenda hujus loci cum prioribus aut sequentibus con- nexione. Lucas enim cum multas Christi sententias reci- tasset, has etiam, quanquam alio forte tempore & occa- sione pronunciatas, huc referendas putavit. Est ergo hoc εἶπε δὲ παραβολὴν αὐτοῖς tale, quale illud κὶ τόδε Φωκυλίδεω. Responderi autem εἶπε Hebræo אמר, quod de nobilibus magistris usurpant Hebræi, cum significare volunt senten- tiam aliquam aut ab illo auctore manasse, aut certe in ore ejus frequentem fuisse. Non est existimandum cum Grotio, hæc non cohærere cum præcedentibus, sed diversas sententias alio forte tempore & occasione dictas consarcinari. Nam quum in confesso sit, eandem concionem montanam à Luca describi, quæ à Matthæo est proposita, & è Matth. VII. constet, Christum de cavendis Pseudoprophetis, quales Pharisæi im- primis tum erant, hortatum esse: paræmia hæc generatim in omnes hypocritas quadrans, maxime qui alios judicant, seipsos non excutiunt, speciali- ter tamen respicit Pharisæos; utpote qui tales hy- pocritæ erant, ac judiciis suis temerariis alios se- ducebant: quos etiam simili ratione, & paræmia cæcos ductores alibi dixit Matth. XV. 14. quemad- modum hoc loco è v. 49. collato cum Matth. VII. 14. seqq. liquet, generalem illam regulam de arbo- re mala Pharisæorum & similium Pseudoprophe- tarum causa traditam esse: quos similis locus Matth. XII. 33. quoque confirmat. Neque ob- scura est συνέχεια harum sententiarum: quia te- merarii ejusmodi judices hypocritæ alios judi- cant, & corrigunt, quum ipsimet cæci sint, neq; vitia sua vel trabem in oculis suis agnoscant: volunt a- lios perfectos esse, quos instituunt, & reformare au- dent, quum ipsi perfecti non sint, non cogitan- tes, quod non sit discipulus supra Magistrum, neque id requiratur, sed sufficiat, si discipulus magistro paria faciat: quibus facete Pharisæi & Scribæ no- tati sunt, qui ductores imperitorum se jactabant, clavemque scripturæ sibi vendicabant, & alios super- ciliose præ se contemnebant, quum ipsimet in rebus divinis vel talpa cæciores essent: à quibus simpliciores pessime seducebantur. Etsi enim hæc sententia, non est discipulus supra Magistrum, alibi ita accipiatur, quod meliori forte ac conditione non sint sectatores præ eo quem sectentur, hic ta- men non sortem respici, uti Grotius vult, sed eru- ditionem vel perfectionem, cum vox κατηρτισμέ- νος docet, tum συνέχεια contextus convincit.

## 6:40
Vers. 40.

The sense of these words is no other than those among Matthew: ἀρκετὸν τῷ μαθητῇ ἵνα γένηται ὡς ὁ διδάσκαλος αὐ- τῦ, X. 25. Here after πᾶς is understood the genitive μαθητῶν, concerning which kind of speaking we have said something on Mark c. IX. 49. But the construction seems to me most clear, which the Syrian also follows: Whoever of the disciples shall be נכון true, upright, which is here translated at its origin κατηρτισμένος, he shall be as the master: that is, he will know that those things are to be done and borne by him which the master has done and borne: for the sentiment is referred to this, not only among Matthew, but also among John in two passages. Therefore ὑπὲρ τὸν διδάσκαλον, which Matthew or Luke say, or μείζων τῦ κυρίε, as John speaks, is not that which is in the Greek verse κρείττονες διδασκάλων. For there it is a matter of a comparison of erudition: here it is indicated that the followers of someone are not in a better lot and condition than he whom they follow. Nor did Irenæus understand this passage otherwise, as is to be seen in the fifth book, chapter XXXI.

Latin:

Vers. 40.

κατηρτισμένος δὲ πᾶς ἔσαι, ὡς ὁ διδάσκαλος αὐτῦ] Non est horum verborum sensus alius quam illorum apud Mat- thæum: ἀρκετὸν τῷ μαθητῇ ἵνα γένηται ὡς ὁ διδάσκαλος αὐ- τῦ, X. 25. Subauditur hic post πᾶς genitivus μαθητῶν, de quo loquendi genere aliquid diximus ad Marcum c. IX. 49. Videtur autem mihi apertissima esse constructio, quam & Syrus sequitur: Quisquis discipulorum erit נכון verus, re- ctus, quod hic ad originem vertitur κατηρτισμένος, is erit ut magister: id est sciet ea sibi agenda & ferenda quæ magi- ster egerit tuleritque: nam huc ea sententia refertur, non apud Matthæum tantum, sed & apud Johannem duobus lucis. Itaque ὑπὲρ τὸν διδάσκαλον, quod dicunt Matthæus aut Lucas, aut μείζων τῦ κυρίε, ut loquitur Johannes, non est illud quod in Græco verfu κρείττονες διδασκάλων. Ibi enim de comparatione eruditionis agitur: hic indicatur non esse meliori sorte ac conditione sectatores alicujus eo quem sectantur. Nec aliter hunc locum intellexit Irenæus, ut videre est libro quinto, cap. XXXI.

## 6:42
Vers. 42. πῶς δύνασαι λέγειν] How do you dare to say?

Latin:

Vers. 42. πῶς δύνασαι λέγειν] Quomodo audes dicere?

## 6:43
Vers. 43.

For it is not a good tree] Although the Syriac and Arabic do not have that γὰρ, yet since the Greek codices prefer it, the Latin has it, and Theophylact acknowledges and interprets it, I dare not delete it: nor is there sufficient cause. Elsewhere we have often noted that among the Hebrews and Hellenists the reasons are given for that which is passed over in silence, but it can be sufficiently understood from the argument of the matter being discussed. Thus here γὰρ is an aetiology of what is passed over in silence. For since the discussion has been about simulators, Christ gives the reason why that mask of holiness cannot be useful for long, because it cannot happen that a disposition is always dissembled. And so if anyone notices, mice are usually betrayed by their own evidence. We have said elsewhere that these apophthegmatic sayings are to be understood ethically, and that for their truth it is sufficient if the outcome often and frequently corresponds. The use of this sentence is similar in Matt. XII. 33. For there too Christ shows that the attempt at simulation is vain. Luke has contracted that passage with the other of Matthew which is in chapter VII, because of the similarity of the argument. Wherefore those things which pertain to the interpretation of this pericope are to be sought from there.

Beza expunged the aetiological particle, relying on the Syriac interpreter, with whom the Arab also agrees, and on the authority of one of his own codices: but Grotius rightly teaches against Beza that it should be retained, based on other Greek codices and the Latin version, as well as Theophylact. However, the reason is not given here why simulation, or the mask of holiness, cannot be useful for long, namely because it cannot happen that a disposition is always dissembled, which is the aetiology Grotius provides here; but since the things which Luke relates must be completed in the Evangelical harmony from Matt. VII. 14 seq., and what he had said in v. 39 specifically concerned the Pharisees and Scribes, the chief hypocrites of that time, therefore Flacius does not wrongly state that this verse 43 and the causal particle have reference to verse 39: and Grotius acknowledges that a similar use of this sentence occurs in Matt. XII. 33, where the discussion is about the doctrine of the Pharisees. Meanwhile, that great maxim about the bad tree, which cannot bear good fruit, is a general application to fruits, such as those of the Pharisees, who, as autumn trees without fruit, twice dead, plucked up by the roots, as St. Jude speaks of false teachers in v. 12, could not produce good fruits of doctrine, serving the glory of the divine name, true holiness of life, and the tranquility of consciences. But Grotius rashly perverts this maxim, as if it were only particular, after the manner of those apophthegms which are to be understood ethically, for whose truth it is sufficient if the outcome often and frequently corresponds: for Christ expressly says in Matt. VII. v. 18, οὐ δύναται, he says, it cannot: he does not speak, therefore, of that which happens often and frequently, but testifies that it CANNOT happen otherwise, and thus teaches that NEVER and NO bad tree, as such, can produce truly good fruits.

Latin:

Vers. 43.

ὐ γάρ ἐστι δένδρον καλὸν] Quanquam γὰρ illud Syrus & A- rabs non habeant, tamen cum Græci codices præferant, habeat Latinus, agnoscat & interpretetur Theophylactus, delere non ausim: neque satis causæ est. Alibi notavimus sæpe apud Hebræos & Hellenistas causas reddi ejus quod subticetur, sed ex argumento rei de qua agitur satis intelligi potest. Ita hic γὰρ est αἰτιολογία t̃ε σιωπωμένε. Cum enim de simulatoribus actum sit, causam reddit Christus, cur diu prodesse non possit illa persona sanctimoniæ, quia fieri non potest, ut semper dissimuletur ingenium. Itaque si quis advertat, plerumque solent suo indicio prodi sorices. Dixi- mus alibi hæc ἀποφθεγματικὰ intelligenda ἠθικῶς, & ad eo- rum veritatem satis esse, si eventus sæpe & frequenter re- spondeat. Similis est hujus sententiæ usus Matth. XII. 33. Nam & ibi Christus ostendit inanem esse simulandi cona- tum. Lucas eum locum cum altero Matthæi qui est VII. capite, ob argumenti similitudinem in unum contraxit. Quare inde petenda quæ ad hujus περικοπῆς interpretatio- nem pertinent.

Particulam αἰτιολογικὴν expunxit Beza fretus Syro interprete, cui etiam Arabs consonat, ac unius sui codicis autoritate: quam vero retinendam esse recte contra Bezam ex aliis codicibus Græcis, & La- tina versione, ut & Theophylacto docet Grotius. Causa autem non redditur hic, cur diu prodesse non possit simulatio, vel persona sanctimoniæ, quod nempe fieri non possit, ut semper dissimuletur ingenium, quam αἰτιολογίαν hic tradit Grotius, sed quum è Matth. VII. 14. seq. complenda in harmonia Evan- gelica sint, quæ tradit Lucas, & quæ v. 39. dixerat, peculiariter spectarint ad Pharisæos & Scribas, hy- pocritarum isto tempore præcipuos, ideo non male Flacius hunc vers. 43. & particulam causalem respectum habere ad vers. 39. statuit: & agnoscit Grotius similem hujus sententiæ usum Matth. XII. 33. occurrere, ubi de doctrina Pharisæorum agi- tur. Interea maxima illa de arbore mala, quæ non possit fructus bonos ferre, generalis, velut ap- plicatio est ad fructus, quales Pharisæorum, qui tanquam δένδρα φθινοπωρινὰ ἄκαρπα δὶς ἀποθά- νοντα, ἐκριζωθέντα, ut S. Judas de falsis doctoribus lo- quitur v. 12. non poterant bonos doctrinæ fructus, gloriæ nominis divini, veræ vitæ sanctitati, & con- scientiarum tranquillitati inservientes proferre. Quam vero maximam temere pervertit Grotius, ac si particularis tantum sit, ad eorum apophtegma- tum modum, quæ ἠθικῶς intelligenda sint, ad quorum veritatem satis est.si eventus sæpe & frequenter re- spondeat: diserte enim Christus Matth. VII. v. 18. ὐ δύναται, inquit, non potest: non loquitur ergo de eo, quod sæpe & frequenter fiat, sed testatur, quod aliter fieri NON POSSIT, adeoque docet, NUNQUAM & NULLAM arborem malam, qua talem, fructus vere bonos proferre.

## 6:46
Vers. 46. ἃ λέγω] Which I command from the Father's will. See Matthew.

Latin:

Vers. 46. ἃ λέγω] Quæ præcipio ex patris voluntate. Vid. Matthæum.

## 6:47
Vers. 47. καὶ ποιῶν αὐτοὺς] ποιεῖν here signifies not a single operation, but the diligent conformation of the whole life, without which the profession of true doctrine profits nothing, nay, it cannot even subsist when tested by adverse circumstances.

Latin:

Vers. 47. καὶ ποιῶν αὐτοὺς] ποιεῖν hic non unicam opera- tionem, sed vitæ totius diligentem conformationem signi- ficat, sine qua veræ doctrinæ professio nihil prodest, imo ne potest quidem rebus adversis explorata subsistere.

## 6:48
Vers. 48. ὃς ἔσκαψε καὶ ἐβάθυνε] A Hebraism: For the Hebrews love to circumlocute with two verbs what might be said by a verb and an adverb. Thus ἔσκαψε καὶ ἐβάθυνε is ἔσκαψε βαθέως, as the Latin interpreter translates it. This comparison designates a zeal for piety, not floating on the surface, but hidden deep within the heart.

Latin:

Vers. 48. ὃς ἔσκαψε καὶ ἐβάθυνε] Hebraismus: Nam He- bræi quod per verbum & adverbium diceretur, duobus ver- bis amant circumloqui. Ita ἔσκαψε καὶ ἐβάθυνε est ἔσκαψε βαθέως, quomodo vertit Latinus interpres. Designat hæc comparatio studium pietatis, non in superficie fluitans, sed alto penitus corde reconditum.

## 7:1 Argument
CHAPTER VII.

ARGUMENT AND DIVISION.

The centurion's servant is healed through the intercession of the Jews: and his faith is proclaimed: The widow's son in Nain is raised to life, and Christ is celebrated as a great Prophet. The disciples of John sent to Christ are instructed, and John is adorned with Christ's eulogy, with the testimony of Malachi (c. III. 1.) confirmed. When the Pharisees rejected the baptism of John, Christ complains of them and of those who reject both Himself and John. Moreover, in the house of Simon the Pharisee, being anointed by a sinful woman, He defends the fact that He admitted it, and forgives her sins.

There are five parts: I. The healing of the centurion's servant, to v. 10. II. The raising of the youth of Nain, to v. 17. III. The instruction of John's disciples with the eulogy of John, to v. 28. IV. A complaint concerning the Pharisees who equally despise John and Christ, to v. 35. V. The anointing and absolution of the sinful woman, to the final v. 50.

PART I. The healing of the Centurion's servant.

Vers. 1. πάντα τὰ ῥήματα αὐτῶ] His dogmas, the summary of which the previous discourse had expressed.

Εἰς τὰς ἀκοὰς τῦ λαᾶ] For these were exoteric words, not esoteric: pertaining to all who wished to be saved: not to the Apostles alone and their successors in the office of teaching.

Latin:

CAPUT VII.

ARGUMENTUM ET PAR- TITIO.

Centurionis servus intercedentibus Iudæis sa- natur: illiusque fides prædicatur: Filius viduæ in Nain resuscitatur, & Christus ut magnus Propheta celebratur. Discipuli Jo- hannis ad Christum ablegati informan- tur, & Johannes elogio Christi ornatur, confirmato Malachiæ testimonio (c. III. 1.) Quum Pharisæi baptismum Johannis re- nuerent, Christus de illis & se, & Jo- hannem reprobantibus queritur. In do- mo autem Simonis Pharisæi à peccatrice unctus, defendit, quod id admiserit, eique peccata remittit.

Partes sunt quinque: I. Servi centurionis sana- tio, ad v. 10. II. Juvenis Nainici resuscitatio, ad v. 17. III. Discipulorum Johannis informatio cum Johanneo elogio, ad v. 28. IV. De Phari- sæis Johannem & Christum pariter spernentibus querela, ad v. 35. V. Mulieris peccatricis unctio, & absolutio, ad v. 50. finalem.

PARS I. Servi Centurionis sanatio.

Vers. 1. πάντα τὰ ῥήματα αὐτῶ] Dogmata sua, quorum summam superior sermo expresserat.

Εἰς τὰς ἀκοὰς τῦ λαᾶ] Erant enim hi λόγοι ἐξωτερικοὶ, non ἀκροαματικοὶ: ad omnes qui salvi esse vellent pertinentes: non ad Apostolos solos & eorum in docendi munere suc- cessores.

## 7:2
Vers. 2. ἤμελλε τελευτᾷν] He was just about to die, קרוב למות. I judge it certain that this is the same history which is narrated by Matthew in chapter VIII, for the reasons which we have brought forward regarding Matthew.

ὃς ἦν αὐτῷ ἔντιμος.] Whom the Lord valued highly. For thus ἔντιμον ποιεῖν is used by the Greeks. I do not think, therefore, that it is correctly translated as 'precious'. For Luke did not intend to signify that this servant could be sold for a high price, but rather commended the kindness of the centurion, who treated his little servant with such a favorable affection, mindful that he is a human being, as Seneca often reminds the Romans, and Philemon once did the Greeks in witty verses: 'Even if someone were a slave, he is none the less a human being, master, if he is a human being.' The wise Hebrew said, 'Let your soul love a sensible servant' (Eccles. VII. 23). Likewise, 'If you have a servant, treat him as a brother': which conform to Paul's precepts on this matter.

Latin:

Vers. 2. ἤμελλε τελευτᾷν] Jam jamque moriturus vide- batur קרוב למות. Eandem hanc esse historiam, quæ à Matthæo narratur cap. VIII. certum arbitror ob eas causas quas ad Matthæum attulimus.

ὃς ἦν αὐτῷ ἔντιμος.] Quem plurimi Dominus faciebat. Ita enim Græcis usurpatur ἔντιμον ποιεῖν. Non puto igitur recte verti pretiosum. Non enim vendi potuisse magno hunc servum Lucas significatum voluit, sed potius bonita- tem commendavit centurionis, qui servulum tam propen- so affectu prosequeretur, memor hominem esse, ut Seneca Romanos sæpe monet, & Philemon olim Græcos facetis versibus: Κἂν δῦλος ἦν τις, ἐδὲν ἧττον δέσποτα Ἄνθρωπος ὗτός ἐστιν, ἐὰν ἄνθρωπος ᾖ. Sapiens Hebræus dixit οἰκέτην συνετὸν ἀγαπάτω σου ἡ ψυχή Eccles. VII. 23. Item εἰ ἔστι σοι οἰκέτης, ἄγε αὐτὸν ὡς ἀδελφὸν: quæ Pauli super hac re præceptis congruunt.

## 7:3
Vers. 3. πρεσβυτέρους τῶν ἰκδαίων] As the magistrates of a town, or the overseers of the Synagogue. For both these and those were called by that name.

Latin:

Vers. 3. πρεσβυτέρους τῶν ἰκδαίων] Ut magistratus oppidi, aut præpositos Synagogæ. Nam & hi & illi eo nomine dicebantur.

## 7:4
V. 4. παρεξῇ] See Mark chapter seven, verse one and twelve.

Latin:

V. 4. παρεξῇ] Vide ad Marcum capite septimo, commate unde imo & duodecimo.

## 7:5
Vers. 5. ἀγαπᾷ γὰρ τὸ ἔθνος ἡμῶν] Namely, on account of the worship of the one God, which alone among so many peoples the Jews almost exclusively professed: very few from other nations, such as that other Centurion in the Acts of the Apostles: and Petronius, the governor of Syria, whom Philo commends for piety and justice: 'For he himself,' he says, 'had, as it seems, some spark of the Jewish philosophy and piety, whether having learned it beforehand on account of his zeal for education,'

so that even from the lands which he governed, in which Jews are very numerous in every city of Asia and Syria, being so disposed in his soul, he was a hearer, a self-prompted learner, and a self-taught student of things worthy of study, as God suggested to him holy thoughts through which, by benefiting others, they would be benefited.

κὴ τὴν συναγωγὴν ἀυτὸς ᾠκοδόμησεν ἡμῖν] At his own expense, perhaps also using the labor of soldiers for that purpose. For the Romans were accustomed to use military hands even for theaters and other substructures, lest idleness should turn into wantonness. Nor is it a wonder if a Roman man spent the care and cost of building a Synagogue, since Augustus himself (whose institutions Tiberius followed) forbade that Jews should be prohibited anywhere εἰς τὰ συνα γώγια συνέρχεσθαι, for these were not to be assemblies of drunkenness and revelry for the purpose of conspiracy to disturb the peace, but schools of temperance and justice, of men practicing virtue.

Latin:

Vers. 5. ἀγαπᾷ γὰρ τὸ ἔθνος ἡμῶν] Nempe ob cultum unius Dei, quem tot inter populos soli ferme Judæi profi- tebantur: ex aliis gentibus perpauci, qualis alter ille in Acti- bus Apostolicis Centurio: & Petronius Syriæ præses, quem pietate & justitia Philo commendat: Α'π' ἔχε, inquiens, καὶ αὐτὸς ὡς ἔοικεν ἔναυσμά τι τῆς Ἰκδαϊκῆς φιλοσοφίας ἅμα καὶ ἐυ- σεβείας, εἴτε καὶ πάλαι προμαθὼν ἕνεκα τῆς περὶ παιδείαν σπεδῆς,

ὥστε καὶ ἀφ' ὧν τῶν χωρῶν ἐπετέπευσεν, ἐν οἷς Ἰυδαῖοι καθ' ἑκάστην πόλιν εἰσὶ παμπληθεῖς Ἀσίας τε καὶ Συρίας, ἅτε κὰ τὴν ψυχὴν οὕτω διατεθεὶς, ἀυτηκόων κὰ αὐτοκελεύστων καὶ αὐτομαθῶν των πρὸς τὰ σπουδῆς ἄξια φοσητοῖς τὰ ἐκαθῶν ἀγαθὰ ὡς ὑπήχει ὁσίας κε γνώμας ὁ θεὸς δι' ὧν ὠφελῦντες ὠφεληθήσονται.

κὴ τὴν συναγωγὴν ἀυτὸς ᾠκοδόμησεν ἡμῖν] Suis impensis, forte & militum eam in rem usus opera. Solebant enim Romani ad theatra etiam aliasque substructiones uti manu militari, ne otium in lasciviam verteret. Nec mirum si Synagoga aedificandae curam ac sumptum impendit homo Romanus, cum ipse Augustus (cujus instituta Tiberius sectabatur) vetuerit necubi Judaei prohiberent εἰς τὰ συνα γώγια συνέρχεσθαι, μὴ γὰρ εἶναι ταῦτα συνόδες μέθης κὰ πα ροινίας ἐπὶ συστάσει ὡς λυμαίνεσθαι τὰ τῆς εἰρήνης, ἀλλὰ διδασκα λεῖα ζωφροσύνης κὴ δικαιοσύνης, ἀνδρῶν ἐπιτηδευόντων τὴν ἀρέ την.

## 7:6
Vers. 6. μὴ σκύλλε] Do not trouble yourself: or do not weary yourself: as the Syrian.

PARS II. The resuscitation of the young man of Nain.

Latin:

Vers. 6. μὴ σκύλλε] Ne tibimet molestus esto : aut ne te fatiga: ut Syrus.

PARS II. Iuvenis Nainici resuscitatio.

## 7:11
Vers. 11. ἐν τῇ ἑξῆς] The Syrian also reads it thus. πόλιν καλυμένην Ναΐν] Jerome ascribes this town to Galilee, and others after him. I do not doubt that it is the same place which Josephus names in Antiquities XX, chapter V, νάι μκες, saying, 'of that which is called Nais.' For he also calls Κεφαρνάμη, that is, Capharnaum, a village elsewhere, and to our writers Bethsaida is sometimes a city, sometimes a village. It seems to stand in the way that Josephus seems to ascribe it not to Galilee, but to the Samaritan region. But if I judge correctly, the passage of Josephus is not intact. For some things seem to be missing to complete the history.

μαθηταὶ] It signifies not the Apostles, but any constant followers.

Latin:

Vers. 11. ἐν τῇ ἑξῆς] Ita & Syrus legit. πόλιν καλυμένην Ναΐν] Galilaeae hoc oppidum adscribit Hieronymus, & post eum alii. Non dubito quin idem sit locus quem Josephus Originum XX. cap. V. nominat, νάι μκες, inquiens, τῆς Νάις λεγομένης. Nam & Κεφαρνάμη id est, Capharnaum, alibi κώμην vocat, & nostris Scriptori- bus Bethsaida modo est πόλις, modo κώμη. Obstare vide- tur quod eam κώμην Josephus adscribere videatur non Gali- laeae, sed Samaritanae regioni. Verum si quid recte judi- co locus Josephi non est integer. Videntur enim ad ex- plendam historiam aliqua deesse.

μαθηταὶ] Non Apostolos, sed quosvis assiduos sectatores significat.

## 7:12
Vers. 12. τῇ πύλῃ τῆς πόλεως] For the tombs of the Jews were outside the city: as we saw in Matthew XXVII. 59. But also for other peoples, whence the word 'to carry out' [efferendi]. And certainly, the reason of public health, which is usually much harmed by the air of tombs, demands this. Wherefore it is the more wonderful that it has pleased almost all Christians that sacred assemblies should be held in the same places in which these corpses are: which, having been introduced long ago in memory of the martyrs, I do not know if it is retained wisely enough.

μονογενὴς] This pertains to signifying the magnitude of the grief. For it passed into a proverb among the Hebrews מספד על היחיד, a lamentation for an only-begotten, Zechariah XII. 10, Jeremiah VI. 26.

κὴ αὐτὴ ἧν χήρα καὶ ὄχλος τῆς πόλεως ἱκανὸς σὺν αὐτῇ] This is the more frequent reading, which the Syrian and the Latin support. Nor do I see what stands in the way. For that 'was' [ἧν] should be understood even where it does not precede is common to almost all languages: but it is most customary for the Hebrews. It is apparent, however, that the funeral was not ignoble, since a large crowd of the city was following the procession.

Latin:

Vers. 12. τῇ πύλῃ τῆς πόλεως] Nam sepulchra Judaeis ex- tra urbem: ut vidimus Matth. XXVII. 59. Sed & aliis po- pulis unde efferendi vox. Et certe ita postulat ratio pu- blicae sanitatis quae multum laedi solet aura sepulchrorum. Quo magis mirum Christianis ferme omnibus placuisse, ut conventus sacri ejusdem in locis haberentur in quibus i- sta sunt cadavera: quod in memoriam martyrum olim in- ductum, nescio an satis sapienter retineatur.

μονογενὴς] Hoc ad luctus magnitudinem significandam pertinet. Nam in proverbium transiit ad Hebraeos מספד על היחיד planctus super unigena, Zachar. XII. 10. Jer. VI. 26.

κὴ αὐτὴ ἧν χήρα καὶ ὄχλος τῆς πόλεως ἱκανὸς σὺν αὐτῇ] Haec frequentior lectio, a qua stant Syrus & Latinus. Nec video qui obstet. Nam ut ἧν subaudiatur etiam ubi non praeces- sit, omnibus ferme linguis commune est: Hebraeis autem usitatissimum. Apparet autem funus non fuisse ignobile cum exsequias populus frequens iret.

## 7:13
Vers. 13. ἐσπλαγχνίσθη ἐπ’ αὐτῇ] The ancients note that in the three miracles which Christ performed after the sermon delivered on the mount, three kinds of God's benefits are shown to us: the first of those which are conferred upon those praying themselves, as that leper whom Matthew mentions: the second of those which others obtain through the prayers of others, an example of which is in the Centurion's servant: the third of those which God bestows out of His own sheer mercy, sought by no prayers: of which thing there is an example in this history. Moreover, the calling of the profane nations to the knowledge of the truth is accustomed to be referred with the best right by the Apostles to such mercy.

μὴ κλαῖε] Not only a represented, as here, but also an expected resurrection ought to diminish for us mourning for the dead. For it is less surprising that the profane nations, who have either no hope or a very uncertain hope of that thing, should pour themselves out immoderately into mourning, as Paul teaches us in 1 Thessalonians 4:13.

Latin:

Vers. 13. ἐσπλαγχνίσθη ἐπ’ αὐτῇ] Notant veteres in tri- bus miraculis quae post sermonem in monte habitum Chri- stus edidit, tria beneficiorum Dei genera nobis ostendi: primum eorum quae conferuntur ipsis orantibus, ut illi vi- tiliginoso cujus meminit Matthaeus: alterum eorum quae per aliorum preces alii obtinent, quorum exemplum est in servo Centurionis: tertium eorum quae nullis precibus quaesita ex mera suapte misericordia Deus largitur: cujus rei in hac historia est specimen. Ad talem autem misericor- diam optimo jure referri solet ab Apostolis gentium profa- narum vocatio ad cognitionem veri.

μὴ κλαῖε] Non tantum repraesentata, ut hic, sed & ex- spectata resurrectio minuere nobis debet luctum ob mor- tuos. Nam profanas gentes quae ejus rei aut nullam aut admodum incertam spem habent, in luctum immodice ef- fundi minus est mirum, ut nos docet Paulus prioris Thessal. IV. 13.

## 7:14
Vers. 14. ἥψατο τῆς σορῦ] The Syriac here, rightly if I am not mistaken, interprets σορὸν as the litter in which the dead were carried out, according to the custom then accepted among the more wealthy. That saying of Martial is well known: 'Do you ask how enviable a litter is to you? You ought not to be carried dead in a six-bearer litter.' But we also learn from Josephus that the Jews were carried out in this way. Christ touched it, however, in order to stop those carrying it: which the following words indicate. Whether He also touched the dead man is uncertain: which, even if He had done so, He would certainly have done nothing in that against the law. For equity itself dictates that he who restores a dead person to life by touching him is not defiled by the touch of the dead, since he removes the very cause of the defilement. Wherefore neither Elijah nor Elisha are to be considered to have acted against the law when they did that. This is a better solution than that brought to the twenty-eighth question of the Orthodox in Justin, where the author, intending to answer, strives to defend Christ as not having been subject to the law from the time he was baptized and began his office: which, however, I do not deny can be softened by a convenient interpretation: since it is otherwise παρακεκινδυνευμένον.

σοὶ λέγω] With that divine power by which he commanded even inanimate things: concerning which matter we have spoken elsewhere, it is God's to call things that are not as though they were, Rom. IV. 17. See Ezech. XXXVII. 4.

Latin:

Vers. 14. ἥψατο τῆς σορῦ] Σορὸν hic Syrus, recte ni fallor, ex more inter opulentiores tunc recepto, lectulum in- terpretatur in quo mortui efferebantur. Notum illud Mar- tialis: Invidiosa tibi quam sit lectica requiris ? Non debes ferri mortuus hexaphoro. Sed & Judaeos ita elatos ex Josepho discimus. Attigit au- tem Christus, ut sisteret ferentes: quod indicant sequentia. An mortuum etiam tetigerit, incertum est: quod, etsi fecis- set, nihil sane in eo fecisset contra legem. Nam ipsa ἐπιεί- κεια dictat eum qui mortuum tangendo in vitam revocet, tactu mortui non pollui, cum causam ipsam pollutionis auferat. Quare nec Elias nec Eliseus cum id fecerunt cen- sendi sunt contra legem fecisse. Haec melior solutio quam illa allata ad quaestionem Orthodoxorum XXVIII. apud Ju- stinum, ubi responsurus auctor defendere nititur Christum ex quo baptizatus & munus suum auspicatus est, legi non fuisse subditum: quod tamen commoda interpre- tatione leniri posse non nego: cum sit alioqui παρακεκιν- δυνευμένον.

σοὶ λέγω] Divina illa potestate qua rebus etiam inaninis imperabat: qua de re diximus alibi, Dei est καλεῖν τὰ μὴ ὄντα ὡς ὄντα, Rom. IV. 17. Vide Ezech. XXXVII. 4.

## 7:15
Vers. 15. ἀνεκάθισεν] He sat up with an erect body.

ἔδωκεν αὐτὸν τῇ μητρὶ αὐτῦ] Confirming by his own act the right of parents. That old manuscript in England expresses it more openly with the word ἀπέδωκε. It may seem strange that this history, so illustrious, was omitted by Matthew and Mark. But it seems to me that both of them were content with one example of life restored in the daughter of Jairus, from which other similar ones could be understood. Which is the more necessary, because in Matthew, Christ says to the legates sent by John, νεκροὶ ἐγείρονται.

Latin:

Vers. 15. ἀνεκάθισεν] Erecto corpore sedit.

ἔδωκεν αὐτὸν τῇ μητρὶ αὐτῦ] Jure parentum facto suo confirmans. Manuscriptus autem ille in Anglia vetus a- pertius id exprimit verbo ἀπέδωκε. Mirum videri potest historiam hanc tam illustrem à Matthæo & Marco omissam. Sed videtur mihi horum uterque contentus fuisse uno ex- emplo redditæ vitæ in Jairi filia ex quo similia alia possent intelligi. Quod eo magis necessarium est, quia apud Matthæum Christus legatis à Johanne missis ait, νεκροὶ ἐ- γείρονται.

## 7:16
Vers. 16. φόβος] See above I. 65.

προφήτης μέγας ἐγήγερται] All those sent by God were called prophets. But they call him great, because not by prayers, not by any superstition of the body, but by a bare command, without any precedent, he had restored a dead man to life.

ἐπεσκέψατο ὁ Θεὸς τὸν λαὸν ἀυτῦ] See above I. 68.

Latin:

Vers. 16. φόβος] Vide supra I. 65.

προφήτης μέγας ἐγήγερται] προφῆται vocabantur omnes divinitus missi. Magnum autem dicunt, quia non pre- cibus, non corporis superstitione, sed nudo imperio, ci- tra omne exemplum, mortuum vitæ reddiderat.

ἐπεσκέψατο ὁ Θεὸς τὸν λαὸν ἀυτῦ] Vid. supra I. 68.

## 7:21
Vers. 21. ἐχαρίσατο] He mercifully bestowed: which the Hebrews call חנן. The LXX are accustomed to translate it ἐλεᾷν, Gen. XXXIII. 5. II. 2. Sam. XII. 22. Ps. XXXVII. 26.

PART III. The instruction of the disciples of John, and the eulogy of John.

Latin:

Vers. 21. ἐχαρίσατο] Misericorditer largitus est: quod Hebræi dicunt חנן. LXX. ἐλεᾷν solent vertere, Genes. XXXIII. 5. II. 2. Sam. XII. 22. Ps. XXXVII. 26.

PARS III. Discipulorum Johannis informatio, & Johan- nis elogium.

## 7:24
Vers. 24. τί ἐξεληλύθατε εἰς τὴν ἔρημον θεάσασθαι] There is the same distinction in Matthew, which I also think should be retained. For Christ asks for the sake of seeing what thing they had undertaken that troublesome journey into desert places. See what is written on Matthew.

Latin:

Vers. 24. τί ἐξεληλύθατε εἰς τὴν ἔρημον θεάσασθαι] Eadem distinctio est apud Matthæum, quam & retinendam cen- seo. Quærit enim Christus cujus rei visendæ causa mole- stum illud iter in loca deserta suscepissent. Vid. quæ ad Mat- thæum.

## 7:25
Vers. 25. ὑπάρχοντες] Since the Latin and the Syriac have read it thus, the other reading διάγοντες, it appears to be an interpretation.

Latin:

Vers. 25. ὑπάρχοντες] Cum ita legerint Latinus & Syrus, alteram lectionem διάγοντες, apparet interpretamentum esse.

## 7:26
Vers. 26. προφήτην] Concerning this passage, see what is written on Matthew.

PART IV. A complaint concerning the Pharisees, who despised both John and Christ.

Latin:

Vers. 26. προφήτην] De hoc loco vide quæ ad Matthæum.

PARS IV. De Pharisæis Johannem pariter & Christum spernentibus querela.

## 7:29
Verse 29. And all the people] This cannot be taken as if spoken by Luke, since John had already been cast into prison, and therefore had ceased to baptize when Christ delivered the preceding discourse: so that, moved by that discourse, no one came to John's baptism. But Christ is narrating what the outcome was of the labor undertaken by John: and the discourse is clearly continuous up to verse 35. All the people, that is, the people of the land, as the Jews used to say, illiterate men: these are opposed to the lawyers, who were trained in the law: just as the tax collectors, believed to be of an impure life, are opposed to the Pharisees, who professed a certain singular and eminent holiness.

Verse 31 teaches that Christ's discourse is not continued up to verse 35. For Luke did not use the particle de in vain; nor would he have inserted these words, 'and the Lord said,' if that were a continuous discourse of Christ from verse 20. Although John had ceased to baptize, the baptism of John did not cease: because he had his own disciples, through whom it could be administered, even though he himself had already been cast into prison.
