We do not, however, object that these things can be referred to the continuation of Christ's discourse, which is found in verses 29 and 30: but that a new discourse, or a new section of the discourse, begins at verse 31: for it is not to be suspected, with Beza, that they were perhaps added by someone, nor are they to be rejected entirely, with Grotius; since they are found in the received Greek and Latin Codices; nor did either Stephanus or Beza himself think they should be omitted, and, as Beza admits, such sections of one and the same discourse occur very frequently in the sacred histories.

They justified God] To justify is very often to approve. God, that is, as follows, the counsel of God; the tax collectors and men of the common people were pursuing with the highest praises and thanks this excellent goodness of God, who, content with repentance, had mercifully decided to forgive all the crimes of their former life, and to give certain assurance of that fact both through John and through him who was pointed out by John.

having been baptized with the baptism of John] He shows how they approved of God's counsel, namely by obeying: for baptism is a sign of repentance.

Latin:

Vers. 29. καὶ πᾶς ὁ λαὸς] Non potest hoc accipi tan- quam à Luca dictum, cum Johannes jam conjectus esset in carcerem, ac proinde baptizare desiisset, cum Christus sermonem præcedentem habuit: ita ut eo quidem sermo- ne commotus nemo ad baptisma Johannis venerit. Sed narrat Christus quis eventus fuerit laboris à Johanne susce- pti: ac plane continua est oratio ad comma usque 35. πᾶς ὁ λαὸς, id est, populus terræ, ut loquebantur Judæi, ho- mines illiterati: Hi opponuntur τοῖς νομικοῖς in lege exer- citatis: sicut τελῶναι vitæ impurioris crediti opponuntur Φαρισαίοις singularem quandam atque eminentem sancti- moniam pollicentibus.

Non continuari orationem Christi usque ad v. 35. docet vers. 31. Nam Lucas particulam δὲ non frustra adhibuit; neque hæc inseruisset, εἶπε δὲ ὁ κύριος, si continua illa esset Christi oratio in- de à vers. 20. Licet vero Johannes baptizare de- sierit, non tamen desiit Baptisma Johannis: quia habuit ille discipulos suos, per quos id admini- strari potuit, conjecto jam ipso in carcerem. Non refragamur tamen hæc referri posse ad con- tinuationem sermonis Christi, quæ vers. 29. 30. ha- beatur: Sed ut nova vers. 31. oratio incipiat, vel nova orationis sectio: Non enim cum Beza suspi- candum ea fortasse ab aliquo adjecta esse, aut cum Grotio prorsus ea reprobanda sunt; siquidem in receptis Codicibus Græcis & Latinis ea habean- tur; neque vel Stephanus, vel Beza ipse ea omit- tenda duxerit, ac fatente Beza occurrant sæpissi- me in sacris historiis istiusmodi veluti sectiones unius & ejusdem sermonis.

Ἐδικαίωσαν τὸν Θεὸν] Δικαιοῦν קדיק sæpissime est ap- probare. Τὸν Θεόν, id est ut sequitur τὴν βουλὴν τοῦ Θεοῦ, Pu- blicani & de rudi plebe homines summis laudibus ac gra- tiis prosequebantur eximiam hanc Dei bonitatem qui pœ- nitentia contentus constituisset prioris vitæ flagitia omnia clementer condonare, ejusque rei fidem certam facere tum per Johannem, tum per eum qui à Johanne mon- strabatur.

βαπτισθέντες τὸ βάπτισμα τῦ ἰωάννε] Ostendit quomodo probaverint Dei consilium, obediendo scilicet: nam bapti- sma indicium resipiscentiæ.

## 7:30
Verse 30. They rejected the counsel of God against themselves] Counsel can signify to the Greeks, as it does to the Latins, either that which one has decided with oneself to do, or that which one judges should be done by another. Either meaning can have a place here. But the former is recognized from the Syriac, which translates it as 'will,' and if I am not mistaken, it is constant with our writers, whether it concerns men, as below XXIII. 51, Acts V. 38, chapter XXVII. 12, 42, I Corinthians IV. 5, or whether it concerns God, as Acts II. 23, chapter IV. 28, chapter XIII. 36, Ephesians I. 11, Hebrews VI. 17. Wherefore, both here and in Acts XX. 27, this meaning seems rather to be taken, so that it signifies the very purpose of God: and in this place, indeed, that purpose of God by which He mercifully decreed to stir up the Jews to repentance through John, having given certain assurance that He would forgive their former faults: as we have already begun to say. I think 'against themselves' should be constructed entirely with that 'counsel,' according to the custom of Luke, who often transposes words, so that it is 'they rejected the counsel of God against themselves': the counsel of God toward them. For 'eis' is accustomed to be put for the Hebrew particle 'le,' as 'to reconcile to himself' in Colossians I. 20. And below IX. 13, 'food for the people,' that is, 'to the people.' For I do not see by what example it is proven that 'eis' here means 'to their own harm,' as pleases some. That 'eis' is put for 'en,' which others prefer here, is both customary among the Greeks and occurs among our own: but usually in the description of a place, as 'he was baptized in the Jordan,' 'he is in the house.' Wherefore this interpretation also, although it pleased the Syriac, does not seem to have a similar example: not to mention that it does not concern what the Pharisees and lawyers thought within themselves, but what they openly testified, for it follows 'not having been baptized by him,' which does not cohere with that sense of silent thought. To reject is rightly translated, if I am not mistaken, as 'to reject,' as below X. 16, John XII. 48. For that is best opposed to the verb 'to justify,' which is to approve and to praise. The rude men of less approved life admired and received with thankful hearts the wise and merciful counsel of God in sending such an excellent exhorter of repentance, with such great promises: on the contrary, those who seemed wiser and holier than the rest despised that very thing, relying on rituals and certain specious deeds. This passage teaches us openly that the counsels of God are not all of one kind. For there are some of His 'wills' which no one has resisted, Romans IX. 19, Isaiah XLVI. 10, Hebrews VI. 17. Although some of these also include a certain 'foreknowledge': as that 'determined counsel' concerning Christ being delivered to death, of which mention is made in Acts II. 23, chapter IV. 28. Justin Martyr in his Apology calls this 'determined counsel' an 'inviolable fate,' of which he gives an example in the decree concerning rewarding those who have chosen honest things, and punishing those who have chosen the contrary. There are, in turn, other counsels of God which leave to us 'that which is in our power': or, as Justin speaks in the cited place, explaining the Christian opinion against the Stoics, 'the power of choice.' These can be, and too often are, rejected by men, like that merciful counsel of God which pertained to the Pharisees no less than to other Jews: whence Christ said in this place 'counsel against themselves,' a counsel pertaining to them and their own salvation. Nor does that make God changeable: for the outcome of the counsel is not suspended, except by that very condition which God willed to be in His counsel: and that for the best reason. For as Justin says, 'it would not be worthy of reward or praise if one did not choose the good of one's own accord,' having been provoked, of course, by the divine benefit. Elsewhere he said: ὧ γὰρ ἦν ἐπαινε τὸν ἰδὶν ἑαυτῶ εἰ ἐκ ἧν ἐπ᾽ ἀμφότερα τρέπεσθαι: to which the most learned Athenagoras has a similar sentiment. Hence Justin also approves that Platonic saying: αἰτία ἑλομένε, and that in the place where he sets forth and defends not his own peculiar doctrine, but the common and agreeing doctrine of all Christians of that age. Prosper beautifully embraces both this kind of divine counsel in one sentence. Those who have spurned the inviting will of God, shall feel the avenging will of God. He said 'spurn' for what is here ἀθετεῖν: for Clement of Alexandria ὑπερηφανεῖν. For thus he says here: ὁ θεὸς ἵνα δέλων ὑὸς ἡμᾶς γενέσθαι βύλεται (you have here βελὴν) οἱ δὲ καὶ υἱοὶ γενέσθαι ὑπερηφανήκασι. In many words Arnobius expresses this same ἀθετεῖν while disputing against the nations: If you have such disdain that you reject the benefit of the gift offered, or rather if you so prevail in wisdom that you call those things which are offered by Christ a game and absurdities, how does the one inviting sin? And soon after, he says, is the grace of divine benevolence to be poured into the lap of you who spurn and flee it? Do you wish to take what is offered, and turn it to your own uses? You will have consulted your own interests: do you spurn, contemn, and despise it? You will have deprived yourself of the convenience of the gift. God brings necessity upon no one, he terrifies no one with imperious dread. For our salvation is not necessary to him.

We agree with Grotius that 'the counsel of God' should be understood rather as God's own purpose or plan than, as Lud. de Dieu and other Calvinists do, as a mandate or preceptive will; and thus it denotes that which God determined with Himself to do, not what He judged ought to be done: who approves this explanation from the Syriac, and from the constant usage of this word βυλὴ in the sacred writings, whether it concerns men, as below XXIII. 51, Acts V. 38, ch. XXVII. 12, 42, 1 Cor. IV. 5, or whether it concerns God, as Acts II. 23, ch. IV. 29, ch. XIII. 36, ch. XX. 27, Eph. I. 11, Heb. VI. 7, so that in this place it signifies that purpose of God by which He mercifully decreed to stir up the Jews to repentance through John, having given assurance that He would forgive their former sins: I add, and through the baptism which He instituted for the remission of sins, that He would grant to them that grace of the remission of sins. But the Pharisees rejected that counsel and purpose of God εἰς ἑαυτὺς, which does not mean 'in themselves,' as Ludov. de Dieu and Beza with the Syriac [think]: which Grotius rightly rejects, both because εἰς is indeed accustomed to be put for ἐν, but mostly in the description of a place, and because it is not a question here of what the Pharisees and lawyers thought within themselves, but of what they made openly manifest, for it follows 'not having been baptized by him,' which does not cohere with that sense of silent thought. Therefore, Beza, not undeservedly, prefers with most others that interpretation of εἰς ἑαυτὺς, that is, 'to their own greatest harm': which is without doubt more convenient than the former. But the Grotian explanation does not seem to be despised, which holds thus: I think εἰς ἑαυτὺς must be constructed entirely with that τὴν βυλὴν, according to the custom of Luke, who often transposes words, so that it may be τὴν ὸ Θεῦ εἰς ἑαυτὺς βυλὴν ἠθέτησαν: The counsel of God towards them. For εἰς is accustomed to be put for the Hebrew particle ל, as 'to reconcile to Himself' Coloss. I. 20, and below IX. 13 'meats to the people,' that is, τῷ λαῷ; finally, he rightly concludes that the word ἀθετεῖν is translated 'to reject,' and from a comparison of Luke X. 16, John XII. 48, and from the antithesis of the word δικαιῦν, which is to approve and praise, he not badly gathers: and thus he concludes against the Calvinists that some counsels of God can be rejected, and yet God does not become mutable, provided that the outcome of the counsel is not suspended except from that very condition which God willed to be in His counsel, praising that of Prosper: 'Those who rejected the inviting will of God, let them feel the punishing will of God.' Concerning which elsewhere. For from there, with Grotius, the freedom of the human will in spiritual matters must be asserted: for even if a man can reject the grace of God towards himself, he cannot, however, accept it by his own powers: we are too prone to evil by nature, but are we therefore also [prone] to good? Original sin brings both, both that we are inclined to evil, and that we are useless for good, Rom. III. 12.

τίνι ἗ν ὁμοιώσω] They cohere with the preceding. Those who thought that Luke interrupted the words of Christ inserted here 'and the Lord said,' to signify that one returns to the discourse of Christ. But many ancient Greek and Latin codices do not have this addition. Neither Ambrose nor Theophylact nor Euthymius read it: but neither does the Syriac, nor the Arab; wherefore I do not hesitate to pronounce it to be an interpolation.

Latin:

Vers. 30. τὴν βελὴν τῦ θεῦ ἠθέτησαν εἰς ἑαυτές] Βελὴ Græcis ut & consilium Latinis significare potest aut id quod secum quis constituit facere, aut quod faciendum alteri censet. Potest utravis significatio hic locum habere. Sed prior illa à Syro cognoscitur qui vertit צבינו & ni fal- lor perpetua est nostris Scriptoribus, sive cum de homini- bus agitur, ut infra XXIII. 51. Act. V. 38. cap. XXVII. 12. 42. I. Corinth. IV. 5. Sive cum de Deo, ut Act. II. 23. c. IV. 28. c. XIII. 36. Eph. I. 11. Hebr. VI. 17. Quare tum hic tum Act. XX. 27. hæc significatio potius sumenda videtur, ut significetur ipsum Dei propositum: & hoc quidem loco illud propositum Dei, quo clementer decrevit Judæos per Johannem ad resipiscentiam excitare; certa fide facta, prio- res culpas se condonaturum: ut jam dicere occepimus. Εἰς ἑαυτὺς omnino construendum arbitror cum illo τὴν βε- λὴν, ex more Lucæ voces sæpe trajicientis, ut sit τὴν τῦ θεῦ εἰς ἑαυτὺς βελὴν ἠθέτησαν: Consilium Dei erga se. Nam εἰς pro ל Hebræorum particula poni solet, ut ἀποκαταλά- ξαι εἰς ἑαυτὸν Coloss. I. 20. Et infra IX. 13. βρώματα εἰς τὸν λαὸν, id est τῷ λαῷ. Quod enim nonnullis placet εἰς ἑαυ- τὺς hic esse idem quod suo malo, non video quo exemplo probetur. εἰς pro ἐν poni, quod alii hic præferunt, & apud Græcos usitatum est, & apud nostros occurrit: sed plerun- que in loci descriptione, ut ἐβαπτίσθη εἰς Ἰορδάνην, εἰς οἶκόν ἐσι. Quare ista quoque interpretatio, quanquam Syro placuit, non videtur simile exemplum habere: ut taceam non de eo agi quod apud se cogitaverint Pharisæi & Legis- periti: sed de eo quod palam testatum fecerint, sequitur enim μὴ βαπτισθέντες ὑπ᾽ αὐτῦ: quod cum illo sensu tacitæ cogitationis non cohæret. Ἀθετεῖν recte ni fallor vertitur rejicere, ut infra X. 16. Joh. XII. 48. Id enim optime op- ponitur verbo δικαιῦν quod est approbare atque laudare. Sapiens & misericors Dei consilium in mittendo tam exi- mio pœnitentiæ hortatore, cum tantis promissis, admirati sunt gratisque animis exceperunt rudes & vitæ minus pro- batæ homines: contra idipsum aspernati sunt hi qui cæte- ris doctiores & sanctiores videbantur: freti ritibus & factis quibusdam speciosis. Docet nos aperte hic locus non u- niusmodi esse Dei consilia. Sunt enim quædam ejus θε- λήματα ὧ ὐδεὶς ἀνθέσηκε, Rom. IX. 19. Es. XLVI. 10 Hebr. VI. 17. Quanquam & horum quædam πρόγνωσιν quandam includunt: ut illa βυλὴ ὡρισμένη de Christo in mortem tra- dendo, cujus mentio est Act. II. 23. cap. IV. 28. Hanc βυλὴν ὡρισμένην Justinus martyr in Apologetico vocat εἱμαρμένην ἀπαράβατον, cujus exemplum ponit in decreto de remunerandis his qui honesta delegerint, puniendis qui contraria. Sunt rursus aliæ Dei βυλαὶ quæ relinquunt no- bis τὸ ἐφ᾽ ἡμῖν: sive, ut Justinus dicto loco Christianam contra Stoicos sententiam explicans loquitur, τὴν προαίρε- σιν. Hæ & possunt, & nimium sæpe solent ab hominibus ἀθετεῖσθαι, ut illud misericors Dei consilium, quod ad Pha- risæos non minus quam ad alios judæos pertinebat: unde βυλὴν εἰς ἑαυτὺς dixit hoc loco Christus, consilium ad ipsos ipforumque salutem pertinens. Neque id mutabilem facit Deum: nam exitus consilii non suspenditur, nisi ab ea ipsa conditione quam consilio suo inesse Deus voluit: idque optima ratione. Nam ut Justinus inquit, ἐκ ἧν ἀξία ἀμοιβῆς ἢ ἐπαίνε ἐκ ἀφ᾽ ἑαυτῦ ἑλόμενον τὸ ἀγαθὸν, provoca- tus jam scilicet divino beneficio. Alibi dixit: ὧ γὰρ ἦν ἐπαινε τὸν ἰδὶν ἑαυτῶ εἰ ἐκ ἧν ἐπ᾽ ἀμφότερα τρέπεσθαι: cui similem sen- tentiam habet doctissimus Athenagoras. Hinc & illud Platonicum Justinus approbat: αἰτία ἑλομένε, idque eo loco ubi non suam peculiarem, sed communem ac consentien- tem Christianorum omnium ejus sæculi doctrinam propo- nit atque propugnat. Utrumque hoc genus consiliorum di- vinorum pulchre una sententia complectitur Prosper. Qui voluntatem Dei spreverunt invitantem, voluntatem Dei sen- tient vindicantem. Spernere dixit quod hic est ἀθετεῖν: Cle- menti Alexandrino ὑπερηφανεῖν. Ita enim hic: ὁ θεὸς ἵνα δέλων ὑὸς ἡμᾶς γενέσθαι βύλεται (habes hic βελὴν) οἱ δὲ καὶ υἱοὶ γενέσθαι ὑπερηφανήκασι. Multis verbis idem hoc ἀθετεῖν Arno- bius exprimit adversus nationes disputans: Si tibi fastidium tantum est, ut oblati respuas beneficium muneris, quin imo si tantum sapientia prævales, ut ea quæ offeruntur à Christo lu- dum atque ineptias nomines, quid invitans peccat? & mox, an, inquit, tibi adspernanti fugientique infundenda in gremium est divina benevolentiæ gratia? Vis sumere quod offertur, at- que intuos usus convertere? Consulueris tibi: aspernaris, con- temnis & despicis? Tu te muneris commoditate privaveris. Nul- li Deus infert necessitatem, imperiosa formidine nullum terret. Neque enim necessaria nostra illi salus est.

Τὴν βυλὴν θεῦ potius de ipso Dei proposito vel consilio accipiendum esse, quam cum Lud. de Dieu aliisque Calvinianis de mandato vel voluntate præ- cepti, adeoque notare id quod Deus secum consti- tuit facere, non quod faciendum censuit, Grotio annuimus: qui è Syro hanc explicationem pro- bat, & è perpetua vocis hujus βυλὴ in sacris u- surpatione, sive cum de hominibus agitur, ut in- fra XXIII. 51. Actor. V. 38. c. XXVII. 12. 42. 1. Cor. IV. 5. sive cum de Deo, ut Act. II. 23. cap. IV. 29. cap. XIII. 36. cap. XX. 27. Ephes. I. 11. Ebr. VI. 7. ut hoc loco significetur illud Dei propositum, quo cle- menter decrevit Judæos per Johannem ad resipiscen- tiam excitare, certa fide facta, priores culpas se con- donaturum: addo, & per baptismum, quem in remissionem peccatorum instituit, se ipsis illam re- missionis peccatorum gratiam concessurum. Il- lud vero consilium & propositum Dei spreverunt Pharisæi εἰς ἑαυτὺς, quod non est in seipsis, ut Ludov. de Dieu, & Beza cum Syro: quod merito reprobat Grotius, tum quia εἰς pro ἐν poni qui- dem solet, sed plerumque in loci descriptione, tum quia non de eo hic agitur, quod apud se co- gitaverint Pharisæi, & Legisperiti, sed de eo, quod palam testatum fecerint, sequitur enim μὴ βαπτισθέντες ὑπ' ἀυτῦ, quod cum illo sensu ta- citæ cogitationis non cohæret. Præfert ergo non immerito Beza cum plerisque aliis illam inter- pretationem εἰς ἑαυτὺς, id est, suo maximo da- mno: quæ sine dubio commodior priori est. Sed nec contemnenda videtur explicatio Grotiana, quæ ita habet: εἰς ἑαυτὺς omnino construendum arbitror cum illo τὴν βυλὴν, ex more Lucæ voces sæ- pe trajicientis, ut sit τὴν ὸ Θεῦ εἰς ἑαυτὺς βυλὴν ἠ- θέτησαν: Consilium Dei erga se. Nam εἰς pro ל Hebræorum particula poni solet ut ἀποκαταλλά- ξαι εἰς ἁυτὸν Coloss. I. 20. & infra IX. 13. βρώματα εἰς τὸν λαὸν, id est, τῷ λαῷ, vocem denique ἀθε- τεῖν recte verti rejici & è collatione Luc. X. 16. Johan. XII. 48. & ex ἀντιθέσἐ verbi δικαιῦν, quod est approbare atque laudare, non male colligit: adeo- que adversus Calvinianos concludit, rejici posse nonnulla Dei consilia, nec tamen Deum mutabilem fieri, siquidem exitus consilii non suspendatur nisi ab ea ipsa conditione, quam consilio suo inesse Deus vo- luit, laudans illud Prosperi, Qui voluntatem Dei spreverunt invitantem, voluntatem Dei sentiant vin- dicantem. Quo de alias. Nam autem inde cum Grotio voluntatis humanæ libertas in spiritualibus adserenda: nam etiamsi homo possit rejicere Dei gratiam adversus se, non tamen eam viribus propriis etiam acceptare potest: ad malum ni- mis quam proni sumus τῇ φύσει, num vero etiam ideo ad bonum? Peccatum originale utrumque infert, & quod proclives simus ad malum, & quod ἄχρηστοι ad bonum Rom. III. 12.

τίνι ἗ν ὁμοιώσω] Cohærent cum præcedentibus. Qui pu- tarunt Lucam interlocutum verbis Christi, infarserunt hic εἶπε δὲ ὁ κύριος, ut significarent rediri ad sermonem Christi. Sed hoc assumentum multi veteres codices Græ- ci Latinique non habent. Neque Ambrosius legit neque Theophylactus neque Euthymius: sed nec Syrus, nec A- rabs quare non dubito pronunciare esse παρεμβεβλημένον.

## 7:32
Vers. 32. ἐκλαύσατε] Matthew [has] ἐκόψατε. Weeping and wailing were accustomed to be joined, as is clear from the Tragedies.

Latin:

Vers. 32. ἐκλαύσατε] ἐκόψατε Matthæus. Solebant conjungi fletus & planctus, ut ex Tragoediis liquet.

## 7:35
Vers. 35. ἐδικαιώθη ἡ σοφία ἀπὸ τῶν τέκνων ἁυτῆς πάντων.] He calls the most wise counsel of God 'wisdom,' first in sending John the herald of repentance with a diet much more severe than that of the Pharisees, who were exceedingly pleased with themselves for their austerity of life: then in sending Jesus, easy and affable. Δικαιῦν, as above, is here also to approve and praise. Those who are fit to recognize divine wisdom are called 'children of wisdom' by a Hebraism: such, however, are those who acknowledge themselves to be unwise and burdened with sins, for the beginning of health is to confess the disease. Such as were these were baptized by John, and more fully taught by Jesus. See what we have said on Matthew.

By Wisdom some understand the Hypostatic wisdom, because the children of wisdom are the children of Christ, who called His faithful ones children. Concerning which in the Paraskev. Anti-Crelliana, Rostochian Dissertations, page 87. Compare what [is said] on Matt. XI. 19. If, however, ἡ σοφία is understood of the counsel of God, it is to be understood not so much of John's more severe diet and of Jesus's affability, as of the fact that God had concluded within Himself the method of leading to salvation through faith in Christ and Baptism as the ordinary medium of salvation.

PART V. The anointing and absolution of the sinful woman.

Latin:

Vers. 35. ἐδικαιώθη ἡ σοφία ἀπὸ τῶν τέκνων ἁυτῆς πάντων.] σοφίαν vocat sapientissimum Dei consilium, primum in mittendo Johanne præcone pœnitentiæ victu multo seve- riore quam esset Pharisæorum, qui vitæ austeritate sibi exi- mie placebant: deinde in mittendo Jesu facili ac comi. Δι- καιῦν, ut supra hic quoque est approbare & laudare τέκνα σο- φίας ex Hebraïsmo dicuntur hi, qui idonei sunt agnoscere divinam sapientiam: tales autem sunt qui se insipientes & peccatis oneratos agnoscunt, nam sanitatis initium est mor- bum fateri Tales qui erant, baptizati sunt à Johanne, plenius edocti ab Jesu. Vide quæ ad Matthæum dixi- mus.

Per Σοφίαν intelligunt nonnulli sapientiam Hy- postaticam, quia τέκνα σοφίας filii Christi sunt, qui fideles suos filios dixit. De quo in Paraskev. An- ti-Crelliana, Dissertationibus Rostochiensibus pag. 87. Conf. quæ ad Matth. XI. 19. Si tamen de consilio Dei accipiatur ἡ σοφία, non tam illud de Johannis victu severiori, & de Jesu facilitate, quam quod de ratione perducendi ad salutem per fidem in Christum, & Baptismum ceu medium salutis ordi- narium, penes se concluserat Deum, intelligen- dum.

PARS V. Mulieris peccatricis unctio & absolutio.

## 7:36
Vers. 36. Ἠρώτα δέ τις αὐτὸν τῶν Φαρισαίων] Simon by name, as is said shortly, who was formerly a leper and, as is credible, healed by Christ, Mark XIV. 3. For the reasons why we should not think the same history is handed down by the four writers have been brought forward at Matthew. Nor did Luke say anything why it should be believed that this happened immediately after the discourses of Christ had been narrated. Wherefore those who think that the order of events was observed here by him judge rightly. For that order is very conspicuous. For an illustrious example is subjoined to the words of Christ. Christ had said that men of a previously less praised life who acknowledge their sins are more fit to accept the benefits of God than those who please themselves more than is right. This history makes for the same thing, as the explanation will show.

We showed at Matt. XXVI. 6 that it is not the same history which is described by the other Evangelists concerning the anointing of Christ in the history of the Passion. If Luke, having neglected the series of times entirely, looked only at the order of events, and immediately related there the examples of the doctrine proposed by Christ that happened to occur, who does not see what a remarkable confusion and uncertainty will arise in the Evangelical history!

Latin:

Vers. 36. Ἠρώτα δέ τις αὐτὸν τῶν Φαρισαίων] Simon nomi- ne, ut mox dicitur, qui olim λεπρὸς & ut credibile est a Christo sanatus Marc. XIV. 3. Nam cur eandem à quatuor scriptoribus historiam tradi existimemus causæ ad Mat- thæum allatæ sunt. Neque Lucas quicquam dixit cur id continuo post narratos jam Christi sermones accidisset cre- dendum sit. Quare recte censent qui rerum ordinem hic ab eo spectatum putant. Est enim is ordo valde conspi- cuus. Nam verbis Christi exemplum illustre subjungitur. Dixerat Christus homines antea minus laudatæ vitæ pecca- ta sua agnoscentes magis esse idoneos ad acceptanda Dei beneficia, quam eos qui sibi plus æquo placent. Eodem facit hæc historia, ut explicatio oftendet.

Non esse eandem Historiam quæ à reliquis Evangelistis de unctione Christi descripta est in historia Passionis, ad Matth. XXVI. 6. oftendimus. Si Lucas negleƈta prorsus temporum serie rerum ordi- nem tantum spectavit, & quæ doctrinæ à Christo propositæ exempla forte occurrerint, eo statim retulit, ubi doctrina illa recensita, ecquis non vi- det, quam insignis confusio, & incertitudo in hi- storia Evangelica oritura sit!

## 7:37
Vers. 37. ἐν τῇ πόλει] That is, in the village. For those are accustomed to be used interchangeably. Bethany is indicated, where this noble woman was, the sister of Lazarus, Mary by name.

ἥτις ἦν ἁμαρτωλὸς] Not a victim of public lust, but otherwise of a life not very chaste; זונה, not קדשה, as the Hebrews distinguish. The Hebrews called such women properly and notably sinners. And what wonder that such fled to Christ, when they also came to the baptism of John? Matt. XXI. 32. Interpreters well advise, however, that either ἦν should have been translated, or certainly ἁμαρτωλὸν, as the Syrian took it, is said improperly, not from the present time, but from a life previously led, as also in Gal. II. 15. In which way the word ἀσεβεῖς is also taken in Rom. IV. 5.

Latin:

Vers. 37. ἐν τῇ πόλει] Id est κώμῃ. Nam solent ista pro- miscue poni. Bethania indicatur, ubi nobiles erat hæc fœ- mina Lazari soror, Maria nomine.

ἥτις ἦν ἁμαρτωλὸς] Non publicæ libidinis victima, sed alioqui vitæ parum pudicæ; זונה non קדשה ut di- stinguunt Hebræi. Tales fœminas Hebræi proprie & insigni- ter peccatrices vocabant. Et quid mirum tales ad Chri- stum confugisse, cum & ad Johannis baptismum vene- rint? Matth. XXI. 32. Bene autem monent interpretes aut ἦν vertendum fuerat, aut certe ἁμαρτωλὸν, ut Syrus ac- cepit improprie dici, non ex præsenti tempore, sed ex vi- ta anteacta ut & Gal. II. 15. Quomodo & vox ἀσεβεῖς su- mitur Rom. IV. 5.

## 7:38
Vers. 38. θριξὶ τῆς κεφαλῆς] The ancients well note that this woman did what Paul wishes all converts to do when he speaks thus: 'As you have yielded your members servants to uncleanness and to iniquity unto iniquity, even so now yield your members servants to righteousness unto holiness' Rom. VI. v. 19. For women of less guarded modesty spend the greatest care on their hair.

Which is the first ornament of beauty, the hair has fallen. Therefore Clement calls the braiding of hair ἑταιρικὰς (harlot-like), Pædagog. III. cap. XI.

ἤλειφε τῷ μύρῳ] Not only the head, which was accustomed to be done for honored men, but even the feet themselves, so that nothing might be lacking to testify to the utmost humility of soul. You may find the anointing of feet even among the Greek comic poets Antiphanes and Cephisidorus. Curtius concerning the Indians: 'Having taken off their sandals, they anoint their feet with perfumes.' Aristophanes set down the three things that are here, washing, anointing of the feet, and kissing, and indeed in the services of women. 'And first my daughter washes me and anoints my feet and stooping down kisses them.' Where the Scholiast says: 'The care by women was ancient, and thus they honored fathers and old men, so that after washing they would anoint their feet.' And he says that Euphronius interprets the 'oily feet' in Homer in this way. And some say that they render it thus.

Latin:

Vers. 38. θριξὶ τῆς κεφαλῆς] Bene notant veteres fecisse hanc mulierem quod omnes conversos facere vult Pau- lus cum ita loquitur: ὥσπερ παρεστήσατε τὰ μέλη ὑμῶν δοῦλα τῇ ἀκαθαρσίᾳ καὶ τῇ ἀνομίᾳ εἰς τὴν ἀνομίαν, οὕτω νῦν παραστή- σατε τὰ μέλη ὑμῶν δοῦλα τῇ δικαιοσύνῃ εἰς ἁγιασμὸν Rom. VI. v. 19. Nam feminæ minus custoditi pudoris maximam comæ curam impendunt.

Quod primum formæ decus est, cecidêre capilli. Itaque Clemens περιπλοκὰς τῶν τριχῶν vocat ἑταιρικὰς, Pæ- dagog. III. cap. XI.

ἤλειφε τῷ μύρῳ] Non caput tantum, quod fieri honora- tis hominibus solebat, sed ipsos etiam pedes, ne quid ad summam animi demissionem testandam deeffet. Pedum unctionem etiam apud Antiphanem & Cephisidorum co- micos Græcos reperias. Curtius de Indis: Demptis soleis, odoribus illinunt pedes. Aristophanes tria quæ hic sunt posuit, ablutionem, pedum unctionem & osculatio- nem & quidem in mulieribus obsequiis. Καὶ πρῶτα μὲν ἡ θυγατήρ με ἀπονίζῃ καὶ τοὺ πόδ' ἀλείφῃ καὶ προσκύψασα φιλήσῃ. ubi Scholiastes: παλαιὰ ἡ διὰ τῶν γυναικῶν τιμελεῖα, κ' οὕτως ἐτιμίλουν τοὺς πατέρας κὶ γέροντας, ὥς ομὲτα τὸ νίψαι ἀλείφειν τοὺς πόδας. Εὐφρόνιθι δὲ ναὶ τοὺς παρ' ὀμήρῳ λιπαροὺς πόδας ὕ- τως ἀποδιδόναι τινας φησί.

## 7:39
Vers. 39. εἰ ἦν προφήτης] Fickle minds easily find that by which they may be offended. For not even the Prophets had known all things; but only those things which it had seemed good to God to reveal to them.

ποταπὴ] Of what life: for it follows ὅτι ἁμαρτωλός ἐστι.

ἥτις ἅπτεται αὐτῦ] For this was a decree of the Pharisees, that others are defiled by the contact of wicked men: which was false. And the caution regarding avoiding the company of such men ought not to have been extended to those already reformed.

Latin:

Vers. 39. εἰ ἦν προφήτης] Leves animi facile inveniunt quo offendantur. Nam nec Prophetæ omnia sciverant; sed ea duntaxat quæ Deo visum erat ipsis aperire.

ποταπὴ] Cujus vitæ: nam sequitur ὅτι ἁμαρτωλός ἐστι.

ἥτις ἅπτεται αὐτῦ] Nam Pharisæorum hoc erat scitum, contactu hominum flagitiosorum alios inquinari: quod falsum erat. Et cautio de vitando talium hominum acces- su non debebat ad jam emendatos porrigi.

## 7:40
Vers. 40. ἀποκριθεὶς ὁ Ἰησοῦς] Intending to show that he knew both who the woman was and who Simon was, not only outwardly, but also in the innermost recess of the heart.

ἔχω σοί τι εἰπεῖν] He courteously asks his host for permission to speak.

Latin:

Vers. 40. ἀποκριθεὶς ὁ Ἰησοῦς] Ostensurus notum sibi tum quæ fœmina tum quis Simon esset, non extra tantum, sed & in recessu intimo pectoris.

ἔχω σοί τι εἰπεῖν] Comiter à convivatore suo postulat lo- quendi veniam.

## 7:41
Vers. 41. δανειστῇ τινι] The Syrian is מרא חובא, that is, Lord of the debt, in Latin, creditor. For even that Latin word, when it pertains properly to a loan, began to be transferred to every cause of owing. Thus also the interpreter of Matthew, what he had called δάνειον, interpreted as τὸ ὀφειλόμενον. Moreover, both words δανειστῆ and χρεωφειλέτα exist in the Greek Prov. XXIX. 13.

- Vers. 42. ἐχαρίσατο] The Latin 'donavit' is good, that is, he remitted it for the sake of a gift, as the Emperors speak in L. Si donationis C. de donationibus. Thus also he who is freed from an obligation seems to have received something, as the rule of law holds.

Latin:

Vers. 41. δανειστῇ τινι] Syrus מרא חובא id est Domino debiti, Latine creditori. Nam & Latina ista vox, cum proprie ad mutuum pertinet, cœpit ad omnem debendi causam transferri. Sic & Matthæi interpres quod δάνειον dixerat, in- terpretatus est τὸ ὀφειλόμενον. Exstat autem vox utraque & δανειστῆ & χρεωφειλέτα in Græco Prov. XXIX. 13.

- Vers. 42. ἐχαρίσατο] Bene Latinus donavit, id est dona- tionis causa remisit, ut loquuntur Imperatores in L. Si do- nationis C. de donationibus. Sic & cepisse videtur qui liberatur obligatione, ut habet juris regula.

## 7:42
τίς ὖν αὐτῶν εἶπε πλεῖον ἀγαπήσει] Christ asks what is probable, not what is necessary. For men are accustomed to judge about men according to that which is probable.

Latin:

τίς ὖν αὐτῶν εἶπε πλεῖον ἀγαπήσει] Quid probabile sit Christus quærit, non quid necessarium. Nam homines de hominibus judicare solent secundum id quod probabi- le est.

## 7:43
Vers. 43. ὑπολαμβάνω] I think it is more correctly translated 'I suppose' than what pleases others, 'I answer.' For the Pharisee is answering what seems probable to him.

Latin:

Vers. 43. ὑπολαμβάνω] Rectius verti puto existimo, quam quod aliis placet respondeo. Nam quid sibi probabile vi- deatur respondet Pharisæus.

## 7:44
Vers. 44. βλέπεις ταύτην τὴν γυναῖκα] Do you see what this woman is doing?

ὕδωρ ἐπὶ τὲς πόδας με ἐκ ἔδωκας] Christ compares Simon to the woman: he had neglected even common duties; she had given extraordinary, and never-before-seen, proofs of her reverence for Christ. The cause of the difference is this, that the woman was conscious of great sins; Simon, being self-satisfied, as if he had less need of Christ, consequently also revered him less. Water was accustomed to be given to those arriving from abroad, as others have proven by several testimonies; to which add the passages 1 Kings XXV. 41, 1 Thess. V. 10. Now Christ had come from Jerusalem to Bethany: for he spent the days teaching in Jerusalem; he would usually withdraw to Bethany in the evenings, as we have seen elsewhere.

Latin:

Vers. 44. βλέπεις ταύτην τὴν γυναῖκα] Vides quid hæc fa- ciat?

ὕδωρ ἐπὶ τὲς πόδας με ἐκ ἔδωκας] Comparat Christus Si- monem fœminæ: ille etiam communia officia neglexerat: hæc eximia, nec unquam visa, documenta reverentiæ suæ in Christum dederat. Causa discriminis hæc, quod mulier peccatorum magnorum sibi esset conscia: Simon sibi sat placens, quasi minus opus Christo haberet, proinde quo- que minus eum reverebatur. Solebat aqua dari peregre advenrantibus, ut aliquot testimoniis alii probarunt: qui- bus adde loca 1. Reg. XXV. 41. 1. Thess. V. 10. Venerat autem Christus Hierosolymis Bethaniam: nam dies Hie- rosolymis docendo transigebat: Vesperis ferme Bethaniam concedebat, ut alibi vidimus.

## 7:45
Vers. 45. φίλημά μοι ἐκ ἔδωκας] This custom also pertains to those arriving from abroad. See what [I wrote] on Matt. XXVI. vers. 49.

- εἰσῆλθον] Since some Greek codices still prefer this reading, and besides the Syrian, the Arab acknowledges it, I judge it to be preferred to the other: although it does not matter much for the sense.

Latin:

Vers. 45. φίλημά μοι ἐκ ἔδωκας] Etiam hic mos ad peregre adventantes pertinet. Vide quæ ad Matth. XXVI. vers. 49.

- εἰσῆλθον] Cum hanc lectionem Græci codices nonnulli adhuc præferant, & præter Syrum Arabs eam agnoscat, præferendam alteri censeo: quanquam ad sensum non multum refert.

## 7:46
Vers. 46. ἐλαίῳ] Although the Hebrews are accustomed to call any ointments whatsoever καταχρησικῶς by the name of oil, as do the Greeks, just as the interpreters note regarding that Homeric εὐῶδες ἔλαιον, nevertheless there is no doubt that in this place common oil ought to be understood. For there is a perpetual ἀντιστοιχία (correspondence). That woman spends tears for washing the feet of Christ: Simon not even water. She is assiduous in kissing the feet of Christ: Simon did not receive Christ with even one kiss of the mouth. She pours precious ointment not only on his head, but also on his feet: He not even on his head with mere oil: which would have been for perfunctory friendship. You may see that oil was accustomed to be poured for guests, also Ps. XXIII. 5, and the passage Ps. XLV. v. 8 looks to the same thing.

Latin:

Vers. 46. ἐλαίῳ] Quanquam solent Hebræi unguenta quevis καταχρησικῶς olei nomine appellare, ut & Græci, quemadmodum notant interpretes ad illud Homeri εὐῶδες ἔλαιον, dubitandum tamen non est quin hoc loco oleum commune intelligi debeat. Est enim perpetua ἀντιστοιχία. Mulier illa lachrymas impendit pedibus Christi proluen- dis: Simon ne aquam quidem. Illa assidua est in pedibus Christi osculandis: Simon ne uno quidem oris osculo Chri- stum excepit. Illa pretioso unguento non caput tantum, sed & pedes perfundit: Ille ne caput quidem mero oleo: quod perfunctoriæ amicitiæ fuerat. Convivis oleum ef- sundi solitum videas & Psal. XXIII. 5. eodemque respicit lo- cus Ps. XLV. v. 8.

## 7:47
Vers. 47. For which reason I say to you, her many sins are forgiven, because she loved much] There are very many interpretations of this passage. Some think that Christ is speaking here of that love which precedes remission. And indeed, that faith which obtains remission is not without love. But that love is usually comprehended more under the name of repentance or even faith, since ἀγάπη is usually said specifically of that more robust love which is accustomed to follow faith and remission, namely the principal part of that holiness to which we are invited by the benefit of remission. Platonists are also accustomed to say that love is twofold, one tender before full knowledge, the other more robust after that same full knowledge. But the name ἀγάπη is more suitable to that more robust love, as can be seen in Rom. XIII. 10, 1 Cor. XIII. 13, Gal. V. 6, and 1 Pet. I. 22, where purification is said to have been made unto love. Add to this that this woman did not, as they suppose, obtain the forgiveness of sins now for the first time. For this event happened a little before the death of Christ: and thus those tears seem to have been born from the heard prediction of his death: and therefore they are accepted by Christ, not as a sign of repentance, but as a sign of love. But long before, this Mary, the sister of Lazarus, had been called blessed by Christ because she applied herself so diligently to his instruction, although Luke narrates this κατὰ προϋστερον in chapter X. 42, placing her name there where the praise of another is alone mentioned: here suppressing it, where there is mention of a former life, just as Mark and Luke are silent about the name of Matthew, where it is a question of the publican being called. Mary was therefore already long since a disciple of Christ, long since dear to Christ, as is also clear from the history of the resurrected Lazarus. Now indeed, that also is difficult, which the patrons of this interpretation say, that the reasoning is inverted by Christ, and whereas he had previously established love as the consequence of forgiveness, he now conversely posits forgiveness as the consequence of love. For certainly, if Christ had wished to infer what seems to them to be the case, he would not seem to have proposed the interrogation and expressed the confession to Simon quite aptly. I also see the ancients using the authority of this passage to prove that love is born from the benefit of remission, not the contrary: Irenaeus lib. III. cap. XXII. Having obtained the gift of incorruptibility from him so that he might love him more. For to whom more is forgiven, he loves more. Cyprian in the excerpts to Quirinus: That God is loved more by him to whom more sins are forgiven in baptism. In the Gospel according to Luke: To whom more is forgiven, he loves more: and to whom less is forgiven, he loves a little. Others think that the remission which has occurred is proven from love as a sign. But Christ does not simply say this, that her sins are already forgiven: but he places emphasis on the word αἱ πολλαὶ, which the preceding interrogation also demanded. And if it were a matter of a sign, it should rather have been said in the following member: ᾧ δὲ ὀλίγον ἀγαπᾷ, ὀλίγον αὐτῷ ἀφίεται. But I will not be longer in refuting the opinions of others: I will say what is most approved by me; let the fair reader judge. The Pharisee had thought that this woman should be rejected from the touch of Christ on account of the impurity of her life: Christ, on the contrary, wished to show that she was more worthy of his touch than those very people who were criticizing this act. For he is most worthy of touch who loves most. But that this should be believed of her, common reason first demanded, teaching that we are loved more by those to whom we have done more good: then the deeds also agreed, which surpassed Simon's pride, namely his mere invitation to dinner, in many respects. Therefore, with these two arguments, common presumption and the evidence of deeds, when Christ had proven her love for him, he refrained from stating the conclusion, as it was self-evident: namely, that this woman was most worthy of his touch. Which very thing he proves more validly by adding an enthymeme, in which both the conclusion and part of the argument are, as usual, left unsaid. This full argumentation would be: For the sake and hope of which deed God forgives many sins, that deed is by no means to be forbidden: But for the sake and hope of this deed, God has forgiven many sins to this woman: therefore it is not to be forbidden. The proposition is of conspicuous truth. The assumption is proven in this way: God is accustomed to forgive great sins, so that he may also obtain works of great love. But this work is such a one. For the sake of obtaining this work, therefore, God forgave many sins. The assumption of this argument had already been proven by the comparison of Simon's deed and the woman's deed. For Simon did not doubt that he had shown a deed of love in giving the little dinner to Christ. But she had done much more. The proposition is consistent with divine goodness and wisdom. It is illustrated from the opposite: for because those to whom less is forgiven love less, therefore it is fitting for divine wisdom to forgive even great and many sins, so that works of extraordinary love may exist. In Valerius Maximus it is: That it is not credible that he whom he loved so much would not be loved in return by him. This exposition seems to me to have nothing forced. For ὗ χάριν for the most part signifies a proposed end to the Greeks. And λέγω σοι is often accustomed to be interposed κατ' ἀπαρένθεσιν, as can be seen in this writer chapter XII. 5, and more openly c. XIII. 24, and c. XXI. 10. But in the forgiving of sins by God, we are taught in many places that works of love are looked upon as the end, some of which we have brought forward regarding those words of Zechariah, that we being delivered out of the hand of our enemies might serve him without fear. Irenaeus also seems to have taken that ὗ χάριν ἀφίωνται in the same way, in the passage already cited: I take ἠγάπησεν indefinitely, without a note of certain time, so that it can be rendered by the present not inappropriately. And ὅτι is the causal particle of that ὗ χάριν. For this reason this and similar deeds are highly esteemed by God, so that he forgives sins in the hope of them, because these deeds are of great love. This, therefore, is a paraphrase of the words of Christ: For the sake of this deed, I say, so that this might indeed come to pass, God has deigned to grant her the grace of sins, which, as you say, are both great and many: nor is that undeservedly: for what appears from this deed, she loves me, and in me God, most ardently. But if less had been forgiven him (as you think less has been forgiven you), he would also love less, just as you love less. You see, therefore, the most equitable reason for the divine counsel.

Grotius deservedly rejects the (Papist) explanation as if it were a matter of love which precedes remission, both because the name ἀγάπης is taken for love following remission, Romans XII. 10, 1 Corinthians XIII. 13, Galatians V. 6, 1 Peter I. 22, where purification is said to have been made, for love, partly because this woman has not now for the first time obtained the forgiveness of sins (which he proves by those arguments that proceed from a false hypothesis about this woman, noted at v. 36 and Matt. XXVI. 6), partly because that is a harsh thing which the patrons of that interpretation say, that the reasoning was inverted by Christ, and that whereas he had previously established love as the consequence of forgiveness, he now places forgiveness as the consequence of love, and partly because the ancients use the authority of this passage to prove that love is born from the benefit of remission, not the contrary; Irenaeus lib. III. cap. 22. Having obtained the gift of incorruptibility from him, that he might love him more. For to whom more is forgiven, he loves more. Cyprian in the excerpts to Quirinus: That God is loved more by him to whom more sins are forgiven in baptism. In the Gospel according to Luke, to whom more is forgiven, he loves more; and to whom less is forgiven, he loves little. Although these things are correct, it is not to be approved that Grotius, with the Papists, also established that love is given which precedes remission, appealing to the Platonic opinion concerning a double love, one tender before full knowledge, the other more robust after that same full knowledge. For what does Plato's opinion have in common with the Christian faith? And although that faith which obtains remission is not without love, because they are simultaneous in time, yet in the order of nature the latter is posterior to the former: nor does love contribute to the remission of sins, but faith alone: nor is love ever proposed as preceding the remission of sins, but always as a consequence. Whence most people establish that remission is proved here from love as a sign a posteriori: which explanation Grotius in vain infringes upon by the fact that it is not said here in the latter member, ὇́ς δὲ ὀλίγον ἀγαπᾷ̃, ὀλίγον αὐτῷ ἀφίεται, but in inverted order, ὧ δὲ ὀλίγον ἀφίεται ὀλίγον ἀγαπᾷ̃. Theophylact certainly thought it should be explained thus: πίστιν ἐνδείξατο πολλὴν, he declared his abundant faith. And the meaning is manifest, in Camerarius's judgment, concerning the similitude. For he to whom a greater debt is forgiven, for that reason loves more the one who conferred that benefit upon him. And this woman declares by offices of highest love how great a benefit she had received, having been freed by Jesus from so many and such grave evils of sins, so that charity or love can in no way be taken as the cause, but as a sign. Then as if one were to say that a servant is magnified by his Master because he is of great worth in his grace. For the cause is not that he is of great worth here, and therefore is magnified, but that is a sign or indication from which there is a conjecture that he is held in high regard by the Master. Which many of the Papists have also acknowledged. Hugo in the Gloss explained; BECAUSE is held SIGNATIVELY, not causally; that is, that it shows the matter to be so, it does not indicate the cause of the matter. Francisc. Toletus the Jesuit in h.l. ann. 73. That BECAUSE signifies the cause not of the matter, but of the proof. For it is an argument from effects and signs. Which he also confirms there by the authority of Gregory the Great, lib. VI. epist. 12; Salmero Tom. 1. pag. 327. Because, he says, because are conjunctions rendering a cause either a priori, as they frequently do, or a posteriori; according to that, many sins are forgiven her, because she loved much. He proves the remission of sins was done from the effect of great love. Similar is that in Ps. XVII. 6. I have cried out, because you have heard me, that is, the effect of your prompt hearing makes me clamorous in prayers, not doubting of the hearing: and in the commentary on 1 John III. disput. III. §. We know: When the Apostle says, we know that we have been translated from death to life: because we love the brothers, he seems to show a sign by which we can know a posteriori that we are fulfilling the commandment of love: just as it is said elsewhere. Many sins will be forgiven, because she loved much, that is, many or more than you, Pharisee, show me signs of love, which posit that the sins had been forgiven previously: just as when we say, this man is merciful and placable, because he spares his enemies, it is an argument from an effect and a certain sign which he produces, of which kind of argumentation there exist many testimonies in the scriptures.

Some observe that the particle ὅτι sometimes signifies wherefore, whence Didacus Stella assigns this meaning: Many sins are forgiven her, wherefore she loved much: according to which meaning he says that no difficulty remains through any reason for doubting: and therefore he infers: Therefore the forgiveness of sins was first, and love followed afterwards, as is evident in the example of those debtors.

It is certainly clear that Christ is not teaching here what is the cause that the woman was justified, or obtained the remission of sins: because the Pharisee did not concede that, but denied it: whence Christ was proving it a posteriori, namely from love, and was illustrating it with the similitude or example of the two debtors: from which it is most manifest that love is not established as the cause of remission: For he loved more, he certainly had a cause for loving, to whom more had been forgiven. Therefore the particle ὅτι is not causal, but rational: and the inference is thus from the antecedents, whence those words ὦ χάριν λέγω Coi, are not to be separated, therefore I say to you, which show the force of the inference, as Flacius taught in the Gloss on this passage.

Grotius, however, having put aside those words, which he pretends should be read in a parenthesis, makes another but very twisted gloss of Christ's words: for the sake of this deed, therefore, so that this might happen (that that woman might anoint me), God deigned to grant her the grace of sins, which are both many and great. For because those to whom less is forgiven love less, therefore it is fitting for divine wisdom to forgive even great and many sins, so that they may be able to provide excellent works of love. Which meaning has hitherto come to no one's mind: and here Grotius presupposes, or assumes, that God forgives us many sins in the hope of our love: when on the contrary God does not forgive and remit sins to us for the hope of his own advantage, but for the sake of our salvation, and out of mere grace, and it is our part to love him and obey his commandments for the sake of gratitude for this grace. Christ designated no other cause of justification or remission of sins than faith alone v. 50. ἡ πίστις σου σέσωκέ σε.

Latin:

Vers. 47. ὗ χάριν λέγω σοι ἀφέωνται αἱ ἁμαρτίαι αὐτῆς αἱ πολλαί, ὅτι ἠγάπησε πολύ] Variæ sunt admodum hujus loci interpretationes. Quidam putant de ea dilectione hic a- gere Christum quæ remissionem antecedat. Et sane fides illa quæ remissionem impetrat sine dilectione non est. Sed ea dilectio solet magis aut pœnitentiæ aut fidei etiam no- mine comprehendi, cum ἀγάπη peculiariter dici soleat quis illa folitior quæ fidem & remissionem consequi solet, pars scilicet præcipua ejus sanctimoniæ, ad quam remissio- nis beneficio invitamur. Solent & Platonici dicere amorem esse duplicem,alterum tenerum ante cognitionem plenam, alterum robustiorem post eandem plenam cognitionem. Illi autem robustiori amori nomen ἀγάπης magis convenit, ut videre est Rom. XIII. 10. 1. Cor. XIII. 13. Gal. V. 6. & 1. Pet. I. 22. ubi purificatio dicitur facta ad dilectionem. Ad- de quod hæc femina, non, ut illi existimant, nunc primum veniam delictorum consecuta est. Accidit enim hæc res pau- lo ante mortem Christi: atque adeo illæ lachrymæ ex audita mortis prædictione natæ videntur: ideoque accipiuntur à Christo, non ut signum pœnitentiæ, sed ut signum dilectio- nis. Multo autem ante Maria hæc Lazari soror à Christo beata erat dicta quod ipsius institutioni tam diligenter im- mineret, quanquam id Lucas narrat κατὰ προϋστερον cap. X. 42. ibi nomen ejus ponens ubi sola alius ejus prædicatur: hic subucens, ubi prioris vitæ sit mentio, quomodo & Mat- thæi nomen reticent Marcus & Lucas, ubi de publicano vo- cato agitur. Erat igitur Maria pridem jam Christi discipu- la, pridem Christo cara, ut & ex Lazari resuscitati historia li- quet. Jam vero & illud durum est, quod dicunt istius in- terpretationis patroni, inverti a Christo ratiocinationen, & cum prius dilectionem statuisset consequens condonatio- nis, nunc vicissim condonationem ponere ut consequens dilectionis. Nam certe si hoc inferre voluisset Christus quod ipsis videtur, non satis apposite videretur interrogationem proposuisse & confessionem expressisse Simoni. Veteres quoque video hujus loci auctoritate uti ut probent dilectio- nem nasci ex beneficio remissionis, non contra: Irenæus lib. III. cap. XXII. Munus incorruptelæ consecutus ab eo ut plus diligeret eum. Cui enim plus dimittitur, plus diligit. Cyprianus in excerptis ad Quirinum: Plus ab eo diligi Deum, cui in baptismo plura peccata dimittuntur. In Evangelio κατὰ Lucam: Cui plus dimittitur, plus diligit: & cui minus dimit- titur modicum diligit. Alii putant ex dilectione tanquam signo probari remissionem quæ contigerit. At Christus non hoc simpliciter dicit jam remissa esse illi peccata: sed ἔμφασιν ponit in voce αἱ πολλαὶ, quod & exigebat antece- dens interrogatio. Et si de signo ageretur, dicendum po- tius in sequente membro fuerat: ᾧ δὲ ὀλίγον ἀγαπᾷ, ὀλίγον αὐτῷ ἀφίεται. Sed longior in refutandis aliorum opinio- nibus non ero: dicam quod mihi maxime probatur; judi- cet æquus lector. Putaverat Pharisæus rejiciendam hanc mulierem à Christi contactu ob vitæ impuritatem: Chri- stus contra ostendere voluit digniorem hanc esse suo conta- ctu quam illi ipsi qui factum hoc reprehenderent. Conta- ctu enim dignissimus ille est qui maxime diligit. Hoc au- tem de illa credi primum communis ratio exigebat, docens magis nos ab iis diligi quibus plus fecerimus boni: deinde congruebant & facta, quæ Simonis fastum, nudam scilicet vocationem ad cœnam, multis partibus superabant. His ergo duobus argumentis, communi præsumtione & fa- ctorum indicio cum dilectionem sui Christus probasset, abstinuit illationem ponere, ut quæ sponte pateret: dignis- simam scilicet hanc feminam esse suo contactu. Quod i- psum validius probat addito enthymemate, in quo iterum & illatio & pars argumenti de more subticentur. Plena ar- gumentatio hæc esset: Cujus facti gratia ac spe Deus multa peccata remittit, id factum minime prohibendum est: Hu- jus autem facti gratia ac spe, Deus multa peccata mulieri i- sti remisit: non est igitur id prohibendum. Propositio con- spicuæ est veritatis. Assumtio hoc modo probatur: Solet Deus remittere magna peccata, ut & consequatur opera magnæ dilectionis. Hoc autem opus tale est. Hujus ergo operis consequendi causa Deus multa peccata remisit. Hu- jus argumenti assumtio jam probata erat collatione facti Simonis & facti mulieris. Nam Simon quin in cœnula Christo danda exhibuisset factum dilectionis non dubita- bat. Illa autem multo plus fecerat. Propositio consen- tanea est bonitati & sapientiæ divinæ. Illustratur autem ex opposito: nam quia quibus minus remissum est minus diligunt, ideo divinæ sapientiæ convenit magna etiam & multa peccata remittere, ut exstare possint eximiæ dile- ctionis opera. Apud Valerium Maximum est: Non esse cre- dibile, ut quem tantopere amaret, ab eo invicem non diligere- tur. Videtur mihi hæc expositio nihil habere violenti. Nam ὗ χάριν plerunqne Græcis finem propositum significat. Et λέγω σοι sæpe κατ' ἀπαρένθεσιν interponi solet, ut videre est a- pud hunc Scriptorem cap. XII. 5. & apertius c. XIII. 24. & c. XXI. 10. In remittendis autem peccatis à Deo ut finem spectari opera dilectionis multis locis docemur, quorum nonnulla adduximus ad illa Zachariæ, ἀφόβως ἐκ χειρὸς τῶν ἐχθρῶν ἡμῶν ῥυσθέντας λατρεύειν αὐτῷ. Irenæus quoque illud ὗ χάριν ἀφίωνται eodem modo accepisse videtur, loco jam citato: ἠγάπησεν accipio ἀορίστως, fine certi temporis no- ta, ita ut per præsens reddi non incommode possit. Et ὅτι est αἰτιολογικὸν illius ὗ χάριν. Nam ideo hoc & huic similia fa- cta magni à Deo æstimantur, ita ut eorum spe peccata re- mittat, quia facta hæc magnæ sunt dilectionis. Est ergo hæc verborum Christi παράφρασις: Hujus inquam facti ergo, ut hoc nimirum fieret, Deus dignatus est illi gratiam facere peccatorum, quæ ut dicis & magna & multa sunt: ne- que id immerito: nam quod ex hoc facto apparet, & me & in me Deum ardentissime illa diligit: quod si minus il- li condonatum esset (ut tu minus tibi condonatum putas) minus quoque diligeret, ut tu minus diligis. Vides ergo consilii divini æquissimam rationem.

Merito reprobat Grotius explicationem (Pa- pistarum) quasi de dilectione agatur, quæ remif- sionem antecedat, tum quia ἀγάπης nomen de consequente remissionem dilectione accipiatur, Ro- man. XII. 10. 1. Corinth. XIII. 13. Galat. V. 6. 1. Petr. I. 22. ubi purificatio dicitur facta, ad- dilectionem, tum quia mulier haec non nunc pri- mum veniam delictorum consecuta est (quod ar- gumentis iis probat, quae ex falsa hypothesi de hac muliere procedunt ad v. 36. & Matth. XXVI. 6. notata) tum quia durum illud est, quod dicunt illius interpretationis patroni, inverti a Christo ra- tiocinationem, & cum prius dilectionem statuisset consequens condonationis, nunc condonationem po- nere, ut consequens, dilectionis tum quod veteres hujus loci auctoritate utantur, ut probent dile- ctionem nasci ex beneficio remissionis, non contra; Irenaeus lib. III. cap. 22. Munus incorruptela consequutus ab eo, ut plus diligeret eum. Cui e- nim plus dimittitur, plus diligit. Cyprianus in excerptis ad Quirinum: Plus ab eo diligi Deum, cui in baptismo plura peccata dimittuntur. In Ev- angelio ad Lucam, cui plus dimittitur, plus di- ligit; & cui minus dimittitur, modicum diligit. Haec quanquam recte sese habeant, non tamen probandum, quod Grotius etiam dilectionem da- ri, quae remissionem antecedat, cum Papistis sta- tuit, ad Platonicam provocans sententiam, de amore duplici altero tenero ante cognitionem ple- nam, altero robustiori post eandem plenam cognitio- nem. Quid enim Platonis sententia cum fide Christiana commercii habet? Etsi autem fides il- la, quae remissionem impetrat, sine dilectione non est, quia tempore simul sunt, natura tamen ordine haec illa posterior est: neque ad remissio- nem peccatorum facit dilectio, sed sola fides: neque uspiam dilectio ut antecedens remissionis peccatorum, sed semper ut consequens proponi- tur. Unde hic ex dilectione tanquam signo a posteriori, remissionem probari plerique sta- tuunt: quam explicationem nequicquam eo in- fringit Grotius, quod hic non dictum sit in po- steriori membro, ὇́ς δὲ ὀλίγον ἀγαπᾷ̃, ὀλίγον αὐτῷ ἀφίεται, sed inversa ratione, ὧ δὲ ὀλί- γον ἀφίεται ὀλίγον ἀγαπᾷ̃. Theophylactus sane ita explicandum duxit: πίστιν ἐνδείξατο πολλὴν, de- claravit copiosam fidem suam. Et est sententia manifesta Camerario judice, de similitudine. Is enim cui condonatur debitum majus, eo nomine magis diligit illum, qui istud beneficium in ipsum contulit. Et mulier haec declarat officiis summi a- moris, quantum beneficium accepisset, tot & tam gravibus peccatorum malis liberata a Jesu, ut cha- ritas seu dilectio nullo modo possit accipi, ut causa, sed tanquam signum. Deinde ac si quis dicat, magnifieri servum a Domino, quod multum ille gratia apud eum valeat. Causa enim non est, quod multum hic valeat, ideo magnifieri, sed signum aut indicium istud est, unde conjectura sit, quod a Domino magni fiat. Quod etiam multi e Papi- stis agnoverunt. Hugo in Glossar. exposuit; QUONIAM tenetur SIGNATIVE, non cau- sative; quod nempe ostendat ita se rem habe- re, non causam rei indicet. Francisc. Toletus Jesuita in h.l. ann. 73. Illud QUONIAM cau- sam significat non rei, sed probationis. Est enim argumentum ab effectibus & signis. Quod etiam auctoritate Gregorii M. lib. VI. epist. 12. ibidem confirmat; Salmero Tom. 1. pag. 327. Quia in- quit, quoniam conjunctiones sunt causam reddentes vel a priori, ut frequenter faciunt, vel a posterio- ri; juxta illud dimissa sunt ei peccata multa, quo- niam dilexit multum. Probat remissionem pecca- torum factam ab effectu dilectionis magna. Si- mile est illud Psal. XVII. 6. Ego clamavi, quo- niam exaudivisti me, id est, effectus promtae ex- auditionis tuae reddit me clamosum in precibus, non dubitantem de exauditione: & in comment. in 1. Joh. III. disput. III. §. Nos scimus: Cum A- postolus ait, scimus quoniam translati sumus de morte ad vitam : quia diligimus fratres, videtur ostendere signum, quo præceptum dilectionis nosse possumus nos implere à posteriori: sicut alibi dicitur. Remittentur peccata multa, quoniam dilexit multum, id est, multa vel plura, quam tu Pha- risæe mihi signa dilectionis ostendis, quæ po- nunt peccata prius fuisse remissa: quemadmo- dum cum dicimus, hic est clemens & placabilis, quia parcit suis inimicis, argumentum est ab effectu & signo certo, quod edit, cujus quidem argumentatio- nis plura extant in scripturis testimonia.

Nonnulli observant particulam ὅτι quandoque significare quamobrem, unde Didacus Stella hunc sensum assignat: Dimissa sunt ei peccata multa, quamobrem dilexit multum: juxta quem sensum nullam manere difficultatem per rationem aliquam dubitandi, ait: ideoque infert: Itaque prius fuit dimissio peccatorum, & postea secuta fuit dilectio, sicut in illorum debitorum exemplo patet.

Id sane liquet Christum hic non docere, quæ causa sit, quod justificata, seu remissionem pec- catorum consecuta sit mulier: quia id non conce- debat, sed negabat Pharisæus: unde id probabat Christus a posteriori, nimirum a dilectione, & il- lustrabat similitudine vel exemplo duorum debito- rum: è quo utique manifestissimum est, non constitui causam remissionis dilectionem: Nam ille magis diligebat, diligendi certe causam habe- bat, cui plus remissum erat. Particula ergo ὅτι non est causalis, sed rationalis: & illatio sic ex antecedentibus, unde illa verba ὦ χάριν λέγω Coi, non sequestranda sunt, idcirco dico tibi, quæ vim illationis ostendunt, uti Flacius in Gloss. ad h. l. docuit.

Grotius vero verbis illis posthabitis, quæ in parenthesi legenda esse fingit, aliam sed valde contortam verborum Christi glossam facit: bu- jus facti ergo ut hoc nimirum fieret (ut me ungeret mulier illa) Deus dignatus est illi gratiam facere pec- catorum, quæ & multa, & magna sunt. Nam quia quibus minus remissum est, minus diligunt, id- eo divina sapientia convenit magna etiam & multa peccata remittere, ut præstare possint eximia dilectio- nis opera. Qui vero sensus hactenus nemini in mentem venit: & præsupponit, vel assumit hic Grotius, Deum multa peccata nobis remittere spe nostræ dilectionis: quum contra Deus non sui com- modi spe, sed nostræ salutis ergo, & ex mera gratia nobis peccata condonet, ac remittat, & no- strum sit gratitudinis causa ob hanc gratiam ipsum diligere, & præceptis ejus morem gerere. Cau- sam autem justificationis, vel remissionis pecca- torum nullam aliam Christus designavit, quam so- lam fidem v. 50. ἡ πίστις σου σέσωκέ σε.

## 7:48
Vers. 48. ἀφέωνταί σου αἱ ἁμαρτίαι] They have already been forgiven by me, who came into the world to testify to them. For Christ either adds these things, or signified them by his countenance and gesture, as the following things show.

Latin:

Vers. 48. ἀφέωνταί σου αἱ ἁμαρτίαι] Pridem remissa sunt per me, qui cum ea protestare in mundum veni. Nam hæc aut addit Christus, aut vultu gestuque significavit, ut sequentia ostendunt.

## 7:49
Vers. 49. τίς ἐστιν οὗτος ὃς καὶ ἁμαρτίας ἀφίησιν] I do not think this is of the calumniating Pharisees: but rather of others who were at the same banquet, who were wondering: which the little word καὶ seems to signify, so that the sense is: Who or how great is this man who even has the right of granting pardon? A similar manner of speaking is below c. 8, 25. Matth. VIII. 27. Mark V. 41. in which places the signification of wondering is manifest.

Latin:

Vers. 49. τίς ἐστιν οὗτος ὃς καὶ ἁμαρτίας ἀφίησιν] Non puto esse Pharisæorum calumniantium: sed potius aliorum qui in eodem convivio erant admirantium: quod significare videtur vocula καὶ, ut sensus sit: Quis aut quantus hic est qui etiam dandæ veniæ jus habet? simile loquendi genus est infra c. 8, 25. Matth. VIII. 27. Marci V. 41. quibus lo- cis manifesta est admirandi significatio.

## 7:50
Vers. 50. ἡ πίστις σου σέσωκέ σε] Do not fear those supercilious censors: do not consider yourself unworthy of my touch. Your faith, having previously worked repentance, absolved you from the crimes of your former life. Tertullian, against Marcion, comments on this passage as follows: 'But even if the stimulus of repentance had come from faith, through repentance, justified by faith, you hear from Him, "Your faith has made you safe," who had announced through Habakkuk, "The just shall live by his faith."' To which perhaps some light is added by Clement of Alexandria, who in Stromata II. 1 speaks thus: 'Repentance is the source and achievement of faith; for if one does not believe that what he was previously held by is a sin, he will not change; and if he does not believe that punishment hangs over the offender, and salvation over him who lives according to the commandments, he will not change even then; and hope itself is already constituted from faith.'

Go in peace) Depart happy, and conscious and certain of your happiness.

Latin:

Vers. 50. ἡ πίστις σου σέσωκέ σε] Noli superciliosos istos censores metuere: noli te indignam meo contactu existi- mare. Fides tua pœnitentiam operata pridem te à vitæ prioris criminibus absolvit. Tertullianus adversus Marcio- nem ita in hunc locum commentatur: Sed & si pœnitentiæ stimulus ex fide acciderat, per pœnitentiam, ex fide justifica- tam, ab eo audiis, fides tua salvam te fecit, qui per Abacuc pro- nunciaverat justus ex fide sua vivet. Cui forte lucis aliquid Clemente Alexandrino, qui Strom. II. 1. ita loquitur: Πί- στεως ἣν πηγὴ ἡ μετάνοια κατόρθωμα· ἐὰν γὰρ μὴ πιστεύσῃ ἁμάρτη- μα εἶναι ᾧ προκατείχετο, ὀυδὲ μεταθήσεται· κἂν μὴ πιστεύσῃ, κό- λασιν μὲν ἐπηρτῆσθαι τῷ πλημμελῦντι, σωτηρίαν δὲ τῷ κατὰ τὰς ἐν- τολὰς βιῦντι, ὀυδ᾽ ὕτως μεταβαλεῖται· ἤδη δὲ καὶ ἡ ἐλπὶς ἐκ πίστεως συνέστηκεν.

πορεύου εἰς εἰρήνην) Abi felix, & felicitatis tuæ conscia & certa.

## 8:1 Argument
CHAPTER VIII. ARGUMENT AND DIVISION.

Christ travels through cities preaching, with the Apostles and certain pious women as companions; a great crowd having gathered, He teaches parables, concerning the seed of the word and the fourfold field, concerning the lamp not hidden, and He warns how they ought to hear: and that they are His brothers and mother who hear the word and do it. Concerning the storm calmed, and the possessed man in the borders of the Gadarenes liberated, while Jesus is preaching publicly, the daughter of Jairus, and the woman with the issue of blood, the latter healed, the former raised to life.

There are four parts: I. The preaching of Christ through cities and villages, and the proposal of certain parables, with exhortation and excitement to hear the word, up to verse 21. II. The calming of the storm, up to verse 26. III. The liberation of the possessed man in the borders of the Gadarenes, up to verse 39. IV. The restoration of the daughter of Jairus and the woman with the issue of blood, the latter to health, the former to life, up to the final verse 56.

PART I. The preaching of Christ through cities, and the proposal of certain parables.

Verse 1. Through every city and village) Lest any Jew might be able to complain that he was passed over, Christ visits not only the cities, into which it was customary to gather from the fields on the Sabbaths, but He visits everyone in their own home.

and the twelve with Him) That they might receive from Him the form of teaching: not that they were teaching while the Master was present. For that was contrary to the ancient custom.

Latin:

CAPUT VIII. ARGUMENTUM ET PAR- TITIO.

Christus peragrat prædicando civitates comiti- bus Apostolis & piis quibusdam fœminis, multa turba congregata parabolas docet, de semine verbi & agro quadruplici, de lych- no non occultato, monetque quomodo audi- re debeant: quodque fratres & mater ejus sint, qui verbum audiunt & faciunt. De tempestate sedata, & obsessio in finibus Ga- darenorum liberato, Jesu publice prædican- te, Iairi filia, & muliere hæmorrhousa, hac sanata, illa resuscitata.

Partes sunt quatuor: Prædicatio Christi per civitates & vicos, & parabolarum quarundam propositio, cum parænesi & excitatione ad au- diendum verbum, ad v. 21. II. Tempestatis seda- tio, ad v. 26. III. Obsessi in finibus Gadarenorum liberatio, ad v. 39. IV. Filiæ Jairı & hæmorrhousæ restitutio, hujus ad sanitatem, illius ad vitam, ad v. 56. finalem.

PARS I. Prædicatio Christi per civitates, & parabola- rum quarundam propositio.

Vers. 1. κατὰ πόλιν καὶ κατὰ κώμην) Ne quis Judæus præte- ritum se queri posset, non urbes tantum obit Christus, in quas ex agris conveniri sabbatis solebat, sed domi suæ o- mnes invisit.

καὶ οἱ δώδεκα σὺν ἀυτῷ) Ut ab ipso acciperent docendi for- mam: non quod docerent præsente magistro. Id enim cum veteri more pugnabat.

## 8:2
Verse 2. Seven demons) There is no need to look for a figure of speech: neither in the word 'demons' since 'evil spirits' precedes: nor in the number seven: since even more demons have possessed one man, as those who called themselves a legion.

Latin:

Vers. 2. Δαιμόνια ἑπτὰ) Non opus est figuram quærere: nec in voce δαιμόνια cum præcedat πνευμάτων πονηρῶν: nec in numero septenario: cum etiam plures dæmones unum hominem obsederint, ut qui se legionem vocabant.

## 8:3
Verse 3. Steward) The Syrian translates it as 'master of the house' or 'steward': the Latin more correctly as 'procurator'. For whom the Latins call the procurator of Caesar, the Greeks call 'epitropos': according to which example the 'logothete' of Herod is here called by the same term. But as for those who seek from this an argument that it is lawful for wives to desert husbands who are aliens to the faith, I do not see what certainty it has. It is more credible either that she is called a wife who had been a widow, or that the husband was not an alien to piety: as God is accustomed to penetrate through certain chinks into courts otherwise too much closed to Him. For even in Nero's court there were not lacking those who favored Christianity, Phil. 4:22.

Susanna) From the lily. For 'shoshannim' and 'shushan' are 'krina' (lilies) to the Phoenicians, as the writer of the Etymologicum rightly says. But also to the Persians, as Athenaeus notes: whence the city Susa, and the ointment 'sousinon' which is 'krininon' (lily-scented).

who ministered to them of their substance) According to the Jewish custom, as Jerome rightly notes, women, especially widows, were accustomed to supply necessities to teachers: which the Apostles followed among the Jews. Paul omitted it among the Gentiles lest he should give an opening for sinister talk. But Christ preferred to admit this benefit than to be a burden to strangers to whom He was arriving, with the company of the Apostles. The best Greek codices, the Syrian, and certain Latin copies have 'to them'.

Latin:

Vers. 3. ἐπιτρόπυ) Syrus vertit רב ביתא οἰκονόμου : re- ctius Latinus procuratorem. Nam quem Latini Cæsaris pro- curatorem, Græci ἐπίτροπον vocant: ad quod exemplum hic λογοθέτης Herodis eodem vocabulo dictus est. Quod autem quidam hinc argumentum petunt, licere uxoribus viros à fide alienos deserere, non video quid certi habeat. Credibilius aut uxorem dici quæ vidua fuerit, aut mari- tum non alienum fuisse à pietate: ut solet Deus rimulis quibusdam in aulas alioqui nimium sibi præclusas pene- trare. Nam & in Neronis aula non defuêre qui Christia- nismo faverent, Phil. IV, 22.

Σωσάννα) A lilio. Nam שושנים & שושן sunt κρίνα Phœ- nicibus, ut recte inquit Scriptor Ethymologici. Sed & Persis ut notat Athenæus: unde urbs Susa, & unguentum σούσινον τὸ κρίνινον.

αἵτινες διηκόνουν αὐτοῖς ἀπὸ τῶν ὑπαρχόντων αὐταῖς) More Judaico ut recte notat Hieronymus mulieres, viduæ præ- sertim, solebant magistris necessaria suppeditare: quod se- cuti sunt Apostoli inter Iudæos. Paulus inter Gentes omi- sit ne sinistterioris sermonis ansam præberet. Maluit autem Christus admittere hoc beneficium, quam cum Apostolo- rum comitatu gravis esse ignotis ad quos adventabat. αὐτοῖς habent Græci codices optimi, Syrus, & Latini exemplaria quædam.

## 8:4
Vers. 4. τῶν κατὰ πόλιν ἐπιπορευομένων πρὸς αὐτὸν) For from all the cities, as he arrived in each, he drew many listeners with him like a dragnet, by the efficacy of his admirable doctrine.

Latin:

Vers. 4. τῶν κατὰ πόλιν ἐπιπορευομένων πρὸς αὐτὸν) Nam ex urbibus omnibus, ut in quamque advenerat, everriculi more multos auditores secum trahebat, admirabilis do- ctrinæ efficacia.

## 8:5
Vers. 5. ὃ μὲν) In this way, as appears from what follows: that is, ὃ μὲν, a part of the seed.

κατεπατήθη) This trampling (as some rightly advise) signifies the custom of the world, which forms a callus against the precepts of piety.

Latin:

Vers. 5. ὃ μὲν) ὡδιτέρως, ut ex sequentibus apparet: id est ὃ μὲν μέρος τοῦ σπόρου.

κατεπατήθη) Hæc conculcatio (ut quidam recte mo- nent) significat consuetudinem mundi ad pietatis præcepta callum obducentis.

## 8:6
Vers. 6. φυὲν) It did not lack all vivid force: for it began to sprout, Matthew says ἐξανέτειλε.

μὴ ἔχειν ἰκμάδα) Moisture is drawn by the root: the root requires deep earth. Therefore these things come down to one thing, ἰκμὰς ἰκμάδα which Luke says, which is the proximate cause τοῦ ξηραίνεσθαι, οὐκ ἔχειν ῥίζαν which Mark says, and οὐκ ἔχειν βάθος γῆς which Matthew says. Thus the poet said concerning vices:

And the tree of evil drives its roots deeper.

Arid places are unfruitful, Jerem. XVII. 6.

Latin:

Vers. 6. φυὲν) Non caruit omni vivida vi: nam enasci cœpit, ἐξανέτειλε inquit Matthæus.

μὴ ἔχειν ἰκμάδα) Humor hauritur radice: radix profun- dam terram postulat. Ideo in unum hæc recidunt, ἰκμὰς ἰκμάδα quod dicit Lucas, quæ est causa proxima τοῦ ξη- ραίνεσθαι, ἐκ ἔχειν ῥίζαν quod Marcus, & ἐκ ἔχειν βάθος γῆς quod Matthæus. Sic de vitiis dixit Poëta:

Et mala radices altius arbor agit.

Loca arida sunt infructuosa Jerem. XVII. 6.

## 8:7
Vers. 7. συμφυεῖσαι) Luke well notes that this seed sprouted, but that the thorns sprouted at the same time, so as to signify a double crop in one man, of which the bad one, if it is not immediately uprooted, suppresses the good one. To someone asking why thorns and tares grow more abundantly than grain, the answer was given that the earth is the mother of thorns and the stepmother of grain, that is, it brings forth thorns of its own accord, but grain only when provoked by the effort of human industry: you might not ineptly say the same of the human mind: for it brings forth those things which are of the flesh of its own accord and without labor, due to the natural commerce of the body: for a better crop, it has need of planting, cultivation, and labor.

Latin:

Vers. 7. συμφυεῖσαι) Bene notat Lucas enatum hoc se- men, sed simul enatas spinas, ut duplicem in homine uno frugem significaret, quarum quæ mala est ni statim evella- tur, bonam opprimit. Quærenti cuidam cur spinæ & lo- lia uberius, quam frumentum nasceretur, responsum est quia terra spinarum mater esset, frumenti noverca, id est spinas suapte sponte proferret, frumentum non nisi huma- næ industriæ conatu provocata: idem de humano ingenio non inepte dixeris: nam ea quæ carnis sunt, ob naturale commercium corporis sponte & sine labore profert: ad me- liorem frugem consitione, cultura & labore opus habet.

## 8:10
Vers. 10. τοῖς δὲ λοιποῖς ἐν παραβολαῖς) Supply πάντα γίνεται, which Mark added.

Latin:

Vers. 10. τοῖς δὲ λοιποῖς ἐν παραβολαῖς) Supple πάντα γίνε- ται, quod addidit Marcus.

## 8:11
Vers. 11. ὁ σπόρος ἐστὶν ὁ λόγος τοῦ Θεοῦ) Which James therefore calls the implanted word, c. I 21.

Latin:

Vers. 11. ὁ σπόρος ἐστὶν ὁ λόγος τοῦ Θεοῦ) Quem propterea λόγον ἔμφυτον Jacobus vocat c. I 21.

## 8:14
Vers. 14. πορευόμενοι) This word is redundant, as it often is in Matthew, πορευθέντες c. IX. 13, c. XXV. 16, and elsewhere. Wherefore the Syriac also omitted it. If it signifies anything, it signifies the passage of time, and nothing more.

ὀυ τελεσφορῦσιν) Those things are called τελεσφόρα by the Greeks which bring their fruit to full maturity and the time of harvest. Therefore Luke himself will now interpret τελεσφορεῖν not as καρποφορεῖν simply, but as καρποφορεῖν ἐν ὑπομονῇ. Hence Sophocles drew the translation in his Omens:

If indeed you have brought forth good things, grant that they be brought to completion.

Josephus also used the word τελεσφορεῖσθαι concerning women who do not miscarry. Luke openly signifies that these were not entirely sterile, but had a sterile outcome: Mark says, ἄκαρπος γίνεται.

Latin:

Vers. 14. πορευόμενοι) παρέλκει hæc vox, ut sæpe apud Matthæum πορευθέντες c. IX. 13. c. XXV. 16. & alibi. Qua- re & Syrus omisit. Si quid significat, significat processum temporis, nec quicquam ultra.

ὀυ τελεσφορῦσιν) τελεσφόρα Græcis dicuntur quæ fructum ad plenam maturitatem & messis tempus perferunt. Ita que Lucas ipse τελεσφορεῖν jam interpretabitur non καρπο- φορεῖν simpliciter, sed καρποφορεῖν ἐν ὑπομονῇ. Hinc tralatio- nem duxit Sophocles de Præfagiis:

Εἰ μὲν πέφητεν ἐσθλὰ, δὸς τελεσφόρα.

Josephus quoque τελεσφορεῖσθαι de mulieribus dixit non ab- ortientibus. Aperte significat Lucas hos non fuisse plane ste- riles: sed sterilem habuisse exitum: ἄκαρπος γίνεται inquit Marcus.

## 8:15
Verse 15. καρδίᾳ καλῇ κὴ ἀγαθῇ) It seems that Luke uses this expression, common indeed but explained more subtly by the philosophers, not without discernment. For when he had discoursed about those who are drawn away from virtue by the fear of inconveniences or by an excessive desire for external goods, he rightly opposes to them τὸν καλὸν κὴ ἀγαθὸν. For if we believe Aristotle, or whoever is the author of the Magna Moralia, ἐστὶ μὲν κακῶς λεγόμενον ἐπὶ τῷ τελέως σπουδαίῳ ἡ καλοκἀγαθία· καλὸς κἀγαθὸς γάρ, φήσιν, ὅταν τελέως σπουδαῖος· ἐπὶ γὰρ τῆς ἀρετῆς τὸ καλὸν κὴ ἀγαθὸν λέγεσιν οἷον τὸν δίκαιον καλὸν κὴ ἀγαθόν φασι, τὸν ἀνδρεῖον, τὸν σώφρονα, ὅλως ἐπὶ τῶν ἀρετῶν, ἐπειδὴ ἦν εἰς δύο διαιρῦμεν, κὴ τὰ μὲν φαμὲν εἶναι καλὰ, τὰ δὲ κὴ ἀγαθὰ. κὴ τῶν ἀγαθῶν τὰ μὲν ἁπλῶς ἀγαθὰ, τὰ δὲ ὄυ· καὶ καλὰ μὲν, οἷον τὰς ἀρετὰς καὶ τὰς ἀπ᾿ ἀρετῆς πράξεις· ἀγαθὰ δὲ ἀρχὴν, πλῦτον, δόξαν, τιμὴν, τὰ τοιαῦτα. ἔστι ὖν ὁ καλὸς κὴ ἀγαθὸς, ᾧ τὰ ἁπλῶς ἀγαθὰ ἐστὶν ἀγαθὰ, κὴ τὰ ἁπλῶς καλὰ, καλά ἐστιν· ὁὶ τοιοῦτος γὰρ καλὸς καὶ ἀγαθός· ᾧ δὲ τὰ ἁπλῶς ἀγαθὰ μή ἐστιν ἀγαθὰ, ἐκ ἔστι καλὸς καὶ ἀγαθός. ὥσπερ ὀὐδὲ ὑγιαίνειν ἂν δόξειεν, ᾧ τὰ ἁπλῶς ὑγιεινὰ μὴ ὑγιεινά ἐστιν. εἰ γὰρ ὁ πλῦτος καὶ ἡ ἀρχὴ παραγινόμενα, τινὰ βλάπτοιεν, ὀυκ ἂν αἱρετὰ εἴη, ἀλλὰ τὰ τοιαῦτα ὅσα ἂν ἀυτὸν μὴ βλάψῃ βυλήσεται ἀυτῷ εἶναι. And shortly after: ᾧ τὰ ἀγαθὰ πάντα ὄντα ἀγαθά ἐστι κὴ ὑπὸ τύτων μὴ διαφθείρεται, οἷον ὑπὸ πλύτε καὶ ἀρχῆς ὁ τοιοῦτος καλὸς κὴ ἀγαθός.

ἐν ὑπομονῇ) This word, frequent among the Hellenists, denotes that constancy which endures among adversities with the hope of better things.

Latin:

Vers. 15. καρδίᾳ καλῇ κὴ ἀγαθῇ) Videtur non sine dile- ctu voce hac vulgo quidem trita sed à Philosophis subtilius explicata uti Lucas. Nam cum de iis disseruisset qui metu incommodorum, aut externorum bonorum nimia cupidi- tate à virtute distrahuntur, his recte opponit τὸν καλὸν κὴ ἀ- γαθὸν.
