Nam si Aristoteli, aut quisquis est Scriptor τῶν ἠθι- κῶν μεγάλων, credimus, ἐστὶ μὲν κακῶς λεγόμενον ἐπὶ τῷ τελέως σπουδαίῳ ἡ καλοκἀγαθία· καλὸς κἀγαθὸς γάρ, φήσιν, ὅταν τε- λέως σπουδαῖος· ἐπὶ γὰρ τῆς ἀρετῆς τὸ καλὸν κὴ ἀγαθὸν λέγεσιν οἷον τὸν δίκαιον καλὸν κὴ ἀγαθόν φασι, τὸν ἀνδρεῖον, τὸν σώφρονα, ὅ- λως ἐπὶ τῶν ἀρετῶν, ἐπειδὴ ἦν εἰς δύο διαιρῦμεν, κὴ τὰ μὲν φαμὲν εἶναι καλὰ, τὰ δὲ κὴ ἀγαθὰ. κὴ τῶν ἀγαθῶν τὰ μὲν ἁπλῶς ἀγα- θὰ, τὰ δὲ ὄυ· καὶ καλὰ μὲν, οἷον τὰς ἀρετὰς καὶ τὰς ἀπ᾿ ἀρετῆς πρά- ξεις· ἀγαθὰ δὲ ἀρχὴν, πλῦτον, δόξαν, τιμὴν, τὰ τοιαῦτα. ἔστι ὖν ὁ καλὸς κὴ ἀγαθὸς, ᾧ τὰ ἁπλῶς ἀγαθὰ ἐστὶν ἀγαθὰ, κὴ τὰ ἁπλῶς καλὰ, καλά ἐστιν· ὁὶ τοιοῦτος γὰρ καλὸς καὶ ἀγαθός· ᾧ δὲ τὰ ἁπλῶς ἀγαθὰ μή ἐστιν ἀγαθὰ, ἐκ ἔστι καλὸς καὶ ἀγαθός. ὥσπερ ὀὐδὲ ὑγιαίνειν ἂν δόξειεν, ᾧ τὰ ἁπλῶς ὑγιεινὰ μὴ ὑγιεινά ἐστιν. εἰ γὰρ ὁ πλῦτος καὶ ἡ ἀρχὴ παραγινόμενα, τινὰ βλάπτοιεν, ὀυκ ἂν αἱρετὰ εἴη, ἀλλὰ τὰ τοιαῦτα ὅσα ἂν ἀυτὸν μὴ βλάψῃ βυλήσεται ἀυτῷ εἶναι. Et mox: ᾧ τὰ ἀγαθὰ πάντα ὄντα ἀγαθά ἐστι κὴ ὑπὸ τύτων μὴ διαφθείρεται, οἷον ὑπὸ πλύτε καὶ ἀρχῆς ὁ τοιοῦτος καλὸς κὴ ἀγαθός.

ἐν ὑπομονῇ) Hæc vox Hellenistis frequens constantiam illam denotat quæ inter adversa durat spe meliorum.

## 8:16
Verse 16. (λύχνε) He has used the name of the genus for the species. For it signifies a μόδιον, which Matthew and Mark express. Regarding the meaning, see under Mark.

Latin:

Vers. 16. (λύχνε) Generis nomen pro specie posuit. Nam μόδιον significat, quod exprimunt Matthæus & Marcus. De sensu ad Marcum vide.

## 8:17
Verse 17. γενήσεται) The future is used in the sense of that which ought to happen, as is often the case. And so, shortly after, he explains the same thing in the potential mood: εἰς φανερὸν ἔλθῃ.

Latin:

Vers. 17. γενήσεται) Futurum ponitur in significatione ejus quod oporteat fieri, ut sæpe. Itaque mox idem ex- plicat modo potentiali: εἰς φανερὸν ἔλθῃ.

## 8:18
Verse 18. ὁ δοκεῖ ἔχειν) We have explained this under Matthew.

Latin:

Vers. 18. ὁ δοκεῖ ἔχειν) Explicavimus ad Matthæum.

## 8:20
Verse 20. λεγόντων) The designation of the persons is missing: because the understanding is easy from that which preceded, διὰ τὸν ὄχλον. The construction is πρὸς τὸ σημαινόμενον.

PART II. The calming of the storm at sea.

Latin:

Vers. 20. λεγόντων) Deest personarum notatio: quia fa- cilis est intellectus ex eo quod præcessit διὰ τὸν ὄχλον. Con- structio est πρὸς τὸ σημαινόμενον.

PARS II. Tempestatis in mari sedatio.

## 8:23
Verse 23. συνεπληρῶντο) A mode of speaking very similar to that Virgilian one: 'jam proximus ardet' [now the nearest burns]. Verse 24. ἐπετίμησε) Thus the Greeks translate יאָגֶר, Ps. CVI. 8. there concerning the sea: here concerning the wind.

PART III. The deliverance of the possessed in the borders of the Gadarenes.

Latin:

Vers. 23. συνεπληρῶντο) Simillimum loquendi genus isti Virgiliano: jam proximus ardet. Vers. 24. ἐπετίμησε) Ita Graeci vertunt יאָגֶר, Ps. CVI. 8. ibi de mari: hic de vento.

PARS III. Obsessi in finibus Gadarenorum liberatio.

## 8:27
Verse 27. ἐκ τῆς πόλεως) The Syriac and Arabic recognize this part as omitted in the Latin. However, that man is to be understood not as having come from the city at that time, but as having been born and raised in the city; which perhaps the interpreter noticed less, and expunged this part as poorly coherent with the history. Soon, when he is described as acting in the manner of a wild animal, 'Itaque rediens' [And so returning] he is described as ἱματισμένος [clothed]. Verse 28. ἑωυήσε) With a most grave adjuration, as we learn from Mark. Verse 29. πολλοῖς γὰρ χρόνοις) I would prefer to explain it through πολλοῖς, which is in Mark: although the Syriac understood it otherwise. εἰς τὰς ἐρήμους) Sometimes into mountainous places, sometimes even into tombs, as Mark teaches. We have noted elsewhere that mountainous places are called ἐρήμος.

Latin:

Vers. 27. ἐκ τῆς πόλεως) Hanc partem Latino omissam agnoscunt Syrus & Arabs. Intelligendus autem est homo ille non ex urbe venisse id temporis: sed in urbe natus atque educatus fuisse: quod forte minus advertit interpres, idque partem hanc ut historiae male cohaerentem expunxit. mox cum ad feri animalis in morem, Itaque rediens describitur ἱματισμένος. Vers. 28. ἑωυήσε) Cum gravissima obtestatione, ut ex Marco discimus. Vers. 29. πολλοῖς γὰρ χρόνοις) Malim exponere per πολλοῖς quod apud Marcum est: quanquam aliter accepit Syrus. εἰς τὰς ἐρήμους) Modo in loca montana, modo in sepulchra etiam ut docet Marcus. Montana ἐρήμος dici alibi annotavimus.

## 8:31
Verse 31. Ἄβυσσον) What the Hebrews call תְּהוֹם, the LXX translate as ἄβυσσον, and that word is mostly used concerning the sea: yet it is also transferred to other things. For even divine judgments were called abysses: because they are unsearchable. In this sense, Paul interprets that which is in Moses, 'who shall descend into the abyss,' as bringing Christ back from the dead: because that place, that is, the seat of the dead, is impassable to us. Furthermore, by the name ἄβυσσον here, ᾅδης is not to be understood, but Tartarus: which two are not correctly confused. For we remember having said elsewhere, and it will have to be repeated below, that they do not pertain to demons, but only to dead men, both good and bad, and indeed only in the intermediate time between death and the resurrection. But Peter, following the example of the Greeks, called Tartarus that region in which impure spirits are kept as if captive until the time of judgment. Nor is there any doubt that it is the same ἄβυσσον here. For also in the Apocalypse of John, chapter XX. 3. where there is likewise mention of chains as in Peter: but the Greeks also called the abysses ταρτάρξε ἄβυσσα χάσματα. Nor do I agree with those who wish Tartarus to be the air.

By ἄβυσσον, if you listen to Grotius, ᾅδης is not to be understood, but Tartarus: because ᾅδης, by his authority, does not pertain to demons, but only to dead men, both good and bad, and indeed only in the intermediate time between death and the resurrection. But Peter, following the example of the Greeks, called Tartarus that region in which impure spirits are kept as if captive until the time of judgment. But even if we concede to Grotius that by the abyss is understood Tartarus here and in Apoc. XX. 3, concerning which 2 Pet. II. 4, it does not appear how ᾅδης is always distinguished from Tartarus.

And if indeed it is sometimes taken for the grave, Job XIV. 13, ch. XVII. 13, and sometimes denotes death, or the state of the dead in general, Gen. XLIV. 29, it must not be denied that it also sometimes occurs for hell, or Tartarus, where demons and damned men are tormented: who are not separated, but are tormented: nor is that to be found, which some wish, that demons in the air possess the bodies of men or beasts, by which they are permitted to visit our regions: unless they are accustomed to wander in the air at the time, whence the Greeks also called them δαίμονες ἠεροφοῖτες, and Paul calls this power granted to demons by God ἐξουσίαν τῷ ἀέρι; and elsewhere τὰ πνευματικά τῆς πονηρίας in the heavens; and that from the most ancient opinion of the Hebrews, which is also to be found expressed in the book Aboth. Where the Tartarus or ἄβυσσος of which there is mention here might be located, there is no great need to investigate. If, however, there is any room for a modest conjecture, I would prefer to place it outside this visible world, as also the region of blessed spirits, which some place in the center of the earth, which is almost the same as saying nowhere. The word ἄβυσσος itself certainly carries a sense of a certain vastness. And one can see ἐν τόπος ὃ τὸ ἔξω τῷ κόσμῳ ἔστιν, that is, that it is outside this world which alone was created for us. Nor perhaps would you wrongly refer to this what is in John ch. XII. 31, νῦν ὁ ἄρχων τῷ κόσμῳ τότε ἐκβληθήσεται ἔξω.

PART IV. The restoration of the daughter of Jairus and the woman with the issue of blood.

Latin:

Vers. 31. Ἄβυσσον) Quod Hebraei תְּהוֹם dicunt, LXX. vertunt ἄβυσσον, & plerunque de mari ea vox usurpatur: solum tamen & ad alia transferri. Nam & divina judicia daemones vocabantur: quia sunt impervestigabilia. Hoc sensu Paulus id quod apud Mosen est τίς καταβήσεται εἰς τὴν ἄβυσσον interpretatur Christum à mortuis reducere: quia & ad hos id est mortuorum sedes nobis est impervia. Caeterum hic ἄβυσσον nomine, non est intelligendus ᾅδης, sed Tartarus: quae duo non recte confunduntur. Nam de sunt alibi dixisse meminimus, & infra repetendum erit, non pertinere ad daemonia, sed tantum ad homines mortuos bonos malosque, & quidem medio duntaxat tempore inter mortem & resurrectionem. Tartara autem Graecorum exemplo Petrus dixit eam regionem in qua impurii spiritus ad tempus judicii velut captivi servantur. Neque dubium est quin idem hic sit ἄβυσσον. Nam & in Apocalypsi Johannis cap. XX. 3. ubi itidem vinculorum est mentio apud Petrum: sed & Graeci ταρτάρξε ἄβυσσα χάσματα dixerunt. Nec illis assentio qui aere esse volunt Tartarum.

Per ἄβυσσον, si Grotium audias, non intelligendus ᾅδης, sed Tartarus: quia ᾅδης, eo autore, non pertinet ad daemonia, sed tantum ad homines mortuos bonos, malosque, & quidem medio duntaxat tempore inter mortem & resurrectionem. Tartara autem Graecorum exemplo Petrus dixit eam regionem, in qua impuri spiritus ad tempus judicii velut captivi servantur. Sed ut per abyssum intelligatur Tartarum hic & Apoc. XX. 3. concedamus Grotio, de quo 2. Petr. II. 4. ita quomodo ᾅδης semper à tartaro distinguatur, non apparet.

Et si enim quandoque pro sepulchro accipiatur, Job. XIV. 13. cap. XVII. 13. nonnunquam & mortem, vel statum mortuorum in genere, Genes. XLIV. 29. notet, negari tamen non debet interdum etiam occurrere pro inferno, vel tartaro, quod daemones & damnati homines cruciantur: qui non separantur, sed cruciantur: neque illud inveniendum est, quod aliqui volunt ut daemonia in aëre hominum aut bestiarum corpora obsideant, quo dovere permitti ut nostras regiones invisant: nisi tempore in aëre ferme vagari solent, unde δαίμονες ἠεροφοῖτες Graeci etiam dixere, & Paulus hanc daemonibus à Deo concessam potestatem vocat ἐξουσίαν τῷ ἀέρι· & alibi τὰ πνευματικά τῆς πονηρίας in vocibus; idque ex vetustissima Hebraeorum sententia, quam & in libro Aboth expressam est invenire. Ubi locorum sit Tartarus aut ἄβυσσος cujus hic sit mentio, nihil valde opus est indagare. Si quis tamen modestae conjecturae est locus, malim extra hunc mundum aspectabilem eum ponere, ut & regionem beatorum spirituum, quam cum quibusdam in centro terrae, quod ferme perinde est quasi nusquam dicas. Ipsum certe vox ἄβυσσος vastitiem quandam sefert. Et videre potest ἐν τόπος ὃ τὸ ἔξω τῷ κόσμῳ ἔστιν, id est quod extra hunc orbem sit qui unus nostros est conditus. Nec male forte huc referas quod apud Johannem est c. XII. 31. νῦν ὁ ἄρχων τῷ κόσμῳ τότε ἐκβληθήσεται ἔξω.

PARS IV. Filia Iairi & hemorrhousae restitutio.

## 8:38
Verse 38. ἐδέσποδε) The Syriac reads it thus: and that is much better than the other reading. Verse 39. καθ' ὅλην τὴν πόλιν) That from which she was sprung, but it also teaches throughout the surrounding cities. Verse 40. ἀπεδέξατο αὐτὸν ὁ ὄχλος) They received him gladly: for that is the force of the word, as in Acts XV. 4, ch. XV. 27. Verse 42. ὡς ἐτῶν δώδεκα) Which age is most subject to the most dangerous diseases διὰ τὴν τῆς ἡλικίας προπὴν [on account of the inclination of the age]. ἀπέθνησκεν) That is, ἵμελλεν ἀποθνήσκειν [was about to die]. For the whole history speaks of her not having died yet when the Father went out: especially that which is below in verse 49. To die, for the philosophers, consists ἐν σιγμῇ [in a moment]. But speaking popularly, one is said to die who seems near to death. συνέπνιγον) This also is said ὑπερβολικῶς [hyperbolically], the sense is as it is in Mark. Verse 43. βίον) Luke calls it here and elsewhere what Cicero calls what Mark said τὰ παρ' ἑαυτῆς, קנינה קלין, as the Syriac translates: the Latin correctly calls it substance. For the name of livelihood is too narrow to fulfill this meaning. See below XV, v. 30.

Latin:

Vers. 38. ἐδέσποδε) Ita legit & Syrus: multoque id praestat lectioni alteri. Vers. 39. καθ' ὅλην τὴν πόλιν) Illam unde erat oriundus, sed & per urbes circumfitas docet. Vers. 40. ἀπεδέξατο αὐτὸν ὁ ὄχλος) Gratanter excepit: ea enim vis est vocis, ut Act. XV. 4. c. XV. 27. Vers. 42. ὡς ἐτῶν δώδεκα) Quae aetas periculosissimae maxime morbis obnoxia διὰ τὴν τῆς ἡλικίας προπὴν. ἀπέθνησκεν) Id est ἵμελλεν ἀποθνήσκειν. Nondum enim mortuam fuisse cum Pater exiret, tota historia loquitur: praecipue id quod est infra commate 49. Mori philosophis consistit ἐν σιγμῇ. At populariter loquendo mori dicitur qui morti vicinus videtur. συνέπνιγον) Etiam hoc dictum ὑπερβολικῶς, sensus est ut apud Marcum est. Vers. 43. βίον) Lucas & hic & alibi Cicero vocat quod Marcus dixit τὰ παρ' ἑαυτῆς קנינה קלין, ut vertit Syrus: substantiam recte Latinus. Nam victus nomen angustius est quam ut hanc significationem impleat. Vide infra XV, v.30.

## 8:47
Verse 47. οὐκ ἔλαθε (לא נשתררה). Verse 41. εἰσελθὼν) The aorist here ought to be translated by the future: so that it is the same as 'about to enter.' This is clear from Mark. καὶ Ἰάκωβον καὶ Ἰωάννην) The Syriac and Latin place this order of names; which I think should be followed since the Greeks also agree.

Latin:

Vers. 47. οὐκ ἔλαθε (לא נשתררה). Vers. 41. εἰσελθὼν) ἀόρισ hic per futurum verti debet: ut sit idem quod intraturus. Liquet id ex Marco. καὶ Ἰάκωβον καὶ Ἰωάννην) Hunc ordinem nominum ponunt Syrus & Latinus; quod sequendum puto cum & Graeci accedant.

## 8:52
Verse 52. ἐκόπτοντο αὐτὴν) The same expression is below in XXIII. v. 27. Briefly said for ἐπ' αὐτὴν as the Apocalypse speaks in I. v. 7 and chapter XVIII. v. 9. The Hebrews also fully say ספר עליו: more briefly ספר לו which the LXX translate as κόπτων αὐτὸν as in 1 Kings XIV. 13, ἦλθε Ἀβραάμ κόψασθαι Σαφράν, Gen. ch. XXIII. 2, and elsewhere. Verse 54. ἐκβαλὼν ἔξω πάντας) Understand from the preceding 'the mourners and the wailers.' Credible. The Arab, along with the Syriac, also acknowledges this part. It is credible that the Syriac [translator], because he did not see how this could be reconciled with what is narrated—that the parents of the girl were present at the miracle, which he [Jesus] later ordered others to do—since there was no difficulty if the words I mentioned were repeated. ἐ δὲ τὸ πνεῦμα αὐτῆς) Luke added this providently so that he might teach that the soul was not of the body, nor something that perishes with the body, but 'its own' [spirit], which after the exit of mortal life is elsewhere than where the body is, for the word 'returned' teaches that. Where it is, it does not matter to know. It is enough that it is in the hand of God, to whom pious people dying commend their spirit to be received for the body at the hour of the resurrection, of which these miracles provided images and a pledge.

Latin:

Vers. 52. ἐκόπτοντο αὐτὴν) Eadem locutio infra XXIII. v.27. Breviter dictum pro ἐπ' αὐτὴν ut loquitur Apocalypsis I. v.7. & cap. XVIII. v.9. Hebraici quoque plene ספר עליו: brevius ספר לו quod LXX. vertunt κόπτων αὐτὸν ut 1 Reg. XIV. 13. ἦλθε Ἀβραάμ κόψασθαι Σαφράν, Gen. c. XXIII. 2. & alibi. Vers. 54. ἐκβαλὼν ἔξω πάντας) Intellige ex superioribus τὰς κλαίοντας κὶ κόπτοντας. Credibile. Partem autem hanc cum Syro Arabs agnoscit quoque. Credibile est eum Syrum quod non videret quomodo hoc conciliari posset cum eo quod narratur parentes puellae miraculo adfuisse, quod adlios etiam postea forstì: cum nulla esset difficultas repetitis quas dixi vocibus. ἐ δὲ τὸ πνεῦμα αὐτῆς) Provide hoc adjecit Lucas ut doceat animum non esset corporis, nec aliquid quod cum corpore intereat, sed αὐτῆς ἄλοντι, quod post exitum vitae mortalis alibi est qua in ubi corpus, id enim docet vox ὑπέστρεψε. Ubi sit non refert scire. Satis est esse in Deo manu, cui morientes pii spiritum suum commendand recipiendum corpori in hora resurrectionis cujus imaginum & pignus ista miracula praebebant.

## 9:1 Argument
CHAPTER IX. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

JESUS, having conferred power over demons and fields, sends out and instructs the Apostles. Fame of him reaches Herod. The Apostles returning report how much they have done. Five thousand men are fed in the desert. The confession of the disciples about Christ delivered by Peter, the prediction of Christ concerning the passion with an exhortation to the cross and confession. The Transfiguration of Christ. Concerning the Father. The lunatic. Repeated prediction of the passion. The thoughts of the disciples concerning primacy, for whom a boy is set as an example. Concerning not forbidding one who is not of the group from casting out demons in the name of Jesus. Hospitality is denied to Christ in Samaria as he is traveling to Jerusalem, on account of which James and John wish to call down fire from heaven, for which they are rebuked and warned about the end of the coming of the Son of Man. to the three wishing to follow Christ and the responses given to them. We constitute two parts of the chapter: The first part contains the Acts before the journey to the third Passover, up to v. 17. The sending out of the disciples, to v. 10. The feeding of the five thousand, to v. 17. In the second part, the Acts begin from the third to the fourth Passover: such as the Confession concerning Christ, with Christ's admonitions, to v. 27. The Transfiguration of Christ, to v. 36. The healing of the lunatic, to v. 45. The correction of the ambition of the Disciples, to v. 50. The refusal of Samaritan hospitality, to v. 56. and the response given to the three wishing to follow Christ, to the final v. 62.

PART I. Concerning the remaining acts up to the third Passover.

(I.) The sending out of the Apostles.

Vers. 1. Τοὺς δώδεκα αὐτοῦ) The differing reading of the codices, since some add μαθητῶν, others ἀποστόλων, is an indication to me that both arose from an interpretation. Luke is accustomed to name the Apostles τοὺς δώδεκα without an addition, as in c. VIII. v. 1. below in verse 12. c. XVIII. 31. c. XXII. 3. 47. Acts VI. 2. as also Paul 1 Cor. XV. 5. Wherefore I do not doubt that it should be read thus here, with the added testimony of the Syriac and Theophylact, as has been noted by others. The Arabic added الرسل ἀποστόλους, whether he who reads it thus did so, or for the sake of explaining the name.

Latin:

CAPUT IX. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

IESUS potestate in daemones & agros collata emittit & instruit Apostolos. Fama ejus ad Herodem pervenit. Apostoli redeuntes quanta fecerint referunt. Quinque millia virorum cibantur in deserto. Discipulorum confessio de Christo à Petro edita, praedictio Christi de passione cum adhortatione ad crucem & confessionem. Transfiguratio Christi. De Patre. Lunatici. Iterata predictio passionis. Cogitationes discipulorum de primatu, quibus puer in exemplum sistitur. De alieno in nomine Jesu daemonia ejiciente non prohibendo. Hierosolymam proficiscienti Christo in Samaria denegatur hospitium, ob quod ignem immiti caelitus volunt Iacobus & Iohannes, ob id reprehensi, & de fine adventus filii hominis moniti. tribus Christum sequi volentibus & re- sponsis iisdem redditis. Partes duas constituimus capitis: Parte prima continentur Acta ante iter ad Pascha tertium, us- que ad v. 17. Emissio discipulorum, ad v. 10. Ci- batio quinque millium, ad vers. 17. Par- te secunda incipiunt Acta a tertio ad quartum Pa- scha: utpote Confessio de Christo, cum Christi monitis, ad v. 27. Transfiguratio Christi, ad v. 36. Lunatici sanatio, ad v. 45. Ambitionis Discipulo- rum correctio, ad v. 50. Hospitii Samaritani de- negatio, ad v. 56. & responsio tribus Christum se- qui volentibus reddita, ad v. 62. finalem.

PARS I. De actis reliquis usque ad Pascha tertium.

(I.) Emissio Apostolorum.

Vers. 1. Τοὺς δώδεκα αὐτοῦ) Differens codicum lectio, cum alii adjiciant μαθητῶν, alii ἀποστόλων, indicio mihi est utrumque natum ex interpretamento. Solet autem Lucas Apostolos nominare τοὺς δώδεκα fine adjectamento, ut c. IIX. v. 1. infra commate 12. c. XIIX. 31. c. XXII. 3. 47. Actor. VI. 2. ut & Paulus 1. Cor. XV. 5. Quare ita hic legendum non dubito, accedente testimonio Syri & Theophylacti, ut ab aliis est notatum. Arabs addidit الرسل ἀποστόλως, live qui ita legit, sive explicandi nominis causa.

## 9:3
Vers. 3. μήτε ἀνὰ δύο χιτῶνας ἔχειν) It depends, if I am not mistaken, on that which preceded, αἴρετε: so that the sense may be: and do not take so much with you, that you individually have two tunics. He understands by tunics those which are sufficient for a man to be well clothed. Concerning the matter itself, see Matthew.

Latin:

Vers. 3. μήτε ἀνὰ δύο χιτῶνας ἔχειν) Pendet, ni fallor, ex illo quod præcessit αἴρετε: ut sensus sit: neque tantum vobiscum sumite, ut singuli bina vestimenta habeatis. Ve- stimenta autem intelligit quæ homini bene vestiendo satis sunt. De re ipsa ad Matthæum vide.

## 9:4
Vers. 4. κἀκεῖθεν ἐξέρχεσθε) Depart from the same place when it is time to move. It appears that the Greeks and the Syrian read it thus; wherefore this reading is to be retained. The sense will be: remain there until you must depart from the city.

Latin:

Vers. 4. κἀκεῖθεν ἐξέρχεσθε) Indidem exite cum migran- dum erit. Apparet ita legisse Græcos & Syrum? quare retinenda hæc lectio. Sensus erit: manete ibi dum urbe exeundum sit.

## 9:7
Vers. 7. διηπόρει) This word of Luke signifies a certain wonder, below XXIV. 4. Acts II. 12. c. V. 24. chap. X. v. 17. Wherefore the Syrian not badly translates it here, as also elsewhere, מתחמר. The Latin translates it as 'was perplexed' in the cited place c. XXIV. 4. Elsewhere 'to be amazed'. The fame of the miracles and the diversity of judgments concerning Jesus so struck anyone that he did not know what to believe.

Latin:

Vers. 7. διηπόρει) Vox hæc Lucæ affonteam quandam admirationem significat infra XXIV. 4. Act. II. 12. c. V. 24. cap. X. v. 17. Quare non male hic, ut & alibi, vertit Syrus מתחמר. Latinus consternatum esse, dicto loco c. XXIV. 4. Alibi stupere. Fama miraculorum & judiciorum de Jesu diversitas ita ullum percellebant, ut quid crederet nesciret.

## 9:8
Vers. 8. ὅτι ς̓ ἀρχαίων) I think that the Prophets who had lived before are called ἀρχαίως: and that this is opposed to the opinion of those who thought Jesus was indeed a Prophet, but a new one, and not seen before. You could otherwise understand ὅτι ς̓ ἀρχαίων as one of those who had been before Elijah: for example, Samuel. For the Hebrews also distinguish the Prophets into the more ancient and the more recent.

Latin:

Vers. 8. ὅτι ς̓ ἀρχαίων) Puto ἀρχαίως dici Prophetas, qui antea vixissent: & id opponi eorum sententiæ qui Jesum Prophetam quidem, sed novum, neque antehac visum exi- stimabant. Posses alioqui intelligere ἵνα ς̓ ἀρχαίων unum ex iis qui ante Eliam fuissent: puta Samuelem. Nam & Hæbræi Prophetas distinguunt in antiquiores & recentiores.

## 9:9
Vers 9. τῷ δι᾿ ἑστῶτ̇) Teaching indeed the same things: but not baptizing as John: but performing miracles, which John did not do.

ἐζήτει ἰδεῖν αὐτόν) So that from his countenance and other signs he might discern whether he was John.

(II.) The feeding of five thousand men.

Latin:

Vers 9. τῷ δι᾿ ἑστῶτ̇) Eadem quidem docens: sed non baptizans ut Johannes: miracula autem edens, quod non fecit Johannes.

ἐζήτει ἰδεῖν αὐτόν) Ut ex vultu aliisque indiciis dignosce- ret an Johannes esset.

(II.) Cibatio quinque millium virorum.

## 9:10
Vers. 10. εἰς τόπον ἔρημον πόλεως καλουμένης Βηθσαϊδά) Into a place which was in the territory of the municipality of the Bethsaidans.

Latin:

Vers. 10. εἰς τόπον ἔρημον πόλεως καλουμένης Βηθσαϊδά) In locum qui in dominio erat municipium Bethsaidenfium.

## 9:13
Vers. 13. εἰ μή τι) An exception regarding what is being fed: Concerning this type of speaking, it has been dealt with elsewhere. It is understood: there is no hope of feeding them.

Latin:

Vers. 13. εἰ μή τι) Exceptio πρὸς τὸ ζωπώμενον: De quo loquendi genere alibi actum est. Subauditur: nulla spes est eos pascendi.

## 9:15
Vers. 15. ἀνέκλιναν ἅπαντας) An explanation of what preceded, ἐποίησαν. For ἀνακλῖναι, just like κατακλῖναι, is taken transitively. Nor does the Syriac read it otherwise. Indeed, many Latin copies also have 'they made them recline'.

Latin:

Vers. 15. ἀνέκλιναν ἅπαντας) Expositio ejus quod præces- sit ἐποίησαν. Nam ἀνακλῖναι, ut modo κατακλῖναι, sumitur μεταβατικῶς. Nec aliter legit Syrus. Imo & Latina mul- ta exemplaria habent discumbere fecerunt.

## 9:16
Vers. 3. εὐλόγησεν αὐτούς) That is, ἐπ᾿ αὐτοῖς, as has been sufficiently stated regarding Matthew.

PART II. OF CHAPTER IX. In which the Acts are begun from the third Passover to the fourth: Whence begins here SECTION III. OF THE ACTS OF THE MINISTRY OF CHRIST. Concerning the Acts from the third Passover of Christ to the fourth. (I). Peter's confession concerning Christ.

Latin:

Vers. 16. εὐλόγησεν αὐτούς) Id est ἐπ᾿ αὐτοῖς, ut ad Mat- thæum satis dictum est.

PARS II. CAPITIS IX. Qua inchoantur Acta a Paschate tertio ad quartum: Unde incipit hic SECTIO III. ACTORVM MINISTERII CHRISTI. De Actis a Paschate Christi tertio ad quartum. (I). Petri de Christo confessio.

## 9:18
Vers. 18. καταμόνας) In seclusion. See what is said at Mark in this place, who himself elsewhere uses this word καταμόνας in a clearly similar way, so as to exclude the crowd, not the disciples, ch. IV. v. 10.

Latin:

Vers. 18. καταμόνας) In secessu. Vide quæ ad Marcum hoc loco, qui ipse alibi simili plane modo vocem hanc κα- ταμόνας usurpat, ut turbam, non ut discipulos excludat, c. IV. v. 10.

## 9:23
Vers. 23. καθ᾿ ἡμέραν) It must be retained entirely. For the Syriac, Arabic, and Latin acknowledge it.

Latin:

Vers. 23. καθ᾿ ἡμέραν) Retinendum omnino. Nam a- gnoscunt Syrus, Arabs, Latinus.

## 9:25
Vers. 25. ἑαυτὸν δὲ) A popular explanation of what he said, 'his soul': for the body is not excluded. And here the Syriac has נפשך.

Latin:

Vers. 25. ἑαυτὸν δὲ) Popularis expositio ejus quod dixit ψυχὴν αὐτοῦ: neque enim corpus excluditur. Et hic Sy- rus habet נפשך.

## 9:26
Vers. 26. ἐπαισχυνθῇ με) We said at Mark that it is something other than what the Latins call 'to be ashamed of' faces, prayers, or faith: for there, to be ashamed is to revere. Here, on the contrary, it signifies to turn away because of a rejected lot. Wherefore a circumlocution is necessary.

(II) The transfiguration of Christ.

Latin:

Vers. 26. ἐπαισχυνθῇ με) Diximus ad Marcum aliud esse quam quod Latini dicunt erubescere ora, preces, fidem: nam ibi erubescere est revereri. Hic contra significat a- versari ob fortem abjectam. Quare circumlocutione o- pus est.

(II) Christi transfiguratio.

## 9:28
Vers. 28. ὡσεὶ ἡμέραι ὀκτὼ) We explained this at Matthew.

Latin:

Vers. 28. ὡσεὶ ἡμέραι ὀκτὼ) Explicavimus ad Mat- thæum.

## 9:31
Vers. 31. ἐν δόξῃ) The one as legislator, the other as the prince of the interpreters of the law, both meanwhile showing ministry to Christ, whom the law and the Prophets serve.

τὴν ἔξοδον) That this type of speaking was customary for the Hellenists has been abundantly shown by others. But also among the Latins, 'exitus' and 'excessus' occur everywhere for death. This locution can be numbered among those which confirm the most ancient tradition concerning the immortality of souls, of which kind some have been observed by Tertullian. Nor, however, does the conjecture of those displease who think there is an allusion to the ἔξοδον of the Israelites out of Egypt. For just as for them the exit out of Egypt was the beginning of liberty, whence Joseph is said to have 'made mention of the departing of the children of Israel', so also death was for Christ the way to glory: and by Christ's example for us: whence also the ancient Christians loved to call death ἔξοδον, 2 Pet. I. 15, which can be seen in Irenaeus, Clement, and others.

These things are well said. Therefore, that immortality of souls and transition to the blessed life was not unknown to the ancients. But that it did not consist in tradition alone, but in the testimony of Scripture, we have shown elsewhere.

πληρῶν) Thus Acts 14:26, 'the work which they fulfilled'.

Latin:

Vers. 31. ἐν δόξῃ) Ille ut legislator, alter ut legis interpre- tum princeps, uterque interim Christo ministerium ex- hibentes, cui serviunt lex & Prophetæ.

τὴν ἔξοδον) Usitatum fuisse genus hoc loquendi Helleni- stis ab aliis abunde ostensum est. Sed & apud Latinos exi- tus & excessus pro morte passim occurrunt. Potest hæc locutio iis annumerari, quæ vetustissimam de animorum immortalitate traditionem confignant, cujus generis ali- quot observatæ sunt a Tertulliano. Neque tamen displicet eorum conjectura qui allusum putant ad Israëlitarum ἔξο dov ex Ægypto. Nam sicut illis exitus ex Ægypto initium fuit libertatis, unde Joseph dicitur μνημονεύσας̾ τῆς ἐξόδου τ̓ υἱῶν Ἰσραὴλ ita & mors Christo via ad gloriam: & Christi exemplo nobis: unde & Christiani veteres amarunt mor- tem ἔξοδον dicere 2. Petr. I. 15. quod videre est apud Ire- næum, Clementem, atque alios.

Optime hæc dicta. Immortalitas ergo illa animarum, & transitio ad beatam vitam non ignota fuit priscis. Quam vero non sola traditione con- stitisse, sed testimonio Scripturæ, alias ostendimus.

πληρῶν) Sic Actor. XIV. 26. ἔργον ὃ ἐπλήρωσαν.

## 9:32
Verse 32. Βεβαρημένοι ὕπνῳ) Thus also Homer: βεβαρηκότες ὕπνῳ.

Latin:

Vers. 32. Βεβαρημένοι ὕπνῳ) Sic & Homerus: βεβαρηκότες ὕπνῳ.

## 9:33
Verse 33. κ̓ ποιήσωμεν) That is, ἵνα ποιήσωμεν. μὴ εἰδὼς ὃ λέγει) Out of amazement, as Mark notes.

(III.) The healing of the lunatic.

Latin:

Vers. 33. κ̓ ποιήσωμεν) Id est ἵνα ποιήσωμεν. μὴ εἰδὼς ὃ λέγει) Præ stupore ut Marcus notat.

(III.) Lunatici sanatio.

## 9:38
Verse 38. ἐπίβλεψον ἐπὶ τ̓ υἱόν μου ὅτι μονογενής ἐστί μοι) It appears that the Latin read it this way. But the Syriac and Arabic read it in this manner: ἐπίβλεψον ἐπὶ μοι, υἱὸς μονογενής ἐστί μοι, so that this is the beginning of the following narrative. Let those who have the means consult the ancient Greek codices.

Latin:

Vers. 38. ἐπίβλεψον ἐπὶ τ̓ υἱόν μου ὅτι μονογενής ἐστί μοι) Ita legisse. Latinum apparet. At Syrus & Arabs hunc in mo- dum ἐπίβλεψον ἐπὶ μοι, υἱὸς μονογενής ἐστί μοι, ut initium hoc sit sequentis narrationis. Consulant verustos codices Græcos si quibus copia est.

## 9:39
Verse 39. κράζει) After this verb the Latin reads τ̓ ῥήσσει, which seems to be an interpretation added from Mark or from that which is below in verse 42. The Syriac seems to have had that same thing before that κ̓ μόγις. μετὰ ἀφροῦ) As I said regarding Mark, it seems the Syriac did not understand the word ἀφροῦ and the verb derived from it, ἀφρίζειν. For in Mark it rendered another word twice: and no less so in this place, unless the codices differ greatly. It is the nature of the raging to foam. Euripides on Agave: 'releasing from foam and rolling her pupils askew.' The same on Orestes in Iphigenia in Tauris: 'foaming at the chin.' Philostratus in the Icon of the raging Hercules: 'spitting out much with foam.' Lucan on the Sibyl: 'Then first the foaming madness flowed through her frenzied mouth.'

(ζυντρίβον αὐτὸν) The other reading, Cυντρίβοντος, is not to be rashly rejected. For τῶ πνεύματος is to be understood. For the genitive is accustomed to be used in that way sometimes, that is, absolutely as they say, even where it was permitted to use the nominative.

Latin:

Vers. 39 κράζει) Post hoc verbum Latinus legit τ̓ ῥήσσει quod interpretamentum esse videtur ex Marco additum aut ex eo quod infra est commate 42. Syrus id ipsum ha- buisse videtur ante illud κ̓ μόγις. μετὰ ἀφροῦ) Ut ad Marcum dixi videtur Syrus vocem ἀφροῦ & verbum inde derivatum ἀφρίζειν non intellexisse. Nam apud Marcum bis aliud verbum reddidit: nec minus hoc loco: nisi valde discrepaverint codices. Spumare furen- tium est. Euripides de Agave ὑπ᾿ ἀφροῦ ἐξίεισα κἀ διαστρόφως κόρας ἑλίσσουσ̓. Idem de Oreste in Iphigenia Taurica τάζων ἀφρῷ γένειον. Philostratus Icone Herculis furentis πολὺ μὲν τὸ ἀφρῷ διαπτύων. Lucanus de Phœbade: Spumea tum primum rabies besana per ora Effluit.

(ζυντρίβον αὐτὸν) Non temere rejicienda est lectio altera Cυντρίβοντος. Subaudiendum enim τῶ πνεύματος. Solet quippe interdum genitivus eo modo, id est absolute ut lo- quuntur, usurpari, etiam ubi nominativo uti licebat.

## 9:42
Verse 42. ἀπέδωκεν αὐτὸν τῷ πατρὶ αὐτοῦ) See above, chapter 11:15.

Latin:

Vers. 42. ἀπέδωκεν αὐτὸν τῷ πατρὶ αὐτοῦ) Vide supra c. XI. 15.

## 9:44
Verse 44. εἰς τὰ ὦτα) The Syriac acknowledges this reading: but so does the Arabic.

(IV.) The correction of the ambition of the disciples.

Latin:

Vers. 44. εἰς τὰ ὦτα) Agnoscit hanc lectionem Syrus: sed & Arabs.

(IV.) Ambitionis discipulorum correctio.

## 9:46
Verse 46. διαλογισμὸς ἐν αὐτοῖς) A dispute, as this word is taken in Phil. 2:14, 1 Tim. 2:8. Therefore, about to indicate thoughts shortly, for the sake of distinction he said διαλογισμὸν τῆς καρδίας. Τὸ, τὶς ἂν εἴη) The 'to' here signifies 'namely' or 'to wit', as below in chapter 22, verse 2. Xenophon: 'he asked what kind of man he might be.' Thus also our author placed 'to' before 'how' below in 20:4 and Acts 4:21.

Latin:

Vers. 46. διαλογισμὸς ἐν αὐτοῖς) Disceptatio, ut hæc vox sumitur Phil. II. 14. 1. Tim. II. 8. Ideo mox cogi- tationes indicaturus discriminis causa dixit διαλογισμὸν τῆς καρδίας. Τὸ, τὶς ἂν εἴη) To hic valet nimirum aut videlicet, ut infra cap. XXII. v. 2. Xenophon ἠρώτησεν ὅτι δὲ τὸ ποδαπὸς εἴη. Sic & τὸ πῶς posuit noster infra XX. 4. & Actor. IV. v. 21.

## 9:48
Vers. 48. τοῦτο) That is, τοιοῦτο, as in Matthew, in which way the Syriac also interprets it here. It is of this kind: love is the same for all. μικρότερος) That is, ταπεινοφρονέστερος, as appears from Matthew.

ῆται] I think this reading, which the Syriac also acknowledges, should be retained. For Christ speaks of a future reward and understands the kingdom as the glory of the kingdom after the resurrection. See what I have said on Matthew.

Latin:

Vers. 48. τοῦτο) Id est τοιοῦτο ut apud Matthæum, quo- modo & hic Syrus interpretatur. Tale est: amor omni- bus idem. μικρότερος) Id est ταπεινοφρονέστερος ut ex Matthæo ap- paret.

ῆται] Retinendam puto hanc lectionem quam agnoscit & Syrus. Nam de futuro præmio Christus loquitur & regnum intelligit gloriam regni post resurrectionem. Vide quæ ad Matthæum.

## 9:49
Vers. 49. ὃς ἀκολουθεῖ μεθ' ἡμῶν] Supply ζὸς, which the Syriac correctly expressed: he does not follow you together with us. Mark ὃς ἀκολουθεῖ ἡμῖν, that is, he is not in our company.

Latin:

Vers. 49. ὃς ἀκολουθεῖ μεθ' ἡμῶν] Supple ζὸς quod recte expressit Syrus: non una nobiscum te sectatur. Marcus ὃς ἀκολουθεῖ ἡμῖν, id est, non est in nostro comitatu.

## 9:50
Vers. 50. καθ' ἡμῶν] What I noted regarding Mark must be repeated here, that not only the Syriac but also the Arabic and the Latin read ὑμῶν. See what I have said there.

(V.) The refusal of hospitality in Samaria.

Latin:

Vers. 50. καθ' ἡμῶν] Quod ad Marcum monui repetendum hic est, ὑμῶν legisse non Syrum tantum sed Arabem quoque & Latinum. Vide quæ ibi diximus.

(V.) Hospitii in Samaria denegatio.

## 9:51
Vers. 51. ἐν τῷ συμπληροῦσθαι τὰς ἡμέρας τῆς ἀναλήψεως αὐτοῦ] Regarding the word ἀναλήψεως, I have spoken at Mark 16:19; it undoubtedly signifies nothing other than being received to God, according to the usage of the Hellenists. Thus it is used of both Moses and Elijah, although they were by no means received in the way that Christ was.

Πληροῦσθαι & συμπληροῦσθαι to the Hellenists, like מָלֵא to the Hebrews, sometimes signifies a limit, sometimes a time not too far removed from a limit, which is how it must be taken here. Thus also Gen. 25:24, 'and her days to be delivered were fulfilled, and there were twins in her womb.' Yet this departure could not have been so far from the death of Christ (which is the beginning of the ἀναλήψεως) that he returned to Galilee after it and undertook a new journey to Jerusalem, as some think. For if Christ did not set out at this time to undergo death, what will be the emphasis in what follows, 'he set his face'? It has moved many that Luke narrates in the following sections not a few things that happened long before this last journey. But we have already often seen that many things are narrated by him as occasion arises, with the sequence of time set aside. The same has happened here, and it is not difficult to conjecture the reason. For when Luke had narrated two notable teachings of Christ, the first of which exhorted the Apostles to avoid ambition, the second to avoid envy, he believed it was a convenient place to add a third admonition against revenge; and so that this might be understood more correctly, he added the circumstances of the event from which that discourse had arisen. Thus also the histories that follow concerning the three men called by Christ are not to be thought to pertain to one and the same time, but have been gathered into one place because of the similarity of the subject matter, so that the impediments which are accustomed to intervene in a vocation might be understood in summary. Having treated these, Luke returns to the thread of the history, and to the vocation of the Apostles, from which he had begun this chapter, he adds the vocation of the other seventy.

This departure is usually referred to the feast of tabernacles, to which John, chapter 7:10, reports that Christ went up. For Luke does not say that those days were already fulfilled, but that this happened while they were being fulfilled. See the Harmony of B. Lyser, ch. 95, and J. Richardson in Ussher, Vol. II, Annals, p. 590. And the Evangelical Harmony testifies that these things do not pertain to the departure for the last Passover, but to the feast of σκηνοπηγίας. Excessive lack of historical sense or disorder is imputed to Luke if it is believed that the last departure to the Passover is designated here. That it finally follows in chapter 19 is clear. St. Luke is a guide of method and order, not a rhapsodic writer.

τὸ πρόσωπον αὑτοῦ ἐστήριξε] The LXX use this expression in Ezekiel and Jeremiah, as others have noted. Elsewhere they say ἐπιστῆσαι τὸ πρόσωπον, as in Lev. 17:10; ἐφιστάναι προσώπῳ, Prov. 21:29; ἑτοιμάζειν τὸ πρόσωπον, Ezek. ch. 4:3; Symmachus, ἐτόλμησε πρόσωπον, Prov. 7:13. These are, however, neutral words, which in most places denote stubborn impudence, but here, and not rarely among the Rabbis, they denote firm constancy of mind.

Latin:

Vers. 51. ἐν τῷ συμπληροῦσθαι τὰς ἡμέρας τῆς ἀναλήψεως αὐτοῦ] De voce ἀναλήψεως diximus ad Marcum XVI. 19. haud dubie ex usu Hellenistarum nihil aliud significat quam ad Deum recipi. Itaque & de Mose & de Elia usurpatur, Quanquam illi neutiquam eo modo sunt recepti quomodo Christus.

Πληροῦσθαι & συμπληροῦσθαι Hellenistis, ut מָלֵא Hebræis, interdum terminum, interdum tempus a termino non nimis remotum significat, quomodo hic sumi necesse est. Sic & Gen. XXV. 4. καὶ ἐπληρώθησαν αἱ ἡμέραι τοῦ τεκεῖν αὐτὴν, καὶ τῇδε ἦν δίδυμα ἐν τῇ κοιλίᾳ αὐτῆς. Neque tamen tam longe hæc profectio à morte Christi (quod initium ἀναλήψεως) abesse potuit, ut post eam redierit in Galilæam, iterumque novum iter Hierosolyma susceperit, quod quidam existimant. Nam si non hoc tempore Christus ad mortem subeundam profectus est, quæ erit ἔμφασις in eo quod sequitur τὸ πρόσωπον αὑτοῦ ἐστήριξε; Movit multos quod Lucas in sequentibus non pauca narrat multo ante iter hoc ultimum gesta. Sed jam sæpe vidimus ex occasione multa ab eo narrari, posthabita temporis serie. Idem hic contigit, nec causam conjectare difficile est. Nam cum duo insignia Christi monita Lucas narrasset, quorum prius ad vitandam ambitionem, alterum ad vitandam invidiam Apostolos hortabatur, commodum esse locum credidit adjiciendæ monitionis tertiæ adversus ultionem; quæ quo intelligeretur rectius, adjecit facti circumstantias, unde in eum sermonem deventum fuerat. Sic & quæ sequuntur historiæ de tribus hominibus à Christo vocatis, non putandæ sunt ad unum idemque tempus pertinere, sed in unum locum conjectæ sunt ob argumenti similitudinem, ut quæ intercedere soleant vocationi impedimenta compendio intelligeretur. Quibus pertractatis redit Lucas ad filum historiæ, & vocationi Apostolorum, unde hoc caput inchoaverat, subjicit vocationem aliorum LXX.

Profectio hæc referri solet ad festum tabernaculorum, ad quod adscendisse Christum Iohannes cap. VII. 10. perhibet. Non enim Lucas dicit, dies illos jam impletos esse; sed factum hoc esse, dum complerentur. Vid. Harm. B. Lyseri, c. XCV. & Iob. Richardsoni apud Usser. Tom. II. Annal. p. 590. Et Harmonia Evangelica testatur non pertinere hæc ad profectionem ad Pascha ultimum, sed ad festum σκηνοπηγίας. Nimia ἀνιστορησία vel ἀταξία Lucæ impingitur, si hic jam profectio ultima ad Pascha designari credatur. Quam demum capite XIX. sequi in aprico est. Dux Methodi & ordinis est S. Lucas: non vero Scriptor rhapsodicus.

τὸ πρόσωπον αὑτοῦ ἐστήριξε] Usurpant hanc locutionem LXX. in Ezechiele & Jeremia, ut alii notarunt. Alibi dicunt ἐπιστῆσαι τὸ πρόσωπον ut Levit. XVII. 10. ἐφιστάναι προσώπῳ Prov. XXI. 29. ἑτοιμάζειν τὸ πρόσωπον, Ezech. c. IV. 3. Symmachus ἐτόλμησε πρόσωπον Prov. VII. 13. Sunt autem voces mediæ, quæ plerisque locis obstinatum inverecundiam, hic vero, & apud Rabbinos non raro, firmam animi constantiam denotant.

## 9:52
Vers. 52. Ἀγγέλους] Perhaps John and James, who are named shortly after.

κώμην] Thus reads Theophylact and Tertullian, who translates it as 'viculum' (little village) against Marcion, IV. The Syriac and Arabic also. For to them, קִרְיָה is more a κώμη than a πόλις. And below there is 'another village.' Nor should it move anyone that someone asks how Christ could have been excluded from a village. For Christ did not wish to occupy hospitality by force; and he who denies hospitality excludes sufficiently.

Σαμαρειτῶν] See below 17:11.

ἑτοιμάσαι] A similar expression is found in Mark, chapter 14, verse 15.

Latin:

Vers. 52. Ἀγγέλους] Forte Johannem & Jacobum qui mox nominantur.

κώμην] Ita legit Theophylactus & Tertullianus qui viculum vertit adversus Marcionem IV. Syrus quoque & Arabs. Nam קִרְיָה illis magis est κώμη quam πόλις. Et infra est ἑτέραν κώμην. Nec movere quenquam debet quod quidam interrogat quomodo ex vico potuerit CHRISTUS excludi. Neque enim vi hospitium occupare CHRISTUS volebat: & satis excludit qui hospitium negat.

Σαμαρειτῶν] Vide infra XVII. 11.

ἑτοιμάσαι] Similis locutio apud Marcum cap. XIV. vers. 15.

## 9:53
Vers. 53. ὅτι τὸ πρόσωπον αὐτοῦ ἦν πορευόμενον εἰς Ἱερου- [salem] That is, ἐτέθη τὸ πρόσωπον ἀυτᾶ εἰς Ἱερκσαλὴμ, as the Syriac translates it here, or ἐδόθη as it is in the Greek version of Jeremiah, chapter 42:15, ἐὰν ὑμεῖς δῶτε τὸ πρόσωπον ὑμῶν εἰς ἀίγυπτον: or ἐτάχθη as it is in 2 Kings 12:17. For all these signify the preparations for a journey. The sense is: He was clearly going towards Jerusalem. For πρόσωπον is everything that is viewed externally or provides an indication, the Hebrews פנים. Thus 2 Chronicles 32:2, τὸ πρόσωπον ἀυτᾶ τῶ πολεμῆσαι ἐπὶ Ἱε- ρυσκλὴμ. And in a similar sense 2 Samuel 17:11, τὸ πρόσωπόν σε πορευόμενον ἐν μέσῳ ἀυτῶν, namely to battle. It seems possible to gather from this passage that the Samaritans acted more humanely toward the Jews than the Jews did toward the Samaritans. For John says of the Jews simply and indiscriminately, and συγχρῶνται Ἰκ- δαῖοι Σαμαρείταις. But the Samaritans here deny hospitality to Christ and his followers, not because they were Jews, which they could certainly have gathered from the speech of those who were sent or even from their dress, as appears in John 4:9, but because they were going to Jerusalem for the sake of religion, by that very fact professing that that place was peculiarly dedicated to worship: which was the chief point of controversy between the Jews and the Samaritans. Wherefore it is no wonder if in matters pertaining to that controversy the Samaritans did not wish to accommodate the Jews in anything. For outside of this controversy, as I have said, the Samaritans seem not to have denied the Jews those things which the reason of humanity demanded. Therefore the woman does not deny water to the Samaritan Christ when he asks; she is more surprised that it is asked of her. And in the parable of the wounded man, Christ sets a Samaritan helping a Jew, not a Jew helping a Samaritan. A more opportune place for speaking about the controversy itself between the Jews and the Samaritans will be at John.

Latin:

Vers. 53. ὅτι τὸ πρόσωπον αὐτοῦ ἦν πορευόμενον εἰς Ἱερου- [... ναλὴμ] Id est, ἐτέθη τὸ πρόσωπον ἀυτᾶ εἰς Ἱερκσαλὴμ, ut hic vertit Syrus, aut ἐδόθη ut est in Græca versione Jerem. cap. XLII. 15. ἐὰν ὑμεῖς δῶτε τὸ πρόσωπον ὑμῶν εἰς ἀίγυπτον : aut ἐτάχθη ut est 2. Reg. XII. 17. Nam hæc omnia iti eris apparatuin significant. Sensus est: Manifestus erant va- dens Hierosolyma versus. Nam πρόσωπον omne id quod exterius spectatur aut indicium præbet, Hebræi פנים. Sic 2. ChnXXXII. 2. τὸ πρόσωπον ἀυτᾶ τῶ πολεμῆσαι ἐπὶ Ἱε- ρυσκλὴμ. Et simili sensu 2. Sam. XVII. 11. τὸ πρόσωπόν σε πορευόμενον ἐν μέσῳ ἀυτῶν, nempe ad prælium. Videtur ex hoc loco posse colligi Samaritanas humanius cum Judæis e- gisse quam Judæos cum Samaritanis. Nam de Judæis dicit Johannes simpliciter & indiscriminatæ, & συγχρῶνται Ἰκ- δαῖοι Σαμαρείταις. At Samaritæ hic hospitium negant Christo ejusque sectatoribus, non quia Judæi erant, quod certe ex sermone eorum qui missi erant aut etiam ex ha- bitu poterant colligere, ut apparet Joh. IV. 9. sed quia Hie- rosolyma ibant religionis causa, eo ipso profitentes eum lo- cum esse adorationi peculiariter dicatum: quod erat præ- cipuum controversiæ caput inter Judæos & Samaritanas. Quare non mirum est si in rebus ad eam controversiam pertinentibus noluerunt Samaritæ Judæis quicquam com- modare. Nain extra hanc controversiam videntur, ut dixi, Samaritæ Judæis non negasse ea quæ humanitatis ra- tio postulabat. Ideo Samaritis mulier aquam Christo pe- tenti non negat; magis eam à se posci miratur. Et in fabula hominis vulnerati ponit Christus Samaritanum Judæo, non Judæum Samaritæ subvenientem. De ipsa Judæorum & Samaritanum controversia opportunior erit dicendi ad Johannem locus.

## 9:54
Vers. 54. πῦρ καταβῆναι ἀπὸ τῶ ὀυρανῶ] Thus the LXX in 2 Kings, chapter 1:10, καταβήσεται ἀπὸ τῶ ὀυρανῶ πῦρ, in the history of Elijah, and indeed in places near Samaria.

ὡς καὶ Ἠλίας ἐποίησεν] Besides the Syriac, the Arabic acknowledges it. And it appears that Tertullian read it so in his time. For Marcion was pressing this passage, to which argument he replies. Wherefore it is credible that it was expunged in the Latin by someone who feared that this passage might favor Marcion: which cause moved others to delete the following words as well. It is a wonder why Tertullian and after him Ambrose say that what the divine history narrates happened to two captains of fifty happened to a false prophet: unless there was an old tradition that those two leaders of the troop were false prophets: which is not incredible.

Latin:

Vers. 54. πῦρ καταβῆναι ἀπὸ τῶ ὀυρανῶ] Ita LXX. 2. Reg. c. I. 10. καταβήσεται ἀπὸ τῶ ὀυρανῶ πῦρ, in Eliæ historia, & quidem in vicinis Samariæ locis.

ὡς καὶ Ἠλίας ἐποίησεν] Præter Syrum Arabs agnoscit. Et Tertullianum apparet suo tempore ita legisse. Urgebat enim Marcio hunc locum, cui argumento ille respondet. Quare credibile est in Latinis ab aliquo expunctum qui verebatur ne locus hic Marcioni faveret: quæ causa alios movit, ut & sequentia delerent. Illud mirandum cur Tertullianus & post eum Ambrosius evenisse dicant Pseu- doprophetæ, quod divina historia narrat evenisse duobus πεντηκοντάρχοις: nisi vetus traditio fuerit duos illos agmi- nis duces fuisse Pseudoprophetas: quod non est incredi- bile.

## 9:55
Vers. 55. ἐκ οἴδατε ὅἰε πνέυματός ἐτε ὑμεῖς] There are those who interpret it: you do not know what spirit becomes you. But it is plainer and simpler to interpret it thus: you do not know what spirit possesses and moves you. Those who are versed in Hebrew letters know how widely the name of spirit extends. In its origin it signifies wind: because of its subtlety, which escapes sight, it is transferred to other things: first to substances. For GOD, good and evil angels, and then the very soul of man are called by that word. Then to accidents. For hunger and pestilence are called πνέυματα in Ecclesiasticus, chapter 39:33, 34. Thus also Paul the Jurisconsult said that a state is contained by one spirit. L. in rem, Digest on the vindication of property, which Conon the Mathematician had called ὑπὸ μιᾶς ἰξέως. But it is most common for that word to be used for the affections of the mind, just as the Apostle Paul said πνεῦμα κατανύξεως after Isaiah in Romans 11:8; thus רוח is used in Proverbs 29:11. Ezechiel 13:3 and elsewhere. The writer of the book of Wisdom says that wisdom is a φιλάνθρωπον πνεῦμα. Thus Clement in his book on Prophecy calls the qualities of the soul πνέυματα. The sense therefore is: You think you are moved by such a Spirit as Elijah was of old, add also Phinehas, Samson, Samuel, Elisha, who exercised the judgments of God with a strong spirit. But you are mistaken. You have indeed zeal, but not according to knowledge, and which therefore is of human affection, not of divine motion, which the following reason proves. This clause with the following one is missing in the manuscript which is in England, perhaps because these things seemed to the copyist to be spoken in anger.

Latin:

Vers. 55. ἐκ οἴδατε ὅἰε πνέυματός ἐτε ὑμεῖς] Sunt qui in- terpretantur: nescitis quis vos spiritus deceat. Sed pla- nius simpliciusque est ita interpretari, nescitis quis vos spiritus habeat atque agat. Sciunt qui in Hebræis literis versati sunt quam late pateat spiritus nomen. Origine sua ventum significat: ob cujus subtilitatem, quæ visum fu- git, ad alia transfertur: primum ad substantias. Nam DEUS, Angeli boni malique, deinde ipse hominis ani- mas eo vocabulo nuncupantur. Deinde ad accidentia. Nam fames & pestis πνέυματα vocantur Eccles. cap. XXXIX. 33. 34. Ita & Paulus Jurisconsultus dixit statud uno spiritu continetur. L. in rem, Digestis de in rem vindicatione, quod Conon Mathematicus dixerat ὑπὸ μιᾶς ἰξέως. Sed maxime usitatum est, ut pro affectibus animi ea vox ponatur, quomodo πνεῦμα κατανύξεως dixit post Esaiam Paulus Apostolus Rom. XI. 8. ita usurpatur רוח Prov. XXIX. 11. Ezech. XIII. 3. & alibi. Scriptor libri Sapientiæ σοφίαν ait esse φιλάνθρωπον πνεῦμα. Sic Clemens libro de Prophetia πνέυματα vocat τὰς ποιότητας τῆς ψυχῆς. Sensus ergo est: Putatis vos agi Spiritu tali quali olim E- lias, adde etiam Phinees, Samson, Samuel, Elisæus qui forti animo Dei judicia exercuerunt. Sed erratis, Ha- betis quidem ζῆλον, sed ἐ κατ' ἐπίγνωσιν, & qui proinde hu- mani est affectus, non divinæ motionis, quod probat ratio sequens. Hoc comma cum sequenti deest in manuscripto qui in Anglia est, forte quod exscriptori hæc aspersus dicta viderentur.

## 9:56
Vers. 56. ὁ γὰρ ὑὸς τῶ ἀνθρώπε ἐκ ἦλθε ψυχὰς ἀπολέσαι, [ἀλλὰ σῶσαι] Thus the Syriac and Latin read, as has been noted by others. Wherefore the fact that ἀνθρώπων is placed by some after ψυχὰς seems to be an interpretation, though an ancient one, since the Arabic also reads it. But as others have noted, and we have said elsewhere, נפשות are the men themselves, not only the better part. And the connection of the words in this place demands this. However, this explanation seems to cohere with the preceding ones in this way: A spirit that is truly divine discerns the moments of times most excellently: the one by which you are now moved does not do this: it is therefore not divine. The assumption is proved, because the reason of the times demands a gentleness much greater than that which was commonly exhibited in the times of the Prophets, since the Messiah himself had been sent not to exercise severe judgments, but for the saving of men, however sinful, sparing no effort to that end, so that he himself would devote himself to that business. The spirit of the law is called the spirit of fear, accommodated to the rationale of those times: the spirit of Christ, which the Apostles ought to have followed, is the Spirit of gentleness and lenity. Although if one examines the things themselves, even setting aside the rationale of the times, there was a great difference between that which Elijah did and that which the Apostles thought should be done: at that time the minions of the court, to whom it was sufficiently clear that Elijah was a Prophet of God, in order to prove their obedience to a king who had lapsed into profane worship, strove to drag the Prophet bound to the king, to the mockery of the true religion. Now those who for some centuries had received from their ancestors that God was to be worshipped in the Garizitan temple, being moreover irritated by the daily insults of the Jews against them, denied to Christ, who was unknown to them, those services which conflicted with their ancestral superstition. This error was more to be pitied than harshly punished. The Gospel indeed has its own weapons of last resort, which Peter exercised against Ananias, and Paul against Elymas: but the Apostles used them when there could be no suspicion of anger vindicating itself under the pretext of God: a color which imposes upon most people too much: they used them against men of stubborn malice, for whom no appearance of ignorance served as an excuse.

Grotius thinks the simpler meaning is this: you do not know what spirit possesses and drives you, rather than if it were rendered: you do not know what spirit becomes you; because those disciples indeed had zeal, but not according to knowledge, of human affection, not of divine motion. But both expositions amount to almost the same thing: namely, they were ignorant, and did not consider, how private vengeance does not become those who have set themselves up as teachers of others: for that Spirit, which they had received, is too holy to serve private desires, an etiology which Grotius extracts from the following: The Spirit, which is truly divine, best discerns the moments of times: The one by which you are now driven does not do that, because the rationale of the times demands lenity, therefore it is not divine, it proceeds from a false hypothesis: as if greater lenity were required in the time of Christ than around the times of the Prophets; since the Messiah was sent not to exercise severe judgments, but to save men, however sinful. For Scripture recognizes no distinction in the times before and after the advent of Christ, regarding the precepts of lenity: and the end of the advent of Christ, the salvation of souls, extends forward and backward, to the times of both the Old and New Testaments equally. The spirit of the law is indeed called the spirit of fear, but the Spirit of Christ is the Spirit of gentleness and lenity: But neither did the spirit of the law pertain only to the times before Christ, since even now those who are outside the grace of Christ are driven by that spirit; nor was the spirit of Christ reserved only for the latest times, because the examples of lenity and gentleness, just as the precepts, shine for us in the O.T., Rom. XV. 4. even by the example of Christ himself, (though under prediction) already proposed in the Old Testament v. 3. from Ps. LXIX. 11. See 1. Pet. III. 4. 5. Rom. XII. v. 19. 20. with a collation made with Deut. XXIII. verse 35. Prov. XV. 21. c. XIV. 29. c. XVI. 37. c. XIX. 11. XXV. v. 14. Eccl. VII. 9. 10. X. 14. Ps. XXXVII. 11. 2. Sam. XVI. 10. Syr. XLV. 4.

The argument of Christ by itself does not need these rugged circumlocutions: Because it is the part of the Son of Man to save, not to destroy souls, it becomes his disciples not to wish that men, however malevolent and inhuman, be consumed by the flame of fire, but rather that they be saved in life, if by chance they might still be converted, and be freed from the destruction of the soul. Thus there is no need with Grotius to interpret souls synecdochically as men, when men and souls are distinguished in the text; for it is said he did not come to destroy the souls of men, so that it is established that souls or lives are here properly regarded as those of men, and not that men themselves are indicated: Whence he did not fear to falsify the original text here for the sake of his gloss, by the omission of the word of men, which all Greek Codices indeed have, as does the Arabic: even if it is not expressed by the Latin and the Syriac. Grotius ought to have thought of what he himself advised at Luke XII. v. 49. Certainly you cannot sufficiently validly prove from those versions that it was read differently in the Greek Codices formerly than it is read now: since interpreters everywhere indulge themselves the right to depart from the letter while the sense is safe. Which observation of his is the more to be observed, the more he himself ignored the same in practice, most frequently gathering a different reading from versions, when they depart from the letter of the Greek Codex.

(VI.) The response given to the three wishing to follow Jesus.

Latin:

Vers. 56. ὁ γὰρ ὑὸς τῶ ἀνθρώπε ἐκ ἦλθε ψυχὰς ἀπολέσαι, [ἀλλὰ σῶσαι] Ita legit Syrus & Latinus, utab aliis est anno- tatum. Quare quod post ψυχὰς à nonnullis est positum ἀνθρώπων, interpretamentum videtur, antiquum tamen, quando & Arabs legit. Sed ut alii notarunt, & nos alibi diximus, נפשות sunt ipsi homines, non sola pars po- tior. Atque id exigit hoc loco verborum connexus. Vi- detur autem hæc αἰτιολογία ita cohærere superioribus: Spiritus qui vere est divinus, optime discernit momenta temporum: vester quo nunc agimini id non facit: none est igitur divinus. Probatur assumtio, quia ratio tem- porum exigat lenitatem multo majorem quam quæ communiter exhibita esset Prophetarum temporibus quippe cum ipse Messias missus esset non ad exer- cenda severa judicia, sed ad homines quamvis peccatores servandos, adeo nulli eam in rem parsurus operæ, ut se- metipse ei negotio esset impensurus. Spiritus legis, spiri- tus timoris dicitur, accommodatus illorum temporum ra- tioni : spiritus Christi, quem sequi debebant Apostoli, Spi- ritus mansuetudinis & lenitatis. Quanquam si quis res i- psas, etiam seposita temporum ratione examinet, multum intererat inter id quod fecit Elias & id quod faciendum censebant Apostoli: illo tempore aulæ mancipia, quibus satis constabat Eliam esse Prophetam Dei, ut obsequium suum regi ad profanos cultus delapso probarent, Prophe- tam ad regem vinctum pertrahere studebant in veræ re- ligionis ludibrium. Nunc illi qui per sæcula aliquot a majoribus illud acceperant, colendum esse Deum in tem- plo Garizitano, quotidianis insuper Judæorum in se con- tumeliis irritati, ea officia Christo incognito negabant, quæ pugnabant cum avita ipsorum superstitione. Mi- serandus magis erat hic error, quam acerbe ulciscendus. Habet quidem & Evangelium sua ultimæ necessitatis te- la, quæ in Ananiam Petrus, in Elymam Paulus exer- cuit: sed usi iis sunt Apostoli ubi nulla esse suspicio pote- rat iracundiæ semet sub Dei obtentu vindicantis: qui co- lor nimium plerisque imponit: usi sunt in præfractæ ma- litiæ homines, quibus nulla species ignorantiæ patroci- nabatur.

Simpliciorem sensum putat Grotius hunc esse: nescitis quis vos spiritus habeat atque agat, quam si reddatur: nescitis quis vos spiritus deceat; quia habuere quidem discipuli illi ζῆλον, sed δ'κατ'ἐπί- γνωσιν humani affectus non divinæ motionis. Sed utraque expositio fere eodem redit: ignorabant nempe, & non considerabant, quam non se alio- rum doctores constitutos deceat privata vindi- cta: Spiritus enim ille, quem acceperant, sanctior est, quam ut privatis cupiditatibus inserviat αἰ- τιολογίᾳ, quam è sequentibus eruit Grotius: Spi. ritus, qui vere divinus est, optime discernit momenta temporum: Vester quo nunc agimini, id non facit, quia ratio temporum exigit lenitatem, non est igitur divinus, è falsâ procedit ὑποθέσει: quasi major lenitas Christi tempore exacta sit, quam circa Prophe- tarum tempora; siquidem Messias missus sit non ad ex- ercenda severa judicia, sed ad homines, quamvis pec- catores servandos. Nam Scriptura nullum in temporibus ante & post adventum Christi agno- scit discrimen, quoad præcepta lenitatis: & finis adventus Christi, salus animarum, porrigit se an- trorsum & retrorsum, ad tempora æque Veteris ac Novi Testamenti. Spiritus legis dicitur quidem spiritus timoris, Spiritus Christi vero Spiritus man- suetudinis & lenitatis: Sed nec spiritus legis tantum pertinuit ad tempora ante Christum, quum etiam- num qui extra Christi sunt gratiam, eo agantur spi- ritu; nec spiritus Christi tantum reservatus fuit temporibus novissimis, quia lenitatis & mansuetu- dinis, ut præscripta, ita exempla in V. T. nobis præ- luceant, Rom. XV. 4. ipsius etiam Christi exemplo, (etsi sub prædictione) in Vet. Test. jam proposito v. 3. è Ps. LXIX. 11. Vid. 1. Petr. III. 4. 5. Rom. XII. v. 19. 20. collatione facta cum Deut. XXIII. vers. 35. Prov. XV. 21. c. XIV. 29. c. XVI. 37. c. XIX. 11. XXV. v. 14. Eccl. VII. 9. 10. X. 14. Ps. XXXVII. 11. 2. Sam. XVI. 10. Syr. XLV. 4.

Argumentum Christi per se manifestum non indiget istis confragosis ambagibus: Quia filii hominis est servare, non perdere animas, discipu- los ejus decet non ignis flamma consumendos homines quamvis malevolos, & inhumanos, sed in vita po- tius servandos optare, si forte adhuc converti, ac ab in- teritu animæ liberari possint. Ita non opus est cum Grotio ψυχὰς de hominibus Synecdochice interpreta- ri, cum homines & ψυχαὶ distinguantur in textu; di- citur enim ὐκ ἦλθε ψυχὰς ἀνθρώπων ἀπολέσαι, ut constet ψυχὰς vel animas hic proprie respici homi- num, non vero homines ipsos indigitari: Unde textu originalem hic fallari in gloslæ suæ gratiam veritus non est, omissione vocis ἀνθρώπων, quam vero omnes Codices Græci habent, ut & Arabs: etsi à Latino & Syro non exprimatur. Cogitasse debe- bat Grotius, quod ipse monuit ad Luc. XII. v. 49. Certe ex illis versionibus aliter lectum olim in Græcis Codicibus, quam nunc legitur, non satis valide evin- cas: cum passim interpretes jus sibi indulgeant sensu incolumi ab apicibus discedendi. Quæ ejus obser- vatio eo magis observanda, quo magis eandem ipse in praxi insuper habuit, frequentissime è ver- sionibus diversam lectionem colligens, cum ab apicibus Codicem Græcorum recedant.

(VI.) Responso tribus Jesum sequi vo- lentibus reddita.

## 9:57
Vers. 57. as they were going on the way] At a certain time, which it was not relevant to describe more precisely. For it seemed good to Luke to connect things of the same kind.

Latin:

Vers. 57. πορευομένων ἀυτῶν ἐν τῇ ὁδῷ] Quodam tempo- re quod proprius describi nihil attinebat. Visum enim Lucæ connectere τὰ ὁμογένεα.

## 9:61
Vers. 61. to bid farewell to those in my house] Some doubt about the persons, whether it should be understood here of things. To me it seems most manifest that it ought to be understood of persons. For to bid farewell used of things is to hold as abandoned: which requires no delay of time since it can be fulfilled with the mind alone. But of persons it is to say goodbye, as Luke uses it in more than one place. And so the Syriac and Arabic have interpreted it. Nor did the ancient Latins understand this passage otherwise. Tertullian against Marcion IV. When he also forbids that third one, who was preparing to bid farewell to his own first, to look back, he follows the sect of the creator. It is added that this history seems to allude entirely to the old history of Elisha. For he, called to the Prophetic office by the casting of Elijah's cloak, prayed for time to greet his parents, in which history Josephus also placed having bidden them farewell. Christ therefore wished to show that the Evangelical ministry, by as much as it was greater than the Prophetic, by so much also was it to be seized more eagerly, with no delay interposed. The expression εἰς τὸν οἶκον for ἐν οἴκῳ occurs so often that it is superfluous to give warning. Not foreign to this passage is what Bardesanes relates among Porphyry concerning the Indians, who wished to be reckoned among the Samanaei (that is the name of the wise men), ὥτε πρὸς γυναῖκα, ὥτε πρὸς τέκνα, εἰ τύχοι κεκτημένοις ἐπιστροφὴν ἤ τινα λόγον ἔτι πεποιηκέναι.

Our blessed Lysserus renders the same opinion, as does also Theod. Beza: it pleased Heinsius, however, to explain ἀποτάσσεσθαι by συντάσσεσθαι: permit me to settle my affairs, or to give final instructions to my family. Schmidius seems to join both meanings, [interpreting] ἀποτάξασθαι not only as saying farewell, but as freeing myself from all things pertaining to an inheritance: But since only one meaning can have a place, we judge the Grotian explanation to be preferred. But as to what seems probable to Grotius, that these who excused themselves were called by Christ for no other purpose than to announce the kingdom of God, and therefore the excuse was rejected for not having obeyed the one calling, and thus also these filled that number of the seventy, of whom Luke subsequently treats, we leave in the middle. Because he has nothing concerning the division of the text.

Latin:

Vers. 61. ἀποτάξασθαι τοῖς ἐν οἰκόν με] Dubitant quidam de personis, an de rebus hic sit intelligendum. Mihi ma- nifestissimum videtur intelligi debere de personis. Nam ἀ- ποτάξασθαι de rebus usurpatum, est pro derelictis habere: quod nullam temporis moram requirit cum solo animo possit expleri. At de personis est valedicere, quomodo Lucas non uno loco usurpat. Atque ita interpretati sunt Syrus & Arabs. Nec aliter Latini veteres hunc locum in- tellexêre. Tertullianus adversus Marcionem IV. Quum & tertium illum prius suis valedicere parantem prohibet retro respectare, sectam creatoris exsequitur. Accedit quod omnino hæc historia ad veterem Elisæi historiam videtur al- ludere. Nam is ad Propheticum munus ab Elia injectu to- gæ vocatus, spatium salutandi parentes oravit, in qua histo- ria etiam Josephus posuit ἀποταξάμενον αὐτοῖς. Voluit igi- tur Christus ostendere Evangelicum ministerium, quanto majus Prophetico esset, tanto etiam avidius arripiendum, nulla interpolita cunctatione. Locutio εἰς τὸν οἶκον pro ἐν οἴκῳ tam sæpe occurrit, ut monere supervacuum sit. Non alie- num ab hoc loco est quod de Indis narrat apud Porphyrium Bardesanes, qui Samanæis (sapientum id nomen) accenseri volebant, ώτε πρὸς γυναῖκα, ὥτε πρὸς τέκνα, εἰ τύχοι κεκτημένοις ἐπιστροφὴν ἤ τινα λόγον ἔτι πεποιηκέναι.

Eandem sententiam reddit B. Lysserus noster, ut & Theod. Beza: Heinsio tamen placuit ἀποτάσσεσθαι per συντάσσεσθαι explicare: permitte mihi, ut de meis statuam, aut suprema meis dem mandata. U- trumque sensum conjungere videtur Schmidius, ἀποτάξασθαι non tantum valedicendo, sed ab omni- bus rebus ad hæreditatem pertinentibus me liberando: Sed quum non nisi una significatio locum habere possit, Grotianam explicationem præferendam censemus. Quod vero Grotio probabile vide- tur, hosce qui se excusarint, non nisi certo consi- lio à Christo vocatos εἰς τὸ ἐπαγγέλλειν τὴν βασι- λείαν τοῦ Θεοῦ, ac proinde excusatio rejiceretur paruis- se vocanti atque adeo & hos implesse numerum illum τῶν ἑβδομήκοντα, de quibus consequenter agit Lucas, in medio relinquimus. Quia de partitio- ne textus nihil habet.

## 9:62
Vers. 62. οὐδεὶς ἐπιβαλὼν τὴν χεῖρα αὑτοῦ ἐπ’ ἄροτρον καὶ βλέπων εἰς τὰ ὀπίσω εὔθετός ἐστιν εἰς τὴν βασιλείαν τοῦ θεοῦ] To put one's hand to the plow for that which is to undertake some work, the Greeks also say. Moreover, in this place there is a certain peculiar force to this similitude. For those plowing must have their eyes directed straight ahead into the furrow, lest, which is the word proper to this thing, they 'delirent' [deviate from the furrow]. For the ancients called a furrow a 'lira'. Wherefore here, as often elsewhere, the 'apodosis' is mixed with the comparison. For the simple proverb would have been: that he who looks back while plowing is not a good plowman. Now with the proverb is signified to what thing the proverb is applied. It is asked whether the kingdom of God in the 'apodosis' is the ministry of announcing the Gospel, or whether it extends more broadly? It seems to me that Christ took the occasion from a particular fact for a general sentiment. For as for him who was called to the ministry of the Gospel all delay was to be rejected, so also for others called to true virtue, that they may be able to attain the kingdom of heaven, that is, the peace of conscience and the possession

Of the Holy Spirit. I am moved by those words βλέπων εἰς τὰ ὀπίσω [looking back]. For they are taken from the history of the destruction of the Sodomites, where the Angels address Lot thus: μὴ βλέψῃς εἰς τὰ ὀπίσω [do not look back] אל תביט אחריך [do not look behind you], to which words, and the punishment which followed even the disobedient wife of Lot, Christ also calls us back below, ch. XVII, 37. Indeed, just as Sodom was set by God as ὑπόδειγμα μελλόντων ἀσεβεῖν [an example of those who would live ungodly], as Peter says, 2 Ep. ch. II, 6, so those who wish to escape the punishment impending over the impious must all, to speak with Paul who looks back to the same history, τὰ μὲν ὀπίσω ἐπιλανθάνεσθαι, τοῖς δὲ ἔμπροσθεν ἐπεκτείνεσθαι, κατὰ σκοπὸν διώκοντες ἐπὶ τὸ βραβεῖον τῆς ἄνω κλήσεως [forgetting those things which are behind, and reaching forth unto those things which are before, pressing toward the mark for the prize of the high calling]. For if, as Seneca says, ambition does not look back, burning with the desire of always attaining greater things, how much more just is it for those to do so to whom immortal glory is proposed? Here, certainly, if anywhere else, that maxim of Roman Law ought to have a place: that nothing seems to have been done as long as there remains something to be done. Nor indeed was it unknown to the Jews what that history signified. For it was sufficiently celebrated by ancient tradition, the ὑπόνοια [allegorical meaning] which, received from the elders, Philo explains to us eloquently: 'For the oracles say that Lot's wife, having turned back, became a pillar of salt. And reasonably and fittingly; for if anyone does not look at the things before, which are worthy of being seen and heard—and these are virtues and the works according to virtues—but looks around at the things behind and at the back, at deaf glory, and blind wealth, and senseless plumpness, and empty beauty of mind, and whatever things are akin to these, pursuing them, he will lie as a soulless pillar, having cast down around himself the counsel and the firm foundation.' And not much differently do some of the Greeks mythologize the fable about Orpheus looking back behind his back. εἰς τὸ ἱερὸν ἐπερχόμενος μὴ ἐπιστρέφου [entering the temple, do not turn back], which Simplicius interprets thus to Epictetus: 'Because one who has set out toward God must not have a double mind, reaching out toward human things.' Among Malchus there exists a similar saying of Pythagoras: 'When departing, do not turn back.' But what has become of those two whose excuse Christ did not admit can be asked. To me it seems probable that they were called by Christ for no other certain purpose than εἰς τὸ ἐπαγγέλλειν τὴν βασιλείαν τοῦ Θεοῦ [to proclaim the kingdom of God]: and therefore, when the excuse was rejected, the caller was obeyed. And thus also this filled that number of the seventy, of whom Luke treats consequently. That ἔνθετός ἐστι [is fit] corresponds to יצלח [is fit/prosperous], which the LXX translate as χρήσιμον ἔσται [will be useful], Ezech. XV. 4.

Latin:

Vers. 62. οὐδεὶς ἐπιβαλὼν τὴν χεῖρα αὑτοῦ ἐπ’ ἄροτρον καὶ βλέπων εἰς τὰ ὀπίσω εὔθετός ἐστιν εἰς τὴν βασιλείαν τοῦ θεοῦ] Manum aratro admovere pro eo quod est opus aliquid ag- gredi, etiam Græci dicunt. Cæterum hoc loco propria quæ- dam hujus similitudinis vis est. Nam arantes oculos pror- sum intentos in sulcum habere debent, ne, quæ vox est ei rei propria, delirent. Liram enim antiqui sulcum vocabant. Quare hic ut alibi sæpe miscetur ἀπόδοσις comparationi. Nam simplex proverbium fuerat: eum qui in arando respi- ciat, non esse bonum autorem. Nunc cum proverbio si- gnificatur cui rei aptetur proverbium. Quæritur regnum Dei ἐν τῇ ἀποδόσει sit ministerium annunciandi Evangelii, an latius pateat? Mihi videtur Christus ex facto particulari oc- casionem sumsisse generalis sententiæ. Nam ut illi ad mi- nisterium Evangelii vocato omnis mora erat rejicienda, ita & aliis vocatis ad veram virtutem, ut adipisci possint regnum cœlorum, id est pacem conscientiæ & possessionem

Sancti Spiritus. Moveor illis verbis βλέπων εἰς τὰ ὀπίσω. Sumta enim sunt ex historia excidii Sodomorum ubi Angeli Lothum ita alloquuntur: μὴ βλέψῃς εἰς τὰ ὀπίσω אל תביט אחריך ad quæ verba & pœnam quæ nec obedientem Lo- thi uxorem secuta est Christus infra quoque nos revocat c. XVII, 37. Nimirum sicut Sodoma à Deo posita est ὑπόδειγ- μα μελλόντων ἀσεβεῖν ut ait Petrus Ep. II. c. II, 6. ita qui effuge- re volunt imminens impiis supplicium, debent omnes, ut cum Paulo ad eandem historiam respiciente loquar, τὰ μὲν ὀ- πίσω ἐπιλανθάνεσθαι, τοῖς δὲ ἔμπροσθεν ἐπεκτείνεσθαι, κατὰ σκοπὸν διώκοντες ἐπὶ τὸ βραβεῖον τῆς ἄνω κλήσεως Si enim, ut Seneca dicit, ambitio non respicit, majora semper consequendi stu- dio flagrans, quanto id æquius est eos facere quibus immor- talis gloria proposita est? Hic sane si usquam alibi locum ha- bere debet illud Juris Romani, nihil actum videri quam diu superest quod agatur. Neque vero Judæis ignotum erat quid illa historia significaret. Erat enim antiqua traditione satis celebrata ἡ ὑπόνοια quam à majoribus acceptam fa- cunde nobis explicat Philo : τὴν γὰρ Λὼτ γυναῖκα κὶ ἐπιστρα- φῆναι εἰς τοὐπίσω φασὶν οἱ χρησμοὶ γενέσθαι στήλην ἁλῶν. Εἰ- κότως δὲ κἀκ προσηκόντως· εἰ γάρ τις μὴ τὰ πρόσω θέατ' ἠγὴ ἀ- κοῆς ἄξια διορᾷ ταῦτα δέ εἰσιν ἀρεταὶ κἀγὶ τὰ κατὰ τὰς ἀρετὰς ἔργα. Περιβλέπεται δὲ τὰ ὀπίσω κἀγὶ τὰ νώτια, κωφὸν δόξαν, κἀγὶ τυφλὸν πλοῦτον κἀγὶ ἀναίσθητον εὐσαρκίαν, κἀγὶ νῦ κενὴν εὐμορ- φίαν, κἀγὶ ὅσα συγγενῆ τούτω μεταδιώκων, ἄψυχος ἀποκείσεται στήλη περὶ ἑαυτὴν καταῤῥίψασ' οἱ γάβουλος κὶ βέβαιον. Nec multo secus Græcorum quidam fabulam de Orpheo post tergum respiciente ἐπυμυθεύονται. Et in Pythagoricorum præceptis erat : εἰς τὸ ἱερὸν ἐπερχόμενος μὴ ἐπιστρέφου quod Simplicius ad Epictetum sic interpretatur : ὅτι τ' εἰς Θεὸν ὁρ- μηθέντα, ὀ χρὴ δίγνωμόν τι ἔχειν πρὸς τὰ ἀνθρωπίνων αἰτεχόμε- νον. Apud Malchum exstat simile Pythagoræ dictum : ἀπο- δημοῦντα μὴ ἐπιστρέφεσθαι. Quid autem duobus his factum sit quorum excusationem Christus non admisit quæri potest. Mihi probabile videtur non nisi certo consilio à Christo vo- catos εἰς τὸ ἐπαγγέλλειν τὴν βασιλείαν τοῦ Θεοῦ : ac proinde cum excusatio rejiceretur, paritum vocanti. Atque adeo & hoc implesse numerum illum τῶν ἑβδομήκοντα, de quibus consequenter agit Lucas. Illud ἔνθετός ἐστι respondet יצלח quod χρήσιμον ἔσται vertunt LXX. Ezech. XV. 4.

## 10:1 Argument
CHAPTER X. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

The 70 disciples are sent out with instruction, where woe is said to Corazin and Bethsaida at the same time, as also to Capernaum: and the return of the 70 disciples is commemorated, with their joy over the subjection of demons, and they are warned about true joy, with thanksgiving rendered to the Father, and about the blessedness which befell them over many Prophets and kings. A lawyer is informed about the love of a neighbor by a parable about a Jew, a Levite, and a Samaritan. JESUS is received into hospitality by Martha: Mary sits at his feet, and listens to him.

There are four parts: I. The sending out of the 70 disciples, up to v. 22. II. The singular blessedness of the disciples, to v. 24. III. The information of the lawyer about the love of a neighbor, to v. 37. IV. The conversation of Jesus with Martha and Mary, to the final v. 42.

PART I. The sending out of the 70 disciples.

Vers. 1. ἀνέδειξεν [appointed] Properly and significantly. For the Greeks use that word in the constitution to offices, as also χειροτονεῖν [to elect/appoint]. Thus also Acts I. 24. ἀνάδειξον ἐκ τούτων τῶν δύο ἕνα [show of these two one]. ἑβδομήκοντα [seventy] Concerning the truth of this reading, because of the agreement of the Greek codices and the Syriac, I do not think there is room for doubt. That the Latin placed LXXII is from nothing else than ancient tradition. For antiquity believed that so many were created by Christ, even the Greeks, who read ἑβδομήκοντα in this place, such as Origen and Epiphanius. Nor indeed rashly: for it was the custom for the Hebrews to name the LXX by a round number, even when it was established that there were LXXII. Thus Josephus himself, to pass over others narrating the same thing, when he had said that men were sent to Ptolemy to translate the books of the law, 'elder men'

ἓξ ἀπὸ φυλῆς ἑκάστης [six from each tribe] he adds: 'But it did not seem necessary to me to declare the names of the seventy elders who brought the law, sent by Eleazar.' But also the Sanhedrin which was constituted by Moses, to whose example Christ chose these, just as he chose the Apostles to the example of the Phylarchs, some Jews have revealed to have been of LXXII heads, among whom is the writer of the Phesictha. Nor are arguments lacking. For there was a report that these also were initially chosen from individual tribes in equal number, although afterwards it is established that the succession was continued without any regard for the tribes. Now indeed there are those who think that Eldad and Medad, inspired by the divine Spirit outside the camp, were above the number of LXX. Others say that Moses and his successors, the princes of the Sanhedrin, are outside the number of LXX, which if we say also of the prince's deputy, who was called אב בית דין [father of the house of judgment], we will have LXXII. But it seems that the number LXX was venerable to the Hebrews even when established in Egypt, as we have noted elsewhere, because of the same number of heads of the family of Jacob when he came into Egypt; the memory of which thing God renewed for them by showing seventy springs in Elim, just as twelve palms shadowed forth the same number of Hebrew tribes. And they followed that number in almost all the greater colleges being erected, as they followed the number XII in the lesser ones. That is apparent from the number of the Interpreters. Josephus also narrates that by the order of Varus, XII legates were sent from the Caesarean Jews to the Ecbatanean Jews: but from the Ecbatanean Jews, LXX men were sent for the sake of clearing themselves, whom Varus slaughtered. And Josephus himself, sent to order the affairs of Galilee, chose for himself LXX assessors from the Galileans. And in the Jerusalem siege, LXX were chosen from the common people εἰς σχῆμα δικαστῶν [in the form of judges]. The ancients are accustomed to compare the offices instituted by Christ with the offices used in the Church after Christ's ascension. And indeed they compare Bishops to the Apostles on account of the exceptional right τῆς χειροθεσίας [of the laying on of hands]: but others compare the deacons to these LXX, as Ignatius does; others the presbyters, as Jerome; others the Chorepiscopi, as the Synod of Neocaesarea: however, it seems to me that the chorepiscopi, whom they also call περιοδευτὰς [itinerant visitors], correspond best to them. For these, having been taken up by the Bishops into a share of their labor, were sent through the fields with the power of teaching. But I admit that both Presbyters and deacons—not all, indeed, but those to whom the power of teaching the people had been granted by the Bishop—are not badly compared to these LXX. Such presbyters are not all, but οἱ κοπιῶντες ἐν τῷ λόγῳ [those who labor in the word].
