Such were the presbyters of old in Alexandria κατ' ἰδίαν ταῖς ἐκκλησίαις ἐπιτεταγμένοι [assigned to the churches individually], as Epiphanius speaks, ἐκκλησίας ἰδίᾳ κατέχοντες κὶ τ' λαὸν συνάγοντες [holding churches individually and gathering the people], as Sozomen says. Eusebius calls them presbyters entrusted with the interpretation of the divine words. Refer here that statement of Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans: 'Let that Eucharist be considered valid which is under the bishop or to whom he himself permits.' Moreover, that these LXX were different grades from the Apostles appears even from the fact that Matthias was promoted from this class εἰς τὴν ἀποστολικὴν ἐπισκοπὴν [to the apostolic episcopate]. Following this example, the seventy bishops who were assessors to the Roman Bishops were long ago called 'libra,' because the Roman libra contained that many solidi.

The integrity of the received Greek text is deservedly recognized: with which agree Tertullian, book IV against Marcion; Jerome, book of Questions to Fabiola II; Ambrose and Theophylact on this passage, as also Eusebius, book I of Church History, chapter XII. But whether the Evangelist used a round number, it is hardly possible to pronounce with certainty: the souls that are said to have come into Egypt were precisely LXX, Gen. XLVI. 27, and the palm trees designated in Exod. XV. last [verse] are just as many, which the blessed Lyserus refers to here, as does Grotius himself: 'It seems, however,' he says, 'that even for the Hebrews established in Egypt, as we have noted elsewhere, the number LXX was venerable on account of the same number of heads of the family of Jacob when he came into Egypt: the memory of which thing God renewed for them, having shown seventy springs in Elim, just as the twelve palm trees shadowed forth the same number of Hebrew tribes.' Grotius adds: 'Moreover, in establishing almost all major colleges they followed that number, just as in minor ones they followed the number XII.' That appears from the number of the interpreters. Josephus also narrates that by the order of Varus, XII legates were sent from the Caesarean Jews to the Ecbatanean Jews; but from the Ecbatanean Jews, LXX men were sent for the sake of clearing themselves, whom Varus slaughtered. And Josephus himself, sent to organize the affairs of Galilee, chose for himself LXX assessors from the Galileans. And in the siege of Jerusalem, LXX were chosen from the common people εἰς σχῆμα δικαστῶν [in the form of judges].

ἀνὰ δύο] Which the Lord had also observed in the Apostles, not only for mutual aid, but also for the assurance of a greater testimony. Thus Moses and Aaron are sent to Pharaoh. The Baptist also sends two to Christ: the Church sends Barnabas with Paul.

πρὸ προσώπου] Who were to perform a similar office to that which the Baptist had performed.

Latin:

CAPUT X. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Emittuntur LXX. discipuli cum instructione, ubi væ Corazin & Bethsaidæ simul dicitur, ut & Capernaumo: reditusque LXX. di- scipulorum commemoratur, cum gaudio ipsorum ob subjectionem dæmonum, & mo- nentur de vero gaudio, cum εὐχαριστίᾳ Pa- tri reddita, deque beatitudine, qua ipsis ob- tigit præ multis Prophetis ac regibus. Le- gisperitus informatur de dilectione proxi- mi parabola de Judæo, Levita, & Sama- ritano. IESUS à Martha hospitio susci- pitur: Maria ad pedes ejus sedet, eique auscultat.

Partes sunt quatuor : I. LXX. discipulorum e- missio, usque ad v. 22. II. Discipulorum beati- tudo singularis, ad v. 24. III. Legisperiti de dilectione proximi informatio, ad v. 37. IV. Jesu cum Martha & Maria collocutio, ad v. 42. finalem.

PARS I. Discipulorum LXX. emissio.

Vers. 1. ἀνέδειξεν] Proprie & significanter. Nam in con- stitutione ad munera eam vocem Græci usurpant, ut & χει- ροτονεῖν. Sic & Act. I. 24. ἀνάδειξον ἐκ τούτων τῶν δύο ἕνα. ἑβδομήκοντα] De lectionis hujus veritate, ob consensum Græcorum codicum & Syri, dubitandum non arbitror. Quod Latinus posuit LXXII. non aliunde est quam ex an- tiqua traditione. Nam tot fuisse à Christo creatos, antiquitas credidit, etiam Græci, qui hoc loco legerunt ἑβδομήκοντα, ut Origenes & Epiphanius. Neque vero temere : Nam moris erat Hebræis LXX. nominare numero rotundo, et- iam ubi constabat esse LXXII. Ita Josephus ipse, ut alios idem narrantes præteream, cum missos ad Ptole- mæum ad vertendos legis libros dixisset πρεσβυτέρους ἄνδρας

ἓξ ἀπὸ φυλῆς ἑκάστης subjicit: ἐμοὶ δὲ ἐκ ἀναγκαῖον ἔδο- ξεν εἶναι τὰ ὀνόματα τ' ἑβδομήκοντα πρεσβυτέρων, οἱ 'ν νόμον ἐκόμιζον ὑπὸ Ἐλεαζάρᾳ πεμφθέντες, δηλῶν. Sed & Syne- drium quod à Mose constitutum est, ad cujus exemplum hos Christus elegit, quomodo Apostolos ad exemplum Phylarcharum, fuisse capitum LXXII. Judæi nonnulli prodiderunt, quos inter Scriptor Phesicthæ. Nec de- sunt argumenta. Nam & hos initio lectos è tribubus singulis pari numero fama habebat, quanquam postea constat continuatam successionem nulla tribuum habita ratione. Jam vero sunt qui Eldadum & Medadum ex- tra castra Spiritu divino afflatos putant fuisse supra nume- rum LXX. Alii Mosem & ejus successores Synedrii princi- pes dicunt extra numerum esse LXX. quod si dicamus & de principis vicario qui dicebatur אב בית דין habebimus LXXII. Videtur autem Hebræis etiam in Ægypto constitutis ut alibi notavimus, venerabilis fuisse numerus LXX. ob to- tidem capita familiæ Iacobi cum in Ægyptum veniret; cujus rei memoriam ipsis Deus renovavit ostensis in Elim septuaginta fontibus, sicut duodecim palmæ totidem tri- bus Hebræas adumbrabant. Ferme autem in omnibus majoribus collegiis erigendis eum numerum sequebantur, ut in minoribus numerum XII. Apparet id ex Interpre- tum numero. Narrat & Josephus Vari jussu ex Iudæis Cæsariensibus missos legatos XII. ad Iudæos Ecbatanenses: à Iudæis autem Ecbatanensibus missos sui purgandi causa homines LXX. quos Varus trucidavexit. Atque ipse Jose- phus missus ad ordinandas res Galilææ ex Galilæis LXX. sibi legit adsessores. Et in obsidio Hierosolymitano LXX. è plebe lecti εἰς σχῆμα δικαστῶν. Solent veteres instituta à Christo munera cum muneribus post Christi ascensum in Ecclesia usurpatis comparare. Et Episcopos quidem com- parant Apostolis propter eximium jus τῆς χειροθεσίας: His autem LXX. alii comparant diaconos, ut Ignatius, alii pres- byteros, ut Hieronymus, alii Chorepiscopos, ut Synodus Neocæsariensis: videntur autem mihi chorepiscopi, quos & περιοδευτὰς vocant, optime illis respondere. Nam hi ab Episcopis in partem sui laboris assumti cum docendi pote- state per agros mitrebantur. Sed & Presbyteros & diaconos, non omnes quidem, sed eos quibus docendi populum potestas ab Episcopo facta esset, fateor his LXX. non male comparari. Tales presbyteri non omnes, sed οἱ κοπιῶντες ἐν τῷ λόγῳ. Tales antiquitus presbyteri Alexandriæ κατ' ἰδίαν ταῖς ἐκκλησίαις ἐπιτεταγμένοι, ut Epiphanius loquitur, ἐκκλησίας ἰδίᾳ κατέχοντες κὶ τ' λαὸν συνάγοντες, ut Sozome- nus. Eusebius vocat πρεσβυτέρες πεπιστευμένος τὴν ἐξήγησιν τ' θείων λόγων. Huc refer Ignatii illud ad Smyrnenses: ἐκείνη βεβαία εὐχαριστία ἡγείσθω ἡ ὑπὸ τ' ἐπίσκοπον ὖσα ἢ ᾧ ἂν αὐτὸς ἐπιτρέψῃ. Diversos autem fuisse gradus hos LXX. ab Apostolis, vel inde apparet quod Matthias ex hac clas- se εἰς τὴν ἀποστολικὴν ἐπισκοπὴν provectus est. Ad hoc exem- plum Romanis Episcopis jam olim LXX. Episcopi adsef- sores libra dicti, quod libra Romana tot solidos contine- ret.

Merito integritas recepti textus Græci agnosci- tur: cum quo faciunt Tertul. l. IV. contr. Mar- cion. Hieron. libr. Manson. ad Fab. II. Ambros. & Theophyl. in h. l. ut & Euseb. l. I. Hist. Eccl. c. XII. Num vero numero rotundo usus Evangelista sit, de eo certo pronunciari vix potest: Animæ utique quæ in Ægyptum venisse dicuntur, præcise erant LXX. Gen XLVI. 27. & palmæ Exod. XV. ult. desi- gnatæ totidem sunt, quas hic refert B. Lyserus, ut & Grotius ipse: Videtur autem, inquit, Hebræis etiam in Ægypto constitutis, ut alibi notavimus, venera- bilis fuisse numerus LXX. ob totidem capita familiæ Jacobi cum in Ægyptum veniret: cujus rei memo- riam ipsis Deus renovavit, ostensis in Elim septuaginta fontibus, sicut duodecim palmæ totidem tribus Hebræas adumbrabant. Addit Grotius: Ferme au- tem in omnibus majoribus collegiis erigendis eum nu- merum sequebantur, ut in minoribus numerum XII. Apparet id ex interpretum numero. Narrat & Jo- sephus Vari jussu ex Judæis Cæsariensibus missos lega- tos XII. ad Judæos Ecbatanenses; à Judæis autem Ec- batanensibus missos sui purgandi causa homines LXX. quos Varus trucidavexit. Atque ipse Josephus missus ad ordinandas res Galilææ ex Galilæis LXX. si- bi legit adsessores. Et in obsidio Hierosolymitano LXX. è plebe lecti εἰς σχῆμα δικαστῶν.

ἀνὰ δύο] Quod & in Apostolis Dominus observaverat, non tantum ad opem mutuam, sed & in majoris testimonii fidem. Ita Moses & Aaron ad Pharaonem mittuntur. Etiam Baptista ad Christum duos mittit: Ecclesia Barnabam cum Paulo.

πρὸ προσώπου] Simili functuros officio quo Baptista fructus fuerat.

## 10:4
Vers. 4. μηδένα κατὰ τὴν ὁδὸν ἀσπάσησθε] A sign of haste, as above IX. 61. These salutations among the peoples of the East were not performed with a light gesture or word, but were delivered with many inquiries and good omens, not without many bowings of the body, kisses, and embraces.

Βαλάντιον] A purse. See Matt. X. צרור Job ch. XIV. v. 17.

Latin:

Vers. 4. μηδένα κατὰ τὴν ὁδὸν ἀσπάσησθε] Festinationis signum, ut supra IX. 61. Salutationes istae apud Orientis populos non fiebant levi gestu verbove, sed multis percunctationibus, bonisque ominibus tradebantur, non sine multis corporis flexionibus, osculis, amplexibus.

Βαλάντιον] Zonam. Vide Matth. X. צרור Job. c. XIV. v. 17.

## 10:6
Vers. 6. ὁ υἱὸς εἰρήνης] That is, worthy of peace, from Matthew: with a mind composed to hear the truth.

Latin:

Vers. 6. ὁ υἱὸς εἰρήνης] Id est εἰρήνης ἄξιος, ex Matthaeo: animo ad verum audiendum composito.

## 10:7
Vers. 7. ἐσθίοντες καὶ πίνοντες τὰ παρ᾽ αὐτῶν] Freely and as if by your own right: which the following words indicate. Τὰ παρ᾽ αὐτῶν, that which is theirs, in a similar manner of speaking as in Mark III. v. 21. And sometimes among the Greeks themselves. Thus the Latin, Syrian, and Arab understand it here.

Latin:

Vers. 7. ἐσθίοντες καὶ πίνοντες τὰ παρ᾽ αὐτῶν] Libere & velut vestro jure: quod sequentia indicant. Τὰ παρ᾽ αὐτῶν quae ipsorum sunt, simili loquendi genere quale Marci III. v. 21. Et apud Graecos ipsos interdum. Ita hic intelligunt Latinus, Syrus, Arabs.

## 10:8
Vers. 8. ἐσθίετε τὰ παρατιθέμενα ὑμῖν] Be content with whatever frugal fare: so that this admonition may differ from the former.

Latin:

Vers. 8. ἐσθίετε τὰ παρατιθέμενα ὑμῖν] Contenti este quamvis frugali apparatu: ut ita differat haec monitio a superiore.

## 10:8
V. 8. ἐθεώρυν] It was when I was seeing. For it must be taken indefinitely, as ἔιδον often is in the Apocalypse. Do not marvel, he says, that the demons yield to your voice. For it is certain to me that the prince of the demons himself is about to fall suddenly from the kingdom which he holds over the human race. See John XII. 31.

ὡς ἀστραπὴν ἐκ τῦ ὐρανῦ] As suddenly, he says, as lightning is accustomed to flash from the sky. A similar comparison is below XVII. v. 24. and Matt. XXIV. 27, where see. This prediction is to be referred to the incredible speed with which the Gospel was propagated through the lands to destroy false religions and all the works of the devil. This was foreshadowed in the fall of the Babylonian kingdom, Isa. XIV. 12.

Others, with Gregory and Theophylact, take it concerning that fall in which Satan, having immediately at the beginning fallen into pride, was cast out of heaven, which Christ as GOD saw, to which interpretation Erasmus also goes, as does Daniel Heinsius: But this sense is a little more remote. Therefore, it pleases others to refer this to the present expedition of the disciples of Christ: as if he were saying, I was seeing, even while I was sending you out, Satan falling like lightning, and all his powers vanishing. Which interpretation B. Lyserus in his Harmony, ch. CIV, most approves of. He does not, however, reject that other explanation, but says it is pious, which pleased Grotius here, that after the coming of Christ, Satan was to be driven out of his kingdom, which he had in the whole world, in which he ruled as if in his own heaven. We consider this to be preferable to the others because of the comparison with Luke ch. XVII. 24 and Matt. XXIV. 27.

Latin:

V. 8. ἐθεώρυν] Fuit cum viderem. Sumendum enim ἀορίσως, ut saepe ἔιδον in Apocalypsi. Nolite mirari, inquit, daemonia vocis cedere. Nam mihi certo constat ipsum Daemoniorum principem subito de regno, quod in genus humanum obtinet, casurum. Vid. Joh. XII. 31.

ὡς ἀστραπὴν ἐκ τῦ ὐρανῦ] Tam subito, inquit, quam fulgur solet e coelo micare. Similis comparatio infra XVII. v. 24. & Matth. XXIV. 27. ubi vide. Referenda haec praedictio ad incredibilem celeritatem propagati per terras Evangelii ad destruendas religiones falsas & omnia opera diaboli. Adumbratum id in casu regni Babylonici Ef. XIV. 12.

Alii cum Gregor. & Theophyl. de eo casu accipiunt, quo Satanas in principio statim in superbiam lapsus e coelo projectus est, quem Christus ut DEUS vidit, quo abit & Erasmi interpretatio, ut & Dan. Heinsii: Sed hic sensus paulo alienior est. Proinde aliis haec referre placet ad praesentem expeditionem discipulorum Christi: quasi dicat, videbam jam ubi vos emittebam, Satanam instar fulguris cadere, omnesque ejus vires evanescere. Quae interpretatio maxime sese probat B. Lysero Harm. c. CIV. Non rejicit tamen illam explicationem, sed piam esse ait, quae hic Grotio placuit, quod post adventum Christi Satanas ex regno suo, quod in toto mundo habuit, in quo tanquam in caelo suo dominatus est, exturbandus sit. Nos hanc caeteris ob collationem Luc. c. XVII. 24. Matth. XXIV. 27. praeferendam ducimus.

## 10:11
Vers. 11. καὶ ὴ κονιορτὸν] As if he were to say: we are so far from having sought any advantages from you, being sent for the sake of your salvation, not our own utility. See what is said on Matthew.

εἰς τὺς πόδας ἡμῶν] Besides the Syrian, the Arab also acknowledges this particle, as does that old manuscript in England.

πλὴν] See regarding this particle what is said on Matthew XI. 22.

Latin:

Vers. 11. καὶ ὴ κονιορτὸν] Quasi dicat: tantum abest ut ulla ex vobis commoda sectati simus, missi vestrae salutis, non nostrae utilitatis causa. Vide quae ad Matthaeum.

εἰς τὺς πόδας ἡμῶν] Praeter Syrum Arabs quoque hanc particulam, & vetus ille in Anglia manuscriptus, agnoscit.

πλὴν] Vide de hac particula quae ad Matthaeum XI. 22.

## 10:16
Vers. 16. ὁ ἀθετῶν ὑμᾶς ἐμὲ ἀθετεῖ] Ἀθετεῖν is ἐξουθενεῖν. An allusion is made to the history in 1 Sam. VIII. 7, where God speaks thus: for they have not rejected (מאסו) you, but they have rejected me.

Latin:

Vers. 16. ὁ ἀθετῶν ὑμᾶς ἐμὲ ἀθετεῖ] Ἀθετεῖν est ἐξουθενεῖν Alluditur ad historiam 1. Sam. IIX. 7. ubi Deus ita loquitur: ὅτι ὖσε ἐξυθενήκασι (מאסו) ἀλλ᾽ ἢ ἐμὲ ἐξυθενήκασι.

## 10:17
Vers. 17. μετὰ χαρᾶς] This does not seem to be placed with a note of reproach. For what follows, πλὴν ἐν τύτῳ μὴ χαίρετε, is to be understood comparatively: therefore it is subjoined: χαίρετε δὲ μᾶλλον. For Christ compares a greater cause of joy with a lesser.

κὰι τὰ δαιμόνια] Not only diseases.

ἐν τῷ ὀνόματί σου] This was the difference between the miracles of Christ and those of the disciples: that Christ performed them by his own power; the disciples by the power of the Master, whose name they also invoked, as can be seen from the Acts, and indeed even from the books of the Jews. Just as demons had hitherto yielded to the name of the God of Israel, so now they yielded to the name of Jesus of Nazareth.

Latin:

Vers. 17. μετὰ χαρᾶς] Non videtur hoc poni cum reprehensionis nota. Nam quod sequitur πλὴν ἐν τύτῳ μὴ χαίρετε comparative intelligendum est: ideo subjungitur: χαίρετε δὲ μᾶλλον. Majorem enim gaudii causam minori Christus comparat.

κὰι τὰ δαιμόνια] Non tantum morbi.

ἐν τῷ ὀνόματί σου] Hoc intererat inter Christi miracula & discipulorum: quod Christus ea faciebat vi propria: discipuli vi magistri, cujus nomen etiam nuncupabant, ut ex Actis, imo & ex Judaeorum libris videre est. Sicut hactenus ad nomen Dei Israelis cesserant daemones, ita nunc ad nomen Jesu Nazareni.

## 10:19
Vers. 19. δίδωμι] As if you were to say, I have not given this only for this mission, but I give it now also for the future, whenever the need so requires.

ἐπάνω ὄφεων καὶ σκορπίων] A manifest allusion to Psalm XCI. v. 12, "You shall tread upon the asp and the basilisk." Although there it is about the protection of divine providence, here it is about a miraculous power: the event corresponded to the words. Tertullian in his Scorpiace: "Faith is a protection to us, if it is not itself struck by the diffidence of immediately signing and adjuring and urging the beast with the heel." In this way, finally, we also often help the Gentiles, having been gifted by God with that power which the Apostle dedicated. And shortly after: "But you: if faith is vigilant, the scorpion is there for a sandal, an anathema struck down." See what is said on Mark near the end: but Christ may also have had regard to the place in Isaiah XI. 8: and all the more so because the disciples are also soon called νήπιοι (infants). The passage in the Greek of Isaiah reads thus: "And a young child shall put his hand on the holes of asps and on the bed of the offspring of asps."

κἀδὲν ὑμᾶς ὀ μὴ ἀδικήσῃ] Thus John in the Apocalypse II. 11, "He who overcomes shall not be hurt by the second death," ch. VI. 6, "Do not hurt the oil and the wine," ch. VII. 3, "Do not hurt the earth," ch. IX. 4, "that they should not hurt the grass." From the species to the genus.

Latin:

Vers. 19. δίδωμι] Quasi dicas, non pro hac tantum legatione dedi, sed do nunc etiam in posterum quandocunque usus ita exiget.

ἐπάνω ὄφεων καὶ σκορπίων] Manifesta allusio ad Psal. XCI. v. 12. ἐπὶ ἀσπίδα καὶ βασιλίσκον ἐπιβήση. Quanquam ibi de tutela divinae providentiae, hic de mirifica virtute agitur: Dictis eventus respondit. Tertullianus Scorpiace: Nobis fides praesidium, si non & ipsa percutitur diffidentia signandi statim & adjurandi ac urgendi bestia calcem. Hoc denique modo etiam Ethnicis saepe subvenimus donati a Deo ea potestate quam Apostolus dedicavit. Et mox: At tu: si fides vigilat, ibidem scorpio pro solea anathema inlisito. Vide quæ ad Marcum circa finem : sed & ad Esaiæ locum XI. 8. respe- xisse potuit Christus : eoque magis quia & mox discipuli vocantur νήπιοι. Locus in Græco Esaiæ sic habet : καὶ παι- δίον νήπιον ἐπὶ τρωγλῶν ἀσπίδων καὶ ἐπὶ κοίτην ἐγγόνων ἀσπίδων τὴν χεῖρα ἐπιβαλεῖ.

κἀδὲν ὑμᾶς ὀ μὴ ἀδικήσῃ] Ita Johannes Apocalypsi II, 11. ὁ νικῶν ὀ μὴ ἀδικηθῇ ἐκ τᾶ θανάτε δευτέρε, c. VI.6. Τὸ ἔλαιον καὶ τὸ οἶνον μὴ ἀδικήσῃς, c. VII. 3. Μὴ ἀδικήσατε τὴν γῆν, c. ΙΧ. 4. ἵνα μὴ ἀδικήσωσι τὸν χόρτον. Ex specie genus

## 10:20
Vers. 20. ὅτι τὰ πνεύματα ὑμῖν ὑποτάσσεται] The unclean ones, of course. For they had just said, "the demons are subject to you."

χαίρετε δὲ μᾶλλον] A more just cause for joy is to have confidence in one's own salvation than to serve the salvation of another: for the latter is the way, the former is the goal. It is more joyful to possess that which is proper to the saints than that which is communicated to others. That joy is subject to the danger of pride; this one subjects a humble and grateful mind to God.

ὅτι τὰ ὀνόματα ὑμῶν ἐγράφη ἐν τοῖς ὐρανοῖς] Just as the Latins say that that which is not durable is written in wind and water, so the Hebrews with a similar sense say it is written in the earth, that is, in the dust. Jer. XVII. 13, "Those who depart from me shall be written in the earth." The opposite of this is to be written in heaven, that is, to be ascribed and destined for eternal life. Moses indeed also mentions the book of the living: but, as the most learned Gerundensis explains, he speaks there according to the custom of those times, popularly about the census of those who lead a happy life in these lands. For it is well known that ספר is called a catalogue by the Hebrews. Nor is that which is in the Psalm to be interpreted otherwise, "Let them be blotted out of the book or census of the living," LXIX. 28. Thus also Ps. CXXXIX, "In thy book all of them are written," seems to be called a census-book of all who are born into this world. But Christ referred all things which were once spoken in figures to eternal life, which he had come to reveal openly to the world. Wherefore those who through faith are engrafted into Him and obtain the right of eternal inheritance, their names are said to be written even now in heaven, as here, or in the book of life. This is that book κατ' ἐξοχήν, in Daniel XII. 1, where Jacchiades is to be consulted; Philipp. IV. 3; to John in the Apocalypse the book of life c. III. 5, c. XX. 12, 15, c. XXI. 27, c. XXII. 9, 19; the book of the Lamb c. XIII. 8, which book is said to be written from the foundation of the world Apoc. XIII. 8 & c. XVII. 8, because, to be sure, all who ever were saints were made perfect through Christ Hebr. XI. 40. To be written, therefore, in heaven, or in the book of the Lamb, or of eternal life, is to be reckoned through the obedience of faith as a son of God, and consequently also an heir Hebr. c. XII. 23. Chrysostom in II. against the Jews [explains] that passage in Daniel, ὁ εὑρεθεὶς γεγραμμένος ἐν τῷ βιβλίῳ, that is, those who are worthy of salvation. For this expression must be referred to the present state, and indeed under an equitable condition, not to the eternal and those pure and peremptory decrees of God. For since among the number of the Apostles there was one son of perdition, who would affirm to us that all the LXXII attained the end to which they were called? Certainly, no prudent person would persuade himself that it was Christ's purpose to make them all certain of that matter. It is much less reasonable to believe this of Paul writing to the Philippians, as he had no certain knowledge of such an outcome. In the constitutions which are called Clement's, book VIII, chapter 1, this very passage which we have in hand is explained thus: Καθὼς ἀυτὸς παιδέυων ἡμᾶς ὁ κύριος δείκνυσι, λέγων μὴ χαίρετε ὅτι τὰ πνέυματα ὑμῖν ὑπακέυσιν, ἀλλὰ χαίρετε ὅτι τὰ ὀνόματα ὑμῶν γέγραπται ἐν τῷ ὐρανῷ· ἐπειδὰν τὸ μὲν ἀυτῇ δυνάμῃ γίνεται, τὸ δε ἡμετέρᾳ ἀνοίᾳ καὶ σπεδῇ δῆλον ὅτι βοηθευμένοις ὑπ' ἀυτῆ. Philo on Abraham: γραφῆς κὴ μνήμης ἄξι@ ὁ ἐνιλπις, ὦ τῆς ἐν χαρτιδίοις τοῖς ὑπὸ ζήψεων διαφθαρησομεν@, ἀλλὰ τῆς ἐν ἀθανάτῳ τῇ φύσῄ παρ' ἧ τὰς σπεδαίας πράξεις ἀναγράφτες εἶναι ζυμβέβηκεν. Similar is that which the Jews hand down, that the names of those who convert the impious are proclaimed by angels in heaven, as can be seen in the book whose name is Golden Apples.

Grotius explains this regarding the state of grace, that to be written in heaven is to be reckoned a son of GOD through the obedience of faith. For, he says, this expression must be referred to the present state, and indeed under an equitable condition, not to the eternal and those pure and peremptory decrees of God. We admit that it cannot be referred to pure or absolute peremptory decrees: because there are no such decrees concerning the salvation of man. Nevertheless, it must be maintained that that inscription is eternal, and that the decree concerning salvation made from eternity, namely of election and predestination, is regarded: because GOD does not finally choose anyone for salvation in time, nor does He write the name of anyone in heaven, or in the book of the Lamb, or in eternal life, but this election and inscription was made ἀπὸ καταβολῆς κόσμε: Eph. I. 4. Apoc. XIII. 8. c. XVII. 8.

The inscription in Dan. XII. v. 4. Phil. IV. 3. 4. is to be understood in no other way than that it was made through eternal election: which passages Grotius connects here, because they treat of eternal life, (although he interprets the former, Dan. XII. v. 14., in his annotations on the Old Testament quite differently) praising Chrysostom in II. advers. Jud. who explains that passage in Daniel: ὁ εὑρεθεὶς γεγραμμένος ἐν τῷ βιβλίῳ τόυτεσιν οἱ σωτηρίας ὄντες ἄξιοι. And Grotius explains being written in heaven in this way, that it is to be ascribed to eternal life, and destined for it. But that this is done in time is nowhere taught, but that it was done from eternity, and before the foundations of the world were laid.

Nor can the Grotian comparison render this opinion doubtful, that since there was one son of perdition in the number of the Apostles, it cannot be certainly asserted that all LXXII disciples were predestined to salvation from eternity: For we do not say that all of them were elect, or that it is Christ's purpose to make them all certain of that thing, because the disciples are taught only what is true and a matter for rejoicing, namely that from that source alone is there solid joy, that someone's name is written in the heavens, nor are the names of all of them said to be written in the heavens; but the expression is indefinite, which is true, even if the discourse is only about some indefinitely. Although indeed Paul was not certain of himself regarding his fellow-workers, whether they were designated in the book of life through eternal election, yet he could have this from divine inspiration which he wrote in Phil. IV. 3; just as he did not have certain knowledge of himself regarding whether they were truly grafted into Christ himself through faith, and had obtained the right of eternal inheritance? Finally, Exod. XXXII. 32. Psal. LXIX. v. 28. it is clear from a comparison of other passages of Scripture that the discourse is not about the census of those who lead a happy life in these lands, as Grotius wishes with the Gerundensian, but about the book of eternal life: for nowhere is a book commemorated in which those who lead a happy life here are written: nor can it be taught from the Scriptures that that temporal happiness was proper to the reason of those times of the Old Testament, as Grotius opined with the Pelagians and Socinians.

Latin:

Vers. 20. ὅτι τὰ πνεύματα ὑμῖν ὑποτάσσεται] τὰ ἀκάθαρτα scilicet. Nam modo dixerant τὰ δαιμόνια ὑποτάσσεται ὑμῖν.

χαίρετε δὲ μᾶλλον] Justior gaudii causa, suæ salutis habere fiduciam, quam alienæ saluti inservire: nam hoc via est, il- lud meta. Lætius id habere quod sanctis est proprium, quam quo l & aliis communicatur. Ista lætitia periculo superbiæ subjacet: illa demissum gratumque animum Deo subjicit.

ὅτι τὰ ὀνόματα ὑμῶν ἐγράφη ἐν τοῖς ὐρανοῖς] Sicut Latini id quod durabile non est dicunt in vento & aqua scribi, ita Hebræi pari sensu dicunt scribi in terra, id est in pulvere.Ier. XVII.13. יסורי בארץ יכתבו ἀφεστηκότες ἐπι τῆς γῆς γρα- φήτωσαν. Huic contrarium est scribi in cælo, id est vitæ æternæ adscribi atque destinari. Meminit quidem & Mo- ses libri viventium: sed, ut explicat doctissimus Gerunden- sis, loquitur ibi pro temporum illorum ratione populariter de censu eorum qui vitam in his terris felicem agunt. Nam ספר vocari Hebræis κατάλογον notissimum est. Neque aliter interpretandum quod in Psalmo est, deleantur è libro aut censu viventium, LXIX. 28. Sic & Ps. CXXXIX. ספר כלם dici videtur liber quasi censualis omnium quæ in hoc mundo nascuntur. At Christus omnia quæ olim in figuris dicta sunt, ad vitam æternam retulit, quam aperte mundo revelaturus venerat. Quare qui per fidem ipsi in- siti jus æternæ hæreditatis consequantur, eorum nomina di- cuntur jamnunc in cælo scribi, ut hic, aut in libro vitæ. Hic est ille liber κατ' ἐξοχήν, apud Daniel, XII. 4. ubi videndus Jacchiades Philipp. IV. 3. 4. Johanni in Apocalypsi liber vitæ c.III. 5.c. XX.12.15.c. XXI.27. c.XXII.9 19.liber agni c. XIII. 8. tuein liber scriptus dicitur ab initio mundi Apoc. XIII. 8. & c. XVII.8. quia scilicet omnes qui unquam sancti fuerunt per Christum ἐτελειώθησαν Hebr. XI.40 Scribi ergo in cælo aut in libro agni, aut vitæ æternæ, est per fidei obe- dientiam censeri Dei filium, ac proinde & hæredem Hebr. c. XII, 23. Chrysostomus in II. adversus Judæos illud apud Danielem, ὁ εὑρεθεὶς γεγραμμένος ἐν τῷ βιβλίῳ, τύτεσιν οἱ ζωτηρίας ὄντες ἄξιοι. Nam ad statum præsentem, & qui- dem sub æqua conditione, non ad æterna eaque pura & peremtoria Dei decreta hæc locutio referenda est. Nam cum in Apostolorum numero unus fuerit υἱὸς ἀπωλείας, quis omnes LXXII. cum ad quem vocati erant finem assecutos nobis affirmet? Certe propositum Christo fuisse, ut ejus rei illos omnes certos faceret, nemo prudens sibi persuaserit. De Paulo ad Philippenses scribente multo minus id par est credi, ut qui nullam habuerit talis eventus certam notitiam. In constitutionibus quæ dicuntur Clementis lib. IIX. c. 1. hic ipse locus quem præ manibus habemus sic explicatur: Καθὼς ἀυτὸς πx παιδέυων ἡμᾶς ὁ κύριος· δείκνυσι, λέγων μὴ χαίρετε ὅτι τὰ πνέυματα ὑμῖν ὑπακέυσιν, ἀλλὰ χαίρετε ὅτι τὰ ὀνόματα ὑμῶν γέγραπται ἐν τῷ ὐρανῷ· ἐπειδὰν τὸ μὲν ἀυ- τῇ δυνάμῃ γίνεται, τὸ δε ἡμετέρᾳ ἀνοίᾳ καὶ σπεδῇ δῆλον ὅτι βοηθευμένοις ὑπ' ἀυτῆ. Philo de Abrahamo: γραφῆς κὴ μνή- μης ἄξι@ ὁ ἐνιλπις, ὦ τῆς ἐν χαρτιδίοις τοῖς ὑπὸ ζήψεων διαφθα- ρησομεν@, ἀλλὰ τῆς ἐν ἀθανάτῳ τῇ φύσῄ παρ' ἧ τὰς σπεδαίας πράξεις ἀναγράφτες εἶναι ζυμβέβηκεν. Simile est quod eo- rum qui impios convertunt nomina ab angelis in cælo prædicari tradunt Judæi, ut videre est in libro cui nomen Poma aurea.

Id explicat Grotius de statu gratiæ, ut scribi in cælo sit per fidei obedientiam censeri DEI filium. Nam ad statum, inquit, præsentem, & quidem sub æqua conditione, non ad æterna, eaque pura & per- emtoria Dei decreta hæc locutio referenda est. Fate- mur non ad pura vel absoluta peremtoria decreta re- ferri posse: quia talia decreta nulla sunt de homi- nis salute. Æternam tamen esse illam inscriptio- nem, & ab æterno decretum de salute factum electionis nempe, ac prædestinationis respi- ci, statuendum est: quia DEUS non in tempore demum quemquam ad salutem eligit, aut in cælo, aut in libro agni, aut vita æterna nomen alicujus scribit, sed electio & inscriptio hæc facta est ἀπὸ κα- ταβολῆς κόσμε: Eph.I. 4. Apoc.XIII.8. c.XVII. 8.

Nec aliter intelligenda inscriptio Dan. XII. v. 4. Phil. IV. 3. 4. quam quod per æternam electionem facta sit: quæ loca conjungit hic Grotius, quod de vita æterna agant, (etsi priorem Dan. XII. v. 14. in annotat. ad Vetus Testamentum longe aliter in- terpretetur) laudans Chrysost. in II. advers. Jud. il- lud apud Danielem explicantem: ὁ εὑρεθεὶς γε- γραμμένος ἐν τῷ βιβλίῳ τόυτεσιν οἱ σωτηρίας ὄν- τες ἄξιοι. Et explicat ita Grotius τὸ scribi in cælo, quod sit, vitæ æternæ adscribi, atq; destinari. Id au- tem in tempore fieri nuspiam traditum, sed ab æ- terno, & ante jacta mundi fundamenta factum esse.

Nec dubiam reddere hanc sententiam potest collatio Grotiana, tum in Apostolorum numero u- nus fuerit υἱὸς ἀπωλείας, omnes LXXII. discipulos ab æterno ad salutem prædestinatos esse certo asseri non posse: Nam neque id dicimus, quod electi o- mnes illis fuerint, aut quod Christi propositum sit, ut ejus rei illos omnes certos faciat, quia quæ vera & gaudendi materia discipuli solum docen- tur, quod nempe inde solidum demum sit gau- dium, quod nomen alicujus in cælis scriptum sit, neque omnium illorum nomina scripta dicuntur in cælis; sed indefinita est loquutio, quæ vera est, etiamsi de nonnullis solum ἀορίστως sermo sit. Etsi vero Paulus de συνέργοις suis, an in libro vitæ per æternam electionem designati sint, ex se certus non fuerit, ex inspiratione tamen divina hoc quod Phil. IV. 3. scripsit, habere potuit; quemadmodum nec de eo certam notitiam ex se habuit, an per fidem Christo ipsi revera insiti, & jus æternæ hæredita- tis consequuti fuerint? Denique Exod. XXXII. 32. Psal. LXIX. v. 28. non de censu eorum, qui vitam in his terris felicem agunt, ut cum Gerun- denfi Grotius vult, sed de libro vitæ æternæ sermo- nem esse, ex collatione aliorum Scripturæ loco- rum liquet: nuspiam enim liber commemoratur in quo scripti, qui hic felicem vitam transigunt: neque illam temporalem felicitatem rationi illorum temporum Veteris Testamenti propriam fuisse, uti cum Pelagianis & Socinistis Grotius opinatus est, e Scripturis doceri potest.

## 10:21
Vers. 21.

ἐν ἀυτῇ τῇ ὥρᾳ) At that time. For no certain moment is indicated. Thus also Matthew ἐν ἐκείνῳ τῷ καιρῷ chap. XI. 25. But Christ came into this thought revolving the counsels of the paternal disposition concerning the salvation of men, and the duties of teacher, priest, and king entrusted to him: as we explained regarding Matthew. For that these things are to be referred to this, the discourse which follows in verses 23 and 24 openly shows. For that also pertains not to any admonitions of piety, but to the mysteries of the kingdom, as a comparison of the other passage in Matthew shows. Nor were these things said at one and the same time: but things which cohered by the argument of the subject matter, Luke in his own manner wove together in one thread.

τῷ πνέυματι) That is, in spirit, as often. For the Syrian and Latin add holy, which the Arab does not recognize: nor does the older part of the Greek codices. It may seem to have been added by those who, with Didymus, thought that as often as the article is added to πνέυματι, the Holy Spirit is understood.

καὶ γραφεὶς πρὸς τὼς μαθητὰς κατ' ἰδίαν, εἶπε πάντα) Since the Syrian and Arab have this particle, it is more credible that it was omitted by others because the same kind of speaking is repeated in the following verse.

Latin:

Vers. 21.

ἐν ἀυτῇ τῇ ὥρᾳ) Ea tempestate. Neque enim certum momentum indicatur. Sic & Matthæus ἐν ἐκείνῳ τῷ καιρῷ cap. XI. 25. Venit autem in hanc cogitationem Christus re- volvens consilia paternæ dispositionis circa hominum sa- lutem, & munia doctoris, sacerdotis, regis sibi mandata: ut ad Matthæum explicavimus. Nam eo hæc referenda et- iam is qui sequitur commate 23 & 24 sermo palam o- stendit. Nam & ille non ad quævis pietatis monita, sed ad regni mysteria pertinet, ut alterius in Matthæo loci col- latio ostendit. Neq; uno eodemq; tempore hæc dicta sunt: sed quæ rerum argumento cohærebant, Lucas more suo uno filo contexuit.

τῷ πνέυματι) Id est animo, ut sæpe. Nam ἁγίῳ quod addunt Syrus & Latinus non agnoscit Arabs: neque Græ- corum codicum pars antiquior. Adjectum ab iis videri po- test qui cum Didymo existimarunt quoties πνέυματι addi- tur articulus, Spiritum S. intelligi.

καὶ γραφεὶς πρὸς τὼς μαθητὰς κατ' ἰδίαν, εἶπε πάντα) Cum habeant hanc particulam Syrus & Arabs, credibilius est ab aliis ideo omissam, quia sequenti commate idem lo- quendi genus repetitur.

## 10:22
Vers. 22.

τίς ἐστι ὁ ὑιὸς) To what end and with what power was he sent? τίς ἐστι ὁ πατὴρ With what goodness, with what justice, with what wisdom: what are his counsels in giving salvation to men or certainly in removing excuse?

ἀποκαλύψαι) And that according to the reason of the times: now a little: more after the resurrection: most after the mission of the Spirit.

That these things are to be understood not only concerning the office of the Son, or the will of the Father, but also concerning the very incomprehensible essence and nature of the Father and the Son, from Matth. XVI. v. 16. 17. & XI. v. 27. Apoc. XIX. v. 12.

it appears. Nor was only a little revealed then concerning the Father and the Son: but since eternal life consists in that knowledge, John XVII. v. 3, which it is certain could have been had even from the Scriptures of the Old Testament, John V. v. 39, 2 Tim. III. v. 15, it is necessary that that knowledge had already been revealed in them. Meanwhile, there is no doubt that the revelation of divine mysteries was made clearer in the New Testament after the Holy Spirit was sent from heaven. We admit a degree of knowledge, but not an essential difference in the things to be believed.

PART II. Concerning the blessedness of the disciples.

Latin:

Vers. 22.

τίς ἐστι ὁ ὑιὸς) Quorsum & qua cum potestate missus? τίς ἐστι ὁ πατὴρ Qua bonitate, qua justitia, qua sapien- tia: quæ ejus consilia in danda hominibus salute aut certe excusatione adimenda?

ἀποκαλύψαι) Idque pro temporum ratione: nunc pau- xillum: plus post resurrectionem: plurimum post missio- nem Spiritus.

Non tantum de officio Filii, aut voluntate Pa- tris, sed de ipsa etiam essentia & natura incompre- hensibili Patris & Filii hæc intelligenda esse, e Matth. XVI. v. 16. 17. & XI. v. 27. Apoc. XIX. v. 12.

apparet. Neque tantum pauxil- lum tum revelatum erat de Patre, & Filio: sed quum in cognitione ea vita æterna consistat Joh. XVII. v. 3. quam è Scripturis etiam Vet. Testam. haberi potuisse constat, Joh. V. v. 39. 2. Tim. III. v. 15. necessum est, eam notitiam in illis jam re- velatam fuisse. Interea dubium nullum est, cla- riorem fuisse factam in Novo Testamento myste- riorum divinorum revelationem, postquam mis- sus de cœlo est Spiritus Sanctus. Gradus notitiæ, non vero essentialem credendorum diversitatem admittimus.

PARS II. De beatitudine discipulorum.

## 10:23
Verse 23. μακάριοι οἱ ὀφθαλμοὶ.

This blessedness is singular: such as that of Mary the θεοτόκος, Luke I. v. 48, c. XI. 27, doing nothing of itself toward obtaining eternal life, for which spiritual vision, which occurs by the eyes of faith, is necessary, John III. v. 15; for bodily vision befell many reprobates who remained unbelieving. But that blessedness is great which is joined with spiritual vision, which therefore many prophets and faithful kings longed for and desired; which, however, was reserved for the Apostles. Let there be noted, therefore, a threefold vision of Christ: 1. Bodily only; such as that of the Jews and Pharisees generally. 2. Spiritual only; such as that of all believers who have not seen Christ in the flesh, the Patriarchs, Prophets, and other righteous men. 3. Spiritual and bodily together; such as that of the Apostles, who both saw Jesus with their eyes and believed in him. Spiritual vision without bodily is sufficient for salvation, John XX. v. 29, but not bodily without spiritual.

PART III. Information of the lawyer concerning the love of one's neighbor.

Latin:

Vers. 23. μακάριοι οἱ ὀφθαλμοὶ.

Beatitudo hæc singularis est: qualis Mariæ θεο- τόκῳ Luc. I. v. 48. c. XI. 27. per se nihil faciens ad consequendam æternam vitam, ad quam spirituali visione, quæ oculis fidei fit, opus est, Joh. III. v. 15. corporalis enim visio multis reprobis obtigit, qui increduli mansêre. Magna autem est illa beatitu- do, qua conjuncta cum visione spirituali, quam ideo Prophetæ multi, ac Reges fideles exopta- runt, & desiderarunt; quæ vero Apostolis refer- vata fuit. Notetur ergo triplex Christi visio 1. Corporalis tantum; qualis erat Judæorum plerun- que & Pharisæorum. 2. Spiritualis tantum; qua- lis est omnium credentium, qui Christum in car- ne non viderunt, Patriarcharum, Prophetarum, aliorumque justorum. 3. Spiritualis & corporalis simul; qualis erat Apostolorum, qui & oculis suis viderunt Jesum, & in eum crediderunt. Spiritua- lis absque corporali sufficit ad salutem, Joh. XX. v. 29. non autem corporalis sine spirituali.

PARS III. Legisperiti de dilectione proximi informatio.

## 10:25
Verse 25.

νομικός τις) One practiced in questions of the law. ἐκπειράζων αὐτόν) Whether he taught anything contrary to the law? τί ποιήσας ζωὴν αἰώνιον κληρονομήσω) Marcion deleted that word αἰώνιον, so that it might seem, as Tertullian speaks, that it was a matter of that life which is promised by the creator in the law. But the same Tertullian rightly refutes that: The Doctor of the law certainly knew how he could obtain the legal life, so that he would not have asked about that whose rules he himself taught. He is inquiring altogether about eternal life, of which the lawyers and Pharisees had conceived a belief from ancient tradition, as we have said elsewhere. When he heard from Christ that this eternal life, not expressed in the covenant of the law itself, was most openly taught and promised, he wished to inquire whether it showed the same road to that life which was shown by the law. Therefore he asks τί ποιήσας. For by doing, that is, by performing those external works prescribed by the law, the lawyers and Pharisees thought that they would obtain not only a happy temporary life, but also immortality. Concerning the precepts of both rites and those pertaining to the civil society of the Hebrews, which are called משפטים and חקת, it is thus pronounced in Leviticus אשר יעשה אתם האדם וחי בהם: ὁ ποιήσας αὐτὰ ἄνθρωπος ζήσεται ἐν αὐτοῖς: Namely, a long life, as the Chaldean Paraphrast rightly interprets in the same place. The same sentiment concerning those same precepts exists in Ezekiel XX. v. 11, and Nehemiah IX. v. 29 refers to the same. And the Apostle Paul uses the same sentiment twice, opposing the works, namely the external ones concerning which the covenant of the law was conceived and in which the Jews trusted, to the faith which consists chiefly in the mind, Rom. X. v. 5, Galat. III. v. 24. The error of the lawyers was clearly pernicious, who thought that eternal life was to be sought by the same reasoning by which immunity from violent death and the happiness of a fleeting life were obtained: proving how false this was, Christ elsewhere denies that those who had remained within that righteousness, namely of deeds, with which the lawyers and Pharisees were content, would reach the heavenly kingdom, Matt. V. v. 20, where see what has been said. Meanwhile, that very thing which was conceived in that popular covenant offered to the wise a signification of more hidden things, namely, of a greater reward to be expected for greater obedience. Tertullian well says: according to the difference in rewards, the difference in works must also be believed. Philo also saw this, who, interpreting the words of the law more mystically, speaks thus: The law says that those who are attached to God live, laying down a necessary and philosophical dogma; for truly the miserable are dead in their souls, but those who have taken the rank assigned by the existing God live a life that is immortal.

Latin:

Vers. 25.

νομικός τις) Exercitatus in legis quæstionibus. ἐκπειράζων αὐτόν) An quid legi contrarium doceret? τί ποιήσας ζωὴν αἰώνιον κληρονομήσω) Illud αἰώνιον dele- bat Marcion, ut videretur, quomodo Tertullianus loquitur, agi de ea vita quæ in lege promittitur à creatore I ngavâ Sed recte id refutat idem Tertullianus: Sciebat utique legis Doctor quo pacto vitam legalem consequi posset, ut non de ea interrogasset, cujus regulas etiam docebat. Quærit omnino de vita æterna, cujus fidem legisperiti & Pharisæi ex veteri traditione conceperant, ut alibi diximus. Hanc vitam æ- ternam in ipso legis fœdere non expressam cum audiret à Christo apertissime doceri & promitti, sciscitari voluit, an iter ad eam vitam idem monstraret quod lege monstraba- tur. Ideo quærit τί ποιήσας. Nam faciendo, id est opera illa externa à lege præscripta præstando, putabant legispe- riti & Pharisæi, se non vitam tantum temporariam felicem, sed & immortalitate consecuturos. De præceptis tum rituum tum ad civilem societatem Hebræorum pertinentibus, quæ vocantur משפטים & חקת, ita pronunciatur in Levitico אשר יעשה אתם האדם וחי בהם : ὁ ποιήσας αὐτὰ ἄνθρωπος ζήσεται ἐν αὐτοῖς: Vitam longævam scilicet, ut ibidem recte interpretatur Paraphrastes Chaldæus. Ex- stat eadem sententia de præceptis iisdem apud Ezechie- lem XX. v. 11. eodemque respicit Nehemias IX. v. 29. At- que eadem sententia bis utitur Paulus Apostolus facta, ex- terna scilicet de quibus conceptum erat fœdus legis, & qui- bus fidebant Judæi, opponens fidei quæ in animo potissi- mum consistit Rom. X. v. 5. Galat. III. v. 24. Pernitiosus plane erat error legisperitorum existimantium, eadem ra- tione vitam æternam patari, qua immunitas à morte vio- lenta & vitæ caducæ felicitas obtinebatur: quam falsi ar- guens Christus alibi negat ad regnum cœleste perventuros, qui intra illam justitiam, factorum scilicet, qua legisperiti & Pharisæi contenti erant, constitissent, Matth. V. v. 20. ubi quæ dicta sunt vide. Interim illud ipsum, quod in fœdere illo populari conceptum erat, sapientibus occultiorum præ- bebat significationem, majoris scilicet præmii exspectandi pro majore obedientia. Bene Tertullianus: pro differentia mercedum, operarum quoq; credenda distantia est. Vidit hoc & Philo, qui verba legis mysticώτερον interpretans ita lo- quitur: ὁ νόμῶ φησὶ τοὺς προσκειμένους τῷ Θεῷ ζῆν, δόγμα τιθεὶς ἀναγκαῖον καὶ φιλόσοφον· ὄντως γὰρ οἱ μὲν ἄθλιοι τὰς ψυχὰς τεθνᾶσιν. οἱ δὲ τὴν παρὰ τῷ ὄντι Θεῷ τεταγμένοι τά- ξιν, ἀθάνατοι βίον ζῶσιν.

## 10:26
Verse 26.

In the law) Christ, intending to show that the law is not opposed but perfected by his own institutions, refers the lawyer to the words of Moses: not indeed those written in the book of Exodus where the covenant is struck and the law proper to the Hebrews is recited, but in Deuteronomy, where Moses, as a faithful teacher of the people, shows what goal the law proposes for itself, and to what it wishes men to be led: namely, to the observation of that law which was given not merely in the times of Moses, but from the beginning of the world, not proper to one people, but common to the whole human race, to which nothing can be added or taken away: and which is situated first in loving God, and then also other men, as joined with us in natural society. See what has been said on this matter at Matt. XX. 36.

How do you read?) You cannot be ignorant of what you yourself read to others and interpret. At the same time, as it seems, Christ showed him the passage from Deuteronomy.

Latin:

Vers. 26.

ἐν τῷ νόμῳ) Christus ostensurus suis institutis legem non oppugnari sed perfici, legisperitum ad verba Mosis rejicit: non illa quidem conscripta in Exodi libro ubi foe- dus pangitur, & lex Hebræorum propria recitatur, sed in Deuteronomio, ubi Moses, ut fidelis populi doctor, monstrat quem scopum sibi lex proponat, quo homines adductos velit: nempe ad observationem legis illius quæ non Mosis demum tempora, sed à mundi initio data est, non uni populo propria, sed communis toti humano ge- neri, cui nec obrogari nec derogari potest: quæque in amando Deo primum, deinde & hominibus alteris, ut naturali nobiscum societate conjunctis sita est. Vide quæ hac de re dicta sunt ad Matth. XX. 36.

πῶς ἀναγινώσκεις) Ignorare non potes quod ipse aliis prælegis atque interpretaris. Simul ut videtur locum Deu- teronomii Christus ei monstravit.

## 10:28
Verse 28.

You have answered rightly) You have well pronounced the words of Moses. It remains that you fulfill them in reality.

Do this and you shall live) Because the lawyer had asked 'by doing what', Christ returns the same word to him, but taken more broadly. Strictly, 'to do' is said of eternal deeds: broadly, it extends even to the internal motions of the mind. It is entirely similar to that in John, where the Jews asking 'what shall we do that we may work the works of God', Christ, seizing upon the little word 'work' but with a slightly changed meaning, answers 'this is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he sent', whereas otherwise the word 'works', taken more strictly for external works considered nakedly and apart from the internal quality of the soul, is in many places opposed to faith, as being situated within the mind.

Grotius, while he here maintains that eternal life is not expressed in the law itself, contradicts the Pelagians and Socinians, and openly contradicts the meaning of the words of the law which are looked to here in Leviticus XVIII. v. 5. Which neither the Chaldean explained as only long life, but as eternal life, and the Apostle in Rom. X. v. 5 and Gal. III. v. 24 interpreted with Christ clearly concerning eternal life. And Grotius rashly takes those words of Lev. XVIII. v. 5, 'he who shall do these things shall live in them', concerning the precepts of rites and those pertaining to civil society, so that he may obtain that only long life is promised to those observing them: when it is clear that they are to be understood concerning moral precepts by Christ here and by the Apostle in the cited places, and indeed also by Ezekiel XX. verse 11 and Nehemiah chapter IX. verse 29. Grotius says that the lawyer wished to inquire in this place whether Christ would show the same road to eternal life that was shown by the law, and that he thought he would attain immortality by doing, that is, by performing the external works prescribed even by the moral law: since therefore Christ in his response looked to those things from the law: 'Do this, and you shall live': how can it be a doubt that, according to the mind of Christ, those words, 'he who shall do these things shall live in them', are to be understood concerning eternal life, and concerning the observance of the moral law at the same time?

But as for the instruction of Christ delivered to the lawyer, it did not consist in what Grotius assumes here, as if a man could indeed aspire to salvation through the external works of the law alone, as the Pharisees and Scribes contended, but that interior obedience and probity of mind is also required: for although he teaches from Deut. VI. that the purity of the internal motions of the mind is also demanded by the law, and that that perfection of the love of God and neighbor, which can be performed by no one after the fall, is required, he by no means delivers this as a way and method of salvation, seeing that it is open to no one, but rather convicts the lawyer of his own weakness and inability to fulfill the law, to the end that he may finally acknowledge that righteousness must be sought outside of himself, and that the law may become for him a tutor unto the Mediator, in whom alone we have the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes, Rom. X. 4. But that Pelagian-Socinian notion is by no means to be admitted, that Christ shows by his institutions that the law is not opposed but perfected, because Christ did not arrive so that he might render the law more perfect, but so that he might procure for us grace and salvation by his obedience, both active and passive.

The Grotian distinction is also vain between those things which are written in the book of Exodus, where the covenant is struck and the law proper to the Hebrews is recited, and those in Deuteronomy, where Moses, as a faithful teacher of the people, shows what goal the law proposes for itself, to which he wishes men to be led, to which Christ here refers the lawyer. For in Exodus and the divine covenant, not only are laws proper to the Hebrews (such as also occur in Deuteronomy) comprehended, but primarily moral precepts, the sum of which consists in that love of God and neighbor which the lawyer here proposed from Deut. 6:5 and Lev. 19:18: which precepts were given not merely in the time of Moses, but from the beginning of the world, and are not proper to one people, but common to the whole human race, which can neither be abrogated nor derogated, as Grotius admits. For who can doubt that the sum of the Decalogue and the moral law is comprehended in those two precepts concerning the love of God and neighbor?

Latin:

Vers. 28.

ὀρθῶς ἀπεκρίθης) Bene pronunciasti verba Mosis. Re- stat ut reipsa impleas.

τοῦτο ποίει καὶ ζήσῃ) Quia legisperitus interrogaverat τί ποιήσας, Christus idem quoque verbum, sed laxius sum- tum illi regerit. Stricte ποιεῖν dicitur de factis æternis: late porrigitur etiam ad internos animi motus. Omnino simile est illud apud Johannem, ubi Judæis interroganti- bus τί ποιῶμεν ἵνα ἐργαζώμεθα τὰ ἔργα τοῦ Θεοῦ, Christus vo- culam ἔργον sed mutato paulum significatu arripiens re- spondet τοῦτο ἐστι τὸ ἔργον τοῦ Θεοῦ ἵνα πιστεύσητε εἰς ὃν ἀπέστειλεν ἐκεῖνος, cum alioqui vox ἔργων strictius sumta, pro ope- ribus externis nude & citra internam animi qualitatem consideratis, fidei, ut intus in animo sitæ, multis in locis opponatur.

Vitam æternam in ipso legis fœdere non expres- sam Grotius cum Pelagianis & Socinianis dum hic statuit, aperte sententiæ verborum legis, quæ hic respiciuntur Levit. XVIII. v. 5. contradicit. Quæ nec Chaldæus de vita longæva tantum, sed de vita æterna exposuit, & Apostolus Rom. X. v. 5. Gal. III. v. 24. cum Christo luculenter de æterna vita interpretatus est. Et temere illa Lev. XVIII. v. 5. qui fecerit hæc vivet in eis, de præce- ptis rituum, & ad civilem societatem pertinenti- bus accipit Grotius, ut vitam longævam tantum promitti obtineat, ea observantibus: quum de præceptis moralibus à Christo hic & Apostolo locis citatis, imo & ab Ezechiele XX. vers. 11. ac Nehemia cap. IX. vers. 29. intelligi in aprico sit. Sciscitari voluisse legisperitum hoc loco, an Christus iter ad vitam æternam idem monstraret, quod lege monstrabatur, & faciendo, id est, opera externa à lege etiam morali præscripta præstando se immorta- litatem consequuturum putasse, ait Grotius: cum ergo Christus illa è lege in responso respexerit: Hoc fac, & vives: quomodo dubium esse potest, ex mente Christi verba illa, qui fecerit hæc, vivet in eis, de vita æterna intelligenda esse, & de obser- vantia simul legis moralis?

Quod autem ad informationem Christi, legis- perito traditam, ea non in eo sita fuit, quod hic assumit Grotius, quasi homo quidem per externa solum opera legis ad salutem adspirare possit, ut Pha- risæi, & Scribæ contendebant, sed requiratur etiam interior obedientia & probitas animi: nam quamvis à lege internorum animi motuum puritatem quo- que postulari, & eam perfectionem dilectionis Dei ac proximi, quæ à nemine post lapsum præ- stari potest, requiri, è Deuter. VI. doceat, hanc tamen salutis viam & rationem, utpote quæ nulli patet, minime tradit, sed convincit potius legis- peritum de imbecillitate sua, & ἀδυναμίᾳ im- plendæ legis, eo fine, ut agnoscat tandem justi- tiam extra se quærendam esse, utque lex ipsi Pæda- gogus fit ad Mediatorem, in quo uno habemus τὸ τέλος νόμου, εἰς δικαιοσύνην τῷ πιστεύοντι, Rom. X. 4. Neutiquam vero Pelagiano-Socinianum il- lud admittendum, Christum ostendere institutis fuis legem non oppugnari, sed perfici, quia non ideo advenit Christus, ut legem perfectiorem redde- ret, sed ut gratiam & salutem nobis obedientia sua tam activa quam passiva compararet.

Vana etiam est distinctio Grotiana inter ea, quæ in libro Exodi scripta, ubi fœdus pangitur, & lex Ebræorum propria recitatur, & quæ in Deute- ronomio, ubi Moses, ut fidelis populi Doctor, mon- strat quem scopum sibi lex proponas, quo homines adductos velit, ad quæ legisperitum Christus hic re- jicit. Nam in Exodo & fœdere divino non tantum leges Ebræis propriæ (quales & in Deuteronomio occurrunt) comprehenduntur, sed imprimis præ- cepta moralia, quorum summa in ea dilectione Dei & proximi consistit, quam Deuter. VI. 5. & Levit. XIX. v. 18. hic proposuit legisperitus: quæ præcepta non Mosis demum tempore, sed ab ini- tio mundi data, non uni populo propria, sed communia sunt toti humano generi, quibus nec obrogari, nec derogari potest, fatente Grotio. Ecquis enim ambigere potest, illis duobus præ- ceptis de amore Dei & proximi summam Decalogi & legis moralis comprehendi?

## 10:29
Ver. 29.

But he, wishing to justify himself, said to Jesus, 'And who is my neighbor?' Christ had wished to lead the lawyer to a confession of his own impotence, so that, having seen what God primarily demanded, and being conscious of how far he was from such a serious and perpetual love, he might suppliantly obtain the help of the divine Spirit, without which such love cannot be admitted into the soul. But he, persisting in Jewish ferocity, wished to parade himself as just and upright before others: for that is what 'to justify' means here. And there is no doubt that he wished to be believed to have loved God sufficiently on account of his exact observance of all the ceremonies. Regarding the neighbor, because it could be doubted how widely that word looked, he demands Christ's interpretation. For if Christ had answered according to the received opinion of those times, that a neighbor was any Israelite, and no one else besides, he thought there was nothing that could be desired of him even in this respect. See what is said at Matt. 5:43.

Latin:

Vers. 29.

ὁ δὲ θέλων δικαιοῦν ἑαυτὸν εἶπε πρὸς τὸν Ἰησοῦν καὶ τίς ἐστί μου πλησίον;) Voluerat Christus legisperitum adducere ad im- potentiæ suæ confessionem, ut viso quid Deus potissimum exigeret, conscius sibi quam longe à tam seria ac perpetua dilectione abesset, supplex divini Spiritus auxilium, sine quo dilectio talis in animum admitti non potest, impetra- ret. At ille in ferocia Judaica perseverans volebat se ju- stum ac probum aliis venditare: id enim hic est δικαιοῦν. Et Deum quidem dubium non est quin satis amatum à se credi vellet ob exactam cæremoniarum omnium observa- tionem. De proximo, quia ambigi poterat quam late ea vox spectaret, interpretationem Christi postulat. Si enim re- spondisset Christus ex recepta eorum temporum senten- tia, proximum esse quemvis Israelitam, nec alium præterea quenquam, arbitrabatur nihil esse quod etiam hac in parte à se desideraretur. Vide quæ dicta ad Matth. V. 43.

## 10:30
Ver. 30.

From Jerusalem to Jericho) Which place is infamous for robberies, as Jerome notes. Whether it takes its name from there, however, can be doubted. For that place is so called in the book of Joshua. But it should be known that in the history of Moses, as also in that of Joshua and Samuel, not a few things are found which appear to have been added long after Moses, Joshua, and Samuel by the prophets or wise men for the sake of explanation. Which could be proven by many arguments, if that were the point. I agree, however, with those who think that a real event is narrated in this passage rather than a fable.

Latin:

Vers. 30.

ἀπὸ Ἱερουσαλὴμ εἰς Ἱεριχὼ) Qui locus latrociniis infa- mis, ut notat Hieronymus. An tamen inde nomen ha- beat מעלי אדמים dubitari potest. Nam is locus ita vo- catur in Josuæ libro. Sed sciendum ut in Mosis ita & in Josuæ & Samuelis historia, non pauca inveniri quæ multo post Mosem, Josuam & Samuelem à Prophetis aut sapien- tibus explicandi causa adjecta appareat. Quod multis ar- gumentis probari posset, si id ageretur. Assentior autem existimantibus hoc loco rem gestam potius quam fabulam narrari.

## 10:31
Ver. 31.

By chance) Which Aristotle calls 'automaton' and describes in Physics II: 'As if someone came for the sake of something, but it happened that he came and did this.' David Kimchi thinks there is the same force in the Hebrew 'petha', which he interprets as 'without intention', as if by choice.

Latin:

Vers. 31.

κατὰ συγκυρίαν) Quod ἀυτομάτον vocat Aristoteles & de- scribit Phys. II. Οἷον ἦλθεν ὁ τύτα ἕνεκα, ἀλλὰ συνέβη ἐλθεῖν καὶ ποιῆσαι τοῦτο. David Kimchi putat eandem vim esse in Hebræo פתע quod interpretatur בלא כונה ὥσπερ προαιρέσεως.

## 10:32
Ver. 32.

He passed by on the other side) He passed by on the opposite path, namely, hurrying from Jericho to Jerusalem. Although Christ's main purpose was to teach that the word 'neighbor' extends more widely than the Jews thought, he nevertheless wished to show in passing that they often do not perform even to those whom they call neighbors that which is the duty of neighbors, that is, friends. For those who attend to things more easily than with their soul easily find an excuse even not to perform deeds: either the journey presses, so that it is not permitted to delay: or they fear their own danger as well: it is credible that these men, the priest and the Levite, pleaded something of this kind. But if their soul had been full of love, full of mercy, both hands and feet would have hastened of their own accord to relieve the misery of the half-dead man. Now, perhaps lightly moved, and with the saying, 'May God have mercy,' they were accelerating their step to the function of their 'ephemeria' (course of service), little mindful of the divine sentence so often inculcated by Christ: 'I desire mercy, not sacrifice.'

Latin:

Vers. 32.

Ἀντιπαρῆλθεν) Præteriit contrario itinere, ab Hieri- chunte scilicet Hierosolyma properans. Quanquam Chri- sto præcipue propositum erat docere latius extendi proxi- mi vocabulum quam Judæi putarent, obiter tamen osten- dere voluit, sæpe ipsas ne iis quidem quos proximos vo- carent præstare id quod esset proximorum, id est, amico- rum. Nam qui facilis magis quam animo attendunt, facile excusationem reperiunt etiam ne facta præstent: aut iter urget, ut morari non liceat: aut suum quoque periculum metuunt: quale aliquid causatos & hos, sacerdotem & Le- vitam, credibile est. At si animus fuisset plenus dilectionis, plenus misericordiæ, & manus & pedes ad sublevandam hominis seminecis miseriam ultro festinassent. Nunc leviter forte moti, & dicto, Deus misereatur, ad ἐφημερίας suæ functionem gradum accelerabant, parum memores divinæ sententiæ à Christo toties inculcatæ: misericordiam malo, quam sacrificium.

Σαμαρείτης] Christ named a Samaritan rather than another foreigner, because the Jews pursued the Samaritans, as apostates, with a more deadly hatred than any others, and therefore removed them further from the name and estimation of a neighbor: and for that reason they imposed that name upon Christ as the highest reproach.

ἐλθεῖν κατ᾿ ἀυτὸν] He approached him more closely.

## 10:37
Verse 37.

ὁ ποιήσας τὸ ἔλεος μετ᾿ ἀυτᾶ] A similar expression above in ch. I, v. 72, 'to show mercy to our fathers.' Christ used admirable prudence, so that he might extort the truth from an unwilling person. If Christ had proposed the narrative about the wounded Samaritan, perhaps the lawyer would have said that an impure man, and one alien to sacred things, should have been neglected. But he could not help but praise the benefit conferred upon a Jerusalemite afflicted by such a grave misfortune. Yet by this circuitous route he is forced to confess what he seemed directly about to deny. For neighbor, friend, and kinsman are relative terms. Wherefore, if that Samaritan acted rightly when he brought aid to a Jew, certainly a Jew will also act rightly if in a similar case he brings aid to a Samaritan. For the bond of nature is equal on both sides, by which alone the Samaritan, and indeed, in the judgment of the lawyer, was laudably moved. Obligations of this kind are mutual: they do not limp. Therefore Christ rightly considers it as established that the perpetual, natural right, common to all men, should be respected, which is in no way abolished by the civil law of the Hebrews; indeed, by which the Hebrew law itself as it were leads us by the hand, that no man is to be considered alien to us who can perceive some aid from us.

πορεύου κὶ σὺ ποίει ὁμοίως] πορεύου here is hortatory, as 'go' in Matthew IX, v. 23. Imitate, says Christ, not the Priest and the Levite, but that Samaritan; and what you wished him to perform for the Jew, perform as a Jew for a stranger, indeed, if the situation so requires, even for a Samaritan. For the laws of nature are immutable. It is easy to say that God is loved by you, but unless you help another man, the image of God, you are caught in a manifest lie. For he who loves the one who commends, loves also those who are commended, 1 John IV. 20.

PART IV. The conversation of Christ with Martha and Mary.

Latin:

Vers. 37.

ὁ ποιήσας τὸ ἔλεος μετ᾿ ἀυτᾶ] Similis locutio supra c. I. v. 72. ποιῆσαι ἔλεος μετὰ τῶν πατέρων ἡμῶν. Admirabili prudentia usus est Christus, ut verum invito extorqueret. Si de Samarita vulnerato Christus narrationem proposuis- set, forte dixisset legisperitus negligendum fuisse hominem impurum, & à sacris alienum. At beneficium collatum in Hierosolymitam tam gravi casu afflictum non potuit non laudare. At hoc ambitu cogitur fateri quod directe vide- batur negaturus. Nam proximus, amicus, cognatus sunt τῶν πρός τι. Quare si Samarites ille recte fecit cum opem tulit Judæo, certe & Judæus recte faciet si in casu simili opem ferat Samaritæ. Nam par utrinque est naturæ vincu- lum, quo uno Samarites, & quidem, judice legisperito, laudabiliter movebatur. Mutuæ sunt istiusmodi obligatio- nes: non claudicant. Merito igitur Christus pro collecto habet si jus perpetuum, naturale, omnibus hominibus commune, respiciatur, quod lege civili Hebræorum mini- me est antiquatum, imo quo lex ipsa Hebræa quasi manu- ducit, neminem hominum à nobis alienum esse censen- dum, qui aliquid à nobis opis sentire possit.

πορεύου κὶ σὺ ποίει ὁμοίως] πορεύου hic hortantis est, ut πο- ρευθέντες Matth. IX v. 23. Imitare, inquit Christus, non Sa- cerdotem & Levitam, sed illum Samariten, & quod illum voluisti præstare Judæo, præsta Judæus extraneo, imo si res ita ferat, etiam Samaritæ. Immutabilia enim sunt na- turæ jura. De Deo dictu facile eum a te amari, sed ni ho- minem alterum, Dei effigiem juves, manifesti mendacii de- prehenderis. Nam qui commendantem amat, amat & com- mendatos Joh. I. Epist. IV. 20.

## 10:42
τὴν ἀγαθὴν μερίδα ἐξελέξατο ἥτις ἐκ ἀφαιρεθήσεται ἀπ' αὐτῆς] Mary, he says, chose this out of many cares and devotes herself entirely to this one thing, the fruit of which is to remain forever. Other things that are cared for are perishable, ephemeral. There are two kinds of pious men: for some cultivate piety in such a way that they simultaneously look after their family, or the state, or anything similar: others, having cast off all that care onto others, devote themselves entirely to prayers and sacred studies. Just as the solicitude of the former is not damnable, so the tranquility of the latter is much more blessed, who begin to lead a heavenly life on earth. And for this reason Paul prefers the celibate life to the married life, 'the unmarried woman cares for the things of the Lord,' namely, solely and with tireless zeal. 'But she who is married cares for the things of the world,' according to those things, of course, which are of the Lord. Mary belonged to the former class; Martha to the latter. Wherefore the ancients do not seem to me to err who place in these two sisters an example of the contemplative and active life: as the Hebrews do in Rachel and Leah. 'For our soul being twofold, and having one part rational and the other irrational, it happens that virtue belongs to each, Leah to the rational, and Rachel to the irrational,' says Philo in his book on the meeting for the sake of preliminary studies, whom Christian writers follow with great consensus.

In this, Grotius followed Cornelius à Lapide, who observed at this passage that Martha bears the type of the active life, and Mary of the contemplative life, while she sits, while she is silent, while she does not answer when interrupted, and who finally, being rapt within, became insensible to things outside. By that example of Mary, the Jesuit wished to honor the idle monastic life, but that is clearly foreign to the nunneries. For Mary hears the sermon sitting at the feet of Christ, as an attentive, doctrine-loving, humble, and obedient disciple, who, as Augustine says in sermon 27 on the words of the Lord, when she was accused by her sister, preferred to commit her cause to the judge than to labor in responding. For she knew that this was not culpable idleness, but the business of businesses, to hear the word of God, to search it, and to store it in her mind: which, as Augustine says again, the more humbly she sat, the more she received: for water flows to the humility of a valley, and runs off from the swellings of a hill. Mary was intent (these are likewise the words of Augustine) on the sweetness of the Lord's word; Martha was intent on how she might feed the Lord; Mary was intent on how she might be fed by the Lord. A banquet was being prepared for the Lord by Martha, in whose banquet Mary was rejoicing. Augustine, Gregory the Great in book 1 of Morals, chapter 1, and Bernard on the Assumption, place here an image of the contemplative and active life. But they did not teach that the contemplative life of monks and nuns is after the manner of Mary, while laypeople are represented by the example of Martha: and the slothful monastic life has no commerce with the zeal of Mary: but there is no doubt that very many laypeople choose that ONE thing necessary more than those enclosed in monastic cloisters. Nor indeed does St. Ambrose in this place admonish only monks, but all Christians, to the Marian zeal of contemplation. Let us also strive to have that which no one can take away from us; so that not a perfunctory, but a diligent hearing is desired. For the seeds of the heavenly word are accustomed to be carried away, if they are sown beside the way. Let the desire for wisdom move you just as it did Mary. For this is a greater, this is a more perfect work, nor let the care of ministry avert you from the knowledge of the heavenly word, nor judge those idle whom you see studying wisdom. For that peaceful Solomon took her to dwell with him. Solomon certainly was not a monk; Nuns did not derive their origin from the Bethany Mary, but from the Vestal Virgins. The Vestal Virgins, says Bebel in De Sacerdot. Rom. page 180, were priests of Vesta, such as Nuns are today.

Latin:

τὴν ἀγαθὴν μερίδα ἐξελέξατο ἥτις ἐκ ἀφαιρεθήσεται ἀπ' αὐτῆς] Maria, inquit, ex multis curis eam elegit & huic uni impense vacat, cujus fructus in æternum mansurus est. Cætera quæ curantur, caduca sunt ἐφήμερα. Hominum piorum duo sunt genera: alii enim ita pietatem colunt, ut simul familiam, aut rempublicam, aut si quid simile est procurent: alii omni illa cura in alios rejecta totos se pre- cibus & sacris studiis devovent. Sicut illorum sollicitudo non est damnabilis, ita horum multo beatior est tranquilli- tas, qui in terris incipiunt vitam agere cælestem. Atq; hoc nomine cælibem vitam nuptæ vitæ præfert Paulus ἡ ἄγα- μῶ μεριμνᾷ τὰ τῶ κυρίε nempe unice atque indeffeffo stu- dio. ἡ δὲ γαμήσασα μεριμνᾷ τὰ τῶ κόσμε juxta ea scilicet quæ sunt Domini. Ad illam classem Maria pertinebat: ad hanc Martha. Quare errare mihi non videntur veteres qui in duabus his sororibus exemplum ponunt, βίε θεωρητικῶ καὶ πρακτικῶ: ut & Hebræi in Rachele & Lea. τῆς γὰρ ψυχῆς ἡμῶν διμερῶς ὑπαρχύσης, καὶ τὸ μὲν λογικὸν, τὸ δ' ἄλογον ἐχύσης, ἀρετὴν ἑκατέρω ὑπάρχειν συμβέβηκε, Λείαν μὲν τῷ λο- γικῷ, τῷ δὲ ἀλόγῳ Ῥαχὴλ, inquit Philo libro περὶ τῆς εἰς τὰ προπαιδεύματα συνόδε, quem magno consensu sequuntur Christiani scriptores.

Sequutus in eo Grotius est Cornelium à Lapi- de, qui ad hunc locum Martham gerere observa- vit typum vitæ activæ, Mariam vitæ contemplativæ dum sedet, dum tacet, dum interpellata non respon- det, quæ denique intus rapta foris insensibilis red- dita fuerit. Illo Mariæ exemplo otiosam mona- sticam vitam cohonestare voluit Jesuita, sed illud plane alienum est à claustris monialibus. Nam concionem audit Mariam ad pedes Christi sedens, ceu attenta, doctrinæ cupida, humilis & obsequiosa discipula, quæ August. term. XXVII. de verb. Do- min. dicente cum argueretur à sorore maluit suam causam judici committere, quam in respondendo la- borare. Noverat enim hoc non esse culpabile otium, sed negotiorum negotium verbum DEI audire, scrutari, animoque recondere: quæ quanto humi- lius, ut iterum Augustinus, sedebat, tanto amplius capiebat: confluit enim aqua ad humilitatem convallis, denatat de tumoribus collis. Erat Maria intenta (verba itidem sunt Augustini) dulcedini verbi Domini, intenta erat Martha, quomodo pa- sceret Dominum, intenta Maria quomodo pascere- tur à Domino. A Martha convivium Domino parabatur, in cujus convivio Maria jucundaba- tur. Vitæ quidem contemplativæ & activæ ima- ginem hic ponunt Augustinus, Gregorius M. l. 1. Moral. cap. 1. Bernhardus de assumpt. sed mona- chorum & monialium vitam contemplativam esse Mariano more, Marthæ autem exemplo Laicos figurari non docuêre: & desidiosa vita Monastica nihil commercii habet cum Mariano studio: Laicos vero plurimos magis UNUM illud necessarium eligere, quam monachicis claustris inclusos, nul- lum est dubium. Nec vero monachos solum, sed omnes Christianos admonet ad studium contem- plationis Marianum S. Ambrosius in h. l. Studea- mus & nos habere, quod nemo nobis possit auferre; non ut perfunctoria, sed diligens audientia desira- tur. Solent enim etiam ipsius semina verba cœlestis æsferri, si secus viam sint seminata. Agat te sicut Mariam desiderium sapientiæ. Hoc enim majus, hoc perfectius opus, nec ministerii cura a cognitione verbi cœlestis avertat, nec arguas eos, &amp; ociosos ju- dices, quos videas studere sapientiæ. Hanc enim sibi cohabitantem Salomon ille pacificus ascivit. Salo- mo certe non erat monachus; Non à Maria Be- thanica, sed à virginibus Vestalibus moniales or- tum traxere. Virgines Vestales, inquit Bebelius de Sacerdot. Rom. pag. 180. fuerunt sacerdotes Vestæ, quales hodie Moniales sunt.

## 11:1 Argument
CHAPTER XI. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

Christ, being asked, teaches his disciples to pray, and makes them certain of being heard by a parable and similitude. He casts out a mute demon, and defends this with an apology against calumnies; teaching, concerning the woman, who are truly blessed: Concerning the sign of Jonah. Concerning the eye, the lamp of the body. At the banquet of the Pharisee, he argues against his hypocrisy, on account of the neglect of interior purification and the chief commandments of God, and his pride; and he reproaches the lawyers for the heavy burdens imposed upon others, and the slaughter of the Prophets from Abel onwards, and their vain boasting of the key of knowledge. Who therefore lie in wait for him.

There are four parts: I. Instruction concerning prayers, to v. 13. II. The casting out of the mute demon with an apology, to v. 28. III. Admonition concerning the sign of Jonah and the light, to v. 36. IV. A grave rebuke of the Pharisees and lawyers, to v. 54.

PART I. Instruction of Christ's disciples concerning prayers.

Vers. 1. Δίδαξον ἡμᾶς προσεύχεσθαι] Teach us a compendium of things to be prayed for. For they were not bound to syllables at that time. Thus it is also credible that a summary of prayers pertaining to repentance was proposed by John: just as this prayer of Christ contains the heavenly kingdom: hence it is called by Tertullian the breviary of the whole Gospel, and by Cyprian the compendium of heavenly doctrine. However, it is entirely credible that things were added in the Greek Codices from Matthew which Luke had omitted, since they do not exist in the ancient Latin ones: that is: who art in heaven. Likewise: thy will be done as in heaven so on earth (which certain Greek Codices also omit) likewise: but deliver us from evil: which themselves also, though not expressed, are contained by force in the other words.

Those words 'teach us to pray', as is evident even from the very sound, introduce not only the matter but also the form of prayers. Because he does not yet teach to pray who only names what things are to be sought: nor did Christ only determine the matter of prayers: but prescribed a formula ἀναρρήδως which is to be used in prayers. That distinction also between what John taught to pray, and what Christ, is of no value: because neither did John preach repentance apart from the kingdom of heaven, but to the kingdom of heaven Matt. III. v. 2. and to the remission of sins Luke III. 3. nor did Christ announce the kingdom of heaven apart from the proclamation of repentance Mark I. 15. both exhorted to repentance and to faith. And in the prayer prescribed by Christ, whatever pertains to repentance is not excluded, but included: for he comprehends it in the sanctification of the divine name, which with us is nothing without repentance; in the coming of the kingdom of God, which has no place unless we perform repentance; and in the performance of the divine will, which also embraces repentance; and not least in the imploring of grace and the remission of sins, which involves trust, the soul of repentance.

That certain things from Matthew have crept into this text of the Lord's Prayer is against the faith of the Greek Codices, which are consistent with themselves as far as all the petitions are concerned: nor are those last words concerning deliverance from evil missing in any Greek exemplar, which the Syriac and Arabic versions also have, even if they have not been found in the Latin Codices. What of the fact that these things which Luke reports were done in another place, at another time, and on another occasion than those in Matthew.

Latin:

CAPUT XI. ARGUMENTUM ET PAR- TITIO.

Christus rogatus docet discipulos suos orare, & certiores ipsos reddit de exauditione para- bola & similitudine. Dæmonium mutum e- jicit, idq; apologia contra calumnias defen- dit; mulierem, qui vere beati sint, docens: De signo Jonæ. De oculo, corporis lumine. In convivio Pharisæi, hypocrisin ejus, ob negle- ctum interioris purgationis, &amp; præcipuo- rum mandatorum Dei, fastumq; arguit, & legisperitos ob onera gravia aliis imposita, ac cædem Prophetarum inde ab Abele iis exprobrat, vanamque jactantiam clavis cognitionis. Qui ideo ipsi insidiantur.

Partes sunt quatuor: I. De precibus informa- tio, ad v. 13. II. Dæmonii muti ejectio cum apo- logia, ad v. 28. III. De signo Jonæ, & lumine commonitio, ad v. 36. IV. Pharisæorum &amp; legis- peritorum gravis increpatio, ad v. 54.

PARS I. Christi discipulorum de precibus informatio.

Vers. 1. Δίδαξον ἡμᾶς προσεύχεσθαι] Doce nos compen- dium rerum orandarum. Neq; enim eo tempore syllabis adstringebantur. Sic &amp; à Johanne credibile est propositam summam precum ad pœnitentiam pertinentium: quomo- do hæc Christi oratio continet regnum cœleste: hinc bre- viarium totius Evangelii Tertulliano dicitur, Cypriano cœlestis doctrinæ compendium. Omnino autem credibile est in Græcis Codicibus adjecta ex Matthæo, quæ Lucas omiserat, cùm non exstent in Latinis antiquis: illud: qui es in cœlis. Item: fiat voluntas tua ut in cœlo ita in terra (quod & Græci Codices quidam omittunt) item: sed libera nos à malo: quæ ipsa etiam, non expressa, vi insunt verbis cæteris.

Verba illa doce nos orare, quemadmodum vel ex ipso sono constat, non tantum materiam, sed etiam formam orationum inferunt. Quia non- dum orare docet, qui quænam petenda sint, deno- minat: neq; Christus tantum materiam orationum determinavit: sed formulam ἀναρρήδως præscri- psit quæ adhibenda in precationibus. Distin- ctio etiam illa inter ea, quæ Johannes orare do- cuerit, &amp; quæ Christus, nauci est: quia nec Johan- nes prædicavit pœnitentiam citra regnum cœlo- rum, sed ad regnum cœlorum Matth. III. v. 2. & ad remissionem peccatorum Luc. III. 3. neq; Christus regnum cœlorum annunciavit citra pœnitentiæ præconium Marc. I. 15. uterq; & ad pœnitentiam hortatus est, & ad fidem. Et in oratione à Christo præscripta nõ excluditur, sed includitur quicquid ad pœnitentiam pertinet: comprehendit enim id in sanctificatione nominis divini, quæ sine pœni- tentia apud nos nulla est; in adventu regni Dei, qui locum non habet, nisi pœnitentiam agamus; & in voluntatis divinæ præstatione, quæ comple- ctitur etiam pœnitentiam; nec non in imploratio- ne gratiæ & remissionis peccatorum, quæ fiduciam involvit, animam pœnitentiæ.

Irrepsisse quædam è Matthæo in hunc textum ora- tionis Dominicæ, contra fidem est Græcorum Co- dicum, qui sibi constant quantum ad omnes peti- tiones: neq; verba illa ultima de liberatione à ma- lo desiderantur in ullo Græco exemplari, quæ ha- bent etiam Syriaca, & Arabica versio, utut in La- tinis Codicibus non inventa sint. Quid quod hæc quæ Lucas refert, alio loco, alio tempore, alia occasione gesta sint, quam illa apud Matthæum.
