## 11:4
ἁμαρτίας] An exposition of that which is in Matthew, ὀφειλήματα.

Vers. 4. καὶ γὰρ ἀυτοὶ ἀφίεμεν παντὶ ὀφείλοντι ἡμῖν] For we also, by your command, forgive injuries to others, on account of the promise of pardon made to us under this condition.

Latin:

ἁμαρτίας] Expositio ejus quod apud Matthæum est ὀφειλήματα.

Vers. 4. καὶ γὰρ ἀυτοὶ ἀφίεμεν παντὶ ὀφείλοντι ἡμῖν] Nam & nos ex tuo præcepto injurias aliis condonamus, ob pro- missionem veniæ sub hac conditione nobis factam.

## 11:5
Vers. 5. χρῆσόν μοι] One is not to be blamed who translates it 'lend to me.' For in Plautus it is, 'If anyone borrows anything, let it be considered lost as if it were one's own.' But that the old interpreter here used 'commodare' (to lend) for 'mutuare' (to borrow), Salvianus, otherwise very skilled in the terminology of law, did the same: 'No one,' he says, 'wishes to be paid what he does not lend.'

Latin:

Vers. 5. χρῆσόν μοι] Non suit reprehendendus qui ver- tit mutua mihi. Nam apud Plautum est, Si quis quid mutuaberit, sit pro proprio perditum. Quod autem commodare pro inutuare hic posuit vetus in- terpres, fecit idem Salvianus juris vocum alioqui peritissi- mus: Nemo sibi solvi vult, inquit, quæ non commodat.

## 11:7
Vers. 7. Τὰ παιδία με μετ᾿ ἐμῦ εἰς τὴν κοίτην εἰσὶ] He signifies that there is no one at home who can give bread to the petitioner without inconvenience, since all had already gone to bed. The Syrian rightly translates παιδία as 'children'; for the name is accustomed to be taken in that way, as in Heb. 2:13-14.

Latin:

Vers. 7. Τὰ παιδία με μετ᾿ ἐμῦ εἰς τὴν κοίτην εἰσὶ] Signi- ficat neminem domi esse qui sine incommodo panes dare petenti possit: cum omnes jam cubitum iissent. Recte autem παιδία liberos vertit Syrus; ita enim sumti id no- men solet, ut Hebr. II 13 14.

## 11:8
Vers. 8. Διάγε τὴν ἀναίδειαν ἀυτᾶ] The Latin translator had not badly rendered it 'improbitatem' (shamelessness). For although it began to be extended further, 'probitas' (probity) is properly αἰδὼς (modesty); thus 'probus' (honest) is opposed to the 'inverecundus' (shameless). Sallust had spoken of Pompey in this sense: 'Of honest face, but shameless mind,' for which it is wrongly read in Suetonius, 'Of shameless face.' But as for what was added a little earlier in the Latin, 'And he will persist in knocking,' I think it was placed there for the sake of explanation, not because it existed in the Greek. But that word ἀναίδειας sufficiently signifies that persistent importunity.

Ὅσων χρήζει] You may even grant more if there is need.

Latin:

Vers. 8. Διάγε τὴν ἀναίδειαν ἀυτᾶ] Non male Latinus verterat improbitatem. Nam quanquam longius porrigi cœ- pit, probitas proprie est αἰδὼς: ita que opponitur probus in- verecundo. Sallustius hoc sensu Pompejum dixerat, Oris probi, animo inserecundo, pro quo male apud Suetonium legitur, Oris improbi. Quod autem paulo ante in Latinis est additum, Et ille perseverabit pulsans, explicandi causa positum puto, non quod in Græcis exstaret. Sed vox illa ἀναίδειας pervicacem istam flag rationem satis significat.

Ὅσων χρήζει] Etiam plus tribuas si opus est.

## 11:9
V. 9. κἀγὼ ὑμῖν λέγω] The comparison is not from a similarity, but from the greater; if an imprudent beggar obtains so much from a man, what will a suppliant and assiduous petitioner not obtain from God?

Latin:

V. 9. κἀγὼ ὑμῖν λέγω] Comparatio est non à simili, sed à majore; si imprudens flagitator tantum obtinet ab homi- ne, quid non à Deo obtinebit supplex & assiduus precator?

## 11:11
Vers. 11. τίνα δὲ ὑμῶν] The words cohere excellently if you interpret τίνα as 'if any,' according to those things which we have said elsewhere. For the sense is, if any of you, who is a parent, should ask his son for bread, will he give a stone to his son?

Latin:

Vers. 11. τίνα δὲ ὑμῶν] Oprime cohærent verba si τίνα interpreteris si quem, secundum ea quæ alibi diximus. Sen- sus enim est, si quem vestrum, qui parens sit, filius suus panem poscat, an is filio lapidem dabit?

## 11:13
Vers. 13. ὁ ἐξ ἐρανᾶ] that is, ἐράνιος, 'the Lord from heaven,' 1 Cor. 15:47. 'Our dwelling place from heaven,' 2 Cor. 5:1.

ἅγιον] Thus the Syrian and the Arab read. To the obtaining of this Spirit, therefore, that formula of prayer is chiefly directed.

That cannot be gathered from these: but only that we can also obtain the gift of the Holy Spirit by prayers, if prayers are made for that reason with confidence.

PART II. The casting out of the mute demon with Christ's apology.

Latin:

Vers. 13. ὁ ἐξ ἐρανᾶ] id est, ἐράνιος, ὁ κύριος ὁ ἐξ ἐρανᾶ, 1. Cor. XV. 47. τὸ οἰκητήριον ἡμῶν τὸ ἐξ ἐρανᾶ, 2. Cor. V. 1.

ἅγιον] Ita legerunt Syrus & Arabs. Ad hunc ergo spiritum impetrandum præcipue directa est illa precandi formula.

Id ex his colligi non potest: sed solum quod etiam Spiritus S. donum precibus impetrari pos- simus, si preces cum fiducia ideo fiant.

PARS II. Dæmonii muti ejectio cum apologia Christi.

## 11:17
Vers. 17. οἶκος ἐπὶ οἶκον] Supply διαμερισθεὶς, which the Syrian rightly expressed. Moreover, οἶκος ἐπὶ οἶκον is said in the Hebrew manner for οἶκος ἐφ᾽ ἑαυτὸν, with the preceding word repeated in place of the relative.

Latin:

Vers. 17. οἶκος ἐπὶ οἶκον] Supple διαμερισθεὶς quod re- cte expressit Syrus. Est autem οἶκος ἐπὶ οἶκον Hebraico more dictum pro οἶκος ἐφ᾽ ἑαυτὸν, antecedente voce repe- tira vice relativi.

## 11:20
Vers. 20. ἐν δακτύλῳ Θεᾶ] He alludes to the history of Exodus, ch. 8, v. 19. Just as then the finger of God working in Moses was a sign of the people being liberated from Egypt, so now the finger of God working through Christ is an effective sign of our liberation from sin, which is the kingdom of God.

The kingdom of God has come upon you] Dan. VII. 22. where in the Greek the same word ἔφθασε.

Latin:

Vers. 20. ἐν δακτύλῳ Θεᾶ] Alludit ad Exodi historiam cap. VIII. v. 19. Sicut tunc digitus Dei in Mose operans si- gnum erat populi liberandi ex Ægypto, ita nunc digitus Dei per Christum efficax signum liberationis nostræ à pec- cato, quod est regnum Dei.

ἔφθασεν ἐφ᾽ ὑμᾶς ἡ βασιλεία τῦ Θεᾶ] Dan. VII. 22. ubi in Græco vox eadem ἔφθασε.

## 11:21
Vers. 21. court] the palace. See the note on the passage in Matt. XXVI. 8.

is in peace] they are in safety.

Latin:

Vers. 21. ἀυλὴν] τὸ βασίλειον. Vide ad locum Matth. XXVI. 8.

ἐν εἰρήνῃ ἐστὶ] in tuto sunt.

## 11:22
Vers. 22. the full armor.] I think that here it is treated of arms properly, because καθωπλισμένος preceded. Opposed to this armor of the Devil is the armor of God described in Eph. VI.

his spoils] This also must be taken in a military sense. Matthew said to plunder the house. Moreover, there was a proverb among the Hebrews הִיקח מִגִבּור מַלְקוֹחַ that is, shall anyone take spoils from a giant, Isaiah XLIX. v. 24. to which allusion is made here.

Latin:

Vers. 22. τὴν πανοπλίαν.] Puto hic de armis proprie agi quia præcessit καθωπλισμένος. Opponitur huic armaturæ Diaboli Dei armatura descripta ad Ephes. VI.

τὰ σκύλα ἀυτᾶ] Etiam hoc sumendum in bellica signi- ficatione. οἰκίαν διαρπάζειν dixit Matthæus. Erat autem proverbium inter Hebræos הִיקח מִגִבּור מַלְקוֹחַ id est μὴ λήψεται τις παρὰ γίγαντος σκύλα, Esaiæ XLIX. v. 24. ad quod hic alluditur.

## 11:24
v. 24. through waterless places. That Satan in truth traverses deserted places which he makes infested and unsafe with his specters, but does not lay aside the desire of again besieging the miserable man, but rather always burns with zeal for a return to his former dwelling, is not an inconvenient explanation. But it is indicated in this way that the matter stands thus with spiritual obsession. In which we leave it to be considered whether by the ἀνύδρους τόπους, which he traverses, can be understood those who are without the water of refreshment outside of Christ, such as Christ wishes to refresh, Matth. XI. Of which kind were the Gentiles, whom he might think of as his own, so that the impure demon would easily cross over into those who had been liberated from the Jews, promising himself a more ready dwelling. For in Gentilism there was then mere dryness, Isa. XLIV. verse 3. This passage is illustrated by the place 2. Pet. II. v. 20. et seqq. Aretius explains the parable at Matth. XII. thus: Dry places are spoken of with respect to Satan, those are such places as exclude him, such as the breasts of the faithful, which burn with hope, faith, charity, &c. ἀνυδρὰ are thirsty, which labor under a penury of water, that is, which are not cold, but are inflamed by the heat of the Spirit of GOD. He wanders through such, but finds no dwelling. That heat of faith, hope, and similar virtues does not endure so unclean a spirit. Let the zeal of Satan be considered, who attempts all things, leaves nothing undone, attempts even the most holy things, so that he may have a place in the human heart. At the same time it is not obscurely demonstrated how Satan can be repelled, namely by faith, by ardent prayer: here 1. Pet. V. v. 9. Resist Satan by faith.

Latin:

v. 24. δι᾽ ἀνύδρων τόπων. Diserta loca quæ infesta & intuta Satanas qui- dem reddat spectris suis transire, sed deside- rium hominem miserum iterum obsidendi non deponere Satanam, quin reditus ad pristinum domicilium studio semper flagret, non incom- moda est explicatio. Sed indicatur ita hic se rem habere cum spirituali obsessione. In qua ἀπόδοσις anne per ἀνύδρους τόπους, quos transit, intelligi possint, qui sine aqua refectionis extra Christum sunt, quales Christus reficere vult, Matth. XI. Cujusmodi erant gentiles, quos ceu suos putet, ita facile transiturus sit impurus daemon in iis, qui e Judaeis liberati erant, paratius domicilium sibi promittens, cogitandum relinquimus. In gentilismo enim tum erat mera siccitas, Esa. XLIV. vers. 3. Pericopen hanc illustrat locus 2. Petr. II. v. 20. seqq. Aretius ad Matth XII. parabolam sic explicat: Arentia loca dicuntur respectu Sata- nae, illa talia sunt loca omnia, quae eum excludunt, qualia sunt pectora fidelium, quae ardent spe, fide, charitate, &c. ἀνυδρὰ siticulosa sunt, quae penuria aquae laborant, hoc est, quae frigida non sunt, calore Spiritus DEI inflammata sunt. Talia pererrat, sed mansionem non reperit. Ille aestus fidei, spei, si- miliumque virtutum non fert tam immundum spiri- tum. Studium Satanae consideretur, qui omnia tentat, nihil non molitur, sanctissima etiam tentat, ut locum habere possit in humano corde. Simul non obscure demonstratur, quomodo repelli Satan possit, fide nimirum, ardenti oratione: hic 1. Pet. V. v. 9. Fide resistite Satanae.

## 11:27
Vers. 27.

μακαρία ἡ κοιλία ἡ βαστάσασά σε] A manner of speaking not unknown to the Greeks also. The writer of the book about Hero and Leander who is accustomed to be called Musaeus: Ὅλβιος ὅς σ᾽ ἐφύτευσε καὶ ὀλβίη ἡ τέκε μήτηρ, Γαστὴρ ἥ σ᾽ ἐλόχευσε μακαρτάτη. You have womb and breasts in the circumlocution of women and below XXIII. 29. In the Talmudic books there is אשרי יולדתו, ὀλβία ἥ σε ἔτικτε among the Greeks.

Latin:

Vers. 27.

μακαρία ἡ κοιλία ἡ βαστάσασά σε] Mos loquendi Graecis quoque non ignotus. Scriptor libri de Ero & Leandro qui Musaeus dici solet: Ὅλβιος ὅς σ᾽ ἐφύτευσε καὶ ὀλβίη ἡ τέκε μήτηρ, Γαστὴρ ἥ σ᾽ ἐλόχευσε μακαρτάτη. Uterum & ubera in circumlocutione foeminarum habes & infra XXIII. 29. In Thalmudicis libris est אשרי יולדתו, ὀλβία ἥ σε ἔτικτε apud Graecos.

## 11:28
Vers. 28.

μενοῦνγε] ἐπανόρθωσις. Not denying what had been said, that the mother was happy by the name of such a birth, which the Angel also and Elisabeth, filled with the Holy Spirit, had said: but adding something greater, namely eternal and solid blessedness, and that it is not situated in this, nor is it proper to Mary.

οἱ ἀκούοντες τὸν λόγον τοῦ Θεοῦ καὶ φυλάσσοντες αὐτόν] To hear the word is to conceive Christ: to observe it is to bring forth. Those who miscarry are in a worse place than if they had not conceived, Matth. VII. v. 27. Roman. II. v. 13. Jac. I. v. 22. For Φυλάσσειν in this place, as also Matth. IX. v. 20. Marc. X. verse 20. Luke below XVIII. v. 21. Acts VII. v. 53. Roman. II. v. 26. Gal. VI. v. 13. is the same as ποιεῖν in other places already mentioned.

PART III.

On the sign of Jonah, and the commotion of the light.

Latin:

Vers. 28.

μενοῦνγε] ἐπανόρθωσις. non negans quod erat dictum no- mine tanti partus felicem esse matrem, quod Angelus quo- que & Elisabetha, Sancto Spiritu plena dixerat: sed majus aliquid addens, beatitudinem scilicet aeternam ac soli- dam, neque in hoc esse sitam, neque Mariae esse pro- priam.

οἱ ἀκούοντες τὸν λόγον τοῦ Θεοῦ καὶ φυλάσσοντες αὐτόν] Au- dire verbum, est Christum concipere: observare est parere. Qui abortiunt pejore loco sunt quam si non concepissent, Matth. VII. v. 27. Roman. II. v. 13. Jac. I. v. 22. Φυλάσσειν enim hoc loco, ut & Matth. IX. v. 20. Marc. X. vers. 20. Lucae infra XVIII. v. 21. Actor. VII. v. 53. Roman. II. v. 26. Gal. VI. v. 13. idem est quod aliis jam dictis locis ποιεῖν.

PARS III.

De signo Ionae, & lumine commotio.

Vers. 30.

ἐγένετο Ἰωνᾶς σημεῖον] See above ch. II. v. 34. & what was said there.

Vers. 30.

ἐγένετο Ἰωνᾶς σημεῖον] Vide supra c. II. v. 34. & quae ini- bi dicta.

## 11:33
Vers. 33.

οὐδεὶς λύχνον ἅψας] Christ, as the wise were accustomed to do, inculcated this maxim more frequently when the occasion was given; and so it is found twice in Luke, which is also fair to understand regarding other maxims. However, it seems to have been said at this time for the explanation of that which had preceded: μακάριοι οἱ ἀκούοντες τὸν λόγον καὶ φυλάσσοντες αὐτὸν. For φυλάσσειν is to bring it about that the light of the word implanted in the soul may appear through works. See what [is said] regarding Matthew.

εἰς κρυπτὸν] Thus the Syriac and Latin: and I prefer that to what other codices prefer, κρύπτην. For εἰς κρυπτὸν here is the same as ὑπὸ κλίνην above, ch. VIII. 16.

Latin:

Vers. 33.

οὐδεὶς λύχνον ἅψας] Sententiam hanc Christus, ut sa- pientes solebant, occasione data saepius inculcabat; itaque apud Lucam bis reperitur, quod & de aliis sententiis par est intelligi. Videtur autem hoc tempore dictum ad explica- tionem ejus quod praecesserat: μακάριοι οἱ ἀκούοντες τὸν λόγον καὶ φυλάσσοντες αὐτὸν. Nam φυλάσσειν est efficere ut lux verbi animis insiti per opera appareat. Vide quae ad Matthaeum.

εἰς κρυπτὸν] Ita Syrus & Latinus: atque id malo quam quod alii codices praeferunt κρύπτην. Nam idem hic est εἰς κρυπτὸν quod supra ὑπὸ κλίνην, c. VIII. 16.

## 11:34
ὁ λύχνος τοῦ σώματος] This maxim is also among those frequently repeated. But it is applied now to the perverse judgments of men concerning Christ, arising from a cloud of passions.

Latin:

ὁ λύχνος τοῦ σώματος] Est & hæc sententia inter sæpe repetitas. Applicatur autem nunc ad perversas hominum de Christo judicationes nascentes ex affectuum nubilo.

## 11:35
Vers. 35.

σκόπει μὴ τὸ φῶς τὸ ἐν σοὶ σκότος ἐστὶ] I praise those who translate 'Consider whether your light is not darkness.' For that is the force of the particle μὴ after the verb σκοπεῖν. Xenophon: 'I consider whether it has been brought or given back.'

Latin:

Vers. 35.

σκόπει μὴ τὸ φῶς τὸ ἐν σοὶ σκότος ἐστὶ] Laudo eos qui vertunt Considera an non lux tua tenebræ sint. Nam ea vis est poculæ μὴ post verbum σκοπεῖν. Xenophon σκοπῶ μὴ ἐπά- γαγον ἦ ἀποδεδωκά.

## 11:36
Vers. 36.

ἔσται φωτεινὸν ὅλον ὡς ὅταν ὁ λύχνος τῇ ἀστραπῇ φωτίζῃ σε] For ἔσται supply σοι. Understand that φωτεινὸς ὅλον as 'the body.' That is, for the whole body will provide you the use which a widely flashing lamp would provide: so there will be nothing that might cause you to stumble. 'He remains in the light and there is no stumbling block in him,' says John, 1 Epist. II. 10. Therefore, Christ here calls the perpetual tenor of life 'the body,' which John in the aforementioned place calls 'remaining in the light,' and in the same Epistle I. 7, 'walking in the light.'

PART IV. A grave rebuke of the Pharisees and lawyers.

Latin:

Vers. 36.

ἔσται φωτεινὸν ὅλον ὡς ὅταν ὁ λύχνος τῇ ἀστραπῇ φωτίζῃ σε] ἔσται supple σοι. illud φωτεινὸς ὅλον intellige τὸ σῶμα. Id est, enim tibi usum præbebit corpus totum lucidum, quem præ- beret late coruscans lucerna: adeo nihil erit quod te offen- dat. ἐν τῷ φωτὶ μένῃ καὶ σκάνδαλον ἐν αὐτῷ οὐκ ἔστιν, inquit Johannes 1. Epist. II. 10. Corpus ergo Christus hic vocat perpetuum vitæ tenorem, quod Johannes d. l. ἐν φωτὶ μέ- νειν, & eadem Epistola I. 7. ἐν φωτὶ περιπατεῖν appellat.

PARS IV. Gravis Pharisæorum & legisperitorum increpatio.

## 11:38
Vers. 38.

ἐβαπτίσθη] that is, he washed his hands. But they prefer to say ἐβαπτίσθη, because the whole hand and part of the arm up to the elbow was not lightly sprinkled, but as it were immersed, so that no filth might adhere. See what [is said] regarding Matt. XV. Mark VII.

πρὸ τοῦ ἀρίστου] For according to the Jewish dogma, all food was unclean without washing.

Latin:

Vers. 38.

ἐβαπτίσθη] id est, ἐνίψατο τὰς χεῖρας. Sed ἐβαπτίσθη di- cere malunt, quia manus tota & brachii pars cubito tenus non leviter perfundebatur, sed quasi mersabatur ne quid sordis adhæreret. Vide quæ ad Matth. XV. Marc. VII.

πρὸ τοῦ ἀρίστου] Nam illotis ex Judaico dogmate omnis cibus erat immundus.

## 11:39
Vers. 39.

νῦν ὑμεῖς] It might seem to be an adversative discourse to what was said before, as if Christ were saying, the soul ought to have been cared for primarily. But now you are occupied with external things. But in that sense, νῦν usually has δὲ attached: as below in chapter XIX, v. 42. Wherefore we shall explain it more correctly thus: As things are now, you care for nothing else than what pertains to outward cleanliness: as if Christ were looking primarily at the customs of the age: as above when he said this generation. He could, however, do so here all the more justly because that tradition was not very ancient.

τὸ ἔξωθεν τοῦ ποτηρίου καὶ τοῦ πίνακος καθαρίζετε] You do just as much as if you were diligently purging what is outside of cups and dishes. For it is a comparison, as we said regarding Matthew.

Τὸ δὲ ἔσωθεν ὑμῶν γέμει ἁρπαγῆς καὶ πονηρίας] A brief discourse which leaves part of the comparison unsaid. For the sense is, as we said regarding Matthew: but just as those cups and dishes, if they were clearly purged on the outside, would be teeming with filth on the inside, so when you are well washed on the outside, your soul is impure with the consciousness of wicked deeds.

Latin:

Vers. 39.

νῦν ὑμεῖς] Posset videri esse adversativa oratio πρὸς τὸ σιντωμένου, quasi diceret Christus, animum præcipue cu- rari oportuit. At nunc in externis occupamini. Sed eo sen- su νῦν solet habere δὲ adjunctum: ut infra cap. XIX. v. 42. Quare rectius sic exponemus: Ut nunc res sunt, nihil aliud curatis quam quod ad exteriorem munditiam attinet: ut fuit potissimum sæculi mores respiciat Christus: ut supra cum dixit γενεὰ αὑτή. Potuit autem hic eo justius facere quia traditio illa non erat admodum antiqua.

τὸ ἔξωθεν τοῦ ποτηρίου καὶ τοῦ πίνακος καθαρίζετε] Tantun- dem facitis, ac si quod extra est poculi & patinarum purge- tis diligenter. Est enim comparatio, ut ad Matthæum di- ximus.

Τὸ δὲ ἔσωθεν ὑμῶν γέμει ἁρπαγῆς καὶ πονηρίας] Breviloqua oratio quæ partem comparationis subticet. Sensus enim est, ut ad Matthæum diximus: sed quasi illa plane exterius purgata pocula & patinæ intus scaterent sordibus, ita cum vos extra bene estis loti, animus vester impurus est flagi- tiorum conscientia.

## 11:40
Vers. 40.

οὐχ᾿ ὁ ποιήσας τὸ ἔξωθεν καὶ τὸ ἔσωθεν ἐποίησε;] First he brings in what is less, at least that the soul, created by the same God, ought to have been cared for alongside the body: intending then to bring in what is greater, that nothing is unclean to the body, as far as salvation pertains to a soul that is well conscious of itself.

Latin:

Vers. 40.

οὐχ᾿ ὁ ποιήσας τὸ ἔξωθεν καὶ τὸ ἔσωθεν ἐποίησε;] Primum in- fert quod minus est, saltem juxta corpus animum curari debuisse ab eodem Deo conditum: illaturus deinde quod majus est, nihil esse corpori immundum, quod ad salutem attinet animo sibi bene conscio.

## 11:41
Vers. 41.

πλὴν τὰ ἐνόντα δότε ἐλεημοσύνην, καὶ ἰδοὺ πάντα καθαρὰ ὑμῖν ἐστιν] This passage is explained in various ways here. But none of the Greeks accepted δότε as indicative, nor does custom allow it, as has been correctly noted by a most learned man. Wherefore it must be accepted entirely as imperative, in the way that the Latin, Syriac, and Arabic [versions] have accepted it. Nor does it please me that this saying be explained ironically: both because that interpretation cannot but seem forced in this place, and because it is probable that the sense is the same as in the words of Matthew, where it is ἵνα γένηται καὶ τὸ ἐκτὸς καθαρὸν, except that there the figure taken from cups and dishes is continued, [while] here the same thing is said more plainly. For the rest of the things are also the same. Wherefore also in these words, τὰ ἐνόντα δότε ἐλεημοσύνην, the same sense is to be sought which is in those words of Matthew, καθάρισον τὸ ἐντὸς. There are those who think τὰ ἐνόντα is the same as τὸ λοιπὸν, that is, the connection of the discourse: but I desire an example of that locution. Add to this that τὸ λοιπὸν cannot have a place here, since what the Pharisees were doing contributed absolutely nothing to true purity. Wherefore it is much more correct that we understand τὰ ἐνόντα to be κατὰ τὰ ἐνόντα, just as the Greeks say τὸν ἐνόντα τρόπον for that which is as much as possible. And so δότε ἐλεημοσύνην τὰ ἐνόντα is, exercise mercy as much as you possibly can. Thus τὰ ἐνόντα corresponds to the Hebrew word מִסַּת in Deut. XVI. v. 10. Tertullian, having followed this sense, translates it, or cites it translated by another, Date quæ habetis. For Luke also said διδόναι ἐλεημοσύνην below in chapter XII. v. 35, for which other writers say ποιεῖν ἐλεημοσύνην. There is no doubt that this exhortation too was common in the mouths of the Hebrews, which the writer of Tobit expressed thus: ἐκ τῶν ὑπαρχόντων σοι ποίει ἐλεημοσύνην: and thus: ὡς σοὶ ὑπάρχει κατὰ τὸ πλῆθος ποίη-

συνεξαυτῶν ἐλεημοσύνη, cap. IV. 79. It remains to see in what sense it is said that all things will be clean to those who perform works of mercy: whether these works are consequent to cleanliness or antecedent to it. For my part, as far as the matter is concerned, I do not doubt that both are true: for certain works of mercy are accustomed to precede that cleansing, and many more and more abundant ones are accustomed to follow it. But the circumstances of this passage, if I am not mistaken, demand the former meaning. For Christ here gives counsel for cleansing the soul: the soul is cleansed through repentance. Repentance has two parts: to desist from evil, in which is also the restitution of things ill-gotten (for the detention of another’s property is also a sin); then to begin some works of better fruit, which the Baptist calls καρποὺς ἀξίους μετανοίας. Among these works, however, works of mercy are most prominent: and so, by synecdoche, the whole of repentance is accustomed to be described by them. Thus Solomon in Proverbs XVI. 6. בחסד ואמת יכפר עון, by truth and mercy iniquity is expiated. Daniel gives the same counsel to Nebuchadnezzar that Christ here gives to the Pharisees: τὰς ἁμαρτίας σου ἐν ἐλεημοσύναις λύτρωσαι, as the Greek version has it in chapter IV, verse 24; looking back to which passage, Salvian greatly accuses those who do not deign to redeem at least by gifts and mercies the things they have committed. ἐλεημοσύνη ἐκ θανάτου ῥύεται, καὶ οὐκ ἐᾷ εἰσελθεῖν εἰς τὸ σκότος, is in Tobit IV, verse 11. ἐλεημοσύνη ἐκ θανάτου ῥύεται καὶ αὐτὴ ἀποκαθαίρῃ πᾶσαν ἁμαρτίαν, in the same book, XII, verse 9. The writer of Ecclesiasticus III, verse 34: πῦρ φλογιζόμενον ἀποσβέσει ὕδωρ, καὶ ἐν ἐλεημοσύναις ἐξιλάσεται ἁμαρτίας: and chapter XXIX, verse 15: σύγκλεισον ἐλεημοσύνην ἐν τοῖς ταμιείοις σου καὶ αὐτὴ ἐξελεῖταί σε ἐκ πάσης κακώσεως. In which sense can also be taken that saying of Peter, ἀγάπη καλύπτει πλῆθος ἁμαρτιῶν, in his first epistle, chapter IV, verse 8; add Isaiah, chapter I, verse 17. In the Constitutions of Clement, book VII, chapter XIII, we also read: ἐὰν ἔχεις διὰ τῶν χειρῶν σου δὸς, ἵνα ἐργάσῃ εἰς λύτρωσιν ἁμαρτιῶν σου. ἐλεημοσύναις γὰρ καὶ πίστεσιν ἀποκαθαίρονται ἁμαρτίαι. Lactantius, book VI: Great is the reward of mercy, for which God promises that He will remit all sins. But those things which follow immediately are even more pertinent to the present passage: Yet do not think that because sins are taken away by giving, license to sin is granted to you; for they are abolished if you give to God because you have sinned, for if you sin with the confidence of giving, they are not abolished. For God desires most of all that men be purged from sin, and therefore He commands them to do penance. But to do penance is nothing other than to profess and affirm that one will sin no further. Add Chrysostom in his oration on why the Devil is allowed to exist, Volume VI, where among the ὁδὸς μετανοίας he commends this one to us. The same author in his second oration on Repentance says, μετάνοια χωρὶς ἐλεημοσύνης νεκρά ἐστι καὶ ἄπτερος. Now what follows, καὶ ἰδὲ πάντα καθαρὰ ὑμῖν ἐστι, is similar to what Paul says, although, due to the difference in times, in a broader sense, πάντα καθαρὰ τοῖς καθαροῖς Tit. I. v. 15. This is surely what Christ means: to amend the body without the soul is useless; but on the contrary, when the soul has been cleansed through repentance, all things not forbidden by God are open for use, so that no stain can be contracted from them.

The ironical exposition, to which the version of B. Luther gives assent, is not so absurd or forced; Ludov. de Dieu also approves of it, comparing that passage in Eccles. II. v. 9. But it is inconsistent with the analogy of faith that all the works of mercy of those who perform them should be the means of cleansing, as if Christ were here giving counsel to change the mind through repentance, which is described συνεκδοχικῶς by works of mercy. For Grotius assumes that certain works of mercy precede a true change of mind: which is false, since there are no works of mercy that do not proceed from faith, through which our hearts must be purified so that pure works may flow from them, Acts XV. v. 9. And where is it that to exercise works of mercy is to change and cleanse the mind through repentance? This is merely ἰδία ἐπίλυσις. The passages Prov. XVI. v. 6. Dan. IV. v. 24. they do not treat of the cleansing of the soul or the expiation of guilt, but of the remission of temporal punishment, which we obtain through alms, beneficence, and sincerity of love. 1. Pet. IV. v. 8. however, the discourse is about covering the infirmities of one's neighbor through charity; and therefore these are ἀλλότρια. The rest from Tob. IV. 11. c. XII. 9. Syr. III. 33. c. 29, 17. are ἔξω τοῦ κάνονος, and are to be explained partly, as we have advised regarding other passages brought forward from Solomon and Daniel, and partly according to the rule prescribed by Christ in Luke XVI. 9.

ὅτι ἀποδεκατῦτε) Why anyone should prefer ὁἱ to ὅτι here, I truly see no probable cause. For ὅτι is placed after οὐαὶ in a similar manner several times in Matthew, chapter XI. v. 21, chapter XXIII. v. 13, 14, 23, 25, 27, 29.

Latin:

Vers. 41.

πλὴν τὰ ἐνόντα δότε ἐλεημοσύνην, καὶ ἰδοὺ πάντα καθαρὰ ὑμῖν ἐστιν] Varie hic locus exponitur. At nemo Græcorum δότε accepit indicative, neque id consuetudo patitur, ut re- cte est a viro doctissimo annotatum. Quare omnino ac- cipiendum imperative, quomodo acceperunt Latinus, Sy- rus, Arabs. Neque placet hoc dictum εἰρωνικῶς exponi: tum quia non potest ea interpretatio hoc loco non coacta videri, tum quia probabile est eundem esse sensum qui in Matthæi verbis, ubi est ἵνα γένηται καὶ τὸ ἐκτὸς καθαρὸν, nisi quod ibi continuatur figura a poculis & patinis sumta, hic res eadem planius dicitur. Nam & cætera omnia eadem sunt. Quare & in istis verbis, τὰ ἐνόντα δότε ἐλεημοσύνην, idem sensus quærendus est, qui est in Matthæi illis καθάρι- σον τὸ ἐντὸς. Sunt qui putant τὰ ἐνόντα idem esse quod τὸ λοιπὸν, orationis scilicet connexionem: sed ejus locu- tionis exemplum desidero. Adde quod nec locum hic ha- bere potest τὸ λοιπὸν, cum id quod faciebant Pharisæi ad veram munditiem nihil plane conduceret. Quare multo rectius est, ut intelligamus τὰ ἐνόντα esse κατὰ τὰ ἐνόντα, quomodo τὸν ἐνόντα τρόπον dicunt Græci, pro eo quod est, quam maxime fieri potest. Itaque δότε ἐλεημοσύνην τὰ ἐνόντα est, exercete misericordiam quantum potestis ma- xime. Ita respondet τὰ ἐνόντα voci Hebrææ מִסַּת Deut. XVI. v. 10. Tertullianus hunc sensum secutus vertit aut ab alio versum citat, Date quæ habetis. Nam διδόναι ἐλεημο- σύνην etiam infra dixit Lucas cap. XII. v. 35. pro quo alii scriptores dicunt ποιεῖν ἐλεημοσύνην. Dubium non est quin hoc quoque monitum tritum fuerit in ore Hebræorum, quod scriptor Tobiæ ita extulit: ἐκ τῶν ὑπαρχόντων σοι ποίει ἐλεημοσύνην: & sic: ὡς σοὶ ὑπάρχει κατὰ τὸ πλῆθος ποίη-

συνεξαυτῶν ἐλεημοσύνη, cap. IV. 79. Super est videre quo sensu dicantur omnia munda futura facientibus opera misericordiae: sint ne haec opera consequentia munditiam an antecedentia. Ego quod ad rem attinet, verum utrumque esse non dubito: Nam & opera quaedam misericordiae mundationem illam antecedere, & multo plura ac uberiora eam consequi solent. Sed loci hujus circumstantiae priorem, ni fallor, significationem postulant. Dat enim Christus hic mundandi animi consilium: mundatur animus per poenitentiam. Poenitentia duas habet partes: à malo desistere, in quo est & restitutio rerum male partarum (nam & detentio alieni peccatum est; deinde inchoare aliqua opera frugis melioris, quos καρποὺς ἀξίους μετανοίας vocat Baptista. In his autem operibus eminent maxime opera misericordiae: itaque ex his συνεκδοχικῶς tota poenitentia solet describi. Sic Solomo in Gnomis XVI. 6. בחסד ואמת יכפר עון in veritate & misericordia expiatur iniquitas. Daniel Nabuchodonosori idem dat consilium, quod hic Christus Pharisaeis: τὰς ἁμαρτίας σου ἐν ἐλεημοσύναις λύτρωσαι, ut habet Graeca versio cap. IV. v. 24. quem locum respiciens Salvianus multum eos accusat qui quae admiserunt, donis saltem ac misericordiis redimere non dignantur. ἐλεημοσύνη ἐκ θανάτου ῥύεται, καὶ οὐκ ἐᾷ εἰσελθεῖν εἰς τὸ σκότος, est apud Tobiam IV. v. 11. ἐλεημοσύνη ἐκ θανάτου ῥύεται καὶ αὐτὴ ἀποκαθαίρῃ πᾶσαν ἁμαρτίαν, eodem libro XII. v. 9. Scriptor Ecclesiastici III, v. 34. πῦρ φλογιζόμενον ἀποσβέσει ὕδωρ, καὶ ἐν ἐλεημοσύναις ἐξιλάσεται ἁμαρτίας: & cap. XXIX. v. 15. σύγκλεισον ἐλεημοσύνην ἐν τοῖς ταμιείοις σου καὶ αὐτὴ ἐξελεῖταί σε ἐκ πάσης κακώσεως. In quem sensum accipi potest & Petri illud, ἀγάπη καλύπτει πλῆθος ἁμαρτιῶν Epistola priore cap. IV. v. 8. adde Esaiam cap. I. v. 17. In Clementis quoque constitutionibus libro VII. cap. XIII. legimus, ἐὰν ἔχεις διὰ τῶν χειρῶν σου δὸς, ἵνα ἐργάσῃ εἰς λύτρωσιν ἁμαρτιῶν σου. ἐλεημοσύναις γὰρ καὶ πίστεσιν ἀποκαθαίρονται ἁμαρτίαι. Lactantius libro VI. Magna est misericordiae merces, cui Deus pollicetur peccata se omnia remissurum. Magis vero etiam ad praesentem locum pertinent, quae mox sequuntur: Nec tamen quia peccata largitione tolluntur, dari sibi licentiam peccandi putes: abolentur enim, si Deo largiare quia peccaveris, nam si fiducia largiendi pecces, non abclentur. Deus enim purgari homines à peccato maxime cupit: ideoque agere poenitentiam jubet. Agere autem poenitentiam nihil aliud est, quam profiteri & affirmare se non ulterius peccaturum. Adde Chrysostomum oratione cur sinatur esse Diabolus Tomo VI. ubi inter ὁδὸς μετανοίας & hanc nobis commendat. Ejusdem est secunda oratione de Poenitentia, μετάνοια χωρὶς ἐλεημοσύνης νεκρά ἐστι καὶ ἄπτερος. Quod autem sequitur καὶ ἰδὲ πάντα καθαρὰ ὑμῖν ἐστι, simile est ei quod dicit Paulus, quanquam, pro temporum diversitate, laxiore sensu, πάντα καθαρὰ τοῖς καθαροῖς Tit. I. v. 15. Hoc nimirum vult Christus: Corpus quidem sine animo emendare inutile est: at contra animo per poenitentiam mundato, res omnes à Deo non vetitae ad usum patent, ita ut nihil inde labis possit contrahi.

Non adeo absurda aut coacta est Ironica expositio, cui annuit B. Lutheri versio; quam probat etiam Ludov. de Dieu, conferens illud Eccles. II. v. 9. Id vero absonum est ab analogia fidei, quod omnia mundi sint facientibus opera misericordiae, quasi daret Christus hic consilium mutandi animi per poenitentiam, quae συνεκδοχικῶς describatur per opera misericordiae. Assumit nempe Grotius opera quaedam misericordiae veram mutationem animi praecedere: quod falsum, quum misericordiae opera nulla sint quae non ex fide proficiscantur, per quam corda nostra purificari oportet, ut opera inde pura redundare possint, Actor. XV. v. 9. Et ubi opera misericordiae exercere est animum per poenitentiam mutare, ac mundare? Est haec mere ἰδία ἐπίλυσις. Loca Prov. XVI. v. 6. Dan. IV. v. 24. non de mundatione animi, aut expiatione culpae, sed de remissione temporalis poenae, quam eleemosynis, beneficentia, & sinceritate dilectionis consequimur, agunt. 1. Pet. IV. v. 8. vero de tegendis proximi infirmitatibus per charitatem sermo est; ideoque haec ἀλλότρια sunt. Caetera è Tob. IV. 11. c. XII. 9. Syr. III. 33. c. 29, 17. sunt ἔξω τοῦ κάνονος, & explicanda partim, uti de aliis locis monuimus è Salomone & Daniele adductis, partim juxta regulam à Christo praescriptam Luc. XVI. 9.

ὅτι ἀποδεκατῦτε) Cur quis hĥc malit ὁἱ quam ὅτι sane nihil probabilis causæ video. Nam ὅτι simili modo post οὐαὶ ponitur apud Matthæum aliquoties, cap. XI. v. 21. cap. XXIII. v. 13. 14. 23. 25. 27. 29.

## 11:42
τὴν κρίσιν) The duties of natural equity. See what [is written] on Matthew.

Latin:

τὴν κρίσιν) Æquitatis naturalis officia. Vide quæ ad Matthæum.

## 11:44
Verse 44.

μνημεῖα ἄδηλα) Buried deep underground, such as there were many in the region of Palestine, as it was ὑπόπετροι (rocky underneath). In Matthew there is another comparison taken from monuments signifying the same thing. It is possible that Christ used now this one, now that one.

It is to be observed here that this is a similar, not the same, discourse as that which is described in Matthew ch. XXIII: which is evident from the circumstance of times, places, and the object, and also from the subject matter itself. See the Harmony of B. Gerhard, ch. CLVIII, near the beginning.

Latin:

Vers. 44.

μνημεῖα ἄδηλα) Penitus sub terram defossa, qualia mul- ta erant in regione Palæstina, ut quæ esset ὑπόπετροι. A- pud Matthæum est alia comparatio à monumentis sumta idem significans. Fieri potest ut modo hanc, modo illam Christus usurpaverit.

Observandum hic similem esse, non eandem concionem quæ apud Matth. c. XXIII. describitur: quod è circumstantia temporum, locorum & ob- jecti patet, nec non ex materia ipsa. Vid. Harm. B. Gerhardi c. CLVIII. sub initium.

## 11:45
Verse 45.

ταῦτα λέγων κ̓ ἡμᾶς ὑβρίζεις) By consequence. For the Pharisees observed the decrees of the lawyers most exactly: the lawyers in turn proclaimed their sanctity with great praises. Thus the mules scratch each other. It may be gathered from this that what the Greek books have in the previous verse, and from them the Syriac and Arabic, γραμματεῖς καὶ Φαρισαῖοι ὑποκριταὶ, was added from elsewhere, for the Latin interpreter does not read it.

The Greek text is wrongly corrected from the Latin version: which, with the agreement of the Codices, and with the Syriac and Arabic interpreters not dissenting, reads those words. Therefore, the lawyers were not noted only by consequence, but expressly: either because the νομικοὶ were themselves γραμματεῖς, which seemed to be the case to Spanheim, Dub. Evang. part II, p. 399, or rather, because the νομικοὶ handed down the ὁμόνια to the Scribes on that point, whom B. Gerhard makes distinct from them in part I of the Harmony of the Gospels, ch. CLVI, p. 1276, in this way: that while all νομικοὶ were indeed γραμματεῖς and νομοδιδάσκαλοι. Cf. Matt. IX. 3, Luke V. 17, not all γραμματεῖς and νομοδιδάσκαλοι were νομικοὶ, but only those who had a place in the great Ecclesiastical Sanhedrin, in whose hands was the Ecclesiastical jurisdiction. John Cameron in his Notes on Matt. ch. XX also distinguishes the Scribes from the interpreters of the Law. But for another reason: namely, that the γραμματεῖς interpreted the law publicly in the Synagogues, performing an Ecclesiastical duty: but the νομικοὶ indeed interpreted the law, but privately: which distinction Spanheim refutes in the place cited. Hottinger teaches that the γραμματεῖς were occupied more in theory, but the νομικοὶ in practice and practical questions, although doubtfully, not definitively, Thes. Phil. p. 75.

Latin:

Vers. 45.

ταῦτα λέγων κ̓ ἡμᾶς ὑβρίζεις) Per consequentiam. Nam Pharisæi exactissime observabant legisperitorum decreta : legisperiti vicissim illorum sanctimoniam magnis laudibus prædicabant. Ita scabunt mutuum muli. Datur hinc col- ligi quod in commate superiore habent Græci libri, & ex illis Syrus & Arabs, γραμματεῖς καὶ Φαρισαῖοι ὑποκριταὶ, aliunde adjectum, nam & Latinus interpres id non le- git.

E Latina versione perperam corrigitur Græ- cus textus: qui consentientibus Codicibus, nec dissentientibus Syro & Arabe interpretibus verba illa legit. Non ergo per consequentiam tantum notati legisperiti, sed expresse: sive quod νομικοὶ fuerint ipsi γραμματεῖς, quod visum fuit Span- hemio Dub. Evang. parte II. p. 399. seu potius, quod Scribis in eo puncto ὁμόνια tradiderint οἱ νο- μικοὶ, quos ab illis diversos facit B. Gerhardus parte I. Harm. Evang. cap. CLVI. p. m. 1276. hoc modo quod omnes νομικοὶ quidem fuerint γραμ- ματεῖς ac νομοδιδάσκαλοι. Conf. Matth. IX. 3. Luc. V. 17. non autem omnes γραμματεῖς ac νομοδι- δάσκαλοι fuerint νομικοὶ, sed illi tantum, qui lo- cum habuerint in Synedrio Ecclesiastico magno, penes quos fuit jurisdictio Ecclesiastica. Johan. Camero in Notis ad Matth. c. XX. Scribas etiam distinguit à Legis interpretibus. Sed alia ratione: nimirum quod γραμματεῖς publice in Synagogis legem interpretati sint, fungentes munere Eccle- siastico: νομικοὶ vero legem quidem interpretati sint, sed privatim: quod vero discrimen refellit l. c. Spanhemius. Hottingerus γραμματεῖς ma- gis in θεωρίᾳ, νομικὺς vero in praxi, & quæstioni- bus Practicis occupatos fuisse docet, quanquam dubie, non definitive, Thes. Phil. p. 75.

## 11:46
Verse 46.

δυσβάσακτα) Thus the Greeks translate נטל Prov. XXVII. 3.

Latin:

Vers. 46.

δυσβάσακτα) Sic Græci vertunt נטל Prov. XXVII. 3.

## 11:47
Verse 47.

οἱ δὲ πατέρες ἡμῶν ἀπέκτειναν αὐτούς) A Hebrew idiom, for which in Latin one should say: whom your ancestors killed: which did not escape the Syriac and Arabic in this place.

Latin:

Vers. 47.

οἱ δὲ πατέρες ἡμῶν ἀπέκτειναν αὐτούς) Hebraica locutio, pro quo Latine dicendum esset quos vestri majores interfece- runt: quod hoc loco Syrum & Arabem non latuit.

## 11:48
Verse 48.

μαρτυρεῖτε κ̓ συνευδοκεῖτε) Thus the Syriac and Arabic read: You bear witness to the deeds of your parents, and you imitate them. Compare this same passage in Matthew.

τῶν πατέρων ὑμῶν) Not only sons of nature, but also of character: so that it cannot but be expected of you what was accomplished by them themselves. See the exposition of the passage on Matthew.

Latin:

Vers. 48.

μαρτυρεῖτε κ̓ συνευδοκεῖτε) Ita legerunt Syrus & Arabs, Testimonium perhibetis de factis parentum, atque ea imi- tamini. Confer hunc ipsum in Matthæo locum.

τῶν πατέρων ὑμῶν) Non naturæ tantum, sed & morum filii: ita ut non possit non à vobis exspectari quod ab ipsis patratum est. Vide expositionem loci ad Matthæum.

## 11:49
Vers. 49.

ἡ σοφία τῦ Θεῦ εἶπεν) God in his counsel thus thought within himself אמר בלבו as the Hebrews say. Concerning these also see the notes on Matthew.

By σοφίαν is understood not the essential wisdom of God, nor God the Father, who is never so called, but the Son of God, the hypostatic wisdom of the Father, whose name this is in Prov. VIII. and elsewhere: and who bears witness of himself, that which is said here of the wisdom of God, in the parallel passage Matt. XXIII. 34. so that we may not doubt that these things are to be understood of him, as the hypostatic wisdom.

Latin:

Vers. 49.

ἡ σοφία τῦ Θεῦ εἶπεν) Deus in consilio suo ita apud se cogitavit אמר בלבו ut Hebræi dicunt. De his quoque ad Matthæum vide.

Per σοφίαν non essentialis Dei sapientia, nec Deus Pater, qui nunquam ita vocatur, sed Filius Dei sapientia Patris hypostatica intelligitur, cujus hoc est nomen Prov. VIII. & alibi : quiq; de se ipso hoc perhibet, quod hic de sapientia Dei dicitur, in loco parallelo Matth. XXIII. 34. ne ambigamus, hæc de ipso, ceu sapientia hypostatica intelligen- da esse.

## 11:51
Verf. 51. τοῦ οἴκου] Just as ναὸς is sometimes the entire structure of the Temple, sometimes that part in which the Priests were, היכל: so οἶκος is taken elsewhere for the whole, here for that same part. See what we said above regarding the chapter.

ἐκζηθήσεται] This is the very word that the dying Zechariah used. ירא יהוה וידרש

Latin:

Verf. 51. τοῦ οἴκου] Sicut ναὸς interdum est tota structura Templi, interdum pars illa in qua erant Sacerdotes, היכל : ita οἶκος alibi pro toto, hic pro eadem illa parte sumitur. Vi- de quæ ad caput diximus supra.

ἐκζηθήσεται] Vox ipsa est qua moriens Zacharias usus .ירא יהוה וידרש

## 11:52
V. 52. ὅτι ἤρατε τὴν κλεῖδα τῆς γνώσεως] The meaning is ambiguous. The Syriac translates it as 'you have stolen,' the Arabic as 'you have seized' or 'you have taken upon yourselves': nor does the Greek language object. For αἴρειν ἄχθος or φορτίον is said with almost the same meaning. Since both can be rightly said of the lawyers, I prefer the former: because I think it corresponds to that which is in Matthew, 'you shut the kingdom of heaven.' For he is rightly said to shut who does not leave the key in the lock. Indeed, an old annotator had explained ἤρατε as ἀκρύψατε, not badly, which also penetrated into the text in some places. Tertullian rightly explains the key as the interpretation of the Scriptures. And it was a custom among the Hebrews, when power was given to someone to interpret the law, to send him, as it were, into possession of the office by giving him a key.

Latin:

V. 52. ὅτι ἤρατε τὴν κλεῖδα τῆς γνώσεως] Ambigua est signi- ficatio. Syrus vertit surripuistis, Arabs arripuistis, aut in vos suscepistis: neque Græcus sermo repugnat. Nam αἴρειν ἄχ- θος aut φορτίον simili ferme significatu dicitur. Cum utrum- que de Legisperitis recte dicatur, prius præfero: quia puto respondere ei quod apud Matthæum est clauditis regnum cælorum. Ille enim claudere recte dicitur qui clavem in sera non relinquit. Vetus quidem annotator ἤρατε exposuerat ἀκρύψατε non male, quod & in textum alicubi penetravit. Clavim autem Tertullianus recte exponit interpretationem Scripturarum. Et mos erat apud Hebræos, eum cui potestas dabatur legem interpretandi, clave data quasi in possessio- nem muneris mittere.

## 11:53
V. 53. δεινῶς ἐνέχειν] The Arabic seems to have read συνέχειν, which some codices have: for it translates it as if you were to say, 'to hold enclosed by a snare.' But this is the more accepted reading, which the Syriac also acknowledges, and it expresses it with words of indignation and anger. Indeed, for Hesychius also, ἐνέχειν is μνησικακεῖν. Thus it would differ somewhat from that which follows, ἐπιστομίζειν.

ἀποστοματίζειν] It does not seem that one should depart from this reading, which so many codices establish. And this is one of the words in which Luke shows an intimate knowledge of the Greek language. For ἀποστοματίζειν is clearly a word taken from the school. Teachers of schools were accustomed to set more advanced students over the younger ones, so that the former might question the latter. That was called ἀποστοματίζειν and μανθάνειν, in which consists that fallacy by which Clinias is deceived by Euthydemus in Plato. For although μανθάνειν is otherwise λαμβάνειν τὴν ἐπιστήμην, in that context it signifies something else, namely, as Socrates explains, ξυνιέναι, that is, to attend to the speaker, or even what he adds, ἐπισκοπεῖν τὸ πραττόμενον ἢ λεγόμενον: just as also in Aristophanes the scholiasts explain μανθάνειν by σκοπεῖν. Whoever has grasped this easily understands the sophisms of Euthydemus: 'Which of the boys were learning the things being recited, the wise or the ignorant?' For Clinias responds well to that peculiar meaning, 'the wise': Aristotle takes from this passage of Plato the refutation by homonymy. For thus he says, 'as those who know learn: for the learned learn the things being recited, for μανθάνειν is homonymous, meaning at one time to understand while using knowledge, and at another to acquire knowledge.' But ἀποστοματίζειν is ambiguous. For it is said both of him who recites, as in Athenaeus and also in the discussion mentioned in Plato: and of him who leads another by questioning, and attends to him as he recites. Three noble grammarians are witnesses. For Hesychius explains ἀποστοματίζειν, or what is the same, ἀποστομίζειν, as ἀπὸ μνήμης ἀξιοῦν λέγειν, that is, to demand that another say something from memory: for thus that ἀξιοῦν must be interpreted, otherwise than the most learned man takes it. Suidas, instead of ἀξιοῦν, said κελεύειν; for to him ἀποστοματίζειν is to command a boy to say certain things from memory. Pollux explains ἀποστοματίζεσθαι as ἐρωτᾶσθαι τὰ μαθήματα. Luke therefore used this word learnedly, to indicate that the Pharisees tried in every way to elicit many things from the mouth of Christ. And thus Euthymius long ago rightly explained this passage. The Syriac rightly expressed the sense with a word for 'to hunt,' and the Arabic with a word that signifies 'to cause someone to delay.' What their purpose was in doing this is shown by the following clause: 'seeking to hunt something from his mouth, that they might accuse him.'

The Vulgate renders the word ἀποστοματίζειν as 'to stop the mouth.' But Grotius, along with Beza, rightly corrects this; ἀποστοματίζειν is one thing, but ἐπιστομίζειν is 'to stop the mouth.' Compare also Casaubon on this passage, if you please.

Latin:

V. 53. δεινῶς ἐνέχειν] συνέχειν, quod quidam codices ha- bent, legisse videtur Arabs: vertit enim quasi dicas, indagi- ne clausum tenere. At receptior ista est lectio quam & Sy- rus agnoscit, & indignandi ac succensendi verbis exprimit. Sane & Hesychio ἐνέχειν est μνησικακεῖν. Ita nonnihil dif- ferret ab eo quod sequitur ἐπιστομίζειν.

ἀποστοματίζειν] Non videtur discedendum ab hac lectione quam tot codices stabiliunt. Et hæc una est vocum in quibus intimam peritiam Græci sermonis Lucas ostendit. Nam ἀποστοματίζειν plane vox est de Schola sumta. Solebant ma- gistri scholarum provectiores discipulos junioribus præfi- cere, ut illi hos interrogarent. Id dicebatur ἀποστοματίζειν & μανθάνειν, in quo consistit fallacia illa qua Clinias decipitur ab Euthydemo apud Platonem. Nam cum μανθάνειν alias sit λαμβάνειν τὴν ἐπιστήμην, in isto aliud significat, nimirum ut Socrates explicat ξυνιέναι id est attendere dicenti, sive e- tiam quod addit ἐπισκοπεῖν τὸ πραττόμενον ἢ λεγόμενον: sicut & apud Aristophanem Scholiastæ μανθάνειν explicant per σκοπεῖν. Hoc qui tenuerit, facile intelligit Euthydemi So- phismata: πότεροι ἐμάνθανον τῶν παίδων τὰ ἀποστοματιζόμενα οἱ Σοφοὶ ἢ οἱ ἀμαθεῖς. Bene enim ad illum peculiarem signifi- catum respondet Clinias, οἱ Σοφοὶ: Aristoteles ex hoc Pla- tonis loco sumit τῶ παρ' ὁμωνυμίαν ἐλέγχω. Ita enim ait οἷον μανθάνουσι οἱ ἐπιστάμενοι: τὰ γὰρ ἀποστοματιζόμενα μανθάνουσι οἱ γραμματικοὶ τὸ γὰρ μανθάνειν ὁμώνυμον, τότε ξυνιέναι χρώ- μενον τῇ ἐπιστήμη, καὶ τὸ λαμβάνειν τὴν ἐπιστήμην. Sed ἀπο- στοματίζειν ambiguum est. Nam & de eo qui recitat dicitur, ut apud Athenæum atque etiam apud Platonem dicta dif- putatione: & de eo qui alteri interrogando præit, eique re- citanti attendit. Testes sunt tres Grammatici nobiles. Nam Hesychius ἀποστοματίζειν, aut quod idem est ἀποστομίζειν, ex- ponit ἀπὸ μνήμης ἀξιοῦν λέγειν, hoc est exigere ut alter quip- piam memoriter dicat: ita enim interpretandum illud ἀξιοῦν aliter quam accipit vir doctissimus. Suidas pro ἀξιοῦν dixit κελεύειν· nam illi ἀποστοματίζειν est κελεύειν ἓν παῖδα λέγειν ἄττα ἀπὸ στόματος. Pollux ἀποστοματίζεσθαι exponit ἐρωτᾶσθαι τὰ μαθήματα. Docte igitur hoc verbo usus est Lucas, ut indicaret Pharisæos omni modo hoc conatos ut multa ex ore Christi elicerent. Atque ita hunc locum pridem recte exposuit Euthymius. Sensum recte expressit Syrus aucu- pandi vocabulo, & Arabs eo verbo quod significat facere ut quis differat. Id quo consilio fecerint ostendit comma se- quens: ζητοῦντες θηρεῦσαί τι ἐκ τοῦ στόματος αὐτοῦ, ἵνα κατηγο- ρήσωσιν αὐτοῦ.

Vocem ἀποστοματίζειν Vulgata reddit os oppri- mere. Sed recte corrigit hoc cum Beza Grotius, ἀποστοματίζειν, sed ἐπιστομίζειν est os opprimere Confer. autem ad h. l. etiam Casaubonus, si placet.

## 12:1 Argument
CHAPTER XII. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

Several thousands having gathered, they are warned about leaven, and to an intrepid confession, with the promise of the Holy Spirit. Christ refuses to be an arbiter in the division of an inheritance: He dissuades from avarice, by the example of the rich steward: He warns about avoiding care for the belly: about giving alms; about servants who are watchful and faithful, and doing the will of the Lord. He teaches about the fire to be kindled on earth; about the Baptism to be received by himself; about the dissension that will arise among household members on his account: about testing the storm and the time; about reconciling with an adversary.

There are six parts: I. Warning about an unhypocritical and intrepid confession, to v. 12. II. Declining the judgment of the inheritance, to v. 14. III. Dissuasion from avarice and care for the belly, to v. 34. IV. Exhortation to watchfulness and faith, to v. 48. V. About the end of the Lord's coming, and the observation of it, to v. 57. VI. Admonition about reconciliation with an adversary, to the final v. 59.

PART I.

Admonition concerning unfeigned and intrepid confession.

Vers. 1. In the myriads of the crowds] Thus the Hebrews say רבבת. The Hellenists say myriads without any other addition, to signify an innumerable multitude, Deut. XXXIII. 2. Psal. III. 7. Dan. XI. 12. It pertains much to the matter that Jesus was seen and heard by so many men. For this is not done in a corner, says Paul, Acts XXVI. 26.

First, beware of the leaven of the Pharisees] A great paradox. For the people especially admired the Pharisees, as can be seen in Josephus. But just as elsewhere he warns his own to beware of the inventions of the Pharisees, so here he warns them not to wish to imitate their masked manners. Both are rightly called leaven: both the incrustation of sincere doctrine, as Gal. V. 9, and manners harmful by example, 1 Cor. V. 6. See what is at Matt. XVI. But that Pharisaic arrogance, which simulation served, approached most closely to the nature of leaven. Philo also in more than one place interprets leaven in the law as the vain swellings of the soul, puffed up by the pride of arrogance. Luke added these things because the subject matter cohered with the previous discourse, not because the series of times required it.

Latin:

CAPUT XII. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Congregatis aliquot millenis, monentur de fermento, & ad confessionem intrepidam, cum promissione Spiritus Sancti. Detrectat Christus arbiter esse in hæreditatis divisio- ne: Dehortatur ab avaritia, exemplo divi- tis villicani: monet de vitanda cura ventris: de dandis eleemosynis; de servis vigilanti- bus & fidis, ac voluntatem Domini facien- tibus. Docet de igne in terris accendendo; de Baptismo à se suscipiendo; de dissidio sui causa inter domesticos orituro: de tempe- state, & tempore probando; de adversa- rio conciliando.

Partes sunt sex: I. Monitio de ἀνυποκρίτῳ & intrepida confessione, ad v. 12. II. Declinatio ju- dicii hæreditatis, ad v. 14. III. Dehortatio ab a- varitia & cura ventris, ad v. 34. IV. Abhortatio ad vigilantiam & fidem, ad v. 48. V. De fine adven- tus Domini, ejusdemque observatione, ad v. 57. VI. Commonefactio de adversarii conciliatione, ad v. 59. finalem.

PARS I.

Monitio de ἀνυποκρίτῳ & intrepida confes- sione.

Vers. 1. ἐν μυριάσι τῶν ὄχλων] Ita Hebræi dicunt רבבת. Hellenistæ μυριάδας sine alio additamento, ad significan- dam innumeram multitudinem, Deut. XXXIII. 2. Psal. III. 7. Dan. XI. 12. Multum ad rem pertinet à tot hominibus visum auditumque Jesum. ὁ γάρ ἐστιν ἐν γωνίᾳ πεπραγμένον τῦτο, inquit Paulus Actor. XXVI. 26.

πρῶτον προσέχετε ἑαυτοῖς ἀπὸ τῆς ζύμης τῶν Φαρισαίων] πα- ράδοξον magnum. Nam Pharisæos imprimis populus ad- mirabatur ut apud Josephum videre est. Sicut autem alibi suos à commentis Pharisæorum ut sibi caveant monet, ita hic ne personatos illorum mores imitari velint. Utrumque recte fermentum dicitur: & sinceræ doctrinæ incrustatio, ut Gal. V. 9. & mores exemplo noxii 1. Corinth. V. 6. Vide quæ ad Matth. XVI. Sed maxime ad fermenti naturam ac- cedebat Pharisæica illa arrogantia, cui simulatio inservie- bat. Etiam Philo non uno loco fermentum in lege interpre- tatur ταῖς τῆς ψυχῆς κεν χαύνοις ἐπάρσεσι, καταληθ' ὑπ' ἀλαζονείας φύσημα. Etiam hæc Lucas addidit quod materia cum su- periore sermone cohæreret, non quod temporum series id exigeret.

## 12:2
Vers. 2. But there is nothing covered] And this which follows is a proverbial saying: often used by Christ, and not always in the same sense: as is wont to happen in adages. Christ had said that simulation was to be avoided: he adds the reason, because it does not happen for those wishing to hide that they always hide. The day, often human, if not, then divine, will betray them.

Latin:

Vers. 2. ὐδὲν δὲ συγκεκαλυμμένον ἐστὶν] Et hoc quod se- quitur dictum proverbiale est: sæpe Christo, nec semper eodem sensu, usurpatum: ut in adagiis fieri solet. Dixerat Christus cavendam simulationem: rationem addit, quia non contingat latere volentibus ut semper lateant. Prodet illos, dies humana sæpe, si non, tuique divina.

## 12:3
Vers. 3. For which things] A manner of speaking quite familiar to the Hellenists: it is mostly used in rendering a cause, as we said above in ch. I. 20. But here I side with those who think it is illative: such as that also in Eph. V. 31, For this cause shall a man leave his father, that is, ἕνεκεν τύτυ as the LXX have it, על־כן.

Whatever you have said in the darkness shall be heard in the light] The second person is to be taken indefinitely, as we have often warned. A similar maxim seems to have been in use among the Greeks. For in the little book which is called Musaeus we read: And in silence the work which you perform, someone hears at the crossroads.

Latin:

Vers. 3. ἀνθ' ὧν] Loquendi genus Hellenistis admodum familiare: Plerumque usurpatur in reddenda causa ut dixi- mus supra c. l. 20. At hic iis accedo qui illativum putant: quale & illud Eph. V. 31. ἀντὶ τύτυ καταλείψει ἄνθρωπος τὸν πατέρα, id est ἕνεκεν τύτυ ut habent LXX. על־כן.

ὅσα ἐν τῇ σκοτίᾳ εἴπατε ἐν τῷ φωτὶ ἀκουθήσεται] Perso- na secunda sumenda ἀορίστως ut sæpe monuimus. Videtur apud Græcos similis γνώμη in usu fuisse. Nam in libello quĩ Musæi dicitur legimus: ἐν δὲ σιωπῇ Ἔργον ὅπερ τελέεις τις ἐνὶ τριοδοισιν ἀκύει.

## 12:4
Vers. 4. But I say to you] Luke has gathered many sayings of different times into one: the coherence of which there is no need to weave. For they are as it were aphorisms.

To my friends] John XV. 15. But I have called you friends, because all things that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you.

And after these things have nothing more to do] This sentiment of Christ is directly opposed to that Aristotelian one: Death is most fearful. For it is the end, and it seems that there is no longer any good or evil for the dead. The passage exists in III, ad Nicom. c. IX.

Latin:

Vers. 4. λέγω δὲ ὑμῖν] Multa diversi temporis dicta in unum congessit Lucas: quorum cohærentiam texere nihil necesse est. Sunt enim velut ἀφορισμοί.

τοῖς φίλοις με] Joh. XV. 15. ὑμᾶς δὲ εἴρηκα φίλες ὅτι πάν- τα ἃ ἤκυσα παρὰ τῦ πατρός με ἐγνώρισα ὑμῖν.

καὶ μετὰ ταῦτα μὴ ἐχόντων περισσότερόν τι ποιῆσαι] Hæc Christi sententia directe opponitur illi Aristotelicæ φο- βερώτατον ὁ θάνατος. πέρας γὰρ κὶ ὐδένι ἔτι τῷ τεθνεῶτι δοκεῖ ὔτε ἀγαθὸν ὔτε κακὸν εἶναι. locus extat III, ad Nicom. c. IX.

## 12:5
V. 5. After killing] Not only the other life but also this one is in the power of God, who can take it away even without the ministry of men when he pleases.

Having authority] Matthew says: being able: but undoubtedly the right and the power of effecting concur here.

Latin:

V. 5. μετὰ τὸ ἀποκτεῖναι] Non vita tantum altera sed & hæc in Dei est potestate, qui etiam citra hominum ministe- rium adimere eam potest quum lubet.

ἐξουσίαν ἔχοντα] δυνάμενον inquit Matthæus: sed nimirum jus & vis efficiendi hic concurrunt.

## 12:6
V. 6. It is not forgotten] לא נשכה that is, it is not outside of care. Thus Ps. IX. 19. In Greek it is, The poor shall not be forgotten to the end. But how mute animals are under the care of God has been treated at Matthew.

Latin:

V. 6. ὐκ ἔστιν ἐπιλελησμένον] לא נשכה id est non est ex- tra curam. Ita Pf. IX. 19. Græce est ὐκ εἰς τέλος ἐπιλησθή- σεται ὁ πτωχός. Quomodo autem muta animantia sub cu- ra sunt Dei, tractatum est ad Matthæum.

## 12:8
V. 8. ἔμπροσθεν τῶν ἀγγέλων τῦ Θεῦ] Matthew [says] ἔμπροσθεν τῦ πατρός! but the mention of angels is also in a similar sentiment in Mark 8:38.

Latin:

V. 8. ἔμπροσθεν τῶν ἀγγέλων τῦ Θεῦ] Matthæum ἔμπροσθεν τῦ πατρός! sed & angelorum mentio in simili sententia a- pud Marcum IX. 21.

## 12:11
Vers. 11.

ὅταν δὲ προσφέρωσιν] It is to be taken impersonally, as if he were saying 'when you are brought'. For what is said several times in the Acts as ἤγαγον, [and] in Matthew as παραδιδόασι and ἄγουσι, here is called προσφέρωσιν.

συναγωγὰς] This pertains to the assemblies of the Jews. See what [is said] regarding Matthew.

Ἀρχὰς] That is, ἡγεμόνας, governors.

τὰς ἐξουσίας] namely, ὑπερεχούσας, as Paul speaks, [or] βα- σιλεῖς [kings] in Matthew.

πῶς ἢ τί ἀπολογήσησθε] What you are to say for yourselves so that you are not thought guilty, and with what caution you are to speak so that the defense itself does not harm you.

ἢ τί εἴπητε] How you are to defend the doctrine which you profess.

PART II. • The declining of a judgment of inheritance.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

ὅταν δὲ προσφέρωσιν] Impersonaliter sumendum, quasi dicat cum sistemini. Nam quod in Actibus aliquoties dici- tur ἤγαγον, Matthæo παραδιδόασι & ἄγουσι, hic dicitur προσφέ- ρυσιν.

συναγωγὰς] Hoc ad conventus Judæorum pertinet. Vi- de quæ ad Matthæum.

Ἀρχὰς] Id est ἡγεμόνας præsides.

τὰς ἐξουσίας] ὑπερεχούσας scilicet, ut Paulus loquitur, βα- σιλεῖς apud Matthæum.

πῶς ἢ τί ἀπολογήσησθε] Quid dicturi sitis pro vobis ipsis ne nocentes putemini, & qua cautione prolaturi ne ipsa de- fensio obsit.

ἢ τί εἴπητε] Quomodo propugnaturi sitis doctrinam quam profitemini.

PARS II. • Declinatio judicii hæreditatis.

## 12:13
V. 13. Διδάσκαλε] It is credible that the Jews were accustomed, in order to avoid the delays of lawsuits, to take as arbiters those whose wisdom and equity were well-known: and especially that disciples willingly stood by the judgment of their masters.

μερίσασθαι μετ᾽ ἐμοῦ τὴν κληρονομίαν] So that he does not withhold more than a just share: and so that he admits to a division on fair conditions.

Latin:

V. 13. Διδάσκαλε] Credibile est Judæos solitos ad fugi- enda litium sufflamina arbitros sumere eos quorum sapien- tia & æquitas erat perspecta: ac præsertim discipulos li- benter stetisse arbitrio magistrorum.

μερίσασθαι μετ᾽ ἐμοῦ τὴν κληρονομίαν] Ne plus justa parte detineat: & ut divisionem admittat æquis conditionibus.

## 12:14
V. 14. τίς με κατέστησε δικαστὴν] The history of Moses is referenced. For when he interposed himself between quarreling Hebrews and recalled them to brotherly love, he heard: τίς σε κατέστη- σεν ἄρχοντα κὶ δικαστὴν ἐφ᾽ ἡμᾶς; [Who made you a ruler and a judge over us?] For the Greek version has it thus, with the same words that are placed here, Exod. II. 14. Therefore, this has the same value as if Christ were saying: I will not commit, ungrateful men, that you may object to me under any pretext what you once objected to Moses. Content to give general precepts which can be very easily accommodated to any matters by those who wish, I will not involve myself in the affairs of individuals.

ἢ μεριστήν] He not only denies that he is a judge, but he does not even desire to be an arbiter. The Greeks call an arbiter διαιτητὴν: but he is rightly called μεριστὴς who is taken as an arbiter for an inheritance to be divided, or for common property to be divided, or for boundaries to be set. And indeed, it is sufficiently manifest that Jesus was bound by no law to undertake such a burden. For he was not appointed to it either by God or by men. Why he did not accept it voluntarily is not stated here, but it is easy to understand. For besides what we have already said about avoiding calumny, little time of life remained for him, which certainly had to be spent on better things, and things that would benefit the whole human race. He who, when he called his disciples, did not permit them to bury their father or to say goodbye to their household, how would he himself have spent his time for teaching on the settling of private controversies? Which gave many an occasion to ask whether the Bishops of the Christians acted rightly in taking upon themselves a burden refused by Christ: which Augustine records that he did with great annoyance, but as if obeying the precepts of the Apostle Paul, and Posidonius testifies concerning him. And before him, Ambrose narrates that he performed the same labor. And the same is found to have been reported about Gregory Neocaesariensis. To judge the matter well, it is important to understand the origin of the thing. The Jews, dispersed through the Babylonian empire, since they considered it a disgrace to their name to refer controversies that arose among them to profane judges who were strangers to the religion of the one God, instituted that they should stand by the arbitrations of their elders as if by judged matters. And if anyone did otherwise, he was judged unworthy of the company of the Jews. He who brings Israelite business to strangers pollutes the name of God, say the teachers of the Hebrews. The same was observed in later times by those who lived under Roman rule outside of Judea (for in Judea they had their own public judges of their own religion), and that custom lasted until Christian times. This is apparent from the law of Arcadius and Honorius which holds as follows: If any of these (Jews), by common agreement, in the manner of arbiters among the Jews, in civil matters only, think that they should litigate, let them not be hindered by public law from choosing their judgment. For let judges execute their sentences as if they had been given by the sentence of a judge-arbiter. And from another of Honorius and Theodosius: if there is any contention between Christians and Jews, let it not be settled by the elders of the Jews, but by the ordinary judges. Whence we learn that such controversies were accustomed to be handled before the presbyters of the Synagogue, namely, the archisynagogues presiding, who surpassed the others in knowledge of the law. The Apostle Paul, following this custom of the Hebrews as one by no means to be disapproved, when he had rebuked the Christian Corinthians for litigating before profane tribunals, wishes the wisest assemblies of the whole [community] to be established for settling controversies of this kind. Those who were called presbyters were undoubtedly the wisest: for the ancients not without reason doubt whether the Church at Corinth had a bishop remaining with them at that time. This cognizance, therefore, belonged to the presbytery, no less than the censure of morals, and if a controversy could not be settled there, the authority of the whole fraternal multitude remained to move him who was more stubborn. It is called, however, the same audience of the Bishop, because the Bishop presided. Constantine and the Emperors who followed him confirmed this custom by law, whence that is from the constitution of Arcadius and Honorius: If any, they say, wish to litigate by consent before the minister of the sacred law, they shall not be forbidden, but the judgment of him sitting voluntarily as an arbiter, in a civil matter only, shall be valid. How much of a burden subsequent times added to the Bishops it is superfluous to recount, since that very thing, ancient and almost necessary, seemed burdensome to every best of Bishops. But no one fails to see that the reason for this custom is by no means as great where Christians hold the empire and public courts, as it was when strangers to the religion held the tribunals. Nor, however, must it be denied that even in Christian empires, love is for the most part better served by friendly discussions than by the delays of lawsuits, the nurses of hatred. Add that there is also less often harm in yielding from one's own in time than in persistently pursuing a lawsuit, however certain the hope of victory. But if anyone should at the same time weigh how much business it is to dispense the divine word rightly, which the Apostles themselves, instructed by such a Spirit, delegated the care of the poor to others so that they could do it rightly, he will easily understand that any others whatsoever should rather be employed in settling the controversies of private individuals than those whom the duty of teaching occupies. It is indeed the duty of these also, nay, of these especially, to cut off discords: but if that can be done by a brief admonition, as Paul reconciles Onesimus to Philemon, not if the intricacies of cases are to be discussed, and the matter of a few should consist in a great waste of time.

PART III. Exhortation against avarice and care for the belly.

Latin:

V. 14. τίς με κατέστησε δικαστὴν] Respicitur Mosis historia. Nam is cum rixantibus Hebræis medium se interponeret & ad fraternum amorem eos revocaret, audivit τίς σε κατέστη- σεν ἄρχοντα κὶ δικαστὴν ἐφ᾽ ἡμᾶς; Ita enim Græca versio habet verbis iisdem quæ hic sunt posita, Exod. II. 14. Tantundem ergo hoc valet quasi dicat Christus: Non committam ut ul- la specie objicere mihi possitis, ingrati homines, quod Mosi olim objecistis. Contentus dare præcepta generalia quæ ad res quasvis accommodari à volentibus facillime possint, singulorum negotiis me non immiscibo.

ἢ μεριστήν] Non tantum negat se judicem esse, sed nec ar- biter esse cupit. Arbitrum Græci διαιτητὴν vocant: sed με- ριστὴς recte dicitur qui familiæ hæreditundæ, aut communi dividundo, aut finibus regundis arbiter sumitur. Et quidem Jesum nullo jure obligatum fuisse ut onus tale susciperet sa- tis est manifestum. Neque enim aut à Deo, aut ab homini- bus erat in id constitutus. Cur sponte non receperit hic non dicit, sed intellectu facile est. Nam præter id, quod jam dixi- mus, de vitanda calumnia, exiguum illi restabat vitæ tem- pus, quod sane impendendum erat rebus melioribus, & toti humano generi profuturis. Qui vocatis discipulis non per- misit sepelire patrem, aut domesticis valedicere, quomodo ipse expendendis privatorum controversiis insumpsisset do- cendi tempora? Quod multis occasionem dedit quærendi rectene fecerint Christianorum Episcopi quod onus à Chri- sto recusatum in se susceperint: quod se fecisse magna cum molestia, sed tanquam præceptis Pauli Apostoli obtempe- rantem memorat Augustinus, & de ipso testatur Posido nius. Atque ante eum eodem se labore functum narrat Am- brosius. Idemque de Gregorio Neocæsariensi proditum inve- nire est. Ad rem bene dijudicanda refert intelligere rei ori- ginem. Judæi perBabylonicum imperium dispersi cum pro- brosum nomini suo existimarent, ortas inter se controver- sias ad judices profanos & à religione unius Dei extraneos deferre, instituerunt suorum seniorum arbitriis quasi rebus judicatis stare. Quod si contra fecisset, is indignus Ju- dæorum consortio judicabatur. Qui adducit negotia Israëli- tica ad extraneos polluit nomen Dei, inquiunt: Hebræorum magistri. Idem posteris temporibus observarunt qui extra Judæam (nam in Judæa suos habebant publicos judices suæ religionis) sub imperio Romano vitam egerunt, dura- vitque is mos ad usque Christiana tempora. Apparet id ex le- ge Arcadii & Honorii quæ sic habet: Si qui vero ex his (Ju- dæis) communi pactione ad similitudinem arbitrorum apud In- dæos in civili duntaxat negotio, putaverint litigandum, sortiti eorum judicium jure publico ne tetentur. Eorum enim sententias judices exsequantur tanquã ex sententia cognitoris arbitri dati fuerunt. Et ex altera Honorii & Theodosii: si qua inter Chri- stianos & Judæos sit contentio non à senioribus Judæorum, sed ab ordinariis judicibg dirimantur. Unde discimus solitas tractari id genus controversias coram presbyteris Synagogæ, præ- sidentibus nimirum archisynagogis, qui cæteris præibant peritia legis. Hunc morem Hebræorum, ut minime impro- bandum sequens Apostolus Paulus, cum reprehendisset Co- rinthios Christianos quod apud prophana tribunalia litiga- rent, sapientissimos cœtus totius vult constitui componen- dis id genus controversiis. Sapientissimi autem erant haud dubie qui presbyteri dicebantur: nam an manentem secum episcopum eo tempore habuerit Corinthi Ecclesia veteres non immerito dubitant. Penes presbyterium igitur fuit hæc notio, non minus quam morum censura, & si ibi componi controversia non posset, supererat totius fraternæ multitu- dinis auctoritas ad permovendum eum qui esset pertina- cior. Dicitur tamen eadem Episcopi audientia, quod Episcœ- pus præsideret. Hunc morem Constantinus & secuti Impe- ratores lege firmarunt, unde illud est ex Arcadii & Honorii constitutione: Si qui ex consensu, inquiunt, apud sacræ legis antistitem litigare voluerint, non vetabuntur, sed experientia illius, in civili duntaxat negotio, vice arbitri sponte residentis judicium. Quantum oneris sequentia tempora Episcopis ad- jecerint supervacuum est commemorare, cum illud ipsum antiquam & pene necessarium, optimo cuiq; Episcoporum grave visum fuerit. Nemo autem non videt, neutiquam tan- tam esse hujus consuetudinis rationem ubi Christiani impe- rium & judicia publica obtinent, ac fuit cum religionis ex- tranei tribunalia obtinerent. Neq; tamen negandum est e- tiam in Christianorum imperiis dilectioni plerumq; rectius consuli per amicas disceptationes, quam per litium moras, odii nutrices. Adde quod & minus sæpe damni est de suo cedere in tempore quam litem pertinaciter prosequi, quan- tumvis certa victoriæ spe. At si quis simul expendat quan- tum sit negotii sermonem divinum recte dispensare, quod ut recte facere possent ipsi Apostoli, tanto instructi Spiritu, curam pauperum aliis delegaverê, facile intelliget quosvis alios potius adhibendos componendis privatorum contro- versiis, quam eos quos docendi munus occupat. Est quidem horum quoq;, imo horum præcipue, discordias præcidere: sed si id brevi admonitione fieri possit, quomodo Onefi- mum Philemoni reconciliat Paulus, non si causæ ambages discutiendæ, & magno temporis dispendio consistat res paucorum.

PARS III. Dehortatio ab avaritia & cura ventris.

## 12:15
V. 15. ἀπὸ τῆς πλεονεξίας] It appears that πλεονεξία is used here, as elsewhere, not for τὴν ἀδικίαν, as some please, but for that very desire of having, of which φιλαργυρία is a species. For just as Christ does not wish the opportunities of protecting one's family to be neglected, so He clearly disapproves of this being pursued intensely so that we may have as much as possible, even if injury is absent. He who was dealt with a little before seems to have provided the material for this discourse, who, when he ought to have asked Christ for the precepts of eternal life, preferred to invoke His help to obtain those things which perhaps were owed to him: but in the meantime, they were not necessary even for this fleeting life: which was a certain indication of a mind caring for such things more than is right.

ὅτι ἐκ ἐν τῷ περισσεύειν τινὶ ἡ ζωὴ αὐτῷ ἐστιν ἐκ τῶν ὑπαρχόντων αὐτῷ] This is the more accepted reading, from which the ancient interpreters do not seem to me to depart. περισσεύειν is taken here entirely intransitively as it is often among the Greeks. Thus Mark c. XII. 24. ἐκ τῶ περισσεύοντος αὐτοῖς. Our author above τὸ περισσεῦσαν αὐτοῖς. & c. XXI. 4. ἐκ τῶ περισσεύοντος αὐτοῖς. The infinitive, however, is placed in the Greek manner in place of a noun or participle. And ἐκ τῶν ὑπαρχόντων is then constructed with that περισσεύειν, in a manner of transposition very familiar to Luke. The sense is quite popular: Life is not helped by the fact that one has more in goods than is enough for the desires of nature: which sense Horace expresses thus: Though your threshing floor should thresh a hundred thousand bushels, your belly will not hold more from this than mine, just as if you should happen to carry a basket of bread on your burdened shoulder among the sellers, you would receive nothing more than he who carried nothing. Or say, what does it matter to one living within the bounds of Nature, whether he plows a hundred or a thousand acres. But it is sweet to take from a large heap. Provided you leave us to draw just as much from a small one, why do you praise your granaries more than our baskets? As if you had need of no more than an urn of liquid, or a cup: and you should say, I would rather take as much from a great river than from this little fountain. Aristotle Nicom. X. 9. ὀ γὰρ ἐν τῇ ὑπερβολῇ τὸ ἄὔταρκες ὐδ᾽ ἡ κρίσις ὐδ᾽ ἡ πρᾶξις.

Latin:

V. 15. ἀπὸ τῆς πλεονεξίας] πλεονεξίαν hic, ut alibi, apparet dici non τὴν ἀδικίαν, ut quibusdam placet, sed ipsum illud habendi studium, cujus species est φιλαργυρία. Nam sicut oc- casiones tutandæ familiæ negligi non vult Christus, ita hoc impense agi ut habeamus quamplurimum, etiamsi absit in- juria, plane improbat. Præbuisse materiam huic sermoni vi- detur ille de quo actum est paulo ante, qui cum à Christo petere debuisset vitæ æternæ præcepta, maluit auxilium e- jus invocare ad ea obtinenda quæ ipsi forte debebantur: at interim ne ad caducam quidem hanc vitam erant ipsi neces- saria: quod certum erat indicium plus æquo talia curantis animi.

ὅτι ἐκ ἐν τῷ περισσεύειν τινὶ ἡ ζωὴ αὐτῷ ἐστιν ἐκ τῶν ὑπαρχόν- των αὐτῷ] Hæc est receptior lectio, à qua mihi non videntur recedere vetusti interpretes. περισσεύειν omnino hic sumitur ἀμεταβάτως ut apud Græcos sæpe. Ita Marcus c. XII. 24. ἐκ τῶ περισσεύοντος αὐτοῖς. Noster supra τὸ περισσεῦσαν αὐτοῖς. & c. XXI. 4. ἐκ τῶ περισσεύοντος αὐτοῖς. Infinitivus autem more Græco ponitur vice nominis aut participii. Et ἐκ τῶν ὑπαρχόν- των tunc construitur cum isto περισσεύειν, trajiciendi more Lucæ perquam familiari. Sensus est admodum popularis: Vitam non juvari ex eo quod quis plus in bonis habeat, quam satis sit ad naturæ desideria: quem sensum ita expri- mit Horatius: Millia frumenti tua triverit area centum, Non tuus hinc capiet venter plus, quam meus, ut si Reticulum panis venales inter onusto Forte vehas humero, nihilo plus accipias, quam Qui nil portarit. Vel dic, quid referat intra Naturæ fines viventi, jugera centum, an Mille aret. At suave est ex magno tollere acervo. Dum ex parvo nobis tantundem haurire relinquas, Cur tua plus laudes cumeris granaria nostris? Vt, tibi sit opus liquidi non amplius urna, Vel cyatho: & dicas, magno de flumine mallem, Quam ex hoc fonticulo tantundem sumere. Aristoteles Nicom. Χ. 9. ὀ γὰρ ἐν τῇ ὑπερβολῇ τὸ ἄὔταρκες ὐδ᾽ ἡ κρίσις ὐδ᾽ ἡ πρᾶξις.

## 12:16
V. 16. ἐυφόρησεν ἡ χώρα] A most learned man rightly notes that ἀγρὸν and χώραν are the same to the Hellenists. This is clear by comparing the passages of Matthew and Luke. For where the former said ἐν τῷ ἀγρῷ c. XXIV. 15. the latter says οἱ ἐν ταῖς χώραις c. XXI. 21. So also John c. IV. 35. θεάσασθε τὰς χώρας: & Jac V. 4. τῶν ἀμησάντων τὰς χώρας ὑμῶν, hence also the name of χωρεπισκόπων.

Latin:

V. 16. ἐυφόρησεν ἡ χώρα] Recte notat vir doctissimus idem esse Hellenistis ἀγρὸν & χώραν. Liquet id collatis Mat- thæi & Lucæ locis. Nam ubi ille dixit ἐν τῷ ἀγρῷ c. XXIV. 15. hic dicit οἱ ἐν ταῖς χώραις c. XXI. 21. Ita & Johannes c. IV. 35. θεάσασθε τὰς χώρας: & Jac V. 4. τῶν ἀμησάντων τὰς χώρας ὑμῶν, hinc & χωρεπισκόπων nomen.

## 12:17
Vers. 17. τί ποιήσω] Behold how care follows increasing money.

πῶ συνάξω τὺς καρπύς μ8] As if there were nowhere those by whom they could be spent to be fed:

Latin:

Vers. 17. τί ποιήσω] Ecce ut Crescentem sequitur cura pecuniam.

πῶ συνάξω τὺς καρπύς μ8] Quasi nusquam essent quibus pascendis possent impendi:

## 12:18
V. 18. καθελῶ με τάς ἀποθήκας κὶ μείζονας οἰκοδομήσω] He tears down, he builds, he changes squares for rounds. The very abundance of produce draws greater expenses with it. There is need not only of larger barns, but also of more servants to guard these things. Basil in his sermon περὶ πλεονεξίας, while he speaks with much singular eloquence against this vice, also says that excellently looking to this passage: καθελῶ με τὰς ἀποθήκας καὶ μείζονας οἰκοδομήσω. ἐὰν δὲ καὶ ταύτας ἐμπλήσῃς τί ποτε ἆρα διανοηθήσῃ, ἤπω πάλιν καθαιρήσεις καὶ πάλιν οἰκοδομήσεις; κὶ τί τότων ἀτοπώτερον, ἀπέραντα μοχθεῖν, οἰκοδομεῖν μετὰ σπεδῆς καὶ μετὰ σπεδῆς καθαιρεῖν; So true is that of Solon: Πλύτε δ᾽ ὐδὲν τέρμα πεφασμένον ἀνδράσι κεῖται.

Τὰ γεννήματά με] γένημα is καρπὸς, says Phrynichus The LXX are accustomed to translate the Hebrew תבואה in this way, as in Exodus 23 and elsewhere. He would have spoken more truly [had he said] the fruits of the earth, the common nurse of men.

κὴ τὰ ἀγαθά με) Not without reason is this added. For that class of men calls riches 'goods,' not only in the popular way of speaking, but because it thinks nothing better than those things. There is an old controversy between the Stoics and the Peripatetics as to whether those things should be called by the name of 'goods' at all. Cicero, following the Stoics in his Paradoxa, says that he requires the prudence of his ancestors, who had called those weak and changeable members of money 'goods': from which opinion the ancient Christians do not depart. For although those things are sometimes called 'goods' in the sacred scriptures, they judge that this is done not properly, as the Peripatetics seem to have thought, but because of a certain similarity to true goods. Wherefore, just as they depart far from the Stoics in other parts, so here they approve of their discourse. Tatian in Aristotle criticizes that he described happiness in those things in which he took pleasure, being too unlearned. The same is to be seen in Clement of Alexandria in more than one place, such as Stromata II. τίνα δὲ τὰ φοβερὰ ὁ νόμος καταγγέλλει κὴ θεασώμεθα τὸ μὲν τὰ μεταξὺ ἀρετῆς κὴ κακίας, οἷον πενίαν κὴ νόσον κὴ ἀδοξίαν κὴ δυσγένειαν κὴ ὅσα παραπλήσια, ταῦτα μὲν κὴ οἱ κατὰ πόλιν νόμοι προτείνουσες ἱκανιώτατοι κὴ τοῖς ἐκ περιπάτε τρία γένη τ' ἀγαθῶν εἰσηγουμένοις κὴ τὰ τούτων ἐναντία λογιζομένοις εἶναι κακὰ ἁρμόδιοι· ἤδε ἡ δόξα· ἀμῖν δὲ ὁ δοθεὶς νόμος· τὰ τῷ ὄντι κακὰ ἀποφύγειν προστάττει μοιχείαν, ἀσελγείαν, παιδεραστίαν, ἄγνοιαν, ἀδικίαν, νόσον ψυχῆς (this passage, badly conceived in published books, ought to be distinguished thus) θάνατον, ὀ τὸν διαλύοντα ψυχὴν ἀπὸ σώματος, ἀλλὰ τὸν διαλύοντα ψυχὴν ἀπὸ ἀληθείας. Elsewhere he says ὅσα τριττὰ εἶναι ἀγαθὰ οἱ περιπατητικοὶ θέλουσι. He himself, following the lead of the sacred scriptures, calls them goods not simply, but with the addition 'goods of the earth.' For thus he says in Paedagogus III. ἢν δὲ ἐσακούσητέ με, τὰ ἀγαθὰ τῆς γῆς φάγεσθε· the instructor says again, calling the goods of the earth human things, beauty, wealth, health, strength, food, for they are goods indeed which neither ear has heard, nor have they ever ascended into the heart, concerning the truly existing kingdom, the truly existing goods, and those awaiting us.
