Origen against Celsus in the fourth book says: that vice is the evil, and the actions according to it, and nothing else according to precise reason: but in the sixth book he says that poverty, diseases, and other things of that kind are called evils catachrestically. He discusses the names of good and evil learnedly and subtly on Psalm 4, writing thus after a long refutation of the Peripatetics: ἀλλ' ἐπείπερ ἴσω ἐν τῇ φράζει ὅτε μὲν κυριολεκτῶν, ὅτε δὲ πυ καταχρηκῶς, ὀ θαυμαστὸν εἴποτε ἐυρήσομεν τὴν τ' ἀγαθῶν κὴ κακῶν προσηγορίαν κειμένην ἐπὶ τ' σωματικῶν. Greek writers often call these goods 'falsely named goods'. Salvianus [calls] those things which are falsely called goods. Theodoret and Chrysostom on chapter 5 to the Ephesians call those things opposed to these 'evils which are thought so by many': what is disease? what is blindness? these are nothing, O man; there is only one evil, to sin.

Latin:

V. 18. καθελῶ με τάς ἀποθήκας κὶ μείζονας οἰκοδομήσω] Diruit, ædificat, mutat quadrata rotundis. Ipsa proventuum ubertas majores secum impensas trahit. Non horreis tantum majoribus, sed & famulis pluribus opus est qui ista servent. Basilius in sermone περὶ πλεονε- ξίας cum multa singulari facundia dicat in hoc vitium, tum illud eximie ad hunc locum respiciens: καθελῶ με τὰς ἀποθήκας καὶ μείζονας οἰκοδομήσω. ἐὰν δὲ καὶ ταύτας ἐμπλήσῃς τί ποτε ἆρα διανοηθήσῃ, ἤπω πάλιν καθαιρήσεις καὶ πάλιν οἰ- κοδομήσεις; κὶ τί τότων ἀτοπώτερον, ἀπέραντα μοχθεῖν, οἰκο- δομεῖν μετὰ σπεδῆς καὶ μετὰ σπεδῆς καθαιρεῖν; Adeo illud So- lanis verum: Πλύτε δ᾽ ὐδὲν τέρμα πεφασμένον ἀνδράσι κεῖται.

Τὰ γεννήματά με] γένημα est καρπὸς, inquit Phrynichus Solent ita LXX. vertere Hebræum תבואה ut Exodi XXIII. & alibi. Verius dixisset τὰ γεννήματα τῆς γῆς, communis hominum nutricis.

κὴ τὰ ἀγαθά με) Non sine causa hoc additum. Nam id hominum genus divitias bona appellat, non tantum populari loquendi modo, sed quod nihil melius istis existimat. Vetus est controversia inter Stoicos & Peripateticos, an omnino res istæ bonorum nomine sint nuncupandæ. Cicero Stoicos in paradoxis sequens a se requirere majorum prudentiam, qui ista imbecilla & commutabilia pecuniæ membra bona appellassent: a qua sententia non abeunt veteres Christiani. Nam quanquam & sacris literis res istæ bona interdum appellantur, id tamen censent fieri non proprie, ut sensisse videntur Peripatetici, sed propter similitudinem quandam cum veris bonis. Quare sicut aliis in partibus a Stoicis longe abeunt, ita hic eorum'orationem probant. Tatianus in Aristotele reprehendit ὅτι τὴν ἐυδαιμονίαν ἐν οἷς ἠρέσκετο περιέγραψε λίαν ἀπαίδευτος. Idem videre est apud Clementem Alexandrinum non uno loco ut Strom. II. τίνα δὲ τὰ φοβερὰ ὁ νόμος καταγγέλλει κὴ θεασώμεθα τὸ μὲν τὰ μεταξὺ ἀρετῆς κὴ κακίας, οἷον πενίαν κὴ νόσον κὴ ἀδοξίαν κὴ δυσγένειαν κὴ ὅσα παραπλήσια, ταῦτα μὲν κὴ οἱ κατὰ πόλιν νόμοι προτείνουσες ἱκανιώτατοι κὴ τοῖς ἐκ περιπάτε τρία γένη τ' ἀγαθῶν εἰσηγουμένοις κὴ τὰ τούτων ἐναντία λογιζομένοις εἶναι κακὰ ἁρμόδιοι· ἤδε ἡ δόξα· ἀμῖν δὲ ὁ δοθεὶς νόμος· τὰ τῷ ὄντι κακὰ ἀποφύγειν προστάττει μοιχείαν, ἀσελγείαν, παιδεραστίαν, ἄγνοιαν, ἀδικίαν, νόσον ψυχῆς (ita distingui locus hic debet male conceptus in editis libris) θάνατον, ὀ τὸν διαλύοντα ψυχὴν ἀπὸ σώματος, ἀλλὰ τὸν διαλύοντα ψυχὴν ἀπὸ ἀληθείας. Alibi dicit ὅσα τριττὰ εἶναι ἀγαθὰ οἱ περιπατητικοὶ θέλουσι. Ipse sacrarum literarum ductum sequens bona vocat non simpliciter ed cum additamento bona terræ. Ita enim ait Pæd. III. ἢν δὲ ἐσακούσητέ με, τὰ ἀγαθὰ τῆς γῆς φάγεσθε· ὁ παιδαγωγὸς πάλιν λέγει γῆς ἀγαθὰ τὰ ἀνθρώπεια ὀνομάζων καλὰ, τὸ κάλλος, τ πλοῦτον, τὴν ὑγίειαν, τὴν ἰσχὺν, τὴν τροφὴν, ἀγαθὰ μὲν γὰρ ὄντως ἃ μήτε ὖς ἤκουσεν, ὔτε ἐπὶ καρδίαν ἀνέβη ποτὲ, περὶ τ' ὄντως ὄντα βασιλεία τὰ ὄντως ὄντα ἀγαθὰ ὄντα κὴ ἀναμένοντα ἡμᾶς. Origenes adversus Celsum libro quarto ait: τὴν κακίαν εἶναι τὸ κακὸν, κὴ τὰς κατ' αὐτὴν πράξεις, κὴ ἄλλο ὀδὲν ὡς πρὸς ἀκριβῆ λόγον: Libro autem sexto paupertatem, morbos & id genus alia ait καταχρητικῶς ὀνομάζεσθαι κακά. Idem erudite & subtiliter de boni malique nominibus disputat ad Psalmum IV. post longam Peripateticorum refutationem ita scribens: ἀλλ' ἐπείπερ ἴσω ἐν τῇ φράζει ὅτε μὲν κυριολεκτῶν, ὅτε δὲ πυ καταχρηκῶς, ὀ θαυμαστὸν εἴποτε ἐυρήσομεν τὴν τ' ἀγαθῶν κὴ κακῶν προσηγορίαν κειμένην ἐπὶ τ' σωματικῶν. Sæpe ψευδώνυμα ἀγαθὰ hæc bona vocant Græci Scriptores. Salvianus ea quæ falso dicuntur bona. His opposita vocat κακὰ τὰ παρὰ πολλῶν νομιζόμενα Theodoretius Chrysostomus in caput V. ad Ephesios: τί δὲ ὁ νόσος; τί δὲ ἡ πώρωσις; ὀδέν ἐστι ταῦτα, ἄνθρωπε, ἐν μόνον ἐστὶ κακὸν, τὸ ἁμαρτάνειν.

## 12:19
V. 19. ἐρῶ τῇ ψυχῇ με] Then, he says, I will enjoy my portion when I have increased my barns: but it was already permitted to do that. There is an old saying: It is too late to live tomorrow, live today. When Pyrrhus was devouring Sicily, Africa, and other things in his hope, Cyneas asked him what he would do if those things had succeeded: we will live afterwards, he said: But this is already permitted, replied Cyneas.

εἰς ἔτη πολλὰ] But no one is so happy that he can promise himself the MORROW. See James 4:14.

ἀναπαύει] He feels from the very torture of his anxieties how sweet is the rest which he cannot provide for himself.

ἐυφραίνε] This word in this place seems to be referred to all other pleasures which are outside of eating and drinking. It corresponds to the Hebrew שמח as can be seen in Ecclesiastes 11:9.

Latin:

V. 19. ἐρῶ τῇ ψυχῇ με] Tunc inquit fruar partis cum horrea auxero: at id facere jam licebat Vetus est dictum: Cras serum est vivere, vive hodie. Pyrrhum, cum Siciliam Africam atque alia spe sua devoraret, interrogavit Cyneas, quid si ea processissent facturus esset: postea vivemus, inquit: At hoc jam licet respondit Cyneas.

εἰς ἔτη πολλὰ] At nemo tam fœlix, CRASTINUM ut possit sibi polliceri. Vide Jac. IV. 14.

ἀναπαύει] Sentit ex ipso sollicitudinum cruciatu quam dulcis sit quies quam præstare sibi non potest.

ἐυφραίνε] Hæc vox hoc quidem loco ad alias omnes voluptates referenda videtur, quæ sunt extra esum potumque. Respondet Hebræo שמח ut videre est in Ecclesiaste XI 9.

## 12:20
Vers. 20. εἶπε δὲ ἀυτῷ ὁ Θεὸς] Not by revealing, but by decreeing. Moreover, the decree is announced quite significantly by way of apostrophe, as in Proverbs 1:26.

ἄφρον] Similar to him who was Nabal in name and in deed, 1 Samuel 25.

ἀπαιτῦσι] The ancients seek in vain about whom this is said. For it is the personal for the impersonal, or the active for the passive, 'your soul shall be required back': but he said 'required back' well, because life was given to be used, it was given to us as a loan without interest.

And those things which you have prepared, whose will they be? Certainly not yours, who, about to die, will not take them away, but others will provide for themselves the use of them. The avaricious stupidity, which has envy joined to it, could not be mocked more effectively than when it is shown that what seems to him the greatest of evils will happen, namely, that another enjoys his things. The Mime says well: The miser does nothing right, except when he dies. Like his pig, of course, no part of which provides any use for itself except after death. The writer of Ecclesiasticus 11:18: There is one who is rich by his carefulness and pinching, and this is the portion of his reward in his saying, I have found rest, and now I will eat of my goods continually, and he does not know what time will pass him by, and he will leave them to others. There are also charming Greek epigrams on this matter: All say you are rich, but I say you are poor, for use is the witness of wealth, Apollophanes.

What you share of them, you have; what you keep for heirs, from then on it becomes another's. You have wealth while being rich, O soul, but you are poor; O rich for your heirs, but poor for yourself.

Let a third, no less elegant, be added: If you live for the long time of a stag or a crow, forgiveness for gathering much wealth. But if you are one of mortals, quickly bringing on old age, let not the gadfly of possessions seize you. Do not let your spirit slip into unbearable pains, so that others may use your goods without limit.

I say to you, miser, the joy of your heir. Snatch, heap up, take away, possess: it must be left behind.

Latin:

Vers. 20. εἶπε δὲ ἀυτῷ ὁ Θεὸς] Non revelando sed decernendo. Decretum autem κατ' ἀποστροφὴν significanter admodum enuntiatur, ut Prov. I. 26.

ἄφρον] Similis illi qui Nabal nomine & re 1. Sam. XXV.

ἀπαιτῦσι] Frustra quærunt veteres de quibus hoc dicatur. Est enim personale pro impersonali, aut activum pro passivo, reposcetur anima tua: Bene autem dixit reposcetur, quia Vita data est utenda, data est sine fœnore nobis Mutua.

ἃ δὲ ἡτοίμασας τίνι ἔσται] Non tibi certe qui ista moriturus non auferes, sed alii usum sui præstabunt. Non poterat efficacius derideri stoliditas avara, quæ conjunctam habet invidentiam, quam cum ostenditur eventurum quod malorum ipsi maximum videtur, ut rebus ejus fruatur alius. Bene Mimus: Avarus, nisi cum moritur, nil recte facit. Suis nimirum instar, cujus nulla pars ullum sui usum præbet nisi post mortem. Scriptor Ecclesiastici XI. 18. ἔστι πλουτῶν ἀπὸ προσοχῆς κὴ σφιγγίας ἀυτῶ, κὴ ἀυτή ἡ μῖρις ἀυτῶ ἀπὸ τῶ μισθῶ ἐν τῷ εἰπεῖν ἀυτὸν, εὗρον ἀνάπαυσιν καὶ νῦν φάγομαι ἀπὸ τ' ἀγαθῶν με ἀδιαλείπτως, καὶ ἐκ οἶδε τίς καιρὸς παραλέυσεται ἀυτόν κὴ καταλείψει ἀυτὰ ἑτέροις. Sunt & lepida in hanc rem Græcorum Epigrammata: Πλωτεῖν φασί σε πάντες, ἐγὼ δέ σε φημὶ πένεσθαι Χρῆσις γὰρ πλώτε μάρτυς Ἀπολλόφανες.

ὧι μετέχεις αὐτῶν σὺ, σὰ γίγνηται ὧν δὲ φυλάττεις Κληρονόμοις, ἀπὸ κὰν γίγνεται ἀλλότρια. Πλυτεῖν μὲν πλουτῶν ἔχεις, ψυχὴ, οἱ πένητος Ὢ τοῖς κληρονόμοις πλέτιε, σοὶ δὲ πένης.

Accedat tertium non minus elegans: Εἰ μὲν ζῇς ἐλάφου ταλαὸν χρόνον ἡὲ κορώνης Συγγνώμη πλεῖστον πλῦτον ἀγειρομένῳ. Εἰ δὲ τις ἐσὶ βροτῶν ὣς αὐτίκα γῆρας ἱάπτων Μή σε γ᾽ ἀπαρεσιων οἶστρος ἕλῃ κτεάνων. Μὴ σὺ μὲν ἀτλήτοισιν ἐν ἀλγίσι θυμὸν ὀλίσσῃς, Χρήσωνται δ᾽ ἄλλοι σοῖς ἀγαθοῖς ἀνίδην.

Tibi dico avare gaudium hæredis tui. Rape, congere, aufer, posside: relinquendum est.

## 12:21
Verse 21. So is he: Such is the end of folly.

And not being rich toward God: I think entirely that being rich is the same as storing up, and therefore toward God is the same as with God. Thus it happens to those who accumulate wealth for themselves and do not labor to have wealth stored up with God, namely, works of mercy, which Christ elsewhere calls treasure in heaven, Matthew 6:20, and also here below in verse 33, the Apostle said being rich in good works, 1 Timothy 6:18.

I do not see why toward God should not be explained as in God, since Grotius has observed more than once that toward is taken for in. But he is rich in God who enjoys the grace of God, trusts in God, is full of God, and of works done in God, and thus is rich in faith, rich in good works, James 2:5, 1 Timothy 6:17. Thus there is no need for those Grotian fractures: Beza seems to say rich in God, who grows daily in the knowledge of God. The Syriac and Arabic also have in God, as does our blessed Luther.

Latin:

Vers. 21. ὅτως ἴσω) Talem habet stultitia exitum.

κὴ μὴ εἰς Θεὸν πλουτῶν) Omnino arbitror πλυτῶν idem es- se quod θησαυρίζων, ac proinde εἰς Θεὸν idem quod παρὰ Θεῷ. Sic illis evenit qui sibi opes accumulant ac non labo- rant ut apud Deum opes repositas habeant, opera scilicet misericordiæ, quos θησαυρὸς ἐν ὀυρανῷ alibi vocat Christus Matth. VI. 20. atque etiam hîc infra 33. πλουτεῖν ἐν ἔργοις καλοῖς dixit Apostolus. I. ad Tim. VI. 18.

Non video cur non εἰς Θεὸν explicandum sit ἐν Θεῷ, quum εἰς pro ἐν accipi non semel observarit Grotius. In DEO autem dives est, qui DEI gratia fruitur, in DEO confidit, plenus DEO, & ope- ribus in DEO factis, adeoque dives fide, dives operibus bonis Iac. II. 5. 1. Tim. VI. 17. Ita non opus illis infractibus Grotianis: Beza πλυτῶν ἐν Θεῷ dici videtur, qui indies augescit in DEI cognitio- ne. Syrus & Arabs habent etiam IN DEO, ut & B. Lutherus noster.

## 12:24
Verse 24. The ravens: Since Matthew named birds in general, it is not without reason that Luke specifically expressed ravens. For Job and the Psalmist proclaim God's special care for the young of ravens; how the teachers of the Hebrews explain this has been noted by others. Certainly, Aristotle notes in more than one place that the young of ravens are driven from the nest by their parents.

Storehouse: Cicero called it a pantry.

Latin:

Vers. 24. τὺς κόρακας) Cum volucres in genere nomina- verit Matthæus, non frustra est quod Lucas corvos speciali- ter expressit. Nam circa corvorum pullos specialem Dei curam Jobus & Psalmographus prædicant; quod quomo- do exponant Hebræorum magistri ab aliis notatum est. Certe Aristoteles non uno loco notat pullos corvorum à suis parentibus nido expelli.

ταμεῖον) Cellam penariam dixit Cicero.

## 12:26
Verse 26. If therefore you are not able to do the least: That is, the lesser thing. It is less to add something to one's stature than to preserve life: if that is not in your power, certainly this is not either. Therefore, do not think your life is safer because you gather such a store of things. Your life is in the hand of God, who, for those who care for eternal things, will not allow temporal things to be lacking while you lead this mortal life. We see both the rich die and the poor survive them by much. See the commentary on Matthew.

Concerning the rest: Concerning the remaining things which are equally placed in the hand of God: so also the Syriac understood it.

Latin:

Vers. 26. εἰ ὖν οὔτε ἐλάχιστον δύνασθε) Id est, τὸ ἔλασσον. Mi- nus est staturæ aliquid adjicere quam vitam conservare: si illud non est in vestra potestate, certe nec hoc quidem est. Quare ne putate vitam vestram ideo esse tutiorem, quod tantam rerum congeratis copiam. Vita vestra in Dei est ma- nu, qui æterna curantibus non patietur de esse temporalia, dum mortale hoc ævum agitis. Videmus & divites mori, & pauperes multo supervivere. Vide ad Matthæum.

περὶ ᾧ λοιπῶν) De reliquis quæ æque sunt in manu Dei posita: ita & Syrus accepit.

## 12:29
V. 29. μὴ μετεωρίζεσθε) Do not be in suspense, do not be distracted by thoughts, as the Syriac translates: Nor does Theophylactus interpret μετεωρισμὸν badly as distraction or the unstable wandering of words, not elation of mind as it pleases some, but anxiety fluctuating miserably between hope and fear. Thus μετεωρισμοὶ ὀφθαλμῶν in Sirach XXVI. 12, the vibration of the eyes.

Latin:

V. 29. μὴ μετεωρίζεσθε) Ne pendete animi, ne distrahibi- ni cogitationibus, ut vertit Syrus: Nec male Theophylactus μετεωρισμὸν interpretatur ὁ περισπασμὸν κό τὴν τῶ λόγων ἄσατον περιφορὰν, non elationem animi ut quibusdam placet, sed anxietatem inter spem metumque misere fluctuantem. Sic μετεωρισμοὶ ὀφθαλμῶν Syrac. XXVI. 12. oculorum vibratio.

## 12:32
V. 32. τὸ μικρὸν ποίμνιον) He addresses all those who had seriously surrendered themselves to his discipline, or were about to surrender themselves: whom he calls a flock, so that they may remember that God is their shepherd not only in a common way, but in a peculiar way, Ps. XXIII. 1. But a little flock, that is, despised, poor, ignoble, not at all fortified by those protections in which others trust. Thus this consolation coheres excellently with the previous discourse.

Εὐδόκησεν ὁ πατὴρ) A signification of benevolence from the nature of the thing, not from the force of the word, has a place here. For ἐυδόκησε joined with an infinitive is nothing other than, it seemed good to him, as we have noted elsewhere.

δῦναι ὑμῖν τὴν βασιλείαν) That eternal kingdom which is accustomed to be described by the name of food and drink, how much more therefore will he give the viaticum of this short life, that is.

Which human nature grieves are denied to it.

Latin:

V. 32. τὸ μικρὸν ποίμνιον) Omnes eos affatur qui discupli- næ suæ serio se tradiderant, aut tradituri essent: quos gre- gem vocat, ut Deum non communi tantum modo, sed pe- culiari suum esse pastorem meminerint, Ps. XXIII. 1. Parvum autem gregem id est contemtum, pauperem, ignobilem, minime munitum iis præsidiis quibus cæteri confidunt. Ita optime hæc consolatio cum sermone priori cohæret.

Εὐδόκησεν ὁ πατὴρ) Benevolentiæ significatio ex rei natu- ra, non ex vi vocis hic locum habet. Nam ἐυδόκησε cum infi- nitivo jungitur, nihil aliud est quam, visum est illi, ut alibi notavimus.

δῦναι ὑμῖν τὴν βασιλείαν) Æternum illud regnum quod cibi & potus nomine describi solet, quanto magis ergo da- bit ανὶ hujus brevis viaticum, id est.

Queis humana sibi doleat natura negatis.

## 12:33
V. 33. πωλήσατε τὰ ὑπάρχοντα ὑμῶν κὰι δότε ἐλεημοσύνην) A Hebrew manner of speaking. The sense is: Rather than be unmerciful to the needy, sell the very bodies of your possessions, so far is it from the case that you should begrudge them whatever overflows from the fruits, just as that rich man mentioned a little before did. You will find a similar kind of speaking below in ch. XXII. 36.

Βαλάντια) Thus Luke calls what Matthew calls ζώνας, as we saw above in ch. X. As far as the matter pertains, βαλάντια signify the same thing as θησαυροὶ. Except that θησαυροὶ are of greater quantity or value, βαλάντια of lesser.

PART IV.

Exhortation to vigilance and faithfulness.

Latin:

V. 33. πωλήσατε τὰ ὑπάρχοντα ὑμῶν κὰι δότε ἐλεημοσύνην) Hebræus mos loquendi. Sensus est: Potius quam immiseri- cordes sitis in egenos, ipsa rerum corpora divendite, tantum abest ut quicquid de fructibus redundat illis invideatis, quemadmodum fecit dives ille paulo ante memoratus. Si- mile loquendi genus reperies infra c. XXII. 36.

Βαλάντια) Ita Lucas vocat quas ζώνας Matthæus, ut vidi- mus supra c. X. Quod ad rem attinet idem significant βαλάν- τια quod θησαυροὶ. Nisi quod θησαυροὶ sint majoris quanti- tatis aut pretii, βαλάντια minoris.

PARS IV.

Adhortatio advigilantiam & fidem.

## 12:35
Vers. 35. ωἱ ὀσφύες περιεζωσμέναι οἱ λύχνοι καιόμενοι)

I entirely think these words pertain to that similitude which is explained in the following verse. For those who wait for the Lord, and ought to be girded high for the undertaking of service, and, if it is night, to have lights ready, so that there may be no delay when the Lord arrives. It is the duty not only of soldiers and travelers but also of those serving to be περιεζῶσθαι τὰς ὀσφύας, as appears in verse 37, and John XIII. 4. Hence Phædrus called the servants girded high. Homer in the Odyssey, book 11: 'Having said this, he quickly girded his tunic with a belt': where Eustathius says it is indicative of haste. Servius on Aeneid VIII: we call those 'præcinctos' who are energetic. Horace: 'one girded higher than we'. To the same, a boy girded high. In Petronius, 'statores' and those girded higher. Whence also in Greek he is called εὔζωνος, not he who has a good belt, but he who is energetic. Philo in his book on Abel and Cain: 'girded about the loins', he interprets as 'having themselves ready for service': in which place he commemorates the Paschal ceremony, to which it seems this also may be an allusion.

Latin:

Vers. 35. ωἱ ὀσφύες περιεζωσμέναι οἱ λύχνοι καιόμενοι)

Omnino puto hæc verba pertinere ad eam similitudinem quæ in sequenti commate explicatur. Nam qui Dominum exspectant, & ad ministerium obeundum alte cincti esse de- bent, &, si nox est, lumina habere parata, ne quid in mora sit cum Dominus advenerit. Non tantum militum & iter facientium sed & ministrantium est περιεζῶσθαι τὰς ὀσφύας, ut commate 37. apparet, & Johan. XIII. 4. hinc alte cin- ctos atrienses dixit Phædrus. Homerus Odysseæ ξ. Ὡς εἰπὼν, ζωστῆρι θοῶς συνέεργε χιτῶνα: ubi Eustathius σπουδῆς δηλωτικὸν. Servius ad VIII. Æneid. præcinctos, strenuos dicimus. Horatius: altius ac nos Præcinctis unum. Eidem puer alte cinctus. Petronio statores & altius cin- cti. Unde & Græce εὔζωνος appellatur non qui bonam zo- nam habet sed strenuus. Philo libro de Abele & Caine: τὰς ὀσφῦς περιεζωσμένους, interpretatur ἑτοίμως πρὸς ὑπη- ρεσίαν ἔχοντας: quo loco Paschalem cæremoniam comme- morat, ad quam hic quoque allusum videri potest.

## 12:37
Verse 37. 'He will gird himself and make them recline': As was done at the Saturnalia in Rome. The sense is, he will show them a new and unusual honor: nor are the parts of the comparison to be pressed further. 'Coming': Approaching closer, as below in XVII. 7. and the same in Acts XXIV. 7.

Latin:

Vers. 37. περιζώσεται κᾲ ἀνακλινεῖ αὐτὸς] Ut Saturnalibus Romæ fiebat. Sensus est, honorem illis habebit novum at- que insolitum: neq; ultra premendæ partes comparationis. παρελθὼν] Accedens propius, ut infra XVII. 7. & idem Act. XXIV. 7.

## 12:38
Verse 38. 'And if he finds them so': 'Watching' must be repeated: so watching, that whether he comes in the dead of night or at the silent hour, the master of the house may find them prompt and ready. Below XXI. 30. 'Watch at every time'. 'Finds': That is, 'should find', he is about to find.

Latin:

Vers. 38. κᾲ εὕρῃ ὕτως] Repeti debet γρηγορῶντας: ita vigi- lantes, ut sive intempesta nocte sive conticinio veniat pa- terfamilias, promtos eos paratosque sit inventurus, Infra XXI. 30. ἀγρυπνεῖτε ἐν πάντι καιρῷ. εὕρῃ] Id est εὕρῃ ἂν, inventurus sit.

## 12:41
Verse 41. 'Are you telling this parable to us, or to all?': I think it is rightly gathered from this, since the prior story had pertained to all, whence also in Mark there is added to it 'what I say to you I say to all, watch', that another was added by Christ, which would properly touch the pastors of the churches.

Latin:

V. 41. πρὸς ὑμᾶς τὴν παραβολὴν λέγεις, ἢ πρὸς πάντας;] Recte hinc colligi puto, cum prior fabula ad omnes perti- nuisset, unde & apud Marcum ei subjicitur ὃ δὲ ὑμῖν λέγω πᾶ- σι λέγω, γρηγορεῖτε, alteram à Christo adjectam, quæ pasto- res Ecclesiarum proprie tangeret.

## 12:42
Verse 42. 'Who then is': A hypothetical, as we have said several times. 'Will appoint': Future in place of the aorist. Matthew says 'appointed': as if he were to say, if any servant is appointed steward of the household, he will be happy if he performs his duty correctly. 'Ration of grain': Thus the LXX said 'to measure out grain' in Gen. XLVII. 12.

Latin:

V. 42. Τίς ἄρα ἐστὶν] ὑποθετικὸν, ut aliquoties diximus. καταστήσει] Futurum vice ἀορίστου. κάλισησε Matthæus: quasi dicat, si quis servus constituitur dispensator familiæ, fœlix erit si munus suum recte obeat. Σιτομέτριον] Sic σιτομετρεῖν dixere LXX. Gen. XLVII. 12.

## 12:46
Verse 46. 'He will cut him in two': Tertullian translates 'to cut in two' in this place as 'to separate', not badly as to the sense. See what is said on Matthew. B. Lyserus explains this word more fully in Harm. c. CX. col. 1590. 'To cut in two' is to cut into two parts: which is the proper punishment for perfidious rebels and traitors to the fatherland. Since, therefore, these also are traitors to the glory of God and the public salvation, they are deservedly subjected to this punishment. They are dissected, however, when first in death the soul is miserably torn away from the body, afterwards they are truly separated from the fellowship of the saints, and finally soul and body are cast into hell, where they will be separated from God forever, and there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. Gen. XV. 10. and Lev. I. 8. the parts of the sacrifices, which were to be burned in the burnt offering and consumed by fire, are called 'dichotomies' (pieces). Likewise Ezech. XXIV. 4. those pieces, which were to be cast into the boiling pot, by which the wrath of God against the rebellious people was declared parabolically, were marked with the same name. Christ therefore wishes to signify that there is in hell a lake of fire burning with sulfur, Apoc. XIX. 20. into which lake these perfidious stewards of the house of God are to be cast, so that thus their portion may be placed with the unfaithful and the damned.

Latin:

V. 46. διχοτομήσει αὐτὸν] Διχοτομεῖν hoc loco segrega- re vertit Tertullianus, ad sensum non male. Vide quæ ad Matthæum. Plenius hoc verbum explicat B. Lyserus Harm. c. CX. col. 1590. διχοτομεῖν est in duas partes secare: quæ pœnæ perfidorum rebellium & proditorum pa- triæ propria est. Cum ergo hi quoque sint gloriæ DEI & publicæ salutis proditores, merito huic pœnæ subjiciuntur. Dissecantur autem quando primum in morte anima à corpore misere divelli- tur, postea vero ipsi à sanctorum consortio sepa- rantur, & tandem anima & corpore in infernum abjiciuntur, ubi à DEO in æternum sejungentur, ibique erit fletus & stridor dentium. Gen. XV. 10. & Lev. I. 8. partes sacrificiorum, quæ in holocau- sto accendendæ & igne absumendæ erant, dicun- tur διχοτομήματα. Item Ezech. XXIV. 4. frustra il- la, quæ in ollam bullientem, qua parabolice ira DEI adversum populum rebellem declarabantur, conjicienda erant, eodem nomine insigniebatur. Vult ergo Christus significare, esse in inferno sta- gnum ignis ardens sulphure, Apoc. XIX. 20. in quod stagnum præcipitandi sint perfidi hi dispensatores domus DEI, ut sic ponatur pars eorum cum infi- delibus & damnatis.

## 12:47
Verse 47. 'And that servant who knew the will': Since Christ had proposed a double story, one which pertained to all Christians, another which pertained to the leaders of the churches, he now shows in what they agree or disagree. They agree in that both the laymen and the leaders will be punished if they have not done their duty: they disagree in that the leaders will be punished more severely, as those to whom generally a greater and more exact knowledge has been given of all those things which pertain indirectly or directly to salvation. Although Christ brought forth this sentiment on this occasion, its force nevertheless extends more widely, as can be understood from the reason subjoined. For the reason which is added is this, that it is just that much be returned by him who has received much. Wherefore some do not altogether badly extend these things to comparing among themselves those who have received the word of the Gospel, and those to whose ears it has not reached. For concerning those who, having heard the Gospel, do not obey, Peter said 'it would have been better for them not to have known the way of righteousness'. Salvianus, book II on Providence: 'And by this we understand that we are much more culpable who have the law of God and despise it, than those who neither have it at all nor know it.' Where also other things are excellently said on this matter. Indeed, no nations can be ignorant of those things which nature itself in a way dictates to men, but they do not know by certain revelation what rewards are established for virtue, what punishments for vices. Although by conjecture perhaps, and by ancient tradition, they attain something of this too, but which is not to be compared at all with that knowledge which has been granted to us by the gift of Christ. Tertullian in his book on Repentance. Since even for those ignorant of the Lord no exception protects them from punishment (because it is not permitted to be ignorant of God, who is established in the open and is comprehensible even from the heavenly goods themselves), how much more dangerous is it to despise Him once known? Philosophers also note that guilt is increased or diminished according to the measure of knowledge. There exists also a saying of Philo on that matter against Flaccus: 'For to him who errs by ignorance of the better, forgiveness is given; but he who sins from knowledge has no defense, having already been convicted in the court of his own conscience.' The Apostle James IV. 17. 'To him who knows to do good and does not do it, to him it is sin.' Salvianus: 'The guilt of a lesser crime is to be ignorant of the law than to despise it.' And elsewhere: 'Ignorance can be forgiven to some extent: contempt has no pardon.'

μὴ ἑτοιμάσας] Supply 'for doing'. But this is well added: for he who prepares himself to do, even if the time or opportunity for doing is lacking, is outside of punishment. Jerome on Matthew XII: 'In the law, works are required, which he who has done will live in them. In the Gospel, the will is sought: which even if it has not had effect, nevertheless does not lose its reward.'

Δαρήσεται πολλὰς] Thus Aristophanes speaks in the Clouds, τυπτόμενος πολλὰς, and Xenophon in the 5th book of the Expedition, ἀνέκραγον πάντες ὡς ὀλίγας παίσας. And Demosthenes on the False Embassy: ξαίνει κατὰ τοῦ νώτου πολλάς. Procopius followed this in the first book of the Vandalic War: ξαίνοντες κατὰ τῶν νώτων πολλάς: so that you may recognize the idiom of pure Greek here no less than elsewhere in Luke. There is an allusion, moreover, to the law in Deut. XXV. 2.

Latin:

Vers. 47. ἐκεῖνος δὲ δοῦλος ὁ γνὺς τὸ θέλημα] Cum du- plicem fabellam Christus proposuisset, alteram quæ ad Christianos omnes, alteram quæ ad Ecclesiarum præposi- tos, pertineret, ostendit jam in quo conveniant ista aut dis- conveniant. Conveniunt in eo quod tam ἰδιῶται quam προεστῶτες plectentur, nisi officium suum fecerint: disconve- niunt in eo quod oi προεστῶτες plectentur gravius, ut quibus communiter major atque exactior data sit scientia omnium eorum quæ ἐμμέσως aut ἀμέσως ad salutem pertinent. Quan- quam autem hac occasione hanc sententiam Christus pro- tulerit, vis tamen ejus latius patet, ut ex subjecta ratione intelligi potest. Ratio enim quæ subjungitur hæc est, quod æquum sit multum ab eo reddi qui multum acceperit. Qua- re non omnino male quidam hæc extendunt ad comparan- dos inter se eos qui Evangelii verbum acceperunt, & eos ad quorum aures idipsum non pervenit. Nam de iis qui audito Evangelio non obediunt dixit Petrus κρεῖττον ἦν αὐτοῖς μὴ ἐπεγνωκέναι τὴν ὁδὸν δικαιοσύνης. Salvianus lib. II. de Pro- videntia: Ac per hoc intellogimus culpabiliores nos multo esse qui legem Dei habemus & spernimus, quam illos qui nec ha- bent omnino nec norunt. Ubi & alia præclare dicta in hanc rem. Non possunt quidem ullæ gentes ignorare ea quæ natura quodammodo ipsa hominibus dictat, sed non norunt certa revelatione, quæ præmia virtuti, quæ pœnæ vitiis sint constitutæ. Quanquam conjectura forte, & veteri traditione aliquid etiam hujus assequuntur, sed quod cum ea notitia quæ nobis Christi munere concessa est, minime sit conferendum. Tertullianus libro de Pœnitentia. Cum etiam ignorantes Dominum nulla exceptio tueatur à pœna (quia Deum in aperto constitutum & vel ex ipsis cælestibus bonis comprehensibilem ignorare non licet) quanto cognitum despici periculosum est? Pro modo scientiæ culpam augeri aut minui etiam philosophi notant. Exstat quoque Philonis dictum ea de re contra Flaccum: τῷ μὲν γὰρ ἀγνοίᾳ τοῦ κρείττονος διαμαρτάνοντι, συγγνώμη δίδοται· ὁ δὲ ἐξ ἐπιστήμης ἀδικῶν, ἀπολογίαν οὐκ ἔχει προεαλωκὼς ἐν τῷ τοῦ συνειδότος δικαστηρίῳ. Jacobus Apostolus IV. 17. εἰδότι τὸ καλὸν ποιεῖν καὶ μὴ ποιοῦντι ἁμαρτία αὐτῷ ἐστιν. Salvianus: Minoris criminis reatus est legem nescire, quam spernere. Et alibi: Ignosci aliquatenus ignorantiæ potest: contemptus veniam non habet.

μὴ ἑτοιμάσας] Supple πρὸς τὸ ποιεῖν. Bene autem hoc additur: nam qui ad faciendum se comparat, etiamsi faciendi tempus aut occasio desit, extra pœnam est. Hieronymus ad XII Matthæi: In lege opera requiruntur quæ qui fecerit, vivet in eis. In Evangelio voluntas quæritur: quæ etiamsi effectum non habuerit, tamen præmium non amittit.

Δαρήσεται πολλὰς] Sic Aristophanes nubibus loquitur τυπτόμενος πολλὰς, & Xenophon V. Exped. ἀνέκραγον πάντες ὡς ὀλίγας παίσας. Et Demosthenes de falsa legatione: ξαίνει κατὰ τοῦ νώτου πολλάς. Secutus Procopius Vandalicorum primo: ξαίνοντες κατὰ τῶν νώτων πολλάς: ut puræ Græciæ locutionem hic non minus quam alibi in Luca agnoscas. Alluditur autem ad legem Deut. XXV. 2.

## 12:48
Vers. 48. μὴ γνοὺς] Through slowness of intellect, or the negligence of teachers, or some other grave cause, provided that the ignorance was not sought out by design, which detracts nothing from the guilt.

ἐδόθη] For his own uses.

ᾧ παρέθεντο πολὺ περισσότερον αἰτήσουσιν αὐτὸν] Again, the personal for the impersonal. The sense is, to whom much has been entrusted, for the uses of others, of course, more will be demanded back from him than from him who received less entrusted to him. What is in Peter, 1st Epistle IV. 10, pertains to this.

PART V. Concerning the proper and accidental end of the Lord's coming.

Latin:

Vers. 48. μὴ γνοὺς] Tarditate ingenii, aut doctorum negligentia, aut alia gravi de causa, modo ne studio quæsita sit ignorantia, quæ de culpa nihil detrahit.

ἐδόθη] In suos usus.

ᾧ παρέθεντο πολὺ περισσότερον αἰτήσουσιν αὐτὸν] Rursum personale pro impersonali. Sensus est, cui commendatum est multum, in usus scilicet alienos, plus ab eo reposcetus quam ab eo qui minus commendatum accepit. Huc pertinet quod apud Petrum est Epistola IV. 10.

PARS V. De fine adventus Domini proprio, & accidentario.

## 12:49
Vers. 49. πῦρ ἦλθον βαλεῖν εἰς τὴν γῆν] Since all the things that follow pertain to the persecutions that would arise on account of the word, I agree with Tertullian, who explains this passage thus: He himself will better interpret the quality of that fire, adding: Do you think that I have come to send peace on earth? I tell you, no, but division. And shortly after: Such as the battle, such also is the conflagration; such as the sword, such is the flame. Moreover, whatever tests the spirits is well compared to fire, 1 Pet. I. 7: that the proof of your faith, being much more precious than gold that perishes, though it is tested by fire, may be found to praise and honor and glory. Menander: Gold indeed knows how to be tested by fire, but goodwill toward friends is judged by time. Ovid: Just as yellow gold is viewed in the fires, so faith must be tested in hard times. But apart from this comparison, adverse things are compared no less to fire than to a flood, Ps. LXVI. 12; Is. XLIII. 2. Christ says, however, that he came for this reason, not because God primarily wills this, but because, having foreseen the characters of evil men and the cruelty that would follow from them, he did not for that reason cease to scatter the truth, intending to use even the work of the wicked for the glory of his name and the purging of the Church. All, says Paul in 2 Tim. III. 12, who desire to live godly in Christ Jesus, will be persecuted.

καὶ τί θέλω;] I think a mark of interrogation should be added. For in these matters no authority of the codices binds us, since the ancient books were without punctuation. The sense is: But what is it that I desire? For an interrogation with the answer following affirms more vehemently. Nor does Theophylact seem to have read and understood it otherwise.

εἰ ἤδη ἀνήφθη] Thus have all the ancient codices, from which there is no cause to depart. The passage, however, has been less correctly understood until now, because it was not observed that εἰ, even with the indicative added, has the same force among the Hellenists as 'would that'. Luke below XIX. 42, εἰ ἔγνως καὶ σὺ, 'Would that you also had known', and XXII. 42, εἰ βούλει παρενέγκειν. LXX Num. XXII. 29, εἰ εἶχον μάχαιραν ἐν τῇ χειρί με, 'Would that a sword were in my hand'. Jos. VII. 7.

O we have been broken and we have been trodden down by the Jordan. Job XVI. 14. If I had spoken to you with words. Isaiah XLVIII. 8. If you had hearkened to my commandments. I wish you had attended to my precepts. The Syrian, although there are those who accept it otherwise, agrees with me. For אלין is accustomed to be used for 'I wish' by the Syrians, as appears in the said place Luke XIX. 42. For it answers to the Hebrew לו or לוא. These words must therefore be translated: I wish now, even now, it were kindled, that fire, to wit, which is to test and purge the flock of Christ: Which the Latin translates: What will I, but that it be kindled, in that it correctly expressed the sense, but did not count the words: just as the Syrian also resolved the present interrogation into a bare affirmation, with equal liberty to that with which in the following clause he rendered πῶς as 'much'. Latin versions older than this Vulgate had 'how I wish that it may burn', or 'how I wish that it may be kindled': correctly as to the sense. But it does not even correspond exactly to the words. For I desire an example that τι is used for πόσον. Certainly, from those versions you could not validly prove that it was read differently in the Greek Codices of old than it is read now, since interpreters everywhere indulge themselves the right to depart from the letter while the sense remains intact.

Latin:

Vers. 49. πῦρ ἦλθον βαλεῖν εἰς τὴν γῆν] Cum quæ sequuntur omnia ad persecutiones verbi causa orituras pertineant, Tertulliano assentior locum hunc sic exponenti: Ipse melius interpretabitur ignis illius qualitatem, adjiciens: Putatis me venisse pacem mittere in terram: non dico vobis sed separationem. Et mox: Quale prælium, tale & incendium, qualis machæra, talis & flamma. Bene autem igni comparatur quicquid adversum animos explorat Petr. ep. I. I. 7. ἵνα τὸ δοκίμιον ὑμῶν τῆς πίστεως πολὺ τιμιώτερον χρυσίου τοῦ ἀπολλυμένου, διὰ πυρὸς δὲ δοκιμαζομένου, εὑρεθῇ εἰς ἔπαινον καὶ τιμὴν καὶ δόξαν. Menander. Χρυσὸς μὲν οἶδεν ἐξελέγχεσθαι πυρὶ, Ἡ πρὸς φίλους δ' εὔνοια καιρῷ κρίνεται. Ovidius: Scilicet ut fulvum spectatur in ignibus aurum, Tempore sic duro est experienda fides. Sed extra hanc comparationem res adversæ non minus igni quam diluvio comparantur, Psal. LXVI. 12. Es. XLIII. 2. Dicit autem Christus ideo se venisse, non quod hoc primario Deus velit, sed quod conspectis hominum malorum ingeniis & secutura inde sævitia, non tamen propterea destiterit verum spargere, usurus scilicet etiam malorum opera ad nominis sui gloriam & Ecclesiæ purgationem. Πάντες, inquit Paulus 2. Tim. III. 12. οἱ θέλοντες εὐσεβῶς ζῇν ἐν χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ, διωχθήσονται.

καὶ τί θέλω;] Interrogationis notam apponendam censeo. Nam his in rebus nulla nos Codicum auctoritas obstringit, cum veteres libri fuerint ἀδιάστικτοι. Sensus est: Quid autem est quod opto? Nam interrogatio subjecta responsione vehementius affirmat. Nec aliter videtur legisse & accepiffe Theophylactus.

εἰ ἤδη ἀνήφθη] Ita habent omnes antiqui codices à quibus nulla est causa recedendi. Locus autem est hactenus minus recte intellectus, quia non est animadversum εἰ etiam addito indicativo apud Hellenistas idem valere quod utinam. Lucas infra XIX. 42. εἰ ἔγνως καὶ σὺ Utinam tu quoque novisses. & XXII 42. εἰ βούλει παρενέγκειν. LXX. Numer. XXII. 29. εἰ εἶχον μάχαιραν ἐν τῇ χειρί με, Utinam machæra mihi esset in manu. Jos. VII. 7.

ῶ κατεμόνιαμεν κὴ κατεπατήθημεν παρὰ τὸν ἰορδάνην. Job.XVI. 14. εἴ τ᾽ ἐναλέμην ὑμῖν ῥήμασι. Esaia XLVIII. 8. εἰ ἤκουσας τῶν ἐντολῶν με Vtinam attendisses præceptis meis. Syrus, quan- quam sunt qui aliter accipiunt, mecum facit. Nam אלין pro utinam poni Syris solet, ut apparet dicto loco Lucæ XIX. 42. Respondet enim Hebræo לו vel לוא. Vertenda igitur hæc verba Vtinam jamjam accendatur, ignis scilicet ille ex- ploraturus & purgaturus Christi gregem: Quod Latinus vertit: Quid volo, nisi ut accendatur, in eo sensum recte expreffit, verba non annumeravit: quomodo & Syrus in- terrogationem præsentem resolvit in nudam affirmatio- nem, pari libertate qua commate sequenti πῶς reddidit multum. Versiones Latinæ hac vulgata vetustiores habe- bant quam volo ut ardeat, aut quam volo ut accendatur: ad sensum recte. Sed verbis ne hoc quidem exacte respondet. Nam ut τι pro πόσον ponatur exemplum desidero. Certe ex illis versionibus aliter lectum olim in Græcis Codicibus, quam nunc legitur, non satis valide evincas, cum passim in- terpretes jus sibi indulgeant sensu incolumi ab apicibus re- cedendi.

## 12:50
Vers. 50. Baptism) See Matt. XX. 22. Mark X. 38. I have a baptism to be baptized with) First in myself, then in my followers. For what happens to them, Christ says happens to himself, Acts XI. 5.

how I am straitened until it be accomplished) Ancient writers often use testimonies from scripture: but in such a way that it appears the codex was not inspected by them, although they render the sentiment quite correctly from memory. Such is that which Irenaeus cites from this place thus: 'I have another baptism to be baptized with and I am very eager for it.' So also Epiphanius against the Arians cites this place far differently than it is, with the addition also of the mention of the cup from the history of Zebedee: which happens to him in citing other places as well, as when he cites those things which are below XXIII. 41. and 44. Wherefore there is no reason why the received reading should be suspect to us on that account. Moreover, there seems to be in the word συνέχεσθαι a certain tacit similitude taken from a pregnant woman who so dreads the labor pains that she nevertheless wishes to be relieved of her burden as soon as possible.

Since therefore Grotius acknowledges that the received reading cannot be safely amended from the citations of the ancients, why did he attempt it so frequently? He is certainly not to be excused in such things, which he himself understood more correctly, as not agreeing in the least.

Latin:

Vers. 50. Βάπτισμα) Vide Matth. XX. 22. Marc. X. 38. ἔχω βαπτισθῆναι) Primum in me ipso, deinde in sectato- ribus meis. Nam quod illis fit sibi fieri Christus dicit A- ctor. XI. 5.

πῶς συνέχομαι ἕως ὅ τελεσθῇ) Veteres scriptores sæpe utuntur testimoniis ex scriptura: sed ita ut appareat codi- cem ab illis non inspectum, cum tamen sententiam satis recte ex memoria reddant. Tale est quod hunc locum ita citat Irenæus: ἄλλο βάπτισμα ἔχω βαπτισθῆναι καὶ πάνυ ἰ- πείγομαι εἰς αὐτὸ. Sic & Epiphanius adversus Arianos lo- cum hunc longe aliter citat quam habet, addita & poculi mentione ex historia Zebedæi: quod illi in aliis quoque lo- cis citandis contingit, ut cum citat ea quæ sunt infra XXIII. 41. & 44. Quare non est quod eo nomine suspecta nobis sit recepta lectio. Videtur autem in verbo συνέχεσθ tacita quæ- dam esse similitudo sumta à prægnante muliere quæ ita partitudinem horret; ut tamen velit quam primum fasce suo levari.

Quum ergo agnoscat Grotius non posse rece- ptam lectionem tuto emendari è veterum citatio- ne, cur id tam frequenter tentavit? Excusandus certe non est in talibus, quæ ipse rectius intelle- xit, minime convenire.

## 12:51
Vers. 51. but rather division) The copies which Tertullian used seem to have had μάχαιραν from Matthew. For he himself suspects that διαμερισμὸν was substituted in its place by Marcion, which does not seem likely: for interpreters here consistently acknowledge διαμερισμὸς.

Latin:

Vers. 51. ἀλλ᾽ ἢ διαμερισμὸν) Videntur exemplaria qui- bus usus est Tertullianus ex Matthæo habuisse μάχαιραν. Nam ipse suspicatur διαμερισμὸν ejus vice substitutum à Marcione, quod non fit verisimile: nam διαμερισμὸς hic constanter agnoscunt interpretes.

## 12:54
Vers. 54. when you see the cloud rising from the west, immediately you say: there will be a shower) Aratus in his Diosemeia: And when turned toward the setting sun, if a cloud darkens the sun, and rays scattered here and there are divided, you would have need of a cloak for the dawn. For natural causes see Theon.

Latin:

Vers. 54. ὅταν ἴδητε τὴν νεφέλην ἀνατέλλουσαν ἀπὸ δυσμῶν, ἐνθέως λέγετε· ὄμβρος ἔται) Aratus Diosemejis: Καὶ δὴ δυομένοι τετραμμένος ἠελίοιο Ην μὲν ὑποσκιάησι μελαντομένη εἰκῆα Ἠελίου νεφέλη, ταὶ δ᾽ ἀμφί μιν ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα Ἀκτῖνες σεσηγὺς ἑλισσόμενοι διχόωνται Η τ᾽ ἂν ἔτ᾽ εἰς ἦῶ σκιαπᾶν κεχρημένος εἴης. Causas naturales vide apud Theonem.

## 12:55
Vers. 55. and when you see the south wind blowing, you say that there will be heat) Because Egypt and further Ethiopia lie toward the south of Judea: whence the winds brought from there bring heat. Thus, on the contrary, northern winds are said to bring cold, Job XXXVII. 9.

Latin:

Vers. 55. καὶ ὅταν νότον πνέοντα, λέγετε ὅτι καύσων ἔσται) Quia Judæa ad meridiem calidissimæ regiones objacent Ægyptus & porro Æthiopia: unde delati venti æstum ad- ferunt. Sic contra venti septentrionales frigus dicuntur ad- ferre Job. XXXVII. 9.

## 12:56
Vers. 56. of the earth) He brought forward nothing about the signs of the earth, but it can easily be supplied from John IV. 36. and Matt. XXIV. 32. this time) The advent of the Messiah, which had certain signs foretold by the prophets. See what [is said] on Matthew.

PART VI.

An admonition concerning the reconciliation of an adversary.

Latin:

Vers. 56. τῆς γῆς) Nihil attulit de terræ signis, sed facile suppleri potest ex Joh. IV. 36. & Matth. XXIV. 32. καιρὸν τῦτον) Adventum Messiæ qui certa habebat signa à vatibus pronunciata. Vide quæ ad Matth.

PARS VI.

De adversarii conciliatione commonefactio.

## 12:57
Vers. 57. and why even of yourselves do you not judge what is right) It is not necessary that arguments be sought from heaven or earth. Take an example from yourselves. For you are not so foolish as to wish to contend in judgment with one who has a certain case that cannot be quashed by any exception. But if you think such a creditor ought to be appeased in time, why do you cease to come to terms with God himself, while it is permitted, while he himself of his own accord offers fair conditions? Matthew indeed uses the same similitude, but, as we have often said, not in the same sense; for there it is a matter of the mutual offenses of men. Moreover, δίκαιον here is not properly what is called just, but what is fitting to be done, and what is agreeable to reason, as Phil. I. 17. and elsewhere. The Latins sometimes call this very thing 'equitable', and here the Syrian does so.

Latin:

Vers. 57. τί δὲ καὶ ἀφ᾽ ἑαυτῶν ἐ κρίνετε τὸ δίκαιον) Non o- ffis est à cœlo aut terra peti argumenta. A vobis ipsis exem- plum sumite. Neque enim tam stulti estis, ut in judicio con- tendere velitis cum eo qui certam habeat actionem nulla exceptione elidendam. Quod si talem creditorem in tem- pore placandum vobis censetis, quid cessatis cum ipso Deo transigere, dum licet, dum æquas conditiones ipse ultro of- fert? Usurpat quidem eandem similitudinem Matthæus, sed, ut fieri sæpe diximus, sensu non plane eodem; ibi enim de mutuis hominum offensis agitur. δίκαιον autem hic non proprie est quod justum dicitur, sed quod fieri convenit, quodque rationi est consentaneum, ut Phil. I. 17. & alibi. Id- ipsum æquum interdum Latini vocant, & hic Syrus.

## 12:58
Vers. 58. ἐπ᾽ ἄρχοντα) ἐπ᾽ signifies, as it is in Matthew and here below, unless you prefer to understand in the Roman manner a magistrate who has the right of granting a judge.

Δὸς ἐργασίαν) Theophylact correctly accepts this Latinism when he brings forward this prior interpretation: Do this in every way so that you may be freed. Which is the very one of Origen. For the latter interpretation of Theophylact is no less forced than what the Syrian placed here; [it is] an ignorance of the Latin language, from which many modes of speaking had then flowed into Greek. ἀπηλλάχθαι ἀp' αὐτοῦ) Thus Aristotle said ἀπαλλάττεσθαι τοῦ χρέος. I would think it is correctly translated here as, that you may extricate yourself from him. τῷ πράκτορι) The LXX translate the Hebrew נוגש as πράκτορας, as in Isaiah 3:12. We have said at Matthew that he is understood to be the one who is called in Latin a collector. Demosthenes: ὧν οὐδεὶς παραδέδωκε τοῖς πράκτορσι τὰ ὀνόματα.

Latin:

Vers. 58. ἐπ᾽ ἄρχοντα) ἐπ᾽ signat, ut apud Matthæum est & hic infra, nisi Romano more intelligere mavis magistra- tum qui dandi judicis jus habet.

Δὸς ἐργασίαν) Latinismum hunc recte accipit Theophy- lactus, cum priorem adfert interpretationem hanc: Omni modo hoc age ut libereris. Quæ ipsa est Origenis. Nam poste- rior Theophylacti interpretatio non minus coacta est, quam quod Syrus hic posuit; Latini sermonis ignorantia, e quo tum multa loquendi genera in Græcum profluxerant. ἀπηλλάχθαι ἀπ' αὐτοῦ) Sic ἀπαλλάττεσθαι τοῦ χρέος dixit Aristoteles. Putem recte hic verti, ut ab eo te expedias. τῷ πράκτορι) Hebræum נוגש πράκτορας vertunt LXX. ut Esaiæ III. 12. Diximus ad Matthæum eum intelligi qui La- tine viator dicitur. Demosthenes: ὧν οὐδεὶς παραδέδωκε τοῖς πράκτορσι τὰ ὀνόματα.

## 13:1 Argument
CHAPTER XIII. ARGUMENT AND DIVISION.

On the occasion of the Galileans killed and slain by the tower of Siloam, Christ exhorts to repentance, with a parable about a fruitless fig tree subjoined: he heals a woman who had a spirit of infirmity for 18 years, on the Sabbath day, and defends this: he proposes parables about the mustard seed and leaven, and directs his journey toward Jerusalem, and discourses about the fewness of those being saved, and the narrow gate, and about not being admitted when the door is shut, but of nations coming from everywhere to the kingdom of God, and the last being first: Which things are to be announced to Herod the fox: and concerning Jerusalem, because it would not be gathered, [it is] to be left desolate.

There are IV parts. I. Exhortation to repentance through examples and a parable, to v. 10. II. Healing of a long-standing infirmity on the Sabbath, with an apology, to v. 17. III. Comparisons of the kingdom of God, and an exhortation to the struggle for its entry, to v. 30. IV. Responses given to the Pharisees concerning Herod and the devastation of Jerusalem, to v. 35.

PART I. Exhortation to repentance.

V. 1. Ἀπαγγέλλοντες) As a new thing which had then happened by chance. περὶ τῶν Γαλιλαίων ὧν τὸ αἷμα Πιλάτος ἔμιξε μετὰ τῶν θυσιῶν αὐτῶν) Not in Galilee: for Pilate had no jurisdiction there: not in Tyrathaba, a village of the Samaritans, as some think: For there is no association of sacred rites for Galileans with Samaritans. Add that not even those Samaritans were killed during sacred rites: for they had not yet arrived at the mountain dedicated to sacred rites. Therefore these things were done at Jerusalem: to which the Galileans were coming for the sake of sacrificing, especially at Passover. But there is no doubt that the faction of Judas the Gaulonite, just as it had its origin in Galilee, so also had many defenders there, who, arriving at Jerusalem, imbued the people with opinions that were opposed to the Roman empire: among which was also this, that sacred rites should not be performed for the Romans, of which controversy Josephus makes mention. It is therefore entirely credible, as most of the Greek interpreters feel, that those whom Pilate suppressed while intent upon sacred rites (the Paschal lamb, for instance) in the very act of stirring up revolution belonged to this sect: just as later the sons of that Judas were suppressed by Alexander the procurator. It is no more surprising that this history was passed over by Josephus than the infanticide at Bethlehem. This may perhaps have been among those things for which the Jews accused Pilate before Caesar. Philo says that Pilate had a disposition that was ἀμείλικτον (implacable). Which the Corban affair and the introduction of the shields, which were mere provocations of the people, sufficiently prove. Under this governor, if it was not safe for anyone to defend that position, ὅτι ἂν ἔξεστι κῆνσον Καίσαρι ἐπικόψαι (that it is lawful to pay tribute to Caesar), no one will be surprised.

That they were of the faction of Judas the Gaulonite is incredible to Grotius, as also to the Greek interpreters, Cyril, Theophylact, Euthymius, and Titus, Bishop of Bostra, whose opinions were opposed to the Roman Empire: concerning not giving tribute to Caesar, and not performing sacrifices for the Romans. But those things are uncertain. Nor is that opinion approved by the blessed Lyser, or even by Dan. Heinsius: who can be compared here. We leave it in the middle. However, that they were killed by Pilate while intent upon the Paschal lamb does not fit the history. Because the time of the Passover had not yet arrived then.

Latin:

CAPUT XIII. ARGUMENTUM ET PAR- TITIO.

Occafione Galilæorum occisorum & per tur- rim Siloah interfectorum, hortatur Christus ad pœnitentiam, parabola de ficu infrugife- ra subjuncta: curat fœminam quæ spiritum ægritudinis 18. annis habuerat, Sabbati die, idque defendit: Parabolas de grano sina- pi, & fermento proponit, & iter versus Hierosolymam dirigit, ac de paucitate sal- vandorum, & angusta porta disserit, deque non intromittendis janua occlusa, venturis vero undecunque gentibus ad regnum Dei, & ultimis primis futuris: Quæ Herodi vul- pi nuntianda: & de Hierosolyma, quia con- gregari noluit, diserta relinquenda.

Partes sunt IV. I. Adhortatio ad pœnitentiam per exempla & parabolam, ad v. 10. II. Sanatio diuturnæ ægritudinis in Sabbato, cum apologia, ad v. 17. III. Comparationes regni Dei, & horta- tio ad agonem pro ejus ingressu, ad v. 30. IV. Pha- risæis de Herode, & Hierosolymæ vastatione red- dita responsa, ad v. 35.

PARS I. Adhortatio ad pœnitentiam.

V. 1. Ἀπαγγέλλοντες) Ut rem novam quæ tum forte ac- ciderat. περὶ τῶν Γαλιλαίων ὧν τὸ αἷμα Πιλάτος ἔμιξε μετὰ τῶν θυσιῶν αὐτῶν) Non in Galilæa: nullum enim ibi jus Pilato: non in Tyrathaba Samaritarum vico, ut quidam existimant: Nulla enim societas sacrorum Galilæis cum Samaritanis. Adde, quod ne isti quidem Samaritæ inter sacra occisi: non- dum enim ad montem sacris dicatum pervenerant. Ergo Hierosolymis hæc acta: quo Galilæi sacrificandi causa ve- niebant, Paschate præsertim. Dubium autem non est quin Judæ Gaulonitæ factio sicut ortum in Galilæa habuerat, ita & multos ibi habuerit defensores, qui Hierosolyma ad- ventantes populum imbuebant opinionibus quæ imperio Romano adversabantur: inter quas & hæc erat, non esse sa- cra facienda pro Romanis, cujus controversiæ Josephus meminit. Omnino ergo credibile est, ut Græcorum Inter- pretum plerique sentiunt, hujus sectæ fuisse quos Pilatus sacris intentos (agno puta Paschali) in ipsa rerum novarum molitione oppresserit: sicut postea ab Alexandro procura- tore oppressi sunt Judæ illius filii. Historiam hanc à Jose- pho præteritam non magis mirum est quam infanticidium Bethlehemiticum. Fuerit hoc forte inter illa quorum Ju- dæi Pilatum apud Cæsarem accusarunt. Ingenium Pilato fuisse ἀμείλικτον dicit Philo. Quod satis evincunt & Cor- banæ invalio, & invectio clypeorum, quæ mera erant po- puli irritamenta. Sub hoc præside si nemini impune fuit θέσει illam defendere, ὅτι ἂν ἔξεστι κῆνσον Καίσαρι ἐπικόψαι, ne- mo mirabitur.

Eos fuisse de factione Judæ Gaulonitæ, incredibile est Grotio, ut & Græcis interpp. Cyrillo, Theophy- lacto, Euthymio, & Tito Bostrorum Episcopo, quo- rum opiniones Imperio Romano adversæ fuerint: de censu Cæsari non dando, & non faciendis sacrifi- ciis pro Romanis. Sed ista incerta sunt. Neq; proba- tur illa sententia B. Lysero, aut etiam Dan. Heinsio: qui hic conferri possunt. Nos eam in medio relin- quimus. Paschali tamen agno intentos occisos esse à Pilato historiæ non congruit. Quia tempus Pa- schatos tum nondum advenerat.

## 13:2
V. 2. more than all the Galileans) Great calamities are indeed usually the punishments of sins, although Christ taught us by the example of the blind man that even this is not perpetual: but the common people for the most part take upon themselves the audacity of judging further, so that they think those to be more wicked than others with whom things go worse, which cruel rashness Job and the writer of the Psalms chastise in many places. Deservedly so: for God often exercises men who are good beyond the common lot with heavy inconveniences. Nor is this only under the new covenant (of which this is as it were a proper dispensation) but also of old, as is most manifest from the example of Job, whom I had begun to speak of, and then also of James, Moses, David, not to mention Isaiah and those who under Antiochus met death for the defense of the truth. Often also the merciful God selects a few from a great crowd of evils, whom He wishes to be a spectacle to the rest, showing in them what all have deserved, as is wont to be done in the decimation of legions. Cyprian: Some are punished meanwhile, so that the rest may be corrected. The torments of a few are examples for all. Salvianus: The pious God, of course, struck a part with the sword of His judgment, so that He might correct a part by example, and prove to all at once both His measure in restraining and His piety in indulging. Where he also illustrates this judgment with some examples of ancient history. And of this kind are those divine judgments which are treated in this place.

ὅτι τοιαῦτα πεπόνθασιν) For there was no doubt among the hearers that both the minds of the powers and natural causes were so governed by divine counsel that nothing could happen which God had not decreed either to do or wisely to permit.

Latin:

V. 2. παρὰ πάντας τοὺς Γαλιλαίους) Soleat quidem magnæ ca- lamitates pœnæ esse peccatorum, quanquam nec id qui- dem esse perpetuum Christus cæci exemplo nos docuit: sed vulgus plerumq; ulterius judicandi sibi sumit audaciam, ut illos cæteris flagitiosiores putet quibuscum pejus agitur, quam crudelem temeritatem multis castigat Jobus & Psal- morum Scriptor. Merito quidem: nam sæpe viros extra communem aleam bonos Deus gravibus incommodis ex- ercet. Neque id tantum sub novo fœdere (cujus hæc velut propria dispensatio est) sed olim quoque, ut illius quem di- cere cœperam Jobi, tum vero & Jacobi, Mosis, Davidis ex- emplo manifestissimum est, ut jam taceam Esaiam atque eos qui sub Antiocho mortem pro veri tuitione oppetiverunt. Sæpe etiam misericors Deus ex magna malorum turba pau- cos seligit, quos cæteris esse velit ostentui, in illis monstrans quid omnes meruerint, ut in legionum decumatione fieri solet. Cyprianus: Plectuntur interim quidam, quo cæteri corri- gantur. Exempla sunt omnium tormenta paucorum. Salvianus: Pius scilicet Deus partem percussit sententia suæ gladio, ut par- tem corrigeret exemplo, probaretq; omnibus simul & coërcendo mensuram & indulgendo pietatem. Ubi & sententiam hanc aliquot veteris historiæ exemplis illustrat. Atque hujus sunt generis divina illa judicia de quibus hoc loco agitur.

ὅτι τοιαῦτα πεπόνθασιν) Neque enim dubium erat apud auditores, & animos potestatum & causas naturales divino consilio ita gubernari, ut nihil evenire possit quod non Deus aut facere, aut sapienter permittere decrevisset.

## 13:3
V. 3. unless you repent, you shall all likewise perish) The whole coherence of the discourse, and what follows concerning the fig tree, certainly persuade me that a common, and indeed visible, punishment impending over the Jewish people is being treated here: although that itself bore the image and omen of eternal punishment. Likewise, he says, you shall perish. See how everything has agreed. For on the day of the Passover a great part were killed in the very temple after the manner of cattle, for the same cause of sedition, which men who were clearly impious veiled under a false pretense of piety.

Latin:

V. 3. ἐὰν μὴ μετανοῆτε πάντες, ὡσαύτως ἀπολεῖσθε) Tota sermonis cohærentia, & quod de ficu sequitur, certo mihi persuadent de communi, & quidem aspectabili pœna Ju- dæorum populo imminente hic agi: quanquam illa ipsa pœnæ æternæ imaginem & omen gessit. Similiter, inquit, peribitis. Vide quam omnia congruerint. Paschatis enim die occisi sunt magna pars in ipso templo pecudum ritu, ob eandem causam seditionis, quam falso pietatis obtentu homines plane impii velabant.

## 13:4
Vers. 4. the tower in Siloam) So it is written twice in John ch. IX. But I also find in Josephus ὑπὲρ τὴν Σιλωὰμ ἐπιστρέφον πηγὴν. Nor otherwise the LXX in Isaiah LX. 8. It appears that it was the custom of that age to sometimes add letters to the ends of words. When it is called by the masculine noun ὁ Σιλωὰμ, it seems that χείμαῤῥος is to be understood. Jerome certainly denies that it was a perennial stream. The Jews reveal that its flow was gentle, and it is proven by the cited place of Isaiah. Josephus calls it γλυκεῖαν κὴ πολλὴν πηγὴν, who also teaches us that the fortifications of the city ran as far as that, among which fortifications was that tower, of which there is speech here.

Ὀφειλέται) A Syriasm. See above XI. 4.

Latin:

Vers. 4. ὁ πύργος ἐν τῷ Σιλωὰμ) Ita & apud Johannem bis scribitur cap. IX. Sed & apud Josephum invenio ὑπὲρ τὴν Σιλωὰμ ἐπιστρέφον πηγὴν. Nec aliter LXX. Esaïæ LX. 8. Apparet ejus seculi morem fuisse, ut literas interdum fini dictionum adjicerent. Cum masculino nomine ὁ Σιλωὰμ dicitur, videtur χείμαῤῥος subaudiri. Jugem certe aquam fuisse negat Hieronymus. Lenem ejus fuisse fluxum pro- dunt Judæi, & dicto Esaïæ loco probatur. γλυκεῖαν κὴ πολλὴν πηγὴν vocat Josephus, qui & munimenta urbis eousque percurrisse nos docet, inter quæ munimenta fuit turris il- la, de qua hic sermo est.

Ὀφειλέται) Syrismus. Vide supra XI. 4.

## 13:5
Vers. 5. unless you repent you shall all likewise perish) You shall perish in a similar way, that is, among the ruins of the whole city, of which that tower bears the image.

Latin:

Vers. 5. ἐὰν μὴ μετανοῆτε πάντες ὁμοίως ἀπολεῖσθε) Peri- bitis simili modo, id est, inter ruinas urbis totius, cujus tur- ris ista imaginem gerit.

## 13:6
Vers. 6. A fig tree) The same meaning as the vineyard in Matt. XXI. 33. Nor did Christ wish anything else to be indicated when He cursed the barren fig tree in Matt. XXI. 19. The vineyard here is the whole human race, in which the fig tree is the Jewish people, offering an excellent hope for itself with its joyful foliage. It is a comparison not unlike that taken from the fig tree in Arrian's Epictetus I. 15. Συκᾶς μὲν καρπὸς ἄφνω καὶ μιᾷ ὥρᾳ ὐ τελειῦται. Γνώμης δ᾽ ἀνθρώπκ καρπὸν θέλεις ἔτω δι᾽ ὀλίγε καὶ εὐκόλως κτήσασθ.

Latin:

Vers. 6. Συκῆν) Eadem significatio quæ vineæ Matth. XXI. 33. Nec aliud indicatum Christus voluit cum ficu ste- rilem devoveret Matth. XXI. 19. Vinetum hic est genus humanum omne, in quo ficus populus Judaicus, læta fron- de spem de se egregiam præbens. Est comparatio non dissi- milis à ficu sumta in Epicteto Arriani I. 15. Συκᾶς μὲν καρπὸς ἄφνω καὶ μιᾷ ὥρᾳ ὐ τελειῦται. Γνώμης δ᾽ ἀνθρώπκ καρπὸν θέλεις ἔτω δι᾽ ὀλίγε καὶ εὐκόλως κτήσασθ.

## 13:7
Vers. 7. three years) Those who refer these to the three years during which Christ taught seem to pay little attention to what follows concerning waiting for a year. For God did not defer the punishments of the Jews after Christ's three years, being prayed to by the pious, for one year, but for forty years. Wherefore it is better that the three years be understood as said because fig trees that are fruitful do not delay their fruit for long. To which three years corresponds all the time before the Baptist and Christ, during which God most patiently awaited the amendment of the Jews. See Isaiah V.

καταργεῖ) The Syrian has placed the very word which Luke wished to express here with the Greek מבטל. For בטל to the Syrian and the Masters of the Hebrews is to hinder. The fig tree draws much sap from the earth, which could have been useful to the vines, and indeed the fig tree itself by its shade harms men. The Jews, having been affected by excellent benefits from God, were so far from being useful to other nations by their shadowy piety that, on the contrary, their life rendered other men more alienated from the true religion. Τὸ γὰρ ὄνομα τῦ Θεῦ δι᾽ ὑμᾶς βλασφη- μεῖται ἐν τοῖς ἔθνεσιν, says Paul in Rom. II. 24.

Latin:

Vers. 7. τρία ἔτη) Qui hæc ad tres annos quibus Christus docuerit, referunt, parum attendere videntur quod sequitur de anno exspectando Neque enim Deus post Christi trien- nium pœnas Judæorum à piis oratus in unum, sed in qua- draginta annos distulit. Quare tres annos satius est dictos intelligi, quod ficus quæ frugiferæ sunt fructum longi9 non differant. Quibus tribus annis respondet omne tempus ante Baptistam & Christum, quo Deus patientissime exspe- ctavit Judæorum emendationem. Vide Esaïæ V.

καταργεῖ) Syrus ipsum verbum posuit quod hic Græco exprimere Lucas voluit מבטל. Nam בטל Syrus & Ma- gistris Hebræorum est impedire. Ficus multum succi è ter- ra haurit, quod vitibus prodesse poterat, quin & ipsa ficus umbra hominibus nocet. Judæi eximiis à Deo beneficiis af- fecti,p/etate umbratica adeo cæteris gentibus utiles non e- rant, ut contra eorum vita homines cæteros à vera religio- ne alieniores redderet. Τὸ γὰρ ὄνομα τῦ Θεῦ δι᾽ ὑμᾶς βλασφη- μεῖται ἐν τοῖς ἔθνεσιν, inquit Paulus Rom. II. 24.

## 13:8
V. 8. I will dig about it) Trenching is applied for this reason, so that the topmost roots may receive both sun and rain. To this can seem to correspond those gifts which the Apostles and their helpers exercised in converting the Jews.

Βάλω κοπρίαν) Trees are manured so that they may be warmed, especially fig trees, as they are colder than others. To this work correspond not badly those great inconveniences of famine, seditions, and others, by which God, in the times of Gaius, Claudius, and Nero, attempted to shake off the lethargy from the Jews. See what is at Matt. XXIV.

Latin:

V. 8. σκάψω περὶ ἀυτήν) Ablaqueatio ideo admovetur, ut summæ radices & solem & imbrem accipiant. Huic vide- ri possunt respondere χαρίσματα illa quæ Apostoli & eo- rum adjutores Judæis convertendis exercuerunt.

Βάλω κοπρίαν) Stercorantur arbores ut calefaciant, ficus præsertim, ut quæ cæteris sint frigidiores. Huic operæ non male respondent magna illa incommoda famis, seditionum atque alia, quibus Deus Caji, Claudii, Neronisque tempo- ribus, veternum Judæis excutere conatus est. Vide quæ ad Matth. XXIV.

## 13:9
Vers. 9. κἂν μὲν ποιήσῃ καρπὸν) Supply from the previous clause ἄφες, leave it, or it is well.

εἰς τὸ μέλλον) I approve this reading which the ancient codices maintain. Paul also uses this manner of speaking in 1 Tim. VI. 9. The Syriac here reads εἰς τὸ μέλλον ζῆν; ἐκκόψεις αὐτὴν

PART II. The healing of a long-standing illness.

Latin:

Vers. 9. κἂν μὲν ποιήσῃ καρπὸν) Subaudi ex superiori com- mate ἄφες relinque, aut bene est.

εἰς τὸ μέλλον) Probo hanc lectionem quam veteres codi- ces tuentur. Etiam Paulus hoc loquendi genere utitur 1.Tim. VI. 9. Syrus hic legit εἰς τὸ μέλλον ζῆν; ἐκκόψεις αὐτὴν

PARS II. Sanatio diuturnæ ægritudinis.

## 13:11
V. 11. πνεῦμα ἔχουσα ἀσθενείας) The word πνεῦμα could indeed be taken after the manner of the Hebrews for the disease itself, according to those things which we have said elsewhere: but since it is openly stated below that this evil was sent by Satan, it is better to understand it in the way Mark IX. 17 spoke of a πνεῦμα ἄλαλον, a demon that hindered the faculty of speech. It was an old opinion of the Jews that many diseases are sent upon men by demons outside of natural causes, as can be seen even from Josephus, and the Hebrew Masters on Ps. XCI. 6. The history of Job and Saul and many narratives in the Gospel confirm this very thing.

συγκύπτουσα) She was stooped. Therefore not ὀπισθότονος, as a learned man wishes, but ἐμπροσθοτονική: not bent back onto the shoulder blades but onto the chest, as Pliny expresses those things. Nazianzenus does not poorly explain συγκύπτειν as κάτω νεύειν. In this sense, συγκύψας προσώπῳ is in the Greek of Job IX. 27. But the LXX use ὀπισθότονοι in Deut. XXXII. 25, where, however, in the Hebrew there is קטב, which most interpret as pestilence; ὀπισθοτονικοὶ are in Latin, if I am not mistaken, obstipi (bent forward).

Ἀνακύψαι) To lift up the head. Thus Aristotle said ἀνακύπτειν πρὸς τὸν ἥλιον. Luke himself below in XXI. 28 explains ἀνακύψαι as ἐπᾶραι τὰς κεφαλὰς. But John also uses it in this sense. The ancients well observe in this woman a certain image of men who, while they ought to raise their faces toward heaven by the argument of their own countenance, carry souls bent down to the earth.

εἰς τὸ παντελὲς) The same manner of speaking in Hebrews VII. 25.

Latin:

V. 11. πνεῦμα ἔχουσα ἀσθενείας) Posset quidem πνεῦμα He- bræorum more pro ipso morbo accipi secundum ea quæ ali- bi diximus: sed cum infra aperte dicatur a Satana immissum hoc malum, præstat ita intelligi quomodo πνεῦμα ἄλαλον dixit Marcus IX. 17. dæmonium quodloque ndi facultatem impediret. Extra causas naturales morbos multos homini- bus immitti per dæmonia vetus fuit Judæorum opinio, ut ex Josepho etiam videre est, & Hebræorum Magistris ad Pf. XCI. 6. Confirmat id ipsum Jobi & Saulis historia & in Evangelio multæ narrationes.

συγκύπτουσα) Erat cernua. Non ergo ὀπισθότονος, ut vult vir eruditus, sed ἐμπροσθοτονική: non in scapulas rugens sed in pectus, ut Plinius ista exprimit. Nazianzenus συγκύπτειν non male exponit κάτω νεύειν. Hoc sensu συγκύψας προσώπῳ est in Græco Jobi IX. 27. At ὀπισθότονοι LXX. usurpant Deut. XXXII. 25. ubi tamen in Hebræo est קטב quod pe- stem plerique interpretantur, ὀπισθοτονικοὶ sunt Latine, ni fallor, obstipi.

Ἀνακύψαι) Caput attollere. Ita ἀνακύπτειν πρὸς τὸν ἥλιον dixit Aristoteles. Ipse Lucas infra XXI. 28. ἀνακύψαι expo- nit ἐπᾶραι τὰς κεφαλὰς. Sed & Johannes hoc sensu usurpat. Bene veteres in hac femina imaginem quandam observant hominum qui cum vultus sui argumento in cœlum erigere deberent, curvas in terram animas gerunt.

εἰς τὸ παντελὲς) Idem loquendi genus adHebræos VII. 25.

## 13:12
προσεφώνησε) Bestowing a benefit voluntarily and unasked: which itself pertains to that which I called the ὑπόνοιαν (suspicion/surmise).

Vers. 12. ἀπολέλυσαι) The past tense for the present, as in Matt. IX. 2, Mark II. 9. For Christ is to be understood as having said these things and at the same time having laid on his hands.

Latin:

προσεφώνησε) Ultro nec rogatus beneficium ingerens: quod ipsum pertinet ad eam quam dixi ὑπόνοιαν.

Vers. 12. ἀπολέλυσαι) Præteritum pro præsenti, ut Matt. IX. 2. Marc. II. 9. Simul enim Christus hæc dixisse, simulque manus imposuisse intelligendus est.

## 13:14
V. 14. ὁ ἀρχισυνάγωγος) The one presiding over the synagogue. Sometimes that word is taken more loosely, so that it also includes the elders, just as we said regarding Matthew. Thus, when there was one στρατηγὸς τῶ ἱερῶ, sometimes that name is communicated to his assistants.

Ἀγανακτῶν ὅτι τῷ σαββάτῳ ἐθεράπευσεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς) Namely, because he placed the height of holiness in rituals: whence he is deservedly called a hypocrite. For those act that fable very well who do not have even a crumb of true love in their minds.

τῷ ὄχλῳ) Accusing Jesus through their side, whom he did not dare to attack openly. This also is done hypocritically and craftily.

ἐργάζεσθαι) And yet it was permitted to take food on the Sabbath: why therefore not also to lay on a hand. The little word תעבד is therefore poorly seized upon, and it could rightly be defended that not even the words of the law pertain to this species of deed: but Christ, omitting subtleties, uncovers the iniquity of the calumny by a most evident comparison.

Latin:

V. 14. ὁ ἀρχισυνάγωγος) ὁ προεστὼς τῆς συναγωγῆς. Inter- dum laxius ea vox sumitur, ut presbyteros quoque com- prehendat, quemadmodum diximus ad Matthæum. Sic cum unus esset στρατηγὸς τῶ ἱερῶ interdum ejus adjutoribus id nomin communicatur.

Ἀγανακτῶν ὅτι τῷ σαββάτῳ ἐθεράπευσεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς) Nimi- rum quia summam sanctimoniæ in ritibus collocabat: un- de merito audit ὑποκριτὴς. Nam illam fabulam optime a- gunt quibus in animo ne mica quidem est veræ dilectionis.

τῷ ὄχλῳ) Per illorum latus Jesum accusans quem palam aggredi non audebat. Etiam hoc ὑποκριτικῶς & vetera- torie.

ἐργάζεσθαι) Atqui cibum sumere sabbato licebat: cur non ergo & manum imponere. Male ergo captatur vocula תעבד recteque defendi poterat ne verba quidem legis ad hanc facti speciem pertinere: sed Christus omissis subtili- tatibus evidentissima comparatione calumniæ iniquitatem detegit.

## 13:15
V. 15. ὑποκριταὶ) The Syrian reads it in the singular: nor is it rare that things are said to one which pertain to him and others.

ἕκαστος ὑμῶν) Of your flock, both of the lawyers and of the Pharisees: for there were smaller sects that felt otherwise, as we have said elsewhere.

Latin:

V. 15. ὑποκριταὶ) Singulariter legit Syrus: neque rarum est, ut uni dicantur quæ ad ipsum aliosque pertineant.

ἕκαστος ὑμῶν) Vestri gregis tum legisperitorum, tum Pharisæorum: nam erant sectæ minores quæ aliter senti- rent, ut alibi diximus.

## 13:16
V. 16. θυγατέρα Ἀβραὰμ) Not content to oppose a human to a beast, which would have been enough, he adds daughter of Abraham, which name was of the greatest value among them. See Matt. III. 9. Luke III. 8. John VIII. 33. Acts XIII. 26. This interpretation is simpler and more correct than that of those who wish the faith of the woman to be considered.

δέκα καὶ ὀκτὼ ἔτη) Not for a few hours, as oxen and asses are bound.

PARS III. Concerning the kingdom of God and the struggle for the same.

Latin:

V. 16. θυγατέρα Ἀβραὰμ) Non contentus hominem pecudi opponere, quod satis fuerat, adjicit filiam Abraha- mi, quod nomen apud illos in maximo fuit pretio. Vide Matth. III. 9. Luc. III. 8. Joh. VIII 33. Act. XIII. 26. Hæc interpretatio simplicior & rectior quam eorum qui fidem fœminæ spectatam volunt.

δέκα καὶ ὀκτὼ ἔτη) Non ad horas aliquot, ut boves & asi- ni ligantur.

PARS III. De regno Dei & agone pro eodem.

## 13:17
V. 17. ἐπὶ πᾶσι τοῖς ἐνδόξοις) He thus calls those things which elsewhere are μεγαλῆια.

Latin:

V. 17. ἐπὶ πᾶσι τοῖς ἐνδόξοις) Ita vocat quæ alibi μεγαλῆια.

## 13:23
V. 23. εἰ ὀλίγοι οἱ σωζόμενοι;) Christ is accustomed to reject curious questions without an answer, as here and Acts I. 7. It concerns us to know what kind are saved, not how many are to be saved, although from the one it is permitted to conjecture the other to some extent. For it pleases few to enter the arduous and equally difficult way.

Latin:

V. 23. εἰ ὀλίγοι οἱ σωζόμενοι;) Solet Christus curiosas quæ- stiones sine responso rejicere, ut hic & Act. I. 7. Nostra refert scire quales serventur, non quot servandi, quanquam ex al- tero alterum conjectare aliquatenus licet. Nam paucis libet viam ingredi arduam æque difficilem.

## 13:24
ἀγωνίζεσθε) Christ openly shows that the number of those to be saved is not defined by a decree excluding every act of the human will, since he invites all to take up the way: but at the same time he shows that the matter is one of great spirit and constancy: for this word indicates that, as also in Colossians ch. I, v. 29.

Vers. 24. ζητήσουσιν εἰσελθεῖν) Supply: to that place to which one cannot go except through the gate, namely, into the heavenly kingdom. There is no one who is not held by the desire for immortality: but it is not present in all, that they are willing on that account to lack the comforts of this age.

Latin:

ἀγωνίζεσθε) Aperte ostendit Christus numerum servan- dorum non esse definitum decreto excludente omnem actum humanæ voluntatis, quando omnes ad capessendam viam invitat: sed simul ostendit rem esse magni animi & constantiæ: id enim verbum hoc indicat, ut & Coloss. c. I, v. 29.

Vers. 24. ζητήσουσιν εἰσελθεῖν) Supple eo quo iri nisi per portam non potest, in regnum scilicet cœleste. Nemo est qui non immortalitatis cupiditate teneatur: sed non o- mnibus extanti est, ut propterea carere velint hujus ævi commodis.

## 13:25
Vers. 25. ἐγερθῇ) Thus the Syriac and the Arab appear to have read the Latin εἰσέλθῃ. But the former is to be preferred: for ἐγείρεσθαι signifies the manner of one proceeding from his seat or bed to shut the door.

ἄρξησθε ἔξω ἑστάναι) A manifest pleonasm which is frequent in Luke, above III. 8, ch. IV. 21, ch. V. 21, ch. VII. 15, 38. Thus also below XIV. 9 and Acts I. 1.

οὐκ οἶδα ὑμᾶς πόθεν ἐστέ) That is, I hold you as strangers.

Latin:

Vers. 25. ἐγερθῇ) Ita Syrus & Arabs Latinum apparet legisse εἰσέλθῃ. Sed illud præferendum: nam ἐγείρεσθαι modum significat de sede sua aut lectulo procedentis ad claudendum ostium.

ἄρξησθε ἔξω ἑστάναι) Manifestus πλεονασμὸς qui Lucæ frequens, supra III. 8. c. IV. 21. c. V. 21. c. VII. 15. 38. Sic & infra XIV. 9. & Act. I. 1.

οὐκ οἶδα ὑμᾶς πόθεν ἐστέ) Id est pro ignotis vos ha- beo

## 13:26
Vers. 26. ἐφάγομεν ἐνώπιόν σου καὶ ἐπίομεν) That is, we lived with you very familiarly: for those are said to eat in the presence of someone who take food together with him, as below XXIV. 43. Which, just as it did not help the Jews who lived with Christ, so it will not profit Christians who do not live like Christians at all to have been participants of the Lord's table: nay, this very thing will aggravate their damnation, as Paul teaches in 1 Cor. ch. XI. 29.

ἐν πλατείαις ἡμῶν ἐδίδαξας) There are many who think themselves righteous by the hearing of the word, when the matter stands far otherwise, Rom. II. v. 13, Jas. I. 22, 23.

Latin:

Vers. 26. ἐφάγομεν ἐνώπιόν σου καὶ ἐπίομεν) Id est admo- dum familiariter tecum viximus: nam φαγεῖν ἐνώπιον τινὸς dicuntur qui una cum eo cibum sumunt, ut infra XXIV. 43. quod sicut Judæos qui cum Christo vixerunt non suble- vavit, ita nec Christianis non Christiane viventibus quic- quam proderit mensæ dominicæ fuisse participes: imo ag- gravabit hoc ipsum eorum damnationem, ut Paulus docet ad 1. Cor. c. XI. 29.

ἐν πλατείαις ἡμῶν ἐδίδαξας) Multi sunt qui auditu verbi se justos existimant, cum longe aliter se res habeat, Rom. II. v. 13. Jac. I. 22. 23.

## 13:27
Vers. 27. ἐργάται) Because the Hebrews use participles for verbal nouns, therefore Luke rightly interprets what is in the Psalm and in Matthew as ἐργαζόμενοι as ἐργάται: for it is not any act, but the pursuit of life that is indicated.

Latin:

Vers. 27. ἐργάται) Quia Hebræi participia pro verbali- bus usurpant, ideo Lucas quod in Psalmo & apud Mat- thæum est ἐργαζόμενοι recte interpretatur ἐργάται: nam non actus quivis sed vitæ studium indicatur.

## 13:28
Vers. 28. Ἀβραὰμ καὶ Ἰσαὰκ καὶ Ἰακὼβ καὶ πάντας τοὺς προφήτας) By whose authority of blood or kinsmen you glory,

Latin:

Vers. 28. Ἀβραὰμ καὶ Ἰσαὰκ καὶ Ἰακὼβ καὶ πάντας τοὺς προ- φήτας) Quibus sanguinis auctoribus aut consanguineis gloriamini,

## 13:30
Vers. 30. εἰσὶν ἔσχατοι) Who now seem most alien from the benefits of God, the Gentiles, whom you despise so greatly.

PARS IV. The answer returned to the Pharisees concerning Herod, and the prediction concerning the devastation of Jerusalem.

Latin:

Vers. 30. εἰσὶν ἔσχατοι) Qui nunc alienissimi à Dei be- neficiis videntur οἱ ἀλλόφυλοι, quos vos tantopere contemni- tis.

PARS IV. Responsum Pharisæis de Herode redditum, & prædictio de Hierosolyma vastatione.

## 13:31
V. 31. προσελθόν τινες Φαρισαῖοι) Who lived in Galilee or Perea. For that is what they mean by saying ἐντεῦθεν. For Herod had no jurisdiction outside those regions. But that there were very many Pharisees not only in Judea, but also in Galilee and elsewhere, this author of ours teaches us, above V. 17.

ὅτι Ἡρώδης θέλει σε ἀποκτεῖναι) From Christ's response it is given, if I am not mistaken, to be understood that these Pharisees did not come of their own accord, nor by their own counsel, but by the instigation of Herod: therefore Christ orders the response to be announced to Herod. It seems, however, that Herod did this out of his own craftiness, so that he might restrain from his borders the one whom he feared to kill, lest he offend the people again, while at the same time striking fear into him. For he wanted him to be as far away as possible, since he was bearing witness everywhere to the innocence of John; and that with great authority, because of the miraculous power that was present with him.

Latin:

V. 31. προσελθόν τινες Φαρισαῖοι) Qui in Galilæa aut Peræa vi- vebant. Nam eo pertinet quod dicunt ἐντεῦθεν. Neque enim extra eas regiones jus ullum erat Herodi. Pharisæos autem non in Judæa tantum, sed & in Galilæa, atque alibi plurimos fuisse docet nos hic noster, supra V. 17.

ὅτι Ἡρώδης θέλει σε ἀποκτεῖναι) Ex responso Christi datur, ni fallor, intelligi, non sponte venisse hos Pharisæos, neque proprio consilio, sed instinctu Herodis: ideo Herodi respon- sum nuntiari jubet Christus. Videtur autem pro vafritie sua hoc fecisse Herodes, ut quem interimere metuebat, ne populum denuo offenderet, eundem tamen injecto metu arceret finibus suis. Volebat enim eum quam longissime abesse qui passim testimonium perhibebat innocentiæ Jo- hannis; idque magna cum auctoritate, ob vim mirificam quæ ipsi aderat.

## 13:32
Vers. 32.
