Tῇ ἀλώπεκι) It is customary for kings to be described by the Prophets with the names of beasts, such as a goat, a ram, a leopard, a bear: and not without reason, because if we look at histories, by far the greatest part strips off humanity and migrates into beastly manners. Thus also Paul describes Nero under the name of a lion. No name was more fitting for Herod than that of a fox: for he was πα- νουργότατος, and mindful of that which Lysander used to say, ὅπου ἡ λεοντῆ μὴ ἐφικνεῖται χρὴ τὴν ἀλωπεκῆν προσράπτειν: composed after the example of the Roman Emperor at that time, who, in order to reign, cherished none of his virtues more than dissimulation. And so you might see him commending himself to the people with great art, as if he were very studious of the Jewish Religion, and fawning servilely upon the Roman Emperor, as if he were most devoted to him, while in the meantime he was pursuing his own affairs in every way. Thus, while secretly fostering the Herodians, a faction of the Sadducees, he meanwhile also made use of the work of the Pharisees. Nor indeed, when Christ designated the Tetrarch with this epithet, is He to be thought to have done anything against the paternal law which exists in Exod. XXII. 28. For since it was the office of the Prophets to rebuke kings themselves with great freedom, as those who were greater than kings in the discharge of their office, Jer. I. 10, it follows from this that that law of Exodus did not apply to them: for an exception for a divine command is inherent in all of God’s positive laws. And the same is most manifest from the examples of Isaiah, Jeremiah, and others. Moreover, in this very passage Christ openly claims for Himself the office of a Prophet. There is in Gregoras an oracle in which a certain Greek Emperor is designated by this very name of fox.

ἰδοὺ ἐκβάλλω δαιμόνια καὶ ἰάσεις ἐπιτελῶ) I do nothing that ought to be called a crime: I harm no one: I cleanse his region of diseases and demons: what then is it that threatens me with death? Christ addresses the Jews similarly in John ch. X. 32.

σήμερον καὶ αὔριον καὶ τῇ τρίτῃ τελειοῦμαι) He signifies an indefinite time, but one known to himself. Thus in Hosea VI, 2. ὑγιάσει ἡμᾶς μετὰ δύο ἡμέρας, ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ τῇ τρίτῃ ἀναστησόμεθα. Those who think that these things were said by Christ entirely at the end are moved by a fragile argument. For they posit that the order of times is observed more strictly by Luke than by the others, which we have shown by many examples not to be the case. Nor is that the force of the word ἑξῆς in the preface of the book: Τελειοῦμαι, however, is an ὑπαλλαγή. For he is said to be consummated whose course is consummated: Τελειοῦται ὁ δρόμος, as our author speaks here in Acts XX. 24. Nor does it seem that Philippians ch. III. 12 should be taken otherwise, where Paul, having taken a simile from runners, adds οὐχ' ὅτι ἤδη ἔλαβον ἢ ἤδη τετελείωμαι.

Latin:

Vers. 32. Tῇ ἀλώπεκι) Solent à Prophetis reges describi bestiarum nominibus, ut hirce, arietis, pardi, urfi: neque im- merito, quia si historias spectemus, pars longe maxima hu- manitatem exuit, & in belluinos mores migrat. Ita & Ne- ronem sub leonis nomine describit Paulus. Herodi nul- lum nomen magis conveniebat quam vulpis: erat enim πα- νουργότατος, & memor ejus quod Lysander dicere solebat, ὅπου ἡ λεοντῆ μὴ ἐφικνεῖται χρὴ τὴν ἀλωπεκῆν προσράπτειν: compositus ad Romani tunc Imperatoris exemplum, qui nullam, ut regnatur, ex virtutibus suis magis quam dissimula- tionem diligebat. Itaque videas eum magna arte & po- pulo se commedasse, quasi Judaicæ Religionis perquam studiosum, & Romano Imperatori adulatum serviliter, quasi ei devotissimum, cum interim omni modo ipsæ res suas ageret. Sic Herodianos partem Sadducæorum clam fovens, interim & Pharisæorum opera utebatur. Neque vero cum hoc cognomento Tetrarcham indigetavit Chri- stus, quicquam censendus est fecisse contra legem pater- nam, quæ exstat Exod XXII. 28. Nam cum Prophetarum munus esset reges ipsos magna cum libertate reprehendere, ut qui majores regibus essent in muneris sui obitu, Jer. I. 10. sequitur hinc illam Exodi legem ad ipsos non spectasse: nam mandati divini exceptio omnibus Dei positivis legib inest. Idemque exemplis Esaïæ, Jeremiæ, atque aliorum manifestissimum est. Prophetæ autem munus hoc ipso loco Christus aperte sibi vendicat. Est apud Gregoram oraculum in quo Imperator quidam Græcus hoc ipso vulpis nomine designatur.

ἰδοὺ ἐκβάλλω δαιμόνια καὶ ἰάσεις ἐπιτελῶ) Nihil ago quod in crimen vocari debeat: noceo nemini: regionem ipsius morbis & dæmoniis purgo: quid ergo est quod mortem mihi minitatur? similiter Judæos alloquitur Christus apud Joh. c. X. 32.

σήμερον καὶ αὔριον καὶ τῇ τρίτῃ τελειοῦμαι) Tempus significat indefinitum, sed sibi cognitum. Sic Oseæ VI, 2. ὑγιάσει ἡμᾶς μετὰ δύο ἡμέρας, ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ τῇ τρίτῃ ἀναστησόμεθα. Quod quidam putant, hæc omnino sub exitum à Christo dicta, fragili moventur argumento. Ponunt enim à Luca pressius quam à cæteris observari temporum ordinem, quod non ita esse multis exemplis apertum fecimus. Neque vero ea est vis vocis ἑξῆς in libri anteloquio: Τελειοῦμαι autem est ὑπαλλαγή. Nam consummari dicitur cujus cursus consummatur: Τελειοῦται ὁ δρόμος, ut noster hic loquitur Actor XX. 24. Neque aliter accipiendum videtur Philipp. c. III. 12. ubi Paulus à cursoribus sumta similitudine subjungit οὐχ' ὅτι ἤδη ἔλαβον ἢ ἤδη τετελείωμαι.

## 13:33
V. 33. καὶ τῇ ἐχομένῃ) Namely, also on that third day at the end of which I shall finally complete my course: whether one chooses to note a certain or an uncertain time.

Grotius wishes to signify that the time is indefinite, but known to Himself, in Christ’s words: comparing Hosea VI. 2. But there the time is expressly defined. Nor is it here entirely ἀόριστον. For by this proverbial expression a small space of time is noted, as Theophylact has interpreted it. Therefore Christ said in the present tense τελειοῦμαι, because the end was imminent. Conf. 2 Tim. IV. 6. There is therefore no need for the enallage of tenses which Grotius invents: where propriety is joined with emphasis. But Camero rightly notes here concerning the present verb, the things which follow: This was the mind of Christ in this place, τῇ τρίτῃ, on the third day, that is, shortly Τελειοῦμαι, I am perfected, for it was necessary that He, before He ascended into heaven, should perform certain duties on earth. And to this John XVII. 4 looked when he testified that he had executed on earth what had been enjoined upon him by the Father, namely because so little time remained, and the passion of Christ, by which he was perfected, was already at hand, he speaks as done what was already in such a state that it was almost done, nor does the voice of Christ on the cross pertain to anything else: it is finished.

πορεύεσθαι) To walk here means to work. John XII. 35 and elsewhere. The sense is the same as in John IX. 4: ἐμὲ δεῖ ἐργάζεσθαι τὰ ἔργα τοῦ πέμψαντός με ἕως ἡμέρα ἐστι. As if he were to say: there is no reason for anyone to threaten me with death at this time and place. Divine providence will never permit Herod that right over me which he claims for himself: I am to die, but where and when the Father shall have willed and I shall have willed. Meanwhile, I shall not desist from miracles, which, the greater they are, the more they torment him.

Id juxta Grotium hic est operari. Sed Heinsius rectius censet τὸ πορεύεσθαι more Ebræorum idem esse, quod ἀπολύεσθαι. Conf. Luc. XXII. 22. Quod τελειοῦσθαι ante dixit.

ὅτι οὐκ ἐνδέχεται) The reason is given why he is not yet to die, that is, why either he himself does not yet wish to die, or even the Father has not yet decreed to permit him to be killed: because it is not fitting for a Prophet to be killed anywhere other than in Jerusalem, which city had, as it were by custom, acquired that right of killing Prophets. Indeed, certain Prophets had been killed outside Jerusalem, but they were few compared to those who had been slaughtered in Jerusalem. It came about, therefore, by divine dispensation, that that city, having neglected all invitations to repentance, should crown its previously committed crimes with this supreme crime, soon to pay the penalty for all its crimes alike.

Drusius gave this reason why it did not happen that prophets were put to death outside Jerusalem: for prophets were not judged except by the judges of the Sanhedrin, who resided at Jerusalem in the chamber of the house. Which is to be noted in the book of precepts 187. 1. They do not judge a tribe which has defected to idolatry, nor a false prophet, nor a high priest, except by the house of judgment of the LXXI. To which also pertains that: Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those who are sent to you.

Latin:

V. 33. καὶ τῇ ἐχομένῃ) Nempe etiam tertio illo die cujus fine demum cursum meum perficiam: sive certum sive incertum tempus notari placet.

Tempus indefinitum, sed sibi cognitum significari Christum vult Grotius: Conferens Os. VI. 2. Sed ibi tempus expresse definitum est. Neque hic plane ἀόριστον. Notatur enim proverbiali hac locutione exiguum temporis spatium, ut interpretatus est Theophylactus. Ideo in præsenti dixit Christus τελειοῦμαι, quod immineret finis. Conf. 2. Tim. IV. 6. Nulla ergo opus temporum enallage, quam fingit Grotius: ubi proprietas cum emphasiconjuncta est. Recte autem hic Camero de verbo præsenti notat, quæ sequuntur: Hæc fuit Christi mens hoc loco, τῇ τρίτῃ, tertia die. hoc est brevi Τελειοῦμαι, consummor, nempe oportebat eum, priusquam in cœlum ascenderet, certis quibusdam officiis perfungi in terra. Atque eo respexit Joh. XVII. 4. quum testatus est se exsecutum esse in terra quod ei injunctum erat à Patre, nempe quia tantillum supererat temporis, atque, jam instabat Christi passio qua consummatus est, factum dicit quod jam in eo fuit ut pene factum esset, nec alio pertinet vox Christi in cruce: consummatum est.

πορεύεσθαι) Ambulare hic est operari. Joh. XII. 35. & alibi. Sensus idem qui apud Joh. IX. 4. ἐμὲ δεῖ ἐργάζεσθαι τὰ ἔργα τοῦ πέμψαντός με ἕως ἡμέρα ἐστι. Quasi dicat: non est quod mihi hoc tempore & loco mortem quisquam minetur. Divina providentia nunquam id jus Herodi in me permittet, quod ille sibi vindicat: moriturus sum, sed ubi & quando Pater voluerit atque ego voluero. Interim non desistam à miraculis, quæ quo sunt majora hoc magis illum excruciant.

Id juxta Grotium hic est operari. Sed Heinsius rectius censet τὸ πορεύεσθαι more Ebræorum idem esse, quod ἀπολύεσθαι. Conf. Luc. XXII. 22. Quod τελειοῦσθαι ante dixit.

ὅτι οὐκ ἐνδέχεται) Causa redditur cur nondum sit moriturus, id est cur aut ipse nondum velit mori, aut etiam pater nondum decreverit permittere ut occidatur: quia non convenit Prophetam alibi occidi quam Hierosolymis, quæ urbs jus illud occidendi Prophetas quasi usu ceperat. Erant quidem & Prophetæ quidam occisi extra Hierosolyma, sed pauci præ iis qui Hierosolymis erant trucidati. Factum igitur est divina dispensatione, ut illa civitas neglectis omnibus ad pœnitentiam invitationibus, ante acta scelera etiam hoc summo scelere cumularet, mox omnium pariter scelerum pœnas luitura.

Causam reddidit Drusius hanc, cur Prophetas interfici non contigerit extra Hierosolymam? Nam Prophetæ non judicabantur nisi à judicibus Sanhedrin, qui Jerosolymæ residebant in exedra domus. Quod notandum in libro præceptorum 187. 1. Non judicant tribum quæ defecit ad idololatriam, neque Pseudo-Prophetam, neque Sacerdotem magnum, nisi per domum judicii LXXI. Quo pertinet & illud, Jerusalem, Jerusalem, quæ trucidas Prophetas, & lapidas eos qui mittuntur ad te.

## 13:34
Vers. 34. Ἱερουσαλὴμ, ἱερουσαλὴμ) I think these were added here by Luke because of the affinity of the subject matter, not because they were spoken by Christ earlier. For the passage seems to be transcribed from Matthew, to whom those things we have noted may be seen.

Latin:

Vers. 34. Ἱερουσαλὴμ, ἱερουσαλὴμ) Puto ob argumenti affinitatem à Luca hoc loco hæc adjecta, non quòd prius à Christo pronunciata fuerunt. Videtur enim transcriptus locus ex Matthæo, ad quem videri possunt quæ notavimus.

## 13:35
V. 35 ἀφίεται ὑμῖν ὁ οἶκος ὑμῶν) Ἔρημος is added here in certain books from Matthew, although the best codices do not have it, and Greek writers, but also certain Latin ones, do not acknowledge it.

Nothing prevents us from believing that these things were said to the Jews on repeated occasions. That those things which were said much later were drawn back to this point because of the affinity of the subject matter cannot be maintained, unless we assert that the order of times was neglected by Luke; which is not to be said rashly. But if the passage is to be called transcribed from Matthew, it will have been either transcribed by copyists, and thus the codices will be corrupt, or by Luke himself: whose task, however, was not to transcribe from elsewhere what he pleased, but to write those things which the Holy Spirit dictated to him. Nor is it indeed new or infrequent for the same things to be said by Christ at different times and places; nay, it is likely that Christ foretold these things not once, but several times at Jerusalem: whence Augustine, book II, On the Consensus of the Evangelists, ch. 7, admits that Christ, approaching Jerusalem, answered such things to those warning him to beware of Herod, as Matthew says he spoke also to the crowds when he had already arrived in Jerusalem. I do not press what Blessed Lyranus thinks, that these things which are recorded as said by Luke, 'you will not see me,' are to be taken in such a way that they were fulfilled at Christ's royal entry into the city, when it was acclaimed to him, 'Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord': which things, however, Matthew reports were said by Christ after his entry into the city. For I acknowledge that these words in Luke are to be understood in the same sense in which they are to be taken in Matthew, where it is most manifest that, because they were uttered after the entry, the fulfillment of those words cannot be sought in the entry. See what has been observed regarding Matthew.

Latin:

V. 35 ἀφίεται ὑμῖν ὁ οἶκος ὑμῶν) Ἔρημος hic in quibusdam libris ex Matthæo adscriptum est, cum optimi codices non habeant, & Græci scriptores sed & Latini quidam non agnoscant.

Nihil obstat quo minus credamus hæc iteratis vicibus Judæis dicta. Ob argumenti affinitatem ea, quæ multo post dicta sunt, huc retracta esse, statui nequit, nisi neglectum à Luca ordinem temporum asseramus; quod non temere dicendum. Transcriptus autem ex Matthæo locus si dicendus, aut à librariis transcriptus, & ita Codices corrupti erunt, aut à Luca ipso: cujus vero non erat transscribere aliunde quæ libuit, sed scribere ea, quæ Sp. S. ipsi dictavit. Neque vero novum aut infrequens est eadem diversis temporibus & locis à Christo dicta, imo verisimile est, Christum non semel, sed aliquoties hæc prædixisse Hierosolymæ: unde August. l. II. de consensu Evang. c. 7. admittit, Christum Hierosolymæ propinquantem talia respondisse monentibus ut caveret Herodem, qualia Matthæus eum dicit etiam turbis loquutum, cum jam pervenisset in Hierusalem. Non urgeo, quod B. Lyranus censet, hæc quæ à Luca dicta memorantur, non videbitis me, ita accipienda, quod in Regio Christi ingressu in urbem, cum acclamatum ei fuit, Benedictus qui venit in nomine Domini, completa sint: quæ vero Matthæus à Christo post ingressum in urbem dicta esse tradit. Agnosco enim eodem sensu hæc verba apud Lucam esse intelligenda, quo accipienda veniunt apud Matthæum, ubi manifestissimum est, quia prolata post ingressum, verborum istorum complementum quæri non posse in ingressu. Vid. quæ ad Matthæum observata.

## 14:1 Argument
CHAPTER XIV.

ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

A man with dropsy is cured by Christ in the house of a Pharisee on the Sabbath, and this is defended, with a warning about not affecting the chief seat, and about inviting the needy, and the parable of the great supper, to which, when the invited guests refused to come, those who were lying in the streets and crossroads were invited, the former being excluded. An exhortation about the method to be undertaken before the preparation of a building and a conflict, and also about tasteless salt.

There are two parts: I. The things done and said in the Pharisee's banquet, up to v. 24. II. Things said to the people about following Christ, with due deliberation, up to v. 35.

PART I.

Deeds and sayings at the Pharisee's banquet.

Vers. 1. εἰς οἶκόν τινος τῶν ἀρχόντων) I think these things happened in Jerusalem: for I see that those who participate in the Sanhedrin are generally called rulers, as below XXIV. 20, John III. 1, Acts ch. III. v. 17.

Τῶν Φαρισαίων) That is, those who were of the number of the Pharisees: for I prefer to take it thus rather than, as some interpreted, the princes of the Pharisees, that is, the primary ones, who would rather be called πρῶτοι Φαρισαίων than ἄρχοντες. No one is ignorant that Greek genitives are accustomed to be taken in this way. John expressed the same sense thus: ἄνθρωπος ἐκ τῶν Φαρισαίων ἄρχων τῶν Ἰουδαίων, chap. III. 1.

It is evident from chap. XVIII. 31 that these things were not done at Jerusalem: for it was there that he finally undertook the journey toward Jerusalem. B. Lyferus thinks they were done while still in Peraea, and not in Judaea, chap. CXIX. Harm. Evang.

x) This is placed for 'that' according to the Hebrew custom, and the following indicative is to be rendered in Latin by the subjunctive.

ἀυτοὶ) The noun Φαρισαῖοι καὶ νομικοὶ is understood, who were present at the same banquet.

παρατηρύμενοι) This word is taken in this way both in Mark III. 4 and above VI. 7. They were observing whether he would do anything alien to the rites pertaining to the Sabbath, which the authority and custom of the masters had introduced.

Latin:

CAPUT XIV.

ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Hydropicus in domo Pharisæi Sabbato à Christo curatus, idque defensum, cum monitione de non affectanda πρωτοκλισίᾳ, & de invitandis egenis, ac parabola de cœna magna, ad quam venire recusantibus convivis invitatis, qui in plateis jacebant & compitis, invitati sunt, prioribus exclusis. Adhortatio de ratione ante ædificii & certaminis paraturam ineunda, nec non de sale fatuo.

Partes sunt duæ: I. τὰ πραχθέντα καὶ λεχθέντα in convivio Pharisæi, ad v. 24. II. Ad populum dicta de Christi sequela, cum justa deliberatione, ad v. 35.

PARS I.

Gesta & dicta in convivio Pharisæi.

Vers. 1. εἰς οἶκόν τινος τῶν ἀρχόντων) Puto Hierosolymis hæc gesta: nam ἄρχοντας plerumque appellari video eos qui synedrium participant, ut infra XXIV. 20. Joh. III. 1. Actor. c. III. v. 17.

Τῶν Φαρισαίων) Id est qui erant ex Pharisæorum numero: ita enim malo accipere quam, ut quidam interpretabantur, Pharisæorum principes, id est primarios qui potius πρῶτοι Φαρισαίων dicerentur quam ἄρχοντες. Græcos autem Genitivos ita accipi solere nemo nescit. Johannes eundem sensum ita expressit ἄνθρωπος ἐκ τῶν Φαρισαίων ἄρχων τῶν Ἰουδαίων, cap. III. 1.

Non gesta haec esse Hierosolymis e c. XIIX. 31. constat: ibi enim aggressus demum est profectio- nem versus Hierosolymam. In Peraea adhuc, non vero in Judaea gesta esse B. Lyferus putat c. CXIX. Harm. Evang.

x) Est hoc Hebraeo more pro ut positum, & sequens in- dicativus Latine per subjunctivum reddendus.

ἀυτοὶ) Subauditur nomen Φαρισαῖοι καὶ νομικοὶ qui eidem convivio intererant.

παρατηρύμενοι) Ita haec vox sumitur & Marci III. 4. & supra VI. 7. observabant numquid facturus esset alienum a ritibus ad sabbatum pertinentibus, quos magistrorum au- ctoritas & usus introduxerat.

## 14:2
Vers. 2. ἔμπροσθεν ἀυτῦ) Who, as is credible, had arrived with the hope of recovering his health.

Latin:

Vers. 2. ἔμπροσθεν ἀυτῦ) Qui spe recuperandae sanitatis, ut credibile est, advenerat.

## 14:3
Vers. 3. εἰ ἔξεστι τῷ σαββάτῳ θεραπεύειν) He proposes a question of disputed law, as it had been accustomed to be done among them.

Latin:

Vers. 3. εἰ ἔξεστι τῷ σαββάτῳ θεραπεύειν) Ut inter ipsos fi- eri consueverat, juris controversi quaestionem proponit.

## 14:4
Vers. 4. οἱ δὲ ἡσύχασαν) For there were dissenting authors. But the more accepted opinion held that it was not lawful to practice medicine on the Sabbath, unless the danger of death were imminent from the delay. Yet equity itself, the best interpreter of laws, suggested that something more should be granted to a man than to a beast: and in such danger, even a beast was cared for on the Sabbath day. We have spoken about this matter elsewhere. Moreover, ἡσυχάζειν for 'to be silent' is frequent among the Hellenists: 1 Macc. I. 3, Isa. XIV. 17.

ἐπιλαβόμενος) Taking hold of him: by which act he showed that the power of healing proceeded from himself: and by the same work he defined the question that had been raised.

Latin:

Vers. 4. οἱ δὲ ἡσύχασαν) Erant enim dissentientes aucto- res. Sed receptior sententia habebat non licere sabbato fa-, cere medicinam, nisi mortis periculum ex dilatione immi- neret. Atqui ipsa aequitas legum optima interpres, suade- bat plus aliquanto dandum homini quam bestiae: in tali au- tem periculo etiam bestiae sabbati die consulebatur. Dixi- mus de hac re alibi. Ἡσυχάζειν autem pro tacere frequens est apud Hellenistas: 1. Macc. I. 3. Es. XIV. 17.

ἐπιλαβόμενος) Attrectans eum: quo facto ostendebat a' se proficisci vim sanandi: eademque opera quaestionem motam definiebat.

## 14:5
V. 5. Τίνος) The same manner of speaking as above XI. 11.

εἰς φρέαρ) Hellenists, by catachresis, use the word φρέαρ for any pit, following the example of the Hebrew באר. In Psalm I, 14 [LV. 24] it is תרדם לבאר שחת, in Greek κατάξεις ἀυτὸς εἰς φρέαρ διαφθορᾶς: in which sense φρέαρ τῆς ἀβύσσου is said several times in the Apocalypse. Luke therefore said φρέαρ, which the interpreter of Matthew called βόθυνον, chap. XII. 11. Christ, however, aptly compared the man with dropsy to a beast to be submerged, just as he compared the woman who was bowed down to a bound beast.

ἀνασπάσει) מסיק. See Dan. VI. 23.

Latin:

V. 5. Τίνος) Idem loquendi genus quod supra XI. 11.

εἰς φρέαρ) Hellenistae per abusionem vocem φρέαρ de quavis voragine usurpant ad exemplum Hebraei באר. In Psalmo I, 14. LV. 24. est תרדם לבאר שחת Graecis κατάξεις ἀυτὸς εἰς φρέαρ διαφθορᾶς: quo sensu φρέαρ τῆς ἀβύσσου dicitur aliquoties in apocalypsi φρέαρ ergo di- xit Lucas, quod Matthaei interpres βόθυνον, c. XII. 11. Ap- posite autem Christus hydropicum submergendae pecudi, ut τὴν συγκύπλουσαν pecudi vinctae comparavit.

ἀνασπάσει) מסיק. Vide Dan. VI. 23.

## 14:7
V. 7. Παραβολὴν) He calls the following admonition thus: because by the example of a banquet-related matter he shows what must be done by us in all of life, and not only before men, but also before God: whence also a general pronouncement is inferred in verse 11, which is repeated below in ch. 18:14. Less, therefore, is said here, more is signified: which is the nature of a παραβολῆς, as the Hellenists use that word. Christ, however, opportunely, having healed the dropsy of the body, also undertakes to heal a double dropsy of the soul: the swelling of pride and the thirst for money.

πῶς τὰς πρωτοκλισίας ἐξελέγοντο) I think this ought to be referred not so much to the deeds as to the disposition of the guests.

Latin:

V. 7. Παραβολὴν) Ita appellat sequentem admonitionem: quia exemplo rei convivalis ostendit quid in omni vita, neq; coram hominibus tantum, sed & coram Deo nobis sit faciendum: unde & generale infertur pronuntiatum com- mate 11. quod repetitum infra est c. XIIX. 14. minus ergo hic dicitur, plus significatur: quod est παραβολῆς, ut eam vo- cem Hellenistae usurpant. Opportune autem Christus sa- nato corporis hydrope sanare etiam aggreditur duplicem animi hydropem, superbiae tumorem & pecuniae sitim.

πῶς τὰς πρωτοκλισίας ἐξελέγοντο) Puto non tam ad fa- cta, quam ad animum convivarum referri hoc debere.

## 14:10
Vers. 10. ἵνα) Resultative, as above μήποτε: although in ἐπιμονῆι it can also be understood in the Ionic manner.

* προσανάβηθι ἀνώτερον) From Solomon 25:7, where it is thus in Greek: 'For it is better for you that it be said to you, Come up, than that you be humbled before the face of a prince.' A parable of the same sense exists in a Jewish book titled 'Electuary of Gems'.

Latin:

Vers. 10. ἵνα) ἐκβατικὸν, ut supra μήποτε: quadquam in ἐπιμονῆι potest etiam Ἰολικῶς intelligi.

* προσανάβηθι ἀνώτερον) Ex Solomone XXV. 7. ubi Graece sic est, κρεῖσσον γάρ σοι τὸ ῥηθῆναι, ἀνάβηθι, ἢ ταπεινῶσαι σὺι ἐν προσώπῳ δυνάστου. Exstat parabola ejusdem sensus in libro Judaico cui titulus Electuarium Gemmarum.

## 14:12
Vers. 12. ἔλεγε δὲ τῷ κεκληκότι ἀυτὸν) Kindly repaying thanks to his host, spiritual things instead of carnal.

Πλουσίους) This word is to be referred to all those things which preceded: friends, brothers, kinsmen, neighbors. Nor, however, does Christ forbid mutual testimonies of friendship among the rich. But he prefers works of mercy by far: as those which are performed for God's sake without hope of human return: for this passage, like many others, is to be understood by comparison. Cicero, 'On Duties', Book 1: 'In bestowing a kindness, this is the greatest duty, that each person should be helped most especially when he is most in need of help: which is done conversely by most people; for they serve most especially those from whom they hope for the most, even if that person does not need their help.' Pliny, Book 9, Epistle 30: 'I want him who is truly liberal to give to friends, but I mean poor friends: not like those people who give most especially to those who are most able to give.'

μήποτε) That is, lest if you are content to do this, your reward be paid to you here. See above 6:23, where he says χάρις for what is here ἀνταπόδομα.

ἀντικαλέσωσι) Let them invite back: for that word in this meaning of a mutual invitation to dinner is most Latin, as others have observed from Lactantius and Nonius. The sense is almost the same as that in Dio Chrysostom, Oration 7: 'as if it were a custom to act precisely and ungenerously regarding poor guests; but to receive only the rich in a friendly manner with gifts and hospitality; from whom, clearly, they themselves expected the same in return.'

Latin:

Vers. 12. ἔλεγε δὲ τῷ κεκληκότι ἀυτὸν) Convivatori suo benigne gratiam rependens, πνευματικὰ ἀντὶ σαρκικῶν.

Πλουσίους) Referenda haec vox ad omnia ea quae praecesse- runt, φίλους, ἀδελφοὺς, (υγγενεῖς, γείτονας. Neque tamen prohibet Christus mutua inter divites amicitiae testimonia. Sed opera misericordiae multo praefert: ut quae sine spe hu- manae vicis Dei causa praestantur: intelligendus enim hic locus, ut alii multi, per comparationem. Cicero de officiis primo: In collocando beneficio hoc maxime officii est, ut quisq; maxime opis indigeat, ita ei potissimum opsitulari: quod contra fit a plerisque: a quo enim plurimum sperant, etiamsi ille his non eget, tamen ei potissimum inserviunt. Plinius lib. IX. Epist. 30. Volo eum qui sit vere liberalis tribuere amicis, sed amicis dico pauperibus: non ut isti qui iis potissimum donant, qui donare maxime possunt.

μήποτε) Id est ne si hoc facere contenti sitis merces ve- stra hic vobis sit persoluta. Vide supra VI. 23. ubi χάρις di- cit quod hic ἀνταπόδομα.

ἀντικαλέσωσι) Revocent: ea enim vox hoc significatu mu- tuae ad coenam vocationis Latinissima est, ut ex Lactantio & Nonio alii observarunt. Sensus ferme idem qui apud Dionem Prusaensem oratione VII. ὡς ἔθινος δὴ ὄντος ὥστε ἀκριβῶς καὶ ἀνελευθέρως πράττειν τὰ περὶ τὺς ξένυς τὲς πένη- τας˙ μόνες δὲ τὲς πλεσίες ὑποδέχεσθαι φιλοφρόνως ξενίοις καὶ δώροις˙ παρ᾽ ὧν δηλονότι καὶ ἀυτοὶ προσεδόκων τὰ ἶσα χῆν.

## 14:13
Vers. 13. call the poor) This word πτωχοὺς must also be referred to all the following, whether they are maimed, or lame, or blind, from whom many shrink as men of ill omen. It has been noted elsewhere that by the Hellenists πτω- χοὺς are called neither strictly the poor, nor always beggars, but those whom the Latins call needy. From this warning of Christ arose the ἀγάπαι, by which wealthy Christians fraternally received poor Christians, which custom, when it became corrupted because the wealthy would feast separately, Paul corrects in his letter to the Corinthians.

Latin:

Vers. 13. κάλει πτωχοὺς) Hoc etiam πτωχοὺς ad sequentia omnia referendum est, sive illi mutili sive claudi, sive cæci, à quibus ut mali ominis hominibus multi abhorrent. πτω- χοὺς Hellenistis dici nec pauperes proprie, nec mendicos semper, sed quos Latini egenos vocant, alibi notatum est. Ex hoc Christi monito natæ ἀγάπαι quibus divites Christiani Christianos pauperes fraterne excipiebant, quem mortem corruptum cum seorsum divites epularentur, ca- stigat ad Corinthios Paulus.

## 14:14
V. 14. in the resurrection of the just) Not only the time, but also the manner of the retribution is signified. The resurrection of the just is the resurrection of life, John V. 24, to which is opposed the resurrection of judgment. But for the most part, resurrection is taken in that better sense. Christ seems here to have alluded to that of the first Psalm, they shall not rise in the counsel of the just, where Symmachus has in the assembly of the just, others in the gathering or congregation. If it is considered a great thing here to be seen in the assembly of the nobles, how much more so in the assembly of those nobles whom God has enrolled in the heavenly court.

Latin:

V. 14. ἐν τῇ ἀναστάσει τῶν δικαίων) Non tempus tantum, sed & modus retributionis significatur. ἀνάστασις δικαίων est ἀνά- στασις ζωῆς Joh. V. 24. cui opponitur ἀνάστασις κρίσεως. Ple- rumque autem ἀνάστασις in partem illam meliorem sumi- tur. Videtur hic Christus allusisse ad illud Psalmi primi οὐκ ἀναστήσονται ἐν βουλῇ δικαίων, ubi Symmachus ἐν συνε- λεύσει δικαίων, alii ἐν συλλόγῳ aut συναγωγῇ. Si magnum hic ducitur conspici in cœtu procerum, quanto magis in cœtu procerum eorum quos Deus cœlesti curiæ ad- scripserit.

## 14:15
Vers. 15. blessed is he who shall eat bread in the kingdom of God) A sentiment frequent among the Rabbis, coming, as is credible, from the times of Ezra. For they used to depict invisible things by the image of visible things.

Latin:

Vers. 15. μακάριος ὃς φάγεται ἄρτον ἐν τῇ βασιλείᾳ τοῦ Θεοῦ) Sententia crebra apud Rabbinos ab Esdræ ut credi- bile est temporibus veniens. Nam τὰ ἀόρατα imagine τῶν ὁρατῶν depingebant.

## 14:17
Vers. 17. the servant) The caller. It appears that it was the custom, which even now flourishes in many places, that those invited would be called again at the very hour of the supper: which very thing is to be observed in Josephus in the history of Esther.

all things are ready) See the notes on Matthew.

ἀπὸ μιᾶς) A solitary expression, in the interpretation of which it is no wonder if scholars today disagree: since long ago the Arab passed over the whole thing, as he is accustomed to do when it is not understood: φωνῆς, which some wish to be supplied, cannot be, since they each brought their own excuses. A man of rare diligence in these matters recently attempted to demonstrate to many that ὥρας is to be understood, after the manner of the Syrians who say מחדא. But that I may pronounce what seems to me to be the case without prejudice to anyone, I cannot perceive how that sense fits this passage. For whether you interpret ἀπὸ μιᾶς ὥρας as at that very time, what emphatic force can that have here, since they could not excuse themselves at any other time than that at which they were being compelled? But if one prefers to interpret it as immediately, not even that fits, for it is no wonder if they wished to excuse themselves, that they excused themselves immediately, as they, being compelled at the very time of the supper, have no space for deliberation. The Syrian himself saw this, who did not translate מחדא here, which he would have done if he could have found a convenient meaning for that word in this place, but מוחך, in which that same most learned man rightly suspects that ל is to be understood. Wherefore, since it is clear even from this that the Syrians were accustomed to speak in this way, what wonder if Luke, a Syrian, imitated the Syrian manner of speaking: yet in such a way that he used the feminine gender: because καρδία, as also ψυχὴ (for it is the same thing which you understand to be suppressed), is of the feminine gender among the Greeks. Our Luke said Μίαν καρδίαν καὶ ψυχὴν in Acts IV. v. 31. Paul also said ψυχὴν μίαν in Philippians I. 27. The sense is that the mind of all was similar. They all act in concert as if in an oil-press, says the most witty writer of Comedies, where he wishes to describe a mind common to all, even those who had not agreed among themselves. But this part of the story signifies not obscurely the magistrates and interpreters of the law of the Jews, who, having been called to repentance formerly by the Prophets, and afterwards by John and Christ, preferred to allege anything at all rather than obey the salutary counsel.

Crocius wishes the word καρδίας or ψυχῆς to be understood, as the Syrian has מוחך, where the word ל is to be understood. He thinks Luke, a Syrian, imitated the Syrian manner of speaking: which, however, he proves by no other example of Syriasms than this one. But why could it not be conveniently supplied by the word γνώμης or βουλῆς, as Beza judged, that is, opinion or counsel, for however they may bring forward different causes, they nevertheless agree in this, that they use their own affairs as a pretext, so that they may not appear at the Supper.

Latin:

Vers. 17. τὸν δοῦλον) Vocatorem. Apparet morem fu- isse, qui nunc etiam multis in locis viget, ut vocati sub ipsam cœnæ horam iterum appellarentur: quod ipsum observare est apud Josephum in Estheris historia.

ἑτοῖμά ἐστι πάντα) Vide ad Matthæum.

ἀπὸ μιᾶς) Locutio μονήρης in qua interpretanda non est mirum si eruditi hodie dissentiunt: cum jam olim Arabs totam præterierit, ut solet non intellecta: φωνῆς quod quidam volunt, suppleri non potest, cum singuli suas ex- cusationes attulerint. Vir raræ in his rebus diligentiæ multis nuper demonstrare conatus est subaudiri ὥρας, ex Syrorum more qui dicunt מחדא. Sed ut quod mihi vi- detur sine cujusquam fraude pronuntiem, non possum perspicere quomodo is sensus huic loco congruat. Nam sive ἀπὸ μιᾶς ὥρας interpreteris eo ipso tempore, quám vim ἐμφατικὴν id habere hic potest, cum non alio tem- pore excusare se potuerint quam quo compellabantur? Sin potius interpretari libet, confestim, ne id quidem quadrat, nec enim mirum, si excusare se vellent, confe- stim se excusasse, qui sub ipsum cœnæ tempus compel- lati non habent deliberandi spatium. Vidit hoc ipse Syrus qui non מחדא hic transtulit, facturus si commo- dam ejus vocis significationem reperire hoc loco potuis- set, sed מוחך in quo idem ille vir eruditissimus recte su- spicatur ל subaudiri. Quare cum vel hinc liqueat ita so- litos loqui Syros, quid mirum si Lucas Syrus Syriacum lo- quendi genus est imitatus: ita tamen ut femininum genus usurpaverit: quia καρδία ut & ψυχὴ (nam perinde est utrum subticeri intelligas) apud Græcos feminini est ge- neris. Μίαν καρδίαν καὶ ψυχὴν dixit Lucas noster Act. IV. v. 31. ψυχὴν μίαν etiam Paulus Philipp. I. 27. Sensus est animum omnibus fuisse similem. Omnes compacto rem agunt quasi in belabro olearii, inquit facetissimus Comœ- diarum scriptor, ubi parem omnibus, etiam qui inter se non convenerant, animum vult describere. Significat au- tem hæc pars fabulæ non obscure Judæorum magistratus & legis interpretes, qui olim per Prophetas, postea per Jo- hannem & Christum ad resipiscentiam vocati, quidvis cau- sare maluerunt, quam salutari consilio parere.

Subintelligi vocem καρδίας vult Crocius vel ψυχῆς, ut Syrus habet, מוחך ubi subaudienda vox ל. Lucam Syrum putat Syriacum loquendi genus imitatum: Quod tamen nullo alio è Sy- riasmo exemplo, quam hoc probat. Quidni vero commode suppleri possit voce γνώμης aut βουλῆς, ut censuit Beza, id est, sententia vel con- silio, utut enim illi diversas causas adferant, in eo tamen conveniunt, quod sua prætexant ne- gotia, quo minus ad Cœnam compareant.

## 14:18
I have need to go out and see it. I ask you, have me excused) Many Latinisms at once. ἔχω ἀνάγκην I have need. Ἐρωτῶ σε I ask you. ἔχε με παρῃτημένον have me excused. You will find ἀνάγκην ἔχειν also below in chapter XXIII, verse 17, 1 Corinthians, chapter VII, v. 37, Hebrews c. VII, v. 27, Jude 3.

Latin:

ἔχω ἀνάγκην ἐξελθεῖν καὶ ἰδεῖν αὐτὸν. Ἐρωτῶ σε, ἔχε με παρῃτημένον) Multi simul Latinismi. ἔχω ἀνάγκην opus habeo. Ἐρωτῶ σε rogo te. ἔχε με παρῃτημένον habe me excusatum. Ἀνάγκην ἔχειν reperies etiam infra cap. XXIII, vers. 17. 1. Corinth, cap. VII. v. 37. Hebr. c. VII. v. 27. Judæ 3.

## 14:19
Vers. 19. Yokes of oxen) Greek enough. Thus also above he preferred to say a yoke of turtledoves rather than two turtledoves, as the LXX had said.

Latin:

Vers. 19. Ζεύγη βοῶν) Satis Græce. Ita & supra ma- luit dicere ζεῦγος τρυγόνων quam δύο τρυγόνας, ut dixerant LXX.

## 14:20
Vers. 20. I am not able to come) He says the same thing as the others, but more rustically. Thus, of those who reject the word of salvation, some wish to appear more polite than others.

Latin:

Vers. 20. ὀ δύναμαι ἐλθεῖν) Idem dicit quod alii sed rusticius. Ita eorum qui sermonem salutis respuunt, alii videri volunt aliis comiores.

## 14:21
Vers. 21. into the streets and lanes of the city) For in these used to sit those who could not sustain themselves by the service of their body.

The poor) Fishermen, tax collectors, and even women of a previously impure life. It must be understood, however, for the most part, not that all the Jews who had believed in Christ were such, but most of them, being despised either because of a rude nature or because of their previous life.

Latin:

Vers. 21. εἰς τὰς πλατείας καὶ ῥύμας τῆς πόλεως) Nam in his sedere solebant qui servitio corporis semet sustentare non poterant.

Τὸς πτωχὸς) Piscatores, publicanos, imo & feminas vitæ antea impurioris. Intelligendum autem ἐπὶ τὸ πολὺ, non quod omnes Judæorum qui in Christum crediderant tales fuerint, sed plerique, aut ob rude ingenium aut ob vitam priorem despecti.

## 14:22
Vers. 22. yet there is room) God had promised a great kingdom to Christ. And so, rather than that he should have few subjects, he relaxes the innermost depths of his mercy, in a manner never seen, never heard.

Latin:

Vers. 22. ἔτι τόπος ἐςὶ) Magnum regnum Christo promiserat Deus. Itaque potius quam paucos ille subditos habeat, laxat intima misericordiæ suæ penetralia, nunquam visa, nunquam audita ratione.

## 14:23
into the roads and hedges) Outside the city, that is, outside the covenant, and where it was possible to see the wretched nations in a manifold labyrinth, wandering and seeking the way of life while straying. Matthew said into the outlets. See what is noted there. Christ seems to have named hedges on purpose, because hedges, as it were, interposed, would seclude foreign peoples from the knowledge of the truth: in which sense Paul uses the word φραγμὸν in Ephesians 2:14.

Compel them to come in), This passage makes me mindful of an excellent doctor among the ancients, who, although he had previously asserted in many books that no one should be compelled to the profession of faith [in which matter he had certainly said nothing that Justin, Athenagoras, Tertullian, Arnobius, Minutius, Lactantius, and as many as had lived before him of any name had not said before him], soon changed his opinion somewhat and put forward the authority of this passage, as if those who constitute hedges ought to be compelled, that is, as he himself interprets, those who seek divisions in the Church. Indeed, even by this example it appears how differently we judge when we look into the things themselves without emotion, and differently when a question of fact arises, from which it happens that second thoughts are not always wiser. The stubbornness of the Donatists expressed this to him, and to press them from all sides, he even snatched up this weapon: although this passage manifestly pertains to the nations who had not yet professed the faith, whom he did not want to be compelled even then, when he thought that Christians ought to be compelled to the unity of profession.

Against the Papists compelling the unwilling to the faith, these things can be opposed, which Grotius, having later become an advocate for the Roman Church, holds here: that according to the opinion of Justin, Athenagoras, Tertullian, Arnobius, Minutius, Lactantius, and others, as many as lived of any name before Augustine, and also of Augustine himself, before the stubbornness of the Donatists expressed another opinion to him, no one should be compelled to the profession of faith: from which, having changed his opinion somewhat, he shows the authority of this passage, as if those who constitute hedges, that is, who seek division in the Church, ought to be compelled, when yet this passage manifestly pertains to the nations who had not yet professed the faith, whom he himself did not want to be compelled even then, when he thought that Christians ought to be compelled to the unity of profession. He adds, moreover, the proof of this opinion, which follows:

And yet, how many things are there in the parables which have a proper sense in the signifying thing, but in the signified thing have only a very figurative one. What of the fact that not even in the story itself can 'to compel' be understood of corporal punishments or threats of punishments: for guests are not accustomed to be compelled in that way, but by importunate urging. Jesus is said to have compelled the disciples to enter the ship, Matt. 14:22, Mark 6:45, which he certainly did neither by pushing nor by pulling, but by the authority of his teaching. Again, those two who were going to Emmaus 'constrained' Jesus to stay with them, by asking insistently, of course. Peter is said to have compelled the nations to Judaism, Gal. 2:14, not by any force, of course, but by example. Thus, therefore, the nations were as if compelled to the faith, while the Apostles and their helpers urged them in season and out of season, 2 Tim. 4:2, besought them through Christ, and added to their words the authority of miracles and the example of a most innocent life: 1. Thess. 2:10. Certainly also in Hermas an angel is introduced speaking thus, I will compel them to believe. And Tertullian said: He who has studied to understand will be compelled also to believe. And the old formula of ecclesiastical prayer has: Before our also compel the rebellious, O gracious one. Cyprian in his tract On Mortality: Gentiles are compelled to believe; by the fear of death, that is. To this kind of compulsion some refer that sign of the πνοῆς βιαίας (violent breath) in the upper room of the Apostles on the day of Pentecost, that is, as Origen interprets it in Against Celsus, of a πνοῆς βιαζομένης (compelling breath) in men, and the things from it.

Thus Grotius. Compare on these matters more fully B. Gerhard, On the Magistrate, § 198. The Canon Law itself, C. Quod autem, Dist. XLV, from Gregory the Great, Book II, Ep. 52: That excellent preacher, he says, says, 'reprove, entreat with all patience and doctrine.' A truly new and unheard-of preaching, which demands faith with lashes. And from the Fourth Council of Toledo, Can. LVI, same distinction, C. Judæis: It teaches that force is not to be brought upon anyone to believe, for God has mercy on whom He wills. Nor does Theophylact in his commentary on this passage explain that ἀναγκασμὸν (compulsion) otherwise than as concerning the power of the Word, to say nothing of others now. Furthermore, Grotius adds these things; which we do not disapprove of in a sound sense.

Certainly those Christians of the early times especially, because of that sudden and extraordinary force of the spirit, can be said to have been as it were drawn by force, which the same Origen affirms of certain ones of his own age, speaking thus: 'Nevertheless it shall be said that many have come to Christianity as if against their will, some spirit having suddenly turned their governing faculty from hating the word to dying for it, and having presented them with visions either awake or asleep.' He says similar things in Homily VII on Luke. Examples, besides that noble one of Paul, can be given from the martyrology, such as the two mimes who, while they were imitating the Christian mysteries in mockery, under Diocletian one, and the other under Julian, were suddenly changed and professed themselves Christians. A similar expression is found in Seneca: 'The mind must be compelled to begin.'

Latin:

Vers. 23. εἰς τὰς ὁδὸς καὶ φραγμὸς) Extra urbem, id est, extra fœdus & ubi miseras gentes videre erat in multiplici Labyrintho, Errare atque viam palantes quærere vitæ. ἐπὶ τὰς διεξόδες dixit Matthæus. Vide quæ ibi notata. De consulto autem φραγμὸς nominasse videtur Christus, quod sepes quasi quædam interpositæ populos extraneos à veri cognitione secluderent: quo sensu vocem φραγμᾶ usurpat Paulus Ephes. II. 14.

Ἀνάγκασον εἰσελθεῖν), Facit hic locus me memorem eximii inter veteres doctoris, qui cum antea multis in libris asseverasset neminem esse ad fidei professionem cogendum [qua in re nihil certe dixerat quod non ante eum dixerant Justinus, Athenagoras, Tertullianus, Arnobius, Minutius, Lactantius, & quotquot alicujus nominis ante vixerant] mutatæ mox nonnihil sententiæ obtendit hujus loci auctoritatem, quasi cogi debeant qui sepes constituunt, hoc est, ut ipse interpretatur, qui divisiones in Ecclesia quærunt. Nimirum vel hoc exemplo apparet quanto aliter judicemus cum res ipsas sine affectu introspicimus, aliter cum facti quæstio incidit, quo fit ut non semper sint σοφώτεραι αἱ δευτέραι φροντίδες. Expressit hoc illi Donatistarum pertinacia, quos ut undique urgeret, etiam hoc telum arripuit: cum tamen hic locus manifesto pertineat ad gentes adhuc fidem non professas, quas ille, ne tunc quidem cogi voluit cum Christianos ad unitatem professionis cogendos arbitraretur.

Pontificiis ad fidem invitos cogentibus violentia adhibita, hæc opponi possunt, quæ Grotius postmodum Romanæ Ecclesiæ advocatus factus hic habet: quod ex sententia Justini, Athenagoræ, Tertulliani, Arnobii, Minutii, Lactantii & aliorum, quotquot nominis alicujus ante Augustinum vixere, nec non Augustini ipsius, antequam aliam sententiam ipsi Donatistarum expressit pertinacia, nemo ad fidei professionem cogendus sit: ex quo mutatæ nonnihil sententiæ hujus loci autoritatem ostendit, quasi cogi debeant, qui sepes constituunt, hoc est, divisionem in Ecclesia quærunt, quum tamen hic locus manifeste pertineat ad gentes adhuc fidem non professas, quas ipse ne tunc quidem cogi voluit, cum Christianos ad unitatem professionis cogendos arbitraretur. Addit autem & ἔλεγχον hujus sententiæ, quæ sequuntur:

Atqui, quam multa sunt ἐν ταῖς παραβολαῖς quæ in re significante sensum habent proprium, in re significata non nisi valde figuratum. Quid quod ne in ipsa quidem fabula ἀναγκάζειν de pœnis corporalibus aut minis pœnarum potest intelligi: non enim eo modo convivæ cogi solent sed importuna flagitatione. Dicitur Jesus coegisse discipulos ut navem intrarent, Matth. XIV. 22. Marc. VI. 45. quod certe nec trudendo nec trahendo fecit, sed magisterii sui auctoritate. Rursum duo illi qui Emmauntem ibant Jesum παραβιάσαντο ut secum maneret, instanter rogando scilicet. Dicitur Petrus gentes coëgisse ad Judaismum, Gal. II. 14. non vi ulla scilicet, sed exemplo. Sic igitur gentes ad fidem quasi coactæ, dum Apostoli eorumque adjutores illis instant ἐυκαίρως, ἀκαίρως 2. Tim. IV. 2. per Christum obtestantur, addunt dictis miraculorum auctoritatem, & innocentissimæ vitæ exemplum: 1. Thess. II, 10. certe & apud Hermam angelus ita loquens introducitur, Cogam eos credere. Et Tertullianus dixit: Qui studuerit intelligere cogetur & credere. Et vetus formula Ecclesiasticæ precationis habet: Ante nostras etiam rebelles compelle propitius voluntates. Cyprianus li- bello de mortalitate: Gentiles coguntur ut credant; metu mortis scilicet. Ad hoc cogendi genus sunt qui referunt signum illud πνοῆς βιαίας in cœnaculo Apostolorum die Pentecostes, id est, ut Origenes ad Celsum interpretatur, πνοῆς βιαζομένης ἐξαφανίσαι τὴν ἐν ἀνθρώποις κακίαν, καὶ τὰ ἀπ' αὐτῆς.

Hæc Grotius. Conf. de his uberiùs B. Gerhard. de Magistrat. §. 198. Jus ipsum Canonicum C. Quod autem Dist. XLV. ex Gregorio M. l. II. Ep. 52. Egregius, inquit, ille prædicator dicit, argue, obsecra in omni patientia & doctrina. Nova vere atq; inau- dita prædicatio, quæ verberibus fidem exigit. Et ex Concilio Toletano IV. Can. LVI. distinct. eadem C. Ju- dæis: Nemini ad credendum vim inferendam esse docet, cui enim vult, miseretur Deus. Nec aliter ἀναγκασμὸν illum explicat Theophyl. in com- ment. ad h. l. quam de virtute Verbi, ut alios jam taceamus. De cætero hæc subjungit Grotius; quæ sano sensu non improbamus.

Certe illi præcipue primorum temporum Christiani, ob vim illam subitam atque eximiam spiritus dici possunt quasi vi pertracti, quod & de quibusdam sui ævi affirmat idem O- rigenes, ita loquens, ὅμως λελέξεται ὅτι πολλοὶ ὡσπερεὶ ἄκοντες προσεληλύθασι Χριστιανισμῷ, πνεύματός τινος τρέψαντος αὐ- τῶν τὸ ἡγεμονικὸν αἰφνίδιον ἀπὸ τοῦ μισεῖν τὸν λόγον ἐπὶ τὸ ὑπερα- ποθανεῖν αὐτοῦ, καὶ φαντασιώσαντος αὐτοὺς ὕπαρ ἢ ὄναρ. Si- milia dicit ad Lucam Homilia VII. Exempla, præter illud Pauli nobile, dari possunt ex martyrologio nonnulla, ut de mimis duobus qui cum Christiana mysteria per ludibrium imitarentur, sub Diocletiano alter, alter vero sub Juliano, subito mutati ac Christianos se professi sunt. Similis est apud Senecam locutio: Cogenda est mens ut incipiat.

## 14:24
Verse 24. (For I say to you) I think the story is continued and that these are the words of the Lord addressing the servants, and testifying that he will never hereafter admit those refusers to his supper.

Latin:

Vers. 24. λέγω γὰρ ὑμῖν) Puto continuari fabulam & ver- ba esse Domini servos alloquentis, & testantis nunquam se posthac illos recusatores à cœnam suam admissurum.

## 14:25
Verse 25. (Great crowds) The bad mixed with the good, as is wont to happen in a large crowd, which gave occasion for the following discourse.

PART II.

Things said to the people concerning following Christ.

Latin:

Vers 25. ὄχλοι πολλοὶ) Mali bonis permixti, ut in grandi turba fieri solet, quod occasionem sequenti sermoni præ- buit.

## 14:26
Verse 26. (comes to me) For the sake of learning. The Jews proposed to proselytes the inconveniences that accompany the law: Christ proposed much greater ones to those following him.

and does not hate) It is certain that this word is taken improperly. For to hate parents is impious, and to hate oneself is among the impossible things, Eph. 5:29. The simplest interpretation is that which explains μισεῖν (to hate) as 'to love less.' For in Matthew it is 'he who loves father or mother more than me,' nor is the Hebrew שנא and the Greek μισεῖν taken otherwise in Gen. 29:31, 33, with all the Hebrews agreeing, for Jacob is not to be thought to have been so cruel as to have held Leah in hatred. So also Deut. 21:15, 17, and Matt. 6:24, and 'hating the soul' in John 12:25, in the way that many also like to understand that which is in Malachi 1:2, from a comparison of the passage in Genesis 25:23, concerning which matter we shall see elsewhere. But that CHRIST warns here that no relationships ought to have so much weight with us that they seduce us from the duty of piety, we have explained elsewhere, having adduced the testimonies of the Philosophers. However, I do not agree with those who refer these things only to the prefects of the churches. For these same things are said in Matthew and Mark to all who wish to follow Christ: nor is there any reason here why a general statement should be taken more narrowly. For that which moves them most, placed below, 'renounces all that he has,' does not have the sense that they themselves think, but one that extends to all Christians.

Grotius here rejected the gloss of the Papists, who refer these things only to the prefects of the churches: to which must also be added those things which will follow in verse 33 in his work.

Latin:

Vers. 26. ἔρχεται πρὸς με) Discendi causa. Judæi proselytis proponebant incommoda quæ legem comitan- tur: Christus se sectantibus multo majora.

καὶ ἐ μισεῖ) Certum est vocem hanc improprie sumi. Nam parentes odisse impium est, semetipsum τ' ἀδυνάτων, Eph. V. 29. Simplicissima interpretatio est quæ μισεῖν ex- ponit minus amare. Nam in Matthæo est ὁ φιλῶν πατέρα ἢ μητέρα ὑπὲρ ἐμὲ, neque aliter sumitur Hebræum שנא & Græcum μισεῖν Gen. XXIX. 31. 33. Hebræis omnibus con- sentientibus, neque enim tam crudelis fuisse putandus est Jacob ut Leam odio habuerit. Sic & Deut. XXI. 15. 17. & Matth. VI. 24. & μισεῖν τὴν ψυχὴν Joh. XII. 25. quomo- do multis placet & illud intelligi quod est in Malachia I. v. 2. ex collatione loci Geneseos XXV. 23. qua de re vi- derimus alias. Quod autem CHRISTUS hic monet nul- las necessitudines apud nos tantum valere debere ut nos ab officio pietatis seducant, explicavimus alibi adductis Philosophorum testimoniis. Illis autem non assentior qui hæc ad solos Ecclesiarium præfectos referunt. Eadem enim hæc apud Matthæum & Marcum dicuntur omnibus Chri- stum sectari volentibus: neque hic quicquam est causæ cur generale dictum sumatur angustius. Nam quod illos maxime movet infra positum ἀποτάσσεται τοῖς ὑπάρχουσιν, non eum quem ipsi putant sensum habet, sed qui ad o- mnes Christianos extenditur.

Glossam Pontificiorum, hæc ad solos Ecclesiæ- rum præfectos referentium, hic rejecit Grotius: quibus addenda etiam illa, quæ v. 33. apud ipsum sequentur.

## 14:27
Verse 27. (and comes after me) Here this expression signifies not just any discipleship, but serious imitation.

Latin:

Vers. 27. καὶ ἔρχεται ὀπίσω με) Hic ista locutio non discipulatum quemvis, sed seriam imitationem signifi- cat.

## 14:28
Vers. 28. For which of you, intending to build a tower) In this and the following comparison, as in many others, the individual parts which pertain to the ὑποτύπωσις (delineation) of the comparison are not to be cut away: but that to which the comparison tends must be looked to. That, however, in this place, is that one who is approaching the profession of Christianity must well weigh the inconveniences and dangers which are accustomed to accompany such a profession, the offenses of relatives, the loss of goods, the perils of life, so that unforeseen missiles may not strike more severely, and so that what one has rashly undertaken, he may desert to his great harm, having become a ῥίψασπις καὶ λειποτάκτης (shield-thrower and deserter). The wise Hebrew well admonishes: My son, if thou come to serve the Lord, prepare thy soul for temptation: which is the best ἐπιμύθιον (moral) of these fables. It is not permitted to say here, any more than in war, I had not thought: but we ought to be so prepared that it may be permitted to us to say,

I have foreseen all things and have gone over them beforehand in my mind.

καθίσας (having sat down) To the table or counting-board. Vers. 31. βουλεύεται (he deliberates) Sallust. Before you begin, there is need of consultation, and after you have consulted, there is need of prompt action. Thucydides, aptly to this subject: Consider the uncertainty of war before you are involved in it. Livy: Propose to your mind both your own strength and the power of fortune and the common Mars of war. Quintilian: It is better to prepare for war than to wage it. Publius Mimus: War must be prepared for with the gods so that you may conquer more quickly.

Latin:

Vers. 28. τίς γὰρ ἐξ ὑμῶν θέλων πύργον οἰκοδομῆσαι) In hac & sequenti comparatione, ut in multis aliis, non sunt resecandæ partes singulæ quæ ad comparationis ὑπο- τύπωσιν pertinent: sed id spectandum quo tendat com- paratio. Id autem est hoc loco, aggredienti professio- nem Christianismi bene expendenda incommoda ac pe- ricula quæ talem professionem comitari solent, offensas propinquorum, bonorum jacturam, vitæ discrimina, ne magis feriant improvisa tela, atque ita quod quis ag- gressus est temere, magno suo malo deserat, factus ῥί- ψασπις καὶ λειποτάκτης. Bene monet Hebræus sapiens Τέκνον εἰ προσέρχῃ δουλεύειν τῷ κυρίῳ ἑτοίμασον τὴν ψυχήν σου εἰς πειρασμόν: quod optimum est harum fabularum ἐπι- μύθιον. Non magis hic quam in bello dicere licet, non putaram: sed ita comparati esse debemus ut dicere nobis liceat,

Omnia præcepi atque animo mecum ante peregi.

καθίσας) Ad mensam sive abacum. Vers. 31. βουλεύεται) Sallustius. Priusquam incipias con- sulto, & postquam consulueris mature facto opus est. Thu- cydides apposite ad hanc materiam: Τὸ πολέμῳ τὸ παρά- λογον ὅσον ἐστὶ πρὶν ἐν αὐτῷ γενέσθαι προδιάγνωθι. Livius: Cum tuas vires tum vim fortunæ Martemque belli commu- nem propone animo. Quintilianus: Prius est parare bel- lum quam exercere. Publius Mimus: Diis apparendum est bellum ut vincas celerius.

## 14:33
Vers. 33. Whosoever does not forsake all his own possessions) Τὰ ὑπάρχοντα (possessions) are those things which we possess, as Matt. ch. XIX. vers. 21, ch. XXIV. vers. 47, ch. XXV. v. 14. Luke above ch. VIII. v. 3, ch. XI. v. 21, ch. XII. v. 15, 33. Below ch. XVI. vers. 1, ch. XIX. vers. 8. Acts ch. IV. v. 32. But from the species the genus is to be understood. For just as above under the example of friends and life, so here under the example of goods, all things are to be understood which are accustomed to be loved in this life. Nor is ἀποτάσσεται (forsake) to be taken otherwise here than ἀπαρνεῖσθαι (to deny) in Matt. ch. XVI. v. 24, Mark VIII. v. 34, and Luke IX. 23. For it is not an act that is designated, but the affection of the mind of one who places all these things below Christ, and is prepared to lose them if they cannot be retained with piety intact. This is what Paul says to the Cor. I. ch. VII. v. 29, 30, that those who have should be as though they had not, those who buy as though they did not possess. Epictetus in the Enchiridion wishes us to be like travelers walking along the shore to whom it may be permitted meanwhile to gather shells, but so that they must be prepared, as soon as the signal to return from the ship is given, to throw them away, lest they delay the ship in any way. Philo: All things are the possession of God, but the use only belongs to creation. For nothing in creation has been firmly sold to anyone, as if they were external things; the possession of the whole is alone strictly firm. To which he says the law concerning the year of Jubilee pertained, so that no one might consider anything his own by full right. οὐ δύναταί μου εἶναι μαθητὴς (he cannot be my disciple) He cannot fulfill the office of a Christian.

Latin:

Vers. 33. ὃς οὐκ ἀποτάσσεται πᾶσι τοῖς ἑαυτοῦ ὑπάρχουσι) Τὰ ὑπάρχοντα sunt ea quæ possidemus, ut Matth. c. XIX. vers. 21. cap. XXIV. vers. 47. cap. XXV. v. 14. Lucæ su- pra c. IIX. v. 3. cap. XI. v. 21. cap. XII. v. 15. 33. Infra cap. XVI. vers. 1. cap. XIX. vers. 8. Actor. cap. IV. v. 32. Sed ex specie genus intelligendum est. Nam sicut supra sub amicorum & vitæ, ita hic sub bonorum exemplo omnia intelligenda sunt quæ in hac vita diligi solent. Neque ἀποτάσσεται aliter hic sumendum quam ἀπαρνεῖσθαι apud Matth. c. XVI. v. 24. Marc. IIX. v. 34. & Luc.IX. 23. Neque enim actus designatur, sed affectus animi isthæc omnia infra Christum ducentis, & parati ea amittere si salva pietate retineri nequeant. Hoc est quod Paulus di- cit ad Cor. I. cap. VII. v. 29. 30. esse debere τοὺς ἔχοντας ὡς μὴ ἔχοντας, τοὺς ἀγοράζοντας ὡς μὴ κατέχοντας. Epicte- tus in Enchiridio similes nos esse vult vectoribus ab lit- tus ambulantibus quibus interim liceat conchas legere, sed ita ut parati esse debeant, simul è nave signum red- eundi datum sit, easdem à se projicere, ne quid navem morentur. Philo: κτῆσις μὲν τὰ πάντα θεοῦ, χρῆσις δὲ μό- νον γενέσεώς ἐστι. Βεβαίως γὰρ οὐδὲν οὐδενὶ πέπραται τῶν ἐν γε- νέσει, ὡς ἂν ἐτὸς ὄντων· ἓν κυρίως βεβαία ἡ τοῦ ὅλου κτῆσις. Quo pertinuisse ait legem de anno Jubilæo ne quis quicquam suum pleno jure arbitraretur. οὐ δύναταί μου εἶναι μαθητὴς) Non potest implere officium Christiani.

## 14:34
Vers. 34. Salt is good) Christ used this adage quite often, as also others of that age. The coherence, however, with the preceding is this: By how much any good thing is better, by so much is the same thing worse when it is bad. Salt, while it retains the nature of salt, is best: the same, if it casts off its nature, is worse than clods and dung. Thus, there is nothing more excellent than the profession of Christianity, if the life corresponds: nothing worse, nothing more harmful if the power is absent from the name, which must necessarily happen to those who are occupied with other things.

ἐν τίνι ἀρτυθήσεται (with what shall it be seasoned) The salt itself, of course, as is clear from Mark, lest anyone take it impersonally: thus the heart and if there are similar parts in which the health of the body is situated, they do not have from where they may recover their lost health.

Latin:

Vers. 34. καλὸν τὸ ἅλας) Adagium hoc sæpiuscule Chri- stus usurpavit, ut & alia ejus sæculi. Cohæren tia autem cum superioribus hæc est: Quo quæque res bona sit, est melior, eo eadem mala est pejor. Sal dum salis naturam retinet, optimum est: idem si naturam suam exuat, pejus gleba & fimo. Ita Christianismi professione nihil excellentius, si vita respondeat: nihil pejus, nihil nocentius si nomini vis absit, quod accidere necesse est aliud agentibus.

ἐν τίνι ἀρτυθήσεται) Ipsum sal scilicet, ut ex Marco li- quet, ne quis impersonaliter accipiat: ita cor & si quæ sunt similes partes in quibus corporis sanitas sita est, sanitatem suam amissam non habent unde recupe- rent.

## 14:35
Vers. 35. Neither for the land nor for the dunghill) That is, it neither produces fruit by itself, nor is it useful to another for fruit. For things sprinkled with salt become sterile, whence places devoted to destruction and taken away from human uses were accustomed to be sprinkled with salt. Such are all Christians of faulty life, useless both to themselves and to others.

He that hath ears to hear, let him hear) See Matt. ch. XI. v. 15.

Latin:

Vers. 35. οὔτε εἰς γῆν οὔτε εἰς κοπρίαν) Id est, neque per se fructus profert, neque alteri ad fructum: prodest. Nam sale conspersa sterilescunt, unde loca devota & humanis ademta usibus sale conspergi solebant. Tales sunt omnes mendosæ vitæ Christiani & sibi & aliis inuti- les.

ὁ ἔχων ὦτα ἀκούειν, ἀκουέτω) Vide Matth. cap. XI. v. 15.

## 15:1 Argument
CHAPTER XV.

ARGUMENT AND DIVISION.

To the Pharisees murmuring because of the reception of sinners, Christ opposes an apology, adorned with notable similitudes, concerning the sheep and the lost drachma, found with joy after the search:

and concerning the prodigal son, and the penitent received into favor by the Father. There are three parts: I. The parable of the lost sheep, to v. 7. II. The parable of the lost drachma, to v. 10. III. The parable of the prodigal son, to the final v. 32.

PART I. The parable of the lost sheep.

Vers. 1. ἦσαν δὲ ἐγγίζοντες] This mode of speaking signifies a continuous and daily action: as we have noted above at IV. 31. and elsewhere.

Latin:

CAPUT XV.

ARGUMENTUM ET PAR- TITIO.

Murmurantibus Pharisæis ob susceptionem peccatorum, apologiam opponit Chri- stus, similitudinibus insignibus orna- tam, de ove, & drachma perdita, cum gaudio post inquisitionem reperta:

deque filio prodigo, ac pœnitente in gra- tiam à Patre recepto. Partes sunt tres: I. Parabola de ove perdita, ad v. 7. II. Parabola de perdita drachma, ad v. 10. III. Parabola de filio prodigo, ad vers. 32. fina- lem.

PARS I. Parabola de ove perdita.

Vers. 1. ἦσαν δὲ ἐγγίζοντες] Actum continuum & quoti- dianum genus hoc loquendi significat: ut supra IV. 31. & alibi monuimus.

## 15:2
V. 2. ὅτι ὗτος ἁμαρτωλὸς προσδέχεται καὶ συνεσθίει αὐτοῖς] We have spoken of the iniquity of this complaint at Matt. ch. IX. 12. All the Jews measured the properties of God, all His effects, and all His counsels solely by the Sinaitic covenant. Wherefore, since that covenant granted expiation only for lesser offenses, they themselves also were implacably angry with all who transgressed against the law, beyond those lesser faults: nor did they give any place for repentance, which error drew others with it: for when certain grave offenses of David and others were narrated in the sacred books, they preferred to elevate them with sought-out colors, rather than to acknowledge the magnitude of the pardon along with the magnitude of the crime. Thus they deny that David's sleeping with Bathsheba was adultery: because, forsooth, those departing for military service were accustomed to leave their wives the freedom of divorce: nor that the homicide he committed against Uriah was such, because kings have the right of using citizens against the enemy at any risk to their lives. There is no doubt that, accustomed to these fictions, they easily cast a veil over their own sins. But how much better it would have been to confess what is true, that many testimonies of divine goodness, in no way circumscribed by that covenant which had been conceived according to the reason of times and men, exist both in our souls and in the writings of the prophets, outside of that covenant? But if God is of such a mind that He willingly receives into favor those guilty of even grave crimes who are led by serious repentance, it is sufficiently clear that it is also our duty to imitate divine clemency in this regard, and therefore not to turn away from those who, after grave wickedness, give hope of amendment, such as were those publicans and other men of less approved life, who, unless they were held by a desire for virtue, would by no means have gathered with such zeal to the teacher of all virtue, called him to themselves, and given audience to his words. Christ confirms God's merciful affection in this matter not from the writings of the ancients, which he could have done, but—which was more popular—by arguments sought from the daily experience of men: and he defends his own action by the example of Him whom it is the highest perfection to imitate. But whatever the hardness of the Jews was then against their own countrymen who had departed from the orbit of the law, the same was their inhumanity after Christ was removed from mortal affairs against foreign peoples, as those who, having fallen into the worship of false gods and other crimes, in their judgment deserved to feel no indulgence from God. Therefore, just as here they complain ὅτι ὗτος ἁμαρτωλὸς προσδέχεται καὶ συνεσθίει αὐτοῖς, so in Acts XI. 3 they write this complaint to Peter, ὅτι πρὸς ἄνδρας ἀκροβυστίαν ἔχοντας εἰσῆλθες καὶ συνέφαγες αὐτοῖς. The matter is clearly similar. For they were accustomed to name the ἐθνικὸς together with the publicans and the ἁμαρτωλοῖς Jews, as can be seen in many places of these writings. Christ, seeing that and foreseeing this, responds to the present calumny in such a way that he simultaneously clears away the future one. Wherefore, the ancients do not seem to me to have erred who, in explaining the following three comparisons, join both interpretations.

Those things which Grotius hands down concerning the Sinaitic covenant are not sound: that all the Jews measured the properties of God, all His affections, and all His counsels solely by the Sinaitic covenant. Wherefore, since that covenant granted expiation only for lesser offenses, they themselves also were implacably angry with all who transgressed against the law, beyond those lesser faults: nor did they give any place for repentance. But was there not also in the Sinaitic covenant a promise of expiation and remission of graver sins concerning the sanctions of the Ceremonial Laws? Was not the expiation of all iniquities made through the scapegoat (hircum ἀποπομπαῖον)?

The passage also which Grotius compares here, Acts ch. XI. v. 3, is certainly different, not clearly similar: for there the Jews wrote the complaint to Peter out of ignorance of the calling of the Gentiles already divinely commanded: here, however, the Pharisees reproached Christ for his association with publicans and sinners out of a mere lust for accusing: by which he himself was not polluted, but he was sacrificing them, and calling them back to fruitfulness.

Latin:

V. 2. ὅτι ὗτος ἁμαρτωλὸς προσδέχεται καὶ συνεσθίει αὐτοῖς] De iniquitate hujus querelæ diximus ad Matth. cap. IX. 12. Judæi omnes DEI proprietates, omnes effectus, omnia consilia ex solo fœdere Sinaitico metiebantur. Quare cum id fœdus non nisi minoribus delictis expiationem concederet, ipsi quoque omnibus contra legem delin- quentibus, extra culpas illas minores, implacabiliter irascebantur: neque ullum dabant pœnitentiæ locum, qui error alios secum traxit: nam cum de Davide atque aliis gravia quædam delicta in sacris libris narrentur, illi eadem quæsitis coloribus elevare maluerunt, quam cum magnitudine facinoris magnitudinem veniæ agnoscere. Ita Davidis concubitum cum Bersabea negant adulte- rium fuisse: quia scilicet in militiam secedentes uxoribus relinquere solebant divertendi libertatem: nec quod in Uriam patravit homicidium, quia regibus jus sit utendi civibus adversum hostem quantovis vitæ ipsorum peri- culo. Dubium non est, quin istis commentis assueti, suis ipsi peccatis facile obducerent tectorium. At quanto fuerat satius, fateri quod verum est, multa extra fœdus illud & in animis nostris, & in vatum scriptis testimonia ex- stare divinæ bonitatis neutiquam circumscriptæ eo fœdere, quod pro temporum atque hominum ratione conceptum fuerat? Quod si Deus eo est animo, ut quamvis gra- vium criminum reos seria pœnitentia ductos libenter re- cipiat in gratiam, satis apertum est nostri etiam esse officii divinam hac in parte clementiam imitari, ac proinde non aversari eos, qui post gravia flagitia spem faciunt emendationis, quales erant publicani illi atque alii vitæ minus probatæ homines, qui nisi desiderio tenerentur virtutis, neutiquam ad omnis virtutis magistrum tanto studio convenirent, eum vocarent ad se, ejus verbis præstarent audientiam. Christus Dei hac in re misericor- dem affectum non ex veterum literis, quod poterat, sed quod erat popularius argumentis ex quotidiana hominum experientia petitis confirmat: suumque factum defendit ejus exemplo, quem imitari summa perfectio est. Quæ autem tunc fuit Judæorum duritas, adversus populares suos qui à legis orbita recesserant, eadem fuit post Chri- stuin exemtum rebus mortalibus eorundem inhumanitas adversus populos exteros, ut qui ad falsorum Deorum cultus aliaque scelera prolapsi, ipsorum judicio nullam deberent Dei indulgentiam sentire. Itaque sicut hic queruntur ὅτι ὗτος ἁμαρτωλὸς προσδέχεται καὶ συνεσθίει αὐ- τοῖς, ita Actor. XI. 3. Petro dicam hanc scribunt, ὅτι πρὸς ἄνδρας ἀκροβυστίαν ἔχοντας εἰσῆλθες καὶ συνέφαγες αὐτοῖς. Res plane similis. Nam ipsi ἐθνικὸς nominare solebant simul cum publicanis & Judæis ἁμαρτωλοῖς, ut multis horum scriptorum locis videre est. Christus illud videns, & hoc prævidens, præsenti calumniæ ita respondet ut simul futu- ram diluat. Quare non videntur mihi errasse veteres qui in sequentibus tribus comparationibus explicandis utram- que interpretationem conjungunt.

Proba non sunt, quæ Grotius de fœdere Si- naitico tradit: Judæi omnes Dei proprietates, o- mnes affectus, omnia consilia ex solo fœdere Sina- itico metiebantur. Quare cum id fœdus non nisi minoribus delictis expiationem concederet, ipsi quoque omnibus contra legem delinquentibus, ex- tra culpas illas minores, implacabiliter irasceban- tur: neque ullum dabant pœnitentiæ locum. An- non vero in fœdere etiam Sinaitico facta est promissio expiationis, & remissionis peccato- rum graviorum circa sanctiones Legum Cere- monialium? Annon omnium iniquitatum expia- tio fiebat per hircum ἀποπομπαῖον.

Locus etiam quem confert hic Grotius Act. c. XI. v. 3. ἀλλότερος certe, non plane similis est: ibi enim ex ignorantia vocationis gentium divinitus jam demandatæ Petro dicam scripsere Judæi: hic vero ex mera criminandi libidine Christo conversationem cum publicanis & pec- catoribus exprobrarunt Pharisæi: qua non pol- luebatur ipse, sed sacrificabat ipsos, & ad frugem revocabat.

## 15:4
Vers. 4. τίς ἄνθρωπος ἐξ ὑμῶν ἔχων ἑκατὸν πρόβατα] It is the same little fable as in Matt. XVIII, but proposed with a slightly different end. There, so that we do not offend in the course toward piety those whom God so greatly wills to be saved; here, so that we do not cruelly turn away those whom God pities. Moreover, the word ἐsὶ ought to be understood after ἄνθρωπος, as also below after that γυνὴ in clause 9. For what is ἦ here, is ἔχει there, which must be translated by 'does not'. Tís isi, that is, εἰ 7is is, as we have said elsewhere as often as.

Latin:

Vers. 4. τίς ἄνθρωπος ἐξ ὑμῶν ἔχων ἑκατὸν πρόβατα] Est eadem fabella Matth. XIIX. sed fine paulo diverso proposita. Ibi ne in cursu ad pietatem offendamus eos quos Deus tantopere vult servatos, hic ne eos crudeliter aversemuur quorum Deus miseretur. Subaudiri autem debet post ἄνθρωπος verbum ἐsὶ ut & infra post illud γυνὴ commate 9. Nam quod hic est ἦ, ibi est ἔχει, quod vertendum est per nonne. Tís isi id est εἰ 7is is, ut alio quoties diximus.

## 15:7
Vers. 7. or over ninety-nine just persons] The particle μᾶλλον, which in the Greek manner is here suppressed in the explanation of the comparison; it is expressed by Matthew in the comparison itself. It is said, however, that there will be greater joy, anthropopathically, because things unexpected or nearly despaired of affect us more. Euripides: 'From things unhoped for, grace is greater to mortals, appearing more than what is expected.' It is added, as the Hebrew Masters not badly note, the more difficult a virtue is, the more beautiful it is: 'It is more joyful whenever honesty costs one much.'

But it is much more difficult to break off the habit of vices than to persist in a probable way of life with an unoffended step. For to many, ignorance of vices stands in place of virtue. But also that can be added which we learned above in ch. IX, that it usually happens that those are more fervent in the pursuit of what is right whom the pain of a past life stimulates. For repentance, as Plutarch teaches, is indeed a saving deity. And there is a saying similar to this in the Gemara on the Sanhedrin, ch. XI. 'In the place where those who do penance stand, there the just will not be able to stand.' 'Peace, peace to the far and the near, says the Lord, that I may heal him.' He puts the far first. Who is the far? He who was far from God. But how the interpreter: 'Great is the virtue of those who do penance, so that no creature can stand in their enclosure.' But just as here heavenly joy is proclaimed over a converted sinner, so on the contrary, the Hebrew masters introduce the angels weeping over the sin of the Hebrews.

οἵτινες ὀ χρείαν ἔχουσι μετανοίας] That is, those who have no need to change their whole way of life: as we explained in Matt. ch. IX. v. 12. Christ, however, opposes ninety just persons to one sinner, not that the matter is so: for very few live according to the norm, but that even if the matter were so, for the sake of that one person a great labor would have to be undertaken: how much more when in a most corrupt age there was such a number of sinners, such a paucity of the just.

PART II. Concerning the lost drachma.

Latin:

Vers. 7. ἢ ἐπὶ ἐννενηκονταεννέα δικαίοις] Particula μᾶλλον quæ more Græco hic in comparationis explicatióne subti- cetur; in ipsa comparatione exprimitur a Matthæo. Di- citur autem majus gaudium fore, ἀνθρωποπαθῶς, quia in- sperata aut prope desperata magis nos afficiunt. Euri- pides: Ἐκ τ’ ἀέλπτων ἡ χάρις μείζων βροτοῖς. Φανεῖσα μᾶλλον ἢ τὸ προσδοκώμενον. Accedit, quod ut Hebræorum Magistri non male notant, virtus quo difficilior hoc pulchrior: Lætius est quoties magno sibi constat honestum.

At multo difficilius est abrumpere vitiorum consuetudi- nem, quam probabili vitæ generi insistere non offenso gradu. Multis enim pro virtute est vitiorum ignoran- tia. Sed & illud addi potest quod supra didicimus c. IX. plerumque fieri ut flagrantiores sint in recti studio, quos anteactæ vitæ dolor stimulat. πάνυ γάρ ἡ μεταμέλεια, ut Plutarchus docet, σώτειρα δαίμων. Estque dictum huic simile in Gemara de Synedrio cap. XI. Quo loco consi- stent pœnitentiam agentes ibi justi non poterunt stare. Pa- cem pacem remoto & propinquo ait Dominus ut sanem eum. Præponit remotum. Quis remotus? qui longe abfuit a Deo. At quem locum interpres: Magna est virtus eorum qui pœnitentiam agunt, ita ut nulla creatura in scepto illorum consistere queat. Sicut autem hic gaudium cœleste prædicatur super converso peccatore, ita contra ob peccatum Hebræi flentes angelos inducunt Hebræorum ma- gistri.

οἵτινες ὀ χρείαν ἔχουσι μετανοίας] Id est, quibus non est opus de toto vitæ genere migrare: ut exposuimus Matth. cap. IX. v. 12. Opponit autem Christus nonaginta justos uni peccatori, non quod ita se res habeat: paucissimi enim ad normam vivunt, sed quod etiamsi ita se res haberet, vel unius illius causa labor magnus fuerit suscipiendus: quanto magis cum corruptissimo sæculo tantus esset pec- catorum numerus, tanta justorum paucitas.

PARS II. De drachma perdita.

## 15:10
Vers. 10. before the 7 angels] Thus 'before the 7 angels' above in ch. XII. 8. a description of the heavenly court.

PART III. Concerning the prodigal son.

Latin:

Vers. 10. ἐνώπιον 7 ἀγγέλων] Sic ἔμπροσθεν 7 ἀγγέλων supra cap. XII. 8. descriptio aulæ cœlestis.

PARS III. De filio prodigo.

## 15:12
Vers. 12. the younger of them] The example of a depraved character is aptly placed in the younger: surely as Theognis sang: 'Youth and young age lighten the mind of a man, and lift the spirit of many into error.' But Homer also had said: 'The minds of younger men are always flighty.' Philo's saying does not depart from this: 'God accepts the younger brother who repents more than him who does not sin at all.'

Δός μοι τὸ ἐπιβάλλον μέρος τῆς ὀσίας] Thus Demosthenes said: 'The portion falling to us.' Aristides on concord to the Rhodians: 'The portion falling to you.' Cicero: 'what falls to me.' The jurisconsults: 'My share.' It is accustomed to be used in those places in which commerce and gainful arts flourish, so that when sons have come to full puberty, if they demand it, parents assign some part of their patrimony, from which the sons may make a profit, which part is imputed to the inheritance after the death of the parents. It is credible that a similar custom, if not among the Jews, certainly among the neighbors of the Jews, the Syrophoenicians, flourished in the times of Christ, since he is accustomed to draw examples and comparisons from common things. I think, however, that in the resigned part regarding the patrimony, one should answer not only with τὸ ἀντεξούσιον, as most of the ancients have depicted it, but with all the good things of God, both common ones, such as the heaven, the stars, the earth, the sea, and what is produced in these, and those peculiar to peoples or men, good health, beauty, strength, excellence of intellect, nobility, riches, and if there is anything similar to these, all of which the greater part of men abuse shamefully.

He divided the life to them) Having entered into a plan, he made a partition of the patrimony. For otherwise the elder son, not separating his part, remained in the paternal family living from the father's, as can be seen below in verse 31.

Latin:

Vers. 12. ὁ νεώτερος αὐτῶν] Apposite in juniore po- nitur exemplum depravati ingenii: nimirum ut Theognis cecinit. Ἥβη καὶ νεότης ἐπικουφίζει νόον ἀνδρὸς, Πολλῶν δ’ ἐξαίρει θυμὸν ἐς ἀμπλακίην.
