Sed & Homerus dixerat: Αἰεὶ δ’ ὁπλοτέρων ἀνδρῶν φρένες ἠερέθονται. Non abit hinc Philonis illud: Θεὸς τὸ μετανοοῦν ἀδελφὸν νεώτερον τῷ μηδόλως ἁμαρτάνειν ἀποδέχεται.

Δός μοι τὸ ἐπιβάλλον μέρος τῆς ὀσίας] Ita Demosthenes dixit: Τὸ ἐπιβάλλον ἐφ’ ἡμᾶς μέρος. Aristides de concor- dia ad Rhodios: τὸ ἐπιβάλλον ἐφ’ ὑμᾶς μέρος. Cicero: quod me contingit. Jurisconsulti: Ratam meam partem. Usurpari solet in iis locis in quibus vigent mercimonia & artes quæstuosæ, ut filiis cum venerint ad plenam pu- bertatem, si id deposcant, parentes assignent aliquam pa- trimonii sui partem, ex qua filii quæstum faciant, quæ pars post parentum mortem in hæreditatem imputatur. Similem morem si non apud Judæos, certe apud Ju- dæorum vicinos Syrophœnicas viguisse Christi tempori- bus credibile est, cum soleat a rebus usitatis exempla & comparationes ducere. Respondere autem in resignifi- cata puto huic parti de patrimonio, non solum τὸ ἀντεξ- ούσιον, ut veterum plerique ἐκτυπώσαντες: sed omnia Dei bona, tum communia, ut cœlum, sidera, terram, mare, & quæ in his gignuntur, tum populorum aut hominum peculiaria, valetudinem bonam, pulchritudinem, robur, ingenii præstantiam, nobilitatem, divitias, & si quid his est simile, quibus omnibus pars hominum major flagitio- se abutitur.

Διεῖλεν αὐτοῖς τὸν βίον) Ratione inita partitionem fecit patrimonii. Nam alioqui major filius partem suam non separans mansit in familia paterna de paterno vivens, ut infra commate 31. videre est.

## 15:13
Verse 13. He traveled into a far country) Aptly to the thing signified: For those who cast off the reverence of GOD are said to be far from God, Psalm LXXIII, verse 27.

He scattered) He squandered. For so the Latins speak, Terence: Before he squanders our twenty minae. Cicero: he was squandering public money. It corresponds to the Hebrew פזר.

Living wastefully) Living wickedly. For Gellius interprets ἄσωτον in Latin as 'nequam' (worthless), quite properly if I am not mistaken. Indeed, Cicero also in the third Tusculan Disputations called wickedness the contrary vice to frugality and thinks the word originated from there, because those who are such have nothing in them, whence they are also called 'nihili' (men of nothing): and the praetor's interdict was conceived thus: Since you are wasting your paternal goods and your own substance by your wickedness. But also 'to live perditely' seems to have the same meaning for the Latins, and not badly to correspond to the Greek ἀσώτως.

Latin:

Vers. 13. ἀπεδήμησεν εἰς χώραν μακρὰν) Apte ad rem significatam: Nam μακρύνειν ἀπὸ τοῦ Θεῦ ἑαυτὸς dicun- tur qui reverentiam DEI exuunt, Psalm LXXIII. vers. 27.

Διεσκόρπισε) Dilapidavit. Ita enim Latini loquuntur, Terentius: Priusquam dilapidet nostras viginti minas. Cicero: dilapidabat publicam pecuniam. Respondet He- bræo פזר.

Ζῶν ἀσώτως) זלל Vivens nequiter. Nam ἄσωτον Gel- lius Latine nequam interpretatur, satis proprie ni fallor. Quippe & Cicero Tusculanarum tertio hequitiam dixit contrarium vitium frugalitati ortamque putat inde vo- cem, quod qui tales sint in iis nequicquam sit, unde & nihili homines dicuntur: & interdictum prætoris ita erat conceptum: Quando tu bona tua patria abitaque nequi- tia tua disperdis. Sed & perdite vivere Latinis eundem sensum habere videtur, neque male respondere Græco ἀσώτως.

## 15:14
Verse 14. And having spent all) Thus Demosthenes also said 'to spend the substance'.

A strong famine) What is said here about the famine, the master, the pigs, the husks, all, if I am not mistaken, pertains to describing for us the misery of those who serve vices. Seneca: It is much more difficult to do those things which you do. For what is more idle than the quiet of the mind, what more laborious than anger? What more relaxed than clemency? What more busy than cruelty? Chastity is free, lust is most occupied; finally, the protection of all virtues is easier: vices are cultivated at great cost. That famous saying of Musonius: pleasure departs, baseness remains, whereas in right actions labor departs, honesty remains.

Latin:

Vers. 14. Δαπανήσαντος δὲ αὐτὲ τὰ πάντα) Sic δαπα- νᾶν τὴν ἐσίαν etiam Demosthenes dixit.

Λιμὸς ἰσχυρὸς) Quæ hic dicuntur de fame, de domino, porcis, siliquis, omnia ni fallor eo pertinent, ut nobis de- scribant miseriam eorum qui vitiis serviunt. Seneca: Multo difficilius est facere ista quæ facitis. Quid enim qui- ete otiosius est animi, quid ira laboriosius? quid clementia remissius? quid crudelitate negotiosius? vacat pudicitia, li- bido occupatissima est, omnium denique virtutum tutela faci- lior est: vitia magno coluntur. Præclarum illud Musonii, abire voluptatem, manere turpitudinem, cum in recte fa- ctis abeat labor, maneat honestas.

## 15:15
Verse 15. He joined himself to one of the citizens) He applied himself to a certain citizen: for so Cicero, Livy, and others speak.

Latin:

Vers. 15. ἐκολλήθη ἑνὶ τῶν πολιτῶν) At civem quendam se applicuit: ita enim Cicero, Livius, atque alii loquun- tur.

## 15:16
Verse 16. Of the husks) חרובא, the Syrian and Arab: whence it appears that the passage is understood by both not of the pods of legumes, but of the fruit of those trees which are properly called siliquiferous, because their fruit is in a pod. Whence the peoples of the East call the fruit חרובא, whence Actuarius made 'karrouba': nor do the French, Spaniards, and Italians call it otherwise now, nor did Theophylact begin otherwise here: and it is noted by Pliny that the siliqua grows most in Syria, which I see is taken as the wild one. The same Pliny treats of chestnuts: Other fodder is produced of its own, with scrupulous rumination even within the kernels of the bark. The very sweet husks seem not to be far from this, except that in them the bark itself is eaten.

Latin:

Vers. 16. ἀπὸ τῶν κερατίων) חרובא Syrus & Arabs: unde apparet utrique intellectum locum non de legu- minum teguminbus, sed de fructu earum arborum quæ propriæ siliquiferæ dicuntur, quia earum fructus in sili- qua est. Unde enim fructum Orientis populi חרובא vocant, unde Actuarius fecit καρρούβα: neque aliter nunc Galli, Hispani & Itali appellant, nec aliter hic cœpit Theo- phylactus: & Plinio notatum siliquam in Syria plurimam nasci, quod de silvatica accipi video. Idem Plinius de castaneis agit: Cætera suum pabula gignuntur, scrupulosa corticis intra nucleos quoque ruminatione. Haud procul ab- esse videantur & pradulces siliquæ, nisi quod in iis cortex ipse manditur.

## 15:17
Verse 17. And coming to himself) He who returns to a good mind is also said by the Latins to return to himself.

Latin:

Vers. 17. εἰς ἑαυτὸν δὲ ἐλθὼν) Ad se redire etiam Lati- nis dicitur qui ad bonam mentem redit.

## 15:18
Verse 18. I will say to him, Father, I have sinned) He does not cast the blame on his age, nor on bad advisors, but prepares a naked confession without excuse. Salvianus well: Whoever excuses himself to himself, accuses himself to God. For he who thinks himself to be something when he is nothing, deceives himself. Therefore, let no one's cause be easy to himself: no one escapes more difficultly than he who has presumed that he will escape. Tertullian: In as much as you have not spared yourself, in that much, believe me, God will spare you. Ambrose: He relieves his errors deeply who burdens himself. Seneca: To perform first the parts of an accuser, then of a judge, lastly of a pleader.

To heaven) Scholars note here that heaven is said for GOD, which I think is true, not antonomastically but synecdochically, so that heaven signifies that power which shines most in heaven, שליטין שמיא as Daniel speaks in chapter IV, verse 23. 1 Maccabees chapter III, verse 18. There is no longer a difference before heaven to save by many or by few. Here 'before heaven' is

לפנו וחוה at the end of the chapter ὡς δ' ἂν ἦ θέλημα ἐν ὀυρανῷ ὕτω ποιήσῃ. Matth. c. XXI. v. 25. τὸ βάπτισμα ἰωάννε πόθεν ἦ; ἐξ ὀυρανῦ ἢ ἐξ ἀνθρώπων.

It does not seem so much a Synecdoche as a Metonymy: since heaven is not taken for the power shining most brightly in heaven, but for God, who is in the heavens.

Latin:

Vers. 18. ἐρῶ ἀυτῷ, Πάτερ, ἥμαρτον) Non in ætatem, non in malos consultores culpam rejicit, sed nudam parat sine excusatione confessionem. Salvianus bene: Quicunque sibi se excusat, accusat Deo. Nam qui se exi- stimar esse aliquid cum nihil sit, seipsum seducit. Nemini itaque facilis sua causa sit: nullus difficilius evadit quam qui se evasurum esse præsumserit. Tertullianus. In quan- tum non pepercerit tibi, in tantum tibi Deus, crede, parcet. Ambrosius: Allebat penitus errores qui ipse se onerat Se- neca: Accusatoris primum partibus fungi, deinde judicis, novissime deprecatoris.

εἰς τὸν ὀρανὸν) Notant hic eruditi cœlum pro DEO dici, quod verum puto, non ἀντονομαστικῶς sed συνεκδοχικῶς, ut cœlum significet eam potestatem quæ in cœlo maxime relucet שליטין שמיא ut Daniel loquitur cap. IV. v. 23. 1. Macc. cap. III. vers. 18. ἐκ ἔτι διαφορὰ ἐναντίον τῦ ἐρανῦ σώζειν ἐν πολλοῖς ἢ ἐν ὀλίγοις. Hic ἐναντίον τοῦ ἐρανῦ est

לפנו וחוה fine capitis ὡς δ' ἂν ἦ θέλημα ἐν ὀυρανῷ ὕτω ποιήσῃ. Matth. c. XXI. v. 25. τὸ βάπτισμα ἰωάννε πόθεν ἦ; ἐξ ὀυρανῦ ἢ ἐξ ἀνθρώπων.

Non tam videtur Synecdoche, quam Meto- nymia: quum cœlum non pro potestate, in cœlo maxime relucente accipiatur, sed pro Deo, qui in cœlis est.

## 15:19
Vers. 19. ὀυκέτι εἰμὶ ἄξιος in the plural) All men are sons of God by birth, as this fable declares, but they fall from that right by alienating themselves from God.

Ποίησόν με ὡς) ποιεῖν signifies to treat, not only with the Dative, but also with the Accusative. Matth. cap. V. 44. καλῶς ποιεῖτε τὲς μισῦντας. Matth. c. XXVII. v. 22. τί ἦν ποιήσω ἰησοῦν ἳ λεγόμενον Χρισόν; Rom. IX. 20. τί με ἐποί- ησας ὕτως;

Latin:

Vers. 19. ὀυκέτι εἰμὶ ἄξιος πληθυντικῶς σκ) Homines o- mnes ortu Dei sunt filii, ut hæc fabula declarat, sed eo jure excidunt semet a Deo alienando.

Ποίησόν με ὡς) ποιεῖν non tantum cum Dativo, sed & cum Accusativo significat tractare. Matth. cap. V. 44. καλῶς ποιεῖτε τὲς μισῦντας. Matth. c. XXVII. v. 22. τί ἦν ποιήσω ἰησοῦν ἳ λεγόμενον Χρισόν; Rom. IX. 20. τί με ἐποί- ησας ὕτως;

## 15:20
Vers. 20. κατεφίλησεν ἀυτόν) Among all the parables of Christ this is certainly excellent, full of emotion, and painted with the most beautiful colors. Moreover, besides the likeness of the whole matter, there seems to be in certain parts also τὸ ἀλληγορύ- μενον. For the kiss is undoubtedly a sign of reconciliation. And so here is declared the supreme goodness of God, who forgives the sins of those led by earnest repentance out of the inner movement of His mercy.

Latin:

Vers. 20. κατεφίλησεν ἀυτόν) Inter omnes Christi para- bolas hæc sane eximia est, plena affectuum, & pulcherri- mis picta coloribus. Videtur autem præter similitudinem rei totius, etiam partibus quibusdam inesse τὸ ἀλληγορύ- μενον. Nam osculum haud dubie fignum reconcilia- tionis. Itaque hic declaratur summa Dei bonitas qui seria pœnitudine ductis peccata remittit ex intimo motu misericordiæ suæ.

## 15:21
Vers. 21. Πάτερ, ἥμαρτον) Even after the announcement of forgiveness to a man, it is expedient for him to acknowledge his guilt. Regarding which matter, that saying of Basil is not unworthy of memory: μὴ γίνε κριτὴς ἄνισος ἑαυτῶ, μηδὲ πρὸς χάριν ἐξέταζε, ὠ μέν τι δοκεῖς ἔχειν καλὸν τῦτο ἐν ψήφῳ τιθείς, τῶν δὲ πταισμά- των ἑκὼν ἐπιλανθανόμενος. Μηδὲ ἐφ' οἷς μὲν σήμερον κατωρ- θῶς μεγαλυνόμενος, μηδὲ ἐφ' οἷς δὲ πρώην καὶ πάλαι κα- κῶς εἰργάσω συγχώρησιν ἑαυτῶ διδύς: ἀλλ' ὅταν σε τὸ παρὸν ἐπάρῃ τὸ παλαιὸν εἰς ἀνάμνησιν ἀγέτω κὴ παῦση τῆς ἀκαιρῦντος φλεγμονῆς. Paul provides a notable example of this modesty in 1. Cor. XV. 9. 1. Tim I. 15. Salvianus: It is not never to have done at all to have ceased doing.

Latin:

Vers. 21. Πάτερ, ἥμαρτον) Etiam post annuntiatam ho- mini remissionem expedit illi culpam suam agnoscere. Quam in rem memoratu non indignum est illud Basilii: μὴ γίνε κριτὴς ἄνισος ἑαυτῶ, μηδὲ πρὸς χάριν ἐξέταζε, ὠ μέν τι δοκεῖς ἔχειν καλὸν τῦτο ἐν ψήφῳ τιθείς, τῶν δὲ πταισμά- των ἑκὼν ἐπιλανθανόμενος. Μηδὲ ἐφ' οἷς μὲν σήμερον κατωρ- θῶς μεγαλυνόμενος, μηδὲ ἐφ' οἷς δὲ πρώην καὶ πάλαι κα- κῶς εἰργάσω συγχώρησιν ἑαυτῶ διδύς: ἀλλ' ὅταν σε τὸ παρὸν ἐπάρῃ τὸ παλαιὸν εἰς ἀνάμνησιν ἀγέτω κὴ παῦση τῆς ἀκαιρῦντος φλεγμονῆς. Exemplum hujus modestiæ insigne præbet Paulus 1. Cor. XV. 9. 1. Tim I. 15. Salvianus: Non est nun- quam omnino fecisse facere cessasse.

## 15:22
Vers. 22. τὴν ςολὴν) Just as the αἱ ἀλληγορίαι are not to be anxiously sought in the parts of comparisons, so here they do not seem to be neglected when the comparison of other passages suggests them. Therefore, ςολὴ seems to signify the continuous innocence of life which, God granting, a grateful mind produces because of the benefit of such great indulgence received. Apoc. VI. 11. c. VII. 13. 14. leads the way to this explanation, with the addition of a passage from the same book c. XIX. 8. & Esaias LII. 1.

τὴν πρώτην) I agree with those who draw this word to excellence, not to time, in the way that the Syrian also understood it. Thus Rom. III. 2. & X. 9. & 1. Tim. I. 15. Likewise Matth. XII. 38. We said something also above VI. 1.

It is more correctly rendered by Theophylact as τὴν ἀρχαίαν: with which Titus of Bostra agrees: bring the first robe, which he lost, namely when he departed from the Father, that is, faith, the knowledge of the truth: and clothe him with it, who stripped himself of it. And Chrysologus: The paternal piety is not content to restore innocence alone, unless it also restores the former honor.

δακτύλιον) Among the Romans a sign of free birth, among the peoples of the East a sign of exceptional dignity. Gen. cap. XLI. v. 42. or even of opulence Jac. cap. II. v. 2. Since, however, the use of a ring among other things is to seal, the ancients do not wrongly think that the gift of the Holy Spirit corresponds to the ring, which seals us, as Paul speaks, 2. Cor. I. 21.

καὶ ὑποδήματα εἰς πόδας) It can be explained from Eph. c. VI. v. 15. ὑποδησάμενοι τὲς πόδας ἐν ἑτοιμασίᾳ τῷ ἐυαγγελίυ τῆς εἰρήνης. Namely, to penitents received into favor God also grants this, that they may be fit to teach others either by voice or certainly by example. David in Psalm LI, when he had prayed for forgiveness and the restoration of the Spirit, promises his effort in teaching and converting other sinners.

Latin:

Vers. 22. τὴν ςολὴν) Sicut non conquirendæ sunt an- xie αἱ ἀλληγορίαι in partibus comparationum, ita hic non negligendæ videntur cum eas aliorum locorum compa- ratio suggerat. Videtur ergo ςολὴ fignificare continuam vitæ innocentiam quam Deo dante parit animus gratus ob acceptum tantæ indulgentiæ beneficium. Præit ad hanc explicationem Apoc. VI. 11. c. VII. 13. 14. addito ejusdem libri loco c. XIX. 8. & Esaiæ LII. 1.

τὴν πρώτην) Assentior ad excellentiam, non ad tem- pus hanc vocem trahentibus, quomodo & Syrus accepit. Sic Rom. III. 2. & X. 9. & 1. Tim. I. 15. Item Matth. XII. 38. Diximus aliquid & supra VI. 1.

Rectius Theophylacto redditur τὴν ἀρχαίαν: cui consonat Titus Bostrensis: afferte primam stolam, quam perdidit, nimirum cum a Patre discessit, hoc est, fidem, cognitionem veritatis: ac induite eum illa, qui eam exuit. Et Chrysologus: Paterna pietas non contenta innocentiam reparare solam, nisi & pristinum restituat hono- rem.

δακτύλιον) Apud Romanos ingenuitatis, apud Orientis populos dignitatis eximiæ fignum. Gen. cap. XLI. v. 42. aut etiam opulentiæ Jac. cap. II. v. 2. Cum autem annuli usus inter alia fit signare, non male veteres respondere an- nulo putant donum Spiritus S. qui nos obsignat, ut loqui- tur Paulus, 2. Cor. I. 21.

καὶ ὑποδήματα εἰς πόδας) Explicari potest ex Eph. c. VI. v. 15. ὑποδησάμενοι τὲς πόδας ἐν ἑτοιμασίᾳ τῷ ἐυαγγελίυ τῆς εἰρήνης. Nimirum pœnitentibus in gratiam receptis etiam hoc Deus concedit, ut apti sint aliis aut voce aut certe exemplo docendis. David in Psalmo LI. cum orasset veniam & restitutionem Spiritus, pollicetur operam suam in docendis, convertendisque aliis peccatoribus.

## 15:23
Vers. 23. ἐυφρανθῶμεν) We said above c. XII. 19. that we see τροφὴν & ἐυφροσύνην distinguished in Acts XIV. 17.

Latin:

Vers. 23. ἐυφρανθῶμεν) Supra diximus c. XII. 19. τροφὴν & ἐυφροσύνην distingui videmus Act. XIV. 17.

## 15:24
Vers. 24. Νεκρὸς ἦν) See at Matt. chap. VIII. vers. 22. The life of the body is the soul, the life of the soul is GOD. Philo, in the first book of his Allegories, defines the death of the soul as the corruption of virtue and the assumption of vice, that is, as he himself explains, when the soul dies to the life of virtue and lives to that of vice. Elsewhere he says that the wicked, even if they drag out their lives to old age, are dead, being deprived of a life with virtue. Likewise, the good and virtue are life, but evil and vice are death. Add Apoc. III. 1. Eph. V. v. 14.

Latin:

Vers. 24. Νεκρὸς ἦν) Vide ad Matth. cap. IIX. vers. 22. Vita corporis animus, vita animi DEUS. Philo ἀλληγο- ριῶν primo, mortem animi definit ἀρετῆς φθορὰν, κακίας ἀνάληψιν, id est ut ipse explicat, ὅταν ἡ ψυχὴ ῾ν ἀρετῆς βίον θνήσκῃ, ῾τ δὲ κακίας ζῇ. Alibi dicit τὺς φαύλες ἄχρι γήρως ὑσάτε παρατείνοντας νεκρὸς εἶναι ᾿η μετ' ἀρετῆς βίον ἀφῃρημένως. Item τὸ μὲν ἀγαθὸν καὶ ἡ ἀρετή, ἐςιν ἡ ζωὴ. Τὸ δὲ κακὸν καὶ ἡ κακία θάνατος. Adde Apoc. III. 1. Eph. V. v. 14.

## 15:25
Vers. 25. He heard music and dancing) The Syrian thought it was hendiadys, because it is choirs that sing together. For a choir is of young men and boys singing, according to Ammonius. Otherwise it signifies a dance, in the way the Arab takes it. Moreover, there was among the peoples of the East a not dishonorable dance, as noted elsewhere.

Latin:

Vers. 25. ἤκουσε συμφωνίας κῂ χορῶν) Syrus putavit esse ἐν διὰ δυοῖν, quia chori sunt qui concinnunt. χόρος enim νέων καῖ παίδων ᾠδόντων Ammonio. Alias χορείαν significat, quo- modo sumit Arabs. Erat autem apud Orientis populos non inhonesta saltatio, ut alibi notatum.

## 15:29
V. 29. Having passed by) He said 'having passed by,' which is more frequently called 'transgressing,' as in the Golden Verses: 'where have I transgressed?'

Latin:

V. 29. παρελθὼν) παρερχοῖς dixit quod frequentius di- citur παραβαίνων, ut in aureo carmine πῆ παρέβην.

## 15:30
V. 30. He who has devoured your living) The 'you' omitted by the Latin translator is correctly acknowledged by the Syrian and the Arab: for it increases the odium of the speech, that he had devoured goods not sought by himself but received from his father.

Latin:

V. 30. ὁ καταφαγών σου τὸν βίον) συ à Latino prætermis- sum, recte agnoscunt Syrus & Arabs: auget enim oratio- nis invidiam, quod ille bona non à se quæsita sed à patre accepta abligurierat.

## 15:31
Vers. 31. You are always with me, and all that is mine is yours) Paulus the Jurisconsult: In one's own heirs, the continuation of ownership appears more clearly to lead the matter to the point that there seems to have been no inheritance, as if these were once masters who are considered masters in a certain way even while the father is alive, whence also the son of the family is called just as the father of the family: hence that expression in the Comedies, 'the younger master.' However, this comparison does not signify that it will grieve those who have always been pious that the penitent are received into grace: but rather that, from this, no ground for just complaint is given. Furthermore, it is a concession. For neither had the Pharisees and the lawyers lived according to the prescription of the divine law, but since they wished to appear as such, Christ, by granting this as it were to them, shows that not even so is there any reason why they should envy the penitent, since nothing is taken away from them by it. Compare what is in Matthew 20:12 and following. Tertullian, in 'On Modesty,' after he had mentioned this passage: He therefore placed them (the Jews) in the parable, not as they were, but as they ought to have been.

Latin:

Vers. 31. σὺ πάντοτε μετ' ἐμοῦ εἶ, καὶ πάντα τὰ ἐμὰ, σά ἐστι) Paulus Jurisconsultus: In suis hæredibus evidentius apparet continuationē dominii eo rem perducere, ut nulla videatur hære- ditas fuisse, quasi olim hi Domini essent qui etiam vivo Patre quodammodo Domini existimantur, unde etiam filius familias appellatur sicut Paterfamilias: hinc illud in Comœdiis, he- rus minor. Non significat autem hæc comparatio, his qui pii semper fuerunt doliturum quod pœnitentes recipiantur in gratiam: sed illud potius, nullam hinc dari juste querendi materiam. Præterea est συγχώρησις. Neque enim Pharisæi & Legisperiti vixerant ad præscriptum divinæ legis, sed cum tales videri vellent, Christus hoc velut illis largiens, ostendit nec sic quidem esse cur veniam invideant pœnitentibꝫ, cum per eam nihil ipsis discedat. Confer quod est Matth. 20, 12. & sequentibus. Tertullianus de pudicitia postquam hujus loci meminerat: Posuit ergo illos (Judæos) in parabola, etsi non quales erant, sed quales esse debuerant.

## 16:1 Argument
CHAPTER XVI. ARGUMENT AND DIVISION.

The parable of the unjust steward, who squandered his master's goods, with an admonition about making friends in time, and about faithfulness, and not serving Mammon: concerning the Pharisees justifying themselves, a pride abominable to God: concerning the kingdom of God suffering violence, and the apex of the Word of God not perishing: concerning divorce: concerning the rich glutton, and Lazarus, the life and end of life of both, and the glutton's vain concern for his brothers in hell.

There are two parts: I. Concerning the unjust steward with the refutation of the Pharisees' illusion, and their just correction, up to verse 18. II. Concerning the rich glutton and the poor Lazarus, up to verse 31.

Vers. 1. Steward) That the Latin translator says 'bailiff' for 'dispenser,' he did so according to the custom of his age. For long before that, that word had begun to be used outside its native sense: indeed, Juvenal even called the prefect of the city a 'bailiff'.

Latin:

CAPUT XVI. ARGUMENUTM ET PARTITIO.

Parabola de injusto œconomo, qui Domini bo- na dilapidavit, cum admonitione de paran- dis tempestive amicis, & de fidelitate, ac non serviendo Mammonæ: de Pharisæis seipsos justificantibus, fastu Deo abomi- nabili: de regno Dei vim patiente, & non perituro apice Verbi Dei: de divortio: de divite epulone, & Lazaro, utriusque vita, & exitu vitæ, ac epulonis irrita in inferno de fratribus solicitudine.

Partes sunt duæ: I. De injusto œconomo cum illusione Pharisæorum retusa, justaque eorum correctione, ad v. 18. II. De divite epulone, & paupere Lazaro, ad v. 31.

Vers. 1. οἰκονόμον) Quod pro dispensatore Latinus inter- pres villicum dicit, more fecit seculi sui. Pridem enim vox illa extra nativum sensum proferri cœperat: quin & præfe- ctum urbi villicum dixit Juvenalis.

## 16:2
Vers. 2. Give an account of your stewardship) He set a time for him to render accounts, upon the completion of which he would depart from his office. The meaning of the disease, and whatever else reminds us of mortality, corresponds to this summons.

Latin:

Vers. 2. ἀπόδος τὸν λόγον σου) Tempus illi præstituit red- dendis rationibus, quibus expunctis ab actu discederet. Huic interpellationi respondentin re significata morbi, & si quid aliud nos mortalitatis admonet.

## 16:3
Vers. 3. He takes away the stewardship from me) As with Shebna, Isaiah 22:19.

I am not strong enough to dig) Thus in Aristophanes' 'Birds,' someone seeking a living by informing defends himself thus: 'For what shall I do? For I do not know how to dig.' And not much different is that of the same: 'But if I were to owe, I would be silent; for I would not be strong enough to play the cithara.'

ἐπαιτεῖν) προσαετεῖν, our author used this for the same thing in ch. 18, 35. Mark 10, 46. John 9, 8. αἰτεῖν ἐλεημοσύνην, our author in Acts 3, 2. Tyrtæus said:

To be a beggar is the most wretched of all things.

Latin:

Vers. 3. ἀφαιρεῖται τὴν οἰκονομίαν ἀπ' ἐμοῦ) Ut Sibnæ, Esaias XXII. 19.

σκάπτειν οὐκ ἰσχύω) Sic apud Aristophanem avibus, qui- dam delaturis victum quæritans ita se defendit: τί γὰρ πά- θω; σκάπτειν γὰρ οὐκ ἐπίσταμαι. Nec multum dissimile illud ejusdem εἰ δ' ὀφείλοιλο, σύγλαυδ' κιθαρίζειν γὰρ οὐκ ἰχύ- σαιμι.

ἐπαιτεῖν) προσαετεῖν pro eodem dixit hic noster c. 18, 35. Marc. 10, 46. Joh. 9, 8. αἰτεῖν ἐλεημοσύνην noster Actor. 3, 2. Tyrtæus dixit:

Πτωχεύειν πάντων ἐς' ἀνηρότατον.

## 16:4
Vers. 4. δέξωνταί με) That is, so that there may be those who receive me. For the noun is understood.

Latin:

Vers. 4. δέξωνταί με) Id est, ut sint qui me recipiant. Nomen enim subauditur.

## 16:5
Vers. 5. βάτους) See Josephus, Antiquities VIII. 2.

Latin:

Vers. 5. βάτους) Vide Josephum antiquæ historiæ VIII. 2.

## 16:6
τὸ γράμμα) The Latin interpreter translated this very well as 'cautionem' (bond/security). For this is what the Jurisconsults call what the Greeks call a 'syngrapha' or 'chirographa'. Tertullian and Salvian also use the word 'cautio' in this sense. But the same interpreter also used 'literas' (letters/documents), which was not bad, except that there was no reason for varying the term. The title of Roman law concerning the obligations of documents (literarum obligationibus) bears witness to this. The word 'tabulae' (tablets), which others prefer, does not signify bonds but the ledger of receipts and expenditures: whence 'novae tabulae', that is, the abolition of debts. It should be noted, however, that it is imagined that this steward had the bonds in his possession, examples of which custom can also be seen in Roman law.

Latin:

τὸ γράμμα) Optime Latinus interpres cautionem vertit. Ita enim Jurisconsulti vocant, quod Græci Syngrapham aut chirographam. Eandem cautionis vocem hoc sensu usurpat Tertullianus & Salvianus. Sed & literas idem interpres, nisi quod nulla erat variandi causa, non male. Testa- tur juris Romani titulus de literarum obligationibus. Ta- bularum vox, quam præferunt alii, non syngraphas sed codicem accepti expensique significat: unde novæ tabu- læ, id est rationum abolitio. Notandum est autem fingi pe- nes hunc dispensatorem fuisse syngraphas, cujus moris exempla etiam in jure Romano conspicere est.

## 16:8
Vers. 8. τὸν οἰκονόμον τῆς ἀδικίας) That is, τὸν ἄδικον, as the Syrian correctly interprets it according to Hebraism. Just as where it is said below ὁ κριτὴς τῆς ἀδικίας, lest anyone think that τῆς ἀδικίας is connected with that ἐπῄνεσεν. Although in an iniquitous act, the Lord could not but approve the shrewdness of the steward, and in this shrewdness lies the force of the parable, not in the wickedness of the act. But the argument is drawn from the lesser. If shrewd wickedness is praised, how much more so is prudence joined with virtue. Thus below in the said chapter 18: If an unjust man is moved by persistent importunity, how much more so is that good God by constant prayer. Similar is what we had above in ch. XI. 13.

ὅτι οἱ υἱοὶ) These are the words of Christ proceeding to the explanation of the parable: therefore, for the sake of interpretation, 'διὸ λέγω ὑμῖν' was added by some, which is sufficiently understood.

τῷ αἰῶνι τούτῳ) Who care for nothing but the comforts of this life. To the Hebrews, בני עלמא.

ὑπὲρ τοὺς υἱοὺς τοῦ φωτὸς) He thus calls all those who have been illuminated by some light, that is, by the knowledge of a better life, of whom, however, a great part neglects to enter the way that leads to the indicated good. Thus, the Jews of old, compared to the nations, could rightly be called sons of light, and now all Christians, 1 Thess. V. 5.

εἰς τὴν γενεὰν τὴν ἑαυτῶν) It is a Hebraism, בתולדתם, that is, in the conducting of their affairs: for the Hebrews also call actions תולדות; that is, γενεὰς, as appears in Gen. 6, 9 and ch. 37, 2, in which place the cause of the descent into Egypt is called the 'generatio' (γενεὰ) of Jacob.

Latin:

Vers. 8. τὸν οἰκονόμον τῆς ἀδικίας) Id est, τὸν ἄδικον, ut recte interpretatur Syrus ex Hebraïsmo. Sicut & ubi in- fra dicitur ὁ κριτὴς τῆς ἀδικίας, ne quis putet τῆς ἀδικίας co- hærere cum illo ἐπῄνεσεν. Quamvis in facto iniquo, non potuit Dominus non probare solertiam dispensatoris, atque in hac solertia sita est vis similitudinis, non in facti improbi- tate. Sed à minori argumentum ducitur. Si laudatur solers improbitas, quanto magis prudentia cum virtute conjuncta. Sic infra dicto capite 18. Si homo improbus assiduis flagi- tationibus movetur, quanto magis bonus ille Deus con- stanti prece. Simile est quod habuimus supra c. XI. 13.

ὅτι οἱ υἱοὶ) Verba sunt Christi pergentis ad explicationem fabellæ: ideo interpretamenti causa adjectum à nonnullis διὸ λέγω ὑμῖν, quod subauditi satis est.

τῷ αἰῶνι τούτῳ) Qui nihil aliud curant quam vitæ hujus commoda. Hebræis בני עלמא.

ὑπὲρ τοὺς υἱοὺς τοῦ φωτὸς) Ita vocat omnes eos qui luce ali- qua, id est vitæ melioris cognitione illustrati sunt, quorum tamen magna pars negligit viam inire quæ ducit ad mon- stratum bonum. Ita olim Judæi comparati nationibus re- cte dici poterant filii lucis, & nunc Christiani omnes, 1. Thess. V. 5.

εἰς τὴν γενεὰν τὴν ἑαυτῶν) Hebraïsmus est בתולדתם, id est in rebus suis agendis: nam actiones etiam Hebræi תולדות; id est γενεὰς vocant, ut apparet Gen. 6, 9. & c. 37, 2. quo loco causa descensionis in Ægyptum vocatur γενεὰ Jacobi.

## 16:9
Vers. 9. κἀγὼ ὑμῖν λέγω) By this connection, Christ signifies that we are not so much the owners of the goods we possess as we are stewards. Philo: 'First, he says, we possess nothing good as our own, but whatever you might think you have, it belongs to another; from which it is gathered that all things are gifts to God, and not of the creation that is with Him and stretches out its hands to receive; second, even if you receive, do not receive it for yourself as a loan or a deposit. Having considered what was given to the one who deposited it, return it as a symbol, having justly and fittingly exchanged an older grace for a newer one that precedes it. For many have become wicked from deposits, misusing the things of others as their own out of boundless greed.' Seneca: 'Why do you spare it as if it were your own? You are stewards.'

ἐκ τοῦ μαμωνᾶ τῆς ἀδικίας) From those goods which are most found among the unjust and are made the most of by the unjust: and by this they are proven not to be true goods. See below v. 11. The Chaldean interpreter of Job also said ממון השקר, the mammon of unrighteousness.

ἵνα ὅταν ἐκλίπητε) Plato called the dead ἐκλείποντας, as the LXX sometimes do. Irenaeus's translator cites this passage thus: 'when you have been put to flight.' And indeed ἐκλείπειν is accustomed to have this meaning as well. But I would prefer that τὰ μαμωνᾶ be understood from the preceding, so that the full expression is ὅταν ἐκλίπητε τὰ μαμωνᾶ, 'when you are destitute of those riches'; nor did the Syrian take it otherwise. For he translates it כד יגמר, that is, 'when it shall have failed,' namely τὸ μαμωνᾶ. This, however, makes well for the comparison, for when one must die, riches leave us, and consequently the stewardship entrusted to us also reaches its end. Martial: 'Seize, heap up, carry off, possess, it must be left behind.'

Δέξωνται ὑμᾶς) That is, 'may they cause you to be received,' and they cause this by being helped by us when they are in need, in much the same way that parents, when honored and observed, are said to prolong life, Exodus 20:12. Furthermore, we ought to remember here also what was said above regarding that passage, πλὴν τὰ ἐνόντα δότε ἐλεημοσύνην, καὶ ἰδὺ πάντα καθαρὰ ὑμῖν ἐστὶν, that such effects are attributed to works of mercy, not as solitary and bare acts, but as companions of true repentance. There are many things in the first book of Salvian against avarice which bring light to these words of Christ: among them also this: 'Therefore, let him offer, even when dying, to free his soul from everlasting punishments, because he can no longer do anything else, at least his substance: but let him offer it, however, with compunction, with tears: let him offer it with sorrow, with mourning: for otherwise what is offered does not profit, because they please not by price but by affection: for it is not the mind of the giver that is commended by the gifts, but the gifts by the mind: nor does money insinuate (that is, commend) faith, but faith commends money.' And by this, he who wishes to profit himself should offer what he offers to God in this way: 'for man does not bestow a benefit upon God in those things which he has given, but God does upon man in those things which He has received, because even what man has is a gift of God and his Lord: and by this, in these things offered by man, man does not return his own, the Lord receives His own.' Therefore, when anyone offers his resources to God, let him not offer as if with the presumption of a giver, but as if with the humility of one paying a debt: nor let him believe that he is absolving his sins, but lightening them: nor let him offer with the confidence of redemption, but with the duty of supplication: nor as if returning the whole debt, but as if desiring to return even a little of a great one, because even if he hands over what he has according to the measure of things, he does not return what he owes according to the magnitude of his sins: and therefore, although he offers, let him pray to God that his slow offering may please Him, lamenting the very fact that he offers late; lamenting and repenting that he did not do so sooner. Tobit

The writer once said: As you have according to your means, do alms from them; if you have little, according to that little do not fear to do alms. For you are storing up a good treasure for yourself against the day of need. Because alms rescues from death, and does not allow one to enter into darkness; for alms is a good gift to all who do it before the Most High. Add what we have said to Matthew chapter VI.20.

into the eternal tabernacles] I think that tabernacles here means nothing other than dwellings: Paul said in 2 Cor. V. 1, an eternal house not made with hands in the heavens, where he also uses the word tabernacle: for there is no allusion here to the tabernacle of the temple as in the Epistle to the Hebrews.

Latin:

Vers. 9. κἀγὼ ὑμῖν λέγω) Hac connexione Christus si- gnificat, bonorum quæ possidentur non tam proprietarios nos esse quam dispensatores. Philo: Πρῶτον μὲν ἴδιον, φησὶν, οὐδὲν ἔχομεν ἀγαθὸν, ἀλλ' ὅτι ἂν νομίσῃς ἔχειν, ἑτέρου παρέρχεσθαι ἐξ ᾧ συνάγεται, ὅτι θεῷ τὰ διδόνθ' εὑρήματα πάντα, ἀλλ' οὐ τῆς μετ' αὐτοῦ καὶ τὰς χεῖρας εἰς τὸ λαβεῖν προτεινούσης γενέσεως· δεύ- τερον δὲ, κἂν λάβῃς, λάβε μὴ σεαυτῷ δάνειον δὲ ἢ παρακαθήκην. νομίσας τὸ δοθὲν τῷ παρακαταθεμένῳ καὶ σύμβολόν τι ἀπόδος, πρεσβυτέραν χάριν χάριτι νεωτέρᾳ προκατάρχουσαν ἀπεκλίσασα δικαίως κὶ προσηκόντως ἀμειψάμενος. πολλοὶ γὰρ ἐκ παρακα- ταθηκῶν πονηροὶ ἐγένοντο, τοῖς ἀλλοτρίοις ὡς ἰδίοις ὑπ' ἀμέτρου τῆς πλεονεξίας καταχρησάμενοι. Seneca: Quid tanquam tuo parcis? procuratores.

ἐκ τοῦ μαμωνᾶ τῆς ἀδικίας) Ex illis bonis quæ maxime in- veniuntur apud injustos & ab injustis maximi fiunt: eoque probantur non esse vera bona. Vide infra v. II. Chal- dæus etiam Jobi interpretes dixit ממון השקר μαμωνᾶ ἀ- δικίας.

ἵνα ὅταν ἐκλίπητε) Plato ἐκλείποντας dixit mortuos, ut LXX. interdum. Irenæi interpres ita citat hunc locum quando fugati fueritis. Et sane solet ἐκλείπειν etiam hunc habere sensum. Sed malim subaudiri ex præcedentibus τὰ μαμωνᾶ, ut plena locutio sit ὅταν ἐκλίπητε τὰ μαμωνᾶ cum divitiis illis destituemini; nec aliter accepit Syrus. Vertit enim כד יגמר, id est, cum defecerit, nempe τὸ μαμωνᾶ. Bene autem hoc ad comparationem facit, nam cum mo- riendum est, relinquunt nos divitiæ, ac proinde finem quo- que accipit credita dispensatio. Martialis: Rape, congere, aufer, posside, relinquendum est.

Δέξωνται ὑμᾶς) Id est efficiant ut recipiamini, id autem efficiunt egenti à nobis adjuti, eo ferme modo quo parentes culti atque observati dicuntur vitam bonis producere Exod. 20, 22. Cæterum meminisse & hic debemus quod di- ctum est supra ad illum locum, πλὴν τὰ ἐνόντα δότε ἐλεημο- σύνην, καὶ ἰδὺ πάντα καθαρὰ ὑμῖν ἐστὶν, operibus misericordiæ non solis atque nudis, sed ut comitibus veræ pœnitentiæ tales effectus tribui. Multa sunt in libro primo Salviani contra avaritiam quæ lucem adferunt his Christi verbis: in- ter ea & hoc: Offerat ergo vel moriens ad liberandam de peren- nibus pœnis animam suam, quia aliud jam non potest, sal- tem substantiam suam: sed offerat tamen cum compun- ctione, cum lacrymis: offerat cum dolore, cum luctu: Ali- ter quippe oblata non prosunt, quia non pretio sed affectu pla- cent: nec enim animus dantis datis, sed animo commenden- tur data: nec pecunia fidem insinuat (id est commendat) sed pecuniam fides. Ac per hoc qui prodesse sibi vult, quæ Deo offert hoc modo offerat: nec enim homo Deo præstat beneficium in his quæ dederit, sed Deus in his homini quæ acceperit, quia etiam quod homo habet Dei ac Domini sui munus est: ac per hoc in his offeruntur ab homine, ho- mo non suum reddit, Dominus suum recipit. Itaque cum offert Deo quispiam facultates suas, non offerat quasi præsumtione donantis, sed quasi humilitate solventis: nec absolvere se peccata sua credat sed adlevare: nec offerat cum redemptionis fiducia, sed tum supplicationis officio: nec quasi totum debi- tum reddens, sed quasi vel parum de magno reddere cupiens, quia etiam si tradat quod habet pro modo rerum, non reddit quod debet pro magnitudine peccatorum: & ideo licet offerat, oret Deum ut lenta sua placeat oblatio, plangens id ipsum quod tarde offert; plangens & pœnitens quod non prius. Tobiæ

Scriptor olim dixerat: ὡς σοὶ ὑπάρχῃ κατὰ τὸ πλῆθος, ποίησον ἐξ αὐτῶν ἐλεημοσύνην· ἐὰν ὀλίγον σοι ὑπάρχῃ κατὰ τὸ ὀλίγον μὴ φοβᾶ ποιεῖν ἐλεημοσύνην. θέμα γὰρ ἀγαθὸν θησαυρίζεις σεαυτῷ εἰς ἡμέραν ἀνάγκης. διότι ἐλεημοσύνη ἐκ θανάτου ῥύεται, καὶ ἐκ ἐᾷ εἰσελθεῖν, εἰς τὸ σκότος· δῶρον γὰρ ἀγαθόν ἐστιν ἐλεημοσύνη πᾶσι τοῖς ποιοῦσιν αὐτὴν ἐνώπιον τῶ ὑψίστου. Adde quæ diximus ad Matthæi cap. VI.20.

εἰς τὰς αἰωνίας σκηνὰς] Σκηνὰς hic nihil aliud esse puto quam habitacula: οἰκίαν ἀχειροποίητον αἰώνιον ἐν τοῖς ὀυρανοῖς dixit Paulus 2. Cor. V. 1. ubi etiam σκήνους vocem usurpat: neque enim ad templi σκηνὴν hic alluditur ut in Epistola ad Hebræos.

## 16:10
V. 10. He who is faithful in a very little, is faithful also in much] Masters are accustomed to test the faithfulness of their servants in a matter of no great value, and from that to make a conjecture about greater things. See Matt. 25, 21. 23. Indeed, in a proverb, a just man is said to desire not even a needle. It is enough, however, if there is some probability in the maxims: for it is not required that they always hold true. The much here is that which is of great value, as much reward Gen. XV. 5.

and he who is unjust in a very little, is unjust also in much] Euripides: For whoever is born to have more, thinks nothing just, nor does he wish to.

Latin:

V. 10. ὁ πιστὸς ἐν ἐλαχίστῳ, καὶ ἐν πολλῷ πιστός ἐστι] Solent heri famulorum suorum fidem in re non magni pretii ex- plorare, atque inde de majoribus conjecturam facere. Vi- de Matth. 25, 21. 23. Sane & in proverbio vir justus dicitur μηδὲ βελόνης ἐπιθυμεῖν. Satis autem est, si in sententiis ali- quid sit probabilitatis: neque enim requiritur ut semper lo- cum habeant. τὸ πολὺ hic est id quod magni est pretii, ut μισθὸς πολὺς Gen. XV. 5.

καὶ ὁ ἐν ἐλαχίστῳ ἄδικος, καὶ ἐν πολλῷ ἄδικός ἐστι] Euripides: Ὅστις γὰρ ἐπὶ τὸ πλέον ἔχειν πέφυκ᾽ ἀνὴρ, οὐδὲν φρονεῖ δίκαιον, οὐδὲ βούλεται.

## 16:11
V. 11. in the unrighteous mammon] See what we said above v. 9. who will entrust the true to you?] Luke declines mammon in a more Greek fashion and understands by the true mammon the gift of God, which is also called the gift of the Holy Spirit. This gift God does not ordinarily grant except to those who for some time have proved themselves to God through works of repentance, in which matter it differs much from those riches which are wont to be sought through illicit means. The word true often has a signification of excellence. See the Gospel of John I.1.

Latin:

V. 11. ἐν τῷ ἀδίκῳ μαμωνᾷ] Vide quæ supra v. 9. τὸ ἀληθινόν τις ὑμῖν πιστεύσει;] Lucas μαμωνᾶ declinat ὠδιτέρως & τὸ ἀληθινὸν μαμωνᾶ intelligit τὴν δωρεὰν τοῦ Θεοῦ quæ & δωρεὰ τοῦ ἁγίου πνεύματος dicitur. Hoc donum or- dinarie Deus non concedit nisi eis qui aliquamdiu per opera pœnitentiæ Deo se probaverunt, qua in re multum distat à divitiis illis quæ per illicita quæri solent. Habet autem vox ἀληθινὸν sæpe excellentiæ significatione. Vid. Evang. Joh.I.1.

## 16:12
Vers. 12. in that which is another's] We saw above that things are called another's by Philo which are entrusted to us by God under the burden of stewardship. Christ opposes to these your own, that which will be to men inalienable, not to be accounted for, proper and perpetual: namely, the possession of eternal life. Nor do I think the same thing is said here as in the previous maxim: there, goods are compared among themselves, greater with lesser, but still such that human faithfulness and industry are required for their use: here, it is a matter of the reward of faithfulness and industry. For it is customary for stewards of a master's affairs to be assigned something for their stewardship, which becomes their own.

Latin:

Vers. 12. ἐν τῷ ἀλλοτρίῳ] Ἀλλότρια etiam supra Philoni vidimus dici quæ nobis a Deo sub onere dispensationis sunt credita. His opponit Christus τὸ ὑμέτερον, id quod homini- bus erit ἀναφαίρετον, ἀνεκλόγητον, proprium atq; perpetuum: vitæ scilicet æternæ possessionem. Neq; enim idem hic puto dici quod in sententia superiore: ibi bona inter se compa- rantur majora minoribus, sed talia tamen ad quorum usum requiratur humana fides & industria: hic de fidei atque in- dustriæ præmio agitur. Solet enim dispensatoribus rerum dominicarum pro dispensatione aliquid assignari, quod ipforum fiat proprium.

## 16:13
V. 13. No servant] See regarding this maxim at Matthew. It is connected very well here to the preceding. For those serve Mammon to whom the chief concern is about riches: and to this concern, illiberality and lack of mercy are usually joined.

Latin:

V. 13. οὐδεὶς οἰκέτης] Vide de hac sententia ad Matthæ- um. Optime autem hic superioribus connectitur. Nam serviunt Mammonæ quibus præcipuum circa divitias est studium: huic autem studio cohærere solet illiberalitas & inmisericordia.

## 16:14
and the Pharisees] As those who were accustomed to join the crowd of listeners, intending to seize an opportunity for calumny: above c. XI. 54.

V. 14. they sneered] They mocked him as teaching things alien to the law, which promises great riches to men. But they understood well enough that no one could either acquire or retain great riches if one had to help the needy with such liberality as Christ's words demanded. Such a severe prescription of liberality could not but be unpleasant or even ridiculous to the greedy. This is what Paul says: the natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God, for they are foolishness to him, 1 Cor. II. 14. Which Lactantius explains thus: The precepts of justice are bitter to the vicious and those living badly. Chrysostom does not badly compare such people to those with vertigo, to whom nothing seems to stand still, or to those with a corrupted palate to whom nothing tastes right. We shall have to sneer also below c. XXIII. 34. Paul also uses the word to sneer. The Greeks in the Proverbs translate the Hebrew with this word.

Not the precepts of the law, which Christ leaves intact, but false opinions and Pharisaical avarice made Christ's prescription unpleasant; which was certainly not alien to the law, but in agreement with it: since in the law we are commanded to love our neighbor as ourselves. Moreover, that mockery is referred not so much to that precept of Christ, as to his Evangelical doctrine, which they turned up their noses at, and met with satires: establishing their own righteousness, as Paul speaks, but not submitting themselves to the righteousness of faith Rom. X. 3.

Latin:

καὶ οἱ Φαρισαῖοι] Ut qui se turbæ audientium jungere so- lerent, captaturi calumniæ occasionem: supra c. XI. 54.

V. 14. ἐξεμυκτήριζον] Irriserunt tanquam docentem a- liena à lege quæ magnas divitias hominibus promittit. Satis autem intelligebant neminem posse magnas divitias aut acquirere aut retinere, si tanta liberalitate succur- rendum esset egentibus quantam Christi verba exigebant. Non poterat avaris non ingrata aut etiam non ridicula esse tam severa liberalitatis præscriptio. Hoc est quod Paulus ait: ψυχικὸς δὲ ἄνθρωπος οὐ δέχεται τὰ τοῦ πνεύματος τοῦ θεοῦ μωρία γὰρ αὐτῷ ἐστιν, 1. Cor. II. 14. Quod Lactantius ita ex- plicat: Amara sunt vitiosis & male viventibus præcepta justi- tiæ. Chrysostomus tales non male comparat vertiginosis, quibus nihil stare videtur, aut palato corruptis quibus nihil recte sapit. Ἐκμυκτηρίζειν habebimus & infra c. XXIII. 34. Voce μυκτηρίζειν utitur & Paulus. Græci in Proverbiis hac voce reddunt Hebræum.

Non legis præcepta quæ sarta tecta relinquit Christus, sed falsæ opiniones & avaritia Pharisaica ingratam faciebant præscriptionem Christi; quæ utique à lege aliena non erat, sed ei consentanea: quum in lege jubeamur proximum diligere sicut nosmetipsos. Cæterum refertur irrisio illa non tam ad præceptum istud Christi, quam ad doctri- nam ejus Evangelicam, quam illi naso suspende- bant adunco, satirisque excipiebant: justitiam e- rigentes propriam, ut Paulus loquitur, justitiæ vero fidei se non submittentes Rom. X. 3.

## 16:15
Vers. 15. who justify yourselves] That is, who sell yourselves as just, as we saw that word accepted c. X. 29. The Pharisees did this with a great effort of ceremonies, which the people admired.

but God knows your hearts] God knows that there is nothing of true holiness in your hearts. Above c. XI. 39. The sacred scriptures often teach us that it is proper to God to inspect hearts. Nazarius in his panegyric: You watch us from on high, God, arbiter of things, and although human minds bear deep recesses of thoughts, the divinity, which is to search everything, nevertheless insinuates itself.

that which is highly esteemed among men, is an abomination in the sight of God] I do not think that pride is properly condemned here. For the sense is, as others have also noted, that many things which seem excellent to men and are placed on high (such as the Pharisaic way of life, which presented a great appearance of holiness) are most displeasing to God because true integrity of soul is absent. I do not doubt that Christ referred to the history in 1 Samuel 16:7, where God declares to Samuel not to look at the height of stature in designating a king (which we read the Ethiopians were accustomed to do), for his estimation does not correspond with the estimation of men: by men, external things are regarded; by Him, the heart itself. What is said there about stature, Christ transferred to actions themselves. There is גבה, which is τὸ ὑψηλόν here.

Latin:

Vers. 15. οἱ δικαιοῦντες ἑαυτοὺς] Id est, qui vos pro justis venditatis, ut eam vocem accipi vidimus c. X. 29. Faciebant autem hoc Pharisæi magno molimine cæremoniarum, quas admirabatur populus.

ὁ δὲ θεὸς γινώσκει τὰς καρδίας ὑμῶν] Deus scit in cordi- bus vestris nihil esse veræ sanctimoniæ. Supra c. XI. 39. Dei esse proprium corda inspicere docent nos sæpe sacræ literæ. Nazarius in panegyrico: Spectas nos ex alto rerum arbi- ter Deus & quamvis humanæ mentes profundos gerant cogita- tionum recessus, insinuat tamen se totam scrutatura divinitas.

ὅτι τὸ ἐν ἀνθρώποις ὑψηλὸν, βδέλυγμα ἐνώπιον τῆ Θεῦ ἐςὶ] Non puto hic proprie superbiam damnari. Sensus enim est, ut & alii notarunt, multa quæ hominibus videantur exi- mia atque in excelso posita (quale erat vitæ Pharisaiæ in- stitutum magnam præferens sanctimoniæ speciem) Deo maxime displicere quia absit vera animi probitas. Non dubito quin respexerit Christus ad historiam 1. Sam. 16, 7. ubi Deus Samueli edicit ne in rege designando respiciat sub- limitatem staturæ (quod Æthiopas factitare solitos legimus) neque enim suam æstimationem congruere cum hominum æstimatione: ab hominibus respici externa: à se cor ipsum. Quod ibi de statura dicitur, Christus ad actiones ipsas transtulit. Ibi est גבה quod hic τὸ ὑψηλόν.

## 16:16
V. 16. The law and the prophets were until John] As if he were saying, do not marvel if greater works of love are now openly required than formerly. For the state of the times demands this. God has never bestowed upon you such great benefits as He now bestows. What is the wonder if He who has bestowed more, requires more of what has been bestowed? The books of Moses and the Prophets, adapted to past times, served as a schoolmaster for children: therefore they overlooked many things and anxiously inculcated that external worship, the observance of which kept you from the superstitions of the Gentiles. From John begins a better age, that age of the kingdom, which therefore demands even better morals. He names John for this reason, because he openly announced that that kingdom had arrived.

An error often noted in Grotius recurs. But did Christ really think that Moses did not require as much love as He Himself required, who in the commandment of love and in works always referred back to Moses, Luke 10, Matthew 22, and could not require greater things than Moses desired? However, this is the coherence: there is no reason for you to consider yourselves righteous because you shine before men with an external appearance of holiness: true righteousness, by which you might stand before God, though indeed handed down by Moses and the Prophets, yet more clearly announced to you by John, is neglected by you: whence you render yourselves unworthy of the kingdom of God: which others, however, receive unto themselves as if by a certain force. But those words καὶ πᾶς εἰς αὐτὴν βιάζεται are not to be taken as Grotius does: The kingdom is not entered except by strenuous labor. For it is not of him who runs, nor of him who wills, but of God who shows mercy, Rom. 9:16. Blessed Polycarp Lyserus correctly expresses the sense in Chapter 122 of his Harmony. Laugh as much as you will, yet know that there remain quite a few others who flock together for the sake of obtaining the kingdom of God, as if contending to snatch it away from others, since none of them wishes to be the last in this pursuit. The little word πᾶς here signifies the promiscuous multitude, which is opposed to the Pharisees and Scribes, and thus is rightly rendered 'everyone.' However, those things which Grotius here again babbles about in the same way as the Pelagians are unworthy of the majesty of the divine law and the promises of the law added to it: 'The law,' he says, 'at least extorted and elicited what could be extorted by the fear of punishments and elicited by the hope of a temporal reward, lest wickedness should reign with the barriers completely broken: It is something to advance thus far, if it is not given to go further.'

and everyone forces his way into it] That kingdom is not open only to the wise, not only to the observers of Pharisaism surrounded by so many of its own rites, as you think, but to all: yet it is not to be entered except by strenuous labor. πᾶς, that is, πᾶς τις, as we said on Mark ch. 9, verse 49. εἰς αὐτὴν βιάζεται, that is, βιαζόμενος ἁρπάζει, as is clear from Matthew. A great thing is being done, a great effort is needed, so that you may obtain that spirit, not of the law, not of servitude, but of the Gospel, but of adoption.

Latin:

V. 16. ὁ νόμος κὶ οἱ προφῆται ἕως Ἰωάννε] Quasi diceret ne miremini si majora dilectionis opera nunc quam olim aperte exigantur. Id enim postulat temporum ratio. Nun- quam tanta in vos Deus beneficia contulit quanta nunc confert. Quid mirum est si qui plus contulit de collato plus exigit? Mosis & Prophetarum libri accommodati anteactis temporibus functi sunt velut puerorum magiste- rio: ideo multa dissimularunt & externum illum cultum, cujus vos custodia à gentium superstitionib. arcebat, sollici- te inculcarūt. A Johanne incipit ætas melior, ætas illa regni, quæ proinde mores etiam meliores postulat. Johannem ideo nominat, quia is adventasse regnum illud aperte nunciavit.

Error sæpius notatus in Grotio recurrit. An vero Christus Mosen non tantam dilectionis postulasse censuit, quantam ipse requirebat, qui in dilectionum præcepto, & operibus ad Mo- sen remisit semper, Luc. 10. Matth. 22. nec ma- jora, quam Moses desideravit, postulare potuit? Cohærentia autem hæc est: non est, quod vos justos esse censeatis, quia externa sanctimoniæ specie coram hominibus fulgetis: vera justitia, qua coram Deo consistatis, à Mose & Prophe- tis quidem tradita, manifestius tamen à Johan- ne vobis annunciata, à vobis negligitur: unde regno Dei vosmetipsos indignos redditis: quod vero alii veluti vi quadam ad se recipiunt. Non autem illa verba καὶ πᾶς εἰς αὐτὴν βιάζεται ita cum Grotio accipienda: Non aditur regnum nisi improbo labore. Non enim est currentis, nec volentis, sed miserentis Dei Rom. IX. 16. Re- cte exprimit sensum B. Polyc. Lyserus C. CXXII. Harmon. Rideatis vos quantum volueritis, tamen sciatis alios satis multos superesse, qui pro conse- quendo Dei regno turmatim confluunt, veluti con- tendentes illud aliis præripere, siquidem nullus ipso- rum in hoc studio postremus esse vult. Vocula πᾶς hic promiscuam multitudinem significat, quæ Pharisæis & Scribis opponitur, adeoque recte redditur quivis. Indigna autem sunt divinæ legis majestate, additisque legis promissionibus, quæ hic Grotius de eadem cum Pelagianis iterum de- blaterat: Extorquebat, inquiens, lex saltem, & eliciebat, quod suppliciorum metu extorqueri & spe temporariæ mercedis elici poterat, ne plane perru- ptis obicibus improbitas regnaret: Est aliqua prodi- re tenus, si non datur ultra.

κὶ πᾶς εἰς αὐτὴν βιάζεται] Regnum illud non solis sapien- tibus, non solis Pharisaisini tot propriis ritibus circumsepti observatoribus, ut vos existimatis, sed omnibus patet: non tamen adeundum nisi improbo labore. πᾶς, id est, πᾶς τις, ut diximus ad Marcum c. 9. comm. 49. εἰς αὐτὴν βιάζεται, id est βιαζόμενος ἁρπάζει, ut ex Matthæo liquet. Magna res a- gitur, magno nisu opus est, ut spiritum illum non legis, non servitutis, sed Evangelii, sed adoptionis consequamini.

## 16:17
Vers. 17. It is easier] A statement about this sentiment is in the commentary on Matthew. Moreover, it coheres very well with the preceding. For Christ, lest what He said be thought to have been said for the purpose of removing the reverence for the Hebrew law from the minds of men, shows on the contrary that nothing of the law will perish. For by His own precepts the law is not abolished but fulfilled. For the law had led to this as a guide: the law wanted this: but since it could not achieve what it wanted because of the natures of men, it at least extorted and elicited what could be extorted by the fear of punishments and elicited by the hope of a temporal reward, lest wickedness should reign with the barriers completely broken. It is something to advance thus far, if it is not given to go further.

πεσεῖν] Among the Hebrews, the word 'to fall' is said of that which lacks its outcome. Joshua 23:14, 1 Samuel 3:19, Romans 9:6.

Latin:

Vers. 17. εὐκοπώτερον ἐςὶ] Dictum de hac sententia ad Matthæum. Cæterum optime cohæret præcedentibus. Nam Christus ne, quæ dixit, ideo dixisse putaretur quo legis He- brææ reverentiam animis hominum eximeret, contra oste- dit nihil legis periturum. Suis enim præceptis non aboleri legem sed consummari. Huc enim lex velut manuduxerat: lex hoc volebat: sed cum quod volebat ob hominū ingenia consequi non posset, extorquebat saltem & eliciebat quod suppliciorum metu extorqueri, & spe temporariæ mercedis elici poterat, ne plane perruptis obicib. improbitas regnaret Est aliqua prodire tenus si non datur ultra.

πεσεῖν] Hebræis cadere verbum dicitur quod suo eventu caret. Josuæ XXIII. 14. 1. Sam. III, 19. Rom. IX. 6.

## 16:18
Vers. 18. πᾶς ὁ ἀπολύων) He illustrates with a notable example what Christ had said. Moses wished for all unnecessary divorces to be abolished, but he could not obtain this without the danger of a greater evil. The law of Christ, gathering a better people with greater aids, openly and clearly forbids what Moses, while disapproving, tolerated. Theophylact does not interpret this passage from Matthew badly, so that ὁ ἀπολύων is understood, namely, as you Pharisees do, not for sufficiently grave causes. For you may understand what the custom of those times was even from Josephus, who, although he everywhere professes himself most observant of the law of his country, thus declares of himself: τὴν γυναῖκα μὴ ἀρεσκόμενος αὐτῆς τοῖς ἤθεσιν ἀπεπεμψάμην, τριῶν παίδων γενομένην μητέρα. See the rest of this argument at Matthew.

PART II. Concerning the rich glutton and the poor Lazarus.

Latin:

Vers. 18. πᾶς ὁ ἀπολύων) Quod dixerat Christus insigni exemplo collustrat. Optabat Moses omnia non necessa- ria divortia tolli, sed hoc obtinere non poterat sine majoris mali periculo. Christi lex majoribus auxiliis populum me- liorem colligens palam & aperte vetat quod Moses impro- bans tolerabat. Hunc autem locum ex Matthæo non ma- le interpretatur Theophylactus, ut intelligatur ὁ ἀπολύων, nimirum ut vos Pharisæi facitis, non satis gravibus de cau- sis. Nam qui eorum temporum mos fuerit vel ex Jose- pho intelligas, qui cum ubique se observantissimum le- gis patriæ profiteatur, ita de se prædicat: τὴν γυναῖκα μὴ ἀρεσκόμενος αὐτῆς τοῖς ἤθεσιν ἀπεπεμψάμην, τριῶν παί- δων γενομένην μητέρα. Cætera hujus argumenti vide ad Matthæum.

PARS II. De divite epulone, & paupere Lazaro.

## 16:19
Vers. 19. ἄνθρωπος δέ τις ἦν πλούσιος) Here Christ returns to the argument from which He had begun His discourse, concerning the use of riches: and He shows that by many followers of Pharisaism, the very law of Moses, set forth in explicit words, is violated in this respect, as if He were saying: there is no need for that law of the new kingdom to condemn you, for whose condemnation the law of Moses alone suffices: the law of the kingdom wishes those who can be relieved by our beneficence to be sought out voluntarily: for their sake we should reduce something of our own comforts, and not wait until they arrive at the extreme line of misery, that is, at beggary: and indeed not only for fellow-countrymen, but for foreigners as well, even if they are not the best, if only for this one reason that they are human beings. But among the Pharisees there were many who were not moderately rich and who openly displayed their opulence with clothing and feasts. How easy it was for them, without any inconvenience to themselves, to at least keep a decent and fellow-citizen, such as Lazarus was at that time, who was daily before their eyes, from beggary, if not to feed him liberally: which certainly not only charity and nature, but that very civil law of the Hebrews given through Moses explicitly commands in Deuteronomy XV. 7, 8. Therefore Christ predicts that it will come to pass that they will not escape those punishments which they themselves admit are established for despisers of the law after this life. Ancient and modern interpreters contend whether what follows here is history or a fable. It seems to me that the author of the responses to the orthodox does not solve this knot badly: for he says it is neither properly a fable nor a history, but rather an ὑποτύπωσιν. Thus masters of eloquence are accustomed to call a narration in which a true thing is depicted with probable colors. Such an ὑποτύπωσις or rather διάτυπωσις (for they wish this to be a more accurate delineation) is that concerning Eleazar, his wife, and seven sons, both in Jason of Cyrene and in Josephus, a man certainly eloquent, whoever he was: for I do not think he is the writer of the Histories. They narrate, however, not only what was done, but also what is believed to have been able to be said or done probably. But this must be added here, that whatever is said about the state after this life, all those things are depicted with express figures after the example of mortal life. These things being understood, the difficulties which have entangled many interpreters are resolved.

πορφύραν) They err who think Herod is designated by the argument of purple. For it was later that it became customary for only Emperors and Kings to use purple, whereas previously others of more luxurious fortune proceeded in that attire. For friends of kings are also called purple-clad everywhere in histories. And the proximity of Tyre provided the Jews with a greater supply of purple. It can be doubted, however, whether the word πορφύρας is used properly here. For the LXX, Josephus, and Philo everywhere place πορφύραν where in the Hebrew there is אַרְגָּמָן. And yet אַרְגָּמָן was not Tyrian purple: for the Tyrians themselves received it from abroad, as Ezekiel XXVII. 7 clearly teaches us. The teachers of the Hebrews wish אַרְגָּמָן to be what is commonly called crimson. I would not even omit that the Syrian retained the word for byssus בּוּצָא, but the Arab the very word for purple أَلْبِرْ فِير, while in the meantime he uses אַרְגָּן, which corresponds to the Hebrew אַרְגָּמָן, for purple, and the other for byssus. That Syrian בּוּצָא is the same from the Hebrew בּוּץ which the interpreters of Chronicles translate as byssus: and the Jerusalem Paraphrast placed that very thing in Exodus XXVIII. 42 for the Hebrew בַּד in the description of breeches: whereas the LXX, Josephus, and Philo are accustomed to place βύσσον where in the Hebrew there is שֵׁשׁ.

εὐφραινόμενος καθ' ἡμέραν λαμπρῶς) The rich man is not accused here of robbery, nor because he brooded over useless gold, like the serpent of the Hesperides, but because he abounded in delights while destitution consumed others, and he is accused as a violator of the old, not the new and more perfect, law. How, therefore, will a large part of Christians escape the punishment inflicted on this rich man?

Latin:

Vers. 19. ἄνθρωπος δέ τις ἦν πλούσιος) Hic Christus ad argumentum, unde sermonem inceperat, regreditur, de usu divitiarum: ostenditque à multis Pharisæismi sectato- ribus hac in parte ipsam Mosis legem dissertis verbis prola- tam violari, quasi dicat: non opus est ut lex illa novi regni vos condemnet, quibus damnandis lex sola Mosis suffi- cit: lex regni vult ultro conquiri eos qui beneficentia no- stra possint sublevari: eorum causa decidere nos aliquid de nostris commodis, neque exspectare dum illi ad extre- mam miseriæ lineam, id est ad mendicitatem, deve- niant: neque vero popularibus tantum, sed alienigenis quoque, etiam non optimis vel ob hoc unum quod homi- nes sint. At inter Pharisæos multi erant non mediocriter divites & qui opulentiam suam vestibus atque epulis palam ostentarent. Quam facile his erat sine ullo suo incom- modo virum probum & popularem quotidie sibi ob oculos versantem, qualis eo tempore erat Lazarus, si non alere liberaliter, certe à mendicitate arcere: quod certe non caritas tantum & natura, sed ipsa illa lex civilis Hebræo- rum per Mosem data exserte præcipit Deuteron. XV. 7. 8. Prædicit igitur Christus futurum, ut non evadant eos pœ- nas quas post hanc vitam legis contemptoribus constitutas ipsi fateantur. Certant veteres novique interpretes id quod hic sequitur historiæne sit an fabula. Mihi videtur Scriptor responsionum ad orthodoxos non male solvere hunc nodum: ait enim nec fabulam esse proprie nec hi- storiam, sed ὑποτύπωσιν potius. Ita solent autem eloquen- tiæ magistri appellare narrationem quibus res vera colori- bus verisimilibus depingitur. Talis ὑποτύπωσις aut potius διάτυπωσις (nam hanc esse volunt delineationem accura- tiorem) est illa de Eleazaro ejus uxore ac septem filiis tum apud Jasonem Cyrenæum, tum apud Josephum vi- rum sane disertum quisquis ille fuit: Historiarum enim scriptorem, hunc esse non puto. Narrant autem illi non tantum quæ facta sunt, sed & quæ dici aut fieri potuisse probabiliter creditur. Sed illud hic addendum est, quæ de statu post hanc vitam dicuntur, ea omnia depingi figuris expressis ad exemplum vitæ mortalis. His intellectis expe- ditæ sunt difficultates, quæ multos interpretes implicitos habuerunt.

πορφύραν) Errant qui Herodem designari putant pur- puræ argumento. Serius enim usitatum est ut soli Impe- ratores & Reges purpura uterentur, cum antea & alii lau- tioris fortunæ eo cultu procederent. Nam & regum amici passim purpurati in historiis vocantur. Et Judæi majo- rem purpuræ copiam fecit Tyri vicinitas. Dubitari tamen potest an vox πορφύρας hic proprie usurpetur. Nam πορ- φύραν LXX. Josephus & Philo ubique ponunt ubi in He- bræo est אַרְגָּמָן. Atqui אַרְגָּמָן non erat purpura Tyria: nam ipsi Tyrii peregre illud accipiebant, ut clare nos do- cet Ezechiel XXVII. 7. Hebræorum magistri אַרְגָּמָן esse volunt, quod carmesinum vulgo dicitur. Ne illud quidem omiserim, Syrum retinuisse byssi vocem בּוּצָא, Ara- bem vero ipsam vocem purpuræ أَلْبِرْ فِير cum interim אַרְגָּן quod Hebræo אַרְגָּמָן respondet, ille pro purpura, hic pro bysso usurpet. Syrum illud בּוּצָא idem est ex Hebræo בּוּץ quod Paral. Interpretes byssum ver- tunt: idque ipsum Paraphrastes Hierosolymitanus posuit Exod. XXVIII. 42. pro Hebræo בַּד in feminalium descri- ptione: cum LXX. Josephus & Philo βύσσον ponere soleant ubi in Hebræo est שֵׁשׁ.

εὐφραινόμενος καθ' ἡμέραν λαμπρῶς) Non accusatur hic dives rapinæ, nec quod inutili auro incubaret, ut Hesperidum serpens, sed quod deliciis afflueret cum alios consumeret egestas, & accusatur ut veteris, non ut no- væ, ejusque perfectioris legis violator. Quomodo igi- tur pœnam huic diviti inflictam evadet pars magna Chri- stianorum?

## 16:20
Vers. 20. ὀνόματι λάζαρος) That is, such as you now see Lazarus. Such is that 'Pone Tigellinum,' it had been odious to assign a name to the rich man, therefore it was enough to say ἄνθρωπός τις. That Tertullian, Prudentius, and others call this same beggar Eleazar is not for nothing. For he who was once accustomed to be called אֶלְעָזָר was called in the times of Christ by a contracted pronunciation לַעְזָר. Therefore the name of Eleazar and Lazarus is the same.

Fuller refutes this in Bald. Walaeus, who may be compared here if one wishes.

πρὸς τὸν πυλῶνα ἀυτοῦ) In the very sight of the rich man, so that he could in no way plead ignorance.

ἡλκωμένος) As men of his fortune are accustomed to contract sores from filth and squalor.

Latin:

Vers. 20. ὀνόματι λάζαρος) Id est, qualem nunc vide- tis Lazarum. Tale est illud Pone Tigellinum, diviti no- men apponere odiosum fuerat, ideo satis fuit dicere ἄνθρω- πός τις. Quod autem Tertullianus, Prudentius, atque alii eundem hunc mendicum Eleazarum vocant, non de nihilo est. Nam qui olim dici solebat אֶלְעָזָר Christi temporibus contracta pronunciatione diceba- tur לַעְזָר. Itaque idem est Eleazari ac Lazari no- men.

Refellit hoc Fullerus apud Bald. Walaeum, qui hic conferatur si lubet.

πρὸς τὸν πυλῶνα ἀυτοῦ) In ipso divitis aspectu ut igno- rantiam causari nullo modo posset.

ἡλκωμένος) Ut solent ejus fortunæ homines sordibus at- que illuvie ulcera contrahere.

## 16:21
Vers. 21. desiring to be fed with the crumbs) Two things are signified here: both the inhumanity of the rich man, who from a larder so wealthy, from a table built up with so many dishes, sent him nothing, and his own immense patience, for whom the height of his desires was to receive only as much as is usually granted to dogs. See Matt. XV. 27.

But even the dogs) As if Christ were saying, so far was the rich man from giving him to be cared for at his own expense, which you remember it is narrated the Samaritan did, that on the contrary the dogs licked him as if he were a corpse. For sacred history narrates in many places that the blood of corpses was accustomed to be sucked by dogs.

Latin:

Vers. 21. ἐπιθυμῶν χορτασθῆναι ἀπὸ τῶν ψιχίων) Duo hic significantur, & divitis inhumanitas, qui de penu tam locuplete, de mensa tot ferculis exstructa nihil illi mise- rit, & ingens ipsius patientia, cui summa votorum fue- rit tantum accipere quantum canibus concedi solet. Vid. Matth. XV. 27.

Ἀλλὰ καὶ οἱ κύνες) Quasi diceret Christus, tantum aberat ut dives illum suis impensis curandum daret, quod Samaritanum fecisse narratum meministis, ut contra canes illum pro cadavere lamberent. Nam cadaverum sanguinem à canibus sugi solitum passim narrat sacra hi- storia.

## 16:22
Vers. 22. to be carried away) Thus in many places the Greek and Latin poets also call the souls released from bodies by the names of the men. Let him who wishes see Homer's nekyia and the sixth Aeneid. Josephus also calls that which appeared to Saul, Samuel. Porphyry, explaining that passage of Homer: 'And there came the soul of Theban Tiresias, holding a golden scepter,' says: 'He purposely changed from the name of the soul to the masculine, so that he might show that the soul was Tiresias.' And at the beginning of the Iliad, Eustathius notes that the word autos sometimes signifies only the soul, sometimes only the body, sometimes the whole man.

by the angels) Behold a sudden change: he who just now had been the laughingstock not only of men but also of dogs, is suddenly honored by the ministry of angels. Moreover, it was an ancient tradition of the Jews that the souls of the pious are led by angels into paradise; the Chaldean Paraphrast mentions this on Canticles IV. 12.

into Abraham's bosom) Most of the ancients think that the region assigned to pious souls is called Abraham's bosom, which the Hebrews called Eden, that is, paradise, and the Greeks called the Elysian fields, and that it is called a bosom just as we speak of a bosom of the sea or of the earth. But those are much more correct who think that not that region, but the most honorable place in that region, is signified. There is no doubt that among all the pious, the Jews attributed the chief place to Abraham, the father of the nation. Hence Christ said elsewhere that many from the Gentiles would recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, describing the joys after this life under the guise of a banquet, as was the custom then received. Now at banquets, the most beloved were accustomed to recline in the bosom of him who was the head of the banquet. Thus John, 'whom Jesus loved, was reclining in his bosom,' chap. XIII. 23. Thus the Son of God is said to be 'in the bosom of the Father,' John I. 18. Therefore, the highest honor of Lazarus is indicated here, as one who in that blessed seat would remain closest to Abraham, whose extraordinary faith and constancy in enduring evils he had imitated. Thus the Hebrews say that Eliezer, formerly the servant of Abraham, rests in Abraham's bosom. Their virtues remain for the good. Thus Abraham's hospitality remains for him.

Grotius thinks that the most honorable place in that region is noted, which the Hebrews called Eden, that is, paradise, and the Greeks called the Elysian fields. But setting aside the fables of the Greeks about the Elysian fields, from wherever they may have their origin, as they have nothing to do with this matter, where we are dealing with the truth of celestial happiness, which is placed in the Holy Scriptures alone, we do not indeed hold paradise and Abraham's bosom to be simply synonyms; yet we judge that being in paradise and being in Abraham's bosom express almost the same thing: for by both phrases celestial beatitude is designated: because the elect in heaven act as if in paradise and the most desired garden of pleasure, and in Abraham's bosom, namely in the bosom of divine grace, into which Abraham, the father of believers, has been received, with pleasure are refreshed by the heavenly. It is called Abraham's bosom not subjectively, as if Lazarus were received by Abraham and into his bosom, but objectively, because that very bosom in which Abraham enjoys happiness, which cherishes Abraham as an object in its embrace, has also received Lazarus, and cherishes the same in a most sweet embrace. Concerning which St. Augustine speaks excellently in book IV de anima: Understand by Abraham's bosom a remote and secret seat of rest, where Abraham is. And therefore it is called Abraham's, not because it is his alone, but because he is set as the Father of many nations, to whom he is proposed as a pattern of faith to be imitated. Therefore Abraham does not cherish Lazarus in his own bosom, but Lazarus is cherished in the same bosom in which Abraham is: which has its name only from Abraham, because he is the Father of believers. Whence it is clear that this phrase does not of itself imply a more honorable place, to be in Abraham's bosom, since all the elect are cherished in that bosom in which Abraham is: Nor is there any reference here either to the custom of those reclining at table, as in Matt. 8, 12, as Camero with Grotius, Heinsius, and others think, or to the bosom of parents, in which children are cherished, as Capellus thinks, for he has not been made the ἐγκόλπιος of Abraham, but the ἐγκόλπιος of God: nor is there anything certain about it, nor can it be persuaded by any reason, that Lazarus obtained a seat next in dignity to Abraham in the heavens, which without doubt is to be assigned to others, far superior to Lazarus, by various merits.

And the rich man died) that 'and' is emphatic, as if he were saying, did those riches profit me against death? Menander: There is no immortality, even if you gather those fabled talents of Tantalus; but you will die and leave these to someone.

Nor was it poorly observed by the ancients that the goodness of God is signified in the fact that Lazarus died before the rich man. For the former was taken away early from the troubles of this age, while for the latter the age was prolonged for repentance.

and was buried) Not even this was added in vain. For it is signified that this final honor befell him despite such great riches.

Latin:

Vers. 22. ἀπενεχθῆναι ἀυτὸν) Ita passim Græci quoque & Latini Poëtæ, animos corporibus solutos hominum nominibus appellant. Videat si cui lubet νεκυίαν Home- ri & sextam Æneidem. Josephus quoque id quod Sau- li apparuit Samuelem vocat. Porphyrius illud Homeri explicans: Ἦλθε δ᾽ ἐπὶ ψυχὴ Θηβαίου τειρεσία. Χρυσέον σκῆπτρον ἔχων. ἐπίτηδες, inquit, ἀπὸ τοῦ τῆς ψυχῆς ὀνόματος εἰς τὸ ἄῤῥενον τὸν μέλεβαλον, ἵνα δείξῃ ὅτι ἡ ψυχὴ ἦν ὁ τειρεσίας. Et ad ini- tium Iliadis Eustathius notat vocem ἀυτὸς modo animam tantum significare, modo corpus tantum, modo totum hominem.

ὑπὸ τῶν ἀγγέλων) En subita mutatio: qui modo non hominum modo, sed & canum ludibrium fuerat, re- pente Angelorum ministerio honoratur. Erat autem ve- tus Judæorum traditio, piorum animas ab angelis dedu- ci εἰς παράδεισον, meminit Paraphrastes Chaldæus ad Can- ticum IV. 12.

εἰς τὸν κόλπον τοῦ Ἀβραὰμ) Putant veteres plerique si- num Abrahæ dici regionem piis animis adscriptam, quam Hebræi עֵדֶן id est παράδεισον, Græci Elysios campos dixe- runt, & sinum dici quomodo maris aut terræ sinum di- cimus. At multo illi rectius, qui non regionem illam, sed in regione illa locum honoratissimum significari pu- tant. Dubium non est, quin inter pios omnes Judæi Abrahamo τῷ ἐθνοπάτορι principem attribuerint locum. Hinc Christus alibi multos ex gentibus dixit accubituros cum Abrahamo, Isaaco & Jacobo, gaudia post hanc vitam, more tunc recepto, sub convivii specie descri- bens. In conviviis autem solebant dilectissimi in sinu e- jus recumbere qui convivii princeps esset. Ita Johannes ὃν ἠγάπα ὁ Ἰησοῦς ἦν ἀνακλινόμενος ἐν τῷ κόλπῳ ἀυτοῦ cap. XIII. 23. Sic Filius Dei esse dicitur εἰς τὸν κόλπον τοῦ πα- τρὸς Joh. I. 18. Indicatur ergo hic summus Lazari ho- nos, ut qui in illa beata sede proximus hæreret Abra- hamo cujus eximiam fidem & in malis perferendis con- stantiam esse imitatus. Sic Hebræi Eliezerem servum quondam Abrahami ajunt in sinu Abrahami requiescere. Bonis suæ virtutes manent. Sic Abrahamo sua hospita- litas.

Locum honoratissimum in regione illa notari pu- tat Grotius, quam Ebræi עֵדֶן id est, παράδεισον, Græci campos Elysios dixere. Sed missis fabulis Græcorum de campis Elysiis, undecunque il- læ originem habeant, utpote quæ huc nihil fa- ciunt, ubi de veritate cœlestis felicitatis agi- tur, in solis literis Sacris posita, non qui- dem Paradisum & sinum Abrahæ simpliciter pro Synonymis habemus, in Paradiso tamen esse, & in sinu Abrahæ, idem fere exprimere cense- mus: Nam utraque phrasi beatitudo cœlestis de- signatur: quia electi in cœlo, ut in Paradiso & horto voluptatis exoptatissimo agunt, & in sinu Abrahæ, in sinu nempe gratiæ divinæ, in quem A- braham Pater credentium receptus est, voluptate cœlesti reficiuntur. Sinus Abrahæ dicitur non subjectivè, quasi ab Abrahamo, & in ipsius sinu receptus Lazarus sit, sed objectivè, quod ille ipse sinus in quo Abraham felicitate fruitur, qui Abrahamum ceu objectum fovet in complexu suo, etiam Lazarum exceperit, eundemq; comple- xu suavissimo foveat. Quo de optime S. Augusti- nus libr. IV. de anima: Sinum Abrahæ intellige re- motam sedem quietis, atque secretam, ubi est Abra- ham. Et ideo Abrahæ dictum, non quod ipsius tan- tum sit, sed quod is Pater multarum gentium sit posi- tus, quibus est ad imitandum fidei principatum propositus. Non ergo Abraham in sinu proprio fovet Lazarum, sed Lazarus in eodem fovetur si- nu, in quo & Abraham: qui solum ab Abraha- mo denominationem habet, quia is Pater est cre- dentium. Unde patet, per se non inferre hanc phrasin locum honoratiorem, in sinu Abrahæ esse, quùm omnes electi in sinu illo, in quo Abraham est, foveantur: Neque hic vel ad morem mensæ ac- cumbentium, uti Matth. 8, 12. sit, respicitur, ut Ca- mero cum Grotio, Heinsio, aliisque, vel ad gremium Parentum, in quo foventur filii, ut Capellus putat, non enim ἐγκόλπιος Abrahami, sed ἐγκόλπιος τοῦ Θεοῦ factus est: neque de eo quicquam constat, aùt ulla id ratione suaderi potest, Lazarum digni- tate proximam ab Abrahamo in cælis consequutum esse sedem, quæ citra dubium aliis, longe superiori- bus Lazaro, qua merita multivaria assignan- da.

Ἀπέθανε δὲ καὶ ὁ πλούσιος) ἐμφατικὸν est illud καὶ quasi dicat mihi illi divitiæ adversus mortem profuerunt Me- nander: Ἀθανασία δ᾽ οὐκ ἔστιν, οὐδ᾽ ἂν συναγάγῃς Τὰ Ταντάλου τάλαντ᾽ ἐκεῖνα λεγόμενα· Ἀλλ᾽ ἀποθανῇ καὶ ταῦτα καταλείψεις τινί.

Nec illud à veteribus male observatum, bonitatem Dei in eo significari quod Lazarus prius, dives poste ius mor- tem obierit. illum enim mature exemtum hujus ævi incommodis, huic ævum ad pœnitentiam proroga- tum.

καὶ ἐτάφη) Ne hoc quidem frustra additum. Significatur enim de tantis divitiis hunc illi honorem postremum con- tigisse.

## 16:23
Ver. 23. and in Hades) This is the only place, if I am not mistaken, in the Holy Scriptures by which many have been moved to think that the place of torment is properly called Hades. But it is most true, as we have said elsewhere, that Hades is a place withdrawn from our sight: and when it is taken of the body, it is the grave in which the body is without the soul, but when of the soul, it is that whole region or state in which the soul is without the body. And so the rich man was indeed in Hades, but Lazarus was also in Hades, with the regions of Hades separated. For both Paradise and Gehenna, or as the Greeks used to say, the Elysian fields and Tartarus, are in Hades. It is a most certain fact that the Greeks spoke thus, whom Virgil follows in the sixth Aeneid. Diphilus: For we believe there are two paths in Hades, one for the just, the other for the unjust. Sophocles' passage is also well known: O thrice-blessed those mortals who, having seen these rites, go to Hades; for to them alone it is given to live there; but for all others, all things there are evil.

Thus also Diodorus Siculus explains the mythology of Hades through the punishments of the wicked and the meadows of the pious.
