Plato says that those who have handed down the mysteries have said that whoever arrives in Hades uninitiated and unfinished will lie in mud, but he who has been purified, arriving there, will dwell with the gods: which sense also exists in Iamblichus. Plutarch also, in his Lucullus, called it a gift in Hades. And that same Iamblichus: We shall receive the rewards of justice in Hades, as the wise poets say. Lest anyone doubt concerning the Jews, I offer Josephus as a surety, who says that Samuel was called up from Hades. The same man, speaking of the Sadducees, says thus: They abolish the punishments and honors in Hades. The same man, when he describes the opinion of the Pharisees: They believe that there is an immortal strength in souls, and that there are judgments and honors under the earth for those who have practiced virtue or vice in life, and that to the former is added eternal imprisonment, but to the latter

ease in freedom from suffering. He openly establishes both punishments and rewards for souls in Hades: and he also calls it under the earth because what is in Hades is accustomed to be called subterranean by the Greeks. Just as Zonaras also, explaining the opinion of the Pharisees, said subterranean judgments, whether because Hades was thought to be truly under the earth, or rather because it is no less out of sight than those things which the innermost recess of the earth hides: for which reason Plutarch said that things inside the earth are called hidden and Hades. Iamblichus called them the courts under the earth. Thus also Pindar, speaking of the Eleusinian mysteries: Blessed is he who, having seen those common things, goes under the earth; he knows the end of life, and he knows the god-given beginning. Plutarch, regarding that passage of Homer: and the soul, flying from the limbs, went to Hades. To the unseen, he says, and invisible, whether one considers it air or a subterranean place. He does not define the place, but proposes a double opinion, one that places Hades under the earth, and one that places it in the spacious fields of the air. The same Plutarch in his 'On the First Cold': the invisible had the name of Hades from the air. Thus also Hippocrates in his book on diet opposes light and Hades. Josephus himself, in another place describing the tenets of the Essenes, says thus: And they declare that for good souls, agreeing with the sons of the Greeks, a life beyond the ocean is laid up, and a place not burdened by rains or snows or heat, but which a mild zephyr always blowing from the ocean cools; but for the wicked they assign a dark and wintry recess full of unceasing punishments. Behold, here he places Hades across the Ocean. Again in another place, the same Josephus, from the same opinion, ascribes the seat for the pious to the most holy place in heaven. But truly these modes of speaking, under the earth, in the air, across the Ocean, and what is in Tertullian across the fiery zone, designate nothing other than the invisible and that which is inaccessible to us. The same Tertullian in his book de anima places torment and refreshment among the dead: In the same place, that the soul is punished and cherished meanwhile in the underworld under the expectation of both judgments, in a certain anticipation and foretaste of it. He has similar things against Marcion IV. Let us add to these the passage of Ambrose in book X of de bono mortis. It had been enough to have said to them (the philosophers) that souls freed from bodies sought Hades, that is, a place which is not seen, which place we call infernum in Latin. Finally, Scripture also named those habitations the storehouses of souls.

Therefore, by ᾅδης Grotius does not understand the place of torment, but that whole region or state in which the soul exists without the body, because ᾅδης is a place withdrawn from our sight, which, when it is understood of the body, denotes the grave, but when of the soul, that region already mentioned: whence he says that the rich man was indeed ἐν ᾅδῃ, but that Lazarus was also ἐν ᾅδῃ, with the regions separated. But although by reason of etymology some derive ᾅδης from τὸ μὴ ἰδεῖν, others nevertheless derive it from ἥδω, I delight, by antiphrasis, because there is no delight there: and those who retain the former derivation wish it to be so called because it is a sad house without the sun, in which there is no light, but mere darkness. But however much the grave may sometimes be indicated by the name שאול, to which the word ᾅδης corresponds among the LXX Interpreters, nevertheless no passage occurs in the New Testament, as B. Gerhard observes in his work on hell §. 5, in which the word ᾅδης cannot be sufficiently conveniently understood as hell. But that by that name a certain common region, in which the souls of both the faithful and the unfaithful are established after this life, is denoted, will never be taught from the Holy Scriptures: which are entirely ignorant of such a common region. Nor is it indicated here by any jot that the soul of Lazarus was ἐν ᾅδῃ, nor is it said anywhere in Holy Scripture concerning the souls of the elect: indeed ᾅδης is explained in this passage as a place of torments, and is separated from the bosom of Abraham and from Paradise by a greatest and insurmountable chasm. It is therefore a paradox, untheological, and a copy, which Grotius hands down here; And Paradise, and Gehenna, or as the Greeks used to speak, the Elysian fields and Tartarus are ἐν ᾅδῃ. But what testimonies does Grotius bring forward for it? from the Greeks

He praises Diphilus, Sophocles, Diodorus Siculus, Plato, Plutarch, Iamblichus, whom he says Virgil followed. But testimonies ought to have been brought forward from the Scriptures, not from profane and exoteric or even poetic and fabulous authors, to whom nothing was certain concerning the heavenly life. Nor is it to be conceded that the phraseology of the Scriptures is analogous to Josephus, or that Scripture is to be explained by Josephus. Tertullian, however, adapted himself to the manner of speaking of the philosophers when he placed torment and refreshment among the shades. But Ambrose, in the cited passage, book on the good of death, ch. X, explicitly alleges the opinion of the philosophers: it had been enough for them (the philosophers) to have said that the soul, freed from the bodies, sought ᾅδην, that is, the place which we call hell in Latin.

ἐπάρας τοὺς ὀφθαλμοὺς ἀυτοῦ) Just as bodily acts are accustomed to be ascribed to God, so too are they to souls freed from the body by a similar figure. Wherefore the argument which Irenaeus and Tertullian seek from this is not sufficiently certain, to prove that after death certain lineaments of the body and images of the limbs remain in the soul: which does not depart far from those things which have been said elsewhere concerning the περὶ τῶν ἀυγοειδῶν σωμάτων (luminous bodies).

Vers. eod. ὑπάρχων ἐν βασάνοις) Just as those who are in prison are accustomed to be tortured before their condemnation, so souls freed from the body, even before the public judgment, cannot but be in most grievous torture, with conscience predicting to them their future sentence: alluding to which Martial wrote: 'And when the Fury has ordered the truth to be confessed, with conscience compelling, he cries out.' Nazianzen, in his second work against Julian, describes the punishments of the wicked, among which he places αἱ ἐν ἀυτοῖς τοῖς δεινοῖς ἐξαγορεύσεις (the confessions in the very torments themselves).

It is certain that not only the torments of conscience are denoted by βασάνες, but the torments of Tartarus: nor can it be admitted that the souls of the unfaithful are tortured by the torments of conscience alone before the public judgment. The present passage certainly teaches otherwise, in which, if anywhere else, the Tartarean torments are described in very emphatic words. For the word ὀδυνῶμαι implies not only the torments of conscience, but most exquisite pains, such as the damned feel in Tartarus: and the feaster exclaims, ὀδυνῶμαι ἐν τῇ φλογὶ ταύτῃ, I am tormented in this flame; which is the flame of Tartarus, that inextinguishable fire; these flames are described, which bring the highest and intolerable heat, such as the damned feel in hell, entirely devoid of any refreshment, whence he would consider it a place of supreme mercy if his tongue could perceive even the smallest drop of water; nor do the terms τῆς βασάνε and τὸ ὑπάρχειν ἐν βασάνοις signify anything other than Tartarus and Tartarean torments. Compare Apoc. 14, 10. 11. c. 20, 10. What else is it to destroy all these things by a figure of fiction than to wish to extinguish the power of infernal fire? And yet Grotius attempts this: he says, he compares the torment of conscience to a burning flame: thus we also say in Latin of those who are tormented in mind: as in Terence, 'uro hominem' (I burn the man). From this, the rest are now feigned consequently: for those who are burned feel thirst most of all in the tongue: thirst is accustomed to be relieved by waters: the minimum of water is as much as adheres to a finger.

ὁρᾷ τὸν Ἀβραὰμ) He says he sees him, because it was probable that he would think of him, and say what he seemed likely to say if he could say it.

Latin:

Vers. 23. καὶ ἐν τῷ ᾅδῃ) Hic unicus, ni fallor, in sacris li- teris locus est quo moti plerique τὸν τόπον τῆς βασάνου pro- prie ᾅδην dici putarunt. At verissimum est, quod alibi dixi- mus, ᾅδην esse locum visibus nostris subtractum: & de cor- pore quidem cum accipitur sepulchrum in quo est corpus sine animo, de animo vero totam illam regionem sive sta- tum in quo est animus sine corpore. Itaque fuit dives quidem ἐν ᾅδῃ, sed fuit ἐν ᾅδῃ etiam Lazarus, distermina- tis ᾅδου regionibus. Nam & Paradisus & Gehenna, sive ut loquebantur Græci, Elysii & Tartara sunt ἐν ᾅδου. Græcos ita locutos res certissima est, quos Virgilius sequitur sex- ta Æneide. Diphilus: Καὶ γὰρ καθ᾽ ᾅδην δύο τρίβους νομίζομεν, Μίαν δικαίων, χατέραν ἀσεβῶν ὁδὸν. Notus & Sophoclis locus: ὢ τρισόλβιοι Κεῖνοι βροτῶν, οἳ ταῦτα δερχθέντες τέλη Μολῶσ᾽ ἐς ᾅδου· τοῖς δὲ γὰρ μόνοις ἐκεῖ Ζῆν ἐστί· τοῖς δ᾽ ἄλλοισι πάντ᾽ ἐκεῖ κακά.

Sic & Diodorus Siculus: τὴν ἐν ᾅδου μυθοποιίαν explicat per ἀσεβῶν τιμωρίας & εὐσεβῶν λειμῶνας. Plato τοὺς τὰς τελετὰς παραδεδωκότας εἰρηκέναι φασιν ὅτι ὃς ἀμύητος καὶ ἀτέλεστος εἰς ᾅδου ἀφίκηται ἐν βορβόρῳ κείσεται, ὁ δὲ κεκαθαρμένος ἐκεῖσε ἀφι- κόμενος μετὰ θεῶν οἰκήσει: qui sensus & apud Jamblichum ex- stat. Plutarchus quoque Lucullo, γέρας ἐν ᾅδου dixit. Et idem ille Jamblichus: τῆς δικαιοσύνης, ὡς φασὶν οἱ σοφοὶ τῶν ποιητῶν, ἐν ᾅδου κομισόμεθα τὰς δωρεάς. De Judæis ne quis dubiret, vadem do Josephum, qui Samuelem ait evocatum ἐξ ᾅδου. Idem de Sadducæis loquens ita ait: τὰς καθ᾽ ᾅδου τιμωρίας καὶ τιμὰς ἀναιροῦσι. Idem ubi Phari zœorum describit sententiam: ἀθάνατόν τε ἰσχὺν ταῖς ψυχαῖς πίστις αὐτοῖς εἶναι, καὶ ὑπὸ χθονὸς δικαιώσεις τε καὶ τιμὰς, οἷς ἀρετῆς ἢ κακίας ἐπιτήδευ- σις ἐν τῷ βίῳ γέγονε, καὶ ταῖς μὲν εἱργμὸν ἀΐδιον προστίθεσθαι, ταῖς δὲ

ῥατώνην τῆ ἀπαθείᾳ. Aperte & supplicia & præmia animis constituit ἐν ᾅδου: idemque vocat ὑπὸ χθονὸς quia quæ ἐν ᾅδου sunt vocari solent ὑποχθόνια Græcis. Sicut & Zonaras sententiam explicans Pharisæorum dixit δικαιώσεις ὑποχθο- νίους, sive quod vere sub terra esse ᾅδης putaretur, sive potius quod non minus extra visum sit quam ea quæ intimo reces- su terra celat: quam ob causam τὰ ἐντὸς γῆς χάθη καὶ ᾅδην ὀνομάζεσθαι dixit Plutarchus. τὰ ὑπὸ γῆν δικαστήρια dixit Jamblichus. Sic & Pindarus de mysteriis Eleusiniis lo- quens: Ὄλβιος ὅστις ἰδὼν ἐκεῖνα Κοινὰ εἶσ᾽ ὑπὸ χθόνα· Οἶδε μὲν βίου τελευτὰν Οἶδεν δὲ διόσδοτον ἀρχάν. Plutarchus ad illud Homeri: ψυχὴ δ᾽ ἐκ ῥεθέων πταμένη ἀϊδόσ δε βεβήκει. Εἰς τὸν ἀειδῆ, inquit, καὶ ἀόρατον, εἴτε ἀέρα θείη τίς εἴτε ὑπόγειον τόπον. Locum non definit, sed duplicem opinionem pro- ponit, tum quæ sub terra tum quæ in spatiosis aëris campis τὸν ᾅδην locat. Idem Plutarchus de primo frigido: ὁ ἀειδὴς τῷ ἀέρων ᾅδου ἐπίκλησιν ἔσχεν. Sic & Hippocrates libro de diæta opponit φῶς & ᾅδην. Josephus ipse alio loco Essæo- rum placita describens ita ait: καὶ ταῖς μὲν ἀγαθαῖς (ψυχαῖς) ὁμοδοξοῦντες παισὶν Ἑλλήνων ἀποφαίνονται τὴν ὑπὲρ ὠκεανον δίαιταν ἀποκεῖσθαι, καὶ χῶρον οὔτε ὄμβροις οὔτε νιφετοῖς οὔτε καύμασι βαρυνόμενον, ἀλλ᾽ ὃν ἐξ ὠκεανοῦ πραὺς ἀεὶ ζέφυρος ἐπιπνέων ἀνα- ψύχει· ταῖς δὲ φαύλαις ζοφώδη καὶ χειμέριον ἀφορίζονται μυχὸν γέμοντα τιμωριῶν ἀδιαλείπτων. Ecce hic trans Oceanum lo- cat τὸν ᾅδην. Rursum alio loco idem Josephus ex eadem sententia sedem piis asscribit χῶρον οὐρανῶ τὸν ἁγιώτατον. Sed profecto ista loquendi genera, sub terra, in aëre, trans Oceanum, & quod apud Tertullianum est trans igneam Zonam, nihil aliud quam τὸ ἀόρατον nobisque inaccessum designant. Idem Tertullianus libro de anima penes infe- ros ponit tormentum & refrigerium: Ibidem, puniri & foveri animam interim in inferis sub exspectatione utrius- que judicii, in quadam usurpatione & candida ejus. Simi- lia habet adversus Marcionem IV. Addamus his Ambrosii locum libro de bono mortis cap. X. Satis fuerat dixisse illis, (philosophis) quod liberatæ animæ corporibus ᾅδην peterent, id est locum qui non videtur, quem locum Latine infernum di- cimus. Denique & Scriptura habitacula illa, animarum promtuaria nominavit.

Per ᾅδην ergo non intelligit Grotius τὸν τόπον τῆς βασάνε, sed totam illam regionem sive statum, in quo est animus sine corpore, quod ᾅδης locus sit visibus nostris subtractus, qui cum de corpore acci- piatur, sepulchrum notet, cum de animo, regionem illam jam dictam: unde divitem quidem ἐν ᾅδῃ fuisse ait, sed fuisse ἐν ᾅδῃ etiam Lazarum, di- sterminatis regionibus. Sed quamvis etymi ra- tione nonnulli ᾅδην περὶ τῶ μὴ ἰδεῖν deducant, alii tamen ab ἥδω delector derivant κατ᾽ ἀντίφρα- σιν, quod nulla ibi sit delectatio: & qui supe- riorem derivationem retinent, ita dici volunt, quod sit tristis, sine sole domus, in qua nulla lux, meræ tenebræ. Utut vero sepulcrum no- mine שאול, cui apud LXX. Interpp. respon- det vox ᾅδης indigitetur quandoque, nullus ta- men in Novo Testam. occurrit locus, observan- te B. Gerhardo de inferno §. 5. in quo vox ᾅδης non possit satis commode de inferno accipi. Quod autem nomine illo regio quædam commu- nis, in qua animæ tum fidelium tum infidelium post hanc vitam constitutæ sint, notetur, nun- quam è S. literis docebitur: quæ communem ejusmodi regionem prorsus ignorant. Neque hic ullo apice indicatur Lazari animam ἐν ᾅδῃ fuisse, aut uspiam in S. Scriptura de electorum animabus id dicitur: imo ᾅδης exponitur hoc loco per locum tormentorum, & maximo & in- superabili hiatu discriminatur à sinu Abrahæ, & à Paradiso. Paradoxon ergo est, ἀθεόλο- γον, & ἀντίγραφον, quod hic tradit Grotius; Et Paradisus, & Gehenna, seu ut loqueban- tur Græci, Elysii & Tartara sunt ἐν ᾅδῃ. Quæ verò testimonia ejus profert Grotius? è Græcis

Diphilum, Sophoclem, Diodorum Siculum, Plato- nem, Plutarchum, Iamblichum laudat, quos sequi Virgilium ait. Sed è Scripturis proferenda erant testimonia, non è prophanis & exotericis aut et- iam Poëticis & fabulosis autoribus, quibus de cœ- lesti vita nihil constitit. Neque ad Josephi Phrasin Scripturæ analogam, aut Scripturam ex Josepho explicandam esse, concedendum. Tertullianus ve- rò attemperavit sese modo loquendi Philosophis, cum penes inferos tormentum posuit, & refrige- rium. Ambrosius vero loco citato, libro de bono mortis c. X. diferte Philosophorum allegat senten- tiam: satis fuerat dixisse illis (Philosophis) quod li- berata anima corporibus ᾅδην peterent, id est, locum quem Latine infernum dicimus.

ἐπάρας τοὺς ὀφθαλμοὺς ἀυτοῦ) Sicut Deo solent asscribi actus corporei, ita & animis à corpore solutis simili figura. Quare non satis certum est argumentum quod Irenæus & Tertullianus hinc petunt, ut probent post mortem in ani- mo manere lineamenta quædam corporis & simulacra membrorum: quod non longe abit ab his quæ περὶ τῶν ἀυ- γοειδῶν σωμάτων dicta sunt alibi.

Vers. eod. ὑπάρχων ἐν βασάνοις) Sicut qui in carcere sunt ante damnationem torqueri solent, ita animi à corpo- re soluti etiam ante publicum judicium non possunt non es- se in cruciatu gravissimo, futuram ipsis sententiam prædi- cante conscientia: quo alludens Martialis: Et cum fateri Furia jusserit verum Cogente clamet conscientia, scripsi. Nazianzenus secundo adversus Julianum describit pœnas improborum, inter quas ab eo ponuntur αἱ ἐν ἀυτοῖς τοῖς δεινοῖς ἐξαγορεύσεις.

Non solum conscientiæ cruciatus per βασάνες, sed tormenta Tartari notari, certum est: neque ad- mitti potest, ante publicum judicium solum crucia- tibus conscientia torqueri animas infidelium. Lo- cus certe præsens aliud docet, in quo, si uspiam a- lias, verbis valde emphaticis tartarei cruciatus describuntur. Nam verbum ὀδυνῶμαι non crucia- tus tantum conscientiæ, sed dolores exquisitissimos, quales in tartaro damnati sentiunt, importat: & exclamat epulo, ὀδυνῶμαι ἐν τῇ φλογὶ ταύτῃ, crucior in flamma ista; quæ flamma tartari est, ignis illius inextinguibilis; describuntur hæ flammæ, quæ æstum summum & intolerabilem inferunt, qualem damnati in inferno sentiunt, omnis refocillationis plane expertem, unde summæ mi- sericordiæ loco haberet, si vel minimam aquæ guttulam lingua persentisceret; neque locus τῆς βασάνε, & τὸ ὑπάρχειν ἐν βασάνοις quicquam aliud quam tartarum, & tartareos cruciatus desi- gnant. Confer. Apoc. 14,10. 11. c. 20, 10. Quæ omnia elidere per Schema fictionis quid aliud est, quam ignis infernalis vim extinguere velle? Et conatur tamen id Grotius: cruciatum, inquit, conscientiæ comparat flammæ urenti: sic & Latine nri dicimus eos qui animi angantur: ut apud Terentium, uro hominem. Hinc jam cætera finguntur consequen- ter: nam hi qui uruntur, maxime sitim in lingua sen- tiunt: sitis solet levari aquis: minimum aquæ est quantum digito adhærescit.

ὁρᾷ τὸν Ἀβραὰμ) Conspicere eum dicit, quod eum co- gitaturum erat probabile, & dicere, quod si dicere posset dicturus videbatur.

## 16:24
Vers. 24. Πάτερ Ἀβραὰμ) He addresses him especially as the prince of the blessed: then as him whose descendant they were accustomed to boast of being. But how different was he, who had received any strangers so kindly?

καὶ πέμψον Λάζαρον) This is because it is credible that those whom they remember to have been treated badly by them are always present to the thoughts of the impious. Statius: 'He looks back at Nero, pale at the sight of his mother's torch.' Plato, describing the torments of impious souls, says: 'They cry out and call, some those whom they killed, others those whom they insulted, and calling, they entreat the wronged to grant them forgiveness.'

ἵνα βάψῃ τὸ ἄκρον τῦ δακτύλε ἀυτῦ ὕδατος καὶ καταψύξῃ τὴν γλῶσσάν μου· ὅτι ὀδυνῶμαι ἐν τῇ φλογὶ ταύτῃ.) He compares the torment of conscience to a burning flame: thus also in Latin we say 'uri' (to be burned) of those who are tormented in mind: as in Terence, 'uro hominem'. From this, the rest are now feigned one by one consequently: for those who are burned feel thirst most of all in the tongue: thirst is accustomed to be relieved by waters: the minimum of water is as much as adheres to a finger. The sense is: the rich man who had once despised Lazarus would now willingly supplicate him, if he could obtain any, even the smallest, relief from such great torments. Similar is what we noted on Matthew 23, 39. Add not dissimilar διατυπώσεις (delineations) in Matthew 7, 22. & 25, 37.

Latin:

Vers. 24. Πάτερ Ἀβραὰμ) Illum potissimum affatur ut beatorum principem: deinde ut eum quo generis auctore gloriari solebant. At quanto ille alius, qui ignotos quosvis tam amice exceperat?

καὶ πέμψον Λάζαρον) Hoc ideo quia credibile est impio- rum cogitationibus semper illos obversari quos ab se male tractatos meminerunt. Statius: Palliduma visa Matris lampade respicit Neronem. Plato cruciatus impiorum animorum describens: βοῶσι, in- quit, καὶ καλῦσιν, οἱ μὲν ὃς ἀπέκτειναν, οἱ δὲ ὃς ὕβρισαν, καλέσαν- τες δ' ἱκετεύουσι τοὺς ἀδικημένους δῦναι σφίσι συγνώμην.

ἵνα βάψῃ τὸ ἄκρον τῦ δακτύλε ἀυτῦ ὕδατος καὶ καταψύξῃ τὴν γλῶσσάν μου· ὅτι ὀδυνῶμαι ἐν τῇ φλογὶ ταύτῃ.) Crucia- tum conscientiæ comparat flammæ urenti: sic & Latinis uri dicimus eos qui animi anguntur: ut apud Terentium, uro hominem. Hinc jam cætera singulatim consequenter s. nam hi qui uruntur maxime sitim in lingua sentiunt: fois solet levari aquis: minimum aquæ est quantum digito ad- hærescit. Sensus est: divitem qui olim Lazarum contem- serat nunc libenter illi supplicaturum, si aliquod vel mini- mum tantorum cruciatuum levamentum possit indipisci. Simile est quod adnotavimus ad Matthæum 23, 39. Adde non dissimiles διατυπώσεις Matth. 7, 22. & 25, 37.

## 16:25
Vers. 25. ἀπέλαβες) ἀπολαμβάνειν here is not to receive back, but to receive fully, in which sense ἀπέχειν is also taken in Matthew 6, 2. 5. 16. Luke above 6, 24.

τὰ ἀγαθά σου) And this emphatically. Those, he says, goods which you considered true, nay, the highest goods, which you used not as entrusted to you under a certain law and manner, but as clearly your own, in which finally you placed your trust. Similar is that of Euripides: 'Κταχθῆ πάμφυν δρῶν γὰρ ὄγκωσαι' (For having done all things, you have been puffed up).

νῦν δὲ ὧδε παρακαλεῖται) That νῦν δὲ shows a wondrous change of fortune. It generally happens, indeed, that those for whom things are best here, for them it is worst in the other life. Whom they would wish never to have shone with proud scepters. Conversely, those whom every kind of evil has exercised here, there perhaps enjoy the best things: so that in this sense also that saying of Heraclitus may be used: we live their death, and we have died their life. That saying of Christ pertains here: blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted. Lactantius, book VI. These are the ways which God has assigned to human life: in which, individually, He shows both good and evil, but in a preposterous and reversed order: for in one He showed temporal evils first with eternal goods: which is the better order: in the other, temporal goods first with eternal evils, which is the worse order, so that whoever chooses present evils with justice may obtain greater and more certain goods than were those which he spurned: but whoever prefers present goods to justice may fall into greater and longer-lasting evils than were those which he fled. Solace is spoken of here, not full retribution, which will happen only when bodies are returned, but a certain expectation of it, sustained meanwhile by great joys: the ancient Latins call this refreshment: Tertullian says that the region in which Abraham is provides refreshment to the souls of the just, until the consummation of things completes the resurrection of all with the fullness of reward, then to appear with the heavenly promise: and he names the same region the temporal receptacle of faithful souls, in which an image of the future is delineated, and a certain bright prospect of both judgments is seen. But just as it is believed both piously and rightly that much good has accrued to pious souls after the death of Christ, so I fear that to describe the degrees, moments, and places of either state is of too curious an audacity. Here that Sophoclean line pleases me: Ἀλλ᾽ οὐ γὰρ ἂν τὰ θεῖα κρύπτοντος θεοῦ Μάθοις ἂν, οὐδ᾽ εἰ πάντ᾽ ἐπεξέλθοις σκοπῶν. to which that saying of Chrysostom, and after him Isidore of Pelusium, seems to allude: ὅταν ἅπερ ὁ θεὸς ἡμᾶς ἠβουλήθη εἰδέναι, ταῦτα βιαζώμεθα μανθάνειν, ὅτε ἐσόμεθα (πῶς γὰρ θεοῦ μὴ βουλομένου;) καὶ τὸ κινδυνεύειν ἡμῖν ἐκ τοῦ ζητεῖν περίεστι μόνον. It is better, says Augustine, treating this argument wisely and modestly, to doubt about hidden things than to litigate about uncertain ones.

Not only is the expectation of retribution or verbal consolation designated: because τὸ ὀδυνᾶσαι is opposed to it. Therefore, if by ὀδύνας are understood the highest pains and torments, so conversely by παράκλησιν a real consolation and highest recreation is indicated. Therefore they are declared blessed, ἀποθνήσκοντες ἀπαρτι, because they are participants in the heavenly beatitude, which consists in the vision and fruition of God, Apoc. XIV. 13. What he says, that much good accrued to pious souls in that blessed age after the death of Christ, is said ἄτερ γραφῆς. And therefore it is believed neither piously nor rightly, because it is nowhere held in the word of God, the sole principle of faith.

Latin:

Vers. 25. ἀπέλαβες) ἀπολαμβάνειν hic non esse recipere, sed plene accipere, quo sensu ἀπέχειν etiam sumitur Matth. 6, 2. 5. 16. Lucas supra 6, 24.

τὰ ἀγαθά σου) Et hoc ἐμφατικῶς. Illa, inquit, bona quæ tu vera, imo summa bona duxisti, quibus usus es non ut tibi creditis sub certa lege ac modo, sed ut plane propriis, in quibus denique fiduciam tuam posuisti. Simile est illud Euripidis: Κταχθῆ πάμφυν δρῶν γὰρ ὄγκωσαι.

νῦν δὲ ὧδε παρακαλεῖται) Illud νῦν δὲ ostendit miram vicis- situdinem. Plerumque sane ita evenit, ut quibus hic optime est, iis in altera vita sit pessime. Quem vellent nunquam sceptris fulsisse superbis. Contra, quos hic omne malorum genus exercuit, ibi forte optima fruuntur: ita ut in hunc quoque sensum usurpari possit illud Heracliti: ζῶμεν τὸν ἐκείνων θάνατον, τεθνήκαμεν δὲ τὸν ἐκείνων βίον. Pertinet huc illud Christi: μακάριοι οἱ πεν- θοῦντες, ὅτι αὐτοὶ παρακληθήσονται. Lactantius libro VI. Hæ sunt viæ quas Deus humanæ vitæ assignavit: in quibus sin- gulis & bona ostendit & mala, sed ordine præpostero atque con- verso: in una enim monstravit temporalia prius mala cum æ- ternis bonis: qui est ordo melior: in altera temporalia prius bona cum æternis malis, qui est ordo deterior, ut quicunque præsentia mala cum justitia delegerit, majora & certiora consequatur bo- na quam fuerunt illa quæ sprevis: quisquis autem præsentia bona præposuerit justitiæ in majora & longiora incidat mala quam fuerunt illa quæ fugit. Solatium dicitur hic, non plena retributio, quæ redditis demum corporibus fiet, sed ejus- dem certa exspectatio, magnis interim gaudiis sustentata: id refrigerium vocant veteres Latini: Tertullianus regio- nem in qua est Abraham ait refrigerium præbere animabus justorum, donec consummatio rerum resurrectionem o- mnium plenitudine mercedis expungat, tunc apparitura cœlesti promissione: eademque regionem nominat tem- porale animarum fidelium receptaculum, in quo delinee- tur futuri imago, ac candida quædam utriusque judicii pro- spiciatur. Sicut autem post Christi mortem piis animis multum boni accessisse & pie & recte creditur, ita utri- usque fortis gradus, momenta, loca describere vereor ne curiosæ nimis sit audaciæ. Placet hic mihi illud Sopho- cleum: Ἀλλ᾽ οὐ γὰρ ἂν τὰ θεῖα κρύπτοντος θεοῦ Μάθοις ἂν, οὐδ᾽ εἰ πάντ᾽ ἐπεξέλθοις σκοπῶν. quo alludere videtur illud Chrysostomi, & post eum Isidori Pelusiotæ: ὅταν ἅπερ ὁ θεὸς ἡμᾶς ἠβουλήθη εἰδέναι, ταῦτα βιαζώμεθα μανθάνειν, ὅτε ἐσόμεθα (πῶς γὰρ θεοῦ μὴ βουλομένου;) καὶ τὸ κινδυνεύειν ἡμῖν ἐκ τοῦ ζητεῖν περίεστι μόνον. Melius est, inquit Augustinus, sapienter & modeste tractans hoc argu- mentum, dubitare de occultis, quam litigare de incertis.

Non tantum expectatio retributionis, aut ver- balis consolatio designatur: quia opponitur ei τὸ ὀδυνᾶσαι. Utergo per ὀδύνας intelliguntur do- lores & cruciatus summi, sic ex adverso per πα- ράκλησιν consolatio realis & recreatio summa indi- gitatur. Ideo μακάριοι beati prædicantur, ἀπο- θνήσκοντες ἀπαρτι, quia cœlestis beatitudinis, quæ in visione & fruitione Dei consistit, parti- cipes sunt Apoc. XIV. 13. Quod ait, piis animis in beato illo seculo multum boni accessisse post Christi mortem, ἄτερ γραφῆς dicitur. Ideoque nec pie nec recte creditur, quod in verbo Dei fidei unico principio nuspiam habetur.

## 16:26
Vers. 26. χάσμα μέγα ἐστήρικται) A Great Chaos, the Latin interpreter, whom I would not wish to be criticized here. For he understood that a certain void interval is signified here, in which sense both χάσμα and χάος are used in the Greek of Zachar. 14, 4. Most frequent, however, is the use of both words where it concerns Hades. Euripides, as we mentioned elsewhere, said ἄβυσσα χάσματα. Seneca, however, called it Chaos in Medea: Noctis alternæ chaos. In Thyestes: Ad chaos inane. Which word Ovid, Silius, and others also use in this sense: Silius describes it the same way: In the middle a vast void stretches far and wide. Seneca thus: Hence ample spaces are loosened in empty places.

Aristotle in Acroamatum IV interprets the place of chaos in Hesiod, not indeed from χάω, as others do, but from χώρειν, whence also χώρημα, deriving that word: which interpretation of Aristotle Philo also recites in On the Incorruptibility of the World. And an old Christian writer against the dogmas of Aristotle, who is read under the name of Justin, approves it. Just as, therefore, they called that which was before this visible world Chaos, so also they called that which is now outside the same world. Many of the philosophers inquired that τὸ κενὸν τοῦ κόσμου κενὸν εἶναι ἄπειρον: but they also called τὸ κενὸν χώραν and διάστημα. Lucretius: The place and space which we call the void. Ibycus: It flies in a foreign chaos. But also Aquila translates the Hebrew תהו in Moses in the history of the world's creation as κένωμα, Theodotion as κενόν. From which Hebrew word, through a metathesis not infrequent, it can be seen that תהום is derived, which the Syriac has here, for which the Arab has لجة, to which another Arabic word هوزة is related, which is also accustomed to be translated as χάος and ἄβυσσος. Tertullian translates χάσμα as deep in this place; and soon after, circumlocuting, he calls it an immense distance of sublimity and depth: also Plutarch in the book On the Delay of the Divine Vengeance in the description of the underworld places a χάσμα μέγα καὶ κάτω διῆκον. Besides these, see the passage of Plato concerning the Armenian Er.

οἱ θέλοντες) That is, even if they wish. Similar is that of Pythagoras concerning souls, that the pure are led to the highest place, but the impure do not even approach those.

Latin:

Vers. 26. χάσμα μέγα ἐστήρικται) Chaos Magnum Lati- nus interpres, quem nolim hic reprehendi. Intellexit enim cafsum quoddam intervallum hic significari, quo sensu & χάσμα & χάος in Græco Zachar. 14, 4. Frequentissimus autem vocis utriusque usus, ubi περὶ ᾅδου agitur. Euripides ut alibi meminimus dixit ἄβυσσα χάσματα. Seneca autem Chaos dixit Medea: Noctis alternæ chaos. Thyeste: Ad chaos inane. Quam vocem hoc sensu Ovidius quoque Silius & alii usurpant: Idem Silius ita describit: In medio vastum late se tendit inane. Seneca sic: Hinc ampla vacuis spatia laxantur locis.

Aristoteles Acroamatum IV, χάος apud Hesiodum locum interpretatur, nimirum non à χάω, ut alii, sed à χώρειν, un- de & χώρημα, eam vocem derivans: quam Aristotelis inter- pretationem & Philo recitat περὶ ἀφθαρσίας κόσμου. Et pro- bat vetus Scriptor Christianus adversus Aristotelis dogma- ta, qui sub Justini nomine legitur. Sicut igitur quod ante mundum hunc adspectabilem erat, Chaos dixere, ita & quod nunc extra eundem mundum est. ińdὸς τοῦ κόσμου κενὸν εἶναι ἄ- πειρον multi Philosophorum sciscebant: atqui τὸ κενὸν etiam vocabant χώραν & διάστημα. Lucretius: Locus ac spatium quod inane vocamus. Ibycus: ποτᾶται δ' ἐν ἀλλοτρίῳ χάει. Sed & Hebræum תהו apud Mosem in historia mundi conditi Aquila vertit κένω- μα, Theodotio κενόν. Ex qua voce Hebræa per metathesin non infrequentem videri potest derivatum תהום quod hic habet Syrus, pro quo Arabs habet لجة cui affinis est altera vox Arabica هوزة quæ & χάος & ἄβυσσος verti solet. Tertullianus χάσμα profundum hoc loco vertit; & mox circumloquens vocat immensam distantiæ sublimitatis ac profunditatis: etiam Plutarchus libro de Sera numinis vindicta in descriptione inferorum ponit χάσμα μέγα καὶ κάτω διῆκον. Præter hæc vide locum Platonis de Ere Ar- menio.

οἱ θέλοντες) Id est, κἂν θέλωσι. Simile est illud Pythago- ræ de animabus, ἄγεσθαι τὰς μὲν καθαρὰς ἐπὶ τὸ ὕψιστον· τὰς δὲ ἀκαθάρτους μήτε ἐκείναις πελάζειν.

## 16:27
Verse 27. ἵνα πέμψῃς αὐτὸν) Namely, him restored to his own body, lest anyone suspect that this deals with the apparitions of souls. But that this is true is shown by what follows below, if someone should rise from the dead.

Latin:

Vers. 27. ἵνα πέμψῃς αὐτὸν) Nempe ipsum corpori suo redditum, ne quis hic de animorum apparitionibus agi suspicetur. Verum hoc esse ostendit quod infra sequitur ἐάν τις ἐκ νεκρῶν ἀναστῇ.

## 16:28
Verse 28. πέντε ἀδελφοὺς) A moderate number to fulfill the representation. Thus also Isaiah 19:18.

ὅπως διαμαρτύρηται αὐτοῖς) That he may bear witness to those things which are done here.

εἰς τὸν τόπον τοῦτον τῆς βασάνου) Which place we have seen called a prison by Josephus. Plato called the same a dungeon. Thus Peter ascribes chains of darkness to the devils, and Jude eternal bonds.

Latin:

Vers. 28. πέντε ἀδελφοὺς) Mediocris numerus ad implen- dam διατύπωσιν. Sic & Esaiæ XIX, 18.

ὅπως διαμαρτύρηται αὐτοῖς) Ut testimonium ferat eorum quæ hic geruntur.

εἰς τὸν τόπον τοῦτον τῆς βασάνου) Quem locum εἱργμὸν apud Josephum vocari vidimus. Plato eundem dixit δεσμωτή- ριον. Sic diabolis Petrus σειρὰς ζόφου, Judas δεσμὰ ἀΐδια asscribit.

## 16:29
Verse 29. ἔχουσι Μωσέα) Whose words exist in dissertation commanding that the needy among the people be helped.

καὶ τὰς προφήτας) As Isaiah, who says to the Jews boasting of their fasts that the best fast is to feed the hungry, to provide hospitality to the outcasts, and to clothe the naked, ch. 58:7.

From Moses and the Prophets, not only could precepts be had concerning mercy to be shown to the needy, but whatever is required for true repentance, whatever for escaping hell, whatever for obtaining eternal salvation. For this reason they are sent to hear Moses and the Prophets.

ἀκουσάτωσαν αὐτῶν) Let them obey their warnings: for that is to hear with profit.

Latin:

Vers. 29. ἔχουσι Μωσέα) Cujus disserta exstant verba præ- cipientia egenis popularibus succurri.

καὶ τὰς προφήτας) Ut Esaiam qui jejunia sua jactantibus Judæis optimum jejunium esse ait, esurientes pascere, ex- torribus præbere hospitium, nudum vestire c. 58, 7.

E Mose & Prophetis non modo præcepta ha- beri poterant de misericordia egenis exhibenda, sed quicquid ad veram pœnitentiam, quicquid ad effugiendam gehennam; quicquid ad conse- quendam salutem æternam requiritur. Ideo enim ad Mosen & Prophetas audiendos remit- tuntur.

ἀκουσάτωσαν αὐτῶν) Illorum monitis pareant: id enim est cum fructu audire.

## 16:30
Verse 30. οὐχὶ) That is, they will not hear them. He knew their disposition from his own.

Latin:

Vers. 30. οὐχὶ) Id est, οὐκ ἀκούσουσι αὐτῶν. De se illorum ingenium noverat.

## 16:31
Vers. 31. If they do not hear Moses and the prophets, neither will they be persuaded if one rise from the dead) Yet it is said of the Tyrians and Sidonians that they would have repented if they had seen the miracles which had been done by Christ in the towns of Galilee. We must answer: first, that all these things are said not absolutely but for the most part: then, that there was a wide difference. The Tyrians and Sidonians were held by great and ancient ignorance. Antiquity had obliterated the old tradition of the Noachides, and long custom had obliterated natural knowledge. Such people are wont to be stirred by miracles. But the Jews, besides those things which were common to the human race, had the law which they themselves confessed was delivered by God and confirmed by many and notable miracles, the fame of which they had received handed down by a continuous succession from their ancestors: and yet they lived their lives against the most manifest words of the law. They could not therefore show either ignorance, or even any probable authority regarding the interpretation of the law, for their fault. Nothing stood in their way except a perverse mind, unwilling to embrace as true, or at least as necessary, those things which they could not argue were false. In such a multitude of men, just as there may be some whom miracles might awaken as if from a deep sleep, so a far greater part is incurably sick. The thing itself shows this. Christ restored to life Lazarus, a namesake of this Lazarus, (and it is not indeed unlikely that Christ looked to this when he said those things). Did the Pharisees obey the warnings of Christ any the more for that? Nay, rather, they devoted their efforts to slaughtering both Christ and Lazarus. Christ himself returned from the dead: there were not a few men as witnesses of this thing, of innocent life, with no reward for lying. This also did not move them to repentance to such a degree that they desired the fame of that event to be extinguished by every means. Lactantius well says: Those who burn with a certain insatiable thirst for avarice and riches, because they cannot live that life which they love with riches or by distributing them with a frugal lifestyle, without doubt say that that evil is false by which they are compelled to renounce their desires. The same: Those who are incited by the roots of lusts (as the Poet says) rush into furies and fire, they certainly say that we bring forward incredible things, because the precepts of continence wound their ears, which prohibit them from their pleasures, to which they have adjudged their soul along with their body. But those who are inflated by ambition, or inflamed by the love of power, have devoted all their effort to acquiring honors, and even if we were to carry the sun itself in our hands, they will not lend belief to that doctrine which commands them, with all power and honor despised, to live humbly, and so humbly that they can both receive injury and refuse to return it if they have received it. These are the men who, with eyes closed, bark in every way against the truth. Salvian: Everything is hard that is commanded to the unwilling: Almost every divine discourse has its rivals; as many kinds of precepts as there are, so many are the adversaries: if the Lord commands that there be generosity in men, the miser is angered: if he demands thrift, the spendthrift curses: the wicked call the sacred discourses their enemies: plunderers shudder at whatever is written about justice: the proud shudder at whatever is commanded about humility: the drunkards turn away when sobriety is proclaimed: the unchaste detest it when chastity is commanded. Soon after: Any wicked person prefers to curse the law than to amend his mind, he prefers to hate the precepts than his vices. Then: I give advice, however, to all to whom the law of God is heavy and burdensome, if they do not refuse to receive it, as to how those things which God commands can be pleasing to them: for all who hate the sacred commandment have the cause of the hatred in themselves: all the disgust is not in the precepts of the law, but in their own morals. For the law is good, but morals are bad, and by this let men change their purpose and their affection: for if they make their morals acceptable, nothing that the good law commands will displease them: for when anyone begins to be good, he cannot but love the law of God, because the holy law of God has within itself that which holy men have in their morals.

Latin:

Vers. 31. εἰ Μωσέως καὶ τῶν προφητῶν οὐκ ἀκούουσι, οὐδὲ ἐάν τις ἐκ νεκρῶν ἀναστῇ πεισθήσονται) Atqui de Tyriis & Sido- niis dicitur pœnitentiam eos acturos fuisse, si miracula vidis- sent, quæ facta erant à Christo in Galileæ oppidis. Respon- dendum: primo dici hæc omnia non ἀποθετικῶς sed κατὰ τὸ πλεῖστον: deinde latum esse discrimen. Tyrii & Sidonii ma- gna ac vetere ignorantia tenebantur. Veterem Noarda- rum traditionem vetustas, naturales notitias longa consue- tudo obliteraverat. Tales solent miraculis excitari. At Judæi, præter ea quæ humano generi erant communia, ha- bebant legem quam ipsi fatebantur à Deo traditam & multis atque insignibus miraculis confirmatam, quorum famam continua successione à majoribus traditam acceperant: & tamen contra apertissima legis verba vitam agebant. Non poterant ergo aut ignorantiam, aut etiam probabilem ali- quam de legis interpretatione auctoritatem, culpæ suæ ostendere. Nihil illis obstabat nisi perversus animus, no- lens ea ut vera, aut certe ut necessaria amplecti, quæ falsi arguere non poterant. In tali hominum multitudine, ut fore sint aliqui quos velut ex alto somno miracula excitent, ita pars longe major insanabiliter ægrotat. Ostendit hoc res ipsa. Lazarum huic Lazaro cognominem, (nec vero dissimile est huc Christum respexisse cum ista diceret) vitæ reddidit Christus. An eo magis Pharisæi monitis Christi obtemperarunt? Imo potius quam id facerent operam de- derunt, ut & Christum & Lazarum trucidarent. Christus ipse à mortuis rediit: testes erant hujus rei viri non pauci, vitæ innocentis, nullo mentiendi præmio. Hoc quoque adeo illos ad resipiscentiam non permovit, ut omni vi fa- mam ejus rei exstinctam cuperent. Bene Lactantius: Qui avaritiæ & opum inexplebili quadam siti flagrant, quia eam non possunt diuitiis aut dilargitis quæ amant tenui cultu vi- tam degere, sine dubio malum id esse falsum quo desideriis suis renuntiare cogantur. Idem: Qui libidinum stirpalis incitati (ut ait Poëta) in furias ignemque ruunt, utique incredibilia nos adferre dicunt, quia vulnerant aures eorum præcepta conti- nentiæ, quæ illos à voluptatibus suis prohibent, quibus animam suam cum corpore adjudicaverunt. Qui vero ambitione inflati, aut amore potentiæ inflammati omne studium ad hono- res acquirendos contulerunt, nec si solem quidem ipsum geste- mus in manibus, fidem commodabunt ei doctrinæ quæ illos ju- bit omni potentia & honore contempto humiles vivere, atque ita humiles, ut & accipere injuriam possint & referre nolint si acce- perint. Ii sunt homines qui contra veritatem clausis oculis quo- quo modo latrant. Salvianus: Totum durum est quicquid im- peratur invitis: Pene omnis sermo divinus habet æmulos suos, quot genera præceptorum sunt, tot adversariorum: si largita- tem esse in hominibus jubet Dominus, avarus irascitur: si par- cimoniam exigit, prodigus execratur: sermones sacros improbi hostes suos dicunt: horrent raptores quicquid de justitia fcribi- tur: horrent superbi quicquid de humilitate mandatur: aver- santur ebriosi ubi sobrietas indicitur: detestantur impudici ubi castitas imperatur. Mox: Mavult quilibet improbus execrari legem, quam emendare mentem, mavult præcepta odisse, quam vitia. Deinde: Do tamen consilium omnibus quibus gravis & onerosa est lex Dei, si accipere non recusant, quemadmodum placere eis possint quæ Deus præcipit: Cuncti etenim qui oderunt mandatum sacrum, causam odii in se ipsis habent: omne fasti- dium non in præceptis legis, sed in moribus suis. Lex quippe bo- na est, sed mores mali, ac per hoc mutent homines propositum & affectum suum: si enim mores suos probabiles esse fecerint, nihil eis quod lex bona præcipit, displicebit: quando enim bonus quis esse cœperit, non potest non diligere legem Dei, quia hoc intra se habet lex Dei sancta, quod homines sancti in moribus.

## 17:1 Argument
CHAPTER XVII.

ARGUMENT AND DIVISION.

Christ teaches his disciples about scandals and brotherly forgiveness, as also, being asked, that he might strengthen their faith, about the power of faith, and about the uselessness of servants, even if they have done all things. Journeying to Jerusalem through Samaria and Galilee, he heals ten lepers, of whom only one, and he a Samaritan, is grateful. But being asked by the Pharisees about the coming of the kingdom of God, he teaches that it does not come with display, and that the coming of the Son of God to judgment will be sudden, comparing those times to the times of Noah and Lot, and warns his disciples about saving the soul.

There are three parts: I. Information about scandals and brotherly forgiveness, as also about the uselessness of servants, to verse 10. II. The healing of the ten lepers, to verse 19. III. The response given to the Pharisees about the coming of the kingdom of God, with a prophecy about the imminent judgment, and necessary exhortation, to the final verse 36.

PART I.

Information about scandals and brotherly forgiveness.

Vers. 1. It is impossible) That is, it is not fitting, as above it is not possible, ch. 13, 33. It is not expedient that men be hindered by the force of divine power from adulterating doctrine, splitting unity, and doing many things which delay others in the course of piety. See at Matt.

It is explained by ἀνάγκη ἐστὶ, it is necessary, in Matt. 18:10. Beza does not establish this sense, it cannot happen that stumbling blocks do not occur. But ἐνδέχεται does not mean it is not, or it never happens. However, the necessity of consequence, and hypothetical, as they call it, is understood, not of the consequent, or absolute. This discourse is similar, yet different, because that one was instituted on the occasion of the contention of the disciples. Here, however, the same admonition is repeated, because nothing is more frequent than to cause scandal to others. And because Christ saw the Pharisees mocking him and envying him on account of his teaching concerning alms and the danger of riches, therefore, lest the disciples be disturbed by this, he warns them about scandals, that while they must indeed happen because of the malice of men, they themselves ought nevertheless to be firmer in faith than to be offended by them.

Latin:

CAPUT XVII.

ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Christus discipulos de scandalis & condona- tione fraterna docet, ut & rogatus, ut fidem confortet, de fidei vi, deque inutilitate ser- vorum, etsi omnia fecerint. Hierosolymam per Samariam & Galilæam tendens decem leprosos sanat, è quibus unus tantum, isque Samaritanus gratus est. A Pharisæis ve- ro rogatus ad adventu regni Dei, id non cum apparatu venire docet, & adventum Filii Dei ad judicium subitum fore, compa- rans illa tempora Noah & Loth tempori- bus, deque anima servanda discipulos monet.

Partes sunt tres: . I. Informatio de scandalis, & condonatione fraterna, ut & servorum inutili- tate, ad v. 10. II. Decem leprosorum sanatio, ad v. 19. III. Responsio Pharisæis de adventu regni Dei reddita, cum vaticinio de judicio imminente, & parænesi necessaria, ad v. 36. finalem.

PARS I.

Informatio de scandalis & condonatione fra- terna.

Vers. 1. Ἀνένδεκτόν ἐστι) Id est, non convenit, ut supra ἐκ ἐνδέχεται c. 13, 33. Non expedit ut vi potentiæ divinæ im- pediantur homines adulterare doctrinam, scindere unita- tem, & plura facere quæ in pietatis cursu alios remorentur. Vide ad Matth.

Exponitur per ἀνάγκη ἐστὶ, necesse est, apud Matth. 18, 10. quem sensum non statuit Beza, con- tingere non potest, ut non eveniant offendicula. Non vero ἐνδέχεται est non, vel nunquam contingit. Necessitas autem consequentiæ, & hypothetica, quam vocant, intelligitur non consequentis, aut absoluta. Concio hæc similis est, diversa tamen, quia illa occasione contentionis discipulorum instituta est. Hic autem repetitur eadem admoni- tio, quia nihil frequentius est, quam alios scandalo afficere. Et quia Christus vidit Pharisaeos se sub- sannare, & invidere sibi, ob doctrinam de eleemo- synis, & de periculo divitiarum, ideo ne discipuli eo turbarentur, monet de scandalis, quod illa qui- dem ob malitiam hominum accidere oporteat, ipsi tamen debeant firmiores esse in fide, quam ut iisdem offendantur.

## 17:2
V. 2. λυσιτελεῖ] The indicative for the potential, as also in that which follows, περιετέθη.

Latin:

V. 2. λυσιτελεῖ] Indicativus pro potentiali, ut & in eo quod sequitur περιετέθη.

## 17:3
V. 3 προσέχετε ἑαυτοῖς) Beware lest you give anyone an occasion to perish, I do not now say by deeds, but even by negligence of duty, not even to those by whom you have been harmed. This is the greatest thing: not to be angry at the one by whom you have been harmed, but even to provide for his salvation, and indeed with the greatest fairness and calmness. Whoever knows how to perform this rightly will neither offend others himself, nor will he be negligent in his duty toward others by whom he has not been provoked by injury.

ἂν ἐπιτίμησον αὐτῷ) By those degrees which are explained in Matthew.

ἐὰν μετανοήσῃ, ἄφες αὐτῷ) Not only that you should not seek vengeance, which you ought not to do even against the contumacious, but that you should admit the one who truly repents into the right of old friendship and familiarity. See Matthew.

Latin:

V. 3 προσέχετε ἑαυτοῖς) Cavete ne cui occasionem detis pereundi, non jam dico factis, sed etiam negligentia officii, ne illis quidem a quibus laesi estis. Maximum hoc est ei a quo laesus sis adeo non irasci, ut etiam saluti ejus consulas, & quidem cum summa aequitate ac placiditate. Hoc qui re- cte praestare norit, neque alios ipse offendet, neque in offi- cio suo circa alios a quibus non est injuria provocatus, ne- gligens erit.

ἂν ἐπιτίμησον αὐτῷ) Iis gradibus qui apud Matthaeum exponuntur.

ἐὰν μετανοήσῃ, ἄφες αὐτῷ) Non modo ut ultionem non expetas, quod facere ne quidem adversus contuma- cem debes, sed ut vere resipiscentem in veteris amicitiae ac familiaritatis jus admittas. Vide ad Matthaeum.

## 17:4
V. 4. ἑπτάκις τῆς ἡμέρας) Very often. For thus the Hebrews speak, Psalm CXIX. 164.

ἐπιστρέψῃ ἐπί σε) ἐπιστρέφεσθαι or שׁוּב or שׁוּב עַל riva. In Hebrew, שׁוּב אֶל with the addition of שׁוּב עַל is to take pains to reconcile someone to yourself, as in Deut. IV. 30. Luke above I. 17. Acts IX. 35. c. XI. 21. and elsewhere.

Latin:

V. 4. ἑπτάκις τῆς ἡμέρας) Saepissime. Ita enim loquun- tur Hebraei Psalm. CXIX. 164.

ἐπιστρέψῃ ἐπί σε) ἐπιστρέφεσθαι vel שׁוּב aut שׁוּב עַל riva. Hebrai- ce שׁוּב אֶל addito שׁוּב עַל est ut aliquem tibi reconcilies operam dare, ut Deut. IV. 30. Lucas supra I. 17. Actor. IX. 35. c. XI. 21. & alibi.

## 17:5
V. 5. πρόσθες ἡμῖν πίστιν) In these narratives which are gathered as if in a medley, no coherence seems to be required. It is credible that the Apostles, often rebuked for their ὀλιγοπιστίαν (little faith), asked Christ to increase the trust in them, by which request they most openly acknowledge the divine power in him. At the same time, this passage refutes that opinion in which Augustine once was when he said: That we believe is our own, but that we do good works is His who gives the Holy Spirit to those who believe, thinking, indeed, as he later interpreted his own error, that faith is not a gift of God, but that the gifts of God are obtained through faith. Rightly, therefore, he corrected it in this manner: Both (both to believe and to work) are His, because He prepares the will, and both are ours, because it does not happen unless we are willing. But lest anyone think that the Greeks, often preaching αὐτεξούσιον (free will), thought otherwise, let him see what we have brought forward elsewhere from Justin and others on this matter.

Those things are not gathered confusedly, but they cohere excellently: For fraternal correction pertains to the teaching concerning scandals: which, if it does not lack its fruit, and he who has sinned against us repents, a readiness for forgiveness is required on our part. But to all these things, since there is need of a firmer faith and true humility, the Apostles ask that their faith be increased, and they are informed by Christ about the power of the same, and are admonished by Christ toward humility. v. 7.

Latin:

V. 5. πρόσθες ἡμῖν πίστιν) In his narrationibus quae velut per saturam sunt congestae, non videtur ulla requiri cohae- rentia. Credibile est Apostolos saepe ob ὀλιγοπιστίαν repre- hensos, postulasse a Christo ut fiduciam in ipsis adaugeret, qua certe postulatione apertissime divinam in ipso poten- tiam agnoscunt. Simul refellit hic locus eam sententiam in qua olim fuit Augustinus cum diceret: Quod credimus nostrum est, quod autem bonum operamur illius est qui cre- dentibus dat Spiritum Sanctum, existimans nimirum ut ipse errorem suum postea est interpretatus, fidem non esse do- num Dei, sed per fidem Dei dona impetrari. Recte igitur id correxit in hunc modum: Vtrumque ( & credere & ope- rari) ipsius est, quia ipse praeparat voluntatem & utramque nostrum, quia non fit nisi volentibus nobis. At ne quis Grae- cos αὐτεξούσιον saepe praedicantes aliter putet sensisse, videat quae alibi ex Justino aliisque in hanc rem adduximus.

Non congesta illa confuse sunt, sed cohaerent o- ptime: Nam ad doctrinam de scandalis pertinet correptio fraterna: quae si fructu suo non careat, & poeniteat, qui adversus nos peccavit, condonationis promtitudo a parte nostra requiritur. Ad haec au- tem omnia, quum fide firmiori opus sit, veraque humilitate fidem sibi augeri petant Apostoli, & de ejusdem virtute a Christo informantur, & ad humilitatem a Christo commonefiunt. v. 7.

## 17:6
V. 6. ὡς κόκκον σινάπεως) See Matthew.

τῇ συκαμίνῳ) This word does not come from the fig tree, as some think; but it is purely Syriac שקמא, to the Hebrews שקמים. It is necessary that the tree be very similar to the mulberry, since not only the Latin, but also the Syrian and the Arab translate it as mulberry. Celsus on medicine, book 3, c. XVIII. Since the Greeks call the mulberry Sycaminum. Moreover, Dioscorides joins μορίας and συκαμινίαν. But what is said here about the Sycaminum is proverbial, by which is signified τὸ παρ' ἀνθρώποις ἀδύνατον (that which is impossible among men). Such is that of Claudian:

A sea fit for fruitful harvests.

By miracles, however, if I may so speak, φυσικὰ (natural), are signified at the same time συμβολικῶς (symbolically) moral miracles, namely the stupendous works of love, of which trust in God is accustomed to bring forth a rich harvest, when it has arrived at its just measure. But Christ invites his disciples to these works in the discourse which is connected with these words.

Latin:

V. 6. ὡς κόκκον σινάπεως) Vide ad Matthaeum.

τῇ συκαμίνῳ) Non venit haec vox a ficu, ut quidam pu- tant; sed est mere Syriaca שקמא, Hebraeis שקמים. O- portet moro admodum similem esse arborem, quando non Latinus tantum, sed & Syrus & Arabs morum vertunt Cel- sus de re medica lib. 3. c. XVIII. Cum Graeci morum Syca- minum appellent. Quin & Dioscorides conjungit μορίας & συκαμινίαν. Quod autem de Sycamino hic dicitur, est pro- verbiale, quo significatur τὸ παρ' ἀνθρώποις ἀδύνατον. Tale illud Claudiani:

Laeta frugibus aptum Aequor.

Per miracula autem, ut ita loquar, φυσικὰ, significantur si- mul συμβολικῶς miracula ἠθικὰ, stupenda scilicet opera di- lectionis, quorum uberem segetem proferre solet fiducia in Deum, ubi ad justam sui mensuram pervenit. Ad haec au- tem opera discipulos Christus invitat eo sermone qui istis verbis connectitur.

## 17:7
V. 7. But which of you.

Since Grotius at length refutes the Papistic heterodoxy concerning the merits of works in relation to this comparison, those things which he hands down here must be carefully observed. For the same things can be opposed to Grotius himself in those matters which he annotated for the consultation of Cassander, in favor of the Papists, and which he attempted to defend against Rivet:

Many of the ancients, among whom is Cyprian, and Theophylact on this passage, extend this comparison even to the most excellent deeds of Christians, teaching that not even in those is there anything for us to boast about, or which we may impute to God. For I judge the true reading in Cyprian to be in the Epistle to the lapsed: 'who have always worked gloriously and grandly in the Church and never imputed their work to the Lord,' as the old editions have it, not as the more recent ones, which omit the negation. For 'to impute' in the Latin language, when it refers to good deeds, is not to accept but to charge as an expense: thus Seneca called the proud and 'imputatores' (imputers), who value their own benefits highly and wish to have others obligated to them on that account; for it is easier, as Chrysostom said, for a humble mind to lead a man to salvation without works than pride joined with works. And there are many things which ought to prohibit us from calling God to account. For first, since He Himself made us from nothing so that we might exist, who would doubt that He can demand from us whatever is in our power, even with no reward proposed? Aristotle said: 'There is no equality toward the double.' Whence he also denies that justice, properly and strictly so called, has a place between master and servant. And indeed, if a servant were entirely the Master's, just as we are God's, he would speak the truth. Do not boast if you have served well; the Sun obeys, the Moon complies. Furthermore, since reason has been given to us, and we have that excellence above other living creatures, should it not be considered as natural for us to live according to reason as it is for beasts to live according to the impulses of nature? But for that reason, no reward is owed to beasts. Thirdly, it ought to come to mind that there is no one to whom unpunished sins have not been forgiven, which, as we said above, even one is enough to prostrate us humbly before God. No one can perform so much that they do not owe more for the benefit of indulgence. Added to this is that even the traces of faults which remain in us after amendment have daily need of divine mercy. The fourth is that the fruits are owed to the sower by every right. But God has sown in us every pursuit of a better life, and that not with a common, but with a truly unusual and unheard-of kindness, when He deigned to raise up the human race, lying in vices, by that admirable calling through Christ, in which respect especially the Apostles call eternal life, as that which follows repentance, a gift and grace. It must be added that now also the Spirit of God excites us to wish to do well, and helps us when we are doing well. To this pertains that saying of Cyprian, repeated so often by Augustine: 'In nothing must we glory, since nothing is our own': and that related one: 'We have read, all that we can is God's.' Salvian: 'Everything, therefore,' he says, 'although offered by some sinner? Nay, nothing, if not with faith: nay, nothing, if not with ambition (that is, supplication and devotion): nay, nothing, if not with prayer: nay, nothing, if not with this mind, that he reckons this very thing among the chief benefits of God, that He gave the mind to offer.' Gregory Nazianzen: 'For when anyone says, he will be so proud of his achievements as to give everything to himself and nothing to the Maker and Teacher and Giver of good things, he teaches by this word, that even to wish well requires help from God.' The fifth is that God, being self-sufficient and in need of nothing, cannot be made more blessed by our works, nor does the fruit of our works redound to Him, so that He could be said to be a debtor on that account. To this pertains that of Job XXXV.7: 'If you have acted justly, what will you give Him, or what will He receive from your hand?' and that of Paul, Rom. XI.34. Who has first given to Him and it shall be repaid to him? With which agrees that of Hierocles: 'Whoever honors God as if He were in need, this man has unknowingly thought himself to be better than God.' Finally, what can be said most truly of sufferings can also be said of even the most excellent deeds: 'that they are not worthy to be compared with the glory that is to be revealed in us,' as the Apostle speaks in Rom. VIII.18. Explaining this passage, Salvian says that every human work is unworthy in comparison to future glory, and rightly so, for what equality can there be between the momentary and the eternal, not to mention those infirmities which intercur in human actions? But all these things, just as they do not take away the modest boldness and confidence and the boasting in God of the pious, so they directly oppose the pride of those who impute merit, nor do they allow God to be considered our debtor except by His merciful promise.

All these things Grotius; who afterwards degenerated from himself, as we have said, and as we have shown in the Exegesis of the Augsburg Confession, Articles IV and XX. But to these he adds what now follows:

Nevertheless, whether these things are proper to this place, without prejudice to the truth and light of things, which ought not to have been enveloped in any mists of disputation, it is permissible to doubt. Many things move me not to think so. First, because here Christ deals with servants who are about to recline after the Master has dined, but elsewhere with servants whom the Master Himself, as soon as He arrives, orders to recline, and He Himself kindly exhibits service to them: above XII. 37. which things in the parable differ much, so they seem also in the ἐπιμισθῳ [wages] to require a different ἀνταπόδοσιν [recompense]. Indeed, Christ himself elsewhere seems to express the other part of the ἀνταπόδοσιν, by a figure taken from this very comparison, when he says that the Apostles will recline at his table, that is, their master's table, below XXII. 30. Another thing is that Christ denies that thanks will be given to those servants of whom he is speaking here, which he himself said elsewhere about those who do good to those who do good to them and love those who love them in return, above c. VI. 32. 33. bidding us think otherwise about those who love their enemies, and exercise beneficence and mercy with no hope of mutual return, not after the example of men, but of the heavenly Father: in the same place 34. 35. 36. The third thing is that ποιεῖν [to do], as we noted above on chapter X of Luke, was understood according to the received manner of speaking as referring to deeds considered nakedly, with whatever intention they may be done: which things, joined together, impel me to believe that it is not a question here of any servants whatsoever, but of those who serve servilely, not (as Terence speaks) liberally. The following will explain this interpretation, which is not destitute of good authors. Let him who is able look at Hermas, book III, c. 5, a writer who is acknowledged to be ancient, and as he is by no means to be equated with the Apostles, so he is of great authority among Irenaeus, Clement, and others. He proposes there a story of a Master who had commanded a servant to fix stakes around a vine, but he had also dug a trench around it and had removed the useless weeds from all sides. Therefore, the Master, granting more than he had promised, writes that he is a co-heir with his son. Wherefore it seems that in those times this comparison was quite common, which, however, is drawn in a different direction in the book of Hermas that exists now.

So far Grotius again. Although he himself denies that the things which he had brought forward above, and which we have opposed to the Papists, are proper to this place, and wishes to argue that Christ is not discussing those things which the faithful do when they are acted upon by the Holy Spirit, but those things which servants do servilely, nevertheless the things which he brings forward in support of this opinion are of no moment; nay, they proceed from a false hypothesis: as if formerly, by the force of the Sinaitic covenant, only external deeds were required, which are noted here by τὰ διαταχθέντα [the things commanded], when on the contrary it is certain, and is deduced by Christ himself from the law, Matt. XXII and Luke X, that an inward love of both God and neighbor was required just as it is required now: and that there is no difference in this between the New and the Old: but that the Old requires perfect obedience from us, while the New demands faith in Christ, in whom we have τὸ πλήρωμα τ̃ νόμꙋ [the fulfillment of the law], and through whose obedience we are constituted righteous, Rom. X. 4, c. V. 18. Therefore, not only must those who, destitute of Evangelical grace, serve servilely, profess what Christ prescribes here, 'we are useless servants, we have done what we ought to have done': but even the faithful themselves, endowed with the Spirit of adoption, such as were the disciples of Christ to whom this doctrine is delivered: who even if they perform all things which they ought to do, that is, even if they love God with all their heart, with all their soul, and with all their strength, and their neighbor as themselves, which is required in the Old covenant if anyone wishes to aspire to salvation through the observance of the law, but can be performed by no one after the fall, they are only useless servants, who can merit nothing by those works of theirs: inasmuch as they are entirely owed to God. Some Papists also acknowledge that those who are called useless here are reborn, because Christ is addressing his disciples, who were already reborn and in grace, such as Stella and Salmero. Nor is the comparison here instituted with a mercenary, to whom something is owed, but with servants and slaves, whose status is not defined by certain terms, but is almost infinite, so that there is no kind of labor which they do not owe. Certainly, no slave merits anything from his master by his labors. Hence the merits of the Papists are forcefully overthrown. First, because we are said to be useless servants even when we have done all things which we ought to have done, namely, useless to ourselves, not to the Master; for he who plows and feeds is certainly useful to his Master, however much he may merit nothing for himself because he is a servant. For if we are useless servants even when we fulfill all things, how much more so when we do not fulfill them! If those, says Stella, who have fulfilled all things ought to consider themselves useless servants, what will be incumbent upon us, who offend in so many things! Furthermore, whoever merits eternal life from God, he is certainly useful to himself. But no one doing all the commandments of God is useful to himself: And whoever is bound to do all the things they do by the right of servitude, they certainly do not merit a reward by their works. Compare what is said about these things toward the end of article VI of the Augsburg Confession in our Exegesis.

Ἀροτριῶντα ἢ ποιμαίνοντα [Plowing or shepherding] Participles placed in the Hebrew manner for verbals: for it is the same as if he had said δῦλον ἀρότην ἢ ποιμένα [a servant plowman or shepherd]. What great thing does he do if he is set to plow, if he plows, or to shepherd, if he shepherds? Nor does it matter much whether we understand by the word δῦλον [servant] a hired minister (as that word is often used in these and the books of the ancient covenant) or indeed one who is in the hand of the Master, provided that we estimate such servitude not according to the custom of barbarian men, but according to equity and goodness and indeed according to the Hebrew law. Chrysippus rightly said that a mercenary minister is a servant for a time: but a perpetual servant is as it were a mercenary to whom food is given instead of money.

Εὐθέως παρελθὼν ἀνάπεσαι [Immediately having come forward, recline] To recline with the head of the family is for sons, not for servants: but servants are accustomed to remain in servitude as long as they serve servilely: to admit servants to the table was a species of manumission, as can be seen in Ulpian in the Institutes.

Latin:

V. 7. τίς δὲ ἐξ ὑμῶν.

Quum circa hanc comparationem Grotius prolixe Papisticam heterodoxiam de meritis ope- rum refellat, ea quae hic tradit, probe observanda sunt. Nam opponi eadem ipsimet Grotio possunt in iis quae ad consultationem Cassandri, in gratiam Papistarum, annotavit, & contra Rivetum tueri conatus est:

Hanc comparationem veterum multi, quos inter Cy- primus, & ad hunc locum Theophylactus, ad præstantissi- ma etiam Christianorum facta extendunt, docentes, ne in illis quidem esse quo nos efferamus, aut quod Deo impute- mus. Veram enim lectionem apud Cyprianum esse arbitror in Epistola ad lapsos : qui in Ecclesia semper gloriose & gran- diter operati sunt & opus suum domino nunquam imputave- runt, ut veteres editiones habent, non ut recentiores, quæ negationem omittunt. Nam imputare in Latino sermone cum ad benefacta refertur, non est acceptum sed expensum ferre: ita superbos & imputatores dixit Seneca, qui magni æ- stimant sua beneficia, & alios eo nomine habere volunt sibi obligatos, facilius enim, ut Chrysostomus dixit, sine operi- bus humilis animus hominem ad salutem perducat, quam cum operibus conjuncta superbia. Multaque sunt, quæ prohibe- re nos debent ne Deum vocemus ad calculos. Primum enim cum ipse nos de nihilo ut essemus fecerit, quis dubi- tet quin quicquid in nostra est potestate exigere à nobis pos- sit, etiam nullo proposito præmio? Dixit Aristoteles : ἐκ ἔστιν ἰσότης πρὸς τὰ ἀντὶ διπλόα. Unde etiam negat inter Dominum & servum jus proprie stricteque dictum locum habere. Et sane si servus totus esset Domini, sicut nos Dei sumus, verum diceret. Ne te jactes si bene serviisti, obsequitur Sol: Obtemperat Luna. Deinde vero cum ratio nobis data sit, idque habeamus eximium supra animantes cæteras, nonne tam naturale nobis censeri debet secundum ratio- nem vivere quam bestiis secundum τὰς φύσεως ὁρμὰς? At be- stiis eo nomine nullum debetur præmium. Tertio in mentem venire debet neminem esse, cui non inulta pecca- ta sint condonata, quod ut supra diximus, vel unum satis est, ut humiles nos Deo substernat. Nemo tantum præsta- re potest quin plus pro indulgentiæ beneficio debeat. Ac- cedit quod etiam quæ post emendationem remanent in nobis culpæ vestigia quotidie opus habeant divina misera- tione. Quartum est quod satori fructus omni jure deben- tur. Deus autem in nobis sevit omne vitæ melioris stu- dium, idque non communi quadam, sed vere insolita at- que inaudita benignitate, cum genus humanum jacens in vitiis, admirabili illa per Christum vocatione erigere digna- tus est, quo præcipue respectu vitam æternam, ut quæ pœ- nitentiam consequitur, donum & gratiam vocant Aposto- li. Addendum quod nunc etiam Dei spiritus nos excitat ut bene agere velimus, bene agentes adjuvat. Huc illud per- tinet Cypriani toties ab Augustino repetitum, In nullo glo- riandum, quando nostrum nihil est: & illud affine? Leiesi, Dei omne quod possumus. Salvianus: Totum ergo, inquit, quamvis peccator aliquis oblatum est? Imo nihil, si non cum fide: imo nihil, si non cum ambitu (id est, supplicio evotio- ne) imo nihil, si non cum prece: imo nihil, si non hoc animo ut hoc ipsum inter præcipua Dei beneficia reputet, quod animum offerendi dedit. Gregorius Nazianzenus: ἐπειδὰν γὰρ εἴπη τινὰ, τεοῦτον μεγαλοφρονῆσετ ἐπὶ τοῖς κατωρθώμασιν, ὥστε τὸ πᾶν ἑαυ- τοῖς διδόναι κὶ μηδὲν τῷ ποιήσαντι κὶ σοφίσαντι κὶ χορηγῷ τῶν καλῶν, διδάσκει τότυτό λόγῳ, ὅτι κὶ τὸ βύλεσθ καλῶς δεῖται τῆς παρὰ Θεῦ βοηθείας. Quintum est, quod Deus ἀυταρκής, ἀνενδεὴς non potest per opera nostra beatior fieri, neque ad eum fru- ctus nostrorum operum redundat, ut dici eo nomine de- bi or possit. Huc illud Jobi pertinet XXXV.7. Si juste ege- ris, quid eo illi donabis, aut quid inde è manu tua accipiet? & illud Pauli Rom.XI.34. τίς προέδωκεν ἀυτῷ καὶ ἀνταποδοθήσε- ται ἀυτῷ; Quibus consonat illud Hieroclis: ὅτις τιμᾷ τὸν Θεὸν ὡς προσδεόμενον, ὗτος λέληθεν ὀιόμενος ἑαυτὸν τῶ Θεῦ εἶναι κρείττονα. Postremo, quod de perpessionibus, idem de factis etiam præstantissimis verissime dici potest ἐκ ἄξια εἶναι πρὸς τὴν μέλλουσαν δόξαν ἀποκαλυφθῆναι εἰς ἡμᾶς ut Apo- stolus loquitur Rom.VIII.18. Quem locum explicans Sal- vianus, indignum esse ad futuræ gloriæ comparationem omne opus dicit humanum, merito sane, quæ enim esse potest æ- qualitas inter momentaneum & æternum, ut jam de illis infirmitatibus taceam quæ humanis actionibus intercur- runt? Hæc autem omnia sicuti non tollunt piorum mode- stam παῤῥησίαν κὶ πεποίθησιν καὶ τὸ ἐν Θεῷ καύχημα, ita dire- cte adversantur imputattici superbiæ, neque patiuntur Deum nobis debitorem censeri nisi ex misericordi promis- sione.

Hæc omnia Grotius; qui postmodum à seipso degeneravit, ut diximus, & in Exegem. Aug. Con- fef. Art. IV. & XX. ostendimus. Hisce autem addit quæ jam sequuntur:

Veruntamen an hæc hujus loci sint propria, salva rerum veritate ac luce, quæ nullis disputationum nebulis obvol- vi debuerat, dubitare fas est. Me ne id putem movent multa. Primum quod hîc Christus de servis agit, qui ac- cubituri sunt postquam Dominus cœnavetit, alibi autem de servis quos ipse Dominus, statim ut advenit, jubet ac- cumbere, atque ipse illis comiter ministerium exhiber: supra XII. 37. quæ ficit in fabula multum differunt, ita- videntur & in ἐπιμισθῳ diversam requirere ἀνταπόδοσιν. Quin ipse Christus alibi videtur exprimere ἀνταπόδοσιν partem alteram, per figuram ex eadem hac comparatione desumtam, cum Apostolos dicit suæ hoc est herili mensæ accubituros, infra XXII. 30. Alterum est, quod Christus negat istis, de quibus hic agitur, servis gratiam habitum iri, quod ipsum alibi dixit de his qui facientibus benefaciunt & diligentes se vicissim diligunt, supra c. VI. 32. 33. aliud nos jubens sentire de iis qui inimicos diligunt, & nulla spe mu- tuæ vicis beneficentiam ac misericordiam exercent, non ad hominum, sed ad cælestis patris exemplum: ibidem 34. 35. 36. Tertium est quod ποιεῖν, ut supra ad caput X. Lucæ an- notavimus, ex recepto loquendi more intelligebatur de fa- ctis nude consideratis, quocunq; tandem animo fiant: quæ inter se conjuncta impellunt ut credam non de quibusvis servis hic agi, sed de iis qui serviunt serviliter, non (ut Teren- tius loquitur) liberaliter. Quam interpretationem non de- stitutam bonis auctoribus sequentia explicabunt. Videat si cui integrum est Hermam libro III. c. 5. Scriptorem quod constat antiquum, & ut Apostolis minime æquandum, ita apud Irenæum, Clementem atque alios magnæ auctorita- tis. Proponit ibi fabulam Domini qui servo imperarat, ut palos circa vitem figeret, ille vero & fossam circumdederat, & herbas inutiles undiq; abstulerat. Itaque Dominus plus quam promiserat præstans illum filio suo scribit cohære- dem. Quare videtur illis temporibus admodum trita fuis- se hæc comparatio, quæ tamen in eo qui nunc exstat Her- mæ libro aliovorsum trahitur.

Hactenus iterum Grotius. Quibus etsi ea, quæ supra adduxerat, quæque Pontificiis opposuimus, ipse hujus loci propria esse neget, ac Christum non de illis, quæ fideles agunt, cum aguntur à Spiritu San- cto, sed quæ servi serviliter agunt, differere velit, non tamen ea, quæ in hanc sententiam adfert, alicujus momenti sunt, imo è falsa hypothesi procedunt: ac si olim vi fœderis Sinaitici externa facta tantum re- quisita fuerint, qua per τὰ διαταχθέντα hic noten- tur, cum ex adverso certum sit, & à Christo ipso ex lege deducatur, Matth. XXII. & Luc. X. intimam tum DEI tum proximi dilectionem requisitam fuisse pariter uti nunc requiritur: nec in eo subesse Novi & Antiqui diversitatem: sed quod Vetus per- fectam obedientiam à nobis requirat, Novum vero fidem in Christum postulet, in quo habemus τὸ πλήρωμα τ̃ νόμꙋ, & per cujus obedientiam justi nos constituimur, Rom. X. 4. c. V. 18. Ideo non tantum il- lis, qui gratia destituti Evangelica serviliter servi- unt, profitendum est, quod hic Christus præscri- bit, servi inutiles sumus, fecimus, quod debuimus: sed ipsismet etiam fidelibus Spiritu adoptionis præditis, quales erant discipuli Christi, quibus hæc doctrina traditur: qui etiamsi omnia præstent, quæ facere debent, hoc est, etiamsi Deum ex toto cor- de, tota anima, omnibusque viribus diligant, & pro- ximum sicut seipsos, quod in Veteri fœdere requiri- tur, si per legis observantiam quis ad salutem ad- spirare velit, à nemine vero post lapsum præstari potest, inutiles tantum servi sunt, qut nihil mereri illis suis operibus possint: utpote quæ Deo debita omnino sunt. Agnoscunt etiam Pontificii nonnul- li, illos qui inutiles hic dicuntur, renatos esse, quia alloquitur Christus discipulos suos, qui renati jam erant & in gratia, utpote Stella & Salmero. Neque comparatio hic instituitur cum mercenario, cui ali- quid debetur, sed cum servis & mancipiis, quorum status non est terminis quibusdam definitus, sed pene infinitus, ut nullum sit laboris genus, quod ipsi non debeant. Nullum certe mancipium mere- tur laboribus suis ab hero. Unde fortiter profli- gantur Papistarum merita. Primo quia tum quo- que dicimur servi inutiles, cum omnia fecimus, quæ facere debuimus, nobis nempe, non Domino inutiles; nam qui arat & pascit, Domino suo utiq; utilis est, utut sibi quia servus est, nihil mereatur. Si enim tum quoq; servi inutiles sumus, cum omnia implemus, quanto magis cum non implemꝫ! Si illi, inquit Stella, se servos inutiles reputare debent, qui o- mnia impleverunt, quid nobis incumbet, qui in tam multis offendimus! Porro quicunque meretur à Deo vitam æternam, is utique sibi utilis est. At ne- mo faciens omnia mandata Dei, sibi utilis est : Et quicunque omnia quæ faciunt tenentur facere ju- re servitutis, illi certe non merentur operibus suis mercedem. Conf. quæ de his sub finem artic. VI. Aug. Confess. in Exegemate nostro.

Ἀροτριῶντα ἢ ποιμαίνοντα] Participia more Hebræo posita pro verbalibus : idem enim est, quasi dixisset δῦλον ἀρότην ἢ ποιμένα. Quid magni facit ad arandum positus si arat, aut pascendum si pascit? Nec multum interest δύλυ voce mi- nistrum conductum intelligamus (ut sæpe ea vox in his & fœderis antiqui libris usurpatur) an vero eum qui in manu sit Domini, dummodo talem servitutem non ex barbaro- rum hominum consuetudine, sed ex æquo & bono atque adeo ex lege Hebræa æstimemus. Chrysippus recte dixit mercenarium ministrum servum esse ad tempus: servum vero perpetuum quasi mercenarium cui pro pecunia victus detur.

Εὐθέως παρελθὼν ἀνάπεσαι] Cum Patrefamilias accum- bere filiorum est, non servorum : solent autem servi in ser- vitute manere quam diu serviliter serviunt: mensæ servos adhibere manumissionis erat species, ut videre est apud Ul- pianum in institutionibus.

## 17:8
Vers. 8. περιζωσάμενος [Having girded himself] Which was the custom of those serving in regions in which they wore more flowing garments. Above XII. 37. See John XIII. 4.

μετὰ ταῦτα] As was the custom of servants or even of those whose labor had been hired.

Latin:

Vers. 8. περιζωσάμενος] Qui mos ministrantium in re- gionibus in quibus demissiores vestes gerebantur. Supra XII. 37. vide Joh. XIII. 4.

μετὰ ταῦτα] Ut mos erat servorum aut etiam eorum quo- rum conducta erat opera.

## 17:9
V. 9. μὴ χάριν ἔχει] The word for reward is taken strictly, so as to signify that which corresponds to labor according to common estimation, in which sense Paul seems to speak: 'to the one who works, the reward is not reckoned according to thanks,' Rom. IV. 4. In this sense, as we remember to have touched upon elsewhere, reward differs from thanks, in that reward looks primarily to the deed, thanks to the spirit itself. Therefore, reward spoken of in this way is owed, even if the servant or hired man did not do what was to be done willingly. But those who do things willingly, and who would wish to do them if they were unable to accomplish what they wished, elicit thanks. But elsewhere the word for reward, in a looser sense, although it signifies a recompense, also signifies a liberal one, which is not the price of a deed, but a mutual expression of kind affection, as in Matthew, and often also in those places where Luke, mindful of literal accuracy, preferred to say thanks: as can be seen in Matt. V. 46, ch. VI. 1, and Luke VI. 31, 32, 33, 34. Luke therefore in this place, according to his custom, opposes thanks to reward.

ὅτι ἐποίησε τὰ διαταχθέντα αὐτῷ] He treats of those things which are carried out by a specific prescription, such as that a plowman plows, that a shepherd pastures, which cannot be omitted without disgrace. He who does these things has a reward: first, that he does not suffer the lash, and second, that he receives his ration. But no thanks are given to him for such labor. This was the state of the Jews, fulfilling the external works of the law moderately, with an unpurified soul.
