ὐ δοκῶ] It is to be understood from the contrary, that the matter would be otherwise if that servant, not with eye-service but with singleness of heart, as Paul speaks in Col. III. 22, had devoted himself in all ways to the honor and advantage of his master, even beyond specific prescriptions. For such servants are accustomed to carry away this thanks, that they obtain freedom, and indeed that they are adopted in the place of sons. Seneca asks whether thanks can be owed to a physician beyond his fee. He rightly answers that it can, if he has treated you not perfunctorily and as he does others, but as a friend, if he has grieved for your ills from the heart. He also teaches that a benefit can be received from a servant: and that because of the affection of a friend, it ceases to be a service. The Hebrew proverb, which Maimonides mentions in the Guide for the Perplexed, book III, ch. 17, also pertains here: 'A reward is given to him who does something unbidden.' Chrysostom VIII. Rom. comparing the ancient Hebrews to Christians: 'And they indeed did everything driven by the fear of punishment, but these spiritual ones by desire and longing, and this they show by even exceeding the commands.'

Latin:

V. 9. μὴ χάριν ἔχει] Mercedis vox stricte sumitur, ut si- gnificet id quod secundum communes æstimationem o- peræ respondet, quo sensu dicere videtur Paulus τῷ ἐργαζο- μένῳ τὸν μισθὸν ὐ λογίζεσθαι κατὰ χάριν, Rom. IV. 4. Hoc sen- su ut alibi attigisse meminimus, distat merces à gratia, quod merces factum respicit præcipue, gratia ipsum animum. Ita- que merces hoc modo dicta debetur, etiamsi servus aut ho- mo conductus quod faciendum est non lubens fecerit. At gratiam provocant qui libenter faciunt, & qui vellent face- re si id quod vellent efficere nequeant. Sed alibi vox merce- dis, laxiore significatu quamvis ἀνταπόδοσιν significat, etiam liberalem, quæ non est facti pretium, sed mutua benigni affectus significatio ut apud Matthæum, sæpe etiam iis in locis ubi Lucas τῆς κυριολογίας memor χάριν maluit dicere : ut videre est Matth. V. 46. c. VI. 1. & Lucæ VI. 31. 32. 33. 34. Lucas igitur hoc loco χάριν suo more opponit μισθῷ.

ὅτι ἐποίησε τὰ διαταχθέντα αὐτῷ] Agit de iis rebus quæ peculiari præscripto peraguntur, ut quod arator arat, quod pastor pascit, quæ prætermitti sine flagitio non possunt. Hæc qui facit, mercedem habet : primo quod flagra non patitur, deinde quod dimensum accipit. Gratia autem nul- la ei ob talem operam habetur. Hic status erat Judæorum legis externa opera mediocriter implentium animo non e- mundato.

ὐ δοκῶ] Ex contrario intelligendum, aliter se rem habi- turam si servus ille non ἐν ὀφθαλμοδυλείαις sed ἐν ἁπλότητι καρδίας, ut Paulus loquitur Col. III. 22. etiam extra peculia- ria præscripta omnibus modis honori & commodis heri se- se impenderit. Tales enim servi gratiam hanc solent repor- tare, ut libertatem consequantur, imo & ut filiorum loco adoptentur. Quærit Seneca an medico possit ultra merce- dem gratia deberi. Recte respondet posse, si non perfuncto- rie & ut cæteros, sed ut amicum te curaverit, si ex animo malis tuis indoluerit. Idem docet & à servo beneficium ac- cipi posse : & quod affectu amici sit desinere esse ministe- rium. Pertinet huc & Hebræorum proverbium, cujus Mai- monides meminit Ducis dubitantium lib. III. c. 17. Ei datur præmium qui quid injussus facit. Chrysostomus VIII. Rom. veteres Hebræos Christianis comparans : κ’ ἐκεῖνοι διὸ φόβῳ τιμωρίας πάντα ἔπραττον ἀγόμενοι, οἱ δὲ πνευματικοὶ ἐπιθυμίᾳ τῇ πόθῳ, καὶ τῦτο δηλῦσι τῷ κὰι ὑπερβαίνειν τὰ ἐπιτάγματα.

## 17:10
V. 10. τὰ διαταχθέντα ὑμῖν] τὰ διαταχθέντα here must be taken strictly, in much the same way as חקים among the Hebrews: concerning which word we spoke above at chapter I. In this number, the ordinances are first those by which something is forbidden to be done: then also those of the commanders which pertain to external deeds, and which are so bound to a certain place or time, or circumstance, that they cannot be omitted without manifest contempt of the divine. In this class I place not only those things which the common law prescribes in common in that manner, but also those which are specially indicated to individual men, such as: You, Abraham, go out from Chaldea: you, Moses, go to Pharaoh: you, Paul, announce the Gospel. He who obeys such prescriptions carries away this reward, that he escapes punishment. An example can be placed in the following history. Those cleansed from leprosy show themselves to the priests by command, but they do not come to give thanks to Christ, which was indeed not similarly commanded, but if they had done so: a grateful mind, like that of the Samaritan, would have obtained greater benefits. The passage is illustrious, I Cor. IX. 16. ἐὰν γὰρ εὐαγγελίζωμαι, οὐκ ἔστι μοι καύχημα. (here he calls καύχημα the hope of having grace from God) ἀνάγκη γάρ μοι ἐπίκειται. (he calls ἀνάγκην an obligation ἐκ διατάγματος, from a special prescription concerning the execution or omission of which there could be no deliberation) οὐαὶ δέ μοι ἐστιν ἐὰν μὴ εὐαγγελίζωμαι (as if he were to say: I could not pass this over with impunity: and therefore I have no grace to be expected from it) εἰ γὰρ ἑκὼν τοῦτο πράσσω, μισθὸν ἔχω. (here he has placed μισθὸν in that broader sense of which we spoke above: if, he says, I do not only what is commanded, but I do it willingly, but I do it eagerly ἑκουσίως καὶ προθύμως, οὐκ ἀναγκαστῶς, as Peter speaks in Ep. II. c. V. 2. in that lies the hope of a great and excellent remuneration) εἰ δὲ ἄκων, οἰκονομίαν πεπίστευμαι (of which, of course, an account must be rendered by me, and for which, if not performed, I am deservedly punished) τίς οὖν μοί ἐστιν ὁ μισθός (here again he calls μισθὸν the τὸ ἀντίδωρον which comes from grace, not from the estimation of the deed) ἵνα εὐαγγελιζόμενος ἀδάπανον θήσω τὸ εὐαγγέλιον τοῦ χριστοῦ (so that while I have the right to demand sustenance, I nevertheless do not use that right for the greater honor of God and the progress of the Church) εἰς τὸ μὴ καταχρήσασθαι τῇ ἐξουσίᾳ μου ἐν τῷ εὐαγγελίῳ (here καταχρῆσθαι, as also in the same epistle I Cor. VII. 31, seems to be not to use badly, but to use in any way, just as the Latins use abuti for things that perish by use) ἐλεύθερος γὰρ ὢν ἐκ πάντων (obligated to no one in this regard) πᾶσιν ἐμαυτὸν ἐδούλωσα, ἵνα τοὺς πλείονας κερδήσω. It is usually asked here whether that which Paul does when he adapts himself to all at his own inconvenience, and even prefers to prepare his living with his own hands rather than be a burden to the Corinthians, was not included in divine precepts. Indeed, if we call everything that is pleasing to God a precept, and also what is generally commanded by God (in the way Christ uses the word ἐντολῆς in Matt. XXII. 36, with a similar allusion to that which we have observed elsewhere in the word ποιεῖν and the noun ἔργον), it cannot be doubted that the scope of the precepts contains this as well. For it proceeded from an intimate love of both God and neighbor, than which there is nothing that is more pleasing to God, nothing that is more required by God. But these precepts are not [to continue the comparison instituted by Christ] as if the Lord were saying to a servant: you feed, you plow: but as if He were inviting them by the hope of great grace to pursue love for Him. God, although He receives no utility from our deeds, nevertheless accepts those things which are performed in this way, that is, outside the necessity of a special prescription and with the determination left to our spontaneity, and thus performed out of true and tireless love, not as servile works, but as the benefits of friends, and as powerful friends are accustomed to do, He repays them both here and in the better life, not according to the worth of the thing, but according to the magnitude of the affection toward Him. Chrysostom on the passage of Paul already produced: τὸ μέν ἐστιν ἐπίταγμα, τὸ δὲ τῆς ἐμῆς προαιρέσεως κατόρθωμα. ἅ μὲν γὰρ ὑπὲρ τὴν ἐντολὴν γίνεται, πο- λὺν ἔχει τὸν μισθὸν κατὰ τοῦτο. And soon after, he says that the statement ἀνάγκη μοι ἐπίκειται was said ὡς ὁ ὑπευθύνῳ ὄντι τοῖς ἐπιταχθεῖσι, κὴ πρὸς ἀντι- διαστολὴν τῆς ἐλευθερίας τῆς ἐν τῷ λαμβάνειν εἱρημένης. A similar sense is in his dissertation in the second sermon on fasting. These are those miracles of faith which, according to the measure of the growing spirit, ought to grow in us. From this arises not a servile demanding of debt, but that ingenuous πεποίθησις κὴ παῤῥησία which addresses God not only as Lord, but also as Father: solicitous about provoking and preserving His love for oneself, secure about the retribution. Clement, Strom. V. τῷ τελείῳ οὐκ ἐν συμ- βολαίοις πολιτικοῖς, οὐδ᾽ ἐν ἀπαγορεύσει νόμῳ, ἀλλ᾽ ἐξ ἰδιοπραγίας καὶ τῆς πρὸς Θεὸν ἀγάπης ἡ δικαιοσύνη. A passage is to be compared in some way to this in Xenophon, where the Syrian, to Hystaspes who was asking why Chrysantas was preferred to him, although he had done all that was commanded diligently, replies: χρυσάντας ἐτοσὶ πρῶ- τον μὲν κ᾿ κληθεὶς ἀνέμεινεν, ἀλλὰ πρὶν καλεῖσθαι παρῆν ἢ ἡμετέ- ρων ἕνεκα· ἔπειτα δὲ οὐ τὸ κελευόμενον μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ ὅτι αὐτὸς γνοίη ἄμεινον εἶναι πεπραγμένον ἡμῖν, τοῦτο ἔπραττεν.

Ἀχρεῖοι ἐσμεν) Some explain this as "we are useless to our master" in the sense which I established a little earlier from the words of Job and Paul. But we noted at Matt. XXV. 30 that the word is Hellenistic, which the Syriac also rendered here as בטילא. It signifies, however, a sluggard: which word, nevertheless, is not used here absolutely, as in the aforementioned place in Matthew, but with a comparison made to servants who do not only execute specific instructions, but also attend to their master’s business night and day, even at their own peril. Plautus in the Stichus has a not dissimilar sentiment: "The servant who always waits to be reminded of his duty, and does not remember to do it of his own will, is not a servant of good character."

and the ancient Hebrews were accustomed to adapt that very thing to that obedience which we owe to God, as can be seen in Maimonides on the rules of repentance, in the last chapter.

ὃ ὠφείλομεν ποιῆσαι) Namely, mercenaries, so that they may obtain an equal reward for their work, servants, both so that they may escape punishment, and so that they may receive the measured amount which is in place of a reward. For between those there is a certain equality, not only from a contract, but

: from the very nature of things: for indeed, in turn, τῷ ἐργαζομένῳ ὁ μισθὸς οὐ λογίζεται κατὰ χάριν, ἀλλὰ κατὰ τὸ ὀφείλημα. For ὀφείλημα is that which Aristotle calls τὸ ἀντιπεπονθὸς. But in the Sinaitic covenant, if not a full ὀφείλημα, it is nevertheless some species of it. For perpetual and diligent obedience to the facts corresponds to some extent to a long and happy life. But in our covenant there is nothing of the sort, in which God looks not at what it is fitting for us to receive, but at what it is fitting for His supreme goodness to give.

PART II. Concerning the ten lepers.

Latin:

V. 10. τὰ διαταχθέντα ὑμῖν] τὰ διαταχθέντα hic stricte sumi debent, eo ferme modo quo חקים apud Hebræos : qua de voce diximus supra ad caput I. in hoc numero ἧ δια- ταγμάτων sunt primum ea quibus aliquid vetatur fieri: dein- de & jubentium illa quæ ad facta exteriora pertinent, quæ- que certo loco aut tempori, aut circumstantię ita alligantur, ut sine manifesto numinis comtemtu omitti nequeant. In hac classe pono non ea tantum quæ lex communis in com- mune ad eum modum præcipit, sed & quæ specialiter ho- minibus singulis indicuntur, ut : Tu Abraham exi è Chal- dæa: tu Moses i ad Pharaonem : tu Paule Evangelium an- nuntia. Talibus præscriptis qui paret, mercedem hanc re- portat quod pœnam evadit. Exemplum poni potest in histo- ria sequente. Purgati à scabie ex imperato ostendunt se Sa- cerdotibus, at gratias Christo actum non veniunt, quod im- peratum quidem similiter non erat, sed quod si fecissent: gratus animus, ut illius Samaritæ, majora impetrasset benefi- cia. Locus est illustris I. Cor. IX. 16. ἐὰν γὰρ εὐαγγελίζωμαι, οὐκ ἔστι μοι καύχημα. (hic καύχημα vocat spem habendæ sibi à Deo gratiæ) ἀνάγκη γάρ μοι ἐπίκειται. (ἀνάγκην vocat obli- gationem ἐκ διατάγματος, ex præscripto speciali de quo ex- sequendo vel omittendo nulla esse poterat deliberatio) οὐαὶ δέ μοι ἐστιν ἐὰν μὴ εὐαγγελίζωμαι(quasi dicat, n n possem hoc impune prætermittere: ideoque nullam inde exspectandam habeo gratiam) εἰ γὰρ ἑκὼν τοῦτο πράσσω, μισθὸν ἔχω. (hic μι- σθὸν posuit latiore illo significatu de quo supra diximus: si, inquit, non facio tantum quod jubetur, sed facio sponte, sed facio alacriter ἑκουσίως καὶ προθύμως, οὐκ ἀναγκαστῶς, ut Petrus loquitur Ep. II. c. V. 2. in eo sita est spes magnæ atq; eximiæ remunerationis) εἰ δὲ ἄκων, οἰκονομίαν πεπίστευμαι (cujus sci- licet ratio mihi reddenda est & qua non obita merito ple- ctar) τίς οὖν μοί ἐστιν ὁ μισθός (hic iterum μισθὸν vocat τὸ ἀντί- δωρον quod ex gratia venit, non ex facti æstimatione) ἵνα εὐαγγελιζόμενος ἀδάπανον θήσω τὸ εὐαγγέλιον τοῦ χριστοῦ (ut cum jus habeam alimenta poscendi, eo tamen jure non u- tar ad majorem Dei honorem & profectum Ecclesiæ) εἰς τὸ μὴ καταχρήσασθαι τῇ ἐξουσίᾳ μου ἐν τῷ εὐαγγελίῳ (hic καταχρῆσθαι, ut & eadem epistola I. Cor. VII. 31. videtur esse non male uti, sed quovis modo uti, quomodo & abuti usurpant La- tini de rebus quæ usu intereunt) ἐλεύθερος γὰρ ὢν ἐκ πάντων (nemini hac in parte obligatus) πᾶσιν ἐμαυτὸν ἐδούλωσα, ἵνα τοὺς πλείονας κερδήσω. Quæri hic solet an non divinis præce- ptis comprehensum fuerit id quod facit Paulus cum se suo cum incommodo omnibus aptavit, atque etiam suis mani- bus victum sibi parare maluit quam Corinthiis oneri esse. Sane si præcepta dicimus omne id quod Deo gratum est, at- que etiam à Deo generaliter præceptum (quomodo Chri- stus vocem ἐντολῆς usurpat Matth. XXII. 36. simili ferme al- lusione qualem in voce ποιεῖν & nomine ἔργον alibi observa- vimus) dubitari non potest quin præceptorum ambitus hoc quoque contineat. Processit enim ex intima dilectione tum Dei, tum proximi, qua nihil est quod Deo esse potius grati, nihil quod magis à Deo postuletur. Sed hæc præcepta non sunt [ut comparationem à Christo institutam prosequamur] quasi dicat servo Dominus: tu pasce, tu ara: sed quasi eos spe magnæ gratiæ ad sectandum in se amorem invitet. Deus quamquam ex nostris factis nihil capit utilitatis, tamen quæ eo modo, hoc est extra specialis præscripti necessitatem & cum determinatione nostræ sponti relicta, sic ex vero at- que indefesso amore præstantur, ea non ut serviles operas, sed ut amicorum beneficia accipit, & ut potentes amici so- lent non pro rei dignitate, sed pro affectus in se magnitudi- ne, & hic & in meliore vita repensat. Chrysostomus ad pro- ductum jam Pauli locum: τὸ μέν ἐστιν ἐπίταγμα, τὸ δὲ τῆς ἐμῆς προαιρέσεως κατόρθωμα. ἅ μὲν γὰρ ὑπὲρ τὴν ἐντολὴν γίνεται, πο- λὺν ἔχει τὸν μισθὸν κατὰ τοῦτο. Et mox illud, ἀνάγκη μοι ἐπίκειται dictum ait ὡς ὁ ὑπευθύνῳ ὄντι τοῖς ἐπιταχθεῖσι, κὴ πρὸς ἀντι- διαστολὴν τῆς ἐλευθερίας τῆς ἐν τῷ λαμβάνειν εἱρημένης. Paris sen- sus apud eum dissertatio altero sermone de jejunio. Hæc sunt illa fidei miracula quæ pro mensura crescentis spiritus crescere in nobis debent. Hinc oritur non servilis debiti fla- gitatio, sed ingenua illa πεποίθησις κὴ παῤῥησία quæ Deum non ut Dominum tantum, sed & ut Patrem compellat: de amore ejo in se provocando, ac conservando sollicita, de re- tributione secura. Clemens Strom. V. τῷ τελείῳ οὐκ ἐν συμ- βολαίοις πολιτικοῖς, οὐδ᾽ ἐν ἀπαγορεύσει νόμῳ, ἀλλ᾽ ἐξ ἰδιοπραγίας καὶ τῆς πρὸς Θεὸν ἀγάπης ἡ δικαιοσύνη. Locus est huic aliquo modo comparandus apud Xenophontem ubi Syrus Hy- staspæ qui imperata omnia sedulo fecerat quærenti cur si- bi Chrysantas præferretur, respondet: χρυσάντας ἐτοσὶ πρῶ- τον μὲν κ᾿ κληθεὶς ἀνέμεινεν, ἀλλὰ πρὶν καλεῖσθαι παρῆν ἢ ἡμετέ- ρων ἕνεκα· ἔπειτα δὲ οὐ τὸ κελευόμενον μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ ὅτι αὐτὸς γνοίη ἄμεινον εἶναι πεπραγμένον ἡμῖν, τοῦτο ἔπραττεν.

Ἀχρεῖοι ἐσμεν) Exponunt quidam inutiles domino su- mus eo sensu quem paulo ante ex Jobi & Pauli verbis ad- struxi. Sed notavimus ad Matth. XXV. 30. vocem esse Hel- lenisticam, quam & hic Syrus בטילא reddidit. Significat autem cessatorem: quæ tamen vox non absolute hic usur- patur, ut dicto Matthæi loco, sed comparatione facta ad servos qui non peculiaria præscripta tantum exequuntur, sed noctu diuq; etiam cum periculo suo attendunt herilibus negotiis. Plautus Sticho non dissimilem habet sententiam: Qui manet ut moneatur semper servos homo officium suum, Non voluntate id facere meminit, servos is habitu haud probu' est:

idque ipsum ad eam obedientiam quam Deo debemus soli- ti sunt aptare etiam Hebræi veteres, ut videre est apud Mai- monidem de regulis pœnitentiæ capite ultimo.

ὃ ὠφείλομεν ποιῆσαι) Nempe mercenarii, ut parem operæ mercedem consequantur, servi, & ut pœnam effugiant, & ut dimensum quod mercedis est loco percipiant. Nam in- ter ista æqualitas quædam est, non ex condicto tantum, sed

: ex ipsa rerum natura: quippe & vicissim τῷ ἐργαζομένῳ ὁ μισθὸς οὐ λογίζεται κατὰ χάριν, ἀλλὰ κατὰ τὸ ὀφείλημα. Est enim ὀφείλημα id quod τὸ ἀντιπεπονθὸς vocat Aristoteles Est au- tem in fœdere Sinaitico, si non plenum ὀφείλημα, aliqua ta- men ejus species. Nam perpetua & diligens factorum obe- dientia vitæ longævæ ac felici aliquatenus respondet. At in nostro fœdere nihil tale, in quo Deus respicit non quid nos accipere conveniat, sed quid summam suam bonitatem de- ceat dare.

PARS II. De decem leprosis.

## 17:11
Verse 11.

διὰ μέσου Σαμαρείας καὶ Γαλιλαίας) Through the very borders of the region of Galilee and Samaria, not directly through Samaria, which is otherwise the shortest route. Josephus, Antiquities XX, ch. V: 'It was the custom for the Galileans, when they came to the holy city for the festivals, to travel through the country of the Samaritans.' The same in his Life: 'I wrote also to my friends in Samaria to take care that their journey might be safe; for Samaria was already under the Romans, and it was necessary for all who wished to depart quickly to travel through it,' just as John also said in IV, 4: 'He had to pass through Samaria.' Add what is above in ch. IX, 51, 52.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

διὰ μέσου Σαμαρείας καὶ Γαλιλαίας) Per ipsa confinia Ga- lilææ & Samaritanæ regionis, non rectà per Samariam, quod alioqui brevissimum iter est. Josephus Originum XX. cap. V. Ἔθος ἦν τοῖς Γαλιλαίοις ἐν ταῖς ἑορταῖς εἰς τὴν ἱερὰν πόλιν παραγενομένοις ὁδεύειν διὰ τῆς Σαμαρέων χώρας. Idem in vita sua : ἔγραψα δὲ κᾀτοῖς ἐν Σαμαρείᾳ φίλοις προνοήσασθαι τῆς ἀσφαλοῦς γενέσθαι τὴν πορείαν αὐτοῖς· ἤδη γὰρ ὑπὸ ῥωμαίοις ἦν ἡ Σαμάρεια καὶ πάντας ἔδει τοὺς ταχὺ βουλομένους ἀπελθεῖν δι᾽ ἐκεί- νης πορεύεσθαι quomodo & Johannes dixit IV, 4. ἔδει αὐτὸν διέρχεσθαι διὰ τῆς Σαμαρείας. Adde quod supra est c. IX. 51. 52.

Vers. 12.

εἰσερχομένῳ αὐτῷ) The present for the future, as the Syriac rightly observes: for those who were polluted with that scab kept themselves outside the towns, Levit. XIII. 46. Josephus on Moses: 'He drove the lepers out of the city entirely, living with no one and differing in nothing from a corpse.' ἕστησαν πόῤῥωθεν) For they were ordered to stand far off from others and to cry out טמא טמא, as can be seen in the cited passage of Leviticus.

Latin:

Vers. 12.

εἰσερχομένῳ αὐτῷ) Præsens pro futuro, ut recte animad- vertit Syrus: nam extra oppida se tenebant qui illa scabie erant polluti Levit. XIII. 46. Josephus de Mose: τοὺς δὲ λε- προὺς εἰς τὸ παντελὲς ἐξήλασε τῆς πόλεως, μηδενὶ συνδιαιτωμέ- νους καὶ νεκρῶ μηδὲν διαφέροντας. ἕστησαν πόῤῥωθεν) Procul enim ab aliis abstare jubebantur & proclamare טמא טמא ut dicto Levitici loco videre est.

## 17:14
Vers. 14.

ἐπιδείξατε ἑαυτοὺς τοῖς ἱερεῦσι) By which saying did he tacitly promise that health would occur on the journey? For they were not shown to the Priest except either to recognize the disease, about which it was sufficiently clear here, or to pronounce the health restored. Moreover, here τοῖς ἱερεῦσι is said for τίνι τῶν ἱερέων. See what [we wrote] on Matt. VIII. 4. At the same time, it is to be noted, which Tertullian did not overlook, that Christ by this act approved the cause of the Jews against the Samaritans in the controversy of the temple: for he does not send the Samaritan, together with the Jews, to the Garizitan priests, but to the Hierosolymitan priests. ἐν τῷ ὑπάγειν αὐτὸς) That is a sign that the confidence of recovering health was conceived by all.

Latin:

Vers. 14.

ἐπιδείξατε ἑαυτοὺς τοῖς ἱερεῦσι) Quo dicto tacite polliceba- tur sanitatem in itinere obventuram? neque enim ostende- bantur Sacerdoti, nisi ut aut de morbo cognosceret, de quo hic satis constabat, aut ut restitutam valetudinem pronun- tiaret. Est autem hic τοῖς ἱερεῦσι dictum pro τίνι τῶν ἱερέων. Vide quæ ad Matth. VIII. 4. Simul notandum est quod non prætermisit Tertullianus, Christum hoc facto causam Ju- dæorum adversus Samaritas in controversia templi probas- se: non enim ad Garizitanos, sed ad Hierosolymitanos Sa- cerdotes Samaritarn simul cum Judæis relegat. ἐν τῷ ὑπάγειν αὐτὸς) Id signum est ab omnibus conceptam recuperandæ valetudinis fiduciam.

δοξάζων τὸν Θεὸν) Namely in Christ, as the following shows.

Vers. 15.

Vers. 16.

Vers. 16.
