## 17:18
Vers. 18.

οὐχ εὑρέθησαν) εὑρίσκεσθαι, as among the Hebrews נמצא is to appear. εὑρέθη μοι ἡ ἐντολὴ εἰς ζωὴν αὕτη εἰς θάνατον Rom VII. 10. σχήματι εὑρεθεὶς ὡς ἄνθρωπος Phil. II. 8. thus Proverb. X, בשפתי נבון תמצא חכמה : ὁ ἀλλογενὴς ὗτος) ἀλλογενὴς corresponds to the Hebrew זר. Josephus also calls the Samaritans ἀλλοεθνεῖς. For the Samaritans were in large part from the Cuthites and other peoples of Assyria, whence they are now also called כותים by the Jews. But some of Israelite stock had mingled themselves with them: whence the occasion was given to the Samaritans, as the situation demanded (just as Josephus narrates), to profess themselves kinsmen of the Jews at one time, and to deny it at another. We learn, however, from Josephus that many Jews, who had sinned against the law of the Sabbath or of foods, had migrated to the Samaritans, and that the city of the Shechemites was inhabited by that class of men. Hence it is that the son of Sirach makes the Shechemites worse than the Garizites, who were Cuthites, as the same Josephus testifies. The words are from Ecclesiasticus 50:27. ἐν δυσὶν ἔθνεσι προσώχθησεν ἡ ψυχή μου· καὶ τὸ τρίτον ἐκ ἔστιν ἔθνος· οἱ κατοικοῦντες ἐν ὄρει Σαμα- ρείας, καὶ οἱ ἄνδρες οἱ κατοικοῦντες Φυλιστιὶμ, καὶ λαὸς μωρὸς ὁ κατοι- κῶν ἐν Σικίμοις. It is a wonder by what argument those Shechemites sold themselves as Sidonians, which Josephus reports.

PART III. Concerning the coming of the kingdom of God.

Latin:

Vers. 18.

οὐχ εὑρέθησαν) εὑρίσκεσθαι, ut apud Hebræos נמצא est ap- parere. εὑρέθη μοι ἡ ἐντολὴ εἰς ζωὴν αὕτη εἰς θάνατον Rom VII. 10. σχήματι εὑρεθεὶς ὡς ἄνθρωπος Phil. II. 8. ita Proverb. X, בשפתי נבון תמצא חכמה : ὁ ἀλλογενὴς ὗτος) Respondet ἀλλογενὴς Hebræo זר. Sa- maritas etiam Josephus ἀλλοεθνεῖς vocat. Erant enim Sama- ritæ magna pars ex Chuthæis & aliis Assyriæ populis, unde כותים nunc quoq; à Judæis dicuntur. Sed quidam Israë- litici generis illis se immiscuerant:unde data occasio Sama- ritis, ut pro re nata (quemadmodum Josephus narrat) co- gnatos se Judæorum modo profiterentur, modo negarent. Discimus autem ex Josepho Judæorum multos, qui in le- gem Sabbati aut ciborum peccassent, ad Samaritas immi- grasse, atque ab eo hominum genere habitatam urbem Si- cimorum. Hinc est quod Sicimitas pejores Garizitanis qui erant Chuthæi, ut idem testatur Josephus, facit Sirachides. Verba sunt Ecclesiastici L. 27. ἐν δυσὶν ἔθνεσι προσώχθησεν ἡ ψυχή μου· καὶ τὸ τρίτον ἐκ ἔστιν ἔθνος· οἱ κατοικοῦντες ἐν ὄρει Σαμα- ρείας, καὶ οἱ ἄνδρες οἱ κατοικοῦντες Φυλιστιὶμ, καὶ λαὸς μωρὸς ὁ κατοι- κῶν ἐν Σικίμοις. Mirum quo argumento Sicimitæ illi pro Si- donus se venditaverint, quod Josephus refert.

PARS III. De adventu regni Dei.

## 17:20
Vers. 20.

ἡ βασιλεία τοῦ Θεοῦ) Of which mention had often been made both by the Baptist and by Christ. The kingdom of God here, as elsewhere, signifies the times of the reigning Messiah. μετὰ παρατηρήσεως) Christ does not deny that there are certain signs of that time that have been brought forth, which he explicitly affirms elsewhere: but he denies that that kingdom would come μετὰ πολλῆς φαντασίας with royal splendor, riches, and triumph, such as the Pharisees expected, and as the Jews still expect today.

Latin:

Vers. 20.

ἡ βασιλεία τοῦ Θεοῦ) Cujus sæpe & à Baptista & à Christo facta erat mentio. Regnum autem Dei hic ut & alibi signifi- cat tempora Messiæ regnantis. μετὰ παρατηρήσεως) Non negat Christus ejus temporis esse quædam indicia prodira, quod alibi diferte affirmat: sed negat illud regnum venturum μετὰ πολλῆς φαντασίας cum re- gio splendore, divitiis, triumpho, qualia exspectabant Pha- risæi, & nunc quoque Judæi expectant.

## 17:21
V. 21. ἰδὺ ἐρῦσιν] There will be nothing to be said. It must be interpreted thus, so that it does not conflict with that which follows in verse 23. ἰδὺ ὧδε καὶ ἰδὺ ἐκεῖ] In that mountain or in that desert, in Cyrene, in the city of Bitter, as the ψευδόχριστοι (false Christs) used to say. Ἐντὸς ὑμῶν ἐστιν] Already among you, that is, in the Jewish people themselves, that kingdom begins to exert its powers, while you are not observing. An evident sign of this thing, however, are the miracles, especially the casting out of demons. Matt. XII. 28. Christ addresses the same Pharisees in this manner: εἰ δὲ ἐγὼ ἐν πνεύματι Θεῦ ἐκβάλλω τὰ δαιμόνια, ἄρα ἔφθασεν ἐφ̓ ὑμᾶς ἡ βασιλεία τῦ Θεῦ, where by the word ὑμῶν the whole of the Jewish people is likewise understood. That ἐντὸς ὑμῶν is rightly translated as in the midst of you. Cf. Matt. XXI. 43.

Latin:

V. 21. ἰδὺ ἐρῦσιν] Non erit quod dicatur. Ita interpre- tandum, ne pugnet cum eo quod sequitur commate 23. ἰδὺ ὧδε καὶ ἰδὺ ἐκεῖ] In illo monte aut in illo deserto, in Cyrene, in urbe Bitter, ut dicebant oi ψευδόχριστοι. Ἐντὸς ὑμῶν ἐστιν] Jam inter vos, id est in ipso populo Ju- daico, regnum illud incipit vires suas exserere, vobis non observantibus. Signum autem hujus rei evidens sunt mira- cula, præsertim ejectio dæmonum. Matth. XII. 28. Chri- stus eosdem Pharisæos hunc in modum alloquitur: εἰ δὲ ἐγὼ ἐν πνεύματι Θεῦ ἐκβάλλω τὰ δαιμόνια, ἄρα ἔφθασεν ἐφ̓ ὑμᾶς ἡ βασιλεία τῦ Θεῦ, ubi voce ὑμῶν similiter populi Judaici uni- versitas intelligitur. Illud ἐντὸς ὑμῶν recte vertitur in medio vestri. Conf. Matth. XXI. 43.

## 17:22
Vers. 22. πρὸς τὺς μαθητάς] To all his followers: addressing the whole Jewish nation in them.

Μίαν τῶν ἡμερῶν τῦ ὑἱῦ τῦ ἀνθρώπυ] What follows below, where mention is likewise made of Τῆς ἡμέρας or ἡμερῶν τῦ ὑἱῦ ἀνθρώπε, causes me to understand by this name that very thing which he just called the kingdom: but in such a way that I think what preceded, ἐντὸς ὑμῶν, must be understood. That kingdom remained in the Jewish people, that is, an invitation to repentance for nearly forty years, towards the end of which time a dark night of calamities followed, concerning which below in verse 34. But during that time of XL years, the kingdom of Christ was most flourishing, and as it were a golden age, with the internal and external gifts of the Spirit appearing everywhere, with pure faith, and fervent love.

καὶ ὐκ ὄψεσθε] When the word of the Gospel shall be taken away from Judea, which will be a certain sign of imminent destruction.

Latin:

Vers. 22. πρὸς τὺς μαθητάς] Omnibus suis sectatoribus: in ipfis totam Judæorum gentem compellans.

Μίαν τῶν ἡμερῶν τῦ ὑἱῦ τῦ ἀνθρώπε] Quæ infra sequuntur ubi itidem mentio fit Τῆς ἡμέρας aut ἡμερῶν τῦ ὑἱῦ ἀνθρώ- πε, faciunt ut hoc nomine intelligam id ipsum quod mo- do dixit regnum: sed ita ut subintelligendum putem quod præcessit ἐντὸς ὑμῶν. Mansit in populo Judaico regnum il- lud, id est invitatio ad resipiscentiam ad annos ferme qua- draginta, sub cujus temporis finem nox atra calamitatum suffessit, de qua infra commate 34. illo autem tempore XL. annorum florentissimum fuit Christi regnum, & aurea velut ætas, spiritus donis internis atque externis ubique ap- parentibus, fide pura, dilectione fervente.

καὶ ὐκ ὄψεσθε] Cum Evangelii sermo è Judæa auferetur, quod certum erit signum imminentis excidii.

## 17:23
V. 23. ἰδὺ ὧδε ἡ ἰδὺ ἐκεῖ] After those times many ψευδόχριστοι (false Christs) will arise, as can be seen in Matthew.

Exposuerat prius, v. 20. & 21. S. Luke had previously explained what Christ answered to the question of the Pharisees, when the kingdom of God would come, namely that the kingdom of God does not come μετὰ παρατηρήσεως, that is, μετὰ πολλῆς Φαντασίας, as Grotius not badly explains, just as the Pharisees were persuaded concerning the coming of the kingdom of the Messiah, namely that the Messiah would come with royal splendor, riches, triumph, dominion, ὐδὲ ἐρῦσιν, there will be nothing to be said, Lo here, or lo there, in that mountain, or in the desert, in Cyrene, in the city of Bitter, as the ψευδόχριστοι (false Christs) used to say, ἐντὸς ὑμῶν ἐστιν, already among you, that is, in the Jewish people themselves that kingdom begins to exert its powers, while you are not observing, as Grotius not badly explains these things. Cf. Beza in h. l. Now the Evangelist relates what Christ said having left the Pharisees to his disciples or followers, addressing them specifically, but not indeed the whole Jewish nation, which is evident from v. 23. Et dicent vo- bis, Ecce hic, ecce illic, ne abeatis, neq; sectemini: & v. 25. Sed prius oportet illum multa pati, & reprobari à natione HAC. Conf. v. 36. 37. What therefore is held concerning the desired ONE DAY of the Son of Man v. 22, is not to be understood of the Jewish people, by whom the Son of Man was not acknowledged, nor were his days, who was truly the Son of Man, the promised Messiah, desired: but of the Apostles and followers of Christ. The days will come, when you will desire to see one day of the Son of Man, and you will not see: which B. Lyserus Harm. CXXVI rightly explained. By the days of the Son of Man he understands that external conversation, by which during the time of his ministry he dared to be familiarly among the Apostles, teaching, admonishing, consoling, feeding, and defending them. Now he complains that those days are not highly esteemed, nay rather that he himself is despised and neglected with his kingdom. But it will shortly come to pass that such dangers and commotions of the world shall arise, that they will wish they could have conversed with him more familiarly for even one day, that they might enjoy his counsel and consolation. Thus also Beza explained it: He speaks of the prior advent of Christ into the world, and says that there will be a time when the disciples, with great sadness of mind, will seek him in his absence in vain. For what is it not probable that they suffered from that night in which he was captured, until that day on which he showed himself to them alive again, nay, indeed, until they were confirmed by the Holy Spirit!

Latin:

V. 23. ἰδὺ ὧδε ἡ ἰδὺ ἐκεῖ] Post illa tempora multi surre- cturi erunt ψευδόχρισοι, ut apud Matthæum videre est.

Exposuerat prius, v. 20. & 21. S. Lucas, quid ad quæsitum Pharifæorum, quando venturum esset re- gnum Dei, responderit Christus, quod nempe re- gnum Dei non veniat μετὰ παρατηρήσεως, hoc est, μετὰ πολλῆς Φαντασίας, ut non male explicat Grotius, quemadmodum Pharisæi de adventu re- gni Messiæ persuasi erant, Messiam nempe venturum cum regio splendore, divitiis, triumpho, dominio, ὐδὲ ἐρῦσιν, non erit quod dicatur, Ecce hic, vel ecce illic, in illo monte, aut in deserto, in Cyreni, in urbe Bit- ter, ut dicebant οἱ ψευδόχρισοι, ἐντὸς ὑμῶν ἐστιν, jam inter vos, id est, in ipso populo Judaico regnum illud incipit vires suas exserere, vobis non observantibus, ut non male hæc exponit Grotius. Conf. Beza in h. l. Jam refert Evangelista, quæ relictis Pharifæis ad discipulos vel sectatores suos dixerit Christus, eosdem compellans specialiter, non vero totam Judæorum gentem, quod patet è v. 23. Et dicent vo- bis, Ecce hic, ecce illic, ne abeatis, neq; sectemini: & v. 25. Sed prius oportet illum multa pati, & reprobari à natione HAC. Conf. v. 36. 37. Quod ergo de defi- derata UNA DIE filii hominis v. 22. habetur, non de Judaico populo intelligendum, à quo non agno- scebatur filius hominis, neq; dies ejus, qui vere Fi- lius hominis erat promissus Messias, desideraban- tur: sed de Apostolis & sectatoribus Christi. Venient dies, quando desiderabitis videre unum diem filii ho- minis, & non videbitis: quæ recte exposuit B. Lyse- rus Harm. CXXVI. Per dies filii hominis intelligit il- lam externam conversationem, qua tempore mini- sterii sui familiariter apud Apostolos, eos docendo, monendo, consolando, alendo, defendendo ausus est. Nunc illos dies non magni reputari, imo se contemni & negligi cum suo regno, conqueritur. Sed brevi e- venturum, ut talia pericula & motus mundi exur- gant, ut optaturi sint se vel unum saltem diem fami- liarius cum eo conversari posse, quo ipsius consilio & consolatione fruantur. Sic etiam exposuit Beza: Lo- quitur de priore Christi adventu in mundum, & tem- pus fore dicit, quo discipuli ipsum absentem magna cum animi tristitia frustra requirant. Nam quid non perpessos fuisse probabile est ab ea nocte qua captus fuit, ad eum usque diem quo se redivivum ipfis exhibuit, imo vero usquedum à Spiritu San- cto confirmarentur!

## 17:24
V. 24. ἐκ τῆς ὑπ᾽ ὀρανὸν εἰς τὴν ὑπ᾽ ὀρανὸν] Understand χώρας (region). So that it may be ἐκ τῆς χώρας εἰς τὰς χώρας from one region, for example Judea, into all the regions which are under heaven. See what I said on Matthew XXVI. 31. ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ αὐτοῦ] ἐν τῇ παρουσίᾳ (in his presence), as Matthew explains. In that span of time, he says, the Gospel will be heard throughout the whole world and will make great progress.

Latin:

V. 24. ἐκ τῆς ὑπ᾽ ὀρανὸν εἰς τὴν ὑπ᾽ ὀρανὸν] Subaudi χώρας. ut sit ἐκ τῆς χώρας εἰς τὰς χώρας ex una regione, puta Judæa, in omnes regiones quæ sub cœlo sunt. Vide quæ dixi ad Matthæum XXVI. 31. ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ αὐτοῦ] ἐν τῇ παρουσίᾳ, ut Matthæus explicat. Illo inquit temporis spatio ederimæ per omnem mundum audietur Evangelium & magnos profectus faciet.

## 17:25
V. 25. πρῶτον δὲ δεῖ] Before that age of the kingdom arrives, the beginning of which was that mission of the Holy Spirit on the day of Pentecost: Christ had to obtain the right of sending this Spirit through death, as has been said elsewhere.

Latin:

V. 25. πρῶτον δὲ δεῖ] Antequam illa ætas regni adveniat, cujus initium fuit missio illa Spiritus Sancti die Pentecostes: Hujus spiritus mittendi jus consequi Christus debuerat per mortem, ut alibi dictum est.

## 17:26
Vers. 26. õτως ἔσται καὶ ἐν ταῖς ἡμέραις τῦ ὑἱῦ τῦ ἀνθρώπυ] Such a conspicuous testimony of divine goodness will deservedly be followed by the rejection of the stubborn, and severe judgments against them, even such as can be seen, such as was the destruction of Jerusalem. For this also pertained to defending the majesty of that kingdom.

Latin:

Vers. 26. õτως ἔσται καὶ ἐν ταῖς ἡμέραις τῦ ὑἱῦ τῦ ἀνθρώπυ] Tam conspicuam divinæ bonitatis testationem merito se- quetur rejectio contumacium, & severa adversus eos judi- cia, etiam quæ conspici possint, quale fuit excidium Hiero- solymitanum. Pertinebat enim & hoc ad tuendam regni istius majestatem.

## 17:27
Verse 27. ἀπώλεσ] All those who have despised the warnings of repentance.

After he had indicated that the day of temporal and external conversation and familiarity would be sought in vain, and on that occasion had warned about avoiding false prophets and false Christs: And they will say, Behold here, or behold there, but do not go away, nor follow them: now he informs his disciples about the spiritual propagation of his kingdom, which is to follow his passion and rejection. We observed at Matthew 24 how the simile concerning the flashing of lightning pertains to a similar prediction, although instituted at another time and on another occasion. Although indeed some refer the same to the bodily advent of Christ for judgment, and there is no light doubt concerning the following comparison of the days of Noah and Lot with the days of the Son of Man, whether it pertains rather to the final advent of Christ, especially because at Matthew 24:37 the days of the Son of Man are compared in like manner with the times of Noah, which passage was shown in the anti-Grotian annotations on Matthew not to pertain to the temporal destruction of Jerusalem, as it might seem to Grotius, but to the final judgment in the destruction of the world: nevertheless, regarding the present discourse and prediction of Christ, that explanation is to be preferred which takes the day of the manifestation of Christ in verse 30 as the day of particular judgment against the Jerusalemites, even though we are not unaware that this prediction is also commonly understood as the day of the final judgment. For since there are two very distinct discourses, there is no need to interpret one by the other: for those places in Luke chapter 17 and Matthew 24 are not parallel. But rather, chapter 21:25 and following below corresponds to this one. Furthermore, Christ had taught about his passion and rejection and the subsequent spreading of the Gospel throughout the world immediately before the preceding information: but the final judgment does not cohere with the passion and rejection of Christ and the spreading of the Gospel, but rather the destruction of the Jews, by whom Christ was rejected along with his Gospel. That exhortation concerning flight pertains to the times of the final destruction of Jerusalem, as is manifest from a comparison of Matthew 24:17-18 with this place in Luke 17:31: which exhortation, however, does not suit the time of the final judgment, which no one can escape. That warning also in verse 33, whoever shall seek to save his life shall lose it, and whoever shall lose it shall bring it to life, suits the time of the siege and destruction of Jerusalem more correctly than the final judgment and the consummation of the age. Nor does it stand in the way that that prediction concerning the two women set at the same mill in verse 35 pertains to the time of the final judgment in Matthew 24:41: because the times of that particular judgment coincide in this part with the day of the universal judgment: and Christ employed similar modes of speaking, predictions, and exhortations in other places because of that suitability: which, however, are to be adapted to their own time, as the reason of it suggests and the circumstances of the passages demand.

Latin:

Vers. 27. ἀπώλεσ] Omnes eos qui resipiscentiæ monita contempserint.

Postquàm indicaræt, frustra à desideratum iri diem temporalis & externæ conversationis, ac familiari- tatis, eaque occasione de cavendis Pseudo-Prophetis, & Pseudo-Christis monuerat: Et dicent, Ecce hic, aut ecce illic, sed ne abite, nec sectemini: jam de spiri- tuali regni sui propagatione discipulos suos infor- mat, quæ sequutura sit passionem, ac reprobatio- nem ipsius. Quo pertinere similitudinem de coru- scatione fulguris, ad similem prædictionem, licet a- lio tempore, & alia occasione institutam, ad Matth. XXIV. observavimus. Quanquam vero nonnulli eandem ad corporalem Christi adventum ad judi- cium referant, & de sequenti comparatione die- rum Noæ & Loth cum diebus filii hominis dubium non leve sit, anne ea pertineat potius ad novissi- mum adventum Christi, maxime quia Matth. XXIV. 37. dies filii hominis cum temporibus Noæ pari li ratione confertur, quem locum non pertinere ad temporale excidium Hierosolymæ, uti Grotio videa- tur, sed ad judicium novissimum in excidio mundi in annot. ad Matth. anti-Grotianis ostensum fuit: præferenda tamen quoad præsentem concionem & prædictionem Christi ea explicatio, quæ diem manifestationis Christi v. 30. accipit de die judicii particularis adversus Hierosolymitanos, etsi non ne- sciamus, communiter de die novissimi judicii hanc etiam prædictionem intelligi. Nam quum duæ di- stinctissimæ conciones sint, non opus est alteram ex altera interpretari: non enim parallela loca illa sunt c. XVII. Lucæ & Matth. XXIV. Sed huic re- spondet potius c. XXI. 25. seqq. infra. Adhæc de pas- sione, & reprobatione sua ac sequutura divulgatio- ne Evangelii per orbem immediate ante præce- dentem informationem Christus docuerat: cum passione vero & reprobatione Christi, ac divulga- tione Evangelii non cohæret judicium novissi- mum, sed excidium Judæorum, à quibus Christus cum Evangelio suo reprobatus est. Adhortatio il- la de fuga ad tempora pertinet ultimi Hierosolymæ excidii, ut è collatione Matth. XXIV. 17. 18. cum hoc loco Luc. XVII. 31. manifestum est: quæ vero adhortatio non convenit tempori novissimi judi- cii, quod nemo effugere potest. Illa etiam commo- nitio v. 33. quicunq; quæsierit animam suam salvam facere perdet illam, & quicunq; perdiderit illam, vi- vificabit eam, rectius tempori obsidii, & excidii Hierosolymitani, quam judicii novissimi, & con- summationis seculi convenit. Neque obstat, quod illa prædictio de duabus in eadem mola constitutis v. 35. apud Matth. XXIV. 41. pertineat ad tempus novissimi judicii: quia conveniunt hac parte tem- pora judicii istius particularis, cum die judicii uni- versalis: & adhibuit Christus ob convenientiam illam etiam in aliis similes loquendi modos, præ- dictiones, & adhortationes: quæ tamen aptandæ sunt suo tempori, prout ratio ejus fert, & circum- stantiæ locorum postulant.

## 17:29
Verf. 29. He rained fire and brimstone) I think that both πῦρ and θεῖον are placed in the nominative. Just as we read among the Latins, stones rained: and in the Apocalypse ἵνα μὴ βρέχῃ ὑετὸς chap. XI, 6. so that the Syrian has expressed the sense rather than the words. Moreover, the memory of this history is preserved even among profane writers, Strabo, Solinus, Tacitus. However, by the name of sulfur, the lightning itself can be understood. For the Greeks also sometimes speak in this way, because lightning has a sulfurous odor and power: indeed the word θεῖον itself, if we look at its origin, can seem to have pertained originally to lightning. See the passage of Philo which we are about to cite.

ἅπαντας) namely, the unrepentant. Christ signifies the same thing by these examples, which Peter expressed in this way when he had mentioned the same examples: οἶδε κύριος εὐσεβεῖς ἐκ πειρασμῷ ῥύεσθαι, ἀδίκους δὲ εἰς ἡμέραν κρίσεως κολαζομένους τηρεῖν. For which end Philo also in his book on the life of Moses brought forward both this history. And indeed he speaks thus concerning the Sodomites: ἐν δὲ τότῳ συνέβαινε τούς τε ἀσεβεῖς ταῖς εἰρημέναις τιμωρίαις κολάζεσθαι, κὰὶγέτις καλοκ᾽ ἀγαθίας διενηνοχότας εὖ πάσχουσιν ἀρετῆς ἐπαξίους ἄθλων τυγχάνοντας· ἐν μέν γε τῇ φορᾷ τῶν κεραυνίων πυρὸς οἰκέτορσιν αὐτοῖς ὅλης χώρας ἐμπιπραμένης, ἕνα μόνον ἀυτὸν μέτοικον ἐπιφροσύνῃ θείᾳ σώζεσθαι, διότι τὸ ἐγχώριον παρανομημάτων ἔδει ἀσπάσασθαι.

Latin:

Verf. 29. ἔβρεξε πῦρ καὶ θεῖον) Puto & πῦρ & θεῖον in no- minativo poni. Sicut apud Latinos legimus, pluerunt la- pides: & in Apocalypfi ἵνα μὴ βρέχῃ ὑετὸς cap. XI, 6. ita ut Syrus sensum potius quam verba expresserit. Est autem hujus historiae memoriae etiam apud profanos scriptores conservata, Strabonem, Solinum, Tacitum. Potest au- tem sulfuris nomine ipsum fulmen intelligi. Nam & Grae- ci interdum ita loquuntur, quia fulmen odorem ac vim ha- bet sulfuream : quin ipsa vox θεῖον, si originem spectemus, ad fulmen primitus pertinuisse videri potest. Vide Philonis locum quem jam jam adducemus.

ἅπαντας) τοὺς ἀμετανοήτους scilicet. Idem his exemplis Christus significat, quod ita extulit Petrus cum eadem exempla memorasset: οἶδε κύριος εὐσεβεῖς ἐκ πειρα- σμῷ ῥύεσθαι, ἀδίκους δὲ εἰς ἡμέραν κρίσεως κολαζομένους τη- ρεῖν. Quo fine etiam Philo libro de Mosis vita utran- que hanc historiam adduxit. Et de Sodomis quidem ita loquitur: ἐν δὲ τότῳ συνέβαινε τούς τε ἀσεβεῖς ταῖς εἰρημέναις τιμωρίαις κολάζεσθαι, κὰὶγέτις καλοκ᾽ ἀγαθίας διενηνοχότας εὖ πάσ- χουσι ἀρετῆς ἐπαξίους ἄθλων τυγχάνοντας· ἐν μέν γε τῇ φορᾷ τῶν κε- ραυνίων πυρὸς οἰκέτορσιν αὐτοῖς ὅλης χώρας ἐμπιπραμένης, ἕνα μόνον ἀυτὸν μέτοικον ἐπιφροσύνῃ θείᾳ σώζεσθαι, διότι τὸ ἐγχώ- ριον παρανομημάτων ἔδει ἀσπάσασθαι.

## 17:30
V. 30. In the day that the Son of man is revealed) Namely, for exercising his judgments upon the despisers of his kingdom. Thus Paul said the wrath of God is revealed from heaven. But the siege of Jerusalem and the evils which followed from it are chiefly understood here, as the following things show, which you would not correctly refer to the universal judgment. Joel also calls this time of divine severity the great and manifest day of the Lord, as Peter explains in Acts II. 20. where this sentence is also read, making for the explanation of the present place, everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved. Meanwhile, we must keep in memory that all those local judgments are images and pledges of the universal judgment.

Latin:

V. 30. ᾗ ἡμέρᾳ τὸ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ἀποκαλύπτεται) Nimirum ad exercenda sua judicia in contemtores regni sui. Sic Pau- lus dixit ἀποκαλύπτεται ὀργὴ Θεοῦ ἀπ᾽ οὐρανοῦ. Obsidium au- tem Hierosolymorum & quae mala ex eo sunt secuta, praeci- pue hic intelligi sequentia ostendunt, quae ad universale judicium non satis recte referas. Joel quoque hoc severita- tis divinae tempus vocat ἡμέραν κυρίου μεγάλην καὶ ἐμφανῆ, ex- plicante Petro Act. II. 20. ubi & haec sententia legitur ad lo- ci praesentis explicationem faciens, πᾶς ὃς ἂν ἐπικαλέσηται τὸ ὄνομα κυρίου σωθήσεται. Interim memoria tenere debemus omnia illa localia judicia imagines & pignora esse judicii universalis.

## 17:31
V. 31. He who shall be upon the housetop) This proverbial expression signifies most certain destruction, and that one must escape most quickly with all delay cut off: not only by the departure of the body but also by the diversity of places, for the following things show that both ought to be joined here, and otherwise it is the custom of the Orientals to join symbols to those things which are through symbols.

Latin:

V. 31. ὃς ἔσται ἐπὶ τοῦ δώματος) Proverbialis haec locutio certissimum exitium significat, & quod praecisa omni mo- ra celerrime sit effugiendum: non solo discessu corporis sed & locorum diversitate, nam utrumque hic conjungi debere ostendunt sequentia, & alioqui mos est Orientalium, τὰ σύμβολα conjungere τοῖς διὰ συμβόλων.

## 17:35
Vers. 35. And the other shall be left) That which is read here in certain codices about those found in the field, no one will doubt was added from Matthew, who will have noticed that the difference between Matthew and Luke in this place is expressly noted by Greek writers.

Latin:

Vers. 35. καὶ ἡ ἑτέρα ἀφεθήσεται) Quod hic in quibusdam codicibus legitur de repertis in agro, ex Matthæo esse adje- ctum non dubitabit, qui animadverterit à Græcis scriptori- bus discrimen hoc loco Matthæi & Lucæ diserte anno- tari.

## 17:36
Vers. 36. Where, Lord?) Where, they say, will this separation of men take place?

ὅπε τὸ σῶμα ἐκεῖ συναχθήσονται οἱ ἀετοί) He said body, where Matthew said corpse: and not without reason: for Porphyry also observes concerning Homer, that he always calls the body of the living δέμας; but that which has already cast off the soul, he calls it σῶμα. As in those verses: Give back my body home. And: The bodies lie uncared for upon the slain in pain. Likewise: For we leave the body in the hall of Circe. Porphyry brings forward this reason: for the same thing, while living, was a bond of the soul to the man; but having died, it is left behind as if it were a tomb. But by this proverb Christ answers the question, signifying that that separation of men will indeed be in Judea, but not only there, but everywhere in places and nations. For that separation ought to extend as widely as the kingdom of Christ was to be extended. Therefore, the kingdom of Christ will not be here, it will not be there, according to the diversity of places, as the Pharisees thought, but it will both be and not be everywhere, according to the discrimination of souls.

Here let those things which we said on Matt. XXVI concerning this proverb be compared again. There is no reason why we should add anything, since we do not here dissent from the interpretation of Grotius.

Latin:

Vers. 36. πῶ κύριε;) Ubi fiet, inquiunt, ista hominum discretio?

ὅπε τὸ σῶμα ἐκεῖ συναχθήσονται οἱ ἀετοί) Σῶμα dixit, quod πτῶμα Matthæus: nec nimirum: nam & de Home- ro Porphyrius observat, ὅτι 7 ζώντων ἀεὶ δέμας προσαγο- ρεύει· τὸ δὲ ἀποβεβληκὸς τὴν ψυχὴν ἤδη ἀυτὸ ἢ σῶμα καλεῖ. ut in illis versibus: Σῶμα δὲ οἴκαδ' ἐμὸν δόμεναι πάλιν. Et: Σώματ' ἀκηδέα κεῖται ἐπὶ κταμένοις ὀδυνῶν. Item: Σῶμα γὰρ ἐν κίρκας μεγάρῳ καταλείπομεν ἡμεῖς. Rationem hanc adfert Porphyrius: τὸ γὰρ ἀυτὸ ζῶντα μὲν τῶ ἀνθρώπῳ δεσμὸς ἦν τῆς ψυχῆς· τελευτήσαντα δὲ ὥσπερεί σῆ- μα καταλέλειπται. Hoc autem proverbio Christus ad inter- rogationem respondet, significans illam discretionem ho- minum futuram quidem in Judæa, sed non ibi tantum, ve- rum ubivis locorum & gentium. Tam late enim patere debebat ista discretio, quam late proferendum erat Christi regnum. Non igitur hic erit Christi regnum, ibi non erit, pro diversitate locorum, ut Pharisæi putarunt, sed ubique & erit, & non erit pro animorum discrimine.

Hic conferantur iterum quæ ad Matth. XXVI. de hoc proverbio diximus. Non est, quod quic- quam addamus, quum hic non abnuamus Grotia- næ interpretationi.

## 18:1 Argument
CHAPTER XVIII.

ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

The parable about always praying, from the widow wearing down the judge with frequent solicitations: and about the prayer of the Publican and the Pharisee in the temple. Little children are brought to Jesus. A certain ruler asking about works necessary to be done for salvation, and boasting that he had kept all the commandments, when he was ordered, having given all his possessions to the poor, to follow Christ, is saddened; Peter, who says that he has followed Christ having left all things, is made certain about the reward. Christ, heading to Jerusalem, prophesies about his passion, death, and resurrection, and heals a blind man near Jericho.

There are two parts: The former is concerning the deeds before the journey to Jerusalem, such as the last Passover, namely concerning the continual prayer, to v. 8, concerning the Pharisee and the Publican, to v. 14, concerning the receiving of the little children, to v. 17, concerning the instruction of the rich ruler, to v. 30. The latter begins those things which pertain antecedently to the last Passover: the prediction concerning the Passion, to v. 34, and the healing of the blind man near Jericho, to v. 43.

PART I. Concerning the remaining deeds before the final journey to Jerusalem.

Ver. 1. Πρὸς τὸ δεῖν) Pertaining to the fact that prayers must always be made.

ἐκκακεῖν) Thus Paul, Eph. 3:13, μὴ ἐκκακεῖν ἐν ταῖς θλίψεσι, 2 Thess. 3:15, μὴ ἐκκακήσητε καλοποιῦντες. Gal. 6:9, τὸ δὲ καλὸν ποιῦντες μὴ ἐκκακῶμεν. The sense is that one must not grow weary in prayers, but must pray, as Paul advises in 1 Thess. 5:17, ἀδιαλείπτως, unceasingly. Thus also Proclus on the Timaeus: χρὴ ἀδιαλείπτως ἔυχεσθαι τῆς περὶ τὸ θεῖον θρησκείας, in which sense he also uses an ancient verse: Δηθύνοντι βροτῷ κραιπνοὶ μάκαρες τελέουσι.

Latin:

CAPUT XVIII.

ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

parabola de semper orando, à vidua judicem obtundente solicitationibus crebris: deque Publicani & Pharisæi oratione in templo. Adferuntur parvuli ad Iesum. Princeps a- liquis quærens de operibus factu necessariis ad salutem, & jactans se omnia præcepta servasse, cum juberetur, omnibus suis pau- peribus datis, Christum sequi, tristatur; Petrus qui se omnibus relictis Christum se- quutum esse ait, de renumeratione certior redditur. Christus Hierosolymam tendens, de passione, morte, & resurrectione sua va- ticinatur, & cæcum prope Iericho sanat.

Partes duæ sunt: Prior est de gestis ante iter Hierosolymitanum, ut Pascha ultimum, utpote de jugi oratione, ad v. 8. de Pharisæo & Publica- no, ad v. 14. de parvulorum assumtione, ad v. 17. de principis divitis informatione, ad v. 30. Poste- rior inchoat ea, quæ ad Pascha ultimum antece- denter pertinent: Prædictione de Passione, ad v. 34. & cæci prope Jericho sanatione, ad v. 43.

PARS I. De gestis ante iter novissimum Hierosoly- mitanum reliquis.

Vers. 1. Πρὸς τὸ δεῖν) Eo pertinentem quod semper preces faci- endæ sunt.

ἐκκακεῖν) Ita Paulus Ephes. III, 13. μὴ ἐκκακεῖν ἐν ταῖς θλίψεσι, 2. Thess. III. 15. μὴ ἐκκακήσητε καλοποιῦντες. Gal. VI. 9. τὸ δὲ καλὸν ποιῦντες μὴ ἐκκακῶμεν. Sensus est, non es- se fatiscendum in precibus, sed orandum, ut Paulus monet 1. Thess. V. 17. ἀδιαλείπτως, indefinenter. Sic & Proclus ad Timæum: χρὴ ἀδιαλείπτως ἔυχεσθαι τῆς περὶ τὸ θεῖον θρη- σκείας, in quem sensum & veteri utitur versu: Δηθύνοντι βροτῷ κραιπνοὶ μάκαρες τελέουσι.

## 18:2
V. 2. τὸν Θεὸν μὴ βοβύμενος) We have spoken of the nature of this comparison at a similar passage in chapter 16.

ἄνθρωπον μὴ ἐντρεπόμενος) Nor was he led by reverence for any man: for concerning God it preceded. Just like the Homeric Cyclops:

Nor would I, avoiding the wrath of Zeus, spare either you or your companions, unless my heart should command me.

Latin:

V. 2. τὸν Θεὸν μὴ βοβύμενος) Cujus generis hæc sit com- paratio diximus ad locum similem in cap. XVI.

ἄνθρωπον μὴ ἐντρεπόμενος) Nec hominis cujusquam reverentia ducebatur: nam de Deo præcessit. Plane ut Cyclops Homericus:

Οὐδ' ἂν ἐγὼ διὸς ἔχθρ ἀλευόμενος πεφιδοίμην, Οὔτε σεῦ, ἠδ' ἑτάρων εἰ μὴ θυμός με κελεύοι.

## 18:3
V. 3. widow] Forsaken, despised, and whom that cruel judge did not respect.

was coming] She kept coming. For the Greeks do not have frequentatives.

avenge me of my adversary] to avenge, or as below and Acts 18:24, to perform vengeance, just as the Latin 'vindicare' is sometimes to take revenge, and sometimes to ward off an injury in any way: which sense fits this place. Cicero defines vindication as that by which we repel force or insult by defending or avenging.

Latin:

V. 3. χήρα] Deferta, contemta, & quam crudelis ille stdeci non faciebat.

ἤρχετο] Ventitabat. Nam Græci frequentativa nō habent.

ἐκδίκησόν με ἀπὸ τῶ ἀντιδίκε με] ἐκδικῇν, aut ut infra & Actor. XVIII. 24. ποιεῖν ἐκδίκησιν, sicut Latinum vindicare, alias est ultionem sumere, alias quovis modo arcere inju- riam: qui sensus huic loco convenit. Cicero vindicationem definit per quam vim aut contumeliam defendendo aut ulciscendo propulsamus.

## 18:4
V. 4. for a time] A phrase familiar to Luke, which by itself signifies neither a long nor a short, but some time. Acts 15:35, 'having spent some time,' and 19:22, 'he stayed for a time in Asia': and the sense of the passage seems to me to demand this more, so that we understand that the daily interpellations could not be endured by that judge for too long.

Latin:

V. 4. ἐπὶ χρόνον] Locutio Lucæ familiaris, quæ per se neque magnum neque parvum sed aliquod tempus signifi- cat. Act. XV. 35. ποιήσαντες δὲ χρόνον, & XIX. 22. ἐπέχε χρό- νον εἰς τὴν ἀσίαν: idque sensus loci magis mihi videtur postu- lare, ut intelligamus non nimium diu potuisse ab eo judice perferri quotidianas interpellationes.

## 18:5
Vers. 5. to the end] Do not agree with those who translate it 'at last.' For it is, as a most learned man has demonstrated by citing several passages, a Hellenistic phrase from the Hebrew לנצח which signifies perpetually, as Ps. 10:19, 13:1, 49:20, and 79:5, 103:9, in which places the LXX also have 'to the end.' Add the passage of Paul, 1 Thess. 3:16, 'but wrath has come upon them to the end.' Nor is that of John, 'he loved them to the end,' to be taken otherwise. The Syrian therefore translates it well as 'at all times,' whom the Arab also follows.

I do not disapprove. The Vulgate and Beza are corrected in this way. Consult here what Drusius has, and de Dieu in Walaeus: as also B. Lyserus, Harm. ch. 127.

weary me] I do not doubt that it is a Latinism, such as there are many in Luke: for 'hypopiazein' literally is to beat black and blue: but 'obtundere' for the Latins is to repeat something to the point of annoyance. Terence: 'You are wearing me out, although I understand.' Cicero: 'If you remember, I will wear you out.' The Syrian therefore expressed the sense well: 'May she be troublesome to me': and the Arab, 'Let her vex me.' I will render justice to her, he says, so that she may never cease to be troublesome to me with her constant importunities.

Latin:

Vers. 5. εἰς τέλος] Noli accedere vertentibus tandem. Est enim, ut vir doctissimus productis locis aliquot de- monstravit, Hellenistica locutio ex Hebræo לנצח quod si- gnificat perpetuo, ut Ps. X. 19. XIII. 1. XLIX. 20. & LXXIX. 5. CIII. 9. in quibus locis etiam LXX. habent εἰς τέλος. Ad- de Pauli locum 1. Thess. III. 16. ἔφθασε δὲ ἐπ' αὐτοὺς ἡ ὀργὴ εἰς τέλος. Nec aliter accipiendum illud Johannis εἰς τέλος ἠγάπησεν αὐτύς. Bene ergo vertit Syrus omni tempore, quem & Arabs sequitur.

Non improbo. Emendatur ita vulgata & Beza. Cons. hic quæ habet Drusius, & de Dieu apud Wa- læum: ut & B. Lyserus Harm. c. CXXVII.

ὑπωπιάζη με] Non dubito quin sit latinismus, quales multi apud Lucam: nam ὑπωπιάζειν ad verbum est obtun- dere: at obtundere Latinis est ad fastidium aliquid repetere. Terentius: Obtundis, tametsi intelligo. Cicero: Si meministis obtundam. Bene ergo sensum Syrus expressit: Molesta sit mi- hi: & Arabs Vexet me. Jus, inquit, illi reddam ne nunquam desinat mihi molesta esse assiduis flagitationibus.

## 18:7
V. 7. of his elect] All the words have emphasis. That just God, that merciful one, will he not ward off injury, not from those whom he despises, but whom he loves, not from those who cause him trouble, but whose prayers he esteems highly. Concerning the word 'elect,' enough elsewhere.

and is he long-suffering over them] That most ancient manuscript in England has it so: Chrysostom reads it so: the Latin interpreter so: the Syrian and Arab so: wherefore I think this reading should be retained: and all the more because those codices that have it otherwise do not have it in the same way; some omit 'and,' others substitute 'and' in its place, so that it appears the passage was variously interpolated by those who did not sufficiently grasp this kind of speaking. Some have thought that 'to be long-suffering over someone' here means to be moved by someone's mercy: which sense, if not directly, certainly by consequence that word has, where it deals with exacting debts or a similar matter, as Matt. 18:26, 29, and the Arab followed this very thing here: for he translates it 'he will help them,' that is, he will repeat the vengeance, tacitly with a negative interrogation. But the word 'long-suffering' cannot be taken in that way here, where it deals with warding off injuries from someone. For there is in that word a signification of delay, which, as it benefits the debtor, so it is burdensome to him who suffers violence. Wherefore the interpretation of the Syrian and the Latin is to be preferred, who do not repeat the negation: the Syrian has 'and will he prolong his spirit over them?' that is, will he be slow in their cause? The Latin: 'and will he have patience in them?' that is, will he be slow in their cause? The son of Sirach removes all doubt, who uses the same kind of speaking in the same matter, undoubtedly from an old proverb to which Christ alluded: 'The prayer of the humble passes through the clouds, and until it draws near he will not be comforted, and he will not depart until the Most High looks upon him, and judges justly and will perform judgment, and the Lord will not delay, nor will the Mighty One be long-suffering over them.' The same is said here, but a verb of the present tense is put for the future. The words that follow declare the same, 'he will perform their vengeance speedily,' he will deliver them quickly, which is opposed to 'being long-suffering'. Nor does the fact that God sometimes suffers his friends to be vexed for a time by the injuries of the wicked force us to depart from this very clear interpretation; for that very time, although it may seem long to those who are suffering, is in reality small, indeed momentary: whence Paul said, 'the momentary lightness of affliction,' 2 Cor. 4:17. Add that that very delay has causes that are salutary to those who are suffering, although often not conspicuous. But it avails much for exciting the constancy of prayers if we trust that we are not only to be delivered, but also to be delivered quickly, even if the deliverance is delayed a little. Thus Hab. 2:3, 'If he makes delay, wait for him, because in coming he will come and will not fail.' Christ himself in the Apocalypse, 'Yes, I am coming quickly,' ch. 22:20.

Latin:

V. 7. τω̂ν ἐκλεκτω̂ν αὐτου̂] Omnia verba ἔμφασιν habent. Deus ille justus, ille misericors, an non arcebit injuriam, non ab iis quos contemnit, sed quos diligit, non ab iis qui mole- stiam ipsi exhibent, sed quorum preces magni æstimat. De voce ἐκλεκτῶν satis alibi.

κὶ μακροθυμῶν ἐπ' αὐτοῖς] Ita habet vetustissimus ille in An- glia manuscriptus: ita legit Chrysostomus: ita Latinus in- terpres: ita Syrus & Arabs: quare hanc lectionem retinen- dam puto: eoq; magis quia qui aliter habent Codices, non habent eodem modo, alii κὶ omittunt, alii ejg loco καὶ repo- nunt, ut appareat varie interpolatum locum ab iis qui lo- quendi istud genus non satis capiebant. Quidam putarunt μακροθυμεῖν ἐπί τινι hic esse misericordia alicujus moveri: quem sensum si non directe, certe ex consequentia habet ea vox, ubi de exigendis debitis aut re simili agitur, ut Matth. XVIII. 26. 29. idq; ipsum hic secutus est Arabs: vertit enim يعانت غليم, id est, ἐκδίκησιν repetita scilicet tacite negativa interrogatione. Sed non potest vox μακροθυμεῖν ita hic accipi, ubi de arcendis de aliquo injuriis agitur. Est enim in ista voce dilationis significatio, quæ ut debitori prodest, ita gravis est ei qui vim patitur. Quare præferenda est Syri & Latini interpretatio qui negationem non repetunt: Syrus ha- bet ומגר רוחה עליהון id est, protrahet spiritum suum er- ga illos? Latinus: & patientiam habebit in illis? id e. in eorum causa lentus erit? Dubitationem omnem eximit Sirachi- des, qui in re eadem idem loquendi genus usurpat, haud du- bie ex vetere proverbio ad quod allusit Christus: προσευχὴ ταπεινῦ νεφέλας διῆλθε, κέἕως συνεγγίσῃ ὐ μὴ παρακληθῇ, κὲ ὐ μὴ ἀποσῇ ἕως ἂν ἐπισκέψηταιὁ ὕψιςφ, κρίνει δικαίως κέ ποιή- σει κρίσιν, κέὁ κύριφ ὐ μὴ βραδύνῃ ὐδὲ μὴ μακροθυμήσῃ ἐπ' αὐτοῖς ὁ κραταιός. Idem hic dicitur, sed præsentis temporis verbum positum est pro futuro. Declarant idem quæ se quuntur verba, ποιήσει ἐκδίκησιν αὐτῶν ἐν τάχει, cito eos li- berabit, quod opponitur τῷ μακροθυμεῖν. Neque discedere ab hac perspicua admodum interpretatione nos cogit, quòd Deus interdum ad tempus amicos suos patitur improbo- rum injuriis vexari; nam illud ipsum tempus, quamvis lon- gum interdum ferentibus videatur, re vera exiguum est imo momentaneum: unde τὸ παραυτίκα τῆς θλίψεως, dixit Paulus 2. Cor. IV. 12. adde quod ipsa illa dilatio causas habet ipsis ferentibus salutares, quanquam sæpe non conspicuas. Mul- tum autem valet ad excitandam precum assiduitatẽ, si confi- damus non tantum liberandos nos, sed & cito liberandos, etiamsi aliquantulum liberatio differatur. Ita Abac. II. 2. Si moram fecerit expecta eum, quia veniendo venit & non trada- bit. Ipse Christus in Apocalypsi, ναὶ ἔρχομαι ταχὺ c. XXII. 20.

## 18:8
V. 8. ἐλθὼν] When the Son of Man shall come to deliver his own: which he will do not only at the time of the universal judgment, but also very often does in this age. Thus, to come is taken in the cited passage of Habakkuk.

ἆρα εὑρήσει πίστιν ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς] Thus also in Habakkuk that constant expectation of deliverance is attributed to faith: for it follows: The just shall live by his faith. And in the Apocalypse, patience and the faith of the saints are rightly joined, XIII. 10. This is the faith that commends prayers: let him ask in faith, says James I. 6. Christ complains that many do not persevere in patient trust, and therefore in prayers until the time of deliverance, which is not far off, arrives. To this also pertains what he says elsewhere, he that shall endure unto the end, the same shall be saved. Faith and a saving birth, as Cyprian testifies, do not vivify by being received but by being kept. This is the work, this is the labor. There will not be lacking, even after Christ, most corrupt ages, such as once the age of the flood, the age of Terah, the age of Amram, the age of Antiochus. See among others 2 Tim. IV. 3, 4.

Latin:

V. 8. ἐλθὼν] Cum veniet filius hominis ad suos liberandos: quod non tantum faciet tempore judicii universalis, sed etiam in hoc sæculo sæpissime facit. Ita venire sumitur di- cto Abacuci loco.

ἆρα εὑρήσει πίστιν ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς] Sic & apud Abacucum con- stans illa exspectatio liberationis tribuitur fidei: sequitur e- nim: Justus sua fide vivet. Et in Apocalypsi recte junguntur ὑπομονὴ καὶ πίστις τῶν ἁγίων XIII. 10. Hæc fides est quæ preces commendat: αἰτείτω δὲ ἐν πίστει, inquit Jacobus I. 6. Con- queritur Christus multos non perseverare in patienti fidu- cia, ac proinde in precibus usque dum tempus liberationis, quod non longe abest, adventet. Huc & illud pertinet, quod alibi dicit, ὁ ὑπομείνας εἰς τέλος, οὗτος σωθήσεται. Fi- des & nativitas salutaris, teste Cypriano, non accepta sed cu- stodita vivificat. Hoc opus, hic labor est. Non deerunt etiam post Christum corruptissima secula, qualia olim seculum diluvii, seculum Tharæ, seculum Amrami, seculum An- tiochi. Vide inter alia 2. Tim. IV. 3. 4.

## 18:9
V. 9. πρός τινας] Luke prudently attaches to the warnings about constant trust a warning about submissive modesty of mind, which has use not only in all of life, but especially in prayers: Christ said these things, however, when he observed certain ones of the Pharisaic sect, as it were, present, whose fierce spirit he was looking into.

τοὺς πεποιθότας ἐφ' ἑαυτοῖς] הַבּוֹטְחִים עַל־נַפְשָׁתָם a similar way of speaking in 2 Cor. I. 9, that we should not trust in ourselves, but in God who raises the dead, although in a different sense: for there it concerns that trust which is accustomed to be placed in natural causes: here it concerns that trust which many, pleasing themselves more than is right, often place in virtues falsely believed in, and by that thing are hindered from fleeing with a humble mind to divine mercy.

ὅτι εἰσὶ δίκαιοι] That is, as if they were righteous, or because they are righteous, in their own estimation, of course: for the words admit both interpretations and the sense falls back into the same thing. Chilo, being asked what was most difficult, replied: to know oneself: for each one adds many things to himself out of self-love. It cannot be that a mind corrupted by self-love does not estimate both its own good qualities above the truth and judge its bad ones to be less than the truth: and conversely, that it does not judge the evils in others to be greater than the truth, and their good qualities to be less than the truth. For as an eye suffused with some humor sees all things not as they are, but according to the quality of that humor, so he who loves himself fashions dreams for himself, and judges all things not from the truth but from his own desire. Wherefore, since it is difficult to keep the middle ground in prayer, just as those whose shoes turn to the right are accustomed to reflect them by pressing much to the left, so it is also right for us to strive toward that side from which we are naturally more averse: for in this direction one errs not only more safely, but also laudably. Chrysostom well says: If you wish to make your good deeds great, do not think them to be great, but confess that you are saved by grace, so that you may make God a debtor to yourself, not only of your good deeds, but also of this gratitude. Macarius: Even if one is chosen by God, let him consider himself rejected in his own eyes, and even if he is faithful, let him consider himself unworthy: for such souls are pleasing to God.

καὶ ἐξουθενοῦντας τοὺς ἄλλους] For it is a consequence that he who admires his own things despises those of others. We have spoken about this matter at Matt. VII.

Latin:

V. 9. πρός τινας] Prudenter Lucas monitis de constante fi- ducia annectit monitum de submissa animi modestia, quæ cum in omni vita usum habet, tum præcipue in precibus: Dixit autem hæc Christus, cum quosdam Pharisæicæ vide- licet sectæ, præsentes conspicaretur, quorum ferocem ani- mum introspectabat.

τοὺς πεποιθότας ἐφ' ἑαυτοῖς] הַבּוֹטְחִים עַל־נַפְשָׁתָם simile loquendi genus 2. Cor. I. 9. ἵνα μὴ πεποιθότες ὦμεν ἐφ' ἑαυτοῖς, ἀλλ' ἐπὶ τῷ Θεῷ ἐγείροντι τοὺς νεκρούς, quanquam in sensu alio: nam ibi de fiducia ea agitur quæ in causis na- turalibus collocari solet: hic de ea fiducia quam multi plus æquo sibi placentes in virtutibus sæpe falso creditis ponunt, eaque re impediuntur ne demisso animo ad divinam mise- ricordiam confugiant.

ὅτι εἰσὶ δίκαιοι] Id est quasi justi essent, aut eo quod justi sint, sua scilicet existimatione: utramque enim interpreta- tionem verba recipiunt & sensus in idem recidit. Chilo interrogatus, quid esset difficillimum, respondit semet nosse : πολλὰ γὰρ ὑπὸ φιλαυτίας ἕκαστον ἑαυτῷ προστιθέναι. Fieri non potest, quin sui amore corruptus animus & bona sua supra verum æstimet & mala vero minora arbitretur: & contra quæ in aliis sunt mala vero majora, quæ bona infra verum. Nam ut humore aliquo suffusus oculus omnia videt non ut sunt, sed pro humoris illius qualitate, ita qui se amat, sibi fingit somnia, resque omnes non ex vero sed ex sua cupiditate judicat. Quare cum medium ἐν εὐγμῇ tenere difficile sit, sicut ii quorum calcei dextorsum ver- gunt, eos solent multum premendo sinistrorsum reflectere, ita & nos æquum est conniti in eam partem à qua sponte nostra alieniores sumus: Nam in hac partem non tutius tan- tum, sed & laudabiliter erratur. Bene Chrysostomus: εἰ βέλει μέγαλά σε ποιῆσαι τὰ κατορθώματα, μὴ νομίζε αὐτὰ εἶναι μέγα- λα, ἀλλὰ χάριτι ὁμολόγει σώζεσθαι, ἵνα ὀφειλέτην ἑαυτῷ τὸν Θεὸν καταστήσῃς, οὐχὶ τῶν κατορθωμάτων μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ ταύτης τῆς εὐ- γνωμοσύνης. Macarius: κἄνπερ ὢν ἐκλεκτὸς τῷ Θεῷ παρ' ἑαυτῷ ἀποδεδοκιμασμένον εἶναι, κἂν ὢν πιστὸς ὡς ἀτάξιον ἑαυτὸν ἡγείσθω˙ τοιαῦται γὰρ ψυχαὶ εὐαρεστοῦσι Θεῷ.

καὶ ἐξουθενοῦντας τοὺς ἄλλους] Consequens enim est ut aliena de- primat qui sua miratur. Diximus de hac re ad Matth. VII.

## 18:10
V. 10. εἰς τὸ ἱερὸν] Because that place was believed to be most acceptable to God for pouring out prayers, 1 Kings VIII. 38, Matt. XXI. 13.

Latin:

V. 10. εἰς τὸ ἱερὸν] Quod is locus ad preces fundendas ac- ceptissimus Deo crederetur, 1. Reg. VIII. 38. Matth. XXI. 13.

## 18:11
V. 11. σταθεὶς πρὸς ἑαυτὸν] I do not think it is signified here that he stood apart from the publican, as if he were unclean. For custom generally held that publicans stood in the court of the Gentiles, and Pharisees in the court of the Israelites, nor was there anything unusual in that, or to be imputed to the Pharisee: he is therefore said to have stood with himself, so that we may understand that the discourse which follows explains his thoughts, as one who was considered to be aware of nothing. See Mark IX. 10, 33, X. 26, XIV. 4, XVI. 3, add 1 Cor. XI. 13, where ἐν ὑμῖν is the same as πρὸς ἑαυτούς in those places.

The sense of the Vulgate and the Arabic is the same. The Syriac, however, with the old Codex of Camerarius and Beza, reads: But the Pharisee standing apart, prayed these things: unless you prefer to interpret the Syriac with Dievius; that Pharisee stood by himself, that is, entirely turned into himself, intent only on himself, and boasting of nothing but himself. Camero understands him to have stood apart, as does Salmasius. Nevertheless, the opinion of Grotius is to be preferred: which also pleased the blessed Luther.

προσηύχετο] And yet the discourse that follows is of the kind that the Hebrews call HODOTH, and the Greeks call doxologies. It must be known, therefore, that under the name of prayer, taken more generally, is comprehended everything by which we address God.

εὐχαριστῶ σοι] The Pharisees did not exclude divine help, as is most evident from Josephus, and as we have mentioned elsewhere. But even those who usurp this name are often ungrateful, when they either attribute the first place in honest actions to themselves and the second to God, or acknowledge common benefits in such a way that they do not flee as suppliants to that peculiar mercy which their sins require. Chrysostom well says against the Jews II: Just as it is the custom for the righteous to be moderate after their righteous acts, so for those

wicked people after their sins to be puffed up. Paulinus in his Letter to Augustine concerning this Pharisee: Not praying that he might be heard, but demanding as if it were a debt of merit, for works that were indeed good, but ungrateful to God, because what justice had built, pride was destroying.

as the rest of men] He sins twice: first because he considers it a great praise not to be in the number of the most wicked, then because he judges so insolently concerning other men, the greatest part of whom he does not know.

and the tax collector] Whom, if there had been any love in him, he ought to have believed was approaching the temple with a purpose of repentance, which his very posture indicated. But if, believing him to be such, he nevertheless insulted him because of his former life, that indeed was even somewhat more atrocious.

Latin:

V. 11. σταθεὶς πρὸς ἑαυτὸν] Non puto hic significari seor- sim illum à publicano, quasi impuro, constitisse. Nam mos id ferebat, ut publicani in atrio Gentilium, Pharisæi in atrio Israëlitarum starent, nec quicquam in eo erat insolitum, aut Pharisæo imputandum: stetisse ergo secum dicitur, ut intel- ligamus eo qui sequitur moneint sermone ejus sensa explicari, ut qui habitus sit nemine conscio. Vid. Marc. IX. 10. 33. X. 26. XIV. 4. XVI. 3. adde 1. Cor. XI. 13. ubi ἐν ὑμῖν idem est quod illis in locis πρὸς ἑαυτούς.

Idem sensus est Vulgatæ & Arabis. Syrus tamen, cum veteri Camerarii Codice, ac Beza legunt, Pha- risæus autem stans seorsim, hæc precatus est: nisi malis Syrum interpretari cum Dievio; Pharisæus ille stabat apud se, id est, totus in seipsum versus, sibi tantum intentus, & nihil nisi seipsum jactans. Seor- sim stetisse ipsum intelligit Camero, ut & Salmasius. Præferenda tamen Grotii sententia: quæ etiam placuit B. Luthero.

προσηύχετο] Atqui is qui sequitur sermo ex eorum est ge- nere quos Hebræi הוֹדוֹת, Græci δοξολογίας vocant. Scien- dum igitur προσευχῶν nomine generalius accepto compre- hendi omne id quo Deum compellamus.

εὐχαριστῶ σοι] Pharisæi non excludebant divinam opem, ut ex Josepho apertissimum est, & nos alibi meminimus. Sed etiam qui nomen hoc usurpant ingrati sæpe sunt, cum aut primas sibi in honestis actionibus, Deo secundas tribuant, aut ita agnoscant beneficia communia, ut ad eam peculia- rem misericordiam qua peccata ipsorum indigent supplices non confugiant. Bene Chrysostomus adversus Judæos II. Ὥσπερ τοῖς δικαίοις ἔθος μετὰ τὰ δικαιώματα μετριάζειν, ὕτω τοῖς

πονηροῖς μετὰ τὰ ἁμαρτήματα ἐπαίρεσθαι. Paulinus in Epistola ad Augustinum de hoc Pharisæo: Non orans ut exaudiretur, sed exigens quasi debitum meriti, pro operibus bonis quidem, sed in- gratis Deo, quia quod justitia ædificaverat, superbia destruebat.

ὥσπερ οἱ λοιποὶ τῶν ἀνθρώπων] Bis peccat: primum quod in magna laude ponit non esse in sceleratissimorum nume- ro, deinde quod de hominibus cæteris, quorum maximam partem non novit, tam proterve judicat.

ἤτῶ καὶ ὁ τελώνης] Quem si quid in ipso fuisset dilectionis, credere debuit resipiscendi proposito ad templum accedere, quod ipse gestus indicabat. Quod si talem credens nihilo- minus ei insultavit ob vitam priorem, id vero aliquanto etiam erat atrocius.

## 18:12
V. 12. I fast twice in the week] Christ does not disapprove of this bodily exercise, although it came not from the prescription of the law, but from voluntary undertaking. Now those days were days of unchangeable fasting, as Epiphanius and Theophylact rightly explain, the second and fifth days, with the books of the Hebrews agreeing: to which also that is to be referred which is in the Constitutions of Clement: and let your fasts not be with the hypocrites; for they fast on the second day of the week and the fifth. The ancient Christians, so that they might not in any part yield to the Jews, from the time when the separation from the Jews had been made throughout the whole world, substituted in the place of these days the fourth and sixth days of the week, which the pagans called Mercury's and Venus's days. Ignatius to the Philippians, do not disregard the fourth and the preparation day, fasting, and bestowing your abundance upon the poor. Clement speaking concerning the truly Gnostic: he himself knows also the enigmas of the fast, of these days, I mean the fourth and the preparation day; for they are named after Hermes, the one, and Aphrodite, the other. Which he explains thus, immediately he fasts according to the life of greed and pleasure at the same time, from which all vices spring. Tertullian: We call the fourth and sixth days of the week stations. How widely that custom extended is testified by Epiphanius arguing against Aëtius: and to whom is it not agreed in all climates of the inhabited world, that the fourth day and the day before the Sabbath is a fast appointed in the Church. The same is testified by Ambrose, Socrates, Augustine, Jerome. That bodily exercise is never condemned by Christ, nor is it to be disapproved of by us, if it is used for a right end and estimated by its own weights, that is, below the works of love. But the Pharisees, entirely occupied in rituals, neglected the more important things. They easily, of course, wrap those ivies around themselves, who have nothing inside but dregs, since the works of true love, especially the assiduous and excellent ones, cannot proceed except from a cleansed soul. Thus happens that old saying, often to be repeated:

The side-work we do as work, And the work we perform as side-work.

I tithe] See concerning this word at Matt. 23:23.

all that I acquire] all that I have. Not only those things which the common people are accustomed to subject to tithes, fruits and crops, but also those things which are of controversial law, for instance smaller herbs, eggs, milk, cheese, rather taking something away from my own comforts than doing anything against the traditions. But how much better was Zacchaeus, who gave half of his goods to the poor. For in those minute things it is very easy to perform something beyond the law: in which, however, the Pharisees placed the sum of a certain singular holiness, the name of which they also preferred.

Latin:

V. 12. Νηστεύω δὶς τῦ σαββάτου] Non improbat Christus hanc σωμασκίαν, quanquam non ex legis præscripto, sed ex vo- luntaria susceptione venientem. Dies autem illi νηστείας ἀν- υπερθέτου erant, ut recte Epiphanius & Theophylactus expli- cant, dies secundus & quintus consentientibus Hebræorum libris: quo & illud referendum quod est in Constitutioni- bus Clementis: αἱ δὲ νηστεῖαι ὑμῶν μὴ ἔστωσαν μετὰ τῶν ὑπο- κριτῶν· νηστεύουσι γὰρ δευτέρᾳ σαββάτων καὶ πέμπτῃ. Christia- ni veteres, ne qua in parte Judæis concederent, ex quo facta erat per totum orbem à Judæis secessio, in horum die- rum locum surrogarunt diem hebdomadis quartum & sex- tum, quos pagani vocabant Mercurii & Veneris. Ignatius ad Philippenses, μὴ παρορᾶτε τέτραδα καὶ παρασκευήν, νη- στεύοντες, πένησιν ἐπιχορηγοῦντες τὴν περιουσίαν. Clemens περὶ τῶ ἀληθῶς γνωστικοῦ loquens: οἶδεν αὐτὸς καὶ τῆς νηστείας τὰ αἰνίγματα, τῶν ἡμερῶν τούτων, τῆς τέτραδος καὶ τῆς παρασκευῆς λέγω· ἐπιφημίζονται γὰρ ἡ μὲν ἑρμῦ, ἡ δὲ ἀφροδίτης. Quod ita explicat, ἀυτίκα νηστεύει κατὰ τὸν βίον φιλαργυρίας τε ὁμῦ καὶ φιληδονίας ἐξ ὧν αἱ πᾶσαι ἐκφύονται κακίαι. Tertullianus: Stationibus quartam & sextam sabbati dicimus. Quam late is mos patuerit testatur Epiphanius contra Aëtium dispu- tans: τίνι δὲ ὐ συμπεφώνηται ἐν πᾶσι κλίμασι τῆς οἰκουμένης, ὅτι τετρὰς καὶ προσάββατον νηστεία ἐστιν ἐν τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ ὡρι- σμένη. Idem testantur Ambrosius, Socrates, Augustinus, Hieronymus. Ista corporalis exercitatio nunquam à Chri- sto damnatur, neque à nobis improbanda est, si recto fine usurpetur æstimeturque suis ponderibus, id est infra opera dilectionis. At Pharisæi toti occupati in ritibus negligebant potiora. Facile scilicet istas hederas sibi circumdant, qui- bus intus nihil est nisi vappa, cum veræ dilectionis opera, assidua præsertim atque eximia, non possint nisi ex animo emundato proficisci. Ita evenit illud veteris sententiæ sæ- pe repetendum:

Τὸ μὲν πάρεργον ἔργον ὡς ποιέμεθα, Τὸ δ᾽ ἔργον ὡς πάρεργον ἐκπονύμεθα.

ἀποδεκατῶ] Vide de hac voce ad Matth. XXIII. 23.

πάντα ὅσα κτῶμαι] כל אשר לי. Non illa tantum quæ vulgus solet decimæ subjicere poma & fruges, sed & ea quæ controversi sunt juris, puta minora olera, ova, lac, caseum, potius meis commodis aliquid detrahens, quam ut quic- quam faciam contra τὰς παραδόσεις. At quanto melius Za- chæus, qui bonorum partem alte am pauperibus dabat. Nam in minutis illis aliquid extra legem præstare perfacile est: in quo tamen Pharisæi summam ponebant singularis cujusdam sanctimoniæ, cujus & nomen præferebant.

## 18:13
Vers. 13.

nor his eyes] I think it refers entirely to a custom common to the Jews and other nations, of lifting the hands to heaven together with the eyes. Concerning the Jews, Philo is a witness: Standing in order along the wall in an orderly manner and lifting their eyes and hands to heaven. Christians followed their custom. Clement Strom. VII. For God hears every unspoken conversation unceasingly. In this way we also lift up our head and raise our hands to heaven. Tertullian also joins both in the passage which we shall cite presently. Concerning the profane nations, for many, one will suffice, Maro.

Stretching his burning eyes to heaven in vain, / Eyes, for bonds restrained his tender palms.

Juvenal:

With face uplifted, this alone, and pale, you pray.

Jeremiah mentions the hands separately in Lamentations III. 41. Thus also Solomon prays with hands spread to heaven, I Kings VIII. Philo the Alexandrian on the Jews: stretching out their hands to heaven. The author of the book On the World: we all men stretch out our hands to heaven. Homer:

- - - And lifting hands to the gods.

Among Latin poets and historians, too, it occurs a hundred times to lift, spread, or stretch out supine hands or palms to heaven, so that to collect the testimonies would be to waste time. For Christians, I will bring forward one from Salvian, book I, On the Government of God: Why do we stretch out our hands to heaven daily? Tertullian alluded to the same thing: The very posture of the praying Christian is prepared for every punishment. Moreover, they testified to their innocence by this position, as Seneca in Oedipus:

I call to witness: it is now permitted to lift to heaven pure hands, fearing no crime. Philo in the cited place: the eyes, trained to look upon things worthy of God; and the hands, because they are clean of gains, undefiled by any pretext for the sake of profit. Paul, I to Timothy II. v. 8: I desire therefore that men pray everywhere, lifting up holy hands without wrath and doubting. Tertullian: Hither, to heaven, looking up, Christians with hands expanded, because they are harmless, with head bare, because we do not blush. Chrysostom, looking to the same, says: For what is the meaning of the stretching out of the hands in prayer? These serve many wickednesses, and he discourses on that matter at length and eloquently in his usual way. The publican, therefore, mindful of his sins, dared not only not to lift his hands to heaven, lest he provoke the wrath of God by false boasting, but not even his eyes: which, although it was properly fitting for the state of one doing penance, was nevertheless wont to be drawn into an example by most Christians. Tertullian: But when we worship with modesty and humility, we commend our prayers to God all the more, not even with hands raised too high, nor even with face lifted in boldness. For that publican, who prayed not only with prayer but also with face humbled and cast down, departed more justified than the most impudent Pharisee. Cyprian in his book on the Lord's Prayer: But when praying, most beloved brethren, let no one be ignorant of how the publican prayed in the temple with the Pharisee: not with eyes impudently lifted to heaven, nor with hands insolently raised, but beating his breast and testifying to the sins shut up within, he implored the help of divine mercy, and while the Pharisee pleased himself, the publican deserved all the more to be sanctified, who prayed thus: who placed his hope of salvation not in the confidence of his own innocence, since no one is innocent, but having confessed his sins, he prayed humbly, and he entreated the one who prays, who always forgives the humble.

He struck his breast] Which gesture of those accusing themselves, as below XXIII. v. 48, the same was observed in the Church of the Christians by those who publicly professed penance.

Be merciful to me the sinner] The Hebrew סלח, which has following it in the dative now a person, now a thing, the LXX translate as to be propitious, Num. XIV. 20, Jerem. XXXI. 34, with the writer to the Hebrews VIII. v. 12 following, to be propitiated, 2 Kings XXIV. 41, to forgive, Deut. XXIX. v. 20, Ps. CIII. v. 3. This very word be merciful exists in Psalm XXV. v. 11, where in the Hebrew it is סלחת, and Dan. IX. 14, where it is סלחה. It seems to me the Syrian did not poorly express the force of the word by חונני. A synonym for this is to make propitiation, by which word the Hellenists render the Hebrew כפר or חטא, which words do not signify the pity or favor of the mind itself, but some act apt for obtaining pity or favor: of which matter, elsewhere. The sense of this whole prayer is taken from the entire Psalm LI.

Latin:

Vers. 13.

ὐδὲ τὲς ὀφθαλμὲς] Omnino puto respici morem Judæis & aliis gentibus communem, tollendi manus ad cælum simul cum oculis. De Judæis testis Philo: Στάντες ἑξῆς κατὰ τοῖχον ἐν κόσμῳ καὶ τὰς ὄψεις καὶ χεῖρας εἰς ὀρανὸν ἀνατείναντες. Horum morem secuti sunt Christiani. Clemens Strom. VII. πᾶσαν γὰρ τὴν ὀδιαίθετον ὁμιλίαν ὁ Θεὸς ἀδιαλείπτως ἐπαΐει. ταύτῃ καὶ προσαναιτείνομεν τὴν κεφαλὴν καὶ τὰς χεῖρας εἰς ὀρα- τὸν αἴρομεν. Conjungit utrumq; & Tertullianus loco quem jam jam citabimus. De profanis gentibus pro multis unus sufficiet Maro.

Ad cælum tendens ardentia lumina frustra, Lumina, nam teneras arcebant vincula palmas.

Juvenalis:

Arrecto vultu solum hoc, & pallidus, oras.

Seorsim manuum meminit Jeremias Threno III. 41. Sic & Solomo passis ad cælum manibus orat, I. Reg. VIII. Phi- lo de Judæis Alexandrinus: προτείνοντες τὰς χεῖρας εἰς ὐρα- νὸν. Scriptor libri de mundo: πάντες ἄνθρωποι ἀνατείνομεν τὰς χεῖρας εἰς τὸν ὐρανὸν. Homerus:

- - - Θεοῖσι δὲ χεῖρας ἀνασχὼν.

Apud Latinos quoque Poetas & historiarum Scriptores centies occurrit, manus supinas aut palmas ad cælum tol- lere, pandere, tendere, ut testimonia congerere sit otio abuti. Pro Christianis unum adducam Salvianum lib. I. de Gub. Dei: Cur ad cælum quotidie manus tendimus? eodem allufit & Tertulliani illud, Paratus est ad omne supplicium ipse habitus orantis Christiani. Testabantur autem hoc situ innocentiam suam Seneca Oedipode:

Testor: licet jam tollere ad cælum pie Puras, nec ullo scelere metuentes manus. Philo dicto loco: τὰς μὲν (scilicet τὰς ὄψεις) ἱκετείας τῷ Θεῷ ἄξια καθορᾷν ἐπαιδευθούσας· τὰς δὲ (τὰς χεῖρας) ὅτι κα- θαρὰι λημμάτων εἰσιν ὑπ᾽ οὐδεμίας προφάσεως τῶν εἰς πορι- σμὸν μιανθεῖσαι. Paulus I. ad Timoth. II. v. 8. βούλομαι οὖν προσεύχεσθαι τοὺς ἄνδρας ἐν παντὶ τόπῳ ἐπαίροντας ὁσίους χεῖρας χωρὶς ὀργῆς καὶ διαλογισμοῦ. Tertullianus: Huc, in cœlum, suspicientes Christiani manibus expansis, quia inno- cuis, capite nudo, quia non erubescimus. Eodem Chryso- stomus respiciens, τί γὰρ βούλεται, inquit, ἐν τῇ εὐχῇ τῶν χειρῶν ἡ ἔκτασις; πολλαῖς πονηρίαις διακονοῦσιν αὗται, & quæ plura more suo facunde in eam rem disserit. Publicanus ergo, peccatorum suorum memor, non modo manus non audebat ad cœlum tollere, ne falsa jactatione iram DEI provocaret, sed ne oculos quidem: quod quanquam pro- prie statui pœnitentiam agentis conveniebat, aliquate- nus tamen in exemplum trahi solebat à plerisque Christia- nis. Tertallianus: Atqui cum modestia & humilitate ado- rantes, magis commendamus Deo preces nostras, ne ipsis quidem manibus sublimius datis, ne vultu quidem in auda- ciam erecto. Nam ille publicanus, qui non tantum prece, sed & vultu humiliatus atque dejectus orabat, justificatior Pha- risæo procacissimo discessit. Cyprianus libro de oratione Do- minica: Adorans autem, fratres dilectissimi, nec illud igno- ret quemadmodum in templo cum Pharisæo publicanus ora- verit: non allevatis in cælum impudenter oculis, nec ma- nibus insolenter erectis, sed pectus suum pulsans & peccata in- tus conclusa contestans, divinæ misericordiæ implorabat auxi- lium, & cum sibi Pharisæus placeret, sanctificari publicanus hoc magis meruit, qui sic rogavit: qui spem salutis non in fiducia innocentiæ suæ posuit, cum innocens nemo sit: sed pec- cata confessus humiliter oravit, & exoravit orantem, qui semper humilibus ignoscit.

ἔτυπτεν εἰς τὸ στῆθος αὐτοῦ] Qui gestus semet accusan- tium, ut infra XXIII. v. 48. eundem observarunt in Chri- stianorum Ecclesia, qui pœnitentiam publice profite- bantur.

ἱλάσθητί μοι τῷ ἁμαρτωλῷ] Hebræum סלח quod modo personam, modo rem in dativo habet sibi subse- quentem, LXX. vertunt ἵλεων εἶναι Num. XIV. 20. Jerem. XXXI. 34. sequente Scriptore ad Hebræos VIII. v. 12. ἱλά- σκεσθαι 2. Reg. XXIV. 41. ἐπιλατεύειν Deuter. XXIX. v. 20. Ps. CIII. v. 3. ipsa hæc vox ἱλάσθητι exstat Psal. XXV. v. 11. ubi in Hebræo est סלחת & Dan. IX. 14. ubi est סלחה. Videtur mihi Syrus non male expressisse vim vocis per חונני. Huic παράνυμον est ἐξιλάσκεσθαι, qua voce Helle- nistæ reddunt Hebræum כפר aut חטא quæ verba non ipsam animi miserationem aut faventiam, sed actum ali- quem aptum impetrandæ miserationi aut faventiæ signi- ficant: qua de re alias. Sensus totius hujus precationis de- sumptus ex toto Psalmo LI.

## 18:14
Verse 14. than that one) I do not doubt that Luke wrote it thus, because both many codices have retained this reading, and it appears that the others were corrupted from it, such as for that one which some books have, and by that one which the Latin reads. But the older Latins read than that one: for Tertullian translates: more justified than the Pharisee, as we have already seen. Cyprian, in the words already cited, describing the whole history, puts: Justified more than that Pharisee: and the Syrian and Arab express the same. Add that Luke also spoke thus above, ch. XIII. 2, 4, where they are called sinners and debtors more than all, who are more wicked than the rest, with than placed for that which is from among the Hebrews, and elsewhere also with, as in Job XXV, where just with God signifies, if he is compared to God. Above we said that to justify is often to approve; therefore the simplest sense of this place is that the humble prayer of the publican, although he had fallen into sins, was more approved by God and more pleasing than that external sanctimony of the Pharisee joined with a certain proud confidence. Origen well, against Celsus, disp. 3: And yet when a sinner, conscious of his own sin, and for this reason proceeding to repent, stands humble over his sins before the one who is thought to be a sinner, but does not think himself a sinner, but is puffed up over certain things which he seems to know in himself to be better, and is swollen with pride over them. Theophylact asks here not without reason what is the cause that the Pharisee is accused of insolence for a few words, when Job, proclaiming so many things about himself, sustains no mark of blame on that account. For the solution of which question, one must see how great is the difference in those deeds. The Pharisee speaks to God and to himself, with no one accusing him, nay, he himself accuses others for his own satisfaction. Job, most gravely accused, as if he were remarkably wicked in comparison with other men, refutes the calumny with the testimony of an innocent conscience: nor does he bring forward slight signs of an upright mind, pure fasts and the exact payment of tithes, with which the Pharisee swells, bearing a mind inwardly full of vices, but those works in which also love & humility, the sister of love, shone forth. Plutarch, in the little book in which he accurately treats this subject of περιαυτολογίας [self-praise], says that there is never a more just occasion for commemorating one's own right deeds than when someone's reputation is being unjustly attacked. Both David and, more openly, Nehemiah commend their services to God, that He might kindly remember them, but only after they had acknowledged their faults, whether common with the people or peculiar to themselves, and had sought pardon from God with humble prayer. The Apostles, however, and Christians conduct themselves much more modestly than those under the old covenant, in the consciousness of such great pardon and benefits received through Christ.

Ὅτι πᾶς ὁ ὑψῶν ἑαυτὸν ταπεινωθήσεται [For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled]) See what we have said at Matt. XXIII. 12 and at Luke above I. 51.

Latin:

Vers. 14. παρ᾽ ἐκεῖνον) non dubito quin ita scripserit Lu- cas, quia & multi codices hanc lectionem retinuerunt, & cæteros inde corruptos apparet, ut ἢ γὰρ ἐκεῖνος quod qui- dam libri habent, & παρ᾽ ἐκείνῳ quod legit Latinus. At Latio- ni vetustiores legerunt παρ᾽ ἐκεῖνον: vertit enim Tertullia- nus: justificatior Pharisæo, ut jam vidimus. Cyprianus in ver- bis jam citata sequentibus totam historiam describens po- nit, Iustificatus magis quam ille Pharisæus: idemq; Syrus & Arabs exprimunt. Adde quod Lucas supra quoq; ita est lo- cutus c. XIII. 2. 4. ubi ἁμαρτωλοὶ καὶ ὀφειλέται παρὰ πάντας dicuntur, qui cæteris sunt flagitiosiores posito παρὰ pro eo quod מן est apud Hebræos, alibi & עם ut Jobi XXV. ubi justus cum Deo, significat, si Deo comparetur. Supra dixi- mus δικαιοῦν sæpe esse approbare; itaq; hujus loci simplicis- simus est sensus, magis probatam esse Deo magisq; placuisse humilem Publicani, quamvis in peccata prolapsi, depreca- tionem, quam externam illam Pharisæi sanctimoniam cum superba quadam confidentia conjunctam. Bene Ori- genes adversus Celsum disp. 3. ἔτι δ᾽ ὅτε ἁμαρτωλὸς, συναι- σθόμενος τῆς ἰδίας ἁμαρτίας, καὶ διὰ τοῦτο πρὸς τὸ μετανοεῖν πο- ρευόμενος· ἐπὶ τοῖς ἡμαρτημένοις ταπεινὸς προΐσταται τῷ ἱλάσ- τον μὲν νομιζομένῳ εἶναι ἁμαρτωλῷ ἐκ οἰομένῳ δ᾽ αὑτὸν ἁμαρ- τωλὸν ἀλλ᾽ ἐπαιρομένῳ ἐπί τισιν οἷς δοκεῖ συνειδέναι ἑαυτῷ κρείτ- τοσι καὶ πεφυσιωμένῳ ἐπ᾿ αὐτοῖς. Quærit hic non abs re Theo- phylactus, quid sit cur ob pauca verba Pharisæus insolen- tiæ arguatur, cum Jobus tam multa de se prædicans nullam eo nomine notam sustineat. Ad cujus quæstionis solutio- nem videndum quanta sit in factis illis diversitas. Pharisæus Deo & sibi loquitur, nemine accusante, imo ipse alios ani- mi gratia accusat. Jobus gravissime accusatus, quasi in ho- minum aliorum comparatione insigniter facinorosus; di- luit calumniam innocentis conscientiæ testimonio: neque levia adfert probi animi signa, pura jejunia & exactam de- cimarum solutionem, quibus turget Pharisæus animura in- terius vitiis plenum gerens, sed ea opera in quibq & dilectio & dilectionis soror humilitas micabant. Plutarchus libello quo materiam hanc περιαυτολογίας accurate pertractat, nu- quam ait justiorem esse occasionem sua recte facta com- memorandi quam cum fama cujusquam injuste oppugna- tur. Commendant & David, & apertius Nehemias Deo sua officia, ut eorum benigne meminerit, sed postquam culpas suas aut cum populo communes aut sibi proprias agnove- rant, & supplici prece à Deo exambiverant veniam. Apo- stoli autem & Christiani, multo quam illi sub veteri federe se gerunt modestius, tantæ veniæ & beneficiorum acce- ptorum per Christum conscientia.

Ὅτι πᾶς ὁ ὑψῶν ἑαυτὸν ταπεινωθήσεται) Vide quæ diximus ad Matth. XXIII. 12. & ad Lucam supra I. 51.

## 18:15
V. 15. τὰ βρέφη [the infants]) Neither the word βρέφη, nor that which is in Mark, ἐναγκαλισάμενος [taking them in his arms], prove strongly enough that infants are being discussed here, as we said at Matthew: see there.

Beza's explanation is more correct here, that they are understood to be very young children, still hanging from the breasts. Compare what was said at Matthew.

Latin:

V. 15. τὰ βρέφη) Neά; vox βρέφη, neq; illud quod apud Mar- cum est ἐναγκαλισάμενος satis valide probant de infanti- bus hic agi, ut ad Matthæum diximus: ibi vide.

Rectius hic se habet Bezæ explicatio, quod in- telligantur teneri, & adhuc ab uberibus penden- tes parvuli. Conf. quæ ad Matthæum dicta.

Concerning those things which pertain to the Passover of Christ that was to be crucified: regarding the beginning of the journey.

Latin:

Vers. 18. ἐπηρώτησέ τις ἀυτὸν ἄρχων) Quæ huc pertinent ad Matthæum vide.

PARS II. CAPITIS XVIII. Profectio ad Pascha ultimum. SECTIO IV. ACTORUM MINISTERII CHRISTI.

De iis, quæ ad Pascha Christi σταυρώσιμον per- tinent: quod ad itineris ingressum.

## 18:31
Vers. 31. τῷ υἱῷ τῷ ἀνθρώπῳ [to the Son of man]) This is the more frequent reading: but it seems he said τελεσθῆναι ἐν τῷ υἱῷ [to be fulfilled in the Son], for ἐν τῷ υἱῷ. Just as below XXII. 32, δεῖ τελεσθῆναι ἐν ἐμοί [it must be fulfilled in me]. Certainly the Syriac and Latin took it thus. Similar is Rom. III. v. 9, τοῖς ἐν νόμῳ λέγει [he says to those in the law], that is, περὶ τῶν ἐν νόμῳ [concerning those in the law].

Latin:

Vers. 31. τῷ υἱῷ τῷ ἀνθρώπῳ) Hæc frequentior lectio: videtur autem eo sensu dixisse τελεσθῆναι ἐν τῷ υἱῷ, pro ἐν τῷ υἱῷ. Sicut infra XXII. 32. δεῖ τελεσθῆναι ἐν ἐμοί. Ita certe ac- ceperunt Syrus & Latinus. Simile est Rom. III. v. 9. τοῖς ἐν νόμῳ λέγει, id est, περὶ τῶν ἐν νόμῳ.

## 18:32
Vers. 32. ὑβρισθήσεται [he will be treated with insolence]) Tribonian in the Institutes: Contumely, which is said to be from despising, which the Greeks call ὕβριν [insolence].

Latin:

Vers. 32. ὑβρισθήσεται) Tribonianus in Institutionibus: Contumelia quæ à contemnendo dicta est, quam Græci ὕβριν appellant.

## 18:34
V. 34. ὀυδὲν τούτων συνῆκαν [they understood none of these things]) By a certain comprehension, that is. The understanding of the words was easy; but they could not see how they agreed with the prophecies delivered concerning the Messiah and the opinions received on that matter. And so it is credible that they were sometimes brought into doubt whether those things were not being said κατ' ἀλληγορίαν [by way of allegory] of some sort.

Κεκρυμμένον ἀπ' ἀυτῶν [hidden from them]) Thus above, παρακεκαλυμμένον ἀπ' ἀυτῶν [hidden from them], c. IX. 45; ἀπέκρυψας ἀπὸ σοφῶν [you have hidden from the wise], c. X. 21. And below c. XIX. 42, νῦν δὲ ἐκρύβη ἀπὸ ὀφθαλμῶν σου [but now it is hidden from your eyes]. Thus ἀπεκρύβησαν ἀπό σου [they were hidden from you], Psal. LXIX. 6. A Hebrew manner of speaking which exists also in Levit. IV. 13, ch. V. 2, Num. V. 13, Job XXVIII. 21, 1 Kings X. 3, and elsewhere.

Latin:

V. 34. ὀυδὲν τούτων συνῆκαν) Certa scilicet' comprehen- sione. Verborum facilis erat intellectus; sed quomodo ea congruerent cum vaticiniis de Messia proditis receptisq; ea de re opinionibus, videre non poterant. Itaque credibile est interdum in dubitationem adductos an non ista dicerentur κατ' ἀλληγορίαν aliquam.

Κεκρυμμένον ἀπ' ἀυτῶν) Sic supra παρακεκαλυμμένον ἀπ' ἀυτῶν, c. IX. 45. ἀπέκρυψας ἀπὸ σοφῶν c. X. 21. Et infra c. XIX. 42. νῦν δὲ ἐκρύβη ἀπὸ ὀφθαλμῶν σου. Sic ἀπεκρύβησαν ἀπό σου Psal. LXIX. 6. Hebraicum loquendi genus quod ex- stat & Levit. IV. 13. cap. V. 2. Num. V. 13. Job. XXVIII. 21. 1. Reg. X. 3. & alibi.

## 18:35
Vers. 35. ἐγγίζειν [to draw near]) See what [is said] at Matthew.

Latin:

Vers. 35. ἐγγίζειν) Vide quæ ad Matthæum.

## 18:39
Vers. 39. "and those going before") The Syrian interprets this as the crowd that was preceding Jesus: thus Matt. XXI. 9. "and the crowds that went before and that followed," where Mark has "and those going before and following."

Latin:

Vers. 39. καὶ οἱ προάγοντες) Interpretatur Syrus de turba quæ Jesum præcedebat: ita Matth. XXI. 9. οἱ δὲ ὄχλοι οἱ προάγοντες καὶ οἱ ἀκολουθοῦντες, ubi Marcus κὴ οἱ προάγοντες καὶ ἀκολουθοῦντες.
