V. 43. "Praise" (Αἶνον) הודות as can be seen in Ps. VIII. 2 & Ezra III. 12.

Latin:

V. 43. Αἶνον) הודות ut videre est Psal. VIII. 2. & Esd. III. 12.

## 19:1 Argument
CHAPTER XIX. ARGUMENT AND DIVISION.

Zacchaeus, desiring to see Jesus, climbs a mulberry tree, and upon Jesus turning aside to him, is converted. A parable about a nobleman entrusting his talents to ten servants, and then demanding an account of how they have traded. Jesus, entering Jerusalem on a donkey's colt, as a King coming in the name of the Lord, is blessed, and rebukes the Pharisees who criticize this in the disciples: And approaching closer to the city, he laments over it and predicts its devastation: he cast the sellers out of the temple, and teaches there, while the Pharisees plot against him in vain.

There are five parts: I. The conversion of Zacchaeus, to v. 10. II. The parable about the nobleman granting certain talents to his servants, to v. 27. III. The acclamation made to Christ as he approached Jerusalem on a donkey's colt, to v. 40. IV. The prediction of the devastation of the city, to v. 44. V. The cleansing of the temple, to v. 48.

Vers. 1. "He was passing through Jericho" (Διήρχετο τὴν Ἰεριχὼ) It seems to cohere in the sequence of time with the previous history. For Jericho was situated between Galilee and Jerusalem: And the things that follow continue that journey.

Latin:

CAPUT XIX. ARGUMENTUM ET PAR- TITIO.

Zachæus Jesum videre discupiens morum con- scendit, & Jesu ad eum divertente conver- titur. Parabola de nobili, decem servis ta- lenta sua credente, & rationem deinde exi- gente, quomodo negotiati sint. Jesus asinæ pullo Hierosolymam ingrediens, tanquam Rex in nomine Domini veniens, benedictus, idque redarguentes in discipulis Pharisæos increpat: Et propius ad urbem perveniens eam deplorat, ejusq; vastationem prædixit: è templo venditores ejecit, ibiq; docet, ne- quicquam ipsi insidiantibus Pharisæis.

Partes quinque sunt: I. Zacchæi conversio, ad v. 10. II. Parabola de Nobili servis talenta aliquot concedente, ad v. 27. III. Acclamatio Christo asinæ pullo Hierosolymam appropinquanti facta, ad v. 40. IV. Prædictio devastationis urbis, ad v. 44. V. Repurgatio templi, ad v. 48.

Vers. 1. Διήρχετο τὴν Ἰεριχὼ) Videtur temporis nexu co- hærere cum historia superiore. Nam Hierichus sita erat in- ter Galilæam & Hierosolyma: Et quæ sequuntur iter illud continuant.

## 19:3
Vers. 3. "who he is" (τίς ἐςι) He desired to know by sight him who was known by fame.

Latin:

Vers. 3. τίς ἐςι) Fama notum vultu noscere cupiebat.

## 19:4
Vers. 4. "running on before" (προδραμὼν ἔμπροσθεν) A manner of speaking similar to that which is above in c. I. 17, "he shall go before him."

Sycomore tree (Συκομωραίαν) "sycomoron; and some also call this sycaminon," says Dioscorides. And indeed, not in one place where the LXX have "sycaminos" have other Greek interpreters preferred to put "sycomoros." The Syrian has לחתה פכירהא which they translate as wild fig, although all the masters of the Hebrews, as also the Arabs, interpret "tut" as mulberry. The Greek name seems to indicate that this tree is so similar to the mulberry that it resembles a fig to some extent. The Arab here has a peculiar name for the tree, "Giumus," which is how Leo calls this tree in his description of Africa, book IX, and says its fruit is similar in taste to a fig, as it is born not among the leaves, but on the very trunk of the tree: and that it is of great height: from which it appears why Zacchaeus sought a vantage point from it. Celsus on Medicine, book III, c. XVIII: "Of a tree growing in Egypt which they call there morosycon."

"that he might see him" (ἵνα ἴδῃ ἀυτὸν) With an affection of true piety, which Christ saw, who "did not quench the smoking flax." Well says the writer of Wisdom, "wisdom anticipates those who desire to be known beforehand."

Latin:

Vers. 4. προδραμὼν ἔμπροσθεν) Loquendi genus simile ei quod supra c. I. 17. προελεύσεται ἐνώπιον ἀυτῶ.

Συκομωραίαν) συκόμορον· ἔνιοι δὲ κὶ τῦτο συκάμινον λέγυσι inquit Dioscorides. Et sane non uno in loco ubi LXX. ha- bent συκαμίνες alii interpretes Græci maluerunt ponere συ- κομόρες. Syrus לחתה פכירהא quod vertunt ficum syl- vestrem, cum tamen omnes magistri Hebræorum, ut & A- rabs תות morum interpretentur. Nomen Græcum in- dicare videtur ita similem moro esse hanc arborem, ut fi- cum aliquatenus referat. Arabs habet hic peculiare arboris جميز, id est, Giumus, quomodo hanc arborem in Africæ descriptione lib. IX. vocat Leo, ficuiq; similem dicit fructus sapore, ut qui non inter folia, sed in ipso arboris trunco na- scatur: esse autem magnæ proceritatis: unde apparet cur inde despectum quæsierit Zachæus. Celsus de re medica lib. III. c. XVIII. Arboris in Ægypto nascentis quam ibi moro- sycon appellant.

ἵνα ἴδῃ ἀυτὸν) Veræ pietatis affectu, quod Christus vidit qui τὸ λίνον τυφόμενον ἐκ ἔσβεσε. Bene scriptor sapientiæ, σοφία φθάνει τὲς ἐπιθυμῦντας προγνωθῆναι.

## 19:5
Vers. 5. "looking up" (ἀναβλέψας) It is well translated in this place, as also in Matt. XIV. 19, as looking up.

"I must stay in your house" (ἐν τῷ οἴκῳ σε δεῖ με μεῖναι) Christ never invited himself to anyone uncalled, except to him who, out of modesty, did not dare to call him.

Latin:

Vers. 5. ἀναβλέψας) Bene hoc loco, ut & Matth. XIV. 19. vertitur suspiciens.

ἐν τῷ οἴκῳ σε δεῖ με μεῖναι) Nulli unquam condixit Christǫ no vocatus, nisi ei qui præ verecundia vocare non audebat.

## 19:8
V. 8. Standing by) Standing by the one teaching before or after a meal.

if I have defrauded anyone of anything) עשק. See above c. III. 14.

I give) As if he were saying, your precepts move me so much that even now I devote myself to works of both justice and also beneficence, both of which he declares by deeds proposed to himself in his mind. That which follows, today, seems to demand this exposition. The mind of Zacchaeus was already prepared somewhat for repentance: but he had not yet fully absorbed his precepts. This remained for him, being prepared to do what he was taught should be done. And in this way it appeared openly how rightly Christ had chosen this host.

fourfold) In imitation of that which was in the law. For he who had stolen a beast, besides an ox, paid fourfold, Exod. XXII. 1. whence the Attic and furthermore the Roman law seems to have taken its origin: I say in imitation, not from the law itself. For first, the law did not bind except those brought to judgment: for this was as it were a penalty for denial: otherwise if anyone before judgment were led by repentance of the deed, he was absolved of guilt, restoring the simple amount and a fifth of the simple, which seems to have succeeded into the place of the uncertain estimation of the damage following the theft, Num. V. 7. Then, the penalty of the fourfold does not have a place except after the alienation of the stolen thing: otherwise the guilty party paying double was freed, Exod. XXII. 4. We learn from the example what must be done by those who repent of their sins. For first, as far as it can be done, damages brought upon others by force or fraud must be repaired, which nature itself dictates, for he does not cease to sin who retains what belongs to another. It is against nature, say the Jurisconsults, for someone to be enriched by another's injury. Furthermore, however, if not necessary, it is nevertheless very useful that he who has sinned, assuming the person of a judge over himself, should himself indicate something for himself in the name of a penalty: by which he may testify how much his sin displeases him: if we judged ourselves, we would not be judged, says Paul 1 Cor. XI. 31. This is among those things about which no defined law exists, but which the Spirit, more powerful than any law, dictates.

To him) Not addressing him, but speaking about him. Such is that which was noted by others, Rom. X. v. 21. and he says to Israel. And in Psalm III. 3. many say to my soul there is no salvation for him in his God. And below XX. 41. he said to them, as we shall say there.

Latin:

V. 8. Σταθεὶς δὲ) Adstans docenti ante vel post prandium.

εἴ τινός τι ἐσυκοφάντησα) עשק. Vide supra c. III. 14.

Δίδωμι) Quasi dicat, ita me movent tua præcepta, ut jam nunc me dedam operibus tum justitiæ, tum etiam be- neficentiæ, quorum utrumq; factis in animo sibi propositis declarat. Hanc expositionem exigere videtur id quod se- quitur σήμερον. Erat jam ante præparatus aliquantum ad pœnitentiam animus Zachæi: sed nondum ejus præcepta plene hauserat. Hoc illi restabat, parato facere quod facien- dum doceretur. Atque hoc modo palam apparuit, quam recte hunc hospitem Christus legisset.

τετραπλᾶν) Imitatione ejus quod erat in lege. Nam qui pecudem, extra bovem, surripuisset, pendebat quadru- plum, Exod. XXII. 1. unde originem sumsisse videtur lex At- tica & porro Romana: imitatione dico, non ex lege ipsa. Nam primum lex non obstringebat nisi in judicium addu- ctos: erat enim hæc velut pœna inficiationis: alioqui si quis ante judicium facti pœnitudine duceretur, is culpa ab- solvebatur, restituens simplum & quintam simpli, quæ vi- detur successisse in locum incertæ æstimationis damni fur- tum consequentis, Num. V. 7. Deinde pœna quadrupli lo- cum non habet nisi post alienationem rei surreptæ: alioqui reus duplum solvens liberabatur, Exod. XXII. 4. Discimus ab exemplo quid faciendum sit iis, quos peccatorum pœni- tet. Primum enim quatenus fieri potest, resarcienda sunt damna aliis per vim aut dolum illata, quod ipsa natura di- ctat, neq; enim peccare desistit qui alienum retinet. Contra naturam est, inquiunt Jurisconsulti, locupletari aliquem cum aliena injuria. Præterea vero, si non necessarium, ad- modum tamen utile est, ut qui peccavit judicis in se perso- nam assumens ipse sibi aliquid indicat pœnæ nomine: quo testetur quantopere sibi peccatum displiceat: εἰ ἑαυτὸς διε- κρίνομεν ἐκ ἂν ἐκρινόμεθα, inquit Paulus 1. Cor. XI. 31. Hoc inter illa est de quibus nulla exstat lex definita, sed quæ po- tentior omni lege Spiritus dictat.

Πρὸς ἀυτὸν) Non illum alloquens, sed de illo loquens. Tale est illud ab aliis annotatum, RomX. v. 21. πρὸς δὲ τὸν Ἰσραὴλ λέγει. Et Psalmo III. 3. πολλοὶ λέγουσι τῇ ψυχῇ μ̄ ὀυκ ἔςι σωτηρία ἀυτῷ ἐν τῷ Θεῷ ἀυτῦ. Et infra XX. 41. εἶπε δὲ πρὸς ἀυτὲς, ut ibi dicemus.

## 19:9
V. 9. to this house) Synecdoche. For house is said for the head of the household: thus above c. X. 5. into whatever house you enter, first say, peace to this house, and if the son of peace is there, your peace shall rest upon him. But Christ seems to have named the house so that he might show the thanks for the hospitality returned. For Christ had said to Zacchaeus, I must stay in your house. Wherefore those things which are accustomed to be brought to this passage concerning the benefits of God to the family of a pious head of a household, although they are true when rightly accepted, nevertheless I do not think they pertain here.

There is no need for Synecdoche, so that we may establish that house is put for the head of the household. And since Grotius acknowledges that the benefits of God sometimes redound even to the family itself of a pious head of a household, why does he reject this sense which the words by themselves render, and fashion a Synecdoche?

forasmuch as he also is a son of Abraham) I cannot approve the opinion of those who think that Zacchaeus was a foreigner, against whom the name itself provides testimony: for it is purely Hebrew, as appears in Ezra II. 9 and VII. 14. Furthermore, those who grumbled do not reproach Christ because he feasts at the house of an uncircumcised man, but because he feasts at the house of a sinner, that is, a Jew indeed, but one living lawlessly. Nor should it move us that he is said to have been a chief tax collector, whom the Hebrews call ריש גבאי. For it was not forbidden for Jews to hold public contracts, especially if any of them had been gifted with Roman citizenship: of which sort it is credible there were quite a few. Josephus, book II of the Jewish War, also teaches us that certain Jews in Judea were Roman knights; for what no one before that time, Florus, dared to do, to scourge men of the equestrian order before the tribunal and to nail them to a cross, of whom even if the race was Jewish, yet at least the rank was Roman. Now taxes were accustomed to be contracted by knights. Finally, that very thing which we had concerning the fourfold [restitution] looks back to Moses, as we have said. The sense, therefore, of these words seems to me to be this: This man, although hitherto because of an impure life unworthy to be called a descendant of Abraham, has now through repentance recovered the right of his former dignity, as if restored to his birthright before God, and therefore is to be reckoned no less a descendant of Abraham in the future than one who is so by the best right, according to that saying, Let there be the same right for the healthy as for the strong. See Ezek. XVIII. Rufinus on the Creed: If the mind in me which has been affected by crime, and in which was the origin of vice, is corrected, why should I not seem to you able to be made innocent, who had previously been a criminal? And thus that which follows will fit together excellently: for the Son of man came to seek and to save that which was lost, that is, the lost sheep of the house of Israel, as it is in Matt. X. 9. It must be held meanwhile, as we also said above, that in those sinners who were equated with foreigners, there was the image of foreigners. Luke alone of these writers uses the word καθότι for ὅτι, and not only here, but also above in ch. I. 7 and Acts II. 24. Elsewhere it is put for καθ' ὅσον, as in Acts II. 4 and ch. IV. 35.

PART II. The Parable of the Nobleman entrusting talents to his servants.

Latin:

V. 9. τῷ οἴκῳ τ́υτῳ) Synecdoche. Domus enim pro pa- trefamilias dicitur: ita supra c. X. 5. εἰς ἣν δ᾽ ἂν οἰκίαν ἐισέρ- χησθε, πρῶτον λέγετε, ἐιρήνη τῷ οἴκῳ τ́υτῳ, καὶ ἐὰν μὲν ᾖ ἐκεῖ ὁ ὑὸς ειρήνης, ἐπαναπαύσεται ἐπ᾿ ἀυτὸν ἐιρήνη ὑμων. Domum autem ideo nominasse videtur Christus, ut ostendat rela- tam hospitii gratiam. Dixerat enim Zachæo Christus, ἐν τῷ οἴκῳ σε δεῖ με μεῖναι. Quare quæ ad hunc locum afferri solent de beneficiis Dei in familiam pii patrisfamilias, quanquam vera sunt recte accepta, tamen huc pertinere non arbitror.

Nulla opus Synecdoche, ut statuamus domum pro patrefamilias poni. Et quum agnoscat Grotius, in familiam etiam ipsam pii patrisfamilias redunda- re nonnunquam Dei beneficia, cur hunc sensum quem verba per se reddunt, reprobat & Synec- dochen fingit?

καθότι καὶ αὐτὸς ὑὸς Ἀβραάμ ἐστι) Probare eorum senten- tiam non possum qui Zachæum putant fuisse ἀλλόφυλον, contra quos ipsum nomen testimonium præbet: est enim pure Hebræum, ut apparet Esdræ II. 9. & VII. 14. Deinde non reprehendunt Christum οἱ διαγογγύζοντες, quod apud in circumcisum epuletur: sed quod apud ἁμαρτωλὸν, id est, Judæum quidem, sed viventem ἀνόμως. Nec movere nos debet quod ἀρχιτελώνης fuisse dicitur, quem Hebræi vo- cant ריש גבאי. Nam Judæis non interdicebatur publica conducere, præsertim si qui eorum erant donati Romana civitate: quales aliquammultos fuisse credibile est. Joseph. lib. de bell. Jud. II. etiam Judæos quosdam in Judæa equi- tes Romanos fuisse nos docet; ὃ γὰρ μηδεὶς πρότερον τότε Φλῶ- ρος ἐτόλμησεν, ἄνδρας ἱππικοῦ τάγματος μαστιγῶσαι πρὸ τοῦ βήματος, καὶ σταυρῷ προσηλῶσαι ὧν εἰ καὶ τὸ γένος Ἰουδαῖων, ἀλλὰ γοῦν τὸ ἀξίωμα ῥωμαικὸν ἦν. Ab equitibus autem con- duci vectigalia solebant. Denique illud ipsum, quod de qua- druplo habuimus, ad Mosem respicit, ut diximus. Sensus ergo horum verborum hic mihi esse videtur: Homo iste, quamvis antehac ob vitam impuram indignus qui Abraha- mi nepos diceretur, jam per pœnitentiam jus dignitatis pri- stinæ recuperavit, natalibus quasi redditus apud Deum, ac proinde non minus nepos Abrahami censendus in posteru quam qui optimo jure, secundum illud dictum, Sanatibus idem jus quod fortibus esto. Vide Ezech. XVIII. Ruffinus ad symbolum: Si animus in me qui criminosus affectus est, & in quo origo fuit vitii, corrigatur, cur tibi non videar posse inno- cens effici, qui prius fueram criminosus? Atque ita optime cohærebit quod sequitur: ἦλθε γὰρ ὁ ὑὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ζητῆσαι καὶ σῶσαι τὸ ἀπολωλὸς, id est, τὰ πρόβατα ἀπολωλότα οἴκου Ἰσ- ραὴλ, ut est apud Matth. X. 9. Tenendum interim, quod supra quoque diximus, in illis peccatoribus, qui extraneis æquabantur extraneorum fuisse imaginem. Vocem καθότι pro ὅτι solus horum scriptorum Lucas usurpat, nec hic tan- tum, sed & supr. c. I. 7. Act. II, 24. Alibi pro καθ' ὅσον poni- tur, ut Act. II. 4. c. IV. 35.

## 19:11
Ver. 11. And as they heard these things) This, of course, which Jesus had said last, that he had come to bring salvation to the descendants of Abraham: whence the Apostles conceived the hope that it would come to pass that Christ, on this journey toward Jerusalem, would enter into the possession of a kingdom both glorious for themselves and salutary for the people. But Christ, rightly indicating future events as is his custom, signifies that the kingdom is indeed owed to him, and not only over the Jews but also over other nations, which had been predicted concerning the Messiah, but that before the full happiness of his kingdom many labors must be undergone by them: and especially that there would be great stubbornness of the Jews against this kingdom.

the kingdom of God to appear) which is also called the kingdom of Israel in Acts I. 6, and elsewhere the redemption for Israel. They were expecting this as imminent from David and other Prophets.

II. ἀκουόντων δὲ αὐτῶν ταῦτα) Hoc nimirum, quod postremum Jesus dixerat, venisse se ut salutem afferret Ab- rahami posteris: unde spem concipiebant Apostoli, futu- rum ut Christus hoc itinere Hierosolyma versus, iniret pos- sessionem regni tum sibi gloriosam, tum populo salutarem. At Christus futura ut solet recte indicans significat regnum quidem sibi deberi, nec in Judæos tantum, sed & in gentes alias, quod de Messia erat prædictum, sed ante plenam ejus regni felicitatem multos labores ipsis subeundos: præcipue vero Judæorum magnam fore adversus hoc regnum con- tumaciam.

## 19:26
Vers. 26.

λέγω γὰρ ὑμῖν) I do not think the Greek codices which the Syrian and Arab used had it otherwise, but for the sake of completing the sense they added 'he said to them,' that is, that king: clearly just as the LXX in a similar place, 2 Kings X. 15, added 'to him.' Moreover, Greeks and Latins are accustomed, when words are exchanged back and forth, to sometimes suppress the names of the persons, which can be sufficiently understood from the utterance itself. But it must also be added that γὰρ in this place is the explanatory particle of what is passed over in silence, such as are often found elsewhere. For it is just as if the Lord were saying: although he has ten minas, nevertheless it must be added to him. For it is just that to him who has and uses, more should be given. Regarding the matter, see Matthew in more than one place.

Latin:

Vers. 26.

λέγω γὰρ ὑμῖν) Non puto aliter habuisse Græcos codices quibus usi Syrus & Arabs, sed supplendi sensus causa addi- derunt ea dixit illis, rex ille scil. : plane sicut LXX. in simili loco 2. Reg. X. 15. addiderunt πρὸς τὸν τὸν οὐ. Solent autem Græ- ci quoque & Latini, ubi verba ultro citroque mutantur per- sonarum nomina interdum subticere, quæ ex ipsa pronun- ciatione satis intelligi possunt. Sed & illud addendum, γὰρ hoc loco esse αἰτιολογικὸν τοῦ σιωπωμένου qualia alibi sæpe. Perinde enim est quasi dicat Dominus: quamvis ille de- cem minas habeat; tamen illi addendum est. Nam id æquum est ut habenti & utenti amplius detur. De re vide Matthæum non uno loco.

Vers. 29.

ὡς ἤγγισεν εἰς Βηθφαγὴ καὶ Βηθανίαν) That is, when he was around those places. For he had passed Bethany. See what was said at Matt. XX. 30. & XXII. Indeed, Petitus observes that there are two Bethanys, of which one, the home of Mary, Martha, and Lazarus, was fifteen stadia from the city: the other, however, situated at the Mount of Olives, was seven stadia away. The day before, he says, the βαιοφορία was the Bethany of Lazarus, John XII. 1. 12. But on this very day of the βαιοφορία he approached Bethphage and Bethany, at the Mount of Olives, Mark XI. 1. Luke XIX. 29. By Bethphage here, however, Petitus understands not a small village, but the field of Jerusalem, in which was Bethany, which is thus distinguished from the other home of Lazarus. Let those things which we said at Matthew be compared here.

Sane Petitus observat duas esse Bethanias, qua- rum una Mariæ, Marthæ, atque Lazari patria di- stabat ab urbe quindecim stadiis: altera vero ad montem Oliveti sita, aberat stadia septem. Pri- die, inquit, βαιοφορίας erat Bethania Lazari, Job. XII. 1. 12. Hoc ipso vero τ̄ βαιοφορίας die as- cessit ad Bethphage & Bethaniam, ad montem Oli- veti, Marc. XI. 1. Luc. XIX. 29. Per Bethphagen vero hic intelligit Petitus non villulam, sed agrum Hierosolymitanum, in quo erat Bethania, quæ ita distinguatur ab altera Lazari patria. Conferantur autem hic ea, quæ ad Matthæum diximus.

## 19:41
v. 41. Ἔκλαυσεν ἐπ' αὐτῇ) The Latin, Syriac, and Arabic versions acknowledge this clause. But Epiphanius testifies that in his time it did not exist in the publicly received copies. His words ἐν ἀγ- νοητῷ are worthy of being noted, if only so that we may see how much the leaders of the Churches permitted themselves. Ὥστε καὶ

“ἔκλαυσε” (he wept) is found in the Gospel according to Luke in the uncorrected manuscripts (this is what he calls copies that had not undergone a critical hand), and the holy Irenaeus uses the testimony in his work Against Heresies against those who say that Christ appeared only in appearance. I do not find this passage in the disputation which Epiphanius mentions, where Irenaeus gathers those passages which the Gnostics abused, not word for word, but with the sense expressed: “For,” he says, “if he wept over Jerusalem, and said, ‘If you had known, even you, today the things that make for peace! But they are hidden from your eyes.’” Since, however, he does not raise a controversy with the Gnostics about the words, but about the interpretation of the words, it is clear that at that time there was no doubt about this reading. Rash and delicate men, to whom it seemed unworthy for Christ to weep, changed it; but they achieved little with this remarkable audacity, since in John there exists “Jesus wept” (ἐδάκρυσεν ὁ ἰησοῦς). The cause of the evil is certain preconceived opinions from the tenets of human wisdom. It was a Stoic maxim: “The wise man pities no one,” for that sect removes the affections from human nature. The Peripatetics thought, a little more wisely, that the affections should be moderated, and that whatever is excessive is a vice. But if it pleases us to listen to the matter itself and the divine will revealed in the Holy Scriptures, we will find that the opinion of the Stoics is to be rejected entirely, but that of the Peripatetics is to be corrected somewhat. For, as Lactantius shows clearly enough in the sixth book of his Divine Institutes, the affections are not to be rooted out, as the Stoics say—for that is to do violence to nature and to drag man into an immovable stupor of mind—nor are they always to be tempered, but directed into the true path. For there is a time when even a moment of joy is vicious; there is a time when even to exult with joy is most criminal. Therefore, those commotions must be assigned to their own matters, their own times, and their own places. Regarding those things which pertain to the honor of God or the eternal salvation of one's neighbor, one cannot rejoice too much, nor is there ever too much grief that arises from the contrary. He who wanders from the path, even if he walks gently, will strike against crags or precipices; he who keeps to the path, even if he has gone more quickly, will not stumble. This, explained by many examples, can be seen in Lactantius. Nor was he the first to initiate this method of philosophizing; for Tertullian also says similar things in his book On the Soul: “Furthermore, when Plato, segregating the rational part to God alone, subdivides two kinds from the irrational, the indignant, which they call θυμικὸν, and the concupiscent, which they call ἐπιθυμητικὸν, so that indeed the former is common to us and to lions, but the latter to flies, and the rational, moreover, to God: I see that I must also retract regarding this, because of those things which are found in Christ.” For behold, this whole trinity is also in the Lord: both the rational, by which he teaches what he discusses, by which he paves the ways of salvation: and the indignant, by which he inveighs against the Scribes and Pharisees: and the concupiscent, by which he desires to eat the Passover with his disciples. Therefore, in our view, the indignant and the concupiscent are not always to be judged as irrational, which we are certain ran their course reasonably in the Lord. Shortly after: “The Apostle also grants us concupiscence: ‘If anyone desires (concupiscit) the office of a bishop, he desires a good work,’ but by saying ‘a good work,’ he shows it is a rational concupiscence.” He also concedes indignation: why not, since he himself took it up? “I wish,” he says, “that they would even cut themselves off who unsettle you.” Indignation is rational when it arises from the affection of discipline. And what follows. In all of which, however, if one attends rightly, he seems to depart from Plato more in word than in the thing itself. For he takes ἄλογον in an opposite sense, whereas Plato takes it negatively, to indicate that power of the soul which does not use reason by itself, but can either obey or rebel against the rational part. Someone might perhaps think that the great philosopher in Christianity, Clement of Alexandria, felt differently about the affections, whose words in Stromata II are these: “Those who speak simply in the discourse of our philosophy say that all the passions are excrescences of the soul, of the soft and yielding part, as it were, imprints of the spiritual powers against which we have our struggle.” But the matter itself shows that by πάθη in that place he does not mean just any affections, but the diseases of the affections: just as many of the Greeks use that word, which has also been noted by Jerome. That passage of Tertullian, which clearly agrees with that of Clement, pertains to the same thing: “The irrational, however, is to be understood later, as that which happened from the instinct of the serpent, that very admission of transgression, and from then on it grew and hardened in the soul like a natural state; because the whole thing happened at the beginning of nature.” But if the affection itself, or even an abundance of affections occupied with honest things, has nothing of vice, certainly neither do the signs of those affections, among which is weeping. Well does Laelius say in Cicero: “For those are not to be listened to who want virtue to be hard and, as it were, iron-like: which is indeed, both in many things and in friendship, tender and tractable, so that friends are, as it were, expanded by good things and contracted by inconveniences.”

Latin:

v. 41. Ἔκλαυσεν ἐπ' αὐτῇ) Agnoscunt hoc comma Latinus, Syrus, Arabs. At Epiphanius testatur suo tempore non ex- stitisse in publice receptis exemplaribus. Verba ejus ἐν ἀγ- νοητῷ digna sunt quæ notentur, vel ob hoc ut videamus quantum sibi Ecclesiarum præpositi permiserint. Ὥστε καὶ

ἔκλαυσε κεῖται ἐν τῷ κατὰ Λυκᾶν ἐυαγγελίῳ ἐν τοῖς ἀδιορθώτοις ἀντιγράφοις (ita vocat exemplaria quæ manum criticam passa non erant) κᾀ κέχρηται τῇ μαρτυρίᾳ ὁ ἅγιος ἐιρηναῖος ἐν τῷ κατὰ ἀιρέσεων πρὸς τὰς δοκήσει τὸν χριστὸν πεφηνέναι λέγον- τας. Locum hunc in ea quam Epiphanius dicit disputatione non invenio, ubi congerit Irenæus ea loca, quibus Gnostici abutebantur, non verbotenus, sed sensu expresso: ἴτι, in- quit, ἐι τῷ προεχόντα ἀυτὸν τῇ ἰερουσαλὴμ δακρύσαι ἐπ' ἀυτὴν κᾀ ἐιπεῖν, ἐἰ ἔγνως κᾀ σὺ σήμερον τὰ πρὸς ἐιρήνην· ἐκρύβη δὲ ἀπὸ σου. Cum tamen non de verbis, sed de verborum interpretatio- ne Gnosticis controversiam moveat, apertum est eo tem- pore de hac lectione non dubitatum. Mutarunt homines temerarii & delicati quibus flere Christo indignum videba- tur: at parum profecerunt hac insigni audacia, cum apud Johannem exitet ἐδάκρυσεν ὁ ἰησοῦς. Causa mali præconce- ptæ quædam opiniones ex humanæ sapientiæ scitis. Stoi- corum erat illud: Sapiens neminis miseretur: tollit enim ea secta affectus de humana natura. Peripatetici paulo sa- pientius moderandos affectus censebant, & in vitio esse quicquid nimium est. At si rem ipsam & divinam volunta- tem in sacris literis revelatam libet audire, inveniemus Stoicorum quidem sententiam plane rejiciendam: Peripa- teticorum autem corrigendam nonnihil. Nam, ut Lactan- tius libro institutionum sexto perspicue satis ostendit, affe- ctus neque evellendi sunt cum Stoicis: id enim est vim in- ferre naturæ, & hominem ad immobilem mentis stuporem pertrahere: neque semper temperandi, sed in veram viam dirigendi. Est enim ubi vel punctum gaudere vitiosum sit; est ubi vel exsultare lætitia maxime criminosum. Quare assignandæ commotiones illæ suis rebus, suis temporibus, suis locis. Ob ea quæ ad honorem Dei, vel æternam pro- ximi salutem pertinent, non potest nimium gauderi, neque nimius unquam dolor est qui ex contrariis nascitur. Qui via aberrat licet leniter eat, in confragosa aut præcipitia impinget; qui viam tenet licet concitatius iverit, non offen- det. Quæ multis exemplis explicata apud Lactantium vi- dere est. Neque ille primus hanc philosophandi rationem iniit: Nam & Tertullianus libro de anima similia dicit: Proinde cum Plato soli Deo segregans rationale, duo genera sub- dividit ex irrationali, indignativum quod appellant θυμικὸν, & concupiscentivum quod vocant ἐπιθυμητικὸν, ut quidem illud commune sit nobis & leonibus, istud vero cum muscis, rationale porro cum Deo: video & de hoc mihi esse retractan- dum, propter ea quæ in Christo deprehenduntur. Ecce enim tota hæc trinitas & in Domino: & rationale, quo docet quæ disserit, quo salutis vias sternit: & indignativum quo invehi- tur in Scribas & Pharisæos: & concupiscentivum, quo Pascha cum discipulis suis edere concupiscit Igitur apud nos non semper ex irrationali censenda sunt indignativum & concupiscenti- vum, quæ certi sumus in Domino rationabiliter decucurrisse. Mox: Dat & Apostolus nobis concupiscentiam, si quis Epi- scopatum concupiscit, bonum opus concupiscit, sed bonum opus dicens rationalem concupiscentiam ostendit. Concedit & indignationem: quidni, quam & ipse suscepit. Vtinam & præcidantur, inquit, qui vos subvertunt. Rationalis est indignatio quæ ex affectu disciplinæ est. Et quæ sequuntur. In quibus tamen omnibus, si quis recte attendat, verbo magis à Platone videtur abire quam re ipsa. Nam ipse ἄλο- γον sumit ἐναντίως, cum Plato sumat ἀποφατικῶς, ad indi- candam eam vim animi, quæ non per se ratione utitur, sed rationali parti aut obtemperare poteit, aut rebellare. Putet forte aliquis aliter de affectibus sensisse magnum in Chri- stianismo Philosophum Clementem Alexandrinum, cujus hæc sunt verba Stromation II. ὁ μὲν ἐν ἁπλῶς λόγῳ τῆς καθ' ἡμᾶς φιλοσοφίας τὰ πάθη πάnta διαπερισώματα τῆς ψυχῆς φασὶν εἶναι τῆς μαλθακᾶς κᾀ εἰκούσης οἱον ἐναποσφραγίσματα τῶν πνευματικῶν δυνάμεων πρὸς ἃς ἡ πάλη ἡμῖν. Sed res ipsa ostendit πάθη eo loco ab ipso dici non affectus quos- vis, sed affectuum morbos: quomodo multi Græcorum utuntur ea voce, quod & Hieronymo est notatum. Eo- dem pertinet & ille Tertulliani locus plane Clementino illi consentiens: Irrationale autem posterius intelligendum est, ut quod acciderit ex serpentis instinctu ipsum illud transgres- sionis admissum, atque exinde inoleverit & conoleverit in ani- ma adinstar jam naturalitatis; quia totum in naturæ primor- dio accidit. Quod si affectus per se aut etiam affectuum übertas honestis in rebus occupata nihil habet vitii, certe nec eorum affectuum signa in quibus est fletus. Bene apud Ciceronem Lælius: Neq; enim sunt isti audiendi qui virtu- tem duram & quasi ferream esse volunt: quæ quidem est cum in multis rebus tum in amicitia tenera atq; tractabilis, ut & bonis amici quasi diffundantur & incommodis contrahantur.

ἐἰ ἔγνως) ἐἰ here is “would that,” as we said above in chapter XII, 49.

where we showed that even with the indicative and the particle ἂν it is used in that sense. κἀγὼ σὺ) Even you, that city above all the cities of the earth beloved by God, the city of David, the royal city, the city dedicated as sacred. καίγε ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ σε ταύτῃ) If not until now, at least now when that day has shone forth, of which it was said: “Tell the daughter of Zion,” Zech. I would only like to be observed here that Grotius acknowledges that Zech. IX. 9 and Isa. LX. 1 are to be taken literally concerning Christ: which is to be noted against him, as he perverts those sayings in their proper place. Compare our annotations on those Prophetic passages. τὰ πρὸς εἰρήνην σε) “I wish,” he says, “you would consider as you ought (for that is ἔγνως) the things that pertain to your safety.” The Son imitates the paternal speech, Deut. XXXII. 29. νῦν δὲ ἐκρύβη ἀπὸ ὀφθαλμῶν σε) With inexcusable ignorance, because you fastidiously reject the light offered, nay, forced upon you. ## 19:47
καθ' ἡμέραν) The same kind of speaking [as in] Matt. XXVI. 25 and above XL. 13 and chapter XVI. 19, from which it sufficiently appears that it is not placed for 'by day,' but for 'daily,' just as the ancient interpreters also understood it. οἱ πρῶτοι τῇ λαῦ) Who elsewhere [are called] οἱ ἄρχοντες, and in the following chapter πρεσβύτεροι, that is, the senators of the great Sanhedrin, as the Syrian also understood it: for the Priests are named particularly because of the excellence of their dignity, the lawyers because of the fame of their learning, as we have also observed elsewhere. But those are called πρεσβύτεροι τῶ λαῦ who were also other πρεσβύτεροι τῶν πόλεων, decurions or councilors. But enough has been said about these elsewhere.

Latin:

καθ' ἡμέραν) Idem loquendi genus Matth. XXVI. 25. & supra XL. 13. & cap. XVI. 19. unde satis apparet non esse positum pro interdiu, sed pro quotidie, quomodo & vete- res interpretes acceperunt. οἱ πρῶτοι τῇ λαῦ) Qui alibi οἱ ἄρχοντες, & capite sequenti πρεσβύτεροι, id est Synedrii magni senatores, ut & Syrus ac- cepit: nam Sacerdotes ob dignitatis excellentiam, legispe- riti ob famam eruditionis peculiariter nominantur, ut & alibi observavimus. πρεσβύτεροι autem τῶ λαῦ dicuntur, qui erant & alii πρεσβύτεροι τῶν πόλεων, decuriones sive βυλευταί. Sed de his alibi satis actum.

## 20:1 Argument
CHAPTER XX. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

Those questioning Jesus as he was teaching in the temple, by what authority he does so, are dispatched through an ἀντερώτησιν [counter-question] concerning the Baptism of John. The parable of the vineyard leased out, the servants beaten, the Son of the Lord himself slaughtered, and the killers slain, with the addition of the prophecy of Psalm (CXVIII.) concerning the rejected stone. The priests and Pharisees strive to lay hands on Christ, they send out spies asking about the tribute to be rendered to Caesar. The Sadducees tempt him concerning the wife of the seven brothers, and are convinced of the resurrection of the dead. The lawyers are confounded by the question concerning Christ as David's son and Lord; the hearers are warned to beware of them.

There are five parts: I. The question concerning the authority of Christ teaching in the temple, to v. 8. II. The parable of the leasing of the vineyard, to v. 18. III. The solution of the question concerning the tribute, to v. 26. IV. The dispatching of the doubt concerning the resurrection of the dead, to v. 38. V. The question proposed to the lawyers concerning the Messiah, and their ambition and avarice, to the final v. 47.

PART I. The question concerning the authority of Christ teaching in the temple.

Vers. 1.

Ἐπέστησαν] They appeared. See at the last chapter of Matthew. The Vulgate and Erasmus agreed. Beza and Ludov. de Dieu, they came upon. The Arab, they stood by. The Syrian, they rose up against him: just as ἐφίστημι is sometimes, I press, I urge, I attack, Acts XVII. 5. See Lud. de Dieu.

Latin:

CAPUT XX. ARGUMENTUM ET PAR- TITIO.

Iesum in templo docentem, qua potestate id faciat interrogantes, per ἀντερώτησιν de Baptismo Iohannis expediuntur. Parabo- la de vinea elocata, servis fustigatis, fi- lio ipso Domini trucidato, & interfecto- ribus occisis, addito Psalmi (CXVIII.) va- ticinio de lapide reprobato. Sacerdotes, & Pharisæi manum Christo injicere sata- gunt, exploratores emittunt de censu Cæ- sari reddendo quærentes. Sadducæi ten- tant ipsum de uxore septem fratrum, & convincuntur de resurrectione mortuo- rum. Legisperiti quæstione de Christo Da- vidis & filio, & Domino confunduntur; illos ut caveant monentur auditores.

Partes quinque sunt: I. Quæstio de potestate Christi docendi in templo, ad v. 8. II. Parabola de vineæ elocatione, ad v. 18. III. Solutio quæ- stionis de censu, ad v. 26. IV. Expeditio dubii de resurrectione mortuorum, ad v. 38. V. Legis- peritis proposita de Messia quæstio, eorumq; am- bitio & avaritia, ad v. 47. finalem.

PARS I. Quæstio de potestate Christi docendi in templo.

Ἐπέστησαν] Apparuerunt. Vide ad Matthæi caput ult. Vulgatus & Erasmus convenerunt. Beza & Lu- dov. de Dieu, supervenerunt. Arabs adstiterunt. Syrus surrexerunt adversus eum: quemadmodum ἐφίστημι interdum est, insto, urgeo, adorior, Actor. XVII. 5. Vid. Lud. de Dieu.

Plutarch on Caesar at the Rubicon: συλλογιζόμενος τὸ μέγεθος τῶν τολμωμένων, that is, revolving in his mind the magnitude of the undertaking.

Plutarchus de Cæsare ad Rubiconem: συλλογιζό- μενος τὸ μέγεθος τῶν τολμωμένων, id est, animo revolvens cœpti magnitudinem.

## 20:19
Vers. 19.

ἔγνωσαν γὰρ] It coheres very well with what precedes. They wanted to kill him because they feared the multitude of the crowd following him. They feared, however, because they understood well enough that they were marked by Christ. See what [is written] at Matthew XI. 18.

The fear of the people was not the cause of the plan to kill Christ, but an impediment, by which they were prevented from laying hands on him themselves: whence they attempt the matter through tunnels and frauds, so that they might confound him before the people, or render him suspect. πρὸς αὐτοὺς] concerning them: as also Acts XXVIII. 25. Thus the Hebrew l. 5, τὸν εἰπε, is also referred to that [passage], 'I will be to him a father'.

Latin:

Vers. 19.

ἔγνωσαν γὰρ] Optime cohæret superioribus. Volebant eum occidere, quia metuebant multitudinem turbæ ipsum sectantis. Metuebant autem ideo, quia se notatos à Chri- sto satis intelligebant. Vide quæ ad Matth. XI. 18.

Populi metus non fuit caussa consilii de Christo interficiendo, sed impedimentum, quo minus ipfi manum injicerent: unde per cuniculos & frau- des rem tentant, ut coram populo ipsum confun- dant, vel suspectum reddant. πρὸς αὐτοὺς] de ipsis: ut & A&t. XXVIII. 25. Sic Hebr. l. 5. τὸν εἰπε refertur etiam ad illud ἐγὼ ἴσομαι αὐτῷ εἰς πατέρα.

## 20:20
Vers. 20.

παρατηρήσαντες] This word is taken absolutely, as also above in c. XIV. 1; however, one must understand there what had been done; here, what he might say: for they sent their explorers to observe that. ἐγκαθέτους] Liers-in-wait: such as those who καθῆνται ἐν ἕδραις ἐνεδρεύοντες. It corresponds to the Hebrew ארבים & אחלים. Salmasius acknowledges that the LXX interpreters in Job XIX. 12, c. XXXI. 9, use this term for crafty men and ambushers who secretly creep up to explore, listen, and test something by which they might do harm: but he denies that this usage of the word is Hellenistic, and wishes it to occur equally among the Greeks. Which, however, he did not prove with suitable passages. δικαίους εἶναι] δικαιοσύνη is taken here in that general sense, so that it comprehends all kinds of duties, in which sense it is often joined with the word ἅγιος. Elsewhere, δικαιοσύνη, φόβος μετὰ τὸν Θεόν. Those of whom it is treated here pretended to be, as the saying goes, of tender conscience, who therefore desired to be fully taught concerning all questions pertaining to conscience. ἵνα ἐπιλάβωνται αὐτᾶ λόγου] Because it is rare that anyone is so prudent that his words cannot sometimes receive a sinister interpretation. ἐπιλαμβάνεσθαι λόγου is said, as below ἐπιλαμβάνεσθαι ῥήματος. Plato similarly, ὑπολάβεστο προφάσεως. τῇ ἀρχῇ τῇ ἐξουσίᾳ τῦ ἡγεμόνος] When controversies about sacred matters do not suffice to oppress the innocent, certain things pertaining to the state are wont to be seized upon.

Latin:

Vers. 20.

παρατηρήσαντες] Absolute sumitur hæc vox, ut supra quoque c. XIV. 1. subintelligendum autem ibi, quid factum esset; hic, quid diceret: nam ut id observarent submitte- bant suos exploratores. ἐγκαθέτους] Subsessores: quales illi qui καθῆνται ἐν ἕδραις ἐνεδρεύοντες. Respondet Hebræo ארבים & אחלים. Subdolos & insidiatores, qui clam subrepunt ad explorandum, auscultandum & tentandum aliquid quo noceant, ita dici à LXX. Interpretibus Job. XIX. 12. c. XXXI. 9. agnoscit Salmasius: negat au- tem usum hunc vocis Hellenisticum esse, vult apud Græcos eundem pariter occurrere. Quod tamen locis idoneis non probavit. δικαίους εἶναι] δικαιοσύνη hic generali illo significatu su- mitur, ita ut omnia officiorum genera comprehendat, quo sensu sæpe jungitur cum voce ἅγιος. Alibi δικαιοσύνη, φόβος μετὰ τὸν Θεόν. Simulabant illi de quibus hic agitur esse se, ut dici solet, teneræ conscientiæ, qui proinde de quæstio- nibus omnibus ad conscientiam pertinentibus plene cupe- rent doceri. ἵνα ἐπιλάβωνται αὐτᾶ λόγου] Quia vix est ut quisquam tam prudens sit, cujus non verba possint interdum accipere sinistram interpretationem. ἐπιλαμβάνεσθαι λόγου dictum, ut infra ἐπιλαμβάνεσθαι ῥήματος. Plato similiter ὑπολάβεστο προφάσεως. τῇ ἀρχῇ τῇ ἐξουσίᾳ τῦ ἡγεμόνος] Cum de sacris con- troversiæ ad opprimendos innocentes non sufficiunt, solent quædam captari ad rempublicam pertinentia.

## 20:22
Vers. 22.

φόρον] The Syrian well translates כסף רישא as poll tax: nor does it seem to me that Luke here has departed from the propriety of the word. For that which is paid for merchandise is properly called τέλος, that which is for lands and heads is φόρος, as the Greek grammarians and Strabo teach: which distinction Paul follows in Rom. XIII. 7.

Latin:

Vers. 22.

φόρον] Bene vertit Syrus כסף רישא argentum capi- tationis: neque videtur mihi Lucas hic descivisse à proprie- tate vocabuli. Nam quod pro mercibus solvitur, τέλος proprie dicitur, quod pro agris & capitibus φόρος, ut do- cent Græcorum Grammatici & Strabo: quod discrimen Paulus sequitur Rom. XIII. 7.

## 20:34
Vers. 34.

οἱ ὑοὶ τῦ αἰῶνος τύτε] Those who lead this mortal life: to whom are opposed οἱ ὑοὶ τῆς ἀνασάσεως. Theodoret well says: ὧ διαρκοῦσιν εἰς ἀεὶ τοῖς θέλω τὴν ἀσώματον φύσιν· ταῦτα τοῖς γὰρ διὰ τῆς διαιρέσεως ἐνδεὴς τῶν ὑπὸ τῷ θανάτῳ τελέντων ἡ φύσις· ἐπειδὴ γὰρ ἐξανδροποδίζε ταυτὴν ὁ θάνατος, ἐσύλησε κυτερα διὰ τῆς παιδοποιίας ἀντεισάγε τὸ δαπανώμενον· οἷόν γάρ τινα ἐπισκευαστὴν ἀθανασίαν ὁ ποιητὴς τῷ θνητῷ ζώῳ τὴν παι- δοποιῖαν ἐμηχανήσατο. Add that [passage] of Athenagoras: ἄνθρω- πον ὡς οἰδεὶς δεῖται τροφῆς, ὡς θνητὸς διαδοχῆς, ὡς δὲ λογικὸς δίκης.

Latin:

Vers. 34.

οἱ ὑοὶ τῦ αἰῶνος τύτε] Qui vitam hanc mortalem agunt: quibus opponuntur οἱ ὑοὶ τῆς ἀνασάσεως. Bene Theodoro- tus: ὧ διαρκοῦσιν εἰς ἀεὶ τοῖς θέλω τὴν ἀσώματον φύσιν· ταῦτα τοῖς γὰρ διὰ τῆς διαιρέσεως ἐνδεὴς τῶν ὑπὸ τῷ θανάτῳ τελέντων ἡ φύσις· ἐπειδὴ γὰρ ἐξανδροποδίζε ταυτὴν ὁ θάνατος, ἐσύλησε κυτερα διὰ τῆς παιδοποιίας ἀντεισάγε τὸ δαπανώμενον· οἷόν γάρ τινα ἐπισκευαστὴν ἀθανασίαν ὁ ποιητὴς τῷ θνητῷ ζώῳ τὴν παι- δοποιῖαν ἐμηχανήσατο. Adde illud Athenagoræ: ἄνθρω- πον ὡς οἰδεὶς δεῖται τροφῆς, ὡς θνητὸς διαδοχῆς, ὡς δὲ λογικὸς δίκης.

## 20:35
Vers. 35.

οἱ δὲ καταξιωθέντες τῦ αἰῶνος ἐκείνου τυχεῖν τῆς ἀνασάσεως τῆς ἐκ τῶν νεκρῶν] αἰὼν ἐκεῖνος is עולם הבא. For ὕτος and ἐκεῖνος are opposites, as we said at Matthew XIV. 36, where ἡμέρα ἐκείνη is ἡ ἡμέρα τῆς ἀνασάσεως. Moreover, there is great force in the word καταξιωθέντες. For those are to be understood as worthy to rise again into blessed immortality, who here have risen from dead works, which is declared also by the following words, ὑοὶ εἰσὶ τῦ Θεῦ. Here they were sons of God by imitating God in their morals; there they will be sons of God by participation in divine happiness, insofar as created nature can receive it. ἐκγαμίσκονται] That ancient manuscript both here and a little later has ἐκγαμίζονται: which is more customary.

Latin:

Vers. 35.

οἱ δὲ καταξιωθέντες τῦ αἰῶνος ἐκείνου τυχεῖν τῆς ἀνασάσεως τῆς ἐκ τῶν νεκρῶν] αἰὼν ἐκεῖνος est עולם הבא. Opposita enim sunt ὕτος & ἐκεῖνος, ut diximus Matth. XIV. 36. ubi ἡμέ- ρα ἐκείνη est ἡ ἡμέρα τῆς ἀνασάσεως. Est autem magna vis in verbo καταξιωθέντες. Illi enim intelligendi sunt digni in bea- tam immortalitatem resurgere, qui hic ex operibus mor- tuis resurrexerunt, quod declaratur & verbis sequentibus, ὑοὶ εἰσὶ τῦ Θεῦ. Hic filii Dei erant Deum moribus imitando, ibi filii Dei erunt felicitatis divinæ participatione, quate- nus eam condita natura recipere potest. ἐκγαμίσκονται] Manuscriptus ille antiquus & hic & pau- lo post ἐκγαμίζονται: quod usitatius.

## 20:36
Vers. 36.

οὔτε γὰρ ἀποθανεῖν ἔτι δύνανται] See what is above and what is at Matthew.

Ἰσάγγελοι γάρ εἰσι] A word coined in the likeness of ἰσόθεοι. The Pythagoreans also used it. Hierocles: 'The discourse exhorts us to revere those men who are ranked among the divine races, the equal-to-daemons and equal-to-angels and similar to the good heroes.' He spoke well, however, in saying ἰσαγγέλους, because Angels in the sacred scriptures are called sons of God, on account of that participation in divine happiness and glory which we have mentioned.

τῆς ἀναστάσεως ὑιοὶ ὄντες] And consequently immortal: for the name ἀναστάσεως here signifies eternal and blessed life: as in Heb. 11:35 and often elsewhere.

Latin:

Vers. 36.

οὔτε γὰρ ἀποθανεῖν ἔτι δύνανται] Vide quæ supra & quæ ad Matthæum.

Ἰσάγγελοι γάρ εἰσι] Vox ficta ad similitudinem ἰσόθεοι. Usurparunt & Pythagorici. Hierocles: τοὺς ἐν τοῖς θείοις γένεσι συντεταγμένους ἀνθρώπους σέβειν ὁ λόγος παραινεῖ, τοὺς ἰσοδαίμονας καὶ ἰσαγγέλους κὶ τοῖς ἀγάθοις ἥρωσιν ὁμοίους. Bene autem dixit ἰσαγγέλους, quia Angeli in sacris literis filii Dei vocantur, ob illam quam diximus divinæ felicitatis & glo- riæ participationem.

τῆς ἀναστάσεως ὑιοὶ ὄντες] Ac proinde immortales: nam ἀναστάσεως nomen hic vitam æternam ac beatam significat: ut Hebr. XI. 35. & alibi sæpe.

ἐπὶ τῆς βάτυ] A brief expression, that is, where he narrates that history concerning the bush. Just as you may not wrongly understand it in Mark as well.

ὡς λέγει κύριον] By narrating, namely, what God had said.

Latin:

Vers. 37.

ἐμήνυσεν] הגיד quod verti solet per ὑποδείκνυσθαι, σημαί- νειν, προλέγειν, ἀποκαλύπτειν.

ἐπὶ τῆς βάτυ] Brevis locutio, id est, ubi illam de rubo narrat historiam. Quomodo & apud Marcum non male accipias.

ὡς λέγει κύριον] Narrando scilicet quod Deus dixerat.

## 20:38
Vers. 38.

πάντες γὰρ αὐτῷ ζῶσιν] The solution of a tacit objection. But they were dead at that time. Indeed, but they live with respect to the power of God, which is able to restore the dead to a better life. For He himself is the one 'calling those things which are not as though they were.' πάντες, those namely, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and those like them.

They are not said to live only with respect to the power of God. But they are said to live in act, and that τῷ Θεῷ: because there in the other life the spirits of the just live fully τῷ Θεῷ, who in this life lived to God, but not without the struggle of the flesh, and therefore not as perfectly as was fitting, and as will happen in the state of perfection. On this passage more fully in Socinismo profligato, in the article on the resurrection of the dead.

PART V. The dispatch of the lawyers.

Latin:

Vers. 38.

πάντες γὰρ αὐτῷ ζῶσιν] Solutio objectionis tacitæ. At- qui mortui tunc erant. Sane, sed vivunt quoad Dei poten- tiam, quæ potest mortuos vitæ meliori reddere. Ipse enim est ὁ καλῶν τὰ μὴ ὄντα ὡς ὄντα. πάντες illi nimirum Abra- hamus, Isaacus, Jacobus & horum similes.

Non dicuntur tantum illi vivere quoad Dei po- tentiam. Sed vivere dicuntur actu, idque τῷ Θεῷ: quia ibi in altera vita plena τῷ Θεῷ vivunt spiritus justorum, qui in hac vita Deo vixerunt, sed non sine lucta carnis, adeoque non ita perfecte, ut par erat, & uti in statu perfectionis id fiet. De hoc loco plenius in Socinismo profligato, in artic. de resurrectione mortuorum.

PARS V. Legisperitorum expeditio.

Verse 47.

προφάσει] That is, ὡς πρόφασιν, so that they might have some pretext for fleecing men, they compose long prayers, and they impute that, forsooth, to others. Thus the Syrian בעלתא and the Latin [translator] at Mark, where I have noted these things, take it here; see [there].

Μακρὰ] Ita legendum non μακρᾷ. Vide quæ ad Marcum.

## 21:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXI. ARGUMENT AND DIVISION.

The needy widow rich in alms. The prediction of the devastation of the temple, and concerning the time, and the things preceding the same, especially the persecution of the Apostles: against which they are fortified: with a warning concerning flight at the time of the siege. Concerning the signs of the final coming of the Son of God, and preparation for the same. Christ teaches by day in the temple: spending the night on the Mount of Olives.

There are four parts; I. The alms of the poor widow is praised, to v. 4. II. The devastation of the temple as well as the city is predicted, to v. 24. III. The signs of the coming of the Lord, and an admonition concerning our preparation, to v. 36. IV. A brief account concerning Christ teaching by day in the temple, v. 37, 38.

PART I. The alms of the poor widow praised.

Latin:

CAPUT XXI. ARGUMENTUM ET PAR- TITIO.

Vidua egena eleemosyna dives. Prædictio de- vastationis templi, & de tempore, & an- tecedentibus ejusdem, imprimis persecu- tione Apostolorum: adversus quam mu- niantur: cum monitione de fuga, tempo- re obsessionis. De signis novissimi adven- tus Filii Dei, & præparatione ad eundem. Christus de die in templo docet: in mon- te Oliveti pernoctans.

Partes sunt quatuor; I. Viduæ pauperis elee- mosyna laudatur, ad v. 4. II. Templi ut & urbis vastatio prædicitur, ad v. 24. III. Signa adventus Domini, & admonitio de præparatione nostri, ad v. 36. IV. Relatiuncula de Christo interdiu in templo docente, v. 37. 38.

PARS I. Vidua pauperis eleemosyna laudata.

εἰς τὰ δῶρα τοῦ Θεοῦ] It should not be doubted that this is a periphrasis for the treasury, which was called synecdochically gazophylacium or corban from the thing contained. Mark ch. VII. v. 11, κορβᾶν ὅ ἐστι δῶρον; Josephus: κορβᾶν δηλοῖ ὡς ἂν εἴποι τις ἐκ τῆς ἑβραίων μεθερμηνευόμενον διαλέκτε, δῶρον Θεῦ.

PART II. Prediction of the devastation of the temple and city.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

εἰς τὰ δῶρα τοῦ Θεοῦ] Dubitari non debet quin hæc sit πε- ρίφρασις τοῦ γαζοφυλακίου. quod συνεκδοχικῶς vocabatur γαζο- bãv aut κορβανᾶ ex re contenta. Marcus c. VII. v. 11. κορ- bᾶν ὅ ἐστι δῶρον, Josephus : κορβᾶν δηλοῖ ὡς ἂν εἴποι τις ἐκ τῆς ἑβραίων μεθερμηνευόμενον διαλέκτε, δῶρον Θεῦ.

PARS II. Prædictio vastationis templi & urbis.

## 21:5
Verse 5.

ἀναθήμασι κεκόσμηται] Philo on Augustus: 'when he almost decorated our temple with the costliness of all kinds of votive offerings.' Josephus: 'for the whole temple had barbarian spoils fixed in a circle.' Among the votive offerings of the temple was a table donated by Ptolemy: but that golden vine, which Tacitus also mentions, stood out most, donated to the temple by Herod the Great, 'a wonder both in size and in art to those who saw it,' as Josephus speaks. This vine had succeeded in the place of another vine which, having been donated to the temple by Alexander, Ethnarch of the Jews, had been taken away from there by Aristobulus and given to Pompey, who placed it in the Capitol at Rome, as the same Josephus teaches us. Strabo says this creation was called τερπωλὴν, from which he who calls himself the son of Gorion made שרמן: that would be in Hebrew עדן, for I do not doubt that this work bore the image of Paradise. Strabo himself doubts whether he ought to call it a vine or a garden: Josephus calls the garden κῆπον. But the Jews say that the Israelite people were signified by this vine, from those things which we read in Psalm 80 and Isaiah 5.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

ἀναθήμασι κεκόσμηται] Philo de Augusto: ὅτε μονονὲ παντοίων ἀναθημάτων πολυτελείαις τὸ ἱερὸν ἡμῶν ἐκόσμησε. Josephus: τῶ δ᾽ ἱερᾶ παντὸς ἦν ἐν κύκλω πεπηγμένα σκῦλα βαρβαρικὰ. Inter ἀναθήματα templi erat mensa donata à Pto- lemæo: sed maxime eminebat vitis illa aurea cujus & Ta- citus meminit, ab Herode magno donata templo θαῦμα καὶ τῷ μεγέθει κὶ τῆς τέχνης τοῖς ἰδῦσιν, ut Josephus loquitur. Successerat hæc vitis in locum vitis alterius quæ ab Alexan- dro Judæorum Ethnarcha donata templo, ab Aristobulo inde ablata & data Pompejo fuerat, qui eam Romæ in Ca- pitolio posuit, ut idem nos Josephus docet. Hoc δημιούρ- γημα Strabo vocatum dicit τερπωλὴν ex quo שרמן fecit is qui se Gorionis filium vocat: id fuerit Hebraice עדן ne- que enim dubito quin id opus imaginem gesserit Paradisi. Strabo ipse dubitat ἄμπελον an κῆπον appellare debeat: Eo Josephus paradisum κῆπον appellat. At Judæi per hanc vi- tem designatum ajunt populum Israëliticum ex iis quæ le- gimus Psal. LXXX. & Esaïæ V.

## 21:6
Verse 6.

ταῦτα ἃ θεωρεῖτε] that is, 'of these things which you see,' as often in these books: but the Latins also speak in this way: as 'The city which I am establishing, it is yours.' Likewise, which approaches more closely; in Plautus: 'These two captives whom you see standing here, those who are standing, they are both standing, they are not sitting.' Wherefore I do not agree with those who insert a question mark. For it is said coldly, 'Are these the things which you see?' Nor indeed did the Syriac understand it otherwise than we say, and the construction is excellent: 'Of these things which you now admire, not a stone will be left upon a stone.' In Matthew it is in the same sense, 'that it may not be left here.'

Latin:

Vers. 6.

ταῦτα ἃ θεωρεῖτε] id est, τότων ἃ θεωρεῖτε, ut sæpe in his libris: sed & Latini ita loquuntur: ut Vrbem quam statuo, vestra est. Item, quod propius accedit; apud Plautum: Hos quos videtis stare hic captivos duos Illi qui astant, ii stant ambo non sedent. Quare non accedo interrogationis notam interponenti- bus. Frigide enim dicitur, hæcne sunt quæ videtis? neque vero Syrus aliter accepit, quam nos dicimus, & optima est constructio: horum quæ vos nunc miramini lapis non relin- quetur supra lapidem. Apud Matthæum est sensu eodem ὃ μὴ ἀφεθῇ ὧδε.

## 21:8
Verse 8.

ὅτι ἐγώ εἰμι] Namely, the Messiah, so that ὅτι may be a mark of mimetic speech. For what others prefer, saying that he is the one who I am, is harsher, if I am not mistaken.

ὁ καιρὸς ἤγγικε] This is what is said in Matthew, 'this generation shall not pass away until all these things happen.' Compare what we said there.

μὴ ὖν πορευθῆτε ὀπίσω ἀυτῶν] Do not follow that kind of impostor.

Latin:

Vers. 8.

ὅτι ἐγώ εἰμι] Nempe ὁ Μεσσίας, ut ὅτι sit nota orationis μιμητικῆς. Nam quod alii malunt, dicentes se esse is qui ego sum, durius est, ni fallor.

ὁ καιρὸς ἤγγικε] Hoc est quod apud Matthæum dicitur, ἡ μὴ παρέλθῃ ἡ γενεὰ ἅυτη ἕως ἂν πάντα ταῦτα γένηται. Con- fer quæ ibi diximus.

μὴ ὖν πορευθῆτε ὀπίσω ἀυτῶν] Ne sectamini id genus im- postores.

## 21:9
Verse 9.

ἀκαταστασίας] He placed this for that which is in Matthew 'rumors of wars,' and in Mark also 'tumults.' I think 'tumults' is correctly translated. Proverbs 26:28, where in the Greek it is ἀκαταστασίας, the Latin interpreter placed 'ruins.' See what is at Matthew 24:6.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

ἀκαταστασίας] Hoc posuit pro eo quod apud Matthæum est ἀκοὰς πολέμων, apud Marcum etiam ταραχάς. Tumul- tus recte verti puto. Prov. XXVI. v. 28. ubi in Græco est ἀκαταστασίας, ruinas posuit Latinus interpres. Vide quæ ad Matthæum XXIV. 6.

## 21:11
Verse 11.

κατὰ τόπες] A similar expression to that which we have often had ἐν χρόνοις, chapter XVIII. 4.

Φοβητρά τε καὶ σημεῖα ἀπ᾿ ὀρανῶ μεγάλα ἔσαι] Namely, a sword hanging over the city from heaven: a flame seen in the temple: the doors of the temple opened of their own accord: chariots and armed phalanxes seen in the clouds: a voice heard in the temple, 'let us depart' with the sound of those exiting: a fanatic man bearing the name of Jesus crying out for four years, αἲ αἲ Ἱεροσολύμοις, αἲ αἲ τῇ πόλει καὶ τῷ λαῷ καὶ τῷ ναῷ: all of which can be seen both narrated and explained in Josephus. Tacitus also mentions a part of these prodigies. However, it seems the Syrian used a codex which had some added words in this place.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

κατὰ τόπες] Similis locutio ei quam sæpe habuimus ἐν χρόνοις cap. XVIII. 4.

Φοβητρά τε καὶ σημεῖα ἀπ᾿ ὀρανῶ μεγάλα ἔσαι] Romphæa scilicet de cælo urbi imminens: flamma in templo visa: fores templi sponte apertæ: currus & armatæ Phalanges conspectæ in nubibus: vox audita in templo, migremus cum exeuntium sono: Fanaticus homo nomen Jesu ferens per annos quatuor clamans, αἲ αἲ Ἱεροσολύμοις, αἲ αἲ τῇ πό- λει καὶ τῷ λαῷ καὶ τῷ ναῷ : quæ omnia & narrata & explicata apud Josephum videre est. Meminit partis horum prodi- giorum etiam Tacitus. Videtur autem Syrus codice usus, qui hoc loco voces aliquot additas haberet.

Vers. 14.

θέσθε ὖν εἰς τὰς καρδίας] Elsewhere he said, τιθέναι ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ, above c. I. 66. Similar is IX. 44, θέσθε εἰς τὰ ὦτα ὑμῶν: elsewhere συμβάλλειν ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ and διατηρεῖν ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ, c. II. 51.

## 21:15
Vers. 15.

στόμα καὶ σοφίαν ᾗ ὐ δυνήσονται ἀντειπεῖν ἢ δὲ ἀντιστῆναι πάντες οἱ ἀντικείμενοι ὑμῖν] To which nothing can be contradicted that has the appearance of truth. This was fulfilled in Stephen, of whom Luke says thus in Acts VI. 10, καὶ ὐκ ἴσχυον ἀντιστῆναι τῇ σοφίᾳ καὶ τῷ πνέυματι ᾧ ἐλάλει. Nor was there any need for them to have curled or affected eloquence for this.

“The myth is the offspring of truth.” See Tertullian on this passage: “What is wiser and more uncontradictable than a simple and open confession in the name of a martyr growing strong with God?” And this is generally the reason why the enemies of truth resort to lashes and the cruelty of tortures, because they find nothing that they can speciously contradict.

Latin:

Vers. 15.

στόμα καὶ σοφίαν ᾗ ὐ δυνήσονται ἀντειπεῖν ἢ δὲ ἀντιστῆναι πάν- τες οἱ ἀντικείμενοι ὑμῖν] Cui nihil contradici possit quod veri habeat speciem. Impletum hoc in Stephano, de quo ita Lucas Act. VI. 10. καὶ ὐκ ἴσχυον ἀντιστῆναι τῇ σοφίᾳ καὶ τῷ πνέυματι ᾧ ἐλάλει. Neque ad hoc opus illis fuit eloquio calamistrato.

Ἀντε͂ς ὁ μῦθος τῆς ἀληθείας ἔφυ. Be e Tertullianus ad hunc locum: Quid sapientius & in- contradicibilius confessione simplici & exserta in martyris no- mine cum Deo invalescentis? Atque hæc plerumque causa est cur ad verbera & suppliciorum sævitiam confugiant ho- stes veritatis, quia quod speciose contradicant non inve- niunt.

## 21:18
Verse 18. “Not a hair from your head shall perish.” A proverbial way of speaking, as if you were to say in Latin, “you shall not suffer even a trifle of loss.” The same expression is in 1 Samuel 14:45, 2 Samuel 14:15, 1 Kings 2:52, and Acts 27:34. However, it is to be understood as loss after accounts have been settled: for to suffer loss for a time is sometimes the greatest gain. Similar is that which is said elsewhere, that all their hairs are numbered before God (Matthew 10:31), because, clearly, if any of them seems to perish for a time, it does not so much perish as it is deposited with God, who is about to return it with interest.

Latin:

Vers. 18. θρὶξ ἐκ τῆς κεφαλῆς ὑμῶν οὐ μὴ ἀπόληται] Pro- verbiale loquendi genus, quasi Latine dicas ne hilum qui- dem damni ferries. Est eadem locutio 1. Samuel. 14, 45. 2. Sam. 14, 15. 1. Reg. 2, 52. & Actor. 27, 34 intelligen- dum autem est damnum post subductas rationes: nam damnum facere ad tempus, maximum interdum est lu- crum. Simile est quod alibi omnes pili ipsorum numerati apud Deum esse dicuntur Matth. 10, 31. quia scilicet si quid ipsorum ad tempus interire videtur, non tam interit quam apud Deum deponitur, qui cum fœnore est reddi- turus.

## 21:19
Verse 19. “Possess your souls.” κτᾶσθε, and what the Syrian has here, קני, I think should be taken here not in the sense of possessing, but of acquiring, as in Matthew 10:9, Acts 1:8, 8:20, 22:28, and often among the LXX. It is the same thing to “save a soul” as to “find a soul” (Matthew 10:39, 16:25), which Luke explains by “to save,” “to keep alive,” rightly: for he truly acquires himself who receives back as his own and perpetual what he has here on loan. The opposite of this is “to forfeit one’s soul” (Mark 8:36). Therefore, it is “in endurance,” by tolerating all adversities, even death if necessary. For: “He who perishes through virtue, does not perish.” Tertullian therefore understood this passage well, translating it more freely or citing it as translated by another: “By tolerance you will save yourselves.” In Matthew and Mark, the same sense is expressed thus: “But he who endures to the end, this one shall be saved.”

Latin:

Vers. 19. κτήσασθε τὰς ψυχὰς] κτᾶσθε & quod Syrus hic habet קני puto hic accipiendum non in possidendi sed in acquirendi significatu, ut Matth. 10, 9. Actor. 1, 8. c. 8. 20. c. 22, 28. & apud LXX. sæpe. Idem est σῶσαι ψυχὴν quod εὑρίσκειν ψυχὴν. Matth. 10, 39. c. 16, 25. quod Lucas exponit per σώζειν, ζωογονεῖν, recte: nam is vere semetipsum ac- quirit, qui quod hic habet commodatum recipit proprium atque perpetuum. Huic contrarium est ζημιῶσθαι τὴν ψυ- χὴν Marci 8, 36. ἐν ὑπομονῇ igitur est, tolerando adversa omnia, etiam mortem si opus est. Nam: Qui per virtutem perbitas, non interis. Bene ergo accepit hunc locum Tertullianus, liberius ita vertens aut versum ab alio citans: per tolerantiam salvos fa- cietis vosmet ipsos. Apud Matthæum & Marcum sensus idem sic effertur: ὁ δὲ ὑπομείνας εἰς τέλος, οὗτος σωθήσε- ται.

## 21:20
Verse 20. “Surrounded by armies.” See above, chapter 19, verse 43. Add that of Josephus: “With astonishment the rebels looked upon the Romans encamping in three divisions.” Therefore, στρατοπέδων is used well, in the plural number.

Latin:

Vers. 20. κυκλωμένην ὑπὸ στρατοπέδων] Vide supra c. 19, v. 43. Adde illud Josephi μετ᾽ ἐκπλήξεως οἱ στασιασταὶ τες ρωμαίες ἀφορῶντες στρατοπεδευομένες τριχῇ. Bene ergo στρα- τοπέδων, multitudinis numero.

## 21:21
Verse 21. “In the countries.” We spoke of this word above, chapter 12, verse 15. But most of the Hebrews did the opposite of what Christ advises, and consequently were shut up in the city as if in a trap.

Latin:

Vers. 21. ἐν ταῖς χώραις] De hac voce diximus supra c. 12, 15. Contra autem quam Christus monet fecerunt ple- rique Hebræorum, ac proinde in urbem velut in nassam conclusi sunt.

## 21:22
Verse 22. “These are the days of vengeance, that all things which are written may be fulfilled.” Josephus: “For the fire had long since been decreed by God against Titus, but fate was present in the cycles of time.”

Latin:

Vers. 22. ἡμέραι ἐκδικήσεως αὗταί εἰσι τῶ πληρωθῆναι πάντα τὰ γεγραμμένα] Josephus: τῶ δὲ ἄρα (Τειτῷ) κατε- ψήφιστο μὲν τὸ πῦρ ὁ θεὸς πάλαι, παρῆν δὲ ἡ εἱμαρμένη χρόνων περιόδοις.

## 21:23
Verse 23. ἀνάγκη. The Greeks call torture ἀνάγκη: and Josephus uses that word in that sense: whence it happened that just as Cάσαν is referred to all evils, especially the more serious ones, so also is ἀνάγκη: which a most learned man has proven in many places. Add, if you please, Tobit 3:6, “Command me to be released from this distress (ἀνάγκης).” Baruch 7:37, “Being in distress (ἀνάγκη) and they did not deliver them.” But also among the paraphrasts of the Old and New Testaments, the word taken from the Greek, אננקי, has the same meaning. Chrysostom on 2 Corinthians 5:5 interprets ἀνάγκας as “unavoidable evils.” “And wrath upon this people.” That is, misery. Thus Matthew chapter 3, verse 8, and above chapter 3, verse 7, “To flee from the wrath to come.” A passage most similar to ours is 1 Maccabees 1:67, “There was great wrath upon Israel exceedingly,” in which way you may not wrongly take that of 1 Maccabees 3:8, “He turned away wrath from Israel.”

Latin:

Vers. 23. ἀνάγκη] Ἀνάγκην Græci vocant τὴν βάσα- νον: in eumque sensum eam vocem & Josephus usurpat: quo factum ut quomodo Cάσαν ad omnia mala, præser- tim graviora, refertur, ita & ἀνάγκη: quod multis locis pro- bavit vir eruditissimus. Adde si placet Tobiæ 3, 6. ἐπίταξον ἀπολυθῆναι με τῆς ἀνάγκης. Baruch. 7, 37. ἐν ἀνάγκῃ ἀνθρώ- ποι ὄντα κ̀ μὴ ἐξίλοντο. Sed & apud paraphrastas Veteris ac Novi Testamenti vox ex Græco desumta אננקי eundem sensum habet. Chrysostomus in II. ad Corinthios cap. 5, 5. ἀνάγκας interpretatur ἄφυκτα κακὰ. καὶ ὀργὴ ἐν τῷ λαῷ τούτῳ] Id est miseria. Ita Matthæus c. 3, 8. & supra c. 3, 7. Φυγεῖν ἀπὸ τῆς μελλούσης ὀργῆς. Locus huic nostro simillimus est 1. Macc. 1, 67. ἐγένετο ὀργὴ μεγάλη ἐπὶ Ἰσραὴλ σφόδρα. quomodo non male sumas & illud 1. Macc. 3, 8. ἀπέστρεψεν ὀργὴν ἀπὸ Ἰσραὴλ.

## 21:24
Verse 24. “They shall fall by the edge of the sword.” “Of those who perished during the whole siege, the number was one million one hundred thousand,” says Josephus, adding later: “Then indeed, as if into a prison, the whole nation was shut up by fate.” In another place, dealing with those killed after the siege: “The number of those who were killed in the battles against the beasts and those burned and those destroyed in the mutual slaughters exceeded two thousand five hundred.”

“And they shall be led captive into all the nations.” “Of all the captives,” he says, “as many as were taken during the whole war, the number nine hundred and seventy thousand was gathered.” That phrase, “into all the nations,” the same most noble writer explains well: “He chose the tallest and most beautiful of the young men and kept them for the triumph. The rest of the multitude over seventeen years of age he bound and sent to the works in Egypt. Titus distributed most of them to the provinces, to be destroyed in the theaters by the sword and by beasts; those under seventeen years of age were sold.” Rutilius Numantianus: “And would that Judea had never been subdued by the wars of Pompey and the power of Titus: the contagions of the excised plague spread more widely, and the conquered nation presses upon its conquerors.”

To this pertains also that of Bardesanes the Syrian:

“On the eighth day they circumcise the male children who are born, not expecting the presence of impiety. And even if they are driven out of their climates, turning aside, led by the law of a foreign land, but whether they happen to be in Syria or in Gaul, or in Italy, or in Greece, or even in Parthia, wherever they may be, they do this.”

“Jerusalem shall be trodden down by the nations.” πατεῖν is to hold by right of victory. Such is that: “The barbarian traveler shall tread upon the ashes here.” Revelation 11:2, “And they shall tread the holy city for forty-two months.” Those foreigners, whom the Hebrews call גוים, are the Romans, Saracens, Franks, Turks,

The word πατεῖν implies more than mere subjection, as noted by Eustathius on Homer's Iliad δ, where it signifies great contempt: so that it is hinted here that that metropolis is to be held as a vile little town, and never to be restored to its former splendor. Let there be applied for בוס he trampled, he trod down, he plundered, Zech. 10:5; for the verb דוש he threshed, he trampled (which is used here by the Syrian): Isaiah 25:10. Moab shall be trampled, as straw is trampled in the mire. It is noted, therefore, not only that Jerusalem is to be brought under the power of the nations, but that it is to be devastated and held in contempt and trampled.

ἄχρι πληρωθῶσι καιροὶ ἐθνῶν] Chrysostom, in his accurate disputation against the Jews, interprets this concerning the time of the universal Judgment: and therefore denies that the Jews are ever to be restored to their homeland. But Origen also, speaking about the Jews against Celsus, had written, θαῤῥῶντες δ' ἂν εἴποιμεν ὅτι ἐδὲ ἀποκαταστήσονται [we would confidently say that they will not be restored], and the writer of Seder Olam defends that very opinion: for he says that after the second ejection from Canaan, the Jewish people will never return there. Others, however, from those things which are in Isaiah ch. 65, ch. 66, Jeremiah ch. 16 and 31, Ezekiel 20, ch. 27, ch. 28, and Hosea 3, v. 3, 4, 5, think otherwise, namely that the Jews, when they have acknowledged Jesus as the Messiah, will recover those goods which God promised to their parents by an eternal, yet condition-containing, covenant. See the words of Moses in Leviticus ch. 26, at the end, and Deuteronomy 30, to which opinion Justin says he adheres in his dialogue with Trypho. Certainly Christ, when asked by the Apostles whether he was now about to restore the kingdom of Israel, did not deny that he would do it, but he did not want the time when it would happen to be inquired of by them: and indeed, partly from these prophecies I have mentioned, and partly from the prerogative of the martyrs in the resurrection (about which there will be a place to speak elsewhere), that opinion concerning the happiness of a thousand years seems to have been fashioned: which great authors Justin and Irenaeus defend as having been received from the successors of the Apostles, whom Melito, Apollinaris, Tertullian, and Victorinus followed: whose opinion, although it seems to have something of human error mixed in (since not everyone explains that happiness in the same way), yet perhaps it is not to be entirely repudiated. There are those who think that passage of the Apocalypse concerning the Euphrates should be referred to this: καὶ ἐξηράνθη τὸ ὕδωρ αὐτῶ ἵνα ἑτοιμασθῇ ἡ ὁδὸς τῶν βασιλέων τῶν ἀπὸ ἀνατολῶν ἡλίου [and its water was dried up so that the way of the kings from the east of the sun might be prepared]. For they think the Israelites are understood by the name of kings. Lactantius also seems to have felt this in the seventh book of his Institutes, ch. 15, when he says that it will come to pass that the empire will return to Asia, and the East will rule again, and the West will serve. See, if you like, what is in the apocryphal book of Esdras which is called the fourth, ch. 13, 43, 47, and compare it with the said passage of the Apocalypse: which opinion, if we accept it, it will be permissible to understand καιρὸς ἐθνῶν [the time of the nations] as the times of divine patience, appointed for the amendment of those who, having professed the name of Christ from among the nations, have departed very far from the discipline of Christ. In which sense we had καιρὸν ἐπισκοπῆς [the time of visitation] concerning the city of Jerusalem above, so that we may understand that God, provoked by the nations, would use a certain new and extraordinary way in converting the Jews to Himself: just as, provoked by the Jews, He drew the nations to His obedience in a similar way. Chrysostom, in the already mentioned disputation, also uses the testimony of Josephus against the Jews as if he too had thought that τὴν ἐρήμωσιν [the desolation] would last without end. But Josephus, just as he dared not promise anything certain to his people, so he did not cast away all hope, as appears even from this passage where, deploring the crimes of the city and the punishment due to them, he addresses it thus: δύναιτο δ' ἂν γενέσθαι πάλιν ἀνώμοισιν, εὐγὲ πότε τὸν πορθήσαντα θεὸν ἐξιλάσῃ [it might be able to become uncursed again, if ever it should appease the God who destroyed it].

The fulfillment of the times of the nations is rightly extended by Chrysostom to the consummation of the age: as also by Euthymius in his commentary on this place. Which sense agrees with the prophecy of Dan. 9:27. It is decreed that the desolation shall persist until the end. By no means, however, can the Jewish opinion concerning restoration be admitted.

Of the Jews into the land of Canaan: regarding which Bede seems to have been somewhat stuck here, nor is that Chiliasm approved by certain of the ancients, which draws its origin from Papias, who was wonderfully prone to accepting fables. Eusebius, book III of the Ecclesiastical History, last chapter; indeed, it proceeded from the false opinion of the Jews concerning the earthly kingdom of the Messiah, and is analogous to it: Lactantius certainly did not hesitate to assert the perception of even bodily delights in that Chiliastic kingdom. That such fables were not entirely displeasing to Grotius appears from the fact that he even appealed here to the most inept inventions of the 4th book of Esdras, ch. 13, 43, 47, and did not fear to compare the same with the Apocalyptic oracles, and thus to favor the bodily return of the Jews, of which there is neither a trace nor a footprint in the whole of Scripture: and which even the Jews themselves reject in the Seder Olam and the Talmud. See Blessed Gerhard on the consummation.

§. 119. Blessed Gerhard dealt with the passage Lev. 26, 41, which the Jews call the golden monkey, and Deut. 30, 3, in the place cited, §. 146. What of the fact that the present passage cannot even be taken with Ambrose concerning the spiritual restoration of the Jews to a spiritual Jerusalem: because the bodily Jerusalem is said to be trampled, and there is no word here about a spiritual Jerusalem: Nor do other oracles of Scripture hand down anything about the same, although authors are accustomed to scrape together many things. Concerning which we have spoken at Hos. 3.

But the fact that Christ, when asked in Acts 1 about the restoration of the kingdom of Israel, did not deny that it would happen, does nothing for this case. For it is one thing not to deny, and another to affirm. He who does not deny, affirms nothing. For he can have a reason why he does not deny, not because he holds it as settled or approves it: but either because he judges it unworthy of a response, or because for the time being he wishes to offer his opinion neither by denying nor by affirming. Furthermore, that Christ says the Father has reserved the times in his own power is not to be applied to the restoration of the kingdom of Israel, because it is a general statement, which could have dismissed the curiosity of the disciples, which was still leaning on a false opinion, even if he did not deign to refute again an opinion that had been refuted more often: or if anyone should judge that it must be applied entirely to the true restoration of Israel, not to that falsely persuaded one, it must be said that there is no need for them to know the times and the opportunity for converting the Israelites or even for establishing the restoration of the spiritual kingdom of Israel through the conversion of the nations, which God has reserved for himself; but as for how much would be necessary regarding these and other things, the Spirit, who was to be poured out upon them, would instruct them sufficiently, when and how he himself was to judge. For it was sufficient that he had reminded them again that the kingdom which Christ was to administer did not pertain only to the Jews, but was to be propagated into Samaria and even to the ends of the earth, even by the Apostles themselves in his own time, when, where, and how it pleased him. The disciples were indeed betraying both their crudeness, in that they were still thinking about an earthly kingdom, and their curiosity, in that they were seeking to know the moments of the times concerning the fulfillment of the prophecies (even if not correctly understood). For the sake of that correction, although he had made it more than once, he promises the Holy Spirit, by whose power they were to be endowed: but he checks this curiosity with a general axiom, that it is not for them to know the times or the moments which the Father has placed in his own power. But what could be extracted from that response of Christ for the restoration of a bodily Israelite kingdom? And is it not sufficiently clear that Christ taught in this way that his kingdom would not be bodily, but spiritual: since he hinted at the nature of his kingdom both by the kind of weapons with which it is to be occupied and propagated, namely that there is no need for arms or external guards, but for heavenly power and the gift of the Holy Spirit, with which the Apostles were soon to be instructed, so that they might be able to speak in various tongues, and perform miracles, and for the glory of the divine name with a great and noble spirit undergo and overcome any dangers: and then by the shown mode of fighting: through these words, And you shall be my witnesses: by which name the office of preaching the Gospel, which the Apostles were to perform, is designated; and then by the description of the boundaries of the kingdom; which the Apostles thought were contained by the borders of the Israelite nation: concerning which see Blessed Arcularius in his Commentary on Acts 1.

PART III. Signs of the coming of the Lord with an admonition concerning pious preparation.

καὶ αἰχμαλωτισθήσονται εἰς πάντα τὰ ἔθνη] τῶν μὲν ἐ͂ν αἰχμα- λώτων πάντων, inquit ille, ὅσα καθ᾽ ὅλον εἰλήφθη τὸν πόλεμον ἀριθμὸς ἐννέα μυριάδες καὶ ἑπτακις χίλιοι συνήχθη: illud etiam, εἰς πάντα τὰ ἔθνη, bene explicat idem nobilissi- mus Scriptor: τῶν δὲ νέων τὺς ὑψηλοτάτυς καὶ καλὺς ἐπι- λέξας ἐτήρει τῷ θριάμβῳ. το͂ δὲ λοιπο͂ πλήθους τὺς ὑπὲρ ἑπτακαί- δεκα ἔτη δήσας ἔπεμψεν εἰς τὰ κατὰ αἴγυπτον ἔργα. πλείστως δ᾽ εἰς τὰς ἐπαρχίας διεδωρήσατο Τῖτος, φθαρησομένυς ἐν τοῖς θεάτροις σιδήρῳ καὶ θηρίοις· οἱ δὲ ἐντὸς ἑπτὰ κ̀ δεκα ἐτῶν ἐπράθησαν. Ru- tilius Numantianus: Atq, utinam nunquam Iudæa subacta fuisset Pompeji bellis, imperioq, Titi: Latius excisæ pestis contagia serpunt, Victoresq, suos natio victa premit.

Huc pertinet & illud Bardesanis Syri: Ἰουδαῖοι πάντες οἱ διὰ Μωσέως δεξάμενοι νόμον τὺς γεννωμένες ἄρρενας παῖδας ἐν

τῇ ὀγδοῇ ἡμέρᾳ ὠλμαΐζουσι περιτέμνοντες, ἐκ ἀσέβειαν παρε- σίαν ἀναμένοντες. κἂν κλίματῶν ἐξωσθῶσιν ἐκτρεπόμενοι, νόμῳ ἀλλοτρίας χώρας ἀγόμενοι, ἀλλ' εἴτε ἐν Συρίᾳ τυγχάνωσιν εἴτε ἐν Γαλίᾳ, εἴτε ἐν Ἰταλίᾳ, εἴτε ἐν Ἑλλάδι κἂν Παρθίᾳ ὅπῃ ἂν ὦσι τοῦτο ποιοῦσιν.

Ἱερεσαλὴμ ἔσαι πατουμένη ὑπὸ ἐθνῶν] πατεῖν est tenere ju- re victoriæ. Tale est illud: Barbarus heic cineres infistet via- tor. Apoc. XI. 7. καὶ τὴν πόλιν τὴν ἁγίαν πατήσουσι μῆνας τεσσα- ράκοντα δύο. Alienigenæ illi, quos Hebræi גוים vo- cant, sunt Romani, Saraceni, Franci, Turcæ,

Plus infert verbum πατεῖν quam nudam subje- ctionem notante Eustachio ad Homer. Iliad. δ. ubi magnum contemtum importat: ut innuatur hic, metropolin istam ceu vile oppidulum haben- dam, nec unquam pristino splendori restituen- dam. Adhibeatur pro בוס conculcavit, pessun- dedit, diripuit, Zach. X. 5. pro verbo דוש trita- ravit, calcavit (quod hic à Syro usurpatum): Esai XXV. 6. Calcabitur Moab, sicut calcatur palea in luto. Notatur ergo non tantum, quod Hiero- solyma sit in potestatem gentium redigenda, sed quod devastanda & contemtui habenda & concul- canda sit.

ἄχρι πληρωθῶσι καιροὶ ἐθνῶν] Chrysostomus in disputatione accurata adversus Judæos interpretatur de tempore Judicii universalis: ac proinde negat Judæos unquam in patriam restituendos.
