Sed & Origenes adver- sus Celsum de Judæis loquens scripserat, θαῤῥῶντες δ' ἂν εἴποιμεν ὅτι ἐδὲ ἀποκαταστήσονται, & eam ipsam sententiam tuetur scriptor Seder olam: ait enim post secundam eje- ctionem è Cananæa populum Judaicum nunquam eo re- diturum. Alii vero ex iis quæ sunt apud Esaiam cap. 65. cap. 66. Jerem. cap. 16. & 31. Ezech. 20. c. 27. c. 28. & Oseam 3. v. 3. 4. 5. aliter existimant, Judæos scilicet cum Jesum Messiam agnoverint recuperaturos ea bona, quæ Deus ipsorum parentibus sempiterno, sed conditionem continente, fœdere promisit. Vide Mosis verba Levitici cap. 26. in fine, & Deuteron. 30. cujus sententiæ se esse dicit in colloquio cum Tryphone Justinus. Certe Chri- stus ab Apostolis interrogatus, an jam restituturus esset re- gnum Israelis, non negavit id se facturum, sed quo id futurum esset tempore, noluit ab ipsis inquiri: & sane parùm ex his quæ dixi vaticiniis, partim ex prærogativa martyrum in resurrectione, (de qua alibi agendi erit lo- cus) concinnata videtur sententia illa, de mille annorum felicitate: quam ut ab Apostolorum successoribus acce- ptam tuentur magni autores Justinus, & Irenæus, quos secuti sunt Melito, Apollinaris, Tertullianus, Victo- rinus: quorum opinio, quanquam admixtum aliquid ha- bere videtur humani erroris, (quando nec omnes illam felicitatem pari modo explicant) forte tamen non in to- tum repudianda est. Sunt qui huic referendum putent illud Apocalypseos de Euphrate: καὶ ἐξηράνθη τὸ ὕδωρ αὐτῶ ἵνα ἑτοιμασθῇ ἡ ὁδὸς τῶν βασιλέων τῶν ἀπὸ ἀνατολῶν ἡλίου. Re- gnum enim nomine Israelitas putant intelligi. Quod sen- sisse &, Lactantius videtur septima institutione cap. 15. cum futurum dicit, ut imperium in Asiam revertatur, & rursus Oriens dominetur, & Occidens serviat. Vide si lubet quæ in Apocrypho Esdræ libro qui quartus dicitur cap. 13, 43. 47. & confer cum dicto Apocalypseos loco: quam sententiam si recipimus, καιρὸς ἐθνῶν intelligere licebit tem- pora divinæ patientiæ, præstituta emendationi eorum, qui ex gentibus Christi nomen professi a disciplina Christi plurimum recesserunt. Quo sensu καιρὸν ἐπισκοπῆς de Hierosolymitana urbe supra habuimus, ut nimirum intel- ligamus Deum irritatum a gentibus modo quodam novo atque extraordinario usurum in convertendis ad se Judæis: sicut ab Judæis irritatus modo simili gentes ad obsequium suum pertraxit. Chrysostomus dicta jam disputatione etiam Josephi testimonio contra Judæos utitur quasi is quoque existimaverit sine fine duraturam τὴν ἐρήμωσιν. At Josephus, sicut nihil certi populo suo ausus est pollice- ri, ita spem omnem non abjecit, ut vel ex hoc loco appa- ret ubi scelera civitatis & pœnam eis debitam deplorans ita eam alloquitur, δύναιτο δ' ἂν γενέσθαι πάλιν ἀνώμοισιν, εὐγὲ πότε τὸν πορθήσαντα θεὸν ἐξιλάσῃ.

Impletio temporum gentium recte à Chrysosto- mo ad consummationem seculi extenditur: ut & ad Euthymio commentar. in h. l. Qui sentus con- gruit vaticinio Dan. 9, 27. Decretum est, ut usque ad finem perseveret desolatio. Nullatenus au- tem admitti potest opinio Judaica de reductione.

Judæorum in terram Canaan: quæ hic Bedæ quodammodo hæsisse videatur, neque Chilia- smus iste quibusdam veterum haud improbatus, qui à Papia ad suscipiendas fabulas mirum quan- tum prono originem trahit. Eusebius libr. III. Histor. Eccles. cap. ult. imo ex Judæorum falsa opinione de regno Messiæ terreno profectus, eidemque analogus est: Lactantius certe cor- porcarum etiam deliciarum perceptionem in re- gno illo Chiliastico adstruere non dubitavit. Quales fabulas non omnino displicuisse Grotio ex eo apparet, quod hic etiam provocavit ad commenta ineptissima libri IV. Esdr. cap.13, 43. 47. eademque veritus non est cum oraculis Apo- calypticis componere, adeoque reditui corpo- rali Judæorum velificari, de quo in tota Scri- ptura nec vola est, nec vestigium: quemque ipsimet etiam Judæi reprobant in Seder olam, & Talmud. Vide B. Gerhardum de consummat.

§. 119. De loco Lev. 26, 41. quem simiam auream Judæi vocant, & Deut. 30, 3. egit B. Gerhard. l. c. §. 146. Quid quod ne quidem de spirituali re- ductione Judæorum ad spiritualem Hierosolymam locus præsens cum Ambrosio accipi possit: quia calcanda corporalis Hierosolyma dicitur, neque verbum de spirituali Hierosolyma hic habetur: Neque de eadem alia scripturæ oracula quicquam tradunt, etsi multa autores corradere soleant. Quo de ad Hos. 3. diximus.

Quod autem Actor. 1. de restitutioni regni Israe- lis interrogatus Christus non negavit eandem futu- ram, id huc nihil facit. Aliud enim est non ne- gare, aliud affirmare. Qui non negat, nihil affirmat. Causam enim cur non neget, habere potest, non quod id ratum habeat, aut approbet: sed vel quod responso indignum judicet, vel quod pro tempo- re sententiam suam neque negando neque affir- mando promere velit. Porro quod ait Christus Patrem in sua potestate sibi tempora reservasse, non applicandum ad restitutionem regni Israelis, quia generale effatum est, quod dimittere potuerat discipulorum curiositatem, quæ adhæc falsa opi- nione nitebatur, etiamsi non dignaretur sæpius refutatam opinionem falsissimam denuo refel- lere: aut si restitutioni Israelis veræ, non illi fal- so persuasæ quis applicandum id omnino cen- seat, dicendum, quod tempora & opportuni- tatem convertendorum Israelitarum vel etiam spi- ritualis regni Israelis restaurationem per conver- sionem gentium instituendi, ipsos scire opus non sit, quæ Deus sibi reservavit, quantum vero de his & aliis opus futurum, Spiritum, qui in eos ef- fundendus erat, eis affatim, quando, & quomodo ipse judicaturus est, eosdem instructurum. Illud enim regnum, quod Christus administraturus erat, non tantum ad Judæos pertinere, sed in Samariam & usque ad ultimas terras propagan- dum esse, etiam per ipsosmet Apostolos suo tem- pore, quando, ubi & quomodo ipsi libuerit, de- nuo monuisse, sufficiebat. Nimirum prodebant discipuli & ruditatem, quod adhuc de regno ter- reno cogitarent, & curiositatem suam, quod tem- porum momenta de implendis vaticiniis (etsi non recte intellectis) scire expeterent. Illius emendationis causa, quamvis à se non semel fa- ctæ, Spiritum S. promittit, cujus virtute induen- di erant: hanc vero curiositatem compescit gene- rali axiomate, quod ipsorum non sit nosse tempo- ra vel momenta, quæ Pater posuit in sua potestate. Quid vero ex ista Christi responsione exsculpi po- terit pro restitutione corporalis regni Israelitici? Et annon satis patet, Christum ita docuisse, re- re- gnum suum non corporale, sed spirituale fore: quum regni sui rationem innuerit tum armorum genere, quo illud occupandum & propagandum fit, quod nempe non armis aut præsidiis externis opus sit, sed virtute cælesti & dono Spiritus S. qui- bus propediem instruendi sint Apostoli, ut & va- riis loqui linguis, & miracula edere, & pro gloria divini nominis magno & excelso animo quævis pericula subire ac superare possint: tum monstra- to pugnandi modo: per ista, Et eritis mihi testes: quo nomine prædicandi Evangelii munus, quo functuri erant Apostoli, designatur; tum termi- norum regni descriptione; quos Apostoli gentes Israeliticæ finibus contineri putabant: de quibus vid. B. Arcularius in Comment. ad Act. I.

PARS III. Signa adventus Domini cum admonitione de pia præparatione.

## 21:25
Verse 25. συνοχὴ ἐθνῶν] Hesychius [defines] συνοχὴ as distress, confusion, anxiety; Paul also uses it in 2 Cor. 11. 4. ἐν ἀπορίᾳ] Thus Paul said ἀπορεῖσθαι in 2 Cor. 4. 8, Galat. 4. v. 20, nor do I think the Syriac read otherwise, but expressed the thing itself with an added gesture. I cannot approve that others read ἀποῤῥοίᾳ. ἠχούσης θαλάσσης] The sea in the Prophetic books signifies the state of the world turbulent with various events: the sound, the tumults stirred up from there. To Porphyry, the sea signifies the material constitution.

Why should the sea not be understood here in its proper sense, from which certainly no necessity compels us to depart? And since the Sun, Moon, and Stars in the heaven above us are to be taken properly, and the earth below us is no less understood here according to the literal sense, why should we descend to a metaphorical meaning when the sea is designated? For it is known what the sound of the sea and the surge is: namely, that it is a sound from the commotion and repercussion of the waves of the sea. It signifies, therefore, that the insane sea will emit wondrous and horrible noises, bellowings, and howlings, because of the most vehement whirlwinds and the commotion of the heavenly powers themselves: for with the higher and heavenly bodies disturbed, the lower and sublunary ones cannot but also be disturbed, the air through the tempests of the winds, the sea through the storms of the waves, etc. See Blessed Gerhard, Harmony of the Gospels, ch. CLXI, p. 782.

καὶ σάλου] Supply ὄντος, that is, in a great agitation of the sea, unless you prefer to interpret σάλον as the seashore, as Polybius understood it: and thus to repeat ἠχοῦντος.

Latin:

Vers. 25. συνοχὴ ἐθνῶν] Hesychius συνοχὴ, ταραχὴ, ἀδη- μονία, utitur & Paulus 2 Cor. II. 4. ἐν ἀπορίᾳ] Sic ἀπορεῖσθαι dixit Paulus 2. Cor. 4. 8. Galat. 4. v. 20. nec puto aliter legisse Syrum, sed rem ipsam expressis- se addito gestu. Quod alios legisse apparet ἀποῤῥοίᾳ pro- bare non possum. ἠχούσης θαλάσσης] Mare in libris Propheticis significat statum mundi variis casibus turbidum: sonus, excitatos in- de tumultus. Porphyrio mare significat τὴν ὑλικὴν σύστα- σιν.

Cur non intelligendum hic mare sensu proprio, à quo ut recedamus nulla sane cogit necessitas? Et quum Sol, Luna, & Stellæ in cælo supra nos pro- prie accipienda, nec minus terræ infra nos κατὰ τὸ ῥητὸν hic intelligatur, cur ad Metaphoricam signi- ficationem descendamus, cum mare designatur? Notum enim est, quid ἦχος θαλάσσης καὶ σάλου sit? quod nempe sonus sit ex commotione & re- percussione fluctuum maris. Significat ergo, ma- re insanum mirificos & horrendos strepitus, mu- gitus atque ululatus editurum, ob vehementissi- mos ventorum turbines, ipsarumque virtutum cœlestium commotionem: turbatis enim supe- rioribus & cœlestibus corporibus non poterunt non etiam inferiora, ac sublunaria turbari, aër per ventorum tempestates, mare per fluctuum procellas &c. Vid. B. Gerhard. Harmon. Evang. cap. CLXI. p. m. 782.

καὶ σάλου] Supple ὄντος, id est, in magna maris agitatio- ne, nisi σάλον interpretari malis oram maritimam, quomo- po accepit Polybius: atque ita repetere ἠχοῦντος.

## 21:26
Vers. 26. ἀποψυχόντων] I think ἀποψύχειν here is as Hesychius interprets it, ἀποπνευματίζεσθαι, to be destitute of spirit, as is accustomed to happen in extreme heat and even in extreme pains.

αἱ γὰρ δυνάμεις τῶν ὀυρανῶν σαλευθήσονται] It is no wonder if the state of the whole world will be most unpeaceful, when the heavenly hosts themselves, that is, the Christian Churches, are to be divided into very many factions, with mutual charity removed; indeed, the matter will come to this, that what ought to be the bond of love will become a pretext for wars. See what [I wrote] on Matthew.

The powers of the heavens are not the Christian Churches: for nowhere are Christian Churches called by that name: nor must one depart to an allegorical interpretation, abandoning the propriety of the words, unless necessity itself compels it. And since Christ is speaking of the peculiar prodigies and portents immediately preceding the final day, what was the point of naming either the depraved state of the world or the factions in the Church, which have flourished in all ages, and long before the final advent? Just as Grotius himself notes at verse 28, and explaining—or rather depraving—the words ἐρχομένων δὲ τούτων γίνεσθαι, [he says] that the state of both the civil empire and the Church would last in such a miserable condition for several centuries. For from the text it is most clear that the discourse is about the signs immediately preceding the consummation of the age. And therefore such things, entirely singular, pre- and supernatural, extraordinary, never heard of before, are without doubt designated for the end time in heaven, on earth, and in the sea, which no mortal before of the heavens, let us understand what the words properly sound, not the ministers of the Word, with Ambrose, not the Angels with Origen, Chrysostom, and Theophylact, not the fictitious motive intelligences of fictitious spheres, with certain Papists, nor with others the elements, which are certainly not the powers of the heavens. But what are precisely denoted by δυνάμεις τῶν ὀυρανῶν, whether accidental powers, influences, and forces, or rather substantial ones, just as the stars themselves are called the hosts of the heavens Gen. 2,1. Deut. 4, 20. Psal. 33,6. or finally whether the firmament of heaven itself is thus designated, because the celestial powers and influences are about to fail, the stars are no longer to remain in their place, the firmament is to be shaken and moved, and by what reason that disturbance and commotion is to behave itself, no one, as we have said, will easily explain. However, those things can perhaps not inconveniently be understood at the same time: because in order for the celestial powers to be moved, the firmament itself must be moved with its host of stars and its powers, by whose seat and order being disturbed, the influx into the lower things is restrained: so that it is noted, all things are meditating ruin 2. Petr. III. 10. Psal. CII. 27.

Latin:

Vers. 26. ἀποψυχόντων] Puto ἀποψύχειν hic esse ut He- sychius interpretatur ἀποπνευματίζεσθαι, spiritu destitui, ut in summo æstu atque etiam in summis doloribus fieri con- suevit.

αἱ γὰρ δυνάμεις τῶν ὀυρανῶν σαλευθήσονται] Non mirum est si mundi totius status erit impacatissimus, cum ipsa agmina cœlestia, id est Ecclesiæ Christianæ in plurimas factiones sint discessuræ, sublata mutua charitate, imo huc res deve- niet, ut quod amoris esse debebat vinculum fiat bellorum titulus. Vide quæ ad Matth.

Virtutes cælorum non sunt Ecclesiæ Christia- næ: neque enim uspiam Ecclesiæ Christianæ ita vocantur: nec ad allegoricam abeundum est in- terpretationem relicta vocum proprietate, nisi ipsa cogat necessitas. Et quum loquatur Christus de peculiaribus proxime antecessuris extremum diem prodigiis & portentis, quid attinebat vel mundi statum depravatum, vel factiones in Ec- clesia nominare, quæ omnibus seculis, & longe ante adventum novissimum viguerunt? quemad- modum adv. 28. Grotius ipse notat, & imperii ci- vilis, & Ecclesiæ statum tam miserandum per secula aliquot duraturum, ita explicans, vel potius depra- vans verba ἐρχομένων δὲ τούτων γίνεσθαι. Nam e textu luculentissimum est de signis proxime an- tecessuris consummationem seculi sermonem esse. Ideoque talia prorsus singularia, praeter- & supernaturalia, extraordinaria, antehac nun- quam audita, extremo tempori propria in coe- lo, terra & mari sine dubio designantur, quae ne- mo mortalium antequam eveniant, plene intel- ligere, aut explicare queat. Per virtutes ergo caelorum id quod proprie voces sonant, non Ver- bi ministros, cum Ambrosio, non Angelos cum Origene, Chrysostomo & Theophylacto, non intel- ligentias orbium fictitiorum motrices fictitias, cum Papistis quibusdam, nec cum aliis elementa, quae utique non sunt coelorum virtutes, intelliga- mus. Quae autem praecise notentur δυνάμεις τῶν ὀυρανῶν, an accidentales virtutes, influentiae, & vi- res, an vero substantiales, uti stellae ipsae dicuntur caelorum exercitus Gen. 2,1. Deut. 4, 20. Psal. 33,6. an denique ipsum caeli firmamentum ita designe- tur, quod defecturae sint vires, & influentiae coe- lestes, stellae non mansurae amplius suo loco, fir- mamentum concutiendum, & commovendum sit, & qua ratione illa perturbatio, & commotio se habitura sit, nemo, ut diximus, facile ex- plicabit. Possunt autem illa fortassis non in- commode simul intelligi: quia ut virtutes coe- lestes commoveantur, firmamentum ipsum com- moveri cum suo exercitu Syderum, & virtuti- bus suis, oportet, quorum sede & serie tur- bata influxus cohibetur in inferiora: ut ita no- tetur, omnia ruinam meditatura 2. Petr. III. 10. Psal. CII. 27.

## 21:27
Vers. 27. τότε) After the fulfilled times of the Gentiles about which above.

Latin:

Vers. 27. τότε) Post impleta tempora gentium de qui- bus supra.

## 21:28
Vers. 28. Ἀρχομένων δὲ τούτων γίνεσθαι) When the status of both the civil empire and the Church will be so miserable for several centuries, a true Christian ought not to despair: If the broken world should fall, the ruins will strike him fearless. Christ, as Tertullian beautifully says at this place, placed in the middle, about to conclude one thing with his advent, that is the inconveniences of the nations, and beginning another, that is the prayers of the Saints.

Ἀνακύψατε καὶ ἐπάρατε τὰς κεφαλὰς ὑμῶν) As those are accustomed to do who expect liberation from a higher place. This is what Paul called ἀποκαραδοκίαν: these things, however, as also those which follow below in verse 34 and thereafter, were spoken in the person of the Apostles to all Christians of all ages. Therefore in Mark it is added ἃ δὲ ὑμῖν λέγω, πᾶσι λέγω.

ἐγγίζει ἡ ἀπολύτρωσις) That full liberation by which death will be triumphed over.

Latin:

Vers. 28. Ἀρχομένων δὲ τούτων γίνεσθαι) Cum & imperii ci- vilis & Ecclesiae tam miserandus erit status per secula ali- quot, desperare non debet vere Christianus: Si fractus illabatur orbis Impavidum ferient ruinae. Christus, ut ad hunc locum pulchre inquit Tertullianus, po- situs in medio, alterum conclusurus adventu suo, id est in- commoda nationum, alterum incipiens, id est vota Sancto- rum.

Ἀνακύψατε καὶ ἐπάρατε τὰς κεφαλὰς ὑμῶν) Ut solent qui de loco superiore liberationem exspectant. Hoc est quod ἀποκαραδοκίαν dixit Paulus: haec autem ut & quae infra se- quuntur commate 34. & deinceps, in persona Apostolo- rum dicta sunt omnibus omnium saeculorum Christianis. Ideo apud Marcum additur ἃ δὲ ὑμῖν λέγω, πᾶσι λέ- γω.

ἐγγίζει ἡ ἀπολύτρωσις) Plena illa liberatio qua mors tri- umphabitur.

## 21:30
Vers. 30. ὅταν προβάλωσιν ἤδη) προβάλωσι, the leaves namely, as the comparison of Matthew 24, 32 and Mark 12, 28 shows. Thus Dioscorides said προβάλλειν ὠτὶς.

Ἀφ' ἑαυτῶν,) That is, with no one to warn, as also above c. 12, 57. But the Syrian reads ἀπ' αὐτῶν, from the trees namely.

Latin:

Vers. 30. ὅταν προβάλωσιν ἤδη) προβάλωσι, τὰ φύλλα sci- licet, ut collatio Matth. 24, 32. & Marci 12, 28. ostendit. Sic προβάλλειν ὠτὶς dixit Dioscorides.

Ἀφ' ἑαυτῶν,) Id est nullo monitore, ut & supra c. 12, 57. At Syrus ἀπ' αὐτῶν legit, ab arboribus scilicet.

## 21:31
Vers. 31. ἡ βασιλεία τοῦ θεοῦ) The tranquil possession of the kingdom: thus the Hebrews often called τὸν αἰῶνα τὸν μέλλοντα. Otherwise, it is signified by these words the time of the Messiah in which that kingdom is acquired.

Latin:

Vers. 31. ἡ βασιλεία τοῦ θεοῦ) Tranquilla regni possessio: ita saepe Hebraei vocabant τὸν αἰῶνα τὸν μέλλοντα. Alias si- gnificatur his vocibus tempus Messiae quo regnum illud ac- quiritur.

## 21:32
Vers. 32. πάντα) All those things which concern the Jews and the destruction of the city, in which there is also a figure of the judgments which God is about to exercise against disobedient nations.

Latin:

Vers. 32. πάντα) Omnia illa quae Judaeos & excidium urbis spectant, in quibus & figura est judiciorum quae Deus adversus gentes immorigeras est exerciturus.

## 21:33
Vers. 33. ὁ ὀυρανὸς καὶ ἡ γῆ παρελεύσονται, οἱ δὲ λόγοι μῦ ὀὐ μὴ παρέλθωσι) Elsewhere we have said it is a Hebraism for πρὶν τοὺς λόγους μου παρελθεῖν, and a proverbial kind of speaking as if you were to say: all things will happen that are said to be impossible, rather than that any of these things which I prophesy should become void. See Matth. V. 18. and above XVI. 15.

It is not a proverbial expression: but a prediction concerning the destruction of the world, with the ἀντιθέσει (antithesis) of the eternity of the Word, such as is in Ps. 102:26, 27, 28; Heb. 1:10; and 1 John 2:17. For because Christ previously dealt with his final coming and the shaking of the powers of heaven, with which shaking and coming of Christ the destruction of heaven and earth will be immediately conjoined, these things, as they sound, are to be taken ϑετικῶς (positively) concerning the passing away of heaven and

earth, and not indeed under an impossible hypothesis, as if it were to be the case (if that could happen) that heaven and earth pass away before anything of those things which Christ said passes away or is not fulfilled, even if this sense was also approved by Euthymius: since the substantial destruction of heaven and earth at the consummation of the age is altogether certain, Ps. 102:26 ff., 2 Pet. 3:7, Apoc. 20:11, ch. 21:1. Excellent is Hilary, Can. 16 on Matthew. He says that heaven and earth, which are considered firm, are not to be future, because from the condition of their creation, that is, having proceeded from nothing, they have this necessity in themselves, that they should not be. But the words of Christ cannot not be, because, derived from eternity, they contain in themselves such power that they remain.

Latin:

Vers. 33. ὁ ὀυρανὸς καὶ ἡ γῆ παρελεύσονται, οἱ δὲ λόγοι μῦ ὀὐ μὴ παρέλθωσι) Alibi diximus Hebraismum esse pro πρὶν τοὺς λόγους μου παρελθεῖν, & proverbiale loquendi genus qua- si dicas: omnia fient fieri quae posse negantur potius, quam horum quae vaticinor quicquam irritum fiat. Vide Matth. V. 18. & supra XVI. 15.

Non est proverbialis loquutio: sed praedictio de interitu mundi, cum ἀντιθέσει aeternitatis verbi, qualis est Psal. 102, 26. 27. 28. Ebr. 1, 10. & 1. Job. II. 17. Nam quod antea Christus de novissimo suo adventu, & de commotione virtutum caeli egerit, cum qua commotione, & adventu Christi con- junctus erit immediate caeli terraeque interitus ϑε- τικῶς haec, ut sonant accipienda de transitu caeli &

terra, non vero sub hypothesi impossibili, quasi futu- rum prius sit, (si fieri id possit) ut cælum & terra transeant, quam ut quicquam de iis, quæ Christus dixit transeat, aut non impleatur, etsi hic sensus Euthy- mio etiam probatus fuerit: siquidem omnino cer- tus sit substantialis interitus cæli & terræ sub con- summationem seculi Psal. 102, 26. seqq. 2. Petr 3,7. Apoc. 20, 11. c. 21, 1. Præclare Hilarius Can. XVI. in Matth. Cælum & terram, quæ firma existimantur, ideo non futura ait, quia ex conditione creationis suæ, id est, profecta de nihilo habent id in se necessi- tatis, ut non sint. Verba autem Christi non posse non esse, quia ex æternitate deducta id in se continent vir- tutis, ut maneant.

## 21:34
V. 34. προσέχετε δὲ ἑαυτοῖς (But take heed to yourselves) Luke loves this manner of speaking, as can be seen in ch. 12:1, ch. 17:3, Acts 5:36, ch. 20:28.

μήποτε βαρυνθῶσιν (lest they be weighed down) βαρύνειν corresponds to the Hebrew הכביד, as can be seen in Exod. 8:15, 32, ch. 9:34; the same is also rendered by σκληρύνειν in Exod. 10:1, and by πωροῦν in Rom. 11:7. Moreover, βαρύνεσθαι among these writers signifies being rendered ἀναισθητεῖν (insensible), Ps. 4:3, 'O sons of men, how long will you be βαρυκάρδιοι (heavy-hearted)?' in which place, as in many others, it appears that the LXX interpreters read not a little differently than the Masoretes teach us to read.

ὑμῶν αἱ καρδίαι ἐν κραιπάλῃ καὶ μέθῃ (your hearts in dissipation and drunkenness) The Greek masters teach that μέθη (drunkenness) and κραιπάλη (dissipation/hangover) differ in that μέθη is the alienation of the mind from present drinking, while κραιπάλη, as Plato speaks, is ἐκ τῆς προτεραίας (from the day before). Or, as the scholiast of Aristophanes says, ἀπὸ χθιζῆς οἰνοποσίας (from yesterday's wine-drinking). There is no doubt, however, that under the name of drunkenness every kind of vice is denoted here which is occupied with pleasures. For because the detriment of reason is more manifest in drunkenness, therefore from that species the whole genus is understood: 'For no one who is drunk, if you examine, is not a slave to having drunk,' as Philemon says. Theognis indeed: 'But whoever exceeds the measure of drink, that man is no longer master of his own tongue nor of his mind.' It is well, however, that 'crapula' (dissipation) is joined to drunkenness, so that from this one most illustrious species we may understand that the power of pleasures is such that not only while we enjoy them do they snatch from us the use of reason, but also for the future they render it more obtuse. For the body, burdened with yesterday's vices, weighs down the soul as well.

καὶ μερίμναις βιωτικαῖς (and with life's anxieties). Concerning honors and riches, which elsewhere are αἱ μέριμναι τοῦ αἰῶνος τούτου (the anxieties of this age).

κ' αἰφνίδιος ἐφ' ὑμᾶς ἐπιστῇ ἡ ἡμέρα ἐκείνη (and that day come upon you suddenly) As once happened to the Chaldean king, Dan. 5. Paul to the Thessalonians 3: 'For when they say peace and safety, then sudden destruction comes upon them.' It is often to be observed that Paul uses the same words that Luke uses, so that it is clearly credible that Paul had written down in Greek certain sayings of the Lord which Luke inserted into his book.

But what kind of consequence is this: Luke often uses the same words as Paul, therefore Luke took his own from the Pauline writings? And whence did Paul have those sayings of the Lord written down in Greek? Or if he had them, why did he not share the same with the Church? The discourse and the words which Luke uses were from Θεοπνευστίᾳ (divine inspiration) and divine inspiration: not from certain apocrypha preserved by Paul.

Latin:

V. 34. προσέχετε δὲ ἑαυτοῖς) Amat Lucas hoc loquendi genus, ut videre est cap. XII, 1. cap. XVII, 3. Actor. V, 36. cap. XX. 28.

μήποτε βαρυνθῶσιν) βαρύνειν respondet Hebræo הכביד ut videre est Exod. 8, 15. 3 2. c. 9, 34. idem & per σκληρύνειν red- ditur Exod. X, 1. & per πωροῦν Rom. 11, 7. Significat autem βαρύνεσθαι apud hos scriptores reddi ἀναισθητεῖν, Psal. 4, 3. υἱοὶ ἀνθρώπων ἕως πότε βαρυκάρδιοι, quo in loco ut multis aliis ap- paret LXX. Interpretes non paulo aliter legisse quam nos legere docent Masoritæ.

ὑμῶν αἱ καρδίαι ἐν κραιπάλῃ καὶ μέθῃ) Magistri Græci tradunt hoc differre μέθην & κραιπάλην, quod μέθη sit ex præsenti potu animi alienatio, κραιπάλη ut Plato loqui- tur ἐκ τῆς προτεραίας. Aut, ut Aristophanis Scholiastes ἀπὸ χθιζῆς οἰνοποσίας. Non dubium autem quin sub vinolentiæ nomine omne vitiorum genus hic denotetur quod circa vo- luptates occupatum est. Nam quia in ebrietate manifestius est detrimentum rationis, ideo ex illa specie genus totum datur intelligi: Οὐδεὶς δὲ μεθύων, ἂν σκοπῆς, Ὃς οὐχὶ δοῦλός ἐστι τοῦ πεπωκέναι, ut Philemon inquit. Theognis vero: Ὃς δ' ἂν ὑπερβάλλῃ πόσιος μέτρον οὐκ ἔτ' ἐκεῖνος Τῆς αὑτοῦ γλώσσης καρτερὸς οὐδὲ νόου. Bene autem ebrietati crapula adjungitur, ut ex hac una spe- cie maxime illustri intelligamus eam vim esse voluptatum, ut non tantum dum iis fruimur, usum nobis rationis eri- piant, sed & in posterum eam reddant obtusiorem. Nam Corpus onustum Hesternis vitiis animum quoque prægravat.

καὶ μερίμναις βιωτικαῖς). Circa honores & divitias quæ ali- bi αἱ μέριμναι τοῦ αἰῶνος τούτου.

κ' αἰφνίδιος ἐφ' ὑμᾶς ἐπιστῇ ἡ ἡμέρα ἐκείνη) Ut olim Chal- dæo regi evenit Dan. V. Paulus ad Thess. III. ὅταν γὰρ λέ- gωσιν εἰρήνη καὶ ἀσφάλεια, τότε αἰφνίδιος αὐτοῖς ἐφίσταται ὄλε- θρος. Sæpe illud observare est, iisnem vocibus uti Paulum quibus utitur Lucas, ut plane credibile sit habuisse Paulum descriptos Græce quosdam Domini sermones quos Lucas libro suo inseruerit.

Quænam vero hæc est consequentia: sæpe uti- tur iisdem verbis Lucas quibus Paulus, Ergo desum- sit sua Lucas è Paulinis scriptis? & unde Paulus ser- mones illos Domini Græce descriptos habuit? aut si habuit, cur non eosdem cum Ecclesia com- municavit? Sermo & voces quibus Lucas utitur è Θεοπνευστίᾳ & inspiratione divina erant: non ex apocryphis quibusdam à Paulo asservatis.

## 21:35
Vers. 35. ὡς παγὶς γὰρ ἐπελεύσεται ἐπὶ πάντας τοὺς καθημένους ἐπὶ πρόσωπον πάσης γῆς (For as a snare it will come upon all who sit upon the face of all the earth) From Isa. 24:17, פח עליך יושב הארץ, in Greek παγὶς ἐφ' ὑμᾶς τοὺς ἐνοικοῦντας ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς (a snare upon you who dwell upon the earth): whence it is clear that καθημένους (sitting) here is the same as ἐνοικοῦντας (dwelling): so that a certain secure habitation fixed upon earthly things is understood in this place. See what we said on Matt. 24:37.

Latin:

Vers. 35. ὡς παγὶς γὰρ ἐπελεύσεται ἐπὶ πάντας τοὺς καθημέ- νους ἐπὶ πρόσωπον πάσης γῆς) Ex Es. 24, 17. פח עליך יושב הארץ Græce παγὶς ἐφ' ὑμᾶς τοὺς ἐνοικοῦντας ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς: unde liquet καθημένους hic esse quod ἐνοικοῦντας: ita ut secura quæ- dam & in res terrenas defixa habitatio hoc quidem loco intelligatur. Vide quæ diximus ad Matth. XXIV. v. 37.

## 21:36
Vers. 36. Ἀγρυπνεῖτε οὖν ἐν παντὶ καιρῷ δεόμενοι (Watch therefore at all times, praying) He commends to us two things, especially necessary for Christian men, προσοχὴν καὶ προσευχὴν (attention and prayer): and not only here, but also elsewhere, Matt. 26:32. And from elsewhere and from here it is to be learned how aptly divine help conspires with human diligence. He who is ordered to watch is not treated as a wooden object movable by foreign nerves: he who is ordered to pray is shown to be in need of divine aid, without which all human industry is vain. That ἐν παντὶ καιρῷ (at all times) is best construed with the verb δεόμενοι (praying), so that it is the same as we are warned above, προσεύχεσθαι πάντοτε (to pray always), ch. 18:1, and with Paul, ἀδιαλείπτως (without ceasing), 1 Thess. 5:17.

ἵνα καταξιωθῆτε ἐκφυγεῖν (that you may be counted worthy to escape) Thus above, 'those who are counted worthy to attain that age.' Paul, 2 Thess. 1:5, 'that you may be counted worthy of the kingdom of God.' Let us learn from this the word

καταξιῶσι, as also δίκαιος which follows in the Epistle to the Thessalonians; and the Latin mereri, is generally not referred to the rigor of human law, but to an estimation tempered by kindness. A great part of our dignity is to confess our indignity ingenuously. ταῦτα πάντα τὰ μέλλοντα γενέσθαι) The fallacies of the ψευδοχριστῶν and ψευδοπροφητῶν: the punishments proper to the Jews or other nations: finally, the common punishments of the impious. καὶ σταθῆναι ἔμπροσθεν τοῦ υἱοῦ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου) This expression designates victory, taken from judgments. Thus in Psalm 1, verse 5, the learned explain that לא יקמו. Thus, of him who had succumbed in judgment, it was said לא היתה לו הקומה רגל. Nahum 1, v. 6, ἀπὸ προσώπου ὀργῆς αὐτοῦ τίς ὑποστήσεται; and Ezra 9, verse 15, οὐκ ἔστι στῆναι ἐνώπιόν σου. In both places in the Hebrew is לעמד that is, ἔμπροσθεν, and here indeed it refers to a judge: elsewhere that לעמד refers to an adversary: as in Wisdom 5, v. 1. τότε scήsεται ἐν παῥῥησίᾳ πολλῇ ὁ δίκαιος κατὰ πρόσωπον τῶν θλιψάντων αὐτόν. The contrary to this is to fall, that is, to be put to shame. Thus also the Latins use to stand and to fall: Securus cadat, an recto stet fabula talo.

PART IV. A short account concerning Christ teaching in the Temple by day.

Latin:

Vers. 36. Ἀγρυπνεῖτε οὖν ἐν παντὶ καιρῷ δεόμενοι) Duas no- bis res commendat; Christianis hominibus apprime ne- cessarias, προσοχὴν καὶ προσευχὴν: nec hic tantum, sed & a- libi, Matth. 26, 32. Et aliunde & hinc discere est quam apte conspiret cum humana diligentia auxilium divinum. Qui vigilare jubetur, non agitur ut nervis alienis mobile lignum: qui precari, ostenditur opis divinæ indigere sine qua inanis est omnis hominum industria. Illud ἐν παντὶ καιρῷ optime construitur cum verbo δεόμενοι, ut idem sit quod supra monemur προσεύχεσθαι πάντοτε, cap. 18, 1. & apud Paulum, ἀδιαλείπτως, I. Thess. V. 17.

ἵνα καταξιωθῆτε ἐκφυγεῖν) Ita supra οἱ καταξιωθέντες τοῦ αἰῶνος ἐκείνου τυχεῖν. Paulus 2. Thess. I. 5. εἰς τὸ καταξιω- θῆναι ὑμᾶς τῆς βασιλείας τοῦ θεοῦ. Discamus hinc vocem

καταξιῶσι, ut & δίκαιος quod in Epistola ad Thessalonicen- ses sequitur; & Latinum mereri, plerumque non ad juris humani rigorem referri, sed ad æstimationem benignitate temperatam. Magna pars est dignitatis nostræ indignita- tem nostram ingenue confiteri. ταῦτα πάντα τὰ μέλλοντα γενέσθαι) Fallacias ψευδοχρι- scῶν καὶ ψευδοπροφητῶν: poenas Judæorum aut alia- rum nationum proprias: postremo poenas communes impiourm. καὶ scαθῆναι ἔμπροsθεν τῦ ὑἱῶ τῦ ἀνθρώπε) Victoriam hæc locutio designat à Judiciis sumpta. Sic Psalmo I. vers. 5. docti exponunt illud לא יקמו. Sic de eo qui Judicio suc- cubuerat dicebatur לא היתה לו הקומה רגל. Ne- hum. I. v. 6. ἀπὸ προσώπε ὀργῆς ἀυτῦ τίς ὑποscήsεται; & Esdræ IX. vers. 15. ἐκ ἐscι scῆναι ἐνώπιόν σε. Utrobique in Hebræo est לעמד id est ἑμπροsθεν, & hic quidem ad ju- dicem: alibi illud לעמד ad adversarium refertur: ut Sa- pientiæ V. v. 1. τότε scήsεται ἐν παῥῥησίᾳ πολλῇ ὁ δίκαιος κατὰ πρόσωπον τῶν θλιψάντων αὐτόν. Contrarium huic est ca- dere, id est pudefieri. Sic & Latini stare & cadere usur- pant: Securus cadat, an recto stet fabula talo.

PARS IV. Relatiuncula de Christo interdiu in Templo docente.

## 21:37
Vers. 37. ἠυλίζετο εἰς τὸ ὄρος τῶν ἐλαιῶν) There is no doubt that it was for the sake of prayer: thus, what he commends to us now in speech, now by his own example, are prayers joined with labor. For he spent the day in labor, the night in prayers. Vers. 38. ὤρθριζε) משכם is the Hebrew to which this Hellenistic word corresponds, as in Exodus 34:4 and elsewhere. 'They gathered at dawn,' translates Tertullian. ὤρθριζε πρὸς αὐτὸν is said concisely, as ὀρθρίζωμεν εἰς ἀμπελῶνας in the Song of Songs 7, v. 12. It appears that that admonition of Christ did not lack fruit: ἀγρυπνεῖτε.

Latin:

Vers. 37. ἠυλίζετο εἰς τὸ ὄρος τῶν ἐλαιῶν) Haud du- bium quin orandi causa: ita quod modo sermone, nunc exemplo suo nobis commendat, preces eum labo- re conjunćtas. Nam diem labori, noćtem precibus impen- debat. Vers. 38. ὤρθριζε) משכם est Hebræum cui hoc Helle- nisticum respondet, ut Exodi XXXIV. 4. & alibi. Dilucu- lo conveniebant, vertit Tertullianus. ὤρθριζε πρὸς αὐτὸν concise dićtum, ut ὀρθρίζωμεν εἰς ἀμπελῶνας Cantico VII. v. 12. Apparet non caruisse frućtu monitum illud Christi: ἀγρυπνεῖτε.

## 22:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXII. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

With the priests and Pharisees anxious about removing Christ, Judas offers himself, promising his betrayal. Peter and John are sent to prepare the Passover, and it is celebrated, and furthermore the Holy Supper is instituted, and the traitor is designated. Concerning the contention of the disciples about primacy. Peter's denial predicted, and the impending passion. Concerning the agony of Christ at the Mount of Olives, and the bloody sweat. The betrayal of Judas, the striking of the servant of the High Priest, and his healing. Christ apprehended, and led to the High Priest: denied three times by Peter: who soon deplores his fall. They mock and strike Christ: He is examined, whether he is Christ; and he professes it openly. There are two parts: The former exhibits the antecedents to the passion, namely, I. The promise of Judas to betray Jesus, to v. 6. II. The eating of the Paschal Lamb, to v. 18. III. The celebration of the Holy Supper, to v. 20. IV. The designation of the traitor, to v. 24. V. Admonition of the disciples contending about primacy, to v. 30. VI. Instruction of Simon concerning the sifting of Satan, with the prediction of the denial, to v. 34. VII. Information of the disciples concerning the danger, to v. 38. The other part concerns the history of the passion itself: in which (I.) The journey to the Mount of Olives, to v. 46. (II.) The betrayal of Judas, to v. 48. (III.) The apprehension of Christ, to v. 54. (IV.) The abduction to the house of the High Priest, in which Peter denied Christ, to v. 62. (V.) The mockery of Christ &

striking, to v. 65. (VI.) The examination of Christ in the Sanhedrin, to v. 71.

PART I. Antecedents of the Passion.

(I.) The pact and promise of Judas concerning betraying Christ.

Vers. 1. Ἡ λεγομένη Πάσχα) For synecdochically the whole ἑορτὴ which was of eight days, was called Pascha from the name of the first day. So also Josephus: τῆς πάσχα προσαγορευομένης ἑορτῆς καθ' ἣν ἔθος ἐστιν ἡμῖν ἄζυμα προσφέρεσθαι. John 18:39, ἔστι συνήθεια ὑμῖν, ἵνα ἕνα ὑμῖν ἀπολύσω ἐν τῷ πάσχα, for which Matthew and Mark have κατὰ ἑορτήν.

Latin:

CAPUT XXII. ARGUMENTUM ET PAR- TITIO.

Sacerdotibus, & Pharisæis solicitis de Christo tollendo, Iudas se offert, traditionem ejus- dem promittens. Emittuntur Petrus & Iohannes ad parandum Pascha, idque ce- lebratur, ac porro S. Cœna instituitur, & proditor designatur. De contentione di- scipulorum de primatu. Petrina abnega- tio prædićta, & imminens passio. De ago- ne Christi ad montem Oliveti, & sudore sanguineo. Proditio Iudæ, percussio servi Pontificis, ejusque sanatio. Christus ap- prehensus, & ad Pontificem dućtus: à Pe- tro ter abnegatus: qui lapsum mox deplo- rat. Illudunt ac percutiunt Christum: Examinatur, an Christus sit; idque palam profitetur. Partes sunt duæ: Prior exhibet antecedentia passionem, utpote I. Judæ de Jesu tradendo pol- licitatio, ad v. 6. II. Agni Paschalis comestio, ad v. 18. III. S. Cœnæ celebratio, ad v. 20. IV. Pro- ditoris designatio, ad v. 24. V. Discipulorum contendentium de primatu commonefaćtio, ad v. 30. VI. Simonis de cribratione Satanæ instru- ćtio, cum prædićtione abnegationis, ad v. 34. VII. Discipulorum de periculo informatio, ad v. 38. Altera pars historiam ipsiusmet passionis concernit: in qua (I.) Profećtio ad montem Oliveti, ad v. 46. (II.) Judæ proditio, ad v. 48. (III.) Christi apprehensio, ad v. 54. (IV.) Ad ædes Pontificis abdućtio, in quibus Petrus Chri- stum abnegavit, ad v. 62. (V.) Christi illusio &

percussio, ad v. 65. (VI.) Christi in Synedrio examinatio, ad v. 71.

PARS I. Antecedentia Passionis.

(I.) Judæ de tradendo Christo pactum, & promissio.

Vers. 1. Ἡ λεγομένη Πάσχα) συνεκδοχικῶς enim tota ἑορτὴ quæ erat dierum octo, ex primi diei nomine Pascha nomi- nabatur. Ita & Josephus: τῆς πάσχα προσαγορευομένης ἑορτῆς καθ' ἣν ἔθος ἐστιν ἡμῖν ἄζυμα προσφέρεσθαι. Joh. 18, 39. ἔστι συνήθεια ὑμῖν, ἵνα ἕνα ὑμῖν ἀπολύσω ἐν τῷ πάσχα, pro quo Matthæus & Marcus κατὰ ἑορτήν.

## 22:3
Vers. 3. εἰσῆλθε δὲ ὁ Σατανᾶς εἰς Ἰούδαν) Just as those who piously obey divine motions finally receive the indwelling Spirit, so those who freely consent to the suggestions of the Devil, finally, God abandoning them, become slaves of Satan: and then Satan is said to enter into them. Thus Paul calls the Devil the πνεῦμα ἐνεργοῦν ἐν υἱοῖς ἀπειθείας, Ephesians 2:2. This order is to be observed in Judas: first, tempted by avarice, he bound himself to theft, and indeed in money destined for the poor, John 12:5; and not having enough of that, the sacrilegious man wanted to appear as the defender of those whom he himself was plundering; admonished by his master, he remitted nothing of his malice: then Satan suggested to him that by betraying Christ he might procure gain for himself: εἰς καρδίαν ἀυτοῦ βέβληκε, says John c. 13, 2. After he had consented to this wicked suggestion, Satan is now said to have entered into him: namely, that he might confirm by a pact what he had proposed in his mind, and it is narrated that he entered into him again, deeply indeed, after that man had hardened his heart against the words of Christ at the supper, John 13:27, so that he might now, indeed, fulfill by the deed itself what he had confirmed by a pact. But to those who deny that the defined decree of God concerning events can be defended otherwise than by saying that this whole malice of Judas ran its course from beginning to end by inevitable necessity, and indeed with God inclining and impelling his very will, it can be said with the best right what Irenaeus wrote to Florinus, who taught similar things: ταῦτα τὰ δόγματα Φλωρῖνε, ἵνα πεπεισμένως εἴπω, ὐκ ἐστιν ὑγιοῦς γνώμης: ταῦτα τὰ δόγματα ἀ- σύμφωνά ἐστι τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ, εἰς τὴν μεγίστη ἀσέβειαν περιβάλλον- τα τὲς πειθομένως ἀυτοῖς· ταῦτα τὰ δόγματα ὐδὲ οἱ ἔξω τῆς ἐκ- κλησίας αἱρετικοὶ ἐτόλμησαν ἀποφήνασθαί ποτέ. These doctrines, Florinus, the elders before us, who also associated with the apostles, did not hand down to you. How much wiser is Euripides: Εἰ θεοί τι δρῶσιν αἰσχρὸν ὐκ εἰσὶν θεοί. And Plato: κακῶν αἴτιον φάναι θεόν τινι γεγονέναι, ἀγαθὸν ὄντα δια- μαχητέον παντὶ τρόπῳ μήτε τινὰ ταῦτα λέγειν ἐν τῇ ἑαυτῶ πόλει, εἰ μέλλει ἐυνομήσεσθαι, μήτε τινα ἀκύειν μήτε νεώτερον μήτε πρεσβύτερον, μήτε ἐν μέτρῳ μήτε ἄνευ μέτρου μυθολογῦντα, ὥστε ὐθ' ὅσια ἂν λεγόμενα εἰ λέγοιτο, ὔτε ξύμφορα ἡμῖν, ὔτε ξύμφω- να ἀυτοῖς.

Latin:

Vers. 3. εἰσῆλθε δὲ ὁ Σατανᾶς εἰς Ἰούδαν) Sicut qui divinis motionibus pie obtemperant tandem accipiunt Spiritum inhabitantem, ita qui suggestionib; Diaboli libere consen- tiunt, tandem Deo eos relinquente mancipia Satanæ fiunt: ac tunc in ipsos ingredi Satanas dicitur. Sic Diabolum Pau- lus vocat πνεῦμα ἐνεργοῦν ἐν υἱοῖς ἀπειθείας Ephes. II. 2. Hunc ordinem in Juda observare est: primum avaritia tentatus furti se alligavit, & quidem in pecunia à pauperibus destinata, Johan. 11, 5. neque id satis habens homo sacrilegus, videri voluit eorum defensor quos ipse spoliabat, à magistro ad- monitus de malitia nihil remisit: tum illi suggessit Satanas, ut Christum prodendo lucrum sibi pararet: εἰς καρδίαν ἀυτῶ βέβληκε, inquit Johannes c. 13, 2. Huic sceleratæ suggestio- ni postquam consenserat, jam intrasse in eum Satanas dici- tur: nempe ut quod animo proposuerat, id pacto firma- ret, iterumque intrasse in eum, penitus scilicet, narratur, postquam iste ad Christi in cœna sermones animum obdu- raverat, Joh. 13, 27. ut jam scilicet quod pacto firmaverat re ipsa impleret. Qui vero definitum Dei decretum de eventibus aliter negant posse defendi, nisi tota hæc Judæ malitia ab initio ad finē dicatur decucurrisse inevitabili ne- cessitate, & quidem Deo inclinante atque impellente ipsius voluntatem, his optimo jure dici potest quod similia docen- ti Florino scripsit Irenæus: ταῦτα τὰ δόγματα Φλωρῖνε, ἵνα πεπεισμένως εἴπω, ὐκ ἐστιν ὑγιοῦς γνώμης: ταῦτα τὰ δόγματα ἀ- σύμφωνά ἐστι τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ, εἰς τὴν μεγίστη ἀσέβειαν περιβάλλον- τα τὲς πειθομένως ἀυτοῖς· ταῦτα τὰ δόγματα ὐδὲ οἱ ἔξω τῆς ἐκ- κλησίας αἱρετικοὶ ἐτόλμησαν ἀποφήνασθαί ποτέ. Ταῦτα τὰ δόγμα- Ἰα οἱ πρὸ ἡμῶν πρεσβύτεροι, οἱ καὶ τοῖς ἀποστόλοις συμβαβηκότες, ὐ παρέδωκάν σοι. Quanto sapientis Euripides: Εἰ θεοί τι δρῶσιν αἰσχρὸν ὐκ εἰσὶν θεοί. Et Plato: κακῶν αἴτιον φάναι θεόν τινι γεγονέναι, ἀγαθὸν ὄντα δια- μαχητέον παντὶ τρόπῳ μήτε τινὰ ταῦτα λέγειν ἐν τῇ ἑαυτῶ πόλει, εἰ μέλλει ἐυνομήσεσθαι, μήτε τινα ἀκύειν μήτε νεώτερον μήτε πρεσβύτερον, μήτε ἐν μέτρῳ μήτε ἄνευ μέτρου μυθολογῦντα, ὥστε ὐθ' ὅσια ἂν λεγόμενα εἰ λέγοιτο, ὔτε ξύμφορα ἡμῖν, ὔτε ξύμφω- να ἀυτοῖς.

## 22:4
Verse 4. καὶ τοῖς στρατηγοῖς) These were in the number of the priests: but they are named peculiarly, because it was incumbent upon their office to seize those who sinned against sacred things: he calls the στρατηγὸς the commander with the assistants added to him. For to each office two men were given as servants, as Josephus teaches us in Antiquities IV. See what we have said on this matter at Matthew ch. XXVI. 45.

Latin:

Vers. 4. καὶ τοῖς στρατηγοῖς) Erant hi in sacerdotum nu- mero: sed peculiariter nominantur, quod eorum officio in- cumberet prehendere eos qui in sacra peccarent: στρατηγὸς vocat τὸν στρατηγὸν cum adjutoribus ei additis. Nam ἑκάστῃ ἀρχῇ δύω ἄνδρες ὑπηρέται ἐδίδοντο, ut Josephus nos docet Originum IV. Vide quæ ad Matthæum hac de re diximus c. XXVI. 45.

## 22:6
Verse 6. ἐξωμολόγησε) Theophilus in the Institutes under the title concerning the obligations of words: ταὶ δὲ ἕτερα μεταφράζονται, πρωμίττις, πρωμίττω· τῦτ' ἔστι, ὁμολογεῖς, ὁμολογῶ. The use of the verb ὁμολογεῖν in this meaning is frequent among the Greek orators, but also among Plato.

(II.) The eating of the Paschal Lamb.

Latin:

Vers. 6. ἐξωμολόγησε) Theophilus in institutionibus ti- tulo de verborum obligationibus: ταὶ δὲ ἕτερα μεταφράζονται, πρωμίττις, πρωμίττω· τῦτ' ἔστι, ὁμολογεῖς, ὁμολογῶ. Frequens usus verbi ὁμολογεῖν hoc significatu apud Græcos oratores, sed & apud Platonem.

(II.) Agni Paschalis comestio.

## 22:7
Verse 7. ἡ ἡμέρα τῶν ἀζύμων) The first of the eight days, on which day the unleavened bread began to be eaten before night. ἐν ᾗ ἔδει θύεσθαι τὸ πάσχα) Mark says, ὅτε τὸ πάσχα ἔθυον, that is, on the day on which it was customary for the Passover to be sacrificed: but concerning these things, see Matthew.

Latin:

Vers. 7. ἡ ἡμέρα τῶν ἀζύμων) Primus dierum octo, quo die incipiebant edi azyma ante noctem. ἐν ᾗ ἔδει θύεσθαι τὸ πάσχα) Marcus inquit, ὅτε τὸ πάσχα ἔθυον, id est quo die de more mactari Pascha solebat: sed de his ad Matthæum.

## 22:8
Verse 8. πορευθέντες) Going right now, without waiting for the afternoon time: thus also shortly: ἑτοιμάσατε without any delay interposed.

Latin:

Vers. 8. πορευθέντες) Jam jam euntes, non exspectato tempore pomeridiano: sic & mox: ἑτοιμάσατε nulla mora interposita.

## 22:14
Verse 14. ὅτε ἐγένετο ἡ ὥρα) When it was time to dine, since it was already late at night, as we said at Matthew. Thus Matthew 14:15, ἡ ὥρα ἤδη παρῆλθεν. Thus Paul Rom. 13:11, ὥρα ἡμᾶς ἤδη ἐξ ὕπνου ἐγερθῆναι. Thus ὥρα πορεύεσθαι in Xenophon: ὥρα δημαγωγεῖν in Plutarch.

Latin:

Vers. 14. ὅτε ἐγένετο ἡ ὥρα) Cum tempus esset cœnandi, quippe multa jam nocte, ut ad Matthæum diximus. Sic Matthæus 14, 15. ἡ ὥρα ἤδη παρῆλθεν. Sic Paulus Rom. 13. v. 11. ὥρα ἡμᾶς ἤδη ἐξ ὕπνου ἐγερθῆναι. Sic ὥρα πορεύεσθαι apud Xenophontem: ὥρα δημαγωγεῖν apud Plutarchum.

## 22:15
Verse 15. ἐπιθυμίᾳ ἐπεθύμησα τῦτο τὸ πάσχα φαγεῖν μεθ' ὑμῶν πρὸ τῦ με παθεῖν) As if he were to say: I have hastened to this supper because the time of death is pressing, which is about to take away from me the opportunity τᾶ πασχαλίζειν μεθ' ὑμῶν. Therefore he gives the reason for the anticipated paschal supper, as in Matthew, ὅτι καιρός

μοῖγ' · ἐσὶ' ἐπιθυμίᾳ ἐπιθυμῆσαι, is to burn with a great desire for some thing, as in Gen. XXXI. 30, for which the LXX said ἐπιθυμίαν ἐπιθυμεῖν, Num. XI. 4. The cause of the desire, however, seems to be explained in the following clause: namely, that Christ desired to explain to them what it was that the Paschal ceremony looked toward most especially, and to fix that in their minds through a visible rite.

Latin:

Vers. 15. ἐπιθυμίᾳ ἐπεθύμησα τῦτο τὸ πάσχα φαγεῖν μεθ' ὑμῶν πρὸ τῦ με παθεῖν) Quasi dicat: festinavi ad hanc cœ- nam quia tempus mortis instat,quod mihi erepturum est fa- cultatem τᾶ πασχαλίζειν μεθ' ὑμῶν. Itaque rationem reddit anticipatæ cœnæ paschalis, ut apud Matthæum, ὅτι καιρός

μοῖγ' · ἐσὶ' ἐπιθυμίᾳ ἐπιθυμῆσαι, est magno rei alicujus de- fiderio flagrare, ut Gen. XXXI. 30. pro quo ἐπιθυμίαν ἐπι- θυμεῖν dixerunt LXX. Num. XI. 4. Causa autem desiderii videtur explicari commate sequenti: nempe quod cuperet Christus ipsis explicare, quid esset quo potissimum respi- ceret Paschalis cæremonia, idque per ritum aspectabilem animis ipsorum infigere.

## 22:16
Vers. 16. ἐκ ἐτι ὐ μὴ φάγω ἐξ ἀυτῶ ἕως ὅτε πληρωθῇ ἐν τῇ βασιλείᾳ τῦ Θεῒ] We began to explain this at Matthew. The sense is: I shall not keep the Passover with you until the Passover is fulfilled. But that will happen in the age to come, which is wont to be called by way of excellence the kingdom of God. It must be known, therefore, that the Passover, although it properly signifies that passing over of the destroyer, yet at the same time and consequently signified the liberation from Egyptian servitude: and, if anyone diligently directs his mind to the places of the sacred context in which mention is made of the Passover, he will for the most part see that it looks not so much to the former as to this latter. Josephus: 'At the feast of unleavened bread which the Jews celebrate, having been released from the salvation of the exodus from the slavery under the Egyptians into the ancestral land.' The same elsewhere: 'The feast of unleavened bread is called Pascha, a memorial of the departure from Egypt.' But all that liberation from Egyptian servitude bore the shadow of a liberation, here indeed from sin, but in the other life from death, the wages of sin: wherefore both of these were mystically figured by the Passover. Philo: 'For the Passover has been ordained for those who have crossed over from passions to the exercise of virtue, having their loins girded, being ready for service, and having the fleshy bulk [I mean the sandals] wrapped around firmly and fixedly, with feet standing, and holding the discipline in hand as a staff for the unerring correction of all things in life, and finally being about to be nurtured into God: for the Passover is called the crossing over of the created and corruptible': and elsewhere, 'For they say that they sacrifice the Passover with haste.' Which, being interpreted, is a passing over, which the mind, employing with an unwavering judgment and an intense eagerness, makes an irrevocable passing over from the passions, [and] the thanksgiving toward God the Savior, who delivered it into the freedom it expected. Again in another place: This is, to speak properly, the psychic Passover, the passing over of all passion and of all sensible things toward the just, which is indeed this and divine. Soon after: This is remission, this is the complete freedom of the soul, casting off the error in which it wandered, and anchoring itself toward the unerring nature. Again in another place: Passover is when the soul practices unlearning the irrational according to passion, and willingly suffers the rational good-passion. To the former transition is to be referred that of Paul: our Passover (that is, the passing over from the old leaven into the new lump) Christ was sacrificed, 1 Cor. V. 7. Origen against Celsus VIII. ὅτι δὲ ὁ νοήσας, that our Passover Christ was sacrificed, and it is necessary to feast, eating of the flesh of the Word, there is no time when he does not perform the Passover, which is interpreted as 'passings-over,' crossing over always in his reasoning and in every word and in every deed from the things of life to God. To the latter, that of John V. 24: 'He who hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life, and does not come into judgment, but has passed over from death into life.' For μεταβέβηκεν is פסח, whence for Philo the Passover is τὰ διαβατήρια, for Josephus and Symmachus ὑπέρβασις. And Christ explains this very thing more broadly in John chapter 6. And lest we be ignorant of how each of these crossings-over happens, Christ expressed this very thing in the consecration of the bread and the cup, by those signs placing before our eyes, as it were, his communion with us and our communion with him, and as it were a corporification: for he himself took our faults upon himself, that we might receive his innocence: he himself underwent death for us, that he might endow us with his immortality. The sense therefore of this passage is: now I celebrate the Passover present and visible with you: hereafter I shall not do so. But the time will come when you will see me again, when the thing itself which the Passover designates will be consummated in you through me, the crossing over from the corruptible to the incorruptible: the beginning of which is in this life the crossing over of the psychic to the spiritual.

Latin:

Vers. 16. ἐκ ἐτι ὐ μὴ φάγω ἐξ ἀυτῶ ἕως ὅτε πληρωθῇ ἐν τῇ βασιλείᾳ τῦ Θεῒ] Exponere cœpimus ad Matthæum. Sen- sus est: ὐ παχαλίσομαι μεθ' ὑμῖν εἰμὴ ὅτε πληρωθήσεται τὸ πάσχα. id autem fiet ἐν τῷ ἀιῶνι τῷ μέλλοντι, qui κατ' ἐξοχὴν solet vocari βασιλεία τῦ Θεῦ. Sciendum ergo Pascha, quan- quam proprie significat transitum illum τῦ ὀλοτρευτῦ, simul tamen & ex consequenti significasse liberationem ex Ægy- ptiaca servitute: ac, si quis diligenter advertat animum ad sacri contextus loca, in quibus Paschatis fit mentio, plerum- que videbit, non tam prius illud quam posterius hoc respici. Josephus: κατὰ τὴν ἑορτὴν τῶν ἀζύμων ἣν ἄγωσιν Ἰυδαῖοι, σω- τήρια ἐξόδε τῆς ὑπ' ἀἰγυπτίοις δυλείας ἀνεθέντες εἰς τὴν πάτριον γῆν. Idem alibi: ἀζύμων ἑορτὴ Φάσκα καλέται, ὑπόμνημα τῆς ἐξ ἀἰγύπτε ἐπάρσεως. Tota autem ista liberatio ex Ægy- ptiaca servitute umbram ferebat liberationis, hic quidem à peccato, in vita autem altera à morte peccati stipendio: quare & per pascha utrumq; hoc μυσικῶς figurabatur. Philo: κὴ γὰρ τὸ πάσχα τοῖς ἐκ παθῶν εἰς ἄσκησιν ἀρετῆς διαβᾶσιν προσε τέτακται ποιεῖσθαι, τὰς ὀσφῦς περιεζωσμένοις, ἑτοίμως πρὸς ὑπη- ρεσίαν ἔχοντας κὴ τὸν σάρκινον ὄγκον, [τὰ ὑποδήματα λέγω, περιει- ληφότας ἀκλινῶς κὴ παγίως, ἑσῶσι τοῖς πόσι καὶ τὴν παιδείαν διὰ χειρὸς ἔχοντας ῥάβδον πρὸς τὴν ἐν τῷ βίῳ πραγμάτων πάντων ἀπταισον καλόρθωσιν, κἀπὶὸ τελευταῖον μέλλοντας εἰς ἐντραφῆναι· διάβασις γάρ ἐστι Θεὸν τῶ γενητᾶ καὶ φθαρτᾶ τὸ πάσχα εἴρηται: & alibi, φασὶ γὰρ μετὰ σπεδῆς θύειν τὸ πάσχα. τὸ δ' ἐστι ἑρμηνευ- θὲν διάβασις, ἣν ἀνενδοίασῳ γνώμῃ καὶ προθυμίας συντόνῳ χρώμενος ὁ νῦς τήντε ἀπὸ τῶν παθῶν ἀμετασρεπτὶ ποίηται διά- βασις, τὴν πρὸς τὸν σωτῆρα Θεὸν ἐυχαρισίαν, ὃς εἰς ἐλευθερί- αν ὦ προσδοκήσασα ἀυτὸν ἐξείλετο. Rursum alio loco: τῦτ' ἐσι κυριως εἰπεῖν τὸ ψυχικὸν Πάσχα, ἡ πάντων πάθος καὶ πάντω ἀιστητῶ διάβασις πρὸς τὸ δίκαιον, ὃ δὴ τοῦτόν ἐσι καὶ θεῖον. Mox, τῦτ' ἐσιν ἄφεσις, τῦτ' ἐλευθερία παντελὴς ψυ- χῆς, ὃν ἐπλανήθητε πλάνον ἀποσεομένης, καὶ πρὸς τὴν ἀπλα- νῆ φύσιν μεθορμιζομένης. Iterum alio loco, Πάσχα δ' ἐσιν ὅταν ἡ ψυχὴ τὸ μεν ἄλογον παθῶς ἀπομαθεῖν μελετᾷ, τὴν δὲ ἔνλογον ἐυπάθειαν ἑκουσίως πάσχῃ. Ad priorem transitum referendum illud Pauli: τὸ πάσχα ἡμῶν (id est ἡ διάβασις ἐκ τῆς παλαίας ζύμης εἰς τὸ νεὸν φύραμα) ἐθύθη χριστὸς, 1. Cor. V. 7. Origenes adversus Celsum VIII. ὅτι δὲ ὁ νοήσας, ὅτι τὸ πάσχα ἡμῶν ἐθύθη χριστὸς, καὶ χρὴ ἑορτάζειν, ἐσθίοντα τῆς σαρκὸς τῦ λόγε ἐκ ἐσι ὅτε ἐ ποιεῖ τὸ πάσχα, ὅπερ ἑρμηνεύεται διαβατήρια, διαβαίνων ἀεὶ τῷ λογισμῷ καὶ παντὶ λόγῳ κὴ πάσῃ πράξει ἀπὸ τῶν τῦ βίε πραγμάτων ἐπὶ τὸν Θεόν. Ad posterio- rem, illud Joh. V. 24. ὁ τὸν λόγον με ἀκέων καὶ πιστεύων τῷ πέμψαντί με ἔχει ζωὴν ἀιώνιον, καὶ ἐις κρίσιν ἐκ ἔρχεται, ἀλλὰ μεταβέβηκεν ἐκ τῶ θανάτε ἐις τὴν ζωὴν. Nam μεταβέβηκεν est פסח unde Pascha Philoni τὰ διαβατήρια, Josepho & Symmacho ὑπέρβασις. Idque ipsuni latius explicat Chri- stus Johannis cap. 6. Ac ne ignoraremus quomodo fiat utraque hæc μετάβασις, expressit hoc ipsum Christus in consecratione panis & poculi, per ea signa nobis velut ob oculos ponens suam nobiscum & nostram secum commu- nitatem & quasi concorpörationẽ: nam ipse culpas nostras in se suscepit, ut nos ipsius innocentiam acciperemus: ipse pro nobis mortem obivit, ut nos immortalitate sua donaret. Sensus igitur hujus loci est: nunc præsens ac conspicuus vobiscum pascha celebro: posthac id non fa- ciam. Sed veniet tempus cum me iterum conspicietis, cum res ipsa quam Pascha designat, in vobis per me con- summabitur τῇ διαβάσῃ [? illegible] φθαρτᾶ εἰς τὸ ἄφθαρτον: cujus in- itium est in hac vita ἡ διάβασις τῶ ψυχικᾶ εἰς τὸ πνευμα- τικόν.

## 22:17
Vers. 17. καὶ δεξάμενος τὸ ποτήριον) According to the custom of the Paschal supper: for it was drunk in a circle several times during the supper, and finally after the supper. Nor is there any reason why we should hold these two clauses suspect, since both Greek and Latin codices acknowledge them, and Arabic ones: but also some of the Syriac: the narrative of Matthew, which recounts these sayings of Christ not in order of time, but for the sake of brevity on occasion, gave some cause for interpolating, concerning which matter we have warned at Matthew.

διαμερίσατε ἑαυτοῖς) As often as the head of the household could not reach the cup to everyone, those nearest passed it from hand to hand to those further away, and that was held to be just as if each had received the cup from the hand of the head of the household.

Latin:

Vers. 17. καὶ δεξάμενος τὸ ποτήριον) Ex more cœnæ pa- schalis: nam & in cœna aliquoties, & postremo post cœ- nam in orbem bibebatur. Nec est, quod duo hæc com- mata suspecta habeamus, cum & Græci codices & La- tini agnoscant, & Arabici: sed & Syricorum nonnulli: interpolandi causam nonnullis præbuit Matthæi narratio, hos Christi sermones non ex temporis ordine, sed brevita- tis causa ex occasione recensentis, qua de re ad Matthæum monuimus.

διαμερίσατε ἑαυτοῖς) Quoties omnibus porrigere po- culum paterfamilias non poterat, proximi remotiöri- bus de manu in manum tradebant, idque perinde habe- batur, quasi singuli ex patrisfamilias manu poculum acce- pissent.

## 22:18
Vers. 18. ἕως ὅτῳ ἡ βασιλεία τῦ Θεῦ ἔλθῃ) See what [we wrote] at Matth.

Others think this circular cup was not Paschal, but a valedictory one, used peculiarly by Christ, to admonish the disciples that this was the last supper, and the last banquet, which he was to celebrate with them in these lands, and in this state indeed: but some, with Tatian and Ammonius, say that this is the very Eucharistic cup which is commemorated in verse 20. And indeed this opinion of Tatian could seem probable for certain reasons. However, we judge the opinion of those who distinguish this circular cup from the Eucharistic one to be truer: because Luke distinctly commemorates both: he indicates not obscurely that the former was also tasted and offered by Christ himself, and thus ordered to go in a circle at the table, and joined with the Paschal lamb in verses 16 and 17; but he teaches that this latter was offered by Christ to the individual disciples after the preceding blessing, once the Paschal Supper was finished. Meanwhile, let us judge that that cup was offered not so much from a rite received among the Jews, which rested on no divine law, but for the sake of a peculiar signification and valediction. For he did not bind himself to Jewish rites which were destitute of divine command.

(III.) The celebration of the Holy Eucharist.

Latin:

Vers. 18. ἕως ὅτῳ ἡ βασιλεία τῦ Θεῦ ἔλθῃ) Vide quæ ad Matth.

Alii poculum circulare hoc non Paschale, sed valedictorium fuisse putant, à Christo peculia- riter adhibitum, ut admoneret discipulos hanc esse ultimam cœnam, & ultimum convivium, quod in his terris, & in hoc quidem statu cum ipsis celebraturus sit: nonnulli vero cum Ta- tiano & Ammonio hoc ipsum esse poculum Eucha- risticum ajunt, quod vers. 20. commemora- tur. Et sane verisimilis ex quibusdam causis vi- deri possit hæc Tatiani sententia. Veriorem tamen censemus eorum mentem qui poculum hoc κυκλικὸν ab Eucharistico distinguunt: quia Lucas distincte utrumque commemorat: illud etiam à Christo ipso gustatum ac propinatum haud obscure indicat, atque ita in orbem men- sæ ire jussum, & cum agno Paschali conjun- ctum vers. 16. 17. hoc vero finita Paschali Cœ- na à Christo singulis discipulis post præviam be- nedictionem præbitum docet. Interim non tam è ritu penes Judæos recepto, qui nulla lege nite- batur divina, quam peculiaris significationis, & valedictionis causa poculum illud propina- tum esse, censeamus, Non enim ritibus Judai- cis sese obstringebat, qui mandato divino desti- tuebantur.

(III.) Sacræ Eucharistiæ celebratio.

## 22:19
V. 19. τὸ ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν διδόμενον (given for you); Paul said κλώμενον (broken): in both, allusion is made to both the bread and the victims. Bread is broken and given: victims also were given by those offering, then they were broken at the altar. Thus also Christ gave his body, when he patiently endured death for our sake, which is said elsewhere dῦναι τὴν ψυχὴν ἀυτῦ, Matthew XX. 28. That same body was also broken, when his hands and feet were pierced with nails, add also the side transfixed. The present is used for the immediate future, as also in the word ἐκχυνόμενον: concerning which matter we have advised at Matthew.

τῦτο ποιεῖτε εἰς τὴν ἐμὴν ἀνάμνησιν (do this in remembrance of me) That is, celebrate by this rite the memory of the death which I am about to undergo. Christ in this place and elsewhere the Apostles bid us remember the death of Christ rather than his life (although also his life), because in his death, both his obedience and his love toward the human race shine forth remarkably.

Latin:

V. 19. τὸ ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν διδόμενον) κλώμενον dixit Paulus: in utroq; & ad panem & ad victimas alluditur. Panis frangitur & datur: victimæ quoque dabantur ab offerentibus, de- inde frangebantur id altari. Ita & Christus corpus suum dedit, cum mortem patienter nostri causa pertulit, quod alibi dicitur dῦναι τὴν ψυχὴν ἀυτῦ, Matthæi XX. 28. fra- ctum quoque est idipsum corpus, cum manus pedesque clavis sunt perfossi, adde & latus transfixum. Præsens po- situm pro proxime futuro, ut etiam in verbo ἐκχυνόμενον: qua de re ad Matthæum monuimus.

τῦτο ποιεῖτε εἰς τὴν ἐμὴν ἀνάμνησιν) Id est hoc ritu celebrate mortis, quam jamjam subiturus sum, memoriam. Christus hoc loco & alibi Apostoli mortis po- tius Christi quam vitæ (quanquam & vitæ) meminisse nos jubent, quia in morte, & obedientia ejus & amor erga genus humanum eximie elucet.

## 22:20
Vers. 20. μετὰ τὸ δειπνῆσαι (after supper) As was the custom of the Jews, just as we have said at Matthew. The same is to be seen as customary also among profane nations. Thus in Virgil in the sacrifice of Evander after the tables are removed it follows: And offer cups with your right hands.

Christ did not distribute the Eucharistic cup according to the custom of the Jews, much less of profane nations, but he here instituted by divine authority a new Sacrament, clearly proper to the New Testament: which has no connection with the Paschal cup introduced by the Jews, nor is it compared without impiety to the rites of profane nations.

τῦτο τὸ ποτήριον ἡ καινὴ διαθήκη ἐν ἁυτῷ ματί (this cup is the new testament in my blood) With a similar locution Stephen said διαθήκης περιτομῆς (covenant of circumcision) Acts 7. 8. that is, περιτομὴν εἰς σημεῖον διαθήκης (circumcision as a sign of the covenant), as we read concerning the rainbow in Gen. IX, 12. or εἰς σφραγῖδα (as a seal) as Paul speaks. Tertullian, citing this passage, does not poorly express the meaning by saying the testament sealed with his blood. The Hebrews say that those things which are sealed with blood cannot be erased. See Esther Rabba.

τὸ ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν ἐκχυνόμενον (which is shed for you) The construction is such as we have already noted several times πρὸς τὸ σημαινόμενον (according to the meaning). For because διαθήκη ἐν ἁιματι (testament in blood) and ἁιμα διαθήκης (blood of the testament) are the same, as Matthew and Mark speak in this place after Moses and Zechariah, therefore he introduced τὸ ἐκχυνόμενον (which is shed) as if he had said ἁιμα διαθήκης (blood of the testament). Thus Matt. 28, 91. when ἐθνη (nations) had preceded, ἀυτὲς (them) follows. Similar are: Where is the crime, who destroyed me? Likewise: Let us each take an equal share: you the one, and I indeed the other. Thus Prov. 4, 13. the construction is as if for ותרפה (and let go) there were written מוסר (instruction). Not dissimilar kinds of speaking are to be observed in Gen. IV. 10. Job. XXIX. 10. ch. XXXII. 7. ch. XXXIII. 2. ch. XXXV. 9. ch. XXXVII. 10. Ps. X. 2.

If this interpretation should prevail, the words will be thus: τῦτο τ' ποτήριον τ' αἷμα τ̃ διαθήκης τ̃ ὑπὲρ ὑ- μῶν ἐκχυνόμενον (this cup is the blood of the testament which is shed for you). That, however, was not τ̃ σημαινόμε- νον (the meaning). For Christ did not intend that: that the cup is his Blood; but that this, which he was offering to be drunk, is his Blood, as the other Evangelists have it. And when the Apostle puts the cup in the place of the subject, he does not say that it is the Blood of Christ, but κοινωνίαν τ̃ αἵματος, the communion of the Blood of Christ, 1 Cor. 10:16. Therefore, it is called τὸ ποτήριον ἐκχυνόμενον, the cup poured out for us: not of itself, but because of the blood which it contains, or by reason of the Blood of Christ, which through this is offered to the Apostles to be drunk. For the cup poured out for us cannot be said to be so because of the wine, which was likewise offered from it: because wine, indeed, was not poured out for us for the remission of sins. And therefore it is said to be poured out for us because of the Blood which Christ offered by means of the cup: But we have dealt with this proposition expressly in the Stereoma of the words of Christ, which may be compared here on page 170 et seqq. of the second edition.

(IV.) The designation of the betrayer.

Latin:

Vers. 20. μετὰ τὸ δειπνῆσαι) Ut mos erat Judæorum, quemadmodum ad Matthæum diximus. Idem videre est & apud prophanas gentes usitatum. Ita apud Virgilium in Evandri sacrificio post mensas remotas sequitur: Et po- cula porgite dextris.

Non ex more Judæorum, nedum gentium prophanarum poculum Eucharisticum distribuit Christus, sed novum plane Sacramentum Nov. Te- stamenti proprium authoritate divina hic insti- tuit: quod nihil commercii habet cum pocu- lo Paschali à Judæis invecto, nec citra impie- tatem cum gentium prophanarum ritibus com- paratur.

τῦτο τὸ ποτήριον ἡ καινὴ διαθήκη ἐν ἁυτῷ ματί μ ) Simi- li locutione διαθήκης περιτομῆς dixit Stephanus Actior. 7. 8. id est περιτομὴν εἰς σημεῖον διαθήκης, ut de iride legimus Gen. IX, 12. aut εἰς σφραγῖδα ut Paulus loquitur. Tertullianus hunc locum citans non male sententiam exprimit dicens testamentum sanguine suo obsignatum. Quæ sanguine signata sunt, deleri non posse ajunt Hebræi. Vide Esther Rabba.

τὸ ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν ἐκχυνόμενον) Constructio est, qualem aliquoties jam annotavimus πρὸς τὸ σημαινόμενον. Nam quia idem est διαθήκη ἐν ἁιματι & ἁιμα διαθήκης, ut hoc loco post Mosem & Zachariam, Matthæus & Marcus loquuntur, ideo τὸ ἐκχυνόμενον intulit quasi ἁιμα διαθήκης dixisset. Sic Matth. 28, 91. cum præcessat ἐθνη sequitur ἀυτὲς. Simi- lia sunt: Ubi est scelus, qui me perdidit? Item: Curemus æquam uterque partem: tu alterum, ego vero alterum. Sic Prov. 4, 13. constructio est quasi pro ותרפה scriptum esset מוסר. Non dissimilia loquendi genera observare est Gen. IV. 10. Job. XXIX. 10. cap. XXXII. 7. c. XXXIII. 2. c. XXXV. 9. c. XXXVII. 10. Ps. X. 2.

Si hæc interpretatio obtineat, ita habebunt ver- ba τῦτο τ' ποτήριον τ' αἷμα τ̃ διαθήκης τ̃ ὑπὲρ ὑ- μῶν ἐκχυνόμενον. Id vero non erat τ̃ σημαινόμε- νον. Non enim Christus id volebat: quod poculum sit Sanguis suus; sed quod hoc, quod præbebat biben- dum, Sanguis suus sit, ut habent rei qui Evangeli- stæ. Et quum Apostolus subjecti locum poculum po- nit, non dicit id esse Sanguinem Christi, sed κοινω- νίαν τ̃ αἵματος, communionem Sanguinis Christi, 1. Cor. X. 16. dicitur ergo τὸ ποτήριον ἐκχυνόμενον, poculum effusum pro nobis: non per se, sed propter ἅιμα, quod continet, vel Sanguinis Christi ratione, qui per hoc populum bibendus Apostolis præbe- tur. Non enim potest poculum effusum pro nobis dici propter vinum, quod ex eo itidem præbeba- tur: quia vinum utique pro nobis in remissionem peccatorum effusum non est. Ideoque dicitur ef- fusum pro nobis propter Sanguinem, quem Chri- stus mediante poculo præbebat: Sed de hac pro- positione egimus ex professo in Stereomate verbo- rum Christi, quod hic conferatur pag. 170. seqq. edit. secundæ.

(IV.) Proditoris designatio.

## 22:21
Verse 21. πλὴν ἰδὲ] Luke connects various sayings of Christ without regard for order. For that matter about the betrayer happened at the proper supper; the admonition about avoiding ambition clearly, as is credible, occurred during the washing between the paschal supper and the proper supper. Thus πλὴν is often a transitional particle for Luke. ἡ χεὶρ τ̃ παραδιδόντος με] I do not think that the hand is taken here for counsel, as in 2 Sam. 14:19. But rather it is said that his hand is on the table with Christ, because he was taking common food with Christ. Matthew: ὁ ἐμβάψας μετ' ἐμῦ ἐν τῷ τρυβλίῳ τὴν χεῖρα.

It is said rashly that Luke had no regard for order. Much more rightly have the more accurate compilers of the Evangelical Harmonies noted that Luke observed the order accurately here. The action with the betrayer did not happen at the proper supper, but after the Eucharist was instituted, as St. Luke reports. For although Matt. 26:21 and Mark 14:18 claim that it happened ἐσθιόντων ἀυτῶν, yet this aorist easily admits the meaning of the past, so that the order of Luke may be preserved; and although it is evident from the Evangelical harmony that not only the common, but also the Sacramental supper had already been finished when Christ indicated his betrayer, yet the table had not yet been removed, but the unleavened bread, wine, and the dipping sauce accustomed to be set out at the feast of the Passover were still on the table, and therefore for that reason the banquet was still continuing.

As for the admonition about avoiding ambition, although it happened at the washing of the feet, yet the washing of the feet was not done before the proper and common supper, but after it, even if before the Sacramental Supper: because in all the ancient codices, with only one exception, John 13:2, it is expressly stated that after the supper was finished, the washing of the feet was instituted. Therefore it did not happen before the common supper. And Christ preferred to perform this after the Supper, so that it might signify that it was done not for the sake of custom and by received habit, but because of a mystery: as He said to Peter: What I do now, you do not know for now, but you shall know hereafter. The particle πλὴν has its full force in this place, concerning which see the blessed Gerhard, Harm. chap. CLXXII, p. 1. The particle πλὴν, 'nevertheless,' by which Luke joins this complaint about the betrayer with the preceding, shows that Christ wished to exaggerate the wickedness and ingratitude of Judas the betrayer by the same: Although I have shown you all huge and clearly singular benefits, by raising you to the pinnacle of Apostolic dignity, by instructing you in my school for over three years, by providing abundantly for you in all necessities, by instructing you in the gift of performing miracles, and just now by admitting you to my table, washing your feet, and distributing to you the most holy Sacrament of my body and blood, yet one of you will betray me, which all sensible people, even with me silent, understand to be a horrible and detestable crime.

Latin:

Vers. 21. πλὴν ἰδὲ] Diversos Christi Sermones nulla or- dinis habita ratione Lucas connectit Nam illud de prodi- tore, in cœna justa contigit; admonitio de vitanda ambitio- ne plane, ut credibile est, in lotione inter cœnam paschalē & cœnam justam. Ita πλὴν sæpe Lucæ est μεταβατικὸν. ἡ χεὶρ τ̃ παραδιδόντος με] Non puto manum hic pro consilio accipi, ut 2. Sam. XIV. 19. Sed potius dici manum ejus esse in mensa cum Christo, quia cibum cum Christo communem sumebat. Matthæus ὁ ἐμβάψας μετ' ἐμῦ ἐν τῷ τρυβλίῳ τὴν χεῖρα.

Nullam habuisse Lucam ordinis rationem, te- mere dicitur. Longe rectius accuratiores Har- moniæ Evangelicæ textores Lucam hic accurate ordinem observasse, annotarunt. Actio cum pro- ditore non in cœna justa, sed post institutam Eu- charistiam, uti refert S. Lucas contigit. Etsi enim Matth. XVI, 21. & Marc. XIV. 18. eam contigisse ἐσθιόντων ἀυτῶν perhibent, hic tamen aoristus si- gnificationem præteriti facile admittit, ut ordo Lucæ servetur; & quamvis ex harmonia Evange- lica constet, non vulgarem tantum, sed & Sacra- mentalem cœnam jam finitam fuisse, cum Christus proditorem suum indicaret, nondum tamen re- mota fuit mensa, sed panis azymus, vinum, & em- bamma in Paschatos festo apponi solitum adhuc in mensa erant, ideoque ea ratione adhuc durabat convivium.

Quod ad admonitionem de vitanda ambitione, etsi ea in lotione pedum contigerit, non tamen pe- dum lotio ante cœnam justam & communem fa- cta est, sed post eandem, utut ante Cœnam Sacra- mentalem: quia in vetustis Codicibus omnibus, uni- co tantum excepto, Joh. 13. 2. diserte habetur ἐκγε- νομένης Cœna facta, lotionem pedum institutā esse. Non ergo ante cœnam communem ea conti- git. Et post Cœnam maluit Christus hoc perage- re, ut non consuetudinis causa, & more recepto, sed ob mysterium id fieri significaret: uti Petro dixit: Quod nunc facio, tu nescis modo, scies autem postea. Particula πλὴν vim suam integram habet hoc loco, de quo B. Gerhard. Harm. cap. CLXXII. p. 1. Particula πλὴν veruntamen, qua Lucas hanc de proditore querelam cum præcedentibus conjun- git, ostendit Christum eadem scelus & ingratitudi- nem Judæ proditoris exaggerare voluisse: Etsi vobis omnibus ingentia & plane singularia beneficia exhi- bui, ad Apostolica dignitatis fastigium vos evehendo, in Schola mea ultra triennium vos instituendo, de necessariis omnibus abunde vobis prospiciendo, dono miracula edendi vos instruendo, ac modo mensæ meæ vos adhibendo, pedes vestros abluendo & sanctissi- mum corporis & sanguinis mei Sacramentum vobis distribuendo, unus tamen ex vobis tradet me, quod esse scelus horribile & detestabile, omnes cordati, etiam me tacente intelligunt.

## 22:22
Verse 22. πορεύεται] הֹלֵךְ, that is, he is dying, as we said in Matthew.

According to that which is determined.

What Grotius holds against the absolute decrees of the Calvinists, even if names are silent, is correct: If you except that which rejects the distinction between the act and the disorder adhering to the act, which, when applied in its proper place, cannot be rejected, and in some places is even absolutely necessary. But this is how Grotius is here.

τῇ ὡρισμένῃ βουλῇ, Acts 2:23. Moreover, in these places ὁρίζειν is the same as προορίζειν, as in Acts 2:23, ch. 10:42, ch. 17:26, 31. But this determined counsel concerning the death of Christ was not without all foreknowledge; indeed, in the cited place of Acts, ὡρισμένῃ βουλῇ and πρόγνωσις are joined. And Justin, in his disputation against Trypho, solves that objection, 'that it was necessary for Christ to be crucified and for those who transgress to be in the race of the Jews,' in this way: 'that God, foreknowing that they would be wicked, did not make them so.' For God, to whom not only those things which are inevitably to be are most well known, but also those which can happen, was not ignorant that there would never be lacking men who would not only not spurn a doctrine of truth contrary to their own advantages, but would also persecute it with cruel hatred. Furthermore, that determined decree is said to have been made concerning the event, not concerning the actions of men, which, when offered, God used for the event. The Apostles clearly distinguish in the hymn which is in Acts 4:28, where Pilate and Herod are said to have gathered together to do ὅσα ἡ χείρ σε θεῦ κὴ ἡ βουλὴ αὐτῦ προώρησε, not to do it themselves, but that it should come to pass. If we ask about the actions themselves of Judas, Pilate, and Herod, it is certain that not even those happened without the Father, since without Him not even a sparrow falls, but the will of God concerning them was permissive, not efficient, which distinction is much more consistent with both the Holy Scriptures and the opinion of all ancient Christians than that which pleases some, who distinguish the action from the vice that is in the action, which in many actions, for instance theft, adultery, and others, the very name of which cannot be understood without vice, is repugnant to the nature of things. Nor are those more to be heard who say that such actions can be procured by God impelling them for a good end, since the end alone cannot make actions right, or even such decrees which antecedently place an absolute necessity upon such actions. Equally to be rejected is the opinion of those who think that God rightly does these things because He is bound by no law: for some things are evil even apart from law, and to procure, while its obligation is placed and remains, that someone should act against the law, is naturally evil and therefore repugnant to the nature of God. Add that, this being posited, the name of sin is rendered empty, since it is impossible to sin in that which the best God has willed us to do by a decree forestalling the freedom of our will. How much more rightly it was to say with Paul εἴασεν ὁ θεὸς τὰ ἔθνη πορεύεσθαι ταῖς ὁδοῖς ἀυτῶν Act. XIV, 16. and if there are any obscure things elsewhere, to expound them according to that form, which we see all the ancients have done.

These are the words of Grotius: who adduced here Clement Strom. VIII. Origen against Celsus VII. where he says that those things which are done wickedly are not ἐκ προνοίας but κατ’ ἐπακολούθησιν: Cyprian, Salvian, Chrysostom, and finally the writer of the responses to the Greeks in the works of Justin: And he refers here also, not undeservedly, to that which all the ancients constantly hand down, that no necessity of acting is imposed upon men by divine foreknowledge: for that would be of no use if foreknowledge itself were supported by purely effective decrees: and that the contrary opinion is found to be condemned everywhere by great consensus. With which compare what we have argued against the Calvinists in Tom. II. Syst. Theol. cap. X. quæst. V. The Grotian words are as follows:

Clement Strom. VIII. Τὸ μὴ κωλύον ἀνενεργητόν ἐσιν. διὸ ἐκ ἔσιν αἴτιον τὸ μὴ κωλῦον, ἀλλὰ τὸ κωλῦον. ἐν γὰρ τῷ ἐνεργεῖν κὴ δρᾶν τι τὸ αἴτιον νοεῖται. Origen against Celsus VII. ὁρᾶτε τὴν ἀτοπίαν ὁ τῦτο λέγων, τῶ πάντα κατὰ γνώμην διοικεῖσθαι τῶ θεῶ. ἀκολυθεῖ γὰρ τῷ λόγῳ κᾀτὰ ἁμαρτανόμενα κᾀ πάντα τὰ ἀπὸ κακίας κατὰ γνώμην διοικεῖσθαι τῶ θεῶ, ὅπερ & ἴαυτον ἐσὶ τῷ, & κωλύοντος τῶ θεῶ γίνεται. Soon after he says that those things which are done wickedly are not ἐκ προνοίας, but κατ’ ἐπακολύθησιν τῶν ἐκ προνοίας. Cyprian: Since He Himself is the Lord, knower, and ruler of the world, and all things are carried out by His will and nod, nor can anything be done unless He has done it or permitted it to be done. Salvian: Divine disposition has ordained some of these things in this way, and has endured some by patience. Chrysostom: ἐδὲν ἀγνοῶντος ἀυτᾶ γίνεται, ἀλλ’ εἰδότος μὲν ἅπαντα, ἐ μὴν πάντα ἐνεργῦντος. The writer of the responses to the Greeks in the works of Justin: συγχωρῇ τε ἡμᾶς πράττειν ἃ ἑκασίως αἱρεόμεθα κακὰ, & διὰ τὴν ἀσθένειαν τῆς ἀυτῦ δυνάμεως, ἀλλ’ ἵνα τὸ ἡμῶν ἀυθαίρετον κᾀ τὸ ἀυτῶ μακρόθυμον δειχθῇ. To this must also be referred that which all the ancients constantly maintain, that no necessity of acting is imposed upon men by divine foreknowledge: for that would be of no use if the foreknowledge itself were supported by purely effective decrees. Origen, disputing against Celsus whether it is rightly said that it was altogether necessary for the aforementioned thing to happen, accurately distinguishes the word altogether. For if he understands altogether as meaning by necessity, we will not grant it to him. For it was possible for it not to happen. But if he says altogether as meaning the same thing which is hindered from being true even if it were possible for it not to happen, it does not trouble the argument. The same Origen had treated this in the third tome on Genesis with not dissimilar words, adding the example of Judas, about whom this passage of Luke is especially concerned: for if altogether is equal to saying that it was fated, so that there is a necessity for the foreknown thing to happen, we do not grant it to him. For we will not say, since it was foreknown that Judas would become a traitor, that there was any necessity for Judas to become a traitor. In that the reproaches and accusations of Judas are written in the prophecies concerning Judas, it will show to everyone his blameworthy nature. But he would not have attached blame to him if he were a traitor by necessity, even if it were not possible for him to become like the rest of the apostles. Soon after: But if anyone will explain that altogether means this, saying that it means that perhaps some things were so, but it was possible for them to happen otherwise, we concede this as true. For it is not possible for God to lie; but it is possible for Him to think about things that are possible to happen and not to happen, that they happen or do not happen.
