Which he pursues more broadly in the same place, not reproved by any of the ancients in this part of the errors: indeed, very many writers have handed down the same thing clearly on this passage: and Chrysostom in his oration on why prophecies are obscure: For foreknowledge, O man, is not the cause of wickedness; God forbid; for it is not compulsive of things that are to be; but only foreknowing. Not because the good One foretold it did that man become a traitor, but because he was about to become a traitor, for that reason the good One foretold it. But the contrary opinion, condemned by great consensus, is to be found everywhere. We have cited the passage of Irenaeus above: to which can be added that of Clement: Before whom the heresies still speak, calling the Almighty good, and free from wickedness and injustice.

But woe to that man by whom he is betrayed] Prosper to the Vincentian objections: The predestination of God neither excited nor persuaded nor impelled the fall of those who fall, nor the malice of the wicked, nor the desires of sinners: but it clearly predestined His own judgment, by which He is about to render to each one according to what he has done, whether good or evil: which judgment would not be at all in the future, if men sinned by the will of God. With which that of Hierocles agrees well: Whatever sins we commit that are within our power, these are referred to our choice. But whatever laws of fate follow the things that have been sinned against by the law of justice, these are referred to fate. But the goods primarily given by God are referred to providence.

(V.) The disciples' discussion about primacy.

Latin:

Vers. 22. πορεύεται] הֹלֵךְ id est moritur, ut apud Mat- thaum diximus.

Κατὰ τὸ ὡρισμένον.

Quæ adversus absoluta decreta Calvinianorum, tacitis etsi nominibus, habet Grotius, recte se ha- bent: Si illud excipias, quod reprobet distinctio- nem inter actum, & actui adhærentem ἀταξίαν, quæ suo loco adhibita rejici non potest, alicubi etiam necessaria omnino est. Ita autem hic Grotius.

τῇ ὡρισμένῃ βουλῇ Act. II. 23. Est autem his locis ὁρίζειν i- dem προορίζειν, ut Act. II. 23. c. X. 42. c. XVII. 26. 31. Sed hoc definitum consilium de morte Christi non erat citra omnem præscientiam, imo conjunguntur dicto loco Actorum ὡρι- σμένῃ βουλῇ & πρόγνωσις. Et Justinus disputatione adversus Tryphonem objectionem illam ὅτι ἐδεῖ τὸν χριστὸν σαυρωθῆναι κᾀν τῷ γένει τῶν Ἰεδαίων εἶναι τὼς παραβαίνοντας, ita solvit: ὅτι προγιγνώσκων ὁ Θεὸς γενησομένως πονηρὸς ἐχ᾽ ὅτι τοιύτως ἐποίησε. Deus enim, cui non ea tantum, quæ inevitabiliter sunt futu- ra, sed & quæ possunt fieri sunt notissima, non ignoravit nunquam defuturos homines, qui doctrinam veri ipsorum commodis adversam, non aspernarentur modo, sed crudeli etiam odio insectarentur. Deinde decretum illud defini- tum dicitur factum de eventu, non de actionibq hominum, quibus oblatis ad eventum usus est Deus. Clare distinguunt Apostoli in hymno, qui est Act. IV. 8. ubi Pilatus & Hero- des coiisse dicuntur, ut facerent ὅσα ἡ χείρ σε θεῦ κὴ ἡ βουλὴ αὐτῦ προώρησε non ἀυτὸς ποιῆσαι sed γενέσθαι. Si de ipsis actionibus Judæ, Pilati, Herodis quæramus, certum est, ne illas quidem contigisse ἄνευ τῦ πατρὸς, cum sine eo ne passer quidem ca- dat, sed voluntas Dei circa eos permittens fuit, non effi- ciens, quæ distinctio & sacris literis & omnium veterum Christianorum sententiæ multo est congruentior, quam ea, quæ nonnullis placet, actionem à vitio quod in actione est discriminantibus, quod in multis actionibus puta furto ad- ulterio, atque aliis, quarum ne nomen quidem sine vitio in- telligi potest, rerum naturæ repugnat. Neque magis an- diendi sunt, qui actiones tales à Deo impellente procurari posse ajunt bono fine, cum solus finis non possit rectas fa- cere actiones, aut etiam talia decreta, quæ antecedenter o- mnino necessitatem ponant talium actionum. Æq; rejici- enda eorum opinio qui Deum recte ista facere arbitrantur, quia nulla teneatur lege: nam quædam mala sunt etiam ci- tra legem, & posita ac manente ejus obligatione procurate, ut aliquis contra legem faciat, naturaliter malum est ac pro- inde naturæ Dei repugnat. Adde quod hoc posito inane redditur peccati nomen, cum peccari in eo non possit, quod Deus optimus voluerit nos facere decreto præverten- te libertatem nostræ voluntatis, Quanto rectius erat cum Paulo dicere εἴασεν ὁ θεὸς τὰ ἔθνη πορεύεσθαι ταῖς ὁδοῖς ἀυτῶν Act. XIV, 16. & siquæ sunt alibi obscura, ad eam formam exponere, quod veteres omnes videmus fecisse.

Hæc Grotius: qui adduxit hic Clementem Stro- mat. VIII. Origenem advers. Celsum VII. ubi ea, quæ fiunt prave, ait non esse ἐκ προνοίας sed κατ’ ἐπακολούθησιν: Cyprianum, Salvianum, Chrysosto- mum, Scriptorem denique responsionem ad Græcos in operibus Justini: Atq; hucrefert etiam non imme- rito illud, quod veteres omnes constanter tradunt ex divina præscientia nullam hominibus imponi agendi necessitatem: id enim nullius foret usus, si ipsa præ- scientia decretis pure effectivis subniteretur: quod- que contraria sententia magno consensu ubique da- mnata inveniatur. Cum quibus confer quæ ad- versus Calvinianos disputavimus Tom. II. Syst. Theol. cap. X. quæst. V. Grotiana ita habent:

Clemens Strom. VIII. Τὸ μὴ κωλύον ἀνενεργητόν ἐσιν. διὸ ἐκ ἔσιν αἴτιον τὸ μὴ κωλῦον, ἀλλὰ τὸ κωλῦον. ἐν γὰρ τῷ ἐνεργεῖν κὴ δρᾶν τι τὸ αἴτιον νοεῖται. Origenes adversum Celsum VII. ὁρᾶτε τὴν ἀτοπίαν ὁ τῦτο λέγων, τῶ πάντα κατὰ γνώμην διοικεῖσθαι τῶ θεῶ. ἀκολυθεῖ γὰρ τῷ λόγῳ κᾀτὰ ἁμαρτανόμενα κᾀ πάντα τὰ ἀπὸ κακίας κατὰ γνώμην διοικεῖσθαι τῶ θεῶ, ὅπερ & ἴαυτον ἐσὶ τῷ, & κωλύοντος τῶ θεῶ γίνεται. Mox ea quæ prave fiunt ait non esse ἐκ προνοίας, sed κατ’ ἐπακολύθησιν τῶν ἐκ προνοίας. Cyprianus: Cum ipse sit mundi Dominus, cognitor, & rector, & cuncta arbitrio ejus & nutu gerantur, nec quicquam fieri possit nisi quod fecerit aut fieri ipse permiserit Salvia nus: Quædam ex his divina dispositio ita ordinavit, quædam patien- tiæ sustinuit. Chrysostomus: ἐδὲν ἀγνοῶντος ἀυτᾶ γίνεται, ἀλλ’ εἰδότος μὲν ἅπαντα, ἐ μὴν πάντα ἐνεργῦντος. Scriptor responsionum adGræcos in operibus Justini: συγχωρῇ τε ἡμᾶς πράττειν ἃ ἑκασίως αἱρεόμεθα κακὰ, & διὰ τὴν ἀσθένειαν τῆς ἀυτῦ δυνάμεως, ἀλλ’ ἵνα τὸ ἡμῶν ἀυθαίρετον κᾀ τὸ ἀυτῶ μακρόθυμον δειχθῇ. Huc referendum & illud quod ve- teres omnes constanter tradunt ex divina præscientia nul- lam hominibus imponi agendi necessitatem: id enim nulli- us erat usus, si ipsa præscientia decretis pure effectivis subni- teretur. Origenes adversus Celsum disputans an recte dicatur πάντως ἐχρῆν γενέσθαι τὸ προειρημένον, accurate vocem πάν- τως distinguit. Εἰ γάρ τὸ πάντως ἀκούει ἀντὶ τοῦ ἠναγκασμένως, οὐ δώσομεν αὐτῷ. δυνατὸν γάρ ἦν καὶ μὴ γενέσθαι. Εἰ δὲ τὸ πάν- τως λέγει ἀντὶ τοῦ ἴσου ὅπερ ἐγκωλύεται ὄντι ἀληθὲς κᾂν δυνα- τὸν ἦ τὸ μὴ γενέσθαι, οὐδὲν λυπεῖ τὸν λόγον. Tractarat idem O- rigenes tomo in Genesim tertio verbis non dissimilibus, ad- dito Judæ exemplo de quo hoc Lucæ loco præcipue agitur: εἰ μὲν γάρ τὸ πάντως ἴσου ἐστὶ τῷ ἐρημένος, ὡς ἀνάγκην εἶναι γε- νέσθαι τὸ προεγνωσμένον, οὐ δίδομεν αὐτῷ. οὐ γάρ ἐροῦμεν, ἐπεὶ προ- έγνωσται Ἰούδαν προδότην γενέσθαι ὅτι πᾶσα ἀνάγκη ἦν Ἰούδαν προδότην γενέσθαι. Ἐν ἦν ταῖς περὶ Ἰούδα προφητείαις μέμ- ψεις καὶ κατηγορίαι τοῦ Ἰούδα ἀναγεγραμμέναι εἰσὶ, παντί τῳ πα- ραστήσει τὸ ψεκτὸν αὐτοῦ. οὐκ ἂν δὲ ψόγον αὐτῷ προσῆπτεν οὐ ἐ- πάναγκες προδότης ἦν κᾂν μὴ ἐνεδέχετο αὐτῷ ὅμοιον τοῖς λοι- ποῖς ἀποστόλοις γενέσθαι Mox: εἰ δέ τις διηγήσεται τὸ πάντως ἴσως καὶ τοῦτο σημαίνειν αὐτὸ λέγων. ὅτι ἴσως μὲν τάδε τινα, ἐνεδέ- χετο δὲ καὶ ἑτέρως γενέσθαι, τοῦτο ὡς ἀληθὲς συγχωροῦμεν. Τὸν μὲν γάρ Θεὸν οὐκ ἐνδέχεται ψεύσασθαι· ἐνδέχεται δὲ περὶ τῶν ἐνδεχο- μένων γενέσθαι καὶ μὴ γενέσθαι φρονῆσαι τὸ γενέσθαι αὐτὰ ἢ τὸ μὴ γενέσθαι. Quod ibidem latius prosequitur, à veterum nullo hac in parte errorum reprehensus: imo plurimi Scri- ptores ad hunc locum idem plane tradiderunt:& Chrysosto- mus oratione cur obscura sint vaticinia: οὐδὲ γάρ ἡ πρόγνωσις, ἄνθρωπε, τῆς πονηρίας αἰτία· μὴ γένοιτο· οὐ γάρ ἐστιν ἀναγκαστικὴ τῶν μελλόντων ἔσεσθαι· ἀλλὰ προγνωστικὴ μόνον. οὐκ ἐπειδὴ προ- εῖπεν ὁ χρηστὸς διὰ τοῦτο ἐγένετο ἐκεῖνος προδότης, ἀλλ' ἐπειδὰν προδότης ἔμελλε γενέσθαι διὰ τοῦτο προεῖπεν ὁ χρηστός. Con- trariam vero sententiam, magno consensu damnatam ubique est invenire. Locum Irenæi supra adduximus: cui addi potest ille Clementis: Ὧι πρὸ Ἰάντης ἔτι Φθέγγονται Φωναὶ αἱ αἱρέσεις, ἀγαθὸν τὸν παντακράτορα κυριντίουσας τῆς γραφῆς κὴ ἀναίτιον κακίας τε καὶ ἀδικίας.

Πλὴν ὀυαὶ τῷ ἀνθρώπῳ ἐκείνῳ δι' οὗ παραδίδοται] Prosper ad objectiones Vincentianas: Non casus ruentium, nec mali- gnitatem iniquorum, neque cupiditates peccantium prædesti- natio Dei aut excitavit aut suasit aut impulit: sed plane præde- stinavit judicium suum, quo unicuique retributurus est prout gessit sive bonum sive malum: quod judicium omnino futurum non esset, si homines Dei voluntate peccarent. Qui cum bene convenit illud Hieroclis: ὅσα μέντοι εἰς ἐφ' ἡμῖν ἁμαρτάνομεν Ταῦτα εἰς προαίρεσιν ἀναφέρεσθ. ὅσα δὲ ἐπὶ τοῖς ἡμαζημένοις καλὰ Ἰὰς τῆς δίκης ἕπεται νόμος εἱμαρμένη. Τὰ δὲ προηγουμένως παρὰ τοῦ Θεοῦ ἐκδιδόμενα ἀγαθὰ, εἰς πρόνοιαν.

(V.) Discipulorum de primatu commonefactio.

## 22:24
ἐγένετο] I think it can be rightly translated as 'had been', for it is not necessary, indeed it is hardly credible, that in such a mournful time their minds were stirred to ambitious strife. But Christ, remembering what they had once disputed among themselves, being about to depart, handed down to his own the precepts of humility just as he did those of love.

The Harmon. Evangel. teaches that this contention arose entirely after the sacramental supper and the manifest intention of Judas the traitor. For there is no reason for us to believe that Luke wished to insert some history that does not pertain here at all; by which reasoning everything could easily be thrown into confusion, and the series of the narrative could never not be called into doubt. But that contention arose without doubt from the fact that Christ made mention of his glorification. For that opinion about the worldly kingdom of Christ, in which each one was eager to obtain the primacy, still clung to the minds of the disciples. Which vain persuasion and rivalry could not be eradicated from the minds and hearts of the disciples even by the most brilliant sermons about the passion. And that Luke used no recapitulation here, and indeed that the contention which is described in Matt. XX. 25 and Mark X. 41 must be held to be different from this one of ours, is clear from the circumstances: Conf. Harm. B. Gerbardi c. CLXXII. p. 115. seqq.

Latin:

ἐγένετο] Puto recte verti posse fuerat, neque enim necesse est, imo vix credibile tam luctuoso tempore va asse animos ambitioso certamini. Sed memor Christus quid olim inter se disceptassent, abiturus, ut dilectionis ita & humilitatis præcepta suis tradidit.

Hanc contentionem omnino exortam esse post cœnam sacramentalem & manifestatam intentio- nem Judæ proditoriam, Harmon.Evangel. docet. Neq; enim est, quod credamus Lucam aliquam hi- storian, huc minime pertinentem, inserere voluis- se; qua ratione omnia facile turbari, & series narra- tionis nunquam non in dubium vocari poterit. Enata autem sine dubio illa contentio inde est, quod Christus mentionem fecerit suæ glorifica- tionis. Hærebat enim adhuc animo discipulorum opinio illa de regno Christi mundano, in quo quisq; τὸ πρωτεῖον obtinere gestiebat. Quæ vana persua- sio, & Φιλονικεία ne quidem luculentissimis con- cionibus de passione eradicari è discipulorum mentibus & cordibus potuit. Et Lucam nulla re- capitulatione hic usum esse, imo diversam plane contentionem illam, quæ Matth. XX. 25. & Marc. X. 41. describitur, haberi debere ab hac nostra, è circumstantiis luculentum est: Conf. Harm.B.Ger- bardi c. CLXXII. p. 115. seqq.

## 22:25
Vers. 25. ἐξουσιάζοντες αὐτῶν] See Matt. XX. 25. ἐυεργέται καλῶνται] You may often find Roman emperors called by this name in Josephus and Philo. It is given also to other kings, as in Plutarch on praising oneself: likewise in Isocrates in the Panathenaicus: In Josephus also Simon the ethnarch is adorned with this title. Christ signifies that such names are often affected by those who in reality consult their own advantages more than those of others (they see therefore what is otherwise a beautiful name, but they do not affect it) but they neglect to do the thing itself. See what we have brought to Matthew: especially what we have cited there from Philo, for it contributes greatly to illustrating this passage. The Hebrews called kings נדיבים beneficent, as in Job XII. 21, XX. 28, and elsewhere.

Latin:

Vers. 25. ἐξουσιάζοντες αὐτῶν] Vide Matth. XX. 25. ἐυεργέται καλῶνται] Sæpe apud Josephum & Philonem re- perias hoc nomine appellari Romanos imperatores. Datur & aliis regibus ut apud Plutarchum de se laudando: item apud Isocratem Panathenaico: Apud Josephum etiam Simon ethnarcha hoc titulo ornatur. Significat Christus nomina ta- lia sæpe ab iis affectari qui reipsa suis magis quam alienis commodis consulant, Vident ergo quid pulchrum sit alio- qui nomen non affectarent) sed facere idipsum negligunt. Vide quæ ad Matthæu: imprimis quod ibi ex Philone addu- ximus, valde enim facit huic loco illustrando. Hebræi re- ges vocabant נדיבים beneficos, ut Jobi XII. 21. XX. 28. & alibi.

## 22:26
Vers. 26. ὁ μείζων ἐν ὑμῖν] Whoever will obtain any office in my kingdom.

γενέσθω ὡς ὁ νεώτερος] Just as those who preside over the Church are called elders, so those who are in the rank of private individuals are called younger, Acts V. 6. and the younger men arose, Paul I Tim. V. 1. Do not rebuke an elder but exhort him as a father; the younger men as brothers. Christ therefore wishes that those set over the Churches should assume to themselves no splendor or advantage as a privilege over the others.

ὁ ἡγούμενος] He seems to be called ἡγούμενος here who has attained a higher rank than the others in the Church, as the Apostles were about to attain, and after them the Bishops: for thus the ancients explain that passage to the Hebrews, obey your leaders. Opposed to these are those who serve, who are in the lowest rank.

Latin:

Vers. 26. ὁ μείζων ἐν ὑμῖν] Quicunque munus aliquod in regno meo obtinebit.

γενέσθω ὡς ὁ νεώτερος] Sicut πρεσβύτεροι vocantur qui Ec- clesiæ præsunt, ita νεώτεροι qui sunt ἐν τάξει ἰδιωτῶν, Act. V. 6. ἀναστάντες δὲ οἱ νεώτεροι, Paulus I. Tim. V. 1. πρεσβυτέρῳ μὴ ἐ- πιπλήξῃς ἀλλὰ παρακάλει ὡς πατέρα· νεωτέρους ὡς ἀδελφούς. Vult ergo Christus præpositos Ecclesiis nihil splendoris aut commodi sibi præcipuum supra cæteros assumere.

ὁ ἡγούμενος] ἡγούμενος hic dici videtur qui in Ecclesia sub- limiorem cæteris consecutus est gradum, ut Apostoli erant consecuturi, & post eos Episcopi: ita enim veteres expli- cant illud ad Hebræos, πείθεσθε τοῖς ἡγουμένοις ὑμῶν. His op- ponuntur οἱ διακονοῦντες qui in minimo sunt gradu.

## 22:27
V. 27. For who is greater] Christ shows the difference between his kingdom and the kingdoms of the world: in the kingdoms of the world the king reclines at the table, others serve: but Christ, the king of the heavenly kingdom, had exhibited service to his subjects during the whole time of his life, and at this very time he was placing that same thing before their eyes through the washing of feet, so that the matter might cling deeply to their memory.

Latin:

V. 27. τίς γὰρ μείζων] Ostendit Christus discrimen sui re- gni à regnis mundi: in regnis mundi rex ad mensam accum- bit, alii ministrant: at Christus rex cœlestis regni toto vitæ tempore suis subditis ministerium exhibuerat, idque ipsum hoc tempore per pedum lotionem oculis subjiciebat, ut res memoriæ penitus hæreret.

## 22:28
V. 28. But you are those who have continued with me] As if he were to say, thus far your affairs are going well enough: I am addressing you who abhor treachery: who have thus far followed me with a faithful spirit.

in my temptations] Temptations are called here adverse things through which constancy is tested, as in Gal. IV. 14, Jas. I. 12, 2 Pet. II. 9, Rev. III. 10. Moreover, Christ is said to have been tempted in Heb. ch. II. 18, ch. IV. 15, insofar as his obedience shone forth through those adversities.

Latin:

V. 28. ὑμεῖς δὲ ἐστε οἱ διαμεμενηκότες μετ᾽ ἐμοῦ] Quasi dicat, hactenus res vestræ satis recte se habent: vos alloquor qui à proditione abhorretis: qui hactenus fideli animo me se- ctamini.

ἐν τοῖς πειρασμοῖς με] πειρασμοὶ hic dicuntur res adversæ per quas constantia exploratur, ut Gal. IV. 14. Jac. I. 12. 2. Pet. II. 9. Apoc. III. 10. Dicitur autem Christus πειρασθῆναι Hebr. c. II. 18. c. IV. 15. quatenus per illa adversa obedien- tia ipsius emicuit.

## 22:29
V. 29. And I appoint unto you, as my Father hath appointed unto me] There is no doubt that διατίθεσθαι here does not mean to bequeath, which does not befit the Father, but to assign by covenant, as appears in the Greek, 2 Chron. VI. 18, in Ps. LXXXIX. 4, כרתי ברית is translated as διεθέμην διαθήκην: just as also some very ancient books have here διατίθεμαι ὑμῖν διαθήκην. Moreover, the words are to be constructed in this way: as the Father hath appointed unto me a kingdom, so I appoint unto you that you may eat and drink at my table, as Theophylact rightly explains. The sense is: Just as the Father assigned a kingdom to me, to be acquired through the endurance of adverse things, so also I assign to you glory next to royal majesty, to be acquired in a similar manner, just as you are partakers of the sufferings, so also of the consolation, 2 Cor. I. 7; if we endure, we shall also reign together, 2 Tim. II. 12. Moreover, it coheres very well with the preceding, where he deterred them from ambition: for those whose glory is laid up in heaven ought not to seek it on earth: Furthermore, the way to glory is humble patience, clearly contrary to ambition.

Latin:

V. 29. κἀγὼ διατίθεμαι ὑμῖν, καθὼς διέθετό μοι ὁ πατὴρ] Du- bium non est quin διατίθεσθαι hic non sit, legare, quod Patri non convenit, sed pacto addicere, ut apparet in Græco, 2. Paral. VI. 18. in Ps. LXXXIX. 4 כרתי ברית vertitur διεθέ- μην διαθήκην: Sicut & libri quidam vetustissimi hic habent διατίθεμαι ὑμῖν διαθήκην. Construenda autem verba sunt hoc modo: καθὼς διέθετό μοι ὁ πατὴρ βασιλείαν κἀγὼ διατίθεμαι ὑ- μῖν ἵνα ἐσθίητε καὶ πίνητε ἐπὶ τῆς τραπέζης με, ut recte exponit Theophylactus. Se: sus est: Sicut Pater mihi regnum addixit, acquirendum per tolerantiam rerum adversarum, ita & ego vobis addito gloriam regiæ majestati proximam simili ra- tione acquirendam, ὥσπερ κοινωνοί ἐστε τῶν παθημάτων οὕτω καὶ τῆς παρακλήσεως 2. Cor. I. 7. εἰ ὑπομένομεν καὶ συμβασιλεύσομεν 2. Tim. II. 12. Cohæret autem optime cum superioribus, ubi eos ab ambitione deterruit: nam quorum gloria in cœlo re- posita est, ii non debent eam in terris quærere: Deinde via ad gloriam est humilis patientia, ambitione plane adversa.

## 22:30
V. 30. That you may eat and drink at my table, in my kingdom] The nobles of a kingdom are accustomed to be known by two marks, of honor and of power. Honor is in the fellowship of the royal table. Power is in the participation of judgments. By these metaphors, the dignity next to royal, as we have said, is described in this place.

(VI.) The prediction of Satan's sifting, and of Peter's denial.

Latin:

V. 30. ἵνα ἐσθίητε καὶ πίνητε ἐπὶ τῆς τραπέζης με, ἐν τῇ βασι- λείᾳ με] Duabus notis solent cognosci proceres regni, ho- noris & potestatis. Honos est in mensæ regalis consortio. Potestas in judiciorum participatione. His translationibus hoc loco describitur dignitas ut diximus regiæ proxima.

(VI.) Cribrationis Satanæ, & abnegationis Petri prædictio.

## 22:31
V. 31. Simon] The Latin and the Syrian read 'Simon'. But the Arab and ancient Latin writers stand by the received reading. Christ addresses all the Apostles in the person of Peter, just as he himself was accustomed to speak for the Apostles: for the things that pertained peculiarly to him, the occasion for them arose from his own response.

he has asked for you] That is, he asked that you be given to him. An allusion to the history of Job, where God says to Satan, 'Behold, all that he has is in your hand.' That is, I give his affairs to you, I permit them to your discretion. Thus Isocrates said: 'But if I should do none of these things, they would demand that I be given over to you.' That is, if I were to do none of these things, they would demand that I be given up by you.

To sift as wheat] He says he asked for this, so that he might be able to shake and agitate you at his discretion. For the infinitive joined to τοῦ is telic in Luke. Σινιάζειν is כרב, which the Septuagint translate as λικμᾷν in Amos IX. 9, but catachrestically: for 'like as in a sieve' follows. Wherefore, since it is credible that the place in Amos is looked to here. The meaning is רדת, which itself is also often translated by λικμᾷν: elsewhere by διασκορπίζειν, ἀπαλλοτριοῦν, καθυβρίζειν.

Latin:

V. 31. Σίμων] Latinus & Syrus legerunt σίμωνι. At à recepta lectione stat Arabs & veteres Latini Scriptores. A- postolos omnes in Petri persona Christus alloquitur, sicut & ipse pro Apostolis loqui solebat: nam quæ ad ipsum peculiariter pertinebant, eorum ex responso ipsius nata est occasio.

ἐξῃτήσατο ὑμᾶς] Id est petiit vos sibi dedi. Allusio ad Jobi historiam, ubi Deus Satanæ הנה כל־אשר־לו בידך. Id est, res ejus tibi dedo, tuo arbitratui permitto. Sic Iso- crates dixit: ἐὰν δὲ μηδὲν τούτων ποιῇ, παρ᾽ ὑμῖν ἐξαιτεῖν. Quod si horum nihil facerem me us dedi à vobis postularent.

Τοῦ σινιάσαι ὡς τὸν σῖτον] Ideo inquit hoc postulavit, ut vos posset pro arbitrio concutere atque agitare. Nam τῦ infini- tivo junctum est τελικὸν apud Lucam. Σινιάζειν est כרב quod λικμᾷν vertunt Septuaginta Amos I IX. 9. sed καταχρηστικῶς: nam sequitur כברא id est in cribro. Quare cum Amosi locum hic respici credibile est. Paris significatus est רדת quod & ipsum sæpe per λικμᾷν vertitur: alibi per διασκορπί- ζειν, ἀπαλλοτριοῦν, καθυβρίζειν.

## 22:32
Vers. 32. But I have prayed for you] That is, for you and the other Apostles. Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans: 'He who prayed that the faith of the Apostles might not fail.' This seems to be the very prayer which exists in John XVII. 9, 'I pray for them,' and 11, 'Holy Father, keep them in thy name,' and 15, 'that thou shouldest keep them from the evil one.'

that your faith may not fail] Ignatius understands ἵνα materially, so that it is that very thing which is asked for. And indeed there is a similar manner of speaking below, 'Pray that you enter not into temptation.' Otherwise it can also be understood telically. But the matter comes to almost the same thing, provided we hold that there is here a similar metonymy to that which was observed in Matt. XXVI. 41, and that Christ wished by this prayer to succor the infirmity of human nature; not of arrogance, not of sloth: therefore Peter, being more confident than was just, is punished by the withdrawal of help. It is usually asked here whether this prayer of Christ in Peter had such an outcome that his faith did not fail. Ancient writers do not speak in the same way: Ambrose says that faith was lost and perished in the denial: Chrysostom denies that the faith failed (ἐκλιπῶσαν τὴν πίστιν), Prudentius says that faith was preserved in his soul, and the sayings of others exist for both opinions. But it appears that the word 'faith' is taken differently by them, which is consistent with the usage of both the sacred scriptures and the common usage of all languages. For the names of virtues and vices sometimes denote the habit (ἕξιν), sometimes the act (τὴν ἐνέργειαν), in which sense Aristotle said that all things are defined by the act (ἄπαντα τῷ ἔργῳ ὁρίζεσθαι), and Tertullian, that with changed qualities the possessions of words are changed: Salvianus: That a name without its act and office is nothing. The act of faith (ἡ ἐνέργεια τῆς πίστεως) failed in Peter for a time: and therefore, unless repentance had come to his aid, he would have fallen into that law which exists in Matthew 10:33 and 2 Timothy 2:12. For it is not enough to believe with the heart unto righteousness, unless confession is made with the mouth unto salvation (Romans 10:10); thus the aforementioned Salvianus says that faith which is not proven by works is to be held as if it were not. But he weakened the habit (ἕξιν), he did not extinguish it: there remained in his soul not a bare assent to perceived truth, but also the purpose of Christianity, although at that moment of time it was ineffective. Cyprian excellently in his letter to Antonius: 'Nor let us think that those whom we see wounded by a deadly persecution are dead, but rather that they lie half-alive: for if they were entirely dead, they would never afterwards become confessors and martyrs.' But since there is in them that which may recover through subsequent repentance, strength is armed for faith and for virtue from repentance. The most holy man understood well that the life and death of the soul and of the body do not behave in the same way: for the body is vivified in a moment and is accustomed to perish in a moment. The soul receives, loses, and recovers life gradually and by parts: which the divine Apocalypse teaches us in chapter 3:2, 'strengthen the things that remain, that are ready to die: for I have not found thy works perfect before God.' Moreover, hasty repentance easily restores dead parts, concerning the utility of which Salvianus says: 'Immediately when they fall, let them rise and straightway meditate on elevation in the fall, and if it is possible in any way by the speed of penitence, let the remedy of the one rising be so swift that the trace of the fallen one can scarcely appear.' Peter did this, and therefore that very thing which failed in him is to be judged as having scarcely failed: and deservedly you may refer to him what the same Salvianus says elsewhere about a sinner who soon performs repentance: 'For he does not utterly harm the Lord's own, for whom propitiation is reserved.' And why more? I think that in the very error he always looked back to Him from whom he could obtain that he might not err any longer.

And thou, when thou art converted, strengthen thy brethren) Most interpret 'when thou art converted' (ἐπιστρέψας) as 'led by repentance.' But that cannot be approved by me: for from the preceding words, danger could be understood, not a fall. Wherefore I prefer to follow others who think it is a Hebraism, such as is in Psalm 84:7, 'thou wilt turn and quicken us' (תשוב תחינו), that is, 'thou wilt quicken us again.' Thus here, 'and thou, when thou art converted, strengthen,' is 'and thou, when thou art again, strengthen.' Thou also, O man, in turn strengthen thy brethren, that is, devote effort so that they may not fail in faith, namely by praying for them, just as I pray for thee, and add also by shining forth with an example.

Latin:

Vers. 32. ἐγὼ δὲ ἐδεήθην περὶ σοῦ] Id est pro te aliisque Apo- stolis. Ignatius ad Smyrnenses: ὁ δεηθεὶς μὴ ἐκλείπειν τὴν πίστιν τῶν Ἀποστόλων. Videtur hæc ipsa esse oratio quæ exstat Joh. XVII. 9. ἐγὼ περὶ ἀυτῶν ἐρωτῶ, & 11. πάτερ ἅγιε τήρησον αὐτοὺς ἐν τῷ ὀνοματί σου, & 15. ἵνα τηρήσῃς αὐτοὺς ἐκ τοῦ που νηροῦ.

ἵνα μὴ ἐκλείπῃ ἡ πίστις σου] Ignatius ἵνα intelligit ὑλικῶς, ut sit ipsum illud quod rogatur. Et sane simile loquendi genus infra, προσεύχεσθε ἵνα μὴ εἰσέλθητε εἰς πειρασμὸν. Potest alioquin & 7ελικῶς intelligi. Sed res eodem ferme recidit, dumillud teneamus esse hic similem μετωνυμίαν qualis observata est Matth. XXVI. 41. & voluisse Christum hac oratione succurrere infirmitati naturæ humanæ; non arrogantiæ, non socordiæ: ideo Petrus æquo confidentior subtractione auxilii punitur. Quæri hic solet an hæc Christi oratio in Petro eventum habuerit talem, ut fides non defe- cerit. Scriptores antiqui non eodem modo loquuntur: fi- dem in negatione amissam esse, periisse dicit Ambrosius: ne- gat ἐκλιπῶσαν τὴν πίστιν Chrysostomus, Prudentius animo dicit servatam fidem, aliorumque exstant dicta in utramque sen- tentiam. Sed apparet fidei vocem ab illis diverse accipi, quod & sacrarum literarum & communi linguarum o- mnium usui convenit. Nam nomina virtutum & vitio- rum modo ἕξιν denotant, modo τὴν ἐνέργειαν, quo sensu ἄ- παντα τῷ ἔργῳ ὁρίζεσθαι dixit Aristoteles, & Tertullianus, mutatis qualitatibus mutari vocabulorum possessiones: Sal- vianus: Nomen sine actu suo atque officio nihil esse. De- fecit in Petro ἡ ἐνέργεια τῆς πίστεως ad tempus: ideoque nisi pœnitentia subvenisset, inciderat in legem illam quæ exstat Matthæi X. 33. & 2. Tim. II. 12. Neque enim satis est corde credi ad justitiam, nisi ore fiat confessio ad salutem Rom. X. 10. ita is quem dixi Salvianus ait fidem quæ per opera non probatur, habendam quasi non sit. At ἕξιν labefactavit, non extinxit: mansit in animo non nuda assensio perceptæ veri- tatis, sed & propositum Christianismi, quanquam eo tem- poris momento inefficax. Cyprianus egregie epistola ad Antonium, Nec putemus mortuos esse, sed magis semianimes ja- cere eos quos persecutione funesta sauciatos videmus: qui si in totum mortui essent, nunquam de eisdem postmodum & con- fessores & martyres fierent. Sed quoniam est in illis quod pœni- tentia sequente revalescat, ad fidem & ad virtutem de pœniten- tia robur armatur. Bene intellexit vir sanctissimus non eodem se modo habere animi & corporis tum vitam tum mortem: nam corpus ut momento vivificatur & momento solet interire. Animus paulatim & per partes vitam acci- pit, amittit & recipit: quod nos docet divina Apocalypsis c. III. 2. στήριξον τὰ λοιπὰ ἃ μέλλει ἀποθανεῖν· ὀ γὰρ εὕρηκά σου τὰ ἔργα πεπληρωμένα ἐνώπιον τοῦ Θεοῦ. Facile autem partes mortuas restituit festinata pœnitentia, de cujus utilitate ita Salvianus: Ilico ubi concidere, consurgant & elevationem protinus meditentur in lapsu, ac si fieri ullo modo pernicitate pœnitudinis potest, tam velox sit remedium resurgentis, ut vix possit vestigium apparere collapsi. Hoc fecit Petrus, & pro- pterea id ipsum quod in eo defecit, vix defecisse censendu est: meritoq; ad eum referas quod alibi de peccatore mox pœnitentiam agente dicit idem Salvianus: Non penitus enim Dominum lædit suum, cui propitiatio reservatur. Et quid plu- ra? puto quod semper in ipso errore respexerit à quo obtinere potuit ne diutius erraret.

καὶ σύ ποτε ἐπιστρέψας, στήριξον τοὺς ἀδελφούς σου) Plerique ἐπιστρέψας interpretantur pœnitentia ductus. Cæterum mihi id probari non potest: nam ex verbis præcedentibus periculum intelligi poterat, non lapsus. Quare alios sequi malo qui Hebraismum putant esse, qualis est Ps. LXXXIV. 7. תשוב תחינו ἐπιστρέψας ζωώσεις ἡμᾶς, id est πάλιν ζωώσεις ἡμᾶς. Ita hic σύ ποτε ἐπιστρέψας στήριξον, est σύ ποτε πάλιν στήριξον. Tu quoque olim vicissim fratres confirma, id est da operam ne in fide deficiant, nempe pro ipsis orans, sicut e- go pro te oro, adde & exemplo prælucens.

## 22:34
Verse 34. Thou shalt deny that thou knowest) A locution similar to that which is above, 'those who gainsay that there is a resurrection' (οἱ ἀντιλέγοντες ἀνάστασιν μὴ εἶναι).

That Grotius says the act of faith (τὴν ἐνέργειαν τῆς πίστεως) failed in Peter for a time, and therefore, unless repentance had come to his aid, he would have fallen into that law which exists in Matthew 10:33 and 2 Timothy 2:12, but that he weakened the habit (ἕξιν) of faith, not extinguished it, this can be admitted concerning dogmatic faith, or bare assent to perceived truth, but not concerning saving faith, and not even concerning the purpose of Christianity, which certainly cannot consist with the denial of Christ: therefore what he says is not simply to be approved, that 'there remained in his soul not a bare assent to perceived truth, but also the purpose of Christianity, although at that moment of time it was ineffective.' Nor indeed would there have been need for the conversion of Peter, if he had retained saving faith, that is, trust in Christ: which, since Grotius understands the following words, 'and thou, when thou art converted, strengthen thy brethren,' he so perverts them that they do not speak of the conversion and repentance of Peter, but are to be explained by a Hebraism, such as is in Psalm 84:7, 'Thou wilt turn and quicken us,' that is, 'thou wilt quicken us again,' in this way: 'and thou, when thou art converted, strengthen,' that is, 'and thou, when thou art again, strengthen.' Thou also, O man, in turn strengthen thy brethren. But why he departs from the customary meaning and explanation, he had no cause to bring forward, except a preconceived opinion: for what he says, that from the preceding words danger alone could be understood, not the fall itself, does not suffice: because even if he had not expressly indicated the fall in the preceding words, this could nevertheless have been tacitly indicated by this word 'convert' (ἐπιστρέψον). But also from the collation of the other Evangelists it is clear that Christ had already openly predicted concerning all, not danger alone but also the fall, Matthew 26:31, Mark 14:27: 'This night all of you shall be offended in me.' The Syriac, the Arabic, and most all interpreters and commentators explain the word concerning the conversion of Peter with us.

(VII.) Information of the disciples concerning the danger.

Latin:

Vers. 34. Ἀπαρνήσῃ μὴ εἰδέναι) Similis locutio ei quæ supra οἱ ἀντιλέγοντες ἀνάστασιν μὴ εἶναι.

Quod Grotius ait defecisse in Petro τὴν ἐνέργειαν τῆς πίστεως ad tempus, ideoq; nisi pœnitentia subvenisset, incidisse in legem illam, quæ exstat Matth. X. 33. & 2. Tim. II. 12. at ἕξιν fidei labefactasse, non extin- xisse, id defide dogmatica, seu nuda assensione perce- ptæ veritatis, non autem de fide salvifica, ac ne quidem de proposito Christianismi, quæ utiq; cum abnegatione Christi consistere nequeunt, admitti potest: ideo non simpliciter probandū, quod ait, mansit in animo non nuda assensio perceptæ veritatis, sed & propositum Christianismi, quanquam eo temporis momento inefficax. Neq; vero opus fuisset conversione Petri, si fidem salvificam retinuisset, hoc est, fiduciam in Christum: quod cum intelligat Grotius verba sequentia κὶ σύ ποτε ἐπιστρέψας στήριξον τὰς ἀδελφούς σου, ita pervertet, quod non de conversione & pœnitentia Petri loquantur, sed per Ebraismum explicanda sint, qualis est Ps. LXXXIV, 7. Ἐπιστρέψας ζωώσεις ἡμᾶς, id est, πάλιν ζωώσεις ἡμᾶς, hoc modo σύ ποτε ἐπιστρέψας στήριξον, id est, σύ ποτε πάλιν στήριξον. Tu quoque olim vicissim fratres confirma. Cæterum cur à consueta significatione & explicatione discedat; causam nullam, præter opinionem præconceptam, adferre habuit: Quod enim ait: ex verbis præcedentibus periculum solum intelligi potuisse, non lapsum ipsum, haud suf- ficit: quia etiamsi expresse lapsum antecedentibus non indicasset, hoc tamen verbo ἐπιστρέψον tacitè idem indicari potuit. Sed & ex aliorum Evange- listarum collatione patet, quod jam apertè de omnibus prædixerit Christus, non periculum so- lum sed & lapsum Matth. XXVI. 31. Marc. XIV. 27. Hac nocte OMNES in me scandalizabimini. De conversione Petri verbum nobiscum explicant Syrus, Arabs & plerique omnes interpretes & commentatores.

(VII.) Discipulorum de periculo informatio.

## 22:36
Verse 36. But now he that hath a purse, let him take it) Christ wished to signify that times were impending far different from those they had experienced until now: for before this there were many who wished them well, who would succor their needs: on the contrary, enemies dared to plot nothing more serious against them: but now, and consequently for them, the most serious things of all were impending: scarcely anyone would be found who would relieve them: on the contrary, they would come into public hatred, so that they would be vexed by anyone with impunity and even with praise. That they may understand this diversity of lot, he first recalls to their memory the very tolerable lot of the past time, which he had once predicted to them, with certain visible signs added, namely, the prohibition against procuring for themselves a bag or a purse or anything similar for future uses: now he indicates a lot far different, even with contrary signs: for he wills that a purse be taken, that a bag be taken, signs of impending penury: nay, and that a sword be sought, a sign clearly of impending danger: for it is customary to go with a sword through places infested by robberies. We have said elsewhere that it was the custom for many nations, but especially for the Jews, to designate more notable things not only by words, but also by conspicuous objects, whence arose the laying on of hands, and many other things of human institution. Concerning the ancient Greeks, Dionysius Thrax the Grammarian: ἐσήμαινον γοῦν οὐ διὰ λέξεως μόνον ἀλλὰ καὶ διὰ συμβόλων. But the Prophets especially made use of this, sometimes by God's prescription, sometimes of their own accord, either themselves doing something which had a signification of a future thing, or commanding others to do so. Examples are I Kings XXII 11, Eph. XX 2, Jer. IX 17, ch. XXVII 2, Ezek. IV 2, ch. XII 7, Os. I 2, Acts XXI 2, and elsewhere. Christ therefore says, if anyone has a purse, let him not leave it at home, but carry it with him. Those who turn the imperative into the future, it is apparent that they are offended by the novelty of a precept not understood by them, but the consensus of interpreters defends the received reading.

ὁμοίως καὶ πήραν) This is said by way of a parenthesis. For the discourse returns to the purse. But Christ admonishes by the way and in passing that a bag will also be needed, since food would otherwise be lacking. Βαλάντιον is כיס, which the Greeks usually translate as μαρσύππιον. Πήρα is ילקוט.

καὶ ὁ μὴ ἔχων) Namely, a βαλάντιον, which those who have some money are accustomed to have. For mention had been interjected concerning the bag, as we have said, which the order of the words also sufficiently indicates. For it is as if he said: whoever has a purse, let him take it: but together with a bag: and whoever does not have one, let him rather sell his garment than lack a sword: for that is the custom to do whenever violence is feared.

πωλησάτω τὸ ἱμάτιον αὐτοῦ) This is not commanded precisely, but comparatively, that is, let him by all means procure a sword for himself, even if by selling his garment if he cannot procure it otherwise.

Latin:

Vers. 36. ἀλλὰ νῦν ὁ ἔχων βαλάντιον, ἀράτω) Significare Christus voluit, longe alia instare tempora quam experti es- sent hactenus: nam antehac multos fuisse qui ipsis bene vel- lent, qui ipsorum subvenirent necessitatibus: inimicos contra nihil in ipsos gravius ausos moliri: nunc autē sibi, & conse- quenter ipsis, instare gravissima quæque: vix quemquam re- pertum iri qui ipsos sublevet: contra venturos ipsos in o- dium publicum, ita ut à quovis impune atque etiam cum laude vexandi essent. Hanc sortis diversitatem ut intelli- gant, primum in memoriam illis revocat anteacti temporis sortem perquam tolerabilem, quam olim ipsis prædixerat, additis signis quibusdam visibilibus, nimirum, vetito ne in futuros usus sibi peram aut crumenam aut simile quid compararent: nunc sortem longe aliam signis etiam con- trariis indicat: vult enim sumi crumenam, sumi & peram, signa instantis penuriæ: quin & quæri gladium, signum sci- licet instantis periculi: nam per loca latrociniis infesta cum gladio iri solet. Diximus alibi morem fuisse multis genti- bus sed Judæis præsertim, res insigniores non verbis tan- tum, sed & conspicuis rebus designare, unde orta manuum impositio, aliaque multa humani instituti. De antiquis Græcis Dionysius Thrax Grammaticus: ἐσήμαινον γοῦν οὐ διὰ λέξεως μόνον ἀλλὰ καὶ διὰ συμβόλων. Sed præcipue id usurparunt Prophetæ modo ex Dei præscripto, modo spon- te sua, aut ipsi facientes aliquid quod rei futuræ haberet significationem, aut alios facere imperantes. Exempla sunt I. Reg XXII 11. Ef. XX. 2. Jer. IX. 17. c. XXVII, 2. Ezech. IV. 2. c. XII. 7. Of. I. 2. Act. XXI. 2. & alibi, Dicit ergo Christus, si quis crumenam habet ne eam domi relinquat, sed secum ferat. Qui imperativum in futurum vertunt, eos apparet offensos præcepti sibi non intellecti novitate, sed lectionem receptam defendit interpretum consensus.

ὁμοίως καὶ πήραν) Hoc dicitur per modum parentheseos. Nam ad crumenam redit oratio. Sed obiter & transcursu admonet Christus pera quoque opus fore, victu alioqui defecturo. Βαλάντιον est כיס, quod μαρσύππιον plerum- que vertunt Græci. Πήρα ילקוט.

καὶ ὁ μὴ ἔχων) Scilicet βαλάντιον, quod habere solent qui aliquid habent pecuniæ. Nam de pera erat interjecta mentio, ut diximus, quod verborum quoque ordo satis in- dicat. Est enim quasi dicat: quisquis crumenam habet su- mat eam: sed simul cum pera: & quisquis non habet, po- tius vestimentum divendat, quam gladio careat: id enim mos est facere quoties vis timetur.

πωλησάτω τὸ ἱμάτιον αὐτοῦ) Hoc non præcise præcipitur, sed comparate, id est omnino gladium sibi comparet vel veste divendita si aliter comparare non potest.

## 22:37
Vers. 37. ἔτι τοῦτο) After many other things endured by me, now that last thing remains, that I be condemned to death as a criminal, whence also those things will follow which pertain to you; for the ignominy and hatred of the master redounds to the disciples.

Τέλος ἔχει) That is, they will now immediately receive an end. Τὰ περὶ ἐμοῦ, namely those things which pertain to the state of my depression.

Latin:

Vers. 37. ἔτι τοῦτο) Post multa alia à me tolerata jam il- lud ultimum restat, ut pro scelerato morti addicar, unde & illa sequentur quæ ad vos pertinent; nam magistri igno- minia atque odium ad discipulos redundat.

Τέλος ἔχει) Id est jam jam finem accipient. Τὰ περὶ ἐμοῦ ea scilicet quæ ad statum depressionis meæ perti- nent.

## 22:38
Vers. 38. ἰδοὺ μάχαιραι ὧδε δύο) They say this, that they may understand whether satisfaction has been made to his command by those two swords. Josephus says that the Galileans were μαχίμους: and it is credible that since the journey from Galilee to the city was infested with robberies, many who set out for the city did so with swords: which can also be gathered from Josephus in several places: who also says that the Essenes went about armed for fear of robbers: and Cyril relates that in his own time it was also customary for this to be done in Palestine on account of wild beasts. The Apostles seem to have followed this custom, not all, but two out of the whole number, one of whom seems to have been Peter, who soon uses a sword, as his own.

ἱκανόν ἐστι) It is sufficient for the signification, for in battle even twelve swords would do nothing against an encroaching multitude of enemies.

He does not say ἱκανοί ἐισι, that is, swords, but ἱκανόν ἐστι, It is enough. Therefore, the Syriac is not correct, they are sufficient. Much less those who, in Theophylact, say this was spoken by irony: But Christ breaks off the discourse: Enough has been said about these things. I see you do not grasp what I mean by my parabolic speech: experience itself and the event will soon reveal its meaning to you. Theophylact handed down this meaning when he said that, when He saw the disciples did not understand the saying, He passes on and allows the event of things to explain the understanding of the words. However, the distortion of Boniface VIII, Bishop of Rome, is inept, who from this proves both the temporal and spiritual sword, or the supreme political and ecclesiastical jurisdiction of the Roman See, C. unam sanctam, de major. & obed. &c. Peter here carried not two swords, but one, and he was ordered to put it back into its sheath.

PART II. OF THE CHAPTER. Pertaining to the

Latin:

Vers. 38. ἰδοὺ μάχαιραι ὧδε δύο) Dicunt hoc, ut intelli- gant an per duos illos gladios satisfactum sit ipsius imperio. Galilæos fuisse μαχίμους ait Josephus: & credibile est cum iter è Galilæa ad urbem infestum esset latrociniis, multos ad urbem profectos cum gladiis: quod & ex Josepho ali- quot locis colligere est: qui & Essenos ait armatos inces- sisse latronum metu: & suo tempore etiam ferarum causa id fieri in Palæstina solitum Cyrillus narrat. Hunc morem secuti videntur Apostoli, non omnes, sed ex omni numero duo, quorum alter fuisse Petrus videtur, qui mox gladio, ut suo, utitur.

ἱκανόν ἐστι) Satis ad fignificationem, nam ad pugnam vel duodecim gladii nihil facerent adverfus ingruentem ho- stium multitudinem.

Non dicit ἱκανοί ἐισι sc. μάχαιραι, sed ἱκανόν ἐξτι. Satis est, Non ergo recte Syrus, fufficientes sunt. Nedum illi, qui apud Theophyl. per Ironiam hoc di- ctum ajunt: Sed abrumpit Chriftus fermonem: Satis est de his dictum. Video vos non affequi quid velim parabolico sermone: ipsa mox experientia & eventus ejus sensum vobis patefaciet. Quem sensum tradidit Theophyl. quando, inquit, vidit discipulos non intelligere dictum, transit, & eventui rerum permittit explicare dictorum intelligentiam. Inepta autem est detorsio Bonifacii IIX. P. R. qui hinc & corporalem & spiritualem gladium seu su- premam jurisdictionem Politicam, & Ecclesiafti- cam Sedis Romanæ probat C. unam sanctam, de ma- jor. & obed. &c. Petrus hic non duos, sed unum geffit gladium, eumq; jussg est recondere in vaginā.

PARS II. CAPITIS. Ad ipsam passionis historiam pertinens. I. Passio Christi ad montem Oliveti.

## 22:40
Vers. 40. προσεύχεσθε μὴ ἐισελεῖν) See what

Latin:

Vers. 40. προσεύχεσθε μὴ ἐισελεῖν) Vide quæ ad Matth.

## 22:41
Vers. 41. ὡσεὶ λίθου βολήν) כמטחוי Gen. XXI, 16. Θεὶς τὰ γόνατα) The common custom of praying was by standing: they prayed on their knees whenever a more serious matter pressed.

Latin:

Vers. 41. ὡσεὶ λίθου βολήν) כמטחוי Gen. XXI, 16. Θεὶς τὰ γόνατα) Communis mos orandi erat stando: in genibus orabant quoties res major urgebat.

## 22:42
Vers. 42. ἐἰ βούλῃ παρενεγκεῖν) That is, would that you were willing to take away: for we have already noted twice that εἶ is so accepted, even when joined with the indicative. This manner of speaking, not being understood, has given occasion for changing the text. Concerning this desire, we have spoken at Matthew.

Latin:

Vers. 42. ἐἰ βούλῃ παρενεγκεῖν) Id est utinam velles au- ferre: nam ita εἶ accipi, etiam cum indicativo conjunctum, jam bis notavimus. Hoc loquendi genus non intellectum mutandæ scripturæ locum præbuit. De hoc desiderio di- ximus ad Matthæum.

## 22:43
Vers. 43. ὤφθη ἄγγελος ἀπ' ὐρανοῦ) Both the superstition and the rashness of those who deleted this clause and the following one concerning the sweat were blameworthy, for no weightier reason than that which we said above was the cause for the deletion of the passage concerning the weeping. For Christ, having been left to the strength of the human nature that was deprived of the divinity dwelling within Him, and consequently having been made a little lower than the angels, had need of the consolation of angels: which is to be observed also in other temptations of Christ, as in Matthew IV. 11. He received similar consolation at another time from a heavenly voice in John XII. 28.

ἐνισχύων ἀυτόν) Recalling to his mind the promised glory and the salvation of the human race, the fruit of this death, by which he was refreshed for a time, he was again permitted to feel sorrow.

Latin:

Vers. 43. ὤφθη ἄγγελος ἀπ' ὐρανοῦ) Illaudabilis fuit & su- perstitio & temeritas eorum, qui hanc particulam & sequen- tem de sudore delevêre, nihilo graviore de causa, quam quo illud quod supra est de fletu deletum diximus. Christus enim destitutę divinitatis in se habitantis virtute humanæq; naturæ relictus, ac proinde ἐλαττωθεὶς βραχύ τι παρ' ἀγγέλους opus habuit angelorum solatio: quod in aliis etiam Christi πειρασμοῖς observare est, ut Matth. IV. 11. Simile solatium alias a voce cœlesti accepit Johannis XII. 25.

ἐνισχύων ἀυτόν) Gloriam promissam & salutem humani generis mortis istius fructum in mentem ipsi revocans, qui- bus ad tempus refocillatus, iterum permissus est mœrori.

## 22:44
V. 44. ἐν ἀγωνίᾳ) The Greeks properly use this word for that movement of the mind toward grave danger which nevertheless would not await fortitude. Porphyry, regarding that passage of Homer: 'Trembling fear seized the limbs of the Trojans each one, and in Hector himself the heart beat in his breast,' says thus: 'For if others trembled before their eyes, he, standing in the danger and being brave, only was in agony.'

That this passage concerning the strengthening by the Angel and the bloody sweat of Christ is authentic, even if it was not found in certain Greek and Latin codices, as Hilary testifies in book X de Trinit. and Jerome in book II contra Pelagium c. 6, which is not to be imputed to the orthodox, with Epiphanius in Ancorat., but to the Docetae and Aphthartodocetae, just as Euthymius in part II of the Panoplia c. 20 revealed a similar mutilation of Scripture by the Armenians, who were infected with the same heresy, and that it is not to be reckoned among the deuterocanonical parts of Scripture with Sixtus Senensis in book I of the Bibl. S. c. 22, but ought to be held as equally canonical as the rest in the Holy Scriptures, this is taught by 1. the unanimous consensus of modern Greek codices 2: the most approved older Greek codices, which Jerome designates in the aforementioned place, and which the authors of the Complutensian edition and also of the King’s work collated, which likewise Theodore Beza and Franc. Lucas Burgensis, and those whom Aldus Manutius in the year 1518 compared, who consistently exhibited this pericope. 3. The consensus of the Syriac, various Arabic, Ethiopic, Persian, Latin, Vulgate, and other German versions, likewise the English, French, Italian, Spanish, Hungarian, Polish, Irish, Icelandic, and Danish versions, whose authors did not find this history lacking in the Greek codices. 4. The testimonies of the most ancient Fathers, who make mention of this history: as for instance in the second century Justin’s Dial. cum Tryph.

Irenaeus, Book III, chapter on heresies, chapter 44. Tatian in the Harmony of the Gospels, Vol. VI of the Library of the Fathers. In the third century, Ammonius of Alexandria, Vol. VII of the Library of the Fathers, and Cyprian on the principal works of Christ. In the fourth century, Athanasius in the Dialogue on the unity of the Deity, etc. Epiphanius, Book II, Vol. 2, heresy 69. Caesarius in the dialogues annexed to the works of Nazianzen, which is falsely believed by some to be his brother's. Jerome, loc. cit., and Chrysostom, homily XXIII on Matthew. In the fifth century, Augustine, Book III on the agreement of the Gospels, and on Psalms 92 and 140. Prosper in the sentences of Augustine, no. 68. Titus of Bostra the younger, commentary on this passage. In the 6th century, Anastasius of Sinai in the Anagogical contemplation of the Hexaemeron. In the 7th century, Bede, commentary on the New Testament. In the 9th century, Rabanus Maurus and his disciple Strabo of Fulda on this passage. Photius, Epistle 133. In the 11th century, Theophylact on this passage, and Anselm in the sermon on the mirror of the Gospel. In the 12th century, Zacharias, Bishop of Chrysopolis, in the book of the Gospels. Euthymius Zigabenus, commentary on the four Gospels. Rupert of Deutz, Book VI on the works of the Lord, chapter 4. Bernard, sermon on the passion of the Lord, etc. Most conjecture that the angel who appeared to Christ was Gabriel, whose name means θε̃υ ἰσχὺν,

But what was this ἰσχύειν [strengthening]? Scholars differ on this. Lyranus says generally that this strengthening by the angel was done in the manner of a servant; others say it was done only externally, not internally, with Fr. Quaresmius, following Thomas, 3rd part, q. 22, art. 4, and Cajetan, which Corn. à Lapide says was done both by praising the extraordinary fortitude of Christ and by setting forth the will of the Father and the fruit that would come from the passion. Regarding the former, Theophilus Raynaud, Book IV, section 1, chapter 4, folio 462, cites Epiphanius in the Ancoratus, that the angel assisted Christ not as a consoler and dispeller of sadness, but as a praiser and herald of his extraordinary fortitude. Regarding the latter, Quaresmius, Vol. III on the wounds of Christ, chapter 3, section 9, cites Salmeron, who says the angel did not bring any strengthening that provided relief, but expressed the Father's will: and Bede, who says he was strengthened, but with such a strengthening that it did not diminish his pain but rather increased it: he was strengthened by the magnitude of the fruit, but without the bitterness of the pain being removed. Seb. Barradius, last volume, folio 250, says the angel is said to have strengthened Christ because he consoled him with words, praises, external appearance, and the wiping away of the bloody sweat, and in other ways unknown to us. Others say he strengthened him only in that he admired and praised the fortitude of Christ and his ready spirit, but the angel provided no consolation in reality, nor did he speak any consolatory words, which Vasquez tries to prove laboriously, part 1 in part 3, d. 56, c. 2. To this are added those who deny that the angel used any words in strengthening Christ, and they judge that he performed the office of a consoler only by assistance, or companionship and the weighing of sorrows, and also by the assumption of a similar habit and gesture, such as if Christ were bending his knees, he himself would also bend his knees, if Christ were prostrate on the ground, he would also prostrate himself, and if Christ were weeping, the angel would likewise weep. But just as B. Klotzius refuted the Spaniard Vasquez by means of other Spanish Doctors in Exercise 18 on the bloody sweat of Christ, thesis 21, and thus taught that the strengthening was done by the proposition of objects, by the contemplation of which the pain in Christ was mitigated, namely the hope of the most joyful catastrophe, that is, the glorious resurrection and the fruit that would redound from the passion, just as Moses and Elijah also spoke with him in the transfiguration about his departure from Jerusalem and strengthened him, Luke 9:31, so not only mere companionship and the mutual weighing of the sorrows which the soul of Christ felt, which not even the whole communion of angels is able to weigh sufficiently, nor could their weighing, however it may be established, whether signified by deed or by words, have contributed anything of moment to the strengthening, nor could the conformation of outward gesture and habit be of any use for τὸ ἐνισχύειν [strengthening]: and these things could easily be snatched away to a fellowship in bearing agonies, if it be said that the angel bent his knees, prostrated himself, wept, or even assumed the habit and gesture of an orator with Christ. Although, however, according to the warning of the ancients, the angel comforted, but did not carry: Is. LXIII. v. 3. Nor indeed does the force and ἔμφασις [emphasis] of the word import only a verbal but also a real comforting, made not by a bare proposition of objects, but also by an interior corroboration of the powers, in which indeed the angel was only engaged διακονικῶς [ministerially]. Truly by the Angel, says the Blessed Klotz, p. 209, Christ was comforted; we constantly assert that strength was truly conferred upon Christ from the eternal treasures of divine power through the ministry of the Angel, with Hieronymus, Cyril, Damascene, Nicetas, Bede, and the Scholastics themselves, Thomas, Perpinianus, Simon de Cassia, Bernardino, and others. Which, after those authors and most others have been adduced, he confirms in these words, p. 211, viz., as the Patriarch Jacob in his struggle with the Angel ἐνίσχυσε μετὰ Θεῦ [strengthened with God] Gen. XXXII. 28, or as it is in Hos. XII. 1, ἐνίσχυσε μετ' ἀγγέλε [he strengthened with the angel], because he was increased in strength and corroborated by the same Angel, his fellow-wrestler, so that he finally emerged a victor, just as Samson, captured and bound by the Philistines, nevertheless by his prayers obtained τὸ ἐνισχύειν [the strengthening] to pull down the columns of the building, Jud. XVI. 28, just as King David, about to fight against his enemies, boasts of the strength divinely granted to him, praying with great confidence to the Lord ἐνισχύσεις με δυνάμει &c. 2 Sam. XXII. 40. Let us think of Christ the Savior in that highest degree of humiliation, struggling with sin, the wrath of God, the curse, and eternal death, as having received from the Angel, the minister of God, not angelic but divine strength, so that he finally emerged victorious, just as it is said of the Israelites fighting against the Benjamite tribe: ἐνίσχυσαν περ' ἑνὸς Ἰσραὴλ, they were strengthened, and the men of Israel. Luth. Das Volck ermannet sich. Jud. XX. 22. Thus it is certain that Christ the Lord received new strength for the angelic presence, and the strengthening made by it, to fight bravely against his enemies: just as God says elsewhere to the Elect: Ἐγώ εἰμὶ ὁ Θεὸς ἐνίσχυσας Es. XLI. 10. For He himself is the one who ἐνισχύει τ υἱὸν Ἰσραὴλ, Joël. III. 16. Thus through the Angel, God the Father inwardly imbued the Son with strength and consolation, by which he became more certain of divine aid and therefore more spirited for the battle. Which the late lamented further explains thus. p. 214. But yet, what we note, Christ was not comforted by the Angel by a bare proposition of objects, as Cajetan asserts with certain recent writers, who understand it in such a way that the Angel only proposed to Christ the objects of consolation, inspiring nothing into him, nor instructing him by any reason or teaching him by interior illumination, but also inwardly in his soul and its faculties filled with comfort, or that the angel suggested a new reason to the intellect and memory of Christ, the actual knowledge of which Christ had suspended for the time, because what Alphonsus Salmeron also confesses, t. 10, tr. 14. The Lord did not concur with the memory of Christ for the recollection of those things which could give him courage, but willed that he should meditate on nothing but the torments and afflictions by which he was to be vexed, or that he proposed a new and singular kind of consolatory expansion and weighing of reason in this or that way, the evidence of which in the soul God the Father, by an admirable counsel, willed to be closed to Christ for that time with some respect to the objects, so that Christ in that deepest κενώσει [emptying] had not so deeply penetrated it, just as it was proposed by the Angel. Christ could indeed, even according to his human nature, in which all the treasures of divine wisdom and knowledge were hidden even in that state as regards κτῆσιν [possession], have comforted himself without the ministry of any man or angel, nor would he have needed any subsidy or ministry of any creature, if only he had willed to exercise fully in that state the Majesty, wisdom, and knowledge communicated to him at the first point of his conception as regards χρῆσιν [use], but he abdicated the plenary use of it, and denied himself the influx of divine powers, and suspended and withdrew for a little while the rays of divine illumination and consolation in his soul, so that in this part also, being tempted, he might become like us in all things except sin. These things are more congruent than the not sufficiently weighed comments of the Jesuits or certain Reformed, in which there is often need of a mind and a just δοκιμασία [testing].

Vers. 44. ἐκτενέστερον προσηύχετο [he prayed more earnestly]) As the pain increased, he intensified the force of his prayer: expressing the same thing also by his gesture: for before he had bent his knees: now he falls prostrate to the ground with his whole body, as we have said from Matthew and Mark: but holy men were accustomed to pray in that position of the body in extreme necessity. Wherefore there were those who here confuse τὸ γόνατα τίθε- σθαι [to place the knees], that is בָּרַךְ [to kneel], and πίπτειν ἐπὶ πρόσωπον [to fall upon the face] or ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς [upon the ground], that is הִשְׁתַּחֲוָה [to bow down], for this is ἐκτενέστερον προσευχομένου [praying more earnestly].

καταβαίνοντες [descending]) Thus the Latin reads: and the sense seems to be clearer: for blood, especially when it falls to the ground, is seen θρομβώδης [clotted]. For θρόμβος [clot] is, even to Galen in the first book on seed, τὸ ἅμα πεπηγός [that which has coagulated]. The Syrian also seems to have read thus: but in such a way as to understand the word ἱδρῶτος [sweat], which kind of speaking is not without example. Aristotle teaches in the third book of the history of animals that it happens to some to ἰδρῶσαι αἱ- ματώδη περιττώματι [to sweat a bloody discharge] because of cachexia and because of the scarcity of heat. Nevertheless, in this place there is nothing from which you can certainly conclude that blood was mixed with this sweat. For, as Theophylact and Euthymius note, it is not said ἐγένετο ἰδρὼς αἵματος [there was a sweat of blood] but ἐγένετο ὁ ἰδρὼς αὐτοῦ ὡσεὶ θρόμβοι αἵματος [his sweat became as it were clots of blood]. Which words indicate that it was true sweat that flowed out, not thin, however, but thick, such as clots of blood are wont to be, since sweat is hardly wont θρομβοῦσθαι [to clot]. Certainly Justin understood it no otherwise in his dialogue with Trypho, who, omitting the mention of blood, thought it enough to have said clots: ἰδρὼς ὡσεὶ θρόμβοι κατεχεῖτο ἀυτοῦ ἐνχομένου [sweat as it were clots flowed down from him]. Such is that: And salty sweat went through the limbs.

He wishes to extenuate or rather to invalidate that miracle concerning the bloody sweat of Christ. In which he had as a predecessor a Syncretist not unlike Georg Calixtus. Whom, however, his admirer Dr. Heinrich Müller, calling him a man superior to all praise, an unpraiseworthy enemy of the Formula of Concord, nay, worthy of all detestation on account of the thefts detected by the blessed Dorsch in the 'Theologus Latro', here abandons in 'Jesu patiente' p. 20. But especially at length, after the blessed Dorsch, in 'Synopsis Theol. Zachar.' c. IX. p. 297. seqq., the blessed Klotz treated it in 'tract. de sudore Christi sanguineo Exerc. IX.' against Grotius, Euthymius, Photius, Pricaeus (he teaches that the matter is doubtful concerning Theophylact), and he warned that the opinion concerning the bloody sweat of Christ was so certain to the venerable antiquity of the Fathers that he pronounced anathema upon those who denied it (among whom Calixtus professed his name), proving the bloody sweat of Christ 1. from the word Θρόμβοι, which is used by Dioscorides, Galen, and Hippocrates concerning the coagulation of blood established outside the vessels; and it was used no differently by Luke the physician of Antioch; especially because 2. the word αἵματος was added: For if he wished to indicate only this, that the sweat was not thin but thick, why did he add the word αἵματος to that θρόμβοι, when from this little word it could have been sufficiently clear that the drops of sweat were coagulated like clots? Or for what purpose did he make mention of drops of blood rather than of other liquid things? And why does he mention blood running down to the ground unless he wished to signify that the sweat had run down with bloody drops so copiously that they flowed from him onto the ground? 3. He confirms this from the nature of blood: whose property it is, when it passes outside the natural vessels deprived of its innate heat, to congeal with cold and go into clots. It is always moist and warm, says Aristotle, as long as it is contained within the body of an animal: But

when it has flowed out, it congeals in all cases except for stags and fallow deer, and if there is anything else of this nature. But watery sweat, as Grotius himself also indicates, is scarcely accustomed to θρομβοῦσθαι (clot), unless perhaps it is stained and mixed with blood. Therefore, it is attributed to watery humor in vain and without foundation, which, according to the letter, from the nature of the thing and the property of the word, should only be attributed to blood. 4. By the Syrian interpreter: who testifies quite clearly that the sweat of Christ, which fell to the ground, was truly bloody, while he translates it in this place thus: And his sweat was as it were great drops of blood and the blood fell upon the ground etc. And indeed that bloody sweat of Christ has always been believed in the Church with great consensus, which why Calixtus and Grotius should have postponed in favor of one Euthymius, let their champions see. Justin Martyr, disciple of the Apostles, asserts this bloody sweat in his Dialogue with Trypho; Irenaeus the Martyr, disciple of Polycarp the Martyr, Bishop of Lyons, whose Greek words are read in the first Dialogue of Theodoret; Ammonius of Alexandria around the year of Christ 226 in the Harmony of the Gospels; Cyprian (or whoever the author of the book of similar age to him may have been) on the Cardinal works of Christ; Caesarius in the Dialogues in Photius, f. 1098; Jerome, book II against Pelagius, ch. 6; Augustine, book 3 on the consensus of the Gospels and in the Enarrations on Psalm 140; Prosper of Aquitaine in the Sentences of Augustine, no. 68; Titus of Bostra in his commentary on Luke; Bede, Vol. V of Works, f. 138; Zacharias Chrysopolitanus in the Evangelists, A.D. 1001; Rupert of Deutz, book VI on the works of the Lord, ch. 4; Bernard, Sermon on the passion of Christ; Suidas under the word Θρόμβοι (clots). To these add the sigh of the Greek Church, sung for many centuries now, διὰ τ᾽ ἀγωνίας τε Σαίματος ἱδρῶτος ρῦσαι ἡμᾶς κύριε (by the agony of Thy bloody sweat, deliver us, O Lord), which it is well known is repeated in our Litany (I believe also in the Church of Helmstedt) in the vernacular language. But what cause, I ask, did that incomparable theologian, superior to all praise, have for departing from the common faith of the Church: that he believed instead that not clots of natural blood, but only copious and thick sweat, as if they were clots of blood, fell to the ground in the agony of Christ? Because, forsooth, it is not plausible that God, beyond what the reason of nature allows, afflicted His Son and immediately through His own power brought upon Him those things which neither the proximity of death apprehended by the mind, nor the cruelty of the Jews could have inflicted. O untimely mercy, by which all mercy is overturned! Who then now believes that God inflicted upon His Son the very punishment of hell, which neither the cruelty of the devil, let alone the Jews, could have inflicted? Will it not be all over with our liberation from eternal death? Will not divine mercy toward us be destroyed, in a manner and fashion entirely Socinian, as being that for which, apart from satisfaction and the full suffering of the punishments due to us, there was no place? For the Socinians also blaspheme that God is to be accused of cruelty on account of such great punishments inflicted upon the most innocent only-begotten Son. Therefore, let Dr. Müller correct his ‡ πανὺ (altogether) here, saying on p. 22: here all things exceed the reason of nature; the efficient cause of the blood bursting forth, which was the burden of sins, the sense of divine wrath, the struggle with the devil, death, and hell; then the form was not blood flowing here, as it is wont to be otherwise, but of thick and condensed drops; then the end, which was the redemption of the whole human race. And in the question. Theological Semi-century, the second, q. xxxix, toward the end: (Christ) sustained not only bodily death, and that by the shedding not of one or another drop, but of his whole blood; but also eternal death, which consists in the struggle of divine wrath according to the judgment of the STRICT judgment of God, where he also praises that of Guillandus on ch. XXVI of Matthew: that Christ, afflicted by the image of death and hell, did not dread death and hell otherwise than if he alone had designated the sins of all men: and therefore took upon himself for our sake the pains of death and hell: What wonder then that those things were inflicted upon him divinely which could not be inflicted by the cruelty of the Jews; since he had to satisfy not the Jews, but divine justice. But he corrected that incomparable theologian (whom one might easily call a Nestorius with the same right, although the blessed Dr. Clotzius did so anonymously in the aforementioned Exercitation. XV. thesis 6, whose refutation, although a little too long, it is worth adding: CHRIST, established in agony, sweated, where in the struggle he was established with all the powers and greater strength of human and angelic nature against death armed with the stings of Satan, of the curse, and of eternal condemnation, and against God Almighty Himself, who was angry on account of sin toward the whole human race, of which he had become the sponsor, and had derived upon himself all the curses and thunderbolts due to us, which to sustain by the powers of our nature alone, if Christ the Lord had been a lover of mankind and supernatural divine virtue had not been added, would have been clearly impossible; for although our Savior acted as a man in the whole act of the passion, it is nevertheless false what a certain most famous man says, that the human nature left to its natural condition suffered as much as it would have suffered if it had neither been personally united with the divinity, nor had known anything of the divine decree. For Christ could not have suffered as much as he suffered, with the human nature remaining safe and alive, unless it had been united with the divinity, sustained by whose infinite strength he suffered, lest he perish; the very words of Christ indicate this, when he says that his soul is sorrowful even unto death, i.e., so surrounded by pain and grief that he must perish unless he is divinely sustained. Isaiah 63:5. Therefore, that also detracts from the value of the passion of Christ, which the SAME most famous man asserts: that it is not plausible that God, beyond what the reason of nature allows, afflicted His Son, and immediately through His own power brought upon Him those things which neither the proximity of death apprehended by the mind nor the cruelty of the Jews could have inflicted. When he wrote these things, he did not think of those utterances of the Holy Spirit: God willed to crush him, God made our sins run into him, it is exacted (punishment from God) and he is afflicted (by God), he himself is the sponsor. And if it is not likely that God afflicted his Son, except as the reason of (human) nature allows, etc., it will likewise not be likely that God was truly angry on account of sins, that Christ truly felt the gravity of divine wrath, that he truly satisfied God for our sins, because such afflictions, which are not on account of the reason of our nature, cannot be satisfactory. B. Klotzius is not wrong about this: for Calixtus is engaged there in his consideration of how far the eternal Son of the eternal Father was willing to humble himself for our sake, and what, although he could have inhibited those infirmities, he nevertheless admitted of his own accord so that he might satisfy for us. But he does not extend that HOW FAR further than the REASON OF NATURE allowed: and that he suffered only AS MUCH as he would have suffered if (these are the explicit words of Calixtus, loc. cit.) the human nature had not been personally united with the divinity, nor had he had any knowledge of the divine decree. But what kind of satisfaction is that to the divinity not united to human nature! What kind of voluntary submission and obedience rendered to the divine will, if he had known nothing of the will and decree of God? Whence one must greatly wonder that Mr. Dr. Müller followed Calixtus here in this, and the same under the eulogy of the incomparable theologian of our century of blessed memory (which certainly no orthodox doctor knowingly and prudently would attribute to such a fierce champion of heretical novelties) in this cause, without any warning to the youth entrusted to his care, stood firm: that namely the decree of the Father concerning satisfaction for the sins of the human race was unknown to Christ, even though he himself professed (p. 15) that God cannot the application of it, because this is against His own justice. Voetius certainly asserts this with Parker and Rivet, that Christ in His soul endured infernal punishments, not only analogically and by compensation or equivalently (which seems to have been the opinion of Vossius, when in l. I. Harm. Evangel. c. XX. §. 17. p. 179. infinite, he says, were the torments of Christ, but not in time, or MAGNITUDE, but in the dignity of the person) but the same, as regards their essence or substance: for He endured, he says, the punishments denounced to Adam, but those were infernal. So that he not only rejected the Papists, who acknowledge only the death and bodily torment of Christ, and none of the soul, except an accidental one from the sympathy of the soul with the body, but also wrote to the English Theologian Bilson, saying that, insisting on the footsteps of the Papists, he contends that all passion of the soul arose from condolence, conjunction, and sympathy with the body, or at least was not undertaken from debt, as our own and in our place, but by Christ's own choice. See p. II. disp. select. p. 106.

For that ὡσεὶ is not of likeness, but of truth, as in Luke XXIV. 2, John I. 14. Henri Estienne, citing the blessed Gerhard, Harm. passion. c. I. col. 17, thinks the particle ὡσεὶ was used to soften what had preceded, namely, that Christ did not simply sweat drops of blood, but as it were clots of blood congealed by terror, because physicians testify that that watery serum in which blood, enclosed in the veins, floats, and by which as a vehicle it is carried into all parts of the body, is the matter of sweat; therefore it is probable that this came out together with the blood, since the Evangelist makes mention of both sweat and blood. Hilary, l. X. de Trinit., says: No one will dare to attribute the sweat of Christ to infirmity, because it is against nature to sweat blood, etc. Whence John Gerhard Vossius, who otherwise willingly adheres to Grotius, here deserted him: For he says, l. I. Harm. Evang. c. XX. p. 177. what is said, ὡσεὶ θρόμβοι αἵματος, that is a bare comparison, which Euthymius wished: or a proverbial hyperbole, as Theophylact believed: but it is to be taken truly and simply. Namely, the blood flowed drop by drop, almost as from those struck by that kind of serpent, from which the name hemorrhoid comes. In Christ, either, the matter of sweat failing, even thinner blood flowed out; as Cajetan wishes: or, mixing itself with the thicker matter of sweat, it made those bloody clots of sweat. See more in Gerhard, loc. cit. Voetius, in his disp. de agon. & desert. Christi, thinks that that bloody gore was natural from a proximate cause: We, he says concerning this sweat, in part II. Disp. select. p. 172. no less than the efflux of blood and water from the side of Christ, we maintain that it was natural, from a proximate cause, that is, although admirable, and a miracle of nature, and indeed even supernatural, if we look at the remote efficient causes and the end. We think we find the proximate cause in the affections and their commotion: affections, I say, partly of sadness and fear, which recall the spirits and blood toward the heart from the exterior parts: partly of love, desire, ardor, and zeal (Luke XXII. 44) which propel the spirits and blood from the heart toward the exterior parts of the body: hence it happened that the blood, agitated back and forth like the Euripus, and thus attenuated, erupted together with the serous humor from the veins through the skin. That such a thing can naturally happen, especially if a rarer texture of the body and skin is added, is testified by

Philosophers and Physicians, etc. Voetius alleges for himself Philip in Consiliis part. I: p. 579, Wendelin in Philosop. moral. l. I. c. 36, and from the Physicians Antonio Satorellus l. XXIII. de Nat. Sanit. c. 12. But that blood should flow through the pores, and indeed thicker and well-consistent, and that in a body suffering from no depraved constitution, is a miracle exceeding nature, which, with Thomas Minadous Rhodiginus, a physician of Udine, in Disp. 1. de sud. sangu. praised by Voetius, Müllerus acknowledges l. c.; and the blessed Klotz solidly proved in Exerc. XVI. that the sweat of Christ was miraculous by reason of the matter, the subject, the quantity, the quality, the consequent coagulation of clots, and the profusion: and that not only against Boetius, Montagu, Gerhard, John Vossius, and the Calvinists, but also against the Papists Lyranus, Cajetan, Barradius, Maldonado, Jansen of Ypres, Corn. à Lap., Barth. Medina, Francis. Collius, Suarez, Tirinus, Drexel, and the sons of physicians, Cyprian Marosa and Hier. Jordanus: with Hilary of Poitiers, X. de Trinit., Titus of Bostra, Zach. Chrysopol., Bede, John Gerson, Simon of Cassia, Gabr. Biel, Corn. Jansen, Bishop of Ghent, Franc. Quaresmius, Salmeron, Didacus Stella, John Raulin, Henr. Harphius, John Osorius, Stanisl. Grodilius, Philip Bosquier the Franciscan, Rainard Landemberg the Augustinian, Thomas of Trujillo the Dominican, Balth. Corderius the Jesuit, and Casp. à Reyes, a physician of Carmona, who in campis Elys. qq. 86. f. 681, affirms that the cause of this sweat was supernatural, and says that the assembly of the Fathers of the Council of Trent had so decreed, and that almost all theologians teach it. There was another greater force, he says, which was able to move the aforementioned sweat, namely, supernatural and divine: Thus the Holy Fathers. The council held at Trent decreed, and almost all theologians teach; and certainly it seems to be confirmed by evident reason that the cause was supernatural, because very copious drops of blood flowed out, running down even to the ground; furthermore, they were drops that came forth from the body, not in the manner of dew as happens in sweat, and as if that mode of exiting does not at all suit the form of sweat: which, if they are joined with the most exact temperament of Christ, subject to no diseases or causes of diseases, it will be easy, nay necessary, to believe that the cause of that sweat was superior and by no means natural, for surely no one has sweated blood drop by drop, but in the form of dew, wherefore both the mode of exiting was particular, and indicated that it had a supernatural cause. See Klotzius, loc. cit., p. 98. Who, on p. 162, adds Joh. Bustanantius of Cambrai and also Calvin, Harm. Evang., fol. 378. If anyone, I ask, today were to emit blood by sweating, and indeed in such quantity that drops should trickle to the ground, it would be an incredible portent. We now subjoin the very declaration of the blessed Klotzius, delivered in Exerc. XIII, thesis 8.
