The most precious blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, which—a thing that can never be said enough—bursting from the veins in that agony, was not impure, corrupt, serous, infected, not vitiated by disease or sickness, which sometimes becomes so watery that as soon as it has flowed from the body it cannot coagulate on account of excessive liquidity, but it was most pure blood, well cooked, digested, perfect in nature, no different from that other which remained enclosed in the veins, differing only a little in heat and rarefaction, preserving the perfect form of blood known by the cooking of heat, retaining its figure intact, true, whole, generous, destined by God through the operation of the Holy Spirit for nourishment for a most generous, most beautiful, and impeccable body, destined by the operation of the Holy Spirit, departing into drops while it emanated from the body, falling to the form of drops, and touching the earth, it concreted and coagulated into clots, which is proper to true, healthy, and pure blood flowing out. And that is an argument for us that the sweat of no man ever could naturally occur. Thomas Minadocus, in book 1 of his Medical Disputations, Disputation I, concerning the bloody sweat, which Voetius cited in the aforementioned place on page 172, although he proves that such a sweat is natural, nevertheless teaches that Christ's bloody sweat was supernatural and miraculous: urging this point in particular: that in the Lord Jesus there could be no bodily infirmity because of the exceptional and superexcellent structure of his body, because of his most perfect and in every respect most absolute constitution, and because of the dignity and nobility of that same body. The blessed Dorscheus, in his Synopsis of Theology, on page 298, likewise urges the excellent temperament of Christ's body, and at the same time the clotted and copious eruption of blood: It is gathered from what has been said, he says, that no slight tincture of sweat arising from serous blood appeared in Christ: nor did an αἱματῶδες περίττωμα διὰ καχεξίαν erupt in his body, as Aristotle observed in his subject in book III of the Parts of Animals, chapter 6, and in book III of the History of Animals, chapter 19, either from a defect of native heat, or from the rarity and looseness of the skin and the opening of the pores, or from a vice of the faculties serving nutrition, namely the expulsive and retentive, but that in the most excellently tempered and healthy body of Christ, true, perfect, and most healthy blood erupted in abundance, and, having congealed into clots due to the coldness of the air, ran down to the ground. But such a clotted, copious, and profuse eruption of the best and most perfect blood in such a body is by no means natural, but clearly supernatural and peculiar in the most profound economic κένωσις of our Savior.

The cause of that prodigious sweat can indeed be established, partly as the supreme fear and anxiety, and the greatest sadness, which, because of the sense of divine wrath and the curse due to the sin of the human race, and the gravity of the torments of hell, occupied our mediator, who was placed in the most strict divine judgment, on every side, so that his soul was περίλυπος even unto death, or lethally; whence it is a wonder that blood was pushed through the pores, since, on the contrary, blood in more severe consternations abandons the outer limbs and runs back into the heart, as if to bring aid to the heart, which is faint and in danger of life due to fear and anxiety: but it is found to be even more wonderful here, how clotted blood could penetrate through the narrow passages of the pores, seeing that it had already congealed into clots in the body of Christ due to that extreme sadness and anxiety: since otherwise fear and sorrow also freeze and constipate the blood: partly, however, the agony and fortitude of Christ, when he was struggling with sin, and the Devil, and the divine wrath itself and eternal death, which, because of the fervent heat, ought to have rarefied and dissolved the blood, but—which increases the power of the miracle—it pushed out whole clots of blood without rarefaction by its own vehemence, so that it is as if fortitude and zeal were mutually struggling with sorrow and anxiety, the latter driving the blood to the heart and constipating it, the former not being so clearly able to rarefy and dissolve the same, yet the blood was still clotted, while the heart, being strengthened and burning with more vehement zeal, was driving and pushing the clots of blood so that they broke forth in great abundance through the pores. To this contributes the fact that Theophrastus Eremus compares agony with anger, and distinguishes it from fear, in that in the latter heat seeks the interior, but in the former it is provoked to the exterior: whence they lean upon the sponge, which Voetius brought forward to teach that the proximate natural cause of Christ's bloody sweat was such; and it becomes clear that not only was the proximate cause, as he wishes, supernatural, but that the miracle must also be located in the proximate cause itself: not only in the cause of both anxiety and sadness, and of zeal and the most powerful agony, but also in the effect of both, the bloody sweat, and its prodigious protrusion. Nor is that declaration of Hieronymus Jordanus, the Göttingen physician, in his book on that which is divine in diseases, chapter 37, page 183, to be admitted: That the blood was first liquefied by the greatest sorrow of the mind, and converted into serum or bloody water (about which the Evangelist has nothing), and soon, in that wonderful agony or most vehement zeal and contention concerning our salvation, was pushed out from the body like a copious sweat, etc. More correctly, other sons of the physicians, as Santorellus reports: Although, they say, it could naturally happen that serous and thin blood might flow through the narrow passages of the skin, thick and clotted blood, however, cannot naturally pass through. Whence also Stephanus Rodericus Castrensis, in his book Quæ ex quibus, book 1, chapter 23, proves that Christ's bloody sweat was by no means natural. In a not dissimilar manner, as we have already done, he explained it after our great Chemnitius, part I, Loc. Comm. page 69, our blessed Gerhard, a supreme and truly incomparable theologian, likewise in chapter II of his Harmony of the Gospels, page 17: In more severe consternations, the blood abandons the outer limbs and runs back into the heart, as if to bring aid to the heart, the citadel of life, but in Christ the blood bursts forth from the heart; for all his strength was broken and blunted, and as it is said in Isaiah 49:4, nature had consumed its strength, therefore it could not contain the blood, but it flowed out in abundance from the whole body as if through a broken dam, and, deprived of natural heat, congealed into clots. That is confirmed by experience, says the blessed Chemnitius in the aforementioned places, that in great consternation a resolution follows, so that the retentive power no longer performs its office, as is evident from the history of Arius. And Epiphanius says that Judas, for the same reason, burst in the middle, following that great resolution from despairing trepidation. Since, therefore, the agony in Christ was quite prolonged, such a dissolution occurred that neither the heart nor the veins retained the blood, but it flowed down as θρόμβοι. That word signifies, moreover, when something distills, and in the very distillation is thickened and congeals through cold, just as in salt mines a salty humor distills, which, when it has become congealed and thickened, is called θρόμβοι ἁλὸς by Suidas. Varinus: θρόμβος is congealed blood. Thus, when that great sadness in Christ had drawn back all the heat, the blood, dissolved into drops, was thickened, and thus flowed out as clotted, congealed blood. But it seems to conflict that in great and sudden consternations, when a vein is cut, blood does not flow out nor is it expelled, but seems to remain as if congealed within the vein itself. But this is the true answer: that in Christ there was not only immense sadness, but also a great struggle joined with consternation, because He willed to render that obedience to the Father, and from these contrary motions, which were most vehement, such an expulsion of congealed and thick blood occurred.

To this cause explained by the blessed Chemnitz, the blessed Gerhard adds another: The compression of the weight pressing upon Him can also be added to the dissolution of strength, so that in this way both causes are joined. For just as a certain heavier burden placed upon us expresses sweat from us, so when those most heavy weights were placed upon Christ at that time—namely, the sins of the whole world, the wrath of God, the curse of the law, and the power of death and the devil—pressed upon Him ineffably, either blood instead of sweat, or blood together with the sweat itself, or first indeed sweat, but afterwards with the anguish increased and the material of the sweat failing, pressed the very blood out of Him. Just as a more intense heat draws forth abundant sweat from us, so the heat of divine wrath drew forth the bloody sweat of Christ. All of which the blessed Clotzius repeated in the aforementioned treatise, and did not disapprove, although he explained the cause of the bloody sweat a little differently in the cited place, p. 192: Namely, that the anguish and sadness of soul arising from the sense of the wrath of God and of sins was the more remote and, as it were, objectively motivating cause, or root, and occasion of this sweat: but the proximate and immediate effective cause of that sweat from within was the agony of Christ, praying at greater length and more intensely, or that which exerted itself in the agony, and the immense and truly divine alacrity and fortitude of soul excited by angelic comfort, which most powerfully thrust forth clots of blood from all the openings of the veins and pores.

II. The betrayal of Judas.

V. 44. ἐν ἀγωνίᾳ) Proprie Græci hanc vocem usurpant de eo motu animi ad grave periculum, qui tamen fortitudi- nem non expectaret. Porphyrius ad illud Homeri: Τρῶας μὲν τρόμος αἰνὸς ὑπήλυθε γυῖα ἕκαστον Ἕκτορί τ' αὐτῷ θυμὸς ἐνὶ στήθεσσι πάτασσε, ita ait, εἰ μὲν γὰρ ἄλλοι πρὸ ὀμμάτων ἕτρεμον, ὁ δ' ἐν τῷ κινδύνῳ και θεστὼς ἀνδρεῖος ὢν, μόνον ἠγωνία.

Angelum qui Christo apparuit pleriq; Gabrielem fuisse conjectant, cujus nomen θε̃υ ἰσχὺν sonat,

Quodnam vero hoc ἰσχύειν fuerit? de eo variant eruditi. Lyranus γενικῶς, confortationem illam angeli factam, dicit, per modum servientis, alii factam exterius solum, non interius cum Fr. Quaresmio, præeunte Thoma 3. part. q. 22. art. 4. & Cajet. quod Corn. à Lapide factum dicit tum laudatione fortitudinis eximiæ Christi, tum propositione voluntatis Patris, & fructus è passione proventuri. De priori Theoph. Raynardus l. IV. sect. 1. c. 4. f. 462. laudat Epiphan. in Ancor. quod affiterit angelus Christo, non ut consolator & tristitiæ depulsor sed ut laudator, & præco eximiæ ejus fortitudinis. De posteriori Quaresmius T. III. de vulner. Christ. c. 3. sect. 9. adducit Salmeronem, qui dicit Angelum non attulisse confortationem ullam dantem refrigerationem, sed expressisse paternam voluntatem: & Bedam, qui confortatus est, inquit, sed tali confortatione, qua dolorem non minuit sed magis auxit: confortatus eum est ex fructus magnitudine, sed non subtracta doloris amaritudine. Seb. Barradius t. ult. f. 250. confortasse, inquit, dicitur angelus Christum, quia eum consolatus est verbis, laudibus, externo aspectu, & sudoris sanguinei abstersione, aliisq; modis nobis ignotis. Alii ita tantum confortasse dicunt, quod fortitudinem Christi & promptum ejus animum admirando laudavit, nullam vero reipsa consolationem adhibuerit Angelus, nec ulla verba consolatoria dixerit, quod operose probare conatur Vasquez p. 1. in p. 3. d. 56. c. 2. Huic accedunt, qui negant ullis verbis in confortando Christo usum esse Angelum, eumque censent solum assistentia, vel societate ac mœrorum ponderatione, nec non habitus ac gestus similis assumtione, ut Christo genua flectente, ipse etiam flecteret genua, Christo humi prostrato se quoq; prosterneret, Christo flente pariter fleret angelus, consolatoris munus peregisse. Sed uti Vasquezium Hispanum ex aliis Doctoribus Hispanicis confutavit B. Klotzius Exerc. XIIX. de sudore Christi sanguineo th. XXI. adeoq; docuit confortationem factam propositione objectorum, quorum intuitu dolor in Christo mitigatus, utpote spei lætissimæ catastrophes, gloriosæ sc. resurrectionis & fructus è passione redundaturi, sicuti Moses etiam & Elias in transfiguratione cum ipso de egressu ejus è Jerusalem collocuti sunt, eumq; confortarunt Luc. IX. 31. ita non solum nuda societas, ac mutua mœrorum, quos anima Christi sensit, ponderatio, quos nec tota angelorum communio satis ponderare valet, neq; eorum ponderatio, qualiscunque illa statuatur sive facto, sive verbis significata, quicquam momenti ad confortationem conferre potuerat, nec gestus- habitusq; externi conformatio ulli ad τὸ ἐνισχύειν esse potuit usui: & facile hæc abripi possent ad so- cietatem in ferendis angoribus, si cum Christo ge- nua flexisse, sese prostravisse, flevisse, vel etiam cū ipso oratoris habitum & gestum dicatur angelus assumpsisse. Quum tamen juxta veterum monitum angelus confortarit, sed non portarit: Es. LXIII. v. 3. Neq; vero solum verbalem sed etiam realem con- fortationem vis & ἔμφασις verbi importat, non nudâ objectorum propositione, sed interiori etiam vi- rium corroboratione, factam, in qua vero angelus tantū διακονικῶς versabatur. Vere ab Angelo, inquit B. Klotz. p. 209. Christum confortatum, vere forti- tudinem ex æternis divinæ potentiæ thesauris per An- geli ministerium Christo collatam constanter asseri- mus cum Hier. Cyrill. Damasc. Niceta, Beda, ipsisq; etiam Scholasticis Thoma, Perpiniano, Sim. de Cassia, Bernbardino & aliis. Quod post autores illos pie- rosq; adductos hisce confirmat p. 211. sc. uti Jacob Patriarcha in lucta cum Angelo ἐνίσχυσε μετὰ Θεῦ Gen. XXXII. 28. sive uti est Os. XII. 1. ἐνίσχυσε μετ' ἀγγέλε, quia ab eodem Angelo collactatore viribq au- ctq & corroboratq, ut tandem victor evaserit, uti Sim- son à Philistais captus & vinctq precibq tamen suis τὸ ἐνισχύειν impetravit, ut columnas ædificii convelleret Jud. XVI. 28. uti David Rex contra hostes præliaturus de fortitudine divinitus sibi concessa gloriatur, ma- gna cum fiducia ad Dominum perorans ἐνισχύσεις με δυνάμει &c. 2. Sam. XXII. 40. ita cogitemus Christum Salvatorem in summo isto exinanitionis gradu cum peccato, ira Dei, maledictione, morte q; æterna collu- ctantem ab Angelo Dei ministro robur non angelicum sed divinum accepisse, ut tandem victor evaserit, uti de Israëlitis contra Benjamiticam tribum decertanti- bus dicitur ἐνίσχυσαν περ' ἑνὸς Ἰσραὴλ confortati sunt ac vir Israel. Luth. Das Volck ermannet sich. Jud. XX. 22. ita certum est Christum Dominum ad An- gelicam præsentiam, factamq; ab ea corroborationem vires novas accepisse, ad fortiter cum hostibus dimi- candum: Vti Deus alias ad Electos dicit: Ἐγώ εἰμὶ ὁ Θεὸς ἐνίσχυσας Es. XLI. 10. Ipse enim est, qui ἐνισχύει τ υἱὸν Ἰσραὴλ, Joël. III. 16. Ita per Angelum Deus Pater Filium interius robore solatioq; perfudit, quo certior de divino auxilio proindeg; ad pugnam animosior fa- ctus est. Quod ὁ μακαρίτης porro ita explicat. p. 214. Sed tamen quod notamus, non nuda objectorū pro- positione Christus ab Angelo confortatus est, uti Caje- tanus asserit cum quibus dam recentioribus, quid ita intelligunt, ut Angelus solum proposuerit Christo obje- cta consolationis nihil in eum inspirans, neque eum instruens ratione aliqua aut interiori illuminatio- ne ipsum docens, sed etiam interius in anima ejusque facultatibus solatio perfusus, vel quod novam ange- lus intellectui & memoriæ Christi rationem suggesse- rit, cujus actualem notitiam pro tempore Christus sus- penderit, quia quod Alphons. Salmeron etiam fatetur t. 10. tr. 14. Dominus non concurrebat cum memoria Christi ad recordationem illorum, quæ animos sibi fa- cere poterant, sed volebat, ut nonnisi tormenta & af- flictiones, quibus erat vexandus, meditarentur, aut quod novam quandam & singularem rationis conso- latoria expensionem & ponderationem hoc illove mo- do proposuerit, cujus evidentiam in anima Christo pro illo tempore aliquo cum objectorum respectu oc- clusam admirando consilio Deus Pater esse voluerit, ut Christus illam in profundissima κενώσει illi adeo & profunde, quemadmodum ab Angelo proponebatur, non penetraverat. Potuisset quidem Christus etiam secundum bumanam naturam, in qua omnes sa- pientiæ & scientiæ divinæ thesauri, etiam in illo sta- tu quoad κτῆσιν reconditi erant, semetipsum citra ullius hominis aut angeli ministerium confortare, nec indiguisset ullo ullius creaturæ subsidio aut mi- nisterio, si modo illam in primo conceptionis puncto sibi communicatam Majestatem, sapientiam & sci- entiam quoad χρῆσιν in illo statu plene exercere vo- luisset, sed abdicavit semetipsum plenario illius usu, & denegavit sibi influxum divinarum virium, sus- penditque & retraxit paulisper radios divinæ collu- strationis & consolationis in anima sua,ut hac etiam in parte tentatus nobis per omnia similis fieret excepto peccato. Hæc magis congruunt quam Jesuitarum aut Reformatorum quorundam non satis ponde- rata commenta,in quibus sæpe νοῦς opus est, ju- staque δοκιμασία.

Vers. 44. ἐκτενέστερον προσηύχετο) Augescente dolore intendebat vim precationis: gettu quoque id ipsum expri- mens: nam ante genua flexerat: nunc toto corpore in ter- ram procumbit, ut ex Matthæo & Marco diximus: eo au- tem situ corporis orare viri sancti solebant in extrema ne- cessitate. Quare erant qui hic confundant τὸ γόνατα τίθε- σθαι, id est בָּרַךְ & πίπτειν ἐπὶ πρόσωπον aut ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς id est הִשְׁתַּחֲוָה, hoc emim est ἐκτενέστερον προσευχομένου.

καταβαίνοντες) Ita legit Latinus: & sensus videtur esse apertior: nam sanguis maxime cum in terram cadit, con- spicitur θρομβώδης. Est enim θρόμβος Galeno etiam in libro primo de semine τὸ ἅμα πεπηγός. Syrus quoque sic legisse videtur: sed ita ut subintelligere vocem ἱδρῶτος, quod loquendi genus exemplo non caret. Docet Aristote- les III. de historia animalium accidere nonnullis ἰδρῶσαι αἱ- ματώδη περιττώματι διὰ καχεξίαν καὶ διὰ τὴν τῆς θερμότητος ὀλιγότητα. Attamen hoc loco nihil est unde certo colligas sudori huic sanguinem fuisse permixtum. Nam,ut Theo- phylactus &Euthymius notant,non dictum est ἐγένετο ἰδρὼς αἵματος sed ἐγένετο ὁ ἰδρὼς αὐτοῦ ὡσεὶ θρόμβοι αἵματος. Quæ verba indicant verum fuisse sudorem, qui emanavit, non tenuem tamen, sed crassum, quales esse solent grumi sanguinis,cum sudor vix soleat θρομβοῦσθαι. Non aliter cer- te intellexit Justinus colloquio cum Tryphone, qui omissa sanguinis mentione satis habuit grumos dixisse: ἰδρὼς ὡσεὶ θρόμβοι κατεχεῖτο ἀυτοῦ ἐνχομένου. Tale illud: Salsusque per artus sudor iit.

Extenuare vel potius evacuare vult miraculum illud de sudore Christi sanguineo. In quo prævium habuit Syncretistam non absimilem Georg. Calix- tum. Quem tamen admirator ejus D. Heinr. Mül- lerus virum omni laude superiorem vocans hostem Formulæ Concordiæ illaudabilem, imo omni de- testatione, ob latrocinia à B. Dorfcheo in Theologo latrone detecta,dignum, hic deserit in Jesu patiente p. 20. Prolixe autem imprimis,post B. Dorfcheum, in Synopsi Theol. Zachar. c. IX. p. 297. seqq. egit B. Clotzius tract. de sudore Christi sanguineo Ex- erc.IX. contra Grotium, Euthymium, Photium, Pri- cæum, (de Theophylacto rem dubiam esse docet) eamque sententiam de sudore Christi sanguineo adeo certam fuisse venerandæ Patrum antiquitati monuit, ut negantibus (inter quos Calixtus suum professus est nomen) anathema dixerit, probans sanguineum Christi sudorem 1. ex voce Θρόμβοι, quæ à Dioscoride, Galeno & Hippocrate de sanguinis extra vasa constituti coagmentatione adhibetur; nec aliter à Luca Medico Antiocheno adhibita; imprimis quia 2. vox αἵματος adjecta: Si enim hoc solum indicare voluit, quod non tenuis sed crassus fu- erit sudor, cur addidit vocem ἅματος ad illud θρόμ- βοι, cum ex hac vocula satis illud potuerit constare, guttas sudoris instar grumorum coagulatas fuisse? aut ad quid sanguinis potius guttarum mentionem fecit, quam aliarum rerum liquidarum? Et cur sanguinis meminit in terram decurrentis nisi signifi- care voluit sudorem sanguineis guttis adeo copiose decurrisse, ut ab ipso in terram defluxerint? 3. Ex natura sanguinis id confirmat: cujus pro- prium est cum extra vasa naturalia calore insito destitutus transit, frigore concrescere & in grumos abire. Humidus & calidus semper est, ait Aristo- teles, quamdiu in corpore animalis continetur: At-

ubi effluxerit, concrescit omnium præterquam cer- vorum & damarum, & si quid aliud natura ejus- modi sit. Sudor autem aquosus uti ipse etiam Gro- tius indicat, vix solet θρομβοῦσθαι, nisi forte san- guine tinctus & permistus sit. Frustra itaque & citra fundamentum aquoso humori tribuitur, quod juxta literam ex natura rei & proprietate vocis nonnisi sanguini tribuendum venit. 4. ESyro inter- prete: qui satis perspicue testatur, sudorem Christi, qui in terram decidit, vere sanguineum fuisse, dum ita hoc loco vertit: Et fuit sudor ejus velut grumi sanguinis & cecidit sanguis super terram &c. Et sane sudor ille sanguineus Christi magno semper consensu creditus est in Ecclesia, quem cur in gratiam unius Euthymii posthabuerit Calixtus, atque Grotius, hyperaspistæ eorum viderint. As- seruit hunc sudorem sanguineum Justinus Martyr Apostolorum discipulus Dial. cum Tryphone, Ireneus Martyr, Polycarpi Martyris discipulus Lugdun. Episc. cujus Græca verba leguntur Dia- logo 1. Christi operibus; Cæsarius in Dialogis apud Phocium f. 1098. Hieronymus l. II. contra Pelag. c. 6. August. l. 3. de consensu Ev- angel. & in Enarr. Psal. CXL. Prosper Aquit. in sentent. August. n. 68. Titus Bostrensis in comment. in Lucam: Beda T. V. Oper. f. 138. Zacharias Chrysopolit. in Evangelist, A. C. 1001. Rupertus Tuitiens. l. VI. de operib. Dom. c. 4. Bernhardus Serm. de pass. Christi Suidas in voce Θρόμβοι. Quibus adde Græcæ Ecclesiæ suspirium multis seculis jam decantatum, διὰ τ᾽ ἀγωνίας τε Σαίμα- τος ἱδρῶτος ρῦσαι ἡμᾶς κύριε, quod in Litania nostra, (credo etiam in Helmstadiensi Eccle- sia) lingua vernacula repeti notissimum est. Quam vero, obsecro, causam à communi Ecclesiæ fide discedendi habuit Theologus ille incomparabilis omniq; laude superior: quod contra crediderit non sanguinis naturalis grumos, sed sudorem solum co- piosum & crassum, ac si sanguinis grumi forent, in terram decidisse in agonia Christi? Quia scil. ve- rosimile non est Deum præterquam naturæ ratio fe- rat, afflixisse Filium suum & immediate per suam ipsius potentiam ea intulisse, quæ nec vicinitas mortis mente apprehensa, nec sævities Judæorum inferri po- tuisset. O intempestivam misericordiam, qua omnis evertitur misericordia! Quis ergo jam cre- dat, Deum inflixisse Filio suo pœnam ipsam infer- nalem, quam nec sævities diaboli, nedum Judæo- rum inferre potuisset? Annon actum ita erit de nostri à morte æterna liberatione? annon profli- gatur divina erga nos misericordia, ausu & more prorsus Sociniano, utpote cui citra satisfactionem & perpessionem pœnarum nobis debitarum ple- nariam, nullus erat locus; Nam & Sociniani Deum crudelitatis arguendum blasphemant, ob tantas Fi- lio unigenito innocentiffimo inflictas pœnas. Ideo corrigat suum ‡ πανὺ hic Dn. D. Müllerus, omnia inquiens p. 22. hic excedunt naturæ ratio- nem, sanguinis prorumpentis tum causa efficiens, quæ erat onus peccatorum, sensus iræ divinæ, lucta cum diabolo, morte & inferno: tum forma non fuit hic sanguis fluens, qualis alias esse solet, sed spissarum & condensatarum guttarum: tum finis, qui erat to- tius generis humani redemptio. Et in quæst. Theol. Semi-centur. altera q. xxxix. sub finem: Non tan- tum mortem corporalem sustinuit (Christus) eamq; effusione non unius vel alterius guttæ, sed totius san- guinis sui; verum etiam æternam, quæ consistit in lu- ctione iræ divinæ secundum sententiam STRICTI ju- dicii Dei, ubi laudat etiam illud Guillandi in c. XXVI. Matth. Christum afflictum imagine mortis & infer- ni, non aliter mortem & infernum horruisse, quam si solus universa hominum peccata designasset : adeog; suscepisse in se nostra causa dolores mortis & inferni: Quid ergo mirum eidem ea divinitus inflicta, quæ à sævitie Judæorum inferri non potuerint; quum non Judæis, sed justitiæ divinæ satisfacere debu- erit. Sed correxit Theologum illum incompara- bilem(qualem etiam quis Nestorium, eodem facile jure dixerit, B. Dn. D. Clotzius licet ἀνωνύμως l. c. Exercit. XV. th. 6. cujus ἔλεγχον etsi paululum prolixiorem adscribere juvat: Constitutus in agonia CHRISTUS sudavit, ubi in lucta omnibus humanæ angelicæque naturæ viribus & robori majori consti- tutus erat contra mortem Satanæ maledictionis & condemnationis æternæ spiculis armatam, contraque ipsum Deum O. M. propter peccati toti generi hu- mano iratum, cujus ipse sponsor factus, omnia nobis debita maledicta & fulmina in sese derivaverat quæ solius naturæ nostræ viribus sustinere Chri- sto Domino si Φιλάνθρωπος fuisset & virtus su- pernaturalis divina non accessisset, plane impossibile fuisset; nam licet in toto passionis actu hominem ege- rit Salvator noster, falsum tamen est, quod vir qui- dam Clariss. ait, naturam humanam naturali con- ditioni relictam tantum doluisse, quant m doluisset si neque cum divinitate personaliter unita fuisset, neg; quicquam de divino decreto cognitum habuisset. Nam Christus tantum quantum doluit dolere non potuisset, salva & viva manente humana natura, nisi cum divinitate unita fuisset, cujus robore infinito sustentatus doluit, ne periret, ipsa Christi verba hoc indicant, cum ait, animam suam esse περίλυπον ad mortem usque h. e. adeo dolore & mærore circumse- ptam, ut pereundum ipsi sit, nisi divinitus sustente- tur. Es. LXIII. 5. Proinde & illud valori passionis Christi derogat, quod IDEM vir Clariss. asserit non esse vero simile, Deum præterquam naturæ ratio ferat afflixisse Filium suum, & immediate per suam ipsius potentiam ea intulisse, quæ nec vicinitas mortis mente apprehensa nec sævitas Judæorum inferre potuisset. Hæc quando scripsit, non cogitavit illa effata Spiritus Sancti, Deus ipsum voluit conterere, Deus incur- rere fecit in ipsum peccata nostra, exigitur (pœna à Deo) & ipse affligitur (à Deo) ipse spondet. Et si non est verisimile Deum afflixisse filium suum, præ- terquam naturæ (humanæ) ratio ferat, &c. pariter verisimile non erit Deum vere propter peccata ira- tum fuisse, vere Christum iræ divinæ gravitatem sen- sisse, vere Deo pro peccatis nostris satisfecisse, quia ejusmodi afflictiones, quæ non sunt propter naturæ no- stræ rationem satisfactoriæ esse non possunt. Hæc B. Klotzius non injuria fane: versatur enim ibi Calix- tus in ejus consideratione quousq; æternus æterni Pa- tri Filius nostri ergo se demittere voluerit, & quid cum infirmitates illas inhibere potuisset, sua tamen sponte ut pro nobis satisfaceret, admiserit. Id vero QUO- USQUE non ulterius extendit, quam qua NA- TURÆ RATIO tulerit: & quod tantum dolu- erit, QUANTUM doluisset, si neque (diserta hæc sunt Calixti verba loc. cit.) cum divinitate persona- liter unita fuisset natura humana, neque quicquam de divino decreto cognitum habuisset. Qualis autem illa satisfactio naturæ humanæ divinitati non uni- tæ! qualis ultronea submissio, & obedientia vo- luntati divinæ præstita, si nihil de voluntate, ac de- creto Dei cognitum habuisset? Unde oppi- do mirari oportet Dn. D. Müllerum in eo se- quutum hic Calixtum, eundemque sub elogio in- comparabilis seculi nostri Theologi beat. memor.. (quod certe hæreticarum novitatum propugna- stori acerrimo nemo orthodoxorum Doctorum sciens prudens tribuerit) in hac causa, citra ullam præmonitionem juventuti fidei suæ creditæ ste- tisse: Quod nempe Christo decretum Patris ignotum fuerit de satisfactione pro peccatis generis humani: quum tamen professus ipse sit p. 15. Deum non posse peccatorum absque satisfactione & illius applicatione impunitum dimittere, quod hoc sit contra ipsius justi- tiam. Voëtius certe ita asserit cum Parckero, & Ri- veto, Christum in anima sua pœnas infernales susti- nuisse, non tantum analogice & per compensationem seu æquivalenter (quæ Vossii videtur fuisse senten- tia, cum l. I. Harm. Evangel. c. XX. §. 17. p. 179. infi- niti, inquit, fuere Christi cruciatus, verum non tem- pore, vel MAGNITVDINE, sed personæ dignitate) sed easdem, quod ad essentiam, seu substantiam ea- rum: pœnas enim, inquit, Adamo denunciatas susti- nuit, at illæ erant infernales. Ut non modo Pontifi- cios rejecerit, qui solam mortem & cruciatum Chri- sti corporalem, nullum vero animæ agnoscunt, nisi ac- cidentalem ex sympathia animæ cum corpore, sed etiam Theologo Anglo Bilsono dicam scripserit, quod Pontificiorum vestigiis insistens, omnem passionem animæ ex condolentia, conjunctione, sympathia cum corpore ortam contendit, aut saltem non ex debito, tanquam nostram, ac nostro loco, sed proprio Christi arbitratu, susceptam. Vid. p. II. disp. select. p. 106.

Nam illud ὡσεὶ non similitudinis est, sed verita- tis, ut Luc. XXIV. 2. Joh. I. 14. Henr. Stephani, citante B. Gerhardo Harm. passion. c. I. col. 17. existimat particulam ὡσεὶ ad leniendum id, quod præcesserat, adhibitam, Christum sc. non simpliciter guttas San- guinis, sed quasi grumos concreti terrore Sangui- nis sudasse, quia testantur Medici, serum illud aqueum cui Sanguis, in venis conclusus, innatat, quo- que velut vehiculo in omnes corporis partes devehi- tur, esse materiam sudoris, ideo probabile est unacum sanguine istud exiisse, cum Evangelista & sudoris & Sanguinis mentionem faciat. Hilar. l. X. de Trinit. Sudorem Christi, inquit, nemo audebit infirmitati de- putare, quia contra naturam est sudare Sangui- nem, &c. unde Joh. Gerh. Vossius, qui alias libenter Grotio adhærescit, eundem hic deseruit: Nec enim, inquit l. I. Harm. Evang. c. XX. p. 177. quod dicitur, ὡσεὶ θρόμβοι αἵματος, id nuda comparatio est, quod voluit Euthymius: vel proverbialis hyperbole, sicut credidit Theophylactus: sed vere & simpliciter capiendum. Nimirum sanguis guttatim manabat, propemodum, sicut ictis ab eo serpentis genere, cui inde hæmorrhoi nomen. In Christo vel, deficiente sudoris materie tenuior etiam sanguis profluxit; ut vult Ca- jetanus: vel, crassiori sudoris materia se permiscens, istos sanguinolentos sudoris grumos effecit. Plura vid. ap. Gerhardum loc. cit. Naturalem fuisse cruorem illum sanguineum ex causa proxima Voëtius disp. de agon. & desert. Christi putat: Nos, inquit de hoc sudore parte II. Disp. select. p. 172. non minus ac ef- fluxum sanguinis & aquæ è latere Christi, statuimus eum fuisse naturalem, ex causa sc. proxima, quamvis admirabilem, & naturæ miraculum, imo & superna- turalem, si efficientes remotas, & finem respiciamus. Causam proximam putamus nos invenire in affecti- bus, & commotione eorum: affectibus, inquam, par- tim tristitiæ & timoris, qui spiritus & sanguinem versus cor ab exterioribus partibus revocat: partim amoris, desiderii, ardoris & zeli (Luc. XXII. 44.) qui spiritus & sanguinem à corde versus exteriores corporis partes propellunt: hinc factum, ut sanguis in- star Euripi vorfum prorsum agitatus, atq; adeo atte- nuatus una cum seroso humore ex venis per cutem eruperit. Tale quid naturaliter posse fieri, imprimis si rarior corporis, ac cutis textura accesserit, testantur

Philosophi, ac Medici, &c. Allegat pro se Voëtius Philippum in Consiliis part. I: p. 579. Wendelinum in Philosop. moral. l. I. c. 36. & è Medicis Antonium Satorellum l. XXIII. de Nat. Sanit. c. 12. Sed sanguinem per poros profluere, & quidem crassiorem ac bene con- sistentem, idq; in corpore nulla prava constitutione laborante miraculum est naturam excedens, quod cum Thoma Minadoo Rhodigino Medico Utinensi Disp. 1. de sud. sangu. à Voëtio laudato, agnoscit l. c. Müllerus; & probavit solide B. Klotz. Exerc. XVI. sudorem Christi miraculosum fuisse ratione mate- riæ, subjecti, quantitatis, qualitatis, consequentis coa- gulationis grumorum & profusionis: idq; non tan- tum contra Boëtium, Montacutium, Gerh. Joh. Vof- sium, Calvinianos, sed etiam contra Pontificios Lyranum, Cajetanum, Barradium, Maldonatum, Jansenium Iprensem Corn. à Lap. Barth. Medinam, Francis. Collium, Suarez, Tirinum, Drexelium & Medicorum filios, Cyprian. Marosam & Hier. Jor- danumi : laudatis in contrarium Hilario Pictav. X. de Trinit. Tito Bostrensi, Zach. Chrysopol. Eeda, Job. Gersone, Simone de Cassia, Gabr. Eiele, Corn. Jansen. Episcopo Gandav. Franc. Quaresmio, Salmerone, Didaco Stella, Joh. Raulino, Henr. Harfio, Joh. Oso- rio, Stanisl. Grodilio, Philip. Bosquier Franciscano, Rainardo Landembergio Augustiniano, Thoma de Trugillo Dominicano, Balth. Cordero Jesuita, Casp. à Reyes Medico Carmonensi, qui in campis Elys. qq. 86. f. 681. affirmat causam hujus sudoris supernatu- ralem fuisse, aitque, ita sanxisse conventum Patrum Trident. Conc. omnesq; fere Theologos docere. Major alia fuit vis, inquit, quæ prædictum sudorem movere valuit, supernaturalis nempe & divina: Ita Sanctorum PP. Tridentini habitus conventus sanxit, & Theologi fere omnes docent; & certe supernatura- lem causam fuisse evidenti ratione videtur confir- mari, quod copiosissime guttulæ sanguinis emanarunt ad terram usq; decurrentes; deinde guttulæ erant, quæ è corpore prodibant, non in roris modum ut in sudore fit, ac si ille exeundi modus sudoris formæ minime con- venit: quæ si cum exactissima Christi temperatura nullis morbis aut morborum causis obnoxia conjun- gantur, superiorem & minime naturalem illius su- doris causam fuisse facile imo necessario credendum erit, nullus quippe sanguinem guttatim sudavit, sed in roris formam, quare & exeundi modus particula- ris fuit, & supernaturalem causam habuisse indica- vit. Vid. Klotzius l. c. p. 98. Qui pag. 162. addit Joh. Bustanantium Camerensem nec non Calvinum Harm. Evang. f. 378. Si quis, inquistem, hodie su- dando sanguinem emittat & quidem tanta copia, ut guttæ in terram destillent, incredibile portentum erit. Subjungimus jam ipsam B. Klotzii declarationem Exerc. XIII. th. 8. traditam. Pretiosissimus Jesu Chri- sti Domini nostri sanguis, quod nunquam satis dici potest in ista ἀγωνίᾳ è venis prorumpens non fuit im- purus, corruptus, scrosus, infectus, non morbo aut æ- gritudine vitiatus, qui adeo interdum serescit, ut simul ac è corpore profluxit propter nimiam aquosi- tatem concrescere nequeat, sed sanguis fuit purissi- mus, bene coctus, digestus, naturæ perfectus, non secus atque alter ille, qui in venis reclusus permansit, solum calore & rarefactione paululum diversus, perfectam sanguinis formam caloris coctione notam conservans propriam, figuram retinens integram, verus, integer, generosus, corpori generosissimo, pulcherrimo, & im- peccabili ad alimentum à Deo per Sp. S. operationem destinatus, in guttas dum è corpore emanaret abiens, ad guttarum formam decidens, terramque in grumos, quod veri, sani & puri sanguinis effluentis proprium est, concretus & coagulatus contingens. Idq; argu- mento nobis est, nulli unquam hominum sudorem talem naturaliter contingere potuisse. Thomas Minadocus l. 1. disput. Med. disput. I. de sudore sanguineo, quem l. c. pag. 172. produxit Voëtius, etsi probet, talem sudorem esse naturalem, Christi tamen sudorem sanguineum supernaturalem & miraculosum esse, docet: haec itidem imprimis urgens: quod in Domino Jesu nulla esse potuerit corporalis infirmitas ob eximiam, & superexcellentem corporis structuram, ob perfectissimam, omnibusq́; numeris absolutissimam complexionem, & ob ejusdem corporis dignitatem, nobilitatemque. B. Dorscheus Syn. Theol. Zach. p. 298. pariter optimum temperamentum corporis Christi, simulque grumosam, & copiosam sanguinis eruptionem urget: Colligitur ex dictis, inquit, quod non levis aliqua sudoris è seroso sanguine oriunda tinctura comparuerit in Christo: nec αἱματῶδες περίττωμα διὰ καχεξίαν in ejus corpore eruperit, sicut Aristoteles lib. III. de partib. animal. cap. 6. & lib. III. Histor. animal. cap. 19. in suo subjecto observavit, aut ex defectu caloris nativi, aut ex raritate, atque laxitate cutis, pororumq́; apertione, aut ex vitio facultatum nutritioni inservientium, expultricis scilicet & retentricis, sed quod in optime temperato sanoque corpore Christi verus, perfectus, saluberrimusque sanguis largiter eruperit, & ex frigiditate aeris in grumos concretus in terram decurrerit. At hujusmodi grumosa, copiosa, & optimi perfectissimique sanguinis in tali corpore profusa eruptio naturalis nequaquam est, sed plane supernaturalis & peculiaris in profundissima κενώσει Salvatoris nostri Oeconomica.

Causa vero sudoris istius prodigiosi constitui potest, partim metus summus & anxietas, atque tristitia maxima, quæ ob sensum iræ divinæ, & maledictionis propter peccatum generis humani, ac cruciatuum infernalium gravitatem, mediatorem nostrum in judicio divino districtissimo constitutum undiquaque occupavit, ut anima ejus περίλυπος fuerit usque ad mortem, vel lethaliter; unde mirum, quod protrusus fuerit sanguis per poros, quum ex adverso sanguis in gravioribus consternationibus exteriora membra destituens, recurrat intra præcordia, veluti suppetias laturus cordi præ metu & anxietate exanimato, & de vita periclitanti: magis autem mirum id hic deprehenditur, quomodo per angustos pororum meatus grumosus sanguis penetrare potuerit, utpote qui in corpore Christi jam ob summam illam mœstitiam & anxietatem in grumos concreverit: quum alias timor & mœror etiam gelet & constipet sanguinem: partim vero agonia & fortitudo Christi, quum luctaretur cum peccato, & Diabolo, ipsaque ira divina & morte æterna, qui ob æstum ferventem rarefacere & resolvere debuisset sanguinem, sed quod miraculi vim auget, citra rarefactionem integros grumos sanguinis, vehementia sua protrusit, ut sit cum mœrore, & anxietate fortitudo & zelus mutuo quasi colluctarentur, illis ad cor propellentibus sanguinem & constipantibus, his rarefacere & resolvere eundem non ita plane valentibus, quin grumosus adhuc esset sanguis, corde tamen confortato, & vehementiori zelo æstuante depellentibus atque protrudentibus grumos sanguinis, ut per poros magna copia prorumperent. Quo facit, quod Theophrast. Eremus agonem cum ira comparat, & à metu distinguit, quod in hoc calor interiora petat, in isto autem ad exteriora provocetur: unde in spongiam incumbunt, quæ Voëtius attulit, ut proximam causam sudoris Christi sanguinei naturalem fuisse doceret; & luculentum evadit, non tantum causam propinquam, ut ille vult, supernaturalem fuisse, sed & mi- raculum in ipsa causa proxima locandum esse: non tantum in causa tum anxietatis & tristitiæ, tum zeli & agonias fortissimæ, sed etiam in ipso utriusq; ef- fectu, sanguineo sudore, ejusque prodigiosa protru- sione. Neque admittenda illa Hieronymi Jordani Physici Gottingensis libro de eo, quod divinum est in morbis cap. 37. p. 183. declaratio: Sanguinem primum præ maximi animi mærore liquefactum, & in serum seu aquam cruentam (de qua nihil habet Evangelista) conversum, mox in mirifico illo agone seu vehementissimo studio, & contentione circa salu- tem nostram instar copiosi sudoris e corpore protrusum esse &c. Rectius alii Medicorum filii, referente Santorello: Quanquam, inquiunt, naturaliter pos- set fieri, ut serosus sanguis, & tenuis per angustos cu- tis meatus fluat, crassus tamen & grumosus natura- liter permeare non potest. Unde etiam Stephanus Roderic. Castr. in libro Quæ ex quibus lib. 1. cap. 23. probat, sanguineum Christi sudorem neutiquam naturalem fuisse. Non absimili, uti a nobis jam factum, ratione exposuit post magnum Chemni- tium nostrum part. I. Loc. Comm. p. 69. summus i- tidem, & vere incomparabilis Theologus B. Ger- hardus noster cap. II. Harm. Evang. p. 17. In gravio- ribus consternationibus sanguis exteriora membra destituens recurrit intra præcordia, quasi arci vitæ cordi suppetias laturus, sed in Christo sanguis a corde prorumpit; fractum enim & retusum fuit o- mne ejus robur, atque ut Esa. XLIX. 4. dicitur, na- tura consumserat fortitudinem suam, ideo sangui- nem continere non potuit, sed is velut perrupto ag- gere largiter ex toto corpore profluxit, & calore na- turali destitutus in grumos concrevit. Illud expe- rientia constat, inquit B. Chemnitius in LL. CC. in magna consternatione sequi resolutionem, ut virtus retentiva non amplius faciat suum officium, sicut patet ex historia Arii. Et Epiphanius dicit, Ju- dam eadem de causa crepuisse medium, sequente illa magna resolutione, ex desperabunda trepidatione. In Christo ergo cum agonia esset prolixior, tanta facta est resolutio, ut nec cor nec venæ sangui- nem retinuerint, sed ii tanquam θρόμβοι decur- rerint. Significat autem illud vocabulum, cum ali- quid distillat, & in ipsa distillatione per frigus spissa- tur & concrescit, ut in salifodinis fossilibus distillat humor salsus, qui cum concretus & spissatus est, vo- cantur θρόμβοι ἁλὸς apud Suidam. Varinus: θρόμβος πεπηγὸς αἷμα. Ita cum in Christo ma- gna illa mœstitia omnem calorem retraxisset, sanguis resolutus in guttas spissatus est, und floß also her- auß geronnen, geliefert Blut. Sed pugnare vi- detur, quod in magnis & repentinis consternationi- bus incisa vena, sanguis non effluit neq; expellitur, sed quasi concretus in ipsa vena consistere videtur. Est autem illa vera responsio: In Christo fuisse non tan- tum ingentem mastitiam, verum etiam magnam lu- ctam cum consternatione conjunctam, quod voluit Patri illam obedientiam præstare, & ex istis contra- riis motibus, qui vehementiores fuerunt, facta est ta- lis expulsio concreti & spissi sanguinis.

Huic causæ a B. Chemnitio expositæ, subjun- git aliam B. Gerhardus: Potest autem virium reso- lutioni etiam compressio ponderis incumbentis addi, ut hac ratione utraque causa conjungantur. Quemadmodum enim gravior quadam sarcina im- posita sudorem nobis exprimit: ita cum gravissima illa pondera Christo tunc temporis imposita, videlicet peccata totius mundi, ira Dei, maledictio legis, mortis ac diaboli potentia ipsum ineffabiliter preme- rent, vel sudoris loco sanguinem, vel una cum ipso su- dore sanguinem, vel primo quidem sudorem, po- stea vero angore aucto & deficiente sudoris mate- ria ipsum sanguinem ei expresserunt. Quemadmodum intensior æstus largum sudorem nobis exprimit: sic æstus iræ divinæ sanguineum Christi sudorem elicuit. Quæ omnia B. Clotzius tract. laudato repetiit, non improbavit, etsi causam sudoris sanguinei paulo aliter l. cit. p. 192. explicuit: Nimirum, quod an- gor & animi mæstitudo ex sensu iræ Dei & peccato- rum suborta remotior & quasi objective motiva, aut radix, & occasio hujus sudoris fuerit: proxima ve- ro & immediate ab intrinseco sudoris illius effectiva ἀγωνία fuerit Christi, prolixius & intensius orantis, vel quæ in ἀγωνίᾳ sese exeruit, & per angelicam confortationem excitata ingens & vere divina animi alacritas & fortitudo, quæ ex omnibus venarum & pororum osculis sanguinis glebas validissime protru- ferit.

II. Proditio Judæ.

## 22:48
Verse 48.

Φιλήματι τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου παραδίδως] Do you hide betrayal under the sign of peace? Do you thus kiss him of whom it is written in Psalm 2:12: Kiss the Son.

III. The apprehension of Christ.

Latin:

Vers. 48.

Φιλήματι τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου παραδίδως] Sub pacis signo proditionem occultas? Sic illum oscularis, de quo scriptum est Psal. II. 12. Osculamini filium.

III. Christi apprehensio.

## 22:49
Verse 49.

εἰ πατάξομεν ἐν μαχαίρᾳ] Doubting between what nature dictated and the often-inculcated precepts of patience, they ask the Lord what is to be done. But Peter, not waiting for the Lord's response, girds himself to repel force with force.

Latin:

Vers. 49.

εἰ πατάξομεν ἐν μαχαίρᾳ] Dubii inter id quod natura di- ctabat & sæpe inculcata patientiæ præcepta, dominum quid faciendum sit rogant. At Petrus non exspectato domini responso ad vim vi arcendam accingitur.

## 22:51
Verse 51.

Ἐᾶτε ἕως τούτου] It is enough that you have progressed this far in returning violence: do not proceed further: stop here: the Syriac rightly expounds this passage in this way.

Latin:

Vers. 51.

Ἐᾶτε ἕως τούτου] Satis est huc usque vos progressos in vi reponenda: nolite ultra progredi: hic consistite: ita hunc locum recte expo sit Syrus.

## 22:53
Verse 53.

Αὕτη ὑμῶν ἐστιν ἡ ὥρα, καὶ ἡ ἐξουσία τοῦ σκότους] This is that time in which power is granted to you, and through you to the prince of darkness, over me, to fulfill the prophecies, of course. This power has hitherto been denied to you; otherwise, you would have apprehended me while I was acting openly among you in the daytime, without arms, without any noise. The word ἐξουσία is taken in this way also in Revelation 9:3, 19.

IV. The leading of Jesus to the house of the High Priest and the denial of Peter therein.

Latin:

Vers. 53.

Αὕτη ὑμῶν ἐστιν ἡ ὥρα, καὶ ἡ ἐξουσία τοῦ σκότους] Hoc est tem- pus illud quo vobis & per vos tenebrarum principi potestas in me conceditur, ad implenda vaticinia scilicet. Hæc po- testas hactenus vobis negata est, alioqui interdiu palam in- ter vos agentem comprehendissetis sine armis, sine ullo strepitu. Vox ἐξουσίαs hoc modo sumitur & in Apoc. IX. 3. 19.

IV. Jesu ad ædes Pontificis deductio & in iisdem Petrinæ abnegatio.

## 22:54
Vers. 54. of the high priest] Of Caiaphas. See the notes on Matthew. Vers. 56. toward the light] By the fire, as in Mark. Looking intently] The propriety of the word requires a circumlocution in the Latin language: for instance, looking with fixed eyes: thus above c. IV. 20. and several times in the Acts. Vers. 59. about one hour] 'About' does not always signify less, but often also a little more than what is said, as we have stated in the notes on c. III. 23. And so it ought to be taken here. See the notes on Matthew. Vers. 61. looked at Peter] Admonishing him silently both of his rash boasting and of the need to hasten his repentance. It is not irrelevant here what Plutarch relates: Polemon, having been merely seen by Xenocrates in the lecture hall and having looked at him, was turned and changed.

V. The mocking and striking of Christ.

Latin:

Vers. 54. τοῦ ἀρχιερέως] Cajaphæ. Vide ad Matthæum. Vers. 56. πρὸς τὸ φῶς] Ad ignem, ut apud Marcum. Ἀτενίσασα] Requirit vocabuli proprietas circumloquu- tionem in Latino sermone: puta, spectans oculis defixis: ita supra c. IV. 20. & in Actis aliquoties. Vers. 59. ὡσεὶ ὥρας μιᾶς] ὡσεὶ non semper minus, sed sæpe & plusculum eo quod dicitur significat, ut diximus ad c. III. 23. Atq; ita hic accipi debet. Vide quæ ad Matthæum. Vers 61. ἐνέβλεψε τῷ Πέτρῳ] Admonens illum tacite & inconsultæ jactationis & maturandæ pœnitentiæ. Non alienum hinc est, quod Plutarchus narrat: Πολέμωνα Ξενο- κράτεις ὀφθεὶς μόνον ἐν τῇ διατριβῇ καὶ ἀποβλέψας πρὸς αὐτὸν ἐτρέψατο καὶ μετέθηκεν.

V. Illusio & percussio Christi.

## 22:63
Vers. 63. and the men who were holding] We have warned in the notes on Matthew that Luke is compelled to go back, because he wished, in the manner of historians, to present the whole narrative concerning Peter in one series. Moreover, the verb עצר is usually translated as to hold, whence is the verbal noun עֹצֶר in Isaiah LIII. 8, where this history is predicted. beating] The Syriac omitted this. Because it follows 'they struck his face'; but it is not a new thing for the species to be named as well when the genus has been named.

VI. The examination of Christ before the Sanhedrin.

Latin:

Vers. 63. κὶ οἱ ἄνδρες οἱ συνέχοντες] Ad Matthæum mo- nuimus coactum Lucam retro gredi, quia historicorum mo- re totam de Petro narrationem una serie exhibere voluerat. Verbum autem עצר verti solet συνέχειν, unde est verbale עֹצֶר apud Esaiam LIII. 8. ubi hæc historia prædicitur. δέροντες] Omisit Syrus. Quia sequitur ἔτυπτον αὐτᾶ τὸ πρόσωπον; sed non est novum genere nominato speciem quoque eximiam nominari.

VI. Christi coram Synedrio examinatio.

## 22:66
Vers. 66. when it became day] When day was approaching: for the aorist is also accustomed to be taken in this way. were gathered] That is, was being gathered. See the notes on Matthew. led him up] This reading seems truer than 'led him away'. For the Sanhedrin was held in a higher portico. Vers. 68. but if I also ask] If I should propose any arguments by which I might prove myself to be Christ. For the Hebrews were accustomed to argue no less than the Greeks by questioning. Sextus the Philosopher often uses it in this way, and hence in Aristotle the fallacy of many questions. Cicero on Fate: Thus they ask: if it is fated for you to recover from this illness, you will recover, that is, for thus they argue. But Christ rightly says they would not answer: for he knew this was their purpose, not that they might refute him with reasons, but that they might oppress him with authority: but even before this, the senators of the same assembly had remained silent when questioned. Above c. XX. 7, 17, 44.

Similarly, the blessed Gerhard in his Harmony of the Passion, c. VI. Even if I were to provide you with an opportunity for further inquiry into the truth, even with pious questions, as was done in Matt. XXI. v. 24, 31, and 40, likewise c. XXII. v. 42, you would not judge me worthy of any answer, nor would you give glory to the truth, so that, acknowledging my innocence, you would dismiss me free. There are, however, those who prefer to take the word 'ask' here in the sense of beseeching, as in John XVII. 9, Acts II. 3, and the word 'answer' in the sense of hearing, in which the word ענה is accustomed to be taken. See 1 Sam. VII. 9, Ps. XXII. 3.

Latin:

Vers. 66. ὡς ἐγένετο ἡμέρα] Cum dies adventaret: nam & ita sumi solet ὁ ἀόριστος. συνήχθη] Id est, ἦν συναγόμενον. Vide quæ ad Matth. ἀνήγαγον] Videtur hæc lectio verior quam ἀπήγαγον. Nam Synedrium habebatur in porticu excelsiore. Vers. 68. ἐὰν δὲ κὶ ἐρωτήσω] Si qua argumenta proponam quibus me Christum probem. Argumentari enim Hebræi non minus quam Græci solebant interrogando. Sæpe ita utitur Sextus Philosophus, & hinc apud Aristotelem falla- cia plurium interrogationum. Cicero de fato: Sic epima interrogant : si fatum tibi est ex hoc morbo convalescere, conva- lesces, id est, sic enim argumentantur. Recte autem dicit Christus non responsuros : sciebat enim hoc illis proposi- tum, non ut se rationibus revincerent, sed ut opprimerent auctoritate : sed & antehac ejusdem consessus senatores in- terrogati siluerant. Supra c. XX. 7. 17. 44.

Similiter B. Gerhardus Harm. de Pass. c. VI. Si vel maxime piis quaestionibus ansam ulterius inqui- rendi veritatem vobis praebere vellem, prout factum erat Matth. XXI. v. 24. 31. & 40. item cap. XXII. v. 42. non tamen ullo me dignum judicaretis responso, nec gloriam daretis veritati, ut innocentiam meam agnoscentes liberum me dimitteretis. Sunt tamen, quibus verbum ἐρωτήσω placet hic potius accipe- re sensu supplicandi, ut Job. XVII. 9. Actor. II. 3. & verbum ἀποκριθῆτε sensu exaudiendi, quo solet verbum ענה accipi. Vid. 1. Sam. VII. 9. Ps. XXII. 3.

## 22:70
Vers. 70. you say] That is, you state the fact, as in Xenophon, 'you yourselves say this, O Socrates'.

that I am he] I think it true that what a most learned man notes here, that 'that' belongs to Christ affirming, not to the repeating of the voice.

Latin:

Vers. 70. ὑμεῖς λέγετε} Id est rem dicitis, ut apud Xeno- phontem αὐτοὶ τοῦτο λέγετε ὦ Σώκρατες.

ὅτι ἐγώ εἰμι] Quod hic monet vir eruditissimus ὅτι esse Christi affirmantis, non repetentis vocem, verum putem.

## 22:71
Vers. 71. we have heard from his own mouth] Namely, blasphemy, which Matthew and Mark express for the sake of clarity: since otherwise it was the custom of the Hebrews to indicate blasphemy by silence rather than by a word.

Latin:

Vers. 71. ἠκούσαμεν ἀπὸ τοῦ στόματος αὐτοῦ] βλασφημίαν scilicet, quod exprimunt Matthaeus & Marcus, perspicui- tatis causa : cum alioqui mos fuerit Hebraeorum βλασφη- μίαν silentio potius quam verbo indicare.

## 23:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXIII.

ARGUMENT AND DIVISION.

Christ is accused before Pilate of sedition against Caesar, and that he makes himself a King: which the latter does not deny: nor yet does Pilate find a cause in him: but they insist, the people having been stirred up, because he had taught throughout Galilee and Judea: whence he is sent to Herod, who was in charge of Galilee: to whom, however, he returns no answer, by whom, having been mocked in a white garment, he is sent back to Pilate, and Pilate testifies that neither he nor Herod finds anything in him of those things which were worthy of death: and therefore that he wishes to release him, according to the custom of the feast: but the assembly crying out again and again that he should release Barabbas and crucify Christ, and when for the third time Pilate denied that he found a cause of death in him, with the clamors overwhelming Pilate, he assented to them, and delivered Christ to their will. When he was being led out to carry the cross, Simon of Cyrene was pressed into service, with a great crowd following, and women lamenting him, whom he warns to weep for themselves and their children, predicting unhappy times. Two evildoers were also led out, in whose midst Jesus was crucified, who indeed prayed for his crucifiers: furthermore, the division of Jesus' garments, and his mockery, and the title placed upon the cross, the blasphemy of one thief, the conversion of the other, to whom paradise is promised; the darkness, and the rending of the veil, and after the spirit was commended to the Father, the death of Christ are recounted. Then the consequences of the death of Jesus are commemorated, the eulogy of the centurion, the wonder of the spectators, and especially the burial cared for by Joseph, the pious Senator of Arimathea, having obtained the body of Jesus from Pilate, with the women inspecting the sepulcher, and returning to prepare spices, but resting on the Sabbath.

There are three parts: (I.) Those things which were done before the crucifixion, namely 1. The proceedings before Pilate, to v. 6. 2. before Herod, to v. 12. 3. The triple testimony of innocence by Pilate to Christ, but returned in vain, with the people shouting crucify, crucify, to v. 23. 4. Pilate's condemnation, to v. 25. (II.) To the crucifixion & death of Christ belong 1. The leading out of Christ with Simon carrying the cross, verse 26. 2. The weeping of the women & the address of Christ delivered to them, to v. 31. 3. The crucifixion between two thieves, to v. 33. 4. The prayer of Christ for his crucifiers, v. 34. 5. The distribution of garments, & the mocking of Christ crucified, to v. 40. 6. The conversion of the thief, to v. 43. 7. The final prayer, & the death of Christ, to v. 46. III. Following the death of Christ on the cross are these: 1. The centurion's confession, v. 47. 2. The wonder of the people & relatives, v. 48. 49. 3. The placing of Christ's body, wrapped, into the sepulcher, to v. 55. 4. The observation of the women, & return into the city, to v. 56.

PART I. The antecedents of the crucifixion & death of Christ.

I. The proceedings before Pilate, the former.

Verse 1. ὤ̀ πλῆθος αὐτῶν] Thus he calls the assembly of the Senators, which the Syrian well translates כנישתהון.

Latin:

CAPUT XXIII.

ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Accusatur Christus coram Pilato seditionis adversus Caesarem, & quod se Regem faciat: quod posterius non diffitetur: nec tamen causam in illo invenit Pilatus : sed instant, populum commotum, eo quod passim in Ga- lilaea, & Judaea docuerit: unde ad Hero- dem, qui Galilaeae praeerat, mittitur: cui vero nullum reddit responsum, a quo illusus veste candida Pilato remittitur, testaturque Pi- latus, nec se nec Herodem quicquam in ipso reperire, eorum, quae morte digna essent: ideoque se illum dimittere velle, pro more festi: coetu autem iterum iterumque claman- te, ut Barrabam dimittat, Christum cruci- figat, ac cum tertia vice negaret Pilatus, se causam mortis in ipso invenire, clamoribus Pilatum obtundente, annuit eidem, Chri- stumque voluntati ipsorum tradidit. Cui cum educeretur ad crucem portandam suc- centuriatus est Simon Cyrenaeus, sequente magna turba, & mulieribus ipsum deplo- rantibus, quas ut se & liberos suos defleant, monet, tempora infelicia praedicens. Educti & duo malefici, in quorum medio Jesus crucifixus est, qui vero pro crucifixo- ribus oravit: porro vestium Jesu partitio, ejusque illusio, & titulus cruci impositus, blasphematio latronis alterius, alterius conversio, cui paradisus promittitur; tene- brae, & scissio veli, & post commendatum Patri spiritum mors Christi recensentur. Tum consequentia mortis Jesu commemo- rantur, Elogium centurionis, admiratio spe- ctatorum, & imprimis sepultura per Jose- phum, pium Senatorem Arimathensem, im- petrato a Pilato corpore Jesu, curata, inspi- cientibus sepulcrum mulieribus, & rever- tentibus ad parandum aromata, sed sabba- to quiescentibus.

Partes sunt tres: (I.) Quae ante crucifixionem gesta, utpote 1. Processus coram Pilato, ad v. 6. 2. coram Herode, ad v. 12. 3. Triplex testimo- nium innocentiae à Pilato Christo, sed frustra red- ditum, populo crucifige, crucifige, clamante, ad v. 23. 4. Pilati condemnatio, ad v. 25. (II.) Ad crucifixionem & mortem Christi spectant 1. Edu- ctio Christi Simone portante crucem, vers. 26. 2. Fletus mulierum & concio Christi ad eas habi- ta, ad v. 31. 3. Crucifixio inter duos latrones, ad v. 33. 4. Oratio Christi pro crucifixoribus, v. 34. 5. Vestium distributio, & illusio Christi crucifixi, ad v. 40. 6. Conversio latronis, ad v. 43. 7. Ora- tio postrema, & mors Christi, ad v. 46. III. Mor- tem Christi in cruce sequentia sunt haec: 1. Cen- turionis confessio, v. 47. 2. Populi & cognato- rum admiratio, v. 48. 49. 3. Corporis Christi in- voluti in sepulcrum repositio, ad v. 55. 4. Mulie- rum inspectatio, & in urbem reversio, ad v. 56.

PARS I. Antecedentia crucifixionis & mortis Christi.

I. Acta coram Pilato priora.

Vers. 1. ὤ̀ πλῆθος αὐτῶν] Ita vocat coetum Senatorum quare bene vertit Syrus כנישתהון.

## 23:2
Verse 2. Διαστρέφοντα τὸ ἔθνος] He is accused of the same crime as Elijah was by Ahab: for there too עכר ישראל the LXX translate ὁ διαστρέφων τὸν Ἰσραήλ. Elijah was calling the people back from the worship of false gods, Jesus from a most corrupt life to the right path. This the wicked call διαστρέφειν, because, forsooth, they do not wish to stir up Camarina.

καὶ κωλύοντα καίσαρι φόρους διδόναι] Because Judas, the author of this doctrine, had come from Galilee, they therefore confidently objected to Christ a crime both most hateful to the Romans and credible in a Galilean: nor were they ignorant of how false it was: but it was convenient for their purpose. It is enough to have objected certain crimes.

Λέγοντα ἑαυτὸν Χριστὸν βασιλέα εἶναι] He also lies who suppresses the truth pertaining to the matter, which the Jewish senators do here. He had said that he was Jesus Christ, that is, the excellent and promised King, but indeed of a heavenly kingdom, which did not stand in the way of the power of the Romans: that not being added, makes the matter appear far different.

Latin:

Vers. 2. Διαστρέφοντα τὸ ἔθνος] Eodem crimine accusatur quo ab Achabo Elias: nam & ibi עכר ישראל LXX. ver- tunt ὁ διασρέφων τὸν Ἰσραὴλ. Elias à falsorum Deorum cultu, Jesus à vita corruptissima populum in rectam viam revoca- bat. Hoc impii vocant διαστρέφειν, quia scilicet nolunt mo- veri Camarinam.

καὶ κωλύοντα καίσαρι φόρυς διδόναι] Quia è Galilaea pro- cesserat Judas hujus dogmatis autor, ideo confidenter ob- jiciebant Christo crimen, & odiosum maxime Romanis & in Galilaeo credibile: neque nesciebant quam id esset fal- sum: sed ita conducebat instituto. Quaedam crimina ob- jecisse satis est.

Λέγοντα ἑαυτὸν Χριστὸν βασιλέα εἶναι] Etiam mentitur qui verum ad rem pertinens subticet, quod hic faciunt Judaei senatores. Jesum Christum se, id est, eximium promissum- que Regem dixerat, sed nempe regni coelestis, quod Ro- manorum potentiz non obslabat: id non additum, facit rem longe aliam videre.

## 23:3
Verse 3. σὺ λέγεις] Jesus confessed the matter, but with the addition of the distinction which the senators had suppressed: I am a King, he said, but not of an earthly kingdom, which John explains.

Latin:

Vers. 3. σὺ λέγεις] Rem fassus est Iesus, sed addita quam senatores suppresserant distinctione: Rex sum, inquiens, sed non regni terrestris quod Iohannes explicat.

## 23:4
Verse 4. ὁ δὲ Πιλάτος εἶπε] Namely, going out to the senators waiting outside, as John teaches us.

οὐδὲν εὑρίσκω αἴτιον] No crime. For the word for fault is usually referred to private offenses. He saw that the confession was so tempered that it did not contain a crime, he saw no proofs: The very demeanor of the man was far removed from the suspicion of affected kingship.

Latin:

Vers. 4. ὁ δὲ Πιλάτος εἶπε] Nempe exiens ad senatores foris exspectantes, ut Iohannes nos docet.

οὐδὲν εὑρίσκω αἴτιον] Nullum crimen. Nam noxae vox ad privata delicta referri solet. Videbat confessionem ita esse temperatam, ut crimen non contineret, probationes videbat nullas: Ipse hominis habitus à regni affectati su- spicione longe aberat.

## 23:5
Verse 5. ἐπίσχυον] They insisted, חזקו Exod. XII. 33.

ὅτι ἀνασείει τὸν λαὸν διδάσκων] When they saw that the crime of affected kingship was not accepted by Pilate, they flee to another which was of an unambiguous deed, but had a question of law: He teaches, they say, certain new things, and not consistent with the opinions accepted among us. Now indeed it is sufficiently known that the people are accustomed to be moved by that thing, and therefore this is opposed to the public tranquility of which you have been appointed guardian. This is the very thing that was objected to Socrates at Athens. Thus also Tertullus accuses Paul, as κινῦντα στάσιν πᾶσι τοῖς Ἰουδαίοις. Celsus also accuses both the Jews, as seditious because they had departed from the institutions of the Egyptians, and the Christians, because they had departed from the Jewish ones.

Beginning from Galilee to this place] If you doubt, you can inquire, not only through Judea, but also through Galilee, the nurse of seditious men, how many followers of his discipline he gathered.

II. Proceedings before Herod.

Latin:

Vers. 5. ἐπίσχυον] Instabant חזקו Exod. XII. 33.

ὅτι αἰνασείει τὸν λαὸν διδάσκων] Cum non recipi à Pilato viderent crimen regni affectati, ad aliud confugiunt quod facti erat non ambigui, sed juris habebat quaestionem: Do- cet, inquiunt, res quasdam novas, neque congruentes cum receptis apud nos sententiis. Iam vero satis notum est, ea re populum commoveri solere, ac proinde adversari hoc publicae tranquillitati cujus tu custos es constitutus. Hoc ipsum est quod Socrati Athenis objectum fuit. Ita & Pau- lum accusat Tertullus, ut κινῦντα στάσιν πᾶσι τοῖς Ἰυδαίοις. Celsus quoque & Iudaeos, ut seditiosos accusat quod ab Æ- gyptiorum institutis recessissent, & Christianos quod à Iu- daicis.

Ἀρξάμενος ἀπὸ τῆς Γαλιλαίας ἕως ὧδε] Si dubitas, inquirere potes, non per Judaeam tantum, sed & per Galilaeam, nutri- cem seditiosorum hominum, quot ille disciplinae suae stipa- tores collegerit.

II. Acta coram Herode.

## 23:7
Vers. 7. Having recognized that he was from Herod's territory] For thus the word authority is taken here metonymically.

he sent him back] He used a proper term of Roman law: for a defendant who has been arrested somewhere is sent back to the judge of either his origin or his residence. Thus Pilate granted to Herod, or the Tetrarch of that place from which Jesus was said to be, the power of taking Jesus away to Galilee, and there, if he wished, of inquiring into his case, as was accustomed to be done among Roman provincial governors, which Theophylact rightly notes here. Celsus in L. Non est dubium D. de custodia rerum: It is usually observed by some, that when he has inquired and decided, he sends him back with a report to him who presides over the province from which the man is: which is to be done for a cause. But here, before he had decided anything, Pilate sends back the defendant: for greater reverence was owed to a king than to a governor. Thus Vespasian permitted the trial of the citizens of Tarichaeae to King Agrippa, in Josephus, Jewish War III, last chapter.

Latin:

Vers. 7. ἐπιγνὺς, ὅτι ἐκ τῆς ἐξυσίας Ἡρώδε ἐστὶν] Cognito ipsum esse ex Herodis territorio. Ita enim μετωνυμικῶς hic sumitur vox ἐξυσίας.

ἀνέπεμψεν αὐτὸν] Propriam Romani juris vocem usur- pavit: nam remittitur reus qui alicubi comprehensus n ite- titur ad judicem aut originis aut habitationis. Itaque Pila- tus Herodi, aut Tetrarchae ejus loci, unde esse Iesus diceba- tur, potestatem permisit Iesum abducendi in Galilaeam, ibi- que si vellet cognoscendi de ejus causa, ut fieri inter Romanos provinciarum rectores solebat, quod recte hic notat Theophylactus. Celsus in L. Non est dubium D. de custodia rerum: Illud à quibusdam observari solet, ut cum cognovit & constituit, remittat illum cum elogio ad eum qui provinciæ præest unde homo est: quod ex caussa faciendum est. Sed hic antequam quicquam constituisset, remittit reum Pilatus: major enim reverentia regi quam præsidi debeba- tur. Sic Vespasianus cognitionem de Tarichææ oppidanis Agrippæ regi permisit, apud Joseph. belli jud. III. c. ult.

## 23:8
Vers. 8. For a long time] That is, from a long time, as he speaks above VIII. 27. to see him] See above ch. IX. 9. he hoped to see some miracle done by him] That he might feast his eyes and mind with a new thing, in the manner of a court. But God is not so prodigal of his power that he wishes it to serve human curiosity. It must be a great matter for which the laws of nature are exceeded.

Latin:

Vers. 8. ἐξ ἱκανοῦ] Id est, ἐκ χρόνων ἱκανῶν, ut loquitur suprà VIII. 27. ἰδεῖν αὐτὸν] Vide supra c. IX. 9. ἤλπιζέ τι σημεῖον ἰδεῖν ὑπ᾽ αὐτοῦ γινόμενον] Ut oculos & animum re nova pasceret, more aulæ. At Deus non ita pro- digus est potentiæ suæ, ut eam inservire cupiat humanæ cu- riositati. Res magna sit necesse est propter quam naturæ leges exceduntur.

## 23:9
V. 9. And he questioned him] Concerning the power which he arrogated to himself.

Latin:

V. 9. ἐπηρώτησεν δὲ αὐτὸν] De potestate quam sibi arrogaret.

## 23:10
V. 10. Vehemently accusing him] The word is of middle usage: for it is also said of Paul, he was vehemently refuting the Jews, Acts XVIII. 28. I think it is rightly translated sharply. The senators, however, were taking pains to make Jesus suspected by Herod also of aspiring to imperial power. For the Davidic kingdom included Galilee no less than Jerusalem.

Latin:

V. 10. Εὐτόνως κατηγοροῦντες αὐτῷ] Vox est usus medii: nam & de Paulo dicitur εὐτόνως διακατηλέγχετο τοῖς Ἰουδαίοις, Act. XVIII. 28. Puto recte verti acriter. Dabant autem ope- ram Senatores, ut Herodi quoque suspectum facerent Jesum affectati imperii. Nam regnum Davidicum non minus Galilæam quam Hierosolyma complectebatur.

## 23:11
Vers. 11. And having set him at naught] Thinking him unworthy of his greatness, if it were believed that he feared a man equipped neither with arms nor with the arts of ruling. This corresponds to the word חזה in Isaiah LIII. 3. with his soldiers] With his attendants, as the Syriac rightly translates. For the Hellenists use army and troop, as the Hebrews use צבא for any retinue. mocking him] Mocking him as a foolish man: for this is the portion of Christ and Christians among that kind of men. a bright garment] The Arab understands it as shining: the Latin as white: neither is sufficiently certain. For as he had said above, of him who was feasting magnificently, that he was clothed in splendor, so also here he understands by bright garment a more splendid robe: just as James also calls the clothing of wealthier men. But here, moreover, it is right to understand a garment more splendid than private attire: for Herod mocked him as one foolishly aspiring to things beyond his grasp, so that the Syriac, which interpreted it as a scarlet robe, may perhaps not have strayed from the truth. One may doubt whether to favor the Latin or the Arab more, because in Acts X. 30 we read that an angel appeared to Cornelius in a bright garment: for a white and shining habit is usually ascribed to angels, as has been noted elsewhere. he sent him back to Pilate] Thinking him unworthy of his anger and therefore not using the benefit of the granted inquiry.

Latin:

Vers. 11. ἐξουθενήσας δὲ αὐτὸν] Indignum sua magnitudine ratus, si crederetur metuisse hominem, neque armis neque regnandi artibus instructum. Respondet hoc voci חזה apud Esaiam LIII. 3. σὺν τοῖς στρατεύμασιν αὐτοῦ] Cum ministris suis, ut recte vertit Syrus. Nam Hellenistæ στρατιὰν & στράτευμα usur- pant, ut Hebræi צבא pro quovis comitatu. ἐμπαίξας] Illudens ei, ut homini fatuo: hæc enim por- tio est Christi & Christianorum apud id genus homines. ἐσθῆτα λαμπρὰν] Fulgentem Arabs intelligit: albam Latinus: neutrum satis certum est. Nam ut supra, de eo qui magnifice epulabatur, dixerat ἐνδυσαμένου λαμπρῶς, Ita & hic λαμπρὰν ἐσθῆτα intelligit vestem splendidiorem: quomodo & Jacobus appellat vestem hominum opulen- tiorum. At hic insuper privato cultu splendidiorem vestem par est intelligi: nam irrisit eum Herodes, ut majora captu suo stulte appetentem, ita ut à re forte non uberraverit Sy- rus, qui vestem coccineam est interpretatus. Dubitare potest Latino magis an Arabi faveat, quod Act. X. 30. le- gimus Angelum Cornelio apparuisse ἐν ἐσθῆτι λαμπρᾷ: Nam solet angelis & candidus & fulgens habitus adscribi, ut alibi notatum est. ἀνέπεμψεν αὐτὸν τῷ Πιλάτῳ] Indignum ira sua ratus ac proinde beneficio indultæ cognitionis non utens.

## 23:12
Vers. 12. And they became friends] Namely, by that kind of friendship which is cemented by common utility and is more correctly called a faction: - - - - By the blow of such a dire treaty, peace is born. - - Vices, though discordant among themselves, easily conspire against virtue. for they were previously in enmity] Because of the Galileans, as is credible, recently slaughtered by Pilate; but also otherwise, hatreds were most easily born between kings and Roman governors out of rivalry, of which matter let him who wishes read a notable example in Philo against Flaccus.

III. Subsequent proceedings before Pilate, with a triple testimony of this innocence of Christ.

Latin:

Vers. 12. ἐγένοντο δὲ φίλοι] Eo nimirum amicitiæ genere quod communi utilitate conglutinatur & rectius factio di- citur: - - - - Tam diri fœderis ictu Parta quies. - - Vitia inter se discordia adversus virtutem facile conspirant. προϋπῆρχον γὰρ ἐν ἔχθρᾳ ὄντες] Ob Galilæos, ut credibile est, a Pilato nuper trucidatos; sed & alias facillime inter Reges & Romanos præsides ex æmulatu odia nascebantur, cujus rei insigne exemplum legat qui volet apud Philonem adversus Flaccum.

III. Acta posteriora coram Pilato, cum tripli- ci hujus innocentiæ Christi testimonio.

## 23:13
Vers. 13. And the rulers] That is, the elders. And the people] He addressed them with the people standing by, see what is said on Matthew.

Latin:

Vers. 13. κὶ τοὺς ἄρχοντας] Id est, τοὺς πρεσβυτέρους. κὶ τὸν λαὸν] Allocutus eos est adstante populo, Vide quæ ad Matthæum.

## 23:14
Vers. 14. ὡς ἀποστρέφοντα τὸν λαὸν] As one who turns the people away from reverence for the Roman empire. Thus Hesychius interprets ἀποστροφὴν as treason. ἐνώπιον ὑμῶν] This is said to the senators. Pilate says that he has investigated the whole matter not only with his own council, but also in the presence of the senators themselves, first indeed when they brought the accused, and again when he himself had proceeded to them. ἀνακρίνας] An investigation having been made. Here too Luke uses the proper term. For it is a judicial word, Acts 4:9, 'if we are being examined today for a good deed.' Acts 25:26, 'so that after the examination has taken place I may have something to write.' Chap. 28:18, 'I was delivered into the hands of the Romans, who, having examined me, wanted to release me.' Plato: 'a judge who is silent for us and does not speak more than the litigants in the examinations.' Plutarch: 'having written how one must examine those who have frequently been among them.' αἴτιον, ὧν κατηγορεῖτε κατ᾽ αὐτοῦ] The cause, of which you accuse him, namely that which pertains to majesty, for that was being urged especially.

Latin:

Vers. 14. ὡς ἀποστρέφοντα τὸν λαὸν] Tanquam qui aver- tat populum a Romani imperii reverentia. Sic ἀποστροφὴν, προδοσίαν interpretatur Hesychius. ἐνώπιον ὑμῶν] Hoc ad senatores dicitur. Ait Pilatus se rem totam inquisivisse non tantum cum consilio suo, sed & coram ipsis senatoribus, primum quidem cum reum ad- ducerent, iterum vero cum ad eos ipse processisset. ἀνακρίνας] Inquisitione facta. Etiam hic κυριολογεῖ Lucas. Nam vox est judicialis Act. IV. 9. εἰ ἡμεῖς σήμερον ἀνακρινό- μεθα ἐπὶ εὐεργεσίᾳ. Act. XXV. 26. ὅπως τῆς ἀνακρίσεως γενο- μένης σχῶ τί γράψαι. cap. XXVIII. 18. παρεδόθην εἰς τὰς χεῖ- ρας ῥωμαίων, οἵτινες ἀνακρίναντές με ἐβούλοντο ἀπολῦσαι. Platos ἄφωνον δ᾽ ἂν δικαστὴς ἡμῖν κὶ μὴ πλείω τῶν ἀντιδίκων ἐν ταῖς ἀνα- κρίσεσι φθεγγόμενον. Plutarchus: γράψας πῶς δεῖ ἀνακρῖναι θαμινῶς ἐν αὐτοῖς γενομένους. αἴτιον, ὧν κατηγορεῖτε κατ᾽ αὐτῦ] Quod ad majestatem sci- licet pertineat, id enim præcipue urgebatur.

## 23:15
Vers. 15. ἀλλ᾽ οὐδὲ Ἡρώδης] If you do not believe me, believe a fellow countryman and a partner in religion. ἀνέπεμψα γὰρ αὐτὸν πρὸς ὑμᾶς] Since this reading is supported by many codices and seems to have pleased the Arab, it does not displease me. For the following parts cohere more correctly. The Syriac reads ἀνέπεμψα γὰρ αὐτὸν πρὸς αὐτόν. οὐδὲν ἄξιον θανάτου ἐστὶ πεπραγμένον αὐτῷ] The Syriac seems to interpret this πεπραγμένον not as done by Jesus, but by Herod concerning Jesus: which sense the Latin version also receives, so that Pilate says this: that Jesus was sent back by Herod without any indictment or sign by which he might be understood to have deserved death, and certainly that ἰδὺ seems to require this sense, which subjects the matter as if to the eyes, and otherwise Pilate would have said the same thing twice: for ὐδὲν εὗρον αἴτιον preceded.

Latin:

Vers. 15. ἀλλ᾽ οὐδὲ Ἡρώδης] Si mihi non creditis, credite populari & consorti religionis. ἀνέπεμψα γὰρ αὐτοὶ πρὸς ὑμᾶς] Hæc lectio cum multis codicibus fulciatur & Arabi videatur placuisse, mihi non displicet. Sequentia enim rectius cohærent. Syrus le- git ἀνέπεμψα γὰρ αὐτὸν πρὸς αὐτόν. οὐδὲν ἄξιον θανάτου ἐστὶ πεπραγμένον αὐτῷ] Videtur Syrus hoc πεπραγμένον interpretari non ab Jesu, sed ab Herode circa Jesum: quem sensum & Latina versio recipit, ut hoc dicat Pilatus: remissum ab Herode Jesum sine ullo ele gio aut figno quo mortem commeritus posset intelligi, & certe hunc sensum requirere videtur illud ἰδὺ quod rem quasi o- culis subjicit, & alioqui bis idem dixerit Pilatus: nam praecessit ὐδὲν εὗρον αἴτιον.

## 23:16
Vers. 16. παιδεύσας] He follows the propriety again: for παιδεύειν corresponds to the Latin 'castigare' (to chastise). Chastisement, however, is properly said of scourging, L. veluti D. de poenis; but it is to be noted that Pilate, having various plans turning in his mind at that time, had proposed to beat Jesus with rods, not as he did later, as if for the sake of holding an examination, but as a punishment: for under Roman laws the punishment was arbitrary if anyone (as Paul the Jurist speaks in his 'Receptae Sententiae') introduced new religions unknown to custom or reason, by which the minds of men might be moved: which Marcus Imperator said: if anyone had done something by which the fickle minds of men might be terrified by the superstition of the divine. This crime, as much as it seemed like treason to Pilate, who wished to satisfy the Jews in any way possible, seemed to fit Jesus better, as those who look to something other than justice are accustomed to seek something to use as a pretext for injury.

Latin:

Vers. 16. παιδεύσας] Iterum proprietatem sectatur: nam παιδεύειν respondet Latino castigare. Castigatio autem de flagellis proprie dicitur L. veluti D. de poenis; sed notan- dum est fuisse tum Pilato varia animo consilia versanti pro- positum flagris Jesum caedere, non ut postea fecit, quasi habendae quaestionis causa, sed pro poena: nimrum legi- bus Romanis arbitraria erat poena, si quis (ut Paulus JĈtus in receptis sententiis loquitur) novas ex usu vel ratione in- cognitas religiones induceret, ex quibus animi hominum moverentur: quod Marcus Imperator dixit: si quis aliquid fecisset quo leves hominum animi superstitione numinis terrerentur. Hoc crimen, quam majestatis videbatur Pi- lato, qui quovis modo satisfacere Judaeis volebat, magis in Jesum congruere, ut solent qui aliud quam jus intuentur quaerere aliquid quod obtendant injuriae.

## 23:18
Vers. 18. αἶρε τῦτον] Concerning this manner of shouting, we have spoken at Matthew.

Latin:

Vers. 18. αἶρε τῦτον] De hoc clamandi modo diximus ad Matthaeum.

## 23:22
Vers. 22. τί γὰρ κακὸν] What evil? There is also here an αἰτιολογία of what is passed over in silence. For it is understood: I will not do what you want: or you are demanding something unjust.

Latin:

Vers. 22. τί γὰρ κακὸν] Quod capital? Est autem & hic αἰτιολογία τῦ σιωπωμένε. Subintelligitur enim: non fa- ciam quod vultis: aut iniquum postulatis.

## 23:23
Vers. 23. κὰι τῶν ἀρχιερέων] The Syriac and Arabic versions acknowledge these words: nor are they superfluous. For it is signified that these men were the leaders in the shouting among the people: which was most unworthy of their gravity.

IV. The condemnation of Christ made by Pilate.

Latin:

Vers. 23. κὰι τῶν ἀρχιερέων] Agnofcunt has voces Syrus & Arabs: neque supervacuae sunt. Significatur enim, hos fuisse in populo ad clamorem praecipuos: quod vel maxi- me indignum erat eorum gravitate.

IV. Christi à Pilato facta condemnatio.

Vers. 24. ἐπέκρινε γενέσθαι] ἐπεκρίνειν here is nothing other than to decree by judging. Thus the writer of 2 Maccabees 4:48 said θάνατον ἐπέκρινε.

Latin:

Vers. 24. ἐπέκρινε γενέσθαι] ἐπεκρίνειν nihil hic est aliud quam judicando decernere. Ita θάνατον ἐπέκρινε dixit scri- ptor 2. Macc. IV. 48.

## 23:25
Vers. 25. τὸν διὰ σάσιν κὰι φόνον βεβλημένον εἰς τὴν φυλακὴν] It is much more ἐμφατικώτερον than if he had simply said Barabbas. Thus Peter in Acts 3:14: 'But you denied the Holy and Just One, and asked for a murderer to be granted to you.'

Vers. 25. τὸν διὰ σάσιν κὰι φόνον βεβλημένον εἰς τὴν φυλα- κὴν] Multo est ἐμφατικώτερον quam si simpliciter dixisset Barrabam. Ita Petrus Act. III. 14. ὑμεῖς δὲ τὸν ἅγιον κὰι δίκαιον ἠρνήσασθε κὰι ἠτήσασθε ἄνδρα φονέα χαρισθῆναι ὑμῖν.

I. Christi eductio.

Vers. 26. ὄπισθεν τῦ Ἰησῦ] See what is at Matthew.
