Vers. 26. ὄπισθεν τῦ Ἰησῦ] Vide quae ad Matthaeum.

II. Fletus mulierum, & Christi ad easdem concio.

## 23:28
Vers. 28. Do not weep for me. Christ considers the custom of men who grieve more for their own evils than for those of others, as if he were saying: if you could see the calamities that hang over you, you would not have the leisure to shed tears for me.

Latin:

Vers. 28. μὴ κλαίετε ἐπ' ἐμὲ] Respicit Christus morem ho- minum de suis quam de alienis malis magis dolentium, quasi diceret: si calamitates quae vobis impendent videre- tis, non vacaret vobis lachrymas mihi impendere.

## 23:29
Vers. 29. In which they will say. Indefinite. That is, when it will be said. Blessed are the barren. Because the pain of seeing children as participants in misery is twofold. Euripides in Alcestis: 'Envying the unmarried and childless among mortals; for one soul is a moderate burden to grieve for beyond itself.'

Latin:

Vers. 29. ἐν αἷς ἐρῦσι] Indefinite. Id est, cum dicetur. μακάριαι αἱ στεῖραι] Quia duplex est dolor liberos videre miseriae participes Euripides Alcestide: Ζηλῶν δ' ἀγάμυς ἀτεκνός τε βροτῶν· Μία γὰρ ψυχὴ τῆς ὑπὲρ ἀλγεῖν Μέτριον ἄχθος.

## 23:30
Vers. 30. To say to the mountains, fall upon us, and to the hills, cover us. From Hosea 10:8, where the discourse is about Samaria, which bore the image of both the depravity and the punishment of Jerusalem: but there the words are transposed: 'they will say to the mountains, cover us, and to the hills, fall upon us.' John interprets the Hebrew 'hills' as 'rocks' in Revelation 6:16: 'they say to the mountains and to the rocks, fall upon us and hide us.' A similar passage is Isaiah 3:19. These expressions are indeed proverbial, but at the same time they were used by Christ for the signification of singular events, so that his foreknowledge might appear more clearly from these sayings. For it was the misery of mothers that they themselves ate their own children because of famine, and when the Roman army occupied the city, very many hid themselves in caves, as can be seen in Josephus.

Latin:

Vers. 30. λέγειν τοῖς ὄρεσι, πέσετε ἐφ'ἡμᾶς, κὰι τοῖς βυνοῖς, καλύψατε ἡμᾶς] Ex Osea X. 8. ubi de Samaria sermo, quae & pravitatis & poenae Hierosolymorum gessit imaginem: sed ibi transpositis vocibus est ἐρῦσι τοῖς ὄρεσι, καλύψατε ἡμᾶς, κὰι τοῖς βυνοῖς πέσετε ἐφ' ἡμᾶς. Iohannes ולגבעות βυνῶν in- terpretatur πέτρας Apoc. VI. 16. λέγυσι τοῖς ὄρεσι κὰι ταῖς πέτραις, πέσετε ἐφ' ἡμᾶς κὰι κρύψατε ἡμᾶς. Similis locus est Esa. III. 19. Locutiones hae sunt quidem proverbiales, at simul à Christo usurpatae sunt ad eventuum singularium si- gnificationem, quo magis ex his dictis ipsius praescientia appareret. Nam & matrum fuit miseria, ut suos ipsae natos prae fame manderent, & occupante urbem Romano ex- ercitu, plurimi se in fpecus abdiderunt, ut apud Iosephum videre est.

## 23:31
Vers. 31. If they do these things in the green wood, what will happen in the dry? Although 'they do' can be referred to the Romans, I think it is more convenient to explain it impersonally, so that the sense is: if this is done (by divine dispensation, of course) in the green wood, what will happen in the dry? Just as Peter says, 'if the righteous is scarcely saved (that is, not without many calamities), where will the ungodly and the sinner appear?' Rabbi Solomon on Numbers 10: When the holy and blessed God executes judgment on the righteous, he is feared, exalted, and praised: for if he does this in them, how much more in the wicked? It appears that this way of speaking was also proverbial. For the Hebrews call good men green wood, and bad men dry. For there is a trite adage among them: if there are two dry pieces of wood and one green, the dry ones burn up that green wood: by which they signify that the good, being fewer, are easily oppressed by the conspiracy of the wicked: but also in Ezekiel 20:47. God threatens that he will cut down every green tree and every dry tree, which he himself soon interprets in chapter 21:3 as the righteous and the wicked. Hermas also uses the same similitude in book 3. But also in Psalm 1, the good man is compared to a green tree, and conversely, trees that are dead are called by both Christ and the Baptist men destitute of piety.

III. The crucifixion of Christ between two thieves.

Latin:

Vers. 31. εἰ ἐν τῷ ὑγρῷ ξύλῳ ταῦτα ποιῦσιν, ἐν τῷ ξηρῷ τι γίνηται] Quanquam potest ποιῦσιν ad Romanos referri, tamen convenientius puto impersonaliter exponi, ut sensus sit: si hoc fit (divina scilicet dispensatione) in ligno humido, quid fiet in arido? quomodo Petrus dicit, εἰ δί- καιος μόλις σώζεται, (id est non nisi per multas calamitates) ὁ ἀσεβὴς κὰι ἁμαρτωλὸς πῦ φανεῖται; Rabbi Salomo ad X. Num. Quum Deus sanctus benedictus judicium facit in justis, timetur, extollitur, & laudatur: Nam si in illu hoc facit, quan- to magis in impiis? Apparet autem & hoc loquendi genus fuisse proverbiale. Nam Hebraei viros bonos ligna viridia vocant, malos arida. Est enim tritum apud eos adagium: si duo fuerint ligna arida & unum viride, arida illud lignum viride exurunt: quo significant facile bonos, utpote pau- ciores, opprimi malorum conspiratione: sed & apud Eze- chielem XX. 47. comminatur Deus excisurum se כָּל־עֵץ יָבֵשׁ pan πᾶν ξύλον χλωρὸν κῂ πᾶν ξύλον ξηρὸν, quod ipse mox cap. XXI. 3. interpretatur justum atque impro- bum. Utitur eadem similitudine & Hermas lib. 3. Sed & in Psalmo I. vir bonus virenti arbori comparatur, contraque arbores emortuæ & Christo & Baptistæ vocantur homines à pietate destituti.

III. Christi inter duos latrones crucifixio.

## 23:32
Vers. 32. Malefactors: for 'nequam' (worthless) is much less; but 'malefici' (sorcerers) are properly those who do harm with evil spells or herbs.

Latin:

Vers. 32. κακῦργοι] Facinorosi: nam nequam multo est minus; malefici autem proprie sunt qui malis carminibus aut herbis nocent.

## 23:33
Vers. 33. The place called the Skull. If the codices supported it, I would read 'of the skulls' (κρανίων), as I suspect the Latin interpreter also read, or 'of the skull' (κρανίε), as Epiphanius seems to have read. Otherwise it will be a metonymy, 'skull' for 'place of the skull,' as it is in the interpreter of Matthew and Mark: but we also read that there was a city in Cephalonia that was called Cranium. Thucydides uses 'Crania' in the plural number.

IV. Christ's intercession for his crucifiers.

Latin:

Vers. 33. τὸν καλύμενον κρανίον] Si codices adstipularen- tur legerem κρανίων, quomodo & Latinum interpretem le- gisse suspicor, aut κρανίε quomodo legisse videtur Epipha- nius. Alioqui erit μετωνυμία, κρανίον pro κρανία τόπῳ, ut est apud Matthæi interpretem & Marcum: sed & in Ce- phallenia urbem fuisse legimus quæ Cranium vocaretur. Thucididi κράνια plurali numero.

IV. Christi pro crucifixoribus intercessio.

## 23:34
V. 34. Father, forgive them. What Christ had warned by word, that one should pray for those who abuse us, he now performs by deed: truly showing himself as the High Priest, whose duty it is to offer for the ignorances of the people. And thus was fulfilled what Isaiah had predicted: 'he will intercede for the transgressors.' But that 'forgive' must be interpreted from the similar prayer of Stephen, 'do not lay this sin to their charge.' Do not impute it, that is, in such a way that you preclude repentance for them by haste to destruction or by the fullest hardening. Justin in his dialogue with Trypho: 'Therefore we also pray for you and for all other men who are hostile to us, that having repented with us, you may not blaspheme Christ Jesus.' And in another place: 'And we do not hate you or those who have assumed such things about us because of you, but we pray that even now all who have repented may obtain mercy from the compassionate and most merciful Father of all, God.' Thus Paul in 1 Timothy 1:13 says that he obtained mercy: because he had done what he had done in ignorance: signifying that he was not hardened for that reason, and that the approach to the truth was not closed to him.

For they do not know what they are doing. Thus Ecclesiastes 4:17. They do not know that they are doing evil. Christ does here what intercessors are accustomed to do: omitting what was to be accused in the deed of the Jews, he refers to that which pertained to diminishing the guilt in some way. It was indeed gross and supine ignorance, and add also that it proceeded from many vices, but yet those who sinned against him whom they had not known were not sinning in the extreme degree. Aristotle in the first book of Rhetoric, and Themistius following him in his oration to Valens, make three kinds of offenses: misfortunes, errors, and injustices: And Themistius says that to misfortunes is owed sympathy and pity (which Diodorus Siculus had also said in his Library, book 13), but to errors is owed rebuke and correction: finally, to injustices is owed condemnation and punishment. This sin of the Jews was not just a mere ἀτύχημα [misfortune], but rather one exceeding even the common lot of ἁμαρτημάτων [sins], and thus it drew something ἐκ τῶ ἀτυχήματος [from the misfortune] mixed into it on account of ignorance: which both Peter acknowledges in Acts III. 17 and Paul in I. Cor. II. 8. And so it is to be seen that many of them were relieved by this prayer of Christ, when, having understood afterwards that the cause of Christ was approved by God, they were led to a serious detestation of their crime. Far different is the case of those who redeemed a lie from the guards with money, or forbade the Apostles to publish the signs of heavenly power. Aristotle taught well in his book on ethics III that ἕτερον εἶναι τὸ δι᾽ ἄγνοιαν πράττειν τῶ ἀγνοῦντα ποιεῖν [it is one thing to act out of ignorance, another to act while ignorant]. For that there are some who indeed sin while ignorant, but not through ignorance, of which thing there is an evident sign if, once the matter is discovered, they do not repent of the deed, which observation of the wisest Philosopher is seen to be wisely adapted to this cause of the Jews in the Responses to the Orthodox, question CVIII, where that writer of great judgment says thus: δεῖχ θήσεως τῆς νομιζομένης γνώσεως διὰ τῆς ἀπο- βάσεως ἀγνοίας ὑπεσχηκότας τῶ πράγματι, ἂν ἐμμείνωσι τῇ ἀυ- τῇ ἀγνοίᾳ ὁ ἀγνοήσας, ἐδεμίαν ἐφέλκεται συγγνώμην, ἀλλὰ τιμωρίαν ἀπαραίτητον [If those who have promised a demonstration of supposed knowledge through the rejection of ignorance persist in the same ignorance, the one who is ignorant draws to himself no pardon, but an inevitable punishment]. And soon after: τὸ ἐξαργυρίζειν ἀυτᾶ (Jesu) τὴν ἀνάςασιν κᾀὶ κωλύειν τὰς ἀποστόλες ἐπι τῷ ὀνόματι ἀυτᾶ μὴ ἐκτελεῖν θεῖα ἔργα ἐν τῇ δυνάμει τῶ θείε πνευματος γινόμενα, ἐκ ἐσιν ἀκσσια ἀγνοιας συγγνώμην ἐφελκομένης, ἀλλ᾽ ἐγνωσμέ- νης ἑκυσίε θεομαχίας τιμωρίαν ἐφελκομένης [To monetize his (Jesus') resurrection and to hinder the apostles from performing divine works in his name, which are done in the power of the divine spirit, is not an act of ignorance drawing pardon, but one drawing the punishment of known, voluntary opposition to God]. For those who ascribed the known works of God to the devil, we do not read that Christ prayed similar things. And when John forbids praying for those sinning unto death, he understands those who now oppose the known truth with a certain purpose of mind, or who contumaciously spurn the warnings of the Church; which kind of men is rightly said to sin unto death, because they are, to speak with Aristotle, ἀνίατοι διὰ τὴν μοχθηρίαν [incurable on account of their wickedness]. Theodoret treats this same argument concerning the manifold kind of sins at the end of his discourse to the Greeks, where he says that it is just that those who openly love and embrace a shameful life, we should abhor: but those whose sins are not ὅλα τῆς γνώμης, we should admonish and support as much as possible.

V. The distribution of Christ's garments, and the mockery of him.

Latin:

V. 34. πάτερ ἄφες ἀυτοῖς] Quod dicto monuerat Chri- stus, orandum ὑπὲρ τῶν ἐπηρεαζόντων ἡμᾶς, id facto nunc præstat: Pontificem se vere exhibens, cujus est munus προ- σφέρειν ὑπὲρ τῶν τῶ λαῶ ἀγνοημάτων. Atque ita impletum est quod prædixerat Esaias לפשעים יפגיע. Illud autem ἄφες interpretandum ex simili oratione Stephani, μὴ σή- ζῃς ἀυτοῖς τὴν ἁμαρτίαν ταύτην. Ne imputa, scilicet in hoc, ut pœnitentiam illis præcludas festinatio exitio aut plenissima obduratione Justinus colloquio cum Tryphone: διὸ κᾀὶ ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν κᾀ ὑπὲρ τῶν ἄλλων ἁπάντων ἀνθρώπων τῶν ἐχθραινόντων ἡμῖν ἐυχόμεθα, ἵνα μεταγνόντες σὺν ἡμῖν μὴ βλα- σφημῆτε τὸν Χρισὸν Ἰησῦν. Et alio loco: κᾀ ἡμεῖς ὑμᾶς κᾀ τὸς δι᾽ ὑμᾶς τοιαῦτα καθ᾽ ἡμῶν ὑπειληφότας & μισῦμεν, ἀλλ᾽ ἐυχόμεθα κᾂν νῦν μετανοήσαντας πάντας ἔλεος τυχεῖν παρὰ τῶ ἐυσπλάγχνε κᾀὶ πολυελέα πατρὸς τῶν ὅλων Θεῦ. Sic Paulus 1. Tim. I. 13. ait se misericordiam consecutum: eo quod ignorans egisset quæ egerat: significans, ideo se non obdu- ratum, non præclusum sibi ad veritatem aditum.

& γὰρ οἴδασι τί ποιε͂σι] Sic Ecclesiastæ. IV. 17. Nesciunt se malum facere. Facit hic Christus quod solent deprecato- res: omisso quod in facto Judæorum erat accusandum, id refert quod ad minuendam aliquo modo culpam pertine- bat. Erat quidem ignorantia crassa ac supina, adde etiam profecta ex multis vitiis, sed tamen non extrema linea pec- cabant qui in eum peccabant quem non pernoverant. Ari- stoteles Rhetor. primo, & eum secutus Themistius oratio- ne ad Valentem, tria faciunt delictorum genera, ἀτυχήμα- τα, ἁμαρτήματα, ἀδικήματα: Et ἀτυχήμασι quidem ait The- mistius deberi τὸ ξυναλγεῖν κᾀντῷ οἰκτείρειν (quod dixerat & Diodorus Siculus Bibliothecæ lib. XIII.) τοῖς ἁμαρτήμασι vero τὸ μέμφεσθαι κᾀὶ τὸ ἐπανορθῶν: postremo τοῖς ἀδικήμασι τὸ καταγινώσκειν κᾀὶ τιμωρεῖσθαι. Judæorum hoc peccatum sicut nudum ἀτύχημα non erat, imo excedensetiam com- munem ἁμαρτημάτων sortem, ita aliquid trahebat ἐκ τῶ ἀτυχήματος ob ignorantiam ei admixtam: quam & Petrus agnoscit Act. III. 17. & Paulus I. Cor. II. 8. Itaque videre est multos eorum hac Christi deprecatione sublevatos, cum intellexissent postea Christi causam Deo probatam, addu- ctos ad seriam facinoris sui detestationem. Alia longe co- rum causa est qui à vigilibus mendacium nummis redeme- runt, aut Apostolis interdixerunt ne ederent cœlestis po- tentiæ signa. Bene docuit Aristoteles libro de moribus III. ἕτερον εἶναι τὸ δι᾽ ἄγνοιαν πράττειν τῶ ἀγνοῦντα ποιεῖν. Nam quosdam esse qui ignorantes quidem peccent, sed non per ignorantiam, cujus rei evidens esse indicium, si eos re comperta facti non pœniteat, quam sapientissimi Phi- losophi observationem ad causam hanc Judæorum sapien- ter aptatam videre est in responsionibus adorthodoxos quæstione CVIII. ubi ita ait quicunque ille est magni judicii scriptor: δεῖχ θήσεως τῆς νομιζομένης γνώσεως διὰ τῆς ἀπο- βάσεως ἀγνοίας ὑπεσχηκότας τῶ πράγματι, ἂν ἐμμείνωσι τῇ ἀυ- τῇ ἀγνοίᾳ ὁ ἀγνοήσας, ἐδεμίαν ἐφέλκεται συγγνώμην, ἀλλὰ τιμωρίαν ἀπαραίτητον. Et mox: τὸ ἐξαργυρίζειν ἀυτᾶ (Jesu) τὴν ἀνάςασιν κᾀὶ κωλύειν τὰς ἀποστόλες ἐπι τῷ ὀνόματι ἀυτᾶ μὴ ἐκτελεῖν θεῖα ἔργα ἐν τῇ δυνάμει τῶ θείε πνευματος γινόμενα, ἐκ ἐσιν ἀκσσια ἀγνοιας συγγνώμην ἐφελκομένης, ἀλλ᾽ ἐγνωσμέ- νης ἑκυσίε θεομαχίας τιμωρίαν ἐφελκομένης. Pro iis, qui cognita Dei opera diabolo ascribebant, Christum similia precatum non legimus: & cum Johannes vetat orari pro delinquentibus ad mortem, eos intelligit qui cognitam jam veritatem certo animi proposito oppugnant, aut mo- nita Ecclesiæ contumaciter spernunt; quod genus hominum recte ad mortem peccare dicitur, quia sunt, ut cum Aristo- tele loquar, ἀνίατοι διὰ τὴν μοχθηρίαν. Tractat idem hoc argumentum de multiplici peccatorum genere Theodore- tus fine orationis ad Græcos, ubi ait, æquum esse, ut eos qui palam amant & amplectuntur vitam turpem, exfecre- mur: eos vero, quorum peccata non sunt ὅλα τῆς γνώμης, moneamus ac sublevemus quantum fieri potest.

V. Vestium Christi distributio, ejusque illusio.

## 23:35
Verse 35.

οἱ ἄρχοντες σὺν αὐτοῖς] It seems to me that the Syrian also read that σὺν αὐτοῖς and expressed it quite correctly by אִנֻּן. For the sense is that not only the common people, but the Senators themselves, whose dignity this least became, as we just noted in a similar case, were cruelly insulting him as he hung there.

ὁ τοῦ Θεοῦ ἐκλεκτὸς] We have spoken of the force of the word ἐκλεκτὸς at Matt. XX. 16; what it signifies properly here, see at Matthew in this place. The Messiah was clearly accustomed to be called by this name among the Jews, which Ebion interpreted perversely to the injury of Christ's birth, whose opinion Epiphanius explains thus: τότε ἕνεκα Ἰησοῦν γεγεννημένον ἐκ σπέρματος ἀνδρὸς λέγουσι καὶ ἐπιλεχθέντα καὶ ἕνεκα κατ᾿ ἐκλογὴν υἱὸν Θεοῦ κληθέντα ἀπὸ τοῦ ἄνωθεν εἰς αὐτὸν ἥκοντος χριστοῦ: From which passage light shines upon two passages of Justin, in the dialogue against Trypho, which are otherwise obscure: ἤδη μέντοι ὦ Τρύφων, I said, it does not destroy the fact that this person (so it should be read, not τοιοῦτον) is the Christ of God, if I am unable to prove that he also pre-existed as the Son of the Maker of all things, being God, and was born a man through the virgin; but if it is proved by all means that this is the Christ of God, whoever this may be, even if I do not prove that he pre-existed and endured to be born a man subject to like passions as we are, having flesh according to the will of the Father, in this it is just to say that I have been mistaken, but not to deny that this is the Christ, if he appears as a man born of men and is proved to have become Christ by election; for there are some, O friends, I said, of our own race, who acknowledge him to be Christ, but declare him to be a man born of men, with whom I do not agree, nor would I, even if most people should say they hold these opinions, since we have been commanded by Christ himself not to be persuaded by human teachings, but by those proclaimed by the blessed prophets and taught by him; and I, Trypho, said, those who say that he was born a man and was anointed by election, and became Christ, seem to me to speak more plausibly than you who say these things which you say. Again elsewhere Trypho speaks thus: καὶ γυμνώσατε αὐτὰ ἑκάστοις λέγοντες αἰδεῖσθαι ὀφείλετε καὶ μᾶλλον ἄνθρωπον ἐξ ἀνθρώπων γενόμενον (the text is corrupt, it should be read: λέγειν τοῦ Ἰησοῦ τοῦτον καὶ ἐὰν ἀποδείκνυτε ἀπὸ τῶν γραφῶν ὅτι αὐτός ἐστιν ὁ Χριστὸς, διὰ τὸ ἐννόμως καὶ τελείως πολιτεύεσθαι αὐτὸν καταξιωθῆναι τοῦ ἐκλεχθῆ- ναι εἰς χριστόν. I have brought these forward the more willingly because they pertain much to the correct understanding of the error of Ebion: and at the same time they show that the use of the word ἐκλέγειν was far different in those times than is now thought.

Latin:

Vers. 35.

οἱ ἄρχοντες σὺν αὐτοῖς] Illud σὺν αὐτοῖς legisse mihi vide- tur etiam Syrus & recte satis expressisse per אִנֻּן. Sensus e- nim est, non plebs tantum, sed & ipsi Senatores, quorum id gravitatem minime de erat, ut modo notavimus in re simili crudeliter insultabant pendenti.

ὁ τοῦ Θεοῦ ἐκλεκτὸς] Quæ sit vis vocis ἐκλεκτὸς diximus ad Matth. XX. 16. quid hic proprie significet ad Matthæum hoc loco. Solebat plane inter Judæos Messias hoc nomine appellari, quod in nativitatis Christi injuriam prave inter- pretatus est Ebion, cujus sententiam ita explicat Epiphanius: τότε ἕνεκα Ἰησοῦν γεγεννημένον ἐκ σπέρματος ἀνδρὸς λέγουσι καὶ ἐπιλεχθέντα καὶ ἕνεκα κατ᾿ ἐκλογὴν υἱὸν Θεοῦ κληθέντα ἀπὸ τοῦ ἄνωθεν εἰς αὐτὸν ἥκοντος χριστοῦ: Ex quo loco lux effulget duobus Justini locis, colloquio adversus Tryphonem, alio- qui obscuris: ἤδη μέντοι ὦ Τρύφων, εἶπον, οὐκ ἀπόλλυται τὸ τοῦτον (ita legendum, non τοιοῦτον) εἶναι Χριστὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ, ἐὰν ἀποδεῖξαι μὴ δύνωμαι ὅτι καὶ προϋπῆρχεν υἱὸς τοῦ ποιητοῦ τῶν ὅλων Θεὸς ὢν καὶ γεγέννηται ἄνθρωπος διὰ τῆς παρθένου· ἀλλ᾽ ἐκ παντὸς ἀποδεικνυμένου ὅτι οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ Χριστὸς ὁ τοῦ Θεοῦ, ὅστις οὗ- τος ἔσται, ἐὰν δὲ μὴ ἀποδεικνύω ὅτι προϋπῆρχε καὶ γεννηθῆναι ἄν- θρωπος ὁμοιοπαθὴς ἡμῖν, σάρκα ἔχων κατὰ τὴν τοῦ πατρὸς βουλὴν ὑπέμεινεν, ἐν τούτῳ πεπλανῆσθαί με μόνον λέγειν δίκαιον, ἀλλὰ μὴ ἀρνεῖσθαι ὅτι οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ Χριστὸς, ἐὰν φαίνηται ὡς ἄνθρωπος ἐξ ἀνθρώπων γενηθεὶς καὶ ἐκλογῇ γενόμενος εἰς τὸ Χριστὸν εἶναι ἀ- ποδεικνύηται· καὶ γάρ εἰσί τινες, ὦ φίλοι, ἔλεγον, ἀπὸ τοῦ ἡμε- τέρου γένους, ὁμολογοῦντες αὐτὸν Χριστὸν εἶναι, ἄνθρωπον δὲ ἐξ ἀν- θρώπων γενόμενον ἀποφαινόμενοι, οἷς οὐ συντίθεμαι, οὐδ᾽ ἂν πλεῖ- στοι ταῦτά μοι δοξάσαντες εἴποιεν, ἐπειδὴ οὐκ ἀνθρωπείοις διδάγ- μασι κεκελεύσμεθα ὑπ᾽ αὐτοῦ τοῦ Χριστοῦ πείθεσθαι, ἀλλὰ τοῖς διὰ τῶν μακαρίων προφητῶν κηρυχθεῖσι καὶ δι᾽ αὐτοῦ διδαχθεῖ- σι· κἀγὼ ὁ Τρύφων, ἐμοί μοι δοκεῖσιν οἱ λέγοντες ἄνθρωπον γε- γονέναι αὐτὸν καὶ κατ᾿ ἐκλογὴν κεχρῖσθαι, καὶ χριστὸν γεγονέναι πι- θανώτερον ὑμῶν λέγειν τῶν ταῦτα ἅπερ φὴς λεγόντων. Rur- sum alibi Tryphon ita loquitur: καὶ γυμνώσατε αὐτὰ ἑκάστοις λέγοντες αἰδεῖσθαι ὀφείλετε καὶ μᾶλλον ἄνθρωπον ἐξ ἀνθρώπων γενόμενον (male coitu legomeno, λέγειν τοῦ Ἰησοῦ τοῦτον καὶ ἐὰν ἀποδείκνυτε ἀπὸ τῶν γραφῶν ὅτι αὐτός ἐστιν ὁ Χριστὸς, διὰ τὸ ἐννόμως καὶ τελείως πολιτεύεσθαι αὐτὸν καταξιωθῆναι τοῦ ἐκλεχθῆ- ναι εἰς χριστόν. Quæ eo libentius adduxi, quod multum perti eant ad recte intelligendum errorem Ebionis: & si- mul usum vocis ἐκλέγειν longe alium fuisse illis temporibus quam nunc putatur, ostendant.

## 23:38
Verse 38.

ἐπιγραφὴ] See at Matthew.

VI. The conversion of the thief.

Latin:

Vers. 38.

ἐπιγραφὴ] Vide ad Matthæum.

VI. Latronis conversio.

## 23:40
Verse 40.

οὐδὲ φοβῇ σὺ τὸν Θεὸν] As if he were to say: It is less surprising that those Jews, secure in their position, behave so cruelly and impiously, but do you also wish to imitate their impiety? He says well φοβῇ τὸν Θεὸν, because he who mocks the dying man despises God.

ὅτι ἐν τῷ αὐτῷ κρίματι εἶ] He said κρίμα in a figurative sense for the punishment which the thieves had in common with Christ, although with unequal merits, as is immediately added by way of correction. This word is used in a similar manner in Matt. XXIII. 14, Mark XII. 40, above c. XX. 47, below c. XXIV. 20, Rom. XIII. 1, 1 Cor. XI. 29.

Latin:

Vers. 40.

οὐδὲ φοβῇ σὺ τὸν Θεὸν] Quasi dicat: Judæos illos secure edita res tam crudeliter atque impie se gerere minus mi- rum est, sed tebine etiam libet eorum impietatem imitari? Bene autem dicit φοβῇ τὸν Θεὸν, quia qui mitens insultat eum contemnit.

ὅτι ἐν τῷ αὐτῷ κρίματι εἶ] κρίμα dixit μετατυπικῶς pro sup- plicio quod latrones habebant cum Christo commune, quanquam disparibus meritis, ut statim κατ᾿ ἐπανόρθωσιν subjicitur. Usurpatur similem in modum vox ista Matth. XXIII. 14. Mar. & XII. 40. supra c. XX. 47. infra c. XXIV. 20. Rom. XIII. 1. Cor. XI. 29.

## 23:41
Vers 41 ἡμεῖς μὲν δικαίως] It is a great sign of repentance to acquiesce in one's own punishment, Lev. XXVI. 41. Another follows, to correct the sinner and defend the oppressed: these were the fruits worthy of repentance.

οὐδὲν ἄτοπον ἔπραξε] From this it is clear that this thief had understood much about the affairs of Jesus: partly, as is credible, before he was captured, and partly in the praetorium itself: but ἄτοπον is αἰσχρὸν: which two things Plato joins somewhere. A certain ancient expositor had explained it as πονηρὸν, which is read in the text of certain books.

Latin:

Vers 41 ἡμεῖς μὲν δικαίως] Magnum est pœnitentiæ signum in pœna sua acquiescere, Lev. XXVI. 41. Accedit & alterum, corrigere peccantem & tueri oppressum: hi e- rant fructus pœnitentiam decentes.

οὐδὲν ἄτοπον ἔπραξε] Hinc liquet latronem hunc multa de rebus Jesu intellexisse: partim, ut credibile est, antequam caperetur, partim in ipso prætorio: ἄτοπον autem est αἰσχρὸν: quæ duo conjungit alicubi Plato. Vetus quidam explicator exposuerat πονηρὸν, quod in quorundam librorum textu le- gitur.

## 23:42
Vers. 42.

Μνήσθητί μου, κύριε, ὅταν ἔλθῃς ἐν τῇ βασιλείᾳ σου] He had heard, as is credible, Jesus professing that a kingdom was owed to him, but not of this world: his great patience in bearing pains, his gentleness toward enemies, and perhaps also certain signs which had then begun to appear, gave assurance to his words: or especially some new and unusual efficacy of divine power, memorable as an example to all ages, stirred this thief to believe a thing most remote from the senses: so that in him shines forth a certain image of that extraordinary and sudden calling which happened to many nations in the age of the Apostles: concerning which matter see what was said above in cap. XIV. 23. I do not think that ἔρχεσθαι ἐν βασιλείᾳ is anything other than ἔρχεσθαι εἰς βασιλείαν, as those are wont to be interchanged among writers. The sense is: when you have attained the possession of that kingdom promised to you by God. Nor indeed does he demand for himself great honors in that kingdom: but mindful of his own unworthiness, he asks only this, that he would be pleased to be mindful of him, knowing it to be royal to do good to others.

Latin:

Vers. 42.

Μνήσθητί μου, κύριε, ὅταν ἔλθῃς ἐν τῇ βασιλείᾳ σου] Audie- rat, ut credibile est, profitentem Jesum fit iregnum debe- ri, sed non hujus mundi: magra ejus in ferendis doloribus patiensia, mansuetudo erga inimicos, forte & signa quæ dam quæ apparere tunc cœperant, dictis ejus fidem conci- liabant: seu præcipue nova atque insolita quædam divinæ virtutis efficacia in exemplum omnibus fæculis memorabi- le, latronem hunc ad credendam rem a sensibus remotissi- mam excitavit: ita ut in ipso imago quædam eluceat ex- traordinariæ illius ac subitæ vocationis quæ Apostolorum sæculo multis gentibus contigit: qua de re vide quæ supra dicta sunt cap. XIV. 23. Non puto aliud esse ἔρχεσθαι ἐν βασιλείᾳ quam ἔρχεσθαι εἰς βασιλείαν, ut solent illa commutari apud scriptores. Sensus est: cum regni illius tibi a Deo promissi possessionem fueris adeptus. Neque vero magnos in eo regno honores sibi postulat: sed indignitatis suæ memor hoc tantum rogat, sui ut memor esse velit, sciens regium esse, aliis benefacere.

## 23:43
Vers. 43. ἀμὴν ἀμὴν λέγω σοι] Christ shows that he is about to say something great.

σήμερον] They have done very badly who have either joined this word with λέγω (which the Syriac openly disapproves) or have interpreted σήμερον as after the resurrection. Christ promises more than was asked: you ask, he says, that I might one day be mindful of you when I have received possession of the kingdom; I will not defer your prayers for so long: but I will present to you a part and the first-fruits of the hoped-for happiness within this very day: die secure, from death divine consolations await you immediately. Moreover, that 'today' is emphatic and is wont to be added to the mention of benefits, as in Jer. I. 10.

μετ᾿ ἐμοῦ ἔσῃ ἐν τῷ παραδείσῳ] There is no doubt that Christ spoke in the way he knew was understood by the thief: παράδεισος is a word, as Pollux truly said, of Persian origin, although the Hebrews also use it, as in Eccl. II. 5, Neh. II. But the Greeks by usage have made this word their own. Cicero, following Xenophon, translates it as an enclosed and diligently planted field: Gellius as a vivarium: the LXX Interpreters translate the Hebrew גן thus elsewhere, as well as in the history of the creation of the world, whence it came about that by a certain special right παράδεισος is called by the Hellenists, and even by Philo, that blessed garden in which God had placed Adam. Afterwards, when the situation demands it, those times—which, as indicated later, were once destined to come—began to be called more closely and distinctly for our use, the happiness after this mortal life, or especially the state of pious minds separated from the body and awaiting the resurrection, by the term used by the Hebrews גן עדן, as the word occurs frequently in this sense in the Talmudic writings. Hence those εὐφημίαι concerning the dead, תהי נפשו בגן עדן, "Let his soul be in the Garden of Eden," and that, כשתהרה ההא צרורו בגן עדן, "May his soul be placed in the Garden of Eden." Indeed, in the customary prayers at the time of death: "May he have a part in Paradise, and also in that future age." And in another formula: "May his soul rest, and may his sleep be in peace, until the comforter comes, who is to bring peace to those sleeping for ages in Hebron. Open the gates of Paradise to him and say peace: Come, you who guard the treasures of Paradise." Thus and in this way Jachiades distinguishes Eden from the state of the resurrection, Dan. VIII. 14. and at the end of the book. Sometimes they call it the lower paradise, because heaven is the upper paradise. To see this, among other things, look at the passage concerning the Essenes in the Salmanticensis. The Hellenists also used παράδεισον with the same meaning: and certain Hebrews used פרדס, which word the Arabic translator also uses in Hebr. XI. 8, dealing with the translation of Enoch. It is not difficult to conjecture the reason for the appellation: for because that place granted to Adam had abounded in all delights, by that likeness they wished to indicate the joyful tranquility of souls: for they interpreted that very garden of Adam συμβολικῶς (symbolically) in that manner. Philo: κατὰ δὲ τὸ θεῖον παράδεισον ἐμψυχῶν, λογικὰ τὰ φυτὰ πάντ᾿ εἶναι συμβέβηκεν, καρπὸν φέροντα τὰς ἀρετὰς, ζωῆς τε ἀπονοίας καὶ ἀφθαρσίας, καὶ πάνθ᾿ ὅ τι ταύτης ὁμοιότροπον (But in the divine paradise of souls, it happens that all the plants are rational, bearing as fruit the virtues, and the contemplation of life and immortality, and everything that is of a similar nature to this). Alibi: λαμβάνοιμεν ἂν τὰς ἀρχὰς, ὃ γενικὰ ἄρετὰ ἀπὸ τῆς ἐδέμ, τῆς τοῦ Θεοῦ σοφίας ἦ χαίρει καὶ γάννυται καὶ τρυφᾷ ἐπὶ μόνῃ τῷ πατρὶ αὐτῆς ἀγαλλομένη καὶ σεμνυνομένη Θεῷ. Rursum alio loco: λέγοιτ᾿ ἂν ἐπ᾿ ὄντων παραδείσῳ φυτὰ εἶναι μηδὲν ἐοικότα τοῖς παρ᾿ ἡμῖν, ἀλλὰ ζωῆς, ἀθανασίας, γνώσεως. Negari ergo non potest quin latro, utpote Judæus, audito nomine גן עדן, additis præsertim designatione temporis, hodie, morte jam imminente, statum illum intellexerit, in quo Abrahami, Isaaci & Jacobi animas esse omnibus Judæis erat persuasum: quasi diceret Christus, non tantum olim cum regnum meum suum accepero, plenitudinem tui ero memor, sed jam nunc magna & ima solatia tibi repræsentabo. Nec sine gravi causa expressum illud, hodie. For the Jews thought that the souls of not just anyone were immediately received into the happy paradise, but only those which departed from this life well purified, πνεύματα δικαίων τετελειωμένων, as the author to the Hebrews speaks in chapter XII. 23. Compare what we have said on Matthew XII. 3. Nor do I think that what is in 2 Cor. XII. 4 should be interpreted otherwise, so that Paul says that those most perfect joys after the resurrection, which are called by the name of the third, that is, the supramundane heaven, were first shown to him by God: and then, lest so long an expectation should torment his soul, also the consolations granted to the pious in the intermediate time, which the Hebrews call גן עדן, the κατάπαυσιν τῷ παραδείσου. We have heard how παράκλησιν was said of the future, that Lazarus was παρακαλεῖσθαι. Nor do I see why what is in the Apocalypse should be taken otherwise: τῷ νικῶντι δώσω αὐτῷ φαγεῖν ἐκ τοῦ ξύλου τῆς ζωῆς, ὅ ἐστιν ἐν μέσῳ τοῦ παραδείσου τοῦ Θεοῦ: especially since Philo also, from the ancient discipline of the Jews, τὸ Let the tree of life be interpreted as the greatest of virtues, piety, through which the soul is made immortal: so that to eat from that tree is to enjoy the happy conscience of right actions: which the same Apocalypse calls being clothed in white robes: and for the sake of explanation it adds, that their works follow them. Nor did the Hebrews use the name of paradise only to express these joys, but even under the image of a garden, they proposed the thing itself to common minds, which could scarcely grasp intelligible things except under the figure of sensible things. Thus Josephus, according to the opinion of the Essenes, calls it a place not burdened by rains or snows or heat, but which a mild Zephyr, always blowing from the ocean, refreshes. Similarly, Justin in his dialogue with Trypho says that the souls of the pious remain in a better place. Tertullian, following the same thing, in the place where he shows that divine truth has been adulterated by the fables of the Greeks: Even if we name paradise, he says, a place of divine amenity destined for the receiving of the spirits of the saints, separated from the knowledge of the common world by a certain wall of that fiery zone, the Elysian fields have occupied the faith. With which it sufficiently agrees that which has been handed down by Diodorus Siculus, that those things which are narrated concerning Hades, came into Greece from the barbarians. Nor is it unworthy of note that the tree of life is mentioned twice in the Apocalypse, but the tree of the knowledge of good and evil nowhere, because the tree of the knowledge of good and evil was, as Philo explains, a σύμβολον of τῆς μέσης φρονήσεως, namely that prudence which is occupied with the things of this age, which it is indeed permitted to use, as is signified by taste and smell, but not to feed upon, that is, to enjoy: for a mind devoted to that pursuit cannot devote as much time as is sufficient to piety: which is shown to us under a figure by the sin of Adam, as Solomon explains in Eccl. VII. 29. τᾶτο ἕυρον ὃ ἐποίησεν ὁ Θεὸς τ' ἄνθρωπον εὐθῆ κὴ ἀυτοὶ ἐζήτησαν λογισμὸς πολλὲς. These cares and distractions from piety will clearly cease ἐν τῷ παραδείσῳ τῷ νοητῷ. Those who added κατέβη εἰς ᾅδε to the symbol of the Christian faith could best defend it with these words of Christ. For if the soul of Christ was ἐν παραδείσῳ, it follows that it was ἐν ᾅδε. For just as the words paradise and Gehenna signify a distinct lot of the good and the bad, so Hades commonly designates the state of souls separated from the body, and is opposed both to this life and to the resurrection, in the way that the sacred scriptures also use Sheol: for Jacob speaks thus: For I shall go down to my son mourning into Sheol; in Greek: that I shall go down to my son mourning into Hades; which cannot be understood of the sepulcher of the body, because Jacob thought his son was not buried, but torn to pieces by wild beasts. Concerning the word Hades we have produced other testimonies of Josephus, Sophocles, Diphilus, and others, but also he who wrote the poems under the title of the Sibyllines in Greek, a man undoubtedly Christian, uses the word Hades in such a way that he derives it from the name of the first parent: nor should the word to descend offend us, for the Greek language had received it to signify the condition of separated souls, for no other reason than that just as the body, after it descends into the sepulcher, is no longer seen, so also the soul having slipped out of the body: wherefore Josephus also says that rewards no less than punishments happen to souls under the earth, which he explains elsewhere as in Hades. In vain, therefore, does Augustine torture himself here, asking how Christ could be at the same time in the underworld, that is, in Hades and in paradise: since the one is included under the other. Nor indeed was the mention of this matter in the symbol superfluous. For since there were various opinions among the pagans concerning the state of souls after this life, it was relevant to the matter that men be taught by the example of Christ that the soul of the dead subsists, that is, that souls are not extinguished with the bodies but are preserved in inconspicuous places. But what we have said concerning the joys of paradise, according to the opinion of the ancients, is to be understood, as I also warned above at chapter XVI, in such a way that they are believed to be great, yet not full: for the fullness of the promises is to be expected in the resurrection, which seems to me to be wisely explained by the writer of the responses to the orthodox, question 76. The question is thus: If before the resurrection there is no recompense of works, what benefit has accrued to the thief before his soul was introduced into paradise, and especially since paradise is sensible, and the essence of the soul is also sensible. He answers: The benefit that accrued to the thief who entered into paradise was to learn by works the profit of faith, through which he was deemed worthy of the gathering of the saints, in which he is kept until the day of the resurrection and recompense, and he has the perception of paradise according to what is called nominal perception, according to which souls see both themselves and the things beneath them. To that which Christ says here with me, Paul seems to allude when he says that he has a desire to depart and to be with Christ, Phil. 1:23. At the same time, however, indicating that just as now after the ascension into the palace of heaven the glory of Christ is greater than it was in the middle time between death and resurrection, so also the joy of those who, having followed Christ, meet death, is increased, and according to the measure and capacity of souls separated from the body they become partakers of the master's happiness: which Theophylact explains here with a not inconvenient similitude. But the ancient Christians were not accustomed to call this state or place of the middle time by the name of heaven, which you may gather even from Justin, who, disputing with Trypho, among other opinions of those who err, also recounts this: that there is no resurrection of the dead, but that as soon as they die their souls are taken up into heaven. The divine Apocalypse describes this state thus: Therefore they are before the throne of God and serve him day and night in his temple, and he who sits upon the throne will dwell over them: within which limits modestly containing ourselves, we have no need to penetrate into those things which are disputed more curiously on this matter between the Greeks and the Latins.

We shall not here contend about the origin of the word παράδεισος, which Pollux assigns to the Persian, and Grotius after him; which the Hebrews in Neh. II. 8, Eccl. II. 5, and the Greeks also used, when the LXX thus translate the word גן, especially in the history of creation, where it treats of the garden of pleasure granted to Adam; which is so called specifically by the Hellenists and Philo. Grotius observes, however, especially that after the times of Ezra, the happiness after this mortal life, but especially the state of pious minds separated from the body and awaiting the resurrection, was called by the Hebrews גן עדן, and that these words frequently occur in this sense in the Talmudic writings, and that thence those euphemisms are derived concerning the dead, תהי נפשו בגן עדן, let his soul be in the garden of Eden, and similar ones. This we readily admit: but we deny what Grotius asserts, that things to happen after this mortal life were formerly indicated only more obscurely and that they began to be called by proper and distinct names only after Ezra: we deny that the happiness after this life and the state of pious minds separated from the body then first began to be known or to be called by peculiar names. But these things are not of this place. Those Grotian points, however, are correct: It cannot be denied that the thief, being a Jew, upon hearing the name גן עדן, especially with the addition of the designation of time, today, with death now imminent, understood that state in which it was believed by all Jews that the souls of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob were: as if Christ were saying, Not only will I be mindful of you one day, when my kingdom shall receive its fullness, but even now I will present to you great and immense consolations.

But as to what he adds, that the Jews thought that the souls of not just any (believers) were immediately received into the happy paradise, but only those who departed from this life well purified, he could not prove that either from the Holy Scriptures (Heb. XII. 23, the just made perfect are opposed to the imperfectly just by habitual or inherent justice, not to those who are such after this life, but who are such in this age) nor from other documents from the Jews who were rightly wise: whatever may be the case regarding the Pharisees or other sects. That distinction also, which he treats here concerning the passage 2. Cor. XII. 4, between the third heaven and paradise, that by the former the most perfect joys after the resurrection are denoted, but in paradise the consolations granted to the pious in the intermediate time, rests on no foundation: since the Apostle rather holds paradise and the third heaven as synonyms, and he was not caught up first into the third heaven and then into paradise, but in one and the same ἁρπαγμῷ (rapture) into the third heaven and into paradise, and in paradise he perceived not only consolations or joys of an inferior order or condition, but ἄῤῥητα ῥήματα ἃ ὀυκ ἐξὸν ἀνθρώπῳ λαλῆσαι (unspeakable words which it is not lawful for a man to utter) 2 Cor. XII. 4. By which words it is certain that truly heavenly goods are described. Cf. 1 Cor. II. 9. Nor is anything else promised through the happiness of paradise in Rev. II. 7 to him who overcomes by faith, namely that the Lord is about to give him φαγεῖν ἐκ τῦ ξύλου τῆς ζωῆς, ὅ ἐστιν ἐν μέσῳ τῦ παραδείσου τῦ Θεῦ (to eat of the tree of life, which is in the midst of the paradise of God), than heavenly beatitude, which is described in the same way in Rev. XXII. 2, and therefore to eat that is not merely to enjoy a happy conscience of good deeds. Furthermore, that the same Grotius says that the Apocalypse calls being clothed in white robes, and for the sake of explanation adds that their works follow them, in that, memory and the true sense of Scripture escape him. For that concerning white stoles is found in Rev. VII. 14, where there is nothing about works following, which is read in ch. XIV. 14 concerning those who die in the Lord, but without any mention of white robes. Nor do those white robes only denote a happy conscience, but they are a sign of victory, happiness, and heavenly joy, which is described more fully there: For they are also said to be before the throne of God, and to serve Him day and night in His temple, and whatever other things are added there, certainly not for the designation of an inferior rather than a heavenly happiness, but so that the blessedness itself and heavenly happiness may be expressed who die in the Lord are called μακάριοι absolutely, Ap. XIX. 13. Compare Acts XXI. 3, where heavenly happiness is described for the same reason.

Finally, Grotius seeks in vain the foundation of this view of his concerning Paradise as a state of intermediate happiness in those words of the Apostles' Creed: κατέβη εἰς ᾅδε; for those do not treat of Christ's soul, but of Christ as a whole, who, having been made alive, or after the making alive of soul and body, descended into the lower regions, demonstrating Himself to be the victor and triumpher over hell to the damned spirits, τοῖς ἐν φυλακῇ, who were shut up in the infernal prison, 1 Pet. III. 18, 19. And that hypothesis and Grotian explanation is discordant, that Christ's soul, which was in Paradise, was ἐν ᾅδη; as if ᾅδης commonly designates the state of souls separated from the body: which hypothesis we have already examined at Luke XVI: and Grotius proves nothing here from those words of the Patriarch Jacob, Gen. XXXVII. 31, ὅτι καταβήσομαι πρὸς ἲυἱόν μου πενθῶν ἐν ᾅδε. For although Jacob believed that his son was not buried but torn by wild beasts, he could nevertheless use this phrase concerning his own descent into the grave, not so that the same thing might be designated, because his body is to be buried or entombed for a like reason, but because it is to be turned into dust, as Ecclesiastes speaks, ch. XII. 7. Just as the son of Sirach testifies concerning all men, that they at length return to the earth and are buried, which is the mother of us all. For although very many are never buried, but are consumed by fire, or devoured by wild beasts, birds, fishes, or even by barbarous men, yet to παντὶ ἀνθρώπῳ, to every man, he assigns ταφὴν εἰς μητέραν πάντων, burial into the mother of all, ch. XLI; and Jeremiah attributes to Jehoiakim the BURIAL of an ass, ch. XXII. 19, although he was not to be placed in any sepulcher.

But although, for the reason Grotius has wished thus far, the joys of Paradise and heavenly joys are not to be distinguished, we do not deny that the state of separated souls differs from the state of consummated happiness, to which the elect will be admitted after the resurrection, however perhaps no one may be able to explain that distinction solidly: and thus far we believe with Grotius that there are great rewards for separated souls, yet not full ones: provided only that separated souls are not excluded from heavenly blessedness: from which the ancient Greeks certainly did not exclude them, whatever may be the case with more recent ones: For Ignatius, writing to the Romans about his martyrdom, says, "Suffer me to behold the pure light." Gregory Nazianzen teaches concerning Gorgonia that she enjoys with the angels the purest illumination of the Trinity, by which it offers itself to be contemplated in its entirety: according to Epiphanius, heresy LXXVIII. against the Antidicomarianites: to enjoy the saints in blessedness is to be in holy mansions, a dance with the angels, a diet in the heavens, glory in incomparable honor, and a perpetual prize in Christ Jesus our Lord: Theodoret, to the Greeks on the Martyrs, book IX, says that their seat is in heaven, and that they are distinguished by eternal crowns. Theophylact openly contradicts Grotius in this place: It must be said that Paradise and the kingdom of heaven are the same: For the thief is in Paradise and in the kingdom, otherwise he would not enjoy the perfect participation of goods.

Finally, although Grotius wishes to appear as if he does not want to penetrate into those things which are disputed more curiously among the (modern) Greeks and Latins concerning this matter, the thing itself nevertheless teaches that the Grotian opinion is not far removed from the sentiment of the more recent Greeks and Armenians, that indeed all souls, however much of the saints, are kept until the last day of judgment in certain hidden receptacles, where they neither see God nor can be called blessed, except in hope: which, however, was not undeservedly reprobated by Innocent III, C. Apostolico X. de Presbytero non baptizato, and in the Council of Florence, session XXV: however much John XXII made the same error his own in the year 1352 and sanctioned it at the University of Paris.

Latin:

Vers. 43. ἀμὴν ἀμὴν λέγω σοι] Ostendit Christus se magni aliquid dicturum.

σήμερον] Pessime fecerunt qui hanc vocem aut cum λέγω conjunxerunt (quod aperte improbat Syrus) aut interpretati sunt σήμερον post resurrectionem. Christus plus promittit quam erat rogatus: rogas inquit, ut olim tui sim memor cum regni possessionem accepero; ego tam diu non differam tua vota: sed partem & primitias speratæ felicitatis tibi intra hunc ipsum diem repræsentabo: morere securus, a morte statim te divina solatia exspectant. Est autem illud hodie ἔμφατικὸν & solet beneficiorum mentioni adjici, ut Jer. I. 10.

μετ᾿ ἐμοῦ ἔσῃ ἐν τῷ παραδείσῳ] Dubium non est quin Christus ita locutus sit quomodo sciebat a latrone intelligi: παράδεισος vox est, ut Pollux vere dixit, Persica, quanquam & Hebræi usurpant, ut Eccl. II. 5. Neh. II. Sed Græci usu hanc vocem suam fecerunt. Cicero apud Xenophontem vertit agrum consseptum ac diligenter consitum: Vivarium Gellius: LXX. Interpretes Hebræum גן ita vertunt alibi, tum in κοσμογονίας historia, unde factum est, ut jure quodam præcipuo παράδεισος vocetur Hellenistis, etiam Philoni, beatus ille hortus in quo Adamum Deus collocarat. Postea ea tempora, cum res postulat, hanc mortalem eventuræ, poscurius olim indicatæ, propius distinctiusque nobis usui appellari cœperunt, felicitas post hanc vitam mortalem, seu præcipue piarum mentium ac corpore separatarum & resurrectionem exspectantium status, voce usitata Hebræis גן עדן ut voce hoc sensu in Thalmudicis scriptis frequentes occurrunt. Hinc illæ εὐφημίαι de mortuo תהי נפשו בגן עדן Sit anima ejus in horto Eden: & illud כשתהרה ההא צרורו בגן עדן animus ejus collocatus esto in horto Eden. Quin solentibus precibus in tempore mortis: partem habeat in Paradiso, nec non in futuro isto seculo: Et in alia formula: Requiescat anima ejus & sit dormitio ejus in pace, donec veniat consolator, qui laus audire pacem pastum seculis dormientium in Hebron. Portas Paradisi aperite ei & dicite pacem: Venite qui custoditis thesauros Paradisi. Sic & ita tum Edenis a statu resurrectionis distinguit Jachiades, Dan. VIII. 14. & in fine libri. Interdum vocant paradisum inferiorem, quia cœlum paradisus superior. Videre hoc est inter alia loco de Esseis apud Salmanticensem. Hellenistæ quoque παράδεισον eodem significatu dixere: & Hebræi quidam פרדס, qua voce & Arabs interpres utitur Hebr. XI. 8. agens de translatione Enochi. Causam appellationis conjectare non est difficile: nam quia locus ille Adamo concessus deliciis omnibus abundaverat, ea similitudine animarum lætam tranquillitatem voluerunt indicatam: nam & ipsum illum Adami hortum συμβολικῶς eum in modum interpretabantur. Philo: κατὰ δὲ τὸ θεῖον παράδεισον ἐμψυχῶν, λογικὰ τὰ φυτὰ πάντ᾿ εἶναι συμβέβηκεν, καρπὸν φέροντα τὰς ἀρετὰς, ζωῆς τε ἀπονοίας καὶ ἀφθαρσίας, καὶ πάνθ᾿ ὅ τι ταύτης ὁμοιότροπον. Alibi: λαμβάνοιμεν ἂν τὰς ἀρχὰς, ὃ γενικὰ ἄρετὰ ἀπὸ τῆς ἐδέμ, τῆς τοῦ Θεοῦ σοφίας ἦ χαίρει καὶ γάννυται καὶ τρυφᾷ ἐπὶ μόνῃ τῷ πατρὶ αὐτῆς ἀγαλλομένη καὶ σεμνυνομένη Θεῷ. Rursum alio loco: λέγοιτ᾿ ἂν ἐπ᾿ ὄντων παραδείσῳ φυτὰ εἶναι μηδὲν ἐοικότα τοῖς παρ᾿ ἡμῖν, ἀλλὰ ζωῆς, ἀθανασίας, γνώσεως. Negari ergo non potest quin latro, utpote Judæus, audito nomine גן עדן, additis præsertim designatione temporis, hodie, morte jam imminente, statum illum intellexerit, in quo Abrahami, Isaaci & Jacobi animas esse omnibus Judæis erat persuasum: quasi diceret Christus, non tantum olim cum regnum meum suum accepero, plenitudinem tui ero memor, sed jam nunc magna & ima solatia tibi repræsentabo. Nec sine gravi causa expressum illud, hodie. Censebant enim Judæi non quorumvis animas statim in felicem paradisi statim recipi, sed eas demum, quæ bene purgatæ ex hac vita excederent, πνεύματα δικαίων τετελειωμένων, ut loquitur auctor ad Hebræos cap. XII. 23. Confer quæ diximus ad Matthæum XII. 3.. Neque aliter interpretandum puto quod est 2. Cor. XII. 4. ut Paulus dicat sibi a Deo primum ostensa illa perfectissima gaudia post resurrectionem, quæ tertii id est supramundani cœli nomine appellantur: deinde vero, ne tam longa exspectati animum cruciaret, etiam solatia piis medio tempore concessa quæ Hebræi vocant גן עדן κατάπαυσιν τῷ παραδείσου. Audivimus παράκλησιν quomodo futura dictum est Lazarum παρακαλεῖσθαι. Neque video cur aliter accipi debeat quod est in Apocalypsi: τῷ νικῶντι δώσω αὐτῷ φαγεῖν ἐκ τοῦ ξύλου τῆς ζωῆς, ὅ ἐστιν ἐν μέσῳ τοῦ παραδείσου τοῦ Θεοῦ: Præsertim cum & Philo ex Judæorum vetere disciplina τὸ δένδρον τῆς ζωῆς interpretetur τὴν μεγίςην τῶν ἀρετῶν θεοσέ- βειαν, δι' ἧς ἀθανατίζεται ἡ ψυχή: ut ex arbore illa vesci sit frui læta recte factorum conscientia: quod eadem Apoca- lypsis vocat indui candidis vestibus: & explicationis causa addit, opera ipsorum ipsos sequi. Neq; nomen tantum pa- radisi usurpabant Hebræi ad hæc gaudia exprimenda, sed et- iam sub horti imagine, rem ipsam proponebant plebejis in- geniis vix capientibus τὰ νοητὰ nisi sub figura τῶν αἰσθητῶν. Ita Iosephus ex Essenorum sententia vocat χῶρον ὄυτε ὄμβροις ὄυτε νιφετοῖς ὄυτε κάυμασι βαρυνόμενον, ἀλλ' ὃν ἐξ ὠκεανᾶ πραὺς ἀεὶ Ζέφυρος ἐπιπνέων ἀναψύχει. Similiter Iustinus colloquio cum Tryphone ait τὰς τῶν εὐσεβῶν ψυχὰς ἐν κρείττονι ποι χώρῳ μένειν. Tertullianus idipsum sequens, quo loco osten- dit veritatem divinam Græcorum fabulis adulteratam: Etsi paradisum nominemus, inquit, locum divine amœnitatis reci- piendis sanctorum spiritibus destinatum, maceria quadam ignee illius Zonæ à notitia orbis communis segregatum, Elysii campi fi- dem occupaverunt. Quicum satis convenit quod à Diodoro Siculo est proditum, ea quæ περὶ ᾅδε narrantur, à barbaris in Græciam pervenisse. Ne hoc quidem notatu indignum bis in Apocalypsi nominari vitæ arborem, nusquam vero arborem scientiæ boni & mali, quia arbor scientiæ boni & mali σύμβολον erat Philone explicante τῆς μέσης φρονήσεως, ejus scilicet prudentiæ quæ circa res hujus ævi occupata est, qua uti quidem licet, ut per gustum & olfactum significatur, at vesci, id est frui, non licet: nam animus ei studio deditus pietati quantum satis est vacare non potest: quod nobis Ada- mi peccato sub figurare ostenditur, explicante Salomone Ec- cles. VII. 29. τᾶτο ἕυρον ὃ ἐποίησεν ὁ Θεὸς τ' ἄνθρωπον εὐθῆ κὴ ἀυτοὶ ἐζήτησαν λογισμὸς πολλὲς. Hæ curæ atque avocamenta pietatis plane cessabunt ἐν τῷ παραδείσῳ τῷ νοητῷ. Qui sym- bolo fidei Christianæ adscripserunt κατέβη εἰς ᾅδε his Chri- sti verbis optime id tueri potuerunt. Nam si Christi anima fuit ἐν παραδείσῳ, sequitur eam fuisse ἐν ᾅδε. Nam sicut παραδείσε & γεέννης vocabula distinctam bonorum malo- rumq; sortem significant, ita ᾅδης communiter designat sta- tum animarum a corpore separatarum, opponiturque tum vitæ huic tum resurrectioni, quomodo & שאול usurpant sacræ literæ: nam Jacob ita loquitur כי־ארד אל־בני אבל שאלה : Græce ὅτι καταβήσομαι πρὸς τ' υἱόν με πενθῶν εἰς ᾅδε; quod de corporis sepulchro intelligi non potest, quia filium non sepultum, sed à feris laniatum Jacob existima- bat. De voce ᾅδε produximus alia testimonia Josephi, So- phoclis, Diphili & aliorum, sed & qui titulo Sibyllinorum carmina Græce scripsit, homo haud dubie Christianus, ita utitur voce ᾅδε, ut quam derivat à primi parentis nomine: neq; offendere nos debet verbum καταβαίνειν, id enim Græ- cus sermo ad animorum separatorum conditionem signifi- candam receperat, non alia de causa, nisi quod quemadmo- dum corpus, postquam in sepulchrum descendit, amplius non conspicitur, ita & animus è corpore elapsus: quare & Josephus præmia non minus quam pœnas animis ait con- tingere ὑπὸ χθόνος, quod alibi explicat καθ' ᾅδε. Frustra ergo hic se cruciat Augustinus, quærens quomodo Christus eo- dem tempore esse potuerit in inferno, id est, ἐν ᾅδε & in pa- radiso: cum alterum sub altero comprehendatur. Neq; ve- ro supervacua fuit in symbolo hujus rei mentio. Nam cum inter paganos variæ essent de animarum statu post hanc vi- tam sententiæ, ad rem pertinebat Christi exemplo doceri homines ὡς ὑφίςηκεν ἡ ψυχὴ τ' ἀποθανόντων, id est, non ex- stinqui cum corporibus animas sed asservari in locis incon- spicuis. Quæ vero de gaudiis paradisi diximus, ex veterum sententia ita intelligenda supra quoq; ad caput XVI. monui- mus, ut magna quidem credantur, non tamen plena: nam plenitudo promissionum in resurrectione exspectanda est, quod mihi sapienter videtur explicare scriptor responsio. num ad orthodoxos quæst. LXXVI. Quæstio sic habet: εἰ πρὸ ἀναςάσεως ἐκ ἔςιν ἡ τ' ἔργων ἀνταπόδοσις, ποῖον τῷ λάςη προσγέγονεν ὄφελος πρὸν τᾶν παράδεισον ἀυτᾶ τῆς ψυχῆς εἰ- σαχθείσης καὶ μάλιςα ὁτι ὁ μὲν παράδεισος αἰσθητὸς, καὶ αἰ- σθητὴ δὲ ἐςι τῆς ψυχῆς ἡ ἐσία. Respondet: ὄφελος γέγονε τῷ λῄςῃ εἰς τὸν παράδεισον εἰσελθόντι τὸ ἔργοις μαθεῖν τῆς πίςεως τὸ ὠφέλιμον, δι' ἧς ἠξιώθη Cυναθροισμαῖθ' τ' ἁγίων, ἐν ᾧ φυλάτ- τεται ἕως τῆς ἡμέρας τῆς ἀνατάσεως τε καὶ ἀνταποδόσεως ἰχεῖ τε τᾶ παραδείσε τὴν αἴσθησιν κατὰ τὴν ὀνοματικὴν λεγομένην αἴ- σθησιν, καθ' ἣν ὁρῶσιν αἱ ψυχαὶ ἑαυτάς τε καὶ τὰ ὑπ' ἀυτάς. Ad illud, quod Christus hic dicit μετ' ἐμᾶ, alludere videtur Paulus, cum dicit se ἐπιθυμίαν ἔχειν εἰς τὸ ἀναλῦσαι καὶ σὺν Χρισῷ εἶναι Phil. I. 23. Simul tamen indicans quemadmo- dum nunc post ascensum in cœli regiam major est Christi gloria quam fuit medio tempore inter mortem & resurre- ctionem, ita auctum quoq; gaudium eorum qui Christum sectati mortem obeunt, & pro modo ac captu animorum separatorum à corpore participes fiunt herilis felicitatis: quod hic similitudine non incommoda Theophylactus ex- plicat. Non solebant autem Christiani veteres hunc sive statum sive locum medii temporis cœli nomine appellare, quod vel ex Justino colligas, qui cum Tryphone disputans inter cæteras errantium opiniones & hanc recenset μὴ ὄντων νεκρῶν ἀνάςασιν, ἀλλ' ἅμα τῷ ἀποθνήσκειν τὰς ψυχὰς ἀυτῶν ἀναλαμβάνεσθαι εἰς τὸν ὀυρανὸν. Hunc statum ita describit divi- na Apocalypsis διὰ τῦτο εἰσιν ἐνώπιον τῦ θρόνε τῦ Θεῦ καὶ λατρεύουσιν ἀυτῷ ἡμέρας καὶ νύκτας ἐν τῷ ναῷ ἀυτῦ, καὶ ὁ καθήμε- νος ἐπὶ τῦ θρόνε σκηνώσει ἐπ' ἀυτός: quibus finibus modeste nos continentes nihil necesse habemus penetrare in ea quæ curiosius hac super re inter Græcos & Latinos disputantur.

De origine vocis παράδεισος Persica, quam assi- gnat Pollux, & ex eo Grotius, hic non contende- mus; quam Ebræi Neh. II. 8. Eccl. II. 5. & Græci quo- que usurparunt, quum LXX. ita vertunt vocem גן, imprimis in creationis historia, ubi de horto volu- ptatis Adamo concesso agitur; qui Hellenistis & Phi- loni ita peculiariter vocatur. Observat autem Gro- tius imprimis, quod post Esdræ tempora felicitas post hanc vitam mortalem sed præcipue piarum men- tium à corpore separatarum & resurrectionem expe- ctantium status Ebræis vocatus sit גן עדן, quodq; hæ vo- ces hoc sensu in Thalmudicis scriptis frequenter occur- rant, atq; inde illi εὐφημισμοί sint de mortuis תהי נפשו בגן עדן sit anima ejus in horto Eden & similes. Quod facile admittimus: Negamus autem quod af- serit Grotius, obscurius olim tantum indicatas res post vitam hanc mortalem eventuras & post Esdram de- mum propriis distinctisq; nominibus appellari cœpisse: negamus felicitatem post hanc vitam statumq; piarum mentium à corpore separatarum tunc demum vel co- gnosci cœpisse, vel peculiaribus vocibus nuncupari. Sed hæc non sunt hujus loci. Recte autem habent sese il- la Grotiana: Negari non potest, quin latro, utpote Ju- dæus audito nomine גן עדן, addita præsertim designa- tione temporis, hodie, morte jam imminente, statum il- lum intellexerit, in quo Abrahami, Isaaci & Jacobi ani- mas esse omnibus Judæis erat persuasum: quasi dice- ret Christus, Non tantum olim, cum regnum meum su- am accipiet plenitudinem, tui ero memor, sed jam nunc magna & ingentia solatia tibi repræsentabo.

Quod vero addit, Judæos censuisse non quorumvis (fidelium) animas statim in felicem paradisi recipi, sed eas demum, quæ bene purgatæ ex hac vita cederent, id probare nec è S. literis (Ebr. XII. 23. justi perfe- cti imperfecte justis habituali vel inhærente justi- tia opponuntur non iis qui tales sunt post hanc vi- tam, sed qui tales in hoc seculo) nec ex aliis docu- mentis potuit è Judæis recte sapientibus: quicquid de Pharisæis, aliisve sectis sit. Illa etiam distinctio, quam circa locum 2. Cor. XII. 4. hic tradit inter ter- tium cælum & paradisum, quod per illud perfectissi- ma gaudia post resurrectionem, in paradiso vero sola- tia piis medio tempore concessa notentur, nullo fun- damento nititur: quum Apostolus potius ut συνώ- νυμα habeat paradisum & cælum tertium, nec pri- mum in tertium cælum, deinde vero in paradisum, sed uno eodemq; ἁρπαγμῷ in cœlum tertium & in paradisum abreptus sit, & in paradiso non tan- tum inferioris ordinis aut conditionis sive solatia si- ve gaudia perceperit, sed ἄῤῥητα ῥήματα ἃ ὀυκ ἐξὸν ἀνθρώπῳ λαλῆσαι 2. Cor. XII. 4. Quibus verbis vere cælestia bona describi, certum est. Conf. 1. Cor. II. 9. Neq; aliud per paradisi felicitatem Ap. II. 7. vincenti per fidem pro- mittitur, quod nempe daturus ipsi Dominus sit φα- γεῖν ἐκ τῦ ξύλου τῆς ζωῆς, ὅ ἐστιν ἐν μέσῳ τῦ παραδείσου τῦ Θεῦ, quam cælestis beatitudo, quæ eadem ratione Ap. XXII. 2. de- scripta est, adeoq; vesci illud non est tantum frui la- tæ recte factorum conscientia. Quod porro Grotius i- dem Apocalypsin vocare indui candidis vestibus, & ex- plicationis causa addere, opera ipsorum eos sequi, ait, in eo ipsum fugit memoria, & verus Scripturæ sensus. Nam illud de candidis stolis habetur, Ap. VII. 14. ubi nihil de operibus sequentibus, quod c. XIV. 14. de bea- tis in Domino morientibus legitur, sed nulla mentione facta candidarum vestium. Neq; illæ candidæ vestes tantum notant lætam conscientiam, sed signum sunt victoriæ, felicitatis & lætitiæ cælestis, quæ uberius ibi describitur: Nam dicuntur etiam esse coram throno Dei, eiq; servire dies & noctes in templo ipsius, & quæ alia illic adduntur, non certe ad inferioris quā cœlestis felicitatis designationem, sed ut exprima- tur ipsa beatitudo, & felicitas cœlestis: unde et- iam μακάριοι absolute dicuntur οἱ νεκροὶ, οἱ ἐν κυ- ῥίῳ ἀποθνήσκοντες Ap. XIX. 13. Cons. Act. XXI. 3. ubi eadem ratione cœlestis felicitas describitur.

Denique frustra hujus suæ de Paradiso ceu statu intermediæ felicitatis fundamentum quærit Grotius in illis Symboli Apostolici verbis: κατέβη εἰς ᾅδε; nam illa non de Christi anima, sed de Christo agunt toto, quod ζωοποιηθεὶς seu post ζωοποίησιν anima & corpore descenderit ad inferos victorem se de- monstrans, & triumphatorem inferni spiritibus damnatis τοῖς ἐν φυλακῇ qui carceri infernali con- clusi erant 1. Pet. III. 18. 19. & absona est illa hypo- thesis & explicatio Grotiana, Christi animam, quæ fuit in Paradiso fuisse ἐν ᾅδη; quasi ᾅδης communi- ter designet statum animarum à corpore separata- rum: quam hypothesin ad Luc. XVI. jam expendi- mus: & nequicquam hic probat Grotius ex illis Jacobi Patriarchæ Gen. XXXVII. 31. ὅτι καταβήσο- μαι πρὸς ἲυἱόν μου πενθῶν ἐν ᾅδε. Etsi enim non sepultum filium sed à feris laniatum crederet Jacobus, poterat tamen hac phrasi uti de descensu suo in sepulchrum, non ut designetur eadem, quod parili ratione humandum vel tumulandum sit cor- pus suum, sed quod convertendum in pulverem sit, ut Ecclesiastes loquitur c. XII. 7. Quemadmo- dum de omnibus hominibus Syracides testatur, quod tandem in terram redeant, ac sepeliantur, quæ omnium nostrum mater est. Etsi enim plurimi non sepeliantur unquam, sed igne crementur, à feris, a- vibus, piscibus, aut barbaris etiam hominibus de- vorentur, παντὶ ἀνθρώπῳ omni homini tamen as- signat ταφὴν εἰς μητέραν πάντων c. XLI. & Jeremias Jojakimo tribuit SEPULTURAM asini c. XXII. 19. etsi nullo sepulchro condendus erat.

Quanquam vero ea ratione, uti voluit hactenus Grotius, discriminanda non sint gaudia Paradisi, & cælestia, statum tamen animarum separatarum dif- ferre à statu consummatæ felicitatis, ad quem electi post resurrectionem admittentur, haud abnui- mus, utut forte nemo discrimen illud explicare so- lide queat: adeoque eatenus cum Grotio magna animarum separatarum credimus præmia, non ta- men plena: dum modo non excludantur animæ se- paratæ à beatitudine cælesti: a qua certe eas non ex- clusêre veteres Græci, quicquid sit de recentiori- bus: Nam Ignatius ad Roman. de martyrio suo scribens, sinite, inquit, me puram lucem aspicere. Gregor. Nazianzenus de Gorgonia docet, eam frui cum Angelis purissima illustratione Trinitatis, qua solimenti totam se contemplandam præbeat: secun- dum Epiphanium hæref. LXXVIII. contra Antidi- co-Marianit: sanctorum frui in beatitudine est in mansionibus sanctis, tripudium cum angelis, diæta in cælis, gloria in honore incomparabili, & perpetua bra- beja in Christo Jesu Domino nostro: Theodoret. ad Græcos de Martyr. l. IX. dicit, quod sedes illorum sit in cælo, & quod æternis insigniti sint coronis. Theo- phyl. aperte in h. l. contradicit Grotio: Dicendum est, idem esse Paradisum & regnum cælorum: Nam latro in Paradiso est, ac regno, alioqui non frueretur perfecta bonorum participatione.

Tandem etsi Grotius videri velit, se nolle in ea, quæ inter Græcos (modernos) & Latinos super hac re curiosius disputantur, penetrare, res ipsa tamen docet, quod à recentiorum Græcorum & Armenio- rum sententia, quod nempe animæ omnes, quan- tumvis sanctorum, usq́; ad ultimum judicii diem ser- ventur in quibusdam abditis receptaculis, ubi nec Deum videant, nec beatæ dici possint, nisi in spe, non multum absit Grotiana opinio: quæ vero non im- merito ab Innocentio III. C. Apostolico X. de Presby- tero non baptizato, & in Concil. Florentino sess. XXV. reprobata est: utut Johannes XXII. eundem erró- rem Anno 1352. suum fecerit, & in Universitate Pa- risiensi sanciverit.

## 23:46
V. 46. παραθήσομαι) I approve this reading all the more because it is read in a similar way in the Psalm among the LXX, but it is the future for the present after the manner of the Hebrews. In the Psalm, David, being placed in the highest dangers, commends his life to divine protection, just as Peter also wishes those who suffer according to the will of God to παρατίθεσθαι τὰς ψυχὰς ἑαυτῶν ἐν ἀγαθοποιΐαις. Furthermore, it is to be observed here also how much more exactly those words fit Christ than David. Among David, רוּחַ is life: among Christ, it is the very mind of man, which the Hebrews properly call by that name; furthermore, to lay down is properly the act of him who has dominion over the thing: but Christ ἐξουσίαν εἶχε θεῖναι τὴν ψυχὴν κὶ πάλιν λαβεῖν αὐτήν, as He Himself professes in John. Stephen is a little different, who, about to die, does not use the word for laying down, but asks Jesus, already made Lord of life and death, to be willing to receive, namely into His custody, his spirit. Justin, in his dialogue with Trypho, says that an example was given to us by Christ: ἵνα ήνίκα ἡμεῖς πρὸς τῇ ἐξόδῳ τῦ βίε γινόμεθα τὰ αὐτὰ αἰτῶμεν τὸν Θεὸν ὸ δυνάμενον ἀποστρέψαι πάντα ἀναιδῆ πο- νηρὸν ἄγγελον μὴ λαβέσθαι ἡμῶν τὰς ψυχάς. Compare that of the Hebrew sage, Wisdom III. 1: δικαίων δὲ ψυχαὶ ἐν χειρὶ Θεῦ, κό ὐ μὴ ἅψηται αὐτῶν βάσανος, and what follows.

PART III. The consequence of the death of Christ.

I. The confession of the Centurion.

Latin:

V. 46. παραθήσομαι) Probo hanc lectionem eo magis quia apud LXX. in Psalmo simili modo legitur, sed est more He- bræorum futurum pro præsenti. In Psalmo David summis in periculis constitutus vitam suam divinæ tutelæ commen- dat, quomodo & Petrus 1ὺὲ πάσχοντας κατὰ θέλημα τῦ Θεῦ vult παρατίθεσθαι τὰς ψυχὰς ἑαυτῶν ἐν ἀγαθοποιΐαις. Cæterum & hic observandum est quanto exactius ea verba Christo quam Davidi congruant. Apud Davidem רוּחַ est vita: apud Christum ipsa mens hominis quam Hebræi proprie eo no- mine appellant, deinde deponere ejus est proprie qui domi- nium rei habet: Christus autem ἐξουσίαν εἶχε θεῖναι τὴν ψυχὴν κὶ πάλιν λαβεῖν αὐτήν, ut ipse apud Johannem profitetur. Paulo aliter Stephanus, qui moriturus non deponendi utitur voce, sed Jesum jam factum Dominum vitæ & mortis rogat ut accipere velit, in suam scilicet custodiam, spiritum ipsius, Ju- stinus in colloquio cum Tryphone exemplum nobis dicit à Christo datum: ἵνα ήνίκα ἡμεῖς πρὸς τῇ ἐξόδῳ τῦ βίε γινόμεθα τὰ αὐτὰ αἰτῶμεν τὸν Θεὸν ὸ δυνάμενον ἀποστρέψαι πάντα ἀναιδῆ πο- νηρὸν ἄγγελον μὴ λαβέσθαι ἡμῶν τὰς ψυχάς. Confer illud Hebræi sapientis Sapientiæ III. 1. δικαίων δὲ ψυχαὶ ἐν χειρὶ Θεῦ, κό ὐ μὴ ἅψηται αὐτῶν βάσανος, & quæ sequuntur.

PARS III. Mortis Christi consequentia.

I. Centurionis confessio.

τύπτοντες ἑαυτῶν τὰ στήθη) With their conscience now beginning to be pricked, which the Apostolic sermon later stirred up more. For these were signs of God, showing aversion to the crime and testifying to the innocence of Jesus.

τύπτοντες ἑαυτῶν τὰ στήθη) Incipiente jam pungi conscientia, quam postea Apostolicus sermo magis excitavit. Signa enim erant hęc Dei, facinus aversantis & Jesu innocentiã testantis.

## 23:53
V. 53. ὗ ὐκ ἦν ἐδέπω ἐδεὶς κείμενος) So that no one might later slander that someone else, and not Jesus, had risen.

## 23:54
V. 54. ἡμέρα ἧν παρασκευὴ) The correct reading: for the whole day was called παρασκευὴ in part, as also in Mark 15:45, John 19:31, 47, and in the edict of Augustus in Josephus. However, the following words show that παρασκευὴ is to be understood here more by reason of the Sabbath than of the feast day.

ἐπέφωσκε) Just as ἐπιφαίνειν is said not only of the sun, but also of the moon and other stars, so too is ἐπιφώσκειν, which means the same thing. For this passage, it will be most appropriate to understand the rising of the stars, the indicator of the evening from which the Jews began their civil day. Tertullian in his book on fasts says this about the Jews: They sigh for the authority of the star that lingers. Learned men have also noted that נגה, which the Syriac has here, is accustomed to be attributed to the moon and other stars. However, ἐπέφωσκε is to be taken as ἤμελλε ἐπιφώσκειν. Just as we have had the present for the future elsewhere: for so much time remained that the women, having returned to the city, could buy spices for themselves.

IV. The observation of the women, and their return to the city.

Latin:

V. 54. ἡμέρα ἧν παρασκευὴ) Recta lectio: nam ex parte to- tus dies παρασκευὴ appellabatur, ut & Marci XV. 45. Joh. XIX. 31. 47. & in edicto Augusti apud Josephum. Intelligi autem hic παρασκευὴν magis ratione sabbati quam festæ di- eę sequentia ostendunt.

ἐπέφωσκε) Sicut ἐπιφαίνειν non tantum de Sole, sed & de Luca aliisq; sideribus dicitur, ita & quod idem valet ἐπιφώ- σκειν. Huic loco convenientissimum erit intelligere stel- larum ortum, indicem vesperæ à qua Judæi diem suum civia- lem inchoabant. Tertullianus libro de jejuniis sic de Ju- dæis: Stellæ auctoritatem demorantis suspirant. Notarunt viri eruditi etiam נגה, quod hic habet Syrus, Lunæ aliis- que sideribus tribui solere. Accipiendum autem ἐπέφωσκε pro ἤμελλε ἐπιφώσκειν. Sicut præsentia pro futuro alibi quoq; habuimus: nam tantum temporis supererat, ut in urbem re- versæ mulieres aromata sibi possent comparare.

IV. Mulierum inspectatio, & in urbem reversio.

V. 56. ἡσύχασαν) As if adjured to let the bridegroom rest until he should rouse himself. Cant. 2:7.

κατὰ τὴν ἐντολήν) According to the commandment of God, from the bond of which Christ had not hitherto released his followers: but had applied to the words a kind and suitable interpretation for the subject matter.

V. 56. ἡσύχασαν) Velut adjuratæ ut quiescere sponsum paterentur, donec ipse semet excitaret. Cant. II. 7.

κατὰ τὴν ἐντολήν) Juxta Dei præceptum, cujus vinculo Christus sectatores suos hactenus non exsolverat: sed verbis benignam & materiæ convenientem adhibuerat interpreta- tionem.

## 24:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXIV.

ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

The women coming early to the sepulcher do not find in it the body of Christ, but two angels appear to them, testifying that Christ has risen, and calling to memory what he had predicted in Galilee concerning his crucifixion and resurrection. These things they reported to the Apostles, but to these they seemed like fables. Peter, however, running to the tomb, finding nothing but the linen cloths, was amazed. But to two going to Emmaus, Jesus draws near, walks with them, and asks about the cause of their sadness: who, reporting to him the deeds and the crucifixion of Jesus, and that they had hoped for the redemption of Israel, and what the women had announced, are rebuked for their unbelief, and being informed from Moses and the Prophets about the passion and resurrection of Christ, they ask that, because evening was approaching, he might stay with them, where, recognized from the customary blessing and distribution of bread, he disappeared. They, however, hastening to Jerusalem, found the Apostles testifying that Christ had appeared to Simon, and reporting what had happened to them on the way, and how he had been recognized by them: but while they are speaking these things, Jesus stood in their midst, and as they thought it was a ghost, he shows his hands and feet, and eats with them, and explains the Scriptures to them concerning the passion and resurrection of Christ, and the proclamation in his name. He promises them power from on high: and having led them out to Bethany, after the blessing, he ascends into heaven, while they return to Jerusalem, and celebrate God.

There are V parts. I. The manifestation of the resurrection made to the women, to v. 12. II. The apparition made to the disciples going to Emmaus, to v. 35. III. The apparition made to the Apostles, to v. 47. IV. The promise of the Holy Spirit, to v. 49. V. The ascension of Christ into heaven, to v. 53.

PART I. The manifestation of the resurrection of Christ made to the women.

Vers. 1. Τῇ δὲ μιᾷ τῶν σαββάτων ὄρθρου βαθέος] Concerning the circumstances of this history, see what [is written] at Matthew ὄρθρου βαθέος, בשפרפרא, at the time when Darius once came to Daniel enclosed in the den, Dan. VI. 19.

καί τινες σὺν αὐταῖς] Some women of Jerusalem who had joined themselves to the Galilean women. For it is not permitted to delete these words, which both very many books and the Syriac and Arabic [versions] acknowledge: which also correctly interpret that τινὲς in the feminine gender.

That there were some women of Jerusalem, appears by no evidence. But Luke here in v. 10 hints that Joanna, the wife of Chuza, Herod's steward, Luke VIII. 3, was present. Others add Susanna, of whom Luke also made mention in c. VIII. 3. Those whom the Holy Spirit does not name, or designate by their place, it is not for us to name or designate.

Latin:

CAPUT XXIV.

ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Mulieres mane ad sepulcrum venientes, in eo non inveniunt corpus Christi, sed apparent illis duo Angeli, resurrexisse Christum te- stantes, & in memoriam revocantes, quæ in Galilæa prædixerat de sui crucifixione & resurrectione. Quæ ea Apostolis nuncia- runt, sed his fabulæ videbantur. Petrus ta- mẽ currens ad sepulcrum, non nisi linteamina inveniens, miratus est. Duobus autem Ema- untem euntibus appropinquat Iesus, cum iis- dem ambulat, & de causa tristitiæ quærit: qui referentes ei gesta & crucifixionem Ie- su, & quod sperarint redemtionem Israelis, ac quæ nunciarint mulieres, redarguuntur ob incredulitatem, & è Mose, & Prophetis de passione & resurrectione Christi infor- mati rogant, ut ob vesperam ingruentem pe- nes ipsos maneret, ubi è solita panis bene- dictione, & distributione agnitus, disparuit. Ipsi vero Hierosolymam properantes, inve- nerunt Apostolos testantes Christum Simo- ni apparuisse, & referentes quæ ipsis in via acciderint, & quomodo ab ipsis agnitus fue- rit: dum autem ista loquuntur, Ie- sus in medio ipsorum stetit, ipsisque putanti- bus spectrum esse, manus & pedes monstrat, & comedit cum ipsis, & Scripturas iisdem exponit de passione & resurrectione Christi, ac præconio in nomine ejus. Promittit ipsis virtutem ex alto: & eductis illis in Betha- niam, post benedictionem, ascendit in cœ- lum, ipsis Hierosolymam reduntibus, Deum- que celebrantibus.

Partes sunt V. I. Manifestatio resurrectionis mulieribus facta, ad v. 12. II. Apparitio facta discipulis Emaunta euntibus, ad v. 35. III. Appa- ritio Apostolis facta, ad v. 47. IV. Promissio Spi- ritus S. ad v. 49. V. Ascensio Christi in cœlum, ad v. 53.

PARS I. Manifestatio resurrectionis Christi mulieri- bus facta.

Vers. 1. Τῇ δὲ μιᾷ τῶν σαββάτων ὄρθρου βαθέος] De circum- stantias hujus historiæ vide quæ ad Matthæum ὄρθρου βα- θέος, בשפרפרא quali tempore Darius olim ad Danielem venit foveæ inclusum, Dan. VI. 19.

καί τινες σὺν αὐταῖς] Hierosolymitanæ aliquot quæ se mulieribus Galilæis adjunxerant. Neque enim delere has voces licet, quas & libri plurimi & Syrus & Arabs agno- scunt: qui & τινὲς illud fœminino genere recte interpre- tantur.

Hierosolymitanas quasdam fuisse, nullo apparet indicio. Johannam autem Chusæ Procuratoris Herodis Luc. VIII. 3. adfuisse Lucas hic v. 10. in- nuit. Adjungunt alii Susannam, cujus mentio- nem etiam Lucas fecit c. VIII. 3. Quas non nomi- nat, aut à loco suo designat Spiritus S. nostrum non est nominare, aut designare.

## 24:12
Vers. 12. ὁ δὲ Πέτρος] Not alone: for below it is said "some of those with us," but accompanied by John. He names Peter, however, rather, because he was the one who penetrated into the cave.

παρακύψας] John uses the same word regarding Magdalene, and then regarding himself, in this history. The LXX are accustomed to translate the Hebrew שקף in this way, which masters explain as looking from a higher place. But παρακύπτειν has a broader meaning for the Greeks, as it does for our own people: just as one may see also in James 1:25 and 1 Peter 1:12. That description of a curious man in Sirach ch. 21:16 pertains very closely to the gesture that is being discussed here: "A fool will peer into a house from the door; but a man who is educated will stand outside." The Syrian and the Arab correctly expressed the force of the word, the former with a word for looking inside, the latter for exploring. See the note on Matthew.

Μόνα] Without the body.

Πρὸς ἑαυτὸν θαυμάζων] These must be joined together as the Syrian did. Thus Luke said διελογίζοντο πρὸς ἑαυτοὺς, above in 20:14.

PART II. The apparition made to the disciples going to Emmaus.

Latin:

Vers. 12. ὁ δὲ Πέτρος] Non solus: nam infra dicitur τινὲς τῶν σὺν ἡμῖν, sed comite Iohanne. Petrum tamen potius nomi- nat, quia is in specum penetravit.

παρακύψας] Eandem vocem de Magdalena, deinde & de se, Iohannes usurpat in hac historia. LXX. ita vertere so- lent Hebræum שקף quod magistri exponunt spectare de loco superiore. Sed latius Græcis patet παρακύπτειν, ut & nostris: quemadmodum videre & Iacobi I. 25. 1. Petr. I. 12. Proxime ad gestum eum de quo hic agitur pertinet illa cu- riosi hominis descriptio apud Syrachidem c. XXI. 16. ἄφρων ἀπὸ θύρας παρακύψει εἰς οἰκίαν· ἀνὴρ δὲ πεπαιδευμένος ἔξω στή- σεται. Vim vocabuli recte expresserunt Syrus & Arabs, ille introspiciendi, hic explorandi verbo. Vide ad Matthæum,

Μόνα] Sine corpore.

Πρὸς ἑαυτὸν θαυμάζων] Conjungenda hæc sunt ut fecit Sy- rus. Sic διελογίζοντο πρὸς ἑαυτὸς dixit Lucas, supra XX. 14.

PARS II. Apparitio facta discipulis Emaunta euntibus.

## 24:13
Vers. 13.

Δύο ἐξ αὐτῶν] Namely, of those whom he had just designated by the name "the rest," from the followers of Christ. The ancients reasonably think that these were of the number of the Seventy, for when they say below "This is the third day that he spends today," they seem to refer to that which Jesus had said to the common people more obscurely, but to them both more openly and more frequently, that he would return to life on the third day. Luke expresses the name of the other below, calling him Cleopas. Many have thought the other to be Luke himself, whom he sufficiently refutes in the preface of his Gospel by distancing himself from the eyewitnesses. Epiphanius thought it was Nathanael, whom others think is one of the Apostolic company who is called Bartholomew by patronymic; in these matters, the most ancient tradition ought to have the greatest authority. And that is that the name of this other was Simon, or, which amounts to the same thing, Simeon. For this is a Hebrew name; the former is a Greek name expressed from the Hebrew. The authority is Origen, who in his book against Celsus says: "And it is written in the Gospel according to Luke, that after the resurrection Jesus, having taken the bread, blessed it, and having broken it, gave it to Simon and to Cleopas." Elsewhere in the same books, but translated into Latin, it is read as Simeon. With whom Ambrose could easily be reconciled, if one were to choose to rewrite Simeon, just as we now read Amaon (which is an unheard-of name). But one must consider, since Origen cites not tradition but Luke himself as the author of his statement, whether he was not deceived by that which is in verse 34 below. For it is possible that in that place some codices had λέγοντες instead of λέγοντας, and whether the Latin and other interpreters read it that way is open to doubt.
