Therefore, that "that the Lord has risen indeed and has appeared to Simon" can be seen as taken by Origen as if it refers to what these two narrated to the Apostles, not what they heard from the Apostles: although, when one examines the matter correctly, the received reading λέγοντας would deservedly be more pleasing: so that by Simon we understand Peter, to whom Paul also testifies that Christ appeared separately.

Vossius repeats most of these things, as many others, from Grotius, Harm. Evang. Book III, ch. 4, § 3. And that he was not Luke is sufficiently clear from Luke 1:2, for which reason Origen and Euthymius falsely make him one of the seventy disciples of Christ, because he openly distinguishes himself from those "to whom he presented himself alive," to whom Jesus had also shown himself to be seen while he was living. But the present companion of Cleopas was without doubt one of the seventy disciples.

Πορευόμενοι ἐν ἀυτῇ τῇ ἡμέρᾳ εἰς κώμην] It is likely that they lived in Emmaus, and returned there after they had spent the Preparation, the Sabbath, and the day after the Sabbath on paschal rites and prayers.

Κώμην] Josephus calls it a village, Pliny a Toparchy. For I do not doubt that it is the same name which is written Emmaus by Pliny and Luke, and Ammaus by Josephus.

Ἑξήκοντα] The Basel edition of Josephus of the year 1544 counts the same number of stadia. Wherefore I do not doubt that what other editions have, τριάκοντα, is corrupt. Moreover, this interval is not so great that they could not have returned from there to Jerusalem before midnight and found the Apostles gathered there, for that distance can be covered in two hours and a little more.

Latin:

Vers. 13.

Δύο ἐξ αὐτῶν] Nempe eorum quos modo λοιπῶν nomine designarat, è sectatoribus Christi. Probabiliter sentiunt ve- teres fuisse hos de numero LXX. cum enim infra dicunt Τρί- την ταύτην ἡμέραν ἄγει σήμερον videntur respicere id quod Ie- sus plebi obscurius, ipsis autem & apertius & sæpius dixe- rat, tertia se die in vitam rediturum. Nomen alterius infra exprimit Lucas, Cleopam vocans. Alterum ipsum Lucam multi putarunt, quos satis ipse refellit in Evangelii antelo- quio ab oculatis testibus se disparans Nathanaelem Epipha- nius putavit, quem alii putant unum esse Apostolicicœtus qui πατρωνυμικῶς Bartholomæus vocatur, in his rebus fama antiquissima maximæ debet esse fidei. Ea autem est nomen huic alteri fuisse Simoni, aut quod eodem recidit, Simeoni. Nam hoc Hebræum est nomen; illud Græcum ex Hebræo expressum. Auctor est Origenes qui in libro adversus Cel- sum: γέγραπται δὲ ἐν τῷ κατὰ Λυκᾶν, ὅτι μετὰ τὴν ἀνάστασιν λα- βὼν τὸν ἄρτον ὁ Ἰησοῦς ἐνλόγησεν καὶ κλάσας ἐπεδίδε τῷ Σίμωνι καὶ τῷ Κλεόπα. Alibi in iisdem libris, sed in Latinum versis, Simeon dictus legitur. Quicum conciliari facile posset Ambrosius, si libeat Simeonem rescribere, uti nunc Amaonem (quod in- auditum nomen est) legimus. Sed cogitandum, quando O- rigenes non famam sed ipsum Lucam dicti sui autorem lau- dat, an non eum deceperit id quod infra est commate 34. Fieri enim potest, ut inibi pro λέγοντας codices quidam ha- buerint λέγοντες, quomodo an non legerint Latinus & alii interpretes dubitari potest. Itaque illud ὅτι ἠγέρθη ὁ κύριος ὄν- τως καὶ ὤφθη Σίμωνι videri potest ita acceptum ab Origene, quasi referatur, quid hi duo Apostolis narraverint, non quid audiverint ab Apostolis: cum tamen recte rem inspicienti merito magis sit placitura recepta lectio λέγοντας: ita ut per Simeonem intelligamus Petrum, cui seorsum apparuisse Christum etiam Paulus testatur.

Repetit hæc pleraque ut alia multa è Grotio Vossius l. III. Harm. Evang. c. 4. §. 3. Et Lucam illum non fuisse satis luculentum est è Luc. I. 2. quem fal- so proinde Origenes, & Euthymius unum faciunt è LXX. Christi discipulis, quia distinguit sese aperte ab iis οἷς ̔η παρέστησεν ἑαυτὸν ζῶντα, quibus etiam Jesus se exhibuerat videndum dum viveret. Præ- sens autem Cleophæ comes sine dubio unus fuit è LXX. discipulis.

Πορευόμενοι ἐν ἀυτῇ τῇ ἡμέρᾳ εἰς κώμην] Verosimile est Em- maunte eos habitasse, atque eo regressos postquam & pa- rasceven & Sabbatum & diem à sabbato primum pascha- libus sacris & precibus impenderant.

Κώμην] χωρίον Iosephus vocat Plinius Toparchiam. Ne- que enim dubito, quin idem sit nomen, quod Plinio & Lu- cæ scribitur Emmaus, Iosepho Ammaus.

Ἑξήκοντα] Totidem stadia numerat editio Iosephi Basile- ensis Anni cIɔ Iɔ XLIV. Quare quod aliæ editiones, habent τριάκοντα vitiosum esse non dubito. Non est autem tantum hoc intervallum, ut non ante medinoctium inde redire Hierosolyma potuerint atque ibi congregatos Apostolos deprehendere, potest enim id spatium duabus & quod ex- currit horis confici.

## 24:14
Vers. 14.

Περὶ πάντων τῶν συμβεβηκότων τούτων] Concerning the life and death of Christ, and concerning those things which the women and Peter and John had reported.

Latin:

Vers. 14.

Περὶ πάντων τῶν συμβεβηκότων τούτων] De vita & morte Christi, & de iis, quæ mulieres Petrusque & Iohannes re- nunciaverant.

## 24:15
Vers. 15.

Συζητεῖν] They were turning over various conjectures in every direction, for that is what συζητεῖν means here, as also in Mark 1:27.

Ἐγγίσας] As if having overtaken them from behind, as is accustomed to happen on the road: whence he also addresses them as if he had heard a part of their conversation.

Latin:

Vers. 15.

Συζητεῖν] Varias conjecturas in omnem partem volve- bant, id enim hic est συζητεῖν, ut & Marc. I. 27.

Ἐγγίσας] Quasi à tergo eos assecutus, ut in via fieri so- let: unde & eos ita affatur quasi partem sermonum audiis- set.

## 24:16
Vers. 16.

ἐκρατοῦντο] They were hindered by divine power from observing more closely those things by which Jesus could be recognized, otherwise disguising himself by his external appearance, as we said regarding Mark.

Latin:

Vers. 16.

ἐκρατοῦντο] Impediebantur vi divina ne propius conside- rarent ea ex quibus cognosci Iesus poterat, cæteroqui ha- bitu externo sese dissimulans, ut ad Marcum diximus.

## 24:17
Vers. 17.

οἱ λόγοι οὗτοι ὣς ἀντιβάλλετε] The words which you are exchanging among yourselves: it is a Latinism, if I am not mistaken.

καὶ ἴστε σκυθρωποὶ] That is, ὄντες σκυθρωποὶ. For the Hebrews are accustomed to speak in this way.

Latin:

Vers. 17.

οἱ λόγοι οὗτοι ὣς ἀντιβάλλετε] Verba quæ inter vos commu- tatis: Latinismus est ni fallor.

καὶ ἴστε σκυθρωποὶ] Id est ὄντες σκυθρωποὶ. Ita enim loqui solent Hebræi.

## 24:18
Verse 18.

ὁ εἷς ᾧ ὄνομα Κλεόπας] The elder of the two, as is credible, to whom the other yielded the role of speaking. It is possible that this is the same person who is called Κλωπᾶς by John with a more contracted pronunciation, whose daughter was Mary the mother of James and Joses.

For the Syrian has קליפא in both places, and the Latin writes Cleophas, which approaches the Syrian pronunciation. Jerome: It is to be noted, however, that the Hebrew language does not have the letter P, but uses פ for it, the force of which the Greek φ sounds. Moreover, Κλεόπας or rather Κλεοπᾶς is the same name as Κλεόπατρος, by the apocope of which we spoke at the beginning of this book. The Macedonian name Cleopatra began to be frequent in Syria and Judea after the Macedonians held Asia. Thus also history calls many women Cleopatras, from the same origin of the name.

Are you the only one who dwells in Jerusalem and have not known the things that have happened] ἐν is missing in most codices. Πάροικος in these books generally signifies one who lives outside his own country, whence sometimes the word ξένος is joined to it, sometimes παρεπίδημος. Thus also Luke said παροικίαν in Acts 13:17 and 1 Peter 1:17. The writer to the Hebrews also uses παροικεῖν. And thus the Syrian, Arab, and Latin have interpreted this word in this place. But if we accept this, it is not to be doubted that it is a Latinism, such as there are many in Luke. For the Romans say that a man is a traveler and a guest in his own city who does not know what is going on. And Emperor M. Antoninus followed this manner of speaking in book 3: 'a stranger to the world who does not know the things that are in the world.' The sense, therefore, may be: Do you alone of all live here as a stranger, so that you are ignorant of things that are known to all? While I would not stubbornly reject this interpretation, I prefer another, which explains παροικεῖν Ἱερεσαλὴμ as dwelling in the Jerusalem territory. For both the authors of Roman law say that the Greek word παροίκους is extended to those who have land within the borders of a town; and ancient Christian writers, even Synods, call the territory that is within the borders of major cities a παροικία, whence whatever was under the care of one Bishop was so called, which they now call διοίκησιν, although that word once had a much wider scope. Nor indeed did only Christians use τὸ παροικεῖν in this sense. But others also, as Herodes the orator when he says that Athens brings many advantages 'not only to those who dwell within, but also to those who dwell nearby': akin to which is what is said in Thucydides, that those who live in the vicinity are said to παροικεῖν, as the scholiast also explains; but also in Josephus, the Jews who lived around Delos are called πάροικοι in the edict of Caesar the dictator, which is read in Antiquities 14.17. This meaning fits this place very well, for Christ was acting as if he himself lived in the territory a little further on from Emmaus, and was therefore heading home, as they were. They wonder, therefore, that one living so near the city should be ignorant of those things whose rumor, given the magnitude of the event, was likely to have been spread far and wide. And thus there will be a Hebraism in these words, which is quite frequent, which you might explain in Greek thus: σὺ μόνος τ̃ παροικέντων ἐκ ἔγνως τὰ γενόμενα; unless one prefers to take παροικεῖν catachrestically for staying even without a domicile, just as the Jews stayed in Jerusalem 'at the feasts': so that Cleopas says: he wonders that anyone could be found among those who are now staying in Jerusalem to whom these things are unknown.

Latin:

Vers. 18.

ὁ εἷς ᾧ ὄνομα Κλεόπας] Senior amborum, ut credibile est, cui alter loquendi partes cessit. Fieri potest, ut idem hic sit qui Iohanni Κλωπᾶς dicitur contractiori pronun- tiatione, cujus filia fuerit Maria mater Iacobi & Iosetis.

Nam Syrus utrobique habet קליפא & Latinus scribit Cleophas quod ad Syriacam pronunciationem accedit. Hieronymus: Notandum autem quod P literam Hebraeus ser- mo non habeat sed pro ipsa utatur פ cujus vim Graecum φ so- nat. Est autem Κλεόπας aut potius Κλεοπᾶς nomen idem quod Κλεόπατρος, per ἀποκοπὴν de qua diximus ad hujus libri initium. Cleopatri nomen Macedonicum in Syria & Judaea frequentari coepit postquam Macedones Asiam tenuere. Sic & multas mulieres Cleopatras vocat historia, eadem nominis origine.

Cù μόνος παροικεῖς ἐν Ἱερεσαλὴμ καὶ ἐκ ἔγνως τὰ γενό- μενα] ἐν deest in pluribus codicibus. Πάροικος in his libris plerumque significat eum qui extra patriam habitat, un- de modo ei adjuncta est vox ξένος, modo παρεπίδημος. Sic & παροικίαν dixit Lucas Actor. XIII. 17. & 1. Petr. I. 17. Scriptor ad Hebraeos etiam παροικεῖν. Atque ita hoc loco vocem hanc sunt interpretari Syrus, Arabs & Latinus. Quod si recipimus, non dubitandum est esse Latinismum quales sunt complures apud Lucam. Nam Romani pere- grinari eum & in urbe sua hospitem esse dicunt qui quid agatur ignorat. Et hoc loquendi genus secutus M. An- toninus Imperator libro III. ξένος κόσμε ὁ μὴ γνωρίζων τὰ ἐν κόσμῳ ὄντα. Sensus ergo sit, Tune solus omnium hic ut peregrinus vivis, utea quae nota sunt omnibus igno- res? Hanc interpretationem ut praefracte improbare no- lim, ita alteram praefero quae παροικεῖν Ἱερεσαλὴμ exponit habitare in agro Hierosolymitano. Nam & Romani juris auctores vocem Graecam παροίκες ad eos extendi dicunt qui in oppidi finibus agrum habent: & Scriptores Chri- stiani veteres, etiam Synodi, παροικίαν vocant agrum qui intra fines est majorum urbium, unde ita appellatum est quicquid unius Episcopi curae suberat, quod nunc vo- cant διοίκησιν, cum olim ea vox multo latius pateret. Ne- que vero soli Christiani hoc sensu usurparunt τὸ παροικεῖν. Sed & alii, ut Herodes orator cum dicit Athenas plurima adferre commoda ὀ μόνον τοῖς ἐνοικῦσιν ἀλλὰ καὶ τοῖς πα- ροίκοις: cui affine est quod apud Thucydidem παροικεῖν dicuntur qui in proximo habitant, ut & scholiasstes expo- nit, sed & apud Iosephum πάροικοι vocantur Judaei qui cir- ca Delum habitabant in edicto Caesaris dictatoris quod le- gitur XIV. Originum XVII. Optime autem huic loco con- venit haec significatio, nam Christus ita se gerebat, quasi & ipse in agro habitaret paulo ulterius Emmaunte, ac proinde domum, ut ipsi, contenderet. Mirantur er- go quod tam prope ab urbe habitans ea ignoret quorum rumorem pro ei magnitudine par erat longe lateque esse sparsum. Atque ita erit Hebraismus in his verbis satis fre- quens, quem Graece ita explices: σὺ μόνος τ̃ παροικέν- των ἐκ ἔγνως τὰ γενόμενα; nisi quis malit καταχρηστικῶς su- mere παροικεῖν pro commorari etiam citra domicilium, sic- ut Judaei Hierosolymis morabantur ἐν ταῖς ἑορταῖς: ut dicat Cleopas: mirari se aliquem inveniri posse eorum qui nunc Hierosolymis versentur quem ista lateant.

## 24:19
Vers. 19.

ποῖα] That is, τίνα, as in Matthew 19:18, chapter 20:36, and elsewhere. What, he says, are those things which you think cannot be unknown to me?

δυνατὸς ἐν ἔργῳ κὶ λόγῳ] Not just any Prophet, but eminent among the Prophets themselves in his manner of teaching and in his deeds. Regarding Moses, Stephen said: 'he was mighty in words and deeds' (Acts 7:22).

ἐναντίον τῦ Θεῦ καὶ παντὸς τῦ λαῦ] We had something similar above in chapter 2:52. ἐναντίον here, like ἔναντι in 1:8, ἐνώπιον in 1:15, and elsewhere, is לפני. But because δυνατὸς preceded here, I think ἐναντίον does not properly signify what Theophylact thinks, and what Paul, following Solomon, does not want to do—'providing for honest things not only in the sight of the Lord, but also in the sight of men' (2 Corinthians 8:21)—but rather the testimony given to him by God through works (in the way that Peter also calls Jesus 'a man approved of God by miracles and wonders') and by men through the faith they had in his speech. The manner of speaking arose from the fact that we bear witness to those things which are in our sight. Akin to this is that in Genesis concerning Nimrod, גבור ציד לפני יהוה, so that we understand him to have been a most powerful warrior (for both Plato and Aristotle compare war to hunting), with God miraculously favoring his arms, undoubtedly to punish the insolence of those peoples who could not bear just liberty. Although I confess that the interpretation of Josephus seems to me not improbable for that passage, who explains לפני יהוה there as 'in defiance and contempt of God.' Because, clearly, Nimrod was of a violent nature, and like Achilles in Horace:

Denying that laws were made for him.

Which kind of men, as we had above, 'fear not God and do not respect man.' Moreover, that לפני is accustomed, according to the diversity of the subject matter, to be taken sometimes in a good sense, sometimes in a bad, as can be seen in the same book of Genesis 6:11, where the human race is said to be corrupt לפני האלהים, that is, to the contempt and anger of the deity. Which I thought to bring up in passing regarding the words of Moses, which are treated in various ways by the Hebrew masters.

Latin:

Vers. 19.

ποῖα] Id est τίνα, ut Matth. XIX. 18. c. XX. 36. & a- libi. Quae, inquit, illa sunt quae putatis mihi ignota esse non posse?

δυνατὸς ἐν ἔργῳ κὶ λόγῳ] Non quivis Propheta, sed inter ipsos Prophetas eminens docendi modo & factis De Mose dixit Stephanus: ἦν δυνατὸς ἐν λόγοις κὶ ἔργοις Actor. VII. 22.

ἐναντίον τῦ Θεῦ καὶ παντὸς τῦ λαῦ] Simile quid ha- buimus supra cap. II. 52. ἐναντίον hic ut ἔναντι I. 8. ἐνώπιον I. 15. & alibi est לפני. Quia vero hic praecessit δυνατὸς, puto ἐναντίον non id proprie significare quod putat Theophyla- ctus & quod post Solomonem Paulus non facere vult, προ- νοεῖν καλὰ ἐ μόνον ἐνώπιον κυρία, ἀλλὰ κὶ ἐνώπιον ἀνθρώπων 2. Corinth. VIII. 21. sed potius testimonium ei datum a Deo per opera (quomodo & Petrus Iesum vocat ἄνδρα ἀπό τῦ Θεῦ ἀποδεδειγμένον δυνάμεσι κὶ τέρασι) Et ab hominibus per fi- dem habitam ejus sermoni. Loquendi genus inde natum quod de iis rebus testimonium perhibemus quae nobis in conspectu sunt. Affine est illud in Genesi de Nembrodo גבור ציד לפני יהוה ut intelligamus eum potentissi- mum fuisse bellatorem (nam & Plato & Aristoteles bellum venationi comparant) Deo arma ipsius mirum in modum fortunante, haud dubie ad puniendam eorum populorum insolentiam qui justam libertatem ferre non poterant. Quanquam fateor non improbabilem mihi videri ad eum locum Iosephi interpretationem qui לפני יהוה ibi ex- ponit πρὸς ὕβριν κὶ καταφρόνησιν τῦ Θεῦ. Quia scilicet fuerit Nembrodus ingenio violento, & ut Achilles apud Hora- tium:

Iura negans sibi nata.

Quod genus hominum ut supra habuimus Θεὸν ὀ φοβῆ- ται κὶ ἄνθρωπον ἐκ ἐντρέπονται. Solet autem illud לפני pro materiae diversitate modo in bonam, modo in malam par- tem accipi, ut videre est eodem libro Geneseos VI. 11. ubi corruptum dicitur humanum genus לפני האלהים, id est ad contemptum atque iram numinis. Quae obiter afferre visum ad Mosis verba ab Hebraeis magistris varie tractata.

## 24:20
Verse 20.

ὅπως τε παρέδωκαν αὐτὸν οἱ ἀρχιερεῖς καὶ οἱ ἄρχοντες ἡμῶν εἰς κρῖμα θανάτε] He treats of the senators of the Sanhedrin, who extorted an unjust sentence from Pilate. See Matt. XX. 19. XXVII. 2.

ἐσταύρωσαν αὐτὸν] That is, they caused him to be crucified: for the Hellenists are accustomed to express in that manner what the Hebrews utter in the Hiphil.

Latin:

Vers. 20.

ὅπως τε παρέδωκαν αὐτὸν οἱ ἀρχιερεῖς καὶ οἱ ἄρχοντες ἡμῶν εἰς κρῖμα θανάτε] De senatoribus Synedrii agit, qui inju- stam sententiam a Pilato expresserunt. Vid. Matth. XX. 19. XXVII. 2.

ἐσταύρωσαν αὐτὸν] Id est effecerunt ut crucifigeretur: nam Hellenistae, quae Hebraei efferunt in Hiphil solent eum in modum enuntiare.

## 24:21
Verse 21.

ἠλπίζομεν] A word indicating a great failure of faith. For what reason was there why they should not still hope, except that the power of God was not sufficiently present to their minds.

ὅτι αὐτός ἐστιν ὁ μέλλων λυτρᾶσθαι τὸν Ἰσραὴλ] Λυτρῦν here is to liberate, just as we said above at I. 68. that λύτρωσιν is taken, and often among the LXX. For it is most certain that the reason for the liberation, situated in this, that he should give himself as a price for the world, was not understood by them at this time: nay rather, they expected an earthly kingdom joined with the amendment of souls. There is therefore in these words a description of the Messiah according to the received opinion of those times, just as above II. 24. προσδεχόμενοι παράκλησιν τῶ Ἰσραὴλ.

Vossius followed Grotius here again: but at Luke II. 25. Simeon, with other believers, expected a spiritual and true λύτρωσιν, in which our salvation is situated; which is most clear from the description of him in v. 25, because he was δίκαιος through faith in Christ and by the illumination and response of the Holy Spirit, v. 26, and concerning the Christ of the Lord from his canticle, v. 29, 30, 31, 32.

Σὺν πᾶσι τέτοις] Σὺν placed for ἐπὶ as על for the Hebrews for עם.

Τρίτην ταύτην ἡμέραν ἄγει σήμερον] The active taken impersonally for the passive, as often. For the sense is, the third day is now being passed, as in Terence: 'This is now the seventh month being passed.' Nor did the Syrian or the Arab read or interpret it otherwise. But I cannot approve the interpretation of those who refer ἄγει to Jesus, for these two are still speaking as if they hoped for nothing from his resurrection, only in the following words they bring forward something of a conjecture, but one in which they show they have little confidence, for which reason they are gravely reproved: it could deservedly be said to them what was said by Spurinna to Caesar: The day has come, it has not gone.

Latin:

Vers. 21.

ἠλπίζομεν] Vox indicans magnum fidei deliquium. Nam quid erat cur non etiamnum sperarent, nisi quod Dei po- tentia non satis ipsis ob animum versabatur.

ὅτι αὐτός ἐστιν ὁ μέλλων λυτρᾶσθαι τὸν Ἰσραὴλ] Λυτρῦν hic est liberare, quomodo & λύτρωσιν sumi diximus supra I. 68. & saepe apud LXX. Nam rationem liberationis in hoc si- tam, ut se daret in pretium mundi, non intellectam ab il- lis hoc tempore, certissimum est: imo potius regnum ter- renum cum animorum emendatione conjunctum expe- ctabant. Est itaque in his verbis descriptio Messiae ex re- cepta eorum temporum sententia, ita supra II. 24. προσδε- χόμενοι παράκλησιν τῶ Ἰσραὴλ.

Sequutus hic iterum Grotium Vossius est: sed Luc. II. 25. Simeon spiritualem ac veram λύτρωσιν expectavit cum aliis fidelibus, in qua salus nostra sita est; quod e descriptione ejus v. 25. quia δίκαιος fuisse per fidem in Christum & illuminatione ac responso Spiritus S. v. 26. de Christo Domini ex cantico ejus, v. 29. 30. 31. 32. luculentissimum est.

Σὺν πᾶσι τέτοις] Σὺν pro ἐπὶ positum ut על Hebraeis pro עם.

Τρίτην ταύτην ἡμέραν ἄγει σήμερον] Activum impersonaliter sumptum pro passivo, ut saepe. Sensus enim est, agitur jam dies tertia, ut apud Terentium: Mensis jam hic agitur septimus. Nec aliter aut legit aut interpretatus est tum Syrus tum Arabs. Eorum vero interpretationem probare non possum qui ἄγει ad Jesum referunt, nam adhuc lo- quuntur hi duo, quasi qui de ejus resurrectione nihil spe- rarent, tantum in sequentibus verbis aliquid adferunt con- jecturae, sed cui se parum confidere ostendunt, quo no- mine graviter reprehenduntur: merito illis dici poterat quod a Spurrina Caesari. Venit dies non abiit.

## 24:22
Verse 22.

Τινὲς ἐξ ἡμῶν] Of our flock and company, as the Syrian and Arab have taken it. Thus below τινὲς τῶν σὺν ἡμῖν.

ἐξέστησαν] Cicero translates ἐκστῆναι in Aristotle's Rhetoric as 'to lead to admiration': but it seems here that such an admiration is in question which renders men ambiguous in judgment: as Luke joined ἐξίστασθαι καὶ διαπορεῖν, Acts II. 12.

Latin:

Vers. 22.

Τινὲς ἐξ ἡμῶν] Nostri gregis ac coetus, quomodo Syrus & Arabs acceperunt. Sic infra τινὲς τῶν σὺν ἡμῖν.

ἐξέστησαν] ἐκστῆναι apud Aristotelem in Rhetoricis Cicero vertit ad admirationem traducere: sed videtur hic de tali agi admiratione quae homines judicii ambiguos reddat: quomodo ἐξίστασθαι καὶ διαπορεῖν conjunxit Lucas, Act. II. 12.

## 24:23
Verse 23.

ὀπτασίαν ἀγγέλων] Concerning Jesus himself being seen, nothing: we have discussed the reasons for the silence in the notes on Matthew. Concerning ὀπτασίας, see above I. 22.

Latin:

Vers. 23.

ὀπτασίαν ἀγγέλων] De ipso Jesu conspecto nihil: Causas silentii ad Matthaeum disquisivimus. De ὀπτασίας vide supra I. 22.

## 24:24
Verse 24.

Τίνες τῶν σὺν ἡμῖν] Peter, whom he just named, and John, whose name he kept silent.

Latin:

Vers. 24.

Τίνες τῶν σὺν ἡμῖν] Petrus quem modo nominavit, & Jo- hannes cujus nomen subticuit.

## 24:25
Verse 25.

Ὦ ἀνόητοι] Thus also Paul addresses the Galatians; therefore, such words are not prohibited in Matthew 5:22, but anger imprudently ejaculating such a word is forbidden. So true it is that deeds are distinguished by the spirit. There is a time when the usefulness of the hearers demands some vinegar.

An intemperate patient makes a cruel physician.

Βραδεῖς τῇ καρδίᾳ] Thus also in Mark 16:14, hardness of heart is joined with unbelief.

ἐπὶ πᾶσιν] Not only those things which concern the glory, but also those which concern the sufferings of the Messiah. It ought not to be our choice to pick out from the Holy Scriptures what pleases us most.

οἷς ἐλάλησαν οἱ προφῆται] If you doubt his own faith, certainly there was no reason for you to doubt the faith of the Prophets. Nor ought you to have been so sluggish as not to have attentively considered their prophecies. Tertullian, arguing against Marcion, cites this passage differently: O foolish and slow of heart in not believing all things which he (namely Jesus) has spoken to you; but it must be known that this passage is cited by him in this way by concession, not from the received Gospel but from Marcion's Gospel, which the conclusion of the book also shows: I pity you, he says, Marcion, you have labored in vain: for the Christ JESUS in your Gospel is mine. That Marcion's edition had it in this place as we have said is gathered from Epiphanius, which I say so that no one, on account of these or similar

Tertullian's citations (for many occur) move the controversy regarding the received reading.

Latin:

Vers. 25.

Ὦ ἀνόητοι] Ita & Paulus Galatas compellat, non ergo Matth. V. 12. voces tales prohibentur, sed vetatur iracun- dia vocem talem imprudenter ejaculans. Adeo verum est animo facta discerni. Est ubi audientium utilitas aceti a- liquid exposcit.

Crudelem medicum intemperans aeger facit.

Βραδεῖς τῇ καρδίᾳ] Sic & apud Marcum XVI. 14. τῇ ἀπι- στίᾳ conjungitur, ἡ σκληροκαρδία.

ἐπὶ πᾶσιν] Non iis tantum quae gloriam, sed & quae per- pessiones Messiae spectant. Non debet nostri esse arbitrii excerpere ex sacris literis, quod maxime placeat.

οἷς ἐλάλησαν οἱ προφῆται] Si de ipsius fide dubitatis, certe de Prophetarum fide non erat quod dubitaretis. Neque tam supinos vos esse oportuit, ut non attente considera- retis eorum vaticinia. Tertullianus adversus Marcionem disputans aliter hunc locum citat: O insensati & tardi corde in non credendo omnibus quae loquutus est ad vos (Jesus scilicet) sed sciendum ita citari ab ipso hunc lo- cum κατὰ συγχώρησιν, non ex recepto sed ex Marcionis Evangelio, quod & libri conclusio ostendit: Miseror, inquit, tui Marcio, frustra laborasti: Christus enim IE- SUS in Evangelio tuo meus est. Marcionis autem edition nem, ita ut diximus, hoc loco habuisse ex Epiphanio colligitur, quod eo dico ne quis ob has aut similes

Tertulliani citationes (plures enim occurrunt) receptæ le- ctioni status controversiam movoat.

## 24:26
Verse 26.

Οὐχὶ ταῦτα ἔδει παθεῖν τὸν χριστὸν καὶ εἰσελθεῖν εἰς τὴν δόξαν ;] And by the decree of the Father often revealed, so that in every respect Christ might become our leader, whom it also behooves to enter διὰ πολλῶν θλίψεων εἰσελθεῖν εἰς τὴν βασιλείαν τοῦ Θεοῦ, as Paul speaks in Acts XIV. 22. Wherefore, that which hindered them from believing that Jesus was that promised Messiah, this very thing ought to have excited them most to believe it.

Latin:

Vers. 26.

Οὐχὶ ταῦτα ἔδει παθεῖν τὸν χριστὸν καὶ εἰσελθεῖν εἰς τὴν δόξαν ;] Et patris decreto sæpe revelato, ut omni ex parte Christus dux noster fieret, quos & ipsos oportet διὰ πολλῶν θλίψεων εἰσελθεῖν εἰς τὴν βασιλείαν τοῦ Θεοῦ, ut loquitur Paulus Actor. XIV. 22. Quare quod illos impediebat quo minus Iesum crederent esse promissum illum Messiam, hoc ipsum illos maximo ad id credendum excitare debuit.

## 24:27
Verse 27.

ἀρξάμενος ἀπὸ Μωσέως καὶ ἀπὸ πάντων τῶν προφητῶν] In which there are certain express prophecies, as in Isaiah and Daniel, and certain ἐν τύποις καὶ συμβόλοις, as the serpent erected by Moses, the expiatory sacrifices which were performed for the people, the affairs of David: the explanation of which Christ handed down to the Apostles, and the Apostles to us. It is credible that a similar mystical explanation of other oracles was also handed down by Christ or his Spirit and preserved as if by hand in the Church: for not everything could be written down: such is that concerning the offering of Isaac, in which even the ancient Jews believed a huge secret lay hidden. But even now they beseech God through that sacrifice, that He may be willing to be propitious to them. Indeed, Isaac is even said by them to have carried his own cross and to have been recovered from the dead. But many pages testify that in later times things were dragged into such fabrications, with a pious mind rather than a praiseworthy success. So great and arduous a thing is it φρονεῖν εἰς τὸ σωφρονεῖν.

I would wish these to be observed: because they serve to refute the glosses of Grotius, who perverts most of the prophecies of the Old Testament concerning the Messiah in his Annotations on the Old Testament, and twists them into another sense. Add, however, to these what he noted at verse 47 in this place: For this, he says, the κήρυγμα of repentance, both other things among the Prophets pertain, and especially the illustrious passage of Isaiah XLIX. 6. It is a small thing that you have chosen me as your servant, to raise up the tribes of Jacob and to convert the desolate ones of Israel: I have also set you as a light to the Gentiles. Add what is cited above in Isaiah LXI. at the beginning in Luke IV. 18. and Psalm XXII. 23. 24. 25. 26. 27. 28.

Latin:

Vers. 27.

ἀρξάμενος ἀπὸ Μωσέως καὶ ἀπὸ πάντων τῶν προφητῶν] In quibus quædam sunt expressa vaticinia, ut apud Esaiam ac Danielem, quædam ἐν τύποις καὶ συμβόλοις, ut serpens à Mose erectus, sacrificium piaculares, quod pro populo peragebatur, res Davidis: quarum explicationem Chri- stus Apostolis, Apostoli nobis tradiderunt. Credibile est aliorum quoque oraculorum similem explicationem mysticam à Christo aut ejus spiritu traditam & per manus quasi conservatam in Ecclesia: neque enim omnia scribi potuerunt: quale illud est de oblatione Isaaci, in quo arcanum ingens latere veteres etiam Iudæi crediderunt. Sed & nunc per id sacrificium Deum obtestantur, ut ipsis es- se velit propitius. Quin & Isaacus illis dicitur crucem suam bajulasse & ex mortuis recuperatus. Sed multa po- steris temporibus ad tales figmentationes pertracta, pio magis animo quam laudabili successu innumeræ paginæ te- stantur. Adeo magna atque ardua res est φρονεῖν εἰς τὸ σω- φρονεῖν.

Hæc observari velim: quia faciunt ad revin- cendas glossas Grotii pleraque vaticinia V. Test. de Messia in Annotatis ad V. T. pervertentis, & in a- lium sensum detorquentis. Adde autem his, quæ ad v. 47. notavit hoc loco: Ad hoc, inquit, pæniten- tiæ κήρυγμα tum alia apud Prophetas pertinent, tum imprimis illustris Esaia locus XLIX. 6. Exiguum est, quod te mihi ministrum elegi, ad suscitan- das tribus Jacobi & convertendos desolatos Israë- lis: Etiam lucem gentium te constitui. Adde quæ sunt Esaia LXI. in principio citata supra apud Lucam IV. 18. & Psalm. XXII. 23. 24. 25. 26. 27. 28.

## 24:28
Verse 28.

ἤγγισαν] Joyful and eager: for a pleasant companion on the road is as good as a carriage, and as they themselves soon confess, the almost extinguished fire of faith had begun to be rekindled within them.

εἰς τὴν κώμην ᾗ ἐπορεύοντο] Emmaus, of course, which he named above: for there is no reason to invent another place here, as some have done.

And he himself made as if to go further] This passage is to be considered more diligently, because Chrysostom draws an argument from here, and Cassian, a disciple of Chrysostom in most things, to prove that a lie is not always illicit, just as Diphilus had once said: I suppose that a lie, when told for the sake of salvation, brings with it nothing difficult.

And Pisander: It is no reproach to speak a lie for the sake of one's life. Nay, and Democritus: One must speak the truth where it is better, from whom Augustine has hitherto dissented, so as to say that there are certain kinds of lies in which there is no great fault, but yet they are not without fault: According to the sentiment of Sophocles: It is not good to speak false things, but for whom the truth brings terrible destruction, it is pardonable to say even that which is not good.

Many pious and learned men dispute about this matter, all of which it is not my intention to gather here. I will advise a few things so that those things which ought to be distinguished may not be confused. First, that must be laid down as certain, that not only lying or feigning, but also dissembling (which thing is undoubtedly indifferent in itself) is not free from grave vice, as often as one tends through that way to the harm of another: which Cicero illustrates with some examples in De Officiis III. Nor is there need to prove this, since it is sufficiently established that acts which are indifferent in themselves are evil, as often as they are employed for an evil end. Therefore, with all depravity of end set aside, it remains to see whether there is any vice in that very thing which is called feigning: in which two things are to be looked at, of which one has the nature of matter, the other of form. I call the exterior act the matter: the intention of the agent the form. The exterior act consists either in deeds or in words; let us treat of deeds first. I say, therefore, that deeds naturally have no signification, unless that which each person wishes: for they do not have signification by institution, unless those deeds which are restricted to a certain signification by divine or human law, under which I also include covenants, and therefore cannot be licitly used with another signification: all other things are free from the bond of a certain signification, even if they are usually accustomed to be used to signify this or that thing. For example: Flight is indeed usually taken as an indication of fear: nevertheless, it is permitted even for one who is not afraid to flee. Circumcision is usually taken as a mark of binding oneself to Jewish rites, yet Paul used it otherwise and rightly, when he wished Timothy to be circumcised. Thus, to advance a few steps (which Christ did here) and to compose the body for walking, although it is accustomed to signify the purpose of a further journey, is nevertheless licitly used even outside such a purpose, because such an act is one to which everyone has a natural right, nor is he bound by any law to that signification. Let someone say here, if not on the part of the matter, certainly on the part of the form, that is, of the intention, there is vice, for this is done, that he who sees it may be deceived by opining, but that I think must be denied. For what is intended here by Christ is the greater utility of those watching, nor did such an opinion follow inevitably from such an act viewed in itself: for they could have opined something else. Let us grant indeed that he knew they would opine otherwise than the matter stood, and did not hinder it: there is no vice in that, if one knows and does not hinder what he was not bound to hinder. But here Christ was not bound to hinder this, because it was not in their interest that it be hindered, nay rather, it was in their interest that it not be hindered. A good man, as Clement of Alexandria says, will do for the benefit of his neighbor alone things which would not be done by him primarily. And these things I would have said concerning simulation, which is situated in deeds, which the Greeks are sometimes accustomed to call oikonomia, which in no way ought to be extended to those gestures which cannot but call men away from true piety. It is not only foolish (says Origen) to pray to statues, but also to pretend, while going along with the multitude, to pray to statues, which those who are of the Peripatetic school do, those who philosophize, and those who embrace the things of Epicurus or Democritus; for nothing spurious ought to underlie the soul of one who is truly pious toward the divine.

Grotius rightly disputes against the sentiment of Diphilus, Pisander, and Democritus, which Chrysostom and Cassian strive to prove from this passage, that a lie is not always illicit, and he teaches that not only is lying and feigning and dissembling not free from grave vice, as often as one tends through that way to the harm of another, but that even with all depravity of end set aside, vice has a place in words and deeds, in lies, simulation, and dissimulation.

Deeds, he rightly observes, naturally have no signification unless that which each person wishes. Yet he also leaves it to the readers to think about this deed of Christ, whether, since with the Greeks pros-poieisthai is to hold before oneself, even where there is no appearance of simulation, it cannot be said that Jesus, just as he was composing his step for a journey, so also truly had determined with himself to go further, unless he were instantly asked to remain. In which way it was also truly said to the Centurion, I coming will heal him. Matt. VIII. 7. namely, if the Centurion wished. And in Mark it is said of Christ that he wished to pass by them c. VI. 48. namely, if he had not been instantly asked to board the ship: for knowledge of a future event does not stand in the way of such a conditional purpose, since even that threat of God, Nineveh will perish within forty days, unless it does penance, namely, had its truth, however much God foreknew this penance. These thoughts were not first Grotius's, as we shall presently say. But since Grotius here further discusses words, in what way vice has a place in them, or sin is committed, so that he may resolve that dispute concerning lies, he discourses learnedly, and we do not withhold our agreement from him in those things which follow:

In words, the difficulty is greater than in deeds: because words, even if not by law, yet by use and custom are accustomed to have a certain signification, by which bond the intercourse and society of men among themselves is in great part contained. But it matters much to what matters words are applied. For some matters are such that by their own nature or by law they require the disclosure of the truth pertaining to that matter. For example: If someone is questioned about the truth of salvation, he is bound to make a profession of it even with danger, both because the honor of God and the eternal salvation of one's neighbor is more worthy than our temporal life, and because Christ expressly commands it: but he who is bound to disclose the truth is without doubt at the same time bound to use words with that meaning which he knows or hopes are understood by the hearers. For otherwise he will not disclose the truth: in this point especially the Priscillianists and certain others formerly condemned by the Church stumbled: which I say, lest anyone drag Chrysostom or Cassian into their company. Clement of Alexandria notes this well, who, when he had conceded a certain συμπεριφορὰν (accommodation) serving the good of others, says that this must be done in such a way that all hypocrisy is absent, διὰ τ᾽ ἐπιρτημένον τοῖς δικαίοις παρὰ τ̃ ζηλόντων κίνδυνον (because of the danger hanging over the righteous from those who seek it). So also when some contract is carried out, both parties are bound to reveal the truth of the things pertaining to the nature of that contract, concerning which matter see the mentioned book of the Offices. And the same must be said about the giving of testimony, as often as someone is obligated to it by equity and good faith. In these cases, therefore, one must speak in the way that words are thought to be understood. Which necessity does not come from the use of words viewed in themselves, but from the quality of the matter which is being transacted. In the rest of discourse there is not the same necessity: for first, that words are not always to be used in the way they signify either from their origin or from more accepted usage, it is superfluous to prove, since, if anyone were to affirm this, he would remove from the nature of things metaphors, catachreses, ironies, hyperboles, litotes, amplifications, and other changes and figures of speech of that kind: in which both human and divine discourse abounds. But not even that can be established here as a perpetual rule, which we said in that former kind of matters, that words are to be used in the way they are known or thought to be understood. For Christ himself also seems to have said certain things to the Apostles, which, while they had a figurative truth, were nevertheless understood by them according to the literal sense of the words, such as about sitting on twelve thrones, and other things of that kind; in which kind of discourse, however, there is no fault. For if you look at the external act, the words were not restricted to that literal meaning: if the internal act, that was not the intention, that the Apostles should be deceived: since in that true sense, but hidden from the Apostles at that time, there was more than in that which they themselves supposed. But where discourse does not receive a meaning that conforms to the truth from the estimation of sound judgment, even if the intention is upright, the far greatest part of the ancient Christians agrees that it is not free from fault: namely because if such discourse is admitted, that bond which unites men to men is in great part removed. For it is not in vain that by a singular gift of God it is granted to men alone to converse with one another. And as far as the intention is concerned, it cannot make an act upright which has, as it were, a crookedness innate to it. Nevertheless, even here a certain exception occurs. For if any are sick with the malady of insanity, such as those possessed by black bile (who generally can hardly be cured of an imaginary disease except by imaginary remedies) or are of that infancy which does not have the use of reason, he who speaks with them can be seen to be placed outside that necessity of adapting words to the things signified: because, clearly, we have no commerce of discourse except with those who are fit to understand the meaning of discourse. And therefore, as far as those destitute of the use of reason are concerned, words seem to be held in the same place as deeds, which we have denied to be restricted to any certain meaning. And in this sense I would easily accept what Plato says, that τὸ ψεῦδος (the lie) is not to be disapproved of, χρήσιμον ὡς ἐν φαρμάκου εἴδει (useful as in the form of a medicine). Following whom, Clement says that a good man must always speak the truth, εἰ μὴ ποτε ἐν θεραπείας μέρει (unless perhaps in the way of treatment), καθάπερ ἰατρὸς πρὸς τοῦ ὄντας ἐπὶ σωτηρίᾳ ψεύσεται ἢ ψεῦδος ἐρεῖ (just as a physician will lie or tell a lie to those who are sick for the sake of their salvation). Where by way of correction he recalls what he had said, that he lies, and says rather that a lie is told by him, because, clearly, the word 'lying' signifies a mind striving to deceive. But as for the fact that Plato equates the rulers of states with physicians in this matter, in that thing he opens too wide a window of license, nor is the reason equal. For the difference of dignity does not remove that equality which nature has established among all men, the greatest part of which consists in the mutual and equal use of discourse, and indeed, as Tertullian said in the Apologetic: No law, that is, civil law, owes the consciousness of its justice to itself alone, but to those from whom it expects obedience. Christians ought also to remember that, since Christ has removed all use of the oath from common discourse, and has substituted in its place a bare affirmation and negation, Christians ought to abhor all perfidy and even vanity no less than other men who have any sense of probity abhor perjury. But to return from this digression to the place which is in hand, although the explanation just brought forward seems to me to have nothing of inconvenience, yet I also leave it to the readers to consider whether, since προσποιεῖσθαι (to pretend) for the Greeks is to make a show of, even where there is no appearance of simulation, it cannot be said

that Jesus, just as He was composing His step for the journey, so also truly had determined with Himself to proceed further, unless He were instantly asked to remain. Just as He also truly said to the Centurion, ἐγὼ ἐλθὼν θεραπεύσω αὐτόν (I will come and heal him), Matt. VIII. 7, namely, if the Centurion wished; and in Mark it is said of Christ that ἤθελε παρελθεῖν αὐτούς (He intended to pass them by), VI. 48, namely, unless He had been instantly asked to board the ship: nor does the foreknowledge of a future event stand in the way of such a conditional purpose, since even that threat of God, 'Nineveh has perished within forty days,' namely, unless it has done penance, had its truth, however much God foreknew this penance.

These thoughts were not primarily Grotius's, since these things had already been explained by others in that manner, see B. Gerhard, Harm. Resurr. ch. VII, p. 290. But he gives the reason why one should not agree with him: But it seems to oppose this opinion that Christ had associated himself with these disciples for the purpose of revealing himself to them at the inn, and that there was no reason why Christ should travel further, since he could have been present in a moment wherever he wished. Therefore, it is more likely and more convenient to the text to establish that Christ simulated with external gestures as if he wished to go further. He adds that a nearly similar example exists in Mark 6:48, where Christ, coming to the disciples laboring on the sea around the fourth watch of the night, wished to pass by, that is, he simulated that he wished to pass by. Wherefore the former explanation of Grotius is more to be approved. Moreover, the intention of Christ must be considered here, who pretends to go further in order to kindle the ardor and desire for himself in these disciples. These Grotian points can be compared with those things which have been said to this effect regarding Abraham, the Egyptian midwives, and Joshua at Gen. 12:13, Ex. 1:19, Josh. 8:15, and elsewhere. For we have explained such things more than once.

Latin:

Vers. 28.

ἤγγισαν] Læti atque alacres: nam comes jucundus in via pro vehiculo est, & ut mox ipsi fatentur, cœperat in ipsis resuscitari prope extinctus ignis fidei.

εἰς τὴν κώμην ᾗ ἐπορεύοντο] Emmaunta nimirum, quam supra nominavit: nam alium locum hic confingendi quod quidam fecerunt, nihil est causæ.

Καὶ αὐτὸς προσεποιεῖτο ποῤῥωτέρω πορεύεσθαι] Locus est hoc diligentius considerandus, quod hinc argumentum petat Chrysostomus & discipulus in plerisque Chrysostomi Cas- sianus, ut probarent non semper illicitum esse mendacium, sicut Diphilus olim dixerat: Ὑπολαμβάνω τὸ ψεῦδος ἐπὶ σωτηρίᾳ, Λεγόμενον οὐδὲν περιποιεῖσθαι δυσχερές.

Et Pisander: Οὐ νέμεσις καὶ ψεῦδος ὑπὲρ ψυχῆς ἀγορεύειν. Quin & Democritus: ἀληθομυθεῖναι χρεὼν ὅπου λώϊον, à qui- bus hactenus dissentit Augustinus, ut dicat quædam esse ge- nera mendaciorum in quibus non sit magna culpa, sed ta- men non sint sine culpa: Ex Sophoclis sententia: Καλὸν μὲν οὖν οὐκ ἔστι τὰ ψευδῆ λέγειν, Ὅτῳ δ᾽ ὄλεθρον δεινὸν ἡ ἀλήθει᾽ ἄγῃ, Συγγνωστὸν εἰπεῖν ἐστι καὶ τὸ μὴ καλόν.

Multa viri pii atque eruditi hac de re disputant, quæ omnia huc congerere animus non est. Pauca monebo ne confun- dantur ea, quæ distingui debent. Primum illud pro certo poni debet non mentiri tantum aut simulare, sed & dissimu- lare (quæ res est haud dubie per se media) vitio gravi non ca- rere, quoties per eam viam tenditur ad alterius damnum: quod exemplis aliquot illustrat Cicero de officiis III. Nec id probari opus, cum satis constet actus per se medios malos esse, quoties malo fine adhibentur. Seposita igitur omni finis pravitate restat videre ecquid in illo ipso quod simulare di- citur, sit vitii: in quo duo spectanda, quorum alterum mate- riæ alterum formæ habet rationem. Materiam voco actum exteriorem: formam intentionem agentis. Actus exterior aut in factis aut in verbis consistit; De factis primum aga- mus. Dico igitur facta naturaliter nullam habere significa- tionem, nisi eam quam quisque velit: Nam ex institu- to significationem non habent, nisi ea facta quæ lege di- vina aut humana, sub qua etiam pacta comprehendo, ad certam significationem restringuntur, ac proinde alio si- gnificatu usurpari licite non possunt: cætera omnia libera sunt a certæ significationis vinculo, etiamsi plerumque so- leant ad hanc aut ad illam rem significandam usurpari. Exempli causa: Fuga solet quidem plerumque ut pavo- ris indicium accipi: attamen etiam non paventi fugere li- cet. Circumcisio solet accipi ut nota se obligandi Iudaicis ritibus, aliter tamen eam usurpavit & recte Paulus, cum Timotheum voluit circumcidi. Ita progredi passus ali- quot (quod hic fecit Christus) corpusque in gressum com- ponere, quanquam itineris ulterioris propositum signifi- care soleat, licite tamen usurpatur etiam extra tale pro- positum, quia actus talis est, ad quem unusquisque na- turaliter jus habet, neque ulla lege ad illam significatio- nem est adstrictus. Dicat hic aliquis, si non ex parte ma- teriæ, certe ex parte formæ, id est, inventionis esse vi- tium, hoc enim agi, ut qui id videt decipiatur opinan- do, id vero negandum arbitror. Nam quod hic intenditur a Christo, est major utilitas spectantium, neque talis opi- natio ex tali actu spectato inevitabiliter sequebatur: pote- rant enim opinari & aliud quippiam. Ponamus sane scis- se eum aliter illos quam res habebat opinaturos, nec im- pediisse: nihil in eo vitii est, si quis sciat nec impediat quod impedire non tenebatur. Hic autem Christus non teneba- tur hoc impedire, quia id impediri illorum non intere- rat, imo potius intererat non impediri. Vir bonus ut in- quit Clemens Alexandrinus, ἐπὶ τῶν πλησίον ὠφελείᾳ μό- νῃ ποιήσει τινὰ ἃ οὐκ ἂν προηγουμένως αὐτῷ πραχθείη. Et hæc quidem dixerim de simulatione, quæ in factis sita est, quam Græci οἰκονομίαν vocare interdum solent, quæ nullo modo extendi debet ad eos gestus qui non possunt non a- vocare homines à vera pietate. Οὐ μόνον τὸ εὔχεσθαι τοῖς ἀ- γάλμασιν (inquit Origenes) ἠλίθιόν ἐστιν, ἀλλὰ γὰρ καὶ τὸ συμ- περιφερόμενον τοῖς πολλοῖς προσποιεῖσθαι τοῖς ἀγάλμασιν εὔχεσθαι, ὁ ποῖον ποιοῦσιν οἱ τὰ ἀπὸ τοῦ περιπάτου, Φιλοσοφοῦντες, καὶ οἱ τὰ ἐπικούρου ἢ δημοκρίτου ἀσπαζόμενοι· οὐδὲν γὰρ νόθον δεῖ ὑπεῖπ- χειν τῇ ψυχῇ τοῦ ἀληθῶς εἰς τὸ θεῖον εὐσεβοῦς.

Recte disputat Grotius contra Diphili, Pisan- dri, Democriti sententiam, quam Chrysostomus & Cassianus ex hoc loco probare satagunt, quod non semper illicitum sit mendacium, ac docet, quod non modo mentiri & simulare ac dissimulare vitio gravi non careat, quoties per eam viam tenditur ad alterius damnum, sed, quod etiam seposita omnifi- nis pravitate in verbis & factis, in mendaciis, si- mulatione, ac dissimulatione vitium locum habeat.

Facta, recte observat, naturaliter nullum habe- re significationem nisi eam quam quisque velit. Id tamen etiam lectoribus circa hoc factum Christi cogitandum relinquit, an cum προσποιεῖσθαι Græcis sit præ se ferre, etiam ubi nulla est species simulatio- nis, dici non possit Jesum sicut gressum ad iter com- ponebat, ita vere etiam secum constituisse ultra progredi, nisi instanter manere rogaretur. Quo- modo & Centurioni vere dicebatur, ἐγὼ ἐλθὼν θεραπεύ- σω αὐτὸν. Matth. VIII. 7. nempe si Centurio vel- let. Et apud Marcum de Christo dicitur ἤθελε παρελ- θεῖν αὐτοὺς c. VI. 48. nempe, nisi rogatus instanter fuiffet, ut navem ascenderet: neque enim tali propo- sito conditionato obstat scientia futuri eventus, cum il- la etiam Dei comminatio, Ninive intra diem quadra- gesimum peribit, nisi pœnitentiam egerit scilicet, veri- tatem suam habuerit, quantumvis hanc pœnitentiam Deo prænoscente. Hæ cogitationes non Grotii primum fuêre, ut jamjam dicemus. Cæterum quum Grotius hic porro de verbis, qua ratione vitium in illis locum habeat, aut peccatum com- mittatur, ut disputationem illam de mendaciis ex- pediat, erudite disserat, calculum ei nostrum non subtrahimus in his, quæ sequuntur:

In verbis, major quam in factis est difficultas: quia ver- ba etsi non lege, usu tamen & consuetudine solent habere significationem certam, quo vinculo magna ex parte con- tinetur hominum inter se consuetudo ac societas. Sed mul- tum refert quibus negotiis verba adhibeantur. Nam quæ- dam negotia talia sunt, ut suapte natura aut lege requirant veri ad id negotium pertinentis patefactionem. Exempli causa: Interrogatus aliquis de vero salutari, tenetur ejus pro- fessionem edere etiam cum periculo, tum quia Dei honos & proximi salus æterna dignior est vita nostra temporali, tum quia Christus id diserte præcipit: qui autem verum pa- tetacere tenetur, sine dubio simul tenetur uti verbis eo signi- ficatu, quo ea scit aut sperat ab audientibus intelligi. Nam alioqui verum non patefaciet: in hanc præcipue partem im- pegerunt Priscillianistæ & alii quidam ab Ecclesia olim da- mnati: quod dico, ne quis in eorum consortium trahat Chrysostomum aut Cassianum. Bene hoc notat Clemens Alexandrinus, qui cum συμπεριφορὰν quandam bono alio- rum inservientem concessisset, ita hoc faciendum ait, ut absit omnis διὰ τ᾽ ἐπιρτημένον τοῖς δικαίοις παρὰ τ̃ ζηλόντων κίνδυνον ὑπόκρισις. Sic etiam ubi contractus aliquis peragitur, pars utraque tenetur veritatem aperire, rerum ad ejus contractus naturam pertinentium, qua de re vide dicto Officiorum li- bro. Idemque dicendum de testimonii dictione, quoties ad eam aliquis ex æquo & bono obligatur. His ergo casi- bus ita loquendum est, quomodo verba intelligi putantur. Quæ necessitas non ex verborum usu per se spectato venit, sed ex negotii, quod agitur, qualitate. In reliquo sermone non eadem est necessitas: nam pri- mum non ita semper usurpanda verba, quomodo aut ex ori- gine sua aut ex usu receptiore significant, probare superva- cuum est, cum, si id quis affirmet, tollat de rerum natura translationes, abusiones vocabulorum, εἰρωνείας, ὑπερβο- λὰς, μειώσεις, ἀυξήσεις, aliasque id genus sermonis mutatio- nes ac figuras: quibus & humanus & divinus sermo abun- dat. At ne illud quidem pro perpetuo statui hic potest, quod in superiori illo negotiorum genere diximus, verba ita usur- panda quomodo sciuntur, aut putantur intelligenda. Nam & Christus ipse quædam videtur dixisse Apostolis, quæ cum veritatem haberent figuratam, ab illis tamen secundum ver- borum proprietatem intelligebantur, ut de sessione in duo- decim sedibus, aliaque ejusmodi; in quo tamen sermonum genere nihil est vitii. Nam si actum externum spectes, non erant verba adstricta ad illam propriam significationem: si actum internum, non ea erat intentio, ut deciperentur A- postoli: cum in illo sensu vero, sed Apostolis ad id tem- pus occulto, plus esset quam in eo, quod ipsi opinabantur. Ubi vero sermo eam, quæ veritati congruat, significatio- nem ex sani judicii æstimatione non recipit, etiamsi recta sit intentio, vitio eum non carere pars Christianorum veterum longe maxima consentit: nimirum quia si talis sermo ad- mittatur, magna ex parte tollitur vinculum illud, quod ho- mines hominibus sociat. Neque enim frustra Dei dono sin- gulari solis hominibus tributum est inter se colloqui. Et ad intentionem quod attinet, ea non potest rectum efficere a- ctum, qui velut agnatam sibi habeat curvitatem. Verun- tamen etiam hic quædam occurrit exceptio. Nam si qui in- saniæ malo ægrotent, ut atra bile perciti (qui fere à morbo imaginoso nisi per remedia imaginosa curari vix possunt) aut ejus sint infantiæ, quæ rationis usum non habeat, apud hos qui loquitur, is positus videri potest extra illam neces- sitatem verba significatis rebus aptandi: quia scilicet sermo- nis commercium non habemus nisi cum iis, qui sermonis si- gnificationem intelligere sunt idonei. Atque ideo illos ra- tionis usu destitutos quod attinet, verba videntur eodem loco habenda, quo facta, quæ ad certam aliquam significa- tionem adstricta esse negavimus. Et hoc sensu facile recepe- rim, quod dicit Plato, non improbandum τὸ ψεῦδος χρήσι- μον ὡς ἐν φαρμάκου εἴδει. Quem secutus Clemens virum bo- num semper ait ἀληθεύειν εἰ μὴ ποτε ἐν θεραπείας μέρει, καθά- περ ἰατρὸς πρὸς τοῦ ὄντας ἐπὶ σωτηρίᾳ ψεύσεται ἢ ψεῦδος ἐρεῖ. Ubi per ἐπανόρθωσιν revocat, quod dixerat, eum mentiri, & ait potius ab eo mendacium dici, quia scilicet vox mentien- di animum fallere studentem significat. Cæterum quod Plato medicis hac in re æquat civitatum rectores, in ea re nimiam licentiæ fenestram aperit, neque par ratio est. Nam dignitatis differentia non tollit eam æqualitatem, quam in- ter omnes homines natura constituit, cujus pars maxima in mutuo & æquali sermonis usu consistit, atque adeo, ut in A- pologetico dixit Tertullianus: Nulla lex, civilis scilicet, sibi soli conscientiam justitiæ suæ debet, sed eis, à quibus obse- quium expectat. Illud quoque Christiani meminisse debent, cum omnem jurisjurandi usum ex communi sermone Chri- stus sustulerit, ejusq; in locum substituerit nudam affirina- tionem ac negationem, non minus Christianos abhorrere debere ab omni perfidia atque etiam vanitate, quam cæteri homines qui modo aliquid habent probitatis abhorrent à perjurio. Sed ut ex diverticulo ad locum qui est in manibus redeam, quanquam allata modo explicatio nihil mihi habe- re videtur incommodi, tamen & illud insuper cogitandum relinquo lectoribus, an cum προσποιεῖσθαι Græcis sit præse fer- re, etiam ubi nulla est species simulationis, dici non possit

Jesum sicut gressum ad iter componebat, ita vere etiam se- cum constituisse ultra progredi, nisi instanter manere roga- retur. Quomodo & Centurioni vere dicebat ἐγὼ ἐλθὼν θερα- πεύσω αὐτόν. Matth. VIII. 7. nempe si Centurio vellet; & apud Marcum de Christo dicitur ἤθελε παρελθεῖν αὐτούς VI. 48. nempe, nisi rogatus instanter fuisset ut navem ascende- ret: neque etiam tali proposito conditionata obstat scien- tia futuri eventus, cum illa etiam Dei comminatio, Ninive intra diem quadragesimum periit, nisi poenitentiam egerit scilicet, veritatem suam habuerit quantumvis hanc poeni- tentiam Deo praenoscente.

Quae cogitationes non Grotii primum fuere, si- quidem jam ab aliis ea ratione haec explicata sint, vid. B. Gerhard. Harm. Resurr. c. VII. p. 290. Qui vero causam cur eidem accedendum non sit, red- dit: Sed huic sententiae adversari videtur, quod Christus eo fine se his discipulis associaverat, ut in di- versorio se iis manifestaret, quodque nulla fuerit causa cur Christus longius proficisceretur, cum in mo- mento adesse potuerit, ubicunque voluerit. Ergo verisimilius & textui convenientius est, statuere quod Christus externis gestibus simulaverit, ac si longius ire vellet. Addit, simile fere exemplum extare Marc. VI. 48. ubi Christus ad discipulos in mari laborantes circa quartam noctis vigiliam veniens voluit prae- terire, id est, simulavit, se velle praeterire. Quapropter prior explicatio Grotii magis pro- banda. Consilium autem Christi hic simul spe- ctandum est, qui prae se fert longius ire, ut ardo- rem & desiderium sui in discipulis hisce accendat. Conferri possunt haec Grotiana cum illis quae de A- brahamo, obstetricibus Aegyptiis, & Josua ad Ge- nes. XII. 13. Ex. I. 19. Jos. VIII. 15. & alibi in hanc sententiam dicta sunt. Plus enim vice simplici ta- lia expedivimus.

## 24:29
V. 29. Παρεβιάσαντο] By asking constantly: Luke also used παραβιάζεσθαι in Acts 16:5 with the same meaning. You have παραβιάζεσθαι in an entirely similar sense in Gen. 19:3 and βιάζεσθαι in Gen. 33:12, Judg. 9:7, corresponding to the Hebrew פצר. See what we said about the verb ἀναγκάζειν above at 14:23.

ὅτι πρὸς ἑσπέραν ἐστὶ καὶ κέκλικεν ἡ ἡμέρα] He did not say the same thing twice, but explained the ambiguous word ἑσπέρας (for the Hebrews use the word ערב for all time in the afternoon) by adding an interpretation. Thus also above at 9:12, what Matthew's interpreter had called ὀψίαν, he interpreted as ἡ ἡμέρα ἤρξατο κλίνειν. The Syriac translates it well: The day is turning toward darkness. Similar is that pastoral invitation in Virgil: 'Yet here you could have rested with me this night.' He added the reason: 'And now the tops of the farmhouses smoke from afar, and the greater shadows fall from the high mountains.'

Moreover, this could have been said emphatically to commend the invitation more, even if the sunset was not so close: so that they could more easily change their plan and soon return to Jerusalem and find the Apostles not yet given over to sleep.

Latin:

V. 29. Παρεβιάσαντο] Constanter rogando: etiam in A- ctis XVI. 5. παραβιάζεσθαι Lucas dixit significatu eodem. Si- mili omnino sensu παραβιάζεσθαι habes Gen. XIX. 3. & βιά- ζεσθαι Gen. XXXIII. 12. Jud. IX. 7. respondentia Hebraeo פצר. Vide quae diximus de verbo ἀναγκάζειν supra XIV. 23.

ὅτι πρὸς ἑσπέραν ἐστὶ καὶ κέκλικεν ἡ ἡμέρα] Non bis idem di- xit: sed vocem ambiguam ἑσπέρας (nam ad exes plum He- braei ערב de pomeridiano omni tempore usurpatur) expli- cavit addito interpretamento. Sic & supra IX. 12. quod Matthaei interpres ὀψίαν dixerat interpretatus est ἡ ἡμέρα ἤρ- ξατο κλίνειν. Bene vertit Syrus: Dies ad tenebras bergit. Si- milis est illa apud Virgilium invitatio pastoralis, Hic tamen hac mecum poteras requiescere nocte. Causam addidit: Et jam summa procul villarum culmina fumant, Majoresque cadunt altis de montibus umbrae.

Potuit autem hoc dictum esse αὐξητικῶς ad commendan- dam magis invitationem, quamvis non tam prope immi- neret Solis occasus: quo facilius mutato consilio mox Hie- rosolyma se recipere & Apostolos nec dum in soporem da- tos invenire potuerunt.

## 24:30
V. 30. Λαβὼν τὸν ἄρτον εὐλόγησε καὶ αὐτὸς ἐδίδε αὐτοῖς] Contrary to the custom of guests: for that was the duty of the host, wherefore by this act he declares himself the Lord and head of the household; which first cast suspicion upon them that this was Jesus, their teacher, who used to perform the rites of the head of the household among the disciples.

Latin:

V. 30. Λαβὼν τὸν ἄρτον εὐλόγησε καὶ αὐτὸς ἐδίδε αὐτοῖς] Prae- ter morem convivarum: erat enim id munus conv oratoris, quare hoc facto se Dominum ac Patremfamilias profitetur; quod primum suspicionem illis injecit esse hunc Jesum, praeeptorem suum, qui inter discipulos solebat patrumfa- milias ritibus defungi.

## 24:31
V. 31. Διηνοίχθησαν οἱ ὀφθαλμοὶ] With the impediments removed, they began to look at him more closely and recognize him, just as in Gen. 21:19 concerning Hagar, 'God opened her eyes and she saw a well of living water.'

Καὶ ἐπέγνωσαν αὐτόν] From his face considered more closely. The mystical interpretation of the ancients does not displease, that Christ is not truly recognized except by those who are in the unity of his body, which is figured by the breaking of bread.

Ἄφαντος ἐγένετο ἀπ' αὐτῶν] How this happened did not begin to be disputed only recently: but long ago it was inquired into with all respect. The Syriac and the Arab seem to think this happened by a sudden change of place: but Epiphanius thinks rather that a darkness was cast over their eyes, as was done long ago by Elisha and by the Angels in the destruction of Sodom. The opinion of Origen seems to have been different from these, who in his accurate disputation against Celsus says that Christ's body during those forty days was ὁρατὸν ὅτ' ἐβούλετο καὶ οἷς ἐβούλετο. For he judges that that very most sacred body was at that time ἐν μεθορίῳ between that which he himself calls the density that perishable bodies have and between natures free from this mortal concretion. Moreover, he explained what he thinks about the Angels at the beginning of the commentary. on Luke: namely that they also become visible or invisible by the sole choice of their own will: The Latin interpreter seems to have been more inclined toward this opinion. I find nothing here to be said that is better than that saying of Basil: not to be over-curious about the how. Of those three modes, just as I see the first two to be more comprehensible, I would not dare to affirm that the third is impossible. For while this dross detains us, we can attain almost nothing that pertains either to the quality of the Angels or even to that of the body which Paul not undeservedly calls spiritual, beyond those things which have been revealed, except by very tenuous conjectures, which ought to put a clasp upon our curiosity. It is clear to me that that ἀπ᾿ αὐτῶν is not brought forward quite aptly for defining the mode of this matter, as if it designated a flight, since it is much more probable that it is a manner of speaking taken from Hebraism, such as above XVIII. 34. κεκρυμμένον ἀπ᾿ αὐτῶν & ΧΙΧ. 42. it was hidden from your eyes, where we have also annotated more passages containing the same locution.

Grotius rightly denies that the third mode is among the impossibilities; And we who would wish to deny to Christ's body that which must be granted to any glorified body, namely that it is visible by substance, even if it is not seen in act, since between the object, which is a spiritual body, and the instrument of vision, which is the earthly eye, there is no proportion. To this also contributes that statement of Augustine to Orosius: The Lord rose with a clarified body, but He did not wish to appear to His disciples in that clarification because they could not behold the clarification with their eyes. And book XXII of The City of God, ch. IX: It is to be believed that the brightness in Christ's body when He rose was hidden from the eyes of the disciples rather than absent. For human and infirm sight would not bear it: For from this it appears that this was not a matter of necessity, that the present sight was [withheld], but of economy and free will, as Thomas advised concerning any glorified body, part III, question 54, article 1: Whoever has a glorified body has it in his power to be seen when he wishes, and when he does not wish, not to be seen. Where, however, he rightly added concerning Christ's body: Christ had this not only from the condition of a glorious body, but also from the power of the Deity, through which it can happen that even non-glorified bodies are miraculously not seen. Nor was the mind of Epiphanius any different from heresy XLII against Marcion: It is clear: It befitted Him who was God, and was transmuting His body into a spiritual one, to show indeed a true body, but to disappear when He wished: because all things are possible to Him: Whence it is gathered against the Calvinists that the body of Christ can altogether be invisibly present somewhere, since it is not only a glorified and spiritual body, but is also united personally to the Word, and subsists in the hypostasis of the Word.

Latin:

V. 31. Διηνοίχθησαν οἱ ὀφθαλμοὶ] Sublatis impedimentis propius eum intueri ac cognoscere coeperunt, ita Genes. XXI, 19. de Agare, ἀνέῳξεν ὁ Θεὸς τοὺς ὀφθαλμοὺς αὐτῆς καὶ εἶ- δε φρέαρ ὕδατος ζῶντος.

Καὶ ἐπέγνωσαν αὐτόν] Ex vultu propius considerato. Non displicet mystica veterum interpretatio, Christum vere non cognosci nisi ab iis qui in unitate sunt corporis illius, quod per panis fractionem figuratur.

Ἄφαντος ἐγένετο ἀπ' αὐτῶν] Hoc quomodo factum sit non nuper demum coepit disputari: Sed olim de istis salva pace quaerebatur. Syrus & Arabs existimare videntur factum hoc subita loci mutatione: At Epiphanius oculis potius obdu- ctam putat caliginem, ut ab Elisao olim & ab Angelis in excidio Sodomorum. Diversa videtur ab his fuisse sententia Origenis qui in accurata adversus Celsum disputatione Christi corpus quadraginta illis diebus ait fuisse ὁρατὸν ὅτ' ἐβούλετο καὶ οἷς ἐβούλετο. Censet enim id ipsum sacratissimum corpus fuisse eo tempore ἐν μεθορίῳ inter eam ut ipse appellat παχύτητα quam habent corpora caduca & in- ter naturas liberas ab hac concretione mortali. De An- gelis autem quid sentiat, explicavit initio commentarii ad Lucam: nimirum eos quoque conspicuos, aut incon- spicuos fieri solo voluntatis suae arbitrio: Videtur Latinus interpres in hanc sententiam fuisse pronior. Ego nihil hic decendum invenio quod melius sit illo Basilii dicto τὸ ὅπως μὴ περιεργάζεσθαι. Ex tribus illis modis, sicut duos priores video esse καταληπτοτέρους, ita tertium esse ἀδύνατον affirma- re non ausim. Nam dum faex ista nos detinet, nihil ferme quod aut ad Angelorum aut etiam ad ejus corporis, quod non immerito πνευματικὸν Paulus vocat, qualitatem perti- neat, extra ea quae revelata sunt, nisi tenuibus admodum conjecturis assequi possumus, quod fibulam imponere de- bet nostrae curiositati. Illud mihi liquet non satis apte ad definiendum hujus rei modum adferri illud ἀπ᾿ αὐτῶν quasi φυγὴν utique designet, cum multo sit probabilius genus esse loquendi ex Hebraismo desumtum, quale supra XVIII. 34. κεκρυμμένον ἀπ᾿ αὐτῶν & ΧΙΧ. 42. ἐκρύβη ἀπ᾿ ὀφθαλμῶν σου, ubi & plura loca annotavimus eandem locutionem continentia.

Recte Grotius tertium modum negat ἐκ τῶν ἀ- δυνάτων esse; Et qui Christi corpori denegare hoc velimus, quod cuivis glorificato corpori conce- dendum, quod scilicet substantia visibile sit, etsi a- ctu non videatur, quandoquidem inter objectum, quod est corpus πνευματικὸν, & inter instrumen- tum visus, quod est oculus terrestris, nulla sit pro- portio. Quo facit etiam illud Augustini ad Oros. Clarificata carne Dominus resurrexit, sed noluit in- ea clarificatione discipulis suis apparere eo quod non possent oculis suis clarificationem aspicere. Et lib. XXII. de Civ. Dei. c. IX. Claritas in Christi corpo- re cum resurrexit, ab oculis discipulorum potius abscon- dita fuisse, quam defuisse credenda est. Non enim eam ferret humanus atque infirmus adspectus: Inde enim apparet, quod hoc non fuerit necessitatis, quod praesens conspectus fuerit, sed oἰκονομίας & liberae voluntatis, ut de quovis corpore glorificato monuit Thomas part. III. quaest. 54. art. 1. Qui- cunque habet corpus glorificatum, in potestate sua habet videri quando vult, & quando non vult non videri. Ubi tamen recte addidit de Christi corpore: Hoc habuisse Christum non solum ex conditione corporis gloriosi, sed etiam ex virtute Deitatis, per quam fieri potest, ut corpora etiam non gloriosa miraculose non videantur. Nec aliam fuisse Epiphanio mentem ex haeres. XLII. contr. Marc. liquet: Decebat i- psum qui Deus erat, & corpus suum in spirituale trans- mutabat, ostendere quidem corpus verum, dispare- re autem quando volebat: quia omnia ipsi possibilia sunt: Unde contra Calvinianos colligitur, quod omnino corpus Christi invisibiliter alicubi prae- sens esse possit, quum id non solum corpus glorifi- catum & πνευματικὸν, sed etiam τῷ λόγῳ unitum sit personaliter, & in hypostasi Verbi subsistat.

## 24:32
Verse 32.

Burning] I do not doubt the truth of this reading since the Syriac, Latin, and Arabic agree. They say this: unless our mind had been dull, we could have recognized Him before He reclined with us from His manner of teaching: for besides the weight of the arguments and the utmost kindness in teaching, there was added a divine efficacy inflaming our souls, such as we were once accustomed to feel when He Himself was teaching. The heat of the heart is a sign of vehement emotion. Thus Psalm XXXIX. 4. My heart was hot within me, my heart was warmed within me.

Latin:

Vers. 32.

Καιομένοι] De lectionis hujus veritate non dubito cum consentiant Syrus, Latinus Arabs. Hoc ajunt: nisi mens fuiffet laeva potueramus eum antequam nobiscum accum- beret agnoscere ex docendi modo: nam praeter argumen- torum pondera & comitatem in docendo summam, acce- debat divina efficacia animos incendens, qualem sentire quondam folebamus ipso docente. Calor cordis vehemen- tis motus indicium. Sic Psalm. XXXIX. 4. חם לבי בקרבי ἐθερμάνθη ἡ καρδία μου ἐντός μου.

## 24:33
Verse 33.

At that very hour] Syriac, that is, immediately. The eleven and those with them] Who were comforting one another in their nocturnal gatherings, John XX. 19. He calls them the eleven Apostles after Judas was cast out, as before the twelve, although perhaps one or two were absent.

Latin:

Vers. 33.

Αὐτῇ τῇ ὥρᾳ] Syrisinus, id est statim. Τοὺς ἕνδεκα κὶ τοὺς σὺν αὐτοῖς] Qui nocturnis coetibus alter alterum solabantur Joh. XX. 19. Undecim vocat Apo- stolos post ejectum Judam ut ante δώδεκα, quanquam for- te unus aut alter aberant.

## 24:34
Verse 34.

Saying] We have said above why this seems to us to be the true reading. The Lord is risen indeed] As if they were saying, the matter now does not rest on the testimony of Magdalene alone or on uncertain conjectures, indeed is truly as Mark XI. 32. To Simon] As the first of the Apostles, most loving of the Lord and struck down by his fall.

Latin:

Vers. 34.

Λέγοντας] Veram hanc esse lectionem cur nobis videatur supra diximus. ἠγέρθη ὁ κύριος ὄντως] Quasi dicant, res jam non nititur solo Magdalenae testimonio aut incertis conjecturis, ὄντως est ἀληθῶς ut Marc. XI. 32. Σίμωνι] Ut primo Apostolorum, amantissimo Domini & ob lapsum perculso.

## 24:35
Verse 35.

ὡς ἐγνώσθη αὐτοῖς ἐν τῇ κλάσει τοῦ ἄρτου] At the table, not before: they accuse their own slowness.

PART III. The apparition made to the Apostles.

Latin:

Vers. 35.

ὡς ἐγνώσθη αὐτοῖς ἐν τῇ κλάσει τοῦ ἄρτου] In mensa non ante: tarditatem suam accusant.

PARS III. Apparitio Apostolis facta.

## 24:36
Vers. 36. Ἔστη] Suddenly, when the doors were shut. εἰρήνη ὑμῖν] That is, Hail, as in Jud. VI. 23. & above X. 5. After these words: ἐγώ εἰμι μὴ φοβεῖσθε, which is now missing in the Greek codices, the Syriac, Latin, and Arabic read: Wherefore it must be seen that it has not slipped out through the carelessness of scribes, since Ambrose also acknowledges it. Let them consult ancient codices if any have the means. I am surprised that a great man says these seem to have been added from John, since they are no more present in John. It is reckless that Grotius dares to correct Greek Codices from Versions, and to prefer the rivulets to the fountain for the sake of purity: which we have often chastised in him himself.

Latin:

Vers. 36. Ἔστη] Subito cum clausæ essent fores. εἰρήνη ὑμῖν] Id est, Avete, ut Jud. VI. 23. & supra X. 5. Post hæc verba: ἐγώ εἰμι μὴ φοβεῖσθε, quod nunc in Græcis co- dicibus deest, legerunt Syrus, Latinus, Arabs: Quare vi- dendum ne elapsum sit scribarum incuria, quando & Am- brosius agnoscit. Consulant antiquos codices si quibus co- pia est. Quod vir magnus ait videri ex Johanne hæc adje- cta miror, cum apud Johannem nihilo magis exstent. Temerarium est, quod audet Grotius Codices Græcos corrigere è Versionibus, frontique rivu- los ratione puritatis præferre : quod sæpe in ipso castigavimus.

## 24:37
Vers. 37.

Ἐδόκουν πνεῦμα θεωρεῖν] What kind of spirit? An evil one, of course. For that kind of spirit was accustomed to appear in the form of dead men: just as most of the Hebrews interpret the story about Samuel being evoked by the Pythoness. In the Gospel of the Nazarenes, which, as we have said, had many things added to Matthew from the tradition of fame, there was in this place instead of the word spirit, an incorporeal demon. And it is therefore less to be rejected that Ignatius, who could have heard the Apostles themselves relating these things, recites the words of Christ refuting this persuasion in this manner: καὶ ὅτε πρὸς τοὺς περὶ Πέτρον ἦλθεν, ἔφη αὐτοῖς, λάβετε, ψηλαφήσατε με, καὶ ἴδετε ὅτι οὐκ εἰμὶ Δαιμόνιον ἀσώματον. πνεῦμα γὰρ σάρκα κᾀ ὀστέα οὐκ ἔχον' καθὼς ἐμὲ θεωρεῖτε ἔχοντα: which passage ought to be the less suspect to us because, as it is now read, it was already praised long ago by Eusebius: just as the passage immediately preceding was by Jerome. Which, if I am not mistaken, pertain not a little to the interpretation of this passage, and the words πτοηθέντες, ἔμφοβοι, τεταραγμένοι in this history do the same. Add what we said at Matth. XIV. 26. to the word φάντασμα. But now he would want the text amended not from Versions, but from the words of an ancient Father. If such license is admitted, what certainty of the true reading will remain? We do not deny that such things can be used for interpretation; but they are by no means to be used for the amendment of the text. For who is ignorant that the Fathers do not always quote the words of Scripture explicitly, but sometimes substitute their own interpretations? Concerning which Grotius himself warned above.

Latin:

Vers. 37.

Ἐδόκουν πνεῦμα θεωρεῖν] Qualem spiritum? malum scilicet. Nam id genus spiritus solebant apparere in specie hominum mortuorum: quomodo Hebræorum plerique historiam de Samuele à Pythonissa evocato interpretantur. In Evangelio Nazaræorum, quod ut diximus multa ex famæ traditione ad Matthæum addita habuit, erat hoc loco pro voce spiritus Dæmonium incorporale. Estque ideo minus repudian- dum, quod Ignatius, qui Apostolos ipsos hæc referentes audire potuit, Christi hanc persuasionem refellentis verba hunc in modum recitat : καὶ ὅτε πρὸς τοὺς περὶ Πέτρον ἦλθεν, ἔφη αὐτοῖς, λάβετε, ψηλαφήσατε με, καὶ ἴδετε ὅτι οὐκ εἰμὶ Δαιμόνιον ἀσώματον. πνεῦμα γὰρ σάρκα κᾀ ὀστέα οὐκ ἔχον' κα- θὼς ἐμὲ θεωρεῖτε ἔχοντα: qui locus eo minus suspectus esse nobis debet quod ita ut nunc legitur, jam olim laudatus sit ab Eusebio: sicut & locus proxime præcedens ab Hierony- mo. Quæ ni fallor ad loci hujus interpretationem non pa- rum pertinent, atque eodem faciunt verba πτοηθέντες, ἔμφο- βοι, τεταραγμένοι in hac historia. Adde quæ diximus ad Matth. XIV. 26. ad verbum φάντασμα. Jam vero non è Versionibus, sed è Patris anti- qui verbis textum emendatum vellet. Qua li- centia si admittatur, quænam lectionis veræ super- erit certitudo? Ad interpretationem adhiberi pos- se talia non negamus; sed ad emendationem textus adhibenda minime sunt. Ecquis enim ignorat, quod Patres non διαῤῥήδην verba Scripturæ adfe- rant semper, sed quandoque sua interpretamenta substituant. Quo de supra monuit ipse Gro- tius.

## 24:38
Vers. 38.

Διαλογισμοὶ ἀναβαίνουσιν ἐν ταῖς καρδίαις ὑμῶν] A locution frequent in the books of the Prophets, which Paul also follows in I. Cor. II. 9. Thus in Latin something is said to come into the mind. But he understands thoughts that are more prone to the worse side. Thus also Dan. II. 28.

Latin:

Vers. 38.

Διαλογισμοὶ ἀναβαίνουσιν ἐν ταῖς καρδίαις ὑμῶν] Locutio in libris Prophetarum frequens, quam & Paulus sequitur I. Cor. II. 9. Sic latine subire aliquid animum dicitur. Cogi- tationes autem intelligit in partem sequiorem proniores. Sic & Dan. II. 28.

## 24:39
Vers. 39. ὅτι πνεῦμα σάρκα καὶ ὀστέα οὐκ ἔχει] Homer, speaking of the souls of the dead: Οὐ γὰρ ἔτι σάρκας τε καὶ ὀστέα ἶνες ἔχουσιν. Maximus Tyrius: οὐ γὰρ σάρκες αἱ δαιμόνων φύσεις. By three arguments Christ refutes that false opinion from the mind of the Apostles, by the judgment of sight, by the judgment of touch, and by the taking of food. Demons are indeed accustomed to appear even in the form of men, but that form does not have solidity, and, if anyone looks more closely with confidence, he will easily find that the form differs from the reality. But terror for the most part prevents the matter from being accurately judged, and if anyone applies touch, the difference will appear much more. For a form fashioned from air (as for the most part) does not suffer touch. Like light winds and most similar to a winged dream. Whence the name φάντασμα is given to images of this kind. Apollonius to Philostratus: λαβὲ μοι, ἔφη, κᾂν μὲν διαφύγω σε εἴδωλόν εἰμί σοι ἐκ Φερσεφάττης ἧκον, οἷα φαίνουσιν οἱ χθόνιοι θεοί· εἰ δὲ ὑπομείναιμι ἁπτόμενον, πεῖθε καὶ Δάμιν ζῆν τέ με κᾂ μὴ ἀποβεβληκέναι τὸ σῶμα. Tertullian, Epiphanius, and others, disputing against Marcion, prove that Christ's body was not a phantom because it could be touched. Someone will object that angels sometimes appeared to pious men, were also touched, and took food, and yet could not be recognized by so many signs; the answer is easy. They were seen, as Tertullian speaks, in true and solid flesh, even if not born, who also says elsewhere, he easily had the power to have given the true substance of flesh, or as its proper author and artificer. But the devil (to continue to speak with the same Tertullian) introduces a phantom of which he cannot provide the reality. But Christ solves that which was occurring to the Apostles concerning a phantom. He does not solve it concerning an Angel, because they did not think that, nor was there indeed any need: for it was certain that Angels do not lie. But he who was appearing professed himself to be Jesus: Therefore he was either a demon, which is proven not to be the case by the application of the judgment of the senses, or Jesus himself.

ANNOTATIONS ON LUKE CH.

Θεωρεῖτε] θεωρεῖν refers not only to sight, but also to other senses, as in John 2:23 and more clearly in Acts 4:13.
