Latin:

Vers. 39. ὅτι πνεῦμα σάρκα καὶ ὀστέα οὐκ ἔχει] Homerus de mortuorum animis locutus : Οὐ γὰρ ἔτι σάρκας τε καὶ ὀστέα ἶνες ἔχουσιν. Maximus Tyrius ὐ γὰρ σάρκες αἱ δαιμόνων φύσεις. Tribus argumentis Christus ex animo Apostolorum refellit falsam illam opinionem, judicio visus accurato, judicio tactus & cibi sumtione. Solent quidem dæmones apparere in spe- cie etiam hominum, sed ea species soliditatem non habet, &, si quis cum fiducia propius intueatur, facile reperiet spe- ciem à re discrepare. Sed terror plerumque impedit, ne res accurate dijudicetur, quod si quis tactum adhibeat multo magis apparebit diversitas. Species enim ex aëre (ut pluri- mum) conformata tactum non patitur. Par levibus ventis volucrique simillima somno. Unde φαντάσματος nomen id genus imaginibus datum est. Apollonius ad Philostratum : λαβὲ μοι, ἔφη, κᾂν μὲν δια- φύγω σε εἴδωλόν εἰμί σοι ἐκ Φερσεφάττης ἧκον, οἷα φαίνουσιν οἱ χθό- νιοι θεοί· εἰ δὲ ὑπομείναιμι ἁπτόμενον, πεῖθε καὶ Δάμιν ζῆν τέ με κᾂ μὴ ἀποβεβληκέναι τὸ σῶμα. Tertullianus, Epiphanius atque alii contra Marcionem disputantes probant Christi corpus non fuisse phantasma quia tangi potuerit. Objiciet aliquis Angelos interdum apparuisse piis hominibus, tactos quo- que & cibum sumsisse neque tamen tot indiciis potuisse co- gnosci, facilis est responsio. Visos eos ut Tertullianus loqui- tur in carne vera & solida etsi non nata, qui & alibi dicit, fa- cile habuit veram dedisse substantiam carnis, vel qua proprius auctor & artifex ejus. Diabolus autem (ut cum eodem Ter- tulliano pergam loqui) phantasma infert cujus non valet veri- tatem. Solvit autem Christus id quod Apostolis occurrebat περὶ φαντάσματος. De Angelo non solvit, quia id non putabant neque vero id opus : Nam certum erat Angelos non mentiri. At is qui apparebat Jesum se esse profiteba- tur : Aut ergo dæmon erat, quod non esse adhibito sen- suum judicio probatur, aut ipse Jesus.

ANNOTATA AD LUCÆ C

Θεωρεῖτε] θεωρεῖν non ad visum tantum, sed & alios sensus refertur, ut Ioh. II. 23. & apertius Act. IV. 13.

## 24:40
Vers. 40. Ἐπέδειξεν] Offering things to be touched, as John teaches in this place, whom see, and at the beginning of the epistle.

Latin:

Vers. 40. Ἐπέδειξεν] Tangenda offerens ut Iohannes do- cet hoc loco, quem vide & epistolæ initio.

## 24:41
Vers. 41. Ἀπιστούντων αὐτῶν] That is, when they were not persuading themselves of the matter as it was with a sufficiently firm mind: for the word ἀπιστίας is taken in this way even in Matthew 17:20.

Ἀπὸ τῆς χαρᾶς] The joy was greater than the mind could contain. Seneca in Thyestes: This peculiar vice follows the wretched, never to trust in happy circumstances. Even if happy fortune returns: yet it is irksome for the afflicted to rejoice. Thus in Aeschylus' Agamemnon, Clytemnestra, when it was announced to her that Troy was captured, says: πῶς φῇς; πέφευγε τοὐπ- πόξ' ἠπιστίας.

Latin:

Vers. 41. Ἀπιστούντων αὐτῶν] Id est cum non satis firmo a- nimo, id quod res erat sibi persuaderent: nam ita vox ἀπι- στίας sumitur etiam Matth XVII. 20.

Ἀπὸ τῆς χαρᾶς] Majus erat gaudium quam quod capere posset animus. Seneca Thyeste: Proprium hoc miseros sequitur vitium, Nunquam rebus credere lætis. Redeat felix fortuna licet: Tamen affictos gaudere piget. Sic apud Æschylum Agamemnone Clytemnestra, cum Troja capta ipsi nunciaretur ait: πῶς φῇς; πέφευγε τοὐπ- πόξ' ἠπιστίας.

## 24:43
Vers. 43. Καὶ λαβὼν ἐνώπιον αὐτῶν ἔφαγεν] Ancient codices should be consulted here as well. For besides the Latin, the Arabic also adds, καὶ λαβὼν τὰ περισσεύματα ἔδωκεν αὐτοῖς. Nor can it be seen as superfluous, since it pertains to a more certain proof of the matter, that the Apostles partook of food in common with him: For Peter urges this very thing in Acts 10:41, we ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead.

Latin:

Vers. 43. Καὶ λαβὼν ἐνώπιον αὐτῶν ἔφαγεν] Consulendi & hic veteres codices. Nam præter Latinum Arabs quoque addit, καὶ λαβὼν τὰ περισσεύματα ἔδωκεν αὐτοῖς. Neque ut supervacuum videri potest, cum ad certiorem rei fidem per- tineat, quod communem cum eo cibum Apostoli sumse- runt: Nam Petrus hoc ipsum urget Act. X. 41. συνεφάγο- μεν καὶ συνεπίομεν αὐτῷ μετὰ τὸ ἀναστῆναι αὐτὸν ἐκ νεκρῶν.

## 24:44
Vers. 44. εἶπε δὲ αὐτοῖς] There follows the summary of the discourses which Jesus had with his Apostles during forty days, which, because they were of the same subject matter, both Mark and Luke—and not only here but in the Acts—recite in a general way. See Acts 1:3.

Οὗτοι οἱ λόγοι] That which you did not believe when I predicted it, or which you did not understand when it was predicted, you now experience in reality. See Matthew 16:21, 17:23, 20:19, Mark 9:31, ch. 10:34, above 9:45, 18:33, 24:7.

ἔτι ὢν σὺν ὑμῖν] Namely, in daily association; for at that time he was present with them only by a special dispensation.

Ὅτι δεῖ] That is, already. Thus Matthew 17:11, Elijah indeed comes first; but δεῖ here refers to the most wise decree of the Father.

καὶ ψαλμοῖς] that is, in the book of Psalms, as above 20:42 and Acts 1:20. Whereby it is more probable that by the most noble part, that whole volume of the Hagiographa is designated, which makes up the third part of the sacred scriptures among the Jews. However, there seems to have been a different division of the books in Josephus's time than is now used, such that the first part consisted of the Pentateuch: the second of all the histories and Prophets, including Daniel: the third of the Psalms, the Proverbs of Solomon, the Ecclesiastes of the same, and the Song of Songs. This third part, comprised of four books as I said, Josephus describes thus: αἱ δὲ λοιπαὶ τέσσαρες ὕμνους εἰς τὸν Θεὸν καὶ τοῖς ἀνθρώ- ποις ὑποθήκας τοῦ βίου περιέχουσι.

Latin:

Vers. 44. εἶπε δὲ αὐτοῖς] Sequitur summa sermonum quos per quadraginta dies Iesus cum Apostolis suis habuit, quos quia ejusdem erant argumenti tum Marcus, tum Lucas neq; hic tantum sed in actis καθολικῶς recitat. Vid. Act. I. 3.

Οὗτοι οἱ λόγοι] Quod prædicenti mihi non credidistis aut quod prædictum non intellexistis, nunc reipsa experimini. Vid. Matth. XVI. 21. XVII. 23. XX. 19. Marc. IX. 31. c. X. 34. supra IX. 45. XVIII. 33. XXIV. 7.

ἔτι ὢν σὺν ὑμῖν] Quotidiano scilicet convictu; Nam tunc tantum κατ' οἰκονομίαν illis aderat.

Ὅτι δεῖ] Id est ἤδη. Sic Matth. XVII. 11. ἠλίας μὲν ἔρχεται πρῶτον, refertur autem δεῖ hic ad patris decretum sapientis- simum.

καὶ ψαλμοῖς] id est ἐν βίβλῳ ψαλμῶν, ut supra XX. 42. & Act. I. 20. Quo probabilius est ex parte nobilissima totum illud volumen ἁγιογράφων designari, quod sacrarum apud Iudæos literarum partem efficit tertiam. Videtur autem a- lia fuisse librorum divisio Iosephi temporibus, quam nunc usurpatur, ita ut prima pars constaret ex Pentateucho: se- cundo ex omnibus historiis & Prophetis comprehenso et- iam Daniele: tertia ex Psalmis, tententiis Salomonis, e- jusdem Ecclesiastæ & carmine Epithalamio. Tertiam hanc partem, quatuor ut dixi libris comprehensam ita describit Iosephus: αἱ δὲ λοιπαὶ τέσσαρες ὕμνους εἰς τὸν Θεὸν καὶ τοῖς ἀνθρώ- ποις ὑποθήκας τοῦ βίου περιέχουσι.

## 24:45
Vers. 45. Διήνοιξεν αὐτῶν τὸν νοῦν τοῦ συνιέναι τὰς γραφάς] The outcome is the best interpreter of prophecies. But not even in this way can it be sufficiently understood what corresponds to what, unless the mind is enlightened by the inspirer of the Prophets through a certain singular gift: which we have noted elsewhere is called interpretation or explanation. Justin in his dialogue with Trypho: Do you think that we would ever have been able to understand these things in the scriptures if we had not received grace from the will of Him who willed them to understand? And elsewhere in the same book: For no such power is in me, but grace from God alone was given to me to understand his scriptures. In the institutions of Clement it is read concerning God: To Him who is able to open the ears of your hearts to receive the oracles of God that have been ministered. Origen IV. On First Principles, speaking of the Sacred writings: 'For the discourse concerning each of these things does not make the most difficult and lofty matters very clear to men.' And what need is there to speak of the prophecies, which we all know to be filled with riddles and dark sayings, and if we reach the Gospels, even the precise mind of those, being as it is the mind of Christ, requires the grace given to the one who has spoken, but we have the mind of Christ. This he then illustrates with examples. The same in the letter to Gregory: 'Attending to the divine reading, seek rightly and according to the faith from God, that which is unswervingly hidden from the many in the divine scriptures: and it is not enough to knock and to seek, for the effort concerning the understanding of these things is also most necessary.' And these things indeed he says concerning the gift of knowledge. For concerning the gift toward faith, we have explained elsewhere what they think. Both gifts are described with similar words. For it is also said to those who first believe in Christ, 'to open the heart' (Acts 16:14). Which Justin called 'the opening of the gates of light'.

Latin:

Vers. 45. Διήνοιξεν αὐτῶν τὸν νοῦν τοῦ συνιέναι τὰς γραφάς] Eventus optimus vaticiniorum interpres. Sed ne sic quidem satis intelligi potest, quid cui rei conveniat nisi mens dono quodam singulari: quod ἑρμηνείας aut ἐπιλύσεως dici notavi- mus alibi, illustretur ab inspiratore Prophetarum. Iustinus colloquio cum Tryphone: οἴεσθε ἂν ἡμᾶς ποτὲ ὦ ἄνδρες νε- νοηκέναι δυνηθῆναι ἐν ταῖς γραφαῖς ταῦτα εἰ μὴ θελήματι τοῦ θελή- σαντος αὐτὰ ἐλάβομεν χάριν τοῦ νοῆσαι; Et alibi eodem libro: οὐδὲ γὰρ δύναμις ἐμοὶ τοιαύτη τίς ἐστιν, ἀλλὰ χάρις παρὰ Θεοῦ μόνη εἰς τὸ συνιέναι τὰς γραφὰς αὐτοῦ ἐδόθη μοι. In Clementis institu- tionibus legitur de Deo: Τῷ δυναμένῳ ἀνοῖξαι τὰ ὦτα τῶν καρδιῶν ὑμῶν εἰς τὸ καταδέχεσθαι τὰ διακονημένα τοῦ Θεοῦ λόγια. Orige- nes IV. περὶ ἀρχῶν de scriptis Sacris loquens: διατὰν οὐδ' ὑπερ- βολὴν χαλεπωτάτην ὕψεσιν τῶν πραγμάτων τοῖς ἀνθρώποις οὐ πά- νυ σαφνίζεται, ὁ περὶ τούτων ἑκάστου λόγος. Καὶ τὶ δεῖ λέγειν περὶ τῶν προφητειῶν ἃς πάντες ἴσμεν αἰνιγμάτων καὶ σκοτεινῶν πεπλη- ρῶσθαι λόγων, καὶ ἐπὶ τὰ εὐαγγέλια τὸ φθάσωμεν κ' ἀκείνων ὁ ἀ- κριβὴς νοῦς, ἅτε νοῦς ὢν χριστοῦ, δεῖται χάριτος τῆς δοθείσης τῷ εἰ- ρηκότι, ἡμεῖς δὲ νοῦν χριστοῦ ἔχομεν. Quod deinde exemplis illustrat. Idem in epistola ad Gregorium: Προσέχων τῇ θείᾳ ἀναγνώσει ὀρθῶς ζήτει καὶ κατὰ πίστεως τῆς ἐκ Θεοῦ ἀκλινῶς τὲ κεκρυμ- μένον τοῖς πολλοῖς τῶν τῶν θείων γραμμάτων: μὴ ἀρκεῖ δὲ τοῦ προύειν καὶ ζητεῖν ἀναγκαιοτάτα γὰρ καὶ ἡ περὶ τοῦ νοεῖν ταῦτα ἕνεξις. Et hæc quidem illi de dono τῆς γνώσεως. Nam de dono πρὸς πί- στιν quid sentiant alibi exposuimus. Utrumque donum simi- libus verbis describitur. Nam & his qui primum in Chri- stum credunt dicitur διανοῖχσαι ἡ καρδία Act. XVI. 14. Quod Iustinus dixit φωτὸς ἀνοιχθῆναι πύλας.

## 24:46
V. 46. 'That Christ should suffer.' We have spoken above concerning the testimonies pertaining to the sufferings of Christ at verse 26 and elsewhere.

And 'to rise from the dead on the third day.' According to the example of Jonah. The deliverances of David and others from extreme dangers had also borne the image of this resuscitation. See Acts 2:25 and 13:35.

Latin:

V. 46. Παθεῖν τὸν χριστὸν] De testimoniis ad Christi perpes- siones pertinentibus diximus supra ad comma 26. & alibi.

Καὶ ἀναστῆναι ἐκ νεκρῶν τῇ τρίτῃ ἡμέρᾳ] Ad Exemplum Io- næ. Hujus resuscitationis imaginem quoque gesserant libe- rationes Davidis atque aliorum è summis periculis. Vide Act. II. 25. & XIII. 35.

## 24:47
Vers. 47. 'And that repentance should be preached in his name.' 'In his name' is rightly explained as by Christ's command, and as if performing his duties, 2 Cor. 5:20: 'We are ambassadors for Christ, as though God were pleading through us; we implore you on Christ's behalf, be reconciled to God.' And so Christ himself is also said to preach the gospel to the nations through his envoys (Eph. 2:17). This announcement has two parts: a demand and a promise: repentance is demanded, under which name all obedience is comprehended: the remission of sins is promised, in which are contained eternal life and its earnest, the Holy Spirit. Both parts are sealed through baptism, as Matthew and Mark teach us. To this preaching of repentance pertain both other things among the Prophets, and especially the illustrious passage of Isaiah 49:6: 'Is it a small thing that you should be my servant, to raise up the tribes of Jacob and to convert the desolate ones of Israel?' I have also set you as a light to the nations. Add what is in Isaiah 61, cited above at the beginning of Luke 4:18, and Ps. 22:23-28.

And 'remission of sins.' Is. 53:12: 'He himself bore the sin of many and will intercede for the transgressors.' Jer. 31:34: 'I will forgive their iniquity and will remember their sin no more.'

To 'all the nations.' Is. 49: 'Listen to me, O islands, and you distant nations.' Hos. 2:23: 'I will call those who were not my people, my people.' Ps. 2: 'I will give the nations as your inheritance.' Joel 3:5: 'Whoever shall call upon the name of the Lord shall be saved.' Malachi 1:11: 'From the rising to the setting of the sun, my name shall be great among the nations.' Dan. 7:14: 'And he gave him power and a kingdom, and all peoples, nations, and languages shall serve him.'

Beginning from Jerusalem. From the city of David, whose throne was promised to the Messiah (Ps. 132, Is. 9:16, and elsewhere); to this point pertain those things in Ps. 2:6: 'I have set my king upon Zion.' Ps. 110:2: 'The Lord shall send the rod of your strength out of Zion.' Is. 2:3: 'Out of Zion shall go forth the law and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem.' Is. 28:16: 'I lay in Zion a stone, a precious stone.' Is. 40:9: 'Go up onto a high mountain, you who bring good tidings to Zion; lift up your voice with strength, you who bring good tidings to Jerusalem.' Isaiah 60:1: 'Arise, be enlightened, Jerusalem,' which the LXX add. Refer here to that which is in Suetonius, namely, the report spread at that time that one would come from Judea who would rule the world.

PART IV. The promise of the Holy Spirit.

Latin:

Vers. 47. Καὶ κηρυχθῆναι ἐπὶ τῷ ὀνόματι αὐτοῦ μετάνοιαν] ἐπὶ τῷ ὀνόματι αὐτοῦ recte exponitur Christi mandato, & quasi vi- ces ejus obeundo, 2. Cor. V. 20. ὑπὲρ χριστοῦ ὖν πρεσβεύομεν, ὡς τοῦ Θεοῦ παρακαλοῦντος δι' ἡμῶν, δεόμεθα ὑπὲρ χριστοῦ καταλλά- γητε τῷ Θεῷ. Itaque & Christus ipse per legatos suos dicitur gentibus εὐαγγελίζεσθαι Eph. II. 17. Hæc annunciatio duas ha- bet partes: postulationem & promissionem: postulatur pœnitentia cujus nomine tota obedientia comprehenditur: promittitur remissio peccatorum, in quo continentur vita æterna, & ejus arrhabo Spiritus Sanctus. Utraque pars per baptismum obsignatur, ut Matthæus & Marcus nos docent. Ad hoc pœnitentiæ κήρυγμα tum alia apud Prophetas perti- nent, tum imprimis illustris Esaiæ locus XLIX. 6. Exiguum est quod te mihi ministrum elegi, ad suscitandas tribus Jacobi & convertendos desolatos Israelis? Etiam lucem gentium te consti- tui. Adde quæ sunt Esaiæ LXI. in principio citata supra apud Lucam IV. 18. & Ps. XXII. 23---28.

Καὶ ἄφεσιν ἁμαρτιῶν] Es. LIII. 12. Ipse tulit multorum peccatum & pro fontibus deprecabitur. Jer. XXXII. 34. Con- donabo iniquitatem ipsorum & peccati ipsorum non recordabor amplius.

Εἰς πάντα τὰ ἔθνη] Es. LXIX. Audite insulæ me, & natio- nes longinquæ. Os. II. 23. Vocabo non populum meum, po- pulum meum. Ps. II. Dabo gentes hæreditatem tuam. Joel. III. v. 5. Quisquis invocabit nomen Dei evadet. Malachiæ I. 11. Ab ortu ad occasum magnum erit nomen meum inter gentes. Dan. VII. 14. Et dedit ei potestatem & regnum, & omnes po- puli, nationes & linguæ ei servient.

Ἀρξάμενον ἀπὸ Ἱερουσαλὴμ] Ab urbe Davidis cujus solium Messiæ erat promissum Ps. CXXXII. Es. IX. 16. & alibi, huc illa pertinent Ps. II. 6. Ego constitui regem meum super Sion. Ps. CX. v. 2. Sceptrum roboris tui mittet Deus ex Sion. Es. II. 3. De Sione exibit lex & verbum Dei ex Hierosolymis. Es. XXVIII. 16. Fundo in Sione lapidem, lapidem pretiosum. Es. XL. 9. Super celsum montem ascende, bonorum nuntia Sion, vocem tuam ve- hementer effer bonorum nuntia Ierusalem. Esaiæ LX. 1. Surge illuminare, Jerusalem scilicet quod addunt LXX. Huc refer illud quod apud Suetonium est vulgatam scilicet eo tempo- re famam, ex Judæa proditurum qui orbi imperaret.

PARS IV. Promissio Spiritus Sancti.

## 24:48
Vers. 48. 'And you are witnesses of these things.' Namely, of my life, death, and resurrection, upon which foundations the whole basis of that announcement is built. But especially the resurrection, as the leader of the Apostles teaches us in Acts ch. 1:21-22. For if Jesus rose, he certainly rose by divine power. And for what purpose could God have done that, except to show openly that what had been announced by him was true, namely, that God's peace—and consequently eternal life—is open to his followers (however damnable their life may have been before). But the resurrection could not be proven except in the way that facts are proven, namely, by the testimony of eyewitnesses, honest men hoping for no advantages from their testimony; however, 'are' (ἐστὲ) is placed here as present for the future 'will be' (ἔσεσθε), as can be seen in Acts 1:8. Thus in the following verse 'I send' (ἀποστέλλω) is placed for 'I will send' (ἀποστελῶ).

The promise of my Father. Namely, so that you may bear that testimony more firmly and constantly against the madness of the world; thus Luke himself explains this in Acts 1:8: 'You shall receive power of the Holy Spirit upon you and you shall be my witnesses, in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria and to the end of the earth.' Where 'and you shall be' (καὶ ἔσεσθε) is in the Hebrew manner, meaning 'so that you may be.' He calls the gift of the Holy Spirit 'the promise of the Father' (ἐπαγγελίαν πατρὸς) promised to him by the Father, so that it might be given by him to the disciples. Thus in Acts 1: 'the promise of the Father which you heard from me.' See Joel 2:28, which is explained in Acts 2; add Isaiah 44:3, Ezekiel 36:26, and John 15:26, 16:7, and Jeremiah 31:33. But he rightly subjoined it to the command of bearing testimony, as if to say: You indeed will bear testimony to me by word concerning the things seen, and I will bear testimony to you within concerning the things hoped for; 'he will bear witness concerning me' (John 15:26).

Latin:

Vers. 48. Ὑμεῖς δέ ἐστε μάρτυρες τούτων] Vitæ nempe meæ, mortis & resurrectionis, quibus fundamentis totum illius annunciationis fundamentum superstruitur. Sed resurre- ctioni præcipue ut nos docet Apostolorum Coryphæus Act. c. I. 21. 22. Nam si Jesus resurrexit, certe resurrexit virtute di- vina. At quorum Deus id fecisse potuit, nisi ut palam often- deret verum esse, quod ab ipso erat annuntiatum, sectato- ribus nempe ipsius (quantumvis antea damnabilis vitæ) pa- tere Dei pacem ac proinde vitam æternam. Resurrectio au- tem probari non potuit, nisi quomodo facta probantur, te- stimonio scilicet αὐτοπτῶν, hominum proborum nulla ex testimonio commoda sperantium; ponitur autem hic ἐστὲ præsens pro futuro ἔσεσθε ut videre est Act. I. 8. Sic in se- quenti commate ἀποστέλλω est positum pro ἀποστελῶ.

τὴν ἐπαγγελίαν τοῦ πατρός με] Nempe quo firmius atque constantius adversus inundi rabiem testimonium illud præ- beatis, ita Act. I. 8. Lucas ipse hoc explicat: λήψεσθε δύνα- μιν τοῦ ἁγίε πνεύματος ἐφ' ὑμᾶς καὶ ἔσεσθε μοι μάρτυρες, ἔν τῇ ἱερουσαλὴμ καὶ ἐν πάσῃ τῇ ἰουδαίᾳ καὶ Σαμαρείᾳ καὶ ἕως ἐσχάτε τῆς γῆς. Ubi καὶ ἔσεσθε more Hebræo est ut sitis: ἐπαγγελίαν πατρὸς vocat donum Spiritus Sancti sibi à patre promissum, ut à se discipulis daretur. Ita Act. I. τὴν ἐπαγγε- λίαν τοῦ πατρὸς ἣν ἠκούσατέ με. Vide Joel. II. 28. quod ex- plicatur Act. II. adde Esaiam XLIV. 3. Ezechiel. XXXVI. v. 26. & Joh. XV. 26. XVI. 7. & Ierem. XXII. 33. Bene au- tem subjunxit mandato ferendi testimonii, quasi dicat: Vos quidem mihi sermone testimonium præbebitis rerum con- spectarum, atque ego vobis intus testimonium præbebo re- rum speratarum, ἐκεῖνος μαρτυρήσει περὶ ἐμοῦ, Ioh. XV. 26.

## 24:49
καθίσατε] That is, do not depart, as interpreted by Luke himself in Acts ch. 1, v. 4. Wherefore I judge this part of the discourse to have been held by Christ after the Apostles had returned from Galilee.

Ενδύσησθε δύναμιν ἐξ ὕψες] ἐνδύειν here corresponds to the Hebrew לבש, which the LXX in Judges 6:34 translate as ἐνδυναμοῖ, but the Hebrews also speak of being clothed with astonishment, shame, or curses, so that it appears that among them everything is said to be put on which does not approach and depart, but adheres thoroughly. John 14:16: 'He will give you another Comforter, that he may abide with you forever.' And by this property this gift is distinguished from the spirit of oversight or of heresies.

ἐξ ὕψες] ממרומים, so also above 1:78.

PART V. The Ascension of Christ into heaven.

Latin:

καθίσατε] Id est μὴ χωρίζεσθε, Interprete Luca ipso Act. c. I. v. 4. Quare hanc partem sermonis à Christo habitam arbitror postquam è Galilæa Apostoli redierant.

Ενδύσησθε δύναμιν ἐξ ὕψες] ἐνδύειν hic respondet Hebræo לבש, quod LXX. Iud. VI. 34. vertunt ἐνδυναμοῖ, sed & in- dui stupore, pudore, diris, dicunt Hebræi ut appareat dici a- pud illos omne id indui quod non accedit & recedit sed pe- nitus adhæret Ioh. XIV. 16. ἄλλον παράκλητον δώσει ὑμῖν ἵνα μένῃ μεθ' ὑμῶν εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα. Atque hac proprietate donum hoc distinguitur à spiritu τῆς ἐπισκοπῆς 7 αἱρέσεων.

ἐξ ὕψες] ממרומים ita & supra I. 78.

PARS V. Ascensio Christi in cælum.

## 24:50
Vers. 50. ἕως εἰς βηθανίαν] To that part of Bethany which was on the Mount of Olives, on which mount Christ had often poured out prayers and tears to the Father, so that the place which had been the witness of his submission might also be the same for his glory. See Acts 1.

Ἐπάρας τὰς χεῖρας αὐτοῦ] It does not signify the simple custom of praying, of which we treated above in 17:13, but the rite of blessing which used to be performed with hands imposed, that is, by the laying on of hands: as can be seen in the history of Isaac, Gen. 27:4, 7, 12, 19, 21, 22.

21. 22. & of Jacob Gen. XLVIII. 9. 14. 15. 16. 17. But as often as a blessing (εὐλογία) had to be imparted to many at once, for the sake of brevity the laying on of hands (χειροθεσία), that is, the stretching out of hands over their heads, for whom prayers were offered, is used. Thus Levit. IX. 22. Aaron lifted up his hands toward the people and blessed them (ἐπάρας Ἀαρὼν τὰς χεῖρας ἐπὶ τ λαὸν εὐλόγησεν αὐτούς). The Bishops of the Christians used this custom both at the beginning and at the end of every assembly: whence Optatus of Milevis reproves Macarius the judge, because although he had spoken to the people of Carthage in the Church, he had done nothing on behalf of a Bishop. His words are in the seventh book of the disputation against Parmenianus: And it is certain that he spoke something among the people: but for the purpose of insinuating some matter, yet not of treating (that is, of teaching), which is the duty of Bishops. For he spoke nakedly as he was able to speak. On the contrary, an Episcopal discourse is proved by being clothed with holiness, namely by a doubled greeting (he calls the blessing (τὴν εὐλογίαν) a greeting here). For a Bishop does not begin to say anything to the people, unless he has first greeted the people in the name of God: the endings are similar to the beginnings, every discourse in the Church is begun in the name of God & is terminated in the name of the same God. Which of you dares to say that Macarius greeted the people in the manner of Bishops? Therefore, since he neither greeted them before he spoke anything, nor dared to greet them, nor laid on his hand, nor offered a sacrifice to God by the Episcopal rite, why is it that you say the Episcopal college is polluted, when you see Macarius is a stranger to every office of Bishops. Light is brought to this passage of Optatus from the ancient constitutions which are read under the name of Clement, but we do not permit laymen to perform any of the priestly works, such as sacrifice or baptism or the laying on of hands or a small or great blessing (ἀλλ᾽ ὔτε λαϊκοῖς ἐπιτρέπομεν ποιεῖν τι ἷ ἱερατικῶν ἔργων οἷον θυ- σίαν ἢ βάπτισμα ἢ χειροθεσίαν ἢ εὐλογίαν μικρὰν ἢ μεγά- λην).

He blessed them (εὐλόγησεν αὐτὸς)] That is, he blessed over them (εὐλόγησεν ἐπ᾿ αὐτούς). Thus Matth. V. v. 14. bless those who curse you (εὐλογεῖτε τὲς καταρωμένες). And often in the LXX, as in the places already cited, to bless (εὐλογεῖν) is sometimes to give thanks, sometimes, as here, to pray.

He blessed them (Εὐλόγησαι αὐτὲς)] He solemnly prayed well for them.

Latin:

Vers. 50. ἕως εἰς βηθανίαν] Ad eam Bethaniæ partem quæ in monte erat Oliveti, in quo monte sæpe Christus preces & lacrymas ad patrem fuderat, ut qui locus submissionis i- psius testis fuerat, idem esset & gloriæ. Vide Act. I.

Ἐπάρας τὰς χεῖρας αὐτοῦ] Non simplex precandi mos si- gnificatur de quo egimus supra XVII. 13. sed ritus εὐλογίας qui fieri solebat manibus impositis, id est διὰ χειρῶν ἐπιθέ- σεως : ut videre est in historia Isaaci Gen. XXVII. 4. 7. 12. 19. 21. 22.

21. 22. & Jacobi Gen. XLVIII. 9. 14. 15. 16. 17. At quoties pluribus simul impartienda esset εὐλογία, compendii causa usurpatur χειροθεσία id est manus protensio super eorum ca- pita, p o quibus preces offerebantur. Ita Levit. IX. 22. ἐπάρας Ἀαρὼν τὰς χεῖρας ἐπὶ τ λαὸν εὐλόγησεν αὐτούς. Eum morem tum initio tum fine cujusque conventus usurparunt Christianorum Episcopi: unde probat Optatus Milevitanus Macarium judicem, quanquam ad populum Carthaginien- sem in Ecclesia verba fecisset, nihil tamen pro Episcopo fe- cisse. Verba ejus sunt disputatione adversus Parmenia- num septima: Et locutum eum esse aliquid in populo constat: sed insinuanda alicujus rei causa non tamen tractandi (id est docendi) quod est Episcoporum. Ille enim nude locutus est sicut loqui potuit. Contra Episcopalis tractatus probatur ab omnibus sanctitate vestitus, salutatione scilicet geminata (salutationem hic vocat τὴν εὐλογίαν) Non enim incipit aliquid Episcopus ad populum dicere, nisi prius in nomine Dei populum salutaverit: similes sunt exitus initiis, omnis tractatus in Ecclesia a nomine Dei incipitur & ejusdem Dei nomine terminatur. Quis ve- strum audet dicere Episcoporum more Macarium populum salu- tasse? Itaque cum nec salutaverit antequam aliquid loque- retur nec salutare ausus sit, nec manum imposuerit, nec sacrifi- cium Deo ritu Episcopali obtulerit, quid est quod dicitis pollui e- piscopale collegium, cum ab omni Episcoporum officio Macarium videatis alienum. Lux huic loco Optati affertur ex consti- tutionibus antiquisquæ sub Clementis nomine leguntur, ἀλλ᾽ ὔτε λαϊκοῖς ἐπιτρέπομεν ποιεῖν τι ἷ ἱερατικῶν ἔργων οἷον θυ- σίαν ἢ βάπτισμα ἢ χειροθεσίαν ἢ εὐλογίαν μικρὰν ἢ μεγά- λην.

εὐλόγησεν αὐτὸς] Id est εὐλόγησεν ἐπ᾿ αὐτούς. Sic Matth. V. v. 14. εὐλογεῖτε τὲς καταρωμένες. Et sæpe LXX. ut locis jam citatis, εὐλογεῖν modo est gratias agere, modo ut hic precari.

Εὐλόγησαι αὐτὲς] Solenniter bene eis est precatus.

## 24:51
Ver. 51. While he was blessing (Ἐν τῷ εὐλογεῖν)] As soon as he had fulfilled that rite while bidding farewell.

He parted from them, and was carried up into heaven (Διέςη ἀπ᾿ αὐτῶν, καὶ ἀνεφέρετο εἰς τ ὀρανὸν)] Thus also in the history of Elijah 2 Kings II. 11. and they were separated from each other and Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven (ויפרדו בין שניהם ויעל אליהו בסערה השמים) where some Greeks say they parted (διέςησαν), others they separated (διεχώρισαν) between them both. You could say more briefly: he went up from them (עלה מעליהם) thus Gen. c. XVII. 22. and God went up from Abraham (ויעל אלהים מעל אברהם) God went up from Abraham (Ἀνέβη ὁ Θεὸς ἀπὸ Ἀβραάμ). Luke himself interprets it Acts I. 9. while they were looking he was taken up, and a cloud received him out of their sight (βλεπόντων αὐτῶν ἐπήρθη, καὶ νεφέλη ὑπέλαβεν αὐτὸν ἀπὸ τ ὀφθαλμῶν αὐτῶν).

Was carried up into heaven (Ἀνεφέρετο εἰς τ ὀρανὸν)] The heaven of heavens, which Paul called far above all heavens (ὑπεράνω πάντων ὀρανῶν) Eph. IV. 10.

Latin:

Vers. 51. Ἐν τῷ εὐλογεῖν] Simul atque ritum illum valedi- cens impleverat.

Διέςη ἀπ᾿ αὐτῶν, καὶ ἀνεφέρετο εἰς τ ὀρανὸν] Sic & in Eliæ historia 2. Reg. II. 11. ויפרדו בין שניהם ויעל אליהו בסערה השמים ubi Græci alii διέςησαν, alii διεχώρισαν ἀνὰ μέσον ἀμφοτέρων. Brevius posses dicere: עלה מעליהם ita Gen. c. VII. 22. ויעל אלהים מעל אברהם Ἀνέβη ὁ Θεὸς ἀπὸ Ἀβραάμ. Interpretatur Lucas ipse Actor. I. 9. βλεπόντων αὐτῶν ἐπήρθη, καὶ νεφέλη ὑπέλαβεν αὐτὸν ἀπὸ τ ὀφθαλμῶν αὐτῶν.

Ἀνεφέρετο εἰς τ ὀρανὸν] τὸν ὀρανὸν τ ὀρανῶν quod ὑπεράνω πάντων ὀρανῶν dixit Paulus Eph. IV. 10.

## 24:52
Ver. 52. Having worshipped him (Προσκυνήσαντες αὐτὸν)] With prostrate body, which they had not done before, since in the days of his flesh (as the writer to the Hebrews speaks) they were admitted to familiar living. Now they do it, having openly recognized his majesty. 2 Cor. V. 16. even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him no longer (εἰ δὲ καὶ ἐγνώκαμεν κατὰ σαρκὰ χρισὸν, ἀλλὰ νῦν ἐκ ἔτι γινώσκομεν).

They returned to Jerusalem (Ὑπέτρεψαν εἰς Ἱερεσαλὴμ)] So also Acts I. 12. It is shown how obedient they were to the word of Christ.

With great joy (μετὰ χαρᾶς μεγάλης)] Because of the understood admirable reason by which the redemption of the human race had been procured, and because of that remarkable promise of sending the Spirit.

Latin:

Vers. 52. Προσκυνήσαντες αὐτὸν] Corpore prostrato quod antehac non fecerant quippe ἐν ταῖς ἡμέραις τῆς σαρκὸς ἀυτᾶ (ut loquitur ad Hebræos scriptor) ad familiarem victum admissi. Nunc faciunt majestati ipsius aperte cognita. 2. Cor. V. 16. εἰ δὲ καὶ ἐγνώκαμεν κατὰ σαρκὰ χρισὸν, ἀλλὰ νῦν ἐκ ἔτι γινώσκομεν.

Ὑπέτρεψαν εἰς Ἱερεσαλὴμ] Ita & Actor. I. 12. Ostenditur quam parentes dicto Christi fuerint.

μετὰ χαρᾶς μεγάλης] Ob intellectam rationem admira- bilem qua procurata erat redemtio generis humani, & ob insignem illam pollicitationem mittendi spiritus.

## 24:53
Ver. 53. And they were continually in the temple (Καὶ ἦσαν διαπαντὸς ἐν τῷ ἱερῷ)] For the Jews were accustomed to pray and also to give thanks to God in the temple rather than elsewhere: especially if anything greater had happened. See above XVIII. 10. Understand continually (Διαπαντὸς) as daily, namely at appropriate times. Thus Peter and John are reported in Acts III. to have gone into the temple about the ninth hour, which was destined for evening prayers. What they did after receiving the Spirit, it is credible that they also did for ten days after the Lord's ascension (ἀνάληψιν): concerning which time these things seem to me to be understood. Nor does it stand in the way that they had their assemblies at that time in private houses, as we are taught in Acts I. 15. for they did the same even after receiving the Spirit, although in the meantime they went to the temple daily Acts c. II. 46. c. III. v. 1. V. 25. XII. 12.

Ludov. de Dieu, however, on Acts 1:13, wishes that word διαπαντὸς to be taken properly, that they were always in the temple, διαμένοντες, remaining, as it is said in Acts 1:13: where Luke says thus: and when they had entered, to wit, into the city, they went up εἰς τὸ ὑπερῷον into the upper room. For he says that the temple had upper rooms, 1 Chron. 28:11 and 2 Chron. 3:9, as also chambers, or rooms, in which not only were the temple guards and the ministering priests and Levites, and the sacred things kept, but also assemblies of religious men were held, where they occupied themselves with sacred things: whence Baruch is said to have read the book of Jeremiah in the chamber of Gemariah, in the house of the Lord, Jer. 36:10, and that the prophetess Anna had such a chamber, Luke ch. 2:26, and that the apostles chose such a place for themselves in the temple and remained there continually προσκαρτεροῦντες ὁμοθυμαδὸν τῇ προσευχῇ & δεήσει, continuing with one accord in prayer and supplication, Acts 1:14. That the Holy Spirit also filled that place or upper room afterwards on the Feast of Pentecost, Acts 2:2, so that by the house there is understood the temple, as the House of the Lord, Hagg. 2:7, 9, or the upper room, or chamber, in which the disciples of Christ were, since such chambers are also called a house by the LXX, Jer. 36:10, 12, 20, 21, ch. 35:4, but not some private house, either of John the Evangelist, as Nicephorus says from Evodius, or of Mary the mother of John, whose surname was Mark, as Beza wishes. Xevius, however, thinks that the aforementioned prophecy of Hagg. 2:7, 9 was fulfilled on the Feast of Pentecost, when the Holy Spirit filled the temple with His glory. But since it is hardly permissible to presume that the disciples of Christ were perpetually tolerated in the temple, and that a special upper room was granted to them there, in which they all remained safe until the time of Pentecost, and they are not said to have been gathered in the temple or any chamber of the temple, but simply in an upper room, Acts 1:13, and Luke reports that the wind filled not the temple, but simply some house, on the Feast of Pentecost, v. 2:2, who without doubt would have made express mention of the temple, as elsewhere, especially in this history of the mission of the Holy Spirit, if it had happened in the temple, the words 'remained always in the temple' are to be understood in no other way than as in Acts 2:46. they are said to have continued daily with one accord in the temple, not because they were always and perpetually in the same place, because it is added that they broke bread from house to house, namely in different houses, but because they were accustomed to meet in the temple at a certain time, every day, as is also observed here by Grotius.

Ἀμήν] Added by the Church, which was accustomed to receive the reading of the Gospel with this acclamation, 1 Cor. 14:16.

We leave this Grotian judgment in the middle. It does not, however, seem to be devoid of probability: because perhaps this little word does not so cohere or agree with the preceding words of the text.

And these things regarding the Gospel of Luke. For the rest, about which one could be advised, can be judged from those things which have been observed regarding Matthew, or even Mark. St. Luke concludes with praise and blessing of the disciples of Christ: May Christ grant that we may be like the disciples of Christ, and always praise and bless God, and finally conclude this life with praise and blessing, so that in eternal life we may sing without end with the holy angels and all the elect:

Blessing, and glory, and wisdom, and thanksgiving, and honor, and power, and might be unto our God for ever and ever, AMEN.

Latin:

Vers. 53. Καὶ ἦσαν διαπαντὸς ἐν τῷ ἱερῷ] Nam in templo potius quam alibi, ut precari, ita & gratias agere Deo Ju- dæi solebant: præsertim si quid majus incidisset. Vide su- pra XVIII. 10. Διαπαντὸς intellige quotidie, temporibus nimirum congruis. Ita Petrus & Johannes Act. III. nar- rantur iisse in templum circa horam nonam, quæ destinata erat precibus vespertinis. Quod post acceptum spiritum fecerunt, idem eos & decem diebus post Domini ἀνάληψιν fecisse credibile est: de quo tempore hæc mihi videntur accipienda. Nec obstat quod cœtus suos eo tempore habue- runt in privatis ædibus, ut docemur Actor. I. 15. nam idem fecerunt & post acceptum Spiritum, quamvis quotidie in- terea & templum adirent Act. c. II. 46. c. III. v. 1. V. 25. XII. 12.

Proprie tamen illud διαπαντὸς accipi vult Lu- dov. de Dieu ad Act. I. 13. quod semper in templo fue- rint, διαμένοντες permanentes, ut Act. I. 13. dici- tur: ubi ita Lucas: & cum intrassent, scil. in ur- bem, ascenderunt εἰς τὸ ὑπερῷον in cænaculum. Ha- buisse enim, ait, templum ὑπερῷα 1. Par. XXVIII. v. 11. & 2. Par. III. 9. ut & cubicula, vel conclavia, in quibus non tantum templi custodes, ac ministri Sacerdotes & Levitæ fuerint, ac res sacræ asserva- tæ, sed & religiosorum hominum conventus habiti sint, ubi sacris vacarint: unde in conclavi Ga- mariæ, in domo Domini, Baruch legisse librum Je- remiæ dicatur Jer. XXXVI. 10. atque tale etiam conclave habuisse Annam Prophetissam Luc. c. II. 26, talemque locum in templo sibi delegisse Apostolos & illic permansisse jugiter προσκαρτε- ροῦντες ὁμοθυμαδὸν τῇ προσευχῇ & δεήσει Act. I. 14. Illum etiam locum vel ὑπερῷον & cœnaculum istud postmodum implevisse Spiritum S. in Festo Pente- costes Actor. II. 2. ut per domum ibi intelligatur templum, ceu Domus Domini Hagg. II. 7. 9. vel cœ- naculum, aut conclave, in quo fuêre discipuli Christi, siquidem & conclavia ejusmodi domus a- pud LXX. vocentur, Jerem. XXXVI. 10. 12. 20. 21. c. XXXV. 4. non vero ædes quædam privatæ, seu Johannis Evangelistæ, uti Nicephorus ex Evodio, seu Mariæ Matris Johannis, cui cognomentum Marci erat, ut Beza vult. Censet autem Xevius vaticinium prædictum Hagg. II. 7. 9. impletum fuisse in Festo Pentecostes, cum Spiritus S. glo- ria sua implevit templum. Sed quum præsumere vix liceat, discipulos Christi perpetuo in templo toleratos, iisdemque peculiare illic cœnaculum concessum fuisse, in quo omnes tuti permanserint usque ad tempus Pentecostes, neque in templo vel conclavi aliquo templi, sed simpliciter in cœnaculo dicantur congregati fuisse. Act. I. 13. nec templum, sed simpliciter domum aliquam ventum replevisse, Festo Pentecostes, Lucas perhibeat v. II. 2. qui procul ambiguo disertam templi mentionem, uti alias, in hac imprimis historia missionis Spiritus S. fecisset, si ea in templo contigisset, διαπαντὸς per- mansisse in templo non aliter intelligendi, quam uti Act. II. 46. καθ᾽ ἡμέραν quotidie perdurantes concor- diter in templo fuisse dicuntur, non quod semper & perpetuo in eodem fuerint, quia additur, quod κατ᾽ οἶκον domatim panem fregerint, in ædibus nem- pe diversis, sed quod certo tempore, singulis diebus convenire in templo consueverint, uti etiam hic Grotio observatum.

Ἀμήν] Additum ab Ecclesiâ, quæ lectionem Evangelii hac acclamatione excipere solebat, 1. Cor. XIV. 16.

Crisin hanc Grotianam in medio relinquimus. Non tamen verisimitudine destitui videtur: quia fortassis verbis textus antecedentibus hæc vocula non ita cohæret, aut congruit.

Atque hæc ad Evangelium Lucæ. Reliqua enim, de quibus moneri poterat, ex iis, quæ ad Mat- thæum, vel etiam ad Marcum observata sunt, ju- dicari queunt. Concludit S. Lucas laude, & bene- dictione discipulorum Christi: Largiatur Christus, ut similes discipulis Christi simus, ac semper laudemus & benedicamus Deum, ac concludamus denique hanc vitam laude, ac benedictione, ut in æterna vita sine fine canamus cum Sanctis Angelis, & electis universis:

Ἡ εὐλογία, κῂ ἡ δόξα, κῂ ἡ σοφία, & ἡ εὐχαρι- στία, καὶ ἡ τιμὴ, καὶ ἡ δύναμις, καὶ ἡ ἰσχὺς τῷ Θεῷ ἡμῶν εἰς τὺς αἰῶνας τ̃ αἰώνων, ἈΜΉΝ.

# John

## 1:1 Introduction
[Abraham Calov, Biblia Novi Testamenti Illustrata (Vol. 1). English: machine translation, The Faith Received (Mere Orthodoxy); the original follows each comment.]
In the name of Jesus. Annotations on the Gospel according to John.

Latin:

I. N. J. ANNOTATIONES IN EVANGELIUM KATA ἸΩΑΝΝΗΝ.

## 1:1 Introduction: Grotian Preface
Grotian Preface.

John, the son of a Bethsaidan fisherman, a fisherman himself, could indeed learn the law as a boy, as was the custom among the Hebrews, but he was not imbued with any Hebrew or Greek literature, unless he drew something of both when he was already older in Asia, where it is sufficiently agreed among the ancients that he spent the greatest part of his life until extreme old age, partly in exile on Patmos, partly before and after that exile at Ephesus. Therefore, whatever was necessary for him for the performance of his Apostolic duty, the Spirit of God supplied, who is accustomed to leave to each person in non-essential matters those things which are proper to him. Hence it happens that there is great simplicity in John's diction above the other Apostles, and his speech is indeed Greek, but clearly shadowed from the Syriac of that century: hence the speech is so broken up, so many copulative conjunctions, so many repetitions of words, which are usually avoided by the Hebrews through less frequent relatives and other shortcuts of speech. What they record that Alexander once said about his friends, that one was a lover of Alexander, another a lover of the king, I think can be applied to the two Apostles of the Lord Jesus, so that we may call Peter most a lover of Christ, and John most a lover of Jesus. For we see many traces of this different affection in both in the sacred books: which the Lord also looking upon, commended the Church to the former in a certain special way, but to the latter, his mother. Authors disagree about the place and time of the writing, with some wishing this book to have been written on Patmos, others at Ephesus, and some indeed thirty and odd years, but others sixty or more years after Christ's ascension into heaven. All, after others, report the chief cause of writing these things to be that he might provide medicine with his authority, which could not but be great among all who profess the Christian name, against the poison already then scattered into the Church. But what errors insinuated themselves into the churches of that century can be understood from those things which we said on Matthew 24:10 and on Mark 1:4. There were Judaizers under the Christian name, about whom not only Paul, but also this one of ours complains in his first Epistle and in the Apocalypse. There were Gnostics mixing philosophy from the Jewish Cabala and the school of Pythagoras and Plato with Christian simplicity, and peddling to the people, not from the Spirit of God but from their own inventions, things about divine emanations and their syzygies and pleromas, and truly walking in those things which they had not seen, as is said in Colossians 2:18, about whom those things which we said on Matthew 24:10 are to be seen. There were also those who preferred to be called followers of John the Baptist rather than of Jesus, to avoid the cross. John saw that all these things had to be met so that the future age would not fluctuate in an uncertainty of opinions: especially indeed the Gnostics who among their aeons named the Word, likewise Life, likewise the Only-Begotten and the Savior, all of which names you may find also in Proclus on Plato's Timaeus and in books of theology: and they said again that one was the maker of the world, another Christ, another Jesus. John is therefore shown to reconcile all these titles to one and the same Jesus Christ, whereby it happens that our Lord is not read to be distinguished by those names among other sacred writers, although they nevertheless handed down the same thing. Nor indeed in this book only, but also in the Epistle and in the Apocalypse, does John expressly attribute the name of Word to Christ, and he calls him the Only-Begotten not only at the beginning of the book, and that repeatedly, but also twice afterwards: and Jesus himself calls himself Life below. The other writers of the Gospels considered it sufficient to indicate Christ's divine nature tacitly, from his admirable conception, from that infinite and most free power to perform miracles, from the insight into the thoughts of others, from those things which happened around his death, resurrection, and ascension into heaven, and finally from the promise of perpetual presence: of sending the Holy Spirit: of forgiving sins: of judging the human race. But John, according to the custom of the times, thought that the name of God should be assigned to him from the very beginning and that the power flowing from an eternal source should be openly handed down. And not only in this way, but also by express comparison he preferred him first to John the Baptist, then to Moses, and also to Abraham. Since this had been the chief cause of writing, he wanted at the same time to narrate things about Christ which had been omitted by the others in such a great abundance of his miracles and sermons, with those things which had been treated by others remaining almost untouched, except insofar as the connection required something of it. But the greatest part of the omitted things falls into the time when John the Baptist was still living. For from here the others almost begin the history of Jesus' miracles, because at that time a greater multitude followed Jesus and was a witness of his deeds.

Latin:

PRÆLOQUIUM GROTIANUM.

JOhannes Bethfaidensis piscatoris filius, piscator & ipse, legem quidem discere potuit puer, ut mos erat Hebreis, cæterum nulla tinctus fuit aut Hebraica aut Græca literatura, nisi si quid utriusq; haufit jam ma- jor natu in Asia, ubi eum maximam vitæ partem ad se- nectutem summam produxisse, partim in Pathmi exsilio, partim ante & post id exsilium Ephesi, satis inter veteres constat. Quare quicquid ei ad Apostolici muneris functio- nem fuit necessarium, supplevit Dei Spiritus, qui idem in re- bus non necessariis solet ea relinquere cuique quæ ei sunt propria. Hinc fit ut supra cæteros Apostolos magna sit in Jo- hannis dictione simplicitas, & sermo Græcus quidem, sed plane adumbratus ex Syriaco illius seculi: Hinc oratio ad- eo intercisa, tot copulativæ conjunctiones, tot repetitiones vocum, quæ per relativa minus frequentata Hebræis & alia dicendi compendia vitari solent. Quod olim Alexandrum de amicis suis dixisse memorant, alium esse φιλαλέξανδρον, alium φιλοβασιλέα, putem ad duos Domini Jesu Apostolos fic posse aptari, ut Petrum dicamus maxime φιλόχριςον, Jo- hannem maxime φιλιησῦν. Nam diversi hujus in utroque af- fectus multa in sacris libris videmus vestigia: quod & Do- minus respiciens illi quidem Ecclesiam præcipuo quo- dam modo, huic autem matrem commendavit. De loco & tempore scriptionis dissentiunt auctores, aliis in Pathmo scriptum hunc librum volentibus, aliis Ephesi, & aliis qui- dem triginta & quod excurrit, aliis vero sexaginta aut am- plius post Christum in cælum evectionem annis. Causam post alios hæc scribendi præcipuam tradunt omnes, ut ve- neno in Ecclesiam jam tum sparso auctoritate sua, quæ apud omnes Christianum nomen profitentes non poterat non ef- fe maxima, medicinam faceret. Qui autem errores in Eccle- sias ejus Seculi se insinuaverint, intelligi potest ex iis quæ ad Matthæum XXIV. 10. & ad Marc. I. 4. diximus. Erant sub Christiano nomine Judaizantes, de quibus non Paulus tan- tum, sed & hic noster in Epistola prima & in Apocalypsi con- queritur. Erant Gnostici ex Cabala Judaica & PythagoræPla- tonisq; Schola philosophiam miscentes simplicitati Christi- anæ, & de emanationibus divinis, earumque syzygiis & ple- romatis, non ex Dei spiritu, sed ex suis commentis, quæ vel- lent populo venditantes vereq; ambulantes in iis quæ non viderant, ut dicitur Col. II. 18. de quibus videnda quæ dixi- mus ad Matth. XXIV. 10. Erant & qui Iohannis Baptistæ se- ctatores quam Iesu dici mallent, ad subterfugiendam cru- cem. His omnibus occurrendum videbat Iohannes ne post futura ætas incerto opinionum fluctuaret: præcipue vero Gnosticis qui inter suos æonas nominabant λόγον, item ζωήν, item μονογενῆ & σωτῆρα, quæ omnia nomina etiam apud Pro- clum ad Platonis Timæum & in Theologiæ libris reperias: & alium rursus dicebant esse mundi opificem, alium Chri- stum, alium Iesum. Ostenditur ergo Iohannes omnes istos titulos uni eidemque Iesu Christo congruere, quo fit ut illis nominibus Dominus noster non legatur insignitus apud a- lios scriptores sacros, cum tamen ste re idem tradiderint. Ne- que vero hoc tantum libro sed & in Epistola & in Apocaly- psi, λόγυ nomen Christo diferte tribuit Iohannes, & μονογενῆ vocat non initio tantum libri, idque iterato, sed & bis post- ea: & ζωὴν infra Iesus ipse se vocat. Cæteri Scriptores Evan- geliorum satis habuerunt Christi divinam naturam tacite indicare, ex admirabili ipsius conceptione, ex infinita il- la ac liberrima vi ad facienda miracula, ex introspectu cogitationum alienarum, ex his, quæ circa mortem, resurre- ctionem & ascensum in cælum acciderunt, ex promisso de- nique perpetuæ præsentiæ: mittendi Sp. Sancti: remitten- di peccata: judicandi genus humanum, At Iohannes pro u- su temporum & ipso initio Dei nomen ei assignandum & vim ex æterno fonte manantem aperte tradendam existi- mavit. Neque tantum hoc modo, sed & expressa collatione eum Iohanni primum Baptistæ, deinde Mosi, sed & Abraha- mo prætulit. Hæc cum scribendi præcipua fuisset causa, eadem opera voluit & de Christo narrare quæ à cæteris in tanta miraculorum & sermonum ipsius copia, prætermissa fuerant, intactis ferme iis, quæ ab aliis tractata erant, nisi quatenus connexio aliquid ejus exigebat. Prætermissorum autem pars maxima in tempus incidit quo Iohannes Baptista adhuc vivebat Nam hinc ferme Iesu miraculorum historiam ordiuntur cæteri, quia eo tempore major multitudo Iesum secuta est & factorum ejus testis fuit.

## 1:1 Introduction: Observations on Grotius's Preface
Observations on Grotius's Preface.

I. On the style of St. John.

On the style of St. John, there is no reason for us to think disparagingly with Grotius, as if there is great simplicity in John's diction, and his speech is indeed Greek, but clearly shadowed from the Syriac of that century, and that because of that the speech is so broken up, so many copulative conjunctions, so many repetitions of words: the cause of which thing he himself indeed gives, but one less worthy of so great an Evangelist: that John was not imbued with any Hebrew or Greek literature, unless he drew something of both when he was already older in Asia. For since St. John received wisdom and speech from the Holy Spirit along with the rest of the Apostles, and wrote no less by His impulse and agitation than he preached, who gave to each as He willed to speak the mighty works of God in tongues, even unknown ones, Acts 2:3 ff., such accusations could hardly be cast without insult to the Holy Spirit Himself, whose amanuensis St. John was. Add, that John with James, on account of the gravity of their speech, were adorned with a special title by Christ, and were called themselves sons of thunder, Mark 3:17. Whence that judgment concerning the Johannine style holds itself more correctly, which is read in Flacius in his gloss p. 422. The speech of John is altogether grand, and at the same time effective, no less than that of Paul: but if one prefers to hear the ancients, in the judgment of Basil, Homily on the beginning of John, in the praises of the Gospel, and in the magnitude of speech, and the gravity of the sentiments, John, the son of thunder, obtains the first place: but the opinion of Chrysostom, in the prolegomena to his commentaries, John sings more sweetly and more usefully than any cithara-player, and any music.

II. CONCERNING THE CAUSE OF THE JOHANNINE GOSPEL-WRITING.

Grotius makes the cause of writing twofold: The former in general holds itself correctly, that indeed all hand down that this was the principal one, that St. John might apply a remedy with his authority to the poison so widely scattered into the Church: but as far as specifically concerns the errors which had to be met, when Grotius recounts sectarians of a triple kind, Judaizers, Gnostics, and those who preferred to be called followers of John the Baptist, rather than of Jesus, to avoid the cross: we find wanting first, that it does not appear from the Johannine Gospel, or even the first Epistle, that it was directed against such as Judaized under the Christian name, such as we know were noted by Paul: as also in the Apocalypse: But as to what he says at Matt. 24:10, that they mixed the Christian religion with Judaism, who acknowledged Judaism as the only cause of salvation, which had been announced both by other Prophets and also by Christ, and he specifically recounts Cerinthus and Ebion, in that Grotius is gravely hallucinating: because that is not an error, that there is a unique way of salvation in the Old and New Testament, but the very divine truth itself: nor for that reason were Cerinthus or Ebion marked for heresy, or for a vicious mixture of Judaism and Christianity, but because they contended that the flesh ought to be circumcised, and other precepts of the law of this kind ought to be kept, as is found in Augustine on heresies, ch. 8 and 10.

Furthermore, as for the Gnostics, whom Grotius says—mixing philosophy from the Jewish Kabbalah and the school of Pythagoras and Plato into Christian simplicity—sold divine emanations and their syzygies and pleromas to the people, and whom he makes Carpocrates the leader of at Matthew 24:11, it will hardly be taught that they flourished even before the Johannine ἐὐαγγελιογραφία (Gospel-writing); since Carpocrates is referred to the beginning of the reign of Antoninus Pius, around the year 109 after Christ suffered, or if he is said to have begun already under Hadrian, as with Theodoret, to the hundredth year after the passion of Christ. See Lamb. Danaeus on Augustine, De haeres. ch. 7. That therefore the Gnostics named among their aeons the Word, likewise Life, likewise the Only-Begotten and the Savior, and said that one was the creator of the world, another Christ, another JESUS, that in no way proves that John wished to teach against them that all those titles correspond to one and the same JESUS Christ; since they rather seem to have impiously and blasphemously derived their aeons from these Johannine ones, and from Platonic ones, though both were their own truly diabolical inventions. Nor is it true, as Grotius says, that the Lord is not read to be distinguished by these names among other Sacred writers; since the name Word also occurs in Luke ch. 1:2 and according to some also in Acts 20:33 and elsewhere regarding Christ, and

the word Savior is a familiar one especially to Paul, Eph. 5:23, Phil. 3:23, 1 Tim. 1:1, 2 Tim. 1:10, Tit. 1:4, ch. 2:13, ch. 3:6, etc. And Grotius himself praises at John 1:1, at the word Word, that not only is the Son of God called דבר (Dabar) by the Hebrews, Ps. 33:6, Ps. 148:8, but also Word by Peter, 2 Ep. 3:5.

Nor indeed, thirdly, could anything be brought forward from antiquity regarding the followers of John, whom Grotius points out, let alone be taught, that the Evangelist sharpened his pen against them. And although he himself preferred Christ not only to the Baptist, but also to Moses and Abraham, that was not done on the occasion of the followers of John, who preferred to cling to him rather than to Christ; but because the history so dictated, as when he reported that the Pharisees attributed the honor of the Baptist to Christ, when Christ appealed to Moses, who wrote about him, and when he testified that he existed before Abraham.

But Grotius here omitted the principal cause of the Johannine Gospel-writing, which Ebion and Cerinthus provided for it. This was that they denied the Deity of Christ and established him as a mere man. Regarding which, Jerome in the prolegomena to Matthew: When John was in Asia, and even then the seeds of the heretics Cerinthus, Ebion, and others were sprouting, who deny that Christ came in the flesh; he was compelled by almost all the Bishops of Asia at that time, and by the embassies of many Churches, to write more deeply about the divinity of the Savior, etc. And Epiphanius, Haer. 51: After Ebion proclaimed Christ to be a mere man out of affection, and Cerinthus and their accomplices in Asia, there the Holy Spirit produced this holy herb or shrub for the world, putting the serpent to flight and destroying the tyranny of the Devil. Compare Eusebius, Book 3, Ecclesiastical History, ch. 18. And prior to all these, St. Irenaeus, Book 3, ch. 3. Since this scope is evident from the Johannine treatment itself and from his clear assertion at John 20:31, it could not be denied here by Grotius himself. The others, he says, the writers of the Gospels, considered it sufficient to indicate Christ's divine nature tacitly from his admirable conception, from that infinite and most free power to perform miracles, from the insight into the thoughts of others, from those things which happened concerning his death, resurrection, and ascension into heaven, and finally from the promise of his perpetual presence, of sending the Holy Spirit, of forgiving sins, and of judging the human race.

But John, according to the custom of the times, thought that the name of God should be assigned to him from the very beginning and that the power flowing from the eternal source should be openly handed down. These are the words of Grotius: who also acknowledged that this was the error of Ebion, refuted by John, that Jesus is a mere man: at John 1:6, that indeed the Ebionites and others falsely said of Christ that he was a mere man. See more on these in Socinismo profligato, Section 1, Member 1.

The later cause of the Johannine writing, according to Grotius, is that he wished to narrate those things about Christ which had been omitted by the others, in such a wealth of his miracles and sermons, with those things which had been treated by others remaining almost untouched, unless the connection required something of it; regarding which cause Jerome says: But they also report another cause for this writing, that when he had read the volumes of Matthew, Mark, and Luke, he indeed approved of the text of the history and confirmed that they had spoken the truth; but that they had woven the history of only one year, in which he also suffered, after the imprisonment of John. Therefore, having omitted the year whose deeds had been set forth by the three, he narrated the deeds of the earlier time before John was shut up in prison, as will be able to be manifest to those who have diligently read the four volumes of the Gospels. Which matter also removes the discrepancy which seems to exist between John and the others. And John [according to] Cosmas Indicopleustes: This Theologian John, he says, the prince of the Evangelists, who was loved by Christ above all others, who reclined on His breast, who finally drew from there, as if from a perpetual fountain, the mysteries of God. To him, therefore, while he was staying in Ephesus, the books of the remaining three Evangelists were presented by the faithful: and when he had read them through, he replied that they were indeed written truthfully, but that nevertheless certain things had been omitted which it was necessary to recount at the same time. Being entreated, therefore, by the faithful, he also published his own work, which in some way is as it were a supplement of the things omitted: such as those concerning the marriage in Cana, concerning Nicodemus, concerning the Samaritan woman, concerning the Nobleman, concerning the man born blind, concerning Lazarus, concerning the indignation of Judas on account of her who had anointed the Lord with ointment, concerning the Greeks who approached, concerning the washing of the feet, and concerning the teachings interspersed, concerning the Paraclete: and especially preaching brilliantly concerning the divinity of Christ, he placed that as the foundation of his work. All of which things indeed had been omitted by others.

III. THE ECONOMY OF THE GOSPEL OF JOHN.

As these things shine with their own light, so it will be worth the effort to add here those things which Matth. Flacius observed concerning the Johannine order: This Evangelist could be divided into two primary parts, into the history of the first three Passovers or years, and the last, in which He suffered. The former part is narrated in the first 10 chapters, the latter in the remaining eleven: the former is again subdivided into three Passovers, so that each encompasses the histories and deeds of the Lord a little before that feast, and soon after it. To the first Passover, therefore, let the first three chapters be referred: where in the first are the testimonies of John concerning Christ, with the calling of certain disciples: In the second is the miracle of the wine changed, and the cleansing of the temple at the Passover: In the third is the conversation with Nicodemus and the new testimony of John concerning Christ, which happened after the first Passover. To the second Passover let the two following chapters be referred; in the former of which indeed is narrated the conversion of the Samaritans, and the healing of the Nobleman's son: but in the latter chapter, which is the fifth, the healing of the man lying in Bethesda, and the dispute which arose from it. To the third Passover let the 5 following chapters pertain: the first of which, the sixth in order, narrates the miracle of the five loaves, the sermon and the contention concerning the heavenly and life-giving bread, soon on that occasion ensuing, which had occurred a little before the Passover. But the remaining four chapters set forth those things which occurred around the following feast of tabernacles: the first and second of which, that is, the VII and VIII, narrate two sermons of Christ delivered in the temple, the former concerning the doctrine and office of the Messiah; the latter concerning the most corrupt nature of man, concerning the sons of the devil and of God, and finally concerning the liberation of the human race through the Messiah. The latter two chapters, IX and X, seem to contain one rather long disputation, held on the occasion of the healing of the man born blind and his excommunication: in the former of which, however, is narrated primarily the contention after the healing between him who was truly enlightened and the now blinded Pharisees, along with Christ's application of that miracle and the whole struggle to his own doctrine and office. In the latter, however, is contained a long and full sermon concerning true and false shepherds and sheep. In which Christ takes away from the Jews and Pharisees the title of shepherds and of the Church of God, and rightfully claims it for himself and his own hearers.

Finally, the latter principal part can rightly be subdivided into those things which were done immediately before his passion, into the passion, and the resurrection. Immediately before Passover were done the raising of Lazarus, which is narrated in the XI chapter. Then the supper held in Bethany, along with the royal entry and the cleansing of the temple, which is narrated in the XII and XIII chapters, the history of the Paschal supper, with the added sayings and deeds of Christ, and especially the washing of the feet. Lastly is the long sermon contained in the three following chapters, XIV, XV, and XVI, and the prayer in the seventeenth. The preceding three chapters therefore contain the long sermon of Christ in such a way that in the first of them are set forth the benefits of the departure or passion of Christ with his members; in the second, the parable of the vine is set forth; in the last, the use of that consolatory doctrine is handed down. Furthermore, the passion itself is narrated in two chapters, XIIX and XIX. The resurrection is narrated and confirmed, along with the added commands of Christ to the Apostles, in the last two chapters.

IV. CONCERNING THE COMMENTATORS ON THE GOSPEL OF ST. JOHN.

Those who have illustrated the Gospel of St. John with commentaries or annotations are listed in the Apparatus of Possevinus, according to alphabetical order: Ægidius Romanus, Agrippa, Albinus, Ambrosius Mediolanensis, Ammonius, Amphilochius, Andreas Cretæ, Anselmus, Antonius Bruich, Apollinaris, Arnobius, Asterius, Aurelius, Augustinus, Basilius, Bernardus, Bessarion, Bonaventura, Bruno Archbishop of Cologne, Catena Græca, Cæsarius, Claudius Guillaudus, Conradus, Cornel. Jansenius, Corn. Musæus, Cyrillus, Didymus, Diegus or Didacus Deza, Diodorus, Dionysius Vasquez Toletanus, Dominicus Nanus, Eusebius Cæsariensis, Euthymius, Fortunatianus, Franciscus Agricola, who reduced the Gospel of St. John into commonplaces, Franciscus Titelmannus, Franciscus Toletus Cardinal, Georgius Trapezuntius, Gilbertus Porretanus, Gregorius Pope, Greg. Corinthi, Guido Perpinianus, Guilelmus Aquisgranensis, Guttierus, Henr. Arnoldi, Hieron. Vida, Innocent Pope, Joach. Abbas, Joh. Arboreus, Ioh. Balbus, Joh. Castellersis, Joh. Christophori, Joh. Gauuer, Joh. Maldonatus, Job. Ridevat Anglus, Johan. Sancta fides, Judocus, Joseph. Typerinus, Isaac, Juvencus, Laur. Justinianus, Ludolph. Cartusianus, Marianus, Michael Massensis, Nonnus Panopolita, Otfridus, Petrus Isusquius, Pet. Scala, Rich. Mediavillanus, Rupertus Gouletus, Seraphinus Capponi a Porrecta, Simon Cassianus, Sim. Cremonensis, Sim. Corroyus, Steph. Polonicus, Tatianus, Theodor. Heracleotes, Theophilus Alexandrinus, Titus, Victor, Zacharias, etc. And Sixtus Senensis praises many of them in his Bibliotheca.

To these, however, must be added Iob. Fetus and Bened. Pererius, besides those who among the Papists have written on the whole New Testament or on the Evangelists. In the Catholic exposition of the Evangelists by Augustinus Marloratus, there were translated from the Reformed commentators on John: Bucerus, Bullingerus, Calvinus, Musculus with the author's annotations; of our own, Brentius alone. Moreover, besides these, there have written on John from our side: B. Erasmus Sarcerius, B. Ægidius Hunnius, B. Chytreus, B. Wigandus, B. Selneccerus, B. Paulus Tarnovius, as also Pelargus, while he was still one of ours; from the Reformed: Cruciger, Polanus, Hemmingius. Dan. Heinsius edited an Aristarchus on the John of Nonnus: Franc. Gomarus presented an illustration of selected passages of John, just as he did for Matthew and Luke.

PART I. OF THE JOHANNINE GOSPEL, containing the history of the first three Passovers.

SECTION I. Pertaining to the first Passover.

Latin:

OBSERVATIONES AD GROTII PRÆLOQUIUM.

I. DE STYLO S. JOHANNIS.

DE Stylo S. JOHANNIS non est quod abje- ctim sentiamus cum Grotio, quasi magna Johannis. sit in dictione ejus simplicitas, & sermo Græ- cus quidem, sed plane adumbratus ex Syriaco illius se- culi, quodque inde oratio adeo intercisa, tot copulativæ conjunctiones, tot vocum repetitiones sint: cujus rei causam ipse quidem hanc reddit, sed tanto Evan- gelista minus dignam: quod JOHANNES nulla tin- ctus fuerit, aut Ebraica, aut Græca literatura, nisi si quid utriusq, haufit jam major natu in Asia. Nam cum à Sp. S. σοφίαν & 5ο'μα cum reliquis Apostolis S. Johannes acceperit, ejusque impulsu & agitatione non minus scripserit, quam prædicarit, qui unicui- que sicut voluit, dedit linguis, etiam incognitis, eloqui magnalia Dei, Act. II. 3. seqq. vix talia ἐγκλήματα, citra contumeliam in ipsummet Spiritum S. cujus amanuensis fuit S. Johannes, jactari poterant. Ad- de, quod Johannes cum Jacobo, ob gravitatem ora- tionis, peculiari elogio ornatus à Christo fuerit, di- ctique sint ipsi filii tonitrui Marc. III. 17. Unde ju- dicium illud de stylo Iohanneo rectius se habet, quod apud Flacium in glossa ejus legitur p. 422. Johannis sermo omnino grandis est, & simul efficax, non minus quam Pauli: at si veteres audire quis malit, Basilio Hom. in princ. Joh. judice, in Evangelii laudibus, & sermonis magnitudine, & sententiarum gravitate Jo- hannes, filius tonitrui, primas obtinet: Chrysostomi vero sententia, in proleg. commentar. Johannes o- mni Cytharedo, omnique Musica suavius utiliusque præcinit.

II. DE ΕΥΑΓΓΕΛΙΟΓΡΑΦΙ'ΑΣ JOHANNEÆ CAUSA.

CAusam scribendi geminam facit Grotius: Prior in genere recte se habet, quod nempe hanc præcipuam fuisse omnes tradant, ut veneno in Ecclesiam tantum sparso auctoritate sua medicinam faceret S. Johannes: sed quod speciatim attinet er- rores, quibus occurrendum fuerit, cum recenset Grotius triplicis generis sectarios Judaizantes, Gnosticos, & qui Johannis Baptistæ sectatores, quam Jesu, dici maluerint, ad subterfugiendam crucem: desideramus primum, quod ex Evangelio Johan- neo, aut etiam prima Epistola, non appareat, id di- rectum fuissecontra tales, qui sub Christiano nomine Judaizarunt, quales à Paulo notatos|novimus: ut & in Apocalypsi: Quod vero ad Matth. XXIV. 10. eos cum Judaismo Christianam religionem misguisse di- cit, qui Judaismum agnovere unicam salutis causam, quæ tum ab aliis Prophetis, tum à Christo etiam esset annunciata, & peculiariter Cerinthum recenset, ac Ebionem, in eo graviter hallucinatur Grotius: quia is non errorest, quod unica salutis via sit in V. & N. Test. sed ipsissima divina veritas: nec ob id Cerinthus aut Ebion hæreseos notati sunt, aut mixturæ Judaismi & Christianismi vitiosæ, sed quod carnem circumcidi oportere, atque alia bujus- modi legis præcepta servari contenderint, ut est a- pud Augustinum de hæref. c. VIII. & X.

Porro quod ad Gnosticos, quos ex Cabala Ju- daica, & Pythagorae Platonisque Schola philoso- phiam simplicitati Christianae miscentes emanatio- nes divinas, earumque syzygias & pleromata populo venditasse, ait Grotius, quorum principem ad Matth. XXIV. 11. facit Carpocratem, vix docebi- tur, eosdem jam ante ἐὐαγγελιογραφίαν Johan- neam floruisse: quum Carpocrates referatur ad ini- tium imperii Antonini Pii, circa annum a Christo passo CIX. aut si cum Theodoreto sub Adriano jam coepisse dicatur, ad annum a passione Christi centesi- mum. Vid. Lamb. Danaeus ad Augustin. de haeres. c. VII. Quod ergo Gnostici inter suos aeonas nomina- runt λόγον, item ζωὴν, item μονογενῆ & σωτῆρα, & alium dixere esse mundi opificem, alium Christum; alium JESUM, id minime probat, quod Johan- nes omnes istos titulos uni eidemque JESU Chri- sto congruere, adversus eosdem docere voluerit; quum illi potius suos aeonas ex istis Johanneis, & e Platonicis, utrisque tamen commentis suis vere diabolicis depravatis, impie & blaspheme dedu- xisse videantur. Neque verum est, quod ait Grotius, Dominum non legi insignitum istis nomi- nibus apud alios S. Scriptores; siquidem & λόγε nomen apud Lucam cap. I. 2. & juxta nonnullos etiam Actor. XX. 33. & alias occurrat de Christo, &

σωτῆρος vox familiaris sit imprimis Paulo, Eph. V. 23. Phil. III. 23. 1. Tim. I. 1. 2. Tim. I. 10. Tit. I. 4. c. II. 13. c. III. 6. &c. Et laudat Grotius ipse ad Joh. I. v. 1. ad vocem λόγου, non tantum דבר dictum esse Ebraeis Filium Dei, Ps. XXXIII. 6. Ps. CXLVIII. 8. sed & λόγον a Petro 2. Ep. III. 5.

Neque vero tertio de sectatoribus Johannis, quos indigitat Grotius, quicquam proferri potuit ex antiquitate, nedum doceri, quod adversus eos calamum strinxerit Evangelista. Et quamvis Chri- stum ipse non Baptistae tantum, sed & Mosi, & Abrahamo praetulerit, id tamen non occasione se- ctatorum Johannis, qui illi, quam Christo, adhaere- scere maluerint, factum; sed quia historiae ita fe- rebant, utpote cum Pharisaeos Baptistae honorem Christi detulisse, cum Christus ad Mosen, qui de se scripserit, provocasse, cum se ante Abrahamum fuisse testatum esse, retulit.

Causam vero praecipuam ἐὐαγγελιογραφίας Jo- hanneae, quam Ebion & Cerinthus ei praebuere, hic praetermisit Grotius. Ea haec fuit, quod ne- garent illi Deitatem Christi, eumque ψιλὸν ἄνθρω- πον constituerint. Quo de Hieronym. in proleg. Matth. Quum Johannes esset in Asia, & jam tunc haereticorum semina pullularent Cerinthi, Ebionis, & caeterorum, qui negant, Christum in carne venisse; coactus est ab omnibus pene tunc Asiae Episcopis, & multarum Ecclesiarum legationibus de divinitate Salvatoris altius scribere, &c. Et Epiphan. haer. LI. Postquam Christum ex affectu nudum hominem prae- dicavit Ebion, & Cerinthus & complices ipsorum in Asia, illic produxit S. S. mundo hanc sanctam her- bam sive fruticem, fugantem serpentem, & Diaboli tyrannidem destruentem. Conf. Euseb. l. III. Histor. Eccl. c. 18. Et his omnibus prior S. Irenaeus l. III. c. 3. Qui scopus quum ex ipsa tractatione Johan- nea, & e luculenta ejusdem asseveratione Joh. XX. v. 31. evidens sit, hic a Grotio ipso negari non po- tuit. Caeteri inquit, Scriptores Evangeliorum satis habuerunt Christi divinam naturam tacite indicare ex admirabili ipsius conceptione, ex infinita illa ac liberrima vi ad facienda miracula, ex introspectu co- gitationum alienarum, ex his quae circa mortem, re- surrectionem, & ascensum in caelum acciderunt, ex promisso denique perpetuae praesentiae, mittendi Sp. San- cti, remittendi peccata, judicandi genus humanum.

At Johannes, pro usu temporum, & ipso initio Dei nomen ei assignandum & vim ex æterno fonte manantem aperte tradendam existimavit. Hæc Gro-tius: qui etiam agnovit Ebionis hunc fuisse errorem à Johanne profligatum, quod Jesus merus homo sit: ad Joh. I. 6. quod nempe de Christo falso Ebionei & alii dixerint, quod fuerit ψιλὸς ἄνθρωπος. Vide de his plura in Socinismo profligato, Sect. I. Membr. I.

Posterior causa scriptionis Joanneæ secundum Grotium est, quod voluerit ea de Christo narrare, quæ à cæteris, in tanta miraculorum & sermonum ipsius copia, prætermissa fuerint, intactis ferme eis, quæ ab aliis tractata erant, nisi quatenus connexio aliquid ejus exigebat; de qua causa ita Hieronymus: Sed & aliam causam hujus scripturæ ferunt, quod cum legisset Matthæi, Marci, & Lucæ volumina, probaverit quidem textum historiæ, & vera eos dixisse firmaverit; sed unius tantum anni, quo & passus est, post carcerem Joannis, historiam texuisse. Prætermisso itaq́; anno, cujus acta à tribus exposita fuerant, superioris temporis antequam Joannes clauderetur in carcerem, gesta narravit, sicut manifestum esse poterit his, qui diligenter quatuor Evangeliorum volumina legerint. Quæ res etiam Diaphonian, quæ videtur Joannis esse cum cæteris, tollit. Et Joannes Cosma Indicopleusti: Hic, inquit, Theologus Johannes, princeps Evangelistarum, qui præ omnibus dilectus est à Christo, qui in ejus pectore recubuit, qui deniq́; inde, tanquam ex perpetuo fonte, mysteria Dei hausit. Huic igitur in Epheso agenti exhibiti sunt a fidelibus reliquorum trium Evangelistarum libri: quos cum perlegisset, vere quidem illos esse conscriptos respondit, sed tamen quædam esse omissa, quæ necesse sit, simul recensere. Exoratus igitur à fidelibus, edidit & ipse suum opus, quod aliquo modo est quasi supplementum prætermissorum: ut sunt de nuptiis in Cana, de Nicodemo, de Samaritana, de Regio, de cæco nato, de Lazaro, de Judæ indignatione ob eam, quæ inunxerat Dominum unguento, de accedentibus Græcis, de lotione pedum, & de documentis interfertis, de paracleto: & præsertim de divinitate Christi luculenter prædicans, id ceu fundamentum sui operis præposuit. Quæ quidem omnia ab aliis prætermissa fuerant.

III. OECONOMIA EVANGELII JOHANNIS.

QUæ uti luce sua radiant, ita operæ pretium erit addere hic ea, quæ Matth. Flacius observavit de ordine Johanneo: Dividi posset hic Evangelista in duas primarias partes, in historiam trium priorum paschatum aut annorum, & ultimi, quo passus est. Prior pars 10. primis capitibus narratur, posterior reliquis undecim: prior rursus subdividatur in tria paschata, ita ut singula complectantur historias & res gestas Domini paulo ante id festum, & mox post illud. Ad primum igitur Pascha referantur tria prima capita: ubi in primo sunt testimonia Johannis de Christo, cum vocatione quorundam discipulorum: In secundo est miraculum vini mutati, & repurgatio templi in Paschate: In tertio est colloquium eum Nicodemo & novum testimonium Joannis de Christo, quæ post primum Pascha acciderunt. Ad secundum Pascha referantur duo sequentia capita; in quorum priore quidem narratur conversio Samaritanorum, & sanatio filii Regii: in posteriori vero capite, quod est quintum, sanatio jacentis in Bethesda, & inde orta disceptatio. Ad tertium Pascha pertineant 5. sequentia capita: quorum primum sextum in ordine, narrat miraculum quinque panum, concionem contentionemque de cælesti vivifico que pane, mox ea occa- sione consecutam, quæ paulo ante Pascha accide- rant, Reliqua vero quatuor capita exponunt ea, quæ eveŋerunt circa secutum festum tabernaculo- rum: quorum primum, & secundum, id est, VII. & VIII. narrant duas conciones Christi in templo habi- tas, priorem de Messiæ doctrina & officio: posteriorem de corruptissima hominis natura, deǫ́ filiis diaboli & Dei, & denique de liberatione humani generis per Messiam. Posteriora duo capita IX. & X. videntur continere unam bene longam disceptationem, oc- casione sanationis nati cæci, & excommunicationis ejius habitam: In quorum tamen priore potissimum narratur post sanationem contentio inter illum ve- re illuminatum, & jam excæcatos Pharisæos, una cum applicatione Christi ejus miraculi, & totius certaminis ad suam doctrinam & officium. In posteriore vero continetur longa & plena concio de veris ac falsis pastoribus & ovibus. In qua Chri- stus aufert Judæis & Pharisæis titulum pastorum ac Ecclesiæ Dei, sibique eum ac suis auditoribus jure vindicat.

Posterior denique principalis pars potest recte subdividi in ea, quæ proxime ante passionem ejus a- cta sunt, in passionem ac resurrectionem. Proxime ante Pascha facta sunt resuscitatio Lazari, quæ XI. capite narratur. Deinde cœna facta in Bethania, una cum regali introitu & repurgatione templi, quæ in XII. & XIII. capite narratur historia cœnæ Pa- schalis, cum adjunctis dictis ac factis Christi, & præ- sertim lotio pedum. Postremo est longa concio tri- bus sequentibus capitibus XIV. XV. & XVI. conten- ta, & precatio unico decimo septimo. Præcedentia igitur tria capita ita continent longam concionem Christi, ut in primo illorum exponantur beneficia abitionis aut passionis Christi cum suis membris; altero parabola vitis exposita: in postremo usus il- lius consolatoriæ doctrinæ traditus. Ipsa porro passio narratur duobus capitibus XIIX. & XIX. Re- surrectio narratur & confirmatur una cum adjun- ctis mandatis Christi ad Apostolos, duobus ultimis capitibus.

IV. DE COMMENTATORIBUS IN EVANGELIUM S. JOHANNIS.

PARS I. EVANGELII JOHANNEI Historiam trium priorum Pascha- tum complectens.

SECTIO I. Ad Pascha primum pertinens.

## 1:1 Argument
CHAPTER I.

ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

The coming into the world of the eternal Word, for the sake of testifying to whom John the Baptist had been sent, and into his own, but acknowledged and received by few, to whom he gave the power of divine sonship. Which coming was brought about through the incarnation: Whence the Word, dwelling among men, manifested his glory, as of the only-begotten Son from the Father, full of grace and truth. Concerning him, however, John testified, and being asked by the Jerusalem Sanhedrin, he gave public testimony both concerning himself, that he is the forerunner of Christ, from Is. (ch. XL. 3), and concerning the Messiah, that he has arisen in their midst, pointing out Jesus arriving on the following day, that he is that Lamb of God bearing the sin of the world, he of whose coming he had spoken, whom he recognized from the descent of the Holy Spirit and the divine oracle. After John had testified again concerning Jesus, on the following day two disciples, among whom was Andrew, followed him, and Simon was brought to him, surnamed Cephas by him, and furthermore Philip and Nathanael, held by Jesus to be a true Israelite, recognized under the fig tree before he was physically present to him, who confesses him for that reason to be the Son of God, that King of Israel: and he receives the promise that he shall see greater things, inasmuch as heaven is now opened, and the Angels of God are to ascend and descend upon the Son of man.

There are three parts: I. The Johannine prologue concerning the coming of the eternal Word into the world and his incarnation, to v. 14. II. The manifold testimony issued by the Baptist, to v. 34. III. The bringing of certain disciples to the recognition of Jesus, namely Andrew, Peter, Philip, Nathanael, and the conversation of the latter with Jesus to v. 51.

PART I. The Johannine prologue concerning the coming of the eternal Word into the world, and his incarnation.

Vers. 1. Ἐν ἀρχῇ] Taken from the Greek of Genesis, just as in turn the Syrian here has placed בְּרֵאשִׁית from the Hebrew.
