I note, however, that the word taken from that place in Scripture is to be understood according to the meaning of that passage. The meaning of the passage of Moses is this: when first God created heaven and earth, the earth was, etc., for the past tense among the Hebrews also has the meaning of a gerund. Then indeed it is the custom for the Hebrews to include the universe under the name of heaven and earth, whence it has come about that the state of the future life is signified by the name of a new heaven and a new earth 2 Pet. III. 12. Apoc. XXI. 1. Therefore ἐν ἀρχῇ is, when first the universe of things began to be created,

ἦν.] He was already then. Thus it is the custom for the Hebrews to describe eternity in popular terms, below XVII. 5. δόξῃ ᾗ εἶχον πρὸ τῦ τὸν κόσμον εἶναι. And Justin said, πρὸ τῦ ποιημάτων, and elsewhere: πρὸ τῦ ἑωσφόρυ κὶ σελήνης. Prov. VIII. The wisdom of God speaks thus: From eternity I had the principality, from the beginning, even before the earth: when there were not yet depths, I was formed, when there were not yet fountains heavy with waters: before the mountains were founded, before the hills I was formed: he had not yet made the earth, and the streets, and the chief parts of the dust of the world: when he prepared the heavens, I was there already. Justin elsewhere, explaining this manner of speaking about the Word, προυπᾶρξε πρὸ τῦν αἰώνων. Athenagoras: ἐξ ἀρχῆς ὁ Θεὸς νῦς ἀΐδιῶ ὢν, εἶχεν αὐτὸν ἐν ἑαυτῷ τῦ λόγον, ἀΐδίως λογικὸς ὢν. Rabbi Eliezer: Before the world was created, there existed a merciful and benign God and his name alone.

What we found lacking in the Grotian explanation of Gen. I. 1, we have stated at that place. Moreover, that the eternity of the Son of God is described here, against the Socinians and their exceptions, has been proven in the Triga Exerc. Selectar. Exerc. II, instituted concerning this passage, in the beginning was the Word. We have defended the passages Joh. XVII. 5. and Prov. VIII. against the same in the tract on the ante-mundane pre-existence of the Son of God, Art. III. p. 96. seqq.

ὁ λόγῃ.] Because Moses had written, God said, let there be light and there was light, and so concerning the rest, hence it came about that the Hebrews called that power of God—without a projection or emanation [for the ancient Christians use these words in this matter]—by which he creates things from nothing and brings about other rare and excellent things, דבר, as can be seen in Ps. XXXIII, 6. CXLIIX. 8. see Maimonides, Guide for the Perplexed, book I. ch. XXIII. LXV. and LXVI. The Chaldeans, not only in those passages but also in others where that word does not exist in the Hebrew, have placed מימרא. Examples are countless, but what is in Isaiah XLV. 12 is most pertinent; in the Hebrew it is read: I made the earth and man upon it, I created. In the Chaldean it is: I in my word made the earth and created men upon it. XLVIII. 13. in the Hebrew it is read: My hand founded the earth, In the Chaldean: By my word I founded the earth. Whom the Apostle Peter followed 2. ep. III. 5. οὐρανοὶ ἦσαν ἔκπαλαι κί γῆ ἐξ ὕδατος, κί διῦδατος συνεστῶσα τῷ τῦ Θεῦ λόγῳ. The same Chaldean paraphrast uses the same word in very many places, where there is talk of miracles, of prophecy, or of the singular help of God: but especially where in the Hebrew there is the face of God, hand, eye. From the ancient books of the Chaldeans, the Greeks cite ἐξ ἕ λόγυ κὶ ἥλιον, κί σελήνη. Hence the writer of the Orphics took: Εἰς δὲ λόγον θεῖον σκέψας, τούτῳ προσέδρευε, Ἰθύνων κραδίης νοερὸν κύτος εὖδ’ ἐπίבαινε Ἀτραπιτῦ· μῦνον δ’ ἐσόρα κόσμοιο ἄνακτα. Εἷς ἐσ’ αὐτοτελής, ἑνὸς ἔκγονα πάντα τέτυκται· The same elsewhere called it αὐδὴν: Αὐδήν ὁρκίζω σε πατρὸς τὴν φθέγξατο πρώτην Ἡνίκα κόσμον ἅπαντα ἑαῖς στηρίξατο βυλαῖς. Following him, Heraclitus, in whom this name is noted by Amelius to exist in that sense? Zeno praised by Tertullian and Lactantius. Tertulliani verba sunt adversus gentes: Among your wise men also, it is agreed that the λόγος, that is, speech and reason, is seen to be the artificer of the universe. For Zeno defines this as the maker, who formed all things in their arrangement. The passage of Zeno, which Tertullian respects, was in his book περὶ ὐσίας, as Laertius teaches us. Seneca, following the Stoics, calls it the making reason, Epist. LXV. Of the number of the Platonists, Amelius—but whom Proclus often complains of defecting from the known Platonists to barbarian philosophy—greatly approved this passage of John, as not only Eusebius notes in the Preparation book XI, but also Augustine in many places. And Cyril against Julian. Plutarch calls it δύναμιν Θεῦ, Symp. VII. ἀναλαβὼν δὲ πά- λιν αὐτῦ Πλάτωνος εἰκότως πατέρα κὶ ποιητὴν τῦ τε κόσμυ, κὶ τῦν ἄλλων γεννητῶν τὸ ἀγέννητον κὶ ἀΐδιον Θεὸν ὀνομάζοντος, ἐ διὰ σπέρματος δὲ κὶ γενόμενον ἄλλῃ δὲ δυνάμει τῦ Θεῦ τῇ ὕλῃ γενόμενον ἀρχὴν ὑφ’ ἧς ἐπαθε κί μετέβαλεν ἐντεκόντος. Thus in the exposition of faith made by Gregory, Bishop of Neocaesarea, ὁ λόγος is called δύναμις τῆς ὅλης κτίσεως ποιητική. Philo, inclining toward Platonic dogmas, since he knew that the exemplar of the world was called λόγος by Plato, used λόγος in that sense himself and was the author of its use by many others, and says that the universe of things was founded through him; he also calls him ὄνομα Θεῦ and εἰκόνα and υἱὸν Θεῦ. Here is rejected by John the figment of the Gnostics who said that the υἱὸν was born after many centuries from the προαρχῆς. Then from the υἱῷ was born the μονογενῆ and from him the λόγον. See Irenaeus at the beginning.

this to that which is said below, that the ὁ λόγος was in the world, made flesh, seen. For he wishes to say that before him he was inconspicuous. For God is called ἀόρατος. I. Tim. I. 17. and to dwell in light inaccessible, 1. Tim. VI. 16. He indicates the same in epistle 42. Καὶ ἡ ζωὴ ἐφανερώθη. And soon: ἥτης ἦν πρὸς τὸν πατέρα, and Ephes. III. 9. Thus below XVII. 5. παρὰ σοι, and when he says he was with the Father, he shows against the Gnostics that the pleroma of the προαρχῆς is not one thing, and that of the λόγου another.

Recte hoc nomen à Grotio deducitur è Genes. c. I. 3. God said, let there be light: concerning which our Anti-Grotian annotations and Commentary on Genesis may be seen, and from Ps. XXXIII. (not likewise from Ps. CXLVIII. 8. where it is a matter of the imperative word, not the hypostatic) and also from the Chaldean מימרא Es. XLV. 12. c. XLVIII. 13. where he notes that the Chaldean followed Peter 2. Ep. III. 5. But the things which he brings from the Greek writer of the Orphics, when he names λόγον and αὐδὴν, word and voice, and others, are either analogous, not the same; or transferred from the Hebrews and Christians to the philosophers, even if not so understood by them. Which are sometimes brought forward by the Fathers κατ' ἄνθρωπων. Thus Tertull. advers. gentes: Among your wise men also, it is agreed that the λόγον, that is, speech and reason, is seen to be the artificer of the universe. For Zeno defines this as the maker, who formed all things in their arrangement. The passage of Zeno, to which Tertullian refers, was in his book περὶ ὀσίας, as Laërtius teaches us, with Grotius observing this here, where he called τὸ ποιοῦν or the efficient cause λόγον, whom Cleanthes, Chrysippus, Archedemus, Posidonius followed, as Laërtius teaches in Zeno, and from him Grotius, book 1, On the Truth of the Christian Religion, in the annotations, p. 32. See also Augustine, book VII of the Confessions, and book X of The City of God, ch. XXIX, where he reports that he heard from Simplicianus, Bishop of Milan, that a certain Platonist had declared that the beginning of the Gospel of John should be written in golden letters and displayed in the most prominent places in all churches.

Therefore, the new Arian Sandius, son of Christopher, the Elector of Brandenburg's secretary, who was removed from office on account of his apostasy to Arminianism, achieves nothing here, although he laboriously strives to prove, by a comparison instituted with the ancient Fathers, that the Arian dogma had prevailed in the Church before the Council of Nicaea, in his Paradoxical Interpretations of the Four Gospels, and especially in the dissertation on the Word subjoined to them. He assumes, of course, as indubitable, as can be seen on p. 151, that St. John accepted the term λόγου in the meaning in which the Rabbis and Platonist philosophers, who had received the doctrine of the λόγῳ from the Jews, commonly understood it. But just as it is not doubtful that the Rabbis received that doctrine from the more ancient Jews, or from the writers of the Old Testament, and that it also flowed in some way from the Jewish Church to Plato and the Platonists, which can be admitted, just as it can also be taught regarding other heads of heavenly doctrine: so it is certain that he borrows light from darkness who wishes to seek from Platonist writers, or even from more recent Rabbis, what should be believed concerning the hypostatic Word, of which the Scripture of the Old Testament and St. John treat. Be it that the Platonist Amelius complained, upon reading the beginning of this Gospel, that John had transferred the mysteries of his master into his own book, and had made what were the arcana of Plato his own and proper to himself, which, however, from his words, 'by Jove, that barbarian agrees with our Plato, the Word of God is established in the order of a beginning,' the heretic gathers nothing at all. For these things report only a consensus; they do not, however, prove that John made the arcana of Plato his own and proper to himself: since from elsewhere those things which he judged to be in conformity with the Platonists, and for which he judged that the words of John should be written in golden letters—concerning which he is praised along with Augustine in the aforementioned place, Eusebius, Preparation for the Gospel, XI. 10, and Cyril of Alexandria, 8, against Julian—John could have had. From those, however, it does not appear how an Arian is going to confirm that the Platonic philosophers derived their doctrine concerning the λόγος from the Jews, much less that John received the word λόγος in the sense in which the Platonists commonly understood it. It is certainly one thing to agree (in some way) that the Word of God was established in the order of a principle, and another to hand down the Word of God and the entire doctrine concerning the Word of God in the same manner. It is one thing to propose certain analogies, another to propose the same things. For it is not difficult to teach how the doctrine concerning certain mysteries of the faith, and particularly concerning the Most Holy Trinity, which they had perhaps received through dealings with the Jewish Church and through report, was changed by Plato and the Platonists, or translated to their own principles and the dreams of their own minds, and then, by the traditions of more recent Rabbis and by Allegorical interpretations, was first involved, then interpolated, and finally variously corrupted and depraved. And we have spoken of these things in a decade of dissertations on the origin, etc., of Matæologies, at Königsberg, in the fatherland of Sandius, formerly proposed publicly: As also in the faith of the Martyrs and Doctors before the Nicene Council concerning the Most Holy Trinity, first delivered at Rostock thirty-six years ago, namely in the thirty-seventh year of this century, and the same was subsequently set forth more fully here at Wittenberg, in a public disputation likewise, against Jonas Schlichtingius of Buckowiez the Socinian, and Henricus Nicolai, who wavered between Catholics, Tritheists, and Arians, and noted in other writings of M. Nicolai detecting and refuting Pyrrhonism. Since these things were not unknown to Sandius, he nevertheless judged that he was foolishly pleading the cause of the Arians if he compiled certain passages from the Platonists—what they (although a great diversity of opinions occurs even among them, and it is difficult to elicit a certain opinion from their perplexed sayings and the wrappings of their secrets) perhaps decided concerning the λόγος—and from that to infer the opinion of the Holy Spirit, which is, as they say, to conclude from the staff to the corner. Therefore, by that laborious collation of Platonic writings, he lost at least his pains and his oil. Nor indeed will those things which have been gathered from Philo the Jew be able to help him much, inasmuch as it cannot be taught that he held or expressed the mind of St. John the Evangelist or of Plato in all things. Therefore, only mere confusions of Christian, Jewish, and Platonic dogma arise from that; but the doctrine of the ancient Church, much less that of St. John and other holy writers, cannot be gathered. Because he praises the writings of Origen (concerning which there was already a great contention in antiquity whether they are interpolated or entirely genuine, just as there was no less, indeed a far graver one, whether Origen held the Catholic faith or whether he interpolated it?) above others on account of their faith, this will certainly profit nothing among those who accuse Origen of heresy, nor even much among those who observe in him testimonies of the faith of the τῆς ὁμουσίας, but who themselves think that something stuck to him and certain others in antiquity from the Platonic Schools. Whence such things, which he has cobbled together without discrimination, with a judgment corrupted by no charm, or certainly by the charm of Arianism, must be discerned with great judgment and accurately tested against the rule of sacred Scripture, as well as against the public Symbols of the ancient Church, if a judgment concerning the Catholic faith is to be made from them. Concerning Origen, Jerome testifies to Magnus that he compared the opinions of Christians and Philosophers among themselves in ten books of Stromata, and confirmed all the dogmas of the Christian religion from Plato, Aristotle, and Cornutus. But who would believe that either Plato and the Platonists, or Aristotle, who was accustomed to go from Plato into all other things, held and handed down all the dogmas of the Christian religion? Origen may therefore have snatched at certain analogous things occurring in the writings of the Philosophers, which Sandius, however, rashly venerates as the very mysteries of the Catholic faith. If it is admitted at all that, as he praises from Philo, Heraclitus followed the dogma of Moses, and that, as he adduces from Origen's book VI against Celsus, Plato learned from certain Hebrews the things that are said in the Phaedrus, and that he stumbled upon the Prophetic writings, which Origen, however, only reports from the account of others; must one therefore learn from Plato or Heraclitus what the opinion of the Old Testament scriptures was, or what the faith of the Israelite Church was, concerning the mysteries of heavenly doctrine, as being purer? And should it not rather be determined as in Eusebius, book XIII of the Preparation for the Gospel, chapter 7, that although Platonic things are in large part derived from the Jews, since, however, philosophy has not kept the purest gold of scripture entirely immaculate, one must have recourse to scripture, which alone is holy and pure.

Furthermore, the Apostate explains on page 155 the passages of the Old Testament and the Targums concerning the hypostatic Word, with which St. John dealt, and acknowledges through the λόγος that the universe was founded, writing thus concerning those in verse 3, πάντα δι ἀυτᾶ ἐγένετο: The Old Testament confirms that all things were made through the Word, in the Word, and by the Word, Ps. XXXIII. 6, Ps. LXX. 9. And the Chaldean Paraphrast on Is. XLV. 12, ch. XLIIX. 13. The Jerusalem Targum, בחכמה, in wisdom God created heaven and earth. So also Peter, 2 Epist. III. 5. But since not only were all things founded through the λόγος, but St. John also openly says, καὶ Θεὸς ἦν ὁ λόγος, and the Word was God, the Word cannot here be viewed as an instrument of creation (which not only the history of Creation and Moses, but the whole of sacred Scripture is ignorant of having been employed in creation), but as the principal cause, because the λόγος is God, and indeed one and the same God with the Father, since there is no other God besides the Father, namely different in essence, nor is any but one God to be believed, as the whole of sacred Scripture intimates; and thus the Arian polytheism has been routed by us in System. Theol. Vol. III and in Natural and revealed Theology; the ὁμουσία of the Son of God with the Father has also been abundantly demonstrated. We have sufficiently taught in the cited writings that those ridiculous exceptions concerning the name Θεὸς placed without the article and concerning the use of the preposition διὰ can in no way refute this. As for the arguments which the Arian Neophyte heaps up to the contrary from the Fathers, Grotius himself, who was far more versed in those same writings (to whom he here appeals), regards them as instances of ἀκυρολογίαις rather than as the settled opinion of those authors, much less as the faith of the early Church, which is rashly estimated from certain private formulas and more unguarded modes of speech used before the controversies arose, and from the use of Platonic philosophy, which was employed less cautiously to express their meaning; concerning which matter we have treated by design in the aforementioned confession of the Martyrs and Doctors of the Church. Cyril of Alexandria, in book III against Julian, reports the opinion of Plato as follows: His father and teacher (Proclus) Plato defined him indeed as the one craftsman who is the cause of all things, whom he also asserts to have been made nearest to the world. Furthermore, he asserts that before him he constituted another GOD, namely the idea of the good.

Furthermore, he has devised a third principle besides, which in order and nature is inferior to those former ones, which he also calls the soul of all things that are. Who would say that this is the very mind of Holy Scripture, who would say it is the faith of the Church of the Old Testament, simple and genuine! Eusebius, at any rate, in book I against Marcellus, ch. 4, p. 23, does not even concede to Origen that he agreed with Plato. Nor, he says, did Origen think about the Principles as Plato did, who, while he acknowledges a single unbegotten principle, without beginning, above all things, establishes that same one to be the Father of one only-begotten Son, through whom all things were made. Let the followers of Arius be called Porphyrians; Sandius boasts that he has taught that they should be so called, according to Socrates, book VI, as a credit to Constantine the Great, he argues. περὶ τ̃ λογ̃ p. 292. because they have followed the doctrine of these: That the true Israelites of the O.T. or Catholic Christians, such as Constantine the Great was, held the dogma of the Platonists or Porphyrians concerning the λόγος, that it was indeed an eternal mind, but a certain pre-eternal one by way of abundance, to which it itself adheres, which Proclus in his book on the Patriarchs or first authors of things reports that Porphyry taught, will be taught at the Greek Calends. Into which parties Augustine is most unjustly dragged by Sandius, because he wrote concerning the Trinity (without citing any chapter or book) that God is something more than a mind, just as much as a man endowed with a mind surpasses brutes lacking a mind. That these things sound concerning the human mind, not the eternal λόγος, no one fails to understand from the very tenor of the words. But that Apostate perverts everything: Nor is it a religion for him to attribute a mind entirely contrary to the holy Fathers, as is the illustrious example in the Parad. Interpr. The passage of Nazianzen from oration XXXIV (which is the second on Theology) brought forward to John 1:9, concerning which heretic. Gregory (he says p. 163) Nazianzen in oration II calls the Son μεγάλε Φωτὸς μικρὸν ἀπαύγασμα, a small radiance of a great light. Oh, the horrible calumny! Nazianzen in that oration is entirely intent on teaching that the Holy Trinity, πρώτην τε & ἀκήρατον φύσιν, that first and purest nature known to itself alone, which is covered by the first veil and hidden by the Cherubim, of which he also prays for μιᾶς θεότητος μίαν ἔλλαμψιν for himself, φράσαι μὲν ἀδύνατον, νοῆσαι δὲ & ἀδυνατώτερον; From which, as from a principal cause and first light, the Angels also are made lights, splendors, intelligent powers, and minds: In this whole contention of speaking, as he himself says, he insists on showing that not even the nature of secondary things (creatures) can be comprehended by the mind and wit of man, let alone that first and only one, τὴν Τριάδα; And although we shall one day know only as much as we have been known, yet in this mortal nature, he says that whatever reaches us is nothing other than a certain small stream, and as it were a small ray of a great light. These things Nazianzen says concerning our knowledge. That he said those things which he says in the place cited concerning the Son of God, that Arian criminalizes with the utmost impudence. From which illustrious specimen, it clearly appears with what honesty the man deals with antiquity. There is, therefore, no reason why we should strive to persuade, with Morainvillerius in his Exam. Philos. Platon. part III, ch. 2, Sect. II, that the Son of God according to the Platonists is the supreme God. Let us grant the Neo-Arian that little glory which he seeks in a honey-cake; that Platonists, Arians, Eunomians, and Muhammadans agree in the doctrine concerning the supreme God and his Word or mind, with which words he sets forth his own ἀπισίαν in Richard's refut. leg. Saracenic. ch. 1, he argues. περὶ τ̃ λόγ̃ page 284. But that the faith of true Israelites and Catholic Christians was the same as the impiety of the Platonists, Arians, and Muhammadans (whose partners we do not envy him) will never be demonstrated. He says he will prove in his tract on the origin of the soul that the Fathers were Platonists up to the fifth century. But there he handed down nothing περὶ τοῦ λόγου or περὶ τοῦ ὁμοουσίου. He brings forward Justin: It is memorable, says the interpreter of the Paradox. p. 303, that Justin writes in his Dialogue with Trypho: ὅτι οὐκ ἀλλότρια ἐστι τὰ Πλάτωνος διδάγματα τοῦ χριστοῦ, that the dogmas of Plato are not alien to Christ (or of Christ). But those things are not contained in the cited dialogue, but in the Apology for the Christians; Nor are they as they are brought forward; for they are cut off, not without deceit, those things by which Justin declares himself. For he professes that he has avoided with all contention being found a Christian, οὐχ ὅτι ἀλλότριά ἐστι τὰ Πλάτωνος διδάγματα τοῦ χριστοῦ, ἀλλ' ὅτι οὐκ ἔστι πάντη ὅμοια: Not indeed that the doctrines of Plato are alien to Christ, but that they are not entirely in agreement with themselves; just as neither are those of others, namely the Stoics, and the Poets, and the Historians. He adds: Whatever therefore has been rightly said by all, is ours, the Christians'. But elsewhere he sufficiently teaches that Plato did not rightly understand what he received from Moses, and that in no way at all could anything be learned about God or the true religion otherwise or from elsewhere than from the Prophets alone, in his Cohort. ad Græcos, Apolog. II, etc., and comparing Plato with Aristotle, he lashes out at him among other things, because just as if he had descended from heaven, and had accurately foreseen the things that are above, he said τὸν ἀνωτάτω Θεὸν ἐν τῷ πυρώδει οὐσίᾳ εἶναι λέγοι, that he said the supreme God is of a fiery essence, Paræn. ad Gentes. Nor indeed does Eusebius, in those books of Ecclesiastical Theology which the Arian praises most highly, admit the same sense of the λόγος which the Platonists had handed down, but he says that the Father existed before the λόγος, or he constitutes the Father and the λόγος as two hypostases, and thus also two Gods or two essences, or he makes the λόγος unlike the Father with the Arians and Eunomians; but he openly contradicts them. One must note here, he says in book II of the Eccles. Theol. ch. XIV, the use, and one must distinguish the new and strange use of that word λόγος, which the Evangelist handed down, speaking indefinitely of the word, but adding a strange and unexpected sense of that word, adapted to its proper force and power. Προσθεὶς δὲ τὸ ξένον καὶ παράδοξον τῆς ἰδιαζούσης αὐτῷ δυνάμεως, in that which he adds: Καὶ Θεὸς ἦν ὁ λόγος. And further: Ὁ δὲ Θεὸς λόγος οὐχ ἑτέρου δεῖται τοῦ προϋποκει- μένου: But God the Word does not need another PRE-EXISTING [being], so that he may be and subsist in it; but he is living and subsisting by himself καθ' ἑαυτὸν, as one who is God. For that he does not deny, but asserts the eternity of the Word against the accusation of Marcellus, he has testified more than once in these books against Marcellus. With a few words inserted, he continues thus in this place: Thus he who grants a God without a λόγος, will entangle himself in an impious and blasphemous dogma, since he admits that God is ἄλογον, inasmuch as he has a λόγος in himself as an Accident: But he is not the λόγος himself. Since it must be confessed altogether that the divine, ineffable, good, simple, uncompounded, uniform, above all things, is God himself: He himself, I say, is αὐτό- λογον, αὐτοσοφίαν, αὐτοφῶς, αὐτοζωὴν, αὐ- τοκαλὸν, αὐτοαγαθὸν, or if anything greater and more excellent than these names can be devised. Nay rather, that which exceeds every mind, surpasses every thought and disquisition of the soul. But [he confesses] his only-begotten Son as the image of the Father, sprung from him: Altogether and in all things most similar to his Begetter, and he believes him to be God, and mind and λόγον, and wisdom and life, and light, the image of that beautiful and good. Not, however, the Begetter himself, but the only-begotten Son of his Father, not indeed himself unbegotten and without beginning: But sprung from him; so that he ascribes the principle of himself to the Father. Further two

He teaches in chapter VII of the same book that he does not introduce two hypostases as two principles, or two unbegotten and unoriginated beings, nor two οὐσίας (essences), and consequently not two Gods, as he teaches in chapter 22, because the Church, which has received the worship of one God, persists in adoring the same God through the Son, his image. But lest anyone object that in chapter 7 he says he does not define the hypostases as ἰσοτίμως (equal in honor), Eusebius had already provided a caveat for this in that same 7th chapter: He says, he commands us to honor him in express words, not as Prophets, not as Angels, or powers similar to Angels, but just as the Father himself: Then indeed he explained his mind in chapter XXIII, namely that he does not wish to introduce two substances set over against each other, equal in honor (δύο οὐσίας ἐξισοτι- μίως ἀντιπαρεξαγομένας ἀλλήλαις εἰσάγη), and therefore not two Gods either. An anonymous author, who added notes to his books against Marcellus, does indeed argue that Eusebius Arianizes. But we already defended his orthodoxy, especially after the Nicene synod, thirty years ago in Theol. Nat. & Revel. p. 17 seqq. This was also subsequently done by the blessed Hülsemann in Dialysi Apolog. p. 99, and by D. Reinboth in Anti-Keddio part II, p. 208. The same was also carried out by the Reformed scholar Pet. Molinæus in his work on the novelty of Popery, book III, c. 2, and from the Catholics by Henr. Valesius in the dissertation on the life and writings of Eusebius prefixed to his Ecclesiastical History, who observes that all Westerners, with the exception of almost only Jerome, feel honorably toward Eusebius; that the Gallican Church even enrolled him in the number of the saints (which he says can be gathered from Victorius Aquitanus, Usuardus, and others), and that Pope Gelasius, in his book on the two natures, ranks him among the Catholics, and that Pope Pelagius likewise pronounces him immune from every stain of heresy, and that therefore it is undoubtedly better that we subscribe to the judgment of our Fathers than to that of the Oriental schismatics. Nor are there lacking those among the Orientals who have felt well toward Eusebius; among them are Socrates and Gelasius of Cyzicus, and in the ecumenical synod the matter was not about Eusebius's faith, except incidentally, but about the worship of images, and it was certainly not done of set purpose, nor was it defined after the cause had been previously examined, nor was any distinction made between his books before and after the Council of Nicaea. Valesius appeals primarily to the books of Eusebius against Marcellus, in which he himself condemned those who said that the Son of God was made from things that did not exist, and that he was when he was not. But Valesius also proved in his Annotations to Eusebius's Ecclesiastical History, p. 191, to book IX, c. 4, that Eusebius held the Catholic faith in his Ecclesiastical History, which was written before the Council of Nicaea was finished, observing these things regarding the words: & αὐτόθεον. This passage is especially to be noted here, in which Eusebius calls Christ αὐτόθεον, that is, God by himself and truly. For this one passage, in my judgment, suffices to repel all the calumnies of those who believed that our Eusebius was stained with the blemish of the Arian dogma. Thus also below he names him on this page τῷ παμβασιλέως κἀ πανη- γεμόνος, and αὐτῷ Θεῷ λόγῳ. This expression is Platonic. For as Plato calls that which is truly and by itself good αὐτοαγαθὸν, so here Eusebius said αὐτοθεὸν of him who is truly and by himself God. Thus Valesius. We have brought forward more proofs of Eusebian orthodoxy in the cited book. All of which, when properly weighed, neither the testimonies of certain ancients produced by Blondell in his book on ecclesiastical writers, p. 895, by Gothofredus in his dissertation on Philostorgius, p. 28, by Theophanes in his Chronographia, p. 22, 28, and by Valesius himself after the cited dissertation, nor the judgments of more recent writers, from whom the Papists are mostly occupied in disparaging the praise of the same Catholic orthodoxy; but they are carried away by the heat of their emotions over the fictitious donation of Constantine the Great, which was passed over by Eusebius, Baronius and Spondanus, at the years 325 and 340, and also Petavius, Tom. II, Dogm. Theol. lib. II, de Trin. cap. 21, 22, are to be noted here

(To which Joh. Dallæus, in book I, de imag. c. 8, did not dare to add his undoubted vote. But they teach that Eusebius should rather be judged from Eusebius himself and the judgment of St. Athanasius. Whence also the blessed Danhavver, although in part II of Christeid. phænom. VIII he favored Eusebius less, in the appendix of the comparison of the Councils of Nicaea and Trent, p. 81 seqq., did not hesitate to stand for Eusebius against Baronius and Scultetus: And the Jena Polyhistor Joh. Andr. Bobsius, in his critical exercise on the preparation for the passage of Fl. Josephus concerning Jesus Christ, published in the year 1668, preferred to choose to suspend judgment, and to confess the sufficiently complex question with Franc. Combefis in his notes to Theophanes, p. 635, rather than to detract from the constancy of Eusebius's Catholic faith after the Nicene Synod. Nor indeed, either from the history of those times, or from the books of Eusebius on the life of Constantine, against Marcellus, against Sabellius, or from any letter of Eusebius, has it been possible to observe thus far that Eusebius never approved from the heart the dogma of the ὁμοεσίε (even though Valesius observes that he never used that word) and the Nicene symbol. But how could Eusebius not have approved the Nicene Symbol, who testifies in book III of the Life of Constantine, c. 3, that all the Bishops who were present at the synod were finally made ὁμογνώμονας & ὁμοδόξες (of one mind and one opinion) on all the disputed points, and praises this synod as an ἐπινίκιον or triumphal one in book IV, 47, and whom Athanasius in his Epistle to the Asians expressly says agreed with the Arians at the beginning, but afterwards subscribed to the Nicene Synod. How could Eusebius have disapproved of the ὁμοούσιον, whom the same holy Father, in his books, as he reports in the cited place, testifies and affirms that there were found certain ancient, learned, and respected Bishops who used the word of coessentiality regarding the divinity of the Father and the Son. And who subscribed to the confession of the Nicene Synod not only regarding the other chapters, but also regarding the ὁμοούσιον, and regarding those things by which the errors of Arius concerning the Son of God were condemned, that he was made from things that did not exist, or from another hypostasis or essence, about which I am silent, as I have spoken in Theol. natur. & Revel. p. 23 seqq. I pass over the fact that Eusebius, when he was accused by Eustathius of innovating the Nicene faith, openly professed that he was not transgressing, but approving the Nicene faith, in Socrates, book 1, Eccl. Hist. c. 18, Sozomen, c. II, 17, to which he also did not hesitate to appeal in his books against Marcellus, as the faith of the Church. But these things concerning those matters: whence it appears that one is laboring in vain, which so laboriously in the interpretation of the paradoxes & the dissertation περὶ τῶ λόγε [on the Word] was sought out and handed down by the Neo-Arian Sandius.

κ] Θεὸς ἦν ὁ λόγος [And the Word was God]. The ancient Hebrews and the first of the Christians judge that as often as any Angel is called יהוה in the sacred books, then it is not my Angel, but He to whom the λόγος [Word] was present, who is understood. Thus Moses Gerundensis interprets that [passage], 'my name is in him,' Ex. 23:21. The Chaldean Paraphrast, Gen. 29:20: 'The word of the Lord shall be God to me.' And Ezek. 1:24, קול שדי [the voice of the Almighty], the Seventy translate as 'the voice of the Word.' But also among Philo, the λόγος is called by the name of God. Chalcidius, in his commentary on the Timaeus, in that place where he professes to explain the eminent doctrine of the holier sect, that is, the Jewish: 'And the reason of God is God, taking counsel for human affairs, which is the cause for men living well and happily, if they do not neglect the gift granted to them by the supreme God.' Tertullian on the same: 'We have learned that He was brought forth from God, and by this bringing forth was generated, and therefore He is called the Son of God and God from the unity of substance, for God is also spirit.' Also when a ray is extended from the Sun, it is a portion from the whole, but the Sun will be in the ray, because it is the ray of the Sun, nor is the substance separated, but extended. The same [author] elsewhere: 'We say He was brought forth from the Father, not separated.' And against Praxeas: 'And never separated from the Father, or another than the Father. This will be the parable of truth, the guardian of unity, by which we say the Son was brought forth from the Father: but not separated.' Soon he says: 'Another by disposition, not another by division.' What is said by Tatian to be γέγονε κατὰ μερισμὸν, ἐ κατ' ἀποκοπὴν [begotten by division, not by cutting off], is called by Justin ἄτμητος κὴ ἀχώριστος πατρὸς δύναμις ὥσπερ τὸ τῶ ἡλίε φῶς [the indivisible and inseparable power of the Father, just like the light of the sun]. To the same [it is] γεγεννημένος κ' κατ' ἀποτομὴν, ὥσπερ ἀπομεριζομένης τῆς τῶ πατρὸς ἐσίας [begotten not by cutting off, just as the essence of the Father is divided]. All of which, as we cannot but stammer in divine matters, have something improper, but must be understood in a manner worthy of God. The same Justin calls Christ Θεὸν ὄντα πρὸ αἰώνων [being God before the ages]. By Theophilus He is called Θεὸς ὁ λόγος κὴ ἐκ τῶ Θεῶ πεφυκώς [God the Word and sprung from God]. Image, character, radiance, with the Apostles as authorities, they often call Him, as do the adjacent writers; likewise δύναμιν, σοφίαν, and if anything similar to these. Tertullian [calls him] the image and person of God. See what we [wrote] on Mark II. 8. Moreover, this manner of speaking is not unlike our own at 2 Cor. III. 17.

These things are to be observed against the corruption occurring throughout the Grotian Annotations on the Old Testament, where he explained those passages in which the Angel is יהוה, not as the Son of God, but as a created Angel: which we have defended in our Anti-Grotius. They are also refuted by the appendix to book IV of the Gospel Explanation, namely the decalogue, in which Grotius, p. 25, understands not only Ex. XX as a created angel pronouncing the law of God, sustaining the person and name of God, but also Gen. XVIII and in other places. How, he says, does he who pronounced the law say, I am יהוה, just as others, who are sent by God for great matters, are called Angels, and allow themselves to be addressed in a similar way. Thus Moses says that God יהוה spoke to him in the bush, Exod. III. 15, and he who had spoken had said that he was, אשר אהיה, which is an explanation of the word יהוה. But Stephen, Acts VII. 30, says that the Angel of the Lord, κυρίου, appeared to Moses in the flame of the bush, and that by the authority of Moses himself, Exod. III. 2. Nor do the most learned of the Hebrews explain similar passages otherwise, where both the name of Angel appears, and yet that Angel speaks as יהוה, and is addressed as יהוה. See Gen. XIX. 13 and 33, compared with the passage at Heb. XIII. 2. Gen. XXII. 15, 17. Josh. V. 14, compared with ch. VI. 1. Judg. VI. 11, compared with v. 14, and ch. XIII. 3, compared with v. 8. 2 Sam. XXIV. 16, compared with v. 17. Thus Grotius is deservedly pitted against Grotius.

Martin Cziechovicius in this place wishes it to be read here, and the word was of God, as in Rev. XIX. 13, and that it stands so in certain Latin MS copies. Of God, not God. But Sandius himself, an Arian, warned here that he ought to have produced in this place where those MSS could be found, if he had wished for credence to be given to his words: adding an observation which is deservedly returned to him and his associates to be observed: By this example, he says, one can see how heretics, if they cannot pervert manifest scripture by interpreting it into their own sense, strive to corrupt the same. Eusebius, book II of Ecclesiastical Theology, ch. XII, expressly warned that John said God. Again, when he said, and the word was with God: he could have said, and the Word of God was with God: But, and God, he says, was the Word, not and the Word of God was God: Lest we should think that that Word of God is significative or effective of an operation, ἵνα μὴ τὸ Θεῢ ἐνέργειάν τινα σημαντικήν τινὸς ἢ ποιητικὴν εἶναι ἀυτὸν ὑπολάβοιμεν.

It is helpful, however, to assert here in a few words the Deity of Christ from its own proper seat and classic passage, regarding the argument derived from the name Θεὸς, and to defend it from the exceptions of the adversaries. From this word, therefore, we conclude as follows:

(1.) He who is called Θεὸς absolutely and simply, and in a proper sense, he is truly God by nature; But Christ is called God absolutely and simply and properly. Therefore. The major premise is proved both from the condition of this name, because it is a name of divine essence, just as man is a name of human essence, and from its appropriation, because it is claimed for the one God alone when it is used absolutely and simply; as is evident from an induction of the places of scripture, and from the nature of its proper signification, which is distinguished by that very fact from improper and metaphorical attribution, because by the former only the true God is designated by essence; whereas by the latter, κατ' ἀναλογίαν, according to similarity, those are called gods who participate in something divine, by which they are in some way similar to the true God. The minor premise is evident from the words themselves, καὶ Θεὸς ἦν ὁ λόγος, and the word was God. For that the name of God is predicated of the Word, that is, of the Son of God, this is taught not only by the article, which testifies that it sustains the place of the subject τῷ λόγῳ; but the whole context proves it: Because the subject, of which it treats, is λόγος, of which the predicates of the context are stated, τὸ εἶναι ἐν ἀρχῇ, τὸ εἶναι πρὸς τὸν Θεὸν, τ᾿ εἶναι Θεὸν, and what are added subsequently, is as clear as that which is most clear, which even Socinus acknowledged against Wujeck, page 313, as did Crellius in his book on God and divine attributes, page 101. The word λόγον, he says, marked with the article, which the word Θεὸς lacks, all interpreters, as far as I know, and other explainers not ignorant of the Greek language, have noted that it holds the place of the subject there. That it is predicated absolutely and simply without an alienating condition, αὐτοψία (direct observation) testifies; that, finally, it is expressed properly, is evident from the fact that no reason persuades, much less compels, one to admit a figurative and improper sense: nay rather, by the same necessity by which the word τοῦ Θεοῦ, immediately preceding and afterwards immediately repeated, is taken properly, by that same necessity, when ὁ λόγος Θεὸς is said, the word Θεῦ must be taken properly. Therefore, just as the Θεὸς, with whom the λόγος is said to have been, is the true God by nature in the preceding verse 1, so also in the present case the word Θεῦ is to be understood as the true God by nature, when it is said λόγος Θεὸς. There is no indication here of a different signification, no reason for disparity. Ὁ λόγος ἦν πρὸς τὸν Θεὸν, κỳ Θεὸς ἦν ὁ λόγος. In a similar way, he is called God with whom the λόγος was, and he himself who was the λόγος with God, whence the whole Church has concluded that the λόγος is God in no other way than God the Father, with whom the ὁ λόγος was from eternity, which we have proven by that preposition, ἐν ἀρχῇ ἦν ὁ λόγος, in a special disputation held on this text.

However, some adversaries take exception to this passage. Enjedinus, Expl. loc. p. 159: (1) objects that the name of God is a name of dignity and office rather than of nature and essence: (2) that it is accustomed to be attributed to various things, Ps. LXXXII, 1 Cor. VIII. (3) that the λόγος is Θεὸν, made by God, Acts II. 36, Heb. I. 9. (4) That this also seems to be confirmed by the fact that Θεὸς is placed here without the article, which Enjedinus says indicates that the supreme God is not signified: Socinus says that the article not being applied to the Greek word Θεὸς clearly demonstrates this against Wujeck, p. 310, because it is certain that the name of God without the article, when it occupies the place of a predicate, is sometimes attributed not only to that supreme God, but also to his creatures, p. 312. Smalcius has similar things, hom. 1 in the beginning of the chapter of John, p. 12, and the remaining adversaries. These, therefore, are the things which the adversaries put forward against our argument, to which we must provide satisfaction.

Resp. to (1.) That the name of God is a name of essence, not only of dignity and office, we have demonstrated in Theol. nat. & revel. c. 3. p. 437. Nor was the discourse in these words concerning his office, but concerning his pre-eternal existence with God the Father and his distinction from the Father by reason of person, which Socinus in the l. c. confesses to be most manifest here when the Word is said to have been with God, as also his communion of Deity with the Father. But that he was conceived and born in a divine manner, and in a certain divine manner designated by Him to perform his office—the things which Smalcius brings forward here—these are ἄπροσδιόνυσα, because the Word was already God while he was in the beginning with the Father, and thus from the beginning of time, nay, from eternity: but it is not a question of this when he was born or designated to his office. Add that he was not God then by reason of his office (without prejudice to the hypotheses. of the adversaries) when he was with God the Father in the beginning: because then he was not yet administering his office, according to their own opinion. That he was conceived in a divine manner does not pertain to his office: nor does designation alone make one actually God of the kind that the adversaries themselves describe. What? That for the same reason God then he was called by John, in the same way as by Thomas in John 20:28, or by Paul in Acts 2:18, or even in Romans 9:5, God blessed for ever. No reason for diversity can be given here: nor is there any intensity or diversity of degrees of perfection in the Deity. Furthermore, we deny that anyone in the New Testament is called God absolutely and simply on account of a divine office alone. Let the adversaries prove it. Nor is the Logos called here only divine, but he is called God, and that absolutely and simply. Finally, he is called God in such a way that the Father was called God. Therefore, he is no less God than the Father himself.

To (2.) I respond (1.) by distinguishing between proper and improper attribution. The name Θεός is indeed improperly attributed to others even outside of God: but properly it is attributed to God alone. But here no reason compels us to abandon the proper meaning. Furthermore (2.) the name Θεός, when placed in the singular number absolutely, without a condition that diminishes or alienates it, never denotes anyone other than the true God by nature. In Psalm 82 it occurs in the plural, as also in 1 Corinthians 8, and in both places a diminishing condition is added, as they call it; here, while θεοὶ λεγόμενοι, they are called gods by name, there, when mention is made of the gods to whom the word of God came, who by divine grace were appointed to a divine office, etc. But here the name Θεός is used simply and absolutely, without a diminishing condition.

To (3.) I respond: the Logos is not said to have been made God in Acts 2:35. But Christ is said to have been made Lord, in his exaltation to the right hand of God, which happened to him according to his human nature, concerning which statement see the examination of Crellius's book, § 38, 225, 239, 246. But here the Logos is said not to have been made, but Θεὸς ἦν, he was God in the beginning of things, namely of all created things, through whom all things were made, whatsoever were made.

Hebrews 1:9 likewise contains no mention of a factitious God; at most Christ, who is designated as God, is said to be anointed by reason of the human nature which the Son of God assumed, Hebrews 2:14, 16. But what does this temporal anointing have to do with the Deity, of which there is talk here, according to which he was with the Father from eternity?

To (4.) I respond: the proof is frivolous, not a demonstration from the article, from which Ejedinus himself says he only seems to confirm it stochastically, to which proof we have cut the nerve in Natural and Revealed Theology, ch. 3, p. 478 et seqq. The force of the word Θεός is the same, whether the article is added or omitted, and it denotes the supreme God no less without the article than with the article. Nor is Christ alone called God without the article, but also ὁ Θεός with the article, John 20:28, Acts 20:28, Titus 2:14, Hebrews 1:8, 1 John 5:20, as also 3:16 according to some codices. But that the article is omitted here and not repeated, this was done partly to avoid confusion of the persons of the Father and the Son, which could have arisen from this if it had been said: ὁ λόγος ἦν πρὸς ὁ θεὸν, ὁ θεὸς ἦν ὁ λόγος: partly for the greater evidence of the preposition, so that it might be more clearly established that ὁ λόγος here holds the place of the subject, to which the article is prefixed, and Θεός that of the predicate: partly to avoid the concurrence of articles, especially because the omission of the article detracts nothing from the proper meaning of the word, just as soon in verse 6 it is said παρὰ Θεῷ and not παρὰ τῷ Θεῷ, where there is no doubt that the supreme God is designated, which can also be seen in verses 12, 13, and 18, τέκνα Θεοῦ ἐκ Θεοῦ ἐγεννήθησαν, and Θεὸν οὐδεὶς ἑώρακε. Is someone other than the supreme God understood here because the article is omitted?

Latin:

CAPUT I.

ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Æterni Verbi, de quo testificandi gratia Iohan- nes Baptista missus erat, adventus in mun- dum, & in propria, sed à paucis agniti, & su- scepti, quibus potestatem dedit filiationis di- vinæ. Qui adventus per incarnationem fa- ctus: Unde Verbum inter homines habitans gloriam suam, tanquam unigenitus Filius à Patre, manifestavit, plenum gratia & veri- tate. De eo autem testificatus Iohannes est, publicumq; rogatus à Synedrio Hierosolymti- tano, testimonium tum de se, quod prodromus Christi sit, ex Es.(c. XL. 3.) tum de Messia, quod in medio ipsorum surrexerit, deposuit, postero die adventantem Iesum demonstrans, quod sit agnus ille Dei portans peccatum mundi, il- le, de cujus adventu dixerat, quem cognovit è descensu Sp. S. & oraculo divino. Postquam Io- hannes iterum de Iesu testatus est, sequenti die duo discipuli, inter quos Andreas sequuti ipsum, adductusque est ad ipsum Simon, Ke- phas ab ipso cognominatus, ac porro Philippus & Nathanael à Iesu pro vero Israëlitahabi- tus, sub ficu, antequam corporaliter eidem adeffet, agnitus, qui profitetur ipsum ideo Dei Filium, Regem illum Israelis: & promissum accipit, quod majora visurus sit, siquidem cœlum jam apertum sit, & Angeli Dei ascen- suri, ac descensuri sint super filium hominis.

Partes sunt tres I. Proœmium Johanneum de æter- ni Verbi adventu in mundum & incarnatione, ad v. 14. II. Testimonium multiplex à Baptista editum, ad v. 34. III. Discipulorum quorundam ad Jesu agni- tionem adductio, nominatim Andreæ, Petri, Philip- pi, Nathanaëlis, hujusque cum Jesu colloquutio ad v. 51.

PARS I. Proœmium Iohanneum de æterni Verbi ad- ventu in mundum, & incarnatione.

Vers. 1. Ἐν ἀρχῇ] Desumtum ex Græco Geneseos, sicut vicissim Syrus ex Hebræo hic posuit בְּרֵאשִׁית. Noto autem scripturæ loco verbum inde sumtum ex sententia illius loci intelligendũ est. Mosi loci sententia hæc est: cum primum cre- avit Deus cœlum & terram, terra erat &c. nam præterita apud Hebræos habent Gerundii etiam significati nem. Tum vero mos est Hebræis, cœli & terræ nomine universum compre- hendere, unde factum est, ut status vitæ futuræ significetur nomine novi cœli & novæ terræ 2. Pet. III. 12. Apoc. XXI. 1. Ergo ἐν ἀρχῇ est, cum primũ rerum universitas cœpit creari,

ἦν.] Jam tum erat. Sic mos est Hebræis æternitatem popu- lariter describere, infra XVII. 5. δόξῃ ᾗ εἶχον πρὸ τῦ τὸν κόσμον εἶναι. Et Justinus dixit, πρὸ τῦ ποιημάτων, & alibi: πρὸ τῦ ἑωσ- φόρυ κὶ σελήνης. Prov. VIII. Dei sapientia sic loquitur: A se- culo habui principatum, à principio, jam ante terram: cum nondum essent voragines, formata sum, cum nondum essent fontes aggravati aquis: antequam montes fundati essent, ante colles sum formata: adhuc non fecerat terram, & pla- teas, & præcipua pulverum orbis: cum præpararet cælos, ibi jam ego. Justinus alibi de verbo hoc loquendi genus ex- plicans προυπᾶρξε πρὸ τῦν αἰώνων. Athenagoras: ἐξ ἀρχῆς ὁ Θεὸς νῦς ἀΐδιῶ ὢν, εἶχεν αὐτὸν ἐν ἑαυτῷ τῦ λόγον, ἀΐδίως λογικὸς ὢν. Rabbi Eliezel: Ante mundum creatum exstitit clemens & benignus Deus & nomen ejus solum.

Quæ in explicatione Grotiana Gen. I. 1. deside- ravimus, ad illud locum diximus. Æternitatem autem Filii Dei hic describi, adversus Socinianos, eorumque exceptiones evictum Triga Exerc. Sele- ctar. Exerc. II. de hoc loco, in principio erat Ver- bum, instituta. Loca Joh. XVII. 5. & Prov. VIII. vindicavimus adversus eosdem in tract. de præex- istentia ante-mundana Filii Dei, Art. III. p. 96. seqq.

ὁ λόγῃ.] Quia Moses scripserat, Dixit Deus, fiat lux & fa- cta est lux, & ita de cæteris, hinc factum est, ut vim sine προ- βολὴν, aut ἀπόῥῥοιαν [has enim voces hac in re Christiani vete- res usurpant] Dei illam, qua res ex nihilo condit, aliaq; rara & eximia efficit, Hebræi appellarent דבר ut videre est Ps. XXXIII, 6. CXLIIX. 8. vide Maimonidem duce dubitantium lib. I. c. XXIII. LXV. & LXVI. Chaldæi non illis tantum lo- cis sed & aliis, ubi ea vox in Hebræo non extat, posuerunt מימרא. Exempla sunt innumera, sed ad rem maxime per- tinet quod apud Esaiam est XLV. 12. in Hebræo legitur: E- go feci terram & hominem super eam ego creavi. In Chaldæo est: Ego in verbo meo feci terram & homines super eam creavi. XLVIII. 13. in Hebræo legitur: Manus mea fundavit ter- ram, In Chaldæo: Verbo meo fundavi terram. Quos secu- tus Petrus Apostolus 2. ep. III. 5. οὐρανοὶ ἦσαν ἔκπαλαι κί γῆ ἐξ ὕδατος, κί διῦδατος συνεστῶσα τῷ τῦ Θεῦ λόγῳ. Eandem vo- cem plurimis in locis usurpat idem Chaldæus paraphrastes, ubi de miraculis, de Prophetia aut singulari Dei auxilio ser- mo est: maxime vero ubi in Hebræo est facies Dei, manus o- culus. Ex veteribus Chaldæorum libris Græci citant ἐξ ἕ λό- γυ κὶ ἥλιον, κί σελήνη. Hinc sumsit Orphicorum Scriptor: Εἰς δὲ λόγον θεῖον σκέψας, τούτῳ προσέδρευε, Ἰθύνων κραδίης νοερὸν κύτος εὖδ’ ἐπίβαινε Ἀτραπιτῦ· μῦνον δ’ ἐσόρα κόσμοιο ἄνακτα. Εἷς ἐσ’ αὐτοτελής, ἑνὸς ἔκγονα πάντα τέτυκται· Idem alibi αὐδὴν vocavit: Αὐδήν ὁρκίζω σε πατρὸς τὴν φθέγξατο πρώτην Ἡνίκα κόσμον ἅπαντα ἑαῖς στηρίξατο βυλαῖς. Hunc secuti Heraclitus, apud quem hoc nomen eo sensu ex- stare notatum ab Amelio? Zeno laudatus à Tertulliano & La- ctantio. Tertulliani verba sunt adversus gentes: Apud vestros quoque sapientes λόγον, id est sermonem atque rationem constat artificem videri universitatis. Hunc enim Zeno determinat fa- ctitatorem, qui cuncta in dispositione formaverit. Locus Zeno- nis, quem respicit Tertullianus, erat in libro ejus περὶ ὐσίας, ut Laertius nos docet. Seneca Stoicos sequens rationem facien- tem vocat Epist. LXV. E Platonicorum numero Amelius, sed quem sæpe à scitis Platonicis ad barbaram Philosophiam de- ficere conqueritur Proclus, hunc Johannis locum valde pro- babat, ut non tantum Eusebius notat in præparatione l. XI. sed & Augustinus pluribus locis. Et contra Julianum Cyril- lus. Plutarchus δύναμιν Θεῦ vocat Symp. VII. ἀναλαβὼν δὲ πά- λιν αὐτῦ Πλάτωνος εἰκότως πατέρα κὶ ποιητὴν τῦ τε κόσμυ, κὶ τῦν ἄλλων γεννητῶν τὸ ἀγέννητον κὶ ἀΐδιον Θεὸν ὀνομάζοντος, ἐ διὰ σπέρματος δὲ κὶ γενόμενον ἄλλῃ δὲ δυνάμει τῦ Θεῦ τῇ ὕλῃ γενόμενον ἀρχὴν ὑφ’ ἧς ἐπαθε κί μετέβαλεν ἐντεκόντος. Sic in exposi- tione fidei facta à Gregorio Episcopo Neocæsariensi ὁ λόγος dicitur δύναμις τῆς ὅλης κτίσεως ποιητική. Philo ad Platonica dogmata deflectens, cum sciret Platoni mundi exemplar λό- γον dici, eo sensu λόγον & usurpavit ipse & multis aliis usur- pandi auctor fuit, & per eum ait conditam rerum universi- tatem, vocat & ὄνομα Θεῦ & εἰκόνα & υἱὸν Θεῦ. Rejicitur hic à Johanne Gnosticorum figmentum qui ἐκ τῖς προαρχῆς post multa secula natum υἱὸν ajebant. Deinde ex υἱῷ natum μονο- γενῆ & ab eo λόγον. Vide Irenæum initio.

hoc ei quod infra dicitur, ὁ λόγος in mundo fuisse, caro fa- ctus, spectatus. Vult enim dicere ante eum fuisse inconspi- cuum. Dicitur enim Deus ἀόρατος. I. Tim. I. 17. & habitare lucem inaccessam, 1. Tim. VI. 16. Idem indicat in epist. 42. Καὶ ἡ ζωὴ ἐφανερώθη. Et mox: ἥτης ἦν πρὸς τὸν πατέρα, & Ephes. III. 9. Sic infra XVII. 5. παρὰ σοι, & cum dicit fuisse apud Patrem, ostendit contra Gnosticos, non esse aliud ple- roma τῆς προαρχῆς, aliud τοῦ λόγου.

Recte hoc nomen à Grotio deducitur è Genes. c. I. 3. Dixit Deus, fiat lux: quo de annot. nostra An- ti-Grotiana & Comment. in Genes. videantur, & è Ps. XXXIII. (non item è Ps. CXLVIII. 8. ubi de ver- bo προστακτικῷ agitur, non de ὑποστατικῷ) nec non è Chaldaico מימרא Es. XLV. 12. c. XLVIII. 13. ubi Chaldeum notat sequutum esse Petrum 2. Ep. III. 5. Sed quæ ex Græco Orphicorum scriptore, cum λόγον & αὐδὴν, verbum & vocem nominat, aliisque adfert, vel analoga, non eadem sunt; vel ab Ebræis & Christianis ad Philosophos traducta, etsi ab iis non adeo intellecta. Qui κατ' ἄνθρωπων à Patribus quandoque adducti sunt. Ita Tertull. advers. gentes: Apud vestros quoque sapientes λόγον, id est, sermonem atque rationem constat artificem videri u- niversitatis. Hunc enim Zeno determinat factitato- rem, qui cuncta in dispositione formaverit. Locus Ze- nonis, quem respicit Tertullianus, erat in libro ejus περὶ ὀσίας, ut Laërtius nos docet, observante hic Grotio, ubi τὸ ποιοῦν seu causam effectricem vocavit λόγον, quem secuti Cleanthes, Chrysippus, Arche- demus, Posidonius, docente Laërtio in Zenone, & ex eo Grot. l. 1. de ver. R. Christ. in annot. p. 32. Vid. & August. l. VII. Confess. & l. X. de civit. Dei c. XXIX. ubi refert, Platonicum quendam profes- sum initium Evangelii Johannei aureis literis conscri- bendum, & per omnes Ecclesias in locis eminentissi- mis proponendum esse, à Simpliciano Mediola- nensi Episcopo se audivisse.

Nihil ergo hic proficit Arianus novellus Chri- stophorus, Christophori Electoralis Brandeburgici Secretarii, sed ob ἀποστασίαν ad Arminianismum, ab officio remoti filius, Sandius, cum operose è Pla- tonicis, collatione cum Patribus antiquis instituta, Arianum dogma ante concilium Nicenum in Ec- clesia obtinuisse, in Interpretat. Paradox. IV. Ev- angeliorum, & imprimis subjuncta de Verbo disser- tatione probare satagit. Nimirum supponit tan- quam indubium, ut p. 151. videre est, D. Johannem vocem λόγου ea significatione accepisse, qua eam communiter intelligebant Rabbini, & Philosophi Platonici, qui doctrinam de λόγῳ Judæis acceptam tulerint. Ast uti hoc dubium non est, à Judæis an- tiquioribus, sive à Scriptoribus Veteris Testa- menti eam doctrinam accepisse Rabbinos, eamq; etiam à Judaica Ecclesia aliqua ratione dimanasse ad Platonem, & Platonicos, admitti potest, quem- admodum etiam de aliis doctrinæ cœlestis capiti- bus id doceri potest: Sic lucem à tenebris mutuari certum est, qui quid de Verbo hypostatico, de quo Scriptura V. Test. & S. Johannes agit, credendum sit, è Platonicis scriptoribus, vel etiam recentioribus Rabbinis petere velit. Esto, quæstus sit Amelius Pla- tonicus, lecto Evangelii hujus principio, Johan- nem in suum ipsius librum transtulisse Magistri sui my- steria, & quæ erant Platonis arcana, sua, propriaq; fecisse, quod tamen è verbis illius, per Jovem barba- rus ille cum nostro Platone sentit, Verbum Dei in or- dine principii esse constitutum, ne quicquam colligit hæreticus. Hæc enim consensum tantum referunt; non autem Johannem arcana Platonis sua, propriaq; fecisse, probant: cum aliunde ea, quæ Platonicis conformia ille censuit, & ob quæ aureis literis ver- ba Johannis conscribenda, quo de cum Augustino l. c. Eusebius præpar. Evang. XI. 10. Cyrill. Alexandr. 8. contra Julian. laudatur, judicavit, Johannes habere potuerit. Ex illis tamen, quomodo A- rianus confirmaturus sit, Philosophos Platonicos doctrinam suam de λόγῳ Judæis acceptam ferre, ne- dum, quod Johannes vocem λόγʊ ea significatione acceperit, qua eam communiter intellexerunt Plato- nici, non apparet. Aliud profecto est, consentire (aliquo modo) de eo, quod Verbum Dei in ordine principii constitutum sit, aliud Verbum Dei & do- ctrinam de Verbo Dei universam eadem ratione tra- dere. Aliud analoga quædam, aliud eadem pro- ponere. Quomodo enim cum à Platone & Pla- tonicis doctrina de quibusdam fidei mysteriis, ac peculiariter de Sacrosancta Trinitate, : quam for- te per commercia cum Ecclesia Judaica, & fa- mam acceperant, commutata, vel ad sua princi- pia, suæque mentis somnia traducta, tum à re- centioribus Rabbinis traditionibus & Cabbalisticis, Allegoricisque interpretamentis involuta pri- mum, deinde interpolata, denique varie corru- pta & depravata sit, haud difficile est docere. Et diximus de his in decade dissertationum de ortu &c. Matæologias, Regiomonti, in patria Sandi, quon- dam publice proposita: Nec non in fide Marty- rum & Doctorum ante Concilium Nicenum de SS. Trinitate primum Rostochii ante hos XXXVI. annos, anno nimirum trigesimo septimo hujus seculi tradita, eademque postmodum hic Wit- tebergæ, disputatione itidem publica, adversus Jonam Schlichtingium à Buckowiez Socinianum, & Henricum Nicolai, inter Catholicos, & Trithei- tas, & Arianos ἐπαμφοτερίζοντα plenius expo- sita, inque aliis scriptis M. Nicolai Pyrrhonismum detegentibus & refellentibus adnerta. Quæ cum ignota non fuerint Sandio, satis tamen se Ariano- rum causam agere infrunite censuit, si loca quæ- dam è Platonicis compilaret, quod illi, (quamvis magna etiam inter ipsos opinionum occurrat di- versitas, & difficile sit certam sententiam è per- plexis eorundem dictis, & arcanorum suorum involucris eruere) forte de λόγῳ statuerint, at- que inde Spiritus sancti sententiam colligere, quod est à baculo ad angulum, ut ajunt, conclu- dere. Illa ergo operosa Platonicorum scripto- rum collatione operam saltim & oleum perdidit. Nec vero multum ipsum juvare poterunt, quæ è Philone Judæo congesta sunt, utpote, quem nec S. Johannis Evangelistæ, nec Platonis mentem per omnia tenuisse aut expressisse doceri potest. Meræ ergo inde confusiones tantum dogmatis Christiani, Iudaici & Platonici oriuntur; non vero doctrina Ecclesiæ veteris, nedum S. Johan- nis, aliorumque sanctorum scriptorum colligi potest. Ob quorum fidem quod Origenis scri- pta, (de quibus interpolatane, an γνήσια omni- no sint, magna jam in antiquitate contentio fuit, uti non minor, imo longe gravior, an- ne Origenes Catholicam fidem tenuerit, an ve- ro interpolarit?) præ aliis laudet, penes illos sane, qui Origenem hæreseos arguunt, nihil proficiet, nec multum etiam apud eos, qui fidei τῆς ὁμουσίας testimonia in illo observant, ipsi autem, aliisque quibusdam in antiquitate è Scholis Platonicis aliquid hæsisse existimant. Unde talia quæ nullo, vel certe Arianismi fasci- no corrupto judicio, sine discrimine, confar- cinavit, magno cum judicio discernenda, & ad regulam Scripturæ sacræ, nec non ad Symbola Ecclesiæ antiqua publica accurate ex- igenda, si de fide Catholica judicium inde fieri debeat. De Origene Hieronymus ad Magnum testatur, eundem in decem Stromatum libris Christianorum & Philosophorum inter se sententias comparasse, & omnia religionis Christia- nae dogmata ex Platone, Aristotele, Numenio, Cornutoq; confirmasse. Ecquis autem credat, vel Platonem & Platonicos, vel Aristotelem, qui à Platone in omnia alia ire consuevit, dogmata Christianae religionis omnia tenuisse ac tradidisse? Rapuerit ergo eo quaedam analoga in scriptis Philosophorum occurrentia Origenes, quae ve- ro temere pro mysteriis ipsismet fidei Catholicae veneratur Sandius. Si omnino admittatur, quod è Philone laudat Heraclitum Mosis dogma se- quutum, & quod ex Origenis lib. VI. contra Cel- sum adducit, Platonem quae in Phedro dicuntur, ab Hebraeis quibusdam didicisse, eundemque in Prophe- tica scripta incidisse, quod tamen Origenes ex a- liorum relatione tantum perhibet; Num ideo è Platone, vel Heraclito, quaenam fuerit sive scri- pturarum Veteris Testamenti sententia, sive fi- des Ecclesiae Israeliticae, de coelestis doctrinae my- steriis purior, discendum? Et non potius cum Eusebio lib. XIII. de praeparat. Evangel. cap. 7. ita statuendum erit, etsi Platonica magnam partem à Judaeis sint derivata, quum tamen Philosophia pu- rissimum scripturae aurum non omnino immaculatum servarit, ad scripturam, quae sola sancta & pura est, recurrendum esse.

Porro explicat Apostata pag. 155. loca Veteris Testament. & Targumica de Verbo hypostatico, quo de S. Johannes egit, & per λόγον agnoscit, conditam universitatem, ad illa vers. 3. πάντα δι ἀυτᾶ ἐγένετο ita scribens: Omnia per Verbum, in Verbo, & Verbo facta esse confirmat Vetus Testa- mentum Ps. XXXIII. 6. Ps. LXX. 9. Et Chaldaeus Pa- raphrastes Es. XLV. 12. c. XLIIX. 13. Targum Hie- rosolymitanum בחכמה in sapientia creavit Deus coelum & terram. Sic etiam Petrus 2. Epist. III. 5. Quum autem non tantum per λόγον omnia condi- ta sunt, sed S. Johannes aperte etiam, καὶ Θεὸς ἦν ὁ λόγος, & Verbum erat Deus inquiat, non potest hic Verbum spectari tanquam instrumen- tum creationis, (quale in creatione adhibitum fuis- se, non tantum historia Creationis, & Moses, sed tota Scriptura sacra ignorat) sed ceu causa princi- palis, quia Deus, & quidem unus idem cum Patre Deus ὁ λόγος, quum alius praeter Patrem Deus, essentia nempe diversus, non detur, nec nisi u- nus credendus sit Deus, tota Scriptura sacra insi- nities docente; adeoque πολυθεότης Ariana à Nobis in System. Theol. Tom. III. & in Theol. Na- turali & revelata profligata; Filii etiam Dei ὁμου- σία cum Patre, demonstrata abunde sit. Qua lu- dicris illis exceptionibus, de nomine Θεὸς absque articulo posito & de Praepositionis διὰ usu nullate- nus elidi posse, scriptis laudatis satis docuimus. Quae vero è Patribus in contrarium coacervat Neophytus Arianus, Grotius ipse, in iisdem longe magis versatus (ad quem hic provocat) pro ἀκυρολογίαις potius, quam constante ipsorum sententia habet, nedum pro fide veteris Ecclesiae, quae temere è quibusdam formulis privatis, & se- curioribus loquutionibus ante mota certamina, & Platonicae Philosophiae usu, ad exprimendam mentem minus caute adhibitis, aestimantur; de quo in confessione praedicta Martyrum & Docto- rum Ecclesiae ex instituto actum. Platonis sen- tentiam ita refert Cyrillus Alexandrinus libr. III. contra Julianum: Pater & Praeceptor ipsius (Pro- cli) Plato unum quidem opificem esse eum definiit, qui causa est omnium, quem & mundo citimum fa- ctum esse asserit. Ante hunc porro DEUM alterum constituisse, nempe boni ideam.

Adhæc tertium insuper principium excogitavit, quod ordine ac natura prioribus illis inferius, quam etiam omnium quæ sunt animam appellat. Hæc quis ipsam scripturæ sacræ mentem, quis Ec- clesiæ Vet. Test. fidem, simplicem ac genuinam esse dixerit! Euseb. utiq; lib. I. contra Marcell. c. 4. p. 23. ne de Origene quidem concedit, quod cum Pla- tone consenserit. Nec ut Plato, inquit, de Principiis Origenes sentiebat, qui principium unicum ingenera- tum, sine principio, super omnia, cum agnoscat, eum i- psum statuit esse Patrem unius unigeniti Filii, per quem omnia facta sunt. Vocentur sane Arii sectatores Por- phyriani; quos ita vocitandos docuisse apud Socratem l. VI. Constantinum M. laudi sibi ducit Sandius dis- fert. περὶ τ̃ λογ̃ p. 292. eo quod horum doctrinam sint sequuti: Veros Israelitas V. T. aut Christianos Catholicos, qualis Constantinus M. erat, Platoni- corum, aut Porphyrianorum dogmati de λόγῳ, quod mens quidem æterna fuerit, sed præeternus περιουσίως quidam fuit, cui ipsa adhæret, quod Porphyrium docuisse Proclus libro de Patriarchis seu primis autoribus rerum perhibet, ad Calendas Græ- cas docebitur. In quas utique partes iniquissime à Sandio abripitur Augustinus, quod de Trinitate (nullo vel capite, vel libro adducto) scripserit, Deum amplius quid, quam mentem esse tantum, quantum homo mente præditus superat bruta mente carentia. Quæ de mente humana, non de λόγῳ æterno so- nare nemo non ex ipso verborum tenore intelli- git. Sed Apostata ille omnia pervertit: Neque reli- gio ipsi est, prorsus contrariam sanctis Patribus af- fingere mentem, ut illustri exemplo est in Parad. In- terpr. locus Nazianzeni ex orat. XXXIV. (quæ est II. de Theologia) adductus ad Joh. I. 9. de quo hæret. Gregor. (inquit p. 163.) Nazianz. orat. II. vocat Filium μεγάλε Φωτὸς μικρὸν ἀπαύγασμα magni lumi- nis parvum splendorem. Proh horrendam calumni- am! Nazianzenus illa oratione totus in eo est, ut S. Trinitatem πρώτην τε & ἀκήρατον φύσιν primam illam & purissimam naturam sibi soli notam, quæ pri- mo velo obtenditur, & à Cherubim obtegitur, cujus & μιᾶς θεότητος μίαν ἔλλαμψιν sibi precatur, do- ceat, φράσαι μὲν ἀδύνατον, νοῆσαι δὲ & ἀδυνατώ- τερον; A qua ceu principe causa & primo lumine lumi- na etiam efficiantur Angeli splendores, intelligentes po- testates, & mentes: In hoc omni, ut ipse loquitur, di- cendi contentione incumbens, ut ostendat, ne ipsam qui- dem secundarum rerum (creaturarum) naturam homi- nis mente atque ingenio comprehendi posse, nedum pri- mam illam ac solam τὴν Τριάδα; Et quanquam nos aliquando tantum cognituri simus, quantum cogniti sumus, in hac tamen mortali natura, quicquid ad nos pertingit, aliud nihil esse, ait, quam exiguum quendam rivulum, & velut parvum lucis magnæ radium. Quæ de nostra scientia Nazianzen. l. c. dicit, ea de Filio Dei ipsum dixisse, summa impudentia criminatur ille Arianus. Ex quo illustri specimine, qua fide homo versetur in antiquitate, liquido apparet. Non ergo est, quod cum Morainvillerio Exam. Phi- los. Platon. parte III. c. 2. Sect. II. suadere annita- mur, Filium Dei juxta Platonicos esse summum Deum. Largiamur Ne-Ariano gloriolam illam, quam in mustaceo quærit; . Platonicos, Arianos, Eunomia- nos, Muhamedanos in doctrina de summo Deo, ejusq; Verbo vel mente convenire, quibus verbis Richardi refut. leg. Saracenic. cap. 1. suam ἀπισίαν effert dis- fert. περὶ τ̃ λόγ̃ pag. 284. Fidem vero verorum Is- raelitarum, & Catholicorum Christianorum eandem fuisse, cum Platonicorum, Arianorum & Mahume- danorum (quos socios ipsi non invidemus) impie- tate nunquam demonstrabitur. Id se proba- turum ait in tract. de origine animæ, Patres usq; in seculum quintum Platonicos fuisse. Sed illic περὶ τοῦ λόγου vel περὶ τοῦ ὁμοουσίου nihil tradidit. Affert Ju- stinum: Memorabile est, inquit interpret. Paradox. p. 303. quod Justin. Dialog. cum Tryphone scribit: ὅ- τι οὐκ ἀλλότρια ἐστι τὰ Πλάτωνος διδάγματα τοῦ χριστοῦ, quod Platonis dogmata à Christo, (vel Christi) non sint aliena. Sed nec habentur illa in dialogo lau- dato, sed in Apolog. pro Christianis; Neque ita ha- bent, ut afferuntur; præcisa enim sunt, non absque dolo, ea, quibus sese declarat Justinus. Profitetur nempe se omni contentione devitasse, ut Christianus inveniretur, οὐχ ὅτι ἀλλότριά ἐστι τὰ Πλάτωνος δι- δάγματα τοῦ χριστοῦ, ἀλλ' ὅτι οὐκ ἔστι πάντη ὅμοια: Non equidem, quod aliena sint à Christo Platonis do- ctrinæ, sed quod sibi ipsis non omnino consenti; sicuti neq; aliorum, Stoicorum videlicet, & Poëtarum, & Hi- storicorum. Addit: Quæcunq; ergo apud omnes recte dicta sunt, nostra Christianorum sunt. Alibi autem satis docet, quod quæ è Moyse accepit Plato, non recte intellexerit, nulloque plane pacto aliter aut a- liunde de Deo vel de recta religione disci quidquam posse, quam à Prophetis solis cohort. ad Græcos A- polog. II. &c. & Platonem cum Aristotele commit- tens, illum inter alia perstringit, quod perinde atq; cœlitus descenderit, atque ea, quæ sursum sunt, accurate perviderit τὸν ἀνωτάτω Θεὸν ἐν τῷ πυρώδει οὐσίᾳ εἶ- ναι λέγοι, summum Deum essentiæ igneæ esse, dixe- rit, Paræn. ad Gentes. Nec vero Eusebius in illis, quos cum maxime laudat Arianus, de Ecclesiastica Theologiæ libris vel eundem τοῦ λόγου sensum ad- mittit, quem Platonici tradiderant, sed prorsus no- vum & inusitatum vel τῷ λόγῳ præextitisse Patrem ait, vel Patrem & λόγον, ut duas hypostases, ita etiam duos Deos vel essentias duas constituit, aut λό- γον à Patre dissimilem facit cum Arianis & Eunomi- anis; sed illis palam contradicit. Animadverten- dus hic, inquit lib. II. Theol. Eccles. cap. XIV. u- sus, & dignoscendus vocis illius λόγου novus & pe- regrinus usus, quem Evangelista tradidit, indefi- nite loquens verbum, adjiciens autem peregrinum & inexpectatum vocis illius sensum, ad vim & vir- tutem propriam ejus adaptatum. Προσθεὶς δὲ τὸ ξένον καὶ παράδοξον τῆς ἰδιαζούσης αὐτῷ δυνάμεως, in eo, quod addit: Καὶ Θεὸς ἦν ὁ λόγος. Et porro: Ὁ δὲ Θεὸς λόγος οὐχ ἑτέρου δεῖται τοῦ προϋποκει- μένου: At Deus Verbum non altero indiget PRÆEX- ISTENTE, ut in ipso sit & subsistat; sed per se καθ' ἑαυτὸν vivens est, & subsistens, veluti qui Deus. Æter- nitatem enim Verbi sese non negare, sed asserere contra Marcelli ἔγκλημα, plus vice simplici in his contra Marcellum libris testatus est. Paucis inter- jectis h. l. sic pergit: Ita Deum qui concesserit sine λόγῳ, impio se atq; blasphemo dogmati implicabit, cum admittat ille Deum ἄλογον, utpote qui λόγον in se habeat tanquam Accidens: Non autem sit ipse λό- γος. Cum omnino fatendum sit, divinum, ineffabi- lem, bonum, simplicem, incompositum, uniformem, su- pra omnia esse ipsum Deum: Ipsum, inquam, αὐτό- λογον, αὐτοσοφίαν, αὐτοφῶς, αὐτοζωὴν, αὐ- τοκαλὸν, αὐτοαγαθὸν, aut si quid hisce nominibus majus & præstantius excogitari queat. Imo vero po- tius, quod excedat mentem omnem, superet omnem cogitationem & disquisitionem animi. Hujus autem Filium unigenitum veluti Patris imaginem, ex ipso or- tum: Omnino & per omnia quam simillimam Se- nitori suo, & ipsum quod credat Deum, & mentem & λόγον, & sapientiam & vitam, & lucem, il- lius pulchri imaginem atque boni. Non tamen i- psummet Genitorem, sed Patris sui Filium unigeni- tum, non ipsum quidem ingenitum & imprin- cipiatum: Sed ex illo ortum; sic ut prin- cipium sui adscribat Patri. Ulterius duas

ὑποστάσεις non inferre duo principia cap. VII, libri ejusdem, aut duos ingenitos & imprincipiatos, nec duas οὐσίας essentias, adeoque nec duos Deos cap. 22. docet, quia Ecclesia, quæ accepit unius Dei cultum, eundem Deum per Filium imaginem suam adorare perseverat. Ne vero ubjiciat quis, quod cap. 7. di- cat, se hypostases non definire ἰσοτίμως honore pares, secundum quid hoc accipiendum esse, tum illo 7. c. Euseb. jam cavit: Disertis, inquit, verbis ipsum ho- norare jubet, non tanquam Prophetas, non velut An- gelos, aut Angelis similes potestates, sed quemadmodum ipsum Patrem: Tum vero mentem suam exposuit cap. XXIII. quod scilicet nolit duas substantias ex adverso introductas, honore pares (δύο οὐσίας ἐξισοτι- μίως ἀντιπαρεξαγομένας ἀλλήλαις εἰσάγη) itaque nec duos Deos. Arguit quidem Eusebium Anony- mus, qui notas libris ejus ad Marcellum subjecit, quod Arianizet. Sed orthodoxiam ejus, imprimis post Nicenam synodum, vindicavimus jam ante XXX. annos in Theol. Nat. & Revel. p. 17. seqq. Quod etiam deinceps factum à B. Hülsem. in Dialysi Apo- log. p. 99. D. Reinboth in Anti-Keddio parte II. p. 208. Idem & è Reformatis Pet. Molinæus in novita- te Papismi l. III. c. 2. è Pontificiis Henr. Vales. disp. de vit. & script. Eusebii Histor. Eccles. præmissa, exequutus est, qui observat, Occidentales omnes uno fere excepto Hieronymo de Eusebio honorifice sentire; Gallicanam vero Ecclesiam eum etiam sanctorum numero adscripsisse, (quod ex Victorio Aquitano, U- suardo, aliisque colligi ait) Gelasium vero P. R. in libro de duabus naturis inter Catholicos referre, ac Pelagium itidem Pontif. ab omni hæreseos labe immu- nem ipsum pronunciare, adeoque satius sine dubio esse, ut Patrum nostrorum, quam ut Orientalium schis- maticorum judicio subscribamus. Neque deesse ex O- rientalibus qui de Eusebio bene senserint; interq́; eos Socratem, & Gelas. Cyzicenum, in synodo vero œcume- nica non de Eusebii fide, nisi obiter, sed de imaginum cultu actum, non certe opera data, aut causa prius co- gnita de illa definitum, nec discrimen inter libros ejus- dem ante & post Concil. Nicen. adhibitum esse. Pro- vocat Valesius imprimis ad libros Eusebii contra Marcellum, in quibus ab ipso damnati, qui dicerent Fi- lium Dei de non exstantibus esse factum, & fuisse, cum non esset. Sed & in Historia Ecclesiastica, ante finitum Concil. Nicenum conscripta, Catholicam fidem te- nuisse Eusebium, in Annotatis ad Histor. Eccl. Eu- seb. p. 191. Valesius probavit ad l. IX. c. 4. hæc obser- vans, ad verba; & αὐτόθεον. Notandum est imprimis hic locus, in quo Eusebius Christum vocat αὐτόθεον, id est, per se, ac vere Deum. Hic enim unius locus, meo quidem judicio, sufficit ad repellendas omnes ca- lumnias eorum, qui Eusebium nostrum Ariani do- gmatis labe aspersum fuisse, crediderunt. Sic etiam infra nominat hac pagina τῷ παμβασιλέως κἀ πανη- γεμόνος, & αὐτῷ Θεῷ λόγῳ. Est autem hæc loquutio Platonica. Nam ut Plato αὐτοαγαθὸν vocat quod est vere ac per se bonum, hic Eusebius αὐτοθεὸν dixit qui est vere ac per se Deus. Hæc Valesius. Documenta ὀρθοδοξίας Eusebianæ plura l. cit. adduximus. Quæ omnia probe ponderata, neque veterum quorun- dam testimonia à Blondello in libr. de script. Eccles. p. 895. Gothofredo in dissert. ad Philostorg. pag. 28. Theophan. in Chronograph. p. 22. 28. ipsoque Va- lesio post dissertationem laudatam producta, ne- que recentiorum judicia, è quibus Papistæ maxi- me in deroganda eidem Catholicæ Orthodoxias laude; sed æstu affectuum ab prætermissam ab Eu- sebio fictitiam Constantini M. donationem, abre- pti occupantur, Baronius & Spondanus, ad anni 325. & 340. nec non Petavius Tom. II. Dogm. Theol. lib. II. de Trin. cap. 21. 22. hic attendenda

(Quibus indubitatum calculum addere non ausus est Joh. Dallæus l. I. de imag. c. 8. Sed Eusebium potius ex ipso Eusebio, & S. Athanasii judicio æstimandum esse docent. Unde etiam B. Danhavver. etsi part. II. Christeid. phænom. VIII. Eusebio minus faverit, in appendice συγκρίσεως Concil. Niceni & Trident. p. 81. seqq. pro Eusebio, contra Baronium & Scultetum, stare non dubitavit: Ac Polyhistor Jenensis Joh. Andr. Bobsius exercit. Critica προπαρασκευαστικῇ in Periocham Fl. Josephi de Jesu Christo Ann. 1668. edita τὸ ἐπέχειν maluit eligere, & implexam satis quæstionem cum Franc. Combefis in notis ad Theophan. p. 635. fateri, quam Catholicæ fidei constantiam post Synodum Nicenam Eusebio detrahere. Neq; vero vel ex historia illorum temporum, vel è libris Eusebii de vita Constantini, contra Marcellum, contra Sabellium, aut Epistola ulla Eusebii id hactenus observare licuit, Eusebium dogma ὁμοεσίε (etsi vocem illam nunquam eum adhibuisse, etiam Valesius observet) & Nicenum symbolum nunquam ex animo probasse. Quomodo vero non probasset Nicenum Symbol. Euseb. qui omnes Episcopos, qui synodo intererant, tandem ὁμογνώμονας & ὁμοδόξες ἐπὶ τοῖς ἀμφισβητημένοις ἅπασιν effectos l. III. de Vit. Constant. c. 3. testatur, & ἐπινίκιον seu triumphalem hanc synodum laudat lib. IV. 47. quemque Athanasius in Epist. ad Asiat. diserte ait, initio quidem cum Arianis consensisse; postmodum autem subscripsisse Nicenæ Synodo. Quomodo improbarit τὸ ὁμοούσιον Eusebius, quem in libris suis ἀξιοπίστως idem S. Pater l. c. perhibet, testatum esse & affirmasse, reperiri quosdam priscos doctos, & spectatos Episcopos alios coessentialitatis voce in Patris & Filii divinitate. Quique subscripsit Synodi Nicenæ confessioni non tantum quoad cætera capita, sed etiam quoad τὸ ὁμοούσιον, & quoad illa, quibus damnabantur errores Arii de Filio Dei, ὅτι ἐξ ἐκ ὄντων ἐγένετο, ἢ ἐξ ἑτέρας ὑποστάσεως ἢ ἐσίας, quo de Theol. natur. & Revel. p. 23. seqq. Taceo, quod Eusebius, cum accusaretur ab Eusthatio, quod innovaret Nicenam fidem, palam professus sit, se non transgredi, sed probare fidem Nicenam, apud Socrat. l. 1. Histor. Eccl. c. 18. Sozom. cap. II. 17. ad quam etiam in libr. contr. Marcell. provocare non dubitavit, tanquam fidem Ecclesiæ. Sed hæc de istis: unde apparet, in spongiam incumbere, quæ tam operose in interpr. parad. & dissert. περὶ τῶ λόγε conquisivit tradiditque Ne-Arianus Sandius.

κ] Θεὸς ἦν ὁ λόγος.] Censent Hebræi veteres & Christianorum primi, quoties Angelus aliquis in sacris libris appellatur יהוה tunc non Angelum meum, sed cui adfuerit ὁ λόγος, intelligi. Sic interpretatur Moses Gerundensis illud, nomen meum in eo est, Ex. XXIII. 21. Chaldæus Paraphrastes Gen. XXIX, 20. Erit verbum Domini mihi in Deum. Et Ezech. I. 24. קול שדי septuaginta vertunt φωνὴν τῶ λόγος. Sed & apud Philon. λόγος vocatur Θεῶ nomine.
