Chalcidius ad Timæum, eo loco, ubi doctrinam eminentem sectæ sanctioris, id est, Judaicæ explicare se profitetur: Et ratio Dei, Deus est humanis rebus consulens, quæ causa est hominib. bene beateq́; vivendi, si non concessum sibi munus à summo Deo negligant. Tertullian. de eod. Hunc ex Deo prolatum didicimus & prolatione generatum, & idcirco filium Dei & Deum dictum ex unitate substantiæ, nam & Deus spiritus. Etiam cum radius ex Sole porrigitur, portio ex summa, sed Sol erit in radio, quia Solis est radius, nec separatur substantia, sed extenditur. Idem alibi: Prolatum dicimus à Patre, non separatum. Et adversus Praxeam: Et nunquam separatus à Patre, aut alius à Patre. Hæc erit parabolæ veritatis, custos unitatis, qua prolatum dicimus Filium à Patre: sed non separatum. Mox dicit: Dispositione alium, non divisione alium. Quod Tatiano dicitur γέγονε κατὰ μερισμὸν, ἐ κατ' ἀποκοπὴν, Justino dicitur ἄτμητος κὴ ἀχώριστος πατρὸς δύναμις ὥσπερ τὸ τῶ ἡλίε φῶς. Eidem γεγεννημένος κ' κατ' ἀποτομὴν, ὥσπερ ἀπομεριζομένης τῆς τῶ πατρὸς ἐσίας. Quæ omnia, ut in rebus divinis non possumus nisi balbutire, habent aliquid ἄκυρον, sed intelligenda θεοπρεπῶς. Idem Justin. Christum vocat Θεὸν ὄντα πρὸ αἰώνων. Theophilo dicitur Θεὸς ὁ λόγος κὴ ἐκ τῶ Θεῶ πεφυκώς. Εἰκόνα, χαρακτῆρα, ἀπαύγασμα, Apostolis auctorib. sæpe vo- ca & proximi scriptores: Item δύναμιν, σοφίαν, & si quid his simile. Tertullianus effigiem & personam Dei. Vide, quæ nos ad Marcum II. 8. Est autem loquendi genus huic no- stro non dissimile 2. Cor. III. 17.

Observanda hæc contra depravationem in An- notatis Grotianis in V. T. passim occurrentem, ubi loca illa, in quibus Angelus יהוה, non de Filio Dei, sed de Angelo creato exposuit: quæ in Anti-Gro- tianis nostris vindicavimus. Revincunt ea etiam appendicem ad lib. IV. Evangel. Explicationem nem- pe decalogi, in qua Grotius p. 25. non tantum Ex. XX. angelum creatum intelligit legem Dei pronuncian- tem, personam nomenque Dei sustinentem, sed & Gen. XVIII. & aliis in locis. Quomodo, inquit, is qui legem pronunciavit, Angelus dicit, ego יהוה, ita & alii, qui ad res magnas à Deo legati sunt Angeli loquuntur, & simili modo compellari se ferunt. Sic Moses in rubo sibi locutum dicit Deum יהוה, Exod. III. 15. & is, qui locutus erat, se dixerat esse, אשר אהיה, quæ vocis יהוה est explicatio. At Stephanus Act. VII. 30. sum, ait, Mosi in flamma rubi Angelum κυρίου Do- mini, idque ipso Mose auctore, Exod. III. 2. Neque aliter Hebreorum doctissimi explicant loca similia, ubi & Angeli apparet nomen, & is tamen Angelus ut יהוה loquitur, & ut יהוה compellatur. Vide Gen. XIX. 13. & 33. collato loco ad Hebr. XIII. 2. Genes. XXII. 15. 17. Jos. V. 14. collato c. VI. 1. Jud. VI. 11. collato v. 14. & c. XIII. 3. collato v. 8. 2. Sam. XXIV. 16. collato v. 17. Ita Grotius cum Grotio merito committitur.

Martinus Cziechovicius in h. l. vult legendum hic esse, & Dei erat ille sermo, ut in Apoc. XIX. 13. & ita extare in quibusdam Latinis exemplaribus MSis. Dei, non Deus. Sed monuit hic Sandius ipse, Arianus; in h. l. produxisse debuisse ipsum, ubi- nam locorum ista MSa. reperiri queant, si fidem ver- bis suis adhiberi voluisset: addens observationem, quæ ipsi & sociis ejus merito reponitur observan- da: Hoc exemplo, inquit, videre licet, quomodo hære- tici, si manifestam scripturam in suum sensum inter- pretando pervertere nequeunt, eandem corrumpere annitantur Eusebius lib. II. de Eccles. Theol. cap. XII. diserte monuit, quod Johannes Deus dixerit. Rursum ubi dixit, & verbum erat apud Deum: potuit dixisse, & Verbum Dei erat apud Deum: Sed &, Deus, inquit, erat Verbum, non & Verbum Dei erat Deus: Ne nos existimaremus, Verbum il- lud Dei operationis significativum aut effectivum esse, ἵνα μὴ τὸ Θεῢ ἐνέργειάν τινα σημαντικήν τι- νὸς ἢ ποιητικὴν εἶναι ἀυτὸν ὑπολάβοιμεν.

Juvat autem hic paucis adhuc asserere Deita- tem Christi è sede sua propria, & loco classico, quod ad argumentum à nomine Θεὸς petitum, id- que ab exceptionibus adversariorum vindicare. Ex hac itaque voce ita colligimus:

(1.) Qui Θεὸς dicitur absolute & simpliciter, sen- suque proprio, is verus est natura Deus; At Chri- stus absolute & simpliciter & proprie Deus dici- tur. E. Major tum è nominis hujus conditio- ne probatur, quod nomen sit essentiæ divinæ, non secus atque homo nomen est essentiæ humanæ, tum ex appropriatione, quod uni soli Deo vindi- cetur, cum absolute & simpliciter adhibetur; quemadmodum ex inductione locorum scriptu- ræ constat, tum è propriæ significationis indole, quæ eo ipso distinguitur ab impropria & meta- phorica attributione, quod illa solum verus Deus designetur per essentiam; hac vero κατ' ἀναλογίαν secundum similitudinem Dii dicantur, qui aliquid participant divini, quo Deo vero aliquo pacto si- miles sunt. Minor ex ipsis verbis constat, καὶ Θεὸς ἦν ὁ λόγος, & verbum erat Deus. Quod enim nomen Dei prædicetur de Verbo, hoc est de Filio Dei, id non solum articulus docet, qui subjecti locum sustinere τῷ λόγῳ testatur; sed totus contex- tus probat: Quia subjectum, de quo agitur, est λόγος, de quo efferri prædicata contextus, τὸ εἶ- ναι ἐν ἀρχῇ, τὸ εἶναι πρὸς τὸν Θεὸν, τ᾿ εἶναι Θεὸν, & quæ deinceps adduntur, tam luculentum est, at- que id quod luculentissimum, quod etiam agno- vit Socinus contra Wujeck. pag. 313. ut & Crell. lib. de Deo & attrib. divin. pag. 101. Vocem λόγον, in- quit, articulo notatam, qua vox Θεὸς caret, subjecti locum ibi tenere omnes, quod sciam, interpretes, aliiq́; explanatores Græcæ linguæ non ignari animadverte- runt. Quod absolute & simpliciter prædicetur si- ne conditione alienante αὐτοψία testatur; quod denique proprie efferatur, inde constat, quod nulla ratio suadeat, nedum cogat, figuratum & improprium admittere sensum: quin imo qua necessitate vox τοῦ Θεοῦ immediate præcedens, ac postmodum statim repetita proprie accipitur, ea- dem etiam, cum ὁ λόγος Θεὸς dicitur, vox Θεῦ proprie accipienda venit. Ut ergo Θεὸς, apud quem λόγος fuisse dicitur, verus est natura Deus in præcedente vers. 1. commate, ita & in præsente Θεῦ vox intelligenda de vero natura Deo, cum λόγος Θεὸς dicitur. Nullum hic di- versæ significationis indicium, nulla disparitatis ratio. Ὁ λόγος ἦν πρὸς τὸν Θεὸν, κỳ Θεὸς ἦν ὁ λόγος. Consimiliter Deus dicitur is, apud quem fuit λό- γος, & ipse qui apud Deum fuit λόγος, unde universa Ecclesia non aliter Deum esse conclusit λόγον, quam Deum Patrem, apud quem ab æter- no fuit ὁ λόγος, id quod præpositione illa, ἐν ἀρ- χῇ ἦν ὁ λόγος inferri disput. peculiari de hoc di- cto habita evicimus.

Excipiunt autem nonnulli adversarii ad hunc locum. Enjedinus Expl. loc. p. 159: (1). obver- tit, Dei vocabulum potius dignitatis & officii esse nomen, quam naturæ & essentiæ: (2.) variis rebus tribui solere, Ps. LXXXII. 1. Cor. VIII. (3.) λόγον esse Θεὸν, à Deo factum, Act. II. 36. Ebr. I. 9. (4.) Id confirmare videri etiam illud, quod Θεὸς hic sine articulo positus sit, quod indicare ait Enjedinus, non significari illum Deum summum: Socinus articulum non appositum Græcæ voci Θεὸς, id plane demonstrare, ait contra Wujeck. p. 310. quia certum sit, nomen Dei sine articulo, cum locum prædicati obtinet, non modo summo illi Deo, sed etiam ejus creaturis aliquando tribui, p. 312. Similia habet Smalc. hom. 1. in prin. cap. Joh. p. 12. & reliqui adversarii. Hæc ergo sunt quæ argumento nostro reponunt adver- sarii, quibus ut satisfiat.

Resp. ad (1.) Dei nomen esse nomen essentiæ, non solum dignitatis & officii, demonstravimus Theol. nat. & revel. c. 3. p. 437. Nec de munere sermo erat in his verbis, sed de prææterna existentiâ apud De- um Patrem & distinctione à Patre, ratione personæ, quam hic apertissimam esse profitetur Socinus l. c. cum verbum dicitur fuisse apud Deum, ut & com- munione Deitatis cum Patre. Quod autem divino modo conceptus fuerit & natus, quodam divino modo ab ipso ad munus suum obeundum designatus, quæ hic adfert Smalcius, ea ἄπροσδιόνυσα sunt, quia Deus jam erat ὁ λόγος, dum erat in principio apud Pa- trem, adeoq; inde à primordio temporis, imo ab æ- terno: non autem de eo agitur, cum natus fuit, vel ad officium designatus. Adde, quod nec muneris ra- tione tum Deus fuerit (salvis hypothesib. adversa- riorum) cum apud Deum Patrem esset in principio: quia tum munus suum nondum administrabat, se- cundum ipsorum sententiam. Quod conceptus fuit divino modo, non pertinet ad ejus munus: nec desi- gnatio sola facit actu Deum tale, qualem ipsi adver- sarii describunt. Quid? quod eadem ratione Deus tum fuerit dictus a Johanne, qua ratione a Thoma Job. XX. 28. vel a Paulo Act. II. 18. aut etiam Rom. IX. 5. Deus benedictus in secula. Nulla hic diversitatis ratio dari potest: nec in Deitate datur intensio, vel graduum perfectionis diversitas. Praeterea negamus, quenquam in N. T. Deum nominari absolute & simpliciter, ob solum munus divinum. Probent adversarii. Nec vocatur hic λόγος solum divinus, sed vocatur Deus, idque absolute & simpliciter. Denique vocatur ita Deus, ut Pater Deus dicebatur. Non minus ergo Deus est, quam ipse Pater.

Ad (2.) Resp. (1.) Distinguendo inter attributionem propriam & impropriam. Improprie quidem aliis etiam extra Deum tribuitur nomen Θεῦ: sed proprie soli Deo. At hic nulla cogit ratio, propriam significationem deserere. Adhaec (2.) nuspiam nomen Θεῦ in singulari numero absolute positum, sine conditione imminuente vel alienante alium quam verum natura Deum denotat. Ps. LXXXII. in plurali occurrit, ut & 1. Cor. IIX. additurque utrobique conditio diminuens, quam vocant; hic dum θεοὶ λεγόμενοι, nuncupative Dii dicuntur, illic cum Deorum mentio fit, ad quos verbum Dei factum est, qui divina gratia muneri divino praefecti sunt &c. At hic simpliciter & absolute Θεῦ nomen adhibetur, sine conditione imminuente.

Ad (3.) Resp. λόγος non dicitur Deus factus Act. II. 35. Sed Christus dicitur Dominus factus, in exaltatione ad dextram Dei, quae ipsi obtigit secundum humanam naturam, de quo dicto vid. exam. libr. Crell. §. 38. 225. 239. 246. At hic λόγος dicitur non factus, sed Θεὸς ἦν, Deus erat in principio rerum scil. omnium creatarum, per quem omnia facta sunt, quaecunq; facta sunt.

Ebr. I. 9. itidem nulla Dei factitii mentio, saltim Christus, qui Deus indigitatur, unctus dicitur, ratione naturae humanae, quam assumsit Filius Dei, Ebr. II. 14. 16. Quid vero haec temporalis unctio ad Deitatem, de quo hic sermo est, secundum quam ab aeterno fuit apud Patrem.

Ad (4.) Resp. Frivola est probatio, non demonstratio ab articulo, unde ipse Ejedinus saltim στοχαστικῶς VIDETUR confirmare ait, cui probationi nervum incidimus Theol. nat. & revel. c. 3. p. 478. seqq. Eadem vis vocis Θεῦ est, sive addatur, sive omittatur articulus, nec minus summum Deum notat sine articulo, quam cum articulo. Nec Christus solum vocatur Deus absq; articulo, sed etiam ὁ Θεὸς cum articulo, Joh. XX. 28. Act. XX. 28. Tit. II. 14. Ebr. I. 8. 1. Joh. V. 20. ut & III. 16. juxta Codices nonnullos. Quod autem hic omittatur, nec repetatur articulus, id factum est partim ob vitandam confusionem personarum Patris & Filii; quae hinc oriri poterat, si dictum foret: ὁ λόγος ἦν πρὸς ὁ θεὸν, ὁ θεὸς ἦν ὁ λόγος: partim ob evidentiam majorem praepositionis, ut luculentius constaret, quod ὁ λόγος hic subjecti locum sustineat, cui praefixus articulus, Θεὸς praedicati: partim ob concursum articulorum declinandum, praesertim quia omissio articuli nihil derogat vocis significationi propriae, uti mox v. 6. παρὰ Θεῷ dicitur non παρὰ τῷ Θεῷ, ubi nullum dubium est, summum Deum designari, quod & v. 12. 13. & 18. videre est, τέκνα Θεῦ ἐκ Θεῦ ἐγεννήθησαν, & Θεὸν οὐδεὶς ἑώρακε. Num hic quia omissus est articulus, alius quam summus Deus intelligitur?

## 1:2
Verse 2. ὗτος ἦν ἐν ἀρχῇ πρὸς Θεὸν. He repeats this because he has already called him God; wishing this, that God is to be understood in such a way that that also remains, that he was with God, that is, that the Logos was not everything that God is. Origen, and others after him, called this the distinction of hypostases. But it is to be noted that this word ὑποστάσεων, as also τριάδος, ὁμουσίας, and certain others, were not used by the first Christians, since Athanasius, the Nicene and Sardican Synods, and some Roman Synods spoke against μίαν ὑπόστασιν, but were taken from Platonic writers with the sense somewhat changed. Among the Platonists there are three ὑποστάσεις: τὸ ἀυτὸν, ὁ νῦς ὁ δημιουργὸς, and τῆς κόσμου ψυχῆς. And because νῦς has a meaning which does not seem to differ from λόγος, and the same νῦς is even called a product by them, therefore many Christians transferred what is said about νῦς by the Platonists to the λόγος or Son. Among the Platonists you may find 3 ὑποστάσεις, three from one. The same: he who raises the monad from the triad and binds the triad from the monad. Similarly, Christians began to speak, as in Lucian, or whoever that author of the dialogue Philopatris is: the high-throned God, the immortal God, heavenly, Son of the Father, Spirit proceeding from the Father, one from three, and three from one. The Hebrew Kabbalists followed both, more Christian in words, more Platonic in sense. For they say: אב אלהים בן אלהים רוח הקדש אלהים שלשה באחד אחד בשלשה:

These things are to be taken with a grain of salt, lest Platonic dogmas be confused with Christian mysteries. For although those words occur most abstractly and formally among the Platonists; yet materially and concretely, as they are applied here to the mystery of the Holy Trinity, such things flowed rather from the true worshippers of God to the Platonists, with the sense of the divine mysteries changed, than vice versa: as is evident even from this, that among the Platonists three ὑποστάσεις are found, τ᾿ ἀυτὸν, ὁ νῦς, ὁ δημιουργὸς, ἡ τῆς κόσμου ψυχὴ.

However these things may be, if the Fathers, informed in the Platonic School, illustrated divine mysteries with the νοήματα of these men (having nevertheless purified them from imperfections) so that they might either more easily lead the Gentiles to our faith, or convince them from their own dogmas; it is nevertheless not to be doubted that the Platonists first received most things from the people of God, which they, indulging their own speculations in their own way, interpolated or recalled to their own concepts; so that the ancient Doctors of the Church deemed it not at all useless that the wealth and vessels be snatched from the Egyptians and subsequently transferred to the uses of the Church. Amelius the Platonist certainly, whose words Eusebius preserved for us in book XI of the Praeparatio, chapter XIX, and Cyril in book VIII against Julian, of whom also from Augustine, book X, chapter 29 of the City of God and book VIII of the Confessions. had his own from John, and cited him under the name of the barbarian: These things, therefore, he says, the λόγος, through whom those things which were made always are, just as Heraclitus also judged: The same indeed, whom that Barbarian indicates in the first founding of things, and even in the unformed state to have stood by, through whom all things were entirely made. Chalcidius in his commentary on the Timaeus praised Moses, because he clearly indicated that, with divine wisdom leading the way, heaven and earth were made, and finally that divine wisdom is the beginning of the universe. We must also take care lest we pour cold water on the Socinians, who slander our doctrine concerning the Most Holy Trinity as having been drawn from the pools of the Philosophers, which Schlichtingius especially cavils at in his preface to all the Prelates of the Churches, prefixed to the disputation on the Trinity instituted against the blessed Meisner. Concerning which we have spoken in the Confession of the Martyrs and Doctors before the Council of Nicaea concerning the Most Holy Trinity. Chrysostom succinctly embraced the opinion of John and the Catholic faith concerning the Son of God from these initial words of the Evangelist in these words: διὰ μὲν γὰρ τ͂ ἐν ἀρχῇ ἦν τὸ ἀίδιον μανθάνομεν, διὰ δὲ τ͂ ἦν πρὸς τ̇ Θεὸν τὸ συναιδιον καὶ ἐνυπόστατον, διὰ δὲ τ͂ Θεὸς ἦν τὸ ἰσοτίθε τ͂ πατρὸς ὀυσίας. For from that which is, In the beginning was, we learn eternity: From that, Was with God, co-eternity and the reality of the person: From that, Was God, the equality of the Father's essence.

Latin:

Vers. 2. ὗτος ἦν ἐν ἀρχῇ πρὸς Θεὸν.] Repetit hoc, quia Deum jam vocavit; hoc volens, ita Deum esse intelligendum, ut & illud maneat, fuisse eum apud Deum, id est, ut non fuerit ὁ λόγος omne id, quod est Deus. Hypostaseon distinctionem Origenes, & post eum alii, vocavere. Sed notandum est, hanc vocem ὑποστάσεων, ut & τριάδος, ὁμουσίας, & alias quasdam non a primis Christianis usurpatas, cum contra μίαν ὑπόστασιν dixerit Athanasius, Synodi Nicena & Sardi- censis; & Romanæ Synodi aliquot, sed desumtas ex Plato- nicis scriptoribus sensu nonnihil immutato. Apud Platoni- cos tres ὑποστάσεις sunt τὸ ἀυτὸν, ὁ νῦς ὁ δημιουργὸς. & τῦ κόσμε ψυχὴ. Et quia rẽs significationem habet, quæ ἀπὸ τῦ λόγε non viderur abludere, & idem vῦς etiam γένημα ipsis dicitur,ideq quæ περὶ νῦς dicuntur Platonicis, multi Christianorum ad τὸ λόγον sive Filium transtulerunt. Apud Platonicos reperias 3 ὑποστάσεις τρεῖς ἐξ ἑνὸς. Ιoem: τ᾽ ἐξαίρων δει τὴν μονάδα τῆς τριάδος ἐξάπτων δὲ τὴν τριάδα τῆς μονάδος. Similiter Christiani loqui cœperunt, ut apud Lucianum, sive quisquis ille est auctor dialogi Philopatridis: ὑψιμέδοντα Θεὸν, Θεὸν ἄμβροτον ὀὐρανίω- να, ὑὸν πατρὸς, πνεῦμα ἐκ πατρὸς ἐκπορευόμενον, ἓν ἐκ τριῶν, χὴ ἐξ ἑνὸς τρῖα. Utrosque secuti Cabalistæ Hebræi, verbis magis Christianos, sensu magis Platonicos. Ajunt enim: אב אלהים בן אלהים רוח הקדש אלהים שלשה באחד אחד בשלשה:

Hæc cum grano salis accipienda, ne confundan- tur dogmata Platonica cum Christianis mysteriis. Nam licet maxime voces illæ abstracte & formaliter apud Platonicos occurrant; materialiter tamen & concrete, qua huic applicantur SS. Trinitatis my- sterio, potius talia à veris Dei cultoribus manarunt ad Platonicos, sensu immutato mysteriorum divi- norum, quam vice versa: ut vel ex eo constat, quod apud Platonicos tres ὑποστάσεις inveniantur, τ᾿ ἀυτὸν, ὁ νῦς, ὁ δημιυργὸς, ἡ τὲ κόσμe ψυχὴ.

Quomodocunque autem ista sese habeant, si Pa- tres in Platonica Schola informati ex istorum νοή- μασι illustrarint divina mysteria (defecatis tamen illis ab imperfectionibus) ut gentiles, aut ad fidem nostram inducerent facilius, aut è propriis do- gmatibus convincerent; dubitandum tamen non est, primum à populo Dei accepisse pleraque Platoni- cos, quæ suo modo propriis indulgentes speculatio- nibus, interpolarunt, aut ad suos conceptus revoca- runt; ut opes, & vasa Ægyptiis eripi deinceps & ad usus Ecclesiæ transferri, haud inutile censuerint veteres Ecclesiæ Doctores. Amelius certe Platoni- cus, cujus verba nobis servavit Euseb. l. XI. Præ- parat. c. XIX. & Cyrill. l. VIII. contra Julian. de quo etiam ex August. l. X. c. 29. de Civit. DEI & l. IIX. Confession. è Johanne sua habuit, eumque sub no- mine τ͂ βαρβάρε adduxit: Hæc itaque, inquit, ὁ λό- γος, per quem semper sunt, quæ facta sunt, quomodo & Heraclitus censuit: Idem profecto, quem Barbarus ille indicat in primo rerum conditu, imo & statu ad- stitisse incondito, per quem omnia omnino facta. Chal- cidius ad Timæum Mosen laudavit, quod aperte in- dicarit, præeunte divina sapientia, cælum terramq; fa- ctam, tandemq; sapientiam divinam esse universitatis primordium. Cavendum etiam ne Socinianis nostram de SS. Trinitate doctrinam è lacunis Philosopho- rum haustam calumniantibus, quod imprimis et- iam Schlichtingius præfatione ad omnes Ecclesiarum Antistites, disputationi de Trinitate contra B. Meis- nerum institutæ præfixa cavillatur, frigidam suf- fundamus. Quo de in Confessione Martyrum & Do- ctorum ante Concil. Nicenum de SS. Trinitate dixi- mus. Sententiam Johannis fidemq; Catholicam de Filio Dei ex his initialibus verbis Evangelistæ suc- cincte complexus est Chrysostomus his verbis: διὰ μὲν γὰρ τ͂ ἐν ἀρχῇ ἦν τὸ ἀίδιον μανθάνομεν, διὰ δὲ τ͂ ἦν πρὸς τ̇ Θεὸν τὸ συναιδιον καὶ ἐνυπόστατον, διὰ δὲ τ͂ Θεὸς ἦν τὸ ἰσοτίθε τ͂ πατρὸς ὀυσίας. Nam ex eo quod est. In principio erat, discimus æternitatem: Ex eo Erat apud Deum, cœternitatem & veritatem personæ: Ex eo. Deus e- rat, Paternæ essentiæ æqualitatem.

## 1:3
Vers. 3. πάντα δι᾽ ἀυτῦ ἐγένετο] Λόγος ἀσωματοποίησιν is found in Philo. The Epistle of Barnabas, when it had treated of the Son of God, calls the Sun the work of his hands. Justin in his first Apology: ὁ λόγος πρὸ τ͂ ποιημάτων κὴ ζυνὼν, κὴ γενώμενῶ, ὅτε τὴν ἀρχὴν δι᾽ ἀυτῦ πάντα ἔκτισε καὶ ἐκόσμησε. Athenagoras: ὁ Θεὸς πάντα διὰ τ͂ λόγε πεποίηκε. Tatian on the same: τ͂τον ἴσμεν τ͂ κόσμs τὴν ἀρχήν. Theophilus: ὁ λόγος ἀυτῦ δι᾽ ἧ τὰ πάντα πεποίηκεν. Irenaeus: The Word of God, through whom all things were made. Tertullian, against the Heretics: That there is one God entirely, and no other besides the creator of the world, who produced all things out of nothing through his Word sent forth first of all. Against Praxeas:

All things were made through the Word. Very often, however, in the Holy Scriptures, it is attributed to that τῷ λόγῳ, so that creation is not taken away from God the Father himself. And thus that which is at the beginning of Genesis in the Jerusalem Paraphrast בחכמה must be understood, and that which is in Philo in the Allegories: Σκιὰ δὲ Θεῦ ὁ λόγος αὐ- τῦ ἐστιν ᾧ καθάπερ ὀργάνῳ προχρησάμενος ἐκοσμοποίει : And concerning Cain: Ὄργανον δὲ λόγος Θεῦ δι᾽ ὗ κατεσκευάσθη, the world, that is to say. Tertullian also called it an instrument, understanding it not as something external, but as connatural, and elsewhere as a minister. By Justin it is called ὑπηρετὴς τῦ ποιητῦ τῶν ὅλων Θεῦ, and more often: by Theophilus, ὑπυργὸς, by Origen, Θεῦ διάκονος. Thus the Latins call both the Word and the Spirit members, pledges, and instruments of God.

It must be repeated here what Grotius warned before: that those things have something ἄκυρον, but are to be understood θεοπρε- πῶς. How, however, the substance of the dogma concerning the Most Holy Trinity was preserved safe among the ancients, even if they varied in modes of speaking, and that those things do not help the Anti-Trinitarians, we have abundantly taught both in the place already cited and in Syst. Theol. Tom. III.

Sandius, in his interpret. parad. on the IV Gospels, at this place, for the sake of his Arminianism, notes that certain Fathers take the word ALL so universally that they have not feared to assert that even the Holy Spirit was made through the Son. He cites Clement of Rome, Constit. VI. c. 11. But he could not have been ignorant that those constitutions are νο- θεύεσθαι, even in the judgment of Bellarmine himself, l. de script. Eccles.: which can be demonstrated with little effort from internal κριτηρίοις, and from St. Athanasius in the synops. script., and the testimonies of others. Nor is it read in those Pseudo-Clementine writings that the Holy Spirit was made through the Son of God, but rather the Holy Spirit is distinguished from other τάγμασι, which are said to have been made through the Son, when he says ἕνα Θεὸν, ἑνὸς υἱῦ Πατέρα, ὐ πλειό- νων, ἑνὸς Παρακλήτε διὰ χριστῦ τ᾿ ἄλλων ταγμάτων ποιητην, one God, the Father of one Son, not of many, the maker of one Paraclete through Christ and of other orders: which can be taken thus: the origin of one Paraclete, that is, but the Effecter of other orders through Christ. He also brings forward Origen, Tom. II. in John, at this place. But he speaks hypothetically: In my judgment, if anyone should say that the Holy Spirit was made, and admits that all things were made through the Word, he must also confess that the Spirit himself was made by the Word. But that the Holy Spirit was made is not to be admitted, nor did Origen profess this here. Finally, he praises Eusebius de Eccles. Theol. lib. II. cap. 23, in which, however, I find nothing of the sort, and from lib. III. cap. 6. Where, he says, the Paraclete Spirit is neither God (that is, the Father) nor the Son, but one of those things which were made through the Son, because all things were made through him. Truly, there he took the name τ̄ γενομένων most broadly (although not appropriately, but entirely ἄτερ γραφῆς & ἀκύρως), by which he embraces all things which have their origin from the Father and the Son in any way, just as the Scholastics say the Holy Spirit is produced by the Son, whom, however, even they distinguish from creatures produced from non-existent things, and there is no doubt that Eusebius distinguishes him, since he refers the Holy Spirit to the most holy Trinity in the same book, cap. V. Who makes his angels spirits: But none of them is to be equated with the Paraclete Spirit, whence he is included in the most holy and most blessed Trinity (τῇ ἁγίᾳ καὶ τρισμακαρίᾳ τριάδι). Naturally, while he wishes to defeat and exclude Sabellianism. The controversies concerning the Deity of the Holy Spirit not yet having been stirred up by the Pneumatomachians, he spoke more incautiously, nor could he assign the distinction of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit so as to guard sufficiently against the essential unity and τῇ ὁμουσίᾳ τῆς Τριάδος. Nor, however, did he deny the Deity of the Holy Spirit, just as he did not that of the Son: otherwise he could not have referred the Holy Spirit with the Son and the Father to that most holy and most blessed Trinity, which he acknowledged to differ greatly from all creatures, and to be alone worthy of worship and veneration. Scultetus indeed confesses, although less fair to Eusebius, that the same man also in the books de præparat. Evangel., such as lib. VII. cap. 45, teaches piously and correctly concerning the Most Holy Trinity that God (the Father) is the Author of all things, that the Word is the second person begotten by the Father, and that the Holy Spirit is to be honored with equal dignity with the Father and the Son. Daniel Chamier also, most versed in the reading of the Fathers, confesses in Panstrat. Cathol. lib. IX. cap. 8. n. 41, that no one has reported anything sinister concerning the faith of Eusebius after the Synod of Nicaea. And indeed, Gregory Nazianzen would not have celebrated Eusebius as an admirable man and most constant in the propriety and confession of the Christian name, in his Monody on the life of Basil the Great, nor would Basil himself, the hammer of the Pneumatomachians, have counted him among the Orthodox Fathers in his book de Spirit. S. ad Amphiloch., if he had fostered the opinion of the Pneumatomachians concerning the Holy Spirit. Finally, we have already warned in confess. Martyr. p. 98, what is to be thought of the ἀκυρολογίαις of Eusebius, and how his writings and those of other ancients are to be read with judgment; who, in the very flight from Sabellian confusion, are believed to have been swept away to the borders of the analogous Arian division formulas, when the limits for both, as far as modes of speaking are concerned, had not yet been sanctioned by public authority or established in the open through more accurate disputations, lest such things be confused with the simple religion of the Catholic faith.

Καὶ χωρὶς ἀυτῦ ἐγένετο ὀδὲ ἓν ὃ γέγονεν.] Where the Holy Scriptures wish to remove every exception, they explain what they have affirmed by the negation of the opposite. Isa. XXXVIII. chap. XXXIX. 4. Jer. XLII. 4. below in verse 20. & 1. Ep. 1. 5. This, however, was done here so that in those things which were created through the Word, those things also might be understood which are not visible to us, Col. I. 16. Even the ages, Heb. I. 2. against the Gnostics, for they wanted there to be one creator of those things which we see, the demiurge, and others of invisible things, each in its own pleroma. Nothing, therefore, except God himself, is excepted from the works of the Word. Moreover, χωρὶς here is the opposite of that διὰ which preceded it. Irenaeus: From all things, however, nothing has been subtracted, but the Father made all things through him, whether visible, or invisible, or intelligible, or temporal, on account of a certain arrangement, or eternal. There is also in it a Hebraism, in that ὀδὲ ἓν, not one thing, is put for nothing, as Ps. CXXXIX, 16. Thus also I. Maccab. VII. 46.

These things of Grotius must be opposed to those trifles which he has concerning the passage Col. I. 16. & Ephes. I. 10. in the Appendix to the IV. Gospels, at the beginning of the Epistle to the Ephesians p. 6. regarding the words τὰ ἐν τοῖς ὀυρανοῖς, not unlike Socinian glosses. Previously, he says, there were factions and rivalries among the Angels on behalf of peoples. See Daniel X. 13. And add Job IV. 18. and those things which Jerome says about the Angels against Jovinian II. and Maximus in the Dialogue, Christ removed those things, having been made King even of the Angels, gathering for himself a people out of so many peoples, to whom the Angels now owe service. Heb. I. 14. See the example Acts V. 19. c. XII. 11. c. XVI. 26. c. XXVII. 23. 44. Add Matth. XVIII. 10. & 1. Cor. XI. 10. where it treats of the Angels of prayer, of whom the Hebrew book Chasidin makes mention, and Tertullian, in the book on prayer, and Philo περὶ φιλανθρωπίας, on humanity, calls them the same ἐφόρους τῇ τῶν σοφῶν ἐμπειρίαν; θεασαμένους μήτι τῆς ᾠδῆς ἐκμελὲς, Inspectors, as the experience of the wise teaches, so that there may be nothing discordant in the song. To the kingdom of Christ, which he has obtained over the Angels, some refer that which is in Col. I. 16. because κτίζειν, to create, often signifies a new ordering; certainly, just as most of the epistles to the Colossians agree with this epistle, so also this passage seems to bring light to it, and in turn to borrow light from it. The Angels are hostile to the Gentiles on account of idolatrous worship, but favor the same when converted to Christ. Those things concerning the factions of good Angels, and concerning their new creation, we have refuted elsewhere. in Natural and Revealed Theology, p. 609. Vol. IV. System of Theology, 469. and in the vindications of the passage Col. I. 15. in Select Exercises, Triga, Exerc. III.

Latin:

Vers. 3. πάντα δι᾽ ἀυτῦ ἐγένετο] Λόγος ἀσωματοποίησιν est a- pud Philon. Epistola Barnabæ cum de Filio Dei egisset, So- lem vocat opus manuum ipsius. Justin. Apologetico priore: ὁ λόγος πρὸ τ͂ ποιημάτων κὴ ζυνὼν, κὴ γενώμενῶ, ὅτε τὴν ἀρχὴν δι᾽ ἀυτῦ πάντα ἔκτισε καὶ ἐκόσμησε. Athenagoras: ὁ Θεὸς πάν- τα διὰ τ͂ λόγε πεποίηκε. Tatian. de eod. τ͂τον ἴσμεν τ͂ κόσμs τὴν ἀρχήν. Theophilus: ὁ λόγος ἀυτῦ δι᾽ ἧ τὰ πάντα πεποίηκεν Irenæus: Verbum Dei, per quem facta sunt omnia. Tertullian, adversus Hæreticos: Vnum omnino Deum esse, nec alium præ- ter mundi conditorem, qui universa ex nihilo produxerit per Verbum suum primo omnium emissum. Adversus Praxeam:

Omnia per sermonem sunt facta. Sæpissime autem in sacris literis διὰ illud τῷ λόγῳ tribuitur, ut ipsi Deo parenti non adimatur creatio. Et sic sumendum id, quod initio Gene- seos est apud Paraphrasten Hierosolymitanum בחכמה, & quod apud Philonem est Allegoriis : Σκιὰ δὲ Θεῦ ὁ λόγος αὐ- τῦ ἐστιν ᾧ καθάπερ ὀργάνῳ προχρησάμενος ἐκοσμοποίει : Et de Caino : Ὄργανον δὲ λόγος Θεῦ δι᾽ ὗ κατεσκευάσθη, mundus sci- licet. Tertullianus quoque instrumentum dixit intelligens non extraneum, sed connaturale, alibi & ministrum. Justino dicitur ὑπηρετὴς τῦ ποιητῦ τῶν ὅλων Θεῦ, sæpius : Theophilo ὑπυργὸς, Origeni Θεῦ διάκονος. Sic Latini & verbum & spiritum vocant membra, pignora, instrumenta Dei.

Repetendum hic, quod monuit antea Grotius: habere illa aliquid ἄκυρον, sed intelligenda θεοπρε- πῶς. Quomodo autem apud veteres substantia dogmatis de SS. Trinitate salva conservata sit, etsi modis loquendi variarint, & quod nihil illi juvent Anti-Trinitarios, cum loco jam citato, tum Syst. Theol. Tom. III. abunde docuimus.

Sandius interpret. parad. ad IV. Evang. ad h. l. in gratiam Arminianismi sui notat, quosdam Patres vocem OMNIA adeo universaliter accipere, ut non veriti sint asserere, etiam Spiritum S. per Filium esse factum. Adducit Clementem Rom. Constit. VI. c. 11. Sed non ignorare poterat, constitutiones illas νο- θεύεσθαι, vel ipsius Bellarm. l. de script. Eccles. judi- cio: quod ex internis κριτηρίοις, & S. Athanasio in synops. script. aliorumque testimoniis facili nego- tio demonstrari potest. Neque id in illis Pseudo- Clementinis legitur, quod Spiritus sanctus per Fi- lium Dei factus sit, sed distinguitur potius Spiritus sanctus ab aliis τάγμασι, quæ dicuntur per Filium facta, cum ἕνα Θεὸν dicit, ἑνὸς υἱῦ Πατέρα, ὐ πλειό- νων, ἑνὸς Παρακλήτε διὰ χριστῦ τ᾿ ἄλλων ταγμάτων ποιητην, unum Deum, unius Filii Patrem, non plurium, unius Paracleti per Christum, aliorum ordinum facto- rem: quod ita accipi potest: unius Paracleti scil. originem, aliorum autem ordinum per Christum Effectorem. Affert & Origenem Tom. II. in Joh. in h. l. Sed is hypothetice loquitur: Meo quidem ju- dicio, si quis dicat factum esse Spiritum sanctum, & admittat omnia per Sermonem facta fuisse, is etiam fateatur necesse est, Spiritum ipsum a Sermone fa- ctum. At Spiritum sanctum factum esse, non ad- mittendum, nec id professus hic Origenes. De- nique laudat Eusebium de Eccles. Theol. lib. II. cap. 23. in quo vero nihil tale reperio, & è lib. III. cap. 6. Ubi, Paracletus, inquit, Spiritus nec Deus est (scil. Pater) nec Filius, sed unum quidem eorum, quæ per Filium facta sunt, quia omnia per ipsum facta sunt. Verum illic τ̄ γενομένων nomen latissime (quanquam haud convenienter, sed prorsus ἄτερ γραφῆς & ἀκύρως) accepit, qua omnia, quæ à Patre & Filio quacunque ratione habent origi- nem, complectitur, uti Scholastici Spiritum S. produci à Filio ajunt, quem tamen à creaturis ex non extantibus, productis, & creatis & hi distin- guunt, & Eusebium distinguere dubium non est, cum Spiritum sanctum ad sacrosanctam Trinita- tem refert libr. eod. cap. V. Qui facit Angelos suos Spiritus: Sed illorum nullus Spiritui Paracleto adæquandus est, unde ille sanctissima & beatissima Trinitate (τῇ ἁγίᾳ καὶ τρισμακαρίᾳ τριάδι) com- prehenditur. Nimirum dum Sabellianismum pro- fligare & excludere vult. Nondum adhuc mo- tis à Pneumatomachis de Deitate Spiritus sancti controversiis, incautius loquutus est, nec discri- men Patris, Filii, & Spiritus sancti ita assignare potuit, ut satis caveret unitati essentiali, & τῇ ὁμουσίᾳ τῆς Τριάδος. Nec tamen Deitatem Spiritus sancti negavit, uti nec Filii: alias Spi- ritum sanctum cum Filio & Patre ad illam san&is- simam & beatissimam Trinitatem, quam ab o- mnibus creaturis maximopere differre, solam- que cultu & veneratione dignam esse agnovit, referre non potuisset. Fatetur sane Scultetus, etsi Eusebio minus æquus, eundem etiam in li- bris de præparat. Evangel. utpote libr. VII. cap. 45. pie & recte de Sacrosancta Trinitate docere Deum (Patrem) esse Autorem omnium, Verbum es- se personam secundam à Patre genitam, Spiritum sanctum pari cum Patre & Filio dignitate honoran- dum. Fatetur & Daniel Chamier in lectione Pa- trum versatissimus, Panstrat. Cathol. lib. IX. cap. 8. n. 41. neminem de Eusebii fide post Synodum Nice- nam sinistri quicquam retulisse. Et profecto haud celebrasset Gregorius Nazianzenus Eusebium, ceu Virum admirabilem & proprietate ac confessione nominis Christiani constantissimum, Monodia in Basilii M. vitam, aut accensuisset Basilius ipse, Pneumatomachorum malleus, eundem Ortho- doxis Patribus libr. de Spirit. S. ad Amphiloch. si de Spiritu sancto Pneumatomachorum sententiam fovisset. Denique monuimus jam in confess. Martyr. p. 98. quid de ἀκυρολογίαις Eusebii ha- bendum, & quomodo ipsius aliorumque vete- rum scripta cum judicio legenda; qui in ipsa Sa- bellianæ confusionis fuga ad confinia analogarum Arianæ divisionis formularum, cum nondum ex- quisite satis limites utrisque, quoad loquendi mo- dos, publica autoritate sanciti, vel per accura- tiores disputationes in aprico constituti fuere, ab- repti creduntur, ne talia cum simplice fidei Ca- tholicæ religione confundantur.

Καὶ χωρὶς ἀυτῦ ἐγένετο ὀδὲ ἓν ὃ γέγονεν.] Ubi omnem exce- ptionem removere volunt sacræ literæ, id, quod affirma- runt, explicant oppositi negatione. Esa. XXXVIII. cap. XXXIX. 4. Ier. XLII. 4. infra commate 20. & 1. Ep. 1. 5. Id autem hic ideo factum, ut in iis, quæ per verbum sunt condita, intelligerentur etiam ea, quæ conspicua nobis non sunt, Col. I. 16. Etiam οἱ αἰῶνες Hebr. I. 2. contra Gno- sticos, nam illi alium volebant esse opificem eorum, quæ cernimus, τὸν δημιεργὸν, alios rerum inaspectabilium in suo quemque pleromate. Nihil ergo, præter ipsum Deum, ab operibus verbi excipitur. Est autem χωρὶς hic oppositum illi διὰ, quod antecessit. Irenæus: Ex omnibus autem nihil sub- tractum est, sed omnia per ipsum fecit pater, sive visibilia, sive in- visibilia, sive intelligibilia, sive temporalia, propter quandam dis- positionem, sive sempiterna. Est & in eo Hebraismus, quod ὀδὲ ἓν, nec una res ponitur pro nulla, ut Ps. CXXXIX, 16. Sic & I. Maccab. VII. 46.

Opponenda hæc Grotiana næniis illis, quas de loco Col. I. 16. & Ephes. I. 10. habet in Appendice ad IV. Evangel. in principium Epistolæ ad Ephesios p. 6. ad verba τὰ ἐν τοῖς ὀυρανοῖς glossis Socinianis non absimilibus. Antea, inquit, inter Angelos factiones erant & studia pro populis. Vide Daniel. X. 13. Et ad- de Job. IV. 18. & ea quæ de Angelis dicit Hieronymus adversus Jovianum II. & Maximus in Dialogo, ea sustulit Christus, Rex factus etiam Angelorum, unum ex tot populis sibi populum colligens, cui Angeli ministe- rium nunc debeant. Hebr. I. 14. Vide exemplum Act. V. 19. c. XII. 11. c. XVI. 26. c. XXVII. 23. 44. Adde Matth. XVIII. 10. & 1. Cor. XI. 10. ubi de Angelis o- rationis agitur, quorum & liber Hebræus Chasidin me- minit & Tertullianus, libro de oratione, Philo περὶ φι- λανθρωπίας, de humanitate, eosdem vocat ἐφό- ρους τῇ τῶν σοφῶν ἐμπειρίαν; θεασαμένους μήτι τῆς ᾠδῆς ἐκμελὲς, Inspectores, ut docet sapientum ex- perientia, ne quid in cantu sit absonum. Ad Chri- sti regnum, quod in Angelos est adeptus, nonnulli re- ferunt id, quod Col. I. 16. quia κτίζειν creare, sæpe ordinationem novam significat, certe ut pleræq; epi- stolæ ad Colossenses cum hac epistola congruunt, ita & locus iste huic lucem adferre, & vicissim ab eo lucem mutuari videtur. Angeli infensi Gentibus ob idolola- tricos cultus favent iisdem ad Christum conversis. Illa de Angelorum bonorum factionibus, & de nova eorum creatione alibi refutavimus in Theol. Naturali & Revelat. p. 609. Tom. IV. Sy- stem. Theol. 469. & in vindiciis loci Col. I. 15. in Ex- ercit. felect. Triga, Exerc. III.

## 1:4
Ver. 4. In him was life] Most frequently the holy writers of the New Testament compare the redemption of the human race to creation, nay, even prefer it, and therefore call it a new creation, 2 Cor. V. 17, Gal. VI. 15. Justin: Christ, being the firstborn of all creation and the beginning, has again become of another race, that which was regenerated by him. Irenaeus III. 11: Signifying that through the Word, through whom God perfected the creation, in this he also bestowed salvation upon men who are in the creation. Thus also Rabbi Lakish, cited in Bereshit Rabba to the passage at the beginning of Genesis, where the Spirit of God is named, says: This is the spirit of King Messiah. John also looks to this, when he attributes both to the same Word, just as at the end of the Apocalypse, in the description of the new World, he uses words taken from the history of the first creation. Wherefore, beware of taking life here as anything other than eternal life. Thus below, Christ says of the Father: He gave to the Son to have life in himself. In the first Epistle V. 11: God gave us eternal life, and this life is in his Son. Nor should you wonder that these things pertain to the Word already made flesh, since he says so much later that the Word was made flesh. For what is said about his having been in the world also pertains to this time. And so that last point is tacitly presupposed here, as being known to all: soon, when the occasion is given, it is explained. And in this kind of discourse, to demand order superstitiously is truly to look for a knot in a bulrush. These things are written as they come, not in a premeditated arrangement. It is said, however, that life was in the Word, because the method of obtaining it was most clearly revealed through the Word. A similar manner of speaking is in Acts IV. 12. At the same time, the Gnostic fiction is destroyed, that the Word is one emanation of God, and Life another. It is proper to John to call Christ the Word, Apoc. XIX. 13, 1 Ep. I. 1, and V. 7.

Although St. John attributes both creation and redemption to the Word, he does not yet discourse here on the work of redemption; nor is there a reason why we should beware of taking this as anything other than eternal life: since it is said simply that life was in the Word, or whatever is of life: namely, natural life no less than spiritual and heavenly. Nor should that be drawn only to the Word already made flesh, or the order be entirely neglected, as if St. John wrote those things confusedly, as they came into his mind. And that explanation is far insufficient, that life was in the Word because the method of obtaining it was most clearly revealed through him, which happened after the incarnation: for these predicates belong to the Word even before the incarnation, that life was in him, and that the life was the light of men. In him was life: because he himself is the true God, and the substantial life itself, or the eternal and living essence, Gen. XVI. 14, XXIV. 62, XXV. 11. Deuter. V. 26, Is. III. 10, Hos. 10, Matt. XVI. 16, and he has a life-giving power in his nature or essence as God, by the force of which we have natural life from him, Acts XVII. 25, and spiritual life, both of the soul, John VI. 63, Eph. II. 5, and of the body in the resurrection, John V. 29, and heavenly life, Apoc. II. 10. But it is primarily the spiritual life of the soul that is treated here, which the Word deigned to restore both meritoriously and effectively; whose merit, indeed, was profitable before he existed, John XIV. 6, 1 John V. 12, 20, which is followed by the resurrection to life, and the heavenly, blessed, and eternal life. See the Sacred Logology of the Blessed D. Balthasar Meisner.

And the life was the light of men] Not only among the Latins and Greeks, but also among the Hebrews, light and life are wont to be joined, as Ps. XXXVI. 10. The sense, however, is this: that that knowledge of eternal life and of the method of obtaining it is a certain light, toward which men can and ought to direct their steps safely. Thus below XI: 10: If anyone walks by day he does not stumble, if anyone walks by night he stumbles. XII. 35: The light is with you, walk while you have the light. Eph. V. 8: Walk as children of light. Here he himself in the first Epistle I. 7: If we walk in the light, as he himself is in the light. And Apoc. XXI. 24: In his light they shall walk. See what we noted on Luke I. 79. The Platonists say the intelligible light is from the Word, as can be seen in Philo on the creation of the world. The Gnostics followed the Platonists; John shows that all these names converge in the one Christ.

Latin:

Verf. 4. ἐν αὐτῷ ζωὴ ἦν] Sæpissime sancti Scriptores novi fœderis redemptionem humani generis conferunt creatio- ni, imo & præferunt, ideoque novam creationem vocant 2. Corinth. V. 17. Gal. VI. 15. Justinus: χριστὸς πρωτότοκος πάσης κτίσεως ὢν καὶ ἀρχὴ πάλιν ἄλλου γένους γέγονεν τοῦ ἀναγεννη- θέντος ὑπ' αὐτοῦ Irenæus III. 11. Significans quoniam per Ver- bum, per quod Deus perfecit conditionem, in hoc & salutem his, qui in conditione sunt, præstitit hominibus. Sic & Rabbi Lakiscti adductus in Bereschit Rabba ad locum initio Ge- nefeos, ubi Spiritus Dei nominatur ait: Hic est spiritus re- gis Messiæ. Hoc & Johannes spectat, cum eidem λόγῳ u- trumque tribuit, sicut & fine Apocalypsis in descriptione Mundi novi, vocabula usurpat desumta ex primæ creatio- nis historia. Quare vitam hic cave aliam accipias, quam vi- tam æternam. Sic infra Christus de Patre: ἔδωκε τῷ υἱῷ ἔχειν ζωὴν ἐν ἑαυτῷ In Epist. prima V. 11. ζωὴν αἰώνιον ἔδωκεν ἡμῖν ὁ Θεὸς καὶ αὕτη ζωὴ ἐν τῷ υἱῷ αὐτοῦ ἐστι. Neque mireris hæc ad λόγον jam carnem factum pertinere, cum tanto post dicat λόγον carnem esse factum. Nam & quod dicitur in mundo fuiffe itidem ad hoc tempus pertinet. Itaque illud ultimum tacite hic præsupponitur, tanquam omnibus notum: mox occafione data explicatur. Et in hoc dissertandi genere or- dinem superstitiose exigere, id vero est nodum quærere in scirpo. Scripta sunt hæc talia pro impetu, non præmedi- tato dispositu. Dicitur autem ἐν τῷ λόγῳ vitam fuisse, quia per τ' λόγον ejus adipiscendæ ratio apertissime revelata est. Simile loquendi genus Act. IV. 12. Simul destruitur Gno- sticonun figmentum, aliam Dei emanationem esse λόγον, aliam ζωήν. Proprium Iohanni est Christum λόγον vocare Apoc. XIX. 13. 1. Ep. I. 1. & V. 7.

Etsi S. Johannes & creationem & redemtionem λόγῳ tribuat, hic tamen de opere redemtionis nondum disserit; neque ratio est, cur cavere de- beamus ne aliam, quam æternam vitam hic acci- piamus: quum ἁπλῶς in λόγῳ vita fuisse dicatur, vel quicquid est vitæ: vita nempe naturalis non minus, quam spiritualis & cælestis: Neque illa tra- henda solum ad λόγον jam carnem factum, aut ne- gligendus plane ordo, quasi confuse illa scripserit S. Johannes, prout in mentem venerint: Et longe insuf- ficiens est illa explicatio, quod in λόγῳ vita fuerit, quia per ipsum ejus adipiscendæ ratio apertissime reve- lata est, quod post incarnationem factum: nam hæc prædicata λόγῳ conveniunt etiam ante ἐνσάρ- κωσιν, quod fuerit in ipso vita, & quod vita fuerit lux hominum. In ipso vita erat: quid ipse verus Deus, & ipsa vita substantialis, seu æterna & vivens essen- tia est, Gen. XVI. 14. XXIV. 62. XXV. 11. Deuter. V. 26. Ef. III. 10. Of. 10. Matth. XVI. 16. & δύναμιν ha- bet ζωοποιητικὴν τῇ Φύσει vel natura ut Deus, vi cujus & naturalem vitam ab ipso habemus Actor. XVII. 25. & spiritualem tum animæ Joh. VI. 63. Eph. II. 5. tum corporis in resurrectione Johan. V. 29. & cæle- stem Apoc. II. 10. de spirituali autem vita animæ hic imprimis agi, quam & meritorie, & effective repa- rare dignatus est λόγος; cujus vero meritum pro- fuit, antequam fuit, Joh. XIV. 6. 1. Johan. V. 12. 20. quam excipit resuscitatio ad vitam, & cœlestis bea- ta, ac æterna vita. Vid. λογολογία sacra B. D. Balthas. Meisneri.

Καὶ ἡ ζωὴ ἦν τὸ φῶς τ' ἀνθρώπων] Non apud Latinos tan- tum & Græcos, sed & apud Hebræos conjungi solent lux & vita, ut Ps. XXXVI, 10. Sensus autem hic est, cognitionem il- lam vitæ æternæ & de ejus adipiscendæ ratione, lucem quan- dam esse, ad quam homines gressus suos tuto dirigere possint & debeant. Sic infra XI: 10. Si quis de die ambulat non offendit, si quis noctu ambulat offendit. XII. 35. Lux vobiscum est, ambu- late dum lucem habetis. Eph. V. 8. ut filii lucis ambulate. Hic i- pse in Epistola prima I. 7. Si in luce ambulemus, sicut ipse est in luce. & Ap. XXI. 24. In luce ejus ambulabunt. Vide quæ notavimus ad Lucam I. 79. Platonici s ἐκ λόγου φῶς τὸ νοητὸν, ut videre est apud Philonem de opificio mundi. Platonicos fequebantur Gnostici, Iohannes ostendit omnia hæc nomina in Christum unum convenire.

## 1:5
V. 5. And the light shines in the darkness] As if he were saying that light is usually brought so that darkness may be illuminated: which also happens to this light. But the darkness here are sinful men having no certain rule for directing their life. Thus Eph. V. 8: You were once darkness: but now you are light. It seems to be an allusion to the light of Isaiah IX. 2.

And the darkness did not comprehend it] It is stated indefinitely, which fits the greatest part. A great part of sinful men did not wish to use the benefit of the light, for the reason that their sins were too pleasing to them: as below III. 20. But here to comprehend means to obtain the fruit of a thing. Thus concerning the knowledge of the law, Ecclus. XV. 7: Unwise men shall not comprehend it. And in the same book XXVII. 8, concerning justice: If you pursue justice, you shall comprehend it. Thus also Rom. IX. 30: He comprehended justice.

He says that this is the sense: that that knowledge of eternal life and of the method of obtaining it is a certain light, toward which men can and ought to direct their steps safely. But John does not say that the knowledge of eternal life is the light: but that life, he says, was the light of men. Which pertains not only to those men who lived after the incarnation of the Word, but to all men. For it is an indefinite and universal assertion, so that no man has ever had light without this life. And the Word is substantial life, just as God is substantial life and light: because God is eternal light, 1 John I. 5, on account of his simplicity, immutability, purity and sincerity, majesty and power: and the Son of God is the brightness of God the Father, Heb. I. 3. Moreover, the Word is not only light in itself, but it is also light for us: or of men: it is not only light essentially, but also effectively: in that it is indeed the light of all men in the world, but especially of the pious in the Church, and of the blessed in heaven: providing to all the light of nature, or of right reason, but to the faithful and the elect the light of grace, and of glory: which is here particularly regarded: whence it is called the light of the world, because it wishes to illuminate all Joh. VIII. 12. and the light of the nations Is. XLIX. 6. Acts XIII. 47. because this light shone in the darkness, because indeed men were involved through the fall in the darkness of the mind and of ignorance Eph. IV. 17. in the darkness of the heart, of sin and of the works of darkness Rom. XIII. 12. in the darkness of eternal damnation Matt. XXII. 13. This light, however, has shone in the darkness for us ever since the preaching of the Proto-Evangelium Gen. III. 15. and its explanation made in all times. And since Saint John uses the present tense Φαίνει, designating a continuous act, and furthermore adds the testimony of John the Baptist concerning this light, he also particularly regards that Φαίνει, by which through his appearance in the flesh 1 Tim. III. 16. he shone upon all men Tit. II. 13. and the light came into the world Joh. III. 19. as also through his preaching in the days of his flesh, and the performance of miracles: by which he flashed on every side; and it still shines even now in the darkness through the diffusion of the word, which is light and a lamp Is. IX. 2. 2 Pet. I. 19., by which it dispels darkness, illuminates minds, warms hearts, refreshes and vivifies.

Latin:

V. 5. Καὶ τὸ φῶς ἐν τῇ σκοτίᾳ φαίνει] Quasi dicat ideo lux affersi solet, ut tenebræ illuminentur: quod & huic luci con- tigit. Sunt autem hic tenebræ homines peccatores nullam certam habentes vitæ dirigendæ regulam. Sic Ephes. V. 8. Fuistis olim tenebræ: nunc autem lux estis. Alludi videtur ad lucum Esaiæ IX. 2.

Kaὶ ἡ σκοτία αὐτὸ ὐ κατέλαβεν] Indefinite enunciatur, quod maximæ parti convenit. Magna pars hominum pec- catorum lucis beneficio uti noluit, ideo quod peccata ipsis nimium allubescerent: ut infra III. 20. Est autem hic κατα- λαμβάνειν fructum rei consequi. Sic de cognitione legis Ec- clef. XV. 7. ὐ μὴ καταλήψονται αὐτὴν ἄνθρωποι ἀσύνετοι. Et eodem libro XXVII. 8. de justitia: ἐὰν διώκης τὸ δίκαιον κα- ταλήψῃ αὐτό. Sic & Rom. IX. 30. κατέλαβε δικαιοσύνην.

Sensum hunc esse dicit: cognitionem illam vitæ æternæ & de ejus adipiscendæ ratione lucem quandam esse, ad quam homines gressus suos tuto dirigere possint & debeant. Ast non ait Johannes, cognitionem vitæ æternæ lucem esse: sed vita illa, inquit, erat lux ho- minum. Quod non ad eos tantum homines, qui post ἐνσάρκωσιν λόγε vixerunt, sed ad omnes ho- mines pertinet. Est enim indefinita & univer- salis assertio, adeo, ut nullus hominum lucem ha- buerit unquam sine hac vita. Et λόγος est vita sub- stantialis, ut Deus vita & lux substantialis est: quia Deus lux æterna est, 1. Joh. I. 5. ob simplicitatem, im- mutabilitatem, puritatem & sinceritatem, majestatem & virtutem: & Filius Dei ἀπαύγασμα est DEI Patris Ebr. I. 3. Non autem tantum in se lux est ὁ λόγος, sed lux est etiam nobis: vel τῶν ἀνθρώπων: non lux tantum est ὐσιωδῶς, sed etiam ἐνεργητικῶς: qua nempe hominum omnium in mundo, imprimis autem piorum in Ecclesia, & beatorum in cælis lux est: omnibus præbens lumen naturæ, vel rectæ rationis, fidelibus autem & electis lumen gratiæ, & gloriæ: quod hic peculiariter respicitur: unde lux mundi dici- tur, quia omnes illuminare vult Joh. VIII. 12. & lu- men gentium Ef. XLIX. 6. Actor. XIII. 47. quia lux hæc in tenebris luxit, quia nempe homines tene- bris mentis & ignorantiæ Eph. IV. 17. tenebris cor- dis, peccati & operum tenebrarum Rom. XIII. 12. te- nebris damnationis æternæ Matth. XXII. 13. per la- psum involuti sunt. Luxit autem in tenebris hæc lux jam inde nobis per Prot-Evangelii prædicatio- nem Gen. III. 15. ejusque explicationem omnibus temporibus factam. Et cum Præsenti utatur S. Jo- hannes Φαίνει, actum continuum designans, ac por- ro subjungat testimonium Johannis Baptistæ de hac luce, respicit peculiariter etiam illud Φαίνει, quo per apparitionem in carne 1. Tim. III. 16. illuxit omni- bus hominibus Tit. II. 13. & lux venit in mundum Joh. III. 19. ut & per prædicationem in diebus car- nis, & miraculorum effectionem: quibus undi- quaque coruscavit; ac lucet etiamnum in tenebris per verbi, quod lux est & lucerna Es. IX. 2. 2. Petr. I. 19. diffusionem, quo tenebras dispellit, mentes illuminat, corda calefacit, recreat & vivificat.

## 1:6
V. 6. Ἐγένετο] He existed in those times, of which it is agreed we are treating: as the Hebrew ויהי is accustomed to be taken:

Ἄνθρωπος] Not the Word: not an Angel; but what the Ebionites and others falsely said about Christ, a mere man, although endowed with the excellent gifts of the Holy Spirit.

Ἀπεσαλμένος παρὰ Θεῦ] He alludes to the passage of Malachi: behold I send my messenger See Matt. XI. 10. and Mark I. 2. Luke VII. 27. Prophets are sent, when they receive a mandate from God.

Ὄνομα αὐτῷ Ἰωάννης] It is a Hebrew custom to put לו for a relative. It would have been customary: To whom the name was John.

Latin:

V. 6. Ἐγένετο] Extitit illis scilicet temporibus, de quibus nos constat agere: ut sumi solet Hebræorum ויהי:

Ἄνθρωπος] Non λόγος: non Angelus; sed quod de Chri- sto falso Ebionæi & alii dicebant, ψιλὸς ἄνθρωπος, quan- quam eximiis Spiritus Sancti dotibus donatus.

Ἀπεσαλμένος παρὰ Θεῦ] Alludit ad locum Malachiæ: ἰδὺ ἐγὼ ἀποστέλλω τὸν ἄγγελόν μου Vid. Matth. XI. 10. & Marc. I. 2. Luc. VII. 27. mittuntur Prophetæ, cum mandatum à Deo accipiunt.

Ὄνομα αὐτῷ Ἰωάννης] לו pro relativo ponere Hebræorum est. Usitatum fuerat: Cui nomen Johannes.

## 1:7
V. 7. ὗτος ἦλθεν εἰς μαρτυρίαν, ἵνα μαρτυρήσῃ] And this is a Hebrew custom, to join verbal nouns with verbs. He tacitly signifies that he was a suitable witness foretold by the prophets, not conceived without a miracle, noble by the austerity of his life, of such liberty that he did not even spare a king.

Περὶ τῦ φωτός] Thus we read of testimony concerning me in Acts XXII. 18. He means this, which he will explain later, that John the Baptist gave this testimony to Jesus, that he himself is the Christ, and therefore that excellent light,

Διαὐτῦ] Namely of the light, that is, into God.

That pronoun does not denote God, but the subject, of which there is discourse here. But it is about John, who is distinguished from the λόγῳ, because he came, that he might bear witness concerning the light, that through it all might believe; in him, namely, who is the true light of men, in whom is life: whence it is added concerning the same John, ὐκ ἦν ἐκεῖνος he was not that light; but that he might bear witness concerning the light. For they were bound to believe in him, the ministry of John serving to that end, concerning whom John was sent to bear witness. But he was bearing witness concerning the λόγῳ, that true light. Therefore they were bound to believe in the λόγον through the same. Cons. v. 12.

Latin:

V. 7. ὗτος ἦλθεν εἰς μαρτυρίαν, ἵνα μαρτυρήσῃ] Et hoc He- bræorum, conjungere verbalia cum verbis. Tacite signi- ficat idoneum fuisse testem prænuntiatum à vatibus, non si- ne miraculo conceptum, vitæ austeritate nobilem, libertatis tantæ, ut nec regi parceret.

Περὶ τῦ φωτός] Sic μαρτυρίαν περὶ ἐμῦ legimus Actorum XXII. 18. Hoc vult, quod postea explicabit, Iohannem baptistam Jesu testimonium hoc præbuisse, ipsum esse Chri- stum, ac proinde eximiam illam lucem,

Διαὐτῦ] Nempe τῦ φωτὸς, in Deum scilicet.

Pronomen illud non Deum, sed subjectum notat, de quo hic sermo. Agitur autem de Johanne: qui distinguitur à λόγῳ, quod venerit, ut testaretur de luce, ut per ipsam omnes crederent; in illum scil. qui vera est lux hominum, in quo vita est : unde de eo- dem Johanne additur, ὐκ ἦν ἐκεῖνος non erat ille lux illa; sed ut testaretur de luce. In illum enim crede- re, ministerio Johannis inserviente, debebant, de quo Johannes ad id missus testabatur. At testaba- tur is de λόγῳ vera illa luce. In λόγον ergo per eundem credere debebant. Cons. v. 12.

## 1:7
Vers. 7. 'For the law was given through Moses.' In passing, the dogma of Ebion is refuted, which makes Jesus posthumous to Moses.

'Grace and truth came through Jesus Christ.' 'Truth,' as we said above, is opposed to the shadow of the law: 'grace' here is especially that abundance of the Spirit poured out everywhere upon Christians, a state unknown to the true law, to which, among other things, he rightly refers that prophecy of Isaiah LV. 13. The Apostle expresses the name of Jesus Christ here for the first time, after he has denoted him by those magnificent titles of his, so that the Church might know that Jesus and Christ are not only not different, as the Gnostics taught, but that Jesus Christ is not someone other than he who is called by the name of 'Word' and 'only-begotten'.

Grotius renders 'grace for grace' as grace because of grace, and explains grace, that is, the gifts of the Holy Spirit, because of grace, that is, granted by God out of mere grace or freely. Others retain that acceptance of the word 'for' as an impulsive cause, but declare the words in another way: grace because of grace: B. Chemnitius, Joach. Camerarius, Paul. Tarnovius, and others explain it in this way: we receive the grace of divine love because of that grace by which the Father loves and accepts his Son, who was made under the law for us, Eph. I. 6, in which way also Francisc. Gomarus has interpreted it, namely, that we receive the grace of justification because of the righteousness performed for us freely by Christ the mediator.

But to Ludovicus de Dieu, that seems far-fetched: He therefore explains grace for grace, that is, one grace for another, the later for the former: For when, he says, he had mentioned the fullness of Christ, he says that not one, but many graces are drawn from it, of which the first is the cause of the second, that of the third, this of the fourth, and so on, the later is always given because of the former, until, with all the gifts of grace completed, blessedness is finally perfected. He adds, however, for the explanation of his opinion, what follows: 'Nor do I think that the right use of grace is looked at here, as if a second grace were given because of it. For that is to recall the mind from Christ to us, when the scope of the Apostle is to fix us entirely in Christ. But I wish the very condition of saving grace to be looked at, which is such that the first draws the other, and because the former was given, the latter is also given, in which continuation of grace I willingly concede that the right use proceeding from grace itself is contained.'

Others explain it thus with Bucer: we receive grace upon grace: by such a phrase, just as Paul says in Rom. I. 17, 'From faith to faith,' i.e., whatever grace and gifts we need for salvation, we receive from his fullness, and his gifts are subsequently increased in us.

Others prefer the meaning of the word ἀντὶ as commutative, that we receive grace for grace, i.e., gratuitous rewards for the first grace of faith: because both faith is grace, and a gift of God, and those rewards are grace, as Augustine explains.

The Papists corrupt that: we receive grace, that is, the habit of love, for grace, i.e., eternal life to be merited: but this is directly against the Apostle in Rom. XI. 6. and against the opinion of Augustine: grace is not grace in any way, if it is not gratuitous in every way.

Finally, others prefer the most accepted meaning of the word ἀντὶ, by which it is the same as in place of, or instead of, which is also its proper and almost perpetual acceptance in the N.T.: in which manner the Greeks, Chrysostom, Cyril, and Theophylact explain it; that in place of the grace of the Old Covenant we receive the grace of the New, or Evangelical, covenant, which interpretation Beza and Scaliger approve, but Lud. de Dieu not undeservedly rejects: I cannot, he says, accede to this opinion, if only because of the following verse, where indeed not the grace of the law is opposed to the grace of the Gospel, but the law is opposed to grace: so that no grace is attributed to the law, and all grace is attributed to Christ alone. For although I confess it to have been a grace that God adorned the Israelite people, above all others, with so perfect a law, and with such holy, good, and just precepts; yet the law itself exhibited no grace, but left it all to Christ, as its end. John proves this, because through Moses, indeed, the law was given, not Grace: but in Christ, both grace and truth have been granted.

The Grotian opinion does not deserve approval: because ἀντὶ χάριτος does not mean freely, or out of grace, and mere goodness, but for grace or in place of grace: whence we cannot accede to the explanation of others, who neglect this proper meaning of the word: which the Syrian expressed with the word חלף, the Arab with بدل; which particles signify commutation, as Dievius admits, by which one thing is substituted in the place of another. Wherefore, other interpretations being dismissed, this seems to us the simplest explanation, that we receive grace in place of or instead of grace, namely the grace of reparation and restitution to salvation, for the grace of primeval creation in the image of God and to eternal life lost in Adam: the grace of Evangelical righteousness, which is through faith, for the grace of primeval righteousness and integrity lost through the fall: which sense is analogous to the explanation of the Greek Interpreters: because primeval righteousness was legal, in whose place, because it was lost, and because of sin, contracted through the fall, it can be found in no mortal, Evangelical righteousness has been substituted: which we receive ἐκ τοῦ πληρώματος αὐτοῦ. (for we grant to Grotius that the particle καὶ in the words καὶ χάριν is exegetical, to be explained by 'namely', and that it is an elegance of the Holy Scriptures to place the same word in a contiguous position with a different sense, which is observed here in the words χάριτος ἀντὶ χάριτος) because that Evangelical grace could not be had from elsewhere, unless ἐκ πληρώματος θεανθρώπου or τοῦ λόγου of the incarnate Word, and this was the cause of the incarnation, that namely in place of the gracious righteousness granted in primeval creation, maliciously lost through sin, sin being expiated, another righteousness might be brought to us, out of mere grace and mercy, Dan. IX. 24. therefore it is added, that the law was indeed given through Moses, from which, however, because righteousness could not be obtained by us, but only our unrighteousness convicted, grace and truth have been obtained for us through JESUS Christ: which is the sum of the proclamation

Evangelical; which the Son of God himself brought forth, as it were, from the bosom of his Father, and manifested to us, when otherwise it would have remained eternally hidden. Conf. Matth. XI. 27. Rom. XVI. 26.

To this sense, Grotius’s explanation of ῥ πληρώματος does not poorly correspond, which signifies τὴν ἀκρὴν μετοχὴν τ̃ θεό- τητο̃, as Origen speaks, as also (the Apostle accepts) Col. I. 19. & II. 9.; just as Clement of Alexandria, Strom. II. πᾶσαι δὲ αἱ δυνάμεις τ̃ πνέυματος συλ- λήβδην μὲν ἕν τι πρᾶγμα γενόμεναι συντελῦσιν εἰς τὸ αὐτὸ τ̃ υἱὸν. For it pleased [God] for this reason, that in him should dwell all the fullness, so that indeed through him all things might be reconciled in him, Col. I. 19. 20. Nor is it inconveniently observed by Grotius, that this ἡ in verse 16, at the beginning, καὶ ἐκ τῦ πλη- ρώματο̃ αὐτῦ, should be connected with the preceding things, which had gone before, before the testimony of the Baptist was inserted, especially with those words, full of grace and truth! Conf. Eph. I. 5.

Latin:

Vers. 7. ὅτι ὁ νόμος διὰ Μωσέως ἐδόθη] In transcursu confoditur Ebionis dogma Jesum Mosi posthumantis.

ἡ χάρις κὶ ἡ ἀλήθεια διὰ Ἰησοῦ χριστῦ ἐγένετο] Ἀλήθεια ut supra diximus opponitur umbræ legis: χάρις hic præcipue est co- pia illa spiritus passim in Christianos effusa, statui veris legis in- cognita, quo præter alias vaticinia recte referat illud Esaiæ LV. 13. Jesu Christi nomen hic primum exprimit Aposto- lus, postquam eum suis illis magnificis titulis denotavit, ut sciret Ecclesia non modo non diversos esse Jesum & Christum ut tradebant Gnostici, sed nec alium esse Jesum Christum quam qui λόγος & μονογενῆς nomine dicatur.

Grotius χάριν ἀντὶ χάριτος reddit gratiam propter gratiam, & exponit gratiam, id est, dona Spi- ritus S. propter gratiam, id est, ex mera gratia seu gratis à Deo concessa. Alii retinent illam vocis ἀντὶ acceptionem pro causa impulsiva, sed alia ratione verba declarant: gratiam propter gratiam: B. Che- mnitius, Joach. Camerarius, Paul. Tarnovius & alii hoc modo explicant: accipimus gratiam dilectionis divinæ propter illam gratiam, qua Pater Filium suum sub lege factum pro nobis diligit, & acceptat, Eph. I. 6. quo fere modo etiam Francisc. Gomarus inter- pretatus est, quod nempe gratiam justificationis propter Christi mediatoris gratis pro nobis præstitam justitiam accipiamus.

Ludovico vero de Dieu id longe petitum vide- tur: Exponit ergo gratiam ob gratiam, id est gra- tiam unam ob alteram, posteriorem ob priorem: Quum enim, inquit, memorasset plenitudinem Chri- sti, dicit hauriri inde non unam, sed plures gratias, qua- rum prima sit causa secundæ, ista tertiæ, hæc quartæ, & sic deinceps semper posterior detur ob priorem, do- nec, completis omnibus gratiæ donis perficiatur tan- dem beatitudo. Addit autem explicandæ sententiæ suæ, quæ sequuntur: Neq; tamen hic rectum gratiæ usum spectari arbitror, quasi ob eum secunda detur gratia. Id enim est mentem à Christo ad nos revocare, quum scopus Apostoli sit, nos totos in Christo defigere. Sed ipsam salutaris gratiæ conditionem spectari volo, quæ ea est, ut prima trahat alteram, & ob datam priorem detur & posterior, in qua gratiæ continua- tione rectum usum ex ipsa gratia proficiscentem conti- neri libenter concedo.

Alii sic explicant cum Bucero: accipimus gratiam super gratiam: tali phrasi, sicut Rom. I. 17. Paulus dicit, Ex fide in fidem, h. e. quicquid gratiæ & dono- rum nobis opus est ad salutem, ex ejus plenitudine ac- cipimus, & ejus dona subinde augentur in nobis.

Aliis placet significatio vocis ἀντὶ commutativa, gratiam pro gratia nos accipere, h. e. præmia gratui- ta pro gratia prima fidei: quia & fides gratia est, ac donum Dei, & præmia illa gratia sunt, uti Augu- stinus explicat.

Pontificii illa depravant: accipimus gratiam, id est, habitum dilectionis, pro gratia, h. e. vita æterna promerenda: sed directe contra Apostolum Rom. XI. 6. & contra Augustini sententiam: gratia non est gratia ullo modo, si non est gratuita omni modo.

Alii denique præferunt significationem vocis ἀντὶ receptissimam, qua idem est quod loco, aut vi- ce, quæ & propria, & fere perpetua est ejusdem in N. T. acceptio: quo pacto Græci, Chrysostomus, Cyrillus & Theophylactus explicant; loco gratiæ Ve- teris fœderis nos accipere gratiam fœderis Novi, vel Evangelici, quam ἔκθεσιν probat Beza & Scaliger, sed non immerito reprobat Lud. de Dieu: non pos- sum, inquit, huic sententiæ accedere, vel ob versum se- quentem, ubi equidem non gratia legis gratiæ Evan- gelii, sed lex gratiæ opponitur: adeo ut legi nulla, Chri- sto soli omnis gratia tribuatur. Etsi enim gratia fuis- se fatear, quod tam perfecta lege; tam sanctis, bonis ac justis præceptis referta, Deus populum Israeliticum, su- pra omnes alios, ornavit; gratiam tamen nullam lex ipsa exhibuit, sed eam Christo totam, tanquam fini suo, reliquit. Id probat Johannes, quia per Mosen, nisi lex data est, non Gratia: at in Christo, & gratia & veritas concessa est.

Grotiana sententia calculum non meretur: quia ἀντὶ χάριτος non est gratis, vel ex gratia, & mera bonitate, sed pro gratia vel vice gratiæ: unde nec a- liorum explicationi accedere possumus, qui hanc significationem vocis propriam negligunt: quam Syrus voce חלף, Arabs بدل expressit; quæ particulæ commutationem significant, fatente Die- vio, qua unum in alterius locum subrogatur. Quapro- pter, missis aliis interpretationibus, hæc nobis vi- detur simplicissima explicatio, accipere nos gra- tiam loco vel vice gratiæ, gratiam nempe reparatio- nis, & restitutionis ad salutem, pro gratia primæva creationis ad imaginem Dei & ad vitam æternam in Adamo deperditæ: gratiam justitiæ Evangelicæ, quæ est per fidem pro gratia justitiæ & integritatis primige- niæ per lapsum amissæ: qui sensus Græcorum Inter- pretum explicationi analogus est: quia justitia pri- mogenia legalis erat, in cujus locum, quia ea deper- dita est, & propter peccatum, per lapsum contra- ctum, in nemine mortalium inveniri potest, surro- gata est justitia Evangelica: quam accipimus ἐκ τοῦ πληρώματος αὐτοῦ. (particulam enim καὶ in verbis καὶ χάριν, ἐξηγητικὴν esse, per videlicet explicandam, & elegantiam S.literarum esse, vocem eandem contiguo loco ponere sensu alio, quæ hic in vocibus χάριτος ἀντὶ χάριτος observetur, Grotio largimur) quia illa Ev- angelica gratia aliunde haberi non poterat, nisi ἐκ πληρώματος θεανθρώπου vel τοῦ λόγου Verbi incar- nati, & hac causa τῆς ἐνσαρκώσεως fuit, ut nempe loco justitiæ gratiosæ in primæva creatione concessæ, per peccatum malitiose deperditæ, peccato expiato, no- bis, ex mera gratia & misericordia, alia adducere- tur justitia Dan. IX. 24. ideo additur, legem quidem per Mosen datam esse, ex qua vero, quia justitia no- bis obtingere non poterat, sed tantum convinci nostra injustitia, gratiam & veritatem obtigisse nobis per JESUM Christum: quæ summa est præconii

Evangelici; quod ipse Filius Dei è sinu Patris sui quasi protulit, nobisque manifestavit, quum cæte- roquin æternum mansisset absconditum. Conf. Matth. XI. 27. Rom. XVI. 26.

Cui sensui non male quadrat explicatio ῥ πλη- ρώματος Grotiana, quod τὴν ἀκρὴν μετοχὴν τ̃ θεό- τητο̃, ut Origenes loquitur, ut & Col. I. 19. & II. 9. (Apostolus accipit) significat; quomodo Clemens Alex. Strom. II. πᾶσαι δὲ αἱ δυνάμεις τ̃ πνέυματος συλ- λήβδην μὲν ἕν τι πρᾶγμα γενόμεναι συντελῦσιν εἰς τὸ αὐτὸ τ̃ υἱὸν. Nam ideo placuit, ut in ipso habitaret tota plenitudo, ut nempe per ipsum reconciliarentur omnia in ipsum Col. I. 19. 20. Nec incommode obser- vatum Grotio, hoc ἡ vers. 16. initio καὶ ἐκ τῦ πλη- ρώματο̃ αὐτῦ, connectendum esse cum superioribus, quæ præcesserant, antequam testimonium Baptistæ in- sereretur, præsertim cum illis, πλήρης χάριτο̃ καὶ ἀληθείας! Conf. Eph. I. 5.

## 1:8
Vers. 8. The light] That excellent light promised through the Prophets, as in Isaiah XLIX. 6. see at Luke II, 32.

Latin:

Vers. 8. Τὸ φῶς] Illa eximia lux promissa per Prophetas, ut Esaïæ XLIX. 6. vide ad Lucam II, 32.

## 1:9
Vers. 9. was the true light, which lighteth] Where the subject is of a different gender than the predicate, there the relative or demonstrative pronouns are placed now in this gender, now in that, as Sed revocare gradum superasque evadere auras, Hoc opus, hic labor est. For the natural construction would have been: this, namely, to escape, is the labor. Thus what we read here is just as if it had been said: He was truly the light, through whom not a few but the whole human race is illuminated. But 'true' is also said of those things which figuratively belong to someone, as Christ is the true vine below XV. 1. His flesh is truly food, below 55. The true bread from heaven, below VI. 32. Thus spiritual goods, the true mammon, Luke XVI. 12. Heaven the true tabernacle, Hebr. VIII. 2. But the true light is the excellent, most excellent light, as also in the first Epistle II. 8.

Every man] Christ is said to have done what he ordered to be done and did through the Apostles. Thus Ephes. II. 17. having come he preached peace to you who were far off. But here Jesus is tacitly opposed to Moses and the other Prophets, who were of benefit to one people only.

coming into the world] The exposition which exists in Cyril and Augustine commends itself greatly to me, that this 'coming' should be referred to 'the light'. For clearly in the same way below III. 19. the light has come into the world. And Christ himself XII. 46. I have come as a light into the world. And below concerning himself XVIII. 37. for this I have come into the world, that I might bear witness to the truth. But this 'to come into the world' is not to be born, (for these two are distinguished XVIII. 37.) but, in the name of God, to appear to men: Thus below VI. 14 the prophet who is coming into the world: And Christ says he was sent by the Father into the world X. 36. & XVII. 18. & similarly that the Apostles were sent by him into the world, in the same place. Therefore it is said here that Christ was given to men for this purpose, that he might benefit them universally.

That explanation of Cyril and Augustine was approved by me also once upon a time, (before it was observed in Grotius) but so that the nativity might be indicated here; which St. John describes in three ways; through the advent of the light into this world, by which, however, it was not recognized v. 9. 10. through the advent into his own, where his own did not receive him, v. 11. but those who did receive him, received the power to be the sons of God, v. 12. 13. & through the incarnation of the Word, where the Apostles saw his glory, as of the only-begotten from the Father, v. 14. Nor indeed are 'for this I was born, and for this I came into the world' John XVIII. 37. distinguished, but are joined by way of explanation. See the dissertation on the pre-existence of the Son of God before Mary, chapter III.

Latin:

Vers. 9. ἦν τὸ φῶς τὸ ἀληθινὸν, ὃ φωτίζει] Ubi subjectum alterius est generis, quam prædicatum, ibi relativa aut de- monstrativa modo hoc modo illo genere ponuntur, ut Sed revocare gradum superasque evadere auras, Hoc opus, hic labor est. Nam naturalis constructio fuerat: hoc sc. evadere, labor est. Ita quod hic legimus, perinde est, quasi dictum esset: Ille vere lux erat, per quem non pauci sed totum genus huma- num illuminatur. Verum autem dicitur etiam de his, quæ fi- gurate alicui competunt, ut Christus vera vitis infra XV. 1. Caro ejus vere cibus, infra 55. Panis verus ex cœlo, in- fra VI. 32. Sic bona spiritualia, verus mammona, Luc. XVI. 12. Cœlum verum tabernaculum, Hebr. VIII. 2. Lux autem vera est lux eximia excellentissima, ut & in Epist. prima II. 8.

Πάντα ἄνθρωπον] Christus dicitur fecisse quod fieri jussit & per Apostolos fecit. Sic Ephes. II. 17. ἐλθὼν εὐηγγελίσατο εἰ- ρήνην ὑμῖν τοῖς μακρὰν. Opponitur autem hic tacite Jesus Mosi & Prophetis aliis, qui uni tantum populo profuerunt.

ἐρχόμενον εἰς ὸ κόσμον] Valde mihi se probat expositio, quæ apud Cyrillum & Augustinum exstat, ut hoc ἐρχόμενον referatur ad τὸ φῶς. Nam plane eodem modo infra III. 19. τὸ φῶς ἐλήλυθεν εἰς ὸ κόσμον Lux venit in mundum. Et ipse Christus XII. 46. ἐγὼ φῶς εἰς ὸ κόσμον ἐλήλυθα. Et infra de se XVIII. 37. εἰς τῦτο ἐλήλυθα εἰς ὸ κόσμον, ἵνα μαρτυρήσω τῇ ἀληθείᾳ. Est autem hic ἔρχεσθαι εἰς ὸ κόσμον, non nasci, (di- stinguuntur enim hæc duo XVIII. 37.) sed, nomine Dei, hominibus apparere: Sic infra VI. 14 ὁ προφήτης ὁ ἐρχόμε- νος εἰς ὸ κόσμον : Et Christus se à Patre missum dicit εἰς ὸ κό- σμον X. 36. & XVII. 18. & à se similiter Apostolos missos εἰς ὸ κόσμον, ibidem. Hoc ergo hic dicitur, Christum in hoc da- tum hominibus, ut eis universim prodesset.

Illa explicatio Cyrilli, & Augustini probata & mihi jam quondam, (antequam observata in Gro- tio) sed ut nativitas hic indicetur; quam tribus modis describit S. Johannes; per adventum lucis in hunc mundum, à quo vero agnitus non est v. 9. 10. per adventum εἰς τὰ ἴδια, ubi οἱ ἴδιοι eum non susce- perunt, v. 11. qui vero susceperunt eum, potestatem acceperunt υἱὸ Ἱητ Θεῦ, v. 12. 13. & per ἐνσάρκωσιν τῦ λόγε, ubi viderunt Apostoli gloriam ejus, velut u- nigeniti à Patre, v. 14. Nec vero illa, ad hoc natus sum, & ad hoc veni in mundum Joh. XVIII. 37. distin- guuntur, sed κατ’ ἐπεξήγησιν conjunguntur. Vid. dissert. de præexist. Filii Dei ante-Mariana cap. III.

## 1:10
Vers. 10. he was in the world] He was present among men: 'world' is used everywhere for men. See 2 Pet. II, 15.

and the world was made through him] Indeed all things were made through him, as we have already heard, but in a special way men. For the Word of God is the pattern of man, as Philo notes. On the creation of the world. Tatian: The heavenly Word, the imitation of the Father who begat him, the image of immortality, made man.

There is no reason why the word 'world' should be taken not properly, but metonymically: for as he came into the world, so also he was in the world: and when the world is said to have been made through him, not only men are understood, but all things, as is evident from the comparison with v. 3. Concerning which more at length against the Socinians in a special Exercise on the beginning of John, which is the second in the select ones.

and the world knew him not] It did not recognize him as its maker.

Latin:

Vers. 10. ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ ἦν ] Interfuit hominibus : κόσμῳ pro hominibus passim sumitur. Vide 2. Pet. II, 15.

καὶ ὁ κόσμος δι’ αὐτῦ ἐγίνετο ] Res quidem omnes per illum factæ, ut jam audivimus, sed speciali modo homines. Nam Θεῦ λόγος est παράδειγμα hominis, ut Philo notat. περὶ κοσμοποιΐας. Tatianus λόγος ὁ ἐπουράνιος τὴν τῦ γεννήσαντος αὐτὸν πατρὸς μίμησιν, εἰκόνα ἀθανασίας, τὸν ἄνθρωπον ἐποίησεν.

Nulla est ratio, cur vox mundi non proprie, sed Metonymice accipi debeat: nam ut in mundum venit, ita & in mundo fuit: & quum mundus dicitur per ipsum factus, non homines tantum intelligun- tur, sed res omnes, ut è collatione v. 3. constat. De quo pluribus adversus Socinianos Exercit. peculia- ri in principium Johannis, quæ altera est in selectis.

καὶ ὁ κόσμος αὐτὸν ὐκ ἔγνω ] Non agnovit ut opificem suum.

## 1:11
Vers. 11. he came into his own] The Jurisconsults teach that that is most naturally ours which we have caused to exist. L. Possideri par. Genera D. de acq. possessione. But 'into his own' is as into his own house as below XVI. 32. Acts XXI. 6. See what is at Luke II. 49.

and his own did not receive him] They did not receive him as Lord. Thus Col. II. 6. But these things also are to be understood of the greater part.

Latin:

Vers. 11. εἰς τὰ ἴδια ἦλθε] Docent Iurisconsulti, id maxime naturaliter nostrum esse quod nos ut existeret effecimus. L. Possideri par. Genera D. de acq. possessione. Est autem εἰς τὰ ἴδια tanquam in domum suam ut infra XVI. 32. Actor. XXI. 6. Vide quæ ad Lucam II. 49.

καὶ οἱ ἴδιοι αὐτὸν ὐ παρέλαβον ] Non receperunt ut Dominum Sic Col. II. 6. Intelligenda autem & hæc de majori parte.

## 1:12
Vers. 12. But as many as received him] He shows here that there were few who are to be excepted from the preceding generality. A similar manner of speaking is in Micah 7:14. Novatian on the Trinity.
