This word is that which is in 'he came unto his own and his own received him not,' for the world was made through him and the world knew him not; to receive (λαμβάνειν) and to take to oneself (παραλαμβάνειν) are the same, to receive as lord.

he gave them power to become the sons of God] Sons, understand the sons of the resurrection, as he explains in Luke 20:36. Our author in 1 Epist. 3:2: 'it does not yet appear what we shall be; but we know that if he shall appear, we shall be like him.' Paul to the Romans 8:23: 'waiting for the adoption, the redemption of our bodies.' Moreover, this power (ἐξουσία) is a right to an inheritance, which also sometimes comes under the name of inheritance, just as he who believes (namely, as it is fitting to believe with a living faith) is said to have eternal life, 3:36. Thus the Jurisconsults: He who has an action to the thing itself, seems to have the thing. But here he said power (ἐξουσία) more properly, because this right is so far from being the thing itself, that the thing may not follow, namely, if perseverance be absent.

Power (ἐξουσία) can be understood either of dignity, namely that he gave us this claim (ἀξίωσιν), preeminence, and dignity, that we might be sons of God: or, as some explain it, of authority, that he granted us a right to an inheritance, or that we might become as the sons of the blessed resurrection. Nonnus explained it in the former way by honor (τιμὴν), as also Chrysostom: 'they are deemed worthy of the same honor.' Compare Heinsius: That something actual is looked to, the word 'were born' (ἐγεννήθησαν) in the following verse 13 confirms: Not that they are to be sons in the future; but that they are already sons is noted. So Cyril, Flacius, Chemnitius, and Nyssenus, etc.

Latin:

Vers. 12. ὅσοι δὲ ἔλαβον αὐτὸν ] Ostendit hic paucos fuisse, qui excipiendi sint ex superiore generalitate. Simile loquendi genus Mich. VII. 14. Novatianus de Trinitate. Verbum hoc illud est, quod in sua venit & sui eum non receperunt, Mundus enim per ipsam factus est & mundus eum non cognovit, idem est λαμβάνειν & παραλαμβάνειν, recipere ut dominum.

ἔδωκεν αὐτοῖς ἐξουσίαν τέκνα Θεῦ γενέσθαι] Filios, intellige fi- lios resurrectionis, ut explicat Luc. XX. 36. noster in 1. Epist. III. 2. ὔπω ἐφανερώθη τί ἰσόμεθα· οἴδαμεν δὲ ὅτι ἐὰν φανερωθῇ, ὅμοιοι αὐτῷ ἐσόμεθα. Paulus ad Rom. VIII. 23. υἱοθεσίαν ἀπεκ- δεχόμενοι, τὴν ἀπολύτρωσιν τῆ σωμάτων ἡμῶν. Est autem hic ἐξουσία jus ad hæreditatem, quod & hæreditatis nomine in- terdum venit, sicut qui credit, (nempe sicut oportet crede- re viva fide) dicitur habere vitam æternam III. 36. Sic Ju- ris-Consulti: Is qui actionem habet ad rem ipsam, rem habere videtur. Sed hic magis proprie dixit ἐξουσίαν, quia jus hoc ad- eo res ipsa non est, ut res possit non sequi, nempe si absit perseverantia.

E'ξουσία intelligi potest vel de dignitate, quod nempe hanc ἀξίωσιν praeeminentiam & dignitatem nobis dederit, ut simus filii Dei: vel ut explicant non- nulli de potestate, quod jus ad hæreditatem, vel ut filii beatæ resurrectionis fiamus, nobis concesserit. Nonnus priori modo exposuit per τιμὴν, ut & Chry- sost. τῆς αὐτῆς ἀξιῶνται τιμῆς. Conf. Heinsius: A- ctuale quid respici verbum ἐξεννήθησαν geniti sunt v. sequenti 13. confirmat: Neque quod olim futuri sint filii; sed quod jam sint filii notatur. Ita Cyrillus, Flacius, Chemnitius & Nyssenus, &c.

## 1:13
Vers. 13. Not of blood nor of the will of the flesh] It is the custom for Hebrews to call a man, especially when compared to God or Angels, 'flesh and blood' (בשר ודם): thus 'flesh' (σὰρξ) and 'blood' (αἷμα) are taken. Matthew 16:17, Galatians 1:16, and elsewhere. Moreover, 'will' (θέλημα) is here for the Hebrew 'desire' (חפץ), which also signifies lust.

nor of the will of man] That this may differ from the former (for there seems to be no explanation (ἐπεξήγησις) here), I think that those are said to be born of the will of man who are made sons of some man not by the natural commixture of sexes, of which we have already treated, but by adoption or institution. We have noted this matter at Matthew 23:9, just as we have also shown at Luke 3:23 how widely the Hebrew 'to beget' (ילד) extends, corresponding to the Greek 'to beget' (γεννᾷν). The Sadducees interpreted the same word 'to beget' (ילד) concerning adoption in Leviticus 18:11; the word 'generations' (תולדות) in Numbers 3:1 must be taken no differently. For nothing concerning the natural offspring of Moses is treated there.

But were born of God] Here, however, he looks not to that adoption which is to be in the other world, but to that which happens here, namely, that we are rendered like to God, not in majesty but in goodness. See what we said at Matthew 5:5 and 45. Thus our author here in the first epistle 3:2, a little before those things which we have already cited: 'now we are the sons of God,' that is, his imitators.

As Gomarus wishes the female to be understood by the name of flesh in the preceding words (without example), so he thinks the male is designated by the word 'man' (ἀνδρὸς). But Beza has already refuted that, acknowledging that by the name of flesh is indicated that foul and impure natural or carnal conception of man, which is everywhere opposed to the spirit, or Job 3:6. B. Luther on Hosea, Vol. VIII, Altenb. p. 609, handed down an interpretation almost similar to the Grotian; yet by the will of the flesh he wishes the voluntary adoption of sons to be looked to, and by the will of man he wishes imitation and exercise without the Holy Spirit to be looked to; and in the explanation of the first chapter of John, Vol. VI, Altenb. p. 1167, he understands by the will of man an honorary title, when, namely, we call Superiors, Magistrates, Teachers, etc., Fathers for the sake of honor, even though they neither begot us nor adopted us as sons. But the explanation of B. Chemnitius is better here: not of bloods: because such are not born by natural generation from believing and holy parents, as the Jews boasted of themselves by carnal lineage: not of the will of either flesh or man; 'Will' signifies the highest zeal and endeavor. The Syrian rendered it 'desire' (צבינא), which signifies choice and free will, to show that by the name of will, 'purpose' (προαίρεσιν) and free will are understood in this place. But 'flesh' is called in Scripture whatever nature can do and effect by its own powers, just as 'the righteousness of the flesh' is called, Hebrews 9:10. And those are called 'men' (viri) by the Hebrews whom other languages call outstanding Heroes. The Syrian rendered it 'man' (גבר), which signifies the strong, the mighty, the powerful, giants, or Heroes, whom the Greeks were accustomed to refer to the number of the Gods by 'deification' (ἀποθέωσιν). And from this word, also mighty works and illustrious deeds are called by the Syrians. The meaning, therefore, is that by no studies, whether common or heroic, works, virtues, merits, or any dignity or excellence of man whatsoever, can true apotheosis be acquired, that is, adoption before God.

Latin:

Vers. 13. οἱ ἐκ ἐξ αἱμάτων ἐδὲ ἐκ θελήματ σαρκός] Mos est Hebræis hominem, præsertim cum Deo aut Angelis comparatum vocare בשר ודם carnem & sanguinem: sic sumuntur σὰρξ & αἷμα. Matth. XVI. 17. Gal. I. 16. & alibi Est autem hic θέλημα pro Hebr. חפץ, quod & libidinem significat.

ἐδὲ ἐκ θελήματ ἀνδρὸς] Ut distet hoc à priori (nulla e- nim videtur esse ἐπεξήγησις) putem, ex voluntate viri eos ge- nitos dici, qui non naturali sexuum commixtione, de qua a- ctum jam est, sed adoptione aut institutione fiunt hominis alicujus filii. Notavimus hac de re ad Matth. XXIII. 9. sicut & ad Lucam III. 23. ostendimus quam late pateat Hebræum ילד respondens Græco γεννᾷν. Eandem vocem ילד de ad- optione Sadducæi, interpretarēbantur Lev. XVIII. 11. neca- liter sumenda vox תולדות Num. III, 1. Nam de naturali Mosis sobole nihil ibi agitur.

Ἀλλ' ἐκ Θεῦ ἐγεννήθησαν] Hic vero respicit non illam ado- ptionem, quæ futura est in altero seculo, sed eam quæ hic fit, quascilicet Deo reddimur similes non majestate sed bonitate. Vide quæ ad Matth. V. 5. & 45. Sic noster hic in epist. prima III. 2. paulo ante ea quæ jam citavimus : νῦν τέκνα Θεῦ ἐσμὲν, jam nunc filii Dei sumus, id est, ejus imitatores.

Ut carnis nomine in verbis præcedentibus Go- marus intelligi vult fœminam, (sine exemplo) ita ἀνδρὸς voce marem designari putat. Sed id repro- bavit jam Beza, agnoscens carnis nomine indigitari fœdam illam & impuram hominis conceptionem na- turalem sive carnalem, quæ spiritui passim oppo- nitur, aut Job. III. 6. B. Lutherus in Hoseam T. VIII. Altenb. p. 609. fere similem cum Grotiana tradidit interpretationem; per voluntatem tamen carnis voluntariam filiorum adoptionem, per voluntatem viri respici vult imitationem & exercitum sine Spiri- tu S. & in explicatione primi capit. Johan. T. VI. Altenb. p. 1167. per voluntatem viri intelligit hono- rarium titulum, cum nempe Superiores, Magistra- tus, Præceptores &c. honoris causa Patres dicimus, etsi nec procrearint, nec adoptarint nos in filios. Præstat autem hic explicatio B. Chemnitii: non ex sanguinibus: quia naturali generatione ex paren- tibus credentibus & sanctis non nascuntur tales, uti Judæi carnali prosapia se efferebant: non ex vo- luntate vel carnis vel viri; Voluntas significat sum- mum studium & conatum. Syrus reddidit צבינא quod electionem & arbitrium significat, ut ostendat, nomi- ne voluntatis προεαίρεσιν & liberum arbitrium hoc loco intelligi. Caro vero in Scriptura vocatur, quicquid natura suis viribus potest & efficit, sicut vocatur justitia carnis, Hebr. IX. 10. Et viri Ebræis vocantur, quos aliæ linguæ præstantes Heroas vo- cant. Syrus reddidit גבר quod validos, fortes, poten- tes, gigantes, seu Heroas significat, quos Græci per ἀποθέωσιν in numerum Deorum referre solebant, Et ab hoc vocabulo, etiam virtutes & res præclare geste Syris appellantur. Sensus igitur est, nullis, vel vulgaribus, vel heroicis studiis, operibus virtutibus, me- ritis, aut dignitate vel præstantia hominis quacunque acqviri posse veram ἀποθέωσιν, hoc est, adoptionem apud Deum.

## 1:14
V. 14. And the Word became flesh] And this is the explanatory reason for the preceding. So that the Word might lift us men up to the divine majesty, He showed Himself in this our weak human nature. Paul in 1 Tim. 2:16: God was manifested in the flesh. For flesh, as we began to say, signifies infirmity and a humble state. Thus Ps. 66:5, 77:39, and elsewhere. Compare Phil. 2:6, 2 Cor. 8:9. The name Son of Man points to the same thing.

Grotius renders it, 'He showed Himself in this our weak human nature,' but that interpretation is such that not even the Socinians themselves reject it. John, however, did not wish to signify here a humble state or infirmity, but the incarnation itself: just as when it is said that He is 'according to the flesh' from the seed of David in Rom. 1:4, it is not indicated according to a humble state, but that He draws His origin from human nature. The humble state was a consequence, and that a voluntary one, of the incarnation of the Word, after He assumed human nature: for He was in the form of God, and from there He freely emptied Himself of divine glory, and assumed the form of a servant, Phil. 2:6, so that in the order of nature the incarnation preceded, and humiliation followed; for the assumption of human nature is prior to the very state of the emptying of the God-man. And therefore the Fathers, whose opinion Grotius himself praises here, understood these things concerning the very becoming man and incarnation. Well, says Justin: 'Since also for our sake He became man (the Word), so that by becoming a partaker of our sufferings He might also effect healing.' Origen: 'From that point the divine and human nature began to be interwoven, so that the human, through communion with the more divine, might become divine, not only in Jesus, but also in all those who, after believing, take up the life which Jesus taught.' Irenaeus: 'The Word,' he says, 'united to His own creation, was made a passible man.' The same elsewhere: 'For this reason the Word became man, so that man, having received the Word and having taken the adoption, might become a son of God.' Tertullian against Praxeas: 'It is consistent that He should be understood to have been made flesh, while He is in the flesh, and is manifested, and is seen, and is handled through the flesh.'

And He tabernacled among us] He dwelt. For thus also those who dwell in heaven are said to tabernacle, Rev. 12:12 and 13:6. 'Among us' you may rightly translate 'between us,' as in Luke 1:29, but it should be noted that by the word 'to tabernacle,' which is the same in sound and meaning as the Hebrew 'shakan,' there is an allusion to the conspicuous presence of the divine majesty which the Chaldean paraphrast also calls 'the glory of the Shekinah': or to a singular operation, both of which the teachers of the Hebrews note are signified by 'shakan,' whence 'Shekinah,' as Maimonides in the Guide for the Perplexed, Book I, ch. 25. Thus what follows coheres well.

And we beheld His glory] That humble state was not without great and certain signs of divine Majesty, which is 'kabod' to the Hebrews, as in Ex. 16:7, 10, 24:16, 17, 29:43, 33:18, 22, 40:31, 32, Lev. 9:6, 23, and often elsewhere. But this glory of Christ appeared not only in that extraordinary transformation on Mount Tabor, in the narrative of which Peter uses the word 'glory' in 2 Pet. 1:17. But also in those things which happened around the passion, in the resurrection and after it, and in the ascension to heaven: indeed, also in the miracles. See below 2:11, 12:23.

As of the only begotten from the Father] What Chrysostom and other Greeks here call 'as' as a definitive, the Hebrews call 'kaph' for truth, which in Latin is rightly translated by 'as.' 'Yachid,' which signifies only-begotten or unique, the Greeks, looking to the sense, translate as 'beloved,' as in Gen. 22:2, 12, and 16, Judg. 11:34, Jer. 6:26, Amos 8:10, Zech. 12:10, or 'loved.' Prov. 4:3, 'desired' Judg. 11:34. Plutarch: 'Homer calls a beloved son, only, late-born, that is, to parents who have no other and will have no others born after.' In the second Odyssey it is 'only, going beloved.' See Matt. 3:17 and Mark 12:6. Thus David calls Solomon his only son, i.e., most beloved, 1 Chron. 29:1, and Solomon himself in the cited place Prov. 4:3. Therefore Christ is rightly called 'only begotten' here, in the meaning we have stated, and to which can be added, because He proceeded from God in a singular way: Justin: 'The only one called properly Son.' And elsewhere: 'The only proper Son to God has been begotten, being His Word and firstborn and power, and by His will having become man.' And in passing, the Gnostics are condemned who made one Word, another only-begotten, another Jesus, which Julian did not fail to note while writing against the Christians. But that 'from the Father,' although it can be referred to 'only begotten' by a construction which is 'according to the meaning,' such as that 'What is that touching of you?', because in a derived noun there is the force of the verb, I would prefer, however, to refer it to 'glory' because of the similar passage of Peter, which we have already begun to note; 'for having received from God the Father honor and glory.'

Thus 'glory from God' below in this book 5:44. Justin notes that the Word is also called the 'glory of God' and the Hebrews, what the Rabbis call 'Shekinah,' explain as 'kabod' as we just said. The confession of Lucian the Martyr exists: 'The Son of God is the unchangeable image of His essence and will and power and glory.' See 2 Cor. 3:9.

When the Greeks translate 'yachid' as 'beloved' in Gen. 22:2, 12, 16, Judg. 11:34, Jer. 6:26, Amos 8:10, Zech. 12:10, the very meaning of the word, which he acknowledges signifies only-begotten or unique, could have taught them that they were not looking at the sense, which Grotius desires. Nor if Christ is called 'only begotten' in that meaning, which Grotius desires, can anything be deduced from it to prove His generation from the Father; although he himself confesses that He is so called because He proceeded from God in a singular way, with these words of Justin added: 'God is the one called properly Son.' Item: 'The only proper Son to God has been begotten, being His Word and firstborn and power.' Nor does he rightly draw that 'from the Father' to 'glory,' since he himself acknowledges it can be referred to the word 'only begotten' by a construction which is 'according to the meaning': because in a derived noun there is the force of the verb. And the comma distinction demands this sense. Nor do those passages 2 Pet. 1:17 John 5:44. To this there are analogies, and all interpreters acknowledge that the only-begotten from the Father is spoken of here: not even excepting the Socinians in the Racovian version of the N.T. and elsewhere.

full of grace and truth] There is no need to interpose a parenthesis: for the Greeks are accustomed to construct the nominative with oblique cases, as we showed at Mark 6:40. And thus our author speaks in the Apocalypse: from Jesus Christ the faithful witness 1:5. See also the passage Eph. 3:17, where after 'of you' follows a nominative. Moreover, 'grace' and 'truth' are joined together below, 17, whence it appears that there is a tacit comparison with Moses, whose law is without grace and the gifts of the Spirit and full of shadows; the law is everywhere opposed to grace in Paul: but also to truth, Rom. 15:8, Heb. 9:24, where truth signifies the very solidity of things, which is sometimes also called the body; see also what is within 4:23. Here is also slaughtered the dream of the Gnostics, for whom 'truth' was something other than the 'Word' or Christ.

PART II. The testimony of John concerning Christ.

Latin:

V. 14. καὶ ὁ λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο] κὴ hic est αἰτιολογικὸν su- periorum. Ut λόγος nos homines ad divinam majestatem e- veheret ipse in imbecilla hac nostra humana natura se ostendit. Paulus ad 1. Tim. II. 16. Θεὸς ἐφανερώθη ἐν σαρκί. Nam σὰρξ ut dicere cœpimus infirmitatein & humilem statum consigni- ficat. Sic Ps. LXVI. 5. LXXVII. 39. & alibi. Conter Philipp. II. 6. 2. Gor. VIII. 9. Eodem spectat nomen filii hominis.

Reddit Grotius, in imbecilla hac nostra humana natura se ostendit, sed ea interpretatio talis est, quam nec ipsi Sociniani reprobant. Johannes vero non statum humilem aut infirmitatem significare hic vo- luit, sed ipsam ἐνσάρκωσιν: quemadmodum cum κτ σάρκα dicitur esse è semine Davidis Rom. I. 4. non in- dicatur secundum humilem statum, sed secundũ na- turam humanam inde ortum trahere. Status humi- lis consequens erat, idq; voluntarium τῆς ἐνσαρκώσεως το̃ λόγε, postquam assumsit humanam naturam: E- rat enim in forma Dei, atque inde libere se evacuavit gloria divina, formamque servi assumsit, Phil. II. 6. ut ordine naturæ præcesserit incarnatio, sequuta sit hu- miliatio; prior enim est humanæ naturæ assumtio ipso exinanitionis θεανθρωπίκ statu; Atque ideo de ipsa ἐνανθρωπήσεs, & ἐνσαρκώσει Patres, quorum hic sententiam laudat ipse Grotius, hæc accepere. Bene, inquit, Justinus: ἐπειδὴ κὴ δι’ ἡμᾶς ἄνθρωπος γέγονεν (ὁ λόγος) ὅπως κὴ τῶν παθῶν τῶν ἡμετέρων συμμέτοχος γενόμενος κὴ ἴασιν ποιήσηται. Origenes: ἀπ’ ἐκείνε ἤρξατο θεία κὴ ἀνθρω- πίνη συνυφαίνεσθαι φύσις, ἵν’ ἡ ἀνθρωπίνη τῇ πρὸς τὸ θειότερον κοι- νωνίᾳ γένηται θεία, ἐκ ἐν μόνῳ τῷ Ἰησᾶ, ἀλλὰ κὴ πᾶσι τοῖς μετὰ τὸ πιτεύειν ἀναλαμβάνεσι βίον ὃν Ἰησᾶς ἐδίδαξεν. Irenæus: Ver- bum, ait, unitum suo plasmati passibilem hominem factum. Idem alibi: εἰς τῦτο γὰρ ὁ λόγος ἄνθρωπος, ἵνα ὁ ἄνθρωπος χω- ρήσας τὸν λόγον κὴ τὴν ὑοθεσίαν λαβὼν ὑὸς γένηται Θεᾶ Tertullia- nus adversus Praxeam: Consequens est, ut sit caro factus intelligatur, dum sit in carne, & manifestatur, & videtur, & contrectatur per carnem.

κὴ ἐσκήνωσεν ἐν ἡμῖν] Habitavit. Nam sic & qui in cœlo ha- bitant σκηνο̃ν dicuntur Apoc. XII. 12. & XIII. 6. ἐν ἡμῖν re- cte vertas inter nos ut Luc. I. 29. sed illud notandum voce σκηνᾶν, quæ eadem sono & significatu est cum Hebræo שכן alludi ad conspicuam divinæ majestatis præsentiam quæ Chal- dæo paraphrastæ etiam כבוד שכינה: aut ad operationem sin- gularem, quorum utrumq; per שכן unde שכינה significa- ri notant Hebræorum Magistri, ut Maimonides duce dubi- tantium lib. I. c. XXV. Sic bene cohæret, quod sequitur.

κὴ ἐθεασάμεθα τὴν δόξαν ἀυτᾶ] Non fuit humilis ille status sine magnis & certis indiciis divinæ Majestatis, quæ כבוד He- bræis, ut Ex. XVI. 7. 10. XXIV. 16. 17. XXIX. 43. XXXIII. 18. 22. XL. 31. 32. Lev. IX. 6. 23. & alibi sæpe. Apparuit gutem hæc Christi δόξα non tantum in illa eximia transfor- matione in monte Taborio, in cujus narratione vocem δό- ξης usurpat Petrus 2. epist. I. 17. Sed & in iis, quæ circa pas- sionem in resurrectione & post eam, & in ascensu ad cœlum acciderunt: imo & in miraculis. Vide infra II. 11. XII. 23.

Ὡς μονογενᾶς παρὰ πατρὸς] Quod hic Chrysostomus & alii Græci vocant ὡς ὁριστικὸν id Hebræi appellant כף לאמתה quod Latine per ut recte transsertur. יחיד quod unigenam aut unicum significat, Græci, sensum respicientes, vertunt ἀ- γαπητὸν ut Gen. XXII. 2. 12. & 16 Jud. XI. 34. Ier. VI. 26. Amos IIX 10 Zach. XII. 10. aut ἀγαπώμενον. Prov. IV. 3. ποθη- τὸν Jud. XI. 34. Plutarchus Ὅμηρος ἀγαπητὸν ὑὸν ὀνομάζει, μο̃- νον τηλύγετον, τῦτεστι μὴ ἔχεσιν ἑτερον γονεῦσι μηδὲ ἕξεσιν ἐπιγεννημένον. In Odyslea secunda est μῦνος ἰὼν ἀγαπητὸς. Vid. Matth. III. 17. & Marc. XII. 6. Sic Solomonem filium suum unicum i. e. dilectissimum vocat David. I. Par. XXIX. 1. & ipse Solomo semet dicto loco Prov. IV. 3. Μονογενὴς ergo hic recte dicitur, Christus eo quem diximus significatu, & cui addi potest, quia singulari modo à Deo processit: Justino: ὁ μόνος λεγόμενος κυ- ρίως ὑός. Et alibi: μόνος ἴδιος ὑὸς τῷ Θεῷ γεγένηται λόγος αὐτᾶ ὑπάρχων κὴ πρωτότοκος κὴ δύναμις, κὴ τῇ βελῇ αὐτᾶ γενόμενος ἄν- θρωπος. Et in transcursu damnantur Gnostici qui alium facie- bant λόγον, alium μονογενῆ, alium Iesum, quod Iulianus con- tra Christianos scribens notare non omisit. Illud autem πα- ρὰ πατρὸς quanquam potest referri ad μονογενᾶς constructie- ne quæ est πρὸς τὸ σημαινόμενον, qualis est illa. Quid tibi illam tactio est? quia in nomine derivato inest vis verbi, malim ta- men referre ad δόξαν ob similem Petri locum, quem jam an- notare cœpimus; λαβὼν γὰρ παρὰ Θεᾶ πατρὸς τιμὴν κὴ δόξαν.

Sic δόξαν παρὰ τοῦ Θεοῦ infra hoc lib. V. 44. Notat Iustinus λό- γον etiam vocari δόξαν Θεοῦ & Hebræi, quod Rabbini vocant שכינה exponunt כבוד ut modo diximus. Luciani Mar- tyris confessio extat: ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ Θεοῦ ὀσίας καὶ βουλῆς καὶ δυνάμεως καὶ δόξης ἀπαραλλακτος εἰκών Vid. 2. Cor. III. 9.

Cum Græci יחיד vertunt ἀγαπητὸν Gen. XXII. 2. 12. 16. Jud. XI. 34. Jerem. VI. 26. Amos VIII. 10. Zach. XII. 10. non respicere eos sensum, quod vult Grotius, ipsa significatio vocis, quam unigenam aut unicum significare agnoscit, docere poterat. Nec si eo significatu Christus μονογενὴς dicitur, quod vult Grotius, quicquam inde ad generationem e jus à Patre probandam deduci potest; quam fateatur ta- men ipse, ita dici, quia singulari modo à Deo processit, additis hisce Justini: ὁ μὲν Θεὸς λεγόμενος κυρίως υἱός. Item: μόνος ἰδίως υἱὸς τῷ Θεῷ γεγέννηται λό- γος αὐτοῦ ὑπάρχων καὶ πρωτότοκος καὶ δύναμις. Neq; recte illud παρὰ πατρὸς trahit ad δόξαν, quum agnoscat ipse referri posse ad vocem μονογενοῦς con- structione quæ est πρὸς τὸ σημαινόμενον: quia in nomine derivato inest vis verbi. Et postulat commatica di- stinctio hunc sensum. Neq; illa loca 2. Pet. I. 17. Joh. V. 44. huic sunt analoga, & agnoscunt omnes inter- pretes unigenitum à Patre hic dici: ne quidem Soci- nianis exceptis in versione N. T. Racoviensi & alibi.

πλήρης χάριτος καὶ ἀληθείας] Non opus est parenthesin in- terponere: nam rectum cum obliquis construere & Græci solent, ut ostendimus ad Marcum VI. 40. Et sic noster lo- quitur Apocalypsi ἀπὸ Ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ ὁ μάρτυς ὁ πιστὸς I. 5. Vide & locum Eph. III. 17. ubi post ὑμῶν sequitur nominativus. Conjunguntur autem & infra χάρις & ἀλήθεια. 17. unde ap- paret tacitam esse comparationem cum Mose, cujus lex ser- me fine venia ac donis spiritus & plena umbris, legi gratia passim apud Paulum opponitur: sed & veritas Rom. XV. 8. Hebr. IX. 24. ubi veritas ipsam rerum soliditatem significat, quæ & corpus interdum vocatur, vide & quod intra IV. 23 Jugula- tur & hic Gnosticorum somnium quibus aliud erat ἀλήθεια quam λόγος aut Christus.

PARS II. Testimonium Iohannis de Christo.

## 1:15
V. 15. John bears witness concerning him] By the public confession of John himself he refutes those who, omitting Jesus, followed John, and wished to be called by his name. 'Bears witness' is in the present tense, because the authority of the testimony endured forever.

and cried out] An allusion to the prophetic predictions concerning John the Baptist.

of whom I said] I said it even before his baptism and now I repeat it before the multitude.

he who comes after me] We have already said that 'to come' is to proceed to the people for the sake of publishing a divine command.

he has become before me] He has been preferred before me, by divine destination, of course, because through him God willed to take away the sins of the world, to judge the world, Acts 2:22, 10:42. Thus Gen. 49:20, where Jacob says he preferred Ephraim to Manasseh, in the Greek it is 'he set Ephraim before Manasseh'.

for he was before me] Two things are to be noted here: First, 'first' for 'prior'; Aristophanes in the Birds: 'and he ruled the Persians first [prior to] Darius and Megabyzus'; below 15:18, 'he has hated me before [prior to] you', that is, 'prior'. Thus 1 John 4:19, 'he himself first [prior] loved us', that is, 'prior'. The second is that 'first' denotes not a precedence of time or place, but an eminence of dignity: In the book of Categories: 'the better and more honorable is thought to be prior'. In Metaphysics 4, ch. 11: 'that which excels in power is prior'. Ulpian on the Oration of Demosthenes against Leptines: 'first not in order but in dignity and authority'. Aristophanes in the Frogs in this sense: 'You think Sophocles prior to Euripides'. Latin grammarians note this regarding that line of Virgil: 'Who first [prior] from the shores of Troy', and, 'And first [prior] Machaon'. And regarding that of Terence: 'or because I am first [prior] with you', and that: 'Nothing prior or stronger'. But why Jesus is more worthy is clear from the above, because he is the only-begotten son; Matthew said 'he is mightier than I' 3:11, whom Mark 1:7 and Luke 3:16 followed.

These things are without doubt pleasing to the Socinians: whose glosses concerning the preexistence of the Son of God we have refuted in Section I, ch. III, IV. And although the word 'he who comes' may be referred by Cyril to the time of preaching, it is nevertheless more correctly explained by Augustine and Epiphanius as referring to his birth: because when Christ is called 'he who comes', his advent is always regarded: and thus it can be translated in the past tense: 'who when he came after me'. But that 'he who' Epiphanius has already denied that 'before me' denotes a more eminent degree of dignity, because we have proven that it implies priority of time, l. c. p. 86, as it is also explained by the Syrian and the Arab. Conf. Jud. I. 23. 1 Reg. III. 12. Marc. I. 2. Lud. de Dieu observed that it is nowhere taken as referring to dignity alone, responding to that passage Gen. XLVIII. 20: The primary sense there is not metaphorical, but literal. See what we have said in the cited place, where we also discussed the exceptions of Enjedinus.

We have also proven that the final clause, 'for he was before me,' is correctly explained with Augustine, Ambrose, and Cyril as referring to priority of time, l. c. p. 90, having likewise discussed the exceptions of Enjedinus, as well as those of Smalcius, which may be seen there.

Latin:

V. 15. Ἰωάννης μαρτυρεῖ περὶ αὐτοῦ] Ipsius Johannis publi- ca confessione eos refellit qui Johannem omisso Jesu secta- bantur, deq; ejus nomine dici se volebant. μαρτυρεῖ autem in præsenti, quia durabat in perpetuum auctoritas testimonii.

καὶ κέκραγε] Allusio ad Prophetica vaticinia de Johanne Baptista.

ὃν εἶπον] Dixi jam ante baptismum ejus & nunc coram multitudine repeto.

ὀπίσω μου ἐρχόμενος] Diximus jam, ἔρχεσθαι esse procedere ad populum, publicandi divini mandati causa.

ἔμπροσθέν μου γέγονεν] Prælatus mihi est, destinatione di- vina scilicet, quia per hunc Deus voluit tollere peccata mundi, judicare mundum Act. II. 22. X. 42. Sic Genes. XLIX. 20. ubi Jacobus dicit Ephraimum anteposuisse Manassi, in Græco est ἔθηκε τὸν Ἐφραὶμ ἔμπροσθεν τοῦ Μανασσῆ.

ὅτι πρῶτός μου ἦν] Duo hic notanda: Primum πρῶτος pro πρότερος Aristophanes avibus: ἦρξε δὲ Περσῶν πρῶτον Δαρείου καὶ Μεγαβύζου infra XV. 18. ἐμὲ πρῶτον ὑμῶν μεμίσηκεν, id est πρό- τερον. Sic prima Epist. IV. 19. αὐτὸς πρῶτος ἠγάπησεν ἡμᾶς, id est, πρότερος. Alterum est, quod πρῶτος non temporis aut lo- ci antegressum, sed dignitatis eminentiam notat: In libro Categoriarum: τὸ βέλτιον καὶ τιμιώτερον πρότερον δοκεῖ. In Me- taphysicis IV. c. XI. τὸ ὑπερέχον τῇ δυνάμει πρότερον. Ulpianus in Orationem Demosthenis in Leptinen: πρῶτον τῇ τάξῃ ἀλλὰ τῷ ἀξιώματι κὶ τῷ κυρῷ. Aristophanes ranis hoc sensu: Σοφοκλέα πρότερον οἴϊ Εὐριπίδου. Notant hoc Latini Gramma- tici ad illud Virgilii: Trojæ qui primus ab oris, &, Primusque Machaon. & ad Terentii illud; aut quia ego sum apud te pri- mus, & illud: Nihil prius aut fortius. Cur autem dignior Jesus, patet ex superioribus, quia filius unigenitus Mat- thæus dixit ἰσχυρότερός μου ἐστιν III. 11. quem secuti Marcus I. 7. & Lucas III. 16.

Socinianis grata hæc sine dubio sunt: quorum vero glossas retudimus de præexistentia Filii Dei Sect. I. c. III. IV. Etsi autem vox ὁ ἐρχόμενος à Cyrillo ad prædicationis tempus referatur, rectius tamen eadem ab Augustino & Epiphanio de nativitate ex- plicatur: quia cum Christus ὁ ἐρχόμενος dicitur; semper adventus ejus respicitur: & sic in præterito verti potest: qui cum post me venerit. Sed illud ἔμ- προσθέν με Epiphanius jam negavit dignitatis gra- dum eminentiorem notare, quod temporis priori- tatem inferre probavimus l. c. p. 86. uti etiam a Sy- ro & Arabe exponitur Conf. Jud. I. 23. 1. Reg. III. 12. Marc. I. 2. Nuspiam de dignitate sola accipi Lud. de Dieu observavit, ad locum illum Gen. XLVIII. 20. respondens: Primarius ibi sensus non est metapho- ricus, sed proprius. Vid. quæ diximus loco cit. u- bi exceptiones etiam Enjedini discussimus.

Postremum etiam membrum ὅτι πρῶτός με ἦν, cum Augustino, Ambrosio, Cyrillo recte de prioritate temporis exponi probavimus l. c. p. 90. discussis itidem Enjedini, ut & Smalcii exceptionibus, quæ ibi videantur.

## 1:16
Verf. 16. 'And of his fullness have we all received' shows the true use of the word 'fullness,' not as signifying some space above the heavens according to the Gnostics, but as 'the peak of the participation of the divinity,' as Origen speaks, as also Col. I. 19 and II. 9. Clemens Strom. II: 'And all the powers of the Spirit, being gathered together in one thing, fell into the same of the Son.' Moreover, this 'and' is to be connected with the preceding things that had come before the testimony of John was introduced, especially with those words 'full of grace and truth.' Conf. Eph. I. 5.

'And grace for grace.' This 'and' is explanatory. It is an elegance of the Holy Scriptures to place the same word in a contiguous passage with a different sense, and this is found in this very word 'grace' in Rom. VI. 15. Where in the first place 'grace' is a gift, in the second it is the benevolence with which God embraces us for Christ's sake, which the Apostle states more distinctly at Rom. XII. 6, 'gifts according to the grace,' and elsewhere without such an allusion, as Eph. III. 7, 'the gift of grace.' Therefore, the Evangelist signifies the gifts of the Holy Spirit freely granted by God to himself and others, the Apostles, and indeed to believers: for I would think that 'for grace' here is nothing other than חנם, that is, not for any merit, but out of mere goodness: which is thus expressed by 'for' (which particle corresponds to the Hebrew תחת), because it contains within itself the negation of price. Thus the Hebrew בגלל is sometimes translated as 'for,' as 'evil for evil' Jer. XI. 17, elsewhere 'grace' 1 Reg. XIV. 16, more often 'through' as Deut. XV. 10, Jer. XV. 4. & elsewhere.

Latin:

Verf. 16. καὶ ἐκ τῦ πληρώματος αὐτῦ ἡμεῖς πάντες ἐλάβομεν] verum usum ostendit vocis πληρώματος non ut secundum Gnosticos spatium aliquod super cæleste significet, sed ut τὴν ἀ- κρὴν μετοχῆς τῆς θεότητος, ut Origenes loquitur ut & Col. I. 19. & II. 9. Clemens Strom. II. πᾶσαι δὲ αἱ δυνάμεις τῦ πνεύματος (υνήθδην μὲν ἐν ἑνὶ πράγματι γενόμεναι συνέπεσαν εἰς τὸ αὐτὸ τ᾽ υἱοῦ. Est autem hoc συν connectendum cum superioribus, quæ præcesserant, antequam testimonium Johannis infereretur, præsertim cum illis πλήρης χάριτος κὶ ἀληθείας Conf. Eph. I. 5.

κὶ χάριν ἀντὶ χάριτος.] Est hic κὶ ἐξηγητικὸν Elegantia est sacrarum literarum vocem eandem contiguo loco ponere sensu alio, Et id in eadem hac voce χάριτος invenitur Rom. VI. 15. Ubi priori loco χάρις est donum, secundo benevolentia, qua nos propter Christum Deus complectitur, quod distinctius enuntiet Apostolus ad Rom. XII. 6. χερισματα κατὰ τὴν χά- ριν, & alibi sine tali allusione, ut Eph. III. 7, δωρεὰν τῆς χάρι- τος. Significat ergo Evangelista dona Spiritus S: sibi aliisq; Apostolis, imo & credentibus gratis à Deo concessa: nam ἀντὶ χάριτος nihil aliud his esse putem quam חנם, id est, non pro ullo merito, sed ex mera bonitate: quod ita per ἀντὶ (quæ particula respondet Hebræo תחת) effertur, quia continet in se negationem pretii. Sic בגלל Hebræum interdum ἀντὶ transfertur ut κακία ἀντὶ τῆς κακίας Jer. XI. 17. alibi χάριν 1. Reg. XIV. 16. sæpius διὰ ut Deut. XV. 10. Jer. XV. 4. & alibi.

## 1:18
Vers. 18. Θεὸν ὐδεὶς ἑώρακε πώποτε] I would think this is the sense: no one has lived so familiarly with God as to perceive his counsels, in which sense Paul said: Who has been a counselor to God, and who has known his mind? Rom. XI. 34. & Matthew: No one knows the Father except the Son, XI. 27. I am led to this also by a passage from Ecclesiasticus, which shows that it was, as it were, a proverb among the Hebrews, and indeed all the more so, because just as the word ἐξηγεῖται follows here, so the word ἐκδιηγήσεται follows there. The passage is XLIII. 35. τίς ἑ- ώρακεν αὐτὸν κέἐκδιηγήσεται; See what we have noted on the cited passage of Matthew. Our author also, or whoever it is in the 3rd epistle, wrote ὐχ ἑώρακε τ̃ Θεὸν, meaning he has not known. And below in chapter III. 32. ὅ ἑώρακε καὶ ἤκυσε, which he certainly knows.

ὁ μονογενὴς υἱὸς, ὁ ὢν εἰς τ̃ κόλπον τῦ πατρὸς) εἰς for ἐν is frequent in others and especially in these books: to be in the bosom is to be nearest and most intimate: it is said of spouses with one another, Deut. XXIIX. 54. 56; of friends, Luke XVI. 22, where we have spoken. See below XIII. 23; of other things, 2 Sam. XII. 3. Also this way of speaking, the bosom of the Father, wrongly usurped by the Gnostics, is here restored to its true and correct sense. See Irenaeus II. 7.

ἐκεῖνος ἐξηγήσατο] ἀπεκάλυψε. Matth. XI. 27. He revealed to the world the counsels of God hidden for so many centuries.

Latin:

Vers. 18. Θεὸν ὐδεὶς ἑώρακε πώποτε] Putem hunc esse sen- sum, nemo cum Deo ita vixit familiariter, ut ejus consilia pervideret, quo sensu Paulus dixit: Quis Deo consiliarius fuit & mentem ejus quis novit? Rom. XI. 34. & Matthæus: Ne- mo patrem novit nisi filius XI. 27. Adducor huc etiam loco Ecclesiastici, qui ostendit quasi proverbium fuisse apud He- bræos, & quidem eo magis, quia ut hic verbum ἐξηγεῖται se- quitur, ita ibi verbum ἐκδιηγήσεται. Locus est XLIII. 35. τίς ἑ- ώρακεν αὐτὸν κέἐκδιηγήσεται; Vide quæ ad dictum Matthæi locum notavimus. Noster etiam aut quisquis etiam est e- pist. III. ὐχ ἑώρακε τ̃ Θεὸν, posuit pronon novit. Et infra cap. III. 32. ὅ ἑώρακε καὶ ἤκυσε, quod certo novit.

ὁ μονογενὴς υἱὸς, ὁ ὢν εἰς τ̃ κόλπον τῦ πατρὸς) εἰς pro ἐν fre- quens & aliis & his maxime libris: in sinu esse est proxi- mum & intimum esse: dicitur de conjugibus inter se Deut. XXIIX. 54. 56. de amicis Luc. XVI. 22. ubi quæ diximus. Vide infra XIII. 23. de rebus aliis 2. Sam. XII. 3. Etiam hoc loquendi genus sinus Patris à Gnosticis male usurpatum ve- ro rectoque sensu hic donatur. Vide Irenæum II. 7.

ἐκεῖνος ἐξηγήσατο] ἀπεκάλυψε. Matth. XI. 27. Consilia Dei tot seculis abscondita mundo patefecit.

## 1:19
Vers. 19. καὶ αὕτη ἐσὶν ἡ μαρτυρία] This also is the testimony of John, not brought forth by chance, but in response to a legitimate interrogation.

Ἰυδαῖοι ἐξ ἱεροσολύμων] That is, the great Sanhedrin, whose seat was at Jerusalem, and whose concern was regarding a true and false Prophet. In a similar way, it is narrated that the Sanhedrin sent to Bar Kokhba to inquire who he claimed to be.

Ἱερεῖς κέ Λευίτας] They had sent the most learned of their assembly: for these men, whose living was from the public treasury, were more free to devote themselves to studies.

ἵνα ἐρωτήσωσιν αὐτὸν, σὺ τίς εἶ; He states the matter briefly, which is understood more fully from what precedes: For they did not ask who he was, that is, what office he performed, but also whether he was the Christ: which Nonnus correctly expresses: Μυστιπόλοι δ᾽ ἐρέεινον ὁμήλυδες ὀξέι μύθῳ, Τίς συ πέλεις, μὴ χρισὸς ἔφυς. It is, however, the custom of the Hebrews to express commands in direct speech, as Exod. III. 14. 2 Kings IV. 16.

Latin:

Vers. 19. καὶ αὕτη ἐσὶν ἡ μαρτυρία] Etiam hoc est testimo- nium Johannis non ex occasione prolatum, sed ad legiti- mam interrogationem.

Ἰυδαῖοι ἐξ ἱεροσολύμων] Id est Synedrium magnum, cujus consessus erat Hierosolymis, quorumque notio erat de vero & falso Propheta. Simili modo ad Barchochebam misisse Synedrium narratur percunctatum quein se diceret.

Ἱερεῖς κέ Λευίτας] Miserant doctissimos sui cœtus: nam hi quibus è publico victus erat liberius studiis vacabant.

ἵνα ἐρωτήσωσιν αὐτὸν, σὺ τίς εἶ; Compendio rem dicit quæ ex superioribus plenius intelligitur: Non enim interroga- runt, quis esset, id est, quo munere fungeretur, sed & an esset Christus: quod Nonnus recte exprimit: Μυστιπόλοι δ᾽ ἐρέεινον ὁμήλυδες ὀξέι μύθῳ, Τίς συ πέλεις, μὴ χρισὸς ἔφυς. Est autem mos Hebræorum mandata exprimere oratione directa, ut Exod. III. 14. 2. Reg. IV. 16.

## 1:20
Vers. 20. κέ ώμολόγησε κέ ὐκ ἠρνήσατο, καὶ ὡμολόγησε] We said above that the negation of the opposite is usually added to an affirmation to crush every exception. Phrases very similar to this are to be found in Job V. 17. 2 Kings XVIII. 36. Moreover, ὡμολόγησε is repeated so that it may be signified that he said the same thing two or three times with great constancy and asseveration: which was the more necessary because that false opinion had already invaded many, Luke III. 15. ὅτι ὐκ εἰμὶ ὁ χρισὸς] He professed that he was not that great Messiah who was expected around those times.

Latin:

Vers. 20. κέ ώμολόγησε κέ ὐκ ἠρνήσατο, καὶ ὡμολόγησε] Supra diximus negationem oppositi addi affirmationi solere ad o- mnem exceptionem elidendam. Locutiones huic persimiles reperire est Job. V. 17. 2. Reg. XVIII. 36. Repetitur autem ὡμολόγησε, ut significetur illum bis tervè idem magna con- stantia atq; asseveratione dixisse: quod eo magis erat neces- sariũ, quia multos jam illa falsa opinio invaserat, Luc. III. 15. ὅτι ὐκ εἰμὶ ὁ χρισὸς] Professus est se non esse magnum il- lum Messiam, qui circa ea tempora expectabatur.

## 1:21
V. 21. Ἠλίας εἶ σύ;] Sent down to earth from that place into which he was caught up. Those who ask this show that they do not know from what father or mother John was born, or they doubt it. See on Matth. XVI. 14.

ὐκ εἰμὶ;] In this sense, of course, in which he was being questioned.

Are you the prophet? The Greeks both read and emphasize the article. Wherefore I might think Jeremiah is understood, concerning whose return a certain rumor was wandering among the Jews. See at Matthew in the stated place. Thus 2 Macc. XV. 14. Jeremiah the prophet of God: it is no wonder therefore that this also is expressly denied by John.

Latin:

V. 21. Ἠλίας εἶ σύ;] In terras demissus ex eo loco in quem raptus est. Qui hoc interrogant ostendunt se nescire quo patre, qua matre natus esset Johannes, aut de eo dubitare. Vide ad Matth. XVI. 14.

ὐκ εἰμὶ;] Hoc nimirum sensu quo interrogabatur.

ὁ προφήτης εἶ σύ;] Græci articulum & legunt & urgent. Quare putem Jeremiam intelligi de cujus reditu rumor qui- dam inter Judæos vagabatur. Vide ad Matthæum dicto lo- co. Sic 2. Macc. XV. 14. Ἱερεμίας ὁ τῦ Θεῦ προφήτης: non mi- rum igitur & hoc diserte à Johanne negari.

## 1:22
Verse 22. Who are you? After the negative responses they wish to elicit an affirmative one, as to what he would call himself in regard to his office.

Latin:

Vers. 22. τίς εἶ;] Post negativas responsiones affirmativam volunt elicere qualem officio se diceret.

## 1:23
Verse 23. I am the voice of one crying. The direct phrasing would have been I am the one crying: but he wished to bring forward the very words of the Prophet Isaiah.

Make straight. The Syrian well translates it 'Level'. See what [I said] at Luke III. 5.

Latin:

Vers. 23. ἐγὼ φωνὴ βοῶντος] Recta locutio fuerat ἐγώ ὁ βοῶν: sed verba ipsa Prophetæ Esaiæ adferre voluit.

εὐθύνατε] Bene Syrus vertit Complanate. Vide quæ ad Luc. III. 5.

## 1:24
Verse 24. From the Pharisees. No wonder: for the greater part of the Sanhedrin was of his sect, as is to be seen in Acts XXIII. The Pharisees thought that no rite which was either commanded by God or

handed down by the elders should be omitted: wherefore they did not think that a baptism should have been added to their rites, unless perhaps by a Prophet. And they asked him and said to him. That is, they questioned him saying,

Latin:

Vers. 24. ἐκ τ̃ Φαρισαίων] Non mirum: major enim Syne- drii pars ejus erat sectæ, ut videre est Actor. XXIII. Pharisæi censebant nullum à se ritum qui aut à Deo præceptus aut à

majoribus esset traditus omitti: quare nec baptismum ad suos ritus addendum fuisse arbitrabantur, nisi forte à Propheta. καὶ ἠρώτησαν αὐτὸν καὶ εἶπον αὐτῷ] Id est interrogarunt dicentes,

## 1:25
Verse 25. Why then do you baptize? With such a solemn and public immersion, which has hitherto been unusual among the Jews: for the Pharisaic ablutions were of another kind: See Mark VII. They were expecting some universal baptism around the times of the Messiah from Zechariah XIII and other places.

In the Prophet Zechariah, therefore, there is a prophecy concerning Christ and his times, and also concerning Baptism: which Grotius denied regarding the place in Zechariah. Compare what we have said at that place.

Latin:

Vers. 25. τί ὖν βαπτίζεις;] Tam solenni ac publica mer- satione, quæ hactenus circa Judæos inusitata: nam ablutio- nes Pharisaiæ alterius erant generis: Vide Marcum VII. Baptismum aliquem universalem circa tempora Messiæ ex- spectabant ex Zachariæ XIII. locis que aliis.

In Propheta ergo Zacharia de Christo ejusque temporibus, nec non de Baptismo vaticinium ha- berur: quod negavit ad Zachariæ locum Grotius. Conf. quæ ad illum locum diximus.

## 1:26
Verse 26. With water. With water alone: to baptize with the Spirit belongs to him whose herald and minister I profess myself to be: which I do, [and] it is a part and beginning of the function commanded to me. See below in verse 33.

The Spirit is not to be separated from water in Baptism, because Baptism consists of water and the Spirit, John III. 5, without the Spirit it would be of no efficacy: And therefore St. John indeed distinguishes himself in this baptism of water, administered by him by the vigor of Prophetic prophecies, from Christ, who was already standing in their midst, as a minister from the Lord, i.e. I indeed, as it was foretold, baptize with water, but know that I am not that promised Messiah, but only his minister, but he himself is already standing in your midst, not to be expected for much longer, whose sandals' straps I am not worthy to untie: But that in this ministry of baptism St. John ascribes to himself only the dispensation of water, and excludes the Spirit from his Baptism, which he was administering, which the Calvinists also contend, does not appear from the text; nor can it be admitted in any way, because it is one and the same action by which Christ dispenses baptism through a minister; and whatever Baptism works, it is not the case that the action of Christ is one thing and that of the minister another, nor is the effect of each different: nor should the ministerial cause be opposed to the principal one in this, but subordinated to it: for the Holy Spirit or his grace is not granted immediately, but through the mediation of the ministry, and through the baptism which the minister dispenses, Acts II. 38.

As for the fact that in this place v. 33 Christ is said to baptize with the Holy Spirit, it refers to the outpouring of the Holy Spirit which took place on the feast of Pentecost, Acts II. 4. He baptized with fire and spirit, as is evident from the parallel passage Matth. III. 11. Some, and among them the blessed Wilh. Lyferus in his disputation on the Postils for the 4th Sunday of Advent, thesis 19, understand this passage, on account of the present tense word βαπτίζων, not as the future miraculous diffusion of the Holy Spirit, but as the present conjunction of water and the Holy Spirit, and that not only by reason of the fruit, but also of the essence, so that we are said to be baptized both with water and the Holy Spirit, and that in one baptism. But the parallel passage favors our explanation.

Latin:

Vers. 26. ἐν ὕδατι] Sola aqua: spiritu perfundere illius est, cujus ego me præconem ac ministrum profiteor: quod fa- cio, pars est & initium functionis ipsi mandatæ. Vide infra commate 33.

Non est sequestrandus Spiritus ab aqua in Ba- ptismo, quia Baptismus ex aqua & Spiritu constat Ioh. III. 5. sine Spiritu nullius futurus efficaciæ: Id- eoque distinguit quidem sese S. Johannes in hoc a- quæ baptismate, vigore vaticiniorum Prophetico- rum à se administrato, à Christo, qui jam in medio ipsorum stabat, ceu ministrum à Domino, q. d. Ego quidem, uti prædictum fuit, aqua baptizo, sed sciatis, me non esse illum promissum Messiam, sed tantum mi- nistrum ejus, ipsum vero jam stare in medio vestrum, non diu adhuc expectandum, cujus non sum dignus sol- vere corrigias calceamentorum ejus: Quod vero in hoc ministerio baptismi S. Johannes sibi solam a- quæ dispensationem adscribat, ac Spiritum à suo Baptismo, quem administrabat, secludat, quod Cal- viniani etiam contendunt, è textu non apparet; nec ullatenus admitti potest, quia una eademq; est actio, qua Christus per ministrum dispensat bapti- smum; & quicquid Baptismus operatur, non au- tem actio alia est Christi, alia ministri, neque alius utriusque effectus: nec opponi in eo debet, sed subordinari causa ministerialis principali: nam non immediate Spiritus S. vel gratia ejus concedi- tur, sed mediante ministerio, & per baptismum, quem minister dispensat, Act. II. 38.

Quod vero hoc in loco v. 33. Christus Spiritu S. baptizare dicitur, id respicit effusionem Spiritus S. quæ in festo Pentecostes facta est Actor. II. 4. cum igne & spiritu baptizavit, ut è loco parallelo Matth. III. 11. constat. Nonnulli & inter hos B. Wilh. Lyferus in disp. Postill. ad Dom. IV. Advent. th. 19. h. l. ob verbum præsens βαπτίζων non de futura miraculo- sa Spiritus S. diffusione, sed præsente aquæ & Spiritus S. conjunctione, idque non tantum ratione fructus, sed etiam essentiæ intelligunt, ut & aqua & Spiritu S. ba- ptizari dicamur, idque in uno baptismo. Sed paralle- lus locus nostræ favet explicationi.

## 1:27
Vers. 27. ὀπίσω ἐρχόμεν@ With preaching and baptism. The passage in Malachi III, 1 is referred to.

ὃς ἔμπροσθέν μου γέγονε] See above 15.

ὗ ἐγώ ἐκ εἰμὶ ἄξι@] See what [is said] regarding Matth. III. 11.

ἵνα λύσω] A despised thing. Gen. XIV. 22.

Τὸ ὑποδημαθ@] A noun of the genus, of which the sandal is a species, which Christ and the Apostles used.

Latin:

Vers. 27. ὀπίσω ἐρχόμεν@] Cum prædicatione & bapti- smo. Respicitur Malachiæ locus III, 1.

ὃς ἔμπροσθέν μου γέγονε] Vide supra 15.

ὗ ἐγώ ἐκ εἰμὶ ἄξι@] Vide quæ ad Matth. III. 11.

ἵνα λύσω] Rem contemptam. Gen. XIV. 22.

Τὸ ὑποδημαθ@] Nomen generis, cujus species sandalium, quo Christus & Apostoli utebantur.

## 1:28
Vers. 28. ἐν βηθαβαρᾷ] The Greeks with great consensus hand down that this reading is the older: nor does it seem to be doubted that it is the same place which is designated below X. 40. For what is here, ὅπου ἦν ὁ Ἰωάννης βαπτίζων, is there ὅπου ἦν ὁ Ἰωάννης τὸ πρῶ- τον βαπτίζων, namely, because after that time he baptized in Salim, in the desert, that is to say, as the other Evangelists speak. Moreover, in the stated passage Joh. X. it is in the Syriac בעברת דיורדנן which also follows the proper name in this place, to explain that πέραν τῶ Ἰορδάνε, since it is properly at the crossing of the Jordan, and that is בית עברה & בית עברח for it is frequently added to the names of a place among the Hebrews. That that place was so at the crossing of the Jordan, that it was across the Jordan, that is, in Perea, is gathered below c. XI. 7. and a map published by the Jews makes it manifest. The name seems to have been given from the history which is in Jos. III. 16. 17. where the word for crossing appears here. And from this and other arguments we conclude that the Syriac, as also the Arabic copy (for both in this place have בית עניה) [was] translated or corrupted from later Greek [copies]. Βηθανίᾳ which in

Josephus is read several times, but it does not pertain here. For it is pe- τ, perhaps from the fruit which grows there, whose name is בּתנים. Nor do I think that בּית־עֲרָבָה, which is Joshua XVIII. 22, or בּית־בּרָה, which is Judges VII, pertains here any more; the former of which is written incorrectly in Greek as βαιθαβαρὰ, when it ought to be written βαι- θαραβὰ, and the latter βαιθηρὰ when it should be read βαιθβηρά. However, some suspicion seems to underlie the place Bethabara. For where the people of God, coming from the desert, crossed into the promised land, there the testimony of John was published, as if making a crossing from the law into the heavenly kingdom. Moreover, we ought not to be surprised that in many Latin Codices Bethania is written instead of Bethabara, since it is frequent that a less known name is changed by scribes into a better known one, as can be seen in the Latin version: I Sam. VI. 6, Cant. II. 17, VI. 12, VIII. 1.

From this Grotian observation, both concerning the Syriac and Arabic copy, as well as the Latin Codices—which are also not very ancient, but translated from later Greek, or even corrupted, and one cannot safely rely on them, since frequent changes by scribes occur in them—it can be established how rashly Grotius often abandons the Greek Codices and prefers the Latin, Syriac, or Arabic ones to them. However, the received Greek reading is rightly retained here, even if it agrees with the Syriac, Arabic, and Latin, as well as with the observation of Epiphanius, that certain Greek autographs read Bethania here.

ὅπου ἦν ἰωάννης βαπτίζων] This phrase generally signifies a quasi-continuous act: where he was then accustomed to baptize.

Latin:

Vers. 28. ἐν βηθαβαρᾷ] Lectionem hanc vetustiorem esse, magno consensu Græci tradunt: Neq; videtur dubitandum, quin idem sit locus, qui infra designatur X. 40. Nam quod hic est, ὅπου ἦν ὁ Ἰωάννης βαπτίζων, ibi est ὅπου ἦν ὁ Ἰωάννης τὸ πρῶ- τον βαπτίζων, nimirum, quia post id tempus baptizavit in Sa- lim, in deserto scilicet, ut alii Evangelistæ loquuntur. Dicto autem loco Joh. X. est in Syriaco בעברת דיורדנן quod & hoc loco post nomen proprium sequitur, ad explicandum illud πέραν τῶ Ἰορδάνε, cum proprie sit in trajectu Jordanis, id autem est בית עברה & בית עברח nam nominibus lo- ci apud Hebræos frequenter additur. Eum autem locum ita fuisse ad trajectum Jordanis, ut trans Jordanem, id est, in Pe- ræa fuerit, colligitur infra c. XI. 7. & manifestum id facit ta- bula a Judæis edita. Videtur nomen inditum ex historia quæ est Jos. III. 16. 17. ubi vox trajectus hic apparet. Et hoc & a- liis argumentis colligimus, Syriacum, ut & Arabicum exem- plar (utrumque enim hoc loco, habet בית עניה) ex serio- ribus Græcis versum aut depravatum. Βηθανίᾳ quod apud

Josephum aliquoties legitur, huc non pertin et. Est enim pe- τ, à fructu forte, qui ibi nascitur, cui nomen בּתנים. Neque magis pertinere huc arbitror aut בּית־עֲרָבָה quod est Jo- suæ XVIII. 22. aut בּית־בּרָה quod est Judic. VII. quorum illud Græcè βαιθαβαρὰ male scribitur, cum scribi debeat βαι- θαραβὰ, & hoc βαιθηρὰ cum legendum sit βαιθβηρά. Videtur autem ὑπόνοια aliqua subesse loco Bethabara. Nam ubi Dei populus ex deserto veniens in terram promissam trajecit, ibi- dem editum est Johannis testimonium, quasi trajectum fa- ciens ex lege in regnum cœleste. Mirari autem non debe- mus, in multis Latinis Codicibus pro Bethabara scriptum Bethania, cum frequens sit, ut nomen minus notum in no- tius à librariis mutetur, ut videre est in Latina versione: I. Sam. VI. 6. Cant. II. 17. VI. 12. VIII. 1.

Ex hac observatione Grotiana, cum de Syriaco & Arabico exemplari, tum de Codicibus Latinis, quod & illa non adeo antiqua, sed ex serioribus Græcis versa, aut etiam depravata sint, neque his tuto niti liceat, quum frequentes in illis occurrant librariorum mutationes, constare potest, quam te- mere sæpe Grotius relinquat Codices Græcos, & iisdem præferat Latinos, Syros, vel Arabicos. Re- cte autem hic retinetur recepta Græca lectio, etsi Syro, Arabi & Latino, ut & Epiphanii consonet observationi, quod ἀυτόγραφα quædam Græca Bethaniam hic legerint.

ὅπου ἦν ἰωάννης βαπτίζων] Phrasis hæc plerunqve actum quasi continuum significat: ubi tum solebat baptizare.

## 1:29
V. 29. ἐρχόμενον πρὸς ἀυτὸν] By divine counsel, so that this testimony might be rendered before the people present, but the occasion of his arrival seems to have been that, just as before baptism, so then he wished to honor the preaching of John among the others.

ὁ ἀμνὸς τῦ Θεῦ] Most pleasing to God, being ἄμωμος καὶ ἄσπι- λος, 1 Pet. I. 18. It is an allusion to the Paschal lamb, Ex. XII. 15. Thus John incidentally shows that Jesus was not baptized for repentance.

ὁ ἄιρων τὴν ἁμαρτίαν τῦ κόσμε] The Hebrew נשׂא, to which the Greek ἄιρειν corresponds, can signify both the obtaining of pardon and the cleansing of souls. That I prefer the latter meaning here is supported by the passage 1 Pet. I. 18, where we are said to be redeemed from vain conversation (idolatry and other flagrant sins) by the blood of the immaculate lamb, by which, clearly, he gave both an example and a testimony of his doctrine. And the passage of this writer of ours, 1 Ep. I. 7, where, if any walk in the light, they are said to be cleansed by the blood of Christ from all sin, that is, by consideration of that dogma which he himself sanctioned by his death, to be drawn back from every kind of offense. Among the prophecies concerning the Messiah, this is also one, that he would be a teacher of the nations and a destroyer of idolatry. Concerning the word κόσμε we have spoken above. ἡ ἁμαρτία is the totality of sins, the body of sin, Rom. VI. 12.

This gloss is Socinianizing. Where Grotius could not show that ἄιρειν, when it corresponds to the word נשׂא and is joined to sin, denotes the cleansing of souls; in 1 Pet. I. 18 that word does not occur: nor are we said to be liberated there through the cleansing of souls, even if we are said to be redeemed from vain conversation, i.e., from the sins which we received by propagation from our parents. For the word ἐλυτρώθητε implies a redemption made by a price, not a cleansing; and the price is expressly added to these, because we are said to be redeemed not with gold and silver but with τι- μίῳ ἅιματι, precious blood: what has this to do with the cleansing of souls? For we follow in that carnal conversation not so much the tradition of our ancestors as the impulse and inclination of a corrupt nature, which also passes to us through paternal propagation, and can be called πατροπαράδοτος. And thus the connection of the Petrine text holds itself very well, as Beza explains: The greater the price by which you have been redeemed from the corruption of carnal life, the more you ought to fear, lest by chance, by returning to the corruption of vices, you offend the soul of your Redeemer. Add that sin is frequently put for the punishment of sin: and therefore we can be said to be redeemed from vain conversation, just as we are redeemed from the punishment of the same. But that interpretation, that we have been redeemed by the blood of the immaculate lamb from vain conversation, idolatry, and other flagrant sins, by which he gave both an example and a testimony of his doctrine, truly Socinianizes: because Christ redeemed us not by example and testimony, but by the price and merit of his blood: nor does his blood καθαριεῖ us (which is a sacrificial phrase) from sin, by consideration of that dogma which he himself sanctioned by his death, to be drawn back from every kind of offense, which is a gloss of the Socinians, even colder than the inventions of Crellius, especially in book 2 on the causes of the death of Christ, but which has expiated our sin, and by that expiation grasped through faith we are justified, and are held as cleansed in the judgment of God. Certainly not by example, not by doctrine confirmed by blood, but by the blood itself, which he shed for us, as that lamb prefigured by the sacrifices of the O.T., he redeemed us and cleansed us from sin. Concerning which, more fully in the refuted Socinianism. Thus also Grotius himself, when he asserted the satisfaction of Christ against Socinus, refuted that gloss in ch. VIII, p. 103. Indeed, even those passages which say we are redeemed from iniquity and vain conversation, such as Tit. II. 14 and 1 Pet. I. 18, pertain to the same thing, since it is most accepted that sin is put for the punishment of sin; and in the passage to Titus the added word καθαρί- ζειν, that is, to expiate, which we will explain below, and in the passage of Peter the mention of the lamb, that is, the victim, make this clear. That this redemption is ascribed to the death of Christ as its cause, since Scripture testifies everywhere, as Eph. I. 7, Rom. III. 24, Heb. IX. 12, not even Socinus could deny that. But how the death of Christ is the cause of redemption, that is the question. For we say that the death of Christ is the cause of redemption because it moved God to liberate us from punishment, but Socinus denies that very thing. And ch. X, p. 137. In the Epistle of John, however, it is altogether absurd to interpret καθαρίζειν as referring to the declaration of cleansing, and not to the cleansing itself, since a little later they are joined, ἀφιέναι & καθαρίζειν v. 9. The Apostle argues from things joined together: If you walk in the light, you have cleansing, that is, remission through the blood of Christ: because sins are not imputed to anyone walking in the light. The preaching of the Baptist, indeed, naming Christ the lamb who takes away the sins of the world, since it looks back to the expiatory sacrifices both of the Hebrews and of the Gentiles, as Socinus acknowledges, clearly does not permit us to interpret taking away sins otherwise than as taking away guilt. For this is what expiatory sacrifices did, but they did not abstract from sinning: as also p. 125. The places in which Christ is called a lamb look to the same thing. Nor would it matter much, even if they were not accustomed in the law to sacrifice lambs for sin. For even so it would have been permitted for holy men to name one animal for another, so that at once the comparison might consist in the general signification of an animal, and yet by naming a lamb rather than a ram or a goat, the innocence of the victim might be expressed. For this reason also Peter added ἀμώμου & ἀσπίλου, 1 Pet. 1:19, and it could at the same time, by a certain brevity of words, look back to the prophecy of Isaiah 53, in whose Greek interpretation there was the word ἀμνός, as appears in Acts 8:32. But furthermore it is clear that a lamb was used in expiating contaminations, Lev. 14:12, Num. 6:12, which contaminations indeed were so far equated to sin in the old law that they even received the name of sin. Whence also that lamb is said in both places to be offered for guilt or a transgression, and in the other place it is expressly added, because he sinned concerning a corpse, Num. 6:11. The effect also is to some extent the same. For the contaminated were not admitted to the society of the Jewish polity, except through such an expiation. Indeed, even the Paschal victim (which it is agreed was for the most part a lamb, Ex. 12:5) had something of an expiatory nature in its first institution. For God says that He, looking at its blood, would turn away from the Hebrews that destruction which they otherwise were going to have in common with the Egyptians (by whose imitation they had contaminated themselves), Exod. 12:13, Heb. 11:28. But also for sin, for instance, of a rash oath, the law shows that a lamb was accustomed to be offered, Lev. 5:4, 6. Moreover, when Christ is called a lamb, Peter shows that a sacrifice is signified, not only by saying we are redeemed by the blood of the lamb,

1 Pet. 1:10, 19. But also John in the Apocalypse in many places, and among others, where he says he was slain, Apoc. 5:6, 9, 12; 13:8. Now a sacrifice cannot be understood as anything other than for sin, because, as Peter testifies, it was redemptive. Such is the only sacrifice for sin. Whence it is more than manifest, when the Baptist said that Christ was the lamb who would take away the sins of the world, John 1:29, that it concerns sins there that are past, not future; and concerns the taking away of guilt through the obtaining of remission before God, but not through the ingeneration of faith. We have also treated of the word נשא there, and specifically of this passage, John 1:29. That phrase is likewise sacrificial: concerning which see Grotius, loc. cit., ch. 1, p. 9. The Hebrews, to signify that which the Latins call 'to pay the penalty,' have no phrase more accepted than this: 'to bear sin'; similar to which is the locution of the Latins, 'to pay for crimes,' that is, the punishments of crimes: 'If anyone shall not have informed against a blasphemer, he shall bear his sin,' Lev. 5:1. 'He who has uncovered the nakedness of his sister, let him bear his sin,' Lev. 20:17. Thus expiatory victims are said 'to carry the iniquities of those who offer them,' Lev. 10:17, because their blood is for the human soul, Lev. 17:11.

Latin:

V. 29. ἐρχόμενον πρὸς ἀυτὸν] Divino consilio, ut hoc testi- monium præsenti coram populo redderetur, sed occasio ad- ventus videtur fuisse, quod sicut ante baptismum, ita tunc prædicationem Johannis inter cæteros vellet cohonestare.

ὁ ἀμνὸς τῦ Θεῦ] Deo gratissimus, quippe ἄμωμος καὶ ἄσπι- λος, 1. Pet. I. 18. Allusio est ad agnum Paschalem. Ex. XII. 15. Sic obiter ostendit Johannes Jesum non in pœnitentiam baptizatum.

ὁ ἄιρων τὴν ἁμαρτίαν τῦ κόσμε] Potest נשׂא Hebræum, cui respondet Græcum ἄιρειν, & veniæ impetrationem significa- re, & animorum emundationem. Ut posteriorem signifi- cationem hic præferam, facit locus 1. Pet. I. 18. Ubi à vana conversatione (idolatria aliisque flagitiis) redempti dici- mur agni immaculati sanguine, quo scilicet doctrinæ suæ exemplum simul & testimonium dedit. Et hujus nostri scri- ptoris locus 1. Ep.I. 7. ubi, si qui in luce ambulant, dicuntur emundari sanguine Christi ab omni peccato, id est confi- deratione ejus dogmatis, quod ipse morte sua sanxit, ab o- mni genere delictorum retrahi. Inter vaticinia de Messia & hoc est, eum fore doctorem gentium & idololatriæ de- structorem. De voce κόσμε supra diximus. ἡ ἁμαρτία est peccatorum universitas, corpus peccati, Rom. VI. 12.

Glossa hæc est Socinizans. Ubi ἄιρειν, cum respon- det voci נשׂא, & peccato jungitur, animorum emen- dationem notet, ostendere Grotius non potuit 1. Pet. I. 18. vox illa non occurrit: neq; liberati ibi dicimur per animorum emundationem, etsi à vana conversa- tione, h. e. à peccatis, quæ per propagationem à pa- rentibus accepimus redemti dicamur. Verbum e- nim ἐλυτρώθητε redemptionem pretio factam infert, non emundationem; & additur his diserte pretium, quia redemti dicimur non auro & argento sed τι- μίῳ ἅιματι pretioso sanguine: quid hoc ad emunda- tionem animorum? Sequimur enim in carnali illa conversatione non tam majorum nostrorum tradi- tionem, quam naturæ corruptæ impetum, & incli- nationem, quæ ad nos etiam transit per paternam propagationem, & πατροπαράδοτος dici pot- est. Et ita συνέχεια textus Petrini sese optime ha- bet, exponente Beza: Quanto majus est pretium, quo redempti estis corruptione vitæ carnalis, tanto amplius timere debetis, ne forte ad corruptelam vitio- rum revertendo, animum vestri Redemtoris offendatis. Adde quod peccatum pro pœna peccati frequenter ponatur: ideoque à vana conversatione redemti dici possumus, qua à pœna ejusdem redemti sumus. Illa vero interpretatio, quod à vana conversatione, idololatria aliisque flagitiis sanguine redemti simus a- gni immaculati, qua doctrinæ suæ exemplum simul & testimonium dedit, vere Socinizat: quia non exem- plo, & testimonio, sed pretio & merito sanguinis sui per nos redemit Christus: neq; sanguis ejus καθαριεῖ nos (quæ phrasis sacrificalis est) à peccato, qua con- sideratione ejus dogmatis, quod ipse morte sua sanxit, ab omni genere delictorum retrahemur, quæ glossa Socinianorum, Crellii imprimis lib. 2. de causis mor- tis Christi, commentis adhuc frigidior est, sed quæ peccatum nostrum expiavit, eaque expiatione per fidem apprehensa nos justificamur, & mundi in judicio Dei habemur. Non sane exemplo, non doctrina sangui- ne confirmata, sed sanguine ipso, quem pro nobis, ut agnus ille, sacrificiis V. T. præfiguratus, effu- dit, nos redemit, & mundavit à peccato. Quo de in Socinismo profligato fusius. Ita & Grotius ipse, cum adversus Socinum satisfactionem Christi as- seruit, glossam illam profligavit c. VIII. p. 103. Quin & illi loci, qui nos ab iniquitate & vana conversatione dicunt redemtos, ut Tit. II. 14. & 1. Pet. I. 18. eodem pertinent, cum peccatum pro peccati pœna poni sit rect- ptissimum: idq́; in loco ad Titum addita vox καθαρί- ζειν, id est, expiare, quam infra explicabimus, & in Pe- tri loco agni, hoc est, victimæ mentio apertum faciunt. Hanc redemtionem morti Christi, tanquam causæ, ad- scribi, cum passim testetur Scriptura, ut Ephes. I. 7. Rom. III. 24. Hebr. IX. 12. ne id quidem inficiari po- tuit Socinus. Sed quomodo causa redemtionis sit mors Christi id est, de quo quæritur. Nos enim ideo causam redemtionis esse mortem Christi dicimus, quod ea Deum moverit, ut nos à pœna liberaret, id ipsum vero negat Socinus. Et c. X. p. 137. In Epistola autem Johannis omnino absurdum est, καθαρίζειν de decla- matione mundationis, non de ipsa mundatione inter- pretari, cum paulo post jungantur ἀφιέναι & καθαρί- ζειν v. 9. Argumentatur Apostolus à conjunctis: Si in luce ambuletis, habetis mundationem, hoc est, re- missionem per sanguinem Christi: quia nemini in luce ambulanti imputantur peccata. Bapistæ vere præ- dicatio, Christum agnum nominantis, qui mundi pec- cata tollat, cum sacrificia expiatoria respiciat tum Hæbræorum, tum Gentium, agnoscente Socino, plane non permittit nos tollere peccata aliter interpretari, quam reatum tollere. Hoc enim faciebant expiatoria sacrificia, non autem abstrahebant à peccando: ut & p. 125. Eodem respiciunt loci, in quibus Christus agnus dicitur. Neque multum ad rem faceret, etiamsi non so- liti essent in lege agni pro peccato immolari. Nam et- iam sic licuisset viris sanctis pro pecude pecudem alte- ram nominare, ut simul & in generali pecudis signi- ficatione comparatio consisteret, & tamen agno potius quam ariete, aut capra nominata innocentia victimæ exprimeretur. Ideo enim & Petrus addidit ἀμώμου & ἀσπίλου, 1. Petr. I. 19. potuitq́; simul & quodam verbo- rum compendio respici ad vaticinium Es. LIII. in cu- jus interpretatione Græca erat vox ἀμνᾶ, ut apparet Act. VIII. 32. Verum insuper liquet, agnum in conta- minationibus expiandis fuisse usurpatum Levit. XIV. 12. Num. VI. 12. quæ quidem contaminationes in lege veteri peccato eousq́; æquabantur, ut & peccati no- men acciperent. Unde & agnus ille in reatum sive de- lictum offerri utrobiq; dicitur, & altero loco diserte additur, quia peccavit circa cadaver, Num. VI. 11. Effectus quoque idem aliquatenus. Nam contaminati non admittebantur ad societatem πολιτείας Judaicæ, nisi per talem expiationem. Quin & Paschalis victi- ma (quam plerumq́; agnum fuisse constat, Ex. XII 5.) in prima institutione aliquid habuit expiatorii. Ait enim Deus, se respicientem ad ejus sanguinem aversu- rum ab Hebræis id exitium, quod alioqui cum Ægyptiis (quorum imitatione se contaminaverant) habituri e- rant commune, Exod. XII. 13. Hebr. XI. 28. Sed & pro peccato puta, temerarii juramenti, agnam of- ferri solitam ostendit lex, Lev. V. 4. 6. Agnus autem cum dicitur Christus, sacrificium notari non tantum Petrus ostendit, redemptos nos dicens agni sanguine,

1. Petr. I. 10. 19. sed & Johannes in Apocalypsi multis locis, atque inter cæteros, ubi mactatum eum dicit Apoc. V. 6. 9. 12. XIII. 8. Sacrificium autem aliud, quam pro peccato, intelligi non potest, quia, Petro teste, fuit redemtorium. Tale est solum sacrificium pro peccato. Unde plusquam manifestum est, cum dixit Baptista, Christum esse agnum, qui auferret mundi peccata, Joh. I. 29. de peccatis ibi præteritis agi, non de futuris; & de auferendo reatu per remissionis impetrationem apud Deum, non autem per fidei ingenerationem. De verbo נשא ibi etiam egimus, & speciatim de hoc loco Joh. I. 29. Phrasis illa itidem sacrificialis est: de qua Grotius loc. cit. cap. I. p. 9. Hebræi, ut significent id, quod Latini dicunt, pœnas pendere, nullam habent phrasin magis receptam, quam hanc, ferre peccatum: cui similis est Latinorum locutio, luere delicta, hoc est, delictorum supplicia: Si quis blasphemum non indicaverit, feret peccatum ipsius, Lev. V. 1. Qui nuditatem sororis suæ retexit, peccatum suum ferto, Levit. XX. v. 17. Sic expiatoriæ victimæ dicuntur, portare iniquitates offerentium, Lev. X. 17. quia sanguis ipsarum est pro anima humana Lev. XVII. 1.

## 1:30
Verse 30. This is he of whom I said, After me comes] See above, com. 15.

Latin:

Vers. 30. ὗτός ἐστι περὶ ὗ ἐγὼ εἶπον· ὀπίσω με ἔρχεται] Vide supra com. 15.

## 1:31
Verse 31. And I knew him not] I think the true interpretation is: I did not know that the Messiah was the expiator of the world and the giver of the Holy Spirit on earth, before God, when he enjoined the command of baptism upon me, both revealed this to me and at the same time designated the person by a sign, namely, that he was the Messiah upon whom I was eventually to see the dove sent from heaven resting.

Others more correctly explain it concerning the knowledge of the vision, as is evident from the following verse: 'I therefore saw.' John certainly knew that the Messiah was in the world, whom, while still enclosed in the womb, he had greeted with a joyful leap: concerning whom he had undoubtedly been taught by Zechariah and Elizabeth, his parents, and other faithful ones: but since he had not yet seen him face to face, he was to be pointed out to him here for the first time, so that he might not err in pointing him out with the same finger. Heinsius and Tarnovius understand it concerning the knowledge of the office of Christ, but it is not to be believed that John was destitute of that when he had already testified concerning Christ several times.

that he might be made manifest to Israel] The baptism was therefore enjoined upon me, so that those whom I baptized, having been instructed concerning repentance, I might send the same to Jesus to receive the most complete instruction, the certainty of pardon, and the Holy Spirit, Acts 19:4. Φανεροῦσθαι is to become known with one's own quality. See below, 7:4; 21:1.

That manifestation took place through the ministry of John, who gave the knowledge of salvation to the people, which consists in the remission of sins, Luke 1:77, not only did he refer them to Christ, so that they might obtain it there. They had, therefore, sufficient instruction from John, they had the certainty of pardon, they had also the Holy Spirit, even if they knew nothing of those extraordinary gifts which began in the solemn outpouring of the Holy Spirit, Acts 2, Acts 19:4.

I came] Sent by God to show myself to the people, as we treated of that voice above.

Latin:

Vers. 31. κ᾿ ἐγὼ ὐκ ἤδειν ἀυτὸν] Veram interpretationem puto, Messiam mundi expiatorem & donatorem Spiritus S. in terris esse, ego nesciebam, antequam Deus mihi, cum baptismi mandatum mihi injungeret, & hoc revelaret, & simul personam indicio designaret, nempe eum esse Messiam, cui visurus aliquando essem supersedentem columbam cœlitus missam.

Rectius alii exponunt de notitia visionis, ut è versu sequenti patet: Ego igitur vidi. Noverat utique Johannes, Messiam in mundo esse, quem in utero adhuc conclusus læto saltu exceperat: de quo à Zacharia, & Elisabetha, parentibus suis, aliisque fidelibus, sine dubio, edoctus erat: sed quum nondum facietenus viderit, hic primum ei monstrandus erat, ut ne in eodem digito demonstrando aberraret. Heinsius & Tarnov. de notitia officii Christi justa intelligunt, sed eà tum destitutum fuisse Johannem, cum aliquoties jam de Christo testatus esset, credendum non est.

ἵνα φανερωθῇ τῷ Ἰσραὴλ] Baptismus ideo mihi injunctus est, ut, quos de pœnitentia institutus baptizarem, eosdem ad accipiendam institutionem plenissimam, certitudinem veniæ & Spiritum S. ad Jesum mitterem, Act. XIX. 4. Φανεροῦσθαι est innotescere cum sua qualitate. Vid. inf. VII. 4. XXI. 1.

Φανέρωσις illa per ministerium Johannis fiebat, qui dedit cognitionem salutis populo, quæ consistit in remissione peccatorum, Luc. I. 72. non solum remisit ad Christum, ut ibi eam consequerentur. Habebant ergo sufficientem institutionem à Johanne, habebant certitudinem veniæ, habebant & Spiritum S. etsi de donis illis extraordinariis, quæ in solemni effusione S. S. ceperunt, Actor. II. nihil scirent, Act. XIX. 4.

ἦλθον] Missus à Deo me ostendi populo, ut de ea voce supra egimus.

## 1:32
V. 32. Descending as a dove] See at Matt. 3:16.

remained upon him] In him the Spirit rested, to be given to no one greater thereafter, indeed not to anyone except through him.

Latin:

V. 32. Καταβαῖνον ὡσεὶ περιστερὰν] Vide ad Matth. III. 16.

ἔμεινεν ἐπ᾿ ἀυτὸν] In illo acquievit Spiritus, nemini posthac majori dandus, imo nec cuiquam nisi per ipsum.

## 1:33
Verse 33. And I knew him not] A repetition of what was said above, which places the matter clearly beyond doubt.

he said to me] When he gave the command to baptize.

Latin:

Vers. 33. κ᾿ ἐγὼ ὐκ ἤδειν ἀυτὸν] Repetitio supra dicti, quæ rem plane extra dubium ponit.

ἐκεῖνός μοι εἶπεν] Cum mandatum baptizandi daret.

## 1:34
Vers. 34. Μεμαρτύρηκα] And I have testified and I testify: after the Hebrew manner, in which the word of the past tense also signifies a permanent act.

ὁ ὑὸς τοῦ Θεοῦ] That most beloved one, that most similar one, finally the only-begotten. The Hebrews also call the שכינה, i.e., the radiance of God.

PART III. The bringing of certain disciples to Jesus.

Latin:

Vers. 34. Μεμαρτύρηκα] Et testatus sum & testor: More Hebræo, quibus vox præteriti etiam permanentem actum significat.

ὁ ὑὸς τοῦ Θεοῦ] Ille dilectissimus, ille simillimus, unigenitus denique. Etiam Hebræi שכינה i. e. τὸ ἀπάυγασμα Θεοῦ vocant.

PARS III. Discipulorum quorundam ad Iesum adductio.

## 1:35
Vers. 35. εἱστήκει] Intent upon his duty.

Latin:

Vers. 35. εἱστήκει] Muneri suo intentus.

## 1:36
Vers. 36. ἐμβλέψας] With eyes intent upon him.

Latin:

Vers. 36. ἐμβλέψας] Intentis in eum oculis.

## 1:38
Vers. 38. Λέγει ἀυτοῖς, τί ζητεῖτε;] Basil: only desire, and God meets you halfway,

He who is the searcher of human hearts, says Chrysostom in this place, he who aptly looks into our thoughts, he asks, not that he may know (for he knows) but that by asking he may bind them to himself and render them familiar, and more attentive, and show that he deems them worthy of his conversation. The thing itself taught them to seek Christ, because they were following Christ, yet he himself asks: What are you seeking? As if he were to say, what are you seeking in me, or what are you seeking me for, what is the cause that you are seeking me? We are accustomed to seek that which we have lost, or also that which we otherwise desire, which we believe to be pleasing, useful, or necessary to us; we do not seek unpleasant and adverse things, but what was more desired and sought after for so many centuries by so many and such great men, by Patriarchs, by Judges, Kings, Leaders, Prophets, by all the Saints of the Old Testament, than that Lamb of God, whom that boundary of the Old and New Testament, holy John, was now pointing out with his finger as present.

Facit] Doubtless they had learned from John the Baptist that this was he from whom the mysteries of the heavenly kingdom were to be drawn.

Latin:

Vers. 38. Λέγει ἀυτοῖς, τί ζητεῖτε;] Basilius: μόνον θέλησον, καὶ Θεὸς προαπαντᾷ,

Qui humanorum cordium scrutator est, ait Chry- sostomus in. h. l. qui cogitationes nostras apte intue- tur, is interrogat, non ut sciat (scit enim) sed ut ro- gando eos sibi devinciat & familiares reddat, atque attentiores, seque suo eos dignari colloquio ostendat. Quærere eos Christum res ipsa docebat, quia Christum sequebantur, quærit tamen ipse: Quid quæritis? quasi dicat, quid in me quæritis, aut quid me, quid causæ, quod me quæritis? Quærere id solemus, quod amisimus, vel etiam quod alias de- sideramus, quod gratum nobis, utile, aut necessa- rium credimus, ingrata & adversa non quærimus, at quid magis desideratum expetitumque fuit tot seculis à tot tantisque viris, à Patriarchis, à Judici- bus, Regibus, Ducibus, Prophetis, Sanctis omni- bus Veteris Testamenti, quam agnus ille Dei, quem nunc præsentem digito demonstrabat Limes ille Vet. & Nov. Test. sanctus Johannes.

Facit] Nimirum ex Johanne Baptista didicerant hunc esse, à quo haurienda essent regni cœlestis mysteria.

## 1:39
V. 39. πῦ μένεις] Where are you staying? For thus the word μένειν is taken in ch. II. 12 and elsewhere. These two did not wish to be hearers of Jesus in just any way, but as more intimate ones, of closer admission,

Latin:

V. 39. πῦ μένεις] Ubi diverteris? Sic enim vox μένειν sumitur c. II. 12. & alibi. Volebant hi duo non quovis modo audi- tores esse Jesu, sed intimioreis, interioris admissionis,

## 1:39
Verse 39. τὴν ἡμέραν ἐκείνην. ὥρα ἦν ὡς δεκάτη) The sense is that they did not depart from there on that day, and consequently they stayed there overnight, because it was already late. See Luke 24:29.

Latin:

Vers. 39. τὴν ἡμέραν ἐκείνην. ὥρα ἦν ὡς δεκάτη) Sensus est eo die inde non discesserunt, ac proinde ibidem pernoctarunt, quia jam serum erat. Vide Luc. XXIV. 29.

## 1:40
V. 40. ἔρχεσθε & ἴδετε. He did not designate the place lest they should have need to investigate, he did not put it off to the time of seeing lest he should disappoint their desire. He did not send them to their own teacher John, in whose school they were being formed, lest he should seem to reject those coming to himself, the supreme Master; but he ordered them to come and see immediately, so that he might not neglect any opportunity for teaching, and might satisfy their desire abundantly.
