He bids them come, although it was the tenth hour, i.e., from the rising of the sun, and evening was approaching, so that he might detain them through the night, and have the opportunity to instruct them all the more richly. While the sun was setting, the never-setting Sun of righteousness was eager to rise for them, because he rejoices as a giant to run his course, Ps. XIX. 6. They did not wish to be troublesome as evening was approaching, therefore they were asking about the dwelling in which he was staying, which was the house of either a kinsman or some other friend, so that they might be able to approach him the next day, and be more fully informed from his familiar conversation. But Christ does not put off the conversation to the following day, or some other more convenient time; but he takes them to himself immediately. Concerning which Chrysostom says in this place: Christ, he says, does not teach the house, but entices those following, showing that he had already received them into his own; he did not say, therefore, that it was unseasonable for them to go to him, but come, he says, he does not say, you will hear tomorrow if you wish, nor did he send them away then, but addresses them as friends bound by long acquaintance. Nor indeed does he only permit them access, but he also promises a vision. Come and see. For he does not only want them to see the place where he is staying, but at the same time gives them hope that they are going to see that which they were seeking. See what you so greatly desire, and by desiring seek. See the most longed-for food of your eyes and souls, see what Kings, what Prophets longed to see, but did not see, Luke 10:24. And since other senses are also usually included with the word for seeing, hearing is certainly not excluded here, because they longed greatly to hear him; conversation and society are not excluded, in which the highest joy was situated, as John testifies, 1 Epist. 1:1. For to see, in the phraseology of Scripture, is to have someone present, to enjoy his appearance and conversation, Acts 8:39, Rom. 1:11. In which way we are also said to see God, Matt. 5:8, Heb. 12:14, and to see the day of Christ, John 8:56, is nothing other than to enjoy his coming and benefits. Finally, knowledge is also noted; see, that is, know, since to see is sometimes the same as to experience and to know, Ps. 34:9, 71:30, Heb. 3:9, 11:5. But Christ immediately takes up disciples for two reasons, as Cyril observes in book 2 on John, ch. 9: first, to teach that no delay is to be praised in seeking good things, since the retardation of utility always brings detriment; second, to show that it is not enough if one has learned where Christ's house, the Church, has been founded, but [it is necessary] if one has come into it through faith and has seen with a fervent spirit what is mystically performed within it. Without doubt, however, that conversation with Christ was most sweet, during which that time was spent in most pleasant dialogues and most wholesome instructions. What a blessed day they had spent, says Augustine in book 2 on ch. 1 of John, what a blessed night! Who is there who can tell us what they heard from the Lord? Let us also build in our own heart and make a house, to which He may come and teach us, and converse with us. These are the words of Augustine.

Latin:

V. 40. ἔρχεσθε & ἴδετε. Non designavit locum ne investigare opus haberent, non distulit in vilen- di opus ne desiderium eorum destitueret. Non misit ad Doctorem proprium Johannem, in cujus schola formabantur, ne ad sese Magistrum sum- mum, venientes reprobare videretur; sed statim eos venire ac videre jussit, ut nullam docendi occa- sionem negligeret, eorumq; desiderio affatim sa- tisfaceret. Venire jubet, licet hora esset decima, ab ortu sc. Solis, & immineret vespera, ut eos per no- ctem detineret, atque eo uberius informandi occa- sionem haberet. Dum Sol occidebat, nunquam occidens Sol justitiæ ipsis oriri gestiebat, quia ad currendum viam ut Gigas exultat Pf. XIX. 6. No- lebant illi molesti esse imminente vespera, ideo de habitatione, in qua morabatur, quæ sive consan- guinei sive amici cujusdam alterius domus fuit, quærebant, ut postero die ipsum accedere, & è colloquio ejus familiari plenius informari possent. At Christus non rejicit colloquium in sequentem diem, aliudve commodius tempus; sed confe- stim adsumit eosdem. Quo de Chrysost. in h. l. Christus, inquit, domum non docet, sed allicit se- quentes, ostendens, jam in suos accepisse; non dixit igitur intempestivum esse, ut ad se proficiscantur, sed venite, inquit, non dicit, audietis cras si quid vultis, neq; tunc missos fecit, sed tanquam amicos longa de- vinctos consuetudine alloquitur. Nec vero tantum accessum ipsis permittit, sed etiam, visionem pro- mittit. Venite & videte. Non enim solum vult ut videant locum ubi maneat, sed spem simul facit, quod visuri sint id, quod quærebant. Videte, quod tantopere desideratis, & desiderando quæritis. Videte oculorum animorumque vestrorum pabu- lum exoptatissimum, videte quod Reges, quod Pro- phetæ videre gestierunt, sed non viderunt, Luc. X. v. 14. & cum videndi voce comprehendi soleant etiam a- lii sensus, non excluditur sane hic auditus, quia au- dire maximopere ipsum gestiebant, non excludi- tur conversatio & societas, in qua gaudium sum- mum situm erat, teste Johanne 1. Epist. I. 1. Videre enim phrasi scripturæ est, aliquem præsentem ha- bere, ejus aspectu & colloquio frui, Act. VIII. 39. Rom. I. v. 11. Quo pacto etiam Deum videre dici- mur, Matth. V. 8. Ebr. XII. 14. & diem Christi videre Job. VIII. 56. nihil aliud est, quam frui ejus adventu & beneficiis. Deniq; notatur etiam cognitio; vide- te, id est, cognoscite, cum videre idem quandoq; sit, quod experiri & cognoscere, Ps. XXXIV. 9. LXXI. 30. Ebr; III. 9. XI. 5. Assumit autem illico Christus di- scipulos duabus de causis, ut observat Cyrillus l. 2. in Joh. c. 9. primo ut doceat nullam esse in quæren- dis bonis moram laudandam, cum utilitatis retardatio semper adferat detrimentum, deinde ut ostendat, non sufficere, si quis ubi Christi domus, Ecclesia fundata sit didicerit, sed si per fidem in eam venerit & quæ mysti- ce in ipsa peraguntur fervente animo viderit. Sine dubio autem suavissima fuit illa cum Christo conversatio, qua dulcissimis colloquiis, sa- luberrimisque instructionibus tempus istud exa- ctum fuit. Quam beatum diem duxerant, ait Augu- stinus lib. 2. in c. 1. Joh. quam beatam noctem! quis est, qui nobis dicat, quid audierunt illi a Domino? Æ- dificemus & nosmetipsi in corde nostro & faciamus domum, quo veniat ille & doceat nos, colloquatur no- bis. Hæc Augustinus.

## 1:40
Verse 40. ἡ. Ἀνδρέας) The Syriac does not poorly construe that ἡ with ὡς which follows.

Most people, along with Chrysostom and Theophylact, believe that the other disciple was St. John himself, because John is accustomed to suppress his own name when he narrates something about himself, and he relates all the circumstances here as if he had been present at those acts and had observed everything with his own eyes. Epiphanius, in Heresy 51, thinks it was either John or his brother James.

Latin:

Vers. 40. ἡ. Ἀνδρέας) Illud ἡ cum ὡς quod sequitur non male construit Syrus.

Alterum discipulum fuisse ipsum S. Johannem, pleriq; cum Chrysostomo & Theophylacto censent, quod Johannes nomen suum subticere soleat, cum de se aliquid narrat, omnesque circumstantias hic ita referat, ac si actibus illis interfuerit, & omnia o- culis usurparit. Epiphanius Hæref. LI. aut Johan- nem, aut Jacobum fratrem ejus fuisse, arbitratur.

## 1:41
Verse 41. εὗτο πρῶτος) That is, πρότερον, as above 15, prior, that is, to his other companion. The Syriac and Nonnus expressed this sense with an adverb in the same sense.

Latin:

Vers. 41. εὗτο πρῶτος) Id est, πρότερον, ut supra 15. prior scilicet altero suo comite. Adverbio hunc sensum ex- pressit Syrus & Nonnus sensu eodem.

## 1:42
εὑρήκαμεν τὸν Μεσσίαν) משיח המלך the Messiah, that King, as the Jews used to speak. Andrew says this because he had found the teachings of Jesus to be in agreement with those things which John had preached about Him. Peter was among those who were awaiting the consolation and redemption of Israel, as it is said in Luke 2:25, 38, and the Kingdom of God, Mark 15:43. Therefore, no news could have come to him that was more joyful.

When the disciples of John had received the talent, they immediately return it multiplied to the Lord, says Cyril. Therefore, Andrew briefly and in summary saved his brother Peter, such a great matter having been signified; we have found, he says, the Messiah, like a treasure hidden in a field or a gem of the greatest value. For this word 'we have found,' according to Chrysostom, belongs to a soul that most desires His coming and expects forgiveness from heaven, at whose coming it exults and is eager to make others participants in the Gospel. Although it is likely that Andrew did not use only these two words, but explained the discourses and doctrine of Christ to his brother at greater length. For the Evangelists are accustomed to indicate only the sum of the matter. It is credible, says Chrysostom, that Andrew narrated more things most suited to persuasion, but the Evangelists sometimes omit many things for the sake of brevity. Nor indeed did Andrew only explain to Simon how he had come to Christ and what he had drawn from His own mouth; but he also brought the same man to Christ, so that he might see, hear, know, and embrace Him in person. For when, as Chrysostom says, Andrew was not sufficient for the narration of such a great light, it was necessary to bring his brother to the fountain itself, with such zeal and alacrity that nothing might turn him away or delay him. This is truly to find the Lord, says Bede in the Vigil of Andrew, to burn with true love for Him, and also to bear concern for the salvation of one's brother. This is the true way of conversion, that others may be led to Christ through the word.

V. 42. ἐμβλέψας) He looked accurately and diligently with eyes that observed not only the face, but also penetrated the soul, and were most burning with love: grammarians note that ἐμβλέπειν is said as if it were βάλλειν ὄπας, to cast one's eyes upon someone. He looks, these are the words of Cyril, as it befits Him who searches the hearts and reins, and He sees, He who is ignorant of nothing, to what great faith and virtue the disciple is about to arrive.

Latin:

εὑρήκαμεν τὸν Μεσσίαν) משיח המלך Messiam illum Regem ut Judæi loquebantur Hoc ideo dicit Andreas, quod dogmata Jesu invenisset congruentia iis, quæ Johannes de eo prædicaverat. Erat Petrus inter eos, qui expectabant con- solationem & redemptionem Israel, ut dicitur Luc, II. 25. 38. Regnum Dei, Marc. XV. 43. Itaque nullus ei nuntius potuit accedere lætior.

Cum accepissent discipuli Johannis talentum, sta- tim multiplicatum illud Domino reddunt, ait Cyrill. Fratrem igitur Petrum Andreas breviter atque in sum- ma tanta re significata servavit, invenimus, inquit, Messiam ut reconditum in agro thesaurum vel maximi gemmam pretii. Hoc enim verbum invenimus se- cundum Chrysoft. animæ est maxime adventum ejus desiderantis & cælitus veniam expectantîs, cujus ad- ventu exultans alios Evangelii gestit fieri participes. Quanquam verisimile sit, non tantum duobus his- ce verbis usum fuisse Andream, sed prolixiuscule sermones & doctrinam Christi fratri exposuisse. Solent enim Evangelistæ summam rei solum indi- care. Credibile est, inquit Chrysost. Andream plura persuasioni maxime accommodata, narrasse, verum Evangelistæ nonnunquam multa brevitatis gratia prætermittunt. Nec vero Andreas expo- suit solum Simoni, quomodo ad Christum perve- nerit & quæ ex ore ipsius hauserit; sed adduxit quoque eundem ad Christum, ut coram ipsum vi- deret, audiret, cognosceret, & amplecteretur. Cum enim, Chrysost. dicente, ad tanti luminis narratio- nem non sufficeret Andreas, ad ipsum fontem fra- trem adducere oportuit, tanto studio & alacritate, ut nihil eum averteret, aut moraretur. Hoc est vere invenire Dominum, ait Beda in Vigil. Andr. vera illius dilectione fervere, fraternæ quoque salutis curam gerere. Hæc est vera conversionis via, ut per verbum alii ad Christum perducantur.

V. 42. ἐμβλέψας) Accurate, & sedulo intuitus est oculis, non faciem solum observantibus, sed ani- mum etiam penetrantibus, & amore longe flagran- tissimis: ἐμβλέπειν Grammatici notant dici, quasi βάλλειν ὄπας, oculos in aliquem conjicere. Aspicit, verba sunt Cyrilli, ut eum decet, qui corda & renes scrutatur, videtq; qui nihil ignorat, ad quantam & fi- dem & virtutem discipulus perventurus sit.

## 1:43
Σίμων) שִׁמְעוֹן hearer: which is the first step of those desiring to learn.

ὑὸς Ἰωνᾶ) בַּר יוֹנָה (See what is said at Matt. XVI. 17. that indeed is son of divine grace: which is the second degree of those already believing.

Σὺ κληθήσῃ κηφᾶς) This is the third degree of those professing with unshaken constancy. You shall be called, that is, in the future, as in Gen. XVII. 5.

As soon as he saw Simon, with no one pointing him out, he recognized his person, and was able to state with certainty his name and his father, nay more, he prophesied concerning the faith and profession of Simon, and concerning his future office and state. Before he had asked anything about him, says Cyril, he calls both him and his father by name, and by this fact he instructs the disciple that he is the one who knows all things even before they happen. It is not a great thing, says Augustine, because the Lord said whose son this man was; what is great to the Lord! He knew all the names of his saints, whom he predestined before the foundation of the world, and do you marvel because he said to one man, you are the son of that man, and you shall be called that: it is great because he changed both the name, and made Peter out of Simon.

He adds the parent, son of Jonah, as if he were saying, although you are an ignoble son of an obscure parent, Simon Bar Jona, you shall also be called Cephas. Some explain the name Jonah as Dove, as if he were called son of a dove to mystically designate simplicity and gentleness, but his parent was called Johanna or gracious, as is held in John XXI. 5. And thus Jerome reads in this place, Epist. 46, and Augustine, whence by contraction he is called Jona, as Drusius observes in book 7 of his Praeterita on this place. Thus, therefore, it is hinted that he has both name and omen and is truly obedient, gentle, and gracious. But the paraphrase of Casaubon: You are like a dove, both timid and of no strength, but look at me, I destine you for an arduous ministry, and I wish to provide strength equal to so great a work, has no place. Exerc. 13 on Ann. Bar. p. 100.

Moreover, when it is asked here whether the name Cephas was imposed on Peter, or whether it was only predicted, to be imposed later, the latter indeed seems to be able to be gathered from Matt. XVI. 18, Mark III. 16. To us, however, the former pleases, with Augustine, book II de consens. Evang. c. 17, book 4 c. 13, since Simon, who is called here to familiar conversation with Christ, when he was called to the Apostleship, had already been named Peter in Matt. IV. 18. But here the office and the future state of Peter are predicted at the same time, namely that he will truly be Cephas, which is not a Greek name from κεφαλὴ, head, as Bellarmine foolishly claims in book 1 de P. R. c. 17, which Johannes Ferus refutes in John I. It is ridiculous, he says, that some interpret Cephas as head. Add also Valla in his declamation on the Donation of Constantine. Cajetan in John I. Undoubtedly, however, this name is of Chaldean origin, which Chemnitz distinguishes from the word Sela and Zur, because these signify an entire crag or rock, but Cepha a certain place on the rock itself, because Christ is the true and solid rock, but not Peter, much less the foundation of the Church, who has his surname from the rock: and he is called Cephas partly because of the perseverance of his faith, for although he fell from faith when he denied Christ, and indeed totally and completely, he did not however fall finally and ultimately, because having been converted he again constantly professed Christ, and did not hesitate to undergo even death for the name of Christ, partly because of the excellence of his office, because he was to be called to the Apostleship, and the Church was to be built upon his confession.

Πέτρ@) It is not an appellative: for the Attic word is never found among the Hellenists: and John himself immediately brought forth the common appellative πέτρα. It is therefore a proper noun but transferred with its meaning into the Greek language.

Some make the name Peter a proper noun in this place, others an appellative: but since the name Simon becomes a proper noun the name Peter is an interpretation of the name Cephas, which however was later used also as a proper name. Grotius denies that it is an appellative. But if it is a proper name transferred with its meaning into the Greek language, which he himself believes, why could an appellative not also be transferred? More correctly former word they think a stone is signified, but by the latter a whole rock, and they explain Simon's name πέτρος, which later became a proper name for him, in such a way that Simon is not the rock itself, but descends from the rock, which B. Luther in the German language renders ein Felser, from the rock [dem Felsen], Tom. VIII. Jen. G. wider das Pabstthumb fol. 226. Augustin. on Matt. XVI. The rock, he says, is the principal name, therefore Peter is from the rock, not the rock from Peter; just as a Christian is not called from Christ, but a Christian from Christ. So also Chrysost. hom. II. on Ps. L. says that he was called Peter because he is τῇ πίςει πεπετρωμέν@, or founded in faith, to which he contributes the fact that Heinsius on Matt. XVI. observes that πέτρον is also explained by Homer as a mountain or rock. Christ therefore predicts that Simon will truly be Peter, ein Felser, who will adhere to the rock Christ with true faith, and will propose the same to the Church by his ministry, which was done by him no less through θεοπνεύςοις writings than by the living voice. Names are usually imposed for the sake of an omen, and examples teach that those to whom new names were imposed were those whom God wished to use for great things; as Chrysostom's observation is useful; that for some names are imposed from birth, as for Isaac and Samson, for others later, as for Abram the name of Abraham, for Jacob the name of Israel, and that this is not done rashly, but so that the appellation may be a perpetual monument of a divine benefit, and that those who were to excel in virtue from an early age had names given to them then, but those who were to progress in the course of their age had them imposed later. But that the name was not changed here for Simon, as the Papists argue to that end (in order to establish Peter's Papacy with this argument, although it is entirely flimsy), but rather that a surname was given to him, is clear even from the fact that the name of Simon was retained afterwards as well, and indeed was used even then, when the Papists pretend that the Papacy was conferred upon Peter, or say it was exercised by him, as John XXI. 15, Acts XV. v. 13, and the passage Acts X. 5 confirms it: call for Simon, who is surnamed Peter, therefore Johannes Ferus in Matt. VI. is rightly called Simon at the beginning, then the surname Peter is added by Christ.

Moreover, from these names can be gathered the heads of doctrine which Christ proposed to his first disciples and especially to Peter at his first introduction, namely that first, by the imposition of a new name, he showed that believers pass into the family of Christ; having received a new name, which the mouth of the Lord named, Is. LXII. 2, Rev. II. 17, and which is written in heaven, Matt. XI. Second, that by the appellation of Peter, Christ taught that he himself is that cornerstone, the foundation of the Church, upon which all must be built up as Peters or living stones, who know how to storm the gates of hell, 1 Pet. II. 2, Matt. XVI. 18. Third, that by the appellation of Peter he insinuated the doctrine concerning the Ministry building upon the rock, as the only foundation, 1 Cor. III. 11. If these things were not so distinctly explained by Christ, they were certainly contained in the words and implicitly insinuated, as Chemnitius believes.

Verse 43. τῇ ἐπαύριον] The day after that on which Simon had approached Christ.

Latin:

Σίμων) שִׁמְעוֹן auditor: qui primus gradus discere cupientium.

ὑὸς Ἰωνᾶ) בַּר יוֹנָה (Vide quæ ad Matth. XVI. 17. id vero est filius divinæ gratiæ: qui secundus gradus jam credentium.

Σὺ κληθήσῃ κηφᾶς) Hic tertius gradus inconcussa constantia profitentium. Vocaberis scilicet in posterum, ut Gen. XVII. 5.

Quam primum Simonem vidit, nemine indicante, personam cognovit, & nomen & patrem ejus certo indicare potuit, imo de fide & professione Simonis, deq; futuro ejus officio & statu vaticinatus est. Antequam aliquid de eo quæsivisset, ait Cyrillus, tam ipsum quam patrem ejus nomine appellat, & hac re instituit discipulum, eum se esse, qui cuncta etiam, antequam fiant, novit. Non magnum, inquit Augustinus, quia Dominus dixit, cujus filius esset iste, quid magnum Domino! Omnia nomina sanctorum suorum sciebat, quos ante constitutionem mundi prædestinavit, & miraris, quia dixit uni homini, tu es filius illius, & tu vocaberis illud: magnum quia mutavit & nomen, & fecit è Simone Petrum.

Addit parentem filius Jonæ, quasi dicat, tu licet obscuri parentis filius ignobilis Simon Bar Jona Cephas etiam vocaberis. Jonæ nomen exponunt nonnulli Columbam, quasi filius columbæ propter simplicitatem & mansuetudinem mystice designandam diceretur, sed parens ejus Johanna dictus fuit sive gratiosus, uti habetur Ioh. XXI. 5. Atque ita legunt h. l. Hieron. Epist. 46. & Augustin. unde per contractionem dictus est Iona, ut observat Drusius l. 7. præterit. ad h. l. Sic ergo innuitur, quod nomen & omen habeat ac vere obediens sit, mansuetus, & gratiosus. Casauboni vero paraphrasis: Columbæ similis es, & timidus & virium nullarum, sed me vide, ego te & ministerio arduo destino, & vires tanto operi pares volo sufficere, locum non habet. Exerc. 13. ad Ann. Bar. p. 100.

Cæterum, cum hic quæritur, num nomen Cephæ Petro sit impositum, an vero tantummodo prædictum fuerit, deinceps imponendum, posterius quidem è Matth. XVI. 18. Marc. III. 16. colligi posse videtur. Nobis tamen prius placet cum August. l. II. de consens. Evang. c. 17. l. 4. c. 13. quandoquidem Simon, qui hic vocatus ad conversationem cum Christo familiarem, cum vocatus est ad Apostolatum, jam Petrus nuncupatus fuerat Matth. IV. 18. Prædicitur autem hic simul officium, ac status Petri futurus, quod nempe vere Cephas futurus sit, quod non est nomen Græcum à κεφαλὴ caput, uti Bellarminus ineptit l. 1. d. P. R. c. 17. quod refellit Iohannes Ferus in Joh. I. Ridiculum est, inquit, quod quidam Cephas per caput interpretantur. Adde & Vallam in declamat. de donat. Constant. Cajet. in Joh. I. Indubie autem hoc nomen originis Chaldaicæ est, quod ita distinguit Chemnitius à voce Sela & Zur, quod hæ rupem integram seu petram significent, Cepha vero locum aliquem in ipsa rupe, quod Christus sit vera & solida petra, non autem Petrus, nedum fundamentum Ecclesiæ, qui à petra agnominationem habet: ac Cephas vocatur partim ob fidei perseverantiam, licet enim exciderit fide, cum abnegaret Christum, & quidem ὁλικῶς ac totaliter, non tamen excidit τελικῶς & finaliter, quia conversus iterum Christum constanter professus est, & pro Christi nomine mortem etiam subire non dubitavit, partim ob officii præstantiam, quia ad Apostolatum vocandus erat, & super confessionem ejus Ecclesia exstruenda.

Πέτρ@) Non est appellativum: nunquam enim vox Attica apud Hellenistas reperitur: & ipse Johannes statim appellativum communiter extulit πέτρα. Est ergo proprium sed translatum cum sua significatione in sermonem Græcũ.

Nomen Petrus alii proprium hoc loco faciunt, alii appellativum: cum vero nomen Simon proprium fit, nomen Petrus interpretamentum nominis Ce- phas est, quod tamen postmodum etiam ceu pro- prium nomen adhibitum est. Grotius appellati- vum esse negat. Sed si proprium est translatum cum sua significatione in sermonem Græcum, quod ipse censet, quidni appellativum etiam transferri potuit? Rectius ergo alii πέτρον & petram distin- guunt, illaq; voce lapidem, hac autem rupem inte- gram significari censent, ac Simonis nomen πέτρος, quod proprium postmodum ipsi evasit, ita expli- cant, quod Simon non ipsa petra sit, sed à petra de- scendat, quod B. Lutherus in Germanica Lingua reddit ein Felser, à petra dem Felsen, Tom. VIII. Jen. G. wider das Pabstthumb fol. 226. Augustin. ad Matth. XVI. Petra, inquit, nomen principale est, ideo Petrus à petra, non petra à Petro; quomodo a Christiano non Christus, sed à Christo Christianus vocatur. Ita & Chrysost. hom. II. in Ps. L. Petrum dictum ait, quod sit τῇ πίςει πεπετρωμέν@, vel in fide fundatus, quo facit, quod Heinsius ad Matth. XVI. πέτρον etiam apud Homerum exponi pro mon- te vel rupe observet. Prædicit ergo Christus Simo- nem vere futurum Petrum ein Felser, petræ Christo vera fide inhæsurum, eandemq; ministerio suo Ecclesiæ propositurum, quod ab ipso non minus θεοπνεύςοις scriptis, quam viva voce factum est. Solent autem nomina imponi ominis causa, & docent exempla, quod, quibus nova nomina imposita sunt, iis Deus uti voluerit ad res magnas; uti utilis est observatio Chrysostomi; quibusdam à nativitate nomina im- poni, ut Isaaco, & Samsoni, quibusdam postmodum ut Abramo, nomen Abrahami, Jacobo nomen Israelis, id autem non temere fieri, sed ut appella- tio sit divini beneficii perpetuum monumentum, & qui ab ineunte ætate debuere virtute pollere, eis tunc indita nomina, qui vero in ætatis progressu profecturi erant, iis postmodum imposita fuisse. Quod autem hic non immutatum Simoni nomen sit, prout Pontifici eo fine disputant (ut hoc argu- mento, quanquam prorsus ficulneo, Petri Papa- tum stabiliant,) sed cognomen ipsi potius datum sit, vel inde liquet, quod Simonis nomen deinceps quoque retentum fuerit, imo etiam tum, ubi Petro Papatum collatum fingunt Papistæ, vel ab eo ge- stum dicunt, adhibitum sit, ut Joh. XXI. 15. Act. XV. v. 13. & confirmat locus Act. X. 5. accerse Simonem, qui cognominatur Petrus, ideo recte Johannes Ferus in Matth. VI. initio vocatur Simon, additur deinde a Christo cognomen Petrus.

Colligi autem possunt ex his nominibus capita doctrinæ, quæ Christus primis suis discipulis & cumprimis Petro in prima ejus adductione pro- posuit, quod scilicet primo impositione nominis novi ostenderit credentes transire in familiam Christi; accepto novo nomine, quod os Domini nominavit, Es. LXII. 2. Apoc. II. 17. quodq; in cœ- lis adscriptum est, Matth. XI. Secundo quod ap- pellatione Petri Christus docuerit, se esse lapidem illum angularem fundamentum Ecclesiæ, cui omnes superædificari oporteat tanquam Petros seu lapi- des vivos, qui expugnare norint portas inferorum, 1. Petr. II. 2. Matth. XVI. 18. Tertio quod insinua- rit appellatione Petri doctrinam de Ministerio ædi- ficante super petram, ceu unicum fundamentum 1. Cor. III. 11. Hæc si non tam à Christo explicata distincte sunt, in verbis certe comprehensa, & im- plicite insinuata fuerunt, censente Chemnitio.

Vers. 43. τῇ ἐπαύριον] Postero die ex quo Simon ad Chri- stum accesserat.

## 1:44
εἰς Γαλιλαίαν] So that from an ignoble region he might gather for himself ignoble disciples, see below VII. 52. Join 1 Cor. I. 28.

ἀκολούθει μοι] With which words Christ calls Philip both to discipleship, so that he might associate himself with his school

and discipline, and to obedience, which is tacitly included in this word, so that he might henceforth comply with him and follow the institutes of his doctrine. Chrysostom asks here why Christ did not call the others himself before anyone followed him of his own accord, but wished to call Philip in this way? He says that Christ did not do the former rashly, but with the highest wisdom. For if he had called some when no one was following of his own accord, one could have doubted their perseverance: but if they had chosen to follow of their own accord, not at all; he gives this reason for the latter, namely that he had Philip better known to himself, as one who was both born and raised in Galilee.

Verse 44. Ἀπὸ Βησαϊδὰ ἐκ τῆς πόλεως] Here ἐξ is redundant, just as below in ch. II. 23.

Some explain that name as house of the hunter, others as house of the provision, ein Haus der Wegsteuer oder Ritterzehrung, as Crell. in Concordant. but because not hunters, but fishermen lived around the lake of Gennesaret, and it descends from צַיִּד, a net, and a hook, by which fish are caught, we think more simply with Chemnitius that Bethsaida is called as if it were the house of nets or hooks, by which fish are caught. Where Chrysostom not inappropriately observes: that Christ demonstrated his power even in this, that from Galilee, a land so sterile, from which neither a Prophet arose, nor anything good, he procured such disciples for himself. The admirable wisdom of the Lord must also be acknowledged, that the first disciples of Christ were gathered from such obscure villages, the Evangelist mentions his fatherland, says Chrysostom, because God chose the weak things of the world.

Latin:

εἰς Γαλιλαίαν] Utex regione ignobili ignobiles sibi di- scipulos colligeret, vide infr. VII. 52. Conjunge 1. Cor. I. 28.

ἀκολούθει μοι] Quibus verbis Christus Philip- pum vocat tum ad discipulatum, ut sese in scholam

& disciplinam suam associarete, tum ad obsequium, quod hac voce tacite comprehenditur, ut scilicet sibi imposterum morem gereret, doctrinæ suæ in- stituta sectaretur. Quærit hic Chrysost. cur Chri- stus alios ipsos non vocavit, priusquam quisquam ipsius sequeretur sponte sua, Philippum autem ita vocare vo- luerit? Prius non temere fecisse Christum, ait, sed summa sapientia. Nam si nemine sponte sua sequente ipse aliquos vocasset, de eorum perseverantia dubita- ri potuisset: at si ultro sequi elegissent, minime; poste- rioris vero hanc reddit rationem, quod scilicet Philippum sibi notiorem habuerit, utpote qui in Ga- lilaea & natus erat, & educatus.

Vers. 44. Ἀπὸ Βησαϊδὰ ἐκ τῆς πόλεως] Hic ἐξ abundat quo- modo infra ir c. II. 23.

Nomen istud exponunt aliqui domum venato- ris, alii domum viatici, ein Haus der Wegsteuer oder Ritterzehrung, uti Crell. in Concordant. at quia circa stagnum Genezareth non venatores, sed piscatores habitabant, & à צַיִּד rete, & hamus, quo pisces capiuntur, descendit, simplicius cense- mus Chemnitio Bethsaida dictam quasi domum retium sive hamorum, quibus pisces capiuntur. Ubi non abs re observat Chrysostomus: Chri- stum etiam in hoc suam demonstrasse virtutem, quod ex Galilæa Terra tam sterili, unde neque Propheta surrexit, neq; quicquam boni, tales sibi compara- ret discipulos. Agnoscenda etiam admiranda Do- mini sapientia, quod ex vicis tam obscuris primi discipuli Christi collecti fuerint, meminit ejus pa- tria Evangelista, inquit Chrysostomus, quod infir- ma mundi elegerit Deus.

## 1:45
Ἀνδρέου καὶ Πέτρου] By the account of whom, as acquaintances, Philip's mind was already somewhat prepared.

Vers. 45. Philip finds.

Philip's obedience is implicitly indicated: in that he followed Him immediately at that one word of Christ, which Chrysostom deems worthy of admiration: how it was that Philip, as well as Peter, could be so easily convinced, not only for the reason that they followed before the signs, but also because they were Galileans, from whom nothing good [was expected]. He gives three reasons concerning Philip: (1.) It is credible that Philip, who had already believed that Christ was to come, had heard from Peter or from John that Jesus is that Christ. (2.) That the discourse of Christ had worked not a little in them; for He knew who would be suitable disciples. (3.) He attributes it to the diligence of Philip, who, having diligently searched the scripture, fervently awaited Christ, according to that common saying: for a diligent man something always remains, and according to the promise of Christ, he who seeks finds, Matt. VII. v. 7. But it pleases our D. Chemnitius above all, that the Evangelist himself seems to indicate that Philip had previously learned from Andrew and Peter those things which they themselves had learned from their conversation with Jesus, and therefore added that Philip was from the city of Andrew and Peter. Whence, already instructed by them, he was ready for obedience to Christ when he was called by Him.

Latin:

Ἀνδρέου καὶ Πέτρου] Quorum ut familiarium relatu præpa- ratus jam nonnihil erat Philippi animus.

Vers. 45. εὑρίσκει Φίλιππος.

Paritio Philippi implicite indicata: quod ad unicum illud verbum Christi statim ipsum secutus sit, quod admiratione dignum censet Chrysosto- mus: quo pacto Philippus ut & Petrus tam faci- le persuaderi potuerint, non tantum ea ratione, quod ante signa secuti sint, sed etiam quod Galilæi fuerint, unde nihil boni. Rationes de Philippo reddit tres: (1.) Credibile esse Philippum, qui jam ante crediderat, quod Christus venturus esset, a Pe- tro vel a Johanne audivisse, quod Jesus sit ille Chri- stus. (2.) Sermonem Christi in eis non parum opera- tum esse; noverat enim qui idonei essent futuri disci- puli. (3.) Tribuit id diligentiæ Philippi, qui se- dulo scripturam scrutatus, fervide Christum expe- ctavit, juxta illud tritum: homini diligenti semper aliquid supcrest, & juxta Christi promissum, qui quærit invenit, Matth. VII. v. 7. Placet autem imprimis D. Chemnitio nostro, quod ipse Evan- gelista videatur indicare Philippum prius ex Andrea & Petro ea, quæ ipsi ex colloquio cum Jesu didicerant, cognovisse, atque ideo addidisse, quod Philippus fuerit ex civitate Andreæ & Petri. Unde jam e- doctus ab illis promtus erat ad obsequium Christi, cum vocaretur ab ipso.

## 1:46
τὸν Ναθαναὴλ] Learned, as the ancients suppose: I will add what I think is credible, that he was instructed by the experts in the law, a privilege which his own humble circumstances had denied to others. His name has the same meaning as the Hebrew Jonathan, the Greek Dositheus, Dorotheus, Theodore, Theodosius: the Latin Adeodatus.

ὃν ἔγραψεν ὁ Μωσῆς ἐν τῷ νόμῳ] In the prophecy of Jacob concerning Shiloh: which he wrote, that is, concerning whom he wrote, as to write for Vario.

καὶ οἱ προφῆται] Especially Isaiah, Malachi, Daniel, it is a circumscription of Christ.

I would wish these things to be noted again against the depravations of the prophecies occurring throughout almost the entire O.T. in the Annotations of Grotius, but especially in the case of Isaiah.

Ἰησοῦν] They indicate to whom they think the title of Christ applies.

Τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ Ἰωσὴφ τὸν ἀπὸ Ναζαρὲθ] Just as they thought Him the son of Joseph according to the opinion of the common people, so also a Nazarene by birth, because He was commonly called so.

V. 46. Can any good thing come out of Nazareth?] Shall I no longer say the Messiah, but rather that some Prophet is expected from there? For the experts in the law were explicitly denying that. See the passage which we have already cited in chapter VII. 52.

Although Augustine, in Tractate 7 on John, thinks this can be taken in an affirmative sense, that something good can come from Nazareth; yet the negative sense is simpler, and it was said thus by Nathanael, both because of the ignobility of the place and because of the wickedness of its inhabitants, on account of which that town was held in ill repute, so that it even passed into a proverb: can anything good come from Nazareth? just as all Galilee had a bad reputation, John VII. 41, 52; and also because of the clarity of the prophetic oracles, which had destined not Nazareth, but Bethlehem, as the homeland of the Messiah, Micah V. v. 2. Therefore Theophylact says that that expression is not one of rejection, but of precision, because it accurately noted the homeland of the Messiah and gave notice of it. For he was, as is clear from Philip's address, well-versed in Moses and the Prophets.

Latin:

τὸν Ναθαναὴλ] Eruditum ut veteres existimant: addam quod credibile puto, à legisperitis institutum, quod aliis sua tenuitas inviderat. Nomen ejusdem sensus cujus He- bræum Jonathan, Græca Dosithei, Dorothei, Theodori, Theodosii: Latinum Adeodatus.

ὃν ἔγραψεν ὁ Μωσῆς ἐν τῷ νόμῳ] In Iacobi vati inio de Si- lo: quam scripsit, id est, de quo scripsit, ut scribere Vario.

καὶ οἱ προφῆται] Maxime Esaias, Malachias, Daniel, cir- cumscriptio est Christi.

Hæc iterum notari velim adversus depravatio- nes vaticiniorum per totum fere V.T.occurrentes in Annotatis Grot. imprimis vero penes Esaiam.

Ἰησοῦν] Indicant cui titulum Christi putent competere.

Τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ Ἰωσὴφ τὸν ἀπὸ Ναζαρὲθ] Sicut Iosephi filium pu- tabant ex vulgi opinione, sic & ortu Nazarenum, quia vulgo sic vocabatur.

V. 46. ἐκ Ναζαρὲθ δύναταί τι ἀγαθὸν εἶναι] Non jam dicam Messias, sed Propheta aliquis inde expectetur? nam id legisperiti diferte negabant. Vide locum quem jam citavimus cap. VII. 52.

Hoc etsi August. tr. 7. in Joh. censeat sensu affirmativo accipi posse, a Nazareth aliquid boni posse venire; simplicior tamen est sensus negativus, dictumque; ita fuit à Nathanaele, tum ob loci ignobilitatem, tum ob incolarum improbitatem, propter quam infame habitum fuit oppidum istud, ut in proverbium etiam abierit: nunquid boni esse potest à Nazareth, prout universa Galilæa male audiebat Joh. VII. 41. 52. tum ob oraculorum Propheticorum perspicuitatem, quæ non Nazareth, sed Bethlehem destinaverant Messiæ patriam, Mich. V. v. 2. ideo Theoph. vocem illam dicit esse non ἀπωσίας, sed ἀκριβείας, quod accurate patriam Messiæ notarit, de eaq; commonefecerit. Fuit enim in Mose & Prophetis, ut ex Philippi alloquio liquet, apprime versat9.

## 1:47
ἔρχου καὶ ἴδε] A frequent expression in the Zohar. You will receive more certain indications from his own speech than can be had from the place of origin. Philip either did not know the traditions of the experts in the law or did not value them too highly.

He appeals to the senses; he does not wish to convince him by arguing, but trusts that he will be convinced by, as it were, ocular inspection: just as Christ had said to Andrew and his companion, come and see: so Philip to Nathanael, come and see. How? Could that be known by the senses? Certainly that was not seen with the eyes of the body, but with the eyes of the mind. Moreover, Christ manifested himself so clearly to his own that they seemed to perceive it with their eyes. Cyril says it excellently in this way; those words: If you see only, if you confer with him in speech, you will most easily agree with me that he is, without a doubt, the one who is expected. But we ought to believe, adds Cyril, that there was a certain ineffable grace in the speech and words of Christ, by which the minds of the hearers were enticed with great pleasure. For it is written that all wondered at the words of grace which proceeded from his mouth, Luke IV. For just as there was virtue in his words for performing divine miracles, so also he had great powers for persuading.

Vers. 47. And he says about him] He said about him, that is, to Andrew and his companion, as also to Peter, who were present with him, but in such a way that it could be heard by Nathanael and Philip as they approached.

Latin:

ἔρχου καὶ ἴδε] Locutio frequens in Zohar. Certiora indicia ex ipsius sermone accipies, quam ex loco origenis haberi possint. Philippus traditiones legisperitorum aut ignorabat aut non nimium magnificiebat.

Provocat ad sensum; non disputando ipsum vult convincere, sed oculari velut inspectione convictum iri confidit: ut Christus dixerat Andreæ & socio ejus, venite & videte: ita Philippus Nathanaeli, veni & vide. Qui? num sensibus cognosci id poterat? non sane id oculis corporis videbatur, sed oculis mentis. Cæterum Christus tam luculenter sese manifestabat suis, ut id oculis usurpare viderentur. Præclare Cyrillus ὧδέ πως; verba illa: Si videris tantummodo, si sermonem cum eo conferas, facillime mihi assentieris, procul dubio ipsum esse, qui expectatur. Credere autem nos oportet, addit Cyrill. ineffabilem quandam gratiam in sermone & verbis Christi fuisse, quibus auditorum animi magna jucunditate allicerentur. Scribitur enim quia omnes admirabantur de verbis gratiæ, quæ exibant de ore ejus Luc. IV. Nam quemadmodum ad facienda signa divina verbis suis inerat virtus, sic etiam ad persuadendum magnas vires habebat.

Vers. 47. Καὶ λέγει περὶ ἀυτõ] Dixit de eo, puta ad Andream & socium ejus, ut & Petrum, qui ipsi aderant, sed ita ut audiri potuerit à Nathanaele & Philippo appropinquantibus.

## 1:48
Ἴδε ἀληθῶς Ἰσραηλίτης] Not all descendants of Israel are worthy of that name, but those who reflect the integrity of Jacob, Rom. IX. 6. Thus are those to be considered the posterity of Abraham who do his works, below c. IIX. 39. In a similar manner of speaking, Plutarch, in his book on Isis, says: an Israelite indeed.

ἐν ᾧ δόλος οὐκ ἐστι] Reference is made to the eulogy given to Jacob, Gen. XXV. 27. אִישׁ תָּם where the Greeks say ἄπλαστος. Aquila says ἁπλοῦς: just as he had translated the same word in the beginning of Job; they translate the same Hebrew word elsewhere as ἄκακον, as in Job VIII. v. 20, Ps. XXV. 21, Prov. VIII. 6. This testimony, however, is borne to Nathanael because he had spoken without giving thanks, which he judged to be in agreement with the sacred scriptures. And yet he came no less, to explore if he could find anything more certain. But if he is such, then he is also blessed according to Ps. XXXII. 2.

The little word ἰδὲ, behold, is used, both for the demonstration of an object, John I. 29, and for the indication of certainty, Eph. VII. 14, and for the sake of attention and the observation of the thing which is proposed, because it is worthy of being noticed, Isa. LII. 13, Zech. IX. 15, Ps. XL. 8, which triple cause has a place here likewise. By the word true Israelite, Nathanael is distinguished from others who were Israelites only according to the flesh, because, namely, he himself is an Israelite also as regards the Spirit and the Promise, Rom. IX. 8, that is, by true faith and sincerity of mind. And therefore Christ adds, in whom there is no guile; not that he is immune from sin, as this phrase is used of Christ in 1 Pet. II. 22, but because of the simplicity and candor of his mind, which is free from hypocrisy, just as Jacob, from whom the Israelites have their name, was a simple and upright man, not of a crafty nature, like Esau, Gen. XXV. v. 27. He signifies, therefore, that he did not expect the Messiah with a hypocritical mind, as the Pharisees, who were panting after external things, but sincerely, in whom he trusted, as a true Israelite. Augustine explains that, in whom there is no guile, in this sense: that Nathanael acknowledged himself a sinner without hypocrisy, in opposition to the Pharisees, who did not acknowledge their sins; but his true and sincere faith and piety are designated, free from fraud and simulation. For guile among the Greeks has its name from δολō̃ν, which is used of dyers who put on a different color: whence guile is defined as being a machination of fraud to circumvent someone, by words or deeds, and it consists either in the heart, and is the very machination of fraud, Matt. XXVI. 4, or in a word, and is a fraudulent lie, or in works, such as is simulation, Acts XXIII. v. 10. And therefore rightly Augustine, in this place guile, he says, is fraud, it is simulation, when someone hides one thing in his heart and speaks another, it is guile; and he is as if he has two hearts; he has one as the bosom of the heart, where he sees the truth, and another bosom where he conceives a lie. Rightly here Cyril, book II on John, ch. XVI: before Christ drew men to faith by the miracle of signs, he showed in another way, and no less wonderfully, that he was God by nature, who had come in human form for the salvation of men. But what was that way? The hidden knowledge of things, which is attributed to God alone. He does not, therefore, flatter Nathanael with little flatteries, but by exposing those things of which he was conscious, namely the hearts of men (which is of God alone), he affirms that he knows them: Cf. 1 Sam. XVI. 7.

Ver. 48. Whence knowest thou me? Having heard that judgment concerning himself, he was asking, whence do you know me? Suspecting perhaps that certain things had been told to the Lord about him by Philip, as Cyril supposes. Or indicating this, whence is this evident to you: have you conversed with me at some time, so that you might know my mind? or have you indeed received this from others?

Latin:

Ἴδε ἀληθῶς Ἰσραηλίτης] Non omnes Israelis posteri digni eo nomine, sed qui Jacobi probitatem referunt Rom. IX. 6. Sic Abrahami posteritas censendi, qui ejus opera faciunt infra c. IIX. 39. Simili loquendi genere Plutarch. lib. de Iside Ἰσιακὸς ὡς ἀληθῶς.

ἐν ᾧ δόλος οὐκ ἐστι] Respicitur elogium Iacobo datum, Gen. XXV. 27. אִישׁ תָּם ubi Græci ἄπλαστος. Aquila ἁπλοῦς: quomodo idem vocem eandem verterat Iobi initio; eandem vocem Hebræam alibi ἄκακον vertunt, ut Iob. VIII. v. 20. Psal. XXV. 21. Prov. VIII. 6. perhibetur autem Nathanaeli hoc testimonium, quia nihil gratiæ dans dixerat, quod sacris literis congruens judicabat. Neque eo tamen minus veniebat, si quid posset certius exploraturus. Si autem talis, ergo & beatus ex Psal. XXXII. 2.

Vocula ἰδὲ ecce adhibetur, tum ad objecti demonstrationem, Joh. I. 29. tum ad certitudinis indicationem, Ef. VII. 14. tum ob attentionem, & rei, quæ proponitur observationem, quod digna sit, quæ advertatur, Ef. LII. 13. Zach. IX. 15. Ps. XL. 8. quæ triplex causa hic itidem locum habet. Voce ve- re Israelita discriminatur Nathanaël ab aliis, qui tantum secundum carnem Israelitæ erant, quod sc. ipse etiam quoad Spiritum & Promissionem Israelita sit, Rom. IX. 8. hoc est, vera fide, animique sinceritate. Ideoque addit Christus, in quo non est dolus; non quod immunis sit à peccato, uti de Christo hæc phrasis adhibetur 1. Pet. II. 22. sed propter animi simplicitatem & candorem hypocriscos expertem, quemadmodum Jacob, à quo nomen habent Israëlitæ, vir simplex & rectus erat, non vafro ingenio, ut Esavus, Gen. XXV. v. 27. Significat ergo, ipsum non animo hypocritico, ut Pharisæi externis inhian- tes, sed sincere expectasse Messiam, in quem confi- debat, ceu verus Israelita. Augustinus illud, in quo non est dolus, explicat hoc sensu; quod Nathanael se peccatorem agnoverit sine hypocrisi, ex oppositione Pharisæorum, qui non agnoscebant peccata sua; sed designatur vera & sincera ipsius fides & pietas, expers fraudis & simulationis. Dolus enim apud Græcos à δολō̃ν, quod de tinctoribus adhibetur co- lorem alium induentibus, nomen habet: unde de- finitur dolus, quod sit machinatio fraudis aliquem circumveniendi, verbis vel factis, & vel in corde con- sistit, estque fraudis ipsa machinatio, Matth. XXVI. 4. vel in verbo, & est mendacium fraudulen- tum, vel in operibus, qualis est simulatio Act. XXIII. v. 10. Ideoque recte Augustin. hoc loco δόλ​୽, in- quit, sraus est, simulatio est, quando aliquis aliquid in corde tegit, & aliud loquitur, dolus est; & tanquam duo corda habet; unum quasi sinum cordis habet, ubi videt veritatem, & alterum sinum ubi concipit menda- cium. Recte hic Cyrillus l. II. in Joh. c. XVI. ante- quam signorum miraculo ad fidem homines traheret Christus, alio quodam modo, nec minus mirabili, natu- ra se Deum esse ostendit, qui humana forma propter salutem hominum venerit. Quis vero ille modus fuit? Occulta rerum cognitio, quæ soli Deo attribui- tur. Non ergo adulatiunculis Nathanaeli blan- ditur, sed ea quorum conscius erat, exponens cor- da scilicet hominum, (quod solius Dei est) se co- gnoscere affirmat: Conf. 1. Sam. XVI. 7.

Vers. 48. πόθεν με γινώσκεις. Audito illo de se judicio, quærebat, unde me no- sti. Suspicatus forte à Philippo quædam Domino de ipso narrata esse, uti autumat Cyrillus. Vel id indicans, unde hoc tibi constat: num mecum con- versatus es aliquando, ut animum meum cogno- sceres? an vero ex aliis hoc acce pisti?

## 1:49
under the fig tree] Whence Philip had called him aside, with no one aware. To be under the fig tree is a sign of a tranquil mind, Mic. IV. 4. and elsewhere to call him who is under the fig tree is a sign of friendship, Zech. III. 10.

I saw thee] I saw your mind and approved it, as in Ps. XVI. as if he were to say, do not think me offended because you raised an argument against my being believed to be Christ.

Here Christ again brings forward three new proofs of his omniscience: (1.) that he heard Philip call him, where it is tacitly implied also that he heard the conversation held with Philip, even though they had the discourse in a secret place alone. (2.) that Nathanael was then under the fig tree. (3.) that he was seen there by him. For he mentions both the time and the place, and the tree, as Chrysostom notes, so that no one might suppose Philip was sent by him, if he had only remembered his journey to Nathanael. Augustine seeks a mystery here: Nathanael, he says, was under the fig tree as if under the shadow of death, the Lord saw him, of whom it was said, to those who sat under the shadow of death, light has arisen: because by leaves other sins are understood, Gen. III. But it is more correctly observed by that mention, that he was under the fig tree, that the state of that time, tranquil, similar to the Solomonic time, 1 Kings IV. 25. is designated, of which this is a periphrasis, that each one might live under his own fig tree, Micah IV. 4. Zech. III. 10. such as it was in the time of the coming of Jesus Christ, who is our peace, Eph. II. 14. and prince of peace, Isa. IX. 7.

Ver. 49. The Son of God] It is the same as Messiah from Ps. II. See what is at Matt. XIV. 33. and XXVI. 63. Therefore follows the King of Israel, another title of the Messiah, Matt. XXI. 5. ch. XXVII. 11. and 42. Mark XV. 32. Nathanael did here what Samuel is commanded to do 1 Sam. XVI. 7. He did not look to those things which seem magnificent to men.

Truly the same is the Son of God, who is the Messiah from Ps. II.

but the Son of God is not the same thing as the Messiah. For the former is a name of nature, the latter of office and of anointing for an office. Which we have observed elsewhere against the Socinians, and also against Grotius. By these signs, therefore, which were by no means deceptive, Nathanael concluded that Jesus was the Christ, having been taught by the scriptures, both because it belongs to God alone to look into the heart, to penetrate hidden and secret things, and to know and understand such things as cannot otherwise be known unless indicated by someone; and because that promised Messiah was not to be a mere man, but true God, the Son of God, the searcher of hearts, and truly omniscient. Regarding the former, see 1 Sam. XVI. 9, 1 Chron. XXVIII. 9, Ps. VII. 10, Jer. XI. 20, ch. XVII. 10, ch. XX. 12; regarding the latter, Is. VII. 14, ch. IX. 6, XXXIII. v. 15; accordingly, he broke out into this confession: Rabbi, you are the Son of God, you are the King of Israel. Chrysostom indeed thinks that Nathanael confessed Christ only as a man, because he adds, you are the King of Israel, since the Son of God is not only King of Israel, but of the whole world; but the Son of God is sometimes described specifically as King in Israel, Ps. II. 6, Mich. V. 2. Sometimes generally, as Lord of the universe, regarding his royal office; nor is that description exclusive, but appropriative, since with a peculiar appropriation Israel pertains to the kingdom of Christ. Nor indeed can it be attributed to Nathanael, whom Chrysostom says is most diligent in searching out the truth, and commends for his knowledge of the scriptures, that he had such ignorance as to suppose that the Son of God, that King of Israel, would be a mere man, and therefore Cyril is more correct on this passage: He knew, he says, well that to God alone are the hearts of men open, and he held that fixed in his mind from the Psalmist, God searching hearts and reins, for to no other, but only to the divine nature, does the Prophet attribute this. When he had perceived that this was in the Lord, he professes him both Master and Son of God and King of Israel. Therefore Christ did not rebuke him because he did not believe, but rather commended his faith, and further corroborated it. Moreover, all those things taken from the Scriptures of the O.T. argue that he was most expert in the Prophetic scriptures, because the Messiah is described as Rabbi, the first Teacher, Deut. XVIII. 18, Is. L. 4, LV. 4; as Son of God, 2 Sam. VII. 14, Ps. II. 7, LXXXIX. 7, Prov. VIII. 23, Mich. V. 2; as King of Israel, Ps. II. 6. Is. IX. 7. Zech. IX. 9.

Latin:

ὑπὸ τὴν συκῆν] Unde eum Philippus solus nemine con- scio avocaverat. Sub ficu agere, signum tranquilli animi, Mich. IV. 4. & alibi vocare eum qui sub ficu est amicitiæ, Zach. III. 10.

ἔιδόν σε] Vidi animum tuum & approbavi, ut Ps. XVI. quasi dicat, ne me putes offensum, quod argumentum ob- jecisti ne Christus crederer.

Tria hic iterum nova suæ πανεπισκοπίας argu- menta profert Christus: (1.) quod audierit Philip- pum eum vocasse, ubi tacite innuitur etiam, quod colloquium cum Philippo habitum audierit, etsi soli secreto in loco sermonem habuerint. (2.) quod sub ficu tum fuerit Nathanael. (3.) quod ibi visus abs se fuerit. Meminit enim & temporis & loci, & arbo- ris, notante Chrysostomo, ne ab ipso quisquam o- pinaretur missum Philippum, si tantum ejus ad Na- thanaelem profečionem meminisset. Augustinus my- sterium hic quærit: Erat, inquit, Nathanael sub ar- bore fici tanquam sub umbra mortis, vidit eum Domi- nus, de quo dictum, qui sedebant sub umbra mortis, lumen ortum est eis: quia per folia alias peccata in- telliguntur, Gen. III. Sed rectius observatur men- tione ista, quod sub ficu fuerit, statum istius tempo- ris, tranquillum, similem Salomonæi temporis 2. Reg. IV. 25. designari, cujus hæc est periphrasis, quod quisque possit degere sub ficu sua, Michæ IV. 4. Zach. III. 10. qualis erat tempore adventan- tis Jesu Christi, qui pax nostra est, Eph. II. 24. & princeps pacis, Esa. IX. 7.

Vers. 49. ὁ ὑός τῦ Θεῦ] Idem est quod Messias ex Psal. II. Vide quæ ad Matth. XIV. 33. & XXVI. 63. Itaque sequi- tur ὁ βασιλεὺς τῦ Ἰσραὴλ, alter Messiæ titulus, Matth. XXI. 25. c. XXVII. 11. & 42. Marc. XV. 11. Fecit hic Nathanaël, quod facere Samuel jubetur 1. Sam. XVI. 7. Non respexit ad ea, quæ hominibus magnifica videntur.

Idem sane ὁ ὑὸς τῦ Θεῦ, qui Messias ex Ps. II.

sed non idem est Filius Dei quod Messias. Illud enim nomen naturæ, hoc officii & unctionis ad of- ficium. Quod alias contra Socinianos, etiam con- tra Grotium, observavimus. Istis ergo indiciis mi- nime fallacibus Jesum esse Christum concludebat Nathanael, è scripturis edoctus, tum quod solius Dei sit cor introspicere, abdita & occulta penetra- re, & cognoscere, ac scire talia, quæ alias nisi indi- cata à nemine sciri possunt; tum quod promissus ille Messias non nudus homo futurus sit, sed verus Deus, Dei Filius, scrutator cordium,, vereq; omni- scius. De priori videatur 1. Sam. XVI. 9. 1. Paral. XXVIII. 9. Psal. VII. 10. Ier. XI. 20. cap. XVII. 10. c. XX. 12. de posteriori Es. VII. 14. c. IX. 6. XXXIII. v. 15. proinde in hanc erupit confessionem: Rabbi, tu es Filius Dei, tu es Rex Israel. Existimat qui- dem Chrysostomus Nathanaelem Christum solum ut hominem confessum esse, eo quod addat, tu es Rex Israel, cum Filius Dei non modo Rex Israel sit, sed universi terrarum orbis; At Filius Dei describitur quandoque specialiter ceu Rex in Israel Psal. II. 6. Mich. V. 2. Quandoque generaliter, ceu Dominus u- niversi, quoad officium suum regium; nec illa descriptio est exclusiva, sed appropriativa, cum peculiari appropriatione Israel ad regnum Christi pertineat. Nec vero tribui potest Nathanaeli, quem in perscrutanda veritate diligentissimum Chrysost. dicit, & à scripturarum cognitione com- mendat, tanta ignorantia, ut opinatus sit, Filium Dei, Regem illum Israelis fore nudum tantum ho- minem, ideoque rectius Cyrillus hunc in locum: Noverat, inquit, probe Nathanael, soli Deo corda hominum patere, ac illud Psalmista infixum animo tenebat, scrutans corda & renes Deus, nulli namque alii, sed divinæ solummodo naturæ hoc Propheta at- tribuit. Id cum inesse Domino perspexiffet, & Ma- gistrum & Filium Dei & Regem Israel profitetur. Id- eo nec Christus redarguit ipsum quod non cre- deret, sed fidem potius ejus commendavit, eamq; ulterius corroboravit. Omnia autem illa è Scri- pturis V. T. desumta eum scripturæ Propheticæ peritissimum arguunt, quia Messias ut Rabbi primus Doctor describitur Deut. XVIII. 18. Es. L. 4. LV. 4. ut Filius Dei 2. Sam. VII. 14. Psal. II. 7. LXXXIX. 7. Proverb. VIII. 23. Mich. V. 2. ut Rex Israel, Psal. II. 6. Esa. IX. 7. Zach. IX. 9.

## 1:50
Ver. 50. πιστεύεις] I think it is rightly read assertively: as below XX. 29, ὅτι ἑώρακάς με πεπίστευκας.

There follows Christ's confirmation, by which he consolidated the disciple who had been received in his faith and confession, having made a promise of a nobler manifestation, in which there is both a commendation of Nathanael's faith: because I said to you, I saw you under the fig tree, you believe; and a promise of more illustrious demonstrations: you will see greater things than these: you are going to be more fervent in faith, as Cyril interprets, when you see greater things than these. For if you were led to faith by one sign, how will you not be better when you behold more wonderful things; and then a designation of a singular specimen, by which he was about to demonstrate himself to be the Son of God.

Μείζω τύτων] By which he may know himself to be King not only of Israel, but also of the angels.

b) d] I think this concerns those things which looked toward exciting greater faith in the disciples, and through them in others, therefore not about the day of judgment.

Latin:

Vers. 50. πιστεύεις] Puto recte legi assertive: quomodo in- fra XX. 29. ὅτι ἑώρακάς με πεπίστευκας.

Sequitur Christi confirmatio, qua discipulum sus- ceptum in fide & confessione sua consolida vit, fa- cta promissione nobilioris manifestationis, in qua tum commendatio habetur fidei Nathanaelis: quia dixi tibi, videbam Te sub ficu, credis; tum pollicita- tio illustriorum demonstrationum: majora his vi- debis: ferventior in fide futurus es, ut interpreta- tur Cyrillus, cum majora his videbis. Nam si uno signo inductus es ad fidem, quomodo non eris melior, quando mirabiliora conspicies; tum designatio speci- minis singularis, quo sese Filium Dei demonstratu- rus erat.

Μείζω τύτων] Quibus non Israelis tantum, sed & angelo- rum Rex cognoscat.

b) d] Puto agi de iis, quæ ad majorem fidem in discipulis, & per eos aliis excitandam spectabant, non ergo de die ju- dicii.

## 1:51
Ver. 51. ἀπαρτὶ ἀνεῳγότα] Preparation for the ὀπτασίας, as we said on Matt. III. 16.

ἀναβαίνοντας κὲ καταβαίνοντας ἐπὶ τὸν ὑὸν τῦ ἀνθρώπυ] It is a σύνχυσις: for ἐπὶ is properly referred to καταβαίνοντας. To ascend and descend, however, signifies ministry, such as the angels exhibited to Jesus in his passion, resurrection, and ascension into heaven. We have said elsewhere that whatever is attributed to God in the Old Covenant, the same is attributed to Christ in the New. Angels ascending and descending minister to God, Gen. XXVIII. 12; what Israel saw there in a dream, the same is said to be about to be seen by the true Israelite while awake; so that he may trust in Jesus himself all the more, just as Israel trusted in God.

Others prefer to render the particle ἐπὶ as "to," along with the Syriac: concerning which see Ludov. de Dieu: the Vulgate, Erasmus, Beza, and the Arab translate ἐπὶ as "upon" or "above." But the Syriac [translates it as] "to"; so that it may be referred as much to those ascending as to those descending, for the descent of the angels, when it is referred to Christ dwelling on earth, is rightly said to be a descent upon him: but their ascent, when it is referred to Christ living in the heavens, is not rightly said to be an ascent upon him: but they are rightly said both to ascend and descend to him. You have ἐπὶ with the accusative for πρὸς, "to," in Luke II. 3 and X. 9.

As for the matter itself, others wish this to be referred not merely to ministry, but explain it concerning some peculiar fact, which has not been expressed by the Evangelist, by which this prediction was fulfilled: Some interpret it not of any fact, but of the future day of the final coming of Christ for judgment, as Gomarus holds: and they judge that the ministry of angels is simply noted metaphorically: by a likeness drawn from the servants of Kings, who are accustomed to ascend and descend, so that they may execute their ministries commanded by the King. Nevertheless (Gomarus adds) that metaphor does not seem necessary, because the discourse is true even in its proper signification; so that the sense may be this: that Christ, as Lord of the angels, surrounded on all sides by their host, will descend from heaven into the air; but the angels, serving his divine command, will descend to the earth primarily to gather the elect and set them before the tribunal of Christ; and ascending to Christ, they themselves will set them there. This is Gomarus. Chrysostom thinks there is no need that we should explain it as referring to the future, or that we should have recourse to unrecorded histories; since both heaven was seen opened at the transfiguration of Christ, and angels descended from heaven at his resurrection. To us, the simplest explanation seems to be that Nathanael, being well-versed in the Law and the Prophets, was recalled by Christ to the type of Gen. XXVIII. shown to Jacob, and that he indicated that he would see or recognize that in himself this type was fulfilled and is being fulfilled, that he is that ladder which reaches from heaven to earth, on account of the hypostatic union of the heavenly or divine, and the earthly or human nature, and that this ladder was erected so that an ἀνακεφαλαίωσις (recapitulation) of all things in heaven and on earth might take place, Eph. I. 10, and that the angels both descend upon the Son of Man (because outside of this ladder no descent would be open to them to us) to provide ministry to the elect, and ascend in turn carrying the souls of the faithful into heaven, Luc. XVI. 22, or that they are said to descend and ascend simply, so that by this phrase their mission and ministry in those things which pertain to our salvation is intimated, just as, by a Hebrew phrase, one is said to come in and go out, Num. XXVII. v. 17, who is diligently occupied in performing his duty for the good of others over whom he is set. Compare B. Chemnit. Harm. Evang. c. XXV.

Moreover, it is helpful to add here what we publicly proposed in this Academy twenty years ago in the Discourses of Christ, chapter VI: The conversation, he says, is directed to those five disciples who had already received some taste of recognition; Amen, Amen I say to you, from now on you shall see heaven opened. In which most sweet and most worthy-to-be-considered promise, it is our intention to note (1.) The formula of asseveration, Amen, Amen. The word ἀμὴν, descending from the Hebrew אָמֵן, which introduces faith and truth: it is sometimes taken nominally, as in Isa. LXV. 15, Apoc. III. 14, sometimes adverbially, so that it is the same as certainly, truly, and that in a double sense; both in the affirmation of those things which are said by us, Matth. XVI. v. 28. Mark 12:43. Then in a vow and wish, Matt. 6:13, and elsewhere throughout, where it is the same as γένοιτο, let it be, as is clear from Deut. 27:15. Most people make this formula, when it is used in the affirmation of some matter, an oath, but it is more correctly established as an asseveration, since among the Hebrews only an asseveration and confirmation is introduced by that word, as R. Mordechai observes in the chapter on concordances, and Jerome agrees in Isaiah, book 8, chapter 25. The Lord often uses this word in the Gospel, Amen, that is, Truly, truly I say to you. This opinion is further confirmed both by the usage of Scripture, because that word nowhere introduces an oath in the O.T., and always, even when it is doubled, imports only a confirmation, as Deut. 27:15, Neh. 8:6, Ps. 41:13, and by the explanation of the Holy Scriptures, because this very word is declared by the little word ἀληθῶς, as is clear from a comparison of Matt. 16:28 with Luke 9:29. Mark 12:43 with Luke 21:3, then the permutation of the particle ναὶ; compare Matt. 23:36 with Luke 11:51, which two particles, ναὶ and ἀμὴν, explain each other mutually, Rev. 22:10, whence that doubled ναὶ is used just as the word ἀμὴν, Matt. 5:37, James 5:12. One will be able to read more about these in Nicholas Fuller, Miscellanea Theologica, book 1, chapter 2. Meanwhile, it does not seem to be denied that that word is like an oath, and obtains equal force in the confirmation of truth in the usage of Scripture: since an asseveration of that kind made by Christ is of no less strength than any oath whatsoever. In which sense Jerome, Commentary on Ezekiel 16, says that in the O.T. the oath of God is, As I live, says the Lord; but in the N.T. he says the oath of God is, Amen, Amen I say to you. Therefore Augustine, tractate 41 on John: In a certain way, he says, if it is right to say so, Amen, Amen I say to you is an oath. If you say with Fuller that God is interposed in every oath as witness and judge, the same is also the case here at least implicitly, because that asseveration is instituted by such a word, from which God is called the God Amen, Isa. 65:16.

(2.) A note of time. Henceforth, which is properly the same as from now on, from this time, Rev. 14:13, by which manner it is designated that they will see that shortly from now, which Christ promises, or it is noted indefinitely that they will see it in its own time thereafter. The former acceptance, however, agrees with the genuine use of the word.

(3.) The prophecy of a future vision, and of its double nature; namely, that they will see both heaven opened and the angels ascending and descending upon the Son of man. Which others take figuratively, that he will openly demonstrate himself to be God, whom alone the angels serve. Others explain it mystically concerning heaven opened to us through Christ, and the entrance laid open to believers, and also concerning preachers, who are also called angels, and ascend, according to Augustine, by imitation, and descend by preaching; they ascend according to Bede where they speak of sublime things, they descend where they speak of humble things concerning Christ. B. Chemnitius understands it concerning the doctrine and fuller knowledge of the person and office of Christ. The interlinear gloss explains it simply concerning the more illustrious miracles by which Christ was about to prove his divinity; others take it according to the letter, either concerning the opening of heaven, which indeed happened but was nowhere included in the writings, but it is not safe enough to take refuge in such unwritten things. Others explain it concerning the opening of heaven that happened at the baptism, and concerning the angels approaching in the desert, Matt. 4:11. But since this concerns a future vision, that interpretation has no place. Therefore others explain it concerning heaven opened in the glorification of Christ, Matt. 17:2. Others concerning the heavens miraculously opened to the protomartyr Stephen, Acts 7:56. Others interpret it concerning the angels at the resurrection and ascension of Christ, Acts 1:10.

Finally, others explain it concerning the final judgment, where with the heavens opened the angels will descend, and the Deity of Christ will be demonstrated most clearly. We think thus: that a more illustrious confirmation of faith is promised here, not only in general, that they will see the Lord from heaven as if the heavens were opened, and will recognize Christ more and more as true God by most abundant proofs, whom the angels deservedly serve; but also that they will enjoy this glory of the Lord with their own eyes as if heaven were truly opened; then in the transfiguration, at which two of these disciples were present, Matt. 17:2; then in the assumption into heaven, attended by the ministry of angels, which all his disciples without doubt beheld, Acts 1:11, where the angels had let themselves down with the heavens opened, which also happened in the passion and resurrection, and the heavens opened themselves again to Christ entering heaven with an angelic retinue, so that the God of glory might enter, Ps. 24; then in the return to judgment, which will be such as the ascension. Concerning which Eusebius: Then, he says, the holy ones will see heaven opened, and the angels ascending and descending, then also Nathanael, who believed so easily, will see greater things, when Christ the Lord will appear in his majesty. The angels therefore descended in his passion and resurrection, which had also happened before in his conception and temptation in the desert, but they ascended in the ascension of Christ into heaven: they will descend and ascend together on the last day. They descended when something had to be announced concerning the Son of man and to be ministered to the faithful: they ascend when they transfer the souls of the faithful into heaven. But these are said to descend and ascend upon the Son of man, not in that sense that this will happen because of the Son of man, that is, for the sake of services to be rendered to him, for his reverence, glory, and majesty, but because Christ is the very ladder upon which they ascended and descended, which the proper force of the preposition ἐπὶ suggests, when someone is said to ascend upon someone. For unless the Son of God had let himself down to earth like that ladder of Jacob, Gen. 28, which he truly wished to recall to the memory of the Israelite Nathanael here, no angel would ever have descended or ascended for the sake of the salvation of men. They confirm this explanation: (1.) the very evidence of the words, which must by no means be abandoned in their literal sense without a compelling reason; and they imply both something that will happen a little later, and a true vision, and not merely some knowledge, and also a true ανάβασιν and κατάβασιν of the holy angels, the heavenly spirits. But with our explanation standing, from now on, or from that time, such a thing began to be fulfilled truly, and subsequently it was fulfilled more and more as the disciples of Christ saw and knew, until it will be fulfilled most fully and most clearly at the final return. (2.) The analogy of Scripture, because it is customary for Christ, when He wishes to demonstrate His Deity, to appeal to His ascension and exaltation, as also to His glorious coming, John III. 13, VI. 62, Luke XXII. 69, where that particle from now on is also found. (3.) The harmony of the fulfillment, since in Scripture such things are read everywhere concerning the ministry of angels rendered to the Son of Man, and still to be rendered at the final coming, so that there is no need to have recourse to unwritten histories. (4.) The meritorious cause of the ascension and descension of the angels, since it is certain that it is only upon this ladder that angels descend and ascend for the sake of our salvation, since the reconciliation of all things which are in heaven and on earth is attributed to Christ, Col. I. 20, and the ἀνακεφαλαίωσις of all things, Eph. I. 10, and it has been truly said by Bonaventure: The ladder of paradise, made in Adam, is repaired in Christ.

(5.) The purpose of the agreement. For to what end does Christ predict both of these things, that both heaven will be opened and that the Angels will ascend and descend upon the Son of man? Certainly to no other end than to teach that by both of these means he will be manifested more illustriously as the Son of God, the promised Messiah, which indeed fits our interpretation perfectly. For by the opening of heaven at the Transfiguration of Christ, and at his ascension into Heaven, Christ was clearly demonstrated to be the Son of God, there by a heavenly voice, here by glorious exaltation. Cf. Rom. 1:4. By the καταβάσεως καὶ ἀναβάσεως (descent and ascent) of the Angels, by which they served him in his Passion and Resurrection, by which they demonstrated his Majesty and Glory with their company, the Son of God was likewise clearly manifested, whom alone the Angels serve, and whom they venerate as Lord, Ps. 97:5, Heb. 1:7. Finally, in the return to Judgment, in both ways, both by the opening of Heaven and by the descent of the angels accompanying Christ, Christ will demonstrate himself to be the Son of God in a most illustrious manner, not only to these disciples, but to all the elect, so that they may recognize in a most perfect way that which they understand here only in part, and there behold through sight what they here apprehend through faith. (6.) The purpose of the type. Since this explanation responds excellently to the Vision made to Jacob Israel, to which Christ refers that true Israelite. For there it was figured how the Angels would ascend and descend upon the Son of man as a ladder reaching from heaven to earth, Gen. 28:12, where one may likewise observe that in the former place mention is made of ascent, in the latter of descent, just as here by Christ, whence we can conclude that Christ alluded to that place. Concerning which see August. lib. 16, de Civ. Dei, cap. 38. By that Ladder is understood the Savior himself, recalling to our memory that in the Gospel, etc.; indeed, something was figured here which pertains to a great Sacrament, and serm. 4 de verb. Domini: The dream of a man would not be written unless a great mystery were signified. (7.) The agreement of interpreters. For, to pass over more recent ones, St. Chrysostom explains the words of Christ thus: To whom the Angels minister, and upon whom they descend and ascend, in what way will he be thought to be (merely) a man? And further: Christ persuades Nathanael with these words to confess him as the Lord of Angels, for as if upon the most beloved Son of the King, the royal Ministers both ascended and descended, the former at the time of the Passion, the latter at the time of the Resurrection and ascension. Cyril. He announces that the Angels will come up and down to the Son of man, ministering, that is, to his commands for the salvation of believers, when he will be most especially believed to be the Son of God. And by this interpretation of ours, not only are the words of Christ retained in their proper sense, but the explanations of most interpreters are joined: If it be said that a richer knowledge of the Son of God was promised here by this twin means of the opening of Heaven and the angelic ascent and descent, as has already been explained. We note further that Christ is called the Son of man where Nathanael had professed him to be the Son of God, so that he might be taught that he is both the Son of man and the Son of God, and that whatever glorious thing befits the Son of God, all this might be insinuated to belong to the Son of man, or to Christ according to his human nature, such as this also is, that the Angels ascend and descend upon him. The appellation of the Son of man is otherwise customary regarding Christ, and to him also in the Evangelical history and in the whole New Testament it is proper, since no one else is called the Son of man, than he alone

Christ. H. Grotius indeed wishes, in his annotations on this place, that by the Son of man in Matt. 12:32 any man whatsoever be understood, and he strives to teach this from a comparison with Matt. 12:8. But there the Sabbath is indeed said to be made for man, but not any man whatsoever, but the Son of man, Christ the Lord, is constituted Lord of the Sabbath. Which words cohere perfectly, because the Sabbath is for the sake of man, not man for the sake of the Sabbath, and who would doubt that the Son of man himself, who is the Son of God, is the Lord of the Sabbath! Be it so, that among the Hebrews בֶּן אָדָם denotes any man, and that sometimes that name is restricted to illustrious men, yet that name is peculiarly appropriated to the Son of God in the New Testament, as is clear from an induction of places, nor can any contrary example be brought forward. The place Matt. 12:32, to which Grotius appeals, is likewise correctly explained of Christ by almost all Interpreters, and the sense is that it is a graver sin against the Holy Spirit than if anyone had affected Christ the Son of man with some blasphemy in the days of his flesh, because sin against the Holy Spirit, specifically so called, brings about the rejection of the means of salvation and the blaspheming of them, and therefore it is not undeservedly considered graver. Moreover, Christ is called by this name (I.) because of the Davidic prediction Ps. 8:3, in which he is called the Son of man, the Holy Spirit being the interpreter, Heb. 2:6. (II.) Because of the Prophetic vision: who is so named in Dan. 7:13, when he saw the Son of man coming in the clouds to the Ancient of days. (III.) Because of the designation of his human nature. For just as Christ is called the Son of God, so that his divine nature may be designated; so also he is called the Son of man, so that his true humanity may be expressed; and just as the former name befits him because of his eternal generation from the Father, so this one befits him because of his temporal generation from his mother; that ὁμοούσιαν with God the Father, this ὁμοουσίαν of Christ with his virgin mother, and therefore with all men, it imports, since he is the true Son of man, the true seed of the woman Gen. III. 15. (IV.) On account of the Exinanition. For since the Hebrews love to speak distinctly of true illustrious men, whom they call sons of a man, and of others less illustrious, whom they call sons of man, by this reasoning is insinuated at the same time the exinanition of Christ, by which he willed to be humbled, so that he was made like a vile servant and the most abject of men, Is. LIII. 4. (V.) On account of the foreshadowing of the office. For just as the Prophet Ezekiel is called the Son of man peculiarly; so also Christ, that great Prophet, willed to be called by this name. But that in Dan. VII. 13. Apoc. 1. 13. ch. XIV. 14. he is said to be like the son of man, either by the likeness itself the truth is expressed, or respect is had to the vision, because that image seen by Daniel and John was like the Son of man, i. e. like to Christ.

Latin:

Vers. 51. ἀπαρτὶ ἀνεῳγότα] Præparatio ad ὀπτασίας, ut di- ximus ad Matth. III. 16.

ἀναβαίνοντας κὲ καταβαίνοντας ἐπὶ τὸν ὑὸν τῦ ἀνθρώπυ] Est σύνχυσις: nam ἐπι proprie refertur ad καταβαίνοντας. Ascen- dere autem & descendere ministerium significat, quale an- geli Jesu exhibuerunt in passione, resurrectione, ascensu in cœlum. Diximus alibi, quæcunque Deo tribuuntur in ve- teri fœdere, eadem in novo Christo tribui. Angeli ascen- dentes & descendentes Deo ministrant, Gen. XXVIII. 12. quod ibi in somnio vidit Israël, idem vigilans visurus dici- tur verus Israëlita; quo magis ipse Jesu confidat, sicut Israël Deo confisus est.

Particulam ἐπὶ alii reddere malunt ad cum Sy- ro: quo de Ludov. de Dieu: Vulgatus, Erasmus, Beza & Arabs ἐπὶ vertunt super, vel supra.
