At Sy- rus ad; ut tam ad ascendentes, quam descendentes referri queat, nam descensus angelorum, quum re- feratur ad Christum in terris versantem, recte dicun- tur super eum descendere: sed ascensus eorum, quum referatur ad Christum in cælis degentem, non recte dicuntur ascendere super ipsum: sed ad ipsum & ascendere & descendere recte dicuntur. ἐπὶ cum accus. pro πρὸς, ad, habes Luc. II. 3. & X. 9.

Quod ad rem ipsam, non ad ministerium modo referri hoc alii volunt, sed de facto quodam pecu- liari explicant, quod ab Evangelista expressum non sit, quo hæc prædictio completa fuerit: Qui- dam non de facto aliquo, sed de futuro demum die ul- timo adventu Christi ad judicium interpretantur, ut habet Gomarus: & Metaphorice simpliciter ange- lorum ministerium notari censent: similitudine à Regum servis deducta, qui ascendere & descendere solent, ut sua ministeria a Rege imperata exequantur. Veruntamen (addit Gomarus) ea Metaphora non videtur necessaria, quia propria significatione vera etiam est oratio; ut sensus hic sit: quod Christus, ut angelorum Dominus, caterva eorum circum- quaque stipatus è cœlo in aerem descendet; An- geli vero divino ejus imperio servientes, ad ele- ctos imprimis colligendos, & coram tribunali Christi sistendos in terram descendent; & ad Chri- stum ascendentes eos ipsi sistent. Hæc Gomarus. Chrysostomus non opus esse censet, ut vel de futuro explicemus, vel ad historias non consignatas re- curramus; siquidem & cælum apertum visum sit in transfiguratione Christi, & de cælo descenderint ange- li in resurrectione ejus. Nobis videtur simplicissi- ma explicatio, quia Nathanael in lege & Prophetis probe versatus fuit, Christum revocasse eundem ad typum Gen. XXVIII. Jacobo ostensum, idque indicasse, visurum vel cogniturum ipsum, in sese impletum esse, & impleri hunc typum, se esse illam scalam, quæ de cælo in terram pertingit, propter unionem hypostaticam cœlestis vel divinæ, & terrenæ vel humanæ naturæ, & hanc scalam erectam esse, ut ἀνακεφαλαίωσις omnium in cælo & in terra fiat. Eph. I. 10. angelique & descendant super Filium homi- nis (quia extra hanc scalam nullus ad nos pateret ipsis descensus) ad ministerium electis præbendum, & ascendant vicissim animas fidelium portantes in cæ- lum, Luc. XVI. 22. vel descendere & ascendere sim- pliciter dicantur, ut hac phrasi innuatur emissio & ministerium eorum, in iis quæ ad salutem nostram faciunt, quemadmodum, phrasi Ebræa, ingredi & egredi dicitur, Num. XXVII. v. 17. qui obeundo officio suo in aliorum bonum sedulo occupatur, quibus præfectus est. Confer B. Chemnit. Harm. Evang. c. XXV.

Addere autem hic juvat, quæ in Eloquiis Chri- sti ante hos viginti annos cap. VI. de hisce publice in hac Academia proposuimus: Conversio sermo- ne ad quinque illos discipulos, qui jam gustum ali- quem agnitionis acceperant, inquit; Amen, Amen dico vobis, a modo videbitis cælum apertum. In qua promissione suavissima & consideratu dignissima notare nobis animus est (1.) Asseverationis formu- lam, Amen, Amen. Vox ἀμὴν ab Ebræa אָמֵן fi- dem & veritatem inferente, descendens: modo nominaliter accipitur, utpote Esa. LXV. 15. Apoc. III. 14. modo adverbialiter, ut idem sit, quod cer- to, vere, idque duplici sensu; tum in affirmatione eorum, quæ à nobis dicuntur Matth. XVI. v. 28. Marc. XII. v. 43. tum in voto & optatione, Matth. VI. 13. & alias passim, ubi idem est, quod γένοιτο fiat, ut liquet e Deut. XXVII. 15. Formulam hanc, cum in affirmatione rei alicujus adhibetur, plerique fa- ciunt juratoriam, at rectius ea asseveratoria sta- tuitur, cum apud Ebræos ea voce solum assevera- tio & confirmatio inferatur, ut observat R. Mar- dochai in cap. concordant. annuitque Hieronym. in Esaiam l. 8. c. 25. Dominus in Evangelio sæpe hoc verbo utitur Amen, id est, Vere, vere dico vobis. Quam sententiam confirmat ulterius tum Scri- pturæ usurpatio, quod nuspiam ea vox in V. T. jus- jurandum inferat, semper etiam cum duplicatur, solum confirmationem importet, ut Deut. XXVII. v. 15. Neh. VIII. 6. Psal. XLI. 13. tum S. S. explicatio, quod hæc ipsa vox per voculam ἀληθῶς declare- tur, ut è collatione liquet Matth. XVI. 28. cum Luc. IX. 29. Marc. XII. 43. cum Luc. XXI. 3. tum parti- culæ và permutatio; Confer Matth. XXIII. v. 36. cum Luc. XI. v. 51. quæ duæ particulæ và & ἀμὴν, mutuo sese explicant, Apoc. XXII. 10. unde æque il- lud và geminatum adhibetur, uti vox ἀμὴν, Matth. V. 37. Jac. V. 12. Legi de his pluribus poterit Nicol. Fullerus in Miscell. Theol. l. 1. c. 2. Interim negandum non videtur, quin vox ea instar jurisju- randi sit, & in veritatis confirmatione parem vim obtineat in usu scripturæ: quandoquidem asseve- ratio ejusmodi à Christo facta non minoris roboris sit, quam juramentum quodcunque. Quo sen- su Hieron. Comm. in Ezech. XVI. in V. T. ait: Dei juramentum esse, Vivo ego dicit Dominus; in N. autem Testam. ait, Dei juramentum esse, Amen, Amen dico vobis. Ideo August. tract. 41. in Joh. Quodammodo, inquit, si dico fas est, juratio est Amen, Amen dico vobis. Si dicas cum Füllero, in omni juramento interponi Deum, ceu testem & judicem, idem etiam hic sit saltem implicite, quia asseve- ratio illa instituitur tali voce, a qua DEUS DEUS Amen denominatur, Es. LXV. v. 15.

(2.) Temporis notam. Posthac, quod proprie idem est, quod à modo, ab hoc tempore, Apoc. XIV. 13. quo pacto designatur brevi abhinc eos id visuros, quod Christus pollicetur, vel indefinite notatur, quod deinceps suo tempore id visuri sint. Prior tamen acceptio usui vocis germano congruit.

(3.) Visionis futuræ prophetiam, ejusque geminæ; quod scilicet visuri sint, & cælum apertum, & angelos ascendentes & descendentes super Filium hominis. Quod alii figurate accipiunt, quod nempe sese a- perte demonstraturus sit Deum, cui soli angeli serviunt. Alii exponunt mystice de cælo nobis per Christum aperto, & ingressu credentibus patefacto, itemque de concionatoribus, qui etiam angeli vo- cantur, & ascendunt, secundum Augustinum, imi- tatione, descendunt prædicatione; ascendunt juxta Bedam, ubi sublimia, descendunt, ubi de Christo di- cunt humilia. B. Chemnitius intelligit id de doctri- na & agnitione uberiori personæ & officii Christi. Gloss. interlinearis exponit simpliciter de miracu- lis illustrioribus, quibus divinitatem suam com- probaturus erat Christus; Alii secundum literam accipiunt, vel de apertione cæli, quæ facta quidem sit, sed nuspiam in scriptis comprehensa, sed ad e- jusmodi ἄγραφα non satis tutum est confugere. Alii de apertione cæli in baptismo facta explicant, & de angelis accedentibus in deserto Matth. IV. v. 11. Sed cum hic de futura visione agatur, interpretatio illa locum non habet. Proinde alii de cælo aperto in glorificatione Christi exponunt Matth. XVII. 2. Alii de cælis miraculose apertis protomartyri Ste- phano, Act. VII. 56. Alii de Angelis in resurrectione & ascensione Christi interpretantur Actor. I. v. 10.

Alii deniq; de extremo judicio exponunt, ubi cœ- lis apertis angeli descendent, Christi q; Deitas lu- culentissime demonstrabitur. Nos ita existima- mus; promitti illustriorem hic fidei confirmationem, non modo in genere, quod cœlis veluti apertis Do- minum de cœlo visuri sint, Christumq; ceu verum Deum magis magisq; documentis locupletissimis agnituri, cui merito serviant angeli; sed etiam glo- riam hanc Domini cœlo vere aperto veluti oculis suis usurpaturi; tum in transfiguratione, cui bini ex his discipulis interfuêre, Matth. XVII. 2. tum in assumptione in cælum, stipata angelorum ministe- rio, quam omnes ejus discipuli sine dubio adspexe- re, Act. I. 11. ubi cœlis apertis demiserant sese Ange- li, quod etiam in passione, & resurrectione factum, & Christo cœlum ingredienti cum angelico comita- tu iterum sese aperuêre cœli, ut Deus gloriæ ingre- deretur Psal. XXIV. tum in reditu ad judicium, qui talis futurus, qualis ascensio. Quo de Eusebius: Tunc, inquit, cælum apertum, & angelos ascendentes & descendentes sancti videbunt, tunc & Nathanaël, qui tam facile credidit, majora videbit, quando in sua majestate Christus Dominus apparebit. Descen- derunt ergo in passione & resurrectione ipsius ange- li, quod antea quoque factum fuit in conceptione ac tentatione ipsius in deserto, ascenderunt vero in a- scensione Christi in cælum: descendent & ascendent simul in novissimo die. Descenderunt cum annun- ciandum aliquid fuit de filio hominis & mini- strandum fidelibus: Ascendunt cum animas fideli- um in cœlum transferunt. Hi vero ἐπὶ supra Filium hominis descendere ac ascendere dicuntur, non eo modo sensu, quod propter Filium hominis, id est, ob servitia ipsi præstanda, ob reverentiam, glo- riam & majestatem ejus, hoc futurum sit, sed quod Christus sit ipsa scala, super quam illi ascenderunt & descenderunt, quod propria vis præpositionis ἐπὶ subinsert, quando quis super aliquem ascende- re dicitur. Nisi enim Filius Dei sese in terram de- misisset instar scalæ illius Jacobeæ Genes. XXVIII. quam hic vero Israelitæ Nathanaeli revocare vo- luit in memoriam, nunquam ullus angelorum de- scendisset vel ascendisset salutis hominum causa. Explicationem hanc confirmant: (1.) ipsa verbo- rum evidentia, quæ proprio sensu citra causam prægnantem nequaquam deserenda; & inferunt tum quoddam paulo post futurum, tum visionem veram, non autem solum cognitionem aliquam, tum etiam veram ανάβασιν & κατάβασιν angelo- rum sanctorum spirituum cœlestium. At stante no- stra explicatione, à modo, vel ab isto tempore tale quid impleri cœpit vere, ac subinde magis magisq; videntibus & cognoscentibus discipulis Christi im- pletum fuit, donec plenissime & luculentissime id implebitur in reditu novissimo. (2.) Scripturæ a- nalogia, quia solenne est Christo, cum Deitatem suam demonstrare vult, provocare ad ascensionem & exaltationem suam, ut & adventum gloriosum, Joh. III. 13. VI, 62. Luc. XXII. 69. ubi etiam parti- cula illa à modo reperitur. (3.) Complementi har- monia, quandoquidem in scriptura passim talia de angelorum ministerio Filio hominis præstito, & adhuc præstando, in adventu novissimo, legantur, ut non opus sit ad historias non-scriptas confuge- re. (4.) Meritoria ascensionis & descensionis an- gelorum causa, cum certum sit, non nisi supra hanc scalam Christum angelos descendere & ascendere, nostræ salutis ergo, quandoquidem Christo attri- buatur reconciliatio omnium, quæ in cœlo & in terra sunt, Col. I. 20. & ἀνακεφαλαίωσις omnium Eph. I. 10. ac vere à Bonaventura dictum sit: Scala paradisi facta in Adamo, reparata est in Christo.

(5.) Finis convenientia. Quo enim fine utrumque hoc prædicit Christus, tum cælum apertum iri, tum Angelos ascensuros & descensuros super Filium hominis? nullo certe alio, quam ut doceat, utroque hoc medio sese illustrius manifestatum iri, ceu Dei Filium, promissum Messiam, quod utique nostræ interpretationi optime congruit. Cæli enim aper- tione in Transfiguratione Christi, & in ascensione in Cælum facta, Christus luculenter demonstratus est Dei Filius, ibi voce cælesti, hic exaltatione glo- riosa. Conf. Rom. I. 4. Angelorum καταβάσεως καὶ ἀ- ναβάσεως, qua inservierunt ipsi in Passione & Resurre- ctione, qua Majestatem & Gloriam ipsius comitatu suo demonstrarunt, pariter Filius Dei luculenter manifestatus est, cui soli Angeli serviunt, eumque ceu Dominum venerantur Ps. XCVII. 5. Ebr. I. 7. Denique in reditu ad Judicium utroque modo & apertione Cæli, & descensu angelorum Christum co- mitantium, illustrissima ratione Filium Dei sese demonstraturus est Christus, non tantum his di- seipulis, sed omnibus electis, ut modo perfectissi- mo id agnoscant, quod hic ex parte tantum intelli- gunt, ibi per speciem intueantur, quod hic per fidem, apprehendunt (6.) Typi congruentia. Cum egre- gie hæc explicatio respondeat Visioni Jacobis Is- raeli factæ, ad quam Israëlitam illum verum re- mittit Christus. Illic enim figuratum fuit, quomodo super Filium hominis ceu scalam de cælo in terram pertingentem ascensuri sint & descensuri Angeli Gen. XXIX. 13. ubi pariter observare licet, quod priori loco ascensionis, posteriori descensionis mentio fiat, perinde uti hic à Christo, unde colligere possu- mus. Christum ad istum locum allusisse. Quo de Au- gust. l. XVI. d. C. D. c. 38. Per Scalam istam intelligi- tur ipse Salvator nobis in memoriam revocans id in Ev- angelio &c. profecto figuratum est hinc aliquid, quod ad magnum pertineat Sacramentum, & serm. 4. de verb. Domini: Somnium hominis non scriberetur ni- si magnum mysterium significaretur. (7.) Interpre- tum consonantia. Nam ut alios mittamus re- centiores, explicat ita fere verba Christi S. Chry- sost. Cui Angeli ministrant, & super quem descendunt & ascendunt, quonam pacto homo (merus) esse existi- mabitur? & porro: Suadet his verbis Christus, ut ipsum Angelorum Dominum confiteatur Nathanael, tanquam enim super dilectissimum Regis Filium regii Ministri, & adscenderunt & descenderunt, hoc qui- dem Passionis, illud Resurrectionis & ascensionis tem- pore. Cyrill. Angelos sursum atque deorsum ad Fi- lium hominis venturos annunciat, mandatis videlicet suis ad salutem credentium ministrantes, quando maxime Filius Dei esse credetur. Atq; hac nostra in- terpretatione non retinentur tantum verba Chri- sti sensu proprio, sed & plerorumq; interpretum explicationes conjunguntur: Si dicatur, cognitionem uberiorem Filii Dei hic promissam fuisse, gemino i- sto medio Cæli aperiundi, & adscensus ac descensus angelici, prout jam expositum est. Id adhuc nota- mus, Filium hominis vocari Christum, ubi Nathanael eum professus erat Filium Dei, ut eundem & homi- nis, & Dei Filium esse doceretur, & quicquid glo- riosi Dei Filio congruit, hoc omne Filio hominis, vel Christo secundum humanam naturam conve- nire insinuaretur, quale etiam hoc est, quod Angeli ascendant & descendant super ipso. Usitata est alias appellatio Filii hominis de Christo, eiq; etiam in hi- storia Evangelica & in toto N. Test. propria, cum nemo alius vocetur Filius hominis, quam solus

Christus. H. Grotius quidem vult, Matth. XII. 32. per Filium hominis hominem quemvis intelligi in an- not. ad h. l. idq; è collatione Matth. XII. 8. docere annititur. Sed ibi Sabbatum quidem propter homi- nem conditum dicitur, at non homo quivis, sed Filius hominis Christus Dominus Sabbati constituitur. Quæ verba optime cohærent, quia Sabbatuin ho- minis causa est, non homo Sabbati causa, & quis ambiget, ipsum Filium hominis, qui Dei Filius est, Sabbati Dominum esse! Sit ita, Ebræis בֶּן אָדָם homi- nem quemvis notare, & quandoque id nominis ad homines illustres restringi, nomen tamen illud pecu- liariter appropriari Filio Dei in N. Test. ex indu- ctione locorum liquet, nec contrarium exemplum ullum adferri potest. Locus Matth. XII. 32. ad quein Grotius provocat, itidem recte de Christo expli- catur à plerisque omnibus Interpretibus, & sensus est, gravius esse peccatum in Spiritum S. quam si quis Christum Filium hominis in diebus carnis blasphemia quadam affecerit, quia peccatum in Spirit. S. speci- fice ita dictum infert mediorum salutis reprobatio- nem, eorumq; blasphemationem, ideoque non im- merito gravius censetur. Vocatur autem Christus hoc nomine (I.) ob Davidicam prædictionem Psal. VIII. 3. in qua Filius hominis vocatus est, interprete Spiritu S. Ebr. II. 6. (II.) Ob Propheticam visionem: qui a Dan. VII. 13. ita nuncupatus est, cum videret Filium hominis venientem in nubibus ad antiquu dierum. (III.) Ob humanæ naturæ designationem. Quemadmodum enim Christus Filius Dei vocatur, ut divina ejus natura designetur; ita & Filius homi- nis nuncupatur, ut vera ejus humanitas exprima- tur; & ut istud nomen ei competit ob generationem à Patre æternam, ita hoc ob generationem à matre temporariam; illud ὁμοούσιαν cum Deo Patre, hoc ὁμοουσίαν Christi cum matre virgine, adeoq; cum o- mnibus hominibus importat, cum verus sit Filius hominis, verum semen mulieris Gen. III. 15. (IV.) Ob Exinanitionem. Cum enim Ebræi distinctim lo- qui ament de veris illustribus, quos filios viri nun- cupant, & de aliis minus illustribus, quos dicunt fi- lios hominis, insinuatur hac ratione simul exinani- tio Christi, qua humiliari voluit, ita, ut instar vilis servi factus est & virorum abjectissimus, Es. LIII. 4. (V.) Ob officii adumbrationem. Ut enim Ezechiel Propheta Filius hominis peculiariter est vocatus; ita etiam Christus, Propheta ille magnus hoc no- mine nuncupari voluit. Quod vero Dan. VII. 13. A- poc. 1. 13. c. XIV. 14. similis dicitur filio hominis, vel si- militudine ipsa veritas exprimitur, vel ad visionem respectus habetur, quod illa imago Danieli ac Jo- hanni visa, Filio hominis, i. e. Christo similis fuerit.

## 2:1 Argument
CHAPTER II. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

Jesus at the Cana wedding, wine failing, turned water into most excellent wine, manifesting his glory by this first miracle, and his disciples believed in him, with whom and his mother he betook himself to Capernaum: Soon however from there he set out to Jerusalem for the Passover, he cast out the sellers and money-changers from the temple according to the prophecy (Ps. LXIX. 10.) But to the Jews demanding a sign he predicted that he would raise up the temple within three days, speaking of the temple of his body: and many having seen his signs believed in his name, but he did not entrust himself to them, for he knew all men. There are three parts: I. The miracle of water turned into wine at the wedding, to v. 11. II. The journey to Capernaum, v. 12. III. Acts at the Jerusalem Passover, to v. 25.

PART I. The first miracle of water turned into wine.

Vers. 1. Τρίτῃ] The third, after Simon had approached Christ, for from here he had already begun to reckon the times above.

Γάμῳ] A banquet, namely a wedding one, the Syrian rightly translates, as has also been noted at Matt. XXII. 2.

ἐν Κανᾷ τῆς Γαλιλαίας] Josephus in his Life: 'I was staying at that time in a village of Galilee, which is called Cana.'

ἦν ἡ μήτηρ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ ἐκεῖ] Joseph having already died, she was a widow, perhaps so that she might arrange what was necessary for the wedding by right of proximity as a matchmaker or wedding-leader.

Latin:

CAPUT II. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Iesus in nuptiis Cananeis deficiente vino a- quam in vinum præstantissimum conver- tit, manifestans gloriam suam hoc primo miraculo, & crediderunt in ipsum discipuli ejus, cum quib. & matre Capernaum se con- tulit: Mox autem inde Hierosolymam ad pa- scha profectus, ejecit venditores & numula- rios è templo juxta vaticinium (Ps. LXIX. 10.) Iudæis vero signum postulantibus prædixit, se templum intra triduum erecturum, lo- quens de templo corporis sui: multiq; visis ejusdem signis in nomen ejus credidere, sed non credidit se ipsis, omnes quippe novit. Partes sunt tres: I. Miraculum aquæ in nuptiis in vinum conversæ, ad v. 11. II. Profectio in Capernaum, v. 12. III. Acta in Paschate Hierosolymitano, ad v. 25.

PARS I. Primum Miraculum aquæ in vinum conversæ.

Vers. 1. Τρίτῃ] Tertia, postquam Simon ad Christum ac- cesserat, nam hinc tempora putare jam supra cœperat.

Γάμῳ] Convivium, nuptiale scilicet, recte vertit Syrus, ut & ad Matth. XXII. 2. notatum est.

ἐν Κανᾷ τῆς Γαλιλαίας] Josephus vita sua διέτριβον δὲ κατὰ τὸ καιρὸν ἐκεῖνον ἐν κώμῃ τῆς Γαλιλαίας, ἣ προσαγορεύεται Κανᾶ.

ἦν ἡ μήτηρ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ ἐκεῖ] Mortuo jam Josepho vidua, for- te ut ea quæ ad nuptias opus erant jure proximitatis ador- naret ut προμνήστρια vel νυμφάγωγος.

## 2:2
Vers. 2. ἐκλήθη δὲ καὶ ὁ Ἰησοῦς] Because perhaps he was not far away. Thus the number of guests seems to have grown beyond expectation.

οἱ μαθηταὶ αὐτοῦ] Those followers named in the first chapter.

Christ appeared at a wedding, because he wished to inaugurate the first rudiments of his power in it with water, as Tertullian speaks in lib. de Bapt. c. 9. For it was fitting, as Cyril of Alexandria excellently says in lib. II. in Joh. c. 21, since he was restoring the whole nature of man for the better, not only to bless those already born, but also to prepare grace for those yet to be born, and to make their entrance into this life holy by the authority of a miracle and his own presence.

Latin:

Vers. 2. ἐκλήθη δὲ καὶ ὁ Ἰησοῦς] Quia forte non longe aberat. Ita videtur crevisse convivarum numerus ultra expectatum.

οἱ μαθηταὶ αὐτοῦ] Sectatores illi primo capite nominati.

In nuptiis Christus comparuit, quia in illis pri- mæ rudimenta potestatis suæ, ut loquitur Tertull. l. de Bapt. c. 9. aqua auspicari voluit. Oportebat e- nim, ut eximie Cyrill. Alex. l. II. in Joh. c. 21. ait, quoniam totam naturam hominis ad melius restaura- bat, non solum natis jam hominibus benedicere, verum etiam nascituris gratiam præparare, & aditum illorum ad hanc vitam autoritate miraculi & præsentia sua sanctum efficere.

## 2:3
Vers. 3. ὑστερήσαντος οἴνου] When it began to fail, and for that reason was being poured more sparingly.

οἶνον οὐκ ἔχουσι] Personal for impersonal. The wine is failing.

Latin:

Vers. 3. ὑστερήσαντος οἴνου] Cum deficere inciperet, eoque infundi parcius.

οἶνον οὐκ ἔχουσι] Personale pro impersonali. Deficit vinum.

## 2:4
Vers. 4. τί ἐμοὶ καὶ σοὶ γύναι] That is, what business does this present to me? Matt. VIII. 29.

Words worthy of note, which are not supplicatory, as Costerus maintains in his homily, p. 283, and ineptly attempts to prove by the words of the demon in Luke IV. 34. For what necessity had the Lord to supplicate his mother, and does the reason added, "my hour has not yet come," in any way present the appearance of a supplication? But they are objurgatory; "what business have I with you," or "what right have you," "why do you intrude yourself," as in similar passages, Jud. XI. 12, 2 Sam. XVI. 10, Ezra IV. 3, Matth. VIII. 29. The form of the words and the reason subjoined teach that this intervention was untimely and by no means appropriate. Christ indeed wished to testify by responding rather harshly in this manner (1.) the majesty of his divinity. Therefore it was also answered, says Greg. M. Ep. 42, "what have I to do with you, woman," as if it were said openly, whence can I perform a miracle, this is from the Father, not from the mother. For from the mother he could die, he who by the nature of the Father was performing miracles. (2.) The dignity of his office, in which he suffers no one to dictate to him. He was subject to his mother until he undertook his office; she used her maternal authority toward him in his private life, but now, when she wishes to use the same in his office, he says, "What have I to do with thee, woman?" Beautifully Chrysostom, hom. 20 in John. He had a care for maternal honor, but far more for the salvation of souls and the common benefit to many, for the sake of which he took on human flesh. These are not, therefore, the words of one speaking too freely to his mother, but words of divine dispensation, that he might admonish that miracles were to be performed according to their dignity. He also taught by this very thing that, in matters which pertain to God or our duty, we should not acknowledge kinsmen or mother. Most excellently, says Bernard, hom. 2 in Dom. I. post Epiph., the Lord taught us not to be more solicitous about our fleshly relatives than religion demands, when he answered even his mother: "What have I to do with thee, woman?" For as long as we are of the world, it is evident that we are debtors to our parents, but after we leave ourselves, we are much more free from their solicitude. Conf. Matth. XII. 18. Luc. XV. 76. Yet it is not to be concluded from this, with Costerus, that those who have devoted themselves to God (he points to Monks and Nuns) cannot be involved in the secular business of friends: since Christ, most devoted to God, Es. XLII. 1. c. XLIX. 6. not only took part in the secular business of a wedding, but also provided peculiar aid, as the Jesuit says. (3.) He keeps the economy properly to Himself, to the counsel or partnership of the administration of which He admits no one, not even His mother. Therefore, He does not suffer anything to be prescribed to Him concerning the supplying of the lack of wine, by which He teaches that He dispenses Himself freely, as He wills, and when He wills in the providence and government of us, Esa. XL. 13. Sap, IX.

Latin:

Vers. 4. τί ἐμοὶ καὶ σοὶ γύναι] Id est, quid negotium mihi ex- hibet? Matth. VIII. 29.

Digna notatu verba, quæ non sunt obsecratoria, ut Costerus vult hom. p. 283. & inepte verbis Dæmo- nis Luc. IV. 34. probat. Quid enim obsecrare neces- se habebat matrem Dominus, & an ratio addita, hora mea nondum venit, ullo modo obsecrationis speciem præfert? Sed sunt objurgatoria; quid mihi tecum negotii, aut quid juris tibi est, quid te ingeris, ut loca similia, Jud. XI. 12. 2. Sam. XVI. 10. Esr. IV. 3. Matth. IIX. 29. Verborum forma & ratio subjuncta, quod intempestiva minimeque conveniens fuerit hæc interventio, edocent. Testari nempe voluit Christus duriuscule hoc pacto respondendo (1.) Divinitatis majestatem. Ideo & responsum est, ait Greg. M. Ep. 42. quid mihi & tibi mulier, ac si aperte diceretur, unde facere miraculum possum, hoc mihi ex Patre non ex matre est. Ex matre enim mori pote- rat, qui ex natura Patris miracula faciebat. (2.) Officii dignitatem, in quo à nemine sibi præscribi patitur. Matri subditus erat, donec officium ag- grederetur, quæ autoritate materna erga ipsum usa fuit in privata vita, jam vero dum eadem uti vult in officio, quid tibi & mihi, inquit, mulier? Pulchre Chrysost. hom. 20. in Joh. Cura ipsi erat ma- ternus honor, sed longe animarum salus, & commu- ne in multos beneficium, cujus gratia humanam car- nem suscepit. Non sunt igitur hæc liberius ad ma- trem loquentis, sed divinæ dispensationis verba, ut admoneret pro dignitate miracula facienda. Docuit etiam hoc ipso, in his, quæ Deum aut of- ficium nostrum attinent, cognatos aut matrem nos non cognoscere. Optime, inquit, Bernhard. hom. 2. in Dom. I. post Epiph. nos docuit Dominus, ne soliciti simus super propinquis carnis nostræ plus, quam Reli- gio postulat, quando ipsi matri etiam respondit: quid mihi & tibi mulier? Quamdiu enim de mundo su- mus, debitores nos esse constat parentibus, at postquam relinquimus nos ipsos, multo magis ab eorum solici- tudine liberi sumus. Conf. Matth. XII. 18. Luc. XV. 76. Non tamen inde cum Costero concludendum, qui se Deo devoverunt (Monachos & Moniales indigi- tat) amicorum negotiis secularibus implicari non pos- se: Siquidem Christus Deo devotissimus, Es. XLII. 1. c. XLIX. 6. non modo interfuerit seculari negotio nuptiali, sed etiam auxilium peculiare, ut Jesuita lo- quitur, præstiterit. (3.) Oeconomias sibi proprie sub- limitatem, ad cujus consilium sive administrationis consortium neminem, ac ne matrem quidem ad- mittit. Ideo præscribi sibi non patitur quicquam de defectu vini supplendo, quo libere se dispen- sare doceat, prout vult, & quando vult in provi- dentia & gubernatione nostri, Esa. XL. 13. Sap, IX.

## 2:5
Vers. 5. ποιήσατε] Taught by the words of the Angel and other signs, and perhaps also by the sayings of her son, that there was nothing so great that could not be expected from him, the mother conceives the confidence that he would not fail to relieve the need and embarrassment of their friends. Therefore, she warns the servants to do whatever Jesus might command, however useless it might seem. See 2 Kings 5:13.

Latin:

Vers. 5. ποιήσατε] Ex Angeli dictis aliisque signis, forte & ex filii sermonibus edocta, nihil tam magnum esse quod non ab ipso posset expectari, fiduciam concipit mater ipsum non defore sublevandæ amicorum inopiæ ac verecundiæ. Ideo famulos monet, ut quicquid jusserit Jesus faciant, quantumve id inutile videatur. Vid. 2. Reg. V. 13.

## 2:6
ὑδρίαι λίθιναι] Not in which they sat to wash themselves, but from which water was drawn to be brought in smaller vessels for the frequent cleansing not only of hands but also of cups. See Mark 7:4. Sedulius calls them cisterns, not incorrectly. Among the Hebrews, צַלַּחַת, which elsewhere signifies a bosom (κόλπος), is translated as ὑδρία; 2 Kings 4:10. In Plutarch, it is named a six-measure hydria in Solon.

κατὰ τὸν καθαρισμὸν] κατὰ not rarely means εἰς, and the Syrian thus understood it here.

τῶν Ἰουδαίων] He adds this because he is writing to Christians, many of whom were called from the Gentiles. Understand, however, the chief of the Jews and most of the lawyers and Pharisees.

The Jews used in their banquets, if you listen to Arias Montanus here, water-jars for washing hands and cups and all vessels, and that was especially observed in wedding banquets, which pertained to joy, because purity is a companion of joy. There were also various baptisms of the Jews; hence, because water was found with more difficulty in those regions, water-jars were placed so that water would always be at hand in them.

μετρητὰς] בַּתִּים as appears in 2 Chronicles 4:5.

δύο ἢ τρεῖς] It is the way of religious witnesses to desire nothing excessive. To the Holy Spirit, who testified properly through John as his minister and amanuensis, the definite measure was not unknown: he speaks, however, disjunctively, because some of these water-jars contained two measures, others three.

Latin:

ὑδρίαι λίθιναι] Non in quibus sedentes lavarentur sed un- de depromta aqua vasis minoribus adferretur ad purgandas subinde non manus tantum sed & calices. Vid. Marc. VII. 4. lacus vocat Sedulius non male. Apud Hebræos צַלַּחַת quod κόλπος sinum alibi significat, vertitur ὑδρία; 2. Reg. IV. 10. Apud Plutarchum nominatur ὑδρία ἐξάχους in Solone.

κατὰ τὸν καθαρισμὸν] κατὰ non raro valet εἰς & ita hic Syrus accepit.

τῶν Ἰουδαίων] Hoc addit, quia Christianis scribit, quorum multi ex gentibus vocati. Intellige autem Judæorum præ- cipuos ac plurimos legisperitos & Pharisæos.

Judæi utebantur in conviviis, si Ariæmontanum hic audias, hydriis ad lavandum manus & calices, & vasa omnia, idque maxime observatum in convi- viis nuptialibus, quæ ad lætitiam pertinebant, quod puritas lætitiæ comes sit. Erant & varia Judæo- rum baptismata, inde, quia in istis regionibus a- qua difficilius inveniebatur, hydriæ positæ erant, ut in illis semper præstò esset aqua.

μετρητὰς] בַּתִּים ut apparet 2. Par. IV. 5. (nite loqui.

δύο ἢ τρεῖς] Religiosorum est testium nihil nimium desi- Spiritui S. qui κυρίως per Johannem testatus est, ceu ministrum & amanuensem suum, non ignota erat definite mensura: loquitur autem disjunctive: quia aliæ ex his hydriæ duas mensuras aliæ tres continebant.

## 2:7
Vers. 7. γεμίσατε] Because they had been emptied by frequent washings.

Although Christ could have produced wine immediately, which seems more wonderful to Chrysostom, or even performed the miracle without the work of the servants, he nevertheless wished to show his power of changing the natures of things and to set up such witnesses of the miracle that it might be more illustriously revealed, since they could testify that they had poured in not wine, but water, so that no fraud, no illusion might be perpetrated, as Chrysostom says.

ὕδατος] With no other liquid mixed in, so that full conviction of the miracle might be established; thus the change was made in the water-jars themselves, not in the cup.

Latin:

Vers. 7. γεμίσατε] Quia crebris lotionibus depletæ erant.

Quanquam poterat Christus immediate vinum producere, quod Chrysostomo mirabilius videtur, aut etiam absq; ministrorum opera miraculum pa- trare, voluit tamen potentiam suam ostendere immu- tandi rerum naturas, tantisq; miraculi testes sistere, ut illustrius id patesceret siquidem illi testari poterant, se non vinum, sed aquam infudisse, ne qua fraus, ne quod præstigium patraretur dicente Chrysostomo.

ὕδατος] Nullo alio liquore admixto, ut miraculo plena fides constaret, ita in ipsis hydriis non in poculo facta mutatio.

## 2:8
Vers. 8. ἀντλήσατε νῦν] Pour out into the cups.

What then? water? By no means, but generous wine, the water having now been turned into wine. How that was done, he does not express, nor is any word read to have been used. This, however, is certain: that the waters were not subtracted and wine substituted in their place (for what need would there have been to pour in water if he had wished to create wine immediately?), but that those very waters in the water-jars were truly changed, and their substance converted into the substance of wine.

Τῷ ἀρχιτρικλίνῳ] To the one in charge of the banquet: the Syrian and certain others wrongly interpret this as the chief guest. It was the duty of this person to run here and there, and to taste the foods and wines beforehand. Wherefore his judgment carries authority, as being both sober and experienced.

Not only because the Architriclinus was able to test the wine better than the others, and because he was in charge of managing the banquet, but also because he knew best that nothing remained, and without a doubt had been anxious in the meantime about supplying the deficiency, and he was also able to discern best the excellence of this wine created by Christ. Nor indeed did He simply make wine, but the best, as Chrysostom rightly says. For such are the miracles of Christ, that things which are perfect by nature are rendered far more beautiful and better. Thus also, when He rendered a distorted limb healthy and strong, by that miracle He demonstrated Himself to be God, the creator of nature. For He manifestly showed that He is the one who irrigates the vineyards and turns rain into wine through the root of the vine, since what is accomplished in the plant over a longer space of time, He performed suddenly at the wedding, as Chrysostom says again. Cf. Psalm 104:15.

Latin:

Vers. 8. ἀντλήσατε νῦν] Defundite in pocula.

Quid vero? num aquam? minime, sed vinum generosum, aqua in vinum jam conversa. Quo- modo id factum sit, non exprimit, neque ullum verbum adhibitum legitur. Id tamen certum est, non subtractas fuisse aquas, & in earum locum vi- num substitutum (quid enim opus fuisset infundi aquas, si vinum immediate creare voluisset?) sed vere illas ipsas aquas in hydriis immutatas, & ea- rum substantiam in vini substantiam conversam.

Τῷ ἀρχιτρικλίνῳ] Τῷ ὁλοπλέρῳ curatori convivii: male Syrus & alii quidam principem convivam interpretantur. Erat hujus nunc huc nunc illuc discurrere, prægustare cibos ac vina. Quare judicium hujus auctoritatem habet, ut & sobrii & periti.

Non tantum quia Architriclinus præ cæteris vi- num probare poterat, & quia curando convivio præerat, sed & quia ipse nihil superesse optime sciebat, ac dubio procul interea solicitus fuerat de defectu fine supplendo, qui etiam optime discer- nere poterat vini hujus à Christo procreati genero- sitatem. Neque vero simpliciter vinum fecit, sed optimum, ut recte Chrysost. Ejusmodi enim Christi miracula, ut quæ, quæ natura perfecta sunt, longe pulchriora, melioraq; reddantur. Ita & alias distor- tum membrum cum sanum validumque reddebat, quo miraculo se Deum, naturæ conditorem, de- monstravit. Manifeste enim ostendit, se eum esse, qui vineas irrigat, pluviam per vitis radicem in vinum vertit, cum quod in planta longiori spatio efficitur, id repente in nuptiis operatus est, dicente iterum Chry- sost. Conf. Psal. CIV. 15.

## 2:9
Vers. 9. τὸ ὕδωρ] See what [is said] at Matthew 26:6.

οἱ δὲ διάκονοι] These words have the force of a perfect participle.

φωνεῖ τῷ νυμφίῳ] Approaching, he calls to the master of the banquet.

Latin:

Vers. 9. τὸ ὕδωρ] Vide quæ ad Matth. XXVI. 6.

οἱ δὲ διάκονοι] Hæc vim habent παρακειμένων.

φωνεῖ τῷ νυμφίῳ] Accedens compellat dominum convivii.

## 2:10
Vers. 10. πᾶς ἄνθρωπος] It is almost so: a universal statement for that which is for the most part.

ὅταν μεθυσθῶσι] When the guests have drunk enough. Thus also the Hebrew שָׁכַר is taken, and the Greek μεθύειν. Which, as we have noted elsewhere, is derived from sacrifices.

ἐλάσσω] The less noble wine.

σὺ τετήρηκας] So he thought, until the miracle was revealed with the consenting testimony of the servants.

Latin:

Vers. 10. πᾶς ἄνθρωπος] Ferme ita sit: Universalis loca- tio pro τῷ ἐπὶ πολὺ.

ὅταν μεθυσθῶσι] Ubi adbiberint convivae. Sic & Hebræum שָׁכַר sumitur, & Græcum μεθύειν. Quod à sacrificiis de- ductum alibi notavimus.

ἐλάσσω] Minus nobile vinum.

σὺ τετήρηκας] Sic existimabat, donec consentiente mini- storum testimonio patefactum est miraculum.

## 2:11
Vers. 11. τὴν ἀρχὴν τῶν σημείων] For before the inauguration of His office they would have been superfluous. The other Evangelists were content to begin from those things which were done before the people after John the Baptist was given into prison. For, although with some omitted, the supply was sufficiently great. And this our own [Evangelist], although he has collected many that were passed over, will nevertheless testify below that miracles were passed over by him as well.

ἐν Κανᾷ τῆς Γαλιλαίας] The article τῷ is missing before ἐν Κανᾷ. This was the first of the miracles in Cana.

τὴν δόξαν αὑτοῦ] His majesty, by which Christ might be recognized, as much greater than Moses, who provided water for the thirsty, as wine is better than water. And by making wine from water, He showed Himself to be the Lord of both this and that creature.

Furthermore, we see here that it is Christ who converts the waters of sadness into the wine of joy, for that very thing is proper to him, because when all things were depraved after the fall, and eternal unhappiness had arisen from thence, liberation was effected by him. He liberated us from hell, etc., no otherwise than Moses did the Israelites from the bitter water by casting in wood, Exod. XV. For Christ is the tree of life, so that our joy may blossom forth from thence. And he performed many things by this sign, for the wedding was sanctified, the curse pronounced upon the woman in Paradise is polluted by the nuptial blessing: the glory of the Savior shines forth; the faith of the disciples is strengthened.

ἐπίστευσαν] They are said to have believed, who believe more firmly.

PART II. Departure to Capernaum.

Latin:

Vers. 11. τὴν ἀρχὴν τῶν σημείων] Nam ante auspicationem muneris supervacua fuissent. Cæteri Evangelistæ satis ha- buerunt ab iis incipere, quæ coram plebe facta sunt post Johannem Baptistam carceri datum. Nam, quamvis ali- quot omissis, satis magna erat copia. Et hic ipse noster cum prætermissa collegerit plurima: tamen a se quoque miracula prætermissa infra testabitur.

ἐν Κανᾷ τῆς Γαλιλαίας] Deest articulus τῷ ἐν Κανᾷ. Hoc in Cana primum fuit miraculorum.

τὴν δόξαν αὑτοῦ] Majestatem suam unde Christus agno- sceretur, tanto Mose major, qui sitientibus aquam præstitit, quanto vinum aqua est potius. Et ex aqua vinum faciens ostendit se & hujus & istius creaturæ Dominum.

Porro videmus hic Christum esse, qui aquas tri- stitiæ in vinum lætitiæ convertit, id ipsum enim ei proprium, quia cum omnia essent depravata post lapsum, indeque æterna infelicitas orta, liberatio ab ipso facta est. Liberavit de inferno nos &c. non aliter ac Moses Israelitas de aqua amara inje- cto ligno, Exod. XV. Christus enim arbor vitæ, ut inde efflorescat lætitia nostra. Et multa hoc signo peregit, nam sanctificatæ sunt nuptiæ, Ma- ledictio in Paradiso mulieri facta benedictione nu- ptiali polluitur: Gloria Salvatoris effulget; Fides discipulorum roboratur.

ἐπίστευσαν] Credidisse dicuntur, qui firmius credunt.

PARS II. Profectio in Capernaum.

## 2:12
Vers. 12. Κατέβη εἰς Καπερναούμ] Into a more famous town, such as were the places accustomed to be chosen by the Prophets.

καὶ ἡ μήτηρ αὐτοῦ, καὶ οἱ ἀδελφοὶ αὐτοῦ] The mother and kinsmen seem to have followed Jesus as if he were departing from them. For they lived at Nazareth.

ἐ πολλὰς ἡμέρας] With the Passover approaching, as follows.

Then, therefore, he did not move into that city, but passing through that city he stayed there only a few days with his companions. This history, therefore, preceded the imprisonment of John, to be distinguished from that migration which is narrated in Matt. IV. 13, Luke IV. 14, and below in ch. IV. 48, as Walæus does from Beza.

PART III. Acts at the Jerusalem Passover.

Latin:

Vers. 12. Κατέβη εἰς Καπερναούμ] In oppidum celebrius, qualia loca eligi à Prophetis solebant.

καὶ ἡ μήτηρ αὐτοῦ, καὶ οἱ ἀδελφοὶ αὐτοῦ] Videntur mater & con- sanguinei Jesum quasi à se abeuntem prosecuti. Nam Nazarethi habitabant.

ἐ πολλὰς ἡμέρας] Urgente ut sequitur Paschate.

Tunc igitur in eam urbe non demigravit, sed per eam urbem transiens aliquot tantum dies ibi cum suis comitibus est commoratus. Hæc igitur historia præcessit Joannis captivitatem, distinguen- da ab ea demigratione, quæ narratur, Matth. IV. 13. Luc. IV. 14. & infra c. IV. 48. uti à Beza Walæus.

PARS III. Acta in Paschate Hierosolymitano.

## 2:13-17
v. 13. 17. Rom. XI. 34. What have I to do with thee, he says to our reason, which desires to insinuate itself into the secrets of the divine economy. (4.) That there is no necessity for an advocate, and that he ought to be called upon in our needs without intermediary patrons. It should be sought from those in need, not from the mother, says Chrysost. hom. 20. in Joh. Salmeron inverts this, Tom. VI. tract. 6., since the first miracle of Christ, the first benefit of his grace on earth, was performed at the intercession of the B. Virgin, we gather that she is that singular advocate for the human race. But since Mary incurred a rebuke here when she wished to intercede, must it not rather be concluded from this that this office does not at all befit her in the presence of Christ? Nor indeed did he perform this miracle because of her intervention, but for the manifestation of his own glory. Of his glory, I say, of his omnipotence, of his most free operation and most gracious assistance, which never deserts or abandons its own. Furthermore, he calls her woman, not mother, because he does not wish to acknowledge maternal authority in this business, but rather judged that he must oppose the Mariolatry which he foresaw, as Epiph. observes, haeres. 79. num. 3. He called her woman, as if prophesying what would be on earth, the kinds of sects and heresies, so that some, admiring the holy one too much, might not slip into this heresy and its ravings. To which heresy Epiphanius opposes this opinion of the Church: In truth she was a virgin and honored, but not given to us for adoration, but she herself adoring him who was born from her own flesh, but for the rest he came from the paternal bosom, and therefore the Gospel diminishes us, because the Lord himself said, what have I to do with thee, woman? Let the Papists note this, who treat Mary with divine worship, as the Rosaries, Hours, the Psalter of Mary of Bonaventure, confirmed by Sixtus IV and Innocent VIII, Offices, Collects, Ave Maria, Salve Regina, the Marian Fraternity, and public daily practice testify. Whence they explain the words of their hymn: Show thyself to be a Mother, that is, Command the Son, and by the right of a mother, order. See concerning the Papal worship of Mary, Andr. Rivet. Apolog. pro Marial. 2.

ὔπω ἥκει ἡ ὥρα με] ὥρα is καιρὸς, a timely time, as Ausonius translates it. Thus below c. IIX. 20. c. XIII. 1. But it was the time for performing the miracle, when it was plain to all that no wine remained, lest the water mixed with wine be believed to be wine. Thus he gives it to be understood that in miracles a benefit is conferred on men incidentally, the chief thing being that the honor of God is manifested. Gregory of Nyssa thought an interrogation should be added to this sentence, so that the sense might be: do you not yet think that the time of my calling has come, so that, emancipated from you, I may obey God alone?

Concerning the word ὥρα, Camerarius can be compared here on this passage. Some have referred it to the hour of death in Chrysostom, but inappropriately, since hour, in the manner of scripture, denotes a convenient and opportune time, Luke XXII. 53. John XIII. 1. Rom. XIII. 11. Rev. XIV. 15. which comes only then, when the lack of wine became openly known, as Theophyl. observes, with Chrysost. leading the way, tr. 8. in Joh. He teaches therefore (1.) that he does not rashly undertake miracles at the prayers of his mother or relatives, but according to the hour defined by his God. (2.) That he does not perform all things at the due time, but not all at once, since there would have been a certain disordered confusion if he had not proceeded in order, as Chrysostom observes. (3.) Christ is subject to no necessity of times, but he himself imposed order on the times, since he is their author, therefore he says, my hour has not yet come, as Chrysostom says again. (4.) Christ teaches moreover to observe certain hours, namely the hour of affliction or temptation, of the cross and misery, and the hour of Assistance, Liberation, Light, Mercy, and Glory. Therefore, in the hour of temptation let us not lose heart, because the hour of liberation will also come, Hab. II. 3. The delay of an answer is not the rejection of the one crying out. He defers, he does not take away, if there is one who endures.

Latin:

v. 13. 17. Rom. XI. 34. Quid mihi & tibi, dicit rationi nostræ, quæ sese in œconomiæ divinæ abdita insi- nuare discupit. (4.) Advocatricis nullam esse necessi- tatem, seque sine mediis Patronis in necessitatibus compellari debere. Ab indigentibus, non à matre id quærendum erat, ait Chrysost. hom. 20. in Joh. In- vertit hoc Salmeron Tom. VI. tract. 6. quoniam pri- mum Christi miraculum, primum in terris gratiæ suæ Beneficium ad B. Virginis intercessionem factum fuit, colligimus singularem illam pro humano genere Ad- vocatam esse. At cum hic reprehensionem Maria incurrerit, dum intercedere voluit, annon con- cludendum potius inde, munus hoc penes Chri- stum ipsi haudquaquam convenire? Nec vero ob ejus interventionem, sed ob gloriæ suæ manifesta- tionem miraculum hoc edidit. Gloriæ, inquam, o- mnipotentiæ, operationis liberrimæ & opitulationis gra- tiosissimæ, quæ suos nunquam deserit aut destituit. Porro mulierem appellat non matrem, quia non vult in hoc negotio maternam agnoscere autorita- tem, sed occurrendum potius censuit Mariolatriæ quam prævidit, ut observat Epiph. hæres. 79. num. 3. Mulierem eam appellavit, quasi prophetans, quæ fu- tura essent in terra, sectarum & hæresium genera, ut ne aliqui nimium admirati sanctam, in hanc hæresin ejusq; deliramenta dilabantur. Cui hæresi opponit Epiphanius hanc Ecclesiæ sententiam: Revera erat virgo ipsa & honorata, sed non ad adorationem nobis data, sed ipsa adorans eum, qui ex ipsius carne genitus est, de cætero vero ex sinubus paternis accessit, & propte- rea Evangelium minuit nos, quod ipse Dominus di- xerit, quid mihi & tibi est curæ, mulier? Notent hoc Papistæ qui Mariam cultu divino afficiunt, u- ti Rosaria, Horaria, Psalterium Mariæ Bonaven- turæ, à Sixto IV. & Innocent. VIII. confirmatum, Officia, Collectæ, Ave Maria, Salve Regina Fraterni- tas Mariana, & publica praxis quotidiana testan- tur. Unde exponunt verba hymni sui: Monstra te esse Matrem, hoc est, Jube Nato, & jure matris impera. Videatur de Mariæ cultu Papali Andr. Rivet. Apolog. pro Marial. 2.

ὔπω ἥκει ἡ ὥρα με] ὥρα est καιρὸς, tempestivum tempus, ut Ausonius vertit. Sic infra c. IIX. 20. c. XIII. 1. Tempus au- tem edendi miraculum erat, ubi plane omnibus constaret nullum superesse vinum, ne aqua vino admixta crederetur. Ita dat intelligi in miraculis beneficium hominibus obiter conferri, præcipuum esse ut Dei honos manifestetur. Gre- gorius Nyssenus putavit addendam huic sententiæ interro- gationem, ut sensus sit: nondumne putas venisse tempus vocationis meæ, ut abs te emancipatus Deo soli paream?

De voce ὥρα conferri hic poterit Camerarius ad hunc locum. Id ad horam mortis apud Chrysosto- mum retulêre nonnulli, sed in congrue, siquidem hora, scripturæ more, tempus notat commodum & opportunum, Luc. XXII. 53. Joh. XIII. 1. Rom. XIII. 11. Apoc. XIV. 15. quod tum demum venit, cum de- fectus vini palàm innotuit, ut Theophyl. observat, præeunte Chrysost. tr. 8. in Joh. Docet itaque (1.) non temere se aggredi miracula, ad preces matris vel cognatorum, sed juxta horam à Deo suo defini- tam. (2.) Omnia debito tempore, non autem simul se- se operari, quoniam inordinata quædam confusio fuiffet, nisi ordine transiisset, ut observat Chrysosto- mus. (3.) Nulli necessitati temporum subest Chri- stus, sed ipse temporibus ordinem imposuit, quoniam autor eorum est, ideo inquit, nondum hora mea venit, ut iterum Chrysostomus. (4.) Docet insuper Chri- stus certas observare horas, nempe horam afflictio- nis seu tentationis, crucis & miseriæ, & horam Opitu- lationis, Liberationis, Lucis, Misericordiæ & Gloriæ. In hora ergo tentationis ne animum despondeamus, quia veniet & hora liberationis, Hab. II. 3. Exaudi- tionis dilatio non est clamantis reprobatio. Dif- fert non auffert, si est qui suffert.

## 2:13
Vers. 13. τὸ πάσχα τ[ῶν] ἰκδαίων] We said above that John was writing to the Churches which were for the most part gathered from the Gentiles. They indeed also celebrated the memory of the Lord's resurrection, to which they gave the name of Passover, as appears from the excellent epistle of Irenæus to Victor, but certainly not in the manner of the Jews. Thus also below in ch. VI. 4.

ἀνέβη εἰς Ἱεροσόλυμα] According to the prescription of the law. See Luke XI. 41.

At the first Passover, which Christ wished to attend, his heroic and divine acts are celebrated by John, the ejection of the merchants and the overturning of the money-changers' tables: which Origen does not hesitate to compare, and Jerome even to prefer to other miracles, and here he thinks a certain fiery and sidereal light shone from the eyes of Christ, and that the divine Majesty shone in his face, which, however, we leave in its place: Furthermore, there is no doubt that by these acts, prophetically, the very casting away of the Jewish nation and the chief reason for the same, namely the profanation of the House of the Lord, was designated (just as by the preceding miracle, according to Cyril, the conversion of the Gentiles was mystically prefigured), as well as certain sayings, partly imperative, partly prophetic. Those are what he said to the sellers of doves: Take these things from here, and do not make the house of my Father a house of merchandise. Concerning these things hereafter.

Latin:

Vers. 13. τὸ πάσχα τ[ῶν] ἰκδαίων] Diximus supra Johannem scribere Ecclesiis quæ maxima parte ex Gentibus collectæ erant. Celebrabant quidem & illæ memoriam resurrectio- nis dominicæ, cui nomen dabant Paschatis, ut ex egregio Irenæi ad Victorem epistola apparet, sed non utique more Judæorum. Sic & infra c. VI. 4.

ἀνέβη εἰς Ἱεροσόλυμα] Ex legis præscripto. Vid. Luc. XI. 41.

In Paschate primo, cui Christus interesse voluit, celebrantur à Johanne tum facta ejus heroica & di- vina, Negotiatorum ejectio & mensarum Numul- lariorum dejectio: quæ Origenes non dubitat con- ferre, Hieronymus etiam anteferre cæteris mira- culis, & hic igneum quoddam ac sidereum radiasse censet ex oculis Christi, divinamq; Majestatem in facie ejus luxisse, quod tamen suo loco relinqui- mus: Cæterum προφητικῶς hisce factis, ipsam gentis Judaicæ projectionem, ejusdemque potis- simam rationem, nempe Domus Domini profanatio- nem designatam esse, nullum est dubium (uti mi- raculo antecedenti, secundum Cyrillum, mysti- ce Gentium conversio præfigurata fuit) tum dicta nonnulla, partim imperativa, partim prophetica. Il- la sunt, quæ ad Venditores Columbarum dixit: Tol- lite ista hinc, & ne faciatis domum Patris mei do- mum negotiationis. De hisce deinceps.

## 2:14
Vers. 14. εὗρεν ἐν τῷ ἱερῷ τὼς πωλῶντας] When Jesus had come to reform the sacred things, he did this twice, testified by a conspicuous sign,

By cleansing the Temple, as the seat of sacred things, around the beginning and around the conclusion of his ministry, he showed that he ended in the same place where he had begun. Others have handed down the later history: John the former, for the reason that Christ had spoken words about the destruction of the Temple on that occasion, which very words, since they were brought against him as a charge, contributed not a little to illustrating the history of the passion. See Matt. XXVI. 61, ch. XXVII. 40.

τοὺς πωλοῦντας] We explained this at Matt. XXI. 12.

Latin:

Vers. 14. εὗρεν ἐν τῷ ἱερῷ τὼς πωλῶντας] Jesus cum venisset ad sacra emendanda bis conspicuo signo testatum hoc fecit,

Templum, velut sacrorum sedem, purgando, circa initium & circa clausulam sui muneris, ut in quo inceperat in eo se desinere ostenderet. Posteriorem historiam alii tradiderunt: priorem Johannes, ideo quod ex occasione Christus verba fecerat de Templi destructione, quæ ipsa verba cum pro cri- mine ipsi objecta sint, non parum faciebant ad illustrandam passionis historiam, Vid. Matth. XXVI. 61. c. XXVII. 40.

τοὺς πωλοῦντας] Explicavimus ad Matth. XXI. 12.

## 2:15
Vers. 15. Φραγέλλιον] The Syrian also has this word. Thus Φραγελλώσας, Matt. XXVII. 26.

ἐκ σχοινίων] Which he had found made there. The writer tacitly implies that the ejection was made, not with a thin whip, but with divine majesty, the whip merely sustaining the sign of divine wrath.

πάντας] The traders themselves. See Matthew, lest anyone refer that 'sheep' only to what follows; for this reason the Syrian correctly inserted a conjunction.

καὶ τὸ κερματιστῶν] He calls those 'collybistae' who made a profit from 'collybistus', that is, the exchange of money. Naturally, those who lived further away from Jerusalem, since they could not conveniently bring the so-called second tithe in its own kind, which they would use at the festivals while they were in Jerusalem according to the command of the law, were able to sell it at home and bring the price, with which similar things to those sold could be bought in the city; and so that it might be carried more conveniently, it had been declared that the price could be carried in silver, either received from the sale or exchanged from the money of the sale. In the temple itself, however, that is, in the mount of the house and in the courts, there were many who made a profit from this business: for some brought cattle and oxen there, which would be sold to those coming from a more remote place and would take the place of the second tithes; others, however, set out small change for exchange with silver brought from the regions. Thus, from that interpretation of the Scribes which we read in the tractate 'Menachoth' concerning the second tithe, there had arisen in the temple an opportunity for avarice and an occasion for trading, which things God had long ago noted by the Prophets as alien to that place, and now Jesus detests with divine authority, as per Arias Montanus and Walaeus.

Latin:

Vers. 15. Φραγέλλιον] Habet hanc vocem & Syrus. Sic Φραγελλώσας, Matth. XXVII. 26.

ἐκ σχοινίων] Quæ facta ibi repererat. Tacite innuit scriptor ejectionem factam, non tenui flagello, sed majestate divi- na, flagello iræ tantum divinæ signum sustinente.

πάντας] Ipsos nundinatores. Vide Matth. ne quis illud πρόβατα ad sequentia tantum referat, ideo Syrus recte copu- lam interjecit.

καὶ τὸ κερματιστῶν] Collybistas vocat eos, qui ex Collybisto, id est, pecuniæ permutatione quæstum faciebant. Nimirum qui longius habitabant à Jerosolymis, cum decimam secun- dam vocatam in proprio genere afferre commode non pos- sent, qua uterentur in festis, dum Hierosolymis essent juxta legis mandatum, poterant domi vendere, & precium defer- re, quo in urbe similes venditis res emerentur; atq; ut com- modius perferretur, precium in argento vel ex venditione accepto, vel ex venditionis ære permutato, ferri posse decla- ratum erat. In ipso autem templo, hoc est, in monte domus, & in atriis erunt multi qui ex hoc negotio quæstum facie- bant: alii enim pecora & boves eo comportabant, quæ ve- nientibus ex remotiore loco venderentur, & decimæ secun- dæ vicem sortirentur: alii vero minutum æs exponebant ad permutationem cum argento à regionibus allato. Ita ex illa Scribarum interpretatione quam legimus id Munacoth tra. Etatu de decima secunda, orta fuerat in templo avaritiæ op- portunitas, & nundinationum occasio, quas res ab illo loco alienas jam olim Deus per Prophetas notaverat, & nunc Je- sus divina autoritate detestatur, ut ex Aria Mont. V V alæus.

## 2:16
Vers. 16. τὰς περιστερὰς πωλοῦσιν] Which, being enclosed, could not be ejected in the same way, but had to be removed.

Adrichomius writes in no. 196 that there were pigeon-rocks in Jerusalem, which could be seen to the south of the Mount of Olives, called in Greek 'peristereon', stony, round, and high, and vaulted, whitened on the outside, and narrow, opening with one small door at the top, in which domestic pigeons were kept, and such a tower often contained even 5000 pigeons. For those who were prevented by sickness or the length of the journey from being able to come to Jerusalem sent money, for which the things that needed to be offered were bought; according to the command of Deut. XIV. 23, 24. Which Walaeus observed here from the Annotations of B. Quistorpius.

Ἄρατε ταῦτα ἐντεῦθεν) Let it be noted here (1.) From where ought they to take them? From the temple, that is: by synecdoche, from the court and the porch of Solomon, into which access was open to all, Acts III. 11. For in it were various buyers and sellers for the purpose and pretext that those who came to the festival might be able to buy cattle for sacrifice; as if no place could be found for buying unless it were the temple. For human reason uses such a pretext. (2.) Who? The sellers of pigeons. Mention is made here both of them and of others who sold sheep, oxen, etc., and of the money-changers, whose tables he overturned and whose money he threw out; the former he ejected with a whip made of cords, which they had used in leading the oxen: the latter, however, he drove out with a word along with their merchandise. Concerning which see Cyril, book II, ch. 20. Just as the Lord commands, and just as the Teacher exhorts to what is fair and just, and exposes their sins, so that, convicted by shame, they may know they are rightly being driven out of the temple. (3.) What ought they to do? Take away the pigeons, so that he might teach that he detests the profanation of the House of God and all Simony, in whatever form it is undertaken. They sell pigeons, according to Aug. tract. 10 in John, who trade in the gifts of the Holy Spirit, who descended upon Christ in the form of a dove.

the house of my Father] He shows that he is occupied in his own place, as sons are accustomed to be on their fathers' estates. See Luke 2:49.

house of merchandise] It is the custom of those who correct rightly to deal first with gentle words: if stubbornness occurs, with harsher ones. See what we noted on Matt. 18:15. Therefore he says here 'house of merchandise.' In the later ejection, 'house of thieves': here he notes the gain, there he expresses more effectively the indignity of gain in a sacred place. See what [is said] on the aforementioned place of Matthew. The argument is taken from the holiness of the place, because that house was sanctified for the worship of God, Deut. 12:5. My Father, he says. Concerning which Cyril: The only-begotten Son, born not by grace, but from the substance of the Father, truly and properly alone calls God his Father, John 3:16, ch. 1:14, Rom. 8:22, 32. Therefore the Father's house was not to be turned into a house of trade. That pollution of the temple was most grave, most unworthy, most scandalous, joined with a false persuasion concerning the peculiar holiness of the cattle and birds standing in the sacred place, and designated under the guise of promoting divine worship. Therefore, it was by no means to be tolerated by him who was Lord of the temple, and had come to purge the sons of Levi, Mal. 3:13. He who wished to make a beginning here from the purging of the temple, as one who was about to repair the entire divine worship and restore heavenly doctrine, so that he might teach that false doctrine and false worship must be reformed before the care and study of true religion is undertaken. Because the end of the temple is the worship of God, therefore the end is overturned by changing it into a house of negotiation, which Christ himself reproves in this place, and frees or purges the temple from that negotiation. Verse 17. And his disciples remembered] They recalled to their memory a famous place of the Psalms and one commonly accustomed to be sung. For it was agreed that the Messiah is described there under the person of David. The Messiah is not described there in Ps. 69:10 under the person of David, but the Messiah speaks there in his own person, nor should those things be drawn to David, as we showed in the annotations on the Psalms. Zeal] Ardent love. Has eaten me up] A saying like that one, 'care consumes the marrow.' Verse 18. They answered] We have said elsewhere that the Hebrew 'wa-ya'anu' as well as the Greek 'apokritheis,' and in Homer 'apameibomenos,' are often said of him who speaks first. What sign do you show us that you do these things?] To remove vicious things in public places belongs to no one except either public authority or divine. The Sanhedrin tolerated these trades, the priests tolerated them. It remained, therefore, that Jesus should profess himself a Prophet. But prophets had to show themselves as such either by predictions or by signs. See 1 Cor. 1:22. Verse 19. Destroy this temple] He addresses the wicked obscurely: for if they had been of a good mind, they would have recognized a miracle in this very act: that one man, instructed by no human powers, had forced such a crowd to yield to his command, moved only by the consciousness of a shameful deed and the sense of divine wrath; we are accustomed to reject foolish men to the end of the work. Thus Christ, although liberal with miracles, frequently refers or rejects [them] to the greatest of miracles and the completion, namely his own resurrection. In the temple, it was believed that there was some power of the divine deity. Thus Solomon prays in Josephus, 'that some portion of God's spirit might dwell in the temple,' book 8.2. Hence, taking the similitude, Christians, to whom the Spirit of God had come, are called the Temple of God, 1 Cor. 3:16, ch. 5:19, 2 Cor. 6:16. How much more, therefore, does this name befit the human nature of Christ, in which not through figures but fully and solidly 'somatikos' (bodily) the divinity had chosen for itself not a temporary but a perpetual dwelling? Col. 2:9. Rabbi Moses Gerundensis: 'Qodesh Qodashim hu ha-Mashiach mequdash mi-benei David'—The Sanctuary of Sanctuaries is the Messiah himself, sanctified from the sons of David. Moreover, the words of Christ are such that they can also be understood of the Temple, for 'lyein' is also to destroy, 2 Pet. 3:10, 12, 1 John 3:8. The imperative, however, is placed here for the potential. Destroy, that is, if you destroy: as 'Pone Tigellinum' (Place Tigellinus), that is, if you place. In three days] Within the third day. I will raise up] And this is ambiguous. For it is also said of buildings to raise up. Thus in a Greek epigram, 'having raised up many houses.' But he said significantly 'egero' (I will raise up) by divine power. Verse 21. He was speaking] He was especially hinting at this. Of the temple of his body] An explanatory genitive, just as we say 'the fountain of Timavus' and many other things, in place of an apposition. The prophecy is twofold, namely concerning the death and resurrection of Christ, on the occasion of a sign, whether from curiosity or from a certain piety, as it seems to some, regarding certain ones present in that assembly. Cf. Matt. 12:40. Which sign, indeed, unless it were to be entirely for the salvation of all, he would never have given to those testifying, as Cyril says. Chrysostom marvels here at his supreme clemency: For what sign was needed, when he was correcting misdeeds and cleansing God's house from such great ignominy? That zeal for the honor of God's house was the greatest sign of virtue, which good men noted. Let the Papists think this is said to them, seeking a sign from Luther. Christ's first prophecy was about death. Destroy, says Christ, this temple, where the word destroy is not that of one commanding, but of one prophesying or narrating. Cf. Job 21:5, ch. 22:21, as the phrases of the Prophets are wont sometimes to pronounce predictions in the imperative mode, Isa. 47:1. He does not impel them to his own slaughter, says Cyril, but he reveals to them what he knew they would do, for their own benefit, if they had had any sense. He understands the temple not properly of the Jerusalem Temple, as the Jews took it, but symbolically of the temple of his body, as the Holy Spirit explains. the Holy Spirit, to whom the body of Christ is a temple because of the expiation made in it, because of holiness, and especially because of the indwelling of the divinity, Col. 2:9, as Ambrose explains in Ps. 4:7. Truly the body of Christ is the temple of God, in which is the purification of our sins; truly that flesh is the Temple of God, in which there could be no contagion; but it itself was the sacrifice for the sin of the whole world. Truly that flesh is the temple of God, in which the image of God shone, and the fullness of the divinity dwelt bodily, since Christ himself is the fullness. He recalls them from the typical temple, in which they boasted so much, to the true Antitype, Heb. 9:14, and at the same time to the most important use of the temple, as that in which the death of Christ and his resurrection especially ought to be preached and foreshadowed. The explanation of R. Menahem in the Talmud, tractate Helech, contributes to this, regarding that prophecy of Amos 9:11, that in the Messiah the tabernacle of David had to fall in death, and in turn be raised up in his Resurrection. The Jews, however, constructed a calumny from this at the Passion of Christ, Matt. 26:61, he himself said, I can destroy the temple of God, which the Holy Spirit himself refutes here. For the destruction of the temple is the death of Christ; when Christ was dead and the soul deserted the flesh, then that temple was destroyed, which was constructed of soul and flesh, says Fulgentius, lib. 3, to Thrasimund, ch. 17.

That the Mosaic Tabernacle, as also the Jerusalem Temple, was a type of Christ is demonstrated (1.) by reason of the efficient cause. For just as God showed the form of the Tabernacle to Moses, and he took care that it be built according to it: so Christ, or the temple of his body, was constructed by the Holy Spirit. (2.) Of the matter, for it consisted of cedar wood and gold: which indicates the twofold nature of Christ. (3.) Of the presence. As God manifested himself in a peculiar way in the tabernacle: so in Christ dwells the whole fullness of the divinity. (4.) Of the Ark of the Covenant and the mercy seat. For there the Laws were kept, etc. So Christ is the true Ark of the Covenant. For in his heart the Laws are inscribed, Ps. 40:9, the true Mercy Seat, Rom. 3:25, Heb. 9. (5.) Of the sacrifice. In the temple sacrifices were offered: so the sacrifice of Christ could not be performed otherwise than in the temple of his flesh. Furthermore, this prophecy seems somewhat obscure, but it has been clarified by the event. Chrysostom asks, however, why Christ did not interpret this speech to the disciples? He himself answers, because the disciples were not yet fit to understand this mystery, much less the crowd. He asks further: how it happened that the disciples were not yet fit? And he provides this reason, because they were held by a false error concerning the worldly kingdom of Christ. But it is also to be noted that at that time the Disciples were Catechumens, who, although they do not immediately understand all the dogmas of the Church, are not for that reason cast out, but are informed more and more. However much they did not understand those things, yet they did not stubbornly deny them.

The second prophecy is about the Resurrection, concerning which Christ prophesies in these words: and in three days I will raise it up. Determining (1.) The time of the resuscitation. ἐν τρισὶν ἡμέραις, in three days, or within three days. For there were not three whole days when the temple of the body was raised, as Alcuin, lib. de div. off. c. de Cœn. Dom., thinks, that Christ lay in the sepulcher for 72 hours; if indeed it is said that Christ was in the heart of the earth for three days and three nights, Matt. 12:39, and even that he rose after three days, ch. 27:63, Mark 8:32, but there μετὰ denotes not after, but within, as Deut. 34:38, Luke 2:46, ch. 22:20. Cf. Mark 8:32, Matt. 16:21. For history teaches that just as he expired at the ninth hour on the day of Preparation, Matt. 27:26, 50, soon after, while that day still lasted, he was buried toward evening, Mark 15:42. Luke 23:54, so that almost three hours of that day remained, and counting, according to the custom of the Jews, the day from that evening to the evening of the following day, the Sabbath, the third day is begun up to the dawn for some hours again, whence the three days of burial must be taken synecdochically, because he rested in the sepulcher for only one whole day and for parts of two days or some hours. (2.) The efficient cause. By the word ἐγερῶ, I will raise up. He indicates himself, both by reason of his divine and his human nature. The proof of his divine nature is that very power of raising his body from death, because this is a truly infinite power proper to God alone, and the raising of Christ from the dead is attributed everywhere to God alone, Acts 2:24, 22, 3:15, 4:10, 5:30, 10:40, 13:30, 17:13. Therefore, an invincible argument is sought here for the divine nature of Christ, which is also said to be demonstrated by the resurrection from the dead, Rom. 1:4. Since by this very great argument, as Chrysostom says, he showed that he was not a mere man, and that death was subject to him, and that he would soon remove its power and most grievous war; but as for his human nature, just as it had the divine power personally communicated to it, and specifically the δύναμιν ζωοποιητικὴν [life-giving power], John 5:23, so his soul is not to be excluded from the vivification of his own body and the raising of the temple, which was done through that divine power. For this reason, the power of both laying down and taking up his life, John 10:17, and the raising of the temple of his body, is attributed to the whole ὑφισαμένῳ [subsistent being]. He raised his own temple, says Cyril, lib. 1 in Es. c. 9, since he himself is the power of the Father. For if he himself is the Resurrection and the life, what then would life require for vivification? And if he is seen to have raised the bodies of others by his own force and power, why should he not raise his own? (3.) The manner and the truth. Ἐγερῶ, I will raise. Just as death was a certain dissolution, so the raising of this building was a new conjunction of soul and body, and the erection of the animated body. For the temple of the body had not been destroyed, but loosened from the soul. Therefore, it is not built anew, but raised, with the union of soul and body restored in turn. But it is absurd, and entirely alien to the words of Christ, that the Racovian Catechism and Melchior Scheffer show that the words of Christ are to be understood thus: I, after I have been raised by the Father, will erect myself, or my body, as if Christ here had claimed for himself not the raising of the body, but the erection of the one already raised. For by this reasoning the words also suffer violence; because he says, I will raise, and not 'I will erect what has been raised by another,' and the force of the miracle is weakened, by which he wished to demonstrate not the Father's, but his own power. (4.) The object. That very temple which was loosened by death was raised by the power of Christ, Ps. 16:10, Acts 2:27, as also Luke 24:39, John 20:20, 21. Epiphanius in Ancor. It is the mark of those, he says, who have a false faith, to say that what fell asleep did not rise again; but it is the mark of believers to say that the same body rose again. The very grain that died rose again, etc. Hence, therefore, it is clear that Christ, by this very statement, made himself the author of his own resurrection from the dead, and thus recalled himself to life, which the Socinians impiously deny and mock; Ostorod. lib. 2 contra Tradel. c. 10, Enjed. in Expl. LL. Script. in h. l., Smaltz. de div. Christi cap. 13, Melch. Scheffer. tr. pecul. de hoc

The argument having been published, by which it was treated concerning several matters by the Faculty of Theology of the University of Königsberg, and published in the second volume of Natural and Revealed Theology on the Augsburg Confession, p. 1289. They object in vain (1.) that the words of Christ are figurative and obscure, because the figure is expressly explained, namely that Christ is speaking of the temple of his body. Nor (2.) can it be excepted: that Christ spoke in such a way out of a necessity of speaking. For what necessity could compel Christ to speak in such a way and not otherwise, and yet not understand it in that way but otherwise? Nor (3.) that he brought these things forth in this way for the sake of the increase of a miracle. For Christ was not accustomed to attribute to himself what was not his own, or to gain authority for himself among the imprudent by ambiguous speech. But how will Enjedinus, Socinus, the Racovians, Smaltzius, Crellius, Scheffer, or other Photinians prove, without begging the question, that he says he himself will raise up the temple of his body in no other way than as the faithful are said to find their soul, Matt. 10:39, or to make it alive, Luke 17:33? Or that which (5.) Socinus does not hesitate to lay down, that Christ is said to raise his body in such a way as the dead are said to rise, as Lazarus is said to have risen elsewhere. For the latter he teaches to obtain life at least by grace and as it were to find it, but the former, not unless recalled to life, does the thing itself teach to rise again, otherwise concerning Christ the author of life, the Lord of death, God blessed forever. Nor is one to depart from the letter unless necessity demands it. But here, in order that we may retain the letter, necessity itself also urges and compels it. For this had to be a proof of divine power, not of the Father, but of Christ, which the Jews themselves were soliciting by asking for it. Finally (6.) against the rest, Enjedinus at last admits that Christ indeed raised himself, but not by his own power. But what kind of declaration of his own divine power would that be, if he had been raised only by another's power? I have power from myself to take up my soul again. Crellius, however, also admits that those passages in John 2 and 10 prove that Christ was the cause of the resurrection, and that it had been placed in his hand, so much so that it could be intercepted by no one. Such is the force of truth! But it is a sign of a desperate cause that Socinus, in his second book against Erasmus on John, p. 114, asserts with profane mouth that the words here are not to be superstitiously observed, since some of them do not agree with the truth in every respect. Just as Socinus blasphemously pronounces concerning that passage in John 10:18: that it perhaps indeed suits Christ that he had the power of taking up his soul again, and that it is said tolerably, l.c. p. 126. Which Scheffer does not fear to affirm; even if it were expressly and several times written in the Scriptures that Christ raised himself, one would still have to doubt it, l.c. p. 33. Is this not setting one's mouth against heaven?

Latin:

Vers. 16. τὰς περιστερὰς πωλοῦσιν] Quæ inclusæ non perin- de ejici poterant, sed amovendæ erant.

Scribit Adrichomius num. 196. quod fuerit Hie- rosolymis petræ columbarum, quæ ad meridiem montis Oliveti conspiceretur, Græce περιστέρεον vo- cata, saxea, rotunda & sublimis, & concameraturis, extrinsecus dealbata, atque angusta uno ostiolo in summitate patens, in qua domesticæ servabantur columbæ, & hujusmodi turris, sæpe vel 5000. co- lumbarum continuerit. Qui enim morbo vel iti- neris longitudine impediti Jerosolymam venire non poterant, mittebant pecuniam, pro qua, quæ offerri debebant, emebantur; Juxta mandatum Deut. XIV. 23. 24. Quæ hic è B. Quistorpii Annotat. observavit Walæus.

Ἄρατε ταῦτα ἐντεῦθεν) Notetur hic (1.) Unde tollere debeant? è templo, id est: Synechdoch. ex atrio & porticu Solomonis, in quem omnibus patebat ádi- tus Actor. III.11. in illo enim erant varii ementes & vendentes eo fine & prætextu, ut qui ad festum ve- nirent, pecora ad Sacrificium emere possent; ac si nullus ad emtionem locus inveniri potuisset, nisi templum. Tali enim prætextu utitur humana ra- tio. (2.) Quinam? Venditores columbarum. Men- tio fit hic tum eorum, tum aliorum qui vendebant oves, boves &c. tum Numulariorum, quorum men- sas evertit, & pecuniam projecit; illos flagello è fu- niculis, quibus in adducendis bobus usi erant, con- texto, ejecit: Istos vero verbo exturbavit cum mercibus suis. Quo de Cyrill. l. II. c. 20. Sicut Do- minus imperat, & sicut Doctor ad æquum & justum hortatur, peccataque illorum exponit, ut pudore convi- cti jure è templo se extrudi cognoscant. (3.) Quidnam facere debeant? Columbas tollere, ut doceret se de- testari profanationem Domus Dei, omnemq; Si- moniam, quocunque schemate susceptam. Colum- bas vendunt, secundum Aug. tr. 10. in Joh. qui Spiri- tus S. in specie columbæ super Christum delapsi donis negotiantur.

τὸν οἶκον τοῦ πατρός με] Ostendit se versari in loco suo, ut fi- lii solent in fundis paternis. Vid. Luc. II. 49.

οἶκον ἐμπορίε] Mos recte castigantium est lenibus primum verbis agere: si contumacia occurrat durioribus. Vide quæ notavimus ad Matth. XVIII, 15. Ideo hic dicit οἶκον ἐμπορίου. In posteriore ejectione οἶκον λῃστῶν: hic quæstum notat, ibi quæstus in sacro loco indignitatem efficacius exprimit. Vi- de quæ ad dictum Matthæi locum. Argumentum est petitum à loci sanctitate, quia domus illa cultui Dei erat sanctificata, Deut. XII. 5. Patris mei, inquit. Quod de Cyrillus: Unigenitus Fi- lius, non ex gratia, sed ex substantia Patris genitus, vere & pro- prie solus Patrem suum Deus appellat, Joh. III. 16. c. I, 14. Rom. IIX 22. 32. Non ergo in Domum mercatus converten- da erat Domus Patris. Pollutio illa templi gra- vissima, indignissima, scandalosissima erat cum fal- sa persuasione de peculiari sanctitate pecudum & a- vium in loco sacro prostantium conjuncta, & sub specie promovendi cultus divini designata. Ideo ab eo, qui Dominus erat templi, & ad purgandum Filios Levi venerat, Mal. III. 13. minime toleranda. Qui à purgatione templi initium hic facere voluit, utpote qui cultum divinum universum reparatu- rus, & doctrinam cœlestem restauraturus erat, ut prius falsam doctrinam, falsumq; cultum reforma- ri, quam religionis veræ curam & studium suscipi debere doceret. Quia finis templi cultus Dei, igi- tur evertitur finis, mutato illo in domum negotia- tionis, quod ipsum hoc loco Christus reprobat, & templum ab ista negotiatione liberat seu purgat. Vers. 17. ἐμνήσθησαν δὲ οἱ μαθηταὶ ἀυτοῦ] Locum celebrem Pfalmorum & cantari vulgo solitum in memoriam sibi re- vocarunt. Nam constabat sub Davidis persona Messiam ibi describi. Non sub Davidis persona Messias ibi Pf. LXIX. 10. describitur, sed loquitur illic ex propria persona Messias, neq; ad Davidem illa trahi debent, quem- admodum in annotatis ad Psalmos ostendimus. ζῆλος] Ardens amor. κατέφαγέ με] Dictum ut illud, est cura medullas. Vers. 18. ἀπεκρίθησαν] Diximus alibi ויענו Hebræum ut & Græcum ἀποκριθεὶς, & apud Homerum ἀπαμειβόμενος sæpe dici de eo qui prior loquitur. τί σημεῖον δεικνύεις ἡμῖν ὅτι ταῦτα ποιεῖς;] In publicis locis tollere vitiosa, nullius est nisi aut publicæ potestatis aut di- vinæ.
