Hæc commercia tolerabat Synedrium, tolerabant sacerdotes. Restabat ergo ut Prophetam se Iesus profitere- tur. At Prophetæ se tales ostendere debebant aut prædictio- nibus aut ostentis. Vid. 1. Cor. I. 22. Vers. 19. λύσατε τὸν ναὸν τοῦτον] Malignos obscure alloqui- tur: nam si probo fuissent animo, in ipso hoc facto miraculu agnovissent: Quod homo unus nullis instructus humanis viribus tantam turbam imperio suo cedere coegisset, sola turpis facti conscientia & divinæ iræ sensu permotos, stultos homines solemus ad operis fine rejicere. Sic Christus, quan- quam liberalis miraculorum, ad maximum miraculorum & complementum, resurrectionem scilicet suam frequentes responsat起こ rejicit. In templo credebatur vis aliqua esse di- vini numinis. Sic Solomon apud Iosephum orat, μοῖραν τινα τοῦ Θεοῦ πνεύματος εἰς τὸν ναὸν ἀποικῆσαι lib. VIII. 2. Hinc simi- litudine sumta Christiani, quibus Dei Spiritus contigerat, Templum Dei dicuntur, 1. Cor. III. 16. c. V. 19. 2. Cor. VI. 16. Quanto magis ergo hoc nomen humanæ Christi natu- ræ competit, in quo non per figuras sed plene ac solide σω- ματικῶς divinitas non temporarium sed perpetuum sibi do- micilium delegerat? Col. II. 9. Rabbi Moses Gerundensis קדש קדשים הוא המשיח מקודש מבני דוד Sanctu- arium Sanctuariorum est ipse Messias sanctificatus de filiis David. Sunt autem verba Christi talia ut & de Templo possint in- telligi, nam λύειν etiam destruere est, 2. Pet. III, 10. 12. 1. Ioh. III 8. Imperativus autem positus hic est pro potentiali. De- struite id est si destruatis: ut Pone Tigellinum id est si ponas. ἐν τρισὶν ἡμέραις] Intra diem tertium. ἐγερῶ] Et hoc ambiguum. Nam & de ædificiis dicitur ex- citare. Sic in Græco epigrammate δώματα πολλ' ἀνεγείρας. Significanter autem dixit ἐγερῶ ego ipse vi divina. Vers. 21. ἔλεγε] Hoc præcipue innuebat. περὶ τοῦ ναοῦ τοῦ σώματος αὐτοῦ] Genitivus ἐξηγητικὸς sicut fon- tem Timavi dicimus & alia multa, vice appositionis. Prophetia gemina est, de morte nempe, & Re- surrectione Christi, occasione signi seu ex curiositate sive è quadam, ut videtur nonnullis, quoad quos- dam in cœtu isto præsentes, pietate desiderati. Conf. Matth. XII. 40. Quod quidem signum, nisi propter salutem omnium futurum omnino esset, nunquam testantibus illis dedisset, dicente Cyrillo. Miratur hic Chrysost. summam clementiam: Quonam enim signo opus erat, cum male- facta corriperet, & Dei domum a tanta purgaret ignominia? Ze- lus ille pro domus Dei honore maximum fuit virtutis signum, quod boni adverterunt. Dictum id sibi putent Papistæ, signum à Luthero petentes. Prima Christi Pro- phetia erat de morte. Solvite, inquit Christus, tem- plum hoc, ubi verbum solvite non est mandantis, sed vaticinantis sive narrantis. Conf. Job. XXI. 5. c. XXII. v. 21. uti solent Prophetarum phrasi quandoque prædictiones imperandi modo pronunciari, Esa. XLVII. 1. Non impellit illos ad cædem suam, ait Cyril- lus, sed quod facturos sciebat, ad utilitatem eorum po- tius, si quid sensus habuissent subaperit. Templum in- telligit non proprie de Templo Hierosolymitano, ut Judæi accipiebant, sed Symbolice de templo corporis sui, ut explicat Spir. S. cui corpus Christi templum est ob expiationem in illo factam, ob sanctitatem, & imprimis ob inhabitationem divinitatis Col. II. 9. ut explicat Ambros. in Ps. IV, 7. Vere templum Dei corpus est Christi, in quo est nostrorum peccatorum purificatio, vere Tem- plum Dei caro illa, in qua nullum potuit esse contagium; sed ipsa pro delicto mundi totius fuit sacrificium. Vere Dei templum caro illa, in qua Dei imago fulgebat, & corporaliter plenitudo divini- tatis habitabat, quoniam ipse Christus est plenitudo. Revo- cat eos à typico templo, in quo tantopere gloriaban- tur ad veram Antitypum, Ebr. IX. 14. ac simul ad potissimum templi usum, utpote in quo præcipue mors Christi ejusdemque resurrectio prædicari, & adumbrari debuit. Facit huc explicatio R. Mena- hem. in Thalm. C. Helech. vaticinii illius Amos IX. 11. quod in Messia tabernaculum Davidis cadere in morte, & vicissim resuscitari in Resurrectione ejus de- buerit. Judæi vero calumniam inde struxerunt in Passione Christi Matth. XXVI. 61. ipse dixit, dissolve- re possum templum Dei, quam diluit hic ipse Spir. S. Templi enim dissolutio est mors Christi, quando mor- tuo Christo anima deseruit carnem, tunc solutum est il- lud templum, quod fuit ex anima carneque constru- ctum, ait Fulgent. lib. III. ad Thras. cap. 17.

Tabernaculum Mosaïcum, ut & Templum Hiero- solymitanum fuisse typum Christi, demonstratur (1.) ratione causæ efficientis. Ut enim formam Ta- bernaculi Deus Mosi monstravit, & iste juxta il- lam ædificari curavit: Sic Christus sive templum corporis ejus à Spiritu S. exstructus est. (2.) Mate- riæ, constabat enim ligno cedrino & auro: quod geminam Christi naturam indicat. (3.) Præsentiæ. Ut Deus peculiari modo in tabernaculo se manife- stabat: Sic in Christo habitat tota plenitudo divi- nitatis. (4.) Arcæ fœderis & propitiatorii. Ibi enim servabantur Leges, &c. Sic Christus est vera Arca fœderis. In corde enim ejus inscriptæ sunt Leges Ps. XL. 9. verum Propitiatorium, Rom. III. 25. Ebr. IX. (5.) Sacrificii. In templo sacrificia offereban- tur: ita non debebat aliter peragi sacrificium Chri- sti, quam in templo carnis suæ. Porro Vaticinium hoc aliquanto obscurius quidem videtur, sed per eventum dilucidatum est. Quærit autem Chryso- stomus, quare Christus orationem hanc discipulis non interpre- tatus sit? Respondet ipse, quia discipuli nondum erant idonei, ad intelligendum istud mysterium multo minus turba. Quærit porro: qui factum sit, quod discipuli nondum fuerint idonei? & hanc suppeditat rationem, quia falso tenebantur errore de regno Christi mundano. Est autem & hoc notandum, quod tum temporis Discipuli fuerint Catechumeni, qui licet non omnia statim Ecclesiæ intelligant do- gmata, propterea tamen non ejiciuntur, sed magis magisque informantur. Utut ea non intellige- bant, attamen nec præfracte negabant.

Altera Prophetia est de Resurrectione, de qua Christus vaticinatur his verbis: & tribus diebus ego excitabo illud. Determinans (1.) Tempus resuscita- tionis. ἐν τρισὶν ἡμέραις, in tribus diebus, sive intra tres dies. Non enim integri erant tres dies, cum exci- taretur corporis templum, uti Alcuin. l. d. div. off. c. d. Cœn. Dom. censet, Christum 72. horis in sepulchro jacuisse; siquidem dicatur Christus tribus diebus & tribus noctibus fuisse in corde terræ, Matth. XII. v. 39. imo etiam post tres dies resurrexisse c. XXVII. 63. Marc. VIII. 32. sed ibi μετὰ non post notat, sed in- tra, ut Deut. XXXIV. 38. Luc. II. 46. c. XXII. 20. Conf. Marc. VIII. 32. Matth. XVI. 21. Historia enim docet, quod uti die Parasceves hora nona exspiravit, Matt. XXVII. 26. 50. mox deinde cum adhuc illa du- raret dies, sub vesperam sepultus fuerit, Marc. XV. 42. Luc. XXIII. 54. ut tres pene horæ istius diei su- perfuerint, & numerato, Judæorum more, die à ve- spera illa ad vesperam sequentis diei Sabbati, tertis dies inchoatur usq; ad auroram per aliquot iterum horas, unde triduum sepulturæ Synecdochice acci- piendum, quia per unum solum integrum diem, & per duarum dierum partes vel horas aliquot quievit in sepulchro. (2.) Causam efficientem. Voce ἐγερῶ ego excitabo. Indicat autem sese, tum ratione divinæ, tum humanæ naturæ. Divinæ naturæ documentum est il- la ipsa potestas excitandi à morte corpus suum, quia hæc vere infinita potentia est soli Deo pro- pria, solique Deo tribuitur passim Christi à mortuis excitatio, Act. II. 24. 22. III. 15. IV. 10. V. 30. X. 40. XIII. 30. XVII. 13. Ideoq; invictum hic argumentum peti- tur divinę Christi naturę, quę demonstrata etiam di- citur per resurrectionem à mortuis Rom. I. 4 Quoniam hoc vel maximo argumento, ut inquit Chrysost. se non esse purum homi- nem, & mortem sibi subesse, & ejus vim & bellum gravissimum, mox sublaturnm ostendebat; Humanæ vero naturæ, uti personaliter communicatam habebat divinam po- tentiam, & speciatim δύναμιν ζωοποιητικὴν Joh. V. 23. ita anima ejus excludenda non est à vivificatione pro- prii corporis & templi excitatione per illam divinã potentiam facta. Idcirco toti ὑφισαμένῳ tribuitur & potestas ponendi sumendiq; vitam. Joh. X. 17. & excitatio tem- pli corporis sui. Excitetit suum ipsius templum, inquit Cyrill. lib. I. in Es. c. IX cum ipse sit potentia Patris Si enim ipse est Resur- rectio & vita, quid tandem adi vivificationem desideraret vita? Et si aliorum corpora excitasse conspicitur, sua et- iam vi & potentia, quidni suum proprium resusci- taret? (3.) Modum & veritatem. Ἐγερῶ, excitabo. Uti mors fuit quædam dissolutio, ita excitatio hu- jus ædificii fuit animæ & corporis nova conjunctio, corporisque animati erectio. Destructum enim non erat corporis templum, sed solutum ab anima. Ideo non de novo ædificatur, sed excitatur, redintegrata vicissim unione animæ & corporis. Ineptum vero est, & à verbis Christi prorsus alienum, quod Cate- chesis Racov. & Melch. Scheffer. verba Christi sic in- telligenda esse ostendunt: Ego postquam resuscitatus fuero a Patre, erigam me, vel corpus meum, quasi Christus hic non excitationem corporis, sed exci- tati erectionem sibi vindicasset. Hac enim ratione & verba vim patiuntur; quia ait, ego excitabo, non autem ab alio excitatum erigam, & vis miraculi e- nervatur, quo non Patris, sed suam ipsius virtutem demonstrare volebat. (4.) Objectum. Illud ipsum templum, quod solvebatur per mortem, excitatum fuit per Christi virtutem Ps. XVI. 10. Actor. II. 27. ut & Luc. XXIV. 39. Joh. XX. 20. 21. Epiphan. in Ancor. Eorum, inquit, qui falsam fidem habent, est, dicere non id quod obdormiit, resurrexit; Credentium autem est dicere, quod idem corpus resurrexerit. Ipsum quod occidit granum resurrexit &c. Hinc ergo li- quet, Christum hac ipsa sententia se authorem re- surrectionis suæ ex mortuis fecisse, adeoq; semet- ipsum in vitam revocasse, quod impie negant qui- dem ac rident Sociniani; Ostorod. l. II. contra Tra- del. c. 10. Enjed. in Expl. LL. Script. in h. l. Smaltz. d. div. Christi cap. 13. Melch. Scheffer. tr. pecul. de hoc

Argumento edito, quo de pluribus actum tr. Germ nomine Facult. Th. Acad. Regiomont. edito & Theol. Natur. & Revel. T. 2. super A. C. p. 1289. Frustra obvertunt (1.) Verba Christi figurata esse atq; obscura, quia figura diserte est explicata, quod nempe loquatur Christus de templo corporis sui. Neque (2.) excipi potest : Christum ex loquendi ne- cessitate ita locutum. Quæ enim necessitas Christum cogere poterat, ut ita & non aliter loqueretur, nec tamen ita sed aliter intelligeret. Nec (3.) quod ob miraculi ἄυξησιν hæc ita protulerit. Non enim sole- bat Christus sibi tribuere, quod suum non erat, aut ambigua oratione sibi apud imprudentes au- toritatem conciliare. Quod autem (4.) se ipsum templum corporis sui excitaturum non aliter di- cat, quam prout fideles animam suam dicuntur inve- nire, Matth. X. 39. vel vivificare, Luc. XVII. 33. quo- modo citra petitionem principii solide, quod con- tendunt Enjedinus, Socinus, Racovienses, Smaltzius, Crellius, Scheffer. aut alii Photiniani probabunt? Vel quod etiam (5.) non dubitat statuere Socinus, ita Christum excitare dici corpus suum, ut mortui re- surgere, ut Lazarus resurrexisse alibi dicitur. Nam illos saltem ex gratia vitam adipisci & velut inve- nire, hos vero non nisi in vitam revocatos docet res ipsa resurgere, secus de Christo vitæ autore, Do- mino mortis, Deo benedicto in secula. Nec est à li- tera discedendum nisi exigat id necessitas. Hic ve- ro ut literam retineamus, ipsa etiam urget, cogitq; necessitas. Debebat enim hoc esse τεκμήριον divi- næ, non Patris, sed Christi potentiæ, quam ipsam Iu- dæi requirendo, solicitabant. Denique (6.) contra reliquos admittit tandem Enjedinus, Christum qui- dem se excitasse, sed non propria virtute. At quænam esset illa declaratio virtutis suæ divinæ, si solum a- liena virtute resuscitatus esset? ἐξουσίαν ἔχω ἀπ' ἐμαυτõ potestatem habeo à me ipso resumendi animam. Crellius autem admittit quoq; id evincere illa loca Joh. II. & X. Christum resurrectionis causam, eamque in illius manu positam fuisse, adeo, ut ipsi ea interverti à nemine posset. Tanta vis est veritatis! Desperatæ autem causæ indicium est, quod Socin. l. II. contr. Erasm. Joh. p. 114. Non esse hic verba superstitiose ob- servanda, quippe quorum aliqua veritati per omnia non conveniant, ore profano asserit. Perinde ut de illo Joh. X. 18. blaspheme Socinus pronunciat : Itidem fortasse quidem Christo convenire, quod habuerit pote- statem resumendi animam, & tolerabiliter id dici l. c pag. 126. Quod Schefferus affirmare non veretur; etiamsi in Scripturis expresse & aliquoties scriptum extaret, quod Christus seipsum resuscitarit, adhuc tamen de eo ambigendum fore l. c. pag. 33. Annon hoc est os in cœlum ponere.

## 2:20
V. 20. Forty and six years) We said at Matt. 24:1 that Herod the Great did not make another Temple by his substructure, but enlarged it. Nor was it destroyed. Therefore the Jews always call it the second Temple from Zerubbabel until the destruction by Titus. But they calculate the times of building under the kings of the Persians more broadly, including also the years in which the work had been interrupted, so that they may make Jesus more odious.

How can 46 years be made up from the time the construction of the second temple was begun, spent on its building under the Persian Kings? Drusius indeed begins the calculation thus: that Cyrus held power for 31 years, Cambyses nine, the Magi seven months: but the building was finished in the sixth year of Darius. But Cyrus did not relax the captivity in the first year of his Persian reign, but of his Monarchy: over which he presided for nine years at most: and if the calculation is subtracted from the time of the Persian rule of Cyrus until the sixth year of Darius Nothus, not 46, but 139 years will result, but if the terminus of the built temple is established as the sixth year of Darius Hystaspis, only 32 years will intervene from the first of the Monarchy of Cyrus, but from the first of the Persian rule, 53 years. Thus the calculation of the construction of the temple of Zerubbabel, which Theodoret nevertheless assumed, does not agree in any way. Beza with other Calvinists, deservedly refuted by Baillie in Book II of his historical work, p. 72, where he also corrected another calculation of Piscator, and again another of Rollock concerning the building of the temple under the Persian Kings. These therefore being left aside, others count these 46 years from the time from which the second temple began to be restored by Herod, i.e., These 46 years the temple has been built, and is not yet perfected, since this renovation began 16 years before the death of Herod, the end of which the birth of Christ slightly preceded, who now, when these things were happening, was about 30 years old. Thus Capellus, with Gwalther, Scaliger, Casaubon, and Diodati preceding, whom Baillie follows; nor do Baronius, Estius, Cornelius a Lapide, etc., proceed by any other path. I simply, says Capellus in Walaeus, accept it concerning the time from which the temple began to be built by Herod, from which (as Josephus testifies) the whole was restored from the very foundations, and made new. But Herod began that work in the 18th year of his reign (calculating, namely, the years of his reign from the time when, having conquered Jerusalem and driven out Antigonus, he occupied the kingdom: and not from the time when he was declared King by the Roman Senate) and therefore 16 years before his death; for he reigned 34 years from the expulsion of Antigonus. But Christ was born toward the end of the reign of Herod, and (as it seems) shortly before his death; but when the Jews were saying these things to Christ, he was just thirty years old; for this happened shortly after the baptism of Christ, namely at the Passover which immediately followed his baptism. Therefore from the first foundations of the temple laid by Herod to that moment when the Jews object this to Christ, 46 years flowed precisely. Furthermore, although Herod is said by Josephus to have finished the structure of the temple in eight years, it is nevertheless plain from the same author that something was always added and built from that time in that temple, and indeed for many years after. For finally in the time of Agrippa the Younger, about sixty years after Christ was born, the whole building of the temple was finished, as the same Josephus testifies, Antiquities book 20, ch. 8. And now at that time the temple was also finished, therefore the people seeing that the craftsmen would be idle, etc. And so the Jews seem to have meant this for themselves here: Already for forty-six years the construction of this temple was begun by Herod, and it is not yet completed: or: For these forty-six years this temple is being built daily, yet it is not yet perfected and finished, but you will restore it, having collapsed, in the short space of three days.

Latin:

V. 20. Τεσσαράκοντα καὶ ἓξ ἔτεσιν) Diximus ad Matt. XXIV. 1. Herodis Magni substructione non effecisse aliud Templum, sed auxisse. Neque enim dirutum fuit. Itaque semper Judæi Templum secundum vocant à Zorobabele ad excidiū Titi. Largius autem computant tempora ædificationis sub Persa- rum regibus, comprehensis etiam annis, quibus interru- ptum opus fuerat, quo majorem Iesu invidiam faciant.

Quomodo possunt anni 46. confici inde à cœ- pta exstructione templi secundi ædificationi ejus impensi sub Persarum Regibus? Drusius sane ita calculum init: quod Cyrus rerum potitus sit annis 31. Cambyses novem, Magi septem mensibus: Sexto au- tem Darii absolutum sit ædificium. Sed Cyrus non re- laxavit captivitatem anno primo regni sui Persici, sed Monarchiæ suæ: cui novem annis ad summum præfuit: & si subducatur calculus à tempore regi- minis Persici Cyri usque ad sextum Darii Nothi, non XLVI. sed CXXXIX. anni prodituri sunt, si ve- ro terminus exstructi templi constituatur sextus Darii Hystaspis, XXXII. tantum anni à primo Monarchiæ Cyri intervenient, à primo vero re- giminis Persici, anni LIII. Ita nullatenus concor- dat calculus exstructionis templi Zorobabelis, quem tamen assumsit Theodor. Beza cum aliis Cal- vinianis, merito refutatus à Bailio L. II. operis hi- stor. pag. 72. ubi etiam alium Piscatoris, iterumque alium Rolloci calculum de templi ædificatione sub Persarum Regibus castigavit. His ergo relictis, aliis annos hosce XLVI. numerant ab eo tempore, ex quo ab Herode restaurari templum secundum cœpit, q. d. Hosce XLVI. annos ædificatum templum, & nondum perfectum est, siquidem XVI. annis ante mortem Herodis cœperit hæc renovatio, cujus excessum paulo antevertit nativitas Christi, qui nunc, cum hæc agerentur, annos circiter XXX. natus erat. Ita Capellus, præeunte Gvaltero, Scaligero, Casaubono, Deodato, quos sequitur Bailius; nec alia incedunt via Baronius, Estius, Cornel. à Lapide, &c. Ego simpliciter, dicit Capellus apud Walæum, accipio de tempore, quo extrui ab Herode cœptum erat tem- plum, a quo (teste Josepho) totum est ab ipsis fun- damentis instauratum, novumque factum. Cœpit au- tem opus illud Herodes anno regni sui 18. (computando scil. regni ipsius annos ab eo tempore, quo expugnatis Hierosolymis & pulso Antigono regnum occupavit: non vero ab eo tempore quo à Senatu Rom. Rex fuit declaratus) ac proinde annis ante mortem XVI. nam à depulso Antigono regnavit annos 34. Christus autem natus est sub finem regni Herodis, & (uti videtur) paulo ante hujus obitum; quum autem Christo ista di- cerent Judæi, natus erat annos duntaxat triginta; hoc enim contigit paulo post Christi baptismum, Paschate nimirum quod proxime secutum est ipsius baptisma. Itaque à primis ab Herode jactis templi fundamentis ad id momentum, quo istud Christo objiciunt Judæi, fluxerunt precise anni 46. Porro etsi Herodes dici- tur à Josepho aunis octo absolvisse templi structu- ram, planum tamen est ex eodem semper aliquid additum & exstructum ab eo tempore fuisse in illo templo imo & pluribus post annis. Nam Agrippæ demum Junioris tempore, sexaginta circiter post Christum natum annis absolutum est totum tem- pli ædificium, teste eodem Josepho Antiq. lib. XX. c. 8. ἤδη δὲ τότε καὶ τὸ ἱερὸν τετέλεστο βλέπων οὖν ὁ δῆ- μος ἀργήσοντας τὺς τεχνίτας &c. Hoc itaque vi- dentur sibi voluisse hic Judæi: Iam ab annis quadragin- ta sex cœpta est ab Herode hujus templi structura, necdum est ab- soluta: vel: Hosce quadraginta sex annos ædificatur quotidie hoc templum, nondum tamen perfectum & consommatum est, tu vero illud brevi dierum trium spatio instaurabis collapsum.

## 2:22
Vers. 22. ὅτε ὖν ἠγέρθη ἐκ νεκρῶν) When not only by the event but also by divine illumination they began to understand the scriptures. See what [I wrote] on Luke ch. XXIV. 45. ἐπίστευσαν) With understanding, that is. τῇ γραφῇ) Of Isaiah, as one who had predicted the glorious life of the Messiah, after he had given himself to death for sinners: which very thing Ps. XVI hints at, taken according to the underlying meaning.

Not only in Isaiah ch. LIII or in Ps. XVI, but in many places the resurrection of the Lord is treated, such as Gen. III. 15, Job XIX. 25, Ps. VIII. 7, Ps. LXVIII. 2, Ps. CX. v. ult., Es. LV. 3. Conf. Acts XIII. 2, 3, 4, Hos. VI. 2, XIII. 14, Mich. IV. 13. Nor only according to the underlying meaning, but according to the literal sense, that Ps. XVI treats of the same has been shown in the defenses of that Psalm. But since Grotius here acknowledges that Isaiah ch. LIII treats of Christ, why does he twist it to the prophet Jeremiah in his annotations on the O.T.

Latin:

Vers. 22. ὅτε ὖν ἠγέρθη ἐκ νεκρῶν) Cum non eventu tan- tum sed & divina illustratione cœperunt scripturas intelli- gere. Vide quæ ad Lucam c. XXIV. 45. ἐπίστευσαν) Cum intellectu scilicet. τῇ γραφῇ) Esaiæ, ut qui prædixerat vitam Messiæ glorio- sam, postquam se in mortem pro peccatoribus dedisset: quod ipsum innuit Ps. XVI. sumptus κατὰ τὴν ὑπόνοιαν.

Non in Esaia tantum c. LIII. aut in Ps. XVI. sed pluribus locis de resurrectione Domini agitur, ut- pote Gen. III. 15. Job. XIX. 25. Ps. VIII. 7. Ps. LXVIII. 2. Ps. CX. v. ult. Es. LV. 3. Conf. Act. XIII. 2. 3. 4. Hos. VI. 2. XIII. 14. Mich. IV. 13. Neq; solum κτ᾽ τὴν ὑπό- νοιαν, sed κτ᾽ τὸ ῥητὸν, Ps. XVI. de eadem agi, in vin- diciis illius Psalmi ostensum est. Esaiæ autem c. LIII. de Christo agere cum agnoscat hic Grotius, cur id detorfital Prophetam Jeremiam in annot. ad V. T.

## 2:23
V. 23. ἐν τῇ ἑορτῇ) We have said what ἑορτὴ is at Matt. XXVI. 5. ἐπίστευσαν) In a persuasive or practical sense, with the understanding convinced, but not also with the will bent toward obedience, which addition makes faith living. See Acts VIII. 13.

Faith is made living, not through the bending of the will toward obedience, but through the apprehension of the merits of Christ: which that bending follows, as the fruit and consequence of true and living faith. And this is the proper and formal practice of faith, namely the apprehension of Christ, John I. 12. But operation through charity is an effect of faith, Galat. V. 6. Whether, however, these had true faith and confidence in

Christ; but whether only a bare συγκατάθεσις [assent] is to be understood in this place, it may be a matter of doubt; Chrysostom, Theophylact, and Nonnus think that they believed only in simulation; but because the Evangelist says they believed in his name, it seems that it should not be taken as referring only to simulation, nor to bare assent, since that phrase is accustomed to be used regarding trust, and the cause of the trust in Christ is added here, namely, that they had seen the miracles of Christ. But when it is subjoined that Christ did not entrust himself to them, it is to be understood of the promiscuous multitude and familiar conversation, that he did not entrust himself intimately to the people as he did to his disciples: because not all among the people were equally affected toward him, even though many believed in him.

Latin:

V. 23. ἐν τῇ ἑορτῇ) Quid sit ἑορτὴ diximus Matth. XXVI. 5. ἐπίστευσαν) πεπρητικῶς ὠ̓ παρακτικῶς, intellectu convicto, non etiam flexa ad obsequium voluntate, quod additamentum fidem efficit vivam. Vide Act. VIII. 13.

Fides efficitur viva, non per voluntatis ad obse- quium inflexionem, sed per meritorum Christi ap- prehensionem: quam illa inflexio sequitur, uti fru- ctus & consequens veræ & vivæ fidei. Et hæc est praxis fidei propria & formalis, apprehensio nem- pe Christi, Joh. I. 12. Operatio vero per chari- tatem effectus est fidei, Galat. V. 6. Utrum au- tem hi veram fidem, & fiduciam habuerint in

Christum; an vero nuda tantum συγκατάθεσις h. l. intelligenda sit, dubium esse queat, Chrysostomus, Theophylactus & Nonnus, simulate tantum illos cre- didisse putant; sed quia Evangelista dicit ἐπίσευ- σαν τὸ ὄνομα αὐτῶ, nec de simulatione tantum, nec de nudo assensu accipiendum id videtur, quum Phra- sis illa de fiducia adhiberi consueverit, addaturque hic fiduciæ in Christum causa, quod nempe vide- rint miracula Christi. Quum vero subjungitur, quod non crediderit se ipsis Christus, intelligendum est de promiscua multitudine, & familiari conversatione, quod populo se intime non crediderit, uti discipu- lis suis: quia non omnes in populo æqualiter ipsi affecti erant, etsi multi in ipsum crederent.

## 2:24
Vers. 24. He did not entrust himself to them) An allusion with a changed meaning of the word, such as in Matt. VIII. 22. He did not commit himself to their faith by daily association, but returned into Galilee, because the opportune time for his death had not yet arrived. He saw that they were not so affected that they would be willing to undergo any danger or ignominy for his sake: because that knowledge did not have a mind loving true piety as its foundation. And now the time of dangers was encroaching. Therefore, in the following chapter, his approach by night is narrated.

Γινώσκειν πάντας [To know all]) Both the evil and those not good enough.

Latin:

Vers. 24. Οὐκ ἐπίsευεν ἑαυτὸν αὐτοῖς) Allusio mutata si- gnificatione vocabuli qualis, Matth. VIII. 22. Non commi- sit eorum fidei quotidianæ convictu, sed rediit in Galilæam, quia opportunum mortis tempus nondum advenerat. Vi- debat eos non ita affectos, ut quicquam aut periculi aut ignominiæ sua causa subire vellent: quia cognitio illa non habebat substructum sibi animum amantem veræ pietatis. Et jam tempus periculorum ingruebat. Ideo capite se- quenti narratur noctu aditus.

Γινώσκειν πάντας) Et malos & non satis bonos.

## 2:25
Vers. 25. That anyone should testify concerning the man) That anyone should betray himself by words or deeds, the man, here is any man whatsoever: concerning which manner of speaking it has been noted elsewhere.

What was in the man) In the innermost part of the heart, which is proper to God. Ps. XXXIII. 15. 1 Kings VIII. 39. and elsewhere, etc.

Latin:

Vers. 25. Ἱνα τις μαρτυρήσῃ περὶ τῶ ἀνθρώπυ) Ut quis se- met dictis vel factis proderet, ὁ ἄνθρωπος, hic est homo quivis: de quo loquendi genere notatum alibi.

Τὶ ἧν ἐν τῷ ἀνθρώπῳ In cordis intimo quod Dei proprium. Pf. XXXIII. 15. 1. Reg. VIII. 39. & alibi, &c.

## 3:1 Argument
CHAPTER III. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

Nicodemus approaches Jesus by night, and is informed by him concerning Regeneration, and also concerning the descent of the Son of man from the heavens, and his exaltation on the cross, as the bronze serpent erected in the desert in the antitype, and the mission of the only-begotten Son of God into the world to the end that, namely, the world might be saved through him, and thus concerning the causes of salvation, as also of condemnation. Jesus baptizes in Judea while John is baptizing in Aenon, whence, a dispute having arisen concerning purification, John testifies that he is not Christ, nor the Messiah, but the forerunner of Christ, and the friend of the bridegroom, who comes from the heavens, and is above all, to whom the Spirit is given not by measure, and all things are delivered into his hands, in whom he who believes has eternal life, and he who does not believe, the wrath of God remains upon him.

There are two parts. I. The colloquy of Nicodemus and Jesus, and his instruction concerning regeneration and the causes of salvation, up to verse 21. II. The dispute concerning baptism, and the testimony of John concerning Christ, the Bridegroom, and the Son of God, and the life to be obtained through faith in him, up to verse 36.

PART I. The colloquy of Nicodemus with Jesus.

Vers. 1. Now there was) There, as the Syriac adds, that is, in the city of Jerusalem, where those things had happened which were narrated a little before.

From the Pharisees) Of the better sect.

Nicodemus by name) The custom had already long since invaded among the Jews of taking Greek names, such as Menelaus, Tryphon, Dositheus.

Ruler of the Jews) That is, one from the great Sanhedrin; see what [I wrote] on Luke 14:1.

Latin:

CAPUT III. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Nicodemus noctu Jesum adit, & ab eo informatur de Regeneratione, nec non de descensu Filii hominis de cælis, ejusque exaltatione in cruce, in antitypo erecti in deserto ænei serpentis, ac missionis Filii Dei unigeniti in mundum fine, ut sc. mundus per ipsum salvaretur, adeoque de causis salutis, ut & conde- mnationis. Jesus baptizat in Judæa Johanne ba- ptizante in Ælon, unde orta disceptatione de purifi- catione, Johannes testatur se non esse Christum, nec Messiam sed prodromum Christi, & amicum spon- si, qui de cælis venit, & super omnia est, cui datus Spiritus non ad mensuram, & omnia in manus tra- dita, in quem qui credit, vitam æternam habet, qui non credit, super eum manet ira Dei.

Partes duæ sunt. I. Colloquium Nicodemi & Jesu, illiusque de regeneratione & causis, salutis infor- mátio, ad v. 21. II. Disceptatio de baptismo, & testifi- catio Johannis de Christo, Sponso, & Filio Dei, ac vita per fidem in ipsam consequenda, ad v. 36.

PARS I. Colloquium Nicodemi cum Jesu.

Vers. 1. Ἦν δὲ) Ibi ut addit Syrus id est in urbe Hierosoly- morum, ubi ea acciderant, quæ paulo ante fuerunt narrata.

Ἐκ τῶν Φαρισαίων) Melioris sectæ.

Νικόδημος ὄνομα) Pridem jam mos invaserat apud Judæos sumendi Græca nomina, ut Menelaus, Tryphon, Dositheus.

Ἄρχων τῶν Ἰυδαίων) Id est unus ex magno Synedrio, vide quæ ad Lucam XIV. 1.

## 3:2
Verse 2. By night) Lest he offend his colleagues who were already ill-disposed toward Jesus. Something similar is said below regarding Joseph of Arimathea at 19:38, and the mention of this Nicodemus follows immediately, with this note added: 'who came to Jesus by night.' It is narrated of Euclid of Megara that when he was forbidden by an edict against the Megarians from coming to Athens openly, he came by night so that he might participate in the counsels and conversations of Socrates.

You have come from God) You have been sent, as above at 1:10 and often elsewhere.

Teacher) With the authority to teach the people. A similar manner of speaking is found below at 12:36.

Unless God were with him) Present to him by His efficacy. See Matthew 28:20. He assumes that Christ does not teach false gods, for except for that one case, one had to believe him who performed miracles. Furthermore, the miracles of Jesus surpassed every power, even the diabolical.

Latin:

Vers. 2. Νυκτὸς) Ne collegas jam Jesu male volentes of- fenderet. Simile quid de Josepho Arimathensi dicitur infra XIX. 38. statimque sequitur hujus Nicodemi mentio, addita hac nota: ὁ ἐλθὼν πρὸς τὸν Ἰησῦν νυκτὸς. De Euclide Megarensi narratur eum cum edicto in Megarenses facto Athenas pa- lam venire vetaretur, venisse noctu ut consiliorum sermo- numque Socratis fieret particeps.

Ἀπὸ Θεῦ ἐλήλυθας) Missus es ut supra, I. 10. & alibi sæpe.

Διδάσκαλος) Cum potestate docendi populum. Simile loquendi genus infra XII. 36.

Ἐὰν μὴ ἦ ὁ Θεὸς μετ᾽ αὐτῦ) Efficacia sua ipsi præsens. Vide Matth. XXVIII. v. 20. Supponit Christum non docere Deos falsos, quo solo excepto credendum erat ei qui miracula e- deret. Deinde miracula Jesu omnem vim etiam diaboli- cam superabant.

## 3:3
Verse 3. He answered) The response tacitly hints at what had been added by Nicodemus: namely, that he wished to know, since Jesus often made mention of the kingdom of heaven while teaching, what the method was for arriving there.

Born from above) Without doubt, ἄνωθεν means 'again,' δεύτερον, as Nicodemus soon understands it, who could not have been deceived by the ambiguous meaning of the word, since in Hebrew or Syriac there is no such ambiguity. Thus the word ἄνωθεν is taken in Galatians 4:9. It exists in that sense in Athenagoras. Thus the Syriac interprets it in this place. Moreover, we have shown at Matthew 13:23 that the words 'to be made' and 'to be born' are accustomed to be used among the Hebrews regarding the formation of the mind. Seneca also uses it regarding the shortness of life: 'We are accustomed to say that it was not in our power what parents we might obtain, [that they were] given to us by chance. But it is permitted to us to be born according to our own will: there are most noble families of intellects; choose into which you wish to be adopted; you will be adopted not only into the name, but into the very goods.' Plutarch says that certain things handed down about Bacchus being torn apart are a 'myth regarding rebirth,' which he interprets as 'a punishment for the irrational and disorderly.' In a similar sense we read in an ancient inscription: 'Reborn forever by the Taurobolium and Criobolium.' And Rabbi Israel, in his book on the soul, calls proselytes 'newly born.' Compare James 1:18, and thus some take [the Hebrew] in Genesis 32:18, where the Greeks [translate it as]... 'Cannot see) To see here is to become a participant, as in Luke 2:26 and below at 8:51.

The kingdom of God) Which begins here through the peace of conscience, and would be completed in the other age through supreme happiness. Christ points out a new thing to Nicodemus, a Doctor of the Law: that henceforth something greater than Judaism is required to produce salvation. See Galatians 6:5, but also that the reward would be greater, the kingdom of heaven, which only then began to be manifested.

It is helpful to repeat here what we once publicly taught regarding these responses of Christ: The first response concerns the necessity of regeneration, verse 3, in which must be noted (1) Christ's Asseveration. 'Amen, Amen, I say to you,' which He prefixes partly because of the dignity of the mystery, for He was accustomed to use this form of speaking when He dealt with matters of the greatest moment and especially those concerning eternal salvation, of which kind is the regeneration of man or the first gate and entrance to eternal salvation; and partly because of the certainty of the matter, signifying that there is absolutely no other method of salvation besides regeneration; [this is] against the Pharisaic opinion, by which Nicodemus was fascinated, that one could approach the kingdom of heaven by the merits of works, so as to show, as Chrysostom says, that he had not yet reached the very vestibule of true knowledge, but was wandering outside the palace, both he and whoever were of the same opinion. (2) The designation of regeneration. Unless one is born from above or again, γεννηθῇ ἄνωθεν. The same generation is called [so] not in the proper sense, as if it were made from the substance of the generating God, and implies being ὁμούσιος with God the Father, such as is the eternal generation of the Son of God, Psalm 2:7, or a certain ἀποθέωσιν, as the Weigelians dream, but figuratively, because it has a certain similarity with generation, by reason of (1) the generating God, who is called our Father on account of our regeneration, 1 Peter 1:3. (2) Men who are regenerated, and are thence called sons of God, not by nature, but by grace. (3) The seed from which we are regenerated, the word of God, both ἀκυστόν or audible, and ὁρατόν or visible, as being the Sacrament of Baptism, Ephesians 5:26. (4) The similarity and participation of the divine nature, which we obtain through regeneration. (5) Spiritual and heavenly life, to which we are reborn, no differently than we obtain earthly life by natural generation. Of production, and the mode of operation. For just as man can contribute nothing to his own carnal procreation, so he can contribute nothing to his spiritual regeneration, since he is spiritually dead, and alienated from the life of God, Eph. II. 3. IV. 7. where, however, this difference between carnal and spiritual generation is to be noted, that while man cannot impede the former, he can not only impede the latter, but often does impede it.

Furthermore, this generation is said to be ἄνωθεν, this ἄνωθεν is from above, or also anew, and afresh. Chrysostom insinuates both meanings of the word, τὸ ἄνωθεν, he says, in this place some explain as from heaven, others as again, so that it may indicate either a supernal or heavenly generation, just as Cyril, Ammonius, and Theophylact explain, which is done by the Father of lights, from whom every good work ἄνωθεν descends, Jas. 1:17, where that word is also accepted in Job 3:13, 19:11, Jas. 3:15, 17, so that it may be distinguished from earthly birth; or a new and repeated birth: according to how that word is used in Gal. 4:9, and is understood here by Augustine, Nazianzen in his Oration on Pentecost, Severus of Antioch, etc. Nor was it understood otherwise by Nicodemus, asking how he could be born again, from which Maldonatus gathers that Christ, speaking in Syriac, used a word that was not at all ambiguous, which signified anew, not from above. For if Christ had said, unless one is born from above, Nicodemus would have sufficiently understood that He was not speaking of carnal generation. But the Formula of Concord rightly observes in the declaration of article 3, p. m. 686. That the word regeneration is not accepted in the same way; for sometimes it is used strictly for rebirth alone, by which we are begotten as Sons of God, by the collation of faith and the powers of believing, so that we may be adopted as Sons of God, Tit. 3:5, 1 Pet. 1:3. But sometimes it embraces in a broader signification even the renewal itself, which is a consequence of regeneration, and differs from it, since in regeneration faith is conferred by which we are justified: but renewal follows justification, by which, being justified and gifted with the Holy Spirit, we are reformed into a new creature, in true justice and holiness; in regeneration the intellect is illuminated, the will is converted to God, so that true recognition and trust may be conceived in us, and through faith we may become children of God, John 1:12. In renewal we are instructed with new strength and faculty, and are made spiritual, so that we may thus become a new creature, and the image of God is restored in us, by which the old man is gradually put off and the new is put on, Eph. 2:10, 4:22, 23. There the faculty of believing is granted, so that we may be recalled to spiritual life; here the faculty of doing good is granted, so that, having been made alive in Christ, we may live according to the spirit, in which way Cyril seems to describe regeneration in a comprehensive sense, book 2 on John, ch. 42. That we therefore become partakers of God, because we acquire through Baptism the Spirit, who proceeds substantially from God, by which, having been reformed into our original beauty and reborn to a new life, we are adopted by God as sons. But regeneration properly so called is the gracious action of God, by which man, flesh born of flesh, by the Spirit of God through the word, or the washing of water in the word, is illuminated with saving knowledge, as regards the will is gifted with trust in Christ, and thus, having been begotten in Him by saving faith, is made alive to spiritual life.

Regeneration properly accepted differs from justification and renewal (1) by reason of the principle and the mode of acting. Because regeneration is the action of God alone, and that intrinsic, and bringing about an intrinsic denomination by reason of the subject which is regenerated, such as illumination and the begetting of faith. Justification, however, is only extrinsic, and brings about an extrinsic denomination, as it is situated in the non-imputation of our injustice and in the imputation of another's justice apprehended through faith. Renewal, however, is indeed intrinsic, but the reborn man concurs with it, and therefore it is not the action of God alone. (2) By reason of the subject, which in regeneration is man, flesh born of flesh, and dead in sins, and destitute of all spiritual powers, Job 3:5, Eph. 2:2. In justification, it is the faithful man, acknowledging sins and believing in Christ, Rom. 3:22. In renewal, it is the justified man, Eph. 4:22, in whom faith is active through love, Gal. 5:6. (3) By reason of the term from which, which in regeneration is original sin, or the privation of spiritual powers, and depraved concupiscence; in justification, it is the guilt of fault and punishment in the judgment of God; in renewal, it is the dominion of sin. (4) By reason of the term to which, which in regeneration is saving faith, or the faithful man recalled to spiritual life, 1 John

ch. 5:2. Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ is born of God, and whatever is born of the spirit is spirit, John 3:6. In justification, it is the justice of Christ imputed, and the sonship of God through faith in Christ. In renewal, it is holiness inherent in us, or a new creature, 2 Cor. 5:17, Gal. 6:15. (5) By reason of the form; because regeneration consists in the illumination of our mind, as regards the mysteries of faith necessary to be believed, and the excitation of trust in our heart, so that we may adhere to God as our Father in the Son, through the Holy Spirit, and rest in Him alone. In a word, in the begetting of the powers of believing and of saving faith. Renewal, however, consists in the liberation of the mind from any other errors whatsoever, and in the rectification and sanctification of the will, so that whatever remains of blindness, ignorance, errors, and vices may be gradually put off, and true wisdom and true justice may be more and more restored, Col. 3:10, Eph. 4:22, 23, 24. That, therefore, happens immediately and once for all, but this happens gradually and successively; that is total and perfect, but this is partial in this life, and imperfect, since we know in part, 1 Cor. 13:12, and the flesh always lusts against the spirit, Gal. 5:17. Therefore we are to be perfected from day to day, 2 Cor. 4:16, and transformed from glory to glory, ch. 3:17. Justification likewise is perfect on account of perfect remission and the imputation of perfect justice. Moreover, since the subject in regeneration, whether man behaves himself merely passively, in justification is partly passive with respect to the benefits which God confers and man indeed receives; but partly in some respect active, whereby, now instructed by faith, he apprehends the grace of God and applies to himself the merit of Christ. In regeneration, faith is considered as a habit infused by the Holy Spirit; but in justification as an act or exercise and function of that habit by reason of its primary operation, namely the apprehension of divine grace; finally, in renovation, as an act by reason of its secondary operation, whereby faith exerts itself through charity. The nature of regeneration consists in the procreation of saving faith, both by the illumination of the mind and by the rectification of the will. The mind is illuminated regarding the articles of faith necessary to be believed. In the heart, confidence is excited, so that we may embrace the paternal love, the redemption of the Son, and the grace of the Holy Spirit offered in the Gospel. In renovation, which belongs to the justified, illumination is given, which purges the mind more and more from errors, ignorance, and blindness, so that we may be restored to the image of the first man, where such things were not found. In renovation, faith itself is not finally begotten, but is already then considered as the mother of all virtues. (6) By reason of order. Because by the order of nature regeneration precedes justification, and justification precedes renovation. For first there is need of regeneration that we may obtain faith: afterwards, when we have been justified through faith, we are renewed by the Holy Spirit and sanctified. Indeed, good works follow the justified, they do not precede the one to be justified, and faith, according to Ambrose, is the mother not only of good works, but also of a good will: yet by the order of time, Regeneration, Justification, and Renovation are simultaneous. And hence it comes about that Regeneration is sometimes called Justification or adoption in the Apology of the Augsburg Confession, and sometimes it is even used for sanctification and renovation itself, in which meaning it is often employed by the Blessed Luther, both in his book on the Councils and the Church and elsewhere, as noted by the Formula of Concord, declaration, article 3, chapter 1. Here we are dealing with Regeneration in its proper and stricter sense, and it is taught how necessary it is that we be instructed by God from heaven with faith, by which we may enter the Kingdom of Heaven. For not to the entry of the Kingdom of Heaven are good works necessary; but faith, which belongs only to the reborn, and therefore there is need of regeneration. John 1:12. 1 John 5:1. (3.) The insinuation of necessity. For regeneration is proposed as necessary (1) universally to all, without distinction; unless one has been reborn, whoever he may be; all who are born carnally have need of spiritual regeneration, because flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of heaven, 1 Cor. 15:50. (2) By reason of the end, namely to obtain eternal salvation: He cannot see the kingdom of God. The 'cannot' implies a simple impossibility, and shuts the door of the heavenly kingdom to all who are not reborn. Now, to see the kingdom of God is said in a Hebrew phrase, that is, to receive it to be possessed, just as the Latins also say: to behold an inheritance; and indeed the kingdom both of grace and of glory.

Latin:

Vers. 3. ἀπεκρίθη) Responsio tacite innuit quod adjectum à Nicodemo fuerat: Nempe velle se scire quandoquidem Jesus regni cœlestis inter docendum mentionem sæpe face- ret, quæ ratio esset eo perveniendi.

Γεννηθῇ ἄνωθεν) Haud dubie ἄνωθεν est iterum, δεύτερον, ut mox accipit Nicodemus qui significatu vocis dubio falli non potuit, cum in Hebræo aut Syriaco non sit ea ambi- guitas. Sic vox ἄνωθεν sumitur Galat. IV. 9. Extat eo sensu apud Athenagoram. Sic hoc loco interpretatur Syrus. Ver- ba autem feri & nasci, solere usurpari apud Hebræos de for- matione animi oftendimus, Matth. XIII. 23. Usurpat & Se- neca de brevitate vitæ: Solemus dicere non fuisse in nostro po- testate, quos fortiremur parentes, forte nobis datos. Nobis vero ad arbitrium nostrum nasci licet: Nobilissimæ ingeniorum fami- liæ sunt: Elige in quam adscisci velis, non in nomen tantum ad- optaberis, sed in ipsa bona. Plutarchus quædam de Baccho dis- cerpto tradita, ait esse μῦθον εἰς τὴν παλιγγενεσίαν, quam in- terpretatur τὸ ἀλόγῳ καὶ ἀτάκτῳ κόλασιν. Simili sensu in anti- qua inscriptione legimus: Taurobolio Criobolioque in æter- num renatus. Et jam Rabbi Israël libro de anima proselytos vocat recens natos. Conf. Iac. I. 18. & sic quidam sumunt ציר יליד Gen. XXXII. 18. ubi Græci ὁσὶν ὲ ἰσπώσαντάσε. Οὐ δύναται ἰδεῖν) ἰδεῖν hic est participem fieri, ut Luc. II. v. 26. infra VIII. 51.

Τὴν βασιλείαν τῦ Θεῦ) Quæ hic inchoatur per parem con- scientiæ, in altero seculo per summam felicitatem absolvere- tur. Rem novam Nicodemo legis Doctori Christus indicat: posthac ad salutem pariendam majus aliquid Iudaismo re- quiri. Vide Galat. VI. 5. sed & præmium fore majus, regnum cœleste, quod tunc demum manifestari cœpit.

Repetere hic juvat, quæ olim publice de his re- sponsis Christi tradidimus: Primum Responsum necessitatem regenerationis concernit, vers. 3. in quo notanda (1) Christi Asseveratio. Amen Amen dico ti- bi, quam præmittit partim ob mysterii dignitatem, hac enim dicendi forma tum uti consuevit, cum de rebus maximi momenti ac æternam imprimis salutem concernentibus egit, cujusmodi est rege- neratio hominis sive prima janua & aditus ad salu- tem æternam; partim ob rei certitudinem, signifi- cans nullam omnino aliam esse salutis rationem, præter regenerationem; adversus Pharisæicam, qua Nicodemus fascinatus erat, opinionem, quod meri- tis operum regnum cœlestis adire quis possit, ut osten- deret, nondum veræ cognitionis Vestibulum ipsum at- tigisse, dicente Chrysost. sed extra regiam oberraie & ipsum, & quicunque eadem essent in sententia. (2) Regenerationis designatio. Nisi quis desuper vel de- nuo natus fuerit, γεννηθῇ ἄνωθεν. Vocatur eadem generatio non sensu proprio, quasi ex substantia Dei gignentis fiat, ac ὁμούσιος cum Deo Patre infe- rat, qualis est æterna Filii Dei generatio, Pf. II. 7. aut ἀποθέωσιν quandam, ut somniant Weigeliani, sed fi- gurato, quod cum generatione similitudinem quandam habeat, ratione (1) generantis Dei, qui Pater noster dicitur, ob nostri regenerationem, 1. Pet. I. 3. (2) hominum qui regenerantur, atq; inde filii Dei vocantur, non natura, sed gratia. (3) Se- minis ex quo regeneramur, verbi Dei, tum ἀκυστέ seu audibilis, tum ὁρατῦ 1. visibilis, utpote Sacra- menti Baptismatis, Eph. V. 26. (4) Similitudinis ac participationis divinæ naturæ, quam per regene- rationem consequimur. (5) Vitæ spiritualis & cœle- stis, ad quam renascimur, non secus atq; naturali generatione vitam terrenam consequimur. (6) Productionis, & modi operationis. Ut enim homo nihil cooperari potest ad sui ipsius carnalem pro- creationem: ita nec quicquam ad spiritualem sui regenerationem conferre potest, cum spiritualiter mortuus sit, & alienus à vita Dei, Eph. II. 3. IV. 7. ubi tamen hæc notanda est differentia carnalis & spiri- tualis generationis, quod illam quidem homo im- pedire non possit, hanc vero non possit tantum im- pedire, sed sæpe numero impediat.

Dicitur porro generatio hæc ἄνωθεν facta, hoc ἄνωθεν est desuper, vel etiam denuo, ac de novo. Quam utramque vocis significationem insinuat Chry- sostomus, τὸ ἄνωθεν, inquit, hoc in loco alii de cœlo, alii iterum exponunt, ut indigitetur vel superna sive cœlestis generatio, quemadmodum explicat Cyrillus, Ammonius, Theophylactus, quæ fit à patre luminum, unde omne opus bonum ἄ- νωθεν descendit, Jac. I. 17. ubi etiam ea vox accipi- tur Job. III. 13. XIX. 11. Jac. III. 15. 17. ut à terrena nativitate discerninetur; vel nova & iterata nativi- tas: prout vox ea adhibetur Gal. IV. 9. & ab Augu- stino, Nazianzeno Or. de Pentec. Severo Antiochen. &c. hîc intelligitur. Nec aliter à Nicodemo intelle- cta fuit, quærente, quo pacto iterum nasci possit, un- de Maldonatus colligit Christum Syriace loquen- tem, verbo minime ambiguo usum fuisse, quod de- nuo, non desuper significaret. Nam si Christus di- xiffet, nisi quis renatus fuerit desuper, satis intelle- xiffet Nicodemus eum non locutum esse de carna- li generatione. Cæterum recte observat Formula Concordiæ in declar. art. 3. p. m. 686. Regenerationis vocem non eodem modo accipi; Interdum enim strictè adhibetur pro sola renascentia, qua gigni- mur Filii Dei, fidei & virium credendi collatione, ut in Filios Dei adoptemur, Tit. III. 5. 1. Pet. I. 3. In- terdum vero ampliori significatione complectitur etiam ipsam renovationem, quæ consequens est re- generationis, & ab ea differt, cum in regeneratio- ne fides conferatur qua justificamur: Renovatio vero Justificationem consequatur, qua justificati & Sp. S. donati in novam creaturam, in justitia, & Sanctitate vera reformamur; in regeneratione intel- lectus illuminatur, voluntas convertitur ad Deum, ut agnitio vera, & fiducia in nobis concipiatur, & per fidem filii Dei evadamus, Joh. I. 12. In renovatione nos nova vi instruimur & facultate, ac spirituales efficimur, ut ita nova creatura evadamus, & imago Dei in nobis restauretur, qua verus homo paula- tim exuitur & novus induitur, Eph. II. 10. IV. 22. 23. Ibi facultas credendi, ut in vitam spiritualem revo- cemur, hic facultas bene operandi, ut vivificati in Christo secundum spiritum vivamus, conceditur, quo pacto Cyrillus sensu complexivo regeneratio- nem describere videtur, l. II. in Joh. c. 42. Dei nos idcirco fieri participes, quoniam Spiritum, qui ex Deo substantialiter procedit, per Baptismum acquirimus, quo in pristinam pulchritudinem reformati & ad novam vitam renati, à Deo in filios adoptamur. Re- generatio vero proprie dicta, est actio gratiosa Dei, qua homo caro de carne natus à Spir. S. per verbum, vel lavacrum aquæ in verbo, cognitione salutari il- luminatur, quoad voluntatem fiducia in Christum donatur, adeoque fide salvifica in ipso procreata ad vitam spiritualem vivificatur.

Differt regenera- tio proprie accepta à justificatione, & renova- tione (1) ratione principii & modi agendi. Quia regeneratio est actio solius Dei, eaque intrinseca, & intrinsecam ratione subjecti denominationem inferens, quod regeneratur, qualis est illumina- tio, fidei procreatio. Justificatio autem solum ex- trinseca est, & extrinsecam infert denominatio- nem, utpote in non-imputatione nostræ injustitiæ & in imputatione alienæ per fidem apprehensæ ju- stitiæ sita. Renovatio autem intrinseca quidem est, sed ad eam homo renatus concurrit, ideo- que non est solius Dei actio. (2) Ratione subje- cti, quod in regeneratione est homo caro de carne na- tus, & in peccatis mortuus, omnibusque viribus spi- ritualibus destitutus, Iob. III. 5. Eph. II. 2. In Justifi- catione homo fidelis, peccata agnoscens & in Chri- stum credens, Rom. III. 22. In renovatione homo ju- stificatus, Eph. IV. 22. in quo fides per charitatem o- perosa est, Gal. V. 6. (3) Ratione termini a quo, qui in regeneratione est peccatum originis, seu privatio spiritualium virium, & prava concupiscentia; in justi- ficatione reatus culpæ & pœnæ in judicio Dei; in renovatione dominatus peccati. (4) Ratione ter- mini ad quem, qui est in regeneratione fides salvifi- ca, vel fidelis in vitam spiritualem revocatus, 1. Ioh.

c. V. 2. Omnis qui credit, quod Jesus est Christus, ex Deo natus est, & quicquid ex spiritu natus est, spi- ritus est, Joh. III. 6. In Justificatione est Justitia Chri- sti imputata, ac filiatio Dei per fidem in Christum. In renovatione est sanctitas nobis inhærens, seu nova creatura, 2. Cor. V. 17. Gal. VI. 15. (5) Ratione formæ; Quia regeneratio consistit in mentis nostræ, quo- ad mysteria fidei creditu necessaria, illuminatione, ac fiducia in corde nostro excitatione, ut Deo ceu Pa- tri nostro in Filio, per Sp. S. adhæreamus, inque eo unice acquiescamus. Uno verbo, virium credendi fideique salvifica procreatione. Renovatio autem consistit in mentis ab erroribus quibusvis aliis libera- tione, ac voluntatis rectificatione ac sanctificatione, ut quicquid superest cæcitatis, ignorantiæ, errorum ac vitiorum, subinde deponatur, ac vera sapientia, veraque justitia magis magisque instauretur, Col. III. 10. Eph. IV. 22. 23. 24. Illa ergo sit statim, ac si- mul & semel, hæc vero paulatim & successive; illa est totalis & perfecta, hæc autem est partialis in hac vita, & imperfecta, siquidem ex parte cognoscimus, 1. Cor. XIII. 12. & caro semper concupiscit adversus spiritum, Gal. V. 17. Ideo de die in diem perficiendi, 2. Cor. IV. 16. de claritate in claritatem transformandi sumus c. III. 17. Justificatio itidem perfecta est ob perfectam remissionem, ac justitiæ perfectæ impu- tationem. Cæterum cum subjectum in regenera- tione, sive homo mere passive se habeat, in justifica- tione partim passivum est respectu beneficiorum, quæ Deus confert, homo vero recipit; partim vero aliqua ratione activum, qua jam fide instru- ctum gratiam Dei apprehendit, meritumq; Christi sibi applicat. In regeneratione fides consideratur ut habitus infusus per Sp. Sanctum; in justificatione au- tem ut actus seu exercitium & functio istius habitus ratione primariæ operationis, gratiæ nempe divi- næ apprehensionis; In Renovatione deniq; ut actus ratione secundariæ operationis, qua fides per cha- ritatem sese exerit. Regenerationis ratio consistit in fidei salvificæ procreatione, tum qua mentis illu- minationem, tum qua voluntatis rectificationem. Mens illuminatur quoad Articulos fidei creditu necessarios. In corde excitatur fiducia, ut pa- ternam dilectionem, Filii redemtionem, & gra- tiam S.S. in Evangelio oblatam amplectamur. In Renovatione quæ justificatorum est, illuminatio da- tur, quæ mentem repurget magis magisque ab er- roribus, ignorantia, cæcitate, ut reparemur ad imaginem primi hominis, ubi talia non invenie- bantur. In renovatione non ipsa fides demum gigni- tur, sed jam tum consideratur ut mater omnium virtutum. (6) Ratione ordinis. Quia ordine naturæ præcedit regeneratio justificationem, & justificatio renovationem. Primum enim opus est regeneratione ut fidem consequamur: post- modum ubi per fidem justificati sumus, renova- mur per Spiritum Sanctum, & sanctificamur. Si- quidem bona opera sequantur justificatum, non præcedant justificandum, ac fides juxta Ambrof. mater sit non tantummodo bonorum operum, sed etiam bonæ voluntatis: ordine tamen temporis simul sunt Regeneratio, Justificatio, & Renovatio. Atque inde adeo sit, ut Regeneratio quandoque dicatur Ju- stificatio vel adoptio in Apol. August. Confess. quan- doque etiam pro ipsa sanctificatione ac renovatio- ne usurpetur, in qua significatione a B. Luthero tum in lib. d. Eccles. & Concil. tum alibi sæpe adhi- betur, notante Form. Concord. decl. art. 3. c. I, Hic de Regeneratione agitur sensu proprio ac strictiori, ac docetur, quam necessarium sit, ut fide a Deo instruamur cœlitus, quo per ean- dem ingrediamur Regnum Cœlorum. Non enim ad ingressum Regni Cœlorum bona opera necessaria; sed fides, quæ non nisi renatorum est, ideoq; regeneratione opus est. Ioh. I. 12. I. J. V. 1. (3.) Necessitatis insinuatio. Proponitur enim rege- neratio necessaria (1) universaliter omnibus, citra distinctionem; nisi quis renatus fuerit, quicunq; ille fuerit; omnes qui nascuntur carnaliter, regenera- tione spirituali opus habent, quia caro & sanguis non potest hæreditate regnum cœlorum, 1. Cor. xv. 50. (2) Ratione finis, ad consequendam nempe sa- lutem æternam: Non potest videre regnum Dei. Tò non potest simplicem infert impossibilitatem, o- mnibusq; non regenitis januam regni cœlestis oc- cludit. Videre autem regnum Dei, phrasi Hebræa di- citur, id est possidendum accipere, uti etiam Latini dicunt: hæreditatem cernere; & quidem regnum tum gratiæ, tum gloriæ.

## 3:4
Verse 4. To be born being an old man] He sets forth an example in himself, who was already an old man.

Latin:

Vers. 4. Γεννηθῆναι γέρων ὢν] Exemplum in se ponit, qui se- nex jam erat.

## 3:5
Verse 5. To be born of water and of the Spirit] He now explains what kind of birth he means, lest Nicodemus be deceived any longer by ignorance of an allegorical expression. It is, however, a hendiadys. For just as 'in spirit and fire' in Matt. 3:11 signifies 'by a fiery spirit,' so here 'of spirit and water' is 'of a watery spirit.' Nor does it stand in the way that a word seemingly limiting the other precedes here. For thus in Acts 17:25, 'life and breath' is the same as 'breath of life' elsewhere, as in Gen. 2:7 and 2 Macc. 7:23, 'spirit and life.' Thus Gen. 3:16, 'conception and pain,' i.e., pain from conception. Thus Col. 2:8, 'through philosophy and empty deceit,' i.e., through the empty fallacies of philosophy. And Matt. 4:16, 'in the region and shadow of death,' the Arab translates 'in the region of the shadow of death.' Again, just as there by a fiery spirit an efficacious spirit is signified, so here by a watery spirit a cleansing spirit is signified. Chrysostom, Homily 31. Scripture sometimes calls the grace of the Spirit fire, and sometimes water. Among Plutarch's Roman Questions we read that fire cleanses, water purifies. In this sense we read of clean waters in Ezek. 36:25, and the knowledge of God is compared to water in Isa. 11:9, Hab. 2:14, and in 1 John 5:9, water is the purity of the Christian life, which together with martyrdom and miracles bears witness to the truth of the dogma. And just as below in chapter 6, it is not indeed a matter of the Eucharist, but the metaphorical expressions have a silent allusion to those signs, because both those signs and these expressions denote the same thing, so here it is not a matter directly of Baptism, but the expressions are alluding to Baptism. See Eph. 5:26 and Tit. 3:5, Heb. 10:22, in which places likewise washing is attributed to the word of the Gospel. Lactantius. Book 5. How much better it is to wash away the mind, which is dirtied by evil desires, and to drive away all vices with one laver of virtue and faith? Whoever has done this, no matter how stained and dirty a body he may bear, is sufficiently pure. If anyone, however, prefers to distinguish these, so that water signifies the flight from evil, and spirit the command to do all things that are best, he will find that by which he may support this opinion.

Grotius explains these by a hendiadys, so that in Matt. 3:11 'in spirit and fire' signifies 'by a fiery spirit,' here 'in spirit and water' is 'of a watery spirit,' and there an efficacious spirit, here a cleansing spirit is signified. But what is a fiery spirit? What is a watery spirit? Where does Scripture speak thus? Or where does it teach that a fiery spirit is an efficacious spirit, and a watery spirit is a cleansing spirit? And what is that distinction of the Holy Spirit, that it is either efficacious or cleansing? Is not the purifying spirit efficacious? Or shall we believe that for cleansing and purification there is no need of efficacy? That statement of Chrysostom, Homily 31, 'Scripture sometimes calls the grace of the Spirit fire, and sometimes water,' has nothing to do with the matter: for it is indeed certain that the Holy Spirit and His power are designated in Scripture now by fire, now by water: but that it is called a fiery and watery spirit will never be taught. Nor does Chrysostom refer there to this passage, but to John 7:38, where the Spirit is metaphorically designated by water, because of the similarity and comparison with water: because water not only purges, but also extinguishes the thirst for temporal things, John 4:14, and makes us fruitful in good works, Isa. 44:3-4. Similarly, it is compared to fire, because it purges us, and makes our opaque hearts bright, and kindles and inflames them. Furthermore, as in Matt. 3:11 Christ is said to baptize with spirit and fire, because He was to bestow the Spirit upon the Apostles through fire and in fiery tongues at the feast of Pentecost, and not only was fire to be poured out, but with the fire the Spirit, Acts 2. Thus in this place, we are said to be reborn of water and spirit, because in Baptism, which is the medium of regeneration of the Holy Spirit, Tit. 3:5, it is not bare water, but with the water the Holy Spirit bestowing efficacy upon Baptism, so that we may be reborn from it. Which we have abundantly proved against the Socinians and Calvinists in the Exegesis of the Augsburg Confession, Art. 9. And these are those clean waters of Ezek. 36:25, nor is anything other than Baptism designated by water in 1 John 5:8, just as by 'the blood' there the Holy Supper is noted, in which the blood of Christ is dispensed: and by 'the spirit' is designated the word, which is spirit and life: John 6, because these are the three that bear witness in the Church in these lands, the Word, Baptism, and the Supper: which are wrongly explained here by Grotius in such a way that water is the purity of the Christian life, blood is martyrdom, and by the name of spirit miracles are noted. Nor indeed in the present passage, John 3:5, is there only an allusion to Baptism, but Baptism is described by the mention of water and Spirit, and is introduced as the medium of regeneration: nor do the passages which Grotius compares here, Eph. 5:26, Tit. 3:5, teach otherwise, but rather confirm this opinion of ours. Heb. 10:22, where washing (and regeneration) is not attributed to the Word of the Gospel, but to Baptism, which is the washing of water in the Word, the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit, and that pure water by which we are cleansed.

Grotius adds another, but more inept gloss of this passage of ours: If anyone should nevertheless prefer to distinguish those things, so that water signifies the flight from evil, but spirit the impulse to do all things that are best, he will find something to support this opinion. But where is it found that water denotes the flight from evil? Where is spirit nothing other than an impulse to do all things that are best? And how are we said to be regenerated from water and spirit, that is, from the flight from evil and such an impulse? Since the flight from evil and the impulse to good presuppose regeneration, they do not constitute it formally, nor are they prior to it in the order of nature.

Addit Grotius aliam, sed ineptiorem hujus no- stri loci glossam: Si quis tamen malit ista discernere, ut aqua significet mali fugam, spiritus vero impetum ad optima quæque agenda, inveniet, quo hanc senten- tiam fulciat. Ubi vero invenitur aqua notare mali fugam? ubi spiritus nihil aliud est, quam impetus ad optima quæq; agenda? & quomodo regenerari dice- mur ex aqua & spiritu, id est, ex mali fuga, & impetu tali? quam fuga mali & impetus ad bonum præsup- ponat regenerationem, non vero constituat eam formaliter, vel prior sit eadem naturæ ordine.

## 3:6
Vers. 6. That which is born of the flesh is flesh] He illustrates the matter by a comparison: that which is born of men by the law of nature performs the actions of natural life. See above v. 13 and Rom. VIII. 5. But this life leads to death Rom. VIII. 6. for it has no right to immortality 1 Cor. XV. 20.

It is said to be flesh, not because it performs the actions of natural life, but because it is corrupted by carnal concupiscence: because we are born such after the fall, John XIV. 2. Ps. LI. 6. Compare John I. 13. Rom. VIII. 5. We are also born of flesh, because we are procreated by carnal parents, who are subject to sin and death: and therefore we are similar to them by nature, Eph. II. 3.

That which is born of the Spirit is spirit] He who has been cleansed by the power of God and has received a divine disposition, leads a divine life. See again above v. 13. See 1 John III. 9. and 1 Peter I. 4. And compare below VIII. 44. Acts XIII. 10. Spirit, that is, spiritual 1 Cor. VI. 17.

To be born of the Spirit is not to be cleansed by the power of God, but to be regenerated by the Holy Spirit, so that those who are children of wrath by nature, by carnal generation, may be children of God through grace and spiritual regeneration. Nor is he who is born in this way called spirit because he leads a divine life, but because he is spiritual, the consequence of which is that he leads a divine life.

Caro esse dicitur, non quod naturalis vitæ actio- nibus fungitur, sed quod concupiscentia carnali cor- ruptum est: quia tales nascimur post lapsum, Ioh. XIV. 2. Ps. LI. 6. Conf. Ioh. I. 13. Rom. IIX. 5. Ex carne etiam nascimur, quia à parentibus carnalibus, pec- cato & morti obnoxiis, procreamur: ideoque iis similes sumus τῇ Φύσει vel natura Eph. II. 3.
