## 3:7
Vers. 7. Do not marvel] Do not marvel like an unbeliever, because this birth does not fall under the eyes, as that natural one does.

Latin:

Vers. 7. μὴ θαυμάσῃς] Ne mireris tanquam incredulus, quia hæc nativitas in oculos non incurrit, ut ista naturalis.

## 3:8
Vers. 8. The wind blows where it wishes] He shows that there are also other things which are not seen, yet truly exist. And because he had begun to speak of the Spirit, he takes an example from the wind, which is also accustomed to be called spirit, as in Gen. VIII. 1. and often elsewhere. Minutius to Octavius: All things are impelled, vibrated, and agitated by wind and blasts, and yet the wind and blast do not come under the eyes. But will is attributed to the wind by personification, just as in Paul, law, sin, and death are introduced personified. The wind moves itself now here, now there. You hear its voice.

You do not know from where it comes] Its origin is not perceived: for some wish it to be a natural flow of air, others exhalations from the earth: and such a diversity of them is found even in the same places that it cannot be referred entirely to the nature of the lands: therefore the origin is sought, it is not seen.

And where it goes] Where is here as below XIII. 36. XVI. 5. and 1 John II. 11. So also where XII. 36. XIV. 4. He means this; it is not known where the wind ends, neither its exit nor its origin comes into view. See Ecclesiastes 11:5. Οὕτως ἐστὶ πᾶς ὁ γεγεννημένος ἐκ τοῦ πνεύματος.] That is, thus is his affair. See Matthew 13:45, Mark 4:26. The actions of those reborn through the Spirit are seen to be wonderful, but the origin itself lies hidden: hidden also is the end toward which it tends, being invisible and of another age. For the end is eternal life, Rom. 6:22. Our life is hidden with God, Col. 3:3.

We omit here the inept and most foolish gloss of a certain Anonymous Arian cited by Sandius. Christ spoke literally about carnal generation. For the first generation is spiritual, the second carnal. The sense, therefore, of Christ's words is: unless one is generated in the flesh, he cannot enter the kingdom of God: and therefore demons cannot enter the kingdom of God, because it is not permitted to them by God to be born a second time, namely in the flesh. By generation, however, according to v. 3, he understands finally that which is carnal, or which is made of water and Spirit, that is, of flesh and Spirit. For water is the principle of carnal generation, from which many of the modern and ancient philosophers have felt that all bodies consist. The sense, therefore, of Christ's words is: unless one is generated of flesh and Spirit; that is, unless one is generated in the flesh, or unless the soul is united to the body, he cannot enter the kingdom of God. To have recited these portents or ravings of errors is to have refuted them.

Moreover, concerning these words of Christ, we have discoursed thus in our 'Elocutions of the Mouth of the Lord', Book I, Chapter X: After Christ instructed Nicodemus—who was very eager for information—in general about the necessity of regeneration, concerning the method of obtaining salvation and specifically about Baptism, which John was administering to those running to him from all sides, while the Pharisees were spurning the Counsel of God against themselves and refusing to receive Baptism, Luke 7:30; and Nicodemus, philosophizing quite crudely about this difficult mystery of faith as if there were need of a new birth from a mother's womb, inquired about the manner, 'How can a man be born again when he is old?'; the heavenly Rabbi Christ expresses the mode of Regeneration more specifically and asserts the Sacrament divinely consecrated for this same cause in the New Testament, nay, asserts its necessity and efficacy. He recalls Nicodemus from the hidden things of nature, which are impervious to human ingenuity, to the mysteries of the supernatural operation of the Spirit, in such a way that he simultaneously convinces the man of his ignorance before he refutes him, and prepares him with reverence for the more sublime mysteries about which he was still to be informed. He prefaces this, however, (1) with the customary formula of asseveration: 'Amen, Amen, etc.', so that he may teach that this truth concerning the Sacrament of Baptismal Regeneration is no less necessary to be believed than the doctrine of Regeneration itself is to be taught. For the doctrine of Baptism is not to be held, with the Socinians, Remonstrants, Calvinists, and Syncretists (Calixtines), as less necessary or not fundamental, but [is to be held] as Christ inculcates it here first to a nocturnal catechumen, who was anxiously seeking the Counsel of Salvation, which the other Pharisees were spurning, for the sake of salutary information; and as the Apostle [does] in Hebrews 6:1-2. διδαχὴν βαπτισμῶν to the foundations, and to the word of the beginning, just as also to the elements of the oracles of God, which were accustomed to be handed down to catechumens in the primitive Church and to be laid down in the place of a foundation; that doctrine is to be held no less necessary for our catechumens after Baptism, when they are informed about the way of salvation, as the means of regeneration by which they were first inserted into Christ, initiated into the Church, and admitted to the kingdom of heaven, and thus rendered more certain of their own regeneration; than it had been for catechumens in the primitive Church, before they were baptized, so that they might pant after this salutary medium, under which name the doctrine of Baptism is also counted among the parts of Christian catechesis in our Church. (II.) The matter of the sacrament of regeneration, from which it consists, and whence our regeneration is made. 'Unless one has been reborn of water and the Spirit.' Which exhibit the matter, both the earthly, true water of Baptism, and the heavenly, the Holy Spirit: and thus they present the Sacrament of Baptism itself. For the Holy Spirit, as Cyprian says in 'On the Baptism of Christ', applies the hand of all goodness invisibly to the visible consecrations, and the fatness of divine unction infuses the fullness of grace with efficacious sanctifications, and consumes and perfects the matter of the Sacrament. When that element of water, says Basil the Great in Psalm 22, has received the Holy Spirit, it is a Sacrament, and it will no longer be water of drinking, but of sanctification. Baptism consists of two things, says Gregory Nazianzen, Orat. 40 on Baptism, namely water and Spirit; the former received in a visible and corporeal manner, the latter, however, concurring invisibly. Whence almost everyone interprets this sentence of Christ concerning Baptism, as Maldonatus confesses with Luther on this passage. Those who explain it otherwise find nowhere to fix their foot, whether they be Calvinists, Socinians, or Arminians. Of these, Zwingli (Book on Baptism, Vol. 2, p. 69) takes water as the knowledge of Christ and the consolation of faith. Calvin (Book 4, Inst. c. 16) interprets water through the Spirit by way of epexegesis. Bullinger (in Decades, Sermon 8) explains the place metaphorically concerning the renewal of the heart through the Holy Spirit. Beza [speaks] of the immense love of God, Peter Martyr ibid. of the grace of God. Cassanus [speaks] of the grace of Regeneration and the Holy Spirit. Gualther understands it of the Word of God. Socinus (Book on Baptism, p. 46) interprets it now as the removal of sins, now as repentance, but then says that regeneration from water is the renewal of the will, and regeneration from the Spirit is the renewal of the intellect. Others wished it to be designated by the water of tribulation or the mortification of the old man, and by the Spirit the renewal of nature. Some think that Christ is pointed out by the Spirit himself. Joh. Gerb. Vossius notes that water and Spirit denote spiritual water. To Hugo Grotius it is watery Spirit, i.e., cleansing Spirit, who nevertheless thinks that by water the flight from evils is also to be understood, and by Spirit, the impulse to do all the best things. What is this other than wishing to mock Scripture? All those glosses certainly collapse by their own vanity. That there is a discourse here about water Baptism is taught both by the very letter of the text, since there is no reason why water should not be understood properly, which has been sanctioned as the medium of regeneration in Baptism, and by the Nicodemic occasion, arising from the Baptism of John, which by the force of the comparison in Luke VII. 30 is admitted by Socinus himself in the cited passage: and by the symphony of other passages of Scripture. Acts XXII. 16. Eph. V. 26. Tit. III. 5. Add that the ancient Doctors of the Church agree on this. Aug. tr. II. in Ioh. Cyrill. Alex. l. T. in Ioh. c. 22. Chrys. hom. 24. in Ioh. Ammon. & Theodor. Mopsuest. in the Roman Chain of the Greeks, citing Maldonatus, as also Euthym. & Theoph. in this passage, indeed even Calvin himself in his Commentary on this passage, Bucer likewise and Maldonatus praising the consensus of the ancients. Vossius, who is most versed in antiquity, confesses that all antiquity understands this passage concerning Baptism, disp. 4. de Bapt. d. 2. (III) The necessity of Baptism. Concerning which, Christ says, He shall not be able to enter the kingdom of God: At the same time implying that Baptism is the first approach and entrance to the heavenly kingdom. This necessity, however, is not absolute, but depends upon the hypothesis of the divine order; to which, although God did not bind himself precisely, he nevertheless willed us to be bound, lest we neglect or despise the medium divinely sanctioned, as was done by the Pharisees, just as Lombard says that the passage is to be understood concerning those who can despise and be baptized; whence the Theological Canon was born:

By the force, therefore, of this Aphorism, Christ's Baptism is ordinarily necessary so that we may enter the Kingdom of heaven; because it is the ordinary medium of Regeneration, without which, as Christ testifies, no one can approach the kingdom of God. And hence it is adorned with most elegant names, such as being called by Justin, in Dial. cum Tryph., the water of life; by Irenaeus, lib. I. c. 18, the baptism of regeneration; by Cyril of Jerusalem, in the preface to the Catechism, the regeneration of the soul; by Optatus of Milevis, etc., an immortal birth; by Cassiodorus, in Cant. VII, the divine fountain by which the faithful are watered; by others, the gate of grace, the entrance to the kingdom of God; by Blessed Luther, the child-bearer of the Celestial Kingdom. The most sweet epithets of Nazianzen in his Oration on Baptism pertain here: that it is a collation of the Spirit, a participation of the Word, a correction of the creature, a deluge of sin, a communication of light, an oppression of darkness, a vehicle to God, a pilgrimage to Christ, the key of the heavenly kingdom, a change of life.

(IV.) The reason for the necessity. Whatever is born of the flesh is flesh. The cause, on account of which there is need for all for Regeneration from water and the spirit, is universal, because all are born in sin, and no one can enter the kingdom of God unless he has been reborn. For flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God, 1 Corinthians c. XV. 45. That which is defiled shall not enter into that City, Revelation XXI. 27.

He is said to be born of the flesh who is propagated in a carnal manner, or is born from parents corrupted and contaminated by sin. For by the name of flesh, human nature is designated synecdochically, Genesis VI. 12, Psalm CXLV. 21, Isaiah c. XL. 5, c. LXVI. 23, Matthew XXIV. 32, Luke III. 6, Romans III. 20. But since here flesh and spirit are opposed and the discourse is about ψιλοῖς ἀνθρώποις (mere men), by flesh is denoted man corrupted through sin. Compare Romans VIII. 1, seqq., Galatians V. 17, chapter VI. 8. Whence Theophylact rightly accepted flesh in this place for the carnal man. The word flesh is taken otherwise when it is opposed to the Spirit, where the discourse is about Christ the God-man. For then the divine and human nature in Christ is designated, see John I. 14, Romans I. v. 4, c. IX. 6, 1 Timothy III. 16, 1 Peter III. 18. In the predicate: It is flesh, human nature corrupted by sin is likewise denoted, so that the sense is: whatever is born from carnal parents, or those contaminated by sin, by carnal propagation, that, through birth or by the force of that carnal propagation, is nothing but flesh. It is not spiritual in any way, but entirely carnal and contaminated and corrupted by sin. A man is not born spiritual or holy from carnal parents, but carnal; as the parents are, such also are the children. Just as Adam in the state of integrity would have procreated children in the image of God, in which he was created: so after the fall he procreated them such as he himself was, in the image not of God, but his own, which he had contracted through sin, Genesis c. V. 1, 3. We are all born such, whence we are all by nature children of wrath, Ephesians II. 3, conceived and warmed in sin, Psalm LI. 7. Unclean, procreated from the unclean, Job XIV. 4. Even if parents are faithful and reborn, the children, however, whom they generate, are not generated according to the spirit, or as they are faithful, but according to the nature in which sin clings, and which is not entirely renewed, but in large part still carnal: therefore, they are not born Saints from Saints, as pleases the Calvinists, but carnal, as Christ teaches here. Nor yet are marriages condemned for this reason, as the Pelagians caviled, whom Augustine solidly refutes in his 2 books to Valerius the Count, On Marriage and Concupiscence. For he rightly notes, l. I. c. V., that the good of marriage cannot be accused by the original evil which is drawn from it, just as the evil of adulteries and fornications cannot be excused by the natural good which is born from them. For just as sin, whether it be drawn from here or there from parents, is the work of the Devil: so man, whether he be born from here or there, is the work of God. He discourses beautifully, especially in c. XXVIII, on this matter: The shameful concupiscence of the flesh is not to be imputed to marriages, but to be tolerated. For it is not a good coming from natural marriage, but an evil approaching from ancient sin: for this reason, therefore, it happens that even from the legitimate marriages of the children of God, not children of God, but children of the age are generated, because even those who generate, if they are already reborn, do not generate from this, that they are children of God, but from this, that they are still children of the age. For it is the Lord's sentence: The children of this age generate and are generated. From which, therefore, we are still children of this age, our exterior man is corrupted; from this also children of this age are generated, and they do not become children of God unless they are reborn: but from which we are children of God, the interior man is renewed from day to day, although the exterior man himself has also been sanctified through the washing of regeneration, and has received the hope of future incorruption. Which he declares in the following chapter by the likeness of the Olive tree, from which a wild olive is born. Just as a wild olive is generated from the seed of a wild olive, and from the seed of an olive tree nothing but a wild olive; although there is a great difference between a wild olive and an olive tree; so also is generated from the flesh of a sinner, and from the flesh of a just man, on both sides a sinner, although there is a great difference between a sinner and a just man.

But not without emphasis did Christ say, τὸ γεγεννημένον, that which is born, so that he might comprehend everything, and the whole that is born. Since this has greater energy: whatever is born of the flesh is flesh, than if he had said: everyone born of the flesh is flesh; for that, that which is born of the flesh, (1.) designates the universality of the supposita, and embraces all men, with no one excepted, except Christ alone, who was not born of the will of the flesh but conceived of the Holy Spirit, and is devoid of all sin. Christ indeed has flesh as regards the substance and truth of human nature, but he was neither born of the flesh, as it is taken in this place, nor is he flesh as regards accidental corruption. But neither is Mary the Theotokos, nor Jeremiah, nor John, nor anyone else excepted. There is no distinction here; all are sinners, Romans III. 22. (2.) It signifies the totality of man; the whole, whatever is born of flesh, the whole man, body and soul, is born of flesh. Not only is the body propagated, but with the body also the soul, inasmuch as it is the πρῶτον δεκτικὸν of original sin. That whole is infected with sin through birth, not only the lower faculties, or the sensitive appetite, as the Papists wish, to whom the Innovators (Calixtines) have hitherto acceded, namely that evil resides in the sensitive appetite, by which we resist the rational appetite, or the rebellion of the same, which, when the intellectual soul infused by God the Creator is united to the body, results from the lower faculties of the soul: as Drejerus contends in deduct. Germ. p. 333. In which way the rational soul will not be corrupted or the subject of original sin or of that depraved congenital rebellion, but that rebellion will reside solely in the sensitive appetite, against which the soul rather struggles as much as it can, inasmuch as its rational appetite is by nature contrary to it, according to this opinion. (V.) The Utility of Regeneration: Concerning which Christ says: That which is born of the Spirit, is spirit. It is said to be born of the Spirit, which is reborn from above by the power of the Holy Spirit. Which likewise concerns the whole man, who must be reborn spiritually through grace, after he has been born carnally; mention is made here indeed of the Spirit alone, inasmuch as he holds the τὸ πρωτεῖον in Baptism, but the medium, water, is not excluded, since that which was already inquired into above with the Spirit. Moreover, it is said that the Spirit is what is born of the Spirit, not through any essential μέθεξιν or participation of the spirit and ἀποθέωσιν or Deification, or through a certain μεταμόρφωσιν or transubstantiation, which the Weigelians dream of. For no change of substance happens here, but the same as flesh is born of flesh, the spirit is reborn of the Spirit. Not through the total abolition of the flesh: for this is not laid aside except with this life. Something of the flesh always still remains, with which the Spirit must needs struggle, Gal. V. 15, Heb. XII. 1, but through the mortification of the flesh and the renewal of the Spirit: not that we are entirely spiritual through the grace of Regeneration, but that we begin to be spiritual while we are renewed, so that we may progress from day to day until we become perfectly spiritual: to which indeed we aspire in this life, but we do not attain it except in the other life. In this sense Cyril of Alexandria, book II on John, ch. 43, says that we are reformed to God through the Spirit and marked with His own character, so that we may be formed in our soul, if I may say so, to His own quality. Let Basil, book I on Baptism, be compared. Whence the utility and Effect of Regeneration is recognized, namely our spiritual renewal, which how it is distinguished from Regeneration has been said before. VI. The condition of the Incomprehensible Mystery. Which Christ explains by the comparison of the wind and its blowing, which no one knows the origin and limit of, even if he hears its sound. Whence it is no wonder if they do not know the reason for spiritual regeneration, even though the same then reveals itself through external signs. Because the grace and operation of that heavenly Flame, the Holy Spirit, is far more inscrutable. If we are ignorant of the reason for natural things and remain stuck in them, what wonder if we cannot comprehend supernatural things, which are as far apart as heaven and earth, nay, God and Nature, the finite and the infinite, the incomprehensible and that which does not exceed every grasp of the creature. Cf. Sirach ch. XVIII. 8. Some of the ancients seem to understand the Holy Spirit by the Spirit, whose origin and limit is unknown. Ambrose, book II on the faith, ch. VII. Hilary, book II on the Trinity. Athanasius, book I on the united Deity of the Trinity. Basil, book V. 9 against the Eunomians. Nazianzen, Or. V on Theology. But this ought not to be admitted otherwise than in the sense that the operation of the Holy Spirit is designated here in a figure. Which most, if I am not mistaken, point out; for Christ speaks of the natural wind, but in such a way that the Spirit figures the supernatural grace by it: and in that sense must be taken those things which Gregory the Great excellently hands down, book XVIII, ch. XIII of the Morals. To hear the voice of the Spirit is, by the power of intimate conjunction, to rise up into the love of the Creator, but no one knows whence it comes, because it is unknown on what occasions it pours itself out to us through the mouths of preachers. And no one knows whither it goes, because while many hear one sermon, it cannot be understood whom it abandons when it casts them off, or in whose heart it rests when it enters. Christ, however, wished to teach how incomprehensible this Mystery is, not only to recall Nicodemus from rash scrutiny and to admonish him to faith and the humility of faith, but also to prepare a way for Himself to recount and humbly receive more sublime Mysteries, without which neither the way of salvation or the Kingdom of God, nor this doctrine concerning Regeneration can be solidly known or apprehended by firm faith, as will be evident from what follows.

The following documents are to be noted from this classic passage,

(I.) The doctrine concerning Baptism is fundamental and necessary. (II.) Baptism is the ordinary medium of Regeneration. (III.) Without Baptism one cannot ordinarily enter the Kingdom of Heaven. (IV.) Yet the Gate of Salvation is not to be rashly closed to the unbaptized, if they are born in the Church. Since God has bound not Himself and His grace, but us, to the media. (V.) The Sacrament of Baptism, if it is to be complete, must consist of true and proper water, as the earthly thing, and the Holy Spirit as the heavenly thing. (VI.) Original Sin is so propagated from parents to descendants that no one who is carnally generated is free from sin. (VII.) Not only the body but also the soul, as the subject of sin, is propagated into the offspring. (VIII.) Therefore, transmission, not the immediate creation of the soul, must be asserted. (IX.) As necessary as the assertion of Original sin is, so necessary is the assertion of the propagation of the soul, unless God is to be established as the cause of sin. (X.) As no one can see this earthly light unless he is born, so no one can see the light of the Kingdom of God unless he is reborn. (XI.) No one ought to be reborn through Baptism or be baptized unless he has been born first into this world. Whence embryos and fetuses only partially born cannot be baptized by water poured on the mother's womb or on the parts delivered, as Aureolus, Ludolph, and Angelus de Clavasio judge, that the part of the fetus brought into the light can be baptized. For rightly St. Augustine, Epist. LV to Dardanus, and Isidore, book I on the Supreme Good, ch. V, say that those who are delivered in the maternal wombs cannot be baptized for this reason, because he who is not yet born according to Adam cannot be reborn according to Christ. Nor can it be called regeneration which generation has not preceded. Which is also the opinion of the Blessed Luther, Vol. XII, Wittenberg, page 292. (XII.) Because of the extreme necessity of Baptism, Baptism is not to be deferred, but conferred on newly born infants. For since they are born flesh of flesh, they have need to be reborn of the Spirit if they are to enter into heaven. But that the kingdom of heaven belongs to infants, Christ testifies with a sonorous voice, Mark X. v. 14. And this has been observed not only by the Apostles, by the power of the universal command of Christ, Matt. XXIX. 19, Acts II. 39, 40, 1 Cor. VII. 14, Col. II. 11, as also Acts XVI. 15, 37, 1 Cor. I. 16, where entire families are read to have been baptized; but also a perpetual practice has obtained in the Church that infants should be baptized. As is manifest from Augustine, Epist. XXIX, as also on Original Sin, ch. XL, Jerome, Ep. to Laeta, Innocent, Epist. XXVI to the Council of Milevis, Theodoret, Epitome of Divine Dogmas, ch. on Baptism. Whence Augustine, in *De Genesi ad literam*, book 10, chapter 33: "The custom of Mother Church in baptizing infants is by no means to be despised, nor in any way to be called superfluous, nor at all to be believed unless it were an Apostolic tradition." Which custom he teaches, in book I *De peccatorum meritis & remissione*, chapter XXVI, was handed down by the Lord and the Apostles, and is observed by the universal Church. Just as long before Augustine, not only did Origen, in book V *ad Rom.*, chapter VI, observe that this tradition proceeded from the Apostles, but Cyprian also, in his epistle to Fidus, book III, as well as Irenaeus, book II, chapter XXIX, taught and demonstrated that infants were to be baptized in their own age. All of which things are so certain that the Pelagians themselves not only conceded that infants were to be baptized, as Augustine testifies in book I *de peccatorum meritis & remissione*, chapter XXVI, but professed it, and that this was done according to

The rule of the universal Church and according to the judgment of the Gospel, just as Augustine observed concerning Celestius in book II against Celestius and the Pelagians. (XII) Therefore, Baptism is not to be deferred until the final moments of life, as was done by some in the ancient Church, nor are only certain days to be fixed for Baptism, as was also observed among some of the ancients until now, so that Baptism might be administered on the feasts of Easter and Pentecost: but Baptism is to be hastened after birth, so that those who are born carnally may be reborn spiritually. Rightly Tertullian in his book on Baptism: Every day is the Lord's, every hour, every time is favorable for Baptism. The Muscovites and Christians in Cranganore, India, are not accustomed to baptize infants before the fortieth day. But because of the various accidents of life, it is better for Baptism to be conferred immediately, lest anyone be deprived of this saving means of Regeneration, which is destined for all. (XIII) Because of the same necessity of Baptism, no one is easily to be excluded from Baptism. Therefore, Baptism is not to be denied either to foundlings born in the Church, nor to others who by legitimate reason, whether by capture or by designation or by right of war, etc., come into the power of Christians, whatever may seem to Calvin, Beza, and Bucanus concerning this matter. The rules of the ancients are to be observed here in Cyprian, book III, Epistle 18, to Fidus. This was our judgment in the Council: that from Baptism and the grace of God, who is merciful and kind and pious to all, no one ought to be prohibited by us. Augustine, on Grace and Free Will, ch. XXII. To some children of infidels this grace is granted, that they be baptized, when by the hidden providence of God they sometimes come into the hands of the pious. Likewise the Fifth Council of Carthage, Canon VIII. It has been decided concerning infants, as often as most certain witnesses are not found who testify without doubt that they have been baptized, nor are they themselves of an age suitable to answer concerning the Sacraments delivered to them, that they are to be baptized without any scruple, lest that trepidation cause them to be deprived of the cleansing of the Sacraments. (XIV) Because of the supreme necessity of Baptism, if ordinary ministers of the word are lacking, it is better for Baptism to be administered extraordinarily by a layman than for the salvation of those to be baptized to be endangered. Just as it is established that circumcision was dispensed by Zipporah and other pious women, Exod. IV. 25, 1 Macc. I. v. 63, 2 Macc. VI. 20. As in the bringing forth of an infant the work of a midwife is necessary, by whose hand he is extracted safely from the womb: so a minister ought to be at hand and ready when he who is involved and entangled in the corruptions of Adam is extracted through the Water of Baptism from original stain. But just as another matron sometimes supplies the place of a midwife and performs the deputy's work, so also another person can, and indeed ought to, supply the place of a minister in a case of necessity, since more is at stake in regeneration to heavenly life than in generation to temporal life. Whence the ancients in necessity admitted the Baptism of laymen, as can be seen from Tertullian, On Baptism, ch. XVI. Otherwise, laymen also have the right: For what is received on equal terms can be given on equal terms. Let it suffice, however, that in necessities you use it wherever the condition of place, or time, or person compels. For then the constancy of the one helping is accepted when the circumstance of the one in danger is pressing, because he will be guilty of a lost man if he has refrained from providing what he could freely provide. And Jerome in the Dialogue against the Luciferians: If necessity compels, we know that it is also permitted for laymen to baptize. For as one receives, so also one can give. We know, he says, whence it is gathered that it was held as undoubted at that time. Similar things are held by Gelasius in his Epistle to all the Bishops throughout

Lucania, the Bruttians, and Sicily: and Isidore, book II, on Ecclesiastical Offices, ch. XXXIV. And from this Gratian gathers in the Canon 'in necess.' on consecration, distinction IV. That when extreme necessity compels, they admit that the administration of Baptism is generally granted to Christian laymen. Not that it is not sometimes permitted, but that it was not observed in all places, but in most, so that no one, as Isidore speaks, might be called away from the world without the saving remedy. Augustine, Vol. VII, against the Epistle of Parmenianus, book II, ch. XIII. If a layman, he says, has given Baptism when compelled by the necessity of a dying person, it is either no sin or a venial one. But do not doubt that the baptized person has then received a legitimate Baptism. Whatever the Council of Elvira may have decreed, that a believer can baptize in necessity, ch. XXXVIII. Whence that which is in the Fourth Council of Carthage, canon C: That a woman should not presume to baptize. is defined, it is to be understood as outside a case of necessity. And therefore Calvin himself, book IV of the Institutes, ch. XV, § 20, acknowledges that it was received by use many ages ago and almost from the very beginning of the Church, that laymen should baptize in danger of death. Nor do they consider gynae-baptism to be illegitimate, having disregarded the contrary opinion of Theodore Beza, part 2, question 139, or that it needs Anabaptism, according to the Anglican Church, as witnessed by Isaac Casaubon in his response to the letter of Cardinal Perron. Gregory, an English Abbot and Theologian, reports in book VI of his questions, lectured upon in the Oxford School, that private dipping was also tolerated for a time in those Churches. The words of the Liturgy of the Anglican Church, in the chapter on private Baptism, are as follows: And let no one doubt that an infant baptized in that way is both legitimately and sufficiently baptized, nor ought he to be rebaptized in the temple. (XV) As we are generated only once, so we are regenerated only once. Whence it is deservedly established that we should not be baptized more than once. However, the Rule of Leo in Ep. XXXVII must be held here: That which is entirely unknown to have been done cannot fall into the crime of repetition, nor should we fear to open the door of salvation to him who is taught never to have entered it before. (XVI) Not Generation, but Regeneration makes Christians. For according to carnal birth we are under no one but the power of the Devil, but through spiritual Regeneration we pass into the kingdom of God. No ones are born Saints or Christians but are made. Although parents may be in the covenant and spiritual from whom we are begotten, we are not however begotten in the covenant or spiritual, but outside the covenant and carnal. But in order that we may be received into the covenant and become spiritual, there is need of regeneration. Moreover, the children of all Christians (not indeed of believers only) are called clean or holy, 1. Cor. VII. 14. not indeed by civil holiness, as household vessels are clean, nor yet by spiritual, which is proper to the Sons of God, but by Ecclesiastical, because they are born in the bosom of the Church and are Candidates for the goods of the Church, which kind of cleanness is not unlike the Levitical, by which some animals were considered clean over others, as Vossius acknowledges, Diss. V. de Bapt. Th. 6. (XVII) Many things are hidden in nature, what wonder if in Scripture? You do not know what is the way of the wind, Ecclesiast. XI. 5. Because you cannot express it definitely. If you are ignorant of natural things which act by necessity, how much more inaccessible will be supernatural things which are of the most free divine dispensation. Job XXXVIII. The Spirit blows where it wills. Maldonatus is not to be heard here, who, being a lover of novelty, speaking of the Spirit as the animal spirit, animates whatever bodies it wills. An explanation too far-fetched, inept. (XVIII) Especially does the mystery of regeneration exceed our comprehension, and therefore it is indeed right to wonder at it, but not to pry into it. But it is one thing to wonder out of ignorance, whether simple or affected, and another out of reverence for a mystery: it is one thing out of unbelief, another out of humility. The former deserves rebuke, the latter praise. And therefore Chrysostom says that this little particle τὸ πῶς to those who are still wise in earthly things. Cyril calls it a Jewish word, and says, there are innumerable things in which, if you seek the how, it will be necessary for you to overturn the entire order. (XIX) The grace of the Holy Spirit is free, and by no means bound to means, subjects, or times. The Spirit blows where He wills. (XX) The communication of the Holy Spirit happens secretly and lies hidden, nor is it manifest in a man before it exerts itself through operations. Luther beautifully says in Eccl. chap. II. 20. Comment. Tom. IV. Lat. Jen. fol. 47. The animal man does not perceive whence an alien and spiritual life may come. For he does not know what kind of life this is. He hears the wind blowing, indeed, but he does not know whence it comes or whither it goes. He hears the voice of the spiritual man, he recognizes his face, his manners, and his gestures, but he does not see whence those words, whence those motions and actions come; because that life is in the heart through faith, where, with the flesh extinguished, Christ reigns with the Holy Spirit, who now sees, hears, speaks, works, suffers, and simply works all things in him, even if the flesh resists. (XXI) One must not doubt the efficacy of the Holy Spirit in the proclamation of the word: even if we are ignorant of whither it goes and what it accomplishes. However much we may not perceive the fruit of our ministry with our eyes or senses, there is nevertheless no reason why we should doubt or despair of the same. For the Spirit blows where He wills, and you do not know whence He comes or whither He goes. Let the faith of the divine promise be more certain to you than what you see with your own eyes. These do not look into the hearts which the Holy Spirit chooses for Himself as temples. For divine truth does not deceive in any way, nor can it deceive; the word which goes forth from my mouth shall not return to me void, Isa. LV. 11. The free operation of the Holy Spirit, because it is for the most part hidden, is not to be entirely despaired of if we do not perceive the progress of the sacred ministry. As ministers of the word are sometimes anxious, let us not believe in senses here, but in the promise of God, and let us rest in that. The grace of the Holy Spirit knows no slow delays.

Mittimus hic ineptam Anonymi cujusdam A- riani à Sandio adducti glossam ineptissimam. Li- teraliter Christus loquutus est de generatione carnali. Prima enim generatio est spiritualis, secunda carna- lis. Sensus itaq; verborum Christi est: nisi quis ge- neretur in carne, non potest intrare in regnum Dei: & propterea Dæmones non possint intrare in regnum Dei, quia non permittitur eis à Deo, ut secundo na- scantur, in carne scilicet. Per generationem autem secundum v. 3. illam demum intelligit, quæ est carnalis, vel quæ fit ex aqua, & Spiritu, id est, ex carne, & Spiritu. Aqua enim est principium generationis car- nalis, ex qua etiam omnia corpora constare, multi ex modernis, & antiquis Philosophis sensêre. Sensus itaque verborum Christi est: nisi quis generetur ex carne & Spiritu; id est, nisi quis generetur in carne, vel nisi anima uniatur corpori, non potest intrare in regnum Dei. Quæ errorum portenta, vel deli- ria recitasse est refutasse.

Cæterum de hisce verbis Christi ita in eloquiis Oris Domini l. I. c. X. disseruimus; Postquam Chri- stus Nicodemum de Salutem consequendi ratione & speciatim de Baptismo, quem Johannes undi- quaque ad ipsum concurrentibus, Pharisæis autem Consilium Dei adversus semetipsos spernentibus, & Baptismum suscipere renuentibus, Luc. VII. 30. informationis perquam cupidum in genere de ne- cessitate regenerationis instruxit; Nicodemus vero de arduo hoc fidei mysterio admodum crasse phi- losophando ac si nova opus sit nativitate ex utero matris, de modo sciscitatus est, quomodo homo de- nuo potest nasci, cum sit senex? Rabbi cœlestis Chri- stus Regenerationis modum specialius exprimit & Sacramentum divinitus, ejusdem causa in N. Test. consecratum adstruit, imo necessitatem atque ef- ficaciam ejusd. adserit. Nicodemum vero à naturæ abditis humano ingenio imperviis ad supernatura- lis operationis Spiritus mysteria ita revocat, ut ho- minem simul de ignorantia convincat, priusquam redarguat, simul ad sublimiora, de quibus adhuc informandus erat, cum reverentia suspicienda my- steria, præparet. Præmittit autem (1.) Asseverationis consuetam formulam: Amen Amen &c. ut scilicet non minus creditu necessariam doceat hanc de Ba- ptismo Regenerationis Sacramento, quam traditu- rus, veritatem quam doctrinam ipsam de Regene- ratione. Doctrina enim de Baptismo non haben- da est, cum Socinianis, Remonstrantibus, Calvini- stis & Syncretistis (Calixtinis) pro minus necessaria, aut non fundamentali, sed cum Christus eandem hic primum inculcet Catechumeno nocturno, Con- silium de Salute, quod cæteri Pharisæi spernebant, salutaris informationis ergo, anxie exquirenri; ac Apostolus Ebr. VI. 1. 2. διδαχὴν βαπτισμῶν τοῖς θεμελίοις, & τῷ λόγῳ τ’ ἀρχῆς, ut & τοῖς στοιχείοις eloquiorum Dei, quæ Catechumenis in primitiva Ecclesia tradi, & fundamenti loco substerni sole- bant, accenseat; non minus necessaria habenda est illa doctrina nostris post Baptismum Catechumenis, cum de via salutis informantur, ut de medio rege- nerationis, quo inserti sunt primum Christo, ini- tiati Ecclesiæ, & admissi ad regnum cœlorum, ad- eoq; de ipsa regeneratione sua certiores reddan- tur; quam fuerat Catechumenis in primitiva Eccle- sia, priusquam illi baptizarentur, ut hoc medium salutare an helarent, quo nomine etiam inter Cate- chumenos cheseos Christianæ partes doctrina de Baptismo in nostra Ecclesia recensetur. (II.) Sacramenti regene- rationis materiam, ex qua constat, & unde nostra fit regeneratio. Nisi quis renatus fuerit ἐξ ὕδατος καὶ πνεύματος. Quæ exhibent, materiam tum terre- nam Baptismi veram aquam, tum cælestem, Sp. San- ctum: Adeoque ipsum Sacramentum Baptismi si- stunt. Spiritus enim Sanctus, ut ait Cypr. de Bapt. Christi, consecrationibus visibilibus invisibiliter ma- num totius bonitatis autor adponit, & plenitudinem gratiæ unctionis divinæ pinguedo sanctificationibus effi- cialibus infundit, & rem Sacramenti consummat ac perficit. Cum istud elementum aquæ, ait Basil. M. in Ps. XXII. acceperit Sp. Sanctum, sit Sacramentum, & jam non erit aqua potationis, sed sanctificationis. Duabus rebus, inquit Gregor. Naz. Or. 40. in Bapt. constat Baptismus, aqua sc. & Spiritu, Illa visibili & corporeo modo accepta, hoc vero invisibili concurrente. Unde hanc Christi sententiam omnes pene de Ba- ptismo interpretantur, ut Maldon. fatetur cum Lu- cero. super h. l. Qui secus explicant, non inveniunt, in quo pedem figant sive Calviniani, sive Socinistæ, sive Arminiani. Ex istis Zuvingl. l. d. Bapt. T. 2. p. 69. aquam de cognitione Christi & consolatione fi- dei accipit. Calv. l. 4. inst. c, 16. aquam per Spiritum κατ᾽ ἐπεξήγησιν interpretatur. Bulling. in dec. Serm. 8. de Spiritu S. locum metaphorice de renovatione cordis per Sp. S. explicat. Beza de immenso Dei amo- re, Pet. Martyr ibid. de gratia Dei. Cassano de Rege- nerationis & Sp. S. gratia. Gualtb. de Verbo Dei in- telligit. Socinus l. d. Bapt. p. 46. Jam de ablatione pec- catorum, jam de pænitentia interpretatur, jam vero regenerationem ex aqua dicit renovationem volunta- tis, regenerationem ex Spiritu, renovationem in- tellectus. Alii per aquam tribulationis aquam seu mortificationem veteris hominis, per Spiritum reno- vationem naturæ designari voluit. Nonnulli per Spi- ritum ipsum Christum indigitari censent. Joh. Gerb. Vossio aqua & Spiritus aquam spiritualem notant. Hugoni Grotio Spiritum aqueum, i.e. Spiritum emun- dantem, qui tamen per aquam etiam malorum fu- gam, per Spiritum, impetum ad optime quæq́; agenda intelligi existimat. Quod quid alius est, quam Scri- pturæ velle illudere? Omnes utiq; illæ Glossæ sua- pte vanitate concidunt. De Baptismo autem aqua hic sermonem esse docet tum ipsa textus litera, cum nulla causa sit, cur non aqua proprie intelligenda sit, quæ tanquam medium regenerationis in Baptismo sancita est, tum occasio Nicodemica, de Baptismo Johannis orta, quæ vi collationis Luc. VII. 30. à Soci- no ipso loco citato admittitur: tum aliorum loco- rum Scripturæ Symphonia. Act. XXII. 16. Eph. V. 26. Tit. III. 5. Adde quod in eo consentiant veteres Ec- clesiæ Doctores. Aug. tr. II. in Ioh. Cyrill. Alex. l. T. in Ioh. c. 22. Chrys. hom. 24. in Ioh. Ammon. & Theodor. Mo- psuest. in Romana Græcorum Catena, citante Maldo- nato, ut & Euthym. & Theoph. in h. l. imo etiam Calv. ipse Comm. in h. l. Bucer. item ac Maldon. con- sensum veterum laudantes. Universam antiquita- tem hunc locum de Baptismo accipere fatetur in anti- quitate versatissimus Voss. disp. 4. de Bapt. d. 2. (III) Baptismi necessitatem. De qua, Non poterit, inquit Christus, ingredi regnum Dei: Simul innuens, Bapti- smum primum esse aditum & introitum ad regnum cælesse. Hæc vero necessitas non absoluta est, sed ab hypothesi ordinis divini pendet; ad quemetsi Deus semetipsum præcise non alligarit, nos tamen adstrictos voluit, ne medium divinitus sancitum, ut à Pharisæis fiebat, negligeremus, vel contemnere- mus, quemadmodum Lombardus locum de illis intelligendum esse dicit, qui possunt contemnere & baptizari; unde natus Canon Theologicus:

Vi ergo hujus Aphorifmi Christi Baptismus ordinarie necessarius est, ut Regnum coelorum ingrediamur; quia est medium Regenerationis ordinarium, si- ne quo, teste Christo, regnum Dei nemo adire potest. Atque hinc elegantissima nomina forti- tur, ut vocetur à Justino, in Dial. cum Tryph. aqua vitae, ab Iren. lib. I. c. 18. baptisma regenera- tionis, à Cyrill. Hierosol. in praef. Catech. regeneratio animae, ab Optato Milev. &c. nativitas immortalis, à Cassiod. in Cant. VII. fons divinus quo fideles ri- gantur, ab aliis porta gratiae, introitus ad regnum Dei, à B. Luthero, puerpera Regni Caelestis. Per- tinent huc Epitheta suavissima Naz. in Orat. ad Bapt. quod sit Spiritus collatio, verbi participatio, figmenti correctio, peccati diluvium, lucis commu- nicatio, tenebrarum oppressio, vehiculum ad Deum, peregrinatio ad Christum, clavis regni caelestis, vi- tae commutatio.

(IV.) Necessitatis rationem. Quic- quid ex carne natum est, caro est. Causa, ob quam omnibus Regeneratione opus est ex aqua & spiritu, universalis est, quod omnes nascantur in peccato, & nemo ingredi possit regnum Dei ni- si renatus fuerit. Caro enim & sanguis regnum Dei possidere non possunt 1. Corinth. c. XV. 45. Non intrabit in Civitatem illam coinquinatum, Apocal. XXI. 27.

Ex carne nasci dicitur, qui car- nali modo propagatur, vel à corruptis pecca- to & contaminatis Parentibus nascitur. Car- nis enim nomine designatur Synecdochice natu- ra humana, Genes. VI. 12. Psal. CXLV. 21. Es. c. XL. 5. c. LXVI. 23. Matth. XXIV. 32. Luc. III. 6. Rom. III. 20. Cum vero hic caro & spiritus oppo- nantur & de ψιλοῖς ἀνθρώποις sermo sit, per car- nem homo per peccatum corruptus denotatur. Con- fer Rom. VIII. 1. seqq. Gal. V. 17. cap. VI. 8. Unde Theophylactus carnem hoc loco recte accepit pro homine carnali. Aliter accipitur vox carnis cum opponitur Spiritui, ubi de Christo θεανθρώπῳ ser- mo est. Tum enim divina & humana natura in Christo designatur, Vid. Joh. I. 14. Rom. I. v. 4. c. IX. 6. 1. Tim. III. 16. 1. Petr. III. 18. In praedica- to: Caro est, itidem denotatur peccato corrupta humana natura, ut sensus sit, quicquid ex paren- tibus carnalibus, vel peccato contaminatis pro- pagatione carnali natum est, id per nativitatem, vel vi carnalis istius propagationis non est nisi ca- ro. Non est spirituale ullo modo, sed totum car- nale & peccato contaminatum, & corruptum. Non nascitur homo spiritualis aut sanctus ex carnalibus parentibus, sed carnalis, quales parentes sunt, tales & sunt liberi. Ut Adam in statu integritatis procreasset liberos, ad imaginem Dei, in qua conditus erat: ita post lapsum procreavit eosdem qualis ipse erat, ad imaginem non Dei, sed suam, quam per peccatum contraxerat Genes. c. V. 1. 3. Tales nascimur omnes, unde omnes Filii irae na- tura sumus Eph. II. 3. in peccato concepti & calefacti, Psal. LI. 7. Immundi ex immundis procreati. Job. XIV. 4. Etiamsi Parentes fideles sint & renati, li- beri tamen, quos generant isti, non secundum spiritum, vel ut fideles sunt, sed secundum na- turam, in qua haeret peccatum, quaeque non est ex asse renovata, sed magna parte adhuc carnalis, ge- nerantur: ideo non nascuntur Sancti ex Sanctis, ut Calvinistis placet, sed carnales, uti Christus hic do- cet. Nec tamen ideo damnantur nuptiae, quem- admodum Pelagiani cavillabantur, quos solide re- fellit August. libris 2. ad Valer. Comitem de Nuptiis & concupiscentia. Nam recte advertit, l. I. c. V. quod ita nuptiarum bonum malo originali, quod inde trahi- tur, non possit accusari, sicut adulteriorum & forni- cationum malum bono naturali, quod inde nascitur, non potest excusari. Nam sicut peccatum sive hinc, sive inde a parentibus trahatur, opus est Diaboli: sic homo sive hinc, sive inde nascatur, opus est Dei. Pul- chre imprimis c. XXVIII. hac de re disserit: Car- nis pudenda concupiscentia non est nuptiis imputan- da, sed toleranda. Non enim est ex naturali connubio bonum veniens sed ex antiquo peccato accedens ma- lum: propter hoc ergo fit, ut & de legitimis nuptiis fi- liorum Dei non filii Dei, sed filii seculi generentur, quia & ii, qui generant, si jam regenerati sunt, non ex hoc generant, quod filii Dei sunt, sed ex hoc quod ad- huc Filii seculi sunt. Dominica quippe sententia est, Filii hujus seculi generant & generantur. Ex quo itaque adhuc sumus Filii seculi hujus, exterior noster homo corrumpitur, ex hoc & Filii hujus seculi gene- rantur, nec nisi regenerantur, Filii Dei fiunt: sed ex quo sumus Filii Dei, interior homo de die in diem re- novatur, quamvis & ipse exterior per lavacrum rege- nerationis sanctificatus sit, & spem futurae incorru- ptionis acceperit. Quod capite sequenti declarat si- militudine Oleae, ex qua nascitur Oleaster. Sicut gi- gnitur ex Oleastri semine Oleaster, & ex Oleae semine non nisi Oleaster; cum inter Oleastrum & Oleam plu- rimum distet; Ita gignitur & de carne peccatoris, & de carne justi utring; peccator, quamvis inter peccato- rem & justum plurimum distet.

Non autem sine emphasifi Christus dixit, τὸ γεγεν- νημένον, quod natum est, ut omne, & totum quod na- scitur, comprehenderet. Siquidem majorem ἐν- έργειαν hoc habeat: quicquid natum ex carne est, caro est, quam si dixisset; omnis ex carne natus caro est, istud enim, quod ex carne natum est. (1.) Vniver- salitatem suppositorum designat, omnesque homi- nes complectitur, nemine excepto, nisi solo Chri- sto, qui non è carnis voluntate natus sed ex Spiritu Sancto conceptus, omnisq; peccati expers est. Chri- stus quidem carnem habet quantum ad substan- tiam & veritatem naturae humanae, sed neque ex carne, uti hoc loco accipitur, natus est, neque caro est, quantum ad accidentalem corruptionem. Non autem excipitur sive Maria Θεοτόκος, sive Jere- mias, sive Johannes, sive alius quisquam. Nulla hic est διαστολὴ, omnes peccatores sunt. Rom. III. 22. (2.) Totalitatem hominis importat; Totum quicquid ex carne natum est, totus homo corpore & anima ex carne nascitur. Non tantummodo propagatur cor- pus, sed cum corpore & anima, utpote quae πρῶτον δεκτικὸν est peccati originalis. Totum illud infe- ctum est peccato per nativitatem, non tantum in- feriores potentiae, aut Appetitus sensitivus, ut Papistae volunt, quibus hactenus accedunt Novatores, (Calixtini) quod nempe in Appetitu sensitivo ma- lum resideat, quo repugnamus appetitui rationali, vel rebellio ejusdem, quae, cum anima intellectualis à Deo Creatore infusa corpori unitur, ex inferio- ribus potentiis animae resultet: ut contendit Dre- jerus in deduct. Germ. p. 333. Quo pacto anima ra- tionalis corrupta non erit aut subjectum peccati originalis vel rebellionis istius pravae congenitae, sed ea rebellio unice residebit in appetitu sensitivo, cui contranitetur anima potius, quantum potest, utpote cujus appetitus rationalis illi per naturam contrarius est, secundum hanc sententiam. (V.) Re- generationis Utilitatem: De qua Christus: Quod ex Spiritu natum est, Spiritus est. Ex Spiritu natum dicitur, quod desuper renatum est virtute Spiritus Sancti. Quod itidem totum hominem respicit, qui spiritualiter per Gratiam renasci debet, postquam carnaliter natus est, Spiritus quidem solius hic men- tio fit, utpote qui τὸ πρωτεῖον obtinet in Baptismo, medium autem aqua non excluditur, quippe, quod supra jam requisitum cum Spiritu erat. Cæterum Spiritus esse dicitur, quod ex Spiritu nascitur, non per aliquam essentialem μέθεξιν vel spiritus participationem & ἀποθέωσιν vel Deificationem aut per quandam μεταμόρφωσιν vel transsubstantiationem, quam Weigeliani somniant. Nulla enim hic substantia fit mutatio, sed idem quod caro nascitur de carne, spiritus renascitur ex Spiritu. Non per totalem carnis abolitionem: Hæc enim non deponitur, nisi cum hac vita. Semper aliquid carnis adhuc superest, cum quo Spiritus colluctari necessum habet Gal. V. 15. Ebr. XII. 1. sed per carnis mortificationem, & Spiritus innovationem: Non quod toti spirituales simus per Regenerationis gratiam, sed quod spirituales esse incipiamus, dum renovamur, ut de die in diem proficiamus, donec perfecte spirituales evadamus: ad quod quidem in hac vita aspiramus, sed non nisi in altera vita id assequimur. Hoc sensu Cyrillus Alex. l. II. in Joh. c. 43. ait, nos per Spiritum ad Deum reformari ac proprio ejus charactere insigniri, ut ad ipsius qualitatem, ut ita dicam, animo formemur. Conferatur Basilius l. I. de Baptismo. Unde utilitas & Effectus Regenerationis agnoscitur, spiritualis nempe nostra renovatio, quæ quomodo à Regeneratione discriminetur, antea dictum est. VI. Incomprehensibilis Mysterii conditionem. Quam explicat Christus collatione venti ejusque flatus, quem nemo ortus, terminique ratione novit: etsi sonitum ejus audiat. Unde non mirum, si non norint rationem regenerationis spiritualis, utut eadem per externa indicia sese deinde prodat. Quia cœlestis illius Flaminis Spiritus Sancti Gratia, & operatio longe magis imperscrutabilis est. Si rerum naturalium rationem ignoramus, & in iisdem hæremus, quid mirum si supernaturalia comprehendere nequeamus, quæ tanto distant intervallo quanto cœlum & terra, imo Deus & Natura, finitum & infinitum, incomprehensibile, & id quod non omnem captum creaturæ excedit. Conf. Syr. c. XIIX. 8. Nonnulli è veteribus per Spiritum, cujus ortus, terminusque ignoratur, Spiritum Sanctum intelligere videntur. Ambros. l. II. de fide c. VII. Hilar. l. II. de Trin. Athan. l. I. de unita Deitate Trinitatis. Basil. l. V. 9. contra Eunomianos. Naz. Or. V. de Theologia. Sed hoc non aliter admitti debet, nisi eo sensu, quod Spiritus Sancti operatio hic in ὑποδόσει designetur. Quod plerique, nisi fallor, indigitant; de vento enim naturali loquitur Christus, sed ita ut Spiritus supernaturalem gratiam eodem figuret: Eoque sensu accipienda sunt, quæ egregie tradit Gregor. M. l. XVIII. c. XIII. Mor. Vocem Spiritus audire est, vi conjunctionis intimæ in amorem conditoris assurgere, sed nemo scit, unde veniat, quia ignoratur, per ora prædicantium, quibus se ad nos occasionibus fundat. Et nemo scitquo vadat, quia dum unam prædicationem multi audiunt, intelligi non potest, quem deserens abjiciat, aut cujus ingrediens in corde requiescat. Voluit autem Christus Mysterium hoc quam incomprehensibile sit, docere, non tantum ut à temerario scrutinio revocaret Nicodemum, & ad fidem fideique humilitatem admoneret: sed ut viam sibi quoque pararet ad sublimiora Mysteria enarranda, & humiliter suscipienda, sine quibus neque via salutis vel Regni Dei, neque hæc de Regeneratione doctrina solide cognosci, aut firma fide apprehendi potest, quemadmodum ex sequentibus patebit.

Documenta ex hoc loco classico notanda sequentia sunt,

(I.) Doctrina de Baptismo fun- damentalis, & necessaria est. (II.) Baptismus or- dinarium medium est Regenerationis. (III.) Si- ne Baptismo non potest ordinarie quis ingredi Re- gnum Cœlorum. (IV.) Non baptizatis tamen, si in Ecclesia nati sunt, temere Janua Salutis non occludenda. Cum Deus non se, gratiamque suam, sed nos ad media alligarit. (V.) Sacra- mentum Baptismi, si integrum esse debeat, vera propriaque aqua, ceu re terrena, & Spiritu Sancto tanquam re cœlesti, constare debet. (VI.) Peccatum Originale a parentibus in poste- ros ita propagatur, ut nemo, qui carnaliter ge- neratur, peccati expers sit. (VII.) Non tantum corpus sed & anima ceu subjectum peccati pro- pagatur in sobolem. (VIII.) Tradux ergo, non vero immediata animæ creatio asserenda. (IX.) Quam necessaria est peccati Originalis as- sertio, tam necessaria est assertio propagationis animæ, nisi Deus statuendus causa peccati. (X.) Ut nemo videre potest hanc lucem terrenam, nisi nascatur, ita nemo Regni Dei lucem videre potest nisi renascatur. (XI.) Nemo renasci de- bet per Baptismum aut baptizari, nisi natus sit prius in hunc mundum. Unde Embryones & Fœtus ex parte tantum nati baptizari non pos- sunt aqua utero materno, aut partibus editis ef- fusa, uti Aureolus, Ludolphus, & Angelus de Cla- vasio censent, partem fœtus in lucem editam baptizari posse. Recte enim S. Augustinus Epist. LV. ad Dardanum & Isiod. l. I. de Summo Bono c. V. qui in maternis uteris editi sunt, ideo baptizari non possunt, quia, qui secundum Adam nondum est natus, secundum Christum non potest renasci. Neque regeneratio potest dici, quam generatio non præcessit. Quæ etiam sententia B. Lutheri Tom. XII. Witteb. pag. 292. (XII.) Ob necessitatem Baptismi summam Baptismus non differendus, sed infantibus recens natis con- ferendus. Cum enim caro de carne nati sunt, opus habent, ut ex Spiritu renascantur, si in cœ- lum ingredi debeant. At infantum esse regnum cœlorum, Christus sonora voce testatur, Marc. X. v. 14. Idque non tantum ab Apostolis, vi universa- lis Christi mandati, Matth. XXIX. 19. observa- tum est Actor. II. 39. 40. 1. Cor. VII. 14. Col. II. 11. ut & Act. XVI. 15. 37. 1. Cor. I. 16. ubi integras le- guntur baptizatæ familias; Sed & perpetua praxis in Ecclesia obtinuit, ut infantes baptizarentur. Quemadmodum ex August. Epist. XXIX. ut & de peccat. Orig. c. XL. Hieron. Ep. ad Letam. In- nocent. Epist. XXVI. ad Concilium Milevitanum. Theod. Epitome Divinorum dogmatum c. de Ba- ptismo, manifestum est. Unde August. de Ge- nesi ad literam l. 10. c. 33. Consuetudo Matris Ec- clesiæ in baptizandis parvulis nequaquam spernenda est, neque ullo modo superflua nuncupanda; Nec omnino credenda nisi Apostolica esset traditio. Quam consuetudinem lib. I. de peccatorum me- ritis & remiss. cap. XXVI. per Dominum & Apo- stolos traditam esse, & ab universa Ecclesia obser- vari, docet. Quemadmodum longe ante Au- gustinum non modo traditionem hanc ab Apo- stolis profectam Origenes lib. V. ad Rom. c. VI. ob- servavit, sed & Cyprianus in Epist. ad Fidum l. III. ut & Irenæus lib. II. cap. XXIX. Infantes baptizandos esse sua jam ætate docuerunt & de- monstrarunt. Quæ omnia adeo certa sunt, ut ipsimet quoque Pelagiani parvulos baptizan- dos esse, non modo concederent, teste Augu- stino lib. I. de peccatorum meritis & remissione c. XXVI. sed profiterentur, & hoc fieri secundum

Regulam universalis Ecclesiae & secundum Evan- gelii sententiam, quemadmodum de Coelestio ob- servavit Augustin. lib. II. contra Caelestium & Pe- lagianos. (XII) Non ergo differendus Baptismus usq; ad extrema vitae tempora, ut a nonnullis in Ecclesia veteri factum, neque certi solum dies Ba- ptismo praefigendi, quemadmodum & adhuc apud veteres quosdam observatum fuit, ut festis Pa- schatos & Pentecostes Baptismus administrare- tur: sed maturandus est post nativitatem Bapti- smus, ut qui nati sunt carnaliter renascantur spi- ritualiter. Recte Tertullianus libro de Baptismo: Omnis dies Domini est, omnis hora, omne tempus favet Baptismo. Moscovitae & Christiani in Cran- ganore Indiae non ante quadragesimam diem ba- ptizare infantes solent. Verum ob varios vitae ca- sus praestat illico conferri Baptismum, ne salutari hoc Regenerationis medio privetur ullus, quod destinatum est omnibus. (XIII) Ob eandem Ba- ptismi necessitatem nemo facile a Baptismo ex- cludendus est. Ideo neque exposititiis in Ecclesia natis, nec aliis qui legitima ratione sive eruptio- ne sive denominatione seu belli jure &c. in pote- statem Christianorum deveniunt, Baptismus de- negandus est, quicquid etiam Calvino, Beza atque Bucano hac de re videatur. Observandae hic vete- rum Regulae sunt apud Cyprianum lib. III. Epist. 18. ad Fidum. Haec fuit in Concilio nostra sententia a Baptismo atq; Gratia Dei, qui omnibus misericors atq; benignus est & pius, neminem pro nos debere prohiberi. Augustinus, de Gratia & lib. Arbit. c. XXII. Aliquibus liberis infidelium praestatur haec Gratia, ut baptizentur, cum occulta Dei providentia in manus piorum quandog; perveniunt. Concilii itidem Carthaginensis V. Can. VIII. Placuit de In- fantibus, quoties non inveniuntur certissimi testes, qui eos baptizatos esse sine dubitatione testentur, neq; ipsi sunt per aetatem idonei de traditis sibi Sacra- mentis respondere, absq; ullo scrupulo esse baptizan- dos, ne ista trepidatio faciat eos Sacramentorum purgatione privari. (XIV) Ob summam Bapti- smi necessitatem, si desunt ministri verbi ordinarii, praestat extraordinarie Baptismum a Laico admi- nistrari, quam baptizandorum salutem periclitari. Quemadmodum constat circumcisionem a Zipo- ra & aliis mulieribus piis, Exod. IV. 25. 1. Macc. I. v. 63. 2. Macc. VI. 20. dispensatam esse. Ut in eductione infantuli obstetriculae opera necefsaria est, cujus manu incolumis ex utero extrahatur: Ita minister ad manum oportet & praesto sit, cum ex labe originali per Aquam Baptismi extrahitur, qui Adami corruptelis involvitur & irretitur. Ut vero obstetricis vices matrona alia quandoque supplet, & vicariam praestat operam, sic & mini- stri vices alia persona in casu necessitatis supplere potest, imo debet, cum plus situm sit in regene- ratione ad vitam coelestem, quam generatione ad vitam temporalem. Unde veteres in necessitate Laicorum Baptismum admiserunt, ut e Tertull. de Bapt. cap. XVI. videre est. Alioquin & Laicis jus est: Quod enim ex aequo accipitur, ex aequo dari potest. Sufficiat autem ut in necessitatibus utaris sicubi aut loci, aut temporis, aut personae conditio compellit. Tum enim constantia succurrentis exci- pitur, cum viget circumstantia periclitantis, quia reus erit perditi hominis, si supersederit praestare quod libere poterit. Et Hieronymus Dialogo ad- versus Lucifer: Si necessitas cogit, scimus & Laicis licere baptizare. Ut enim accipit quis, ita & dare potest. Scimus, inquit, unde colligitur id pro indubitato tum habitum fuisse. Similia ha- bent Gelasius Epistol. ad universos Episcopos per

Luraniam, Brutios, & Siciliam: & Isidorus lib. II. de offic. Ecclesiast. cap. XXXIV. Atque ex hoc colligit Gratianus Canone in necess. de consecrat. distinct. IV. Cum extrema cogit necessitas, Laicis Christianis plerumque concedi Baptismi admini- strationem, fatentur. Non quod quandoque id non liceat, sed quod non in omnibus locis, sed plerisque id ita observatum fuerit, ne quisquam, ut loquitur Isidorus, sine remedio salutari de seculo avocetur. Augustin. Tom. VII. contra Ep. Parmenii l. II. cap. XIII. Si Laicus, inquit, Baptismum per- eunti necessitate compulsus dederit, aut nullum, aut veniale delictum est. Baptizatum autem tum Ba- ptismum legitimum accepisse nihil dubita. Quod- quod Concilium Ileberitanum fidelem posse bapti- zare in necessitate decreverit, cap. XXXVIII. Un- de quod in Concilio Carthaginensi IV. can. C. Ne mulier baptizare præsumat. definitum, extra neces- sitatis casum intelligendum est. Ideoque Calvinus ipse lib. IV. Instit. cap. XV. §. 20. Multis abhinc secutis & ab ipso fere Ecclesiæ exordio usu receptum agnoscit, ut in periculo mortis Laici baptizarent. Neque Gynæcobaptismum posthabita Theodor. Bezæ parte 2. quæst. 139. contraria sententia, pro illegitimo habent, aut Anabaptismo indigere cen- sent Anglicanæ Ecclesiæ teste Isaaco Casaubono re- sponso ad epistolam Cardinalis Perronii. Priva- tam etiam tinctionem ad tempus toleratam fuisse in illis Ecclesiis, refert Gregorius Abbas Theologus Anglus, lib. VI. quæstionum, in Schola Oxoniensi prælectarum. Verba Liturgiæ Ecclesiæ Anglicanæ, cap. de privato Baptif. ita habent: Nec dubitet quis- quam, quin infantulus eo modo baptizatus & legi- time & sufficienter baptizetur, neque debet in templo rebaptizari. (XV) Ut semel tantum generamur, ita semel tantum regeneramur. Unde merito san- ctum est, ut non sæpius quam semel baptizemur. Tenenda autem hic Leonis Regula Ep.XXXVII. Non potest in iterationis crimen devenire, quod fa- ctum omnino nescitur, nec vereamur huic salutis januam aperire, quam nunquam ante docetur in- gressus. (XVI) Non Generatio, sed Regenera- tio Christianos facit. Nam secundum nativita- tem carnalem non nisi sub potestate Diaboli su- mus, sed per Regenerationem spiritualem trans- imus in regnum Dei. Non nascuntur ulli Sancti aut Christiani sed fiunt. Etsi parentes in fœdere, & spirituales sint à quibus progeneramur, non ta- men in fœdere aut spiritales generamur, sed ex- tra fœdus & carnales. Ut autem in fœdus recipia- mur, & spiritales evadamus regeneratione opus est. Mundi autem vel sancti dicuntur Christia- norum omnium, (non vero fidelium solum) libe- ri, 1. Cor. VII. 14. non quidem sanctimonia civili, ut vasa domestica munda sunt, neque tamen spi- rituali, quæ Filiorum Dei propria est, sed Eccle- siastica, quod nascantur in gremio Ecclesiæ, & Candidati sint bonorum Ecclesiæ, cujusmodi mundities non absimilis est Leviticæ, qua animalia alia præ aliis munda censebantur, ut agnoscit Vos- sius, Diss. V. de Bapt. Th. 6. (XVII) Multa in na- tura sunt abscondita, quid mirum si in Scriptura? Venti quæ sit via ignoras, Ecclesiast. II. 5. Quia de- terminate eam exprimere nequis. Si naturalia ignoras quæ ex necessitate agunt, quanto magis impervia erunt supernaturalia quæ liberrimæ sunt dispensationis divinæ. Job. XXXVIII. Spiritus ubi vult spirat. Maldonatus hic non audiendus, qui novitatis amans, Spiritus, de spiritu animali loquens, animat quæ vult corpora. Explicatio ni- mis longe petita, inepta. (XVIII) Captum no- strum excedit imprimis regenerationis myste- rium, ideoque mirari id quidem fas est, sed non rimari. Aliud autem est mirari per ignorantiam seu simplicem, seu affectatam, aliud per mysterii reverentiam: Aliud ex infidelitate, aliud ex humi- litate. Prius reprehensionem, posterius laudem meretur. Ideoque particulam istam τὸ πῶς Chry- sostomus dicit, non esse multum credentium, sed ad- huc terrena sapientium. Judaicum Cyrillus ver- bum nominat, & innumerabilia, inquit, sunt, in quibus si quodammodo quæris universam evertere seriem tibi necessum erit. (XIX) Spiritus Sancti Gratia libera est, minimeque astricta ad media, subjecta, aut tempora. Spiritus ubi vult spirat. (XX) Spiritus Sancti communicatio occulte fit ac latet nec prius in homine, quam se per operatio- nes exerat, patet. Pulchre Lutherus in Eccl. cap. II. 20. Comment. Tom. IV. Lat. Jen. fol. 47. Ani- malis homo non percipit unde eveniat aliena & spi- ritualis vita. Nescit enim qualis hæc sit vita. Ven- tum quidem audit sonantem, sed unde veniat, aut quo vadat, nescit. Audit vocem spiritualis hominis, agnoscit faciem, mores & gestus ejus, sed unde illa verba, unde illi motus & actiones veniant, non vi- det; quia vita illa est in corde per fidem, ubi extincta carne regnat Christus cum Spiritu Sancto, qui jam videt, audit, loquitur, operatur, patitur & simplici- ter omnia operatur in ipso, etsi caro reluctetur. (XXI) Non ambigendum de Spiritus Sancti effi- cacia in præconio verbi: Etsi quo vadat, & quid præstet ignoremus. Utut fructum ministerii no- stri oculis aut sensibus nostris haud usurpemus, non est tamẽ quod de eodẽ dubitemus, aut despe- remus. Spiritus enim ubi vult spirat, & nescis unde veniat aut quo vadat. Certior sit tibi permissionis divinæ fides, quam ipsis quod tuis vides oculis. Hi non inspiciunt corda, quæ eligit Spiritus San- ctus sibi in templa. Nec enim ullatenus fallit aut fallere potest veritas divina, non revertetur va- cuum ad me verbum, quod egreditur ex ore meo, Esa. LV. 11. Spiritus Sancti libera operatio, quia plerumque occulta, non plane desperanda, si non sentiamus sacri ministerii profectum. Uti verbi ministri quandoque soliciti sint, sed hic non sensi- bus, sed promissioni Dei credamus, eoq; acquie- scamus. Nescit tarda molimina Spiritus S. gratia.

## 3:9
Πῶς δύναται ταῦτα γενέσθαι;] It is that of one hesitating.

Latin:

Πῶς δύναται ταῦτα γενέσθαι;] Hæsitantis est.

## 3:10
Vers. 10.

Latin:

Vers. 10.

## 3:10
Σὺ εἶ ὁ διδάσκαλος τῦ Ἰσραήλ;] That notable man among the experts of the law,

Καὶ ταῦτα ᾇ γινώσκεις;] Have you not read what Jeremiah and Ezekiel promised concerning the creating of a new heart in the times of the Messiah? Could God, by breathing into Adam, confer upon him natural life: and will He not be able to confer supernatural life with a better spirit? Are you so fixed in those Pharisaical cleansings of the body that you think of nothing more sublime?

It was not only in the times of the Messiah that a new heart was to be created: for all at all times who wished to enter into the kingdom of God had need of regeneration and renewal. But shall we exclude the Patriarchs and other pious men of the O.T. from the kingdom of God? Or did they enter into the kingdom of God without regeneration? The former is repugnant to the words of Christ, Matt. VIII. v. 11. The latter to this assertion of Christ, John III. vers. 3.

Latin:

Σὺ εἶ ὁ διδάσκαλος τῦ Ἰσραήλ;] Ille insignis inter legis- peritos,

Καὶ ταῦτα ᾇ γινώσκεις;] Non legisti, quæ Jeremias & E- zechiel promiserunt, de corde novo creando Messiæ tem- poribus? Potuit Deus inspirando in Adamum, vitam ei naturalem conferre: & non poterit meliore spiritu conferre vitam supernaturalem? Adeo defixus es in Pharisaicis illis mundationibus corporis, ut nihil sublimius cogites?

Non Messiæ demum temporibus cor novum cre- andum erat: nam regeneratione & renovatione o- pus habuêre omnes omni tempore quicunque in regnum Dei ingredi voluêre. Num vero Patriar- chas, aliosque pios V. T. regno Dei excludemus? aut num sinè regeneratione illi in regnum Dei in- gressi? Prius repugnat verbis Christi Matth. VIII. v. 11. Posterius huic Christi asseverationi, Joh. III. vers. 3.

## 3:11
Vers. 11.

ὃ οἴδαμεν λαλῦμεν] It is a proverbial expression of those testifying to something certainly, which Christ applies to Himself.

ὃ ἑωράκαμεν] I have certainly known the counsel of the Father concerning the changing of the souls of men. See above I. 18.

There is no reason to depart to a figurative expression, since these things can be understood properly, just as the blessed Chemnitius explained them in Harm. c. XXVIII. c. 274; those words, We know and We have seen, properly belong to Christ, as he says in John c. VIII. v. 38: I speak what I have seen with my Father: and Matt.

XI, v. 27. No one knows the Father, except the Son, John I. v. 8. No one has seen God: the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has declared him. For the prophets spoke those things which they learned from the inspiration of the Spirit, and which they heard from revelation: but we testify to what we know, what we have seen. He speaks, however, in the plural, because in John VIII. v. 16 he says: I am not alone, but I, and the Father who sent me. Likewise v. 17. He who sent me is with me, and has not left me alone. And the testimony of two is true. Likewise: The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, Luke IV. v. 12. Chrysostom therefore and Cyril rightly explain the plural number in this passage, just as in John XIV. v. 23. We will come, and will make our abode. And Genesis I. v. 26. Let us make man. This is therefore a notable commendation of this doctrine, both concerning the regeneration of the Spirit and its external ministry: namely, that it was decreed in the secret counsel of the divinity, and announced through the Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, conscious of and the interpreter of all the secrets of the divinity.

8 λαμβάνετε] You and your other colleagues and countrymen do not fully admit it into your minds.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

ὃ οἴδαμεν λαλῦμεν] Est proverbialis locutio certo aliquid testantium, quam Christus sibi applicat.

ὃ ἑωράκαμεν] Certo cognovi consilium Patris de mutan- dis hominum animis. Vide supra I. 18.

Non est, ut ad figuratam loquutionem abeamus, quum proprie intelligi hæc possint, quemadmo- dum ea B. Chemnitius Harm. c. XXVIII. c. 274. ex- posuit; Verba illa,Scimus & Vidimus, Christo pro- prie conveniunt, sicut inquit Joh. c. VIII. v. 38. Ego quæ vidi apud Patrem meum, loquor: & Matth.

XI, v. 27. Nemo novit Patrem, nisi Filius, Joh. I. v. 8. Nemo Deum vidit: unigenitus Filius, qui in sinu Patris est, ipse enarravit. Prophetæ enim ea, quæ ex afflatu Spiritus didicerunt, & quæ ex revela- tione audiverunt, locuti sunt: sed nos, quæ scimus, quæ vidimus, testamur. Loquitur autem plurali- ter, quia Joh. VIII. v. 16. inquit: Non sum solus, sed ego, & qui misit me Pater. Item v. 17. Qui mi- sit me, mecum est, & non reliquit me solum. Et duorum testimonium verum est. Item: Spiritus Domini super me, Luc. IV. v. 12. Chrysostomus er- go & Cyrillus recte hoc loco pluralem numerum ex- ponunt, sicut Joh. XIV. v. 23. Veniemus, & mansio- nem faciemus. Et Genes. I. v. 26. Faciamus homi- nem. Insignis ergo hæc commendatio est hujus doctri- næ, & de regeneratione Spiritus, & de externo ejus ministerio: quod scilicet in arcano divinitatis consi- lio decreta, & per Filium, qui in sinu Patris omnium secretorum divinitatis conscius est & interpres, e- nunciata est.

8 λαμβάνετε] Non penitus in animum admittitis vos a- liique Collegæ & populares vestri.

## 3:12
Vers. 12.

εἰ τὰ ἐπίγεια εἶπον ὑμῖν] If I have explained the matter to you by a comparison of things which we experience daily, namely natural birth and the wind. Thus to speak κατ' ἄνθρωπον in Gal. III. 15 is to take similitudes from human affairs.

καὶ ὁ πιστεύετε] And not even then do you understand me, adapting myself to you, as above II, 22.

ἐὰν εἴπω ὑμῖν τὰ ἐπεράνια] With the figures removed, the language of Angels.

Grotius refers these to the manner of proposing: but τὰ ἐπίγεια, καὶ τὰ ἐπεράνια do not indicate the manner of proposing, but the things themselves which are proposed. And therefore it should be believed that earthly things are rather compared with heavenly things, with Chrysostom and Cyril; those things which concern us on earth, with those which pertain to the mysteries of the Trinity in the heavens: because those things which concern our carnal generation and spiritual regeneration are not by far as sublime and as abstruse (speaking comparatively) as those super-celestial mysteries concerning the divine essence and the persons or distinct hypostases in the same: concerning which he now brings forward certain things in the following, as if for the sake of example, concerning the Son of God, his descent from the heavens, and existence in the heavens while he was acting on earth, and also his ascension into heaven and how the Father gave his only-begotten Son to the world, and likewise how he willed the same to be exalted on the cross for the sake of our life and salvation: which present the foundation and the meritorious cause at the same time of our regeneration and entry into the kingdom of God.

Latin:

Vers. 12.

εἰ τὰ ἐπίγεια εἶπον ὑμῖν] Si rem vobis explicavi compa- ratione rerum quas quotidie experimur, nempe naturalis nativitatis & venti. Sic κατ' ἄνθρωπον λέγειν Gal. III. 15. est similitudines sumere à rebus humanis.

καὶ ὁ πιστεύετε] Et ne sic quidem aptantem me vobis in- telligitis, ut supra II, 22.

ἐὰν εἴπω ὑμῖν τὰ ἐπεράνια] Remotis figuris, lingua An- gelorum.

Refert hæc Grotius ad modum proponendi: at τὰ ἐπίγεια, καὶ τὰ ἐπεράνια non modum proponen- di, sed res ipsas, quæ proponuntur, indicant. Ideo- que componi potius terrena cum cælestibus, cum Chrysostomo & Cyrillo, credendum; ea quæ nos in terris concernunt, cum illis, quæ SS. Trinitatis mysteria in cœlis attinent: quia quæ carnalem no- stram generationem & spiritualem regenerationem concernunt longe tam sublimia, tamque abstrusa non sunt, (comparate loquendo) quam illa super- cælestia mysteria de divina essentia & personis vel hypostasibus distinctis in eadem: de quibus in se- quentibus quædam jam, veluti exempli causa, profert, de Filio Dei, ejus è cælis descensu, & exi- stentia in cælis, cum in terris ageret, nec non ascensu in cælum & quomodo Pater Filium suum unigeni- tum mundo dederit, quomodo item eundem in cruce exaltari, vitæ ac salutis nostræ causa voluerit: quæ fundamentum, & causam meritoriam simul exhi- bent regenerationis nostræ, & introitus in re- gnum Dei.

## 3:13
Vers. 13.

ἐδεὶς ἀναβέβηκεν εἰς τὸν ἐρανὸν] He is said to ascend into heaven who penetrates the secrets of heaven, Prov. XXX. v. 3. As far as heaven is distant from the earth, so far are divine counsels from human ones, Isa. LV. v. 9. That which is near us, obvious, plain, known, is said not to be in heaven, so that one must ascend to it, Deut. XXX, 12. Rom. X, 6. Thus, generally, to enter into the sanctuary is taken, Ps. LXXIII. 17.

ὅ ἐκ τῷ ἐρανῦ καταβὰς] Who has been granted to us by the singular gift of God, as below VI. 58. Jas. I. 17. III. 15. 17. Thus 1 Cor. XV. 47. the second man, the Lord from heaven. Thus the baptism of John is from heaven, Matt. XXI. v. 25. Jerusalem, which descends from heaven, Rev. III. v. 12. ch. XXI. 2. 10. Tertullian in the Apologeticus: Your law has erred: I think it was conceived by man, for it did not fall from heaven. Arnob. b. VII. Hear, I desire something to have fallen from heaven.

ὁ ὢν ἐν τῷ ἐρανῷ] If the πολίτευμα, that is, the conversation of Christians is said to be in heaven, how much more so that of Christ, who always looked into the inmost parts of the Father? Thus above c. I. 18. ὁ ὢν εἰς τὸν κόλπον τῦ πατρός. See what is there.

Although there are not wanting those who explain these things metaphorically: yet because one should not depart from the literal meaning without cause, and it is sufficiently known from other places of Scripture what is understood by the ascent of the Son of Man into heaven, and what by the descent from heaven, and A little later, concerning the gift of the only-begotten Son of God, it is discussed; deservedly these things are explained in their proper and received sense, along with most interpreters, Augustine l. 1 de peccat. c. 31, Chrysostom, Theophylact, Bede, Rupert, and others, namely that no one ascends into heaven by their own virtue, except that Son of man Dan. VII. 14, by whose merit and virtue it is necessary for those to ascend who ought to enter into heaven: inasmuch as he is not a mere man, but the Lord from heaven, 1 Cor. XV. 47, and descended from heaven for us men and for the sake of our salvation, whom God gave to the world as his only-begotten Son out of mere love and grace, so that to all who believe in him, access to heaven might be opened through him; who neither ascend without him, and through faith in him are one with him 1 Cor. VI. 17. And thus, with him ascending and having entered into heaven, they are seated with him in the heavenly places, Eph. II. v. 6, whence they have need of regeneration, by which they may become one with Christ through faith, who wish to ascend into heaven, so that his righteousness may be imputed to them, and by the same they may enter heaven itself. The same Son of man, even though he was on earth, dealing with Nicodemus, as far as the property of human nature and visible local presence is concerned: yet he was truly in heaven then, as far as the communion of heavenly and divine majesty is concerned, by which he had the whole fullness of divinity dwelling in him, Col. II. v. 9, and as far as his illocal presence ἐν αὐτῷ τῷ λόγῳ, by virtue of the hypostatic union, because there is one and the same hypostasis of the human and divine nature, and it is present ἀδιαστάτως to the human and divine nature, so that where the divine nature is, there also the human must necessarily be present inseparably, which together with the same constitutes one ὑφιστάμενον. Nor indeed is ascending into heaven, Deut. XXX. 12, or even Prov. XXX. v. 3, to penetrate the secrets of heaven, but in the former place it is taken properly, that there is no need for an ascent into heaven so that we may know the will of God, since his word is near to us: in the latter, however, by ascent into heaven and descent from heaven, the omnipresence of God is designated, who fills heaven and earth no less by divine ἀδιαστασία than by divine ἐνεργείᾳ; for God is present here and everywhere powerfully, Jer. 23, 24.

Latin:

Vers. 13.

ἐδεὶς ἀναβέβηκεν εἰς τὸν ἐρανὸν] Ascendere in cælum di- citur, qui arcana cæli penetrat, Prov. XXX. v. 3. Quantum cælum à terra distat, tantum consilia divina ab humanis, Esa. LV. v. 9. Quod prope nos est, obvium, planum, co- gnitum, id dicitur non esse in cœlo, ut eo sit ascendendum, Deut. XXX, 12. Rom. X, 6. Sic ferme ingredi in sanctua- rium sumitur, Psal. LXXIII. 17.

ὅ ἐκ τῷ ἐρανῦ καταβὰς] Qui singulari Dei dono nobis concessus est, ut infra VI. 58. Jac. I. 17. III. 15. 17. Sic 1. Cor. XV. 47. ὁ δεύτερος ἄνθρωπος, ὁ κύριος ἐξ ἐρανῦ.
