Sic Johan- nis baptisma ex cœlo, Matth. XXI. v. 25. Jerusalem, quæ descendit ex cœlo, Apoc. III. v. 12. c. XXI. 2. 10. Tertul- lianus in Apologetico: Lex tua erravit: puto ab homine concepta est, neque enim de cœlo ruit. Arnob. l, VII. Au- dite, desidero cælo aliquid lapsum.

ὁ ὢν ἐν τῷ ἐρανῷ] Si Christianorum πολίτευμα, id est, con- versatio dicitur esse in cœlo, quanto magis Christi, qui sem- per introspexit Patris intima? Sic supra c. I. 18. ὁ ὢν εἰς τὸν κόλπον τῦ πατρός. Vide quæ ibi.

Etsi non desint, qui Metaphorice ista ita expli- cent: quia tamen non est citra causam disceden- dum à proprietate literæ, & satis ex scripturæ aliis locis notum est, quid per ascensum Filii hominis in cælum, quid per descensum è cælis, intelligatur, ac paulo post de donatione Filii Dei unigeniti agi- tur, merito haec sensu proprio & recepto, cum ple- risque Interpretibus, Augustino l. 1. de peccat. c. 31. Chrysostomo, Theophylacto, Beda, Ruperto, aliisque explicantur, quod nempe nemo propria virtute in coelum afcendat, praeter Filium illum hominis Dan. VII. 14. cujus merito & virtute afcendere oportet, qui in coelum ingredi debent: utpote qui non est merus homo, sed Dominus de coelo, 1. Cor. XV. 47. & de coelo descendit propter nos homines & nostrae salutis gratia, quem ceu Filium unigenitum mun- do ex mera dilectione, & gratia dedit Deus, ut omnibus qui in ipsum credunt, per ipsum pateat aditus in coelum; qui nec sine ipso afcendunt, & per fidem in ipsum unum sunt cum eo 1. Cor. VI. 17. & ita ipso afcendente, & ingresso in coelum, cum eodem in coelestibus collocati sunt, Ephes. II. v. 6. unde regeneratione opus habent, quo cum Chri- sto unum fiant per fidem, qui afcendere in coelum volunt, ut ipsius justitia ipsis imputetur, eademque coelum ipsi ingrediantur. Idem Filius hominis etsi in terra erat, cum Nicodemo agens, quantum ad naturae humanae proprietatem & visibilem localem praesentiam: vere tamen in caelo tum erat, quan- tum ad majestatis coelestis & divinae communionem, qua in se habitantem totam divinitatis plenitudi- nem habebat, Col. II. v. 9. & quantum ad illocalem praesentiam ἐν αὐτῷ τῷ λόγῳ, vi unionis hypostati cae, quia una eademq; naturae humanae & divinae est hypostasis, & ἀδιαστάτως adest humanae divinae na- turae, ut, ubi divina est natura, ibi etiam humana, quae cum eadem constituit unum ὑφιστάμενον, in- separabiliter adesse necessum sit. Neq; vero afcen- dere in coelum, Deuter. XXX. 12. aut etiam Prov. XXX. v. 3. est arcana caeli penetrare, sed in priori loco pro- prie accipitur, non opus esse ascensu in caelum, ut voluntatem Dei cognoscamus, quum verbum e- jus prope nobis sit: in posteriori vero per ascensum in coelum & descensum de caelo omnipraesentia Dei de- signatur, qui caelum & terram replet non minus ἀδιαστασία, quam ἐνεργείᾳ divina; Enter praesen- tes Deus hic & ubiq; potenter, Jer. 23, 24.

## 3:14
Vers. 14.

καὶ καθὼς) He continues to say how God was about to effect this new birth of men, not by the mere teaching of JESUS himself, but by such a one, to which he himself was about to provide both an example and a testimony by his own death, so that no just occasion for doubting, either concerning the truth or the possibility, might be left.

ὕψωσε) There is no doubt that Christ is looking back to his cross, in which sense the word ὑψῶσαι is also found below in chapter VIII. 28 and XII. 32, 34. That serpent was set up, as the history of Moses speaks, על-נס Num. XXI. 8, 9. That נס, however, Rabbi Solomon interprets as פרק, a fork. And what is here in Syriac for ὑψῶν is רים, which Kimchi interprets as זקף, whence comes the word זקיפה, which signifies a cross to the Syrians. Justin in his 2nd Apology writes: λαβὼν τὸν Μωσέα χαλκὸν καὶ ποιῆσαι τύπον σταυρᾶ, κ᾿ τῦτον στῆσαι ἐπὶ τῇ ἁγίᾳ σκήνῃ.

τὸν ὄφιν) That is, the salutary image of a serpent, a harmful creature. Thus Christ without sin, in the likeness of sinful flesh, Rom. VIII. v. 3, nay even numbered among the wicked, Mark XV. 28, Luke XXII. v. 37, from the serpent of disease, medicine through a serpent, through man sin and death, through man justification and resurrection, Rom. V. v. 18, 1 Cor. XV. v. 21. Concerning this serpent of Moses, Philo in his book περὶ γεωργίας brings forward these things, which you may best adapt to Christ: Τῦ Μωσέως ὄφιν (φαμεν) τῆς ἡδονῆς ἐναντίαν διάθεσιν, καρτερίαν παρ᾿ ὃ κὴ τῆς χαλκᾶ κραταιοτέρας ὕλης κατεσκευασμένον εἰσάγεται. τὸ γὰρ ἄκρως καταθεασάμενον τὸ τῆς καρτερίας εἶδος κ᾿ ἂν οἱ δεδηγμένοι πρότερον ὑπὸ τῶν φίλτρων, ἡδονῆς τυγχάνοι, ζῆν ἀναγκαῖον. ἡ μὲν γὰρ ἐπανατείνεται ψυχῇ θάνατον ἀπαραίτητον, ἐγκράτεια δὲ ὑγείαν καὶ σωτηρίαν προτείνῃ βία. ἀντιπαθὲς δὲ ἀκολασίας φάρμακον κὴ ἀλεξίκακον σωφροσύνη. What we said, that this bronze serpent (for such it was made, so that I might the more prefer that which refers to the color of bronze) bore the image of Christ in this, that it was other than it appeared, Justin rightly noted against Trypho, speaking thus concerning that serpent: ἀναίτιός ἐσιν ἀδικίας. It is to be noted, however, so that its power may be more consistent with the comparison, that the sight of the serpent was indeed the condition and way to salvation, but the salutary power was properly from divine grace. The Hebrew Sage XVI. 5, 6, 7: καὶ γὰρ ὅτε αὐτοῖς δεινὸς ἐπῆλθε θηρίων θυμὸς, δαγμασι τε σκολιῶν διεφθείροντο ὄφεων, ἢ μέχρι τέλους ἔμεινεν ἡ ὀργὴ σε, ὡς νυθεσίαν δὲ πρὸς ὀλίγον ἐταράχθησαν, σύμβολον ἔχοντες σωτηρίας εἰς ἀνάμνησιν ἐντολῆς νόμῳ σου, ὁ γὰρ ἐπιστραφεὶς, ὐ διὰ τὸ θεωρούμενον ἐσώζετο, ἀλλὰ διὰ σὲ τὸν πάντων σωτῆρα. Ἐν τῇ ἐρήμῳ) In this vast place, full of poison, in which is the figure of the world in the times of Christ, which was most corrupt. Οὕτως) With a similar effect: which is explained in the following clause.

Ὑψωθῆναι) On the cross, as we have already shown. Δεῖ) By the decree of the Father. We have the same thing on this matter in Matt. XXVI. 54, Mark VIII. 32, Luke IX. 22, XVII. 25, XXIV. 6, XXVI. 54, below XII. 34, and elsewhere. τὸν υἱὸν τῆ ἀνθρώπε) A man indeed, but an innocent one. This gloss concerning the end and fruit of the death of Christ is Socinian. It does not sound of testimony, nor of example, but of the merit of Christ: because he did not suffer and was not exalted on the cross for us for the sake of testimony or example; but so that he might satisfy for us, and acquire eternal life for us. For in his cross is our salvation: in his death our life. And that type tends to this. For through Christ's suspension on the cross, medicine, salvation, and life come to us meritoriously. Which Grotius himself asserted against Socinus in his tract on the satisfaction of Christ, opposed to the same. Concerning the word ὕψωσις, we approve what Grotius has. Moreover, that euphemism of John, by which he uses the suspension of the cross, or rather of Christ himself, seems to have been employed also because through it Christ was exalted on the cross, even if beyond the intention of the Jews; since he became the Savior of the world, and entered into his glory through his passion.

Latin:

Vers. 14.

καὶ καθὼς) Pergit dicere, quomodo novam hanc homi- num nativitatem effecturus esset Deus, non nudo ipsius JESU dogmate, sed tali, cui & exemplum, & testimonium ipse sua morte esset praebiturus, ne qua justa relinqueretur, aut de veritate, aut de possibilitate, dubitandi occasio.

ὕψωσε) Dubitandum non est, quin Christus ad crucem suam respiciat, quo sensu vox ὑψῶσαι & infra reperitur cap. VIII. 28. & XII. 32. 34. Impositus est serpens ille, ut Mosis historia loquitur, על-נס Num. XXI. 8. 9. Illud autem נס Rabbi Salomo interpretatur פרק furcam. Et quod hic in Syriaco est pro ὑψῶν רים, id Kimchi interpretatur זקף unde est vox זקיפה quae crucem Syris significat. Justi- nus Apologetico 2. scribit λαβὼν τὸν Μωσέα χαλκὸν καὶ ποιή- σαι τύπον σταυρᾶ, κ᾿ τῦτον στῆσαι ἐπὶ τῇ ἁγίᾳ σκήνῃ.

τὸν ὄφιν) Id est, effigiem serpentis salutarem, animan- tis noxii. Sic Christus sine peccato, in similitudine carnis peccati, Rom. VIII. v. 3. imo & annumeratus improbis, Marc. XV. 28. Luc. XXII. v. 37. ex serpente morbi, per ser- pentem medicina, per hominem peccatum & mors, per hominem justificatio & resurrectio, Rom. V. v. 18. 1. Cor. XV. v. 21. De hoc serpente Mosis Philo lib. περὶ γεωργίας haec adfert, quae ad Christum optime aptes: Τῦ Μωσέως ὄφιν (φαμεν) τῆς ἡδονῆς ἐναντίαν διάθεσιν, καρτερίαν παρ᾿ ὃ κὴ τῆς χαλκᾶ κραταιοτέρας ὕλης κατεσκευασμένον εἰσάγεται. τὸ γὰρ ἄκρως καταθεασάμενον τὸ τῆς καρτερίας εἶδος κ᾿ ἂν οἱ δεδη- γμένοι πρότερον ὑπὸ τῶν φίλτρων, ἡδονῆς τυγχάνοι, ζῆν ἀ- ναγκαῖον. ἡ μὲν γὰρ ἐπανατείνεται ψυχῇ θάνατον ἀπαραίτητον, ἐγκράτεια δὲ ὑγείαν καὶ σωτηρίαν προτείνῃ βία. ἀντιπαθὲς δὲ ἀκολασίας φάρμακον κὴ ἀλεξίκακον σωφροσύνη. Quod di- ximus serpentem hunc aeneum (talis enim factus erat quo magis praeferrem qui aeri concolor referret) in eo Christi gessisse imaginem, quod alius erat quam videbatur, recte notavit adversus Tryphonem Justinus de eo serpente sic loquens: ἀναίτιός ἐσιν ἀδικίας. Notandum autem quo ma- gis vis sua comparationi constet, adspectum quidem ser- pentis fuisse conditionem & viam ad salutem, vim autem salutarem proprie fuisse a divina gratia. Sapiens Hebraeus XVI. 5. 6. 7. καὶ γὰρ ὅτε αὐτοῖς δεινὸς ἐπῆλθε θηρίων θυμὸς, δαγμασι τε σκολιῶν διεφθείροντο ὄφεων, ἢ μέχρι τέλους ἔμεινεν ἡ ὀργὴ σε, ὡς νυθεσίαν δὲ πρὸς ὀλίγον ἐταράχθησαν, σύμβολον ἔχοντες σωτηρίας εἰς ἀνάμνησιν ἐντολῆς νόμῳ σου, ὁ γὰρ ἐπιστραφεὶς, ὐ διὰ τὸ θεωρούμενον ἐσώζετο, ἀλλὰ διὰ σὲ τὸν πάντων σωτῆρα. Ἐν τῇ ἐρήμῳ) In hoc loco vasto, pleno veneni, in quo figura mundi Christi temporibus corruptissimi. Οὕτως) Simili effectu: quod sequens commate explicatur.

Ὑψωθῆναι) In cruce ut jam ostendimus, Δεῖ) Patris decreto. Eadem nos hac de re apud Matth. XXVI. 54. Marc. VIII. 32. Luc. IX. 22. XVII. 25. XXIV. 6. XXVI. 54. infra XII. 34. & alibi. τὸν υἱὸν τῆ ἀνθρώπε) Hominem quidem, sed innocentem. Sociniana est haec glossa de fine & fructu mortis Christi. Non de testimonio, non de exemplo, sed de merito Christi haec sonat: quia non passus & exaltatus est in cruce pro nobis testimonii aut exempli causa; sed ut satisfaceret pro nobis, & vitam nobis acquireret aeternam. In ejus enim cruce nostra est salus: in ejus morte nostra vita. Atq; huc tendit typus ille. Per Christi enim suspensionem in cruce medicina, salus, & vita nobis obtingit meritorie. Quod Grotius ipse contra Socinum tract. de satisfact. Christi eidem opposito asseruit. De voce ὕψωσις probamus, quae habet Grotius. Caeterum Euphemismus ille Johannis, quo de crucis suspensio utitur, vel potius ipsius Christi, videtur etiam ideo adhibitus, quia per illam in cruce exaltatus est Christus, etsi praeter intentionem Judaeorum; quum factus sit mundi Salvator, & gloriam suam ingressus per passionem sit.

## 3:15
V. 15. ἵνα πᾶς He continues to explain the causes of the Decree already indicated. ὁ πιστεύων εἰς ἀυτὸν: Not in any way whatsoever, but with faith and trust admitted deeply into the heart: for such things as are necessary for eternal life follow of themselves from it. However, these things are to be understood concerning the believer as is fitting, in the way and for as long as he is such. Concerning these matters, we have previously handed down these things in the Utterances of the mouth of the Lord. Responding to Nicodemus, who was repeating nothing but his 'How? How?', Christ dealt with him, as with a most eager disciple of instruction and salvation, in three ways: (1) He gravely reproved his ignorance and unbelief: 'Are you the teacher of Israel?' ὁ διδάσκαλος τῆ Ἰσραὴλ κατ' ἀντονομασίαν, that man who teaches all of Israel, and the most learned of any in the Israelite people, and do you not know this? All teachers in Israel were bound to set forth to others the mystery concerning carnal generation, spiritual regeneration, and heavenly salvation, and to explain the prophecies of the Prophets, among which were primarily those handed down concerning Baptism, read in Ezek. XXXVI. 35, Zech. XIII. 1. Whence this ignorance was deservedly reproved, although it seems to be the voice of one grieving rather than of one harshly reproving. For he grieves that the matter in Israel has been brought to such a point that even the highest Rabbis are ignorant of such necessary dogmas. Whence Chrysostom, Euthymius, and Theophylact say that Christ argued not the malice, but the simplicity of Nicodemus. Moreover, he adds a repeated confirmation, 'Amen, Amen I say to you, because we speak what we know, and we testify what we have seen, and you do not receive our testimony.' For the third time he repeats his Amen, so that he may refute the 'how' of Nicodemite unbelief. Moreover, he joins with himself the Holy Spirit who had descended upon him in Baptism and by whom he had been anointed, or even at the same time God the Father, who was not leaving him alone, John VIII. 16. Therefore he speaks in the plural, 'what we know, we speak,' etc., to indicate the mystery of the divine persons. As the blessed Luther rightly observes in his commentary on Gen. XXXV. (1) because an enallage of number is not to be invented, as Enjedinus wishes, and Calixtus, who follows his lead, where no pregnant cause for the same can be given. (2) Christ wished to oppose the testimony of several persons many Pharisees rejecting these things. (3) He was accustomed thus to join Himself with the Father in testimony, Joh. VIII. 16, 18, and to appeal to the testimony of the Holy Spirit, Joh. XV. 26. (4) These are the witnesses in heaven, or heavenly ones, who bear testimony in the cause of our salvation, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit, 1 Joh. V. v. 7. What therefore prevents us from believing that they are designated by these? (5) They are accustomed to be joined elsewhere, as similar passages of plural expression are a proof, Gen. I. 26, c. III. 22, c. XI. 7, Esa. VI. 9, XLI. 21, seqq. (6) That eternal vision belongs peculiarly to the Holy Spirit likewise and to the Son, Joh. V. 19, and ακουσ. XVI. 13. But if you should say that it does not befit the Father or the first person, those words could be accepted as a certain γνωμη, because the testimony is made only concerning things known, which are just as certain as those which we see with our eyes; indeed, since all things are most known to God and are most clearly perceived in His eternal vision and intuition, why should we not say that the Father also saw these things from eternity? To know and to speak certainly befits all the persons of the Holy Trinity. (7) Thus the Ancients explain it. St. Cyril on this passage says that because the Savior naturally has the Father and the Holy Spirit in Himself, He brought forth the persons of those testifying in the plural number. Chrysostom, Euthymius, Rupert, etc., agree with him. (8) If you depart from this interpretation, you will have nothing certain. Some say that Christ joined Himself with the other Prophets and with John, but because He spoke here with supreme authority: Amen, Amen I say to you, He is not to be considered to have joined Himself with others. Others wish to speak in the plural for the sake of authority. But this is altogether unusual for Christ, as Maldonado observes. He therefore wishes Him to speak Himself, generally concerning all good witnesses and concerning the whole subject matter of similar testimonies, that is, we are not accustomed to testify except to what we know and have seen. And therefore you should believe that I know this for certain, but that is equally unusual. We acquiesce, therefore, in the explanation of the Ancients. Christ thus meets this incredulity of Nicodemus in such a way that He simultaneously insinuates a more sublime mystery and recalls Nicodemus from earthly to heavenly things. If I have told you earthly things, and you do not believe. He joins the other unbelievers also with Nicodemus. But some, as Chrysostom notes, judge "earthly things" to be spoken of the wind, in this way: if you do not believe an example taken from earthly things, how will you believe higher things? But Chrysostom understands the passage concerning Baptism more correctly, whether because it is performed on earth, or because he so designates it in comparison to the ineffable nature of His own generation; likewise Origen, Ammonius, Cyril, Euthymius, and Augustine: The sense, therefore, is, if you do not believe the earthly things and those which have been ordained on earth for the sake of your salvation, and which are easily accessible, such as was Baptism, when ordained by God with the Word and the Ministry, which three are said to bear witness on earth, 1 John 5:8, how much less will you believe if I tell you of the heavenly, sublime mysteries concerning those who bear witness in heaven, 1 John 5:7? However, He did not say, you do not understand, but you do not believe. For indeed, as Chrysostom observes, he who does not understand things difficult to the intellect is deservedly accused of ignorance, but he who does not accept things that are understood not by reason but by faith is convicted no longer of stupidity but of incredulity.

(II.) He brings forward the heavenly mystery concerning the Son of man, in order to set forth the meritorious cause of regeneration, and no one has ascended into heaven, etc. Truly this is a heavenly mystery, because here are things merely heavenly; the descent from heaven, the ascent into heaven, the presence of the Son of man in heaven. And thus all things cohere most excellently. For not only is an example of heavenly mysteries brought forward, but also the foundation of our regeneration is set forth, and the approach to the kingdom of heaven through Baptism. No one has ascended into heaven by his own power; only the Son of man, who descended from heaven for the sake of our salvation, ascended into heaven after the work of redemption was accomplished, and thus was able to open it by his own merit; because he is not a mere man, but as the Son of man he possesses the divine majesty and glory communicated to him, so that by the power of the same, while he was acting on earth, he was present in heaven and endowed with heavenly glory at the same time. Chrysost. Theophyl. & Euthymius wishes the second verse to be considered here, so that Christ may show that He excels the Prophets by a great kind of distinction. Maldonatus renders this connection: since it is necessary to know the divine mysteries, through faith in which you may arrive at salvation, you cannot know them from any other than from Me, because no one has ascended into heaven, etc., which he illustrates with the Hebrew phrase, "Who has ascended into heaven?" that is, "Who can know divine things?" Deut. XXX. 11, so that the sense is: No one can penetrate to those things which are heavenly except Him who descended from heaven. As Junius, Heinsius, and indeed even Chemnitius explain it. But Augustine, and with him Bede, more correctly mark it as a confirmation of the preceding: That whoever wishes to enter into heaven must become one with the Son of Man, that is, a member of Him, which happens when one is reborn of water and the Spirit. See August. l. de Peccat. Merit. & Remiss. c. 31. & Tr. 12. in Joh.

Expendendum autem hic (1) Syncategorema, Nemo: by which it is designated that no mortal has ever ascended by his own power; Enoch indeed ascended, Elijah ascended into heaven, but they were translated by divine power, they did not ascend by their own. Although indeed the Angels both ascend and descend Gen. XXVIII. 12, yet that ascension is not majestative, nor meritorious, of which there is discourse here, but it is done for the sake of ministry. That one, however, can be attributed to no one, save to the one and only Son of man, who for us and for our salvation, as is held in the Nicene Creed, descended from heaven.

(II.) The subject is the Son of man, who is said to have descended from heaven, to be in heaven, and to be about to ascend into heaven. But since the Son of man is a concrete term denominated from the human nature, designating his person, in which the divine and human nature concur, the subject must be understood in different ways according to the nature of the different predicates.

The Son of man, therefore, is said to have descended from heaven, not because the human nature was brought down from heaven, as the Valentinians and Apollinarius once invented, as Theophylact testifies: and as the Anabaptists and Schwenckfeldians dream today concerning the flesh of Christ: inasmuch as it was assumed from Mary the θεοτόκω, Luke 1:35, Galatians 4:4. Nor because Christ as man was previously in heaven, through a prior ascent into heaven, which the Socinians imagine, but because the Son of God descended from heaven, and by that very descent was made the Son of man. Whence, on account of the identity of the person and the communication of idioms, the Son of man is said to have descended. Compare Augustine, loc. cit.

Furthermore, the Son of man is said to be about to ascend into heaven not according to the divine nature, which is everywhere by essence, nor according to both, because a true and real ascent does not befit the divine nature, but according to the human nature, according to which he suffered, died, and was buried, and rose again from the dead, and thus ascended into heaven, and sits at the right hand of God.

Finally, the Son of man is said to be in heaven not according to the divine nature only, for this would not be unique, indeed he was never not in the heavens in that way, but also by reason of the human nature, which is truly a wonderful and heavenly mystery. For here is asserted the glory and majesty of the divine nature, which was required not only for a glorious ascent into the heavens, but also for the truly divine work of redemption. Since indeed the Son of man willed to be crucified for the salvation of the whole human race and to be exalted on the cross, so that all might have eternal life through faith in him. Thus, he who was on earth through the infirmity of the flesh, the same was in heaven through the divinity participated by the flesh, as Aug. says, loc. cit. He calls himself the Son of man in all those predicates, because he was comparing himself with other men, and asserts that no one except himself has ascended.

(III) There are three predicates. To Castellio and Enjedinus, this whole sentence is obscure and abrupt, indeed the whole conversation with Nicodemus; but it is no wonder to them, because they are blinded by the spirit of darkness, so that the light itself seems obscure to them; the first predicate is

ἀναβέβηκεν: He ascended into heaven, which is not to be understood as a mental ascent or knowledge of heavenly things, with Junius or Enjedinus, because the propriety of the word itself, which is not to be set aside without cause, as well as the opposition of the descent, and also the comparison of the present in heaven, testifies. For just as he truly descended from heaven, and is truly in heaven, not only mentally, so he also truly ascended into heaven. Nor is it about an ascent made through the hypostatic union, as Maldonatus wishes; for this refers to a descent from heaven rather than an ascent. Nor is it about a rapture of Christ into heaven before the passion and the prophetic office, which the Socinians dream of: since he entered into heaven only once, and that after his passion, Hebr. IX. 12. but about the true and real and unique ascent of Christ into heaven, described in Luke XXIV. and Acts I.: outside of which the Holy Scriptures acknowledge no ascent of Christ. No one has ascended into heaven, says Christ, because hitherto no one has ascended (whence he used the past tense: by which, however, the continuous fruit of the ascent is simultaneously designated) and in such a way no one is to ascend hereafter, with the sole exception of Christ, who by his ascent unlocked heaven for us. The second is καταβὰς: he descended from heaven, which is said of the Son of man, not by reason of regeneration, as Enjedinus foolishly claims, that descending from heaven is explained through the spiritual man, 1 Cor. II. v. 14, so that by descent a heavenly birth is signified, and by ascent the understanding of heavenly things. Which gloss agrees neither with the words nor with the matter. Since, just as Christ was not reborn, there is no doubt that many were reborn before Christ. Nor (2) by reason of a local descent from heaven, from where he had previously been assumed, just as he is read to have descended from a mountain; but by reason of the incarnation, namely that through the descent the Son of man was made the Son of God, and he descended from heaven, not by changing place, but by assuming human flesh on earth, and manifesting himself in it. For God is said to descend from heaven when he manifests himself on earth, Gen. II. 6, ch. XVIII. 31, Exod. XIX. 18. But this is a most significant Φανέρωσις, which was made in the incarnation, 1 Tim. III. 16, 1 John I. 2, ch. III. 5, 8. Just as the incarnation is also described through an exit from God, John XIII. 3, ch. XVI. 28, ch. XVII. 8. Nor, however, do we deny that an emptying is also designated, inasmuch as it is joined to the incarnation. The third predicate is, ὁ ὢν ἐν ὀυρανῷ. Which the Socinians wish to be rendered, who was in heaven, but it must be rendered, by the force of grammar, in the present, who is in heaven, since Christ intends this, that the Son of man was then in heaven, while he was acting here on earth with Nicodemus, as the words themselves sound. Which, however, is not to be understood with the Zwinglians through Alloeosis concerning the divine nature, nor with Enjedinus concerning the enjoyment of the knowledge of heavenly things. For that the conversation of the pious is said to be in heaven, Phil. III. v. 20, and we are placed in heavenly places, Eph. II. 6, that is ἀλλότριον here. There the discourse is about mere men, both because they ought to lead a heavenly life and aspire to heaven, and because they have obtained access to the heavenly kingdom in Christ. Here, however, the majesty of Christ is set forth, belonging to him μονοτρόπως & ἐξαιρέτως. ὀὐδεὶς NO ONE. These things, therefore, are proper to him alone, but not common to others. How, therefore, is this to be understood? By reason of the divine glory communicated to Christ, as he is the Son of man, or according to his human nature, which by the force of the personal union possesses divine glory, so that he is also present in heaven ἀδιαςάτως & ἀδιασπάσως. For the flesh is nowhere absent from the λόγῳ after it was assumed into the ὑπόςασιν of the λόγῳ.

(IV.) The confirmation subjoined, which is sought from Moses, and indeed from a most illustrious type, which without doubt was not unknown to the Rabbis, or ought to have been, Num. XXI. 9. inasmuch as from it is proved, not only that the Son of man by his passion, and subsequent ascension, ought to have opened heaven, but the means also is shown, through which access is granted to us, namely Faith in Christ the Son of man, which is not kindled in us except through regeneration. The reason for the type consists in these things: (I) As regards the subject to be saved; just as in the desert all were to be healed who had drawn deadly poison from those fiery serpents, and that on account of rebellion against God, because they were unwilling to be content with the food granted by God: so is designated here partly the fault of men, Apostasy from God: partly the punishment, that we have been made liable to death, through the poison infused by the infernal serpent, when the Protoplasts were not content with the granted fruits of paradise. Furthermore, as the bite of the fiery serpents caused intolerable heat, unquenchable thirst, horrible death, whence they are called burning serpents, Num. XXI. v. 6. ἰόβολοι δράκοντες, Wis. XVI. 20. So also sin brings in a truly intolerable heat, namely the burning of conscience, likewise an unquenchable thirst, on account of the lack of divine consolation, and finally a horrible death, not only temporal, but also infernal, Rom. VI. v. last. That in this way the condition of the subject to be regenerated and saved, of whom he had pronounced, That which is born of the flesh is flesh, had been insinuated by Christ through the present type.

(II.) As to the Remedy brought, that was for the Israelites then the bronze serpent, σωτήριος exalted in the desert: a remedy is prepared for us also through the exaltation of Christ on the cross. Christ is therefore compared with the bronze serpent (I) by reason of form, the form of a serpent was chosen then because a serpent is a vile and despised worm, on account of the state of Christ's emptying, by which he was made most abject, Isa. LIII. I am a worm, he says, and not a man, Ps. XXII. v. 7. then because the serpent is cursed by God, Gen. III. v. 16. Since Christ also was made a curse, Gal. III. v. 13. (II) By reason of matter. A bronze serpent had to be erected, not indeed on account of any power of bronze, since rather, as Rabbi David Kimchi says, such is the nature of glowing bronze, that if anyone bitten by a serpent looks upon it, he dies immediately. But on account of the type, that, just as that one appeared fiery on account of its redness, so Christ had to be scorched on the altar of the cross by the fire of divine wrath, and be purified by his own red blood. Then indeed, just as it is contrary to nature that poison inflicted by a serpent should be removed by bronze material, so it is clearly contrary to human reason that blessing and life should be procured for us through Christ cursed and dying on the wood. Justin observes in his 2nd Apology for the Christians, that Moses made the figure of the cross out of bronze, so that the cross of Christ might be designated, which we leave in its place. But Christ made mention of exaltation, That the serpent was erected and lifted up on high, so that it could be seen by all the people scattered throughout the camp for more than three miles, so also was Christ lifted up on the cross, John 12:32. Since he was suspended there like a miserable worm and a serpent, so that just as there was a common remedy for all the wounded from the one erected serpent: so the common salvation of all might be restored by the death of the one Christ. Cyril of Alexandria beautifully says on this passage: The serpent signifies sin, that cruel thing destructive to man, which was devouring the whole human race, attacking the soul of each one with various bites, and pouring out a manifold poison of wickedness, which had grown so strong that it could not be avoided by us otherwise than by heavenly aid. God the Word was therefore made in the likeness of sinful flesh, that he might condemn sin in the flesh, as it is written, and that to those looking upon him with more intent faith, or with an inquiry into divine doctrines, he might exist as the reconciler of eternal salvation. Augustine, Tractate 12 on John: because in their serpent, death was figured through the image of a serpent. The bite of serpents is lethal, the death of the Lord is vital; the serpent is hung up, so that the serpent may have no power: What is this? Death is hung up, so that death may have no power. Petrus Galatinus, book VI, On the Arcane Truths of the Catholic Faith, chapter XVII, cites Rabbi Simeon Ben Joahi, that the tree on which the bronze serpent was erected had been cut from the tree of life in paradise; but these are Rabbinic wrappings mixed with inventions; the wounding did not come from the tree but from the suspended serpent, and that not only naturally, but supernaturally and miraculously, by the power of divine ordinance, Wisdom 16:6-7. That everything was done as a type of a future thing, whence the sign was ordered to be erected, Numbers 21:4. Therefore Justin challenges Trypho the Jew in the Dialogue, p. 25, to explain another reason for this sign, primarily because Moses had forbidden a likeness to be made, and the Jewish interlocutor acknowledged that no other reason could be given: You have spoken truly, he says, for we have no reason that we can give. For I myself have sometimes asked our teachers about this, but none explained the reason. Which Tertullian urges against the Jews, chapter X. The same Moses again, after the prohibition of any likeness of anything, why did he propose the bronze serpent placed on wood in the habit of one hanging as a salutary spectacle for Israel, at that time when they were being exterminated by serpents after idolatry? except that this pointed to the Lord's cross, by which the serpent, the Devil, was made public, and for everyone injured by such snakes, that is, his angels, salvation was effected by being intent upon the sacraments of Christ's cross from the sinfulness of their offenses. For whoever looked upon it then was freed from the bite of the serpents.

(III) As regards the manner of healing, Christ expresses the same, both by the word of lifting up, and by the subsequent words, That everyone who believes in him may not perish, but have eternal life. For although Christ was truly lifted up on the cross, when he was suspended on the wood, yet not without singular cause did he use the word of lifting up here: namely, so that it might be simultaneously implied how this lifting up on the cross ought to be truly lifted up, which was done through the lifting up into heaven, and the preaching in the whole world. To which John 12:32 also looks. Cyril of Alexandria notes this in book II on John, chapter L. But that the serpent was lifted up on high denoted that the passion of Christ would come into that knowledge, so that, as he himself also had predicted, there is no one who is ignorant that he suffered on the cross. Chrysostom says on this passage, he does not say to be suspended, but to be lifted up. So that it might seem neither ignominious to the hearers nor abhorrent to the figure. But these reasons are not sufficient unless the former ones are joined. Here is signified specifically 1. The nature of faith through the looking at the bronze serpent. For this consists in the fact that we look at Christ suspended for us on the cross: And so, just as looking is by the reception of the species, not by the emission of rays: so also faith, by which we look at Christ, happens by receiving and apprehending Christ and his passion, not indeed by emitting rays of majesty. For faith is the spiritual eye of the soul. Chrysostom explains this elegantly in Homily 26 on John. How can those who believe in the crucified one be saved, since he did not free himself from death? Deservedly, therefore, he brings forward the ancient history. For if the Jews, looking at the image of the bronze serpent, were freed from death, how much greater a benefit will those who believe in the crucified one enjoy. You see how the figure agrees with the truth. There the Jews escaped death, but temporal. Here the faithful escape eternal death. There the suspended serpent healed the strikes of serpents: Here Jesus, affixed to the cross, cured the wounds of the incorporeal serpent. There those looking with bodily eyes obtained bodily health, here they obtained the remission of all sins with incorporeal eyes. There the bronze was suspended in the image of a serpent. Here the Lord's body formed by the Spirit. The serpent there bit and the serpent healed. Here death destroyed and death saved. Furthermore, the serpent that was killing raged with poison, the one that was freeing, with none. Therefore, death destroyed sin, the Lord's death had it as the serpent's poison, all that, just as the bronze serpent took away the poison. Let Athanasius, Tom. II, against those who denied the human nature of Christ, p. 304, be compared.

II. The object of saving faith is the crucifixion and death of Christ for the salvation of the world. Just as its proper and formal act is the apprehension of the same. Just as the object of the Israelites' looking was the serpent lifted up in the desert, the head of all, says Gregory of Nyssa in his Life of Moses, almost near the end, what we believe in this article of the Christian profession is to look with firm and straight faith into the passion of Christ, who suffered for us. The cross indeed is the passion, wherefore he who looks at the cross, as history testifies, the poison of desires cannot harm him. Augustine, book I, On the Merits of Sins, chapter XXXI: What is, he says, the lifted-up serpent, but the death of Christ in that mode of signifying by which that which is effected is signified by the efficient cause. For from the serpent came death, who persuaded man of the sin by which he would deserve to die. The Lord, however, did not transfer sin into his own flesh like the venom of a serpent, but only transferred death, so that he might be in the likeness of sinful flesh, punishment without fault; whence in the flesh of sin both fault and punishment might be loosed. Just as, therefore, then he who looked upon the exalted serpent was both healed from the venom and freed from death. So now he who is conformed to the likeness of Christ's death through faith and his baptism is freed both from sin through justification and from death through resurrection.

(III) The application of faith. For just as the suspended serpent was a common remedy, but did not profit except those who looked upon it. So Christ provided a common remedy of salvation by his meritorious passion, but the application must be made through faith. Nicetas explains this in Oration XLII of Gregory Nazianzen, No. XLIX: We too offend God and fall into the bite of spiritual serpents, which, striking us through every kind of sin, afflicted us with death. But in what way have we obtained salvation? We too have looked upon the serpent on the wood, that is, by gazing upon Christ himself and believing in him, we obtain salvation.

(IV) The power of faith and its cause. Just as the power of healing uniquely depended there for the Israelites upon divine ordination: thus also faith works salvation not because of its own dignity but because of divine ordination. John chap. VI. verse 40. What was then exalted, says Epiphanius in Heresy XXXVII. by Moses, brought about healing through inspection, not because of the nature of the serpent but because of the good will of God, who through the serpent then worked as a remedy for those bitten. And just as in the exaltation of the serpent healing happened to those bitten; so in the Crucifixion of Christ Redemption was made for our souls from the bites of sin inflicted upon us.

(V) The energy of Faith. Salvation must be attributed to the Merit of Christ, which Faith apprehends, however else it may be. Whence also those who are of very weak faith, nonetheless obtain life, because salvation depends not on the quantity, strength, or merit of faith, but on the merit of the death of Christ: Just as those who looked at the bronze serpent with weak, languid, wavering eyes, and eyes swimming in death, recovered no less than the rest who looked with a stronger gaze. Only the sincerity of faith is required; Firmness is not desired, as if weak faith were of no value here. For the power of salvation arises not from faith, but from the object which faith apprehends. To those looking upon him with sincere faith, eternal salvation is generously shown, says Cyril on this passage.

(VI) That salvation is to be claimed for Faith alone without the cooperation of works, we are taught also by this type. For as the mere looking at the serpent, without any work, restored health to the Israelites, so that the serpents entangled in the hands and feet of the sick would fall off, provided they looked at the bronze serpent: so the mere looking of faith, without our works, renders salvation. Ambrosius excellently, and from him the Augsburg Confession, Article 6. This is established by GOD, that he who believes in Christ may be saved without work by faith alone, freely receiving the remission of sins; which truly golden saying must be diligently observed because of the Sophists, Papists, Photinians, and Innovators.

(VII) But as it was necessary for those who neglected the divinely shown means to perish: so it must be that all perish who despise Christ crucified for us, or are offended by the vile appearance of this saving means, 1. Peter chap. I. verse 7. 8.

(VIII) Finally, as the healed were led into the Land of Canaan, in which they were immune from the bites of the fiery serpents: So there will be no more fear, no danger from the infernal serpent in the land of the heavenly promise, into which we are led, justified by faith through Christ, Apocal. XXI. 4.

And thus the Doctors commonly explain this type. Yet Tertullian, in the book on Idolatry, chap. 5, insinuates that another reason for the same can be given, which Greg. Nazianz. exhibits in Oration II. on Easter: But is the bronze serpent suspended against the bites of serpents, not only as a type of Christ who suffered for us, but as an antitype, and does it bring salvation to those who look upon it, while it is believed that he is not enjoying life, but is dead and has destroyed the powers subject to him in the meantime, being indeed oppressed and extinguished as he deserved. Thus, therefore, through the suspended bronze serpent, the Theologian understands the Devil suspended and extinguished through the death of Christ, whose Epitaph he adds in the same place. All of which Nicetas (the Paraphrast of Nazianzen) explains indeed excellently. However, the interpretation of the other Doctors of the Church is simpler and more convenient, by which the suspended serpent is understood not as the Devil extinguished through the cross of Christ, but as Christ himself, exalted on the cross, since Christ himself makes the same type of his exaltation on the cross, and the proper object of faith is not the extinction of the Devil, but the crucifixion of Christ, by which same thing sin was expiated and the tyranny of the Devil extinguished.

The following lessons of this Pericope can be noted. (I) There are two principles of error in matters of faith. (a) ignorance of scripture, which Christ reproaches the Sadducees with: You err, not knowing the Scriptures, Matth. XXII. verse 29. (β) unbelief, that faith is not applied to those things which have been handed down in the scriptures, John III. v. 12. Let Is. LIII. 1, Rom. X. 16, 1. Peter II. 8 be compared. (II) The knowledge not only of original sin, but also of heavenly regeneration and the satisfactory merit of Christ, was incumbent upon the Israelites in the Old Testament, because they obtained salvation by the same faith as we, Acts XV. 11, Ephes. IV. 6. Hence the Master in Israel is rebuked, because while he ought to have taught others these things, he himself was ignorant of them. (III) Plural expressions used about GOD designate the mystery of the plurality of persons in GOD, and since they occur here and there in the Old Testament, therefore it is undoubted that in the Old Testament this mystery was also proposed. See B. Luther, Commentary on Genesis chap. XXXV. and our disputation on the plurality of divine persons. (IV) The remarkable love of mankind of GOD is to be noted, that the persons of the divine Sacrosanct Trinity wished to take the place of witnesses concerning our eternal salvation, so that we might not disdain to believe the mysteries of faith. For the Father testifies here and there in the Old Testament, the Son especially in the New Testament in the days of his flesh, the Holy Spirit has testified by the inspiration of both Testaments, made to the Prophets and Apostles, testifies through the scriptures, and seals that testimony in hearts like a pledge, 1. Corinth. I. v. last. The whole Sacrosanct Trinity testified in the Baptism of Christ, testifies in our Baptism, and finally testifies in his coming to us and the indwelling of our heart. Hence John appeals to the three witnesses in heaven, in this cause of salvation, 1. John V. v. 7. (V) Earthly are those things which are required on our part, the hearing of the Word & the use of the Sacraments, etc. Although divine effects follow. But divine are those things which on the part of GOD have been conferred and are conferred for salvation, that highest love of GOD, from which He gave the Son of GOD, the coming of the Son from the heavens, the incarnation, passion, death, resurrection, and ascension into the heavens, as also the mission of the Holy Spirit, and His gracious operation. For these are merely divine, to which our works can contribute nothing. (VI) The highest and most eminent Articles of faith are, the descent of the Son of man from heaven, likewise the Majesty and omnipresence of the same in heaven and on earth, as also the glorious ascension into heaven, which it is necessary to believe for salvation, for those who are ignorant of them or deny them, cannot sincerely, and as is fitting, believe the person or office of Christ. (VII) The type of the bronze serpent teaches that the Mystery of universal salvation was proposed to the Israelites clearly enough, and was to be believed by them no less explicitly. Because in that type it was permitted to discern clearly both the state of the subject to be led to salvation, regarding guilt and punishment, and the condition of the remedy, which is prepared in the passion and death of Christ; then the manner of Application, which is done through faith, the nature, force, character, and ἐνέρ- γειαν (energy/operation) of which faith they were insinuating. There is no doubt that all those things were explained to the Israelites by the Doctors. For this figure was proposed to them for this reason, that through faith in Christ, here shadowed forth, they might be saved, and this Salvation, thus shadowed forth to them, might be explained for the sake of confirming faith in the Messiah. Let John V. 39, Rom. X. 4, c. XV. 4, 1 Cor. X. 11 be compared. And who would doubt that the Priests and Prophets, in whom was the Spirit of Christ, 1 Pet. I. 11, handed down to the people that very thing which God intended through this type, and for whose sake He proposed the same, in the same manner as it was done by Christ! For either this was the very intention of God proposing it, which Christ here expounds, or it was another. If another, Christ did not propose it correctly. If it was the same, then it could not but have been handed down by the Spirit of Christ, who was in the holy men of God. Otherwise God would have been in vain, while He proposed the type with the intention that they should believe in the Messiah shadowed forth by the type, and obtain salvation. Hence it is that Christ, in his disputation with the Israelite Teacher, assumes as undoubted that that signification of the Type ought to have been certain and most especially perceived by all. (VIII) Our salvation is situated in the suspension of the crucified Christ. Compare 1 Cor. I. 18, 21, 30, ch. II. 2, 7, 2 Cor. V. 5, 21, Rom. V. 18, 19, having instituted a collation with the head Phil. II. 8, Rom. III. 22, seq. If the serpent affixed to the wood conferred health upon the sons of Israel, says Ambrose, Serm. LV, how much more does the Lord, crucified on the gallows, provide salvation to the people! And if the figure profited so much, how much do we believe the truth has profited: Blessed Macarius beautifully says regarding this matter, after he explained this type, Homil. XI, In the dead body there is life, here is Redemption, here is light. Here the Lord approaches death and disputes with it, and commands that it cast out souls from hell and death, and restore them to Him. Behold, death, struck by these things, goes to its ministers, and gathers all the powers and Princes of malice, brings out the Chirographs (handwritings of debt), and says: Behold, here they obeyed my word, Behold how mortals worshipped us? But God, who is a just judge, there shows His justice, saying to it: Adam obeyed you and you obtained from thence his whole heart: Humanity complied with you, but what has my body committed? This is devoid of sin. That body of the first Adam is obligated to you and by right for that reason you obtain his Chirographs. But all bear witness to me that I have not sinned, therefore I am not obligated to you at all, and that I am the Son of God. I redeem, therefore, the body sold to you by the first Adam, I dissolve your Chirographs; for I have satisfied for the debts of Adam (ἀπέδωκα τὰ χρέα τῦ Ἀδὰμ) while I was crucified, and descended into hell. And I command you, Hell, darkness, and Death, send forth the souls of Adam included. And so at length the infernal powers, struck with fear, restore the included Adam. (IX) As from the wood came perdition through the serpent, so from the wood through Christ, shadowed forth in the brazen serpent, came liberation. For dissolving, says Irenaeus l. V, the disobedience which from the beginning was made in the wood, He became obedient even unto death, even the death of the cross, and healing that disobedience made in the wood. (X) One may behold here the Ladder of Heaven: Whose extremes are God the Lord of Heaven, and Man cast down because of sin and precipitated to hell. The matter, from which the ladder consists, is most divine, both the Divine nature of the Son of God, and His Holy Humanity. Form: It is a personal union, or the coupling of the divine and human nature into the unity of a suppositum. Whence arises the unity of the ladder through which the ascent to God lies open. The extreme degrees are the descent from heaven of the Son of God or the incarnation: and the ascent into heaven, or the exaltation. John XVI, 28. The middle ones

Nativity, life, obedience, Passion, Crucifixion, death, burial, descent into hell and Resurrection. The use and end is that we may ascend through the same ladder into heaven, outside and beyond which no access lies open to God, John XIV. 6. The Ladder of Paradise broken in Adam is repaired in Christ, says Bonaventure. The medium by which we are elevated, and the degrees we ascend, is the Word of God extended to us from heaven on the part of God, both audible and visible; through which, on our part, faith is ascended, so that by the same, adhering to the word, they may be drawn in that ladder by God, and being drawn we may arrive in heaven. But Angels ascend and descend upon the same ladder, not that Christ the Mediator was given to them, and through Him access lies open to them into heaven, but because by descending they announce to us heaven opened and join ministers to us on earth, Matt. XVIII. 10, Heb. I. 14. By ascending they also transport us with them into heaven, Luke XVI. 22. All of which things were prefigured in the ladder seen by Jacob, Gen. XXVIII. 12, with Christ as the interpreter, John I. 51. If a collation with this saying, John III. 13, be instituted, so that thus no one truly ascends into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man, who is in heaven, and who through faith is one with the Son of man. 1 Cor. VI. 17. And these things are from our lectures.

Latin:

V. 15. ἵνα πᾶς Decreti jam indicati causas explicare pergit. ὁ πιστεύων εἰς ἀυτὸν: Non quovis modo, sed penitus in cor admissa fide & fiducia: nam talis quae est eam caetera ad vitam aeternam necessaria per se sequuntur. Intelligenda autem haec de credente ut oportet, qua & quamdiu talis est. De his in Eloquiis oris Domini antehac ista tradidimus. Nicodemo nil nisi suum Quomodo? Quomodo? ingeminanti respondens Christus cum eo, ceu informationis, & salutis discipulo cupidissimo, tria egit, (1) Ignorantiam & incredulitatem ipsius graviter reprehendit: Tnne Magister Israel? ὁ διδάσκαλος τῆ Ἰσραὴλ κατ' ἀντονομασίαν ille qui totum Israel docet, & doctissimum quemq; in populo Israelitico, & hoc ignoras? Magistri in Israel universi tenebantur aliis mysterium de carnali generatione, spirituali regeneratione, ac coelesti salute proponere, ac vaticinia Prophetarum, inter quae imprimis erant quae de Baptismo tradita, Ezech. XXXVI. 35. Zach. XIII. 1. leguntur, exponere. Unde merito haec ignorantia redarguebatur, quanquam videatur potius vox dolentis esse, quam acerbe reprehendentis. Dolet enim eo rem perductam esse in Israel, ut summi etiam Rabbini talia tamq; necessaria dogmata ignorent. Unde Chrysostomus, Euthymius, & Theophylactus Christum non malitiam, sed simplicitatem Nicodemi arguiffe ajunt. Addit autem iteratam confirmationem, Amen, Amen dico tibi, quia quod scimus loquimur, & quod vidimus testamur, & testimonium nostrum non accipitis. Tertia vice suum Amen ingeminat, ut τὸ πῶς Nicodemicae incredulitatis refellat. Conjungit autem secum Spiritum S. qui super ipsum in Baptismo descenderat & quo unctus erat, vel etiam simul Deum Patrem, qui eum non solum relinquebat, Joh. VIII. 16. Ideo in plurali ait, quod scimus, loquimur, &c. ad indicandum divinarum personarum mysterium. Ut recte observat B. Lutherus comment. in Gen. XXXV. (1) quia non est fingenda Enallage numeri, ut vult Enjedinus, & qui ei pollicem premit Calixtus, ubi nulla causa praegnans ejusdem dari potest. (2) Opponere Christus voluit plurium personarum testimonium plurib. Pharisaeis ea reprobantibus. (3) Consuevit sic conjungere se cum Patre in testificatione, Joh. VIII.16.18. & ad testimonium Spiritus S. provoca- re, Joh. XV. 16. (4) Hi sunt testes in coelo, vel coe- lestes, qui in causa salutis nostrae testimonium per- hibent, Pater, Verbum, & Spiritus S. 1. Joh. V. v. 7. Quid ergo obstat, quo minus eos his designatos credamus? (5) Conjungi alias illi solent, ut do- cumento sunt loca similia pluralis locutionis, Gen. I. 26. c. III. 22. c. XI. 7. Esa. VI. 9. XLI. 31. seqq. (6) Spiritui S. pariter & Filio competit peculiariter illa aeterna visio, Joh. V. 19. & ακουσ. XVI. 13. Quod si dicas, Patri sive primae personae eam non conve- nire, accipi possent verba illa tanquam γνωμη ali- qua, quod de notis tantum testificatio fiat, quae ae- que certa sunt, ac quae oculis videmus, imo cum Deo omnia notissima & in visione ac intuitu aeter- no perspectissima sint, quidni haec etiam Patrem ab aeterno vidisse dicamus? Scire utiq; & loqui o- mnibus SS. Trinitatis personis competit. (7) Sic explicant Veteres. S. Cyrillus in h. l. quia Salvator Patrem ac Spiritum S. in seipso naturaliter habet, plurali numero personas testantium protulit. Cui annuit Chrysostomus, Euthymius, Rupertus, &c. (8) Ab hac si recedas interpretatione nil certi habebis. Quidam Christum se cum caeteris Pro- phetis & cum Johanne conjunxisse dicunt, sed quia hic ex summa autoritate locutus: Amen, Amen dico vobis, non censendus est, se cum aliis conjun- xisse. Alii Autoritatis gratia pluraliter loqui vo- lunt. Quod vero prorsus insolitum Christo est, sentiente Maldonato. Hic ergo vult loqui ipsum, generaliter de omnibus bonis testibus, & de omni si- milium testimoniorum materia, id est, non solemus testari nisi quae scimus ac vidimus. Ideoq; credas me certo id scire, sed aeque id insolitum est. Acquie- scimus ergo Veterum explicationi. Huic itaque incredulitati Nicodemi sic occurrit Christus, ut simul sublimius mysterium insinuet, & a terrenis ad coelestia Nicodemum revocet. Si terrena dixi vobis, & non creditis. Conjungit cum Nicodemo caeteros quoque incredulos. Terrena autem, no- tante Chrysostomo, nonnulli de vento dicta arbi- trantur, hoc modo, si exemplum a terrenis sum- tum non creditis, quo pacto altiora credetis? Sed rectius de Baptismo intelligit Chrysostomus, sive quod in terra perficiatur, sive quod ad suae ipsius generationis ineffabilis comparationem ita appel- let; ita & Origenes, Ammonius, Cyrillus, Euthym. & Augustinus: Sensus ergo est, si terrena & ea quae in terris salutis vestrae causa ordinata, facileque ob- via, non creditis, qualis erat Baptismus, cum Ver- bo & Ministerio divinitus ordinatus, quae tria in terra testificari dicuntur, 1. Joh. V. v. 8. Quanto minus credetis, si coelestia sublimia mysteria de iis, qui in caelo testificantur, 1. Joh. V. v. 7. vobis dixero? Non autem dixit, non intelligitis, sed non creditis. Siquidem, ut observat Chrysosto- mus, qui intellectu difficilia non intelligit, merito ignorantiae accusatur, qui vero, quae non ratione sed fide intelliguntur, non accipit, non amplius stul- titis sed incredulitatis arguitur.

(II.) Caeleste Mysterium de Filio hominis affert, ut causam regenerationis meritoriam exponat, & nemo ascendit in caelum, &c. Vere hoc coeleste mysterium est, quia hic mere coelestia; Descensus e caelo, ascensus in caelum, praesentia Filii hominis in caelo. Atq; ita omnia cohaerent optime. Non enim tantum exemplum affertur coelestium myste- riorum, sed & fundamentum exponitur nostrae re- generationis, & aditus per Baptismum ad regnum coelorum. Nemo ascendit in caelum propria virtute; solus Filius hominis qui de cœlo descendit nostræ sa- lutis causa, peracto redemptionis opere adscendit in cœlum, adeoq; aperire id merito suo potuit; quia non est merus Homo, sed ceu Filius Hominis divi- nam majestatem & gloriam communicatam pos- sidet, adeo, ut ejusdem vi, cum in terris ageret, in cœlis præsto ac cœlesti gloria simul præditus esset. Chrysoft. Theophyl. & Euthymius respici hic volunt versum secundum, ut monstret Christus magno discriminis genere se Prophetas antecellere. Maldo- natus hanc reddit connexionem, cum necessarium sit divina cognoscere mysteria, per quorum fidem ad salutem perveniatis, non potestis ea ex alio quam ex me cognoscere, quia nemo in cœlum ascendit &c. quod illustrat phrasi Hebræa, quis ascendit in cœlis? id est, quis potest res divinas cognoscere Deut. XXX. 11. ut sensus sit: Neminem ad ea, quæ sunt cœlestia pe- netrare præter eum, qui è cœlo descendit. Uti & Ju- nius, Heinsius, imo & Chemnitius explicat. Sed re- ctius Augustinus, & cum eo Beda confirmationem superiorum signant: Quod quisquis introire velit in cœlum, unum quoddam cum Filio hominis, id est, membrum illius fieri debeat, quod fit cum ex aquâ & Spiritu renascitur. Vid. August. l. de Peccat. Merit. & Remiss. c. 31. & Tr. 12. in Joh.

Expendendum autem hic (1) Syncategorema, Nemo: quo designatur neminem unquam morta- lium adscendisse suapte virtute; Ascendit quidem Enoch, ascendit Elias in cœlum, sed isti translati sunt virtute divina, non ascenderunt propria. Quanquam vero Angeli & ascendant & descendant Gen. XXVIII. 12. ea tamen ascensio non est majesta- tiva, neque meritoria, de qua hic sermo est, sed ministerii causa fit. Illa vero nemini tribui potest, quam uni & soli Filio hominis, qui propter nos & nostram salutem, ut in Symbolo Niceno habetur, descendit è cælo.

(II.) Subjectum Filius hominis est, qui de cælo descendisse, in cælo esse, & in cælum ascensurus di- citur. Cum vero Filius hominis concretum sit à natura humana denominatum sui personam desi- gnans, in qua divina & humana natura concurrunt pro ratione diversorum prædicatorum, diversi- mode subjectum accipiendum erit.

Filius ergo hominis descendisse dicitur de cælo, non quod hu- mana natura de cœlo traducta sit, ut olim Valenti- niani, & Apollinarius commenti sunt, teste Theo- phylacto: & hodie Anabaptistæ & Schwencfeldia- ni de carne Christi somniant: Utpote quæ è Maria θεοτόκω assumpta est Luc. I. 35. Gal. IV. v. 4. Nec quod antea in cælo fuerit Christus qua Homo, per ascensum priorem in cœlum, quem fingunt Soci- nistæ, sed quod Filius Dei de cœlo descenderit, ac ipso descensu Filius hominis factus. Unde propter identitatem personæ ac communicationem idioma- tum Filius hominis descendisse dicitur. Confer. Augustin. loc. cit.

Porro Filius hominis in cœlum ascensurus dicitur non secundum divinam natu- ram, quæ ubiq; est per essentiam, neq; secundum utramq;, quia divinæ naturæ non convenit verus & realis ascensus, sed secundum humanam natu- ram, juxta quam passus, mortuus est, & sepultus, & resurrexit à mortuis, atque ita ascendit in cœ- lum, sedetq; ad dexteram Dei.

Deniq; Filius ho- minis in cælo esse dicitur non secundum divinam tantum naturam, hoc enim singulare non erat, imo ita nunquam non in cœlis fuit, sed ratione hu- manæ etiam naturæ, quod vere est mirabile ac cœ- leste mysterium. Asseritur enim hic gloria & ma- jestas divinæ naturæ, quæ non ad ascensum in cœ- los solum gloriosum, sed & ad opus redemptionis vere divinum requirebatur. Siquidem Filius ho- minis pro salute totius generis humani crucifigi & in cruce exaltari voluit, ut omnes per fidem in ipsum vitam æternam haberent. Ita qui in terra erat per carnis infirmitatem, idem ipse erat in cælo per participatam carni divinitatem, dicente Aug. loc. cit. Dicit autem hic se Filium hominis in omni- bus illis prædicatis eo, quod se cum aliis homini- bus compareret, neminemque præter se ascendisse asserat.

(III) Prædicata tria sunt. Castellioni & Enjedi- no, tota hæc sententia obscura est & abrupta, imo tota collocutio cum Nicodemo; Sed non mirum iis, quia spiritu tenebrarum excæcati sunt, ipsam lucem obscuram videri; primum prædicatum est

ἀναβέβηκεν: Ascendit in cælum, quod non de ascen- su mentali seu cognitione rerum cælestium cum Ju- nio, aut Enjedino accipiendum esse ipsa vocis pro- prietas, quæ citra causam deferenda non est, ut & oppositio descensus, nec non collatio præsentis in cælo testatur. Quemadmodum enim vere de- scendit de cælo, vere in cælo est, non tantum men- taliter, ita & vere ascendit in cælum. Nec de ascen- su per unionem hypostaticam facto, ut Maldonatus vult; hanc enim descensus è cælo refert potius quam ascensus. Nec de raptu Christi in cælum ante pas- sionem & munus propheticum, quem Socinistæ somniant: siquidem non nisi semel in cælum in- gressus sit, idq; post passionem suam, Hebr. IX. 12. sed de ascensu Christi in cælum vero, ac reali eoq; unico, Luc. XXIV. Act. I. descripto: extra quem nullum Christi ascensum agnoscunt sacræ literæ. Nemo ascendit in cælum, inquit Christus, quod hactenus nemo ascenderit (unde præterito verbo usus est: quo tamen simul continuus ascensus fru- ctus designatur) ac taliter nemo ascensurus sit de- inceps, solo excepto Christo, qui suo ascensu cæ- lum nobis reseravit. Secundum, est καταβὰς: de- scendit de cælo, quod de Filio hominis dicitur, non ratione regenerationis, ut ineptit Enjedinus, descen- dere de cælo explicari per hominem spiritualem, 1. Cor. II. v. 14. ut per descensum nativitas cœlestis, per ascensum intellectio rerum cælestium significe- tur. Quæ glossâ, neq; verbis convenit, neque rei. Siquidem ut Christus non fuit renatus, ita ante Christum renatos plurimos fuisse nullum est du- bium. Nec (2) ratione localis è cælo, quo prius as- sumptus fuerit, descensus, quemadmodum de mon- te descendisse legitur; sed ratione incarnationis, quod nempe per descensum Filius hominis factus sit Filius Dei, atque è cælo descendit, non locum mutando, sed carnem humanam in terra assumen- do, inq; ea sese manifestando. Dicitur enim Deus de cælo descendere cum se in terra manifestat, Gen. II. 6. c. XVIII. 31. Exod. XIX. 18. Hæc autem maxi- me insignis est Φανέρωσις, quæ in incarnatione fa- cta, 1. Tim. III. 16. 1. Joh. I. 2. c. III. 5. 8. Quemadmo- dum & incarnatio describitur per exitum a Deo, Joh. XIII. 3. c. XVI. 28. c. XVII. 8. Neq; tamen ne- gamus exinanitionem quoq; designari, utpote quæ incarnationi conjuncta est. Tertium prædicatum est, ὁ ὢν ἐν ὀυρανῷ. Quod Socinistæ reddi volunt, qui erat in cælo, sed reddendum, vi Grammaticæ, in præsenti, qui est in cælo, cum hoc intendat Christ9, Filium hominis tum in cælo fuisse, dum in terris hic ageret cum Nicodemo, ut verba ipsa sonant. Quod vero non intelligendum cum Zwinglianis pet Allæosin de divina natura, neque cum Enjedino de fruitione cognitionis rerum cœlestium. Quod enim piorum conversatio in cælis esse dicitur, Phil. III. v. 20. nosq; collocati in cælestibus, Eph. II. 6. id hic ἀλλότριον est. Ibi de meris hominibus sermo est, tum quod vitam cœlestem agere de- beant, & ad cœlum aspirare, tum quod aditum ad regnum cœleste consecuti fuerint in Christo. Hic vero majestas Christi exponitur, μονοτρόπως & ἐξαιρέτως ipsi conveniens. ὀὐδεὶς NEMO. Hæc ergo ipsi uni propria sunt, non autem aliis com- munia. Quomodo ergo id intelligendum? Ra- tione gloriæ divinæ Christo, ut est Filius hominis, seu secundum humanum naturam communicatæ, quæ vi unionis personalis divinam possidet glo- riam, ut & in cœlo ἀδιαςάτως & ἀδιασπάσως præsto sit. Nuspiam enim caro abest à λόγῳ post- quam in ὑπόςασιν τῷ λόγῳ assumta est.

(IV.) Subjuncta confirmatio, quæ è Mose petita est, & quidem à typo præclarissimo, qui sine dubio Rabbinis non incognitus fuit, aut esse debuit, Num. XXI. 9. utpote è quo probatur, non solum quod Filius hominis passione sua, & subsequente ascensione cœlum debuerit patefacere, sed me- dium etiam ostenditur, per quod aditus nobis conceditur, Fides nempe in Christum Filium ho- minis, quæ non nisi per regenerationem in nobis accenditur. Ratio typi in his consistit: (I) Quan- tum ad subjectum salvandum; quemadmodum in deserto sanandi erant omnes, qui ab ignitis isti serpentibus venenum mortiferum hauserant, id- que propter rebellionem adversus Deum, quod ci- bo divinitus concesso contenti esse nollent: ita designatur hic partim culpa hominum Apostasia à Deo: partim pœna, quod morti obnoxii facti, si- mus, per venenum ab infernali serpente infusum, cum non contenti essent Protoplasti concessis pa- radisi fructibus. Porro ut morsus serpentum igni- torum conciliabat calorem intolerabilem, sitim inexplebilem, mortem horribilem, unde dicuntur serpentes inflammantes, Num. XXI. v. 6. ἰόβολοι δεά- κοντες, Sap. XVI. 20. Ita & peccatum infert calo- rem vere intolerabilem, æstum nempe conscientiæ, sitim item inexplebilem, ob defectum consolatio- nis divinæ, & mortem denique horribilem non temporalem solum, sed & infernalem, Rom. VI. v. ult. Ut hoc pacto insinuata fuerit à Christo, per typum præsentem conditio subjecti regenerandi & salvandi, de quo pronunciarat, Quod ex carne natum est, caro est.

(II.) Quod ad Remedium allatum, id erat Isra- elitis tunc serpens æneus, σωτήριος in deserto ex- altatus: paratum & nobis remedium per exalta- tionem Christi in cruce. Confertur ergo Christus cum serpente æneo (I) ratione formæ, Serpentis forma eligebatur tum quod serpens vilis & con- temptus sit vermis, ob exinanitionis Christi sta- tum, quo factus est abjectissimus, Esa. LIII. Ego vermis, inquiens & non homo, Psal. XXII. v. 7. tum quod serpens maledictus sit à Deo, Gen. III. v. 16. Quandoquidem & Christus sit factus male- dictio, Gal. III. v. 13. (II) Ratione materiæ. Æ- neus erigi debuit serpens non quidem ob vim a- liquam æris, cum potius, ut Rabbi David Kimchi, ea sit æris candentis natura, ut si quis à serpente morsus illud intueatur, actutum moriatur. Sed ob typum, quod, uti ille igneus visus est ob rubedi- nem, sic Christus debuerit in ara crucis igne divi- næ iræ ustulari, ac rubicundo suo sanguine per- purari. Tum vero quemadmodum naturæ adver- sum est, per æneam materiam venenum tolli à ser- pente illatum, ita plane adversum est humanæ ra- tioni, per Christum maledictum ac morientem in ligno nobis benedictionem ac vitam conciliari. Justinus observat Apologia 2. pro Christianis, quod Moses figuram crucis ex ære fecerit, ut scilicet crux Christi designaretur, quod suo loco relinquimus. Christus autem exaltationis mentionem fecit, quod serpens erectus, atque in sublimi exaltatus fuerit, ut ab omni populo per castra ultra tria milliaria diffusa videri potuerit, ita & Christus ex- altatus est in cruce, Joh. XII. 32. Quandoquidem ibi miseri vermiculi ac serpentis instar suspensus fuerit, ut quemadmodum commune remedium erat ab uno erecto serpente omnibus sauciatis: ita unius Christi morte communis omnium salus reparetur. Pulchre Cyrillus Alexandr. in h. l. Ser- pens peccatum significat, sævum illud & homini exitiosum, quod universum genus humanum depa- scebatur, variis morsibus uniuscujusq; animam appe- tens, & multiplex nequitiæ venenum effundens, quod in tantum invaluerat, ut aliter à nobis vitari non pos- set, quam ope cælesti. Factus est ergo Deus Verbum in similitudinem carnis peccati, ut damnaret pecca- tum in carne, sicut scriptum est, & respicientibus in ipsum intentiori fide, aut divinorum dogmatum in- quisitione, æternæ salutis conciliator existeret. Au- gustinus Tr. 12. in Joh. quia in serpente illorum per serpentis effigiem figurata est mors. Morsus serpen- tum lethalis, mors Domini vitalis; Appenditur ser- pens, ut nihil valeat serpens: Quid hoc est? Appen- ditur mors, ut nihil valeat mors. Petrus Galatinus l. VI. de Arcanis Cath. verit. c. XVII. adducit Rab- bi Simeon Ben Joahi, quod arbor in qua serpens æneus erectus fuit, excisa fuerit ab arbore vitæ in paradiso; sed hæc involucra sunt Rabbinica com- mentis mixta, non ab arbore sed à suspenso ser- pente sauciatio obtingebat, idq; non modo natu- rali, sed supernaturali & miraculoso, vi divinæ or- dinationis, Sap. XVI. 6. 7. Quod omne factum est ob typum rei futuræ, unde signum erigi jubebatur, Num. XXI. 4. Ideo Justinus provocat Tryphonem Judæum in Dialogo p. 25. ut aliam hujus signi ra- tionem edisserat, imprimis quia Moses similitudi- nem fieri prohibuerit, & agnovit Judæus collocu- tor aliam rationem reddi non posse: Veræ, inquit, dixisti, non enim habemus quam reddamus ratio- nem. Nam & ipse aliquoties de hoc Magistros no- stros sum percontatus, nullus autem rationem expli- cuit. Quod urget Tertullianus advers. Judæos c. X. Idem rursus Moses post interdictam omnis rei simi- litudinem, cur æneum serpentem ligno impositum pendentis habitu in spectaculum Israeli salutare pro- posuit, eo tempore, quo à serpentibus post idolola- triam exterminabatur? nisi quod hic dominicam cru- cem intentabat, qua serpens Diabolus publicabatur & læso cuique ab ejusmodi colubris, id est, Angelis ejus, à delictorum peccantia ad Christi crucis sacra- menta intento, salus efficiebatur. Nam qui in illam tunc respiciebat, à morsu serpentium liberabatur.

(III) Quod ad modum sanationis attinet, expri- mit eundem Christus, tum voce exaltationis, tum verbis subsequentibus, Ut omnis qui credat in ipsum, non pereat, sed habeat vitam æternam. Quanquam enim vere exaltatus sit in cruce Chri- stus, dum suspensus est in ligno, non tamen sine causa singulari hic usus est voce exaltationis: ut nempe simul involveretur, quomodo hæc in cru- ce exaltatio vere exaltari debeat, quod factum est per exaltationem in cœlum, & prædicationem in mundo universo. Quo & respicit Joh. XII. v. 32. Notat id Cyrillus Alexandr. lib. II. in Joh. cap. L. Quod autem in sublime serpens exaltatus fuit, in eam cognitionem, passionem Christi perventuram denotabat, ut sicut ipse quoque prædixerat, nemo sit, qui in cruce passum fuisse ipsum ignoret. Chrysofto- mus in hunc locum ait, non dicit suspendi, sed ex- altari. Ut neq; auditoribus ignominiosum neq; à fi- gura abhorrens videretur. Sed hæ rationes suffi- cientes non sunt, nisi priores conjungantur. De signatur autem hic specialiter 1. Fidei natura per intuitum serpentis anei. Hæc enim in eo sita est, quod intueamur Christum in cruce pro nobis suspensum: Adeoq; ut intuitus sit per receptionem speciei, non per emissionem radiorum: ita & fides, qua intuemur Christum, fit recipiendo & appre- hendendo Christum, ejusq; passionem, non vero emittendo radios majestatis. Fides enim est oculus spiritualis animæ. Eleganter id exponit Chrysost. Homil. 26. in Joh. Quomodo possunt in crucifixum credentes salvi fieri, cum se à morte non liberarit, merito ergo in medium adducit historiam veterem. Nam si ad anei serpentis simulacrum aspicientes Ju- dæi à morte liberabantur, quanto majori, qui in crucifixum credunt, beneficio fruentur. Vides ut fi- gura veritati consentiat. Illic effugerunt mortem Judæi, sed temporalem. Hic sempiternam fideles. Illic ictus serpentium suspensus serpens sanabat: Hic incorporei serpentis plagas Jesus cruci affixus cura- vit. Illic corporeis oculis suspicientes corporis salu- tem, hic incorporeis omnium peccatorum remissio- nem consecuti sunt. Illic suspensum erat æs in serpen- tis effigiem. Hic dominicum corpus à Spiritu for- matum. Serpens illic mordebat & serpens sanabat. Hic mors perdidit & mors salvum fecit. Adhæc, qui interimebat serpens, veneno sæviebat, qui libera- bat, nullo. Itaq; perdidit mors peccatum, tanquam serpentis venenum habuit Domini mors, id omne, ut æneus serpens venenum abstulit. Conferatur Athanas. Tom. II. contra eos, qui humanam Christi naturam negabant, p. 304.

II. Objectum fidei salvificæ est Christi pro sa- lute mundi crucifixio & mors. Quemadmodum actus ejus proprius & formalis est apprehensio e- jusdem. Perinde ut objectum intuitus Israëlita- rum erat serpens in deserto exaltatus, caput omnium, inquit Gregorius Nyssenus de vita Mosis, ferme circa finem, quod in hoc Christianæ professio- nis articulo credimus, est firma rectaq; fide in passio- nem Christi respicere, qui pro nobis passus est. Crux vero passio est, quare qui crucem respicit, ut historia testatur, ei venenum cupiditatum obesse non potest. Augustinus lib. I. de peccatorum meritis c. XXXI. Quid est, inquit, exaltatus serpens, nisi mors Chri- sti eo significandi modo, quo per efficientem id quod efficitur, significatur. A serpente quippe mors venit, qui peccatum, quo mori mereretur, persuasit ho- mini. Dominus autem in carnem suam non pec- catum transtulit tanquam venenum serpentis, sed tantum transtulit mortem, ut esset in similitudine carnis peccati, pœna sine culpa; unde in carne pec- cati & culpa solveretur & pœna. Sicut ergo tum qui conspiciebat exaltatum serpentem & à veneno sanabatur, & à morte liberabatur. Sic nunc qui conformatur similitudini mortis Christi per fidem baptismumque ejus & à peccato per justificationem & à morte per resurrectionem liberatur.

(III) Fidei applicatio. Ut enim serpens sus- pensus commune erat remedium, sed non prode- rat, nisi eis qui aspiciebant eundem. Ita Christus commune salutis remedium præstitit passione sua meritoria, sed applicatio fieri debet per fidem. Explicat id Nicetas in oratione XLII. Gregor. Na- zianzen. Num. XLIX. Deum nos quoq; offendimus atq; in spiritualium serpentum morsum incidimus, qui per omne peccati genus nos ferientes morte affi- ciebat. Quo autem modo salutem consecuti sumus? Aspeximus & ipsi serpentem in ligno, hoc est, Chri- stum ipsum intuentes atque in eum credentes salu- tem nanciscimur.

(IV) Fidei vis & causa ejus. Quemadmo- dum unice illic sanationis vis Israëlitis depen- debat ab ordinatione divina : sic & fides non ob sui dignitatem sed ob ordinationem divinam salutem operatur. Johann. cap. VI. vers. 40. Quod tunc exaltatum est, inquit Epiphanius Hæresi XXXVII. à Mose, per inspectionem faciebat sa- nationem, non propter serpentis naturam sed ob bo- nam Dei voluntatem, qui per serpentem tum com- morsis velut remedium operabatur. Et quemadmo- dum in exaltatione serpentis sanatio commorsis fie- bat; sic in Crucifixione Christi Redemptio facta est animis nostris à morsibus peccati nobis illatis.

(V) ἐνέργεια Fidei. Salus accepta ferenda est Merito Christi, quod apprehendit Fides, quomo- docunque sese de cætero illa habeat. Unde & illi, qui fide admodum infirma sunt, nihilo secius vi- tam consequuntur, quia non à fidei quantitate, robore, aut merito, sed à merito mortis Christi sa- lus dependet : Perinde uti illi, qui infirmis, languidis, nutantibus & morte natantibus ocu- lis aspiciebant serpentem æneum, non minus, quam reliqui validiori aspectu intuentes conva- luere. Sinceritas tantum fidei requiritur; Fir- mitas non desideratur, quasi infirma fides hic nihil valeat. Non enim à fide, sed ab objecto, quod apprehendit fides, vis salutis oritur. Re- spicientibus in eum fide sincera æterna salus largiter ostenditur, ait Cyrillus in hunc locum.

(VI) Soli Fidei salutem vindicandum esse ci- tra συνέργειαν operum, hoc etiam typo doce- mur. Ut enim solus intuitus serpentis, absque ullo opere, sanitatem Israëlitis restituit, ut serpentes ægrorum manibus ac pedibus impli- cati deciderent, dummodo hi serpentem æ- neum intuerentur: ita fidei intuitus solus, abs- que operibus nostris, salutem reddit. Præcla- re Ambrosius & ex illo Augustana Confess. Ar- ticulo 6. Hoc constitutum est à DEO, ut qui credit in Christum, salvus sit sine opere sola fi- de, gratis accipiens remissionem peccatorum; quod dictum vere aureum ob Sophistas, Pa- pistas, Photinianos, & Novatores, sedulo est ob- servandum.

(VII) Ut vero eos qui negligebant medium divinitus monstratum, perire oportuit : ita per- eundum & omnibus est, qui Christum pro no- bis crucifixum aspernantur, vel vili hujus me- dii salutiferi specie offenduntur, 1. Petr. cap. I. vers. 7. 8.

(VIII) Denique ut sanati ducebantur in Terram Canaam, in qua immunes erant ab igni- torum serpentum morsibus : Ita nullus amplius metus, nullum à serpente infernali periculum erit in cœlestis promissionis terra, in quam justificati fide per Christum deducimur, Apocal. XXI. 4.

Atque ita communiter Doctores explicant hunc typum. Aliam tamen ejusdem rationem dari posse insinuat Tertullianus, libro de Ido- latria, cap. 5. quam exhibet. Greg. Nazianz. Oration. II. in Pascha: An vero serpens æneus ad- versus serpentum morsus suspenditur, non tan- tum ut Christi pro nobis passi typus, verum ut antitypus, atque iis qui istam intuentur, salutem affert, dum non vita frui, sed mortuus esse ac sub- ditas sibi potestates secum interimere creditur op- pressus nimirum & extinctus sicut merebatur. Sic ergo per serpentem æreum suspensum intelligit Theologus Diabolum suspensum & extinctum per Christi mortem, cujus Epitaphium ibidem subjicit. Quæ omnia eximie quidem explicat Nicetas (Paraphrastes Nazianz.) Cæterum sim- plicior & convenientior est reliquorum Eccle- siæ Doctorum interpretatio, qua serpens suspensus non Diabolus per crucem Christi extinctus, sed ipse Christus, in cruce exaltatus intelligitur, siquidem Christus ipse eundem typum facit suæ exaltationis in cruce, nec objectum fidei proprium sit Diaboli extinctio, sed Christi crucifixio, qua eadem peccatum expiatum, Diaboli tyrannis extincta est.

Documenta hujus Pericopes hæc notari possunt sequentia. (I) Duo sunt erroris in rebus fidei principia. (a) ἄγνοια seu ignorantia scripturæ, quam Christus Sadduceis exprobrat: Erratis ignorantes Scripturarum, Matth. XXII. vers. 29. (β) ἀπιστία, incredulitas, quod iis, quæ in scripturis tradita sunt, fides non adhibeatur, Iohann. III. v. 12. Conferatur Es. LIII. 1. Romon. X. 16. 1. Petr. II. 8. (II) Israëlitis in Veteri Testamento incumbebat cognitio non tantummodo peccati originalis, sed & regenerationis cœlestis, & meriti Christi satisfactorii, quia eadem, qua nos fide, salutem adepti sunt, Actor. XV. 11. Ephes. IV. 6. Hinc reprehenditur Magister in Israël, quod cum alios ea docere debuerit, ipse ea ignorarit. (III) Plurales locutiones de DEO adhibitæ mysterium pluralitatis personarum in DEO designant, & cum in Vet. Testam. passim occurrant, ideo indubium est, in Vet. Testamento etiam propositum esse hoc mysterium. Vid. B. Lutherus Comment. in Genes. cap. XXXV. & disput. nostræ de plural. person. divin. (IV) Notanda insignis DEI Φιλανθρωπία, quod divinæ Sacrosanctæ Trinitatis personæ testium locum subire voluerint de salute nostra æterna, ut mysteria fidei credere ne dedignemur. Pater enim testatur passim in Vet. Testament. Filius imprimis in Nov. Test. in diebus carnis suæ, testatus est Spiritus Sanctus utriusque Testamenti inspiratione, Prophetis & Apostolis facta, testatur per scripturas, idque testimonium obsignat in cordibus arrhabonis instar, 1. Corinth. I. v. ult. Tota Sacrosancta Trinitas testata est in Baptismo Christi, testatur in Baptismo nostro, testatur denique in adventu ad nos cordisque nostri inhabitatione. Hinc ad tres testes in cœlo provocat Johannes, in hac salutis causa, 1. Joh. V. v. 7. (V) Terrena sunt ea quæ ex parte nostri requiruntur, Verbi auscultatio & Sacramentorum usus &c. Etsi effectus divini consequuntur.
