Divina vero sunt quæ ex parte DEI collata sunt & conferuntur ad salutem, summa illa DEI charitas, ex qua Filium DEI dedit, Filii ex cœlis adventus, incarnatio, passio, mors, resurrectio & in cœlos ascensio, ut & Spiritus Sancti missio, ac gratiosa operatio. Hæc enim mere divina sunt, ad quæ nostra nihil conferre potest opera. (VI) Summi ac eminentissimi fidei Articuli sunt, descensus Filii hominis de cælo, Majestas item & omnipræsentia ejusdem in cælo & in terra, nec non gloriosa ascensio in cælum, quos omnino credere oportet ad saltem, qui eos enim ignorant aut negant, Christi personam aut officium fincere, & ut par est, credere non possunt. (VII) Typus ænei serpentis docet, Israëlitis universæ salutis Mysterium aperte satis propositum, nec minus explicite ab iisdem credendum fuisse. Quia illo in typo luculenter cernere licuit tum subjecti ad salutem perducendi statum, qua culpam & pœnam, tum remedii conditionem, quod in Christi passione & morte paratum est; Tum Applicationis rationem, quæ fit per fidem, cujus fidei naturam, vim, indolem atque ἐνέρ- γειαν infinuabant. Illa omnia quin fuerint Israe- litis à Doctoribus declarata, dubium non est. Ideo enim iis proposita erat hæc figura, ut per fi- dem in Christum hic adumbratum salvarentur, atque hæc Salus ipsis ita adumbrata explicaretur fidei in Messiam confirmandæ causa. Conferatur Joh. V. 39. Rom. X. 4. c. XV. 4. 1. Cor. X. 11. Et quis ambiget Sacerdotes atque Prophetas in quibus Christi Spiritus fuit, 1. Petr. I. 11. illud ipsum, quod intendebat Deus, per hunc typum, & cujus causa eundem proponebat, populo eadem ratione, quemadmodum id à Christo factum, tradidisse! Nam aut hæc ipsa fuit intentio Dei proponentis, quam hic Christus edisserit, aut alia. Si alia, Chri- stus eam non recte proposuit. Si eadem ipsa, Ergo non potuit ea à Spiritu Christi, qui in Sanctis Dei viris erat, non tradita esse. Alias Deus frustra fuis- set, dum typum proposuit, ea intentione ut in Messiam typo adumbratum crederent, ac salutem consequerentur. Hinc est, quod tanquam indu- bium sumat Christus in disputatione cum Magi- stro Israelitico, quod ea Typi significatio omnibus debuerit certa maximeque perspecta esse. (VIII) In suspensione Christi crucifixi salus nostra sita est. Confer. 1. Corinth. I. 18. 21. 30. cap. II. 2. 7. 2. Cor. V. 5. 21. Rom. V. 18. 19. instituta collatione cum ca- pite Phil. II. 8. Rom. III. 22. seq. Si affixus serpens, inquit Ambros. Serm. LV. ligno filiis Israel contulit sanitatem, quanto magis salutem præstat populo Do- minus in patibulo crucifixus! Et si figura tantum profuit, quantum profuisse credimus veritatem: Pulchre hac de re B. Macarius postquam hunc typum explicuit Homil. XI. In corpore mortuo vita est, hic Redemptio, hic lumen. Hic accedit ad mor- tem & disputat cum ea Dominus, ac mandat, ut eji- ciat ex inferno & morte animas, ac reddat eas sibi. Ecce hæc hisce perculsa adit ministros suos, congre- gatque omnes potestates ac Principes malitiæ, depro- mit Chirographa, & dicit: Ecce hic obedierunt ver- bo meo, Ecce quomodo adorarunt nos mortales? Deus autem, qui est justus judex, illic ostendit justitiam suam, dicens ei: Paruit tibi Adam & obtinuisti inde omne cor ejus: Optemperavit tibi humanitas, meum autem corpus quidnam commisit? Hoc peccati est expers. Corpus illud primi Adæ obligatum tibi est & jure ob id ejus Chirographa obtines. Mihi autem o- mnes testimonium perhibent, quod non peccaverim, ergo nihil tibi obligatus sum, & quod sim Filius Dei. Redimo ergo corpus tibi venditum à primo Adamo, dissolvo tua Chirographa; ego enim satisfeci pro debi- tis Adæ (ἀπέδωκα τὰ χρέα τῦ Ἀδὰμ) dum crucifi- xus sum, & in infernum descendi. Et mando vobis, In- ferne, tenebræ, & Mors, emittite animas inclusas Adæ. Sicq; tandem infernales potestates metu perculsæ re- stituunt inclusum Adam. (IX) Ut à ligno perser- pentem perditio, ita à ligno per Christum in ser- pente æneo adumbratum facta est liberatio. Dis- solvens enim, inquit Irenæus l. V. eam, quæ ab initio in ligno facta erat inobedientiam, obediens factus est usque ad mortem, mortem autem crucis, eamque in ligno factam inobedientiam sanans. (X) Scalam Cœli hic intueri licet: Cujus extrema sunt Deus Cœli Dominus, & Homo abjectus ob peccatum & præcipitatus ad infernum. Materia, unde con- stant scala, divinissima est, tum Divina Filii Dei na- tura, tum Sancta ejus Humanitas. Forma: Unio est personalis, vel copulatio divinæ & humanæ natu- ræ in unitatem suppositi. Unde unitas scalæ oritur per quam ascensus patet ad Deum. Gradus extre- mi sunt descensus è cœlo Filii Dei vel incarnatio: & ascensus in cælum, vel exaltatio. Joh. XVI, 28. Medii st

Nativitas, vita, obedientia, Passio, Crucifixio, mors, sepultura, discensus ad inferos & Resurre- ctio. Usus & finis est, ut ascendamus per eandem scalam in coelum, extra & praeterquam nullus ad- itus patet ad Deum, Johan. XIV. 6. Scala Paradisi fracta in Adamo reparata est in Christo dicente Bo- naventura. Medium quo elevamur, gradusque conscendimus, ex parte Dei coelitus nobis porre- ctum est Verbum Dei, tum ἀκουστὸν tum ὁρατόν; per quod ex parte nostri ascenditur fides, ut per ean- dem verbo adhaerescentes in scala illa attrahantur à Deo, & attracti perveniamus in coelum. Ascen- dunt autem & descendunt super eandem scalam Angeli, non quod iisdem Christus Mediator da- tus sit, ac per eundem aditus ipsis pateat in coelum, sed quia descendendo annunciant nobis coelum referatum & adjungunt nobis ministros in ter- ra, Matth. XVIII. 10. Ebr. I. 14. Adscendendo etiam nos secum transportant in coelum, Luc. XVI. 22. Quae omnia praefigurata sunt in scala Jacobo visa, Genes. XXVIII. 12. interprete Christo, Joh. I. 51. Si collatio cum hoc dicto, Joh. III. 13. institua- tur, ut ita nemo vere ascendat in coelum nisi qui descendit è coelo Filius Hominis, qui in coelo est, & qui per fidem unum est cum Filio hominis. 1. Co- rinth. VI. 17. Atque haec è praelectionibus No- stris.

## 3:16
Vers. 16.

ἠγάπησεν ὁ Θεὸς] Individual words have emphasis. GOD, that Lord of all, loved, and indeed first: our 1 Epist. IV. 10, 19.

τὸν κόσμον) Not the Jews only with whom He had some covenant, but the whole human race entirely, overwhelmed by sins. 1 John V. 19, with the addition of Rom. V. 8 and Eph. II. 12.

Ὥστε τὸν υἱὸν αὑτοῦ τὸν μονογενῆ) Paul Rom. VIII. 32: ὅς γε τοῦ ἰδίου υἱοῦ οὐκ ἐφείσατο. It was not enough to have said son unless he had added only-begotten. There is an allusion to the history of Abraham Gen. XXII. 12.

ἔδωκεν) Understand freely, provoked by no merits, πα- ρέδωκε Paul in the said place and often elsewhere, he speaks obscurely about his death, openly about eternal life, so that he may lift up spirits.

Latin:

Vers. 16.

ἠγάπησεν ὁ Θεὸς] Singula ἔμφασιν habent. DEUS o- mnium ille Dominus dilexit, & quidem prior: noster I. Epist. IV. 10. 19.

τὸν κόσμον) Non Judaeos tantum quibuscum foedus habebat aliquod, sed omne omnino genus humanum, peccatis obrutum. I. Johann. V. 19. addito Rom. V. 8. & Ephes. II. 12.

Ὥστε τὸν υἱὸν αὑτοῦ τὸν μονογενῆ) Paulus Rom. VIII. 32: ὅς γε τοῦ ἰδίου υἱοῦ οὐκ ἐφείσατο. Non satis erat filium dixisse nisi addidisset unigenitum. Allusio est ad Abrahami historiam Gen. XXII. 12.

ἔδωκεν) Intellige gratis nullis meritis provocatus, πα- ρέδωκε Paulus dicto loco & alibi saepe, de morte sua ob- scure loquitur de vita aeterna aperte, ut animos eri- gat.

## 3:17
Vers. 17.

ἵνα κρίνῃ τὸν κόσμον) GOD is often described as an avenger in the Old Testament: therefore, those conscious of their sins could deservedly expect the Son to come to exact penalties in the name of the Father. For κρίνειν is κατακρίνειν as in I Corinthians XI. 32, Hebrews XIII. 4, but κατακρίνειν is both to condemn and to exact penalties.

Σωθῇ] May have life, as the Syriac explains it thus.

Latin:

Vers. 17.

ἵνα κρίνῃ τὸν κόσμον) DEUS saepe ultor describitur in veteri pagina: itaque conscii peccatorum merito ex- pectare poterant Filium venire ad poenas patris nomine exigendas. Nam κρίνειν est κατακρίνειν ut I. Corinth. XI. 32. Hebr. XIII. 4. at κατακρίνειν est & damnare & poe- nas exigere.

Σωθῇ] Vitam habeat ut sic explicat Syrus.

## 3:18
Vers. 18.

ὁ πιστεύων εἰς αὐτὸν οὐ κρίνεται) He is snatched from the common destruction.

ὁ δὲ μὴ πιστεύων, ἤδη κέκριται) It is an old saying: The guilty man condemns himself on the day he sins. Thus in the Roman Laws: you have subjected yourself to punishment: and those who form a wicked plan are said to be deservedly punished by their own [act]. But add what we noted at Matthew chapter XXV, verse 32.

ὅτι μὴ πεπίστευκεν εἰς τὸ ὄνομα μονογενοῦς υἱοῦ τοῦ Θεοῦ) Because he was unwilling to believe or trust in Him who so openly reflects the divine truth and goodness and seals it with His own death, which the following [verses] show proceeds from a very wicked mind.

Latin:

Vers. 18.

ὁ πιστεύων εἰς αὐτὸν οὐ κρίνεται) Eripitur communi exi- tio.

ὁ δὲ μὴ πιστεύων, ἤδη κέκριται) Dictum est vetus: Illo nocens se damnat quo peccat die. Sic in Legibus Romanis: ipse te poenae subdidisti: & qui sceleratum capiunt consilium suo. merito puniri dicun- tur. Sed adde quae ad Matth. cap. XXV. vers. 32. nota- vimus.

ὅτι μὴ πεπίστευκεν εἰς τὸ ὄνομα μονογενοῦς υἱοῦ τοῦ Θεοῦ) Quod veritatem & bonitatem divinam tam aperte referenti & morte sua obsignanti nec credere, nec confidere vo- luerit, quod ex pessimo animo proficisci sequentibus o- stendit.

## 3:19
Vers. 19.

Αὕτη δὲ ἐστιν ἡ κρίσις) In this they are αὐτοκατάκριτοι, condemned internally by their own judgment.

τὸ φῶς ἐλήλυθεν εἰς κόσμον] Christ with His most pure doctrine, as above I. 10. Compare Isaiah IX. 2 and chapter XLII, verse 16. They ought to have sought the light: it was offered to them of its own accord.

ἠγάπησαν οἱ ἄνθρωποι μᾶλλον τὸ σκότος ἢ τὸ φῶς] Μᾶλλον here is of opposition, not of comparison; men (that is, the great part of men, as above I. 12) preferred darkness to light. Thus 2 Timothy III. 4. Thucydides: μᾶλλον βούλομαι τοῦτο ἀντὶ ἐκείνου: I prefer this rather than that. Understand τὸ σκότος here as a way of living supported by no rule, which is clearly described in Ephesians II. 3; thus below VIII. 12, XII. 35, I Epistle I. 6, II. 11, Eph. V. 11.

For their works were evil) Understand not only the works in which they had lived before the light had shone upon them, but also those in which it pleased them to remain, and they favored the disease.

Latin:

Vers. 19.

Αὕτη δὲ ἐστιν ἡ κρίσις) In hoc sunt αὐτοκατάκριτοι, intus suopte judicio damnati.

τὸ φῶς ἐλήλυθεν εἰς κόσμον] Christus cum suo purissi- mo dogmate, ut supra I. 10. Confer Esaiam IX. 2. & cap. XLII. vers. 16. Quaerere lucem debuerant: ultro ipsis ob- lata est.

ἠγάπησαν οἱ ἄνθρωποι μᾶλλον τὸ σκότος ἢ τὸ φῶς] Μᾶλ- λον hic oppositionis est, non comparationis praetulerunt homines (id est magna pars hominum, ut supra I. 12.) te- nebras luci Sic 2. Tim. III. 4. Thucydides: μᾶλλον βούλο- μαι τοῦτο ἀντὶ ἐκείνου: hoc prae illo malo, τὸ σκότος hic in- tellige vivendi rationem nulla regula subnixam, quz lu- culenter describitur Ephes. II. 3. sic infra VIII. 12. XII. 35. I. Epist I. 6. II. 11. Eph. V. 11.

ἧν γὰρ πονηρὰ αὐτῶν τὰ ἔργα) Intellige non modo opera in quibus vixerant, antequam lux affulsisset, sed & ea in quibus manere ipsis placebat, favebant morbo.

## 3:19
ver. 19. Our salvation in the other life will be situated, both in an immunity of every kind from sins and their punishments: and in the most perfect fruition of God. Whence a diversity arises, as regards the salvation of this life and the other. For in this life we are not yet entirely immune from sins, even if we are freed from the guilt of sin. Nor are we entirely exempt from the punishments of sins; for although those, insofar as they are formally punishments, do not lie upon the justified: yet the material of punishments, such as are afflictions, calamities, and finally death itself, still threatens them. But in the other life we shall be entirely immune from sins as to guilt, dominion, sense, root, and incentive, and also from the punishments both material and formal. Furthermore, in this life we do indeed enjoy God, but through faith in Christ. Hence we are endowed with the most perfect Righteousness before the tribunal of God, namely the Righteousness of Christ, than which a more perfect cannot be given: But it is in us only λογιστικῶς (imputatively): but the inherent righteousness which redounds into us from thence, by which, beholding the perfect Glory of the Righteousness of Christ with unveiled face, we are transformed into the same image, is here imperfect in many ways, so much so, that we have need to be transformed from glory to glory, more and more by the Lord the Spirit, until we aspire to the most perfect glory of the other life, 2. Corinth. ch. III. ver. 18. In that blessed life, therefore, we shall enjoy God not through faith and imputation, but through vision and blessed contemplation face to face. Therefore, the righteousness of Christ, consisting of his active and passive obedience, will not only belong to us λογιστικῶς through imputation, but that righteousness will be perfect which will inhere in the elect through the perfect conformation of their mind and will with the divine mind and will and the consummated restoration of the divine Image. You say: Is not the righteousness eternal which Christ brought back for us, Dan. ch. IX. ver. 24. Shall we not shine with the righteousness of Christ forever? Will the adornment with which Christ decorates us, that wedding garment at the heavenly marriage of the Lamb, not cover us any longer, nor shine in us? Let us answer, certainly, but in a far more perfect way. For here we are clothed with the same only through faith, here the same shines in us only as it is imputed to us, or also as some splendor excited thence by the Spirit of the Lord shines in us, so that the clarity of the restored image may shine forth not entirely nothing: Since faith generates and emits from itself certain rays of that clarity, through love toward GOD and neighbor, to which, however, the manifold darknesses of errors and sins are still mixed. The matter will be otherwise in the other life. There we shall not be clothed through faith with the righteousness of Christ, nor will the obedience of Christ be imputed to us by a mere λογισμὸν alone through the mediation of faith, not that the λογισμὸς and imputation of God has an end, or is not eternal; for it remains, and thus the righteousness of Christ is transcribed to us for eternity: just as it was transcribed from eternity in our predestination to life: although faith ceases in eternal life as to its act, yet not as to the divine intuition or fruit, 2 Corinth. chap. XIII. vers. 13. 2 Corinth. chap. V. vers. 7. which also did not exist from eternity, except by reason of προγνώσεως and intuition in the decree of the election of GOD: But because the fruit and effect of the imputation of righteousness, which here itself explains by the partial restoration of the divine image, whence our inherent righteousness is only imperfect, there will be the fullness of the divine Image and most perfect inherent Righteousness; and that Christ, apprehended here through faith, dwelling in us by means of faith, that we may be filled with all the fullness of God, Eph. there in us immediately, is not only going to surround us with the most perfect and most full light of his meritorious active and passive obedience, and in an inexplicable way to us (for he is our mediator and priest forever, the redemption which he found, the Righteousness which he brought back, is eternal), but also with the immense Glory of his Deity, which he has in common with the Father and the Holy Spirit, as GOD by essence, as man by the Grace of personal union, is so going to shine in us, that from this the perfect image of GOD, the consummated Righteousness and Holiness, may shine forth. Finally, the end of our salvation is the Glory of GOD, that the Fatherly love of GOD may be celebrated eternally, as well as the brotherly redemption of the only-begotten Son of GOD, as also the heavenly Calling and Conversion of the Holy Spirit, and the infinite grace to be given to us in salvation and the most gracious communication of himself by the Holy Trinity. For this is our full joy, as Augustine says in book 1 of the Trinity, ch. 8: Than which there is nothing greater, to enjoy the Holy Trinity, GOD, in whose image we were made. How great will that happiness be there, says Augustine again in book 22 of the City of God, ch. 30, where there will be no evil, no good will be hidden, there will be leisure for the praises of GOD, who will be all in all; for what else will be done, where there will be no sloth, nor will there be any laboring under any need, I do not know. These things concerning the causes of salvation.

Now, therefore, the cause of perdition cannot be hidden: which is truly not to be imputed, with the Calvinists, to the absolute decree of GOD, whether of reprobation or of the preterition of the greater part of mankind. For Holy Scripture knows no such thing: nor to the inequality of the grace of GOD, or the particularity of the merit of CHRIST: for CHRIST acknowledges no inequality of Grace, nor difference in merit and Redemption, as far as the ordinary economy of salvation is concerned; he teaches that the whole world was so equally loved by GOD, that the only-begotten Son of GOD was spent for it all equally. Which will of GOD, revealed in the Gospel, it is our duty to venerate, and not to hunt here for another hidden will in GOD. But neither is the cause of destruction to be sought in the calling of the HOLY SPIRIT. Since the same word and the same Sacraments are dispensed to believers and unbelievers, and the same saving Grace is exhibited to all through the same Ministry without discrimination; that grace is dispensed to the Elect Ἀμέσως (immediately) smacks of the Schwenckfeldian separation of the Spirit from the word, an Enthusiastic illumination apart from the word and the ministry of the word, but of this elsewhere. It remains, therefore, that the blame for perdition lies solely in men. Since it is to be sought neither in the unequal grace of GOD, nor in the disparate Redemption of CHRIST, nor in the diverse ordinary Economy of calling. This is what is said in Hos. 13:9, Thy salvation is from me, O Israel, thy perdition from thyself.

Now, therefore, the matter concerns the Judgment of GOD against the unfaithful. For after CHRIST said that he was sent into the world, not that he might judge the world, but that the world might be saved through him, lest anyone think that there is now no judgment to be feared, and that salvation certainly comes to all: CHRIST explains whence it happens that, nevertheless, many are judged, and who in truth are to be immune from Judgment, who indeed are already judged, and upon whom the judicial sentence of the law has its full force, John ch. 3, v. 18 seq.

To be observed here (I.) is the true and only cause of immunity and exemption from Judgment, which is faith in CHRIST; He who believes in him is not judged, says Christ. Judgment is understood both as condemnation, when those who are condemned are said to be judged, and as the legal judicial sentence, which strikes all who do not persist in all things which are written in the book of the law, Deut. ch. 27, last verse. Immune and exempt from both Judgments are those who believe in CHRIST, both from the condemnatory sentence of the law, and from the actual condemnation itself, to which they were liable according to the sentence of the Law. The cause is because Christ, in whom we believe, underwent that judgment in our place, having been made a curse for us, that he might free us from the curse. Gal. ch. 3, v. 13. He himself willed to be condemned by the judgment of GOD as a criminal in our stead, lest we, who were truly criminals, should have need to be judged and condemned. But that CHRIST underwent the Judgment for all is undoubted, because he took upon himself the sins of all, he laid down his life for all; just as he was given to the whole world, and came into the world, that the world might not be judged, so he was made a propitiation for the sins of the whole world, 1 John ch. 2, v. 2. Whence all can apply this liberation to themselves, lest they have need to come into judgment. St. Athanasius explained this excellently in his work On the Incarnation of the Word, Vol. 1 of his works, p. 72. Whom it is helpful to hear here: As therefore the debt for all had to be paid, and all were bound to die, therefore it remained that the only-begotten Son of GOD should offer a sacrifice for all, delivering his own Temple to death for all, by which he might make all unliable and free from the old transgression. For there was need of death, and it was necessary that death be brought in for all, that what was owed by all might be paid. Wherefore the Word, because it could not die, being immortal, took to itself a body that could die, and offered that as its own for all, so that by being joined in body to all, it might, by suffering death for all, restrain him who has the power of death, that is the Devil, and might deliver those, as many as through fear of death were subject to death throughout their life. Certainly, the common Savior of all having died for us, we no longer die by death according to the threat of the Law, as once we did, as many as trust in CHRIST JESUS. For that very condemnation has been obliterated. Moreover, with corruption ceasing and being abolished, we are dissolved according to the bodily nature of our mortality only until that time which GOD has willed to be defined for each one, so that we may be rendered partakers of a better resurrection. All these things St. Athanasius, not only powerfully asserting the universal Redemption of Christ, but also illustrating the whole business of our salvation.

(II.) The contrary cause of judgment. He who does not believe is already judged. He is said to be judged in the past tense, because the Judgment already passed by the law presses upon him, nor is he freed from it. For although liberation from the curse of the law has been obtained for him, from which he could apply it to himself, and was owed through faith: Yet he does not enjoy it, because he does not embrace the liberation by faith: Not otherwise than if a λύτρον (ransom) had been paid for a captive, but this payment is despised, so that the liberated man prefers to remain in captivity, from which, unless he were to treat the λύτρον as worthless, he could have departed. The true and only cause, therefore, of the judgment of condemnation is unbelief. The cause of the curse of the law is sins: but the proper and formal cause of being left under the curse of those who have been liberated by the λύτρον of Christ the Redeemer is not sins, since they have been redeemed from that: But unbelief, because they do not apply that redemption to themselves, but despise it, and thus remain under the judgment from which they could have been immune. It is therefore manifest again that those were liberated through the merit of Christ, for they could not, through unbelief, despise the λύτρον paid for them, much less be condemned on account of that contempt, namely for the reason that they do not believe in this liberation of theirs accomplished through Christ, if they had not truly been redeemed by him; unless one wishes to say that they ought to believe, which is not true at all, and are therefore condemned because they do not believe that very thing, which however is not consistent, namely that they do not believe that Christ died for them and made satisfaction.

(III.) Confirmation of this cause; because he does not believe in the name of the Only-begotten Son. For if faith in the name of the Only-begotten Son of God, who was sent so that the world might not be judged but saved, through whom alone liberation reaches us, is required for the actual enjoyment of liberation, it is necessary that all who do not believe in the name of the only-begotten Son are already judged, and remain eternally under the condemnatory judgment of the Law. By which very fact all Pagans, Turks, Jews, I add also Arians and Photinians, are proscribed from the enjoyment of eternal salvation to eternal perdition. For none of them believes in the name of the only-begotten Son of God. Turks blaspheme the generation of the Son of God. Jews accept neither the Son of God nor the Mystery of Redemption. Arians make Christ a creature produced from non-entities, and not truly a Son generated from the substance of God the Father. Photinians, although they profess the true and natural Son of God in words, do not however call him so except by reason of his temporal nativity, but with impious daring they oppose the eternal generation from the substance of the Father, for which, however, Christ is uniquely called the only-begotten Son of God. For how, says Cyril of Alexandria in book XII of the Thesaurus, chapter XV, will the true fruit of a Begetter be anything other in Nature than his begetter? For since the Father is God by nature, the Son will also be God by nature. Otherwise he will be of lesser dignity than his creature. For creatures produce from themselves fruit consubstantial to themselves: but God, according to these men (he means the Arians), will not generate a GOD by nature from himself, which is utterly absurd. And book I on John, chapter 3. If the only-begotten Son truly shone forth from God the Father, it is necessary, even for those unwilling to confess it, that he is from the substance and nature of the Father, for that is what true Filiation signifies; But if he is not from the substance of the Father according to nature, he will not even be truly the Son? For who, says Athanasius in Oration III against the Arians, hearing the name Son, does not immediately think of him as being something proper to the paternal essence? For as Hilary says in book VIII on the Trinity: Human sense excludes this from intelligence, that something born should be different from the nature of its origin. Whence Augustine in the book against the sermon of the Arians, chapter 36, Vol. VI. of the Works: If any of those were to say that his son was not of the same nature as himself, but of a different one, the son would prefer to be disinherited by him than to think this; how great, therefore, is the impiety with which those are blinded who, while they confess the only-begotten Son of God, do not wish to confess him of the same nature as the Father, but of a different and unequal one, and in many things and ways dissimilar, as if he were not born of GOD, but created by him from nothing. Nor is Christ only called Son, but begotten Son, and that which is truly begotten arises from the very substance of the begetter, says Cyril of Alexandria, Dial. 3 on the Trinity. Who finally will not be consubstantial to the Begetter, if he is in truth a Product, and as it were a certain natural fruit of the Begetter, says the same Cyril in book X of the Thesaurus. Nor is he called only begotten, but also μονογενὴς only-begotten, because he is one and alone begotten from the substance of the Father. Eunomius contended that he was called the μονογενῆ (only-begotten) Son because he alone was procreated by the sole Father, while the rest were made by the Father through him: Truly he should have been called μονοκτιστὸς (only-created), not μονογενὴς (only-begotten). Nor is he called μονογενὴς because he was begotten by the sole one, but because he is the only one who was begotten: Which emphasis of the word Chrysostom explains in book IV on the Incomprehensible, against the Eunomians. The word Son is present, and it is present in men and in Christ. But in us by a certain abuse of language, in Christ however properly. But the word only-begotten is his alone, because namely he is the one and only one begotten; and it does not fit any of the others, not even by abuse of language. And Basil in his Oration on faith. Therefore, as he is Son, he says, he possesses naturally what belongs to the Father: but as he is only-begotten, he comprehends all things in himself, dividing nothing with another. Furthermore, since we are commanded to believe in the Son of God, it is necessary that the Son of God himself be true God; since one must not believe except in the true God. Since we are commanded to believe in the name of the Son of God, what else is designated than the majesty of God? Since the majesty of God is accustomed to be insinuated through the name of God, Ps. 79:9, Ps. 110:9, Isa. 36:23. But to believe in the name of the only-begotten Son of God is not only to acknowledge that Christ is that only-begotten Son of God whom GOD the Father sent into the world as Savior, and who gave himself for the life of the world, but also to trust in him and his merit as the only Redeemer, by which alone we are liberated from the guilt of eternal judgment. Compare John 21:25, Acts 4:12, chapter 10:43. But this meaning is to be sought not so much from the distinct usage of the word 'to believe,' which Augustine otherwise inculcates not unprofitably—namely, that it is one thing to believe God, another to believe to God, and another to believe in God—since these phrases are sometimes interchanged. See Exord. XIV. v. 20. 31. 1. Paral. XXI. v. 20. Rom. IV. v. 3. as from the underlying subject matter and the explanation of Holy Scripture. Therefore, when we are commanded to believe in the name of the Son of God, not only assent is assigned, but primarily trust, which Scripture teaches everywhere is to be placed in Christ; indeed, it establishes salvation in Him. Such trust is therefore understood as that which is to be shown to God. Nor is any distinction of the object of trust as ultimate or non-ultimate to be admitted here in any way, as if God were the ultimate object of trust, and the Son of God not the ultimate and intermediate one. For in the same way we are commanded to believe in the Son of God, and in the name of the Son of God, as in God, and in the name of God, John XIV. 1. Just as in the same way we are baptized in the name of the Son and of the Father, Matt. XXIX. 19. and the Son is to be honored in the same way as the Father, John 5:23.

Thus the cause of the judgment of condemnation is established, which here is unbelief in general, not only actual, but whatever it may be, whether original or habitual. For it is certain that some are condemned not only on account of actual contempt of the Gospel and unbelief, but also on account of original and habitual [unbelief]. Let infants dying outside the Church be an example, whom, however, if the discussion is about all in general, we judge should be committed to the judgment of God; and among adults, those who perhaps, through the fault of their ancestors, were deprived of the Gospel and did not hear it: although even these are not free from actual guilt and unbelief, because they did not seek the Gospel, which they ought to have sought and could have. Therefore, unbelief taken γενικῶς (generally) remains the immediate, proximate, and adequate cause of condemnation. Meanwhile, we do not deny that sins are a remote and immediate cause; for sins of themselves merit condemnation, but on account of the intervention of the merit of Christ, actual condemnation follows not because of sins, but because of infidelity toward Christ. That is according to the judgment of the Law: This by the power of the Doctrine of the Gospel, which, even if it does not abolish the Law, nevertheless, if it is received by faith, derogates from the condemnation of the Law: if not, the effect of the Law is left intact. And this is why the final judgment is to be instituted according to either the Law or the Gospel as the norm. According to the Law, as regards the condemnatory sentence, which, by the power of the curse of the Law, awaits the infidels, because the judgment from which men are exempted through faith in Christ is left upon the infidels. Just as, on the contrary, the faithful will be absolved according to the Gospel. Hence the Holy Spirit is said to convict the world of sin, because it does not believe in Christ. On which words Augustine. Tractate 95 on John. This sin, he says, he placed as if before the others, because while this remains, the others are retained, and when this departs, the others are remitted. To this effect, Blessed Luther, Vol. II, Latin, Jena, on the Babylonian Captivity, fol. 271: No sins, he says, can condemn a baptized person, except unbelief alone; all others, if faith returns or stands in the divine promise made to the baptized person, are in a moment absorbed by that same faith, nay, by the truth of God, because He cannot deny Himself; if, however, you have confessed Him and have faithfully adhered to the One promising. For just as faith alone justifies and saves, although good works are not excluded from the justified, but are connected to faith, so unbelief alone condemns, although it is never without sins; yet the reason is different in this, that sins by their nature merit condemnation, but from an accident they do not inflict it unless they redound from infidelity and are its fruits; but good works by their nature can neither merit justification or salvation, nor contribute anything to it, even if they proceed from faith, as it is the office of faith alone to apprehend grace, justice, and salvation. The cause of this is that we find the matter of condemnation in ourselves, but we have the necessity to seek that of true justice and salvation in another, namely in Christ alone, Phil. 3:9 seq.

(IV.) The equity of the divine judgment, concerning which verse 19 is treated, is such that every cause is removed from God and the guilt is transferred to man. This is the condemnation, that light has come into the world: Thus the cause is removed from God; and men loved darkness rather than light: thus the guilt is transferred to men. This, says Christ, is the condemnation, that is, the cause of condemnation by a metonymy of the effect, as in Rom. 7:7, The Law is sin, or the cause of sin. Κρίσις (judgment) is taken for the other species of judgment, condemnation. Light is understood as Christ, that true Light, which came into the world, that it might illuminate every man, John 1:9. The Holy Spirit delights in this appellation of Light when He treats of Christ, Isa. 9:1, ch. 49:6, ch. 60:1, John 1:9, ch. 9:5, ch. 8:12, ch. 12:35, 36, 46, 47, etc. Therefore it is worthy of consideration, but Christ is called Light (1.) ὐσιωδῶς (essentially) and essentially, because He is that eternal Light, in which there is no darkness, 1 John 1:5, James 1:17, on account of the simplicity, purity, holiness, divine omniscience, majesty, and perfection of the divine essence; whence Irenaeus, lib. 2, cap. 6: God is all eye, all light. And Cyril, lib. 1, in John, cap. 8: The Son indeed is the true light, but the creature is light by illumination through grace; therefore, it is one thing for the true light to be light by nature, which illuminates the nations with light, and another for the creature, which is illuminated. (2.) Ὑποστατικῶς (hypostatically) on account of His personal origin. Thus He is called Light from Light, as God from God in the Nicene Creed, because He proceeds from the eternal light as the ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης πατρικῆς (radiance of the Father's glory), Heb. 1:3, ἀπαύγασμα φωτὸς ἀϊδίου (radiance of eternal light), Wis. 7:26. Not that there are two lights, of which one is kindled by the other, as a certain Hierax dreamed: but that the Son is the word, light, and splendor, from the true light, God the Father, with the unity of the essence of Light and divine Majesty saved. Concerning which beautifully St. Athanasius, Tr. 4, against the Arians: It is not, he says, as someone might have said, two lights. Yet there are two, the Sun and the splendor, but one light of the Sun in the splendor itself, everywhere light. By the same reason, the divinity of the Son is the divinity of the Father, whence it is also indivisible and thus one God, and no other besides Him. Wherefore when the true Light, says Cyril, lib. 1, in John, cap. 7, has shone forth from the true Light, the Son will not be numbered with the Light, but is rightly believed to be consubstantial with the Father. But by this word is excellently designated the generation of the Son of God from the Father, and His eternity, immutability, purity, immanence, and inseparability, and finally the ὁμοουσία (consubstantiality) and unity of substance. ἐνεργητικῶς, or efficiently on account of illumination. Because the Son is light, both of all in the world, and of the faithful in the Church, and of the blessed in glory; As the light of the Sun suddenly spreads itself, puts darkness to flight, illuminates all things, warms the earth, makes the seed grow, exhilarates living creatures, and makes the Sun itself visible: So the Son of God through the Word, which is called Light Ps. 119:105 and light Isa. 9:2, spreads the knowledge of himself through the proclamation and Writings of the Apostles, who themselves are also called the light of the world, Matt. 5:14, dispels darkness through the removal of ignorance, illuminates minds through the true knowledge of God, warms through ardent love, refreshes through living consolation, exhilarates the sad through the hope and taste of eternal life, and exhibits himself with the Father and the Holy Spirit as the true light, Matt. 11:25. But the Light is said to have come into the world, not because it was not in the world before, but because it appeared in the world in a peculiar way, when the world had deprived itself of the true Light: Since through sin, as an aversion from that true Light and from the Father of lights, it had been wrapped in darkness. The Light came into the world through the incarnation; when the incorporeal Light of the divinity, as Gregory the Great speaks, he assumed a body of humanity; thus the light came into the world, when it arose in the world in the lower hemisphere, and when the Orient from on high visited us, Is. 9, 2. Luke 1, 78. When the Sun of Righteousness arose, Mal. 4, 2. Therefore his birth is described by the rising of the Light, Is. 60, 1. John 12, 46. He came indeed into the world even before his advent in the flesh through the protoevangelium, the announcement, frequent appearance, the mission of the Prophets, and the preaching of the Word, but primarily he came into the world through his appearance in the flesh: then he shone in the darkness by preserving [it] on earth; by preaching, by performing miracles, by sending the Apostles into the world surrounded by darkness, and by illuminating all things everywhere with his light.

This denotes at the same time the state of the world, such as it was outside of Christ after the fall, because man, deprived of the true light, remained in mere darkness, namely in the darkness of ignorance and of the mind, John 12, 35. Eph. 4, v. 18. c. 5, 8. In the darkness of malice or of sins or of the heart, Rom. 13, 12. In the darkness of misery and affliction, Is. 9, 2. In the darkness, finally, of the exterior damnation and hell, Matt. 22, 13. For although some little sparks of concreated light remained, namely of natural notions, those were so far from being sufficient for beholding or attaining that true light, that they were all but completely extinguished by the darkness of ignorance and of sins: which, although they are not entirely nothing in natural and moral matters, yet in supernatural and spiritual matters they must be held as absolutely nothing, left outside that true light. Moreover, our spiritual misery and especially sin is compared to darkness; because as darkness separated from light obscures all things, begets cold and stiffness, sadness and horror: so sins separate from God, the true light, obscure the mind with errors, make the heart cold so that it stiffens toward good works, and produce mere anguish and torments.

Finally, the cause of Christ's advent is insinuated in these words, that he came as a light into the world, to perform that which light performs for dark places, that he did not come to increase or bring darkness, but to dispel it, not to blind, but to illuminate. Although by accident the blinding of many occurred, John 12, 40. Whence does this happen? Men loved darkness more than light: they were more delighted by the darkness of ignorance and iniquity than by the light of truth and holiness. That indeed seems clearly alien to reason, that anyone should be more delighted by darkness than by light. But the cause was the snatching away of the eyes of the mind, and the blinding done by Satan, 2 Cor. 4, 4, as also the pleasing titillation of the works of darkness to the flesh, since the flesh lusts against the spirit, Gal. 5, 17. It is evident, however, thus clearly the equity of the divine judgment against the incredulous. With these words, says Chrysostom, Homily 37, he takes away every excuse from the unfaithful. For if he had come to demand an account of works and to punish errors, one could certainly be excused if he did not follow him. But if he came to divide the light from the darkness, who will pity him who, having known the light, persists in remaining in the darkness? And a little later, indeed, says Chrysostom, he came not to judge nor to inquire, but to forgive sins, and to bestow salvation through faith. If he had come to judge, he would have some excuse. For who, conscious of any guilt, is accustomed to flee a judge: but to indulgence even the erring come to meet him. Why therefore he came to grant indulgence, it was consistent that those conscious of many crimes should show themselves with a ready mind, as was done by the publicans and sinners. If I had not come, says Christ, John 15, 22, and had not spoken to them, they would not have sin. For indeed he who dwells in darkness, with the light failing, is perhaps worthy of some pardon: but he who, when the light arrives, follows darkness, truly carries with him the proof of an evil and depraved mind. Cyril has it thus regarding this matter; If when they could come to the light, they preferred to lie in darkness, how are they not to be condemned themselves, who by their own depraved judgment choose for themselves torments, preferring worse things to better, and preferring darkness to light. August. tract. 12 in John. As much as is in the physician, Christ came to heal the sick man: he kills himself who does not wish to keep the physician's precepts: the Savior comes into the world, why is he called the Savior of the world? unless to save, not to judge the world; if you do not wish to be saved by him, you will be judged by yourself.

(V.) A fuller declaration, who those are who have hatred for the light; whom Christ describes a posteriori, namely from sins and evil actions as the consequences of incredulity: For their works were evil. For everyone who does evil hates the light. By which words he indicates those who persist in malice, as Chrysostom says: For indeed Christ came to grant indulgence, so that he might forgive old sins and make man more cautious for the future. For from evil works comes the contempt of light and incredulity; just as from good works the admission of light and faith is gathered. And what else is sin but the contempt of God, as Bernard says, sermon 32, on the manner of living well. What are sins but works of darkness, Rom. 13, 12. Which proceed from the spirit of darkness, Col. 1, 13, are carried out in darkness, 1 Thess. 5, 5, are nothing but the privation of true light, that is, they are darkness, 1 John 1, 5, 6. and they precipitate [one] into eternal darkness, 2 Pet. 2, 17. Moreover, Christ's statement is a general gnome about the custom of the impious and hypocrites, that everyone who does evil flees the light. For nature has imbued every evil, says Tertullian in Apolog. chap. 2, with either fear or shame. Finally, evildoers are eager to hide, avoid appearing, tremble when caught, deny when accused, and do not easily or always confess even when tortured. The incredulous hate the light of Christ, the Sun of righteousness, his doctrine as well as his presence, because it exposes their evil works. The world hates me, says Christ, because I testify of it, that its works are evil, John 7, 7.

(VI.) Finally, an illustration made from the contrary. But he who does the truth comes to the light, that his works may be manifested, because they are done in God. The Hebrews call a just and right work truth, Psalm XXIV. 2. Therefore, those are said to do the truth who devote effort to the truth and to truly good works; since these are nothing without true repentance, Augustine rightly says, he who does the truth accuses his own evil deeds in himself, he does not spare himself, he does not forgive himself, so that God may forgive, because he also wants God to forgive, he himself forgives. And he comes to the light to whom he gives thanks, because He showed him what he had hated in himself. They do not flee the light, but rejoice to come to the light, who are true children of the light, and walk in the light, so that their works may be set forth in clear light. Since truth fears nothing more than to be hidden. The cause is because such works are done in God, who is the true light, that is, with God as the author, according to GOD, and in God through that mutual spiritual περιχώρησιν, by which God is in the faithful, and they themselves are in God. The cause, therefore, to conclude the sum of Christ's words, of condemnation, just as Felargius himself infers in his Commentary on this passage. The only cause, I say, of condemnation is the love of darkness, and that which is perpetually combined with it, unbelief. And lest anyone object that it is the work of God that we believe, John 6:29, that faith is not of all, 2 Thess. 3:2, but of those to whom God has given it, Phil. 1:29, and therefore that those to whom faith has not been given are unjustly condemned: Pelargus replies that faith is indeed θεόδοτον [God-given]: meanwhile, the means by which He wills to confer faith are open to all, namely the external hearing of the word, serious reading and meditation upon it, and the external exercises of piety; the light of the Gospel is offered to all through preaching. But because men of their own spontaneous malice close their eyes and ears, flee the light, and delight in darkness—that is, in idolatry, ignorance, and the works of darkness, or sins—therefore they are justly damned, God not causing or infusing that unbelief, but punishing it by a most just judgment, and indeed eternally. As also Ambrose says, Sermon VIII on Psalm 118. The Sun of righteousness has risen for all, has come for all, has suffered for all, and has risen for all. If anyone, however, does not believe in Christ, he deprives himself of the general benefit, just as if someone were to exclude the rays of the sun by closing the windows. These are the words of Pelargus, which are deservedly opposed to other Calvinists. To which sentiment Irenaeus speaks excellently against the Heresies of Valentinus, book IV, ch. 76: 'Those who have fled the light will justly inhabit the darkness; and just as in this temporal light, those who flee it consign themselves to darkness, so that they themselves are the cause that they are deprived of the light and inhabit the darkness, and the light is not the cause of such a state, as we have said before: So also, because they flee the eternal light of God, which contains all good things in itself, they are themselves the cause that they inhabit eternal darkness, deprived of all good things, having become for themselves the cause of such a habitation.' For Scripture here removes all blame from God and imputes it entirely to man. See Prov. 1:24, Isa. 65:12, Hos. 4:6, 13:9, Matt. 22:4, 23:37, Acts 13:46. Therefore Origen rightly says in his Epistle to Titus: 'No man, he says, has been delivered by God to perdition: but each one of those who perish perishes by his own negligence and fault.' Nor is there here any distinction between God's negative or privative reprobation and positive, or between preterition and pre-damnation. Because for the same reason that someone is deprived of eternal salvation, for that same reason he is also reprobated to eternal death, and vice versa. St. Irenaeus has summarized the sum of the matter in the aforementioned place. God, foreknowing all things, prepared suitable habitations for both: to those indeed who seek the light of incorruptibility, who run to it, He kindly grants that light which they desire; but for others who despise it and turn themselves away from it and flee it, and as it were blind themselves, He has prepared darkness, which is consistent with those who oppose the light. And these things have been delivered before concerning this classic passage, and now are not rashly repeated here.

PART II. A discussion concerning Baptism, and the testimony of John concerning Christ as the bridegroom and Son of God.

Latin:

vers. 19. Salus nostra in altera vita sita erit, tum in omnimoda a peccatis, eorumque pœnis immuni- tate: tum in perfectissima Dei fruitione. Unde diversitas oritur, quantum ad salutem hujus, & alterius vitæ. In hac enim vita nondum à peccatis prorsus immunes sumus, etsi à peccati reatu liberemur. Nec à peccatorum pœnis ex- empti prorsus; quamvis enim illæ in quantum pœnæ sunt formaliter haud incumbant justifica- tis: Materiale tamen pœnarum, ceu sunt affli- ctiones, calamitates, mors denique ipsa, adhuc imminet iisdem. In altera autem plane à pec- catis quantum ad reatum, dominium, sensum, ra- dicem, & fomitem, nec non à pœnarum tum ma- teriali, tum formali immunes futuri sumus. Porro in hac vita fruimur quidem Deo, sed per fidem in Christum. Hinc Justitia instructi sumus perfectissima coram Dei tribunali, Justi- tia nempe Christi, qua dari perfectior non po- test: Sed ea nobis tantum λογιστικῶς (impu- tative) inest: quæ vero exinde in nos redun- das inhæsiva justitia, qua Gloriam Justitiæ Christi perfectam retecta facie speculantes, in eandem transformamur imaginem, multis mo- dis hic imperfecta est, adeo, ut à claritate in claritatem, magis ac magis subinde à Domino spiritu transformari necessum habeamus, donec ad perfectissimam claritatem alterius vitæ aspire- mus, 2. Corinth. cap. III. vers. 18. In illa ergo beata vita fruemur Deo non per fidem & impu- tationem, sed per visionem & beatam contem- plationem a facie ad faciem. Non ergo justitia Christi, obedientia ejus activa & passiva con- stans, tum λογιστικῶς nobis solum conveniet per imputationem, sed perfecta erit illa, quæ in e- lectis hærebit Justitia per mentis atque volunta- tis ipsorum perfectam cum divina mente ac vo- luntate conformationem ac consummatam Ima- ginis divinæ restaurationem. Dicis: Annon vero æterna est Justitia, quam Christus reduxit nobis Dan. cap. IX. vers. 24. Annon Justitia Christi fulgebimus in æternum? Num ornatus, quo nos condecorat Christus, vestis illa nu- ptialis in Agni nuptiis cœlestibus non obteget nos amplius, nec resplendescat in nobis? Re- spondeamus utique, sed modo longe perfe- ctiori. Hic enim vestimur eadem tantum per fidem, hic refulget eadem solum in nobis, qua imputatur nobis, aut etiam qua splendor a- liquis inde à Spiritu Domini excitatus in nobis micat, ut imaginis restitutæ claritas non plane nulla effulgescat: Siquidem fides gignat & emittat de sese radios quosdam illius claritatis, per dilectionem erga DEUM & proximum, quibus tamen tenebræ errorum & peccatorum multivariæ adhuc admixtæ sunt. Secus sese res habebit in altera vita. Ibi non vestiemur per fidem Justitia Christi, nec imputabitur nobis obedientia Christi per nudum tantum λογισμὸν mediante fide, non quod λογισμὸς & impu- tatio Dei finem habeat, aut æterna non sit; Manet enim illa, atque ita nobis in æternum transcribitur Christi Justitia: Quemadmodum ab æterno in prædestinatione nostri ad vitam transcripta fuit: etsi fides cesset in æterna vita quantum ad actum, non tamen quoad divi- num intuitum aut fructum, 2. Corinth. cap. XIII. vers. 13. 2. Corinth. cap. V. vers. 7. quæ nec ab æterno fuit, nisi ratione προγνώσεως & intuitus in decreto electionis DEI: Sed quod fructus & effectus imputationis Justitiæ, qui hic sese partiali divinæ imaginis reftauratione explicat, unde non nifi imperfecta est inhæsiva nostra ju- stitia, ibi futurus sit plenitudo Imaginis divinæ & Iustitiæ inhærens perfectissima; Quodque Chri- stus per fidem hic apprehensus mediante fide in nobis habitans, ut impleamur omni Dei pleni- tudine, Ephes. III. v. 16. 19. fine fidei interventu, & immediate illic in nobis habitaturus, non tan- tum obedientiæ suæ meritoriæ activa & passiva luce plenissima nos circumfusurus sit perfectis- sima, nobisque inexplicabili ratione, (est enim mediator & sacerdos noster in æternum, redem- tio, quam invenit, Iustitia, quam reduxit, æter- na est) sed & immensa Deitatis suæ Gloria, quam cum Patre & Spiritu Sancto communem habet, ut DEUS per essentiam, ut homo per unionis personalis Gratiam ita in nobis coru- scaturus, ut hinc refulgeat perfecta DEI ima- go, consummata Justitia & Sanctitas. De- nique finis salutis nostræ est Gloria DEI, ut æternum celebretur Paterna DEI dilectio, nec non unigeniti Filii DEI fraterna redemtio, ut & Spiritus Sancti superna Vocatio & Conver- sio, & infinita Sacro-Sanctæ Trinitatis in sa- lute nobis donanda gratia & gratiosissima sui communicatio. Hoc enim plenum nostrum gau- dium, ut inquit Augustinus lib I. de Trinitat. cap. 8. Quo amplius non est frui Sancta Trini- tate DEO ad cujus imaginem facti sumus. Quan- ta erit illic felicitas, inquit iterum Augustinus lib. 22. de Civit. DEI cap. 30. ubi nullum erit malum, nullum latebit bonum, vacabitur DEI laudibus, qui erit omnia in omnibus; Nam quid aliud agetur, ubi neque ulla desidia cessabitur, neque ulla indi- gentia laborabitur, nescio. Hæc de causis salu- tis.

Jam ergo latere causa perditionis non possunt: quæ vere non imputandæ cum Calvinianis, DEI absoluto decreto, sive reprobationis, sive præteri- tionis maximæ partis hominum. Tale enim nullum novit Scriptura Sacra: Nec gratiæ DEI inæqualitati, aut meriti CHRISTI particula- ritati: nullam enim, quantum ad ordina- riam salutis ὀικονομίαν, Gratiæ inæqualitatem, nec in merito & Redemtione differentiam CHRISTUS agnoscit, totum mundum ex æquo ita dilectum à DEO docet, ut toti illi ex æquo impensus fuerit Filius DEI unigeni- tus. Quam in Evangelio revelatam DEI vo- luntatem, nostrum est venerari, nec abscon- ditam hic aliam in DEO voluntatem venari. Sed neque in vocatione SPIRITUS SAN- CTI causa interitus quærenda est. Siquidem verbum idem, eadem Sacramenta dispensentur credentibus & incredulis, omnibusque exhi- beatur per idem Ministerium eadem salutife- ra Gratia sine discrimine; Ἀμέσως gratiam pe- culiarem dispensari Electis, Schwenckfeldianam resipit separationem Spiritus à verbo, Enthu- siasticam illuminationem citra verbum & ver- bi ministerium, sed de hoc alias. Relinqui- tur ergo, culpam perditionis unice sitam esse in hominibus. Siquidem ea nec in gratia DEI inæquali, nec in dispari CHRISTI Redem- tione, nec in vocationis Oeconomia ordinaria diversimoda quærenda sit. Hoc est quod Hos. XIII. v. 9. dicitur, Salus tua ex me, perditio ex te Israel.

Jam ergo de Judicio DEI adversus infideles agitur. Postquam enim CHRISTUS se missum in mundum dixit, non ut judicaret mundum, sed ut salvaretur mundus per eum, ne quis existimet, nullum jam metuendum es- se judicium, omnibus certo obtingere salutem: Exponit CHRISTUS, unde fiat, quod ni- hilo secius multi judicentur, & qui revera à Judicio immunes sint futuri, qui vero jam ju- dicati sint, in quos vim suam integra habeat le- gis judicialis sententia, Joh. cap. III. vers. 18. seq.

Observanda hic (I.) vera & unica immunitatis & exemtionis à Judicio causa, quæ est fides in CHRISTUM; Qui credit in ipsum, non judi- catur, inquit Christus. Judicium intelligitur tum condemnationis, cum judicari dicantur illi, qui condemnantur, tum sententia judiciaria le- galis, quæ omnes ferit non persistentes in o- mnibus, quæ in libro legis scripta sunt, Deut. cap. XXVII. vers. ult. Ab utroque Judicio im- munes, atque exempti sunt, qui in CHRI- STUM credunt, & à condemnatoria legis sententia, & à condemnatione ipsa actuali, cui secundam Legis sententiam obnoxii erant. Cau- sa est, quia Christus, in quem credimus, ju- dicium illud nostri loco subiit, factus pro no- bis maledictum, ut nos à maledictione liberaret. Gal. cap. III. vers. 13. Ipse condemnari voluit Judicio DEI ceu reus nostri vice, ne nos, qui vere eramus rei, judicari, & condemnari opus haberemus. Pro omnibus autem Judicium obiisse CHRISTUM, indubium est, quia omnium in sese peccata suscepit, pro omnibus vitam suam posuit; quemadmodum datus erat toti mundo, & in mundum venit, ne judica- retur mundus, ita pro totius mundi peccatis fa- ctus est propitiatio, 1. Joh. c. II. v. 2. Unde omnes hanc liberationem sibi applicare possunt, ne in judicium venire necesse habeant. Præclare id exposuit S. Athanasius de Incarnatione Verbi, Tom. I. operum p. 72. Quem hic audire juvat: Quemadmodum igitur debitum pro omnibus sol- vendum erat, debebant autem omnes ut more- rentur, ideoque reliquum erat, ut Filius DEI u- nigenitus pro omnibus sacrificium offerret, pro omni- bus Templum suum morti tradens, quo omnes inobnoxios & liberos à veteri prævaricatione efficeret. Morte enim opus fuit, & mortem pro omnibus inferri necesse erat, ut quod ab omnibus debitum erat, lueretur. Quamobrem Verbum, quia mori non potuit, utpote immortale, corpus sibi sumpsit, quod mori poterat, illudque ut suum pro omnibus obtulit, ut ita pro omnibus, omnibus ipse corpore conjunctus mortem patiens compesceret eum, qui habet mortis imperium, hoc est Diabolum, in liberaret illos, quotquot formidine mortis servi- tuti mortis per vitam erant obnoxii. Certe com- muni omnium Salvatore mortuo pro nobis, jam non ulterius, sicuti olim, secundum Legis com- minationem morte morimur, quotquot in CHRI- STO IESU confidimus. Obliterata est enim illa ipsa condemnatio. Cœterum nos corruptione desinente & abolita pro ratione corporea nostræ mortalitatis solummodo ad id tempus dissolvimur, quod DEUS unicuique definitum esse voluit, ut resurrectionis melioris compotes reddamur. Hæc omnia S. Athanasius, non modo potenter uni- versalem Christi Redemtionem asserens, sed etiam totum salutis nostræ negotium illu- strans.

(II.) Contraria judicii causa. Qui non credit, jam judicatus est. Judicatus dicitur in præterito, quod Judicium à lege jam latum ipsam premat, nec ab il- lo liberetur. Quamvis enim parta ipsi sit liberatio à maledicto legis, unde illam applicare sibi poterat, & debebat per fidem: Ea tamen non fruitur, quia fide non amplectitur liberationem : Non secus ac si pro captivo λύτρον solutum sit, hæc vero solutio contemnator, ut in captivitate re- manere liberatus malit, è qua, nisi susque de- que haberet λύτρον, egredi poterat. Causa ita- que vera & unica judicii condemnationis est in- credulitas. Maledictionis legis causa sunt pecca- ta: sed relictionis sub maledictione illorum, qui per Christi Redemptoris λότρον liberati sunt, propria & formalis causa non sunt peccata, si- quidem ab illa redempti sint: Sed incredulitas, quod redemptionem illam sibi non applicent, sed contemnant, atque ita sub judicio maneant, à quo immunes esse poterant. Manifestum er- go iterum est, liberatos illos fuisse per Christi meritum, non enim per incredulitatem con- temnere λύτρον pro se persolutum, nedum ob contemtum illum condemnari possent, ideo scilicet, quod non credant in hanc per Chri- stum factam sui liberationem, si vere ab ipso redempti haud essent; nisi quis dicere velit, ipsos credere debere, quod minime verum est & eapropter condemnari, quod idipsum non credant, quod vero consentaneum non est, quod nempe non credant, Christum pro se mortuum esse, & satisfecisse.

(III.) Causa hujus confirmatio; quia non cre- dit in nomen Unigeniti Filii. Si enim ad libe- rationis actualem fruitionem requiritur fides in nomen Unigeniti Filii Dei, qui missus est, ut mundus non judicaretur, sed salvaretur, per quem solum nobis obtingit liberatio, necesse est, omnes, qui non credunt in nomen unige- niti Filii, jam judicatos esse, ac sub judicio Le- gis condemnatorio æternum manere. Quo ipso à salutis æternæ fruitione ad æternam perditio- nem proscribuntur omnes Pagani, Turcæ, Ju- dæi, addo & Ariani, ac Photiniani. Nullus enim eorum in nomen unigeniti Filii Dei cre- dit. Turcæ generationem Filii Dei blasphe- mant. Judæi nec Filium Dei, nec Mysterium Redemptionis suscipiunt. Ariani Christum creaturam faciunt ex non-Entibus productam, non vero Filium ex substantia Dei Patris gene- ratum. Photiniani, etsi verum & naturalem Dei Filium verbis profiteantur, non tamen ni- si ratione nativitatis temporalis ita vocant, æter- nam vero generationem è substantia Patris impio ausu oppugnant, ob quam tamen unice Chri- stus Filius Dei unigenitus dicitur. Quomodo enim verus Genitoris fructus, ait Cyrillus Alexan- drinus lib. XII. Thesauri cap. XV. aliud Natura, quam genitor suus erit? Quum enim Pater na- tura Deus sit, erit Filius quoque Deus natura. Aliter minoris erit dignitatis, quam creatura suæ. Creatura enim consubstantialem sibi fructum ex se ipsis producunt: Deus autem secundum istos (Arianos intelligit) non natura DEUM ex se generabit, quod absurdum penitus est. Et lib. I. in Johan. cap. 3. Si ex Deo Patre unigenitus Fi- lius vere effulsit, etiam nolentes confiteri oportet, ex substantia naturaque Patris ipsum esse, id enim Filiatio vera significat; Quod si ex substantia Pa- tris secundum naturam non est, nec vere quidem Filius erit? Quis enim, inquit Athanasius orat. III. contra Arianos, audiens nominari Filium, non statim de eo cogitat eum proprium quoddam esse paternæ essentiæ? Nam ut Hilarius lib. VIII. de Trinitate, ait: Intelligentiæ istud humanus sensus excludit, ut aliquid a natura originis suæ nascendo diversum sit. Unde Augustinus libro contra sermonem Arianorum cap. 36. Tom. VI. Operum: Si quis istorum Filium suum non cujus ipse esset, sed diversae diceret esse naturae, exhae- reditari ab eo mallet Filius, quam hoc putare; quanta itaque impietate isti caecantur, qui cum confiteantur unigenitum Dei Filium, nolunt ejus- dem naturae, cujus Pater est, confiteri, sed diver- sae atque imparis, & multis rebus, modisque dis- similis, tanquam non de DEO natus, sed ab illo de nihilo creatus. Neque vero Filius tan- tum dicitur Christus, sed genitus Filius, id ve- ro, quod vere gignitur, ex ipsa gignentis sub- stantia oritur, ait Cyrillus Alexandrinus Dial. 3. de Trinit. Qui tandem Genitori consubstantialis non erit, si revera Genimen est, ac velut natu- ralis quidam fructus Genitoris, ait idem Cyrillus lib. X. Thesauri. Nec genitus dicitur solum, sed & μονογενὴς unigenitus, quod unus & solus ex sub- stantia Patris genitus sit. Eunomius μονογενῆ Fi- lium dici contendebat, quod Solus a solo Patre procreatus sit, cum reliqua per ipsum a Patre facta sint: Verum ita dicendus fuisset μονοκτι- στὸς Vnicreatus, non μονογενὴς Unigenitus. Nec vero μονογενὴς dicitur, quod a solo genitus sit, sed quod solus genitus sit: Quam emphasin vo- cis explicat Chrysost. libr. IV. de incomprehensi- bili, contra Eunomeos. Vox ista Filius inest, & hominibus inest & Christo. Sed nobis abusio- ne quadam, Christo vero proprie. At vox uni- geniti ipsius est solum, quia scilicet ipse unus & solus genitus est; neque aliorum ulli, ne quidem abusione, convenit. Et Basilius Oratione de fide. Ut ergo Filius est, inquit, naturaliter, quae Patris sunt, possidet: ut autem unigenitus, o- mnia in seipso comprehendit, nihil cum altero di- videns. Porro cum credere jubeamur in Filium Dei, oportet ipsum Dei Filium verum Deum esse; Siquidem non nisi in verum Deum cre- dendum sit. Cum jubeamur credere in nomen Filii Dei, quid aliud quam majestas Dei desi- gnatur? Siquidem per nomen Dei majestas Dei insinuari soleat, Psal. LXXIX. 9. Psal. CX. 9. Esa. XXXVI. 23. In nomen autem Filii Dei unigeniti credere, non est tantum agnoscere, Christum es- se Filium illum Dei unigenitum, quem DEUS Pater misit mundo Salvatorem, quemque pro mundi vita sese tradidit, sed etiam in ipsum, ejusque ceu unici Redemptoris meritum, con- fidere, quo solo ab aeterni judicii reatu libe- ramur. Confer Johan. XXI. ult. Actorum IV. 12. cap. X. 43. Quae vero significatio non tam ex distincto vocis credere usu, quem alioquin non inutiliter inculcat Augustinus, quod nempe aliud sit, credere DEUM, aliud credere Deo, aliud credere in Deum, petenda, quandoqui- dem hae phrases permutentur nonnunquam. Vid. Exord. XIV. v. 20. 31. 1. Paral. XXI. v. 20. Rom. IV. v. 3. quam ex substrata materia & explicatione Scripturae sacrae. Cum ergo in nomen Filii Dei credere jubemur, non assensus tantum, sed im- primis fiducia assignatur, quam in Christum collocandam esse passim Scriptura doces, imo in eo salutem constituit. Intelligitur itaque fi- ducia talis, qualis Deo exhibenda est. Neque hic ullatenus admittenda distinctio objecti fidu- ciae ultimi, vel non ultimi, ac si Deus ulti- matum fiduciae objectum sit, non ultinatum & intermedium Filius Dei. Eodem enim mo- do in Filium Dei credere jubemur, & in no- men Filii Dei, ut in Deum, & in nomen Dei Joh. XIV. 1. Quemadmodum eodem modo in no- men Filii & Patris baptizamur, Matth. XXIX. 19. ac similiter honorandus est Filius ac Pater, Joh. V. vers. 23.

Ita constat causa judicii condemnationis, quæ hic in universum incredulitas non tantum actualis, sed quæcunque seu originalis sive habitualis. Siquidem non solum ob actualem Evangelii contemptum, & incredulitatem, sed etiam ob originalem & habitualem quosdam condemnari certum. Exemplo sint infantes extra Ecclesiam morientes, quos tamen, si de omnibus universim sermo sit, Judicio Dei committendos censemus; & ex adultis illi, qui forte culpa Majorum privati Evangelio, id non audiverunt: tametsi & hi non vacent actuali culpa, & incredulitate, quod non quæsiverunt Evangelium, quod inquirere debebant, & poterant. Manet ergo incredulitas γενικῶς accepta causa immediata, proxima & adæquata condemnationis. Interim peccata causam remotam esse & immediatam non abnuimus; peccata enim merentur per se condemnationem, sed ob interventum meriti Christi, non propter peccata, sed propter infidelitatem in Christum sequitur actualis condemnatio. Illud juxta sententiam Legis: Hoc vi Doctrinæ Evangelii, quod etsi non tollat Legem, effequi tamen Legis condemnationi derrogatur, si fide suscipiatur: Sin minus, integer relinquitur Legis effectus. Atque hoc est quod judicium novissimum vel juxta Legem vel juxta Evangelium ceu normam instituendum sit. Juxta Legem, quantum ad sententiam condemnatoriam, quæ, vi maledicti Legis, infideles manet, eo quod judicium, cui eximuntur homines per fidem in Christum, super infideles relinquatur. Quemadmodum contra secundum Evangelium absolventur fideles. Inde dicitur Spiritus sanctus ἐλέγχειν mundum de peccato, quod non credat in Christum. In quæ verba Augustin. Tract. 95. in Iohan. Hoc peccatum, inquit, quasi præ cæteris posuit, quia hoc manente cætera detinentur, & hoc discedente cætera remittuntur. In quam sententiam B. Lutherus Tom. II. Latin. Ienens. de captivitate Babylon. fol. 271. Nulla, inquit, peccata baptizatum condemnare possunt, nisi sola incredulitas, cætera omnia, si redeat, vel stet fides in promissionem divinam baptizato factam, in momento absorbentur per eandem fidem, imo veritatem Dei, quia seipsum abnegare non potest; Si tamen eum confessus fueris, & promittenti fideliter adhæseris. Ut enim sola fides justificat & salvat, etsi non excludantur à justificatis bona opera, sed fidei connexa sint, ita sola incredulitas condemnat, etsi nunquam sit sine peccatis; dispar tamen in eo est ratio, quod peccata natura sua mereantur condemnationem, ex accidente vero non inferant, nisi ex infidelitate redundent, ejusque fructus sint, Bona opera autem natura sua nec mereri justificationem aut salutem, nec quicquam ad eam conferre possunt, etiam si ex fide proficiscantur, utpote cujus solius officium est, gratiam, justitiam & salutem apprehendere. Causa hæc est, quia materiam condemnationis in nobis invenimus, veræ autem justitiæ & salutis in alio quærere necesse habemus, in solo nempe Christo, Phil. III. vers. 9. seq.

(IV.) Æquitas divini judicii, de qua vers. 19. ita agitur, ut removeatur omnis causa à Deo, & transferatur in hominem culpa. Hæc est condemnatio, quod lux venit in mundum: Ita removetur causa à Deo; & homines magis dilexe- runt tenebris quam lucem : ita transfertur cul- pa in homines. Hæc est, inquit Christus, con- demnatio, id est, causa condemnationis per meto- nymiam effecti, ut Rom. VII. 7. Lex peccatum est, vel causa peccati. Κρίσις judicium pro altera specie judicii condemnatione accipitur. Lux in- telligitur Christus, Lux illa vera, quæ in mun- dum venit, ut illuminet omnem hominem, Joh. I. v. 9. Delectatur Spiritus sanctus hac appella- tione Lucis cum de Christo agit, Esa. IX. 1. cap. XLIX. 6. cap. LX. 1. Joh. I. 9. cap. IX. 5. cap. VIII. 12. cap. XII. v. 35. 36. 46. 47. &c. Digna ergo est consideratione, dicitur autem Christus Lux (1.) ὐσιωδῶς & essentialiter, quia est æterna illa Lux, in qua non sunt tenebræ 1. Joh. I. 5. Jac. I. 17. ob essentiæ divinæ simplicitatem, puritatem, san- ctitatem, divinam omniscientiam, majestatem & perfectionem; unde Irenæus lib. II. cap. 6. Deus totus oculus, totus lumen est. Et Cyrillus lib. I. in Johan. cap. 8. Filius quidem lux vera est, crea- tura autem ejus illuminatione per gratiam lux est, aliud ergo natura lux vera est, quæ gentes luce illustrat, aliud creatura, quæ illustratur. (2.) Ὑποστατικῶς ob personalem originem. Ita vocatur Lumen de Lumine, ut Deus de Deo in Niceno Symbolo, quod ab æterna luce pro- deat ceu ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης πατρικῆς Hebr. I. c. 3. ἀπαύγασμα φωτὸς ἀϊδίου, Sap. VII. 26. Non ut duo lumina sint, quorum alterum ab altero accensum sit, ut Hierax quidam somniavit: sed ut Filius verba lux & splendor sit, ex luce vera, Deo Patre, salva Lucis essentiæ & Majestatis di- vinæ unitate. Quo de pulchre S. Athanas. Tr. IV. contra Arian. Non est, inquit, ut quispiam dixerit duo lumina. Duo tamen sunt, Sol & splendor, una vero Solis lux in ipso splendore ubi- que lucis. Eadem ratione Filii divinitas Patris est divinitas, unde & indivisibilis est atque ita unus Deus, atque non alius præter ipsum. Quare cum Lux vera, inquit Cyrillus lib. I. in Johan. cap. 7. ex vera Luce Filius effulserit, non connumerabitur Luci, sed Patri consubstan- tialis jure creditur, Designatur autem hac vo- ce eximie generatio Filii Dei a Patre, ejusque æternitas, immutabilitas, puritas, immanentia & inseparabilitas, ὁμοουσία denique & substan- tiæ unitas. (3.) ἐνεργητικῶς, vel efficienter ob illuminationem. Quia Filius lux est, tum o- mnium in mundo, tum fidelium in Ecclesia, tum beatorum in gloria; Ut Solis lux subito se diffundit, tenebras fugat, omnia illustrat, ter- ram calefacit, sementem vegetat, animan- tia exhilarat, Solem ipsum visibilem reddit: Ita Filius Dei per Verbum, quod Lumen voca- tur Psal. CXIX. v. 105. & lux Esa. IX. 5. notitiam sui diffundit per præconium & Scripta Apostolo- rum, qui ipsi quoque lux mundi dicuntur, Matth. V. 14. tenebras dispellit, per igno- rantiæ sublationem, mentes illuminat, per veram Dei agnitionem, calefacit per ardentem dilectionem, reficit per vivam consolationem, tristes, exhilarat, per spem & gustum vitæ æ- ternæ, seque cum Patre & Spiritu sancto, ceu veram lucem exhibet, Matth. XI. 25. Lux au- tem venisse in mundum dicitur, non quod an- tea in mundo non fuerit, sed quod peculiari ra- tione in mundo apparuerit, cum mundus Lu- ce vera semetipsum privasset: Siquidem per peccatum ceu aversionem a vera illa Luce & a Patre luminum tenebris involutus fue- rit. Venit Lux in mundum per incarna- tionem; cum Lux incorporea divinitatis, ut Gregor. M. loquitur, corpus assumsit humanita- tis; ita venit lux in mundum, cum in Hemisphæ- rio inferiori mundo exorta est, & cum visitavit nos Oriens ex alto Es. 9, 2. Luc. 1, 78. Cum Sol Justitia exortus, Mal. 4, 2. Ideo per exortum Lucis nativitas ejus describitur, Es. 60, 1. Joh. 12, 46. Venit quidem in mundum etiam ante adventum in carnem per πρωτευαγγελίαν annunciationem, frequentem ap- paritionem, Prophetarum missionem, & Verbi prædicationem, sed imprimis venit in Mundum per apparitionem in carne: tum luxit in tenebris conservando in terris; prædicando, miracula e- dendo, Apostolos in orbem terrarum tenebris circumfusum emittendo, omniaque undiquáque luce sua collustrando.

Denotatur hoc simul status mundi, qualis ex- tra Christum fuerit post lapsum, quod homo vera luce destitutus in meris tenebris hæserit, in tene- bris nempe ignorantiæ, & mentis Joh. 12, 35. Eph. 4. v. 18. c. 5, 8. In tenebris malitiæ vel peccatorum sive cordis, Rom. 13, 12. In tenebris miseriæ & afflictionis, Es. V. 13. In tenebris denique exterioribus damna- tionis & gehennæ, Matth. XXII. 23. Quanquam enim scintillulæ aliquæ lucis concreatæ supererant notio- num nempe naturalium, illæ tamen ad lucem istam veram aspiciendam, vel consequendam tan- tum abest ut suffecerint, ut à tenebris ignorantiæ etiam & peccatorum tantum non penitus extin- ctæ fuerint: quæ uti in rebus naturalibus & mora- libus non plane nullæ sint, in supernaturalibus tamen, & spiritualibus prorsus nullæ haberi debent, extra lucem illam veram relictæ. Con- sertur autem tenebris miseria nostra spiritualis ac cumprimis peccatum; quia ut tenebræ separatæ à luce cuncta obscurant, frigus & rigorem, tristi- tiam & horrorem gignunt: sic separant peccata à Deo, vera luce, mentem obscurant erroribus, cor frigefaciunt, ut ad bona opera rigeat, merosque angores & cruciatus procreant.

Causa denique adventus Christi his verbis in- sinuatur, quod venerit ceu lux in mundum, id præ- stiturus, quod lux præstat locis caliginosis, quod non venerit, ut tenebras augeret, vel afferret, sed discuteret, non ut excæcaret, sed ut illuminaret. Quamvis ex accidenti evenerit multorum excæ- catio Joh. XII. 40. Unde hoc evenit? homines tene- bras magis amabant quam lucem: magis delecta- bantur tenebris ignorantiæ & iniquitatis, quam luce veritatis & sanctitatis. Id vero plane vide- tur à ratione alienum, quemquam magis delectari tenebris quam luce. Sed in culpa erat oculorum mentis ereptio, & excæcatio per Satanam facta, 2. Corinth. IV. 4. ut & grata carni operum tenebra- rum titillatio, cum caro concupiscat adversus spi- ritum, Gal. IV. 17. Patet autem ita luculenter æ- quitas judicii divini adversus incredulos. His verbis, inquit, Chrysostom. Homil. XXXVII. omnem auferat infidelibus excusationem. Nam ad ope- rum rationem si exigenda & errata punienda ve- nisset, posset sane quis excusari, si eum non seque- retur. Sin vero ad dividendam lucem à tenebris, quisnam ejus miserebitur, qui cognita luce in tene- bris potius manere perseverat? Et paulo post, pro- fecto, inquit Chrysostomus, non ad judicandum ne- que ad inquirendum venit, sed ad dimittenda pec- cata, & ad salutem per fidem largiendam. Si ju- dicatum venisset, haberet aliquid excusationis. Quis enim alicujus culpæ conscius est, judicem fugere so- let: Indulgentia autem errantes quoque obviam fiunt. Cur ergo ad indulgendum venit, consenta- neum erat, ut plurimorum criminum conscii, prompto animo se exhiberent, ut à publicanis & pec- catoribus factum. Si non venissem, inquit Chri- stus, Joh. 15 32. & non locutus fuissem eis, peccatum non haberent. Siquidem qui in tenebris versatur, deficiente lumine fortassis aliqua venia dignus est: Qui vero adveniente luce tenebras sectatur, mali profecto, pravique animi præ se fert argumentum. Cyrillus hac de re ita habet; Si cum ad lucem venire poterant, in tenebris jacere maluerunt, quomodo non sunt ipsi condemnandi, qui pravo sibi judicio crucia- tus adsciscunt pejora melioribus, & tenebras luci anteferentes. August. tract. 12. in Joh. Quantum in medico est, sanare venit Christus ægrotum: Ipse se interimit qui præcepta medici servare non vult: Ve- nie Salvator in mundum, quare Salvator dictus est mundi? nisi ut salvet, non ut judicet mundum, sal- vari non vis ab ipso, ex teipso judicaberis.

(V.) Uberior declaratio, quinam illi sint, qui lucem odio habeant; Quos à posteriori describit Christus, à peccatis nempe & actionibus malis ceu consequentibus incredulitatis: Erant enim opera eorum mala. Omnis enim, qui male agit, odit lucem. Quibus verbis eos indicat, qui in malitia perseverant, uti Chrysost. dicit: Siquidem ad indul- gendum venerit Christus, ut peccata vetera dimitte- ret & in posterum hominem cautiorem redderet. Ex operibus enim malis contemptus lucis & increduli- tas; quemadmodum ex bonis operibus lucis admis- sio & fides colligitur. Et quid aliud peccatum est nisi contemptus Dei, ut ait Bernhard. sermon. XXXII. de modo bene vivendi. Quid peccata sunt nisi opera tenebrarum Rom. 13, 12. Quæ à spiri- tu tenebrarum proficiscuntur, Col. I. 13. in tene- bris peraguntur 1. Thess. V. 5. nihil nisi privatio veræ lucis, hoc est, tenebræ sunt, 1. Joh. I. 5. 6. & ad tenebras æternas præcipitant, 2. Petr. II. 7. Est autem dictum Christi Gnome generalis de impiorum & Hypocritarum consuetudine, quod omnis qui male agit, lucem fugiat. Omne enim malum, inquit Tertullianus in Apolog. cap. 2. aut timore aut pudore natura perfudit. Denique malefici gestiunt latere, devitant apparere, tre- pidant deprehensi, negant accusati, ne torti qui- dem facile aut semper confitentur. Oderunt in- creduli Solis justitiæ Christi lucem, doctrinam pariter atque præsentiam ejus, quia patefacit mala eorum opera. Odit me mundus, inquit Christus, quia ego testor de eo, quod opera ejus mala sint, Joh. VII. 7.

(VI.) Denique illustratio à contrario facta. Qui autem facit veritatem, venit ad lucem, ut mani- festentur opera ejus, quia in Deo sunt facta. Ve- ritatem Ebræi vocant opus justum & rectum, Psal. XXIV. 2. Veritatem ergo facere dicuntur, qui veri- tati & operibus vere bonis operam navant; Quæ cum sine vera pœnitentia nulla sint, ideo recte Augustinus, qui veritatem facit, inquit, accusat in se mala sua, non sibi parcit, non sibi ignoscit, ut Deus ignoscat, quia & vult ut Deus ignoscat, ipse ignoscit. Et venit ad lucem cui gratias agit, quod illi, quod in se odisset, ostendit. Illi non fugiunt lucem, sed gaudent venire ad lucem, qui lucis veri filii sunt, & in luce ambulant, quo opera eorum in clara exponantur luce. Siquidem veritas ni- hil magis metuat, quam abscondi. Causa est, quia opera talia in Deo, qui vera lux est, facta sunt, hoc est, Deo autore, juxta DEUM, & in Deo per mutuam illam περιχώρησιν spiritualem, qua Deus est in fidelibus, & ipsi sunt in Deo. Causa er- go, ut concludamus summam verborum Chri- sti, damnationis, quemadmodum Felargius ipse infert in Comment. in h. l. Sola, inquam, damnatio- nis causa est amor tenebrarum, & qua illi perpetuo conjuncta incredulitas. Et ne quis objiciat opus Dei esse ut credamus Johan. VI. 29. fidem non esse omnium 2. Thess. III. 2. sed eorum, quibus donavit Deus Phil. I. 29. ideoque inique condemnari eos, quibus data non sit fides: respondet Pelargus: fi- dem sane esse θεόδοτον: media interim, quibus con- ferre vult fidem, patere omnib. auditum nempe ex- ternum verbi, seriam lectionem, & meditationem e- jus, & externa pietatis exercitia offerri omnib. lucem Evangelii per prædicationem. Quia vero homines spontanea malitia oculos & aures claudunt, lucem fugiunt & tenebris delectantur, hoc est, idololatria, ignorantia, & operibus tenebrarum, sive peccatis, idcirco juste damnari, Deo incredulitatem illam non efficiente, non infundente, sed justissimo judicio pu- niente, & quidem æternum. Uti etiam ait Ambros. serm. VIII. ad Psal. 118. Sol justitiæ omnibus ortus est, omnibus venit, omnibus passus est, & omnibus resurrexit.
