Si quis autem non credit in Christum, generali beneficio se ipse privat, ut si quis clausis fene- stris Solis radios excludat. Hæc Pelargus, quæ aliis Calvinistis merito opponuntur. In quam senten- tiam præclare Irenæus adversus Hæres. Valent. l. IV. c. 76. Qui fugerunt lumen juste inhabitabunt tene- bras, quemadmodum autem in hoc temporali lumi- ne, qui fugiunt illud, ipsos se tenebris mancipant, ut ipsi sibi causa fiant, quod destituantur à lumine, & inhabitant tenebras, & non lumen causa est bujus- modi conversationis, quemadmodum prædiximus: Sic æternum Dei quod fugiunt lumen, quod continet in se omnia bona, ipsi sibi causa sunt, ut æternas inha- bitent tenebras, destituti omnibus bonis, sibimetipsi causa bujusmodi habitationis facti. Culpam enim omnem à Deo hic removet Scriptura, eamque in solidum imputat homini. Vid. Prov. 1, 24. Es. 65, v. 12. Hos. 4, 6. c. 13, 9. Matth. 22, 4. c. 23, 37. Actor. 13, 46. Ideo recte Origenes in Epistolam ad Titum. Nemo, inquit, hominum à Deo in perditionem tradi- tus est: sed unusquisque pereuntium sua negligen- tia perit & culpa. Neque hic ulla distinctio inter Dei reprobationem negativam, vel privativam, & positivam aut præteritionem & prædamnationem. Quia ob quam causam quis salute æterna privatur, ob eandem quoque ad æternam mortem repro- batur, ac vice versa. Summam rei hisce complexus est S. Irenæus loc. cit. Deus omnia præsciens utrisque aptas præparavit habitationes, iis quidem qui inqui- runt lumen incorruptibilitatis, qui ad id recurrunt, benigne donans hoc, quod concupiscunt lumen; aliis vero id contemnentibus & avertentibus se ab eo & id fugientibus, & quasi semetipsos excæcantibus congruentes lumini adversantibus præparavit tene- bras. Atque hæc de loco isto classico antehac tra- dita sunt, nunc haud temere huc repetita.

PARS II. Disceptatio de Baptismo, & testificatio Ioban- nis de Christo sponso & Filio Dei.

## 3:20
Vers. 20. For everyone who does evil hates the light) It is a proverb taken from the common people. Euripides, Iphigenia: for the night is for the thief, but the light is for the truth. Philo on Caligula: to him the light of the sun is altogether unwelcome, but not so to those who, if there is anything darker than darkness, are in the disposition of their deeds. And shortly after: since good things require the brightness of midday for display, but shameful things, they say, require the remotest parts of Tartarus. Similar is that proverb: those who get drunk, get drunk at night. Hence the 'tenebriones' (lurkers in darkness) and 'lucifugæ' (light-shunners). Xenophon, Cyropaedia II: those who wish to do wrong seem to do so more when they are in the dark. And on Agesilaus: it is fitting for shameful deeds to be hidden, but for a life of beauty, the light provides more adornment. Seneca, Ep. CXXII: The light is burdensome to a bad conscience. See an excellent explanation of this passage in Chrysostom on chapter IV to the Ephesians, II. 19.

that his works may not be exposed) Nor may the baseness of the life he leads appear to himself. Eph. VI. 13. But all things when they are exposed by the light are made manifest.

These things pertain not so much to those very people who commit evils, lest the baseness of them appear to themselves, as to others by whom they might be either confounded or dragged to punishment.

Latin:

Vers. 20. Πᾶς γὰρ ὁ φαῦλα πράσσων μισεῖ τὸ φῶς) Proverbium est ex vulgo desumtum. Euripides Iphigenia: κλέπτων γὰρ ἡ νὺξ: τῆς δὲ ἀληθείας τὸ φῶς. Philo de Caligula:ἐκεῖνῳ δὲ ἡλίου ἡ φῶς συνόλως ἀσπασόν ἐστιν, ἀλλὰ οὐχὶ τοῖς, κἄν εἴ τι σκότυς ἀφεγγέστερον, εἰς τὴν τῶν ἰκτόρων ἔγων διάθεσιν. Et mox ἐπειδὴ τὰ μὲν καλὰ περιαυγείας μεσημβρινῆς δεῖται πρὸς ἐπίδειξιν. Τὰ δὲ αἰσχρά, φασιν, ἐσχατιᾶς ταρτάρῥ. Simile proverbium illud: οἱ μεθυσκόμενοι νυκτὸς μεθύουσι. Hinc tenebriones lucifugæ. Xenophon de Cyri Instit. II. οἱ διὰγυόμενα ῥαδιοργεῖν πῶς μᾶλλον δοκεῖν ὥσπερ οἱ ἐν σκότη ὄντες. Et de Agesilao: αἰσχυργίᾳ μὲν τὸ ἀφανίζεσθαι πρέπειν, τῷ δὲ εἰς κάλλος βίῳ τὸ φῶς μᾶλλον κόσμον παρέχειν. Seneca Ep. CXXII. Gravis malæ conscientiæ lux est. Vide egregiam hujus loci explicationem apud Chrysostomum in caput IV. ad Ephes. II. 19.

ἵνα μὴ ἐλεγχθῇ τὰ ἔργα αὐτοῦ) Nec sibi ipsi appareat vitæ, quam ducit, turpitudo. Eph. VI. 13. τὰ δὲ πάντα ἐλεγχόμενα ὑπὸ τοῦ φωτὸς φανεροῦται.

Hæc non tam ad eos ipsos, qui patrant mala, ne sibi ipsis eorum turpitudo appareat, quam ad alios pertinent, à quibus vel confundi, vel ad pœnam trahi possint.

## 3:21
Vers. 21. But he who does the truth) He who acts sincerely: Thus 2 Kings XX. 3, to walk in truth is explained as with an upright heart. Add Ps. XXV. 5, LXXXVI. 11, Proverbs XXVIII. 16. It is joined with light in Ps. XLIII. 3, Ephes. V. 8, 9. And in this epistle I. 1. 6. Understand this also as the light after it has shone: for the resolve to amend one's life is described by these words.

comes to the light) Philo in the cited passage: good things require the brightness of midday for display. Plutarch: no one wraps darkness around good works.

that his works may be made manifest) So that he himself may examine and direct these works according to that doctrine, for he does not fear the examination.

that they have been wrought in God) 'en' for 'kata', according to the nature and will of God, thus 'en kyrio' (in the Lord) 1 Cor. VII. 39.

It is pleasing to add here what we once proposed concerning this classic passage, which is almost the most important among the 'logia' or Oracles of the mouth of the Lord. Christ now approaches the root of the cause, and with the veil of the Old Testament removed, openly explains the mystery of universal salvation, with all its causes elucidated, and at the same time, the causes of the damnation of men set forth in opposition. Chrysostom renders this coherence: Do not wonder that I must be exalted, so that you may be saved. For so it seems to the Father, who loved you so much that He gave His Son for servants, and indeed ungrateful ones. But let us examine the weight of the words. For individual words, as Chrysostom again warns, have great force. They express: I. The beginning of salvation, the love of God the Father, gratuitous and immense. So God loved the world. The grace and love of God is the source of all our salvation. There was no cause for this love, because nothing worthy of love could be found in us, who were worthy only of hatred and wrath. Therefore, out of mere grace, God loved us. By which name 'agape', the love of God, is proclaimed here. For 'agapan', according to Phavorinus, is 'agein' (to lead), namely, 'eis to pan' (into the whole), that is, to be carried toward the beloved object with one's whole soul and in every way. Otherwise, it is called 'oiktirmos' or the mercy of God, Luke VI. 36. And here are also commemorated the 'ta splanchna eleous', the bowels of mercy, an explanation of the elegant Hebrew word 'rachamim', designating uterine or maternal mercy, Ps. LI. 7, Luke I. 13, concerning which see more at length in T. 2, Syst. Theol. c. II. Paul proclaims in Eph. II. 7, the 'hyperballonta plouton tes charitos autou en chrestoteti', the superabundant riches of His grace in His kindness, and testifies that God Himself commends His charity toward us in that He willed to have mercy on us while we were still sinners, Rom. V. 8.

II. The object of love. By the word κόσμος, beyond controversy, human beings are designated, not indeed angels. Furthermore, that only the elect are indicated here from among human beings, some of the Calvinists contend sharply, primarily Beza in his notes on 1 John 2:2; Piscator in his notes on this passage and 1 John 2:2; Altingius in his Loci Communes, Heidelberg, part 2, book 4, page 400; Johannes Maccovius, Collegium on Predestination, disputation 12, page 36; Antonius Walaeus in his Loci Communes, page 288; Wendelin in Christian Theology, book 1, chapter 17, page 284; which Friedrich Spanheim fervently asserts above others in his Exercitation on Universal Grace, page 732, who also, which you might wonder at, attempted to demonstrate particular grace from this passage. But it is too manifest that the elect alone cannot be understood here by the word world, but rather that all human beings are denoted by Christ. These reasons can be noted: (1) Nowhere in the whole Scripture does the word κόσμος denote the elect alone; that meaning is deservedly rejected as merely arbitrary and precarious. (2) When the word world is used regarding human beings, it either denotes all human beings generally, or specifically the reprobate; but that it is not taken specifically regarding the reprobate here is beyond controversy. (3) The discussion here is absolutely about the world, nor does any reason for restriction appear as to why it should be determined to the elect alone, which argument Heinrich Bullinger deservedly urges in the Calvinist school in his commentary on this passage: if he had said human beings, we could have understood the just and the good; again, it would have been permitted to understand human beings of this or that order, status, or age: but now he has said world; he says to John: the world is placed in the evil one; therefore, by the word world he signifies not human beings of one age, sex, or order, but all human beings of all ages, and those dwelling in the world and subject to sin. (4) The world is also dealt with here διαστατικῶς (distinguishingly), because, namely, it was corrupt and lay in extreme misery through the deadly strikes of the infernal serpent. Wherefore the word world can by no means be understood as the faithful or the elect, which argument Johannes Bergius urges in his explanation of this saying, German, page 7. Nor indeed does Christ understand the elect only by the world here, as they are already separated from the world, but the whole human race taken universally, as it lies in sin, and as it is commonly called through the Gospel to repentance and faith in Christ. (5) That world which did not exist before and outside the mission and redemption of the Son of God cannot be understood here at all: because, therefore, the discussion here is about a world to be redeemed, not a world already redeemed and enjoying redemption. But the world of the elect or the faithful did not exist at all before or outside the mission of the Son of God, for faith presupposes the redemption which it apprehends, and therefore it cannot be prior to redemption. (6) The discussion is about that world which was under sin, the power of Satan, and eternal condemnation, and thus stood in need of a Redeemer and redemption. But the world of the faithful is no longer under sin, the power of Satan, and eternal condemnation, where God is said to have reconciled (redeemed) the world; it is not to be disputed regarding the reprobate, nor regarding the elect, says Musculus on 2 Corinthians 5:17. (7) The type of the bronze serpent confirms this, because that remedy was proposed not as a particular but as a universal one to all bitten Israelites, by which they could recover from the poisonous strikes of the serpents, but not to certain ones only who were peculiarly beloved; hence the grace which came to human beings in Christ is not particular, but consecrated to the whole human race bitten by the infernal serpent. (8) The love of God is extolled by the emphatic particle with singular emphasis and admiration. Thus God loved the world, concerning which Chrysostom can be seen on this passage, wherefore it can neither be restricted nor determined, nor ought it to be. (9) That world is understood here as loved by God, to which He gave His Son as Redeemer, whom He gave not to the elect or the faithful alone, but to all the descendants of Adam, Genesis 3:15, and to all the peoples of the earth, chapter 22:18, concerning which Johannes Grotius, Commentary on Titus 2, page 357: God loved the whole the world and destined the Son for it, why therefore should I accept love for the elect alone, I do not find a suitable reason. He had promised the seed of the woman to the whole world, Gen. III. 15. therefore He gave Him to the whole world. Then Christ gave Himself and thus made satisfaction not for a few, but for the whole world or the entire human race, or all men, 1. Tim. II. 6. Heb. II. 9. 1. John II. 2. and that sufficiently, with an actual sufficiency. So far Grotius. (10) Just as all are subject to perdition outside of Christ, so Christ is said to be given to all, and to the whole lost world, so that whoever among those lost ones believe in Him may not actually perish, but obtain eternal life, whence rightly Christopher Pezelius in the explanation of this passage p. 291. the world signifies, by synecdoche, the whole human race, which is contaminated by sin, and to which the wrath of God and eternal punishment is due. (11) The discourse here is about that world which can be divided into believers and non-believers, those who are judged and those who are not judged, those who perish, and those who do not perish, but have eternal life. But the world of the elect cannot be divided into believers and non-believers etc. Therefore, which argument Bergius urges in the explanation of this saying in German p. 8. That this is the genuine interpretation, he says, of the words of Christ, it may be manifest, both from these words, by which eternal life is promised to all men commonly, if only they believe in the Son, and from the following, where this world is divided into two parts, of which one believes in the Son, therefore embraces the love of God, light, life and salvation, but the other does not believe etc. (12) Those who are judged from the world, for this very reason are said to be judged, because they do not believe in Christ given to the world, so that the world might be saved through Him. But whoever ought to believe in Christ the Savior and through faith in Him obtain salvation, they are certainly bound to believe that Christ was given to them, that He redeemed them, died for them, and was made a propitiation, whence we argue further; Whatever the reprobate are bound and commanded to believe, that must be true. But the reprobate are bound and commanded to believe that Christ was given to them as Savior and died for them; Therefore it must be true that Christ was given to the reprobate as Savior and died for the reprobate. Further: For what the reprobate are damned, that it pertains to them by the intention of God, is certain. But the reprobate are damned because of the grace of God and the redemption of Christ neglected, therefore. Rightly Crocius in the Prussian conversion p. 2. c. 6. p. 472. How all are bound to embrace by faith what does not pertain to all under the condition of faith: how the reprobate can be damned because of unbelief, if in no way at all Christ died for them, no one is damned, except because of the neglect of that thing, which in some way pertains to him (13) Having dismissed the opinions of the Fathers, who are all to a man in agreement with us, and acknowledge here the universal love of God, we bring forward only Augustine, whom the Particularists, as also the Innovators (I point to the Calixtines) wish here to depart into a different view, who in sermon 128 de tempore: Let us read, he says, in the Scriptures, that the salvation of the whole human race has been redeemed by the blood of the Savior, for the Evangelist John says in ch. III. for Christ did not come into the world to judge the world etc. See therefore that money not so much a small portion of a field bought, as the abundant possession of the whole world. Let Tractate 12 on John be compared, on the words of ch. 3, 17. God did not send His Son etc. Therefore as much as it is in the Physician to heal, He came to heal the sick man, he destroys himself, who does not wish to keep the precepts of the Physician etc. But the sick man was the whole human race, and from it the reprobate destroy themselves, while they neglect the salvation of the Physician. (14) To whom, because the chief of the Reformers interpret the word world as all men, Calvin himself, the Antipelanus of them, in his Commentary on this passage, says he applied a universal note, both so that he might invite all indiscriminately to the participation of life, and so that he might cut off excuse from the unbelievers: to the same also pertains the name of the world, which he used before. And in ch. I. 29. When he says, the sin of the world, he extends this grace to the whole race then indiscriminately. also in the Harmony published in the year 1555, in the exposition of the Genealogy of Christ, p. 28. although, he says, from the time when God had made His covenant with Abraham, the Redeemer had been promised peculiarly to his seed, we know however that immediately from the fall of the first man it was necessary for all, just as He was then destined for the whole world. Finally in the book on predestination p. 917. There is no controversy, he says, that Christ came to expiate the sins of the whole world, but that solution immediately occurs, that whoever believes in Him may not perish, but have eternal life. Nor indeed is it asked now what kind of Christ is, or what He may avail by Himself, but to whom He offers Himself to be enjoyed. Phil. Melanchthon in the body of Doctrine, which most Calvinist Churches and especially the Anhalt and Bremen ones today accept, as a Symbolic Writing in the Books. Commentary under the title on the Gospel has this: But we establish that the promise of the Gospel is universal, for just as the preaching of repentance is universal, so the preaching of the remission of sins is universal. To this are gathered the universal sentences about the Gospel, which exist here and there in the Scriptures, as John III. So God loved etc. also in Paul, He concluded all under sin. But that not all obtain the promises of the Gospel, it happens because not all believe. The Palatine Theologians in the Refutation. In the Golden Ladder and Aureolus on the death of Christ, published in German in the year 1592, p. 55, they say regarding the saying of Christ in John 3: whereas with Beza the word 'loved' is interpreted especially concerning the peculiar love of God toward believers and the elect, it is entirely clear and necessary that the word 'world' signifies indefinitely all and every kind of believer from the whole world; we, however, gladly following the common exposition concerning the general love of God toward the whole human race, interpret the word 'world' universally concerning all men in general. Just as it is understood in that manner by Calvin himself in Harm. p. 35, Wolfgang Musculus on John p. 71, Zanchius in Miscell. p. 282, and many others. Why, therefore, do they object Beza to us more than John or others? The Theologians of Great Britain: George of Llandaff, John Davenant, Samuel Ward, Thomas Goad, Walter Balcanquall in their judgment on the second Article of the Remonstrants. God, they say, having pitied the fallen human race, sent His Son, who gave Himself as the price of redemption for the sins of the whole world. The Belgian Doctors and Professors of Leiden and Franeker, Francis Gomarus, John Polyander, Antonius Thysius, Antonius Walaeus, as also Lubertus Sibrandi, explain it in this place concerning all the descendants of Adam and thus all men in the judgment presented at Dordrecht concerning the second article. We confess, they say, that the merit and value of the death and satisfaction of Christ is of such great price that it is sufficient not only to expiate all the sins of men, but also to save all the descendants of Adam, however many more there might be, provided they embraced it with true faith. John 3:16. To whom also are added, among the more ancient, Henry Bullinger on this place, praised before, and Rudolph Gualther in his exposition on 1 John 2. Homily 5: He wished to use the word 'world' so that we would not think anyone excluded from the merit of Christ, just as the Lord Himself says: 'So GOD loved the world.' And the whole Scripture proves that such promises pertain to all men, etc. Christopher Pezel in his explanation of this passage warns that we should not allow this quality and universal promise to be evaded or undermined by any tricks of cavillers, etc. William Perkins in his Golden Chain, ch. 31, p. 72, accepts this statement concerning the whole human race. Bartholomaeus Pitiscus, Professor at Heidelberg, in a sermon on John 3, p. 7, interprets it concerning the whole world and all men. Abr. Scultetus, in his Scholastic exposition of the Gospels for the second day of Pentecost, says: Who is the world that is loved by this Lord? It is the miserable and sin-contaminated human race, which has fallen away from God, etc. Raphaël Eglinus, in his disputation on the covenant of God, p. 40, acknowledges that a common remedy is here opposed to a common fall, and that the love of God toward the world—that is, toward the whole human race fallen into misery by the craft of Satan—is proclaimed. Wolfg. Musc. likewise in John asserts this opinion at length, as does also Hieron. Zanch. in his Miscellanies. p. 282, as well as Zacharias Ursinus in his Exegesis of the Heidelberg Catechism, and others. Then, among the more recent and modern writers, the Syncretists and hypothetical universalists, one and all, who defend the universal grace of God with us, appeal to this passage above all others. See Paulus Steinius in his Evangelical Ecclesiastical Fraternity, part 1, p. 734; Joh. Crocius in his Ladder of Salvation, published in German in 1638, p. 631, from the Hessians; Joh. Bergius from the March, in his German explanation of this saying; Gerhard de Neufuille, disputation 1 on predestination, from the Bremensians; and especially Ludovicus Grocius in his Syntagma Theologiae, p. 1031, and in his dyodecade of disputations, p. 475: The word 'world' is taken here universally, he says, for the whole human race, which by nature lies in sin, etc., who expressly confirms this opinion and brings forward, among others, Ursinus in the place cited. Ursinus, he says, a theologian remote from party spirit, takes the word 'world' with the Apostle John, not for the elect alone, as certain more recent writers interpret, but for the whole fallen human race, to which we deservedly subscribe. Concerning the Anhaltines, see the brief and clear repetition of the orthodox Confession, which the churches of the principality of Anhalt embrace, 1581, art. II, on predestination, p. 44. Moses Amyraldus has set forth at length, against Spanheim, the opinion of the French of Saumur and especially of their teacher Joh. Cameron, as well as of his colleague Testard, that the whole human race is comprehended by the word 'world.' To say nothing, finally, of Joh. Maccovius himself, who in his Coll. on predestination, disp. 12, p. 36, interprets this passage concerning the whole human race.

III. The most ample gift: That he gave his only-begotten Son. A more eminent and divine gift he could not give. For he did not give an angel or an archangel, nor some man endowed with divine majesty, who are also called sons of God (Job 38:7; Ps. 82:6), but that is said metaphorically; but his very own Son, properly so called, or his own (Rom. 8:32), not one out of many, but the only-begotten of the same essence as himself he gave. For the Son of God was not made but begotten (Ps. 2:7; Prov. 8:33), and indeed by a proper generation, which imports the communication of the same essence with the relation of paternity and filiation, and a most singular manner, so that he alone and uniquely is begotten by God the Father. Therefore he is called μονογενὴς or only-begotten: for he is the only-begotten whom the Father begat as the only one, says Hieron. ad Helvid. c. 5, and this is confirmed by the origin of the word, its native signification, and common sense, as well as the perpetual usage of Scripture, which nowhere attributes the word μονογενὴς except to the only Son. Add the exaggeration of the love of God, which Cyrillus Alexandrinus excellently urges here in his book 2 on John, c. 51: for if, as you (Arians) say, he is not from the substance of the Deity, he cannot be the Son of God according to nature, and so that wonderful love of the Father will appear to be nothing. For he gave a creature for creatures, not the true Son. But in what manner God gave his only-begotten Son is to be gathered from what precedes, namely, that he did not give him in just any way, but that he might be lifted up as the serpent in the desert, or be nailed to the cross. For he gave him to the world when he sent him into the world through the incarnation; he gave him when he subjected him for the world to the law through servile subjection (Gal. 4:4); he gave him when he delivered him to death for the world through vicarious satisfaction (Rom. 8:22). Whence the scope of the love of God the Father, who gives the Son, and the liberation of the Son, who redeems the world, is equal, as will be taught in the following verse, 17.

IV. The most gracious covenant. By which he demands nothing else from us than faith; that everyone who believes in him, etc. He does not, I say, demand the obedience of the moral law, he does not demand Levitical sacrifices, or anything similar that we could contribute from our own, he requires faith alone, so that by it we may receive this most gracious love of his, this most precious redemption of his Son, and place our trust solely in the only-begotten Son, the savior of the world, delivered for us. But he demands it from us in such a way that he also wills to work it in us through the Holy Spirit, since that is not in our power, but of divine grace and power. Nor, however, does he only will that everyone who believes in him should have life through him, but he also wills that all should believe in him; he also wills, as far as it is in him, to work faith in all and to lead all to faith. He does not will faith only preceptively or approbatively, but he also wills faith communicatively and effectively, by destining and offering the means of faith to all and by them intending faith in them.

The more recent Calvinists, and especially the Syncretists, and the Hypotheticals, such as the Bremensians, Berliners, Hessians, and the French of Saumur, and likewise some Britons, indeed concede that Christ was sent for all, that Christ redeemed all, that eternal salvation was procured for all, and that the salvation of all was intended by this mission and redemption: but under the hypothesis, if all believe. In the Synod of Dort, which presents public judgments, these things can be observed most especially regarding this matter. The theologians of Great Britain in the judgments of the foreigners concerning the second Article, p. 90. Salvation, they say, is a thing promised in the new covenant, nor is it promised except under the condition of faith: Since, therefore, not all men have faith in Christ, under whose condition alone salvation is promised, it is certain that the death of Christ did not obtain for all, but only for the faithful, a restoration into a state of grace and salvation. This is the opinion of the Hessians, p. 97. That the value, dignity, and sufficiency of the death of Christ are so great that through it all men, provided they truly believe in Christ, can be reconciled to God and obtain the remission of sins. From the Bremensians, Matthias Martinius in the judgments on the second Article, p. 116, thesis 23. Christ, he says, has merited the favor of God for all, if they actually believe, and thus from the favor of God [obtain] righteousness and life, etc. Ludovicus Crocius in his judgment, p. 127, thesis 2, says that not only the counsel, scope, and intention of God the Father delivering the Son to death, but also of the Son undergoing death, is to acquire, obtain, and merit for all and each of the sinners by that most precious death and passion, that if they repent, when they are capable of his doctrine and believe in Christ, they can be reconciled with God and receive the remission of sins. Item, in the dyodecade of dissertations, p. 491. God wills all men to be saved, provided they fulfill the covenantal condition. And p. 594, he says that Christ is the Redeemer and Savior of all men and of each one, even of those who do not become partakers of salvation, so that He died for all and each, and merited the remission of sins and reconciliation with God under the condition of faith. From the Marchians, Mr. Joh. Bergius in a Disputation held at Königsberg in the year 1621 argued thus: Whatever promises are determined by the condition of faith, in these no difference can be given. All Evangelical promises are determined by the condition of faith, therefore in Evangelical promises no difference can be given. He pursued his opinion at greater length in a German sermon on this saying. From the French, John Cameron in his miscellaneous works, Epistle on the Satisfaction of Christ, p. 531 of his works. He describes it thus: Scripture, he says, teaches us God's antecedent love, so that it contains certain degrees, of which the first is this, that Christ was given both to the Gentiles and to the Jews, but with this condition, if they believe in Him. This degree is described in that famous passage: God so loved, etc. John III. By a similar formula of speaking, by which it could be said: That a King so loved the Parisians, that he granted pardon to those who asked. Here by the name of Parisians I understand all Parisians, although I assert that immunity is proposed to no one absolutely, but with the condition, if they as suppliants ask for pardon. In respect of this degree, God is said to have given Christ for the life of the world, to will the salvation of all, insofar as He indeed calls all to repentance, some by the law of nature, this being written, others by the preaching of the Gospel. Moses Amyraut in his defense against Spanheim adorned, section 4, thus explains the opinion of the Hypotheticals: They say, therefore, that God, moved by His philanthropy and mercy for the human race, decreed from eternity to send His Son into the world, who, having performed satisfaction for sins, would acquire the remission of sins and eternal salvation for all under this law, if they would embrace Him through faith; nor would they disdain to be partakers of such great salvation. They establish, therefore, indeed, that God both willed in some way, and that men likewise could all be saved, provided they believed, but they add besides that God, no longer by His Φιλανθρωπία, for that is indeed common, but by a certain singular kind of love and mercy, through a motion, selected some from the universality of men, to whom He might grant faith, with the intention that He might most certainly lead them to salvation. And section 21. Christ, when He obtained redemption for all, indeed had that end, that it might be applied to all, that is, that it might be communicated to all in act, provided they did not reject its communication; if they did reject it, He did not will it to be communicated. Thus, therefore, stands the opinion of the Hypothetical Calvinists.

But concerning this matter it must be established thus: (1) We acknowledge that the federal promises promising us salvation under the New Testament are conditional, or include the hypothesis of faith, but a distinction must be made between the antecedent and the consequent will; for thus by the antecedent will that condition is not regarded, but in the consequent, by which salvation is promised only to believers or under the condition of faith in Christ. (2) The antecedent will, even if strictly speaking it is not absolute, is yet truly and absolutely universal, reaching and extending itself to all men, because God wills the salvation of all men, not indeed only under the condition of faith if they believe, but not even absolutely, but truly under a certain order (τάξει) of means; therefore this will of GOD is not absolute, but ordered, if we wish to speak properly; but it is by no means conditional, as the Hypothetical Calvinists wish. Absolute is accustomed to be opposed not only to hypothetical or conditional, but also to ordered, and defined by some order (τάξει), just as against the Calvinists we deny that election is absolute, because it is defined by the order (τάξει) of divine dispensation and of the causes which

God foresaw. The term, therefore, is ambiguous, and so it is better to abstain from it. (3) But if we wish to use this term here, lest we err, we must distinguish with Mr. Dr. Joh. Behm, of blessed memory, disp. 2 on the difference of Evangelical promises, aph. 5, between the antecedent will of God, by which it is considered either by reason of its first origin and internal cause, in which way he says it is independent and absolute, as Damascenus said it was ἐξ αὐτῦ καὶ ἀφ' ἑαυτῦ, from and of Himself, or by reason of event and execution; thus he says it is dependent on the order (τάξει), and therefore not so much conditional as ordered or modified. For whatever will is described in the word of God (1) in an ordered manner (2) so that with this order excluded or despised God does not will to confer salvation upon men (3) and is so constituted that it can be rejected and hindered by men by actual malice and contumacy in respect of the salutary effect, that is ordered and modified, and not indeed absolute. The will of God concerning the salvation of all and each of men is such: (α) God does not will the death of the one dying, yet not absolutely but in an ordered manner through the ordinary means of conversion, that he may be converted and live; (β) he who has not believed will be condemned, he who does not believe is already judged. Whence Mr. Dr. Behm concludes, he who wills all to be saved, and in turn from all these some are judged and damned because they do not believe, his will concerning the salvation of men is in no way absolute but ordered. (γ) The will of God can be rejected, Prov. I. 25, Luke VII. 30, therefore it is not absolute. Which l. c. Mr. Dr. Behm treats this at length. (δ) When the will of God is called antecedent and conditional by certain orthodox [theologians], the term condition is taken crudely and somewhat loosely, in this sense: that God wills the salvation of all not absolutely, but in an orderly manner, namely under this order, that they repent and believe in Christ; but not in the Calvinist manner, that He wills it only conditionally if all believe, but does not will that all believe, but rather out of an absolute good pleasure wills that only the elect believe. It is therefore safest of all, as Mr. Dr. Behm also advises, that we separate ourselves both in mind and tongue from the Calvinists in this part, and not call the antecedent will of God and the promises consistent with this will conditional, but teach with Scripture: that God wills all men to be saved, in this order, that they believe, or as Paul says, that they come to the knowledge of the truth 1 Tim. II. 4. or as Peter 2. Ep. III. 9. that they repent, or as Ezech. XXXIII. 11. that they be converted and live. (ε) The antecedent will of God does not include only an affection of pity and a gracious and saving love of all, hypothetically, if all believe, but also that gracious will by which God desires that all believe; that is, God not only wills that all be saved under the hypothesis if they believe, but He wills both, that all believe and that all be saved, because both are joined together in the Scriptures, Ezech. XXXIII. 11. 1. Tim. II. 4. etc. (ζ) God does not will the salvation of all under some unperformable condition, or such as might be in our own powers (which is Pelagian, against which Amyraldus nevertheless did not sufficiently guard himself) or which He Himself might not will to effect in all, by virtue of an absolute decree: but under that condition (if a condition is to be established here) which He wills to work in all. (η) Nor is this only a will of sign, of command, of declaration, of approbation, but it is a will of good pleasure, of counsel, and of gracious divine intention joined with a communicative affection, by which God, as far as it lies in Him, desires the faith and salvation of all to be promoted. (θ) Therefore the antecedent will of God, which is to be carefully observed, is not only joined with the affection of love, mercy and ardent desire, but it includes at the same time the good pleasure, counsel, purpose, and decree of God, which thesis, having been prolixly asserted, see if you please in the same Mr. Dr. Behm, aph. 6. This is what the Formula of Concord, in the solid repetition of Art. XI, p. 802, attributes to the antecedent will as well: counsel, purpose, and decree. (i) This grace, common to all men, is not only objective, as Amyraldus wishes, by which the object is offered to them only extrinsically, but also subjective, in so far as he wishes to confer the power of God, by the force of which the proposed object is insinuated into the mind, and faith is excited. Let the defense of Amyraldus against Spanhem, Sect. II, and others be seen. What is that objective grace of mere offering without the affection of collation?

It must therefore be said: that God, as far as the antecedent will is concerned, so wills the salvation of all men, that he not only desires all to be saved if they believe; but that he also has the mind of expending and communicating to all the means of salvation, so that thus there may be established in God a universal and indiscriminate affection of the gracious collation of the means of salvation. (1.) He who indiscriminately and universally wishes to show mercy graciously to all, he also indiscriminately wishes to confer upon all the means of salvation, and faith itself as well. For he who wills the end, also wills the means leading to the end. But the former is true of God, Rom. XI. v. 32, therefore the latter is also. (2.) He who wills all men to be saved, and to come to the knowledge of the truth, he wills not only that all men be saved if they believe, but he also wills to confer upon all men the means of salvation, and faith itself, because without them they can neither come to the truth nor be saved. But God wills both, namely that all men be saved, and then also that all come to the knowledge of the truth, 1 Tim. II. 4. Therefore. (3.) He who does not wish any to perish or die, but seriously wishes all to come to repentance and to live, he also wishes to bestow upon all, if they do not have it in their own powers, the means necessary for conversion. But the former is true of God, 2 Pet. III. 9, Ezech. XIII. 23, XXXIII. 11. Therefore the latter is also. (4.) Those whom Christ wished to be gathered in a saving manner, he had a serious mind to confer upon them the means necessary and sufficient for a saving gathering. But Christ wished the refractory Jews to be gathered in a saving manner, Matth. XXIII. 37. Therefore. (5.) Those whom God invites with the intention that he may refresh them, to them not only is objective grace exhibited; but subjective grace must also be conferred. For that refreshment is subjective grace. But he invites all men with the intention that he may refresh them, Matth. XI. 28, and that they themselves may enjoy heavenly food and drink, Es. LV. 12. Therefore. (6.) Those whose hearts God graciously knocks upon, to the end that he may be let in and celebrate the Supper with them, he intends to confer upon them both faith and salvation. But God graciously knocks upon the hearts not only of the elect but also of the reprobate, Apoc. III. 30. Therefore. (7.) To whomever God exhibits, presents, and offers faith and the remission of sins, he also intends to confer it upon them seriously and with an internal good pleasure of the heart; which must be asserted entirely, unless that external calling is feigned to be hypocritical, joined with an affection clearly disparate and contrary. But God offers it to all men, therefore it is said in Acts XVII. 31, πίστιν παρασχὼν πᾶσιν, to offer or exhibit faith to all, or even to present and provide. Col. I. 28. To admonish all men so that all may be presented perfect in Christ Jesus. Joh. I. 6. and 7. to exhibit the testimony of the Gospel to all, so that all may believe, etc. Therefore. (8.) Whoever has given Christ the Redeemer to all men, so that through faith in him they may have eternal life, he not only wished all to be saved if they believe, but he wished entirely that all should believe and be saved. He not only wished the salvation of all, but he also wished the means of salvation to be communicated to all. For he destined the Savior for all, so that not only might eternal life be acquired for all, but also gracious illumination, faith, and conversion, so that through it they might aspire to eternal life. Whence we further collect: To whomever Christ by his death acquired the grace of illumination and the gift of faith, to them God wishes to confer this grace of illumination and saving faith. But Christ acquired this grace for all, certainly not under the condition if all believe; for what would this be, to acquire faith for all, if all have faith? The minor is proved; for to whomever that grace is offered, it must have been acquired by the death of Christ. But he grants that the same is offered to all, Amyraldus with the Socinians. Therefore. (9.) If God gave his only-begotten Son to all men out of a most ardent affection of love, so that all might be saved through him, then without doubt he has a gracious affection toward all to confer upon them those things which make for salvation. The reason for the consequence rests upon the Apostolic assertion Rom. VIII. 32, for if God delivered up his Son for us, how will he not also with him freely give us all things! (10.) He who announces the word of faith to all men, so that through it we may obtain faith and salvation, he not only wishes that all be saved if they believe, but that all should entirely believe, and he intends to confer upon all not only salvation, but also faith for salvation. But God announces the word of faith to all men, so that through it they may obtain faith and salvation, which is therefore called ῥῆμα τῆς πίστεως, Rom. X. 8, λόγος τῆς πίστεως, 1 Tim. IV. 6, ἀκοὴ πίστεως, Gal. III. 2, for no other reason certainly than because God wishes through it to work faith in those to whom it is preached. It is called the seed of regeneration, 1 Pet. I. 23, which by the force of the δυνάμεως πλαστικῆς, those to whom it is preached ought to be, and can be, regenerated. (11.) Whoever offers the means of salvation to all for this end, that all may through them be converted, illuminated, regenerated, and led to eternal salvation; he not only wishes their salvation if they are converted or believe; but he also wishes to work conversion, illumination, regeneration, faith, and salvation in them through those means. The reason for the consequence is this, because those ἀποτελέσματα are not in the faculty of the receiving subject, but depend solely upon the power and grace of God working. The intention of God, therefore, would be vain, unless God himself willed to effect those things through means destined for this end. But God offers the means of salvation to all for that end; as those against whom we are arguing here undoubtedly acknowledge. (12.) Whoever are condemned for the reason that they have rejected the grace of God and the operation of the Holy Spirit, intending conversion and salvation, in them it is certain that God willed to effect conversion: for the grace which they reject, and on account of which rejected grace they are condemned, that grace God certainly willed to be bestowed upon them: for no one can despise or reject that which does not pertain to him, much less can or ought he to be condemned for rejecting it. But the reprobate are condemned for the reason that they reject the grace of God, etc. See Ps. XCV. 8. Is. LXV. 2. Matt. XXIII. 37. John III. 36. Acts VII. 51. (13.) If God also willed in some way that all be saved, that is, under the condition of faith provided they believe, he certainly did not will that non-believers be saved, such as are countless, namely all those to whom he did not will to grant faith. But those whom God seriously wills to be saved, those he not only wills to be saved, but wills to save; nor only to be saved or to save under this or that condition, but also to bestow upon them the condition under which they can be saved, since He knows that without this they cannot be saved. Whom would a wise man consider to seriously wish to give a benefit to all, and indeed under a condition not performable by those to whom he wishes to give it, and which they cannot have except from him alone he is unwilling to confer that condition upon countless others? If GOD has willed to grant faith absolutely to certain ones only, and not likewise to others, He certainly in reality did not will to have mercy on all unto salvation: For since no one can obtain salvation without faith, and that is from the sole efficiency of God, and He was unwilling to apply that in countless others, namely in those whom He did not choose, and thus passed over, He surely did not will to have mercy on such unto salvation, which Spanheim rightly urges against Amyraut in Exercit. de grat. univers. pages 80, 88, and 118. (14.) Whatever opinion turns Evangelical promises into mere commands, that is not undeservedly rejected. But this opinion of the Hypotheticals turns Evangelical promises, by which God promises the grace of illumination, conversion, and regeneration of faith if anyone hears His word and uses the offered means, into mere commands, since it is feigned that God indeed wishes, commands, and orders that men believe, be regenerated, and be converted, but does not wish to work those things in those whom He commands them. (15.) Whatever doctrine renders divine Grace merely deceptive and illusory, and attributes contrary wills to God, that is deservedly rejected. But is not the Grace of God rendered merely illusory by this doctrine, if indeed it is said that God wishes the salvation of all men if they believe, but does not wish that all believe, nay, that from His absolute good pleasure He wishes that only the peremptorily elect believe; is not a contrary will attributed to God, who seriously wishes the salvation of the reprobate if they are converted and believe, but does not wish to work faith and conversion in the reprobate, nay, has rejected the same from this grace, by which alone faith and conversion are produced? These things are so manifest that in the same School of Calvin, for this very reason, this opinion is contradicted, and it is vehemently and not undeservedly attacked. Let us hear Spanheim, l. c. sect. 4, p. 104. If the reason for the salvation of the elect is also placed in faith, and the cause of faith in the sole efficiency and mercy of God; and God was unwilling to apply this efficiency concerning the greater multitude of men, which however could not be supplied by any works from elsewhere, what does it help those in whom God was unwilling to exert this efficiency, that the mercy of God and His serious and indeed ardent [desire] for saving them and the redemption of Christ performed in that name are inculcated μετα πολλῆς Φαντασίας (with much show), when nevertheless nothing is more certain or inevitable than that such will perish? And p. 113: What profit is it therefore, or can it be, for such that Christ is sent, who acquires the remission of sins and salvation under the condition of faith for those who were passed over from eternity, whom Christ testifies He never knew, Matt. VII. v. 23, and thus who were certainly and inevitably to be unbelievers, and for that reason infallibly to be damned, and indeed by an eternal decree? How can this be consistent with the will to save such under a condition? I adjure anyone in whose mind there resides at last some reverence, whether such a volition can or ought to be attributed to God, by which not even any wise man would be deceived. Spanheim declares this by the simile of Amyraut himself, p. 139. The simile which the learned man brings forward concerning a girl whom a suitor wishes to marry under the condition that she be endowed with this or that dowry, to speak most mildly, is little to the point and in reality feigns God to be acting not seriously but illusorily. For if it is known to the suitor that the girl lacks that dowry, and that it cannot be had unless he gives it, and yet he is unwilling to give it, he in reality deludes that girl, and will by no means wish to take her as a wife if he testifies that he does not wish to take her unless she is endowed with that dowry and possessed of those conditions: ought that which convicts a human actor or buffoon to be attributed to God? Another simile illustrates the matter, page 170. Who, I ask, would consider a King or Prince to seriously propose to all and each of his subjects a prize or some κειμήλιον (treasure) under the condition that they run in the circus, look at the goal, and carry this or that token, when nevertheless he knows that many of them are paralytic, blind, and who neither have nor can have that token by any reason, nay, when he knows that no one can have it unless he gives it, but has determined to distribute it only to certain selected ones? Finally, p. 543, he illustrates that matter with another simile: Who will say that a Physician seriously wishes to heal a madman, if a certain remedy is to be received, and the Physician knows that he cannot wish to receive it, and is unwilling to remove that madness and aversion, although he could remove it? Therefore, in the preface recounting the occasion of the exercise, he considers that this method of Amyraut, if you examine the secrets more closely and deeply, leaves nothing except bubbles and inanities, since he denies to it that without which no mortal will obtain salvation unto eternity. And in another preface to the Reader, he says that this doctrine is like the Colossus of Nebuchadnezzar, having a golden head, but a body disparate to itself and ending in base metal. Virgins, he says, the poets once fashioned, which ended in a fish or a serpent: the same has place here, and as the Sodomite apples, beautiful in color, vanish at a touch into ashes and cinders; so that specious and pompous grace! when examined more deeply, at last departs into a mere mockery and into vain proclamations of the tongue. And further: If we believe the tenets of that method, God wishes the salvation of all and does not wish it, calls and does not call, man can convert himself and cannot, can be saved and cannot. You would call this Theology hanging and supported by no prop, it wavers so. Nor is this only the judgment of Spanheim; the very same censure is found in the Theological Faculty of Leiden, which Spanheim prefixed to his Exercise, subscribed by Joh. Polyander à Kerckhoven, Andreas Rivetus, and Jacobus Triglandius: We cannot wonder enough, they say, why they do not acknowledge the same free dispensation of God in the paternal love of the Father and the fraternal redemption of the Son, which they say they acknowledge in the heavenly calling of the Spirit and the application of that love and redemption, or why, when they extend the former two, namely love and redemption, to all men in general, they so openly contract the application of both. We cannot see how the former cohere with the latter and the latter with the former: nay, how these are not clearly overturned by those, or those by these. What of the fact that Spanheim appeals to the judgments not only of the Leidensians, Polyander, Walaeus, Thysius, Triglandius, Bogermannus, Malcovius, Schotanus, Gomarus, and Altingius, as also of Andreas Rivetus and the Churches and Academies that professed their grief over this new method at the Synod of Alençon, in his Exercise, page 35, but also observes that the same men judge those heads of Amyraldus not only alien to Scripture and the Synod of Dort, but also erroneous and dangerous, and to that judgment The Utrecht Academy [holds that] theologians as well as the Synods of the churches in the federated provinces [should] accede and agree. To which we finally add the Confession of Amyraut, who in his defense, p. 19, acknowledges that his opinion is hindered by inextricable difficulties.

But enough of this new discovery. We return to our text in which (V.) it is necessary to weigh the most salutary end of Christ's mission, and that [is] both ultimate and intermediate. The ultimate is that all who believe in him should not perish, but have eternal life; which is therefore twofold: first, privative, that we may not perish, or liberation from perdition; by which word is not understood total destruction and the extinction of soul and body, but death and eternal condemnation, which those who undergo are said to perish, because there is no salvation there, but mere destruction, concerning which Augustine, book 13, On the City of God, 11: there will not be men before death, nor after death, but always in death, and by this never living, never dying, but dying without end; for it will never be worse for man in death than where death itself will be without death. And Gregory the Great, book VI of the Morals, ch. 39: Death without death happens to the miserable, because death destroys but does not extinguish. This eternal death is therefore called destruction. Matt. VII, v. 31 [sic]; Mark I, 34; John XVII, 11; Acts VIII, 20; Rom. ch. IX, 32; Phil. I, 28, etc. Then [it is] positive, the possession of eternal life; for just as we have not only been liberated by Christ from condemnation, but eternal salvation has also been acquired for us, so through faith in Christ we obtain not only immunity from condemnation, but also eternal salvation, which is therefore called the end of faith, 1 Pet. I, v. 9. From the immediate opposition of both of which it is clear that no intermediate state is given between hell or eternal death, and heaven or eternal life. Verse 17 exhibits the intermediate end of the mission. For God did not send the Son into this world so that he might judge the world, but that the world might be saved through him, if this is taken concerning the meritorious cause of salvation, namely that that mission was not made to the end that it might only reveal that the world was concluded under sin, and judge the world, but that it might acquire salvation for the world, that it might save the world meritoriously. Although the words can be understood concerning the actual leading to salvation, not concerning the mere acquisition of salvation, so that the sense is that this was the intention of God the Father in the mission of his only-begotten Son, not that he might argue, judge, or reprobate the world, but that the universal world might be saved through him, both by merit and by efficacy, and thus be led to salvation by the virtue of his merit. Concerning which Cyril of Alexandria, book 2 on John, ch. 52, beautifully [says]: for I am not sent, he says, to condemn the world like Moses, nor to hand down commands for the reproof of sins, nor to perform a servile ministry, but that through mercy befitting God, as Son and Heir of the Father, I might vindicate men from servitude, the condemning law having been changed into justifying grace, and thus I might snatch the human race from the bonds of sins. Therefore I came to save, not to condemn. Thus this universal love of God is confirmed by the salutary end of Christ's mission, namely that he was sent not to judge the world or the human race, or for condemnation, but that the world or the human race might be saved through him; and thus he came for the salvation of the whole human race. Wherefore we have in this place a clear testimony of the divine salutary intention in the mission

of the Son, and not a particular one, concerning only a few in the human race, but universal, simply pertaining to all men. Nor can this opinion, written with the rays of the Sun, be eluded, whether by the restriction of the absolute Calvinists to the smallest particle of the world, since it is too manifest that, as the world was to be judged because of sin, so the Son of God came not to judge it, but to save it: or by the hypothesis of the moderates, Syncretists, or Hypothetical Calvinists, who indeed say the whole world was redeemed by Christ, but under the condition, if namely the whole world believed, and thus they fabricate a certain hypothetical redemption. Matthias Martinus in his judgment on art. 2 of the Synod of Dort, thesis 21, in the acts p. 116, explains himself thus: The Lord merited grace for all men, but not that which depends on singular election for all; which, therefore? That which is promised under the condition of faith. Ludov. Crocius, thesis 3 of his judgment: CHRIST, he says, from his and the Father's counsel, suffered and died, and by his death and passion most sufficiently merited for all and each of sinful men that, if only they repent and believe, they can be reconciled to God and restored to his grace and bosom, but he actually reconciled only the elect to God by his passion and death, and restored them to his bosom. He has set forth this opinion of his more prolixly in dissertations 10 and 11 of his Dyodecas. He distinguishes, namely, between the universal satisfaction performed for all and each of men, and the actual acquisition of the remission of sins, which he makes proper to the elect alone: Whence Andr. Rivetus, dissertation 6 on redemption, thesis 11, judges that that opinion agrees in sense with other Reformed [theologians], even if it differs in the manner of speaking, since they deny that Christ died equally for the impious and the pious, which judgment Crocius does not deny is consistent with the truth, page 596. Moses Amyraut, in his defense, sections 24 and 25, who says indeed that salvation was acquired for all by way of satisfaction, but that faith was obtained for the elect alone by way of final cause, and that that impetration was made absolutely and not conditionally, and in that matter he differs vehemently from the impetration of salvation, since salvation was so impetrated that it was offered under the condition of acceptance: but faith was impetrated not that it might be offered under the condition of accepting, but that it itself might be the condition through which salvation is received. Therefore Amyraut makes a twofold redemption, one universal, the other particular: one absolute, the other conditional, section 17. He likewise assigns in the same place a twofold account of Destination and Redemption: particular, insofar as it has the decree concerning the bestowing of faith conjoined with it; universal, insofar as that decree is separated from it. Wherefore in Sect. 19 he explains himself thus: that Christ indeed ἁπλῶς redeemed the children of God, but for the rest conditionally, that if they believe they might be freed from death: and that the destination of the death of Christ to the elect includes within itself the decree of election, whereas as regards others the decree of election is segregated from the counsel of the death of Christ.

But that Christ did not satisfy for all only conditionally if they should believe, nor did He acquire salvation for the elect alone by way of a final cause, but for all, and therefore as regards the intention of Redemption and the merit of Satisfaction He died equally and indifferently for all men, without distinction, and indeed to this end, that all might apprehend by faith the satisfaction rendered for all; this is confirmed by these arguments. (1.) Because Scripture nowhere proposes a twofold satisfaction, one absolute, the other conditional, nor is there even a γρῦ of such a conditional satisfaction or redemption, which the hypotheticalists assign, in the sacred writings. Deservedly, therefore, that is rejected as a Calvinistic figment of the brain. (2.) The sacred writings openly teach that Christ died for all men not ἀνίσως or unequally, but παρέρισως or equally; therefore Christ is said here to be given as Savior to the whole world, and to have come into the world to save the whole world. No difference is assigned here, as regards the end of Christ's mission and the redemption of men, between the elect and the non-elect, but he is said to be given to all and sent to all for the purpose that he might redeem all, and that all might be saved through him. If one and the same is the end of Christ's passion, both as to the thing and as to the manner of the thing, with respect to the whole world, and thus also with respect to believers and unbelievers, then certainly the redemption was not made in view of and under the hypothesis of faith. But one and the same is the end of Christ's passion both as to the thing and as to the manner of the thing; therefore he is called the Savior of the world, John ch. IV, v. 33, 1 John ch. IV, 14, and to have given his flesh for the life of the whole world, John ch. VI, v. 15, and to have reconciled the whole world, 2 Cor. V, 19, that is, to have acquired life and reconciliation for the whole world; no difference is established here again between the elect and the non-elect; life and reconciliation are implied to have been acquired for all equally: therefore, which is especially to be observed, he is called the propitiation not for believers only, but for the sins of the whole world, 1. John II, 2, so that as regards the expiation of sins and the acquisition of grace, it is implied that he satisfied equally for the sins of all and of the whole world. Therefore, finally, he is said to have given himself as a redemption for all, 1 Timothy II, v. 6, to have tasted death for all, Heb. II, 9, delivered to death for all, Rom. ch. VIII, v. 32, and died for all, so that it is as if all had died equally, 2 Cor. V, 14, 15, which certainly cannot be asserted if he had died absolutely for the elect alone, and only conditionally for the rest. For thus it would not be as if all had died when he died, but only as if the elect had died, provided he did not satisfy for all equally. (3.) When he is said to be sent into the world to save the world, or delivered for the life of the world, or made a propitiation for the whole world, a distinction cannot surely be established here between the elect and the non-elect, since election is posterior in the order of reason to redemption itself and reconciliation in the Divine Decrees, and follows the πηγύνασιν of faith, which must be placed into the redemption itself, so that we may be in the number of the elect: Thus reprobation, without doubt, even by the admission of the hypotheticalists themselves, is posterior to redemption, as it follows incredulity toward Christ and his merit; for they are reprobated, who are reprobated, because they do not believe that Christ redeemed them. For whatever is posterior to redemption itself, that cannot vary redemption itself and discriminate it in itself or determine it conditionally. But the difference of faith and incredulity of the elect and likewise of the reprobate is posterior to the Redemption of Christ, therefore the difference of faith and incredulity of the elect and likewise of the reprobate cannot vary the redemption of Christ and discriminate it in itself, nor can faith determine the same conditionally. (4.) If equally

Christ expiated the sins of all, then he also acquired salvation for all equally. But he expiated the sins of all equally, because, since we all equally like sheep have gone astray, GOD equally cast the sins of all upon him, Isa. LIII, v. 6, and he equally bore the sins of the whole world, John ch. I, 29, 1 John II, 2. For whose sins were cast upon Christ, it can in no way be said that these were simply excluded from the fruit of the passion by an absolute denial of faith. (5.) If the efficacy of the merit of Christ is one and the same, produced and acquired for all indiscriminately by the death of Christ, then it is not to be limited by the same condition of faith, or to be established as absolute for some, but hypothetical for the rest. But the antecedent is true. For those who are commanded to believe in the merit of Christ, to them certainly the efficacy of the merit of Christ pertains. But all are commanded to believe in the merit of Christ, and the reprobate are damned because they do not believe in it. John ch. III, v. 18, 2 Peter II, 1. (6.) By whatever merit illumination and faith have been acquired for all, just as salvation itself, by that same merit salvation cannot be said to have been acquired for all only under the hypothesis of faith, since that very hypothesis, namely faith, has been acquired for all by the same. But by the merit of Christ, illumination and faith have truly been acquired for all, just as salvation itself. For what is there of spiritual grace that has not been acquired by Christ, with whom all things are given to us, Rom. VIII, v. 31, therefore he is also called the true light, which illuminates every man, John ch. I, v. 9, meritoriously, that is, and imputatively, because he merited illumination for all, and whence is the gift of faith, if not from the merit of Christ? Whence is it that faith is offered to us all, through the word and Sacraments, Luke ch. XXIV, v. 42, Acts ch. XVII, v. 31, if not because Christ merited that grace for us all? Since as we have said, (which we repeat again because it is especially to be observed,) no grace comes to us except through and on account of the merit of Christ. But whatever has been acquired through the death of Christ, that the merit of Christ cannot render determined or conditional. For a subsequent act of something cannot determine the act itself as such conditionally. The gift of faith is acquired through the death of Christ. Therefore. Finally, for whomever sins have been expiated, for them also faith has been acquired entirely, since Christ not only expiated evils, but also acquired goods, among which the first is faith. But Scripture testifies with a resounding voice that sins have been expiated for all. 2 Cor. V, 19, 1 John II, v. 2, etc. (7.) Those for whom the λύτρον was truly and in the very act paid, and not merely a payment destined under some condition, they are truly and in the very act redeemed; and redemption is not merely destined for them under some condition. But the λύτρον was truly and in the very act paid for all men, as the Apostle testifies, 1 Tim. II. 6, 2 Cor. V. 14. (8.) Thus, if Christ is the Redeemer of anyone under the condition that he believes Him to be such for himself, faith would certainly create its own object. But the consequent is absurd, because in order for someone to be able and bound to believe this, it is necessary first that Christ be his Savior. For the object is said to precede the act which is directed toward it. Nor indeed is our faith the cause of Christ’s death, but its effect: nor is it because a man believes that Christ died for him, but because Christ died for him, hence it comes about that he believes: just as it is not because someone receives a λύτρον that it is paid

ANNOTATIONS ON JOHN

for himself, it is paid, but vice versa, therefore what is paid for himself can be accepted by him as paid in full for himself. (9.) If the acquisition of Salvation is distinguished in this from its application itself, that the former is not conditional, but the latter includes a condition, it can by no means be said that the redemption of Christ was made under a hypothesis, for what else is the redemption of Christ than the acquisition of salvation? Now, however, in the entire Scripture this distinction is inculcated, of acquisition, salvation, and application, so as to make the former common to all, but the latter proper as to the very act of the believers, and so as to include a condition for the latter, while on the contrary it never proposes the former as conditional, nay, it makes that former one posterior to the latter. (10.) If the redemption of Christ is at least hypothetically universal, it is not really universal. For an act having an attached condition is not only incomplete, but if that condition is by the very fact, or even in potentiality, nothing, then in reality that act will be nothing. Now, however, the meritorious act of Christ, according to the opinion of the Hypotheticals, has an attached condition, which with respect to the reprobate is by the very fact nothing, and impossible. For the impious cannot believe by their own powers, nor does God wish to bestow grace upon them so that they might be able. (11.) To wish to save someone only under the condition of faith, but not to save them in act, is not to be their savior, but to be able to be: Nay, to wish to save someone under an impossible condition is not to seriously wish to be someone's savior. Add (12.) That the redemption made by Christ was in itself absolute and consummated on the cross, and ought not to be called such insofar as some embrace it; for it was absolute before many (or any) even embraced it, nor is it absolute or not absolute by the fact that some embrace it and others do not; but it ought rather to be called efficacious or not efficacious: as Spanheim has it in Exerc. de Grat. univers. page 725.

But let these things be said concerning that new controversy. But before we return to the text, we shall briefly illustrate the causes of salvation proposed here in summary. The efficient cause is designated, both the principal one, the Paternal love of God, and that universal, embracing the whole human race, signified by the name of the world: and the meritorious satisfaction of the Son of God given to the world and for the world, and the Instrumental one, Faith in Christ the only-begotten Son of God. If the material cause is considered by reason of the divine intention, it concerned not just a small part of the world but the whole world. Since God gave his Son to the whole world, which, having been concluded under sin, was subject to condemnation by the force of the law: even if by reason of actual fruition, none but believers actually obtain the salvation procured by Christ. The formal cause of salvation is exemption from destruction, and the fruition of eternal life: That we may not perish in sins, the remission of sins provides; that we may have eternal life, the donation of eternal righteousness provides. For the kingdom of God or eternal life is Righteousness, Rom. ch. XIV. ver. 17. Our salvation, therefore, in this life is situated in Justification, which consists partly in the non-imputation of our sins, partly in the imputation of the righteousness of Christ, since we are not only to be freed from sins, that we may not perish, but also to be endowed with perfect Righteousness, that we may obtain eternal life, which, since it is not found in all, the righteousness of Christ must be apprehended, by which alone we are constituted righteous before God, Rom. ch. V.

Vers. 21. ὁ δὲ ποιῶν τὴν ἀλήθειαν) Qui sincere agit: Sic 2. Reg. XX. 3. ambulare in veritate exponitur, integro corde. Adde Psal. XXV. 5. LXXXVI. 11. Proverb. XXVIII. 16. Conjungitur cum luce Ps. XLIII. 3. Ephes. V. 8. 9. Et in hujus epist. I. 1. 6. Hoc quoque intellige, lux postquam affulsit: nam consilium emendandæ vitæ his verbis describitur.

ἔρχεται πρὸς τὸ φῶς) Philo dicto loco: τὰ καλὰ περιαυγείας μεσημβρινῆς δεῖται πρὸς ἐπίδειξιν. Plutarchus: οὐδεὶς τῶν καλῶν ἔργων τὸ σκότος περιβάλλει.

ἵνα φανερωθῇ αὐτοῦ τὰ ἔργα) Ut ipse hæc opera ad illud dogma exploret ac dirigat, neque enim formidat examen.

ὅτι ἐν θεῷ ἐστιν εἰργασμένα) ἐν pro κατὰ secundum naturam ac voluntatem Dei, sic ἐν κυρίῳ I. Cor. VII. 39.

Addere hic libet, quæ de loco hoc classico, & fere præcipuo inter τὰ λόγια vel Eloquia oris Domini quondam proposuimus. Arce causæ jam aggreditur Christus, & remoto V. T. velo aperte explicat universæ salutis mysterium, causis ejusdem omnibus enucleatis, & ex adverso simul causis damnationis hominum traditis. Cohærentiam hanc reddit Chrysostomus. Ne mireris, quod exaltari debeam, ut salvemini. Ita enim Patri videtur, qui adeo vos dilexit, ut pro servis, & quidem ingratis, Filium daret. Sed dispiciamus verborum pondera. Etenim singula verba, ut iterum Chrysostomus monet, magnam vim habent. Exprimunt autē I. Salutis principium, Dilectionem Dei Patris, gratuitam & immensam. Sic Deus dilexit mundum. Gratia & dilectio Dei fons est omnis salutis nostræ. Nulla dilectionis hujus causa fuit, quia in nobis nihil dilectione dignum reperiri potuit, qui odio & ira tantum digni eramus. Ideo ex mera gratia Deus nos dilexit. Quo nomine prædicatur hic ἀγάπη, Dilectio Dei. Ἀγαπᾶν enim secundum Phavorinum est ἄγειν scil. εἰς τὸ πᾶν, hoc est toto animo, omniq; modo in rem dilectam ferri. Alias vocatur οἰκτιρμος seu misericordia Dei, Luc. VI. 36. Ac commemorantur hic etiam τὰ σπλάγχνα ἐλέυς viscera misericordiæ, elegantis vocis Ebrææ רַחֲמִים uterinam seu maternam misericordiam designantis explicatione, Ps. LI. 7. Luc. I. 13. de quibus prolixius vid. T. 2. Syst. Theol. c. II. Paulus prædicat Eph. II. 7. τὸ ὑπερβάλλοντα πλῦτον τῆς χάριτος αὐτοῦ ἐν χρηστότητι, superabundantes divitias gratiæ in benignitate ipsius, ac testatur, quod Deus ipse commendat suam charitatem erga nos in eo, quod nostri misereri voluerit cum adhuc peccatores essemus, Rom. V. 8.

II. Dilectionis objectum. Voce κόσμυ designantur citra controversiam homines, non vero Angeli. Cæterum ex hominibus solos electos hic indigitari, acriter contendunt nonnulli è Calvinianis, imprimis Beza in notis ad 1. Joh. II. 2. Piscator in no- tis h. l. & 1. Joh. II. 2. Altingius in LL. CC. Heidelb. p. 2. L. 4. p. 400. Joh. Maccovius, Colleg. de prædest. d. 12. p. 36. Ant. Walæus in LL. CC. p. 288. Wende- lin. in Chr. Theol. l. 1. c. 17. p. 284. quod fervide præ aliis Frid. Spanb. Exerc. de grat. univers. p. 732. asse- ruit, qui etiam, quod mireris, ex h. l. gratiam par- ticularem demonstrare conatus est. Sed nimis ma- nifestum est, hic non posse electos solos voce mun- di intelligi, verum omnes homines à Christo de- notatos esse. Rationes hæ notari possunt (1) Nus- piam in tota scriptura vox κόσμος solos electos no- tat, significatio ea ut mere arbitraria & precaria merito rejicitur. (2) Vox mundi cum de homini- bus sermo est aut generaliter omnes homines no- tat, aut speciatim reprobos, hic vero de reprobis speciatim non accipi, extra controversiam est. (3) Agitur hic absolute de mundo, nec ulla apparet re- strictionis ratio, cur ad solos electos determinari debeat, quod argumentum merito urget in Schola Calvini Heinr. Bulling. Comm. in h. l. si homines di- xiffet, justos & bonos intelligere potuissemus, rursus hujus vel illius ordinis status aut ætatis homines in- telligere licuisset: jam vero dixit mundum; ad Johan- nes ait: mundum in maligno positum esse; mundi ergo vocabulo significat nec unius ætatis, sexus aut ordinis homines, sed omnes omnium ætatum homines, eosq; in mundo versantes & peccato obnoxios. (4) De mundo etiam διαστητικῶς hic agitur, quia scil. corruptus erat, atque per serpentis infernalis ictus mortiferos in extrema miseria jacebat. Quapro- pter vox mundi nequaquam de fidelibus vel ele- ctis intelligi potest, quod argumentum urget Job. Bergius, in expl. dicti hujus Germ. p. 7. Nec vero Chri- stus per mundum hic intelligit electos tantum, prout jam à mundo separati sunt, sed totum genus huma- num universe sumtum, prout in peccato jacet, & pro- ut communiter per Evangelium ad pœnitentiam & fidem in Christum vocatur. (5) Qui mundus non fuit ante & extra missionem ac redemtionem Filii Dei, ille hic nequaquam intelligi potest: quia igitur hic de mundo redimendo, non redemto & redemtione fruente. At mundus electorum vel fidelium ne- quaquam fuit ante vel extra missionem Filii Dei, fides enim præsupponit redemtionem, quam ap- prehendit, ideoq; redemtione prior esse non po- test. (6) de eo mundo sermo est, qui erat sub pecca- to, potestate Satanæ, & condemnatione æterna, adeoq; Redemtore & redemtione indigebat. At mundus fidelium non amplius est sub peccato, po- testate Satanæ, & condemnatione æterna, ubi Deus mundum reconciliasse, (redemisse) dicitur, neg. de reprobis, neg. de electis disputandum, ait Mu- scul. in 2. Cor. V. 17. (7). Confirmat id typus serpentis ænei, quia enim illud remedium non particulare sed universale omnibus Israëlitus sauciatis propo- situm, quo ab ictibus serpentum venenatis conva- lescere possent, non autem certis tantummodo quibusdam peculiariter dilectis; hinc gratia quæ in Christo hominibus obtigit, non particularis est, sed toti humano generi morsu serpentis infer- nalis sauciato consecrata. (8) Extollitur Dei dile- ctio per particulam ἐπιτατικὴν cum singulari ἐμ- φάσει & admiratione. Sic Deus dilexit mundum, qua de videri potest Chrysost. in h. l. quapropter re- stringi aut determinari, neque potest neque debet. (9) Mundus is hic intelligitur à Deo dilectus, cui dedit Filium suum Redemtorem, quem vero non electis aut fidelibus solis sed omnibus Adæ posteris, Genes. III. vers. 15. omnibus terræ po- pulis cap. XXII. 28. dedit, quo de Johan. Gro- tius, Com. ad Tit. II. pag. 357. Deus dilexit totum mundum & ei destinavit Filium, cur igitur dilectio- nem de solis electis accipiam, causam idoneam non invenio. Toti mundo promiserat semen mulieris, Gen. III. 15. toti igitur mundo dedit. Deinde Christus se dedit adeoque satisfecit non pro paucis, sed pro mundo universo seu toto humano genere, sive omni- bus hominibus, 1. Tim. II. 6. Ebr. II. 9. 1. Johan. II. 2. idque sufficienter, sufficientia actuali. Hactenus Gro- tius. (10) Ut omnes perditioni obnoxii sunt ex- tra Christum, ita omnibus, totique mundo perdi- do Christus datus dicitur, ut quicunque ex perdi- tis illis in ipsum credunt actu non pereant, sed vi- tam æternam consequantur, unde recte Christo- phorus Pezelius in explicatione h. l. p. 291. mundus significat, κατ' συνεκδοχὴν, totum genus humanum, quod contaminatum est peccato, & cui debetur ira Dei & pœna æterna. (11) De eo mundo hic sermo est, qui dispesci potest in credentes & non creden- tes, eos, qui judicantur & non judicantur, eos qui pereunt, & qui non pereunt, sed habent vitam æter- nam. At mundus electorum non potest dispesci in credentes & non credentes &c. E. quod argu- mentum urget Bergius in explic. hujus dicti germ. p. 8. Hanc esse genuinam interpretationem, inquit, verborum Christi manifestum sit, tum ex his ver- bis, quibus communiter omnibus hominibus, si mo- do in Filium credant, vita æterna promittitur, tum ex sequentibus, ubi hic mundus in duas partes divi- ditur, quarum una in Filium credit, ideo dilectio- nem Dei, lucem, vitam & salutem amplectitur, al- tera vero non credit &c. (12) Illi qui judicantur e mundo, hanc ipsam ob causam judicari dicun- tur, quod non credant in Christum mundo datum, ut mundus salvetur per ipsum. At quicunque crede- re debent in Christum Salvatorem & per fidem in ipsum salutem consequantur, illi utique credere tenentur, Christum sibi datum esse, se redemisse, pro se mortuum, & propitiationem factum esse, unde argumentamur porro; Quicquid reprobi tenentur ac jubentur credere, id verum sit oportet. At Christum sibi datum esse Salvatorem ac pro se mortuum esse, reprobi tenentur ac jubentur cre- dere; Verum ergo esse oportet, Christum repro- bis datum esse Salvatorem ac pro reprobis mortu- um esse. Ulterius: Propter quod reprobi damnan- tur, id ad ipsos ex intentione Dei pertinere, certu est. At propter gratiam Dei & redemptionem Christi neglectam reprobi damnantur, E. Recte Crocius conversione Prutenica p. 2. c. 6. p. 472.
