Nor indeed should this be called the first journey of Jesus: because that of the other Evangelists is joined to his temptation in the desert, and there his first arrival in Galilee is clearly designated, and illustrated by the testimony of Isaiah c. 9, 1. Matt. 4, 15. The history of the imprisonment of the Baptist is therefore deservedly placed before the withdrawal of Christ from Judea, and therefore the words of our Evangelist are to be understood thus, that the Pharisees had heard that Jesus was making more disciples and baptizing than John, namely, before he had been imprisoned. Conf. Harm. B. Chemnitz, chap. XXXI. and XXXII.

Latin:

CAPUT IV. ARGUMENTUM ET PAR- TITIO.

Iesus ob Pharisæos relicta Judæa in Galilæam se conferens per Samariam in Sichar, ad pu- teum Iacobi, cum muliere Samaritana, à qua aquæ potum petierat, colloquitur de aqua viva, quæ in vitam æternam scaturit, quæ aquam illam expetit, admonita de quinq; maritis, & sexto viro, non proprio marito, marito, agnoscit eum Prophetam & quærit de loco adorationis, informatur autem de Patre ubique jam invocando, & de Messia, quod nempe ipse Messias sit, qui cum ea loquebatur. Quæ id civibus suis annunciat. Interim monent discipuli Christum de cibo, quibus imminentem Messem spiritualem prædicit: Samaritani credunt in ipsum, tam ob ea quæ retulerat mulier, tum imprimis ob Verbum ejus: Iesus in Galilæam, non tamen in urbem patriam, quia Propheta non est acceptus in patria, tendens, ibi suscipitur, & in Cana Reguli filium in Capernaum decumbentem, ad intercessionem patris isto verbo, filius tuus vivit, sanat, qui eadem hora domi convaluit: quod ita factum esse resciscens Pater cum tota domo sua in Iesum credidit: idq́; alterum miraculum ejus in Galilæa fuit.

Partes sunt quatuor: I. Colloquium Jesu cum Samaritana, ad v. 30. II. Colloquium cum discipulis de cibo, & de messe spirituali, ad v. 38. III. Samaritanorum ad Jesum conversio, ad v. 42. IV. Filii Reguli in Capernaum decumbentis in Cana sanatio, ad v. 54.

Vers. 1. Ἔγνω) Divina cognitione.

ὅτι ἤκουσαν οἱ Φαρισαῖοι) Ii maxime, qui in Synedrio erant Hierosolymitano. Vide supra c. 3, 1. Sadducæi omnes ritus lege non præscriptos pari loco habebant. Quare nec baptismum Jesu, nec Johannis curabant, non magis, quam Pharisæorum cæremonias.

ὅτι Ἰησοῦς) Ἰησοῦς positum pro ἀυτὸς, ut sæpe apud Hebræos.

πλείονας μαθητὰς ποιεῖ κὶ βαπτίζει) Plures habet discipulos, & solenniter eos initiat.

ἢ Ἰωάννης) Putem cum hæc acciderunt vixisse tunc adhuc Johannem Baptistam, & aliud hoc esse iter quam quod ab aliis Evangelistis describitur. Tanto major in Jesum invidia erat quam in Johannem, quanto plures habebat sectatores. Et Johannis quidem honos nati ex sacerdotali familia aliquatenus ipsum ornabat sacerdotium: & tamen hujus quoque baptismum repudiarunt Pharisæi Luc. 7, 30. At in Jesu Galilæo, de plebe, ut putabatur, omnis honos detrimentum erat publicæ auctoritatis.

Non apparet causa, cur aliud hoc iter in Galilæam sit, quam quod ab aliis Evangelistis, puta Matth. 4, 12. Marco 1, 14. Luc. 1. 3. descriptum, & utrum horum prius dicendum? Illud aliorum Evangelistarum prius statui nequit, quia tum traditus jam erat Baptista, cum id Christus susciperet, teste Matthæo: audiens autem Jesus quod Iohannes traditus esset, ἀνεχώρησεν secessit in Galilæam. Neq; vero hoc primum iter Jesu dicendum: quia illud aliorum Evangelistarum tentationi ejus in deserto subjungitur, & illic primus adventus ejus in Galilæam luculenter designatur, & testimonio Esaiæ c. 9, 1. illustratur Matth. 4, 15. Historia ergo captivitatis Baptistæ merito collocatur ante secessum Christi ex Judæa, ideoq; verba Evangelistæ nostri sic accipienda, Pharisæos audivisse, Iesum plures facere discipulos & baptizare, quam Iohannes scil. antequam captivaretur, fecisset. Conf. Harm. B. Chemnitii cap. XXXI. & XXXII.

## 4:2
Vers. 2. Καίτοιγε Ἰησοῦς ἀυτὸς ἐκ ἐβάπτιζεν) We said above c. III. 22.

Casaubon rightly: Although not Christ himself, but his disciples were baptizing; yet it was Christ's, whence the baptism of the disciples is both believed and called: concerning which matter it is pleasing to bring forward a very elegant passage of Tertullian. Thus he in the book on Baptism: But behold, they say, the Lord came, and did not baptize. For we read: And yet he did not baptize, but his disciples: as if John had truly predicted that he himself would baptize with his own hands. It is not, however, to be understood in that way, but said simply in common parlance. Just as it is, for example, the Emperor proposed an edict, or, the prefect beat with clubs. Does he himself propose, or does he himself beat? He is always said to do it, for whom it is performed by another. It is similar to what the Jurists teach. That he is seen to do it, who does it through another, as in Law XXII. §. 1. de liberali causa. See Walæus.

Latin:

Vers. 2. Καίτοιγε Ἰησοῦς ἀυτὸς ἐκ ἐβάπτιζεν) Diximus supra c. III. 22.

Recte Casaubonus: Etsi non Christus ipse, sed ejus discipuli baptizabant; Christi tamen, unde discipulorum baptismus & creditus est & vocatus: qua de re placet perelegantem Tertulliani locum proferre. Sic ille in libro de Baptismo: Sed ecce, inquiunt, venit Dominus, & non tinxit. Legimus enim: Et tamen is non tingebat, sed discipuli ejus: quasi revera ipsum suis manibus tincturum Iohannes prædicaffet. Non utiq; sic intelligendum est, sed simpliciter dictum more lo- communi. Sicut est, verbi gratia, Imperator propo- suit edictum, aut, præfectus fustibus cecidit. Nun- quid ipse proponit, aut nunquid ipse cædit? Semper is dicitur facere, cui præministratur. Simile est, quod JCti tradunt. Videri eum facere, qui per alium facit, ut in Lege XXII. §. 1. de liberali causa. Vid. Walæus.

## 4:3
Vers. 3. ἀφῆκε τὴν Ἰουδαίαν) In which they had the most power, being in control of the courts, with the Romans permitting it.

Arias Montanus provides another reason besides this, according to Walaeus: Namely, that the Pharisees might understand that he was not contending with John out of a desire for rivalry, nor to stir up a new sect of the Pharisees themselves, but to leave to John his own duty of baptizing and preaching repentance, which was being promoted by him, not attacked; and the aim of both was the same in such preaching: and therefore he left Judea and went again into Galilee, so that he might promote his ministry there, which pertained not only to the Jews, but to all Israelites, and to those who had perished from the house of Israel. For meanwhile, as long as John lived, he was to perform his duty of bearing witness concerning Jesus Christ.

and he went away again into Galilee) Where Herod was reigning, whose anger against John had not yet flared up. Thus, without loss to his preaching, he consulted his own safety for a time.

Latin:

Vers. 3. ἀφῆκε τὴν Ἰουδαίαν) In qua illi plurimum pote- rant judiciorum compotes, Romanis id permittentibus.

Aliam præterea causam reddit Arias Montanus apud Walæum: Ut scilicet intelligerent Pharisæi il- lum non studio contendendi cum Johanne, aut no- vam sectam Pharisæorum ipsorum æmulatione susci- tare, sed relinquere Johanni suum munus baptizan- di, & pœnitentiam prædicandi, quod à se promove- batur, non autem impugnabatur; & idem erat u- triusque studium in hujusmodi prædicatione: ideoque reliquit Judæam, & abiit iterum in Galilæam, ut ibi ministerium suum promoveret, quod non ad Judæos tantum, sed ad omnes pertinebat Israelitas, & eos, qui perierant de domo Israel. Interea enim Johannes dum viveret, suo munere functurus erat testimo- nium reddendi de Jesu Christo.

καὶ ἀπῆλθε πάλιν εἰς τὴν Γαλιλαίαν) Ubi Herodes regna- bat, cujus ira in Johannem nondum exarserat. Ita fine da- mno prædicationis ad tempus sibi consuluit.

## 4:4
V. 4 And he was passing through Samaria) Understand by Samaria that part of the promised land in which the Assyrians had remained after the Jews, returning from Babylon, had recovered the rest formerly possessed by the ten tribes. For the name of the city, once the capital of the kingdom, remained for the region. Through this, however, was the journey from Jerusalem into Galilee and vice versa. See what we have brought forward at Luke 17:11.

Latin:

V. 4 Διήρχετο δὲ διὰ τῆς Σαμαρείας) Samariam intellige il- lam partem terræ promissæ in qua manserant Assyrii post- quam cætera à decem tribubus olim possessa Judæi à Baby- lonia reduces receperant. Ab urbe enim olim regni capite nome mansit regioni. Per hanc autem Hierosolymis in Gali- læam & contra iter erat. Vide quæ attulimus ad Luc. 17, 11.

## 4:5
Vers. 5. he comes therefore into a city of Samaria) He calls the territory of the city a city here. We noted a similar thing at Luke 11:7.

called Sychar) Most Greek codices and the Syriac have Sychar. And it is read thus in the Latin, and Jerome notes that it was read so in his time. Other codices have Sychar, and the Arab follows these. And indeed the permutation of the vowel is not new; thus Simon and Symeon are written, and this very city is written Sichem and Sychem. Jerome thinks that the writing of 'as' instead of 'im' is a fault of the scribes: others more correctly think it is a pronunciation corrupted by time, just as from Belial was made Beliar and similar things. This city is usually called Sikima in Greek inflection, concerning which and that whole tract there exist verses by the Greek poet Theodotus in his book about the Jews, which Eusebius cites in Preparation for the Gospel, book IX, ch. 1, but they are corrupt, and I judge they should be emended thus: 'And it was good and rich in goats and high. A long road led to the city from the field; here and there thickets warded off the path. And very near to it two fortified mountains appeared.' Abounding in grass and wood; and in the middle a narrow path is cut like a furrow; above, holy Sichem appears, a sacred city, built low under the root; and around it the smooth foothills are deserted.

Those two mountains which loom over Sichem are Gerizim, about which we shall hear now, and Ebal. See Benjamin in his itinerary. Epiphanius wrongly denies this with weak arguments. But this city is significantly named, as a rival to Jerusalem in religion.

There is no doubt that it is the same city which is called Sichem in the Old Testament: Thus the ancient histories concerning Sichem (Gen. 33:19, ch. 34:1, ch. 37:12) fit here, because Jacob lived there with the twelve Patriarchs, worshipped, and bequeathed the estate to Joseph. The bones of Joseph also were buried in that part of the field, because of faith and the expectation of the Messiah (Josh. 24:32). Not far from Sichem, as Jerome writes, Melchizedek had lived in Salem, and the blessings had been recited on the nearby mountain (Deut. 27:5, Josh. 8:30). And the Baptist had recently baptized in Aenon, near Salim close to Sichem. Sichem was a royal city in the time of the Judges, which Abimelech leveled to the ground (Judg. 9:45). Jeroboam, however, rebuilt it (2 Kings 12:25) and used it for a royal seat. Whence perhaps that valley was called royal. Afterwards, Omri built the city of the same name, Samaria, on Mount Ephraim (2 Kings 16:24). And the following Kings of the Israelites used that city, which was called Samaria from then on, for a royal seat. Josephus, however, writes that in the time of Alexander the Great, Samaria was the metropolis that it was Sichem again. After the times of the Evangelists, however, Sichem was restored again, and with its name changed was called Neapolis, which was the fatherland of Justin Martyr, and it retained that appellation even in the time of Jerome. That that Sichem was situated not far from Mount Gerizim, on which we have said the temple of the Samaritans was built, is gathered from Judges ch. IX, v. 7, where the voice of one standing on the summit of the mountain is heard in this very city of Sichem: as B. Chemnitius observes.

to the parcel of ground that Jacob gave to Joseph) Gen. XLVIII. 22. In the exposition of this passage, it does not please me that some think this field was taken by force by Simeon and Levi when they were plundering Sichem. For Jacob disapproved of that deed, mixed as it was with treachery. Nor would I any more think it was occupied by neighbors upon the departure of Jacob, and then recovered by arms by Jacob upon his return, as some invent. For the strength of Jacob and his family was not such that they would dare anything against their neighbors in open war, since that very thing which Simeon and Levi had dared was not done except by deceit and by the occasion of sickness. Wherefore it is more likely, just as this gift did not have effect until after the promised land was occupied by arms, as can be seen in Joshua XXIV. 32, so Jacob in his hope anticipated this victory, and attributed to himself what his descendants were going to do, and in the prophetic manner declared in the past tense that which he saw would certainly come to pass.

Compare what is said about these things in the Commentary on the passage of Genesis.

Latin:

Vers. 5. ἔρχεται ἦν εἰς πόλιν τῆς Σαμαρείας) πόλιν hic vocat civitatis territorium. Simile notavimus ad Luc. XI. 7.

λεγομένην Συχάρ) Σιχὰρ habent Græci codices plerique & Syriacus. Et sic in Latinis legitur & suo tempore lectum no- tat Hieronymus. Alii codices Συχὰρ & hos sequitur Arabs. Et vocalis quidem permutatio non nova, sic Σίμων & Συ- μεὼν scribitur, & hæc ipsa urbs Σιχὲμ & Συχὲμ. Pro ιμ au- tem quod ας scribitur putat librariorum vitium esse Hiero- nymus: alii rectius pronunciationem corruptam tempori- bus putant, ut ex Βελίαλ factum est Βελίαρ & similia. Σίκι- μα Græca flectione plerumque hæc urbs appellatur, de qua totoq; eo tractu exstant versus Theodoti Poetæ Græci libro de Judæis, quos citat Eusebius præparationis lib. IX. c. 1. sed corruptos, quos sic emendandos censeam: Ἡδ' ἄρ' ἔην ἀγαθή τε κὴ αἰγίνομος κὴ ὑψηλή. Ὠδέ μιν ἔσκεν ὁδὸς δολιχὴ πόλιν εἰσαφικέσθαι Ἀγρόθεν' ὠδέποθι δρία λαχνήεντ' ἀπόεργεν Ἐξ αὐτῆς δὲ μάλ' ἄγχι δύ' ὄρεα φαίνοτ' ἐρυμνά. Ποίης τε πλήθοντα καὶ ὕλης˙ τῷ δὲ μεταξὺ Ἀτραπιτὸς τέτμητ' ἀραὴ ἀυλάκις' ὕπερθεν Ἡ δἱερὴ Σίκιμον καταφαίνεται ἱερὸν ἄστυ Νέρθεν ὑπὸ ῥίζῃ δεδμημένον˙ ἀμφὶ δὲ τείχη Λισσὸν ὑπώρειαι ὑποδεδραμέται εἰσιν ἔρημοι.

Montes illi duo qui Sicimis imminent, suntGarizim, de quo jam audiemus, &Hebal. Vide Benjaminem itinerario. Male id negat Epiphanius levibus argumentis. Significanter autē nominatur hæc urbs, ut Hierosolymis in religione æmulæ.

Eandem esse civitatem, quæ in V. Test. Sichem vocatur, dubitandum non est: Ita priscæ historiæ de Sichem Gen. 33, 19. c. 34, 1. c. 37, 12. huc quadrant, quod Jacob cum duodecim Patriarchis ibi habi- tarit, adorarit, prædium Josepho legarit. Ossa etiā Josephi in ea parte agi, propter fidem & expecta- tionem Messiæ sepulta fuerunt, Jos. 24, 32. Non procul etiam à Sichem, sicut Hieron. scribit, in Sa- lem, Melchisedech habitaverat, & in monte vicino benedictiones Deut. 27, 5. Ios. 8, 30. recitatæ fue- rant. Et Baptista nuper in Ænon, circa Salim pro- pe Sichem baptizaverat. Fuit autem Sichem regia civitas tempore Iudicum, quam Abimelech solo æquavit, Iud. 9, 45. Jerobeam vero rursus eam æ- dificavit 2. Reg. 12, 25. & pro regia sede ea usus fuit. Unde forsan vallis illa regia vocata est. Postea Am- ri ædificavit in Ephraim monte Someron civitatem ejusdem nominis, 2. Reg. 16, 24. Et ea civitate, quæ inde Samaria appellata fuit, sequentes Reges Israe- litarum pro regia sede usi sunt. Josephus vero scri- bit, tempore Alexandri Magni Samariæ Metropolin rursus fuisse Sichem. Post Evangelistarum vero tempora Sichem iterum fuit restaurata, & mutato nomine dicta Neapolis, quæ patria fuit Justini Martyris, & Hieronymi adhuc tempore appella- tionem illam retinuit. Fuisse autem Sichem illam non procul positam à monte Garizim, in quo templum Samaritanorum extructum fuisse dixi- mus, colligitur ex IX. c. Judicum v. 7. ubi vox stan- tis in vertice montis in ipsa hac civitate Sichem exauditur: ut observat B. Chemnitius.

τῶ χωρίῳ ὅ ἔδωκεν Ἰακὼβ Ἰωσήφ) Gen. XLVIII. 22. in cujus loci expositione non placet, quod quidam putant à Simeo- ne & Levi hunc agrum manu captum, cum Sicima diripe- rent. Nam id factum perfidia mixtum improbavit Jaco- bus. Neque magis putem discessu Jacobi à vicinis occu- patum, deinde à Jacobo reverso armis recuperatum, quod quidam fingunt. Neque enim ea fuit vis Jacobi ejusque fa- miliæ ut aperto bello quicquam in vicinos auderent, cum illud ipsum quod Simeon & Levi ausi fuerant non factum sit nisi dolo & per morbi occasionem. Quare verisimilius est, sicut donatio hæc effectum non habuit, nisi postquam terra promissa armis occupata est, ut videre est Josuæ XXIV. 32. ita Jacobi spe antecepisse hanc victoriam, sibique tribue- re quod sui posteri facturi erant & præterito tempore enun- tiare more Prophetico, id quod certo eventurum videbat.

Confer quæ de his ad locum Geneseos in Com- mentario.

## 4:6
V. 6. Jacob's well) It was a pit, as we shall soon see, situated to the south of the city, as those experienced in the places note. But it is the custom of the Hebrews to call every spring a fountain. We noted this at Mark V. 29. However, that this well was dug by Jacob was not evident from the sacred scriptures, unless one wishes to draw in here that passage of Deuteronomy, 'Jacob's fountain for grain and wine,' but rather from ancient report, as with many other things.

Being wearied from the journey) The truth of human nature is indicated.

he sat thus) Carelessly, as the place had offered itself. Not unlike that in Acts XX. 11.

by the well) ἐπὶ is על which means at or near. Thus Exodus II. 15, וישב על הבאר, he sat by the well, to which history allusion is made here.

About the sixth hour) See above I. 39. He shows the cause of the thirst, because he had both made a long journey and it was now midday.

Latin:

V. 6. πηγὴ τοῦ Ἰακώβ) Puteus erat, ut mox videbimus, situs ad Austrum ab urbe ut notant locorum periti. Sed He- bræis mos est omnem scatebram fontem vocare. Notavi- mus ad Marc. V. 29. A Iacobo autem effossum hunc pu- teum ex sacris scriptis non constabat, nisi quis trahere huc velit illud Deuteronomii πηγὴ Ἰακὼβ ἐπὶ σίτῳ καὶ οἴνῳ, sed vetere fama, ut alia multa.

Κεκοπιακὼς ἐκ τῆς ὁδοιπορίας) Indicatur veritas humanæ naturæ.

ἐκαθέζετο οὕτως) Incuriose, ut se locus obtulerat. Non dissimile illud Act. XX. 11.

ἐπὶ τῇ πηγῇ) ἐπὶ est על quod valet ad vel juxta. Sic Exod. II. 15. וישב על הבאר ἐκάθισεν ἐπὶ τῦ φρέατος ad quam historiam hic alluditur.

Ὡσεὶ ἕκτη) Vide supra I. 39. Causam sitis ostendit, quia & multum itineris fecerat & jam erat meridies.

## 4:7
V. 7. There comes) A chance event is indicated, but one directed by divine counsel.

A woman of Samaria) A Samaritan woman, as John speaks soon after: for ἐκ in this place is put for the Hebrew מ, signifying origin or habitation. Thus ἀπὸ in Matthew XXVII. 57. But understand Samaria here again as the region.

Casaubon explains this more fully. Rightly, he says, did Lyranus and many after him observe that the word Samaria is not the name of a city, but of a people or region. The reason, however, is: because it is not likely that the inhabitants of the city of Samaria would have come to fetch water to the town of Sychar, or Sichem; which was distant from Samaria, according to Benjamin of Tudela, שני מוכאור, two miles, as some interpret that word: or two leagues, as Arias Montanus translates. In whichever way you take it, the interval will be too long for it to seem probable that the inhabitants of Samaria went to Sichem to fetch water. Therefore, Samaria in this verse is the city of Sychar itself; and verses 28 and 30 are to be understood of the same: And similarly the word Samaritan in this history is more often used for Sichemite. But the Evangelist seems to have used this common appellation rather than the proper one, because the hatreds between those two peoples were better expressed by that word; which was especially relevant to the matter.

Ἀντλῆσαι ὕδωρ) With a water jar, of course, as was the custom, below in clause 28. Gen. XXIV. 15. Nonnus: 'having the accustomed pitcher.' Thus in Homer's Odyssey, book 7: 'Like a maiden, a young girl carrying a pitcher.'

Δός μοι πιεῖν) From the urn already filled.

The cause of this request was, on the one hand, true thirst from fatigue and the heat of the sun around midday—for it was about the sixth hour of the day—and the absence of the disciples who might provide a drink; and on the other hand, it was a foreshadowing of his own mystical thirst, by which he thirsted for the salvation of the wretched woman; for he who sought to drink was thirsting for the faith of the woman herself, as Augustine has it in Tractate 15 on John. Whence it is by no means to be conceded to Salmeron that Christ begged, much less that he provided an example here for the useless order of mendicant monks: for Pererius proves in this place that Christ and his disciples were not accustomed to seek their living by begging from door to door: nor did he have need of mendicancy, he who could draw forth water as he wished, or even live without the drinking of water, just as he testified in verse 32 that he was in no way in need of food offered by the disciples: He did not beg, but asked that water be given to him, primarily so that he might conveniently lead the woman to the thirst for the water of life. For he was accustomed to seize occasions for saving instruction from things that had occurred, as was done from food and the impending harvest in the other part of the chapter, and likewise in chapter VI, on the occasion of the feeding, the discourse concerning the heavenly manna was held. Some, such as Ambrose, Bede, Maximus, Euthymius, and Thomas, think that Christ did not ask for that water which the woman understood, but for spiritual water. But in truth, the woman could not provide spiritual water, nor did Christ have any need to ask it of her: and just as true thirst is gathered from the fatigue of Christ, so there is no doubt that Christ asked here for water from Jacob's well, nor did the Samaritans understand it otherwise than as Christ eventually led her to the mystical water. Moreover, these words, 'give me to drink,' teach not only the true humanity of Christ and his state of κένωσις (emptying), but primarily also the end of the same, to which Christ perpetually recalls us, namely, satisfaction for the gluttony of our first parents and our own. He thirsts himself, so that he may expiate the thirst and heat of perverse concupiscence: He thirsts so that we might not have need to thirst eternally, Luke XVI. 24. For he who thirsts here is not a mere man, but he who provides drink to all. He thirsts who gave Israel drink in the desert, 1 Cor. X. 4. For they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them; it went with them, as the Syrian interprets.

Latin:

V. 7. ἔρχεται) Indicatur casus, sed divino consilio di- rectus.

Γυνὴ ἐκ τῆς Σαμαρείας) Σαμαρῖτις, ut mox loquitur Io- hannes:nam ἐκ hoc loco ponitur ut מ Hebræum significans originem vel habitationem. Sic ἀπὸ Matth. XXVII. 57. Sa- mariam autem hic iterum regionem intellige.

Explicat id uberius Casaubonus, Recte, inquit, observavit Lyranus & multi post illum, vocem Sama- ria non esse nomen civitatis, sed gentis vel regionis. Ratio autem est : quia non sit verisimile, urbis Sama- riæ incolas aquatum ventitasse ad oppidum Sichar, si- ve Sichem; quod à Samaria distabat, autore Benjami- no Tadelensi שני מוכאור duo milliaria, ut qui- dam interpretantur illam vocem: vel duas leucas, ut Arias Montanus vertit. Utro modo accipias, longius erit intervallum, quam ut videri queat probabile, in- colas Samariæ Sichemo aquam petiisse. Est igitur Sa- maria in hoc versu, ipsa urbs Sichar; & de eadem versus 28. & 30. sunt intelligendi: Ac similiter vox Samaritanus in hac historia sæpius pro Sichemita. Videtur autem Evangelista hanc potius communem appellationem, quam propriam usurpasse, quia odia inter illas duas gentes ea voce melius exprimebantur; quod ad rem cumprimis faciebat.

Ἀντλῆσαι ὕδωρ) Cum hydria scilicet, ut moris erat, in- fra commate 28. Gen. XXIV. 15. Nonnus ἠθάδα κάλπιν ἔχουσα. Sic apud Homerum Odysseæ η: Παρθενικῇ εἰκῦα νεήνιδι κάλπιν ἐχόσῃ.

Δός μοι πιεῖν) Ex urna jam impleta.

Petitionis hujus causa erat, tum sitis vera à de- fatigatione Solisque æstu circa meridiem, erat e- nim hora fere sexta oriunda, & discipulorum, qui potum præberent absentia, tum mysticæ etiam si- tis suæ, qua miseræ fœminæ salutem sitiebat ad- umbratio; qui enim bibere quærebat, fidem mulie- ris ipsius sitiebat, ut habet Augustinus Tract. 15. in Job. Unde nequaquam Salmeroni conceden- dum Christum mendicasse, nedum inutili Mona- chorum mendicantium ordini exemplum hic prę- buisse: Non enim Christum & discipulos ejus soli- tos victum ostiatim mendicando quærere, Pererius in hunc locum probat: Neq; opus habuit mendicita- te, qui aquam educere, ut voluit, potuit, vel etiam absque aquæ potu vivere, quemadmodum cibo à discipulis oblato se minime egere v. 32. testabatur: Non mendicavit, sed dari sibi postulavit aquā, im- primis ut ad sitim aquæ vitæ mulierem commode perduceret. Consuevit enim è renata occasiones informationis salutiferæ captare, uti è cibo & im- minente messe in altera capitis parte factum, item c. VI. occasione cibationis concio de manna cælesti habita. Nonnulli utpote Ambrosius, Beda, Maxi- mus, Euthymius & Thomas existimant non petivil- se Christum illam aquam, quam mulier intellexit, sed aquam spiritualem. Verum enim vero spiritua- lem aquam nec mulier præbere poterat, nec Chri- stus ab eadem petere opus habebat: & uti è defati- gatione Christi vera sitis colligitur, ita nullum du- bium est, aquam è fonte Jacobæo hic petiisse Chri stum, nec aliter id Samaritis intellexit, quam dein- de demum ad aquam mysticam Christus deduxit. Docent autem hæc verba, da mihi bibere, non tan- tum veram Christi humanitatem statumque κενώ- σεως, sed imprimis quoq; finem ejusdem, ad quem nos perpetuo revocat Christus, satisfactionem nempe pro ingluvie primorum Parentum & nostra. Sitit ipse, ut sitim & ardorem pravæ concupiscen- tiæ expiet: Sitit ne nos æternum sitire opus habea- mus, Luc. XVI. 24. Sitit enim hic non homo me- rus, sed is qui potum præbet omnibus. Sitit qui Israëlem in deserto potavit 1. Cor. X. 4. Bibebant enim de spirituali petra quæ sequebatur eos; ibat cum iis, ut Syrus interpretatur.

## 4:8
V. 8. Οἱ γὰρ μαθηταὶ αὐτῶ) The disciples were not present to bring a pitcher to him from elsewhere. And on this occasion, the modesty of the woman, whom Christ was about to lead to a better way of life, was consulted. It seems that at this time Christ had as yet few disciples before the twelve were chosen.

Latin:

V. 8. Οἱ γὰρ μαθηταὶ αὐτῶ) Non aderant discipuli, qui ur- ceum ipsi aliunde adferrent. Et hac occasione consultũ est pudori mulieris, quam Christus ad meliorem frugem erat perducturus. Videtur hoc tempore Christus discipulos ad- huc paucos habuisse ante electos duodecim.

## 4:9
V. 9. Ἰουδαῖος ὢν) The dialect also distinguished the Ephraimites from other Israelites, Jud. XII. 6, and the Galileans from the Jews, Matt. XXVI. 73. How much more the Samaritans from a Jew? It is credible that there was also some difference in their clothes, just as they differed in many rites: as is noted in the book Musar.

ὐ γὰρ συγχρῶνται Ἰυδαῖοι Σαμαρείταις) What is called κολλᾶσθαι in Acts IX. 26, that is, to associate in a friendly way, which the tradition of the lawyers interpreted in such a way that it was indeed permitted to buy necessities, but not permitted to accept any favor from a Samaritan. But Christ rightly rejected such traditions, which were supported neither by the law of God nor by fair reason. The law forbids no commerce with a foreigner (I except the peoples condemned by divine sentence) as long as one abstains from forbidden foods. Reason dissuades nothing other than what could lead the weak away from the worship of God, for which reason the Hebrews note that it was forbidden to drink wine with an idolater, not by law but by the caution of the learned, lest contagion be contracted through too familiar association. The Samaritans, however, were so superstitious that upon seeing a Jew they would exclaim, 'Do not touch.' But these words are those of the Evangelist, who is giving the reason for what the woman had said. A similar parenthesis occurs shortly after in IV. 24.

A threefold Samaritanism is to be observed here: The first is Jeroboamic, admitting the worship of calves, 1 Kings XII. 32. The second is Cuthite, gentile, worshipping the idols of the heathens at the same time, 2 Kings XVII. The third is Garizitan, regarding the ἐθελοθρησκείαν (will-worship) of worshipping God not in the Jerusalem temple, but on Mount Gerizim. See Josephus, Antiquities, book XI, ch. 7 and 8.

Latin:

V. 9. Ἰουδαῖος ὢν) Dialectus etiam Ephraimitas ab aliis Israëlitis Jud. XII. 6. & Galilæos à Judæis distingvebat. Matt. XXVI, 73. Quanto magis Samaritani à Judæo? Credibile est & in vestibus aliquid fuisse discriminis, ut multis ritibus dif- crepabant: ut notatur in libro Musar.

ὐ γὰρ συγχρῶνται Ἰυδαῖοι Σαμαρείταις) Quod κολλᾶσθαι dicitur Actor. IX. 26. id est amice uti, quod legisperitorum traditio sic interpretabatur, ut emere quidem necessaria li- ceret, at beneficium à Samarita ullum accipere non lice- ret. Sed tales traditiones neq; lege Dei neq; æqua ratione subnixas merito Christus repudiavit. Lex nullum cum alie- nigena vetat commercium (populos divina sententia da- mnatos excipio) dum cibis vetitis abstineatur. Ratio non aliud dissuadet, quam quod infirmos à Dei cultu posset ab- ducere, quam ob causam notant Hebræi vetitum cum ido- lolatra vinum bibere, non lege sed eruditorum cautione, ne familiari nimium consuetudine contagium contrahere- tur. Samaritæ vero adeo erant superstitiosi, ut viso Judæo exclamarent, ne attinge. Verba autem hæc Evangelistæ sunt rationem reddentis ejus quod fœmina dixerat. Similis pa- renthesis mox occurrit IV. 24.

Triplex hic observandus Samaritanismus: Pri- mus Jerobeamicus, cultum vitulorum admittens, 1. Reg. XII. 32. Alter Chuthæus gentilis, Ethnicorum idola simul colens, 2. Reg. XVII. Tertius Garizita- nus quoad ἐθελοθρησκείαν colendi Deum non in templo Hierosolymitano, sed in monte Garizin. Vid. Josephum l. XI. Antiq. c. 7. & 8.

## 4:10
V. 10. εἰ ᾔδεις τὴν δωρεὰν τῶ Θεῶ) If you understood how great this is: namely, the opportunity which God now provides to you, however much you are a Samaritan woman. Thus in Eph. II. 8, the evangelical calling is called the 'gift of God.'

Τίς ἐστι) Who and how great.

When the woman wondered how he, being a Jew—as appeared from his dress and speech, which were different from the Samaritans, who were Chaldean in origin—could ask a drink of her: since, according to the traditions of the Jews, as Arias Montanus observes, it would not be lawful for them to receive food as a gift from the Samaritans, or to drink from the same cup as them: On account of the different religion of the Assyrians who worshipped false gentile deities alongside the God of Israel 2 Kings 17: Christ answered if you knew the gift of God & who it is who said to you give me to drink, you would ask, and he would give you living water. By the gift of God he does not understand God's gifts in general, as Theophylact does, nor himself as the incarnate Son of God, as some recent writers do, nor the Holy Spirit as it seemed to Augustine and Rupert: But this very grace, which then befell her, that such a benefit is exhibited to the Samaritan woman herself from heaven: If you knew this, and therefore understood, who it is that asks water of you. What follows, the Vulgate renders thus, perhaps you would have asked of him. Whence Maldonatus gathers the faculty of free will. But from the hypothetical proposition if you knew this gift of God, nothing can be inferred. For the unregenerate are destitute of that knowledge, and therefore since there is no desire for what is unknown, they cannot desire the living water, of which they are ignorant. We see, however, how much the gift and benefit of God; with Christ himself as the herald, the manifestation of Christ ought to be valued: it is called δωρεὰ; which happens gratuitously, and cannot be bought for a price. Acts 8:20. And concerning the gift of the Holy Spirit. Acts 2:28. 10:45. concerning the gift of justification. Rom. 5:15, 17. concerning the heavenly gift. Heb. 6:4. it is used. All of which are obtained freely and by grace. That it is said to be exhibited to us δωρεάν freely, which we in no way deserve. Matt. 20:8. 2 Thess. 2:8. Rev. 21:6, etc. 22:17. Which may be noted against the Popish merit of congruity. Just as this benefit came to the Samaritan woman gratuitously, because Christ manifested himself to her: so whatever things make for life are given to us only and entirely gratuitously. 2 Pet. 1:3 and we are said to be justified δωρεὰν freely by his grace Rom. 3:24.

˝Έδωκεν ἁν σοι ὕδωρ ζω̃ν] Water has a varied meaning in various places. In this place and in the Apocalypse several times I do not doubt that the Evangelical dogma is signified, namely insofar as it contains those things which are necessary and sufficient for producing eternal salvation. I have as a primary argument for this matter that which is read below in verse 34, which we shall use presently. Nor do the ancients depart much from this, such as Cyprian in his Epistle to Caecilius, who take it concerning baptism: for baptism is the solemn profession of that dogma. Philo in Allegories on Moses in Midian: ἐκάθισεν ἐπὶ τυ̃ φρέατος ἐνδεχόμενος τι ὁ θεὸς ἀνομβρή- σει πότιμον τη̃ διψώση καὶ ποθώση ψυχη̃ τὸ ἀγαθὸν ἀναχωρει̃ μὲν ἀπὸ τη̃ς ἀδίκου καὶ ἡγεμονικο̂ς τω̃ν παθω̃ν δόξης.

By this living water Grotius understands the Evangelical dogma, others the grace and mercy of God on account of the Son our Mediator to be applied by the Holy Spirit in our hearts through faith in the sense of the wrath of God, so that the desire and thirst for any other things besides that grace of God may cease: as the blessed Tarnovius explains: Cyprian in his Epistle to Caecilius wishes Baptism to be designated: others interpret it concerning the Holy Spirit: But we easily agree that the truly Evangelical doctrine, which is concerning that mercy of God, and the merit of Christ to be drawn by the mouth of faith and applied to us, is designated: since the doctrine concerning the remission of sins is often proposed in the Prophets under the metaphor of the thirst of a sterile or arid land, and of water that refreshes, revives, and makes grow, Is. 12:3, 35:7, 44:3, 55:1, Jer. 2:13, Ez. 47:1, Joel 3:18, Zech. 14:8. as the blessed Chemnitius observes: Which water, drawn through faith, causes the dire thirst excited by the recognition of sins and the sense of the wrath of God to begin to be quenched in this life, so that we may not be tormented by it forever, Luke 16:14. But let us have eternal life, and enjoy the crystalline river of living water forever Rev. 22:1, and so let it be for us a fountain springing up into eternal life. Since therefore wisdom testifies in Sirach 24:29, they who drink me shall yet thirst, it is insinuated that it is not a lack, but a spiritual desire that grows from time to time, so that the more those spiritual waters are drunk, the more they are thirsted for. Whence it is rightly noted by Grotius that there is an emphasis in the word shall spring up: for waters are accustomed to spring up to the height of their origin. Because that water overflows from heaven into us, and springs up again even to heaven. Nor is that ὃ μὴ διψήση εἰς τὸ αἰῶνα badly compared with chapter 6 verse 35. ὁ πιςέυων εἰς ἐμὲ ἰ μὴ διψήσῃ πώποτε are compared, so that it may be concluded from that, that that water is that which is believed for salvation, which once drawn is not to be drawn again, but only to be retained. Perhaps, however, those sentences can be subordinated if it is understood here first, and properly as the grace of the Holy Spirit, as appears both from the promises of the Old Testament Is. 44:3, Ez. 36:25, 27, and especially from the declaration of the same made in the place parallel to this one of ours. John 7:38, 39. He who believes in me, as the scripture says, rivers of living water shall flow from his belly. But he said this concerning the Spirit whom those who believe were to receive. With which also the Type of Ez. 47:9 agrees. For living water flowing from the true temple of the body of Christ John 2:31, and also from the temple of the mystical body of the Church through the word into us, is the Holy Spirit and his grace, which is compared to water for these reasons.

(1) As water quenches thirst, so the Holy Spirit can quench the thirst for spiritual goods, which believers pant for. Ps. 42:2, Is. 55:1, by satisfying us with the same Matt. 5:6, as Christ says afterwards, he who drinks of the water that I shall give shall not thirst forever. (2) As in the heat water refreshes and restores us, so the Holy Spirit tempers the heat of divine wrath in us and refreshes us with sweet cooling. (3) On account of fruitfulness Is. 44:3, 4. For through the grace of the Holy Spirit, as Cyril has in book 2 chapter 82, human nature, irrigated from aridity and unfruitfulness to the pristine beauty and greenness of its powers, flourishes with a great number of virtues and produces most sweet fruits through Charity toward God. To which it contributes that the Holy Spirit quenches the ardor of conscience and the thirst for temporal things in us. (4) Just as water washes and cleanses the body, so by the grace and regeneration of the Holy Spirit we are cleansed from our sins. (5) Add that through the affection of love, the Holy Spirit joins man with God and his neighbor, etc.

He calls it living water, that is, according to the interpretation of Chrysostom, that which always springs forth, not standing water, such as is in lakes, but springing, because the grace of the Spirit always makes the soul agile for good, as Theophylact observes. Therefore, the Holy Spirit is called living water not only essentially, because He is life itself, but also efficiently, because He makes us participants of spiritual and eternal life, and thus Athanasius de nat. hum. suscepta, Ambrose l. II. de Sp. S. c. XXIX, Cyril, Chrysostom, and Theodoret on this passage, Basil on Ps. XLV, Bede, Theophylact, Euthymius, Rupert, etc., explain it concerning the Holy Spirit. Irenaeus l. III. c. XIX, dealing with this living water, institutes a comparison of this kind: Just as a single mass cannot be made from dry wheat without moisture, nor one loaf of bread, so neither could we, being many, become one in Christ Jesus without the water which is from heaven: And just as dry earth, if it does not receive moisture, does not bear fruit; so also we, being at first dry wood, would never bear the fruit of life without the voluntary rain from above.

Christ made Himself the giver of this living water for three reasons. 1. By reason of principle and origin. For He presents Himself here as the fountain of living water, from which the Holy Spirit overflows and has His origin, concerning which Chrysostom elegantly says, for this reason, he says, the Savior shows Himself to be the fountain of life, and the living water to be the Holy Spirit. Likewise, the Father is the fountain of living water, the river proceeding from the fountain is the Son, the water of the river is the Holy Spirit. Therefore, the Spirit is said to ἀναβλύζειν, to spring forth from the Son. Cyril in his Epistle to Nestorius and in book III of his Commentary on John speaks of the outpouring of the Holy Spirit from the Son no less than from the Father. Epiphanius, Heresy LXIX, of the Arians. A fountain from a fountain from the Father and the only-begotten Son.

ANNOTATIONS ON JOHN

He names the Holy Spirit. Athanasius, in his work on the assumption of human nature, proves from these words of Christ, and also from Ps. 36:10, that the Son is the fountain of the Holy Spirit. These things excellently confirm the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Son according to the opinion of the ancient Greek Doctors, because the Son is πηγὴ, the Fountain of the Holy Spirit, because He proceeds from Him, just as the Greeks otherwise designate the Father as the fountain of the Holy Spirit. Athanasius, in the second Dialogue on the Trinity: 'For as a fountain does not produce the water it emits from an external source, but has it springing forth from itself: So also God: He is the Fountain of the Holy Spirit and is believed not to assume Him from an external source, but to cause Him to flow from Himself,' and to that extent the word of procession ἐκπορεύσεως is explained by Chrysostom in his Homily on the Holy Spirit, that He proceeds like water flowing from a fountain, as is said of Paradise, 'a river goes out from Eden,' etc. Just as in Rev. 22:1. The crystalline river, designating the Holy Spirit, is said to be ἐκπορευόμενος, proceeding from the throne of God and of the Lamb, on account of the eternal procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son. (II) By reason of merit and acquisition. For whatever grace Christ bestows upon us, He bestows by the virtue of His merit, as He in whom God freely gives us all things, Rom. 8:32, in whom we are blessed with every spiritual blessing, Eph. 1:3. Rightly, therefore, does Christ say, 'I will give,' because He Himself acquired this gift for us, and thence received the promise of the Holy Spirit from the Father, that is, the power of giving the Holy Spirit, as He had promised, Acts 2:33. (III) By reason of the gift and communication: because He Himself communicates the Holy Spirit to us, just as He gave the same to His disciples, John 20:22. He Himself sends and pours out the same from heaven, Luke 24:49, John 15:26. Nor indeed is the Holy Spirit communicated only κατ' ἐνέργειαν, according to efficacy, but also κατ' ὀυσίαν, according to essence, if indeed the Spirit Himself is said to be given to us as living water, to be sent as our Paraclete, to be gifted in such a way that He dwells in us, John 14:39, Rom. 8:11, 1 Cor. 3:16. We receive the Holy Spirit Himself, Rom. 8:25. God sends the Spirit of His Son into our hearts, in whom we cry Abba Father, Gal. 4:6. Therefore, the ancient Doctors assert ὁμαθυμαδὸν (with one mind) that not only gifts but the Holy Spirit Himself is communicated to us. Basil, book V against Eunomius: 'Life,' he says, 'which the Spirit emits for the production of another life, is not at all separated from Him, but just as fire is partly the heat which is inherent in it, and partly that which water provides: So the Spirit both has life in Himself, and those who are partakers of Him possess divine and heavenly life.' If fire, says Cyril of Jerusalem, Catechesis 17, when it is a body entering into a body, thus operates without any impediment, as you see, why do you wonder if the Holy Spirit enters into the interior of the soul? And hence Augustine concludes: that Christ is God, because the Holy Spirit bestows God upon us, book XV on the Trinity, ch. XXVI. 'How is He not God who gives the Holy Spirit? Nay, how great a God is He who gives God?' Cyril of Alexandria, book II on John, ch. II, teaches that we become partakers of the divine nature because the Holy Spirit is given to us, using an elegant similitude. For if the fragrance of aromatics expresses its own power into garments, and in a way transforms into itself those things in which it is present, how could the Holy Spirit not be able, since He exists naturally from God, to make those in whom He dwells partakers of the divine nature through Himself?

Furthermore (II) it can also be explained concerning the word of the Gospel, insofar as the Holy Spirit unites Himself to His word, and does not communicate Himself to us immediately, but anointed with the word and through the medium of the word. Whence the word is living and effective, Heb. 4:12. The law of the Spirit of life, Rom. 8:3. The power, Rom. 1:16, nay, the Spirit and life through and because of that gracious union of the Spirit with the word; for the power of the Holy Spirit is not one thing and that of the word another, but it is one and the same power, which is in the Holy Spirit originally, but in the word communicatively. For divine power is only one and indivisible; whence it cannot be said that the power of the word is instrumental and that of the Holy Spirit principal, even though the word may be called, by reason of the external economy primarily, an instrument of the Holy Spirit, just as the visual power of the soul and of the eye is one, and the eye is not called an instrument by reason of the visual power communicated to it, but by reason of the bodily members, concerning which compare our System, Tom. I, ch. IV, quest. XXV. concl. III. & IV. p. 710. And thus by living water Ammonius, Euthymius, and also Theodoret in Ps. 1 understand the word of the Gospel.

By the same reason (III) it can be explained concerning the Sacrament of Baptism, insofar as the Holy Spirit, as the true water of life, unites Himself not only to the word but also to Baptism, and indeed to this in a peculiar sacramental manner, on account of which union whatever efficacy exerts itself in Baptism has the Holy Spirit as its Author, nor is it attributed to the water of baptism otherwise than because the Holy Spirit has joined Himself with that water, Tit. 3:5. Moreover, they interpret the words of Christ concerning the water of baptism: Justin Martyr in his Dialogue with Trypho, Cyprian in his Epistle to Caecilius, Ambrose in book I on the Holy Spirit, ch. XIX, Maximus in his sermon on Almsgiving, Augustine in sermon XCII on the times, Prosper in book I on the promises, ch. I, which sense we do not disapprove, provided that by living water is understood not the element of water itself, but the Holy Spirit who presents Himself to it in Baptism. Therefore Rupert beautifully says on this passage: 'What is the water if not that grace of the Holy Spirit which is received in the Baptism of Christ?' The water is the Holy Spirit, this water is God, this water is a fountain in the heart of God the Father, it is a torrent of glory in all the Angels, it is an inundation of life in the elect, which, having been drunk by anyone, leaps back to its eternal Matrix, the abyss of divinity.

(IV.) Christ as living water is explained by Epiphanius, Heresy 74, as also in the Ancoratus. Likewise by Procopius on Isaiah 7, and others. Nor is there any doubt that Christ communicates himself to us when he offers us living water, because the Holy Spirit makes us participants through the Word and Sacraments in the merit of Christ, and in the salvation obtained through him, and indeed in our Savior himself. Furthermore, the very term 'living water' signifies the Holy Spirit immediately, as we have said. The thing signified, however, consequently implies the presence and efficacy of the Savior, because the Holy Spirit is living water to us when he makes us partakers of our life, which is Christ, and communicates to us the life obtained through him. For the life which God gave us is in his Son, 1 John 5:11. Hence, just as he is the bread of life, so he is most rightly called the water of life, as Epiphanius, loc. cit., concludes.

Latin:

V. 10. εἰ ᾔδεις τὴν δωρεὰν τῶ Θεῶ) Si intelligeres, quantum hoc sit: Occasio nempe, quam tibi nunc Deus præstat, quantumvis Samaritidi. Sic Eph. II, 8. δῶρον Θεῶ dicitur vocatio Evangelica.

Τίς ἐστι) Quis quantusque.

Cum mulier miraretur, qui ipse Judæus, ut ex ha- bitu & sermone à Samaritanis, origine Chaldæis diverso apparebat, potum abs se peteret: Siquidem per traditiones judæorum, ut observat Arias Mon- tanus, non liceret his cibos à Samaritanis dono ac- cipere, aut ex eodem cum ipsis poculo bibere: Ob diversam Assyriorum falsa gentilium numina jux- ta Deum Israëlis colentium 2. Reg. XVII. religio- nem: Respondit Christus si scires donum Dei & quis sit qui dixit tibi da mihi bibere,tu rogares, & da- ret tibi aquam vitæ. Per donum Dei non intelligit in genere Dei dona,uti Theophylacto, non seipsum in- carnatum Dei Filium, ut recentioribus nonnullis, non Sp. S. ut Augustino & Ruperto visum: Sed hanc ipsam gratiam, quæ ei tum obtigit, quod tantum beneficium ipsi Samaritidi cœlitus exhibeatur: Si nesses hoc,adeoq; intelligeres,quisnam abs te aquam petat. Quæ sequuntur, Vulgata ita reddit, tu forsan petiisses ab eo. Unde Maldonatus colligit liberi ar- bitrii facultatem. Sed ex hypothetica propositione si nesses hoc Dei donum,nihil inferri potest. Illa enim notitia destituuntur non renati, proinde cum i- gnoti nulla sit cupido, desiderare aquam vivam, quam ignorant, non possunt. Videmus autem quantum Dei donum atq; beneficium; præcone ipso Christo, æstimari debeat Christi manifestatio: δωρεὰ dicitur; Quod gratuito contingit,neq; pre- tio emi potest. Act.VIII.20. Et de Spirit. S. dono. Act.II.28. X.45. de dono justificationis. Rom. V. 15. 17. de cœlesti dono. Ebr.VI.4. adhibetur. Quæ o- mnia gratis & ex gratia obtingunt. Quod δωρεάν gratis nobis exhiberi dicitur, quod nullatenus me- remur. Matth.XX.8. 2. Thess. II.8. Ap.XXI.6. &c. XXII.17. Quæ contra meritum congrui Papisticum notentur. Uti hoc beneficium gratuito Samarita- næ obvenit,quod Christus se ipsi manifestavit: ita non nisi gratuito prorsus donantur nobis,quæcunq; ad vitam faciunt. 2.Petr. I. 3. ac δωρεὰν gratis per gra- tiam ipsius justificari dicimur Rom. III. 24.

˝Έδωκεν ἁν σοι ὕδωρ ζω̃ν] Aqua variis in locis variam habet significationem. Hoc loco & in Apocalypsi aliquoties non dubito quin significetur dogma Evangelicum, nempe qua- tenus ea continet, quæ ad salutē æternam pariendam neces- saria sunt ac sufficiunt. Argumentum ad eam rem præcipuũ habeo id quod infra legitur v1.34. quo jam jam utemur.Nec multum hinc abeunt veteres, ut Cyprianus Epistola ad Cæ- cilium,qui de baptismo accipiunt: nam baptismus est istius dogmatis solennis professio. Philo Allegoriis de Mose in Madian: ἐκάθισεν ἐπὶ τυ̃ φρέατος ἐνδεχόμενος τι ὁ θεὸς ἀνομβρή- σει πότιμον τη̃ διψώση καὶ ποθώση ψυχη̃ τὸ ἀγαθὸν ἀναχωρει̃ μὲν ἀπὸ τη̃ς ἀδίκου καὶ ἡγεμονικο̂ς τω̃ν παθω̃ν δόξης.

Per aquam hanc vivam dogma Evangelicum in- telligit Grotius, alii gratiam & misericordiam Dei propterFiliumMediatorem nostrum à S. S. in cor- dibus nostris per fidem in sensu iræ Dei applican- dam,ut desiderium & sitis quarumcunque aliarum rerum præter illamDei gratiam cesset: ut explicat B. Tarnovius: Cyprianus Epist. ad Cæcil. Baptisma designari vult:alii de Spiritu S. interpretantur:Sed facile annuimus doctrinam vere Evangelicam, quæ est de misericordia illa Dei, meritoq; Christi fidei ore hauriendis nobisq; applicandis designari: si- quidem doctrina de remissione peccatorum in Pro- phetis sæpe proponatur sub metaphora sitis terræ sterilis seu aridæ, & aquæ refrigerantis, refocillantis, vegetantis, Es.XII.3. XXXV.7. XLIV.3. LV.1. Jer.II. 13. Ez.XLVII.1. Joel.III.18. Zach.XIV.8. ut obser- vatB.Chemnitius: Quæ aqua per fidem hausta fa- cit,ut dira sitis agnitione peccatorum, & sensu iræ Dei excitata in hac vita restingui incipiat,ne in æ- ternum illa torqueamur, Luc. XVI.14. Sed habea- mus vitam æternam, & fruamur crystallino fluvio vivæ aquæ in æternum Ap. XXII.1. adeoq; sit nobis fons scaturiens in vitam æternam. Quum ergo sapi- entia testatur Syr.XXIV.29. qui bibent me, adhuc si- tient, non inopia, sed desiderium spirituale subinde crescens,ut quo plus sunt potæ plus sitiantur aquæ illæ spirituales,insinuatur. Unde recte à Grotio nota- tur emphasis in voce saliet: solent enim aquæ salire ad altitudinem usq; suæ originis. Quia aqua illa de cœlo in nos redundat, & salit iterum in cœlum us- que. Nec male illa 8' μὴ διψήση εἰς τὸ αἰῶνα cũ c. v1. 35. ὁ πιςέυων εἰς ἐμὲ ἰ μὴ διψήσῃ πώποτε confe- runtur, ut concludatur inde, quod aqua illa sit id quod creditur ad salutem, quod semel haustũ am- pli9 hauriendum non est, sed retinendum tantum. Forte autem sententiæ illæ subordinari possunt si intelligatur hic I. πρώτως, ac proprie Sp. S. gratia, ut apparet cum è promissionibus V. T. Es. XLIV. 3. Ez. XXXVI. 25. 27. tum imprimis è declaratione eorundem in loco Parallelo huic nostro facta. Joh. VII. 38. 39. Qui credit in me, sicut dicit scriptura, flu- mina fluent è ventre ejus vivæ aquæ. Hoc autem dixit de Spiritu quem accepturi essent credentes. Quibus consonat etiam Typus Ez. XLVII. 9. Aqua enim viva è templo vero corporis Christi Joh. II. 31. nec non è templo corporis Ecclesiæ mystici per ver- bum redundans in nos Sp. S. est ejusdemq; gratia, quæ aquæ ob has causas comparatur.

(1) Ut aqua sitim restinguit, ita Sp. S. sitim bonorum Spiritua- lium, quæ anhelant credentes. Ps. XLII. 2. Es. LV. 1. nos satiando iisdem, restinguere potest Matth. V. 6. ut i Christus postmodum ait, qui bibet ex aqua quam ego dabo non sitiet in æternum. (2) Ut in æstu aqua re- frigerat, & reficit nos, ita iræ divinæ æstum in nobis temperat Sp. S. nosq; refocillat dulci refrigerio. (3) Ob fructificationem Es. XLIV. 3. 4. Per gratiam e- nim Sp. S. ut Cyrill. l. II. c. LXXXII. habet, natura humana ab ariditate & infœcunditate ad pristinam virium pulchritudinem & viriditatem irrigata, magno virtutum numero floret & Charitate erga Deum suavissimos fructus producit. Quo facit quod Sp. S. ardorem conscientiæ & sitim rerum tempo- ralium in nobis restinguat. (4) Sicut corpus abluit & mundat aqua, sic gratia & regeneratione Spirit. S. mundamur à peccatis nostris. (5) Adde quod per affectum amoris, hominem conjungat Sp. S. cum Deo & proximo, &c.

Aquam autem vivam dicit, h. e. interprete Chry- sostomo, quæ semper scaturit, aquam non stantem, qualis in lacubus est, sed scaturientem, quia Gratia Spiritus semper agilem ad bonum facit animam, ut observat Theophylactus. Aqua ergo viva dicitur Sp. S. non tantum essentialiter, quia ipsa vita est, sed & efficienter, quia vitæ Spiritualis & æternæ nos par- ticipes facit, atq; ita de Sp. S. exponunt Athanasius de nat. hum. suscepta. Ambros. l. II. de Sp. S. c. XXIX. Cyrill. Chrys. & Theodorent. in h. l. Bas. in Ps. XLV. Be- da, Theophyl. Euthymius, Rupertus &c. Irenæus l. III. c. XIX. de hac aqua viva agens, ejusmodi instituit comparationem: Sicut de arido tritico massa una fie- ri non potest sine humore, neq; unus panis, ita neq; nos multi unum in Christo Jesu fieri poteramus sine aqua, quæ è cœlo est: Et sicut arida terra, si non percipiat humorem, non fructificat; sic & nos lignum aridum existentes primum, nunquam fructificaremus vi- tam, sine superna voluntaria pluvia.

Datorem autem aquæ hujus vivæ se fecit Chri- stus, ob tres causas. 1. Ratione principii & originis. Sistit enim sese hic tanquam fontem aquæ vivæ, ex quo redundat Sp. S. atq; originem suam habet, quo de eleganter Chrysostomus, ob id, inquit, Salvator ostendit seipsum fontem esse vitæ, & aquam vivam esse Sp. S. Item fons aquæ vivæ Pater est, flumen ex fonte procedens, Filius aqua fluminis Sp. S. Ideo di- citur Spiritus ἀναβλύζειν scaturire ex Filio. Cyrill. in Epist. ad Nestorium & in lib. III. Comment. in Joh. dicit πρόχευσιν profundi ex Filio Sp. S. non minus quam ex Patre. Epiphanius Hæres. LXIX. Ariano- rum. Fontem ex Fonte ex Patre & unigenito Filio

ANNOT. AD JOHANNIS

Spiritum S. nuncupat. Athan. de suscept. hum. nat. ex his verbis Christi, nec non ex Ps. XXXVI. 10. probat, Filium esse Spiritus S. fontem. Quæ eximie confirmant processionem Sp. S. ex Filio è Veterum Doctorum Græcorum sententia, quod Filius sit πηγὴ, Fons Sp. S. quia procedit ex ipso, quemadmodum alias Patrem ideo fontem Sp. S. indigitant Græci. Athanas. Dialogo secundo de Trinitate. Nam ut fons, quam emittit, aquam eam non extrinsecus efficit, sed à seipso scaturire faciens habet: Sic & Deus: Fons est Sp. S. & creditur non extrinsecus ipsum assumens, sed ex seipso manare faciens, & eatenus vox processionis ἐκπορεύσεως à Chrysost. Homilia de Sp. S. explicatur, quod procedat velut aqua à fonte manans, uti de Paradiso dictum, fluvius egreditur ex Edem &c. Quemadmodum Ap. XXII. 1. Fluvius crystallinus Spiritum S. designans, dicitur ἐκπορευόμενος procedens ex throno Dei & agni ob æternam processionem Sp. S. à Patre & Filio. (II) Ratione meriti & acquisitionis. Quicquid enim Christus largitur nobis Gratiæ, virtute meriti sui largitur, utpote in quo nobis omnia Deus χαρίζεται Rom. VIII. 32. in quo benedicimur omni benedictione spirituali, Eph. I. 3. Jure ergo Christus dicit, ego dabo, quia ipse acquisivit nobis hoc donum, indeq; accepit promissionem Sp. S. à Patre, hoc est, potestatem dandi Sp. S. uti promiserat, Act. II. 33. (III) Ratione doni & communicationis: quia ipse communicat nobis Sp. S. uti discipulis suis eundem dedit, Joh. XX. 22. Ipse mittit & effundit eundem cœlitus Luc. XXIV. 49. Joh. XV. 26. Nec vero tantum communicatur Sp. S. κατ' ἐνέργειαν quoad efficaciam, sed & κατ' ὀυσίαν, quantum ad essentiam, siquidem ipse Sp. S. dicatur nobis dari ceu aqua viva, mitti ceu Paracletus noster, donari ita, ut habitet in nobis Joh. XIV. 39. Rom. IIX. 11. 1. Cor. III. 16. Accipimus ipsummet Sp. S. Rom. VIII. 25. Deus mittit Spiritum Filii sui in corda nostra, in quo clamamus Abba Pater, Gal. IV. 6. Ideo ὁμαθυμαδὸν veteres Doctores asserunt, non dona tantum sed ipsummet Sp. S. nobis communicari Basil. l. V. contra Eunom. Vita, inquit, quã ad alterius vitæ productionem Spiritus emittit, ab ipso minime separatur, sed quemadmodum ignis partim est calor, qui inest ipsi, partim ille, quem aqua præbet: Ita Spiritus & ipse in seipso vitam habet, & qui participes ipsius sunt, divinam cælestemque possident vitam. Si ignis, inquit Cyrillus: Hierof. catech. XVII. cum sit corpus in corpus ferri ingrediens, sic absq; ullo impedimento, ut vides, operatur, quid miraris, si Sp. S. in animæ interiora ingreditur? Atque hinc concludit Augustinus: Christũ Deum esse, quod Spiritus S. Deum nobis largiatur l. XV. de Trinit. c. XXVI. Quomodo Deus non est qui dat Spiritũ S. imo quantus Deus est qui dat Deum, Cyrillus Alexandr. lib. II. in Joh. c. II. docet, nos participes fieri divinæ naturæ, quia donatur nobis Sp. S. eleganti usus similitudine. Nam si Aromatum fragrantia propriam vim in vestes exprimit, & ad se quodammodo trãsformat ea in quibus inest, quomodo non possit Sp. S. quandoquidem ex Deo naturaliter existit, divinæ naturæ illos participes facere per seipsum in quibus insit?

Porro (II) de verbo Evangelii quoque explicari potest, quatenus Sp. S. sese verbo suo unit, nec immediate nobis se communicat, sed unctus verbo & mediante verbo. Unde verbum vivum est & efficax, Ebr. IV. 12. Lex Spiritus vitæ Rom. VIII. 3. Potentia, Rom. I. 16. imo Spiritus & vita per & propter unionem illam gratiosam Spiritus cum verbo; nec enim alia Sp. S. alia verbi, sed una eademq; virtus est, quæ Spiritui S. originaliter, verbo a. communicative inest. Virtus enim divina non nisi una est, & indivisibilis; Unde dici nequit, virtutem ver- bi esse instrumentalem, Sp. Sancti principale, tamet- si verbum dici possit ratione externae imprimis oi- κονομίας Instrumentum S. Sancti uti una est virtus visiva animae atq; oculi, nec oculus ratione virtutis visivae sibi communicatae instrumentum dicitur, sed ratione membrorum corporeorum, quo de conferatur System. nostri Tom. I. c. IV. quaest. XXV. concl. III. & IV. p. 710. Atq; ita per aquam vivam verbum Evangelii intelligunt Ammonius, Euthymius ut & Theodoretius in Ps. I.

Eadem ratione (III) De Sacramento Baptismi explicari potest, quatenus nempe Sp. S. vera aqua vitae se non tantum verbo, sed Baptismo quoque unit, & huic quidem peculiari sacramentali ratio- ne, ob quam unionem quicquid efficaciae in Bapti- sma se exerit, Autorem habet Sp. S. nec aliter aquae baptismatos tribuitur, quam quia Sp. S. cum aqua illa sese conjunxit, Tit. III. 5. Interpretantur autem verba Christi de aqua baptismatos: Iustinus Mar- tyr. Dialogo cum Tryphone, Cyprianus Epist. ad Ce- cilium. Ambros. l. I. de Sp. S. c. XIX. Maximus sermo- ne de Eleemosyna, Aug. serm. XCII. de tempore. Pro- sper l. I. de promissionibus c. I. quem sensum non re- probamus, modo per aquam vivam non ipsum a- quae elementum, sed qui ei se Baptismo sistit, Sp. S. intelligatur. Ideo pulchre Rupertus in hunc loc. Quae est aqua nisi illa, quae in Baptismo Christi per- cipitur Sp. S. gratia? Aqua haec Sp. Sanctus est, aqua haec Deus est, aqua haec in corde Dei Patris fons est, in omnibus Angelis torrens gloriae est, in electis homi- nibus inundatio vitae est, quae à quocumque bibita fuerit ad Matricem suam aeternam, divinitatis abys- sum resilit.

(IV.) De Christo aqua viva explicatur ab Epiph. haeres. 74. ut & in Ancorato. Nec non à Procopio in Es. VII. aliisque. Neque dubium est, Christum sese nobis ipsum communicare, cum aquam vi- vam nobis praebet, quia Spiritus Sanctus nos per Verbum & Sacramenta participes facit meriti Christi, ac salutis per eum partae ipsiusque adeo Salvatoris nostri. Caeterum vox ipsa aquae vitae Spi- ritum Sanctum, uti diximus, immediate significat. Res autem significata consequenter importat prae- sentiam & efficaciam Salvatoris, quia Spiritus San- ctus nobis aqua vitae est, cum nos vitae nostrae, quae Christus est, consortes reddit, vitamque per ipsum partam nobis communicat. Vita enim quam dedit nobis Deus, est in Filio ejus, 1. Ioh. V. 11. Hinc ut panis illa vitae est, ita & aqua vitae rectissime dici- tur, uti Epiph. loc. cit. colligit.

## 4:13
V. 13. Διψήσει πάλιν) If he lives: because by its own nature this water is such that it does not have an effect unless it is temporary. For it is digested and excreted.

Latin:

V. 13. Διψήσει πάλιν) Si vivat: quia sua natura talis est haec aqua ut effectum non habeat nisi temporarium. Dige- ritur enim & excernitur.

## 4:14
V. 14. Ὀυ μὴ διψήσῃ εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα) Below 6:34, 'he who believes in me shall never thirst.' Therefore, here the water is that which is believed unto salvation, which once drunk need not be drunk again, but only retained. There is nothing that can be added to it, unlike the precepts of human wisdom, which have no end: therefore the more it is drunk, the more the thirst grows. Of this there is discourse in Eccles. XXIV. 30. Cyprian in the cited place: Everyone who drinks of this water will thirst again: but whoever drinks of the water that I shall give will never thirst. By which also the baptism of saving water is signified, which is taken once and not repeated again. Indeed, baptism, as we have said, is a profession of a dogma, which it suffices to have drunk once. Chrysostom on the penultimate chapter of the first to the Corinthians, ὦ γὰρ ἀυτὸ δεῖται τὸ δόγμα μαθεῖν ἀλλ' ὑπομνησθῆναι καὶ διορθωθῆναι.

A fountain of water springing up into eternal life) This alone without other knowledge suffices for the begetting of eternal life. See above I. 4. below VI. 68 XII. 50. XVII. 4. XX. 31. Hebr. IV. 12. And the emphasis is on the word spring up: for waters are accustomed to spring up to the height of their origin. The passage of the Song of Songs IV. 15 looks to this mystically.

Latin:

V. 14. Ὀυ μὴ διψήσῃ εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα) Infra VI. 34. ὁ πιστεύων εἰς ἐμὲ ἐ μὴ διψήσῃ πώποτε. Ergo hic aqua est id, quod cre- ditur ad salutem, quod semel haustum amplius haurien- dum non est, sed retinendum tantum. Nihil est quod ei adjici possit, aliter quam in humanæ sapientiæ præceptis, quorum nunquam finis est: ideo quo magis ea bibitur eo magis crescit sitis. De ea sermo est Eccles. XXIV. 30. Cy- prianus dicto loco: Omnis qui biberit ex aqua ista, sitiet iterum: qui autem biberit ex aqua quam ego dedero, non sitiet in æternum. Quo & ipso baptisma salutaris aquæ significatur, quod semel sumitur nec rursus iteratur. Nimirum baptismus ut diximus professio est dogmatis, quod semel hausisse suf- ficit. Chrysostomus ad caput penultimum prioris ad Corin- thios, ὦ γὰρ ἀυτὸ δεῖται τὸ δόγμα μαθεῖν ἀλλ' ὑπομνησθῆναι καὶ διορθωθῆναι.

Πηγὴ ὕδατος ἁλλομένε εἰς ζωὴν αἰώνιον) Hoc solum sine alia cognitione sufficit ad pariendam vitam æternam. Vi- de supra I. 4. infra VI. 68 XII. 50. XVII. 4. XX. 31. Hebr. IV. 12. Et emphasis est in voce saliet: solent enim aquæ salire ad altitudinem usque suæ originis. Spectat huc mystice lo- cus Cantici IV. 15.

## 4:15
V. 15. Lord) Thus the Hebrews also addressed strangers for the sake of honor. See below XX. 15.

that I may not thirst nor come here to draw) She silently shows her need, which compels her to undergo the labor which she would prefer to be relieved of.

Since the Samaritan woman understood nothing but carnal things concerning the water of life, and therefore expostulated with Christ as to how he could provide living water, when he had neither a bucket nor a drawing vessel, as Augustine calls it, and the well was very deep, from which Jacob the Patriarch himself, whom the customary boastfulness of the Samaritans called their father, could not find a better one there for the use of himself and his own, Christ, having left that invidious contention with Jacob, repeats his promise at least, and again recalls her to the spiritual water, teaching that it differs immensely from the elemental; for of this he says: everyone who drinks from it will thirst again, but of that: but whoever drinks of the water that I shall give him will never thirst, but the water that I shall give him will become in him a fountain of water springing up into eternal life. The difference is sought from the effect, and it is twofold. I. that this water extinguishes thirst, so that he who drinks from it does not experience thirst. That, however, is not explained in the same way: Augustine interprets it concerning the thirst of the body, which the blessed will not feel after death. Tract. XV. in John. Similarly Rupert, who takes it then concerning bodily thirst, while he takes it concerning the full satiety of the soul, which will appear in the glory of God. The water which Jesus gives extinguishes the thirst of body and soul utterly into eternity, so that he does not thirst, burning among the dead, or burn while thirsting, but with the Lamb as guide proceeds to the fountains of the waters of life, etc. This is a true but not full interpretation, since from the fact that someone drinks this water, the quenching of thirst is promised to him immediately, not finally in the other life: indeed, the fountain of water which rises up in us when we are watered with this water is distinguished from eternal life itself, into which it is said to spring and bubble up. Cyprian takes it concerning the non-iteration of Baptism, Epist. LXIII. that he does not thirst, and that the baptized do not thirst forever, because baptism is taken only once. Ambrose also leans toward this, as does Augustine in sermon XCII. de tempore: He teaches, he says, one Baptism, which does not allow any of us to thirst after having entered the Sacrament of the eternal fountain and the heavenly cup. But here, unless perhaps by consequence it is gathered from that, that the grace of the Holy Spirit received in Baptism is by its nature sufficient for quenching thirst, and on the part of God is without repentance, Rom. XI. 29. Others understand it only of the thirst for bodily goods and carnal pleasures. But thirst here indicates those goods which all the pious ought to desire. Calvinists commonly interpret it concerning Grace that is absolutely unlosable, that once drunk, it suffices forever: nor do they ever experience thirst again who have once drunk this spiritual water. But in truth it must be observed that the discourse here is about the water of this living nature and its own proper virtue in itself, not about the event in any given subject. That this water is so constituted that by its native virtue it can quench thirst, so that he who drinks it may not thirst again, unlike elemental water, which even if it quenches thirst, yet thirst easily arises again, for which reason at least the nature of this water is described, that it differs greatly from natural water. Since that does not profit unless it is consumed and digested, and hence thirst arises again, because the water is consumed by the heat of the stomach: But this Spiritual water is neither consumed nor corrupted, indeed it has the power of preserving us from corruption, and therefore once drunk it suffices forever, provided it is not vomited up again or cast out. Although therefore by its nature it possesses this virtue of satisfying thirst, it is nevertheless necessary that it remain in us, and become a fountain of water springing up into life, if it is to satisfy forever. For the virtue is inseparable from the water itself, and therefore it is not to be vomited out, which happens through sins against conscience. Whence we are warned not to cast out or quench the Spirit. 1. Thess. V. 29. Eph. IV. 30.

Wherefore there is required not only some drinking of this living water of the Holy Spirit, but also the preservation of it once drunk, for which end it is to be drunk repeatedly through the mystical channel of the Word and Sacraments. Just as a medicinal drink has the power of healing, it certainly cannot exercise it if the sick person immediately vomits up the same draught; so the drink of living water is to be retained, and for this to happen, the channels are not to be neglected, through which its continuous influx is derived into us. And truly of this water can be said that which is in Eccles. XXIV. 29. He who drinks it will still thirst for concupiscence and ardor desiring a more abundant refreshment. For here too, the more that is drunk, the more the water is thirsted for. And thus one does not thirst anymore as if for lack of refreshment or defect of saving drink.

II. That this water may become a fountain springing up into eternal life, even unto heaven. The metaphor is taken from fountains that eject water high up, which happens because of the abundance and gushing of the waters. Water ascends to its own place, and ascends as high as the altitude of the place from which it flows. The grace of the Holy Spirit, flowing from God, ascends to God and springs up into heaven. Who, therefore, would thirst, who has a fountain in his bowels springing up so high? Moreover, this fountain does not differ from the water itself which is drunk, except that by this a more abundant supply and efficacy of the water is designated. For the more greedily it is drunk, the more abundantly it is poured forth, and the more effectively it exerts itself. Its effect extends into eternal life, as far as the nature of the water is concerned; although it does not gush forth to that extent in all subjects, namely when the fountain fails or rather is blocked and dried up by their own fault.

Latin:

V. 15. Κύριε) Sic ignotos quoque Hebræi honoris cau- sa compellabant. Vide infra XX. 15.

ἵνα μὴ διψῶ μηδὲ ἔρχωμαι ἐνθάδε ἀντλεῖν) Inopiam suam tacite ostendit, quæ cogat subire laborem quo levari mallet.

Cum Samaritana de aqua vitæ non nisi carna- lia saperet, atque propterea cum Christo expo- stularet, quomodo aquam vivam præbere valeat, cum neque situlam vel hauritorium, ut vocat Au- gustinus, habeat, & profundus admodum sit pu- teus, quo Jacobus ipse Patriarcha, quem con- sueta Samaritanorum jactantia patrem suum di- ceret, meliorem istic, ad sui suorumque usum, invenire nequiverit, Christus invidiosa illa con- tentione cum Jacobo relicta, promissum saltem suum repetit, denuoque ad aquam spiritualem revocat, immensum eam ab elementari distare docens; de hac enim dicit: omnis qui ex illa bi- berit, sitiet iterum, de ista vero: qui autem biberit ex aqua quam ego dabo ei, non sitiet in æternum, sed aqua quam ego dabo ei, fiet in eo fons aquæ sa- lientis in vitam æternam. Differentia ab effe- ctu petita est, eaque gemina. I. quod aqua hæc sitim extinguat, ita, ut qui ex ea bibit, sitim non experiatur. Id vero non eodem explicatur modo: Augustinus de corporis siti, quam beati post mortem non sensuri sint, interpretatur. Tract. XV. in Johan. Similiter Rupertus, qui tum de corporali siti, dum de animi plena satietate, quæ apparebit in gloria Dei accipit. Aqua quam Jesus dat, corporis & animi sitim in æternam fundi- tus extinguit, ut non sitiat, apud inferos ardens, aut ardeat sitiens, sed agno duce pergat ad vitæ fon- tes aquarum &c. Vera hæc sed non plena inter- pretatio, siquidem ex eo statim, quod quis hanc aquam bibat, promittatur ipsi sitis restinctio, non demum in altera vita: imo fons aquæ qui in nobis exsurgit, cum hac potamur aqua, distingua- tur ab ipsa æterna vita, in quam ipsa salire & sca- turire dicitur. Cyprianus de non iteratione Baptismi accipit, Epist. LXIII. non sitire illum, & non si- tire in æternum baptizatos, quia tantum semel ba- ptisinus sumitur. Huc etiam abit Ambrosius ut & Augustinus serm. XCII. de tempore: Unum, inqui- ens, Baptismum docet, qui post ingressa æterni fon- tis, & cælestis poculi Sacramentum unumquemque nostrum sitire non patitur. Sed hic nisi forte per consequentiam inde colligatur, quod Spiritus Sancti gratia in Baptismo accepta & natura sua suf- ficiens sit, ad restinguendam sitim, & ex parte Dei ἀμεταμέλητος, Rom. XI. 29. Alii de siti bono- rum tantum corporalium & voluptatum carnalium intelligunt. Sed sitis hic indigitatur eorum bono- rum quæ desiderare pii omnes debebant. Calvi- niani communiter interpretantur de Gratia pror- sus inamissibili, quod ea semel pota, in æternum sufficiat: neq; iterum sitim experiantur unquam qui semel aquam hanc spiritualem hauserint. Ve- rum enim vero observandum, quod sermo hic sit, de aqua hujus viva natura & virtute propria in se, non de eventu in quolibet subjecto. Aquam hanc ita esse comparatam, ut nativa sua virtute si- tim restinguere valeat, ne sitiat amplius, qui eam hauriat, secus atque elementaris aqua, quæ etiam- si sitim restinguat, facile tamen iterum sitis exo- ritur, quapropter natura saltem hujus aquæ de- scribitur, quod à naturali aqua plurimum distet. Siquidem illa non prosit, nisi consumatur dige- raturque, atque hinc sitis exoritur iterum, quod aqua calore stomachi consumatur: Hæc vero Spi- ritualis aqua, nec consumitur, nec corrumpitur, imo nos à corruptione præservandi vim habet, ideoque semel pota in æternum sufficit, dummo- do iterum non evomatur, aut ejiciatur. Quan- quam ergo natura sua hac virtute sitim explendi polleat, necesse tamen est, in nobis maneat, & fons fiat aquæ in vitam salientis, si in æternum ex- plere debeat. Virtus enim est ab ipsa aqua insepa- rabilis, ideoque non evomenda est, quod fit per peccata contra conscientiam. Unde monemur ne Spiritum ejiciamus, vel extinguamus. 1. Thess. V. 29. Eph. IV. 30.

Quapropter requiritur aquæ hujus vivæ Spi- ritus Sancti non solum aliqua potatio, sed etiam se- mel haustæ conservatio, quo fine per canalem my- sticum Verbi & Sacramentorum subinde haurien- da est. Utut potus medicus vim habeat medendi, exercere eam certe non potest si ægrotus eundem haustum illico evomat; ita retinendus est potus aquæ vivæ, quod ut fiat, non negligendi canales sunt, per quos continuus ejus affluxus in nos deri- vatur. Et vere de hac aqua dici potest illud Eccles. XXIV. 29. Qui biberit eam adhuc sitiet ob concupi- scentiam & ardorem refectionem uberiorem de- siderantem. Nam & hic, quo plus sunt pota, plus siti- untur aqua. Et sic non sitiat amplius quis velut ob carentiam refectionis vel defectum potus salutaris.

II. Qud aqua hæc in fontem evadat salientem in æternam vitam, usque in cœlum. Metaphora desumitur à fontibus alte aquam ejaculantibus, quod fit propter copiam & scaturiginem aqua- rum. Aqua ad locum suum ascendit, & tantum a- scendit, quanta altitudo loci est unde fluit. Gratia Spiritus Sancti à Deo manans ad Deum ascendit, & in cœlum salit. Quis ergo sitiat, qui fontem in visceribus habeat tam alte salientem? Cæterum hic fons non differt ab ipsa aqua, quæ bibitur, nisi quod aquæ hujus largior copia & efficacia per eundem designetur. Quanto enim avidius bibitur, tanto largius affunditur, tanto efficacius exerit sese. Cujus effectus in vitam æternam se porrigit, quantum ad naturam aquæ attinet; tametsi non in omnibus subjectis, quando nempe culpa illorum fons deficit vel potius obturatur & exsiccatur, eo usque scaturiat.

## 4:16
V. 16. Call your husband) It is not sufficiently decorous for a bride to confer a benefit upon a husband who is unaware.

Not for the sake of decorum, but in order to lead the sinner to the knowledge of Himself, and to have an opportunity of revealing Himself, the Lord said these things; therefore, it is not so much the prudence and modesty of Christ that is to be observed here with Maldonatus, as the true method of dealing with those to be converted that is to be learned, who are first to be taught concerning the highest end, namely eternal life: then to be led into the recognition of their own misery; afterwards to be instructed in the recognition of the Savior, as the blessed Tarnovius observed in his commentary, pp. 376, 391.

Latin:

V. 16. Φώνησον τὸν ἄνδρα σου) Non satis decorum est, nu- ptæ beneficium conferre marito inconscio.

Non ob decornm, sed ut ad sui cognitionem adduceret peccatricem, & occasionem se patefa- ciendi haberet, hæc dixit Dominus, non ergo tam prudentia & modestia Christi cum Maldonato hic observanda, quam vera agendi cum convertendis ratio discenda, qui prius de fine summo nempe vita æterna docendi: deinde in suæ miseriæ agni- tionem deducendi; postea in agnitionis Salvatoris informandi, ut observavit B. Tarnovius in com- ment. p. 376. 391.

## 4:18
V. 18. For you have had five husbands) From whom you freed yourself by divorce contrary to the law of Moses. For that law permitted a husband to dismiss a wife, but not a wife to depart from a husband, which, however, the custom of later times had introduced, as is to be seen in Josephus, who notes the first example from which that custom began.

οὐκ ἔστι συ ἀνὴρ) According to the law. ἐ γνήσιος ἔστιν ἀκοίτης, Nonnus. Doubtless as I understand it, because she was still held bound to another man, not having received a bill of divorce. Samaritz if any had sprung from Jacob, they were held by the very law of birth by the law of Moses: The others, because they had received the law and had professed by circumcision that they would live according to it, Gal. V. 3.

Others, with Chrysostom and Maldonado, prefer to understand five fornicators, which the blessed Tarnovius thinks is more consistent with the text: because (1) Christ would have revealed nothing hidden if he had said they were her five legitimate husbands, which was known to all her fellow citizens. (1) The woman herself also, v. 29, invites her fellow citizens to see the man who had indicated everything she did, not only with this fornicator, but also with the preceding ones. (3) Finally, the particle καὶ implies that both the present one and the past ones were of the same condition. The blessed Chemnitz does not reject either opinion: Christ orders her husband to be summoned, so that he may thus lead her into the acknowledgment of her sins and the wrath of God. For after five, whether legitimate marriages repudiated, or after five concubinages, the old woman was still living in fornication. For the conjunction κὶ can be taken either as adversative, namely, you have had five legitimate husbands, but he whom you now have is not your legitimate husband; or if κὶ is taken simply, the sense will be, Previously you have had five illegitimate husbands, and not even he whom you now have in your old age is your legitimate husband. Christ, however, wanted such to be the firstfruits of the foreigners, whom he first called to his kingdom, so that we may know that it is given not out of merit, but out of grace, so that no one may boast, but that every mouth may be stopped. For that is why in this place the gift of God is offered first not to the honest citizens of Samaria, but to a worn-out harlot.

Latin:
