V. 18. Πέντε γὰρ ἄνδρας ἔχες) A quibus te divortio con- tra legem Mosis liberasti. Nam ea lex marito permittebas uxorem dimittere, non autem uxori discedere à marito, quod tamen posteriorum temporum mos introduxerat, ut apud Josephum videre est, qui notat exemplum primum unde is mos cœperit.

οὐκ ἔστι συ ἀνὴρ) Secundum legem. ἐ γνήσιος ἔστιν ἀκοίτης, Nonnus. Nimirum ut ego accipio, quia alii viro obligata adhuc tenebatur, non accepto libello dimissionis. Samaritz si qui à Jacobo orti erant ipso nascendi jure lege Mosis tenebantur: Cæteri, quia legem receperant & secundum eam se victuros circumcisione erant professi, Gal. V. 3.

Alii cum Chrysostomo, & Maldonato Scortatores quinque intelligere malunt, quod textui congruëntius putat B. Tarnovius: quia (1) nihil occulti revelasset Christus, si quinque legitimos eos maritos fuisse dixisset, quod notum erat omnibus ejus civibus. (1) Ipsa etiam mulier v. 29. invitat populares, ad videndum hominem, qui indicaverit omnia, quæ fecit, non tantum cum hoc scortatore, sed etiam cum præcedentibus. (3) Denique particula καὶ innuit, & præsentem, & præteritos, fuisse ejusdem conditionis. B. Chemnitius neutram sententiam reprobat: Christus jubet accersi maritum ejus, ut ita ducat eam in agnitionem peccatorum & iræ Dei. Nam post quinque, vel legitima conjugia repudiata, vel post quinque concubinatus, vetula adhuc vivebat in scortatione. Nam conjunctio κὶ potest accipi vel pro adversativa, quinque viros scilicet legitimos habuisti, sed ille, quem nunc habes, non est legitimus tuus vir; vel si κὶ simpliciter accipiatur, sensus erit, Antea quinque viros illegitimos scilicet habuisti, & ne ille quidem, quem nunc in senectute habes, legitimus tuus vir est. Tales autem voluit Christus esse primitias alienigenarum, quos primo ad regnum suum vocavit, ut sciamus, donari illud non ex dignitate, sed ex gratia, ne quis glorietur, sed ut omne os obstruatur. Ideo enim hoc loco donum Dei primo non honestis Samariæ civibus offertur, sed exoleto scorto.

## 4:19
V. 19. ὅτι προφήτης εἶ συ) For it is the work of prophets to reveal hidden things. Therefore, she consults him as a Prophet about the controversy long agitated, showing twice that she is not a despiser of God, both when she acknowledges these crimes, and when she consults him not about light matters, but about those which pertain to God and his worship.

Latin:

V. 19. ὅτι προφήτης εἶ συ) Prophetarum enim est abdita revelare. Ideo ut Prophetam consulit de agitata diu controversia, bis ostendens Dei contemtricem se non esse, & cum crimina hæc agnoscit, & cum non de rebus levibus, sed de his, quæ ad Deum ejusque cultum pertinent, eum consulit.

## 4:20
V. 20. οἱ πατέρες ἡμῶν) We have said that the Samaritans wanted to be considered as Hebrews. But since she is in some way pleading the cause of her own people here, I shall refer that πατέρες ἡμῶν to the most ancient times, just as that manner of speaking is also used by Archidamus in the speech which is in Thucydides, book two. What many write about Isaac being sacrificed here is vain: for that was done on Mount Moriah, Gen. XXII, 2. But it is true that an altar was built by Abraham not far from Shechem some time before the offering of Isaac, Gen. XII. 6, 7. Then also by Jacob, Gen. XXXIII, 18. Moreover, in those times, altars were accustomed to be built in places closest to the sky: which is also noted by Strabo. Added to this is that on that mountain the blessings of the law were pronounced, Deut. XI. 29.

ἐν τῷ ὄρει τύτῳ) He points with his finger to Mount Gerizim, where Sanballat had built a temple in the times of Alexander the Great, and although Hyrcanus had destroyed that temple, sacred rites had nevertheless not ceased to be performed there in the same manner. That mountain was also called ᾿Αγάριζος with the addition of הר in which there is the meaning of mountain. Thus in Revelation XXI. 16, ᾿Αρμαγεδδὼν הר מגדו, thus in Tacitus, Annals XV, the fortress Arfamosata הר שמשת Mount of the Sun.

ὅπε δεῖ προσκυνεῖν) Understand to worship with offered victims and other public rites, which God had willed to be done in only one place, namely that which he himself would designate in his own time, Deut. XII. 14, 26. ἅμαλι ταυρείη, said Nonnus here.

Grotius refers this to the most ancient times, that Abraham built an altar not far from Shechem, Gen. XII. 6, 7, as did Jacob, Gen. XXXIII. 18. But that he says that in those times altars were accustomed to be built in places closest to the sky is from a childish persuasion, as if mountains were closer to the sky and to God than valleys, which is against Jer. XXIII. 24. The sum of the response to the controversial question, and the appeal to antiquity, is this, as interpreted by our blessed Chemnitz: That one must judge not by examples, but by laws, as is commonly said. Therefore, the examples of the Fathers, where we do not have the same command, nor the same spirit, are not to be imitated without judgment, which ought to be formed from the Word of God. For without doubt the Patriarchs undertook such things by the special direction of the Holy Spirit. Likewise, that times are to be distinguished. For the Fathers before the law did not have a command concerning the Jerusalem temple and Levitical ceremonies, which command was given later, and in the New Testament that command concerning Levitical worship has now been abrogated. If these times are confused, a zeal without knowledge of examples which is not approved by God can easily be admitted. Christ has encompassed all these things in that brief and memorable sentence: You do not know what you worship, that is, although you may have a good intention and direct your worship to God, and even use the examples of the Fathers as a pretext: yet because your worship is instituted without the manifest word of God, you do not know what you worship. Among the Jews, who are truly pious, because they have the certain word of God concerning their worship, they know what they worship. But the hour is at hand, he says, of the abrogation of the Levitical Priesthood: and if anyone after that abrogation should wish to worship God with Levitical rites, he will sin no less than you Samaritans with your zeal without knowledge of the Fathers.

Latin:

V. 20. οἱ πατέρες ἡμῶν) Diximus Samaritas pro Hebræis censeri voluisse. Cum autem causam aliquo modo hic agat suorum, illud πατέρες ἡμῶν ad antiquissima tempora referam, quomodo id loquendi genus & Archidamus usurpat in oratione, quæ est apud Thucydidem secundo. De Isaaco hic sacrificato quod scribunt multi vanum est: id enim factum in monte Moria Genes. XXII, 2. At illud verum, non procul Sicimis altare ab Abrahamo structum aliquanto ante oblationem Isaaci Gen. XII. 6. 7. Deinde & à Jacobo Gen. XXXIII, 18. Solebant autem illis temporibus altaria strui in locis cœlo proximis: quod & Straboni notatum. Accessit quod in illo monte pronunciatæ erant benedictiones legis Deut. XI. 29.

ἐν τῷ ὄρει τύτῳ) Digitis monstrat montem Garizim ubi templum Sanbelletes struxerat Alexandri Magni temporibus, & quanquam id templum diruerat Hyrcanus, sacra tamen ibidem eodem more fieri non desierant. Vocatus is mons & ᾿Αγάριζος addito הר in quo montis est significatio. Sic in Apocalypsi XXI. 16. ᾿Αρμαγεδδὼν הר מגדו fic apud Tacitum Annalium XV. castellum Arfamosata הר שמשת Mons Solis.

ὅπε δεῖ προσκυνεῖν) Intellige adorare oblatis victimis aliisque ritibus publicis, quod uno tantum in loco, eo nempe, quem suo tempore designaturus esset ipse, fieri Deus voluerat Deut. XII. 14. 26. ἅμαλι ταυρείη dixit hic Nonnus.

Ad antiquissima hoc refert Grotius tempora, quod Abraham non procul Sicimis altare struxerit, Genes. XII. 6. 7. ut & Jacobus Genes. XXXIII. 18. Quod autem ait illis temporibus altaria consuevisse strui in locis cælo proximis, à puerili est persuasione, quasi montes cœlo & Deo propriores sint, quam valles, quod est contra Jer. XXIII. 24. Summa autem responsionis ad controversiam quæstionem, & provocationem ad antiquitatem hæc est, interprete B. Chemnitio nostro: Non exemplis, sed legibus judicandum esse, sicut vulgo dicitur. Ideo exempla Patrum, ubi non idem mandatum, non eundem spiritum habemus, non esse sine judicio, quod ex Verbo Dei formari debet, imitanda. Sine dubio enim Patriarchae speciali Sancti Spiritus di- rectione talia suscepêre. Item tempora esse discer- nenda. Patres enim ante legem non habuerunt mandatum de templo Hierosolymitano, & de Levi- ticis ceremoniis, quod mandatum postea datum fuit, & in Novo Testamento mandatum illud de Leviticis cultibus jam abrogatum est. Si haec tem- pora confundantur, facile potest admitti κακοζη- λία exemplorum quae Deo non probatur. Haec o- mnia Christus complexus est brevi & memorabili illa sententia: Vos nescitis, quid adoretis, hoc est, li- cet bonam habeatis intentionem & dirigatis cul- tum ad Deum, praetexatis etiam exempla Patrum: tamen quia sine manifesto verbo Dei cultus vester institutus est, nescitis quid adoretis. Inter Judæos, qui vere pii sunt, quia habent certum verbum Dei, de suis cultibus, sciunt, quid adorent. Adest autem, inquit, hora abrogationis Sacerdotii Levitici: & si quis post eam abrogationem voluerit Leviticis ritibus Deum colere, non minus peccabit, quam vos Samaritani κακοζηλία Patrum.

## 4:21
V. 21. Believe me) Since you hold me for a Prophet, in whom you are not deceived.

is coming) The present for the immediate future. See Matt. XXVI. 27. So below in verse 25, the Syrian translates: the older Latin codices also in the same place: will come.

Neither in this mountain nor in Jerusalem will you worship) Namely, as I have said, with a certain special rite; Philo II. Alleg. of the Laws: the base man thinks God is in a place, not containing, but contained. At the same time, the impending desolation of both places is tacitly hinted at.

the Father) He tacitly hints at the sweetness of the new covenant when he calls God Father, Rom. VIII. 15. Gal. IV. 6.

Latin:

V. 21. Πίστευσόν μοι) Quando me pro Propheta habes, in quo non falleris.

ἔρχεται) Praesens pro proxime futuro. Vide Matth. XXVI. 27. sic infra commate 25. vertit Syrus: Latini quoq; codi- ces antiquiores ibidem: veniet.

Οὔτε ἐν τῷ ὄρει τύτῳ οὔτε ἐν Ἱεροσολύμοις προσκυνήσετε) Nempe ut dixi eximio quodam ritu, Philo II. Alleg. legis: ὁ φαῦλος δοκεῖ εἶναι ὁ Θεὸς ἐν τόπῳ μὴ περιέχοντα, ἀλλὰ περιε- χόμενον. Simul tacite innuitur imminens utrique locorum vastitas.

τῷ πατρὶ) Tacite novi fœderis suavitatem innuit, cum Deum patrem vocat, Rom. VIII. 15. Gal. IV. 6.

## 4:22
V. 22. You do not know) Some think that God was considered corporeal by the Samaritans: but this they had in common with not a few Jews. Others think that the God of Israel was considered not as the God of the universe, but of one region. For thus they are thought to have believed of old, those who first dwelt there of the Assyrians, but as is credible, not yet having accepted the law, 2 Kings XVII. It seems more credible to me that, just as the Son is said to have seen God because He knew His secrets, above I. 18, so the Jews are said to have known God, because they had learned His will, where and how He wished to be worshipped, not only from the Law, but also from the Prophets: whom the Samaritans rejected, but by the warning of the Prophets David had proposed to build a temple in Jerusalem, and Solomon built it.

we worship) He counts Himself among the Jews: for the woman had already shown that she held Him for a Jew.

what we know) His will having been known, as we have said, through the prophets.

Not only where and how God wished to be worshipped, as Grotius explains, but the very object of adoration, as the Samaritans did not know it, so the Jews, among whom Christ counted Himself, being imbued with the true religion by the Prophets, knew it well: That namely they are bound to worship the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit as the true God.

salvation is from the Jews) There, after the temple was built, a perpetual succession of priests remained, which the Jews urge against the Samaritans in this very controversy. Joseph. Antiq. XIII. 16. The prophets honored that temple with their presence. By which signs God shows that the knowledge of His will is to be sought from there, not from the Garizitans; and for that reason He also wished the Evangelical dogma to be preached in that temple by Christ and the Apostles, according to that which had been predicted through Malachi III. 1.

Latin:

V. 22. ὏ οὐκ οἴδατε) Putant quidam à Samaritis Deum habitum corporeum: sed hoc illis commune cum Judæis non paucis. Alii Deum Israelis habitum pro Deo non uni- versi, sed unius regionis. Ita enim olim existimasse censen- tur, qui primi Assiriorum ibi habitaverunt, sed ut credibile nondum lege suscepta 2. Reg. XVII. Credibilius mihi vide- tur sicut vidisse Deum Filius dicitur, quod arcana ejus no- verit, supra I. 18. ita novisse Deum dici Judæos, quia volun- tatem ejus, ubi & quomodo coli vellet non ex lege tantum cognoverant, sed & ex Prophetis: Quos Samaritæ rejiciebat, Prophetarum autem monitu templum Hierosolymis struc- re proposuerat David, struxit Salomo.

ἡμεῖς προσκυνῦμεν) Judæis se accenset: nam jam osten- derat mulier, se eum pro Judæo habere.

ὃ οἴδαμεν) Cognita, ut diximus, per prophetas ipsius vo- luntate.

Non tantum ubi & quomodo coli vellet Deus, ut Grotius exponit, sed ipsum objectum adorationis, uti Samaritæ nesciebant, ita Judæi, quibus se Chri- stus accensebat, vera religione imbuti à Prophetis probe noverant: Quod nempe Patrem, Filium & Spiritum S. ut verum Deum colere teneantur.

ἡ σωτηρία ἐκ τῶν Ἰυδαίων ἐστιν) Ibi post structum templum perpetua mansit sacerdotum successio, quod urgent Judæi adversus Samaritas in hac ipsa controversia. Joseph. Antiq. XIII. 16. Illud templum præsentia sua honestarunt prophe- tæ. Quibus signis ostendit Deus, cognitionem voluntatis suæ indidem, non à Garizitanis petendam; ac propterea etiam in eo templo à Christo & Apostolis prædicari voluit Evangelicum dogma, juxta id quod prædictum erat per Malachiam III. 1.

## 4:23
V. 23. But the hour is coming and now is) Now signifies the time immediately impending; as if he were to say, it will be, nay, it is already at hand. The same expression below V. 25. refer 'but' to that which preceded concerning adoration not being bound to either temple.

The true worshippers) True here are the excellent, pleasing to God before others, we said above I. 9.

in spirit) With a pure mind, as it is in the Latin verse, which Persius called the composition of his mind and the law of the soul. Hierocles: You will honor God best if you liken your mind to God. Shortly after: The divine thought, constantly established, joins itself to God; for it is necessary that the like should go to the like; whence the wise man is not only called a priest, only

He alone is dear to God, he alone knows how to pray; for he alone knows how to honor who does not confuse the worth with the one being honored; and he who primarily offers himself as a sacrifice and fashions his own soul as a divine image and prepares himself as a temple for the reception of the light of God now. For what such thing will you take from the matter lying in the midst, which you might fashion as an image akin to God or a gift able to be offered to him? Which things must necessarily happen upon the rational essence having been purified; for as the same men say, God has no place on earth more appropriate than a pure soul. Clemens Alexandrinus book VII. Therefore they are servants and ministers of God, who offer the most free and most royal service, that which is through a God-fearing mind and knowledge. See Rom. I. 9. II. 29. 2. Cor. III. 6.

It is not adequately or sufficiently explained by a pure mind, much less do Hierocles, Persius, or other profane writers contribute here, who knew what it is to worship in spirit and truth just as well as the most ignorant. But what that is, is learned no more correctly than from the antithesis of the worship of the Jews and Samaritans, of which he had spoken: the worship of the latter was supposititious and hypocritical; the former was done only under shadows and figures. Spirit, therefore, is opposed to hypocrisy, truth to shadows and figures: worship must be done in spirit, so that it is commanded by the Spirit, and defined in the Word of the Spirit: it does not consist in external motions, or appearance, and outward simulation, but in true internal motions of the faithful heart excited by the Holy Spirit; which the flesh or the reason of man cannot effect or elicit, but they must be the fruits of the Spirit, who illuminates the mind, creates a clean heart, and works in us the interior motions of the heart, devotion, groans, sighs, and works of religious worship, invocation, prayers, adoration, of which there is nothing among the nations. Among the Jews, indeed, under the Old Testament, the pious also worshipped God spiritually, but many stuck in external rites, and were persuaded that they could serve God with them, without interior motions, Ps. L. 14. Is. LVIII. 7. In the New Testament, however, Christ teaches that that worship, clothed in Levitical ceremonies and external rites, is about to cease, that the old figures and shadows are to be abrogated, and that God is henceforth to be worshipped in truth without those shadows. Compare concerning the phrase in spirit Matth. XXII. 43. Joh. III. 6. Rom. VII. 5. VIII. 14. Gal. VI. 6. Concerning the other, in truth Joh. I. 17. Eph. IV. 24.

And in truth) Not in figures but in solid things, such as prayers, thanksgivings, martyrdoms, works of beneficence. For we showed that the word truth is taken in this way I. 17. Not far from here goes that saying of Philo about God in the book 'The worse are wont to plot against the better': 'which he genuinely embraces as worship, and genuine are those of the soul bringing a bare and sole sacrifice, truth.' Those Jewish rites indeed had their utility for turning the people away from foreign worship and at the same time for preparing minds for greater things: but after the chief part of piety had begun to be placed in them, they were now to be rooted out like tares obstructing the true crop. This was done first indeed by the publication of Christian liberty (which is called the time of correction, Heb. VIII. 10.) then also by the destruction of the temple, both the Garizitan and the Hierosolymitan.

He seeks such) Such he loves and desires most highly, 'he embraces' as Philo said.

Latin:

V. 23. Ἀλλ’ ἔρχεται ὥρα καὶ νῦν ἐστιν) Νῦν significat tem- pus de proximo imminens; quasi dicat, erit, imo jamjam erit. Eadem locutio infra V. 25. ἀλλὰ refer ad id quod præ- cessit de adoratione neutri templo adstringenda.

Οἱ ἀληθινοὶ προσκυνηταὶ) Ἀληθινοὶ hic sunt eximii, Deo ante alios grati, diximus supra I. 9.

ἐν πνεύματι) Pura mente ut est in Latino versu, quod com- positum ejus fasque animi dixit Persius. Hierocles. Τιμήσεις ὤς Θεὸν ἄριστα ἐὰν τῷ Θεῷ τὴν διάνοιαν ὁμοιώσῃς Mox: Τὸ δὲ ἔν- θεον φρόνημα διαρκῶς ἡδρασμένον, συνάπτει Θεῷ χωρεῖν γὰρ ἀνάγ- κη τὸ ὅμοιον πρὸς τὸ ὅμοιον’ ὅθεν κὴ μόνον ἱερεὺς ὁ σοφὸς λέγεται, μό-’

μόνῳ θεοφιλὴς, μόνῳ εἰδὼς εὔξασθαι· μόνῳ γὰρ οἶδε τιμᾷν ὁ τὴν ἀξίαν μὴ συγχέων τῷ τιμωμένῳ· καὶ ὁ προηγουμένως ἱέρειον ἑαυτὸν προσάγων καὶ ἄγαλμα θεῖον τεκταίνων τὴν ἑαυτοῦ ψυχὴν κὴ ναὸν εἰς ὑποδοχὴν τοῦ Θεοῦ φωτὸς ἑαυτὸν παρασκευάζων νῦν. Τί γὰρ τοιοῦτον προλάξεις ἀπὸ τῆς ἐν μέσῳ κειμένης ὕλης, ὃ τῷ θεῷ προσφυὲς ἄγαλμα ἐργάσῃ ἢ δῶρον αὐτῷ ἰνῆσαι δυνάμενον; ἃ δὴ ἐπὶ τῆς λογικῆς οὐσίας καθαρθείσης συμβαίνειν ἀνάγκη· ὡς γὰρ οἱ αὐτοὶ ἄνδρες φασὶ ψυχῆς καθαρᾶς τόπον οἰκειότερον ἐπὶ γῆς Θεὸς οὐκ ἔχει. Clemens Alexandrinus libro VII. θεράποντες ἄρα κὴ θεραπευταὶ τοῦ Θεοῦ, οἱ ἐλευθερικωτάτην κὴ βασιλικωτάτην θεράπειαν προσάγοντες τὴν διὰ τῆς θεοσεβοῦς γνώμης, τε καὶ γνώσεως. Vide Rom. I. 9. II. 29. 2. Cor. III. 6.

Non adæquate aut sufficienter exponitur pura mente, multo minus huc Hierocles, Persius, aut alii prophani Scriptores faciunt, qui quid in spiritu & veritate adorare sit, juxta cum ignarissimis noverant. Quid autem illud sit, non rectius, quam ex antithesi cultus Judæorum & Samaritanorum, de quo dixerat, addiscitur: quorum hic cultus erat supposititius & hypocriticus: ille tantum sub umbris & figuris fiebat. Spiritus ergo hypocrisi, veritas umbris & figuris opponitur: in spiritu fieri debet cultus, ita ut a Spiritu mandatus sit, & in Verbo Spiritus definitus: non in externis motibus, aut specie, ac simulatione exteriori consistat, sed in veris internis a Spiritu S. excitatis fidelis cordis motibus; quos caro aut ratio hominis non potest efficere, aut elicere, sed oportet esse fructus Spiritus, qui mentem illuminat, cor mundum creat, & in nobis interiores motus cordis, devotionem, gemitus, suspiria & opera religiosi cultus, invocationem, preces, adorationem operatur, de quibus nihil apud gentes. Inter Judæos sane sub Vet. Test. coluerunt etiam pii Deum spiritualiter, sed multi in externis ritibus hærebant, illisq; Deo se servire posse, sine interioribus motibus, persuasi erant, Pf. L. 14. Es. LVIII. 7. In Novo vero Test. docet Christus cultum illum, ceremoniis Leviticis & externis ritibq vestitum cessaturum, figuras & umbras veteres abrogatum iri, Deumq; in veritate sine istis umbris deinceps colendum esse. Confer de Phrasi in Spiritu Matth. XXII. 43. Joh. III. 6. Rom. VII. 5. VIII. 14. Gal. VI. 6. De altera, in veritate Joh. I. 17. Eph. IV. 24.

Καὶ ἀληθείᾳ) Non in figuris sed rebus solidis, quales sunt preces, gratiarum actiones, martyria, opera beneficentir. Nam veritatis vocem sic sumi ostendimus I. 17. Non longe hinc abit Philonis illud de Deo lib. pejores insidiari melioribus: οἷς γνησίως μὲν θεραπείας ἀσπάζεται γήσιοι δ' εἰσὶν αἱ ψυχῆς ψιλὴν κὴ μόνην θυσίαν φερόσης ἀλήθειαν. Ritus illi Judaici suam quidem habuerunt utilitatem ad avertendum populum ab extraneo cultu simulq; ad præparandos animos ad majora: sed postquam in illis præcipua pars pietatis collocari cœperat, evellendi jam erant ut veræ frugi obstans lolium. Factu autem hoc primum quidem publicatione Christianæ libertatis (quod tempo correctionis dicitur, Heb. VIII. 10.) deinde etiam destructione templi & Garizitani & Hierosolymitani.

Τοιούτους ζητεῖ) Tales summe amat ac desiderat, ἀσπάζεται ut dixit Philo.

## 4:24
V. 24. God is Spirit) Mind, as Cicero says, loosened and free, separated from all mortal concretion. God is soul, as in the Latin poem. Like things rejoice in like things: wherefore he is not delighted by corporeal worship, neither by itself nor primarily.

in spirit and truth one must worship) With the distinction of places removed, just as that of the three. Menander: 'Everything is a temple to the good word; for it is the mind that will speak to God.' Clemens in the cited place: 'Every place is sacred to the one who is, in which we receive the thought of God.' Cicero on the nature of the gods II: 'But the worship of the gods is the best and also the most chaste and most holy, and most full of piety, that we may always venerate them with a pure, whole, incorrupt mind and voice.' The same on the Laws II: 'The law commands to approach the gods chastely, namely with the mind in which all things are.' Seneca cited by Lactantius: 'Do you wish to think of God as great and placid and to be revered with gentle majesty? As a friend and always near: not to be worshipped with immolations and much blood: for what pleasure is there from the slaughter of the innocent? But with a good mind, with a pure and honest purpose? Temples are not to be built for him with stones piled to a height: he is to be consecrated in each person's own breast.' Thus he shows that there is no reason for the woman to torment herself about that old controversy, since that privilege about which there was a dispute is soon to cease entirely.

Latin:

V. 24. Πνεῦμα ὁ Θεός) Mens, ut Cicero inquit, soluta & libera segregata ab omni concretione mortali. Deus est animus ut in Latino Carmine. Similia similibus gaudent: quare corporeo cultu, nec per se nec præcipue delectatur.

ἐν πνεύματι κὴ ἀληθείᾳ δεῖ προσκυνεῖν) Sublatis ut tribus ita & locorum discrimine. Menander. πᾶντ' ἐςὶ τῷ καλῷ λόγῳ ἱερὸν· ὁ νῦς γάρ ἐσιν ὁ λαλήσων θεῷ. Clemens dicto loco: πᾶς ἐν κὴ τόπος ἱερὸς τῷ ὄντι, ἐν ᾧ τὴν ἐπίνοιαν [τοῦ Θεοῦ λαμβάνομεν. Cicero de natura deorum II. Cultus autem Deorum est optimus idemq; castissimus atq; sanctissimus, plenissimusq; pietatis, ut eos semper pura, integra, incorrupta & mente & voce veneremur. Idem de Legibus. II. Caste jubet lex adire ad Deos, animo videlicet in quo sunt omnia. Seneca a Lactantio citatus: Vultis vos Deum cogitare magnum & placidum & majestate leni verendum? amicum & semper in proximo: non immolationibus & sanguine multo colendum: quæ enim ex trucidatione immerentium voluptas est? sed mente bona, puro honestoq; proposito? Non templa illi congestis in altitudinem saxis struenda sunt: in suo cuiq; consecrandus est pectore. Sic ostendit non esse quod mulier se de veteri illa controversia torqueat, cum brevi cessaturum sit omnino id privilegium, de quo certabatur.

## 4:25
V. 25. That the Messiah is coming) That Shiloh preached to Jacob, whose time she had heard from common report was now at hand.

the one called Christ) A parenthesis of the Evangelist, as above 10. He will announce to us all things) The opinion had not yet been born then, which later Jews invented out of hatred for us, that the Messiah would not be a Prophet. Similar is what the Jews say today about Elijah, 'Elijah will come, and will reveal all things.' Thus also in the times of the Asmoneans, controversies were deferred to the coming of a prophet, 1. Macc. IV. 46. XIV. 41. Understand 'all things' which we seek to know. V. 26. I am.) That is, I am he, as below XVIII. 5. A great reward is given to the simplicity of the woman, because Jesus first makes his dignity known to her. When the woman still persisted in a carnal sense, 'Lord give me this water, that I may not thirst, nor come to draw.' The Lord, tolerating the error with the greatest gentleness, judged that it should be removed by a gracious revelation of himself rather than by laborious contention: And therefore he manifests himself first by the knowledge of hidden things, then by the designation of the time of the Messiah's advent, and finally by an open declaration that he himself is the Messiah. Where two parts or degrees of repentance can be noted: to acknowledge and confess sins, and to believe in Christ. The Savior led this harlot to the former when he commanded her husband to be summoned, so that by this as a kind of occasion of the law she might be driven to the acknowledgment of sin: Go, call your husband, and come here. For we do not think that he ordered the husband to be called solely under some pretext, either of communicating this gift to her husband, as Chrysostom and Euthymius wish, or so that the woman might be taught through him, which pleases Cyril and Augustine. and Theophylact wish, or so that the woman might be taught through the same, which pleases Cyril and Augustine, he ordered the husband to be called, but so that he might have an occasion to declare to her whatever she had done in her whole lifetime, as Ammonius teaches, or to bring her back to repentance. And not without reason do Chrysostom and Euthymius observe here both the prudence and the modesty of Christ, that he did not do this at the beginning of the conversation, but when a certain occasion was sought, as the matter itself demanded, or at least when it seemed very opportune to say it. Therefore, when the woman denied that she had a husband, 'You have said well,' says Christ, 'that I have no husband, for you have had five husbands, and the one you now have is not your husband; you have said this truly.' Augustine, Athanasius, Hilary, Bede, Euthymius, and Nonnus understand these as legitimate husbands. Chrysostom more correctly [understands them as] illegitimate and adulterous, because Christ would have revealed nothing hidden if they had been legitimate husbands: that would have been notorious to all the citizens; but the woman confesses in verse 29 that he had revealed hidden things: 'Come and see a man who told me all things that I have done'; and the connection indicates that the others were of the same kind as this present man. Thus, therefore, from the knowledge of hidden things, the Samaritan woman gathers that this interlocutor is a Prophet, and she proposes to him a case of conscience or a question, agitated for many centuries now between the Jews and the Samaritans, whether one ought to worship on Mount Gerizim, which the Samaritans commonly believed the ancient fathers had done, because Moses had promulgated the blessings there in Deut. 27, as Cyril observes in this place, or whether, as the Jews wished, in Jerusalem? Therefore Christ took from there an occasion to manifest himself further, from the article of the present time: 'Woman, believe me, the hour is coming when you will worship the Father neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem.' And at the same time, informing her most fully about the proposed case, that the worship performed in Jerusalem, by the rite of the Jews, had been restricted only to a certain time: Which time has now arrived, in which the ceremonial and typical things were to have an end. That the distinction between the Jews worshipping in Jerusalem and the Samaritans, who performed their worship on Mount Gerizim, and indeed even of all the Gentiles, was now to cease. And that all from everywhere without distinction would worship, not idols, not an unknown God (Θεὸν ἄγνωστον), but that true God whom

He indicates by the name of Father, either taken essentially, as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are our Father, by reason of creation, redemption, and regeneration, not only for this life, but primarily for eternal; or personally, as Father expresses the first person of the Deity, but connotes the others: because in that sense he is not Father, unless he who has a Son, and from whom the Spirit proceeds, whence Cyril of Alexandria notes this in lib. 2. on John c. XCII. How wonderfully the woman is invited by the Savior's speech to think something about the Son of God; for he called God Father, furthermore, Father cannot be understood unless he has a Son. Hence he refutes the Samaritans, you worship what you do not know, because they did not serve God the Father, but mixed the God of Israel with idols, and did not have the true worship of God, but one devised by their own ἐθελοθρησκείᾳ. Thus far, therefore, the Jews excelled, who had the true worship of the true God from the word of God, which had been entrusted to them, Rom. III. 2.

Let it therefore be noted in these words of Christ: I. The certainty of the prediction. Believe me. For he would not demand faith, unless he were indicating a certain thing and one worthy of faith: just as for this reason the word of God is called πιστὸς λόγος, 1 Tim. IV. 9. cap. III. 1. He wants this also to be believed, because it was of the greatest importance that it be believed that the ceremonies of the Old Testament would no longer endure: that the distinction of the Jews from the Samaritans and Gentiles was about to cease entirely.

II. The designation of time. The hour comes, by synecdoche he calls the time that is imminent and at hand: just as he adds later: The hour comes and now is: because the time of the Messiah had been so predicted in the Old Testament, namely that the distinction of peoples and places would cease, so that worship pleasing to God could be performed everywhere, Zech. XIV. Mal. I.

III. The prediction itself. That worship of God is not to be instituted any longer on this mountain, on which the Samaritans had built a temple similar to the Jerusalem one, see Joseph. Ant. lib. II. cap. 8., or in Jerusalem in the temple of Zerubbabel, which he designates by the name of adoration (synecdoche), because the chief among the external works which are performed for God is adoration. Which is also to be opposed to the Papists, who bind the worship of God and religion in the time of the New Testament to certain places, and therefore persuade pilgrimages to such places as being holier than others under the opinion of worship and merit.

IV. The description of the Samaritans. You worship what you do not know; destitute, that is, of the word of God. Whoever does not worship God the Father, worships what they do not know, they are ignorant of whom they ought to worship, and thus are deservedly held as idolaters. Such, therefore, are the Gentiles, the Mahometans, the modern Jews, and add also the Photinians. For these are ignorant of or deny the Father. This Samaritanism or mixed religion is also reproved, by which the true worship of God is mixed with the false, and a temperament of true and false religion is sought: which is accustomed to be called Samaritanism. Since a mixture of that kind was introduced among the Samaritans at the first time of Jeroboam in the thirtieth year after the temple was founded: afterwards under Shalmaneser, 2 Kings XVII., about 520 years later it was restored again, and finally after 400 years it was further consummated by Sanballat, with a temple built on Mount Gerizim near the city of Puchimitica in emulation of the Jerusalem one.

V. The commendation of the Jews. We worship what we know. In which words the plural, we worship, either declares only the genus, and does not include the person speaking: or that Christ spoke according to the opinion of the woman, with Chrysostom and Theophylact.

it must be said. For because he was held for a Jew and a common man, he therefore joins himself with the Jews. For among them alone at that time was the true worship of the true God. They knew both whom they ought to worship and how, Ps. CXLVII. 19. For them also a certain place was defined for divine worship by the command of God himself, Deut. XII. 5. XIV. 33. 2 Sam. VII. 34. 2 Chron. VI. 6. Ps. LXXVIII. 68. This communication, however, detracts nothing from the Deity of Christ; for he communicates himself to those who worship, as Cyril says, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit is worshipped as much by the Angels as by us. Let the adversaries show, however, with all Holy Scripture turned over, where worship is attributed to the Word and Son of God naked in the flesh. Does he not use the plural number, we worship, and number himself among the servants? Are these things said by a man of servitude? For since he assumed the form of a servant, he undertook a ministry fitting for a servant. For does he not attribute a certain spiritual thing, and is not adoration a certain profession of servitude? Thus far Cyril.

VI. The particular reason for the commendation. Because salvation is from the Jews. Which salvation, which Jesus, the Savior of the world, brought forth, or Jesus himself, who is the salvation of all, Gen. XLIX. 10. or which proposes that salvation to us, Holy Scripture, the word of salvation and life, entrusted to the Jews, Rom. III. 2. For that salvation is from the Jews, which has been acquired for us by Christ; Jesus came forth from them, and the announcement of salvation was first made to them, and from them it was derived to the remaining nations, Isa. II. 3. Luke XXIII. 47. From them also had to come forth he who is our one salvation, Rom. IX. 5. Luke II. 30. Finally, among them the tables of salvation, τὰ λόγια τῦ Θεῦ, had to be kept, Rom. III. 2. Thus, therefore, he recalls the woman to himself, the true salvation, and at the same time Christ teaches the chief head, that for adoration and worship or true religion, the doctrine concerning the Messiah and his salvation is most necessary, being destitute of which, it is necessary to dwell in darkness and worship what they do not know. The connection of the words, therefore, and the argument of Christ is this: Those who do not acknowledge, or are ignorant of the salvation which is from the Jews, namely Christ the author of salvation, and his merit, they do not acknowledge the true God, and thus worship what they do not know; therefore, the worship of all those who do not acknowledge Christ as the true salvation is condemned here.

VII. Repetition, confirmation, and illustration of the prediction. But the hour comes, and now is, when the true worshippers shall worship the Father in spirit and in truth: Rightly Cyril on this passage. By these things he signifies the time of his advent in which he insinuates that the figures of the law are to be transformed into truth, and the shadow in worship into a spiritual and pleasing norm of living to God the Father through Evangelical doctrine. We note 1. here the Subject of worship, 2. the Act, 3. the Object, 4. the Mode, 5. and its Cause and Argument.

I. The Subject are true worshippers. By which a distinction is established between the worshippers or cultors of God. For not all are ἀληθινοὶ true, or those who worship whom they ought to worship, and as he is to be worshipped. Therefore, not anyone who pours out prayers, or invokes a Deity, is to be held as a true worshipper. There are those who invoke false Idols, Deities, and demigods. These are not true worshippers but idolaters. There are those who indeed worship God, but not in a divine and due manner, whether because they institute worship not according to the prescription of the word, but out of their own will and superstition, or because they do not perform it with true devotion of mind, humility, and faith. He also opposes true worshippers to those who served only shadows, and stuck mostly to externals, as the Pharisees and most of the Jews at that time: so that he may designate those who, having dismissed those shadowy things, render and offer to God internal, spiritual worship prefigured by that other worship, not that true worshippers of the Father were lacking in the Old Testament, but that under the New Testament true worshippers are to worship God everywhere in the world without the observation of those shadows.

II. The verb προσκυνεῖν expresses the act, which is to show reverence by the bowing of the body and genuflection, Matt. II. v. 11, Rev. III. v. 19, and cf. Matt. IX. v. 18, Mark V. 32. But since worship is either civil, which is offered to creatures because of finite excellence, or religious, which is offered to God because of infinite excellence, it is manifest that here religious worship owed to God alone is indicated, Matt. IV. v. 10, whether it be exhibited by the mind, by due acknowledgment of divine excellence or devoted inclination of the will, or by external reverence and veneration.

III. The object is the Father or, as it is explained in v. 24, ὁ Θεός. Both names are common to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, since it is taken essentially in this place. For the object of adoration is not the person of the Father alone, but also the Son, whom all the angels also adore, Ps. XCVI. 8, Heb. I. 6, who is to be honored as the Father, John V. v. 23, as also the Holy Spirit, whom we profess and invoke in Baptism equally with the Father and the Son, Matt. XXVIII. 29, as also in our vows and prayers, 2 Cor. XIII. v. 13, Rev. I. v. 4. That adoration is without doubt predicted here which is already being performed everywhere in the world for so many centuries since Christ was born. Indeed, the public prayers and δοξολογίαι of the Church confirm that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are to be adored. Not those which were received after the Council of Nicaea or Constantinople, but as Basil the Great in his book on the Holy Spirit S. ch. XXIX demonstrates, even those which were used in the Church at all times before that.

IV. The mode is that worship ought to be done in Spirit and truth, which some understand by a hendiadys as in the Spirit of truth. To this returns the interpretation of those who take Spirit and truth from Rom. I. v. 9, Rom. II. v. 39, 2 Cor. III. v. 9 as the same thing. Others wish Spirit to be opposed to flesh or carnal rites, and truth to figures and shadows and the hypocrisy of external actions. Others understand by Spirit and truth the Holy Spirit and the Son of God, as Athanasius in his Epistle to Serapion. But since this mode of adoration is expressed by these two words, therefore to adore in Spirit is when we pray with a contrite and humiliated spirit and true repentance, Ps. LI. 19, Isa. LXVI. 2, cf. Gen. XVIII. 21, 2 Chron. XXXIII. 2, Joel II. 13, Luke XVIII. 7. When we pour out prayers through the spirit of faith and a faithful heart without wavering or doubt, 2 Cor. IV. 13, Jas. I. v. 6. True παῥῥησία of being heard, John XVI. v. 24, Rom. X. 14, Eph. III. 12, Heb. IV. 16, ch. XI. 6. When we pray with a holy heart sanctified by the Spirit, and lift up holy hands, Eph. I. 15, Job IX. 31, 1 Tim. II. 8. Thus the word ἐν πνεύματι is taken equally with the efficient cause of spiritual adoration pleasing to God, the Holy Spirit, who as the Spirit of prayers teaches us to pray, Zech. XII. v. 10, interceding for us, Rom. VIII. 27, while, namely, He makes us intercede and cry Abba Father, Rom. VIII. 15, Gal. IV. 5, as Ambrose in book III on the Holy Spirit, ch. XII, explains this word. They also designate the mode of adoration, that it ought to be done spiritually, and with a spiritual, penitent, faithful, and holy mind. Therefore, the Arians foolishly denied that the Spirit is God, because we ought to adore God not the Spirit, but in the Spirit. For it is wrong to oppose the Spirit as Author, Teacher, and Mover or cause of prayers to the object of adoration. Since God is both the efficient cause of adoration and its proper object. II. By the other word ἐν ἀληθείᾳ it is expressed that adoration ought to be done according to the will of God and the word of truth, 1 John V. 14, so that we pray only for that which is agreeable to the will of God, Jas. IV. 3, and as God teaches and requires it, setting neither mode nor time for God: but committing all things to the divine will, Judith VIII. 11, 14, Dan. III. 18. And so we should not be sluggish in prayers, but persist in praying, Dan. VI. v. 10, Luke VI. 12, ch. XVIII. 1, Rom. XII. 12, 1 Thess. V. 16, then also that prayer ought to be done with true devotion of heart, and without hypocrisy, Matt. VI. 6, Lam. III. 4, Hos. VII. 14, so that we cry out not so much with the mouth as with the heart, Exod. XIV. 15, 1 Sam. I. 15, Ps. CXLV. v. 18, Isa. XXVI. 16, ch. XXIX. 13. Thus far not badly Origen, Novatian, Hilary in book 2 on the Trinity, Chrysostom, Cyril in this place. Procopius, Euthymius, and Theophylact observe that truth is here opposed to figures, because, namely, the time has come when public worship of God will not be restricted to a certain place, nor performed by legal ceremonies and sacrifices, but by truth, or those things which were signified by figures. In which way the ancients did not adore in truth, that is, without figures, even though they adored truly, not hypocritically.

V. A twofold argument for this adoration is brought forward. The one from the will of God. For the Father also seeks such as adore him in Spirit and truth. He indeed once wished to be worshipped with shadows, but before the body was exhibited: now when it has been exhibited, he does not require figures: and God is delighted not with external things, but with internal and spiritual worship, Ps. LI. 19, Heb. XIII. 15. The other argument is sought from the nature of God. God is a Spirit, and those who adore him must adore in Spirit and truth. The reason for the consequence is because God, as a spiritual nature, requires spiritual worship of the mind, and does not desire external worships. Just as also those external rites were not instituted for God's sake, nor accommodated to the nature of God, but rather to the nature of men and the condition of the time, in which things to be prefigured were not yet exhibited, cf. Ps. L. 13, Isa. I. 11, ch. LXVI. 1, seqq. But as the spiritual nature of God is immutable and always remains the same: so under the Old Testament God, if you consider his nature, could not be delighted by external worship in itself, but only insofar as it was ordered toward internal worship and served faith. In those words πνεῦμα ὁ Θεὸς some make the Holy Spirit the subject, with Athanasius in his book on the common essence of the Trinity. Others more correctly establish God as the subject here, as the added article shows; and thus it teaches that the incorporeal nature of God is asserted here. For God is called Spirit not because he is of a merely more subtle, albeit corporeal nature, as Crellius of the Photinians says in his book on God and his Attributes, p. 107, calling God a spirit in the sense in which air is called a spirit; but because he is devoid of a body, and is plainly immaterial and of a spiritual nature. For if God were endowed with some body, even if it were subtle, this argument of Christ would have no force, that God is to be worshipped not with corporeal rites, but in spirit; thus Ammonius rightly says in the Greek Catena: God is called Spirit, he says, not as wind, but as an incorporeal and life-giving substance. Deservedly, therefore, are those rejected who, along with pagan idolaters, establish a corporeal God: the Rabbis who establish corporeal members, Tertullian against Praxeas c. VII who establishes a body, Arnobius book III against the Gentiles, Lactantius on the way of God c. 18 who establish a figure of a body. The Manichaeans who establish corporeal parts, the Vadians and Anthropomorphites who establish a human figure, the Messalians who establish a sensible nature, the Mahometans attributing a corporeal essence to God; just as Conrad Vorstius, arguing that a body can be attributed to God, lib. de Deo & attrib. pag. 151. Whom Alstedius in vain attempts to excuse, pag. 55. Theol. Natur. All these can be seen refuted in Tom. II. System. Theol. c. III.

The woman being thus informed about the worship of God, since she did not deny it, but said that the Messiah, whom some take the word ἔρχεται in verse 25 to mean in the future, as if he were about to come shortly: or that he had already come, from common report or even from the preaching of John, presupposing the Mosaic scripture, which the Samaritans revered, and believed that he would come to the Samaritans also, and would explain all things, he removes the veil and openly manifests himself to her, saying, I am he, who speaks with thee. Thus, therefore, he wished to lead her gradually to faith. 1. By the power of his word exerted in the mind of the Samaritan woman, the foundation being laid, upon which a solid faith in the Messiah could afterwards be built: Believe, says Augustine, what you hear: what you seek: what you see? Interpreters ask why he never professed this so openly to the Jews, as he did here to the Samaritan woman, since he came especially for their sake? Origen, Ammonius, Chrysostom, Theophylact, Euthymius say that the Jews for the most part asked with a malicious mind, but this woman with a desire to learn. We admit this, yet we do not ascribe to the woman any merit of simplicity with Salmeron. It was done so that, through the Samaritan woman as an intermediary, her fellow citizens might be led to faith, whom Christ foresaw would believe. Just as the outcome taught, they believed first through the report of the woman, and afterwards, having heard Christ himself, were confirmed in the faith. They indeed believed through the woman, but then they believed in Christ through himself, just as Augustine in chapter V of the Epistle of Manichaeus (Epistola Fundamenti) professes that he believed the Church through the Catholics, even though scripture itself is sufficient in itself to procure authority and faith for itself. Concerning which, against the Pontificians, it is treated in Crit. Sacr. p. 332.

Latin:

V. 25. ὅτι Μεσσίας ἔρχεται) Siloh ille Jacobo prædicatus, cujus tempus jam instare, ex communi fama acceperat.

ὁ λεγόμενος χριστὸς) Parenthesis Evangelistæ, ut supra 10. Ἀναγγελεῖ ἡμῖν πάντα) Nondum nata tunc erat opinio, quam in nostri odium posteriores Judæi confinxerunt Mes- fiam non fore Prophetam. Simile est quod hodie de Elia di- cunt Judæi, Elias veniet, & revelabit omnia. Sic & Asmonæo- rum temporibus controversiæ in adventum prophetæ reji- ciebantur, 1. Macc. IV. 46. XIV. 41. πάντα intellige, quæ scire expetimus. V. 26. ἐγώ εἰμι.) Id est ego is sum ut infra XVIII. 5. ma- gnum præmium simplicitati mulieris redditur, quod ei pri- mum Jesus dignitatem suam cognitam facit. Cum adhuc in carnali sensu perstitit mulier, Do- mine da mihi hanc aquam, ut non sitiam, neque veni- am haurire. Dominus summa lenitate errorem to- lerans, gratiosa potius sui revelatione, quam ope- rosa contentione tollendum eum duxit : Ideoq; se- se primum rerum occultarum notitia manifestat, tum temporis Messiæ adventus designatione, denique aperta patefactione, quod ipse Messias sit. Ubi duæ partes resipiscentiæ aut gradus notari possunt, agno- scere, & confiteri peccata, & credere in Christum. Ad priorem perduxit hoc scortu Servator, cum man- davit accersi maritum, ut hac tanquam occasione quadam legis ad agnitionem peccati adigeretur, Vade, voca virum tuum, & veni huc. Non enim pu- tamus, quod solum prætextu aliquo sive commu- nicandi doni hujusce marito ipsius, ut Chrysost. Euthym. & Theoph. volunt, sive ut per eundem mulier doceretur, quod Cyrillo & Augustino pla- cet, vocari maritum jusserit, sed ut occasionem haberet declarandi illi, quicquid toto vitæ tempo- re egerat, ut Ammonius docet, vel reducendi ean- dem ad pœnitentiam. Nec immerito hic & pruden- tiam, & modestiam Christi observant Chrysost. & Euthym. quod non sub ingressum colloquii id fe- cerit, sed quæsita quadam occasione, quid dictu- rus esset, reipsa postulante, vel certe admodum o- portune id dicere videretur. ubi ergo mulier se vi- rum habere negaret, bene, inquit, Christus, dixisti, quia non habeo virum, quinq; enim viros habuisti, & quem nunc habes non est vir tuus, hoc vere dixisti. Vi- ros legitimos Augustinus, Athanasius, Hilarius, Be- da, Euthymius & Nonnus intelligunt. Rectius Chry- sost. illegitimos & scortatores, quia nihil occulti re- velasset Christus, si legitimi fuissent viri: notorium id fuisset omnibus civibus, fatetur autem mulier v. 29. occulta eundem revelasse: venite & videte hominem, qui mihi dixit omnia, quæ feci: & nexus indicat, ejusdem generis cæteros fuisse, cum hoc præsente viro. Ita ergo ex abditorum notitia col- ligit Samaritana hunc collocutorem Prophetam esse, eique casum conscientiæ vel quæstionem in- ter Judæos & Samaritanos, multis jam seculis a- gitatam proponit, an adorandum sit in monte Ga- rizim, quod patres antiquos fecisse, vulgo cre- debant Samaritani, eo quod Moses illic benedi- ctiones promulgarit Deut. XXVI. uti Cyrillus in h. l. observat, an vero, uti Judæi volebant, Hiero- solymis? Ideo Christus ulterius sese manifestan- di occasionem inde cepit, à temporis præsentis articulo: Mulier, crede mihi, venit hora, qua neque in hoc monte, neque Hierosolymis adorabitis Patrem. Simulque de proposito casu plenissime eam informans, quod adoratio Hierosolymis fa- cta, ritu Judæorum, ad certum tantum tem- pus adstricta fuerit: Quod tempus jam adve- nit, quo ceremonialia ac typica finem habitura. Quod discrimen Judæorum Hierosolymis adoran- tium, & Samaritanorum, qui in monte Garizim cultum suum peragebant, imo & Gentilium o- mnium cessaturum jam sit. Quodque omnes undi- quaque sine discrimine veneraturi sint, non idola, non Θεὸν ἄγνωστον, sed illum verum Deum, quem

Patris nomine indigitat, seu essentialiter accepto, qua Pater, Filius & Spiritus S. sunt Pater noster, ratione creationis, redemtionis & regenerationis, non ob hanc tantum vitam, sed imprimis ob æter- nam; sive personaliter, qua Pater primam perso- nam Deitatis exprimit, sed cæteras connotat: quia Pater eo sensu non est, nisi qui habet Fi- lium, & à quo procedit Spiritus, unde animad- vertit vult hic Cyrillus Alexandr. lib. 2. in Johan. c. XCII. Quomodo mirabiliter ut de Filio Dei ali- quid cogitet oratione Servatoris mulier invitetur; Patrem enim Deum appellavit, Pater porro nisi ei Filius sit intelligi nequaquam potest. Hinc redar- guit Samaritanos, vos adoratis quod nescitis, quia ipsi non serviebant Deo Patri, sed commiscebant Deum Israelis cum idolis, neque verum Dei cul- tum habebant, sed propria ἐθελοθρησκείᾳ excogi- tatum. Hactenus ergo Judæi præstabant, qui ve- rum veri Dei cultum ex verbo Dei, quod ipsis concreditum erat, Rom. III. 2. habebant.

Notetur itaque in his Christi verbis I. Prædi- ctionis certitudo. Crede mihi. Non enim fidem postularet, nisi rem certam atque fide dignam in- dicaret: quemadmodum ideo Dei verbum πιστὸς λόγος dicitur, 1. Tim. IV. 9. cap. III. 1. Credi & hoc vult, quia maximopere intererat, ut hoc cre- deretur non amplius duraturas Veteris Testam. ceremonias: Discrimen Judæorum à Samaritanis & Ethnicis plane cessaturum.

II. Temporis designatio. Venit hora per synec- dochen tempus quod imminere, ac præsto esse di- cit: quemadmodum postea addit: Venit hora & nunc est: quia ita prædictum erat in Veteri Testa- mento tempus Messiæ, desiturum nempe discri- men populorum atque locorum, ut ubique cul- tus Deo gratus præstari possit, Zach. XIV. Mal. I.

III. Ipsa prædictio. Quod non amplius in monte isto, in quo templum Hierosolymitano si- mile extruxerant Samaritani, vid. Joseph. Ant. lib. II. cap. 8. vel Hierosolymis in templo Zerobabelis cultus Dei instituendus sit, quem nomine adora- tionis Synecd. designat, quia præcipuum inter opera externa, quæ Deo præstantur, est adoratio. Quod etiam Papistis opponendum, cultum Dei & religionem tempore Novi Testamenti locis quibusdam alligantibus, atque idcirco peregrina- tiones ad talia loca ceu aliis sanctiora sub opinio- ne cultus & meriti suadentibus.

IV. Samaritanorum descriptio. Vos adoratis quod nescitis; destituti scilicet Dei verbo. Qui- cunque non adorant Deum Patrem, adorant quod nesciunt, ignorant, quem adorare debeant, adeoque pro idololatris merito habentur. Tales ergo gentiles Mahometani, Judæi hodierni, adde & Photiniani sunt. Hi enim ignorant vel abne- gant Patrem. Reprobatur hoc etiam Samarita- nismus vel miscella religio, qua verus Dei cultus cum falso commiscetur, & temperamentum veræ & falsæ religionis quæritur: quod Samaritanismus dici consuevit. Siquidem mixtura ejusmodi pe- nes Samaritanos primo tempore Jerobeami anno trigesimo post templum conditum invecta: post- modum sub Salmanassare, 2. Regum XVII. annis circiter 520. iterum restaurata, ac denique post 400. annos ulterius à Saneballat consummata templo in monte Garizin civitati Puchimiticæ vi- cino ad æmulationem Hierosolymitani extructo.

V. Judæorum commendatio. Nos adoramus quod scimus. In quibus verbis pluralis, nos adora- mus vel genus tantum declarat, non personam com- prehendit loquentem: vel ex mulieris opinione lo- cutum esse Christum cum Chrysost. & Theophyl.

dicendum. Quia enim pro Judæo, & communi ho- mine habebatur, ideo se cum Judæis conjungit. Penes hos enim solos tum erat, verus veri Dei cul- tus. Illi sciebant, & quem adorare debebat & quo- modo Pf. CXLVII. 19. illis etiam certus erat defi- nitus locus ad cultum divinum ex ipsius Dei man- dato Deut. XII. 5. XIV. 33. 2. Sam. VII. 34. 2. Chron. VI. 6. Pf. LXXVIII. 68. Hæc vero communicatio nihil derogat Deitati Christi; adorantibus enim, uti Cyrillus ait, seipsum communicat, qui cum Pa- tre & Spiritu S. tam ab Angelis, quam à nobis adora- tur. Ostendant autem adversarii, omni Scriptura S. revoluta, ubi Verbo & Filio Dei carne nudo adora- tio tribuatur. Nonne enim plurali numero utitur, nos adoramus, & servis se annumerat. Hæc à servi- tutis homine dicuntur? Cum enim servi formam as- sumserit, servo conveniens ministerium suscepit. Annon enim spirituale quoddam tribuit, & servitu- tis quædam professio adoratio est? Hactenus Cyrill.

VI. Commendationis peculiaris ratio. Quia sa- lus ex Judæis est. Quæ salus, quam peperit Jesus, Salvator mundi, vel ipse Jesus, qui salus omnium est, Gen. XLIX. 10. vel quæ eam salutem nobis pro- ponit, Scriptura S. verbum salutis & vitæ, concre- ditum Judæis Rom. III. 2. Illa enim salus ex Judæis est, quæ nobis à Christo acquisita est; Jesus ex ipsis prodiit, & annunciatio salutis ipsis primum facta, & ab illis derivata est in reliquas gentes, Esa. II. 3. Luc. XXIII. 47. Ex illis etiam prodire debuit is, qui est una nostra salus Rom. IX. 5. Luc. II. 30. De- nique penes ipsos asservari debebant salutis tabu- læ τὰ λόγια τῦ Θεῦ Rom. III. 2. Sic ergo ad se, ve- ram salutem, revocat mulierem, docetque simul Christus præcipuum caput, ad adorationem & cultum vel religionem veram, necessariam maxi- me esse doctrinam de Messia ejusq; salute, qua de- stitutos in tenebris versari oportet & adorare quod nesciunt. Nexus verborum ergo & argumentum Christi hoc est: Qui non agnoscunt, vel ignorant salutem, quæ ex Judæis est, Christum nempe salu- tis autorem, ejusq; meritum, illi verum Deum non agnoscunt, adeoq; adorant quod nesciunt; damna- tur ergo hic eorum omnium cultus, qui Christum ceu veram salutem non agnoscunt.

VII. Prædictionis repetitio, confirmatio & illu- stratio. Sed venit hora, & nunc est, quando veri adoratores adorabunt Patrem in Spiritu & verita- te: Recte Cyrillus in h. l. Per hæc adventus sui tem- pus significat in quo figuras legis in veritate, & um- bram in cultu spiritualem & placentem Deo Patri vivendi normam per Evangelicam doctrinam transmutandam insinuat. Notamus 1. hic adora- tionis Subjectum, 2. Actum, 3. Objectum, 4. Mo- dum, 5. ejusque Causam & Argumentum.

I. Subjectum sunt veri adoratores. Quo discri- men statuitur inter adoratores vel cultores Dei. Non enim omnes sunt ἀληθινοὶ veri, seu qui ad- orant, quem adorare debent, & prout adoran- dus est. Non ergo quivis qui preces fundit, vel Numen invocat, pro vero adoratore habendus. Sunt qui falsa invocant Idola, Numina, & Dea- stros. Hi non sunt veri adoratores sed idololatræ. Sunt qui Deum quidam adorant, sed non divino debitoq; modo, sive quod non juxta verbi præscri- ptum, sed ex proprio arbitrio & superstitione cul- tum instituant, seu quod vera animi devotione, hu- militate, ac fide id non præstent. Opponit etiam veros adoratores illis, qui umbris tantum servie- bant, & in externis potissimum hærebant, ut Pha- risæi & è Judæis plerique isto tempore: ut designet eos, qui umbratilibus istis dimissis internum, spi- ritualem, per illum præfiguratum cultum præstant Deo & exhibent, non quod in Veteri Testamento veri adoratores Patris defuerint, sed quod sub Novo Testamento ubivis terrarum citra observa- tionem istarum umbrarum veri adoratores Deum culturi sint.

II. Actum exprimit verbum προσκυνεῖν, quod est corporis incurvatione & genuflexione reveren- tiam exhibere, Matth. II. v. 11. Apoc. III. v. 19. & conf. Matth. IX. v. 18. Marc. V. 32. Cum autem oratio vel civilis sit, quæ creaturis defertur ob ex- cellentiam finitam, vel religiosa, quæ defertur Deo ob infinitam excellentiam, manifestum est, hic religiosum soli Deo debitum cultum indicari. Matth. IV. v. 10. seu exhibeatur mente, debita ex- cellentiæ divinæ agnitione aut voluntatis devota inclinatione, seu externa reverentia & venera- tione.

III. Objectum est Pater vel uti v. 24. explica- tur ὁ Θεός. Quod utrumque nomen commune est Patri, Filio & Spiritui Sancto, cum essentialiter hoc loco accipiatur. Adorationis enim objectum non sola persona est Patris, sed & Filius, quem ad- orant quoque omnes angeli, Psal. XCVI. 8. Ebr. I. 6. qui honorandus est ut Pater, Joh. V. v. 23. ut & Spi- ritus Sanctus, quem in Baptismo juxta cum Patre atque Filio profitemur, & invocamus, Matth. XXVIII. 29. ut & in votis ac precibus nostris 2. Cor. XIII. v. 13. Apoc. I. v. 4. Ea hic sine dubio adoratio prædicitur, quæ in orbe terrarum undiquaque per tot sæcula inde à nato Christo jam peragitur. Ea vero adorari Patrem, Filium & Spiritum Sanctum publicæ Ecclesiæ preces ac δοξολογίαι confirmant. Non quæ post concilium Nicenum vel Constanti- nopolitanum receptæ fuêre, sed uti Basil. Magnus lib. de Spir. S. c. XXIX. demonstrat, etiam quæ ante illud in Ecclesia omni tempore usurpatæ.

IV. Modus est, quod in Spiritu & veritate fieri debeat adoratio, quod quidam intelligunt per Hendyaden in Spiritu veritatis. Quo redit eorum interpretatio, qui Spiritum & veritatem è Rom. I. v. 9. Rom. II. v. 39. 2. Cor. III. v. 9. pro eodem ha- bent. Alii Spiritum volunt opponi carni seu riti- bus carnalibus, veritatem figuris & umbris, ac hypocrisi externarum actionum. Alii per Spiri- tum & veritatem intelligunt Spiritum Sanctum & Filium Dei, uti Athanasius in Epistola ad Serapio- nem. Sed cum hic modus adorationis duabus istis vocibus exprimatur, idcirco adorare in Spiritu est cum spiritu contrito atq; humiliato veraque pœni- tentia oramus, Psal. LI. 19. Esa. LXVI. 2. conf. Gen. XVIII. 21. 2. Chron. XXXIII. 2. Joel. II. 13. Luc. XVIII. 7. Cum per spiritum fidei & corde fideli pre- ces fundimus citra fluctuationem vel dubitatio- nem, 2. Corinth. IV. 13. Jac. I. v. 6. Vera παῥῥησία de exauditione certi, Joh. XVI. v. 24. Roman. X. 14. Eph. III. 12. Ebr. IV. 16. c. XI. 6. Cum sancti- ficati per Spiritum sancto corde oramus, sanctas- que manus attollimus, Eph. I. 15. Job. IX. 31. 1. Tim. II. 8. Ita vox ἐν πνεύματι juxta cum causa efficiente spiritualis adorationis Deo gratæ Spiritu Sancto, qui nos ceu Spiritus precum orare docet, Zach. XII. v. 10. interpellans pro nobis, Rom. VIII. 27. dum sc. nos interpellare facit, & clamare Abba Pater, Rom. VIII. 15. Gal. IV. 5. uti Ambros. l. III. de Spir. S. c. XII. vocem hanc exponit. Modum quoq; designant adorationis, quod ea spiritualiter, ani- moque spirituali, pœnitente, fideli & sancto fieri de- beat. Inepte ergo Ariani Spiritum negabant esse Deum, quia non Spiritum, sed in Spiritu Deum adorare debemus. Perperam enim Spiritus pro Autore, Doctore, & Motore seu causa precum op- op- ponitur objecto adorationis. Siquidem Deus & causa efficiens adorationis sit & proprium ejus ob- jectum. II. Altera voce ἐν ἀληθείᾳ exprimitur, quod adoratio debet fieri secundum Dei volunta- tem & verbum veritatis, 1. Joh. V. 14. ut id tantum oremus, quod voluntati Dei consentaneum est, Jac. IV. 3. & prout id Deus docet atque requirit, Deo neque modum, neque tempus statuentes: sed omnia divinæ voluntati committentes, Judith. VIII. 11. 14. Dan. III. 18. Adeoque non remissi red- damur in precibus, sed instemus orando, Dan. VI. v. 10. Luc. VI. 12. c. XVIII. 1. Rom. XII. 12. 1. Thess. V. 16. tum quoque quod oratio fieri debeat vera cordis devotione, & absque hypocrisi, Matth. VI. 6. Thren. III. 4. Os. VII. 14. ut non tam ore quam cor- de clamemus, Exod. XIV. 15. 1. Sam. I. 15. Psal. CXLV. v. 18. Es. XXVI. 16. c. XXIX. 13. Hactenus non ma- le Origenes, Novatianus, Hilarius lib. 2. de Trinit. Chrysost. Cyrill. in h. l. Procop. Euthym. & Theoph. veritatem figuris hic opponi observant, quod nem- pe tempus venerit, quo non certo loco adstringe- tur publicus Dei cultus, neque legalibus ceremo- niis & sacrificiis peragetur, sed veritate, seu rebus iis, quæ per figuras significatæ sunt. Quo pacto in veritate non adorarunt veteres, hoc est, sine figu- ris, tametsi vere, non hypocritice adorarint.

V. Argumentum geminum hujusce adoratio- nis affertur. Alterum à Dei voluntate. Nam & tales Pater quærit, qui adorent eum in Spiritu & veritate. Umbris quidem coli olim voluit, sed priusquam corpus exhiberetur: nunc ubi id exhi- bitum est, figuras non requirit: & delectatur Deus non externis rebus, sed interno & spirituali cultu, Psal. LI. 19. Ebr. XIII. 15. Alterum Argumentum petitur à natura Dei. Spiritus est Deus, & eos, qui adorant eum, in Spiritu & veritate oportet ad- orare. Ratio consequentiæ est, quia Deus ceu spi- ritualis natura, spiritualem animi cultum requirit, non vero externos cultus desiderat. Quemadmo- dum etiam externi isti ritus non Dei causa institu- ti, nec ad Dei naturam accommodati fuêre, sed potius ad naturam hominum & temporis, quo res adhuc præfigurandæ nondum exhibitæ erant, con- ditionem, confer Psal. L. 13. Esa. I. 11. c. LXVI. 1. seqq. Uti autem spiritualis Dei natura est immuta- bilis eodemq; modo semper se habet: ita sub V. T. Deus, siquidem naturam ejus respicias, cultu ex- terno per se delectari non potuit, sed quantum ille ad internum ordinabatur, ac fidei inserviebat. In verbis illis πνεῦμα ὁ Θεὸς nonnulli subjectum fa- ciunt Spiritum Sanctum cum Athanas. lib. de com- mun. Essent. Trin. Alii rectius hic subjectum Θεὸς uti Articulus adjectus docet, constituunt; adeoq; incorpoream Dei naturam hic adstrui docet. Di- citur enim Deus Spiritus non quod subtilioris tan- tum, etsi corporeæ naturæ sit, uti è Photinianis Crell. lib. de Deo & Attrib. p. 107. Deum dicit Spi- ritum, eo sensu, quo aer spiritus vocatur; sed quod corporis expers, ac plane immaterialis, & spi- ritualis naturæ sit. Si enim Deus corpore quodam, ur ut subtili, præditus esset, nulla hæc ratio Chri- sti foret, quod non corporeis ritibus, sed spiritu colendus sit Deus; ita recte Ammonius in Catena Græca: Spiritus, inquit, vocatur Deus, non ut ven- tus, sed ut incorporea & vivifica substantia. Me- rito igitur reprobantur cum Paganis idololatris Deum corporeum constituentibus Rabbini mem- bra corporea, Tertull. contra Prox. c. VII. corpus Arnob. l. III. contra gentes. Lactant. de via Dei c. 18. figuram corporis. Manichæi partes corporeas, Va- diani & Anthropomorphitæ figuram humanam, Messaliani sensibilem naturam, Mahometani cor- poream eflentiam Deo affingentes; ut & Conra- dus Vorstius corpus Deo tribui posse disputans lib. de Deo & attrib. pag. 151. Quem nequicquam excusatum it Alstedius pag. 55. Theol. Natur. O- mnes hi refutati videri possunt Tom. II. System. Theol. c. III.

Informata ita mulier de cultu Dei, cum illa non abnueret, sed Messiam, quem vel venturum bre- vi, uti nonnulli verbum ἔρχεται vers. 25. in futuro accipiunt: vel jam venisse, ex communi fama sive etiam concione Johannæa, præsupposita scriptu- ra Mosaica, quam suspiciebant Samaritani, & ad Samaritanos quoque venturum credebant, omnia expositurum diceret, remoto velo, aperte se ei- dem manifestat, Ego sum, inquiens, qui loquor te- cum. Ita ergo gradatim eam ad fidem perducere voluit. 1. Verbi sui virtute in animo Samaritanæ exerta, fundamento jacto, cui postmodum super- strui poterat solida in Messiam fides: Crede, in- quit, interprete Augustino, quid audis: quid quæ- ris: quid vides? Quærunt interpretes cur nun- quam Judæis tam aperte id professus sit, quod hic Samaritanæ, cum eorum potissimum causa vene- rit? Origenes, Ammonius, Chrysostomus, Theophy- lactus, Euthymius, Judæos plerumque maligno animo, mulierem autem hanc discendi studio in- terrogasse ajunt. Quod ita admittimus, ut nullum tamen simplicitatis meritum mulieri cum Salmero- ne adscribamus. Factum id, ut Samaritana mulie- re mediante, ad fidem perducerentur concives, quos credituros prævidebat Christus. Quemad- modum eventus docuit, per relationem mulieris eos primum credidisse, postmodum Christo ipso audito in fide confirmatos esse. Credidere illi qui- dem per mulierem, sed Christo deinde credidere per se, sicut Augustinus cap V. Epist. fundamenti profitetur se per Catholicos credidisse Ecclesiæ, utut scriptura ipsa in sese sufficiens sit, ad autoritatem fidemque sibi conciliandam. De quo contra Pon- tific. actum in Crit. Sacr. p. 332.

## 4:27
Vers. 27.

κ' ἐπὶ τούτῳ) While Jesus is speaking, as the Syriac interprets. οἱ μαθηταὶ ἀυτᾶ) See above v. 8. ἐθαύμασαν ὅτι μετὰ γυναικὸς ἐλάλει) For it was contrary to the custom of both the Hebrews and Jesus: nor could they conjecture the subject of the conversation, since Jesus was accustomed to speak of nothing but heavenly things, of which they could not believe the Samaritan woman was eager to learn. ὐδεὶς μέντοι εἶπε) Reverence forbade them to be curious. τί ζητῆς) What do you ask of her, food or drink?

Latin:

Vers. 27.

κ' ἐπὶ τούτῳ) Dum loquitur JEsus, ut Syrus interpretatur. οἱ μαθηταὶ ἀυτᾶ) Vide supra v. 8. ἐθαύμασαν ὅτι μετὰ γυναικὸς ἐλάλει) Nam præter morem id erat & Hebræorum & Jesu: nec conjicere poterant ser- monis materiam, cum Jesus nihil nisi cœlestia solitus esset loqui, quorum discendorum avidam esse Samaritidem credere non poterant. ὐδεὶς μέντοι εἶπε) Reverentia vetabat esse curiosos. τί ζητῆς) Quid ab ea poscis, cibum an potum?

## 4:28
Vers. 28.

Ἀφῆκεν ἓν τὴν ὑδρίαν) See above vers. 7. The mind is shown to be kindled with a zeal for divine things, so that she forgot the very thing for which she had come. Thus the disciples are noted to have followed Jesus, leaving their nets, Matt. IV. 20. τοῖς ἀνθρώποις) that is, to those there.

Latin:

Vers. 28.

Ἀφῆκεν ἓν τὴν ὑδρίαν) Vide supra vers. 7. Ostenditur a- nimus accensus rerum divinarum studio ita ut id ipsum oblivisceretur, ob quod venerat. Sic notantur discipuli Jesum secuti omissis retibus, Matth. IV. 20. τοῖς ἀνθρώποις) id est, τοῖς ἐκεῖ.

## 4:29
Vers. 29.

πάντα ὅσα ἐποίησα) The series of my life, which he could not know in a human way.

PART II. Conversation with the disciples about food and the spiritual harvest.

Latin:

Vers. 29.

πάντα ὅσα ἐποίησα) Vitæ meæ seriem quam scire huma- nitus non potuit.

PARS II. Colloquium cum discipulis de cibo & de messe spirituali.

## 4:31
Vers. 31.

Ἠρώτων) ἐρωτᾷν is used everywhere for to ask, as in chapter IV. 40, 47, c. XVI. 16. We noted this at Luke IV. 38. Chrysostom says το ἠρώτων here is to beseech in their local dialect. The disciples had brought lunch from the city: therefore they invite him to eat, not doubting that he had contracted hunger from the long journey.

This meaning, says de Dieu, is unusual among approved Greek authors, where it is used only for to ask, to inquire, and is opposed to ἀποκρίνεσθαι, to answer. This is a Hellenism of the language. For שׁאל in Hebrew means both to ask, and to pray, to request, to seek. Hence Psalm CXXII. v. 6. שׁאֲלוּ שְׁלוֹם

שַׁאֲלוּ שְׁלוֹם יְרוּשָׁלָיִם to request, to wish for, to obtain by prayers the peace of Jerusalem, LXX. ἐρωτήσατε τὰ πρὸς εἰρήνην τὴν Ἱεροσαλὴμ. See also Psalm XXXV. 13.

Latin:

Vers. 31.

Ἠρώτων) ἐρωτᾷν pro rogare passim sumit, ut cap. IV. 40. 47. c. XVI. 16. Notavimus ad Luc. IV. 38. Chrysostomus το ἠρώτων ἐνταῦθα παρακάλειν ἐστὶ τῇ ἐγχωρίῳ ἀυτῶν φωνῇ. Attulerant discipuli ex urbe prandium: itaque invitant ut vescatur, non dubitantes quin ex multo itinere famem con- traxisset.

Inusitata, inquit de Dieu, hæc significatio apud probatos autores Græcos, ubi tantum pro interrogare, sciscitari usurpatur, opponiturq; ei ἀποκρίνεσθαι respondere. Hellenistica hoc linguæ est. Nam שׁאל Hebrais & interrogare, & orare, postulare, petere significat. Hinc Psal. CXXII. v. 6. שׁאֲלוּ שְׁלוֹם

שַׁאֲלוּ שְׁלוֹם יְרוּשָׁלָיִם postulare, optare, precibus impetrate pa- cem Hierosolymae, LXX. ἐρωτήσατε τὰ πρὸς εἰρή- νην τὴν Ἱεροσαλὴμ. Vide & Psal. XXXV. 13.

## 4:32
Verse 32.

Ἐγὼ βρῶσιν ἔχω φαγεῖν) Christ gives an example to his own so that they may always prefer spiritual things to temporal ones. Compare the history of Samuel, 1 Sam. XVI. 11. Therefore, although hungry, he delays his meal because of the offered opportunity of teaching the Samaritans. ἔχω φαγεῖν I have something to eat, as ἔχοντα λαλῆσαι, who had something to say, Acts XXIII. 18. and ἔχω λέγειν below c. XVI. v. 12. Otherwise ἔχω καταφαγεῖν in Isocrates is I have something that I may eat. It is, however, a custom for the Hebrews to call that by which the desire of the soul is satisfied בָּרוֹת, just as the Latins also say the food of souls. See Psalm XIX. 11.

ὕκ οἴδατε) You do not consider, you do not attend.

Latin:

Vers. 32.

Ἐγὼ βρῶσιν ἔχω φαγεῖν) Dat Christus exemplum suis ut semper spiritualia temporalibus anteferant. Confer hi- storiam Samuelis 1. Sam. XVI. 11. ideo quamvis esuriens differt prandium ob oblatam occasionem docendi Sicimi- tas. ἔχω φαγεῖν edendum habeo, ut ἔχοντα λαλῆσαι, qui ha- bebat quid dicendum, Actor. XXIII. 18. & ἔχω λέγειν in- fra c. XVI. v. 12. Alioqui ἔχω καταφαγεῖν apud Isocratem est habeo quod edam. Mos est autem Hebraeis בָּרוֹת vo- care id, quo desiderium animi expletur, sicut & Latini di- cunt pastum animorum. Vide Psal. XIX. 11.

ὕκ οἴδατε) Non consideratis, non attenditis.

## 4:33
Verse 33.

μήτις) Has anyone from the city brought us something without our knowing? They say this because they wonder why the meal is being delayed.

Latin:

Vers. 33.

μήτις) An quis ex urbe nobis inscius? Hoc ideo dicunt, quia mirantur differri prandium.

## 4:34
Verse 34.

τὸ θέλημα τῶν πέμψαντός με) The command enjoined upon me. Thus below c. V. 30. c. VI. 38. 39. 40.

τελειώσω αὐτῶ τὸ ἔργον) The work of calling sinners to repentance: to which the command tends below c. XVII. 4.

While Christ is still talking with the Samaritan woman, the disciples return from the city and invite him to take food, the table having been prepared, saying, Rabbi, eat: but Christ answers, I have food which you do not know of: the disciples ask among themselves mutually: Has anyone brought him food? What wonder then, says Augustine, if that woman did not understand about the water, just as his disciples did not understand about the food. On this occasion, Christ wished not only to inform them about his spiritual food, but also about the imminent Evangelical harvest. There are therefore two memorable things here: 1. The explanation of the food in which Christ took the greatest delight, which is the administration of his office. My food, he says, is to do the will of him who sent me, to finish his work. He thus designates both the operation proper to himself: To do the will of the Father, by whom he had been sent; namely, the Prophetic Office; and the work and effect, which he rejoiced to finish as the result of that office, namely, the conversion of men, and consequently their eternal salvation. For this was the highest pleasure for Christ, to execute the will of the Father and to work for the salvation of men. It is called food by way of comparison. For just as the hungry seek food, and having received it are satisfied and filled with joy: so Christ sought nothing with greater appetite than to execute the will of the Father, he hungered for nothing more than the salvation of men, by which one thing he is most intensely satisfied and delighted. For this food is taken for a sweet and pleasing thing, with which one is delighted, Job XX. 14. For he was occupied in instructing the woman, who was a stranger to the faith, which was to him like the sweetest food. But the disciples did not know this: Therefore, he says, I have food that you do not know. From which it is gathered 1. How greatly Christ is delighted by the conversion of men, to such an extent that nothing is more pleasing and agreeable to him, and nothing does he hunger or thirst for more than our salvation. Christ calls the salvation of men food, says Chrysostom, Homily XXXIII on John, to show how great a care and desire for our salvation he holds. Similarly Cyril, book II on John, chapter 103. From this we learn how great is the love of GOD toward men. For he calls the conversion of lost men his food: Our salvation is to him as it were the seasoning of the Father's will, which makes that, in itself most sweet, even sweeter to him. 2. With what pleasure and delight we ought to execute the parts of our duty, especially that which pertains to propagating the kingdom of GOD, so that nothing may be more pleasing to us. Conf. Romans XII. v. 7. Philippians II. verse 10. 1. Thessalonians II. 19. chapter III. v. 8. Psalm XIX. v. 10. & 11.

As masters of the world, says Ammonius, Christ accustomed his disciples to postpone bodily food to the will of God and the salvation of men. Ambrose illustrates this in his work On Elijah and Fasting, chapter III, with the example of the angels. For not every food is material, nor is every food bodily. There is also the food of the mind, with which the soul feasts: of which the Lord speaks: My food is that I should do the will of my Father. This is the food of the angels, that they should serve the divine command: they have no care for tables: no use for banquets: no stored-up feasts: no drink of wine or strong drink: no distension of the body: no offense of the belly. Thus Ambrose. Such food will be the hidden manna in the other life, where nothing will be more pleasant to us than this food of the angels, Rev. 2:7.

Latin:

Vers 34.

τὸ θέλημα τῶν πέμψαντός με) Mandatum mihi injunctum. Sic infra c. V. 30. c. VI. 38. 39. 40.

τελειώσω αὐτῶ τὸ ἔργον) Opus vocandi peccatores ad poenitentiam: quo mandatum tendit infra c. XVII. 4.

Dum colloquente adhuc Christo cum Samari- tide revertuntur e civitate discipuli, eumque ad- ornata mensa ad cibum capiendum invitant, Rabbi comede: Christus vero respondet, cibum habeo, quem vos nescitis: quaerunt discipuli inter se mu- tuo: Numquis ipsi cibum adduxerit? Quid mi- rum ergo, inquit Augustinus, si mulier illa non in- telligebat aquam, ceu discipuli ejus non intelligebant escam. Hac occasione Christus non tantum de ci- bo suo spirituali informare eos voluit, sed etiam de imminente messe Evangelica. Habentur ergo duo hic ἀξιομνημόνευτα: 1. Explicatio cibi, quo maxi- me delectatus fuit Christus, qui est administratio officii. Cibus meus est, inquit, ut faciam volunta- tem ejus, qui misit me, ut perficiam opus ejus. Desi- gnat ita tum operationem sibi propriam: Facere vo- luntatem Patris, a quo missus erat; Officium nem- pe Propheticum; tum opus & effectum, quod per- ficere gaudebat ceu ἀποτέλεσμα officii illius con- versionem nempe hominum, & consequenter aeter- nam salutem. Haec enim summa voluptas fuit Christo, exequi voluntatem Patris & operari salu- tem hominum. Dicitur cibus per similitudinem. Ut enim cibum expetunt esurientes, eoque acce- pto saturantur, & laetitia implentur: Ita Christus nihil majori appetitu expetiit, quam exequi vo- luntatem Patris, nihil magis esuriit, quam salutem hominum,qua una re exsatiatur, ac deliciatur im- pensissime. Accipitur enim cibus hic pro re suavi & grata, qua quis delectatur, Job. XX. 14. Occu- pabatur enim in informanda muliere, a fide alie- na, quod ipsi instar cibi suavissimi erat. Hoc au- tem nesciebant discipuli: Ideo, inquit, cibum ha- beo quem vos nescitis. Unde colligitur 1. Quan- topere Christus delectetur conversione homi- num, adeo ut nihil ei gratius, ac jucundius sit,ni- hilque magis esuriat aut sitiat, quam salutem no- stram. Hominum salutem, inquit Chrysost. Homil. XXXIII. in Johan. Christus cibum vocat, ut quanta salutis nostrae cura & desiderio teneatur ostendat. Similiter Cyrill. lib. II. in Johan. cap. 103. Hinc discimus, quanta sit erga homines DEI charitas. Cibum enim suum vocat perditorum hominum conversionem: Salus nostra veluti condimentum paternae voluntatis ipsi est, quae illam per se sua- vissimam, ipsi reddit suaviorem. 2. Quanta vo- luptate & delectatione partes muneris, impri- mis, quod ad propagandam regnum DEI facit, exequi debeamus, nequicquam gratius nobis sit. Conf. Roman. XII. v. 7. Philipp. II. verf. 10. 1.Thess. II. 19. cap. III. v. 8. Psalm. XIX. v. 10. & 11.

tanquam Magistros orbis terrarum, inquit Ammo- nius, assuefecit Christus discipulos suos corporalem cibum Dei voluntati, hominumque saluti postponere. Illustrat id Ambrosius de Elia & Iejunio cap. III. exemplo Angelorum. Nam omnis esca materia- lis nec omnis cibus corporalis. Est & cibus mentis, quo epulatur anima: de quo agit Dominus: Meus cibus est, ut faciam voluntatem Patris mei. Hic ci- bus Angelorum est, ut famulentur divino imperio: Nulla iis cura mensarum: Nullus conviviorum usus: nulla reposita epulæ: nullus vini potus aut si- cera: nulla distensio corporis: nulla ventris offensio. Hæc Ambrosius. Talis cibus erit Manna abscondi- tum in altera vita, ubi nihil jucundius erit nobis hoc Angelorum cibo, Apoc. II. 7.

## 4:35
Verse 35.
