οὐχ ὑμεῖς λέγετε) You have been accustomed to console yourselves for the labors of sowing with this hope. The opposite member below in verse 37 shows this. Similar is that saying, 'When evening has come, you say, fair weather,' and what follows, Matt. 16:2, where in a similar way one ascends from a statement about temporal things to greater ones.

ἔτι τετράμηνόν ἐστι) It is a Hebraism for 'after four months the harvest is at hand.' Thus Jonah 3:4. But an old manuscript without ἔτι has τετράμηνός ἐστι, perhaps from the Calends of Nisan, which is the beginning of the year.

How can these four months be counted from the Calends of Nisan or Abib to the harvest, when in the following chapter 5:1 Grotius understands by the feast the feast of the Passover, and immediately after that feast the barley harvest in Judea began or was imminent, Exod. 13:4, ch. 30:11, 12, Lev. 16:10, Num. 28:26, Deut. 16:9? Therefore these things were said in the month of Casleu or November, or rather Thebith or December, and not in the month of Nisan. I know what Heinsius has found new here, what Dievius has conjectured, what Samuel Petitus, and from him B. Quistorpius: but none of them proves itself to us. What Heinsius assumes from the heat that wearied the Savior, that it was summer, is frivolous. For the Evangelist does not establish summer as the cause of thirst, but weariness from the journey, v. 6.

ὀφθαλμοὺς ὑμῶν) The eyes of the mind.

θεάσασθε τὰς χώρας) As widely as you can extend the gaze of your mind, for the calling not only of the Jews and Samaritans, but also of the Gentiles is hinted at.

λευκαί εἰσι πρὸς θερισμόν) What the Latins call 'to turn yellow': just as he passes from the food of the body to the food of the mind, so he passes from the temporal harvest to the spiritual. A similar translation is in Matt. 9:37. He indicates, however, that many minds are teachable.

Latin:

Vers. 35.

οὐχ ὑμεῖς λέγετε) Soliti estis laborum sationis hac spe solari. Id ostendit membrum oppositum infra 37. Simile est illud ὀψίας γενομένης, λέγετε, εὐδία & quæ sequuntur. Matth. XVI. 2. ubi similiter à locutione de rebus tempora- libus ad majora adscenditur.

ἔτι τετράμηνόν ἐστι) Hebraismus est pro post quatuor men- ses instat messis. Sic Jonæ III. v. 4. At manuscriptus vetus sine ἔτι habet τετράμηνός ἐστι, forte à Calendis Nisan, quod anni initium.

Quomodo à Calendis Nisan, vel Abib quatuor hi menses ad messem numerari possunt, cum se- quenti cap. V. v. 1. per festum intelligat Grotius festum Paschatos, & festo illo statim messis hordea- cea in Judæa inierit, aut imminuerit, Exod. XIII. v. 4. cap. XXX. v. 11. 12. Levit. XVI. vers. 10. Num. XXVIII. 26. Deut. XVI. v. 9. Quapropter men- se Casleu vel Novembris, vel Thebith, potius aut Decembris hæc dicta sunt, non vero mense Nisan. Novi, quid hic novi invenerit Heinsius, quid con- jectarit Dievius, quid Samuel Petitus, & ex eo B. Quistorpius: Sed nihil eorum se nobis probat. Quod Heinsius assumit ex æstu, qui fatigarit Sal- vatorem, æstatem colligi frivolum est. Nam non æstas causa sitis ab Evangelista constituitur, sed fa- tigatio ex itinere. v. 6.

ὀφθαλμοὺς ὑμῶν) Mentis oculos.

θεάσασθε τὰς χώρας) Quam late potestis aciem animi ex- tendere, vocatio enim non Judæorum tantum, & Samari- tanorum, sed & Gentium innuitur.

λευκαί εἰσι πρὸς θερισμόν) Quod flavescere dicunt Lati- ni: sicut à cibo corporis ad cibum animi, ita à messe tempo- rali ad spiritualem transit. Similis translatio Matth. IX. 37. Indicat autem ingenia multa esse docilia.

## 4:36
Verse 36. ὁ θερίζων μισθὸν λαμβάνει) The payment of wages by farmers is deferred until after the harvest.

συνάγει καρπὸν εἰς ζωὴν αἰώνιον) Those whom he reaps he brings into the heavenly kingdom, as if into a barn.

ἵνα καὶ ὁ σπείρων ὁμοῦ χαίρῃ καὶ ὁ θερίζων) That the glory of the saints of the Old and New Covenants may be one, Heb. 11:40. ἵνα here is consecutive. The passage in Amos 9:13 pertains mystically to this.

Latin:

Vers. 36. ὁ θερίζων μισθὸν λαμβάνει) Solutio operarum ab agricolis post messem differtur.

συνάγει καρπὸν εἰς ζωὴν αἰώνιον) Quos metit eos infert regno cœlesti, tanquam horreo.

ἵνα καὶ ὁ σπείρων ὁμοῦ χαίρῃ καὶ ὁ θερίζων) Ut Sanctorum veteris ac novi fœderis una sit gloria, Hebr. XI. 40. ἵνα hic est ἐκβατικὸν. Huc mystice pertinet locus Amosi IX. 13.

## 4:37
Verse 37.

ὁ λόγος ἐστὶν ἀληθινὸς) That is, that old saying holds true here.

ἄλλος ἐστὶν ὁ σπείρων καὶ ἄλλος ὁ θερίζων) A proverb which is noted to have prevailed also among the Greeks: 'Others sow, and others in turn shall reap.' And in the Knights of Aristophanes: 'reaping another's harvest.' Similar to this: 'You have roused a hare for others.' And that one: 'Thus you, not for yourselves.'

Latin:

Vers. 37.

ὁ λόγος ἐστὶν ἀληθινὸς) Id est dictum illud vetus hic lo- cum habet.

ἄλλος ἐστὶν ὁ σπείρων καὶ ἄλλος ὁ θερίζων) Proverbium quod & apud Græcos obtinuisse notatum est: Ἄλλοι μὲν σπείρουσ᾽, ἄλλοι δ᾽ αὖ ἀμήσονται. Et equitibus Aristophanis : τ' ἀλλότριον ἀμῶν θέρος. Cui si- mile: Aliis leporem excitasti. Et illa: Sic vos non vobis.

## 4:38
Vers. 38.

Ἀπέστειλα ὑμᾶς) That is, I have destined to send. Thus Matt. X. v. 5. 16.

Ἄλλοι κεκοπιάκασι) The field has been tilled by the Prophets, who not only in Judea, but also through various dispersions among the nations, had stirred up men by voice and writings to the worship of the one God, which is the seed of the Evangelical harvest. Thus κοπιᾷν is taken in 1 Tim. II. 6.

εἰς τὸν κόπον αὐτῶν εἰσεληλύθατε) That is, into the field labored upon by them, as in the poet: '...The joyful crops and the labors of oxen.' Thus κόπος seems to be taken in 2 Cor. X. 15.

It is commonly said at the time of sowing, there are still four months and the harvest comes. But now, when he had scarcely made a sowing in Samaria in this one woman, 'Lift up,' he says, 'your eyes and you will see the whole region already whitening for the harvest,' not a few fellow-countrymen as the first-fruits of the future conversion of the Samaritans; see how quickly they have ripened for the spiritual harvest. For the fellow-citizens were about to rush there immediately after the woman's report, as Christ foresaw, whom he preferred to instruct, having been brought by the woman, than to take the food brought by the disciples. And since this was his highest joy, he also urges the disciples to gladness, because they can not only rejoice with the Prophets who did the sowing, but also enjoy a more ample joy. For the Apostles reap what they did not labor for, whereas on the contrary the Prophets, who indeed labored in the sowing, did not so much celebrate that ample harvest themselves as they predicted it was to be celebrated. We note here (I.) the common proverb, 'Do you not say, commonly, that there are still four months and the harvest comes?' Origen accepted this concerning the long time, according to the disciples' opinion, still remaining for the spiritual harvest; which opinion, as to the matter, does not conflict with our already provided paraphrase. However, the explanation of Cyril, Chrysostom, Augustine, Bede, and Theophylact regarding the corporal harvest, which Christ, as we have said, compares to the spiritual, is closer. But he implies that this does not have some months remaining, but is already at the door. Maldonatus wishes it to be a Hebrew proverb, by which it is signified that there is enough time for us to think about doing some thing. For between sowing and harvest there generally intervene four months, since the former was done in the month of November, the latter at the end of April, as can be seen in Exodus XXXIV. 22 and Leviticus XXII. But the matter comes to the same thing.

(II) Indication of the spiritual harvest: Lift up your eyes and see the regions, because they are already white for the harvest. They are commanded to lift up the eyes not only of the body, but also of the mind, so that they may see the approaching Samaritans, whence the ripeness of other regions for the harvest is not obscure, because the Samaritan region, especially alienated from the faith, was already whitening for the harvest, prepared for receiving the Gospel. The harvest of the Gospel is spoken of by metaphor concerning the harvest of preaching and the conversion of men, as in Matt. IX. 37, Luke X. 11. For just as in the harvest sheaves are gathered from the fields and brought into the threshing floor, so a great assembly was to be gathered from the field of the world into the threshing floor of the Church. Cf. Matt. III. 12, Luke III. 17.

(III) The fruit of the reapers. And he who reaps receives wages and gathers fruit unto life eternal. Both the wages and the fruit of the Apostles are designated. Wages is the reward which they receive for their labor, which comes under the name of wages, namely on account of the promise made to those who labor, and on account of the relation to the labor: not that there is a just proportion here, but that it is rendered for labors, nevertheless, whatever had been promised in the likeness of wages. Conf. Dan. X. 3. Matth. V. 2. 2. Tim. IV. 7. 1. Pet. V. 4. 2. Cor. III. 8. But the fruit, which is gathered unto life eternal, can be understood of converted men, because conversion is the fruit of the Gospel, and the converted are like a crop sprouting from the seed of the Gospel, which fruit Christ designated as to be gathered unto life eternal Matth. XIII. verse 38. And who would desire a more joyful fruit of the reapers? Moreover, Teachers, as spiritual reapers, gather this fruit or crop unto life eternal when they collect those called into the spiritual kingdom of God: which reapers the angels will one day gather into the heavenly kingdom.

IV. The joy of those who labor. That both he who sows and he who reaps may rejoice together. For those who sow not for themselves but for the master, rejoice when it is reaped, because they not only congratulate the master, but also themselves for the happy yield, and for the fruit of their labors, some part of which redounds to the workers as well, when the farmer brings the wages due to the workers at the harvest; the joy is common at the time of harvest, Isa. 9:3. Otherwise, not joy, but sorrow arises, when some sow and others reap, Isa. 65:22, when, namely, enemies reap what they did not sow. Cyril of Alexandria speaks beautifully of this common joy of the Prophets and Apostles in this place: Nor will the reapers alone rejoice in this reward, but because they will gather what was sown by the labor of the Prophets, they will triumph in one celebration with them. He points out the Apostles as the reapers, but the Prophets themselves are those who sowed; from the happy harvest, joy arises for both.

Let it be noted, V., the distinct office of the Prophets and Apostles. Lest it seem that the discourse was about a corporal harvest, Christ himself instituted the application, having first set forth a common proverb which they were accustomed to use, when one had labored and another was receiving the fruit of the labors. For in this is the true word, because one is he who sows, and another is he who reaps. The labor of sowing is most difficult, and is undertaken with uncertain hope of yield. The harvest is easier and more pleasant because of the certain yield. I sent you to reap that for which you did not labor; others labored, and you have entered into their labors. He openly indicates here that it is the Prophets who labored in the sowing. But that this happiness falls to the Apostles, that they should now celebrate the harvest, is explained by Origen, Chrysostom, Augustine, and especially Irenaeus, book IV, ch. 40. Who then, says Irenaeus, are those who labored, who served the dispositions of God. It is manifest that the Patriarchs and Prophets, who also prefigured our faith, and disseminated into the earth the coming of the Son of God, who and what he would be, so that those who were to be future men, having the fear of God, might easily receive the coming of Christ, instructed by the Prophets. They labored, however, by preparing that people for the Messiah, with prophecies, types, and figures, and also by exciting the desire for his coming: whence the labor and the yield of the Apostolic ministry was happier. Which Irenaeus teaches excellently by the example of the Ethiopian Eunuch: Nothing else was lacking to him, he says, who had been pre-catechized by the Prophets, he did not lack knowledge of God the Father, nor the disposition of conduct, but only the coming of the Son of God; which when he had briefly learned, he went on his way rejoicing, about to be a herald in Ethiopia of the coming of Christ. Wherefore Philip did not labor much concerning him, because he was prepared in the fear of God by the Prophets. And not dissimilarly, Cyril says: The intellectual seeds and spiritual ears of corn are those who, cultivated by the voice of the Prophets, arrive at the faith of Christ, which crop whitens then, when the mind is already mature, that is, ready to receive the faith of Christ and the true religion. The reaping sickle, however, is the splendid preaching of the Apostles, which, cutting the hearers away from legal figures, transfers them to another Church of God. Where, crushed by the labor of virtue, they are made into shining wheat and worthy of the divine barn. Irenaeus gathers from this that the God of the Old and New Testament is the same, against Marcion. Since by the same one both the Prophets were sent to sow and the Apostles to reap in the same field. Furthermore, that Christ sent the Prophets, who says, I sent you, Ammonius and Leontius infer, because both the reapers and the sowers are sent by the same Master of the house.

PART III. The conversion of the Samaritans to Jesus.

Latin:

Vers. 38.

Ἀπέστειλα ὑμᾶς) Id est, destinavi mittere. Sic Matth. X. v. 5. 16.

Ἄλλοι κεκοπιάκασι) Subactum est arvum à Prophetis, qui non tantum in Judæa, sed & per dispersiones varias apud gentes voce ac scriptis homines ad unius Dei cultum excitarant, quod semen est Evangelicæ frugis. Sic κοπιᾷν sumitur 1. Tim. II. 6.

εἰς τὸν κόπον αὐτῶν εἰσεληλύθατε) Id est in arvum ab ipsis laboratum, quomodo apud Poëtam: - - - Sata læta boumque labores. Sic κόπος sumi videtur 2. Cor. X. 15.

Vulgo dici solet tempore sementis, quatuor men- ses adhuc sunt & venit messis. Nunc autem ubi vix sementem in Samaria in una hac muliere fecit, Levate, inquit, oculos & videbitis, jam ad messem albescere totam regionem, populares non paucos ejusdem primitias futuræ Samaritanorum con- versionis, videte quam cito maturuerint ad mes- sem spiritualem. Siquidem concurfuri erant illico post relationem mulieris concives, uti prævidebat Christus, quos à muliere adductos informare ma- lebat, quam cibum à discipulis allatum capere. Atque cum hoc summum esset ejus gaudium, ad lætitiam quoque hortatur discipulos, quod non modo cum Prophetis, qui sementem fecerunt, gaudere possint, sed etiam ampliori lætitia fruan- tur. Siquidem Apostoli metant quod non labo- rarunt, cum è contrario Prophetæ, qui in semente quidem laborarunt, messem vero illam amplam non tam celebrarint ipsi, quam celebrandam præ- dixerint. Notamus hic (I.) vulgatum proverbium, Nonne vos, vulgo, dicitis, quod adhuc quatuor men- ses sunt & messis venit; id de longo tempore, juxta discipulorum opinationem, ad spiritualem mes- sem adhuc restante, Origenes accepit: quæ senten- tia quoad rem nostræ jam traditæ paraphrasi non repugnat. Propinquior tamen est Cyrilli, Chryso- stomi, Augustini, Bedæ, Theophylacti explicatio de messe corporali, quam Christus, uti diximus, spi- rituali comparat. At hanc non restare menses ali- quot, præ foribus eandem jam esse innuens. Mal- donatus vult, Proverbium esse Hebræum, quo signi- ficetur satis esse temporis, ut de re aliqua facienda cogitemus. Siquidem inter sementem & messem plerumque quatuor menses interveniant, cum illa facta fuerit mense Novembri, hæc exeunte Aprili, uti Exodi XXXIV. 22. Levit. XXII. videre est. Sed res eodem recidit.

(II) Messis spiritualis indicium: Levate oculos vestros & videre regiones, quia albæ jam sunt ad messem. Oculos non tantum corporis, sed & mentis attollere jubentur, ut videant adventan- tes Samaritanos, unde aliarum regionum matu- ritatem ad messem colligere haud obscurum est, quod Samaritana, maxime à fide aliena, jam ad messem albesceret, parata ad suspiciendum Evan- gelium. Messis Evangelii dicitur per metaphoram de messe prædicationis & conversionis hominum, ut Matth. IX. 37. Luc. X. 11. Quemadmodum enim in messe manipuli ex agris colliguntur, & in aream conferuntur, ita tantum colligendus erat cœtus ex agro mundi in aream Ecclesiæ. Conf. Matth. III. 12. Luc. III. 17.

(III) Messorum fructum. Et qui metit, mer- cedem accipit & congregat fructum in vitam æter- nam. Designatur Apostolorum cum merces, tum fructus. Merces est præmium, quod pro labore accipiunt, quod mercedis nomine venit, nempe ob promissionem laborantibus factam, & ob rela- tionem ad laborem: non quod proportio justa hic sit, sed quod pro laboribus tamen reddatur, quic- quid instar mercedis promissum fuerat. Conf. Dan. X. 3. Matth. V. 2. 2. Tim. IV. 7. 1. Pet. V. 4 2. Cor. III. 8. Fructus vero, qui in vitam æternam congregatur, intelligi potest de hominibus con- versis, quia conversio est fructus Evangelii, & conversi sunt instar segetis è semente Evangelii progerminantis, quem fructum in vitam æternam congregandum designavit Christus Matth. XIII. vers. 38. Et quis messorum lætiorem fructum ex- optaret? Congregant autem fructum vel segetem istam in vitam æternam Doctores, ceu messores spirituales, cum vocatos in regnum Dei spirituale colligunt: quos messores novissimi Angeli in re- gnum cœleste congregaturi olim sunt.

IV. Laborantium gaudium. Ut & qui seminat simul gaudeat & qui metit. Qui enim non sibi sed hero seminant, gaudent cum metitur, quia non modo gratulantur hero, sed & sibimetipsis de proventu felici, & de laborum fructu, quorum pars aliqua ad operarios quoque redundat, cum agricola mercedem operariis ad messem debitam defert; commune est tum gaudium messis tempore Esa. IX. 3. Alias non gaudium, sed mæror oritur, cum alii seminant, alii metunt, Esa. LXV. 22. cum nempe hostes metunt quod non seminarunt. Pulchre de hoc communi Prophetarum & Apostolorum gaudio Cyrillus Alexandr. in h. l. Nec soli hac mercede lætabuntur messores, sed quia labore Prophetarum seminata colligent, in una celebritate cum illis triumphabunt. Messores indigitat Apostolos, Prophetæ vero ipsi sunt, qui seminarunt, utrisque ex felici messe oritur gaudium.

Notetur V. distinctum Prophetarum & Apostolorum officium. Ne de messe corporali sermo esse videretur, applicationem Christus ipse instituit, præmisso tamen communi proverbio, quo uti consueverant, cum alius laborarat: alius autem laborum fructum percipiebat. In hoc enim est verum verbum, quia alius est qui seminat, & alius est qui metit. Labor sementis difficillimus est, & incerta spe proventu suscipitur. Messis facilior & ob certum proventum jucundior. Ego misi vos metere, quod vos non laborastis, alii laborarunt, & vos in labores eorum introistis. Aperte hic indicat Prophetas esse, qui laborarint in semente. Apostolis vero eam obtingere felicitatem, ut messem jam celebrent: quemadmodum explicant Origenes, Chrysostomus, Augustinus, & imprimis Irenæus lib. IV. c. XL. Qui ergo sunt, inquit Irenæus, qui laboraverunt, qui dispositionibus Dei deservirunt. Manifestum est, quia Patriarchæ & Prophetæ, qui etiam præfigurarunt nostram fidem, & disseminaverunt in terram adventum Filii Dei, quis & qualis erit, uti qui posteriores erant futuri homines, habentes timorem Dei, facile susceperint adventum Christi, instructi a Prophetis. Laborarunt autem illud præparando populum ad Messiam, vaticiniis, typis & figuris, nec non excitando desiderium adventus ejus: unde felicior erat & labor & proventus ministerii Apostolici. Quod egregie docet Irenæus exemplo Eunuchi Æthiopis: Nihil aliud deerat ei, inquit, qui a Prophetis fuerat præcatechizatus, non Deum Patrem, non conversationis dispositionem, sed solum adventum ignorabat Filii Dei; quem cum breviter cognovisset, agebat iter gaudens præco futurus in Æthiopia adventus Christi. Quapropter non multum laborabat circa eum Philippus, quia erat in timore Dei præparatus a Prophetis. Nec absimiliter Cyrillus Sata, inquit, intellectualia, & spicæ spirituales sunt, qui Prophetarum voce culti ad fidem Christi perveniunt, quæ seges albescit tunc, cum jam maturus, id est, promptus ad suscipiendam fidem Christi, & religionem veram animus est. Messoria vero falx est Apostolorum splendida prædicatio, quæ a legalibus figuris auditores abscindens ad aliam Ecclesiam Dei transponit. Ubi labore virtutis contriti fulgens in triticum ac divino dignum horreo efficiuntur. Colligit inde Irenæus eundem esse Deum Veteris & Novi Testamenti, adversus Marcionem. Siquidem ab eodem & Prophetæ ad seminandum & Apostoli ad metendum in eundem agrum missi sint. Adhæc Christum Prophetas misisse, qui ait, ego misi vos, infert Ammonius & Leontius, quia ab eodem Patrefamilias & messores & seminatores mittuntur.

PARS III. Samaritanorum ad Iesum conversio.

## 4:39
Ver. 39.

Many believed in him. The following shows that this is to be understood of the Sichemites before they had left the city. Behold the fulfillment of that which had been said concerning the Messiah.

Testifying that he told me. They believed the woman as one who would not spare herself: and they rightly judged that to know secrets was something divine. There is here, however, as often, direct speech for indirect. For in Latin we would say, because of the word of the woman testifying that her deeds were told to her by Jesus.

Latin:

Vers. 39.

πολλοὶ ἐπίστευσαν εἰς ἀυτὸν] Ostendunt sequentia, intel- ligendum hoc de Sicimitis antequam exiissent urbe. Ecce complementum ejus quod de Messia dictum erat.

Μαρτυρούσης ὅτι εἶπέ μοι] Mulieri credebant ut quæ sibi non parceret: & arcana nosse divinum esse aliquid recte judicabant. Est autem hic, ut sæpe directa oratio pro in- directa. Nam Latine diceremus, ob sermonem mulieris testantis sua facta sibi ab Jesu indicata.

## 4:40
Ver. 40.

They asked. Thus above 31.

Μείναι παρ' ἀυτοῖς] that he might lodge with them, as above I. 39.

Καὶ ἔμεινεν ἐκεῖ δύο ἡμέρας] He did not indulge them for more than two days, so that he might moderate the matter, lest he either despise the Samaritans who were eager to learn, or seem to prefer them to the Jews. He had previously forbidden the disciples to stay in Samaritan towns, but only for a time. He himself was forbidden by no law from approaching them.

Others give different reasons for the two-day stay: namely, that this ought to have been only a prelude to the calling of the Gentiles, not the fullness itself; and that the Lord already knew the sufficiently firm faith of the Samaritans, which reason Augustine presents in tract. XVI on John.

Latin:

Vers. 40.

ἠρώτων] Sic supra 31.

Μείναι παρ' ἀυτοῖς] ut apud se diverteret, ut supra I. 39.

Καὶ ἔμεινεν ἐκεῖ δύο ἡμέρας] Non plus biduo illis indul- sit, ut rem temperaret, ne aut Samaritas discendi avidos contemneret, aut Judæis præferre videretur. Discipulis antehac vetuerat morari in Samaritanis oppidis, sed ad tem- pus. Ipse nulla lege eos adire vetebatur.

Alias biduanæ tantum commorationis causas reddunt alii: utpote quod hoc præludium tantum esse debuerit vocationis gentium, non ipsa pleni- tudo; & quod Dominus jam satis firmam Samari- tanorum fidem norat, quam rationem exhibet Augustinus tract. XVI. in Johannem.

## 4:41
Vers. 41.

Διὰ τὸν λόγον ἀυτᾶ] Without miracles, which shows great docility in the Samaritans, a presage of that which was to be expected from the Gentiles.

Latin:

Vers. 41.

Διὰ τὸν λόγον ἀυτᾶ] Sine miraculis quod magnam in Samaritis docilitatem monstrat, præsagium ejus, quod à Gentibus erat expectandum.

## 4:42
Vers. 42.

ἐκ ἔτι διὰ τὴν σὴν λαλιὰν] Understand, not so much, a manner of speaking common both in others and especially in these writers. And note the argument of faith. What he had just called λόγον, he now calls λαλιὰν. Elsewhere it is a certain property of the speaker, as below c. VIII. 43, Matth. XXVI. 73, Marc. XIV. 70; thus שמע in Isa. XI. 3 is translated λαλιὰ. So also Psal. XIV. 4, λαλιὰ for the Hebrew אָבֵל, where in Latin it is speech as here. For the Hebrew דבר it is found in Job XXXIII. 3, Eccles. III. 18, cap. VII. 15, Cant. IV. 3. See also Marc. XV. 12. The ancients noted in this Samaritan woman a figure of the Church, which leads us to the divine word: we believe in the word especially because of the majesty and holiness of the word itself. Compare I. Reg. X. 6, 8.

Which is to be noted against the Papists, who suspend the authority of the divine word from the Church, urging to that effect the saying of Augustine, l. contr. epist. fundam. c. 5: 'I would not believe the Gospel, unless the authority of the Church moved me': concerning which, however, see what we have said in Tom. I. on Augustine's Confessions, or Crit. Sacr. page 302 seq., and the dissertation of the Blessed Lord D. Dorscheus on the authority of the Church, or an explanation of those words of St. Augustine.

Ἀληθῶς ἐστιν] Just as you remembered that he had preached himself to us. For this must be tacitly understood, although it is not narrated. For who would believe that the woman kept silent about this? And it is to be noted that the Samaritans were not offended by the lowliness of his appearance.

ὁ σωτὴρ τῶ κόσμο] Thus 1. Ioh. IV. 14. He is called by Paul the savior of all men, 1. Tim. IV. 10. Whence did the Samaritans know this? Because Jacob had said concerning Shiloh, that is, the Messiah, that the nations would gather to him, Gen. XLIX. 10.

PART IV. The healing of the nobleman's son lying sick in Capernaum, in Cana.

Latin:

Vers. 42.

ἐκ ἔτι διὰ τὴν σὴν λαλιὰν] Intellige, non tam, loquendi genet e & in aliis & in his maxime scriptoribus usitato. Et nota argumentum fidei. Quod modo λόγον dixerat, nunc λαλιὰν vocat. Alibi est proprietas quædam loquen- tis ut infra c. VIII. 43. Matth. XXVI. 73. Marc. XIV. 70. sic שמע Esa. XI. 3. vertitur λαλιὰ. Sic & Psal. XIV. 4. λαλιὰ pro Hebræo אָבֵל, ubi Latine loquela ut hic. Pro Hebræo דבר reperitur Job. XXXIII. 3. Eccles. III. 18. cap. VII. 15. Cant. IV. 3. Vide & Marc. XV. 12. Notarunt veteres in hac Samariti de Ecclesiæ esse figuram, quæ nos adducit ad ver- bum divinum: nos verbo maxime propter ipsius verbi ma- jestatem & sanctitatem, credimus. Confer I. Reg. X. 6. 8.

Quod contra Pontificios notandum, qui auto- ritatem verbi divini suspendunt ab Ecclesia, in eam sententiam urgentes dictum August. l. contr. epist. fundam. c. 5. Evangelio non crederem, nisi Ecclesiæ me commoveret autoritas: de quo vero vi- de quæ diximus Tom. I. in August. Confess. vel Crit. Sacr. pag. 302. seq. & B. Dn. D. Dorschei dissertatio- nem de autoritate Ecclesiæ, sive explicationem eo- rum verborum S. Augustini.

Ἀληθῶς ἐστιν] Sicut tu eum de se prædicasse nobis me- morasti. Hoc enim tacite subintelligendum est quanquam non narratur. Quis enim credat hoc reticuisse fœminam? Et notandum tenuitate cultus non offendi Samaritas

ὁ σωτὴρ τῶ κόσμο] Sic 1. Ioh. IV. 14. Paulo dicitur σωτὴρ πάντων ἀνθρώπων. 1. Tim. IV. 10. Unde hoc sciebant Sa- maritæ? quia de Siloh, id est, Messia, Iacob dixerat ad eum concursuras gentes, Gen. XLIX. 10.

PARS IV. Filii Reguli in Capernaum decumbentis in Cana sanatio.

## 4:43
Vers. 43.

εἰς τὴν Γαλιλαίαν] That is, into the territory of Galilee, not into the towns. Just as the word Ἰουδαία is taken above in ch. III. 22. Since, however, it was said above that the home of Jesus was at Nazareth, a reason had to be given why he did not go straight from the Samaritan region to Nazareth.

Latin:

Vers. 43.

εἰς τὴν Γαλιλαίαν] Id est, in agrum Galilææ, non in op- pida. Sicut vox Ἰουδαία sumitur supra c. III. 22. Cum autem supra dictum sit, domicilium Iesu fuisse Nazarethi, ratio reddenda fuit cur non recta ex Samaritana regione Naza- rethum perierit.

## 4:44
Vers. 44.

Αυτὸς γὰρ Ἰησῦς ἐμαρτύρησεν] As if he were saying, he did not go to Nazareth for this reason, because he knew he would be despised there, on account of the memory of his humble upbringing: just as he himself was sometimes accustomed to preach. For that word ἐμαρτύρησε does not have a mark of a specific time: therefore nothing prevents Christ from having said it somewhat later, namely at that time, the narrative of which is in Matt. XIII. v. 57 and Mark VI. 4, where see the notes. I clearly do not approve of the fact that some here understand 'fatherland' to be that region in which Bethlehem was. For that had not yet become known: so that he could not be despised there on account of familiarity or upbringing.

Having departed from Samaria, Christ came into Galilee; among his τὰ λεχθέντα, however, let it be observed in particular

A proverb concerning the fellow-citizens of Prophets. For Jesus himself testified that a Prophet has no honor in his own country. He testified this not only by deed or by avoiding his country, as Tarnovius maintains, but by an express statement, which is read also in Matt. XIII. 57, Mark VI. verse 4, Luke IV. v. 24. We note in this place I. The occasion of this testimony. Those who take it from Judea, with Origen, say this, that having left that country in which Bethlehem was, his native land, he now turned himself into Galilee. Others interpret it of all Galilee with Augustine, that Christ foresaw that, however much the Galileans might receive him at the beginning, that honor would not be lasting, since he did not make as much progress there in the space of several days as he did in two days among the Samaritans; others interpret it of the country of his residence, Capernaum, such as Chrysostom, Euthymius, and also Tarnovius, because he passed by that place as well. But it is better to explain it with Cyril as referring to the city of Nazareth, which is specifically called his country, because he did not go to it, but met it as he was leaving Samaria, having directed his journey rather toward Cana, because a Prophet is not accepted in his own country. The emphasis of the word ἐν τῇ ἰδίᾳ πατρίδι teaches this, the course of the journey confirms it, and especially the repetition of the same proverb and the event itself in Luke IV. v. 24. For the ungrateful Nazarenes confirmed the truth of Christ's prediction by his ejection. II. The meaning and truth of the proverb. Which is not to be taken absolutely, since sometimes Prophets have been held in reverence even in their own country, but as the usage of proverbs dictates: which are understood of those things which for the most part happen, and is confirmed by the examples of the Prophets in the Old Testament, who were almost nowhere less valued than in Judea and among their own people, and also by daily experience. The cause; which can be given as threefold: first, innate envy, because it is almost natural, as Jerome says in Matt. XIII, for citizens always to envy citizens: then, the familiarity of conversation, because custom is wont to breed contempt, especially when youthful pursuits are thought of and familiar conversations are remembered. For, as Jerome has it in the cited passage, they do not consider the present works of the man, but remember the fragility of his infancy. Then also, the perversity of the human mind, because we prefer most things that are rare and exotic to domestic ones. See Theophylact on Matt. XIII. IV. The use of the proverb. That we should not have a fixed mind intent solely on our country, for although we were born there first, the reason of the divine will and glory must be held before all things, and the utility of the Church must be looked to, which can be hoped to be greater where honor and authority are stronger: for preaching cannot bear fruit there where the preacher is despised, says Cyril in this place; then if we are despised in our country, let us consider that the same happened to Christ, let us leave it with Christ, and let us not doubt that hospitality is prepared for us elsewhere among strangers and foreigners, if we are held in low esteem among our own hosts, just as other Galileans received Christ honorably when he was rejected in Nazareth. Joseph in Egypt, Jonah among the Ninevites, Daniel among the Babylonians, were held in higher esteem than among their own people; Plutarch observed this long ago. book on Exile, Of the most prudent and wisest men, you will find very few in whom their country has been a source of happiness in their fostering or care.

Latin:

Vers. 44.

Αυτὸς γὰρ Ἰησῦς ἐμαρτύρησεν] Quasi dicat, ideo Naza- rethum non iit, quod ibi se contemni sciret, ob memoriam humilis educationis: sicut ipse interdum prædicare solebat. Illud enim ἐμαρτύρησε non habet certi temporis notam: ita- que nihil obstat quo minus id post aliquanto Christus dixe- rit, eo nempe tempore, cujus narratio est apud Matth. XIII. v. 57. & Marc. VI. 4. ubi notata vide. Plane non probo quod patriam hic quidam intelligunt eam regionem, in qua Bethlehemum erat. Nam id nondum innotuerat: ita, ut ibi ob familiaritatem aut educationem contemni non posse.

Samaria egressus Christus in Galilæam venit in- ter τὰ λεχθέντα autem ejus observetur inprimis

Parœmia de Prophetarum civibus. Ipse enim Je- sus testatus est, quod Propheta in patria honorem non habeat. Testatus est non facto tantum seu evi- tatione patriæ, ut vult Tarnovius, sed expresso di- cto, quod legitur etiam Matth. XIII. 57. Marc. VI. vers. 4. Luc. IV. v. 24. Notamus hoc loco I. Te- stificationis hujus occasionem. Qui de Judæa ac- cipiunt cum Origene, hanc dicunt, quod relicta ea, in qua Bethlehem erat, patria ipsius, nunc in Galilæam se converterit. Alii de Galilæa tota cum Augustino interpretantur, quod præviderit Christus, utut initio suscepturi sint Galilæi hono- rem illum non stabilem futurum, ubi plurium die- rum spatio non tantundem profecerit, quantum per biduum apud Samaritanos; alii de patria in- habitationis Capernaum interpretantur, utpote Chrysostomus, Euthymius, ut & Tarnovius, quod & eandem præterierit. Sed præstat cum Cyrillo explicare de urbe Nazareth, quæ peculiariter pa- tria ejus dicitur, quod eandem non adierit, sed cum ipso eidem Samaria excedenti obvenerit, iter suum potius versus Canam direxerit, quia in pa- tria acceptus non est Propheta. Docet hoc verbi emphasis ἐν τῇ ἰδίᾳ πατρίδι, confirmat cursus iti- neris, & imprimis repetitio ejusdem Parœmiæ ac eventus ipse Luc. IV. v. 24. Siquidem prædictio- nis Christi veritatem ingrati Nazaræi ejectione ejusdem confirmarunt. II. Sententiam & veri- tatem proverbii. Quod non absolute accipiendum, cum quandoq; Prophetæ etiam in patria reveren- ter sint habiti, sed ut fert proverbiorum usus: Quæ intelliguntur de iis, quæ ut plurimum fiant, & ab exemplis Prophetarum in Veteri Testamento, qui fere nusquam minus in pretio fuêre, quam in Judæa, & apud suos, nec non experientia quoti- diana confirmatur. III. Causam; quæ triplex da- ri potest, tum ingenita invidia, quod propemodum ut Hieronym. in Matth. XIII. ait, naturale sit, ci- ves semper civibus invidere: tum familiaritas con- versationis, quod consuetudo contemptum pare- re soleat, maxime quando cogitantur studia ju- venilia, & familiares conversationes recordantur. Non enim, uti loco citato Hieronymus habet, consi- derant præsentia viri opera, sed fragilitatem recor- dantur infantiæ. Tum etiam ingenii humani per- versitas, quod pleraque τὰ σπάνια & exotica præ- feramus domesticis. Vide Theophyl. in Matth. XIII. IV. Usum proverbii. Ne fixam mentem habea- mus in patria unice intentam, cui etsi primo nati simus, divinæ tamen voluntatis & gloriæ ante omnia habenda est ratio, & utilitas spectanda Ec- clesiæ, quæ major sperari potest, ubi potior est honor & autoritas: prædicatio enim fructum ibi facere non potest, ubi prædicator contemnitur, in- quit Cyrillus in h. l. tum si contemnamur in patria, cogitemus Christo idem obtigisse, cum Christo relinquamus eam, neque dubitemus alibi inter ignotos, & exteros parata nobis hospitia, si penes hospites nostros ἄτιμοι habeamur, quemadmo- dum honorifice suscepere Christum alii Galilæi cum in Nazareth reprobaretur. Joseph in Ægy- pto, Jonas penes Ninivitas, Daniel apud Babylonios, longa impensius habiti, quam inter suos, id ob- servavit jamdudum Plutarch. lib. de Exilio, Ex prudentissimis & sapientissimis paucissimos reperias, in quib. fovendis aut curandis patria fuerit felicita.

## 4:45
V. 45. ἐδέξαντο) They received him hospitably. For not as much testimony is rendered to them as to the Samaritans.

οἱ Γαλιλαῖοι) Those who inhabit the field and the villages.

πάντα ἑωρακότες) Slower than the Samaritans, who had placed their faith in him without having seen any miracles.

ἃ ἐποίησεν ἐν ἱεροσολύμοις) Above ch. I. 23. II. 2.

ἦλθον εἰς τὴν ἑορτὴν) As the law commanded.

Latin:

V. 45. ἐδέξαντο) Hospitaliter acceperunt. Neque enim tantum illis testimonium redditur quantum Samaritis.

οἱ Γαλιλαῖοι) li qui agrum & vicos habitant.

πάντα ἑωρακότες) Tardiores Samaritis, qui nullis con- spectis miraculis fidem ei adhibuerant.

ἃ ἐποίησεν ἐν ἱεροσολύμοις) Supra c. I. 23. II. 2.

ἦλθον εἰς τὴν ἑορτὴν) ut lex præcipiebat.

## 4:46
Vers. 46. ἦλθεν ὖν) When he wished to betake himself from the country into the town, not even then did he betake himself to Nazareth, but to Cana.

τὶς βασιλικὸς) This reading relies not only on the better faith of the codices, but also on the authority of the Syriac and the Arabic; in Syriac it is עבד מלכא, a minister of the King; in Arabic, أدنس ملكي, a man of the King; in 3 Esdras VIII. 69 it is read τοῖς βασιλικοῖς οἰκονόμοις. I think this man was in charge of collecting the taxes for Herod the Tetrarch (whom the Galileans, for the sake of honor, called King, Matt. XIV. 9, Mark VI. 14): from which he was later instructed, the Roman Centurion acting in the same town conceived an excellent opinion of Jesus.

Casaubon has this to say about it: It is an old question in what sense the word βασιλικὸς is to be taken in this passage. Chrysostom offers a double interpretation; either because he was himself of the royal lineage, of royal blood; or he had some other dignity of office that was called by this name. Or that he was endowed with some dignity by which he was so called: that is, on account of which he himself was so called; for instance, a Royal Procurator, or a Royal Chamberlain: which would pertain to the court and service of the King or Tetrarch of Galilee, who was Herod Antipas. In this sense Jerome translates it: Palatine; and I think this is the truest of all. For who does not know that everywhere among the Greeks, by the appellation of τῶν βασιλικῶν, the courtiers and ministers of Kings are understood? Although the Roman Emperors had deprived the sons of Herod the Great of the title of Kings, and had ordered them to be called Tetrarchs, there is no doubt that they were still often called Kings by their own people: And the Evangelists speak in this way, Matt. XIV. v. 9, Mark VI, and elsewhere. Josephus also speaks thus: for Hyrcanus, whom Pompey had deprived of the royal name and had wished to be content with the honor of High Priest, is called βασιλεὺς even afterwards, as on p. 430 and 431. If, therefore, you were to translate ἦν τὶς βασιλικὸς not badly, it would be, there was a certain courtier. Compare also Heinsius on this passage.

ἐν Καπερναὺμ) Whether you refer this to the father, or to the son, or to both, it must be held entirely that this royal minister lived not in Cana but in Capernaum, from where the servants soon meet him.

Latin:

Vers. 46. ἦλθεν ὖν) Cum ex agro in oppidum recipere se vellet, ne tum quidem Nazarethum se recepit, sed Canam.

τὶς βασιλικὸς) Hæc lectio non tantum meliorem codi- cum fide nititur, sed & Syri & Arabis autoritate, Syro est עבד מלכא minister Regis, Arabi أدنس ملكي homo Regis, 3. Esdr. VIII. 69. legitur τοῖς βασιλικοῖς οἰκο- νόμοις. Puto hunc Herodis Tetrarchæ (quem Galilæi ho- noris causa Regem appellabant, Matt. XIV. 9. Marc. VI. 14.) vectigalibus colligendis fuisse præpositum: Ex quo edo- ctus deinde Centurio Romanus in eodem agens oppido, egregiam de Iesu opinionem concepit.

De eo ita habet, Casaubonus: Vetus est quæstio, quo sensu accipienda sit vox βασιλικὸς hoc loco. Chry- sostomus duplicem interpretationem affert; vel quia esset ipse τῦ γένες τῦ βασιλικῦ, regii sanguinis; ἢ ἀξίωμά τι ἀρχῆς ἕτερον ὕτω καλύμβρον εἶχε. Vel quod aliqua præditus esset dignitate, qua sic vocare- tur: hoc est propter quam ipse sic vocaretur; puta, Procurator Regius, vel Cubicularius Regius: quod pertineret ad aulam & ministerium Regis sive Te- trarchæ Galilææ, qui erat Herodes Antipas. Hoc sensu Hieronymus. Palatinum vertit: atque hoc omnium verissimum puto. Nam quis nescit, passim apud Græcos appellatione τῶν βασιλικῶν, intelligi Regum aulicos & ministeria? Etsi autem Romani Imperatores filios Herodis Magni Regum appella- tione privaverant, & Tetrarchas esse dici jusserant, quin tamen à suis Reges sæpe dicerentur, nullum du- bium est: Et ita loquuntur Evangelistæ, Matth. XIV. v. 9. Marc. VI. & alibi. Sic & Josephus lo- quitur: nam Hircanus, quem Pompejus regio nomi- ne privaverat & honore Summi Pontificis voluerat esse contentum, βασιλεὺς illi nuncupatur etiam post- ea, ut p. 430. & 431. si igitur ἦν τὶς βασιλικὸς non male verteres, erat quidam aulicus. Confer. & Hein- sius in hunc locum.

ἐν Καπερναὺμ) Sive hoc ad patrem, sive ad filium refe- ras, sive ad utrumque, omnino tenendum est hunc regium ministrum non in Cana sed Capernaum habitasse, unde mox ipsi famuli occurrunt.

## 4:47
Vers. 47. εἰς τὴν Γαλιλαίαν) For the fame of Christ was preceding him as he arrived in those territories.

ἵνα καταβῇ) It is said by the Hebrews to descend even for one who goes into a higher place, Judg. XV. 11. But I think he is looking here not so much at the position of the city as of the region. For Capernaum was closer to the river.

Drusius has this to say in this place: Capharnaum was situated on a mountain: it should have been said, therefore, that he went up. Perhaps that courtier lived on a lower part of the mountain. Or this knot must be untied in another way. For we read in Judg. ch. XV. 11, they went down to the top of the rock. Conversely, Jos. VII. 24, They made them go up into the valley of Achor. For one descends into a valley from a mountain. But one ascends into it from another lower place. Xenophon, a Greek author, said ἀνάγω for ἀπάγω, I lead up for I lead away.

Ἰάσηται αὐτῦ τὸν ὑιὸν) All the ancient interpreters read αὐτῦ, not αὐτὸν, which is why that is more correct. He suspected something good about Jesus, as if the present could heal the present. Compare 2 Kings V. 11. And note how much greater the faith of the alien Centurion was, Matt. VIII. 8.

ἤμελλε γὰρ ἀποθνήσκειν) He was near to death, as the Syrian translates. Thus in the Tragedy, 'For I was about to kill you, husband, as you say.' If it was probable that it would happen that he would kill you, Luke VIII. 42 said ἀπέθνησκεν for the same. Otherwise, it could also be taken as 'he seemed to be dying,' in the way the Scholiasts note that μέλλειν is used by Homer.

Latin:

Vers. 47. εἰς τὴν Γαλιλαίαν) Fama enim in eos fines Chri- stum adventantem præcurrebat.

ἵνα καταβῇ) dicitur Hebræis descendere etiam qui it in locum superiorem, Iudic. XV. 11. Sed hic non tam urbis quam regionis situm respiciputo. Erat enim Capernaum propius flumen.

Drusius ita habet hoc loco: Capharnaum erat in monte sita: dicendum ergo erat, ut ascenderet. Forte aulicus ille in decliviore loco montis habita- bat. Aut aliter solvendus hic nodus. Nam legimus Judic. c. XV. 11. descenderunt in summitatem petræ, Contra Jos. VII. 24. Ascendere fecerunt eos in val- lem Achor. Nam in vallem ex monte descenditur. Sed ex alio loco depressiore ascenditur in eam. Xeno- phon autor Græcus ἀνάγω dixit pro ἀπάγω, subdu- co pro abduco.

Ἰάσηται αὐτῦ τὸν ὑιὸν) αὐτῦ non αὐτὸν legerunt omnes veteres interpretes, quare id rectius. Aliquid boni de Iesu suspicabatur, quasi præsens præsentem sanare posset. Con- fer 2. Reg. V. 11. Et nota quanto major Centurionis alie- nigenæ fides fuerit Matth. VIII. 8.

ἤμελλε γὰρ ἀποθνήσκειν) Proximus erat morti, ut vertit Syrus. Sic in Tragœdia ἐγὼ γὰρ σ' ἔμελλον ὡς σύ φης κτείνειν πόσιν. Si probabile erat futurum, ut te occideret, ἀπέθνησκεν pro eodem dixit Lucas VIII. 42. Alioqui posset & sumi pro videbatur mori, quomodo μέλλειν apud Homerum poni notant Scholiastæ.

## 4:48
Vers. 48. Ἐὰν μὴ σημεῖα καὶ τέρατα ἴδητε, ὐ μὴ πιστεύσητε) You, he says, O Jews, are so hard-hearted that although you have one preaching the most holy things, although you have testimony from John the Baptist, you do not believe unless you see healings and portents. For τέρας here seems to be more than σημεῖον, as also in Matt. XXIV. v. 24, Rom. XV. v. 29, 2 Cor. XII. 12, 2 Thess. II. 9, Heb. II. 4. Although elsewhere the order of the words is inverted. Compare what we said above in ch. II. v. 18, and contrast the readiness of the Samaritans to this hardness of the Jews. Note also that this very minister of the king is said not to believe, because he did not believe sufficiently: and his fault is noted, who demanded a miracle for the sake of his own temporal good, not for the sake of proving a doctrine.

Latin:

Vers. 48. Ἐὰν μὴ σημεῖα καὶ τέρατα ἴδητε, ὐ μὴ πιστεύσητε) Vos, inquit, Iudæi tam duri estis ut quamvis sanctissima prædicanti, quamvis testimonium habenti à Iohanne Ba- ptista, non credatis nisi conspectis sanationibq & portentis. Videtur enim τέρας, hic plus esse quam σημεῖον, ut & Matth. XXIV. v. 24. Rom. XV. v. 29. 2. Cor. XII. 12. 2. Thess. II 9. Hebr. II. 4. Quanquam alibi vocum ordo invertitur. Con- fer quæ diximus supra c. II. v. 18. & huic Iudæorum duritiæ facilitatem Samaritanorum oppone. Nota item hunc ipsum regis ministrum dici non credere, quia non satis credebat: & vitium ejus notari, qui miraculum exigeret sui tempo- ralis boni non probandi dogmatis causa.

## 4:49
Come down before he dies) He is still concerned only with his own, and thinks weakly of Jesus, as if He could not be of help while absent: much less does he suspect that one who is dead can be raised, which is a most robust faith, Heb. 11:19.

Latin:

Κατάβηθι πρὶν ἀποθανεῖν) Adhuc & suum tantum curat & tenuiter de Jesu sentit, quasi absens prodesse non possit: multo minus suspicatur mortuum posse resuscitari, quæ ro- bustissima est fides, Hebr. XI. 19.

## 4:50
Ver. 50. Go) What the Jews say, Go in peace, this is, be of good courage. See Luke 7:50.

lives) He is well. A locution most customary among the Hebrews. So below v. 52. Josh. 5:8.

1. Regarding the origin of this nobleman, Cyril and Jerome make him a Gentile; others, because the Jews were accustomed to seek signs, make him a Jew. 2. Regarding his status, the Vulgate version calls him a nobleman, as if βασιλίσκος were read; but since βασιλικὸς, royal, is held, he is to be understood as a minister with the Syriac interpreter, whom Origenes and others more correctly judge to have been in charge of the city of Capernaum in the name of Caesar, or Herod, whom Luke in chapter 7:3 makes a prefect of Herod. B. Chemnitz calls him a courtier of Herod, or a Palatine, that is, someone from the palace or court of the King, in Isa. 65. Others interpret the word as being of royal blood with Baronius, but less congruously. We note only in the words of Christ to this prefect, or Palatine, who, excited by the fame of the miracles, hastened to Christ because his son was lying at the point of death, both an exploratory rebuke and a supportive confirmation of faith: for Christ first rebuked him as he was asking that He come down and heal his Son, v. 48. Unless you see signs and wonders, you do not believe. Maldonatus and Emanuel Sa wish this to be said not by way of reproach, but by way of declaration, as if He were saying, I am compelled because of your infirmity to perform miracles, because if I did not, you would not believe Me. But the rebuke is sufficiently open, not as if the nobleman were still entirely incredulous, but because his faith was quite languid, because he wanted Christ to come down with him, and indeed quickly, lest his Son die in the meantime: which indeed shows he did not yet believe that Jesus was the Messiah, but nevertheless held Him for some distinguished Prophet. He was therefore teaching by this rebuke. I. The sins of hearers, even those established in great authority, such as that Palatine was, are to be rebuked, Isa. 58:1, Jer. 15:2, 1 Tim. 5:20, 2 Tim. 4:2. Thus Nathan rebuked David, Elijah Ahab; Isaiah Hezekiah, 2 Kings 20:36. The Baptist openly rebukes Herod. II. It is the duty of hearers to receive rebukes with a grateful mind, Ps. 131:5, Prov. 27:5, 6. Who will not bear a physician giving wholesome advice? Nor does he know the danger of sin, says Basil, nor the profit of repentance, who is affected with sadness against him who has rebuked him. III. The Word of God is to be believed simply as being worthy of all trust, even if we do not see what the word teaches or promises. Faith is of those things which you do not see, τῶν οὐ βλεπομένων, Heb. 11:1. To believe what you see outwardly and perceive in reality is not that faith which Scripture celebrates. Blessed are those who believe and do not see, John 20:29. IV. We are for the most part so affected that we require signs and wonders, and we do not indeed refuse to believe God, yet we tacitly and obliquely include this condition, that we see His presence and help. V. Signs are not to be requested rashly. The requesting of miracles is illicit, whether it be done out of diffidence with Zechariah, Luke 1:18, 30, or out of curiosity, with Herod. But it is impious if it be done out of a desire to slander, with the Pharisees, Matt. 12:38. But God Himself sometimes commanded that miracles be requested for the confirmation of faith, Isa. 7:13, and they were sometimes requested by the faithful, by Abraham, Gen. 15:18, Gideon, Judg. 6, Hezekiah, 2 Kings 20:9. Furthermore, today, after God has spoken to us most recently through His Son, Heb. 1:1, since He does not act immediately or extraordinarily, and no promise of signs exists, one must acquiesce

the Word of God having been confirmed long ago by many miracles. VI. The Papists wrongly contend that miracles are necessary so that faith in doctrine may be conciliated. The Mainz theologians in their animadversions to Anti-Becanus, p. 121. Truly, unless Christ and the Apostles had performed those portents for the sake of producing faith, the Jews were certainly not bound to believe, but could by right and merit refute the Gospel with an argument taken from the antiquity of the Synagogue. But in truth, miracles had indeed been necessary for Christ because of the promises concerning the Messiah being manifested through miracles, Isa. 35:5, John 15:24, but they were not necessary because of the faith and authority of Christ's doctrine, which is of itself worthy of all trust and builds up faith for itself; nor did Christ always perform miracles where He preached, as his own fatherland is an example. John the Baptist was distinguished by no miracles; were they therefore not bound to apply faith to his doctrine? Adam Conzen admits in his Commentary on John 4:48, that the testimony of the Baptist was authentic, so that those who had been instructed by him were bound to believe. But he says that a new sign is now needed, if indeed we interpret the scriptures in a new way. But the doctrine of John concerning the coming of the Messiah was also new, a new Sacrament, a new Chair in the desert, a new ambassadorial office, and therefore he was also held as an innovator, Luke 7:30, 33, and yet he did not need miracles to assert his new doctrine. Furthermore, we do not concede that our doctrine is new, which is that of Christ Himself and the Apostles, abundantly confirmed by their miracles.

VII. Miracles are not marks of the Church. Bellarmine includes them in the same list of marks (1.) But marks ought to be perpetual: here, however, Christ wishes to be believed, even if signs and wonders are not seen, nor was any promise made about perpetuating them: nor are they necessary after the doctrine of Christ was sufficiently confirmed by miracles through the Apostles. Augustine, book XXII of The City of God, chapter 7. I could say, he says, that they were necessary before the world believed, in order that it might believe. Whoever, however, requires these prodigies in order to believe, he says, is himself a great prodigy, who does not believe while the world believes. Signs were given for the sake of the unbelieving, as the Apostle testifies in 1 Cor. 14:22; therefore, those who demand signs must be infidels. And for that reason, Lorinus on the Acts of the Apostles, p. 94, and Toletus, book IV of his Instruction, chapter 3, teach that miracles are not now necessary. Didacus Stella on Luke 2. He declares this with a simile: When a boy begins to walk, he is helped by a walker, which would be a hindrance to an adult; so, if miracles were performed now, men would stumble at it and say that our faith was not yet well confirmed. Beware, therefore, lest you seek signs. (2.) Marks should be proper, not common. But miracles are common to false prophets and to the Antichrist himself, Matt. 7:22, 2 Thess. 2:4, Apoc. 13:13. (3.) Marks ought to be infallible and indubitable; but miracles do not prove doctrine infallibly; indeed, they prove nothing if they do not have the truth of doctrine joined to them, Deut. 13:2. Therefore, Maldonatus on Matt. 7, p. 137, admits that an argument taken from miracles, even true ones, is not entirely necessary. Joseph Acosta, book III on the Last Times, chapter 3, says that miracles are entirely vain and empty unless they are approved by Scripture, that is, unless they have doctrine conformable to Scripture. But that Scripture itself, by itself, is the most invincible argument. And this is what Chrysostom urges here, that we should attend not to signs but to doctrine. Ferus agrees in his Commentary on chapter 24 of Matthew: not doctrine from miracles, but miracles are to be judged from doctrine.

There follows II. The assistance of Christ, by which he primarily confirmed his faith. For when he urged by praying, 'Lord, come down before my son dies,' the Lord Jesus said, 'Go, your son' lives. This is a most sweet opposition; the courtier urges, come down Lord. The Lord says, I will not come down, yet go; the courtier, before my son dies. The Lord: Your son does not die, he already lives. He testifies therefore that he has already helped him while locally absent, whom the man supposed he could not help except by coming down. the certainty of the help, and he himself be refreshed by the restoration of his son. But he also refreshes the parent, before he sets himself on the way, with a word of promise, so that he may not fail on the way, because of a word of rebuke, therefore he adds, Your son lives. For that word Go, is not of one rebuking or chiding, as Maldonatus wishes, as if he were saying, go you unbeliever, see, experience, that your son lives, and believe. But it is the word of one raising up and comforting, so that he may go confidently, and rejoice in the restoration of his son. The word חָיָה he lives, by Hebraism, is the same as he recovered, 2 Kings 1:2, Ps. 70:20, Ps. 137:7; he uses however not the future, he will live, but the present, so that not natural health, but divine operation may be recognized. Maldonatus applies this to the consecration of the Eucharist, which, as here by saying Your son lives, he himself was made healthy; so there by saying this is my body, the body of Christ was made, which was bread. Truly by those words, Your son lives, the healing was not performed, but only indicated, which is to be attributed to the nod and simple will of Christ, nor if the healing had been performed here by that word, could transubstantiation be inferred through the words of the Eucharist, because having weighed the tenor of the institution, only a sacramental union is to be inferred. We are taught however here: (I.) That Christ does not reject weak faith. Weak faith is also from God, who distributes to each one his own measure, Eph. 4:7. Rom. 12:3, it is also truly faith, Mark 9:29, it is truly acceptable to Christ, who came for the sake of the weak, Isaiah 61:2, Matt. 11:28. He does not extinguish the smoking flax, Isaiah 42:3, nor does he reject anyone coming to him, John 6:37, whose power is perfected in the weak, 2 Cor. 12:9, and he perfects and confirms and consolidates us, 1 Pet. 5:10. Let us only pray with the disciples: Lord, increase our faith, Luke 17:5, all strength of faith is from Christ, whom it apprehends; but even a small faith apprehends Christ, just as a sick hand can also apprehend the gift of a rich man. (II.) Christ often performs more than we ask, and helps better than we desire; the courtier asked that he would come down, so that his son might not die, but the son could have succumbed before Christ arrived there; therefore he himself brings it about immediately, so that the son, already near to death, may be well: He was asking that he would help by coming down: Christ however demonstrates that he, visibly absent, can help as present, and helps by the very act. Let human sloth blush, says Augustine in chapter 39 on the words of the Lord, he wishes to give more than we wish to receive, he wishes to show mercy more than that misery wishes to be freed. Bernard, sermon V on the triple mode of praying, warns, before it has gone out from our mouth, God commands it to be written in his book, and we can undoubtedly hope. Because he will either give what we ask, or what he knows is more useful, Matt. 7:7, John 14:13, ch. 15:7, Rom. 8:26, 28. (III.) The end of Christ's help is the confirmation of our faith. He helps in such a way as he knows it serves to help our faith. When asked by the courtier he did not want to come down. To the centurion, however, not asked, he promised that he wanted to come, Matt. 8:7. How so? There he wanted to increase a small and weak faith, without the help of coming down, which he would have confirmed by his descent in his unbelief, as if he could not have helped except by coming down. Here he wanted to bring into the light a great faith lying in secret. Because in the centurion, says Chrysostom, faith was being perfected, therefore he said he would go, so that we might recognize the man's faith. But the courtier was still imperfect, therefore he was pushing Christ with all effort to come down, and he did not yet know that he also had the power to cure while absent. What he could do, therefore, he showed, so that what the centurion felt by himself, this one (the courtier) might be taught without Jesus approaching. (IV.) God in place of answering sometimes deals more harshly with us, so that the vices which contaminate faith may be corrected. As examples here with the courtier are Jacob, Job, David, the Canaanite, etc.

ἐπίστευσεν ὁ ἄνθρωπος τῷ λόγῳ) This second degree of belief shines forth. He believes that Jesus says true things: that health was restored to his son by his power, or he does not yet believe, or he doubts.

Latin:

Vers. 50. πορεύου) Quod Judæi dicunt, Vade in pace, hoc est bono animo esto. Vide Luc. VII. 50.

ζῆ) Valet. Locutione Hebræis usitatissima. Sic infra v. 52. Jos. V. 8.

Regulum hunc 1. quoad originem Cyrillus, & Hieronymus Ethnicum, alii, quia signa Judæi pe- tere solebant, Judæum faciunt. 2. Quoad statum, Vulgata versio Regulum dicit, quasi legatur βασι- λίσκος; Sed cum habeatur βασιλικὸς Regius, mi- nister cum Syro interprete intelligendus, quem ci- vitati Capernaum Cæsaris, Origenes, alii re- ctius Herodis nomine præfuisse censent Chusan, à Luca præfectum cap. 7, 3. Ἐπίτροπον Herodis facit B. Chemnit. Hieronymus Aulicum dicit Hero- dis, vel Palatinum, hoc est aliquem è Palatio, seu aula Regis in cap. 65. Esa. Alii de Sanguine Regio interpretantur vocem cum Baronio, sed minus congrue. Notamus solum in Christi ver- bis Præfecti, vel Palatini hujus, qui ob filium ad mortem decumbentem ad Christum miraculo- rum fama excitatus properavit, tum explorato- riam objurgationem, tum opitulatricem fidei con- firmationem: rogantem enim, ut descenderet ac sanaret Filium redarguebat primum Christus v. 48. Nisi signa & prodigia videritis, non creditis. Mal- donatus & Emanuel Saa volunt, non reprehendendo hoc dici, sed pronunciando, quasi dicat, cogor pro- pter infirmitatem vestram facere miracula, quia si non facerem, mihi non crederetis. Sed aperta est satis redargutio, non quasi Regulus adhuc plane incredulus, sed quod fides ejus admodum langui- da fuerit, quia volebat Christum secum descende- re, & quidem cito, ne interea moriatur Filius: quod quidem nondum crediderit, Jesum esse Messiam, sed tamen pro insigni aliquo Propheta habuerit. Docebat itaque hac reprehensione. I. Peccata auditorum, etiam in magna autoritate constituto- rum, qualis erat Palatinus ille, redarguenda esse, Esa. 58, 1. Ierem. 15, 2. 1. Tim. 5, 20. 2. Tim. 4, 2. Sic Nathan Davidem, Elias Achabum: Esaias Eze- chiam, 2. Reg. 20, 36. Baptista Herodem aperte re- darguit. II. Auditorum est objurgationes grato animo suscipere, Psal. 131, 5. Prov. 27, 5. 6. Quis Medicum salutaria monentem non feret? Neque periculum, inquit Basil. peccati novit, neque pœni- tentiæ lucrum, qui tristitia afficitur contra eum qui increpavit. III. Verbo Dei ceu ἀξιοπίστῳ simpli- citer credendum est, etiam si non videamus, quæ verbum docet, vel pollicetur. Fides est eorum, quæ non vides, τῶν ὀυ βλεπομένων, Hebr. XI. 1. Credere quod exterius videas & reipsa sentias non est illa fides, quam Scriptura celebrat. Beati qui credunt & non vident Ioh. 20, 29. IV. Plerumque nos ita affecti sumus, ut signa & prodigia requiramus, & credere Deo quidem non recusemus, tacite tamen & oblique hanc conditionem includamus, ut præ- sentiam & auxilium ejus videamus. V. Signa te- mere postulanda non sunt. Illicita est miraculo- rum postulatio, sive è diffidentia fiat cum Zacharia Luc. 1, 18. 30. sive è curiositate, cum Herode. Impia autem, si è calumniandi fiat libidine cum Pharisæis, Matth. 12, 38. Ad confirmationem vero fidei & po- stulare miracula quandoque jussit Deus ipse, Esa. 7, 13. & postulata nonnunquam sunt à fidelibus, Abrahamo Gen. 15, 18. Gideone Iud. 6. Ezechia 2. Reg. 20, 9. Cæterum hodie postquam novissime locutus nobis est Deus per Filium Ebr. 1, 1. cum non agat immediate aut extraordinarie, neque promissio ulla signorum extat, acquiescendum est

Verbo Dei olim miraculis plurimis confirmato. VI. Perperam Papistæ contendunt, necessaria esse miracula, ut fides doctrinæ concilietur. Mogunti- ni in animadversionibus ad Anti-Becan. p. 121. Sa- ne nisi Christus & Apostoli fidei facienda causa ea portenta patrâssent, non tenebantur profecto Judæi credere, sed poterant jure merito argumento ab anti- quitate Synagogæ petito Evangelium refellere. Ve- rum enim vero necessaria quidem fuerant Christo miracula ob promissionum de Messia per miracula manifestando veritatem, Es. 35, 5. Joh. 15, 24. non autem necessaria fuerunt, ob doctrinæ Christi fidem & autoritate, quæ per se ἀξιόπιστος ipsa sibi fidem adstruit; nec semper ubi prædicavit Christus mi- racula patravit, ut exemplo est patria ejus. Johan- nes Baptista nullis claruit miraculis, num ideo do- ctrinæ ejus fidem non tenebantur adhibere? Fate- tur utiq; Adamus Conzen Comment. in Joh. 4, 48. testimoniu Baptistæ ἀυτενθικὸν fuisse, ut qui ab i- pso instructi fuerint, credere tenentur. At novo si- gno opus jam esse ait, siquidem novo modo interpre- mur scripturas. Verum etiam nova erat Johannis doctrina de messiæ adventu, novum Sacramentum, nova in deserto Cathedra, novum officium πρεσβευ- μετικὸν ideo etiam pro novatore habebatur, Luc. 7. ℣. 30. 33. nec tamen miraculis egebat ad asserendam novam doctrinam. Cæterum non concedimus, nostram doctrinam esse novam, quæ ipsius Christi & Apostolorum, miraculis eorundem abunde co- firmata.

VII. Miracula non sunt notæ Ecclesiæ. Bel- larm. notis eadem accenset (1.) At notæ debent esse perpetuæ: hic vero Christus credi vult, etiamsi signa & portenta non videantur, neq; de illis per- petuandis ulla facta est promissio: nec necessaria illa sunt postquam satis per Apostolos doctrina Christi miraculis firmata est. August. lib. XXII. de Civ. Dei cap. 7. Possem dicere, inquit, necessaria fuisse priusquam crederet mundus ad hoc ut crede- ret. Quisquis autem ad hæc prodigia ut credat, in- quit, magnum ipse est prodigium, qui mundo cre- dente non credit. Signa data sunt ob incredulos, teste Apostolo 1. Cor. IV. 22. infideles itaque oportet esse qui signa postulant. Ideoque Lorinus ad Acta Apostol. p. 94. Toletus l. IV. Instructionis c. 3. docent, miracu- la nunc non esse necessaria. Didacus Stella in Luc. 2. Simili id declarat: Puer quando ambulare incipit, adjuvatur vehiculo, quod adulto esset impedimento, ita homines, nunc si miracula fierent, in id offende- rent, & dicerent fidem nostram nondum bene esse confirmatam. Cave igitur ne signa quæras. (2.) Notæ propriæ sint, non communes. At miracula falsis Prophetis & Anti-Christo ipsi communia sunt, Matth. 7, 22. 2. Thessal. 2, 4. Apocal. 13, 13. (3.) Notæ debent esse infallibiles & indubitatæ; At miracula non probant infallibiliter doctrinam, imo nihil probant, si non conjunctam habeant doctrinæ veritatem, Deut. 13, 2. Ideo Maldonatus ad Matth. 7. p. 137. fatetur, non omnino necessarium argumentum sumi è miraculis etiam veris. Josephus Acosta lib. III. de temporib. noviss. cap. 3. Miracula omnino vana esse ait, & inania nisi Scriptura appro- bentur, hoc est, habeant doctrinam Scripturæ con- formem. Scripturam vero ipsam per se, invictissi- mum esse argumentum. Atque hoc est quod sua- det hic Chrysostomus, non signa sed doctrinam no- bis attendendam esse. Astipulatur Ferus in Com- ment. cap. 24. Matth. non doctrina ex miraculis sed miracula ex doctrina æstimanda sunt.

Sequitur II. Christi opitulatio, qua fidem ejus imprimis confirmavit. Cum enim instaret pre- cando, Domine descende, priusquam moriatur Fi- lius meus, Dominus Jesus, Vade, inquit, Filius tuus vivit. Suavissima haec oppositio ; Palatinus urget , descende Domine. Dominus inquit , non descen- dam, vade tamen; Palatinus, priusquam moriatur filius meus. Dominus: Filius tuus non moritur , jam vivit. Absentem ergo localiter se opitulatum jam esse testatur , quam non nisi descendendo juvare posse , homo illi opinabatur. Imperat , Vade, ut agnoscat actutum auxilii certitudinem, & restitu- tione filii reficiatur ipse. Sed & reficit parentem , antequam se in viam conferat verbo promissionis , ut ne deficiat in via , ob verbum objurgationis , ideo addit, Filius tuus vivit. Verbum enim illud Vade, non est reprehendentis, aut objurgantis, uti Maldo- natus vult , quasi dicat, vade incredule, vide, experi- re, Filium tuum vivere, & crede. Sed est verbum erigentis & consolantis , ut eat confidenter, & filii sui restitutione gaudeat. Verbum חָיָה vivit per He- braismum idem est , quod convaluit 2. Reg. 1. 2. Ps. 70, 20. Psal. 137, 7. utitur autem non futuro, vi- vet , sed praesenti, ne naturalis valetudo, sed divina operatio cognoscatur. Maldonatus applicat hoc ad consecrationem Eucharistiae , quod uti hic dicen- do Filius tuus vivit , sanus ipse factus est; ita illic dicendo hoc est corpus meum , corpus Christi fa- ctum sit , quod panis erat. Verum verbis illis, Fi- lius tuus vivit, sanatio non facta, sed solum indi- cata est , quae tribuenda nutui & voluntati Christi simplici, neque si hic verbo illo facta esset sanatio, inferri posset, per verba Eucharistiae transsub- stantiatio, quia pensi habito institutionis tenore , inferenda tantum est sacramentalis unio. Doce- mur autem hic : (I.) Christum fidem infirmam non abjicere. Fides infirma a Deo etiam est, qui uni- cuique suum metrum dividit, Eph. 4, 7. Rom. 12, 3. vere etiam fides est, Marc. 9, 29. vere Christo ac- cepta est, qui propter infirmos venit Esai. 61, 2. Matth. 11, 28. Fumigans non extinguit linum Esa. 42, 3. nec quemquam ad se venientem rejicit, Joh. 6, 37. cujus virtus in infirmis perficitur, 2. Cor. 12, 9. nosque perficit & confirmat & consolidat , 1. Petr. 5, 10. Oremus modo cum discipulis : Do- mine, adauge nobis fidem, Luc. 17. 5. omnis fidei vis est a Christo , quem apprehendit; Christum au- tem etiam apprehendit exigua fides , quemad- modum donum divitis etiam manus aegrota ap- prehendere potest. (II.) Christus saepe plus prae- stat, quam nos rogamus, & melius juvat, quam de- sideramus, Palatinus rogabat, ut descenderet , ne moreretur Filius , at succumbere poterat Filius , antequam eo veniret Christus ; actutum ergo ef- ficit ipse, ut valeat filius jamjam morti vicinus : Ille petebat , ut descendendo opitularetur : Chri- stus autem se visibiliter absentem, praesentem opi- tulari posse demonstrat, actuque ipso opitulatur. Erubescat humana pigritia , ait cap. 39. de verbis Domini Augustinus , plus ille vult dare , quam nos accipere , plus vult ille misereri, quam illa miseria liberari. Bernhard. sermon. V. de triplici orandi modo , monet , priusquam egressa ab ore nostro Deum eam jubere scribi in libro suo, & indubitan- ter nos sperare posse. Quia aut dabit quod petimus, aut quid novit utilius , Matth. 7, 7. Johan. 14, 13. cap. 15, 7. Rom. 8, 26. 28. (III.) Finis auxilii Chri- sti est, fidei nostrae confirmatio. Sic juvat, uti no- vit fidei nostrae juvandae id inservire. Cum Palati- no hoc rogatus descendere noluit. Ad Centurio- nem vero non rogatus se venire velle promisit , Matth. 8, 7. Qui ita ? Ibi exiguam fidem & infir- mam augere voluit, sine descensu juvandi, quam descensu suo in infidelitate sua confirmasset, quasi non nisi descendendo juvare potuisset. Hic fi- dem magnam in occulto latentem in lucem pro- pro- ducere voluit. Quia in Centurione, inquit Chry- foft. fides perficiebatur, ideo se iturum dixit, ut viri fidem cognosceremus. At Regulus adhuc imperfe- ctus erat, propterea omni studio Christum impelle- bat, ut descenderet, neque adhuc noverat, absentem quoque habere potestatem curandi. Quid ergo posset, ostendit, ut quod per se sentiebat Centurio, hic (Regulus) non accedente Jesu erudiretur. (IV.) Deus loco exauditionis aliquando durius nobis- cum agit, ut vitia, quæ fidem contaminant, corri- gantur. Uti exemplo sunt cum Palatino hic Ja- cob, Hiob, David, Cananæa, &c.

ἐπίστευσεν ὁ ἄνθρωπος τῷ λόγῳ) Secundus hic gradus credulitatis elucet. Credit vera dicere Jesum: virtute e- jus valetudinem filio redditam, aut nondum credit, aut du- bitat.

## 4:51
V. 51. ἀπήντησαν αὐτῷ) On the journey from Cana to Capernaum. V. 52. τὴν ὥραν) So that he might understand whether it corresponded to that time, in which Christ had ordered him to be of good cheer.

Latin:

V. 51. ἀπήντησαν αὐτῷ) In itinere Cana Capernaumum. V. 52. τὴν ὥραν) Ut intelligeret an congrueret in id tem- pus, quo Christus ipsum bene animatum esse jusse- rat.

## 4:52
κομψότερον ἔσχε) He was somewhat better: Lexicographers explain it as ἐλαφρότερον.

ἀφῆκεν αὐτὸν ἡ πυρέτος) He did not recover little by little, but the fever left him suddenly.

Latin:

κομψότερον ἔσχε) Meliuscule se habuit: ἐλαφρότερον ex- ponunt Lexicographi.

ἀφῆκεν αὐτὸν ἡ πυρέτος) Non paulatim revaluit, sed subi- to eum reliquit febris.

## 4:53
Vers. 53. ὅτι ἐν ἐκέινῃ τῇ ὥρᾳ) Supply, that was done: and therefore he recognizes not only his knowledge, but also his power.

ἐπίστευσεν αὐτὸς) The third degree of faith, by which he seems to have already held Jesus plainly for the Messiah and professed himself his disciple.

and his whole house) As many as had the use of reason. Similar examples of families converted with the father of the family himself leading the way can be seen, Acts 16, 14. 15. 34. ch. 18, 8.

Latin:

Vers. 53. ὅτι ἐν ἐκέινῃ τῇ ὥρᾳ) Supple, id factum est: ac proinde non scientiam tantum ejus, sed & potentiam agno- scit.

ἐπίστευσεν αὐτὸς) Tertius gradus fidei, qua videtur Je- sum jam plane pro Messia habuisse & professum se ejus di- scipulum.

καὶ ἡ οἰκία αὐτϿ ὅλη) Quotquot erant rationis usum ha- bentes. Similia exempla familiæ, patre ipso familias præ- eunte conversæ, videre est, Act. 16, 14. 15. 34. c. 18, 8.

## 4:54
Vers. 54. this again a second time) Refer this to that which follows, having come out of Judea into Galilee. For he had done many things in Jerusalem. John seems to add this, however, to signify that these were the first miracles done in the region of Galilee, and therefore prior to those which are narrated by Matthew ch. IV. 7 and others.

Latin:

Vers. 54. τῦτο πάλιν δεύτερον) Refer ad id, quod sequitur ἐλθὼν ἐκ τῆς Ἰυδαίας εἰς τὴν Γαλιλαίαν. Nam Hierosolymis plura fecerat. Videtur autem hoc addere Johannes, ut significet, hæc prima esse signa facta in regione Galilææ, ac proinde priora iis quæ à Matthæo cap. IV. 7 & aliis nar- rantur.

## 5:1 Argument
CHAPTER V. ARGUMENT AND DIVISION.

Jesus, having set out for the feast to the pool in Bethsaida, where the sick were healed when an Angel stirred the water, heals a lame man of 38 years on the Sabbath with a single word, whom the Jews rebuke because he was carrying his bed, but he is warned by Jesus not to sin again once restored to health, and he indicates to the Jews that he had been healed by Jesus, who were seeking to kill him. But Jesus testifying that he works with the Father, they are exasperated because he makes himself equal to God, calling him Father, which Jesus defends, saying that he does all things which the Father does, and that he gives life to whom he wills, as does the Father, that all judgment has been given to him by the Father, so that the Son may be honored as the Father, and that by hearing his Word and having faith, eternal life is had, and that those who are in the tombs will be resurrected when the voice of the Son is heard, some to life, others to judgment, that he seeks the will of the Father, and that John has testified concerning him, and his works testify more, and the Father has testified, and therefore the scripture must be searched because it testifies of him, so that they may have life. But when the Jews do not receive him, he teaches that they are accused by Moses, who wrote of him.

There are two parts: I. The healing of the lame man in Bethsaida, to v. 15. II. The Apology of Jesus against the Jews persecuting him, to v. 47.

PART I.

The healing of the lame man in Bethesda.

Ver. 1. A feast of the Jews) Writers dispute here which feast day this was: and they calculate the times with conjectures, it is wonderful how uncertain. If we follow the authors, the most ancient is Irenaeus, who in book II, chapter 39, says this is the Paschal feast. If we attend to the manner of speaking, we certainly show that the Passover is designated by this name, Matt. 26, 5. Nor should it move us that this article is not added to the noun ἑορτὴ. For clearly in the same way ἑορτὴ without the article signifying the Passover is required in Mark 15, 6; Luke 18, 17.

The feast of the Passover is altogether to be understood in this place, with Irenaeus, book II, chapter 39, who says, 'Christ went up for the second time to the feast day of the Passover in Jerusalem, when He healed the paralytic who was lying by the pool'; with B. Luther, Chemnitz, Pelargus, Scaliger, and Johann Molther in his 'Mathematical and Historical Disquisition on the different eating of the Paschal lamb celebrated by Christ and the Jews,' th. 92 and 103; with Toledo on this passage, and Baronius, even though Chrysostom, Cyril, and Epiphanius, as also Theophylact, Euthymius, and Lyranus, stand for the feast of Pentecost, and others for the Feast of Tabernacles. For since three years and a half were assigned to the Ministry of Christ, Dan. IX. 24, and those are believed to be described by John through the Passovers, it is necessary that no other feast be understood here than the Passover. For in John II. 13, the first is openly named. The third is commemorated in John VI. 4. Finally, the fourth is had in John XI. 16. It is necessary, therefore, that the second be designated here. Add that no other feast is designated by the name ἑορτῆς alone, except the Passover, Matt. 27, 15; Luke 2, 42; John 11, 56; and chapter 12, 12; and that John alone distinctly noted all the feasts of the Passover celebrated during the course of Christ's preaching, as Eusebius observes in book VIII of the 'Demonstratio Evangelica'.

of the Jews) Thus above c. 2, 13. the passover of the Jews &c.

Latin:

CAPUT V. ARGUMENTUM ET PAR- TITIO.

Jesus ad festum profectus ad piscinam in Beth- saida, ubi Angelo commovente aquam sana- bantur ægroti, claudum 38. annorum Sab- bato uno verbo sanat, quem Judæi, quod le- ctum suum portaret, redarguunt, à Jesu autem monetur, ne restitutus sanitati de- nuo peccet, indicatque Judæis, se à Jesu sa- natum esse, qui quærebant ut ipsum interfi- cerent. Jesu autem testante, quod cum Pa- tre operetur, exacerbantur, quod se Deo, Patrem eum dicens, æqualem faciat, quod vero defendit Jesus, omnia se facere, quæ fa- ciat Pater, ac vivificare, quos vult, uti Pa- ter, omne judicium sibi à Patre datum, ut honoretur Filius, sicut Pater, ac per Verbi sui auditum, & fidem haberi vitam æter- nam, Filiique voce audita resuscitatum i- ri, qui in monumentis sunt, alios ad vitam, alios ad judicium, se Patris voluntatem quærere, deque se testatum esse Johannem, ac magis testari opera sua, testatum Pa- trem, atque ideo scrutandam esse scriptu- ram, quod de se testetur, ut vitam habe- ant. Quum vero Judæi ipsum non susci- piant, à Mose, qui de se scripsit, eos accu- sari, docet.

Partes sunt duæ: I. Claudi in Bethsaida sanatio, ad v. 15. II. Jesu contra Judæos ipsum persequen- tes Apologia, ad v. 47.

PARS I.

Claudi in Bethsaida sanatio.

Vers. 1. Ἑορτὴ τῶν Ἰουδαίων) Disputant hic scriptores, quis hic dies festus fuerit: & tempora suppurant conjecturis mirum quam incertis. Si autores sequimur, vetustissimus est Irenæus qui lib. II. cap. 39. Paschale hoc festum ait. Si loquendi morem attendimus sane Pascha hoc nomine designatum ostendimus, Matth 26, 5. Nec movere nos debet quod hic Articulus non est additus nomini ἑορτὴ. Nam plane eodem modo ἑορτὴ sine articulo Pascha significans requiritur Marci 15, 6. Luc. 18. 17.

Omnino festum Paschatos intelligendum hoc loco cum Irenæo lib. II. cap. 39. qui, secunda, inquit, vice ascendit Christus in diem festum Paschæ in Hierusalem, quando Paralyticum, qui juxta natatorium jacebat, sanavit; B. Luthero, Chemnitio, Pelargo, Scaligero, Johan. Molthero disqu. Mathem. & Histor. de diverso esu agni Paschal. à Christo & Judæis celebrat, th. 92. & 103. Toleto in h. l. & Baronio, utut Chrysostomus, Cyrillus, & Epiphanius, ut & Theophylactus, Euthymius, Lyranus, stent pro festo Pentecostes, alii pro Festo Scenopegias. Nam quum Ministerio Christi assignati fuerint tres anni cum dimidio Dan. IX. 24. & descripti illi à Johanne credantur per Paschata, necesse est hic non aliud intelligi festum, quam Paschatos. Nam Joh. II. 13. primum aperte nominatum est. Tertium Joh. VI. 4. commemoratur. Quartum denique habetur Joh. XI. 16. Necessum ergo est, ut hic secundum designatum sit. Adde quod nullum aliud festum solo ἑορτῆς nomine designetur, nisi Paschatos, Matth. 27, 15. Luc. 2, 42. Johan. 11, 56. & cap. 12, 12. quodque solus Johannes omnia Paschatos festa curriculo prædicationis Christi celebrata distincte notarit, observante Eusebio libr. VIII. demonstr. Evangel.

τῶν Ἰουδαίων) Sic supra c. 2, 13. πάσχα τῶν Ἰουδαίων &c.

## 5:2
Ver. 2. by the sheep market) ἐπὶ as the Hebrew על for 'at' or 'near'. 'ἐπὶ πριάμοιο θύρῃσι' in Homer: at the doors of Priam. Thucydides said 'ἐπὶ ποταμῷ' for 'παρὰ ποταμῷ' (by the river). One must understand here 'πύλῃ' (gate), which is read expressed in Nehem. 2, 1; c. 12, 38. By this, victims were led into the city.
